If the hypothesis is supported, the coefficient on this term should be positive and significant. All lower-order interaction terms are included in the regressions.
time_window: three years pre- to three years post-spin-off

description: Indicator variable taking the value one in the three years after the completion of a spin-off, and zero in the three years before its completion. After 1, After 2, and After 3 are indicator variables respectively taking the value one in the first, second, and third year after the completion of a spin-off and zero in the three years before its completion; these replace After in the intertemporal-trend models.
time_window: three years before to three years after spin-off completion

description: A count of the number of business segments operating within a company, measured for parent firms in the year prior to the completion of their spin-offs and for control firms in the same fiscal year as their matched parent firms. #Segments squared is the squared term of #Segments, and the two are interacted with After and Median Segment Industry q to test the inverted-U-shaped prediction.

Monthly sum of political campaign contributions made by a firm's top management team and political action committee (normally controlled by senior executives) to state legislators, to the governor, and to candidates for election, in the state in which the utility operates. The average value of monthly contributions in the sample is $2,589, or approximately $31,000 annually.

Firm-specific count of intervenors that were active in the most recent rate review for a firm, measured from the number of intervenors that participated in every formal regulatory review of the firm's regulated rates since 1980. The average value is 7.4 intervenors with a standard deviation of 6.2, and the measure is lagged because it refers to the prior rate review.

The average number of days that the commissioners of the state Public Utility Commission have been in their positions. The mean value is 1,676 days (just over 4.5 years) with a standard deviation of 923 days.

The average number of days that Public Utility Commission commissioners have remaining until their reappointment dates. The mean value is 930 days (about 2.5 years) with a standard deviation of 319 days.

The measure is constructed in two stages following the FSR patent-level measure. In the first stage, the ease of recombination of a technological subclass is the number of different subclasses that have been combined with it, normalized by the number of patents in which that subclass has been used. In the second stage, the interdependence of a patent is the average of the inverted ease-of-recombination scores for the subclasses on that patent. The industry-level measure is the average of the patent-level measure among the patents classified under the same four-digit SIC code, using Silverman's concordance to map patent classifications to industry classifications. A time-invariant version is set at its 1988 level and a time-varying version is updated annually as patents accumulate; the equations themselves are not readable in the text provided.
time_window: 1988-1996; the 1988 level uses patents with application years between 1901 and 1988

description: MeanQ is the natural log of the average Qit within each four-digit SIC code industry. Qit is calculated as the sum of firm market value (share price multiplied by outstanding shares) and the book value of long-term debt, preferred stock, and net current liabilities, all divided by the total asset value of the firm for each firm in each year.

Firm-level profitability is the natural log of Qit, where Qit is the ratio of the market valuation of the firm to the value of tangible assets (Tobin's q). Qit is calculated as the sum of firm market value (share price multiplied by outstanding shares) and the book value of long-term debt, preferred stock, and net current liabilities, all divided by the total asset value of the firm for each firm in each year of the sample.

A binary indicator distinguishing industries with greater patent effectiveness, based on the threshold established by Cohen et al. (2002). Industries with effectiveness greater than 41% as shown in their Table 1 are coded as 1, and 0 otherwise. All models using it use time-varying interdependency, and sample size changes as a result of the matching between ISIC and SIC codes.

Cumulative actual minus expected stock return for firm i for days t1 to t2. Expected returns come from a Fama and French four-factor model (with the Carhart momentum factor) estimated over the period t - 255 to t - 11 relative to the event day t = 0, where the intercept is the daily abnormal return. CAR is computed for each stock over event windows of varying lengths, with ( - 2, + 2) chosen as the focal event window.
time_window: event window ( - 2, + 2) around the announcement; estimation period t - 255 to t - 11

description: Structural topic modeling (STM) is used to analyze announcement-related media coverage, with three topics chosen because this approach offers the highest semantic coherence score. STM assigns probability distributions across topics to each media report, and the identified topics were labeled business impact, announcement reasoning, and sustainable initiatives. The measure sums the daily averages of probabilities for the business impact topic across all media coverage in the event window.

Estimated scope 1 and 2 (for carbon neutrality) and scope 1-3 (for net-zero) CO2 equivalent emissions in metric tons from the LSEG database, aligned with the scopes the firm commits to eliminating. The values are scaled by firm size.
time_window: at the time of the event

description: The number of days since the first carbon goal announcement by any firm within the same industry, based on the exact date each firm made its first public carbon goal announcement identified through internet and Factiva searches. Firms are assigned to nine industries, and timing effects are studied relative to industry peers.

The event is a firm's first public carbon goal announcement (carbon neutrality or net-zero), identified for S&P 500 firms through Google searches, the Wayback Machine and Factiva. The exact announcement date defines event day zero for the event study; 188 announcements from 2018 to 2024 form the sample, and the effect on Hypothesis 1 is read from the average CAR.

Dummy indicating whether the potentially citing inventor has prior patenting experience in the technology class of the deceased patent. Experience is read from the first Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) subsection of any prior patents of the inventor at risk for citing, during the specified time period, and remains independent of the deceased patent's classification. Inventors with any experience in the same CPC subsection are coded one and those with no experience in that subsection are coded zero.
time_window: prior patenting up to the grant date of the potentially citing patent

description: Dummy equal to one if the potentially citing inventor lives within radius r of a living coinventor of a deceased inventor, and zero for a citing inventor residing within the same-sized radius around the deceased inventor. Radii from 10 to 100 miles are estimated separately, and citing inventors living in overlapping regions of the radii around the deceased and living coinventors are excluded.

Dichotomous dependent variable taking the value of one in case of an observed citation to patent p and zero otherwise. It indicates a cite that comes from an inventor i residing within radius r of the location of inventor j on the multi-author deceased patent p within a time window of t since grant of p.
time_window: 10 years since grant of the cited patent

variable_name: recent experience (<5 years) vs. less recent experience (5-10 years)
description: Potentially citing inventors are separated into those with more versus less recent experience. Recent experience is defined as having applied for at least one prior patent with the same CPC subsection as the deceased patent within five years before the grant date of the potentially citing patent, excluding the potentially citing patent itself. Less recent experience uses the identical definition applied to the 5-10 year window before that grant date; the estimated interaction terms of both groups are then compared.
time_window: 0-5 years vs. 5-10 years before the grant date of the potentially citing patent

description: Deceased patents are split into those classified in one technological field versus those spanning more than one field. In the sample, 54% of deceased patents stay within one CPC section, 39% cover two fields, 5% cover three fields, and 2% cover three or more fields; the interaction terms of Equation (2) are then compared across the two groups.

Within-firm knowledge diffusion is measured as citations from a patent within the same firm. The analysis sample is split to include potentially citing inventors from the same or different firms as the deceased patent, and the citation propensity around still-living versus deceased coinventors is estimated within firms.
time_window: 10 years since grant of the cited patent

description: A variable equal to one for periods after the severance pay reform was enacted in 2011, which was applicable only to workers hired after November 2011 and reduced severance pay. The reform affected only new hires across all firms, so the variable identifies individuals hired under the lower termination cost regime.

Equals one for individuals who join a new venture, defined as a firm five years old or younger, rather than an incumbent firm, and zero otherwise. Each observation represents a new hire identified in the QDP annual snapshots.

Equals one for female employees and zero for male employees. Gender is measured and reported by the Quadro de Pessoal, which identifies individuals as a woman or a man but does not identify additional genders.

Defined as whether the focal employee was a startup owner at any point during the five years preceding the hiring year. To address potential endogeneity, the authors also measure it for the year immediately preceding the sample period.
time_window: five years preceding the hiring year

description: Measured as the percentage of female employees in the industry where the employer operates during the hiring year. Industries are defined using the two-digit Portuguese Classification of Economic Activities (CAE2 Rev. 3).

Measured as the percentage of female employees among all startup employees in the industry where the employer operates during the hiring year. Industries are defined using the two-digit Portuguese Classification of Economic Activities (CAE2 Rev. 3).

A treatment dummy equal to 1 if the store is in the treatment group, in which store managers were granted full authority to make hiring decisions, and 0 for control stores, which retained the centralized HR-led hiring process with limited managerial discretion. Stores were randomly assigned to the two groups.

The log of a worker's average monthly sales, used as the dependent variable for new hires (Columns 1) and for all workers (Column 3) in the productivity regressions. Pretreatment data were used for observational analysis and treatment-period data were used for experimental analysis.

The average monthly probability of receiving product returns, defined as the share of months with at least one return. Product returns provide insight into service quality, signaling potential customer dissatisfaction or product mismatches.

The authors compare the distribution of employee productivity under LMH by manager type, reporting that the distribution of employee productivity was more dispersed for both high- and low-performing managers, and that even the best managers sometimes hired low performers. The text does not state a formula or a specific variance variable.

Calculated from purchasing records for January 2016 through August 2018 to capture active returning customers. According to the firm, an active returning customer has a cumulative purchasing record of at least ¥10,000 and has visited a store within the past six months.

Used as a proxy for the precision of the local manager's information, on the reasoning that managers with longer tenure are likely to have accumulated more contextual knowledge about the store and its customers, improving their ability to assess applicant fit.

Baseline store sales used as a proxy for alignment between managerial and firm incentives; the authors argue that stores or managers with poorer baseline performance may face greater incentive alignment issues.

The distance between a store and the company's regional headquarters, used as a proxy for incentive alignment because it is presumably more difficult for the firm to monitor stores that are geographically farther away.

Measured as the ratio of active customers to store personnel, it captures the opportunity cost of managers' recruiting time; managers of stores with higher customer-employee ratios are likely to be busier and face greater opportunity costs associated with hiring.

Store managers' self-reported overall job satisfaction, collected in the pre-RCT and post-RCT surveys (August 2018 and September 2019). In the post-RCT survey, managers were also asked about their attitudes toward LMH and about potential mechanisms.
time_window: pre- and post-RCT surveys (August 2018 and September 2019)

description: Nutritionists' self-reported overall job satisfaction, collected in the pre-RCT and post-RCT surveys (August 2018 and September 2019). Nutritionists were also asked about their perceptions of managerial support and communication frequency.
time_window: pre- and post-RCT surveys (August 2018 and September 2019)

description: Total monthly sales generated by all store staff, used in log form as the store-level outcome. The analysis uses monthly store sales from January 2016 through August 2019.

Dummy equal to 1 if the lab pair becomes colocated because of the moves, and set back to 0 when the labs are separated again. It identifies the within-pair effect on outcomes after labs become colocated because of the asbestos removal, relative to their before period. Lab pairs are colocated when they are in the same tower or corridor building.
Dummy equal to 1 when a previously colocated pair is separated because of the moves and 0 otherwise. It captures the reverse change in proximity within a lab pair during the asbestos-removal period.
Dummy equal to 1 if the lab pair collaborates in the focal year and 0 otherwise. Collaborations between labs are identified from coauthored publications of the two labs.

Number of collaborations between the two labs in the focal year, estimated with OLS and with a Poisson specification with fixed effects. The Poisson specification with fixed effects drops all lab pairs where collaboration is never observed.

Lab pairs that have an above-the-median similarity in keywords (or in cited references) are classified as facing lower search costs ex ante, since they are more likely to overlap in topics and the literature they cite; lab pairs that have below-the-median similarity are classified as experiencing higher search costs ex ante. The cosine similarity between the vectors of keywords (or of references cited) used by each lab is calculated excluding all direct collaborations and is measured before the moves start.

Cosine similarity between the vectors of cited references used by each lab in a given year, which captures the extent of overlap in backward cites for a specific lab pair in a given year. Coauthored papers between the focal labs are dropped so the vectors of cited references are based on independent publications. It is used as a dependent variable in the analysis of research trajectories.

Cosine similarity between the vectors of keywords used by each lab, computed in the same way as the cited-references measure (author and index keywords retrieved from Scopus). Coauthored papers between the focal labs are dropped so the vectors are based on independent publications.

Number of publications by the lab pair in the focal year within the first (lowest) quartile of the citation distribution, conditional on collaboration in the focal year. Citation data is obtained from Scopus and quartiles for the citation distribution are built by year using a large sample of articles in the relevant fields of science.

Number of publications by the lab pair in the focal year within the fourth (highest) quartile of the citation distribution, conditional on collaboration in the focal year. Citation data is obtained from Scopus and quartiles for the citation distribution are built by year using a large sample of articles in the relevant fields of science.

Maximum number of citations received by the publications of the lab pair in the focal year, conditional on collaboration; used to explore the right tail of the outcome distribution, including for pairs split by ex ante search costs. Citation data is obtained from Scopus.

Dependent variable: the average price charged for one room-night by each hotel in each monthly observation, between January 2002 and July 2009. Hotels report to STR the average room-night price received and the number of room nights sold on each day. Regressions are estimated on every monthly price observation of every dual-distribution chain hotel.

Key independent variable: equals 1 if a hotel is managed by a franchisee and equals 0 if the hotel is company-managed. The STR census classifies the organizational form of each property as 'company-managed,' 'franchised,' or 'independently managed'; the analysis focuses on the first two categories. The variable is treated as endogenous in the 2SLS regressions.

variable_name: Upper tier brands / Lower tier brands
description: Brands are classified into four STR-defined quality categories: upper upscale, upscale, midscale, and economy. The first two categories are combined as the 'upper tiers' and the latter two as the 'lower tiers.' The pricing regressions are estimated first on the pooled population and then separately on the upper tier and lower tier subsamples.

Firm size was measured by number of employees and is empirically treated both categorically and log linearly in the data analysis. A cutoff of 250 employees was utilized in categorical analyses, consistent with evidence of a plateauing of size-related contract differences between 100 and 500 employees. Data on the number of employees at an employee's site was also collected.

variable_name: Individual performance based, group performance based, and equity contract attributes
description: The degree to which an employee's contract is individual performance based was measured through responses on seven-point Likert-type scales to the accuracy of two statements about whether compensation is primarily based on seniority in the firm and on individual performance. The degree to which the contract is output based was measured through similar responses to statements about basing compensation on the performance of the project or organizational unit and on the overall performance of the firm. Respondents were also asked to indicate whether they had an equity stake in their employer and, if so, what percentage of the firm's equity they own.

Measures were constructed with multiple items when possible, and items were standardized and weighted equally in constructing composite measures. Awards, performance ratings, and self-rating of performance are overall measures of performance at a common employer. Skill specialization measures uniqueness of an engineer's skills. Master's education, doctorate, and scholastic achievement are education-related ability measures. Counter offer amount and search time are indications of an employee's value as perceived internally and externally. Patents and publications are further indications of the possession of valued skills or information and superior ability.

Effort was measured with a self-assessment of time and effort relative to colleagues and to the general population of engineers, and with the estimated number of hours worked per week in job-related activity. A parallel measure asked former employees to estimate the number of hours they worked while at Company A or Company B.

The models regress yearly salary (as of June 1987) on tenure, experience, engineer type, location, firm size, and various performance, ability, skill, and effort measures, together with interaction terms between small and large firm categories and each performance correlate.

Performance contingent contracts should involve greater risk for employees; this contract risk was measured in part as the perceived risk of job loss through bankruptcy or layoff. Bankruptcy likelihood was measured as the respondent's estimate of the likelihood of the firm going out of business within the next three years, and layoff likelihood as the estimate of the likelihood of being laid off within the next two years. Equity held by an employee is in part a measure of contract risk.
time_window: next three years (bankruptcy); next two years (layoff)

description: Market share, MS, is defined as the firm's share of prescription drug sales of total domestic market volume. The temporal mean for each firm was computed over each period for which a stable strategic group structure was observed, and the averages were compared across strategic groups.
scale: share of total domestic market volume
time_window: temporal mean over each period of stable strategic group structure (1963-1969, 1970-1974, 1975-1979, 1980-1982)

description: Weighted segment share, WSS, measures the extent to which firms dominate the market segments in which they compete, and was constructed from firm drug sales in therapeutic categories and total prescription drug sales. The paper's formula for WSS was not readable in the available text; the components the authors list are drug sales of firm i in therapeutic category j, total prescription drug sales of firm i, and total market volume of therapeutic category j.
time_window: temporal mean over each period of stable strategic group structure

description: AROS was defined as the ratio of net income before interest and taxes for the pharmaceutical operations to total drug sales for the firm. The measure was adjusted for inflationary changes by restating depreciation charges, and R&D expenses were restated from expense to a depreciation of capitalized R&D. Because most firms are diversified and the drug asset base was unavailable, the study had to rely on a return on sales measure.
scale: ratio of income to drug sales
time_window: temporal mean over each period of stable strategic group structure

description: Risk measures were obtained by calculating the standard deviation about the temporal mean for each of the three performance measures (MS, WSS, AROS) for each firm in each period of stable strategic group structure.
time_window: each period of stable strategic group structure

description: Risk-adjusted measures of performance were obtained by dividing average firm performance for each of the three indicators by their respective standard deviation.
time_window: each period of stable strategic group structure

variable_name: Strategic group membership from cluster analysis
description: Group membership is derived by cluster analysis (Ward error sum of squares, with MANOVA on cluster centroids to pick the number of clusters) of firms' standardized, period-averaged strategy variables, within subperiods of stable strategic group structure identified by testing equality of variance-covariance matrices over time. The strategy variables describe scope commitments (market segment focus, ethical and generic drug markets, foreign sales) and resource commitments (R&D and marketing).

Respondents reported on questionnaires given once each week on random days for ten weeks their technical communication with other projects only, excluding written and/or social communication. Seventy-two percent of all communication reported was mentioned by both parties. The data were averaged over the ten weeks and the average frequency of communication per person per project per week was used as the measure.

Centrality of the project within the network of the projects in the sample was measured by the average number of responses per person per project; the number of other project members multiplied by their percentage and then divided by the total number of project members. Centrality was defined as the ratio of the number of researchers who actually direct communication to the members of the project's research team to the total number of researchers. Of the question asking how communication with each scientist usually originates, only the second classification, 'He or she initiated the contact,' was used as the measure; 92 percent of communications were identified by both parties.

Each project was evaluated independently by an average of four observers, the top managers responsible for and familiar with the projects, who rated the technical performance of the project on a 5 point Likert type scale ranging from (1) very low to (5) very high. The observers' ratings were averaged to determine the overall project performance score; the evaluations of the four managers were highly correlated (Spearman-Brown reliability = 0.89).

Project members' demographic information, including age, was collected with the questionnaires; the median age of the project members was 42 years. The regressions of the sociometric variables on the frequency and centrality of communication use the project participants' average age.

Respondents' educational attainment was collected with the questionnaires: of the total of 146 researchers, 51 had received their doctoral degrees, 58 had master's and 37 had bachelor's degrees. The variable is entered as 'Education' in the regression of the sociometric variables on the frequency and centrality of communication; the coding scheme is not stated in the text.

Year-end market price divided by book value of equity. Intrinsic value cannot be observed, so the authors follow the argument that market value provides an unbiased measure of intrinsic value and use the market price to book ratio to represent the intrinsic valuation ratio (V/B).

Three measures of Return on Equity reflecting different time horizons and weights. ROE1 is year-end net income divided by year-beginning equity; ROE2 is the past three-year average of ROE1; ROE3 is the past three-year average of ROE1 with unequal weights of 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5 assigned to year t-2, year t-1 and year t respectively.

Cost of Equity = Risk-free Rate + Systematic risk (equity risk premium). The year-end long-term Government Bond yield is used as the risk-free rate and the Value Line Beta as the measure of systematic risk, with two alternate measures of the equity risk premium corresponding to Ibbotson and Sinquefield's arithmetic and geometric means.

Five growth measures: growth in dividends per share, growth in sales, growth in earnings per share, growth in assets and growth in equity per share. Each measure reflects the average annual growth rate over the past three years.
Aggressive technology policy measured on the mail questionnaire. The authors define an aggressive technology policy as a preemptive, long-range strategy for technological innovation.
Diversification into nonfood markets, measured on the mail questionnaire and used as an exogenous variable in the causal model.
Organization size measured as the natural logarithm of the number of year-round employees.

Concentration of specific technical and engineering group(s), measured on the mail questionnaire; treated as a function of technology policy, diversification and organization size in the causal model.
Number of new products introduced in the last two years, a dependent variable in the mail survey causal model.
Number of radical (new to industry) processes adopted during the past three years, a dependent variable in the mail survey causal model.
Number of incremental processes adopted during the past three years, a dependent variable in the mail survey causal model.

A scale measuring three categories of adoption for 13 packaging technologies. The technologies include rectangular cans, ovenable glass pans, trays, aseptic packages, and paperboards. The measure was included on both the mail questionnaire and the interview schedule.

variable_name: Stage of adoption for the retort pouch
description: A single-item adoption scale for the consumer retort pouch running from rejected to implemented. The measure was included on both the mail questionnaire and the interview schedule.

variable_name: Familiarity and use of retortable packaging
description: Familiarity or use of retortable packaging technology, measured on the mail questionnaire and used as a dependent variable in the causal models.

variable_name: Sum of staged adoption behaviors, CRP
description: A set of behaviors, decisions and events that were factor analyzed into stages of adoption-implementation for the retort pouch. This measure was included only in the interviews.
Market dominated growth strategy, measured with the interview data and treated as an exogenous variable in the interview causal model.
Structural complexity, one of the three dimensions of organization structure measured with the interview data.
Formalization, one of the three dimensions of organization structure measured with the interview data.
Centralization, one of the three dimensions of organization structure measured with the interview data; low values indicate decentralization.
Presence of an innovation champion, here the champion of the consumer retort pouch. Measured with the interview data; multiple respondents were used where available.

Degree of fit between an organization and a specific technology, scaled on two dimensions, economic attributes of congruence and general attributes, both with respect to the consumer retort pouch. Data were collected from key organization members.

Traditional structural arrangements are represented by the three known dimensions of organization structure, structural complexity, formalization and centralization (low centralization meaning decentralization), measured with the field interview data on 56 food processing firms and used as separate variables in the causal models.

Principal investigators reported the frequency of communication, initiation of communication and the amount of written communication with other principal investigators. Based on their responses the principal investigators were classified into high, moderate and low frequency of communication levels, and zero order and partial correlations with project success were computed for each category.

Obtained as a ratio of the number of the principal investigators who actually direct communication at the project principal investigator to the total number of the principal investigators in the related projects.

Measured by the principal investigator's report on his/her contacts with other sources of information such as the National Sea Grant Office, industry, government agencies, and others. The number of sources that interacted with each category were divided by six (the total number of sources of information); these computed indices were measures of diversity of communication.

The amount of written communication of the principal investigators was considered as the measure of the formality of communication. Correlations with project success were computed for very low, low, moderate and high formality categories.
scale: categories: very low to high formality

description: The principal investigators, the program directors, and the project monitors were independently asked to indicate the success of the project. All dependent variable measures were factor analyzed using principal component analysis, which extracted a single factor accounting for 94% of the variance, and a single index of project success was computed using factor score coefficients and used as the project success measure in the analysis.
Computed by taking the average sum of the individual project's centrality for each network.
Computed likewise to aggregate centrality, by taking the average sum of the individual project's formality of communication for each network.
Computed likewise to aggregate centrality, by taking the average sum of the individual project's diversity of communication for each network.

Measured by the principal investigator's interactions with other principal investigators within the network of related projects (meeting during the past year to discuss respective projects, joint programs related to projects, other interactions). Only reciprocal relations between the principal investigators were used in computing scores, and a single index of cohesiveness was computed using factor analysis score coefficients.
Project success for the aggregated level was computed by taking the average sum of individual project successes for each network.

A surrogate measure of the existence of an organizational need, capturing the complexity of the software development environment as reflected by typical project length, cost and effort. Three items were combined (alpha = 0.80): the percentage of projects requiring more than six months for development, more than 25 man-months of effort, and more than $20,000 development cost. The authors note that this measure does not capture the full essence of the need-recognition component of 'push-pull' theory.

Means recognition reflected simply whether or not the respondents were familiar with a practice (a yes-no response). These responses were then summed to obtain measures of overall recognition (all six practices), technical recognition (the three technical practices), and administrative recognition (the three administrative practices). The authors note that this construct and its measure create an obvious bias toward empty support of 'push-pull' theory: unrecognized means will obviously not be reported as being used.

Software managers characterized each of the practices along a Likert-like scale according to six items. A factor analysis of the six items resulted in all loading on a single factor (with all factor loadings between 0.71 and 0.89), and the internal consistency of this attitude measure over all six practices was 0.97. Three measures were obtained by summing across all six characteristics: one for all six practices, one for the three technical practices, and one for the three administrative practices.

Each software development group's receptivity toward change was measured by having each of the software managers characterize their software group, using a modification of an instrument developed by Siegel and Kaemmerer (1978). The four items used addressed the degree to which an organization was flexible and continually adapted to change, examined its most basic assumptions, searched for fresh ways of looking at problems, and dealt with new problems and tasks constructively. The authors note that this measure does not explicitly measure group receptivity toward change; rather, it captures the software manager's perception of the software group's overall receptivity to change.

Each software group's use of the practices was ascertained by asking respondents to describe the extent to which each was currently applied within their organizations, using six responses coded respectively as the integers 1-6: not used at all; a few people/projects are experimenting with it; a few people/projects regularly use it; a number of people/projects regularly use it; most people/projects regularly use it; and usage has become standard. Three measures were computed: the sum over all six practices (overall use), the sum over the three technical practices (technical use), and the sum over the three administrative practices (administrative use).

Data were collected regarding the adoption of six modern software practices; the first three (top down development, structured design, structured review) can be categorized as technical process innovations and the latter three (chief programmer team, configuration management, unit development folder) as administrative innovations. Separate dependent variables were formed by summing use over each subset of three practices, yielding technical use and administrative use in addition to overall use.

The dependent variable, described as simply an arithmetic average of the scores on the innovation, proactiveness, and risk-taking variables. The authors report a Cronbach alpha of 0.88 for the seven-item entrepreneurial variable and note that aggregate entrepreneurship correlates significantly with each of its three components.

One of the three dimensions of entrepreneurship, covering the firm's product-market and technological innovation. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score, and the authors report that it correlates significantly with the aggregate entrepreneurship variable.

One of the three dimensions of entrepreneurship: coming up with proactive innovations and beating competitors to the punch rather than imitating their moves. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score, and the authors report that it correlates significantly with the aggregate entrepreneurship variable.

One of the three dimensions of entrepreneurship: the firm's willingness to undertake somewhat risky ventures. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score, and the authors report that it correlates significantly with the aggregate entrepreneurship variable.

variable_name: Locus of control of the leader
description: Measured using Rotter's well-known internal-external scale. The more internal the executive, the more he feels he has control over his environment and his destiny; executives who believe outcomes are due to chance or to elements beyond their control are less likely to be innovative, proactive and risk taking. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.

The degree to which decision making power is centralized in the hands of one or two top administrators; high centralization is practical in simple, undiversified firms. Together with small size it served as a classification criterion for Simple firms. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.

The extent to which the firm scans its environment to discover important challenges and opportunities. In Simple firms it represents the chief executive's knowledge of customer wants, sources of supply, and competitor strategies. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.

The extent to which the firm makes use of technocrats such as scientists and engineers in creating product and technological innovations; in Simple firms it reflects the frequency with which leaders are in touch with scientists, engineers or even marketing experts. High technocratization was a classification criterion for Organic firms, and scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.

The extent to which the firm's product-market strategy is explicitly and formally elaborated, as opposed to residing as the implicit and often vague vision of the leaders. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.

The extent to which an established strategy tends to guide decision making and is resistant to change. Strategies that are carefully integrated are well established and regularly direct decisions. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.

The extent to which the firm's environment is dynamic, where customer tastes, product-service technologies, and competitive weapons often change unpredictably. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.

The extent to which the firm's markets are hostile; ease of entry makes markets hostile and the small size of firms leaves them susceptible to threats from competitors. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.
The diversity of the firm's market; managers in such markets find themselves dealing with a rather diverse array of customers. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.

The extent to which the organization is differentiated, so that individuals and departments with very different abilities coexist in response to the diverse contingencies posed by the environment; it allows a greater diversity of talent and experience within the organization. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.

The extent of extensive and open internal communication among organizational members so that they can work jointly on complex innovative projects. Open internal communications served as a classification criterion for Organic firms. Scale items were averaged to obtain the variable score.

variable_name: Organization structure variables (scanning, controls, communication, centralization, technocratization, differentiation, integration)
description: Organizational structure is represented by a set of questionnaire-based structural scales: scanning, controls, open internal communication, centralization, technocratization, differentiation and integration. Multi-item scale items were averaged to obtain each variable score, and each variable was correlated with entrepreneurship within each firm type.

The sample was divided into two groups by organizational age. The first group includes 17 older manufacturing organizations, 15 or 88 percent of which were established at least 10 years before the study. The second group includes 14 younger firms, 11 or 79 percent of which were established within six years. Age itself refers to the number of years since the organization established production facilities for the product lines covered in this study.

One of the two indices of complexity, measured by the scales developed by Hage and Aiken. The structural variables were measured at the level of the work group because they are related to operations technology, which reflects work flow patterns.
The second index of complexity, measured by the scales developed by Hage and Aiken at the level of the work group.

One of the two indices of formalization, which refers to the degree of codification specifying who is to do what, where, and when. Measured by the scales developed by Hage and Aiken at the level of the work group.
The second index of formalization, measured by the scales developed by Hage and Aiken at the level of the work group.
A measure of centralization, which refers to the hierarchy of authority and decision making in the organization, measured by the scales developed by Hage and Aiken at the level of the work group.
A measure of centralization, measured by the scales developed by Hage and Aiken at the level of the work group.

Integration refers to the structural devices designed to integrate the workings of various subsystems to attain the common goals of the organization, measured by the scales developed by Hage and Aiken at the level of the work group.

Adaptability refers to the degree of flexibility in operations technology and was measured by an eight-item workflow scale developed by the Aston Group. Data for these variables were obtained through interviews with production managers of the organizations under study. Continuity reflects inversely the degree of adaptability and was therefore not reported.

Measured by a six-point scale: an organization which performs a simple assembly operation of 100 percent foreign parts for foreign-designed products was scored 1, while an organization that produces products which are unique and entirely different from the existing products of the advanced economies was scored 6.

The number of technological changes in products and processes during one year, measured using the total number of changes that have occurred in the previous five years divided by the number of years that each change has been in effect. Information on innovation was first obtained from each organization's new product catalogues and development and engineering records, and then verified through interviews with principal members of the engineering and/or R&D department.
Size refers to the number of workers in the organization.

The task environment was delineated into 20 subcomponents, each measured by a five-point Likert scale through interviews with top management. The supplier component index was obtained by summing only those subcomponent variables that are positively correlated with the sum.
scale: five-point Likert scales for subcomponents; summed component index

description: One of the environmental component indices, formed by summing only those subcomponent variables that are positively correlated with the sum. Each subcomponent was measured by a five-point Likert scale through interviews with top management.
scale: five-point Likert scales for subcomponents; summed component index

description: One of the environmental component indices, formed by summing only those subcomponent variables that are positively correlated with the sum. Each subcomponent was measured by a five-point Likert scale through interviews with top management.
scale: five-point Likert scales for subcomponents; summed component index

description: One of the environmental component indices, formed by summing only those subcomponent variables that are positively correlated with the sum. Each subcomponent was measured by a five-point Likert scale through interviews with top management.
scale: five-point Likert scales for subcomponents; summed component index

description: One of the environmental component indices, formed by summing only those subcomponent variables that are positively correlated with the sum. Each subcomponent was measured by a five-point Likert scale through interviews with top management.
scale: five-point Likert scales for subcomponents; summed component index

description: Centralization was measured, a = 0.69, by summing responses indicating the location (programmer/analyst, project manager, software development manager, a superior) of decision responsibility for eight common activities. The scale is the author's own composite; no range is stated.

Formalization was reflected, a = 0.76, by the number of tasks from a list for which standards currently existed. The tasks listed are project control, feasibility study, budget estimation, schedule estimation, requirements analysis, system design, program design, coding, testing, documentation, and conversion. No range is stated.

Initiation was reflected by the number of practices each respondent recognized (a 0-3 range), measured here over the three technical MSP. For those practices recognized, respondents were asked to describe the extent each was currently being applied.

Adoption was measured as the proportion of recognized practices in use beyond an experimentation stage (a 0-1 range), measured here over the three technical MSP. The response categories used to describe application extent ranged from 'not used at all' to 'usage has become standard'.

Implementation was taken as the average extent adopted practices were being used (a 3-6 range), measured here over the three technical MSP. The extent responses cover not used at all; a few people/projects experimenting; a few people/projects regularly using it; a number of people/projects regularly using it; most people/projects regularly using it; and usage has become standard.

Initiation was reflected by the number of practices each respondent recognized (a 0-3 range), measured here over the three administrative MSP. For those practices recognized, respondents were asked to describe the extent each was currently being applied.

Adoption was measured as the proportion of recognized practices in use beyond an experimentation stage (a 0-1 range), measured here over the three administrative MSP. The response categories used to describe application extent ranged from 'not used at all' to 'usage has become standard'.

Implementation was taken as the average extent adopted practices were being used (a 3-6 range), measured here over the three administrative MSP. The extent responses cover not used at all; a few people/projects experimenting; a few people/projects regularly using it; a number of people/projects regularly using it; most people/projects regularly using it; and usage has become standard.

The presence of a mechanistic overlay was identified by whether analysts/programmers were maintained as fixed teams, i.e., a formal structure existed through which innovations could be channeled, or were assigned to new projects on an as-needed basis.

The presence of an organic overlay was identified by the existence of a formal group whose organizational role was to search for methods to improve the software development process and introduce these methods throughout the software group, i.e., a venture group.

variable_name: Initiation, adoption and implementation of modern software practices
description: Innovative behavior is measured in three phases for six modern software practices (three technical, three administrative): initiation (number of practices recognized, 0-3), adoption (proportion of recognized practices used beyond experimentation, 0-1) and implementation (average extent adopted practices are used, 3-6), reported by the software development manager.

A semantic differential item asking what top management concentrates its attention on, anchored at management of the business at one end and political negotiations and relations with the public at the other. Responses were recorded on a continuum of seven equal intervals between the two end positions and quantified assuming interval scales. Higher values indicate a stronger political orientation of management.
scale: seven equal intervals between two end positions

description: A semantic differential item asking whether, in managing the business, top management focuses on the needs of the enterprise or on the needs of the customers. Responses were recorded on a continuum of seven equal intervals between the two end positions and quantified assuming interval scales. Higher values indicate a stronger external orientation in business management.
scale: seven equal intervals between two end positions

description: A semantic differential item asking whether, in political negotiations and relations with the public, top management focuses on the needs of the enterprise or on the needs of the public. Responses were recorded on a continuum of seven equal intervals between the two end positions and quantified assuming interval scales. Higher values indicate a stronger external orientation in political management.
scale: seven equal intervals between two end positions

description: A semantic differential item about what the goals of the organization are concerned with, ranging from attempting to maximize profits each year at one end to attempting to maximize gross sales each year at the other. Responses were recorded on a continuum of seven equal intervals between the two end positions. Higher values indicate a greater emphasis on sales goals.
scale: seven equal intervals between two end positions

description: A semantic differential item about prices in relation to costs, ranging from relatively low at one end to relatively high at the other. Responses were recorded on a continuum of seven equal intervals between the two end positions. Higher values indicate higher prices relative to costs.
scale: seven equal intervals between two end positions

description: A semantic differential item about the organizational goals, ranging from stable at one end to unstable at the other. Responses were recorded on a continuum of seven equal intervals between the two end positions. Higher values indicate less stable goals, so the measure runs opposite to goal stability.
scale: seven equal intervals between two end positions

description: A semantic differential item about the objectives and policies of the enterprise, ranging from specific and clearly stated at one end to general and vague at the other. Responses were recorded on a continuum of seven equal intervals between the two end positions. Higher values indicate less clear goals, opposite to goal and policy clarity.
scale: seven equal intervals between two end positions

description: A semantic differential item about the intervals at which performance evaluation takes place, ranging from regular intervals at one end to irregular intervals at the other. Responses were recorded on a continuum of seven equal intervals between the two end positions. Higher values indicate less regular evaluation, opposite to regularity of performance evaluation.
scale: seven equal intervals between two end positions

description: A semantic differential item about what management does when initiating a new plan which can benefit from political support, ranging from act first then ask for support at one end to ask for support before acting at the other. Responses were recorded on a continuum of seven equal intervals between the two end positions. Higher values indicate greater cultivation of support before action.
scale: seven equal intervals between two end positions

description: A semantic differential item about where top management is recruited from, ranging from business firms at one end to public organizations at the other. Responses were recorded on a continuum of seven equal intervals between the two end positions. Higher values indicate more top managers recruited from public organizations.
scale: seven equal intervals between two end positions

variable_name: External orientation of management (items X2 and X3)
description: External orientation of management is measured with two semantic differential items on seven-interval scales: external orientation in business management (needs of the enterprise versus needs of customers) and external orientation in political management (needs of the enterprise versus needs of the general public). The two items are used as moderators of the political orientation effects.

Projects were coded as having a gatekeeper when they contained at least one individual who was in the top fifth of their intradepartment communication distribution and who was also in the top fifth of the extra-organizational communication distribution, that is, internal stars who also maintain a high degree of extra-organizational communication. Gatekeepers were identified in 21 projects and 40 projects had no gatekeepers.
scale: binary: projects with gatekeepers vs. projects without gatekeepers

description: Each department manager (n = 7) and laboratory director (n = 2) was interviewed separately and asked to evaluate the overall technical performance of all projects with which they were technically familiar; managers who could not make an informed judgement were asked not to rate the project. Each project was independently rated by an average of 4.7 managers on a seven-point scale from very low to very high, and the individual ratings were averaged to yield overall project performance scores (range from 3.0 to 6.4; median of 4.6).
scale: seven-point scale (very low to very high); observed range 3.0 to 6.4

description: Respondents selected the task category that best characterized the objectives of their project, choosing among basic research, applied research, development and technical service, and indicated on a three-point scale how completely the project's objectives were represented by the selected category; the twelve possible answers were scored along a single scale ranging from completely basic research to completely technical service. Respondents also indicated what percentage of their project's work fell into each of the four categories, and a weighted average of the percentages was calculated for each respondent; the scored responses to the two questions were averaged (Spearman-Brown reliability = 0.91) and individual responses were pooled to project scores. The distribution of project task scores clustered into three categories: Research (basic and applied research), Development, and Technical Service.
scale: single scale from completely basic research to completely technical service; clustered into Research, Development, Technical Service

description: Six mutually exclusive communication measures were operationalized for each project: communication within the project; communication to other areas within the project's department; communication to other areas in the laboratory; communication to areas in the larger organization; communication to external professionals outside the parent organization, including consulting firms, universities and professional societies; and communication to external operational areas, including suppliers, vendors and customers. Extra-organizational (i.e. external) communication is the sum of the reported communication to professional and operational areas. Project communication is the average absolute amount of technical communication per person per project over the fifteen weeks, obtained by pooling individual responses.

variable_name: Mean absolute change in project funding (D; adjusted version Da)
description: Mean over all projects of the absolute dollar change in project funding between two decision points in the budget cycle, establishing the average magnitude of actual dollar changes. The text states that D is the mean of absolute funding changes over all projects and that X(i,j) is the funding of project i at point j (or k) in the cycle; the printed formula is not readable in this text. An adjusted version, Da, is computed after project funding levels are adjusted for changes in total budget.
time_window: between decision points in the budget cycle (June 1968-April 1971)

variable_name: Mean absolute percent change in project funding (DP; adjusted version DPa)
description: Mean over all projects of the absolute percent change in project funding between decision points, taken project by project, establishing the average relative change in actual project funding. The printed formula is not readable in this text. An adjusted version, DPa, is computed after project funding levels are adjusted for changes in total budget.
time_window: between decision points in the budget cycle (June 1968-April 1971)

variable_name: Pearson product moment correlation between funding distributions
description: Pearson product moment correlation coefficients calculated between pairs of points in the cycle in order to measure the degree of similarity in funding distribution. In the refinement phase the correlation is in excess of 0.97 for all pairs of comparisons and in the apportionment phase it equals or exceeds 0.94.
time_window: between pairs of decision points in the budget cycle

variable_name: Test statistic t for the linear trend coefficient
description: Multivariate test of the hypothesis that adjusted project funding data are of a linear form over the thirteen sequential points, with x(j) a (181 x 1) vector of adjusted project funding levels, y an unknown vector of constants, B an unknown vector of trend coefficients and e(j) a vector of unobservable errors. The printed equations are not readable in this text; estimating the parameters from the differenced data gives t = 101.9, which the authors describe as very low.
time_window: thirteen sequential points of the budget cycle

variable_name: Organizational level of the decision entity
description: The hierarchical entity making a change in project funding. Four hierarchical levels participate directly in the refinement stage: agency headquarters, the research organization director, division chiefs, and subordinate units. Reallocation actions are identified by hierarchical level rather than date, and the apportionment phase involves only agency headquarters and the research organization director.

variable_name: Budget cycle phase and decision event
description: Codification of the points in the cycle at which funding decisions are made. Four hierarchical levels participate directly in the refinement stage, which has five identifiable points; following refinement there are six entries into the budget cycle during apportionment; the last stage, reallocation, follows apportionment with changes initiated by each organizational entity. The sequential points of the cycle are indexed j = 1, 2, ..., 13.
level: decision event within the budget cycle

variable_name: Project funding level (smaller versus larger projects)
description: Relative change in project funding is compared between smaller (lower funded) and larger (higher funded) projects. If the absolute percent change in adjusted project funding is evenly distributed over small and large projects, the mean absolute percent change in adjusted funding equals the mean absolute change in adjusted funding divided by average adjusted project funding, the latter two in units of $1,000; the comparison of mean change and mean percent change provides a measure of the relative impact on large versus small projects.
time_window: between decision points in the budget cycle

description: Project funding at the final decision event of the cycle, consisting of the released program following reallocation by all entities. It is compared with the entries in the first two phases, and the authors note that the final allocation was 21 percent lower than the budget sought at the beginning of the cycle.

The total research budget at each decision event of the cycle; changes in it are generally beyond the control of the hierarchical entities studied. Project funding levels are adjusted for changes in total budget in constructing the adjusted change measures.

variable_name: pre- to post-test gains in achievement scores
description: All pupils were pre-tested during the initial weeks of school and post-tested during the last weeks of school using the Comprehensive Test of Basic Skills, a widely-used achievement measure. Pre- to post-test gains were computed as changes measured by the achievement test; reading gains are reported as years of growth. The high-growth group was formed from those children with the highest growth in reading skills (N = 230).
time_window: pre-test at the start of the school year, post-test in the last weeks of the school year

description: Computed from parent responses to a series of questions posing twelve decisional situations which occur in school systems in general and which did occur with reference to the project in particular. Respondents indicated whether they currently participated in and whether they desired to participate in each decision; the index of satisfaction with current decisional participation levels was computed by summing over the number of decisions in which each person currently participated and those in which he or she wished to participate and then computing the absolute differences between these two figures. The same index was computed for general school issues; the reported parent figures for project issues are used here.

Computed from teacher responses to a series of questions posing twelve decisional situations which occur in school systems in general and which did occur with reference to the project in particular. Respondents indicated whether they currently participated in and whether they desired to participate in each decision; the index of satisfaction with current decisional participation levels was computed by summing over the number of decisions in which each person currently participated and those in which he or she wished to participate and then computing the absolute differences between these two figures. The same index was computed for general school issues; the reported teacher figures for project issues are used here.

It was anticipated that the degree of authoritarianism exhibited by teachers and parents would be related to their willingness to accept change and innovation. A shortened version of the F-scale was employed for this purpose, administered to both teachers and parents.

Interpersonal trust was measured by a scale derived from the work of Kluckhohn and Murray which focused on beliefs concerning the fundamental cooperativeness and trustworthiness of human nature. The higher an individual scored, the greater the interpersonal trust.

Prior research indicated that teachers are differentially involved in three separate and independent dimensions of their job: the child-related portion, the administrative portion, and the professional development portion. These three dimensions were measured through the use of 18 Likert-type items which elaborated the scale employed by Lodahl.

variable_name: Perceived Job Tension and Teacher Commitment
description: Job tension was measured with the scales reported by Kahn et al. and Lichtman, involving responses on a five-point scale to various aspects of job-related tension; the greater the numerical score, the greater the tension experienced by each teacher. Teacher commitment to the employing school district was ascertained, following Becker, from questions focused on the inducements necessary for a teacher to leave employment in the district; responses to a slight increase in pay, a slight increase in status, a position allowing slightly more creativity, and a position in which individuals are slightly more friendly were summed to indicate commitment levels.
scale: five-point scale (job tension); summed inducement responses (commitment)

description: Both teachers and parents were asked to rank order how a series of role performers—including school principals, superintendents, the community, and the teacher herself—currently influenced daily teaching activities. This ranking yielded an indication of perceived current teacher autonomy levels; the higher the rank, the more autonomous the teacher was perceived.

variable_name: Attitude Toward the School System (desirability and importance)
description: Semantic differential attitudinal scales developed by Osgood, Succi, and Tannenbaum were used, yielding three general factors of meaning: one factor indicating the individual's judgement concerning the desirability of various school system issues, another indicating the judgement concerning the current existence of each condition, and a third indicating its importance. Attitudinal data were also gathered for performance contracting and the school principal, and from both teachers and parents.

Binary variable that takes the value '1' for teams that are located within 100 miles of a mass shooting or domestic terrorism event for 30 days following the event, and '0' otherwise. Only events with human casualties were included, and events occurring in both databases were removed. Terrorist incidents carried out by foreign groups were excluded.

Spline function representing performance relative to aspirations using the score differential between the team of interest and their opponent: coded as the absolute difference in scores when performance falls short of aspirations, and as 0 when performance is above aspirations.

Score differential between the team of interest and their opponent when performance exceeds aspirations, coded as 0 when performance is below aspirations. A Valence indicator taking the value '0' when performance is below aspirations and '1' otherwise accompanies the spline specification.

Binary variable equal to '1' if the offensive team opts to play on a fourth down ('go for it') and '0' otherwise; punting and kicking a field goal are treated as the less risky options. Fourth-down decisions from preseason games and overtime periods were excluded.

Total length in years of professional residence of the coach in the affected area, collected from pro-football-history.com and pro-football-reference.com. Used to split the sample at the median coach tenure.

variable_name: Decision-maker proximity to the site of violence
description: Distance in miles between a team and a violent traumatic event, employed as a measure of salience; teams within a 100-mile radius are compared with teams located farther away in 100-mile bands up to 500 miles. Higher distance corresponds to lower proximity.

Four items adapted from the state regulatory focus scale of Godollei and Beck (2020), designed to assess respondents' current state rather than a trait-level regulatory focus (alpha = .86; e.g., 'I focus on attaining my goals and aspirations'). Items were assessed on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much).
time_window: measured at the end of the study, after the risk-taking task

description: Four items adapted from the state regulatory focus scale of Godollei and Beck (2020) (alpha = .78; e.g., 'I focus on minimizing losses'). Items were assessed on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much).
time_window: measured at the end of the study, after the risk-taking task

description: Measured as the number of cards participants chose to select in each of three rounds of a game adapted from the cold version of the Columbia Card Task; of 32 cards, 30 were gain cards and two were loss cards. Each gain card selected yielded 10 points, but selecting a loss card gave zero points for that round, so selecting more cards was riskier. Risk-taking in round 1 served as a baseline before feedback, and rounds 2 and 3 captured the joint effects of the manipulations.
Same state regulatory focus measure as in Study 1 (alpha = .92), measured immediately after the manipulation of traumatic event salience and before the risk-taking task.
time_window: measured immediately after the salience manipulation, before the risk-taking task

description: Same state regulatory focus measure as in Study 1 (alpha = .88), measured immediately after the manipulation of traumatic event salience and before the risk-taking task.
time_window: measured immediately after the salience manipulation, before the risk-taking task

description: Measured as the number of grids participants chose to attempt to solve in each of three rounds of a real-effort task adapted from Abeler et al. (2011), in which they counted zeros in grids full of numbers under time pressure. Participants stated in advance how many grids they would attempt; if they solved all attempted grids within 45 seconds the grids were added to their cumulative points, otherwise they received zero points for the round, so attempting more grids was riskier. Risk-taking in round 1 served as a baseline before feedback.

The number of new products previously launched by divisions other than the one associated with the focal project, using knowledge from startups found by the focal scout. The authors focus on new products launched because these complete integration projects exposed scouts to the entire process, enabling the development of knowledge and relationships. The variable was mean-centered to facilitate interpretation of the results.

A dummy variable set to 1 if the external knowledge integration process in the focal division culminated in the launch of a new product and to 0 otherwise. The dependent variable refers to 'new product' but includes both products and services, as in this setting these are often bundled in the same offering.

Captures the similarity between the focal startup's technology and that of startups that the focal division worked with earlier, measured as the extent of overlap between a startup's patents and those of startups previously selected by the focal division, in terms of patent classes. For each startup's patents, the corresponding technology classes were identified using the Cooperative Patent Classification; vectors of patent distributions across these classes were constructed and their similarity measured via angular separation. The formula is unreadable in the text and was not restated in prose. This formula yields an index, with a higher value representing greater startup technological similarity. The authors used the full set of listed four-digit patent classes and all patents filed prior to being identified by the focal scout, and mean-centered the variable.
time_window: all patents filed prior to the startup being identified by the focal scout

description: Evaluates overlap in product market between the focal division and those with which the focal scout gained experience. Product-market overlap between each division-year pair was first calculated using yearly data on each division's product lines and market segments from Telcorp's annual reports, using the Jaccard index. The division(s) and year(s) in which the scout had gained experience prior to the focal observation were then identified. The variable is time-variant and compares the focal division with the ones with which the scout gained experience, in terms of product-market overlap at the time when experience was gained; it takes the value of 0 if there is no scout experience with other divisions. The variable was mean-centered.
time_window: at the time when experience was gained, before the focal project

description: LDA is used to identify the topics founders and the market discuss each quarter within each market, producing time series of quarterly topic proportions; log odds of these proportions are modeled in a vector autoregressive (VAR) system with two lags estimated for each startup and each quarter. Cumulative impulse response functions are then computed, and founders leading the market discussion is measured as the cumulative change in market discussion following a permanent 10-percentage-point increase in founder discussion five quarters earlier.
time_window: quarterly, from one year before founding up to 28 quarters later

description: Built from the same LDA topic time series and startup-specific VAR models as founders leading the market discussion. Founders following the market discussion is the cumulative change in founder discussion after a permanent 10-percentage-point increase in market discussion, computed through cumulative impulse response functions.
time_window: quarterly, from one year before founding up to 28 quarters later

description: New product introductions in a quarter are identified using Crunchbase news coverage data, which provides a list of articles for each startup. The authors read the title and excerpts of these articles and identify the ones that refer to the introduction of new products or new refinements for existing products; when multiple articles cover the same product, it is counted as just one.

Market attention is measured with the organic traffic to the startup's website each quarter, that is visits that come to a website via unpaid search results, from Semrush data. To account for skewness, market attention is logged.

Time is the quarterly time variable in the growth curve model; variables are centered at their grand mean and the first quarter in which a startup is observed (the quarter of its founding) is coded equal to 0, so that simple effects of the independent variables can be interpreted as their effects on initial market attention.

Participants were asked in Wave 1: 'Which of the following labels describes your political views best?' Participants who responded 'conservative' were coded as -1 and 'liberal' as 1. This binary measure of ideology was the focal independent variable.
time_window: Wave 1 (one week before the activism manipulation)

description: The same binary self-identification measure as in Experiment 1a was used: participants selected the label that best described their political views, coded conservative as -1 and liberal as 1.
time_window: Wave 1 (one week before the activism manipulation)

description: The same binary measure of political ideology used in Experiments 1a and 1b was used as the main measure, with conservative coded as -1 and liberal as 1.
time_window: Wave 1 (one week before the activism manipulation)

description: Participants in the societal well-being condition were asked to think of one important reason why businesses should pursue activities that promote societal well-being rather than focusing only on activities that generate profits, and to write about this reason in a text box before completing the rest of Wave 2. Participants in the control condition were not given this task. The manipulation check showed that participants in the societal well-being condition were more likely to agree that businesses should focus on societal well-being than were control participants.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions. In the liberal (conservative) CEO activism condition they read 'As CEO, Ben Smith has been vocal in his public support of various politically liberal (conservative) causes.' In the no CEO activism condition they read 'As CEO, Ben Smith has not made any public statements on political issues.'

Participants were randomly assigned to read that CEO Ben Smith has publicly opposed state laws banning transgender people from using public restrooms that conform with their gender identity (liberal activism), has publicly supported such laws (conservative activism), or has not publicly voiced support for any political causes, including those related to transgender people (no activism).

Participants were randomly assigned to read that CEO Dave Baker has publicly urged the U.S. congress and state legislatures to pass more gun control laws (liberal activism), more gun rights laws (conservative activism), or has not publicly voiced his support for any political causes, including on the topic of guns (no activism).

A five-item scale developed by Highhouse, Lievens, and Sinar (2003) was used to measure job seekers' intention to pursue employment at the firm. Items included 'I would accept a job offer from Solaris' and 'I would make Solaris one of my first choices as an employer'; the scale had an alpha of .87.

Following research on petitions, participants were asked to provide their email address if they were interested in applying to the job so that they could be sent more detailed information about the application process. Responses that entered an email address were coded as 1 and responses that did not as 0.
scale: binary (0 = did not provide email, 1 = provided email)

description: After seeing the description about the CEO, participants were shown pictures of the type of soap the company sells and answered a single question commonly used in the marketing literature: 'How likely are you to purchase XYZ products the next time you are purchasing soap?'

The dollar sum of a company's violation penalty amounts in a given calendar year, expressed as a percentage of the company's revenues for that fiscal year according to Compustat. One unit of violation intensity corresponds to 1% of the firm's annual revenues. The variable is normalized by firm revenues because employees are expected to perceive violation intensity relative to organizational size. It remains highly skewed even after normalization.
scale: percentage of annual firm revenues (one unit = 1%)

description: The count of all employee job spells at each company that have end dates in a given calendar year, aggregated from U.S.-based individual employee job spell records to the company level using Revelio Labs company identifiers. Instances where an employee's subsequent job spell is also at the same company are omitted to exclude internal job moves.

The count of states in which a firm experiences violations during each calendar year, based on the geographic locations of the firm's facilities responsible for each of its violations. It captures the extent to which a firm's violation events in a given year are distributed across a geographical footprint. The variable ranges from 0 to 30, with an average of 1.1 violation locations per firm-year.

The number of years between the current year and the last time that the focal firm experienced violations of the same or greater intensity, up to five years earlier.
