A five-year cutoff is used to account for the natural cycling of employees and because employees may forget violations after five or so years. The variable ranges from 0 to 5, with an average value of 4.2.

The number of new violation categories a firm enters in a given year, relative to its own violation history over the previous five years. Violation Tracker's 121 specific offense types were grouped, with the help of ChatGPT and manual review, into 28 broad categories. The measure ranges from 0 to 4 in the dataset, with a mean value of 0.18.

Total U.S. dollar amount of marijuana products sold by dispensaries to consumers each month. The distribution of sales exhibited moderate positive skewness and leptokurtic characteristics, so the authors applied a Box-Cox transformation; a cube-root transformation was optimal for normalizing the distribution, and the transformed variable is used in all analyses.

County-level percentage of Black residents, measured using one-year estimates from the American Community Survey. Black Americans are identified as the primary market-stigmatized group in Washington's marijuana market.

For each dispensary and observation period, the percentage of terms from the medical dictionary in the dispensary's product names and descriptions, calculated by dividing the number of terms from that dictionary by the total number of terms in the same text and multiplying by 100. The medical dictionary covers terms related to medicine (e.g., 'patient', 'medical', 'rx', 'pharmacy') and medical conditions (e.g., 'pain', 'cancer', 'ADHD', 'disease', 'syndrome'). The three language variables are not mutually exclusive and each has a value between 0 and 100.

For each dispensary and observation period, the percentage of terms from the wellness dictionary in the dispensary's product names and descriptions, calculated by dividing the number of terms from that dictionary by the total number of terms in the same text and multiplying by 100. The wellness dictionary contains language associated with quality-of-life improvements (e.g., 'creativity', 'ease', 'focus', 'relaxation', 'stress-relieving'). The three language variables are not mutually exclusive and each has a value between 0 and 100.

For each dispensary and observation period, the percentage of terms from the vice dictionary in the dispensary's product names and descriptions, calculated by dividing the number of terms from that dictionary by the total number of terms in the same text and multiplying by 100. The vice dictionary includes terms associated with the illicit market (e.g., slang such as 'trees' or 'nugs') and intoxication (e.g., 'euphoric', 'buzzed', or 'couchlock'). The three language variables are not mutually exclusive and each has a value between 0 and 100.

County-level percentage of Hispanic residents, measured using one-year estimates from the American Community Survey, included to test the theory's application to a group whose connection to the market stigma is less straightforward.

County-level percentage of Asian American residents, measured using one-year estimates from the American Community Survey, included as a theoretically grounded comparison group whose stigma content is distinct from that associated with the marijuana market.

The sum of backward citations in the acquirer's patent applications to the partner's patents within a five-year interval following the date of the target's acquisition. Only citations to patents of the partner that were not previously cited by the acquirer are considered, and the acquirer's citations to the partner's patents previously cited by the target are excluded, as are citations in patent co-applications between the target and the acquirer and between the acquirer and partners. Each citation is weighted by a factor of (1 - r)^t, with r an annual discount rate of 10% and t the difference in years between the priority dates of the citing and cited patents.
time_window: five years following the acquisition date

description: A binary variable indicating whether an observation features the actual partner or the matched pseudo-partner ('0' = pseudo-partner, '1' = actual partner). Actual partners are those with whom the target formed an alliance in the decade preceding its acquisition; pseudo-partners are identified through a two-step matching procedure on firms listed in Compustat, first by propensity-score matching on firm size, performance, R&D intensity, and solvency and then by selecting the firm with the highest knowledge base relatedness to the actual partner.
time_window: alliances formed in the decade preceding the acquisition

description: The count of backward citations in the target's patent applications to the partner's patents during the five years following the alliance announcement; if the alliance preceded the acquisition by fewer than five years, citations during the period between the alliance announcement and the acquisition date are counted. Citations in patent co-applications between the target and the acquirer or the partner are not considered. A 10% annual discount rate is applied to attach greater weight to knowledge flows more likely to have occurred in proximal connection with the alliance's activities.
time_window: five years following the alliance announcement (or until the acquisition date if shorter)

description: Jaffe's cosine index of the extent to which the acquirer and the partner file patents in similar technology classes, where the technology class is the subclass of the International Patent Classification. The index measures the angular separation between the vectorized distributions of the acquirer's and the partner's patent applications across patent classes over a five-year period following the acquisition, after removing patent co-applications between the acquirer and the target. Scores range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater knowledge base relatedness.

The overlap in the acquirer's and the partner's historical four-digit primary SIC codes and their product-market similarity at the time of the acquisition. The SIC-code overlap is coded as 0 if the firms' SIC codes have no common digits, 0.2 for a first-digit match, 0.4 for a two-digit match, 0.6 for a three-digit match, and 0.8 for a four-digit match; the Hoberg and Phillips product-market similarity score (ranging from 1/7 to 1) is multiplied by 0.2 and added to the SIC overlap score. The variable takes a maximum value of 1 and a minimum of 0.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: Measured from changes in the composition of the executive boards of the target and the acquirer in the post-acquisition period, using positions with seniority ranks 'executive director' and 'senior manager'. It is computed as the number of directors transitioning from the target to the acquirer's board (DTA) divided by the total number of unique positions on the acquirer's board prior to the acquisition, minus the number of directors transitioning from the acquirer to the target's board (DAT) divided by the total number of unique positions on the target's board prior to the acquisition. A positive value indicates a greater degree of target autonomy.

Binary indicator equal to 1 when the focal firm listed a competitor that was peripheral in year t but grew to become (and remained) prominent by year t + 5. Peripheral competitors are those not listed by any other firms in the focal firm's industry segments; prominent competitors are those in the top 25th percentile in indegree centrality in at least one of the focal firm's industry segments. Built from yearly segment-level perceptual competition networks constructed from 10-K competitor lists.
time_window: year t, with prominence assessed by year t + 5

description: Count of competitors listed only by the focal firm in year t, used as the mediator in the mediation analysis.

The average number of prior firm affiliations across the top management team. The number of unique firms in each TMT member's work history (excluding the current firm) is counted and averaged across the team.
The average tenure at the focal firm across the top management team. For each TMT member the total number of years worked at the focal firm is summed and averaged across the team.

The average number of prior industry affiliations across the top management team. For each team member the four-digit Global Industry Categorical Standard is recorded for each prior firm, and the number of unique industries represented in the work history (excluding infrastructure software) is counted and averaged across the team.

The average tenure in infrastructure software across the top management team. For each TMT member the total number of years worked at any infrastructure software firm is summed and averaged across the team.

We operationalized the residual value available to equity stakeholders as net profit margin, measured as the ratio of net profit to total sales. Net profit captures the remaining revenue after all expenses are deducted. We calculated this measure as the proportion of total sales so that the value is not skewed by firm size. All ratios were winsorized at 5% of their empirical distributions to mitigate the effect of extreme values.
scale: ratio of net profit to total sales

description: To test Hypothesis 1, the authors created binary indicators comparing conventional firms with worker cooperatives and multistakeholder cooperatives, as well as worker with multistakeholder cooperatives. For the switcher subgroup they constructed two indicators: the first equal to 1 if a conventional firm became a worker cooperative (0 otherwise), and the second equal to 1 if it became a multistakeholder cooperative (0 otherwise). In the cross-sectional models the structure variable takes a value of 0 for conventional firms and 1 for worker cooperatives, or 0 for conventional firms and 1 for multistakeholder cooperatives, depending on the model.

variable_name: count of stakeholders with governance rights
description: To analyze the factors driving coordination costs, the authors used the count of stakeholders with governance rights, which in their data ranges from 3 to 10. It captures the number of stakeholders with governance rights in firms with broadened stakeholder governance.

The Blau index of stakeholder diversity increases with both the number of stakeholders and the evenness of the distribution of governance rights among them, so a higher value indicates that decision-making power is more evenly shared among contracted stakeholders.

For Hypothesis 1b, the authors calculated supplier representation as the percentage of governance rights allocated to suppliers. These continuous measures reflect the level of control these contracted stakeholders had over multistakeholder cooperatives.

For Hypothesis 1b, the authors calculated employee representation as the percentage of governance rights allocated to workers. These continuous measures reflect the level of control these contracted stakeholders had over multistakeholder cooperatives.

For suppliers, the authors calculated supplier fixed claim, defined as the ratio of total input costs to total sales. These measures capture how firm resources are allocated to input costs, reflecting stakeholders' financial and economic demands. All ratios were winsorized at 5% of their empirical distributions.
scale: ratio of total input costs to total sales

description: For workers, the authors calculated worker fixed claim, which is the ratio of total wages to total sales. These measures capture how firm resources are allocated to labor expenses, reflecting stakeholders' financial and economic demands. All ratios were winsorized at 5% of their empirical distributions.
scale: ratio of total wages to total sales

description: To evaluate coordination costs, the authors calculated the log of annual meeting duration for a subsample of multistakeholder cooperatives. For this subset of firms they collected archival annual meeting records, which are publicly available and include the duration of the meetings. Computing the total duration of annual meetings in minutes for each year enabled them to quantify the time spent on internal coordination activities among various stakeholders with residual control rights.

The authors measured firm maturity as the number of years that the firm had operated as either a conventional firm, a worker cooperative, or a multistakeholder cooperative. This measure enabled them to include both de novo and switcher worker and multistakeholder cooperatives.
time_window: years since founding or since transition

description: To proxy firm-specific investments, the authors computed intangible asset intensity, defined as the ratio of the stock of intangibles to total sales. This measure captures the importance of a firm's investments in intangibles - such as training, research, and development - that complement the firm-specific investments made by contracted stakeholders. These investments provide an indirect yet effective proxy for firm-specific investments made by contracted stakeholders.
scale: ratio of stock of intangibles to total sales
time_window: annual; lagged stock of intangibles used in models

description: The authors used a dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if a region was in recession after the financial crisis, and 0 otherwise. Their measure identified regions that had not recovered by 2012, meaning their GDP per capita in 2012 was still lower than in 2007, contrasted with a control group of regions that had exceeded their 2007 GDP per capita by 2012. The results are compared over three years (2010-2012).

To assess firm survival, the authors used a binary measure, firm closure, indicating whether a firm closed in a given year, coded 1 if a firm ceased operations in a given year. In the FICUS-FARE panel, a firm is considered to have exited when it no longer reports economic activity, which may occur through judicial liquidation or bankruptcy, voluntary dissolution, or merger or absorption. Treating all exit modes as loss of survival is conceptually appropriate because the theorizing focuses on the firm's persistence as an organization that provides value to stakeholders.

Subjective social class origins measured with the survey item: 'Which of the following best describes your family's socioeconomic situation while you were growing up: lower class (bottom 20%), working class (20%-30%), middle class (30%-80%), upper class (80%-90%), or highest class (top 10%)?' Using established cutoffs, CEOs were coded as having lower social class origins (1) if they indicated that their parents were either lower class or working class, and 0 otherwise.
scale: binary (1 = lower or working class origins, 0 = otherwise)

description: A single-factor measure of CEO greedy behavior computed using principal components analysis with varimax rotation to combine three proxies of greedy behavior. The first proxy is the annual dollar amount of compensation not classified as salary, bonuses, or long-term incentive compensation, such as personal use of company-owned homes and aircraft. The second proxy is the discrepancy between the payment allotted to the CEO and the cash compensation allotted to the second-highest-paid executive. The third proxy, CEO overpayment, is the proportion of a CEO's pay that cannot be explained by organizational, contextual, or experiential factors, calculated as the residual of regressing CEO tenure, CEO compensation, CEO duality, firm size, board independence, firm risk, ROA, sales growth, and firm fixed effects onto total direct compensation. The single factor had an eigenvalue of 1.38, accounting for 44% of the unique explanatory variance, and the measure was winsorized at the 1% level.

An adjusted internal CSR measure, based on the Thomson Reuters ASSET4 database, used to capture CEOs' prosocial behavior. The measure was adjusted to include only indicators under the CEO's purview, and indicators that represented board or shareholder actions were excluded; details about the measure are provided in Appendix A in the Additional Materials.

Operationalized based on performance-related dismissals within the focal CEO's two-digit industry peer group each year, identified using the CEO turnover database compiled by Gentry et al. (2021). The variable was coded 1 only when two conditions were met: (1) at least one other CEO in the industry was dismissed for poor performance, and (2) the focal CEO's performance fell below the industry median; it was coded 0 otherwise.
scale: binary (1 = performance-related peer dismissal and focal CEO below industry median performance, 0 = otherwise)

description: Measured using ExecuComp data on each CEO's past vested stock option holdings. Following Phua, Tham, and Wei (2018), CEO overconfidence was coded as 1 when a CEO chose not to exercise stock options that had increased in value by at least 67% since the grant date, with five years remaining on at least two occasions; the cutoff is grounded in the rational stock options model. Using this method, 62 out of 135 CEOs in the sample were identified as overconfident.

The authors qualitatively coded CEO interviews from TV and podcasts and identified instances in which individual CEOs expressed a resource insecurity mindset. Indicators of resource insecurity included personal insights (e.g., 'Normal is being cash-strapped. That's just the way of life.') and occupational experiences (e.g., 'Leading an organization is like being hit by one wave, and just as you think you're emerging from it, there's another bigger one right behind it.'). The final sample consisted of 177 handcoded interviews, totaling 314,780 spoken words and involving 90 CEOs, using one observation per CEO; for the time-varying measures the mean across each CEO's tenure was taken. Variables were standardized to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

Measured by counting instances where the CEO held a leadership role in a nonprofit organization. Executive profiles were examined using BoardEx, LinkedIn, and Bloomberg, and company names were cross-referenced with the U.S. Internal Revenue Service database of nonprofit organizations. CEOs were classified as philanthropically involved if they served as a board member, trustee, or in another key role within a nonprofit organization. Charities were classified using a computer-aided keyword search of their names and descriptions according to nine United Nations Sustainable Development Goals; charities focused on vulnerable populations specifically included those focusing on children, women, unhoused people, the disadvantaged, and people with disabilities. Yearly philanthropic involvement was tracked using the initial date of involvement; in the sample, 21% of CEOs were involved with at least one qualifying charitable organization (32% of yearly observations).
time_window: yearly, tracked using the initial date of involvement

description: Cosine similarity between the text of a game's feature-update announcements and the text of users' prior reviews, with documents represented as TF-IDF-weighted unigram vectors after lower-casing, removal of punctuation and stop words, and Porter stemming. Update texts retain only sentences signalling substantive feature or gameplay changes; user reviews up to but not including the current month are aggregated as the comparison text. In the cross-sectional data the value is the mean similarity between each month's update text and cumulative prior reviews, and a higher value indicates a greater degree of feedback incorporation.
time_window: mean over Early Access months, with cumulative prior reviews up to the current month

description: One minus the statistical overlap between the distribution of a game's reviewers across market segments and the distribution of all Steam reviewers across those segments. Segments are created by applying UMAP to reduce 42 user-level variables to 10 dimensions and then K-means clustering all 4 million users on SteamDB into five distinct market segments. If the game's reviewer distribution were identical to the broader Steam population the measure would be 0, and if maximally dissimilar it would be 1; in the cross-sectional sample the measure ranges from .08 to .73.

Base-game sales revenue during the first six months post-launch after leaving Early Access. Revenue is computed from SteamSpy average daily ownership estimates per calendar month: the number of new owners in a month is the average number of owners minus the previous month's average number of owners, multiplied by the average price for that month; when the number of owners decreased revenue was set to zero. The measure captures only base-game sales, not subscription fees or extra-content sales.
Number of positive reviews divided by total reviews in the Early Access period.

For each CVC's parent firm i in focal year t, the firm's knowledge domain (its 'knowledge space') in year t-5 is identified as all patents the firm cited up to year t-5, excluding patents owned by firm i. The number of citations that this knowledge space received from other firms (excluding firm i) is calculated in year t-5 and in year t, and the variable is the degree of change in the number of citation counts between the two years. A larger value indicates a greater decline in the utility or relevance of the firm's knowledge space due to technological developments in the field.
time_window: five-year interval from t-5 to t

description: The volume of a venture's inventive activity, reflecting its yearly production of successful patent applications, that is, patent applications that were eventually granted.
The technological impact and knowledge spillovers of the venture's patents, measured as the annual number of forward citations received by the venture.

The extent of competition faced by the CVC's parent, captured by the 1 - Herfindahl-Hirschman (1 - HHI) index of industry j in year t. Industry classifications are defined using Standard Industrial Classification codes at the three-digit level, and each firm's market share is its annual net sales divided by the total sales of the whole industry.

A social network-based measure calculated with the eigenvector centrality measure of Bonacich (1987), indicating the position an organization holds in the network of relationships as a function of both its direct and indirect ties in the VC syndicate network; the relationship matrix counts coinvestments between two VC firms during the last five years. For each venture-year, the maximum prominence value among all IVCs that invested in the venture in that year is used.
scale: maximum centrality each year is scaled to one across all VCs

description: The number of newly appointed female director(s) within a focal firm in year t. A female director counts as newly appointed if she did not serve on the board in the previous year but joined in the current year. A one-year lag structure is applied, so appointment in year t predicts changes in CEO pay in year t+1; the independent variable spans 2010-2016.

The log difference in CEO total compensation between year t and year t+1. Total compensation includes salary, bonus, and the value of long-term incentive grants, calculated using the Black-Scholes method. The measure is industry-adjusted by subtracting the industry-level raises, computed as the log difference in average CEO compensation in the firm's primary two-digit SIC industry between year t and year t+1. The dependent variable spans 2011-2017.
A dichotomous variable measured in year t. It is coded 1 if there were no women on the board before the appointment (year t-1) and 0 if at least one female director was already on the board.

variable_name: At or above industry norms on diversity
description: The focal firm's female board representation is compared with the average female board representation in the focal firm's primary industry in year t-1. The variable is coded 1 when the percentage of women on the board of the focal firm is equal to or greater than the industry average and 0 otherwise.
CEO gender in year t+1 is a dichotomous variable coded 1 for male CEOs and 0 for female CEOs.

The difference between the total number of external board seats held by male directors and female directors, divided by the number of male directors in the focal firm in year t. Higher values indicate that male directors hold more external board seats relative to female directors, capturing relative influence in group decision-making.

Measured using the stability index recommended by Crutchley, Garner, and Marshall (2002), which assesses the degree to which group membership remains consistent over time; the authors use one minus the stability index as the index of male directors' membership instability. The stability index ranges from 0 to 1 with higher values indicating greater stability, and it is built from the number of male directors in years t-1 and t and the numbers of male directors present in one year but not the other. The formula as printed is unreadable in the extracted text.
Placeholder duplicate record is not used; the measure of female director appointment is reported under m_female_appointment.

Calculated as the CEO's dollar value contributions to the Republican Party minus the CEO's dollar value contributions to the Democratic Party, all divided by the CEO's dollar value contributions to both political parties. This results in a continuous measure in which scores closer to 1 represent greater affiliation with the Republican Party and scores closer to -1 indicate greater affiliation with the Democratic Party. The score is calculated across each two-year election cycle and then averaged across all election cycles for each CEO.
time_window: averaged across all two-year election cycles

description: Conformity is measured as the extent to which the focal firm's repertoire of competitive actions is similar to the average repertoire in the firm's industry, using Euclidean distance. The difference between the focal firm's total number of instances of each competitive action in each of the eight action categories and the industry's average in each category is squared, the resulting scores are summed, and the square root of the total value is taken. Given that Euclidean distance measures how different the focal firm's repertoire is from the industry, the final value is multiplied by -1 such that lower values represent less conformity with the industry and higher values indicate more conformity.

Measured as the ratio of the number of Democratic-leaning CEOs in the focal firm's industry to the number of Republican-leaning CEOs, excluding the focal firm CEO's party affiliation. Each CEO was dichotomized as Democratic Party leaning if their party affiliation score was less than or equal to zero, or Republican Party leaning if their party affiliation score was greater than zero. Higher values indicate a higher concentration of CEOs who prefer the Democratic Party. The variable was winsorized at 5% due to several outlying observations.

Long-term investor value appropriation captures the extent to which CEOs create value for the firm as represented by backward-looking net present value of stock market returns over time. It is measured three years after the focal year given the measure is particularly appropriate for medium and long time periods of around three or more years.
time_window: three years after the focal year

description: Short-term firm performance is captured using net income, a commonly used proxy for firm performance that does not account for value creation in the long term because it relies on backward-looking accounting data that is limited to the prior fiscal year.

The full Pd score from the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory, which consists of 50 items in the original MMPI. The score was obtained from the Finnish Defense Forces for male CEOs who were drafted into military service between 1982 and 2000; men typically undergo call-up testing at approximately 18 years of age, so most CEOs in the sample were born between 1964 and 1982. The sample is restricted to firms led by male CEOs.
time_window: measured at approximately age 18; drafts between 1982 and 2000

description: A spline variable that equals the historical aspiration level minus ROA when ROA is below aspirations, and zero otherwise. Aspirations are based on the firm's past performance in ROA; the authors state that higher values of the updating weight give more weight to recent performance and that the model fit is highest for a weight of 0.5, which they set. The formal equation for the aspiration update is not legible in the text as provided.

A spline variable that equals ROA minus the historical aspiration level when ROA is above aspirations, and zero otherwise. It is built from the same historical aspiration level based on the firm's past ROA. The formal equation for the aspiration update is not legible in the text as provided.

A composite measure of expenditures associated with uncertain returns: capital investments and foreign operations. Each variable was scaled by annual sales and their common component was extracted using principal component analysis. Risk-taking is measured at time t+1.

R&D intensity is calculated as the ratio of R&D expenditure to total annual sales, following prior studies, and is used as the measure of R&D search. In the robustness section the authors also operationalize R&D search using industry-adjusted R&D intensity, calculated as the difference between the ratio of the focal firm's R&D expenditures to total annual sales and average industry R&D intensity.

Performance below historical aspiration, equal to the difference between the focal firm's performance and the corresponding historical aspiration level if firm performance is less than the historical aspiration level, and zero otherwise; the absolute value of this variable is included in the regression models. Performance is measured as return on assets, the ratio of net income to total assets for each year, and a firm's historical aspiration in a given year is the weighted average of the prior period's historical aspiration and the previous performance of the focal firm, with the weight a estimated by searching parameter values in increments of 0.1 and choosing the value with the highest model log-likelihood, which yielded a value of 0.3. The aspiration formula itself is not readable in the provided text.

Performance below social aspiration, equal to the difference between the focal firm's performance and the corresponding social aspiration level if firm performance is less than the social aspiration level, and zero otherwise; the absolute value of this variable is included in the regression models. A firm's social aspiration is defined as the average performance of its industry peers, including both domestic and foreign-owned firms, with industry measured by three-digit National Industrial Classification codes. The aspiration formula itself is not readable in the provided text.

A dummy variable identifying firms that were founded in the pre- and post-reform periods. A firm that was founded in the pre-reform period is coded as 1, whereas a firm that was founded in the post-reform period is coded as 0.

A dummy variable classifying industries as more- or less-protected through their import penetration ratios, which are influenced by both tariff- and nontariff-based import barriers and are calculated at the two-digit NIC code level. Industries whose import penetration ratios are lower than the median value are assigned the value of 1, indicating more protected industries, whereas those whose values are higher than the median value are assigned the value of 0, representing less-protected industries.

Category spanning of a restaurant, constructed following Kovács and Hannan (2015) from the number of cuisine categories offered by the restaurant and the average distance between those categories. The average distance is based on cosine similarity for pairs of categories in a yearly co-occurrence matrix, so that categories that co-occurred frequently in a focal year contributed less than categories that rarely co-occurred that year. The formula itself is not readable in the provided text.

Number of gourmet food trucks in each metro-year from 2008 to 2013, measured from data collected from Twitter's API that were prepared to exclude conventional food trucks such as hot dog and ice cream stands. Because GFTs did not emerge until 2008, prior years were filled as zero; the variable was lagged by one year and standardized.
time_window: lagged one year; 2008-2013 with zeros filled for prior years

description: Average yearly Yelp customer rating of a brick-and-mortar restaurant in the seven metropolitan areas from 2005 to 2014. The authors aggregated 1,661,893 ratings, ranging from 1 for 'completely dissatisfied' to 5 for 'completely satisfied', assigned to 34,727 restaurants to yield 141,123 restaurant-year observations.

Indicator variable distinguishing restaurants in the lowest price segment (Price 5 1) from those in higher price segments (Price 5 2, 3, or 4), used to test whether organizations sharing salient attributes with GFTs benefit more from their spillover. In the sample, 49.5% of the restaurants belonged to the lowest price segment and 50.5% to the higher price segments.
scale: 1 = lowest price segment, 0 = higher price segments

variable_name: New form basic condition / New form plus condition
description: Dummy indicators for randomly assigned treatment conditions in which respondents read a short vignette about gourmet food trucks as a new organizational form that emphasizes spanning in its products. The new form plus condition added that GFTs are able to offer better value for price than many restaurants because of their streamlined operations.

Average of responses to three questions asking how appealing a generic restaurant offering fusion food that spans two, three, and more than three culinary categories is, measured on a 7-point Likert scale (Cronbach's alpha = .90).

Scientific articles and conference papers on FPD technologies written by researchers in FPD firms, downloaded from INSPEC using keywords derived from interviews with engineers and managers of FPD companies. In total 3,448 such articles constituted the citation database, and 100 U.S. and 100 Japanese corporate articles were selected into each of the two matched sets.

Publications on FPD technologies written by university researchers, drawn from a set of 3,500 randomly selected publications by university researchers. From this pool, 100 U.S. and 100 Japanese academic articles were matched to corporate articles in each of the two matched sets.

variable_name: total number of citations by firm-based scientists
description: For each of the 400 articles in each matched set, database searches identified all instances in which the article was cited by a researcher in an FPD firm. Instances in which a corporate researcher cited an article written by a researcher in his or her own firm were deleted. This total was the dependent variable for Hypotheses 1 and 2.

variable_name: citations by industrial researchers outside the author's country
description: The total number of citations by industrial researchers housed in R&D facilities located outside the author's country of residence. This was the dependent variable used in Hypothesis 3.

variable_name: time lag for citation from abroad
description: The average number of years between the publication date of an article and its citation by industrial researchers outside the author's country; used as the dependent variable in Hypothesis 4.

Articles in each matched set were assigned to a national sample according to whether their authors were based in the United States or Japan, and separate one-way analyses of variance were conducted for each country. To test Hypothesis 5, the difference between citations to each university article and to its corporate match was computed and the sample was split at the median into 1969-82 and 1983-89.

A dichotomous variable based on a review of the laws of incorporation for each state to determine whether it had adopted an other-constituency statute. A company incorporated in a state with such a statute was coded 1, and a company in a state without such a statute was coded 0.

A dichotomous variable differentiating more regulated from less regulated industries, using Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) primary industry codes. Heavily regulated industries were specified as those in the 4000 or 6000 SIC categories (transportation, utilities, banking, and finance) or in the 2830 category (pharmaceuticals); the variable was coded 1 for heavy regulation and 0 for less regulation.
Measured as the natural logarithm of the number of employees, following previous board studies.

variable_name: Proportion of stakeholder directors on a board
description: The number of nonshareholder stakeholder directors divided by the total number of directors on a board. To classify stakeholders, the authors reviewed the texts of various states' other-constituency statutes and the stakeholder management literature, distinguishing between private stakeholders (those who had business relationships with a corporation, for instance customers, suppliers, and creditors) and public stakeholders (such as government officials, academics, and community representatives). Each director was categorized on the basis of occupation and/or the affiliation with the company noted in the company proxy.

variable_name: Proportion of stakeholders on major board committees
description: For each of the four major board committees-audit, compensation, executive, and nominating-the numbers of public and private stakeholder directors on the committee were divided by the total number of directors on the committee. The proportion of stakeholder representation on each committee was analyzed separately.

Proxy statements and annual reports were reviewed to determine whether a company had a committee with a stakeholder orientation, such as a public policy, social responsibility, or contributions committee. This variable was coded 1 if a company indicated such a committee and 0 if it did not.

Average of the extent to which respondents agreed that e-filing had increased worker productivity, reduced errors in return preparation and filing, routinized return preparation, enabled wage reductions for return preparation staff, enabled careful monitoring of return preparation work, and improved the quality of the return preparation product and service. Respondents indicated agreement on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree); the scale had a coefficient alpha of .87.

Average of the extent to which respondents agreed that e-filing had increased the revenues of the firm, increased the firm's competitiveness, enabled the firm to diversify into new businesses, and increased the firm's market share. Respondents indicated agreement on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree); the scale had a coefficient alpha of .84.

Average of four items: perceived competitive benefits from adoption of the new ITs, perceived competitive disadvantage from nonadoption, perceived threat from introduction of the new ITs into the industry (reverse-coded), and perceived opportunity from introduction of the new ITs into the industry. Responses were on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree) and the scale had a coefficient alpha of .77. A high score indicates framing the new ITs as an opportunity, and a low score indicates framing the new ITs as a threat.

Average of three modified items from Milliken's (1990) measure of effect certainty: the extent to which respondents were certain that the new ITs would play an important role in their industry, the extent to which they were certain the new ITs would affect their companies in the future, and how much of an impact they felt the new ITs would have on their companies in the future. Responses were on a seven-point scale.

Average of responses on a seven-point scale to three modified questions from Milliken's (1990) instrument: the perceived difficulty in weighing various alternatives in responding to the introduction of the new ITs, the respondents' confidence about how to respond if these new ITs became important, and their perceived need to guess when responding in the absence of indications about what to do. The first and last items were reverse-coded; the scale had a coefficient alpha of .67.

variable_name: perceived similarity of the new ITs to e-filing
description: An item asking respondents to indicate the extent to which they perceived e-filing technology as similar (1 = extremely dissimilar, 7 = extremely similar) to each of five new ITs; responses to the five items were averaged to obtain a score on the variable.
Measured as the percentage of returns filed electronically by the company in the previous tax-reporting year (1993-94).

variable_name: proactive information seeking about new ITs
description: Average of responses on a seven-point scale to four items assessing the extent to which a company kept in touch with the IRS on developments in information technologies for return filing, monitored what ITs its competitors in the industry were adopting or developing, monitored developments in IT that might potentially affect its business, and surveyed its customers to assess their expectations in terms of IT-based services. The scale had a coefficient alpha of .70.

variable_name: Threat/opportunity framing, effect certainty and response certainty
description: Strategic issue interpretations of the new information technologies are assessed with three survey scales: threat/opportunity framing, effect certainty and response certainty, each analyzed as a separate dependent variable.

Multi-item measure built from the business strategy questionnaire: 18 items (6 on the entrepreneurial dimension, 4 on the engineering dimension, 8 on the administrative dimension) asking respondents to position their firms on a scale of 1 to 7 initially constructed so that low values matched a defender strategy and high values a prospector strategy; the pattern was inverted for questions 3, 5, 6, 9, 13, 15, and 16 to avoid skewing answers. The rating was calculated as the arithmetical mean of the item ratings after eliminating two items that displayed negative correlations with the total score, and the scores were standardized in each sector to give a relative indicator of proactivity.
scale: 1-7 per item; final score standardized within sector

description: Factor score on the first natural environmental approach, derived from principal components analysis with standardized varimax rotation of the 14 natural environmental practice items; items were answered on a scale from 0 ("We have not addressed this issue at all and have no plans to do so in the near future") to 7 ("We are the leaders on this in our sector") and ratings were standardized by sector. The variables with high loadings were natural environmental training for executives and for other personnel, and, to a lesser extent, natural environmental audits and participation in government-subsidized natural environmental programs.
scale: item answers 0-7; factor scores standardized by sector

description: Factor score on the second natural environmental approach, derived from the same principal components analysis with varimax rotation of the 14 natural environmental practice items; ratings were standardized by sector. The key loadings were pollution damage insurance, discharge controls and filters, and residue recycling, that is, traditional natural environmental methods generally subject to public regulations.
scale: item answers 0-7; factor scores standardized by sector

description: Factor score on the third natural environmental approach, derived from the same principal components analysis with varimax rotation of the 14 natural environmental practice items; ratings were standardized by sector. The main influences were natural environmental aspects in administrative work, a total quality program with natural environmental aspects, and product-life-cycle analyses, that is, modern voluntary and preventive improvements.
scale: item answers 0-7; factor scores standardized by sector

description: Each entity's four-digit SIC code was linked with its rating in a 1991 list of the aggregate R&D intensity of U.S. firms. R&D intensity was defined as R&D investment expressed as a percentage of net sales averaged for each industry. Figures published by Schonfeld and Associates were used, and these numbers were the most complete data published for each four-digit SIC code.

A variable was constructed representing investment ventures involved with auto or steel manufacturing (1 = involvement, 0 = no involvement) to represent potential political influence factors. Legislators have threatened or implemented import restrictions for both of these industries.
A variable was included to represent whether direct investments were new companies (1) or acquired (0).

Data from Dodwell Marketing Consultants, the Japan External Trade Organization, and the Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry were used to determine if any Japanese parent of an entity produced a product in Japan that was similar to the entity's product or products in the United States (1 = Japanese parents with similar products, 0 otherwise).
scale: 1 = Japanese parents with similar products, 0 otherwise

description: One of the three ownership-structure groups in the discriminant analysis. A partial ownership firm was one owned just by Japanese companies and other investors (not by other companies): either an existing company in which a substantial block of stock had been purchased by a Japanese company or a start-up in which substantial amounts of stock were held publicly or privately by individuals. Percentages of Japanese and U.S. ownership were derived from the Japan Economic Institute data.
scale: categorical group (joint venture, partial ownership, total ownership)

description: One of the three ownership-structure groups in the discriminant analysis. A joint venture was defined as a manufacturing firm and separate legal entity, with a Japanese parent or parents and a U.S. or non-U.S. parent or parents, established in the United States. Following Hennart, joint ventures are those in which one or more Japanese parents own between 5 and 95 percent of the equity; the authors note that joint ventures include partial ownership in free-standing firms as well as minority ownership in ongoing concerns.
scale: categorical group (joint venture, partial ownership, total ownership)

description: One of the three ownership-structure groups in the discriminant analysis. Ownership of between 95 and 100 percent of equity was considered total ownership, following previous research. Seventy-one percent of the direct Japanese investments captured in the data set involved total ownership.
scale: categorical group (joint venture, partial ownership, total ownership)

description: The year of the Japanese investment, included in the discriminant analysis to control for cohort effects.

In the 1984 wave, CEOs were presented with characterizations of the four Miles and Snow strategic types, labeled Hospitals A through D and worded for use in the hospital industry. Each CEO indicated the type to which his or her hospital was currently most similar using a seven-point scale: a rating of 1 or 2 represented the defender, 3, 4, or 5 the analyzer, and 6 or 7 the prospector; CEOs who viewed their organizations as lacking consistent strategies indicated similarity to the reactor, which was not on the scale, and a 'not applicable' response was also available. The responses were collapsed into the four Miles and Snow nominal categories for analysis. The measure was previously validated by comparison with archival product-market data.
scale: seven-point scale collapsed into four nominal categories

description: In the 1986 wave, each CEO was asked to identify the hospital's business strategy of two years ago (time 1), using the same strategy typology. The 1986 measure was the same as the 1984 measure except that 'operated two years ago' replaced 'now operates'. Responses were classified into the same four Miles and Snow nominal categories.
scale: seven-point scale collapsed into four nominal categories

description: A dummy variable coded from annual firm data: zero in the before-acquisition period and one in the after-acquisition period. Acquired companies were identified through Standard and Poor's COMPUSTAT research files and matched to their acquirers using Moody's Industrial Manual and the Federal Trade Commission's Large Merger Series. The procedure is described as similar to Hoskisson's (1987) approach to measuring the longitudinal effects of M-form structural change.
time_window: up to three years before and three years after the acquisition; year of acquisition excluded

description: Financial statement figures for the acquiring and acquired firms were combined in the preacquisition periods, and R&D intensity was measured as total R&D expenditures divided by total sales. Because firm R&D intensity was strongly positively related to industry R&D intensity, average industry R&D intensity was subtracted from the combined R&D intensity of each acquiring and acquired firm. Industry R&D intensity was the weighted average of the two firms' dominant two-digit SIC industries, with sales in the last years before acquisition used as weights for all post-acquisition years; studied firms were not used in calculating their industry averages.
time_window: up to three years before and three years after the acquisition; year of acquisition excluded

description: Patent data were collected from BRS Information Technologies PATDATA and CASSIS/CDROM, both based on information from the Patent and Trademark Office of the U.S. Department of Commerce; two data bases were used to ensure accuracy, currency, and effective aggregation to a firm level. Because there was a strong relationship between total number of patents and firm size, patent intensity was measured by dividing the total number of patents a firm held by its annual sales.
time_window: up to three years before and three years after the acquisition; year of acquisition excluded

description: Categorical dependent variable dividing the firms into leaders, followers, and free riders. A code of 2 for "leader" indicates that a firm petitioned the ITC either alone or with a few other firms, and a code of 1 for "follower" shows that a firm decided to participate in the petitioning process through a trade association. A code of 0 for "free rider" designates firms that decided not to participate even though their industry was involved in an ITC petition filed either by leaders or by government agencies.
A firm's dependence on a product for which a petition was filed, measured as the ratio between sales of the product and total sales.

One of two measures of organizational slack suggested by Chakravarthy (1986), measured by a firm's return on assets. It indicates how much discretion managers have in allocating resources to political activities.
One of two measures of organizational slack, measured as the ratio of a firm's long-term debt to stockholders' equity. A firm's debt-to-equity ratio indicates its ability to raise long-term capital.
Firm size, the third indicator of resource constraints, measured as total assets.
A dummy variable indicating whether the firm had a Washington office at the time a petition was filed, included to examine a firm's past ability to make political investments.
time_window: at the time a petition was filed

description: The number of firms in an industry that produced the product for which the ITC reported a filing, used to measure the effects of industry structure on firm political activity.

Firms were classified into Rumelt's categories of corporate diversification strategy: single business, dominant business, related diversification, and unrelated diversification. As in Montgomery and Singh (1984), Rumelt's (1974) categories were used; 133 firms were available from Rumelt's (1978) classifications and 143 additional firms were classified by the author from annual reports and SEC 10-K reports. Strategy was entered as a nominal variable with dummy variables representing each strategy category.

Data on systematic risk were obtained from the Value Line Investment Survey (1974). The authors define systematic risk as a firm's total return relative to that of the market as a whole. The text does not describe the specific estimation procedure beyond the source.

Current or retired managers of the organization or of one of its subsidiaries were classified as inside directors; outside directors did not currently hold, nor had they previously held, management positions within the company for which they were serving as director. The number of outside members was divided by the total number of directors to obtain a proportion for each firm. Because the data are longitudinal and slight changes in board composition are common from year to year, the percentages of outsiders from 1980 to 1984 were averaged, so the proportion represents the average proportion for each firm during the five years.

For Hypothesis 2 the independent variable is binary, so a dummy variable was used, with firms having a majority (> 50%) of outsiders on their boards coded 1, and firms where outsiders were a minority coded 0.

The dependent variable is the total number of instances in which firms were found guilty in litigated cases, were parties to nonlitigated consent decrees, or were involved in unsettled cases in which the court found substantial merit to the charges against the cited firms. The areas of litigation considered were price discrimination, tying arrangements, refusal to deal, exclusive dealing, franchise violation, price fixing, foreclosure of entry, reciprocity, acquisitions, allocation of markets, monopoly, conspiracy, and illegal mergers.

Names and titles in Standard & Poor's Register of Corporations were compared to determine whether a single individual served as both CEO and chairman or whether separate individuals held these positions between 1980 and 1984. Because changes took place over time, only firms that consistently maintained either dual or separate status throughout the relevant dates were used for further analysis.
Dichotomous variable indicating whether the firm has a medical department, measured in the 1979 survey of Illinois firms.
Dichotomous variable indicating whether the firm is unionized, measured in the 1979 survey of Illinois firms.

Measured as the number of job categories reported by the firm. No firm reported less than 4 categories or more than 10; thus the variable was used as a limited range interval variable, and an organization with 10 job categories was considered most complex.
Dichotomous measure of firm location, distinguishing urban from other locations; the text does not state which value is coded 1.
Firm size was measured as the number of employees. Because of the highly skewed distribution of size (skewness 4.68), the natural logarithm of size was used in the analysis.

Dichotomous dependent variable. Program adoption was defined in the questionnaire as the existence of a formal program consisting of either written procedures, a special office, or a coordinator for employees with emotional, personal, alcohol or drug problems; firms with either alcohol specific or employee assistance programs were used in the analysis. Of the 173 firms, 68 had adopted programs and 105 had not.
Dichotomous dependent variable, indicated if the firm's basic insurance plan specifically covered reimbursement for alcoholism treatment.
Dummy variable added as an explanatory variable in the program adoption model, coded 1 if insurance was adopted prior to program adoption, and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: boundary spanning as a percentage of time
description: Subjects were asked to record the number of hours they had in an average week with each of nine categories of environmental constituencies (customers/clients, suppliers/vendors, interviewing new employees, bankers/lawyers/accountants, business/professional/trade associations, regulators/government/union officials, outside stockholders or creditors, competitors, and other business related activity). The sum of the hours spent in these activities divided by the number of hours worked per week measures how intensive the owner/operator's boundary spanning activity is. Customer/client figures were not included in the calculation of the variables used in the statistical tests.

The sum of the number of contacts the owner/operator reported in an average week across the same nine categories of environmental constituencies; the authors describe it as an extensive measure. Customer/client figures were not included in the calculation of the variables used in the statistical tests.

Operationalized by the Schroder sentence completion test. Subjects responded to three sentence items: 'Rules...', 'When I am in doubt....', and 'When I am criticized....'. Responses are scored along a 7-point Likert scale; the criterion for scoring is the complexity with which the answers are structured, and the two highest scores are averaged for the final score.

A 16-item questionnaire developed by Budner, measuring the tendency to perceive ambiguous situations as sources of threat. Budner reported reliabilities of the scale ranging from .39 to .62 and admitted that the low reliability was because of the multidimensionality of the variable; the reliability for the subjects in this study was alpha = .56.

Performance was measured by three criteria: net addition to retained earnings, current sales, and the gross economic benefits accruing to ownership for 1981. The gross economic benefits measure was constructed by prorating by percentage of ownership the owner's draw, fringe benefits, cash dividends, and net additions to retained earnings; it represents the total economic benefits available to ownership, adjusted for more than one equity position.

A dummy variable taking the value 1 when a firm classified itself as having diversified since 1968-1969, and 0 otherwise. Firms were asked whether they had diversified during the period 1968-1969 to 1977-1978.

The percentage of a firm's total sales in 1977-1978 attributable to diversification undertaken since 1968-1969, as reported by diversifying firms (the same percentage was also requested for 1974-1975).

Return on Total Assets = [Earnings (after tax) + Interest]/Total Assets. It attempts to measure the total after-corporate tax return on the total capital invested in a firm by shareholders and lenders. Average rates of return are computed for each group over the whole period and each subperiod.

Return on Equity = Earnings (after tax)/Shareholders' Equity. It is a measure of the return on shareholders' equity in a firm and of the success of management in managing a firm on behalf of its shareholders. Average rates of return are computed for each group over the whole period and each subperiod.

Risk is measured in two ways: as the relative variability of each profitability ratio through the coefficient of variation, and as the relative variability in earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) and in earnings after tax (EAT). The coefficient of variation of EBIT measures operating or business risk; the coefficient of variation of EAT is a relative measure of business and financial risk.
Debt Ratio (1) = Total Debt/Total Assets. It measures the proportion of a firm's investment in its assets financed by debt. Group averages are reported over the whole period and the two subperiods.

Debt Ratio (2) = Interest Bearing Debt/Total Assets. It measures the extent of usage of interest bearing debt in financing assets, and is described as a measure of the success of the firm in raising fixed interest debt.

Compound rates of growth computed for the two groups over the whole period and each subperiod for earnings after tax, total assets, market capitalization, and the profitability ratios (return on total assets and return on equity). G is the compound rate of growth in assets over the period.
Average firm size over the period, measured by assets, used as an explanatory variable in the profitability regressions. In the simple tests firms were split at the median firm size for the period.

Respondents answered 43 Likert-type questions (24 single-response and 19 multi-item) describing how comprehensive their firm would be if it faced the scenario problem. In single-response questions the alternative answers were arranged from least to most comprehensive and scaled from 1 to 5 or 7. Three kinds of scores were used: a firm score on each of the 43 questions, a comprehensiveness score for each of the four steps of the theoretical model, and a single overall score that represented the comprehensiveness of a firm's overall strategic decision process, computed as the mean of the four step scores. Individual responses were aggregated within firms to the organization level.

variable_name: average after tax return on assets
description: Average after tax return on assets during the most recent five years. It was obtained as an indicator of how efficient firms were in managing their assets, and a five-year average was used to insure that it reflected sustained performance and was not a one-time aberration.
Percentage change in gross sales during the most recent five years. It was included as a measure of effectiveness because it provides an indication of long term viability.

Executives read a five-page decision scenario depicting a paint and coatings manufacturer facing a major problem and responded to 43 Likert-type questions describing how comprehensive their firm would be if it faced the same situation. Responses were aggregated within each firm on each of the 43 questions. Three kinds of scores were used: a firm score on each of the 43 questions (24 single-response and 19 multi-item), a score for each of the four steps of the theoretical model, and a single overall score, yielding 48 scores. All responses were scaled from 1 to 5 or 7.

Average after-tax return on assets during the most recent five years, used to assess how efficient firms were in managing their resources. Partial correlations controlling for size were computed between this measure and the comprehensiveness measures.

Percentage change in gross sales during the same five-year period, included as a measure of long term viability or effectiveness. Partial correlations controlling for size were computed between this measure and the comprehensiveness measures.

variable_name: regulation uncertainty under the Radiation Control for Safety and Health Act
description: Measured by the annual frequency of activities such as standards promulgation and enforcement actions as reported in the Bureau of Radiological Health's annual reports. It is one of the five industry-level variables, common to all firms within a year, measured from 1962 through 1977.

Measured by industry sales' volatility, computed from the annual percentage change in the industry's value of shipments adjusted for inflation (Pfeffer & Salancik, 1978). It is one of the five industry-level variables, common to all firms within a year.

Measured from the market concentration of the four largest firms, using indices reported by the Bureau of the Census every four years; intervening years were estimated by interpolation. It is one of the five industry-level variables, common to all firms within a year.

Measured by the annual number of 4-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes each firm participated in each year. It is one of the six variables measured uniquely for each of the seven firms each year.

variable_name: percentage of outsiders on the board of directors
description: The percentage of outsiders, measured by the annual number of board members who were not and had not been company officers (Pfeffer, 1972). It is used as a cruder indicator of indirect control because data on organizational structure, such as the number of technical marketing directors, were not available.
Measured by the annual total number of board members (Pfeffer, 1972). It is one of the six variables measured uniquely for each of the seven firms each year.

variable_name: relevant X-ray industry trade association memberships
description: Trade associations were identified from the 1980 questionnaire responses and verified with annual trade association membership lists. Unlike the other variables it exhibited little variation (trade association memberships).

Measured by each firm's annual patent applications in patent class 250 (radiant energy). Questionnaire responses were used to verify that patent applications were a meaningful measure of new product invention in this industry and that development of new products was important for each firm's economic success.

Measured by each firm's annual total sales, the measure of three alternatives that had the highest intercorrelation: total sales correlated higher with total assets (r = +.91) and total employees (r = +.92) than assets and employees did with each other (r = +.82).

variable_name: diversification, outsiders on the board, board size, trade association memberships
description: The less risky strategic alternatives were measured by four firm-level variables, each analyzed separately in the path model: the annual number of 4-digit SIC codes a firm participated in (diversification), the percentage of outsiders on the board, total board size, and the firm's relevant X-ray industry trade association memberships. Data were annual for seven firms from 1962 to 1977.

The average seller concentration ratio (ASCR) for each two-digit SIC industry divided by its corresponding average buyer concentration ratio (ABCR). ASCR is a sales-weighted average of the four-firm seller concentration ratios of the industry's four-digit product classifications; ABCR is computed from input-output tables as the sales-weighted average of the four-firm seller concentration ratios of the top three consuming industries. Industries with POW below 2.5 are classified as holding low power positions and those above 2.5 as holding high power positions.

Each merger is classified by the FTC into one of five primary merger strategies according to the primary strategic relationship between the acquiring and acquired firm: horizontal, vertical, product extension, market extension, and conglomerate. For the analysis, horizontal, market extension and vertical integration mergers were recorded as Type I strategies, while nonmarket (product) extension and conglomerate mergers were designated Type II strategies.

The classifying variable was the percent of sales derived from new products for this business minus the percent of sales derived from new products for the three largest competitors. A defender is a business whose relative new product activity is -5 or less (in an industry in which industry innovation is 0, a business with the lowest possible score of 0 is classified as a defender); a prospector is a business whose relative new product activity is +5 or more. Businesses with moderate scores, which might be called analyzers, were excluded.
scale: percentage; defenders -5 or less, prospectors +5 or more

description: One of the three performance measures, and the most conventional measure of current business performance. Like all accounting measures it suffers from varying depreciation, inventory, and lease valuation methods, a problem minimized by the use of four-year averages.

One of the three performance measures; cash flow indicates the extent to which the company currently is reaping more money than it is putting into the business. Like ROI it suffers the limitations of any accounting measure, which the use of four-year averages helps minimize.
One of the three performance measures; market share change indicates the growth of the business and its fitness for the future.

The environments of the businesses were categorized according to life cycle stage as reported by the respondents. The study used businesses in the growth and maturity stages of the life cycle; sample sizes in the introductory and decline stages were too small to allow meaningful analysis.

Category of the business's industry according to the extent of product innovation, as reported by respondents. Industries with moderate innovation scores (1 percent to 5 percent) were excluded from the analysis; the dividing lines were chosen to capture roughly the bottom 40 percent and top 40 percent of PIMS businesses on this variable.

For the matched-pair analysis, a defender was defined as a business whose new product sales were below 1 percent for all four years, and a prospector as a business whose new product sales were above 10 percent for all four years. A total of 74 matched pairs of businesses pursuing these extreme, persistent strategies were identified within the same 4-digit SIC codes.
scale: new product sales below 1 percent (defender) or above 10 percent (prospector) in each of four years

description: Product research and development expenditures as a percentage of sales, compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.
Marketing expenses—sales force, promotion, and marketing administration—as a percentage of sales, compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.

A relative measure of the extent to which the business is integrated forward, indicated by whether it handles its own selling, warehousing, and distribution. Compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.
A relative measure of the extent to which the business is integrated backward toward its sources of raw materials, compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.
Gross fixed assets per employee, compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.
Value added per employee, compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.
The utilization level of the business's capacity, compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors; the businesses operated at around 73 percent to 74 percent.
Average compensation rates, considered relative to competitors and compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.
The business's overall direct costs, considered relative to competitors and compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.
The portion of total R&D expenditures devoted to process improvements, compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.
The business's prices relative to those of competitors, compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.
The business's quality relative to competitors, compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.
The business's service relative to competitors, compared across the matched pairs of defenders and prospectors.

Hospitals were classified as proprietary (profit) or nonprofit institutions. To obtain two organizational samples with highly similar domains, only short-term, general, nongovernment, nonreligious, nonteaching hospitals with 100 to 300 beds were included. The American Hospital Association's 1978 Guide to the Health Care Field was used to identify hospitals that met these criteria.

variable_name: Perceived power of the medical staff, forced choice
description: Respondents evaluated each of the 27 potential power holders by means of a 5-point scale that ranged from "no influence at all" to "a great deal of influence." The ratings for the medical staff were averaged across each economic orientation and then rank ordered to provide a power hierarchy for each economic orientation.
level: individual respondent, aggregated by economic orientation

variable_name: Units of influence allocated to the medical staff
description: Respondents allocated a theoretical 100 "units of influence" among the 27 groups and individuals in any manner they desired. The allocations for the medical staff were averaged across each economic orientation and then rank ordered to provide a power hierarchy.
level: individual respondent, aggregated by economic orientation

variable_name: Perceived power of the board of trustees, forced choice
description: Respondents evaluated each of the 27 potential power holders by means of a 5-point scale that ranged from "no influence at all" to "a great deal of influence." The ratings for the board of trustees were averaged across each economic orientation and then rank ordered to provide a power hierarchy for each economic orientation.
level: individual respondent, aggregated by economic orientation

variable_name: Units of influence allocated to the board of trustees
description: Respondents allocated a theoretical 100 "units of influence" among the 27 groups and individuals in any manner they desired. The allocations for the board of trustees were averaged across each economic orientation and then rank ordered to provide a power hierarchy.
level: individual respondent, aggregated by economic orientation

variable_name: Perceived power of the hospital administrator, forced choice
description: Respondents evaluated each of the 27 potential power holders by means of a 5-point scale that ranged from "no influence at all" to "a great deal of influence." The ratings for the hospital administrator were averaged across each economic orientation and then rank ordered to provide a power hierarchy for each economic orientation.
level: individual respondent, aggregated by economic orientation

variable_name: Units of influence allocated to the hospital administrator
description: Respondents allocated a theoretical 100 "units of influence" among the 27 groups and individuals in any manner they desired. The allocations for the hospital administrator were averaged across each economic orientation and then rank ordered to provide a power hierarchy.
level: individual respondent, aggregated by economic orientation

description: Number of employees of the succession company, collected from Standard and Poor's Register of Corporations (1980). Because of the extreme skewness typically encountered, all size data were subjected to logarithmic (base-10) transformation for analysis.

Total sales of the succession company, collected from Standard and Poor's Register of Corporations (1980). Because of the extreme skewness typically encountered, all size data were subjected to logarithmic (base-10) transformation for analysis; the median split analyses are based on the total sales metric.

The coding of successor type is binary; an inside successor is a person promoted from within the executive span of the predecessor, and outside succession occurs when the newly appointed CEO was not in the predecessor's span. Succession information was derived from daily reports in the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by corporate 8K reports; only the CEO successions of parent companies were considered.

Companies in the population were classified by the market on which they were listed: the New York Stock Exchange, the American Stock Exchange, or the over-the-counter market listed by the National Association of Securities Dealers. The analyses contrast NYSE companies (N=103) with non-NYSE companies (N=78).

Firms were classified by whether their stock was publicly traded. The 32 privately-held firms contacted constituted the entire list of privately-held manufacturing or food processing companies with over 500 employees listed in the Corporate Report Fact Book (1978) for the Ninth Federal Reserve District, of which 18 agreed to participate. The chief executive officer of the privately-held firm identified competitors, and a like-sized publicly-held competitor was used as the match.

The least squares growth rate for sales over the previous five years, 1974 through 1978, estimated from the regression of the logarithm of sales on year; the slope coefficient is expressed as percent growth per year.
The mean square error of the least squares growth calculation for sales over the previous five years.

The CEO's perception of how important a role potential growth in sales played, on average, in the five key decisions he had identified earlier in the interview. Each of 11 strategic factors was rated on a 10-point scale with anchor points characterizing the factor from crucial to low importance, and the responses on each factor were averaged across the five decisions.
The CEO's perception of how important a factor consistency of sales had been, on average, in the specific key decisions, rated on the 10-point importance scale and averaged across the five decisions.

The CEO's opinion of the importance that forecasts of near-term earnings had on the specific decisions he had earlier identified as important, rated on the 10-point importance scale and averaged across the five decisions.

An index developed from the CEO's description of the company's accounting policies. It was comprised of policies on inventory valuation, depreciation, and the attitude toward decisions to expense or capitalize investments.
The CEO's impression of the firm's pricing relative to competition, aimed at maximizing internally generated cash flow rather than growth.

variable_name: reliance on subjective judgment in decisions
description: CEO-reported items, each the CEO's perception of how important the factor was, on average, in the specific major decisions he had identified: considerations of product quality, product appearance or other subjective properties, and gut feel.
Five-year averages extracted from accounting data, computed for current assets, fixed assets, and total assets.
Ratio of hourly (i.e., non exempt) employees per dollar of sales. The data were extracted from company records and averaged over five years.
The CEO's perception of how important constraints on the ability to raise capital were on the major decisions, rated on the 10-point importance scale and averaged across the five decisions.

An adaptation of an existing formalization instrument (Price, 1972) which asks the CEO whether certain formal written documents exist and the extent of distribution of those documents, together with the proportion of management positions covered by written job descriptions and the importance of an explicit ROI calculation in each major decision.

Participativeness was measured with an instrument developed by Likert (1967) that characterizes the firm's management style as System I, II, III, or IV. The test compared the dispersion of scores of privately-held and publicly-held firms using the f-ratio.
scale: Likert System I, II, III, IV

description: An index of formal education was developed for each second-level manager consisting of one point for each year of postsecondary education plus one point for each academic degree. This index was averaged across all the second-level managers.

variable_name: ratio of administrative and professional personnel to sales
description: Ratio of administrative and professional (i.e., exempt) personnel to sales. The ratio was extracted from company records and averaged over the prior five years.

Firms were assigned to the OBSP (experimental) group if their SBDC consulting met a decision rule: the consulting had to address business level strategy issues, include thorough analysis and decision making in two or more functional areas, involve 10 or more contact hours between client and consultants, and include three or more substantive contact periods.
