Firms in the two control groups did not engage in SBDC consulting.

variable_name: net profit before taxes divided by sales (NPOS)
description: Net profit before taxes divided by total sales, taken for the matching pre-OBSP and post-OBSP time periods. The change (absolute increase) in NPOS between the two periods is the profitability measure used to test Hypothesis 1, and the pre-OBSP level was used to compare the OBSP group with the control groups.
time_window: matching pre-OBSP and post-OBSP time periods

description: Net profit before taxes plus owner compensation divided by total sales, taken for the matching pre-OBSP and post-OBSP time periods. The absolute increase in ROS between the two periods is the profitability measure used in the multivariate test of Hypothesis 2.
time_window: matching pre-OBSP and post-OBSP time periods

description: Total sales for the post-OBSP time period (adjusted for inflation) minus total sales for the matching pre-OBSP time period, divided by total sales for the matching pre-OBSP time period. Percentage change was used rather than absolute change to control for size differences between firms.
time_window: matching pre-OBSP and post-OBSP time periods

variable_name: absolute increase in sales per employee
description: Sales per employee for the post-OBSP time period (adjusted for inflation) minus sales per employee for the matching pre-OBSP time period. Because sales per employee is a ratio, absolute change was used rather than percentage change.
time_window: matching pre-OBSP and post-OBSP time periods

variable_name: percentage increase in the number of full-time equivalent employees (FTEs)
description: Number of full-time equivalent employees for the post-OBSP time period minus the number of FTEs for the matching pre-OBSP time period, divided by the number of FTEs for the matching pre-OBSP time period. Percentage change was used to control for size differences between firms.
time_window: matching pre-OBSP and post-OBSP time periods

description: In Hypothesis 2, effectiveness was operationalized as a multivariate concept, assessed with four change measures between matching pre- and post-OBSP time periods: percentage change in total sales, absolute change in return on sales, percentage change in the number of full-time equivalent employees, and absolute change in sales per employee.
time_window: matching pre-OBSP and post-OBSP time periods

description: Each firm was classified into one of three diversification strategy categories: related-constrained, related-linked, or unrelated. The related-constrained and related-linked firms represent all of Rumelt's original sample for which data were available on the COMPUSTAT tapes; for the unrelated category additional firms were randomly drawn from the Fortune 500 to obtain a comparable sample size. The appropriateness of the classification was verified for the 1973-1977 time period, and firms were removed whenever substantial doubt existed.

Return on assets defined as net income after taxes but before extraordinary items divided by total assets. A return was calculated for each of the years 1973-1977 and then an average ROA across the years was determined. The 5-year time period was chosen as a long term measure of performance.
The same return on assets measure computed with the pharmaceutical firms removed from the sample; ROA1 refers to the variable when the pharmaceutical firms were not included.

Risk measured by the standard deviation of the ROA figure across the 5-year time period. The standard deviation was chosen because it or its square, the variance, is a standard measure of dispersion and hence risk.

The same risk measure, the standard deviation of ROA across the 5-year period, computed with the pharmaceutical firms removed from the sample; RISK1 refers to the variable when the pharmaceutical firms were not included.

Grand strategy was measured on a nominal scale using four strategy classifications derived from Glueck (1976, 1980): stability, internal growth, external acquisitive growth, and retrenchment. Each executive chose the single dominant strategy of the firm; executives were not allowed to combine the strategies. The operational definition of each strategy type is given in the text (for example, a retrenchment strategy is one in which the firm tries to improve performance by scaling down the level and/or scope of its product/market objectives by cutting back in costs and by reduction in the scale of operations through divestment of some units or divisions).

Executives were asked to rate a normative list of 55 key result areas on a 7-point Likert-type response mode ranging from "completely strategically insignificant" to "of the greatest strategic significance." To obtain a relative strategic importance score for each function, these ratings were grouped by function and summed, producing a score for each of seven functions (GENA, PROD, ERD, MKT, FIN, PER, PGR). Six items on which the interjudge correlations were low were deleted and new interjudge reliability scores were obtained.

Type of production system was measured by using Woodward's (1965) classification scheme, which classifies firms as unit and small batch, large batch and mass production, or continuous process. Firms were allowed to specify another type of production system if one of the three classifications was inappropriate, but this option was not exercised.

PEU was measured with Miles and Snow's (1978) instrument, which includes 6 scales (total of 25 items) covering major dimensions of an industrial firm's environment. Scale items were measured using a 7-point response mode ranging from "predictable" to "unpredictable." The PEU score was computed by obtaining the average item score per scale and summing the six scale scores.

variable_name: growth in sales and growth in return on equity
description: Annual reports or financial statements were obtained beginning with the first year of the five years and extending two years beyond the end of the period, giving seven years of data. Logarithmic averages of the growth in sales (revenues) and the growth in return on equity were taken for the seven years. Firms with sales growth of less than 8 percent (the average rate of inflation) and an average decrease in R.O.E. were classified as low performers; firms with real growth in both indicators were classified as high performers.
scale: growth rates; classifications of high and low performance
time_window: seven years (first year of the five-year period plus two years beyond)

description: Because confidentiality was guaranteed, performance was measured with chief executives' reports on a 7-point scale comparing the firm's performance over the last five years relative to competitors on growth in sales/revenues and return on equity, where 1 indicated poorer and 7 better vis-a-vis competitors and 4 no change. Firms with scores of 5 or more on both indicators were high performers; those with scores of 3 or less on both were low performers.
scale: 7-point (1 = poorer vis-a-vis competitors, 4 = no change, 7 = better vis-a-vis competitors)

variable_name: performance data for the published sample
description: Reliable performance data came from Moody's and S&P, published corporate histories, and annual reports. Periods were rated as improving or declining when both sales growth and R.O.E. moved in the same direction over the duration of the period plus the following two years; the performance criteria were the same in real terms as those for the Canadian sample.
time_window: period plus the following two years

variable_name: correlations among changes in structural variables
description: Product-moment correlation matrices were computed for the successful and unsuccessful subsamples, with the upper row of coefficients per variable for the successful sample and the lower row for the unsuccessful sample. Artificial variables were formed by taking an arithmetic average of the variables within each of the four categories (uncertainty reduction, differentiation, integration, dual function) so that high correlations among them indicate that the categories tend to change together to the same degree.

variable_name: correlations among changes in structural variables
description: The same procedure as for the Canadian sample was applied to the Australian subsamples: product-moment correlation matrices for the successful and unsuccessful subsamples and artificial averaged variables for each category whose intercorrelations summarize across-category concerted change.

variable_name: correlations among changes in structural variables
description: Correlations among changes in the nine published-data variables were computed for the successful and unsuccessful subsamples, together with correlations among the averaged category variables that summarize overall across-category concertedness.
time_window: periods defined by the scoring heuristic

description: A computer count of the scores along each variable for each subsample was made. Scores of 1 (maximum decrease) and 7 (maximum increase) were counted as very extreme changes; scores of 1, 2, 6, and 7 were counted as extreme increases and decreases. Percentages of extreme and very extreme scores were computed per scale and averaged for each subsample.
scale: 7-point change scale (1 = maximum decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = maximum increase)

description: The same count of extreme (1, 2, 6, 7) and very extreme (1, 7) change scores was made for the Australian subsamples, with percentages reported per scale and averaged for each subsample.
scale: 7-point change scale (1 = maximum decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = maximum increase)

description: Percentages of extreme (1, 2, 6, 7) and very extreme (1, 7) change scores were computed for the nine variables of the published data subsamples.
time_window: periods defined by the scoring heuristic

variable_name: standard deviations of the change scores
description: Standard deviations were computed along the change scores for each variable separately for the successful and unsuccessful subsamples. Variances were compared with an F test using N-1 and N-1 degrees of freedom.

variable_name: standard deviations of the change scores
description: Standard deviations along the change scores were computed for the Australian successful and unsuccessful subsamples and compared with F tests.

variable_name: standard deviations of the change scores
description: Because the published data used ordinal rather than interval scales, the F statistic was considered inappropriate; as a rough guide standard deviations were calculated for the nine variables of the published sample.
time_window: periods defined by the scoring heuristic

description: Change over the last five years on seven questionnaire scales of uncertainty reduction devices: formal rules and policies in capital budgeting, formal rules and policies in personnel management, constraints limiting managerial discretion, group decision making, scanning of markets via formal staff activities, informal scanning of markets by managers, and briefings by field personnel. Responses were given by chief executives. The scales were not combined into constructs and were analysed individually in the correlation matrices.
scale: 7-point change scale (1 = great decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = great increase)

description: The identical survey instrument was used, so the same seven uncertainty reduction scales measured change over the last five years for the Australian firms.
scale: 7-point change scale (1 = great decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = great increase)

variable_name: changes in delegation, scanning, and analysis
description: Each period of history was scored for changes in nine structural variables, of which the uncertainty reduction variables are delegation, scanning, and analysis. Two independent case raters assigned scores on 7-point ordinal scales after reading the published histories, where 1 indicated a great decrease, 4 no change, and 7 a great increase.
scale: 7-point ordinal change scale (1 = great decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = great increase)
time_window: periods defined by the scoring heuristic

description: Change over the last five years on five questionnaire scales of differentiation devices: number of staff departments, number of profit centers, delegation of authority for strategic decisions, organizational differentiation, and influence of technocrats in decisions. Responses were given by chief executives and the scales were analysed individually.
scale: 7-point change scale (1 = great decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = great increase)

description: The identical survey instrument measured the same five differentiation scales of change over the last five years for the Australian firms.
scale: 7-point change scale (1 = great decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = great increase)

variable_name: changes in centralization, differentiation, and technocratization
description: Of the nine structural variables scored for each period of history, the differentiation variables are centralization, differentiation, and technocratization. Scores were assigned on 7-point ordinal scales by two independent raters.
scale: 7-point ordinal change scale (1 = great decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = great increase)
time_window: periods defined by the scoring heuristic

description: Change over the last five years on three questionnaire scales of integration devices: formal task forces and committees, frequency of meetings and communications, and formal controls. Responses were given by chief executives and the scales were analysed individually.
scale: 7-point change scale (1 = great decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = great increase)

description: The identical survey instrument measured the same three integration scales of change over the last five years for the Australian firms.
scale: 7-point change scale (1 = great decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = great increase)

variable_name: changes in integration, internal communications, and controls
description: Of the nine structural variables scored for each period of history, the integration variables are integration, internal communications, and controls. Scores were assigned on 7-point ordinal scales by two independent raters.
scale: 7-point ordinal change scale (1 = great decrease, 4 = no change, 7 = great increase)
time_window: periods defined by the scoring heuristic

description: Firms were classified into three planning classes from questionnaire responses: Class 1 (nonplanners) with no formal long-range planning process; Class 2 (incomplete planners) with a written long-range plan covering at least three years ahead but not meeting all the requirements of Class 3 planners; and Class 3 (complete planners) with the most comprehensive, systematic, future-oriented long-range planning process. Class 3 planners prepare a written long-range plan for at least three years into the future, quantify objectives and goals, prepare pro forma financial statements over the planning horizon, have mechanisms for scanning the external environment, plan for virtually all facets of their operations in a systematic way, and have procedures for monitoring performance against the plan. The final sample consisted of 78 planners selected from Class 3 and 51 Class 1 nonplanners.
scale: three classes (1 = nonplanners, 2 = incomplete planners, 3 = complete planners)

description: Residuals are calculated from the one-factor market model relating each security's monthly return to the observed average monthly return on a value-weighted market portfolio of all NYSE assets, so that the effects of general market factors are abstracted from. Each security's residuals are cross-sectionally averaged over all securities in the sample for each month relative to the month strategic planning was adopted, defined as month zero. July was selected as month zero because only the year of adoption is known from the survey. The expected value of the average residual is zero, and significant deviations are interpreted as associated with the initiation of strategic planning.
level: firm-month residual, averaged cross-sectionally by event month
time_window: relative months -60 to +120 around month zero

description: Beta is the slope parameter b, from the one-factor market model, estimated by regressing security returns on market returns over 60 months of prior return data. To account for a changing beta, a beta was calculated for every month using five years of prior return data, so that to estimate beta in month t, months (t - 60) through (t - 1) of return data were used. For each firm a preplanning beta was calculated for relative month -36 and postplanning betas for relative months +67 and +120, giving a total of 181 betas per firm including month zero, subject to data availability.

The rate of technological change was operationalized as the change in productivity in the organization's primary industries. Rates of productivity change (1959-1969) obtained from a Bureau of National Affairs publication for the 4-digit SIC codes representing each firm's major outputs were averaged to give a score for technological change.

The extent of computer use in clerical functions, such as payroll, inventory control, and production scheduling. The authors describe it as the actual degree of use of the computer, i.e., the number of functions computerized.

A dummy variable indicating whether a given organization did or did not have its own data processing facilities on the premises. A number of the organizations using computers did not have their own facilities and instead used data processing facilities located at corporate headquarters.

An index of the degree of use of mass production techniques based on Woodward's (1965) scale of production continuity. Because many firms in the study actually used a mix of the different categories, a weighted average of the relative importance of each category was computed to arrive at the index.

The degree of horizontal differentiation or functional specialization was assessed by counting the number of staff specialties, from a specific list of 17 staff functions, that were performed by at least one full time specialist.
The degree of vertical differentiation, or vertical span, was simply the number of levels in the hierarchy from chief executive to bottom level employees.

Based on the Aston scale, formalization was measured by the degree to which the employees' roles were formally defined by official documents such as job descriptions, standard operating procedures manuals, and the like.

Twelve personnel-related decisions were chosen from a list of typical management decisions developed by the Aston researchers. For each decision the level at which authority to make it resided was established by questioning executives at the top two levels: if the decision had to be referred to a higher authority by the CEO it was scored as a zero, if the CEO made it himself it received one point, if he delegated it to the second level it scored two points, and when second level executives also delegated the decision it received three points. The final index was the total points for the twelve decisions.

Eleven operations-related decisions were chosen from a list of typical management decisions developed by the Aston researchers. For each decision the level at which authority to make it resided was established by questioning executives at the top two levels, with scores of zero to three depending on whether the decision was referred above the CEO, made by the CEO, delegated to the second level, or further delegated. The final index was the total points for the eleven decisions.

The general staff size included the number of employees in 10 of the 17 functions and therefore came closest to the aggregate measure of the size of a general supportive component or administrative staff used in previous research. The natural logarithm was used in all statistical analyses for the staff size measures.

The development staff size indicated the number working on the development of material resources (e.g., research and development), as well as human resources (e.g., employee training and development). The natural logarithm was used in all statistical analyses for the staff size measures.

The planning and control staff size included the number employed in quality control, production planning and control, and market or strategic planning functions. The natural logarithm was used in all statistical analyses for the staff size measures.

The maintenance staff size included the number engaged in maintenance of plant and equipment as well as employee health and welfare; the maintenance staff is primarily concerned with the work flow. The natural logarithm was used in all statistical analyses for the staff size measures.
The span of control at the bottom level, i.e., of first line supervisors, was assessed as an indicator of structure and is considered relatively more concerned with the work flow.

Employees were asked to state how many shares of stock they had personally bought when the company was purchased. The number of shares owned is the major independent variable for Hypotheses 1 and 2 and is used to interpret the meaning of ownership. All employees, whether stockowners or not, are included in this analysis.

Groups of stockholders and nonstockholders were compared on ownership perceptions; there were 24 employees (16 production workers and 8 office workers) who did not own stock in the plant. Because ownership may reflect itself in the act of purchasing rather than in the amount of capital invested, the simple fact of holding stock is treated as a separate aspect of ownership.

Perception of ownership was measured by asking about the extent to which one as an individual owned the company. The response scale ranged from 1 ("No, there is no real ownership") to 6 ("Yes, there is real ownership"). Subjects also were asked to state how much employees as a group and how much management owned the plant, using the same scale.

Labor-management partnership was assessed by a 3-item scale comprised of items designed to measure various aspects of a partnership, extracted from a factor analysis of 40 items. Each item was measured on a 6-point scale, where response alternatives ranged from 1 ("Strongly disagree") to 6 ("Strongly agree"). The internal consistency estimate, using the Spearman-Brown prophecy formula, was .79.

Subjects stated how much influence or say each of three groups had over decisions about each of seven issues and, in a different section, how much influence or say the different groups should have, using a 6-point scale ranging from 1 ("Virtually no say at all") to 6 ("A great deal of say"). The three groups were employees as a group not through the union, the union through collective bargaining, and management. Of the seven issues, the two concerning wages and pensions were combined into one scale and investments, planning, and company profit decisions were combined into a policy scale.

variable_name: Power difference between management and labor
description: Partnership beliefs (controlling for role ambiguity, work alienation, and possible interactions) were regressed on the difference between the power management should have and the power labor (represented by the union) should have over each of the four areas of decision making; a difference in power preferences for management and union indicates a lack of interest in power equalization. Workers were also separated into a high partnership group with scores of 5 or 6 on a 6-point scale and a low partnership group with scores of 1 and 2 and compared on their power preferences for labor and management.
scale: difference score between preferred management power and preferred labor power

description: Subjects were classified into four occupational interest groups: blue-collar, white-collar, middle managers, and top managers. The managerial group was divided because middle managers were responsible only for day-to-day operations and did not play a role in top level decision making.

The company's degree of diversification, classified among Wrigley's (1970) strategic categories on an ordinal scale, which the authors treat as the company's strategy. The scale was developed from responses on strategy given in the structured interviews.

An ordinal scale for the degree of divisionalization of structure, ranging from low for functional, through geographically divisional, then product divisional, to highest for product and geographically based divisional structures.
The number of levels within the core workflow hierarchy, used as the measure of the chief executive's vertical span of control.
The number of specialist staff officers reporting to the chief executive at the head office, used as the measure of the chief executive's lateral span of control.
Size is captured by three measures that are themselves strongly intercorrelated: net capital employed, annual sales, and number employed.
The number of separate sites operated by the company. Service companies tend to have more operating sites than manufacturing ones.
The geographical dispersion of the company's major operations or of its site locations.

A scalar measure of the match between the strategy and structure scales, devised to incorporate the assumptions implicit in the strategy/structure school; details may be found in Grinyer et al. (1978).

Average return on capital employed, computed both over four years and over two years. Average ROI is among the variables with missing values, the highest number being 19 for the 4-year averages, which reduced the cases available to merely 29.
Growth in profits and ROI, and growth in capital employed, sales, and numbers employed. Growth in net profit between 1969 and 1973 and growth in ROI between 1972 and 1973 are among the measures used.

variable_name: standard deviation of ROI (variability of ROI)
description: The standard deviation of return on capital employed, computed together with the four-year average ROI and subject to the same missing values.
Classification of the company as service, manufacturing, or a combination of both. Of the companies, 25 percent were in service industries, 43 percent in manufacturing, and 32 percent in both.

variable_name: market share in most important market
description: The company's share of its most important market, used together with market rank and dependence on major customers as a cluster of variables expected to reduce the hostility of environmental pressures.
The number of sources of important adverse impacts on the market for the companies' three most important product lines in the previous three years; it measures past market turbulence.
The number of expected sources of adverse market turbulence in the next three years; expectations were obviously conditioned by perceptions of past experience.

A 5-point ordinal scale of the perceived need for new product innovation, ranging from not worthwhile to essential for survival, taken as a rough proxy for the degree of new product competition in the company's major markets.
A Likert-type scale measuring the perceived rate of technological change in the industry.
An ordinal scale based on interviewees' perceptions of the difficulty of obtaining alternative supplies of raw materials and brought-in components.

Firms were classified in terms of core technology using the typology developed by Woodward (1958), which identifies three categories — small batch or unit production, large batch or mass production, and process production — forming a scale of technical complexity. The upholstered furniture industry represents small batch or unit technology and the soft drink bottling industry represents continuous process technology. In each firm the researchers studied the manufacturing process and the subsidiary tasks necessary for primary objectives by observation, interviews, and collection of industry data, together with the number and nature of decisions at each management level, the cooperation required among the management team, and the control exercised by senior executives.
scale: three-category scale (small batch/unit, large batch/mass, process)

variable_name: use of part-time and temporary workers
description: The amount of use of part-time and temporary workers for the calendar year 1976 was used as the dependent variable, collected as the amount of part-time and temporary man-hours for each firm. Four separate categories of part-time and temporary workers were used: permanent part-time, temporary company payroll, occasional part-time, and temporary outside agency. Results for each firm were standardized by dividing the total number of part-time and temporary worker man-hours by the total number of full-time plus part-time and temporary man-hours.

Measured by the score obtained on Duncan's perceived environmental uncertainty instrument (1971) as modified by Downey (1974). The questionnaire was administered to decision makers who had the authority to approve the use of part-time and temporary workers. The instrument is designed to measure both internal and external uncertainties; respondents were asked to select the three most important factors they consider in their decision to use part-time and temporary workers.

Measured by the average number of employees the organization had available to do its work for the 1976 calendar year, i.e., the number of full-time employees. Firms within each technology group were divided into large and small size subgroups based on the 1972 Census of Manufacturers.

Total number of full- and part-time employees including owners, transformed to a logarithm for analysis. Range, mean and standard deviation are reported in Table 1 for this study and for the Dewar and Hage sample.

Variety of possible customer needs that the firm can satisfy through products and services sold, coded in three categories: 3 = services (motel, restaurant, bank, etc.); 2 = general goods (hardware, department, clothing, etc.); 1 = specialty goods (jewelry, flowers, health foods, etc.). The authors consciously attempted to duplicate Dewar and Hage's reported measure despite the very different sectors of operation.

Number of occupational specialties that represent distinctive types of knowledge and training, such as manager, sales clerk, bookkeeper, janitor, secretary, security guard, cook, mechanic, teller. These are not simply job titles: 'restaurant busboy' and 'restaurant dishwasher' constitute a single specialty whereas 'insurance broker' and 'insurance salesperson' constitute two specialties.

Number of departments or work units distinguished by the presence of a supervisory position that has primary responsibility for overseeing the work of the unit. The measure was constructed to duplicate Dewar and Hage's reported measure.

A planning questionnaire of closed-ended questions asked respondents to specify the existence and extent of use of various factors in their long-range planning process. A multiple cutoff system classified a firm into Class 1 (no formal long-range planning process), Class 2 (a written, documented plan including the specification and selection of objectives and goals, the selection of long-range strategies, and a determination of future resources required), or Class 3 (all Class 2 items plus procedures for anticipating or detecting errors in the plan and correcting them on a continuing basis, plus some attempt to account for factors outside the immediate environment of the firm). A firm was placed into the next lower class if any of the requirements for a class were not met.

Respondents indicated on a 4-point scale ("never" to "frequently") the relative frequency with which each of a listed set of items had been considered in long-range planning decisions made in the past year. To obtain scores for the simple-complex scale, the total number of items checked as "frequently considered" was tallied and multiplied by the square of the number of different factor categories in which those items appeared. A separate score was calculated for the internal and external environments and added together for a total score.

Those factors identified by respondents as being "frequently" considered in the most recent planning period were tested for importance in several earlier periods: respondents checked, from several choices, those earlier periods in which the respective factor had also been considered important. The environment was classified as stable to the extent that the same factors had remained important over the last several planning periods. Scores for the stable-unstable scale were obtained from a weighted average of the "frequency of consideration" values added to a weighted average of the "consistency of importance" column, with separate scores for the internal, external, and total environment; the exact formula could not be read from the paper's rendering, so the specification is recorded as a gap.

Scores on the complexity and stability measures were calculated for each firm, the firms were ranked and dichotomized into equal groups (median splits), and each firm was grouped into simple-stable, simple-unstable, complex-stable, or complex-unstable categories. Because the four categories were viewed as benchmarks along a continuum with the extremes representing the ends, the two middle categories were combined into one category relabeled compound-complex. Each firm was thus finally classified into one of three categories of organizational environment, and a separate score for the internal, external, and total organizational environment was calculated and used to test each hypothesis.

An index built from the planning questionnaire items asking whether the firm employs, on a regular basis, a mathematical model or the computer in any phase of its long-range planning process and whether the firm employs outside consultants to assist in the planning process. Positive responses were scored and summed, and firms were classed as never, sometimes, or frequently using these methods.

An index built from planning questionnaire items on who is responsible for the long-range planning of the firm at the corporate level, the direction of information flow emphasized by the planning process (upward, downward, or both), and whether plan information is available only to management or also to the public. Points were summed and firms were classed as relatively closed, intermediate, or relatively open.
The length of time the formal long-range planning process had been in use, taken from the planning questionnaire item asking how long the company has prepared a long-range plan, in years.

The planning questionnaire asked whether the company prepares a written long-range plan covering a stated minimum period and, if so, what time period the plan covers. Responses were grouped into ordered classes of planning horizon, and the same categories were used for the analysis.

Built from the planning questionnaire item asking whether the long-range plan contains procedures for anticipating or detecting differences between the plan and actual performance and for preventing or correcting these differences, and, if yes, how frequently this is done. Responses were grouped into ordered categories of review frequency.

An index built by scoring the quantified objectives named in the planning questionnaire, computed separately for "tangible goals" such as sales, earnings, return on investment, products, plant expansion, and equipment acquisitions and for "intangible goals" such as capital growth, share of market, hiring and training of key management personnel, corporate acquisitions, research and development, and social, technological, and labor/personnel trends. Firms were classed along a range from longer-range plans with few tangibles addressed to immediate plans with many tangibles addressed.

A second scoring of the same planning questionnaire objectives, counting only the tangible, near-term objectives for which quantified objectives were reported, used together with the immediacy measure to capture whether planning premises support more immediate and tangible goals as opposed to longer-range and intangible goals.

Number of different persons occupying the department head position during the period 1954 to 1974. No count was taken of acting heads substituting for a permanent head on leave; other acting heads were counted. Data were obtained from the university archives; the average number of administrators in the 20 departments during the period was 4.2.

An archival index built from the number of words used by dissertation writers to abstract their dissertations, where fields with more developed paradigms communicate more economically, and from the maximum chaining of course prerequisites, where longer chains indicate a more shared paradigm. Ranks on the course chaining measure, after removing variations attributable to the task interdependence measure, were added to the abstract length ranks to obtain an overall estimate of paradigm development. In the analysis of administrative change, a dummy variable was coded 1 for low paradigm departments and 0 for others.
time_window: Dissertation Abstracts International (1975); course catalogs 1961-1963 and 1972-1974

description: Derived from the structure of course prerequisites: the percentage of a department's courses listing at least one other departmental course as a prerequisite, reflecting the probability that any teaching activity of a department will have to be coordinated with another teaching activity. Data were obtained from the university course catalogs for 1961-1963 and 1972-1974. The departments' percentage of courses with prerequisites ranged from 34.4 percent to 98.7 percent, with a mean of 80.0 percent and a median of 72.4 percent.

A resource scarcity index derived by taking the rank difference between each department's rank on size and its rank on grants, classifying departments according to their pooled interdependence for resources. In the analysis of administrative change, a dummy variable was coded 1 for high interdependence departments (above the median) and 0 for others.

A dummy variable coded 1 for turbulent years and 0 for others. The years of turbulence were defined as 1959-1963 (for the period of expansion), 1968-1970 (for the war years), and 1970-1974 (for the period of decline); the periods of normalcy were defined as 1954-1959 and 1964-1968.

Whether the administrative position was a headship (indefinite term, terminated voluntarily or by a two-thirds vote of the faculty) or a chairpersonship (specific term, usually three years, renewable by vote). Eight of the 20 departments had chairpersons at least once during the 20 years, and altogether 22 of the 84 administrators had been chairpersons.

For the analysis of the probability of administrative change, the task and resource interdependence measures were combined into a single index; a dummy variable was coded 1 for high interdependence departments (above the median) and 0 for others.

The CDQ presents 12 hypothetical situations; each item requires the respondent to choose between a safe alternative and a more attractive but risky one and to indicate the lowest probability of success sufficient for him to select the risky alternative. The CDQ score summarizes the responses made to a particular set of 12 choice dilemmas. A maximum score of 120 is possible, and 12 is the minimum score; lower scores are associated with less conservatism in risk taking situations.

Participants who within the three months prior to the study ceased working for their employers and at the time of the study owned as well as managed business ventures; owners who were employed elsewhere were eliminated. The entrepreneurial group was compared with two groups of managers who had also changed positions within three months prior to the study, one group having changed organizations and the other having changed positions within an organization.
time_window: three months prior to the study

description: A transition score is the difference between the score for a variable at the end of a transition period and its score at the beginning, normalised on a 7-point scale as Vi = ((Vi2 - Vi1)/2) + 4. A variable is counted as changing continuously over two consecutive transition periods if its transition score is greater than or equal to four for both periods, or else less than or equal to four for both periods. A computer program counted, for each nonenvironmental variable, the number of continuous and reversed links across temporally adjacent period pairs.
scale: binary indicator derived from 7-point transition scores

description: A transition score is the difference between the score for a variable at the end of a transition period and its score at the beginning, normalised on a 7-point scale as Vi = ((Vi2 - Vi1)/2) + 4.
