description: Physical capacity, measured as the total number of schools in the school district. One of the four measures of size used in the study.

The total number of instructional personnel, which includes teachers, librarians, guidance counselors, audiovisual personnel, psychologists, and secretaries and clerks associated with instruction. Treated separately from noninstructional personnel because they are likely to affect different administrative personnel.

The total number of noninstructional personnel, which includes health, food service, operation of plant, maintenance, and transportation personnel, as well as secretaries and clerks not associated with instruction. Treated separately because they are likely to affect different administrative personnel.
Volume of inputs, measured as the total enrollment in grades kindergarten through twelve. Changes in enrollment were also used to categorize school districts as growing or nongrowing.
Discretionary resources, measured as the total revenues from federal, state, and local sources.

Administrators categorized as instructional: assistant superintendents, principals, vice principals, and the directors and supervisors of personnel involved with instruction (e.g., librarians). Assignment of personnel to categories is based on the assignments found in the Maryland Department of Education annual reports.

Administrators categorized as noninstructional: superintendents, assistant superintendents, and the directors and supervisors of noninstructional personnel (e.g., maintenance). Assignment of personnel to categories is based on the assignments found in the Maryland Department of Education annual reports.

Personnel requiring knowledge and skills acquired through formal training including skills in education or education psychology; these include librarians, counselors, psychologists, and audiovisualists but not teachers.
Those professional personnel assigned to instruct students.
Those involved with servicing the instructional function.
Those who service all functions other than instruction.
Personnel other than secretaries/clerks who are classified in health and food services, pupil personnel, operations and maintenance of plant, and transportation.

Districts were categorized on the basis of change in enrollment: a declining school district is one that realized a decrease in enrollment every year since 1968, a growing district one that realized an increase in each year, and districts with a combination of increases and decreases were classified as mixed. This definition produced 6 growing, 11 declining, and 7 mixed school districts. Change in enrollment is also the measure used by administrators when discussing growth and decline.

Executive tenure was the years spent as chief executive as of December 1972, taken from McEachern. It is the dependent variable in the regression equations, denoted T, the number of years served by 1972.

variable_name: ownership classification (owner managed, management controlled, externally controlled)
description: A firm was classified as externally controlled if a group or individual held 4 percent or more of the common stock and was not part of the firm's management; as owner managed if the chief executive owned, directly or through immediate family, 4 percent or more of the stock; and as management controlled when no single group or individual owned 4 percent or more of the stock. In the regressions, 0-1 dummy variables were used: OM for owner managed firms and MC for management controlled firms.

variable_name: proportion of inside directors on the board
description: The proportion of insiders on the board was the proportion of directors who were managers in 1972. Interaction terms were computed by multiplying the proportion of inside directors by measures of profit margin.
The firms' net income as a percentage of sales (profit margin) averaged for the period 1965-1973, taken from reports in Value Line Investment Survey. It is denoted PM in the regression equations.

variable_name: average firm profit margin compared to industry (PMI)
description: A ratio of the firm's profit margin compared to the profit margin average for the industry during the period 1965-1973, constructed using Value Line's information on industry. It is denoted PMI in the regression equations.

variable_name: profit margin prior to administrative change (PAC)
description: A third measure of profit margins was computed for those firms that changed executives during the period, namely, the margin prior to the administrative change. It is denoted PAC in the regression equations.
time_window: years prior to an administrative change during 1965-1973

description: Capital market performance was estimated by McEachern as the combined rate of return on common stock for the period 1963 through 1972, considering all dividends as being reinvested in the stock of the firm throughout the period.

A rating of SP success based on three independent judges' forced choice paired comparisons of the success of 13 companies' SPs. Raters were asked to contrast organizations on the extent to which the full effort, experience, creativity, and innovative ability of the entire work force, through the use of the Scanlon Plan, are directed toward increasing the organization's total effectiveness. The interrater reliabilities were .89, .93, and .89 and the composite rating had a reliability of .97 by the Spearman-Brown prophecy formula. Thirteen companies were ranked on SP success with 1 = highest SP success.
time_window: at the time corresponding to the time the survey data were collected

description: Whether the SP was subsequently abandoned or retained, available for 22 companies of the sample.
time_window: after the questionnaire data were collected

description: Measured by averaging responses across all employees to a 5-item scale that has been used in previous research (White & Ruh, 1973), adapted from Vroom (1960). Internal consistency reliability (alpha) was .81 (9 companies).
Total number of employees (23 companies). The companies ranged in size from 23 to 3,000 employees with a median of 150.

variable_name: time (number of years a company has had the SP)
description: Number of years a company has had the Scanlon Plan (23 companies).

Measured by averaging responses from all persons with supervisory responsibilities to a 27 Likert-type item scale developed by Miles to assess attitudes relating to his human resources management style (Miles, 1965). Reliability alpha was .94.
Measured by using only the responses of the most senior executive(s) to the same Miles instrument (18 companies).

variable_name: reward for following participative management policies (R)
description: Measured by averaging responses across all managers to six yes/no items regarding the extent to which they thought they would be recognized and not criticized for following participative management policies. The items were taken from the same Miles instrument as the managerial attitude data; alpha was .75 (18 companies).

Measured by averaging responses across employees to a 9-Likert-type item scale concerning the extent to which the employees thought the SP would contribute to achieving various desirable outcomes (alpha = .91; 2 companies). The measurement was taken prior to implementing the SP.

The amount of money allocated to an agency for the 1972-73 fiscal year by the state or federal government. The individual employment service offices did not have a separate budget; their operating expenses were figured by multiplying their number of staff times an average salary and overhead amount supplied by the state office.

Staff members were asked how often they dealt with aspects of their clients' lives: medical problems, family relationship, other social problems, economic problems, educational needs, experience, psychological characteristics, plans, and dreams. Four response categories ranged from 'every time we meet with them' to 'never'.
scale: 4 response categories from 'every time we meet with them' to 'never'
level: staff members aggregated to the agency

description: The total number of local organizations, public and nonprofit, with which a focal manpower organization interacts. The size of the organization set was computed by counting the number of organizations checked on the master list.

The concentration of the set was computed using Herfindahl's 'H' statistic, which increases in value as the organizations in the set are concentrated in a few sectors. Organizations on the master list were classified into nine categories, or sectors, comprising the agency's task environment.
The average number of civic action organizations (e.g., NAACP, Settlement House Board) the staff members belong to. Responses were aggregated from the entire staff.
level: staff members aggregated to the agency

description: The average number of previous jobs the staff held in employment service, other manpower organizations, business organizations, public agencies, education organizations, and other community service type organizations. Responses were aggregated from the entire staff.
level: staff members aggregated to the agency

description: The number of regularly scheduled meetings within an organization per month.

The staff members' average response regarding how often they participated in making four decisions: to promote any of the nonclerical staff, to hire new staff members, to adopt new policies, and to adopt new programs. Responses were coded on a 5-point scale from 'never' to 'always'.
level: staff members aggregated to the agency

description: The relationship between the perceived importance of the organizations in the nine sectors of the task environment and the number of linkages with organizations in each sector, measured by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient between the two sets of nine scores for each of the focal manpower organizations. The variable is labelled INSTVALUE, for instrumental value.

The perception of the organization's control over its environment was measured by asking the agency's director to respond to a survey question with a 7-point response scale ranging from 'the environment dominates the organization' to 'the organization dominates its environment.'
scale: 7-point response scale from 'the environment dominates the organization' to 'the organization dominates its environment'

description: A rating of the perceived importance of each of the nine sectors for the successful fulfillment of the agency's mission was obtained from the agency's director. Each sector was rated on a 7-point scale, and directors were not informed of the particular sector into which each organization on the master list had been classified.
level: agency (director's rating of each of nine sectors)

variable_name: institutional centralization measures (hierarchy of control index; average number of hierarchical levels)
description: Institutional measures were computed from information obtained from a questionnaire, identical to that used by Sathe in his interviews, given to the head of each department. The centralization measures are Samuel and Mannheim's (1970) hierarchy of control index and the average number of hierarchical levels from each department member to the department head.

variable_name: questionnaire centralization measures (centralization scale; participation in decision making scale)
description: Questionnaire measures were obtained from responses of department members to a perceptual structure scale based on Sathe's (1978) scale; each respondent was treated equally, scores were totalled, and an average was computed to establish department scores. The centralization measures are a slightly longer (six versus five items) version of Sathe's centralization scale of comparable reliability (KR-8 of .799 versus Sathe's .864) and a participation in decision making scale of four items (KR-8 of .855).

variable_name: Inkson, Pugh and Hickson's (1970) documentation index
description: Institutional measure of formalization computed from information obtained from a questionnaire, identical to that used by Sathe in his interviews, given to the head of each department.

A slightly longer version (six versus four items) of Sathe's rules and procedures scale of comparable reliability (KR-8 of .793 versus Sathe's .826). Obtained from responses of department members, with each respondent treated equally, scores totalled, and an average computed to establish department scores.

variable_name: institutional differentiation measures (number of functions; number of job titles; functional diversification index)
description: Institutional measures of differentiation computed from information obtained from a questionnaire, identical to that used by Sathe in his interviews, given to the head of each department. They are the number of discrete functions in each department performed by at least one specialist, the number of job titles, and Samuel and Mannheim's (1970) functional diversification index.

A shorter version (three versus four items) of Sathe's division of labor scale with comparable reliability (KR-8 of .726 versus Sathe's .704). Obtained from responses of department members, with each respondent treated equally, scores totalled, and an average computed to establish department scores.
Size was measured as the logarithm of the total number of full time personnel in the department.
Technology was measured with a routineness scale (KR-8 of .853) administered to department members. A department technology score was computed by averaging the responses of department members.

Environmental uncertainty was measured using Sathe's (1974) scale administered to department heads. Sathe's uncertainty scale is a modification of Duncan's (1971) and has a higher level of internal reliability (KR-8 of .909).

variable_name: questionnaire measures of centralization, formalization and differentiation
description: Emergent structure was measured with questionnaire scales answered by department members and averaged to a department score: a centralization scale and a participation in decision making scale, a rules and procedures scale (formalization), and a division of labor scale (differentiation), all based on Sathe's scales.

variable_name: subunit size, technology and environmental uncertainty
description: Organizational context was operationalized as three control variables. Size was the logarithm of the total number of full time personnel in the department; technology was a routineness scale averaged over department members; environmental uncertainty was Sathe's scale (a modification of Duncan's) administered to department heads. The three were statistically controlled in partial correlations.

variable_name: institutional measures of centralization, formalization and differentiation
description: Designed structure was measured with institutional measures computed from a questionnaire given to each department head: Samuel and Mannheim's hierarchy of control index and average hierarchical levels (centralization), Inkson, Pugh and Hickson's documentation index (formalization), and the number of discrete specialist functions, number of job titles and functional diversification index (differentiation).

Each organizational unit was classified by its combination of complexity, change rate, and routineness of problem/opportunity states into one of the eight cells of the typology presented in Figure 1. The text does not state the cutoffs used to define low and high values on each dimension.

The CEO first identified the factors and components in the environmental list that had to be taken directly into consideration in making decisions. Factors located in the internal environment received a weighting of 1 and those in the external environment a weight of 2, and the number of components was squared: [(factors, weights assigned according to location) x (components)2]. This scheme was used to arrive at an overall measure of the complexity dimension.

A change rate index was computed for each unit by multiplying the frequency of changes by the magnitude of each change; frequency and magnitude were each rated on 5-point scales. Changes in the internal environment received a weighting of 1 and those in the external environment a weighting of 2, and the weighted products were summed. The displayed formula for the index was not extractable from the text.

The dimension was analyzed in terms of the variability of the stimuli, the analyzability of the stimuli, and the amount of discrepancy between environmental demands and the organizational unit's capacity. The scores on the three variables were correlated, then combined and averaged to form a routineness dimension.

Duncan's (1972) operationalization of perceived environmental uncertainty was adapted for use in this study. Scores on the three components comprising uncertainty were calculated according to the formulae suggested by Duncan and were correlated; given the high correlations they were combined and then averaged to form an overall uncertainty index ranging from 1 through 5. A score of 5 indicates high certainty; a score of 1 indicates high uncertainty.

Departmental structure was measured in terms of standardization, formalization, role specialization, and decentralization in decision making, scored according to the formulae suggested by the developers of the respective instruments. The scores were correlated and, given the high correlations, combined and averaged to form an overall departmental structure score ranging from 1 through 5. A score of 5 indicates a highly mechanistic structure; a score of 1 indicates a highly organic structure.

The respondent indicated on a 5-point scale, ranging from less than one year to more than four years, the time perspective adopted by his department in planning future policies and goals to be pursued by the department. A score of 5 indicates a long ranging planning perspective; a score of 1 indicates a short ranging planning perspective.

The respondent indicated on a 5-point scale, ranging from 1 = 'Very seldom (changes to less than 20 percent of the original plans)' to 5 = 'Very often (changes to more than 80 percent of the original plans)', the frequency of changes to existing departmental plans and programs over the lifetime of such policies and programs.
time_window: over the lifetime of the policies and programs

variable_name: mean frequency of technical communication outside of the organization
description: Each professional was asked to specify individuals with whom he had work related oral communication on a given sampling day; these sociometric data were collected on a randomly chosen day each week for 15 weeks, with equal representation of weekdays. Respondents reported all oral work related communications within and outside the laboratory, whom they talked to, and how many times; strictly social contacts and written communications were excluded. Each communication was coded for content, and problem definition or evaluation, idea generation and information location were later aggregated as technical communication. Reported communications were normalized to an average frequency per 10 sampling days, yielding a project measure of the average absolute amount of technical communication per person per project over 10 weeks, focused on communication between project members and professionals outside the organization.
time_window: 15 weeks of sampling, normalized to an average frequency per 10 sampling days

variable_name: degree to which external communication is skewed across project members
description: To test the role specialization ideas, the degree to which external communication was skewed across project members was computed for each project. Substantial positive intraproject skew in external communications indicates reliance on gatekeepers for technical information; when gatekeepers do not exist the skew in external communication is not substantial and extra-organizational communication is more evenly distributed. The text does not give the formula of the skew coefficient.

All group managers and both laboratory directors were interviewed individually and asked to evaluate the technical performance of all projects with which they personally were technically familiar, using the dimensions developed with top level managers. Each project was rated independently by an average of 4.7 managers on a 7-point scale (from very low to very high), and the individual ratings were averaged to yield overall project performance scores. Project performance was categorized as either high or low by splitting the scores at the median.
scale: 7-point scale from very low to very high

description: Respondents were asked to select the category that best characterized the objectives of their project and to indicate, on a 3-point scale, how completely the project's objectives were represented by the selected category; the 12 possible answers were arranged and scored along a single numerical scale ranging from completely basic research to completely technical service. In a separate question respondents indicated what percentage of their project's work fell into each of the four content categories, and a weighted average of the percentages was calculated for each respondent to yield a score comparable with the task dimension question. The scored responses to the two questions were averaged, and project measures were calculated by averaging the individual members' scores; on the basis of this measure projects were categorized as research, development, and technical service.
scale: single numerical scale from completely basic research to completely technical service

description: Size of the school district is measured as the number of students. Number of students is frequently used in studies of educational organizations and represents the demands placed upon such organizations by the community. In this sample of high school districts, number of students is correlated .9 with number of teachers.

Revenues per pupil are the measure of district affluence. Revenues per pupil control for the size of the district and indicate whether the relative size of the total resource pie is larger or smaller than other districts.

variable_name: percentage of teachers with a master's degree
description: Educational level of employees in the technical core is measured as the percentage of teachers in the district who have a master's degree.

Proportion of total salaries paid to classroom teachers. The primary function of high schools is classroom teaching, so resources devoted to that activity are considered allocated to the technical core. The relative allocation to a given department is measured by the percentage of resources received by the department, not the absolute dollar amount.

variable_name: administration, clerical and maintenance (proportion of total salaries)
description: The proportion of resources allocated to clerical, maintenance and administration combined, which indicates the relative cost of all overhead activities in the district. The administrative function involves supervision and coordination; the clerical function includes clerical and secretarial support for teachers and administrators; the maintenance function includes personnel who handle operation and maintenance of buildings, equipment and grounds.

variable_name: auxiliary educational services (proportion of total salaries)
description: Proportion of total salaries paid to provide services to students in support of classroom education. This category includes guidance and psychological counseling, librarians, health, teacher aids, and audio-visual services.

variable_name: other student and community services (proportion of total salaries)
description: Proportion of total salaries paid to personnel involved in other student and community programs, which include adult education, summer school, lunch, athletics, manpower development and training, and economic opportunity project.

Division self-containment was classified using two measures, division self-containment and functions centrally performed, which were significantly negatively correlated but not consistently associated with any of the other retained measures. Crosstabulation of the two component measures yielded three classes: low, high, and overlaid self-containment; the overlaid class covers observations in which divisions had most of the functions necessary to operate in their business environments but which also contained a wide range of specialized, central service units.

Twelve coordinative devices were rated; because some could be substitutes for one another, responses were subjected to a principal components analysis, which produced four factors. Factor scores for each company were computed as unweighted means of the high loading items, and indices of complexity of coordinative devices were constructed by summing the four factor scores. The distribution approximated normal and was broken into three categories (low, 7.2-11.25; medium, 11.26-14.75; high, 14.76-18.7).
time_window: 1970 and 1974; the two samples were combined for the factor analysis

description: Divisionalization was classified using three measures—number of divisions, size of average division, and division product scope—which were significantly correlated with one another and not consistently associated with other dimensions. Classificatory breaks were based on crosstabulation of the three component measures, and it was decided that little would be gained by employing more than the high and low classes.

The measures of organizational characteristics were collapsed into a taxonomy of nonoverlapping (either/or) organizational choices by first identifying the number of dimensions of organizational choice implied by the data and then determining the number of categories of choice for each dimension. The resulting taxonomy contained 18 possible types of divisionalized organization, 15 of which were required to classify the 75 situations in the data base; six organization types accounted for 66 percent of the companies in each sample.

Respondents used five-point scales to rate the influence typically exerted by five different general management levels on "the broad policy decisions which affected the activities of their companies' divisions." The levels were top level corporate executives (chairman, president, executive vice president), corporate staff officers and their staffs, group vice presidents, the division general manager, and persons one level below the general manager.
level: company (perceived influence rating reported for the company)

description: The number of personnel employed in corporate-level technological staffs for every $100 million of corporate sales. A corporate technological staff was counted as any group engaged in basic research, engineering, product development, or process improvement that met three conditions: less than 50 percent of its activities resulted in direct external sales, its activities were designed to benefit at least half of the firm's operating divisions, and no more than 50 percent of its activities were undertaken for the exclusive benefit of any one operating division. Groups doing occasional minor research for other divisions, groups selling a substantial part of their output to outside customers, and groups concentrating on a single division were excluded.
scale: persons per $100 million of corporate sales

description: The Supervisory Behavior Description Questionnaire developed by Fleishman (1972) was used to measure leader initiating structure. Subordinates described their supervisor's leadership style, and all questionnaire data are presented as average data for each county director/agency. Scored using a five-point response mode.

The Supervisory Behavior Description Questionnaire developed by Fleishman (1972) was used to measure leader consideration. Responses of the leader's direct subordinates were averaged for each director/agency. Scored using a five-point response mode.

The Job Descriptive Index developed by Smith, Kendall, and Hulin (1969) was used, containing measures of five dimensions of job satisfaction. The JDI used standardized scoring, unlike the other respondent-based measures. Subordinate responses were averaged for each director/agency.

The measure was adapted from an instrument developed by Arvey and Mussio (1973) to operationalize constructs pertaining to the expectancy model of motivation. Three aspects were operationalized: expectancy (E), an abbreviated model (ΣI·V), and the full model (E×ΣI·V). Scored on a five-point response mode and averaged across the leader's direct subordinates for each director/agency.
A 13-item scale factorially derived by Rizzo, House and Lirtzman (1970). Scored on a five-point response mode and averaged across the leader's direct subordinates for each director/agency.

A single-item question: "In the past six months, how often have you seriously considered the possibility of getting a job elsewhere?" Response choices ranged from "not at all" to "very frequently." Scored on a five-point response mode and averaged across the leader's direct subordinates for each director/agency.
scale: not at all to very frequently (five-point)

description: Three objective measures were obtained from the state office: total turnover rate, the ratio of the total number of full-time employees who left the agency for any reason during the past 12 months to the total number of authorized full-time agency employees; resignation rate, the same ratio for voluntary resignations; and transfer rate, the same ratio for voluntary transfers to other organizations within the state merit system.

variable_name: Performance appraisal of the agency director
description: The agency director's most recent performance evaluation obtained from the state office. It included graphic ratings on quality of work, quantity of work, cooperation, initiative, maintenance of equipment and supplies, the manner in which the county director directed, reviewed and checked the work of the unit, and sometimes an optional trait added by the rater. The measure was the average rating across all traits, with a potential range from 0 to 3.

Organizational size was measured as the number of full-time organization members. The contingency variable was dichotomized on an a priori basis after a review of relevant literature suggested that 20 or more members was a critical point at which organizational formalization increases dramatically, giving small agencies (less than 20 full-time members) and large agencies (20 or more full-time members).

The number of members in the local administrative bureaucracy. The authors report that the size of these administrative bureaucracies varied from 44 to 1,530, that the mean number of members was 245.7 with a standard deviation of 271.4, and that the variable was transformed into its natural logarithm prior to statistical analysis.

Width was measured by the number of departments in the organization. A department was defined as any unit having at least two persons and two levels, the head of which reported to the mayor, administrator or an alderman. The organizations varied from three to 12 departments, with a mean of 7.16.

Vertical differentiation was measured by counting the number of levels in each department from the department head to the lowest level worker and then calculating the average for all departments. Organizational scores ranged from 2.50 to 6.0, with a mean of 3.64.

An index based on six questionnaire items about the nature of respondents' tasks. Items were coded (1) 'definitely true,' (2) 'more true than false,' (3) 'more false than true,' and (4) 'definitely false,' unless otherwise stated, and several items are marked as reversed; one item asks whether the work is very routine (coded as 4), routine (3), nonroutine (2), or very nonroutine (1). Cronbach's alpha was .70 for department head routinization and .73 for subordinate routinization, and separate department head and subordinate scores were computed.

An index built from the reported authority of organizational actors in making 18 strategic decisions concerned with policy matters. Department heads and their subordinates were asked whether they could not or could make decisions in these areas. Cronbach's alpha was .8981 for department heads and .8687 for subordinates, and separate department head and subordinate scores were computed.

Each respondent was asked to report the number of contacts with persons in other public services during a typical week as well as the number of contacts with persons outside the public sector during a typical week. These were summed for each person, and then level-specific boundary spanning scores were constructed by taking the average for all department heads and the average for all subordinates. Cronbach's alpha was .7812 for department heads and .5484 for subordinates.

Respondents were asked to report the number of contacts either in face to face meetings or by telephone with persons at the same level, at a lower level and at a higher level in the organization in a typical week. Organizational scores for department heads were computed by averaging the responses of all department heads, giving dimensions for upward, lateral, downward and total communication.

Respondents were asked to report the number of contacts either in face to face meetings or by telephone with persons at the same level, at a lower level and at a higher level in the organization in a typical week. Organizational scores for subordinates were computed by averaging the responses of all subordinates, giving dimensions for upward, lateral, downward and total communication.

variable_name: population of the area serviced by the bus system
description: One of the two measures of size, the population of the urban area serviced by the bus system. The text does not state where these population figures were obtained.

variable_name: number of buses owned by the system
description: The second measure of size, the number of buses owned by the transit system. It reflects the size of the transit system itself rather than the size of the geographical area where the organization exists, and research on size has normally dealt with organizational size. The correlation between the two size measures is .89.

Built from the 60 common decisions identified in the questionnaire, for which respondents indicated the locus of the final decision. The number of final decisions made at each level was multiplied by a weight assigned to that level and summed for all levels. A weight of five was given the top level and a weight of one the bottom level, with intermediate levels weighted equidistantly for the number of levels in that structure, so that measures are comparable across organizations with varying numbers of levels.

The proportion of final decisions made by the resident operations manager and his staff, including any decisions delegated by him to his subordinates, based on the 60 common decisions identified in the questionnaire. It focuses on a single organizational level, avoiding possible confounding effects of the number of levels.

The number of hierarchical positions counted on the organization chart provided by each property. In all cases the level of the resident operations manager was the lowest and the mayor and city council or transit authority was the highest.

Each of the systems in the sample was classified as one of three types (I, II or III) according to whether upper and middle management are existing government entities or a specially created transit board or authority, with slight variations in the names and titles given to the different units.

The perceived prestige ranking was obtained from the Carpenter et al. (1974) survey of accounting educators, who assessed the quality of accounting faculties in departments offering doctoral degrees, and an overall top 20 ranking was developed. A clear separation was indicated between the perceived prestige of the top five departments and the remainder of the top 20. The prestige ranking is separated into three groups: the top five (higher prestige schools), the next 15 (intermediate prestige schools), and the nontop 20 (lesser prestige schools).

variable_name: degree of coalition formation among accounting departments
description: Coalition formation among accounting departments is measured by the degree of hiring by each department (for its faculty) of the accounting doctoral graduates of other departments. Hiring is not necessarily restricted to initial hirings but is reflected in the current location of each graduate, so that coalition formation between departments is operationalized as the number of accounting faculty in a specific department who graduated from another specific department. The top 20 departments were surveyed to discover the university where each faculty member earned his (her) doctoral degree and in which year it was obtained; for the remaining departments this was taken from Hasselback (1974).
level: department pair (origin department of degree, employing department)

description: The degree of vertical integration (inbreeding) within each accounting department is reported for the three prestige groups. The first line of the table gives the number of faculty currently employed by the same department from which they obtained their doctoral degree, broken down by higher, intermediate and lesser prestige departments.

The top 20 departments were divided into three geographic groups: a Western group (Stanford, Berkeley, Washington, and UCLA), a Midwestern group (Chicago, Illinois, Michigan State, Ohio State, Northwestern, Michigan, Minnesota, and Kansas), and an Eastern group (Cornell, Harvard, Columbia, MIT, Penn State, and Penn). Texas and North Carolina did not fit readily into any of the groups and were excluded from this analysis.

variable_name: openness to programs of interhospital cooperation
description: The dependent variable was based on responses to a question concerning cooperation and coordination with other hospitals; the question wording as printed in the text is garbled. The response categories ranged from "very low" (1) to "very high" (5).

variable_name: perceived level of hospital task accomplishment
description: Developed from a question asking how well the respondent feels the hospital is presently accomplishing each of five task activities. Respondent scores were summed using response categories ranging from "hardly at all" (1) to "exceptional" (5).
scale: 1 (hardly at all) to 5 (exceptional), summed across items

description: An index based on a sum of scores across four criteria of participation in health-related professional activities at the national level. The criteria concern memberships maintained in national professional health associations, attendance of national professional association meetings, office or committee appointments, and publication in professional health administration journals.
scale: index summing scores of 0-3 on three criteria and 0-1 on one criterion

variable_name: Index of state and local professional activity
description: Constructed by summing scores (0,1) on each of four criteria of participation at the state and local levels. The criteria concern state hospital association meetings and appointments and local hospital council or association membership and appointments.
scale: index summing 0,1 scores on four criteria

description: A summary scale representing the respondent's sharing of five categories of information. Response categories ranged from "never" (1) to "very frequently" (5). The five items constituted a Guttman scale with a coefficient of reproducibility of .937.
The total number of hours from a nominal forty hour week the respondent spends on three categories of interaction with extrahospital elements.
scale: hours from a nominal forty hour week

description: A summary score of the degree of importance placed by the respondent on each of three hospital task activities. The response categories ranged from "very low" (1) to "very high" (5).
scale: 1 (very low) to 5 (very high), summed across items

description: Developed from responses to a question asking the degree of influence the respondent feels each of three individuals or groups should have over hospital goals and policies. Scores were summed using response categories ranging from "none" (1) to "very high" (5).

Measured by a shortened version (18 items) of Likert's organizational characteristics questionnaire, three items per each of six climate dimensions. The 20-point, equal-interval, graphic rating scales had values ranging from 0.0 (complete nonsupportiveness) to 20.0 (maximum supportiveness); scales for the 18 items were randomly reversed and Likert's System 1-4 titles were not used. Responses were scored to the nearest one-tenth, and a manager's climate score was the average of the 18 items.

For each of seven MBO effectiveness dimensions a statement was prepared and the respondent indicated his agreement/disagreement with it on an equal-interval graphic rating scale ranging from 0.0 (strong disagreement) to 20.0 (strong agreement), with responses scored to the nearest one-tenth.

Type of work was classified as line or staff, differentiated on the basis of whether the job essentially contributed directly to the products or service of the company (line) or indirectly in more of an advisory capacity (staff).
This variable was divided into middle and lower management; the former group included department, district, and manager levels and the latter group consisted of first-line supervisors.

Measured by an eight-item instrument developed by Vroom dealing with the frequency with which an individual engages in independent behavior and the satisfaction he gets from independent behavior. Each of the eight items had five possible responses, with one point assigned to the response indicating the lowest need for independence and five points to the response indicating the highest need. Managers with a score of 25 or less were classified in the low need group and those with a score of 29 or more in the high need group.
scale: eight items, each scored 1 to 5; scores grouped as low (25 or less) or high (29 or more) need

variable_name: connectedness and density indices of the opinion/advice sociogram
description: The existence of a community was assessed against four criteria: informal communication channels linking firms together (connectedness in the graph theoretic sense), density resembling known social groupings, interconnections shown to be other than random, and frequency-of-use data indicating regular use. Two computed indices were used for density: Proctor and Loomis' measure of group expansiveness, the average number of other firms with which each firm is in direct contact, and an index created by the author based on the average and the range of the path lengths connecting each member to every other.

Respondents were asked (a) whether in their initial search process they had contacted any other sources for information about the innovation and, if so, from which competitive firms; (b) whether, after their decision to adopt, any firms had contacted them for information and which; and (c) whether they had regular opinion/advice relationships with any specific firms. The general opinion/advice nominations received in response to the third question were used to construct sociograms (directed graphs based on sociometric data), beginning with reciprocated relationships and expanding stepwise until all respondents and even nonrespondents were included.

variable_name: firm size and type of business
description: Firms were classified by size and type of business. Firms in Network A were all 'Big Steel' firms, including the six largest firms in the industry; firms in Network B were almost without exception Mini-Mills, many of them belonging to a trade association of such small firms, to which no firm in Network A belonged. Firms in Network B were substantially smaller than those in Network A, and a test of the difference in sales volume between the members of the two networks, using Student's t, showed the difference to be significant beyond the .01 level.

variable_name: number of firms contacting the firm for information about the innovation
description: The data were generated through analysis of the first and second sociometric questions. For each firm the authors counted the number of firms adopting earlier which contacted the firm, the number of firms adopting later than the firm and contacting it, and the total number of firms contacting it for information about the innovation. Firms were classified into early or later adopter categories, the first 7 to adopt being designated early adopters on the basis of the median time of adoption minus one year.

Firms were termed high on centrality or low on centrality based on the number of opinion/advice nominations received, and the mean time of adoption of the two groups was compared. Firm size was correlated with the number of nominations received and was held constant in a partial correlation between centrality and time of adoption.

The time of adoption was based on the date that a decision was made to adopt the innovation, not the date of its installation, which followed by as much as two years. For the analysis of opinion leadership, firms were also classified into early and later adopter categories, the first 7 to adopt being designated early adopters based on the median time of adoption minus one year.

Responses to the single questionnaire item asking the extent to which the manager was interested in the operator's general welfare. Operators indicated their opinions on five-point Likert-type scales.

variable_name: assessments of managers' behavior with respect to safety matters
description: Subordinates' responses to four questionnaire items assessing how their manager behaves with respect to safety matters, each answered on five-point Likert-type scales. The item means for the two groups are reported in Table 2.

Single questionnaire item asking the operator to what extent he feels his work environment is safe, answered on a five-point Likert-type scale. A lower score indicates a perception of a safer environment.

variable_name: You are exposed to safety hazards during your daily work?
description: Single questionnaire item asking the operator to what extent he feels he is exposed to safety hazards during his daily work, answered on a five-point Likert-type scale.

variable_name: You, personally, have a chance of being involved in an accident at work?
description: Single questionnaire item asking the operator to what extent he feels he personally has a chance of being involved in an accident at work, answered on a five-point Likert-type scale.

An inside successor is a person promoted from the executive staff of the predecessor; an outside successor is anyone not in the predecessor's executive staff, so that a company member promoted to president who formerly was not a member of the executive staff is classified as an outside successor. The executive staff is defined as those individuals holding administrative positions directly accountable to the president of a large corporation: chairman of the executive committee, executive vice president, group vice president, senior vice president, functional vice president, controller, treasurer, and corporate secretary.

A modification of Fiedler's semantic differential scale for measuring LPC; twelve adjective pairs (helpful-unhelpful, efficient-inefficient, open-closed, and so on) were used after four of Fiedler's 16 bipolar adjective pairs were eliminated. A large loading to the favorable side of the adjective continuums produces a high LPC score, indicative of an employee oriented style of leadership, while the negative end forms a low LPC score, indicative of a task oriented leadership style. Words of positive connotation were not necessarily placed on the left side of the questionnaire to reduce respondent bias toward successively marking the same space.

A modification of Haire and associates' measure of the amount of need satisfaction a manager derives from his job, with six items designed to generate data on the relative importance of social, esteem, and autonomy need satisfaction. For each item the respondent reports (a) how much of the need there is now and (b) how much there should be, and the discrepancy between the two is calculated for each of the six items. Positive discrepancies indicate basic satisfaction and negative discrepancies indicate dissatisfaction; the net value of these discrepancies gives rise to the total need satisfaction of the respondent, so higher scores mean less need deficiency.
scale: six items, each with a now and a should-be amount

variable_name: Percent change in executive personnel and formal administrative positions
description: The percent change in the number of subordinates within the executive group over a two year period (1972 and 1973) following succession, a percentage measure used because larger firms have a greater number of positions than do smaller firms. The study also includes within the measure of organizational change the percent change in the number of formal administrative positions within two years (1972 and 1973) after succession. The two measures of change are combined into a unidimensional scale.

Uncertainty was measured by the number of major product changes made by an organization during the past five years. To be considered a 'major' product change, a change had to fit at least two of three criteria. The median number of major product changes was one, and the range was zero to 50 product changes.

The chief executive and two of his immediate subordinates each described the management system of the organization on a 22-item, Likert-type instrument whose items were based on work by Duncan, Hall, and Galbraith. A factor analysis routine using a varimax, orthogonal rotation yielded three factors: impersonal hierarchy (11 items), group decision making (3 items, 11.0 percent of the variance), and rules for decision making (4 items, 8.4 percent of the variance), together accounting for 72.4 percent of the total variance. Scores for the organizations were ranked for each of the three factors and dichotomized into equal high and low groups; organizations were classified as organic if two or more factors were in an organic direction and mechanistic if two or more factors were mechanistic.
scale: five-point scale ranging from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree'

description: Congruency was determined by classifying those organizations which were in the predicted direction for type of management system and uncertainty on two or more factors as congruent, and those organizations not in the predicted direction for two or more factors as noncongruent.

Economic success was measured by four empirical indices adapted from Lawrence and Lorsch: sales volume in units, total unit production costs, controllable costs (only those affected by the organization's operations), and contribution to company profit (not considering fixed costs and depreciation). The percentage changes for each of these variables over a five-year period were obtained. A fifth measure asked for a subjective assessment of total organizational success by the chief executive, a current percentage rating of the organization compared to ideal performance in the particular industry. An organization was assigned to the high economic success category if three or more of the criteria were high, and to the low category if three or more criteria were low.
scale: percentage changes; percentage rating of current performance compared to ideal performance

description: Project personnel were asked to rank, in order of importance, the reasons they usually comply with the requests of project managers; this influence method corresponds to the item 'I feel he has the formal authority.' A rank of 1 constitutes the most important reason for compliance and 8 the least important. The item parallels legitimate power in French and Raven's typology.
level: project personnel (rankings; correlations computed across the 22 project teams)

description: Measured by three of the ranked reasons for compliance: perceived influence over salary, over promotion, and over future work assignments. Together these items parallel reward power in French and Raven's typology. Rankings run from 1 (most important reason for compliance) to 8 (least important).
level: project personnel (rankings; correlations computed across the 22 project teams)

description: Measured by the ranked reason for compliance 'I feel he can apply pressure or penalize me in some way.' The item parallels coercive power in French and Raven's typology. Rankings run from 1 (most important reason for compliance) to 8 (least important).
level: project personnel (rankings; correlations computed across the 22 project teams)

description: Measured by the ranked reason for compliance 'I respect him and place confidence in his special knowledge and advice.' The item parallels expert power in French and Raven's typology. Rankings run from 1 (most important reason for compliance) to 8 (least important).
level: project personnel (rankings; correlations computed across the 22 project teams)

description: Measured by the ranked reason for compliance 'He has established a personal friendship with me.' Rankings run from 1 (most important reason for compliance) to 8 (least important).
level: project personnel (rankings; correlations computed across the 22 project teams)

description: Measured by the ranked reason for compliance 'I feel the things he asks me to do are professionally challenging.' Rankings run from 1 (most important reason for compliance) to 8 (least important).
level: project personnel (rankings; correlations computed across the 22 project teams)

description: Project personnel indicated on a four-point scale how frequently they met the requests of their project manager with maximum effort (1 indicates a low degree and 4 a high degree of support). For purposes of correlational analysis the project personnel of each project manager were grouped together and a group mean was determined for each of the 22 project teams.

A slightly modified four-item Likert-type scale developed by Patchen. The four items deal with how often project personnel feel time drags on their job, how involved they are in their job versus other interests, how often they do extra work that is not required, and how hard they feel they work in comparison with others doing the same type of work. The scores on each item were summed to obtain an index which could range from 4 (low involvement) to 20 (high involvement); a group mean was determined for each of the 22 project teams.

A slightly modified three-item Likert-type scale developed by Patchen, used as a measure of the openness of upward communications. The three items deal with how free project personnel feel to disagree with their project manager, how frequently they have disagreed with him about some policy or work procedure, and how frequently they have expressed disagreement to him on a face-to-face basis. The scores on each item were added to obtain a willingness-to-disagree index ranging from 3 (low willingness to disagree) to 18 (high willingness to disagree); a group mean was determined for each of the 22 project teams.

The superiors of the project managers were asked to provide a ranking of the project managers reporting to them in terms of their overall effectiveness in carrying out assigned projects. There were three superiors who had approximately the same number of project managers reporting to them (seven, seven, and eight).

variable_name: project support, project involvement and willingness to disagree
description: Project climate was measured by three team-level variables taken together: degree of support (how often personnel met the manager's requests with maximum effort, four-point scale), project involvement (four-item Patchen index, range 4 to 20) and willingness to disagree as openness of upward communication (three-item index, range 3 to 18). Each was a group mean for the 22 project teams.

Eighteen items dealing with authority, control, and autonomy, selected because they were related directly to the Proposition and because the Matrix model predicted differential responses to them by technology; they represent all relevant items in the survey that deal with authority, control, and autonomy. Items are mostly five-point scales anchored 'Great Deal' to 'None' and zero-to-ten scales anchored 'Never' to 'Always' or 'Completely by me' to 'Completely by someone else'. The analysis compares mean responses across the three technology cells within each sample grouping.

The authors jointly classified a sample of 828 department managers on the basis of their self-report of the predominant task and personnel characteristics of the people in their departments (task units) according to the Matrix model. Task and personnel characteristics did not include those associated with the Matrix Heuristic design, so the 828 task units could be assigned only to the Routine, Engineered, or Craft cells.

Each of the 14 plants was divided into two groups, those with direct and those with indirect labor, giving 25 groups. An index of modal technology for the direct and indirect groups was generated from the company's job code classification as reported by each department manager; the 25 groups were arrayed from low to high technology and three clusters were identified by inspection and classified as low (Routine), medium (Engineered), and high (Craft) technology. The seven remaining groups were omitted from the analysis.

Respondents were first level managers (supervisors and project leaders) and second level managers (managers of first level managers) drawn from the same seven of the fourteen plants and the same groups; the analysis compares how much autonomy the second level management people perceive relative to first level management across the Routine, Engineered and Craft designs.

Sum of the three points which make up the control curve. Each point is the mean response of one managerial echelon (top, middle, lower) to how much say or influence it has in determining work goals, answered on a five-point scale from one 'usually has a great deal of say' to five 'usually has no say at all'. Plants were ranked on this attribute and the rankings dichotomized into high and low at the median rank.
scale: five-point scale per echelon point, summed over three echelons

description: Calculated by fitting a least squares regression line to the three points which comprise the control curve, i.e. the slope of the curve. Plants were ranked on this attribute and dichotomized at the median rank into a distribution approximating power equalization versus one approximating bureaucratic.

The sum of the deviations among the three pairs of points at each hierarchical level for the set of control curves. Plants were ranked on this attribute and dichotomized at the median rank into high and low concordance.

variable_name: Index scores on the ten criterion measures
description: One hundred items tapping relevant aspects of satisfaction and organizational functioning were factor analyzed with an orthogonal routine, where a meaningful factor required an eigenvalue of at least 1 and items loading at least .50; 26 factors accounted for 58 percent of the variance and ten were retained as criterion dependent variables. Index scores were calculated for each factor by a linear summation of the raw scores on items loading .50 or greater, after modification for scale length and direction. Alpha coefficients were calculated, yielding a mean alpha of .73, and intercorrelations indicated the variables are generally independent.

variable_name: cell classification of task units (Routine, Engineered, Craft)
description: The authors established a decision rule to assign the 828 task units into the appropriate cell according to the primary task performed in each unit. The nature of the tasks was reported by each first-level manager in terms of one of the company's 14 numerical job classification codes, which order job specifications and operative qualifications. Because the task characteristics of the sample did not include those described by the Heuristic strategy, the task units could only be assigned to Routine, Engineered, and Craft cells: 246 departments were assigned to Routine, 278 to Engineered, and 304 to Craft.

Responses of the first-level manager of each task unit to 18 items taken from a comprehensive 250-item management attitude survey. Items were selected if the item content was directly related to Proposition I and if differential predictions about task unit manager response could be made from the model. The items concern the degree of say, authority, and freedom the respondent and his manager have in decision areas such as salary increases, work goals, job decisions and schedules, and the extent to which the manager directs, insists on standard procedures, encourages objectives, seeks opinions, or requests information. Individual items rather than factor scores were used because several items are moderately correlated and load on the same factors.
level: task unit (as perceived by its manager)

variable_name: proportion of employees under a centralized personnel function
description: Number of state employees working under a centralized personnel function expressed as a per cent of the state's total number of employees, as reported by respondents and tabulated by state. A state is treated as having a centralized personnel function when at least two-thirds of the total state employees are serviced in a single bureau of the state government, the service to include at a minimum the compilation of employee eligible lists. For the urban-rural comparison, states were classified as having (Yes) or not having (No) a centralized personnel function.

variable_name: proportion of employees under a comprehensive merit system
description: Number of state employees covered by a comprehensive merit system expressed as a per cent of the state's total number of employees. Coverage of at least two-thirds of the state's total employees under a merit system is used as the criterion for a comprehensive merit system. For the urban-rural comparison, states were classified as having (Yes) or not having (No) a comprehensive merit system.

The state is classified as urban when the population proportion living in urban areas is 60 per cent or greater; a rural state is defined as a state in which the population proportion living in rural areas is 40 per cent or greater. States were then grouped as urban or rural for the comparison of proportions.

variable_name: employees organized for collective bargaining purposes
description: Formally organized employee groups formed for collective bargaining about terms and conditions of employment permitted by state law; a state has large numbers of employees organized when at least one-third of the state's total employment is in such organizations. Reported separately as numbers and per cents of employees organized and unorganized. Only twenty-five states reported the number of employees involved in labor unions or public employee associations.

Interorganizational conflict is measured by the level of market channel conflict, using a modification of an instrument used by Walton, Dutton, and Fitch in their analysis of lateral interdepartmental conflict-cooperation. Salesmen and organizations are observed as percentages placed along a six-point scale with 'conflict' and 'cooperation' as the two poles, across information, structure, and attitude measures. Each observed call, combined with historical information given by the salesman, was considered an interorganizational conflict episode, and market channels were then ranked according to their level of interorganizational conflict into high conflict and low conflict channels.
scale: six-point scale with 'conflict' and 'cooperation' as the two poles

description: ILP is measured by a specially constructed four item index offered as an operational approximation of the linking process factors identified by William G. Scott. Each item asks how frequently a described situation occurs, answered on a six-point frequency scale ranging from 'always' to 'never'. The four sets of responses are summed into an index of ILP, and the index is divided into 'high' and 'low' levels corresponding to the upper and lower halves of the scale.
scale: six-point frequency scale (always, very frequently, frequently, infrequently, very infrequently, never)

description: Exchange is measured by a self-rating of productivity by salesmen, an instrument based upon a study by Pym and Auld, because the level of an individual salesman's productivity is taken as a proxy measure of interorganizational exchange. Each salesman rated himself in terms of quantity and quality of performance by comparing himself with other salesmen in his company doing similar work. Those who ranked themselves near the top were categorized as 'high' producers and all others as 'low' producers.

Experimental organizations of eleven members were established with two, three, or four levels; each structure was replicated once. The difference in levels required adjustment in the individual tasks and in the formal channels of communication and authority.

Profit for each trial was computed by determining the sales revenue for a given output and subtracting the production, inventory and lost sales costs. The profit results are arrayed by cycle (6 decisions) and total (36 decisions) as percent of profit attained by cycle.
time_window: per decision/cycle; 6 cycles of 6 decisions, 36 decisions total

description: The time required to reach a decision in each trial; mean time per decision in minutes was computed for each structure and compared by Duncan's Multiple Range Test.
The number of errors made in each trial, aggregated as the mean number of errors per decision for each structure, compared with Duncan's Multiple Range Test.

A modified version of the questionnaire employed by Porter and Lawler was administered after each experiment; a rating scale with responses from a minimum value of 1 to a maximum value of 7 was associated with each question. A mean score for each structure for each question and for the total questionnaire was prepared and tested by t tests.

Points are awarded after each quarter of play for six objectives — share of the market, inventory, cash, profit, owners' equity, and dividends — on numerically weighted scales, and the total of these values is the game performance score. The weight each objective carries depends on the policies the game manager selects. The score was used as the criterion variable and correlated with the students' records and test scores.
time_window: twelve quarterly decision periods (a simulated three-year trial)

description: Points are awarded after each quarter of play for six objectives — share of the market, inventory, cash, profit, owners' equity, and dividends — on numerically weighted scales, and the total of these values is the game performance score. Indicates whether a startup was female- or male-led, taking the value of 1 for female-led startups and 0 for male-led startups. Independent coders hand-collected founders' gender using publicly available images (e.g., LinkedIn profiles, startups' websites); for the remaining founders the authors used pronouns listed in PitchBook biographies and, if needed, name-based inference. For team-founded startups, gender was classified based on the founder designated as the primary contact, typically the CEO who led the pitch.

Takes the value of 1 for startups selected for admission in the shortlisting stage and 0 otherwise. It is the binary evaluative outcome of the shortlisting stage, aggregated from judges' independent evaluations into selection by NVA's overseeing committee.

Takes the value of 1 if a startup was selected as a winner (and allocated funding) in the winners stage and 0 otherwise. It is the binary evaluative outcome of the final, binding stage of the competition.

Each judge independently rated each startup's overall quality on a 0 to 5 scale, indicating whether it should be selected: 0 (''definitely don't recommend''), 1 (''strongly don't recommend''), 2 (''don't recommend''), 3 (''recommend''), 4 (''strongly recommend''), and 5 (''definitely recommend''). Each startup was independently assessed by multiple judges per stage and judges could not see one another's ratings.

Each startup's written application included a one-paragraph description, which the authors converted into numerical embeddings capturing semantic context. Conceptual distance is the average cosine distance between each startup and all other startups in the same industry-year, standardized within industry-year, so a value of 0 indicates average differentiation and higher values indicate greater differentiation from peer startups.

Gender differences in the amount of funding allocated to startups named as winners. Winners could receive up to $100,000 in equity-free funding according to their ratings by judges, and the committee allocated the limited funding based on the competition's results. The dependent variable is used in logged form.

The number of months a startup's website remained active after the competition, tracked from the competition date through September 2025 using ping data from the Wayback Machine, assuming that website shutdown typically coincides with business closure. A site was coded as ''closed'' after 12 consecutive months without ping data; website redirects to a new domain were treated as continued activity. Models use the logged value.
time_window: from the competition date through September 2025

description: The same standardized measure of differentiation from same-industry-year peers is used in the shortlisting stage, both as a main effect and in an interaction with Female-led to test whether returns to unconventionality vary by founder gender.

Number of SOEs each year in an industry, defined at the three-digit SIC level; the count includes firms in the sample (established in or after 1998) as well as firms established before 1998. All density measures were expressed in thousands of firms.
time_window: t, lagged one year in the hazard models

description: Number of COEs each year in an industry, defined at the three-digit SIC level, constructed in the same way as SOE density and including firms established before 1998. All density measures were expressed in thousands of firms.
time_window: t, lagged one year in the hazard models

description: Number of POEs each year in an industry, defined at the three-digit SIC level, constructed in the same way as SOE density and including firms established before 1998. All density measures were expressed in thousands of firms.
time_window: t, lagged one year in the hazard models

description: Coded 1 if a focal firm at time t did not exist in the database at time t + 1, and 0 otherwise; exit may occur through bankruptcy, acquisition, or (for non-SOEs) sales falling below 5 million RMB for two consecutive years. Exit identification relied on the firm identifier and other registered information; merger cases in which the acquiring party could not be clearly identified were excluded, about 2 percent of the sample. This variable is the dependent variable in the hazard model for the state-owned enterprise population.

Coded 1 if a focal firm at time t did not exist in the database at time t + 1, and 0 otherwise; exit may occur through bankruptcy, acquisition, or (for non-SOEs) sales falling below 5 million RMB for two consecutive years. Exit identification relied on the firm identifier and other registered information; merger cases in which the acquiring party could not be clearly identified were excluded, about 2 percent of the sample. This variable is the dependent variable in the hazard model for the collectively owned enterprise population.

Exit identification relied on the firm identifier and other registered information; merger cases in which the acquiring party could not be clearly identified were excluded, about 2 percent of the sample. This variable is the dependent variable in the hazard model for the privately owned enterprise population.

One measure of label ambiguity, built on a label's contrast, or how clearly a label is defined relative to other labels in its environment. An organization's grade of membership in a label is the number of times it mentioned the label in press releases divided by the number of times it mentioned any label, for each year, and takes values between 0 and 1; fuzzy density is the sum of the grades of membership of organizations that affiliate with the label, and contrast is fuzzy density divided by support (the number of organizations claiming non-zero membership). Fuzziness is the opposite of contrast, so when fuzziness is high a large number of affiliated organizations also identify with at least one other label. An organization's value is a weighted average that sums the product of its grade of membership in a label with the label's fuzziness. The equations themselves are not readable in the text.
time_window: measured at the start of each time period

description: One measure of label ambiguity, built on a label's contrast, or how clearly a label is defined relative to other labels in its environment. An organization's grade of membership in a label is the number of times it mentioned the label in press releases divided by the number of times it mentioned any label, for each year, and takes values between 0 and 1; fuzzy density is the sum of the grades of membership of organizations that affiliate with the label, and contrast is fuzzy density divided by support. Fuzziness is the opposite of contrast. An organization's value is a weighted average that sums the product of its grade of membership in a label with the label's fuzziness. The equations themselves are not readable in the text.
time_window: measured at the start of each time period

description: An alternate measure of ambiguity that builds on fuzziness but also takes into account whether a label overlaps with many different labels. It is computed by multiplying fuzziness by the natural log of the number of distinct other labels members identified with. An organization's value is a weighted average that sums the product of its grade of membership in a label with the label's leniency. The equations themselves are not readable in the text.
time_window: measured at the start of each time period

description: The number of labels the organization claimed in a given year, used to measure label spanning. Because the distribution was skewed, the natural log is used, consistent with previous studies on organizational categorization.
time_window: measured at the start of each time period

description: The number of labels the organization claimed in a given year, used to measure label spanning. Because the distribution was skewed, the natural log is used, consistent with previous studies on organizational categorization.

description: Inverse rank is 500 minus the rank of the organization in Software Magazine's Software 500, so that a higher inverse rank is associated with a more positive consumer evaluation; in every year the highest inverse rank is 500. The range of values for inverse rank is between 1 and 500. Consulting companies were not included in the analysis.

Whether an organization received venture capital funding in the current year. This is a binary variable for which 0 indicates the organization did not receive venture capital funding in the focal year, and 1 indicates that it did receive funding. Only venture capital deals were included.

The event of interest was the defection of clients from Arthur Andersen, and the dependent variable is the unobserved hazard rate of defection. The week of defection is defined as the calendar week in which a firm officially announced that Arthur Andersen had been dismissed, as announced in the 8K filing (regardless of when the 8K was filed) with the SEC. Firm event histories were split into one (calendar) week spells.
time_window: weekly spells from week 1 (October 15, 2001) to week 46 (August 31, 2002)

description: Binary variable coded one if public pension funds holding at least $100 million in equity assets, such as CalPERS, together owned more than 5 percent of the shares in a firm. This definition excludes smaller pension funds with less than $100 million in equity because they do not have to file 13Fs and report to the SEC in which firms they have invested. Institutional ownership was restricted to public pension funds because they are the most active investors and are less susceptible to pressure from management than corporate pension funds.

Analyst coverage is defined as the number of security analysts who issued earnings forecasts or investment recommendations for a given client in the last half of 2001. Most analyst coverage is positive coverage (more than 95 percent) because analysts traditionally have been reluctant to issue negative investment recommendations.

Binary variables were used as indicators of the stock exchanges on which firms were listed, using NASDAQ as the comparison group (NYSE, AMEX, and OTC). The variables for American Stock Exchange (AMEX) and over-the-counter (OTC) were entered as control variables.

Media coverage of prior defections was defined in terms of the number of articles mentioning firms that defected from Arthur Andersen published weekly in the Wall Street Journal. The WSJ was chosen because it is published daily, has a national subscriber base, and is a trusted source of information in the business community. Only WSJ articles that mentioned actual defections were counted, excluding articles only mentioning that firms were monitoring the situation, considering defecting, or had made contingency plans. The variable was updated weekly and lagged one week.

A large firm was defined as a Fortune 500 firm, and the variable focuses on the weekly defections of Fortune 500 firms. Based on their sales, 100 Arthur Andersen clients made the Fortune 500 list in 2001, with Enron being the largest (#5) and Hilton Hotels the smallest (#499). The variable was updated weekly and lagged one week.

A binary variable was used to distinguish between firms whose directors (executive and non-executive directors) were on the board of directors of firms that already had defected from Arthur Andersen. It was rare for firms to be interlocked with more than one prior defector, which suggests that a binary variable is most appropriate. The variable was updated weekly and lagged one week.

Firms registered with the SEC have to disclose the annual audit and non-audit fees they paid to their auditor in their proxy statements (DEF 14A). The natural logarithm of audit fees was regressed on various measures of audit difficulty and audit risk, and the ratio between actual audit fees and predicted audit fees was used as a measure of the extent to which firms paid higher or lower than expected audit fees.
