Audit difficulty was measured as firm size (assets), diversification (entropy measure), internationalization (proportion of revenues from international operations), proportion of receivables to assets, proportion of inventory to assets, and fixed effects for industry; audit risk measures included return on assets, a binary variable indicating if the firm had experienced a loss in the prior three years, and a binary variable indicating if the firm had received a qualified audit opinion the previous year.

The index is based on the number of decisions in each of the 21 categories of market-oriented action for each airline in year t. Because the average number of decisions differs across categories, scores for each type of action were standardized across all airlines and years so that rare decisions are weighted more heavily than common ones; the sum of these standardized scores is divided by the log of revenue passenger miles, a common industry measure of scale of operations, to render the index comparable across firms of different scale. The quotient was converted to a positive number by adding a constant large enough to allow the natural log to be taken, and the sign of the Activity index is reversed so that it measures competitive inertia rather than activity level. The correlations among the 21 types of actions produce a Cronbach alpha of .79.

A version of the inertia index computed only from tactical actions, defined as actions not involving significant long-term commitments of fixed assets and deemed to have a less permanent impact on the firm. The 21 generic action types were classified as strategic or tactical by three raters working independently, with total agreement among the raters, and the classification was confirmed by a questionnaire sent to six management professors with expertise in competitive strategy and the airline industry.

A version of the inertia index computed only from strategic actions, defined as actions involving significant investments in fixed assets, people, or structure, relatively long time horizons, considerable financial expenditures, and important and relatively irreversible departures from the status quo. Seven kinds of actions were deemed strategic: mergers and acquisitions, hub creations, feeder and interindustry alliances, new services, frequent flyer programs, and new airplane purchases.

Performance was measured by operating revenue per available seat mile flown, R/ASM. The authors state that this index reflects both the load factor of an airline and the revenue produced thereby, and that it is updated for most airline executives very frequently, so it can have a rapid impact on strategy; measures such as return on equity or return on assets were avoided because they are calculated too rarely and are influenced by factors having little direct connection with the actions incorporated in the inertia measure.
time_window: annual, current year and one-year lag

description: A composite index assessing the number of different airports served by each airline and the number of competitors faced by each airline. Information was obtained from the U.S. Department of Transportation's publication Airport Activity Statistics of Certified Route Carriers; the authors state these numbers indicate the variety of markets and passengers served and hence the diversity of competitive conditions and customer demands that airlines must confront.
Measured by the level of growth in total industry business volume, assessed by the annual change in total revenue passenger miles for the entire domestic airline passenger business.

A company's breadth of competitive experience was assessed as competitive inertia during the previous year, giving an overall assessment of the company's level of activity in the past. To establish robustness the authors also assessed experience using simply a count of the number of types of actions made by a firm in the preceding year, with almost identical results.
Firm age was measured in years.
Size was measured simply as the natural log of the number of full-time employees.

The number of years the incumbent has served as CEO, used as the duration measure in all models estimated. CEOs appointed prior to 1960 are subject to left-truncation: data on prior CEO tenure were recorded for all incumbents in 1960 and only the remainder of the CEO's tenure was included in the sample.

Return on assets was used as the performance measure and was adjusted for industry average. Financial data used were lagged one fiscal year, and the best fit was obtained for the single one-year lag of the ROA variable. The correlation between adjusted and unadjusted ROA was .94.
The number of years of the CEO's board tenure before first becoming CEO. This variable was measured in logarithmic form by taking the natural log of the variable plus 1.
The proportion of all directors first appointed during the CEO's incumbency.
The number of outside board members divided by the total number of directors.
The number of board members, both insider directors and outside directors.
A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 when the chairman of the board of directors differs from the CEO, and 0 otherwise.

CEO succession events were coded from Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors based on changes in the names of the relevant officers. A succession variable that takes the value of 1 if a succession event occurs, and 0, otherwise, is included for comparison.

Dependence relations between each pair of decision makers were defined using path distances in the dependence network, assuming that constraint is a negative function of the number of steps between ego and alter. Four levels of dependence were defined: one-step or direct dependence, two-step dependence, three or more steps, and no dependence. The longest observed chain was eight steps.
scale: four categories: one-step, two-step, three or more steps, no dependence

description: Direct cooptive efforts were coded as present when either a political tie or a confidential discussion tie existed between ego and the alter. Confidential discussion ties were self-reported sociometric nominations of people with whom the respondent regularly has confidential discussions on topics affecting his or her performance as a decision maker, counted as present if either member of the dyad cited the other. Political ties were identified through joint membership in one of the three groups that participated in the 1990 elections to the board of the core firm, supplemented by faction leaders' lists of followers and by field observation of two further political clusters. In the analysis of cooptive efforts by level of dependence, the two indicators were combined into four categories: joint tie, confidential tie only, political tie only, and none.

Two-step cooptation was coded as present when both a political tie and a confidential tie existed between ego and actors on whom the alter depends, that is, actors separated by two steps from ego in the dependence network. The joint tie was used as an indicator of two-step linkages to eliminate potentially spurious cases by requiring a strong, definite bond between the parties.

Ties were coded as conflictive if either ego or alter cited the other party as someone who had troubled him or her in the performance of his or her role or as someone whose influence on a key issue he or she actively tried to neutralize. Two sociometric indicators were used to maximize the reliability of the coding, capturing ongoing friction in the relation rather than the direction of the conflict; the two measures correlate at r = .30 (p < .001).

Dummy variable for the ith pharmaceutical firm's choice of undertaking the jth R&D project. It was coded 1 if the firm's R&D on the project was completely internal and 0 if the project involved an external source. In the few cases involving two established firms, the case was treated as external/collaborative when there was evidence that both firms were contributing R&D. In 47 percent of the cases the pharmaceutical firm was doing the R&D project internally.

For each project, the number of new biotechnology firms with R&D programs in the same therapeutic application, since new biotechnology firms are the overwhelmingly dominant source of external biotechnology R&D. The variable is specified in log form because an additional supplier has a smaller effect on small-numbers-bargaining hazards as the number of suppliers grows. The therapeutic application of each project is recorded in Table 1.

For each project, the number of established pharmaceutical companies (all firms except new biotechnology firms) attempting to develop or commercialize the same product or other products within the same area of therapeutic application. New biotechnology firms were not counted as rivals because they have generally lacked the capabilities to commercialize products on their own, and the measure was aggregated over the entire world market. It is specified in log form for the same reason as the SUPPLIERS variable.

Ratio of the number of the firm's own R&D pharmaceutical products in development in 1982 to all of its pharmaceutical products in development in 1982, where 'own R&D' means products originating from the firm's own R&D laboratories and the denominator includes products from internal and external sources. The year 1982 was chosen to avoid simultaneity with the dependent variable, and because of long R&D cycles the construct picks up decisions made over the previous five-to-seven-year period. A value closer to 1 indicates a firm that has tended to be more vertically integrated into traditional pharmaceutical R&D.

Number of completed R&D projects by firm i in biotechnology category j, where j varies across the projects in the sample; the number of completed projects is taken as an indicator of the firm's accumulated experience in biotechnology R&D. Completed projects were identified by generating, from the data sources, lists of biotechnology products each firm had in clinical development, awaiting regulatory approval, or already on the market as of 1986 and determining whether each originated in-house. Each project was classified into one of six technological categories.

The percentage of each firm's total sales attributable to its pharmaceutical business, gathered from annual reports; for the Japanese firms the data were drawn from The Japan Company Handbook for the years 1982-1985.

Firm size measured in terms of pharmaceutical sales rather than total corporate sales, because economies and diseconomies of internal organization should occur at the business unit rather than the corporate level. A quadratic specification was used to allow for the possibility that the direction of the effect changes with size, and SALES-only, log(SALES), and no-size specifications were also estimated. Data on sales were available from annual reports and The Japan Company Handbook.

A dummy variable for the country of the plant, entered in the additive models that permit intercepts (means) to differ between countries while constraining slopes to be the same. The table note gives its coding as 1 for a U.S. plant and 0 for a Japanese plant, so the variable is reverse-coded relative to the construct as named here.

Aston functional specialization scale: the proportion of 20 functions that are the sole responsibility of at least one individual, assigned as full-time responsibilities. Where employees had other responsibilities as well, the specialty was coded as absent. The authors report that three-quarters of the functions listed are assigned to specialists in the U.S. plants and less than one-third in the Japanese plants.

Number of units one level below the plant manager. In both countries the authors coded as departments all groups shown by the organization chart as one level below the manager of the organization studied. The count is taken from organization charts and informant reports.

Number of units below department level; the authors coded as sections all units from the next level below departments on down. Some section heads in Japanese organizations report directly to the factory chief executive even though their status is two levels down, and such units were still counted as sections.
Number of hierarchical levels from the lowest direct worker to the highest manager in the plant.

The plant manager's span of control, i.e., the number of subordinates reporting to the chief executive of the plant. The authors report that the chief executive's span of control is wider in the Japanese sample by a net 1.44 subordinates.
Average first-line supervisor's span of control. The authors report that first-line supervisory spans appear just slightly larger in Japan, with a difference nowhere near significant.

Ratio of managers to the total number of employees in the plant. The authors use it, together with the production-worker ratio, to test whether Japanese companies have leaner or more manager-heavy hierarchies.

Ratio of clerical workers to the total number of employees in the plant, treated by the authors as an indicator of file keeping and formal communications. The Japanese plants had a net 4 percent more clerical employees than the U.S. plants, a difference not significant in the unadjusted means but highly significant in the regression coefficient paired with the dummy for country.
Aston formalization scale: the proportion present of a total of 28 written documents.

Variant of the Aston centralization scale consisting of 37 decision items, each scored for the level in the organization with the formal authority to make the decision: 1 (direct worker), 2 (first-line supervisor), 3 (middle manager), 4 (department head), 5 (plant manager), or 6 (company official above the plant manager). The total score is computed as the mean of the 37 items.
scale: mean score on a 1-6 level code

description: Variant of the Aston centralization scale consisting of the same 37 decision items, each scored for the level at which, in practice, the decision was usually made, using the same codes as for formal authority. The total score is computed as the mean of the 37 items.
scale: mean score on a 1-6 level code

description: The proportion of a total of 37 decisions that top management reported were made in the ringi fashion, measured in the Japanese plants. In the U.S. sample informants were asked the substitute question of whether the same decisions were made by a group rather than an individual; the authors state that these are not parallel indices.

Proportion of employees surveyed in the plant who reported that they were members of quality circles, obtained from questionnaires administered to representative samples of employees from all administrative levels and major departmental groupings. The measure limits the sample to the 52 U.S. and 46 Japanese plants from which questionnaire data could be obtained. Seventy-six percent of the Japanese sample of 3,735 employees reported QC membership, against 27 percent of the 4,567 U.S. employees.

Sum of the plant manager's ratings of the extent of custom (1 = not at all, 5 = a great deal) and small batch technologies on the same scale. The custom and small batch indicators were combined into one unit-weighted scale, the two items correlating at .394.
Sum of the plant manager's ratings of the extent of large batch and mass production technologies on a 5-point scale; the two indicators were combined into one unit-weighted scale.
Plant manager's rating of continuous process technology on a 5-point scale.

Automation scale: the sum of scores indicating the most automatic machinery in the plant and the automation level of the bulk of the machinery (hand tools and manual machines = 0; computer control = 5).
scale: sum of two scores from 0 to 5

description: Aston workflow rigidity scale: the proportion applicable of eight statements characterizing the rigidity and interdependence of workflow processes. Among the items in the scale is minimizing buffer stocks between stages of processing.

Six variables (V1-V6) were used to operationalize capacity. The first four, growth in sales, growth in price-cost margin, growth in total employment, and growth in value added, were specified as the rate of growth (regression coefficient) divided by the mean value of the dependent variable over a ten-year period. Growth in the number of establishments was measured as the average annual percentage change over an eleven-year period because annual data were not available. Industry sales concentration was operationalized as the proportion of the total value of shipments accounted for by the eight largest companies.

Eight variables were used to operationalize the homogeneity-heterogeneity and concentration-dispersion dimensions of complexity (V7-V10, V16-V19). For three of the four variables used for homogeneity-heterogeneity the Gibbs-Martin formula was used, incorporating both structural differentiation and distributive differentiation. Concentration of industry inputs and outputs reflected the extent to which a large portion of an industry's input was supplied by, or purchased by, relatively few industries, and diversity of industry products measured the degree to which output was concentrated within a few seven-digit SIC products or evenly spread among many. The specialization ratio measured the proportion of the value of shipments accounted for by the one primary product by which establishments were assigned to the classification, and the Gibbs-Martin formula was also used to measure geographical concentration of industry sales, value added, employment, and establishments.

Five variables (V11-V15) were used to operationalize environmental stability-instability, four of which used the same data sources as four of the capacity variables. Stability-instability was measured by the dispersion about the regression line obtained when each dependent variable was regressed on time over the period 1968 to 1977, a form of measurement consistent with the view of instability as unsystematic, unpredictable change. Technological instability was operationalized as the percentage of scientists and engineers in the total number of employees. Turbulence was measured in two ways from input-output data: the sum of all direct and indirect requirements placed on an industry if every industry increased its output by one unit and the sum of indirect requirements, and the proportion of industry output sold to other industries for further processing and the proportion sold for investment.

The relative measure is the percentage of innovations adopted from the total innovations available for adoption during a specific period. For example, the relative score of technical innovations from 1975-1979 for a library is the number of technical innovations that it adopted during 1975-1979 divided by the number of all technical innovations available during 1975-1979, multiplied by 100. Sixty-seven innovations, 40 technical and 27 administrative, were the subject of analysis, and technical innovations are those pertaining to technical service areas such as acquisition, circulation control, cataloging, and reference services. The relative rather than the absolute measure was used in operationalizing the degree of organizational lag.

The relative measure is the percentage of innovations adopted from the total innovations available for adoption during a specific period, computed separately for administrative innovations. Administrative innovations comprise the introduction of a new management system, administrative process, or staff development program, affecting the library's social system. The relative rather than the absolute measure was used in operationalizing the degree of organizational lag.
Organizational lag for a given period was measured by the (absolute) difference between the relative measures of technical and administrative innovations in that period.
time_window: 1975-1979 (period for which the relationship with performance was analyzed)

description: A composite objective measure formed from three performance indicators, each of which was divided into four levels of a frequency distribution (the first to the fourth quartile) to create a four-point performance scale. The analysis showed that the three performance indicators of the efficiency measure were highly intercorrelated, and the mean of the three indicators was therefore used to represent a composite measure of efficiency. This was the measure used to analyze the relationship between performance and organizational lag.

Three indicators based on assessments made by library directors of the performance of their libraries, computed for the 1980-1982 period. An approach similar to the one used by Lawrence and Lorsch was used to ask directors to rate their libraries' overall performance, extent of services, and quality of services against those of other public libraries of the same type and size.

Measured by two indicators: the focal agency's dependence on the member agency and the member agency's dependence on the focal agency, each answered for every relationship by the respective respondents. The measure is assessed at time 1 and again at time 3.

Measured by two indicators: the extent to which the focal agency and the member agency provide the same services, and the extent to which they serve the same clients. Assessed at time 1 and again at time 3.

Measured by two indicators: the frequency of written communications and the frequency of phone calls between the parties to the relationship. The authors report the variable for time 1, time 2, and time 3.
time_window: t1, t2 and t3 (March 1974, January 1975, August 1976)

description: Measured by two indicators: the extent to which the agreement between the parties is written and the extent to which it is legal. Assessed at time 1.
Measured by two indicators: the extent to which the parties agree on service goals and the extent to which they agree on the focal agency's methods. Assessed at time 2 and again at time 3.

Measured by a single indicator, the degree of money flows from one agency to the other; the authors note that monetary transactions is one of the three variables measured with one indicator rather than two. Assessed at time 2.
Measured by a single indicator, the degree of client referral between the two organizations; one of the three variables measured with one indicator rather than two. Assessed at time 2.

Measured by a single indicator, the frequency of the funding agency's site visits, which serve both to evaluate contract compliance and to provide technical assistance and training; one of the three variables measured with one indicator rather than two. Assessed at time 2.
Measured by two indicators: the extent to which the relationship is perceived as worthwhile and the extent to which it is perceived as productive or effective. Assessed at time 3.

A scale measuring the degree to which the establishment had an ILM, built from interview questions. An establishment scored a 1 on each of seven items: (1) followed an established promotion-from-within policy, (2) had promoted most employees with at least five years of service at least once, (3) filled all or almost all jobs from within, (4) offered entry-level jobs with at least some promotion potential and requiring no prior work experience and no more than high school graduation, (5) offered entry-level jobs with some promotion potential and requiring no prior work experience except such educational qualifications as graduation from junior college or a college degree, (6) frequently promoted unskilled laborers to semiskilled jobs (manufacturing establishments only), and (7) frequently promoted semiskilled laborers to skilled jobs (manufacturing establishments only). The ILM score of the establishment was the number of items on which it scored 1 divided by the number of items on which it had nonmissing values; establishments having missing values on more than three items were excluded. Cronbach's alpha for this variable was .67.
A dummy variable referring to whether or not the establishment offered vestibule training, i.e., training given before the worker assumed the full duties of the position.
The degree to which the establishment offered formal employer-supported on-the-job training. The variable has a range of 0-3, where 0 means that no training is provided.

The degree to which the establishment offered or required any training outside the establishment. The variable has a range of 0-3, where 0 means that no training is provided; such training is likely to be associated with more general skills.

An additive scale comprising seven dichotomous items. An establishment scored a 1 on the following items if, during 1960-1966, it built a new plant, remodeled an old plant, installed new equipment, modernized equipment, significantly changed internal operating procedures, eliminated inefficient working arrangements (work rules and loose production standards), or changed materials used in the production process. The technology score of an establishment was the number of items on which it scored 1 divided by the number of items for which it had nonmissing values; establishments having missing values on any of the seven questions were excluded. Cronbach's alpha for this index was .72.

Industrial sector was coded as 1 if the establishment operated in one of the industries classified as 'core' by Tolbert, Horan, and Beck (1980); a 1 means the establishment operated in the core, a 0 means it was at the periphery.
A dummy variable indicating whether or not the establishment was part of the government.
A dummy variable indicating whether or not the establishment reported having a personnel department.
Unionization was measured by the percentage of employees covered by a collective bargaining agreement.

Organizations answering 'yes' to the question 'Have you ever found it difficult to recruit within a reasonable length of time the number of workers you wanted to hire?' scored 1 for having recruitment difficulties.
Size of establishment was measured by the natural logarithm of the number of employees in 1967.
Growth was coded as 1 if the establishment reported a significant increase in the number of employees since 1960.
Decline was coded as 1 if the firm reported a significant decrease in the number of employees since 1960.
Type of establishment was coded using a dummy variable; 'branch' was coded as 1 if the establishment was part of a larger organization (but not a headquarters unit).

Each Letter to Shareholders was parsed into sentences and every instance of causal attribution was retained, with the effects coded as good news or bad news and the causes classified by locus of causality as internal or external. A cause was considered internal when referring to factors internal to the organization, and external when arising from factors external to the organization. The frequencies of the self-serving cells (internal causes for good news and external causes for bad news) in each combination of performance and context were totalized and transformed into a proportion of the total amount of attributions of their respective column.
level: coded causal attribution, aggregated by company performance-context combination
time_window: years of the annual reports (2002 and 2003)

description: Net income was used as the proxy for performance. Companies were separated by their respective combination of performance (negative or positive) and external context, forming the groups NB (negative performers in the bad year), NG (negative performers in the good year), PB (positive performers in the bad year) and PG (positive performers in the good year). Companies were selected on the criterion that information about net earnings was available for 2001, 2002 and 2003 in the Economatica database.

variable_name: External context (bad year versus good year)
description: A good year and a bad year were selected using the per capita gross domestic product and the Ibovespa (Bovespa index) as proxies. 2002 was chosen as the bad year and 2003 as the good year; in 2002 the per capita GDP decreased 0.32% and the Ibovespa showed a negative variation of 17 percentage points, while 2003 had a 4.19% increase in the per capita GDP and a positive variation of 97.33 points in the Ibovespa.
The Letters to Shareholders of the sampled companies were collected for the years of 2002 and 2003, the bad and the good year respectively, and analyzed separately for each year.

Institutions were classified by their division in football and basketball: major in both sports, major in only one sport (mixed), or minor in both sports. Until 1972 the NCAA had university (major) and college (minor) levels, determined by choice of opponents, granting of athletic scholarships, size of athletic program, and self-designation. Membership in the 1961-1962 year was used for calculating the probabilities involved in examining Hypothesis 1.

Dummy variable coded 1 for institutions belonging to an athletic conference and 0 for nonconference institutions. Conferences were defined by the existence of a central administrative office and the determination of conference football and basketball champions at the time. Conference membership was used as a measure of competitiveness.

variable_name: Detected violations / number of times sanctions received (0, 1, 2 or more)
description: Institutions were coded by whether they had ever been penalized and how many times (0, 1, or 2 or more) over the period; the reported figures are the proportions of institutions at each level of competition in each category. Only cases in which a violation was detected and publicly penalized are recorded, so the data represent those cases publicly penalized.

Poll rankings 1 through 10 were recorded from 1947-1972 for all university division schools ranked, giving 10 points for first and 1 point for tenth position. Associated Press year end poll rankings in football and basketball were taken to be a measure of visibility and, in the long run, athletic prestige.

variable_name: Number of years ranked in the five years prior to the violation
description: The number of years an institution appeared in the national rankings in the five years before the violation, taken as a measure of visibility in the analysis of sanction severity.
time_window: five years prior to the violation

description: Penalties were ranked in order of severity according to the NCAA sanctioning procedure. Categories run from reprimand, censure, reprimand and censure, probation 1 year or less, probation 2 years, probation 3 years, and probation more than 3 years to permanent and temporary suspension from the NCAA. The suspension categories were theoretically available but were not used, and probations usually included exclusion from championship competition and restriction of television appearances.

The number of constitutional and bylaw provisions violated in each case was summed, and separate totals were kept for infractions involving illegal financial and nonfinancial inducements to athletes. Aid-related infractions indicated violations of the basic recruiting regulations. Infractions were classified into 23 specific categories before being grouped as aid-related or nonaid-related.

Alterations in the pattern of rankings for all NCAA members in football and basketball were recorded for each year in the twenty-year period. Whenever changes of seven places or more in either direction appeared, the number of places changed was noted; a team going from off the top ten list to number three in one year would have improved at least seven places in ranking.
scale: count of places changed in ranking
time_window: each year of the twenty-year period, 1952-1972

description: The academic excellence of each institution was estimated using the "College Admissions Selector" in Barron's handbook for 1972, which placed academic institutions in nine categories ranked by the degree of competition for admission; 1 is the most competitive category. Academic competitiveness was used as a measure of dependence upon goals mediated by the association, and those with high academic rankings (1 = highest) were considered less dependent.

Agency executive directors were asked to list the number of people, both full- and part-time, currently employed by their agency. The item was later used, together with board influence, board linkages, agency–United Way board cooptation and number of clients, in the standardized five-item links-with-the-community scale used in the regression equations.

Executive directors were asked how many people worked for their agency over the past fiscal year as volunteers. Volunteers had to have worked at least 8 hours per month to qualify. The variable was retained as a separate variable in the regression equations after factor analysis.

The actual number of clients served by each agency over the past year was obtained from agency records. The item was used, together with board influence, number of employees, board linkages and agency–United Way board cooptation, in the standardized five-item links-with-the-community scale.

Names of all people serving on each agency's board of directors were obtained from each agency, and a scale was constructed by averaging two standardized items: the percentage of an agency's board members listed in the city's 1973 Social Register, and the percentage of board members residing in high income areas, defined as areas with a mean family income of at least $15,000 per year. The measure was also one of the three items combined into the establishment-in-the-community scale.

Agency executive directors were given a list of all United Way agencies and were asked to list the seven agencies which they felt had boards of directors with the most influence in the community. A score was assigned to each agency consisting of the number of times the agency was mentioned by all executive directors, ranging from zero to 38. The item was also one of the five items in the links-with-the-community scale.
scale: count of mentions by all executive directors (0 to 38)

description: Each agency executive director was asked to indicate the number of programs conducted over the past year for which there was joint participation between his or her agency and any other organization, the total number of different organizations involved in these joint programs, and the number of United Way agencies involved. The items were standardized and then averaged to form a three-item scale.

A count was made of the number of linkages between an agency's board and the boards of all other agencies affiliated with United Way; an agency scored each time one of its own board members was also represented on the board of another United Way agency. The item was also included in the links-with-the-community scale.
A count was made of the number of an agency's board members who also served on the board of directors of United Way. The item was also included in the links-with-the-community scale.

The number of years the agency had been serving the community, obtained from United Way records. It measured the agency's establishment within its domain in the community and was also one of the three items combined into the establishment-in-the-community scale.

The number of years the agency had been affiliated with United Way, obtained from United Way records. It measured the agency's establishment within its domain within the United Way support network and was also one of the three items combined into the establishment-in-the-community scale.

Each agency executive director was asked to compute the percentage increase or decrease in the number of clients served by their agency over the past three years. The figure was based on agency records for clients served in 1973 and in 1976, and two- or one-year growth figures were used for the few agencies not in existence in 1973.

Computed by dividing the total dollar budget from all sources (1976) by the number of clients served by each agency (1976). High costs per client were taken to indicate relatively intensive and comprehensive services.

variable_name: Net dependence of an agency on United Way
description: The difference between the percentage of an agency's total budget funded by United Way (dependence of the agency on United Way) and the percentage of United Way's total allocations going to that agency (dependence of United Way on the agency). The percentages were first standardized on their own means and then averaged over a three-year period (1974-1976) before subtraction; for a few new agencies data were available for only two years. Since low dependence indicates high potential power, the scores were transposed so that a high value reflects power.

variable_name: Percentage of an agency's budget request met by United Way
description: The percentage of each agency's United Way budget request actually funded by United Way was computed for each of three years (1974-1976), and a mean of the three yearly figures (two years for a few new agencies) was then computed to reduce the effect of yearly fluctuations. Data were obtained from United Way records.

variable_name: Percentage increase in an agency's United Way funding
description: The yearly percentage increase (or decrease) in each agency's United Way funding for three years (1974-1976) was computed and averaged, again to minimize the effect of yearly fluctuations resulting from unusual circumstances. Data were obtained from United Way records.

variable_name: Perceived power I (assessed agency's ease in obtaining funding)
description: The executive director of each agency was asked to indicate the extent of agreement with statements that his or her agency could readily obtain funding from United Way to cover increases in client needs, for new programs, and to cover increased administrative expenses. Possible responses ranged from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree); responses were standardized and then averaged to form a three-item scale.

variable_name: Perceived power II (agency's ability to influence United Way, as assessed by United Way staff)
description: Each of five United Way staff members working directly with the agencies studied listed the agencies with which he or she worked and indicated the extent to which each agency was able to successfully influence United Way in order to meet its own budget needs, influence meaning the extent to which the agency's policies, views and actions had some impact on the final fund allocation decision. Possible responses ranged from 1 (virtually no influence) to 5 (a great deal of influence).
scale: 1 (virtually no influence) to 5 (a great deal of influence)

variable_name: Agency power relative to United Way (five measures: potential power, enacted power I and II, perceived power I and II)
description: Agency power was measured with five indicators: potential power (net dependence of the agency on United Way), two measures of enacted power (percentage of the budget request funded and percentage increase in the United Way allocation, averaged over 1974 to 1976), and two measures of perceived power (executive directors' ratings of their ability to obtain funding and United Way staff ratings of agency influence). Data came from agency and United Way records and from interviews.
scale: five separate measures (percentages, dependence index, rating scales)

variable_name: perceived distinctive competence (strength/weakness ratings of ten functions)
description: Respondents rated each of ten broad functions as a 'strength,' 'weakness,' or 'OK' (average) in their company. The functions were (1) general management; (2) financial management; (3) marketing/selling; (4) market research; (5) product research and development; (6) engineering, basic and applied; (7) production; (8) distribution; (9) legal affairs; and (10) personnel. By assigning 'weakness' a score of 1, 'OK' a score of 2, and 'strength' a score of 3, distinctive competence was assumed to be measured by a quasi-interval scale. Since factor analyses indicated that each item tapped different distinctive competences, reliability coefficients were not computed.

Top managers assessed the strategies of their own organizations using descriptions of the four strategies in the Miles and Snow (1978) typology, which yielded a nominal scale. For the analysis of strategy and performance, each organization's strategy was determined by calculating the mode of its top managers' evaluations of strategy for their organization. Use of the mode was legitimated by an analysis of variance showing substantial agreement on strategy among top managers within a given organization (F = 2.9, p < .001).
level: individual top manager; organization for the performance analysis

variable_name: ratio of total income to total assets
description: An objective measure of profitability, the ratio of total income to total assets, was used as a surrogate of overall organizational performance. This ratio was chosen because more commonly used ratios are subject to wide variation in accounting practice, even among organizations within the same industry, and because it was believed to be sensitive to differences in strategy and distinctive competence while being relatively unaffected by differences in accounting methods. The ratio was computed for 1975, the year corresponding to the questionnaire on managerial perceptions.

variable_name: top managers' rankings of distinctive competence
description: To identify patterns in distinctive competence across the four strategies, a simple ranking of top managers' perceived distinctive competences was made, showing the four highest-rated strengths of each strategy by industry. The data also were subjected to simple correlational analysis as well as factor analysis (varimax rotation) to determine the factor loadings on perceived strengths by strategy type. Only the Defender and Prospector strategies showed satisfactory ratios between sample size and number of items for factor analysis.

variable_name: distribution of perceived strategies by industry
description: Strategy distribution was the count of top managers in each of the four industries who typed their organization as Defender, Prospector, Analyzer or Reactor from the Miles and Snow descriptions, compared within and across industries.

An index constructed from three variables: the average length in words of dissertation abstracts in each field, the average length in pages of dissertations of each field, and the length of the longest chain of prerequisite courses in the field. The composite index reflects the overall level of paradigm development of the discipline. Departments are ranked from most to least highly developed.
The length of the longest chain of prerequisite courses in the field on the larger of the two campuses, used as a more localized indicator of the level of paradigm development.

Size was measured as the average number of full-time-equivalent regular faculty in the department during the period 1967-1976. Only regular faculty were included, not teaching assistants, part-time lecturers, or other non-ladder faculty.

A weighted rank measure computed for the average faculty composition during the period 1967-1976, defined as (Assistant Profs + 2*Associate Profs + 3*Full Profs) divided by the total number of Assistant, Associate, and Full Professors.

The change in the proportion of total faculty by department from 1967 to 1976. For each year the number of faculty in the department was divided by the total number of faculty in all studied departments on the same campus, and the 1967 figure was compared to the 1976 figure.

The average tenure of department heads in each department was computed by dividing the length of time (ten or twenty years) by the number of heads who served during the period in question. Only actual successions were counted; an acting head appointed while a head was on leave was not counted as an additional succession event.

Resource scarcity is indexed by the comparison of the two ten-year periods: the percentage increase in university budget and in budget for the departments examined, less the rate of inflation as measured by the gross national product price deflator, are reported for the first and second ten-year periods, with the second period showing greater financial stringency.

Work motifs were coded from how the heads of firms responded to the open-ended question "How do you define a successful project?", sometimes clarified by the follow-up question "What do you aim for in your work?" Content analysis of the answers revealed 13 distinct categories, and each principal's responses were coded as a set of 13 dummy variables indicating the presence or absence of a particular motif. Four motifs mentioned by too few principals and three categories with high intercorrelations were eliminated, leaving six categories in the analysis.

The number of architectural awards won by the firm during the past five years. In analyzing the effects of other factors on innovation the actual number of awards was used as a raw variable; in comparing firms by successful innovation the sample was divided into firms that had won awards and firms that had not.

The total number of units under the top executive, split in one analysis into the number of divisions responsible for the primary activities of design and production and the number of additional staff units engaged in support activities such as client contacts, legal services, research, and the coordination of construction activities.
Based on the list of "comprehensive services" developed by the American Institute of Architects, the variable tells how many of 16 different services the firm was able to provide.

variable_name: Nonprivate clients; joint ventures; consultant use
description: The percentage of 1973 projects commissioned by other than private individuals indicated the scale of projects and the complexity of design and production problems. Whether or not the firm entered into a joint venture with another architectural or other type of firm during 1973 was another aspect. Consultant use is the average use over 15 types of consultants, computed as the sum over 15 types divided by 15.

The number of full-time equivalent staff. Because data were collected over a three-month period, possible effects of seasonal and economic fluctuations were eliminated by asking for information on size as of April 1, 1974.
A dummy variable indicating whether or not the staff had access to a computer.
A dummy variable indicating whether or not the firm had written personnel rules and regulations.
A dummy variable indicating that advertising was used to hire new architects, included in the analysis as an index of impersonal recruitment.

Clerical personnel as a percentage of all administrative staff, computed from census occupational counts for each industry and census year. The authors state that this structural ratio measures the level of bureaucratization and is given for selected Canadian and American industrial sectors. The formula as printed in the text is garbled in the source and cannot be reliably reproduced.

Professional personnel as a percentage of the authority structure, computed from census occupational counts for each industry and census year. The authors state that this structural ratio measures the development of staff or professional structures. The formula as printed in the text is garbled in the source and cannot be reliably reproduced.

Dummy variables identifying the era in which an industry was established: PREF equals 1 if the industry is prefactory and 0 otherwise; EARN equals 1 if the industry dates from the early nineteenth century and 0 otherwise; RAIL equals 1 if the industry is of railroad age and 0 otherwise. The modern age is treated as the base case.

Dummy variables for the census period of the observation: SIX equals 1 if the observation is 1961 U.S. or 1960 Canada data and 0 otherwise; SEV equals 1 if the observation is 1971 U.S. or 1970 Canada data and 0 otherwise. The 1950 and 1951 census years are treated as the base years.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the industry was in Canada and Canadian-controlled and 0 otherwise, in which case the comparison observation is the same industry in the United States. An interaction term of Canadian control with the later census year was also included.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the industry was in Canada and foreign-controlled and 0 otherwise, in which case the comparison observation is the same industry in the United States. An interaction term of foreign control with the later census year was also included.

variable_name: Clerical as % Administrative and Professional as % Authority
description: Structure was measured with two census-based ratios by industry and census year: clerical personnel as a percentage of all administrative staff (bureaucratization) and professional personnel as a percentage of the authority structure (development of professional staff).

Change in enrollment, measured as average daily attendance computed over the full academic year. AE is the difference between enrollments in the 1971-1972 school year and the 1970-1971 school year; the change terms span one year rather than the full two-year period because hiring decisions for a school year are made in the preceding spring. Enrollment data come from yearly reports prepared by the Bureau of School Apportionments and Reports.
Changes between 1971 and 1972 in revenues from federal sources, measured in tens of thousands of dollars. The model also includes the lagged level of federal revenues (FED).

Changes between 1971 and 1972 in revenues from the state, measured in tens of thousands of dollars. Much state funding is in the form of block grants, which augment local revenues. The model also includes the lagged level of state revenues (STA).
Changes between 1971 and 1972 in revenues from local sources, mainly property taxes, measured in tens of thousands of dollars. The model also includes the lagged level of local revenues (LOC).
The supportive component, defined as PROF + A + NPS. Personnel components were defined in terms of full-time equivalents and measured in the second year of the academic cycle.
T = number of classroom teachers, including substitutes; the direct component in this analysis. The personnel components were defined in terms of full-time equivalents.

PROF = the professional staff; certified employees who perform nonteaching services for pupils in direct contact with them. Examples given are guidance counselors, librarians and school nurses. Measured in full-time equivalents.

A = administrators narrowly defined; certificated employees who do not provide a service directly to pupils. Examples given are principals, superintendents and financial officers. Measured in full-time equivalents.

NPS = nonprofessional staff; employees whose jobs do not require educational certification. Examples given are janitors, cafeteria workers excluding dieticians, clerks and secretaries. Measured in full-time equivalents.

A binary variable: growing districts are those that increased, and declining districts those that decreased, in enrollment between 1971 and 1972 and between 1972 and 1973. The variable was used to split the sample into growing and declining subsamples.

Recent experience of the district in tax elections, measured as a nominal scale. It was scored as a 'fail' when the district attempted to raise the tax rate in 1970, or 1971, or 1972 or in all of them, and failed. It was scored as a 'pass' if it succeeded in any single instance, even if it failed in the others. It was scored as a 'no election' district if it never called an election in one of these years. TAX is therefore a composite of the district's experience over three years, pooled because in any given year only about one-fourth of the districts have an election.
scale: nominal, three categories (fail, pass, no election)

variable_name: teachers, professional staff, administrators, nonprofessional staff and supportive component
description: Personnel components were measured in full-time equivalents for each school district: classroom teachers (T, direct component), professional staff (PROF), administrators (A), nonprofessional staff (NPS) and the supportive component (SUP = PROF + A + NPS), following Freeman and Hannan (1975).

An index developed by Gibbs and Posten reflecting the division of labor in terms of how evenly employees are distributed among the occupations in a work organization; the formula is not readable in the text. Forty-two departments staffed by at least one person in at least one newspaper in the sample were used. The score reflects the actual distribution of personnel compared to a perfectly uniform distribution; the more the actual distribution approximates uniformity, the higher the index, up to a maximum of 1.00.

The number of departments staffed in a newspaper, used as a second measure of differentiation reflecting the functional distinctiveness among departments. It is not related empirically to the staff distribution index, the correlation for all 72 newspapers being .175.

A multiple-item measure obtained from a factor analysis of indicators of dominance; the highest loading items refer to the number of agencies or activities in a city that are nationally organized or have national implications. The standardized factor scores obtained were used as indices in the analysis.

A multiple-item measure obtained from the same factor analysis of dominance indicators; the highest loading items refer to locally organized activities such as retail trade. The standardized factor scores obtained were used as indices in the analysis.

A multiple-item indicator derived from the factor analysis reported in Table 1, built from per capita ratios of leisure services. High-scoring centers had large, diverse leisure economies with both personal entertainment facilities (restaurants and nightclubs) and mass entertainment facilities (motion picture theaters). The standardized factor scores obtained were used as indices in the analysis.

An aggregate socioeconomic index developed by Shevsky and Bell, computed as the arithmetic mean of two ratios: the number of professional, managerial, and similar workers per 10,000 employed people in a metropolitan area and the number of people over 25 years old who had completed 12 or more years of school per 1,000 people in that age category. Higher index scores mean a proportionately larger middle class population; the index was converted to z-scores.

A multiple-item measure built from approximately seven potential indicators selected for the concept and factor analyzed using orthogonal, varimax rotation. Indicators were converted to per capita ratios before factor analysis, except when the conversion was not applicable. The standardized factor scores obtained were used as indices in the analysis.

A multiple-item measure built from approximately seven potential indicators selected for the concept and factor analyzed using orthogonal, varimax rotation. Indicators were converted to per capita ratios before factor analysis, except when the conversion was not applicable. The standardized factor scores obtained were used as indices in the analysis.

A two-firm concentration ratio computed for each metropolis: the proportion of total newspaper circulation, morning and evening, accounted for by the two largest newspapers (including suburban papers) in a metropolitan community. When morning and evening papers had different names but were jointly owned, their combined circulation was treated as one firm. A two-firm ratio was selected after inspecting the circulation data. It is used as the criterion of environmental competitiveness, so higher values mean less competition.

The measure employed to capture the proportional discretionary allocation of resources is the previous total legislative funds budget; if administrators decide to allocate discretionary funds in a "fair share" way, one method would be to grant increases of a fixed proportion to all subunits in proportion to the previous total budget. The variable is the subunit's total legislative funds budget in the previous year.

Relative workload was measured as student credit hours weighted by level of instruction per full-time equivalent faculty; weights employed were those used by the university administration in workload calculations. The workload measure was lagged one year on the grounds that these measures, not workload in the current year, were the measures available at the time of budget determination.

Change in total workload during the previous year (t-2 to t-1), also weighted to reflect the level of instruction, captures change in total performance or contribution of the subunit. The measure was lagged in the same manner as relative workload to reflect data available to administrators at the time of budget formulation.

Relative power within the political structure is inferred from a measure of participation in the University Senate, the primary instrument of faculty governance at the University of Minnesota. The relative power of academic subunits was measured in terms of the proportion of membership positions on standing Senate committees held by members of the subunit; this measure was lagged in analyses to reflect power at the time of budget decisions.

Power based upon relationships with important interests external to the university was analyzed with two different measures, one of which indicates whether or not an independent advisory board external to the university was associated with a subunit. Affiliation with an advisory board indicates a base of influence external to the university, which can exert pressure upon the university administration favorable to the subunit; the measure was lagged.

The second external measure is the amount of matching funds granted a subunit from an external source; only matching funds, not grants and contracts, were considered, since matching funds require a commitment of resources within the university as a condition for receipt of the external funds. Matching funds were not lagged, since, presumably, they affect university allocations during the year of the grant.

Total budget increment of legislative funds to a subunit minus systemwide increments, that is, the portion of the annual subunit budget increment beyond the increment specified in systemwide decision guidelines, which is controllable by the administration or the subunits. Only this measure is utilized in the study to test for the presence of coalitional behavior in budget decision making.

variable_name: Periods of relatively abundant and relatively scarce resources
description: The years 1964-1975 are classified into periods of relatively abundant and relatively scarce resources based upon legislative treatment of university requests; appropriations for 1971-1974 severely curtailed previous patterns of university growth and appropriations for 1975 followed more closely the pattern prior to 1971. Separate analyses were conducted within the two periods to investigate the impact of the availability of resources upon decision processes.

variable_name: period of relative stringency versus period of relative plenty
description: The study compared four academic years, the first two (1964 and 1966) representing a period of relative plenty in the university and the second two (1971 and 1973) a period of relative stringency. Responsiveness between 1971 and 1973 was compared with responsiveness between 1964 and 1966, so that the period stands for the severity of the financial environment.

For each department and each of eight curriculum variables, raw values were tabulated for each year in a 30 x 8 x 4 array and change between the second and first year of each period was computed; the change was expressed as relative change ranging from +1 to -1 by dividing the algebraic difference between the second and first years by their sum. The change in the 1960s was subtracted from the change in the 1970s to form a difference score that could vary from +2 to -2, and only the sign of this difference was retained: 1 if the department was more responsive between 1971 and 1973 than between 1964 and 1966, 0 if less responsive, and 1/2 if there was no difference. A department's row total across the eight variables is its responsiveness score.
scale: per-variable sign codes 0, 1/2, 1; departmental score 0 to 8
level: department-year (aggregated to department and to variable)
time_window: change within 1964-1966 and within 1971-1973, compared across the two periods

description: Departments were ranked using two standard rankings, Carter (1966) and Roose and Andersen (1970). Eighteen departments were ranked on one or both rankings and 16 on both; departments were ordered on the basis of the mean of their reputational rankings, with ties resolved by weighting the more recent (1970) ranking slightly more than the earlier one.

Each professional's communication activity was separated into mutually exclusive communication domains and this study arbitrarily defined internal stars as those individuals in the top fifth of the intradepartment communication distribution. Because one department was substantially larger than the other six, it was excluded from these analyses; fifty stars were located by these methods.

Amount of work-related oral communication that each professional reported with professional areas outside the organization, namely universities and professional societies, reported for one selected day per week over 15 weeks. The tables report the median absolute amount of such communication over the 15-week period for stars and nonstars.

Amount of work-related oral communication that each professional reported with operational areas outside the organization, namely suppliers, vendors, and customers, reported for one selected day per week over 15 weeks. The tables report the median absolute amount of such communication over the 15-week period for stars and nonstars.

Amount of work-related oral communication that each professional reported with areas in the larger organization (outside the laboratory), reported for one selected day per week over 15 weeks. The tables report the median absolute amount of such communication over the 15-week period for stars and nonstars.

Amount of work-related oral communication that each professional reported with other areas of the laboratory, that is, outside his or her own department, reported for one selected day per week over 15 weeks. The tables report the median absolute amount of such communication over the 15-week period for stars and nonstars.

variable_name: number of boundary roles per project
description: Boundary roles were isolated by taking those internal communication stars which were also connected strongly to an external information domain, that is, in the top fifth of the external communication distribution. The mean number of such roles per project is reported for different task areas, environmental conditions, and amounts of task interdependence, with standard deviations in parentheses.

Respondents answered two questions about their work: in which of four categories (basic research, applied research, development, technical services) they would place the objectives of their work, and roughly what percentage of the work required to accomplish the task's objectives falls in each of the four categories. Individual responses to the two questions correlated highly (Spearman-Brown reliability = .91), so individual task scores were the average of the two questions, and project scores were calculated by pooling individual scores. Project task scores fell into three distinct areas: research, development, and technical service.

Each respondent answered how rapidly he or she saw the demands of the job changing, that is, the extent to which techniques, skills, or information needed for the project were changing. Fifty-eight projects provided usable responses and project scores were calculated by pooling individual scores.
scale: 5-point scale from 1 'to a very little extent' to 5 'to a very great extent'

description: Respondents indicated on scales the degree to which their work was interrelated with the work of technical personnel in other departments and with the work of technical personnel in the organization but outside of the laboratory. Fifty-eight projects provided usable responses and project scores were calculated by pooling individual scores; interdependence is the sum of laboratory and organizational interdependence.
scale: 10-point scales, 1 = very low interrelationship, 5 = moderate, 10 = very high interrelationship

description: All group managers (N=7) and both laboratory directors (N=2) were interviewed individually and each was asked to evaluate the overall technical performance of all projects with which he was technically familiar. An average of 4.7 managers independently rated each project on a seven-point scale, and the individual ratings were averaged to yield overall project scores.

Respondents reported how frequent contact is between their organization and the other organization, on a seven-point scale from almost never (1) to daily (7). The dependent variable is the average of the responses of the community organization and the employment service in each relationship, which reduces the perceptual bias of either respondent. For the chi-square analysis the scores on this dimension were divided at the median.

Respondents reported the extent to which their organization benefits in attaining its goals as a result of its interaction with the other organization, on a seven-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = very great extent). The scores of the community organization and of the employment service were used to classify each relationship as high or low on benefits by a median split.

The community organization and employment service scores on benefits from interaction were classified according to whether each organization reported high or low benefits, producing the four conditions shown in the Figure. Cell A is mutual high benefits, Cell B is the asymmetrical condition where the community group benefits but the employment service does not, Cell C is the reverse condition, and Cell D is no or low interdependence. Cells B and C are the asymmetrical relationships used in the tests of Hypothesis 4.

Respondents reported the extent to which the goals of the other organization, as they understand them, are compatible with the goals of their own organization, on a seven-point scale from not compatible (1) to extremely compatible (7). Each side of the relationship reported its own perception of goal compatibility.

Respondents reported how much influence the other organization has on the decisions reached when representatives of the two organizations meet to discuss issues of mutual concern, on a seven-point scale from none (1) to very much (7).
Respondents reported how important the other organization is for the operations of their own organization, on a seven-point scale from not important (1) to extremely important (7).
Respondents reported the extent to which they see their organization's relationship with the other organization as a form of bargaining, on a seven-point scale from not at all (1) to very much (7).

Respondents reported the extent to which the other organization has attempted to interfere with the attainment of the goals of their own organization in areas of overlapping interest, on a seven-point scale from never (1) to frequently (7).
Respondents reported the extent to which tension exists between their organization and the other organization, on a seven-point scale from none (1) to a great deal (7).

Respondents reported the extent to which there are agreements between their organization and the other organization, coded as no agreement (1), informal agreement (2), or formal agreement (3). The authors report that formalization does not discriminate between the cooperative and conflictual dimensions and is not included in the remainder of the analysis.

Respondents reported how the terms of their organization's interaction with the other organization are set: completely by them (1), mostly by them (2), mutually (3), mostly by us (4), completely by us (5). The authors report that reciprocity does not discriminate between the cooperative and conflictual dimensions and is not included in the remainder of the analysis.

Composite of six measures: participation in work decisions, formalization (reverse scored), hierarchy of authority (reverse scored), impersonality (reverse scored), division of labor, and participation in strategic decisions. Five of the measures are taken from Duncan (1971); the sixth is a questionnaire item on the extent of the subject's participation in strategic decisions. The mean score across the relevant questions of the structure instrument was used as the score for each measure, and because the factor loadings were all high, all six measures were included; the unweighted mean scores on each measure were then averaged to obtain an organicness score for each individual's work unit, and the average of these organicness scores for all individuals in a unit was used as the organicness score for that unit. These unit organicness scores ranged from 38 to 72 on a 0 to 100 scale, with a mean of 58 and a median of 57.

Measured by seven questionnaire items of the form, "How often do you know what to expect in your dealings with other people or organizations?" Responses were collected on a 0 to 100 scale anchored at five points: never, seldom, sometimes, often, and always. A factor analysis indicated that each question loaded on the first factor with a loading of from .37 to .75, and all seven questions were used as measures of the composite variable; the seven unweighted scores were added together and their mean value used as the PEU score for each individual. These PEU scores ranged from 34 to 93, with a mean of 42 and a median of 41 on a 0 to 100 scale.
scale: 0 to 100 (anchored at never, seldom, sometimes, often, always)

description: Composite variable created from eight questionnaire questions about hours of formal meetings, hours of informal face-to-face or telephone conversations, and times of formal and informal written communications, each asked separately for contacts outside the work group but within the larger organization and for contacts outside the organization altogether. A factor analysis indicated that each of the eight questions loaded on the first factor with a loading of from .44 to .83, so the eight unweighted scores were added together and their sum used as the boundary-spanning activity score for each individual. These values ranged from 0 to 242, with a median score of 26 and an average score of 46.

A ward-level index built by applying nurse-panel task predictability scores for each of 71 surgical operations to the ward's distribution of patients across those operations and dividing by the total number of patients in each ward. Every eighth day over a four-month period each surgical patient was classified into one of 71 operations or one of four residual categories. Scores for the operations ranged from a low of .26 for open heart surgery for valvular or vascular disease with cardiopulmonary bypass to a high of 7.72 for proctoscopy and sigmoidoscopy without biopsy.

Derived from the head nurse's identification of the type of care predominating on each ward, one of eight types, rank ordered by the authors' estimate of the variety, timing, and ordering of care tasks on each type of ward. A score of 1 was assigned to intensive care wards as experiencing the least predictable level of workflow and a score of 8 to mental health wards as the most predictable.
The total number of fulltime equivalent staff members employed on each ward.
The proportion of the ward's total staff, excluding clerical personnel, who were registered nurses. These data were obtained during interviews with the head nurses.

An index of current professional activity of the ward's nurses combining three indicators: staff nurse (including practical nurses) membership in professional associations; number of professional courses taken during the past year for which certification was received or which significantly enhanced professional knowledge, exclusive of in-service training; and number of articles in professional journals read per month. Responses were averaged across nurses in each ward and, since the indices were not highly correlated, converted to standard scores and combined into a single index. For the courses indicator only, attention was restricted to day-shift nurses.
time_window: past year for courses taken; per month for articles read

description: An index of differentiation developed by Gibbs and Martin: D = 1 - [ΣX²/(ΣX)²], where X is the number of staff members in each job title present on the ward and the summations are taken across all job titles. The larger the number of positions and the more even the distribution of persons among them, the higher the score. Job categories and numbers of staff in each position came from an organization chart constructed during the interview with each head nurse.

Based on the first three decision items: hiring a replacement staff nurse for the ward, adding a new staff nurse position to the ward staff, and determining the appropriate disciplinary action for a staff nurse who has committed a serious medication error. Influence of staff nurses and of the head nurse on each decision was rated on a five-point scale; staff nurse ratings on a ward were averaged and combined with the head nurse's ratings with a weight of four to the staff nurse ratings and one to the head nurse. Differences in influence scores for head nurse and staff nurses were converted to standard scores and summed.

Based on the fourth decision item, changing the nursing care system on the ward, for example, to adopt team nursing, and left to stand alone as an indicator of the centralization of policy decisions. Centralization was calculated by subtracting the influence score for the staff nurses from the influence score for the head nurse, using the same weighting of head nurse and staff nurse ratings.

A single measure formed by combining eight items on how explicit procedures were, asked of staff nurses by questionnaire and of each head nurse by interview. Head nurse responses were weighted one to four relative to staff nurse responses, and all eight items were then combined.

variable_name: proportion of industry i's total joint venture activity that was with industry j (vij)
description: A 21 x 21 industry matrix (441 cells) was created with the industries each partner could come from listed vertically and horizontally. Each joint venture except those between firms in the same industry entered the matrix twice, once above and once below the diagonal. The number of joint ventures in each cell was transformed into proportions by dividing by the row totals, giving the proportion of industry i's total joint venture activity that was with industry j.

The proportion of industry i's purchases within the set of 21 industries made from industry j. Computed on a proportional basis consistent with the method used for computing the dependent variable, from input-output tables showing resource flows among sectors of the American economy.

The proportion of industry i's sales made to industry j. Computed on a proportional basis consistent with the method used for computing the dependent variable, from input-output tables showing resource flows among sectors of the American economy.

The proportion of industry i's total transactions made with industry j, including both sales and purchases. Computed on a proportional basis consistent with the method used for computing the dependent variable, from input-output tables showing resource flows among sectors of the American economy.
Data on industry concentration were obtained from Weiss (1963), whose measures are adjusted for geographic market areas and for aggregation effects.

variable_name: proportion of total employment engaged in research and development (scij)
description: The measure of the technological intensity of the industry was the proportion of scientists and engineers in research and development to total industry employment in 1969. The number of scientists and engineers was obtained from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (1969) and total industry employment from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Handbook of Labor Statistics (1972).

variable_name: proportion of labor input and capital intensity of the industry
description: Data on the proportion of labor input and the capital intensity of the industry were obtained from the Internal Revenue Service Statistics of Income, Corporation Tax Returns for the years 1963 to 1967. A five-year average was taken to provide reliable estimates for the variables.

variable_name: proportion of industry i's joint subsidiaries that were in industry j
description: Only joint subsidiaries in manufacturing or oil and gas extraction were considered, yielding 145 joint subsidiaries in manufacturing, each with two or more parents. Each joint subsidiary leads to two data points in a matrix of industry of parent by industry of joint subsidiary, one for each partner. Numbers were transformed into proportions by dividing by the row totals.

The proportion of industry i's purchases from industry j, computed on a proportional basis consistent with the method used for computing the dependent variable, from input-output tables of resource flows among sectors of the American economy. Used in the individual-industry correlations of parent-progeny patterns.

The proportion of industry i's sales to industry j, computed on a proportional basis consistent with the method used for computing the dependent variable, from input-output tables of resource flows. Used in the individual-industry correlations of parent-progeny patterns.

The proportion of industry i's total transactions with industry j, including both sales and purchases. Used as the transactions variable in the regression of the proportion of parents from one industry with joint subsidiaries in another industry, and in the individual-industry correlations.

Industry concentration obtained from Weiss (1963), whose measures are adjusted for geographic market areas and for aggregation effects. Used in the parent-progeny analysis, where it was less important than transactions interdependence.

variable_name: proportion of total employment engaged in research and development (scij)
description: The proportion of scientists and engineers in research and development to total industry employment in 1969; its coefficient in the parent-progeny regression is statistically significant at less than the .01 level.

The number of members in the local administrative bureaucracy. The size of these administrative bureaucracies varied from 44 to 1,530 members, with a mean of 245.7 and a standard deviation of 271.4, indicating considerable skewness, so the variable was transformed into its natural logarithm prior to statistical analysis.

The number of departments in the organization; a department was defined as any unit having at least two persons and two levels, the head of which reported to the mayor, administrator or an alderman. The organizations varied from 3 to 12 departments, with a mean of 7.16 and a standard deviation of 2.22. In the analysis the residual of this measure after the effect of organizational size had been removed was used.
