The number of levels in each department counted from the department head to the lowest level worker, averaged for all departments. Organizational scores ranged from 2.50 to 6.0, with a mean of 3.64 and a standard deviation of .87. In the analysis the residual of this measure after the effect of organizational size had been removed was used.

The measure of role specialization developed by Pugh, Hickson, and their associates (1969), reflecting the number of specialized roles across 16 functional areas. Organizational scores varied between 0 and 21, with a mean of 9.1 and a standard deviation of 5.1. In the analysis the residual of this measure after the effect of organizational size had been removed was used.

variable_name: Average span of control of middle echelon
description: The number of subordinates who reported directly to each department head was determined, and the mean for all departments was taken for each organization. The mean for the 44 organizations was 4.32, with a standard deviation of 1.33 and a range from 2.20 to 7.27. Because span of control correlated very poorly with size, the residual was not computed for this measure.

An index of the degree of routinization of work processes based on six questionnaire items, including 'People here do the same job in the same way every day' (reversed) and 'The same steps must be followed in processing every piece of work' (reversed). Responses were coded (1) 'definitely true', (2) 'more true than false', (3) 'more false than true', (4) 'definitely false' unless otherwise indicated, and the items were equally weighed in constructing level-specific measures. Separate scores were computed for the middle and lower echelons; Cronbach's alpha was .70 for middle-echelon and .73 for lower-echelon routinization.
level: organization (separate scores for middle and lower echelons)

description: An index reflecting the degree of autonomy of action which the individual actor has in his particular work activity, and hence the degree to which action is constrained, based on four questionnaire items: 'People here are allowed to do almost as they please' (reversed), 'How things are done here are left pretty much up to the person doing the work' (reversed), 'A person can make his own decisions without consulting anyone else' (reversed), and 'Most people here make up their own rules' (reversed). Items were equally weighed in constructing level-specific measures, with separate scores for middle and lower echelons; Cronbach's alpha was .66 for the middle echelon and .65 for the lower echelon. Higher scores indicate greater autonomy, that is, less formalized work processes.
level: organization (separate scores for middle and lower echelons)

description: An index of the degree to which organizational actors followed specific rules and regulations, based on six questionnaire items including 'I always stick to the letter of the rules' (reversed), 'We have procedures here for every situation' (reversed), and 'I always have to follow strict operating procedures at all times' (reversed). Items were equally weighed in constructing level-specific measures, with separate scores for middle and lower echelons; Cronbach's alpha was .87 for middle-echelon and .81 for lower-echelon rule observance.
level: organization (separate scores for middle and lower echelons)

description: Respondents were asked to report the number of contacts, either in face-to-face meetings or by telephone, with persons at a higher level in the organization in a typical week. Separate means were computed for the middle and lower echelons.
level: organization (separate scores for middle and lower echelons)

description: Respondents were asked to report the number of contacts, either in face-to-face meetings or by telephone, with persons at the same level in the organization in a typical week. Separate means were computed for the middle and lower echelons.
level: organization (separate scores for middle and lower echelons)

description: Respondents were asked to report the number of contacts, either in face-to-face meetings or by telephone, with persons at a lower level in the organization in a typical week. Separate means were computed for the middle and lower echelons; of the three communication directions downward communication had the greater volume and the consistently strong relationship with influence.
level: organization (separate scores for middle and lower echelons)

description: An index constructed from respondents' answers to whether they had (1) 'no', (2) 'little', (3) 'some', (4) 'quite a lot of' influence on 18 strategic decisions. All items were weighed equally and an average was computed for each person; then in each organization an average score was computed for all persons at the middle echelon (department heads) and another average score for all lower-echelon persons. Cronbach's alpha was .95 for lower-echelon and .95 for middle-echelon influence in strategic decisions.
level: organization (aggregated from individual respondents, separately for middle and lower echelons)

description: An index constructed from respondents' answers to whether they had (1) 'no', (2) 'little', (3) 'some', (4) 'quite a lot of' influence on five work decisions concerning work using the same response categories. All items were weighed equally and an average was computed for each person; then in each organization an average score was computed for all persons at the middle echelon (department heads) and another average score for all lower-echelon persons. Cronbach's alpha was .87 for lower-echelon and .90 for middle-echelon influence in work decisions.
level: organization (aggregated from individual respondents, separately for middle and lower echelons)

variable_name: width, average number of levels and role specialization
description: Structural complexity was measured by three variables: horizontal differentiation as the number of departments reporting to the mayor, administrator or an alderman; vertical differentiation as the average number of levels; and role specialization using the Pugh, Hickson and associates measure of specialized roles across 16 functional areas.

Individuals named the five people with whom they worked most closely; to determine isolation from official control these five work contact names were examined to determine how many were in positions of authority. The less contact reported, the more pronounced the isolation. For cross-tabulation purposes the data were condensed into three categories separately for each organization, so that high isolation meant no overlapping contacts were reported and low isolation meant four or five overlapping contacts were reported.

The five named work contacts were examined to determine how many also appeared in response to a sociometric question asking who, in the respondent's opinion, exercised most actual control in the organization. The less overlap, the more isolation on this dimension; for cross-tabulation the data were condensed into three categories within each organization.

The five persons listed as close friends were compared with the five work contacts to determine isolation from friends. An individual could score from 0 (none of his work contacts involved people who were also friends) to 5 (all five work contacts involved people also named as friends). For cross-tabulation the data were condensed into three categories within each organization.

The five persons listed as those whose professional judgement is most respected were compared with the five work contacts to determine isolation from respected coworkers. For cross-tabulation the data were condensed into three categories within each organization.

A composite score combining the scores on the four isolation measures, measuring the amount of working contact members had, overall, with their own selection of friends, respected coworkers, actual control nominees, and official administrative authority figures. The most isolated person was one who had no contact with any of the four categories of personnel; the least isolated was the one who reported some working contact with members of all four categories.

A second composite isolation score based on the total number of times members were listed by others as persons with actual control, as friends, as persons whose professional judgement is respected, or as work contacts who are useful sources of information; the emphasis is on the number of choices received from others. The most isolated member (least interpersonal attractiveness) received no choices on any of the four criteria; the least isolated (most interpersonal attractiveness) was not passed over by others on any of the four dimensions. A high score means high attractiveness and therefore low isolation, so its correlations are generally opposite in sign to those of overall isolation.
Number of years of formal education, used as one measure of expertise.
A measure of expertise based on reports of specialized training for an occupation over and above ordinary formal education.

Based on official title, position and duties, specifically exercising supervisory authority over the work of others. Other measures of status used to test Hypothesis 2 were professional standing, formal education, specialized professional training and sex.
Measured by a combination of occupation, training and job duties in the organization; the four categories used corresponded basically to clerical, service, technical, and professional.
Sex was measured ordinally (with male high) to reflect differences in freedom and privileges.

The five organizations were classified into three types: two highly professionalized social and survey research organizations (one semiautonomous survey research unit attached to a private university and one autonomous survey organization); two semiprofessional public-service organizations (a public school system in a small town and an alcoholism rehabilitation program); and one commercial research unit of a large national food-processing and marketing organization.

Index of forces favorable to unfreezing, calculated for each project from the final questionnaire items. After scale improvement the U+ category contained eight items, retained because of their correlations with their category index. Each item was rated on a five-point scale.
scale: five-point scale from (1) "the statement accurately depicts what occurred" to (5) "the statement accurately depicts the opposite of what occurred"

description: Index of forces unfavorable to unfreezing (resistance to unfreezing), calculated for each project from the final questionnaire items. After scale improvement the U- category contained eight items, retained because of their correlations with their category index. Each item was rated on a five-point scale.
scale: five-point scale from (1) "the statement accurately depicts what occurred" to (5) "the statement accurately depicts the opposite of what occurred"

description: Index of forces favorable to moving, calculated for each project from the final questionnaire items. After scale improvement the M+ category contained six items, retained because of their correlations with their category index. Each item was rated on a five-point scale.
scale: five-point scale from (1) "the statement accurately depicts what occurred" to (5) "the statement accurately depicts the opposite of what occurred"

description: Index of forces unfavorable to moving (resistance to moving), calculated for each project from the final questionnaire items. After scale improvement the M- category contained six items, retained because of their correlations with their category index. Each item was rated on a five-point scale.
scale: five-point scale from (1) "the statement accurately depicts what occurred" to (5) "the statement accurately depicts the opposite of what occurred"

description: Index of forces favorable to refreezing, calculated for each project from the final questionnaire items. After scale improvement the R+ category contained eight items, retained because of their correlations with their category index. Each item was rated on a five-point scale.
scale: five-point scale from (1) "the statement accurately depicts what occurred" to (5) "the statement accurately depicts the opposite of what occurred"

description: Index of forces unfavorable to refreezing (resistance to refreezing), calculated for each project from the final questionnaire items. After scale improvement the R- category contained eight items, retained because of their correlations with their category index. Each item was rated on a five-point scale.
scale: five-point scale from (1) "the statement accurately depicts what occurred" to (5) "the statement accurately depicts the opposite of what occurred"

description: Index of level of success calculated for each project from items derived from the content units relevant to measuring the success of a project. A five-point, behaviorally based scale was used for four items on level of success, each rating point giving a measure and/or a description of sample behavior.

Managers were asked: "How often do you see each of the people who reports directly to you?" with response 7 = "They are almost never out of my sight," and 1 = "I see each person less than once a week." The item was administered only to the 329 managers.

Everyone, managers and "others," was asked: "How often does your immediate supervisor check to see what you are doing on the job?" with response 8 = "Can see me almost all the time," and 1 = "Checks once a week or less."

Managers were asked: "When you are evaluating the people who report directly to you for raises or promotions, how much weight do you give to their output records?" with response 7 = "Decision based entirely on output records" and 1 = "Output records are not considered at all in the decision." The item was administered only to the 329 managers.

Everyone was asked whether records are kept for each employee showing his or her output, such as sales volume, selling cost, number of parcels handled, and, if yes, "When you are being evaluated for a raise or promotion, how much weight does your supervisor give to the records of your output?" with response 7 = "Decision is based entirely on output records," and 1 = "Output records are not considered at all in the decision."

Managers were asked: "How much can you tell by watching the people who report directly to you while they are working?" with response 4 = "I can tell exactly whether they are doing their jobs properly or not," and 1 = "I can't tell anything about how well they are doing their job by watching them."

Everyone was asked: "Regardless of whether or not your supervisor checks often, how familiar is your supervisor with your on-the-job performance?" with response 5 = "Very familiar," and 1 = "Not familiar at all."
Respondents were asked: "To what extent does your performance depend upon how well others do their job?" with response 5 = "A very great deal," and 1 = "Almost none."
Respondents were asked: "What percentage of your time on the job do you spend carrying out routine tasks?"

Respondents were asked: "How long do you think it would take an inexperienced person to learn the basics necessary to handling your job?" with response 1 = "1 month or less," and 5 = "More than one year."

All respondents were placed in one of seven levels through a comparison of job title with organization charts. Levels 1-5 were within the stores; levels 6 and 7 were within the corporations that owned the stores and were excluded from the study.

A dummy variable representing membership in either Company A (approximately 2,000 employees) or Company B (approximately 8,000 employees). There were 785 respondents from two stores owned by Company A and 1,613 respondents from three stores owned by Company B.

The orientation measure was based on the proportion of total income derived from production activities. Organizations with half or more of their income from production activities were classified as production-oriented; those with less than half of their income from this source were classified as rehabilitation-oriented.

Organizations were divided into an earlier and a later period of founding. The dividing line for the earlier and later period of workshops was 1946, so that workshops founded before and during World War II were distinguished from those founded after World War II.

Workshops were distinguished by whether they had any income from grants, that is, none versus some. Of the workshops with a rehabilitation orientation, 15 had no income from grants and 49 had some; of those with a production orientation, 39 had no income from grants and 20 had some. Grants received by all of the organizations in the sample accounted for only 5.4 percent of total income.
scale: dichotomous (none vs some income from grants)

description: Each city official was asked to rate the importance he or she felt should be given to each of 14 goals on a seven-point scale. The individual respondent ratings of the 14 goals were normalized to a mean of zero and a variance of unity, the standard deviation of these normalized scores was computed for each goal across all respondents within a city, and these standard deviations were summed across the 14 goals as an overall measure of goal incompatibility. Cronbach's alpha coefficient for the index was .36. The 25 goals initially assembled were reduced to 14 after a pretest.

Each city official was asked to rate on a seven-point scale the amount of authority that each of five different decision-making units had in making decisions on five sets of issues in collective bargaining, that is, 25 ratings per official. The individual ratings for each decision-making unit on each issue were averaged across respondents within a city, the variance was calculated for each issue, and these five variances were summed as the measure of dispersion of power. The larger the sum, the less dispersed the power among the units. Cronbach's alpha obtained by aggregating across the five issues was .36.

City officials were asked to rate on a seven-point scale the extent to which the policies they advocated in bargaining were controlled by each of the five decision-making units. A variance in city scores was computed; the higher the variance, the less dispersed the control among the decision-making units.

The authority ratings that each respondent assigned to the various decision-making units on the five issues were first converted to ranks and then the Kendall coefficient of concordance was computed for each issue across respondents. An overall measure of jurisdictional ambiguity for a city was computed by summing the five coefficients; the lower the sum, the more jurisdictional ambiguity. Cronbach's alpha for this index was .79.
scale: sum of five Kendall coefficients of concordance

description: City officials were asked to rate the extent to which the union relied on threats to engage in job actions, or threats to use the state dispute-resolution procedures. For each city the score for each of the two methods was obtained by summing the ratings across officials, and these two ratings were then summed to obtain an index of the amount of pressure within formal negotiations. Cronbach's alpha coefficient for this measure was .40.
scale: index (sum of two ratings summed across officials)

description: City officials were asked to rate on a seven-point scale the amount of conflict they experienced with each of the other decision-making units. The individual responses were aggregated into a city score for each item and an index was obtained by summing these scores across decision-making officials. Cronbach's alpha for conflict across decision-making units was .62.

City officials were asked to rate on a seven-point scale the amount of conflict among city decision-making units in making decisions on each of the five bargaining issues. The individual responses were aggregated into a city score for each item and an index was obtained for conflict across issues by summing these scores. Cronbach's alpha for conflict across issues was .68.

variable_name: dispersion of power, dispersion of control, jurisdictional ambiguity and pressure within negotiations
description: Ability to interfere with goal attainment was operationalized through four situational factors measured from city officials' ratings: dispersion of power, dispersion of control, jurisdictional ambiguity, and pressure within negotiations. Each was computed at the city level from the officials' responses.

Perceptions of organizational climate measured with a questionnaire developed by Douglas McGregor for use in team building, asking respondents to rate trust, support, communication, understanding of objectives, commitment to objectives, handling of conflict, utilization of resources, control methods, and organizational environment. Administered anonymously just before and immediately after the involvement of the outside consultants, in January 1970 and March 1971, to approximately 90 production foremen. Separate t-tests with one-tail tests of significance were computed for each item; the text does not report the response scale.

Perceptions of the behavior of the immediate supervisor measured with a questionnaire developed by Ed Nevis for use in OD projects and modified for this study, asking employees to describe their supervisors relative to listening, expressing ideas to others, influence style, decision making, relations with others, task orientation, handling of conflict, willingness to change, problem solving, and self development. Administered anonymously before and after the involvement of the outside consultants, in January 1970 and March 1971, to approximately 90 production foremen. Separate t-tests with one-tail tests of significance were computed for each item; the text does not report the response scale.

Data on the rate of production were collected on a daily basis and then averaged across the 41 months and the three time periods (before, during, after). The analysis is based on separate one-tail t-tests on the period data, performed separately for the day and night shifts. The variable is the average number of units produced per month.
scale: average number of units produced per month
time_window: 41 months covering the periods before, during, and after the interventions

description: The variance for the production index was computed and 95 percent confidence intervals were established for the period before intervention by shift and compared with the variance in the period after. Following the procedure outlined by Hays, the confidence intervals were used to judge whether the variances before and after could be drawn from the same population, and F-ratios were computed.
time_window: period before versus period after the interventions

description: Data regarding the level of quality were collected on a daily basis and then averaged across the 41 months and the three time periods. The variable is the average number of units produced per month which did not require repair or rework. Separate one-tail t-tests were performed on the period data for the day and night shifts.
scale: average number of units produced per month not requiring repair or rework
time_window: 41 months covering the periods before, during, and after the interventions

description: The variance for the quality index was computed and 95 percent confidence intervals were established for the period before by shift and compared with the variance in the period after, as a basis for judging whether the variances before and after were drawn from the same population; F-ratios were significant at the .07 level.
time_window: period before versus period after the interventions

description: Monthly profit or loss data for this index were averaged across the three time periods and separate one-tail t-tests were performed to determine if significant change had taken place. The variable is the average monthly profit or loss (performance to budget).
time_window: 41 months covering the periods before, during, and after the interventions

description: The OD intervention was the plant's organization development program for production supervisors and managers, a six-phase sequence (initial diagnosis, team skills training, data collection, data confrontation, action planning, team building and intergroup building) run with outside consultants from January 1970 to March 1971. Outcomes were compared before, during and after the program.

Respondents rated on anchored 7-point scales the extent to which each of five major technologies was used in the manufacturing process of their firm. The ratings were differentially weighted—custom 1, small-batch 2, large-batch 3, mass-production (assembly-line) 4, and continuous-process 5—then aggregated and divided by the sum of the weights to secure an index of how mass-output oriented the firm's technology was.
scale: index built from five 7-point ratings (1 = not applicable, 7 = almost exclusively used)

description: The president rated on a 7-point scale the extent to which the firm engaged in each of eight integration activities, from 1 = the firm does not engage in the activity at all to 7 = engages in it fully, that is, to the full extent of its requirements. The ratings for the eight items were averaged to secure the firm's index of vertical integration.

The president rated on a 7-point scale the extent to which the chief executive officer of the firm had delegated decision-making authority in each of nine strategic areas of decision making, from 1 = no delegation of authority from the top to 7 = complete delegation of authority. The ratings for the nine areas were averaged to secure an index of delegation of decision-making authority by the chief executive.

Ratings were obtained from the president on the use in his firm of each of nine controls, on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 to 7 (7 = used fully). The ratings for the nine controls were averaged to secure an index of the extent to which sophisticated controls were employed in the firm.

variable_name: firm size (natural logarithm of annual sales)
description: The size of the firm was measured by taking the natural logarithm of its annual sales. A natural logarithm was used to dampen the great variability in firm sizes.

variable_name: average profitability of firm (return on net worth)
description: The firm's long-term profitability was measured by averaging the highest rate of profit on net worth with the lowest such rate during the previous five years. Before-tax profit rates rather than after-tax profit rates were used to improve interfirm comparability.

Each department head, or a close assistant, rated the power of each of the subunits, including his own, on a 7-point scale ranging from a great deal to very little power, with a column for a don't know response. Respondents were told that power was the ability of the department to affect decisions so that they conformed more closely to what the department wanted, and the departments were listed in random order.
scale: 7-point scale ranging from a great deal to very little power

variable_name: membership on the University Research Board
description: Subunit representation on important university committees during 1958-1970 was used as an indicator of subunit power, with membership on the University Research Board treated as a separate power measure. Committee membership may be both a source of power and an outcropping indicating the relative influence of organizational subunits.
Proportional representation of the subunit on all of the important university committees included in the study during the period 1958-1970, used as the third indicator of subunit power.

variable_name: proportion of faculty supported by restricted funds / proportion of restricted funds received
description: From archival records, the proportion of total grants and contracts a particular department received, restricted funds in the budget categories, and the proportion of faculty supported by restricted funds were obtained for the 13-year period 1958-1970. In the regressions on subunit power, faculty funded by restricted funds, that is grants and contracts, was the best predictor.

variable_name: proportion of advanced graduate instructional units taught
description: From archival records the proportion of undergraduate and graduate students taught by the department was obtained for the 13-year period 1958-1970. In place of the actual number of graduate students, the proportion of advanced graduate instructional units taught was used, a variable highly correlated with the number of graduate students.

variable_name: number of undergraduate instructional units taught
description: From archival records, the proportion of undergraduate students taught by the department, used as an objective measure of the department's contribution of undergraduate instruction.

For the 17 departments in which rankings were available, data on national prestige were obtained from the studies conducted by the American Council on Education (Cartter, 1966; Roose and Andersen, 1970). Because only 17 departments in the sample represent disciplines rated by the American Council on Education, analyses including national rank use only these 17 departments.

variable_name: department head's assessment of the subunit's relative contribution of resources
description: Each department head interviewed was asked to assess the extent to which his department contributed each of seven resources compared to other departments in the university. The scale used was a 5-point rating scale ranging from 1 for much more than average to 5 for much less than average.
scale: 5-point rating scale, 1 = much more than average to 5 = much less than average

description: As part of the interviews, department heads were asked to rank seven resources in terms of how scarce they were, with the rankings proceeding from 1 for the most scarce to 7 for the least scarce. The average ranking of each resource was taken as the estimate of its relative scarcity, on the assumption that averaging individual responses yields an accurate ranking of relative scarcity.
scale: rank 1 = most scarce to 7 = least scarce

description: In the same interview, department heads were asked to rank the same seven resources in terms of their criticality, from 1 for the most critical resource to 7 for the least critical. Criticality was defined for respondents as the extent to which the resource is absolutely necessary for the effective operation of the department.
scale: rank 1 = most critical to 7 = least critical

variable_name: objective criteria indicators for the four resources
description: Indicators of objective criteria for allocating the four resources were obtained from discussions with persons involved in the allocation decisions and represent the bases they articulated as reasonable. The principal criterion for summer faculty fellowships and appointments to the Center for Advanced Study is faculty membership, indicated by the number of full-time equivalent faculty in the department, with the department's American Council on Education rating employed as the indicator of quality. For graduate fellowships and Research Board grants, the criterion is the proportion of advanced graduate instructional units taught, with national rank in 1969 as the indicator of quality.

variable_name: correlations of power measures with proportional resource allocations
description: The use of power is assessed by the simple and partial correlations between the three measures of subunit power and the proportional allocations of the four resources to departments, and by multiple regressions of the average proportional allocation of each resource on power and the objective criteria. Allocated resources were defined proportionally, so departmental allocations are represented as proportions allocated to each of the 29 departments in a given year; partial correlations control first for the objective bases of allocation and then additionally for the national ranking of the department.

Each of the 48 mainland states was characterized using Elazar's classification of states into three pure political culture types. Where Elazar classified a state traditionalistic, traditionalistic-individualistic, or traditionalistic-moralistic, it was categorized here as having a traditionalistic political culture.

Walker's composite innovation score was derived by calculating the time it took a state to adopt each of 88 programs as a percentage of the time it took for all states to adopt the program, summing and averaging across program areas, and subtracting the average from one so that higher scores indicated higher levels of state innovation. The states were ranked from the highest to the lowest score, with the most innovative state assigned the rank of 1 and the least innovative state the rank of 48. Median rank of the innovation score was then calculated for the states of each political culture type.

variable_name: ratio of organization budget to total state expenditures
description: Agency directors were asked in round numbers what the total budget for the planning or development organization was for the fiscal year ending in 1963. This amount was divided by the total expenditures of the state for the fiscal year ending in 1962, the nearest year for which data were obtainable. The ratio thus formed was multiplied by 10,000 for convenience and then averaged for the various types of organizations and the various political cultures.
time_window: organization budget for fiscal year ending 1963 over state expenditures for fiscal year ending 1962

variable_name: proportion of first choices of abstract activities
description: Directors checked the activities their organization undertook and ranked in order of importance the five most important activities of the organization, with the most important function ranked 1. Each activity was classified in advance as concrete, intermediate, or abstract. An indicator of the importance of each kind of activity was derived by counting the number of times an activity of that kind was ranked 1 and dividing by the number of possible first choices, which equals the number of organizations. The resulting proportion measures the importance attributed to activities of various kinds and could be averaged for each type of activity, kind of organization and political culture.

variable_name: presence of a parent board or commission
description: Directors were asked whether the planning or development agency was at present under a parent board or commission, checking the one most correct statement among no parent board or commission, yes there is a parent board or commission, or other described by the respondent. The responses permitted the derivation of a percentage for each type of organization in each of the three political cultures that could be taken as an index measuring the presence of supervisory boards.

A preliminary question in the survey required agency directors to identify their organization as a planning organization, one which gave primary emphasis to planning, or as a development organization, one which gave primary emphasis to development. Where the director indicated that equal emphasis was given to planning and development, the agency was termed a miscellaneous organization.

Quantity of job performance in the production departments, measured by averaging weekly production levels expressed as a percentage of engineering standards. A random-sample eight-week average prior to the MBO program served as the T0 measure, and the same random-sampling procedure was used at the other data points. The performance data were adjusted for leaves of absence, machine down time, and other recorded work stoppages under the control of the operating employees. The measure ranged from 29.8 percent to 147.4 percent of standard; higher figures mean greater output.

Quality of job performance in the production departments, measured alongside the quantity measure from weekly production data based on randomly selected eight-week periods. The quality measure ranged from 6.9 percent to 18.3 percent. Lower figures mean better quality or fewer defective parts found by quality control.

Primarily an indication of the number of formal union-recognized grievances filed by production operating employees in the three plants; only those grievances presented in writing to the first-line supervisors were recorded. A randomly selected sample of eight weeks was used to tabulate the grievance rate, which ranged from 32 to 104. Lower figures mean fewer grievances filed.

Measured by the proportion of hours absent to total hours worked for each time period for which data were collected, with adjustment for vacations and layoffs. The measure ranged from .24 to .68. Lower figures mean less absenteeism.

Through a projection of market-share trends, the top-level executives established a standard market-share percentage for each territory, which served as an objective or target for the salesmen; the target was given an index of 100. The indicator ranged from 68.4 percent to 137.2 percent during the 36-month study period; randomly selected eight-week periods were used in generating the data. Higher figures mean better sales performance.

Calculated by adding the salesmen's expenses for a period to their compensation and dividing this by the total sales volume generated. This figure was then expressed as a percentage against a budgeted amount allocated for selling expenses. The selling-cost measure ranged from 87.8 percent to 158.4 percent of the budgeted amount. Lower figures mean better sales performance.

Used to measure the performance of salesmen in generating orders, calculated by dividing the number of orders a salesman secured in a given period by the number of visits made. The ratio ranged from .12 to .94. Higher figures mean a better sales-to-visit ratio.

A performance indicator calculated by taking the total sales volume generated in a period and dividing it by a potential sales volume available. The index ranged from .68 to 1.74. Higher figures mean more of the potential market secured.

variable_name: variable reinforcement schedule in plant E2
description: Positive reinforcement was a variable schedule applied only in plant E2 for a six-month period between T3 and T4, delivered as letters, meetings, memos and telephone discussions to MBO participants. Plant E1 and the comparison plant had no such schedule.

variable_name: MBO program (experimental plants E1 and E2 vs comparison plant)
description: MBO was a program implemented in two experimental plants (E1 and E2), with training and full implementation at top, middle and lower management levels, while the comparison plant had no MBO program. Performance was observed at time points up to 36 months after.

variable_name: Scale and diversification of municipal government
description: A dichotomous index scoring cities above the median number of municipal employees per capita and above the median in similarity of municipal expenditure per capita across standard budget categories (thirty-seven cities) versus all other cases (ninety-three cities). The number of municipal employees per capita measured scale and the degree of similarity among rankings of 1960 per capita expenditures for education, fire protection, health, highways, police protection, sanitation, and welfare indicated diversification.

A dichotomous index distinguishing the seventy-six cities for which one or more community-wide associations were mentioned, by persons other than their functionaries, from the remaining fifty-four cities. The mentions came from essay answers by knowledgeable informants to form letters mailed early in 1961 asking about citizen participation, civic pride, cohesion, conflict, and the distribution of power.

The number of general, short-term, nonproprietary hospitals in the city in 1960. The authors state that this was the measure of need, and that while the sheer number of organizations affects the need to establish formal relationships, the national emphasis upon interorganizational relations in health services is likely to intensify the effect of numbers upon perceptions of need.

Presence in 1969 of a local association to which at least some of the hospitals belonged, according to a list provided by the American Hospital Association. Of the 130 cities, forty-six had hospital councils, thirty-four of which were established after measurement of the hypothesized independent variables and the particular control variables that proved to affect outcome, so that all forty-six councils and then the thirty-four newer ones could be predicted in separate analyses.
time_window: 1969 (councils formed after 1960; newer councils formed after mid-1961)

description: Cities were scored according to whether they had Neighborhood Youth Corps projects that were part of a complex interorganizational network (twenty-nine cities) versus all other cases (101 cities). The complex form involved sponsorship established over 1964-1966 by a federation of local organizations and two federal agencies, the U.S. Department of Labor and the U.S. Office of Economic Opportunity through local Community Action Agencies.

Categorization of each department by the ownership of its general hospital: governmentally controlled city and county hospitals (n = 47) and Veterans Administration hospitals (n = 43), and profit (n = 76) and nonprofit (n = 172) private general hospitals.

The number of beds devoted solely to inpatient psychiatric care, taken directly from the Inventory of Psychiatric Services. The authors treat bed capacity as organizational size, noting that patient census is limited only by bed capacity.

The total number of discharges from each inpatient department for the year 1969 divided by department size, providing a utilization or turnover ratio of output per bed. No re-admission data were available, so the gross discharge figure could not be adjusted for re-admissions.

All expenditures directly attributable to the inpatient psychiatric service for the year 1969, including direct salary expenses, equipment for inpatient care and other operating expenditures excluding overhead, divided by the total number of discharges from the department for the year.

All expenditures directly attributable to the inpatient psychiatric service for the year 1969 divided by the number of patient days. The authors note patient days are slightly inflated, and cost per day slightly deflated, as a function of rate of discharge.

Total staff man-hours, full time and part time, of administrative personnel worked for the inpatient psychiatric department during the week of January 11, 1970, divided by department size to give hours per unit of size.

Total staff man-hours, full time and part time, of professional staff worked for the inpatient psychiatric department during the week of January 11, 1970, divided by department size to give hours per unit of size. The Inventory listed man-hours by type of staff, denoting totals such as hours of psychiatrists, psychologists and other professionals.

Whether the psychiatric department had restrictions as to type of patient served, taken as the existence of diagnostic input restrictions by which the department restricts and homogenizes its input. Examination for the existence of diagnostic restrictions revealed no differences in their occurrence as a function of hospital ownership.

Whether an outpatient department or service existed, taken as a mixture of input and output buffers: it can act as an input buffer when the inpatient department receives patients for whom outpatient care is inappropriate, and it can smooth output when it provides follow-up service allowing earlier release.

The number of directors on the organization's board, used as the dependent variable in the board size equations and correlated with sales, debt-equity, local regulation and national regulation. The paper writes the variable as ND in the regression equation, but does not otherwise describe how the count was obtained.

The proportion of board members that are current managers in the organization or retired or former managers of the same organization, with subsidiary organizations assumed to be within the organization under consideration. The actual percentage of insiders of each company is compared with the percentage predicted by the estimated equation to form DIF.

variable_name: percentage of board members representing financial institutions
description: The percentage of the board of directors composed of representatives of financial institutions, where financial institutions include banks, investment banks, stock brokerages, and investment companies.

variable_name: percentage of attorneys on the board
description: The percentage of the board of directors composed of attorneys. The paper states that the appearance of attorneys on boards is related to the debt-to-equity ratio, to national regulation, and to the percentage of inside directors, but gives no further detail on how the percentage was computed.

The need for access to capital markets is represented by the debt to equity ratio for the organization; it was felt that firms with relatively large debt in their capital structure would face greater financing problems and would have more frequent need to refinance or adjust their capital structure.

variable_name: dummy variables for local regulation (LR) and national regulation (NR)
description: Regulation is coded with dummy variables: a dummy variable indicating whether or not the firm is locally regulated, included in the equation for the number of directors, and a dummy variable representing whether or not the organization was regulated nationally, included in the equation for the percentage of inside directors.

The size of the organization is measured by its total sales volume in millions of dollars; in terms of impact on the external environment this seemed a more meaningful figure than the related value of total assets. Data are for the year 1969.

For each company, the absolute value of the difference between the actual percentage of insiders and the percentage predicted for that company by the estimated board-composition equation. The predicted values were computed from the pooled experience of the randomly sampled companies, on the belief that the resulting relationship would more closely approximate a preferred relationship than any single datum point.

variable_name: income to sales (I/S) and income to equity (I/E) relative to industry standards
description: Two measures of company performance commonly used in evaluating organizations: the ratio of net income to sales, which tells how well the company is performing relative to its sales volume, and the ratio of net income to stockholders' equity, which tells how well it is utilizing stockholders' investment. The refined test compares these measures to measures for the organization's industry as a whole, with industry standards derived from Dun and Bradstreet's Key Business Ratios in 125 Lines wherever possible and from the Internal Revenue Service in other cases.

Index computed by multiplying the number of decision factors (F) that decision unit members identified as taken into consideration in decision making by the squared number of environmental components (C) in which those factors are located. Squaring the number of components weights the dissimilarity of factors located in different components. The factors taken into consideration in decision making were identified by an interview prior to administering the questionnaire, using the environmental components in Table 1 as a guide, so that the number of factors may vary across decision units.

The scores obtained on the two subdimensions of the static-dynamic dimension are added together to obtain the decision unit's static-dynamic index. The first subdimension is measured by asking respondents how often each of the factors they identified as important in decision making changes, on a five-point scale of (1) never, (2) almost never, (3) sometimes, (4) frequently, and (5) very often. The second subdimension is measured by asking respondents how often they consider new and different factors in decision making, on the same five-point scale; individual responses are averaged to form the unit's score.
scale: five-point scale (1) never, (2) almost never, (3) sometimes, (4) frequently, (5) very often

description: The scores of the three components of uncertainty are added to form a total uncertainty score. The first dimension, lack of information regarding the environmental factors associated with a given decision-making situation, contains six scale items; the second dimension, not knowing the outcome of a specified decision in terms of how much the organization would lose if the decision were incorrect, also contains six scale items. The third dimension is derived by weighting the respondent's certainty about the effects of a given factor by the range of the certainty estimate (1 - range of certainty estimate) and averaging over the number of factors taken into consideration. Each item is averaged over the factors taken into consideration, and individual responses are pooled to form the decision unit score.
scale: five-point response scale for the first two dimensions

description: Four of the eight experimental groups performed the pretask with all five members present, including an internal associate dean who had participated with the group; in the four other groups the associate dean was external and was presented to his group as a new appointment to the faculty after the pretask. Each associate dean was trained in either a planning-programming or a conventional budgeting method, giving a two-by-two factorial design with four cells and two groups in each cell.

Three forced-choice questionnaire items on conflict in the group: conflict with other members of the faculty (scored 1 for a great deal, 3 for sometimes, and 5 for never), whether the respondent's role forced him to take contradictory positions with regard to budgetary decisions (a binary 1, 2 scale), and the general level of conflict in the faculty group (1 for a great deal, 2 for a fair amount, 3 for almost no conflict). Mean scores were computed for groups with internal and external associate deans and compared.
scale: 1-5 on the first item; 1-2 on the second; 1-3 on the third

variable_name: Perceived tension between dean and associate dean
description: A single questionnaire item asked subjects: "To what extent do you think there was tension between the dean and the associate dean in your faculty group!" Mean scores for groups with an external associate dean and groups with an internal associate dean were computed and compared.
Questionnaire measure of the perceived threat to the harmony of the group, reported as group means and variances for groups with internal and external associate deans.

variable_name: Perceived threat to individual and group authority
description: Questionnaire measures of the perceived threat to each individual's authority and to the authority structure of the group, reported as means and variances for groups with internal and external associate deans.

variable_name: Perceived threat to individual and group effectiveness
description: Questionnaire measures of the perceived threat to individual effectiveness and to group effectiveness, reported as means and variances for groups with internal and external associate deans.

variable_name: Perceived helpfulness of budgetary approach used
description: Questionnaire item on whether the budgeting method used was a help or a hindrance in preparing the group's budget documents, used as a rough indication of the method's acceptance by group members; group means were compared between groups with internal and external associate deans.

Questionnaire item asking members how closely their group followed the budgeting method introduced by its associate dean; groups with external associate deans reported following the method quite closely as compared to fairly closely for groups with internal associate deans.

Subjects were asked to rank the other members of their group in order of influence, from 1, most influential, to 5, least influential; mean scores for deans and associate deans in the two kinds of groups were calculated and compared.

Measure constructed from several questions about the work, including the question 'Would you describe your work as being very routine, somewhat routine, somewhat nonroutine, or very nonroutine?' together with four items developed by Hall (1963); the items loaded together in a factor analysis of various aspects of organizational behavior and seem to represent a separate and distinct dimension representing the routineness of work. Respondents replied definitely true, true, false, or definitely false to each of Hall's questions. Organizational scores were computed by first averaging the means of each social position and then averaging across positions; the organizational scores ranged from 1.31 to 2.46 on a scale that could vary from 1.00 to 4.00.

variable_name: degree of participation in organizational decisions
description: Measure of the degree of participation in decision-making about basic organizational issues, built from staff responses and aggregated to the organization. The authors refer to Aiken and Hage (1968) for the construction of the measure.
Indicator of formalization based on staff responses to questions about whether the organization has a rules manual. Routine work is correlated with this indicator at r=.51.

Indicator of formalization based on staff responses to questions about whether the organization has job descriptions, which together with the rules manual are described as two basic mechanisms for establishing organizational control. Routine work is correlated with this indicator at r=.53.

variable_name: degree of specificity of job descriptions
description: Measure of the degree to which work procedures are specified in job descriptions; it measures how concrete the job description or procedural manual is. Items were obtained in a factor analysis of several batteries of tests developed by Hall (1963) and are described in Aiken and Hage (1968). Routine work is correlated with this measure at r=.61.

Measure of whether or not there are rules for the job occupants, that is, how well defined the job is; the authors distinguish it from specificity by noting that the former measures rules and the latter work procedures. Items from Hall's (1963) batteries, described elsewhere in Aiken and Hage (1968). Routine work has little impact on this measure.

Measure of the enforcement of the rules, that is, the degree of surveillance. Items from Hall's (1963) batteries, described elsewhere in Aiken and Hage (1968). Routine work has little impact on this measure (r=.20).
Measure of the amount of professional training of the staff, one of the measures of the degree of complexity of the organization. Organizations with routine work have less well trained staff.
Measure of the amount of professional activity, described by the authors as the third measure of complexity. Routine work does not seem to affect it.
Measure of the diversity of occupational specialties in the organization, one of the measures of the degree of complexity. Routine work appears to have little relation with it.

Measure of the degree of affect toward supervisors, obtained from a factor analysis of scales developed by Seeman and Evans (1961) in their study of the stratification of medical goals. There is almost no relation between this measure and routineness (r = .09).

Measure of the degree of social distance between supervisors and staff, obtained from the same factor analysis of scales developed by Seeman and Evans (1961). There is only a very weak positive relationship between routineness and this measure.

variable_name: degree of hierarchy of authority in work decisions
description: Measure of autonomy in work decisions used in the study, described by the authors as the hierarchy of authority. There was no correlation (r = -.02) between this measure and the degree of routineness of work.

Scale built from a series of paired comparisons in which respondents selected the goal their organization was emphasizing at the time of the interview; the efficiency of operation was one of the four goals presented. In each of the three comparisons made, ten points were assigned if the respondent selected the goal and five points if he said half and half or gave both goals equal weight, so the scale varies from zero to thirty. The ordering of presentation of pairs was randomized. The degree of routineness and this goal are related.

Scale built from the paired comparisons in which respondents selected the goal their organization was emphasizing; the morale of the staff was one of the four goals presented. Ten points were assigned in each of the three comparisons if the respondent selected the goal and five points if he said half and half or gave both goals equal weight, so the scale varies from zero to thirty. The inverse relationship between routineness and this goal is r=-.37.

Scale built from the paired comparisons in which respondents selected the goal their organization was emphasizing; the development of new programs or services was one of the four goals presented. Ten points were assigned in each of the three comparisons if the respondent selected the goal and five points if he said half and half or gave both goals equal weight, so the scale varies from zero to thirty. There is no correlation between this goal and the routineness of work (r=-.05).

Scale built from the paired comparisons in which respondents selected the goal their organization was emphasizing; the effectiveness of client services was one of the four goals presented. Ten points were assigned in each of the three comparisons if the respondent selected the goal and five points if he said half and half or gave both goals equal weight, so the scale varies from zero to thirty. There is no association between routineness and this goal (r=.00).

Measure of the emphasis on the quality of client service as a product goal; in order to measure product goals as described by Perrow, respondents were additionally asked whether the organization placed greater emphasis on the quantity of clients served or on the quality of client service. The hypothesis is moderately supported by the data (r =-42), with more routinized technology associated with less emphasis on the quality of service and more emphasis on the number of clients served.

Each respondent made sociometric choices for social contact and for three forms of technical information flow: technical discussion, critical incident information, and new research ideas. The number of choices overlapping between two networks was compared with the number expected by chance, computed from a binomial probability model based on the number of choices each respondent made; the observed and expected distributions were compared by means of a one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.

In laboratory A organizational relationships were taken directly from the departmental organization chart, the work group consisting of a first-line supervisor and those reporting to him. In laboratory B, where no organization chart existed, respondents were asked to name the people they considered members of their present work group, and consideration of formal structure was restricted to ad hoc project groups.

One of the four questions asked of each respondent dealt with the social relations within the laboratory, and the arrows in the sociogram indicate the direction of choices in social contact. The resulting socialization network is treated as the informal organization of the laboratory.

The eight respondents most frequently chosen for technical discussion, that is at least one standard deviation above the mean for the laboratory (six or more choices), are treated as the stars of the technical discussion network. A second set of key-position individuals consists of the seven people cited by respondents as the source of critical incident information.

variable_name: number of technical and professional and scientific periodicals read
description: The names of all technical periodicals to which each respondent subscribed or read regularly were obtained, and those sponsored by engineering and scientific societies were separated out in the analysis. The communication characteristics of members at key positions are reported in the table as percentages above the median for the laboratory.
scale: number of periodicals read (reported as percentage above the median)

variable_name: use of personal friends outside the laboratory as sources of information
description: In laboratory B additional questions dealt with individual information-gathering behaviour, including technical reading habits, amount of technical discussion, and contact with members of other organizations. Respondents indicated their use of personal friends outside the laboratory and of technical specialists within the laboratory as sources of information; values are reported as percentages above the median for the laboratory.

Members of the laboratories were classified according to whether they held the doctorate degree; in laboratory B the Ph.D. versus non-Ph.D. distinction exemplifies a status differential in the communication network.

Organizational slack was measured by the hospital occupancy rate, the proportion of the total annual hospital bed-days which were in use during the year. The use of this measure assumes that the costs necessary to maintain hospitals of similar size and function are relatively constant, and that differences in organizational slack will result from differences in income. Economic profitability is termed by the authors the ideal measure of organizational slack, but was not available.

A composite of two pharmacy performance measures. Drug cost per in-patient day is the cost of drugs dispensed to in-patients for the latest fiscal year divided by total in-patient days, with economic orientation assumed to increase as this ratio decreases. Drug inventory turnover rate is the cost of drugs for the latest fiscal year divided by the average value of the drug inventory, with economic orientation assumed to increase as this ratio increases. Normalized scores for drug cost and drug turnover were averaged to arrive at the hospital's economic orientation score.

variable_name: frequency of trial of new drugs
description: The new drugs released by national drug manufacturers between January 1962 and May 1964 were listed in a questionnaire, and chief pharmacists of the hospitals were asked to indicate which of these drugs had ever been ordered in their hospitals.

Promptness of trial was traced by means of audits of purchase invoices for a sample of six drugs (declomycin, librium, aldactone, aldomet, prostaphyllin, and valium). The raw score was the elapsed time in days between the date of market release of a drug and the date of first purchase; for each drug the raw score was normalized in relation to the scores of all hospitals for that drug and, because proportions exhibit heterogeneity of variance, an arc-sine transformation was applied. The normalized scores for the six drugs were pooled, so that the relationships are based upon 136 observations.
time_window: drugs released in late 1959 and early 1960 and since 1962

description: The residual difference between the actual number of levels in a department and the number of levels expected, given the regression equation relating the size of a department to the number of levels in it. The residual number of levels equals Ya - .00272 x - 3.649, where Ya is the actual number of levels and x is the total number of employees. Hierarchical differentiation is low when this expression is less than zero and high when the expression is positive.

The residual difference between the actual number of divisions in a department and the number of divisions expected, given the regression equation relating the size of a department to the number of subunits in it. The residual number of divisions equals Y1 - .00723 x - 5.027, where Y1 is the actual number of divisions and x is the total number of employees. Functional differentiation is low when this expression is less than zero and high when the expression is positive.

variable_name: authority of division heads to make decisions and policy of department heads in delegating authority
description: Informants were asked what kinds of decisions division heads can make without the approval of the head of the department, specifically about work assignments, budget allocations, or accounting procedures. About half said division heads could decide about work assignments only, and half said division heads had authority over budget allocations or accounting procedures, or both. Over 60 percent of informants also volunteered a statement of their policy in delegating authority, ranging from making all decisions to having decisions made at the lowest possible level.

The presence of written rules governing promotions was used as the indicator of accessibility of the rules. Departments were classified as having written regulations that specified the criteria for promotions or as not having them.

Informants were asked about the relative weights of examinations and personal evaluations in deciding about promotions; in the average department examinations counted about one-third. Departments were classified by whether examinations counted less than one-third or one-third or more in promotion decisions.
scale: less than one-third vs. one-third or more

description: Informants were asked about the relative weights of examinations and personal evaluations in deciding about promotions; in the average department evaluations counted about one quarter. Departments were classified by whether evaluations counted less than one-third or one-third or more of the promotion decision.
scale: less than one-third vs. one-third or more

description: The measure is based on how evenly production personnel are distributed throughout the total number of production occupations, using the formula developed by Gibbs and Martin, where D is the division of labor and X the number of persons in an occupation; the exact algebraic formula is not legible in the text. The value of D is zero when all employees are in the same occupation and is maximum when personnel are evenly dispersed; because Dmax is a function of the total number of occupations (N) in the industry (Dmax = 1 - 1/N), D values are adjusted by dividing each D by Dmax, and D/Dmax is the actual measure used. The D/Dmax values for the 41 industries are listed in column 2 of Table 2.
The measure of industry size is the total number of craftsmen, operatives, and laborers in each industry, so that overall industry size refers to production personnel (PP), not to total personnel.

The measure of administrative personnel is the ratio of the total number of administrative personnel to production personnel (A/PP), that is, the ratio between the total number of managerial, clerical, and professional personnel and the total number of craftsmen, operatives, and laborers.
The ratio of managerial personnel to production personnel is used as the measure of managerial hierarchy.
The ratio of clerical personnel to production personnel is used as the measure of formal communication structure.
The ratio of professional personnel to production personnel is used as the measure of professional authority.

The certainty of the three subenvironments was measured by the rate of change in environmental conditions, the certainty of information at a given time about environmental conditions, and the time span of definitive feedback from the environment. Data about these subenvironments were collected in interviews with the top executives in each organization, and the ranking of each subenvironment along the three dimensions was summed to provide at least a crude estimate of relative certainty.

Each basic subsystem was seen as coping with its respective segment of the total external environment: the market subenvironment for the sales subsystem, the technical-economic subenvironment for the production subsystem, and the scientific subenvironment for the research subsystem. The character of each of these sectors was described from interviews with top executives.

One of the three dimensions along which the subenvironments were ranked from interviews with top executives: the modal time span of definitive feedback from the subenvironment on the results of subsystem behavior. Feedback was reported to be available on a regular basis, often weekly, in the market subenvironment, on a daily basis in the technical-economic subenvironment, and only after a project was entirely completed in the scientific subenvironment.

A four-point scale, ranging from most controlling to least controlling, was developed for each of six structural characteristics, and a structural score was computed for each subsystem in all organizations by adding the scores on all six characteristics. Data on these characteristics were gathered from organizational documents or, when these were not available, by interviewing subsystem managers about organizational practices.
scale: four-point scale per characteristic, summed over six characteristics (low score indicates low structure)

description: The interpersonal orientation of members of the several subsystems was measured by using the Least Preferred Coworker instrument developed by Fiedler. This semantic differential scale measures the respondent's interpersonal style on a continuum from primary concern with task accomplishment to primary concern with social relationships.
scale: semantic differential continuum from task concern to social concern

description: The time orientation of members of the different units was measured with a question which asked for an estimate of the percentage of total time used working on activities affecting the organization's profits within a specific time period: less than one month, one month to one year, and one year to five years.

A list of ten criteria which managers might consider in making decisions relevant to product and process innovation was developed to measure this goal orientation; three of these criteria related to factors in each of the three subenvironments, and one criterion related to the total environment was not used in this analysis. Respondents were asked to select from these ten criteria the three most important considerations in making decisions, and then the next three most important.

To test hypothesis 5 the degree of differentiation in the four subsystem attributes between pairs of subsystems with high requisite integration was measured by computing the differences in each attribute score for each pair of relevant units. The range of differences for all six organizations in each attribute was divided into quintiles, and each quintile was assigned a unit of differentiation score from one (least differentiated quintile) to five (most differentiated quintile); these scores were summed across the four attributes for each pair.
scale: one to five per attribute, summed across four attributes

description: The effectiveness of integration was measured by asking respondents for their evaluation of the state of interdepartmental relations between all the pairs of subsystems, the evaluation being made on a seven-point scale ranging from sound, full unity of effort in obtaining innovations is achieved (1) to could not be worse, bad relations, serious problems exist in getting innovations, which are not being solved (7). Respondents tended to use only the upper part of this scale, and mean scores of 2.5 or more for a pair of relationships seemed to indicate appreciable difficulties in achieving integration.

Interviews with top executives provided information on the requirements for integration in this environment, indicating whether task characteristics made it possible for subsystems to operate independently or required continual collaboration. This information was used to identify the pairs of subsystems having a similar, high degree of requisite integration, on which the differentiation-integration analysis was conducted.

It was possible to secure indices of performance such as change in profits over the five years prior to the study, change in sales volume over the same period, and percentage of current sales volume accounted for by products developed within the last five years. The six organizations were ranked in each of these indices and these rankings were then totaled as a crude measure of the total performance of the organization; the rankings were checked against the chief executives' subjective appraisals.
time_window: five years prior to the study

description: In all the organizations except organization II there were integrative subsystems whose members had the function of integrating the sales-research and the production-research subsystems; in organization II there was also a formally established integrative subsystem, but it functioned somewhat differently and might be termed an integrative role set. In addition, four of these organizations had integrating teams with representatives from each of the basic subsystems and the integrative subsystems.

The six organizations were all operating in a chemical processing industry characterized by relatively rapid technological change and product modification and innovation; according to top executives, the dominant competitive issue was the development of new and improved products and processes, which seemed to require organizations to achieve a high degree of both differentiation and integration.

The methods used for measuring structure, and time, goal, and interpersonal orientations were also used for this analysis. The midpoint of the range of scores in each attribute was computed for the basic subsystems being integrated, and the difference between the score for the integrative subsystem and the midpoint was then computed to determine how closely the integrative subsystem approached an intermediate position; for time and goal orientations the differences on the relevant dimensions were summed to get a single score.

Members of each organization were asked, How much say or influence do you feel each of the units listed below has on product-innovation decisions? Each subsystem was included, and responses were made on a five-point scale ranging from little or no influence to a very great deal of influence. The mean scores for each subsystem within each organization were then ranked.
scale: five-point scale from little or no influence to a very great deal of influence

description: Data about the basis of influence was collected in interviews from responses to questions about the role of the integrative subsystem. Comments were classified according to whether the integrators' influence was attributed to their knowledge and competence in dealing with problems associated with the environment or almost entirely to their position, either because of the formal authority of the position or because of close proximity to top management.

One question asked respondents to select from a list of possible criteria for evaluation the three most important factors used by their supervisors to evaluate their performance; the criteria were own individual accomplishments, performance of subordinates, performance of the product group, how well you get along with others in your own department, and how well you get along with members of other departments. Respondents ranked their three choices most important (1), second most important (2), and least important (3), and the mean score for the integrators in each organization was computed.
scale: rank of 1 to 3 among selected criteria

description: The question used to determine the relative influence of the integrative subsystem was also used to derive the data for this determinant, with scores ranging from little or no influence (1) to a very great influence (5). Mean influence scores were computed for each organization.
scale: five-point scale from little or no influence (1) to a very great influence (5)

description: Data about the locus of pertinent knowledge was obtained in interviews with top managers in all six organizations. To measure influence in each subsystem, respondents were asked to indicate for their own subsystems, How much say or influence each of the levels has on product innovation decisions? The scale used was five points ranging from little or no influence to a very great deal of influence, and the data were analysed to determine if the levels where influence was concentrated were also the levels with the required knowledge.
scale: five-point scale from little or no influence to a very great deal of influence

description: Respondents indicated on a five-point scale, from very typical behavior, usually occurs to behavior which never occurs, to what extent each of twenty-five aphorisms described typical ways of handling conflict in their organization. The data were factor analyzed using an orthogonal rotation; factor III described the confrontation mode of conflict resolution.
scale: five-point scale from very typical behavior to behavior which never occurs

description: Index based on four questions about how frequently the respondent participates in decisions to hire new staff, on the promotion of professional staff, on the adoption of new policies, and on the adoption of new programs. Respondents were assigned numerical scores from 1 to 5 depending on whether they answered never, seldom, sometimes, often, or always; an average score was computed for each respondent and the data were then aggregated into organizational scores by computing the mean of each social position and averaging the position means.

Index computed by first averaging the replies of individual respondents to five statements about reliance on the chain of command for work decisions. Responses could vary from one (definitely false) to four (definitely true); the individual scores were then combined into an organizational score by the social-position averaging procedure.

Index based on five questions about whether jobs are specified by rules. Replies were scored from one (definitely true) to four (definitely false), and then each respondent's answers were averaged and combined into an organizational score.
Index computed by averaging the responses to two statements about the supervision of job occupants for conformity with rules. The scale range is not stated in the text.

Measured by asking respondents to report their major duties and classifying each respondent according to the type of occupational speciality, e.g., psychiatrist, rehabilitation counselor, teacher, nurse, social worker; the number of professional occupational specialities in the agencies studied ranged from one to eighteen.

Index of the amount of college training as well as other professional training, scored 0 for lack of training beyond a college degree and lack of other professional training, 1 for lack of training beyond a college degree but other professional training, 2 for training beyond a college degree and lack of other professional training, and 3 for training beyond a college degree and other professional training. The agencies studied varied between 0.7 and 2.3 on this measure on a scale with a possible range of 0 (low) to 3 (high).
