Index based on the number of professional associations in which the respondents were involved, the number of meetings attended, and the number of offices held or number of papers given at professional meetings: one point for belonging to a professional organization, one point for attending at least two-thirds of the previous six meetings of the professional organization, and one point for presenting a paper or holding an office in a professional organization. The maximum score was three points and the minimum score was zero; the scores of the organizations studied varied from .9 to 2.5.

A Likert internal-consistency scale consisting of a series of statements related to the dimension of hierarchy of authority. Employees indicated how accurately each statement described their own organization. For the interdepartmental comparison, the departmental score was the mean of the respondents' scores in each department; for the hierarchical comparison, scores were split at the median of all scores on the dimension into high and low perceived bureaucratization.
level: individual respondent (aggregated to department or hierarchical group)

description: A Likert internal-consistency scale consisting of a series of statements related to the dimension of division of labor based upon functional specialization. Employees indicated how accurately each statement described their own organization. Departmental scores were the means of respondents' scores; for the hierarchical comparison respondents were split at the median into high and low perceived bureaucratization.
level: individual respondent (aggregated to department or hierarchical group)

description: A Likert internal-consistency scale consisting of a series of statements related to the system of rules covering the rights and duties of positional incumbents. Employees indicated how accurately each statement described their own organization. Departmental scores were means of respondents' scores; hierarchical comparison used a median split into high and low perceived bureaucratization.
level: individual respondent (aggregated to department or hierarchical group)

description: A Likert internal-consistency scale consisting of a series of statements related to the system of procedures for dealing with work situations. Employees indicated how accurately each statement described their own organization. Departmental scores were means of respondents' scores; hierarchical comparison used a median split into high and low perceived bureaucratization.
level: individual respondent (aggregated to department or hierarchical group)

description: A Likert internal-consistency scale consisting of a series of statements related to the impersonality of interpersonal relationships. Employees indicated how accurately each statement described their own organization. Departmental scores were means of respondents' scores; hierarchical comparison used a median split into high and low perceived bureaucratization.
level: individual respondent (aggregated to department or hierarchical group)

description: A Likert internal-consistency scale consisting of a series of statements related to selection for employment and promotion based upon technical competence. Employees indicated how accurately each statement described their own organization. Departmental scores were means of respondents' scores; hierarchical comparison used a median split into high and low perceived bureaucratization.
level: individual respondent (aggregated to department or hierarchical group)

variable_name: Departmental task type (Type I / Type II)
description: Each of the ten organizations' departments was divided into categories of nonuniform or social tasks (Type II) and uniform or traditional tasks (Type I). The categorization was based on the background information on departmental affiliation given by respondents in the questionnaire. Only three organizations had departments in the Type II category, and the Type I departments were compared with the Type II departments of the same three organizations, giving a total of sixteen departments.

Respondents were classified into executive and nonexecutive categories on the basis of their own listing of their hierarchical position in the background questionnaire. Although more hierarchical levels were present in most organizations, insufficient respondents in several possible categories led to grouping respondents into these two categories; executives from all ten organizations were combined into one category and nonexecutives into another.

variable_name: department A versus department B (job classification)
description: Employees are grouped by the technology of their department. Department A jobs represent highly skilled crafts in which difficult skills are applied to produce a whole or almost whole complex product; department B jobs are unskilled and semiskilled, composed of automatic and semiautomatic tasks in which the employee for the most part feeds the machines. The researcher's assumption of differences is based upon management's job-classification structure, and the difference is verified from the employees' point of view through their reports of variety, routine and job satisfaction.

The need to produce high-quality work is inferred from an individual content analysis made of each interview. The percentage of employees in each department who report such needs is compared between departments.

variable_name: desire to learn more about the job
description: One measure of involvement in the kind of work is the extent to which the individual expresses a desire to learn more about his particular job or jobs within the same family of jobs. The percentage of employees expressing this need in each department is compared.

variable_name: potency of the need for money / money liked best about the company
description: A scale of degree of potency is used, with 0 for no potency, 1 for regular potency, 2 for high potency, and 4 for extremely high potency; zero and regular potency are grouped as low potency and high and extremely high potency as high potency. Two further indicators are used: whether money is reported as the thing the employee likes best about the company, and the employees' satisfaction with their wages.
scale: 0 = no potency, 1 = regular potency, 2 = high potency, 4 = extremely high potency

variable_name: needs allied to the mature and infant sides of the personality model
description: Interview responses are coded into needs along the personality-growth model and the percentage of employees in each department reporting each need is compared. Reported needs include needs for variety and challenge in their work, relative independence (control over their work world) and the potency of relative independence, the need to initiate action for others, the need for routine work where the employee does a few and similar things all the time, the need to be left completely alone, and the need to receive directions and to be passive.

Inferred from the employees' reports of the abilities they have to offer: reporting that they have many abilities to offer that are very important to their company or any other company, as opposed to reporting that they have nothing much to offer except a few abilities learned on the job, which they classify as simple, unimportant and easily learned by anyone.

Data collected by the cost-control department: at the beginning of each month each department defines for itself the standards it believes reasonable in terms of spoiled work and extra operations, and at the end of the month the department's estimated score is compared with its actual performance. If the total amount is higher than the estimated score, a minus sign is placed before the difference. The formula given for this comparison is not legible in the available text.
time_window: monthly (estimate at the beginning of each month, compared at the end of the month)

variable_name: willingness to blame themselves for errors
description: Employees report what they see as the cause of errors: that errors are probably the result of their own haste to get out a particular quantity to earn a particular rate for the day, or that other departments are to blame for the cause of errors, waste and scrap. Departmental percentages are compared.

variable_name: close friendships formed in the plant
description: Employees report whether they do not form close friendships or whether they have made very close friendships while working in the plant. Years of service did not differ significantly between the two groups.

Employees are asked to discuss their activities outside the plant and the responses are coded into two general categories. The first category includes activities that do not require much creative thought and permit an individual to be passive, quiet and alone (for example, watching TV, staying at home and reading the papers, trimming the lawn, working around the house). The second category includes activities that require more skill and are viewed by people as challenging (for example, cabinet making, electrical work, plumbing and reading). Percentages of employees in each category are compared between departments.
The incidence of absenteeism, turnover and transfer in the two departments is so low that the company does not keep central records of it, so the departments cannot be compared on this measure.

variable_name: desire for upward mobility and involvement in company problems
description: Employees report whether upward mobility is possible and whether they desire it, and how much they agree that upward mobility is not possible, was once possible, but is no longer desired. Involvement in the interests of the plant is measured by asking what information employees would like to have about the company that would help them understand it better and contribute more directly to its growth, and whether they have suggestions to improve their responsibility.

Assessed from the state of unionization in the company: no union exists within the company, and a number of attempts to unionize the plant have failed, having met equal resistance from employees in departments A and B.

Board Size was operationalized, as in other studies, as the total number of board positions, from the Governance Survey. Board Size Squared was calculated as the square of Board Size and was used to test the prediction of a curvilinear relationship between board size and strategic change.

Precise data on the average tenure of board members were unavailable; Board Tenure was measured as the maximum number of years that a board member could sit on the board, a proxy the authors expect to be highly correlated with average board tenure. Board Tenure Squared was the square of this measure and was used to test the curvilinear prediction.

Respondents indicated how many board members were less than 30 years of age, between 31 and 50, between 51 and 70, and 70 years of age and over. From these data Board Member Age was calculated as the percentage of board members who were greater than 50 years of age. Board Member Age Squared was calculated as the squared term of this measure.

Board members were classified into one of 14 mutually exclusive occupational groups. Occupational Heterogeneity was calculated as the percentage of members in each of the 14 groups squared, and then summed; the theoretical range runs from close to 0 (14 equally represented occupational groups) to 1 (a single occupational group). Occupational Heterogeneity Squared was also calculated to test Hypothesis 4.

Following Alexander et al. (1993), this measure was calculated as the proportion of board members whose primary occupations were of a business or legal nature, namely other hospital CEOs, nonhospital corporate executives, independent business people, banker/financiers, and lawyers. Representation in these five occupational categories was contrasted to membership in nine other categories such as educator, nurse, government official and religious leader.

Respondents indicated which of eleven issues occupied most of their board's time over the past year. Of the 11 issues, three were explicitly strategy related: (1) diversification, mergers, and joint ventures, (2) strategic planning, and (3) hospital's competitive position. A dichotomous measure was created, with 1 indicating that one of the three strategy-related issues occupied most of the board's time, and 0 indicating that primary attention was devoted to a nonstrategic issue.

Comprehensiveness of CEO Evaluation was calculated as the total number of criteria explicitly used by the board to evaluate the CEO's performance. The variable ranged from zero, when no formal evaluation mechanism was used, to ten, indicating that all ten criteria in the survey were explicitly considered.

A Board Power index was calculated as an aggregate of four indicators of the board-CEO relationship: whether the CEO was or was not a member of the nominating committee that selected board members (CEO exclusion indicates board power); whether the CEO did not participate in developing the hospital's mission statement; CEO tenure, which is inversely related to board power and was reversed scored; and the extent to which the CEO was excluded from board votes. Board Power was calculated as the sum of the standardized measures.

A service added between 1985 and 1990 that one-third or fewer of the hospitals offered in 1985 was assigned a weight of three; a weight of two was assigned to services offered by between one-third and two-thirds of hospitals, and a weight of one to services provided by greater than two-thirds of hospitals. The weighted 1985 count of all services provided was subtracted from the weighted 1990 change score, and the difference was divided by the weighted score for services originally offered in 1985, giving the proportional change from 1985 to 1990. The measure is sensitive to both service additions and divestitures.

variable_name: difference between product market diversification at the focal firm and diversification of director home companies
description: Non-directional difference computed by subtracting product market diversification of the focal firm in the prior year from the average home company diversification of manager-directors on the board in the prior year, and squaring the difference. Product market diversification itself is operationalized with the entropy measure, which takes into account the number of segments in which a firm operates and weights each segment according to its contribution to total sales.

variable_name: difference between geographic diversification at the focal firm and diversification of director home companies
description: Non-directional difference computed by subtracting geographic diversification of the focal firm in the prior year from the average home company diversification of manager-directors on the board in the prior year, and squaring the difference. Geographic diversification is operationalized with the composite measure validated by Sullivan (1994), which sums the ratio of foreign sales to total sales, foreign assets divided by total assets, and the number of country subsidiaries as a percentage of the highest value in the sample.

variable_name: average product market diversification of director home companies
description: Average level of product market diversification at manager-director home companies just prior to succession, measured in the prior year and operationalized with the entropy measure, which takes into account the number of segments in which a firm operates and weights each segment according to its contribution to total sales.

variable_name: average geographic diversification of director home companies
description: Average level of geographic diversification at manager-director home companies just prior to succession, measured in the prior year and operationalized with the composite measure validated by Sullivan (1994), which sums the ratio of foreign sales to total sales, foreign assets divided by total assets, and the number of country subsidiaries as a percentage of the highest value in the sample.

variable_name: product market diversification of the new CEO's prior employer
description: Level of product market diversification, operationalized with the entropy measure, of the firm where the new CEO was previously employed, measured in the year prior to the year of employment.
time_window: year prior to the year of employment

variable_name: geographic diversification of the new CEO's prior employer
description: Level of geographic diversification, operationalized with the composite measure validated by Sullivan (1994), of the firm where the new CEO was previously employed, measured in the year prior to the year of employment.
time_window: year prior to the year of employment

variable_name: product market diversification of the new CEO's board ties
description: Average product market diversification, operationalized with the entropy measure, of other Fortune/Forbes companies where the new CEO served as an outside director, measured in the prior year.

variable_name: geographic diversification of the new CEO's board ties
description: Average geographic diversification, operationalized with the composite measure validated by Sullivan (1994), of other Fortune/Forbes companies where the new CEO served as an outside director, measured in the prior year.

variable_name: product market diversification of the focal firm following succession
description: Level of product market diversification of the focal firm, operationalized with the entropy measure, estimated in year t+2 while controlling for the prior value in t-1 so that the model estimates change in strategy.

variable_name: geographic diversification of the focal firm following succession
description: Level of geographic diversification of the focal firm, operationalized with the composite measure validated by Sullivan (1994), estimated in year t+2 while controlling for the prior value in t-1 so that the model estimates change in strategy.

Binary variable coded as 1 in a given year if a new CEO from outside the organization was hired in that year, and as 0 otherwise. The event-history model predicts the likelihood of outside succession versus inside succession or no succession, treating succession as a repeatable event.

Firm performance measured with return on equity as an accounting-based measure and Jensen's alpha as a market-based measure, averaged over the prior two years, and combined into a single index using principal components analysis. In testing interaction effects, the performance index was inverted so that higher values signify lower performance.

The value of the performance variable for the individual director's home company, used to weight each director's home firm diversification score in the interaction terms: each director's home firm diversification score was multiplied by the value of the performance variable for their home company and the products were summed across directors.
Measured as the number of years the director had been employed at their current home company, used to weight each director's home firm diversification score in the interaction terms.

variable_name: Current Knowledge learned from Foreign Parents
description: A five-item scale based on Likert-type responses to the question 'To what extent have you learned from your foreign parents (a) new technological expertise, (b) new marketing expertise, (c) product development, (d) managerial techniques, and (e) manufacturing process'. Responses run from 1 = little to 5 = to a great extent, giving the scale a possible range of 5-25. The Cronbach's alpha for these five items was 0.96.

Two scales were used. The IJV's performance in specific areas was assessed using four five-point Likert items (1 = poor to 5 = excellent) on increasing business volume, increasing market share, achieving planned goals, and making profits. General performance was assessed using a three-item scale summarizing how the Hungarian parent, foreign parents, and IJV general manager evaluate the IJV's overall performance. Factor analysis revealed both sets of items were unidimensional; responses were standardized and added to create an overall IJV Performance Index (alpha = 0.87).

The level of trust between parents was measured using a single item, with 1 = low level of trust and 5 = high level of trust. The authors note that what matters most at any given point in time is the partners' overall confidence in one another's trustworthiness.
Relevant prior knowledge was measured using the same five-item learning scale, but utilizing data from the 1993 study. The Cronbach's alpha for the five learning items in that survey was 0.88.

variable_name: Cultural Compatibility of the domestic and foreign parents
description: Measured by reverse scoring a two-item scale (1 = little to 5 = very much) on the extent to which cultural misunderstandings and cultural differences have been issues in the IJV (alpha = 0.91). The distribution of the scale was positively skewed, so the log of the measure was used in the analyses.

variable_name: Relatedness of IJV's and Foreign Parent's Businesses
description: Measured by reverse scoring a single item for unrelatedness, in reverse form coded 1 = related and 0 = unrelated.

A three-item scale of 5-point Likert-type items based on agreement with normative statements on the extent to which the IJV is flexible and adapting to change, is creative, and rewards performance (alpha = 0.67; possible range 3-15).

A six-item scale of 5-point Likert-type items that summarizes the degree to which the foreign parent(s) contribute sales/marketing support, managerial resources, administrative support, emotional support, training, and time to the IJV (alpha = 0.82; possible range 6-30).

variable_name: Education and Training by Foreign Parents
description: Measured by a single item on the extent to which managers in the IJV were given education and training by the foreign parents (1 = little to 5 = great extent).
Measured with a single item on the IJV's use of formal goals and objectives (1 = either or both written, 0 = neither written).
scale: 1 = either or both written, 0 = neither written

variable_name: Specialization by Foreign and Domestic Parents
description: Measured using a single item on the extent to which the foreign parent(s) provides technology to the IJV while the domestic parent provides the manufacturing capability (1 = little, 5 = great extent).

A scale of six Likert-type items (alpha = 0.75; possible range 6-30) on the degree to which the IJV's business strategy entailed differentiation over the past two years. The items assessed the degree to which the IJV had emphasized developing new products, promotion and advertising expenditures above industry average, a broad product line, extensive customer service capabilities, highly trained personnel, and strong influence over the channels of distribution.
A two-item scale of 5-point Likert-type items on how effective the IJV was in the prior year in providing adequate worker training and improving management skills (alpha = 0.72; possible range 2-10).

variable_name: Relative absorptive capacity (Prior Knowledge, Cultural Compatibility, IJV-Foreign Parents Relatedness)
description: Relative absorptive capacity was operationalized with three separate variables entered together in the learning model: prior relevant knowledge from the foreign parents (the 1993 learning scale), cultural compatibility of the parents (two-item scale, reverse scored), and relatedness of the IJV's business to the foreign parents' business as a proxy for shared dominant logic.

variable_name: international strategy (cluster membership: global or multidomestic)
description: Four statements were constructed that measured whether competition was predominantly global or local and whether the corporate strategy was focused on achieving economies of scale or on achieving local differentiation. These questions were subjected to cluster analysis and a two-cluster solution resulted in clusters that could easily be identified as global and multidomestic. For each headquarters the authors verified whether subsidiaries were classified in the same cluster; the limited number of divergent cases were recoded to the cluster that contained the majority of subsidiaries. In total, 101 subsidiaries were classified as multidomestic and 186 as global.

The entry mode is captured by a dummy variable that takes the value of one if the entry is made by acquisition and zero if the entry is made by greenfield. To ascertain the entry mode, respondents were asked whether the subsidiary had been acquired by another owner after its foundation. The overall sample included 97 acquisitions and 190 greenfields.

Based on a review of over 15 publications on control mechanisms, four main categories of control mechanisms were identified: personal centralized control, bureaucratic formalized control, output control and control by socialization and networks, each being composed of 2-4 individual control mechanisms. The questions used by Martinez and Jarillo (1991) were adapted and supplemented to measure these mechanisms. The items formed a reliable scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.74) and were averaged to form a composite score for the level of control.

Three questions were used to assess the presence of expatriates in a given subsidiary: the nationality of the managing director, the number of top five jobs held by expatriates, and the total number of expatriates working in the subsidiary. Since the number of expatriates might be influenced by the size of the subsidiary, the number of expatriates was calculated as a percentage of the total workforce of the subsidiary. Because the items had different scales they were standardized before they were averaged to form a composite score for the level of expatriate presence.

Local responsiveness was measured with four items asking for the percentage of local R&D and local production incorporated in products sold by the subsidiary and the percentage of products and marketing that was substantially modified for the local market. The items formed a reliable scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.73) and were averaged to form a composite score for the level of local responsiveness.

To test the hypotheses with regard to subsidiary development, the authors calculated the time for which subsidiaries had been under ownership of headquarters at the time of the study. For greenfields this was the year of data collection minus the year in which they were established; for acquisitions this equated to the year of data collection minus the year in which their current owner had acquired them.

The headquarters-subsidiary relationship is studied through three elements: the level of control exercised by headquarters through the different types of control mechanisms, the level of expatriate presence in the subsidiary, and the level of local responsiveness that headquarters allows to the subsidiary. Each element is measured as a composite score formed from the survey items described for control, expatriate presence and local responsiveness.

Composite measure of competitive strategy built from questions regarding the extent of usage of specific competitive tactics relevant to marketing differentiation, innovative differentiation and low cost, adapted from Dess and Davis (1984) and Miller (1988). Confirmatory factor analysis of a second-order structure supported the intercorrelation of the individual strategy dimensions, and the composite measure of Strategy was developed by averaging the respective individual items. Items used a five-point scale anchored much less than competitors to much more than competitors.
scale: 5-point Likert scale (1 = much less than competitors ... 5 = much more than competitors)

description: Composite measure built from items covering organizational, marketing and technical capabilities; CEOs were asked to indicate the extent to which each constitutes a particular strength relative to competition. Organizational capabilities denote managerial competencies, knowledge and skills of employees, efficient organizational structure, organizational culture, efficient coordinative mechanisms, strategic planning procedures and ability to attract creative employees; marketing capabilities were measured with items such as privileged relationships with customers and suppliers, market knowledge, control over distribution channels and a strong installed customer base; technical capabilities were measured with three items (efficient production department, technological capabilities and infrastructure, economies of scale and technical experience). Confirmatory factor analysis supported the second-order structure and the composite was formed by averaging the respective items.
scale: 5-point Likert scale (1 = much weaker than competitors ... 5 = much stronger than competitors)

description: Composite of four items adapted from Achrol and Stern (1988) gauging the intensity of competition the firm faces in its major market served. Price competition did not survive the preliminary scale purification procedure and was therefore not included as a measurement component of the construct, so the measure captures non-price competition.
scale: 5-point Likert scale (1 = very weak competition ... 5 = very fierce competition)

description: Single-item question asking the respondent to evaluate the difficulty of entering the industry, referring to the situation confronted by the firm in its major market served. Higher values indicate more difficult entry.
scale: 5-point scale (1 = very easy to enter ... 5 = very difficult)

description: Single-item question asking the respondent to evaluate the threat of substitutes faced by the firm, referring to the situation confronted by the firm in its major market served. Higher values indicate a greater threat.
Measured as the percentage of sales made to the three biggest buyers of the firm in its major market served. Higher values indicate greater dependence on, and hence bargaining power of, buyers.

Single-item question asking the respondent to evaluate the firm's bargaining power over suppliers, reverse scored to indicate the power of suppliers. Higher values indicate greater supplier bargaining power.
scale: 5-point scale (1 = very weak ... 5 = very strong), reverse scored

description: Composite of perceptual items reflecting market share, absolute sales volume, increase in market share and sales. Managers were asked to indicate their firm's performance relative to competition over the last three years period, in order to avoid bias from temporal fluctuations and to proximate a notion of sustainability of performance. The items were placed in a different part of the questionnaire relative to the strategy and resources and capabilities items to mitigate potential autocorrelation effects.
scale: 5-point scale (1 = much below the average ... 5 = much above the average)

description: Composite of three perceptual items reflecting return on equity, profit margin and net profits relative to competition. Managers were asked to indicate their firm's performance relative to competition over the last three years period. The items were placed in a different part of the questionnaire relative to the strategy and resources and capabilities items to mitigate potential autocorrelation effects.
scale: 5-point scale (1 = much below the average ... 5 = much above the average)

variable_name: Composite market performance and composite profitability
description: Firm performance was operationalized as a two-dimensional perceptual construct. Composite profitability combined three CEO-rated items (return on equity, profit margin, net profits) and composite market performance combined items on market share, sales volume, increase in market share and sales, all relative to competition over the last three years.

Revenues per room, an industry standard performance measure, computed as a hotel's revenues scaled by its number of rooms, measured for each establishment in each fiscal quarter. The authors argue that agglomeration production effects should lower costs while demand effects should raise revenues, so revenues per room should capture agglomeration gains for demand.

The fraction of firms in the market that are greater in size than the focal hotel, computed at the five-digit zip code market level. It varies for each hotel in a market: for the largest hotel in a market it is zero and for the smallest hotel it is equal to one.

The fraction of chain affiliated firms in the market, computed at the five-digit zip code market level. The fraction can be based upon either the count of competitors or the count of rooms in the market, which are highly correlated; the reported results are based upon count of competitors. FRA HAIN is market invariant, the same for all hotels in a given market.

Equals 1 if the establishment is chain affiliated. Affiliation is determined by examining establishments' names and comparing them to a comprehensive hotel brand name list taken from Conlin (1999), which Conlin constructs by reviewing Lodging Hospitality, a trade magazine for the lodging industry.

variable_name: size class dummy variables (SIZE1 through SIZE10)
description: Dummy variables for ten size classes defined in fixed twenty-five room increments: SIZE1 is 25-49 rooms, SIZE2 is 50-74 rooms, SIZE3 is 75-99 rooms, and so on, with SIZE10 being greater than 249 rooms. Size class dummies are used instead of a continuous size measure because the dependent variable is total revenues divided by size, and because several levels of minimum efficient scale may exist.
scale: dummy (0/1) for each of ten room-count classes

description: Markets are split into rural versus suburban/urban using PROC CLUSTER in SAS with density (population per square mile) as the clustering criterion, which maximizes between group variation while minimizing within group variation. The authors adopt a split between rural and suburban of 975 people per square mile; the average for markets defined as rural is only 113 people per square mile.

Similarity in chain affiliation to the market was tested with the interaction of the establishment's chain dummy (CHAIN) and the fraction of chain-affiliated hotels in the zip code market (FRA HAIN), in rural markets.

variable_name: Size class dummies interacted with fraction of larger hotels (SIZE4567 x FRA GTSZ, SIZE890 x FRA GTSZ)
description: Similarity in size to the market is tested through interactions between grouped size class dummies (sizes 4 to 7 and 8 to 10, with sizes 1 to 3 as the base) and the fraction of hotels in the zip code market larger than the focal hotel (FRA GTSZ). The coefficients show which size classes gain from larger hotels in the market.
scale: interaction of dummies with a fraction

description: Continuous variable measured in years for the hospital director. It was constructed from VHA internal personnel files for years 1988 through 1998 to identify the relevant demographic characteristics of the director at each VHA hospital for each three-month interval during the study; values change in the first three-month period following the departure of an existing director and the appointment of a new one.
time_window: 1988-1998; values assigned for each three-month interval

description: Continuous variable measured in years for the hospital director; hospital positions held since joining VHA were obtained from VHA internal personnel files and used to construct the director's organizational tenure at each hospital for each three-month interval during the study.
time_window: 1988-1998; values assigned for each three-month interval

description: Dichotomous variable, whether or not the director held a graduate degree. Two primary groups of VHA directors are identified: those who worked their way up VHA's career ladder without the benefit of a graduate degree, and those who earned a graduate degree.
scale: dichotomous (graduate degree vs no graduate degree)
time_window: 1988-1998; values assigned for each three-month interval

description: A dummy variable that indicated whether at each three-month interval during the study period a hospital's director had prior TQM exposure before assuming the directorship at the focal hospital; created to assess the effect of director transfers.
time_window: 1988-1998; values assigned for each three-month interval

variable_name: percentage of hospitals in its service complexity group that had adopted TQM
description: For each hospital in the study, the percentage of hospitals in its service complexity group that had adopted TQM was computed at each three-month interval during the study. Hospitals were classified into high, moderate and low service complexity categories from a VHA data base; none of the hospitals changed their classification during the study period.

variable_name: percentage of hospitals in its referral network that had adopted TQM
description: A unique primary referral network was constructed for each VHA hospital: every VHA hospital from which the focal hospital received at least ten percent of the total referrals it received from other VHA hospitals over a 12-month period, and every hospital to which it sent at least ten percent of the total referrals it sent over a 12-month period. Referrals were identified in the Patient Treatment File where a patient was discharged from one VHA hospital and admitted to another on the same day; for each hospital the percentage of hospitals in its referral network that had adopted TQM was computed at each three-month interval.
time_window: referral networks reconstructed for each year of the study period; adoption percentages at each three-month interval

variable_name: dummy variable for demonstration-site presence in referral network
description: Demonstration-site hospitals were first removed from the data base; a dummy variable was then included for each remaining hospital indicating for each three-month interval whether a hospital with demonstration-site status existed within its patient referral network. VHA headquarters selected twelve of its hospitals that were early adopters of TQM as demonstration sites.

variable_name: percentage of private-sector hospitals in the county that had adopted TQM
description: Annual survey estimates, by county, of the percentage of private hospitals that had adopted TQM beginning in 1989 through 1998 were obtained from an AHA survey; since these adoption rates were available on an annual basis only, linear interpolation was used to compute cumulative rates of adoption for each three-month period, matched with the counties in which VHA hospitals were located.

Dichotomous variable (1 = adoption, 0 = no adoption). Survey questionnaire data were used to determine whether and when TQM adoption had occurred; adoption was specified as an event within three-month intervals throughout the study period, with a code of one assigned for each hospital at the three-month interval that covered the documented date of adoption.

Dummy variable coded 0 to indicate a privately owned firm and 1 to indicate an SOE. There were no firms with hybrid ownership structures in the sample. Majority foreign-owned firms were excluded; some private firms had nominal foreign investment of typically 10 percent or less of total paid-up capital.

Competitive intensity measured using the Herfindal index. Market share data were obtained from Markets and Marketshares, a CMIE report that provides annual market statistics on over 300 product groups in the manufacturing sector.
Return on sales, one of two commonly used profitability indicators in this stream of literature used to compare SOEs and private firms. The text does not give the formula.
Return on investment, one of two commonly used profitability indicators in this stream of literature used to compare SOEs and private firms. The text does not give the formula.

Indicator of operational efficiency measured as a ratio of cost of goods sold (direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overheads) to sales. It provides an intermediate range of comparisons relatively well insulated from extraneous effects such as administered output prices and social costs.

Number of breakthrough patents in the chemical industry in any year that were created by the focal firm. For every year the patents applied for in that year were sorted on the basis of their citation weights and the top 1 percent were identified as breakthrough patents, so each patent is compared only with patents of its own application-year cohort. The variable is a count taking only nonnegative integer values and is the dependent variable of the study.

Number of new technology classes entered by a firm in the previous 3 years, computed from the U.S. patent system's technology classification and the firm's prior patenting history. A firm was considered to have entered a new technology class when it first applied for a patent in a class in which it had not patented in the previous 4 years, the presumption being that a technology unused for 4 years is unfamiliar to the firm.

Number of a firm's patents that cite technology that is on average less than 3 years old, based on the ages of the prior-art patents cited by the firm's patents. The measure captures the degree to which the firm experiments with leading-edge or nascent technologies.

Number of a firm's patents that cite no other patents, patents being required to indicate their prior technological lineage by citing the patents they build on. Patents citing no other patents indicate no discernible technological antecedents, so creating many such patents is taken to reflect a firm's willingness to adopt a pioneering or unprecedented innovation approach.

A 7-item scale adapted from Covin and Slevin's (1989) entrepreneurial orientation scale. All items used 5-point Likert scales. The scale captures the extent to which the firm identifies and responds to partnering opportunities.

Respondents rated their performance, relative to their competitors, on market share, sales growth, market development, and product development. Ratings used a 5-point Likert scale with the anchors 'Much Worse' and 'Much Better' to control for industry effects.
A 3-item scale adapted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993) and Dickson and Weaver (1997). All items used 5-point Likert scales.
A 4-item scale adapted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993) and Dickson and Weaver (1997). All items used 5-point Likert scales.

A 3-item scale adapted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993) and Dickson and Weaver (1997). The scale includes items on firms' ability to predict the competitive landscape, the rate of new entrants, and the actions of competitors; all items used 5-point Likert scales.

The logarithmic transformation of sales used as the measure of size. The firms range in size, in U.S. dollars, from a minimum of $18 million to a maximum of $30 billion (median = $120 million); employment ranges from 50 to 131,000 employees (median = 800).

Count of the strategic alliances a traditional pharmaceutical firm has entered into with providers of biotechnology. The total is further split into exploration and exploitation alliances, and each alliance is classified along the value chain of a fully integrated biopharmaceutical company using BioScan's qualitative firm-level alliance descriptions.

Count of technology-oriented alliances, coded as alliances focused on drug discovery and development as well as clinical and commercial manufacturing. Of the 889 alliances, 317 were exploration alliances.
Count of market-oriented alliances, coded as alliances focused on clinical trials, FDA regulatory management, and marketing and sales. Of the 889 alliances, 589 were exploitation alliances.

The number of new biotechnology products the firm had introduced into the market up until December 1997, which marks the publication date of the BioScan industry directory used for the study. New biotechnology products include new biotechnology-based drugs and in vivo diagnostics; the sample is limited to in vivo therapeutics because firms in that segment face extensive regulatory reporting requirements.

A financial performance index constructed for each firm based on its average firm ROE for 1998 and 1999. When testing the performance hypothesis, 1997 firm ROE is included as an independent variable (lagged firm performance) to control for specification bias arising from unobserved heterogeneity.

variable_name: entrepreneurial orientation (composite of innovativeness, risk-taking propensity, proactiveness)
description: Entrepreneurial orientation is measured by three dimensions. Innovativeness is measured by two indices: the number of R&D employees in 1997 and the number of products/services that created a new market niche, penetrated established markets successfully, or significantly substituted imports from foreign countries in 1998; the two standardized scores are added. Risk-taking propensity is measured by the number of risky R&D projects in 1997 and expenditure on those risky R&D projects in 1997; the two standardized scores are added. Proactiveness is measured by the number of first mover pursuing projects and first mover pursuing project expenditure in 1997; the two standardized scores are added. The three dimensions are then standardized and a single composite indicator is created by multiplying each standardized score by its corresponding factor loading and adding them up.

Technological capabilities are measured by three indices: the number of technologies that were internally developed, including the number of patents obtained or submitted until the end of 1997; the number of utility models and designs that were registered to the Korean Patents Administration at the end of 1997; and the number of foreign and domestic quality assurance marks acquired until the end of 1997. Each index is standardized by its mean and standard deviation, and a single factor is produced by multiplying each standardized score by its corresponding factor loading and adding them up.

variable_name: financial resources invested during the development period
description: The variable is measured by the amount of total R&D investment, advertising expenditure, and market research investment in 1997. The logic is that organizational performance largely depends on the amount and appropriate timing of financial resources invested during the development period.

Partnership-based linkages are measured by four indices: the number of other firms with which the focal firm has a strategic alliance for marketing or technology development; the number of venture capital firms that invested equity in the focal firm; the number of collaborating R&D projects and technology exchange programs with universities or research institutes; and the number of entrepreneurial associations in which the entrepreneur of the start-up actively participated.

Sponsorship-based linkages are measured by two indices. The first reflects sponsorship from commercial banks and consists of the frequency with which financial institutions named the focal firm a 'promising small enterprise' and the number of financial services firms from which the focal firm received a loan with a below market rate in 1997; the standardized scores are combined by multiplying each by its factor loading and adding them up. The second reflects sponsorship from Korean governmental agencies and comprises the frequency with which Korean central or local governmental agencies named the focal firm a 'promising small enterprise' and the number of government-sponsored research projects carried out in the focal firm, alone or with other organizations, during 1997; the standardized scores are combined by factor loadings.

Performance is measured by sales growth—the sales volume of years 1998 and 1999 subtracted by the sales volume of years 1996 and 1997. The independent variables are assumed to have their influence on a start-up's performance during the subsequent 2 years. Sales volume data were collected from the KSMBA web site and, when unavailable there, through telephone interviews with CEOs.

Treated as a dummy variable in the analysis by assigning a value of one to IPO firms with founder CEOs and a value of zero to firms with nonfounder CEOs. Forty-eight percent of the IPO firms in the sample had CEOs who were also the firms' founders, and the remaining 52 percent had nonfounder CEOs.

Calculated by subtracting the initial stock offer price from the closing price on the first day of trading, then dividing this figure by the initial offer price. An unretained wealth figure of zero (14 percent of the sample) implies the initial offer price perfectly mirrors the first-day closing market value; figures greater than zero (81 percent of the sample) imply underpricing; figures less than zero (5 percent of the sample) imply the stock was overpriced. The authors also refer to this variable as the underpricing ratio.

Consistent with Megginson and Weiss's (1991) approach, measured by summing the value of the IPO deals underwritten by the investment banking firm during the sample period, then dividing this figure by the total value of all IPO deals completed during this same period.

variable_name: proportion of insiders on the board of directors
description: Calculated as the ratio of board members currently serving as firm officers to total board members. It was treated as a control variable when not being examined as a potential moderator.

Two statements reflecting the extent to which the relationship is characterized by personal, social ties between the young technology-based firm and the customer; the dimension of social capital was modeled after Nahapiet and Ghoshal (1998) and Tsai and Ghoshal (1998). Statement-style items were measured on a scale from 1 = do not agree to 7 = completely agree.
scale: 1 = do not agree to 7 = completely agree

description: Three statements reflecting the extent to which the young technology-based firm perceives trust between itself and the key customer. The first item was adopted from Heide and Miner (1992) and the other two from Tsai and Ghoshal (1998). Statement-style items were measured on a scale from 1 = do not agree to 7 = completely agree.
scale: 1 = do not agree to 7 = completely agree

description: Two statements reflecting the degree to which the key customer relationship provides the young technology-based firm with a network of customer contacts; the construct was designed based on Larson (1992) and Uzzi (1997). Statement-style items were measured on a scale from 1 = do not agree to 7 = completely agree.
scale: 1 = do not agree to 7 = completely agree

description: Four statements reflecting the technological and market knowledge that a young technology-based firm may acquire from the key customer, based on Huber (1991), Nooteboom et al. (1997) and von Hippel (1988). Statement-style items were measured on a scale from 1 = do not agree to 7 = completely agree.
scale: 1 = do not agree to 7 = completely agree

description: Respondents estimated how many new products, services, or technologies their firm had developed specifically as a result of the key customer relationship; responses ranged from 0 to 40, with a mean of 2.3. The natural log of this measure was used in the analyses to compensate for skewness.

Three statements regarding the extent to which the firm's technology is a source of competitive advantage for the firm, designed based on Wernerfelt (1984) and Conner (1991); the company's technology was defined for respondents as 'the company's technological skills and knowledge as well as the products, services, and processes based on these skills and knowledge.' Measured on a 7-point scale (mean 4.83).

variable_name: overall sales and marketing costs as a percentage of total sales revenue
description: Overall sales and marketing costs measured as a percentage of total sales revenue in 1997; the natural logarithm was used to compensate for the effects of a few firms with very high costs as a percentage of sales. Self-reported figures were validated against secondary sales cost data from the FAME data base.

variable_name: Social interaction, relationship quality, customer network ties (set of three)
description: Social capital in the key customer relationship was measured with three survey dimensions: social interaction (two statements), relationship quality or trust (three statements) and customer network ties (two statements), answered by managing directors of young technology-based firms. The three were modeled as separate predictors.

variable_name: Number of new products developed, technological distinctiveness, sales and marketing cost percentage (set of three)
description: Knowledge exploitation was operationalized as three outcome variables: the number of new products developed as a result of the key customer relationship, technological distinctiveness of the firm, and overall sales and marketing costs as a percentage of sales revenue. They were modeled as three separate dependent variables of knowledge acquisition.

The count of establishments of a particular type operating in a given year; the number of corporate units tallies the restaurants owned and operated by the franchiser. The variable is logged to account for decreasing returns to scale.

The count of establishments of a particular type operating in a given year; the number of franchise units counts the restaurants run by independent owner-operators. The variable is logged to account for decreasing returns to scale.

The number of states in which a chain operates provides the measure of geographic dispersion (environmental heterogeneity). This count is logged because the degree of heterogeneity likely exhibits decreasing marginal effects.

Sales in constant 1992 dollars provide the dependent variable for the growth models. Sales growth is used because franchising agreements typically maximize franchisers' earnings when their franchisees maximize sales.

The error term of the growth model is parameterized as a function of a vector of independent variables and a random term, giving simultaneous estimation of the mean and the variance using maximum likelihood. Factors that reduce risk generate negative coefficient estimates, while those that increase risk elicit positive effects on the variance.

Operationalized as the gross book value of depreciable assets per establishment for each venture's entered industry, consistent with the measure proposed by Koch (1974) and with the argument that economies of scale are strongly associated with large firm size as indicated by asset levels per establishment.
Operationalized as the gross book value of depreciable assets per employee for each venture's entered industry.

Operationalized as the advertising intensity ratio, i.e., advertising expenditures divided by sales revenue for each venture's entered industry. Following Robinson and McDougall's (1998) classification scheme, firms were grouped according to their industry's advertising intensity ratios, and industries with high and low degrees of product differentiation were then combined into one category representing high barriers to entry, while industries with moderate degrees of product differentiation comprised the category representing low barriers to entry.
scale: two categories (high or low vs. moderate advertising intensity)

variable_name: stage of the industry life cycle
description: Two researchers independently categorized the industry life cycle stage for each firm using information contained in each firm's IPO prospectus supplemented by industry growth rate information contained in Dun's Industry Norms and Key Business Ratios; initial agreement between the two raters was 87 percent. Because the sample had relatively few firms entering in the introductory or decline stages, the introductory and growth stages were combined into one category representing entry early in the life cycle, and the maturity and decline stages were combined into one category representing entry later in the life cycle.
scale: two categories (early vs. later life cycle stage)

description: Competitive scope was classified into three categories based upon the venture's breadth of product/market offerings as compared to its competitors: narrow-lower relative product/market offerings; intermediate-comparable product/market offerings; or broad-higher relative product/market offerings. Two researchers independently categorized the competitive scope for each firm using information contained in each venture's IPO statement, with initial agreement of 80 percent and differences resolved through discussion.

Operationalized by taking the average of ROS for the first three complete fiscal years following a venture's IPO. The logit transformation was utilized for the ROS variable, which is appropriate for data bound above and below such as percentages.
time_window: first three complete fiscal years following the IPO

description: Operationalized as the increase in stock price from the end of the first full fiscal year following the venture's IPO to the end of the fourth full fiscal year (as adjusted for stock splits) plus average dividends over the 3-year period. The measure was adjusted to reflect changes in the S&P 500 Index for comparable time periods for each venture, and the logarithmic transformation was utilized for this positively skewed variable.
time_window: from the end of the first full fiscal year following the IPO to the end of the fourth full fiscal year (3-year period)

description: Sales growth of each venture was operationalized as the average of annual sales growth over the first three complete fiscal years following the venture's IPO.
time_window: first three complete fiscal years after IPO

variable_name: Economies of scale, capital requirements and product differentiation (set of three)
description: Entry barriers were operationalized as three industry-level variables for each venture's entered 4-digit SIC industry: economies of scale (gross book value of depreciable assets per establishment), capital requirements (gross book value of depreciable assets per employee) and product differentiation (advertising intensity ratio). They were entered as separate predictors.

A 1-0 dummy variable equal to 1 for the 58 firms with a capitalization in the top, 4A category; the other 207 firms are treated as the omitted reference group. Capitalization was taken from the 1948 volume of Thomas' Register, or from the last volume in which a firm was listed as a radio producer if it was not listed in 1948; each TV entrant had the same capitalization at entry as in the 1948 volume.
time_window: 1948 (or last listing as a radio producer)

description: A 1-0 dummy equal to 1 for the 79 firms in either of the first two product categories of Thomas' Register: descriptions such as 'home', 'household receiver' or 'combination with phonograph' (interpreted as radios for the home), and receivers not designated as being for home use, which the authors suspect were also largely produced for the home. The remaining firms form the omitted reference group.
A 1-0 dummy equal to 1 for the 65 firms in the third category, firms without any description, which the authors interpret as typically producing (home) radios that required no further explanation.

The number of years the firm produced radios, computed by subtracting the year it was first listed in the Thomas' Register category 'Radio Apparatus: Complete Sets, Outfits, etc.' (started in the 1922 volume) from the last year it was listed in 1944-47. Values range from 0 to 25, with a mean of 6.6 and a median of 4.

A 1-0 dependent variable for entry into TV set production among the 265 firms listed as radio producers in the 1945-48 volumes of Thomas' Register; the Television Factbook listings indicate that 56 of the 265 entered. One radio producer that entered television manufacture by acquisition in 1949 was excluded as ambiguous.

Cox proportional hazards model of the annual hazard of entry for all 176 entrants into TVs over 1946-89, h_it = f(t)exp(b'x_i). The covariates are the 4A size dummy, the years of radio production variable, and a dummy equal to 1 for entrants that produced radios in 1945-48, which the authors interpret as measuring the effects of experience in producing home radios. Foreign firms entering U.S. production were excluded.

Cox proportional hazards model of the hazard of a firm exiting the industry in year t given survival to year t, estimated on the 134 firms that entered TVs by 1951 to avoid radio experience proxying for time of entry. Covariates are the 1-0 radio dummy, the 4A size dummy, and years producing radios; firms acquired by other TV producers were treated as censored exits. In a second specification the radio and size dummies are allowed to affect the hazard differently in 1948-54, 1955-64 and 1965-89.

variable_name: log of TV set market share
description: Three OLS regressions of the log of firm TV market share in 1951-53, 1959-60 and 1970 on the 4A dummy and years of radio production. Because market share data exist only for a few leading producers, almost all 4A prior radio producers, the radio dummy was inestimable and the analysis compares 4A radio producers with all other firms combined. Small firms with unreported market shares were assigned average values of the market share not allocated to specific firms, and only firms surviving in each year were included; the log was used to reduce skewness.

Levy's (1981) series on major product innovation through 1979, compiled from interviews with TV executives, in which each innovation is dated and attributed to one or more firms. The annual rate for each firm was computed by summing its number of innovations and dividing by the number of years it was a TV set producer for which innovation data were available.

A list the authors constructed by using the Industrial Arts Index (later Applied Science and Technology Index) to look up trade articles related to TV set manufacturing and examining them for references to new methods in TV set production; each innovation was classified by date and manufacturer(s) and given a 1-7 point subjective estimate of its impact on manufacturing costs. Of about 210 relevant indexed articles, 198 were obtained and analyzed, yielding 264 process innovations by U.S. firms, with credit divided evenly where multiple firms were credited. The focus is on years through 1957; annual rates divide the sum of innovations by years as a producer with data available.

The product and process innovations data were combined to compute an overall rate of innovation for each firm over the period 1948-79, used in the hazard model testing Hypothesis 5. The variable has a standard deviation of 0.85.

A rating developed by Willard (1982) for the 19 principal color TV producers he analyzed, assigning each firm a value of 0 to 3 based on expert opinion regarding its commitment to innovation. A second dummy variable equal to 1 for firms not rated by Willard, presumably the least committed to innovation among the producers in the color era, was included alongside the rating.

A multi-indicator factor model of the CEO's external directorate network built on CEO outside corporate directorships collected from proxy statements. Seven indicators were created: a simple count of the number of directorships held (span of the network); two prominence measures (the number of directorships with Fortune 1000 firms and the average net sales of each directorship held); the average profitability of each directorship, operationalized as return on equity; and three relational measures of centrality (degree, betweenness and closeness) computed with the UCINET network analysis program on a model of pairwise ties among all members of the Fortune 1000 and then matched to each CEO. When a CEO had multiple outside directorship ties, indicators reflect the mean score for all ties held by that person. Only corporate ties were coded.

CEO compensation was measured using Finkelstein and Boyd's (1998) two-indicator factor model using the logarithms of total cash compensation and long-term compensation. Long-term pay was valued using the discount valuation method. These data were drawn from proxy statements.
Diversification was measured using Palepu's (1985) dt entropy measure for total diversification. The COMPUSTAT business segment database and company 10-K reports were used to create this variable.

Strategic similarity was measured with three items from five-point scales: whether the businesses sold to similar customers, operated in similar geographic markets, and competed directly with each other. The three dimensions are customers, geographic markets, and competition.

A set of items measured the magnitude of resource redeployment to the target along four resource dimensions: product innovation, manufacturing know-how, marketing expertise, and brand redeployment. A five-point scale measured the magnitude of resource redeployment along each dimension, and the responses along the four resource dimensions were combined to create the variable.

A set of items measured the magnitude of resource redeployment to the acquirer along four resource dimensions: product innovation, manufacturing know-how, marketing expertise, and brand redeployment. A five-point scale measured the magnitude of resource redeployment along each dimension, and the responses along the four resource dimensions were combined to create the variable.

Four items based on Datta's categorization and scale of resources that firms tend to divest following acquisitions, using seven-category response scales for percentage reductions of each type of resource. The four items recorded percentage reduction of facilities and workforce for manufacturing, distribution, sales networks, and administrative services for the targets. Each item represents the mean values on each dimension for the target.
scale: seven-category response scale for percentage reductions

description: Four items based on Datta's categorization and scale of resources that firms tend to divest following acquisitions, using seven-category response scales for percentage reductions of each type of resource. The four items recorded percentage reduction of facilities and workforce for manufacturing, distribution, sales networks, and administrative services for the acquirers. Each item represents the mean values on each dimension for the acquirer.
scale: seven-category response scale for percentage reductions

description: The resource asymmetry variable combined four items: product innovativeness, manufacturing know-how, commercial dynamism, and product quality. It is a latent variable of the structural model and is entered as an influence on resource redeployment.

variable_name: extent of direct competition (structural equivalence matrix in terms of customer overlap)
description: Computed as structural equivalence between pairs of the 100 supplier banks based on their patterns of ties with all 4088 customer banks, creating a 100 x 4088 matrix of ties. Pearson product-moment correlation was used for each pair of customer profiles to obtain a correlation coefficient in each cell of the 100 x 100 structural equivalence matrix. A high correlation between a pair of banks on their customer profiles indicates that they compete directly for business from many of the same customer banks.

Four dimensions of alertness were computed for each of the 100 supplier banks and standardized with z-scores: extensiveness of information scanning (number of different banks called), global scope (number of different countries called), maintenance of multiple weak ties, and probability of bridging structural holes. A dissimilarity matrix for each pair of banks was created by computing the Euclidean distance between them using all four variables. The greater the number in each cell, the greater the dissimilarity between the two banks on alertness.

The number of outgoing conversations initiated by each supplier bank for each of the 24 hours was correlated with market volatility for each hour, yielding a correlation coefficient for each bank that reflects its speed of response to market volatility. Market volatility was measured as the standard deviation of the variation in the bid dollar-mark prices for each of the 24 hours. The correlation coefficient was used to create a dissimilarity matrix in terms of the Euclidean distances between pairs of banks on this variable.
scale: Euclidean distance on hourly correlation coefficients

description: A matrix of shared country of location was created by coding the cell between each pair of banks as '1' if the banks were located in the same country and '0' otherwise. The 100 supplier banks were located in 24 countries.

The locations of the banks were divided into three time zones on the basis of countries that were 4 hours or more away from Greenwich Mean Time, roughly an Asian, a European and an American time zone. The cell between each pair of banks was coded '1' if the banks were located in the same time zone and '0' otherwise.

variable_name: shared location in a primary cluster
description: Primary cluster was operationalized as a dummy variable with value 1 if the bank was located in London, New York or Tokyo. A matrix of shared location in a cluster was created from these data, coding each pair of banks '1' if both were located in any of the primary clusters.

Established scale (see Narver and Slater, 1990) used to measure market orientation. It is composed of three first-order components: competitor orientation (CO), customer orientation (CU), and interfunctional coordination (INT). Responses were given on seven-point Likert scales anchored by 'strongly disagree' and 'strongly agree'.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: Five items from Naman and Slevin's (1993) entrepreneurship scale. The items are: 'We believe that wide-ranging acts are necessary to achieve our objectives'; 'we initiate actions to which other organizations respond'; 'we are fast to introduce new products and services to the marketplace'; 'we have a strong proclivity for high risk projects'; and 'we are bold in our efforts to maximize the probability of exploiting opportunities'. Seven-point Likert scales anchored by 'strongly disagree' and 'strongly agree' were used.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: Established scale used to measure innovativeness (see Hurley and Hult, 1998). The items focus on the degree to which the SBU encourages the introduction of new ideas and processes, i.e., the 'openness to innovation' aspects of the innovation process. Seven-point Likert scales anchored by 'strongly disagree' and 'strongly agree' were used.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: Established scale used to measure organizational learning (see Hult, 1998; Hult et al., 2000). It involves the development of new knowledge in the MNC's SBUs, which is generated and disseminated throughout the MNC to achieve a greater degree of shared knowledge among the participants. Seven-point Likert scales anchored by 'strongly disagree' and 'strongly agree' were used.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: A higher-order latent variable estimated in LISREL with the four capabilities (market orientation, entrepreneurship, innovativeness, and organizational learning) as first-order indicators. It is the latent, intangible construct through which the four capabilities are related to performance.

Five-year average change in return-on-investment, one of three objective performance indicators. The data pertained to the years 1995-1999. ROI5 is a measure of the SBU's performance, as each SBU is directly responsible for its own performance.

Five-year percentage change in income, one of three objective performance indicators. The data pertained to the years 1995-1999. INCOME5 is a measure of the SBU's performance, as each SBU is directly responsible for its own performance.

Five-year percentage change in stock price, one of three objective performance indicators. The data pertained to the years 1995-1999. STOCK5 is a measure of the firm's performance, reflecting the SBU's contribution to the overall performance of the firm.

A dummy variable set equal to 1 if product i is a new name brand and 0 otherwise, i.e., if it is an extension. For the purposes of measurement only the product and not the firm name is used in determining whether a product is an extension or a new name brand.

variable_name: first year real dollar advertising expense (AD)
description: Real dollar advertising spent on new product i during its first full year on the market, measured in thousands of dollars. The reported annual figure was divided by the number of months the cereal had been available and then annualized; for cereals introduced during the last two months of the year the next calendar year's advertising data were used.
time_window: first full year on the market

description: The long-run average of the market size divided by the number of products in segment s over the two prior periods. Because the fixed cost of introducing a brand regionally may differ, the number of products is set equal to the number of nationally advertised products, so the ratio measures the fixed cost of introducing a nationally advertised brand.
time_window: average over the two prior periods

description: The market share of the product that is just profitable, proxied by the product with the lowest pound sales (and separately the lowest dollar sales) that survived in the market for at least 5 consecutive years, following the survivor test. Products with sales below either of these levels are too low to cover fixed costs; the estimates ranged between 1 and 7 percent of market size depending on the segment.
time_window: at least 5 consecutive years of survival

description: Lagged market size multiplied by the expected market growth rate, where the expected market growth rate for segment s at time t is assumed to equal the average growth rate of the last three periods.
time_window: average growth rate of the last three periods

description: The dollar or pound size of the market, entered in the entry models in lagged form. The authors estimate the models separately with pound and with dollar market size variables.

A latent variable set equal to 0 if there is no entry in segment s, 1 if an extension is introduced, and 2 if a new name brand is introduced in the segment. In the two-option entry model it is set equal to 1 if a firm enters segment s at time t and 0 otherwise. When a manager chose to enter with both an extension and a new name brand, whether the earliest product entry was an extension or new name brand determined the coding.

Using the average values of the independent variables and the estimated coefficients of the multinomial logit model, the authors compute the probability of no entry, extension entry and new-name entry; conditional on entry, the probability that an extension is introduced is used as evidence that extensions enter when new-name entry is unprofitable and thus preempt subsequent entry.

Abnormal return refers to the difference between the stock market return associated with the announcement of the firm's participation in a JV (actual return) and the firm's historical return (normal return). The abnormal return on day t for each firm i was computed as ARit = Rit - (ai + bi/Rmt), with ai and bi estimated from the market model appraised over a 200-day period beginning 51 days before the announcement. For each firm, abnormal returns were cumulated over a 2-day announcement period comprising the announcement day and the following day.

Partner-venture business relatedness was measured in terms of similarity between the firm's and the venture's products, markets, manufacturing technologies, and science-based research. The study's first author scored relatedness on a 5-point scale (1 = least related; 5 = most related) for each of these four dimensions; the sum of these scores constituted the relatedness variable.
scale: 5-point scale per dimension (1 = least related, 5 = most related), summed

description: Partner-partner business relatedness was measured in terms of similarity between the partners' products, markets, manufacturing technologies, and science-based research. The study's first author scored relatedness on a 5-point scale (1 = least related; 5 = most related) for each of these four dimensions; the sum of these scores constituted the relatedness variable. Four objective SIC-based measures of business relatedness were also constructed to ascertain validity, but the subjective measures were used in the empirical analysis.
scale: 5-point scale per dimension (1 = least related, 5 = most related), summed

description: A firm's previous JV experience was operationalized in terms of the frequency of a firm's participation in international JVs during the period beginning 1986 until the time of the firm's JV formation announcement. Higher frequencies denoted greater JV experience, and vice versa.
time_window: from 1986 until the JV formation announcement

description: Relative partner size was operationalized as the negative logarithmic value of the absolute difference between the number of employees of a JV's partners. A logarithmic scale was used to reduce the variance in partners' size, and the scale was multiplied by (-1) so that higher values indicated greater similarity between the firm sizes of a JV's partners.

Cultural relatedness between international JV partners was operationalized in terms of the Kogut and Singh (1988) index, defined as the negative, cumulated deviation between variance-adjusted culture scores of a venture's partners. The variance-adjusted scores are inverted so that higher values indicate greater relatedness between partners' national cultures.

Political risk in JV host countries was operationalized in terms of 'transfer risk', even though political risk is a multidimensional construct, such that higher values denoted greater host country political risk. Data were obtained from annual scores reported in the Planning Review.

The level of competition faced by U.S. partners in their core business was constructed as a set of two dichotomous variables: LOCOMP = 1 if competitive pressures on a firm were low, and 0 otherwise; HICOMP = 1 if competitive pressures on a firm were high, and 0 otherwise. The variables were built by content analysis of descriptive information provided in Value Line reports for the quarter preceding the JV announcement, analyzed for negative and positive indicators of competitive pressures. Where the tone of an analyst's report was nonmonotonic, both variables assumed zero values, which defines the base category.

Firm-level R&D intensity minus industry-level U.S. R&D intensity matched with each specific line of business, defined at the 3-digit SIC level. R&D intensity was defined by firm-level expenditures on R&D deflated by total sales, measured at time t-1 of the investment. Because line of business spending on R&D was difficult to gather, firm-level R&D intensity was substituted, assuming firm-level spending contributes equally to technological knowledge in each line of business.
level: entry (firm matched to 3-digit SIC line of business)

description: Dummy variable indicating whether the entry into the United States took place in a new line of business for the firm.
