Based on line of business information at the 3-digit SIC level, entries in a new line of business were assigned a value of one while entries in incumbent lines were left as zero.

Composite index of cultural distance formed by calculating the squared terms of the deviation of the cultural index of each country from the United States for each of Hofstede's four indices (Power Distance, Individualism, Uncertainty Avoidance, and Masculinity), then taking the square root of the sum of the four squared deviation terms. A similar composite index was used by Kogut and Singh (1988).
level: home country of the investing firm

description: Dummy variables built from Ronen and Shenkar's nine cultural groups, which the authors used to supplement Hofstede's indices. The home countries in the sample were divided into five groups: the United Kingdom in the Anglo cluster; Japan in the Far Eastern cluster; Germany and Switzerland in the Germanic cluster; France, Italy, and Belgium in the Latin European cluster; and Norway, Sweden, Denmark, and Finland in the Nordic group. The Germanic cluster is the reference group and dummy variables are created for the four others.
level: home country of the investing firm

description: Preinvestment experience of international experience, operationalized as the ratio of sales in the North American region to total sales, measured at time t-1 of investment. Because of inconsistencies in the way firms report geographic sales, the measure captures sales in the North American region, which includes Canada as well as the United States.

Categorical dependent variable with three outcomes: greenfield investment (setting up a new plant or other establishment from scratch), acquisition (purchase of a controlling interest in a local firm), and joint venture (pooling of assets of two or more firms in a common and separate organization). Greenfield investment is the reference option in the multinomial logit model, so coefficients describe the relative risk of acquisition or joint venture versus greenfield.

variable_name: Subsequent entry vs. first firm entry
description: Dummy variable distinguishing entries in Sample B and Sample C from entries in Sample A in the whole sample, capturing whether firms with prior entry experience have different preferences toward entry modes than firms without prior entry experience. The sequence of entry is also used to split the data into Sample A (first entry for the firm in manufacturing during the study period), Sample B (first entries in each line of business other than the firm's first entry), and Sample C (all subsequent entries in lines of business).

variable_name: First Firm Mode Acquisition, First Firm Mode Joint Venture
description: Two dummy variables identifying whether the first entry at the firm level was an acquisition or a joint venture. Together with the two line-of-business dummies, they were devised to reflect how the earlier choice of entry mode can shape the mode of later entries; two of the four dummies were used for Sample B and all four for Sample C.
time_window: first entry in the study period

variable_name: First LOB Mode Acquisition, First LOB Mode Joint Venture
description: Two dummy variables identifying whether the first entry at the line of business level was an acquisition or a joint venture. They were used together with the firm-level dummies to test the tendency of subsequent entries in a line of business to use the same mode as the first entry in that line of business.
time_window: first entry in that line of business

description: Each business unit was rated on the Shortell and Zajac orientation toward change scale, on which Defenders are coded '1' (low orientation towards change), Analyzers '2' (the midpoint) and Prospectors '3' (high orientation towards change). The ratings were based on a combination of expert interviews and archival sources covering criteria such as orientation towards new products and innovation, stage in the life cycle, market context, investment allocations, orientation toward costs and strategic objectives; a co-author independently classified the divisions and the scores were reviewed and vetted by key decision-makers within the firm.
scale: 1 = Defender, 2 = Analyzer, 3 = Prospector. Direction: higher = more prospector (defender to prospector scale)

description: Position in the hierarchy was coded as a continuous variable ranging from 0 (Employees) to 7 (Managing Director). Both companies used the same hierarchical structure with identical levels and designations. The authors chose a continuous variable over dummy indicators because the latter are less parsimonious, less powerful and more problematic in the study of interaction effects. Data were obtained from company records.

Total base salary taken from personnel records, with a log transform applied to normalize the distribution. Base salary is reported in the tables in relative numbers (base = 100 for strategic orientation 'Defender' at hierarchical level '1').

Total bonus pay taken from personnel records. Archival measures of pay free the study from nonrespondent or common method bias; bonus is reported in the tables in relative numbers only, for confidentiality reasons.
The degree of leverage, defined as the ratio of bonus to base pay, computed from the two archival compensation variables.

The tenure of the head of production for each studio, measured as the number of years since his appointment to that position. Information was obtained from several accounts of the histories of the major studios. Because studios could only have a single production head at any given time, the measure allows each studio head's performance to be assessed for each year.

The sum of the absolute values of the interyear differences in the percentage of films made in each genre. The percentage of films in each genre is the number of films made in each genre divided by the number of films made by that studio in that year. It reflects all of the shifts in the distribution of films across genres and is the broadest measure of experimentation.

A count of the number of new film genres that a firm takes on in a given year. To rule out trivial departures in the film mix, a genre was counted as new only if it included at least two films for the year, and a new genre was defined as one in which the studio had not made any films in the prior year.

variable_name: percentage of films in new genres (PCNEW)
description: The total number of films in all genres that had not been used in the previous year by the studio, expressed as a percentage of the total number of films produced by that studio in that year. It indicates the relative emphasis placed on films in new genres.

An annual measure of average profits per film for each studio, used to evaluate the performance of each studio head for each year. Because profits are to some extent a function of production costs, the authors controlled for production costs as an independent variable rather than expressing profits as a fraction of costs. Data on production costs, sales and profits were obtained from Moody's Industrial Manuals and company financial reports, adjusted for the consumer price index, and adjusted to reflect only film production and distribution for studios in other businesses.

A sample of 114 '.com' name changes was obtained by examining announcements in newswires and newspapers. Private companies, non-'.com' name changes, firms not public prior to the change, changes from one '.com' name to another, product- or subsidiary-level changes, announcements with confounding events in a three-day window and cases without available returns were deleted, leaving 59 unique announcements. The exact announcement date was pinpointed using multiple sources.

Abnormal returns are computed using the Nasdaq Composite Index and the Nasdaq Computer Index as benchmarks and are additionally adjusted by subtracting an equally weighted portfolio return for all firms in the same 4-digit SIC code excluding sample firms. Returns are cumulated over a three-day (-1, +1) window around the announcement. Because many firms are thinly traded, non-parametric generalized sign and rank tests are used, and median returns are emphasized over means.

The average trading volume in the pre-event period (days -100 to -10) is compared to the event-period volume for each firm, and a ratio of event-period volume to non-event-period trading volume is calculated. Under the null hypothesis of no change in trading volume this ratio equals one. T-tests and Wilcoxon rank tests are used to test whether the mean or median differs from one, and medians are emphasized because extreme values influence the means.
time_window: event days -1, 0 and +1 versus pre-event days -100 to -10

description: A dummy variable coded 0 for image-only name changes and 1 for other strategies, based on coding of press releases and articles, quarterly reports and company websites in the year prior to the name change. Name changes preceded by internet-related acquisitions, closings of retail outlets, or alliances with other internet firms were classified as strategic name changes; those with no such detectable activity were classified as image only. Two raters coded all cases and agreed on 50 of the 61 cases, an interrater reliability of 82%.
time_window: year prior to the name change

description: Acquisitions were classified into those that involved firms with overlapping business units and those that did not, at the 4-digit SIC code level. This classification produced the 'overlapping' (consolidation-oriented) and 'no overlapping' (diversification-oriented) categories compared in the analysis.

A second classification checked whether the acquiring and target firms were both in defense-dependent industries. Defense-dependent industries were identified from data compiled by the Department of Defense, and the sample of acquisitions was divided into defense-defense acquisitions and defense-civilian acquisitions.

variable_name: abnormal stock market returns (cumulative abnormal returns)
description: Risk-adjusted returns computed with the market model, estimated over 250 days (-800 to -551 relative to the announcement) and then used to subtract expected returns from actual returns during a window around the event; the daily abnormal returns are added up to obtain cumulative abnormal returns. Results are reported for a 3-day window because results from a 3-day and a 5-day window were identical. Significance is tested by standardizing individual securities' abnormal returns with their standard errors and summing them.
time_window: 3-day window around the acquisition announcement (-1 to +1)

variable_name: pretax operating cash flows normalized by the market value of assets
description: Operating cash flows are sales, minus cost of goods sold and selling and administrative expenses, plus depreciation and goodwill expenses, normalized by the market value of assets (book values of debt are used instead of market values). Each year's data were adjusted by the average profitability and cash flow figures of the industry. Up to 5 years of data were used for the pre- and post-acquisition values, year 0 being the year of the acquisition.
time_window: -5 to -1 and 1 to 5 relative to the acquisition year

description: Acquisitions are assigned to the growth period (1978-86) or the decline period (1987-92) of the defense sector, and the performance measures of the two periods are compared.

variable_name: number of business units in the firm
description: Firms were disaggregated into categories representing different levels of scope, formed on the basis of the number of business units in which the firm was active. The reported breakdowns contrast single-segment and multisegment firms.

Computed following Lindenberg and Ross (1981) with additional approximations: the year-end market value of the firm is the sum of the market values of common stock, preferred stock and debt, with the market value of common stock computed as outstanding shares times price per share and the market values of debt and preferred stock approximated by their book values. Replacement costs of net plant, equipment and inventories are obtained with Lindenberg and Ross's algorithm, adjusting for price level changes, depreciation and technological changes, with annual depreciation, the inventory valuation method and the GNP deflator taken into account. It is used in cross-sectional comparisons of levels rather than changes over time.

A dummy variable set to 0 when firms had headquarters in Japan or Germany (i.e., bank-based system) and to 1 if companies were headquartered in the United States or the United Kingdom (i.e., market-based system). For the models incorporating the corporate governance systems, the bank-based system was used as the basis for comparison.

variable_name: country dummies (Japan, Germany, the United Kingdom, the United States)
description: Three dummy variables indicating whether the sampled firm was headquartered in Japan, Germany, the United Kingdom, or the United States, used to analyze governance effects by country rather than by each system. Japan was used as the base for comparisons.

Constructed as the percentage of the number of rivals that invested simultaneously in a product-market during an observation year. It tests whether firms are more likely to invest when they see more of their rivals investing, regardless of how much capacity these rivals are adding.
Measures the percentage of total capacity that was added simultaneously by rivals, directly measuring the amount of capacity added by rivals.

A binary choice measure set equal to 1 for all observations where firm i expanded in a particular product-market either by adding a new greenfield plant or by expanding one or more of its plants' production capacity by more than 5 percent, and otherwise. De-bottlenecking was excluded from the total set of capacity expansions because it does not represent a major, discrete investment.

A proxy for free cash flow: the average of the log of net corporate profits in the 2 years prior to the observation year, taking into account the lead time in capacity expansion. Data on divisional performance and on corporate cash flow were scarce across the financial databases used, which is why the proxy was adopted.
time_window: 2 years prior to the observation year

variable_name: Rivals' simultaneous investment (RIVAL1, RIVAL2) and their interactions with governance system
description: Bandwagon behavior is captured by the effect of rivals' simultaneous investment on a firm's probability of expanding capacity in a product-market. RIVAL1 is the percentage of rivals that invested in the same product-market during the observation year and RIVAL2 is the percentage of total capacity added simultaneously by rivals. They were interacted with the governance system dummy in the expansion model.

Dummy variable for the vertical scope of alliance activities, created from information in the SDC database. SCOPE is set to one when alliance activities include manufacturing and/or marketing in addition to collaborative R&D, and zero for alliances involving R&D activities exclusively.
Dummy variable for alliance governance mode, created from information in the SDC database. GOVERNANCE equals 0 when the alliance is organized by contract and 1 when organized by equity joint venture.

Simple measure capturing whether allying firms have their primary operations in the same industry. MARKET OVERLAP is set to 1 if both partner firms have their primary operations in the same 4-digit SIC code and 0 otherwise; for multilateral alliances it is set to 1 if at least two of the partner firms have the same primary 4-digit SIC.

Dummy variable coded 1 for alliances involving firms headquartered in the same country and 0 if allying firms are headquartered in different nations. It is used to proxy for geographic market competition, on the assumption that firms headquartered in the same country perceive each other to be more direct competitors.

Dummy variable based on the 1997 Red Herring listing of the Top 100 Technology Companies, which represents the leading public and private technology firms in the editors' opinion. LAGGARDS equals one if none of the alliance partners appear in the Red Herring list of top technology companies, and zero otherwise.

Each partner firm's technological portfolio is generated by measuring the distribution across patent classifications of the patents applied for in the 4 years prior to alliance formation, captured by a multidimensional vector where each element is the number of patents assigned to the firm in a patent class. The extent of overlap is then computed from these vectors: the measure normalizes the length of the within-class vectors to one and captures the angle between the firm vectors. It varies from zero (no overlap in partner firms' areas of technological expertise) to one (complete overlap) and is not sensitive to the total number of a firm's patents within a class. For alliances involving more than two firms, the measure is calculated for every combinatorial pair and averaged.
level: alliance (firm pair, averaged for multilateral alliances)

description: Count of each firm's pharmaceutical patents granted in the 10 years prior to the launch of the new product that are assigned to the same therapeutic area as the new product introduction. USPTO therapeutic subclasses within Class 514 were mapped onto the IMS therapeutic areas to build the variable. One was added to each count and the variable was log-transformed to correct for its skewed distribution.
time_window: 10 years prior to the launch of the new product

description: Count of each firm's pharmaceutical patents granted in the 10 years prior to the launch of the new product that are assigned to therapeutic areas other than the one of the new product introduction. Built from the same USPTO Class 514 patent data and IMS mapping scheme as proximal technological experience. One was added to each count and the variable was log-transformed to correct for its skewed distribution.
time_window: 10 years prior to the launch of the new product

description: Total product years of market experience that the introducing firm accumulated in the focal therapeutic area in the 10 years prior to a new product's introduction. A firm is considered to have more experience if it has produced and sold more products, and if those products have been on the market for longer periods of time. The count (plus one) was logged to account for its skewed distribution.
time_window: 10 years prior to the launch of the new product

description: Total product years of market experience that the introducing firm accumulated in therapeutic areas other than the focal area in the 10 years prior to a new product's introduction. A firm is considered to have more experience if it has produced and sold more products, and if those products have been on the market for longer periods of time. The count (plus one) was logged to account for its skewed distribution.
time_window: 10 years prior to the launch of the new product

description: Total sales of a new product in its first full year on the market. Because the sample of introductions covers a 6-year window, each sales figure was converted into 1986 dollars using the annual pharmaceutical producer price index obtained from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Because its distribution is highly skewed, the real sales variable was log-transformed to generate the dependent variable.
time_window: first full year on the market

description: The dependent variable is whether a transfer event occurred between a focal project team in the local subsidiary and one of the other 40 subsidiaries. The project manager indicated the percentages of a project's total hardware and software and the percentage of the project's total technical know-how and information that came from other subsidiaries, and which subsidiary the transfer involved. The variable was dichotomized, set to 1 if the project manager reported a transfer from another specified subsidiary and 0 otherwise. In all, 54 of the 121 project teams experienced between one or three transfer events, with a total of 87 such events.

A dyadic variable that took a value of 1 if there was a match between at least one competence listed by the target subsidiary and the focal team, and zero otherwise. A list of 22 technological competencies in which one or more subsidiaries had developed a particular competence was generated with three senior corporate R&D managers; the R&D managers of each of the 41 subsidiaries indicated their subsidiary's competencies on the list and the project managers of the 121 projects indicated which competencies the project required. Of the 4840 dyads, 42 percent were coded as having related competencies.

Measured as the number of direct air miles between the city where the office of the project team was located and the city of the target subsidiary in the dyad. The measure was logged because individuals most likely do not perceive that the burdens of travel increase linearly with air miles. The shortest dyadic distance was 0 (located on the same site) and the longest was 10,512 miles, with a median value of 1072 miles.

Constructed from the cultural indices developed by Hofstede, following prior measures by Kogut and Singh and Barkema and Vermeulen: the differences in the five national attributes between pairs of relevant countries were computed and the Euclidean distance was calculated, with each index divided by the variance of that index across all countries in the sample. The measure assigns to a subsidiary the national cultural characteristics of the country in which it is located and computes the distance between focal and target subsidiaries in a dyad, and was set to zero if the dyad did not cross national borders. Among international dyads the smallest cultural distance was 0.4 and the largest 4.9, with a mean of 0.95.
Recorded whether the office of the focal project team and the location of the target subsidiary were located in different countries. Of all the dyads, 48.3 percent crossed national borders.

A three-level measure of formal proximity constructed from the two hierarchical levels in the company: 0, only integrated at the top (President's office); 1, integrated at the business group level; and 2, integrated at the division level. Of all the dyads, 72 percent were at level 0, 25 percent at level 1, and the remaining 3 percent at level 2. An alternative measure denoted whether the focal team and the target subsidiary were in the same business group (scored 1) or not (scored 0).

Obtained from the network survey to the R&D managers, who were asked: 'Over the past 2 years, are there any units [subsidiaries] from whom your unit [subsidiary] regularly sought technical and/or market-related input?' The R&D manager also reported how many years each relation had been in existence, and only relations that had existed prior to the start of a focal product development project were included. Of all the dyads, 12 percent had an informal relation.
time_window: Relations existing prior to the start of the focal project

description: A 0-1 variable which equals 1 if a subsidiary that existed but did not do any R&D at time t-1 does R&D at time t. 328 of the 989 affiliates were assigned R&D responsibilities during the time window 1990-96.

variable_name: U.S. MNCs' host country R&D (MNC spillover variable)
description: The lagged sum of all R&D conducted in the same country and industry as the focal subsidiary by other U.S. MNC subsidiaries. The variable was constructed out of the sample by using BEA data on the entire population of U.S. MNC subsidiaries in each country-industry. A log transformation is used to mitigate heteroscedasticity.

The lagged sum of all R&D conducted by firms in the host country, other than U.S. MNCs, in the industry of the focal subsidiary. It is constructed by subtracting from the total R&D expenditures the R&D conducted by subsidiaries of U.S. MNCs; data on the R&D activities of local firms come from the OECD ANBERD database. A log transformation is used.

variable_name: interfirm dispersion of U.S. MNCs' host country R&D
description: Measured as 1 - sum of squared p_i, where p_i is each subsidiary's proportion of total R&D in the same country and industry as the focal subsidiary by all U.S. MNCs. The measure can range from 0 (extreme concentration of R&D) to 1 (extreme dispersion of R&D). It is constructed only for U.S. MNCs' R&D because firm-level data on the R&D activities of other firms in each host country are unavailable.
Measured as the lagged proportion of the subsidiary's total sales revenues which are derived from sales in the host country.
Constructed as the lagged sum of the MNC's direct and indirect ownership share in the focal subsidiary. Parent MNCs have, on average, a 98 percent ownership stake in the subsidiaries.

variable_name: increase in the MNC's ownership stake
description: A dummy variable which equals 1 if the MNC's ownership stake in the focal subsidiary increases between time t-1 and time t; otherwise it is zero. In 2 percent of the cases (i.e., 46 cases) parents increased their ownership stake during the period under study.
Measured as the lagged sum of exports and imports between the MNC's U.S. operations and its foreign subsidiaries divided by the total sales of the U.S. operations.

The lagged count of the MNC's foreign subsidiaries which already have R&D responsibilities. The square of this variable is also included to test for an inverted-U shaped relationship. Parent MNCs have, on average, about 10 foreign R&D units.

The number of successful semiconductor patents applied for by the subsidiary in a given year t. Patents are allocated to the MNC based on the ownership of the patents (assignees) and within an MNC to specific subsidiaries based on the geographic location of the inventors. Patent counts were computed only for semiconductor patents, classified using USPTO technology class information; 20 broad technology classes covering the semiconductor spectrum were used. The patent application date of successful patents indicates the year of innovation, and the counts were adjusted by a yearly factor based on total semiconductor patents filed, with 1981 as the base.

The number of patents successfully applied for by the MNC as a percentage of total worldwide semiconductor patents applied for in year t - 1. It is calculated as the number of semiconductor patents applied for by MNC i in year t - 1 divided by the total number of semiconductor patents applied for in year t - 1, times 100, using the 53,062 patents belonging to each MNC.

The number of patents successfully applied for by the host country as a percentage of total worldwide semiconductor patents applied for in year t - 1, constructed from the 197,796 patents belonging to each of the host countries in the 1981-92 period.

An index measuring the distribution of the MNC's patents for every year across the 20 semiconductor classes, where the firm is located in a multidimensional technology space captured by a K-dimensional vector of the fraction of its patents in each patent class. The printed formula (MNC diversity = 1 - [(sum over k of fikt-1)...]) is not fully readable in the text. The measure ranges from 0 to 1: 0 indicates complete concentration in a single technology class and 1 indicates maximum diversity of innovations across the technology classes.

An index analogous to MNC diversity, constructed from the proportion of the host country's patents in each semiconductor class in year t - 1. The measure ranges from 0 to 1: 0 indicates complete concentration in a single technology class and 1 indicates maximum diversity of innovations across the technology classes; the printed formula is not fully readable.

variable_name: Subsidiary knowledge linkages with the MNC
description: The number of other subsidiaries in the MNC cited by the subsidiary in year t - 1, built from the 1,250 patents cited by every original patent filed by the subsidiary in the sample (cited patents filed 1971-92).

variable_name: Subsidiary knowledge linkages with the host country
description: The number of host country firms cited by the subsidiary in year t - 1, built from the patent citations of the subsidiary's original patents.

Experience in a given context for firm i in year t is defined as the sum over years from the start year to year t minus one of the number of new drugs discovered by and launched in that context. Experience in 'Old Japan' increments from 1960 to 1980 and then ceases to increment thereafter. The historical experience of firms from 1960 to 1981 is used in the cross-section to predict innovative capability.

Cumulative overseas experience of the firm in the Southern European or 'Catholic' group of countries (Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, and Switzerland), computed as the sum of discoveries launched in those countries. These nations are argued to be the ones most 'proximate' to Japan.

Cumulative overseas experience of the firm in the Anglo-Nordic or 'Protestant' group of countries (Australia, Canada, Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and the United States), computed as the sum of discoveries launched in those countries. These markets are 'distant' from Japan in institutional terms.

variable_name: Southern European vs. Anglo-Nordic grouping of foreign markets
description: The 13 sample nations foreign to Japan are split into an Anglo-Nordic or 'Protestant' group and a Southern European or 'Catholic' group. The Southern European nations are argued to be more 'proximate' to Japan than the more stringently regulated Anglo-Nordic nations, based on premarket regulation, drug spending, polypharmacy, and side-effect reporting.

The number of new drugs discovered by the firm, counted cumulatively for 1982 to 1995 and analysed as a single normally distributed random variable. Innovations are disaggregated into local drugs (never launched outside Japan), mid-diffusion drugs (launched in two to five countries) and global drugs (launched in five or more foreign nations out of a possible 13).

Corporate sales data are used to measure the extent of corporate operations outside the focal industry of ethical pharmaceuticals. Firms are described as significantly diversified when ethical pharmaceutical sales range from 35 to 65 percent of corporate sales; for example, only about 65 percent of Tanabe's corporate sales are in ethical pharmaceuticals.

The age of each of the 38 firms is computed using the first year of discovery of any new drug as the birth year for the firm. The oldest firm in the sample is Tanabe Seiyaku, founded in 1678 as a wholesale pharmacy.

Experience in the pre-1981 domestic Japanese context: for firm i and year t it is the sum over years from the start year to year t minus one of new drugs discovered by and launched in that context. It increments from 1960 to 1980 and then ceases to increment, and in the panel the historical experience of each firm up to year T minus one is used to predict innovations in year T.

Experience in the domestic Japanese context after the 1981 change in the institutional environment: it is zero until 1980 and then increments from 1981 to 1995 as the firm's discoveries are launched in Japan. The domestic context in Japan changed fundamentally after 1981, so the sample period was split in 1981 to distinguish the old and new contexts.

Experience overseas for firm i in year t in the Southern European or 'Catholic' markets (Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, and Switzerland), calculated as the sum of the firm's discoveries launched in those countries. In the panel this variable is expressed in logarithms.

Experience overseas for firm i in year t in the Anglo-Nordic or 'Protestant' markets (Australia, Canada, Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and the United States), calculated as the sum of the firm's discoveries launched in those countries.

The annual number of new drugs discovered by firm i in year t, denoted N it, treated as a Poisson-like discrete random variable drawn from the linear exponential family. The variable is highly skewed, with most firms discovering no new drugs, and its variance is heteroskedastic, with means and variances positively related.

Corporate operations outside the focal industry of ethical pharmaceuticals, measured from corporate sales and diversification data. In the panel this variable is expressed in logarithms and enters in interaction with domestic and Southern European experience.

Measured as the average number of prior-art patents cited by a firm in its patents each year. Firms that cite many patents as precursors of their own inventions are likely to be working in relatively well-exploited areas of technology and more likely to face technology exhaustion. Four lagged versions reflecting period t, t-1, t-2 and t-3 values were constructed.

The average number of scientific non-patent references in the firm's patents that year: total number of scientific publications cited by a firm's patents in year t+1 divided by the number of patents obtained by the firm in the same year. Non-patent citations were categorized into scientific books, journal articles, conference proceedings, technical documents and commercial documents; only the first three categories are used. Citations to non-scientific documents such as commercial brochures, patents and standards are excluded. This variable is also used as an independent variable predicting firm innovation, in count form as the total number of journals, books and conference proceedings in the previous year.

Measured through the firm's patenting across nations each year, using Blau's index of diversity, computed as one minus the sum over countries of the squared proportion of the firm's patents in each country. High scores indicate geographically more diverse search. For Hypothesis 2 the difference between period t+1 and period t values of the index is used; in predicting firm innovation the variable is used in levels form. Geographic location is determined by the location of the inventor documented in the patent, using the first inventor when there are several.

The number of countries in which each sample firm has a presence through either a subsidiary or an affiliate company, recorded in the annual editions of the Who Owns Whom directories and collected yearly from 1982 to 1992. Because Hypothesis 2 predicts that changes in presence lead to changes in search, the difference between period t and period t-1 values of the presence variable is used as international product-market change; four alternative lagged versions (t to t-1, t-1 to t-2, t-2 to t-3, t-3 to t-4) were computed.
time_window: 1982-1992; t-1 to t changes and four lags

description: Measured as the number of successful patent applications, or granted patents, for firm i in year t+1. Following the standard innovation production function approach, the count of inventions is modeled as an outcome of total inputs such as R&D.

A centralization scale that increases with overall R&D centralization, coded 1 = decentralized; 2 = decentralized hybrid; 3 = balanced hybrid; 4 = centralized hybrid; 5 = centralized. The authors note the measure implicitly assumes that the distance between each adjacent organization form is the same, but it has the advantage of ease of interpretation. Hybrids were classified by the ratio of corporate to divisional researchers estimated from the Directory of American Research and Technology (above 1.3 = centralized hybrid, below 0.7 = decentralized hybrid, between 0.7 and 1.3 = balanced hybrid).

variable_name: Centralized, Decentralized, Centralized Hybrid, Decentralized Hybrid, Balanced Hybrid (categorical dummies)
description: Five categorical variables capture each R&D structure type: Centralizedk equals 1 if firm k has a centralized R&D structure and 0 otherwise, Decentralizedk equals 1 if firm k has a decentralized structure, Centralized Hybridk equals 1 for a centralized hybrid, Decentral Hybridk equals 1 for a decentralized hybrid, and Balanced Hybridk equals 1 for a balanced hybrid. Decentralized is the omitted category in the empirical estimations.

The proportion of firm k's 1994 R&D budget that was provided by corporate HQ, as opposed to being provided directly by the business units. It is computed as the proportion of R&D funding allocated by corporate HQ divided by the sum of the proportion allocated by corporate HQ and the proportion allocated by business units. External funding was excluded because it was zero for most firms and less than 6 percent of total funding for the rest; for hybrid firms the proportions were combined using weighted averages of the funding proportions reported by recipient R&D group.

For an individual patent, the number of citations received as of December 31, 1999, used as the traditional proxy for its overall impact. When these citations are averaged at the firm level the variable becomes continuous rather than an integer, so negative binomial estimation is not appropriate; one-sided tobit estimation is used.

Construction entails identification of all citations made to a focal patent, identification of the technology class of each citing patent, and calculation of a technological diversity index equal to one minus the Herfindahl concentration index of these technology classes. The measure equals 0 when a focal patent is cited only by patents from a single technology class; the more diverse the technologies citing a patent, the broader its impact. Hall's small-numbers correction multiplying the measure by N/(N-1), where N is the number of citations received, is applied.

Measured for each focal patent as one minus the proportion of citations made by that patent that are self-citations, that is, citations to patents assigned to the same firm that developed the focal patent. It thus captures the degree to which a focal patent cites prior art from outside rather than within the firm.

Constructed analogously to the breadth of impact measure, but based on the technology classes of the patents cited by the focal patent rather than those citing it: one minus the Herfindahl concentration index of the technology classes of the cited patents. The summation is smaller, and the measure larger, the more diverse the technologies cited by a patent. Hall's N/(N-1) small-numbers correction is applied.

The number of application categories (e.g., word processor, spreadsheet) in which a given product is classified. Categories are drawn from The Software Catalog: Microcomputers classifications, with some categories combined for the analysis.

The number of application categories in which the firm has a product classified. Categories are drawn from The Software Catalog: Microcomputers classifications, with some categories combined for the analysis.
The number of computing platforms (e.g., Apple II, Apple Macintosh, IBM-PC) that a product is classified under. Platforms are drawn from The Software Catalog: Microcomputers classifications.
The number of computing platforms under which the firm has at least one product classified. Platforms are drawn from The Software Catalog: Microcomputers classifications.
The number of products that the firm has on the market. It is used to operationalize the final dimension of scope at the firm level.
The number of niches, defined as the intersection of category and platform, in which the product is classified. It is used to operationalize an additional dimension of scope at the product level.

Standard entropy calculation of -sum[pi ln(pi)], where pi is the probability that the product is classified in a particular category and the sum is over the categories; the average over the firm's products is the firm-level Category Entropy. Firms that tend to offer products integrated over multiple categories have greater category entropy.

Standard entropy calculation of -sum[pi ln(pi)], where pi is the probability that the product is classified under a particular platform and the sum is over the platforms; the average over the firm's products is the firm-level Platform Entropy. Firms that tend to offer each product across several platforms have greater platform entropy, i.e. lower platform focus.
A count of new products introduced by the firm. It is one of the firm-level variables describing adjustments in product variety.
A count of categories in which new products are introduced, summed over the new products, at the firm level.
A count of platforms in which new products are introduced, summed over the new products, at the firm level.

A count of the number of new categories the product was made available for during the 'spell'-that is, during successive publications of The Software Catalog: Microcomputers. Product-level New Category Entry is also aggregated to the firm level.

A count of the number of new platforms the product was made available for during the 'spell'-that is, during successive publications of The Software Catalog: Microcomputers. Product-level New Platform Entry is also aggregated to the firm level.
A count of the new category/platform combinations the product was made available for during the spell.

Observations for a firm begin when the firm first appears in The Software Catalog: Microcomputers and continue until the firm no longer appears. The variable is coded as zero during the observations when the firm appears and coded '1' when the firm exits. For interpreting the results the authors reversed the signs so that in the tables positive coefficients correlate with survival.

Observations for a product begin when the product first appears in The Software Catalog: Microcomputers and continue until the product no longer appears. The variable is coded as zero during the observations when the product appears and coded '1' when the product exits. For interpreting the results the authors reversed the signs so that in the tables positive coefficients correlate with survival.
The median rate of sales growth (annualized) of companies in the industry between t-2 and t, calculated from firm-level data on the 21 industries in the sample.

The absolute difference in the industry growth rate from t-2 to t-1 versus from t-1 to t; an industry that grew 2.00 percent and then shrank 3.00 percent receives a score of 5.00. It captures unpredictable growth or shrinkage of industry demand.
The median R&D/sales ratio for t-1 of companies in the industry, used as an indicator of technological intensiveness.
The log of company sales in t-1, used as an indicator of organizational size and task demands. Other size indicators, such as assets and employees, yielded similar results.
Measured as by Palepu (1985), using an entropy measure based on the firm's dispersion of sales across 4-digit SICs within the firm's 2-digit SICs.
A count of the number of acquisitions in t-1 that were at least 2 percent of the size of the focal firm, drawn from Securities Data Corporation's Merger and Acquisition Database.
A dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO was board chairman in year t.
Coded to 1 when the CEO had spent more time in finance, accounting, or law positions prior to becoming CEO, indicating a background in peripheral functions.

Coded 1 if the CEO had never held the title of COO or President prior to being CEO, i.e., lacked prior firm-wide operational experience. A continuous version, number of years served as COO, gave unchanged results.
Coded to 1 if the CEO joined the firm within 2 years of becoming CEO, and zero otherwise, following prior research on CEO outsiders.

Coded 1 whenever someone other than the CEO held the title COO and/or President and was serving primarily as COO rather than as heir apparent. If someone other than the CEO held the title President or COO and was no more than 4 years younger (or was older) than the CEO, that person was coded as a COO; if the person was more than 4 years younger than the CEO, he or she was coded as an Heir Apparent.

CEOs with 3 or more years of observed tenure were classified by their tenure-long COO experience: those who never had a COO during their observed tenure are COO-averse, and those who had COOs for over 50 percent of their tenures are COO-prone. The dummy variable distinguishes COO-prone from COO-averse CEOs.

Return on assets, an accounting-based performance indicator; the average performance of each COO-prone and COO-averse CEO across his or her entire observed tenure in the data panel. Prior-year firm ROA and industry ROA were included as controls.
time_window: CEO's observed tenure (prior-year and industry ROA as controls)

description: Market-to-book value of common equity, reflecting the stock market's assessment of the health and prospects of the firm; the average performance of each CEO across his or her entire observed tenure. Prior-year firm MTB and industry MTB were included as controls. The two performance measures are not redundant.
time_window: CEO's observed tenure (prior-year and industry MTB as controls)

description: The dependent variable is the cumulative abnormal daily stock returns observed at the time of the downsizing announcement. Event study methodology common to financial research was used to calculate the CAR over a narrow 3-day event window that included the day prior to, the day of, and the day following the announcement in the Wall Street Journal.
time_window: 3-day event window (day -1, day 0, day +1 relative to the announcement)

description: The level of downsizing was operationalized as the percentage reduction in total employees in the firm as announced in the Wall Street Journal. As a step to create the squared term, the first-order term was first mean-centered. The squared term of LD was entered alongside the first-order term in the curvilinear test.

Using a 0/1 binary variable, downsizing announcements that signaled a low reallocation strategy (broad-based, across-the-board) were coded as 0 and those that signaled a high reallocation strategy (more targeted area or specific unit) were coded as 1. Two independent raters analyzed each announcement regarding the firm's reallocation strategy; initial interrater reliability was 0.90 and total agreement was achieved through discussion by the raters.

The use of distinct disengagement incentives was identified by evaluating the announcements, and the variable was coded as 1 if disengagement incentives were offered and 0 otherwise. Two independent raters analyzed and scored each announcement; the initial interrater reliability was 0.97, with total agreement achieved through interrater discussions.

Coded '1' if the pharmaceutical firm exited a biotechnology partnership, and '0' otherwise. In the hazard rate models the dependent variable is the hazard rate of divesting an equity alliance, and right censoring is incorporated for agreements still held at the end of the period. The authors report 62 divestitures among the 76 terminations identified.

Coded '1' if the pharmaceutical firm acquired their biotechnology partner, '0' otherwise. In the hazard rate models the dependent variable is the hazard rate of acquiring a majority stake of the biotechnology partner. The authors report 14 instances in which the pharmaceutical firm bought out the biotechnology partner.

Following Elton and Gruber, uncertainty is measured as the monthly standard deviation of the returns of an industry index. Because the existing biotechnology indices started later and covered only one to four labs, the authors built a new capital-weighted index based on 10 public biotech companies that were public during the whole period, selected to have a similar number of companies within each major subject grouping. Daily stock prices were gathered from CRSP, monthly values were taken from the last tradable day of the month, and the index was adjusted in response to new stock offerings.

Dyadic measures of technological overlap among biotechnology partners in a portfolio are calculated first: technological overlap of partner a in portfolio is the ratio of common technological domains among partners a and the other partner divided by the number of total technological domains of a; this is converted to a distance by taking one minus this ratio. Where there are more than two partners in the portfolio, the authors use the minimum of the distances for partner a, which constitutes the measure of portfolio distance used to test Hypothesis 2. Technological domains are those identified by BioScan.
level: equity alliance (partner dyad within a pharmaceutical firm's portfolio)

description: Measured by one minus the ratio of common technological domains of the pharmaceutical firm and one of the partners in its portfolio divided by the total number of technological domains of the pharmaceutical firm. Lower values of partner distance suggest a higher possibility of redeploying assets from the pharmaceutical firm to the biotechnology partner, and the variable is used to test Hypothesis 3. Technological domains are those identified by BioScan.

The number of citations an article received in the top 40 management journals over a 72-month period following the article's publication. The figure was first adjusted by deleting self-citations and then by weighting citation counts by the average rating given to the citing journal in a large study of journal reputations. A log transformation was performed on the variable prior to the analysis because visual inspection of the distribution revealed skewness and kurtosis.

After reading each summary, judges provided an overall evaluation of its relevance by circling a number along a single Likert-type scale with anchors (1) 'No contribution to the practice of management,' (4) 'neutral,' and (7) 'Very significant contribution to the practice of management.' Where more than one panelist rated an article, an average of the global ratings was used. The global ratings were collected before judges completed the dimensional rating sheets.

An additive scale comprised of two items, each rated on a Likert-type scale with anchors 'Completely Disagree' (1), 'Neutral' (4), and 'Completely Agree' (7). The items capture Davis's (1971) core idea that interesting things are different and new and the idea that extending or clarifying knowledge makes it more useful and thus more interesting to practitioners. The Pearson correlation coefficient between the two items is 0.864.
A single item measured on a Likert-type scale with anchors 'Completely Disagree' (1), 'Neutral' (4), and 'Completely Agree' (7).

Respondents' report of whether their firm had managed to achieve a better environmental protection record compared with other organizations in their industrial sector. Assessed with a single indicator in the structural equation model, with measurement error fixed at 20 percent of the indicator variance. All items are respondents' opinions on a 5-point Likert-type scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

variable_name: champions' individual commitment to environmental initiatives
description: The champion's level of commitment to environmental initiatives, measured with a single indicator in the structural equation model. The measurement scale was set by fixing the indicator loading at 1.0 with a fixed measurement error variance. All items are respondents' opinions on a 5-point Likert-type scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

variable_name: respondents' expectancy to achieve their initial goal
description: Obtained as the geometric mean of respondents' scores on two 5-point Likert scale statements: 'My organization cannot act on its own to improve environmental performance because we have insufficient resources' and 'My organization cannot act on its own to improve environmental performance because we must remain competitive'. Internal reliability for the two-item scale was 0.75. Higher item scores indicate lower expectancy, so the scale is reversed relative to the construct as named.
scale: geometric mean of two 5-point Likert items (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Perceived strategic commitment of the upper echelons to environmental protection, assessed with a single indicator in the structural equation model. The indicator loading was fixed at 1.0 and measurement error was fixed at 25 percent of the indicator variance. All items are respondents' opinions on a 5-point Likert-type scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

variable_name: diffusion and integration of environmental values
description: Perceived diffusion and integration of environmental responsibilities/values among organizational members, assessed with a single indicator in the structural equation model. The indicator loading was fixed at 1.0 with a fixed measurement error variance. All items are respondents' opinions on a 5-point Likert-type scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

Respondents' perceptions of the formalization of environmental responsibilities within the organization, assessed with a single indicator in the structural equation model. The indicator loading was fixed at 1.0 and measurement error was fixed at 15 percent of the indicator variance. All items are respondents' opinions on a 5-point Likert-type scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

Indicator for the 227 sample firms that change from reporting one business segment to reporting two or more in Compustat between 1980 and 1992. Each sample firm is matched to single-segment industry peers.

Current year R&D expense divided by assets. Measured at the year-end prior to the diversification event (Year 0), and also for Years -3 to +3. The comparison holds when only reported R&D is used, or when missing data on R&D expense are assumed to be zero.

Continuous index using data from firms' patents. Each patent's International Patent Class (IPC) is used to generate a distribution of patent equivalents across industries. The resulting measure is a concentric index of diversification of the patent portfolio across industries, with the focal industry defined as the primary segment SIC code. Greater specialization appears as a lower value for this index.
Current-year firm ROA is net income over total assets; segment ROA is segment operating profits over segment assets, as reported in Compustat.
time_window: year prior to and year after diversification

description: Market-to-book ratio computed as (market value of common stock + book value of preferred stock + book value of debt) divided by book value of total assets, where market value of common stock equals price at year-end times shares outstanding.
time_window: year prior to and year after diversification

description: Defined using a Herfindahl index based on segment assets in the first year after diversification.

Categorization of sample firms into acquisition/merger or internal growth, confirmed using Lexis/Nexis articles, information on acquisitions from SDC, and annual reports. Regression uses dummy variables for announced and unannounced internal growth relative to the excluded acquisition category.
Identified as any firm that has the highest market share in its 4-digit SIC code, using revenue data from the Compustat Industrial Segment files for the year just prior to diversification.

The market value of the company's shares, used as the dependent variable in both value models. Data on the market value of the company shares were extracted from the Daily Bulletin of the Madrid Stock Exchange.

The percentage of common shares held by shareholders that own significant shares. It is entered in the value model together with its square, which allows the authors to explicitly test the monitoring and expropriation effects and to optimally determine the breakpoint of the value-concentration relationship.

The percentage of common shares held by insiders. It is entered in the value model together with its square and its cube, which allows the authors to test a cubic form of the value-insider ownership relationship and to derive its breakpoints.

Calculated through a two-step procedure: the trend line for monthly averages of the Equity Price Index was first regressed from December 1988 through December 1999; the operational measure is then the ratio of DataStream's index average value for the third month prior to the effective date of acquisition announcement to the Equity Price Index trend value (from the above regression) for that month. The 3-month period is an allowance for decision lead time. A value of greater than 1 represents a bullish market whereas a value of less than 1 represents a sluggish market.
time_window: third month prior to the effective date of acquisition announcement; trend regression December 1988 through December 1999

description: CAR values for individual acquisitions were calculated by following the standard procedure adopted by many previous studies, using daily equity price data extracted from the DataStream online system over the window of -9 to +1 days. The estimation of the model parameters was based on 90 days of data prior to the window. The authors assume the Singapore equity market is efficient.
time_window: -9 to +1 days around the acquisition announcement; 90 days prior to the window for parameter estimation

description: Net income before taxes divided by average capital, surplus, and reserves, as defined by OSFI for the general insurance industry. All independent and control variables were measured in year t and the dependent variable in t + 1 to avoid causal ambiguity.

The entropy measure, calculated from p_ik, the percentage of premiums collected by firm i in the kth market niche (k = 1, 2, ..., 205). The entropy measure has become the standard for research into the link between diversification and performance. Hypothesis 1 predicts that the coefficient of this variable is positive.

For each focal insurer, the number of market niches in which the focal firm competes with its rivals, calculated as the average of MMCij, the number of market niches shared by firms i and j, across the total number of firms sharing at least one market niche with firm i. Hypothesis 2a proposes that the coefficient of this variable is positive.

The MMC per rival variable weighted by Sij, the similarity between firms i and j in cultivating the same locations of industry resource space; the authors describe it as the interaction term between Sij and MMC per rival. Hypothesis 2b proposes that the coefficient of this variable is positive.

The niche overlap index between firms i and j calculated by Sohn's (2001) method, from p_ik, the proportion of firm i's insurance premium collected from the kth market niche, p_jk, the proportion of firm j's premiums from the kth market niche, and w_k, the total premium collected by all firms from the kth market niche. It was entered into the analysis as a control variable and is the component variable of the interaction term.

Calculated from p_ik, the proportion of firm i's insurance premium collected from the kth market niche, multiplied by the summation over market niches l of r_kl, the relatedness index between market niches k and l derived by Sohn's method. The authors describe the variable as an interaction term in which the effect of p_ik on firm i's performance depends on the degree of market niche overlaps with other insurers.

The technical education variable indicates whether a technical education (technical high school or technical associates degree) is required. It also reports the degree to which direct labor employees have technical degrees even if they are not required. The human capital variables are coded as yes/no or with a three-point ordinal scale typically expressed as high/medium/low.
The screening test variable is a simple binary variable that indicates whether the fab uses a test to screen for technical skills in the hiring process.

variable_name: human resource training (SPC training, vendor training, multiple machines qualification)
description: The statistical process control (SPC) training variable refers to whether equipment operators are required to undergo on-the-job training in statistical process control procedures related to their job tasks; it also indicates the degree to which the fab considers SPC training to be a priority. The vendor training variable reports simply whether operators receive equipment-specific training from a vendor. The multiple machines qualification variable reports the average number of machines that an operator is qualified to operate within his or her area and is measured with a three-point scale.

Human resource deployment is operationalized as the proportion of operators that participate in problem-solving teams and the proportion of operator time spent troubleshooting process control problems. The troubleshooting measure reports the estimated average share of their time that equipment operators spend troubleshooting 'out-of-control' situations with their equipment.

The prior experience variable measures whether firms require experience for hiring and the degree to which employees have previous experience in their production area, semiconductor manufacturing, and unrelated manufacturing.
The operator turnover variable is the average annual percentage of full-time equivalent (FTE) operators that are replaced.

Defect density (the Murphy defect density parameter) is the dependent performance variable used to measure learning and is chosen to control for the influence of die size on die yield. The fabs reported either their monthly die yield or defect density; when die yield was reported it was converted to the Murphy defect density using Equation 4, and when fabs reported defect densities using a formula different from the Murphy model the defect density was converted to die yield and then converted to the Murphy defect density. Defect density is an appealing measure of learning because virtually all defects are the result of some lack of knowledge and, as knowledge grows, defects fall, resulting in direct reductions in manufacturing cost.

A dichotomous variable coded from content analysis of the CEO narratives submitted with the Entrepreneur of the Year nomination. Two coders identified future-tense sentences referring to plans for growth and coded them as market or product expansion logics; '1' indicates the presence of a market expansion logic in a firm's narrative and '0' its absence. Market expansion and product expansion are not mutually exclusive, so some firms may have pursued both logics.

A dichotomous variable coded from content analysis of the CEO narratives submitted with the Entrepreneur of the Year nomination. Future-tense sentences about plans for growth were coded into market and product expansion logics; '1' indicates the presence of a product expansion logic in a narrative and '0' its absence. The two logics are not mutually exclusive categories.

Calculated as the difference between working capital available and working capital required, where working capital available is a firm's current assets (cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, inventory, marketable securities) and working capital required is a firm's current liabilities (accounts payable and accrued expenses). Positive financial slack implies excess resources not being used productively; negative slack implies the firm is stretching its resources. Values are taken at the end of the calendar year prior to the nomination year.
time_window: end of the calendar year prior to the nomination year

description: Calculated using an equation that the supplied text does not render; from the prose, the measure is based on the number of employees relative to sales, inverted from the sales/total employees productivity ratio so that larger values indicate greater levels of slack. Slack is measured relative to a target, the total employees/sales ratio for all firms in the company's four-digit SIC industry, giving an indicator of whether a firm has above- or below-average slack in human resources relative to industry norms.
time_window: end of the calendar year prior to the nomination year

description: The dependent variable is the 2-year cumulative percentage growth in sales during the year the narrative was written and the year following the narrative year, computed with an equation the supplied text does not render. The growth measure encompasses a 2-year time period because measurements were taken at the end of each year, with t-1 the end of the year just prior to when the narratives were written and t+1 the end of the following year.
time_window: from the end of the year prior to the narrative year to the end of the year following the narrative year (2 years)

description: Acquisition performance is measured as the difference between return on assets (ROA) of the acquiring bank 3 years after the acquisition and 1 year before the acquisition, adjusted so that the same variation in the ROA of local competitors is subtracted from it. Competitors are benchmarked in seven geographic areas of the United States (New England, North Atlantic, South Atlantic, Mid-west, South, Rocky Mountains, Pacific) and one in Canada.
time_window: 3 years after vs. 1 year before the acquisition

description: Acquisition experience is computed as the number of acquisitions completed by the acquiring firm before the focal acquisition. The Acquisition History Profile collected the list of all acquisitions completed by the responding institution since founding or since a merger of equals, allowing the complete stock of prior acquisition experience to be constructed for each observation.

Knowledge codification is measured as the sum of acquisition tools developed by the acquiring firm at the time of the focal acquisition, tools that are specific to different parts of the acquisition process, including financial evaluation, due diligence, conversion of information systems, human resources integration, and sales/product integration. The Acquiring Bank Questionnaire asked whether each item was developed and, if so, when it was developed.

Integration was measured with a single scale collected with the Acquisition History Profile instrument. For each acquisition respondents answered the question 'To what extent were the systems, procedures and products aligned or centralized?', with possible answers 0 (few or no features were aligned or centralized), 1 (only selected systems, procedures or products were aligned or centralized), 2 (many but not all systems, procedures, and products were aligned or centralized), and 3 (all systems, procedures, and products were completely integrated).

Replacement was measured with a four-point scale on which respondents answered the question 'To what extent has the executive leadership of the acquired bank been changed after the acquisition?'. Alternative answers were 0 (no substantial change), 1 (some changes), 2 (many changes), and 3 (virtually all the top management team was changed). The word 'change' was substituted for 'replacement' because the latter was deemed too negative.

The pre-acquisition quality of the acquired firm's resource endowment was measured by asking about the performance level of the target bank prior to the acquisition, on a scale anchored at -2 (the acquired institution was bankrupt), -1 (it was a poor performer), 0 (it was an average performer), +1 (it was a good performer) and +2 (it was an outstanding performer).

An adaptation of the measure developed by Hitt and Ireland (1985), consisting of 12 items rated by the local authorities' general managers on a 7-point scale. Cronbach's alpha of this measure is 0.88.
scale: 7-point scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree

description: A measure with three dimensions: education, work experience, and competence of the firm's members. Respondents evaluated four items relating to education and work experience and eight items relating to competence on a 7-point scale. Cronbach's alpha for this measure is 0.80.
scale: 7-point scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree

description: Based on the model developed by Eden and Moriah (1996), consisting of seven items that cover four aspects of the auditing system: teaching, motivating, deterrence, and process improvement. One item is reverse-scored. Cronbach's alpha for this measure is 0.89.
scale: 7-point scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree

description: A development of the model presented by Kitay and Marchington (1996) consisting of nine items covering the degree of trust and satisfaction in the relations between the management and employees, the degree to which labor relations are planned and managed, and the extent to which the labor relations system pursues the principles of safety, fairness, individualism, and democracy. Cronbach's alpha for this scale is 0.93.
scale: 7-point scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree

description: Based on Denison's (1990) model with its four hypotheses (involvement, consistency, adaptability, and mission); eight items represent the four ingredients of the model, rated on a 7-point scale. Cronbach's alpha for this measure is 0.81.
scale: 7-point scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree

description: An integration of two measures: a city reputation survey and the reputation survey of Fortune magazine, adapted to the unique function of the local authorities in Israel. The measure consists of four items based on the corporate reputation survey and five items based on the city reputation survey, rated on a 7-point scale. Cronbach's alpha for this measure is 0.82.
scale: 7-point scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree

description: The proportion of self-income in the local authority's overall income as reported in its regular budget. Self-income consists of all the income (taxes, grants, and fees) that the local authority collects directly from its residents, businesses, and other assets within its jurisdiction; overall income in the regular budget consists of property taxes, fees, surcharges, general grants, financing from ministries, and single sources of income. The closer the ratio to unity, the greater the fiscal strength (health) of the local authority.

The proportion of the current year's actual collecting (the total amount of income that was collected by the local authority) in the total income theoretically collectable during the current year. Actual collecting consists of property taxes, water, and sewage fees; the total income to be collected consists of accumulated debt from earlier years, the current year's 'income to be collected' minus discounts and cancellation of self-income.

The ratio of the number of permanent residents net of the number of job seekers (monthly average) to the number of permanent residents. The total number of permanent residents consists of all the permanent residents and migrants in Israel, including permanent residents who were away from Israel for less than 1 year during the survey that collected the data for this measure.

Consists of two ratios: development expenditure ratio (the ratio between the total amount of expenses aimed at local development and the number of permanent residents) and local services' expenditure ratio (the ratio between the budget expenditures on services and the number of permanent residents). Cronbach's alpha of this measure is 0.87.
The ratio between the number of permanent residents at the end of the current and previous year. A strong local authority is likely to exhibit an increase in its permanent population.

Intangible organizational elements were measured as six survey-based scores from the local authorities' general managers: managerial capabilities, human capital, perceived organizational reputation, internal auditing, labor relations and organizational culture. Each used a 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree) and entered the models separately, with interactions among them.

Respondents self-typed their business unit into one of the Miles and Snow business strategy types using the self-typing paragraph approach commonly used in strategic management research. The Miles and Snow strategy type descriptions were taken from James and Hatten (1995).
scale: four categories (Prospector, Analyzer, Differentiated Defender, Low Cost Defender)

description: Cluster membership from a K-means cluster analysis performed on 11 marketing activity scales that were formed by factor analysing 76 items describing separate marketing activities. Four clusters were selected as the starting point, consistent with the number of business strategy types, and were labelled Aggressive Marketers, Mass Marketers, Marketing Minimizers and Value Marketers.

A 7-point measure of profitability taken from Babakus et al. (1996). Respondents indicated how well their business unit had performed on profitability compared to the industry average and compared to business unit objectives over the past 24 months.

A 7-point measure of market performance taken from Babakus et al. (1996). Respondents indicated how well their business unit had performed on market share compared to their major competitor and compared to business unit objectives over the past 24 months.

Coded one if the ultimate parent firm is foreign owned and zero if it is U.S. owned. Ultimate parent and home nation were identified from the Dun and Bradstreet data, and nationality was individually verified where the data base did not list one. Seventeen percent of the establishments in the sample are foreign owned.

Count of the number of performance criteria with which each facility must comply (the number of permits issued to a facility) under the Clean Water Act. The minimum value is zero, the maximum is three, and the mean is 0.43.

Chemicals are weighted by toxicity using the reportable quantities (RQ) measure from the CERCLA statute, and the toxicity-weighted chemical waste generated by the facility is summed in each year and logged. Because waste generation is strongly influenced by product and operation size, the authors estimate a waste production function relating the log of facility size to the log of aggregate toxic waste generation by 4-digit SIC code within each year, and the standardized residual between observed and predicted waste generation measures relative generation.

Standardized residual between the observed and predicted amount of waste processed by the facility, where the amount processed is the log of the sum of all toxicity-weighted pounds processed on and offsite. Predicted values come from the same waste production function approach using facility size and 4-digit SIC code within year.

Standardized residual between the observed and predicted amount of waste processed onsite by the facility, where the amount processed onsite is the log of the sum of all toxicity-weighted pounds burned, recycled, or otherwise treated. Predicted values come from the waste production function using facility size and 4-digit SIC code within year.
For each year, a normalized deviation for each country's oil price relative to all other countries in the sample, built from the OECD Environmental Data annual compendium reports.

Annual percentage of glass and cardboard recycled in each country, calculated from OECD data, expressed as a deviation measure relative to other countries in the sample. The authors also calculated annual spending on all waste processing (public and private) as a percentage of GNP; the two measures are highly correlated, and the recycling measure is reported.

Accounting-based performance measure obtained from the Nikkei NEEDS tapes for each year in the 1986-97 period. ROA and ROS were highly correlated and generated similar findings; the reported tables are confined to the results for ROA.

The percent of parent firm sales that were derived from export revenues. This variable was derived from annual export and revenue information found in the Nikkei NEEDS tapes. Independent variables are lagged one year in the models.

Count of the number of FDIs in which the parent firm had a 10 percent or greater equity share, derived from the Toyo Keizai directory for the 1986-97 period. This count and the number of countries measure are highly correlated and were entered separately in parallel sets of models.

Count of the number of countries in which the firm had FDIs, derived from the Toyo Keizai directory for the 1986-97 period. Entered separately from the number of FDIs measure in parallel sets of models because the two are highly correlated.

Based on the identity of equity joint venture partners, the number of Japanese-local (J-L) equity joint ventures and the number of host countries in which the firm had J-L equity joint ventures were counted and then divided by the total number of subsidiaries to derive J-L joint venture intensities by subsidiaries and by host countries. Both variants were computed annually for 1986-97 and entered separately in the models; all non-Japanese partners were coded as local partners.

Based on the identity of equity joint venture partners, the number of Japanese-Japanese (J-J) equity joint ventures and the number of host countries in which the firm had J-J equity joint ventures were counted and then divided by the total number of subsidiaries to derive J-J joint venture intensities by subsidiaries and by host countries. Both variants were computed annually for 1986-97 and entered separately in the models.

Financial leverage is defined as the ratio of debt to equity. The measure includes the use of fixed charge securities in the form of fixed-charge debt and preferred stock. The financial leverage measure for each firm was averaged over a 4-year period to control for spurious events (1989-92).

Industry values of shipment were regressed over 5 years against time (1988-92), and the standard error of the regression coefficient related to a time dummy variable divided by the average value of the industry's shipments produced a standardized index of environmental dynamism. The variable was centered by subtracting its mean before the interaction term was formed.

ROA is operationalized as income before extraordinary items divided by total assets (which includes current assets, net property, plant and equipment, and other noncurrent assets as identified by the firms). The data were averaged over a 5-year time period from 1989 to 1993.

ROI is operationalized as income before extraordinary items divided by total invested capital (which includes total long-term debt, preferred stock, minority interest, and total common equity). The data were averaged over a 5-year time period from 1989 to 1993.

Product lines offered by each firm were noted in the baseline year (1978 or 1983) and recorded again in 1995, so that lines dropped, retained and added could be identified. Reconfiguration is greater when organizations retain fewer product lines and/or add more product lines over time, and the authors compare the percentages of lines dropped, retained and added across targets, acquirers, nonacquirers and continuing businesses.

variable_name: retention or disposal of a target's product line
description: For every acquisition case in the sample of firms operating in 1978 and/or 1983, the product lines belonging to the target immediately prior to the acquisition were observed and coded 0 or 1 depending on whether the acquirer retained the lines in 1995. If the initial acquirer was acquired in turn, the authors determined whether the ultimate acquirer retained the lines in 1995.
