variable_name: target-acquirer resource overlap and distinction (deepening variables)
description: Focal line overlap captures whether or not an acquirer possessed the product line before the acquisition. Complementary line overlap is the number of lines shared by acquirer and target, excluding any focal overlap. Category overlap records the number of overlapping categories, excluding the focal category. The authors expect the overlap variables to show a positive relationship with line retention.

variable_name: target-acquirer resource overlap and distinction (extension variables)
description: Target line distinction and acquirer line distinction record the number of nonoverlapping lines at the target and at the acquirer. Target category distinction and acquirer category distinction record the number of nonoverlapping categories at the target and acquirer. The authors expect the distinction variables to have positive estimates but to be smaller relative to those of deepening.
Firms operating in the 1978 and 1983 panels were tracked and the authors found which had been acquired by 1995, identifying firms that became acquisition targets.
Firms operating in the panels were tracked and the authors found which had pursued acquisitions by 1995, identifying firms that themselves undertook acquisitions.

Firms were clustered into three strategic groups using a two-step clustering approach, hierarchical clustering followed by k-means with initial centers taken from the first step (Ward's clustering method). The hierarchical step used visual inspection of tree-plots to determine the appropriate number of clusters; five outliers were eliminated and the clustering procedure was repeated on the final sample. Three groups with significantly different strategic competitive profiles emerged.

A composite reputation measure for each firm was generated by standardizing the numeric equivalents of the letter opinion level assigned the firm by each rating agency (A. M. Best, Standard & Poor's, and Weiss Ratings) and then averaging the standardized values. Weiss rates firms on 16 levels (A+ = 16 down to F = 1), Best on a 15-level modified A-F scale, and S&P on an 18-level basic A-C pattern. The reliability coefficient for this three-item set of observations indicates an alpha of 0.768.

Measures the proportion of personal lines business relative to total net premiums written. Personal lines are products primarily sold to individuals, such as home owners and private passenger auto, whereas commercial lines are sold to businesses.
Measures the proportion of property lines business relative to total net premiums written. Property exposures are direct and associated indirect losses suffered by the primary policyholder.

Measures the proportion of business derived from financial lines relative to total net premiums written; financial lines include fidelity coverage, surety and performance bonds, mortgage guaranty, and credit insurance.
A Herfindal index is used to measure the extent of firm diversification across lines of business. Higher index values indicate greater diversification.
The natural log of total admitted assets is employed in order to mitigate adverse effects of skewness in insurer size that exist across the industry.
scale: natural log of total admitted assets

description: A binary variable proxies strategic differences in owner/managerial incentives between stock and nonstock ownership forms. Following Mayers and Smith (1981), stock insurers whose ultimate parent is in fact a mutual or other nonstock form are coded as nonstock firms; the text does not state which value of the binary variable indicates which form.
Age is calculated as 1996 (the year of analysis) less the year of incorporation.

A binary variable (agency = 1; nonagency = 0) depicts whether an agency (indirect) or nonagency distribution system is utilized. Agency systems channel products to customers through independent agents and/or brokers; direct writers use exclusive agents, salaried employees, and/or mass merchandising techniques.
Captured by the difference between total direct premiums written and net premiums written (i.e., after reinsurance ceded), divided by net premiums written.

Calculated as net earned premiums (that portion of total policy premiums written where the contracted obligation for coverage already has been provided as amortized over the life of the policy) divided by policyholder surplus (the accounting difference between available asset base and total firm liability obligations).

Represents total investments other than government and investment grade corporate securities divided by aggregate government and investment grade corporate securities. The proportion of more risky investments (e.g., mortgages, junk bonds, commercial real estate) to relatively safe investments differentiates strategic investment choices.

Indicator variable that is set to 1 for founder-managed firms and 0 for nonfounder-managed control firms. Founder-managed firms were identified by selecting all firms in Forbes magazine's annual CEO compensation report that classified the CEO as the firm's founder.
time_window: first year the firm appeared on the Forbes list during the 1980-91 period

description: Three-year holding period returns were computed for each firm by compounding monthly stock returns, representing the return on a hypothetical $1 investment in the firm's stock at the beginning of the 3-year period. The 3-year performance measurement period followed the first instance of the founder-managed firm's inclusion on the Forbes list during the 1980-91 data collection years.
The natural logarithm of the firm's market capitalization, used as the firm size variable. Market capitalization data were obtained from the CRSP data files.

The natural logarithm of the difference between the year firm i enters the sample and the year of the firm's incorporation. Data on the year of the firm's incorporation were gathered from Moody's manuals.

The survey listed 19 distinct work-life activities and asked respondents to indicate which were currently offered by the organization. The index is the sum of the number of programs listed in the survey that were offered by the organization, so its potential range is 0 to 19. Cronbach's alpha reliability is 0.77.

The same composite work-life index (sum of the 19 listed programs offered by the organization) is used as the predictor in the productivity equation. In the interaction models the index was centered by subtracting the mean value of the variable for each score prior to calculating the multiplicative interactions. Findings for the log-transformed index were virtually identical to those for the nontransformed index, and the nontransformed data are reported.

Respondents indicated the percentage of employees in each of eight categories, and the percentage of professionals was used in the analysis. The categories were supervisory/managerial, administrative, sales, professional, technical/technical support, skilled crafts, secretarial/clerical, and other.

The percentage of professional employees reported by respondents is entered as a main effect and interacted with the work-life index in the productivity equation. In the interaction models the variable was centered by subtracting its mean prior to computing the interaction term.
The dummy variable for 'career ladders' is coded as 1 if the company has formal employee advancement programs.

The career ladder dummy (1 if the company has formal employee advancement programs) is entered as a main effect and interacted with the work-life index in the productivity equation; the components were centered before the interaction was calculated.
Respondents indicated the percentage of workers who were female.

The percentage of female workers is entered as a main effect and interacted with the work-life index in the productivity equation. The variable was centered by subtracting its mean before the interaction term was computed.

Productivity is measured as the logarithm of sales per employee for the public for-profit firms in the database, taken from a separate archival source to minimize common method variance. Financial services firms were removed from the productivity equations because sales per employee is not as good a proxy for productivity in that sector.

Coded '1' if a firm's head office is in the cluster (Toronto), and '0' otherwise. Data for this measure came from the Investment Funds Institute of Canada (1998a), company data (annual reports, etc.), BellCharts (1997), and Pape (1997).

Built from survey questions about executives' friendships, information, and advice networks. Where more than one executive from a firm responded, responses were pooled such that a tie is recorded if any executive reported such a tie, and each of the friendship, information, and advice networks was mapped in a 77 x 77 matrix. The three matrices were summed and dichotomized to record whether or not a tie existed, symmetrized, and in-degree was measured by summing the columns to yield the number of firms tied to each firm.

Built from three measures of institutional ties (IFIC Board of Directors ties, IFIC Management Committee ties, and IFIC Retail Council ties), each recorded as a symmetric 77 x 77 matrix coded '1' if a tie existed between firms and '0' otherwise. The matrices were summed into the Institutional Tie matrix, whose cells are valued from '0' (none of the three ties present) to '3' (all three present), which was then dichotomized and its columns summed for each firm.

Industry experts responded to three statements about each fund company ('This firm often leads the industry at (1) introducing new products/ (2) introducing new services/ (3) adopting new technologies.'), scored on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (strongly agree) to 5 (strongly disagree). Innovation is the summed and averaged responses received from all respondents for each firm; because Innovation was reverse scored, the results were reverse-coded as Innovativeness.

The tests of centrality effects on firm performance used firm innovativeness as the outcome: industry experts rated each fund company on three statements (leads the industry at introducing new products, new services and adopting new technologies) on a 5-point scale, averaged across respondents and reverse-coded so high values mean more innovative (alpha = 0.93).

variable_name: Size of the company, defined as the volume of deposits at the end of 1994
description: Strategic groups are defined by company size, defined as the volume of deposits at the end of 1994. The limits of separation are set to find a certain homogeneity of size in each category: large (deposits > 2 billion pesetas), medium (415,000 million pesetas < deposits < 2 billion pesetas) and small (deposits < 415,000 million pesetas). The resulting groups are the big six (41.04 percent of the total market), 27 medium-size entities (35.64 percent) and 113 small entities (21.12 percent).

variable_name: Response to competitive actions between strategic groups
description: Built from the news items on competitive actions and responses: the actions of each strategic group that attracted a response from another group are counted and expressed as horizontal and vertical percentages for each pair of groups. Responses were identified by selecting news items containing expressions such as 'in response to...', 'following...', 'under pressure from...', 'reacting to...', and then looking for the news of the initial action to which each response referred. The authors report detecting 126 actions (38 of which provoked at least one response) and 82 responses across the 146 entities.

The average delay time, in days, of the responses of an entity to the actions of its competitors in a year. Because response time varies with the type of initial action, response time was first regressed (OLS) on type of action for all years and companies and the average residual of all a company's responses in a given year was used as that company's response time for that year; the ANOVA and Mann-Whitney tests are calculated with these residuals, whereas the tables show number of days as it is more intuitive.

A subjective estimation by an agent (strategic group) of the effect of a 1 percent increase in the amount offered over the increase in the amount offered by another agent (strategic group). It is estimated by maximum likelihood for two systems of behaviour equations per size group, semi-logarithmic (1) and logarithmic (2), each with 14 unknown parameters; the semi-logarithmic specification is selected by the Akaike criterion. The model specifies parametrically the conjectures of the benchmark entities (the greatest-size entity in each group plus the smallest entity in the sample) and expresses the conjectures of non-benchmark entities as linear combinations of them. A negative conjectural elasticity indicates competition and a positive one collusion, both with reference to the Cournot situation; the coefficients of the small group could not be estimated because of singularity problems.

variable_name: industry factors (Industry Maturity, Entry Barriers, Competitive Power)
description: Sixteen survey items based on Porter's industry analysis framework and Scherer's reviews of empirical findings in industrial organization economics, framed as questions on a 1-5 scale. A factor analysis of the responses produced six factors with eigenvalues exceeding one; after a scree curve analysis suggested the eigenvalues and explained variance began to level after the third factor, factors four through six were incorporated into the first three based on their second-best factor loadings. The final three factors used in the hypothesis testing were Industry Maturity, Entry Barriers, and Competitive Power.
scale: 1-5 Likert-type scale (5 = agree strongly, 1 = disagree strongly)

description: One of the three industry factor scales retained after the factor analysis of the 16 survey items and labeled Industry Maturity by the researchers on the basis of its underlying component variables. The reliability coefficients for the first three industry factors fell between 0.65 and 0.75, which were taken as adequate to constitute meaningful industry factors.

One of the three industry factor scales retained after the factor analysis of the 16 survey items and labeled Entry Barriers by the researchers on the basis of its underlying component variables. The reliability coefficients for the first three industry factors fell between 0.65 and 0.75, which were taken as adequate.

One of the three industry factor scales retained after the factor analysis of the 16 survey items and labeled Competitive Power by the researchers; the authors note that five variables comprise this factor, with rivalry, the threat of substitutes, power relative to customers, and power relative to suppliers collapsing into it.

A scale formed from three survey questions on a Likert-type 1-5 scale, addressing 3-year profitability, sales growth, and overall financial performance. The Cronbach alpha reliability coefficient for the performance scale was 0.89, within generally accepted limits.
time_window: 3-year performance reported at the time of the survey

description: One of the three performance questions making up the performance scale, addressing 3-year profitability on a Likert-type 1-5 scale. The authors report results for profitability variance separately from the overall performance measure.

One of the three performance questions making up the performance scale, addressing sales growth on a Likert-type 1-5 scale. The authors report results for sales growth variance separately from the overall performance measure.

Proportion of affiliated directors serving on the audit committee. Directors were classified as affiliated according to Securities and Exchange Commission Regulation 14A, Item 6(b) guidelines, covering employment by the corporation or an affiliate within the last 5 years, close family relationships, customer/supplier/banker/creditor affiliations, investment banking relationships, control person status, and association with a law firm engaged by the corporation. Data were collected for the 5 years prior to the actual bankruptcy filing date from corporate proxy filings.
time_window: 5 years prior to the bankruptcy filing date

variable_name: percentage common stock held by institutional investors
description: The percentage of the firm's common stock held by institutional investors, collected for the 5 years prior to the actual bankruptcy filing date from Standard and Poor's Corporation Security Owner's Stock Guide.
time_window: 5 years prior to the bankruptcy filing date

description: Sample firms either filed a bankruptcy petition during the study period (coded 1) or they did not (coded 0). Bankrupt firms were identified in a multistage process, beginning with all firms with assets greater than $100 million at the time of their Chapter 11 filing, which are tracked by New Generation Research and published in the Bankruptcy Yearbook and Almanac.

Those bankrupt firms filing a prepackaged plan were coded as 1 and those bankrupt firms not filing a prepackaged plan were coded as 0. Prepackaged plans were provided by The Bankruptcy Yearbook and Almanac.

variable_name: length of time spent in reorganization
description: An interval level variable measured in days, provided by The Bankruptcy Yearbook and Almanac. The bankrupt firms in the sample represent reorganizations ranging in length between 35 days and just under four years.

Standardized abnormal returns generated as a result of the acquisition announcement, estimated with event study methodology; the event window is the day of the event (Day 0). Scholes-Williams betas are used, and the Patell test is extended with the Boehmer, Musumeci, and Poulsen cross-sectional variance adjustment; serial dependence is corrected with the Mikkelson and Partch procedure.

variable_name: acquisitions of online firms by offline firms
description: Subsample of the acquisition events in which an online firm was acquired by an offline firm, identified by classifying acquirers and targets as online or offline with two independent raters. This subsample comprises 435 of the acquisition events.

variable_name: acquisitions of online firms by online firms
description: Subsample of the acquisition events in which an online firm acquired another online firm, based on the same rater classification of acquirers and targets. This subsample comprises 363 of the acquisition events.

A dummy variable identifying acquisitions announced before March 2000, regressed on the standardized abnormal returns for the two samples to test whether a differential effect exists before and after the stock market correction.

An index variable computed by summing the inversed standardized (Z-score) firm and industry tenure of the new CEO, defining a continuum from new CEOs who have a greater combination of firm and industry tenure to those who have no experience in the firm and the industry. Firm tenure carries more weight in the measure, because the concept of successor origin puts heavier weight on firm experience for a new CEO's insiderness.
scale: index of inversed standardized tenure scores

variable_name: change in composite post-succession firm performance
description: A composite measure computed by summing the standardized (Z-score) change in a firm's two operational performance indicators, industry-adjusted return on assets (ROA) and industry-adjusted return on sales (ROS), and a market-based performance indicator, industry-adjusted total shareholder return (TSR), from the time of succession until 3 years later. The change in composite firm performance rather than the absolute measure is used as the dependent variable.
time_window: from the time of succession until 3 years later

description: Measured by the volatility of demand across time, by regressing a variable for each year (time) on a variable for revenue per available seat miles in the airline industry and for value of shipments in the chemical industry. Five years of data were used for each equation; the volatility of demand measure is the standard error of the regression slope coefficient divided by the mean value of the dependent variable.
Measured using the same regression model as turbulence, where munificence is the regression slope coefficient divided by the mean value of the dependent variable, indicating a growth-based measure.

A composite measure constructed by summing the standardized (Z-score) average growth (or decline) in a firm's industry-adjusted ROA, ROS, and TSR for 2 years before the succession event occurred. It was also included as a control variable to address the potential threat of the regression-to-the-mean effect.

A variation of Finkelstein and Hambrick's strategic persistence measure using six strategic indicators: advertising intensity, R&D intensity, plant and equipment newness, nonproduction overhead, inventory levels, and financial leverage. The firm's three-year variance for each strategic dimension was computed, the industry average variance was subtracted from the firm's variance score for each dimension to control industry effects, and the industry-adjusted variance scores for the six indicators were summed to yield an overall strategic change measure.
time_window: t-1 through t+1 (three years around the succession)

description: The percentage of entering executives was calculated by counting the number of executives per firm who were not on the team the last year the predecessor held office (t-1) but on the team the following two years (t and t+1), divided by team size. The percentage of exiting executives was calculated by counting the number of executives listed in t-1 but not in t and t+1, divided by team size. The overall percentage of change in teams averages the percentages of team entries and exits.
time_window: from t-1 to t+1 relative to the succession year

description: The industry sectors were coded into three categories in which privately owned profit-seeking (medical electronic) firms were coded as 1, privately owned non-profit organizations (private universities) were coded as 2, and publicly owned non-profit organizations (public universities) were coded as 3. The variable distinguishes profit seeking from non-profit organizations and, within the non-profit category, privately owned from publicly owned organizations.

The same three-category sector code distinguishes privately owned organizations from publicly owned organizations: privately owned profit-seeking medical electronic firms and privately owned non-profit private universities on one side, publicly owned non-profit public universities on the other. Codes were 1 for private profit-making firms, 2 for private non-profit universities and 3 for public non-profit universities.

Respondents rated the perceived impact of each of several specific influence strategies on a +10 to -10 scale where +10 indicates a very positive impact, 0 indicates no impact, and -10 indicates a very negative impact. Principal component analysis with varimax rotation produced a first factor labelled 'information' that included the strategies for preparing detailed technical reports, personal visits, testimony and contacting colleagues of regulators, and the strategies within the factor were summed to produce the information scale (alpha = 0.74).
time_window: at the time of the survey, 1980-1981

description: Respondents rated the perceived impact of each of several specific influence strategies on a +10 to -10 scale where +10 indicates a very positive impact, 0 indicates no impact, and -10 indicates a very negative impact. The second factor, labelled 'pressure', included pressure strategies such as originating letter-writing campaigns, contacting third party organizations, contacting third party individuals and organizing media campaigns, and the strategies within the factor were summed to produce the pressure scale (alpha = 0.73).
time_window: at the time of the survey, 1980-1981

variable_name: organization size (total number of full-time employees, logged)
description: Organization size was operationally measured as the total number of full-time employees for each organization. Size for each medical electronics firm was determined from Poor's Directory whereas size for each university was determined from data published by the American Association of University Professors. The natural logarithm of size was used to linearize this variable in order to more closely meet the assumptions of the linear regression model.
scale: count of full-time employees; natural logarithm used in regressions

description: Dependence was operationally measured as the proportion of financial resources controlled by regulations to the total financial resources available to the organization at the same time, collected for 1977 from archival sources. For medical electronics firms, each firm's market share was multiplied by the industry value of shipments to determine total sales in the medical electronics industry, which became the numerator in relation to total sales in 1977; for universities, the proportion of federal research dollars in relation to the university's total budget was used. In both cases the measure represents the proportion of total revenues that were derived from a regulated source.

Organizational fear of retaliation by regulatory agencies was measured by two questionnaire items that were summed (alpha = 0.72). The two items were responded to on a five point scale of importance in shaping the institution's regulatory response to specific regulations (5 = extremely important to 1 = not at all important). The first item asked the importance 'that fears of strong, negative response from my organization to the proposed regulation would aggrevate our relations with the federal government'; the second asked the importance of 'the fear that a strong, negative response from this organization might jeopardize future government support'.
scale: five point importance scale, summed across two items
time_window: at the time of the survey, 1980-1981

variable_name: Perceived impact of influence strategies (eight strategy items and information and pressure scales)
description: Perceived impact of influence strategies was measured with items adapted from Aplin and Hegarty (1980). Respondents rated the impact of each of eight strategies (letter campaign, technical reports, personal visits, testimony, colleague contact, third party individuals, third party groups, media campaign) on a +10 to -10 scale. Two scales, information and pressure, were also formed from the items.

Mergers are classified into four relatedness categories using the FTC's categorization: product concentric mergers; horizontal and market concentric mergers; conglomerate mergers; and vertical mergers. Horizontal and market concentric mergers are combined because there is little distinction between the two, given the increasing ease with which a firm can geographically expand its markets. The classification is described as a crude but readily available objective measure of merger relatedness.
The same FTC-based classification of mergers into product concentric, horizontal and market concentric, conglomerate, and vertical categories is applied to the sample of acquired firms.

Abnormal returns are the residuals from a market model estimated by longitudinally regressing 60 months of monthly returns beginning 67 months before the merger transaction month for the pre-merger period, and again beginning 5 months after the transaction month for the post-merger period; the 12 months surrounding the transaction month are excluded. Residuals are standardized and adjusted following Brown and Warner (1980) and cumulated over windows. Pre-merger CARs are reported, as are post-merger CARs for 1-18, 19-37, and 38-64 months after the merger.
time_window: 60-month estimation windows; pre-merger and post-merger windows of 1-18, 19-37 and 38-64 months

description: To construct the difference measures, a turning month of market awareness to the merger is identified from marked changes in the trend of the portfolio's pre-merger cumulative average residuals, and was noticed about 28 months before the merger for the grouping depicted. A paired-difference score for firm i is the average monthly change in its abnormal rate of return, computed by subtracting the average abnormal monthly return of the non-merger control period (67 months before the merger through 1 month before the turning month) from the average abnormal return of the merger impact period (the turning month through 1 month before the merger). The score is averaged with those of other firms of the same merger type to form APD; CPD equals APD multiplied by the number of months in the merger impact period.
time_window: control period -67 months to turning month minus 1; merger impact period turning month to 1 month before the merger

variable_name: CAR and CPD premiums of acquired firms
description: Premiums to the stockholders of acquired firms are measured by the cumulative abnormal return (CAR) and by the cumulative paired-difference measure (CPD), using the same market-model procedures as for acquiring firms, and are reported by merger type.

Abnormal returns were calculated only for IBM using the market model, estimated with daily returns for the period 1 January 1977 to 31 December 1978 obtained from CRISP (504 trading days). The regression had an R-squared of 0.193 and an F value of 119.998, significant at 0.0001; the beta was significant at 0.0001 while the intercept was not significant. The abnormal return for each event date was computed as the forecast error, with a Student-t statistic and a one-tailed significance test.
time_window: estimation period 1 January 1977 to 31 December 1978; event dates 1979-1984

variable_name: event history of IBM's moves into the PBX industry
description: News items and articles referring to IBM and the telecommunications industry were compiled from a thorough search of the 1968-84 Predicasts F&S Index and the Wall Street Journal Index; each report was read to ascertain its relevance to IBM's entry into the PBX industry, and 16 such events beginning with IBM's formal announcement of its intention to enter the U.S. PBX industry were listed. The events were grouped for expositional convenience into internal developments (announcements, statements by the company or investment analysts indicating possible entry, creation of a new division or unit, R&D commitments, new products, new manufacturing processes) and external transactions (co-operative marketing, technology development or manufacturing agreements, joint-ventures, licensing agreements, minority equity participation with firms in the target industry other than the target firm).

Measure of total innovation created by summing across all 55 innovation items (the 34 technical and 21 administrative items). Items were developed from interviews with bankers and were checked by respondents as in use or not. Alpha for the total index was 0.91.

Index of technical innovation formed by summing across 34 items covering products/services, marketing, computerized retail customer applications, delivery systems and operations, and office automation. The CEO checked (0 = no; 1 = yes) those which were in use at his bank. Alpha = 0.87.

Index of administrative innovation covering staffing, attitude assessment, planning, compensation and training. Because these items involve human resource practices they were completed by the human resource executive, and an index was formed by summing across the items. Alpha = 0.79.

Mean age of the top management team members. Each member's current age was reported by the human resources executive from personnel documents, and the team mean was computed. The average age of the 1220 executives on the teams was 45.42 years.

Heterogeneity of team members with respect to age. For interval-level variables with a theoretically fixed zero point, the coefficient of variation (the standard deviation divided by the mean) provides a direct method for obtaining a scale invariant measure of dispersion, and it is used here for age and tenure.

Average number of years team members had been employed at their current bank, computed from the year each person joined the bank. The executives had been employed at their current firms 14.79 years on average.

Heterogeneity of team members with respect to organizational tenure, measured by the coefficient of variation (the standard deviation divided by the mean), the scale invariant measure of dispersion used here for age and tenure.
Average education level attained by team members. Education level attained was reported in six fixed categories ranging from 'high school' to 'doctorate'.
scale: six categories from high school to doctorate

description: Heterogeneity with respect to the major field of study for the highest degree earned. For categorical variables, Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity (1 - sum pi squared) is used, where p is the proportion of group members in a category. A total of 17 categories were provided, of which 10 were specific to business and seven were non-business fields; differences between any two business-related topics were treated as equivalent to differences between a business major and a major outside of business.

Heterogeneity among team members with respect to their functional background experiences. The functional area in which each person had the most experience was reported using 12 fixed categories chosen on the basis of pretest interviews with bank executives, and Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity (1 - sum pi squared) was used to measure dispersion.

variable_name: size of golden parachutes (in terms of the number of years' salary)
description: The dollar size of golden parachutes provided for top management expressed in terms of the number of years' compensation of top executives as reported in the proxy statement. The measure is linked to the latest annual salary of the executives when a change in control occurs, and thus reflects its value adjusted for annual salary differences.

variable_name: GP number (number of executives covered by golden parachutes)
description: The number of executives covered by the golden parachute contract, an indicator of how far the protection is distributed within a company. In the sample the number of executives covered ranged from 1 to 99, with an average of 10 and a standard deviation of 14.37.

variable_name: average absolute tenure of top executives
description: The human asset investment of the executives and its related hazard of loss of employment are measured as the average absolute tenure of the top executives of the company. Average absolute tenure and relative tenure are highly correlated and are entered individually into the regression models.

variable_name: ratio of the average tenure of the top five executives to the average tenure of individual outside directors
description: The information asymmetry between top management and the board is measured in terms of the ratio of the average tenure of the top five executives (including the CEO) to the average tenure of individual outside directors. This measure is used in models as an alternative to average absolute tenure.

variable_name: percentage of stock owned by the management team
description: Top management team incentives are indicated by the percentage of stock owned by the management team as reported in the proxy statement.

variable_name: concentration of stock ownership not owned by management
description: The level of concentration of stock ownership not owned by management is measured as the sum of all blocks of stock ownership greater than 5 percent. The 5 percent cut-off is used following the guideline by the SEC as an indicator of significant stock ownerships.

variable_name: proportion of outside directors on the board
description: Board characteristics are measured in terms of size, the proportion of outside directors, and the proportion of inside directors sitting on the executive compensation committee. This variable is the proportion of outside directors on the board.

variable_name: proportion of inside directors sitting on the executive compensation committee
description: The proportion of inside directors sitting on the board's executive compensation committee. For the three firms in the sample that did not have any compensation committee, the authors assume that all board members were involved in decisions about top executive compensation, so the proportion of inside directors in the compensation committee equals the proportion of inside directors on the board.

A dummy variable that is one if a company did experience a takeover threat and zero otherwise. Takeover threat is measured conservatively as an actual transfer of stock ownership of greater than 5 percent of the total stock of the firm to the potential acquirer and the filing of a 13D statement with the SEC, at least a year in advance of the date of acceptance of the golden parachute proposal.
time_window: up to 1 year before adoption of the golden parachute

description: Board characteristics are measured in terms of size, the proportion of outside directors, and the proportion of inside directors sitting on the executive compensation committee. This variable is the size of the board of directors.

A factor score obtained by principal components factor analysis of the nine underlying heterogeneity indicators, with the solution rotated by the varimax method. The second factor loaded on variation in age, tenure with the firm, variation in tenure with the firm, and tenure with the top management group. It was computed separately for the inclusive and the exclusive definition of the top management group. The underlying indicators came from 10,960 individual-level executive observations.
time_window: each of the eight time periods, 2-year intervals from 1967

description: A factor score from the same varimax-rotated principal components analysis of the nine indicators. The first factor loaded mostly on the two indicators of occupational diversity and, for the inclusive group, also on the two indicators of educational diversity. Diversity on the categorical dimensions was measured with a Blau form and a Shannon form, each taking a value of zero when all group members fell in one category.
time_window: each of the eight time periods, 2-year intervals from 1967

description: A factor from principal components factor analysis of six performance indicators. The first factor loaded very highly on earnings/sales, earnings/net worth, earnings/equity, and earnings/total capital, and was labeled short-term performance. Data came from the Value Line computer tapes for firms still independently operated in 1982 and, for firms that had declared bankruptcy or been acquired, directly from annual reports or from summaries in Moody's Industrial Manuals.

The second factor from the principal components factor analysis of the six performance indicators. It had high loadings on the price/book value indicator and the price/earnings ratio, and a less substantial loading on the earnings/sales ratio, and was labeled expected long-term performance. The same data sources as for short-term performance were used.

Market share for the preceding period was subtracted from current market share, the absolute value was taken, and these values were summed within the industry for each year to give uncorrected rivalry. Two indicators of rivalry were then obtained per industry and year by dividing uncorrected rivalry by either the four-firm or the eight-firm concentration ratio. Because there were only two indicators, the standardized indicators were added to obtain an overall indicator.

For each year of interest a count was made of the number of articles published by the Wall Street Journal during the year and indexed within the food or oil industry sections, and a measure was taken of the amount of space allocated to each of the two industries in the New York Times index. There being only two indicators, the standardized indicators were simply added to obtain an overall indicator.
time_window: each of the years of interest over 1967-1981

description: Participants indicated their nationality, and national differences were used as a proxy for cultural differences. Culture is defined by country cluster, based on previous cross-national research attributing similar managerial values and beliefs to similarities in national culture: North American (U.S. and Canada), Anglo (U.K.), northern European (Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Austria), Latin European (France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Portugal), and Nordic (Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland). The 303 participants represent 16 countries.

Membership in the Latin European country cluster (France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Portugal) as distinguished from the other four clusters in the Tukey HSD comparisons of cluster means. Latin European managers were compared with managers from other cultures.

Interpretation items in a questionnaire containing 36 items using a seven-point Likert scale, designed to assess issue interpretations, e.g. whether the issue is a 'crisis'. Each interpretation item was analyzed separately by analysis of variance to assess the overall impact of national culture, and differences between cluster means were then tested with the Tukey studentized range test.

Single questionnaire item asking whether the issue is a threat, rated on a seven-point Likert scale, following the Essex Bank Case. The item was analyzed by analysis of variance across country clusters and cluster means were compared with the Tukey studentized range test.

Single questionnaire item asking whether the issue is a 'crisis', rated on a seven-point Likert scale, following the Essex Bank Case. The item was analyzed by analysis of variance across country clusters and cluster means were compared with the Tukey studentized range test.

Response items in the same 36-item, seven-point Likert questionnaire assessing recommended responses to the potential repeal of the McFadden Act, e.g. 'Begin major changes in organizational design'. Each response item was analyzed separately by analysis of variance to assess the overall impact of national culture, and differences between cluster means were tested with the Tukey studentized range test. Items include internally oriented actions, externally oriented actions and proactive behaviors.

variable_name: cluster solution for each informant's rating grid
description: Each informant's grid of ratings of the focal bank holding companies along his own dimensions was cluster analyzed using SAS CLUSTER with three algorithms: average linkage, centroid and Ward's method. Three decision rules determined the number of clusters for each informant's data: adopt cluster solutions at large breaks in the dendrograms, avoid solutions that produce one-firm groups, and choose solutions with high interpretability based on informants' qualitative comments. Solutions of two or three clusters were obtained from all but one informant, and the three algorithms yielded exactly the same clusters in the data from 17 of the 23 informants.

variable_name: number and percentage of informants assigning each BHC to each cluster
description: For each focal bank holding company, the number and percentage of informants who assigned it to each of the three clusters commonly observed in the data were tabulated. Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 each contained a core group of BHCs assigned to the same cluster by all informants rating that company plus a secondary group clustered with the core by more than 65% of the informants; Cluster 3 exhibited neither a core nor as strong a secondary group. Individual assignments were also compared with the cluster expected if group assignments are shared across all industry participants.

Informants were presented with triads of bank holding company names and asked the way or ways in which two of the BHCs were more similar strategically and how the third was different, which elicited the bipolar dimensions each strategist uses to differentiate competitors. Each informant was then randomly assigned to one of four groups and rated an overlapping subsample of 12 of the 18 focal BHCs along his own dimensions using 11-point scales. The procedure yielded 23 rating grids, one per informant, where each grid has as many rows as the informant's elicited dimensions and as many columns as the firms he felt knowledgeable assessing.

1986 return on assets for each focal bank holding company. The average ROA of Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 was compared using a t-test of group mean differences for small samples, and the two groups were significantly different in 1986. Because many of the focal BHCs were acquired in 1987 and did not report independent ROA figures, profitability differences could not be meaningfully compared for later years.

variable_name: independence or acquisition and type of acquirer
description: Whether each focal bank holding company remained independent or was acquired after the interviews, and, if acquired, what type of firm made the acquisition, for example an international bank holding company or a bank holding company headquartered in the midwestern United States. Ownership changes occurring after the interviews were tracked up to 5 years after the executive assessments.
time_window: up to 5 years after the interviews (to 1991)

description: For each firm, data were collected on the average assets, average sales, and average production in units over the period 1981-87. These three standardized variables were combined in a simple additive scale, SIZE, as the final indicator of size.
The average market share of each firm from 1981 to 1987 in the three main markets of the world: Western Europe (M/ShareE), the U.S.A. (M/ShareUS), and Japan (M/ShareJP).
The construct was operationalized by counting the number of segments in which the firm had a significant presence. The segments are small, medium, large, specialty, and all-terrain vehicles.

Two industry experts rated all firms in the sample on a scale of 1 (much lower than industry average) to 5 (much higher than industry average) in terms of 'the relative technological sophistication in their manufacturing operations.' The average of the two ratings was used as the final indicator.
scale: 1 (much lower than industry average) to 5 (much higher than industry average)

description: Operationalized in a manner similar to relative technological sophistication: the same two experts rated firms on (a) relative overall efficiency in managing manufacturing operations (MFEFFIC), (b) relative overall effectiveness in managing human resources (MGHRES), and (c) relative speed in developing and introducing new products (SPEED). The average score of the two raters was used for each dimension, and ORGCAP is the average of these three dimensions.
scale: 1 (much lower than industry average) to 5 (much higher than industry average)

description: The capability is measured in terms of the firm's average labor cost, which is the weighted average of its production in different countries and the labor cost in each of those locations.

The standardized strategic capability variables were used as attributes in a hierarchical clustering algorithm to identify strategic groups, and a one-way ANOVA tested differences in the various strategic capabilities across strategic blocks. It was the view of the expert informants that, taken together, these variables provide a comprehensive set of indicators of the important strategic capabilities in the automobile industry.

The standardized capability variables were used as attributes in a hierarchical clustering algorithm employing the complete linkage method and Euclidean distances. Using a cut-off Euclidean distance of 1.0, eight strategic groups were obtained; the eight firms that could not be used as cases because of incomplete data were classified into three additional strategic groups based on limited data, giving 11 strategic groups for all 35 firms.

CONCOR is a hierarchical clustering algorithm that successively splits the firms into a larger number of blocks of firms with a similar pattern of relationships until a specified number of blocks has been formed, operating on the basis of convergent correlations. Six blocks were identified.

The complementarity index has a value of 1 if all the firms in a block belong to different strategic groups (an ideal type of the complementary block), and zero if all the firms in a block belong to the same strategic group and they are all linked to each other (an ideal type of the pooling block). The index only applies to non-zero blocks. The equation itself is not legible in the text; the text states that the index uses the number of strategic groups, the density of linkages of the subgraph formed by those firms in the block that belong to each strategic group, and the number of firms in the block.

Prominence within each block was studied in terms of the relative degree of each actor inside the block; relative degree is a measure of the fraction of all possible intra-block ties that a firm has, frequently used to measure power or prominence. Freeman's measure of graph centralization was also calculated for the subgraph of relations within each strategic block and used as an indicator of the concentration of prominence or power in each block.

The density matrix shows the densities of ties within and across blocks; taking the density of the second block as a cut-off point yields an image matrix of the block structure. Only one out of 15 possible inter-block links was observed.

Linkages were rated for strength from 1 (weak) to 9 (strong) using Contractor and Lorange's assessment of the inter-organizational interdependence created by different types of linkages. These ratings formed a symmetrical adjacency matrix with Aij = Aji representing the strength of the linkage between firm i and firm j; when firms had multiple linkages, Aij represents the strongest linkage between them, and the diagonal cells were assigned a value of 10.

variable_name: Entry mode (dependent variable = 1 for own entry and = 0 for joint venture/affiliate)
description: Binary variable representing the mode chosen for each entry, equal to one for a wholly-owned venture and zero for a collaborative arrangement. It was constructed from the 292 cases of entry into 13 new product markets, of which 157 (53.8%) were wholly-owned.

Total branches divided by total assets, as of January 1987 at the start of the deregulated era. Used as a proxy for the firm-specific asset of a branch network of retail outlets allowing cross-selling.

Total headquarters staff divided by total assets, as of January 1987, as a proxy for management team capacity in the sense of Penrose (1959). The authors note that a mere number count cannot distinguish differences in managerial quality.
Advertising expenditure divided by total assets in 1985-86, the last years for which full advertising data were made public. Brandname capital is proxied by the expenditure used to maintain it.

Firm size, the one firm-level characteristic not deflated by total assets. Entered as a continuous variable in the probit models, with a squared SIZE**2 term added to test for nonlinearity; descriptive comparisons are made in size quartiles.

Accumulated surplus divided by total assets as of January 1987, representing each society's relative availability of funds for investment. Deflated by total assets because it is considered size-related.

After-tax profits to assets, averaged over the 2 years prior to deregulation. The authors note that average profitability is a very imperfect proxy for the marginal profitability of new investments, but it is all that is available because post-tax data were available on a uniform basis.

Binary product-level variable equal to one for those products which involved extending credit, zero otherwise. The products coded as credit-extending are unsecured loans, credit cards, stockbroking and property development.

Binary product-level variable equal to one for those products which, according to industry sources, required a particularly large initial fixed investment, zero otherwise. The products coded as high fixed cost are estate agents, current accounts, ATMs and stockbroking.

Binary product-level variable for those products covered by the 1986 Financial Services Act, zero otherwise. The Act required sellers of selected products, including investment advice, general insurance and pension plans, to opt for either tied or independent intermediary status.

Latent construct measured with five indicators: CEO duality, coded 1 if the CEO also served as board chair and 0 otherwise; the ratio of insiders on the board, computed as the number of insiders (directors who are also members of a firm's management) divided by the total number of board members; the percentage of common stock owned by the board of directors, excluding stock owned by the CEO; the number of owners of 5 percent or more of a firm's stock (or their agents) who sit on the board; and director compensation, measured as the sum of annual retainer plus per-meeting fees. A confirmatory factor analysis of the board control submodel was used to assess how strongly the indicators load on a single factor.

Total cash compensation, the sum of salary and bonus, used as the dependent variable. Salary and bonus were not coded separately since less than one-third of the sample reported separate data. As recommended by Finkelstein and Hambrick (1989), the logarithm of compensation was used to reduce heteroscedasticity.

Firms were divided into one of six groups on the basis of whether or not they exhibited competence in none, one, two, three, four or all five of the strategy-making modes. A firm was defined as possessing competence in a given mode if its value fell into the upper one-third of the sample distribution for the mode in question. The six groups were Low Capability, Singles, Doubles, Triples, Fours and High Capability.

One of five performance factors derived from 13 questionnaire items. Respondents assessed their company's performance on current profitability compared to that of other companies in the same market and at a similar stage of development, on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (low performer) to 7 (high performer). The 13 items were factor analyzed and five valid and reliable factors emerged.

One of five performance factors derived from 13 questionnaire items, tapping indicators related to sales growth and market share in existing businesses. Respondents compared their company's performance with that of other companies in the same market and at a similar stage of development on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (low performer) to 7 (high performer).

One of five performance factors derived from 13 questionnaire items, tapping indicators related to the future positioning of the firm such as new product development and diversification into new businesses. Respondents compared their company's performance with that of other companies in the same market and at a similar stage of development on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (low performer) to 7 (high performer).

One of five performance factors derived from 13 questionnaire items, tapping indicators related to quality such as product quality, employee satisfaction and overall quality. Respondents compared their company's performance with that of other companies in the same market and at a similar stage of development on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (low performer) to 7 (high performer).

One of five performance factors derived from 13 questionnaire items, tapping indicators related to social responsiveness such as environmental and community concerns. Respondents compared their company's performance with that of other companies in the same market and at a similar stage of development on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (low performer) to 7 (high performer).

Firm size was operationalized as the natural log of total employment for the firm in 1988. For the size contingency analysis the sample was split into small firms (between one and eight employees), medium-sized firms (between 8 and 50 employees), and large firms (50 or more employees).

One of the unidimensional environmental factors that emerged from factor analysis of twelve questionnaire items on the firm's competitive environment. Two of the twelve items used a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (poor economic outlook) to 5 (excellent economic outlook); these two items were used to operationalize munificence. The competitive environment was considered munificent for firms registering a value above the midpoint of the scale and hostile below the midpoint.
scale: 5-point scale (1 = poor economic outlook, 5 = excellent economic outlook) for the munificence items

description: As suggested by Emery and Trist (1965), the measure for Turbulence was constructed by combining the Dynamism and Complexity factors together into a single index; Dynamism is a multidimensional factor comprised of change and the unpredictability of change. A firm was considered to be in a turbulent environment if the respondent perceived the competitive environment to be simultaneously complex and dynamic, that is if the two indices registered above the scale midpoints.
scale: combined index of two factor scores (dichotomised at scale midpoints)

description: One of five factors that emerged from a principal components analysis with oblique rotation of seventeen projective questionnaire items tapping strategy-making process; the CEO responded to each item on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) through 7 (strongly agree). The factor clearly reflects the Command mode postulated in the Hart (1992) framework.
scale: factor score from 7-point Likert items (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

The factor clearly reflects the Symbolic mode postulated in the Hart (1992) framework.
scale: factor score from 7-point Likert items (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

scale: factor score from 7-point Likert items (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

scale: factor score from 7-point Likert items (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

The factor clearly reflects the Generative mode postulated in the Hart (1992) framework.
scale: factor score from 7-point Likert items (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: The text defines this variable as a diluted ownership structure reflected by a large number of shareholders. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as current first generation majority owners. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as current first generation senior executives. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as original founders who are still partners or shareholders. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text uses firm age; the sample average age was 26.6 years and ranged from 1 year to 240 years. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as the range of managerial functions currently operated. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as the proportion of managerial functions that are the sole responsibility of one person. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as high levels of delegation of managerial functions to individuals. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text only lists the variable name in the hypothesis and states that it is defined in the Appendix. It is used in the correlation and regression analyses.

The text defines this variable as regular and frequent meetings with professional advisors: banker, accountant and lawyer. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as regular and frequent meetings with customers and suppliers. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as whether management has undergone some form of management training. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as financial investment received from a large number of sources, not including overdraft facilities from banks. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as non-manual control technology for the major manufactured product lines. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations for manufacturing firms.
The text defines this variable as relatively mature pieces of production equipment. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as the use of sophisticated technology in the control of the administration base. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as location in the south of England, specifically the standard regions of East Anglia, the South East and the South West. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as whether the firm has taken advantage of government training schemes. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as whether the firm has taken advantage of government grants. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as the number of major product lines or major service groups. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as the number of new major product lines or major service groups introduced during the previous year. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as the percentage of sales revenue accounted for by the major product line or service group. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as the diversity of the firm's customer base. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as the number of significant new customers added over the previous year. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as the number of suppliers from which the firm purchases goods and services. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as the extent to which the firm's supplier base is becoming more diverse and wider in scale. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as the extent to which the firm sells the majority of its products and services in nationwide or overseas markets rather than local or regional markets. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text defines this variable as the extent to which the firm is not exclusively supplied by local suppliers. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.
The text defines this variable as the number of direct competitors faced by the firm. The main analysis uses it as a small firm characteristic in correlation and regression equations.

The text uses the total number of employees as one of three surrogates for comparative growth. It is used as a dependent variable in correlation, regression, chi-squared and analysis of variance tests.

variable_name: level of sales for the last financial year (Y2)
description: The text uses the level of sales for the last financial year as one of three surrogates for comparative growth. It is used as a dependent variable in correlation, regression, chi-squared and analysis of variance tests.

variable_name: level of profitability for the last financial year (Y3)
description: The text uses the level of profitability for the last financial year as one of three surrogates for comparative growth. It is used as a dependent variable in correlation and regression analyses.
The text uses the owner-manager's rating of the business's profit performance relative to competition, with the categorical scores good, about average, or poor. It is used in chi-squared analyses.

Product innovativeness combines three items: Robertson's tripartite 'newness to the market', the three-part 'newness to the firm', and Booz, Allen & Hamilton's six-part 'level of innovation'. The first two items were measured on a three-point scale and the third on a six-point scale; the items were respectively standardized to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, and the mean of the three standardized items represents product innovativeness (Cronbach alpha = 0.82). Excluding any of the three items reduced the alpha coefficient.
scale: standardized Z score with mean 0 and standard deviation 1

description: The number of firms involved in the product introduction. Because there were too few cases of three or more cooperative firms, the variable was collapsed into two categories: cases of a single firm offering a new product and cases of multiple firms offering a new product.
scale: binary: single firm vs. multiple firms

description: Strategic linkage between cooperating firms, classified into two categories: vertical cooperations (links were not between similar functions, i.e. distribution arrangements) and horizontal cooperations (links were between similar functions, i.e. R&D consortium). Single-firm cases are essentially a form of vertical cooperation within the company and are thus considered vertical.
Size of the firm, coded as large = Fortune 500 or Fortune International 500, small = otherwise, and mixed = at least one firm in each firm size category.
Product type, coded as Type B versus Type M industries, following Kodama's distinction between mechatronics (Type M) and biotechnology, pharmaceutical and chemical (Type B) products.
scale: categorical: Type B vs. Type M

description: Agreement between the firm's industry and the product's industry; the variable captures whether the product is offered in the firm's own industry or outside it.

Agreement or accord between the cooperating firms' industries, coded as intraindustry versus interindustry cooperation; added in the second phase, where single-company product introductions were discarded.
Month in which the product was introduced, coded with September 1988 = 1 and an increment of 1 per month onward.

Nationality of the firm. European-Japanese cooperations and U.S.-European-Japanese cooperations were deleted because there were too few cases, so the categories analyzed were (1) European, (2) Japanese, (3) U.S., and (4) crossnational (U.S. with one or more foreign partners).

variable_name: percent of the firm's stock held by outside institutions
description: The percent of the firm's stock held by outside institutions-banks and trust companies, pension funds, savings and loan associations, insurance corporations, and mutual fund management institutions. A 3-year mean of institutional stockholdings was computed for each firm over 1983-85, and the two firms with the highest and the lowest mean in each industry were selected. The log transformation of the ownership measure was used in the analysis to account for skewness in the ownership data distribution.

variable_name: long-term debt as a percent of the firm's total capital
description: Long-term debt as a percent of the firm's total capital, measured as a 3-year mean over 1983-85, following similar measures used in earlier studies of corporate strategy and capital structure.

variable_name: return on assets, return on equity, price-earnings ratio, total stock return
description: Four measures of financial performance, each based on 3-year means over 1983-85: percent of return on assets (ROA), an accounting measure of the efficiency with which corporate assets are managed; percent return on equity (ROE), a measure of the efficiency with which shareholders' investments are managed; price-earnings (P-E) ratio, which reflects a relative value of the firm's stock in the market; and percent of total stock return, which captures income to shareholders in the form of dividends and capital gains due to share price increases.

variable_name: percent of stock held by corporate executives
description: Annual data on the percent of the firm's stock held by corporate executives, averaged over 1983-85. The log transformation of the ownership measure was used in the analysis to account for skewness in the ownership data distribution.

variable_name: percent of stock held by family owners
description: Annual data on the percent of the firm's stock held by family owners, averaged over 1983-85. The log transformation of the ownership measure was used in the analysis to account for skewness in the ownership data distribution.

variable_name: percent of stock held by insider-institutions
description: Annual data on the percent of the firm's stock held by insider-institutions, averaged over 1983-85. The log transformation of the ownership measure was used in the analysis to account for skewness in the ownership data distribution.

variable_name: firm loadings on 'ideal firm' components / mixed strategy indicator
description: Within each pooling period variable scores are standardized and a 0-type principal-component analysis is performed on the covariance matrix, retaining three significant components. The loadings of each firm on the significant 'ideal firm' components within each pooling period are averaged, and firms with high loadings (>±0.4) on more than one ideal type are interpreted as exhibiting mixed strategies.

Strategic group membership coded 1, 2 or 3, obtained by subjecting the averaged firm 'strategic vectors' of loadings on the three significant components to k-means type cluster analysis within each pooling period. Three distinct clusters are identified in each time-series pool and one-way ANOVA of firm loadings by group shows significant F-scores in all cases.
time_window: group structure derived within each pooling period

description: Period-average worldwide sales, used as an independent variable in the logit estimations of DFP. The authors report that the strategic groups explain a large share of the variance in period-average worldwide sales, so that firms of similar size tend to group together.
time_window: period average for each contextual period

description: Dummy variables indicating the possession of resources related to DFP skills: use of DFP in other markets (ODFP; No = 0, Yes = 1) and other DFP in the U.S. (ODFPUS; No = 0, Yes = 1). They are significant when tested alone but lose significance when GROUP is added to the logit model.

U.S. sales to global sales ratio, described as a measure of strategic resource focus on the U.S. market and of dependency on the U.S. auto market. It is not significant alone, is marginally (0.10) significant with GLOBAL, and is not significant with GROUP.

Choice of investment versus exports modelled as a dummy variable DFP, with values of 0 for trade and 1 for direct foreign production. None of the firms rely totally on DFP in the U.S. market, but the decision to use DFP indicates a shift in the planned structure for the host market; the test focuses on 1980-1985, during which five firms began to manufacture part of their product line in the U.S.
time_window: observed for each year; test period 1980-1985

description: Annual percentage increase in market share, where the relevant market is that for foreign autos in the United States. Percentage change in market share removes size effects which would dominate in measures of actual unit sales or simple change in market share, and the effect of a 'rising tide' of increasing foreign car sales over time on all firms is eliminated.
time_window: measured for each contextual period (1974-79 and 1980-85)

variable_name: Strategic orientation (five composite scales and cluster membership)
description: Industry-specific, multi-item, 7-point anchored Likert-type scales operationalized five measures of strategic orientation; a composite measure was obtained for each scale by averaging the individual item raw scores. Firms were divided into different clusters based on the five measures using a K-means clustering algorithm, yielding Prospectors, Defenders and Reactors.
scale: 7-point anchored Likert-type scale (1 = 'significant decrease in emphasis', 4 = 'no change', 7 = 'significant increase in emphasis')

description: Four measures were used: CEO cash compensation, CEO salary, CEO annual bonus, and average executive team cash compensation. CEO cash compensation was defined as the sum of annual salary, bonus and fringe benefits. The executive team consisted of the officer group (typically vice-presidents and more senior managers) for whom corporate proxies provided compensation data. All four measures were expressed in 1987 dollars using the GNP Implicit Price Deflator.

Dummy indicators of the existence of the different types of outcome-based compensation plans for executives: a bonus plan equals 1 if an annual bonus plan for executives existed, a stock option plan equals 1 if a stock option plan existed, a long term plan equals 1 if a long-term incentive plan existed, and a total incentive plan equals 1 if either a bonus plan or a stock option plan or long-term incentive plan existed.
The proportion of outcome-based cash compensation was measured by dividing CEO bonus by CEO cash compensation.

Environmental change was operationalized as two time periods of the sample years: 1978-82, when the utilities were effectively regulated, and 1983-87, when they were increasingly deregulated and faced a rapidly changing environment. Period was a factor in the repeated measures analysis of compensation.

Events that were evidence of outcomes were coded as either positive (good news or successful accomplishments), negative (bad news), or mixed (results indicating elements of both success and failure); events coded as 'mixed' were not included in developing the dichotomous variable. Outcomes include both tangible results of entrepreneurs' courses of action and less tangible value judgments about the success or failure of venture activities by corporate sponsors and entrepreneurs. Of the 719 total events, 341 include changes in outcomes, 232 (68%) of which were judged negatively, while 109 (32%) were judged to represent positive outcomes. Events were aggregated into monthly counts for the time series equations.

The directions of the actions that occurred in each event were coded according to whether they represented an expansion (addition, elaboration, reinforcement), contraction (subtraction, reduction, deemphasize), modification (revision, shift, correction), or persistence (in current direction) of the course of action under way. Because trial-and-error learning consists of realizing which course of action to pursue and which to avoid, modification events were combined with contraction events to develop a composite measure of 'change'. The coded events were aggregated into monthly counts; continuation events total 456 and changing events total 263 over the 12 years.

When a resource controller or CIP entrepreneur stated plans or outcome criteria that were different from the past, the event was coded as a shift in plans. Shifts in plans and associated outcome criteria occur in 7% of all 719 events during the 12-year period. Events were aggregated into monthly counts for the time series equations.

When corporate sponsors were behaviorally involved in an event, it was coded as such. SP is the monthly count of the number of times corporate sponsors were involved. Corporate sponsors' involvement occurred in 10% of all 719 events during the 12-year period. Events were aggregated into monthly counts for the time series equations.

When an event involved a change in the activities occurring external but reported as relevant to CIP (including changes in competitors' technology and industry structure), it was coded as an environmental event. External environmental events occurred in 13% of all 719 events during the 12-year period. Events were aggregated into monthly counts for the time series equations.

Ambiguity was treated as a condition that differed by venture period rather than as a scored variable. The expansion period (1980-85), when ambiguity about multi- versus single-channel cochlear devices was present, and the contraction period (1985-89), when it disappeared, were analyzed in separate time series regressions.

Respondents indicated the degree of importance they generally place on each listed factor in their business strategy on a 1 (not at all important) to 7 (extremely important) scale. The authors state that the aggregate of four indicators was used to measure the construct, with a reliability (Cronbach's alpha) estimated at 0.782. The individual indicators are not reproduced in the available text.

Respondents indicated the degree of importance they generally place on each listed factor in their business strategy on a 1 (not at all important) to 7 (extremely important) scale. The authors state that the aggregate of three indicators was used to measure the construct, with a reliability (Cronbach's alpha) estimated at 0.741. The individual indicators are not reproduced in the available text.

Respondents rated the impact of electronic filing on competition in the market for tax-related services for individuals once electronic filing is fully implemented, on a 1 (low impact) to 7 (high impact) scale. The authors state that the aggregate of five indicators was used to measure the construct, with a reliability (Cronbach's alpha) estimated at 0.762. The individual indicators are not reproduced in the available text.

Respondents indicated the degree of opportunity or threat posed by the factor for their business operations, where an opportunity implies the business can exploit it to gain relative advantage over competitors and a threat implies the business is likely to be more negatively affected, on a 1 (great threat) to 4 (neutral) to 7 (great opportunity) scale. The authors state that only one indicator was used because they sought to measure the perceived attractiveness of a specific technological innovation to a specific firm, and that a higher score indicates a more positive effect valence.
