Respondents indicated the likelihood that their organization would adopt each of the listed responses, on a 1 (not at all likely) to 7 (extremely likely) scale. The authors state that the aggregate of three indicators was used to measure the construct, with a reliability (Cronbach's alpha) estimated at 0.933. The individual indicators are not reproduced in the available text.

Measured as the percentage of returns filed electronically during the tax filing season that followed a year after the IRS had introduced electronic filing. Data were collected from the IRS regarding adoption of electronic filing by each firm in the sample. The authors used the subset of the sample that had the opportunity to file electronically during the next season, since the dependent variable is irrelevant for firms that did not have the choice to file electronically.
time_window: tax filing season one year after the survey (1988)

variable_name: Efficiency orientation and service quality orientation (set)
description: Competitive posture was represented by two survey-based orientations, efficiency orientation (four importance items) and service quality orientation (three importance items), each rated on a 1 to 7 scale of importance in the firm's business strategy. They entered the path model as two separate exogenous variables.

Coded from the annual cause maps of each firm. Two coders identified causal assertions in the letters and linked the concepts into maps, achieving 93.4 percent agreement on the codes and 93.0 percent agreement on whether a causal statement had been made. Seven protocols identified significant change across maps: new or deleted concepts, replacement of a specific concept with a more general term, introduction and sustained use of new categories, the degree of linkage or disruption of existing causal chains, sign reversals between established relationships, changes in lists of examples or subsets, and the amount of continuity from one map to the next. Changes that do not involve many linkages are treated as incremental (low level) learning; additions producing new clusters or a major proportion of altered map are treated as more significant (high level) change.

variable_name: strategic renewal versus decline (firm fate and strategic action)
description: The two firms were selected because, despite being matched on geography, size, and traffic base, they experienced different fates: the C&NW remains viable today while the Rock Island sought bankruptcy protection in the mid-1970s and ceased to exist. Major changes in mental models were reflected in proactive strategies: after the 1956 shift the C&NW made plans for reducing costs, raising productivity, and increasing maintenance-of-way, whereas the Rock Island delayed maintenance-of-way, did little to control costs, and after 1964 pursued a merger with the Union Pacific.

variable_name: environmental munificence (relative prosperity of the two firms)
description: Munificence is characterized through the firms' relative prosperity. The Rock Island enjoyed relatively high performance in the early 1950s due to post-war economic prosperity and a surge in business activity associated with the Korean War, while the C&NW did not experience the same degree of prosperity; this relative prosperity may have accounted for the Rock Island's tendency to view traffic declines as a temporary economic adjustment.

variable_name: concepts about environmental change in the maps (competition from trucks, airlines, barges, and pipelines)
description: Detection of environmental change is coded as the presence of concepts in the firm's map that deal with changes in its environment. For the Rock Island, eight concepts in the 1950 letter to shareholders are concerned with competition from trucks, airlines, barges, and pipelines, though these trends are not associated with a larger shift in the environment; threats from increased competition begin to disappear from the Rock Island's map in 1954. For the C&NW, declines in traffic were seen as important concepts signaling permanent changes in the environment requiring internal change.

variable_name: signs of unlearning and learning in the maps
description: Coded from the maps as the continual addition and deletion of concepts (the experimentation associated with learning), the generalization of specific concepts, the sustained use of new variables, and whether the new map refreezes. The C&NW exhibits definite signs of unlearning and learning before the 1956 succession and continues to add new concepts and connections afterwards, while the Rock Island shows little or no evidence of experimentation and moves from one 'frozen' state to the next.

Acquired companies were the experimental group; the control group was 30 companies not involved in a merger during the same time period, drawn from the Standard and Poor's Stock Guide, distributed over the New York and American Stock Exchanges and of comparable asset size.

The percentage of a company's top management team that had departed, computed at each of the 5 years following the merger (experimental group) or the time of initial observation (control group). Each executive was identified by name, age and position from the company's 10-K or proxy statement, and the parent company's human resources officer reported whether the executive was still employed and, if not, the date of departure; control executives were tracked directly in 10-Ks or proxy statements. Data are available for 55 acquisitions, with complete management team data on 50 acquisitions; five companies sent incomplete data.
time_window: 5 years from the date of the merger or the time of initial observation

variable_name: type of merger or acquisition (FTC categories)
description: Acquisitions were classified using the Federal Trade Commission's five-fold category system based on the primary economic relationships established between the parent firm and the target firm: horizontal, vertical, product extension, market extension and unrelated. The four types of related acquisitions were compared with the unrelated acquisitions, and the five categories were also compared with one another.

Managers were divided into a presidential group of presidents, CEOs, or chairmen of the board and a vice-presidential group of vice-presidents, senior and executive vice-presidents, controllers, secretaries, and treasurers, based on the position recorded for each executive at the time of the merger.

The average elapsed time from the acquisition date until departure, in months, computed for the managers who turned over within 5 years of the merger: 55 of the 142 presidents, CEOs, or chairmen of the board and 168 of the 619 vice-presidents and other officers.

A three-item scale, developed by Khandwalla (1976/77), used to measure environmental hostility; respondents rated the external environment within which their firm operates. The respondents' ratings on these three items were averaged to arrive at a single index for each firm. The higher the index, the more hostile the firm's environment.

A seven-item scale developed by Khandwalla (1976/77) that measures organicity, that is, the extent to which organizations are structured in organic versus mechanistic manners. Respondents indicated on seven-point Likert-type scales the extent to which each item characterizes the structure of their firm. Each firm's mean rating on these seven items was used as that firm's organicity index; the higher the index, the more organic the firm's structure.
scale: seven-point Likert-type items; index range 1.29 to 7.0 (mean 5.07, standard deviation 1.10)

description: A nine-item scale assessing the firm's reliance on innovation, proactiveness, and risk-taking; the first three items assess the tendency toward innovation, the second three the proactive orientation, and the third three the risk-taking propensity. Items were adapted from existing instruments (items 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8) or are original (items 4, 5, 6 and 9). Respondents characterized their firms' strategic posture on these nine items and the mean rating was used as the firm's score; the higher the score, the more entrepreneurial the strategic posture. All items loaded above 0.5 on a single factor (average loading 0.66).
scale: item ratings; index range 1.22 to 6.78 (mean 4.33, standard deviation 1.23)

description: A modified version of an instrument developed by Gupta and Govindarajan (1984). Respondents first indicated on a five-point Likert-type scale, ranging from 'of little importance' to 'extremely important', the degree of importance their firm attaches to each of nine financial performance criteria; they then indicated on another five-point scale, ranging from 'highly dissatisfied' to 'highly satisfied', the extent to which the firm's top managers are currently satisfied with their firm's performance on each of these same criteria. The 'satisfaction' scores were multiplied by the 'importance' scores to compute a weighted average performance index for each firm.

Respondents were asked to rate the extent to which they agreed or disagreed that various statements were descriptive of their firms' current overall business strategy, including reliance on various business practices and competitive tactics. The rating scales for these statements ranged from 'strongly disagree' (= 1) to 'strongly agree' (= 5). Zero-order correlations between these ratings and performance were computed separately for firms above and below the mean hostility value.

The interviews gave an exhaustive list of 120 variables describing buyers' behavior in the stainless steel industry and of 91 variables in the corrugated cardboard paper industry. Fifty-seven variables were common to both industries; 34 were specific to the corrugated cardboard paper industry and 63 were specific to the stainless steel industry (concerning technical specifications). Variables were measured on ten point scales, except purchased products variables measured by percentages of each product category.
scale: ten point scales; purchased products measured by percentages

variable_name: market segments (groups resulting from cluster analysis)
description: For each industry an ascendant hierarchical cluster analysis was performed on the set of variables to define segments, i.e. groups of customers having similar purchasing behaviors; analyses of variance of all the active variables between the groups were then made to test the significance of inter-group differences (F test). The paper industry analysis shows 15 main market segments and nine particular cases; the stainless steel analysis results into 20 market segments and 21 particular cases.

The interview variables cover key purchasing criteria on which customers evaluate suppliers' offers, measured on ten point scales. Averages have to be compared with the buyer's expectations on lowering prices measured on the same scale, and standard deviations indicate the dispersion of buyers' judgements.

The main differentiation sources were selected after evaluation among key purchasing criteria (average scores measured on 10-point scales, standard deviations). The sources common to both industries are punctuality of deliveries, quick response to unexpected orders, quick answers to requests, product quality regularity and short delivery times, ranked among the most important criteria.

variable_name: probability of imitation by other competitors
description: For each potential differentiation source found through the market studies, the experts were asked which means would be adequate to implement these strategies, what the approximate cost of implementation would be, what (subjective) probability of imitation by other competitors they would forecast, and how to defend from such imitations.

Ten variables described the firm's position on differentiation criteria: product relative quality (four variables among which was a product quality index); the firm's position on delivery times, technical services and other services (and a 'product environment index' combining them); product innovation; and a composite differentiation index. The composite differentiation index is built from the product quality index, the product environment index and product innovation.

Product relative quality was described by four variables among which was a product quality index; it is one of the ten variables describing the firm's position on differentiation criteria contained in the postal questionnaire.
An index combining the firm's position on delivery times, technical services and other services, part of the ten variables describing the firm's position on differentiation criteria.
Product innovation, one of the ten variables describing the firm's position on differentiation criteria in the postal questionnaire sent to firms.

variable_name: profitability index (return on sales, return on investment)
description: The firm's performance was evaluated through market share variation and profitability: return on sales, return on investment and a profitability index. The profitability index was the dependent variable of the stepwise multiple regression, with the product quality index, the 'product environment' index, product innovation and the firm's cost position as independent variables.

The firm's performance was evaluated through market share variation and profitability; market share variation is the variation of the firm's market share, used as an outcome and correlated with the product relative quality index.

variable_name: Key purchasing criteria with low dispersion across buyers (Table 3)
description: Industry-wide differentiation sources were identified from interview data with buyers as key purchasing criteria rated on 10-point scales whose averages and standard deviations across buyers indicated that current offers were not optimal for most customers (e.g., punctuality of deliveries in stainless steel, paper quality regularity in corrugated cardboard).

variable_name: Discriminant dimensions of expected improvements across customer clusters
description: Segment-specific differentiation sources were identified by a hierarchical cluster analysis of buyers' expected improvements on key purchasing criteria (10-point scales), followed by a discriminant analysis between the groups that gave the most discriminant dimensions and positioned the groups on them. These dimensions were read as possible segment-specific differentiation strategies.
scale: cluster analysis and discriminant functions on 10-point rating items

description: Both PIMS data bases contain a measure of order of entry which identifies three categories-namely, pioneers, early followers and late entrants. The two samples have very similar distributions on this variable: 30 percent of the start-up businesses claim to have been pioneers, 30 percent early followers and 34 percent late entrants, while the corresponding percentages for the adolescent sample are 34, 33 and 34.

Market share is one of the performance measures used to compare the three entrant groups. It is the dependent variable in the regression equations because it is much more highly correlated with order of entry and with the other independent variables than any of the measures of profitability.

Profitability is one of the performance measures used to compare the three entrant groups, alongside market share. The authors also discuss pioneers' high return in relation to the highly negative return on sales and cash flow to investment ratios in the start-up sample.

Three measures of scale were included-namely, the breadth of the product line offered by the new business, the depth and breadth of its market distribution (an index combining the number, size and spread of customers), and the size of its production capacity relative to the market. The presence or absence of patent protection was also included in this category.

These variables describe the level and types of resources that a new business has available to it by virtue of its ownership characteristics. They include the size and the diversity of the parent firm's activities, the possibility of buying materials or selling output internally, and the opportunity to share existing production facilities or distribution channels.

These variables measure the ongoing competitive position of the business relative to competitors. They include the level of marketing expenditure (a composite of advertising, selling and promotion), product quality and customer support services, price, and direct manufacturing costs; the latter two variables are ratios measuring the position of the reporting business relative to its three largest competitors.

For each year from 1971 to 1986, a discrete (yes/no) measure capturing whether the organization added any business program for the first time ever. The addition of a business program is measured when a college grants a degree in this category of majors for the first time.

For each year from 1971 to 1986, a discrete (yes/no) measure capturing whether the organization added any graduate program for the first time ever. The addition of graduate programs is measured based on administrators' responses to the annual HEGIS questions on the institution's highest level of offering.

variable_name: moving from single sex to coeducation
description: For each year from 1971 to 1986, a discrete (yes/no) measure capturing whether the organization changed from a single sex to a coeducational institution, for the first time ever. The switch to coeducation is measured based on administrators' responses to the annual HEGIS questions on the gender of the student body.
The endowment measure is endowment divided by enrollment (i.e., adjusted for organizational size). The ratio is computed as the market value of endowment divided by enrollment.
The debt measure is divided by total assets; the debt ratio is computed as debt divided by total assets.

An industry-specific measure for reputation: Cass and Birnbaum's six-point selectivity index, where a higher score indicates greater selectivity. The index is recognized as an authoritative source in evaluating the reputation of colleges.
Organizational size is measured in terms of full-time equivalent (FTE) enrollment.
Organizational age, which the authors describe as self-explanatory.
The two relevant region variables are coded as dummy variables (Northeast and West-Southwest).
The dichotomous (yes/no) measure of organizational death, coded as such when enrollment and revenues both drop to zero.
time_window: lagged 1 and 2 years behind the predictor variables

description: A continuous performance measure: the proportional change in enrollment from the prior to the current year.
time_window: lagged 1 and 2 years behind the predictor variables

description: A continuous performance measure: change in operating margin, where operating margin captures financial viability and is measured as (operating revenue-operating expenses)/operating revenues.
time_window: lagged 1 and 2 years behind the predictor variables

description: The standard deviation of return on assets during the prior 10-year period.
The standard deviation of the firm's weekly stock market returns during the prior 10-year period.
Calculated as total current and long-term debt divided by total common equity.

A continuous measure of the proportion of CEO total compensation comprised of long-term incentive grants, calculated as the value of CEO long-term incentives divided by total compensation (i.e., cash compensation plus the value of long-term incentives). LTI compensation includes grants of multiyear performance incentives, such as performance shares, performance units, and restricted stock.

variable_name: proportion of CEO total wealth change from noncash sources
description: The natural log of the percentage of CEO total compensation derived from noncash sources, capturing the amount of a CEO's total income that is 'at risk'. The measure is constructed as (the value of CEO long-term incentives plus the change in value of stock held by the CEO for the year) divided by (cash compensation plus the value of CEO long-term incentives plus the change in value of stock held by the CEO for the year); the formula as printed is split across paragraphs.

variable_name: percentage of a firm's equity held by the CEO
description: The percentage of a firm's equity held by the CEO, used as a third measure of managerial incentives and as the firm's level of CEO equity ownership.
Indicates the portion of the board composed of outside directors.
Calculated as the percentage of common stock owned by outside directors.
A dichotomous variable coded '1' if a nondirector stockholder owns at least 5 percent of the common stock, and '0' otherwise.
Captures the separation of the CEO and board chair positions, a dichotomous variable coded '1' if the CEO and board chair positions were separate and '0' otherwise.

Calculated using Jacquemin and Berry's entropy measure, which takes into account the number of segments in which a firm operates and the relative importance of each segment as a portion of total sales.

Counts of 'important' patent grants, counted by year of application, where a patent is defined as important if it was granted in two of the three major markets: the U.S.A., Japan and the European Community. Derwent Publications produced the counts broken down by therapeutic class using their proprietary classification and search software.

The stock of patents obtained in each research program, calculated by assuming a 20 percent depreciation rate for knowledge. The authors reason that firms with competencies in a particular disease area are more likely to have obtained patents in that area historically; they note the coefficient resembles a lagged dependent variable.

Constructed from the interview transcripts using a 5-point Likert scale, where the firm was coded 5 if standing in the larger scientific community was a dominant criterion for the promotion of scientific personnel and 1 if an individual's publication record and reputation in the wider community were not significant factors in promotion decisions.

Measured on a 5-point Likert scale, where in any given year a firm scored 5 if problem-solving within the cardiovascular research programs appeared to be characterized by frequent exchange of rich, detailed information across disciplinary or disease area boundaries and 1 if there was very little communication within the program or across programs within the firm.

Measured on a 5-point Likert scale, where for any given year a value of 5 was assigned if global research was managed as a seamless whole under a single director, while a value of 1 was assigned if geographically dispersed research units were managed through entirely separate organizations within the firm.

Scored on a 5-point Likert scale, where in any given year a firm scored 5 if resource allocation within research was entirely controlled by a single individual and 1 if resource allocation was entirely decentralized and managed through a governing committee.

Proportion of the executives of the acquired firm present at the time of the acquisition who had departed by the end of the second postacquisition year. Executives counted were officers holding a title above the rank of Vice-President or inside directors, or both, identified through public filings made prior to the acquisition; departure information was gathered from postacquisition firms by phone or written request, yielding data on 451 executives in 96 acquired firms.

The percent of the More-Senior group that had departed within 2 years was calculated, where More-Senior executives are those holding the titles Chairman, Vice-Chairman, President, CEO, or COO. More-Senior executives comprised 36 percent of the sample of executives.

The percent of the Less-Senior group that had departed within 2 years was calculated, where Less-Senior executives are those not holding the titles Chairman, Vice-Chairman, President, CEO, or COO. Less-Senior executives comprised 64 percent of the sample of executives.
Executives who held any of five titles were classified as 'More-Senior': Chairman, Vice-Chairman, President, CEO, and COO; the remainder were classified as 'Less Senior.'

Calculated as the average within rater difference between rated performance at t = 4 and rated performance at t = 0; negative values imply performance declines and positive values imply improvement. The reliability coefficient for this measure was 0.848.

Raters were asked 'How would you rate the profitability of [the acquired firm] at the time the deal was made (in 19-);' on a 7-point scale with anchors 'very poor' and 'very good.' Six executives from the acquiring firm and six security analysts who specialized in the acquiring firm's securities were selected as informants for each acquisition; the average number of respondents was 4.02 per acquisition. The reliability coefficient for performance at t = 0 was 0.852, and its correlation with preacquisition return on equity was 0.573.
time_window: at the time the deal was made (t = 0)

description: Raters were asked to rate the profitability of the acquired firm 'Four years later (in 19-)' on a 7-point scale with anchors 'very poor' and 'very good.' The reliability coefficient for postacquisition performance (t = 4) was 0.846.

Coded 1 if any member of the acquired firm's top management team received corporate-level officership and/or directorship in the postacquisition firm, and 0 otherwise. This condition was evaluated by examining the first annual report or proxy statement filed by the acquiring firm following the acquisition event, so status bestowal did not reflect rewards for eventual good postacquisition performance outcomes.

Two judges independently categorized each acquisition from business descriptions of the merging firms in Moody's Industrial Manuals as 'Related' if the firms served the same or similar customers or produced the same or similar products, and otherwise as 'Unrelated'; they disagreed on only 6 of 96 observations, and conflicts were resolved. Firms categorized as Related were then examined using CRSP SIC codes, and when both firms were in the same dominant 4-digit SIC industry the acquisition was classified as 'Horizontal.' Thus three categories were measured via two dummy variables: 'Unrelated' coded 1 if classified Unrelated and otherwise 0, and 'Horizontal' coded 1 if classified Related and CRSP provided the same 4-digit SIC code and otherwise 0; 'Other-Related' was the omitted category. The sample included 18 Horizontal, 48 Other-Related, and 30 Unrelated acquisitions.

Dummy variable for the organizational status of a production, with studio production serving as the reference category (ORG = 0 for studio films). Films were classified as studio or independent productions from Warner Brothers records on the organization and management of production.

Production cost of each film, collected from audit reports at Princeton and verified by comparing them to detailed expense ledgers and reports at the University of Southern California. Expenditures on each project were tracked from the initial acquisition of rights through shipment of a final print. Dollar figures were adjusted to 1967 equivalents using a CPI inflator. In the descriptive analysis, values adjusted for the effect of year of production are used.

The portion of box office receipts remitted to the distributor, described as the primary measure of performance because it is a direct indicator of public response to films and the indicator typically tracked in the film industry. In the descriptive analysis, values adjusted for the effect of year of production are used.

variable_name: margin of gross over production cost (MARGIN)
description: The difference between the distributor's gross revenues and the production cost of the film, which is less sensitive to production expenditures and introduces some control for them.
The ratio of the margin of gross revenues over production cost to production cost, which provides adjustment for the scale of projects.

variable_name: estimate of the cash flow to the distributor from each film (CASHFLOW)
description: An estimate of the cash flow to the distributor from each film, described by the authors as a relatively crude measure that takes account of the differences in the structure of payoffs associated with independent and internal production and provides some indication of the profitability of films.

Variance of the performance variables for independent and studio films, compared with F-ratios for homogeneity of variance, together with Kolmogorov-Smirnov probabilities for goodness of fit of the cumulative distributions of the two groups. Variance in market performance is used solely as a measure of variability in audience appeal, not as a measure of risk.

A factor composed of two survey items using a 7-point Likert scale on which high scores represent significant board pressure or involvement in the decision to restructure or acquire business units. The responses to the two items were summed to obtain a scale score.

Operationalized as the ratio of outside members divided by total board size. Outside directors were identified as those directors with no personal or professional relationship with the firm, other than in their capacity as directors.
Equity interests for outside directors were obtained from proxy statements and operationalized as the sum of their equity holdings divided by common shares outstanding.
Equity interests for top management were obtained from proxy statements and operationalized as the sum of their equity holdings divided by common shares outstanding.

A factor composed of three survey items describing the importance of different control system types on a 7-point Likert scale. Level of strategic control in the pre-restructuring period was measured using a survey item anchored by decreased emphasis and increased emphasis relative to the post-restructuring period, and the change in strategic control was used to adjust the current measure to obtain a measure of pre-restructuring emphasis.

The mean number of years in which individuals were a member of the top management team, collected for members of the top management team from the proxy statement and Dun & Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Managements.

The mean number of years in which individuals were employed by the firm, collected for members of the top management team from the proxy statement and Dun & Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Managements.
The mean number of years in which individuals served on the board of directors, collected for board members from the proxy statement and Dun & Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Managements.
Operationalized as the coefficient of variation, i.e., the standard deviation divided by the mean board tenure.

variable_name: variance in mean top management team tenure
description: Operationalized as the coefficient of variation, i.e., the standard deviation divided by the mean top management team tenure.
Measured using the average number of years of education of top management team members.

The percentage of total outstanding common voting shares owned by insiders of the firm. The data are based on 13G filings with the SEC, which require that all officers and directors of a public corporation report their purchases and sales of stock in the firm, and were constructed from the Value Line Investment Survey for 1981. Log-transformed in the regressions to correct for skewness.
The percentage increase or decrease in insider ownership between 1981 and 1987, constructed from Value Line Investment Survey data. Log-transformed in the regressions to correct for skewness.

The percentage of outstanding common voting shares that were held by owners of 5 percent or more of the firm's common shares. Blockholdings reported in Value Line are based on the SEC's 13D reporting requirements.
A binary variable which has a value of 1 if a blockholder bought into a firm that did not have a blockholder at the beginning of 1981, and 0 if otherwise.
The percentage of common voting shares managed by institutions, reported in Value Line and based on the SEC's 13(f) reporting requirements.
The percentage increase or decrease in institutional ownership between 1981 and 1987, based on institutional share ownership reported in Value Line.

Downsizing is measured as the percentage change in firm sales between 1981 and 1987, as reported in COMPUSTAT. The authors use both sales and employee measures because each captures a different dimension of inefficiency stemming from overexpansion: firms may increase their efficiency by cutting back on marginal sales, or they may maintain their sales levels but reduce employees to improve labor productivity.

Downsizing is measured as the percentage change in firm employees between 1981 and 1987, as reported in COMPUSTAT. It is used alongside the sales measure because it captures the labor-productivity dimension of inefficiency stemming from overexpansion. Found to be skewed and log-transformed in the regressions.

Change in total diversification is measured using the sales and employee-weighted Herfindahl-Hirschman indices of concentration, following Comment and Jarrell (1992). These data were obtained from TRINET, Inc.'s Large Establishment Database. The authors note that change in total diversification is measured as increases in focus.

variable_name: Percentage change in the specialization ratio
description: The specialization ratio measures the importance of the core business of the firm; it is estimated as the proportion of total firm sales accounted for by the sales of the largest line of business, defined by four-digit SIC code. The measure used is the percentage change in this ratio, measured using TRINET data.

variable_name: Percentage change in the related ratio
description: The related ratio measures the importance of the core of related businesses of the firm; it is estimated as the proportion of total firm sales accounted for by the sales in the firm's largest industry, defined by two-digit SIC code. The measure used is the percentage change in this ratio, measured using TRINET data.
Estimated as the proportion of sales of all four-digit SIC lines of business divested between 1981 and 1987 to total firm sales in 1987. Found to be skewed and log-transformed in the regressions.

Financial restructuring is first measured as the percentage change in the proportion of cash flow paid out by firms in dividends and interest, as reported in COMPUSTAT. Cash flow is measured with the formula developed by Lehn and Poulsen (1989): revenues minus cost of goods sold, interest payments and taxes, with no deduction for depreciation. To avoid bias from economic cycles, the change is estimated between two periods, 1976-80 and 1981-87; the printed formula for this change is garbled in the text.

Following the agency theory argument that financial restructuring is intended to reduce inward investment, reductions in inward investment are measured as the percentage change in average annual additions to property, plant, and equipment between 1976-80 and 1981-87.

To capture changes in the rate at which cash flow is reinvested, the authors estimate the change in the average annual proportion of cash flow invested in property, plant, and equipment between 1976-80 and 1981-87.

Corporate restructuring is operationalized as the set of portfolio restructuring measures (change in sales and employees, change in diversification, specialization and related ratios, divestiture activity) and financial restructuring measures (change in payouts, investment and investment rate) between 1981 and 1987, each analyzed as a separate dependent variable in OLS regressions. Data come from COMPUSTAT, TRINET and Value Line.

A winner was defined as an organization whose product was awarded the first prize in an event. Organizations that won second and third places were not treated as winners because some competitions did not award second and third prizes. The natural logarithm of cumulative victories plus unity was computed for each firm to allow valid observations for organizations with zero victories, and this measure was lagged by a year.

The exit rate is the probability of an organization experiencing an event in the interval from t to t + s given that an organization was at risk at time t. An exit was defined as bankruptcy, cessation of operations, or withdrawal by an organization, and mergers were not defined as exits. In the exponential specification the transition rates are postulated to be log-linear functions of the covariates; the event history of an organization was split into yearly spells to allow for time-varying covariates, and each spell was coded as right censored unless a firm exited.
A variable called STARTUP was created to account for de novo organizations. Startup organizations were expected to exit at a higher rate than pre-existing organizations.

The natural logarithm of the number of accumulated contests was computed and lagged by a year. Data on hill climbing, fuel economy, endurance, and speed contests organized during 1895-1912 were collected from the Horseless Age; the sample consisted of 381 contests organized in the United States.

Each firm's annual share of industry sales revenue in each year that the business participated in the industry. Annual business sales information was available for larger participants, and linear interpolation was sometimes used to estimate values for missing years; minor participants were assigned a market share of 0.1 per cent. The variable is lagged one year, as 'Lag share', when used as an independent variable in the survival analyses.
scale: share of industry sales revenue (per cent)
time_window: annual; lagged one year in the survival analyses

description: One-year spells (record years) created for each firm beginning with its entry year and continuing until it exited or until the end of the study period, giving 585 record years in total. The measure takes a value of 1 if the firm continued to operate at the end of the year (right-censored) and 0 if the firm shut down its business during the year, a procedure known as spell-splitting. Firms that sold their pacemaker businesses were treated as right-censored cases.

Number of times that a firm was among the first to introduce incremental innovations, created from published product line information. The count starts with the second year in which the firm participated in the industry and is updated for each year that the firm operated. Firms were credited as being among the first when their products incorporated the incremental change during the first year the innovation was offered in the market. The variable is lagged one year with respect to the dependent variable.
time_window: time-varying, updated annually; lagged one year

description: Number of times that the firm introduced competitors' innovations during the second or third year after the innovation became available, recorded as a time-varying accumulated count that is updated for each year the firm operated and lagged one year with respect to the dependent variable. Years 2 and 3 were combined for convenience of presentation; similar results were obtained when variables were specified for each year.
time_window: time-varying, updated annually; lagged one year

description: Number of times that the firm introduced competitors' innovations in the fourth year or later after the innovation became available, recorded as a time-varying accumulated count that is updated for each year the firm operated and lagged one year with respect to the dependent variable.
time_window: time-varying, updated annually; lagged one year

description: Combines the first to market and adoption variables to record the number of times that a firm either was among the first to introduce or adopted an incremental innovation. The variable is time-varying, updated annually, and used in the survival analysis.
time_window: time-varying, updated annually; lagged one year

description: Number of firms offering incremental innovations that the firm had been among the first to introduce, averaged by the value of the 'First to market' variable. Firms that had not been among the first to introduce as of the current record year received the average value of the competition variable, which included all record years of incumbents that never introduced an incremental innovation. The variable is time-varying and lagged one year with respect to the dependent variable.
time_window: time-varying, updated annually; lagged one year

description: Number of competitors offering similar products, defined equivalently for total introductions and used in the dissolution analysis. The competition variables were lagged by one year with respect to the dependent variables.
time_window: time-varying, updated annually; lagged one year

variable_name: entry rates of second sources into technological communities
description: The dependent variable is the rate at which second sources enter a technological community, estimated as an event count with the Poisson model. The unit of analysis is each community, which has an observation for each quarter that it is in existence. Two analyses are performed, one with the sponsor forming the center of the community and one with the design forming the community center. Entry dates are quarterly.
The number of community members was the number of firms belonging to a community, including both the sponsor and the second sources. The independent variables were all lagged by one quarter.

Community density was simply defined as the number of technological communities in the market other than the focal community. It is computed separately for the analyses in which communities are defined at the level of the sponsor and those in which the design is the unit of analysis. It is entered linearly in one model and with a squared term in another.

variable_name: number of second sources outside the community
description: The number of second sources outside the community was computed by summing second source density across all communities at each point in time and subtracting the number of second sources in the focal community.

Any community whose primary design was based on RISC technology was given a value of one for this dummy variable. RISC is treated as an architectural innovation because the linkages between the software and hardware components of the processor changed.

Installed sales base equals the total value of all products ever sold by the community, so it reflects the cumulative history of the community. Quarterly sales for each community were constructed from quarterly product shipment data supplied by the data research firm multiplied by pricing information from EDN's Annual Survey of Microprocessors, with annual price data converted to quarterly by interpolating between years. Shipment data covered only 20 of the 30 communities; 1.25 percent of total calculated sales was equally allocated to the missing communities' sales values.

variable_name: community's sales in the previous quarter
description: A second measure of dominance, the community's sales in the previous quarter, which reflects the community's recent performance rather than its cumulative history. It was built from the same quarterly product shipment data and EDN price information used for the installed sales base.

Using the dates of innovations, a clock was constructed for each community which was reset to zero each time there was an innovation; the clock was collinear with age until a community introduced its second innovative product. Innovation of Type I occurred when a community member, usually the sponsor, shipped a product technologically superior to anything previously produced by the community; for sponsor-defined communities, Innovation Type II also counted the introduction of a new design or an improvement in an existing design. The technological ranking of a product was determined by consulting Money's Microprocessor Data Book and descriptions of products in EDN's Annual Survey of Microprocessors.

Each executive was asked to evaluate the 30 scenarios and rate both the attractiveness of the relationship and the probability that they would pursue such a relationship on a seven-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (very low) to 7 (very high). The numbers reported for these two questions were added together to create the dependent variable, 'evaluation of the opportunity' (alpha = 0.95).

variable_name: significance of the technology to current strategy
description: One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the significance of the technology to the company's strategy. Each of the 17 criteria was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high) across the 30 scenarios.

variable_name: existing skill capability to develop the technology
description: One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the firm's existing skill capability to develop the technology. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high). Both the factor and the square of the factor were entered into the analysis.

variable_name: life cycle phase of the technology
description: One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the life cycle phase of the technology to be developed. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the compatibility of operating and management styles of the firm and the potential partner. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the number of other potential partners for developing the technology. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the level of asset-specific investments required by the cooperative project. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the information availability relative to the partner. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high); the squared term of the factor was used to test the curvilinear prediction.

variable_name: favorability of potential partner's cooperative history
description: One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the favorability of the potential partner's cooperative history. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

variable_name: potential to learn from the relationship
description: One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the potential to learn from the collaborative relationship. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

variable_name: importance of learning by doing of the technology
description: One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the extent to which the technology requires 'learning by doing'. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the potential for broad corporate application of the technology. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

variable_name: ability to patent protect the technology
description: One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the potential for gaining patent protection for the technology. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the availability of technological substitutes. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the potential of the collaboration for decreasing development risk. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the total expected cost for developing the technology. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

variable_name: contingency of cost commitments on outcomes
description: One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the degree to which cost commitments for the technology can be made contingent on outcomes. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

One of the 17 informational criteria used to describe the scenarios; it represents the potential for increased exposure to related markets. Each criterion was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high).

Executives were asked to report the number of levels between them and their firm's CEO; the further the executive was from the CEO, the higher the number (CEO = 0). The variable was entered into a hierarchical regression after the control variables and situation-specific factors.

Executives denoted their primary work experience by marking one of five categories: engineering and R&D, general management, finance and accounting, marketing, or other. Each was coded as a dummy variable in the analysis and the dummies were entered as a block following the controls and specific factors.

Executives provided the number of years they had worked in the firm's primary industry. Interaction terms were generated between industry tenure and the various factors used to describe the collaborative opportunity and entered into the model following all other variables.

variable_name: number of significant factors per subject
description: Stepwise regression entered only the information that was statistically significant at p < 0.05 for each executive's individual model, and the number of significant criteria entering into an individual model was counted. The average number of significant factors per subject for the final sample was 3.7; in the aggregated hierarchical regression nine of the 17 factors were significant at the 0.05 level.
scale: count of significant criteria (0 to 8 per executive)

description: The organization's strategy was identified based on interviews, annual reports, and survey items of strategy content incorporated into the questionnaire; the strategy-content measures were based on the strategy variables identified in Segev (1989), and means on each item were generated from multiple middle manager respondents. The top manager of each organization was surveyed on strategy content and, with middle manager responses, provided the basis for self-typing. Each author reviewed the cases to corroborate the student's classification; the authors' independent assessments matched for all 25 firms.

Weighted, additive scale computed from the item loadings of the final factor analysis for the championing factor. Items asked respondents to rate how frequently they performed each activity on 5-point Likert-type items (1 = never, 5 = very frequently); the frequency scale was intended to capture the extent to which managers perceived the roles to be part of their work activity.
scale: 5-point Likert-type frequency scale (1 = never, 5 = very frequently)

description: Weighted, additive scale computed from the item loadings of the final factor analysis for the synthesizing factor. Items asked respondents to rate how frequently they performed each activity on 5-point Likert-type items (1 = never, 5 = very frequently). Two of the original synthesizing items loaded on championing as well as synthesizing, and the other loaded on championing rather than synthesizing.
scale: 5-point Likert-type frequency scale (1 = never, 5 = very frequently)

description: Weighted, additive scale computed from the item loadings of the final factor analysis for the facilitating factor. Items asked respondents to rate how frequently they performed each activity on 5-point Likert-type items (1 = never, 5 = very frequently). Two of the original facilitating items were dropped and one became part of the implementation scale.
scale: 5-point Likert-type frequency scale (1 = never, 5 = very frequently)

description: Weighted, additive scale computed from the item loadings of the final factor analysis for the implementation factor. Items asked respondents to rate how frequently they performed each activity on 5-point Likert-type items (1 = never, 5 = very frequently). The item 'Encourage informal discussion ...' loaded on implementing rather than facilitating.
scale: 5-point Likert-type frequency scale (1 = never, 5 = very frequently)

description: Single global item similar to that used in previous research: 'Overall, how involved are you in the creation and implementation of the organization's strategy?', rated on a 5-point scale from 1 = not at all to 5 = to a great extent.
scale: 1 = not at all, 5 = to a great extent

description: Counts the number of firms exiting a particular market segment in any given year. Entered in the models as a linear term and a squared term to capture non-monotonic rate dependence, and interacted with firm niche overlap density. The variable is lagged by one observation period.

An indicator variable that marks up observations in which a firm's mid-niche falls in different market segments between two consecutive years and in which that firm's niche midpoint changes between two consecutive years. The measure ensures that the firm itself must change its niche for a segment move to be observed and eliminates events driven solely by shifts in segment boundaries.

Count of firms whose niches overlap at least partly with the niche of a focal firm, measuring the extent of competitive intensity experienced by the firm. It is included as a baseline covariate and interacted with the number of departing peers. The variable is lagged by one observation period.

variable_name: position in the market center segment (MCS)
description: An indicator of whether the firm's position falls in the market center segment, included to get at the difference between the resource-rich market center and the two peripheries. In the failure-rate analysis the variable is entered together with its interaction with industry concentration. All independent variables in the event-history file are lagged by one observation period.

variable_name: position in the low periphery; position in the high periphery
description: Indicator variables for whether the firm's position falls in the low periphery segment or in the high periphery segment, tested in separate failure-rate models each with its interaction with industry concentration.

The ratio of the annual production of the four largest firms to total industry output. The authors note the measure applies directly to concentration in the market center while allowing peripheral segments to develop independently. It is used as a control in the transition-rate analysis and as the moderator of segment position in the failure-rate analysis.

The failure rate of U.S. automobile manufacturers, estimated with piecewise exponential models in which position in the market center and position in each periphery are entered with their interactions with industry concentration. In the transition analysis, the likelihood of position move out of the segment and the likelihood of organizational failure are modeled as competing risks.

variable_name: M&A shareholder gains (dollar-weighted cumulative abnormal returns)
description: Cumulative abnormal returns for the acquiring firm over a three-day window surrounding the announcement of the deal, incorporating the day before and the day after the announcement. Abnormal returns are the firm's returns minus expected returns, with the market-model parameters estimated by regressing the firm's returns on market returns for a period of 240 to 40 days preceding the announcement of the M&A event. The CARs are weighted by the market value of the firm two days prior to the announcement.
time_window: three-day event window (day before to day after the announcement)

description: The number of institutional investors that own stock in both the acquiring firm and the target firm, obtained by extracting the ownership portfolios of both target and acquiring firms and counting the number of matching owners for both firms at the end of the quarter immediately preceding the announcement of the deal.
time_window: end of the quarter immediately preceding the deal announcement

description: The sum of ownership stakes at the acquiring firm of all owners that held stock in both the acquiring and the target firm at the end of the quarter preceding the announcement of the deal.
time_window: end of the quarter immediately preceding the deal announcement

description: The number of independent directors serving on the board, divided by the total number of directors. The board information was obtained from the IRRC Director database.
time_window: end of the year preceding the M&A event

description: The number of directors serving on the board, extracted from the IRRC Director database, used to capture the board's ability to ensure that management decisions support the interests of shareholders.
time_window: end of the year preceding the M&A event

description: Indicator variable equal to 1 if the CEO is also the chair of the board and 0 otherwise, derived from the title of the executive obtained from Execucomp.
time_window: end of the year preceding the M&A event

description: The percentage of outstanding shares owned by the CEO at the end of each fiscal year, relying on data obtained from Execucomp, used as an indicator of incentive alignment.
time_window: end of each fiscal year preceding the M&A event

description: The Black-Scholes value of the options granted to the CEO during the year, obtained from Execucomp. Because the variable was skewed and kurtotic, a natural logarithmic transformation was applied.
time_window: the year preceding the M&A event

description: Return on assets minus the social aspiration level, where the social aspiration level is set to the median ROA of the shipping firms in the same nation as the focal firm. To focus the analysis on performance below the aspiration level, performance is specified as a spline function with separate slopes above and below zero, and the variable below the aspiration level is the one used to test Hypothesis 3.

The logarithm of the total fleet of the firm, measured as a count of ships as in the dependent variable. This variable tests Hypothesis 2 and is used in the interaction variable that tests Hypothesis 1.

The number of used ships acquired during the focal year; the variable counts only used ships because they can be acquired quickly, allowing easy linking of cause and effect through the one-year lag of dependent variables. Acquisition of new ships is excluded because it is a lengthy procedure with difficult-to-specify lags, but the analysis controls for the same-year deliveries of new ships on order.

The proportion of the current fleet in the ship types acquired in the focal year, calculated by multiplying the proportion of the current fleet in each ship type with an indicator variable of whether an acquisition was made in the same ship type, and summing these products. It varies between zero (all acquired ships have types new to the firm) to one (all existing types of ships are acquired). The measure treats all categories of ships as equally different from each other.

A logit regression was estimated on an indicator variable of whether the firm made any acquisitions, and an inverse Mills' ratio with Lee's (1983) correction was calculated and entered into the rigidity regression to take selectivity into account.

A set of dummy variables that takes into account whether the firm is the pioneer, the second entrant, the third entrant or a late follower, with the last category serving as the base case. Entry into the second generation is taken as the starting point because acceptance of the first generation was scarce among consumers.

Switching costs are calculated for each period and each firm's customer installed base following Shy's (2002) method, which requires measures of sizes and prices. Sizes enter through the installed bases of the operators, that is, their number of users, and prices are taken from Average Revenue per User (ARpU). The measure is intended to reflect the cost of changing brands for an average user.
Market share is the number of users subscribed to the services of operator i in country j divided by the total number of users in country j. Quarterly information is used.
The profitability of firm i is measured through the variable EBITDA, calculated by Merrill Lynch by dividing total EBITDA by total revenues. Quarterly information is used.

Firm-specific returns are measured as firms' return on assets (ROA) for the year, less the industry norm ROA for the year, where the industry norm is the median ROA in the three-digit NIC industry. Firm-specific ROA values greater than 0 indicate superior firm-specific profits, and the analysis models only observations where prior-year profits were above the industry norm. The coefficient of lagged firm-specific returns measures the regression relationship between firm-specific returns across time periods and is the measure of sustainability, with larger values indicating greater sustainability of abnormal profits (a lower rate of decay or convergence toward the industry norm).

An index that tracks pro-market changes in laws and regulations governing product, capital, and labor markets. It is based on established measures that track liberalization of foreign direct investment regulations, tariff reductions, strengthening of intellectual property laws, strengthening of shareholder and creditor protections, and the liberalization of labor laws and restrictions.

An indicator variable with a value of 1 for firms classified as affiliates of a business group by the Center for Monitoring the Indian Economy (CMIE), and 0 otherwise. Its direct effect is encompassed by the firm fixed effects rather than estimated separately because of its time-invariant nature.

An indicator variable with a value of 1 for firms classified as affiliates of a foreign firm by the Center for Monitoring the Indian Economy (CMIE), and 0 otherwise. Its direct effect is encompassed by the firm fixed effects rather than estimated separately because of its time-invariant nature.
An indicator variable with a value of 1 for firms reporting nonzero R&D expenses in the year and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: M&AD (greater investment in marketing and advertising)
description: An indicator variable with a value of 1 for firms reporting marketing and advertising expense to sales ratios that are greater than the industry mean in the year, and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: mean performance on the source and transfer tasks
description: Participants received a score after each decision trial for the performance of their team; higher scores were achieved by meeting production targets for the production team or meeting run targets for the cricket team. Scores on the two tasks were in equivalent units for comparison, and the performance scores were averaged across all 20 decision trials to compute the mean performance outcomes for both the source and transfer tasks. Transfer was assessed by comparing the mean performance of the two order conditions on each task.

variable_name: transfer performance on the cricket team task
description: Performance on the cricket team transfer task was the average across all 20 decision trials, calculated exactly as described for Study 1. Transfer was also assessed with Murdoch's (1957) formula for the percentage and direction of transfer by comparing transfer performance with the performance of the 16 Study 1 participants who completed the cricket team task as the source task; in the regression model, mean performance across all 20 decision trials on the cricket team transfer task was the dependent variable.
time_window: averaged across all 20 decision trials of the transfer task

description: Task variation was manipulated through changes to the employees managed by experimental group participants in decision trials 6-13 of the production team source task. In the control condition participants managed the same five employees throughout the 20 decision trials; in the experimental condition two of the employees were changed at decision trial 6 and then changed back to the original employees at decision trial 14. The task reverted back to the control level from decision trial 14.
time_window: decision trials 6-13 of the source task

variable_name: performance on the production team source task
description: Performance on the simulation tasks was calculated exactly as described for Study 1 with one change: the individual decision trial data were averaged to compute mean performance across three trial blocks for the production team task. Block 1 included decision trials 1-5, block 2 included decision trials 6-13, and block 3 included decision trials 16-20; the data for trials 14 and 15 were excluded from the final analysis as they were influenced by lagged effects from the variation manipulation trials.
time_window: decision trials 1-20 of the source task, aggregated into three trial blocks

description: Knowledge of the underlying structural relations of the source task was assessed using 12 questionnaire items presented after participants finished working on the production team source task. These 12 items were derived directly from the underlying equations of the simulation; participants were asked to respond with true or false after each statement. Two items referred to knowledge about the allocation of employees to jobs, three about the use of feedback, four were concerned with goals, and a further three with the provision of rewards. An overall knowledge score was computed by taking the sum of correct answers to the 12 items.
time_window: after completion of the production team source task

description: A measure of how much decision makers engaged in systematic search of the problem space was derived from each participant's decision data; systematic search involves unconfounded changes made to decision variables within each block of trials, an unconfounded change being one in which only one variable at a time is changed within a decision trial. The systematic search strategy measure was computed as the number of unconfounded changes made across each of the four decision categories (employees, goals, feedback, and rewards) divided by the number of changes it was possible to make within each decision category for each trial block, and these trial block proportions were added together for the final measure.
time_window: across trial blocks of the source task

description: The CEO first identified the members of the TMT and then classified each manager's dominant functional expertise into five areas. Diversity was quantified using Blau's heterogeneity index; a high score on this index indicates high functional diversity.

Assessed with three items following methods developed by Jehn (1995). Both the CEO and the CTO indicated the extent (1-7) to which each statement described their TMT's decision making over the previous three years, and the two sets of responses were averaged. Cronbach's alpha was 0.84.

Assessed with four items following methods developed by Jehn (1995). Both the CEO and the CTO indicated the extent (1-7) to which each statement described their TMT's decision making over the previous three years, and the two sets of responses were averaged. Cronbach's alpha was 0.92.
Following Smith, Collins, and Clark (2005), the CEO indicated the number of innovations developed over the previous year in four categories, and the four numbers were summed up.

Adapted from Tan and Litschert (1994). The CEO indicated how predictable the firm's competitive environment had been over the previous three years in six aspects (1-7, 7 as 'highly unpredictable'); the six ratings were averaged and had a Cronbach's alpha of 0.66.

Following Li and Atuahene-Gima (2001), the CEO indicated the extent to which the government and its agencies had provided support to the firm over the previous three years in four areas. Cronbach's alpha for this scale is 0.79.

Host country de facto property rights protection is observed with four different measures, of which the Rule of Law index of the World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators is the one used in the main specification that tests Hypothesis 1. The index measures the quality of contact enforcement, property rights, police and courts, as well as the likelihood of crime and violence. The composite measure ranges from approximately -2.5 to 2.5, with higher values corresponding to stronger protection.

The similarity weighted experience measure of firm i in relation to host country j, built from the firm's home country and its network of global subsidiaries drawn from the Directory of Corporate Affiliations. The numerator captures the extent of operations in a country, while the denominator captures the similarity of the country with the target host country. The final measure is the average value of experience across all other countries.

A binary measure of whether a firm made a greenfield investment in the information services sector in a host country in a given year. It takes the value of '1' if a firm made an investment in a new greenfield project in a host country in a given year, and '0' otherwise. The unit of analysis is the firm-host country-year.

Firms' stock of publications collected over a 10-year window up to the collaboration date from the ISI Science Citation Index; the window was chosen to allow firms' publication output to translate into reputational effects. All publications were weighted by the number of citations they received in the Web of Science database (as of April 2010) and depreciated at a yearly rate of 10 percent. Corporate publications were aggregated at the parent level after taking into account mergers and acquisitions, divestitures and name changes.
time_window: 10-year window up to the collaboration date

description: Scientists' lifetime publications collected from the ISI Science Citation Index, weighted by the number of citations they received in the Web of Science database (as of April 2010) and depreciated at a yearly rate of 10 percent.

Firms' patents collected over a six-year window prior to the contract time and weighted by the citations they received as of June 2010, with a 10 percent annual depreciation rate, to control for variation in patent quality. Corporate patents were aggregated at the parent level, accounting for the firm's corporate structure during the relevant time window. The text does not name the patent data source.
time_window: six-year window prior to the contract

description: Scientists' patents collected over a six-year window prior to the contract time and weighted by the citations they received as of June 2010, with a 10 percent annual depreciation rate. The text does not name the patent data source.
time_window: six-year window prior to the contract

variable_name: entropy index of diversification (firm knowledge base)
description: Breadth of a firm's knowledge base measured by an entropy index of diversification based on the distribution of the firm's patents across technology domains defined by the inventive IPCR patent classes. The index equals the sum over domains of f_i multiplied by ln(1/f_i), where N is the total number of technological domains in which the firm has been patenting and f_i is the fraction of patents in the i-th category. The index takes higher values as firm knowledge becomes more diversified, so the measure is coded opposite to the specialization construct.
time_window: based on the firm's patents in the relevant window

variable_name: entropy index of diversification (scientists' knowledge base)
description: The knowledge-diversification index of the university scientists is defined in the same way as the firm index, with scientific domains replacing technological domains. Scientific domains were identified in the MEDLINE database of the National Library of Medicine, where NLM specialists classify each article according to the Medical Subject Headings (MESH) thesaurus; a combination of MESH descriptors and MESH qualifiers was treated as constituting a scientific domain, and MESH categories that do not reflect substantive scientific information were eliminated. Higher values indicate a more diversified knowledge base, so the measure is coded opposite to the specialization construct.
time_window: based on the scientist's publications up to the collaboration date

description: Multi-item measure developed by Schilke and Goerzen (2010) with a five-dimensional, second-order structure. The dimensions are interorganizational coordination, alliance portfolio coordination, interorganizational learning, alliance proactiveness, and alliance transformation. A composite score of the construct is computed as the simple average of its dimensions' items. The measure was corroborated by correlating it with the firm's prior R&D alliance experience.

Multi-item measure relying on the measurement items introduced by He and Wong (2004). The items gauge the extent to which a firm routinely carries out innovation projects aimed at entering new product domains. The measure was triangulated with archival information on R&D intensity.

Competitive advantage is operationalized as a two-dimensional construct with the first-order dimensions of strategic performance (qualitative dimension) and financial performance (quantitative dimension), both measured in comparison to competition. The six items for the two performance dimensions were adapted from Jap (1999) and Weerawardena (2003). The measure was collected in a separate survey three years after the survey of the independent variables.
time_window: t=2, three years after the first survey

description: Multi-item measure of the volatility and unpredictability of the firm's external environment, using items developed by Miller and Friesen (1982) and Jap (1999). The perceptual measure was validated against two archival indexes of instability in sales and net assets.

The change between the 'before' and 'after' cross-citation rates of partner firms' patents; a cross-citation rate is the rate of citation of one firm's patents in new patents applied for by the partner firm, taken as a measure of the extent of interfirm knowledge transfer and of technological overlap. 'Before' rates are computed from patents applied for after 1 January 1979 and issued before 31 December 1984; 'after' rates from patents with applications dated after 1 January 1987 and issued prior to 1 December 1994. Negative values indicate divergent development and positive values convergent development.
Firm's pre-1985 cross-citations of its partner firm's patents, used as a narrowly focused measure of absorptive capacity. Entered as a continuous variable in the models of firm-level learning.
A dummy variable indicating alliances that involve shared equity by partner firms, as against contract-based alliances.

A dummy variable indicating 'unilateral' contract-based alliances (technology licenses, R&D contracts and second-source agreements), contrasted with bilateral contract-based alliances such as cross-licensing, joint development and technology sharing agreements.

The firm's R&D intensity in 1985, drawn from Compustat for U.S. firms and from Compact Disclosure's 'Worldscope Global' data base for non-U.S. firms; used as an additional measure of absorptive capacity.

The natural logarithm of the firm's sales in 1985, drawn from Compustat for U.S. firms and from Compact Disclosure's 'Worldscope Global' data base for non-U.S. firms; used as an additional measure of absorptive capacity.
A dummy variable designating Japanese companies, used to test whether Japanese firms absorb more capabilities from alliances with U.S. firms than other foreign partners.
The absolute value of the difference between post- and prealliance cross-citation rates for a firm pair, compared between alliance partners and nonallying pairs.
A dummy variable equal to 1 for the 792 alliance pairs and 0 for the 858 nonallying pairs in the control sample.

Hypothesis 1 is tested by comparing knowledge sharing in the semiconductor industry with that in steel. The authors document the faster pace of technological change in semiconductors with relative patenting activity by pairs of similarly sized steel and semiconductor companies and with R&D expenditure to sales, which was almost 8 percent in semiconductors in 1994 compared with 0.5 percent in steel.

variable_name: importance of sources of technical information
description: Respondents rated nine possible sources of technical information on a 7-point scale where 1 represented 'not at all important' and 7 represented 'very important'. For comparison with the steel study the semiconductor sample was limited to the 53 respondents from 21 U.S. IC companies. The survey also produced rankings of preferred knowledge sharing vehicles linking the respondent with another IC company and with equipment vendors. In the semiconductor sample, 57 percent rated technologists at other companies as an important source of technical information, meaning that they scored this source 5 or above on the 7-point scale.

The number of times the respondent was approached by someone outside of his or her company for technical advice or technological information in the year previous to the survey year, coded into the categories Never, 1-5, 6-10, 11-15, or 16 or more times. It is used as a dependent variable in the ordered logit analyses.
time_window: year previous to the survey year

description: The number of times the respondent provided the requested information, coded into the categories Never, Less than Half, About Half, More than Half, or Always. It is used as a dependent variable in the ordered logit analyses.
scale: ordered categories (Never; Less than Half; About Half; More than Half; Always)
time_window: year previous to the survey year

description: Whether the respondent had participated in cross-company knowledge sharing; 71 percent of the U.S. semiconductor respondents had done so, compared with 83 percent of the respondents from the steel study.

Whether the respondent worked for a U.S. or a Japanese company. Of the 134 respondents, 96 worked for U.S. companies and 27 worked for Japanese companies; the larger sample used for the logit analysis contained 123 respondents from Japanese and U.S. companies.
Whether the respondent's company provided training on how to control sensitive information.

variable_name: rewards for presenting papers at professional conferences
description: Whether the respondent's company included paper presentations at professional conferences in pay or promotion decisions.
