Response to the question 'to gain access to the complementary knowledge of other participants', reported on a 5-point Likert scale where 1 = not important and 5 = very important. The answer is given by a company for a particular R&D consortium.

Average of the Likert-scale scores on two questions: 'to share fixed costs among participants and realize economies of scale in R&D' and 'to avoid wasteful duplication of research by dividing the tasks among participants', each scored 1 = not important to 5 = very important.
Difference between the measure of the skill-sharing motive and the measure of the cost-sharing motive. Its range is from -4 to 4.

Response to the questionnaire question 'How wide was participation from other industries?' scored 1 = from single industry to 5 = wide variety of industries. Responses of 3 or less are classified as homogeneous and responses of 4 or more as heterogeneous; the split was determined by the mean of the overall scores.

variable_name: diversity measures (DT, DU, 2- and 3-digit product counts)
description: Palepu's total (DT) and unrelated (DU) entropy measures and Montgomery's 2- and 3-digit product count measures, calculated for each R&D consortium by using the 3-digit SIC codes of the participating firms' main businesses, assuming that each firm has an equal share in an R&D consortium. The heterogeneity/homogeneity distinction is determined by splitting the full sample in half by the means of these measures.
Total project budget for a project, in real terms as of the project's first year.

Likert scale score on the response to project-related R&D spending as a percentage of the government budget per firm on the project. R&D spending is measured as a percentage of the government outlay per firm on the project because firms would not disclose absolute expenditures for each R&D activity.

Operationalized as a discounted sum of the number of units operated by chain i over its history to the year before the current year, where the discount depreciates past operating experience to account for antiquation due to environmental change or decay due to forgetting. The square of the variable (Own Operating Experience 2) is also included to test for a U-shaped influence. In the reported models operating experience is discounted by the square of the age of the experience.
time_window: from the chain's founding to the year before the current year

description: The number of the nine census regions in which the chain operates, used as the operationalization of geographic generalism. The modal number of regions for a chain is one, representing 5,676 observations, and only 308 observations (2.8%) represent chains operating in more than six census regions.

A discounted accumulation of all the units other chains have operated during the focal chain's life, computed from the year of the organization's entry to the year before the current year, where the industry mass is the total number of units in all chains during the year less the number of units of the focal chain. Operating experience is discounted by the square of the age of the experience.
time_window: from the organization's entry to the year before the current year

description: Defined using the industry experience since entry equation but with the number of chain failures in year t as the numerator, so it is a discounted accumulation of the industry's failures during the focal chain's life. Competitive experience is discounted by the square root of the age of the experience.
time_window: from the organization's entry to the year before the current year

description: A discounted accumulation of industry mass from the first year of the industry's experience to the year before the focal organization's entry, with Mt and the discount factor as in the industry experience since entry equation.
time_window: from the industry's first year to the year before the organization's entry

description: Defined using the industry experience at entry equation but substituting the number of failures in a year for the industry mass, giving the discounted accumulation of industry failures up to the year before the organization's entry.
time_window: from the industry's first year to the year before the organization's entry

description: A chain is coded as failing when it ceases to operate at least three units. Failure is modeled through the instantaneous rate of failing given that the chain was operating at t; chains that leave the industry by merging or being absorbed (44 cases as opposed to 705 failures) are treated as right censored. Life histories are broken into 1-year spells so that time-varying covariates can be incorporated.

Dummy variable that takes the value 1 if the founding team is politically heterogeneous, that is, composed of at least one Democrat and one Republican, and 0 otherwise (all founders registered with the same party). Teams enter the sample only if all founders could be identified as Democrats or Republicans, and firms whose founders changed party affiliation since 2015 were dropped.
time_window: one observation per organization (L2 data current as of July 2023)

description: Dependent variable in the logistic regression on the likelihood of team formation, set to 1 for teams in the authors' dataset and 0 for randomly constructed counterfactual teams; the counterfactual sample was created by randomly assigning founders within states to founding teams (with variants randomizing nationally or within state, industry, gender, age, race, and experience cells) and combined with the actual data.

Dummy variable indicating whether a startup has ceased operations or remains operational (including being acquired). The active status of the company's website was verified and cross-referenced with PitchBook, and in rare cases where a company was listed as operating but evidence indicated closure the firm's status was adjusted. In this venture-backed sample, closure typically represents failure to achieve product-market fit or investor expectations rather than successful lifestyle businesses chosen by founders.

The logarithm of the total amount of funding received, in USD. For companies lacking funding data on Crunchbase, a total funding of zero dollars was assigned. It is analyzed both including firms with zero funding and excluding them.

Crunchbase does not display an exact employee count but provides an estimated range (e.g., 1-10 or 501-1000); the authors approximated employee count by calculating the logarithm of the midpoint number of employees as shown by Crunchbase (e.g., ln(5.5) or ln(750.5)).
Dummy variable indicating whether the startup has been sold to another entity or not, where not acquired includes both operational and closed startups.

Crunchbase Rank is determined by Crunchbase's proprietary algorithm that takes into account the number of connections of a profile within the platform, the amount of community engagement, funding events, news articles, acquisitions, and more. A higher (worse) rank is associated with political heterogeneity, and the authors caution that this proprietary measure should be interpreted cautiously.

Founders were classified as Democrats or Republicans using L2 voter registration data. Crunchbase and L2 were merged by exact matching on standardized first and last names (punctuation, accents, middle names, and suffixes removed) and US state addresses, retaining only unambiguous matches and adding manually verified fuzzy matches; this uniquely identified 30% of the founders in L2. Only Democrats and Republicans were considered, and firms whose founders changed political identity since 2015 were dropped.
time_window: L2 data current as of July 2023, compared with L2 data from 2015

description: A three-step text measure built from earnings call transcripts. First, using the relevant strategy category dictionaries, LIWC software produced counts of the words and the percentage of words associated with each strategy category within a transcript. Second, the proportions of words in the transcripts (prepared comments and managers' responses) pertaining to each of the six relevant strategy category dictionaries were divided by the total number of words in the dictionary to create normalized word proportions. Third, the six normalized word proportions associated with growth were summed.

A validated dictionary-based measure of curiosity applied to the text of analyst questions in the Q&A portion of the earnings call, assessing the frequency of word use from a dictionary of 76 words that align with an individual's expression of curiosity. The percentage is multiplied by 100.
time_window: Q&A portion of the earnings call

description: The analytical thinking measure from LIWC applied to analysts' language, providing a score between 0 and 100, with low scores indicating informal, intuitive thinking and high scores indicating formal, logical thinking. The variable is a composite measure of articles and prepositions minus pronouns, auxiliary verbs, adverbs, conjunctions, and negations.
time_window: Q&A portion of the earnings call

description: Each firm-quarter's mean sell-side analyst rating from IBES, using the first rating issued after the earnings call. Ratings follow the standard 1-5 scale (1 = Buy, 3 = Hold, 5 = Sell); lower scores indicate more favorable assessments.
time_window: first rating issued after the earnings call

description: The 12-month forward stock price forecast from IBES, averaged across all analysts covering the firm and scaled by dividing by 100. This provides a continuous, more fine-grained indicator of analysts' expectations about future firm performance following the call.

IBES data on analysts' 12-month forward stock Price Forecast and earnings per share forecasts are used to develop a mean value of the PE ratio across all analysts in the month of the pertinent earnings call, which is then divided by 100.

IBES data on analysts' 12-month forward dividend yield forecasts are used to develop a mean value of dividend yield across all analysts in the month of the pertinent earnings call, which is then multiplied by 100.

Indicator for whether the subject was randomly assigned to see a social media message from the CEO supporting gun rights. In the non-activism control condition, respondents were shown a product page from the Bean Brigade website with generic product information only. Randomization into this condition, and into the private/public condition, occurred at the level of participant pairs and produced four study conditions: Private Control, Private Activism, Public Control, and Public Activism.
scale: binary indicator (1 = saw the CEO activism message)

description: Indicator for whether the subject made a private or public (i.e., observable to their study partner) choice of winning either a 12-ounce bag of Bean Brigade coffee or a bonus payment. Subjects in the public choice condition were told that their choice and the information about Bean Brigade coffee would be shared with their partner. Subjects in the private condition were given the same choice without seeing a message about its observability.

Indicator for whether a subject chose Bean Brigade coffee over the bonus payment in the second survey. The choice was real: the chance of winning was 1 in 12 for both the coffee and the bonus, and subjects who chose the coffee and won received a coupon code redeemable on the Bean Brigade website while those who chose the cash bonus and won were paid via the Prolific platform. The bonus offered was randomly set to one of five values: $0.25, $0.50, $1.00, $2.00, or $4.00, with both people in each pair offered the same bonus.

Variable based on the question of whether the subject believed gun policy in the United States should be stricter, should be less strict, or is about right. The authors use this categorical variable to examine interactions between study condition and participants' views on gun policy, separately analyzing treatment effects by this variable.
scale: categorical: more strict, about right, less strict

description: In the follow-up survey, subjects rated the importance of the beliefs and values of Bean Brigade's CEO in their choice between the coffee and bonus on a 5-point scale ranging from 'Not at all important' to 'Extremely important'. The authors compare the mean importance of this factor across study conditions.
scale: 5-point scale from 'Not at all important' to 'Extremely important'

description: In the follow-up survey, subjects rated the importance of expressing their own beliefs and values in their choice between the coffee and bonus on a 5-point scale ranging from 'Not at all important' to 'Extremely important'. The authors compare the mean importance of this factor across study conditions.
scale: 5-point scale from 'Not at all important' to 'Extremely important'

description: In the follow-up survey, subjects rated the importance of how their partner would react to their choice in their choice between the coffee and bonus on a 5-point scale ranging from 'Not at all important' to 'Extremely important'. The authors compare the mean importance of this factor across study conditions.
scale: 5-point scale from 'Not at all important' to 'Extremely important'

description: In the follow-up survey, subjects rated the importance of the likely quality of Bean Brigade's coffee in their choice between the coffee and bonus on a 5-point scale ranging from 'Not at all important' to 'Extremely important'. The authors report that the coffee's perceived quality is not more important to people in the treatment conditions.
scale: 5-point scale from 'Not at all important' to 'Extremely important'

description: Index formed from questionnaire items rated on 5-point Likert scales; factor analysis with varimax rotation produced three factors used as constituency-building indices. The credibility index captures shareholder attitudes concerning the credibility of corporate management. Mean scores on each index were calculated to quantify respondents' attitudes. A questionnaire printing error at Corporation VI made it impossible to calculate a credibility score for that firm, so sample sizes for analyses involving credibility were lower.
scale: 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Index formed from Likert-scale questionnaire items; captures shareholder attitudes concerning corporate political activism in general. The authors note that its internal reliability (Cronbach's alpha) was somewhat lower than desired but acceptable for an exploratory effort. Mean scores on each index were calculated to quantify respondents' attitudes.
scale: 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Index formed from Likert-scale questionnaire items; captures shareholder attitudes concerning their own involvement and participation in the political activities of the corporation. Its internal reliability was somewhat lower than desired but acceptable for an exploratory effort. Mean scores on each index were calculated to quantify respondents' attitudes.
scale: 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Variable distinguishing shareholders who acknowledged receiving public policy information from any corporate source from those who had not. About 68 percent of respondents reported receiving such information, most of it in annual reports and infrequent ad hoc communications rather than formal constituency programs. It was used as an independent variable in t-tests and in multivariate regression with dummy variables.

Variable representing membership in Corporation I, the only corporation in the study with a well-developed, 5-year-old constituency program. It was included as an independent variable in the regression testing Hypothesis 4.

Classification variable used in three-way analysis of variance and Duncan's multiple range test to compare shareholder subgroups. The authors describe it as one of the shareholder characteristics generally available to the corporation.

Classification variable used in three-way analysis of variance and Duncan's multiple range test to compare shareholder subgroups. The authors describe it as one of the shareholder characteristics generally available to the corporation.

Classification variable used in three-way analysis of variance and Duncan's multiple range test to compare shareholder subgroups. The authors describe it as one of the shareholder characteristics generally available to the corporation. Annuitants, shareholders retired from the corporation, were one group compared.

variable_name: Credibility, legitimacy and shareholder involvement indices
description: Constituency-building attitudes are measured by three indices from a shareholder questionnaire with Likert items: credibility of corporate management, legitimacy of corporate political activism, and shareholder involvement in the corporation's political activities. The indices came from a factor analysis and each is analyzed separately as a dependent variable.

New product outputs is the simple average of new product sales as a percent of total sales for 1975 and 1976. It was used as the dependent variable in the first of the three approaches, with R&D inputs (RDIN) included as a control variable in the model.

The residual after regressing R&D inputs on new product outputs, so that R&D inputs absorb their full influence on new product outputs. For example, a business spending an average of 1.0 percent of sales on product R&D between 1971 and 1974 would have an expected new product sales rate in 1975-76 of 4.87 (2.85 + 2.02 x 1.0); a business whose actual new product sales rate were 8 percent would have an innovative efficiency of 3.13 (8-4.87).

Innovative efficiency (IE) divided by the amount of new products that would be expected on the basis of R&D inputs alone. The business in the example would have an innovative efficiency percentage of 64 percent (3.13/4.87), which meets the criticism that innovative efficiency needs to be examined in terms of relative magnitude.

The percentage of sales the three largest competitors derive from new products (introduced within the past three years). Only the 1971 figure was used, since the figure for any later year could include sales from new products still counted as new products in the years of new product outputs, 1975-76.
Survey item: "Have there been major technological changes in the products offered by the business or its major competitors during the last eight years?" Coded 0 = no, 1 = yes.
The market share of the business divided by the total shares of the three largest competitors. It is used as an indicator of size, since data on absolute size are not available in the PIMS data base.

Survey item: "Relative to the weighted average of the product lines of the three largest competitors, estimate the breadth of the product line of this business," coded 1 = narrower, 2 = same, 3 = broader.

The percent of sales the business derives from new products minus the percent of sales the three largest competitors derive from new products. Only the 1971 figure was used because later years could include products still counted as new in the output years.
The sum of errors from a four-year least-squares fitting of R&D/sales.
Survey item: "Compare the degree of forward integration of this business relative to its three largest competitors," coded 1 = less, 2 = same, 3 = more.

Survey item: "Are installation, repair, customer education, and other product-related services provided to end users ... ?" coded 1 = of relatively little or no importance, 2 = of some importance, 3 = of great importance.
scale: 1 = little or no importance, 2 = some importance, 3 = great importance

description: Survey item: "Approximately what percent of total sales of this business are made to other components of the same corporation?"
The percentage of all employees covered by collective bargaining agreements.
Gross book value of all fixed assets divided by revenues.
Net book value of fixed assets divided by gross book value of fixed assets.

INSIDER1 is the number of directors who were current employees of a firm divided by the total number of directors. Two alternative measures were also derived from the same director data: INSIDER2 is the number of directors who were current or former employees divided by the total number of directors, and INSIDER3 is the number of directors whose status was current employee, ex-employee, employee of a customer or a supplier, employee of a firm's investment bank or corporate counsel, or employee of its parent company or a subsidiary, divided by the total number of directors. INSIDER1 corresponds to the technical or narrow definition of inside directors, and INSIDER3 counts all affiliated directors as insiders.

variable_name: percentage of stock owned by a board
description: The percentage of stock owned by a board was measured in terms of shares owned by directors divided by total shares outstanding. It was calculated for each director from the number of shares owned reported in the proxy statements.

Firm size was measured in two ways: (1) book value of total assets, and (2) rank within the Fortune 500, based upon sales volume, or FORTUNE. The logit model focused on Fortune 500 sales volume rank as the measure of size.

Four measures of financial performance were initially employed: operating income divided by total assets (ROA); net income divided by common equity (ROE); operating income divided by sales; and the excess value ratio (EXCESS), the difference between the total market value of a firm (market value of equity and book value of debt) and the book value of its assets, normalized by sales. EXCESS proved to be the only significant financial performance variable in the logit regression.

Financial leverage was measured by interest-bearing debt divided by total assets. The correlation between leverage and incidence of golden parachutes was weak and insignificant, and the variable was eliminated from further analyses.

Proxy statements for the firms in the sample were examined for evidence of granting golden parachutes, narrowly defined as a guarantee of severance pay after a triggering event related to a change in control, even in cases of voluntary termination. Existence of a golden parachute agreement, or GOLDENP, was a categorical variable set to 1.0 if firms had no such agreement and 2.0 if they did. Of the 406 firms for which adequate data were available, 52 had such agreements with their executives.

ROE data were collected from Compustat reports on the 96 subject companies for the three years prior to the successions. ROE here is income before extraordinary expenses and discontinued operations divided by common equity as reported. The authors combined these data to create a continuous variable, average ROE for the presuccession period.

variable_name: common stock performance (slope of end-of-month closing stock prices)
description: For each subject company, end-of-the-month closing stock prices for the three years prior to succession provided a vector of 36 data points. Each vector was subjected to a regression analysis to determine the slope of the standardized regression equations; a negative slope indicated that performance had been falling over the three-year period and a positive slope indicated rising performance. These slope values were used as continuous variables in the logit analysis.
scale: slope values ranging from an extremely poor -.93 to an excellent .56
time_window: three years prior to succession (36 monthly observations)

description: Succession is binary since any replacement must be either an insider or an outsider. The variable was coded as a dummy with 0 = inside and 1 = outside, derived from the inside or outside succession dichotomy.
time_window: the one year period in which the successions occurred

variable_name: Average ROE and slope of common stock prices (three years before succession)
description: Organizational performance before succession is measured with two indicators for the three years prior to the succession: average return on equity (income before extraordinary expenses and discontinued operations divided by common equity, from Compustat) and common stock performance as the slope of a standardized regression on 36 end-of-month closing prices (CRSP). Each is tested separately against the inside or outside succession dummy.

Starting from all strategic attributes prominent in past PIMS studies, the authors discarded variables with very restricted distributions (typically, nominal and ordinal scales for which one answer appeared over 80 percent of the time) and variables that were highly intercorrelated (above .40), leaving a set of 20. Table 1 lists these variables under categories set forth in a previous study. The intercorrelations among the 20 attributes for the overall sample were all less than ±.40.

ROI was the performance measure used as the dependent variable. Four-year averages were used, which helped to minimize its accounting-related limitations. No additional performance measures, such as cash flow and changes in market share, were considered.

Defines the broad sector of a business' basic market. Because there were basically two possible classes, the cut point was evident: consumer versus industrial product. Industrial (high) covers capital goods, raw materials, components, supplies, and consumable products.

Describes the stage of development of the products and services sold by a business over the last three years. Growth (low) was coded for markets growing at more than 10 percent annually in real terms, with technology or competitive structure still changing; mature (high) for growth below 10 percent per year, with products familiar to the vast majority of users and technology and competitive structure reasonably stable. Businesses in the emerging and declining stages were excluded because of very small sample sizes.

Defined by the question, "Has there been a change in technology of the product or production process in the past eight years?" Cut points for the low and high subsamples were established by judgment, guided by major inflections or breakpoints in frequency distributions.

Defined by the question, "How often do this business' end users typically purchase its products or services?" Frequently purchased (low) was coded as once per month or more often; infrequently purchased (high) as once every year or less often.

Defined by percent of industry sales by the four largest competitors. Cut points for the low and high subsamples were established by judgment, guided by major inflections or breakpoints in frequency distributions.

Ten-year average annual variability from the trend line in primary demand. Cut points for the low and high subsamples were established by judgment, guided by major inflections or breakpoints in frequency distributions.

Proportion of total annual purchases by average immediate customers. Cut points for the low and high subsamples were established by judgment, guided by major inflections or breakpoints in frequency distributions.

Defined as percent of sales from superior products plus percent from inferior products. Cut points for the low and high subsamples were established by judgment, guided by major inflections or breakpoints in frequency distributions.

Industry sales in the United States accounted for by establishments outside the United States. Cut points for the low and high subsamples were established by judgment, guided by major inflections or breakpoints in frequency distributions.

Total annual share-point movements among the top four competitors, summed over a four-year period. Cut points for the low and high subsamples were established by judgment, guided by major inflections or breakpoints in frequency distributions.

The contingency variable is operationalized as ten PIMS variables (user sector, life cycle stage, technological change, purchase frequency, concentration, demand instability, dollar importance to customers, product differentiability, industry imports, share instability). Each splits the sample into low and high subsamples, and Chow tests compare how strategic attributes relate to ROI across the subsamples.
scale: binary low/high split of each variable

description: Fifteen indicators of life-cycle stage were gathered from Likert-type questions on formal structure definition, adherence to formal structure, type of structure, formality of communication, reward system, budgets and planning horizons, top-level staff composition and top-level decision making, plus interview and secondary data on firms' ages, sizes, and rates of growth. Multiple manager responses were aggregated into organizational composite scores, the 15 indicators were reduced to five principal factors by principal components analysis, and firms were classified into three stage groups by several cluster techniques (6 organizations in stage 1, 13 in stage 2, and 8 in stage 3).

Time, measured in terms of how many game sessions participants experienced, was used as a surrogate for specific stages. Pretesting indicated four stages: organizational start-up (sessions 1 and 2), mobilization and turnaround (sessions 3, 4, and 5), growth in resources and performance indicators (sessions 6 and 7), and a period in which growth slowed. Data were collected after game sessions 2, 5, 7, and 10.

variable_name: importance points assigned to the technical efficiency folder
description: Managers were told that each of three unlabeled folders held five kinds of information and were asked to distribute 100 importance points among the five kinds of information within each folder, then to distribute 100 additional importance points among the three folders on the basis of which folders would be most important to them in making the decision. The authors took the folder-level approach in their initial test because it directly reflected the three priorities; one folder contained five kinds of technical efficiency information.
scale: 100 importance points distributed among the three folders

variable_name: importance points assigned to the organizational coordination folder
description: Managers distributed 100 importance points among the five kinds of information within each folder and then 100 additional importance points among the three folders based on which folders would be most important to them in making the decision. One folder contained five kinds of information reflecting the organizational coordination priority, and the authors used the folder-level importance values in their initial test.
scale: 100 importance points distributed among the three folders

variable_name: importance points assigned to the political support folder
description: Managers distributed 100 importance points among the five kinds of information within each folder and then 100 additional importance points among the three folders based on which folders would be most important to them in making the decision. One folder contained five kinds of information reflecting the political support priority, and the authors used the folder-level importance values in their initial test.
scale: 100 importance points distributed among the three folders

description: Department managers responded on four occasions to forced-choice questions indicating how much emphasis each priority received during the previous game session. Three questions asked them to distribute up to 100 importance points to indicators of all three priorities and two additional questions asked them to distribute 100 points between only technical efficiency and organizational coordination indicators, giving five measures of technical efficiency. Composite scores were formed by averaging all the priority indicator scores across all questions for game sessions 5, 7, and 10.

Department managers responded on four occasions to forced-choice questions indicating how much emphasis each priority received during the previous game session, distributing up to 100 importance points to indicators of all three priorities in three questions and 100 points between technical efficiency and organizational coordination indicators in two questions, giving five measures of organizational coordination. Composite scores were formed by averaging all the priority indicator scores across all questions for game sessions 5, 7, and 10.

Department managers responded on four occasions to forced-choice questions indicating how much emphasis each priority received during the previous game session; the questionnaire design yielded three measures of the political support priority. Composite scores were formed by averaging all the priority indicator scores across all questions for game sessions 5, 7, and 10.

Nine strategy variables were selected from a set of 17 variables that measure parts of business-level strategy. Three criteria were applied: representation of each of the four broad theoretical dimensions of strategy, lack of multicollinearity, and maximum R-squared with ROI with the fewest possible variables. The final combination of nine strategy variables accounted for 40 percent of the variance in ROI.

The overall measure of environment is a discrete variable with eight categories: emerging, fragmented, fragmented with auxiliary services, global importing, global exporting, stable, mature, and declining. Every business unit was classified into one of these categories according to its pattern on 17 environmental components representing characteristics of market structures; the categories were developed through cluster and discriminant analysis of the 17 environmental components.

Return on investment (ROI) is the criterion variable predicted from the strategy variables, the environmental categories, and their interaction. The authors report the adjusted R-squared for each set of predictors; the strategy variables accounted for 40 percent of the variance in ROI, the environmental categories 2 percent, and the interaction terms 0 percent.

For each of six functions (manufacturing, marketing/sales, R&D, purchasing, government liaison, other administrative activities), respondents answered two questions on 5-point scales: the importance of the function in implementing the SBU's strategy and the extent of resource sharing between the focal and one or more other SBUs. Using the data on the importance of various functions as weights, the authors derived a weighted-average measure of the extent of resource sharing for each SBU.
scale: component items on 5-point scales (importance: 1 = of little importance to 5 = extremely important; sharing: 1 = almost none to 5 = a very great deal)

description: On each of 12 performance dimensions respondents rated their SBUs' performance relative to superiors' expectations on a 5-point scale ranging from not at all satisfactory to outstanding. Using as weights the data on dimensional importance that came from validating the competitive strategy index, the authors obtained a weighted-average effectiveness index for each SBU.
scale: 5-point scale from not at all satisfactory to outstanding

description: Respondents used a 5-point scale, ranging from significantly lower to significantly higher, to position their products relative to competitors' in two areas: performance and price. The sum of responses to the two items is the measure of the focal SBU's competitive strategy, with higher values indicating a strategy stronger on differentiation and lower values indicating a strategy stronger on low costs.

Respondents indicated the number of years spent with their current firms. The responses were coded as 0 = less than 1 year, 2 = 1 to 3 years, 5 = 4 to 6 years, 8 = 7 to 9 years, 11 = 10 years or more.
scale: coded 0 = less than 1 year, 2 = 1 to 3 years, 5 = 4 to 6 years, 8 = 7 to 9 years, 11 = 10 years or more

variable_name: general manager's years on current job
description: Respondents indicated the number of years spent on their current jobs. The responses were coded as 0 = less than 1 year, 2 = 1 to 3 years, 5 = 4 to 6 years, 8 = 7 to 9 years, 11 = 10 years or more.
scale: coded 0 = less than 1 year, 2 = 1 to 3 years, 5 = 4 to 6 years, 8 = 7 to 9 years, 11 = 10 years or more

description: Respondents indicated whether their bonuses were calculated strictly by formula, or whether superiors determined all or some percentage in a discretionary manner. The measure is the percentage of bonus decided in a discretionary manner, ranging from 0 to 100 percent.

Respondents indicated if the sizes of bonus pools from which they received shares were based solely on their own SBU's performance (coded as 1) or on the performance of a larger organizational grouping including their own and other SBUs (coded as 2).
scale: coded 1 = own SBU's performance only, 2 = performance of a larger organizational grouping

description: Three items from Van de Ven and Ferry's 6-item instrument were used to assess the respondents' satisfaction with their job contexts: satisfaction with current job, career progress made in this organization up to now, and chances for career advancement in this organization in the future. The measure is an additive one.

The structural variable for integrative liaison devices. In the principal components analysis of structural variables it loaded on the first factor, formal integration, together with the formalization variables. The authors report that this variable had the strongest relationship with the rationality factor.
Four formalization variables that the authors report combine with the integration variable to form the first structural factor, formal integration.

The second structural factor, with its primary negative loadings on centralization, the ratio of administrative to total personnel, and mechanization of production. It captures intensity of administration, the extent to which upper level managers control an organization. High values on the factor indicate decentralization, the reverse of the construct as named.
The third structural factor, related to number of operating sites, vertical span of control, ratio of clerical to total personnel, and to a lesser degree level of specialization.

The first strategy-making factor, which included the variables of analysis, future orientation and planning, explicitness of strategy, and systematic scanning of the environment. It represents systematic, analytical decision making.
The third strategy-making factor, reflecting interaction among decision makers; it relates positively to bargaining and inversely to consensus versus individual decision making.
The second strategy-making factor, reflecting assertiveness, with associated variables being proactiveness and risk taking.

Three indices of performance: CEOs' reports on a 7-point scale of how their firms performed over the last five years in terms of long-term profitability relative to their industry's average; actual average annual growth rates in net income; and average rates of return on investment for the previous five years, both from financial statements. A principal components analysis of the three variables produced a first component on which relative profitability, growth in income, and ROI had loadings of 0.70, 0.66, and 0.83, accounting for 54 percent of the variance.
scale: 7-point scale for relative profitability; growth and ROI are rates

description: Innovation was measured using five-year averages of research and development expenses as a percentage of sales. The authors describe this as a good measure of complex innovation because it gauges real expenditures rather than subjective assessments by managers.
Number of employees was the measure of firm size. The sample was bifurcated according to firm size, measured by numbers of employees, into approximately equal subsamples.

variable_name: relative percentage change in yearly acquisition of advertising revenues
description: Yearly advertising revenues for each station were estimated by multiplying the station's market share by total advertising expenditures in the market. The percentage change in advertising revenues from the previous year was then calculated and adjusted by subtracting the mean percentage change in revenues for all stations competing in the market. Market shares came from A. C. Nielsen Company surveys and total market advertising expenditures came from Federal Communications Commission documents.
time_window: change from prior year to current year

description: Each reported resource exchange was assigned a value of 1 and a value of 0 was assigned where no resource exchange was reported; the values were summed across all exchanges. Data were collected from Television Factbook from 1965 to 1980.

Resource exchanges were first classified into four cells based on transactional flow and transactional content. Complexity was computed as C = (sum of Ii squared) / L squared, where Ii is the number of resource exchanges within the ith category and L is the total number of linkages established by a station across all categories. The higher the calculated value, the more similar a station's resource exchanges are to one another; the lower the value, the more complex its resource exchanges are, with values ranging from 0 to 1.0.

The complexity measure was trichotomized into equal thirds and a dummy variable was created for similar linkages. A complexity score of greater than or equal to .38 was considered to indicate similar linkages, and L2a was coded 1; stations falling between the cut-points form the omitted variable category.

The complexity measure was trichotomized into equal thirds and a dummy variable was created for diverse linkages. A complexity score of less than .31 was considered as indicating diverse linkages, with L2b coded 1; stations falling between the cut-points form the omitted variable category.

Measured by the absolute percentage change in advertising expenditures within a market from the prior year. Markets with stable rates of growth or decline in advertising expenditures suggest high predictability of revenues, and large percentage increases or decreases indicate uncertainty. Each station received the appropriate score for its particular market.
time_window: change from prior year to current year

description: Calculated by dividing total market advertising expenditures by the total number of households in a market, and then dividing this value by the total number of stations competing in the market. A low value indicates that advertising expenditures per person are scarce relative to the number of stations operating in the market; a high value indicates munificence.

Measured on the basis of demographic distributions of age, education, and wealth within a market's Standard Metropolitan Statistical Area using Gibbs and Martin's (1962) formula. Because U.S. Census data are collected once a decade, each complexity measure was interpolated using the average increase or decrease of value over the ten years, and the three measures were combined into a single index. A high complexity score suggests a demographically homogeneous market and a low value a heterogeneous or differentiated market.

Each of the three networks studied used a different transactional form. One manufacturer owned the dealerships and they sold only the manufacturer's products (corporate network); in the second the dealerships were autonomous organizations linked to the manufacturer through exchanges alone (conventional network); in the third the dealerships were not owned by the manufacturer but were tied to it by contracts and sold only the manufacturer's product (contractual network).

A 20-item instrument developed from prestudy interviews with managers of 12 dealerships, 4 from each network. Managers were asked to circle the number that best describes the extent to which they feel the manufacturer influences their decisions for each issue, on a 5-point scale (1 = no extent, 2 = little extent, 3 = some extent, 4 = much extent, 5 = great extent). The items were all highly correlated and were combined into a single scale, with reliabilities ranging from .88 to .97 for the three networks.

A 20-item instrument developed by reviewing the three manufacturers' programs for and policies on providing support to their dealers and by prestudy interviews. Managers were asked to circle the number that best describes the extent to which they feel they rely upon the manufacturer for each of the services listed, on a 5-point scale (1 = no extent, 2 = little extent, 3 = some extent, 4 = much extent, 5 = great extent). Items were highly correlated and were combined into one scale (alpha = .88-.96).

Number of joint programs each dealer was involved in, obtained by providing managers with examples of programs most likely to reduce dependence on the manufacturer (joint advertising, joint purchasing, joint storage) and asking in how many they were involved. Contacts with industry elites were measured similarly, by giving examples of influential industry figures (company executives, trade association officers, board members, bank officers) and asking for the average monthly number of personal contacts. Number of customers, number of years in business, number of employees, and market share were obtained from dealers' records. Market share was measured on a 4-point scale (1 = below 10%, 2 = 10-15%, 3 = 16-20%, 4 = above 20%).
scale: market share: 1 = below 10% to 4 = above 20%; other indicators are counts

description: Estimated abnormal returns computed with the time-event method: parameters are estimated over an estimation (baseline) period consisting of the previous year, and the prediction errors of the analysis (focal) year are cumulated to yield the CPE. Abnormal return is the difference between the actual return and the normal return estimated from the market model. CPEs were calculated for 1977 and 1980 for the main analysis and, to estimate the incidence of truly abnormal performance, for all years from 1976 through 1981.
time_window: one-year estimation (baseline) period and one-year analysis (focal) period; focal years 1977 and 1980; CPEs also calculated for 1976 through 1981

variable_name: percentage of change in salary compensation
description: Percentage of change in salary compensation for the top corporate executive listed for each company. Because changes in salary do not occur until the year after a year in which a raise is given, the change is calculated for 1978 versus 1977 and, with the same one-year lag, for 1981 versus 1980. The use of percentage changes instead of absolute changes eliminated the need for a firm-size variable.

variable_name: percentage of change in bonus compensation
description: Percentage of change in bonus compensation for the top corporate executive listed for each company. Because bonuses are normally paid near the end of the year, the change is calculated for 1977 versus 1976 and for 1980 versus 1979. Salary and bonus are reported and analyzed separately, so that salary data can be adjusted for the time lag.

Dummy variable introduced to discriminate between the bull market and the bear market. It is coded 1 for 1977 (bear market) and 0 for 1980 (bull market) and is included in the regression equations in order to test for the overall effects of the market.

The F.T.C. classified each merger according to the primary strategic relationship between the acquiring and acquired firms into five basic merger strategies: horizontal, vertical, product-concentric, market-concentric, and conglomerate. The authors collapsed the F.T.C.'s five-strategy scheme into Lubatkin's (1983) four-strategy scheme by pooling horizontal and market-concentric mergers into one type designated single-business mergers; related mergers are those sharing related production or marketing technologies and unrelated mergers are those with dissimilar products and markets.

The three components of risk were estimated using Lubatkin and Shrieves's (1986) market model, in which the monthly rate of return on the acquiring firm's common shares is regressed on the average monthly rate of return of all NYSE traded securities listed on the CRSP returns file. Unsystematic risk was defined by the standard deviation of the error term over the 60-month estimation period. A difference score was computed for each acquiring firm by subtracting the premerger estimate of unsystematic risk from its respective postmerger measure; a positive difference score means that risk has increased.
time_window: 60 months premerger beginning 67 months before the merger month and 60 months postmerger beginning 5 months after, excluding 12 months surrounding the transaction month

description: A systematic-risk difference score was computed for each acquiring firm by subtracting the premerger estimate of the historic parameter b (beta) from its respective postmerger measure, using the same market model and 60-month estimation periods. The difference score represents the change in each firm's systematic risk characteristics due to merging.

A total-risk difference score was computed for each acquiring firm by subtracting the premerger estimate of total risk from its respective postmerger measure. Total risk was defined as the standard deviation of a firm's excess returns, or a firm's returns in excess of the risk-free rate, less the standard deviation of the market's excess returns; the normalizing procedure helps to control for changing market-wide influences.

A leverage difference score was computed for each acquiring firm by subtracting each five-year premerger estimate of leverage from the firm's five-year postmerger estimate. Leverage was defined as the book value of a firm's long-term debt divided by the book value of its total assets. The leverage analysis covers the 114 mergers in the full group of 297 that are listed on COMPUSTAT data files for the five years before and after the year of a merger.
time_window: five years before and five years after the merger

variable_name: bear market subgroup / bull market subgroup
description: The group of 297 mergers was split into two independent parts in order to isolate possible changes in merger outcomes due to economic cycles. The bear-market subgroup consists of 80 mergers completed during the periods designated by the Department of Commerce to be periods of market decline; the bull-market subgroup contains 134 mergers completed between December 1961 and December 1973 during periods of stability or growth.

variable_name: Large mergers sample (297 mergers, pre versus post event)
description: Mergers are the 297 large acquisitions of 1954 to 1973 drawn from the FTC large merger series (assets of at least 10 million dollars) in which the acquirer owned more than 50 percent of the target and was NYSE listed for the required months before and after. Each merger is treated as an event, and risk is compared between the premerger and postmerger periods around the merger month, by merger type and market period.
time_window: 1954-1973; 60 months before and after the merger month

description: A typology of implementation approaches constructed from the documentary record and the interviews. The primary distinction was between rule-bound behavior, operationally defined as compliance with the standard technical specifications, and autonomy, defined as customizing those guidelines through the adoption of unique, plant-specific characteristics. Rule-bound responses included obedience, matching the NRC's standards, and incremental adjustment; autonomous responses included modification, combination, planning, and anticipation. At least three members of the research team independently classified the safety review systems of the plants they had visited, and the classification was checked with NRC officials and with the interviewed safety review staff.

variable_name: unsafe events attributable to human error in 1982
description: The number of unsafe events attributable to human error that occurred in 1982, taken from license event reports. Events attributable to human error, such as failure to follow a procedure, constitute anywhere from a third to a quarter of the total number of reports. The author assumed that events occurring in 1981 came before the implementation of the new safety review systems and that events occurring in 1982 came after implementation.

The plant's prior safety record, measured by the number of safety events that had occurred in 1981, that is, before the implementation of the new safety review systems. Autonomy was significantly correlated with a low occurrence of events in 1981 and 1982.

Capacity ratings show the percentage of electric power that a nuclear power plant has generated in a particular period in comparison with the amount that it could generate given its overall capacity. They were examined to correct for different amounts of on-line time and other operational features that can affect the number of events a plant has, because a plant can have few events simply because it has been shut down for a significant period of time.

CEOs were asked to select the one of four unlabeled descriptions of a firm and its situation that most closely described their own firm. The descriptions corresponded to the stages of growth outlined in the model. The stage measure preceded the problem measure in the questionnaire.
time_window: current stage at the time of the survey (late 1982)

description: Scale score calculated using a unit weighting of the means of the problem ratings loading on the factor. Each problem was rated by the CEO on a 1 to 7 scale in terms of its current dominance to the firm.
time_window: current dominance at the time of the survey (late 1982)

variable_name: sales and marketing factor scale score
description: Scale score calculated using a unit weighting of the means of the problem ratings loading on the factor. Each problem was rated by the CEO on a 1 to 7 scale in terms of its current dominance to the firm.
time_window: current dominance at the time of the survey (late 1982)

description: Scale score calculated using a unit weighting of the means of the problem ratings loading on the factor. Each problem was rated by the CEO on a 1 to 7 scale in terms of its current dominance to the firm.
time_window: current dominance at the time of the survey (late 1982)

description: Scale score calculated using a unit weighting of the means of the problem ratings loading on the factor. Each problem was rated by the CEO on a 1 to 7 scale in terms of its current dominance to the firm.
time_window: current dominance at the time of the survey (late 1982)

description: Scale score calculated using a unit weighting of the means of the problem ratings loading on the factor. Each problem was rated by the CEO on a 1 to 7 scale in terms of its current dominance to the firm.
time_window: current dominance at the time of the survey (late 1982)

description: Scale score calculated using a unit weighting of the means of the problem ratings loading on the factor. Each problem was rated by the CEO on a 1 to 7 scale in terms of its current dominance to the firm.
time_window: current dominance at the time of the survey (late 1982)

description: The magnitude of change in automaticity was measured as the percentage of change from 1973 to 1981 in a plant's manufacturing-equipment automaticity scores. Automaticity was measured by Amber and Amber's (1962) scale of automaticity, and the measure identified manufacturing process innovations that have been implemented rather than simply adopted. The measure was geometrically weighted, giving disproportionate weight to machines at the highest levels of the automaticity scale, and the weighted proportions were summed to obtain an overall automaticity score; the change score compares the 1981 score with the 1973 score.

A scale that summed the standardized scores of five technology measures: Woodward's technical complexity scale, machine automaticity (1973), percentage of mechanical material-transfer devices, work-flow rigidity, and percentage of sales of standardized products. All of the measures were based on 1973 data.
scale: scores ranged from -4.4 (low production-system development) to 6.5

description: Complexity was the percentage of professional and technical employees at a plant, a measure of the degree to which labor was divided on the basis of specialized knowledge. The factories had an average of 8.86 percent of employees in professional-technical occupations, with a range of 0 to 38.5 percent. All structural measures were based on the 1973 data collected by Blau and his colleagues.

Decentralization referred to the locus of decision-making authority within a plant; items measuring decentralization were divided into strategic and line-operating classes of decisions. Practically speaking, most strategic decisions are shared by the highest executive and the executive one level below the highest executive, and strategic decisions were considerably more centralized than line-operating decisions. All structural measures were based on the 1973 data collected by Blau and his colleagues.

Decentralization referred to the locus of decision-making authority within a plant; items measuring decentralization were divided into strategic and line-operating classes of decisions. Operational decisions are typically made at the production-head level, and line-operating decisions were considerably more decentralized than strategic decisions. All structural measures were based on the 1973 data collected by Blau and his colleagues.

A measure, developed by Blau and his colleagues and based on the Aston studies' measurement of the concept, of the extent to which activities were prescribed in an organization. Most plants were moderately formalized (mean = 4.74), and scores ranged from 0 to 9 (highly formalized). All structural measures were based on the 1973 data collected by Blau and his colleagues.

Effectiveness data were collected on ten performance dimensions. On each dimension SBU general managers rated, on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from "significantly below average" to "significantly above average," the SBU's performance relative to corporate standards. Each respondent then rated each of the ten dimensions on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from "not important" to "extremely important." With the data on dimensional importance as weights, a weighted average performance index was obtained for each SBU.
scale: 7-point Likert scale for performance; 5-point Likert scale for importance weights

description: SBU general managers were asked to position their products relative to those of leading competitors in six areas, using a 7-point Likert scale ranging from "significantly lower" to "significantly higher." The scores for the six items were summed for a combined scale. The response set was polarized so that high values indicated a strong differentiation strategy and low values indicated a strong low-cost strategy.
scale: 7-point Likert scale per item; summed six-item scale

description: SBU general managers were asked the Hopwood (1972) question on the three factors that count the most in how their superior evaluates their performance, ranking the three most important items. A continuum of evaluative style was constructed: 5 = neither meeting the budget nor running the unit efficiently ranked among the top three criteria; 4 = efficiency but not budget ranked among the top three; 3 = both ranked among the top three but efficiency higher than budget; 2 = both ranked among the top three but budget higher than efficiency; 1 = budget but not efficiency ranked among the top three. Low values indicated great importance attached to meeting a budget in evaluating an SBU manager's performance.

SBU general managers were provided with a list of operating decisions that could affect SBU performance and, using an approach similar to Hofstede's (1967), indicated on a 7-point Likert scale the typical influence they had in affecting the outcome of each decision, from "decision taken by you without consulting your superior" to "your opinion is not asked, decision is not explained to you." Responses on the four questions were summed to create an index of decentralization for each respondent.
scale: 7-point Likert scale per decision; summed four-item index

description: Rotter's (1966) internal-external scale was used. Of the 29 original items, fillers, items referring to schoolrooms and teachers, items about control over political and world events, and items on interpersonal control were excluded, leaving an 11-item scale. Each manager was asked to indicate which of the two statements in each item he or she more strongly believed to be the case. Responses to the 11 items were summed to form a total internal-external control score, with high values indicating an internal locus of control and low values indicating an external locus of control.

Scores on the three administrative mechanisms were standardized, with scores ranging from -1.00 to +1.00, to bring all variables to a uniform scale, and theory-based ideal profiles of the administrative mechanisms were developed for the low-cost and differentiation subgroups. The degree of fit for any given SBU was measured as the euclidean distance between that SBU's scores and the scores of its ideal type, identified on the basis of the focal SBU's strategy.
scale: euclidean distance between standardized mechanism scores and ideal profile scores

description: Coded binarily, with 1 for adoption of a proposal to provide top management with golden parachutes and 0 for no adoption. Firms were identified through proxy statements filed with the SEC.

Coded 1 if a company had experienced a takeover threat and 0 otherwise. A takeover threat was measured as actual transfer of ownership of more than 5 percent of the total stock of a firm to a potential acquirer and the filing of 13D statements with the SEC at least a year before acceptance of a golden parachute proposal; recorded from 13D filings and summarized articles in the Wall Street Journal Index.
time_window: up to one year before adoption of a golden parachute contract

description: The size of a firm's board, collected from proxy statements.
time_window: the year before golden parachute adoption or the corresponding period for other firms

description: Board composition in terms of ratios of inside to outside directors, collected from proxy statements; the variable in the model is the percentage (proportion) of outside directors.
time_window: the year before golden parachute adoption or the corresponding period for other firms

description: CEO influence measured as the ratio of a CEO's tenure to the average tenure of a firm's outside directors.
time_window: the year before golden parachute adoption or the corresponding period for other firms

variable_name: percentage of stock owned by management team
description: The percentage of stock owned by a top management team, obtained from the proxy statement in the section discussing stock ownership of officers and directors.
time_window: the year before golden parachute adoption or the corresponding period for other firms

variable_name: cumulative blocks of shares owned by major nonmanagement shareholders
description: The sum of all blocks of stock ownership greater than 5 percent, which measured the concentration of stock in nonmanagement hands.
time_window: the year before golden parachute adoption or the corresponding period for other firms

description: A variant of the measure developed by Pugh, Hickson, Hinings, and Turner (1968). It is constructed by summing 31 specialization items, each indicating the existence or absence of at least one full-time individual exclusively charged with a particular specialized activity; the reported alpha is .90.
The scale gives the number of nonwork-flow functions in which at least one specialist held a recognized professional qualification. Child (1973) developed this measure; the reported alpha is .81.

The abbreviated scale of formalization developed by Inkson, Pugh, and Hickson (1970), scored with the same procedure those authors used; the reported alpha is .88. The text does not list the individual items.

A subset of 14 decision items originally developed by Pugh and colleagues (1968) to measure centralization and later used by Inkson and coauthors (1970) to represent organizational autonomy. Each item is scored on a 5-point scale indicating, in ascending order, the hierarchical level at which the decision is made; the reported alpha is .89.

A subset of 6 decision items covering strategic marketing and financial decisions, identified by factor analysis of 20 decision items. Each item is scored on a 5-point scale indicating, in ascending order, the hierarchical level at which the decision is made; the reported alpha is .81.

A composite measure developed through principal component analysis of ten 5-point scales; three address the extent of perceived competition (prices, promotion, product quality) and seven the extent of perceived constraints (financial institutions, local governments, central governments, international bodies, buyers, suppliers, trade unions). Items were scored from 1, very little, to 5, very great; the first principal component, with an eigenvalue of 2.74, provides an overall measure of perceived environmental pressure.
scale: principal component scores of ten 5-point scales (1 = very little to 5 = very great)

description: The rate of change of demand for the industries' products and services was used to represent the extent of environmental munificence or scarcity, measured as growth of sales over 1973-77 using published industry sales data in constant prices. Four industries experienced sales increases of between 4.2 and 34.6 percent and their 25 companies operated in munificence; four other industries experienced declines of between 2.5 and 39.6 percent and their 20 companies operated in scarcity. A dummy variable coded 0 for munificence and 1 for scarcity was used in the regressions.

The degree of automation of the bulk of the equipment a firm used in operations, following Pugh and colleagues (1969); it is a subscale of their operations technology measure. It measures operations technology on a 6-point scale ranging from use of hand tools and manual machines (0) to use of computer-controlled cognitive machines (5), and it correlated strongly with measures of work-flow rigidity (r = .59) and work-flow integration (r = .81).
Size was measured as the logarithm of the number of employees in a firm.

A membership shift is a cluster analytic assignment of a firm to a different group than it had been in during the prior year, so at most one shift per firm per year. Mobility rates are computed as shifts between groups relative to the maximum observable shifts, adjusted for the number of firms in the pair of groups.

Two indicators were used jointly to identify periods of economic stability, growth, and decline: capacity change, the change in the number of industry rigs, and capacity utilization, the proportion of total rigs that were working. These indicators demarcate a stability period (1966-1973), a growth period (1973-1981), and a decline period beginning in 1981.

Strategic groups are defined by cluster analysis on seven standardized group-defining variables: product-line diversity, technological capability, global spread, vertical integration (oil-company and national-government dummies), and marketing orientation (proportions of the fleet contracted to major oil companies and to national oil companies). Group 2 (contingency strategy) is treated as similar to groups 1 and 3, whereas groups 1 and 3 are treated as the less similar pair.

Several executives in each firm read a decision scenario describing a firm in their industry facing a major problem and then answered 43 Likert-type questions (24 single-response and 19 multiitem) describing the process their firm would use. The overall measure was developed by calculating the mean response of a firm's participants to each of the 43 questions, taking the mean of the 10 or 11 questions specific to a particular step of the decision process to obtain a firm-level score for each of the four steps, and deriving the overall score as the mean of the four steps. Responses were aggregated within firms to the organization level.

Calculated by subtracting the overall comprehensiveness score obtained in the pertinent earlier study from that obtained in the present study. A positive change score indicates that a firm became more comprehensive and a negative score that it became less so; the score was derived from two aggregated, multi-respondent measures with high interrater agreement.
scale: change on the comprehensiveness scale; plus or minus 6 represented the largest possible change
time_window: four or six years between the original study and the present study

description: Number of full-time employees, a common indicator of size used in the earlier studies, provided the basis for the change measure. Change in size was measured as the percentage increase or decrease in the number of full-time employees from the original study to the present study. The authors note that size measures tend to be correlated; the correlation between number of employees and volume of sales was .85 or higher in each industry.
time_window: from the original study to the present study

description: Respondents in both the earlier studies and the present one specified the number of years they had worked in their firms. Change in intrafirm tenure was computed by subtracting the average number of years executive-team members reported in the earlier study from the average number reported in the present study; a positive difference indicates an increase and a negative difference a decrease in mean tenure. Length of service is the common definition of tenure and tenure has been used as a measure of intrafirm socialization.
time_window: from the original study to the present study

description: Each firm's list of participants represented the CEO's characterization of the top management team at a particular time, so changes in that list were used as an indicator of executive-team continuity. The measure was the proportion of a firm's executives whom the CEO identified in the present study who had also been identified in the first; the higher the proportion, the more continuity in an executive team.
time_window: from the original study to the present study

variable_name: average after-tax return on assets adjusted for extraordinary items
description: A measure of economic performance used in the earlier studies, again used for the four or six years since those studies. The periods of interest were 1982-85 for paint and coatings and 1980-85 for forest products. Change in performance was measured as average ROA for the years of the present study less that for the earlier one.
time_window: 1982-1985 for paint and coatings; 1980-1985 for forest products

description: The authors compared the four items that loaded most heavily on the stability dimension in Dess and Beard's work - industry sales, cost-price margin, value-added, and employment - across the interim years. In forest products each item exhibited continued volatility, while in paint and coatings all but one of the items showed modest but consistently linear increases, indicating that the two environments continued their previously established patterns of stability and instability.
time_window: decade ending in 1979 and the interim years since the original studies

description: For a dyad, the ratio of the number of routes in which dyad members were both significant competitors having at least 10 percent of the total passengers to the total number of routes in which the dyad members were significant competitors with all other trunk airlines. Data came from the CAB's Origin-Destination Survey of Airline Passenger Traffic.

For a dyad, the ratio of the number of a dyad member's indirect interlocks within the dyad to its total number of indirect interlocks with all other trunk airlines. Indirect interlocks include directors or executives who also sit on the board of a third firm, in any industry.

A measure based on annual earnings, using earnings before interest and taxes as a composite measure of financial volatility and calculating differences between adjacent years to distinguish unexpected changes from trends. It was calculated for two five-year periods, the five years before 1970 and the five years before 1982.
time_window: five years before 1970 and five years before 1982

description: The great circle distance, the shortest distance over the surface of the globe, between the cities housing the headquarters of the firms in each dyad. For the general linear model the distance was split into high and low categories.

The ratio of total debt to total assets for each firm, chosen over the debt-to-equity ratio because that ratio is nonlinear and overstates dependency at high debt levels. Changes between 1970 and 1976 and between 1976 and 1982 were used.

For each airline, the ratio of direct interlocks with financial sector institutions (banks, investment companies, or insurance firms) to the total number of direct interlocks with all firms. Direct interlocks include both shared directors and executive interlocks.
The average before-tax return on stockholders' equity over five years.

Observations were made in the period 1970-76, treated as a period of relatively low financial dependence, and in 1976-82, treated as a period of high financial dependence. Industry debt ratios obtained from Standard & Poor's Industry Survey were used to document the general deterioration of the industry's financial situation.

The dependent variable is the number of voluntary social service organizations founded in each quarter between January 1970 and December 1982. Founding was dated by formal incorporation. Separate series were constructed for specialist and generalist foundings, giving 52 periods of data for each.

The number of foundings in the population in the period before the outcome period; the authors computed values lagged one time period for all independent variables because instantaneously acting influences seemed unlikely. Both the linear and squared terms were used to capture curvilinear effects.

An organization was defined as disbanded when it ceased to exist as a legal entity, so mergers counted as organizational disbandings. The frequency of disbandings is the quarterly number of disbandings in the population from January 1970 to December 1982, taken from the Provincial Index of Incorporated NonShare Corporations; since only annual disbanding data were available, disbandings were prorated by quarters. The variable is lagged one period and both linear and squared terms were used.

Density is the total number of organizations alive at a given time in the population. The authors express density in a period in relation to density in the preceding period together with lagged foundings minus lagged disbandings; the printed formula is garbled. The variable is lagged one period and both linear and squared terms were used.

variable_name: Opportunities for Youth and Provincial Restraint dummies
description: Two dummy variables represent the two major institutional changes occurring during the observation period, with 1 indicating existence of the period and 0 otherwise. The Opportunities for Youth period (1971-1975) legitimated the creation of new voluntary social service organizations and created new government-supplied resources; the Provincial Restraint period (1976-1981) emphasized fiscal restraint and improving the productivity of existing organizations rather than creating new ones. Both dummies were lagged one time period.
time_window: Opportunities for Youth 1971-1975; Provincial Restraint 1976-1981, lagged one period

description: Organizations offering services in a single domain were designated specialists and those offering services in three or more domains were designated generalists; organizations operating in two domains, termed quasi generalists, were excluded from the study. Trained coders using archival data on services provided classified the organizations, and the classification was corroborated with other independent archival sources and with the questionnaire, which asked respondents to indicate from a listing of various domains whether they offered services in one or more of them. The coding involved only counting the number of domains in which an organization offered services.

The nine items in the scale assessing the information processing of top management teams were drawn from Duncan (1973, 1974) and coded so that high scores indicated a high capacity for information processing. Items use a 7-point Likert response format and were averaged to calculate the variable score. An example item is 'To what extent is there a free and open exchange of ideas among team members about strategic issues?'

Using the Annual Guide Book's 54 service or facility categories, a profile of service offerings in 1983 and 1987 was constructed for each hospital, following Hambrick's (1979, 1981) method. Service additions were weighted according to how innovative they were: a service added by 1987 that 50 or fewer hospitals offered in 1983 received a weight of three, one existing at 51 to 100 hospitals received a weight of two, and one existing at 100 or more received a weight of one. The difference between the number of services offered in 1983 and the summed weights of the services offered in 1987 was the measure of service and product innovativeness; hospitals with high scores were considered domain-offensive and those with low scores domain-defensive.

Five questions were posed to identify the extent to which a CEO would use each label to describe the case scenarios, based on the questionnaire used by Jackson and Dutton (1988). After reading each case scenario respondents were asked, for example, 'To what extent would your hospital label the situation as something positive.' The continua were scaled so that high ratings indicated that respondents labeled the case situation as positive. Items used a 7-point Likert response format and were averaged, and responses were averaged across the two cases within each hospital.

Five questions were posed to identify the extent to which a CEO would use each label, based on Jackson and Dutton's (1988) questionnaire; respondents were asked, for example, whether they 'feel that benefits will come from the situation.' The continua were scaled so that high ratings indicated that respondents labeled the case situation as a gain. Items used a 7-point Likert response format, were averaged within the scale, and were averaged across the two cases.

Five questions were posed to identify the extent to which a CEO would use each label, based on Jackson and Dutton's (1988) questionnaire; respondents were asked, for example, whether they 'feel it can manage the situation instead of the situation managing it.' The continua were scaled so that high ratings indicated that respondents labeled the case situation as controllable. Items used a 7-point Likert response format, were averaged within the scale, and were averaged across the two cases.

The 16 information items used to construct each of the case scenarios were presented to the respondents, who were asked to indicate the extent to which the hospital would use each to clarify and define the strategic situation presented; for example, 'To what extent would you use the information that indicated that HMOs have penetrated 20 percent of the market in your area?'
