Items used a 7-point Likert response format and were averaged, and responses were averaged across the two cases within each hospital.

The logarithm of the time that had elapsed between the cessation of the federal loan program in 1983 and an HMO's conversion. Conversion time was measured in six-month intervals, with the last ending in June 1987. Data from organizations that had not converted by June 1987 were right-censored.

Age, the number of years in operation, was taken directly from the Interstudy census. Values for the independent variables were calculated for 1983, when the federal government announced the end of its loan program for nonprofit HMOs.

Size was measured by the logarithm of the number of members enrolled in an HMO, as reported in each Interstudy census. The logarithm was used because size was expected to have a marginally decreasing effect.

Structure was measured as a dichotomous variable. Individual practice associations, which are organized around solo and single-specialty practices, were coded 0 for a low level of system coupling; prepaid group plans (staff, group, and network plans) were coded 1 for a high level of system coupling.
Utilization, the ratio between the number of days of service rendered by an HMO and its number of members, measured the extent to which members used available services.
Case load, the ratio between the number of members enrolled in an HMO and its number of physicians, measured the efficiency with which an HMO used its physicians.
Federal qualification was a dichotomous variable, with 1 signifying federal qualification and 0 signifying no federal qualification.

Physician availability was the number of physicians in a state per 100,000 residents. Task environment variables were measured at the state level, with each HMO assigned to the state in which its headquarters are located.
Market saturation was the ratio of HMO enrollees in a state to the total state population. It was measured at the state level.
Entry rate was the ratio of the number of HMOs entering a state market to the number of HMOs existing in that market. It was measured at the state level.
Chain membership was a dichotomous variable with 1 signifying membership in a national chain and 0 signifying no membership. National chains operate HMOs in two or more states.
For-profit status was the ratio of the number of for-profit HMOs to the total number of HMOs in a state. It was measured at the state level.

State law was a dichotomous variable, with 1 referring to location in a state having statutes specifically permitting conversion and 0 referring to location in a state without such statutes. Data on supportive state legislation were drawn from Dunn and colleagues (1986).

Mode of entry was a binary variable, with 1 for direct entry and 0 for acquisitive entry. An entry was classified as acquisitive if a new product line matched one described as part of the business of a firm acquired by the entrant the year before the new product line first appeared. Observations that could not be traced to any acquisition after accounting for all acquisitions were assumed to represent direct entries.

A diversification profile of entrants before and after diversification moves was obtained with Berry's rectangular approximation. The distance of new industry i from the firm's largest business was coded 0 if i and b were in the same four-digit SIC code, 1 if they were in the same three-digit SIC code, and so on. The degree of unrelatedness of an entry move was defined as the diversification value one year after the entry minus the diversification value the year before, so large values represent a highly unrelated diversification move; sales attributable to a new entry were measured one year after the move.
time_window: one year before and one year after the diversification move

variable_name: ratio of long-term debt to the market value of a firm
description: Long-term debt divided by the market value of the firm, a standard measure of liquidity used to represent internal funds and to measure leverage directly. The lower the value of the variable, the lower the risk of a firm's debt and the higher its liquidity. Debt and market value were computed from annual reports and the Standard and Poor's Security Stock Guide for the year before an entry.

variable_name: relation of a firm's current ratio to the entered industry's current ratio
description: The entrant's current ratio divided by the current ratio of the entered industry, used to capture short-term debt and working capital. A high value for the relation to the industry current ratio represents low risks for lenders of short-term operating funds and a high level of working capital. The industry data were from the IRS Source Book of Income Statistics.

The ratio of a firm's average stock price the year before a diversification move to its average stock price two years before. The higher the value of this variable, the cheaper it is for a company to use stock as a medium of exchange.
time_window: one year before vs two years before the diversification move

description: The percentage of sales captured by the four largest firms in an industry, obtained from the Census of Manufacturers for 1958 and 1963. Large values for this variable indicate that a few large competitors may retaliate against a direct entry.
The growth rate of sales one year prior to an entry year, used to approximate expected growth rates. Growth was computed from sales data reported in the IRS Source Book of Income Statistics.
time_window: one year prior to an entry year

description: Each policy declaration was classified by trained judges as either accommodative or defensive, using the authors' definitions of the two signal types. In the regression model a dummy variable represented the type of signal, its value set to 1 for an accommodative and 0 for a defensive signal. Of the 112 observations, all judges agreed on the classification of 87.
time_window: day of and day before the announcement

description: Each crisis was assigned to one of three types-accidents, scandals, or product safety and health incidents-based on the crisis's effects on victims and what could plausibly be said about its causes. The authors examined major case books and monographs and focused on 15 of the 27 crises they found described; because only five accidents were found, two severe airline crashes were included.

The expected return for each policy declaration was estimated with a market model in which the expected return equals an intercept plus a beta coefficient times the return on a standard market index plus a residual. The estimation period began 244 trading days before each postcrisis announcement and ended 6 days before it. The abnormal return is the actual return minus the expected return, and the average impact of the announcement on the day before it appeared in the Wall Street Journal and on the day of its appearance is used.
time_window: 244 trading days before the announcement through 6 days before it (estimation); day before and day of the announcement (event window)

description: Interviewees described the most significant strategic decision made in their organizations over the study period, and in the course of that description the decision duration was identified. Durations ranged from 1 month to 24 months; because decision duration reflects the slowness of a decision, the scale was reversed by subtracting decision duration from 25, yielding a metric in which high values reflect fast decisions and low values slow decisions.

CEOs were asked to identify and discuss each of the alternatives that were simultaneously considered in making the decision studied. As a reliability check, one or two other organization members were also queried about the alternatives considered; in all but one organization the CEO reliably estimated the number of alternatives, and in that one instance follow-up interviews resolved the discrepancy.

Measured as the principal component of the average board member's tenure on the board, average age, and average years of working experience in the focal industry in 1986, derived from factor analysis with varimax rotation. The factor loadings for the three variables were .943, .847, and .417, and the factor's eigenvalue was 1.831; the industry familiarity loading was above the heuristic level of .4 and was retained on theoretical grounds.
Calculated by averaging each organization's return on assets over the study period, 1985 through 1987.
Computed by averaging the annual sales growth rate from 1984 through 1987.

Operationally defined as industry growth coupled with changes in technology and such other disruptive forces as governmental regulations. Industry growth was measured with archival data as change in industry employment and change in industry sales; technological change was measured with a seven-point, one-item scale assessing 86 executives' perceptions of the pace of technological change in their industries, averaged for each of the three industries and found to differ significantly (p < .05); additional competitive, technological, and governmental discontinuities were described qualitatively from archival data. On this basis one industry was classified as high-velocity, one as medium-velocity, and one as low-velocity, relative to one another; in the regressions environmental velocity was represented as +1 for the biotechnology subsample, 0 for the hospital subsample, and -1 for the textile subsample.

The difference between internally generated cash and power plant construction expenditures, divided by stockholder equity, converted to a percentage, and used as a three-year moving average. Internally generated cash adds depreciation, other noncash charges, and the proceeds from sales of company property, facilities, and investments to net income. The authors note data collection constraints precluded a finer-grained measure, but the variable correlates .82 with investment report-based cash flow measures for the industry.
time_window: three-year moving average; lagged one year relative to the event year

description: The dependent variable is the earliest date on which a utility's announcement of the intention to form divisions appeared. Announcement of the intention to adopt was chosen over actual adoption because actual dates depend on state regulatory proceedings; the event is modeled as the hazard rate of adoption.

The total number of different four-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes in which first-tier subsidiaries were active, less those numbers accounted for by vertical integration. The authors did not make more detailed measures because the SIC codes did not capture that all subsidiaries were unregulated and fundamentally distinct from the parent company and each other.

A second measure of diversification, made possible by the requirement that utilities state their equity in subsidiary companies on annual reports to federal agencies. It is the total equity position in nonvertical subsidiaries divided by stockholders' equity, converted to a percentage.

variable_name: change in the logarithm of compensation
description: The dependent variable is the change in the logarithm of compensation from 1986 to 1987. Three measures of compensation were used: cash compensation (salary, bonuses, and deferred amounts); cash compensation plus stock options valued with the Black-Scholes model; and cash compensation plus stock options valued at the closing market price for the year in which options were granted. Only options granted during the study period were valued, and each measure was adjusted for inflation to represent 1986 constant dollars using the Consumer Price Index.

The accounting-based performance measure is net income divided by average total assets, based on financial data for 1986. It was also examined relative to industry and relative to the prior fiscal year, 1985.

The market-based performance measure is market return in fiscal year 1986, computed from stock prices and dividends per share adjusted for stock dividends and splits. It was also examined relative to industry and relative to the prior fiscal year, 1985.

For each firm, expenditure on a decision variable (R&D or advertising, standardized as a proportion of net sales) was regressed on industry expenditure for 1982 to 1985 to obtain time series OLS coefficients, which were used to predict the firm's 1986 expenditure. The unique portion of the CEO's decision is the residual, and the absolute value of that residual was used to construct the measure; a logarithmic transformation was applied for the analysis.

The proportion of the passengers served by an airline in the year an action was taken that were affected by the action. For example, if an airline served 250,000 passengers in a particular year, of whom 50,000 were affected by an action, a competitor dependence measure of 0.2 was assigned to this airline for this action. The competitors affected by each action were the airlines providing service in at least one studied airport affected by the action, that is, the 37 U.S. large air traffic hubs.
time_window: the year an action was taken

description: A composite index for each of 13 generic competitive moves, constructed by averaging respondents' ratings on 14 dimensions of irreversibility, such as investment required, organizational disruption, and degree of industry publicity. Respondents rated each dimension on a five-point scale (1, very low; 5, very high) for each competitive move, and the index is the average rating of a move across dimensions. The reliability of the irreversibility index yielded a Cronbach alpha of .91.
scale: five-point scale (1, very low; 5, very high)

description: A dichotomous variable in which 1 represents a competitor who could have responded but did not respond, and 0 represents response. If a competitor was reported in Aviation Daily as reacting to an action, it was identified as an actual responder.
The number of days between the date a specific action was first reported in Aviation Daily and the date that journal first made public the competitor's response to the action.
time_window: days between action report and response report

description: A measure based on the concurrence of the types of an action and a response; if the response was of the same type as the action (for example, a price cut responding to a price cut), it was identified as a matching response.

The classification of all actions and responses into 13 generic types allowed price moves to be distinguished from other types of competitive moves. Price actions were included only when they had a change magnitude greater than 10 percent.

Monthly data on passenger shares for airlines making competitive moves; increases and decreases in share for each attacking and responding airline were calculated as a percentage of total passengers. The percentages were measured at three points in time: the end of the month in which a move was made, one month after the move was made, and two months after the move was made, presented as one-, two-, and three-month lags.
time_window: end of the month of the move; one month after; two months after

variable_name: attacker, responder, and early versus late responder
description: Attackers are the firms that initiated the 856 actions; responders are the competitors reported in Aviation Daily as reacting to an action; nonresponders are airlines that could have responded but did not. Early versus late responders were distinguished by the response delay variable.
Contrast between the initiators of competitive actions and the competitors that responded to them, used in mean difference tests of market share changes.

A scale composed of two variables: (1) the number of links between stages of production, which indicated increased complexity, and (2) Gort's (1962) measure of constrained vertical diversification, which indicated decreased complexity. The scale was constructed by subtracting the second variable from the first after standardizing (x = 0, s.d. 1) the items; coefficient alpha for the scale was .87. The number of vertical links was computed by identifying whether the firm had sales in each of the areas represented by the boxes in the value-added chain diagram and counting every arrow connecting two boxes in which sales existed. Gort's measure was sales in ancillary activities divided by the quantity of total sales less the sales in the core product group, with single-product firms assigned a score of one.
scale: standardized items (x = 0, s.d. 1) combined by subtraction

description: Betas computed from a regression model based on monthly stock market returns from the CRSP tapes for the 60 months ending on December 31, 1985. Beta was computed for each firm using the standard CAPM model R - Rf = a + b x (MR - Rf), where R is return on common stock including capital gains and dividends, Rf is the risk-free rate established using short-term treasury bill rates from CRSP, and MR is the average return of the market portfolio. The returns of an equally weighted portfolio of all stocks traded on the New York Stock Exchange were used as the market proxy, and a high beta indicated high vulnerability to economy-wide changes and therefore high risk to shareholders.

A modification of Altman's (1983) Z-score, defined as Z = (1.2 x LIQ) + (1.4 x RE) + (3.3 x ROA) + (0.6 x MED) + (1.0 x CAPINT). Because some of the regression models included measures of debt to equity and sales to assets, the last two items were eliminated to form a modified Z-score for use in the statistical tests. A high Z indicates a low risk of default; the modified Z was correlated almost perfectly (r = .94, p < .0001) with the original Z.

Measured using the weighted average of the volatility for each of the four-digit SIC product lines in which a firm operated, each volatility weighted in proportion to the percentage of sales in the category. The weightings were based on averaging 1983 and 1985 category sales percentages reported in the Trinet data base. The measure of volatility was the intertemporal variance in the average return on equity (ROE) for firms in each SIC category, as reported in Dun & Bradstreet's Industry Norms and Key Business Ratios.

Measured as the average 1985 environmental growth rate in all the four-digit SIC product lines in which a firm operated, weighted in proportion to the percentage of the firm's sales in each category as reported in the Trinet data base. The environmental growth rate was calculated from the total product sales of all firms in each SIC category reported in such U.S. government publications as the Annual Survey of Manufacturers; in sum, a measure of industry sales growth rate.

Total employment data for companies were obtained for the pre-downturn and downturn years identified by respondents, from COMPUSTAT, or where unavailable from Moody's manuals or Standard & Poor's Register, always using the same source for both years of a given company. The variable is the percentage change in total company employment between the pre-downturn year and the downturn year, and is described as a coarse-grained measure that can capture countercyclical hiring for a broad range of key employees.

variable_name: Percentage change in employment of managers and professionals (managers-officials)
description: A second questionnaire asked respondents to report from EEO-1 forms the numbers of managers-officials a company employed in the downturn year it had identified and the year before the downturn. The variable is the percentage change in the employment of managers-officials between those two years, giving a finer-grained measure of countercyclical hiring because the strategy is envisioned as applying to managers and professionals.
time_window: year before the downturn to the downturn year

variable_name: Percentage change in employment of managers and professionals (professionals)
description: A second questionnaire asked respondents to report from EEO-1 forms the numbers of professionals a company employed in the downturn year it had identified and the year before the downturn. The variable is the percentage change in the employment of professionals between those two years, giving a finer-grained measure of countercyclical hiring because the strategy is envisioned as applying to managers and professionals.
time_window: year before the downturn to the downturn year

description: Two items were combined to provide a subjective measure of countercyclical hiring. Respondents rated the extent to which their companies practiced (or emphasized) countercyclical hiring of managerial and professional personnel during the last economic downturn in their predominant industries, on seven-point scales with 1 = little extent (or emphasis) and 7 = great extent (or emphasis). Coefficient alpha was .84, and the correlation of .62 between the ratings of the two respondents from each company supported convergent validity.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 = little extent (or emphasis), 7 = great extent (or emphasis)

description: Two items were used to tap the importance of human resource planning for avoiding shortages of qualified personnel, on seven-point scales (1 = very unimportant, 7 = very important). Coefficient alpha was .87 and convergent validity was .58.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 = very unimportant, 7 = very important

variable_name: Human resource planning's link with strategy
description: Two items were used, one assessing human resource planning's link with strategic planning and one assessing its input to strategic planning, on seven-point scales (1 = very weakly or very little input, 7 = very strongly or very great input). Coefficient alpha was .92 and convergent validity was .61.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 = very weakly (or very little input), 7 = very strongly (or very great input)

description: Two items asked to what extent higher-quality entry-level and experienced applicants encouraged countercyclical hiring, on seven-point response scales with 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring and 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring. Coefficient alpha was .86 and convergent validity was .84.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring, 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring
time_window: conditions at the time of the downturn

description: A single item was used to determine facilitation of affirmative action, on a seven-point response scale with 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring and 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring. There was insufficient variance to use test-retest correlation, but 68 percent of respondents made identical ratings on the test and retest and 84 percent differed by no more than one point; convergent validity was .52.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring, 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring
time_window: conditions at the time of the downturn

description: One item asked to what extent maintenance of a regular age distribution encouraged countercyclical hiring, on a seven-point response scale with 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring and 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring. Sixty-seven percent of respondents made the same responses on the test and retest, and 83 percent differed by no more than one point.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring, 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring
time_window: conditions at the time of the downturn

description: Two items assessed the influence of the facilitation of employee development programs and of career planning, on seven-point response scales with 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring and 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring. Coefficient alpha was .82 and convergent validity was .61.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring, 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring
time_window: conditions at the time of the downturn

description: Financial performance data were obtained from the 1990 CRSP monthly tape files, using the common stock monthly return observations corresponding to the downturn year reported by each company. Monthly return observations were converted into annual values by continually compounding the monthly rates of return, and a market-adjusted return was constructed by deducting the CRSP market index from a company's annual return; this derived excess return for the downturn period measures company financial performance.

A single item assessed the influence of cost considerations, on a seven-point response scale from 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring to 7 = strongly encourage. Items making up the inhibiting variables were reverse-coded, so that strongly discourage had a value of 7 and strongly encourage a value of 1. Test-retest reliability was .78, although convergent validity was .33.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring, 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring (reverse-coded)
time_window: conditions at the time of the downturn

description: Two items asked to what extent risk-averse decision makers and organizational resistance influenced countercyclical hiring, on seven-point response scales; coefficient alpha was .65 and convergent validity was .54. As an inhibiting variable it was reverse-coded, so that strongly discourage had a value of 7 and strongly encourage a value of 1.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring, 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring (reverse-coded)
time_window: conditions at the time of the downturn

description: The influence of inaccurate human resource forecasting and lack of forecasting was assessed with two items on seven-point response scales; coefficient alpha was .83 and convergent validity was .53. As an inhibiting variable it was reverse-coded, so that strongly discourage had a value of 7 and strongly encourage a value of 1.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 = strongly discourage countercyclical hiring, 7 = strongly encourage countercyclical hiring (reverse-coded)
time_window: conditions at the time of the downturn

variable_name: degree of focus on customer segments
description: Computed in two steps from the CEO questionnaire: first, the entropy due to multiple customer segments served by each business of the firm; second, a weighted average degree of focus for the firm using the revenue shares of the businesses in total firm revenues as weights. CEOs listed the top ten businesses and top ten customer segments and entered the proportion of total firm revenues obtained from each business and each customer segment, plus for each business the proportion of its revenues obtained from each customer segment. High values on the measure indicate low degrees of focus.

variable_name: degree of focus on internal capabilities
description: CEOs listed each firm's top ten businesses and identified significant resources shared between each pair of businesses, where significant resources were described as physical plant or equipment, personnel's specialized knowledge or skills, or special routines or repertoires. From these data, sets of businesses that shared resources were identified, and an entropy measure of focus on internal capabilities was computed from the revenue share of these sets of businesses in total firm revenues. High values on the measure indicate low degrees of focus.

variable_name: degree of focus on geographic regions
description: The third data matrix was identical to the matrix for customer segments except that geographic regions replaced customer segments; nine regions were listed: North America (the United States and Canada), South America, the USSR and Eastern Europe, Western Europe, the Pacific Rim, China, other Asian countries, Africa, and Australia and New Zealand. An entropy measure of degree of focus on geographic regions was computed exactly as was the measure for degree of focus on customer segments. High values on the measure indicate low degrees of focus.

variable_name: industry- and risk-adjusted return on equity
description: Return on equity was used as the accounting-based measure of firm performance, averaged over the five years 1983-87. Both firm and industry five-year average ROE over 1983-87 were divided by an accounting-based measure of systematic risk, defined as the ratio of the covariance of a firm's return on equity with the return on equity obtained on a broad market portfolio of stocks to the variance of the return on equity of the market portfolio; a risk-adjusted, weighted average industry ROE was then computed using the firm's 1987 proportion of revenues from its activities in each industry and subtracted from the risk-adjusted firm ROE.

The ratio of the market value of equity to its book value, computed as the average market value of equity divided by the average book value of equity in 1987, with opening and closing values averaged for the year, and adjusted for industry participation differences using the same industry-adjustment approach as for ROE. No risk adjustment was applied because the market-to-book measure needs none.

A stock-market-based measure of operating performance obtained as the estimate of the intercept in a regression of firm returns on market returns, both computed in excess of the risk-free rate, using daily firm and stock-market returns for 1987 and the 12-month treasury bond rate for each month of 1987 to obtain the risk-free rate. Jensen's alpha compares the performance of a firm to that of firms in an unmanaged portfolio with similar market risk.

Based on the National Union Survey question 'How frequently has your union used nontraditional membership categories such as associate members?' Unions that indicated using such membership categories were contacted again to ascertain the nature of these programs, and published information on associate member programs was also consulted. A dichotomous variable was created indicating whether a union had a program meeting the study's criteria (1 = associate membership program, 0 = no program).

The percentage change in a union's membership between 1983 and 1987. For AFL-CIO unions, the numbers of members reported for per capita payment purposes in 1983 and 1987 were used; for nonaffiliates, membership figures were taken from Gifford (1984, 1988).

A two-item index taken from the National Union Survey (alpha = .66). The items assessed the degree to which a union stressed collective bargaining alone or several strategies, including bargaining, organizing, and political activities. High scores indicated a reliance on a broader scope of strategies.

The logarithm of union membership (in thousands) in 1985, derived from the same data as membership change. Membership levels do not necessarily connote resources, but other measures of size, including assets and membership levels, tend to be highly correlated with membership.

The proportion of a union's National Labor Relations Board certification elections that were held in prospective 'professional and/or technical' and 'office, clerical, and other white collar' collective bargaining units between 1977 and 1985.
The logarithm of the number of votes cast for a union in failed union certification campaigns, calculated from the same election data used for knowledge worker organizing.

A dummy variable indicating whether a union operated primarily in construction, based on primary jurisdiction assignments derived from information regarding industrial distributions of members (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 1980: Appendix I) and similar information based on large samples of bargaining agreements. Coded 1 for unions with a primary jurisdiction in construction, 0 otherwise.

A three-item index constructed from the National Union Survey (alpha = .69). The items assessed the degree to which a union limited staff and rank-and-file member participation in policy decisions. Based on 1990 data but treated as a relatively stable organizational characteristic.

variable_name: participation in the AFL-CIO Committee on the Evolution of Work
description: Determined from the committee's 1985 report, coded 1 for participation and 0 otherwise.
A variable recording whether a change in CEO had occurred at the start of the period. Periods of succession are compared with periods that did not follow succession.
time_window: measured at the start of each period

description: A composite factor score for the power concentration dimension, calculated using only variables with absolute value loadings of 0.70 or more on that factor. The underlying variables were rated on seven-point scales at the beginnings and ends of periods, and change across the period is the dependent variable.
scale: seven-point ratings (1 = much lower, 4 = about average, 7 = much higher)
time_window: beginning and end of each period

description: A single composite factor score combining the highly correlated intelligence systems and intended rationality variables, which loaded on the same factor. It was calculated using only variables with absolute value loadings of 0.70 or more on the factor, and change across the period is the dependent variable.
scale: seven-point ratings (1 = much lower, 4 = about average, 7 = much higher)
time_window: beginning and end of each period

description: A composite factor score for the structural complexity dimension, calculated using only variables with absolute value loadings of 0.70 or more on that factor. Change across the period, in absolute value, is the dependent variable in the tests of change.
scale: seven-point ratings (1 = much lower, 4 = about average, 7 = much higher)
time_window: beginning and end of each period

description: A composite factor score for the competitive aggressiveness dimension, calculated using only variables with absolute value loadings of 0.70 or more on that factor. Change across the period, in absolute value, is the dependent variable in the tests of change.
scale: seven-point ratings (1 = much lower, 4 = about average, 7 = much higher)
time_window: beginning and end of each period

variable_name: Absolute change in the four factor scores
description: Organizational change is the absolute value of the change over each period in the four composite factor scores (power concentration, information processing, structural complexity, competitive aggressiveness). The scores come from seven-point ratings of firm variables made by raters from corporate histories, and the absolute values capture change in either direction.

Return on equity (ROE) calculated as income before extraordinary items and discontinued operations divided by common equity as reported during the fiscal year prior to the year of the succession. Each firm's ROE was then adjusted by its industry's average ROE by subtracting the industry's ROE from that of the firm and dividing the result by the standard deviation in industry ROE. Industry was defined at the two-digit Standard Industrial Code (SIC) level.
time_window: fiscal year prior to the year of the succession

description: The intercept term of the Capital Asset Pricing Model, used as an operational definition of market return and as an estimate of shareholder returns relative to an unmanaged portfolio of stocks of similar market risk. It was estimated by regressing each firm's daily stock returns (appreciation plus dividends) against the daily stock returns of a value-weighted CRSP portfolio used as a proxy for the return of all risky assets over a 100-trading-day window ending 50 trading days before a succession event.
time_window: 100-trading-day window ending 50 trading days before a succession event

description: Calculated as the covariance between a firm's return and a value-weighted market portfolio and estimated by the slope coefficient of the same regression model used to estimate Jensen's alpha. The return on an unmanaged portfolio of stocks of similar market risk served as the benchmark.
time_window: same 100-trading-day estimation window as Jensen's alpha

description: By construction, variance in shareholder returns that could not be explained by movements in the market (the residuals) and thus was specific to the firm under consideration. The return on an unmanaged portfolio of stocks of similar market risk served as the benchmark.
time_window: same 100-trading-day estimation window as Jensen's alpha

description: A binary (0,1) variable; an outsider was defined as any successor with less than two years of service in the firm he or she headed. Fifty-two outsider selections were identified in the data, 11 percent of the succession events.

Coded on the basis of the different possible associations a former CEO can have with a firm after succession has occurred, using a five-level classification scheme (relay, normal retirement, early retirement, death or poor health, and dismissal); a binary dismissal/nondismissal measure was used when testing for a moderating effect. A succession event was categorized as a dismissal if all officership and directorship connections between a firm and its outgoing CEO were severed at the time of the succession.
scale: 0,1 (dismissal/nondismissal in tests; five-level classification in descriptive analyses)
time_window: at the time of the succession

description: An indicator variable coded 1 if a person in a firm other than the incumbent CEO was the president and otherwise coded 0.
A dummy variable coded 1 if the outgoing CEO at the time of a succession also held the title 'chairperson' and coded 0 if a person other than the incumbent held that title.
time_window: at the time of a succession

description: Indicator variable that equaled one if an organization failed in any period and zero if it survived to operate in the next period. Measured at the end of each one-year period.
time_window: measured at the end of each one-year period

description: A set of dummy variables measuring the exits of the presidents of the firms studied. Each dummy variable was set equal to one during the period between the ith and (i+1)th succession event and equal to zero otherwise; the maximum number of succession events studied was four. Measured at the beginning of each one-year period.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each one-year period

description: A set of dummy variables measuring the exits of vice presidents, treasurers, secretaries, and general managers, combined into one group because no data were available to differentiate meaningfully among them. The exit of any one of these was sufficient to code a managerial succession event. Each dummy variable was set equal to one during the period between the ith and (i+1)th succession event and zero otherwise.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each one-year period

description: A pair of variables recording elapsed duration in years since the most recent presidential and managerial succession events. Following Carroll (1984) and Amburgey and colleagues (1993), the clock was set equal to zero until the first succession occurred; it then recorded the time elapsed since succession in years, and was reset to zero if another succession occurred.
Age measured in years since founding, updated each year and included among the control variables measured each year.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each one-year period

description: R&D intensity was calculated in the traditional manner by dividing R&D expenditures by sales for each line of business. The measure is the variance of these intensity values across the lines of business of the firm, used as a measure of dispersion in resource allocations. All variables were averaged over the study period.
time_window: averaged over 1984-90 (seven years); three-year periods in the early/late split tests

description: Capital intensity was calculated in the traditional manner by dividing capital expenditures by sales for each line of business. The measure is the variance of these intensity values across the lines of business of the firm, used as a measure of dispersion in resource allocations. All variables were averaged over the study period.

Return on assets was used as the measure of financial performance. The dependent variable is industry-adjusted: a weighted average of the ROA of the dominant four-digit industry of each firm, excluding the firm's own financial figures, was subtracted from firm ROA prior to analysis. All variables were averaged over the study period.

Obtained by calculating the number of lateral policy and budget committees in a municipal authority as a percentage of the number of separate departments it had. A high value indicated a high integrative effort.

Calculated as the absolute number of departments based upon a program rather than a functional-service basis. A functional-service organization would have departments such as engineering, planning, and architecture, whereas a program organization would have a department of technical services combining the previously separate units into team-based units. A high value indicates high use of the program criterion.

Measured as the extent to which certain policy and managerial issues were routed through interdepartmental structures. The distinction sought was whether issues were routed through a management team with multiprofessional membership or handled exclusively within a given professional department. The range of possible ratings for each issue was from 0 to 3, with a high rating indicating a corporate pattern of interaction; ratings were based upon the number of professions involved in discussing each issue, and the organization's interaction score was the total for the seven issues.
scale: each issue rated 0-3; organization score is the total across seven issues

description: Measured as the extent to which an organization employed eight techniques whose use constituted part of the wider debate on the applicability of corporate planning and budgeting to municipal authorities. Organizations were rated on a three-point scale (yes = 3, partly = 2, and no = 1) for each technique. The higher the rating, the greater the use of rational analysis within a resource allocation system.
scale: three-point scale per technique (yes = 3, partly = 2, no = 1) across eight techniques

description: Measured as the extent to which an organization had explicit procedures for three items: overall environmental scanning, an explicit meta-policymaking system covering the organization as a whole, and explicit environmental scanning procedures within each department. Organizations were rated on each item in terms of the same three-point scale (yes = 3, partly = 2, no = 1).
scale: three-point scale per item (yes = 3, partly = 2, no = 1) across three items

variable_name: clan versus bureaucratic form of appraisal
description: Indexed as the extent to which a department head's policies and program were scrutinized using a common format of cross-organizational goals and priorities rather than professional goals relevant to a single department. Bureaucratic control was defined as occurring when departmental policies and appraisals were subject to examination by corporate bodies such as management teams, corporate evaluation groups, and policy committees; clan control was seen as occurring when departments were allowed to operate according to their own internal standards.

variable_name: classification as within an archetype (corporate bureaucracy or heteronomous professional bureaucracy)
description: Standardized scores were computed for each variable using a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 15, to enable comparisons across variables and across time periods with regard to the extent to which organizations were in an archetype. An organization was classified as within the corporate bureaucracy archetype if it scored two-thirds of a standard deviation or more above the mean on each variable, achieving a score of 60 or more, and as within the heteronomous professional bureaucracy archetype if it scored two-thirds of a standard deviation or more below the mean on each variable, achieving a score of 40 or less. An organization was classified as within an archetype if all its structures and systems were consistent with the theoretical template.
scale: standardized scores, mean 50 and standard deviation 15; archetype cutoffs at 60 or more and 40 or less

description: A track is the temporal association of an organization with one or more archetypes; it is about the extent to which an organization remains over time within the assumptions and parameters of a given archetype or moves between archetypes. The authors used the tracks of the 24 organizations across the three survey points to distinguish organizations that remained within the same archetype throughout, organizations that began within or close to an archetype and stayed within it over subsequent survey periods (relative inertia), and the few organizations that reoriented from one archetype to another.

Organizational design is measured by six indicators of structure and systems: ratio of integration to differentiation, criteria of differentiation, interaction pattern, degree of rational analysis, extent of assertiveness, and clan versus bureaucratic appraisal. They were coded from interviews and documents of 24 municipal authorities and standardized (mean 50, SD 15), then used to classify organizations into archetypes.

Configurations derived each year by cluster analysis of standardized values of ten grouping variables, one from each construct category drawn from prior strategic groups studies, using the complete linkage method and (for confirmation of membership) the k-means iterative partitioning FASTCLUS procedure; the number of clusters was chosen by visual inspection of tree-plots and checked by randomly splitting the hospital population into two subgroups. Total assets was dropped from the clustering variables because its correlation with number of beds exceeded .85 in each year.

Configurations derived each year by clustering hospitals on two theory-based dimensions of competitive strategy: source of competitive advantage, measured as the percentage of routine patient days, and breadth of operations, measured as the total number of services offered by the hospital from the AHA list. The same clustering procedures were used as for the inductive approach, and four configurations were found in each year of the study for all full and split sample solutions.

Each hospital was assigned to one of the four deductively defined configurations each year: entrepreneurs/r-specialists (innovation on nonroutine services, narrow breadth), prospectors/r-generalists (innovation, broad breadth), defenders/K-specialists (efficiency on routine services, narrow breadth), and analyzers/K-generalists (efficiency, broad breadth). Membership was based on the two clustering dimensions, with the iterative partitioning assignment used where the two clustering procedures disagreed.

Five performance measures used in prior configurations-performance studies: net patient revenue per bed (sales), return on equity (equity and investment), return on assets (asset-related measures), profit per discharge, defined as net in-patient revenue minus in-patient cost divided by total facility discharges (margin and profit), and average occupancy (overall performance). Total assets and profit per discharge were excluded from subsequent analyses because the correlation between return on assets and profit per discharge increased from .61 in 1986 to .83 in 1990. These variables served as the dependent variables in the MANOVAs.

variable_name: number of configurations identified per year
description: The count of clusters produced by the clustering procedures for each approach in each of the five years studied. Over the five-year period the inductive approach yielded a minimum of three configurations and a maximum of five, whereas the deductive approach yielded four configurations in each year for all full and split sample solutions.

Configurations are the hospital clusters derived each year by two approaches: an inductive cluster analysis of ten standardized grouping variables, and a deductive clustering on two theory-based competitive strategy dimensions that yields four configuration types. Each hospital is assigned to a cluster each year.

Expansion projects were coded as belonging to one of four categories: horizontally related (coded 1) if the expansion took place within the Dutch equivalent of an SIC three-digit category; related (2) if it took place within a two-digit SIC category; unrelated (3) if none of the other three categories applied; vertically related (4) if it took place within a firm's value-added chain. The unrelated category is the omitted contrast in the hazard models. Assignment to the vertical category was based on a judgment as to whether intracompany transfers of goods and services could take place, as annual reports do not give data on actual transfers.
An expansion was coded as domestic (1) if it was implemented within the Netherlands and as foreign (2) if it occurred elsewhere, including in a European Union country.

An expansion was coded as an acquisition (1) if it entailed the takeover of an existing firm or a business unit and as a start-up (2) if it did not. The authors note that the mode of expansion was defined unequivocally from primary sources rather than by an arbitrary cutoff on the share of sales accounted for by mergers and acquisitions.

Full ownership (1) was coded if an expansion was 100 percent controlled by the diversifier; majority ownership (2) if the diversifier owned between 50.1 and 100 percent of the equity; equal ownership (3) if the diversifier had a 50 percent stake; and minority ownership (4) if the diversifier owned less than 50 percent of the expansion's equity. The results section reports estimations using three ownership dummies and a separate estimation involving a single dummy in the 50 percent category.

Longitudinal learning was measured as a three-year (or five-year) moving average of previous projects' longevity, treated as a proxy of a firm's past diversification success. For each new project this average covered strings of three (or five) years, up to the year prior to a new expansion's onset, and was lagged one time unit to offset the overlap between this covariate and the hazard of new expansions. Any expansion lasting more than three years was treated as having lasted three years to accommodate the calculation of three-year moving averages. The first three years of the period were used to construct a baseline for each firm, which removed 80 observations from the data.
time_window: three-year moving average, lagged one time unit; a five-year average used as a sensitivity analysis

variable_name: Duration of expansion project (hazard of dissolution)
description: The dependent variable is the hazard that an expansion project is dissolved; the duration of a venture is construed as a measure of process, and long-enduring projects were deemed viable unless there were indications in an annual report that a venture had languished, while an expansion dissolved after problems were reported was classified as a failure. Acquisitions of firms or business units were not classified as failures or deaths. Projects still in existence in 1988 were right-censored.
time_window: from the project's initiation until dissolution or censoring in 1988

description: One of five decision criteria embedded in the text of each acquisition scenario. It was specified as the extent to which the sharing or exchange of critical skills, capabilities, or resources between the acquiring and acquired organizations was necessary to achieve the acquirer's goals in the acquisition.

One of five decision criteria embedded in the text of each acquisition scenario. It was specified as the extent to which the success of the acquisition depended on unique capabilities of the acquired organization that would be jeopardized by loss of independence.

One of five decision criteria embedded in the text of each acquisition scenario. It was specified as the degree to which the management of the acquiring organization tolerated and valued a diversity of values, philosophies, and beliefs.

One of five decision criteria embedded in the scenarios, defined as the difference in size of the two organizations, measured as number of employees. Because pretesting indicated that associating size directly with the names of the hypothetical organizations reduced confusion, this information was listed at the top of each scenario.

One of five decision criteria embedded in the text of each acquisition scenario. It was specified as the extent to which the acquirer and the acquired organization had compatible ideas about the goals each was trying to achieve through the acquisition and the means to achieve those goals.

Respondents made a unidimensional global judgment about integration and responded to six items regarding integration of financial resources and risk, policies and procedures, personnel, physical resources, decision making and control structures, and culture. Each dependent variable used a seven-point Likert scale representing the extent to which the decision maker would integrate the acquired organization (0 = no extent, 6 = a very great extent; responses were subsequently recoded to range from 1 to 7). Factor analysis extracted a single factor on which all items including the global rating loaded, a single response scale was created, and reliability analysis produced a Cronbach's alpha of .90; the scale, including the global integration measure, was used as a simple multi-item scale measure of level of integration.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (0 = no extent to 6 = a very great extent, recoded 1 to 7)

description: Reported by each respondent on the personal profile page of the questionnaire as acquisition experience both as acquirer and acquiree. Data were logarithmically transformed prior to investigating their effects. The average level of respondent acquisition experience was 12 acquisitions, with a range from 1 to more than 100 and a median of 6.

Reported by each respondent on the personal profile page as the number of employees of his or her organization. Data were logarithmically transformed prior to the analysis. Respondents' organizations ranged from 6 to 25,000 employees, with an average of 1,938 and a median of 700.

Reported on the personal profile page as the respondent organization's major industrial classification, coded as manufacturing, 1; service, 2. Of the 56 organizations represented, 33 were in service industries and 23 were in manufacturing.

Primary information about the pace of decision making was derived from scenario responses. Respondents recorded the number of days that their firms would most likely take to reach decisions on each of six events as they occurred, capturing the perceived speed of decision making.

Three 5-point Likert questions about the respondents' firms' decision-making speed; an index of responses served to validate the primary measure of organizational decision speed. The second pace measure was repeated with the questions reordered in the follow-up phone survey to form a third measure of pace.
A measure of cognitive complexity developed from a Bieri grid. In previous research on managers, this instrument had a test-retest reliability of .82.
Measured as a respondent's number of years of formal education beyond high school.
scale: years of education beyond high school

description: A six-item index of self-reported willingness to use intuition in actual business situations and reported use of intuition in the iterative acquisition scenario.
Considered a reflection of intuition, acquisition experience was measured with two questions.
Following Williams (1965), the authors measured risk propensity using the Job Preference Inventory.
A three-item measure of optimism concerned with attitudes about the future and personal expectancies, used to assess tolerance for risk (Carver & Scheier, 1981).
A 13-item measure of psychological flexibility (Gough, 1987) included as a measure of tolerance for risk.
A 12-item measure of energy and activity developed using the Jenkins Activity Scale (Jenkins, Zyzanski, & Rosenman, 1971).
An 11-item assessment of locus of control (Rotter, 1966; Smeltz, 1990) used as a second measure of propensity to act.
Centralization was measured through five Likert-scale questions that probed the degree to which a respondent's firm engaged in delegation and consensus seeking.
Formalization was measured as the degree to which firms engaged in long-term, explicit planning, with five items informed by Olian, Sims, and Smith (1991).

An indicator variable coded 1 for related acquisitions and 0 for unrelated acquisitions. Two panels of three academics unfamiliar with the rest of the research classified each acquisition using information about the acquirers' and targets' revenue sources, products, markets, and production processes drawn from business and industry indexes and directories, published articles, and telephone conversations with firm employees and trade associations. An acquisition was judged related if at least 70 percent of the acquiring firm's revenues came from a business area related by product, market, or production process to a business of the acquired firm.
The number of acquisitions made by an acquiring firm during the four years prior to the purchase of a focal acquired firm. The information was obtained from Mergers & Acquisitions.
time_window: four years prior to the focal acquisition

description: The ratio of the acquired firm's revenue to the acquiring firm's revenue, with information from COMPUSTAT and other published data sources. To model the hypothesized curvilinear relationship, the square of that ratio was also included as an explanatory variable.

A panel of three faculty members in strategic management, strategic marketing, and finance, unfamiliar with all other parts of the research, evaluated the success of each acquisition on a seven-point scale ranging from 1, very unsuccessful (no significant financial or strategic benefits), to 7, very successful (significant financial or strategic benefits). Evaluations were based on excerpts from published accounts of the acquisition results by industry experts, stock analysts, and business writers; duplicate information appearing to come from the same press release was excluded. Acquisition performance was deemed the mean value of the three academics' ratings; Ebel's measure of interrater agreement was .94.
time_window: from the announcement of an acquisition to 7.6 years after its consummation

description: Dependent variable coded "1" if an alliance involved the use of equity and "0" if it did not. An alliance was coded as equity based when a public announcement said that an equity joint venture had been created or that a firm had taken a substantive minority position in another with the intent of pursuing joint projects. The distinguishing characteristic is that equity sharing creates shared ownership and, beyond a minimum threshold, reduces exposure to opportunistic behavior.

Coded 1 if the alliance encompassed an R&D component (basic R&D, product development, or elements of both) and 0 otherwise. An alliance was labeled as including R&D only if a public announcement clearly stated that the agreement encompassed joint product development or basic R&D. Non-R&D alliances typically involved joint production or marketing. This variable is used as the measure of high transaction costs.
Number of prior alliances two firms had had since 1970; the variable took a zero value for a first-time alliance.

Number of prior equity alliances between two parties, taking a zero value for a first-time alliance of the given type. It includes both the situation in which there are only prior equity alliances and that in which there have been mixed alliances.
Number of prior nonequity alliances between two parties, taking a zero value for a first-time alliance of the given type. It does not include situations with mixed alliances.
Dummy variable indicating whether an alliance was domestic or international, coded 1 for partners of differing nationalities and 0 for partners of the same nationality.

The number of partners in an alliance was computed; because the alliances in the sample were either bilateral or trilateral, the variable was recoded as a dummy with a value of 1 if an alliance was multilateral and 0 if it was bilateral.

Firm performance was defined as average income growth during the five years prior to the measurement. Income growth over a five-year time horizon provides an indication of the extent to which resource stocks have been deployed and of the market reaction to that deployment. The measure was taken from 10-K reports as compiled by Compact Disclosure.
time_window: five years prior to the measurement

description: Respondents indicated the location and the extent to which each of nine functional activities is coordinated across country locations, choosing among "performed in one country," "performed in multiple countries and managed nationally," "performed in multiple countries and coordinated within regions," and "performed in multiple countries and coordinated globally." The responses for all nine activities were summed to create an index; a low score indicated little international interdependence and a high score extensive interdependence.
scale: summed index of nine four-category activity items

description: Rotter's (1966) E Scale, as modified by Govindarajan (1988), was used to measure each CEO's locus-of-control type. Responses to 11 items are summated to provide a total internal-external score, with high values indicating an internal locus of control and low values an external locus.

The shortened version of Form F of the Myers-Briggs Problem-Solving Styles Indicator was used; the short form asks respondents a series of forced-choice questions, instructing them to "indicate which response comes closest to how you usually feel or act." The authors do not describe how the information-gathering subscale score is formed.

The shortened version of Form F of the Myers-Briggs Problem-Solving Styles Indicator was used; the short form asks respondents a series of forced-choice questions, instructing them to "indicate which response comes closest to how you usually feel or act." The authors do not describe how the information-evaluation subscale score is formed.

Each respondent was asked to "summarize the functional areas of your career assignment" using a three-point scale in which 0 equaled "have not been assigned to this functional area" and 2 was "have spent an extensive amount of time in this functional area." A cluster analysis algorithm minimizing within-group variance relative to between-groups variance produced a four-cluster solution: broad-based, marketing management, technical management, and core business. In data analyses, each type of functional experience was coded as a dummy variable.
scale: 0-2 per functional area; cluster membership coded as dummies

description: Each respondent was asked to indicate his or her total accumulated experience in an international function or in a function that included international responsibilities, using Likert-type response categories.
scale: 1 = less than 1 year, 2 = 1 to 3 years, 3 = 4 to 6 years, 4 = 7 to 9 years, 5 = 10 to 12 years, 6 = 13 to 15 years, 7 = 16 years or more

description: Each respondent was asked to indicate the total accumulated time spent on overseas assignments, using Likert-type response categories.
scale: 1 = less than 1 year, 2 = 1 to 3 years, 3 = 4 to 6 years, 4 = 7 to 9 years, 5 = 10 to 12 years, 6 = 13 to 15 years, 7 = 16 years or more

description: All variables were standardized; ideal profiles of CEO characteristics were developed for high and low international interdependence contexts on the basis of the congruence hypotheses, and cluster analysis segmented firms into the two contextual conditions on the basis of the international interdependence variables. A distance-effectiveness index was calculated for each CEO by measuring the Euclidean distance between the theoretical profile and the CEO's actual ratings on the various dimensions; the closer the characteristics to the ideal profile, the smaller the distance.

Empirically derived profiles based on the two firms with the best performance in each group were also examined: distance measures were recalculated and the correlation between each distance measure and performance reassessed. This procedure yielded weaker results than the theoretical specification.

The change in debt was measured as the difference between the total debt-to-equity ratio of a firm one year after its LBO and one year prior to it. Total debt was used rather than long-term debt because a portion of the debt structure may consist of very short-term (3-6 month) bridge loans. Although all LBOs involve an increase in the debt-to-equity ratio, the magnitude of the increase varies significantly from case to case.
time_window: one year prior to one year after the LBO

description: The change in management stockholdings was measured as the difference between the ratio of the value of management-owned shares or share equivalents (sometimes referred to as 'shadow stock') to total capitalization (total debt plus total equity) one year after and one year prior to an LBO. Total capitalization was used rather than total equity since a majority of equity is swapped for debt in a leveraged buyout, and because error in estimating the correct discount rate would compound any unreliability inherent in estimating book value at the time of the buyout. The data were obtained from respondent reports of the percentages one year before and one year after the LBO; on average, mean management stockholdings increased from 14.2 to 35.7 percent after an LBO.
time_window: one year prior to one year after the LBO

description: The efficiency goals scale contained three items - profitability, profit growth, and cash flow - and measured the emphasis on efficiency goals, with the value of the scale being the mean score for all items it included. Respondents marked the importance of each performance criterion before and after the LBO was completed (1 = most important, 5 = irrelevant). Values were calculated for one year prior to an LBO and one year after it, and the change in emphasis was computed by subtracting the one-year-prior score from the one-year-after score, so a high positive result indicates that efficiency goals became more important after the buyout.
time_window: one year prior to one year after the LBO

description: The growth goals scale contained two items, sales growth and market share, with the value of the scale being the mean score for all items it included; the higher the score on this scale, the greater the importance of these criteria as goals. Respondents marked the importance of each performance criterion before and after the LBO was completed (1 = most important, 5 = irrelevant). The change in emphasis was calculated by subtracting the one-year-prior score from the one-year-after score.
time_window: one year prior to one year after the LBO

description: The change in the diversified scope of a firm was measured using a Herfindahl index of diversification, where t is the year of firm i's LBO and S is the share of firm i's total sales from the ith four-digit SIC industry group; the formula as printed is partly unreadable. The data required to calculate this measure were from the survey. Change in diversified scope was then measured as the absolute change in the value of the Herfindahl index between t-1 and t+1.
time_window: t-1 to t+1, where t is the year of the LBO

description: Two scales measured the extent of decentralization within a firm, and the value used to represent each scale was the mean score for all items it included. Operating decentralization contained seven items and strategic decentralization four items; the strategic decentralization scale captures the extent to which corporate decisions are shared with lower-level managers after an LBO. Respondents indicated the degree to which each decision was the sole responsibility of the executive office before and after the LBO (1 = always an executive office responsibility, 3 = responsibility shared with lower level managers, 5 = never an executive office responsibility). Changes in decentralization were calculated in the same way as the change in goals, with higher values indicating higher decentralization.
scale: 1 = always an executive office responsibility, 3 = responsibility shared with lower level managers, 5 = never an executive office responsibility
time_window: one year prior to one year after the LBO

description: This scale contained seven items and the value used to represent the scale was the mean score for all items it included. A negative score indicated a decrease in hierarchical complexity. Respondents were asked to recall, to the nearest percentage, the degree the organization design items had changed one year after the LBO (1 = increased by 66-100%, 4 = no change, 7 = decreased by 66-100%).
scale: 1 = increased by 66-100%, 4 = no change, 7 = decreased by 66-100%

description: Change in performance was measured by the difference between the labor productivity of a firm one year after and one year prior to its LBO. Labor productivity was measured by earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) over total labor costs, using labor costs rather than number of employees as the denominator in order to account for variations among firms' salary structures. To account for effects not captured by productivity changes, the change in return on sales (ROS), defined as EBIT/total sales, was also measured; ROS was used rather than ROI or ROE since equity is typically reduced drastically in an LBO firm. The data came from the survey.
time_window: one year prior to one year after the LBO

description: The leveraged buyout is the event that defines the sample: 450 LBOs completed between 1986 and 1989 identified from the Mergers and Acquisitions database, which defined an LBO as a merger deal with 80 percent or more of total value debt-financed. Outcomes are compared one year before and one year after the buyout.
time_window: 1986-1989 buyouts; one year before to one year after

variable_name: standard deviation among analysts' earnings forecasts
description: Industry information-processing load was measured as the standard deviation among earnings forecasts made by institutional brokers. The reported standard deviations were averaged over an industry's firms over 1976-91 to arrive at the industry standard deviation, and the 268 industries in the database were sorted in ascending order. Cutoffs of 0.53 (light) and 0.91 (heavy) standard deviations were used to form the three groups.

Market model parameters were estimated for each firm over 45 days' returns, from 60 days before the event to 15 days before it, using a value-weighted index. The abnormal return is the actual return during the event period minus the return predicted by the market model; the prediction error represents the market value impact of the announcement. The authors examined several event windows, including the standard two-day window.
time_window: 45-day estimation period from day -60 to day -15; several event windows around the announcement

description: Percentage change in salary and bonus between a past and a present year, computed using the decimal equivalent of the percentage because percentage change adjusts for salary differences across individuals; Forbes reports CEO salary in thousands of dollars. Before the regressions the variable was transformed to the arcsine of its square root so that the linear model meets the assumption of homoscedasticity.
time_window: one-year change between a past and a present year

description: Earnings per share divided by the common stockholder's equity per share. The decimal equivalent rather than the percentage was used for consistency with the dependent variable.
time_window: one-year lag in the main models

description: Net (after-tax) income divided by sales before extraordinary items; Forbes excludes extraordinary revenues that are not considered part of normal operations, such as the sale of a subsidiary business unit. Although Forbes reports net profit in percentages, the decimal equivalent was used.
time_window: one-year lag in the main models

description: Growth of earnings per share between the past and the present year, transformed to a decimal equivalent.

Orthogonal factor obtained from a factor analysis of the performance variables; its highest factor loadings are net profit, return on equity, and earnings per share. Only factors with eigenvalues greater than one were retained, and the factor scores were used as independent variables predicting salary change.

Firm performance divided by industry-median performance or by market-median performance, so that a firm performing above the median yields a value greater than one and a firm below the median yields a value lower than one or a negative value; alternatively, ordinal ranks of performance based on a firm's relative position within the sample, within an industry, or within a year. Negative industry or sample medians were handled by adjusting all affected numerators and denominators by the absolute value of the industry or sample median plus one to avoid division by zero.
time_window: concurrent, with one-year lagged performance and scale factors

description: Net sales of a firm before extraordinary revenues, reported in millions of dollars for each firm; used as the measure of firm size (scale).
time_window: one-year lag in the main models

description: Orthogonal factor obtained from a factor analysis whose highest factor loading is sales; retained because its eigenvalue exceeded one and used as an independent variable predicting salary change alongside the performance factor.

Factor score of the fourth factor from an exploratory factor analysis (principal factors method with promax rotation) of a 25-item strategy-making instrument adapted from Hart (1991), which used five-point Likert-type scales rated from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.' The factor includes items indicating established and narrowly defined strategy-making processes. CEO responses were used to represent this variable in order to minimize common method variance. Cronbach's alpha for the significant variables was .64.

Executives assessed their organization's performance over the past five years relative to competitors on three performance indexes, each measured on a seven-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1, 'low performer,' to 7, 'high performer.' The three categories were combined into a firm-level score by averaging the responses of the executives other than the CEO.

Respondents identified the variable that best described the current stage of their organizations' development, with choices including pre-start-up, start-up, accelerated growth, steady growth, stability, and decline. Averaged responses of the executives other than the CEO were used, and the averaging made it necessary to treat stage of development as an interval variable.

Three items measuring executives' perceptions of environmental dynamism on seven-point semantic differential scales anchored by descriptive phrases. Averaged responses of the executives other than the CEO were used at the firm level.

Three items relating to customer buying habits, competition, and technological requirements, each measured on a seven-point scale. Averaged responses of the executives other than the CEO were used at the firm level.

Factor score of the first factor from the exploratory factor analysis (principal factors method with promax rotation) of the 25-item strategy-making instrument with five-point Likert-type scales. The factor includes variables indicating a participative management style; two variables with significant negative loadings may be considered the obverse of participation.

Factor score of the second factor from the exploratory factor analysis (principal factors method with promax rotation) of the 25-item strategy-making instrument with five-point Likert-type scales. The factor includes variables suggesting strategy making characterized by innovation, risk taking, and entrepreneurship, plus one variable with a significant negative loading indicating an approach contrary to experimentation.

Factor score of the third factor from the exploratory factor analysis (principal factors method with promax rotation) of the 25-item strategy-making instrument with five-point Likert-type scales. The factor suggests an external orientation toward adapting to customer needs and responding to supplier feedback and environmental cues.

Each firm's distribution of performance levels for a period was tested against the group distribution of performance levels for that period using the nonparametric Kolmogorov-Smirnov two-sample test. Firms found to have statistically significantly different distributions (alpha = .05) were set aside and the process repeated until the group of firms sharing the main distribution stabilized; the excluded firms then formed the basis of a second group, and the iterative process continued until no further inclusions or exclusions could be made. The grouping was confirmed with discriminant function analysis in a confirmatory mode, with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov-derived performance groups as the grouping variable and the first two moments of the distributions, mean and variance, as the independent variables.
time_window: five-year periods spanning 1973-1991 (up to 15 distributions per firm per measure)

description: Ordinal time series analysis, a technique based on state-determined systems that can deal with missing observations caused by firms entering and going out of business, was used to compute transition matrixes and total weighted uncertainty statistics showing the frequency of shifts from one performance group to another in the next time period. The performance groups were compressed into five nonoverlapping supersets in each industry, each author independently classifying them and discrepancies being resolved by choosing the classification that minimized the Euclidean distance between group centroids. The observed transition matrixes were compared with a benchmark stable matrix by computing minimum discriminant information statistics.

ROA was collected for all firms for the years 1973 to 1991 inclusive from the COMPUSTAT PC-Plus database. It was selected because all prior research on the predictive validity of strategic groups and all five of the antecedent studies employed a measure of accounting returns, most often ROA.

Tobin's q was operationally defined as the ratio of market to book value. This ratio has been shown to be theoretically equivalent to Tobin's q as well as empirically equivalent; it has a correlation greater than .92 with all alternative measurements. The Tobin's q samples were slightly smaller across the board than the ROA samples because the measure required multiple data items.

Board power relative to the CEO was measured four ways. Separation of the CEO and board chair positions is a binary variable coded 1 if the CEO was not also chairperson. Board tenure relative to the CEO is the average tenure of the firm's directors divided by the CEO's tenure.
