Independent outside directors is the proportion of outside (nonemployee) directors appointed before the CEO began his or her tenure divided by the total number of board members. Outside directors' stock ownership is the portion of total common stock owned by outside directors. For the interaction tests, the three continuous variables (board tenure relative to CEO, independent outside directors, and outsider stock ownership) were each converted to Z-scores and summed into a single composite measure of relative board power.

Several dichotomous measures were created, each coded 1 if the existing CEO was replaced by an individual possessing a different demographic trait and 0 otherwise, for functional background, degree type (presence or absence of an advanced management degree) and educational affiliation (presence or absence of an Ivy League degree). Change in age was measured simply as the new CEO's age minus the prior CEO's age. A composite measure was coded 1 if the new and old CEOs differed across all three categorical variables (functional background, educational degree type and educational affiliation).
scale: binary (1 = different trait), except age change in years

description: Four measures of demographic similarity were constructed for each company in each year by aggregating the similarity of all CEO-board member dyads. Age similarity used an analog of the Euclidean distance measure (the coefficient of variation), and the resulting measure was converted to an indicator of similarity by subtracting each firm's coefficient from the highest value in the sample. For the categorical variables a variant of Blau's index of heterogeneity was applied, indicating the squared proportion of CEO-board dyads sharing the ith category. Continuous indicators of change in demographic similarity were created by subtracting similarity with the old CEO from similarity with the new CEO, and change in similarity across multiple dimensions was calculated by standardizing each change-in-similarity variable and summing them.

Two performance measures were used: excess stock returns, a market-based measure calculated as cumulative daily stock returns (capital gains plus dividend payouts) in excess of returns on a market portfolio of stocks with similar systematic risk, and return on assets, an operating measure. Both used the average value for the prior three years, year t-4 to year t-1 inclusive. For the interaction test the two measures were standardized by converting each to a Z-score, summed into a single composite measure, and subtracted from the highest value in the sample so that higher values reflect lower performance.
time_window: average of year t-4 to year t-1

description: A binary variable indicating successor origin, coded 1 if the new CEO was hired from outside the organization and 0 otherwise.

Three items from a scale developed and used by Jehn (1992, 1994) that loaded heavily on a single factor and produced a subscale reliability coefficient of .79. Responses were recorded on five-point, Likert-type scales. Individual responses were averaged to form the team-level variable.

Four items from a scale developed and used by Jehn (1992, 1994) that loaded heavily on a single factor and produced a subscale reliability coefficient of .86. Responses were recorded on five-point, Likert-type scales. Individual responses were averaged to form the team-level variable.
The same three cognitive conflict items were measured by survey in the smaller sample, with the same measurements taken in both samples.
The same four affective conflict items were measured by survey in the smaller sample, with the same measurements taken in both samples.

Three items asking team members to rate, on a scale ranging from 1, "poor," to 4, "excellent," the overall quality of the decision, the quality of the decision relative to its original intent, and the quality of the decision given its effect on organizational performance. The items loaded on a single factor and produced a reliability coefficient of .91. Individual responses were averaged to form the team-level variable.

Each manager was asked to allocate ten points to six different areas such as "cost control and efficiency" and "new customer/market development" to indicate how heavily those concerns influenced the decision in question. For each team, the sum of the squared differences on the six items was divided by the team's size to produce a distance score representing disagreement among members. The distance score was subtracted from a constant so that the more similarly a team's members understood their decision, the higher their understanding score.

Items adapted from Wooldridge and Floyd (1990). The responses to questions like "How much did you personally argue for the alternative that became the final decision?" and "How consistent was the final decision with your own personal priorities and interests?" were recorded on five-point scales. The items all loaded on a single factor and produced a reliability coefficient of .88.

Two items adapted from Schweiger and colleagues (1986, 1989) and Priem, Harrison, and Muir (1995). The responses to the questions "Did you enjoy working with the group on ...?" and "...reached?" were recorded on five-point scales. The items loaded on a single factor and produced a reliability coefficient of .73.

In the smaller sample the outcome data were collected verbally: each manager was read the items used to measure decision quality in the first sample and asked to respond. Transcripts were scored by a panel of three doctoral students using the same scales; interrater reliabilities averaged .93 and were averaged to produce a set of quantified responses.

In the smaller sample the outcome data were collected verbally: each manager was read the items used to measure understanding in the first sample and asked to respond. Transcripts were scored by a panel of three doctoral students using the same scales; interrater reliabilities averaged .93 and were averaged to produce quantified responses.

In the smaller sample the outcome data were collected verbally: each manager was read the items used to measure commitment in the first sample and asked to respond. Transcripts were scored by a panel of three doctoral students using the same scales; interrater reliabilities averaged .93 and were averaged to produce quantified responses.

In the smaller sample the outcome data were collected verbally: each manager was read the items used to measure affective acceptance in the first sample and asked to respond. Transcripts were scored by a panel of three doctoral students using the same scales; interrater reliabilities averaged .93 and were averaged to produce quantified responses.

Industry concentration was measured as the four-firm concentration ratio (Harrigan, 1981) for 1977, 1982, and 1987. Data were measured at the four-digit level and obtained from various volumes of the U.S. Census of Manufactures.

Capital intensity was defined as a ratio of an industry's gross book value of assets to the value of annual shipments, again for 1977, 1982, and 1987. Data on industry gross book values of assets were measured at the four-digit level and obtained from various volumes of the U.S. Census of Manufactures.

Industry growth was defined as average annual rate of growth in the value of shipments (adjusted for inflation) for the five years preceding 1977, 1982, and 1987 (Dess & Beard, 1984). Data on annual values of shipments were measured at the four-digit level and obtained from various volumes of the U.S. Census of Manufactures.

Demand instability was measured as the coefficient of variation of the annual values of shipments over the same three periods (Haleblian & Finkelstein, 1993). Data on annual values of shipments were measured at the four-digit level and obtained from various volumes of the U.S. Census of Manufactures.

Product differentiation was defined as the degree of average advertising intensity in an industry over the three five-year periods (Rajagopalan & Prescott, 1990). Advertising intensity was obtained at the three-digit level from the Troy Almanac of Key Business and Industrial Financial Ratios.

CEO firm tenure was defined as the number of years a CEO had served in a firm (Michel & Hambrick, 1992). CEO data were collected for three years, 1977, 1982, and 1987. Both the education and experience measures came from Finkelstein (1988); all four CEO characteristics were computed from data obtained from Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management and Who's Who in Finance and Industry.

CEO educational level was measured on a seven-point scale based on the highest degree earned by a CEO (1 = high school, 2 = some college, 3 = undergraduate degree, 4 = some graduate school, 5 = master's degree, 6 = attended doctoral program, and 7 = doctorate). Finkelstein (1988) was the source of the measure.

Throughput functional orientation was a continuous measure defined as the number of years spent in functional categories 1, 2, or 5 expressed as a percentage of the total number of years spent in categories 1 through 6; a CEO with a rating of 70 percent on throughput functional background would automatically be assigned a score of 30 percent on the output measure. The paper's list of functional categories is partly unreadable in the text; the readable categories are production/operations, finance/accounting, marketing and sales, and planning and general management.

CEO functional heterogeneity was defined as 1 - sum of p_i squared, where p_i was the proportion of a total career spent in each of the seven functional areas identified above (Blau & Schwartz, 1984). The higher the score on this index, the lower a CEO's functional specialization.

Drawing on a procedure suggested by Venkatraman and Ramanujam (1986), three financial measures of performance (return on sales, return on equity, and return on assets) were standardized within each firm's industry (four-digit SIC) and then averaged to create a composite measure of firm performance for each year. Three-year averages of the composite measure were used.
time_window: three-year averages for each focal period

variable_name: CEO tenure, education, throughput functional orientation, functional heterogeneity
description: CEO characteristics are four variables: firm tenure in years, educational level (seven-point scale of highest degree), throughput functional orientation (share of career in production, finance or accounting, and planning categories), and functional heterogeneity (1 minus the sum of squared career proportions across seven functional areas). Each is a separate dependent variable, collected for 1977, 1982 and 1987.

The ratio of the number of new franchised outlets established to the number of new company-owned outlets established for the period prior to the one under study; for example, to predict ten-year growth and survival, the number of franchised outlets created during the first nine years was divided by the number of company-owned outlets created in the same nine years. A constant of 0.1 was added to both the numerator and the denominator before division to ensure that a divisor of zero never occurred.
time_window: period prior to the period under study (one to nine years)

description: The logarithm of the change in the number of outlets in a system from 1983 to the year under investigation. A constant of 55 was added to all cases because some franchisors had negative growth, so that a log transformation could be calculated.
time_window: 1983 to the year under investigation (one to ten years)

description: The existence of the organization in the year under investigation. Firms were categorized as nonsurvivors in a given year if three conditions were met: they were not listed in the sources, attempts to contact them at their last known addresses or telephone numbers failed, and information about the firms did not appear in Franchise Annual or Entrepreneur Magazine.
time_window: year under investigation (one to ten years)

description: Computed by aggregating the market domain overlaps of the focal firm with all other firms in the industry. For each market m, an indicator set to one if firm i is active in market m at time t is multiplied by an indicator set to one if firm j is active in market m at time t; these contacts are summed over markets and other firms and divided by the number of markets served by the focal firm. Values were computed yearly for each airline based on the routes it operated at the start of each observation year and multiplied by 100 for rescaling.
scale: zero to the number of firms in the industry (minus one)

description: The number of firms j that contact the focal firm i in market m and that are multimarket contacts (i.e., encountered in at least one market other than m) is scaled by the number of markets firm i serves and by the number of multimarket competitors it faces on the route. Market-specific values were assigned for each airline and route in the risk set based on the routes airlines flew at the start of each observation year and multiplied by 100 for rescaling.
scale: zero to the total number of firm i's markets

description: Defined for each route as the number of airlines serving route m at the start of each year. To permit the hypothesized curvilinear effects, the variable was specified as a quadratic by including both linear and squared terms, divided by 10 for rescaling.

Defined for each route m as the maximum proportion of routes connecting to the origin and destination of that route flown by any airline at the start of each year. Its interaction with multimarket contact was included in the analysis.

Defined for each route m using the Herfindahl index for that route at the start of each year, multiplied by 100 for rescaling. The index is computed from the proportion of routes connecting to the origin and destination of route m flown by each airline i and the total number of airlines having routes connecting to that origin and destination. An interaction with multimarket contact was included in the analysis.

Modeled as the instantaneous transition rate at which an airline enters one or more new routes between t and t+dt, conditional on being at risk. Market entry was modeled as a competing risk to firm failure, and the event history of each firm was broken into yearly observations in which the firm was at risk of market entry or exit.

Modeled as the instantaneous transition rate at which an airline exits one or more current routes between t and t+dt, conditional on being at risk. Market exit was modeled as a competing risk to firm failure, with each firm's event history broken into yearly observations.

A dichotomous dummy variable for relatedness measured the traditional Rumelt way: firms classified as related take the value 1, and firms classified as unrelated or dominant take the value 0. Single-business firms were excluded from the analysis.
An SIC-based index of total diversification calculated from a firm's sales across four-digit SIC industry segments, used as an alternative traditional measure of relatedness.

A dummy variable that takes the value 1 if a firm has adopted the CM-form structure and 0 if it has not. Classification used questionnaire responses and Williamson and Bhargava's scheme, with CM-form involving centralized strategic and financial control and head-office intervention in operating decisions.
Profitability defined as return on sales. Data on ROS came from COMPUSTAT. The main regressions use ROS 1988; additional analyses report profitability for 1986, 1987, and 1988.

A firm's expenditure on media advertising expressed as a percentage of the total sales of the product lines classified to each market. It captures the importance of mass-market brand building and skills in building brands.
The proportion of product lines belonging to a given industry for which users generally purchase less than once per year. It measures the requirement for and ease of building customer relationships.
The percentage of products that pass through one or more intermediaries before reaching final users, rather than being sold directly to users by the manufacturer.
Total marketing and sales expenditures other than expenditures for media advertising, expressed as a percentage of sales. It captures the proportion of marketing effort directed toward distributors.
The proportion of highly skilled jobs in an industry as a percentage of total employment.

A scale designed for this study from themes in prior research on rationality; after coefficient alpha analysis, five items remained and items that did not correlate well with the scale were dropped (alpha = .80). Items include the degree to which decision makers collected and analyzed information and used quantitative analytic techniques. Item means were calculated across informants on each team and then averaged across items to form the scale; the scale was found to be unidimensional by principal components analysis with varimax rotation.
time_window: first interview wave, as soon as possible after the decision was made

description: A scale designed for this study; after reliability analysis four of five items remained (alpha = .66). The retained items cover the extent to which decision makers sought to maximize their own interests, had hidden agendas, and employed power and negotiation in making decisions. Item means were calculated across informants on each team and averaged across items; the scale was unidimensional and independent of procedural rationality.
time_window: first interview wave, as soon as possible after the decision was made

description: In the first interview wave informants identified objectives for the decision and allocated 100 points among them by importance, and specified complete success and complete failure for each objective to serve as scale anchors. In the second interview wave informants rated the extent to which each objective had been attained on a scale from 1 (complete failure) to 7 (complete success). Effectiveness for each informant was calculated as the weighted sum over objectives of the objective's total weight times its degree of attainment, and the decision score is the average across informants.
scale: 1-7 for each objective; anchored by complete failure and complete success specified in the first interview
time_window: objectives and weights from the first interview wave; attainment ratings from the second wave one to two years later

description: In the first interview wave informants suggested environmental factors that would influence the effectiveness of the decision, identified the best and worst realistically possible values of each factor, and allocated 100 points among the factors by importance; these weights were averaged across respondents. In the second wave informants rated how favorable each factor had been using seven-point scales anchored by the best and worst values from the first interview. The favorability score is the sum over factors of the factor's total weight times its favorability, and individual scores were averaged to form decision-level scores.
scale: 7-point response scales anchored by the best and worst values specified in the first interview
time_window: factors and weights from the first interview wave; favorability ratings from the second wave one to two years later

description: In the first interview wave informants identified issues important for implementing the decision; all issues mentioned by a team's informants were included in that team's second-wave questionnaire. Two seven-point questions were asked per issue: how well the issue had been addressed during implementation and how important the issue had been for the success of the decision. The resulting index of implementation quality weighted by importance was divided by seven to create a range consistent with the other scales, and scores were averaged across informants.
scale: 7-point response scales for quality and importance
time_window: issues from the first interview wave; quality and importance ratings from the second wave

description: Environmental instability encompasses both market and technological instability and was measured following the authors' earlier approach in Sharfman and Dean (1991). The market component replicates Dess and Beard's (1984) measure using Census of Manufactures data: value-of-shipments instability and number-of-employees instability were each calculated as the standard error of the regression slope over the years 1973-82 divided by the mean. The technological component is the average number of patents granted in the industry from 1973 through 1982. The overall score was created by standardizing and summing the components.

Equity ownership of the firm by corporate insiders, that is, its top executives and the members of their boards of directors. Ownership data were obtained from the Value Line Investment Survey. In the piecewise linear regressions the variable is partitioned into a low-end segment (below 7.5 percent) and a high-end segment (7.5 percent and above).
time_window: 1986 and 1992 (with the same measure used in the lagged analysis)

variable_name: corporate risk taking (standard deviation of analysts' forecasts of earnings per share)
description: The standard deviation of financial analysts' forecasts of earnings per share, taken as an ex ante proxy for income uncertainty. The authors note that the advantage of this measure is that it is an ex ante proxy for income uncertainty, and that management and analysts' forecasts are highly correlated. The measure reflects the uncertainty in the firm's future income stream that results from risk-taking decisions.

Equity ownership of the firm by blockholders, obtained from the Value Line Investment Survey. The variable is entered in the cross-sectional regressions both contemporaneously and lagged by two years.
time_window: 1986 and 1992 (with the same measure used in the lagged analysis)

description: Equity ownership of the firm by institutional investors, obtained from the Value Line Investment Survey. The variable is entered in the cross-sectional regressions both contemporaneously and lagged by two years.
time_window: 1986 and 1992 (with the same measure used in the lagged analysis)

description: Tobin's q, defined as the market value of a firm standardized by the replacement cost of its assets, calculated from COMPUSTAT files. It is used as a dichotomous moderator: firms with q's in excess of unity represent the group with growth opportunities, and the remaining firms (q of unity or less) comprise the group lacking profitable investment projects.
All remuneration in the form of salary and bonus, collected from annual proxy statements. The natural logarithm of cash compensation was used in the reported analyses to reduce heteroscedasticity.

The value of all long-term, contingent pay in the form of stock options, performance unit or share plans, restricted stock, and long-term management incentive plans, collected from annual proxy statements. Stock options were valued at 25 percent of their exercise price, performance plans by multiplying performance units or shares by target or actual payout values, and restricted stock by the number of shares granted times the grant-date share price; the natural logarithm was used in the reported analyses.
The sum of cash compensation and long-term compensation; the natural logarithm of total compensation was used in the reported analyses.

Number of businesses was determined for each firm by counting the number of four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes reported in Standard & Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors and Executives.

Coded 1 for firms pursuing conglomerate diversification and 0 for firms pursuing related patterns of diversification. Firms were identified as conglomerates using the Business Week and Forbes annual surveys of corporations.
A count of the number of corporate officers in each firm, obtained from Standard & Poor's Million Dollar Directory.

Annual capital equipment expenditures divided by sales, obtained from COMPUSTAT. Unlike capital intensity measures, this activity-based measure captures the magnitude of consequential, nonroutine decisions made by a top executive in the recent past.
Annual R&D expenditures divided by sales, obtained from COMPUSTAT.
Dichotomous variable with a value of 0 if the parent firm exited from the entered industry between 1982 and 1986 and 1 if it remained in the industry as of 1986. The data were derived from Trinet.

Growth over four years [(sales at t2/sales at t1)], where t2 was the year (1986) in which entrants' performance was evaluated and t1 was the first year (1982) in which the sales of the entrant businesses were available in Trinet. The data were derived from Trinet.
Market share at t2 over market share at t1. The data were derived from Trinet.

Industry asset intensity was calculated as minimum efficient scale (MES) multiplied by the cost disadvantage ratio (CDR). MES was measured as the median plant size in the industry and CDR was obtained by dividing sales per employee for plants in the third quartile by sales per employee for plants in the first quartile. The data were derived from Trinet.
Selling and distribution expenses per unit of sales in the destination industry. The data were obtained for the year 1977 from the Federal Trade Commission's Line-of-Business report.
Advertising expenditures per unit of sales in the destination industry. The data were obtained for the year 1977 from the Federal Trade Commission's Line-of-Business report.
R&D expenditures per unit of sales in the destination industry. The data were obtained for the year 1977 from the Federal Trade Commission's Line-of-Business report.
Combined market shares of the top four firms in the destination industry. The data on this variable were obtained from the Census of Manufacturers.
Dollar sales made during an entrant's first year of operations. The data were obtained from Trinet.
Industry shipments in 1982 over industry shipments in 1977. The source for these data was the Census of Manufacturers.

Measured as the absolute difference, with respect to each of advertising, R&D, and fixed asset intensity, between the firm's activity level and the activity level in the entered industry. The formula was |Firm_f - Industry_f|, where f represents functional intensity. The data used to compute functional dissimilarity variables were obtained from FTC-ALB, COMPUSTAT, and Trinet.

Computed using a modified version of the concentric diversification index: product relatedness = sum over parent industries l of (P_kl × d_il), where P_kl is the percentage of firm k's sales in industry l and d_il is a weight whose value is 2 if entered industry i and industry l are within the same three-digit SIC code, 1 if they are within the same two-digit SIC code, and 0 if they are in different two-digit SIC industries. Larger values indicate greater product relatedness. The data were obtained from Trinet.

A composite index for each headquarters-subsidiary country pair based on the deviations from one another on each of Hofstede's four cultural dimensions (individualism, masculinity, uncertainty avoidance, and power distance), using a procedure similar to one developed by Kogut and Singh. The formula corrects for the variance of each cultural dimension and averages across the four dimensions.

An index patterned after the Roth and Morrison (1992) subsidiary scale. Executives were asked to indicate the extent to which eight statements described the responsibilities of their subsidiary, using a five-point scale (1 = not at all characteristic to 5 = extremely characteristic); the responses were averaged to create an overall lateral centralization score. Internal reliability was acceptable (alpha = .90).
scale: five-point scale (1 = not at all characteristic to 5 = extremely characteristic)

description: Measured by the senior manager's commitment to headquarters using a scale adapted from Gregersen and Black (1992), which was developed from previous studies measuring organizational commitment. The internal reliability for the parent commitment scale was alpha = .83.

An aggregate agency problem index created using the three agency components (cultural distance, lateral centralization, and parent commitment). Observations scoring in the middle third were dropped to better distinguish differences between firms on the agency index.

Measured by the percentage of total senior management compensation paid through a short-term bonus plan, a long-term bonus plan, a short-term equity plan, and a long-term equity plan. The scale was based on similar measures used in the Balkin and Gomez-Mejia (1987) and Galbraith and Merrill (1991) studies and was self-reported by each subsidiary senior manager.

Measured using a scale adapted from Balkin and Gomez-Mejia (1990). For both salary and incentives, respondents were asked to rate the compensation level of their subsidiary as compared to that of competitors.

The senior management pay mix scale was modified to capture the percentage of total compensation paid by the subsidiary through incentive-based compensation forms (using the four plans detailed above) to all employees.

Respondents reported the percentage weight given to individual performance, subsidiary performance, regional performance, and corporate performance as a basis for evaluating their performance for salary adjustments. The construct was the aggregate percentage of the salary adjustment criteria given to regional and corporate performance.

An alignment, or fit, measure was calculated for the remaining firms within each agency-problem group, based on the Euclidean distance over the range of compensation components from the empirically derived ideal profile (defined by the top five performers in the high and low agency-problem groups). A significant negative correlation between the fit index and subsidiary effectiveness would support the alignment hypothesis.

A multidimensional scale with performance dimensions taken from similar measures used in studies examining business unit or profit center performance. For each of ten dimensions, respondents rated the performance of their subsidiary relative to superiors' expectations on a five-point scale ranging from 1, 'not at all satisfactory,' to 5, 'outstanding.' An average effectiveness index was created for each foreign subsidiary using the reported performance on each dimension.
scale: five-point scale (1 = not at all satisfactory to 5 = outstanding)

description: A count of the antidumping and countervailing duty petitions a firm filed against alleged unfair trade practices of foreign steel producers in a year. Unfair trade petition filings were found in the Federal Register and in U.S. International Trade Commission reports. The one escape clause petition filed over the period, by Bethlehem Steel and the United Steel Workers of America in 1984, is not included with the antidumping and countervailing duty petitions.

The extent of a firm's appearances, through its representatives, at congressional hearings on trade protection. Congressional hearings were located through the Congressional Information Services Congressional Masterfile 1 and 2, and data were subsequently obtained from the full texts of the hearings. Testimony is the second of the two forms the authors use to measure corporate political involvement.

The firm's market share in the steel industry, used as the indicator of the firm's relative size in the industry. Financial and market share data were gathered from company 10-K and annual reports. The prose does not state further details of construction.

The extent of the firm's related business diversification, entered as a firm-level strategic variable in both equations. The prose reports only that it was not statistically significant; it does not describe how the variable was constructed.

A dummy variable for the existence of a Washington, DC, lobbying office. The authors note that all of the large integrated steel firms—except, until recently, the Inland Steel Company—had Washington lobbying offices, and the smaller firms did not.

The current ratio is used as the indicator of the availability of slack resources within the firm. The prose reports that it was not statistically significant in either equation and gives no further details of construction.

variable_name: import penetration (share of imports in the U.S. market)
description: The level of import penetration into the industry, described in the prose as the share of imports in the U.S. market. Industry data were found in secondary sources, including reports from the American Iron and Steel Institute and the U.S. Department of Commerce Bureau of Economic Analysis. The authors note that domestic consumption and import penetration were measured in such a way that they were mathematically related.

variable_name: level of domestic steel demand (domestic consumption)
description: The level of domestic demand for steel products, referred to as domestic consumption and as the level of domestic steel demand. Industry data were found in secondary sources, including reports from the American Iron and Steel Institute and the U.S. Department of Commerce Bureau of Economic Analysis. The authors note that this variable and import penetration were measured in such a way that they were mathematically related, raising collinearity concerns.

Internal career opportunities referred to the extent to which a bank had an internal career ladder or internal career opportunities and was measured as the mean of four 7-point Likert-type items. Higher scores indicated the existence of a well-defined internal career and staffing system with greater opportunities. One of the items was reverse-coded before scoring.

The degree to which training, both formal and informal, was provided for employees in a job was assessed using the mean of four Likert-type items. Higher scores reflected more extensive and formalized training programs for employees.

Appraisal was defined as the degree to which performance appraisals focused on output or results measures rather than on behavioral measures and was calculated as the mean of two items. Higher values represented a greater reliance on results or output measures.

Profit sharing was measured with a single item that asked respondents the extent to which employees received bonuses based on an organization's profit. Higher responses represented a greater use of profit sharing in a bank.

Employment security was conceptualized as the degree to which an employee could expect to stay in his or her job over an extended period of time and was measured as the mean of four items. Higher scores represented a greater degree of employment security.

Employee participation, or voice, was defined as the degree to which employees were allowed to have input into their work and the degree to which the organization valued their input; it was measured as the mean of four items, with higher scores reflecting a greater amount of participation and voice.

Job description referred to the extent to which jobs were clearly and precisely defined. This measure was computed as the mean of four items and scored so that higher values reflected a higher degree of job description (more tightly defined jobs). One item was reverse-coded before scoring.

Following previous contingency interpretations of Miles and Snow's theory, the strategic contingency variable was defined as rate of product/market innovation. Innovation was measured as the mean of six Likert-type items adapted from Segev (1989), each using a seven-point Likert-type response scale. A second, larger set of strategy measures (six innovation items plus nine additional items adapted from Segev, 1989) was also collected for the configurational tests.

Return on average assets is one of two financial measures important to the banking industry used as a dependent variable. The financial measures were obtained from the Sheshunoff Bank Search database, and the measures of ROA were the year-end measures for 1992, the year in which the surveys were completed.

Return on equity is the second financial measure important to the banking industry used as a dependent variable. The financial measures were obtained from the Sheshunoff Bank Search database, and the measures of ROE were the year-end measures for 1992, the year in which the surveys were completed.

Ideal-types fit was used to test Hypothesis 3 and was operationally defined as the additive inverse of the deviation between a real organization's employment system and the ideal employment system that the organization most closely resembled. The computation of the final similarity index was restricted to the HR practice measures. The values for the ideal employment system profiles were theoretically specified and operationally defined using the profile values, with the market-type and internal systems specified as plus or minus one standard deviation from the mean of each variable.

Contingent ideal-types fit, used to test Hypothesis 4, was measured as the additive inverse of the deviation between an organization's employment system and the ideal employment system that was appropriate for the ideal strategic type most similar to the organization's strategy. The computation of the final similarity index was restricted to the HR practice measures, and the ideal strategic profiles were operationally defined as the values for each ideal type reported by Segev (1989).

Contingent hybrid-types fit, used to test Hypothesis 5, was defined as the additive inverse of the deviation between the organization's employment system and a hybrid ideal employment system most consistent with the organization's strategy. The hybrid systems are combinations of the initial ideal-type employment systems that define a continuum, and the computation of the final similarity index was restricted to the HR practice measures.

Strategic HR practices are measured by seven survey scales answered by each bank's HR contact: internal career opportunities, training, results-oriented appraisals, profit sharing, employment security, participation (voice), and job descriptions. Each is a mean of Likert-type items (profit sharing is a single item), tested individually and together.

Additive index combining the scales selective staffing, selection for technical and problem-solving skills, comprehensive training, training for technical and problem-solving skills, developmental and behavior-based performance appraisal, external equity, group incentives, skill-based pay, and salaried compensation. The additive approach means a firm can raise its index either by using more practices or by using them in a more comprehensive and widespread manner. The index's Cronbach alpha was .68.

Additive index combining the scales selection for manual and physical skills, policies and procedures training, results-based performance appraisal, individual equity, individual incentives, and hourly pay. The index's Cronbach alpha was .61.

Managers assessed their plant's current performance relative to other firms in its industry on eight items: product quality, employee morale, on-time delivery, inventory management, employee productivity, equipment utilization, production lead time, and scrap minimization. The measures were assessed in both waves of questionnaires and averaged over the two time periods (t and t + 1.5 years). Principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation produced three stable factors used as the dependent variables in the regressions.
time_window: two waves approximately 1.5 years apart, averaged

description: One of three performance factors from the factor analysis of the self-report performance items, represented by product quality and on-time delivery. Managers assessed their plant's performance on these items relative to rivals within their industry, and the items were averaged over the two survey waves.
time_window: two waves approximately 1.5 years apart, averaged

description: One of three performance factors from the factor analysis of the self-report performance items, represented by employee morale and employee productivity. Managers assessed their plant's performance on these items relative to rivals within their industry, and the items were averaged over the two survey waves.
time_window: two waves approximately 1.5 years apart, averaged

description: One of three performance factors from the factor analysis of the self-report performance items, represented by equipment utilization and scrap minimization; the authors also refer to it as equipment efficiency. Managers assessed their plant's performance on these items relative to rivals within their industry, and the items were averaged over the two survey waves.
time_window: two waves approximately 1.5 years apart, averaged

description: One of four factors from principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation of the 31 manufacturing strategy items; the cost dimension was made up of items dealing with low labor, material, and unit costs. Each strategy factor had an eigenvalue above 1.00 and a Cronbach alpha greater than .70.

One of four factors from principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation of the 31 manufacturing strategy items; it was comprised of virtually every quality-related item on the list. Two quality-related items, solving customer problems immediately and meeting customer expectations, loaded on both quality and a second factor and were not included in the scale. Each strategy factor had an eigenvalue above 1.00 and a Cronbach alpha greater than .70.

One of four factors from principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation of the 31 manufacturing strategy items; it involved releasing new products and making deliveries on time, scaling production up or down quickly, and generally being flexible. The high productivity item also loaded on this factor. Each strategy factor had an eigenvalue above 1.00 and a Cronbach alpha greater than .70.

One of four factors from principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation of the 31 manufacturing strategy items; it contained items related to adjusting product mix, handling nonstandard orders, and making products to order in small lots. Each strategy factor had an eigenvalue above 1.00 and a Cronbach alpha greater than .70.

variable_name: Human-capital-enhancing and administrative HR system indices
description: HR systems are measured by two additive indices of survey scales: a human-capital-enhancing index (selective staffing, technical skill selection, comprehensive training, developmental appraisal, group incentives, skill-based pay, and others) and an administrative index (manual skill selection, procedures training, results-based appraisal, individual incentives, hourly pay, and others). Plant managers answered the items.

variable_name: Cost, quality, delivery flexibility and scope flexibility strategy factors
description: Manufacturing strategy is measured by 31 survey items on competitive priorities. Principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation yielded four factor scales: cost, quality, delivery flexibility, and scope flexibility, each entered as a moderator.

Computed as the sum of ratings on several items coded 1 if the firm engaged in the practice and 0 if not: strategy and mission statements cited employees as a competitive advantage; a training program for employees was mentioned; an officer with responsibility for human resource management was present; full-time employees rather than temporary or contract employees were regularly used; and the firm's employee relations climate (0 for poor or satisfactory, 1 for good, 2 for excellent relations). Values on the summed variable ranged from 0 to 6. Internal reliability statistics could not be calculated because the measure is summated.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Computed by adding responses to dummy indicators: stock options for all employees, stock options for key employees and management, profit sharing for all employees, profit sharing for key employees and management, and other forms of group-based incentives (gainsharing, customized rewards) for all employees or for management. Values ranged from 0 to 5.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: All firms still in business at year-end 1993 were coded as survivors. Survival status was identified by searching an on-line database of current public firms, supplemented with Compact Disclosure and the Directory of Obsolete Securities, and by phone calls to numbers in the prospectuses. Merged firms were considered to be nonsurvivors.

The premium is the amount of the stock price that is above and beyond the book value, representing the perceived potential value of a firm. To standardize the premium across all firms it was divided by the total share price: percent price premium = (stock price - book value)/stock price.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Calculated as initial stock price over book value. Using initial stock price measured the reaction of the initial investors (primarily institutional investors) to a firm; the higher the ratio, the more the firm is valued.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Captures the number of applicants considered for each position filled by an organization for three different types of employees: those in the occupation most directly involved with the organization's primary product (core employees), those in the occupation of the respondent to the GSS, and managers. The standard scores for the logged value of these responses were averaged to form the index.

A 3-item index of the extensiveness of employee training: whether the organization had provided any formal job training in the past two years, the number of employees that had received formal training in that time period, and respondents' views on the overall effectiveness of their training programs. The measures were standardized and averaged to create the index.
scale: effectiveness item ranged from 1, "not at all effective," to 3, "highly effective"; index standardized and averaged

description: A 3-item index that reports respondents' perceptions of how important job performance is in determining the earnings of the three primary occupational groups (core employees, the respondent's occupation, and managers).
A dummy variable indicating the existence of a formal procedure for resolving disputes between employees and supervisors or co-workers.

An 8-item scale indicating the level at which important organizational decisions rest, such as hiring or performance evaluation. The variable is scaled so that the lowest value occurs if the CEO makes these decisions and higher values occur if the decisions are made by someone lower in the organization.
scale: 8-item scale, lowest value = CEO makes the decision, higher values = decisions made lower in the organization

description: A 5-item index that captures the existence of opportunities for promotion from within. For each item, response options were "yes" and "no," coded 2 and 1, respectively.
The number of occupation levels in the organization between the highest and lowest jobs, capturing the extent to which organizations are able to provide promotion opportunities.

Constructed from seven NOS items assessing respondents' perceptions of their firm's performance over the past three years relative to that of similar organizations; items concern issues such as product quality, customer satisfaction, and new product development. Answers were given on Likert scales ranging from 1, "worse," to 4, "much better."

Available only for profit-making organizations; constructed from four questions concerning respondents' perceptions of their firm's performance over the past three years relative to product market competitors, focusing on economic outcomes such as profitability and market share. Answers were given on Likert scales ranging from 1, "worse," to 4, "much better."

variable_name: number of practices above the sample median
description: A variable indicating the number of practices for which each firm was above the sample median, with a range from 0 to 7. A significant positive coefficient on this variable, with all other HRM practices controlled, would reflect the magnitude of any synergistic effect of investing widely in such practices; transformations including individual dummies and a spline function were also examined.

variable_name: interactions among the HRM practice variables
description: Moderated or interactive specifications in which the returns to one HRM practice, such as training, are allowed to vary across the level of another practice, such as staffing selectivity. Interactions were examined within each HRM practice category (employee skills, motivation, and the structure of jobs and work) and between categories; multicollinearity precluded evaluating them all simultaneously.

variable_name: announcement of an early retirement program
description: Announcements were located in four newspapers through the DIALOG system of the National Newspaper Index for 1982 through 1992; companies not publicly traded on the New York or American Stock Exchange were removed, as were first announcements that told of the results of an already completed early retirement program and those contaminated with other contemporaneous company information. The final sample included 51 announcements, and day 0 is defined as the announcement day.

A regression equation of daily stock returns against the return on a market index becomes the predictive model used to predict normal returns around announcements; the difference between the actual and the normal returns is a security's prediction error, or abnormal return. These were averaged on each day in the test interval and accumulated over various intervals to provide mean cumulative abnormal returns, and Dodd and Warner's test statistic Z was used to determine whether the CARs differed from zero. The largest reaction occurred over the interval days -5 to -2.
time_window: event windows around day 0 (notably days -5 to -2, also -20 to -1, -240 to -20, 20 to 240, and 241 to 460)

description: Each firm's income statement was examined and its profit margin (net income divided by net sales revenue) computed in the year of the early retirement program's announcement (year 0) and for two years prior to the announcement (year -2); the change in the profit margin from years -2 to 0 was also used.

variable_name: abnormal stock returns in the year preceding the announcement
description: Abnormal stock returns measured over the period days -240 to -20 relative to the announcement; thirty of the 51 firms experienced negative CARs during this period, and the measure rests on the assumption that poor prior financial performance will negatively affect a firm's stock prices.

The collected news stories were examined for the stated reasons for the early retirement programs, yielding two major categories, cost cutting and reorienting; 31 of the firms specifically indicated cost cutting as their motive. In some statistical tests a dummy variable taking the value of 1 when a firm stated cost cutting as a motive was included.

The institutional rationale was also tested by dividing the sample into two equal groups based on announcement timing: half of the sample announced the programs prior to January 30, 1987, and half announced them later. Firms announcing in a good economic climate may be demonstrating a commitment to growth, whereas those announcing in a poor climate may be making short-sighted attempts to cut costs.

variable_name: percentage of employees eligible for an announced program
description: A variable measuring the percentage of employees eligible for an announced early retirement program was included to test Hypothesis 3. The average percentage of eligible employees was 2.93 percent, but the statistic ranged from small programs that rounded to 0 percent up to those including 33 percent of a firm's employees.

Each of eleven bank asset strategy variables, measured as a proportion of total assets, was compared to the industry mean value for that variable and expressed as a standard deviation. The absolute values of the standard deviations for all the strategy variables were totaled for each bank, giving a holistic measure of deviation, and the total was multiplied by -1 to create a scale on which more positive numbers indicate greater conformity.

Regulators assess a bank's financial capital position by classifying it into three ordered discrete categories on the basis of capital ratios and categories specified by regulatory agencies; banks in lower categories are not fully endorsed and are subject to increased regulatory scrutiny. From 1985 through 1988 they used the total capital ratio. The variable is coded (0, 1, 2), with fully endorsed banks having the highest coding (2).

A dichotomous variable built from the record of on-site examination enforcement actions obtained from LEXIS; enforcement actions require the bank to take certain actions such as curtailing lending to a certain industry or firing top management. Banks not subject to an enforcement action during a year were given a rating of 0; banks under an enforcement action were given a -1.

Recording units, each comprising an individual bank in a single article, were rated as endorsing or challenging the subject bank's legitimacy. The Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance was used to create annual measures of public endorsement for each bank, measuring the relative proportions of endorsing and challenging recording units for each bank in a year. The measure has a meaningful zero point when there are equal numbers of endorsing and challenging recording units and is bounded by 1 and -1.

Acquisition intensity was operationally defined using two indicators: the number of acquisitions completed and the percentage of sales acquired. The number of acquisitions was the total number of business units acquired during the restructuring period; the percentage of sales acquired was the acquisition price of the unit divided by the acquiring firm's total sales during the previous year, summed over the years the firm acquired businesses.
time_window: first three years of the study period beginning with the onset of restructuring through 1991

description: Divestiture intensity was defined using two indicators: the number of divestitures made and the percentage of sales divested. Number of divestitures was the total number of business units sold through sell-offs, buyouts, or equity carve outs, or spun off, during restructuring; the percentage of sales divested was the sales price of a sold unit divided by its total sales for the previous year, summed over the years a firm restructured. In the absence of a publicly reported price, the unit's prior-year sales were used as a proxy for the price.
time_window: first three years of the study period beginning with the onset of restructuring through 1991

description: Strategic controls used by top management to process external and internal information in order to evaluate business unit strategy and allocate resources were measured with three survey items indicating emphasis on using strategic controls in evaluating division managers' strategies and performance on a seven-point Likert scale. The coefficient alpha for this scale was .72.

The financial control factor was composed of four items modified from a scale reported in Hill and colleagues (1992), assessing the importance of financial control measures and procedures in evaluating divisional managers' performance on a seven-point Likert scale. The coefficient alpha for this scale was .70.

External innovation was composed of three items from the survey instrument asking to what extent a firm had made external acquisitions of new products, external acquisitions to develop new processes, and external acquisitions to build new markets. These three items describe the importance of external innovation to the firm on a seven-point Likert scale; the coefficient alpha was .73.

Internal innovation was defined with two variables measuring different dimensions of the construct: firm R&D intensity and new product intensity. R&D intensity was a firm's reported R&D expenditure per $1,000 of sales. New product data came from Dialog's PTS New Product Announcements database, scanned for 1991-92 to obtain the number of new products introduced; the mean number of new product announcements over the two years was divided by mean annual firm sales to adjust for size effects, a variable referred to as new product intensity.
time_window: internal innovation data collected in the period 1991-92

variable_name: difference between realized market share and expected share (attraction model residual)
description: Realized market share and a firm's price vector in each technology generation were used to estimate expected share with an attraction model, which produces share estimates bounded by 0 and 1 that sum to 1. Brand dummies were included for ten firms that consistently had high market shares over the ten years studied. The dependent variable is the difference between a firm's predicted market share in each year and its realized market share, which may be positive or negative; the bigger the difference, the greater the share that cannot be explained through relative pricing alone.

A counter that began at 0 the year any firm introduced a new microprocessor. The counter was increased by 1 for every year that a firm produced microcomputers but offered none of the latest generation, and it was reset to 0 each time a new generation of microprocessors appeared.
The portion of other firms in a firm's niche whose most advanced computer was at least one technology generation older than the focal firm's.
The portion of other firms in a firm's niche that offered a model from a newer generation than the focal firm's.

Simple euclidean distance, summing the difference between a firm's vector in the ten-dimensional market space used in clustering and that of each other firm. For the test of Hypothesis 4, differentiation within a niche was defined as the Z-score of distance from each firm to the others in its niche.
The Z-score of all distances among each firm and all others outside its niche, based on the cluster variables.

A dichotomous dummy variable. Any firm that was not in the same niche cluster in year t - 1 and year t was considered to have switched niches in year t, either because the niche continued but the firm moved to another one, or because the niche in year t did not continue into year t + 1. Each firm is assigned the value 0 (no switching) in its first year of shipping.
time_window: year t relative to year t - 1

description: A counter equal to 1 at initial entry or in any year in which the firm switches niches, incremented each year that the firm's niche in year t equals its niche in year t - 1.
A simple count of the number of other firms in each firm's niche.

For each niche in each year, the ratio between demand among all firms in the niche and the number of firms occupying the niche (demand per firm within the niche), divided by the same number for the previous year. A missing value was substituted for the first year in the study, so the measure captures year-to-year growth in per-firm demand within a niche.
time_window: year t relative to year t - 1

description: For each niche, the number of firms that had been in the niche in both year t and year t - 1 divided by the number of firms in the same niche in year t.
time_window: year t relative to year t - 1

description: The number of firms in the market outside a given firm's niche. This is a measure of marketwide competition and complements niche density.

variable_name: organizational source (new entrant vs. former sponsor)
description: Firms were classified by whether they had previously introduced an original microprocessor design: new entrants versus former sponsors. The average number of new designs introduced by new entrants per year over the period was compared with the average number introduced by former sponsors, using a t-test for difference in means.

Firms in the industry introduced a total of 38 different designs over the study period; all but 8 of these were introduced by new sponsors. The number of designs and the number of sponsors were tracked over the time period of the study.

variable_name: density of design communities / density of sponsor communities
description: The density of design communities was operationally defined as the number of designs currently in the market, and the density of sponsor communities was measured as the number of sponsors in the market; both were updated quarterly. The linear and squared terms of these densities were entered in the event-count models.
time_window: measured one quarter before the dependent variable

variable_name: count of the number of sponsors entering in each quarter
description: The dependent variable was defined as a count of the number of sponsors entering in each quarter, because new sponsors will have no market history. Entries were defined as occurring when a firm first put a product into production.

For design communities, the number of second sources copying each design was determined and then summed across all designs to compute the number of second sources supporting design communities. For sponsor communities, the number of second sources copying any of the designs of each sponsor was determined and summed across all sponsors.

Following Tushman and Anderson (1986), a dummy variable was coded one after a single technological community achieved a 50 percent or greater market share, and zero otherwise. In this market, Intel captured 50 percent of the market in the first quarter of 1984, largely because of the success of the IBM personal computer. The measure was derived from the community sales figures and was included in models estimated over 1971-1989.
scale: 0/1 (one after a community reaches 50 percent market share)

variable_name: market share of the largest community
description: The market share of the largest community was computed as a calculation akin to a one-firm concentration ratio, and was computed separately for communities defined by sponsor and those defined by design. Models using this concentration measure were estimated from 1984 onward, the point at which the Intel community captured 50 percent of the market.

Because of the relatively low number of events, Hypothesis 5 was tested in two parts: a dummy variable indicating that one community captured over 50 percent of the market's sales was inserted into the model, and the sponsors entering the market after 1984, the year that Intel-compatible processors captured 50 percent of the market, were then qualitatively examined to determine if most of them were specialists. All 11 of the new entrants' processors were specialized, serving the segment of the market in which performance had the highest priority.

The density, that is the number of brewing firms in the population, in the year in which the organization was founded. Density in any given year was calculated from the event-history data as the numbers of foundings and deaths. In the breweries analysis the highest and mean observed densities at founding were 2,726 and 346, and the implied mortality multipliers of organizations born in those periods are compared.

The density, that is the number of newspapers in the population, in the year in which the organization was founded, derived from the event-history data on foundings and deaths. In the newspaper analysis the highest and mean observed densities at founding were 125 and 44, and the implied mortality multipliers of organizations born in those periods are compared.

Competitive intensity at founding was calculated as the aggregate age of all competitors in the industry in the year of founding. The highest and mean competitive intensity periods are described as 46,168 organization-years and 5,978 organization-years respectively.

Competitive intensity at founding was calculated by summing the ages of all competing newspapers in the year of founding. The highest and mean competitive intensity environments are described as 1,280 organization-years and 280 organization-years respectively.

Following Carroll and his collaborators, a dummy variable for years of political turmoil was included in the mortality models for newspaper organizations. In the analysis of founding conditions, organizations are distinguished by whether they were founded in periods of political turmoil.

The instantaneous death rate of the ith organization at age t, modeled with Makeham's law, which contains three vectors: the beta vector associated with the initial mortality rate, the alpha vector associated with the asymptotic mortality rate, and the gamma vector measuring the speed with which the asymptotic death rate is reached. The printed equation is garbled in the text; founding conditions enter the model through these vectors. Each organization's life history was divided into a series of annual spells, with all but the last spell treated as right-censored, and organizations still alive at the end of the observation period were censored on the right.

The instantaneous death rate at organizational age t, modeled with Makeham's law, whose beta vector is associated with the initial mortality rate, alpha vector with the asymptotic mortality rate, and gamma vector with the speed at which the asymptotic death rate is reached. Life histories were divided into annual spells and treated as right-censored except for the final spell.

The age of the organization, that is, the time elapsed since founding, updated at the beginning of each year. Time-varying covariates such as age were assumed to change as annual step functions and to be constant within years. Observed organizational ages in the American brewery population varied from 0.5 to 133 years.

The age of the organization, that is, the time elapsed since founding, updated at the beginning of each year and assumed to be constant within years. Observed organizational ages in the Argentine newspaper population varied from 0.5 to 61 years.

variable_name: density, competitive intensity and political turmoil at founding
description: Adverse founding conditions were indexed by three conditions in the year of founding: organizational density (number of firms in the population), competitive intensity (aggregate age of competitors), and, for the newspaper population, a political turmoil dummy. Each enters the Makeham mortality model as a founding-condition covariate for the brewery and newspaper populations.

The aggregate of the organizational niche overlaps of the focal organization with those of all other members of its population, computed yearly for each organizational niche by profit orientation using Equation 1 and the organizational niche overlap weights from Table 2. Organizational niches are defined by the ages of children a center is licensed to enroll and by profit status. Local measures were computed from DCCs operating in each of the six cities and diffuse measures from DCCs operating in all the other cities.
level: organizational niche by city by year

description: The aggregate of the resource nonoverlaps, the number of organizations whose resource requirements do not overlap with those of the focal organization. It is computed as the number of DCCs in the sector minus overlap density. Local and diffuse versions were computed from the geographic locations of DCCs, as for overlap density.
level: organizational niche by city by year

description: Computed yearly for each organizational niche by profit orientation using Equation 3 and the organizational niche nonoverlap/overlap ratios from Table 3. It is the sum of an organization's ratios of organizational niche nonoverlap to overlap with all other potentially competing population members, i.e., those whose niche overlap with the focal niche is more than zero. Local and diffuse versions were computed from the geographic locations of DCCs.
level: organizational niche by city by year

description: The number of purchase-of-service agreements between day care centers and the Children's Services Division of Metropolitan Toronto, a government agency with a metropolitan jurisdiction, counted at the start of each year as reported in either the Day Nurseries Information System or the Directory and computed separately for nonprofit and for-profit DCCs. To test the predicted inverted U-shaped effect, the measure was modeled as a quadratic by including both relational density and relational density squared, with the squared term divided by 1,000. Local and diffuse versions were computed from DCCs' geographic locations.
level: organizational niche by city by year
time_window: measured at the start of each year

description: The number of site-sharing arrangements, which permit a day care center to operate within the physical facilities of another legitimated community organization such as a community center, public school, or church, counted at the start of each year and computed separately for nonprofit and for-profit DCCs. For the predicted inverted U-shaped effect the measure was modeled as a quadratic, with the squared term divided by 1,000. Local and diffuse versions were computed from DCCs' geographic locations.
level: organizational niche by city by year
time_window: measured at the start of each year

description: The dependent variable is the yearly numbers of nonprofit and for-profit DCC foundings that occurred in each organizational niche in each of Metropolitan Toronto's six constituent cities. Date of founding is defined as the year in which the Ministry issued the original operating license or the year of first appearance in the Directory.
level: organizational niche by city by year

description: Day care centers' organizational niches are described using their license specifications and profit status; centers are classified as nonprofit or for-profit, and the density, founding, and relational density measures were computed separately for the nonprofit and for-profit sectors. Founding counts are reported separately for the two sectors.

The first of three factors (five items, alpha = .76) obtained from a varimax-rotated factor analysis of 14 survey items on corporate entrepreneurship; executives rated their firms' actual, rather than preferred, entrepreneurial activities on a five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). The items covered the creation and introduction of products, emphasis on R&D investments, and commitment to patenting.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: The second factor (five items, alpha = .70) from the varimax-rotated factor analysis of the corporate entrepreneurship items, capturing a firm's venturing activities such as entry into new business fields by sponsoring new ventures and creating new businesses. Rated by executives on the same five-point actual-activity scale.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: The third factor (four items, alpha = .73) from the varimax-rotated factor analysis of the corporate entrepreneurship items, covering strategic renewal efforts aimed at revitalizing a company's ability to compete and redefining its business domain by eliminating unprofitable operations while improving internal efficiencies. Rated by executives on the same five-point actual-activity scale.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: The number of outside directors divided by the total number of directors on a board, averaged over the 1988-90 period. Directors were considered outsiders when they were not former employees (officers) of a firm or its subsidiaries (divisions), did not possess contractual relationships with it, or were not associated with a major supplier to the company.
The sum of outsiders' equity divided by a company's common shares, averaged over the 1988-90 period.

The percentage of a company's total stock held by its senior executives, defined as vice presidents and those in higher offices, averaged over the 1988-90 period. Data were available for only 127 companies.
The percentage of a company's stock held by long-term institutional investors, a group that included mutual, pension, and retirement funds, averaged over the 1988-90 period.
The percentage of a company's stock held by short-term institutional owners, a group that covered investment bankers and private funds, averaged over the 1988-90 period.

A four-item survey index (alpha = .71) for which respondents were asked to focus on their firm's major industry over the three-year period before data collection. The items followed a five-point response format (5 = strongly agree, 1 = strongly disagree) and the average score on the items was entered into the regression analyses.
scale: five-point response format (5 = strongly agree, 1 = strongly disagree)

description: Corporate entrepreneurship was measured with a 14-item executive survey rated on five-point scales. Factor analysis gave three factors: innovation (5 items, alpha .76), venturing (5 items, alpha .70) and strategic renewal (4 items, alpha .73), which were used as the dependent variables.

Number of years a venture persisted. Following earlier research, the authors used longevity as the dependent (independent) variable, arguing that although it is not a perfect performance measure, previous studies have shown it provides the best estimate of managers' perceptions of the success of an expansion and that it correlates with financial performance.
Measured as the number of previous international wholly owned subsidiaries a firm had had by the time of a new affiliate's founding.
level: firm (at the time of a new affiliate's founding)

description: Measured as the number of previous domestic joint ventures a firm had had by the time of a new affiliate's founding.
level: firm (at the time of a new affiliate's founding)

description: Measured as the number of previous international joint ventures a firm had had by the time of a new affiliate's founding.
level: firm (at the time of a new affiliate's founding)

description: Measured with Kogut and Singh's (1988) index, an aggregate of the four dimensions of culture outlined in Hofstede (1980). The index is an arithmetic average of the deviations of each country from the index of the Netherlands along Hofstede's four cultural dimensions, divided by the variance of the index for the dimension.
level: host country relative to the Netherlands

description: Two multiple-item scales (r = .57) derived from Terpstra and Simonin's (1993) taxonomy of strategic alliances. The first manifest variable, Y1, represents the level of experience with five different structural collaborative forms, rated on a seven-point scale for each form, and is computed as the mean of all these ratings. The second, Y2, represents the level of collaborative experience with ten different functional collaborative modes across the value chain, rated on similar scales, and is the mean of these ratings.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = not at all, 4 = moderate, 7 = a great deal)

description: Five factor scores (alpha = .82) capture the essence of this complex and multifaceted construct. A factor analysis with the maximum-likelihood extraction method and direct oblimin rotation was performed on a set of 20 measures corresponding to the assessed level of corporate expertise with each listed aspect of collaborative know-how on a seven-point Likert-type scale. The analysis generated five factors with eigenvalues greater than 1.0 that accounted for more than 70 percent of the total variance, and additive factor scores were computed for each observation to obtain the five manifest variables.

A set of three items (alpha = .87) capturing the extent to which the alliance under consideration contributed to a variety of tangible benefits: generating profits for the parent company, improving market share, and sustaining competitive advantage. All values were recorded on a seven-point perceptual scale (1 = not at all, 4 = moderate, 7 = a great deal).
scale: seven-point perceptual scale (1 = not at all, 4 = moderate, 7 = a great deal)

description: Three single-item scales (alpha = .75) measuring intangible collaborative benefits related to learning issues: learning about interfirm cooperation, learning specific skills and competencies held by the partner, and learning skills and competencies independent of the partner. The format follows the construct previously described for tangible benefits.
The number of countries in which the firm had established subsidiaries at the time of the expansion. It is a count measure of the diversity of the national settings in which the firm operates.
time_window: at the time of the expansion

description: The number of three-digit Standaard Bedrijfs Indeling (SBI) codes in which the firm was active at the time of the expansion. A squared term of this count measure was also entered in the models to capture the curvilinear relationship.
time_window: at the time of the expansion

description: A venture was called an acquisition if it entailed the takeover of another company (or one of its business units) in which the Dutch firm did not previously have an ownership stake. It was called a start-up if it was a subsidiary newly established by the Dutch firm, alone or with one or more partners. In the models, start-up is coded 1.

An expansion was coded as horizontal if it took place within the same three-digit SBI category as the core activities of the firm, as related if it took place within the same two-digit SBI category but not in the same three-digit category, as vertical if it took place within the firm's value-added chain, and as unrelated if none of the other three categories applied. Three dummy variables for horizontal, related, and vertical expansions were entered in the models, with unrelated as the omitted category.
time_window: at the time of the expansion

description: A variation of Sullivan's (1994) composite measure that gauges internationalization on three theoretically distinct dimensions. The first dimension, foreign sales, is the ratio of foreign sales to total sales; the second, foreign production, is foreign assets expressed as a percentage of total assets; the third, geographic dispersion, is the number of countries in which a firm had subsidiaries expressed as a percentage of the highest number of countries with subsidiaries represented in the sample. The three variables were summed to form the composite measure, which has a theoretical range of 0 to 3 and demonstrated high interitem reliability (alpha of .86) and loaded on one factor.

The proportion of total compensation paid in long-term forms (e.g., stock options, restricted stock, and long-term incentive plans), calculated as long-term compensation divided by total compensation. Long-term forms of compensation were valued at the present value provided by a company in its proxy statement. Stock options were valued using the SEC method, in which the potential value of stock options is estimated by subtracting the option grant price from the estimated stock price in ten years and discounting this difference at 5 percent per year to the present year.
The logarithm of the total of all forms of compensation granted to the CEO during 1992.
