A dummy variable indicating whether a CEO also occupied the position of chairperson of the board (1 = yes). Duality signified that one individual occupied both positions.

Two measures were used to gauge the robustness of TMT size effects. First, TMT size was measured as the count of the total number of officers in a firm. Second, executive team size was measured as the number of executives who were in the top two tiers of executive management. The top tier was defined as a firm's chairman, vice chairman, CEO, president, chief operating officer, and chief financial officer; the second tier was defined as those executives holding the next highest titles (e.g., executive vice presidents or vice presidents).
The number of members of a board of directors.

The proportion of board members who were outsiders, where insiders were executives of a firm who also served on the board of directors and outsiders were board members not otherwise employed by the firm.
Measured as the total number of colleges in a focal college's consortium. Time-varying over the 1971-86 study period. Independent variables were lagged four years relative to the adoption event.
The standard deviation of the enrollments of the colleges in an association. One of two time-varying measures capturing heterogeneity within a consortium.
The standard deviation in the tuition charges of the colleges in an association. One of two time-varying measures capturing heterogeneity within a consortium.
Measured as the time since a consortium's founding. In the few cases where colleges entered a consortium after its founding, time spent in the consortium was used to measure age.

Inferred when a college granted, for the first time, a bachelor's degree in any of five broad curricular areas. The authors examined first-time adoption of any of the five programs and also modeled adoption of each program separately.

The number of colleges in an association that had previously adopted a specific program (e.g., business), used to predict the subsequent adoption of that program by a focal college. In the model of first-time adoption of any program, the variable contained the number of colleges in an association that had previously adopted any of the five programs. Several independent variables were logarithmically transformed because of skewed distributions.

The mean enrollment of other colleges within an association that had previously adopted a particular program, used as a measure of adopters' size. Logarithmically transformed because of skewed distribution.

The prestige of earlier adopters was measured in terms of their mean score on a recognized annual reputational ranking, specifically adopters' average scores on Cass and Birnbaum's (1971) selectivity index.

The mean percentage of their total degrees that previous adopters granted in the program in question. Popularity of a new program (its ability to attract students) is described as one of the clearest measures of its effectiveness as an adaptive response. Time-varying.

Previous adopters' total first-time freshmen divided by total enrollment. New enrollment growth is described as at least a partial function of the type of curricula a college offers and a central strategic concern of small college administrators. Time-varying.

Adopters' total degrees granted divided by total enrollment. Retention is described as an outcome of great concern to small college administrators and strongly affected by the curriculum offered. Time-varying.

Similarity was calculated by (1) creating a vector of difference scores between the focal organization and previous adopters, (2) transforming these differences into absolute values, and (3) taking the mean of these absolute differences. Time-varying.

Similarity was calculated by (1) creating a vector of difference scores between the focal organization and previous adopters, (2) transforming these differences into absolute values, and (3) taking the mean of these absolute differences. Time-varying.
scale: mean absolute difference in tuition charges

variable_name: performance below aspiration level, or budget deficit
description: An indicator variable set when a focal college suffered a budget deficit in a given year, that is, when total expenditures exceeded total revenues. The authors argue the deficit-surplus line is a reasonable threshold for nonprofit colleges. To test the implied interaction, a series of interaction terms was created as the product of the deficit indicator and the number of previous adopters (number of adopters by budget deficit).

A competitor-dyad-specific measure summing over markets (routes) in the set of markets served by firms i and j the product of the centralities of route m to each airline's network and indicator variables set equal to 1 if the airline is active in route m at time t and 0 otherwise. Route centrality is defined as the proportion of an airline's routes that connected with route m. For CACs that met each other in one or no routes, multimarket contact equals 0; more generally, the higher the value, the higher the level of multimarket contact.

Dichotomous dependent variable coded 0 for each firm in a dyad prior to initiation of multimarket contact. If a firm acted to initiate multimarket contact, the variable was coded 1 for that firm and remained 0 for the other; if both firms acted to create multimarket contact at the same time, it was coded 1 for both. Once a dyad had established multimarket contact, it left the risk set for initiation.

Dichotomous repeatable-event dependent variable coded 0 for firms i and j in all dyads having already established multimarket contact. If a firm acted to increase the number of market contacts in a dyad, the variable was coded 1 for that firm and left 0 for the other; if both firms acted simultaneously, it was coded 1 for both. Dyads remained in the risk set unless the firms served identical markets or severed their multimarket contact.
Airline i's (competitor j's) number of routes was defined as the total number of markets an airline served at the start of each observation year.

Airline i's (competitor j's) entries into competitor j's (airline i's) routes were defined as occurring in the first year an airline was reported in the OAG as flying one of a given competitor's incumbent routes.
time_window: first year of entry, updated annually

description: Airline i's (competitor j's) average route capacity was defined as the average size of the human population residing at the origin and destination (county or district) of airline i's routes at the start of each observation year, based on the 1980 Census of Population.

Measured as the total available-seat-miles flown by airline j in the prior year, logged to normalize the distribution. Available-seat-miles is an input measure of airline operations, the total number of seat-miles it is possible for an airline to sell.

Airline operational performance was measured on a yearly basis using competitor j's passenger load factor, that is, revenue-passenger-miles divided by available-seat-miles. Revenue-passenger-miles, an output measure, is the funds an airline generates selling tickets.

variable_name: average multimarket contact in other dyads
description: The average multimarket contact in other competitor dyads at the start of each year, that is, average multimarket contact in dyads not involving either airline i or competitor j. This variable reflects the extent to which frequency-based copying of other competitors' multimarket contact motivates initiation and expansion of multimarket contact.

variable_name: average multimarket contact by large (small) airlines in other dyads
description: The average multimarket contact for large (small) firms in other dyads at the start of each year. Large (small) firms were defined as those above (below) the mean total available-seat-miles flown by all CACs in the prior year.
time_window: start of each year; firm size from the prior year

variable_name: average multimarket contact by high-performing (low-performing) airlines in other dyads
description: The average multimarket contact for high-performing (low-performing) firms in other dyads at the start of each year. High-performing (low-performing) firms were those above (below) the mean passenger load factor (revenue-passenger-miles divided by available-seat-miles) for all CACs in the prior year.
time_window: start of each year; performance from the prior year

variable_name: average MMC by airline i with competitors other than j
description: Airline i's average multimarket contact in all its dyads with competitors other than j, based on the routes airline i flew at the start of each year. Support for the experiential-learning hypotheses required positive coefficients for this variable.

variable_name: interaction of average MMC by airline i with competitors other than j and average MMC by competitor j with airlines other than i
description: The interaction of average multimarket contact by airline i with competitors other than j and average multimarket contact by competitor j with airlines other than i, defined analogously. Positive coefficients for this interaction term would signify higher rates of initiating (expanding) multimarket contact when both i and j have greater experience with multimarket contact through their other competitive relationships. The main effect of average multimarket contact by competitor j had to be included to obtain an unbiased estimate of the interaction.

A dummy variable indicating whether a firm had expanded outside the United States during the period 1989 through 1993, coded 0 for no and 1 for yes. Data were gathered from texts and tables in annual reports and 10-Ks.

A four-item scale drawn from an expert panel survey, preceded by the stem "Comparing this company to all other food service operations". The items ask how long it would take to train competent assistant managers, how long it would take to train competent hourly employees, how difficult it would be to communicate job requirements to unit-level managers, and how difficult it would be to include all of the unit manager's job tasks in an operations manual. Seven-point Likert response formats were used. Alpha equaled .86.
level: firm (ratings by expert panelists, average number of ratings per chain 9.3)
time_window: survey constructed in 1994, assumed to portray conditions in 1989

description: A four-item scale drawn from the expert panel survey, preceded by the stem "Comparing this company to all other food service operations". The items ask how difficult it would be to use the company's kitchen equipment for another food service format, how difficult it would be to use the company's dining room decor for another food service format, how difficult it would be to convert an average unit's building and grounds to another type of business, and how customized the kitchen equipment is for the company. Items had seven-point Likert response formats with anchors comparable to those for specific knowledge. Alpha equaled .85.
time_window: survey constructed in 1994, assumed to portray conditions in 1989

description: An indicator of the firm's ability to raise capital in equity markets: when investors share optimism concerning a firm's future, share prices are bid up, making capital easier to raise. Measured in 1989 and obtained through Compact Disclosure. A negative relationship with expansion through franchising was expected.

As debt rises, a firm's ability to meet its financial obligations is reduced and debt financing becomes increasingly expensive and difficult to locate, so a positive relationship with expansion through franchising was expected. Measured in 1989 and obtained through Compact Disclosure.

Access to liquid capital measured by dividing the sum of cash and marketable securities by the number of outlets in a chain. If a firm holds deposits of cash and securities that are large relative to its size, it is less likely to suffer from capital scarcity, so a negative relationship with expansion through franchising was expected. Measured in 1989 and obtained through Compact Disclosure.

Return on assets used to assess financial performance, with the average ROA during 1988 and 1989 used to guard against one-year outlier performances. Strong financial performance should reduce the need for capital from franchisees, so a negative relationship with expansion through franchising was expected. Obtained through Compact Disclosure.

The relative importance of franchising and company ownership, computed as the percentage of total growth achieved through franchising. The printed equation is garbled in the text, but the result of the equation is the percentage of total growth achieved through franchising. Only activity between 1989 and 1993 was included, and data were gathered from texts and tables in annual reports and 10-Ks.

The dependent measure was computed as the number of new franchised outlets divided by the sum of new franchised outlets plus new company-owned outlets over the 1989-1993 period; the printed equation in the text is garbled, and the authors state that the result of this equation will be the percentage of total growth achieved through franchising.

The set of markets served by a focal firm except the focal market was divided into those with strong resource-sharing opportunities with the focal market and those with weak resource-sharing opportunities. The number of markets in the strong subset is markets served (strong resource sharing) and the number in the weak subset is markets served (weak resource sharing); the difference in the effects of these two variables reflects the impact of strong versus weak resource-sharing opportunities.

Following prior research, a count measure of multimarket contact was used. For a focal airline route, the number of markets in which the airline met a specific rival outside the focal market was first counted. Since a focal market-unit can meet multiple focal-market rivals, the variable was computed as the average number of multimarket contacts with all focal-market rivals (e.g., rivals met in 100 and 300 other markets give a measure of 200).

Efficiency was measured as cost per revenue-passenger-mile, the cost of flying a paying passenger in a given airline route divided by the distance between the endpoint cities, stated in cents per mile. Because airlines do not report actual costs per revenue-passenger-mile for each route, the value was constructed as the product of cost per available-seat-mile and the inverse of the route load factor; airline-route load factor was calculated from the load factors of the segments used, and route cost per available-seat-mile was estimated from firm-level and route-level data following Brander and Zhang.

Yield was used to capture lack of rivalry and was defined as revenue per revenue-passenger-mile, the average price paid by customers in an airline route divided by the distance between the endpoint cities, stated in cents per mile. Higher yields reflect less intense rivalry, so the variable is reversed relative to the intensity-of-rivalry construct.

Airlines report profitability only at the airline level, so the Lerner index was constructed at the airline-route level from yield (price per revenue-passenger-mile) and cost per revenue-passenger-mile. The Lerner index, a popular measure of economic performance in industrial economics, is the price-cost margin divided by the price. The authors note it is equivalent to return on sales, and the sales-weighted average of the index across an airline's routes correlated .90 with firm-level ROS.

variable_name: rivals' noncontact markets served (strong resource sharing)
description: The number of markets served by focal-market rivals but not by the focal firm was divided into those with strong resource-sharing opportunities with the focal market and those with weak opportunities. Rivals' noncontact markets served (strong resource sharing) captured the number of markets in the strong subset and rivals' noncontact markets served (weak resource sharing) the number in the weak subset; the effect was evaluated from the difference in the effects of these two measures. Variables for a given rival were first computed and then averaged across all focal-market rivals.

Each docket sheet contained numerical codes indicating what a dispute was about (for instance, breach of fiduciary duty, inspection of books and records, rightful board of directors); the authors counted the number of different codes to determine the number of issues in dispute.

The authors recorded the date of the filing of a complaint and the date of the resolution of the dispute (the date of the chancellor's deciding opinion for Chancery-decided cases, the date listed on the voluntary settlement for settled cases) and subtracted the filing date from the resolution date. Because there were large variations, the measure was logarithmically transformed for hypothesis testing.

The docket sheets included separate entries listing the attorneys for the plaintiffs and defendants, each lawyer listed by a four-digit number; the authors counted the number of codes to determine the number of lawyers involved for each disputant.
The number of lawyer codes listed on the docket sheet as representing the defendant in the dispute.

The type of settlement was coded as a Chancery decision or a voluntary settlement. The first was coded when the final document in the case was a memorandum opinion from the chancellor; the second when the final document noted a 'stipulation among the parties for dismissal.'

variable_name: plaintiff documents and defendant documents scales
description: All docket entries were sorted into three mutually exclusive piles representing the Chancery, the plaintiff, and the defendant. The authors counted the number of docket entries made by each disputant and measured the height of the paper piles; because the number and the height of docket entries were highly correlated, the two measures were standardized and summed into plaintiff documents and defendant documents scales, regarded as absolute measures of corporate voice or expression.

The proportion of docket entries relative to the total number of docket entries made in the case by the disputants and the proportion of the height of the docket entries relative to the total height of paper, both coded from the perspective of the plaintiff so that a higher number indicated a larger proportion of the documentation came from the plaintiff. The two proportional measures were arc-sine transformed and averaged to obtain the plaintiff proportion of documents.

The coding was drawn from court documents: for Chancery decisions the docket sheet included a synopsis of the chancellor's opinion, and the opinion was read when the summary was unclear; outcomes unclear even after reading the entire opinion were coded as missing. Outcomes were coded as (1) completely favoring the defendant, (2) mostly favoring the defendant, (3) compromise, (4) mostly favoring the plaintiff, and (5) completely favoring the plaintiff; voluntary settlements were coded on the same scale.
scale: 1 (completely favoring the defendant) to 5 (completely favoring the plaintiff)

description: The authors looked for a special code on the docket sheet indicating any case that was appealed to the Supreme Court of the State of Delaware. If the code was present, then the chancellor's decision had been appealed, and the absence of compliance was inferred.

Size was the total assets of a firm for the year in which a dispute was filed; most of this information came from the Compact Disclosure database, but because many corporations are privately held, total asset information was not uniformly available. Because there were large variations in the sample, the total assets measures were logarithmically transformed.
time_window: year in which the dispute was filed

description: The total number of newly created competitive actions, regardless of type, carried out by each leader and challenger in a given pair-year. A relative measure was calculated as the number of total new actions for the leader minus the number of total new actions for the challenger, so a positive score indicates that the leader executed more competitive actions than the challenger in the same industry-year.

Time elapsed, measured in days, between the date of a competitive action carried out by the leader and the date of a preceding competitive action carried out by the challenger, with a similar measure calculated for the challenger. Where a firm carried out two or more successive moves before the alternate firm acted, the chronological midpoint of the sequence captured the elapsed time. Relative action timing is the annual average action timing measure for the leader (in days) minus the average annual measure for the challenger.

Within-firm action concentration measured with the action analogue of the Herfindahl index, in which action categories serve as the dimension of diversity and the square of the share of a firm's actions in each action category is summed. A firm with a high action simplicity score favored just a few action types, while a low score indicates a broad range of action types. Relative action repertoire simplicity is the difference between the leader's and the challenger's individual simplicity scores.

Between-firm action differentiation calculated by summing, across all action categories for each industry-year, the squared differences in the proportions of competitive actions carried out by the leader and the challenger, a Euclidean distance measure across competitive actions of many types. High dissimilarity scores indicate that leader and challenger differ in the competitive actions each implements; low scores indicate similar strategic choices.

Individual market shares for leader and challenger were calculated from sales totals reported in the business and geographic segment files of COMPUSTAT. Relative market share is derived from the logarithm of the ratio of the leader's market share to the challenger's market share, which reduces to a market share difference score for each time period. The rate of erosion of the market share gap is the change in the market share gap from year to year, where positive values indicate a narrowing gap and negative values represent a widening gap.
time_window: change from year to year over 1987-93

description: Dethronement was a dichotomous variable coded 1 for industry-years in which a leader was dethroned and 0 for industry-years in which no dethronement occurred. Its occurrence also identified the leader's duration or tenure in years at the top, which was used in the event history analysis.

One of the five stakeholder relationship items consistently reported in the KLD database for 1991-96. Firm actions toward employees are rated by KLD analysts on a five-point scale, where -2 suggests negative actions toward the stakeholder group and +2 suggests positive actions. Ratings rely on primary and secondary data on roughly 650 U.S. firms.

One of the five stakeholder relationship items consistently reported in the KLD database for 1991-96. Firm actions toward the diversity stakeholder area are rated by KLD analysts on a five-point scale, where -2 suggests negative actions toward the stakeholder group and +2 suggests positive actions.

One of the five stakeholder relationship items consistently reported in the KLD database for 1991-96. Firm actions toward local communities are rated by KLD analysts on a five-point scale, where -2 suggests negative actions toward the stakeholder group and +2 suggests positive actions.

One of the five stakeholder relationship items consistently reported in the KLD database for 1991-96. Firm actions toward the natural environment are rated by KLD analysts on a five-point scale, where -2 suggests negative actions toward the stakeholder group and +2 suggests positive actions.

One of the five stakeholder relationship items consistently reported in the KLD database for 1991-96. Firm actions on product safety/quality are rated by KLD analysts on a five-point scale, where -2 suggests negative actions toward the stakeholder group and +2 suggests positive actions.
The cost efficiency measure was the ratio of the cost of goods sold to total sales; a smaller value indicates better firm operating efficiency, so a negative relationship with ROA is expected.
Total firm assets for a given year divided by the number of employees for that year. The capital intensity variable was divided by 100 so that the means of the capital variables were roughly similar.
Net capital expenditures made by a firm in a given year divided by its sales for that year. The variable was multiplied by 100 so that the means of the capital variables were roughly similar.

The differentiation measure was the ratio of general, selling, and administrative expenses to total sales, capturing a firm's willingness to spend on marketing- and selling-related activities in an effort to differentiate itself from its rivals.
Financial performance was operationally defined as return on assets (ROA), computed as the ratio of operating income to total assets.

variable_name: strategy variables (cost efficiency, capital intensity, capital expenditures, selling intensity)
description: Firm strategy was measured with Hambrick's (1983) operational definition of strategic resource allocation. Cost efficiency, asset parsimony (capital intensity and capital expenditures) and differentiation (selling intensity) were computed from financial data.

Stakeholder relationships were measured with Kinder, Lydenberg, Domini ratings of firm actions toward five stakeholder groups: employees, natural environment, diversity, customers (product safety/quality) and community. Each was a separate rating variable in the regressions.

A composite indicator of relative customer service performance formed by adding together, with equal weight, the annual standardized values of five customer service indicators. Three of the indicators (complaints to OFWAT, inadequate water pressure, and supply interruptions) were expressed as 100 percent minus the reported percentages published by OFWAT so that higher values are associated with better customer service; the other two were ratings on a five-point scale. The five variables could not be simply aggregated because their measurement units differed, so each was transformed into an annual standardized value before aggregation. In model 2 the five individual standardized customer service variables were entered separately.
time_window: annual, coinciding with the firm's accounting year from April 1 to March 31

description: The dependent variable in the profits models, defined as company j's posttax profits for the year deflated by the book value of shareholders' equity (issued share capital plus reserves), minus the sector-average profits/equity for the same period. Firm-level fixed effects, firm size and differences in capital structure were included as controls.

The dependent variable in the shareholder returns models, defined as firm i's returns over time t minus the sector-average returns for the same period. The returns for each company and the sector-average returns were calculated as natural logarithms. Returns were measured over two different periods: the month in which the regulator released the customer service findings (announcement month model), and the subsequent one-year period from April 1 to March 31 (annual returns model).
time_window: the customer service announcement month (late November or early December) and the subsequent annual period from April 1 to March 31

description: Ethics-responsible informants assessed the frequency with which 'communications which remind them about ethics and conduct issues' were received by employees at four ranks: high-level management, middle management, low-level management/supervisory personnel, and nonsupervisory employees. Answers were given on a five-point Likert scale: 1 'not at all'; 2 'only at hiring'; 3 'every few years'; 4 'every year'; and 5 'two times per year.' Cronbach's alpha was .90 across the four questions.

Measured with three five-point Likert items (1, strongly disagree; 5, strongly agree) asking informants whether 'assessment of a person's ethics is a formal part of performance appraisals,' 'people get formally evaluated on the ethics of their behavior,' and 'supervisors are asked to formally assess the ethical performance of their people.' Cronbach's alpha was .82.

Four five-point Likert items (1, strongly disagree; 5, strongly agree) assessed managers' awareness of and familiarity with the USSC guidelines, covering whether executive meetings and communications discussed the impact of the guidelines as well as the respondent's self-assessed personal familiarity with them and sense that USSC requirements informed company ethics practices. Cronbach's alpha was .78. Reported mean was 3.59, s.d. = 1.03.

Count of newspaper article abstracts appearing in Newspaper Abstracts from early 1989 through October 1994 that suggested (1) violations of law (such as discrimination in hiring or firing and fraud), (2) threat to the general public (for instance, safety failures), (3) ruthless or deceptive business practices, or (4) hints of undisclosed impropriety. Two trained research assistants followed common written guidelines; one of the authors repeated the search for 10 percent of the companies evaluated by each assistant, with interrater agreement of 70 and 71 percent.

variable_name: Presence at Conference Board ethics meetings
description: Company attendance at the Conference Board's annual ethics meetings held prior to survey administration, measured using conference registration lists for 1992, 1993, and 1994. A company was counted as exposed to this standard-setting influence if it appeared on the registration list for one or more of these conferences.

variable_name: Top management commitment to financial and strategic concerns
description: Ethics-responsible officers rated the extent to which various subjects are a topic of conversation for the top management team on a five-point Likert scale from 'never' (1) to 'very frequently' (5), with higher frequency interpreted as a sign of greater concern for and commitment to the topic. Topics indicating commitment to financial, strategic, and operational matters were financial performance, strategy and planning, stockholders and investors, and productivity and efficiency. Cronbach's alpha was .68, which the authors note likely reflects the diverse range of topics included.

Ethics-responsible officers rated the extent to which ethics-related subjects are a topic of conversation for the top management team on a five-point Likert scale from 'never' (1) to 'very frequently' (5), with higher frequency interpreted as a sign of greater concern for and commitment to the topic. Topics indicating commitment to ethics were 'doing the right thing,' 'seeking the good of society,' 'treating people fairly,' 'the company's role in society,' and 'valuing integrity as much as profits.' Cronbach's alpha was .85.

Coded from the "Management" section of each prospectus as whether or not the firm had a senior HRM executive on its top management team, that is, a vice president of HRM who reported to the CEO. Coded 1 = yes, 0 = no.
time_window: at the time of the initial public offering

description: Year-end 1996 stock price, the primary dependent variable. After initial stock price (adjusted for splits, buybacks, and any other changes that affected unit price) is controlled for, the variable should reflect the increase in value of a firm in the first three years following its IPO.

Year-end 1996 earnings per share, a measure of internal performance often used by analysts and investors to assess the future value of a firm. Earnings per share at the time of the IPO was included as a control variable rather than using change scores.

Sales data for 1992-95 were obtained from COMPUSTAT and the percentage change in sales was calculated for two periods, 1992-93 and 1992-95. The first measure was included so that the measure would be consistent with the other data obtained at the time of each firm's IPO; the second was added because low variance prior to the IPO was expected.

Company size obtained from the prospectus, measured as number of employees at the time of the offering. Because the distribution was skewed, the logarithm of the number of employees was used in the analyses.
time_window: at the time of the offering

description: Each respondent estimated the ages of the oldest and youngest members of his or her team. The difference between these numbers was the age range and the mean of the two numbers estimated the mean age; the age range divided by the estimated age mean approximates a coefficient of variation. Members' coefficient of variation estimates were averaged to obtain team age diversity (eta-square = .41, above the .20 criterion for aggregation).
Respondents reported how long they had been working for their companies. Company tenure diversity was computed as the coefficient of variation of company tenure among TMT members.

Respondents reported the highest educational degree they had attained. To be consistent with Smith and colleagues (1994), highest degree was transformed into years of formal education and the group's coefficient of variation was computed to estimate education-level diversity.

Respondents indicated which of seven categories reflected their functional specialty. Functional background diversity was then computed using Blau's index (1 - sum of squared proportions of respondents in each category).

Using a version of Duncan's (1972) scale, respondents indicated whether each of ten environmental factors had undergone a major (greater than 10 percent), nonpredictable and noncyclic change during the 1991 calendar year. For each team the authors summed the number of factors marked as changing by at least one member and as not changing by at least one member, statistically controlled this sum for the number of respondents, and saved the residuals as PEU diversity.

Each team member considered one recent, important strategic decision and rated the level of debate that occurred using four Likert-type items (Cronbach's alpha = .75). Individual responses were added to obtain individual-level debate perception scores, and individual-level scores were averaged within each team to obtain team-level scores (eta-square = .46).

Each team member described the same decision process in terms of comprehensiveness using three scale items based on Miller's (1990) comprehensiveness measure (Cronbach's alpha = .78). Individual perceptions were aggregated; the eta-square of .39 indicates that aggregation was statistically permissible.

Change in gross profit expressed as a percentage of sales between 1990 and 1991. Respondents reported 1991 gross profit, before executive draw, as a percentage of sales, and whether 1991 gross profit was higher or lower than 1990 gross profit and by how many percentage points. The change-in-profitability figure was standardized by dominant product line (passive components, semiconductors, or printed circuit boards).

Change in gross sales from 1990 to 1991 expressed as a percentage of 1990 sales, reported by respondents on a nine-point scale. As with change in profitability, the measure was standardized by dominant product line.
scale: 1 (down more than 25 percent) to 9 (up over 25 percent)

variable_name: TMT diversity variables (age, tenure, education, functional background, PEU)
description: TMT diversity was measured as five separate diversity variables computed from team members' survey responses: age, company tenure, education level, functional background, and perceived environmental uncertainty (PEU) diversity. Each was tested for interaction with debate.

A count of the number of two-digit ISIC-equivalent industries in which a group is involved. The calculation includes the industries of all group members, including those that were not in the sample, on the grounds that this inclusion provided a more complete picture of the total unrelated diversification of a group. For unaffiliated firms it is the number of two-digit ISIC-equivalent industries in which the firm is present.

ROA is defined as [net income + interest x (1 - tax rate)]/[total assets], where an average tax rate is estimated for each firm. It is used as the firm-level performance measure in the year-by-year and panel regressions.

A dummy variable indicating whether the firm is affiliated with a business group; the authors refer to its coefficient as the non-diversification-related group effect. The estimate on this dummy is reported as always positive, and its yearly value is used to trace the decline of the group effect over time.

A time trend inserted in the panel regressions, used as a proxy for the ensemble of changes in the Chilean institutional context because a time trend is statistically significant for 10 of the 13 contextual variables and the variables are highly correlated. The group dummy is interacted with this time trend to test whether the group effect declines over time.

variable_name: employment (downsizing measured as change in the logarithm of a firm's number of employees)
description: Following Bethel and Liebeskind (1993), downsizing was measured in terms of changes in the logarithm of a firm's number of employees. All regression models were estimated in levels with a lagged dependent variable as a regressor, so that a negative and significant beta coefficient means an increase in the regressor would increase the extent of downsizing, and a positive and significant beta means the regressor works against downsizing. The authors note that the signs on the predicted effects in the results table are reversed, since the hypotheses refer to downsizing while the table uses employment change. The reduction in the number of observations from 150 to 103 is due to missing data.
time_window: 1994, 1996, and 1997 (ownership, industry, and control variables lagged one year)

description: An index of an industry's real output in the three countries between 1993 and the measurement point expressed as a percentage of the 1993 level. It was built from officially reported national statistics and IMF staff country reports on annual industrial output and indexes of each industry's real output between 1993 and the measurement point. Initially two measures (industry decline at t-1 and industry decline squared) were used; because they were highly correlated, restrictions of equality of the absolute values of the coefficients were imposed and the two measures were replaced with the single change-in-industry-decline measure, with industry and control variables lagged one year.
time_window: 1993 to the measurement point; one-year lag

description: Data from all three countries were combined, and dummy variables for country were used to control for systemic differences between individual countries not captured by the other independent variables, with Belarus as the reference category.

Ownership interests were measured with three continuous variables representing the percentages of the company's voting shares held by institutional investors, outside private individuals, and managers, respectively; ownership by employees was omitted to avoid collinearity because ownership shares sum to unity. Both managerial equity and its square were entered, with one-year lags, to capture the predicted curvilinear relationship. Because of suspected collinearity between the ownership variables, separate tests were conducted using a full regression model and two reduced models with restrictions on the coefficients of the managerial ownership variables.

A continuous variable representing the percentage of the company's voting shares held by institutional investors, such as banks, investment funds, and foreign companies, with a one-year lag. Ownership by employees was omitted to avoid collinearity because ownership shares sum to unity.

A continuous variable representing the percentage of the company's voting shares held by outside private individuals, with a one-year lag. Ownership by employees was omitted to avoid collinearity because ownership shares sum to unity.

The sum of the equity holdings of Japanese parents that were members of the same horizontal keiretsu. The variable has a lower limit of 0 and an upper limit of 100, which makes the double-censored Tobit procedure appropriate. An alternative specification grouped ownership into three ordinal categories (minority joint venture, co-owned or majority joint venture, and wholly owned subsidiary), but only the Tobit results are reported.

A measure of the extent to which a change in the preferences of any one branch of government (executive, lower and upper legislative chambers, judiciary, and subfederal institutions) may lead to a change in government policy. It identifies the number of independent branches of government with veto power over policy changes, assumes preferences and the status quo policy are independently and identically drawn from a uniform, unidimensional policy space, and is modified for alignment across branches and for preference heterogeneity within legislative branches. Possible scores range from 0 (minimal risk) to 1 (extremely risky).

A measure of perceived legal barriers to equity ownership by foreign firms, taken as the average response of a panel of 2,515 executives surveyed for the World Economic Forum's World Competitiveness Report to the statement 'Foreign investors are free to acquire control in a domestic company'. A logarithmic transformation of these scores is used.

Research and development expenditures as a percentage of sales, used as an imperfect proxy for the private expropriation hazard of technological leakage. The measure is a five-year (1992-96) average of data from Kaisha Zaimu Karute. The authors note it is also a proxy for firm-level research capabilities.

The advertising-to-sales ratio, adopted as an imperfect proxy of the extent of private expropriation hazards of free riding on brand name and reputation. The measure is a five-year (1992-96) average of data from Kaisha Zaimu Karute. The authors note it is also a proxy for firm-level marketing capabilities.

The logarithm of the number of subsidiary years of experience the parent firm had in the focal host country, based on the extent of its investment activity at the date of a subsidiary's founding. A subsidiary year was one year of operations by one subsidiary. Experience of current subsidiaries and of subsidiaries the parent had owned and exited prior to 1997 was included.
time_window: measured at the date of a subsidiary's founding

description: The logarithm of the number of subsidiary years of experience the parent firm had in a given industry, based on the extent of its investment activity at the date of a subsidiary's founding. A subsidiary year was one year of operations by one subsidiary. Experience of current and exited subsidiaries was included.
time_window: measured at the date of a subsidiary's founding

description: The logarithm of the number of subsidiary years of experience the parent firm had in countries other than the focal host country, based on the extent of its investment activity at the date of a subsidiary's founding. A subsidiary year was one year of operations by one subsidiary. Experience of current and exited subsidiaries was included.
time_window: measured at the date of a subsidiary's founding

description: A dummy variable coded 1 when a sogo shosha was the largest Japanese equity holder in the subsidiary. Nine sogo shoshas (Itochu, Kanematsu, Sumitomo Corporation, Tomen, Nichimen, Nissho Iwai, Marubeni, Mitsui & Co., and Mitsubishi Corporation) were identified as listed under industry code 40101 (general trading companies).
A dummy variable coded 1 when a sogo shosha had an ownership position lower than that of another Japanese firm.

A dummy variable for overseas operations in which a partner from one of the big six horizontal keiretsus (Mitsubishi, Mitsui, Sumitomo, DKB, Fuyo, and Sanwa) took an equity stake but no sogo shosha was active, created to separate the effects of keiretsu membership from sogo shosha ties.

The total number of research institutes that, from 1985 up to the decision year (1990, 1991, or 1992), were listed in the MPH records as involved in the research for other approved compounds in the same therapeutic category. The variable was specified in natural logarithmic form for the estimations because the effect of an additional supplier was expected to have less impact at higher levels. The authors note the measure is likely conservative because it includes only institutes involved in previously approved compounds.

The number of firms that, from 1985 to the decision year, were listed in the MPH records as producers of other compounds in the same therapeutic category. The variable was specified in natural logarithmic form. The authors note it understates the number of firms producing in each category because approvals predating the database are not covered.

Dichotomous variable coded 1 if the firm was located in one of 7 of China's 30 province-level administrative regions categorized as highly competitive on the basis of both regional and firm performance: Liaoning, Shandong, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Sichuan, and Guangdong. These regions account for a little more than 50 percent of China's total pharmaceutical production, sales, and profits, and 62 of China's top 100 firms in terms of sales are located in them.
Dummy variable coded 1 if the focal compound j was in the same therapeutic category i in which the firm had a previously approved compound, up to and including the decision year for compound j.
time_window: up to and including the decision year for the compound

description: Dummy variable set equal to 1 for generic compounds, based on the MPH's categorization of a compound's newness. A compound was categorized as a me-too drug if another firm was already producing it. A value of 1 therefore indicates low technical uncertainty.
time_window: at the time of the compound's development

description: Dummy variable indicating whether the firm had been recorded as the sole research organization for a compound in any therapeutic category prior to the development of compound j.
time_window: prior to the focal compound's development

description: Dichotomous variable set equal to 1 if the firm was not included as one of the organizations involved in the compound's development, and 0 otherwise; it represents the buy outcome. Transfer served as the comparison group in the multinomial logit estimation.
Dichotomous variable set equal to 1 if both the firm and a research institute were listed as involved in the compound's development, and 0 otherwise; it represents the ally outcome.
Dichotomous variable set equal to 1 if the firm was the only organization listed as involved in the compound's development, and 0 otherwise; it represents the make outcome.

variable_name: net sales of the top ten business groups as a percentage of GDP
description: The total net sales of each of the top ten business groups in a given country was divided by the country's gross domestic product. This ratio provides a repeated measure of the importance of business groups relative to the size of an economy that is comparable across countries at each level of the top ten ranking.

variable_name: stock market capitalization as a percentage of GDP
description: The most widely used indicator of the development of financial markets was chosen as the proxy for market failure theories, which point to underdeveloped financial markets as a reason for the creation of business groups. Higher values of the indicator mean less market failure.

Hofstede's (1991) power distance index was used to measure the prediction that vertical or hierarchical societies foster business groups. The index captures the extent to which relationships in a society are based on autocratic and paternalistic assumptions and is frequently used in the international management literature.

variable_name: inverse of Henisz's index of political constraints
description: State autonomy was measured with the inverse of Henisz's (1999) index of political constraints based on the Polity III database (Gurr, 1990, and subsequent electronic updates).

variable_name: general government consumption as a percentage of GDP
description: State size was measured with general government consumption as a percentage of GDP.

Calculated as the absolute difference between Z-scores (standardized values) for imports of consumer goods and passenger cars and Z-scores for total exports. Imports of consumer goods and passenger cars rather than total imports were used so as to capture to what extent a country protected its domestic firms.

Calculated as the absolute difference between Z-scores for inward and outward stocks of foreign direct investment. The indexes of asymmetry in foreign trade and investment are significantly correlated with each other, and therefore they were not entered simultaneously in the analysis.

variable_name: firms affiliated to one of the 30 largest business groups
description: For each of the 100 largest nonfinancial firms by total sales in each country and year, the authors coded whether a firm was affiliated to one of the 30 largest business groups in the country, to a foreign multinational enterprise, or to the state. The residual category includes companies affiliated to a group that was not among the top 30, worker-owned cooperatives, family firms, and firms with dispersed control. Rankings were obtained from a combination of sources, and multiple reference sources and field interviews were used for coding.

Respondents were asked what percentages of their firms' sales had previously been made in the industries of the acquired SOEs. The measure follows the continuous measures used in diversification research that measure the sales of merging firms in common SIC codes.

Two independent judges evaluated each case, using survey information on the industry of the acquirer and of the target firm, for an upstream or downstream relationship between the two firms. The judgments resulted in 94 percent agreement. The variable was coded 1 if the experts agreed that an up- or downstream relationship existed between the merging firms and 0 otherwise.

Respondents were asked to what degree financial goals had existed for the managements of the SOEs before acquisition and to what degree management rewards or reprimands had depended on financial performance. The higher an SOE was rated on these combined items, the higher the assumed degree of organizational fit. Nine-point Likert response formats were used and Cronbach's alpha for the measure was .56.

Respondents were asked to specify the financial investments their firms had made in the acquired SOEs as a percentage of the sales of an acquired firm for each year since acquisition. These figures were then averaged and logarithmically transformed to smooth skewness.

The survey asked for both the total number of an SOE's employees and the number who had to be guaranteed employment, because the number required to be retained depends on the size of the acquired firm.
Respondents were asked what percentage (if any) the selling government was still holding in a former SOE.

Country risk was measured with the country risk measures provided by the Institutional Investor. The annual country credit risk rating is based on information provided by 75 to 100 leading international banks and uses a scale from 0 to 100. The March 1995 ratings were used, recoded so that 0 represented the least risk.

Respondents rated the approximate annual change in total sales of the acquired SOE in 1994 on a seven-point scale, where 7 stood for a value greater than 25 percent, 6 for greater than 20 percent, and so forth, and 1 indicated negative sales growth. Pretax data were requested.

Respondents rated the return on assets of the acquired SOEs on a seven-point scale, where 7 stood for a value greater than 25 percent, 6 for greater than 20 percent, and so forth, and 1 indicated negative ROA. Pretax data were requested.

Respondents rated sales, market share, pretax return on sales, and pretax return on total capital invested, each relative to premerger performance, on Likert scales. Cronbach's alpha for this four-item relative performance scale was .85; the measure directly compares the performance of an acquired SOE to its premerger performance.
time_window: after acquisition, relative to premerger levels

description: The R&D expenditure divided by total sales, measured at time t. The authors use it, together with advertising intensity, as a proxy for intangible knowledge-based resources.
The advertising expenditure divided by total sales, measured at time t. It is used as a proxy for intangible knowledge-based resources.

Current assets divided by current liabilities, measured at time t. It is one of the indicators of the availability of capital raised by a firm, and a positive sign with respect to firm performance was expected.

Long-term debt to equity, measured at time t. A high debt-to-equity ratio limits a firm's ability to finance its investment by borrowing, so a negative sign with respect to firm performance was expected.

The weighted average of the R&D intensity of all other firms in firm i's business group, where the weighting factor is sales. For firm i it is computed as the sum over other firms j of R&D intensity times the weight, where the weight is firm j's sales as a proportion of the aggregated total sales of all other firms associated with the same business group, measured at time t.

The weighted average of the advertising intensity of all other firms in firm i's business group, where the weighting factor is sales measured at time t; the calculation is analogous to that for the group R&D variable.

The weighted average of the liquidity ratios of all other firms in firm i's business group, where the weighting factor is current liability. The group liquidity variable for firm i is computed as the sum over other firms j of liquidity times the weight, where the weight is firm j's current liability as a proportion of the aggregated total current liabilities of all other firms associated with the same business group, measured at time t.

The weighted average of the leverage ratios of all other firms in firm i's business group, where the weighting factor is equity base. The group leverage variable for firm i is computed as the sum over other firms j of leverage times the weight, where the weight is firm j's equity as a proportion of the aggregated total equity bases of all other firms associated with the same business group, measured at time t.

The debt guarantee supplied to group members divided by the equity base of the providing firm, measured at time t. It is one of the measures of the outflow of financial resources from a firm to its affiliates.

The equity participation of group members divided by the equity base of the provider, measured at time t. It is one of the measures of the outflow of financial resources from a firm to its affiliates.

The debt guarantee received from group members divided by the equity base of the recipient, measured at time t. It is one of the measures of the inflow of financial resources to a firm from its affiliates.

The equity participation by group members divided by the equity base of the recipient, measured at time t. It is one of the measures of the inflow of financial resources to a firm from its affiliates.
The amount of sales to affiliated companies divided by the total sales of a firm, measured at time t.
The amount of purchases from affiliated companies divided by the total sales of a firm, measured at time t.

A firm's return on invested capital, defined as the sum of net income before tax plus interest payments, deflated by total assets, measured at time t. The authors state that this measure captures operating efficiency without being biased by the relatively high debt-to-equity ratios common in Korean firms.

Firms were classified by the market context of their home country. Firms from Mexico, Poland, and Romania represented emerging markets, and firms from Canada, France, and the United States represented developed markets; countries from two world regions were selected to control for potential regional geographic idiosyncrasies. Separate models were estimated for the emerging and developed market subsamples and the two were compared.

One of the 14 partner firm characteristics used as an independent variable. The cases were constructed by varying the levels of the 14 independent variables randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 14 partner firm characteristics used as an independent variable. The cases were constructed by varying the levels of the 14 independent variables randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 14 partner firm characteristics used as an independent variable. The cases were constructed by varying the levels of the 14 independent variables randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 14 partner firm characteristics used as an independent variable. The cases were constructed by varying the levels of the 14 independent variables randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 14 partner firm characteristics used as an independent variable. The cases were constructed by varying the levels of the 14 independent variables randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 14 partner firm characteristics used as an independent variable. The cases were constructed by varying the levels of the 14 independent variables randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

A two-item scale on which executives rated each of the 30 potential partners described in the cases: the attractiveness of the firm described as a partner and the probability that the respondent would recommend an alliance with the firm described. Both items used a seven-point Likert-type scale and were averaged to form the dependent variable; the correlation between the two items was .87.

The degree of resource commitment to technology transfer, measured by two items: the Japanese parent has provided technology (y1) and the Japanese parent has sent skilled engineers and product managers to the JV (y2). Responses were recorded on a five-point Likert scale.
The timing of entry, measured by a single item: entry into the Chinese market through the JV is much earlier (or later) than its rivals. Responses were recorded on a five-point Likert scale.
Perceived economic performance, measured with items on a five-point Likert scale with coding ranging from 1 (poor) to 5 (extremely good).
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = poor, 5 = extremely good)

description: The strategic importance of a JV to the Japanese parent, measured by items x1 (role: the JV plays a significant role to the Japanese parent's overall global strategy) and x2 (definition: the role that the JV is expected to play for the Japanese parent is clearly defined). Responses were recorded on a five-point Likert scale.

The extent of a Japanese parent's control within a JV, measured by items x3 (post: Japanese expatriates occupy significant management posts in the JV), x4 (equity: the extent of equity share owned by the Chinese partner, 0-100%), and x5 (chairman: the chairman of the JV is Chinese, no=0, yes=1).

The availability of supporting infrastructure in local markets, measured by items x6 (protection: legal protection of intellectual property rights, patented technology and trademark is sufficient), x7 (recruit: it is easy to recruit skilled local human resources), and x8 (infrastructure: local distribution network and infrastructure are well developed). Responses were recorded on a five-point Likert scale.
Employee retention likelihood, measured by a single item on a five-point Likert scale.
Overall satisfaction, measured by a single item on a five-point Likert scale.

variable_name: ties with top managers at other firms
description: Respondents were asked to circle the number best describing the extent to which top managers at their firm had utilized personal ties, networks, and connections during the past three years with top managers at buyer firms, supplier firms, and competitor firms. Answers to the three questions were averaged to create a composite measure.
scale: seven-point Likert scale, from 'very little' to 'very extensive'

description: Respondents were asked to circle the number best describing the extent to which top managers at their firm had utilized personal ties, networks, and connections during the past three years with political leaders at various levels of the government, officials in industrial bureaus, and officials in regulatory and supporting organizations such as tax bureaus, state banks, and commercial administration bureaus. The three answers were averaged to approximate ties with officials.
scale: seven-point Likert scale, from 'very little' to 'very extensive'

description: Respondents were asked to provide their firm's average market share in the industry during the past three years, in percent. In the cover letter respondents were asked to refer to their industry associations' reports, which follow four-digit Chinese Industrial Classification groups, and to report a firm's sales divided by its industry's total sales as reported by the association.

Respondents were asked to provide their firm's average return on assets during the past three years, in percent. ROA was chosen as the financial measure because equity contributions for a majority of Chinese firms are historically ambiguous and because return on sales significantly correlates with market share.
Ownership was defined by a dummy variable, coded 1 for state-owned enterprises and 0 for non-SOEs. Of the responding firms, 71 were SOEs and 56 were non-SOEs.
Business sector was measured by a dummy variable, coded 1 for manufacturing and 0 for service. Sampled firms included 99 manufacturers and 28 service firms.
Firm size was defined by the number of employees. Sampled firms had a range of 50 to 6,000 employees, with a mean of 377.

Industry growth was measured by the compound growth rate of pretax profits during 1993-95. The industry growth rates had a range of -14 to 63 percent, with a mean of 9.31 percent during the study period. Before-tax profits were used instead of after-tax profits because different industries in China have different rates of taxation.

Assessed with items adapted from Lewin and Yang (1992). The variable reflects the beliefs of management regarding the importance of human resources and people as a source of competitive advantage (Butler et al., 1991). The text does not state the number of items or the response scale.

Measured with a Likert scale adapted from studies by various authors (Arthur, 1992; Dess & Davis, 1984; Hambrick, 1983; Snell, 1992; Snow & Hrebiniak, 1980). The items reflect such aspects of organizational strategy as the variety of products or services and the level of product or service quality. Low values represent narrow and stable strategic positions, and high values represent a broad range of products, varied customer tastes, and high-quality postures.

Measured with a Likert scale developed specifically for this study but based on the work of Taira (1994) and Hammer and Champy (1993). Low values represent a traditional bureaucratic structure with slow service and many handoffs, and high values reflect flexibility, rapid decision making, and a strong customer orientation.

Measures different components of a firm's HRM strategy as applied to its nonsupervisory production workers: the degree to which the firm relied upon extensive training, empowerment, highly selective staffing, performance-based pay, and broad job design. High values from all these areas are consistent with a high-involvement strategy, and low values are consistent with a control strategy. Highly selective staffing and extensive training were assessed on six-category Likert scales using items adapted from Snell and Dean (1992); empowerment was measured by a seven-item, six-category Likert scale; performance-based pay by a three-item scale with a six-point Likert scale reflecting the degree of the linkage of performance and pay level; and broad job design by a three-item scale reflecting the extent to which jobs involved multiple skills and competencies.

Items adapted from Khandwalla (1977). Only the externally oriented and largely market-focused indicators were used in forming the performance scale; the authors used a single, global measure of organizational performance. Perceptual measures were used because comparable objective measures were difficult to find for both multinational and indigenous firms and because Asian firms often do not accurately disclose financial performance.

variable_name: choice of area for new branch establishment
description: For each new branch, the chosen area among 20 alternatives is the dependent variable, estimated by a conditional logit model; the data have 824 choices with 20 alternatives each and the model predicts the alternative actually chosen. The benefit of an area is specified as a function of population, own branches, and competitors in the focal area and of own branches in neighboring areas.
time_window: choice year (all covariates lagged one year)

description: Counts all branches in an area per year, entered as a linear and a squared effect; a positive linear and negative squared effect would indicate an inverted U-shaped relation. It includes branches of banks headquartered outside Tokyo and branches founded before the start of the study.
Counts all bank headquarters in the area per year, entered as a linear and a squared effect. It is separated from branch density to allow each form to have different coefficient estimates.

Each branch in an area is given a weight equal to its firm's size, measured as its number of branches, and these weights are summed by area. A positive estimate would indicate that the branches of large banks were more likely to attract imitations.
A count of all offices (banks or branches) of the same bank in a given area. A positive estimate supports Hypothesis 3.
A count of all offices of the same bank in areas adjacent to a focal area, with area adjacency given by a proximity matrix coded from historical maps. A positive estimate supports Hypothesis 4.

A count of the number of offices in an area owned by banks that a focal bank had contact with in two or more areas. Bank offices are partitioned into those owned by banks with multipoint contact, those with single-point contact, and those with no prior contact (the omitted category).

A count of all offices in the area owned by banks that the focal bank had contact with in just one area. A positive estimate would show that areas with more offices of banks with which a focal bank can establish a mutual forbearance relation are more attractive.

Bank size is measured as the number of offices; it was mean-deviated and interacted with the momentum and forbearance variables, so main effects describe a bank of average size. Bank size itself was not entered into the model because the conditional likelihood model only estimates coefficients of covariates that differ across areas in a single choice.

Eight work-family policies were coded 1 if a company had the policy and 0 if it did not: on-site day care, help with day care costs, elder care assistance, information on community day care, paid parental leave, unpaid parental leave, maternity or paternity leave with reemployment, and flexible scheduling. A principal component factor analysis with varimax rotation yielded three factors (leave policies, traditional dependent care, and less traditional dependent care), and standardized values for the three were entered in a cluster analysis. Four cluster groupings were identified, ranging from organizations in which all categories are relatively scarce to organizations in which all three categories are prevalent.

A seven-item measure (alpha = .87) of perceived firm performance assessed relative to that of other firms doing the same kind of work. Items include the quality of products, the ability to attract essential employees, and relations between management and employees. This dependent variable was also assessed in a separate ANCOVA including both nonprofit and for-profit firms.

A four-item measure (alpha = .85) of perceived market performance assessed relative to that of other firms, including items related to marketing and market share. The market performance items were only available for profit-making firms.
A two-item measure (r = .75) of a firm's percentage increase in sales and profits over the last 12 months. These items were only available for profit-making firms.
Measured as the logarithm of total employees.
Measured as the natural logarithm of 1991 minus the founding year.
Measured as the percentage of women in core positions, defined as jobs that are directly involved with the main product or service of a firm.

variable_name: innovation (composite of R&D spending and number of patents)
description: A composite measure computed by adding standardized values of R&D spending and number of patents, with separate composites computed for 1992 and 1993. R&D spending is the company's annual R&D expenditures in millions of dollars; number of patents is the annual number of company patents. Firm size was controlled for scale effects on R&D spending and number of patents.
time_window: 1992 and 1993 (year prior to the pay year)

variable_name: innovation (composite of R&D spending and number of patents)
description: The same composite measure, computed by adding standardized values of R&D spending and number of patents, constructed separately for the control sample of low-technology firms.
time_window: 1992 and 1993 (year prior to the pay year)

description: Total cash compensation received by the CEO during a specific year, consisting of annual salary and bonus, taken from the Forbes data set and reported in thousands of dollars for 1993 and 1994.
Total cash compensation received by the CEO during a specific year, consisting of annual salary and bonus, taken from the Forbes data set for the control sample and reported in thousands of dollars.

Equity-based compensation of the CEO, valued at the number of shares multiplied by 25 percent of the exercise price, following the approach used by Lambert, Larcker, and Weigelt and by Finkelstein and Boyd. Data came from proxy statements for 1993 and 1994.
Equity-based compensation of the CEO in the control sample, valued as the number of shares multiplied by 25 percent of the exercise price, with data taken from proxy statements.

Whenever possible, life cycle was computed as the difference between the year an article was first published on a fashion and the year in which publications on the fashion first dropped to zero. Only management fashions that had actually peaked by the conclusion of the study period were included in analyses in which life span was assessed.

variable_name: number of years it took the fashion to peak
description: An alternative measure of the life span of a management fashion, computed as the number of years it took the fashion to peak.

variable_name: year in which a fashion was introduced
description: The year in which a fashion was introduced, taken as the year an article was first published on the fashion.

Rated on a five-point scale where 1 = easy and 5 = hard, assessing the degree to which implementation of a fashion in organizations is difficult. Ratings were made by three of the authors and an outside expert judge; final ratings were made through consensus building after each judge had made an independent assessment.

Rated on a five-point scale where 1 = narrow and 5 = organizationwide, assessing the degree to which a fashion targets (or affects) specific people, project teams, or departments as opposed to an entire organization. Ratings were made by three of the authors and an outside expert judge through consensus building.

Rated on a five-point scale where 1 = more on lower levels and 5 = more on management, focusing on whether successful implementation of a fashion demands more effort, responsibility, and persistence from upper management than from those lower in an organization's hierarchy. Ratings were made by three of the authors and an outside expert judge through consensus building.
scale: 1 = more on lower levels to 5 = more on management

description: Rated on a five-point scale where 1 = not at all radical and 5 = extremely radical, representing the degree to which a fashion encourages divergence from established management thinking. Ratings were made by three of the authors and an outside expert judge through consensus building.
scale: 1 = not at all radical to 5 = extremely radical

description: Rated on a five-point scale where 1 = not at all and 5 = extremely, based on Abrahamson's (1997) explanation of normative rhetoric; it represents the degree to which a fashion addresses the needs, concerns, and motivations of an organization's staff. Ratings were made by three of the authors and an outside expert judge through consensus building.

Rated on a five-point scale where 1 = not at all and 5 = extremely, representing the degree to which a fashion focuses on enhancing the output and productivity of an organization, drawn from Abrahamson's (1997) explanation of rational rhetoric. Ratings were made by three of the authors and an outside expert judge through consensus building.

Rated on a five-point scale where 1 = not at all and 5 = extremely, relating to the degree to which a fashion is likely to create apprehension, anxiety, and consternation among the members of an organization. Ratings were made by three of the authors and an outside expert judge through consensus building.

Rated on a five-point scale where 1 = blamed and 5 = blameless, representing the degree to which a fashion represents management as responsible for the creation of organizational ills that have given rise to the need to adopt the fashion. Ratings were made by three of the authors and an outside expert judge through consensus building.

variable_name: number of articles in which a fashion was the main subject
description: Collected through a manual search/count of volumes of the Business Periodicals Index published annually from the mid 1950s to the late 1990s. A fashion had to be the main subject of the article to be counted. The number of articles is used as a proxy for degree of implementation and measures interest in a fashion.
Trade balance, taken from the International Statistics section of the Council of Economic Advisers' Economic Report of the President, used as an indicator of overall global competitiveness.
time_window: each year of the study period

description: Corporate profits, taken from the Corporate Profits and Finance section of the Economic Report of the President, used as a benchmark of organizations' financial health.
time_window: each year of the study period

description: Per unit labor costs, taken from the Production and Business Activity section of the Economic Report of the President, used as evidence of efficiency.
time_window: each year of the study period

description: Data on management consulting industry revenues, collected to gain insight into the degree to which management fashion implementation may be supply-driven. Historical data were collected from the Statistical Abstract of the United States, Historical Statistics of the United States, and the Economic Report of the President for each year of the study.
time_window: each year of the study period

description: The number of mergers and acquisitions in each year of the study period, collected to reflect structural alterations. Historical data were collected from the Statistical Abstract of the United States, Historical Statistics of the United States, and the Economic Report of the President for each year of the study.
time_window: each year of the study period

description: Calculated as sales in a given foreign country expressed as a percentage of a firm's total sales. Foreign sales data were collected for the sixth year of each firm's operation from the firms' sixth-year annual reports, with COMPUSTAT PC+ used to determine which firms had entered foreign markets.
time_window: sixth year of each firm's operation

description: The average of risk ratings published in Euromoney, Institutional Investor, and the Wall Street Journal. These publications present annual ratings of countries based on composite measures of both political and economic risk; the average had a reliability of .96.
level: country (applied to each foreign market entry)

description: A five-level variable indicating entry mode commitment risk in a given foreign market, ordered from exporting, licensing, foreign sales office, joint venture, to solely owned foreign production subsidiary. In the order listed, each mode represents increased complexity, increased commitment of resources and therefore increased market and political risk.
time_window: sixth year of each firm's operation

description: A firm-level count of the number of foreign markets in which each firm operated in its sixth year.
time_window: sixth year of each firm's operation

description: Four industry experts independently classified each firm's strategic actions for each year of the study into the categorical variables excess capacity, international economies of scale, dynamic capabilities, innovation, and no focus. Each firm was represented by a vector of 13 yearly observations and the sequences of strategic actions formed firm-by-firm strategic paths; hierarchical clustering on rater-by-rater distance matrices using the average linkage method produced nine distinct patterns, of which the third pattern is the hypothesized sequencing.

Firm growth was the dependent variable, measured as change in three size dimensions over the period of interstate deregulation: total sales, number of employees, and total assets, taken from annual reports and 10K reports. The pattern means for the three measures of the dependent variable were compared across the resource-based sequencing patterns.

Adapted from Covin and Slevin's (1989) semantic differential items, with word and sentence changes to enhance understanding in the Chinese context, for example "placed emphasis on developing new products through allocation of substantial financial resources" and "developed a large variety of new product lines." Respondents rated their firm relative to its major competitors over the last three years. Confirmatory factor analysis showed all items loaded on their respective construct with large and significant loadings.

Respondents rated their firm's performance relative to its principal competitors over the last three years. The measure is composed of five financial and four market performance measures, which the authors combined into a single variable because they were highly correlated (r = .66, p < .001).

A new measure created specifically for the study. It captures the extent to which the competitive behavior of firms in the market is opportunistic, unfair, or even unlawful; respondents rated the degree to which statements described their firm's environment.
