A new measure created specifically for the study. It reflects the extent to which administrative institutions such as government departments provide support for firms, for example helping the firm obtain licenses for imports of technology, manufacturing and other equipment.

Adapted from past research (e.g., Miller, 1987), with four items adapted but only two retained, yielding an alpha of .50. It refers to the degree of change and unpredictability of a market environment.

Adapted from the extant literature, with word and sentence changes to enhance understanding in the Chinese context. It captures cooperative agreements with other firms to develop and market new products, such as entering cooperative agreements to design and manufacture new products, collaborating to market new products, and jointly distributing and providing support services for new products.

A new measure created specifically for the study. It captures the extent to which top management over the last three years cultivated personal connections with officials of government and its agencies, maintained good relationships with officials of state banks and other government financial agencies, and devoted substantial resources or money to building relations with top government officials.

Heterogeneity of inputs was measured by counting every commodity category used by an industry in the 1992 Benchmark Input-Output tables. Heterogeneity of demands was measured by identifying every commodity category produced by each industry and then, for each of those categories, all purchasing industries, so that the count includes every industry customer for every commodity category produced. Both measures were standardized and aggregated into a multidimensional construct.

Dollars spent on contract work as a percentage of the total cost of materials for an industry. Data were obtained from the 1997 Census of Manufacturers and converted from the seven-digit NAICS level to the four-digit SIC level using NAICS-SIC concordance tables.

Percentage-based variables for each industry were created by dividing employment in each alternative work arrangement by total employment in that industry. The two arrangements used, which were the most explicitly temporary, were contract agency work and temporary help agency work. These measures were then aggregated to create an index of use of alternative work arrangements.

Counts of strategic alliances by industry, formed from the primary SIC code of each partner in each alliance, divided by the number of firms in an industry to get a measure of the degree of alliance formation. Data on alliances formed in 1997 were used.

A measure of overall modularity created by standardizing each of the three previous dependent variables and then combining them, with the three dimensions equally weighted. The formula is the sum of the z-scores of percent use of contract work, percent use of alternative work arrangements, and degree of alliance formation for each industry.

A dummy variable (0 = "no," 1 = "yes") indicating whether each industry had a registered member of the American National Standards Institute that developed and administered standards for that industry.

Average total factor productivity (TFP) growth rate over 1980-94 at the four-digit SIC level, as reported in the Bartelsman-Gray database. TFP growth is based on a five-factor production function (capital, production worker hours, nonproduction workers, nonenergy materials, and energy) and is calculated as the growth rate of output (real shipments) minus the revenue-share-weighted average of the growth rates of each of the five inputs.

Three measures were standardized and combined (alpha = .89): number of industry competitors, the inverse of the four-firm market concentration, and the inverse of the Herfindahl-Hirschmann index of market share. The number of firms in each industry was averaged over the five-year period 1992-96 as reported by Dunn & Bradstreet; market concentration and the Herfindahl-Hirschmann index were obtained from the U.S. Census of Manufacturers for 1992.

Calculated as the percentage of team members' total years of experience accrued in international assignments. The top management team was defined as the top two tiers of an organization's management, yielding teams of approximately six members. Teams were assessed in 1988 and 1993.
time_window: 1988 and 1993 (two years before each global strategic posture observation)

description: Educational background was a categorical variable; using Wiersema and Bantel's (1992) coding scheme, executives' educational backgrounds were classified as in the arts, the sciences, engineering, business and economics, or law. TMT members with M.S. or B.S. degrees, and those with Ph.D. degrees in the sciences, were coded as science specialists. The degree of heterogeneity was calculated using Blau's (1977) index, 1-Σ(Pi)², where Pi is the percentage of individuals in the ith category.

Functional background was a categorical variable; team members' functional backgrounds were coded as being predominantly marketing, distribution, sales, research and development, production, engineering, finance and accounting, law, or general. The degree of heterogeneity was calculated using Blau's (1977) index, 1-Σ(Pi)², where Pi is the percentage of individuals in the ith category.

Calculated using the coefficient of variation of a TMT's firm tenure (standard deviation divided by the mean). The coefficient of variation is preferred among inequality measures when interval-level data such as age or time are used.

A composite measure based on Sullivan's (1994) measure of firm internationalization. The indicators of its three dimensions-foreign sales (ratio of foreign sales to total sales), foreign production (foreign-owned assets as a percentage of total assets), and geographic diversity (presence in any of Ronen and Shenkar's ten cultural zones, each zone counted as .10)-were summed because each indicator had the same metric and the three were highly correlated. The higher the number, the more expansive the firm's posture; each component is a ratio variable ranging from 0.0 to 1.0, so the composite ranges from 0.0 to 3.0. To reduce the effects of annual aberrations, values were averaged over 1990 and 1991 and over 1995 and 1996.

A variation of the environmental instability measure developed by Dess and Beard (1984), capturing the volatility of a firm's net sales in each of its four-digit SIC industries. A variable for each year was regressed on a variable for net industry sales, using five years of data for each equation, following the equation yt = b0 + b1t + at, where y is industry sales, t is year, and a is the residual; volatility was the standard error of the regression slope coefficient divided by average sales. Greater environmental uncertainty is indicated by larger values of volatility, and values were averaged for the two-year period between the TMT and global strategic posture measurements.
time_window: five-year windows preceding each measurement; values averaged for the two-year period between the TMT and global strategic posture measurements

description: Human capital was measured on two dimensions: quality of the law school attended by partners (a proxy for articulable knowledge and prestige) and total experience as partners in the focal firm (a proxy for firm-specific tacit knowledge). For each firm, an average ranking of the law schools from which all the partners had graduated was calculated (total ranking, reverse-scored, divided by the number of partners). Average firm-specific experience as a partner was computed by dividing total experience reported by all responding partners by their number. The two dimensions were factor-analyzed and combined using standardized factor scores.

Leverage was defined as the total number of associates in a firm divided by the total number of partners, indicating the average number of associates assigned to each partner; it represents the structure of the primary human capital in these firms. The measure was transformed using a logarithmic transformation.

Service diversification was measured with a Herfindahl index, computed as the sum of squares of the proportion of total lawyers in the five largest practice areas of each law firm. Because this value is inversely related to diversification, the value of the variable was subtracted from 1.

A Herfindahl index was calculated for the proportion of lawyers in the four largest branch locations (in separate cities). Only domestic branches were included in the calculation. To ensure that high values represented greater diversification, the variable was subtracted from 1.

Firm performance was defined as the ratio of net income to total firm revenue, derived from a profitability index reported annually by the American Lawyer, the API, which is the ratio of profits per partner to revenue per lawyer. The authors recalculated the index by removing the number of partners from the numerator and the number of lawyers from the denominator; the resulting measure can be interpreted as return on sales.

Entry modes were initially classified as exporting, licensing, operation of foreign sales offices, joint venturing, or operation of wholly owned subsidiaries. Entries involving licensing or joint venturing, which required collaboration with outsiders, were treated as collaboration. A dummy variable was created for each firm and was coded 1 if it used an entry mode involving collaboration or 0 otherwise.
time_window: sixth year of each firm's operation

description: Profitability was measured as the average return on sales (ROS) within each foreign market during years 6, 7, and 8 of each firm's existence. For each entry, data were collected regarding profit generated from that market and sales there.
time_window: years 6, 7, and 8 of each firm's existence

variable_name: sales growth in each foreign market
description: Sales growth in each foreign market was calculated on an annual basis from year 5 to year 8 of each firm's existence, adjusted by subtracting the industry average growth rate during the same time period, and the results for the three time periods were averaged. The formula compares the change in foreign market sales with the change in industry sales for years 6, 7, and 8.
time_window: year 5 to year 8 of each firm's existence

description: For each firm, R&D intensity was measured by computing the ratio of R&D expenses to sales. The resulting quotient was then adjusted for industry effects by subtracting the industry average R&D intensity. Industry-average data were collected from aggregate data provided on COMPUSTAT PC+ for each firm's four-digit primary SIC code.
time_window: sixth year of each firm's operation

description: For each firm, advertising intensity was measured by computing the ratio of advertising expenses to sales. The resulting quotient was then adjusted for industry effects by subtracting the industry-average advertising intensity. Industry-average data were collected from aggregate data provided on COMPUSTAT PC+ for each firm's four-digit primary SIC code.
time_window: sixth year of each firm's operation

description: Respondents were instructed to assess results achieved by their project over the last two months. A rating of 1 indicated that results were far worse than expected, and a rating of 5 indicated that results were far better than expected. These assessments were applied to ten generic objectives common to new business development projects. Item scores were averaged across a project's members and then totaled and averaged across items to obtain an overall grand average.

Respondents were asked to position their projects between two semantic differentials, with a value of 1 indicating lower autonomy and a value of 5 indicating greater autonomy. The construct covers autonomy with respect to goals, roles, and authority structures. Responses were averaged across a project's members and across items.

Respondents were asked to position the typical way people handled operational tasks between two semantic differentials. A rating of 1 positioned a project closer to the "supervised" end of the dimension, and a rating of 5 positioned the project closer to the "autonomous" end. Responses were averaged across a project's members and across items.

Respondents were asked to provide a rating in response to the question, "To what extent are the following project characteristics or factors new to your firm at the moment?" A value of 1 meant "to no extent (not new at all)," and a 5 meant "to a very great extent (entirely new)." The measure captures newness in the product, technology, resources employed, or markets sought. Responses were averaged across a project's members and across items.

In-degree centrality represents the total number of units from which a focal unit has received knowledge. Respondents selected from a list of all units those units that provide their unit with new knowledge or expertise when seeking technical advice inside the organization, and the opposite question was also asked. A knowledge transfer relationship between units i and j was treated as valid if unit i indicated it had provided knowledge to unit j and unit j confirmed receiving knowledge from unit i; with multiple respondents per unit the relationship was valid if indicated by any respondent of the source unit and confirmed by any respondent of the recipient unit. Using validated data, a relational matrix of interunit links was constructed for each company, with the i,jth cell coded 1 if unit i provided its knowledge to unit j.

Following Cohen and Levinthal (1990), R&D intensity is defined as R&D expenditure divided by sales and is used to measure absorptive capacity at the business unit level. Data on R&D expenditure and unit sales were obtained through corporate internal records. Consistent with the data collection period of the other independent variables, 1996 R&D intensity was used.

The innovation achieved rate is the number of new products introduced in a unit in a particular year divided by the unit's target number in that year. Innovation targets were assessed and negotiated between unit managers and corporate managers each year, who considered business unit strategic priorities and industry-related factors when setting them. The achieved rates for all units were collected for the time period 1997-98 through corporate internal records.

The profitability achieved rate is a unit's return on investment in a particular year divided by its target return in that year. Profitability targets were assessed and negotiated between unit managers and corporate managers each year, who considered business unit strategic priorities and industry-related factors when setting them. The achieved rates for all units were collected for the time period 1997-98 through corporate internal records.

Organizational age was defined as the number of days that a fund family had been in existence. The natural logarithm of age was used because the difference between age 365 days and age 565 days is not the same as the difference between age 1,000 days and age 1,200 days. The variable was measured annually and lagged by one year.

The external connections of a mutual fund family were measured by counting the number of subadvisors it used; if a fund family employed only one subadvisor, its external connections would take on a value of 1. The authors measured external connections as the natural logarithm of the number of ties to subadvisors, to account for nonlinear effects. The variable was measured annually and lagged by one year.

A dummy variable coded 1 if a focal fund family had introduced a new mutual fund, following Boeker's (1997) definition wherein product innovation occurred when a given product offered in a particular year had not previously been offered. A fund family was defined as having introduced a new mutual fund if it entered any of the 33 mutual fund categories maintained by Morningstar. The variable was measured annually and lagged by one year.

A dummy variable coded 1 when a focal fund family recruited a portfolio manager employed in a stock fund in another fund family. Because investment advisors can simultaneously be involved in several fund families, a recruitment event includes only moves in which a portfolio manager changed fund families and also changed advisors. The analyses were conditioned on a fund family already being in existence, and a recruitment event was defined as the entry of executives other than the founder of a fund family. The variable was measured annually and lagged by one year.
The number of days a recruit had served as a portfolio manager in the open-ended mutual fund industry; days are the unit of this variable.

The percentile ranking of the latest annual performance of the fund from which a recruit originated among all other funds with the same investment objective; percentile rankings based on annual performance were chosen rather than three-year and five-year performance because annual performance determines the status of managers among investors. When a manager managed more than one fund, the average percentile ranking of those funds was used. For ease of interpretation, the authors reverse-coded Morningstar's rankings, so that higher rankings equated higher performance.
time_window: latest annual performance at the time of recruitment

description: The total net asset value of the fund at which a recruit last worked. If a recruit had worked for multiple funds, the authors added up their net asset values.
The number of days in which the fund that had last employed a recruit had been in existence.

variable_name: recruit tenure, competitor fund performance, size and age
description: Recruit characteristics were captured by four variables describing hired portfolio managers and their previous employers: recruit industry tenure, recent performance of the origin fund, size of that fund, and age of that fund. They were entered as the recruit-expertise predictors of product innovation.

Coded 1 if a new fund had a portfolio manager who was shared by this fund and an existing fund or funds; coded 0 if the new fund had a portfolio manager dedicated solely to it. The sample was restricted to new funds managed by a single portfolio manager.

If the investment objective category of the product-line extension matched that of existing funds in the fund family, the portfolio managers currently working with these funds were classified as having current related experience. It was calculated as the total number of days that all the managers with current related experience worked on funds in the same investment category as the product-line extension, including funds in other fund families in the industry and even with interruptions. The measure was taken as of the day before the starting date of the new fund and was logged.
time_window: as of the day before the starting date of the new fund

description: Portfolio managers' experience was classified as previous and related if they had previously worked (but were not currently working) on a fund in the same objective category as the product-line extension at any time in their careers. The measure was the number of days managers in the fund family had worked in the investment objective category of the new fund in the past (not currently), including all industry experience even if there were interruptions. It was measured as of the day before the starting date of the new fund and was logged.
time_window: as of the day before the starting date of the new fund

description: All other managers were classified as having unrelated experience. The measure was the total industry experience of all managers in the fund family with unrelated experience, taken as of the day before the starting date of the new fund and logged.
time_window: as of the day before the starting date of the new fund

description: Task complexity was assigned a 1 for an equity fund (high task complexity) and a 0 for a bond fund (low task complexity). Equity funds are more complex because investment in equities requires more information processing than investing in bond funds, and portfolio managers have greater discretion and a greater variety of securities from which to choose. The authors note they could not measure task complexity at the level of the new fund and used investment objective category as the archival proxy.

Institutional influence coded in terms of a period effect. It was a dummy variable coded 1 for years following the major shift in 1965, the year in which Medicare and Medicaid were inaugurated, and 0 before. The coding rests on the observation that 1965 reflects the major shift in the stability and coherency of institutional processes in this field.

Measured by the number and types of health-related regulatory bodies operating in various capacities at the federal level. The measure includes departments, bureaus, offices, and independent boards and commissions. The data were originally collected by Scott and colleagues (2000).

The number of specialties and subspecialties in existence each year of the study period. Recognition of an area by the American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS, 1996) was the criterion for inclusion of a specialty or subspecialty. Subspecialties extending from each area grew from 38 to 96 during the sample period; the measure does not include foundings of specific specialty associations.
time_window: each year of the study period

description: As an indicator of the movement toward a greater public voice in the institutional logics of health care, the number of popular magazines devoted to health-related issues was tracked. Public attention was measured as counts from the Reader's Guide to Periodical Literature, which offers a cumulative index to periodicals of general interest published in the United States since 1900. These counts were standardized by the total number of titles indexed each year.
time_window: annual counts over the study period

description: Yearly count of foundings of identity-based associations, defined as field-authorized professionals and occupational groups. A founding was recorded when an association name appeared for the first time in one of the archival sources. The name, type of membership, and activity areas were used to categorize associations; the initial seven categories were recoded so that categories of physician associations, medical professional associations, nonmedical professional associations, and associations of organizations were classified as identity-based.

Yearly count of foundings of advocacy-based associations, formed on the basis of advocacy or claims making on behalf of interested roles in the field. A founding was recorded when an association name appeared for the first time in one of the archival sources. Public interest or advocacy groups and funds, centers, or foundations were classified as advocacy-based.

Density was calculated as cumulative yearly sums of foundings minus failures for the population of identity-based associations. A squared (quadratic) term for all densities was also calculated and divided by 1,000 for ease of computation. These measures were used to measure cross-density effects as well.

Density was calculated as cumulative yearly sums of foundings minus failures for the population of advocacy-based associations. A squared (quadratic) term for all densities was also calculated and divided by 1,000 for ease of computation. These measures were used to measure cross-density effects as well.

Performance-contingent compensation measured as pay mix: total variable pay (bonuses, LTIP, and stock option awards) divided by total pay. Contingent forms of pay were lagged one year since these forms of pay are determined and awarded in the year following the year in which they are earned; the ratio was then averaged over the five-year study period.
time_window: 1994-98, averaged over five years; contingent pay lagged one year

description: Total CEO compensation combined cash and noncash forms of income: salary, bonus, long-term incentive pay (LTIP), the value of stock options awarded, and all other pay. Contingent forms of pay were lagged one year; these forms of pay were summed annually and averaged over the five-year study period.
time_window: 1994-98, averaged over five years; contingent pay lagged one year

description: One of two market-based measures of firm risk taken from the CAPM, which was estimated using five years (1994-98) of monthly stock price and treasury bill data.
The second market-based measure of firm risk taken from the CAPM, which was estimated using five years (1994-98) of monthly stock price and treasury bill data.

Calculated similarly to the market risk measures but with quarterly ROA replacing stock price in the model: quarterly firm ROA was regressed on the quarterly average ROA of all S&P 500 firms. The parameter estimate from this model becomes the measure of systematic income risk.

Calculated similarly to the market risk measures but with quarterly ROA replacing stock price in the model: quarterly firm ROA was regressed on the quarterly average ROA of all S&P 500 firms. The error term from this model becomes the measure of unsystematic income risk.

Firm performance measured as total stock returns over the five years of the study, included to allow for comparison with prior research. Total stock return includes the appreciation of stock price over the period plus dividends paid.

variable_name: systematic and unsystematic market and income risk
description: Firm risk was measured with four variables: systematic market risk (beta), unsystematic market risk (sigma), systematic income risk and unsystematic income risk. The market measures came from the CAPM using five years (1994-98) of monthly stock data, and the income measures used ROA in the same model.

The survey provided data on executives' salaries and bonuses. Cash compensation was computed as the sum of base salary and annual bonus, and the sum was then "logged" so that extreme values would not bias the results. Cash compensation was lagged one year by gauging it at time t + 1 (salary paid at t + 1 plus bonus paid at t + 1 based on performance at time t), while all other variables were gauged in the preceding year at time t.

For each individual in the survey, the company provided information on the functional department, broken out by the category that the employee worked in. Dummy variables denote an employee's functional position. Finance position included finance executives, controllers, treasurers, payroll managers, cash managers, and budget managers; marketing position included marketing, sales, and advertising; all engineering and research and development executives were grouped into research and development position. Individuals were coded into the international responsibility position category if they reported having any international responsibilities, part- or full-time, and this position classification superseded the other possible functional classification for a given executive. Positions in general administration, operations, and law collectively constituted the omitted category.

Four categories of strategic resource allocations were examined: (1) financial (the logged value of capital expenditures and absolute level of diversification calculated as the number of four-digit SIC codes reported by a firm), (2) marketing (the logged value of advertising expenses), (3) research & development (the logged value of R&D expenses), and (4) international (the logged value of foreign sales). In general, the larger the value of a strategic resource allocation variable, the greater a firm's dependence on the functional area corresponding to that allocation variable.

A dummy variable was created in which 1 equals "CEO same," and 0 equals "CEO different." The Forbes annual compensation survey categorizes CEO functional background into categories ranging from "administrative" to "technical" and identifies a single background for each CEO; potential areas of similarity in ten Forbes categories were clustered into six groups: administration, finance and investments, legal, operations, research and development, and retail, sales, and marketing. Two raters coded the similarity scheme and reached full agreement.

Executives' organizational rank was captured with dummy codes for levels 2 and 3, excluding level 1 (the CEO); level 4 was the omitted category. Level 2 includes the most senior executives (chief operating officer, chief financial officer, president, division president), level 3 the next tier such as senior and executive vice presidents, and level 4 higher-level vice presidents.

Education was simply measured as years of formal education, so those with high school educations would have 12 years and those who stopped after completing their undergraduate degrees would be coded as having 16 years. Work experience was computed as age minus education minus 6, assuming individuals started their formal educations at age six and began working immediately after completing their educations; firm tenure was also examined and produced no substantive differences. Both education and work experience were modeled with squared terms to account for their likely curvilinear (inverted U-shaped) effects on pay.

The market price of the firm's stock at the beginning of each month was subtracted from the weighted average strike price of all the CEO's option grants, and the measure was assessed monthly. The strike price of each option grant was weighted by the number of options associated with the grant, and the weighted average of all grants was used. Positive values indicate the degree to which a CEO's options are underwater.
scale: dollar spread (may be positive or negative)

description: A dummy variable for whether or not an option-repricing event occurred during a monthly spell between July and December 1998. A repricing event was coded as having occurred if any prior option grant offered to a firm's CEO was reported as being repriced during the last six months of 1998.

The percentage of outstanding voting shares owned collectively by all institutions at the beginning of the period of study. The measure was converted to a natural logarithm, with a value of one added to all observations before logging because some companies had zero institutional ownership.
time_window: beginning of the period of study

description: The percentage of outstanding voting shares owned by a firm's CEO at the beginning of the period of study.
time_window: beginning of the period of study

description: Three variables were used to measure CEO structural power: a dummy for CEO duality, the number of board members appointed after the CEO took office, and a dummy for whether or not the company had a staggered board. Classifying directors into different groups and staggering the elections of the classes so that only a minority of a board can be voted out in any one year makes it more difficult to take over a company and oust its CEO.
scale: two dummy variables and a count

description: Visibility was assessed as the net sales of a firm in fiscal 1997 plus the total cash compensation (1998 base salary + 1997 annual bonus) of the CEO. Sales was used as a proxy for firm size, a use well established in the literature and consistent with prior repricing research.
time_window: fiscal 1997 sales; 1998 base salary and 1997 annual bonus

description: The compounded survival rate of PA-firms divided by the compounded survival rate of non-PA-firms from 1925 to the year under consideration, indicating the extent to which PA-firms enjoyed a higher survival rate than non-PA-firms. Firms that changed their organizational structures in the corresponding period were excluded from the calculation.
time_window: compounded from 1925 to the year under consideration; lagged by one observation period

description: The compounded growth rate of PA-firms divided by the compounded growth rate of non-PA-firms from 1925 to the year under consideration, indicating the extent to which PA-firms enjoyed a higher growth rate than non-PA-firms. Growth rates are averages weighted by firm size, and firms that changed their organizational structures in the corresponding period were excluded.
time_window: compounded from 1925 to the year under consideration; lagged by one observation period

description: Identified by investigating the status of accountants in firms: if a firm had at least one associate accountant for the first time in its history, the adoption of a partner-associate form was flagged. Having adopted the PA-form, a firm was removed from the data set because it was no longer a candidate for mimetic adoption; nonadopters and firms that dissolved or were acquired were right-censored.
time_window: one- to five-year observation intervals from 1925 to 1990

description: Measured by counting the number of ties that accountants at a specific firm had with accountants in PA-firms: the summation over all accountants at a firm of the ties-to-adopters measure used for exposure to the adoption norm. Ties were traced through career changes: when two accountants were affiliated with a firm in any overlapping period, they were assumed to have network ties with each other thereafter. Indirect ties were not considered.
time_window: ties at time t; lagged by one observation period

description: For each accountant the number of ties to accountants in PA-firms was divided by the total number of ties to accountants in other firms, and individual exposure was aggregated to the firm level to produce a proxy for firm-level exposure to the adoption norm. An accountant outside a particular firm could contribute more than one tie to the index.
time_window: at time t; lagged by one observation period

variable_name: percentage of adopters among similarly sized firms
description: Size similarity was defined as the ratio of the size of another office to the size of the focal office, with firm size measured by the number of accountants; all values falling within the range of 0.5 to 2.0 comprised a size cohort. The cohort was used to determine the percentage of similarly sized firms that had a PA-form.
time_window: corresponding observation period; lagged by one observation period

variable_name: percentage of adopters among geographically proximate firms
description: Measured by the percentage of PA-form adopters in the province in which a focal firm had the largest number of offices for the corresponding observation period.
time_window: corresponding observation period; lagged by one observation period

description: For each firm-year observation, coded as 1 if the firm exited the market in a given year, and as 0 otherwise. A firm was treated as exiting when it disappeared from the industry listing; identifiable mergers were treated as the continuance of the larger firm and the exit of the smaller firm.
time_window: each year of a firm's existence, 1908-1991

variable_name: life cycle phase (growth phase vs. mature phase)
description: The growth phase was measured as the period between commercialization of an industry and the transformation of entry barriers, when entry significantly declines; the mature phase was measured as the period after that point, including the period of suppressed entry and the subsequent resurgence in entry. A generalized discriminant analysis procedure was applied to each industry's data on annual gross entry rates to determine the delineating year.

For each year of a firm's existence, age was calculated as the number of years since the time of industry entry. To account for nonlinear effects of age, both age and age squared were included in the model.
time_window: each year of a firm's existence

description: Firm size was measured as the asset size listed in the Thomas Register for each year of a firm's existence; asset size is reported in categories of current dollar assets. The data on size were adjusted for inflation and the logarithm of asset size was used in the analysis.
time_window: each year of a firm's existence

description: The logarithm of rank of entry, where rank is measured by the year in which a firm entered an industry relative to the time of commercial introduction. Because observations were pooled across industries, the scale was standardized by dividing the year of firm entry by the year of an industry's transition between phases before taking the logarithm.
time_window: year of firm entry relative to industry commercialization

variable_name: relative density and relative density squared
description: Relative density was defined as the density in a particular year divided by the peak density observed in an industry. To account for nonlinear effects, both contemporaneous density and contemporaneous density squared were used in the model.

Two questions using seven-point semantic differential bipolar scales with a 'not applicable' category, with comparative wording relative to competitors. The measure was anchored to the midpoint of the time period, creating a lag of several years between the assessment of installed base and the lockout. A value of 1 corresponded to a very large installed base and 7 to a small installed base. Items for the factor were averaged for subsequent analysis, and the variable was coded so that an increase should show an increase in the probability of lockout.

Two questions using seven-point semantic differential bipolar scales with a 'not applicable' category, with comparative wording relative to competitors, asked only for technologies that require complementary goods. A value of 1 corresponded to wide availability of complementary goods and 7 to little availability. Items for the factor were averaged for subsequent analysis, and the variable was coded so that an increase should show an increase in the probability of lockout.

A composite of two measures: the firm's investment in research and development related to the product technology relative to that of competitors, and the degree to which the firm emphasized learning or development of new capabilities. The two items were measured on seven-point semantic differential bipolar scales and were averaged for subsequent analysis. Actual research expenditures were not used because firms do not report R&D expenditures consistently, not all learning is accrued through R&D projects, and R&D is not reported for separate product categories.

Two questions using seven-point semantic differential bipolar scales with a 'not applicable' category and comparative wording relative to competitors. A value of 1 corresponded to very early entry and 7 to late entry. Items for the factor were averaged, and entry time was entered into the model once untransformed and once squared to test a U-shaped relationship. To reduce collinearity between the timing variables, they were first centered by subtracting the mean response of 2.90.

A dichotomous variable coded 0 or 1, used to minimize ambiguity by selecting only extreme cases of lockout. The original lockout cases were screened so that the lockout resulted from reasons related to technology standards (verified through news retrieval sources) and met a minimum threshold of failure: either the technology was withdrawn from the market, or the sponsoring firm had conceded defeat in a market and ceased promotion of the product.

Dummy variable coded 1 for relay succession and 0 otherwise. A succession was classified as relay when the new CEO was an executive of the given firm with firm tenure of at least two years at the time of succession and was the heir apparent to the predecessor CEO, identified as having had the title of president or COO or both before the succession occurred.
The total number of executives other than an incumbent CEO who had the position of executive vice president (EVP) or higher in the year prior to a succession.

Measured using three dimensions: return on assets (ROA), return on sales (ROS), and the ratio of market value to the book value of shareholders' equity. The average for the three years prior to succession was calculated for each measure and then standardized within the sample; the average of the three standardized dimensions yielded a composite measure.

Measured with the same procedure as presuccession firm performance applied to corresponding data for the three years after a succession occurred; the composite averages the standardized ROA, ROS, and market-to-book dimensions.

Following Finkelstein and Hambrick's (1990) measurement of strategic persistence, six strategic dimensions were used: advertising intensity (advertising/sales), research and development intensity (R&D/sales), plant and equipment newness (net P&E/gross P&E), nonproduction overhead (SGA expenses/sales), inventory levels (inventories/sales), and financial leverage (debt/equity). A firm's presuccession three-year variance was computed for each dimension, variance scores were standardized within the sample, and the average of the six standardized dimensions yielded the composite.

Measured in a similar fashion to presuccession strategic instability, using the six strategic dimensions and their standardized three-year variances, with corresponding data for the three years after a succession.

Following Dess and Beard (1984), measured as a composite of instability in sales growth and employment growth in an industry at the four-digit SIC level. Instability in industry sales was calculated as the standard error of the regression slope coefficient divided by the mean value of sales in the three years prior to succession, and instability in industry employment was calculated with the same procedure; the two standardized dimensions were averaged.

Measured similarly to presuccession industry instability, as the composite of standardized instability in industry sales growth and industry employment growth, with corresponding data for the three years after a succession.

An individual's dissimilarity to the rest of the team. For age, the mean squared Euclidean distance from each incumbent team member j; for the three dichotomous categorical variables (career path, industry experience, academic status), 1 minus the squared proportion of team members with the same background (Blau's index). Each of the four distance measures was standardized and their average was used as the overall demographic distance measure. Distances were calculated for all executive management team members, both migrants and incumbents.
level: individual (entrant or team member at risk of exit)

variable_name: exit from top executive management team
description: The instantaneous rate of individual exit from a top executive management team, where t represents a manager's tenure on the team. Estimated as piecewise constant rate exponential models with the covariate effects specified as log-linear functions; team histories were split into yearly intervals and time-varying covariates updated at the beginning of each interval, with robust standard errors taking the clustering of observations on individuals into account. Tenure was split into four durations: zero to three, three to five, five to ten, and more than ten years.

The proportion of board members originating from inside a company subtracted from the proportion of management team members originating from inside the company, with the proportions weighted by average top team and board tenure, respectively. The same procedure was followed for industry experience, and the two measures were standardized and summed to obtain one proxy for the executive management team's relative power.

Organizational performance was measured as yearly gross return on sales and as the difference in ROS from year t - 1 to year t, thus including the effect of both the absolute level of and the change in a firm's performance.

A Herfindahl index (the sum of squared proportions) on the spread of firm turnover in ten different activities was calculated and subtracted from 1. The measure does not weight for the relatedness of the ten activities.

Each firm's yearly net turnover growth rate subtracted from those of its four Big Five competitors combined, on the idea that crowding occurs, and competitive pressures are most severely felt, when a focal company's growth lags behind that of its major competitors.

A clinical area was classified as a functional structure if clinical professionals for that area reported through a traditional hierarchy to managers of departments for their respective clinical disciplines. It was classified as a product-line structure if the professionals reported to a manager outside the traditional discipline-based hierarchy who had budget authority and accountability for producing a largely comprehensive set of patient care services for that clinical area. For multivariate analyses a dichotomous variable assigned product line a value of 1 and functional a value of 0. Only clinical areas that had had the same structure in place for at least 12 months prior to data collection were included.
time_window: structure in place for at least 12 months prior to data collection; classified in 2001

description: A four-item scale concerning the extent to which professionals met the needs and expectations of patients, constructed by integrating and modifying items from scales previously used to assess effects of cross-functional structures. An example item is 'Patients and their families are satisfied with the services provided in the clinical units I service.' Each item had a five-point response set based on level of agreement/disagreement, and the variable was included in the multivariate analyses as a continuous measure.

A three-item scale concerning the extent to which professionals developed new ideas for improving patient care. An example item is 'We are always developing new practices and better ways of caring for patients in the clinical units I service.' Each item had a five-point response set based on level of agreement/disagreement, and the variable was included in the multivariate analyses as a continuous measure.

A four-item scale concerning the extent to which individuals had opportunities for developing knowledge and skills for their careers. An example item is 'I regularly have opportunities for professional development.' Each item had a five-point response set based on level of agreement/disagreement, and the variable was included in the multivariate analyses as a continuous measure.

A four-item scale concerning an employee's general satisfaction with his/her job. An example item is 'All things considered, I am satisfied with my job.' Each item had a five-point response set based on level of agreement/disagreement, and the variable was included in the multivariate analyses as a continuous measure.

A categorical variable gathered from the firm's archival records in consultation with the R&D manager who served as liaison for the study. Projects were coded as ongoing, completed, or terminated. When collecting each panel of data, the status of each project that had been ongoing at the last panel was verified with the liaison.

A measure completed by project team members that assessed the extent to which management strongly advocated the pursuit of a product development project. Higher scores indicate that a project was strongly supported and given a higher priority by management. Between-project variability was significant (F = 6.22, p < .01), and the median rwg was .88. The appendix gives the items and response scales.

A ten-item measure adapted from previous work on R&D management, responded to by the team leader and a department head. A higher score indicates that a respondent perceived the project as more likely to achieve its technical and commercial objectives. Between-project variability was significant (F = 3.35, p < .01), and the median rwg was .99.
scale: 0-100% and 1 = "not at all" to 5 = "to a great extent"

description: A four-item measure adapted from Green et al. (1995) of the speed at which the science and technology being used in the new product development project was emerging in the general scientific community, responded to by a senior R&D manager. A higher score indicates that the focal area of science and technology knowledge was rapidly developing. This measure was collected annually as opposed to every six months; where the R&D executive provided data only in panels 1 and 3, the fill-forward option in STREG replaced missing data in panels 2 and 4.

A five-item measure adapted from Green et al. (1995) that assessed the experience a firm had in commercializing such a product, responded to by team members, with a higher score indicating that the firm had more experience. Between-project variability was significant (F = 3.10, p < .01), and the median rwg was .91.

A ten-item measure that assessed the experience a firm had with the science and technology germane to the project being assessed, responded to by team members, with a higher score indicating that the firm has more experience. Between-project variability was significant (F = 2.02, p < .01), and the median rwg was .95.

A nine-item measure that assessed the magnitude of the resource commitment made to a project, responded to by team members, with a higher score indicating a greater resource investment in the project. Between-project variability was significant (F = 2.31, p < .01), and the median rwg was .96.

Target R&D intensity is measured as R&D expenditures divided by sales. The authors note that this variable does not capture all forms of knowledge intensity but is a well-accepted measure useful for the inquiry. Firm R&D intensity was available for 2,313 transactions that could be cross-referenced in COMPUSTAT.

SDC provided an indicator variable for lockup agreements. Agreements stipulating both lockup options and lump-sum payments were coded as lockup agreements, and other cases were recorded as zero. Either may discourage bidding wars by granting an advantage to a favored bidder.

A dummy variable coded via four steps: the SDC database indicated the presence of a rival or rivals; the database was indexed by target and events were coded as bidding wars when rivals were found; all management buyouts were researched in the archives of 6,000 newspapers to identify rival bidders; and 150 randomly selected cases were researched in the news archives to check for miscoding, with no incorrectly coded observations of bidding wars found. The process did not capture informal expressions of interest or bids withdrawn before any public announcement.

The SDC database reports whether managers participated in each transaction; in other cases buyers were listed as "private investors," a category that sometimes includes managers. In both situations the news archives were searched to identify the extent and nature of management participation. A transaction was coded as an MBO if news accounts confirmed that management's bid was not a defensive response to another bid and that management would have gained control of the firm if their bid succeeded.

Stocks of organizational knowledge were measured in terms of the demographic work experience, years in the industry, of each responding TMT member and knowledge worker. Years of industry experience were averaged for TMT members and knowledge workers across respondents from the same firm to arrive at organizational scores.

variable_name: years of post high school education
description: Stocks of organizational knowledge were measured in terms of the formal education, years of post high school education, of each responding TMT member and knowledge worker. Years of education were averaged for TMT members and knowledge workers across respondents from the same firm to arrive at organizational scores.

Functional heterogeneity was measured with Blau's (1977) heterogeneity index: (1 - sigma i squared), where i is the proportion of the group in the ith category. A high score on this index indicates variability in functional backgrounds among respondents, or functional heterogeneity; a low score represents greater functional homogeneity.

TMT members and knowledge workers were asked about their relationships with each of 13 categories of alters and to identify the number of direct contacts they had for each category. The sum of contacts across each category was the total number of contacts for each respondent, and the measure was the average number of TMT and knowledge worker contacts across respondents. Because the average number of contacts was not normally distributed, the natural logarithmic transformation of the average number of contacts was used in the statistical analyses.

Following Burt and Minor (1983), network range is conceptualized as the number of different status groups (categories of alters) accessed by a network. Thirteen categories of alters were identified, and network range was measured as the proportion of categories to which an organization had at least one link.

Respondents identified the number of contacts within each alter category that were critical to achieving the company's goals and answered questions about those important relationships. Strength of ties was an index including the mean duration of relationship, frequency of interaction, and emotional intensity of these key contacts. Duration was the average number of months the relationships had existed, frequency the average number of contacts per month, and emotional intensity the average response on a five-point scale to how close the relationship was. The three items were standardized and combined in a linear additive index at the firm level of analysis.

Measures of climate were collected from the surveys of knowledge workers, using items from O'Reilly, Chatman, and Caldwell's (1991) instrument. Climate for risk taking was measured with a five-item scale. Respondents assessed their agreement, from 1 = 'strongly disagree' to 5 = 'strongly agree', with statements about their organization's climate. The scale showed good reliability (alpha = .88) and support for aggregation (ICC[1] = .22, ICC[2] = .73).

Measures of climate were collected from the surveys of knowledge workers, using items from O'Reilly, Chatman, and Caldwell's (1991) instrument. Because the original teamwork factor comprised only two items, a third item was developed. Respondents assessed their agreement, from 1 = 'strongly disagree' to 5 = 'strongly agree', with statements about their organization's climate. The scale showed good reliability (alpha = .87) and support for aggregation (ICC[1] = .25, ICC[2] = .71).

Measures were provided by the surveys of the knowledge workers. Fifteen five-point-scaled questions measured the extent to which respondents had access to people or groups with specialized information, were able to absorb and combine information that had been exchanged, and anticipated value from the exchange and combination process. A first-order factor analysis showed 12 items loaded on a single factor with an eigenvalue of 5.73, so the 12 items were combined into a single measure for each individual (alpha = .87), with support for aggregation (ICC[1] = .37, ICC[2] = .74).

variable_name: number of new products and services
description: The measure was the number of new products or services an organization had introduced in the most recent year. These data were collected during the interviews with the CEOs. The measure was significantly correlated with the average percentages of sales spent on R&D (r = .35, p < .01), the number of personnel assigned to R&D (r = .44, p < .01), and sales growth (r = .41, p < .01).

Binary variable that took on a value of 1 if a facility was ISO 14001 certified during a particular annual period, and 0 otherwise. Certification occurs at the facility level and was gathered from a database of ISO 14001-certified facilities.

The natural logarithm of the great circle distance (in miles) from the supplying facility to the nearest member of its major buying industry. Longitude and latitude for each facility came from TRI data, and the major buying industry (the one accounting for the largest percentage of sales) for each selling industry was determined from Bureau of Economic Analysis input-output tables. Supplying facilities were identified by their four-digit SIC code.

The percentage of all goods produced by members of an industry that is shipped to buyers outside of the United States. The variable was created using input-output data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis.

Binary variable that took on a value of 1 if a supplier and a potential buyer (as determined by the Bureau of Economic Analysis input-output tables) were owned by the same corporate parent as the focal facility.

An estimate of the log percentage of each dollar produced by each industry (each SIC code) shipped to a vertically integrated buyer. First, pairs of supplying and buying industries were identified using Bureau of Economic Analysis data; for each supplying industry, the entire 1996 Dun & Bradstreet database of 500,000 facilities was used to calculate the percentage of suppliers owned by a corporation that also owned a facility in the buying industry. Because the volume of exchanges between industries differs widely, this percentage was weighted using shipment data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis input-output tables and then logged to reduce skew.

Binary variable coded 1 if the sources a facility reported for changes to production processes provided evidence of a functioning environmental management system. Since 1991 facilities have reported such changes and their sources as part of their annual TRI submissions. The sources of changes indicating evidence of an operating EMS were internal pollution prevention opportunity audits, materials balance audits, participative team management, and employee recommendations under a formal company program.

The standardized residual, or deviation, between observed and predicted waste generation given a facility's size and industry sector. Waste generation was the toxicity-weighted sum of all Toxic Release Inventory waste generated by the facility in the year, with toxicity measured using the inverse of CERCLA reportable quantities; size was the estimated number of employees at the facility. The sign of the residual was reversed to reflect the fact that more waste than predicted for a facility represented poorer environmental performance.

The number of WOFS entries per year into a particular industry from a particular home country was tabulated; the WOFS form was defined in terms of 100 percent foreign ownership. Foreign entry data were aggregated from the subsidiary level to the home country and industry level, so the unit is the home country-industry-year cell.
Total number of wholly owned foreign subsidiaries from the same home country in the same industry (Community I), counted in the previous year.
Total number of wholly owned foreign subsidiaries from the same home country but in different industries (Community II), counted in the previous year.
Total number of wholly owned foreign subsidiaries in the same industry but from different home countries (Community III), counted in the previous year.
Total number of foreign joint ventures in Community I (same industry and home country), counted in the previous year. The squared term of this variable tests the competition effect.

variable_name: Local acceptance of the WOFS form
description: A keyword search of the People's Daily index identified a total of 644 articles related to FDI in China over 1979-95. Two researchers working independently coded all articles, identifying whether an article addressed issues related to wholly owned foreign subsidiaries in China and, if yes, whether the coverage was favorable or unfavorable to the WOFS form; the raters agreed on about 91 percent of the cases. The number of articles endorsing wholly owned foreign subsidiaries published in the previous year was used as the proxy.

Total operating expenses and management fees divided by total assets, from which the mean expense ratio of all funds in a product category is subtracted, giving a relative cost measure. The authors state that this variable was reverse-coded for ease in interpretability, and that because expense ratios include some marketing expenses, money management related expenses explain much of the variation across funds.

The percent change in net asset value from the previous year, from which the mean performance of all funds in a product category is subtracted to provide a relative fund performance measure. This standard measure excludes flows of assets into and out of funds due to consumer purchases and redemptions of shares, and the authors state that the variable was reverse-coded for ease in interpretability.
time_window: previous year; lagged one year, updated annually

description: A 0/1 dummy variable that tracks whether a new contract to an independent professional money management firm was established by an existing mutual fund, enabling estimation of the probability that a mutual fund established such a contract. Each fund can theoretically experience multiple events.
A dummy variable coded 1 if a mutual fund was categorized as a growth fund in the Wiesenberger Investment Companies Yearbook, and 0 for nongrowth funds.
A dummy variable that took a value of 1 if a mutual fund was located in Boston.
A dummy variable that took a value of 1 if a mutual fund was located in New York.

Respondents were asked, in questions separate from those about vertical partnerships, to indicate the degree to which they were committed to establishing a set of behavioral norms in their horizontal partnerships, as gauged by their efforts to (1) share information, (2) assist each other, and (3) promote fair sharing of cost savings and benefits arising out of joint efforts. The first two items were adapted from Heide and John (1992) and Artz and Brush (2000); the third was adapted from Ring and Van de Ven (1992). Item responses were scaled from 1 ('not at all') to 5 ('to a high extent'), and respondents were asked to consider the past three years of their relationships.
scale: 1 ('not at all') to 5 ('to a high extent')
time_window: past three years of the relationships

description: Respondents were asked, in questions separate from those about horizontal partnerships, to indicate the degree to which they were committed to establishing a set of behavioral norms in their vertical partnerships, as gauged by their efforts to (1) share information, (2) assist each other, and (3) promote fair sharing of cost savings and benefits arising out of joint efforts. The first two items were adapted from Heide and John (1992) and Artz and Brush (2000); the third was adapted from Ring and Van de Ven (1992). Item responses were scaled from 1 ('not at all') to 5 ('to a high extent'), and respondents were asked to consider the past three years of their relationships.
scale: 1 ('not at all') to 5 ('to a high extent')
time_window: past three years of the relationships

variable_name: pooling of demand with peer firms for specialized services
description: To measure the degree to which firms shared resources, respondents were asked the degree to which their firms pooled demand with other peer firms for specialized services such as the efforts of Fundación ExportAR, which assigned a foreign ministry counselor to assist furniture makers in (1) contacting potential foreign customers through their web of consulates in other countries, (2) coordinating and financing their showing products in international fairs, and (3) promoting the country image of Argentina.
scale: 1 ('not at all') to 5 ('to a high extent')

description: To gauge productivity, respondents indicated the number of inventory turns necessary to support 12 months of sales, a metric associated with the performance of production systems. A second measure, the percentage of goods delivered when promised, was highly skewed; because the analysis required normally distributed data, it was dropped from the study.
Rate of 'catalogue turnover,' defined in the survey as both the percentage of revenue from new products and the percentage of new products in a firm's catalogue.
SMEs' access to global markets was measured as the percentage of a firm's total sales that was in foreign markets.

Organizational size is the logarithm of own premiums, which equals total premiums minus premiums reinsured. Each firm's size was adjusted by subtracting a social aspiration level defined as a weighted average of the size of all other sampled firms, with a weighting factor that let corporate form and market niche overlap affect similarity judgments. The difference between actual size and the aspiration level was entered as a spline, and this variable is the part entered when size was below the aspiration level.
time_window: one-year lag of all independent variables

description: Organizational size is the logarithm of own premiums, which equals total premiums minus premiums reinsured, adjusted by subtracting a social aspiration level computed as a weighted average of the size of all other sampled firms. Because the difference between actual size and the aspiration level was entered as a spline, separate variables were entered when size was above and when it was below the aspiration level; this variable is the part entered when size was above the aspiration level.
time_window: one-year lag of all independent variables

description: Performance was operationalized as the loss ratio, the losses on own premiums divided by own premiums, which is a reverse-coded performance measure because managers seek to minimize losses. The loss ratio was adjusted for the aspiration level by subtracting the previous year's loss ratio, and this value was included as loss ratio increase.

An indicator variable set to 1 when the loss ratio was higher than the prior year's loss ratio, that is, when performance was below the aspiration level. This variable was the main effect for the interaction variables used to test whether the reactions to size were different when performance was below the aspiration level.

Firm growth is the ratio of next-period and current-period size, and firm growth rate is this ratio minus 1. The model is made linear by taking logarithms, so the logarithm of size at time t + 1 is specified as a linear function of the covariates and the logarithm of size at time t.

Associated firms were identified by searching the proxy statements of the 30 accused firms for director interlocks to them; all firms in the second group had at least one interlocking director. The number of interlocks between accused and associated firms was also recorded from the associated firms' proxy statements as a control.

Cumulative abnormal return for an associated firm over a two-day event window running from day -1 (one day prior to an allegation) to day 0 (the day of the allegation); the event dates used were the allegation dates on which the respective accused firm experienced reputational penalties. Abnormal returns are computed from a market model estimated over the 300 to 100 trading days prior to the event window, using the value-weighted CRSP index as the market portfolio, and daily abnormal returns are summed over the event window. Confounding announcements one day before, on, and one day after the event date were excluded. The text presents the abnormal return, market model and CAR expressions in equation form.
Dummy dependent variable coded 1 if an associated firm had a significant, negative CAR over the two-day event window and 0 otherwise; 45 (18.4%) out of the 244 associated firms were coded 1.

variable_name: audit committee chair of associated firm
description: Dummy variable indicating whether an interlocking director held the position of audit committee chair in the associated firm (1, yes; 0, otherwise), extracted from the proxy statements of associated firms.

variable_name: corporate governance committee chair of associated firm
description: Dummy variable indicating whether an interlocking director held the position of corporate governance committee chair in the associated firm (1, yes; 0, otherwise). Publicly listed firms adopt different names for their corporate governance committees, so any board committee dealing with governance issues, such as the compensation of executives, the nomination of directors, or other duties involving the formulation or implementation of corporate governance policies, was defined as a corporate governance committee.

variable_name: audit committee chair of accused firm
description: Dummy variable indicating whether an interlocking director held the position of audit committee chair in the accused firm (1, yes; 0, otherwise); these board positions were the exception to the rule that independent variables were extracted from the proxy statements of associated firms.

variable_name: corporate governance committee chair of accused firm
description: Dummy variable indicating whether an interlocking director held the position of corporate governance committee chair in the accused firm (1, yes; 0, otherwise).
Variable extracted from the proxy statements of associated firms indicating whether the associated firm had an independent board chair; the text does not state its coding.

The number of independent directors divided by the total number of directors in an associated firm. An outside director was classified as independent if the associated firm's proxy statement did not identify the director as having any direct or indirect business relationship with the firm.
The total percentage of shares held by all the independent directors in an associated firm.

The total percentage of shares held by public pension funds (such as New York State Teachers' Retirement System and CalPERS) and professional investment funds (such as FMR Corp. and Nicholas-Applegate Capital Management) in an associated firm. Other institutional investors, such as banks, insurance companies, and private pension funds, were excluded.
The total percentage of shares held by all inside directors (including the CEO) in an associated firm. A squared term for this variable was also entered to test for a curvilinear effect.

Each executive's functional areas were weighted equally, since information on time spent in each function was not available, to compute an intrapersonal functional diversity score for each TMT member; the scores were then averaged across the team following Bunderson and Sutcliffe (2002). The measure was normalized so that, for the entire sample, it ranged from 0 (low intrapersonal functional diversity) to 1 (high intrapersonal functional diversity).

Each executive's dominant functional background was classified into one of eight tracks, and a version of the Herfindahl-Hirschman index was used to capture dominant functional diversity at the TMT level. The index was calculated as 1 - sum of Si squared, where Si is the proportion of a TMT in the i-th category, and can vary between 0 and 1, with values close to 1 indicating higher diversity.

Derived from information on the work address of each TMT member from the S&P Register of Corporations, Directors, and Executives and cross-checked with a variety of other sources. Colocation was calculated with a variant of the Herfindahl-Hirschman index as the sum of Li squared, where Li is the proportion of a TMT in the i-th geographic location.

Following Carpenter and Fredrickson (2001), net sales for all Compustat firms in each four-digit SIC industry were summed by year, and five years of industry-level data were used to gauge uncertainty for the sixth year. For each year and industry, the five previous years' industry sales were regressed on year, and environmental uncertainty was measured as the standard deviation of the regression coefficient divided by industry-average sales over the five-year period.
time_window: five prior years of industry sales (e.g., 1985-89 for 1990)

description: Firm performance was calculated as ROA, captured as annual income before extraordinary items and discontinued operations divided by net assets, averaged over times t + 1 and t + 2. To control for potential industry effects, the corresponding industry-average ROA was subtracted from each firm-level measure.

Optimism was measured using Scheier et al.'s (1994) six-item Life Orientation Test-Revised (LOT-R). Responses were given on a scale from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree,' and were summed into an overall score; high scores indicated a generalized feeling of optimism about the future, and low scores indicated a more pessimistic outlook. The measure produced a Cronbach's coefficient alpha of .80 in the current study.

A single survey item asked respondents to report 'the number of new ventures started prior to the founding of your current business.' Responses ranged from 0 to 6, with nearly half of the respondents (n = 91) having previously founded a business. The authors used the actual number of new ventures started rather than dummy-coding previous founding dichotomously.

Industry-level rate of unpredicted change measured as the standard errors of four regression slopes, in each case with time as the independent variable and industry revenues, number of industry establishments, number of industry employees, and research and development intensity as dependent variables. Following Sharfman and Dean (1991), time was regressed against these variables for the most recent ten-year period, and an index of the standard errors of the regression slopes divided by their respective means was used as the indicator of unpredicted change for each variable. These figures were then standardized and summed into an overall index of environmental dynamism, which produced a Cronbach's coefficient alpha of .69.

One of two objective growth measures of new venture performance, obtained from Dun & Bradstreet. The measure was calculated as the average annual revenue growth over the two years immediately following the collection of the survey data; lagged performance data were used in order to enhance the ability to draw causal inferences.
time_window: two years immediately following survey data collection

description: One of two objective growth measures of new venture performance, obtained from Dun & Bradstreet. The measure was calculated as the average annual employment growth over the two years immediately following the collection of the survey data; lagged performance data were used in order to enhance the ability to draw causal inferences.
time_window: two years immediately following survey data collection

description: Analysts' quarterly earnings forecasts taken from the I/B/E/S database. To test Hypothesis 1, the authors took the median value of the most recent quarterly earnings forecasts for a company; to test Hypothesis 2, the most recent quarterly forecast issued by an analyst for a company; and to test Hypotheses 3, 4 and 5, the first forecast after the survey date of each analyst who covered a firm. In the board composition models the earnings forecast variable is inverted so that higher values indicate less positive forecasts.
time_window: most recent quarterly forecast before the survey date; first forecast after the survey date

description: Stock recommendations divided into five categories: 1 = 'strong sell,' 2 = 'sell,' 3 = 'hold,' 4 = 'buy,' 5 = 'strong buy.' To test Hypothesis 1 the authors took the average value of analysts' most recent recommendations for a firm; to test Hypothesis 2 they used the most recent recommendation issued by a focal analyst for a focal company; and to test Hypotheses 3, 4 and 5 they created dichotomous variables indicating whether a particular analyst had issued an upgrade or a downgrade of a focal firm's stock during the 12 months after the survey date.
scale: 1-5 categories for recommendations; dichotomous for upgrade/downgrade
time_window: 12 months after the survey date for upgrade/downgrade indicators

description: The number of outside directors without known employment or business ties to the firm for which they were directors (other than their directorship) divided by the total number of board members. In the simultaneous equations models the authors estimated the number of formally independent directors and the number of dependent directors separately rather than the ratio.

A survey scale developed by Westphal (1999) on which CEOs and outside directors reported the board's involvement in control of management decision making. Interitem reliability was high in this sample (alpha = .88) and kappa coefficients were greater than .75, suggesting a high level of agreement between CEOs and outside directors about level of board control. In the primary analyses CEO responses were used and board control was measured at time t+1.
time_window: t+1 (year after the year in which analyst appraisals were measured)

variable_name: CEO social influence over the nominating committee
description: The proportion of the firm's nominating committee members with friendship ties to the CEO. Friendship ties were measured with a survey scale prompting CEOs to indicate whether each board member was (1) 'among your closest friends,' (2) 'a friend, but not among your closest friends,' (3) 'less than a friend but more than an acquaintance,' or (4) 'an acquaintance'; interrater agreement was high (weighted kappa = .88).

variable_name: CEO verbal impression management about board control
description: A six-item scale assessing the extent to which CEOs engage in verbal impression management directed toward analysts about board propensity to control management decision making. Respondents indicated how frequently during the prior year they had sought to persuade or convince analysts that their boards engaged in independent control, and two questions directly assessed the objective behind the CEOs' communications; respondents answered separately for each security analyst with whom they had communicated during the past 12 months (alpha = .87).

Number of shares owned by dedicated institutional owners in a given firm-year divided by the total number of shares outstanding for the same firm-year. Owners with at least 1 percent equity were included and were classified annually as dedicated, transient, or quasi-indexer following Bushee's (1998) classification system. Values refer to shares owned at the end of the year prior to the year in which competitive actions occurred.
time_window: end of the year prior to the year of the competitive actions

description: Number of shares owned by transient institutional investors divided by the total number of shares outstanding for a given firm-year. Owners with at least 1 percent equity were included and were classified annually as dedicated, transient, or quasi-indexer following Bushee's (1998) classification system. Values refer to shares owned at the end of the year prior to the year in which competitive actions occurred.
time_window: end of the year prior to the year of the competitive actions

description: A headline was coded as a strategic competitive action when the reported action involved a significant commitment of specific assets, was difficult to implement, would not yield payback for a long time, and was difficult to reverse. Each strategic action was coded by two researchers on four characteristics (commitment of resources, difficulty of implementation, time horizon, irreversibility) using a five-point scale (1 = 'very low/short,' 5 = 'very high/long'). Each individual strategic action was multiplied by its weighted significance, and these results were summed annually by firm.
