Measured as a count variable of the total annual number of tactical competitive actions, following prior competitive dynamics research. Examples of tactical actions include pricing changes and incremental service improvements. No weighting of these actions was required.

A six-item measure assessing the extent to which a joint venture received support from its foreign parent in each of the following areas: product technology, operations technology, operations support, sales/marketing, administrative support, and training. Responses were on a 1 to 5 scale from 'little support' to 'strong support'. The composite reliability was .87, and empirical support for one underlying factor suggested that parent firms tend to use packages containing all six resource types.

Joint venture managers evaluated the influence that the Hungarian parent, the foreign firm, and JV managers had over eight issues by dividing 100 percent among the three groups. The issues were financing, product technology, process technology, operations, sales/marketing, management decisions, administrative support, and pricing decisions. The values on these issues for the foreign parent were combined; the composite reliability was .89.
scale: percentage of influence divided among three groups

description: The respondent was asked how key managers in the Hungarian parent would rate the performance of the joint venture, how key managers in the foreign parent would rate the joint venture's performance, and how the respondent would rate the joint venture's performance (1 to 5, 'poor' to 'excellent'). A fourth item was an aggregate measure in which the respondent rated the firm's performance for the last year on seven activities (1 to 5, 'poor performance' to 'excellent performance'; alpha = .82). Each of these four items was standardized and combined; the composite reliability was .88.
time_window: last year for the aggregate performance item

description: An index of the knowledge a joint venture acquired from its foreign parent. Six items, each with the frame 'to what extent have you learned from your foreign parent,' appraised technological expertise, marketing expertise, product development, foreign cultures and tastes, managerial techniques, and production processes. The composite reliability was .88.

A dichotomous variable indicating the sample to which a joint venture belonged. A 0 indicated a member of the early transition phase sample (the 1993 data), whereas a 1 indicated a member of the late transition phase sample (the 2001 data).
scale: 0 = early transition phase (1993), 1 = late transition phase (2001)

description: Following Dunbar (2000), the authors computed a bank's specialization with a Herfindahl index over the seven market segments in which banks underwrote public offerings. The formula is displayed as an equation: kit is the number of deals in which bank i participated in a given period t and Sj is the number of deals in sector j that bank i participated in. When the measure approached 0 the bank underwrote deals in all seven market sectors and was thus a generalist; when it approached 1 the bank was a specialist. The main effects were centered on industry yearly means before interactions were constructed.

Burt's (1992: 52-53) network efficiency measure, referred to by the authors as structural holes and computed with UCINET. A high value meant that a bank's network contained a large proportion of otherwise disconnected partners, that is, that the bank was located in an open network. The measure was centered on industry yearly means before interactions were constructed.

To measure banks' market shares at time t, the authors allocated the inflation-adjusted dollar value of each offering made during the previous year among the members of the syndicate that underwrote the deal. If a deal involved only one bank as lead manager, that bank was assigned 100 percent of the offering's dollar value; for deals with multiple syndicate members, the lead bank received 50 percent of the underwriting value and the remaining value was split equally among the other members. Each bank's deal values were then divided by the total value of public offerings at time t. The dependent variable is the natural log of market share plus one.

A control for a bank's exposure to market segments with volatile demand for new securities. Using five-year moving windows, the authors computed the standard deviations and means of the counts of offerings in all seven sectors and weighted a bank's exposure to segments by the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean count of offerings it made in that segment; the formula is displayed as an equation. The higher the value, the larger the changes in demand in the market segments to which a bank was exposed.

A dummy variable that measured whether a firm's CEO won any medal in March of each year. It was used to assess whether certification had a positive impact on firm performance (Hypotheses 1a and 1b) and the immediate effect of winning a medal early in the year on that year's total compensation to the CEO (Hypothesis 2). The authors did not distinguish among gold, silver and bronze medals because there was only one gold medal winner each year and a relatively small number of silver medals, and because analysts and CEOs first decided which contestants would win a medal of any type.

variable_name: Medals won in previous five years
description: This variable captured the number of medals a CEO had won over the previous five years, reflecting the authors' reasoning that the effects of certification on compensation were likely to extend beyond one year and that winning multiple medals would increase the impact of certifications on compensation. It was interacted with performance (measured as both ROE and stock return) to test Hypothesis 3.

variable_name: Annual market return (total yearly stock return)
description: Compounded market returns measured as the total yearly stock return of the company, with reinvestment of dividends assumed, using the formula (price end - price beginning + dividends)/price beginning. The measure was obtained from the COMPUSTAT database.

Annual return on common equity, described as a measure of how well a company is using the equity provided by stockholders and commonly used as a basis for awarding incentive pay. The measure was obtained from the COMPUSTAT database.

Excess returns are a firm's actual return minus its expected return. Expected returns were calculated in two ways using the EVENTUS program: with the market model, in which regression analysis relates a firm's return to that of the S&P 500 index using daily returns over an estimation period ending 46 days before the event and extending back 255 days prior to the event, and with market-adjusted returns, which subtract the return of the market during each day of the event period from the firm's daily returns. The resulting excess returns were used to calculate average daily excess returns by summing the average excess returns over the event window, and t-statistics assessed whether these excess returns differed significantly from 0.
time_window: one-, two- and three-day event windows after the announcement, and long-term windows from three days after certification to 30, 90, 180 and 240 days later

description: A CEO's total direct compensation included salary, bonus, the value of restricted stock grants, options granted during the year (valued by the Black-Scholes method), long-term incentive payouts that year, and all other types of cash compensation paid in that year. As in other studies, this variable was transformed into its natural logarithm so that extreme values would not unduly bias the analysis. Data were gathered from the EXECOMP database.

A dichotomous variable set equal to 1 if an agency was public in year t. An agency was considered to be public if its stock was traded independently. The value of the variable was changed in the year a firm's public/private status changed; years of IPOs were excluded from the analyses because the ownership regime was ambiguous in those years.

The primary measure of growth is an agency's percent annual change in revenue. Growth rate appeared to be the most reasonable measure of overall agency performance in this sample, given the absence of financial data on private firms. Two alternative proxies, survival and revenue per employee, were considered but not used as the primary measure.
Firm size was measured as the logarithm of global revenue, adjusted to 1982 dollars.

Creativity was measured as the winning of awards for creative excellence, measured as the number of Clio and Art Director's Club of New York (ADCNY) awards an agency won in a given year. Almost all the awards are intended to recognize creativity rather than marketing effectiveness, and panels of judges comprised of prominent creative personnel from multiple agencies determine these awards. No Clio data were available for 1979, so all 1979 observations were excluded from models using awards measures.

The difference between an agency's actual awards and a predicted number of awards based on a negative binomial model in which awards was regressed on firm size, year fixed effects, and firm growth rate. This construction was used to control for agency size and year effects and to compare the mean award rates of public and private agencies.

The number of citations received by a focal patent from firms other than the one holding the patent, counted in each year after its application year. Self-citations—citations by a firm to its own earlier patents—were omitted. Application year rather than grant year was used to track the vintage of a technology.
time_window: each year after a patent's application year through 1999

description: Indicator variable set to 1 for observations occurring after a patenting firm had exited the industry and to 0 otherwise. Exit was defined as the cessation of a firm's operations in the disk drive industry; acquisitions were not counted as exits.

variable_name: firm age at the time of a patent
description: Calculated by subtracting the year of firm entry into the disk drive industry from the application year of the patent.
time_window: at the time of the patent application

description: The proportion of citations in a patent that were to the firm's own prior patents, corresponding to the self-citation ratio calculated in the NBER database. The larger the value, the more an innovation drew upon the firm's internal knowledge base. The lower bound of the NBER estimate of self-citations was used.
time_window: at the time of the patent application

description: The number of inventors listed on a patent application, used as an indication of the size of the team involved in the innovative research being patented.
time_window: at the time of the patent application

description: Corresponds to the originality score calculated in the NBER data, which counts the number of citations a patent makes within each of the three-digit patent classes and thus captures how widely it draws on technological areas. The modified measure multiplies the original measure by n/(n-1), where n is the number of citations made by a patent.
time_window: at the time of the patent application

description: The dependent variable is the hazard rate of response: the likelihood that a response will be observed at time t, given that no response occurred prior to time t. Each action taken by one firm against another established an opportunity to respond in every host country in which both rival firms competed, and time was measured as the number of days between a rival firm's action against a focal firm and the subsequent response action of the focal firm against the same rival. Observations in the countries where the response took place were coded as responses (failures) and all others as censored; observations still unresolved were right-censored at December 31, 2001.
Geographic distance was measured as the logarithm of the number of kilometers between the capital cities of an MNE's home country and the country of interest.

Geographic distance was measured as the logarithm of the number of kilometers between the capital cities of an MNE's home country and the country of interest; for this variable the country of interest is the initiating country where the rival's attack took place.

Assessed with three variables from the Executive Opinion Survey of the World Economic Forum, which collects the perceptions of 4,000 top executives about the competitive characteristics of 59 countries. Average responses to the statements about administrative procedures, government regulations, and irregular payments were reverse-coded to reflect MNE managers' perceptions of restrictions on their business, then factor-analyzed into a composite measure. The same measure, for different countries, gauges host and home government constraints.

The same composite measure built from three reverse-coded Executive Opinion Survey items was used, albeit for different countries, to gauge home government constraints, that is, constraints in the MNE's home country.

To capture subsidiary control, the authors used the percentage of a subsidiary's equity held by its MNE headquarters. Higher operational control is argued to result from having a greater ownership in a foreign venture.
Gauged as the proportion of a responding MNE's sales that occurred in the initiating country.
A dummy variable indicating whether or not the focal host country was also the initiating country.

The dyadic measure developed by Baum and Korn (1999), which takes into account the strategic significance (centrality) of each country the two firms compete in, where centrality is the proportion of each firm's total sales represented by each country. Indicator variables are set equal to 1 if the two firms are active in a market and 0 otherwise; the level of multimarket contact is computed for each pair of firms at time t.

Dummy variable for franchised establishments, coded 1 for 'franchised' and 0 for 'not franchised'; the company-owned ownership form is the omitted category. Whether a unit was franchised or company-owned in a certain quarter was determined using the brand name, the owner address, and information from the Directory of Hotel & Lodging Companies.

The Herfindahl index, calculated on the basis of the capacity share (number of rooms available) of all firms in a market; the market is defined as the zip code area in which the focal hotel is situated. The interacting variable was centered on its mean.

The primary dependent variable was the average price for a hotel room, measured as an average for each hotel establishment for each three-month period; the natural logarithm of price was used because price followed an approximate lognormal distribution. In reality the price per night usually fluctuates according to length of stay, room size, day of the week and season, which the averaged measure does not capture.

variable_name: rivals' price per room per night
description: The average price the rival hotels in the same market charged, calculated by dividing the sum of rivals' quarterly revenues in a specific market by the total number of room nights sold by rivals in the same period and market. Both a zip code and a firm-centric market definition were used.

Revenues per available room, typically abbreviated as 'RevPAR' by industry practitioners, calculated by dividing the total quarterly revenues by the number of rooms that were available at a focal hotel.

Royalty fee per brand as a percentage of revenues, taken from the annual 'Franchising Supplement' of Hotel & Motel Magazine over the 1997-2002 study period. Because franchise fees were relatively stable and changes were reflected only in new contracts signed after the changes, average franchise fees per brand over the six-year period were used. The variable was centered on the mean for franchised units and set to zero for company-owned establishments.

Count of project investments announced by foreign-domiciled MNCs for developing country i in year t, collected from the Thomson SDC project finance investment database, which compiles regulatory filings and media reports covering dates of project announcement, financing and construction, estimated dollar costs, and lead and junior sponsor syndicate information. Sample projects were sponsored by MNCs domiciled outside the project host country. The mean value of the dependent variable is 2.65, with a standard deviation of 3.40, a minimum value of 0, and maximum value of 19; the average announced investment project is worth approximately $500 million.

Expectations takes on three possible values related to three expected electoral outcomes MNCs might consider: 1 indicates MNC expectations that right-wing parties and policies will prevail, -1 indicates expectations that left-wing parties and policies will prevail, and 0 indicates there is no clear MNC expectation of either right- or left-wing parties and policies coming to power (a close call). MNC expectations during election year t are assumed not to be systematically different from results observed on election days, so the variable is measured by noting election day victors, their partisan orientations, and their victory margins, defined as differences in percentage points between winning and second-place candidates in a final round of voting. Right-wing victories by substantial margins are coded 1, left-wing victories by substantial margins are coded -1, and victory margins of less than 3 percent are close call elections no matter the winner and coded 0.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the incumbent is right-wing and 0 if left-wing. Electoral incumbents and challengers from right-wing and centrist party orientations were aggregated into a single right-wing bloc following the DPI's partisan classification criteria. Approximately 76 percent of the country-year observations involve countries with right-wing incumbents.

A count of optics-related words appearing in the letters to shareholders of each company, normalized by the total number of words in the letter to produce a measure of emphasis on optics relative to other themes. A coding list was developed from the ground up and coding identified the context-specific use of words. The counts were lagged three years because responses to changes in CEO attention are not instantaneous.

Estimates of the amounts of total sales coming from carriers only, constructed from communications sales information based on Compustat segment data where available and supplemented by reports of communications sales from company press releases, media reports and analysts. The portion of these sales specifically made to carriers was adjusted using estimates of emphasis on carriers based on coding by three industry experts. The higher this number, the greater a firm's incentive to invest in optics; the value was logged and entered with a three-year lag.

A measure of the number of years a firm had had an optical product in the market. The data for the timing of launch of the first optical product were developed from company new-product announcements and the CorpTech Directory, using survey responses by participating firms. The variable was entered with a three-year lag.

variable_name: optical patenting emphasis (optical patents as a percentage of total patents)
description: Calculated as a count of all optical patents, based on primary patent class, in the application year of each patent, normalized by a count of a firm's total patents in all classes. The three-digit USPTO classes associated with optics in communications are 356 (optics: measuring and testing), 359 (optical systems and elements), 372 (coherent light generators), and 385 (optical waveguides). The measure ranges from 0 to 100 percent and models are censored at 0 and 100 percent.
time_window: measured in the patent application year

variable_name: Number of related acquisitions since last restructuring
description: Count of the number of horizontal, vertical, and related diversified acquisitions made since the year of a firm's most recent restructuring; the count is reset to 0 in the case of organizational restructuring. An acquisition was coded as horizontal if it took place within the same three-digit SBI code as the firm's core activities, as related-diversified if within the same two-digit SBI code, and as vertical if within the firm's value-added chain.

Firm performance measured through return on assets (ROA). The authors chose ROA because abnormal returns did not serve their purpose of studying when and how synergies are unlocked over time, and because ROA is the least sensitive to biases due to changes in leverage or bargaining power caused by acquisitions. ROA served as the dependent variable in the performance models and as a control in the restructuring models.

A binary measure that equaled 1 if a firm's annual report showed that it undertook organizational restructuring in a given year. The authors first identified all firm-year observations in which restructuring activity took place at the divisional level, which can take the form of creation, elimination, merger, or split-up, and then assigned 1 to those cases in which divisional restructuring spanned multiple divisions and/or the firm transformed its formal structure, switching between functional, product-divisional, geographic area, or matrix structures.

variable_name: Number of related acquisitions between last two restructurings
description: A count variable reporting the total number of related acquisitions a firm had undertaken between its most recent restructuring and the one prior to that (i.e., between the last two restructurings). It differs from the count of acquisitions since the most recent restructuring in that it covers the interval between the last two restructurings.

A clock variable measuring the number of years elapsed since a firm's most recent restructuring; in the event of restructuring, the clock was reset to 0. It serves as the (inverse) indicator of acquisition intensity in the interaction with the number of related acquisitions: the wider the time interval over which a firm undertakes acquisitions, the lower the acquisition intensity.

Measured as the natural logarithm of the total number of acquisitions undertaken by a firm since 1966. The logarithm was used because it captured the decreasing marginal returns that experiential learning is subject to.
Measured as the natural logarithm of the total number of restructurings since 1966.

Binary indicator coded 1 if a potential comanager's status score is at least 0.85. Status was measured with Bonacich's (1987) eigenvector measure of network centrality, calculated from the yearly underwriting management networks in the bond market for investment banks and from the yearly underwriting management networks in syndicate lending for commercial banks. Status scores in each area were divided by the highest status score in that area so that the two rankings are comparable.

Binary indicator coded 1 for low-status banks, defined as banks with maximum status scores of 0.10. Banks identified as secondary investment banks and commercial banks with relative status scores similar to those of the secondary investment banks were excluded from the low-status category.

Network constraint of the potential comanager's ego network, defined from the proportion of a bank's network resources invested in each contact. The measure approaches 0 when ego networks are unconstrained and reaches the maximum of 1 when they are fully constrained. Because constraint varied considerably from year to year for the smaller banks, it was smoothed by using three-year rolling averages.

Binary variable coded 1 if a potential comanager was a commercial bank (an entering firm) and 0 if it was an investment bank (an incumbent firm). A significant positive main effect implies inclusion of entering commercial banks, a significant negative main effect implies exclusion, and an insignificant main effect implies a blind strategy.

Dichotomous dependent variable coded 1 if a given lead manager/comanager dyad was realized and 0 otherwise. The lead manager chooses the rest of the management group, and the observed bond issues had between one and ten comanagers, most with fewer than three.

Measured with 11 survey items about the extent to which different areas or activities had been combined. The 11 items were summarized into four indicators: employee integration depth (three items averaged), production integration depth (two items averaged), marketing integration depth (three items averaged), and systems integration depth (three items averaged).
Measured with the response to a survey question regarding the length of the integration process.

Measured with two indicators, one a survey response and the other derived from EDGAR. Changes were measured in the top five executives, and changes made immediately after an acquisition were not considered so as to isolate turnover during the integration after an initial postacquisition TMT was in place.

Measured with survey data using three questions developed to assess the attention paid to customer needs during acquisition integration, highly similar to the items used by Homburg and Bucerius (2005).

Importance-weighted measures calculated by multiplying the goal importance score by the goal achievement score for each objective, with both measured on a seven-point Likert scale and the achievement measure rescaled to a -3 to +3 scale. Comprised of two indicators: consolidation of similar units, and knowledge transfer from acquirer to target.
scale: goal importance and achievement on a seven-point Likert scale; achievement rescaled to -3 to +3; indicator is the product of the two
time_window: at the time of the acquisition and the level of achievement reported later

description: Importance-weighted measures calculated by multiplying the goal importance score by the goal achievement score for each objective, with both measured on a seven-point Likert scale and the achievement measure rescaled to a -3 to +3 scale. Comprised of three indicators: expansion into new customer and/or geographic market segments, cross-selling, and market share growth.
scale: goal importance and achievement on a seven-point Likert scale; achievement rescaled to -3 to +3; indicator is the product of the two
time_window: at the time of the acquisition and the level of achievement reported later

description: Measured with two indicators of the acquirer's three-year postacquisition abnormal stock returns: monthly cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) for the period beginning one month prior to the acquisition announcement date and ending 36 months later, and Jensen's alpha calculated over the same window. All data came from CRSP, with the CRSP equally weighted index used as the benchmark portfolio.
time_window: from one month before the acquisition announcement through 36 months after

description: The dependent variable was the acquisition hazard rate. Announcements of one or more acquisitions during a year were coded as an event, irrespective of whether the announced acquisitions were completed or how many acquisitions a focal firm announced. Events included deals classified by SDC as mergers, acquisitions of majority interest, and acquisitions of assets; SDC tracks transactions involving at least 5 percent of the ownership of a company and valued at $1 million or more, and after 1992 deals of any value (including undisclosed values) were covered.
scale: event indicator (announcement of one or more acquisitions = 1)

description: An aspiration proxy based on a firm's own prior performance. Performance was measured as return on assets in period t-1, and the aspiration levels were obtained from the prior period (t-2). The difference between a firm's performance and its aspiration level (historical) was the firm's attainment discrepancy. Historical and social attainment discrepancy were highly correlated (.71 for firms below their aspirations), so separate models were estimated with each.
time_window: performance at t-1, aspiration at t-2

description: An aspiration proxy based on the performance of a typical firm in the same industry: the performance of the median firm in the same four-digit SIC category in the prior year. Performance was measured in period t-1 and the aspiration level was obtained from the prior period (t-2). The difference between the firm's performance and its social aspiration level was its attainment discrepancy.
time_window: performance at t-1, aspiration at t-2

description: Absorbed slack was measured as the ratio of selling, general, and administrative expenses (SGA) to sales. The authors assumed that unabsorbed and potential slack are more directly relevant to initiating acquisitions than absorbed slack, but used all three measures.
The measure of unabsorbed slack was the current ratio, i.e., current assets divided by current liabilities.

For potential slack the authors used the ratio of debt to equity as an inverse indicator, so a high debt-to-equity ratio indicates low potential slack. This is why the coefficient on this proxy is negative.

Altman's Z-score was created from firms' accounting information regarding working capital, retained earnings, earnings before interest and taxes, market value of equity, and sales, calculated as (1.2 x working capital divided by total assets) + (1.4 x retained earnings divided by total assets) + (3.3 x income before interest expense and taxes divided by total assets) + (0.6 x market value of equity divided by total liability) + (1.0 x sales divided by total assets). An Altman Z-score of 1.8 was used as a cutoff; firms below that score were considered to be close to bankruptcy, and those above, as distant from bankruptcy.

Preexisting prestige was measured by separately counting, and then aggregating, the number of prestigious executives, prestigious outside directors, and prestigious VCs in place at the end of each prior month. The three types of preexisting prestige were standardized by transforming them into Z-scores and combined into a single preexisting prestige index; the Cronbach alpha for the three indicators was .71.
time_window: end of each prior month within the final year

description: The preexisting prestige index was inverse-coded to generate the measure of the scarcity of preexisting prestige, so that a higher score indicates that a firm had a relative lack of preexisting prestige.
time_window: end of each prior month within the final year

description: Urgency was measured as the inverse of the number of months remaining until the IPO registration date. For each month, the number of months remaining until IPO registration was calculated and then subtracted from 12 (urgency = 12 - months remaining), so higher values indicate greater urgency.
time_window: each month in the 12 months prior to IPO registration

variable_name: number of prestigious executives hired each month
description: A count of the number of prestigious executives hired by each firm in each month during the last year prior to IPO registration, based on the month and year they joined the firm as reported in the offering prospectus. Executives included all members of the top management team listed in the IPO prospectus; an executive was considered prestigious if he or she possessed one or more of the indicators of prestige.
time_window: each month in the year prior to IPO registration

variable_name: number of prestigious outside directors hired each month
description: A count of the number of prestigious outside directors hired by each firm in each month during the last year prior to IPO registration, based on the month and year they joined the firm as reported in the offering prospectus. Outside directors included directors who were not current or prior executives of the company (or their family members), or representatives of venture capitalists invested in the IPO firm; a director was considered prestigious if he or she possessed one or more of the indicators of prestige.
time_window: each month in the year prior to IPO registration

description: A dummy variable coded 1 if a hired executive was prestigious, and 0 otherwise. This measure was used to test the compensation hypotheses.
time_window: the year prior to IPO registration

description: The total compensation paid to each executive hired during the year prior to IPO, equal to the sum of annual salary, bonus, all other compensation (insurance premiums, retirement contributions, etc.), and the value of stock options granted. The measure was transformed into its natural logarithm; stock option value was calculated as mandated by the SEC assuming a 10 percent compounded annual stock price appreciation until option expiration.
time_window: the year prior to IPO registration

description: A weighted count capturing the number of electronic services a focal credit union offered in a given time period and how 'new' these innovations were in the relevant population. The authors first counted how many of eight services (account aggregation, bill payment, electronic cash, merchandise purchase, new share accounts, member application, Internet access services, and electronic signature authentication/certification services) a credit union offered in each time period. They then computed a time-varying weight for each e-service based on its diffusion, defined as (1 - p_it), where p_it is the percentage of sample credit unions offering service i at time t, so that less diffused services have higher values for degree of newness. Innovation adoption is the client firm's sum of electronic services offered multiplied by the degree of newness of each service varying by time period; the variable is continuous, with higher values indicating greater innovation adoption.
scale: continuous weighted count; lower limit 0, upper limit 8
time_window: eight semiannual periods, June 2001-December 2004 (independent variables lagged one period)

variable_name: Technology solution provider technical experiential diversity
description: Assesses experience in dealing with different types of technological innovations. The authors first determined the different electronic services offered by each credit union client of a provider in each period and then aggregated these services by type at the technology solution provider level for each time period. They then calculated the measure as 1 minus the Herfindahl index, so that higher values reflect greater diversity. Including all electronic services that a provider's clients offered in a given period, both those adopted in prior periods and those adopted in the current period, captures cumulative experience with different technological innovations. The measure equals 0 when all clients in a technology solution provider's portfolio offer only one type of electronic service and increases as the services offered by a provider's clients become more varied.
time_window: lagged one time period; cumulative within period

variable_name: Technology solution provider organizational experiential diversity (size)
description: Uses a coefficient of variation based on client firm sizes, computed as the standard deviation of a technology solution provider's clients' assets divided by the mean for each time period. Because the coefficient of variation is scale-invariant, the authors use a standardized coefficient of variation to control for number of clients. Higher values of the coefficient of variation indicate greater diversity in firm size among technology solution providers' clients. The authors discounted the technology solution provider organizational experiential diversity measure linearly over three time periods, weighting the last period's experience by three-thirds, the previous period by two-thirds, and the period before that by one-third.
time_window: lagged one time period; linearly discounted over three time periods

variable_name: Technology solution provider organizational experiential diversity (performance)
description: Uses a coefficient of variation of clients' performance, measured as delinquent loans divided by total loans, a measure the NCUA uses to monitor and assess a credit union's asset quality. Higher values indicate greater diversity in asset quality among clients. The authors report the standardized measure, and discounted the technology solution provider organizational experiential diversity measure linearly over three time periods, weighting the last period's experience by three-thirds, the previous period by two-thirds, and the period before that by one-third.
time_window: lagged one time period; linearly discounted over three time periods

description: Measured as a client's marketing expenses, which include advertising, publicity, and promotion, divided by total revenues. Because a firm's absorptive capacity accumulates over time and decays as experience ages, the authors discounted marketing intensity linearly over the prior three time periods.
time_window: lagged one time period; linearly discounted over the prior three time periods

description: For carrier i on route j, the sum of all contacts between carrier i and other carriers on route j, over all routes, during a month, divided by (n - 1), where n is the number of carriers on the route. The normalization sets average multimarket contact equal to 1 for any carrier on any route when the carrier does not meet any of the carriers on that route on any other route.

variable_name: average multimarket contact on low-concentration and high-concentration routes
description: Separate measures of average multimarket contact for contacts on low- and on high-concentration routes. The sample was split into low- and high-concentration routes using the median Herfindahl index value on nonmonopoly routes, and monopoly routes were excluded because there are no multimarket contacts on them. For each carrier-route, contacts were summed separately over routes whose Herfindahl index was below and above the median and normalized by dividing by (n - 1), where n is the number of carriers on the route.
The number of minutes late (or early) that a flight arrives at the gate relative to its scheduled arrival time, averaged over all of a carrier's flights on a particular route during a month.

variable_name: percentage of flights arriving at least 15 minutes late
description: The proportion of a carrier's flights on a route in a month that arrived at the gate at least 15 minutes late, which is the DOT's usual definition of a late flight.

variable_name: percentage of flights arriving at least 30 minutes late
description: The proportion of a carrier's flights on a route in a month that arrived at the gate at least 30 minutes late.
The scheduled time for a flight, used as the dependent variable in the direct test of whether the level of multimarket contact influences flight schedule length.

variable_name: Herfindahl index for a given route
description: A standard measure of concentration: the sum of the squared market shares for each firm serving a route. The authors state that market share for firm i is the firm's number of emplanements on the route divided by the total number of emplanements, and also state that the index was constructed using carriers' shares of flights on the route during a month. Routes were divided at the median Herfindahl value on nonmonopoly routes into low-concentration and high-concentration sets for the contact-route measures.

A count of the number of distant scientists hired in the three years prior to each time of measurement, using a three-year rolling window. A hired scientist's technological distance from the hiring firm is the angle between the firm's aggregated technological position and the scientist's aggregated backward-citation vector prior to recruitment; a scientist is coded as distant when this distance is greater than one standard deviation above the mean.

A dichotomous dependent variable that equals 1 when a new patent's angular distance from the patenting firm's existing technological position exceeds the average distance by more than one standard deviation, and 0 otherwise. Technological position is a 22-dimension vector of the percentage of a patent's backward citations in each technological area, aggregated over the firm's patents in the previous three years. Angular distance is used rather than Euclidean distance because it estimates divergence from an existing technological trajectory.
time_window: updated with every patent application; firm position aggregated over the previous three years

description: A weighted index of inventors' patenting activity, based on a Herfindahl-type index of the number of patents held by the most prolific inventors in the firm, with a correction that increases the value for firms with fewer scientists to avoid bias. A higher value means innovative productivity is more centered around one or a few prolific scientists. The number of scientists involved in patenting is counted with a five-year rolling window and the index is updated with every new patent application.

A nonbiased Herfindahl index for citations, following Hall (2002), computed from the number of patents the firm holds in each of 22 technological fields at time t and subtracted from 1, with an adjustment that assigns a higher value to the index when firms have fewer patents. The index can range between 0 and 2, and the authors state that a smaller index indicates the firm undertook a broader search. The firm's technological portfolio is updated with each patent application.

A Teachman entropy index used as a measure of the degree of technological diversity of the hiring firm; it was selected because the theoretical model used the Herfindahl index, and it generates two coefficients entered in the second-stage model as instruments in the first-stage selection equation.

Respondents rated their knowledge of three areas relevant in new firms in different sectors on a scale from 1, 'very little knowledge,' to 5, 'very high knowledge.' For each area the authors generated a dummy denoting whether a founder possessed at least a medium level of knowledge (coded 1), and created the linear sum of all three dummies. A founder with at least medium knowledge in all three areas scores 3; one with at least medium knowledge in two areas scores 2.
time_window: reference period of the 2005 survey (prior to firm founding)

description: Measured as the highest position a respondent had attained, with response categories 'technical employee, nonleadership position,' 'technical employee, leadership position,' 'management employee, nonleadership position,' 'management employee, leadership position,' and 'other.' Responses in the 'other' category were coded by the authors and three organizational scholars into leadership and nonleadership groups. From these data a dummy was created, coded 1 if a founder had obtained leadership experience in a previous work activity and 0 otherwise.
time_window: prior work activity before firm founding

description: Built from ZEW panel data on the average employment size of new firms founded in Germany in 2001 in each of 197 five-digit industry codes, tracked for each business year (2001, 2002, 2003) so that it matched the time frame of the study. Because the ZEW data were based on headcount regardless of type of employment, one person (the founder) was subtracted from the average employment size to match the dependent measure, which captures only jobs created for individuals besides founders. The yearly updates also take into account that some firms in the 2001 cohort failed over time.

Respondents stated the number of full-time employees, part-time employees, mini-job employees (employees with salaries lower than 400 euros per month), and freelancers working for their firms in each of the three years covered by the study. For each business year the different types of jobs were summed to arrive at the total employment count; for example, one full-time employee and three freelancers in the first year gives an employment count of four.
time_window: each of the three business years 2001, 2002, 2003

description: A dummy variable coded 1 to indicate a state that allowed statewide branching and 0 otherwise. Annual state-level legal-environment histories were constructed for all 48 states; the definitions of the branching types vary somewhat state-to-state and coding relied on the precedent set by the Federal Reserve Bulletin and previous research.
time_window: annual, 1896-2001 histories; lagged one year in the analyses

description: The percentage of bank locations in a given state that were outside of a bank's headquarters location. It is described as a direct measure of the extent to which banks relied on outlying locations, and the data come from annual counts of branches at the state level indicating whether or not branches are in banks' head-office cities.

Total banking assets in each state for each year from 1896 through 1978 divided by the total number of banking locations for that year, including both the headquarters and the branches. It is used to estimate whether states had banks with greater or lesser degrees of focus on large locations.
State nonurban (i.e., rural) roadway mileage obtained from various issues of Highway Statistics. These data became available at the state level in 1923 and the series was extrapolated back to 1896.
time_window: annual, 1896-1978 (data available at state level from 1923, extrapolated back to 1896)

description: The percentage of the state's population living in urban areas. Population data were collected at ten-year intervals beginning in 1900, with intervening years interpolated.
time_window: annual, 1900-1978 (ten-year census intervals, intervening years interpolated)

description: The number of banks in a given state, log-transformed to correct a skewed distribution.
The number of farms in a given state, log-transformed to correct a skewed distribution, collected from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's historical database on farms.

The value in billions of US dollars of an automaker's investment in a given country if it made an investment in that country during a given year, and a value of 0 otherwise. Amounts reported in other currencies were transformed into U.S. dollars using prevailing exchange rates in the year of the investment; when only added capacity was reported, the investment value was estimated by regressing other investments in the sample on their added production capacities; for joint ventures each automaker was assigned the reported amount, or an equal share when unreported.
scale: billions of US dollars, censored at zero

description: A dichotomous indicator taking a value of 1 when a particular automaker made an investment in a particular country in a particular year, and a value of 0 otherwise. It was coded to account for the possibility that the reported (and estimated) investment amounts were unreliable.

Residualized and transformed total country sulfur dioxide (SO2) emissions, used as a proxy for environmental regulations because data on applicable emission standards were unavailable for most countries. Total country SO2 emissions were regressed on country size (GDP), manufacturing intensity (the fraction of GDP that was manufacturing output), fossil-fuel intensity (the ratio of fossil fuel to hydroelectric production of electricity) and the number of automobiles per capita; the residuals represent indicators of the laxity of country environmental regulation, were normalized to fall between 0 and 1 and reverse-scored by subtracting from 1, so that higher numbers indicate more stringent environmental regulations.

The absolute value of the difference between the environmental institutional strength of a focal country and that of an automaker's home country. Environmental institutional strength was computed by averaging the normalized number of environmentally focused international nongovernmental organizations per capita with country environmental stringency.

A relative institutional distance measure computed by subtracting the strength of a focal country's environmental institutions from the strength of an automaker's home country's environmental institutions. Environmental institutional strength averages the normalized number of environmental international nongovernmental organizations per capita and country environmental stringency.

The absolute value of the difference between the environmental institutional strength of a focal country and the weighted average of the institutional strength of all countries in which an automaker had invested in the previous five years, weighted by the fraction of the automaker's production that occurred in that country.

A relative institutional distance measure computed by subtracting the strength of a focal country's environmental institutions from the weighted average of the environmental institutional strength of the countries the automaker had invested in over the previous five years (weighted by the fraction of the automaker's production that occurred in that country).

The fraction of an automaker's automobile plants that had obtained the environmental management system standard, ISO 14000 certification, by the end of the year, calculated for that year because certification is a 12- to 18-month process. The variable ranges from 0, for an automaker that has not certified any of its assembly plants, to 1, for an automaker that has certified all of its plants.

Percentage of a firm's board made up of executives actively involved with the business at the time of the IPO. Individual biographical data were used to identify persons whose job titles identified them as actively affiliated with the firm and also serving on the board, such as executive officers or scientific officers. For spline analyses, variables represented three ranges: 0 to 49 percent, 50 to 75 percent, and greater than 75 percent.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Twenty-four-month compounded holding period returns for sample firms' shares beginning on the second day of trading after the IPO. HPRj represents the 24-month compounded return earned on a $1 investment in firm j made on the day following the first day of trading. If a firm was delisted because it was acquired, HPR was estimated for the months prior to delisting; in bankruptcy, HPR was coded as a total loss.
time_window: 24 months beginning on the second day of trading

description: Industry-level environmental munificence defined as the regression slope of industry aggregate sales for the five-year period ending in the year of the sample firm's IPO, divided by the mean value of the industry's five years of sales. Data were taken from U.S. Census Bureau publications.
time_window: five-year period ending in the IPO year

description: Standard error of the regression coefficient of a focal industry's five-year growth divided by the mean value of five-year sales.

Five-year average industry-level patent counts from the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office reports for the three-digit SIC codes represented in the sample, averaged over the five years ending in the IPO years.
time_window: five-year period ending in the IPO year

description: Percentage of the workforce in each three-digit SIC industry represented in the sample made up of scientists and engineers, taken from the U.S. Bureau of Labor's Report on National Industry-Specific Occupational Employment & Wage Estimates.
Average number of SIC codes, both primary and secondary, listed for firms in Compustat for each primary three-digit SIC code represented in the sample.

Dispersion index of the geographic operations of industries represented in the sample, calculated as DIj = Σ Rij² / (Σ Rij)², where Rij is the number of regions in which firm i in industry j operated in its IPO year, based on Compustat's geographic segments variable ranging from 1 to 5.

A dummy variable with 1 designating full statewide banking and 0 otherwise, measured at the bank's founding. It was built from annual, state-level histories of the legal environments of all 48 states from 1896 to 2001, created by examining more than 15 secondary sources and, in many cases, actual state statutes. The authors note that limited statewide banking was typically quite restricted, so it was grouped with the 0 category.
level: state-year (assigned to each bank at founding)
time_window: state-year histories 1896-2001; value at the bank's founding year

description: A dichotomous variable with 1 indicating that a bank acquired another bank in a given year and 0 otherwise. Banks are defined at the highest level of ownership, with all subsidiaries included in one observation corresponding to the primary bank. The authors dichotomized rather than counted acquisitions because their theory concerns the propensity to acquire, because more than 80 percent of positive bank-year observations were 1, and to avoid multiple counting of acquisitions of multi-entity banks.

A principal component factor score of the extent of highway development for each state-year, computed from two state-year measures: annual state-level capital spending on roadways and annual state-level highway maintenance, culled from Highway Statistics. Both measures correlate at .97 and each correlates at .95 with total highway mileage at the national level; because the data extend back only to 1921, values were extrapolated back to 1896. The state-year value corresponding to a bank's founding is used.
level: state-year (assigned to each bank at founding)
time_window: state-year, extrapolated back to 1896; value at the bank's founding

description: Measured as the percentage of the state population that lived in urbanized areas in a given year. The requisite data were obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau at ten-year intervals beginning in 1890, with intervening years linearly interpolated. The state-year value corresponding to a bank's founding is used.
level: state-year (assigned to each bank at founding)
time_window: state-year, ten-year intervals from 1890 with linear interpolation; value at the bank's founding

description: Measured as the number of national Grange family members per state at the founding of a bank, using data from Tontz (1964), which presents Grange membership at 12 points in time between 1875 and 1960, with intervening years linearly interpolated. No state-level data exist after 1960, so banks founded after 1960 were treated as if there were no Grange presence at founding.
level: state-year (assigned to each bank at founding)
time_window: 1875-1960 with linear interpolation; value at the bank's founding

description: Measured as the number of farms in a given state compared to the overall population (i.e., farmers per capita), using data from the USDA National Agriculture Statistics Service covering 1890 to the present. Firms founded prior to the start of the data series were assigned the value at the start of the series.
level: state-year (assigned to each bank at founding)
time_window: 1890 to present; value at the bank's founding

description: Measured as the political support garnered by Progressive political candidates, defined as any party that had the word 'Progressive' in its name, in elections for national offices (president, senator, representative) in each state at the founding of a bank. The data were obtained from ICPSR study 7757; elections occur every two years and intervening years were interpolated.
level: state-election year (assigned to each bank at founding)
time_window: elections every two years with interpolation; value at the bank's founding

description: Adoption was inferred when a college first reported the existence of an administrative position with the title 'vice president for enrollment management' or some close approximation thereof. The authors focus on the initial adoption of the structure.

Assessed with three measures: average faculty salary (standardized within years to control for inflation), tenure-track faculty to student ratio, and research budget. Research budget was captured with an indicator variable (0, 1) because roughly two-thirds of the sample colleges provided no research funding. Faculties that are relatively better paid, more permanent, larger, and better supported in their academic pursuits are expected to be more powerful and professional ones.

variable_name: has admissions dean; admissions officer tenure
description: Gauged using data about admissions directors' titles and lengths of tenure. A significant percentage of admissions directors (20%) had the title 'dean of admissions,' taken as evidence of greater authority and professionalization, giving a has admissions dean variable. Admissions officer tenure was also included, with the expectation that a director's influence would increase with time in office. Missing tenure values were replaced with zeroes and a dummy variable denoted these observations.
Captured the percentage of a school's total revenues that come from sources other than tuition, calculated as (total revenues - tuition revenues) / total revenues.

Measured with geographic dispersion of the student body, calculated using data from the IPEDS 'residency survey,' which requires schools to report the home states of their incoming students. A Herfindahl index measured the geographic concentration of a school's student body (across all 50 states); the variable was then reverse-coded so that higher values reflect greater dispersion (the obverse of concentration).
Indicates the number of professional programs that a school adopted between 1971 and 1985.
The authors describe this measure as self-explanatory; it was used to test the hypothesis that colleges with longer-tenured presidents are less likely to adopt the enrollment management structure.

variable_name: president from school with enrollment management structure
description: The authors describe this measure as self-explanatory; it indicates whether a college's president had migrated from a previous adopter of the enrollment management structure.

variable_name: cumulative prior adoption of enrollment management at the field level
description: Captures the overall percentage of liberal arts colleges that had adopted the structure as of time t-1; a standard measure in institutional diffusion studies.

variable_name: percentage of direct competitors previously adopting the enrollment management structure
description: Direct competitors were identified using three criteria: geographic overlap, tuition similarity, and similarity in selectivity. A school's group of direct competitors was defined as the five other schools with the highest degree of geographic overlap that were also within one standard deviation of the focal school on the other two dimensions. The measure is the percentage of these direct competitors that had previously adopted the enrollment management structure.

variable_name: mean tuition discount rate of direct competitors
description: The mean tuition discount rate of a focal college's group of five direct competitors; tuition discounting is the core practice of enrollment management. Data for this variable were missing for 1997 through 2001 because the federal government did not release finance data in those years, and the missing values were filled in using linear interpolation between the 1996 and 2002 values.

A five-point measure of a college's overall selectivity in admissions, obtained from Peterson's Guide to Colleges. Because status is relatively stable, the 1987 measure was used throughout. A squared term (selectivity squared) was included to test the more specific argument that middle-status colleges are the most vulnerable to enrollment management adoption.
A late period dummy variable, defined as the latter half of the 20 year study period (1997-2006), interacted with the variables used to test Hypotheses 8-10.

Count of the press releases issued by a focal firm that include one or more of three types of defensive statements: assertions that organizations in the field perform more reliably than organizations in other fields, placement of blame for accidents or poor safety performance on actors or forces outside of organizations in the field, and communication of gains made or planned in the industry. Press releases and other official statements issued by panel companies were collected through searches for press releases and articles including keywords such as spokesperson, spokeswoman, spokesman, and company official; releases that directly discussed issues related to railroad safety or accident performance were retained, yielding 347 unique releases, of which 296 contained qualifying statements.

Count of the number of accidents (in hundreds) involving other firms, and not the focal firm, during a prior year. Accidents covered are those railroads are required to report, involving fatalities, significant injuries, or damage above an established value, such as derailments, hazardous material spills, and impacts with pedestrians or motorists. For the models testing core similarity the variable was split into accidents at other firms offering passenger service and accidents at other firms without passenger service; for the models testing similarity with external events it was split into collisions and noncollisions.

Ratio of negatively toned articles about safety for all companies (excluding the focal firm) to total articles about any issue. Articles were gathered as a stratified random sample of all print media pertaining to the company panel, excluding press releases; all editorials, commentary, or front-page stories mentioning a relevant company name entered, plus 33 percent of general news stories naming a relevant company in the headline or lead paragraph, and all articles when fewer than five were available in a company-year. Safety-focused articles were rated negative when they presented evidence that safety practices or reliability were being contested by any constituents, positive when they presented endorsements, and neutral if no main stance could be discerned.

variable_name: issue scrutiny at the focal firm
description: Ratio of negatively toned articles about safety pertaining to the focal firm to total articles about any issue pertaining to that firm, calculated similarly to the fieldwide scrutiny variable. The underlying articles were read and coded for tenor (negative, positive, or neutral) with intercoder agreement checks.

variable_name: interaction of passenger service revenue with accidents at other passenger service providers
description: The focal firm's own passenger service revenue (in millions) was interacted with the variable tracking accidents at other firms that offered passenger service; a higher value on the interaction indicates greater core similarity with accident-prone firms, reflecting a higher level of passenger service provision along with a greater number of accidents at other passenger service providers.

variable_name: interaction of the focal firm's collisions with other firms' collisions
description: The focal firm's experience with collision accidents was interacted with the variable tracking collision accidents elsewhere in the field, where collisions exclude those arising through equipment problems, operator error, or track and signal defects. A higher value on the interaction indicates greater similarity, reflecting more accidents across the field that could involve external forces combined with increases in the firm's own experience with similar accidents.

Count of the distinct mechanisms of action underlying drugs in a focal drug's therapeutic class in a given year. Mechanisms capture the key pharmacological and physiological knowledge underlying drugs and spawn substitute innovations competing for dominance in a therapeutic class. Competing mechanisms rather than the drugs that rivals had already created were counted so as to capture the substitution threat inherent in mechanisms that had yet to spawn many drugs.

For each patent in the sample, observations were created for each year following the year that the USPTO granted the patent to a firm. The dependent variable was set to 1 if the firm filed a lawsuit against another firm for infringement of the focal patent in a given year and to 0 otherwise.
time_window: yearly following the year of patent grant

description: Dummy variable set to 1 if the Pharmacy Times' annual listings indicated that the drug protected by the focal patent was one of the top 100 best-selling drugs and to 0 otherwise.

Coded from 1 to 3 on the basis of three key events: issuance of the earliest patent protecting a drug, application for FDA approval, and FDA approval. The lower the variable's value, the earlier the innovation was in its life cycle.

Dummy variable set to 1 if the drug that a patent protected was the first one to draw on a new mechanism of action in its therapeutic class and to 0 otherwise. Data on drugs introduced prior to 1980 were also gathered, since drugs applying a mechanism may have existed before the 1980-2004 period.

Change in the number of independent directors, captured by subtracting the number of independent directors at time t -1 from the number of independent directors at time t. The RiskMetrics database distinguishes three types of directors: executive directors, linked directors (former employees or nonemployees with business or family ties to the focal firm), and nonaffiliated directors; only directors without family or business ties to the firm were coded as independent.

An index formed by standardizing the individual measures of demographic similarity (age, functional background, industry background, and education) and combining them with a standardized measure of shared directorships and shared educational affiliation; the resulting measure was multiplied by -1 to create the final measure of social independence. Prior social ties were measured as the proportion of CEO-director dyads in which the CEO had served on another board with the director and as the count of directors who attended the same educational institution as the CEO. Similarity on categorical attributes used a variation of Blau's heterogeneity index, equal to the squared number of CEO-board member dyads sharing a particular category, while age similarity used a Euclidean distance measure.

Computer-aided content analysis with the LIWC program, which counts the number of words from predefined dictionaries appearing in a given text. For each article LIWC produced a score reported as the percentage of words from the positive emotion dictionary. Positive media coverage was equal to the mean LIWC score for the positive emotion category from all articles about a sample firm in a given year, using the subsample of articles screened by keyword search on the name of each sample CEO and the name of the company.
time_window: articles in a given year; lagged one year in models where media coverage predicts outcomes

description: Computer-aided content analysis with the LIWC program, which counts the number of words from predefined dictionaries appearing in a given text. For each article LIWC produced a score reported as the percentage of words from the negative emotion dictionary. Negative media coverage was measured as the mean LIWC score for the negative emotion category from all articles about a sample firm in a given year, using the subsample of articles screened by keyword search on the name of each sample CEO and the name of the company.
time_window: articles in a given year; lagged one year in models where media coverage predicts outcomes

description: Computer-aided content analysis with the LIWC program. Positive media coverage was equal to the mean LIWC score for the positive emotion category from all articles about a sample firm in a given year, using the subsample of articles that Factiva's 'intelligent indexing' classifies in the 'managerial issues' category, which contains articles related to corporate governance, executive pay, and management philosophy.
time_window: articles in a given year; lagged one year in models where media coverage predicts outcomes

description: Computer-aided content analysis with the LIWC program. Negative media coverage was measured as the mean LIWC score for the negative emotion category from all articles about a sample firm in a given year, using the subsample of articles that Factiva's 'intelligent indexing' classifies in the 'managerial issues' category, which contains articles related to corporate governance, executive pay, and management philosophy.
time_window: articles in a given year; lagged one year in models where media coverage predicts outcomes

description: Coded using the 'resignation' variable from ExecuComp; a dummy variable coded 1 if the reason for departure given in that database was 'resigned.'

Includes CEO salary, short-term bonus, and the value of long-term incentive grants made in a particular year. Long-term incentive grants include stock options, valued using the Black-Scholes method; performance shares and restricted stock were valued at the market price on the date of a grant.
time_window: grants made in a particular year

description: Following prior research, measured as the proportion of total compensation consisting of long-term incentive pay.

Indicator variable coded 1 if the political party that ruled the state was different from the one that ruled nationally or if it was not part of the national ruling coalition, and 0 otherwise. The definition is consistent with the methods of previous studies in political science.
A bank's expanding in a state in a particular year, represented as a count of the number of branches opened annually by each bank in each of the 24 states.

variable_name: reduction in political competition in a state
description: Measured as the number of years the incumbent ruling party had ruled the state continuously. If an incumbent party had been in power continuously for three years in a state, this variable was coded 3.
Indicator variable coded 1 if a government entity had a majority ownership share in a particular bank and 0 otherwise. Various governments had majority ownership shares in 32 percent of the banks.

variable_name: proportion of business from focal state
description: Coded as the ratio of a bank's branches in a focal state to its total number of branches in all states in a particular year.

Content analysis of the negative social evaluations of arms producers conveyed publicly by authoritative international newspapers. The 12 newspapers were searched for articles containing at least one keyword expressing criticism or condemnation, at least one sampled firm's name or variant, and the words weapon*, arm*, military, defense, or defence; every time disapproval was conveyed about a firm in an article excerpt, 1 was added to the dependent variable (2,014 excerpts were coded). Content disapproving of poor performance and content disapproving of a firm in relation to a lawsuit regarding corporate misconduct were excluded. The variable was logged because it was skewed to the right.

Percentage of an arms producer's yearly output devoted to the civilian product category, computed as civilian sales divided by civilian plus arms sales, multiplied by 100. Higher values indicate a greater dilution of the association with the stigmatized arms category.

Proportion of nonstigmatized ('clean') customers in a firm's portfolio in any given year. Stigmatized customers were identified with the Political Terror Scale, which ranges from 1 to 5; any country receiving a 4 or a 5 in a given year was considered a stigmatized customer, and the measure is the annual proportion of customers that did not receive a PTS score of 4 or 5. Higher values thus indicate that association to stigmatized customer categories is more diluted.

Category saliency is described as essentially unobservable and difficult to measure, so the authors used the 9/11 terrorist attacks as an exogenous shock to category saliency and ran separate models for the pre- and post-9/11 periods to test Hypothesis 2. The field research and a content analysis of U.N. Security Council annual reports indicate that customer categories became more salient after 9/11 while the 'weapons' and 'civilian' industry categories became less salient.

Current wealth is calculated using a variable from the Execucomp database: the number of options from each option grant, multiplied by their corresponding spread (for in-the-money options) on the final day of the fiscal year. The cash value of stock options held by CEOs is treated as a heuristic for estimating the current wealth inherent in their options. A first-stage regression predicting option values from lagged firm and executive characteristics is used to retain predicted valuations as an endogeneity control.
time_window: final day of the fiscal year; lagged independent variables

description: The authors estimate the future increase in the value of a CEO's stock options over and above their present-day value by increasing the stock price at the average increase in the Dow over the period of the study, 6.8 percent, over the remainder of the life of the CEO's options, deducting the present-day stock price, and multiplying by the number of options held. The number of options held is the sum of unexercisable and exercisable stock options reported in Execucomp; price is the firm's stock price at the end of the fiscal year; average time to expiry was calculated using the estimation technique of Core and Guay (2002).
time_window: remaining life of the options; end of fiscal year stock price

description: Three strategic risks were factor-analyzed: R&D expense, capital expenditures, and long-term debt, each taken from the relevant category within Compustat and measured in millions of dollars. The factor analysis produced a single factor; the authors calculated a single risk-taking variable as the standardized factor score for this common factor, where a higher score is interpreted as greater risk taking. Unscaled measures of the dependent variables are used, with firm size controlled directly in the model instead.

A binary measure coded as 1 if a firm's options are traded on any US equity options exchange, and 0 if not. If the options are publicly tradable, it provides the CEO with easy access to buying put options. This measure is positively correlated with the use of hedging and reflects the cost and ease of hedging.

For those firms that have their equity options publicly traded, the authors use options trading volumes to measure the liquidity of the options market. This liquidity measure also reflects the cost and ease of hedging. Because this measure is often reported as a missing value when the volume of option trading is low or nonexistent, it covers a subset of the total sample.

A dummy code indicating three consecutive years of share price decline, coinciding also with three years of decline in ROA. Both accounting (ROA) and market-based (share price) measures of CEO performance are used, given that both influence CEO dismissal. A dummy is used because there is no theoretical or empirical basis for thresholds in stock price decline or ROA that trigger CEO dismissal and because negative values in an interaction term can lead to analysis and interpretation problems.

Percentage of directors with backgrounds in the financial sector, excluding banking. The group-level measure is a simple combination of dichotomous individual measures; teams with a higher proportion of financial directors are assumed to be more influenced by financial assumptions, priorities, and norms.

Percentage of directors with banking experience. Banking experience is considered a measure of financial embeddedness because directors with banking experience are chosen generally not because of their community involvement but because of their banking and financial skills, and because board members, not bankers on management teams, are the key to banks' community orientation.

Percentage of directors on corporate boards. Corporate board experience is considered a good measure of embeddedness in the financial logic because legal principles and taken-for-granted assumptions of corporate governance imply that boards of directors exist ultimately to protect the financial interests of shareholders.

Proportion of directors who listed some involvement in volunteer community boards, whether social, civic, professional, or economic. This variable is continuous, going from 0 to 100 percent, and is described as a revealed preference measure of community identity.

variable_name: time elapsed from filing to establishment or withdrawal
description: Time elapsed, in days, from the filing of a bank charter application to the opening date of the bank for groups that succeeded in opening, and, for groups that failed, to the date of their withdrawal. For successful groups, longer elapsed time is a proxy for greater difficulty and lower likelihood of success in establishing their banks because the organizing funds get depleted; among groups that ultimately withdrew, the time elapsed is an indication of resiliency.

Dummy variable with a value of 1 for banks not established or withdrawn by August of 2008, since banks that were still in the process of being established as of September of 2008 were much less likely to get established.

The article reports results for founding teams highly embedded in both community and financial logics from models that include interaction effects, and reports the interaction of that combined embeddedness with the crisis variable. The text does not describe how the combination of the two embeddedness measures is computed beyond the interaction terms.

Implicit prices for IT hardware are used to calculate the nominal value of different IT components for each year, and these nominal values are deflated using appropriate price indices from the BEA. Following Hitt and Brynjolfsson (1996), total IT capital stock is the sum of IT hardware and three times the IT labor cost, where IT labor cost is the number of IT employees in the firm multiplied by industry-average labor compensation. The IT capital stock is divided by the total number of employees in the firm, and the logarithm value of this per-employee IT capital stock is the measure of aggregate IT capital.
scale: logarithm of per-employee IT capital stock

description: Vertical integration is constructed in three steps. First, the primary segment (the four-digit NAICS segment with the highest sales) and all secondary segments of each firm are identified from the COMPUSTAT segment database. Second, the vertical relatedness between a secondary segment in industry j and a primary segment in industry i is calculated from the IO use table using the dollar values of each industry's output required to produce the other's total output. Third, each firm's vertical integration is assessed by aggregating these relatedness values with weights equal to the ratio of each secondary segment's sales to the total sales of all secondary segments.

Horizontal complementarity is calculated in a four-step process from the IO use table. For each industry, the percentage of its output supplied to each intermediate industry is computed, and the correlation coefficient between these output shares is calculated for each pair of industries; the same is done for the percentage of each industry's input from each intermediate industry. The complementarity coefficient between two industries is the average of the two correlation coefficients.
