Indicator that equals 1 if a marriage equality decision had been enacted as of month-year t in the headquarter state of firm i in cohort c, and 0 otherwise. Treated firms are compared to control firms headquartered in states with no marriage equality decision by the end of the cohort estimation window. Settlement dates were originally obtained from Wikipedia and compared with dates appearing in peer-reviewed academic articles.
time_window: four years before and four years after the settlement

variable_name: Firm's collective action frames (relative to individual action frames)
description: A dictionary-based continuous measure of the relative use of collective action versus individual action frames. Keywords for each frame were identified by human coding of a subsample of 2,143 tweets and 6,441 press release titles and elaborated with latent Dirichlet allocation topic modeling over the whole corpus. The frequency of collective action frame words is divided by the sum of collective action and individual action frame word frequencies, retaining observations where only collective action frames are used.

variable_name: BOD and CEOs' liberal political ideology
description: A firm's directors' and CEO's dollar amount of donations to Democratic candidates divided by their total donations. Because donation data are available only in even-numbered years, the subsequent even-numbered year's score is applied to the preceding odd-numbered year. Donations are averaged over the previous three years and the resulting average is lagged by five years.

An average of Bonica's (2013) campaign finance ideology scores for political action committees whose ultimate organization belongs to a given industry at the two-digit standard industrial classification (SIC) level. The measure applies a 10-year lag and a five-year moving average.
time_window: five-year moving average, lagged ten years

description: An average of Bonica's (2013) campaign finance ideology scores of political candidates in the state, used to gauge the ideological preferences of the electorate. Because CF scores are available only in even-numbered years, scores from the preceding even-numbered year are used for the subsequent odd-numbered year, with no lag and a two-year moving average.

variable_name: issue-aligned advocacy organizations in the firm's headquarter state
description: A dummy variable coded 1 if two or more issue-aligned advocacy organizations operated in a firm's headquarter state, and 0 otherwise. The value of 2 is used as the cut-off because the distribution of organizations across state-years is highly skewed.

Family firms are defined as those owned by a family, involving two or more family members. The family firm dummy variable was coded as 1 or 0 and was used to construct merger types (family–family; family–nonfamily; nonfamily–nonfamily).

variable_name: Merger (family–family merger; family–nonfamily merger; nonfamily–nonfamily merger)
description: A merger occurs when firms cease to exist and are subsumed into a combined entity. A merger between two family firms was defined as a family–family merger (coded as 1 or 0), a merger between a family firm and a nonfamily firm as a family–nonfamily merger (coded as 1 or 0), and a merger between two nonfamily firms as a nonfamily–nonfamily merger (coded as 1 or 0). In the mediation models family–family merger is the omitted reference category, so the other two dummies are measured relative to it.

Measured as 1 minus the percentage reduction in the number of employees dismissed in the combined organization in the years after the merger. In the main models the job security variable was lagged by one year relative to the merger.

Post-merger performance captured as the merged firm's return on assets (ROA), an indicator of how profitable a company is relative to its total assets, adjusted for industry using the four-digit SNI code. In the main models the post-merger performance variable was lagged by one year relative to the merger.

Variation in the clone game keywords relative to the original game, measured with the angular separation of the game keyword vectors after constraining the core features to be the same, so that it captures deviations in peripheral features. The proximity measure equals 1 when the original and clone have an identical set of keywords and is bounded between 0 and 1; the deviation for a pair is computed by subtracting the proximity from 1. The final measure for the innovator that released the original is constructed by aggregating the individual pair deviations across the pool of near-clone games.
level: original game (aggregated over its pool of near-clones)
time_window: clone games released at least three months after the original and no later than three months before the sequel

description: The quality of the innovator's sequel game is measured with the average critics' rating scores listed in MobyGames and Metacritic. The scores are weighted averages of normalized rankings from individual critics, weighted by each critic's rating history, accuracy, and variance.

The main measure is a simple average of the imitator firms' market shares in the focal genre in year y - 1, where y indicates the year in which the focal imitation game was released. For instance, if the clones were produced by three firms each holding 10% of the market share in the focal genre in the prior year, the measure would be 10.
level: imitator pool of the original game
time_window: year before the focal imitation game's release

variable_name: Loss of tacit product-specific knowledge (development unit change)
description: Coded 1 if the development unit that developed the sequel game is different from the unit that developed the original, and 0 otherwise. Unit name changes are excluded, but reorganizations due to a merger or acquisition between game studios are included.

Our unit of analysis is the dyadic relationship between firm i and nonprofit j in year t, from 2010 to 2017. The outcome variable is a dummy variable that takes the value of '1' each year if the firm and nonprofit have a partnership together and '0' if they do not. It was created by coding firms' annual reports and, where available, their corporate foundations' reports, using natural language programming to identify mentions of listed nonprofits. All mentions were coded as partnerships in the main analyses.
Dummy variable that assumes the value of '0' for the years 2010 through 2013 (before Carwash) and '1' for the years 2014 through 2017 (after Carwash). It assesses the impact of Operation Carwash.
Dummy variable coded '1' if the firm was directly implicated in Operation Carwash from that year onwards and '0' otherwise. This concerned the eight firms listed previously in Appendix A.
Dummy variable coded '1' if the firm had more than 49.9% government shares and '0' otherwise. It measures whether firms were indirectly tainted through state ownership.

Count of the political positions that corporate board members held. It was built by searching board members' résumés for keywords identifying political connections, drawing on prior classifications. A political tie was identified if a board member ever held an elected or appointed office in local, state, or national government or if they occupied a managerial position in a state-owned company.

Dummy variable coded '1' if the nonprofit corresponds to the trade association categorization and '0' otherwise. All other social missions are coded '0,' since the authors theorize that they face a lower risk of being co-opted by corporate political interests after revelations of a government corruption scandal.

Dummy variable coded '1' if the nonprofit is an education and research nonprofit and '0' otherwise. E&R nonprofits were defined to include only those subcategories involved in research (e.g., universities, research institutes, think tanks), not schools that solely provide education services. All other social missions are coded '0.'

Measured in four steps. First, Factiva was searched for Brazilian media articles mentioning the nonprofits at risk of corporate partnerships, yielding 324,150 articles from 2010 to 2017. Natural language processing identified instances where a nonprofit's name appeared within 14 words of job titles held by government actors at Brazil's local, state, and national levels; only the first mention connecting a nonprofit and government actor within an article or across articles referencing the same subject on the same date was retained. LIWC was then used to retain only positive relationships, using a 60% cutoff. The variable designates the number of cooperative relationships between a nonprofit and political actors in a year.
scale: number of cooperative relationships; text notes it ranges from 0 to 1

description: Composite scale built from 13 items measuring the extent to which a business model leverages novelty as a design theme. The strength of each item in a given business model was measured using Likert-type scales and coded into a standardized score; after coding, the item scores were aggregated into an overall score for the composite scale using equal weights. The measure was validated with a standardized Cronbach alpha of 0.72 and with confirmatory factor analysis and partial least squares.
time_window: one measurement per firm, collected between May 2000 and June 2001

description: Composite scale built from 13 items measuring the extent to which a business model leverages efficiency as a design theme. The strength of each item in a given business model was measured using Likert-type scales and coded into a standardized score; after coding, the item scores were aggregated into an overall score for the composite scale using equal weights. Internal consistency was a standardized Cronbach alpha of 0.69, and the measure was further validated by confirmatory factor analysis and partial least squares.
time_window: one measurement per firm, collected between May 2000 and June 2001

variable_name: logarithm of the market value of a firm's equity
description: The market value of equity at a given date is the number of shares outstanding multiplied by the firm's stock price, taken from the combined CRSP and Datastream databases. The logarithm of the market value of equity was calculated in order to comply with the normality assumption of ordinary least squares regression. The dependent variable was measured at various points in time (annual average, average during Q4, and the last day of trading of Q4) and in the years 1999 and 2000.
scale: logarithm of market value of equity
time_window: 1999 and 2000 (annual average, Q4 average, last day of Q4 trading)

variable_name: time period of dependent-variable measurement (1999 versus 2000)
description: Because the business model construct spans industry boundaries and many sample firms span multiple industries, the authors could not define an industry-level variable capturing resource munificence. They therefore measured the dependent variables in time periods sufficiently distinct in terms of environmental resource munificence: 1999 (and Q4 1999 in particular) was a time of relatively high munificence for entrepreneurial firms in the sample, whereas 2000 (and Q4 2000 in particular) was a time of relatively low munificence, following the worldwide crash of high-tech stocks in March 2000. Munificence was thus operationalized by the time period in which performance was measured rather than by a separate firm- or industry-level variable.

The weakness of an interdivisional tie is measured as the average of the frequency and closeness scores as reported on 7-point Likert-type scales by the R&D managers in the network survey. A division's tie weakness score is the average weakness of all its ties to other divisions in a given year, and the score is lagged by one year before being assigned to the projects of that division. Licensing agreements and participation in enduring cross-divisional technology groups were coded 1 if present and 0 otherwise and included in the network.

The number of months from the start of concept development to market introduction for a given project. Starting time is defined as the month when a dedicated person started working part or full time on the project, and the end date is the date on which the product was released to shipment; for on-going and canceled projects the time to the end of the study period or to cancellation is used.

A three-item 7-point Likert-type scale measuring the extent to which the knowledge transferred from the source division to the receiving project team was not fully documented, insufficiently explained in writing, and was mainly personal practical know-how. The measure consists of the average of the responses to the three questions, and the Cronbach alpha for this scale is .81.

Project managers were asked whether the 'ware' that was leveraged could function as 'stand alone' or was dependent on other components or products in those divisions, with anchors 'highly dependent' and 'mainly stand-alone'. The question was asked for both software and hardware and the measure is the average of the responses to the two questions. Information was missing for seven project teams, so a dummy variable (dummy-dependent) was entered, coded 1 if there was missing information and 0 otherwise.
scale: 7-point scale (anchors: highly dependent to mainly stand-alone)

description: Knowledge complexity is entered in the models through its two dimensions, the noncodified knowledge scale and the dependent knowledge measure, each interacted with tie weakness. The two knowledge complexity variables are reported separately and are set to zero when the main effect of tie weakness is interpreted in isolation, i.e., when the knowledge to be transferred is highly codified and mainly stand-alone.

The number of successful patent applications, or granted patents, for firm i in year t. The granted patent carries the date of the original application, which was used to assign a granted patent to the year in which it was originally applied for. Only chemicals patents were counted, identified from the technology-class information on the patents; the patent count assigns to the firm all chemicals patents issued solely to it or its subsidiaries and half of the chemicals patents issued jointly to the firm and a partner or to joint ventures of the firm.
time_window: Patent years 1982-1992; covariates lagged one year

description: The count of the direct ties maintained by a firm in any year: the number of direct partners of the focal firm, i.e., its degree centrality in the network. Hypothesis 1 predicted a positive impact of this variable on patenting frequency.
time_window: 1981-1991, lagged one year before patent counts

description: Three alternative measures capture a firm's reach in the network through its indirect ties. The first is a simple count of indirect ties, computed as the number of other firms in the network tied to the focal firm at path distances of two or greater, excluding direct ties. The second is Burt's frequency-decay distance-weighted count, which attaches weights of the form 1 - [f_i/(N+1)] to each tie, where f_i is the total number of nodes that can be reached up to and including path distance i and N is the total number of firms reachable by the focal firm in any number of steps, so that ties at progressively longer path distances receive progressively smaller weights. The third, a refinement of the frequency-decay measure, weights each node by the number of patents applied for by that firm in the period, multiplying the vector of Burt's frequency-decay weighted path distances by the vector of patent counts.
scale: count (weighted counts for the distance-weighted and distance-and-information-weighted versions)
time_window: 1981-1991, lagged one year before patent counts

description: The ratio of nonredundant contacts to total contacts for the ith firm (Burt, 1991), computed from the proportion of i's relations invested in the connection with contact q, the marginal strength of the relationship between contact j and contact q, and the total number of contacts for firm i. Higher values reflect firms whose ego networks are rich in structural holes, i.e., whose partners are not connected to each other; if all of a firm's partners are unconnected the index takes a value of 1, and for firms without any partners the index is set to 0. The measure was computed with STRUCTURE (Burt, 1991).
time_window: 1981-1991, lagged one year before patent counts

variable_name: change in dollars invested in each of eight markets
description: The independent variable is diversifying and is measured as change in the dollar amounts invested in each of the eight earning-asset markets. These are actual increases or decreases in investments, calculated after correcting for inflation with the GNP deflator index. For models of financial performance, all changes are calculated over six-month periods between June 1977 and December 1986; for models of failure, some periods are six months long (June 1977 through December 1983), while others are three months long (December 1983 through March 1987). Data on change in asset portfolios are taken from the detailed balance sheets given for each firm.
time_window: six-month periods June 1977-December 1986 for performance; six- and three-month spells June 1977-March 1987 for failure

description: The first measure of financial performance is the level of reserves or net worth, computed as assets minus liabilities. It is a stock variable that assesses a firm's capital adequacy, meaning capital not committed to cover current obligations and therefore available to handle unanticipated outlays. If a thrift's net worth declines below a threshold of 6 percent of its total assets, the firm is considered to be insolvent. The variable is measured at the end of a period and, like all other dollar amounts, is adjusted for inflation using the GNP deflator index.

The second measure of financial performance is net income, computed as total income minus total expenses. It is a flow variable that assesses the profitability of each period's operations. Net income, like all other dollar amounts, is adjusted for inflation using the GNP deflator index.

The dependent variable is the instantaneous rate of merger or dissolution, and the failure variable is coded one if a firm fails during the period under study and zero if it continues to operate. Three types of exits were grouped together under organizational failure: mergers explicitly labelled as FHLBB- or FSLIC-supervised, outright liquidations, and mergers of firms with zero or negative net worth. For cases in which archival sources do not classify thrift mergers as voluntary or involuntary, any merger in which the disappearing firm was technically insolvent (zero or negative net worth) was classified as involuntary.

The degree to which new markets are related to residential mortgages is assessed qualitatively, based on similarity of the three dimensions of domain (products sold, clients served, and technology employed). Five of the seven new markets are classified as related diversification (nonresidential mortgages, mortgage-backed securities, consumer nonmortgage loans, cash and investment securities, and equity investments in service corporation subsidiaries) and two as unrelated diversification (commercial nonmortgage loans and direct investments in real estate).

variable_name: rate of entry into each of the six new markets
description: For each new market, the authors observed whether or not a firm entered the market by investing over 5 percent of its assets in the market. A firm's market entry behavior was coded zero if it had not yet passed the 5-percent threshold and one if it had, and a firm remained in the data set until it first exceeded the threshold. The dependent variable is the instantaneous rate of entry, the hazard rate of change.
scale: 0/1 entry indicator underlying the hazard rate

description: A count of thrifts, newly founded or established, active in the market above the 5-percent threshold that were within a size-localized window around the focal firm. Size was measured in terms of asset base in millions of dollars and corrected for inflation using a GDP deflator index; the window runs from .5 Si to 1.5 Si, so the measure varies from firm to firm. Models included both linear and quadratic terms to test for curvilinear effects.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each period

description: A count of thrifts with investments above the 5-percent threshold that were in the top quartile for size (assets) in each product market studied in each period. Models included both linear and quadratic terms for this density.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each period

description: A count of thrifts with investments above the 5-percent threshold that were in the top quartile for return on assets in each product market studied in each period. Return on assets is described as the best measure of thrift performance. Models included both linear and quadratic terms for this density.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each period

variable_name: dummy for potential entrant in the top quartile for organizational size
description: A dummy variable indicating whether or not a potential entrant was in the top quartile for organizational size, interacted with large-firm market density to test hypothesis 3b. Linear and quadratic terms for the interaction were included to test for curvilinear effects.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each period

variable_name: dummy for potential entrant in the top quartile for profitability (return on assets)
description: A dummy variable indicating whether or not a potential entrant was in the top quartile for profitability (return on assets), interacted with profitable-firm market density to test hypothesis 3a. Linear and quadratic terms for the interaction were included to test for curvilinear effects.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each period

description: The insider ratio was calculated as the number of employee directors divided by the total number of board members. Data on board structure were obtained from corporate proxy statements.
CEO-board-chairman duality is a binary variable, coded as one if a CEO was also chairman of the board, and zero otherwise.

Relative CEO-board tenure was calculated as the average board tenure of directors divided by the CEO's tenure. The measure is the inverse of the construct as named here (CEO tenure relative to board tenure).

Directors' stock ownership was measured as the percentage of total common equity owned by non-CEO directors. Because stock ownership can also be an important source of power for the CEO, the authors adjusted for CEO ownership in measuring this variable.

Coded as one if both the CEO and the new director had primary experience in the same functional area. Functional backgrounds were consolidated into three core areas: output functions (marketing and sales), throughput functions (operations, R&D, and engineering), and peripheral functions (primarily law, finance, and accounting); each director's primary functional area was the area in which he or she had the most experience. Coding was based primarily on current and prior job titles while also considering other aspects of employment history, and the correlation between two coders' ratings for a random sample of 75 directors was .88.

Coded as one if the CEO and the new director shared the same educational category. Educational background was divided into four categories: (1) less than a bachelor's degree; (2) less than a master's degree; (3) less than a doctoral degree; and (4) a doctoral degree.

Coded as one if the CEO and the new director differed by less than one standard deviation (7.8 years, calculated from the pooled sample of directors). In a separate model a more restrictive definition of age similarity (five years or less) was used.

Coded as one if CEOs and new directors were both insiders or both outsiders, and zero otherwise. Directors were coded one if the director was not an employee of the organization, and zero otherwise; CEOs were coded as outsiders if they were not employed by the company or any of its subsidiaries prior to becoming CEO.

Measured with an analog of the euclidean distance measure (i.e., the coefficient of variation) commonly used in research on organizational demography, using the ages of the new director and of existing board members (excluding the CEO). The measure was converted to an indicator of similarity by subtracting each firm's coefficient from the highest value in the sample.
level: board-new director dyad aggregated to firm
time_window: year of appointment (board members in that year)

description: Calculated as a variant of Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity, defined as the squared proportion of dyads sharing the same category. For functional background, the measure indicates the squared proportion of dyads in which both individuals have primary experience in the same core functional area.
level: board-new director dyad aggregated to firm
time_window: year of appointment (board members in that year)

description: Calculated in the same way as functional background similarity (board), using the squared proportion of dyads sharing the same educational category.
level: board-new director dyad aggregated to firm
time_window: year of appointment (board members in that year)

description: Calculated in the same way as functional background similarity (board), using the squared proportion of dyads sharing the same insider/outsider status category.
level: board-new director dyad aggregated to firm
time_window: year of appointment (board members in that year)

description: Four measures of change in CEO-board similarity were constructed for each year as similarity in the current year minus similarity in the prior year; the measures of absolute CEO-board similarity are analogous to the measures of CEO-new-director similarity. Since increases in the four measures were highly correlated (Pearson correlation coefficients > .6 in all cases), a single measure of increased similarity was created by summing the z-scores of all four change variables.
time_window: change from year t-1 to year t

description: Total compensation comprises base salary, annual bonus, and the total value of long-term incentives granted in a given year. Stock options were valued using the Black-Scholes (1973) method, and other grants such as restricted stock and performance shares were valued according to the market price at date of grant; all compensation values were adjusted for inflation to represent 1990 constant dollars using the CPI. Change in total compensation was measured as the logarithm of compensation in the subsequent year minus the same measure in the prior year, indicating the growth rate in total compensation.
time_window: change from year t to year t+1

description: Compensation contingency was calculated for each year as the total value of long-term incentive grants divided by total compensation. Change in compensation contingency was calculated for each year as contingency in the subsequent year minus contingency in the prior year. Short-term bonuses were not included in this measure.
time_window: change from year t to year t+1

description: Institutions were stratified by public and private control and a random sample was drawn within each stratum. In the ordered probit models control is used as a predictor of the number of administrative offices and is also interacted with the measures of dependence; the text refers to the predictor as public control. The paper does not state explicitly how the variable is coded numerically.

One of four primary sources of support used to measure dependence: the proportion of the institution's total revenues derived from government appropriations. This is described as a source of support traditionally viewed as a mainstay of public institutions.

One of four primary sources of support used to measure dependence: the proportion of the institution's total revenues derived from government grants and contracts. The authors note that although public and private institutions have both received government grants and contracts for research since World War II, government grants are treated here as technically a public source of support.

variable_name: gifts and grants from private sources
description: One of four primary sources of support used to measure dependence: the proportion of the institution's total revenues derived from gifts and grants from private sources, a category associated with private status.

One of four primary sources of support used to measure dependence: the proportion of the institution's total revenues derived from self-generated funds, defined as tuition, fees, and endowment income, a category associated with private status.

Count of the administrative offices with primary responsibility for dealing with sources of public funding. From the list of coded administrative positions, six were selected as having major responsibility for managing relations with external sources of financial support, and three of them measure this dependent variable. The dependent variable can assume one of only four possible values (0-3). Each office serves a variety of functions, not all directly involving funding relations.

Count of the administrative offices with primary responsibility for the management of private-funding sources. From the list of coded administrative positions, six were selected as having major responsibility for managing relations with external sources of financial support, and three of them measure this dependent variable. The dependent variable can assume one of only four possible values (0-3).

For analyses of questionnaire responses, centrality was represented as a dichotomous variable depending on the group into which a unit fell. Academic units were categorized as 'core' and all other units as 'peripheral.' Core units are those whose functions are essential to the central mission of an institution.

variable_name: Relative change in unit's share of the general budget
description: The relative share of internal institutional resources acquired by a unit, especially money, space, and campus location. The study focuses on the relative change in a unit's share of the general budget. For analyses of questionnaire responses, resource allocations was represented as a dichotomous variable depending on whether the unit fell into a gainer or loser group.
scale: dichotomous gainer/loser for group analyses; budget change for regressions

variable_name: Tapping external academic resources (core unit environmental power index)
description: Index of environmental power for core units. Two questions were combined: substitutability, the relative ability to bring in each of 13 environmental resources compared with other similar units on a 5-point scale; and criticality, the importance of each resource to the institution on a 5-point scale. Importance ratings were used to weight the contribution responses in developing indices of environmental power. The core index is called 'tapping external academic resources' because of its items.

variable_name: Tapping external financial resources (peripheral unit environmental power index)
description: Index of environmental power for peripheral units, constructed from the same substitutability and criticality questions as the core index. The peripheral index is called 'tapping external financial resources.' At least in current times of financial stress, peripheral gainers acquire internal budget resources by attracting much-needed financial support.

variable_name: Institutional power index for core units
description: Summary index of institutional power questionnaire items. Respondents compared their unit with other similar budgetary units on 14 listed characteristics and a general item on present power within the institution, using a 5-point scale. The index construction distinguished gainers from losers separately for core and peripheral units. For core units, positive items measured aspects of a unit's present internal ties, such as administrative support, constituent service, and general visibility.

variable_name: Institutional power index for peripheral units
description: Summary index of institutional power questionnaire items, constructed similarly to the core index. Respondents compared their unit with other similar budgetary units on 14 listed characteristics and a general item on present power within the institution, using a 5-point scale. The index construction distinguished gainers from losers separately for core and peripheral units.

Respondents indicated on a 5-point scale, where 1 = Very Little or Not at All and 5 = Very Much, how much they use each of eight strategy categories when preparing their unit's annual budget. The main analyses added these strategy categories to environmental and institutional power in multiple regressions.
scale: 5-point scale (1 = Very Little or Not at All, 5 = Very Much)

description: For each top manager recruited from another semiconductor firm, the author created a vector of dummy variables for the product markets the top manager's former firm competed in and the focal firm did not currently compete in. The effects of a top manager move remained in effect for a three-year period and were assumed constant over that period.

Dichotomous variable representing the event of entry into a market that was new for a particular semiconductor firm. An entry event occurred if, for a given product, a firm did not offer that product in the prior year and entered that product market in the current year; the dependent variable was coded 0 for each firm/product/year record if the firm did not enter and 1 in the year it did enter. Each product market was dropped from the risk set after the focal firm entered it.

The functional experience of the recruited top manager, coded into one of five areas: research and development, product engineering, marketing, sales, and all others. To test hypothesis 2, the first two categories (R&D and product engineering) were tested together as R&D/engineering, and the second two (marketing and sales) together as marketing/sales.

Dummy variables for the formal position, or rank, of the executive in his or her previous organization, using three categories: chief executive or president (CEO); directly reporting to the CEO (one level below the CEO) (direct reports); and more than one level below the chief executive (not a direct report). There were only six instances of a chief executive moving to a new firm as a top manager, one of which resulted from an acquisition.
The executive's tenure was measured as his or her years of experience in the semiconductor industry.
time_window: at the time of the move

description: The relative size of the organization the executive came from, measured as the revenue of his or her prior employer divided by the revenue of the firm he or she moved to, both measured in the year the executive moved.
The average organizational tenure of the entire top management team, based on biographical data available from the market research firms and the firms themselves.
The standard deviation of the top management team tenure distribution.
The total number of individuals reporting to the chief executive, excluding strictly administrative or support personnel.

Euclidean distance between the avenue and street locations of a newly founded hotel and those of neighboring established hotels, using positions within the Manhattan street-avenue grid. For hotels in Lower Manhattan, where streets are laid out irregularly, comparable street and avenue locations were assigned by extrapolating from actual distances (about 1/20th of a mile between streets and 1/5th of a mile between avenues). To account for the close proximities of Lexington, Park, and Madison avenues, hotels on those avenues were coded 3.5, 4, and 4.5 on the avenue measure. Values were computed and analyzed based on the 5, 10, and 15 hotels geographically nearest the founding.
scale: Euclidean distance in street/avenue grid units (blocks, in 'as-the-crow-flies' units)
time_window: at the time of the focal hotel's founding

description: Euclidean distance in number of rooms between a newly founded hotel and its neighboring established hotels at the time of the focal hotel's founding. Hotel size was measured each year as the number of rooms operated, the standard measure of size in the hotel industry, and linear interpolation was used for a few years in which size data were missing. Values were computed and analyzed based on the 5, 10, and 15 hotels physically closest to the newly founded focal hotel.
scale: Euclidean distance in number of rooms
time_window: at the time of the focal hotel's founding

description: Euclidean distance in average advertised daily room rate, in constant dollars, between a newly founded hotel and its neighboring established hotels at the time of the focal hotel's founding. Hotel price was measured each year as the average advertised daily room rate in constant dollars, and linear interpolation was used for a few years in which price data were missing. Values were computed and analyzed based on the 5, 10, and 15 hotels physically closest to the newly founded focal hotel.
time_window: at the time of the focal hotel's founding

description: Product distance from incumbents was measured on two dimensions, hotel size (number of rooms) and hotel price (average advertised daily room rate in constant dollars). Each was the Euclidean distance between a newly founded hotel and its neighboring established hotels at founding.

The survey first asked respondents to indicate whether their hospital had engaged in twenty different quality practices covering team structures, statistical tools and process heuristics, training, quality reports and benchmarking. Conformity was measured by coding whether a hospital used a particular practice, then calculating the percentage of other hospitals adopting TQM in the same or earlier time period whose response (use/do not use) matched the focal hospital's response; these percentages were summed across the twenty practices.
time_window: 1993 survey, responses compared with other adopters in the same or earlier time period

description: A separate measure asked respondents whether their TQM program followed one of the standard approaches (Crosby, Deming, or Juran), a combination of these approaches, some other nonstandard approach, or no particular approach. Programs in the latter three categories are viewed as more customized than programs conforming to a single standard approach. This measure was coded 1 if hospitals used a particular, standard TQM model and 0 otherwise.

The time of TQM adoption was divided into three categories: within two years, between two and four years previous, and more than four years previous to data collection in 1993. This time variable effectively divides early and late adopters at approximately the midpoint of the observed adoption period, with an additional category for the relatively few hospitals that adopted earlier.

Measured as a count variable equal to the number of alliance partners who adopted TQM prior to the focal firm. The measure includes ties to other hospitals adopting prior to the focal hospital, even for those adopting in the same category of adoption period.

Measured in the same way as alliance ties: a count of fellow system members who had adopted TQM prior to the focal hospital. As with alliance ties, ties to hospitals adopting prior to the focal hospital are included even when both years fall in the same adoption-period category.

Hospital legitimacy was measured with the overall JCAHO rating, ranging from 0 (no compliance) to 100 (perfect compliance), calculated as a composite of 83 individual scores measured as 1 = substantial compliance, 2 = significant, 3 = partial, 4 = minimal, and 5 = no compliance. Based on this overall evaluation, JCAHO accredits organizations achieving acceptable levels of performance.

A survey measure assessing the perceived impact of TQM on costs, the frequency of errors and inappropriate treatment, hospital-physician relations, physician, nurse, and staff turnover, and patient satisfaction. The reliability of this scale was satisfactory (alpha = .88) and factor analysis confirmed that all items loaded on a single factor.

Return on equity, an archival measure of hospital profitability, calculated for the year following TQM adoption. ROE is described as a meaningful measure of performance for all hospitals in the sample, including not-for-profits.
An archival measure of productivity: the number of full-time equivalent employees per 100 admissions, calculated for the year following TQM adoption. This measure assesses productivity.

An effect-coded dummy variable for the industry of the sending firm, coded -1 for nonfinancial interlocks and 1 for financial interlocks. It is used as a predictor of the reconstitution of the broken tie.

An effect-coded dummy variable for type of ownership control, coded -1 for family-controlled firms and 1 for management-controlled firms. Control was determined from the classifications of Larner, Burch, Kotz, and Herman, with the authors deriving their own classifications for the years not covered by these studies; firms classified as financially controlled were treated as management-controlled.
An effect-coded dummy variable for whether the broken tie was part of a multiple interlock, coded 1 for a multiple tie. It is used as a predictor of the reconstitution of the broken tie.
The number of directors on a firm's board in a given year. The distribution was right-skewed, so its values were transformed to logarithms (base 10).

The number of years that a tie had existed prior to its disruption, measured by tracing each interlock formed prior to 1955 back to its original starting date. The distribution was right-skewed, so values were transformed to logarithms (base 10).

The dependent variable in the analysis of all broken ties: whether a broken tie was reconstituted in the same direction with the same firm. Of the 255 broken ties in the analysis, 35 (14 percent) were reconstituted this way. The log-odds of reconstitution is the dependent variable in the logistic regression equation.

In the analysis restricted to financial interlocks, whether the broken tie was reconstituted directly with the same financial corporation. Among the 81 financial interlocks in the data set, 27 (33 percent) were directly reconstituted with the same financial corporation; functionally reconstituted financial ties are treated as discontinued in the analysis of direct reconstitution.

In the analysis restricted to financial interlocks, whether the broken tie was reestablished with another financial institution. Of the 81 financial interlocks, 12 (15 percent) were reconstituted with another financial institution.

A variable recording whether the industrial firm had a known business relation with the financial institution with which the tie was disrupted, culled from Moody's Industrial Manual. It includes the financial's being in any way involved in a firm's public offering of stocks or bonds, and covers underwriting, trusteeship, transfer agency, or registrar.

variable_name: number of financials' representatives on the board
description: The number of representatives of financial institutions on the board at the time of the tie disruption, examined to see if an increase in the number of financial directors increases their power and thereby the likelihood of direct reconstitution.
time_window: at the time of the tie disruption

variable_name: change in the firm's debt ratio
description: The change in the firm's debt ratio, computed as long-term debt plus current liabilities divided by total assets, from the previous year. Each figure was standardized to the thirty-year mean debt ratio for the particular firm by taking its difference from the thirty-year mean.
time_window: change from the previous year; standardized to the thirty-year mean

description: Technical complexity of the plant's production process in 1972, operationalized by a seven-category version of Woodward's original eleven-category technical complexity scale. Woodward's first two categories were consolidated and her last two categories merged, and the two mixed types of production were eliminated. The seven categories, arranged in order of increasing technical complexity, are complex units, fabrication, small batch, large batch, large batch with large-batch assembly, mass, and process.

Technical complexity of the quality-control function, measured as the percentage of product inspections done by measuring devices or machines in 1972 rather than by manual techniques. The more quality control is dominated by tools or machines, the more technologically sophisticated and complex the function is taken to be.

Structural complexity measured as the number of plant divisions in 1972, where divisions are major structural subunits whose heads report directly to the plant manager. Since many plants in the sample were functionally designed, this is described as a partial proxy for the number of specialties present, i.e., complexity of knowledge.

Ratio of full-time supervisors to remaining (nonsupervisory) plant employees in 1972, multiplied by 100 to yield a percentage figure. Full-time supervisors include all managers and foremen who customarily direct the work of two or more other people and whose major responsibility is supervising their work rather than sharing in its performance; administrators in headquarters units are excluded. Nonsupervisory employees are used as the denominator to avoid embedding the number of supervisors in both numerator and denominator.

Percentage change in plant size (total number of employees) from 1967 to 1972, computed as [(SIZE72 - SIZE67)/SIZE67] x 100, which initially yielded a measure of growth on which high positive values indicated growing plants. This variable was then reverse scored by subtracting each value from zero to create an interval measure of decline, so that low (negative) values indicate growing plants and high (positive) values indicate declining plants. Increasing values therefore indicate an increasing tendency toward organizational decline.

variable_name: proportion of outside directors who were family of management
description: Proportion of outside directors who were family of management, aggregated per board from individual data collected for the companies' 759 outside directors. Data were collected from proxy materials and cross-validated against Standard and Poor's and Moody's Industrial Manual.
time_window: year of greenmail announcement, or the year following the raider's acquisition for the control sample

description: For each of the 759 outside directors, the board composition of the director's principal company was examined to identify whether members of the target company's management were among the board members. The data were recorded from Standard and Poor's Industrial Guide and aggregated per board.
time_window: year of greenmail announcement, or the year following the raider's acquisition for the control sample

variable_name: proportion of outside directors who had contracts with the company
description: Proportion of outside directors who were contractually linked to the company, directly or through affiliated organizations, aggregated per board from individual data collected for the companies' 759 outside directors. Data were collected from proxy materials.
time_window: year of greenmail announcement, or the year following the raider's acquisition for the control sample

description: Proportion of outside directors on the board, aggregated per board from individual data collected for the companies' 759 outside directors. Outside directors were defined as all directors who were not employed full-time by the company or who had not retired from employment with the company. Data were collected from proxy materials.
time_window: year of greenmail announcement, or the year following the raider's acquisition for the control sample

variable_name: average proportion of company equity held by outside directors
description: Average proportion of company equity that was held by the board's outside directors, aggregated per board from individual data collected for the companies' 759 outside directors. Data were collected from proxy materials.
time_window: year of greenmail announcement, or the year following the raider's acquisition for the control sample

variable_name: proportion of outside directors with executive experience
description: Proportion of outside directors who had executive experience in other companies, aggregated per board from individual data collected for the companies' 759 outside directors. Data were collected from proxy materials.
time_window: year of greenmail announcement, or the year following the raider's acquisition for the control sample

description: Group outcome coded by whether the company privately repurchased stock at a premium above the market price in a greenmail transaction. The greenmail-paying sample comprised 53 boards identified as having allowed greenmail payment amid reported rumors or explicit threats for a takeover or proxy fight by a minority stockholder; the resisting sample comprised 57 boards that resisted greenmail under the same circumstances. Repurchases involving 5 percent or more of outstanding equity were included, and the terms and prevalence of takeover threats were verified through original Wall Street Journal articles.

Total number of district and school administrators. School administrators include principals and assistant principals; district administrators include superintendents, assistant superintendents, and special services administrators. Collected by the EEOC, Fall 1976.
Total number of teachers in the district, including elementary and secondary school teachers and teacher aides. Collected by the EEOC, Fall 1976.
Total administrative expenditures as measured by the Bureau of the Census in the 1976-77 Survey of Local Government Finances.
Total instructional expenditures, also measured by the Bureau of the Census in the 1976-77 Survey of Local Government Finances.
Total revenue received by the district directly from the state. All revenue variables were collected by the Bureau of the Census in the 1976-77 Survey of Local Government Finances.
School district revenue derived from local sources, including the property tax, the parent government funding (local city or county), and revenue from other school districts.
School district revenue from the ESEA, the NDEA, Federal Vocational Programs, School Lunch monies, and direct federal aid through Public Laws 815 and 874.

Federal funds linked to the recent reforms of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA), separated from all other federal funds to permit a test of the idea that ESEA funding produces especially large effects on administrative expansion.

All federal funds other than those linked to the ESEA reforms, comprising the older federal programs such as NDEA and vocational education, School Lunch monies, and direct federal aid through Public Laws 815 and 874.

Wirt's (1978) measure of the programmatic authority of the state department of education. Wirt did content analyses of state law, involving items such as accreditation, textbook, and attendance requirements, and combined these into an index varying between 0 and 6. In the analyses its effect is estimated with the interaction of this variable with the enrollment of the district.
Total revenue received by the district directly from the state, taken from the Bureau of the Census 1976-77 Survey of Local Government Finances and used in the expenditure equations.
School district revenue derived from local sources, including the property tax, the parent government funding, and revenue from other school districts, used in the expenditure equations.
School district revenue from the ESEA, the NDEA, Federal Vocational Programs, School Lunch monies, and direct federal aid through Public Laws 815 and 874, used in the expenditure equations.
Federal funds linked to the recent ESEA reforms, broken out from all other federal funds in the expenditure equations to test their especially large effects on administrative expansion.
All federal funds other than those linked to the recent ESEA reforms, used in the expenditure equations.

Wirt's (1978) index of the programmatic authority of the state department of education, varying between 0 and 6, used in the expenditure equations with its effect estimated through interaction with district enrollment.

ESEA federal funding was district revenue from the newer Elementary and Secondary Education Act programs, separated from other federal funds such as NDEA and vocational programs. The same variable is on file as ESEA funds.

Firms were classified into three categories adapted from Rumelt's typology: single and vertically integrated (combining single-business firms with less than 5 percent of their sales outside their major business and vertically integrated firms with at least 70 percent of sales from a single integrated production technology), dominant and related, and unrelated and conglomerate (less than 70 percent of sales in related business lines). Although the ultimate classification is determined by sales, acquisition patterns, significant mergers and acquisitions, legal proceedings, company name changes and formal statements by executives were used to determine the timing of changes in strategy.
time_window: at the end of each former CEO's tenure

description: Functional specialization (production, sales, general management, finance, law), based on the CEO's education and career positions, was combined with institutional specialization (company, industry, generalist experience) into a 15-cell specialization matrix; a log-linear analysis of the simultaneous associations between functional specialization, institutional specialization and corporate strategy was used to create a three-category typology of core, administrative and environmental specialists. The typology divides the total sample of 544 CEOs into approximately equal groups.

The successor's specialization was recorded for each of the 370 cases of CEO succession using the same three-category typology of core, administrative and environmental specialists that was applied to the former CEO. Succession was defined as actually occurring when the successor was given the title of CEO.
Functional specialization was divided into five categories, production, sales, general management, finance, and law, and was based on the CEO's education and career positions.

Institutional specialization measured the institutional experience of a CEO with three categories: company experience (entire working life in one company), industry experience (entire working life in one industry but more than one company), and generalist experience (working life in a number of industries and companies).

variable_name: fragmentation of institutional decision making (survey measure)
description: Measured from survey data by calculating the distributional inequality of influence within each domain of decision making across the 14 state agencies, using the Shannon-Weiner information index calculated as the index in which P_a represents the proportion of total institutional influence accounted for by agency a. Extreme fragmentation is found when influence is evenly distributed across the 14 agents; the extreme of centralized decision making is found when one agent has all the influence. The index was calculated separately for each decision domain.

Archival county statistics routinely report the number of villages in a county, including a breakdown of the number of villages with autonomous village councils. The more autonomous councils there are, the more fragmented decision making is at the local level. Two specifications were used, the raw counts of each type of village and the percentage of villages with autonomous councils.

Archival county statistics report the number of villages with councils common to more than one village. Common councils would seem to indicate less fragmentation and greater centralization. The measure is probably confounded by a possible higher total number of councils, so specifications using raw counts and percentages of village types were used.

Linkages were counted as the number of enterprise exchange partners a cooperative had in the past year for both supplies and sales, collected by the research team member from the accounting files of the cooperatives. A disaggregated version of this variable allowed analysis of linkages in supplies and sales separately.

Linkages outside the basic functional area were defined as enterprise exchange partners for nonagricultural purchases and sales, since many cooperatives are diversified into other spheres. The measure was collected from the accounting files of the cooperatives.

Respondents were asked to assess on a 5-point scale the extent of competition with other cooperatives for the purchase and sale of products and services (5 = strong competition, 1 = weak). The question was asked separately for a variety of different products and services, and the measure of the dependent variable was constructed by adding the responses for each of the 31 questions.
scale: 5-point scale per item (5 = strong competition, 1 = weak), summed over 31 items

description: The administrative component was measured using the ratio of nonmanual workers to all workers. Because the range of this variable is restricted, it was transformed with a logit operation before analysis, as suggested by Tukey (1977), to extend the range of the ratio variable, bounded by 0 and 1, while preserving the order.
scale: ratio bounded by 0 and 1, logit transformed

description: The reported CEO's compensation (salary and bonus) in thousands of dollars from Business Week's May 6, 1985 survey, used in conjunction with information available in each company's proxy report. It is the dependent variable in the regressions.

Firm size was measured in three ways: sales in millions of dollars, assets in millions of dollars, and number of employees. Financial data and the number of employees were obtained from Fortune's annual listing of the largest industrial corporations.
Profitability was assessed as return on equity for 1984.

Nine industry dummy variables were constructed as controls. The nine industries selected were those with a maximum number of firms per industry represented, and the omitted category in the regressions is conglomerates.

As an indication of the accumulated on-the-job learning or human capital of each CEO, the number of years that each individual had been with the firm and in the position was obtained from Dun's Million Dollar Directory.

The number of vice presidents for each firm was obtained from Standard and Poor's 1985 Register of Corporations, Directors and Executives and from the number given on the proxy statement. The former includes all individuals with the title of vice president, while the latter is the firm's reporting of executive officers with significant responsibility as required under SEC regulation.

variable_name: gap between CEO and average VP compensation
description: Averages of vice-presidential pay computed from proxy and 10K reports were used to indicate the gap between CEO and average vice president compensation for testing the tournament model. In the regressions the average VP salary was entered as an independent variable instead of using the gap measure as the dependent variable, and equivalent results were obtained using the actual gap between the salaries of CEOs and vice presidents. Two possibilities were examined: the gap between CEO and top vice-president compensation and that between the CEO and the larger vice-presidential group.

variable_name: average salary of top VPs and average salary of executive officers
description: The average pay of the senior vice presidents was computed from the highest paid vice presidents in the firm, with the number used varying from one to four depending on how many ranked among the five highest paid officers. For the executive officers of the corporation an average was computed for the group as a whole, representing the mean compensation for the vice presidents defined under SEC reporting regulations as having significant responsibility.

variable_name: compensation committee salary; highest salary on compensation committee
description: Data on the compensation committee, including salary levels for board and committee members, were obtained from the proxy and 10K reports of both the focal corporation and the corporations for which the outside directors worked. Data could be collected only for those outside directors who were executives in publicly held firms, giving compensation data on roughly 50 percent of compensation committee members.

variable_name: outside directors' salary; highest salary of outside directors
description: Data on the board of directors, including the number on the board, the number of outside directors, directors' fees paid by the corporation, and salary levels for board members, were obtained from the proxy and 10K reports of both the focal corporation and the corporations for which the outside directors worked.

A firm was classified as state-owned if more than 50 percent of its equity was owned by a government, following Zif (1981). Ownership data were obtained from several issues of the Financial Times Oil and Gas International Yearbook, which details capital structure information on industry firms.

A firm was classified as publicly traded if its shares were traded on a stock exchange and if it was not majority government-owned. Ownership data were obtained from several issues of the Financial Times Oil and Gas International Yearbook.

A firm was classified as privately held if its shares were not traded on a stock exchange and if a majority of the shares were not government-owned. Ownership data were obtained from several issues of the Financial Times Oil and Gas International Yearbook.

Measured as the change in number of rigs in a firm's fleet between year t and year t + 1 divided by the number of rigs in the firm's fleet in year t. Annual measures of each variable were averaged over the life of a firm to obtain one measure per firm, and the latter was employed in the analyses.
time_window: annual measures averaged over the life of the firm, 1966-1984

description: Measured as the number of countries in which a firm had operations. Annual measures of each variable were averaged over the life of a firm to obtain one measure per firm.
time_window: annual measures averaged over the life of the firm, 1966-1984

description: Measured as the number of rigs a firm had in its domestic market divided by the total number of rigs in the firm's domestic market. Annual measures of each variable were averaged over the life of a firm to obtain one measure per firm.
time_window: annual measures averaged over the life of the firm, 1966-1984

description: Measured as the number of rig types in a firm's fleet. Four types of rigs existed in the industry: barges, jack-ups, drillships, and semisubmersibles. Annual measures of each variable were averaged over the life of a firm to obtain one measure per firm.
time_window: annual measures averaged over the life of the firm, 1966-1984

description: Measured as the number of rigs overseas contracted to state-owned customers divided by the number of rigs a firm had operating overseas. The overseas customer variable was missing for firms without international operations.
time_window: annual measures averaged over the life of the firm, 1966-1984

description: Measured as the firm mean of the proportion of years in a rig's life it was contracted to the same customer. The customer stability variable was available only for firms that had operations in more than one year.
time_window: annual measures averaged over the life of the firm, 1966-1984

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if the firm had a drillship rig or semisubmersible rig in its fleet, and 0 otherwise. Drillships and semisubmersibles drill while afloat and embody a more complex technology than bottom-supported barge and jack-up rigs, to cope with greater susceptibility to tide, wave, and weather conditions and to permit drilling at greater water depths.
time_window: annual measures averaged over the life of the firm, 1966-1984

description: Measured as the mean number of years of employment in the firm of top-management-team members in year t. Tenure in the company was adopted because it was the tenure variable most highly correlated with other tenure measures (tenure in position, tenure in the top-management team, and tenure in the industry), which yielded generally very similar patterns.

Composite measure of the extent to which a firm's strategy remains fixed over time, built from six strategic indicators. Treating t as the focal year, the firm's five-year (t-1 through t+3) variance for each strategic dimension was computed; variance scores were standardized by industry using data points from sample firms only and multiplied by minus one to bring the measures in line with the concept of persistence (absence of strategic variance over time), and the six standardized indicators were summed into an overall measure, Strategic Persistence 1 (SP1). Because advertising and R&D intensity had considerable missing data, an alternative measure, Strategic Persistence 2 (SP2), was developed based only on the other four indicators; the missing data reduced the N for SP1 to 155.

Measures the degree to which a firm's strategy matches the average strategic profile of its competitors in the same industry, using the same six strategic dimensions as the strategic persistence measure but assessing strategy at one point in time (year t). Each strategic dimension was standardized by industry using data points from sample firms only; the absolute difference between a firm's score and the average score for all sample firms in that industry was calculated; these absolute differences were multiplied by minus one to convert their meaning to conformity, and summed. Strategic Conformity 1 (SC1) summed all six indicators and Strategic Conformity 2 (SC2) summed items 3 through 6; missing data reduced the N for SC1 to 155.

Analogous to strategic conformity but assesses the extent to which a firm's performance aligns with the average of its competitors in the same industry. Three indicators were used because of the weaknesses inherent in any one measure of performance; items were standardized by industry, absolute differences were calculated, multiplied by minus one, and summed to yield an overall measure of Performance Conformity (PC).

Industries were selected to represent low-, moderate-, and high-discretion environments using product differentiability, growth, demand instability, low capital intensity, and low degree of regulation as the primary indicators of environmental discretion. The computer industry was selected as the high-discretion industry, the chemical industry as moderate discretion, and the natural-gas distribution industry as the low-discretion industry. In the moderation models, two dummy variables identify the computer and chemical industries, with natural-gas distribution as the reference category.
scale: dummy variables (1 = computer industry; 1 = chemical industry)

description: Calculated as the number of employees in the firm in year t (in thousands). Firms with many employees face bureaucratic momentum and often have severe difficulties effecting change, inhibiting managerial discretion; alternative measures of size, such as sales and assets, were highly correlated with the number of employees. Size is also entered as a control variable in regressions on tenure.

The annual working capital ratio (working capital/sales), which assesses the cushion a firm has to meet needs and opportunities on a short-term basis and which enhances managerial discretion. The conventional measure of longer-term slack, equity/debt, was not used because its reciprocal was included in the computation of the dependent variable indices. Slack is also entered as a control variable in regressions on tenure.

variable_name: mean number of new designs per year
description: The mean number of new product or process models introduced per year in each era. The mean number of new designs per year during eras of ferment was compared with the mean during eras of incremental change. Testing was limited to the cement and minicomputer industries and the glass industry was not used in testing hypothesis 1.

variable_name: time to standard (length of the era of ferment)
description: The era of ferment was defined as the period from the year a discontinuous innovation was first introduced to the year a single design first achieved a 50-percent market share, including endpoints. Its length in years for each discontinuity is reported as the time to standard.

The period following the emergence of a dominant design and preceding the next technological discontinuity. Table 5 partitions the total advance within a technology cycle into the discontinuity, the era of ferment, and the era of incremental change.

A dominant design was defined as a single configuration or a narrow range of configurations that accounted for over 50 percent of new product sales or new process installations and maintained a 50-percent market share for at least four years. Archival sources were used to identify every new cement kiln installed after a discontinuity and every minicomputer sold after a discontinuity, permitting the specification of the year that a particular design achieved a 50-percent market share.
time_window: at least four years of 50-percent share

description: Each discontinuity was classified by whether it built on existing know-how (competence-enhancing) or rendered it obsolete (competence-destroying). Such data on technical competence were unavailable for these historical innovations, so the assessment rested on the judgment and informed argument of the historian, described for every discontinuity in the Appendix.

Each of the sixteen discontinuities was classified as competence-destroying when it rendered obsolete the expertise required to master the technology it replaced. The classification of each case is described in the Appendix.

variable_name: year sales of new technology peaked
description: The year in which sales of all versions of the new technology peaked following each technological discontinuity, in constant dollars for minicomputers and in new machine installations for cement and glass. This was compared with the year the dominant design emerged.

variable_name: performance of the dominant design vs. maximum value in the year of dominance
description: For each dominant design, its performance (measured in barrels per day, containers per minute, square feet per hour, or CPU speed) was compared with the maximum value of that measure achieved in the year the design achieved dominance. If the frontier value exceeded the value for the dominant design, at least one rival design was superior to the industry standard on the criterion measured.

variable_name: newcomer / incumbent classification of early adopters
description: A firm was considered to have entered an industry when it sold its first minicomputer, barrel of cement, sheet of glass, or container. For each technological cycle, a firm was classified as an incumbent if it entered the industry before the discontinuity and otherwise as a newcomer. The decision rule was to use the maximum number of pioneers that could be identified reliably, up to a pool of five firms, with ties included.

variable_name: proportion of total advance attributable to each phase
description: For each of 11 discontinuities where data were available, the proportion of total advance within each cycle attributable to the discontinuity, advances during the era of ferment, and advances during the era of incremental change. To be conservative, all progress following the float-glass and solid-state discontinuities was assigned to the era of incremental change even though no dominant design emerged.

variable_name: innovation advancing the performance frontier by a new design
description: A technological discontinuity was an innovation that advanced the performance frontier by a significant amount through a new product or process design. The authors tracked the state of the art each year and counted only peaks tied to new designs, giving 16 discontinuities.

variable_name: High versus low appropriability classification of discontinuities
description: Each technological discontinuity was classified as occurring under high or low appropriability. The two cases in which technological competition was constrained by patent protection (continuous forming and float glass) were treated as high appropriability and the remaining fourteen as low appropriability when testing whether a dominant design emerged.

Number of sentences in a letter to shareholders referring to customers or to general economic factors affecting demand. Measured in absolute terms, as a proportion of the total number of sentences in the letter, and as a focus measure (sentences on output as a proportion of sentences on output, input, and internal environments). The output/input emphasis measure equals output focus minus input focus, so that a high score means management emphasized the output environment over the input environment.
time_window: each of the five years preceding the bankruptcy (T-5 to T-1)

description: Number of sentences in a letter to shareholders referring to creditors and suppliers. Measured in absolute terms, as a proportion of the total number of sentences in the letter, and as a focus measure (sentences on input as a proportion of sentences on output, input, and internal environments).
time_window: each of the five years preceding the bankruptcy (T-5 to T-1)

description: Number of sentences in a letter to shareholders referring to owners, employees, and top managers. Measured in absolute terms, as a proportion of the total number of sentences in the letter, and as a focus measure (sentences on internal matters as a proportion of sentences on output, input, and internal environments).
time_window: each of the five years preceding the bankruptcy (T-5 to T-1)

description: Output attention plus input attention. The external/internal emphasis measure equals (output focus plus input focus) minus internal focus, so that a high score means management emphasized the external environment over the internal environment.
time_window: each of the five years preceding the bankruptcy (T-5 to T-1)

description: Firms that filed a Chapter X or XI bankruptcy petition between 1972 and 1982, each matched with a surviving firm of similar size and product/market environment five years prior to the bankruptcy. Matches were required to be prospering, either exhibiting profitability in the top half of their industries in the year of the bankruptcy or surviving at least three years beyond the bankruptcy date.

variable_name: difficulty of agreement on the allocation of adjustment costs
description: Two indicators: (1) the difficulty of agreement with the supplier on the allocation of costs due to engineering changes for the part and (2) the difficulty of agreement with the supplier on the allocation of costs due to changes in material costs for the part, each measured on a 7-point Likert-type scale. Because the correlations between the two variables were not high enough to suggest a strong coefficient of reliability and their correlations with other variables differed in magnitude, the authors predicted each indicator separately rather than treating them as a single latent variable, and estimated the covariance between their measurement errors.

Two indicators: the extent to which the production of the part requires technical labor skills that are relatively unique to the supplier and the extent to which the production of the part requires manufacturing equipment that is relatively unique to the supplier, each measured on a 7-point Likert-type scale.
Whether the supplier invested in new technology to increase the likelihood of being selected as a supplier for this category of part, measured as yes or no.

The extent to which there are enough potential suppliers to ensure adequate competition at the commodity level for the provision of the input, measured on a 7-point Likert-type scale. The authors chose the variable that was most correlated with Walker and Weber's (1984) supplier market competition construct (r = .975).

Each sampled input was classified by whether it was procured from an internal component manufacturing division operated as a profit center or from an outside supplier in a relational contracting relationship. The two groups were compared by constraining a parameter to be equal across groups and then allowing it to differ between them.

The dependent variable is the instantaneous rate of failure of a child care service organization, modeled as a log-linear function of the covariates. Each CCSO event history is broken down into one-year observations in which the CCSO is at risk of failure, and each annual spell is treated as right-censored unless the CCSO fails. A CCSO was defined to have failed on the earliest date of closing reported in the MCSS archives or Directory listings.

Organizational age was defined as the number of years since a CCSO was founded. For CCSOs founded during 1979-1987 the founding date was the year the MCSS issued the original operating license; for CCSOs founded during 1971-1978 it was the year the CCSO first appeared in the Community Information Center's Directory.

Organizational size was defined as the maximum capacity specified in a CCSO's annual operating license. As a result of the Day Nurseries Act, licensed capacity is highly correlated with many aspects of organizational size, including enrollment, number of qualified and unqualified program staff, and size of physical facilities, playground, and equipment inventory.

For day cares, generalism was set equal to the number of age ranges a day care was licensed to serve in each year of its existence. A CCSO's license specifies the particular age range(s) that it may enroll, and CCSOs licensed to serve multiple age ranges must maintain separate configurations of human and material resources for each. A separate analysis showed that this measure does not spuriously capture the effects of operating in specific combinations of age ranges.

A dummy variable set equal to 1 for nonprofit CCSOs and 0 for profit-oriented CCSOs. In the child care sector, influential institutional constituents and the public have been increasingly opposed to for-profit child care, and for-profit CCSOs are perceived as providing poorer quality care.

The SSA linkage variable was set equal to 1 for CCSOs with site-sharing arrangements and 0 otherwise. SSAs were defined to start in the year they were first reported in the MCSS archives or Community Information Center Directory; all SSAs were established at the time of founding and no CCSOs broke an SSA by moving location.

The POSA linkage variable was set equal to 1 in each year a day care had a purchase of service agreement with the Municipality of Metropolitan Toronto Children's Services Division and 0 otherwise.
