POSAs were defined to start in the year they were first reported in the MCSS archives or Community Information Center Directory, and over 95 percent of day cares that established POSAs did so in their first year.

Day care and nursery densities were defined as the number of each type of CCSO at the start of each observation year. Density-squared terms (divided by 1000 for rescaling) were included in the models to control for the nonmonotonic relationship between density and failure rates proposed by Hannan and Freeman.

Archival data were collected on all age-range changes each day care made between 1971 and 1987, and two dummy variables were constructed. In each year prior to the occurrence of a change the dummy variables were set equal to 0; after a change (if any) the dummy variables were set equal to 1.

Firm performance was measured as annual sales growth compared to average sales growth for the semiconductor industry. It was operationalized as industry-adjusted average performance for two years, the year prior to the dismissal event and the year of the dismissal event, because organizations do not ordinarily react to poor performance within a very short time by replacing their chief executive. The information was provided by two of the market research firms, as well as by the firms themselves.
time_window: two years: the year prior to the dismissal event and the year of the dismissal event

description: Firms were identified as having had poor performance in each year that their performance was below the average for the industry for that year. Below-average performance was then coded as a dummy variable, coded 1 for a year of poor performance and 0 otherwise, and placed in an interaction term with chief executive power. The continuous measure of performance was used to control for the main effects of performance.

Chief executive dismissal was measured on an annual basis for each firm and coded 1 if a dismissal occurred, and 0 otherwise. In identifying the chief executive, the individual responsible for the operation of the organization was distinguished; where the title chief executive officer referred to an investor with little operating authority, the chief operating officer was treated as the chief executive. Dismissals were identified by two market research firms that kept records of all chief executive and top management dismissals.

Top management dismissal was measured on an annual basis for each firm. Of the 244 firm-years (out of 1,050 total) in which any top managers were dismissed, there were only 28 cases in which more than one top manager was dismissed; because multiple dismissals occurred relatively infrequently, and to distinguish more clearly between no top manager dismissal versus any top manager dismissal, the variable was measured dichotomously, coded 1 if any top manager was dismissed, and 0 otherwise.

Board composition measured the proportion of inside members of the board of directors. Information on the board of directors for each firm in the study was compiled by the market research firms, with additional information made available by the organizations themselves.

Board loyalty measured the proportion of directors appointed during the tenure of the current chief executive. Because longer-tenured chief executives will have had more opportunity to appoint more board members, chief executive tenure was controlled for.
Insider loyalty measured the proportion of directors appointed during the tenure of the current chief executive who were insiders.

Ownership dispersion was measured as the converse of ownership concentration. It was operationalized as one minus the proportion of total firm ownership held by the four largest owners. Historical ownership data was provided by the market research organizations and the semiconductor firms.
scale: proportion (1 minus the top-four ownership share)

description: Chief executive ownership was measured as the proportion of total firm ownership held by the chief executive. Historical ownership data was provided by the market research organizations and the semiconductor firms.

Successor origin, measured for each firm each time a succession event occurred, was coded 1 if the successor was from outside the organization, and 0 otherwise. An insider is a person promoted from within the firm; an outside succession occurs when a newly appointed chief executive is appointed from outside the firm.

Board membership measured the proportion of top managers who were members of the board of directors. This variable was examined in tests of the dismissal of top managers reporting to the chief executive.

Appointed by the chief executive measured the proportion of top managers appointed during the tenure of the current chief executive. This variable was examined in tests of the dismissal of top managers reporting to the chief executive.

Chief executive power was represented by board and ownership characteristics: proportion of insiders on the board, board loyalty, insider loyalty, ownership dispersion and chief executive ownership. Each was interacted with below-average performance in the dismissal models.

The dependent variable is the probability of mortality, studied with a logit regression model in which x is a vector of time-constant and time-varying covariates. Disbandings were defined as liquidation, forced merger, or voluntary merger. SLAs with negative or zero net worth under GAAP, SLAs under the Management Consignment Program, SLAs subject to regulatory intervention, and mutual-to-stock reorganizations were not treated as disbandings.

A dummy variable constructed to account for structural differences between the two forms: 1 stood for stocks and 0 for mutuals. The structural differences between the forms are institutionalized in the chartering procedures of federal and state-level regulators.

variable_name: local and nonlocal densities of financial intermediaries
description: Density, or the number of existing organizations in a population, was used as a measure of competition. Local and nonlocal densities of SLAs, commercial banks, life insurance companies, and mutual savings banks were computed. The local density of each intermediary was the number of organizations of that type in existence in the state in which the focal SLA was based; the nonlocal density was the number of organizations in states other than the one in which the focal SLA was located. No second-order density terms were computed.

Environmental variability was defined as variation in six-month T-bill rates. The measure was the coefficient of variation for each year from 1960 to 1987; as the authors write it, V = sigma over x, where x is the mean net savings inflows over the period and sigma is the standard deviation of the time series over the period. The operationalization is described as similar to that of Freeman and Hannan (1983).

A period dummy created to account for the advent of deregulation from 1980 on, marking the period in which legislation, interest-rate variability, and new intermediaries dramatically altered the asset powers and opportunities available to SLAs.

Euclidean distance of a focal organization's position in the distribution of organizational size (number of rooms operated) from the positions of all others in the population at time t; large values imply less intense competition. The measure was calculated as of the beginning of each calendar year and divided by 100 for rescaling.
time_window: beginning of each calendar year, updated annually

description: Window-based Euclidean distance in which the focal hotel is assumed to compete only with organizations within a competitive window set as ±size/2 of the focal hotel's own size, so that a 100-room hotel competes with hotels from 50 to 150 rooms. Distances to organizations outside the window have no effect on the measure. Calculated at the beginning of each calendar year and divided by 100 for rescaling.
time_window: beginning of each calendar year, updated annually

description: Euclidean distance in the two-dimensional Manhattan street-avenue grid between the focal hotel's location and the locations of all other hotels in the population at time t, with street number divided by four to equalize the physical distance scales of the street and avenue measures. Grid positions were assigned by extrapolating the existing street-avenue grid to parts of Manhattan not covered by it. Calculated at the beginning of each calendar year and divided by 100 for rescaling.
time_window: beginning of each calendar year, updated annually

description: Window-based Euclidean distance in which the focal hotel competes only with hotels inside a geographic competitive window: avenue i ± 3 avenues and street i ± 25 streets. Combined, these windows approximate the east-side-west-side and uptown-midtown-downtown distinctions commonly used for Manhattan. Calculated at the beginning of each calendar year and divided by 100 for rescaling.
time_window: beginning of each calendar year, updated annually

description: Euclidean distance between the focal hotel's average advertised daily room rate in constant dollars and the prices of all other hotels in the population at time t; for years in which price data were missing, linear interpolation was used. Calculated at the beginning of each calendar year and divided by 100 for rescaling.
time_window: beginning of each calendar year, updated annually

description: Window-based Euclidean distance in which the focal hotel competes only with hotels priced within ±price/2 of its own price, so that a hotel with a $300 room rate competes with hotels priced between $150 and $450 and a $50 hotel competes with hotels from $25 to $75. Calculated at the beginning of each calendar year and divided by 100 for rescaling.
time_window: beginning of each calendar year, updated annually

description: Failure was defined as the cessation of hotel services for short-term visitors. Changes in name or ownership were not counted as failures. The date of failure was the year a hotel was permanently delisted from the Red Book; when Red Book listings differed from other sources, a hotel was defined to have failed in the first year it was permanently delisted from two or more of the archival sources. A hotel was defined to have been founded in the year it first appeared in any archival source.
scale: event indicator (failure in a one-year spell)

description: Total assets in millions of dollars, taken from the FHLB's Financial Reports and corrected for inflation using a GNP deflator index. The authors deliberately do not take the logarithm of size; they deviated each variable from its mean across all observations on a firm to estimate firm-specific fixed effects.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each six-month period (t-1)

description: The level of a firm's investment in the nonresidential mortgage market--mortgages on commercial, industrial, and undeveloped property--observed at the end of each six-month period, with the beginning-of-period level included as a lagged dependent variable in the partial-adjustment model. Dollar amounts are adjusted for inflation with a GNP deflator index and deviated from firm means for fixed-effects estimation.
time_window: end of each six-month period, June 1977-December 1986

description: The level of a firm's investment in mortgage-backed securities--securities consisting of bundles of residential mortgages--observed at the end of each six-month period, with the beginning-of-period level entered as a lagged dependent variable. Amounts are inflation-adjusted dollars deviated from firm means.
time_window: end of each six-month period, June 1977-December 1986

description: The level of a firm's investment in consumer nonmortgage loans--including secured automobile and home equity loans, unsecured education, car, and vacation loans, and open-ended credit card and overdraft services--observed at the end of each six-month period, with the beginning-of-period level as a lagged dependent variable.
time_window: end of each six-month period, June 1977-December 1986

description: The level of a firm's investment in commercial lending--very short-term unsecured commercial paper and longer-term secured loans--observed at the end of each six-month period, with the beginning-of-period level as a lagged dependent variable.
time_window: end of each six-month period, June 1977-December 1986

description: The level of a firm's direct investment in real estate--land held for development and resale--observed at the end of each six-month period, with the beginning-of-period level as a lagged dependent variable.
time_window: end of each six-month period, June 1977-December 1986

description: The level of a firm's investment in investment securities--securities issued by government agencies and corporate stock--observed at the end of each six-month period, with the beginning-of-period level as a lagged dependent variable.
time_window: end of each six-month period, June 1977-December 1986

variable_name: Equity investments in service corporation subsidiaries (SCo)
description: The amount of a thrift's assets invested in service corporation subsidiaries--vehicles for activities such as real estate development and sales, property management, insurance, accounting and tax services, and escrow and trust services--observed at the end of each six-month period, with the beginning-of-period level as a lagged dependent variable.
time_window: end of each six-month period, June 1977-December 1986

description: One of four indicators of CEO influence. It is typically argued that as tenure increases, CEOs acquire personal power by populating boards with supporters while gaining expert power through an increased familiarity with the firm's resources. It was collected for each year.

variable_name: insider ratio (ratio of inside to outside directors)
description: The ratio of inside to outside directors on the board, one of four indicators of CEO influence. Agency theorists and advocates of board reform typically assume that outside directors will be less conciliatory than insiders toward CEOs. It was gathered at three-year intervals beginning in 1971.
time_window: gathered at three-year intervals beginning in 1971

variable_name: appointment of outside directors (number of outside directors appointed after the CEO)
description: The number of outside directors appointed after the CEO, a related measure of influence proposed by Wade, O'Reilly, and Chandratat; it represents a modification of the insider ratio. It was gathered at three-year intervals beginning in 1971.
time_window: gathered at three-year intervals beginning in 1971

description: Whether the CEO serves simultaneously as CEO and chairman of the board; in that case the CEO should have greater stature and influence among board members. It was collected for each year.

A firm is coded as having adopted an LTIP if it adopted a new performance plan aimed at adding multiyear performance incentives, such as performance shares or performance units, to a CEO's compensation contract; introduction of a performance plan is a necessary and sufficient condition for LTIP adoption. The date of adoption was recorded as the date of the annual meeting, and adoption was treated as an absorbing state.

A dichotomous measure, coded as 1 if any units or shares were granted during the year of adoption or the year thereafter, and 0 otherwise. An observation period of two years rather than just one year was used because some companies make long-term incentive grants biannually.
time_window: year of adoption and the year thereafter

variable_name: average annual grant value as a proportion of total compensation
description: The average annual grant value, as a proportion of total compensation, calculated for the two-year period following adoption. The value of restricted stock grants was included in calculating the size of LTIP grants, and the Consumer Price Index was used to adjust all compensation values for inflation to represent 1990 constant dollars. Valuation formulas are shown in the Appendix.
Total returns were calculated as capital gains plus dividends accrued during the year, divided by share price at the beginning of the year, and were lagged by one year.
The accounting-based measure of prior performance, lagged by one year.
A continuous measure of time of adoption, with values ranging from 1, when adoption was in 1972, to 19, when adoption was in 1990.

The two primary debt markets are treated as differing in uncertainty, the non-investment-grade debt market being the higher-uncertainty market and the investment grade market the lower-uncertainty one. The analysis is run separately for each market, and in the pooled analysis market type is interacted with the six variables reflecting the reliance on previous exchange partners and status.

The number of times that the lead manager has occupied a subordinate management position on an offering led by the potential co-manager over the past two years. Its coefficient denotes the tendency of the lead manager to reciprocate for management opportunities that have been provided to it by the potential co-manager over the past two years.

variable_name: prior tie between the issuing corporation and the potential co-manager
description: The number of times that the potential co-manager has occupied a management position on any offering that the issuing corporation has made over the previous two years. The authors justify it by noting that an issuer with a strong relationship with a bank may insist upon that bank being used as a co-manager.

Status is measured with Bonacich's c(a,p) measure applied to a relational matrix R that is 0 along the main diagonal and in which cell r_ij is the proportion of offerings in which banks i and j jointly appear in nonmanagement positions and i appears in a bracket above that occupied by j. The measure is based only on tombstones collected from the Wall Street Journal in 1981 and is standardized such that a score of 1 means that a bank has approximately average status. In the models the status of the lead manager and of the potential co-manager enter as separate spline variables.
scale: standardized status score with 1 equal to approximately average status

variable_name: dual spline specification of lead manager and co-manager status
description: Status-based homophily is tested with a spline specification using one coefficient for the effect of the lead manager's status when it is less than the potential co-manager's and another when it is greater, and one coefficient for the effect of the potential co-manager's status when it is less than the lead manager's and another when it is greater. Status-based homophily implies that the coefficients are positive when the focal bank's status is lower and negative when it is higher.

variable_name: distribution of offerings across high- and low-status banks
description: Market concentration is described by the proportion of offerings led by the highest-status banks in each market: 96 percent of the investment grade offerings were led by one of the 21 highest-status banks, in contrast to 71 percent of the offerings in the non-investment-grade market. It is also described by the change in offerings co-managed between the 1981-1982 and 1985-1986 periods, where the average bank in the high-status group increased the number of offerings it co-managed by 199 percent and the average bank in the lowest-status group by 162 percent, with a correlation of .23 between status and the percent increase across the 55 banks.

The dependent variable was the hospital's primary cesarean section rate. This primary rate measure excludes cesareans performed because of a prior cesarean, called repeat cesareans, because this rule applied regardless of risk and because information about previous cesareans was unavailable.

Hospital-level measure of the riskiness of each hospital's birthing population, built from recorded measured risks: labor complications and low fetus weight. The measure is the percentage of women in a given hospital and in a given year having these risk characteristics, representing the overall likelihood that a hospital faced measured risks in the patients it treated.

Hospital-level measure of the riskiness of each hospital's birthing population, built from recorded inferred risk characteristics: age (under 18 or over 34) and parity (first birth or sixth or more). The measure is the percentage of women in a given hospital and in a given year having these risk characteristics.

Hospital characteristics were measured by six categorical variables created by crossing hospital ownership charters, billing contract method, and teaching status. Not all logically possible types are represented in the California data: no major teaching-center hospitals are chartered as HMOs or for-profits, and no for-profit hospitals in California during this period contracted with patients on a prepaid insurance basis. In the regressions, dummy variables define the hospital types, with nonprofits as the base compared with the other types.
Hospitals are classified by their charter of incorporation as for-profit, nonprofit, or government. The California data include data on hospital ownership.

Whether the hospital operates on a fee-for-service basis, contracting with a patient on a per-service basis, or on a prepaid insurance basis. All HMO hospitals in the sample are in the Kaiser system, which is nonprofit; no for-profit hospitals in California during this period contracted on a prepaid basis.

Teaching hospitals were defined as members of the Council of Teaching Hospitals (COTH). Members of COTH must sponsor or participate significantly in at least four active accredited residency programs, and all the teaching hospitals in the sample have residencies in obstetrics. Teaching status was obtained from American Hospital Association publications and matched to the California data.

A z-score representation of the difference between the proportion of patients at risk and the proportion so treated, normalizing the difference in proportions with the standard deviation of the proportion at risk; the printed formula is not fully legible. Lower scores indicate that fewer risky patients are treated relative to the proportion at risk; higher scores indicate that more are treated.

The number of research and development ties a firm has, capturing the extent of its involvement in the core activities of the industry. It is used as a dependent variable measured at time t + 1 and as a predictor measured at time t.
time_window: measured at time t as a predictor and at time t + 1 as a dependent variable

variable_name: Number of ties of each type (other than R&D)
description: The disaggregated number of ties for each stage of the product life-cycle, used to capture the non-R&D network activity in which firms are involved; the authors view these efforts as a way to exploit R&D discoveries and thus as a complement to R&D networks.

The range of ties that a firm is engaged in at any given time. Portfolio diversity is computed for each firm in each year as each type's proportion of the firm's total number of ties squared and summed over all types and subtracted from 1, equivalent to Blau's index of heterogeneity. It is treated as a continuous random variable bounded in the interval [0, 7/8].
The time since inception of a firm's first R&D alliance, computed for each firm in each year as the current date minus the date at which the firm's initial R&D tie was formalized.
time_window: time since first R&D alliance, measured at time t

description: An additional measure of experience at managing ties: the time since inception of a firm's first tie for any purpose other than R&D, computed for each firm at time t as the current date minus the date at which the firm's first nonresearch alliance was formalized.
time_window: time since first non-R&D alliance, measured at time t

description: Centrality of a firm gauged locally, such that a firm's centrality is the number of other firms connected to that firm, ignoring how well those partners are connected. A connection between two DBFs was counted when there was a direct tie and when the DBFs were linked at degree distance two through a common partner. Measures of central connectivity were computed using UCINET IV.

A measure of centrality based on the concept of closeness, which captures independence from the control of others; computed for each firm as the reciprocal of the sum of the degree distance to each other firm. A high closeness score means a firm has access to many other DBFs and is not dependent on specific others for access to information.

A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if a firm is in the main connected component and 0 if not; a firm in the main component is considered much more centrally connected than an isolate. A component is defined as a group of n firms, each of which has a connection to at least one other firm in the group, with connections either direct or at degree distance two.
The reported number of employees at time t + 1, used as a measure of firm size and as one of the two indexes of growth.
A dummy variable that takes on the value of 1 if the firm is publicly traded at time t + 1 and 0 otherwise; used as the second index of growth.

Park development is operationalized with expenditure data for the Ontario Niagara Park, from the annual reports of the commissioners, and for the State Reservation in New York, from the Laws of New York and directly from the reservation. Expenditure figures were converted to constant 1983 U.S. dollars and accumulated over time and depreciated to represent in each year the current value of past capital investments in a park. Because the capital investment component of expenditures could not be identified in all years, the proportion (52 percent) of expenditures that were for capital investment in the years in which the distinction could be made was applied to all years, and an annual depreciation rate of 10 percent was used.

The dependent variable is the instantaneous rate of failing, defined as the limiting probability of a failure between t and t + t given that the hotel was operating at t, calculated over t. Failure is coded when the hotel ceases operation, but not when it changes ownership or changes name. The life histories of each hotel were broken into one-year spells to incorporate time-varying covariates, yielding 14,280 spells.

The dependent variable is the number of foundings in a year in one of the hotel subpopulations at Niagara Falls. Because there is no identifiable organization before a founding, an aggregate unit of analysis is used. Because tests indicated overdispersion of a variance-mean ratio linear in the mean, negative binomial models (Cameron and Trivedi's Negbin II) were estimated using LIMDEP.

Own density is the number of organizations in the focal hotel's subpopulation; a second-order term, own density squared, is also included. The failure rate is predicted to decrease with own density and increase with own density squared.

Other density is the density of the other hotel subpopulation; a second-order term, other density squared, was included to test for a possible nonmonotonic effect, and was dropped in models in which it was not significant.

Density at the time of the focal organization's founding, measured within the hotel's own subpopulation; it is predicted to increase the failure rate because organizations founded in environments of intense competition are forced into unattractive niches.

Density at the time of the focal organization's founding, measured in the rival subpopulation; the resources for founding and much of the relevant strategic space are partitioned by the border, so it was predicted not to influence failure.

The number of failures in the previous period in the focal hotel's own subpopulation, entered together with a second-order term, own failures squared at t-1; the prediction is a nonmonotonic effect, first increasing then decreasing the failure rate.

The number of failures in the previous period in the other subpopulation, together with a second-order term, other failures squared at t-1; the same nonmonotonic pattern as for own failures was predicted because signaling and resource implications of past events should extend across the border.

Age enters the piecewise exponential model through age periods: the age range is divided at k points, creating k age periods, and constants (baseline mortality rates) are estimated for each age period. Confidence in any result for age is tempered because size had to be estimated for many spells.

Size is measured as the number of rooms; preliminary analysis showed the number of rooms to be best for explaining the failure of Niagara Falls hotels. Size data were found for 85 percent of Ontario hotels but only 31 percent of New York hotels, and hotels that left no record of their size were assigned a size of 30 rooms, about half the average size of other Niagara Falls hotels.

Hotels are classified by the type term used in the firm's name into house, hotel, motel, inn, and other, where other is the omitted category and includes types such as lodge that have too few instances to be modeled separately.

The Euclidian distance in miles between the hotel and the falls. An interaction between distance to the falls and calendar time was also included to test whether the advantage of proximity decreases over time.

The average of the Euclidian distance in miles between the focal hotel and all other hotels that existed in the year; for hotels on different sides of the Niagara River the distance between them was calculated by way of the major bridge. An interaction between distance to competitors and calendar time was also included.
The number of other hotels within a half-mile of the focal hotel.
The year of the observation minus 1885, included to capture trends in the failure rate that are a function of historical time.

Park development was split into own-side and other-side park variables. Own-side development was the accumulated, depreciated (10 percent a year) value of capital expenditure on the park on the hotel's side of the border, in constant 1983 dollars.

Failure was recorded as the year a hotel was permanently delisted from the Redbook; if Redbook listings differed from those in the other archival sources, a hotel was recorded as failed in the first year it was permanently delisted from two or more of the archival sources. Each hotel's history is broken down into one-year spells in which the hotel is at risk of failing, and each spell is considered right-censored unless the hotel fails, which allows the time-varying independent variables to be updated annually. The hazard rate is the instantaneous rate of failure, estimated in a piecewise exponential model in which constants (baseline mortality rates) are estimated for each of several preselected age periods.

A dummy variable set equal to zero until the occurrence, if any, of a chain affiliation; thereafter it was set equal to one and reset to zero if the affiliation was subsequently lost. A second dummy, ex-component hotel, was constructed analogously based on the loss of chain affiliation, and two time-clock variables tracked the natural logarithm of the number of years since a hotel last acquired or lost a chain affiliation. Together the dummy and time-clock variables capture the main and time-varying effects of chain affiliation and loss.

variable_name: initial local experience and incremental local experience
description: A chain's operating experience in Manhattan is a function of the number of component hotel-years it operated in Manhattan during its past history, with a discount weight that depreciates values of experience as a function of their age to account for antiquation or decay of knowledge. Initial local experience is the affiliated chain's cumulative operating experience in Manhattan at the time the relationship was established; incremental local experience is that cumulative experience at the start of each year minus appropriately discounted initial experience. Both variables were set equal to zero until a chain affiliation was established, were reset to zero if the affiliation was severed, and were reset to the experience of the new chain when a component changed chains. Four specifications of the discount factor were estimated, and the analysis uses the square-root-of-age discount.

variable_name: initial nonlocal experience and incremental nonlocal experience
description: A chain's operating experience outside Manhattan is a function of the number of component hotel-years it operated outside Manhattan during its past history, discounted in the same way as local experience. Initial nonlocal experience and incremental nonlocal experience were computed in the same way as the corresponding local experience variables, using the nonlocal experience equation.

variable_name: number of Manhattan rooms a chain operated (natural logarithm)
description: Measured as the natural logarithm of the number of Manhattan rooms a chain operated at the start of each year.

variable_name: number of Manhattan hotels a chain operated
description: Measured as the number of Manhattan hotels a chain operated at the start of each year.

Computed for each chain at the start of each year as the percentage of a hotel chain's components that had the same name as the focal component. This modifies Ingram's (1996b) chain-level measure, which was based on the most common name in the chain, so that the sharing of the focal component's name is captured.

variable_name: independent hotel density and independent hotel mass
description: Independent hotel density is the total number of independent hotels existing in Manhattan at the start of each year. Independent hotel mass is the total number of rooms in independent hotels existing in Manhattan at the start of each year, from which each independent hotel's own number of rooms was subtracted so that mass reflected the number of rooms operated by other hotels; a natural logarithm transformation of mass was used. Own-type and other-type density and mass variables were interacted with the component hotel dummy variable.

variable_name: component hotel density and component hotel mass
description: Component hotel density is the total number of component hotels existing in Manhattan at the start of each year. Component hotel mass is the total number of rooms in component hotels existing in Manhattan at the start of each year, from which each component hotel's own number of rooms was subtracted so that mass reflected the number of rooms operated by other hotels; a natural logarithm transformation of mass was used.

The purchase price per target share minus the pre-takeover ("unaffected") stock price, divided by the pre-takeover price. The pre-takeover price is the target's stock price 30 days prior to the first date on which a potential takeover of the target was announced in the Wall Street Journal Index; the purchase price is the price at which the acquisition was consummated, and when stock rather than cash was offered the market value of stock offered per target share was used as the numerator. The premium was adjusted for the movement in the Standard and Poor 500 Index, an adjustment the authors report correlated at over .90 with the unadjusted premiums.
time_window: 30 days prior to the first takeover announcement; consummation price

description: Stockholder returns for the twelve months prior to the date used to determine the unaffected stock price. Stockholder returns were calculated as stock price appreciation plus returns from dividends (assuming dividends are immediately reinvested in the stock), divided by the initial stock price.
time_window: twelve months prior to the unaffected stock price date

description: The aggregate favorability of all CEO press accounts: the sum of the scores for all articles about a CEO over the three years leading up to the acquisition. Articles specifically attributing organizational outcomes to CEOs or otherwise commenting on CEOs' performance were identified in seven major newspapers through Lexis/Nexis and in magazines through ABI Inform; 138 articles were identified and independently coded by two researchers. Articles were scored 3 points for unequivocally favorable, 2 points for on balance favorable with some critical remarks, 1 point for neither positive nor negative, -1 point for on balance negative with some positive comments, -2 points for unequivocally negative, and zero points for the 45 CEOs who received no press reports.
scale: sum of article scores (each article scored -2 to 3)
time_window: three years leading up to the acquisition

description: A measure of CEO self-importance calculated as CEO cash compensation divided by the compensation of the second-highest-paid officer in the firm.

A composite measure of hubris derived from factor analysis of the three hubris indicators. With an oblique rotation method incorporating a maximum likelihood procedure, the three variables formed a single factor with an eigenvalue of 1.48, explaining 50 percent of the variance; the factor loadings were recent acquiror performance = 0.46, media praise = 0.85 and CEO relative pay = 0.74. These weightings were used to construct an overall hubris index.
A dummy variable coded 1 when the board chair and CEO were the same individual and 0 otherwise.
The number of executive directors divided by the total number of directors.

The number of shares owned by all outside directors divided by the total number of company ordinary shares; to convey "smallness of director holdings" the authors used the natural logarithm of the reciprocal of outside director holdings.

Cumulative abnormal returns for the period immediately surrounding the takeover news: from five days prior to the first takeover announcement to five days after the consummation of the acquisition. Cumulative abnormal returns were measured using the market model, with parameters estimated over the 300 trading days prior to the last unaffected stock price.
time_window: from 5 days before the first takeover announcement to 5 days after consummation

description: Cumulative abnormal returns for the period from 30 days prior to the first takeover news to 331 trading days later, including more delayed market responses and presumably postacquisition developments. Estimated with the market model over the 300 trading days prior to the last unaffected stock price.
time_window: from 30 days prior to the first takeover news to 331 trading days later

description: For each firm I summed foundation disbursements and direct cash contributions and, because of yearly fluctuations, averaged this sum across 1979, 1980, and 1981 and then across 1987, 1988, and 1989. Figures from 1987-89 were converted into 1980 dollars using the producer price index. Since the variables were highly skewed, natural logs were computed. Donated goods, volunteer time, and sponsorships were not included.

Dummy variable for period used in the pooled model, together with multiplicative interaction terms between each substantive regressor and YEAR. If the effect of a regressor differs across periods, the interaction coefficient is significant.

Company representatives estimated the percentage of sales in 1980 and 1981, and again in 1988 and 1989, that went to households or consumers; data were obtained on 66 of the 69 firms in 1981 and 73 of the 76 firms in 1989. Where self-reports were missing, the firm's primary industry was coded and that industry's dependency on consumer sales was assessed with an input-output based percentage. Because the zero-order correlations between the Dun and Bradstreet and Standard and Poor's percentages were so high, the two were averaged.

The average number of employees was divided by the average value of total assets, computed for 1979 through 1981 and for 1987 through 1989. Data were taken from various editions of the Corporate Report Factbook.
The natural log of employees averaged across 1979-81 and across 1987-89 was the indicator of firm size.
scale: natural log of number of employees

description: Two sets of measures of company performance were computed. First, simple ratios of pretax net income (averaged over each three-year period) to revenues, total assets, and equity; pretax net income came from 10-K reports and the denominators from the Corporate Report Factbook. Second, ratios of after-tax net income to revenues, total assets, and equity for 1979, 1980, 1987, and 1988 separately, averaged within each period. The same three ratios were examined for firms of comparable size (based on total assets) in the company's primary industry (four-digit code) using Dun and Bradstreet's Industry Norms (1981) and Business Ratios (1989), and companies were coded as at or above the 75th percentile (4), between the 50th and 75th (3), between the 25th and 50th (2), and below the 25th percentile (1). Summary performance measures averaged the three ranks based on Dun and Bradstreet's industry codes and the three ranks based on Standard and Poor's SICs.

From proxy statements for 1980 and 1988 I gathered the percent of stock owned by the single largest shareholder other than the CEO, the largest family shareholder group, and the single largest corporate shareholder; where proxy statements were unavailable, data for an adjacent year were substituted. All four ownership variables were recoded as dichotomies (0 through 9.9 percent = 0; > 10 percent = 1). LGINVEST was coded 1 if any type of outside interest (a person, family group, or corporation) owned 10 percent or more of the company's stock and 0 otherwise.

The percent of stock owned by the CEO, gathered from proxy statements for 1980 and 1988, recoded as a dichotomy with 0 through 9.9 percent coded 0 and more than 10 percent coded 1. In the panel analysis this item was instead treated as an interval variable, because no company in the panel went from weak CEO control (< 10 percent) to strong CEO control (> 10 percent).
scale: dummy (0/1) in the cross-sectional analysis; percent in the panel analysis

description: The CEO (or president) of the firm in late 1979 and 1987 was identified from the Corporate Report Factbook, and birthplace was obtained from various volumes of the Corporate Report Factbook and phone calls to corporate staff. A dummy variable was coded 1 if the CEO was born in Minneapolis, St. Paul, or their suburbs and 0 elsewhere.

Philanthropic leaders were identified by asking samples of 90 prominent citizens in 1981 and 108 in 1989 to name those very instrumental in raising corporate contributions; those with three or more votes were dubbed 1981 and 1989 philanthropic leaders. Leaders were handed a list of the study companies and asked to check those where they knew personally an officer or board member, producing a rectangular array whose column sums divided by the number of elite respondents give NETPCT. ELITSUM sums the number of shared memberships between each CEO (or spouse) and the leaders across area metropolitan and country clubs (CLUBSUM), Fortune 500/50 boards (FORTSUM), and the eight most prestigious cultural organization boards (CULTSUM). Because the pooled correlation between ELITPROX's two components was .785, a principal components analysis was performed and factor scores assigned to each case; the first eigenvalue was 1.78 and explained 89.0 percent of the variance, with factor loadings of .943.

The log of total contributions in 1987-89 is the dependent variable of the panel model, with the log of total contributions in 1979-81 as a predictor. Both were coded the same way as in the cross-sectional analysis.

The change in a firm's performance score between 1979-81 and 1987-89, entered as a change score in the panel models and, in the interaction models, multiplied by elite proximity. Coded the same as in the cross-sectional analysis.
The change in the natural log of employees between 1979-81 and 1987-89, entered as a change score in the panel models and in the interaction models. Coded the same as in the cross-sectional analysis.
scale: change in natural log of number of employees

description: The change between 1979-81 and 1987-89 in the dummy indicating whether a large outside investor owned 10 percent or more of the firm, entered as a change score and in interactions with elite proximity. A one standard deviation above the mean indicates firms went from having no large outside investor to having one.

The change between 1979-81 and 1987-89 in the CEO's stock ownership, treated as an interval variable rather than dichotomized because no company in the panel went from weak CEO control (< 10 percent) to strong CEO control (> 10 percent). Entered as a change score and in interactions with elite proximity.
scale: change in percent of stock owned

description: Contemporaneous elite proximity measured in 1987-89, already standardized, used as the base predictor in the interaction models testing hypothesis 8; change in elite proximity between the two periods was also examined in the panel models. Variables were not centered before computing the interaction terms because ELITPROX was already standardized and change scores had a meaningful zero.

Measured as the number of prior adopters of the practice, in this case the number of other firms that used each of the 63 investment banking firms during the past three years. Three years was used on the assumption that any indicator of the experience of other firms that is more than three years old is too old to influence the acquiring firm.

variable_name: average asset size of the other firms using each investment banker
description: Average asset size of the other firms using each of the 63 investment bankers. Because the size distribution was skewed, the log of the size variable was taken prior to analysis.

variable_name: average profitability of the other firms using each investment banker
description: A variable reflecting each firm's return on equity (ROE) was first created. Since profitability varies widely by industry, the average ROE for all other firms in the same industry was subtracted from that variable. These industry-adjusted values were then averaged across the other firms using each of the 63 investment bankers.

For each acquisition, the average of the acquisition premiums associated with each of the 63 investment bankers during the prior three years. The premium paid for the target company was calculated as the percentage difference between the final price per target share paid by the acquiring firm and the target's stock price four weeks before the offer announcement.

The maximum premium paid on an acquisition that each investment banking firm was associated with during the past three years, used to measure very high premiums. Premiums are calculated as the percentage difference between the final price per target share and the target's stock price four weeks before the offer announcement.

The minimum premium paid on an acquisition that each investment banking firm was associated with during the past three years, used to measure very low premiums. Premiums are calculated as the percentage difference between the final price per target share and the target's stock price four weeks before the offer announcement.

Measured by the variation in analysts' estimates of the value of the target firm involved in each acquisition. The measure was the coefficient of variation, i.e., the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean, of the analysts' projected target EPS estimates for the year of the acquisition, measured as of December 31 of the year before the acquisition.
time_window: December 31 of the year before the acquisition

description: Measured by the range (high versus low) of premiums associated with each investment banker during the prior three years. If an investment banker is associated with widely varying outcomes (premiums), it is more difficult to interpret the impact of that investment banker on prior deals.

variable_name: whether a given investment banking firm was selected
description: Each observation was coded 1 if that investment banking firm was selected to advise on the acquisition, and 0 otherwise. Each acquisition contributed 63 observations to the analysis, and acquirers selected an average of 1.7 investment bankers per acquisition.

variable_name: number of railroad charters granted by the legislature each year
description: Annual count of railroad charters granted by the Massachusetts legislature, taken from the state's annual railroad reports and cross-checked against the Acts and Resolves of the General Court and, for the early period, Poor's (1860) manual. Charters granted to local street car lines and charters granted to incumbent firms when they acquired other firms or entered receivership were excluded. The year of the first founding, 1825, was omitted because its value is constrained to be greater than zero, and annual counts rather than exact charter dates were analyzed.
Binary variable representing the public capitalization policy regime, which extends from the industry's beginning to 1871, when Massachusetts legislation curtailed public capitalization.
Binary variable representing the pro-cartel policy regime, which extends from the year after rate regulation legislation, 1872, to 1896.
The antitrust regime (1897-1922) is the omitted category of the binary policy regime variables. It begins with the Supreme Court enforcement of the Commerce and Sherman acts in 1897.
Five binary variables representing the periods identified by economic historians, omitting the first period: 1825-1860, 1861-72, 1873-1893, 1894-1913, and 1914-1922.

Following prevailing practice, density is the number of firms surviving at year's start, calculated as cumulative foundings minus cumulative failures. An alternative measure, independent density, is the number of autonomous firms at the beginning of the year, computed as simple density minus the number of wholly leased firms; this alternative did not perform as well as density in the analysis.

variable_name: lagged foundings and lagged foundings squared
description: Lagged foundings and lagged foundings squared serve as independent variables; the quadratic form captures the inverted U-shaped effect expected of prior foundings.

A railway fails when it declares bankruptcy, enters receivership, or is acquired by another firm; acquisitions, while not technically failures, are treated as such to replicate previous studies. Railroads that expired without experiencing any of these events are coded as failed in the year the railroad permanently halted construction, ceased to operate, or last recorded legal action. Lagged failures were entered with a squared term in equation (3), but only the linear term was retained in the reduced model because only the first term showed a significant effect.

The vitality of the British capital market is operationalized as the number of months the economy held steady or grew in the previous year. Each variable was constrained to range from 0 to 12, and years in which the U.S. was at war were set to zero because wars interrupted capital flows.

The vitality of the U.S. capital market is operationalized as the number of months the economy held steady or grew in the previous year. Each variable was constrained to range from 0 to 12, and years in which the U.S. was at war were set to zero because wars interrupted capital flows.

Mileage mass is the total operating track mileage in the commonwealth at the beginning of the year; revenue mass is gross industry revenues. Both were collected from the state's annual railroad reports, supplemented by other sources, with mileage corrected in places with data from Poor's (1860) manual. Each measure was logged to replicate previous studies.

Capital mass, the measure most commonly used in previous ecological studies, is the cumulative capitalization of the industry, collected from the state's annual railroad reports and supplemented by other sources. The measure was logged to replicate previous studies.

variable_name: Herfindahl concentration index (with four-firm and eight-firm concentration ratios)
description: Four-firm and eight-firm concentration ratios reflect the proportion of total industry revenues accruing to the largest four and eight firms, respectively. The Herfindahl concentration index is the sum of the squares of the market shares of operating firms and is constrained to range from 0 to 1; the market share of a railroad is its annual sales divided by total industry sales. Figures come from railroads' annual reports to the commonwealth.

The measure of importation was limited to those top management team members who within the previous 10 years were hired from firms whose primary industry was the same as the focal firm's. Each of these executives received a score of 1 (i.e., one intraindustry tie), which was then adjusted for recency by a factor taking the form (10 - firm tenure)/10; thus an executive who had been with the focal firm for five years received an importation score of .5. Tie totals were divided by top management team size.

To capture active participation and interaction, rather than nominal membership alone, the measure counted the number of trade association leadership positions held by executives. Tie totals were divided by top management team size.

Measured like intraindustry importation, using a count of extraindustry hires added to the top management team within the previous 10 years, adjusted for recency by the factor (10 - firm tenure)/10, and divided by top management team size.

This measure was a count of all top management team members' directorships in outside firms, divided by top management team size. Fewer than 10 percent of these ties were to firms operating in the same industry, and these were excluded, ensuring that the measure reflects only extraindustry linkage.

variable_name: outside directors serving on the focal firm's board
description: This variable was measured by counting all outside directors with primary responsibilities outside of the focal firm's industry, excluding the very few within-industry directorships, and dividing by top management team size.
To measure these ties, the authors counted top executives' memberships in industry-spanning associations such as the Conference Board and the Business Roundtable, divided by top management team size.

Following Finkelstein and Hambrick (1990), each strategic indicator was standardized by industry for each year of study (mean = 0; standard deviation = 1) and the absolute difference of each firm's score from the industry averages was calculated. A single composite indicator of conformity was created by summing together all six difference measures (Cronbach alpha = .62) and multiplying by minus one to convert the construct's meaning to one of conformity. Strategic conformity was measured at time t+2.

Performance was measured as the firm's average return on assets (ROA) in years t+2 and t+3. A common gauge of organizational profitability, ROA captures the degree to which management has effectively deployed firm assets. Because it is widely acknowledged that extraneous factors can introduce variability into single-year measures, two-year averages were used.

A dummy variable was used to designate environmental uncertainty, coded 0 for the stable food industry and 1 for the uncertain computer industry. The two industries differed substantially over the study period, with the computer industry characterized by rapid technological change, volatile growth, and demand instability, in contrast to the significantly less turbulent branded foods industry.
scale: 0 = stable food industry; 1 = uncertain computer industry

description: Measured as the percentage of people in the sample with lower levels of education than the entrepreneur in the observation. Education was identified in nine categories, and the variable ranges from 0 to 1 and is scaled based on the empirical distribution of education.
Coded 1 if the entrepreneur had 'supervised managers' as the highest level of management experience achieved, with 'supervised no one' as the reference group.
Coded 1 if the entrepreneur had 'supervised others' as the highest level of management experience achieved, with 'supervised no one' as the reference group.
The number of prior full-time jobs held by the entrepreneur, segmented into five discrete categories: 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4, or 5 or more jobs.

The entrepreneur's previous experience with (a) customers, (b) suppliers, and (c) products and services, each measured individually on a 5-point Likert scale and then combined (Cronbach alpha = .8723), recoded to the 0-1 range.

Coded 1 if the entrepreneur's most important goal in starting a new venture was 'to let you do the kind of work you wanted to do' or 'avoid working for others'; coded -1 if the entrepreneur responded 'to make more money than you would have otherwise' or 'to build a successful organization'; and 0 if the goal was 'other.'
A dummy variable that takes into account the parents' history in an entrepreneurial venture.

The age recorded at the time of the first questionnaire. To avoid multicollinearity between age and age squared, age was operationalized as deviation from the mean (36 years) and age squared as the square of such deviation.

For those firms that survived and returned the 1987 questionnaire, the amount of money (in the form of salaries, perquisites, and dividends) the entrepreneur withdrew from the venture during the third year. Money taken out was reported as being within a range between predetermined bounds, and it represents the overall returns to the entrepreneur for both the financial and human capital invested in the venture.

The latent construct of threshold performance, which is never directly observed. It is derived from comparisons of economic performance and venture discontinuance and estimated through the maximum likelihood tobit equation on threshold.
A binary variable representing the exit decision of firm n: 0 if the firm continued, 1 if it was discontinued.

Dependence on organizations with different ideologies was operationalized as the amount of short-term debt owed to banks. Short-term loans, which are due on demand or in less than one year, provide the bank with the greatest amount of leverage because it is when loans are due and renewals and extensions are being negotiated that the bank's power to make credit contingent on concessions by the kibbutz is greatest. Banks are treated as ideal-type capitalist organizations that represent a different ideology than the socialist kibbutzim.

variable_name: economic cost of not hiring labor
description: Estimated as the marginal product of labor for each kibbutz in each year minus the average wage rate in Israel for that year. The marginal product of labor was estimated with a classic Cobb-Douglas production function, separately for agriculture and industry, using revenue, investment in equipment and amount of labor, with fixed effects for kibbutz and year. The figures for agriculture and industry were converted to constant dollars and averaged with weights based on the proportion of the kibbutz's revenue that came from agriculture and industry.

The degree of ideological adherence of the kibbutz was operationalized by federation affiliation. Dummy variables for Artzi and Meuchad were included and interacted with the dependence and economic cost variables; the excluded category includes primarily kibbutzim of the Ichud federation, but also a very small number of other kibbutzim that were less adherent to the self-labor principle. On the ideological adherence scale for the self-labor principle the Ichud is the most lenient, the Artzi the strictest and the Meuchad in between, a ranking based on expressed ideology and not on observed usage of hired labor.

Expenditures for outside laborers were divided by the average wage rate in Israel over the period studied to estimate the number of hired laborers, and this number was divided by the total labor used by the kibbutz. It is a continuous measure of the extent to which a kibbutz implemented or failed to implement a practice dictated by its ideology, and it has been used as a dependent variable in previous studies of kibbutzim and other cooperative organizations. Total labor includes only labor at productive activities on the kibbutz, the activities for which hired labor is normally used.

The same percentage of hired labor used as the dependent variable, read as the extent to which the kibbutz implemented or failed to implement the practice dictated by its ideology: a higher percentage of hired labor means less implementation of the principle of self-labor. Hired labor was estimated by dividing expenditures for outside laborers by the average wage rate in Israel and dividing by total labor used by the kibbutz.

The performance measure is the 12+ Metro audience share (Monday-Sunday, 6 AM-midnight), the average proportion of all listeners over 12 years old tuned in to the focal station during the broadcast week. The social aspiration level is the mean share of all stations in the market: the numerator is the sum of the shares of the local commercial stations with measurable influence, and the denominator is the number of local commercial stations with measurable influence. The key relative performance variable is defined as share minus the social aspiration level, entered as a spline so that the coefficient can change at the aspiration level point.
time_window: annual audience measurement, formed as an average of the spring and fall ratings books for markets surveyed at least twice a year and as the spring ratings book for markets surveyed only once a year

description: The historical aspiration level uses the audience share and makes an exponentially weighted moving average of the share experienced by the focal station, with an adjustment parameter a giving the weight to the current performance. The relative performance variable is defined as share minus the historical aspiration level, entered as a spline so that the coefficient can change at the aspiration level point; the value a = 0.1 is used in the reported tables.
time_window: annual audience measurement, exponentially weighted moving average of experienced performance

description: The most inclusive event consists of all changes in format or production, effectively counting all entries in the M Street Journal; this is called all changes. The outcome is the binary variable (no change or change) at a specific time, predicted in a given year by last year's performance and current market conditions. Four subevents partition the events: innovative format, satellite format entry, production change, and new format.

A count of the format changes by other stations in the local market in the previous year. The market change variables test how information about opportunities affects change, so only recent events were added.
A count of all format changes in markets in which the focal corporation had stations, except changes in the focal market and by its own stations.

A count of the station's own format changes during the past two years. The station and corporate change variables test how capabilities affect change, so a two-year span was used to capture a longer period of buildup and retention.
A count of the format changes made by the other stations in the focal corporation during the previous two years.

Alliances were classified into three categories arrayed in increasing order of hierarchical controls: contractual alliances, minority equity investments, and joint ventures. The variable was coded 0 for contractual alliances, 1 for minority equity investments, and 2 for joint ventures.
scale: 0 = contractual alliance, 1 = minority equity investment, 2 = joint venture

description: Two dummy variables capture the anticipated type of interdependence of an alliance, classified from the strategic rationales given by each partner for its participation at the time of announcement. Each alliance was coded as involving reciprocal, sequential, or pooled interdependence using Thompson's distinction, and an alliance was conservatively coded with the highest level of interdependence anticipated by either partner. The default category is pooled interdependence.
scale: 0/1 dummies with pooled interdependence as the default category
time_window: at the time of alliance announcement

description: A measure to capture the presence of a technology component within the alliance, coded 1 = technology component and 0 = no technology component. Non-R&D alliances typically included those that primarily involved production, distribution, or marketing.

Sector dummy variables capture systematic differences in appropriability regimes across industries, with biopharmaceuticals as the default sector. Prior research suggests that biopharmaceuticals has the strongest appropriability regime and automotives the weakest, with new materials lying in between.
scale: 0/1 dummies with biopharmaceuticals as the default sector

description: An indicator recording the number of prior alliances the two firms had entered into since 1970, used as an indicator of trust between them. A value of 0 denotes a first-time alliance.
scale: count of prior alliances; 0 = first-time alliance

description: Three dummy variables indicating whether an alliance was between partners in the USA, Europe, or Japan, used to capture trust. The default was a cross-region alliance, with 1 = partners of that region and 0 = partners of different regions.
scale: 1 = partners of that region, 0 = partners of different regions

description: The number of partners in the alliance was computed and recoded as a dummy variable, with a value of 1 if an alliance was multilateral and a value of 0 if it was bilateral.

A factor score from an exploratory factor analysis of seven binary accreditation indicators. Factors were extracted via principal components with eigenvalues greater than 1 and varimax rotation; polychoric loadings produced virtually identical scores. The factor scores were computed via the Bartlett method and normalized as z-scores.

A factor score from an exploratory factor analysis of seven binary accreditation indicators. Factors were extracted via principal components with eigenvalues greater than 1 and varimax rotation; polychoric loadings produced virtually identical scores. The factor scores were computed via the Bartlett method and normalized as z-scores.

A binary indicator of exit from the hospital population. Exit events included dissolutions, acquisitions by other hospitals, transformations into other organizational forms, and equal-status mergers. The survivor models estimate mortality rates.

A period indicator for the era of federal involvement, used in interaction with technical legitimacy to test the moderating effect of centralized funding decisions. The period is compared with the professional dominance era (1945-1965) and the managed competition era (1983-1990).

A period indicator for the era of managed competition, used in interaction with managerial legitimacy to test the moderating effect of formalized organizational interdependence. This era is characterized by widespread provider linkages and exchange relations.
A count of hospital organizations in the SMSA and its square, included in survival models to capture form-level cognitive legitimacy and competitive dynamics.

The time since the founding of a hospital. For those organizations undergoing equal-status mergers, the old organizational event histories were coded as exits and the time clock of the new merged hospital was set to zero.
A binary distinction between general hospitals and specialist hospitals. The specialist category included children's, orthopedic, TB, and maternity hospitals, among others.

Interaction terms between institutional periods and hospital ownership types (for-profit, nonprofit, government). The conformity of mission with the regime is inferred from the sign and significance of ownership coefficients in each period.

variable_name: technical and managerial legitimacy factor scores
description: Normative legitimation was measured by accreditation and membership indicators that grouped into two factor scores, one for technical functions and one for managerial functions. These scores were used in the survival models.

An analyst is identified as covering a firm if he or she publishes at least one earnings forecast for that firm and is then designated as an industry specialist based on the number and proportion of the firms in that industry that he or she covers. Coverage mismatch for a firm in an industry varies from a score of zero, indicating that the firm has succeeded in attracting the maximum number of industry specialists, to a score of 1, meaning that it has failed to attract any of these analysts. The firm-level measure is a weighted average of the segment-level scores, where the weight is the proportion of total sales (or assets, if sales data are unavailable) that the segment represents.
time_window: t-1 (one year before the time of potential divestiture)

description: The coverage mismatch of a segment is computed as for the firm and then expressed in terms of its deviation from the firm-level measure.

The excess value of a firm is the log-ratio ln[V/I(V)] comparing the firm's actual value V, measured as its total capitalization, to an imputed value I(V). I(V) is calculated by taking the median value-to-sales ratio for single-segment firms in each industry, applying it to each of the segments of a multi-industry firm, and then summing to generate an imputed value for that corporation. Discrepancies between summed segment-level sales and total sales are corrected by eliminating the 5 percent of firms for which the discrepancy is greater than 1 percent.
The ratio of the firm's earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) to its assets.
The segment's ratio of earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) to its assets, expressed as a deviation from the firm's mean level.

The median ratio, taken over all single-segment firms in the corresponding industry, of a firm's total value or capitalization (the market value of a firm's common stock plus the book value of its debt) to its sales. Sales rather than another performance measure is used because the sales-based measure has produced the most robust results in previous research; to increase reliability, the median ratio for the corresponding 2-digit industry is used when there were fewer than four single-segment firms in a 3-digit industry.
The firm's expenditure on research and development in the segment, expressed as a deviation from the firm's mean level.

A segment's prevalence score is the mean relatedness of that segment to all other segments of the firm, using the interindustry prevalence structure T derived following Teece et al. (1994). The firm-level measure is the weighted average of the prevalence scores across the firm's segments, with weights equal to the ratio of the segment's reported sales (or assets, when available) to total firm sales (or assets).
For the segment-level measure, the firm-level measure is subtracted from a segment's prevalence score.
The segment's percentage of the firm's total sales, expressed as a deviation from the firm's mean level.
The age of the segment, expressed as a deviation from the firm's mean level.

Indicator of whether a firm exited a 3-digit SIC industry (segment) by the subsequent fiscal year. Breaks of one or two years in the publication of segment data are coded as missing rather than as divestitures; when a 3-digit SIC code disappeared from a firm's profile of segments and a segment with the same 2-digit SIC code emerged to replace it, the new segment is coded as a continuation rather than a divestiture. Divested segments were removed from the analysis in all years subsequent to divestiture.

variable_name: Percent of program adoptions by school selectivity group
description: Measures the extent to which schools within each of the four status groups have adopted a recycling program. The four stable status groups were derived from a hierarchical cluster analysis in UCINET based on school selectivity. The variable is lagged by one year in the models.

A standard dummy variable, coded as one for the most highly selective group and zero otherwise. It was constructed from selectivity data coded annually on a continuous four-point scale, with four being the most selective, taken from two published guides used for cross-checking.
A dummy variable indicating whether a college or university is public or private. It is one of the invariant dummy variables not lagged in the models.

Captures if and when a college or university created an environmental major. It is a time-varying covariate developed by systematically coding whether a school had an official major related to environmentalism as reported in the two published guides from 1975 to the present, using two sources for cross-checking.
time_window: 1975 to the present; lagged by one year

description: A time-varying dichotomous variable that captures if and when a college or university student environmental group was a member of the Student Environmental Action Coalition through official membership, providing an objective indicator of a school's propensity to experience student advocacy of recycling. Annual membership data were provided by the SEAC from its inception in 1989.

The dependent variable records whether a campus recycling program, if and when created, was staffed by creating a new full-time position within the facilities management department. This is one of two destination states estimated in the competing risk formulation, with its own set of rates and parameters. Data were obtained through the survey of Great Lakes colleges and universities.

The dependent variable records whether a campus recycling program, if and when created, was staffed by giving recycling duties to an existing facilities employee as an additional obligation. This is the second destination state estimated in the competing risk formulation, with its own set of rates and parameters. Data were obtained through the survey of Great Lakes colleges and universities.

The event analyzed is the adoption of an authorized recycling program of either staffing form. Data are organized to include yearly observations on each school in the population until a recycling program was adopted, yielding 2,530 school-year observations. Analyses begin in 1975, when the first authorized recycling program in the population was created, to avoid left-censoring.

Subjective measure derived from a question asked of company respondents: "To what extent could you rely on existing knowledge to build the first product?", followed by the prompt "That is, you did not have to create extensive new technical knowledge." The question was reversed-scored in the original; a 0 indicated all new knowledge was created and a 10 indicated the firm used nearly all existing knowledge. For the analysis the scale was inverted to indicate increasing degrees of innovativeness. Values: 0 = low new knowledge creation; 5 = moderate knowledge creation; 10 = extensive knowledge creation.

Subjective measure derived from the question "To what extent did you synthesize existing knowledge to produce your first product?", followed by the prompt "That is, you used existing knowledge in unique combinations." A zero indicated no synthesis and a 10 indicated extensive synthesis.

Objective measure of technological innovation based on an industry-wide comparison: the minimum feature size in microns, a physical specification of the degree of miniaturization of the circuit designs created by the semiconductor companies. Semiconductor circuit design technology advances toward increasingly smaller units, so the smallest micron sizes represent state-of-the-art designs. The expected effect on waiting time to first shipment is negative: the smaller the micron line width, the longer the waiting time.

The number of months from the month and year of founding (birth) until the month and year of first shipment for revenues. The data source is the principal's interview. For firms that dissolved before first shipment, cases that are right-censored in the event-history analysis, the waiting time is equal to the number of months since founding, or age at the last observation point.
time_window: from founding to first shipment or end of observation

variable_name: average number of years of semiconductor industry experience on the founding team
description: The average number of years of semiconductor industry experience on the founding team obtained prior to founding the current new venture, defined as years spent as an employee of a merchant producer of semiconductor devices. This was calculated as the arithmetic mean of the individual founders' semiconductor industry experience.

variable_name: prior experience in a start-up company
description: Calculated as the proportion of founding managers who had previously worked in a start-up firm during its first twelve months after founding. The variable ranges from 0 to 1, with 0 indicating that none of the entrepreneurs had previous start-up experience and 1 indicating that all members of the founding team had previous start-up experience.

The extent to which members of the founding team had worked together in a prior employment setting, calculated as the proportion of entrepreneurs who had worked with any of the others prior to founding the new venture. The variable ranges from 0 to 1, where 0 indicates that none of the founders had previously worked together and 1 indicates that all had worked together. For single-founder organizations, this variable is 0.

Dichotomous dummy variable for which 1 indicates the presence of both marketing and manufacturing positions in the founding structure and 0 indicates the absence of the two positions. The founding organizational structure was coded from the principal's interview, in which respondents were asked who had the highest level position in the organization at founding, what it was called, and who reported to each position. The same dummy represents the presence of the manufacturing position used in the joint-presence prediction.

Dichotomous dummy variable for which 1 indicates the presence of both marketing and manufacturing positions in the founding structure and 0 indicates the absence of the two positions. The founding organizational structure was coded from the principal's interview, in which respondents were asked who had the highest level position in the organization at founding, what it was called, and who reported to each position. The same dummy represents the presence of the marketing position used in the joint-presence prediction.

The basic data were total costs and expenses, by year (12-month increments). The measure was total costs and expenses during the research and development period, divided by the number of months from founding to the month of the first shipment. For companies that did not ship during the period of observation, the figure is total costs and expenses until the end of the observation period divided by the number of months in the period. This value was then logged, creating a logged monthly rate of spending during the period for all cases.
scale: logged monthly rate in millions of dollars
time_window: research and development period (founding to first shipment or end of observation)
