description: The proportion of the firm owned by venture capital investors during the first year of the new venture's life. Data come from the financial questionnaire, which asked for the percentage of ownership, by year, across several categories of potential owners, including venture capital firms. The variable has a potential range of 0 to 1.
time_window: first year of the new venture's life

variable_name: proportion of outside investors on the board of directors
description: Calculated from data gathered during the principal's interview; the board membership was traced over time from founding to the date of the interview. For each member of the founding board the respondents were asked whom he or she represented, when he or she joined, whether he or she had left the board, and whether he or she was an investor. The number of members on the board of directors at founding and the number of members who were outside investors were counted, and the proportion of outside investors was calculated.

variable_name: number of competitors in the market
description: Munificence was measured by number of competitors in the market. Competitor data were provided by the market-research firms Dataquest and Integrated Circuit Engineering, which specialize in collecting data on the segments of the semiconductor industry's markets. During the principal's interview respondents were asked how they would describe their market niche in the first year they shipped product, or their targeted market if they had not yet shipped. The number of competitors in a market was then linked to each case by the new venture's self-defined market niche or targeted market.
time_window: first year of shipping (or targeted market)

variable_name: cohort's average waiting time to first shipment
description: Calculated as the average number of months to first shipment for all other companies founded in the same year as the focal organization, not including the focal firm. This produces a mean waiting time for each of the birth-year cohorts from 1978 to 1985, customized to the individual firm.

variable_name: number of acquisitions by the focal firm
description: The number of acquisitions completed by the focal firms during the randomly selected year was obtained from the Journal of Mergers and Acquisitions. The number of acquisitions completed by the focal firms in the selected year ranged from zero to nine, and 82 percent of the focal firms completed either zero or one.

variable_name: number of current-year horizontal acquisitions by the focal firm
description: Each acquisition by the focal firm was classified as horizontal, vertical, or conglomerate. An acquisition was coded as horizontal when the two-digit industry code of the acquiring firm matched that of the acquired firm; the industry of almost all acquired firms was available from either the M&A database or COMPUSTAT.

variable_name: number of current-year vertical acquisitions by the focal firm
description: An acquisition was coded as vertical when the industry of the acquiring firm either sold more than 5 percent of its output to or received more than 5 percent of its input from the industry of the acquired firm. The input-output numbers were obtained from the input-output tables published annually by the Survey of Current Business.

variable_name: number of current-year conglomerate acquisitions by the focal firm
description: Acquisitions that were neither horizontal nor vertical were coded as conglomerate. The authors note that the coding scheme will classify some acquisitions as conglomerate that are really horizontal or vertical, and that any misclassifications work against finding effects.

variable_name: number of acquisitions by the tied-to firms
description: Interlock data were collected by obtaining the names of all inside directors, their titles and director ties from the proxy statements of the focal firm; each firm for which these managers served as director was checked against the M&A database. The number of acquisitions by these tied-to firms during the sampled year and three years before the sampled year was used to create the tied-to firm acquisition variables.
level: firm (tied-to firm), aggregated to the focal firm
time_window: sampled year and three years before

variable_name: number of prior horizontal acquisitions by the tied-to firms
description: The type of acquisition completed by the tied-to firm was coded the same way as that of the focal firm, with horizontal acquisitions identified by matching two-digit industry codes of acquiring and acquired firms.
time_window: sampled year and three years before

variable_name: number of prior vertical acquisitions by the tied-to firms
description: The type of acquisition completed by the tied-to firm was coded the same way as that of the focal firm, using the input-output criterion between the acquiring and acquired firm's industries to identify vertical acquisitions.
time_window: sampled year and three years before

variable_name: number of prior conglomerate acquisitions by the tied-to firms
description: The type of acquisition completed by the tied-to firm was coded the same way as that of the focal firm; acquisitions that were neither horizontal nor vertical were coded as conglomerate.
time_window: sampled year and three years before

description: Network centrality was calculated as the sum of ties for all inside directors of a firm, minus any duplicated ties, i.e., when two directors of the same firm sit on the same board. The number of ties to other firms ranged from zero to fifteen.

variable_name: acquisitions by tied-to banks versus tied-to nonbanks
description: Ties were classified by the industry of the tied-to firm, and the largest proportion of ties (22 percent) are to commercial banks. The number of acquisitions completed by the tied-to firms was separated into two variables, one representing the number of acquisitions completed by banks during the three years before the sampled year and the other representing the number of acquisitions completed by nonbanks over that period.
time_window: three years before the sampled year

variable_name: period dummy and period by tied-to firm acquisitions interaction
description: To test for differences in imitation over time, the sample was split into two periods; the split occurred between 1986 and 1987, right after the peak of the 1980s merger wave. A dummy variable for period and an interaction variable (period by number of acquisitions by the tied-to firms) were created.

variable_name: focal-firm acquisitions classified by whether tied-to firms acquired in that industry
description: The number of acquisitions by the focal firm were classified by whether the tied-to firms acquired in that industry or not. This analysis was performed for the 72 pairs of firms in which both the focal and tied-to firms completed one or more acquisitions.
time_window: selected year and prior three years

variable_name: industries in which the tied-to firms acquired
description: The industries in which the tied-to firms are acquiring, determined from the industry of the acquired firms; used to classify whether focal-firm acquisitions occurred in the same industry as tied-to firm acquisitions.
time_window: selected year and prior three years

variable_name: prior acquisitions by the focal firm
description: Prior focal firm acquisition activity was the number of acquisitions completed by the focal firm in the year before the current year. It was used as the predictor of tied-to firms' current acquisitions in the reversal test of imitation.

Annual sales revenue achieved by a business in a particular product market, recorded for each record year, measured in millions of dollars and deflated by the Producer Price Index with a 1967 base year. For about 15 percent of the record years, sales information was not available for some minor participants with low sales in the product markets, and these were assigned a business sales value of 1 percent of market share in the relevant product market. Linear interpolation was used to impute annual business sales for about 10 percent of the record years involving businesses with partially missing sales information.

The number of years that each firm had participated in the product market, recorded for each record year as a time-varying measure of business age. The age variable was multiplied by the start-up firm and diversifying-entrant dummy variables to create age variables for each type of firm.

variable_name: start-up firm and diversifying-entrant dummy variables
description: Dummy variables distinguished between start-up firms and diversifying entrants. The business age and sales variables were multiplied by the start-up firm and diversifying-entrant dummy variables to create age and size variables for each type of firm.

One of two 0-1 dummy variables recording whether a firm exited a product market in a given calendar year, referred to as a record year. The first variable recorded cases in which businesses shut down, defined as a participant's operations in the United States ceasing, either through bankruptcy or withdrawal from the product market, and not being sold to another company as ongoing operations. Business divestiture is treated as a right-censored case in dissolution models.

The second of two 0-1 dummy variables recording whether a firm exited a product market in a given calendar year, identifying cases in which businesses were sold as individual operating units. An exit was classed as a divestiture if a participant was sold to another organization or underwent a management buyout and either retained the same name or was reported to continue operations as a recognizable entity. Business divestiture was recorded at the business level, so the 43 cases in which several businesses were sold at the same time were treated as right-censored cases rather than as business divestitures; single and multibusiness divestitures were combined when comparing the likelihood that diversifying entrants and start-up firms sell their businesses.

Percentage of time spent on the predevelopment phase, from the start of the project to the development of basic product requirements, as designated by the respondent management group. Computed by dividing the total reported time spent on planning the product by the total elapsed time, from the start date to the end date, of the development project.
time_window: from project start to end date

description: Number of stages of the product development process in which suppliers actually participated. Involvement is defined as having one or more employees of a supplier as recognized members of the product development team, actively participating in team meetings and design activities.

Percentage of design engineers on the product development team (electronic, mechanical, and manufacturing process) who used computer-aided design systems when designing on the project. A second, less direct measure was the rating by respondents of the importance of increasing CAD usage to decreasing product development time.
scale: percentage; second measure a 5-point Likert scale (1 = not at all important, 5 = very important)

description: Sum of the overlaps (in months) across the six phases of the product development project, divided by the total development time. Higher percentages of overlap reflected more project overlap.

Whether personnel from specific functions were involved on the product development team during the various stages of product development. For each phase the total number of functions was calculated, and the final measure adds the total number of functions in every phase. Involvement is defined as having one or more members of the function as recognized members of the product development team, including active participation in team meetings and design activities.
A 5-point Likert scale asking whether the product development personnel were rewarded for meeting the schedule deadlines during the course of the project.
time_window: during the course of the project

description: How many iterations occurred in the development of the product, with an iteration defined as a redesign of at least 10 percent of a product's parts. The measure was adjusted by the average number of iterations for each industry segment by dividing the difference between the number of design iterations for a project and the average number of iterations of its corresponding industry segment by the average number of iterations in the industry segment.

Percentage of time that is spent on testing the designs, measured by dividing the total reported time spent on testing the product (from start to end date) by the total elapsed time, from the start date to the end date, of the development project.
time_window: from project start to end date

description: The respondent group first provided the number of formal milestones for the project, with a milestone defined as an officially scheduled project review point, and was then asked the average time (weeks) between these milestones during the project. The measure was adjusted by industry segment in the same way as the number of design iterations.

Asked the respondent group where in the SBU hierarchy the project manager reported, coded 1 if he or she reported directly to the SBU manager (the highest reporting relationship) and 0 if the reporting relationship were with someone lower in the SBU hierarchy. As a second measure, power was assessed by whether or not the project manager was the final decision maker on the key issues of budget, team composition, and the project timetable.
scale: 0/1 dummy; second measure based on final decision making on budget, team composition, and timetable

description: Duration relative to the average development time of all projects in its industry segment. The duration of each project was measured by the start and end dates of the project, where the start of a project was marked by the time at which the first meeting was held to consider the development of this specific product and the ending date was the date at which product stabilization was reached. The relative development time was calculated by dividing the difference between each project's duration and the average project duration of its corresponding industry segment by the average project duration of its industry segment.

Dichotomous dependent variable coded 1 if an agency theory explanation was used in the proxy statement announcing the new LTIP, and 0 otherwise. Three people independently coded the relevant sections of all proxy statements that included some explanation, making two sequential and dichotomous choices: whether an agency theory explanation was used, then whether a human resource management explanation was used. The unit of analysis is the entire proxy statement.

Dichotomous dependent variable coded 1 if a human resource management explanation was used in the proxy statement announcing the new LTIP, and 0 otherwise. Coders were instructed to answer the agency question before proceeding to the human resource question, and coders also noted whether some other explanation was used. The unit of analysis is the entire proxy statement.

Dichotomous dependent variable coded 1 if both an agency and a human resource management explanation were used in the proxy statement, and 0 otherwise, based on the same coder classifications. Because the use of two explanations was coded 1 in all three analyses, the descriptive statistics showing the percentage of agency, HR, and dual explanations exceed 100 percent. The unit of analysis is the entire proxy statement.

Variable indicating time of adoption, with values ranging from 1 (adoption in 1976) to 15 (adoption in 1990). To test the hypotheses relating intermediate levels of the variables to the use of both explanations, the variable was converted into raw deviation form (the absolute value of the raw deviation).

Used as a market-based measure of firm performance, calculated as capital gains plus dividends accrued/paid during the year, divided by share price at the beginning of the year. Performance was measured in the year of adoption. Results were not sensitive to alternative operationalizations such as average stock returns over the past three or five years.

Used as an operating measure of firm performance. Performance was measured in the year of adoption. Results were not sensitive to alternative operationalizations such as average return on assets over the past three or five years.

A variant of Blau's index of heterogeneity, defined as the squared proportion of CEO-board-member dyads sharing the same functional background category, where the category proportion is taken over dyads. Various functional backgrounds were consolidated into three core areas: output functions (marketing and sales), throughput functions (operations, research and development, engineering), and peripheral or staff functions (law, finance, accounting). Firms whose data were missing were included only if complete demographic data were available for at least three-quarters of the outside directors in each year.

The portion of CEO-board-member dyads in which both individuals have the same type of degree. Degree type was measured as the highest obtained university degree and was divided into five categories; when specialties were not listed, B.S. and M.S. degrees were classified as science degrees.
The portion of CEO-board-member dyads in which both individuals attended the same educational institution, at the undergraduate or graduate level.

Measured with an analog of the euclidean distance measure (the coefficient of variation) commonly used in research on organizational demography, where the coefficient is computed from the CEO's age and the ages of the directors excluding the CEO. The measure was converted to an indicator of similarity by subtracting each firm's coefficient from the highest value in the sample.

The portion of CEO-board-member dyads sharing the same demographic category for at least three of the four dimensions. To create this variable, a dichotomous measure of age similarity was first created, coded 1 for a given dyad if the individuals differed in age by less than one standard deviation and 0 otherwise.
A binary variable coded 1 if a CEO is not also chairman of the board, and 0 otherwise. It was collected for each year.
Measured as the percentage of common stock owned by non-CEO directors divided by the percentage held by all directors, including the CEO. Stock ownership data were collected for the year of adoption.

Indicates the portion of the board composed of outside directors appointed after the CEO. Data on outsiders were gathered at three-year intervals beginning in 1976. Higher values indicate a larger portion of the board beholden to the CEO for their position.
Measured in years. It was collected for each year.

variable_name: raw deviation form of the board power variables
description: To test the hypotheses relating intermediate levels of the variables measuring time, firm performance, relative CEO-board power, and demographic similarity to the use of both explanations, each independent variable was converted into raw deviation form, i.e., the absolute value of the raw deviation. In the dual-explanation analysis, intermediate levels of board power were indicated by the appointment of outside directors, CEO tenure, and relative director and CEO stock ownership; separate CEO and board chair, a categorical variable, was excluded from this specific analysis.

Count of thrifts born each calendar year; to translate these counts into rates the models control for industry density, the number of firms at the beginning of each year. A second set of models counts the managerial jobs created each year by organizational founding and controls for the number of managerial jobs in the industry at the beginning of the year.

Count of thrifts dissolved each calendar year; to translate these counts into rates the models control for industry density, the number of firms at the beginning of each year. A second set of models counts the managerial jobs destroyed each year by organizational dissolution and controls for the number of managerial jobs in the industry at the beginning of the year.

Count of thrifts merged each calendar year, with the focal organization's own acquisitions subtracted from the industry total so that the impact of other firms' mergers can be estimated separately; rates are obtained by controlling for industry density. A parallel specification counts the managerial jobs that disappeared through merger, again subtracting jobs acquired by the focal organization.

For each acquiring organization, the number of firms acquired; a second specification counts the managerial jobs acquired, that is, the number of managerial jobs in firms that were acquired in the year before they were absorbed. These quantities separate the effects of own merger from the effects of other firms' mergers on surviving organizations.

Count of managers entering each surviving organization each year, where surviving organizations are those that operate the year after the mergers or dissolutions under study occurred. Each organization's entry count was standardized by controlling for number of managers.

Count of managers exiting each established organization each year, where established organizations are those that operated for at least one year prior to the year under study. For acquiring organizations, employees transferred directly from acquired entities were distinguished from other employees. Each organization's exit count was standardized by controlling for number of managers.

Mean firm tenure of managerial employees, measured at the end of each calendar year. For organizations that acquired other organizations, mean tenure was measured for all managerial employees except those transferred directly from acquired entities.
time_window: measured at the end of each calendar year

description: The standard deviation of individual employees' years of tenure, the dispersion component of the firm's length-of-service profile. The coefficient of variation, the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean, is described as the most straightforward scale-independent measure of dispersion, but the multivariate models estimate the standard deviation of tenure and control for mean tenure so that results are easier to interpret. For acquiring organizations the standard deviation was measured for all managerial employees except those transferred directly from acquired entities.
time_window: measured at the end of each calendar year

description: Size was measured in terms of number of managerial employees. Stock variables such as firm size were measured at the beginning of each calendar year.
Age was measured in years and controls for the variety of transformations that organizations go through over the course of their lives.

variable_name: counts of thrift foundings, dissolutions and mergers
description: Ecological processes were measured by counts of thrifts born, merged and dissolved each calendar year, with industry density controlled to turn counts into rates. A second specification counted the managerial jobs created and destroyed by these events.

variable_name: manager entry and exit counts, mean tenure and tenure dispersion
description: Personnel flows were counts of managers entering and exiting each organization per year, standardized by number of managers. Tenure distributions were mean firm tenure and the coefficient of variation of managers' tenure.

From the event-history data, the authors aggregated the number of wineries founded at any time in a given year in each state. The annual number of foundings was then subdivided by organizational form to obtain separate series for farm wineries and mass-production wineries.

Following Hannan and Freeman, density was operationalized as the number of wineries ever to operate in a particular state in a given year, regardless of how long. This total count was broken up by organizational form to obtain farm winery density.

The niche creation process was captured by the volume, in millions of gallons, of wine imports. Data on the volume of wine imports were taken from annual volumes of the Wines & Vines Annual Statistical Survey and were available for 1934-1990.

A four-firm concentration ratio based on the share of industry storage capacity accounted for by the largest four firms. The authors used the capacity-based measure because it was available over the entire 1940-1990 period; a sales-based measure available for 1963-1990 averaged 50.2 percent and was highly correlated with the capacity measure.

A 0,1 variable indicating the existence of a farm winery law in a given state. Information on farm winery laws came from descriptions of state laws and regulations in the annual directories of Wines & Vines, from Adams (1985, 1990), and in some cases by contacting state alcoholic beverage control agencies.
A form-specific density measure for mass-production wineries within each state, calculated from the event-history data using the number of wineries ever to operate in a state in a given year.

Centralization was measured using the full form of the Aston instrument. Interviewees identified the lowest level in the organization where 37 specific decisions were made and could be acted upon, coded 0 = operator level, 1 = supervisory level, 2 = workflow subunit level, 3 = all workflow activity level, 4 = whole unit level, 5 = level above the chief executive officer level. Scores could range from 0, decentralized (all decisions made at the operator level), to 185, centralized (all decisions made above the chief executive officer).

This was measured by the Aston scale identifying the number of job levels from the direct workers (e.g., tellers, clerks) to the chief executive, excluding deputies to, assistants to, and secretaries. If there was more than one line from top to bottom, the longest line was used.
This variable refers to the number of functions to which a full-time employee was assigned. It was measured by the 16-item Aston functional specialization scale.

Formalization refers to the availability of organization charts, written operating instructions, written terms of reference or job descriptions, written policies, and a workflow or production schedule. It was measured by the Aston formalization scale, in which scores ranged from 0 (no written documents) to 44 (all of the above documents available).

Managerial employees' reactions were measured by self-reports on the measure 'satisfaction with work' from the Job Description Index. Only the evaluative items of work satisfaction, as identified by Ferratt, Dunham, and Pierce (1981), were used. These items ask the respondent to indicate agreement, disagreement, or indecision on five adjectives describing their current work.
scale: agreement, disagreement, or indecision on five adjectives

description: The number of promotions was the number of partners listed as associates in the prior year's directory. Counts were constructed by matching each lawyer listed in a firm across consecutive annual directories. The dependent variable is truncated with a lower bound of zero.

The number of lateral entries was the number of partners who were not listed as associates in the prior year's directory. Counts were constructed by matching each lawyer listed in a firm across consecutive annual directories. The dependent variable is truncated with a lower bound of zero.

Differentiation was the number of fields in which a law firm claimed expertise. The directory reports the areas of law in which the firm claims expertise and the number of lawyers in each area, divided into partners and associates.

The proportion of lawyers in litigation was the ratio of the number of lawyers listed as being in litigation relative to the total number of lawyers in the firm. The field counts come from the firm's entry in the NALP directory, divided into partners and associates.

Growth was the difference between size in the current year and size in the prior year, divided by the size in the prior year. Law firm size was coded as the total number of partners and associates in the firm for a given year.
The partner-to-associate ratio is self-descriptive, formed from the numbers of partners and associates reported for the firm. In the models the ratio is lagged one year.
The number of partners exiting was the number of partners who were listed in the prior year's directory but not listed in the current year.

For each law firm, the number of linkages was the number of corporations listing the law firm as its outside counsel or listing a member of the law firm on its board of directors. The data were compiled from reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The measure was available only for 1979 and 1980, so values for 1981 and 1982 were calculated with a first-order regression.

The addition of major clients was measured as the change in the number of client linkages between years. Since the measure for client linkages was available only for 1979 and 1980, a first-order regression on lagged client linkages, lagged partners, lagged exits, lagged promotions and lagged firm age was used to calculate values for 1981 and 1982.
time_window: one-year change; values calculated for 1981 and 1982

description: Ten items (Cronbach alpha = .93) following the influence-strategies format developed by Kipnis, Schmidt, and Wilkinson (1980), tailored to the faculty role through personal interviews. Three basic tactics were identified: influencing the decision criteria for choosing dean candidates, soliciting support from administrators, and lobbying other faculty to support a specific candidate. Faculty members indicated how often they observed other faculty members using each listed political behavior. The measure is the mean response for all respondents in each college, with higher scores indicating more political activity; the measure does not capture the intent of the faculty members engaging in the activities.

Five items (Cronbach alpha = .84). Respondents indicated the degree to which departments worked together in five basic decision areas affecting all departments in the college. The decision areas were selected because they occur in all colleges, are not mandated by day-to-day technology, and are likely to affect future relationships between departments. The interdependence measure is the mean response for all respondents in each college, with higher scores indicating more interdependence; it assesses the extent to which faculty actually do work interdependently, not their need to interact.

Four items (Cronbach alpha = .84), based on Tannenbaum's (1968) control-graph approach to decision centralization, with a format similar to measures developed by Beyer and Lodahl (1976) for university settings. Respondents indicated the amount of influence each of five hierarchical levels had in each of four decisions affecting faculty teaching and research. The centralization measure is the degree of kurtosis in the influence curve for each college, with high positive values associated with centralized (i.e., narrowly dispersed) decision making.

Nine items (Cronbach alpha = .85). Faculty members rated the importance of several attributes characteristic of an effective dean, representing either an internal, administrative/managerial orientation or an external, research orientation. Individual faculty member ratings were converted into a rank order and a college score calculated using Kendall's coefficient of concordance. Since the coefficient of concordance is a measure of association, high scores indicate more consensus on the desired characteristics for a new dean.

Measured by the ratio of the number of degree programs to the number of departments in a college, with higher values indicating more specialization. The measure is intended to capture the prevailing level of skill specialization among faculty members, providing a finer scale than a simple count of departments.

Measured by the ratio of the number of universities from which faculty members had received professional degrees (e.g., Ph.D., D.B.A., and Ed.D.) to the number of faculty members in a college. The higher this ratio, the more heterogeneous a faculty is with respect to its members' institutional training. The measure reflects differences among faculty members in addition to those resulting from departmental specialty.

A scale of corporate profitability for the 157 nonfinancial corporations, built from three measures: return on shareholders' investment, return on assets, and net interest on assets. Three-year averages were used for each measure to smooth out short-term anomalies. The three measures were highly correlated (intercorrelations greater than 0.8; Cronbach's alpha = 0.99) and were combined as the sum of the three standardized variables.

variable_name: identical tie received from a financial
description: An interlock between a financial and a nonfinancial corporation was considered broken when the interlocking director no longer appeared on one of their boards for reasons other than mergers, takeovers, and bankruptcies. It was considered replaced if a new interlock appeared within two years of the time of breakage; the replacement required to operationalize an identical tie was a new interlock in the same direction between the given pair of firms. This variable records whether the nonfinancial received such an identical tie from a financial, compared with nonfinancials that did not.
time_window: 1963 and 1968; replacement within two years of breakage

variable_name: identical tie sent to a financial
description: An identical tie is a broken interlock that has been replaced within two years by a new interlock in the same direction between the same pair of firms. This variable records whether the nonfinancial sent such an identical tie to a financial, compared with nonfinancials that did not.
time_window: 1963 and 1968; replacement within two years of breakage

variable_name: all directional interlocks between financials and nonfinancials
description: Presence of all directional interlocks between financials and nonfinancials, regardless of whether these interlocks were subsequently replaced, when accidentally broken, by a new interlock in the same direction between the same pair of firms. Separate categories record interlocks from financial to nonfinancial and from nonfinancial to financial.

variable_name: percentage of stock owned by the CEO or president
description: The percentage of voting stock owned by the CEO or president, gathered from each firm's 1980 proxy statements. The raw variable was highly skewed and was recoded into four values: less than 1 percent = 1; 1 to 4.9 percent = 2; 5 to 19.9 percent = 3; 20 percent or more = 4. Actors reported as owning less than 1 percent of the voting stock were recorded as owning .9 percent, and those reported as owning less than .01 percent were rounded up to .01 percent.

variable_name: percentage of stock owned by the single largest individual shareholder other than the CEO (recoded)
description: The percentage of voting stock owned by the single largest individual shareholder other than the CEO, gathered from 1980 proxy statements. The raw variable was highly skewed and was recoded as a dichotomous variable: less than 5 percent of stock owned = 1; 5 percent or more of stock owned = 2.

variable_name: percentage of stock owned by the single largest corporate shareholder (recoded)
description: The percentage of voting stock owned by the single largest corporate stockholder, gathered from 1980 proxy statements. The raw variable was highly skewed and was recoded as a dichotomous variable: less than 5 percent of stock owned = 1; 5 percent or more of stock owned = 2.

variable_name: percentage of stock owned by the single largest family group (recoded)
description: To derive a measure of family control the authors examined each firm's proxy statements for any immediate kin relationship among the officers, board members, or individuals holding more than 5 percent of the company's stock, and tallied the stock each family member owned as well as stock held in trust for family members. Where two or more family groups were present, only the group with the greatest number of shares was tallied. The raw variable was highly skewed and was recoded as a dichotomous variable: less than 5 percent of stock owned = 1; 5 percent or more of stock owned = 2.

variable_name: cross-classifications of the four ownership variables
description: Three new factors created as cross-classifications of the four ownership variables (CEO ownership and individual, corporate, and family-group ownership), each dichotomized at the 5 percent threshold. The resulting cells were labelled the 'managerial firm', 'agency firm', 'entrepreneurial firm' and 'partnership firm'. In the cross-classification of CEO and family group ownership there were no instances in which the CEO owned 20 percent or more of the company's stock and a family group owned more than 5 percent.

variable_name: log of average annual total contributions, 1979-1981
description: The natural logarithm of the firm's average annual total tax-deductible cash contributions for the years 1979, 1980 and 1981, gathered during on-site interviews for the original study. This logged average is the dependent variable in the regressions and the criterion variable in the multiple classification analyses.

variable_name: dummy variable indicating if the firm rationalized contributions as enlightened self-interest
description: A dummy variable indicating whether the firm rationalized its contributions as enlightened self-interest. To recover the rationale, those responsible for contributions in each firm were asked why they believed their company gives money to nonprofit charitable organizations and how important contributions are for realizing corporate objectives. Twenty-seven different reasons were identified and grouped into five general categories, one of which was 'Enlightened Self-Interest'.

A factor score combining two indicators of executive-elite social linkage. The first is a score based on the number of citations a firm received when 26 living philanthropic leaders, named by three or more of the 80 surveyed community elite, were given the list of 209 publicly held corporations and asked to check off firms in which they knew personally an officer or board member on a first-name basis. The second counts the boards and clubs shared by each CEO and the philanthropic elite (or their wives), constructed from the rosters of the area's major metropolitan clubs, the two most prestigious country clubs, the boards of the eight most prestigious cultural organizations, and the boards of the 21 Fortune 500 and Fortune 50 firms headquartered in the Twin Cities. The zero-order correlation between the two measures was .717 and principal components analysis combined them into a single construct, with factor scores assigned to each firm.

variable_name: sample variance of each organizational attribute within each collective
description: To test the isomorphism hypotheses, the sample variance of each of the four typology clusters identified by the network analysis was calculated for each of the four attributes. The larger the value of the sample variance, the lower the degree of isomorphism within a collective for each attribute. The variances were calculated after controlling for sponsorship, regulation, and affiliation by taking the variance of the residuals from regressions of each attribute on the three environmental factors.

The five binary adjacency matrices were stacked to produce an N x 5 matrix and clustering was done on all five matrices concurrently using Ward's minimum-variance method with a structural equivalence criterion. The clustering yielded four collectives: the confederate collective (high equivalence, intracluster interaction), the conjugate collective (nonequivalence, intracluster interaction), the agglomerative collective (structural equivalence and no intracluster interaction), and the organic collective (nonequivalence and no intracluster interaction, drawn as a random subset of noninteracting, nonequivalent organizations).
Measured by asking respondents to identify from a list of 16 goal areas (e.g., job counselling, research, training, medical advice, other) the services in which they were involved.
scale: count of goal areas from a list of 16

description: Measured by asking respondents to indicate from a list of 12 areas of specialization (e.g., dealing with insurance requirements, public relations, advertising) whether or not these functions were specialized; the measure is the sum of the specialized functions identified.
scale: sum across a list of 12 specialization areas

description: A list of 25 decision areas (e.g., salaries of operatives, training methods, buying procedures) was presented to respondents, and they were asked to identify the level at which each decision was made.
scale: level of decision making for 25 decision areas

description: The formalization measure asked respondents to indicate whether or not the organization had each of a set of written formal devices, such as a formal organization chart, written contracts of employment, operating instructions, information booklets, manuals of procedures, policies, schedules, and research programs.

Ownership type was assessed by two items. The first asked whether there was 'any single individual or institution outside the firm which owns 5 percent or more of the company's stock'; a firm was classified as owner-controlled when there was a yes response and management-controlled when there was a no response. The second item evaluated if the firm was owner-managed by asking if there was any individual within the firm (e.g., the CEO) that owned 5 percent or more of the company's stock; no firm in the sample was owner-managed.

A set of items about the processes used to establish CEO pay in the firm, on which respondents indicated the extent of agreement on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree. Items worded to reflect lower monitoring and incentive alignment were reverse-scored so that 5 represents high monitoring and 1 low monitoring, and all items were averaged into a single composite scale labeled monitoring. A principal axis factor analysis yielded only one factor with an eigenvalue greater than 1.0 and the a priori monitoring and incentive-alignment scales were very highly correlated (r = .81).
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = low monitoring, 5 = high monitoring)

description: A compensation-risk score for bonuses, calculated by averaging the responses to three items, each measured on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from low (1) to extremely high (5): variability, downside risk, and long-term orientation. Bonuses were defined as cash awards to the CEO during a specific short-term period (e.g., annually). A high compensation-risk score indicates that the policies that govern, and the criteria for awarding, bonuses provide for greater managerial risk bearing.

A compensation-risk score for long-term income, calculated by averaging the responses to three items, each measured on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from low (1) to extremely high (5): variability, downside risk, and long-term orientation. Long-term income was defined to include stock options, stock appreciation rights, stock purchase plans, stock awards, performance share plans, phantom stock plans, and other related long-term income programs. A high score indicates that the policies governing long-term income provide for greater managerial risk bearing.
The CCO was asked to indicate the relative influence exercised by the CEO on CEO compensation on a 5-point scale ranging from none to very high.
scale: 5-point scale ranging from none to very high

description: The CCO was asked to indicate the relative influence exercised by outside consultants on CEO compensation on a 5-point scale ranging from none to very high.
scale: 5-point scale ranging from none to very high

description: The CCO was asked to indicate the relative influence exercised by major stockholders on CEO compensation on a 5-point scale ranging from none to very high.
scale: 5-point scale ranging from none to very high

variable_name: influence of the board of directors
description: The CCO was asked to indicate the relative influence exercised by the board of directors on CEO compensation on a 5-point scale ranging from none to very high.
scale: 5-point scale ranging from none to very high

description: The CCO was asked to indicate the relative influence exercised by the compensation committee on CEO compensation on a 5-point scale ranging from none to very high.
scale: 5-point scale ranging from none to very high

variable_name: influence of the chief compensation officer
description: The CCO was asked to indicate the relative influence exercised by the chief compensation officer on CEO compensation on a 5-point scale ranging from none to very high.
scale: 5-point scale ranging from none to very high

description: Coded as 1 if an incumbent used direct distribution before the emergence of a new subfield and 0 if it used independent sales representatives. If no information about sales type was available (about 20 percent of the cases), a firm was assumed to use sales representatives; an assumed-distribution-system dummy flagged those cases.
time_window: before the emergence of a new subfield

description: The year that a firm began selling diagnostic imaging equipment anywhere in the world was subtracted from the year that products in a new subfield were first sold to U.S. buyers. It is a measure of a firm's specialized reputation with users.
time_window: from first worldwide imaging sales to first U.S. sales of the new subfield

description: Recorded the firm's share of sales across all subfields during the year before a new subfield emerged. It is associated with possession of other specialized assets, such as research, development and manufacturing systems.
time_window: the year before a new subfield emerged

description: Defined as the number of multiple-subfield incumbents during the year before a subfield emerged, where such firms were those participating in at least two subfields of the imaging industry. The measure was chosen because multiple-subfield status was positively correlated with possession of specialized assets.
time_window: the year before a subfield emerged

description: Incumbents were divided into three classes: industry sales leaders (at least 3 percent of industry market share during the year before a new subfield emerged, all multiple-subfield incumbents), multiple-subfield followers (in at least two subfields but under 3 percent share), and single-subfield followers (one subfield and under 3 percent of sales). Each effect variable was set equal to the number of multiple-subfield participants if the potential entrant was of that class and 0 otherwise.
time_window: the year before a subfield emerged

description: Coded as 1 if the potential entrant participated in a threatened subfield and 0 otherwise. Incumbents of the electrodiagnostic subfield were threatened by the emergence of ultrasound instruments, nuclear medical imaging producers by CT, x-ray equipment manufacturers successively by CT, magnetic resonance and digital radiographic instruments, and CT in turn by magnetic resonance and digital radiography.
time_window: at the emergence of the new subfield

description: Coded as 1 if a firm that manufactured imaging systems during the year before a new subfield emerged entered the new subfield at any subsequent time, and 0 otherwise. The entry variable also served as a right-censored dummy variable for the entry-timing analysis.
time_window: from subfield emergence through end of 1988

description: Recorded the number of years an industry incumbent waited before entering an emerging subfield, with the count starting at 1 for a firm that entered during the first year. If a firm had not entered by the end of 1988 but continued to participate in the industry, the waiting period was set equal to 1989 minus the subfield introduction year; if a firm left the industry before entering, the waiting period was the year following its exit minus the subfield introduction year.

Presence of a director of unit management (DIRECTOR), presence of a department of unit management (DEPARTMENT), and placement of the program under a new administrative hierarchy rather than the existing nursing hierarchy (HIERARCHY). For the scale items, HIERARCHY was coded 1 = unit manager reports to the new hierarchy, 0 = unit manager reports to old nursing hierarchy, and DIRECTOR and DEPARTMENT were coded 1 = present, 0 = absent. The three indicators form a reliable scale (Cronbach's alpha = .74 and .78 in 1972 and 1978, respectively).

The unit manager's relationship to the head nurse on the patient unit, elicited with response categories 3 = superior to head nurse, 2 = peer, 1 = subordinate to head nurse. For scale purposes the item was dichotomized as 1 = unit manager is superior to head nurse, 0 = unit manager is peer of or subordinate to head nurse. When the unit manager is superior to the head nurse, the unit manager is a "matrix boss" and the head nurse is a "shared subordinate" or "two-boss manager," supervised by both the unit manager and nursing supervisor.
scale: 1 = subordinate to head nurse, 2 = peer, 3 = superior to head nurse

description: Additive scale reflecting the total number of nonnursing personnel categories over which the unit manager has some supervisory authority on the unit (alpha = .65). It also indicates the degree to which unit managers supervise nonnursing personnel on the patient unit. For the scale it was coded 1 = unit manager supervises one or more persons from other departments, 0 = unit manager supervises no personnel.

The number of administrative and policy areas the unit manager has responsibility for, including developing administrative rules and procedures for the patient unit, preparing its budget and maintaining statistical records, designing unit plans and programs, and coordinating all personnel. There are no indicators of the degree to which influence is shared between the nursing and administrative hierarchies. For the scale it was coded 1 = unit manager makes decisions in one or more administrative-policy areas, 0 = unit manager makes no decisions in these areas.

Dual support systems are indicated by the presence of separate education (TRAINING) and development (CAREER PATH) programs for unit managers. The two indicators are only weakly related to one another, and dual support systems is the only hypothesized element that fails to appear empirically. These two measures reflect one type of dual support system found in both business and hospital settings.

Internal diffusion is indicated by the unit manager's geographic realm of responsibility: the proportion of inpatient units (%UNITS) and beds (%BEDS) each unit manager supervises, and by the program's spread across all hospital inpatient units (%TOTAL UNITS) and ancillary areas (ANCILLARY AREAS). The two indicators of the geographic realm of responsibility form a reliable scale (alpha = .77 and .83); %UNITS and %BEDS are highly interrelated, only moderately associated with %TOTAL UNITS, and not associated with ANCILLARY AREAS.

Temporal duration and coverage are indicated by the number of days in a week that unit managers provide inpatient coverage on the day shift (DAYS), evening shift (EVENINGS), and night shift (NIGHTS). These indicators reflect whether unit management operates around the clock and throughout the week. The three indicators form a moderately reliable scale (alpha = .72 and .64 in 1972 and 1978, respectively).

A scale score assigned to each program on the basis of the total number of items passed among the five indicators of structural differentiation, dual authority, and decision-making influence, i.e., INFLUENCE, DIRECTOR, DEPARTMENT, HIERARCHY, and SUPERVISION; the scale was chosen because it is consistent with the unidimensional and cumulative character of the scale, and it correlated highly (r = .85) with an alternative scale scored by the most complex item passed. The high coefficient of reproducibility indicates that a program's complexity score predicts its pattern of scores on the five indicators, and the moderately high coefficient of scalability indicates unidimensional and cumulative properties. RELATION TO HEAD NURSE was omitted from the scale because of its low bi-serial correlation with the sum of the other items (.00 in 1972, .19 in 1978).

The age of the matrix program, used in simple correlations with the complexity scale in both 1972 and 1978; the year in which programs started is available from the earlier diffusion panel. Similar results were obtained when program age and each of the indicators of matrix structure were correlated.

The dependent variable of the event-history model, the log of the matrix lifetime, regressed against the complexity scale and several measures of internal diffusion and temporal coverage measured in 1972. Program structure is last observed in 1978 and survival and failure data are available through 1979, with no left-censoring of observations; the parametric model is fit to right-censored failure-time data.

Diversity among the organizational elements relevant for hospital decision making was operationalized by four indicators: the number of different inpatient units; the volume of outpatient care (as a proportion of admissions); the volume of emergency care (as a proportion of admissions); and the presence of a medical school affiliation. Data for these measures were taken from the 1972 Annual Survey conducted by the American Hospital Association. These indicators were used in a regression model to predict the level of program complexity in 1972.

No environmental or hospitalwide measures of task uncertainty are available from the AHA Annual Survey; two additional measures of diversity, the number of different psychiatric services and the number of different intensive care units (ICUs) offered by the hospital, were included because they may also reflect the degree of technological uncertainty on specific clinical areas. Hospitals that offer more psychiatric services and ICUs are assumed to exhibit a greater degree of task uncertainty because they treat more patients with uncertain, unstable, and variable conditions that require continual feedback and processing of information in the course of treatment.

Measured as a three-year average of percentage changes in unit sales for the entire minicomputer-producer population, including both start-up and established firms. The three-year average covered the year preceding each company's birth through the year following its birth. Unit sales rather than dollar sales were used to avoid potential confounding influences of price differences among companies; unit and dollar sales were correlated at r = .914.
level: Industry, aligned to each firm's founding year
time_window: Three-year average covering the year before through the year after each firm's birth

variable_name: Competitive concentration (percentage changes in concentration ratios)
description: Measured as a three-year average of percentage changes in four-firm unit sales concentration ratios, calculated for the same three-year window used for market demand. Percentage change is calculated as the change in concentration from one year to the next over the concentration of the earlier year, so it reflects both the direction and relative magnitude of changes in competitive conditions.
level: Industry, aligned to each firm's founding year
time_window: Three-year average covering the year before through the year after each firm's birth

description: Coded as the number of segments in which a company competed for each year of its existence, using six application segments that industry documents and analysts universally described: severe environments; scientific and engineering laboratories; industrial automation and process control; communications management; distributed data processing; and small business systems. Firms producing for more than one application segment but developing products for a single industry were coded as competing in only one segment. Start-up strategy was measured for the year in which a firm first achieved a strategy sustained for at least three years (age three for most firms); for the 17 firms that did not live to three years, the last year of existence was used.
time_window: Year of first stable strategy (age three, or last year of existence for firms not surviving to age three)

description: Coded as a count of the number of distinct product lines that the company offered during each year of its existence, taken from census listings published in the EDP Industry Report. Lines were not distinguished on the basis of targeted market segments; companies routinely marketed the same line to several application segments and multiple lines in a single segment. The variable was correlated with the number of sales offices maintained by a firm and the percentage of revenues assigned as R&D and selling expense (.59, .49, and .52, respectively). Strategy was measured at the year of first stable strategy.
time_window: Year of first stable strategy (age three, or last year of existence for firms not surviving to age three)

description: A firm was coded as surviving if it remained an independent producer of minicomputers from birth through the end of the study; survival is coded as 1 and all other fates (failure or acquisition) are coded as 0. Acquired firms were treated as failures after comparing their market shares and returns on assets with those of independent firms and examining their subsequent disposition. Five organizations founded after 1976, which could not have survived five years given 1981 as the end of the observation period, were dropped from the analyses.
scale: Binary (1 = survived five years as an independent minicomputer producer, 0 = failure or acquisition)

description: The period during which the semiconductor firm was incorporated. The industry's development was divided into four periods: the Military Market (1958-1966), the Commercial Market (1967-1973), Price Competition (1974-1979), and the Custom Market (1980-1985). Because the variable is categorical, one control category was used for dummy coding to prevent model overspecification.

Measured categorically as the primary functional experience of the entrepreneur, prior to starting the new firm, within the areas of research, design, and development; manufacturing and production; or marketing, sales, and customer service. In all but one firm the founder's primary work experience could be categorized as coming from within one of these three broad functional areas. One control category was used for dummy coding to prevent model overspecification.

The relative level of staffing in the research and development function, measured as the proportion of the total workforce engaged in research and development. Both current staffing and staffing at founding were measured, and staffing is one of three measures used to assess the importance of each of the three functions.

variable_name: Perception of research and development importance
description: The entrepreneur or a member of the founding team was asked to judge the relative importance of the three operational functions by weighting each functional area so that the weights total 100 percent. Respondents were first asked about the current importance of the three functions and then asked to recall their importance at founding; in approximately 75 percent of the firms the entrepreneur or a founding-team member was interviewed, otherwise the current president or a top executive with knowledge of the founding.
scale: 100 percentage points allocated across the three functions

description: The proportion of subunits with a direct reporting relationship to the president of the organization that were engaged in research and development. Proportions were calculated by counting the total number of subunits with a direct reporting relationship to the president that were involved in the activity and dividing by the total number of subunits reporting to the president.

The relative level of staffing in manufacturing and production, measured as the proportion of the total workforce engaged in manufacturing and production. Both current staffing and staffing at founding were measured, and staffing is one of three measures used to assess the importance of each of the three functions.

variable_name: Perception of manufacturing and production importance
description: The entrepreneur or a member of the founding team was asked to judge the relative importance of the three operational functions by weighting each functional area so that the weights total 100 percent. Respondents were first asked about the current importance of the three functions and then asked to recall their importance at founding.
scale: 100 percentage points allocated across the three functions

description: The proportion of subunits with a direct reporting relationship to the president of the organization that were engaged in production and manufacturing. Proportions were calculated by counting the total number of subunits with a direct reporting relationship to the president that were involved in the activity and dividing by the total number of subunits reporting to the president.

The relative level of staffing in marketing and sales, measured as the proportion of the total workforce engaged in marketing and sales. Both current staffing and staffing at founding were measured, and staffing is one of three measures used to assess the importance of each of the three functions.

variable_name: Perception of marketing and sales importance
description: The entrepreneur or a member of the founding team was asked to judge the relative importance of the three operational functions by weighting each functional area so that the weights total 100 percent. Respondents were first asked about the current importance of the three functions and then asked to recall their importance at founding.
scale: 100 percentage points allocated across the three functions

description: The proportion of subunits with a direct reporting relationship to the president of the organization that were engaged in marketing and sales. Proportions were calculated by counting the total number of subunits with a direct reporting relationship to the president that were involved in the activity and dividing by the total number of subunits reporting to the president.

The absolute value of the difference between the organization's measure of founding functional importance and current functional importance for each of the three functional areas; for staffing this yields three of the nine difference scores estimated for each organization.
time_window: from founding to the time of the interview

description: The absolute value of the difference between the respondent's rating of founding functional importance and the rating of current functional importance for each of the three functional areas; for perceptions this yields three of the nine difference scores estimated for each organization.
time_window: from founding to the time of the interview

description: The absolute value of the difference between the organization's founding top-management structure measure and its current top-management structure measure for each of the three functional areas; for top-management structure this yields three of the nine difference scores estimated for each organization.
time_window: from founding to the time of the interview

description: For each year of operation, firms were characterized as poor performers if their rate of sales growth was more than one standard deviation below the average sales growth of the sample in that year. The number of years of poor performance was summed over the number of years the organization had been in existence and divided by the number of years of operation. Performance was reverse-coded in the reported results, with higher performance scores representing better performance. Sales were used rather than profits because many semiconductor manufacturers operate at a low level of profitability while building market share.
time_window: each year of the firm's operation since founding

description: The number of years since the organization was incorporated.

The proportion of the firm's lifetime that the entrepreneur had worked in the firm, measured as the number of years the entrepreneur remained with the firm after founding, divided by the age of the firm.
time_window: from founding to the time of the interview

description: The proportion of firm ownership initially held by members of the founding group. This information was unavailable from two firms.

Importance of each of three functions (R&D, manufacturing and production, marketing and sales) at founding and currently, assessed with three separate measures: the share of the workforce in the function, the respondent's weighting of the functions to total 100 percent, and the share of the president's direct reports that are in the function. This yields nine measures of functional importance.

Context variable built from OAI questionnaire items; the text states that eight items were used for the task uncertainty scale, of which four are reproduced. The reproduced items ask how often difficult problems with no immediate or apparent solutions arose in the past three months, how much the same the day-to-day situations and problems are (reverse scored), how frequently exceptions requiring substantially different methods or procedures arise, and how often about the same work methods or steps are followed from day to day (reverse scored). Responses of unit members and supervisors were aggregated to the work-unit level.

Interorganizational dependence and interunit dependence were averaged to create the horizontal dependence measure. The dependence scales each comprised three items asking how much the respondent has to depend on people in other units of the office, the Administrative Office, or people in other organizations outside the Job Service Division to obtain the materials, clients, or information needed to do the work; how much they have to rely on those people to perform the next steps in the process after finishing their part of the job; and a third set of parallel items. Responses were aggregated to the work-unit level.

Each of the seven design variables was standardized (mean = 0; standard deviation = 1) and then a simple average was taken on the seven scores, with standardization and supervisory discretion negatively weighted. A negative score indicates a design that is predominantly mechanistic, and a positive score a predominantly organic design. The resulting measure had a mean of -.02, a median of -.04, a standard deviation of .5, and ranged from -1.25 to 1.51.

The fit measure is calculated by computing, for each unit, the Euclidean distance over the range of standardized design measures from the relevant appropriate pattern of design; the composite measure reflects the extent to which each unit deviates from a pattern of design known to produce high performance under similar contextual conditions, and it is then correlated with performance. Ideal profiles were derived empirically from the mean design scores of high-efficiency units (units scoring at least one-half a standard deviation above the mean on efficiency), and the sample was randomly split so that profiles were created on one group and tested on the other (69 units). Two measures of deviation were compared: one based on four ideal profiles, one per contingency type, and one based on ideal profiles derived only from the unconflicted contexts (Types 1 and 4), with Type 2 units measured against the Type 1 profile and Type 3 units against the Type 4 profile.

Obtained from organizational performance records for each of the 230 Wisconsin units and consisting of the amount of output produced per full-time equivalent position. Relevant output criteria were developed for each unit type following lengthy interviews and consultation with office and unit personnel and are the same as those used by the Federal Department of Labor for allocating resources to state and local agencies, for example the number of initial and continued claims taken and processed, the number of disputed claims resolved, the number of job seekers placed, or the number of individuals counseled. An N-score transformation (to which a constant of 5 was added) was computed to establish a common criterion for comparison, creating a ratio scale of unit performance.

Units were split at the median on task uncertainty and on horizontal dependence to form four contingency types. Types 1 (low task/low dependence) and 4 (high/high) are unconflicted and Types 2 (low task/high dependence) and 3 (high task/low dependence) are conflicted.

Amount of corporate contributions nonprofit j reported receiving from corporation i in 1984, originally collected in nine response categories. The nine categories were recoded to three: low donations (less than $3,000), medium donations ($3,000-$30,999), and high donations ($31,000 and up). The variable is the response variable in all nine models.

Each of the 26 interviewed members of the corporate philanthropic elite was handed a list of the 326 nonprofits and asked to indicate which organizations they recognized, thought essential, and regarded as outstanding. Each nonprofit received a score of 1, 2, or 3, and the responses of the 26 informants were aggregated into a score for each nonprofit. Scores were dichotomized at the median so that the second category is highly recognized and viewed as important by the elite.
scale: 1-3 aggregated score, dichotomized at the median

description: Factor scores from a principal components analysis combining two indicators into a single construct. The first indicator is the number of philanthropic leaders who checked a given firm as one in which they personally knew an officer or a board member. The second is the number of clubs and boards a firm's CEO shared with members of the elite, built from rosters of metropolitan and country clubs and of prestigious cultural organizations and Fortune firms. The factor scores were dichotomized at the median.

Giving officers in 61 of the 75 firms were asked to check off the nonprofits they recognized, those they felt provided very essential services to the community, and those they felt had achieved extraordinary accomplishments. This produced three binary arrays that were summed into a single rectangular array with values 0, 1, 2, and 3 in the cells; nonrespondents' rows received missing data codes.

Binary adjacency matrix summarizing linkages among those responsible for corporate giving programs. In each firm the principal functionary responsible for corporate contributions was asked whether he or she knew someone personally in other area firms who was responsible for corporate contributions; staff in two companies were linked only if staff in both companies acknowledged knowing someone in the other firm. Because data were available for only 61 officers, a number of cells were assigned a missing-data code.

Binary matrix constructed from rosters of the boards and executives of Fortune 50 and Fortune 500 firms and of the most prestigious cultural organizations and private clubs in the Twin Cities; the cell equals 1 if the two CEOs belonged to the same boards or clubs over the period from 1977 to 1981 and zero otherwise. There were no missing data.

Symmetric adjacency matrix among donees built from nonprofit administrators' lists of the names of those who sat on their boards of directors, after checking on the names; 1 indicates that two nonprofits had the same individual(s) on their boards and zero that they did not. There were no missing data.

Weighted sum giving the number of officers in other firms, known by the donation officer of firm i, whose firm gave money to nonprofit j in 1980, weighted by the size of the gift. The variable was coded so that it has three categories with roughly one-third of the dyads in each ordinal category; a low value indicates that the companies in the networks of firm i gave little or no money to nonprofit j, a high value that they did.

Weighted sum giving the number of CEOs who share club and board memberships with the CEO of firm i whose firm gave money to nonprofit j in 1980, weighted by the size of the gift. Coded into three ordinal categories with roughly one-third of the dyads in each; a low value indicates that the companies in the CEO's network gave little or no money to the nonprofit, a high value that they did.

Weighted sum giving the number of nonprofits that interlock with nonprofit j and that received a gift from corporation i in 1980, weighted by the size of the gift. Coded into three ordinal categories; a low value indicates that the NPOs that interlock with nonprofit j received little or no money from corporation i, a high value that they did.

Indirect network variable that takes into account the 1980 gifts of companies linked indirectly (at a graph distance equal to two) to donor i in the officer network. Coded into four ordinal categories with roughly an even number of dyads in each; low values mean that corporations linked indirectly to firm i did not give much money to nonprofit j, high values that they made substantial donations.

Indirect network variable examining the 1980 gifts of companies linked indirectly (at a graph distance equal to two) to donor i in the CEO network. Coded into three ordinal categories with roughly an even number of dyads in each; low values mean that indirectly linked corporations gave little money to the nonprofit, high values that they gave substantial donations.

Indirect process variable examining the 1980 gifts received by nonprofits linked indirectly (at a graph distance equal to two) to donee j in the nonprofit network. Coded into four ordinal categories with roughly an even number of dyads in each; low values mean that nonprofits linked indirectly to nonprofit j received little from corporation i, high values that they received substantial donations.

Multiplicative term aggregating the attitudes toward nonprofit j of donation officers linked to the donation officer of firm i, built from the officer network and the summed recognition/esteem matrix. The variable is ordinal and coded to have four categories with roughly equal numbers of dyads in each; a low value indicates that those in the network of the donation officer of firm i have low recognition and regard for nonprofit j, and a high value indicates high recognition and regard.

The amount of ITC included in the current year's calculation of net income on the financial statements stated as a percentage of total net income in the current year. This proxy was used because for early years the amount of ITC received in the current year was not reliably available.

Percentage changes in the earnings per share of the firm over the five fiscal years up to and including the current fiscal year. The mean percentage change in this series was multiplied by its variance; thus, a large negative number implies that the firm had a mean change that was negative, as well as a large variance in those changes. This variable was expected to have a negative effect.
time_window: five fiscal years up to and including the current fiscal year

description: For all firm fiscal years ending within a particular calendar year, the median total assets was determined; this was subtracted from the total assets of each firm in that year and the difference was divided by the median total assets. A negative value means the firm was smaller than the median sample firm in a given year; a positive value implies the opposite.

Dummy variable coded one if the firm was categorized as managerially controlled in the fiscal year in question, and zero otherwise. For fiscal years 1962-1972 the measurement was based on Kotz's (1978) classification; for fiscal years 1972-1977 it was based on Herman's (1981) classification; for years after 1977 a firm was coded as under management control if no individual owned 5 or more percent of the voting stock according to the 10-K report.

Two measures were used. The first is a dummy variable called DR, which indicates whether debt restrictions were mentioned in the notes to financial statements in the annual report; it was coded one if such restrictions were mentioned and zero otherwise. The second variable, URRE, measured the differential importance of these restrictions across firms by computing the proportion of the firm's total retained earnings that are not restricted by debt covenants; it was expected to have a negative effect.
Dummy variable coded one if incentive-compensation schemes were mentioned in either the 10-K or annual reports and zero otherwise.

Dummy variable indicating whether the observation represents a firm fiscal year ending in calendar year 1964, the year in which the APB prohibition against the FTM ended. In a model including FY64 and LATE, the years 1962 and 1963 are the omitted category, measured by the constant.
Dummy variable indicating whether the firm was under the jurisdiction of the Interstate Commerce Commission in the fiscal year represented by the observation.
Dummy variable indicating whether the firm was under the jurisdiction of the Federal Power Commission in the fiscal year represented by the observation.

Dummy variable for fiscal years ending during calendar years between 1965 and 1984, testing whether firms that did not adopt the FTM in 1964 were imprinted with the Deferral Method and less likely to adopt the FTM in subsequent years.
Dummy variable coded one if the firm's auditor in a given fiscal year was one of the Big Eight firms that supported the prohibition, and zero otherwise.

The proxy is the coefficient of variation of capital expenditures over the five periods up to and including the current fiscal year, called VCE. Because the hypothesis predicted a negative effect from 1962 to 1964 and a positive effect from 1965 to 1984, two variables were created: EVCE equals VCE from 1962 to 1964 and is zero if the year is later than 1964; LVCE equals VCE from 1965 to 1984 and is zero if the year is earlier than 1965.
time_window: five periods up to and including the current fiscal year

description: The top-management team was operationalized as the officers of the corporation listed in the annual report. Turnover was measured as the percentage of the current year's top-management team who were not members of the top-management team in the previous year. Two variables were created: ECHMT represents management turnover from 1962 to 1964 and is zero if the year is later than 1964; LCHMT represents management turnover from 1965 to 1984 and is zero if the year is earlier than 1965.
time_window: current fiscal year relative to the previous year

description: Coded zero if the firm maintained the DM during the fiscal year; coded one if the firm adopted the FTM during the year in question. Firms that adopt the FTM are included up to and including the year of adoption; after that they are removed from the sample, so that years in which the use of the FTM was maintained are not mixed with years in which it was adopted.
