Cases are all realized ties—every instance in which a lead investor invited another VC firm and that firm accepted; controls are potential co-investment ties that could have occurred but did not, matched at a 1:10 ratio on the same lead VC and target company.
time_window: first round in which each non-lead invested

description: Proportion of venture-backed firms that went public in the prior year headquartered in the same Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA) as each target company. It was computed for the year before the potential investment in target company z and is intended to capture fashion-like investor enthusiasm for particular regions; as a proportion it theoretically ranges from zero to one.

Proportion of venture-backed firms that went public in the prior year and that operated in the same VentureXpert 1-digit industry category as each target, computed for the year before the potential investment. The authors state that this variable captures the widely documented fashions that define industry-specific market bubbles.

Ordinal count (1st, 2nd, 3rd, ...) of the current financing round, logged because the distribution of rounds is highly skewed. Because uncertainties about the investment target and the probable need for future resource contributions from syndicate members decline in later rounds, late-round syndicates offer more conducive settings for distant relations.

Count of the number of new investors involved in the syndicate in each financing round, logged because the count is highly skewed. The authors chose the number of new members rather than all investors in a round based on their discussions with venture capitalists, who think about the size of a syndicate in terms of the number of new members they recruit.

Count of the number of investors, excluding the potential syndicate partner (j), with whom the lead VC firm has previously invested (i.e., shared a prior direct tie). The variable is highly skewed but because many cases have zero values it was transformed with a square root function rather than the natural log.

variable_name: level of media attention to a boycott
description: The level of media attention granted to a particular boycott, operationalized as the number of newspaper articles discussing a boycott prior to a concession or occurring during the six-month time period following the announcement of the boycott. Newspaper articles were located by searching for the word 'boycott' in the text of articles from five national newspapers and were read and coded to match the article to company-specific data.
time_window: six-month window following the boycott announcement, or up to the concession

description: Computed using COMPUSTAT data on net sales. The variable measures the change in net sales (in millions) from two years prior to the boycott to the year in question and was reverse coded so that a positive value of the variable implies a larger decline in sales. A positive coefficient for this variable would indicate that a decline in sales positively influences the likelihood of concessions.
time_window: from two years prior to the boycott to the year in question

description: Computed using Fortune magazine's list of the 'Top 100 Most Admired Companies' in the United States. The variable was calculated using an ordinal transformation of the raw scores, resulting in four ordinal values: the lowest ordinal value, 0, signifies that the firm did not make the top 100 list, and the highest ordinal value, '3,' indicates that the firm had a reputation score of greater than 7. The reputation decline variable was calculated by measuring the change in reputation value from two years prior to the boycott to the year in question and, like the sales decline variable, was reverse coded so that a positive value implies a larger decline in reputation.
time_window: change from two years prior to the boycott to the year in question (Fortune's admiration index is taken in the prior year, lagging the variable by one year)

description: Binary dependent variable indicating a recognition by the corporation of the boycotters' demands and a public expression of conformity to those demands, excluding attempts by the target to demobilize the activists without making any real changes. Information on concessions came from an additional search of newspaper articles relating to the boycotts conducted using the Factiva database, with a six-month time window beginning with the first announcement of the boycott.
time_window: six-month window beginning with the first announcement of the boycott

variable_name: activism-resistant and activism-prone prior adopter categories
description: A company's perceived orientation toward activism was coded from a content analysis of major newspaper and magazine articles published between 1985 and 2005 that described each firm's response to activists targeting it. Firms were coded activism resistant when an article conveyed that the firm was among the last in a targeted group to adopt the advocated practice (or never adopted it) or that it proactively resisted activist demands; they were coded activism prone when the firm was among the first in a targeted group to agree to demands or when the article attributed the change partly or wholly to activist pressure. Firms that did not meet either criterion were assigned to the mainstream category, which constitutes the risk set, while all three categories were included in the influence set; discrepancies between the two coders were coded as neither resistant nor prone.
scale: three categories (activism resistant, activism prone, mainstream)

description: The date of domestic partner benefit adoption was taken from data provided by the Human Rights Campaign and verified when possible through the GLBT employee group survey; adoption data were also available from the human resources survey for the year 2000 as a third check, and few discrepancies were found. Year of adoption was the temporal unit of analysis because benefit changes are generally made once per year in most firms, preceding the annual employees' open enrolment window.

A time-varying covariate reflecting the formation of GLBT employee groups, with the presence and formation date of groups within each firm taken from the employee group survey. Group formation dates were found for 111 of 115 firms with known groups. Where a group formed after the firm adopted benefits, the group formation score was recoded to zero to exclude groups that could not logically have influenced the adoption decision, and a simple spell-splitting procedure accounted for variation over time.

Respondents to the human resources manager survey were asked, 'Please name two or three other employers to which you compare your health benefits (for example, Fortune 500 companies).' Responses pertained to healthcare benefits generally, not to domestic partner benefits, which ensured that the network was exogenous to the practice under consideration. The majority of responses referenced companies that also responded to the survey, but alters not in the Fortune 500 sample frame were also included in the network analysis. The network was entered into the social proximity vector, used to restrict contagion in the benchmarking model, and used to construct eigenvector centrality scores.

For each firm in the influence set, the CSR score was constructed by summing that firm's performance on four positive and four negative items provided in the KLD database. All raw items are binary, so the possible range for each firm extends from -4 to +4. The composite CSR score was entered directly into the infectiousness vector.

In the heterogeneous diffusion model, the infectiousness vector represents the strength of a prior adopter's influence on other firms, modelled alongside the focal firm's propensity and susceptibility and the social proximity of the adopter-focal pair. Characteristics of prior adopters, including activism-prone and activism-resistant dummy measures and CSR scores, were entered in this vector to model the influence of prior adoption events in the field. The baseline model excludes infectiousness vector variables.

Measured, following Dobrev, Kim, and Hannan (2001), as the count of firms whose niches overlap with the niche of the focal firm. Niches are defined on the technological dimension of engine horsepower, and the variable is updated yearly as a time-varying covariate lagged by one observation period.

A density measure for the number of firms operating in each of the market segments (low periphery, market center, high periphery). The variable is measured for the firm's origin segment and is lagged by one observation period.

A dummy variable that equals unity when a firm's mid-niche falls in different market segments between two consecutive years and when that firm's niche midpoint changes between two consecutive years. This ensures that a firm itself must change its niche for a segment move to be observed and eliminates events in which moves between market segments are an artifact of shifts in the boundaries of the market segments while the firm niche remains unchanged.

The dependent variable is the rate at which Korean firms formed cross-border strategic alliances. Korean firms continue to report details of alliances involving any significant foreign sources of equity investment to the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Energy. Pure technology purchasing agreements and other one-time transactions were excluded, as were cases of outward foreign direct investment by Korean firms in other emerging economies. The alliance data were cross-checked against leading Korean business periodicals, company reports, and local and foreign analyst reports.

variable_name: CEO or chairman born in Choongchung
description: A time-varying indicator coded for each year on whether the company's CEO or chairman had been born in the central-western region of Choongchung. Data on managerial demography came from three newspaper Web sites and the leading credit information agency, Korea Information Service.

variable_name: CEO or chairman born in Gangwon
description: A time-varying indicator coded for each year on whether the company's CEO or chairman had been born in the northeastern region of Gangwon. Data on managerial demography came from three newspaper Web sites and the leading credit information agency, Korea Information Service.

variable_name: CEO or chairman born in Jeolla
description: A time-varying indicator coded for each year on whether the company's CEO or chairman had been born in the Jeolla region. Data on managerial demography came from three newspaper Web sites and the leading credit information agency, Korea Information Service.

variable_name: CEO or chairman attended Daegu's Kyungpook High School
description: Data were collected for each year on whether a firm's CEO or chairman had attended Daegu's Kyungpook High School. Data on managerial demography came from three newspaper Web sites and the leading credit information agency, Korea Information Service.

variable_name: senior manager attended Busan High School
description: For Busan High School, data were collected on whether a senior manager at the level of general manager or higher had attended Busan High School, because although large numbers of executive vice presidents and other senior managers had attended Busan High School, for some years only a small number of CEOs and chairmen had that social tie. Data on managerial demography came from three newspaper Web sites and the leading credit information agency, Korea Information Service.

variable_name: CEO or chairman served as an officer of the FKI
description: Each firm in the sample was coded for whether its CEO or chairman had a connection as an officer of the leading business association, the Federation of Korean Industries (FKI), for every year between 1987 and 2003. Data on managerial demography came from three newspaper Web sites and the leading credit information agency, Korea Information Service.

variable_name: CEO or chairman born in North Korea
description: A time-varying indicator coded for each year on whether the company's CEO or chairman had been born in North Korea. Data on managerial demography came from three newspaper Web sites and the leading credit information agency, Korea Information Service.

variable_name: CEO or chairman with prior ministerial or senior bureaucratic experience
description: The study examined the value of having senior managers with prior ministerial experience, and also measured whether the CEO or chairman served as a mid-ranking bureaucrat or higher in the national government. Each firm in the sample was coded for whether its CEO or chairman had such a connection for every year between 1987 and 2003. Data on managerial demography came from three newspaper Web sites and the leading credit information agency, Korea Information Service.

variable_name: Political capital variables (set of elite network tie indicators)
description: Political ties were measured with a set of time-varying firm-year binary indicators coded for 1987 to 2003: whether the CEO or chairman was born in a given region (Jeolla, Choongchung, Gangwon, North Korea), attended a regional high school (Kyungpook, Busan), served as an officer of the Federation of Korean Industries, or had prior ministerial or senior bureaucratic experience. Each indicator was interacted with dummies for the three political regimes.

Number of new industrial robots introduced by each sample firm each year. To qualify as new, each product had to differ in technical or physical characteristics from the producing firm's previous products; an existing product introduced in a new geographical area did not qualify. To qualify as an industrial robot, a product needed to be programmable to move a gripper or tool through space to accomplish a useful industrial task.

Improvement in product design characteristics important to users, calculated annually for each firm. The authors compared the average performance characteristics of firm i's new products in year t with the average performance characteristics of new products introduced in the industry the previous year, for repeatability, speed, load capacity, and degrees of freedom. They identified differences between year t and year t-1 values divided by year t-1 values for each characteristic and took the average of the four ratios.

Proportion of prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that were neither in its own nor in its rivals' past five years' knowledge bases nor in its rivals' knowledge bases in the current year. The denominator is the total number of prior-art patents the focal firm cites in the current year.
time_window: current year, lagged as five-year moving average of years t-1 through t-5

description: Proportion of prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that were not in its rivals' but were in its own past five years' knowledge bases. The denominator is the total number of citations by the focal firm.
time_window: current year, lagged as five-year moving average of years t-1 through t-5

description: Proportion of prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that were not in its rivals' but were in the firm's own past five years' knowledge base and were used in the current year by both. The denominator is the total number of citations by the focal firm.
time_window: current year, lagged as five-year moving average of years t-1 through t-5

description: Proportion of prior-art patent citations in the firm's rivals' current-year patents that could not be found in the rivals' past five years' technological knowledge bases nor in the focal firm's knowledge bases in the current year or earlier. The denominator is the total number of prior-art patents rivals cite in the current year.
time_window: current year, lagged as five-year moving average of years t-1 through t-5

description: Proportion of prior-art patent citations in rivals' current-year patents that were in the rivals' but not in the focal firm's past five years' knowledge bases and were not used by the focal firm in the current year either. The denominator is the total number of citations by rivals.
time_window: current year, lagged as five-year moving average of years t-1 through t-5

description: Proportion of prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that were in rivals' knowledge bases during the past five years but not in the firm's knowledge base and were used in the current year by both. The denominator is the total number of citations by the focal firm.
time_window: current year, lagged as five-year moving average of years t-1 through t-5

description: Proportion of prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that were not in its own nor in its rivals' past five years' knowledge bases but were used in the current year by both. The denominator is the total number of citations by the focal firm.
time_window: current year, lagged as five-year moving average of years t-1 through t-5

description: Proportion of prior-art patent citations in the focal firm's current-year patents that could be found in its own and in its rivals' past five years' knowledge bases and were used again in the current year by both. The denominator is the total number of citations by the focal firm.
time_window: current year, lagged as five-year moving average of years t-1 through t-5

description: CEOs indicated how much importance should be assigned to each item when making critical management decisions, using a 7-point scale ranging from 'none: of no importance' to 'of most importance: should be considered more important than all other considerations.' Three items measured economic values, such as 'effect on firm profitability.' The measure forms a latent construct in the structural model, with loadings between .55 and .85.

CEOs indicated how much importance should be assigned to each item when making critical management decisions on a 7-point scale ranging from 'none: of no importance' to 'of most importance.' Five items measured stakeholder values, such as 'employee relations issues (well-being, safety, working conditions)' and 'welfare of the local community.' One item (contribution to the economic welfare of the nation) did not achieve an adequate loading and was dropped from the measurement model.

Subordinates indicated their level of agreement with items describing their respective CEOs on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree.' The visionary leadership measure included items such as 'anticipates; attempts to forecast events,' 'considers what will happen in the future,' and 'clearly articulates his/her vision of the future.' Responses were aggregated to the firm level, justified by intraclass correlations.

Subordinates rated their agreement that items describe their CEO on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree.' The autocratic leadership measure consisted of four items, such as 'tells subordinates what to do in a commanding way' and 'forces his/her values and opinions on others.' Responses were aggregated to the firm level.

A second group of subordinates reported their 'reactions to, and views of, this organization' rather than their effort in relation to the leader, rating agreement on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree.' The measure consisted of four items, such as 'Others are stimulated to put forth efforts above and beyond the call of duty and make personal sacrifices' and 'I contribute to this organization 100% of my ability.' One item pertains to the extra effort of others to mitigate social desirability bias, and the measure taps the self-sacrifice aspect of extra effort. Responses were aggregated to the firm level.

Following Dess and Robinson's recommendations, respondents assessed organizational performance on a 7-point scale in terms of gross return on investment and sales growth relative to their competitors. The authors combine sales and return on investment to capture a broad, internally controlled concept of performance, arguing that comparison to close competitors controls for exogenous industry and environmental influences. The measure was validated in a small subsample of 13 firms, correlating .41 (p < .05) with an objective performance measure. Responses were aggregated to the firm level.

Dichotomous variable with a value of one if the investor made an equity investment in the venture as part of the venture's first round of professional investments and zero otherwise. Each occurring dyad was matched with ten random non-occurring dyads through choice-based sampling, and the resulting sample was corrected for the difference in the proportion of positive outcomes.

Identical to the primary dependent variable, except that it takes on a value of one if an investment was made as part of a second or later round of investments and zero otherwise. Choice-based sampling and rare-event corrections were applied as in the primary sample.

Dichotomous variable with a value of one when a tie existed and zero otherwise. A founder's direct tie was measured by whether a founder had previously founded another venture in which the potential investor had made an equity investment. Founders' biographies from archived Web sites were used to identify any prior ventures they had started, and the VentureXpert database was used to identify the professional investors investing in these prior ventures.

Dichotomous variable with a value of one when a tie existed and zero otherwise. A founder's indirect tie was measured by whether the potential investor had previously co-invested with another professional investor that possessed a direct tie with one or more of a venture's founders.

A factor score obtained from a factor analysis, using the principal factor method with promax rotation, of three measures: the percentage of founders that attended an elite university for either their undergraduate or graduate degree (elite universities classified using the designations of Useem and Karabel); whether at least one founder had a relevant graduate degree, i.e., a Master's or Ph.D. in a related science or engineering discipline, measured as a 0/1 variable; and the number of venture-capital-backed startups previously founded by members of the founding team that had either been acquired or gone public. Only one factor had an eigenvalue greater than 1, and all three measures loaded on this single factor.

A factor score obtained from a factor analysis, using the principal factor method with promax rotation, of three dichotomous 0/1 measures: whether one or more of the team's founders had been a manager at a public company; whether the founding team was functionally diverse, including at least one founder who had previously managed a group, one who had an engineering background, and one with marketing experience; and whether two or more of the founders had previously worked together. Only one factor had an eigenvalue greater than 1; the loadings suggest that public management experience and functional diversity are the strongest determinants.

Computed yearly from 2000 through 2005 for each investor as the eigenvector centrality in the co-investment network of all the potential professional investors over the previous five years, because it weights each tie by the connected investor's centrality. The five-year time horizon was chosen to ensure that co-investment ties were recent and for consistency with the prior literature on co-investment network centrality. The networks included all U.S. investors listed in VentureXpert as being active during the relevant time period.

The similarity between founder entrepreneurial human capital and investor status, computed by taking the ratio of the lower of the two compared values (i.e., either the relevant measure of founder human capital or investor status) divided by the larger of the two values, after both measures were normalized to range from 0 to 1. The measure ranges from 0, indicating no similarity, to 1, indicating complete similarity; for dyads in which the compared measures both equal 0, the similarity measure was set to 1.

The similarity between founder managerial human capital and investor status, computed with the same ratio-based similarity measure as for entrepreneurial human capital: the lower of the two normalized compared values divided by the larger, ranging from 0 (no similarity) to 1 (complete similarity), and set to 1 when both compared measures equal 0.

The number of products that a venture had released at the time of the focal investment round relative to the number of products released by the other new organizations in the sample when they were the same age, computed as [p_v - min(p)] / [max(p) - min(p)], where p_v is the number of products the venture had released when it formed the focal round and p is a vector of the number of products released by the rest of the ventures in the sample when they were the same age. Product release dates were gathered from archived versions of the ventures' Web sites, and the measure was normalized across the sample to range from 0 to 1.
time_window: at the time of the focal investment round

description: The number of awards that a venture had received at the time of the focal round relative to the awards received by other ventures in the sample when they were the same age, calculated using the same method as for venture product accomplishments and also normalized to range from 0 to 1. Information on awards, including dates, came from the news and events sections of the ventures' archived Web sites.
time_window: at the time of the focal round

description: The similarity between organizational product accomplishments and investor status, calculated using the same ratio-based similarity comparison as used for founder human capital and investor status similarity (lower value divided by higher value of the two normalized measures).

The similarity between organizational award accomplishments and investor status, calculated using the same ratio-based similarity comparison as used for founder human capital and investor status similarity.

Age was measured as the number of years that a venture had existed at the time of the focal investment round. It was included to control for the reduced risk associated with investing in older ventures and was interacted with the founder-related variables to test hypothesis 5.
time_window: at the time of the focal investment round

description: A binary variable with a value of 1 if the investor had previously invested in the venture and a value of 0 otherwise.
A binary variable with a value of 1 if the investor had previously co-invested with one or more of the venture's previous professional investors and a value of 0 otherwise.
Measured with the same ratio-based similarity measure, by dividing the lesser of the potential investor's status and the highest status of the existing investors by the greater of these two values.

The dependent variable in the recruitment models is whether a publicly held American corporation was formally visited as a benchmarking partner in a given Team Challenge. Two risk sets are used: the Compustat 6000, consisting of publicly held American corporations whose annual sales were greater than two million dollars and whose workforce numbered at least 180 employees during the period, and publicly held members of the Fortune 500.

Each manager was presented with a list of the firms that his or her team had benchmarked and asked 'How influential were the examples provided by the following external companies for the development of your team's thinking and recommendations?' Managers scored firms on a 5-point scale from 'no influence' to 'extremely influential,' and perceptions of the impact of each visited firm were averaged to the team level, giving a continuous measure between 1 and 5.

When teams offered policy recommendations they named the organizations they regarded as models of best practice and/or where they had witnessed the practices they recommended; best practice citations counts the number of times each visited company was described as a source of best practice in connection to specific policy proposals in team reports.

Board interlock equals 1 if Global Financial's senior executives and inside board members served on a firm's board, if that firm's executives served on Global Financial's board, or if Global Financial's outside board members served on that firm's board. All firms that had a board interlock to the bank within a five-year window ending with the year of the relevant challenge were included.
time_window: five-year window ending with the year of the relevant challenge

description: Same region is a binary indicator that equals 1 for companies headquartered in New York, where Global Financial is based, or in the states of Connecticut and New Jersey, which adjoin the New York metropolitan area.

Executive migration is a binary indicator based on the prior corporate homes of the bank's top management team; career histories of Global Financial's executive officers were retraced using internal publications, the databases ABInform, Hoovers, and PRNewswire, as well as the search engine Google. All firms in which Global Financial's current executives had been employed within the last five years were coded as being linked to the bank via a management tie, and analyses focus on in-migration ties.

Competitor identifies those companies with businesses in any of the two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) categories in which Global Financial operates: depository institutions, non-depository credit institutions, and security and commodity brokers. Competitors do not include firms in other financial segments or firms whose financial activities were modest enough relative to their overall operations not to be identified in SIC classifications.

A binary indicator equaling 1 if a benchmarked firm scored among the top 100 on Fortune magazine's reputational measure in the year before it was benchmarked. Fortune polls samples of up to 11,000 executives, directors, and market analysts to evaluate firms within their industry, and the measure can be interpreted as a measure of status equivalence as well as a marker of organizational prestige.
time_window: year before the firm was benchmarked

description: State-level membership data obtained from the Sierra Club, which over the period of the study was one of the three largest environmental social movement organizations in the United States. The authors argue that membership reflects the size and strength of the Sierra Club more accurately than other measures such as the number of Sierra Club chapters in a state. Membership data were only available from 1982 to 1993, and the analyses focused on these years. All independent and control variables were lagged one year.

The dependent variable is registration with FERC by an entrepreneur or entrepreneurial team, which signals intent to build but does not necessarily mean that the facility will become operational. FERC required all ventures seeking qualifying-facility status under PURPA to file a notice reporting basic facts about their proposed facility; registration required the applicant to determine technology type, facility size, relationships with utility incumbents, and approximate location. In the event history analysis each filing within each state was treated as a founding event and split by state-year, giving 666 filing events in 50 states over 14 years.

Constructed by summing state laws, agency rules, and commission policies that had been enacted or adopted with the intent to increase electricity conservation and the generation of renewable energy within a state. Policies included inverted rate structure, solar and waste heat utilization policies, load management, tax incentives for investment in wind energy, defined avoided costs, and use of a standard contract. If the state had a given policy in place, that state received a '1' for that policy; these scores were then summed for each state-year. The variable was lagged one year.

Obtained from the U.S. Department of Energy as the number of acres of available land in each state that had wind quality rated at a wind class greater than 3, i.e., wind speeds greater than 6.4 meters/second. The variable was lagged one year.

Calculated as the number of people in each state employed in technical fields relevant to wind energy technology, using the Standard Industrial Classification code as a guide. Five major industry groups were included: engines and turbines, electric transmission and distribution equipment, electronic components and accessories, miscellaneous electrical machinery, and aircraft and parts. Missing data points were filled in by linearly interpolating values within a state over time using the Stata ipolate command; the five industry group variables were then summed by state. The variable was lagged one year.

The amount of net electricity imports into a state, used as a proxy that measures the degree to which a state is unable to generate sufficient electricity to meet electricity demand. Data come from the United States Department of Energy. The variable was lagged one year.

variable_name: yearly count of patents assigned to the DBFs
description: Yearly count of patents assigned to the dedicated biotechnology firms, categorized by application date rather than issue date because that date best reflects when the research was completed. Patent counts were extracted from the United States Patent and Trademark Office database and matched to firm-level and network data. Nearly 7,300 (N = 7,299) patents were issued to the 371 firms between 1988 and 1999, with a mean yearly volume of 2.4 patents per firm and a standard deviation of 8.2; the counts are highly right-skewed and the median is 0.0 patents per year.

Continuous, yearly firm-level measure of geographic distance based on Sorenson and Audia's (2000) localized geographic density measure: the average distance from a focal firm to every other alter firm in each year in the database, with the weighting variable set to one. Firm locations were coded from the postal zip code of the firm's headquarters, and distances in miles on a curved surface were computed from latitude and longitude using spherical geometry. The measure increases in magnitude as a firm's proximity to other companies in the industry increases; normalized proximity statistics are presented to account for the changing number of firms per year.

Continuous, firm-level measure of geographic proximity to universities and research hospitals and institutes, computed with the same localized density equations, this time calculating the distance from a focal firm to all public research organizations in the biotechnology industry. The measure captures closeness to potential sources of knowledge spillovers and its value decreases as the distance between a focal firm and a public research organization grows. Because none of the public research organizations changed locations during the time period, nonnormalized measures are presented.

Bonacich's (1987) power centrality measure, in which the strength of a focal firm is recursively defined by the sum of the power of its alters, calculated using the full global network of firms and partners regardless of geographic distance or location. The network of formal contractual relationships among DBFs and partner organizations was coded from BioScan by start date and duration, and a link exists whenever a DBF and a partner have one or more ties between them. In models that include local centrality, global position was recalculated with all local ties removed; the percentage of companies with non-zero power centrality ranges from 60 percent in 1988 to 91 percent in 1999.

Bonacich's power centrality calculated using only ties in a focal firm's regional network, for the Bay Area, Boston, and San Diego regions. The three local networks collectively involve 193 DBFs, 41 public research organizations, one government lab, and 99 venture capital firms during this time period. Local centrality increases in magnitude as a focal firm connects to neighbors who are themselves well connected to other organizations in the region.

variable_name: percentage of family members in the inner circle
description: Inner circle members coded as having family ties to the key leader, including immediate family members (son, daughter, husband, wife, father, and mother) and close relatives such as brother, sister, son-in-law, daughter-in-law, sister-in-law, brother-in-law, nieces, and uncles. For each relationship category the authors calculated the percentage of members with such relationships in the inner circle as (number of members of a certain relationship category) / (size of the inner circle - 1), because the key leader does not have one of the four relationships with himself. Strangers are the omitted category. All relationships fall into only one of the four categories.
time_window: coded in 1973, 1977, 1981, 1986, 1990 and 1994 and extended at time t to t+1 for the intervening years

variable_name: percentage of prior social ties in the inner circle
description: Inner circle members coded as having prior social relationships with the key leader, including distant relatives (clan members and in-laws outside a spouse's blood relatives), friends, classmates, colleagues, and business partners of the key leader who had worked with him prior to serving in the current inner circle. Calculated as the number of members of this relationship category divided by the size of the inner circle minus one. Strangers are the omitted category.
time_window: coded in 1973, 1977, 1981, 1986, 1990 and 1994 and extended at time t to t+1 for the intervening years

variable_name: percentage of common-identity ties in the inner circle
description: Inner circle members coded as strangers with common identity: alumni of the same school as the key leader and people from the same hometown. Calculated as the number of members of this relationship category divided by the size of the inner circle minus one. Strangers are the omitted category.
time_window: coded in 1973, 1977, 1981, 1986, 1990 and 1994 and extended at time t to t+1 for the intervening years

description: Business group performance is gauged by return on assets, which takes into account the efficiency of using the firm's assets and hence reflects a firm's profitability. For the years before 1980, when ROA was not reported in the directory, the authors calculated ROA as net income divided by total assets.

A dummy variable distinguishing the institutional periods: 1987 marked the beginning of sea changes in Taiwan, so the 1988-1996 period was coded as the post-transition period and the 1973-1986 period as the pre-transition period.

variable_name: Having a woman in a partner position
description: A dummy variable capturing whether or not a firm had a woman partner, followed annually until one of the firm's partners was a woman. The variable equals one for the firm-year in which there is a woman partner, and the firm then exits the risk set. Sex of attorneys was determined from first names, confirmed with photographs where possible, and any gender-neutral name was classified as male unless a photograph proved otherwise.

variable_name: Institutionalized female leadership (proportion of years the parent had women partners)
description: The proportion of years that there was a woman partner in the parent firm, beginning with the parent firm's first year and ending with the year the founder departed. The variable ranged from zero (the parent firm never had any women partners before the founder left) to one (the parent firm had at least one woman partner in each year from its birth until the founder left).
time_window: from the parent firm's first year until the year the founder departed

variable_name: Institutionalized female subordination (proportion of years the parent had women associates)
description: The proportion of years that a parent firm had women associates, coded as an indicator of how institutionalized women in subordinate positions were. Years of women associates are measured controlling for the existence of women partners.
time_window: from the parent firm's first year until the year the founder departed

variable_name: Number of years the founder worked with women partners
description: The number of years the founder worked when there were also women partners in the parent firm.
time_window: founder's tenure in the parent firm

variable_name: Number of years the founder worked with women associates
description: The number of years the founder worked when there were also women associates in the parent firm.
time_window: founder's tenure in the parent firm

description: A variable that equals one if the founder was a former associate and zero if the founder was a former partner. It is interacted with each of the institutionalization variables.

The absolute value of the difference between the parent's leverage ratio at the time of the founder's departure and the progeny's leverage ratio, where the leverage ratio is the associate-to-partner ratio. The greater the difference in leverage ratios, the fewer routines are transferred from the parent to the progeny. In about 10 percent of cases the progeny had multiple parents and the parents' leverage ratios were averaged.
time_window: parent's leverage ratio at the time of the founder's departure

description: Dummy variables distinguishing different types of progeny from de novo firms, which are the reference category: whether the firm is any type of progeny (has a parent firm in Silicon Valley), and dummies separating progeny whose parents had institutionalized female leadership, progeny whose parents had institutionalized female subordination, and progeny from parents with no history of women in leadership or subordinate positions.

variable_name: weekly count of newspaper mentions of 'the Skandia scandal'
description: The main independent variable is the weekly count of newspaper mentions of 'the Skandia scandal' in Dagens Industri, the most widely read daily business newspaper, and Dagens Nyheter, the most widely read daily general newspaper. Two coders working independently coded each occurrence of the phrase. As a sensitivity test the authors also estimated models using an alternative measure giving the average tenor of all articles in a week.
time_window: coded from December 1998 through December 2004; weekly counts

description: The logarithm of the total sale amount in Swedish Kronor (plus one, because sales can equal zero) of the focal fund. These are sales from the investor's point of view and hence are transaction withdrawals from the fund manager's point of view. The logarithm was taken because the distribution is skewed and a logarithmic response function fits the data better than a linear one.

Net transactions, buys minus sells. Both tails of the distribution are heavy, so the authors used a logarithmic transformation on each side of zero but preserved the sign: if the untransformed variable was x, the variable equals sign(x) times ln(abs(x) + 1). Higher values mean less withdrawal of money from the fund.

The authors stratified the sample by organizational form to compare the effects of the scandal on all organizational forms with subsidiaries offering mutual funds, although some forms had fewer members than others. In the pooled analysis each organizational form is given a separate intercept and the scandal count is entered as an interaction with organizational form, with no main effect of the scandal count.
scale: categorical (insurance, pension, big bank, small bank, foreign, independent)

variable_name: asset size difference (square root of size difference from Skandia)
description: The size of the mutual fund firm is the total assets under management (not only assets under management in the PPM system) from a database maintained by MoneyMate (Sweden), an independent industry observer. These data were then used to construct a variable set to the square root of the size difference of the focal firm and Skandia. Higher values mean less similarity in size to Skandia.

The percentage of real estate holdings to the total assets held by each parent corporation. The mutual funds in the data do not hold real estate, nor do the mutual fund management firms, so the real estate holdings belong to a parent or sibling of the mutual fund management firm in the corporate structure. The data were collected from the statistics of the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority and the Swedish Insurance Association and were updated annually.

Consumer quality ratings of the firms in the sample from the Swedish Quality Index (SQI), an independent quality-rating institute that carries out consumer surveys on industry sectors to measure consumers' perceptions of quality in various dimensions. The quality index is constructed on the basis of an annual survey of 4,500 individuals using a partial least squares analysis. Ratings are available for all Swedish banks and insurance firms from 1998 onwards; when the rating was missing it was set to the mean and an indicator variable for missing rating was set to one.

The transnational's host market local (non-export) sales divided by the total local sales achieved by foreign transnationals in that same industry and host market. The result is a continuous measure bounded between 0 and 1 that indicates the relative host market prominence of the foreign transnationals in the sample.
level: firm by industry by host market

description: Calculated based on the total number of IGOs in which the transnational's home and host countries share joint membership, following Ingram, Robinson, and Busch (2005). The average value of this measure over a three-year period is used, and the variable is scaled by its standard deviation.

The home share in total exports from the host divided by the home share in total exports from the world. If the numerator is greater than the denominator the ratio exceeds 1 and the host is treated as more export dependent on the home, compared with the world. The average value of this measure over a three-year period is used.

A simple average of two categorical variables created to indicate the extent and significance of immigration flows from home-to-host and host-to-home countries. A value of 2 is assigned if immigration was significant enough to be considered formative of the destination country's people, 1 if immigration was sizable but not formative, and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: proportion of WCTU members in a state
description: The annual number of dues-paying members of local WCTU chapters (unions) in each state divided by the total state population. The data came from the Minutes of the Convention of the National Woman's Christian Temperance Union (1874-1920).

variable_name: number of American Medical Association members per state
description: A count of AMA members per state, used to capture the amount of resources available for lobbying and temperance endorsement. Information on AMA state membership came from the Transactions of the American Medical Association (1869-1920).

variable_name: percentage of all counties in adjoining states that had enacted state and county prohibition laws
description: For each focal state, the percentage of all counties in adjoining states that had enacted state and county prohibition laws. The authors orthogonalized the interaction variables involving this measure and WCTU proportion.

variable_name: logged accumulative time since scientific temperance instruction was enacted
description: The number of years a state had in place mandatory scientific temperance instruction, logged as a cumulative learning measure. Because once a state mandated STI the passage of time should result in a progressively larger proportion of the population that had received pro-temperance instruction, the authors followed past research on individual learning in using logged accumulative time.

variable_name: proportion of counties with prohibition laws in a state
description: For states that had not passed statewide laws, the proportion of counties that had passed prohibition laws; when states passed laws applying to all counties, the measure was coded as 1. Information came from a public-use dataset of county- and state-level prohibition laws.

Each brewery was assigned a value of 1 for each year that it was in operation and 0 for the year that it failed, if this occurred. Because the period begins in 1870 and the first brewery was founded in 1633, the data in the event history analysis are left-censored.

variable_name: number of soft drink manufacturer foundings
description: For each state-year, the number of soft drink manufacturer foundings calculated from a dataset providing founding date, address, ownership, date of failure, and products for over 20,000 soft drink bottlers. Roughly 13 percent of the bottlers in the sample manufactured soft drinks under franchise contracts and were included in the analyses.

On-site emissions were weighted using the Human Toxicity Potential factor, assigning each chemical separate values for different media of release; after weighting each chemical by its corresponding HTP value, results were aggregated across chemicals, first at the facility level and then by parent company. Cancer and noncancer values were used separately to calculate two variables. As these variables were highly skewed, they were log-transformed (after adding 1). The measures were reversed by multiplying them by -1 so that bigger values are associated with better environmental performance. Given a Cronbach's alpha of 0.91, both measures were standardized and averaged to create the final environmental performance measure, averaged for the period 1999-2002.
Firm type was a dummy variable that assumed the value 1 if the family owned at least 5 percent of the company's stock, and 0 otherwise.

The measure is based on the absolute distance in miles between the headquarters of firm i and subsidiary j, weighted by the number of employees of subsidiary j divided by the economically active population of the zip code area of subsidiary j, and summed over all subsidiaries. Distance between headquarters and subsidiaries was calculated with the Spheresoft Zip Code Tools as the straight-line distance across the globe.
A dummy variable that assumed the value of 1 if the CEO belonged to the family that controlled the firm, and 0 otherwise.
A dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO held both the CEO and board chair positions, and 0 otherwise.
The CEO's percentage of ownership in the firm.

Dichotomous variable coded 1 in the years after a facility disclosed one or more regulatory violations under the U.S. EPA Audit Policy and formally committed to self-regulate, and 0 beforehand. The variable was always coded 0 for facilities that never disclosed violations under the Audit Policy.
time_window: coded 1 in the years after the disclosure year, 0 beforehand

description: Dichotomous variable based on a facility's regulatory inspection on a given date, coded 1 when the inspection resulted in no compliance violations (i.e., was 'clean') and coded 0 when the inspector cited the facility for one or more violations. Data on Clean Air Act inspections and violations come from the EPA's AIRS database.

variable_name: targeted by a Compliance Incentive Program
description: Facilities targeted by a U.S. EPA Compliance Incentive Program in the disclosure (or match) year, identified from EPA data obtained via Freedom of Information Act requests; the H1 subsample consists of facilities that disclosed without such a direct regulatory threat, defined as those not targeted by a Compliance Incentive Program in the disclosure (or match) year.

variable_name: number of inspections in the two years prior to the disclosure (or match) year
description: Heavy regulatory monitoring is defined as at least two inspections during the two years prior to the disclosure (or match) year, constructed from CAA regulatory inspection data obtained from the U.S. EPA's AIRS database.
time_window: two years prior to the disclosure (or match) year

description: Calculated as the average number of times a facility in each industry (2-digit SIC code) was inspected in each state and year, using facility industry identifiers from the agency's Facility Registry System. Facilities were classified as being in heavily monitored industries when their industry inspection intensity exceeded the median industry inspection intensity level for its state-year, focusing on the year prior to each facility's disclosure (or match) year.
scale: average number of inspections (dichotomized above/below state-year median)
time_window: year prior to the disclosure (or match) year

description: Operationalized as no compliance violations or enforcement actions in the year in which the facility disclosed to the Audit Policy or in either of the previous two years; compliance data were obtained from the U.S. EPA's AIRS and ICIS databases.
time_window: disclosure year and the two preceding years

description: Because traditional indicators of legitimacy could not be used, as they focus on large numbers of firms and the density of a population, the authors developed an alternative indicator: the widespread commercialization and consumer adoption of a new market product. In the analyses this threshold demarcates the emergence period (1999-2001) from the early growth period (2003-2005), with 2002 identified as the tipping point at which satellite radio was legitimated.

variable_name: identity claims ('what we do' and 'who we are')
description: To test shifts in identity claims the authors coded statements of 'what we do' and 'who we are' in the press releases. Coding rules specified unique instances per release, and the authors focused on patterns in the number of codes per release, comparing mean instances across periods.

To test patterns in language, labeling, and framing the authors coded linguistic framing, which they refer to broadly as 'metaphor,' including framing that referenced the market category as a whole and framing that referenced the individual firms. Coded categories included category framing and firm-specific framing.

To test patterns in announced affiliations the authors coded announcements that emphasized the prominence of alliance partners and their sanctioning of the collective practices of the category, cataloguing instances in which announcements emphasized the advantage to the category while suppressing individual firm advantages and instances that emphasized advantages to the individual firms while suppressing collective or categorical advantages, such as exclusive endorsements.

variable_name: analyst report codes (category versus individual firms)
description: Two codes distinguished whether attention in analysts' reports was directed toward the category as a whole or toward the individual firms. The authors also analyzed the ratio of competitor to focal-firm mentions in reports on a focal firm. Only the body of each report was coded, disregarding tables, figures, and disclaimers.

The authors graphed the pattern of daily stock returns for the satellite radio firms over time and used the Zivot-Andrews procedure to analyze the cointegration of firms' stock values over time. The procedure normalizes differences in the magnitude of the firms' stock returns over time, which could be masked in the visual plot when an actual break occurs.

The authors searched three major newspapers for articles in which the headlines named the category as a whole ('satellite radio') or the firms individually, and analyzed references to 'satellite radio' only in the headlines (with no mention of either firm), comparing the proportion of such headlines across periods.

Interquartile range of the Polity score within the group of states. The Polity score rates states each year on a scale of -10 to 10 based on the presence of democratic institutions and the absence of autocratic ones, and measures the competitiveness of elections and constraints on executive authority. The interquartile range is chosen because it is a robust measure of divergence within a group that is relatively invariant with group size.
Mean of the direct-line distance between each pair of states in the group. Higher values indicate greater dispersion of the group rather than greater proximity.
Percentage of dyads within the group that had engaged in militarized interstate disputes with each other in the previous 10 years.

Measure of the extent to which states within a group are dependent on trade with each other, based on Gleditsch's dyadic trade data. The variable is entered in the models as the logged average dyadic trade.

variable_name: average dyadic IGO ties within group
description: Mean of the dyadic tie strength between each pair of states in the group. Dyadic tie strength is defined as the number of IGOs in which the two states of the dyad share a membership.

Counts the IGO memberships of group members that do not contribute to IGO ties within the group. For a given state, an IGO membership that is not shared by any of the other states in the group is counted in full, while memberships that form ties with some but not all group members are counted proportionally. Together with average dyadic IGO ties within group, it decomposes each member's IGO memberships into those that create contact within the group and those that do not.
Based on the total number of NGO memberships of the citizens of each state in the group, as coded by Hafner-Burton and Tsutsui, averaged over the group and entered in logged form.
Mean of the Polity score within the group of states, capturing the average level of democracy of the states rather than their similarity.

Dependent variable coded 1 for groups of states that experienced an IGO founding in a given year and 0 for the ten matched samples from the risk set that did not experience a founding in that year. An IGO is treated as founded in the year it actually began operations.

Interquartile range of the Polity score within the group of member states of the focal IGO. The Polity score rates states each year on a scale of -10 to 10 based on the presence of democratic institutions and the absence of autocratic ones. The interquartile range is a robust measure of divergence within a group that is relatively invariant with group size.
Mean of the direct-line distance between each pair of member states of the focal IGO. Higher values indicate that the members are more widely dispersed rather than more proximate.
Percentage of dyads among the members of the focal IGO that had engaged in militarized interstate disputes with each other in the previous 10 years.
Measure of the extent to which the member states of the focal IGO are dependent on trade with each other, based on Gleditsch's dyadic trade data, entered in the models as a logged average.

variable_name: average dyadic IGO ties within group
description: Mean of the dyadic tie strength between each pair of member states of the focal IGO, where dyadic tie strength is the number of IGOs in which the two states of the dyad share a membership.

Counts the IGO memberships of the focal IGO's member states that do not contribute to IGO ties within the membership group. A membership that is not shared by any other member of the group is counted in full, and memberships that form ties with some but not all group members are counted proportionally.
Based on the total number of NGO memberships of the citizens of each member state of the focal IGO, as coded by Hafner-Burton and Tsutsui, averaged over the members and entered in logged form.
Mean of the Polity score across the member states of the focal IGO, capturing the average level of democracy of the members rather than their similarity.

Failure event defined as the IGO ceasing to exist outright or being merged into another IGO, but not as being replaced by a new IGO; replacements were treated as right-censored non-failures. Each IGO's life history was broken into one-year spells to incorporate time-varying covariates.

The purchase price per target share paid by the acquiring firm less the target's pre-acquisition stock price, divided by the pre-acquisition stock price. The target's pre-acquisition stock price was taken 30 days prior to the acquisition announcement date to avoid bias from the run-up in a target's stock due to the anticipation of an acquisition.
time_window: 30 days prior to the acquisition announcement date

description: The organic growth of all banks in existence during the study period was first measured as the annual compound growth rate of a bank's total assets during the three years prior to the focal year minus any growth in total assets resulting from mergers and acquisitions during the period. Relative social organic growth was then calculated by taking the three-year organic growth of the focal bank and subtracting the average three-year organic growth of its peer banks, defined as all banks in existence that operated in all the states in which the focal bank operated in a given year. The variable was log-transformed to model the non-linear relationship with acquisition premium.
time_window: three years prior to the focal year

description: An acquirer's past level of organic growth was measured by an exponentially weighted moving average of the acquirer's organic growth in the past, with the weighting factor set to 0.3, which provided the best model fit among alternative weighting factors. Relative historical organic growth was operationalized by subtracting an acquirer's historical organic growth from its current year's organic growth, and the variable was then log-transformed to model the non-linear relationship with acquisition premium.
time_window: current year relative to history; weighting factor 0.3

description: The three-year acquisition dependence of all banks in existence was first measured as the total amount of growth in total assets that a bank realized via acquisitions during the three-year period prior to the focal year as a percentage of the total amount of growth in total assets during the same period. Relative social acquisition dependence was then calculated as the three-year acquisition dependence of a focal bank minus the average three-year acquisition dependence of all banks that also operated in the states in which the focal bank operated. The variable was reverse-coded so that small values represent high desperation and was log-transformed to model a non-linear relationship with acquisition premium.
time_window: three years prior to the focal year

description: Operationalized as the difference between an acquirer's current year's acquisition dependence and its historical level of acquisition dependence, which was measured in the same way that historical organic growth was created. The variable was reverse-coded so that small values represent high desperation and was log-transformed to model a non-linear relationship with acquisition premium.

Measured by the discounted sum of the number of intraindustry acquisitions that a bank in the sample made since 1988, the year in which the CEBA and the Douglas Amendment were enacted. Because the value of experience depreciates over time, the value of each experience was discounted using the age of the experience as the discount factor.
time_window: since 1988, discounted by age of experience

description: Measured by the total number of acquisitions for which the focal acquisition advisor served as advisor in the commercial banking sector between 1988 and the focal acquisition, counting advisor experience only when it was specific to the commercial banking industry. The variable was discounted using the age of each experience to account for the depreciation of the value of experience over time.
time_window: 1988 to the focal acquisition, discounted by age of experience

description: The logged sum of R&D, capital expenditures, and acquisitions in a given year, following Sanders and Hambrick (2007). Across all firm-years, each of the three forms of risky spending contributed roughly equally to aggregate annual spending; standardizing the three elements was not necessary.

The target firm's share price was noted four weeks prior to the date on which the takeover was first announced, and the acquisition premium was computed as the purchase price minus the pre-takeover price divided by the pre-takeover price.
time_window: year leading up to the acquisition

description: Two industry-adjusted indicators measured in year t+n-1: Total shareholder returns (TSR), calculated as year-end share price minus year-beginning price plus dividends paid, all divided by year-beginning share price; and Return on assets (ROA), calculated as net income divided by assets. The industry average for the year was subtracted to obtain industry-adjusted performance indicators.
Total shareholder returns (TSR) for the year leading up to the acquisition, calculated as in Study 1. As in Study 1, industry averages were subtracted to obtain industry-adjusted TSR.
time_window: year leading up to the acquisition

description: Two indicators measured in t+n-1. Media praise for the CEO was assessed by content analysis of prominent newspapers and business magazines; articles with evaluative comments about the CEO were rated from -2 (very critical) to +2 (unequivocally favorable), and each year's media praise was the sum of ratings of all evaluative articles, with zero for CEOs with no evaluative articles. Media awards were counted with one point for every award received in a given year.
scale: media praise: -2 to +2 per article; awards: count

description: Media praise for the CEO measured in the year leading up to the acquisition using the same content-analysis method as Study 1. Two independent raters coded all articles, and interrater agreement was high.
time_window: year leading up to the acquisition

description: Simple mean of four standardized unobtrusive indicators: prominence of the CEO's photograph in the company's annual report, prominence of the CEO in press releases, relative cash pay, and relative non-cash pay. The measure was averaged over years t+1 and t+2 of the CEO's tenure, omitting the first year.

Same method as in Study 1, relying on four unobtrusive indicators: prominence of the CEO's photograph in the company's annual report, prominence of the CEO in press releases, relative cash pay, and relative non-cash pay. Narcissism scores for each CEO were computed by averaging the four measures, after standardization.

Categorical dummy identifying early entrants with 80 percent or more of their first-five-year flat panel patents in plasma technology. Used together with enter with LCD (omitted category), enter with both, and the late entrant dummy in the count models of annual LCD patenting.

Ratio of LCD patents to all flat panel display patents in the early entrants' first five years in the industry; used as a continuous, initial test of hypothesis 1. It was set to 1 for all late entrants, an effect dummied out by the late entrant dummy.
Categorical dummy identifying early entrants with 80 percent or higher share of LCD patents in their first five years at entry. This is the omitted category in the count models of LCD patenting.

Categorical dummy identifying early entrants whose share of LCD patents in their first five years fell between the high-LCD and high-plasma cutoffs, i.e., firms that invested in both competing technologies at entry.
scale: dummy (1 = early supporter of both technologies)

description: Dummy equal to one for firms whose first flat panel display patent was filed after 1982, i.e., firms entering after the technological uncertainty had been resolved in favor of LCD.

Annual count of LCD patents the firm applied for and later received, based on patent families from Derwent rather than individual patents. Because the firm's LCD patent stock is controlled for, the models predict differences in the growth rate of that stock for firms making different initial technological choices. Observations with no patenting were retained with a zero.

Dummy noting whether the firm had any plasma patents in the given year, measured from 1989 to 2003 during plasma's renaissance, because more than 88 percent of firms had no plasma patents in this period.

Stock of the firm's patenting in general flat panel patents, patents Derwent classifies as applying to both LCD and plasma displays (e.g., glass, power supply, driver circuitry). Logged for overdispersion and lagged one year.

Dummy identifying firms with experience as incumbents in the television, computer, or watch industries before their entry into flat panel displays, used as a commercialization measure of complementary assets based on pre-entry experience.

Regulatory distance is computed with a Mahalanobis distance measure across six dimensions of industry regulation, measuring the distance between each country and Brazil, the reference country, and is then aggregated to the firm level by multiplying the firm's country investment presence matrix by the country distance vector. Three weighting approaches capture home-country effects (all weight on the home country), host-country effects (all weight on prior host countries), and combined experience effects (equal weight on home and host countries), and additional variants capture the minimum distance and the sign of regulatory distance (stronger or weaker industry regulation than Brazil's). The portfolio of prior investments is recorded for t <= 1998 and updated annually to include new subunits acquired globally during the study. The squared distance term gives only a positive measure of distance, so the sign of regulatory distance distinguishes environments with stronger regulation from those with weaker regulation than Brazil's.
time_window: prior experience recorded for t <= 1998 and updated annually

description: The time to failure event is a firm's exit from Brazil, measured at the firm/parent/year level, where firm survival in period t is coded (0) and failure is coded (1). Each exit was examined to determine the reason for it, and failures were limited to exits driven by financial underperformance in earnings projections, difficulty securing capital to continue the investment, lack of understanding of local institutions, or related situations. Three independent coders assessed failure cases with 100 percent interrater reliability. The event is modeled in an accelerated failure time specification in which a positive and significant coefficient decelerates time to fail.

Breadth of experience measures the dispersion of types of host-country regulatory experience prior to entering Brazil (t < 1998) using a coefficient of variance approach, which focuses on the central tendency of dispersion in experience rather than the simple standard deviation. Standardized regulatory scores are used to compute the dispersion in types of regulation across all home and host-country regulatory environments. The time-varying measure is updated annually to include new host-country subunit entries.

Depth measures the frequency of each of the six regulatory dimensions summed across countries that exactly matched (within +/- .1 of the regulatory dimensional scores) the regulatory environment in Brazil. Firm scores are based on the fraction of replication of Brazil's regulatory environment (100 percent redundancy = 1) and the depth within each of the replicated dimensions (1/6 for each replicated dimension). Conservative estimations added fractional redundancies of the same type only after all six dimensions were replicated. Depth scores ranged from 0 (e.g., SK Telecom, 1998) to 2.5 (e.g., Telefonica, 2004).
time_window: prior experience before entry into Brazil

description: In the loss-of-control models the predictor of interest was whether the firm was family owned (coded as 0) or not (coded as 1). In the performance-hazard and venturing-risk analyses, family owned was measured as 1 if the mill remained in family hands or 0 if the mill became part of a cooperative.
time_window: annual, measured at the start of each year

description: Obtained from the registry for those mills designated as family owned, using three mutually exclusive categories: Family Stage I, corresponding to those owned and managed by the founding family (1 if yes, 0 otherwise); Family Stage II, corresponding to those owned and managed by the non-founding extended family (1 if yes, 0 otherwise); and Family Stage III, corresponding to those owned by the non-founding extended family but managed by hired non-family executives (1 if yes, 0 otherwise).
time_window: annual, measured at the start of each year

description: Measured each year as a dichotomous variable. A mill was coded as 1 whenever it voluntarily decided to change status from a privately owned independent firm to a cooperative; mills that decided to remain independent in a given year were coded as 0.

Estimated with an event history analysis in which the endogenous variable is the duration or waiting time until the firm disappearance event occurs; the instantaneous hazard rate r(t) is the probability that an olive oil mill fails between t and t + dt given that the organization was operating at t. A semiparametric Cox model was used so that no distribution of waiting time had to be chosen, estimated by maximum partial likelihood.

A comparison of current with past performance, assessed as the percentage increase or decrease in tons of olives sold, computed as the natural logarithm in tons of olives sold at t + 1 divided by tons of olives sold at t. A score of 0 means that the target was achieved; the magnitude of positive (above 0) or negative (below 0) scores indicates the distance from achieving the target.

A comparison of the focal firm's performance in each time period with the average performance of other firms in the sector in the same time period, calculated for each firm as the annual percentage difference in tons of olives (in logarithmic form) sold by that firm and the average sold by other similar oil mills. The magnitude of positive or negative percentage scores indicates the extent to which the firm fell behind or exceeded the performance target of referent firms.

Calculated for each firm as a measure of venturing risk by dividing the standard deviation in tons of olives sold by the average tons of olives sold. The coefficient of variation normalizes the standard deviation of performance by mean performance and was used as an indicator of venturing risk.

Twelve survey questions were used as indicators of a manufacturer's performance in the procurement relationship, designed to measure the buyer's satisfaction with the exchange relationship. Factor analysis returned a two-factor solution, with nine items loading unequivocally on the first factor and two on the second; the two items loading on the second factor measured interorganizational conflict and were dropped. The first nine items were averaged to create the composite performance measure.

An exploratory factor analysis of thirteen items reflecting different aspects of the supplier's and manufacturer's dependence yielded two factors, one reflecting the supplier's dependence and one reflecting the manufacturer's dependence. Items were standardized and averaged to construct the two dependence scales, and the joint dependence variable was constructed by adding the measures of the manufacturer's and the supplier's dependence.

A scale constructed from the items that loaded uniquely on the second factor of an exploratory factor analysis of thirteen dependence items, reflecting the magnitude of exchange, the concentration of exchange, the availability of alternative sources of exchange, and the magnitude of transaction-specific investments. Items were standardized to eliminate differences in variance due to scaling and averaged.

A scale constructed from the items that loaded uniquely on the first factor of an exploratory factor analysis of thirteen dependence items, reflecting the magnitude of exchange, the concentration of exchange, the availability of alternative sources of exchange, and the magnitude of transaction-specific investments. Items were standardized and averaged.

A spline specification of dependence asymmetry. The values of (D S - D M), the difference between the supplier's and the manufacturer's dependencies on each other, were first calculated and then recoded to equal (D S - D M) if (D S > D M) and zero if otherwise. Thus the measure captures the supplier's excess dependence on the manufacturer. The sample returned 72 dyads in which a supplier held a dependence advantage.

A spline specification of dependence asymmetry. The values of (D M - D S) were calculated, keeping the original values if (D M > D S) and letting them equal zero if otherwise. Thus the measure captures the manufacturer's excess (net of the supplier's) dependence on the supplier. The sample returned 79 dyads in which a manufacturer held a dependence advantage.

Ten survey items reflecting the degree of the supplier's involvement in various aspects of cooperative exchange, the degree of joint problem solving, and the adaptability of partners in the relationship. Three items reflecting the treatment of problems of joint responsibilities, the degree of joint improvement of operations, and the degree of joint involvement in forecasting commodity requirements did not load highly and uniquely on the factor and were excluded; the rest were averaged to construct the scale. Items 1-7 were measured on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = 'Not at all involved' to 7 = 'Involved to a great extent' and items 8-10 on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 = 'Strongly disagree' to 7 = 'Strongly agree'.

A scale constructed from six items that correspond closely with those used by other scholars investigating interorganizational trust. Principal component analysis revealed that all items overwhelmingly loaded on a single factor.

From thirteen survey items reflecting the kinds of information exchanged and the level of detail, timeliness, and accuracy of the information exchange, an exploratory factor analysis rendered a two-factor solution. One item reflecting the degree of marketing information exchange did not load uniquely and was excluded; the items loading on factor 1 were averaged to measure the quality of information exchange as reflected by its level of detail, timeliness, and accuracy. Items 11-13 were measured on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = 'Poor' to 7 = 'Excellent'.

The items that loaded on the second factor of the two-factor solution of the information exchange items were averaged to measure the scope of information exchange as reflected in the frequency of exchanged information of various types. Items 1-10 measured the kinds of information exchanged on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = 'Not at all exchanged' to 7 = 'Exchanged very frequently'.

variable_name: difference between directors' concern about strategy and perception of others' concern
description: In the primary board-level models, two records were created per firm: one with directors' concern about strategy and one with directors' perception that other board members were concerned about strategy.
