A new variable was set equal to the concern value in the first record and the perceived-concern value in the second record and regressed on a dummy variable for record type, with control variables; a positive and significant dummy coefficient indicates pluralistic ignorance. Aggregation to the board level was supported by rwg indices and significant ICCs.

Multi-item scale from the survey questionnaire. Items include the extent to which the director is concerned about the viability of the current corporate strategy and the extent to which the director is comfortable with the current strategy. Factor analysis showed the items loaded on one factor, and inter-item reliability was high, with alpha of .94. The measure was aggregated to the board level, supported by an rwg index of .93 and a significant ICC.
scale: 5-point scale with endpoints 1 = "Not at all" and 6 = "Very much so" and "Somewhat" at the midpoint, as printed

variable_name: perception that other board members are concerned about strategy
description: Multi-item scale from the survey questionnaire. Items ask the director to assess whether other directors are concerned about the viability of the current corporate strategy and whether other directors are comfortable with the current strategy. Factor analysis showed the items loaded on one factor, and inter-item reliability was high, with alpha of .88. The measure was aggregated to the board level, supported by an rwg index of .94 and a significant ICC.
scale: 5-point scale with endpoints 1 = "Not at all" and 6 = "Very much so" and "Somewhat" at the midpoint, as printed

description: Multi-item scales in the initial survey and the follow-up survey gauge the extent to which directors have expressed concern about strategy during the 12 months preceding the survey. Factor analysis loaded the items on a single factor; inter-item reliability was high, with alpha of .94 for the initial survey and .93 for the follow-up survey. Interrater reliability was supported by weighted kappa values above .75 for all four survey items and an ICC of .90.

variable_name: density of personal friendship ties among outside directors
description: Respondents were asked to consider their personal relationship with each of the other outside directors, listed by name, and to indicate whether they considered each person to be an acquaintance or a personal friend. Density of friendship ties was measured as the number of such ties between outside directors divided by the number of possible ties. In the primary analyses, data on friendship ties one year prior were used.
scale: ratio of actual ties to possible ties
time_window: one year prior to the survey

description: Homogeneity was measured on each demographic characteristic using a variant of Blau's index of homogeneity, where P is the proportion of outside director dyads sharing the ith category. The categories are the same functional background, primary industry of employment, gender, and educational affiliation (having or not having an Ivy League degree). Functional background was classified into throughput functions, output functions, and peripheral functions.

variable_name: change in product market diversification and geographic diversification
description: Product market diversification was measured using the entropy measure, which operationalizes diversification according to the number of segments in which a firm competes and the relative contribution of each segment to total sales. Geographic diversification used Sanders and Carpenter's abbreviated version of Sullivan's validated scale, with three components summed into a composite measure. In the primary models, strategic change was estimated by measuring diversification in a subsequent year, year t+3, and controlling for the prior value as an instrumental variable.

variable_name: return on equity relative to historical and competitor averages
description: Firm performance was operationalized as return on equity. Prior firm performance was measured as average return on equity during the prior three-year period, t-3 to t-1. Competitor performance was measured as the average return on equity of firms with the same primary Standard Industrial Classification code. Firms were treated as below aspiration levels when performance was below the firm's historical average and below the average performance of competitors.

variable_name: number of direct ties to the distributor
description: Count of the principals' films over the prior three years carried by the same distributor as the current one. Because of the skew in its distribution, one was added to the count and the resulting number was transformed by the natural log. Quadratic terms were investigated in all models, but the reported models use logged counts.

The film's budget or negative cost in units of logged dollars, taken from information recorded in the Internet Movie Database. Films produced outside the United States were excluded because costs differ across countries and foreign currencies are difficult to translate, leaving budget information for a subset of 1,269 films. The authors note that they could not determine what portion of the budget comprised payments to the principals.

The number of screens on which a film played in its first week of exhibition, used as a measure of the level of resources allocated to promoting a film because distributors do not systematically report marketing expenditures. It was transformed with a natural log function to adjust for skew and to account for decreasing returns.

A moving average of total box office receipts across all films for a three-week window centered around the film's release date during the previous three years, used to capture whether a distributor released a film during a high-demand period. The three-week average accommodates the movement of holidays from year to year, and using three prior years of data minimizes the effect of outliers. It was transformed with a natural log function.

The logged box office receipts of the film, the most direct measure of film performance. Because contracts allocate revenue to exhibitors and distributors as percentages of overall receipts, all participants wish to maximize sales, and box office sales remain the critical measure of success.

Organizational growth was operationalized using annual operating expenditures as reported by respondents, who almost always referred to audited statements, tax forms, or other written records. Expenditure data were collected for 1980 through 1988 and 1991 through 1994 and converted into 1994 dollars using the producer price index. In the growth models the log(10) of expenditures was used because the error terms for the intercept and the two linear effects were highly skewed with raw expenditure data.
scale: dollars (1994 dollars); log(10) in the growth models

description: Tally of the number of urban elites who, in 1981 and 1989, mentioned an organization as providing essential services or as having achieved outstanding accomplishments in its field, and of the number of nonprofit managers who, in 1984 and 1988, said an organization had adapted well since 1980 or was well thought of by corporations and foundations. The four indicators correlated all over .88 and were combined by factor analysis; because of multicollinearity the natural logs of the reputational indicators were factor analyzed and the factor scores used as measures of organizational status in the growth models.

For each organization, the number of elite respondents who said that they supported the organization in some capacity (donations, volunteer work, consulting, board memberships) or that they or their families had used its services was tallied. Because the support and use items were highly correlated (.912 in 1980 and .920 in 1988), principal components analysis was used to combine the two items into a single construct and the factor scores served as the indicator of the nonprofit's ties to urban elites.

Organizational respondents reported the panel nonprofits to which they gave or from which they received information, the nonprofits to which they sent or from which they received personnel, clients, facilities or supplies, and the nonprofits in which they knew a manager or staff member personally; a '1' was recorded for each such tie and the three asymmetric matrices were added and symmetrized (summing x ij and x ji), giving cell values from 0 to 6 in 1984 and 1988 and 0 to 2 in 1994. Bonacich's (1972) eigenvector centrality, in which ego's ties are weighted by alter's ties to others, was computed on the entire network in 1984, 1988, and 1994 and standardized scores were computed.

Principal components analysis of the proportions of revenue from fees/sales and from donations and the proportions of personnel who were employees and volunteers, extracting one factor for each of 1980, 1988, and 1994. Factor scores were used as the measures of nonprofit type, and the 1994 factor scores were multiplied by -1 to make them consistent with the other two years; high scores indicate donative and low (negative) scores commercial inputs.

variable_name: Change in percent of gifts/grants and change in percent of employees/volunteers
description: Difference scores computed by subtracting the percentages in 1980 from the percentages in 1988 and the percentages in 1988 from the percentages in 1994 for the percent of funding that came from private gifts/grants and for the percent of personnel that were employees or volunteers. In the text the sentence describing the second difference score is garbled, so the exact quantity differenced for gifts/grants cannot be read with certainty from the prose.

Difference scores computed by subtracting the percent of fees/sales in 1980 from the percent of fees/sales in 1988 and the percent of fees/sales in 1988 from the percent of fees/sales in 1994. Table 3 reports results only for the differences in the percent of fees/sales across the two periods, because none of the other difference scores were associated with any of the dependent variables.

The degree to which a community is characterized by the presence of organizational populations that supply inputs to the focal population. It weights, by the dollar value of inputs the focal population acquires from a population divided by the dollar value of sales that population makes to all organizational populations, the density of that population in the community divided by the total density in the community, summed over all nonfocal populations. It equals zero if a community has no organization that supplies inputs to instruments producers, and uses proportions rather than absolute counts to avoid overwhelming the measure with metropolitan size.

The degree to which a community is characterized by the presence of organizational populations that purchase goods from the focal population, measured with the same weighting equation as supplier symbiosis. The difference is that the dollar value of sales from the focal population to a population and the dollar value of purchases made by that population from all organizational populations enter the weights; proportion of sales made to the focal population is used because suppliers who depend more on the focal population pay more attention to the relationship.

The weighted sum, across nonfocal populations, of each population's share of the community's total density times its similarity to the focal population. Similarity is an instance of structural equivalence operationalized as a Euclidean distance converted into a similarity based on transaction profiles with suppliers, taking the value of one if a population and the focal population have identical profiles; because similarity in transactions with suppliers correlates strongly with similarity in transactions with purchasers, only the supplier-side similarity is used.

An event-count variable of autonomous establishments present only in the second year of each two-year period, identified by comparing two consecutive years of establishment data. Foundings are dated 1978 for the 1976-1978 period and so on for 1980, 1982, 1984, 1986 and 1988, giving six two-year waves of observations for the United States.

The occurrence of the first founding of an instruments manufacturing company in a community that had no instruments manufacturers at the beginning of the observation period; LMAs are removed from the sample when the first founding takes place. The probability of this infrequent event is modeled with Poisson models, and left-censoring is addressed with a variable recording the local density of instruments manufacturers in 1973.
time_window: two-year waves from 1978 to 1988, with 1968 and 1973 left-censoring checks

description: The count of all establishments of the focal population in the community, including both autonomous units and branches. It is included together with its squared term, which the authors include for completion and comparability, although the dataset does not allow a proper test of density dependence at the local community level because many LMAs had organizations in existence at the start of the study period.

variable_name: Nonlocal density weighted by geographic distance
description: A time-varying measure in which each nonlocal instruments organization's contribution is weighted by the inverse of the geographic distance between its community and the focal community, and the weighted contributions are summed across all nonlocal instruments organizations. Geographic distances are computed from the center point of each LMA using spherical geometry to take into account the curvature of the earth. Smaller values on this variable indicate greater geographical distance from instruments manufacturers located outside the community, so it enters the models both as a control for spatial interdependence and as the moderator in the initial-founding analysis.

variable_name: Community's dominant population weighted by unrelatedness
description: The organizational population with the largest share of resources in each LMA is identified as the one with the highest ratio of its aggregate wages to total community wages, using Bureau of Labor Statistics wages data. A measure of unrelatedness is obtained by averaging three indicators of supplier symbiosis, purchaser symbiosis and supplier commensalism after standardizing and transforming them to vary between zero and one, and subtracting this average from one. The ratio of the dominant population's wages to total community wages is then weighted by this degree of unrelatedness, so that the more unrelated the dominant population the more positively it is weighted.

A five-item index of unobtrusive indicators, calculated as the simple mean of the five measures after standardization (mean = 0; s.d. = 1) for each CEO. The five indicators are the prominence of the CEO's photograph in the annual report (four points if alone and more than half a page, three if alone and less than half a page, two if photographed with one or more fellow executives, one if no photograph); the number of times the CEO was mentioned by name in company press releases divided by total press-release words in thousands; the number of first-person singular pronouns divided by the sum of first-person singular and plural pronouns in interview transcripts; the CEO's cash compensation divided by that of the second-highest-paid executive; and the CEO's non-cash compensation divided by that of the second-highest-paid executive. The correlations among the indicators were all positive and significant, the Cronbach alpha for the standardized values was .75, and a confirmatory factor analysis met recommended standards.
scale: index of standardized indicator values (Cronbach alpha .75)
time_window: averaged over the second and third years of each CEO's tenure (t + 1 and t + 2)

description: Absolute change (without regard to direction) between the prior year (t + n - 1) and the focal year (t + n) was calculated on four resource allocation indicators: advertising intensity (advertising/sales), research and development intensity (R&D/sales), selling, general, and administrative expenses/sales, and financial leverage (debt/equity). Each dimension was standardized over all observations (mean = 0; s.d. = 1), and the four standardized indicators were summed into a composite measure. The four indicators yielded a one-factor solution with an eigenvalue of 1.91 explaining 47.7 percent of the variance.
time_window: annual change from t + n - 1 to t + n

description: The extent to which a firm changed its portfolio of businesses from one year to the next, using four-digit SIC codes. The measure is the sum of all SICs added and dropped between the prior year (t + n - 1) and the focal year (t + n); for example, a company that added two new SICs and dropped one SIC would receive a score of three.
time_window: annual change from t + n - 1 to t + n

description: A simple count of the number of acquisitions made by the firm in each focal year (t + n), taken from the SDC merger and acquisitions database.
The ratio of the combined revenues of all acquisitions to the revenues of the acquiring firm, measured for each focal year (t + n) as a measure of the aggregate size of acquisitions.

Return on assets was calculated as net income divided by assets for each year (t + n). The industry average ROA was computed for each year, and the measure is the firm's absolute difference from the industry average; directionality was not considered because the authors were interested strictly in deviations from central performance tendencies in the industry.

Total shareholder returns were calculated as change in share price plus dividends divided by start-of-year share price for each year (t + n). The industry average TSR was computed for each year, and the measure is the firm's absolute difference from the industry average; directionality was not considered.

The absolute difference in the firm's return on assets between the prior year (t + n - 1) and the focal year (t + n). Directionality was not considered because the authors were interested strictly in the magnitude of the annual performance swing for each firm.
time_window: annual change from t + n - 1 to t + n

description: The absolute difference in the firm's total shareholder returns between the prior year (t + n - 1) and the focal year (t + n). Directionality was not considered because the authors were interested strictly in the magnitude of the annual performance swing for each firm.
time_window: annual change from t + n - 1 to t + n

description: CAR sums the daily abnormal returns for a 26-day window around the protest event, comprising the twenty days prior to the protest (day -20) and the five days following it (day +5). The daily abnormal return is the difference between the actual daily stock price return and the expected return, with the coefficients of the expected return equation estimated over a 239-day period prior to the beginning of the event window and the market return taken as the equally weighted daily return for all firms in the CRSP index. A negative CAR indicates that the firm exhibited returns below what would be expected based on past performance.
scale: percentage change in stock price relative to expected return
time_window: 26-day window (day -20 to day +5) around the protest

description: Total number of people involved in the protest divided by 1,000. Information on this variable came from the New York Times articles used to generate the protest event data set.

variable_name: number of social movement organizations sponsoring the protest
description: The number of social movement organizations that were recorded as sponsoring a protest. Information on this variable came from the New York Times articles used to generate the protest event data set.

variable_name: labor and consumer issue dummy variables
description: Two dummy variables that equal 1 if labor or consumer issues were mentioned during the protest itself and 0 otherwise. These protests did not include labor strikes or other union-sponsored events; they were generated by activists in the social movement sector sympathetic with labor causes but not union-driven.
A dummy variable indicating whether the protest was associated with a consumer boycott. In the data set, 7 percent of the protests were coupled with a consumer boycott.

A dummy variable indicating whether the protest targeted an institutionalized organizational program, policy, or practice, such as hiring policies or investment practices. Issues not considered institutionalized features of the organization include decisions like changing a pricing scheme or releasing a new product.

The number of paragraphs in the New York Times article dealing with the protest event. All protest events in the data set had sufficiently high media salience to have been covered by a national newspaper, so the measure captures variation in the extent to which the media focused on a given event.
The number of articles in the New York Times citing the target firm in the year preceding the protest event window.
time_window: one year preceding the protest event window

description: Cash flow is a firm's operating income plus depreciation value divided by the firm's common shares. This measure is then adjusted for the industry mean cash flow for that given year (cash flow minus mean industry cash flow). Cash flow is used as an indicator of performance because research shows that cash flow is often managed by firms to create the outward appearance of elevated financial performance, and it captures the extent to which firms have excess resources with which to absorb potential costs.

variable_name: Protest event (New York Times protest event data set)
description: Each protest event targeting a publicly traded U.S. corporation was drawn from content-coded New York Times articles (1962-1990) as part of a larger protest event data set. Only public events involving more than one person were kept, giving 342 events, and the event date anchors the stock return window.

Coded 0 in each month a firm remained alive and 1 in the month the firm died. Firms were assumed to enter the industry as of the release date of their first film and to die as of the release date of their last film. Monthly spells were used; for the small number of films with a release year but no month, months were assigned by working through the alphabetical listing within each year, forward in even-numbered years and backward in odd-numbered years. The longest period between films of any firm was 24 months, so films were collected through 1922 to limit right-censoring.

Dummy coded zero for all firms during months prior to January 1909 and after October 1915. It was coded 1 for firms that were alive and MPPC members only during the months of effective market control (January 1909 to October 1915). A negative, significant value of the coefficient was interpreted as support for H1.

The total number of short films produced by the MPPC during the preceding twelve months divided by the total number of short films produced by all firms in the population during the same twelve months. It was coded zero in months outside the period of MPPC market control. A positive, significant value of the coefficient was interpreted as support for H2.

Coded zero outside of the period of MPPC market control. During the period of market control it equals the cumulative count, as of the previous month, of the number of lawsuits brought by the MPPC against any other firms. Federal lawsuits were collected using Lexis-Nexis. A positive coefficient on this variable was interpreted as support for H3.
time_window: cumulative as of the previous month, within January 1909-October 1915

description: Set to zero outside of the period of MPPC market control and equal to the cumulative count, as of the previous month, of the number of lawsuits in which the MPPC was named as defendant during the period of market control. A negative coefficient on this variable was interpreted as support for H4.
time_window: cumulative as of the previous month, within January 1909-October 1915

description: Equal to zero in months when the MPPC did not have market control; during the period of market control it equals the cumulative difference in the occurrence of trust framing and patent framing as of the end of the previous month. Counts were updated in each month when an article appeared and were taken from the 35 New York Times articles, published between January 1909 and October 1915, in which MPPC activities were the primary focus. Two readers achieved 100 percent agreement in independently counting the occurrence of the words in five randomly chosen articles, and in classifying injunctions as for or against the MPPC. Initial values start out negative, indicating predominance of the patent framing, but by mid-1913 trust framing words come to predominate and the variable becomes positive; because larger values are associated with greater frequency of trust framing, a negative result for this variable supports H5.
time_window: cumulative as of the end of the previous month, within January 1909-October 1915

description: Equals the number of feature-length films made in each month by each firm. Because this is a count variable, both Poisson and negative binomial specifications were estimated; the results indicated that the dependent variable was more dispersed than would be true for the Poisson specification, so the negative binomial specification was used.
Coded one for MPPC firms from January 1911, the first month in this analysis, until October 1915, and zero otherwise. A significant, negative effect indicates support for H6.

The hazard that a VC firm terminates investment in a venture at time t. A VC-venture investment relationship was coded as terminated if the VC firm did not appear in any of the subsequent investment rounds or if the focal round was also the final round of financing for the venture; in the former case the event was assumed to occur at the earliest round date at which the VC no longer appeared as an investor, and in the latter 482 days after the final round of financing.

The hazard of a successful exit for a venture at time t, with IPOs and acquisitions considered successful exit events. The time variable measures the time in days from a venture's founding date until the IPO or acquisition date, and ventures that did not achieve a successful exit event by December 2004 were considered unsuccessful and at risk for termination.

The number of rounds of financing a venture received from each VC firm, entered also in squared form and centered by subtracting the respective means. Two or more consecutive rounds listed within a 90-day period were aggregated and treated as a single round.

The number of all VC professionals employed in the firm, counting managing partners, general partners, senior principals, principals, associates, and managing directors, used as a proxy for the extent of intraorganizational politics. The measure is time-varying and was compiled for the years 1989, 1994, 1999, and 2003.

The total number of VC firms that had invested in the venture as of the focal round, used as a proxy for co-investor pressure. It is a time-varying, cumulative count of VC investors that participated in prior financing rounds or the focal round.

A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if the VC is in the top 5 percent of Bonacich's eigenvector centrality measure in the co-investment network. The centrality score was calculated for each year using co-investment matrices from the three most recent years and ranges between zero (for isolated firms with no contacts) and one (for firms that syndicate with other central actors).

The difference between the focal round year and the fund vintage year, where VentureXpert defines fund vintage year as the year of fund formation and first takedown of capital or the year the fund made its first investment into a portfolio company. If a firm invested in the venture through multiple funds, the age of the oldest fund, which is closest to liquidation, was used.

variable_name: adoption of a direct voting system
description: Dependent variable coded 1 if a given university replaced the appointment system with a direct voting system in a particular year of presidential selection, and 0 otherwise. Because presidential selections are held every four years, only presidential selection years were included in the event risk-set, so a university founded before 1985 made a decision a maximum of four or five times during the study period. The data covered all 192 universities in Korea and totaled 649 observations; 80 universities replaced their appointment system with a direct voting system.

Measures whether political opportunities for change were created in a university in terms of the agency power structure after political democratization. If a university was a public one, it was coded as 1, and otherwise as 0. A public university was audited and supervised by the Ministry of Education without a board of trustees, and since democratization the government has not directly governed public universities, so they lost a powerful incumbent who would otherwise champion the traditional appointment system.

Measured by the presence or absence of a faculty council that could promote the establishment of a direct voting system. If a university had a faculty council in a particular year of presidential selection, it was coded as 1, and otherwise as 0. The faculty council is not part of the formal university structure but a voluntary association or social movement organization founded through long, painstaking processes.

Coded 1 if challengers in a university employed conflict tactics such as open confrontations like picketing, demonstrations, sit-ins, strikes, street rallies and marches, boycotts, public protests, and physical clashes in the presidential selection years, and 0 otherwise. Information was gathered through content analyses of three major and six minor nationwide daily newspapers; through the extensive search, 27 universities were found to have experienced such conflicts.

The total number of universities that had adopted a direct voting system since 1985 as of the previous year. Field-level institutional dynamics were measured in two ways: this cumulative count and the number of universities that adopted direct voting systems in the previous year.

Facilities were classified into those using green fuels and those using brown fuels. Following the U.S. Department of Energy and industry analysts, green fuel types are biomass/biogas, geothermal, small hydro, solar, and wind; the remaining fuel types—fuel oil, natural gas, coal, waste natural gas, nuclear, other waste, and 'other'—are brown. There were cogenerators and small power producers in both categories.

variable_name: founding event indicator (green or brown technology)
description: One observation was created for every founding event of the focal type, meaning green- or brown-technology founding. The start date of each event was the day on which the previous founding event of the same technology type occurred; the end date was the day on which the focal founding event occurred. Two dependent variables were coded as one whenever the focal type of firm (using green or brown technology) was founded, and zero otherwise.

Calculated as the heterogeneity of foundings in California and New York every six months between January 1, 1980, and December 31, 1992, using an index where P_it is the proportion of all foundings in a focal state during the six-month period t with form i (Blau, 1977). The index measures the probability that randomly sampled pairs of firms being founded in any given period will have different forms. The minimum value is zero when all foundings in a period are of a single form, and the index approaches one as more forms are founded.

Average avoided costs paid by utilities during each six-month period, gathered from the California Public Utility Commission and the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority. In California, regulators generally calculated avoided costs for each utility as a function of fuel prices and construction costs for new plants; in New York, regulators set avoided costs at the same level for all utilities in the state. The variable was lagged six months.
Coded one when the federal government offered a 10-percent investment tax credit for all qualifying facilities from 1978 to 1985, and zero otherwise. It was lagged six months.
Set to one after the May 16, 1983 Supreme Court decision upholding PURPA's mandatory-interconnection and avoided-cost provisions, and zero before. It was lagged six months.

Measured as the number of facilities that had contracts with utilities in a focal state, based on records of all power sold on the wholesale market by independent power producers. A squared term for sector density was also created to capture possible competitive effects.

Count of positive and neutral articles on the independent-power sector in three major newspapers (Wall Street Journal, New York Times, Washington Post) and three business-oriented journals (Economist, Business Week, Newsweek). Purely negative articles were rare and excluded from the analysis. The variable was lagged six months.

Dummy variables set equal to one a year after association founding and zero before that date, for the Independent Energy Producers Association of California (IEPA, founded May 15, 1982) and the Independent Power Producers of New York (IPPNY, founded June 17, 1986).

The number of nonlocal ties formed in a given year divided by the number of new ties formed in the same year. A syndicate tie was defined as nonlocal when, in all prior observation years, the focal bank was separated from the partner by a path length greater than two. Because the variance of a proportion depends on its value, the proportions were normalized using the arcsine-root transformation.

Spline variable for the failure range, equal to the bank's relative historical performance (the performance metric at t minus its historical aspiration at t) for observations in which that value is less than zero and zero otherwise; for ease of interpretation it was reverse coded so its values were positive. Historical aspirations were computed as a weighted moving average of experienced performance, with the reported models using an updating parameter of a = .5. It was computed for two performance metrics, market share and network status, and lagged one year for model estimation.
time_window: t, lagged one year for model estimation

description: Spline variable for the success range, equal to the bank's relative historical performance for observations in which that value is greater than zero and zero otherwise. Historical aspirations were computed as a weighted moving average of experienced performance, with the reported models using a = .5. It was computed for two performance metrics, market share and network status, and lagged one year for model estimation.
time_window: t, lagged one year for model estimation

description: Spline variable equal to the bank's relative social performance (the performance metric at t minus its social aspiration at t) for observations in which that value is less than zero and zero otherwise; for ease of interpretation it was reverse coded so its values were positive. Social aspirations were based on the current performance of other banks in the network; the reported models weighted the peer group by size similarity. It was computed for market share and network status and lagged one year.
time_window: t, lagged one year for model estimation

description: Spline variable equal to the bank's relative social performance for observations in which that value is greater than zero and zero otherwise. Social aspirations were based on the current performance of other banks in the network; the reported models weighted the peer group by size similarity. It was computed for market share and network status and lagged one year.
time_window: t, lagged one year for model estimation

description: Measured for a given year using the inflation-adjusted dollar value of the syndicates in which the bank participated in that year. Based on norms identified in interviews with bank managers, 50 percent of the underwriting value was allocated to the lead bank and the remaining value was split equally among the co-lead banks. Three alternative specifications were computed and, because the average correlation among them was 0.98, the 50-50 specification was used.

Bonacich's (1987) eigenvector centrality computed on the symmetric syndicate tie network for each four-year moving period and assigned to the final year of the period (e.g., the 1952-1955 network for 1955). The measure was normalized by dividing it by the maximum difference in each four-year network to facilitate comparisons over time.

A discounted cumulative count of the products that were internally selected out of the firm's portfolio over the years of its life, lagged by one year so that it was not confounded with selection events at time t. Each year's selection count is multiplied by a discount weight that depreciates the value of selection events across time, and because some firms had no selection events in their first few years, 1 was added to the event summation before logging it. In the selection models goodness of fit was best using a discount value of 0.9.
time_window: cumulative over firm life, lagged one year

description: A measure coded in the same way as cumulative internal selection: a discounted, lagged cumulative count of the products the environment selected out of the firm's portfolio while the firm survived, with the event summation logged after adding 1. The same discount weight of 0.9 was used in the selection models.
time_window: cumulative over firm life, lagged one year

description: An internal selection event was designated in year t if a product's sales were zero in year t+1, the firm survived, and the product's sales had not declined by at least 50 percent from their rolling historical peak. Products that survived only one year could not show a sales decline, so the average first-year sales of all new products introduced in the same year was calculated and an internal event was coded if the product survived one year and exceeded that average. Internal selection events were mutually exclusive competing events, right-censored whenever another event type occurred or the product had positive sales in the final year of observation.
time_window: annual, year t with outcome in t+1

description: A partial external selection event was coded in year t if the firm survived but the annual sales of the focal product were zero in year t+1 and that product's sales in year t had declined at least 50 percent from their rolling historical peak. For products that survived only one year, a partial external selection event was coded if first-year sales were below the average first-year sales of all new products introduced in the same year. The variable was right-censored when another type of event occurred and in the final year of observation.
time_window: annual, year t with outcome in t+1

description: A full external selection event was coded when a focal product's host firm died, thus eliminating its entire portfolio; that happened in year t if each of a firm's products had zero sales in year t+1. It was modeled as a competing event alongside internal and partial external selection. There were 1,289 full external selection events in the product-year analyses.
time_window: annual, year t with outcome in t+1

description: To buttress the product-level analyses of full external selection, the authors used Cox models to assess organizational failure rates; because failures are not repeated events, those models did not contain fixed effects. The firm-year failure analyses contain 576 failure events, and the model drops product size and product age while still controlling for firm size and the average age of the products in the portfolio.

The number of new product introductions was the dependent variable in testing hypotheses 5a and 5b, obtained for each firm in each year using the product introduction dates in the IDC data. The one-year lag of that count was also included to help control for unobserved heterogeneity across firms. The counts were modeled with negative binomial models that account for overdispersion, a first-order autoregressive process, and robust variance estimates.
time_window: firm-year, with a one-year lagged count also included

variable_name: occurrence of exit of marketing managers
description: Exit events were coded as occurring in year t when a manager was listed as an employee of a firm in year t but was not listed as an employee of the same firm in year t+1. Exchange managers in client firms were identified from job titles in the Marketing functional category (jobs with responsibilities for marketing, sales, brand management, and advertising). The main models use the occurrence of exit events, aggregated to the firm-year and lagged one year.

variable_name: occurrence of exit of agency exchange managers
description: Exit events were coded as occurring in year t when a manager was listed as an employee of a firm in year t but was not listed as an employee of the same firm in year t+1. Exchange managers in agencies were identified from job titles in three functional roles: account services, creative, and other boundary spanners. Because functional roles in agencies are highly differentiated, mobility was analyzed separately for each functional category; the main models use the occurrence of exit events aggregated to the firm-year and lagged one year.

variable_name: occurrence of promotion of marketing managers
description: Promotion events were coded as occurring in year t when managers were observed at a specific job level in year t but at a hierarchically higher job level in year t+1 (e.g., vice president in year t and senior vice president in year t+1). Job levels are well defined in these firms, making identification of promotion straightforward. Client exchange managers were identified by the Marketing functional category; the main models use the occurrence of promotion events aggregated to the firm-year and lagged one year.

variable_name: occurrence of promotion of agency exchange managers
description: Promotion events were coded as occurring in year t when managers were observed at a specific job level in year t but at a hierarchically higher job level in year t+1. Agency exchange managers were identified in the account services, creative, and other boundary-spanning functional roles, and mobility was analyzed separately for each functional category. The main models use the occurrence of promotion events aggregated to the firm-year and lagged one year.

Size was measured as the annual gross revenue for clients in the focal year. A log transformation was used before entering size into the analyses because the variable is highly skewed. Both first- and second-order effects were included to account for the possibility that the effects of bureaucratization and decentralized decision making vary non-monotonically over the full range of firm size.

Size was measured as the annual gross revenue for agencies in the focal year. A log transformation was used before entering size into the analyses because the variable is highly skewed. Both first- and second-order effects were included.

The number of market ties was determined from the Advertiser Red Book as the number of agencies used by clients each year. It was entered as a moderator of the mobility effects and also controlled for as an alternative explanation for dissolution.

The number of market ties was determined from the Agency Red Book as the number of clients listed by agencies each year. It was entered as a moderator of the mobility effects and also controlled for as an alternative explanation for dissolution.

variable_name: dissolution of client-agency market ties (client firms)
description: Dissolution was defined as a market tie that exists in year t but not in year t+1 and was recorded as occurring in calendar year t when the name of an exchange partner appeared in the directory in year t but not in year t+1. Dissolution was defined conservatively as completely severed ties, excluding decreases in tie strength such as losing one account of a multi-account relationship. The data were aggregated to the firm level and recorded for each year; because the client firm data fit a binary distribution (89 percent of the observations were either 0 or 1), logistic regression was used to estimate the likelihood of any dissolutions occurring per client firm per year.

Dissolution was defined as a market tie that exists in year t but not in year t+1 and was recorded as occurring in calendar year t when the name of an exchange partner appeared in the directory in year t but not in year t+1. Dissolution was defined conservatively as completely severed ties. The data were aggregated to the firm level; because market tie dissolution is such a frequent event for agencies, the data fit a Poisson distribution and Poisson regression was used to estimate counts of dissolution events per agency per year, with tests and corrections for overdispersion.

A yearly proportion of the adherents of Catholicism, Protestantism, Orthodox Christianity, Judaism (for the 1976-2000 years), and Islam (for 1976-2000) in an MSA. The number of adherents of these denominations was summed across all counties in the MSA and divided by the total population of the MSA. The variable was updated annually and lagged by one year.

A yearly proportion of the adherents of LDS, Buddhism, Hinduism, Judaism (for 2001-2004), and Islam (for 2001-2004) in an MSA. Built by dividing the number of adherents of these denominations in an MSA by the total population in that MSA, updated annually and lagged by one year.

The STATA command geonear was used to identify the nearest neighbors using geodetic distances, and all MSAs that bordered a focal MSA were coded as neighbors. For each focal MSA, the number of neighboring MSAs whose proportion of religious adherents opposed to biotherapeutics was greater than the focal MSA's by at least 15 percent was summed and then divided by the total number of neighboring MSAs.

Counts the number of identified newspaper pages for a given MSA each year, based on a search of over 26,000 local and national newspapers archived on Newspapers.com for pages that included at least one word/bigram from each of three lists covering social movement events, biotherapeutics, and religious denominations; the social movement and biotherapeutics words had to occur in the same sentence. The search identified 3,281 newspaper pages, and the variable ranges from 0 to 41 newspaper pages per MSA-year.
The U.S. dollar amount invested by venture capitalists in the biotherapeutics firms in an MSA each year, obtained from the Venture Expert database. The variable was logged to adjust for skewness.
The U.S. dollar amount of grants given by the National Institutes of Health to firms and research organizations in an MSA each year. The variable was logged to adjust for skewness.

A time-invariant variable measuring an MSA's number of universities with biotechnology-relevant graduate programs (biochemistry, cellular/molecular biology, and microbiology) with scholarly quality reputation rankings of 4.0 or higher in the 1982 National Research Council Survey.

Constructed by counting the number of all biotherapeutics firms that entered a particular MSA each year. A firm was identified as having entered the biotherapeutics industry in a region when a new firm was founded in a region to develop biotherapeutics products; an established firm entered the biotherapeutics industry in an MSA by creating a new division, subsidiary, or joint venture, or through the acquisition of or merger with an existing biotherapeutics firm; or an established biotherapeutics firm relocated from one MSA to another.

Quality of nursing care was assessed with the Rush-Medicus Nursing Process Monitoring Methodology, which evaluates nursing processes including assessment, planning, intervention, and evaluation of patient care. The instrument contains 365 questions drawing data from patient records and from interviews with both patients and nurses, with a subset of 8 to 41 questions used for any particular patient. Two pairs of trained registered nurses collected data on 340 patients in the 27 subunits at different times of day and days of the week. Subunit quality scores can range from 0 to 100; in this study scores ranged from 66.16 to 90.66.

Technology was measured with the 21-item instrument developed by Leatt and Schneck (1981), each question using a 5-point scale with 1 for routine and 5 for nonroutine, to solicit respondents' opinions about task behavior. Subunit scores were created for the three technology scales by calculating the mean responses of nursing personnel within each subunit. The reliability of the uncertainty scale in this study was .62.

Technology was measured with the 21-item instrument developed by Leatt and Schneck (1981), each question using a 5-point scale with 1 for routine and 5 for nonroutine, to solicit respondents' opinions about task behavior. Subunit scores were created by calculating the mean responses of nursing personnel within each subunit. The reliability of the instability scale in this study was .86.

Technology was measured with the 21-item instrument developed by Leatt and Schneck (1981), each question using a 5-point scale with 1 for routine and 5 for nonroutine, to solicit respondents' opinions about task behavior. Subunit scores were created by calculating the mean responses of nursing personnel within each subunit. The reliability of the variability scale in this study was .77.

Structure was measured with an instrument developed by Leifer and Huber (1977) on the basis of Duncan's (1971) findings and adapted to the nursing context; 12 items loaded significantly on three factors, each item using a 5-point Likert scale. Items that were reverse-scored in the analysis are indicated with an (R), and the scoring was such that 1 = mechanistic structure and 5 = organic structure. Subunit scores were created by calculating the mean responses of nursing personnel within each subunit; the reliability of the vertical participation scale in this study was .74.

Structure was measured with an instrument developed by Leifer and Huber (1977) and adapted to the nursing context; 12 items loaded significantly on three factors, each item using a 5-point Likert scale. Items that were reverse-scored in the analysis are indicated with an (R), and the scoring was such that 1 = mechanistic structure and 5 = organic structure. Subunit scores were created by calculating the mean responses of nursing personnel within each subunit; the reliability of the horizontal participation scale in this study was .63.

Structure was measured with an instrument developed by Leifer and Huber (1977) and adapted to the nursing context; 12 items loaded significantly on three factors, each item using a 5-point Likert scale. Items that were reverse-scored in the analysis are indicated with an (R), and the scoring was such that 1 = mechanistic structure and 5 = organic structure. Subunit scores were created by calculating the mean responses of nursing personnel within each subunit; the reliability of the formalization scale in this study was .61.

variable_name: fit between instability and vertical participation
description: Fit is the absolute difference between the values for technology and structure, computed as the absolute difference between the subunit instability score and the subunit vertical participation score. Technology variables were scaled so that low numbers represented routine technologies and structure variables were scaled so that low numbers represented mechanistic structures. Using the Cohen and Cohen formula for reliability of difference scores, reliability coefficients of .66, .72, and .67 were found for the three fit variables in this study.

variable_name: fit between variability and horizontal participation
description: Fit is the absolute difference between the values for technology and structure, computed as the absolute difference between the subunit variability score and the subunit horizontal participation score. Technology variables were scaled so that low numbers represented routine technologies and structure variables were scaled so that low numbers represented mechanistic structures. Using the Cohen and Cohen formula for reliability of difference scores, reliability coefficients of .66, .72, and .67 were found for the three fit variables in this study.

Fit is the absolute difference between the values for technology and structure, computed as the absolute difference between the subunit uncertainty score and the subunit formalization score. Technology variables were scaled so that low numbers represented routine technologies and structure variables were scaled so that low numbers represented mechanistic structures. Using the Cohen and Cohen formula for reliability of difference scores, reliability coefficients of .66, .72, and .67 were found for the three fit variables in this study.

Four task difficulty items followed Perrow's (1967) concept of analyzability (e.g., the extent to which individuals use standard methods). Items were measured on 7-point Likert scales and grouped by factor analysis with varimax rotation; selected items loaded at > .40 on one factor.

Two interunit interdependence items concern change in policies and procedures induced by other subunits, a concept that applies to both B->A and A->B work flow sequences. An item measuring this concept's complement, change induced in other subunits, was omitted from the analysis. Items were measured on 7-point Likert scales and grouped by factor analysis with varimax rotation.

Four boundary-spanning activity items measured the frequency and time spent in interactions with members of other units. Items were measured on 7-point Likert scales and grouped by factor analysis with varimax rotation.

Frequency of participation was measured for each of four decisions on a scale ranging from almost always to almost never; two of the decisions were task-related and two concerned personnel. A fifth item concerned influence in changes in methods initiated by subordinates. Items were measured on 7-point Likert scales and grouped by factor analysis with varimax rotation.
scale: 7-point Likert; almost always to almost never

description: Autonomy was a composite of two items reflecting independence of action generally and two items referring to independence in handling nonroutine decisions; two of these specifically referred to independence from supervisors or specialists in making decisions. Items were measured on 7-point Likert scales and grouped by factor analysis with varimax rotation.

Calculated as one minus the ratio of nonnuclear power generation to the total energy output of a utility for 1980; the index measures the percentage of a utility's total energy output provided by nuclear power and thus the utility's reliance on nuclear power to satisfy energy demand. Data on total energy output came from Federal Energy Regulatory Commission records.

The percentage of growth in earnings from 1975 to 1980, calculated by dividing 1975 earnings by the figure for 1980, using the standardized balance sheet and income statement that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission calculated for all nuclear utilities before 1981.

Ratio of total hours of operation to the total hours a plant could have operated if it had not experienced a forced shut-down. Raw data for 1981 were adjusted to eliminate hours of nonoperation due to outages for such reasons as scheduled maintenance, refueling, and retrofitting.

Count of violations at severity levels 1, 2, 3, and 4 for 1981, taken from computerized NRC files. The six severity categories were collapsed into major and minor categories to minimize possible misclassifications, and only 1981 data were used because the bases for some violations categories were adjusted after 1981.

Count of violations at severity levels 5 and 6 for 1981, taken from computerized NRC files. Minor violations included failures to follow administrative procedures and maintenance schedules and inadequate record keeping. The six severity categories were collapsed into major and minor categories to minimize possible misclassifications, and only 1981 data were used.

A search of case notes on the organizations in the data bank for five events that commonly occur when conflict has reached sufficient intensity to prejudice organizational performance: recent turnover attributable to internal politics or incompatibilities; apathy or fatalism about external threats attributable to excessive infighting; inability to reach consensus on how to implement needed strategic or operational changes; recent intervention by external entities attributable to internal inability to make or implement decisions; and the presence of easily identifiable opposing internal factions. Organizations in which at least one event was clearly present were classified as high conflict and those in which such events were clearly absent as low conflict; two additional raters independently reviewed the case studies and agreed except in the case of one low-conflict organization, which was dropped along with one randomly chosen high-conflict organization.

Managers from 19 of the 22 organizations provided their perceptions of conflict levels on a Likert scale of 1 to 6. These scores were significantly correlated with the number of events indicating disruptive conflict taken from the case studies.

Responses to the question asking the number of contacts with each other individual in an average week were entered as an adjacency matrix; groups were identified with CONCOR and the sociomatrix was divided into groups of ten or fewer individuals. Ties between groups involving contacts occurring six or more times in an average week were counted as external strong ties; totals and proportions of external ties that are strong were computed for the high- and low-conflict organizations.

Ties within CONCOR groups involving contacts occurring six or more times in an average week were counted as internal strong ties. The analysis compares the number and percentage of internal strong ties and the proportion of strong ties that are internal across the high- and low-conflict organizations.

CONCOR groupings were placed together in an adjacency matrix, and a density table was made by dividing the sum of contacts in each region by the number of possible relationships; values above and below the grand mean of the matrix were denominated as one and zero blocks, producing a blockmodel, or reduced-form image. Blockmodels of each organization were compared to identify recurring structural patterns in the high- and low-conflict organizations.

Dichotomous dependent variable, the probability that a company had resisted greenmail. Companies were classified as greenmail payers if between 1979 and 1983 they had privately repurchased 5 percent or more of their outstanding equity at a premium above the market price from a dissident stockholder who threatened management with a takeover or a proxy fight, and as resisters if they faced a comparable threat from one of eight notorious raiders but did not repurchase.

The value of the outside directors' common stock divided by their annual cash compensation for board membership, aggregated and averaged across each board's outside directors. Board compensation included annual retainers and the annual sum of fees for perfect attendance; the dollar value of equity was based on the company's stock price 30 days before a 13D filing.
time_window: the year in which a greenmail transaction was announced or the year following a raider's acquisition of stock as reported in a 13D report

variable_name: variation in outside directors' equity holdings
description: Heterogeneity of outside directors' equity holdings measured with Theil's index of dispersion, defined as T = 1/n sum (X_i/mu) log(X_i/mu), which Allison recommended when a variable has a diminishing marginal utility or when its utility or value is irrelevant to the analysis, as is the case for measures of income or social rewards.

Outside directors' tenure was defined as the total number of years a director had served on a board; the measure was aggregated and averaged across each board's outside directors. The quadratic function of this variable was included to test the curvilinear effect.

The level of heterogeneity in outside directors' tenure was calculated with the coefficient of variation-the standard deviation divided by the mean-which Allison recommended as the best direct scale-invariant measure of dispersion when a variable does not have a diminishing marginal utility.

Occupational variation was defined using the standard deviation of the eight job categories into which principal occupations were classified: executive, retired executive, lawyer, banker, consultant or certified public accountant, academic, professional director, or one of a mixed group of public jobs including work in politics, sports, religion, and show business.

The dollar value of stock and options owned by the company's top three executives divided by the combined amount of their annual salaries and cash bonuses. In testing the interaction effects, the ratio was represented by a dichotomous dummy variable set equal to 1 if the ratio was below the median value of the variable's frequency distribution and to 0 for values above the median.

The numbers of diagnostic categories and intervention roles indicated by each worker were taken as a percentage of the total number on a list in the item. The two scores were summed to get an individual's scope of service score, individuals' scores were averaged to obtain organizations' scores, and organizational units were then aggregated to the interorganizational system level.
level: individual, aggregated to organization and then to interorganizational system

description: Responses to the first questionnaire item on intensity of service were averaged to the organization level and organizational units were then aggregated to the interorganizational system level. The text reports no further item wording or formula for this measure.
level: individual, aggregated to organization and then to interorganizational system

description: Responses to the first questionnaire item on clients' volitional status were averaged to the organization level and organizational units were then aggregated to the interorganizational system level; in the results the variable is described as the percentage of involuntary clients in a system. The text reports no further item wording or formula for this measure.
level: individual, aggregated to organization and then to interorganizational system

description: Three percentages for three types of task integration were averaged to the organizational level, with three types of client flow weighted as follows: sequential = .75, reciprocal = 1.5, and collective = 3; the three weighted scores were then summed to obtain the task integration score for each organization, and organizational units were aggregated to the interorganizational system level.

The variable was computed by taking each organization's administrator's response for each of three methods (if there was more than one administrator, their scores were averaged); each of the three scores was weighted, with impersonal = 0, personal = 1.5, and group = 3, and the weighted scores were summed to obtain an administrative coordination score for each organization, with organizational units then aggregated to the interorganizational system level.

Conflict is one of the nine concepts measured by the two questionnaires and was measured with the second questionnaire administered to employees of member organizations at staff meetings, with individual-level data aggregated by averaging across individuals and then across organizational units to the system level. The text reports no item wording or formula for this measure; the Appendix, from which the method for each measure is reported and which is partly garbled in the text, gives the particular method used.
level: individual, aggregated to organization and then to interorganizational system

description: Symmetrical type matrixes were created from data on the number of clients referred and accepted by each organization serving each client type, obtained in the initial survey of organizations. The MacKenzie algorithm was then used to compute a centralization index representing the degree to which a core agency dominated a system, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0.

The index is the ratio of the number of organizations within a system performing a single function to the number of organizations in the system performing multiple functions, derived from data obtained in the initial survey of organizations.
The score is the average number of different services provided by each organization in a system, derived from data obtained in the initial survey of organizations.

A case was defined as a company that had dissolved its relationship with its independent auditor and had therefore employed a new audit firm; a control was a company that had retained its auditor. Dissolution was defined as a change in the identity of the client's auditor, except when the change was associated with the incumbent auditor's merger or acquisition, the incumbent auditor's cessation of practice, or a merger of the client firm. Cases were identified using corporate annual reports, 10-K statements, Moody's manuals, the Standard and Poor's register, and Who Audits America. A set of 170 controls was frequency matched to the 170 cases on the year of the switch and on company size, yielding a study group of 170 switchers and 170 nonswitchers.

variable_name: change in the ratio of receivables to assets
description: The ratio of receivables to total assets, one of the measures of difficult-to-audit assets, was computed for the year of the event (t) and the preceding year (t-1). The measure is the absolute value of the difference between the two ratios, because either increases or decreases in resource requirements can affect the likelihood of switching. Data came from annual reports, 10-K statements, and COMPUSTAT.

variable_name: change in the ratio of inventories to assets
description: The ratio of inventories to total assets was computed for the year of the event (t) and the preceding year (t-1). The measure is the absolute value of the difference between the two ratios, since either increases or decreases in resource requirements can affect the likelihood of switching. Data came from annual reports, 10-K statements, and COMPUSTAT.

variable_name: change in the ratio of foreign assets to total assets
description: The ratio of foreign to total assets was computed for the year of the event (t) and the preceding year (t-1). The measure is the absolute value of the difference between the two ratios, because either increases or decreases in resource requirements can affect the likelihood of switching. Data came from annual reports, 10-K statements, and COMPUSTAT.

An auditor's industry-specific revenues were estimated by summing the square root of the assets of the auditor's clients in a given two-digit SIC industry; market share is the ratio of the revenue earned by a firm to total revenues of all auditors in that industry. Change in resource provisions was operationally defined as the absolute value of the percentage change in market share from t-2 to t-1, a window chosen to ensure that shifts in market share did not result from the dissolution events under investigation. The absolute value was used because either increases or decreases in resource provisions are argued to affect the likelihood of dissolution.

All auditors operating in a client's industry constitute its set of alternatives, so industry concentration statistics measure the audit market, an increase in concentration implying a decrease in the set of available alternatives. The Herfindahl statistic was calculated by squaring each auditor's market share in a given industry and summing over all audit firms active in the industry, with industries classified by two-digit SIC codes. Change is measured as the absolute value of the change in the index from t-2 to t-1, because both increases and decreases in the alternative set are argued to increase the probability of dissolution.

variable_name: tenure of the chief executive officer
description: The number of years that the chief executive officer had served in any of the boundary-spanning positions since the beginning of the auditor-client relationship. A separate variable was used to represent the attachment associated with each critical boundary-spanning position, and these officers' tenures were used as specific measures of individual attachment.
time_window: since formation of the auditor-client relationship

variable_name: tenure of the chief financial officer
description: The number of years that the chief financial officer had served in any of the boundary-spanning positions (chief executive, financial, or accounting officer) since the beginning of the auditor-client relationship. A separate variable was used to represent the attachment associated with each critical boundary-spanning position.
time_window: since formation of the auditor-client relationship

variable_name: tenure of the chief accounting officer
description: The number of years that the chief accounting officer had served in any of the boundary-spanning positions since the beginning of the auditor-client relationship. A separate variable was used to represent the attachment associated with each critical boundary-spanning position.
time_window: since formation of the auditor-client relationship

variable_name: average tenure of the members of the audit committee or board
description: The average number of years that members of a firm's audit committee (or the board as a whole if no audit committee existed) had served on the board of directors since the beginning of the auditor-client relationship. The members of the audit committee of a firm's board of directors are among the boundary spanners critical to auditor-client relationships.
time_window: since formation of the auditor-client relationship

description: The number of consecutive years that an incumbent auditor had provided an independent assessment of a client's financial statements. The measure follows from the cumulative feature of attachments: structural attachment is likely to increase with the duration of a relationship. Data sources were annual reports, proxy statements, and Moody's Manuals.

variable_name: Change in resource fit variables (set of seven absolute change measures)
description: Change in resource fit was measured as a set of absolute year-to-year changes in its components: client resource requirements (ratios of receivables, inventories and foreign assets to total assets), auditor resource provisions (auditor's industry market share), and the client's set of alternatives (industry Herfindahl concentration). The set was tested jointly and individually against auditor switching.

A regression of daily stock returns against the return on a market index is used to predict normal returns for a period of 30 days before and 30 days after the Wall Street Journal announcement. The difference between actual and normal returns is the prediction error, which is averaged across firms on each day and accumulated over intervals to give mean cumulative prediction errors. Dodd and Warner's (1983) z statistic is used to test whether MCPEs differ from zero. Intervals reported are days -30 to -2, days -1 to 0, days -5 to +5, and days +1 to +30.
time_window: 30 trading days before to 30 days after the announcement; announcement period days -1 to 0

variable_name: type of firing announcement (presence of permanent replacement information)
description: Each firing announcement was read and classified according to whether information about a permanent replacement was given. Some firings were announced simultaneously with a permanent replacement, some with a temporary replacement, some with no replacement information followed later by a successor announcement, and some as departures only.
time_window: announcement date (subsequent appointments occurred on average 111.5 calendar days after the firing announcements in the original population)

description: Replacement announcements were classified as naming an insider or an outsider, with outsiders defined as having had no previous employment with the company or any of its subsidiaries. Counts of insider and outsider appointments accompanying firings were compared with those for 282 other appointment announcements.
time_window: announcement of the replacement (concurrent with or subsequent to the firing)

description: Companies were assigned to one of three groups: target companies challenged by a raider, their size-matched competitors, and a size-matched control group. The factor was coded as target (1), competitor (2), or size-matched control (3). Turnover was referenced against the cohort of officers and directors incumbent at the time of a given 13D filing and against a similar cohort incumbent five years before the filing.

Each company's monthly market-adjusted return was computed as the simple excess return compared with the value-weighted market index for that month from the CRSP data base; cumulative abnormal returns were formed by summing the relevant abnormal monthly returns for intervals of one year and two, three, four, and five years prior to the 13D filing and five years prior to the filing. For the factorial design these measures were recoded into a dichotomous variable by comparing a company's cumulative abnormal returns with the market average. The reported analyses use the two-year cumulative performance measure.
time_window: one to five years prior to (and five years prior to) the 13D filing

description: Annual turnover rates were established for officers, the top executives without positions on their employer's board, including chairpersons, chief executive officers, presidents, executive vice presidents, senior vice presidents, and treasurers. Annual turnover was computed as the difference between consecutive cumulative turnover rates and expressed as a percentage of the turnover within the total group of officers and directors.
time_window: five years before to five years after the raider's 13D filing (T-5 to T+5)

variable_name: annual turnover rate for inside and outside directors
description: Annual turnover rates were established for inside directors, top executives with board positions, and outside directors, board members without executive positions in the company on whose board they sat. Turnover data were obtained by tracking top management and board composition, and annual turnover was computed as the difference between consecutive cumulative turnover rates, expressed as a percentage of the turnover within the total group of officers and directors.
time_window: five years before to five years after the raider's 13D filing (T-5 to T+5)

description: Heterogeneity of a top management team was calculated with the coefficient of variation, a measure of dispersion for interval-scaled data calculated by dividing the standard deviation by the mean for a group. Age data for all 220 managers were taken from 1980 registry data and aggregated within each top management team.

Heterogeneity of a top management team was calculated with the coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean for the group. Organizational tenure data for all 220 managers came from 1980 registry data.

Heterogeneity of a top management team was calculated with the coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean for the group. Executive committee tenure data for all 220 managers came from 1980 registry data.

University prestige was determined by classifying universities into one of ten ranks based on rates of acceptance as listed in the nationwide rankings of universities. Team heterogeneity was then calculated with the coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean for the group.

At the individual level a distance measure, or measure of isolation, was used to capture the degree of membership in a cohort. An individual's distance score directly reflects the absolute distance of that person from every other individual in a group.

At the individual level a distance measure, or measure of isolation, was used to capture the degree of membership in a cohort. An individual's distance score directly reflects the absolute distance of that person from every other individual in a group.

At the individual level a distance measure, or measure of isolation, was used to capture the degree of membership in a cohort. An individual's distance score directly reflects the absolute distance of that person from every other individual in a group.

At the individual level a distance measure, or measure of isolation, was used to capture the degree of membership in a cohort. An individual's distance score directly reflects the absolute distance of that person from every other individual in a group.

At the organizational level, turnover represents the proportion of the top management team in 1980 that were no longer with the organization in 1983. A second measure, turnovers under age 65, represents the proportion of the top management team in 1980 that were no longer with the organization in 1983 and were less than 65 years of age in 1983.

At the individual level, turnover is a dichotomous variable, coded 0 if no turnover occurred, and 1 if turnover occurred, for the period 1980 to 1983. Turnover under age 65 represents a second measure of turnover for individuals less than 65 years of age in 1983.

A dichotomous variable coded 1 for all firms for the year of a technological discontinuity (1960 or 1972) and for each of the four years following, and 0 for all other years. Two technological discontinuities were identified: the introduction of computerized long kilns in 1960 and the introduction of suspension preheating in 1972. The four-year window allows for the non-immediate diffusion of these technologies.
time_window: year of discontinuity plus four following years

description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 for the year of a regulatory event and for a two-year adjustment period, and 0 otherwise. Three regulatory events were identified: base-point pricing ruled illegal in 1947, the Federal Highway Act in 1956, and the Federal Trade Commission ruling that cement firms could not own concrete interests in 1967. The adjustment period was made shorter for regulatory jolts than for technological discontinuities.
time_window: year of jolt plus two following years

description: Coded to reflect a reorientation in either a previous or current year, so as to test the effect of reorientations in time t-1 or t on team change in time t. A reorientation was defined as having occurred when both strategy (adding cement types and brands, adding cement plants or distribution centers) and structure (divisionalizing, adding functions, adding or consolidating senior positions) changed over no more than two years.
