The variable was built from firm-level historical data coded by three independent coders.

Coded 1 if a CEO left in a current or previous year and 0 otherwise. When there was no CEO title listed for the team, CEO succession was coded 1 if the chairperson of the board left the firm; if there was no CEO and no chairperson, it was coded 1 if the president left. The measure thus reflects succession of the highest-ranking team member.

Defined as the number of years between consecutive reorientations. In the year a reorientation occurs, time since reorientation is reset to 0. The years between birth and a firm's first reorientation are also coded 0 to account for the difference between organizational evolution with no past experience and evolution with previous history.

Defined as the number of years elapsed since any of the identified jolts (technological or legal-regulatory) had occurred, with the value set equal to 0 in the year an external jolt occurred. Although technological discontinuities were modeled separately from other types of jolts, one measure was used because the inertial effects of time were expected to be similar for all types of exogenous jolts.
Measured as the number of years a given person was CEO. When a change in CEO (or top executive) occurred, CEO tenure was set back to 0 in that year.
time_window: years as CEO in the firm

description: Defined as the total number of reorientations in which a given CEO was present and in the CEO role. Reorientations that occurred while the person was on a firm's executive team but not the CEO were not counted, and reorientations the CEO directed in other firms were not counted because those data were unavailable.

variable_name: number of executives in, number out, total fluctuation
description: Change in an executive team was measured by counting in each year for each firm the number of executives who were not on the team the previous year (number entering) and the number of executives listed in the prior year but not in the current year (number exiting). The absolute numbers of executives entering and exiting were added to obtain total fluctuation in a given year. Each of the three measures was standardized by the size of the team in that year.

variable_name: functional heterogeneity and coefficient of variation in team tenure
description: Heterogeneity was captured by the coefficient of variation in team tenure, calculated by dividing the standard deviation of a variable by its mean, and by functional heterogeneity. Function was identified by job title and functional heterogeneity was calculated using the Gibbs-Martin index, where p_i is the proportion of team members in each functional category i and n is the total number of categories; lower values reflect lower heterogeneity, or higher homogeneity. The functional categories were finance and accounting, production and operations, research and development, special services (such as transportation, public relations, and distribution), marketing, and general management; titles identifying no function were placed in the general category.

Mean team tenure was calculated for each team for each year by taking the average of all individual members' tenures on their team. All of a team's members, including the firm's CEO, were included in measures of tenure if the individuals were reported on the executive team for a given year.

An 18-item scale assessing the extent to which a plant had implemented and integrated computer technologies for manufacturing such as CAM and MRPII. Respondents were plant managers and operations managers; because interrater reliability was acceptable, the responses were averaged within each plant.

A 10-item scale measuring the extent to which a plant used techniques to promote continuous improvement, doing things right the first time, and devotion to fulfilling customer needs. Respondents were the plant managers and quality managers, and responses were averaged within each plant.

A 5-item scale measuring the extent to which a plant attempted to cut costs through reducing inventories and lead times between orders and deliveries through adjusting numbers of suppliers, sizes of deliveries, total numbers of parts, and so forth. Responses of plant managers and production control managers were averaged within each plant.

A 10-item scale measuring the extent to which a job was mentally demanding and involved many different tasks, clients, methods, and procedures. Respondents were the three functional managers and the six nonmanagerial employees, and the measures of job characteristics were based on the mean of their responses within each plant.

A 7-item scale measuring the extent to which a job required interaction and collaboration with others. Respondents were the three functional managers and the six nonmanagerial employees, and responses were averaged within each plant.

A single item asking the extent (1 = not at all, 5 = extensively) to which the pay method was utilized. Each functional manager responded according to the practices used in his or her function, and the corresponding personnel manager separately noted the compensation practices used in each function to corroborate the responses; the compensation measures were based on the mean of the functional manager's and the human resources manager's responses.

A single item asking the extent (1 = not at all, 5 = extensively) to which the pay method was utilized, answered by the functional manager for his or her function and separately by the personnel manager for corroboration. The measure is based on the mean of the two respondents' answers within the plant.

A single item asking the extent (1 = not at all, 5 = extensively) to which hourly wages were utilized, answered by the functional manager for his or her function and separately by the personnel manager for corroboration. The measure is based on the mean of the two respondents' answers within the plant.

A single item asking the extent (1 = not at all, 5 = extensively) to which salary was utilized, answered by the functional manager for his or her function and separately by the personnel manager for corroboration. The measure is based on the mean of the two respondents' answers within the plant.

A single item asking the extent (1 = not at all, 5 = extensively) to which seniority-based pay was utilized, answered by the functional manager for his or her function and separately by the personnel manager for corroboration. The measure is based on the mean of the two respondents' answers within the plant.

A single item asking the extent (1 = not at all, 5 = extensively) to which skill-based pay was utilized, answered by the functional manager for his or her function and separately by the personnel manager for corroboration. The measure is based on the mean of the two respondents' answers within the plant.
A natural logarithmic transformation of a plant's number of full-time employees, obtained from Standard & Poor's Directory of Corporate Affiliations.
A one-item scale asking if a plant manager reported to another manager at a location remote from the plant site (0 = no, 1 = yes).
A one-item scale asking whether a plant's work force was represented by a union (0 = no, 1 = yes).

An 8-item scale assessing productivity, lead time, quality, inventory management, and so forth. It was measured from plant managers and treated in the analysis as a source of inertia that moderates the manufacturing-compensation relationship.

Six single-item measures of how extensively each pay method was used in the plant: individual incentives, group incentives, hourly wages, salary, seniority-based pay and skill-based pay. Each was rated 1 (not at all) to 5 (extensively) by functional managers and corroborated by personnel managers, and averaged within plant. Each practice was analyzed separately.

Issues were measured by the extent to which they were interpreted as strategic. For each of the six issues, a four-item, seven-point scale assessed strategic interpretation, with items scaled so that higher ratings indicated that an issue was perceived as strategic; a sample item asks the extent to which the institution would consider the issue as one that has consequences for the institution's position in the marketplace. Across all six content areas the strategic scale items exhibited an internal consistency of .88, and the alphas for the six subscales ranged from .73 to .86. For the hypothesis tests, responses regarding the interpretation of all six issues were combined.
scale: 1, "to a small extent," to 7, "to a great extent"
level: individual respondent (item average across the six issues)

description: Issues were measured by the extent to which they were interpreted as political. For each of the six issues, a four-item, seven-point scale assessed political interpretation, with high ratings indicating that an issue was perceived as political; a sample item asks the extent to which the institution would consider the issue an area in which there is conflict within the administration over control of the issue. Together the political scale items across the different issues exhibited an alpha of .92, and the alphas for the six subscales ranged from .73 to .81. For the hypothesis tests, responses regarding the interpretation of all six issues were combined.
scale: 1, "to a small extent," to 7, "to a great extent"
level: individual respondent (item average across the six issues)

description: A seven-item scale (alpha = .88) based on Thomas and McDaniel's (1990) work, measuring the perceived formality, interaction, and degree of participation among the top managers involved in executive decision processes. The items were scaled so that high values represented low formality, high participation, and high interaction, indicating an information-processing structure with high capacity. Responses referred to team characteristics and were aggregated within universities before being assigned to each individual.
scale: 1, "to a small extent," to 7, "to a great extent"

description: A four-item scale (alpha = .71) measuring the extent of political activity using the attributes Pfeffer (1981) suggested: goals and preferences, coalitions, information requirements, and information use. The items were scaled so that high ratings represented high levels of political activity. Responses referred to team characteristics and were aggregated within universities before being assigned to each individual.
scale: 1, "to a small extent," to 7, "to a great extent"

description: A scale adapted from Milliken's (1990) work, described by the authors as a six-item scale (alpha = .82), referring to a top management team's beliefs about various facets of its organization's cultural values; the appendix lists five items. High values indicated a strong identity, that is, a more widely held and understood sense of uniqueness. Responses were aggregated within universities before being assigned to each individual.
scale: 1, "to a small extent," to 7, "to a great extent"

description: Executive level data were collected from self-report information through the questionnaire and coded into three levels, with CEO or president equal to +1, executive vice president or chief academic officer equal to 0, and chief of admissions or chief financial officer equal to -1.
Position tenure was the number of years a respondent had been in a current position, collected from self-report information through the questionnaire.
Institutional tenure was the number of years a respondent had been at his or her present institution, collected from self-report information through the questionnaire.

Academic background was a respondent's area of formal education, collected from self-report information through the questionnaire and coded -1, liberal arts, including psychology, sociology, art, music, and theology; 0, hard sciences, including biology, chemistry, physics, and math; +1, business and related fields, business administration, economics.

Size was calculated by collapsing the nine size groupings used in the United States Department of Education's Digest of Educational Statistics. Because the resulting distribution of sizes was markedly skewed (Kolmogorov-Smirnov Z-test = 4.80, p < .001), a logarithmic transformation was applied to the observed values. Size, type, and ownership data were obtained from the Higher Education Publication's (HEP) 1990 Higher Education Directory.

Type was coded in terms of the highest degree offered, with bachelor's degree equal to 1, master's degree equal to 2, and Ph.D. or postdoctoral degrees equal to 3. Size, type, and ownership data were obtained from the Higher Education Publication's (HEP) 1990 Higher Education Directory.
Ownership was coded as either public (1) or private (2). Size, type, and ownership data were obtained from the Higher Education Publication's (HEP) 1990 Higher Education Directory.

Issue content was operationalized as six issues selected from interviews, a literature search and an expert panel ranking: faculty satisfaction, minority issues, external funding, student educational satisfaction, changes in academic programs, and changes in student enrollment. Each issue was rated on strategic and political interpretation scales and used in the configurational analysis.

variable_name: Individual-level variables (executive level, position tenure, institutional tenure, academic background)
description: A set of four self-reported top manager variables entered together as a block: executive level (CEO or president, executive vice president or chief academic officer, chief of admissions or chief student affairs officer), years in current position, years at the institution, and academic background (area of formal education).

A set of three institution characteristics entered together as a block: size (collapsed Department of Education size groupings), type (highest degree offered) and ownership (public or private), taken from the 1990 Higher Education Directory.

Each top management team member indicated the number of years spent in each of eight different functional areas. The diversity measure was constructed with the Euclidean distances among the top management team members, averaged to the level of the team.
Each top management team member indicated the date he or she became a member of the team. An average tenure score was computed for each executive team.
Scanning was assessed with six questionnaire items based on the work of Glick and colleagues (1990) and of Fahey and King (1977). The scale had a coefficient alpha of .88.
Performance monitoring was assessed with a four-item scale based on the work of Eisenhardt (1989). The scale had a coefficient alpha of .80.
Centralization was assessed using a seven-item scale adapted from Glick and colleagues (1990). The scale had a coefficient alpha of .74.

Perceived instability was originally assessed with nine Likert-type questionnaire items, rated on seven-point scales, based on the work of Duncan (1972) and Bourgeois (1985). Two items were omitted because they were found to have low item-total correlations. The revised scale had a coefficient alpha of .71.

Perceived munificence was assessed through seven questionnaire items the author developed, based on the work of Glick, Huber, Miller, Doty, and Sutcliffe (1990). The scale had a coefficient alpha of .88.

The instability of each industry was measured by taking the mean of three indexes measuring instability in industry sales, capital expenditures, and net assets. To compute each index, the variable was regressed on a variable representing the time period, and the index is a function of the standard error of the regression divided by the mean level of the dependent variable. All indexes were first computed at the level of the individual business segment and then averaged to produce an industry-level value, and each participating business segment was assigned its industry's instability score.

Three munificence indexes (sales, capital expenditures, and net assets) were averaged to create an overall industry-level munificence measure. Each index represented the unstandardized regression coefficient from a time-trend regression analysis divided by the mean of the dependent variable of the regression, so that the steeper the regression slope, the higher the level of growth. Indexes were computed at the level of the individual business segment and then averaged to produce an industry-level value.

The firm-level perceived environmental instability scores were standardized to z-scores and subtracted from the already standardized archival instability scores. The absolute value of the difference provides a measure of a firm's perceptual divergence from its true relative position, so the higher the score the greater the divergence. This score was then subtracted from a constant to derive a congruence rather than a divergence measure, so that the higher the score the greater the congruence between perceived and actual instability.

The firm-level perceived environmental munificence scores were standardized to z-scores and subtracted from the already standardized archival munificence scores. The absolute value of the difference measures a firm's perceptual divergence from its true relative position, so the higher the score the greater the divergence. This score was then subtracted from a constant to derive a congruence rather than a divergence measure, so that the higher the score the greater the congruence between perceived and actual munificence.

Dichotomous variable with 0 representing women and 1 representing men. The variable was entered into each logistic regression equation after the set of experience-based director characteristics, so that any significant main effect of sex indicates influence on membership odds after other measured differences in directors' characteristics have been accounted for.

variable_name: Committee membership (audit, compensation, executive, finance, nominating, public affairs)
description: The committee membership variables for the audit, compensation, executive, finance, nominating, and public affairs committees were measured dichotomously, with 0 representing nonmembership and 1 representing membership. A separate logistic regression equation predicts the odds of an individual's membership on each given committee, with odds defined as the probability of serving on the committee divided by the probability of not serving on the committee.

Dichotomous variable with inside directors coded 0 and outsiders coded 1. Inside directors are defined as all current or former employees of a company or its subsidiaries and all relatives of such persons; all other directors are defined as outsiders.
Tenure on a board, measured in years. It was entered as a continuous independent variable in the logistic regression equations predicting committee membership.

Dichotomous variable with directors whose primary employer was a corporation, financial institution, or law firm classified as holding business occupations (1) and all other directors categorized as holding nonbusiness occupations (0).
The total number of concurrent directorships of other corporations or financial institutions a director held, entered as a continuous variable in the logistic regression equations.

The total number of concurrent directorships or trusteeships of political, cultural, educational, religious, or other nonprofit institutions a director held, entered as a continuous variable in the logistic regression equations.

A set of five director variables entered together as a block in each logistic regression predicting committee membership: director type (inside vs outside), board tenure in years, occupation (business vs nonbusiness), number of business interlocks, and number of nonbusiness interlocks.

A scale constructed by averaging the questionnaire items whose standard scores loaded unambiguously at .30 or greater on the first factor extracted by principal component analysis with varimax rotation. The items cover a formal job design program, enhanced selectivity in hiring, training hours per employee, quality of work life programs, quality circles, labor-management teams, information-sharing programs, formal grievance procedures, and profit- and gain-sharing plans. Questions were asked separately for exempt and nonexempt employees and each response was weighted by the proportion of employees in each category affected. Cronbach's alpha for the scale was .67.

A scale constructed by averaging the questionnaire items whose standard scores loaded unambiguously at .30 or greater on the second factor, comprising a narrowly focused set of practices designed to recognize and reinforce desired employee behaviors. Responses were asked separately for exempt and nonexempt employees and weighted by the proportion of employees in each category affected. Cronbach's alpha for the scale was .66.

Assessed with a single questionnaire item: "What is your average annual rate of turnover?" The question was asked separately for exempt and nonexempt employees, and the level of turnover for each firm is the weighted average across these categories. The measure includes both voluntary and involuntary departures, and the data were collected in a period of widespread corporate downsizings.

The logarithm of sales per employee, described as a widely used measure of organizational productivity adopted to enhance comparability with prior work. Total employment used in the denominator was taken from the questionnaire, and sales come from the financial data. Models specifying productivity as the logarithm of net income per employee produced very similar results.

The logarithm of Tobin's q, calculated by dividing the market value of a firm by the replacement cost of its assets; conceptually q is a measure of the value added by management. The calculations were taken from Hall and colleagues. Both contemporaneous and subsequent (t + 1) year values were used.

variable_name: gross rate of return on capital (GRATE)
description: An accounting measure of profits calculated by dividing cash flow by gross capital stock, described as a better measure of accounting profits than return on assets or return on equity because it is not as greatly affected by depreciation or other noncash transactions. The calculations were taken from Hall and colleagues.

variable_name: interaction between human resources policy consistency and each practices scale
description: The first measure of internal fit as moderation consists of the interaction between the degree of human resources policy consistency and the respective High Performance Work Practices factor scales. Human resources policy consistency was assessed with a Likert-scale survey item: "How would you describe the consistency of your human resource policies across any divisions or business units your firm may have?" The author notes the measure has restricted range because firms that by definition do not adopt human resource policies consistently were excluded from the sample.

variable_name: interaction of the employee skills and organizational structures and employee motivation scales
description: The second measure of internal fit as moderation consists of the interaction between the two factor scales. It rests on the assumption that the returns from investments in employee skills and organizational structures will be higher to the extent that firms have also devoted significant resources to employee motivation, and the author describes it as superior to the first internal fit measure in that it does not exhibit the psychometric problems outlined above.

The internal fit-as-matching variable, computed as the absolute value of the difference between a firm's scores on the employee skills and organizational structures and employee motivation scales; internal fit as matching occurs if a firm is consistently low, medium, or high on both factors, so a lower score indicates greater fit.

variable_name: interaction of the proportion of sales from differentiation or focus strategies with each practices scale
description: The first measure of external fit as moderation indicates the correspondence between each firm's competitive strategy and its system of High Performance Work Practices; the proportion of sales derived from either a differentiation or focus strategy was interacted with scores on the employee skills and organizational structures and employee motivation scales respectively. The author assumed that a predominantly differentiation or focus strategy would require more intensive investments in High Performance Work Practices than would a cost leadership strategy.

variable_name: interaction of the strategic HRM index with each practices scale
description: The second measure of external fit as moderation is based on a behavioral indication of the emphasis each firm placed on aligning its human resource management practices and competitive strategy. Respondents indicated whether or not they attempted to implement each of seven strategic human resource management activities for all employees, and an index was constructed by adding the number of affirmative responses (alpha .69). To test the expectation that the returns from investments in both factors will be greater when firms explicitly attempt to link human resources and business objectives, each firm's score on the strategic HRM index was interacted with each factor score.

Calculated by taking the absolute value of the difference between the Z score of the proportion of sales resulting from a differentiation or focus strategy and the respective factor scores; the variable indicates the degree to which firms adopting differentiation or focus strategies also employ high levels of High Performance Work Practices and vice versa, with a lower score indicating greater fit.

variable_name: proportion of annual sales derived from each competitive strategy
description: To provide an estimate of a firm's competitive strategy, each respondent indicated the proportion of its annual sales derived from each of Porter's types: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus. Because the responses were constrained to equal 100 percent, the proportion of sales derived from cost leadership equals 1 minus (differentiation + focus), so models were estimated separately for each strategy type and a dummy variable was also created that equaled 1 if the combined value of differentiation plus focus was greater than 67 percent.
scale: proportion of annual sales, constrained to sum to 100 percent

variable_name: proportions of years of experience in each functional area
description: For each executive the authors computed the ratio between years in a particular functional area and total years of work experience in all functions, including the nonfunctional category general administration. Data on years of work experience in accounting, finance, marketing, personnel, production and operations, research and development, and sales came from the final questionnaire mailed six months after the last interview. Two sets of combined categories were used: set 1, output experience (sales and marketing) and throughput experience (production-operations and accounting), following Hambrick and Mason's functional tracks; set 2, customer experience (marketing, including sales), operations experience (production-operations), financial experience (finance and accounting) and technology experience (research and development), following Kefalas and Schoderbek. Personnel experience was omitted from the analyses because only 8 of the 63 executives had experience in that area and it was never their most extensive experience.
scale: proportion of total years of work experience

variable_name: number of changes perceived in each environmental sector
description: Each change reported in the interviews was coded by an interviewer into one of 12 categories; environmental changes were coded into one of the ten environmental sectors shown in the Appendix. The number of changes each executive perceived in each sector was used as a dependent variable, and sectors with fewer than 24 changes were not included in the analysis. Because the distributions of the dependent variables were highly skewed toward low frequencies, the frequencies were transformed by adding 1 to each frequency and taking the natural logarithm of this sum.
time_window: previous 6 months for each of three interviews, covering a contiguous 18-month period

variable_name: number of changes perceived in each effectiveness category
description: Each effectiveness change reported in the interviews was coded into one of four categories based on Quinn and Rohrbaugh's model of organizational effectiveness: open systems (growth, resource acquisition, and external support), rational goal (productivity and efficiency), internal process (stability and equilibrium), and human relations (value and development of human resources). The internal process category had a frequency below 20 and was omitted from the analyses. Frequencies were transformed by adding 1 and taking the natural logarithm.
time_window: previous 6 months for each of three interviews, covering a contiguous 18-month period

variable_name: natural logarithm of the number of employees
description: Cause was measured with the natural logarithm of the number of employees in an organization.

variable_name: percentage of employees who were women
description: Constituents was defined as the percentage of an organization's employees who were women.

variable_name: percentage of managers who were women
description: A second operational definition of constituents was the percentage of an organization's managers who were women.
Content was a dichotomous variable coded "1" if an organization was in the public sector.

variable_name: percentage of organizations that acquiesced in the intersection of the organization's census region and industry
description: Control was measured with three variables assessing the degree of work-family program diffusion in a focal organization's organizational field: the percentage of organizations that acquiesced in the organization's industry, in the organization's census region, and in the intersection of the organization's census region and industry. A finding that the percentage of adopters in the intersection of industry and region positively influences responsiveness could not be explained by regional or industry differences and thus would support the institutional control argument; the industry and region percentages serve as controls.

variable_name: attention to practices in other organizations
description: Context was assessed by the response to a direct question about the degree to which an organization paid attention to practices in other organizations like it when evaluating its performance.

variable_name: unemployment rate for women in the organization's industry
description: Countervailing power was the unemployment rate for women in the organization's industry.

variable_name: problems when employees with young children miss work
description: Benefits from work-family responsiveness was assessed via the response to a direct question about the degree to which an organization had problems when employees with young children missed work because child-care services were not available.

The dependent variable, responsiveness to work-family issues, was coded into four groups: "3" if an organization acquiesced, "2" if it compromised, "1" if it avoided, and "0" if it defied institutional pressure. The coding considered three classes of benefits: dependent care services (on-site day care, subsidized day care away from the workplace, assistance with aging parents), flexible workplace options (flextime, working at home, paid paternity leave), and cheap responses (information about child care in the community, unpaid paternity leave). Organizations were treated as following acquiescence when they had at least one benefit in each of the two expensive categories, compromise when they offered at least one benefit from one expensive category and at least one cheap response, avoidance when they offered only cheap responses or only one category of expensive benefit with no cheap response, and defiance when they offered no work-family benefits at all. The same coding was used in four logit models predicting the likelihood that an organization used each strategic response.

Downside risk specified as a second-order root lower partial moment of below-target annual ROA observations. For each year, the downside performance discrepancy is the aspired-to target return minus the actual return when the target exceeds the actual return, and zero otherwise; these discrepancies are aggregated into a root lower partial moment over the five-year period. The target level is the average performance of all firms in the firm's two-digit SIC industry in the previous five-year period, with aspirations updated annually. First- and second-order root lower partial moments were computed, and only the second-order measures were retained for the analyses.
time_window: five-year period; target based on prior five-year industry performance

description: Return on assets, measured as the firm's average ROA over the five-year period. The authors chose ROA over ROE because ROA does not vary with changes in financial leverage. In the risk equation, average return in a period is used to explain risk in the subsequent five-year period.

Recoverable slack was measured using accounting ratios, each normalized by dividing the firm's ratio by the two-digit SIC industry average ratio for that year. The three normalized recoverable slack indicators load on a single factor and are combined into an aggregate measure as an unweighted sum of the three standardized recoverable slack indicators for a given year. The slack measure used for model estimation is a firm's mean recoverable slack calculated over a five-year period.

The common standard deviation of return on assets over a five-year period; a trend standard deviation around the firm's returns time trend was also computed. Five years of returns data were required to calculate the standard deviation measures.

Timeliness of feedback was manipulated by having two of the entrepreneurs provide a feedback comment after each trial and two provide no comments; subjects received the performance data on all companies, so only the timeliness of the feedback varied. A single 7-point Likert-type item measuring the extent to which subjects thought the entrepreneur provided them with timely feedback served as the manipulation check.

Feedback was measured by four items developed by the authors assessing the extent to which CEOs had provided the investor with timely feedback on strategic decisions and venture performance over the prior 12 months. All responses were on five-point Likert-type scales.
level: venture capitalist reporting on one portfolio venture

description: Influence was manipulated by varying the extent to which entrepreneurs followed subjects' advice: two of the entrepreneurs followed the buying strategy recommended by the subject and two followed a strategy in direct opposition to it. Two 7-point Likert-type items assessing the perceived influence subjects had over entrepreneurs' decisions served as the manipulation check for influence.

Influence was measured by four items assessing the extent to which the venture capitalist could influence the strategic direction and decisions of the CEO; these were adapted from Lind, Lissak, and Conlon (1983). Responses were on five-point Likert-type scales; one item asking whether the CEO ignored the investor's advice is reverse-coded.
level: venture capitalist reporting on one portfolio venture

description: Procedural justice was measured by two 7-point Likert-type items assessing perceptions of the extent to which the entrepreneur treated the subject fairly in the course of decision making, adapted from Lind, Kurtz, Musante, Walker, and Thibaut (1980).

Procedural justice was measured by four items adapted from Lind and colleagues (1980) assessing the fairness of the procedures used by a CEO to conduct board meetings and make strategic decisions, on five-point Likert-type scales.
level: venture capitalist reporting on one portfolio venture

description: Trust in the entrepreneur, adapted from Roberts and O'Reilly (1974), was measured by three 7-point items assessing subjects' trust in the entrepreneur.

The four-item measure of trust, adapted from Roberts and O'Reilly (1974), concerned venture capitalists' assessment of the extent to which they believed a CEO to be honest, sincere, and trustworthy. Responses were on five-point Likert-type scales.
level: venture capitalist reporting on one portfolio venture

description: Commitment to decisions was measured by two 7-point Likert-type items adapted from Earley and Lind (1987) regarding subjects' commitment to the decisions made by the entrepreneur.

Commitment to decisions, based on Earley and Lind (1987), was measured by three items assessing the extent to which venture capitalists supported the strategic directions taken by the CEOs, on five-point Likert-type scales.
level: venture capitalist reporting on one portfolio venture

description: Monitoring was assessed by the number of times subjects inquired about the performance of the company; subjects could purchase an outcome report at a cost of $20 per inquiry and could inquire as often as they desired.
time_window: across all trials of the simulation

description: Frequency of monitoring was measured by two items, developed for this study, assessing the extent to which the investors sought additional performance reports and documentation, on five-point Likert-type scales.
level: venture capitalist reporting on one portfolio venture

description: Investing was measured by the total amount of money subjects invested in a venture across all trials.
time_window: across all trials of the simulation

description: Investing was measured by four items, developed for this study, assessing whether the investors had taken or would take every opportunity to invest in the venture, on five-point Likert-type scales.
level: venture capitalist reporting on one portfolio venture

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 if a store is under the outcome-based incentive plan and 0 otherwise. The plan paid each salesperson a base wage equaling an hourly rate times hours worked plus a cash bonus if quarterly sales exceeded a prespecified goal, was identical in structure at all stores that implemented it, and applied to all sales consultants and all merchandise sold at those stores. Fifteen of the 34 stores implemented the plan and the other 19 provided a natural control group.

Weighted index of the number of competitors in each store's trade area. Competitors were classified by the company into three categories, high-end, middle, and low-end, with weights of 3, 2, and 1 respectively, so that close high-end competitors were weighed much more than discount stores. The measure is constant over time for each store.

Principal component combining four demographic variables measured for the trading area of each store: median household income, median age, percentage of the population with college education, and percentage of white-collar workers in the population. Only one principal component emerged with an eigenvalue greater than one. The measure is constant over time for each store.

Ratio of the number of managers supervising the salesforce to the number of sales consultants at each store. The variable used in the estimation model is the level of supervisory monitoring existing prior to plan implementation, computed as the average monthly ratio for 1987, the year prior to the implementation of the incentive plan.

Average monthly sales per square foot for each store, computed by dividing the sales of each store by its area. The measure is a monthly time series of 77 months of data drawn from the company's general financial ledgers.

Store profit measured as store sales revenues less the cost of goods sold and all store-level expenses, including the salaries and bonuses of sales consultants and managers and support expenses such as security, displays, promotions, and administration. Profitability per square foot was measured over 65 months.

Annual measure of customers' satisfaction with salesforce service for each store, constructed by averaging customer responses to four survey questions identified by the company's customers as important. The company computed an overall store weighted-average response as (100 x percent of store responses stating strongly agree) + (70 x percent of store responses stating agree), based on between 300 and 900 customer surveys per store each year. Responses were made by checking boxes on a four-point scale.

An index of overlap between the backgrounds of a CEO and the chair of his compensation committee. Four dummy variables were used: employment at the same firm (contemporaneous or noncontemporaneous), attendance at the same educational institution as an undergraduate or graduate student, number of shared Fortune 500 board memberships, and number of shared memberships on other boards. Each individual measure was first standardized and then combined to form the index used to test Hypothesis 1.

An index built by counting the total numbers of corporate board memberships, trusteeships, social club memberships, and the prestige of the undergraduate institution attended (Harvard, Yale, or Princeton coded 2; any of the other 11 high-prestige institutions coded 1; nonelite background coded 0). To test Hypotheses 2a and 2b, each CEO's raw score on each measure was standardized using the mean and standard deviation for CEOs only, and the standardized results were summed to form the global status index.

An index built by counting the total numbers of corporate board memberships, trusteeships, social club memberships, and the prestige of the undergraduate institution attended. The chair's raw scores were standardized using the mean and standard deviation for compensation committee chairs only and then summed to form the global status index used to test Hypotheses 2a and 2b.

To test Hypothesis 3a, CEO and compensation chair raw scores on each of the four status measures were standardized using the mean and standard deviation of the full sample (all CEOs and compensation chairs combined) and summed to produce a status index for each individual. For each dyad, the CEO's local status index was compared to his chair's. The local status dummy variable equals 1 when the CEO's local status index is greater than the chair's index and 0 if the CEO's local status index is lower than the compensation chair's.

Four dummy variables capturing the relationships of a CEO and a compensation chair to their own groups and to the other member of the dyad. Each individual's global status index was first compared with his group mean: the dummy equals 1 if the CEO's status exceeds the mean for all CEOs in the sample and 0 if it falls below, with the same procedure followed for compensation chairs. The CEO and chair dummies were then compared within dyads; for example, the high-CEO/low-compensation chair relational status dummy equals 1 when the CEO is of high status relative to other CEOs and is paired with a chair of low status relative to other compensation chairs.
The logarithm of the CEO's cash compensation (base and bonus) for the year 1984, obtained from the 1985 Business Week survey and checked against firm proxy statements.

Ownership status of the business unit, classified into state-owned, collective-hybrid, and private companies. Ownership status and industry were initially identified from insurance company records and then confirmed during interviews. In the analysis, two dummy variables were used to compare each ownership type against the other two.

Assessed with the question, "How important is the relationship to you?" Executives rated relationships on a range from 1, "not important," to 4, "vitally important." Each executive assigned each of his or her connection cards to a response category.
Assessed by the executives' responses to the statement, "This relationship is useful as a defense against threats," with response options from 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree.

Measured by responses to "What is the primary reason for the person's usefulness?" Responses were coded as 1 for "important connections in government" or as 0 for any of the following: "important connections in key companies," "important connections elsewhere in this company," "controls financial resources," "access to customers," "technical or professional knowledge," and "I have to go through this person."
Measured by asking, "To what extent do you trust the person?" with response options from 1 = deeply distrust to 5 = trust completely.

Assessed by the question, "People in business relationships often give one another gifts. Could you categorize these relationships by the form of gift giving between you and the other?" Coded 1 = give connection nonreciprocated gifts or 0 = do not give connection gifts or give mutual gifts. The authors focused on nonreciprocated gift giving because they were testing the hypothesis that executives in less structurally secure situations would have more need to strengthen their guanxi via giving gifts.

variable_name: coefficient of variation of exempt employment
description: The coefficient of variation in number of exempt employees over the study's time frame, calculated by dividing the employment-level standard deviation by the employment-level mean. The statistic standardizes the variation units across firms of all sizes. It was used as the dependent variable in the tests of Hypotheses 1a and 1b.

variable_name: coefficient of variation of total employment
description: The coefficient of variation in total number of employees over the study's time frame, calculated by dividing the employment-level standard deviation by the employment-level mean. It was used as the dependent variable in the test of Hypothesis 2a.

variable_name: coefficient of variation of nonexempt employment
description: The coefficient of variation in number of nonexempt employees over the study's time frame, calculated by dividing the employment-level standard deviation by the employment-level mean. It was used as the dependent variable in the test of Hypothesis 2b.

For each employee, each firm designated base pay and a total amount of bonus payments made during the past year; bonus pay was typically a function of individual and business performance combined. The ratio of bonus to base pay for each individual was used in residual estimation, in which each individual-level compensation variable was regressed on education, potential labor market experience (and its square), firm tenure (and its square), job tenure (and its square), number of levels between the individual's job and the board of directors, and number of managerial levels supervised. Individual residuals were then averaged across individuals within an organization to create the organization-level measure of emphasis on short-term bonus pay.
time_window: compensation measured at time t+1 relative to performance at time t

description: Operationally defined as the average number of employees eligible for performance-based payments that would not be available to those employees during the next year. Although the organizational average was constructed from a yes or no indicator for each employee, the residual estimation (controlling for human capital and job characteristics) and subsequent averaging across individuals and within firms result in an interval measure of the organization's emphasis on long-term incentives. The measure was based on managerial data but was treated as representing exempt compensation for the tests of Hypotheses 1a and 1b.
time_window: compensation measured at time t+1 relative to performance at time t

description: Institutional influences were coded in terms of period effects. The variable nationalism, used to assess the main effect of the impact of sociocultural norms, was a dummy variable coded 1 for years marked by nationalism (1840-1917) and 0 otherwise. The authors note that period effects only indirectly capture nationalism and that attempts to derive other indicators failed because reliable data over the historical period were not available.

To assess the extent to which the intensity of nationalism varied over time, four subperiods of nationalism were constructed after historical analysis and interviews. Each was a dummy variable coded 1 for years within the subperiod and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: language of publication (Finnish-language paper versus Swedish-language paper)
description: Two destination states for founding were constructed, Finnish-language paper and Swedish-language paper. Language of publication was entered as a dummy variable coded 1 for papers printed in Finnish and 0 for papers printed in Swedish; this dependent variable allows for the testing of the institutional arguments made in the study as it is an indicator of institutional norms of nationalism.
level: newspaper founding event (population-year and city-year destination state)

description: Founding is the start of a newspaper's publication and is a characteristic of the population of newspapers; the instantaneous probability of a newspaper's being founded is estimated. The data are coded as a single series of repeatable events, and the rate of occurrence is taken as a log-linear (exponential) function of the independent variables. Parameter estimates were obtained by maximum likelihood in the RATE program, and simple exponential models were used because prior work on this data set failed to support age parametric dependence.

A variable that captures whether the populace of a locale was predominantly Swedish speaking: 1 indicates Swedish speakers exceeded Finnish speakers, 0 indicates otherwise. It was used together with nationalism in an interaction to test the local-level prediction that Finnish-language founding rates rise even in predominantly Swedish-speaking locales.

variable_name: reputation (expanded Fortune scale); management-quality reputation variable
description: Reputation was measured as a multidimensional construct based on an expanded version of the eight-item Fortune scale, with respondents rating their alliance partner relative to other firms in its industry. The three hypothesized dimensions are product quality (seven items, alpha = .90), management (nine items, alpha = .90), and financial performance (three items, alpha = .65). Because product quality and management are highly correlated, a linear combination of these two dimensions (the average of management and quality ratings) was used in subsequent analyses.
scale: 1 = worst in industry, 5 = about average, 10 = best in industry
level: firm (respondent firm's partner in the alliance)

description: Prior relationship between partners was measured by seven items indicating the extent to which the two firms had a prior affiliation as customer and supplier, competitors, or partners of another type (alpha = .43; the low alpha is not surprising because one firm's prior relationship with another as a customer would not be expected to correlate with a prior relationship as a competitor). The seven items were averaged to reflect the degree to which any type of prior affiliation existed.

Data on the degree of shared decision making were gathered in the second round of surveys, in mid-1995, at the same time as the alliance outcomes. The text of this paper does not describe the items or the response scale used for this variable.

The similarity scale was based on ten items that asked respondents to indicate the similarities between their firm and its partner on a range of organizational attributes. Exploratory factor analysis supported two types of similarities; five items load on similarities in strategic content (alpha = .72). Respondents indicated the degree to which the operations of their firm are similar to those of the partner firm; these items were reverse-coded in analyses.
scale: 1 = very similar, 7 = not at all similar (reverse-coded in analyses)

description: The second factor from the ten-item similarity scale consists of five items covering organizational processes (alpha = .82). Respondents indicated the degree to which the operations of their firm are similar to those of the partner firm; these items were reverse-coded in analyses.
scale: 1 = very similar, 7 = not at all similar (reverse-coded in analyses)

description: The primary alliance outcome measure was a three-item scale reporting performance as perceived by a partner organization in the alliance, reflecting overall satisfaction with the alliance, the degree to which it has met the goals of the partner, and its contributions to the partner's core competencies (alpha = .87). The three items were averaged as an overall outcome indicator. Termination of an alliance was not necessarily equated with failure.

As a second alliance outcome measure, data on initial satisfaction were gathered as part of the first survey. This single item asked partners to assess their level of satisfaction in the first year of an alliance.
time_window: first survey, 1994 (first year of the alliance)

description: Joint equity position was used as a measure of administrative form. If equity in the relationship and outcomes were shared to any extent by the partners, the alliance was coded 1 (47 percent of transactions); if one partner maintained all equity and proceeds were shared by some predetermined contractual method, the alliance was coded 0 (53 percent). There was no significant difference in administrative form between cross- and within-border transactions.
scale: 0 = one partner maintained all equity, 1 = equity in the relationship and outcomes shared to any extent by the partners

description: Measured as the difference between an S&L's ROA and the average ROA of S&Ls located in the same state, with both measured in the same year. ROA was used because managers commonly use this measure to assess relative performance, and a statewide average was used because the performance data firms use for comparisons are published by states using state-level data.

The ratio of real estate owned to total mortgage loans held. The authors use this measure because it indicates the amount of foreclosed real estate an institution has recorded for nonperforming borrowers; relaxing credit standards or poor underwriting can result in higher incidences of loan foreclosure and ultimately increase the amount of repossessed real estate held by an S&L.

Measured as an institution's cost of district Federal Home Loan Bank (FHLB) advances. Conventional deposits from local markets are a financial institution's primary source of financing, but S&Ls frequently rely on FHLB advances to meet operating expenses, lending commitments, and deposit withdrawal requests. This source is primarily short-term and is sensitive to interest-rate changes, so its use increases an institution's interest-rate risk.
The ratio of liquid assets to total assets.

Measured as the ratio of general and administrative overhead expenses to total assets. This ratio is squared in the model because the prediction is for a fully convex relation whereby high and low levels of slack correspond to high risk and moderate levels of slack correspond to low risk.

A dummy variable coded 1 for stockholder-controlled S&Ls and 0 for mutual, depositor-owned institutions. Parameter estimates associated with this dummy variable indicate how realized credit and interest-rate risks in stock S&Ls differ from those in mutual firms.
Measured using a ratio of total liabilities to estimated tangible GAAP assets, consistent with prior S&L research that used ratios of net worth to assets or liabilities or of debt to assets.

A dummy variable set to 1 for FHLB districts 4, 7, 9, and 10 and to 0 otherwise. The four districts had been independently identified as having had less supervisory control over S&Ls during the 1980s, a view verified by comparing the 12 districts one by one against the district exhibiting the lowest average realized risks.

A dummy variable coded 1 for state S&Ls and 0 for federal S&Ls, used to model investment regulation, since state-chartered institutions generally enjoyed more liberal limits on their investment powers.

Firm performance was captured through operating cash flow, measured as the ratio of operating cash flows to total assets. This measure is less susceptible to manager manipulation than return on assets (ROA) and is insensitive to the accounting principles or reporting rules adopted by a firm.

A five-item index that taps environmental heterogeneity and its associated information-processing demands. Two items assess industry size (number of establishments and number of employees), two assess regional dispersion in industrial production (one based on establishments, the other on employees), and one assesses the percentage of workers not covered by a collective bargaining agreement. Values were created on the full set of two-digit SIC industries and then mapped to unions by two-digit SIC codes.
level: two-digit SIC industry, mapped to national union

description: A seven-item index that assesses the availability of external resources to support growth. Annual values for each item from 1983 to 1987 were transformed into natural logarithms and regressed on a linear time trend (and a constant) for each separate two-digit industry; the growth measures used in the composite were the antilogarithms of the regression slope coefficients. Items relate both to demand for and costs of union services and to industry growth in general.
level: two-digit SIC industry, mapped to national union

description: A seven-item index that captures unexpected change in external conditions, using the same seven items as the munificence measure. It consists of the antilogarithms of the standard errors on the linear time trend coefficient from the regression analyses described above, providing a measure of discontinuity that allows similar scores for environments that present similar patterns but start at different base levels.
level: two-digit SIC industry, mapped to national union

description: A 14-item index (alpha = .79) composed of NUS responses and data coded from union constitutions, on which level had the most authority (i.e., the vertical locus of authority) over goal formation for six union activities, including organizing, bargaining, and politics. The NUS items ask which group has the most say or influence for each activity, with responses coded 1 = executive board to 6 = rank-and-file members. The constitution items code which level has control over negotiations, formulation of bargaining demands, strike initiation, strike termination, and negotiating personnel, and whether the national union must approve contracts and local bargaining demands.

A 13-item index (alpha = .63) based exclusively on union constitutions, tapping two key dimensions of democratic structure: the degree to which members participated in or had direct influence over union decisions and leaders, and the degree of independent countervailing sources of power within the union. Items 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, and 10 were reverse-coded for the composite measure.

A five-item index (alpha = .71) comprised of NUS items and archival data that emphasize the degree of departmentalization, divisionalization, and functional specialization within a union. Two NUS items ask whether the union has special national-level units other than locals for particular constituents and whether it has intermediate bodies between the national and the local. Three archival items are the number of intermediate units, the number of departments listed for each union, and the number of staff.

A nine-item index (alpha = .65) made up exclusively of NUS items that assess four areas: standardization, formalization, communication, and coordination. Items are five-point accuracy, agreement, or planning scales; item 3 was reverse-coded for the composite and items 7, 8, and 9 were reverse-coded for the composite measure.

A three-item index (alpha = .69) made up exclusively of NUS responses that tap the degree to which decision making is spread throughout an organization, adapted from Knoke (1990). Respondents indicate agreement with statements about whether major policy decisions are made only after wide consultation at all levels, whether power over major policy decisions is concentrated in the hands of a few people, and whether leaders sometimes make decisions that have little support from the rank and file. Item 1 was reverse-coded for the composite measure.

A three-item index (alpha = .92) that taps the scope of operations and internal resources of the union. The NUS item asks roughly how many members the union currently represents; the archival measures are total assets and total dues receipts as reported by LM-2 Form data tapes (three-year average, 1988-90).

The natural logarithm of membership per local, where membership per local is national union membership as reported in the NUS divided by the number of affiliated local unions reported in archival sources. Two sample unions lacked traditional locals and were assigned values near zero (.0001) before taking the logarithm.

A two-item index (alpha = .84) that assesses the breadth of two-digit SIC industries in which a union actively sought members from 1986 through 1990. One item is the number of two-digit SIC industries in which the union held at least one NLRB election; the second is the proportion of all NLRB elections held outside the four two-digit SIC industries in which the union held the greatest number of elections. The second item was reverse-coded for the composite.

A three-item index that measures diversity in three member attributes: race, gender, and white-collar/blue-collar employment, assuming that members who differ on these attributes have different work-related interests. The measure takes on its highest value in a union in which the percentages of women, minority members, and white-collar employees are each equal to 50 percent. Its internal consistency was low (alpha = .45), which the authors attribute to its elements being causal rather than effect indicators.

A three-item index (alpha = .72) designed to capture the extent to which a primary jurisdiction can generate locals with members who are capable of effectively participating in democratic decision making. Higher average earnings per employee suggest higher worker skill and education levels, and high earnings and large establishments suggest a greater ability to create locals with the financial resources necessary to participate in national forums and governance bodies.
level: two-digit SIC industry, mapped to national union

description: Actual pay at time t minus predicted pay of executive i at time t using the sample and separately estimating annual equations. The predicted pay level was the predicted pay level at time t derived from estimating an ordinary least squares regression on the executives' current cash compensation level using t − 1 firm size and performance measures and board characteristics as explanatory variables; the estimated pay anomaly experienced by each executive at time t was the residual from this model.
time_window: time t, with predictors lagged t − 1

description: Actual pay at time t minus predicted pay of executive i at time t using a pay-level model in which pay is a function of firm size, with the parameters of the model separately estimated using all Times 1,000 firms in each sector and re-estimated each year. The comparison pay level was derived by estimating an OLS regression relationship between cash pay and firm size for each sector for each year, using all firms in that sector that were on the Times 1,000 list.

Actual pay at time t minus predicted pay of executive i at time t based upon the Times 1,000 sector-average pay of highest-paid directors. The comparison measure of cash compensation was simply the sector average of all Times 1,000 firms in each sector for each year, similar to the Smith and Szymanski (1995) model, with data obtained from Datastream.

variable_name: logarithm of change in total cash compensation
description: The logarithm of change in compensation, In[pay t + 1] − In[pay t], where pay t + 1 and pay t are the actual cash compensation payments to executives reported at times t + 1 and t. Cash compensation here is total cash compensation, salary plus bonus, for the company's highest-paid executive director, estimated for the highest-paid executive director in each firm.

The same one-period logarithmic change in cash compensation, applied to salaries only rather than salary plus bonus, for the company's highest-paid executive director. Because information on the split between the highest-paid directors' salaries and cash bonuses was collected from the published financial accounts for the three years from 1992 onward but Datastream does not make this distinction, the salary-only change models that included the lagged performance variables could only be estimated for two years, 1992-93 and 1993-94.

The total responsiveness score was obtained by summing the five subscores (leave, flexible work, dependent care, financial benefits, and miscellaneous benefits) after standardizing them for the number of questionnaire items in each subscore. The maximum possible score was five and the coefficient alpha for the overall scale was .90. The subscores were built from questionnaire items about which benefits and policies the company offered and whether each was available to all employees.

variable_name: percentage of female employees on the firm's current payroll
description: Respondents indicated the percentage of female employees on the firm's current payroll. This was used as a measure of resource dependence on female labor.
time_window: current payroll at the time of the survey

variable_name: change in the percentage of employees who were women
description: Respondents indicated the percentage of female employees on the payroll five years earlier as well as currently; the change in the percentage of employees who were women was computed from this information.

Respondents indicated whether the top management groups for their organizations included any women, any individuals who were parents of children under 18 in dual-career families, any single parents, or any individuals with known elder care responsibilities. A dummy variable was created to indicate whether the top management team had any individuals of any of these types who might be likely to raise work and family issues.

The industry in which the company operated was used to capture industry-level institutional effects. Interindustry comparisons focused on the three industry sectors with the largest representation in the sample: manufacturing, finance, insurance and real estate, and health care.

Respondents selected the geographic region in which their company operated from eight possible regions; because samples in some regions were small, the eight regions were grouped into five clusters: the Northeast, the Midatlantic, the Midwest, the West, and the South. Each region was treated as a dummy variable and the Midatlantic was omitted from the analysis.

Respondents indicated whether their companies conducted surveys of employees' needs and what other methods they used for learning about employees, such as exit interviews, informal contact, written suggestion programs, and an other category. The measure was created by summing the items asking about surveys and exit interviews, as these loaded most strongly on the information-gathering factor extracted by factor analysis.

variable_name: mention of an increase in the number of women
description: From an open-ended question about the changes in the U.S. workforce composition that had most affected their firms in the prior five years, this variable was the sum of the number of times a respondent mentioned either an increase in the number of women in management positions in his or her firm or an increase in the number of women in the organization in general.

variable_name: mention of changes in family structure
description: From the same open-ended question, this variable was the sum of the number of times a respondent mentioned an increase in employees in dual-career families or increases in the workforce's demand for more flexibility, help with child care, changed benefits, and so forth.

Respondents judged how likely the growing number of dual-career couples and single employees with responsibility for the care of children and/or adult dependents would be to impact the productivity, rates of absenteeism, turnover, refusals of relocation offers, and organizational commitment of their workforces if not responded to adequately. Responses were on a seven-point scale (1 = unlikely, 7 = extremely likely) for each of the effects; factor analysis indicated that all items loaded onto a single factor and the coefficient alpha was .86.

Dissent within strategic decision-making teams was measured by two items based on Rahim's (1982) Intragroup Conflict Inventory. The items asked the extent to which strategic decision makers openly expressed a difference of opinion during the process of making the decision. Responses were summed and aggregated to the team level.
scale: seven-point Likert-type, anchored 1 'to a small extent', 4 'to a moderate extent', 7 'to a large extent'
time_window: during the focal strategic decision-making process

description: The loyalty items were based on Butler's (1991) Conditions of Trust Inventory and measured the characteristic of disinclination toward opportunism. Responses were on a seven-point Likert-type scale anchored 1 'strongly disagree', 4 'neither agree nor disagree', 7 'strongly agree', and negatively worded items were reverse-coded so that more of the attribute corresponded to a higher value. Sum scores were calculated and aggregated to the team level.

The competence items were based on Butler's (1991) Conditions of Trust Inventory and measure the extent to which team members were perceived as being skillful and reliable in performing their jobs. Responses were on a seven-point Likert-type scale anchored 1 'strongly disagree', 4 'neither agree nor disagree', 7 'strongly agree', and negatively worded items were reverse-coded. Sum scores were calculated and aggregated to the team level.

Commitment to the identified strategic decision was measured by adapting six items from the short form of the Organizational Commitment Questionnaire developed by Mowday, Steers, and Porter (1979). The wording was changed to reflect team members' attitudes toward the strategic decision rather than their organization, so that the items measured the extent to which team members were willing to stick with the decision through implementation and exert effort to see it implemented. Responses were on a seven-point Likert-type scale and summed and aggregated to the team level.

The quality of the identified strategic decision was measured by seven items derived from recommendations of Tilles (1963) and Schweiger and colleagues (1986) for assessing the quality of strategic decisions. The items asked team members' perceptions of the quality of the information used in making the decision, whether the decision fit their hospital's current strategy, whether the decision was financially responsible, and whether the decision contributed to the hospital's overall effectiveness. Responses were on a seven-point Likert-type scale and summed and aggregated to the team level.

Single item selected from multiple items developed for stakeholder power, using the item with the highest interitem correlation. CEOs rated the item for each of Freeman's five generic stakeholder groups on a seven-point Likert scale, with reference to their interactions with the group during the past month.

Single item selected from multiple items developed for stakeholder legitimacy, using the item with the highest interitem correlation. CEOs rated the item for each of Freeman's five generic stakeholder groups on a seven-point Likert scale, with reference to their interactions with the group during the past month.

Single item selected from multiple items developed for stakeholder urgency, using the item with the highest interitem correlation. CEOs rated the item for each of Freeman's five generic stakeholder groups on a seven-point Likert scale, with reference to their interactions with the group during the past month.

Single item: 'This stakeholder group was highly salient to our organization (definition: received high priority from our management team).' CEOs rated the item for each of Freeman's five generic stakeholder groups on a seven-point Likert scale, with reference to their interactions with the group during the past month.

variable_name: cumulative number of stakeholder attributes above threshold
description: Following Mitchell and Agle's decision structure, the absence or presence of the stakeholder attributes was quantified relative to a threshold value for each attribute, set at the mean value on that attribute in the sample. The cumulative number of stakeholder attributes above the threshold level for each stakeholder was then regressed against the salience of that stakeholder.

Computed as the sum of four Rokeach items: 'a comfortable life (a prosperous life),' 'helpful (working for the welfare of others),' 'compassion (feeling empathy for others),' and 'wealth (making money for myself and family).' The Likert scales for the comfortable life and wealth items were reversed so that higher values indicate more other-regarding values. Respondents rated each item on a seven-point Likert scale from 1 (least important) to 7 (most important).
scale: 1 = least important to 7 = most important; sum of four items

description: A single scale combining items from the economics and ethics scales of a shortened Aupperle CSR instrument. The ethics items represent an other-regarding posture and the economics items represent a self-interested posture; the economics items were reversed by subtracting their ratings from zero and then added to the ethics items to form the values scale.

Four measures from the KLD social index: employee relations (combining employee relations and treatment of women and minorities), community relations, environment, and products. Each was measured on a five-point scale ranging from -2 to +2 and industry-adjusted by subtracting or adding the industry mean for each measure. Ratings were averaged over 1996 and 1997 unless data were unavailable for 1996 or the CEO had assumed the position during 1996, in which case only 1997 was used. An overall CSP measure was the aggregate of the four measures.
time_window: 1996 and 1997; averaged over two years unless data were unavailable or CEO took office in 1996

variable_name: return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE)
description: ROA and ROE were obtained from COMPUSTAT for 1996 and 1997 and averaged over the two years unless the CEO had assumed the position in 1996, in which case only 1997 was used. Industry effects were controlled by subtracting the average industry ROA and ROE, based on the firm's dominant four-digit Standard Industrial Classification code, from each firm's ROA and ROE.
time_window: 1996 and 1997; averaged over two years unless CEO took office in 1996

variable_name: Corporate social performance and corporate financial performance
description: Corporate performance was measured with two sets of variables: industry-adjusted KLD ratings of employee relations, community relations, environment and products (corporate social performance, averaged over 1996 and 1997), and industry-adjusted ROA and ROE from COMPUSTAT averaged over 1996 and 1997.

CEO values were measured with two surveyed scales: a sum of Rokeach items on self-interested versus other-regarding values (comfortable life, helpful, compassion, wealth, with the first and last reversed), and a single Aupperle scale combining ethics items with reversed economics items (alpha = .86). Both were analyzed separately.

The plant managers were requested to allocate 100 points across five subcategories of environmental technologies based on total use of capital, operating, and managerial resources over the last two years. The sum of values reported for product and process adaptation technologies was the pollution prevention index, which was rescaled to range from 0 to 1.

From the same forced-choice allocation of 100 points across five subcategories of environmental technologies, the sum for remediation and end-of-pipe technologies was the pollution control index. The index was rescaled to range from 0 to 1.

Because of the forced-choice instrument, the management systems index was equal to 100 minus the sum of the pollution prevention and pollution control indexes. The index was rescaled to range from 0 to 1.

Managers assessed how well their plants were performing relative to their competitors at the time of the survey on a seven-point Likert-type scale (much worse than competitors, 1; about the same, 4; much better than competitors, 7). Scale items for four factors were reproduced from the second round of the international survey used by the Global Manufacturing Research Group: two items for cost, one for product quality, three for speed, and three for flexibility performance. Factor analysis on the nine items confirmed four factors; the items for each factor were averaged.
time_window: at the time of the survey (1994)

description: Objective measures were requested both at the time of the survey and two years earlier (1992): first-pass quality, the percentage of products that meet quality standards after all operations are initially completed; delivery speed (days); on-time delivery; and throughput time (days). Each of the three objective measures of speed performance was significantly correlated in the expected direction with its respective perceptual scale item, whereas first-pass quality did not correlate significantly with the perceptual measure of quality.

The total environmental release and transfer of hazardous pollutants was analyzed at the plant level and termed TRI releases. Data were extracted for 1992 and 1994, and the 1992 data were corrected for changes in production volume over the two-year period. A natural logarithmic transformation was used because of the enormous variation and heteroscedasticity; for nonreporting plants an estimate equal to the reported minimum was used.

Following Daft and colleagues' formula, the sum of the rate-of-change items and the complexity items was multiplied by the sum of the importance items to create the strategic uncertainty variable: strategic uncertainty = (rate of change + complexity) x importance. It is built from 21 items, 7 per environmental variable.

Using a matrix format, the frequency with which participants collected or received information about each of the seven environmental sectors was measured on a five-point scale (5 = daily, 4 = weekly, 3 = monthly, 2 = a few times per year, 1 = less than once a year). Four matrixes, one for each mode of information scanning, contained 7 items each, for a total of 28 items measuring scanning, and the format allowed examination of frequency on a per sector or per information mode basis, as well as total scanning across all sectors and modes.
