scale: 5 = daily, 4 = weekly, 3 = monthly, 2 = a few times per year, 1 = less than once a year

description: Respondents evaluated the accessibility of each information mode on a five-point scale adapted from Culnan (1983; 5 = extremely accessible, 1 = not very accessible at all), resulting in a four-item measure of total perceived accessibility.
scale: 5 = extremely accessible, 1 = not very accessible at all

description: Frequency of scanning of personal sources of information, built from the personal external and personal internal matrixes of the scanning instrument. Each matrix contains seven items, one per environmental sector, rated on the five-point frequency scale (5 = daily, 1 = less than once a year).
scale: 5 = daily to 1 = less than once a year

description: Frequency of scanning of impersonal sources of information, built from the impersonal external and impersonal internal matrixes of the scanning instrument. Each matrix contains seven items, one per environmental sector, rated on the five-point frequency scale (5 = daily, 1 = less than once a year).
scale: 5 = daily to 1 = less than once a year

description: Frequency of scanning of external sources of information, built from the personal external and impersonal external matrixes of the scanning instrument. Each matrix contains seven items, one per environmental sector, rated on the five-point frequency scale (5 = daily, 1 = less than once a year).
scale: 5 = daily to 1 = less than once a year

description: Frequency of scanning of internal sources of information, built from the personal internal and impersonal internal matrixes of the scanning instrument. Each matrix contains seven items, one per environmental sector, rated on the five-point frequency scale (5 = daily, 1 = less than once a year).
scale: 5 = daily to 1 = less than once a year

description: The seven environmental sectors rated by respondents are political/legal, competition, economic, sociocultural, technology, customer/market, and resources; the authors compare sectors classified as task environment and general environment sectors when ranking them by perceived strategic uncertainty.

Seven items, one for each environmental sector, measured on Daft and colleagues' five-point Likert scale (5 = very high, 1 = very low) and defined as the frequency and speed of change in the trends, issues and conditions in each environmental sector.

Seven items, one for each environmental sector, measured on a five-point Likert scale (5 = very high, 1 = very low) and defined as the number and diversity of events occurring in environmental sectors outside the operations of the company; the measurement focused on heterogeneity.

Seven items, one for each environmental sector, measured on a five-point Likert scale (5 = very high, 1 = very low); respondents were asked how important they consider each environmental sector to be in accomplishing their company's goals.

The venture creation decision was measured with a dichotomous variable (coded yes/no) based on a positive response to either one of two questions. The two questions capture a completed venture creation decision and a reasonable experiential period in which venturing scripts could develop, be validated, and mastered.

Measured with a paired script cue approach: respondents selected between a script-consistent expert cue and a socially desirable distracter cue. Selection of a script cue consistent with expert mastery was coded 1, and selection of a distracter was coded 0. Because the items are independent pieces of evidence, they are formative indicators and were added together to create interval-scaled variables. The summed scale was recoded into high, medium, and low categories for hypothesis tests.
scale: summed 0/1 cue items, recoded into high, medium, and low categories

description: Measured with the same paired script cue approach; selection of a cue consistent with expert mastery was coded 1 and distracter selection was coded 0. The independent formative items were summed into an interval-scaled variable, which was then recoded into high, medium, and low categories for the analysis.
scale: summed 0/1 cue items, recoded into high, medium, and low categories

description: Measured with the paired script cue approach; expert-consistent cue selection was coded 1 and distracter selection was coded 0. The formative items were added together into an interval-scaled variable and recoded into high, medium, and low categories for hypothesis tests.
scale: summed 0/1 cue items, recoded into high, medium, and low categories

description: The cultural value dimension of individualism was measured with Hofstede's (1980) ordinal assessment for six of the countries; China's score was approximated using McGrath, MacMillan, Yang, and Tsai's (1992) study. Countries were recoded into high, medium, and low groupings on the basis of proximity of country scores: the United States, Canada, and Australia comprised the high-individualism group, Japan and Mexico the medium-individualism group, and Chile and China the low-individualism group.
scale: ordinal country scores recoded into three groups

description: The cultural value dimension of power distance was measured with Hofstede's (1980) ordinal assessment for six of the countries, with China's score approximated using McGrath, MacMillan, Yang, and Tsai's (1992) study. Countries were recoded into low, medium, and high power distance groupings: the United States, Canada, and Australia (low), Japan and China (medium), and Chile and Mexico (high).
scale: ordinal country scores recoded into three groups

variable_name: Individualism and power distance country groups
description: Cultural values were measured as the individualism and power distance of the respondent's country, using Hofstede's (1980) scores for six countries and an approximated score for China. Countries were recoded into high, medium and low groups on each dimension.
scale: ordinal country scores recoded to 3 groups

description: Cognitive scripts were measured indirectly with a paired script cue approach: respondents chose between a script cue consistent with expert mastery (coded 1) and a socially desirable distracter (coded 0). The items were summed into interval-scaled scores for arrangements, willingness and ability scripts, which were then recoded into high, medium and low.

An index following Zajac and Westphal (1996) that combines the three most widely used measures of CEO power: the proportion of the firm's outstanding shares held by the incumbent, the incumbent's tenure as CEO in years, and a dummy variable for CEO duality (1 if the CEO was also board chair, 0 otherwise). The stockholding proportion and tenure were standardized and summed, and the duality dummy was then added to the index. Because the index was used in interactions, the final measure was standardized to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

An index derived in a manner similar to CEO power. The percentage of outside directors on the board during each year was standardized and became the first component. The proportion of the firm's outstanding shares owned by outside directors and the proportion of shares held by large outside owners (those holding at least 5 percent of outstanding shares) were summed, and this sum, standardized, became the second component. The two standardized components were summed to create the index, and the final measure was then standardized for use in interaction terms.

Each firm's ROA was calculated as income before extraordinary items and discontinued operations divided by net assets as reported during the fiscal year prior to the year in which the dependent variable (heir apparent status) was recorded. Given the diversity of industries in the sample, industry-average ROA for that year was calculated at the two-digit SIC level and deducted from the firm's ROA. The measure was standardized to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
time_window: the fiscal year prior to the year the dependent variable was recorded

description: Daily returns to shareholders from CRSP tapes were compounded over each fiscal year; these returns are already adjusted for dividends and stock splits, so the compounded measure reflects the returns shareholders realized at the end of a fiscal year from a $1.00 investment made on the first day of the fiscal year. This return was then adjusted for a parallel level of return that would have been realized if $1.00 had been invested in a fully diversified portfolio rather than in the firm's stock alone. Because the measure was used in interaction terms, it was standardized to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

The number of years the heir apparent was employed in the firm at the time he or she became the heir apparent. This treatment creates a fine-grained distinction between insider and outsider heirs apparent; 30 heirs apparent in the sample came directly to the position from outside their firms, that is, their company tenure was 0.
time_window: at the time of appointment as heir apparent

description: Coded 1 if the heir apparent was also a member of the firm's board of directors and as 0 otherwise.

Examining the officer lists in annual reports at the end of each fiscal year, the authors used a categorical variable to denote heir apparent status, with 0 representing a non-event-occurrence observation or a right-truncated observation (the heir apparent continued in the existing position), 1 representing promotion to the CEO position, and 2 representing exit from the firm. These three categories comprised the dependent variable in the event history analysis, with the holding position as the comparison group; among the 382 heir-apparent-years there were 286 non-event-occurrence or right-truncated observations, 65 promotions, and 31 exits.

The same categorical dependent variable of heir apparent status was used for the exit outcome: 0 for a non-event-occurrence or right-truncated observation (the heir apparent continued in the existing position), 1 for promotion to the CEO position, and 2 for exit from the firm. Exit was modeled simultaneously with promotion as a competing event relative to continuation. Of the 31 heir apparent exits, 9 occurred along with a CEO succession and 22 occurred before a CEO succession.

A cumulative count of instances of institutional activism. Each firm was assigned a value of 0 for 1986, and after the firm's first instance of activism the count was set to 1, after the second instance to 2, and so on. Instances included announced opposition to management, initiation of a shareholder proposal, announcement of direct negotiation with management, and initiation of proxy contests, identified from media and governance publications and cross-verified against proxy statements by three raters whose combined ratings were used.
time_window: cumulative through year t-2 in the decomposed model

description: The number of instances of institutional activism taking place in a given year (year t-1), as distinguished from cumulative institutional activism. The same set of activism actions was used and identified with multiple raters from the media and governance publications and cross-verified against proxy statements.
Total expenditures in research and development expressed as a percentage of sales. Data were obtained from COMPUSTAT. The measure is the dependent variable in the R&D inputs models.

The number of new products announced by a firm in a year, identified by examining announcements in the Wall Street Journal Index. A team of three knowledgeable raters not involved in formulating the hypotheses independently evaluated the entire set of announcements; their ratings had a within-group interrater reliability of 0.85 and the combined ratings were used to develop the final measure.

Proxy-based activism included instances initiated through the formal proxy machinery, including shareholder proposals and proxy contest initiations. Non-proxy-based activism included public announcements or instances of negotiation reported in the press. Activism was separated into these two categories in the models of R&D inputs.
A dummy variable with a value of 1 if Tobin's Q (the ratio of market value of assets to their replacement value) exceeded 1 and 0 otherwise.

A dummy variable that took on a value of 1 for firms in high-tech industries with firm R&D intensity below the industry average, based on the primary two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code, and 0 otherwise.
The percentage of ownership by institutions that engage in activism.
The number of directors without affiliations to a firm as a proportion of the total number of directors, calculated with the procedure described by Daily and Dalton (1994).

Estimated with data envelopment analysis, following past research on investor-owned utilities. Total sales and dispositions of energy in megawatt hours were used as outputs; the inputs were spending on total production, transmission, distribution, and general plant plus the total number of employees and the amount of purchased power. The efficiency scores ranged from a minimum of 0.32, on a scale of 0 to 1, to a maximum of 1.00, and the mean score for the 150 electric utilities was 0.78.

Air pollution was the ratio of each utility's air pollution plant value to total plant value and water pollution was the ratio of each utility's water pollution plant value to total plant value. These variables captured utilities' investment exposure to different types of pollution control requirements, with firms' spending on different types of pollution control activities serving as a proxy for differences in the flexibility of various regulations.

Waste pollution was the ratio of waste pollution plant value to total plant value. It captured utilities' investment exposure to solid waste pollution control requirements, whose regulations the authors describe as flexible and granting discretion.

Four items assessed the importance, in a given project, of team members' demonstrating an understanding of project objectives, technical knowledge, awareness of project details, and devoting sufficient time to the project. Items were rated on a scale ranging from 1, 'not very important,' to 5, 'very important.' Responses of project informants were averaged to form project-level scales.
scale: 1 = not very important to 5 = very important
time_window: surveys every six months; analyses used time 1, time L - 1, and time L panels

description: Four items gauged the importance, in a given project, of the project schedule, interim goals, and test results for tracking progress. Monitoring items were rated on a scale ranging from 1, 'not very important,' to 5, 'very important,' and were averaged across respondents to the project level.
scale: 1 = not very important to 5 = very important
time_window: surveys every six months; analyses used time 1, time L - 1, and time L panels

description: A three-item measure assessed the degree to which teams received useful information from regulatory and marketing personnel on technical and commercial issues. Items were rated from 1, 'little useful information,' to 5, 'much useful information,' and averaged across respondents to the project level.
scale: 1 = little useful information to 5 = much useful information
time_window: surveys every six months; analyses used time 1, time L - 1, and time L panels

description: Three items measured the extent to which corporate executives, an expert review board, and divisional development research personnel reviewed the project. Items were rated from 1, 'never evaluate,' to 5, 'often evaluate,' and averaged across respondents to the project level.
time_window: surveys every six months; analyses used time 1, time L - 1, and time L panels

description: Three items measured the extent to which team members felt they had decision-making authority and accountability. Items were rated from 1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'a great deal,' and averaged across respondents to the project level.
scale: 1 = not at all to 5 = a great deal
time_window: surveys every six months; analyses used time 1, time L - 1, and time L panels

description: Three items gauged whether management was becoming more involved in project details (for instance, altering the budget and priorities) and providing feedback and technical and commercial information. Items were rated from 1, 'never,' to 5, 'often,' and averaged across respondents to the project level.
time_window: surveys every six months; analyses used time 1, time L - 1, and time L panels

description: A seven-item technical knowledge measure gauged the probability that a project would yield valuable technical knowledge, suggest new markets, promise a major breakthrough or an incremental advance, and help in ongoing projects. Respondents assigned probabilities between 0 and 100 percent, and the measure used the averaged judgments of the project manager and his or her department head.
time_window: time L - 1 and time L panels

description: Four items assessed the probability that the project would meet its commercial objectives—that is, develop a product with reasonable manufacturing costs that could gain its projected market share. Respondents assigned probabilities between 0 and 100 percent, and the measure used the averaged judgments of the project manager and his or her department head.
time_window: time L - 1 and time L panels

description: Three items assessed the extent to which a project was progressing within projected cost levels. Items were rated from 1, 'way under budget,' to 5, 'way over budget,' and the measure used the averaged judgments of the project manager and his or her department head; higher values therefore indicate poorer budgetary efficiency.
scale: 1 = way under budget to 5 = way over budget
time_window: time L - 1 and time L panels

description: A two-item measure labeled on time gauged whether the project was meeting its schedule, rated from 1, 'way behind schedule,' to 5, 'way ahead of schedule.' The measure used the averaged judgments of the project manager and his or her department head.
scale: 1 = way behind schedule to 5 = way ahead of schedule
time_window: time L - 1 and time L panels

description: Ten reverse-coded items indicated the degree to which team members were familiar with the science and technology used in a project and the division's level of expertise in this area, so that technical uncertainty was a function of (low) familiarity. Median splits on a project's scores at each panel created three categories: projects with decreasing technical uncertainty were coded -1, projects with unchanging uncertainty were coded 0, and projects facing rising uncertainty were coded 1.
time_window: scores at time 1, time L - 1, and time L

description: Five reverse-coded items assessed a firm's experience commercializing (manufacturing, packaging, advertising, selling, and distributing) products like the developing product, so that commercial uncertainty was a function of (low) experience. Because commercial uncertainty remained stable over time, three categories were formed: low, unchanging (coded 1); varied or changing (coded 0); and high, unchanging (coded 1).
scale: three categories (low unchanging = 1, varied or changing = 0, high unchanging = 1)
time_window: scores at time 1, time L - 1, and time L

variable_name: Emergent style (monitoring understandings, information gathering, participative control)
description: Emergent project management style was measured with three survey scales, one per activity: monitoring understandings (4 items), information gathering (3 items) and participative control (3 items). Items were rated on 1 to 5 scales and averaged across respondents to the project level.

variable_name: Project performance (technical knowledge, commercial objectives, within budget, on time)
description: Project performance was measured with perceptual measures from the averaged judgments of the project manager and his or her department head: technical knowledge and commercial objectives (innovation facets, probabilities from 0 to 100) and within budget and on time (efficiency facets, 1 to 5 ratings).

variable_name: Planned style (monitoring milestones, formal review, directive control)
description: Planned project management style was measured with three survey scales, one per activity: monitoring milestones (4 items), formal review (3 items) and directive control (3 items). Items were rated on 1 to 5 scales and averaged across respondents to the project level.

Defined by the first year that a professional finance association was in existence. For each year, each business and professional association in existence was coded, enabling disaggregation of the professional and business subpopulations; coding was done by consulting the association yearbooks and government surveys that describe what associations do and whom they represent, and phone calls were made in difficult cases. The dependent variable is the annual count of foundings in the professional subpopulation.
level: field-year (annual foundings in the professional finance association population)

variable_name: Percent change in market concentration for financial intermediaries index (reverse-coded)
description: For each year a Herfindahl index, which equals the sum of the squared market shares of all the actors in an industry or field, was calculated from assets managed by all financial intermediary types (insurers, commercial banks, mutual funds, and so forth). The index is constrained to be between 1 and 0, and the closer it is to 1 the more concentrated the market. The variable is the percent change in this index; a decline in the index indicates the fall of commercial bank dominance and a general rise in competition among intermediary forms. This variable was reverse-coded for the purposes of testing Hypothesis 1.
scale: percent change in a Herfindahl index (0 to 1)
time_window: 1945-1993 (measured as change; all independent variables are lagged by one year)

variable_name: Percent change in use of the term "financial services"
description: The growing pervasiveness of the retail-oriented market logic was tracked by calculating the percent change in use of the term "financial services" in 139 economic journals whose 1969-93 issues are contained in the database EconLit. The variable is measured in change terms because the absolute levels are less important than the degree to which use of the term is increasing.

variable_name: Growth rate of portfolio management knowledge
description: The percentage of articles published in the Journal of Finance that focused on portfolio management. The series was calculated from 1946, the publication year of volume 1 of the journal, through 1983 using the journal's 1985 cumulative index, which categorized articles in a fashion that enabled calculation of this variable. The author supplemented this time series by coding articles that focused on portfolio management from 1984 through 1993.

Standardized scores were calculated from the absolute values of change on each scale, standardized to a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1; a mean of these scores was generated to indicate the relative amount of change that took place in each group between 1984 and 1986, 1986 and 1988, 1988 and 1992, and 1992 and 1996. A positive score indicates above-average change activity and a negative score lower-than-average change activity. Absolute values were used because some scales changed in a negative direction and some organizations experienced reversals.
time_window: change between consecutive data collection points (1984-86, 1986-88, 1988-92, 1992-96)

description: To gain this designation an organization had to achieve, and maintain until 1996, executive office archetype status, and it had to have started the transition from a position outside the embryonic executive office archetype so that the change counted as radical. Archetypal status was allocated to an NSO displaying appropriate scores on 11 or more of the 14 scales.

Five scales: technical specialization was determined by the number of teams an NSO operated, the number of coaches used, the breakdown of the coaching staff by technical expertise and gender, and the existence of committees involved with national team administration. Support staff specialization, professional specialization, and volunteer specialization recorded whether positions of given types existed; for these three scales the response categories were 'yes,' 'no,' and 'not applicable.' Number of committees was a single-item measure of the total number of subunits and committees.
scale: yes/no/not applicable for three scales; counts for the others
time_window: measured at each data collection point (1984, 1986, 1988, 1992, 1996)

description: Five scales of between four and ten items each, covering administrative operations, athlete services, evaluation procedures, support operations, and decision making. They measured the extent to which an NSO made use of formal plans, policies, and procedures and engaged with formal monitoring, evaluation, and communication systems. Responses ranged from a simple 'yes,' 'no,' or 'not applicable' designation to a Likert-type rating from 0, indicating that no formal procedures existed, to 4, indicating that extensive formal procedures were in place; informants also reported whether their NSO had become more or less formalized since the previous data collection.
scale: 0 (no formal procedures) to 4 (extensive formal procedures) on Likert-type items; yes/no/not applicable on others
time_window: measured at each data collection point (1984, 1986, 1988, 1992, 1996)

description: Four scales of six decision-making items each, covering topics central to the organization such as selection of national team athletes, participation in national team training programs, selection of coaches, development of coaches and officials, and which athletes receive direct federal funding. The final decision maker scale recorded the level at which a decision was made, scored from 6 (volunteer board of directors) down to 1 (a non-organization member). The levels in making decision scale measured the number of individuals from differing hierarchical levels involved in each decision; professional decisions counted the key decisions made by professional staff; and decisions without volunteers counted the key decisions into which volunteer members had no input.
scale: 1-6 for the final decision maker scale; counts for the other scales
time_window: measured at each data collection point (1984, 1986, 1988, 1992, 1996)

description: Using a multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) and polynomial contrasts, the authors examined the trend toward the means for each scale over each time period. A significant t-value indicates rejection of the null hypothesis that the variable changed in a nonlinear manner, so a significant t shows a linear trend and a nonsignificant t suggests a nonlinear trend such as a quadratic, cubic, or quartic curve, indicating delays, reversals, and/or oscillations.

Radical transformation was identified from archetype classification on 14 specialization, formalization and centralization scales. An organization with 11 or more appropriate scale scores had full archetypal status, and the 8 organizations that moved from outside the executive office archetype in 1984 to full status by 1996 were classed as having made a radical transition (group 1).

The high-impact element, decision-making structure, was measured with four centralization scales of six decision items each: final decision maker (level at which decisions were made), levels involved in making decisions, number of decisions made by professional staff, and number of decisions without volunteer input. A decision-making formalization scale was also used.
A dummy variable, coded 1 indicating that the CEO of a sample company had exercised stock options during a focal year, and 0 indicating otherwise.

The percentage of shares owned by a CEO, net of options exercised during the year. To examine curvilinear relationships with stock option exercise, a quadratic term, the square of the CEO's ownership percentage, was also included in the analysis. Continuous variables were centered around the mean following Aiken and West (1991:130).
The difference in a CEO's equity ownership percentage between 1995 and 1996.
A dummy variable coded 1 for a negative change in CEO equity from 1995 to 1996.
A firm's annualized market performance for three years (1996 to 1998). The measure parallels that used by Carpenter and Yermack (2000).
A firm's average return on assets over the subsequent three years (1996 to 1998).

CEO origin was classified into three categories: intrafirm, intraindustry, and outside-industry. Intrafirm succession was defined as one in which an executive with firm tenure of at least two years had been promoted to the CEO position. Among the 220 successions, there were 132 intrafirm successions.

Intraindustry succession was defined as one in which the successor CEO had firm tenure of less than two years but had industry tenure of at least two years in the same four-digit industry that the hiring firm was in. To classify the industry origin of a new CEO, the authors obtained a new CEO's work history and ascertained whether the CEO had prior work experience of at least two years in the four-digit industry of the hiring firm. Among the 220 successions, there were 34 intraindustry successions.

An heir apparent was identified as any officer who was the only person in the firm holding the title of president or of COO or both and who was at least five years younger than the incumbent CEO. The variable was coded 1 if, in the year preceding succession, there was such an individual in a firm, and 0 otherwise. Four cases in which a president/COO had firm tenure of less than two years were recoded as having no heir apparent.
The total number of executives, other than a firm's current CEO and heir apparent, who were also members of the board of directors.

Six strategic dimensions were used to create a composite measure. Treating t as the succession year, a firm's presuccession five-year variance was computed for each strategic dimension; variance scores for each dimension were standardized by the sample and multiplied by -1 to bring the measures in line with the concept of persistence; the average of the six standardized dimensions yielded the overall measure.
time_window: t-4 through t, where t is the succession year

variable_name: number of similarly sized and larger firms in an industry
description: Operationally defined as the natural logarithm of the number of firms in a focal firm's primary industry whose sales in the year prior to succession were equal to or larger than half of the focal firm's sales. Firm size data were obtained from COMPUSTAT.

The same six strategic dimensions used for strategic persistence were used. Variance within the similarly sized and larger firms for each strategic dimension was computed for the year prior to a succession; variance scores were standardized by the sample and multiplied by -1 to bring the measures in line with the concept of homogeneity; the average of the six standardized dimensions yielded the overall measure.

Measured via the same six strategic dimensions. A focal firm's score on each strategic dimension (for the year prior to succession) was first standardized by its industry and then multiplied by -1 to bring the measure in line with the concept of conformity (an absence of difference from other firms in the industry); the average of the six standardized dimensions yielded the overall measure.

The event is a firm's announcement in the Wall Street Journal of a work-family human resource initiative. Two researchers identified the announcements with 88.8 percent interrater agreement, and disagreed-upon announcements were coded by forced rater agreement. Announcements were classified into dependent care, flexible work arrangements, family stress, and general work-family categories. The reported analyses use only announcements without confounding events (n = 130).

Excess returns were calculated as the difference between the actual firm return and the firm's expected value, where expected value comes from the relation between the firm's shareholder return and the return of an equally weighted diversified portfolio of AMEX, NYSE and Nasdaq stocks estimated over 255 trading days. The dependent variable was either the excess return for the three possible one-day windows or cumulative excess returns for the various two- and three-day windows around the announcement.
time_window: one-, two- and three-day event windows; 255 trading days estimation period

description: A dummy variable assigned a value of 1 if the firm was classified as within a high-tech industry and a 0 otherwise. High-tech industries are those in which the number of research and development workers was at least 50 percent higher than the average proportion of all industries surveyed.

variable_name: proportion of women in an industry
description: Using the three-digit SIC code, the proportion of female employees, expressed as a percentage, within an industry one year prior to a work-family announcement. A one-year-lagged value of the variable was included in the analyses.

Using the three-digit SIC code and industry-level unemployment rates, the industry unemployment rate one year prior to a work-family announcement. In the analyses the lagged unemployment rate was expressed as a percentage.

A dummy variable constructed to account for pre- and postlegitimation effects, assigned a value of 0 if an event occurred prior to 1981 and a value of 1 if it occurred in 1981 through 1996. A linear extrapolation from the estimate that approximately 80 percent of large firms had at least one work-family program in 1987 suggests that half of Fortune 500 firms had instituted a program by 1981.

Using the previous audit of each unit as the baseline, changes in organizational structure (consolidation of previously separate activities and new reporting relationships), unit manager, and technology (new major hardware or software) were identified from operating data provided to audit teams. Each type of change was coded as a binary variable (0 = 'no change'; 1 = 'change'), and the overall level of change was measured as a simple count of the different types of changes in each unit, varying from 0 to 3.
time_window: between the previous audit of the unit and the current audit

description: Latent errors were identified by content-analyzing the standardized internal audit reports of each unit; a latent error was any segment that described deviations from procedures and policies. A second analysis of 20 randomly chosen reports (25 percent of the sample) by an independent rater yielded an interrater agreement (Cohen's kappa) of .84.

The risk level for each unit was measured on a seven-point scale developed by a centralized risk management unit at the NAFI, with 7 denoting a high-risk unit (such as foreign exchange trading) and 1 denoting a low-risk unit (like savings accounts operations). The rating was determined on the basis of the total dollar value of the unit's transactions and the specific types of risks inherent in its operations (for instance, liquidity risk, market risk, and exchange risk).

A dichotomous measure based on the section of each prospectus detailing the stock options granted to a firm's CEO in the year prior to its IPO. The text states that 0 equals stock option compensation in the year prior to an IPO and 1 equals the presence of stock option compensation in that time period.

The value of stock option grants in the year prior to the IPO, calculated as mandated by the SEC on the assumption that a firm's stock price will appreciate at a compounded rate of 10 percent annually until the date of expiration. If a CEO was granted more than one set of options in the year prior to an IPO, the individual option grants were summed.

The Black-Scholes valuation of the stock options granted to a CEO in the year preceding an IPO. Because IPO firms have never been publicly traded, the median stock return variation for each firm in an IPO firm's primary industry (two-digit SIC code) in the year prior to the IPO date was used as a proxy for volatility; the interest rate was the yield of the ten-year U.S. treasury bond on the first day of the month of each firm's IPO. Dividends were not included because IPO firms rarely issue dividends, and separate grants were valued and then summed.

The percentage of equity owned by a CEO; the authors relied on the fraction of firm equity a firm's CEO retained after its IPO. Where a CEO owned less than 1 percent of a firm's outstanding equity, that percentage was assumed to equal zero.

Calculated as stock price less book value over stock price, where the stock price equals the stock price at the time of the IPO (the offer price) and book value is the book value of the firm's equity as reported in its financial statements. These data were collected from the prospectuses.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Size was the number of full-time employees at a work site. A logarithmic transformation was applied to induce normality. The variable was collected during all waves and was time-varying.

Respondents were asked in all waves: 'What degree of overall impact does employee drug abuse have on your workplace?' (4 = 'major,' 3 = 'moderate,' 2 = 'minor,' and 1 = 'none'). It is a single-item, time-varying covariate.

Turnover was measured as the average annual rate of voluntary employee exits (average annual voluntary turnover) for a work site. Turnover data were collected in all waves, and the variable was time-varying.

Data on the percentage of male employees at each establishment were collected during all waves. These figures were averaged over time, so the variable was treated as time-invariant; the test-retest reliability for this variable was .82.

variable_name: Year of adoption of applicant drug testing
description: Each HR manager was asked if his or her work site had adopted drug testing of applicants at all interviews, and if the answer was yes, the year of adoption was asked. Since respondents were asked for the year of adoption in all four waves, reliability was checked by comparing responses and differences greater than one year were examined case by case until the inconsistency was resolved.
time_window: waves 1987-88 to 1995; adoption years from 1970 onward

variable_name: Year of adoption of Employee Assistance Program
description: The same respondents were asked for this information in all four waves, and reliability was checked by comparing responses. Figure 1 shows the cumulative number of employers with pre-employment drug-testing programs and those with EAPs by year of adoption.
time_window: waves 1987-88 to 1995; adoption years from 1970 onward

description: Time-varying covariates for the density of adoption of both EAPs and drug testing were calculated for all waves by geographical area. To calculate area densities, each workplace was first coded as located in 1 of the 12 labor markets in Georgia defined by Tolbert and Killian (1987), who used census-based commuting time to identify counties with shared commuting patterns of employees. The variable was calculated as the number of establishments with drug testing (or an EAP) divided by the total number of establishments in the sample from each focal labor market.

Industry densities were the proportions of employers nationwide that had EAPs or drug tests. This information was obtained from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and supplemented with more recent industry percentages for the years 1992-93. Industry type for each workplace was defined via NAICS code, as were the BLS statistics.

Abstracts of periodical articles for which substance abuse treatment or drug testing was listed as the subject were examined via ABI/Inform for 1970 through 2001. Following Abrahamson and Fairchild's (1999) methodology, the total number of words for each year and the total number of words in each content category were counted using the program General Inquirer, which uses the Harvard-IV dictionary and links words within articles to content categories; examples of positive words are 'acceptable,' 'fair,' and 'suitable.' Because the number of articles increased over time, the word counts in each content category were normalized by dividing by the number of articles for each year.

The same content analysis counted the words in the 'negative' content category in the abstracts of periodical articles on substance abuse treatment or drug testing; examples of words the program considers negative are 'abandonment,' 'fail,' and 'objection.' As with positive discourse, counts were normalized by dividing by the number of articles for each year because the number of articles increased over time.

To test Hypothesis 2, a period effect for the federal War on Drugs was coded, assigning the years up to 1986 a value of 1 to represent the time before the War on Drugs declaration; other years were coded 0.

Because the rate of adoption was not linear, the study period was examined in segments. For drug testing, three dummy variables were created, one for 1970-85 adoption, one for 1986-90 adoption, and one for 1991-95 adoption; for EAPs the periods were constructed so that early adoption extended through 1982, with an acceleration phase and a late phase. Moderation was tested by creating variables in which each independent variable interacted with dummy variables for the period.

variable_name: Cumulative implemented suggestions (logged, lagged one month)
description: The cumulative number of employee suggestions implemented at the plant since the gainsharing program began, lagged by one month and entered as a natural logarithm in the regression models. In the depreciation models the authors used a depreciated version in which the depreciation factor lambda is multiplied by the number of cumulative suggestions each period and the resulting product is added to the number of new suggestions implemented in the same period. Data were taken from the plant's suggestion log, which recorded the date each suggestion was submitted, the action taken on it, and the date each accepted suggestion was implemented.
time_window: lagged by one month; cumulative from January 1989

description: Actual cost per unit produced each month, determined by dividing the total costs of production by the number of standard units produced, and entered as a natural logarithm in the regression models. The cost data covered all direct and indirect labor (including overtime), maintenance material, perishable tools, spoilage (scrap), rework (returns), supplies, and other miscellaneous production-related expenses; certain fixed costs for equipment, facilities, and materials were excluded. Managers allocated standard labor hours to each product using standard industrial engineering procedures, so the measure controlled for the effect of monthly fluctuations in product mix on unit costs.

A constant parameter with values between 0 and 1 that is multiplied by the number of cumulative suggestions each period, with the resulting product added to the number of new suggestions implemented in the same period. When lambda equals 1 no depreciation of past knowledge has occurred; when lambda is less than 1 only a fraction of the performance impact of the stock of previous suggestions carries over to subsequent periods. Because theory did not specify an exact rate, the authors estimated lambda with an empirical search, setting it to values from .025 to 1 in increments of .025 across 40 separate regression equations and selecting the value that maximized model fit based on the maximum-likelihood function, and then calculated a 99 percent confidence interval around the point estimate.

A dummy variable coded 1 if a firm received any media coverage on a given day. The authors used a dichotomous variable so that event history modeling techniques could be applied. Only 14 instances out of more than 13,000 firm-day observations involved two media mentions on a given day, and no company received more than two mentions a day.
time_window: post-IPO period (61 trading days after the IPO)

description: The percentage of the total shares a firm has offered that are traded on a given day. Higher turnover indicates greater investor attention to the company. Calculated over days 2-61.

The total number of articles about a firm published from 12 months prior to the IPO's registration with the SEC until two days before the observation day. Pre- and post-IPO articles were aggregated to better capture the level of accumulated media attention. If multiple articles were published about a company on a given day, they are captured in the measure.
time_window: from 12 months prior to SEC registration until two days before the observation day

description: The percentage of IPO shares traded on the day the offering company goes public. The number of shares traded on the day of an IPO is typically much higher than the number traded on subsequent days, so high levels of trading on the first day can be highly salient to investors.
The daily post-IPO media coverage measure lagged by one day, capturing the most recent attentional choices the media could observe.
Daily turnover lagged by one day, capturing the most recent attentional choices investors could observe.

A dummy variable coded 1 if a firm received media coverage containing a positive evaluative statement about the firm on a given day. A trained coder assessed each article as positive, negative, or neutral in its discussion of the company; neutral statements simply reported facts. Articles with relatively equal instances of positive and negative references were coded as neutral. There were no instances in the sample of a company receiving more than one positive article on a given day.

A firm's daily return, which is the percent change in stock price from the end of the prior day to the end of the current day. Daily returns were calculated from day 2 through day 61 because the first day's return is the degree of underpricing an IPO experienced.
Measured the same way as cumulative media coverage and reflects the total number of positive articles about each IPO firm.
time_window: from 12 months prior to SEC registration until two days before the observation day

description: Equals the percent change in stock price ((price end - price initial) / price initial x 100) on the first day of public trading. Underpricing was used to operationalize available investor evaluations because large deviations from expectations (i.e., high underpricing) are likely to be highly salient.
The daily positive post-IPO media coverage measure lagged by one day, capturing the most recent evaluative choices the media could observe.
Daily return lagged by one day, capturing the most recent evaluative choices investors could observe.

A refinement of a larger instrument developed by Podsakoff et al. (1990), limited to one page for the executives surveyed. Five major factors emerged from the refined instrument, and a global variable labeled 'total charisma' was computed as the sum of the raw scores of all the questionnaire items. Individual managers' responses were combined into a single measure of charisma for each CEO; the global scale had an alpha of .94, ICC(1) of .34, ICC(2) of .90, and r*wg(J) of .80.

Measure developed by Ramanujam, Venkatraman, and Camillus (1986), based on four questions assessing a firm's increase in sales, earnings, market share, and return on investment in relation to its competitors since the time of its CEO's ascension. Items were measured on a seven-point Likert scale ranging from 'much better' to 'much worse' and loaded on a single factor. Constructed as the average of the sum of the raw scores for the four items, with alpha of .90, ICC(1) of .69, ICC(2) of .89, and r*wg(J) of .86.
time_window: since the time of the CEO's ascension

description: The cumulative stock return of each firm was measured over the prequestionnaire period (from the announcement of a new CEO until the questionnaires were completed in 1992) and the postquestionnaire period (from 1992 until the same CEO's departure or until the end of 1999, whichever was first). The corresponding average cumulative stock return of the firm's industry, defined by four-digit SIC code, was subtracted to obtain the industry-adjusted stock return, which was then annualized.

Income before extraordinary items divided by the total assets of a firm in a year. Data were obtained from the COMPUSTAT database for each firm for the years of the sample period; the annual measure was corrected by subtracting industry averages and averaged over the pre- and postquestionnaire periods.

Income before extraordinary items divided by the total stockholder equity of a firm in a year. Data were obtained from COMPUSTAT for each firm for the years of the sample period; the annual measure was corrected by subtracting industry averages and averaged over the pre- and postquestionnaire periods.

Income before extraordinary items divided by the net sales of a firm in a year; this measure corresponds to the net profit margin used by Waldman et al. (2001, 2004). Data from COMPUSTAT were corrected by subtracting industry averages and averaged over the pre- and postquestionnaire periods.

Constructed for each firm as the percentage change in sales dollars (or revenues) from one year to the next. COMPUSTAT data were corrected by subtracting industry averages and averaged over the pre- and postquestionnaire periods.

Objective measure of environmental uncertainty used as a proxy, estimated as the annualized standard deviation of daily stock returns of a firm adjusted for average industry volatility, measured over the postquestionnaire (performance) period. It is interpreted as the collective assessment of uncertainty by stock market participants rather than the assessment of managers.

A composite index of the status conferred by three external audiences on individuals. The individual variables used for the composite index were director status, lead actor 1 status, and lead actor 2 status, each coded on a 1-4 scale: 1, no recognition of high status by any of the three audiences; 2, recognition by one of the three; 3, recognition by two of the three; and 4, recognition by all three. The three measures were multiplied to create a single composite measure in which higher values meant higher status, and the quadratic term of the index was used to test for a curvilinear relationship.
scale: 1-4 on each of three audience measures, multiplied into a composite index

description: A count of the number of newcomers included in a film, ranging from 0 to 5, based on the five most important creative and technical personnel categories. An individual was considered new if he or she had not been employed in the industry before 1926. Higher values of the index implied higher exploration.

A composite of three submeasures scored over five dyads: c1, the proportion of dyads containing at least one new resource; c2, the proportion of dyads presenting new combinations of old resources; and c3, the proportion of dyads that were old combinations of old resources. After applying a weight of +1 to c1, 0 to c2, and -1 to c3, the authors computed an average value that ranged from -1 to +1 with 0.2 intervals; higher values indicate higher exploration. A combination was considered new if it had never been employed in the industry before 1926.

Two dichotomous variables represent the hierarchical solutions adopted to coordinate production of a film. The first variable took the value 1 if a film was coordinated by a unit producer, and 0 otherwise (two-layer structure). The second variable took the value 1 if the film was coordinated by a unit producer plus an associate, and 0 otherwise (three-layer structure). The central producer structure (one-layer) was the reference category.

variable_name: team mechanisms (the average score on communication and cohesion)
description: TMT members rated both communication and cohesion on a response scale ranging from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 6, 'strongly agree,' and ratings were averaged to create team-level variables. Confirmatory factor analysis showed that communication and cohesion empirically loaded on one factor in this sample, which the authors call 'team mechanisms,' and this combined factor was used in all subsequent analyses. In the regression models the variable entered is the average score on communication and cohesion.

The authors assessed communication using the four items from the Lester, Meglino, and Korsgaard (2002) scale that focus on communication rather than coordination. Items were, 'Members are willing to share information with other team members about our work,' 'Members of this team enjoy talking to each other,' 'When members talk to each other, there is a great deal of understanding,' and 'Team members are comfortable talking to each other about what needs to be done.' Across TMT members, the reliability of the scale was .92 at the individual level and .97 at the team level, and checks for aggregation yielded acceptable values.

The authors combined three underlying facets identified by Beal et al. (2003) to comprehensively assess team cohesion, including measures of social cohesion (Seashore, 1954), group pride (Festinger, 1950), and team commitment (Kirkman & Rosen, 1999). Items included, 'Members of this team get along with each other very well,' 'I really value being a member of this team,' and 'My team members are all committed to our team.' Across all TMT members, the reliability of the 13-item scale was .93 at the individual level and .97 at the team level, and checks for aggregating team cohesion yielded acceptable values.

The authors measured interdependence with 12 items, 9 from Campion et al.'s (1993) scale, and 3 new items added to enhance reliability (the original alphas ranged from .59 to .68). Items focused on the extent to which tasks performed by members were interrelated within a team and whether member goals, rewards, and feedback were related to the team's objectives and success. Examples included, 'I do very few activities that are not related to goals of the senior management team' and 'Within my team, work performed by other team members is dependent on another's work.' The scale reliability was .80 at the individual level and .95 at the team level, and checks for aggregating team interdependence were acceptable.

CEOs completed Kirkman and Rosen's (1999) six-item measure of team performance. Examples of items are, 'This team meets or exceeds its goals' and 'This team completes its tasks on time.' The alpha reliability for this measure was .81. Ratings were made on a six-point scale, and relying solely on CEO ratings was intended to rule out common method bias as an explanation for relationships with performance.

The authors assessed firm performance the year following survey administration using data provided by the National Credit Union Administration, which uses four key financial ratios of performance: net worth to total assets, which assesses capital adequacy; delinquent loans to total loans and net charge-offs to average loans, which both assess asset quality; and return on average assets (ROA), which assesses earnings. Each score was converted to a Z-score, and the final score reflects the mean over these four measures of organizational performance for the year following the TMT surveys. The alpha reliability for this measure was .65.

Measured as the average of eight items that address the fairness of various procedures used in formulating and managing an alliance, governing exchange, and executing joint decisions and contracts, all on a seven-point Likert scale; one questionable item was omitted from the analysis. The final score was computed in two steps: the mean of the two parties' perceived procedural justice, weighted by the interparty agreement index (r wg) between the two parties.

Measured as the average of four items that capture the fairness of reward and return sharing in view of each party's contributed resources, continued commitment, amount of effort, and level of responsibility, all on a seven-point Likert scale. The final score was the mean of the two parties' perceptions weighted by the interparty agreement index (r wg).

Measured as the average of six items that reflect interpersonal and interactional treatment, all on a seven-point Likert scale. The final score was the mean of the two parties' perceptions weighted by the interparty agreement index (r wg).

Assets turnover was defined as average annual sales divided by average total assets over the three-year period (1998-2000). It was measured with archival data collected from the Jiangsu Commission of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation, obtained from a separate, archival source in an effort to reduce common method variance.

Collected in the initial survey, which asked alliance CEOs questions concerning goal differences between parties. The variable was used to divide the total sample at its mean (4.70) into a high goal difference group (n = 67) and a low goal difference group (n = 60).

The Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ Form 5X) measured the four components of transformational leadership: an eight-item scale for idealized influence and four-item scales for inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration. Respondents indicated the frequency with which each item described their CEO on a five-point Likert response scale (1 = 'not at all,' 5 = 'frequently, if not always'). A higher-order transformational leadership factor explained the common variance among the four components, so ratings were aggregated over dimensions (alpha = .94) and averaged over raters.
level: individual (VP ratings of the CEO), averaged across raters to the leader/team level

description: Three-item scales assessed the importance of each of the seven CEO-identified credit union goals (21 items overall), and each item was rated by all members of a TMT, including the CEO, on a five-point scale (1 = 'strongly disagree,' 5 = 'strongly agree'). High ratings indicated that a respondent believed the specific goal was an important one to which the organization was devoting time and effort. A confirmatory factor analysis of the 21 items showed that seven goal factors captured the variance among the items.

A dyadic goal importance congruence score was calculated for each CEO-VP dyad using the D-statistic, computed as the square root of the sum of the squared differences between VP goal importance ratings and CEO goal importance ratings. The D-statistic was multiplied by -1 so that a high score indicates high levels of similarity about the importance of specific organizational goals between a CEO and an individual VP.

A standard deviation was calculated from the goal importance ratings provided by all TMT members (including the CEO) for each of the seven goals; the standard deviations were then summed, and the sum was multiplied by -1. A high score on this variable implies high goal importance congruence among all TMT members.

A composite of three VP attitudes, all measured on a five-point response scale (1 = 'strongly disagree,' 5 = 'strongly agree'): a five-item overall job satisfaction measure, the nine-item short form of the Organizational Commitment Questionnaire, and three items from the Job Diagnostic Survey assessing satisfaction with the CEO. A higher-order factor analysis showed that a general attitudes factor explained the variance among the three attitudes, and the composite scale exhibited high reliability (alpha = .94).

CEOs rated the performance of each VP using an 11-item scale adapted from existing measures and following Campbell's (1990) performance taxonomy. Items assessed four primary aspects of performance: task performance, communication, teamwork, and leadership. A higher-order factor analysis revealed that a single overall performance factor explained the variance among the four performance factors, and the overall performance scale exhibited high reliability (alpha = .93).

Archival measures of ROA for 2004 were collected from the National Credit Union Administration one year after the second survey administration. The credit union CEOs in the preliminary survey had identified ROA as the most commonly used measure of organizational performance in the industry.

Multi-item measure of the degree to which firms relied on behavioral norms of information exchange, flexibility, and solidarity. Informants indicated the degree to which they were committed to (1) sharing information on plans and schedules, (2) being transparent in regards to intent, (3) being flexible (illustrated in the survey as preferring to work out a new deal when an unexpected situation arises rather than holding each other to the original agreement), and (4) practicing reciprocity and procedural justice in negotiating shares of efforts and results. Responses were tracked on a scale from 1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'to a large degree,' and all measures were standardized.
scale: 1 (not at all) to 5 (to a large degree)
time_window: past three years of the relationship

description: Multi-item measure based on the view that the more contingencies a contract covers, the more complete it is. Informants indicated their level of agreement with the stem statement, 'The supply contracts between your firm and THIS customer fully and clearly specify . . .' for each of three dimensions. Responses were tracked on a scale from 1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'to a large degree,' and all measures were standardized.
scale: 1 (not at all) to 5 (to a large degree)
time_window: past three years of the relationship

description: Multi-item measure of the degree to which human knowledge, skills, physical, and dedicated assets were customized to serve the unique needs of the informant's focal ('THIS') customer. Informants assessed four categories of assets and routines. Responses were tracked on a scale from 1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'to a large degree,' and all measures were standardized.
scale: 1 (not at all) to 5 (to a large degree)
time_window: past three years of the relationship

description: Multi-item measure following the authors' definition of complexity. Respondents agreed or disagreed with the statement, 'To the best of your knowledge, compared to other parts supplied to THIS customer by other firms, the production and exchange of this product is complex because they involve . . .' three characteristics. Responses were tracked on a scale from 1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'to a large degree,' and all measures were standardized.
scale: 1 (not at all) to 5 (to a large degree)
time_window: past three years of the relationship

description: Because exchange renegotiations tend to involve labor-related costs, the authors gauged the amount of time a firm spent preparing for and actually renegotiating supply arrangements and the amount of effort spent in resolving conflicts in the negotiations. They measured the amount of excessive bargaining sessions before efficiently reaching a deal, the amount of excessive haggling in negotiations, and the degree to which partners got agitated with each other. Responses were reverse-coded on these 'costs' to capture 'efficiencies.' Responses were tracked on a scale from 1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'to a large degree,' and all measures were standardized.
scale: 1 (not at all) to 5 (to a large degree)
time_window: past three years of the relationship

description: Following management science work on supply chain performance evaluation, the authors measured the number of inventory turns to support 12 months of sales and the percentage of goods delivered on time. Construct validity analysis suggested that the two performance dimensions measured the same underlying construct. All measures were standardized.
time_window: past three years of the relationship

description: Measured as the difference between the most recently reported earnings and the median earnings for the same period forecast by all analysts who covered a focal firm for whom data were available. The authors state that the variable is inverted so that higher values indicate lower earnings relative to forecasts.

variable_name: announcement of a diversifying corporate acquisition
description: Dichotomous variable coded 1 if a focal firm announced such an acquisition in the prior year and 0 otherwise. Acquisitions were coded as 'diversifying' when the primary two-digit SIC code of the acquiring firm did not match that of the acquired firm; analyst assessments of relatedness on a four-point scale provided additional evidence for the validity of this measure.

Multi-item survey measure of the extent to which top executives granted favors to individual security analysts who covered their firms, asked for up to three firms per analyst and over the relevant time period (since the firm's most recent earnings announcement, since the analyst's most recent recommendation, since an acquisition announcement, or in the prior six months). Some items used a five-point Likert-type response format, other items elicited an 'agree'/'disagree' response, and a series of questions asked how many times executives had performed specific favors; respondents could also list other favors. Using these responses the authors calculated the number of favors granted to the focal analyst by executives at the focal firm; factor analysis loaded the favor-rendering items on one factor and Cronbach's coefficient alpha for the scale was .88.
time_window: since the firm's most recent earnings announcement; since the analyst's most recent recommendation; since a diversifying acquisition announcement; prior six months (varies by survey)

description: Multi-item survey measure of analysts' personal access to top executives, asked since an analyst's most recent recommendation regarding a focal firm; some items asked analysts to assess the general level of personal access to executives at the focal firm and others asked whether they had been denied access in specific ways, and respondents could list specific instances in which they were denied access. The authors calculated the number of instances in which analysts were denied personal access to executives at the focal firm (subsequent to the most recent recommendation and in the previous six months), so higher values indicate less access; factor analysis loaded the count variable and other survey items on one factor and Cronbach's alpha was .93.
time_window: since the analyst's most recent recommendation and the previous six months

variable_name: awareness of another analyst's loss of favors or executive access
description: Survey scale of 'yes' or 'no' questions asking whether analysts were aware of another instance in which an analyst had lost executive favors or personal access to top executives after downgrading a focal firm's stock, for example having difficulty gaining access to top executives after downgrading their stock, having received fewer favors from executives after downgrading the firm, seeming to get blacklisted after issuing a downgrade, being unable to get access after downgrading, or stopping receiving favors after downgrading.

Categorical variable distinguishing three levels of All-America status (1 = 'first team,' 2 = 'second team,' and 3 = 'third team'), based on Institutional Investor's annual survey of large institutional money managers, in which the top three finishers in each industry are designated first, second, and third team All-Americans. Higher values therefore indicate lower status.
scale: 1 = first team, 2 = second team, 3 = third team

description: Operationalized as the total number of analysts employed at the analyst's firm.

Dichotomous variable coded 1 if a focal analyst's most recent stock recommendation involved a downward change from the previous recommendation. In the primary analyses stock recommendations were divided into three basic categories: buy, hold, and sell.
Dichotomous measure coded 1 if a focal analyst downgraded a focal firm's stock during the 12 months after the survey.

Tenure in government service, used as the measure of the depth of a former government official's human and social capital. In calculating service tenure the authors included any time in government service at the local, state, or federal level; in most cases the majority of tenure was accumulated at the last position held in federal government service. Data came from the Lexis-Nexis congressional database, which contains detailed biographies on each government official.

Each individual was categorized on the basis of his or her last position before exiting federal service as a set of three indicator variables coded as 1, indicating membership in the category, and 0 otherwise. The authors expected presidential cabinet members to have the greatest breadth of human and social capital, followed by senators and representatives, respectively.

variable_name: hazard function stratified by breadth (analysis time)
description: To capture whether a former government official's likelihood of accepting an outside board appointment depreciates over time, the authors modeled the hazard function stratified by the former official's breadth of human and social capital after removing the impact of chronological age. Time starts on the date of departure from government service.
time_window: date of departure from office to December 31, 2003, or death

description: A time-varying predictor coded as 1 if none of the three branches of the government were controlled by the individual's political party affiliation, and 0 otherwise. It was built from three dummy variables identifying whether the former government official was of the same political party as the one in control for each branch of government: Senate, House, or White House.
scale: 1 = none of the three branches controlled by the individual's party; 0 = otherwise

description: The key dependent variable, set to 1 when the authors observed a former government official joining the board of a U.S. public corporation as an outside director, and 0 otherwise. It was identified by consulting the Thompson SDC database of SEC filings and news accounts in LexisNexis Universe and other public records.
scale: 1 = joined a board as an outside director; 0 = otherwise

description: A formative six-item scale that relates to resource provision (procurement costs), production process (efficiency of operations, quality of final products), customers (responsiveness, delivery reliability), and financial performance (return on sales). Because a supply chain disruption can have a variety of possibly uncorrelated negative outcomes, a formative model is appropriate; the formative index was created as the unweighted linear sum of the measurement items. Measures refer to the situation after the event.

Buffering was measured with three items reflecting the activities of insulating the firm from its task environment. The activities were derived from the extant supply chain risk management literature and from preliminary interviews, and the items refer to activities that a focal firm pursued or intended to pursue in response to the supply chain disruption of interest. The measure refers to the situation after the event.

Bridging was measured with five items reflecting collaborative supply chain initiatives, improved information exchange, and stricter monitoring of the focal exchange partner. The activities were derived from the extant supply chain risk management literature and from preliminary interviews, and refer to activities that a focal firm pursued or intended to pursue in response to the supply chain disruption of interest. The measure refers to the situation after the event.

Dependence on the exchange partner was measured by a scale proposed by Jap and Ganesan (2000). This four-item scale assesses a firm's inability to replace a given exchange partner, to find an alternative partner, and to achieve its goals in the event that the relationship is terminated. The measure refers specifically to the situation before the supply chain disruption.

A new five-item firm-level scale developed by leveraging items from a scale measuring organizational error management culture and a scale measuring climate for initiative. The adopted and newly developed items reflect the zeal to learn from supply chain disruptions and a state of permanent alertness and dynamic awareness, and were formulated to focus on behaviors rather than on beliefs to reduce proneness to social desirability bias. The measure refers to the situation after the event.

Trust was treated as a second-order factor along two first-order dimensions, credibility and benevolence, using a scale developed by Doney and Cannon (1997). Credibility comprises three items that assess the likelihood that the exchange partner will keep its promises and honor its commitments; benevolence comprises three items that assess the degree to which the exchange partner engages in actions that support the business activities of the focal firm. For final estimation trust was formed as the average of the average scores of credibility and benevolence (all unweighted), and the measure refers specifically to the situation before the supply chain disruption.

Prior experience refers to the number of supply chain disruptions that the focal firm incurred during the prior year related to the product line that was most involved in the specific supply chain disruption. Following Rossiter (2002), a single item was used to measure this variable, which was logarithmically transformed prior to subsequent model estimation. The measure refers specifically to the situation before the supply chain disruption.
time_window: the prior year, before the supply chain disruption

variable_name: CEO social identification with the corporate elite
description: Factor score estimated with the Bartlett method from survey items adapted from Mael and Ashforth's (1992) group identification scale and from Bergami and Bagozzi (2000). One question asks respondents to assess the extent of overlap between their self-definition and the corporate elite using a pictorial display, and another uses a standard Likert-type format. A confirmatory factor analysis showed the items loaded on the same factor, and the scale alpha was .86.
scale: agree/disagree and Likert-type items; pictorial overlap item

description: Count variable indicating the total number of occasions on which a focal CEO provided social support to (1) a fellow member of an informal support group and (2) a fellow CEO-director over the 12 months after CEO identification was measured. Items asked about specific kinds of moral support (e.g., reassuring the recipient that the issue reflects the pressures of being CEO) and informational support (e.g., offering advice on how to cope with the matter, referring the person to someone who could help). Responses of providers and recipients showed intraclass correlations of .85 to .94; alphas ranged from .84 to .93.

Total number of occasions during the prior 12 months on which (1) other informal support group members and (2) fellow CEO-directors who experienced the same problem as the focal CEO provided social support to the CEO; support is aggregated across help providers. The survey asked CEOs to indicate whether others who provided support had mentioned that they previously experienced a similar problem.

Factor scores from three survey scales gauging the extent to which CEOs were experiencing each personal problem: strained marital relations, strained relations with a child, and health problems of a loved one. The items were adapted from scales on the quality of marital and other personal relationships in the counseling psychology literature. Interitem reliabilities were .91, .93, and .94 for the three scales, and CFA showed that the items loaded on three different factors as expected. Measures were lagged by one year.

Factor scores from the short form of the Profile of Mood States (POMS) Depressive Mood Scale and a short form of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression (HAD) Scale. The HAD Scale includes seven Likert-type items (e.g., 'Worrying thoughts go through my mind'; 'I can sit at ease and feel relaxed'; 'I feel tense or wound up'), and the POMS Scale prompts respondents to rate their feelings over the prior week on a list of eight adjectives (e.g., 'unhappy,' 'worthless,' 'hopeless') from 0 ('not at all') to 4 ('extremely'). CFA showed the items loaded on different factors as expected, with alphas of .82 and .86.
scale: 0 (not at all) to 4 (extremely) for POMS adjectives; Likert-type items for HAD

description: Survey scale adapted from measures of interpersonal behavior validated in the leader-member exchange literature, with wording modified using pretest feedback. In the primary analyses the average response to each question among managers and directors at the same firm was calculated. CFA indicated the items loaded on a single factor and interitem reliability was acceptably high (.83-.90); intraclass correlations with focal CEOs ranged from .82 to .93.

Survey scale adapted from measures of interpersonal behavior validated in the leader-member exchange literature, with wording modified using pretest feedback; responses of managers and directors at the same firm were averaged in the primary analyses. CFA indicated a single factor and interitem reliability of .83-.90.

variable_name: seeking input from lower-level managers in making strategic decisions
description: Survey scale adapted from measures of interpersonal behavior validated in the leader-member exchange literature; responses of managers and directors at the same firm were averaged in the primary analyses. CFA indicated a single factor and interitem reliability of .83-.90.

variable_name: seeking information from lower-level managers about progress in implementing corporate strategies
description: Survey scale adapted from measures of interpersonal behavior validated in the leader-member exchange literature, with wording modified using pretest feedback; responses of managers and directors at the same firm were averaged in the primary analyses. CFA indicated a single factor and interitem reliability of .83-.90.

variable_name: soliciting advice and counsel from outside directors
description: Westphal's (1999) survey measure of CEO advice seeking from board members, answered by outside directors. In the primary analyses the average response to each question among directors at the same firm was calculated. CFA indicated a single factor and interitem reliability of .83-.90, and intraclass correlations with focal CEOs ranged from .82 to .93.

variable_name: CEO overall effectiveness as a corporate leader
description: Survey scale adapted from standard measures of leader effectiveness (Eagly et al., 1995), including agree-disagree items and five-point Likert-type items, evaluated by independent directors. The average response to each question among directors at the same firm was calculated. CFA indicated the items loaded on one factor with interitem reliability of .93, and weighted kappas ranged from .86 to .92.
scale: five-point Likert-type items and agree/disagree items

variable_name: five interpersonal leadership behaviors (mentoring, encouraging, input seeking, information seeking, advice seeking)
