description: Measured as the set of five discretionary behaviors, each with its own survey scale: mentoring lower-level managers, encouraging lower-level managers, seeking input from lower-level managers, seeking information from them about strategy implementation, and soliciting advice from outside directors. Scales were adapted from leader-member exchange measures or Westphal's (1999) advice-seeking measure, and responses of managers and directors at the same firm were averaged. Each scale loaded on a single factor (alphas .83 to .90).
level: CEO (rated by managers and directors at the same firm)

description: Ethnicity data from the NHS National Staff Survey in 2007 were used, with respondents choosing from a list of ethnic background options; the five main groupings (white, mixed, Asian/Asian British, black/black British, and other) were used. Blau's index was computed for each hospital as a measure of variety, an indicator of variability in categories interpreted as the probability that any two individuals come from separate categories. A perfectly homogeneous group would have an index of 0 and a perfectly heterogeneous group with an infinite number of equally represented categories an index of 1. Blau's index ranged from .05 to .69 across the focal hospitals, and the proportion of white staff ranged from 43 to 98 percent (mean = 85%).

Data from the most recent U.K. census (2001) informed the ethnic makeup of each 'LSOA' (lower super output area), a spatial unit covering on average around 1,500 people. GIS mapping was used to calculate the distance to each hospital for each LSOA population-weighted centroid, and LSOAs were assigned to the closest hospital geographically; where an organization included more than one hospital building, the total of all LSOAs mapped to any hospital within the organization was taken to be the local community. Blau's index was then calculated in the same way as organizational diversity; it ranged from .01 to .68, and the proportion of white community members ranged from 42 to 99 percent (mean = 91%).

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov Dn statistic, most often used to test the representativeness of a sample for a given population, compares the cumulative distribution of employees in the first x ethnic groups (ordered by frequency) with the cumulative distribution of the community in the same first x groups. It describes the maximum discrepancy between the profile of an organization and the profile of a community, being at its minimum when the profiles are exactly matched and at its maximum when no correspondence exists. For the organizational profile the data were restricted to doctors and nurses, the two groups with most contact with hospital inpatients. To ensure the variable could be interpreted as representativeness, it was reversed before being included in the analysis.

Fourteen questions from the 2007 NHS Acute Inpatient Survey asking about the manner in which hospital staff treated patients were selected for factor analysis; an example item is 'Overall, did you feel you were treated with respect and dignity while you were at the hospital?' For each question a score between 0 and 100 was published for each organization, where 0 represents all patients giving the least favorable response possible and 100 the most favorable response possible. One factor accounted for 64 percent of the variance and all items loaded significantly onto it, with Cronbach's coefficient alpha of .95, so a single score represented civility toward service recipients. The organizational aggregate score was reliable (ICC2 = .94) and within-organization agreement was high (r wg(j) ranging from .83 to .97, mean = .91).

One of the two ratings produced by the Annual Health Check, assessing the overall quality of services provided, rated on a four-point ordinal scale containing the ratings 'weak,' 'fair,' 'good,' and 'excellent.' The outcome is indicative of the extent to which each organization is meeting the government's core standards and making and sustaining improvements in priority areas. In 2007-08, 4 percent of organizations were considered weak with regard to quality of care; 17 percent, fair; 49 percent, good; and 30 percent, excellent.
scale: four-point ordinal: weak, fair, good, excellent

description: The second rating produced by the Annual Health Check, rated on the same four-point ordinal scale. The use of resources outcome draws from financial audits to assess each organization's financial reporting, management, and standing, and the economy, efficiency, and effectiveness of the resources utilized. In 2007-08, 8 percent of organizations were considered weak; 32 percent, fair; 21 percent, good; and 39 percent, excellent.
scale: four-point ordinal: weak, fair, good, excellent

description: A multi-item scale including three continuous-scale indicators that gauge the number of occasions on which other board members mentored a focal first-time director on how to participate in board discussions and the amount of time devoted by other directors to such mentoring, plus a series of questions about whether other board members provided mentoring about specific aspects of the participation process, used to derive four dichotomous measures. In the primary analysis the dichotomous indicators were included together with the three continuous-scale indicators in the confirmatory factor analysis, using an asymptotic distribution-free estimator. The items loaded on a single construct with standardized factor loadings above .85 and interitem reliability of .92.
time_window: six-month period prior to the survey (survey six months after the focal director's appointment)

description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if the focal director was a woman. Data on the gender of corporate directors were provided by a large management consulting firm.
A dichotomous variable coded 1 if the focal director was a racial minority. Data on the race of corporate directors were provided by a large management consulting firm.

variable_name: presence of a female incumbent director (dichotomous)
description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if there was a woman among incumbent directors. Very few boards in the sample included more than one incumbent director from the same minority-status group; in separate models the presence of another director from the same minority group was measured using count variables.

variable_name: presence of a racial minority incumbent director (dichotomous)
description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if there was a racial minority among incumbent directors. Very few boards in the sample included more than one incumbent director from the same minority-status group; in separate models the presence of another director from the same minority group was measured using count variables.

variable_name: number of board appointments at other firms
description: A count variable indicating the number of board appointments acquired by a focal first-time director at other firms in the population, examined in the primary analysis over the subsequent two-year period. In other analyses a dichotomous variable coded 1 if the director received an appointment during the subsequent two-year period was used.
time_window: two years subsequent to the survey date

description: A survey measure of director-decision control behavior developed and validated by Westphal and Stern (2007), included in the initial surveys of incumbent board members and in follow-up surveys of first-time directors and incumbent board members one year after appointment. Items asked about director behavior over the prior six-month period; in the primary analysis the average responses of incumbent directors were used. The scale had interitem reliability of .90 and interrater reliability (weighted kappa) of .82.
time_window: one year after appointment (t + 6 months to t + 12 months); six-month period

variable_name: Number of new knowledge elements explored
description: The frequency of a researcher's exploratory innovation, indicated by the number of knowledge elements that were explored, advanced, and incorporated into his or her inventions and were new to the firm's extant stock of knowledge. A knowledge element (an industrial subclass) was considered newly explored if it was absent from the firm's stock of knowledge between 1976 and 1995 but present in the observation period 1996-2000. The 844 researchers in the sample were granted 2,836 patents in the latter period, containing 1,653 industrial subclasses new to the firm's stock of knowledge.
time_window: 1996-2000, compared with the firm's stock of knowledge 1976-1995

variable_name: Structural holes in the firm's knowledge network
description: The average extent to which knowledge elements tied to a researcher's knowledge elements are disconnected, without having been combined in previous inventions. The firm's knowledge network was built from patenting data between 1976 and 1995, with a tie between two knowledge elements (industrial subclasses) copresent in a patent; dyadic constraints and aggregate constraint Ci were computed and structural holes Si was obtained by subtracting Ci from 2; the average of these values over the knowledge elements in a researcher's knowledge portfolio is the explanatory variable.

variable_name: Degree centrality in the firm's knowledge network
description: The average degree centrality of a researcher's knowledge elements. The degree centrality (the number of combined knowledge elements) of each knowledge element in the firm's knowledge network between 1976 and 1995 was computed first, and then the values of the knowledge elements in a researcher's knowledge portfolio were averaged.

variable_name: Structural holes in the firm's collaboration network
description: The extent to which a researcher's network contacts are disconnected. A firm-wide collaboration network among researchers was constructed from patenting data between 1991 and 1995, with a collaboration tie between two researchers listed among a patent's authors; dyadic constraints were summed into an aggregated constraint measure and the structural holes value was derived by subtracting the aggregated constraint from 2.

variable_name: Degree centrality in the firm's collaboration network
description: The number of collaboration partners that a researcher had between 1991 and 1995. On average, a researcher had about five network contacts, with a standard deviation of 5.31.

variable_name: Charisma (difference between the Democrat and Republican candidate charisma scores)
description: A charisma score was derived from the candidates' nomination acceptance speeches by two trained graduate students who independently coded each speech at the sentence level for the presence or absence of nine charismatic rhetorical tactics, summing the frequency of use of each item. To ensure maximum reliability, the mean score across the two coders was used for analyses. The variable used in the models is the difference score between the Democrat and the Republican candidate, so a positive value indicates that the Democrat candidate employed more rhetorical items than did his Republican counterpart.
time_window: nomination acceptance speech in the election year

description: The absolute difference of the out-of-sample predictions of the Fair econometric model of the Democratic vote share subtracted from 50% (Performance signal = |V_hat - 50|); it is the predicted margin of victory when only attributional processes (the economy) are considered. Values close to 0% indicate a small margin of victory and therefore ambiguous performance signals, while values moving away from 0% indicate clear economic signals.
time_window: out-of-sample prediction for the election year

variable_name: Economic variables (G, P, Z) multiplied by incumbency I
description: G is the growth rate (at an annual rate) of real per capita GDP in the first three quarters of the election year; P is the absolute value of the GDP deflator (inflation rate at an annual rate) covering the current administration up to the election; Z is the number of quarters in which the growth rate of per capita GDP exceeded 3.2% at an annual rate, a 'good news' variable. Because the dependent variable is the Democratic vote share, the variable I (= 1 if the presidential incumbent is a Democrat, -1 if a Republican) determines the direction of the effect of the three economic variables, with which it is multiplied.
time_window: first three quarters of the election year (G); current administration up to the election (P, Z)

description: The dependent variable is the share of the two-party U.S. presidential popular vote received by the Democratic candidate, considering only the Democratic and Republican contenders and excluding third parties. Higher values indicate greater success in leader (or party) selection.
scale: share of the two-party popular vote

description: CEO charisma was manipulated in three ways: directly through the CEO statement read by the anchor, in terms of how many charismatic rhetorical tactics were used (six versus none, with both versions having the same number of sentences and words); indirectly via how others (the news anchor) described the leader; and indirectly through descriptions about the CEO in an interview given by a former employee.

variable_name: Firm performance signals (clearly good, ambiguous, clearly poor)
description: Firm performance was manipulated through (a) presenting stock price over the last quarter on a graph where it was either increasing by about 8%, decreasing by about 8%, or being almost constant (ambiguous signal); (b) analysts' recommendations (buy, hold, sell); and (c) the recommendations of the finance specialist interviewed on the show (buy, hold, sell).
scale: three conditions: clearly good, ambiguous, clearly poor

description: After watching the newscast, participants were asked to first imagine that they were on the board of directors of the company and then to vote on whether the current CEO should be reappointed or replaced; it was this binary decision that was modeled as the selection decision.

Alignment is the closeness of each orchestra's repertoire to the repertoires of other orchestras in the same season, computed as the sum of squared distances between (a) the proportion of the orchestra's total number of performances devoted to each composer whose works were performed by any orchestra during the season and (b) the proportion of other orchestras' performances of each composer's works. To construct repertoire alignment, this distance measure was scaled by its maximum possible value and the negative of the logged scaled distance was computed. The measure has a zero lower bound and takes higher values as the distance gets smaller and the orchestra's repertoire becomes more aligned with the average repertoires of all other orchestras.

Conventionality captures the extent to which the orchestra's programming choices focus on a subset of highly salient composers emblematic of the field; to measure this bias in each season, the composer shares of each orchestra's annual performances were regressed on the composer shares of performances at other orchestras. The slope of the regression line is interpreted as the measure of conventionality: a slope exceeding 1 indicates an above-average commitment to canonical composers, while a slope less than 1 indicates a below-average commitment.

An inter-orchestra diffusion network of newly introduced composers was built for every season, with nodes being orchestras and tie values a function of the total number of composers entering the repertoire of an adopter orchestra after they were first introduced by an introducer orchestra, as well as the speed at which those composers were incorporated; adoption counts decline steadily with time and become null five years or more after the introduction. Status is measured with Bonacich and Lloyd's (2001) eigenvector-like measure of centrality for non-reciprocal ties based on the cumulative diffusion networks of new composers over the previous 25 years, assigning a higher score to nodes tied to central nodes. Because status is a relative measure, the variable is centered on its annual mean and standardized.
time_window: cumulative networks over the previous 25 years

description: Bonacich and Lloyd's (2001) centrality scores computed in the inter-director diffusion network of new composers, an interpersonal rather than interorganizational network in which the nodes are the musical directors in charge of concert programming decisions. The values of the ties are calculated as functions of the number of new composers introduced by musical director i and later performed by musical director j, as well as how soon musical director j adopted those new composers.

variable_name: founding of a cooperative association in a municipality in the focal year
description: Indicator of whether a retail cooperative was founded in a municipality in the focal year, used as the dependent variable in the founding analysis. The founding data come from the Cooperative Association in Norway and were supplemented and cross-checked with annual reports of its predecessor organization and a monograph on cooperatives in Norway. Cooperatives were coded to 1950 municipality boundaries using the postal code of their modern location or a match of the geographical name of their founding location. The founding probability is modeled with a complementary log logistic model.

Municipality Spanish Flu mortality per 1,000 individuals as reported by Mamelund (2003), following his procedure of adding mortality attributed to Spanish Flu and pneumonia because some Spanish Flu cases had pneumonia as the final cause of death. Cases were reported by doctors at the medical district level (corresponding to one or more municipal units). A Pearson residual from a first-stage equation predicting Spanish Flu mortality is included in the founding models to address possible endogeneity.

variable_name: Pearson residual for cooperative form diversity in 1917
description: Civic capacity is treated as the unobservable associated with the diversity of nonprofits. A Blau (1977) measure of organizational diversity (one minus the sum of squared proportions) of non-profit forms in 1917 for each community was modeled as a function of the same variables used to model cooperative founding, and a Pearson residual for cooperative form diversity in 1917 was extracted and used as a proxy for civic capacity. The residual shows the extent to which a community has a more diverse set of community organizations than expected from its characteristics. The authors report similar results when the Blau measure of non-profit diversity is included instead of this residual.

Formed as the (negative) sum of below-zero deviations in the three years before the focal year, using data on annual deviations from the monthly mean temperature in April for five geographical regions in Norway. Higher values on this variable indicate more severe recent spring frost.
time_window: three years before the focal year

description: The extent to which the timing of a specific performance of a routine matches the timing of its previous performances. The authors constructed a time index for street locations of the collection truck at 10-minute intervals, compared the focal performance with each prior performance within the previous 30 days, counted matches within a +/- 30 minute window, scaled matches by possible matches, and averaged across all comparisons. Minimum value is 0 and maximum value is 1.

variable_name: customer reports of missed waste collection service
description: Count of customer reports of missed waste collection service for a route, aggregated beginning with the collection day and ending with the sixth day after it. The measure is a reverse indicator for effectiveness because it reflects problematic routine performance and excludes follow-up calls. For a day of waste collection service on a route, the range of complaints was 0 to 11.
time_window: collection day through six days after

description: A reverse indicator of multiplicity in the timing of routine performances. It captures the average matching in timing across past routine performances for a route within the past 30 days, using time indexes with street locations at 10-minute intervals and counts of matches when the truck was on the same streets at the same times or 10, 20, or 30 minutes earlier or later. Matches are scaled by the number of 10-minute intervals in which a waste collection was made for the earlier performance in each comparison. Minimum value is 0 and maximum value is 1.

For a given zip code, the percentage of customers that are government employees at any level—city, county, state, or federal. The authors matched waste collection routes to the dominant zip code and assigned the corresponding Census data to route performance observations.
time_window: averaged proxies for 2005 from 2000 Census and 2010 Census or 2011 estimates

description: For a given zip code, the percentage of the population that is 65 years or older. The authors used this as an indicator of co-present point of view because retirement decreases external work-related routines and responsibilities, thereby increasing co-presence.
time_window: averaged proxies for 2005 from 2000 Census and 2010 Census or 2011 estimates

description: Binary variables indicating whether the focal performance of waste collections was during a holiday week and took place either on, or following, a major holiday (Thanksgiving and Christmas) or a minor holiday (Labor Day, Columbus Day, and Veterans Day).

variable_name: Proportion of the agency workforce in the store
description: Company headquarters maintained monthly reports of the number of agency workers and regular employees in each store. The sum of the two equaled the size of the total workforce in each store, and the proportion of the agency workforce was the number of agency workers divided by the total workforce. To obtain a reliable measure, the numbers reported in three months of the first quarter in each year were averaged.

variable_name: Workplace identification of the regular workforce
description: Identification of employees with their workplace (i.e., store) measured with Mael and Ashforth's (1992) six-item scale, which is consistent with the notion of organizational identification. The scale asked how members viewed their relationship to their immediate workplace - their store - where they were employed. To obtain the measure for each store, ratings were averaged over all employees in the store (ICC1 = .15; ICC2 = .67; rWG(J) = .80; Cronbach's a = .85).
time_window: survey administered in June-July each year

description: Assessed by adopting the three-item measure of shared vision developed by Pearce and Ensley (2004), adjusted to refer to the instrumental value of using the agency workforce as opposed to vision in general. Regular employees of each store rated the extent to which their store manager shared the value of using agency workforce with them. Ratings were averaged over all regular employees within each store (ICC1 = .29; ICC2 = .70; rWG(J) = .86; Cronbach's a = .90).
time_window: survey administered in June-July each year

description: Measured with Dumas, Phillips, and Rothbard's (2013) three-item valid scale of integration practices, which is based on behaviors such as participation in company social events. Both regular and agency workforces were asked to rate the extent to which social integration activities were initiated in the workplace. Ratings were averaged over all workplace workers (i.e., agency and regular workforces) within each store (ICC1 = .19; ICC2 = .70; rWG(J) = .89; Cronbach's a = .82).
level: store-year (aggregated from regular and agency workers)
time_window: agency survey in April-May and regular survey in June-July each year

description: Captures how well the store workforce interacts with and treats customers. It is measured by 'secret shoppers' from an outside assessment agency who come to the store every month and pretend to be shoppers. They evaluate (a) service provider appearance, (b) willingness to provide prompt service, (c) the provision of professional information, (d) degree of kindness, and (e) degree of personal attention. Each aspect is rated and the scores are averaged into a single monthly score for each store; the score was obtained after the four-month lag from the completion of the regular workforce survey.
time_window: monthly, obtained four months after the regular workforce survey

description: The percentage of total sales in the store accounted for by its private-label products as opposed to name-brand versions of the same items. The store makes more profit from private-label products, and the main sales task of the store's workforce is to persuade customers to shift purchases from brand-name items to their private-label counterparts.
time_window: obtained from the company's accounting department

description: Regular workforce participants were asked to assess the item 'My job in this store is secure' on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). It was included as a competing threat-based explanatory mechanism in the moderated mediation model analyses.
time_window: survey administered in June-July each year

description: Regular workforce participants were asked to assess the item 'I am satisfied with the opportunities for advancement in this store' on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). It was included as a competing threat-based explanatory mechanism in the moderated mediation model analyses.
time_window: survey administered in June-July each year

description: Based on eight resource allocation indicators from Compustat: advertising intensity (advertising expenditure / sales), R&D intensity (R&D expenditure / sales), overhead efficiency (selling, general, and administrative expenses / sales), capital intensity (fixed assets / total employees), plant and equipment newness (net plant and equipment / gross plant and equipment), financial leverage (total debt / shareholder equity), acquisition intensity (acquisitions / firm market value), and foreign income intensity (foreign income / firm total income). The authors calculated the standardized absolute difference between the firm's score for each of the eight variables and their industry means for each year, then summed the eight standardized absolute differences for each firm-year. All firm-year variables were windsorized at the 1% level.
time_window: one-year lag; measured from two years prior to each CEO's start through 2014 or the end of tenure

description: A dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO was non-Caucasian or female, and 0 otherwise. CEO gender (male or female) and ethnicity (Caucasian, African American, Asian, Hispanic, Native American, or other non-Caucasian ethnicity) were identified using Execucomp data supplemented by information from firm websites and Bloomberg.com. Gender and ethnicity were combined because neither indicator had sufficient representation to estimate effects separately.

Created from two forms of self-promotion: the total number of firm press releases mentioning the CEO in a given year, and the number of tweets that mentioned the CEO (for firms with Twitter accounts, including tweets from CEOs' personal accounts where they existed). In years where neither the firm nor the CEO had a Twitter account, the CEO was given a score of 0. Both the press release measure and the Twitter measure were standardized for each year and added together to create the overall CEO self-promotion score.

An annual celebrity rating built from 11 standardized volume-of-media-attention indicators and a positive valence measure. Each indicator was standardized by year and the 11 standardized values were summed into a volume of media attention score; valence was the average positive affect ratio of all media coverage in a year (LIWC positive affect divided by total affective content), standardized by year. Volume and valence scores were rescaled to be positive, multiplied to generate volume x valence scores, divided by the highest score for a CEO that year and multiplied by 100. The top quartile of scores in a year separated noncelebrities from celebrities, with A-list celebrities as the top 10% and B-list celebrities as the next 15%; the categories were assigned values of 2 (A-list), 1 (B-list), and 0 (noncelebrity).
time_window: each year in office, excluding the CEO's year of appointment, through 2014

variable_name: Brokerage structure inequity in knowledge recombination opportunity
description: Built in three steps. First, for each broker i-alter j dyad the authors evaluated whether the broker has an advantage in knowledge recombination, capturing the broker's citations to alter j over a rolling five-year window up to year t normalized by the broker's total citations net of self-citations, compared with the alter's citations to the broker normalized by the alter's total citations net of self-citations; a value of 1 is assigned for the dyad if the broker recombines more knowledge than the alter, and 0 otherwise. Second, a value of 1 is assigned if the broker recombined the knowledge of both alter firms in the triad in a single patent over the rolling five-year window. The final triad-level measure is the summation of the values from the two steps, ranging from 0 (no imbalance) to 3 (broker recombines more than both alters and recombines both alters' knowledge).
time_window: rolling five-year window up to year t; independent variables lagged one year

description: A dummy equal to 0 in the year the brokerage triad first appears and, for other years, retained at 0 if the triad appears consecutively each year without any change in its structure since its first appearance. It is operationalized as 1 for the year in which the triad status quo changes and thus brokerage decays, i.e., when one of the two broker-alter ties dissolves or the triad closes.

The authors used the spherical law of cosines formula to calculate the great-circle distance between the broker firm's and each of the alter firms' subsidiaries, or the firms themselves, whichever was directly involved in the alliance at time t, using latitudes and longitudes in radians. Where more than one alliance existed simultaneously between an alter and the broker, they took the mean of the distances; they then took the mean of the Alter1-Broker and Alter2-Broker distances and divided it by 1,000 to obtain the measure in thousand-mile units.
time_window: at time t; lagged one year

description: Operationalized with three measures: Investment Attractiveness, rated on a 5-point Likert scale from 1 (definitely unattractive) to 5 (definitely attractive); Amount Invested, the investment amount reported by respondents (if any) and winsorized at the 95th percentile (£10,000); and Expected Investment, the product of the previous two measures.

The same three measures as Study 1: Investment Attractiveness, Investment Amount, and Expected Investment. The descriptive statistics report attractiveness on a 7-point scale (mean 4.91 out of 7) and an average investment of £1,421.
Failure equals 1 where the previous venture failed and 0 if it succeeded.
Failure equals 1 where the previous venture failed and 0 if it succeeded.

Skill equals 1 if the respondent was presented with a treatment indicating entrepreneurial skill and 0 otherwise. In Study 1 the skill cue was inclusion of the entrepreneur's Forbes '30 Under 30' recognition in the Q&A section; the cue was absent otherwise.

Skill equals 1 if the respondent was presented with the skill cue and 0 if the respondent was presented with a nonskill cue. The skill cue was the entrepreneur's Forbes '30 Under 30' recognition; the nonskill cue consisted of statements about the founder's commitment, passion, and excitement.

CFO speeches were extracted from the managerial discussion section of conference calls. Exhibited optimism was estimated as the percentage of positive emotion words to the total number of words spoken, and risk-taking, promotion focus, and future focus were measured with the same procedure using the LIWC risk focus, future focus, and Gamache et al. (2015) promotion focus dictionaries; a weighted average across all CFO speeches in a year was taken for each attribute. Principal component analysis was conducted on the four language attributes and the data were recast along the first two principal component axes to obtain the index.
time_window: year in which the firm signed the debt contract

description: The number of covenants used in a debt contract was counted. The measure is unweighted because the relative importance of each clause was either unclear or did not provide additional information in prior contract research. Covenants require the borrower to maintain certain accounting measures of financial health, and lenders obtain the right to accelerate the debt or renegotiate if the threshold is violated.

All speeches by each CEO of the sampled firms were extracted during the year in which the firm signed the debt contract with the bank. Principal component analysis was used to develop an index of CEO language based on the same four dimensions used for CFO function-based language incongruity (optimism, risk-taking, promotion focus, and future focus), and this index represents corresponding CEO language.
time_window: year in which the firm signed the debt contract

description: News article information was collected from the Dow Jones edition of the RavenPack database; articles with the topic of business and a relevance score of 100 were selected. The text-based composite sentiment score (CSS) offered by RavenPack was used to evaluate the sentiment of each news article, examining emotionally charged words and phrases and estimating short-term market effects. The CSS ranges between 0 and 100, with a value higher than 50 indicating positive sentiment and lower than 50 denoting negative sentiment; the average CSS of all business news articles related to the firm for each year was computed.
time_window: per year in the sample period

variable_name: Receiving service from a cashier with a disability
description: Dummy variable coded 1 for the disability group (customers who checked out with a cashier with a hearing disability, identifiable via interaction and an 'I cannot hear' badge on the uniform) and 0 for the nondisability group. During data collection 100% of cashiers with a hearing disability wore the badges, and 169 (53%) participants checked out with them.

Customers were asked 'How satisfied are you with the cashier's service today?', with response options ranging from 1 (very dissatisfied) to 7 (very satisfied). This measure of service satisfaction serves as the contact quality measure in the retail setting.

Items from Fiske et al. (2002) were used to measure competence on a 7-point Likert-type scale (1 definitely not to 7 definitely yes); a total of nine items measured competence and warmth together. A sample item is 'As viewed by society, how competent are people with physical disabilities; e.g., hearing impairment?'. Cronbach's alpha was .88.
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale, 1 definitely not to 7 definitely yes

description: Items from Fiske et al. (2002) were used to measure warmth on a 7-point Likert-type scale (1 definitely not to 7 definitely yes); a total of nine items measured competence and warmth together. A sample item is 'As viewed by society, how sincere are people with physical disability; e.g., hearing impairment?'. Cronbach's alpha was .96.
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale, 1 definitely not to 7 definitely yes

description: Walsh and Beatty's (2007) 15-item customer-based corporate reputation scale measuring five reputation dimensions; a sample item is 'The company treats its customers in a fair manner.' A more parsimonious second-order factor model treats corporate reputation as a single factor; Cronbach's alpha for the scale was .94. Items were measured on a 7-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale, 1 strongly disagree to 7 strongly agree

variable_name: Service from a person with a disability (experimental condition)
description: Random assignment to one of three 30-second checkout video vignettes: a cashier with a hearing disability (wearing an 'I cannot hear' badge), a cashier using a wheelchair (indicating paraplegia), and a cashier without disabilities (control condition). In the analyses two dummies are used, one for hearing disability and one for using a wheelchair, against the control group.

CSR was measured with a three-item scale (Wagner, Lutz, & Weitz, 2009), for example 'Supermarket is a socially responsible company'. Pretest alpha was .93 and posttest alpha was .96; items were measured on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
scale: 7-point Likert scale, 1 strongly disagree to 7 strongly agree

description: Participants completed the same customer-based reputation measure as in Study 1 (Walsh & Beatty, 2007). Pretest and posttest Cronbach's alphas were .98; items were measured on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
scale: 7-point Likert scale, 1 strongly disagree to 7 strongly agree

description: Similar to Colella and Varma (1999), participants indicated how well an average (a) person who is deaf or (b) person with paraplegia (requires a wheelchair for mobility) can perform a cashier job relative to an average person without a disability. The scale ranged from 0 to 100, with 0 indicating they cannot perform the job and 100 meaning they can perform the job just as well as an average person without a disability.

Two items from Yoon, Gurhan-Canli, and Schwarz (2006) measured sincere motives - Supermarket hires people with disabilities because 'they have genuine concerns for people with disabilities' and 'they sincerely care about people with disabilities'. The correlation between the two items was r = .91, p <= .001.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 strongly disagree to 7 strongly agree)

description: Two items adapted from Vlachos, Tsamakos, Vrechopoulos, and Avramidis (2009) measured egoistic motives - Supermarket hires people with disabilities because 'they want to benefit from tax incentives' and 'they are taking advantage of it to help their own business'. The correlation between the two items was r = .62, p <= .001.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 strongly disagree to 7 strongly agree)

description: Companies are assigned to one primary basic category at a minimum (and potentially more basic categories) and one or more subcategories. To test the hypotheses the population was decomposed into three mutually exclusive cases: subordinate category spanning (SubCS) when a company was assigned to more than one subordinate category but only one basic category (30.7% of observations); basic category spanning (BCS) when it belonged to more than one basic category (46.3% of observations); and basic category membership (BCM) when it was assigned to only one basic category and one subordinate category (23.0% of observations).

The company's pre-money value, that is, the value prior to receiving a capital infusion, determined at the investment stage of the VC process. Because the pre-money value is skewed to the right, the authors log-transformed the variable.

The lead investor's past experience in the target company's primary basic industry, calculated as the number of investment rounds the lead investor has participated in by investing in companies in the same primary basic category as the target company during the six years preceding the deal year. The average nonlogged expertise score is 30.00 (SD = 55.86); the variable was log-transformed because it is highly skewed to the right.
time_window: six years preceding the deal year

description: Participants were randomly assigned to one start-up's category membership condition among three: subordinate category spanning (SubCS: microfinance or credit risk), basic category spanning (BCS: finance or information technology), or basic category membership (BCM: finance). All other features of the start-up profile were identical across conditions and applicable to any classification label.

Participants were asked: 'Would you recommend investing in the start-up?' (0 = not at all, 9 = strongly). Participants' scores represent the valuation variable. Across conditions, valuation has a mean of 4.75 (SD = 1.62).

Items adapted from Fleck and Quester (2007) and Rifon et al. (2004). Participants indicated the extent of their agreement with six statements: 'The industrial categories that the company uses . . . (a) go well together, (b) match together, (c) are compatible with each other, (d) are a good fit, (e) are congruent with each other, (f) are an appropriate combination' (0 = I completely disagree, 9 = I completely agree). The scores for the six items were averaged (Cronbach's alpha = .95); across conditions congruence has a mean of 5.52 (SD = 1.36).

A 12-item questionnaire was developed to measure participants' expertise, following established research. Participants earned one point for each correct answer, and the total number of points was used as a finance expertise score. Participants whose scores were greater than or equal to the median (5 out of 12 possible points) were considered experts; the sample comprised 155 nonexperts (50.49%) and 152 experts (49.51%).
Participants were randomly assigned to a condition of category membership, either subordinate category spanning (SubCS) or basic category spanning (BCS), identical to those found in Study 2.
The same variable of valuation as in Study 2. Across all the conditions, valuation has a mean of 5.70 (SD = 1.80).
Perceived congruence uses the same items as in Study 2 (Cronbach's alpha = 0.97) and it has a mean of 6.38 (SD = 1.64).

The same expertise measure as in Study 2; participants whose expertise scores were equal to or above the median (i.e., 5 out of 12 possible points) were classified as experts. Experts comprised 52.02% of the sample (n = 206), whereas nonexperts comprised 47.98% of the sample (n = 190).

Participants were asked to solve a series of eight verbal analogies, being exposed either to analogies within the same domain (e.g., 'Blindness is to sight what deafness is to -') or to analogies across different domains (e.g., 'Blindness is to sight what poverty is to -'). This variable took a value of 1 if the participant was assigned to the across-domain condition and 0 if the participant was assigned to the within-domain condition.

Measured with the coefficient of variation. The authors first calculated each group's average pay level by averaging all group members' monthly payrolls (base pay plus PFP). They then generated a store-level variable by dividing the store standard deviation in the groups' averaged pay levels by the store mean of all groups' averaged pay levels.

Measured with the coefficient of variation. The authors calculated the standard deviation of the total pay level within each group and divided it by the group members' average total pay level, then averaged all groups' WGPD to obtain each store's overall WGPD.

Employees rated their perceptions of distributive justice regarding pay on the four-item scale developed by Colquitt (2001), with sample items such as 'Our work outcomes (such as pay and pay raise opportunities) reflect the effort we have put into our work'. Items were rated on a 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) scale (alpha = .94). The store-level distributive justice climate variable was generated by averaging all employees' distributive justice perceptions at the store level.

Group leaders evaluated their group members' altruistic behaviors toward other group members within the store using two items from Farh and colleagues' altruism scale in the Chinese context, with modified instructions and referent. Items were rated on a 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) scale (alpha = .87), and all group leaders' responses were averaged to reflect the store's level of intergroup helping.

Objective data obtained from the HR department at the headquarters of the retail company. Each store's voluntary turnover rate was calculated by dividing the number of departing employees who left their stores voluntarily by the total number of employees working in the store in January 2018.

Obtained from the company archive and measured by the extent to which the store's first half-year goal was met in 2018. This index was used for the company's resource allocation decisions, such as compensation budgets, and was standardized by headquarters for confidentiality.

Store managers evaluated their stores' overall productivity and effectiveness in accordance with the objective achievement and progress in organizational goals set by the province management team, using the seven-item organizational performance scale developed by Sparrowe et al. (2001). Items were rated from 1 (very poor) to 5 (outstanding) (alpha = .91); for stores with two or more managers, their scores were averaged.

Employees' perceived pay dispersion, measured by modifying existing measures to fit the research context, with three items rated from 1 ('very small') to 7 ('very large') (alpha = .92). All employees' individual scores were averaged to reflect the branch's overall BGPD.

Employees' perceived within-group pay dispersion, measured with three items rated from 1 ('very small') to 7 ('very large'). Employees' individual scores were first averaged to reflect the size of WGPD for the service/marketing group to which they belonged inside a branch (alphas = .96 and .94), and the two groups' WGPD values were then averaged to reflect each branch's overall WGPD.

Employees' justice perceptions of the pay distribution, measured with four items following prior research, rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) (alpha = .96). All employees' responses were averaged to reflect the branch's distributive justice climate.

For each store-month, the dismissal rate is the ratio of the number of dismissals in a store due to employee poor performance, poor attendance, lack of integrity, or violations of organizational rules and policies to the number of store employees in that month. The store-month population counted all employees who worked at the store in that month without exiting the unit; employees who left at any point during the month were not counted.

The layoff rate is the ratio of the number of nontemporary workers who were involuntarily terminated due to the elimination of their positions to the number of employees who worked in the store in that month; temporary and seasonal positions were excluded. The layoff announcement rate was measured as the layoff rate three months later, assuming that employees were informed about layoffs within their units approximately three months before the events occurred.
time_window: three months before the layoff event

description: The store-level voluntary turnover rate for each store-month is the ratio of the number of voluntary turnover events in a store to the average number of store employees. Common reasons for voluntary turnover included personal reasons, career advancement, returning to school, and job dissatisfaction.

Personnel data included supervisor evaluations, which were the supervisors' overall evaluation of how employees contributed to the business's success and workers' citizenship behavior on a five-point scale, with higher numbers indicating higher levels of performance. Because the evaluation occurs annually, performance data exist only for employees who had been with the organization for at least one year. The high-performance variable equals 1 if employee performance is above the unit's average and 0 otherwise; the low-performance variable is its opposite. These dummies were interacted with individual-level turnover dummies (dismissals, layoff announcements, voluntary turnover) and aggregated to the unit-month level to measure the rate of each turnover event for high and low performers.
scale: five-point scale; dummy variables for high versus low performance

description: The store-month level hiring rate is the ratio of the number of new hires in a store to the number of store employees in that store-month. Only external hires who joined the unit from outside the organization were included; rehired employees, transfers, and promotions were not considered new hires.

Ego network density of the focal MSA: the ratio of in-degree ties formed by VC firms that invested in the focal MSA's adjacent MSAs but resided in other adjacent MSAs to the number of all possible MSA pairs in the focal MSA's ego network, excluding the focal MSA. It is built on a directed ego network capturing the directionality of resource flows and is calculated with UCINET 6 using a five-year moving window (1990-1994 data for 1994). The variable was mean-centered in the regression analyses.

Total number of new business establishments in each MSA at time t, obtained from county-level U.S. Census Bureau data aggregated to the MSA level. Following established practice, the variable was transformed by taking its natural logarithm to normalize the skew.

Number of publicly traded companies per 100,000 population in each MSA at time t-1, compiled from Compustat and aggregated to the MSA level to ensure commensurability across MSAs. The variable was mean-centered.

Total congregational membership per 10,000 population, calculated by the U.S. Religion Census from county-level counts of congregations, members, adherents, and attendees and aggregated to the MSA level; the higher the index, the greater the level of religiosity. Data from the 1990, 2000, and 2010 surveys were used and missing data for intervening years were interpolated at time t-1, and the variable was mean-centered.

The measure weights the volume of analyst coverage a firm has received by the analyst's expertise in the firm's industry, approximating 'the centrality of the focal firm in the security analyst coverage network'. The authors counted the number of firms each analyst covered in a 3-digit SIC industry during the previous year, assigned a value of 1 to the analyst covering the largest number of firms in each industry, and used the number of firms they covered to normalize the number of firms all other analysts covered in a given industry, creating analyst expertise scores that ranged from 0 to 1. These scores were aggregated by firm-year and used as the firm status measure; firms with no analyst coverage were coded 0.
time_window: previous year (analyst coverage); aggregated by firm-year

description: The authors first dichotomized the status scores of all firms with at least one analyst covering them at the 90th percentile to identify high-status firms, then counted the number of data breaches involving high-status firms within the focal firm's 3-digit SIC industry during the 365 days preceding the focal firm's breach disclosure. Only past breaches covered in at least one article were used, and each incident was discounted by dividing it by the number of weeks from the focal incident before aggregating. A focal firm's own past breaches were excluded from the measure.
time_window: 365 days preceding the focal breach disclosure

description: Operationalized as the number of data breaches involving high-status firms outside the focal firm's industry during the 365 days preceding the focal firm's breach disclosure. As with insider breaches, only past breaches covered in at least one article were counted and each incident was discounted by dividing it by the number of weeks from the focal incident before aggregation.
time_window: 365 days preceding the focal breach disclosure

description: An ordered variable coded 0 if a breach did not receive any media coverage, 1 if it was covered but the volume of coverage was below the 95th percentile in the sample (40 articles), and 2 if the volume of media coverage was above or equal to the 95th percentile. Media coverage was collected as articles about the data breach incidents published during the two weeks following the incidents' disclosures from all English-language outlets registered with Factiva, and articles were manually identified and limited to those about the focal breach incident.
scale: 0 = no media coverage, 1 = moderate media coverage, 2 = scandalized
time_window: two weeks following the breach disclosure

description: Count of articles, news wires, and press releases covering cases of abuse as reported on BishopAccountability; the variable is coded only to include the first instance of media coverage for each accused individual in the database that took place within the diocese during the previous decade, without regard for follow-on coverage of the same incident. It therefore counts articles that report a not previously known occurrence of misconduct within the diocese published in the previous 10 years. In the models it is logged.

A Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) of ethnic diversity, defined in the [0;1] range and taking a value of 1 when homogeneity is greatest. It is calculated based on ethnic groups reported in U.S. Census Bureau data; to obtain a diocese-level measure, the number of individuals belonging to each ethnic group is summed across counties belonging to the same diocese before calculating the HHI, using data collected as part of the relevant decennial Census. For consistency only the groups reported in 1980 are considered.

The ratio between the number of Catholics within the diocese, obtained through survey data made available by the ARDA, and the total population of the diocese computed from U.S. Census Bureau data for the same year. The rationale is that the degree to which organizational members have ties to the community and the strength of such ties are likely to be greater where Catholics are more heavily represented.

For each year in the observation window, the number of organizations corresponding to the relevant NAICS codes is summed to obtain a total count of the number of social and voluntary organizations within the county, which include religious, civic, political, and social associations, as well as professional and labor organizations, gyms, bowling centers, golf courses, and sports teams or clubs. Because the study takes place at the diocese level, figures are aggregated by summing the number of organizations for all counties within a diocese, and the variable is finally normalized by dividing it by the diocese population count, making it comparable across dioceses and over time.
time_window: each year in the observation window

description: Predecessor race was coded 0 for White predecessors and 1 for Black predecessors. Combined with the dependent variable, which distinguishes Black from non-Black (White) successor appointments, it captures racial similarity between predecessor and successor; the authors note that findings are identical, though reversed, when White coach appointment is used as the focal dependent variable.

Measured as the prior coach's win-loss record, which reflects the objective team winning percentage for the season leading up to the new coaching appointment (i.e., the year prior to succession). Data on team winning percentage were received directly from staff at the NCAA. Independent variables are mean-centered in the analyses.
time_window: the season leading up to the new coaching appointment (the year prior to succession)

description: The dependent variable is leader selection, coded as 0 for non-Black coach appointments and 1 for Black coach appointments. Because the possible appointment outcomes are binary, the findings are identical, though reversed, when White coach appointment is used in place of Black coach appointment.
time_window: the coaching appointment following each succession event

description: Participants were randomly assigned to a condition in which the predecessor and candidate were either racially dissimilar (coded as 0) or racially similar (coded as 1), implemented with photos of either a phenotypically Black or White male in the predecessor and candidate profiles. In the racial similarity (dissimilarity) condition, the predecessor and leader candidate were the same race (different races); participants who incorrectly responded to either manipulation check question were removed.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two predecessor performance conditions: low performer (coded as 0) or high performer (coded as 1). In the low [high] performance condition participants were told that based on performance reviews the predecessor was a low-performing [high-performing] leader who was extremely ineffective [effective] at communicating goals and tasks, that the employees in the marketing department often underperformed [overperformed], and that the department failed to meet [always met] its performance goals.
Participants responded to the question 'How likely would you be to hire Candidate 1?' on a range of 1 (definitely not) to 7 (definitely) to assess their willingness to select each leader candidate.

Consistent with prior research, false alarms were used as the measure of transference: the probability of erroneously recognizing traits of the predecessor as traits of the candidate. Participants completed a 12-item memory recognition task rated on a scale of 1 (confident that this item was not presented) to 4 (confident that this was presented); half of the items had been presented to describe the past leader but not the candidate. The scale was dichotomized so that scores of 1 and 2 indicated the participant was not confident the item was presented and scores of 3 and 4 indicated confidence, and six dichotomous measures were averaged into a single continuous variable ranging from 0 to 1, where higher scores indicate more erroneous generalization from predecessor to candidate.
scale: continuous, 0 to 1 (averaged from six dichotomous items)

description: Participants were randomly assigned to a condition in which the predecessor and candidate were either racially similar (yes) or racially dissimilar (no), using a 2 (racial similarity: yes or no) x 2 (predecessor performance: low or high) between-subjects design.
Participants were randomly assigned to a low or high predecessor performance condition in a 2 (racial similarity: yes or no) x 2 (predecessor performance: low or high) between-subjects design.

Participants answered 'How likely would you be to hire the candidate?' on a 1 (definitely not) to 7 (definitely) scale, and also completed a choice set question in which they had to select between one of three candidates: an Asian, Black, or White candidate; one of the candidates in the choice set was the candidate they had been randomly assigned to evaluate earlier.
Participants were given the same memory recognition task from Study 2 to assess transference.

Participants were randomly assigned to a condition with a predecessor (either Jon Ossoff, who is White, or Raphael Warnock, who is Black) and a candidate (either a White, Black, or Asian male candidate) who were either racially similar or racially dissimilar.
scale: binary: racially similar or racially dissimilar

description: For the measure of evaluators' familiarity with the predecessor, participants who were residents of the U.S. state of Georgia were coded as familiar with the predecessor (1) and residents in non-Georgia southeastern states as unfamiliar (0).
scale: binary: 1 = Georgia resident (familiar), 0 = non-Georgia southeastern state resident (unfamiliar)
time_window: at the time of data collection (Spring 2021)

description: Participants were tasked with evaluating a leader candidate who was seeking to fill a public office (U.S. senator for the state of Georgia) and reported their selection of the candidate.
Participants engaged in a memory recall task that was identical to the task in Study 2 to assess transference.

variable_name: racial and gender similarity of candidates
description: Participants read the profile of an Asian female predecessor and a profile of one leader candidate (either an Asian female, Asian male, or Black female), so that candidates varied in whether they shared the predecessor's race and gender.
Participants were asked to evaluate fictitious candidates who were seeking to replace a predecessor for the role of vice president of marketing.
Participants engaged in a memory recall task that was identical to the task in Study 2 to assess transference.

Total compensation is ExecuComp data item TDC1, the dependent variable for all core regressions. It is winsorized at the top and bottom 1%; because the distribution remains skewed after winsorizing, the authors transform it by taking the natural logarithm.
time_window: Executive-year observations from three years before to three years after the job change in most models

description: Dummy variable that equals 1 if the executive moved across industries, and 0 otherwise. Firms are classified with the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), and the authors use the first two NAICS digits, which designate the business sector, to operationalize industry change. In the models the variable is interacted with post-job-change, a dummy that equals 1 for the periods after a job change (the treatment period).

Two dummy variables operationalize the status difference between the origin and destination industries: status-leaper takes the value 1 for all observations associated with an executive who moved to a higher-status industry, and status-leaker takes the value 1 if the industry-changing executive moved to a lower-status industry. Industry status is proxied by Gallup's annual industry prestige rankings, for which industry prestige scores are calculated by subtracting total negative responses from total positive responses to the question asking respondents to rate each business sector, yielding annually updating rankings from 2001 to 2014; for 1999 and 2000 job changes the earliest available (2001) rankings are used.
time_window: Annual rankings, 2001-2014, matched to each job-change year

variable_name: proportion of women partners in the firm
description: Measured as the proportion of women partners in the firm in the previous year. Senior women constitute only 20% of partnership roles on average in the data. The variable was lagged by one year, and its values were confirmed against the National Law Journal's Female Scorecard.

Measured as the average score across six internally oriented diversity practices reported in the Vault/MCCA survey. Each practice was coded 0 if the firm indicated that the initiative had not been implemented and was not a current priority, 1 if the firm indicated that it was currently addressing and implementing that practice, 2 if the diversity practice had already been completed in the past, and 3 if the firm had already implemented the practice and was continuing to prioritize and address it.

variable_name: number of full-time job offers extended to women candidates for the entry-level associate position
description: Count of the number of full-time job offers extended to women candidates for the entry-level associate position in the year. The total number of offers made for first-year associate positions in that year was included as a control.

variable_name: proportion of women across the diversity and hiring committees
description: Measured as the proportion of women across the diversity and hiring committees, which firms self-report in the Vault/MCCA survey. The diversity committee recommends actions and monitors diversity and hiring efforts, while the hiring committee makes final hiring decisions; both are typically chaired by senior partners and may include attorneys from various ranks. The variable was lagged by one year.
Gender as indicated by each user on the Y Combinator Cofounder Matching platform. Women entrepreneurs were coded as a '1' and men entrepreneurs were coded as a '0'.

Text analysis of users' descriptions of what they were looking for in a cofounder. A dictionary of 172 words or word roots associated with a high interdependent self-construal was created following the recommended procedure and uploaded into LIWC. Because the distribution of the score was skewed, the natural log of one plus this score was used.
scale: natural log of one plus dictionary score

description: Text analysis of users' descriptions of their cofounder preferences using an interpersonal attraction dictionary of 209 words or word roots, built deductively from prior theory, inductively by scanning the corpus, and validated by subject matter experts. LIWC produced a score representing the proportion of dictionary words to the total words in the description; because the distribution was skewed, the natural log of one plus the score was used.
scale: natural log of one plus dictionary proportion

description: Text analysis of users' descriptions of their cofounder preferences using a resource-seeking dictionary of 228 words or word roots, built deductively from prior theory, inductively by scanning the corpus, and validated by subject matter experts. LIWC produced a score representing the proportion of dictionary words to the total words in the description; because the distribution was skewed, the natural log of one plus the score was used.
scale: natural log of one plus dictionary proportion

description: A discrete ordinal index of legitimacy ranging from 0 to 4, built from four factors relating to legitimacy: whether the entrepreneur attended a university in the top 10 of the U.S. News & World Report's 2021 rankings, whether the entrepreneur has a terminal degree such as a PhD or MD, whether the entrepreneur has work experience at one of the 'big five' tech giants (Amazon, Apple, Facebook, Google, Microsoft), and whether the entrepreneur has prior entrepreneurial experience. Zero if the individual exhibited none of the factors, adding one for each factor exhibited.
Respondent gender taken from the Prolific database of respondents' demographic information. Women respondents were coded as a '1' and men respondents were coded as a '0'.
Three survey items developed by Cross et al. (2000), rated on a 7-point Likert scale (alpha = .846). The mean of participants' responses was calculated and then the score was standardized.

Attribute importance scores generated for each respondent by a hierarchical Bayesian multinomial logit model, which represent the percent of the variation in utility influenced by each attribute. The scores for the 'shared personal values' and 'easy to talk to' attributes were summed to generate an overall importance score for interpersonal attraction, and the scores were standardized.

Attribute importance scores generated for each respondent by a hierarchical Bayesian multinomial logit model, which represent the percent of the variation in utility influenced by each attribute. The attribute importance scores for the 'skill set' and 'startup experience' attributes were summed to generate an overall importance score for resource seeking, and the scores were standardized.

Experimental manipulation: respondents randomly assigned to the 'high legitimacy' condition were coded as '1' and respondents randomly assigned to the 'low legitimacy' condition were coded as '0'. The high legitimacy condition conveyed a degree from a prestigious university, an industry award, and endorsements from key industry stakeholders; the low legitimacy condition stated that the respondent did not possess these signals.

Participants reported their gender, choosing among 'male', 'female', 'other', and 'prefer not to answer'; all respondents answered either 'male' or 'female'. Women entrepreneurs (those who indicated 'female') were coded as a '1' and men entrepreneurs (those who indicated 'male') were coded as a '0'.

Text analysis of entrepreneurs' pitches, which occurred before the networking event. The interdependent self-construal dictionary created in Study 1 was used to analyze the transcribed text of each entrepreneurial pitch; because the distribution was skewed, the natural log of one plus this score was used, and the measure was standardized.
scale: natural log of one plus dictionary score, standardized

description: A composite score created for each dyad measuring the level of interpersonal attraction of the cofounder, incorporating information on the cofounder's interpersonal motives, agreeableness, and the cofounder's expression of interest in working with the entrepreneur. The measure was standardized.

A composite score created for each dyad measuring the resource level of the cofounder, incorporating information on the cofounder's functional skill set, industry experience, and entrepreneurial experience. The measure was standardized.

Organizational achievements were captured by asking entrepreneurs to select from a list of 10 startup activities (e.g., prototype developed, first customer acquired, business plan complete) completed before the beginning of the incubator program; the number completed was counted and standardized. Founder-related aspects of legitimacy were captured by the number of years of entrepreneurial experience for each entrepreneur, standardized. The mean score of these two measures was calculated to measure legitimacy.
time_window: before the beginning of the incubator program

variable_name: Focal firm-broker tie reinitiation (Reinitiation and Days)
description: Because the authors use a parametric event history estimator, the dependent variable has two components. Reinitiation is a dummy coded '1' when the focal alter reinitiated a tie with the broker firm during the observation period and '0' otherwise. Days measures the time-to-event outcome, that is waiting time until the event of tie reinitiation occurs, or otherwise time until censoring occurs (the event is not observed for a particular case). Observations for brokers with no reinitiations were treated as right censored.

Trust violation is coded '1' for a specific exchange (i.e., voyage) if in any deal its shipbroker partner has mediated a follow-on deal between a charterer and a shipper in which the charterer is using the focal firm's ship to transport the shipper's cargo, and '0' otherwise. In cases of trust violations the focal firm just rents out the ship to a charterer brought in by the shipbroker but does not directly transport cargo for a shipper, so the focal firm knows that a potential cargo exists but the broker has directed it to the charterer instead.
A dummy with a value of '1' if both the focal firm and its broker partner firm are collocated in Copenhagen and '0' otherwise.

Relational embeddedness measures the frequency of the focal firm-shipbroker relationship, that is the cumulative index of the total number of deals since the focal firm and the shipbroker started working together. The frequency-based and duration-based measures are not included together because of their high correlation.

variable_name: Number of new business registrations in a county in a month
description: Count of new business registrations in a county in a month, taken from Minnesota Secretary of State records. Branches of existing businesses, re-registrations such as an ownership change, and resurrection of an expired registration are excluded, so only new registrations are counted as founding events. For the linear fixed effects models used as main models the natural log of this variable is the dependent variable; count and generalized linear model panel specifications use the plain count.
time_window: monthly; five years before the September 2019 intervention through March 2020

description: A binary independent variable whose default state is 0 for all nonmetro counties before September 2019. It is set to 1 for a county from September 2019 onwards if one or more EEAs from that county attended the intervention, so it varies by county and by time.

variable_name: Number of community improvement and business associations in the county
description: Count of community improvement associations such as chambers of commerce in a county, treated as a source of preexisting organizational competence, knowledge, and ties relevant to entrepreneurship. The data come from the IRS Business Master Files for 501(c) organizations, aggregated from Form 990 and 990-EZ filings.
The Gini coefficient of income inequality in the county, gathered from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey, used to gauge the community's level of generalized social trust.

Indicator that the two employees share membership in the same disciplinary department, the authors' example of a formal collective focus. Every faculty member at the university belongs to at least one disciplinary department; the department selects new hires and, along with the administration, controls the definition of employee duties, pay, and benefits.

Indicator that both employees are substantively affiliated with the same one of the three interdisciplinary research centers (Biotech Center, Environmental Center, International Studies Center) in a given year. Substantive affiliation requires being listed as 'affiliated faculty' or 'center faculty' on the website or in the annual report and engaging in at least one other center-based activity, such as giving a seminar or applying for an internal grant.

Indicator that an employee holds a joint appointment to more than one disciplinary department. These individuals are paid by both departments and hold defined responsibilities and duties in each. The individual holding the joint appointment is taken to share this type of membership with all others in the department of interest.

Indicator that an employee holds one or more courtesy appointments in departments outside his or her primary disciplinary department. The salary is paid entirely by the primary department and all contractual responsibilities fall in the primary department; the employee is invited to attend meetings and activities in the courtesy department but holds no contractual obligations there. The individual holding the courtesy appointment is taken to share this type of membership with all others in the department of interest.

Binary indicator of whether a new coauthorship tie formed between employees i and j in year t, estimated over all potential undirected dyads. Ties are considered at risk only if the tie had not existed at any prior time; the analysis starts in 1999 while data from 1993 to 1998 are used to drop dyads that had collaborated in earlier years.

Binary indicator of whether a new collaboration tie formed between employees i and j in year t through applying together for a grant proposal, estimated over all potential undirected dyads. Ties are considered at risk only if the tie had not existed at any prior time; the analysis starts in 1999 while data from 1993 to 1998 are used to drop dyads that had collaborated in earlier years.

Yearly count of publications authored by a faculty member, used as one of the two activities of interest in the individual-level productivity models. The authors assessed solo activities separately from collaborative activities to determine whether focal memberships affect these activities in different ways.

Yearly count of grants proposed by a faculty member, used as one of the two activities of interest in the individual-level productivity models. The authors assessed solo activities separately from collaborative activities to determine whether focal memberships affect these activities in different ways.

Organizational mortality is modeled as the instantaneous mortality rate, the probability that an organization dies between t and t + dt, allowed to vary as a function of age. The rate is estimated with a generalized Gompertz specification, r(t) = exp[beta'X(t)]exp(gamma t); the life history of each organization is segmented into one-year intervals so that covariates can be updated from year to year. Age is computed by subtracting the year of founding from the year of each observation.
time_window: one-year intervals over the study period

description: Organizational mortality is modeled as the instantaneous mortality rate estimated with the generalized Gompertz specification, with each organization's life history segmented into one-year intervals so that covariates can be updated annually. For Iowa, the year of founding or mortality is the first or last year a company is listed in the Annual Assessment, and age is the year of observation minus the year of founding.
time_window: one-year intervals over the study period

description: Density is defined as the number of organizations in each sample area at the start of each year. For each organization in the sample, the density of magneto companies is measured with two terms: local density, the number of magneto companies in the organization's counties of operation, and nonlocal density, the number of geographically distant magneto companies not operating in the same county or counties.
time_window: annual, at the start of each year

description: Annual count of the companies using common-battery power technology in the sample area. In the models this density term is entered as a main effect and also interacted with a common-battery dummy variable, so that its effect on common-battery companies can be separated from its effect on other companies.
time_window: annual, at the start of each year

description: Annual count of the common-battery companies operating multiple exchanges in communities more than 30 miles apart. In the models estimated on the subset of common-battery companies, this density is entered as a main effect and in interactions with the multi-exchange dummy variable, its interaction with the multi-exchange dummy capturing competition within the multi-exchange population.
time_window: annual, at the start of each year

description: Annual count of the common-battery companies operating in only one community, or in geographically adjacent communities within a 30-mile radius. In the models estimated on the subset of common-battery companies, this density is entered as a main effect and in interactions; single-exchange companies are the omitted category in the dummy variable, so the interaction term gives the relative effect of multi-exchange density on single-exchange companies.
time_window: annual, at the start of each year

description: Respondents were asked if the job was supposed to be temporary, seasonal, or permanent at the time when the most recent incumbent was hired. Jobs were classified as temporary if they were either temporary or seasonal; 10 percent of jobs were temporary and 5 percent were seasonal. Temporary job is a binary variable, coded 1 if the job was temporary or seasonal and 0 if the job was permanent.
Independent contractor is a binary variable, coded 1 if the establishment used independent contractors and 0 if it did not.

Benefit costs were not measured in the survey, so data on industry benefit levels were used as a proxy for firm benefit costs. Industry benefits, at the two-digit Standard Industry Classification (SIC) level, were measured as the ratio of total employee-benefit costs to payroll in 1980.

Firm-specific training was a job-level measure and was assessed as the sum of the number of hours of three types of training received by the typical job incumbent after hiring: formal training, informal training by managers, and informal training by coworkers.
