Variation in employment was measured as the coefficient of variation in establishment employment on six dates: July 1979, December 1979, July 1980, December 1980, July 1981, and December 1981.
Unionization is the percentage of workers in the establishment covered by collective bargaining agreements in 1981.

Government oversight of affirmative action was measured at the industry (two-digit SIC) level as the percentage of workers in an industry employed in firms that must file EEO-1 reports. The greater the percentage of workers employed in firms required to file reports on affirmative action compliance, the higher the level of government scrutiny of employment practices in the industry.
The establishment-level measure was the extent to which the establishment had bureaucratic termination procedures, measured as the amount of paperwork needed to fire an employee on a 1-4 scale.
The job-level measure was the number of weeks a job's probationary period lasted. The authors note that use of probationary periods is strongly related to other bureaucratic hiring standards.
Establishment size is the number of employees on the date the survey was administered in 1982.
Multiple-site establishments were identified by a binary variable, coded 1 if the firm had any other divisions or subsidiaries located outside of the SMSA and 0 otherwise.

Interpersonal complexity is an occupational-level measure taken from the 4th edition of the Dictionary of Occupational Titles (DOT). All complexity measures were reverse-coded so that higher complexity scores indicate more complex jobs.

Informational complexity is an occupational-level measure taken from the 4th edition of the Dictionary of Occupational Titles (DOT). All complexity measures were reverse-coded so that higher complexity scores indicate more complex jobs.

Technical complexity is an occupational-level measure taken from the 4th edition of the Dictionary of Occupational Titles (DOT). All complexity measures were reverse-coded so that higher complexity scores indicate more complex jobs.

For each attribute dimension, the authors computed correlations between the ratings for each of that dimension's attributes and the ratings for the attributes of all other dimensions and averaged the absolute values of these correlations. They averaged across a dimension's attributes to obtain a composite index of centrality for each dimension.
The average absolute correlation between a dimension's attribute ratings and the ratings on the seven self-categorization items, averaged across the attributes within the dimension.

Managers categorized their own firm using the categories obtained from the interviews, rated how well their firm fit each of the seven summary categories, and the authors used cluster analyses to derive a six-category solution that best fit the self-categorizations. The six categories are handknitters, fashion handframe knitters, traditional handframe knitters, upmarket fully fashioned manufacturers, midmarket firms, and mass-market cut-and-sew contractors.

Respondents checked which of the 261 listed firms in the industry were competitors that they often considered when setting prices, developing products, and marketing their knitwear. A cell in the 89 x 89 rivalry matrix was coded 1 when the row firm cited the column firm as a competitor, 0 otherwise, and densities are the ratio of actual to possible ties; main diagonal entries are within-category densities and off-diagonal entries are directional between-category densities.

The absolute value of a firm's distance from the category mean on each of the 14 attributes that make up the size, location, knitting methods, assembly methods, and product style dimensions, averaged across the 14 ratings. Smaller values of AVGDIS imply that a firm was representative of the category.

The log of the sales variable. Managers provided total sales for the most recent full year of operations using eleven-pound-Sterling categories from '£50,000 or less' to 'over £40 million', and this sales item constituted the measure of organizational size.
scale: eleven sales categories from £50,000 or less to over £40 million
time_window: most recent full year of operations

description: The number of other firms within the same category that a respondent cited as a rival, standardized by dividing this number by n - 1, where n is the number of firms in the category. The larger the number, the greater the rivalry between a firm and others in the same category.

The number of other firms within the same category that cited the respondent's firm as a rival, again standardized by dividing this number by n - 1. The larger the number, the greater the rivalry between a firm and others in the same category.

Factor scores on a single principal component from a factor analysis of six establishment-level measures of the promotion system: percentage of jobs in promotion ladders; natural logarithm of average ladder length (jobs not in ladders assigned a length of one); percentage of jobs with promotion prospects; percentage of bottom-level jobs; percentage of jobs that could not be entered from outside the establishment; and percentage of jobs in structured promotion ladders. The component captured 70.1 percent of the total multivariate association. High scores denote establishments with proportionately more jobs in ladders, longer average ladders, a higher percentage of nonentry jobs, and proportionately more jobs above the bottom level, in structured ladders, and not dead-ended.

Average within-establishment training and experience required for its jobs. Required orientation time, in-plant training time, on-the-job training time, and time required in other positions in the establishment were added for each job as estimated by the Employment Service analyst; the sum was converted into the metric by which specific vocational preparation (SVP) is measured in the DOT (ranging from 1 to 9) and then averaged across all jobs in the establishment. The authors note the variable was measured imperfectly.
Job-level indicator of training and skill requirements drawn from Employment Service staffing schedules and job analyses.
Measured as the natural logarithm of the total number of workers in the establishment.
Binary variable coded zero if the establishment was an independent firm and one otherwise, used as a crude proxy for bureaucratization.
Binary variable coded one if any portion of the line workforce was unionized and zero otherwise.

Series of nonexclusive binary variables adapted from Woodward (1965): unit-craft technology only; unit-craft technology in conjunction with another technology; batch or mass production; process technology only; and process technology in conjunction with another technology.

Series of six nonexclusive binary variables based on SIC codes, used as a proxy measure for the tangibility of the organization's outputs: manufacturing; government; agriculture; wholesale or retail trade; services; and social-overhead-capital.
Measured as the percentage of women working in the jobs analyzed by the Employment Service in each establishment.
Measured by the percentage in each establishment of each occupational category, based on three-digit DOT codes; some categories with very small percentages of jobs were combined in the analyses.

variable_name: Occupational composition (professional, technical, clerical, sales, and service)
description: Measured by the percentage in each establishment of each occupational category, based on three-digit DOT codes; some categories with very small percentages of jobs were combined in the analyses.

Job-level indicator of occupational type drawn from Employment Service staffing schedules and job analyses, based on three-digit DOT codes; categories include professional, technical, managerial, clerical, sales, business services, personal services, transportation, extraction, and production, with line production jobs as the omitted category in the regressions.

Job-level indicator of job size drawn from Employment Service staffing schedules and job analyses. The authors note that if an organization or job ladder has a constant span of control, the measure of job size is perfectly correlated with level in the hierarchy, so the size of the job indicates its level within the promotion hierarchy.

The complexity of workers' informational and technical duties was operationalized by job ratings on the DOT measures of 'data' and 'things,' respectively. Because of gender biases in the third edition of the DOT, values were truncated at 6 for 'data' and 7 for the 'things' item, and the original scales were inverted so that large-scale values denote complex involvements by workers.
scale: truncated DOT scales (data up to 6, things up to 7), inverted

description: Job-level indicator of gender composition drawn from Employment Service staffing schedules and job analyses; the analyses distinguish jobs held exclusively by men from jobs held exclusively by women.
Binary variable coded 1 if the job was in a promotion ladder and 0 otherwise.
For jobs in ladders, a binary variable coded 1 if the job was on the bottom level of the ladder and 0 otherwise; defined as missing for jobs not in promotion ladders.
For jobs in ladders, a binary variable coded 1 if the job could be entered from outside the establishment and 0 otherwise; defined as missing for jobs not in promotion ladders.

For jobs in ladders, a binary variable coded 1 if the job had additional mobility opportunities (i.e., was not dead-ended at the top of a ladder) and 0 otherwise; defined as missing for jobs not in promotion ladders.

The number of distinct administrative titles used to classify workers in an establishment was compared with the number of distinct tasks identified by the Employment Service analyst. The latter was measured as the number of unique detailed (six-digit) DOT occupational codes used to enumerate the establishment's jobs, so that fragmentation equals J/O, where J is the number of unique job titles within the organization and O is the number of unique detailed DOT occupational codes. The dependent variable was transformed logarithmically (base e).
Organizational scale was measured by the natural logarithm of establishment employment.

The modal technology in each enterprise was coded from qualitative materials obtained from Employment Service analysts and classified into categories derived from Woodward. Unlike Woodward, organizations were not restricted to one technology category; each organization could also receive a secondary technology score if one applied. The regressions reported include binary variables indicating if the primary technology was craft, mass, or process, and binary variables denoting whether the primary or secondary technology was batch, extractive, or service.

For establishments bearing second-edition DOT titles, jobs were assigned a score of 2 for skilled, 1 for semiskilled, and 0 for unskilled positions, and the mean was computed within each enterprise and converted to z-scores relative to other cases with second-edition DOT occupational data. Among cases with third- or fourth-edition DOT codes, the mean of workers' scores on the 'things' dimension, a measure of the complexity of workers' relationships with things on the job, was computed and normalized relative to all other organizations with third- or fourth-edition data, with the 'things' scale truncated at 7 to correct for gender biases in the third-edition DOT.

variable_name: average training time (specific vocational preparation, SVP)
description: Skill levels were measured by the average training time (specific vocational preparation, or SVP) obtained from job analysis information and aggregated to the establishment level. The measure of SVP includes general training, so that its net effect, controlling for technical skill and the percentage of non-entry-level jobs, captures the relative importance of general skills in an organization.

variable_name: percentage of line workers in non-entry-level jobs
description: The presence of internal labor market arrangements was measured by the percentage of line workers in non-entry-level jobs, that is, jobs above the bottom of an internal career ladder, based on staffing schedule information aggregated to the establishment level.

variable_name: percentage of workers in professional, technical, and managerial occupations
description: Occupational composition was measured as the percentage of workers in professional, technical, and managerial occupations, obtained from job analysis and staffing schedule information aggregated to the establishment level. Production, transportation, and extractive jobs are the omitted category in the models.

The effect of having a specialized personnel function was measured by a binary variable coded 1 for establishments with 100 or more employees and at least one full-time person engaged in personnel activities, based on detailed occupational codes. In the sample, specialized personnel roles occurring in organizations with fewer than 100 employees were typically payroll clerks and the like.

Establishments were coded 1 on a binary variable for unionization if there was any evidence that a significant percentage of the enterprise's line workers were covered by a collective bargaining agreement. Because nonunion firms in highly unionized sectors are likely to resemble their unionized counterparts, enterprises were also coded 1 if they were nonunion but in a sector of California's economy that was highly unionized as of 1973; industry sectors were coded as highly unionized if 45 percent or more of their labor force was unionized.
time_window: July 1973 for the industry unionization data

description: Based on detailed SIC codes, organizations were classified into major industrial sectors and binary variables denote industrial location. A few establishments operated in more than one sector or belonged to both the state and social overhead capital sectors as operationalized, so the binary variables are not entirely exclusive.

variable_name: average size of enterprises in the organization's industry
description: The average size of enterprises in the organization's industry, the proxy for the tendency toward isomorphism within organizational fields, was measured from annual County Business Patterns data for California, ascribing the relevant figure to each enterprise. The variable was transformed logarithmically (base e), since absolute differences in an industry's average firm size are expected to have diminishing effects on the division of labor.

Market scope was coded on a four-point scale used to measure the breadth and complexity of the environment: 1 = local (city, county, SMSA); 2 = state; 3 = regional; 4 = national or international. It was coded from qualitative materials obtained from Employment Service analysts.

variable_name: percentage of workers in sales occupations
description: Occupational composition was measured as the percentage of workers in sales jobs, obtained from job analysis and staffing schedule information aggregated to the establishment level.

A binary variable coded 1 if the firm relied principally on craft technology or was one or more standard deviations above the sample mean in terms of average training time (specific vocational preparation). Though not perfect, this operationalization seemed to capture enterprises whose production workers had unusually high amounts of general human capital.

Managers rated each of 56 issue characteristics for how well the characteristic fits their understanding of a strategic issue that is a threat, on a 7-point scale anchored 'not a threat; fits a nonthreat extremely well' (-3), 'can't tell' (0), and 'threat; fits a threat extremely well' (+3). The 56 characteristics included 28 pairs of attribute antonyms and were ordered randomly. Mean ratings across respondents were used to plot the characteristics.

Managers rated the same 56 issue characteristics for how well each fits their understanding of a strategic issue that is an opportunity, using parallel wording to the threat rating scale. Characteristics were ordered randomly for the rating task. Mean ratings across respondents were used to plot the characteristics.

Information condition created by embedding in the scenario a subset of issue characteristics selected from the threat-distinctive region of the Study 1 map, i.e., characteristics consistent with threat and discrepant from opportunity. Issue characteristics were not italicized in the scenarios read by study participants. All participants were exposed to all information conditions.

Information condition created by embedding in the scenario a subset of issue characteristics selected from the opportunity-distinctive region of the Study 1 map, i.e., characteristics consistent with opportunity and discrepant from threat. Issue characteristics were not italicized in the scenarios read by study participants.

Information condition in which the issue characteristics embedded in the scenario are consistent with both threat and opportunity and discrepant from neither. Characteristics for the ambiguous condition were highlighted in the Study 1 map and have been described in detail above.

Information condition defined by two criteria: the issue characteristics were rated near zero (-.50 < mean < .50) for both threat and opportunity, and the threat and opportunity ratings for these characteristics were not significantly different from each other (p > .05, two-tailed paired t-test).

variable_name: "Does this represent a threat for us?"
description: After reading each scenario, respondents answered question #3, 'Does this represent a threat for us?', answered using a scale of 1 (definitely no) to 5 (definitely yes). Each participant provided a rating under each of the eight information conditions. The other questions were included to add face validity to the task and to minimize participants' sensitivity to the research questions.

variable_name: "Does this represent an opportunity for us?"
description: After reading each scenario, respondents answered question #7, 'Does this represent an opportunity for us?', answered using a scale of 1 (definitely no) to 5 (definitely yes). Each participant provided a rating under each of the eight information conditions.

Bargaining without being covered by a law, measured as the number of years the city had bargained with the police department and was not covered by a law as of 1971, 1976, and 1981. Including this variable enables comparisons of this type of union-city relationship to the reference category of nonbargaining cities.

The number of years the city bargained with police and was covered by a law not providing for interest arbitration in each of the three data years. It measures the first type of mandated relationship.
The number of years the city bargained with police and was covered by a police arbitration law as of 1971, 1976, and 1981. It measures the second type of mandated relationship.
The log of per capita police department expenditures, constructed from data on police department expenditures and city population. All monetary variables were transformed into constant 1971 dollars.

The log of police expenditures per full-time police employee, constructed from data on police department expenditures and full-time police employment. All monetary variables were transformed into constant 1971 dollars.

The log of the number of sworn police officers employed per capita. Sworn police officers, regardless of rank or uniformed status, are trained in law enforcement procedures and practices, given arrest powers and weapons, and permitted to use force in the performance of their duties.

The log of the number of police civilian employees per capita. Police civilian employees is a heterogeneous category that includes all other employees of the police department (clerical, custodial, mechanical/technical, and administrative).

Police expenditures as a percentage of total city expenditures, constructed from data on police department expenditures and total city expenditures. It captures the police department's share of the city budget.

The log of per capita total city expenditures, used to examine overall city budgets and assess possible responses to the cost pressures generated by bargaining relationships. All monetary variables were transformed into constant 1971 dollars.

Weight was measured as perceived subunit power: clinic staff rated the power of each subunit on a scale of little influence (1) to a great deal of influence (5), and the power weight of each subunit was the mean score each subunit received from all members of the clinic. Scope was measured by the number of decisions in which a subunit participated (participation power), assessed by observing decision-making processes and from interviews with clinic staff. Because the two measures were highly correlated (r = .85) and could not be validly distinguished, they were combined into a single index of power.
time_window: measured at T1 and T2, two years apart

description: Six elements of the clinics' environment were rated by subunit heads and headquarters executives for level of uncertainty according to variability in outcomes, from no variations (1) to high, unpatterned variation (6), and for criticality, from not critical (1) to highly critical (7); the uncertainty level of each outcome was the mean variability rating weighted by the mean criticality rating. Subunit coping with the six areas was rated from 1 (no coping) to 5 (high coping), with the category of absorbing the effects of variations given a double weight, using interviews, observations, and analysis of clinic records. Each variable was first divided into quartiles and combined into a sequence of 16 categories ranging from high coping with high uncertainty (16) to low coping with low uncertainty (1), with uncertainty given priority over coping; each subunit was scored by its location on this sequence.

Since the number of actual workflow links between subunits was a constant (reciprocal links), perceived pervasiveness was measured by asking staff in each clinic to rate each subunit's relations with the others and the work interaction among subunit heads, on a scale of hardly any work relations (1) to very extensive work relations (5). Perceived pervasiveness was supplemented by observed pervasiveness: observers rated each subunit's workflow pervasiveness on the same 5-point scale, and the observed ratings were combined with the two perceived pervasiveness ratings into a single workflow pervasiveness index. The other dimension of centrality, immediacy, did not yield adequate results because all subunits were rated low on it.

Actual nonsubstitutability was measured by objective indicators such as the level of formal education and experience required for a job within the subunit, difficulty in hiring (length of time positions have been vacant), existence of formal prerequisites for hiring (e.g., registered nurses only), and number of subunit tasks contracted out, collected from records of the organization and supplemented by headquarters executives; except for experience requirements and length of time position has been vacant, which correlated poorly with the others, these variables were transformed into standard scores and combined. Assessed nonsubstitutability was measured by observers rating subunits on substitutability from within the subunit itself, substitutability of the activities of one subunit by those of another, and substitutability of a subunit by entities outside the clinic, combined into a scale. The mean standardized scores of all nonsubstitutability items were combined into a single nonsubstitutability index.

variable_name: Control over structural conditions (coping with uncertainty, centrality, nonsubstitutability; also combined into control over contingencies)
description: The three structural conditions, control over coping with uncertainty, centrality (workflow pervasiveness) and nonsubstitutability, were each assessed by subunit ratings using at least two methods (interviews, questionnaires, observations, records) at both time points. They were used separately as predictors of subunit power and, because they were highly correlated, also combined into a single measure of control over contingencies.
scale: subunit ratings on three conditions; combined index
time_window: two data collections two years apart

description: A dummy variable coded one if any contractual agreement potentially provides the CEO with a payment contingent upon a change in control of the company, zero otherwise. The data were obtained from the 1984 proxy statement for each company.
Measured as the log of sales in 1984; the logarithm was used so that extreme values would not bias the results.
A dummy variable used for firms designated as owner-controlled if at least 5 percent of the stock was beneficially owned by an individual or organization; other firms are management-controlled.

Computed for 1984 by taking the difference between a firm's total market value (market value of equity plus book value of liabilities) and the book value of its assets, normalized by sales. The lower a firm's EXCESS value, the greater the threat of a takeover.

variable_name: number of boards the CEO serves on
description: The number of corporate boards on which the CEO serves, obtained from 1984 proxies. Only major boards were counted, specifically those listed in Moody's industrial, finance, or transportation manuals, because the variable was meant to measure prestige.
Defined as the board tenure of the CEO divided by the average board tenure of the other directors. Data were obtained from 1984 proxies.

variable_name: number of outsiders appointed after the CEO
description: The number of directors classified as outsiders who were appointed after the CEO; with the size of the board held constant, the coefficient on this variable effectively represents the percentage of the board composed of outsiders appointed after the CEO. Directors were classified as outsiders if they had never worked for the firm or one of its subsidiaries in a high-level executive position.
The CEO's board tenure, obtained from 1984 proxies. The paper does not state the units in which it is measured.

Papers linked with political parties constitute the group of organizations with interorganizational linkages. Dummy variables were included for each type of paper other than general-content papers, which are the excluded category; the party-affiliated dummy marks papers affiliated with a political party.

Failure was defined as the permanent cessation of a newspaper's publication. Temporary suspensions, whether voluntary or through government suppression, were not included as failures, nor were permanent suppressions by the Tsarist regime or the republic; the five instances in which a newspaper was sold but continued to publish were also not counted as failures.

The single-attribute-change variable was coded as 1 if the newspaper had experienced a single attribute transformation within the previous five years and as 0 otherwise. A single attribute change is a transformation in which only one attribute such as frequency of publication was altered.

The multiple-attribute-change dummy variable was constructed in the same way as the single-attribute-change dummy, coded 1 if more than one attribute was altered in the same issue within the previous five years and 0 otherwise. As many as five characteristics were changed simultaneously.

Environmental shocks were represented by a set of period-effect dummy variables. The authors describe periods of restrictive press laws and repression by the Tsars (a priori censorship and foreign-news censorship), the Years of Oppression, three wars and the Great Depression. The text states the set comprises seven dummy variables but names more periods than seven.

Dependent variable: the rate of transition to adoption of a poison pill. Adoption dates or dates of first public announcement were supplied by the IRRC Corporate Governance Service and cross-checked against a Merrill Lynch Capital Markets internal document for the period up to May 1986. Adoption of any type of poison pill is treated as equivalent, i.e., the board's adoption, without shareholder approval, of a device that raises barriers to takeover, and adoption is treated as a fatal, nonrepeatable event. Firms were considered at risk starting just prior to the first adoption and were dropped from the risk set upon adoption.

The proportion of all outstanding shares held by all officers and directors of the firm according to the proxy statement dated closest to January 1, 1986. Where Compact Disclosure reported shares held by insiders but not total shares outstanding, COMPUSTAT's figure for the relevant period was used; where insider holdings were missing, the proxy statement was consulted directly. Stock options were not included in the measure.
time_window: proxy statement dated closest to January 1, 1986

description: A dummy variable indicating whether the firm had adopted a golden parachute contract for top executives, taken from IRRC published data. The measure was available for 1984, 1986, and 1987 and was lagged in the analysis.

The percentage of shares held by all large (5 percent or more) blockholders, calculated as the sum of all shares held by large holders divided by the number of shares outstanding, multiplied by 100. Measured as of the first quarter of 1986.

The percentage of directors that were executives of the firm, from board composition data in the proxy statement dated closest to January 1, 1986, as reported in Compact Disclosure. Inside board members were those Disclosure identified as executives of the firm, and a computerized matching procedure comparing apparent outside directors against a separate comprehensive list of officers for each firm identified several dozen more executives.
time_window: proxy statement dated closest to January 1, 1986

description: Board interlocks is the sum of all nonduplicated ties the firm's board had to all other boards in an expanded sample of firms: the total number of other boards each director sat on, summed across all directors, minus duplicated ties. The measure used in the analyses is the natural log of the number of interlocks plus unity, because of the extremely skewed distribution, which also allows valid values for firms with zero interlocks; it implicitly assumes decreasing returns to further interlocks. Data quality was ensured by computerized routines and multiple hand-checks against Standard and Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors and Executives.
time_window: proxy statement dated closest to January 1, 1986

description: The number of the focal firm's interlock partners that had previously adopted a poison pill, calculated quarterly; the analyses used the natural log of this number plus unity because the measure is highly skewed by a handful of outliers. By definition the measure is monotonically nondecreasing over time, and it is constrained to be less than or equal to the firm's total number of interlocks.
time_window: calculated quarterly, measured as of the beginning of each spell

description: The percentage of firms in the focal firm's primary 2-digit SIC industry that had adopted a poison pill as of the beginning of the current quarter, calculated in three-month increments. Primary industry is defined by the 2-digit category in which the firm made most of its sales.

variable_name: number of days until the firm became subject to a tender offer from a nonmanagement group
description: The dependent measure is the number of days from 1 January 1980 until the firm became subject to a tender offer from a nonmanagement group, if ever. Firms not subject to a tender offer, and firms delisted from COMPUSTAT for reasons other than a successful tender offer, were considered right-censored. For firms that received more than one tender offer, the date of the first offer was used.

Annual data on the market-to-book ratio were obtained from COMPUSTAT and calculated for each year from 1979 through 1989 for firms that did not receive tender offers; for target firms they were calculated until the last point prior to the tender offer at which data were available. Each firm's data were lagged one year, so that the risk in a given year depended on the value measured at the beginning of the spell.

Annual return on equity was obtained from COMPUSTAT and calculated for each year from 1979 through 1989 for non-target firms and up to the last point prior to the tender offer for target firms. The values were lagged one year in the models.

Cash flow is measured as income before extraordinary items divided by market value, taken from annual COMPUSTAT data. Values were calculated for each year from 1979 through 1989 for non-target firms and until the last point prior to the tender offer for target firms, and were lagged one year in the models.
A dummy variable representing free cash flow, coded as unity if the firm was above the median on the cash flow measure and below the median on the capital structure measure, and zero otherwise.

variable_name: debt or capital structure (long-term debt/market value)
description: Capital structure is measured as long-term debt divided by market value, from annual COMPUSTAT data. Values were computed for each year from 1979 through 1989 for non-target firms and until the last point before the tender offer for target firms, and were lagged one year in the models.

Age was calculated using data on the year of founding, usually reported as the year of original incorporation, from Standard & Poor's Encyclopedia and Moody's Industrial Manual for 1980. Because the additional effect of age on organizational inertia should decrease with age, the measure of age was logged, assuming that organizations become inert at a decreasing rate as they age.

Because firm-level measures of workforce seniority do not exist at the needed scale, average tenure (the average number of years employees spent with their current employer) was calculated by industry from the January 1981 Current Population Survey. Industries are defined at approximately the 3-digit SIC level, so the analyses assume that a firm's average tenure is close to that of its primary 3-digit industry. Only full-time wage earners in the civilian labor force were included, leaving 61,470 individuals.
Growth in employment was calculated as a percentage change in the number of employees for each year, using annual COMPUSTAT data.

A dummy variable coded as unity if the firm operated in an industry that was above the median in tenure and the firm was at or below the median (zero) in employment growth, and zero otherwise. This interaction term was used to test the joint effect of a highly tenured workforce and low growth.

Using data on dominant ownership blocks in 1980 from the Corporate Data Exchange Stock Ownership Directory, firms were coded as family-controlled if the largest ownership block (other than the company's own pension plan, ESOP, or other stock ownership plan) was greater than 5 percent and was controlled by a family or individual. Management control, with no owner possessing more than 5 percent of the firm's equity, was the omitted category.

Based on the Corporate Data Exchange Stock Ownership Directory for 1980, firms were coded as bank-controlled if the largest ownership block was greater than 5 percent and was controlled by a commercial bank. Management control, with no owner possessing more than 5 percent of the firm's equity, was the omitted category.

Total interlocks was measured as the number of other firms in the interlock sample with which the firm shared at least one director. Board data for 1982 were coded from Standard & Poor's Directory of Corporations, Directors, and Executives for 1983, and the same procedures and sample were used to create interlock data for 1986 from Compact Disclosure. Because these data were unavailable before 1982, models with these variables were estimated only for 1983-1990, using the 1982 data for firm-years 1983-1985 and the 1986 data for firm-years 1986-1990.
time_window: 1982 and 1986 board data applied to 1983-1990 firm-years

description: The interlock variable for ties sent by banks was coded as unity if the firm's board had at least one member who was an executive of one of the sampled commercial banks, and zero otherwise. The interlock sample included the union of the firms in the 1980 or 1986 Fortune 500 largest industrials and the Fortune 50 largest commercial banks, 25 largest diversified financials, 25 largest retailers, and 25 largest transportation companies for 1986 for which board data were available.
time_window: 1982 and 1986 board data applied to 1983-1990 firm-years

description: Total compensation is the sum of salary, annual bonus, and the authors' valuations for stock options, performance plans, phantom stock, and restricted stock. Stock options were valued at 25 percent of their exercise price; grants associated with performance plans or phantom stock plans were valued by multiplying the number of performance units, performance shares, or phantom shares by their respective target values; grants of restricted stock were valued by multiplying the number of restricted shares by the price per share at the date of grant. Dollar amounts are expressed in 1990 dollars.

Indicator variables identify the executive's position in the hierarchy: Div equals one if the executive is a divisional CEO and zero otherwise, Grp equals one if the executive is a group CEO and zero otherwise, and CEO equals one if the executive is the corporate CEO and zero otherwise. The plant manager is the omitted executive position, so the intercept refers to that position.

variable_name: Remp, Paext, Ceop, Extp, Perext, Int5p, Ext5p
description: Managerial power is captured by seven surrogates. Ceop is the percentage of outstanding shares owned by the corporate CEO and his or her immediate family; Paext is the percentage of external board members appointed after the present CEO assumed office; Remp is the number of employees in the executive's unit relative to total corporate employees for group, division, and plant executives; Extp is the percentage of outstanding shares owned by external board members; Perext is the percentage of the board that is external; Int5p equals one if a non-CEO internal board member owns at least 5 percent of the shares; and Ext5p equals one if an external party or blockholder owns at least 5 percent of the shares. Remp, Paext, and Ceop are assumed to be positively associated with managerial power, whereas Extp, Perext, Int5p, and Ext5p are assumed to be inversely related to it. Ceop and Paext were not used for group, division, and plant executives because they are unique to the corporate CEO.

Performance is measured by accounting return on assets (Roa), computed as the ratio of earnings before extraordinary items to total assets and obtained from the 1987 Compustat files; for group, division, and plant managers performance is the segment return on assets (Unroa) of the segment in the same two-digit SIC code as the unit, computed as segment operating earnings divided by segment assets. A second performance measure is the firm's real stock market return (Ret). Return on assets is inflation-adjusted by multiplying earnings by the current consumer price index and total assets by the consumer price index five years prior; stock returns are also converted into real terms. Because the surveys provide compensation payments or grants for 1982 to 1984, the associated performance measure was computed for 1981 to 1983.

Each dyad-year record was dichotomously coded for a dependent variable indicating whether the members of the pair of firms entered an alliance with each other in the given year. No dyad experienced more than one alliance in a given year.

Each industry panel was segmented into distinct organizational niches by entering firms' industry subsegment and national origin into a hierarchical clustering algorithm employing complete linkage and Euclidean distances. Strategic interdependence is coded 1 if the firms in a dyad belonged to different niches and 0 if they belonged to the same niche.

The number of prior ties between the firms in a dyad, computed in UCINET IV from the yearly adjacency matrixes of alliance activity through the year prior to the given year. Multiple ties between the same two firms were captured with a Guttman scale reflecting the strongest alliance the firms had formed, and a squared term for repeated ties was used to assess a damper effect.
time_window: all alliance activity until the year before the given year

description: The interaction of the number of prior third partners each pair of firms shared and a dummy variable indicating whether a dyad had a previous direct tie or not (1 = no prior tie, 0 = prior tie). The interaction term is thus positive only when there were third-party ties but no direct ties between the two firms.
time_window: all alliance activity until the year before the given year

description: The shortest path between two firms in the relevant network of prior alliances, computed with the distance routine in UCINET IV, which calculates all path distances as the sum of values of all links and then estimates the path with least distance. For the weighted matrixes the reciprocals of the weights were taken, so that stronger ties implied shorter distances.
time_window: all alliance activity until the year before the given year

description: Records the time elapsed since the prior alliance between two firms, which is set to 0 at the outset. If a subsequent alliance occurred between the firms, the variable is reset to 0 and again captures the time elapsed since the latest alliance. A quadratic term was also included in the model.

The central dependent variable is an index (sum), which is the sum of the number of the programs listed in Table 1 that are offered by the establishment. This sum can range from zero to nine. The Cronbach's alpha for the index is .75. The model is estimated with ordinary least squares.
The survey asked about the percentage of the establishments' core employees who were women. The variable is the percentage of the core labor force that is female.

For four labor force concerns the variable measure is the response on a 5-point scale to the question about how serious are the difficulties which are attributable to family issues. The scale for each question was 'not serious,' 'slightly serious,' 'moderately serious,' 'very serious,' and 'extremely serious.'

The establishment was asked how difficulties associated with work/family conflicts were expected to evolve, looking ahead five years; the variable future measures the response of the establishment on this 3-point scale (more difficulties, about the same level of difficulties, or less difficulties).

ladder measures where the establishment is on a 5-point scale assessing the extent of preference for insiders in filling job openings, where the value of 5 indicates that such a preference is extremely important. This variable measures whether ports of entry are limited in the establishment.
A similarly structured variable that measures the extent to which seniority is used as the criterion for determining which insider gets promoted to fill vacancies.
HR takes the value of 1 if the establishment had a human resources department, defined as a person or group of persons whose only responsibility was human resource issues.

The respondent assigned a value of 100 points to the goal of limiting the growth of wage and benefit costs over the next five years and then assigned points to several other objectives relative to that goal. One objective was 'obtaining or maintaining a committed and cooperative workforce over the next five years'; commit is the number of points assigned to this objective relative to the 100 points for limiting wage growth.

Captures the extent of employee discretion in carrying out work assignments. The variable indicates where on a 5-point scale the establishment is in response to a question about the extent of discretion core employees have in deciding 'the best way to accomplish their assignments' (the value of 5 indicates complete discretion).

Data were collected on whether any core employees were involved in problem-solving groups/quality circles and, if so, what percentage was involved. The percentage of core employees involved in the practice ranges from 0 to 100. The interviewer defined the practice as 'Quality programs where employees are involved in problem solving.'

Data were collected on whether any core employees were involved in total quality management and, if so, what percentage was involved. The percentage of core employees involved ranges from 0 to 100. The interviewer defined the practice as 'Quality control approach that emphasizes the importance of communications, feedback, and teamwork.'
Categorical variable that takes the value of 1 if the business establishment provides formal training to its executives and professionals on a regular basis, and zero otherwise.
Categorical variable that takes the value of 1 if the business establishment provides formal training to its clerical, sales, and production workers on a regular basis, and zero otherwise.
The number of executives and managers divided by total employment in the business establishment.
The number of professional and technical employees divided by total employment in the establishment.

Following Hodson (1983), market concentration was measured by an industry concentration ratio, with industry sales concentration measured as total sales of the largest eight firms in an industry, divided by total sales of all business establishments in that industry. Due to data limitations, industry sales concentration was measured at the 2-digit SIC level.
Firm size is the natural logarithm of the total number of employees in the firm in 1986. In the analysis, the term firm refers to the corporation as a whole.
Percentage union was measured by the percentage of employees under collective bargaining agreements in the business establishment.

Following Averitt's (1968) definition, regulated industry identifies a set of industries from which regulatory presence can be inferred, with a value of 1 if the business establishment is in transportation, utility, or communication industries, and zero otherwise.

The strength of government presence was measured by government purchase, which is industry output sold to government, divided by total industry output. Government purchase was measured at the 3-digit Standard Industry Classification (SIC) level.

As in Pfeffer and Cohen (1984), decline is a categorical variable measuring previous workforce reductions in business establishments that takes the value of 1 if employment had decreased 10 percent or more between 1984 and 1986, and zero otherwise. The employment-decline threshold of 10 percent or more for decline was chosen after examining linear and curvilinear relationships, as well as other threshold levels, which produced no significant effects.

Dichotomous dependent variable for transition-assistance benefits (outplacement and/or retraining assistance) for salaried employees, with 1 indicating the presence of these benefits and 0 indicating their absence.
Dichotomous dependent variable for severance pay for salaried employees, with 1 indicating the presence of these benefits and 0 indicating their absence.
Dichotomous dependent variable for transition-assistance benefits for hourly workers, with 1 indicating the presence of these benefits and 0 indicating their absence.
Dichotomous dependent variable for severance pay for hourly workers, with 1 indicating the presence of these benefits and 0 indicating their absence.
Dichotomous dependent variable for advance notification for hourly workers, with 1 indicating the presence of these benefits and 0 indicating their absence.

Measured by five dichotomous dependent variables, each coded 1 if the establishment provides the benefit and 0 otherwise: transition assistance for salaried employees, severance pay for salaried employees, transition assistance for hourly workers, severance pay for hourly workers, and advance notification for hourly workers. Each was analyzed in a separate logistic regression using the establishment survey.

Two dummy variables record whether or not the changes had occurred, taking the value of 0 until the occurrence of a change and the value of 1 thereafter, regardless of the number of changes. These variables captured the average effect of all changes, net of other factors. Each was also allowed to interact multiplicatively with organizational age.

In both cases the value of the clock is 0 until the occurrence of a change; the clock then records the elapsed time since the change, and if another change of the same type occurs the clock is reset to 0 and then again records the elapsed time. The elapsed time represents the number of days since an event, rescaled by dividing by 1000, and the clock values were logged for the analysis.
The basic time unit used to construct the spells was the day; age was rescaled by dividing by 1000 and the natural logarithm of age was used in the models.

Two variables count cumulative occurrences of the different types of changes; they take on the value of 0 until the first change, the value of 1 until the second change, a value of 2 until the third change, and so on.

Each change dummy was allowed to interact multiplicatively with organizational age. The resulting interactions take the value of 0 prior to the first change and the value of age thereafter, so that if the first change occurs early in the life cycle age is lower and the change in the hazard and change rates are smaller, and if the first change occurs later in the life cycle age is higher and the change in the rates is greater.

Failure was an event in the event history of each newspaper, defined as the voluntary and permanent cessation of publication. Involuntary suppressions by the state were not counted as failures. The data came from the bibliography of Finnish newspapers.

The total amount of money borrowed, both short-term and long-term, including public bond issues. It was divided by total assets to control for firm size, and the dependent variable and all independent variables affected by inflation were adjusted to constant dollars (1967 = 100).

Anticipated earnings was the product of the firm's profitability and growth in the period leading up to the year in question, each averaged over the previous three-year period. Cost of capital was measured by Moody's bond rating (with missing values predicted from a linear function of the debt ratio and dividends per share). Because the two operationalizations are in very different units, each was transformed to standardized scores and the standardized score for cost of capital was subtracted from the standardized score for anticipated earnings, creating the ERB variable.
time_window: three-year period prior to the year coded

description: Operationalized in terms of retained earnings, the amount of internal funds left after a corporation has paid its stock dividends for the year, divided by total assets to control for firm size. The variable was lagged by an interpolated half-year, averaging the previous and current years' values.

Following Fligstein (1987), operationalized as the employment background of the person identified as being in control of the firm. CEOs with previous positions exclusively in finance and/or accounting were coded as finance CEOs; those with backgrounds in finance and other areas (such as sales, marketing, or production) were coded as having backgrounds in general management. The presence of a finance CEO was a dummy variable coded 1 for yes, and it was measured with a straddled lag.

Initially computed as the number of directors whose principal affiliation was with a commercial bank, an insurance company, or an investment bank or diversified financial corporation, with principal affiliation determined by identifying the individual's full-time position. Because the number may be confounded by board and firm size, the authors collapsed financial representation into a dummy variable coded 1 for the presence of one or more financial representatives on the firm's board; equations with the proportional variable gave virtually identical results.
scale: dummy (1 = one or more financial representatives)

description: Whether a firm had an employee stock ownership plan was a dummy variable coded 1 for yes.

The number of risk factors described in the IPO registration statement, where top management must explicitly list and discuss the risk factors facing the IPO firm. Because personal legal liability stemming from the Securities Act of 1933 is imposed on top management's presentation of risk factors, differences in the number of risks described capture fundamental differences in the riskiness of IPO firms. Higher values indicate greater risk.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Dichotomous measure of the choice of a best-efforts or firm-commitment offering contract in the IPO underwriting. The measure takes the value of 1 for firm commitment and 0 for best efforts; because firms choosing best-efforts contracts are riskier relative to those choosing firm-commitment contracts, higher values indicate lower risk.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Measure of firm risk derived from the reported profitability or unprofitability of the IPO firm. The variable is coded 0 for profitable and 1 for unprofitable; a documented minimum inflow from operating activities suggests that firm risk will be lower than for firms that did not report any measured earnings.

Constructed by regressing the actual after-market standard deviation from the post-IPO market on the three previous risk measures (profitability indicator, number of risks disclosed, and type of underwriting contract) for all firms; the expected after-market standard deviation is the predicted value of this cross-sectional regression. The measure reflects the composite of the three risk measures along with the actual variability of share price for the post-IPO firm, and higher levels suggest higher levels of firm risk.
time_window: post-IPO market, combined with the three pre-IPO risk measures

description: Dichotomous measure indicating whether stock options were used to compensate the top management group (1 = yes; 0 = no). The presence or absence of options is explicitly discussed in every firm's registration statement with the SEC, and the authors' reading of the registration statements revealed that the granting of stock options was almost always limited to the top management group.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The percentage of IPO firms' equity held by the top management group. The individuals in the top management group and their equity holdings before the IPO are explicitly identified in the IPO registration statements.

variable_name: noncash incentive portion of total compensation
description: The percentage of total executive compensation derived from noncash sources, constructed as (the value of managers' stock options + the change in value of stock held by the manager in the pre-IPO year) / (cash compensation + the value of managers' stock options + the change in value of stock held by the manager in the pre-IPO year). Stock options were valued using the Black-Scholes (1973) option pricing model; no adjustment was made for dividend yield because IPO firms rarely pay dividends, the risk-free rate was estimated with the average market yield on government securities of similar maturity to the option, and the variance of stock price was estimated using the 20-day after-market standard deviation. The managers' equity value change was estimated by computing the difference between the first-day bid price and the contributed capital per share divided by the age of the firm multiplied by the number of equity shares held by the managers.
time_window: pre-IPO year and first-day after-market price

variable_name: ratio of outside directors to total directors
description: The ratio of the number of outside directors to total directors (i.e., inside and outside directors), a measure commonly used by researchers to measure corporate control.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The proportion of outside owner-directors (i.e., directors who are also shareholders) to total directors.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Dichotomous measure of the presence (1 = yes; 0 = no) of a shareholder with large equity holdings (>5 percent; 0 otherwise) who is not on the board, i.e., a blockholder.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Dichotomous measure capturing whether the IPO firm is venture-backed (1 = yes; 0 = no).
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Dichotomous CEO/chairman variable indicating whether the CEO position is separated from the chairman of the board position (1 = yes; 0 = no).
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The number of ISO 9000 certificates in each country and year, taken from an annual survey initiated by Mobil Corp. and then continued by ISO. The reference month for the number of certificates was December of each year, except for 1992 (January 1993), 1993 (September), and 1994 (June), due to irregularities in the original survey. The variable is non-negative, integer-valued, overdispersed, and longitudinal.

General government consumption, obtained from the CD-ROM of the World Bank's 1999 World Development Indicators, normalized by gross domestic product to control for the size of each country's economy. The authors acknowledge that this variable includes expenses other than those incurred by the government as a buyer, but argue that a larger government presence still implies a larger base of transactions with commercial entities. Entered into the analyses in logarithmic form and measured with a one-year lag.

The value of inward foreign direct investment stock, obtained from the United Nations' World Investment Report for 1994-1999, normalized by gross domestic product to control for the size of each country's economy. Used to measure the coercive effect of the presence of foreign multinationals. Entered into the analyses in logarithmic form and measured with a one-year lag.

variable_name: articles on operations, engineering, manufacturing, and quality per capita
description: Count of articles on "operations," "engineering," "manufacturing," and "quality" authored by residents of each country during each year, using the Science Citation Index. Coauthored papers by residents in different countries were attributed to each of the countries. The number of articles published in academic, technical, and trade journals is treated as an indicator of knowledge exchange and exposure among members of a community to a certain practice or idea. Normalized by population to control for the size of the country and entered into the analyses in logarithmic form.

For country i at time t, the strength of trade ties between country i and every other country j (country i's trade with country j as a proportion of country i's total trade) is squared and multiplied by the number of ISO 9000 certificates in country j as of the previous year, and these products are summed over all other countries. The cohesion effect is highest when a country has strong trade ties with other countries that have a large number of certificates as of the previous year. The measure is non-negative but has no upper bound.

For each country i and year t, export and import industry share vectors were constructed indicating the share of each of the 34 industry categories in country i's total exports and imports; the two vectors were stacked to form a single vector. The measure multiplies the Pearson correlation coefficient between the industry share vectors of countries i and j in year t-1 by the number of certificates held by country j in year t-1, summed over j. The correlation indicates the extent to which two countries compete in the same industries regardless of whom they trade with. The measure is not bounded and can be negative or positive.
time_window: trade vectors at t-1; certificates at t-1

description: A 13-item scale intended to capture the three component behaviors of ingratiation: other-enhancement, opinion conformity, and favor rendering. Items were adapted from measures developed by Westphal (1998) and Kumar and Beyerlein (1991) and respondents reported the number of times a specific behavior occurred during the prior twelve months. Factor analysis with promax rotation produced one ingratiation factor with item loadings greater than .5, and the scale's interitem reliability was Cronbach's α = .90; factor scores were estimated using the Bartlett method.

variable_name: appointment at a board where the CEO serves as an outside director
description: A dichotomous measure indicating whether the focal manager was appointed to a particular board (x_j) where the CEO served as director at the time of the survey. Appointments were examined at all firms in the Forbes listing of large and medium-sized U.S. firms for which data were available, over the two-year period subsequent to the survey.

variable_name: appointment at a board to which the CEO is indirectly connected
description: A dichotomous measure indicating whether the focal manager was appointed to a board to which the CEO was indirectly connected, that is, a board where a fellow CEO-director on the nominating committee of x_j served as an outside director. Appointments were examined over the two-year period subsequent to the survey.

variable_name: degree from an elite undergraduate institution
description: A dummy variable indicating whether the manager held a degree from an elite undergraduate institution, using elite designations taken from prior research on the corporate elite.

variable_name: MBA degree from an elite graduate school of business
description: A dummy variable indicating whether the manager held an MBA degree from an elite graduate school of business, using elite designations taken from prior research on the corporate elite.

variable_name: member of an exclusive social club
description: A dummy variable indicating whether the manager was a member of one or more of the most exclusive social clubs in the U.S., as designated in prior research on the corporate elite.

variable_name: listed in the Social Register and/or attended an exclusive preparatory school
description: A dummy variable indicating whether the manager was listed in the Social Register and/or attended an exclusive preparatory school, with exclusive preparatory school designations taken from prior research on the corporate elite.

variable_name: minority status with respect to ethnicity and/or gender
description: A dummy variable indicating minority status with respect to ethnicity and/or gender. Because every CEO in the sample was a white male, demographic dissimilarity from the CEO is effectively equivalent to having minority status.

A standardized factor score computed from four dichotomously coded variables (1 if present; 0 otherwise): presence of strategic planning, conduct of an independent financial audit, collection of quantitative data for program evaluation, and use of consultants. Because these variables were binary, the authors used a matrix of tetrachoric correlation coefficients among the four variables to extract factor loadings via a principal components method; all four variables loaded strongly on one single general factor. The obtained factor loadings were used to compute the factor score, which was then recalculated as a z-score.
time_window: consultants in the past three years; other practices at time of interview

description: A sum of five binary variables, coded 1 when present and 0 otherwise, summed for each organization to measure the level of organizational professionalism. The index was constructed so that an organization that is staffed and run only by paid personnel and managed by a full-time, paid executive director receives the highest score, and a volunteer-based organization without a formal executive director position receives the lowest score.

A dummy variable for organizations whose executive directors or board chairs had professional degrees of any kind. For organizations without a formal executive director position, the educational background of the chair of the board of directors was coded.
A dummy variable covering a range of general management degrees, including Master's of Business Administration, Master's in Public Administration, and nonprofit management.
A dummy variable for all professional degrees that are neither managerial nor sovereign, such as education, clinical psychology, criminology, social work, and public health.
A dummy variable for the ideal-type professions of law (J.D.), medicine (M.D.), divinity (M.A. in Divinity), and academe (Ph.D.).

A dummy variable measuring whether nonprofit managers, staff, and volunteers attend workshops or conferences to further hone their skills, in substantive areas or in management-related areas. Interviewees were asked whether they or their management staff attend workshops, conferences, or training courses to help manage the organization.

A dummy variable measuring whether nonprofit managers, staff, and volunteers attend management development training or workshops, such as executive programs in nonprofit strategy or board governance. Training courses attended were researched and coded to determine the kinds of training provided (management, substantive, or both).

A dummy variable measuring whether nonprofit managers, staff, and volunteers attend training and development in substantive areas, differentiated from management-related workshops or classes. Training courses attended were researched and coded to determine the kinds of training provided (management, substantive, or both).

Dummy indicating hybrid organizations, defined as any firms that combined more than one of the 219 industry categories identified in the Reference Book during the postbellum period. Approximately 83 percent of firms were listed with only one explicit category, slightly over 15 percent were listed with two, 1 percent with three, and only .05 percent with four explicit categories.

The frequency with which a particular form or combination is encountered in the Dun Reference Book, measured in 1,000s. It was included both as a general control and as an interaction term with hybridity to assess whether form frequency is particularly relevant for the coverage and evaluation of hybrid enterprises.

Dummy indicating firms that were assigned a residual category ('&c.', etcetera) in addition to one or more explicit industry categories, denoting an ambiguous product line or service for a multiproduct enterprise. In the sample, the classification of 9 percent of all firms was marked with an etcetera.

From 1885 on, identified as instances in which credit reporters attempted to ascribe a second-order category to a hybrid business, but the multiple lines of business could not be mapped to a single trade group. Before 1885, the same procedure was applied counterfactually to identify boundary violations that would be at odds with the later second-order classification system.

Firms were ranked into seven credit categories, ranging from A1 (a respected firm with unlimited credit) and 1 or 1.5 (strong credit) down to 2 or 2.5 (good credit), 3 (fair credit), and 3.5 (an undesirable credit report). For analysis the ratings were reverse-coded into an ordinal scale ranging from 1 (undesirable report) to 7 (unlimited credit).

Indicator of whether an enterprise received credit coverage from a Dun correspondent; in 20 percent of the cases in the Reference Book an enterprise received no credit coverage. Credit rating and coverage were analyzed jointly within a selection model as well as modeled separately.

For every brokerage firm in a given year, the author gathered the stock price, prior year's earnings, and forecasted annual earnings of every stock it covered and calculated each stock's PEG score as (stock price/earnings)/earnings growth rate. A one-way analysis of variance was performed on the PEG scores of each brokerage firm in a given year using the broker's rating categories as the groups of interest, and the resulting F-test was converted to a p-value so that scores are comparable across firms with different rating systems. A higher p-value indicates a less significant difference among category means and therefore greater ambiguity.

Using Thomson Financial's SDC Platinum New Issues database, the author counted the number of new issues - venture capital and non-venture-capital-backed initial public offerings as well as equity issues for established organizations - in which a given brokerage firm participated during the prior year. The raw count of underwriting was divided by 100.
The total number of underwriting deals of the brokerage firm was divided by the number of equities it covered, capturing the amount of underwriting relative to the amount of equity coverage.

Binary indicator variable that takes the value of 1 if a fund is represented by a placement agent, and 0 otherwise. Data were collected primarily from the Funds in Market database and matched by fund and firm name to all funds listed in VentureXpert for 2001-2006, with supplemental searches of firm Web sites, industry newsletters, and LexisNexis.

Total amount of capital raised by the time the fund closes, in hundreds of millions of U.S. dollars; this is the empirical measure for organizational size, since firms that raise more capital are generally larger organizations in terms of assets under management and number of employees. When sources disagreed, the largest fund size reported was coded; when fund size was unavailable but the firm's target fund size was, the target fund size was coded. The variable was squared to test Hypothesis 1a.

Count of previous funds raised by each firm plus one; this is the measure for organizational experience, since firms that raised more funds in the past possess more experience with raising funds from limited partners. Data were obtained from VentureXpert or the Galante Directory. The variable was squared to test Hypothesis 1b.

Bonacich centrality in a symmetric firm-by-firm matrix of all venture capital and private equity investments in U.S. companies; each cell originally equals 1 if firms i and j both invested in the same company in the previous five years and 0 otherwise, and the matrix is updated annually. To reduce multicollinearity, the dichotomous co-investment indicators were replaced with the geometric mean of the number of companies in which both firms invested before computing Bonacich centrality. To test Hypothesis 1c, one was added to the measure and the sum squared.

Binary indicator variable that takes the value of 1 if fund i is represented by placement agent j, and 0 otherwise. The sample starts with the 64 represented funds, each matched with all placement agents active in the year the focal fund closed.

Total amount of capital raised by the time the fund closes, in hundreds of millions of U.S. dollars, used as the measure of organizational size in the dyadic matching models, where its interaction with placement agent reputation is estimated. The variable is unadjusted here and the squared term is not included in the matching models.

Count of previous funds raised by each firm plus one, used as the measure of organizational experience in the dyadic matching models, where its interaction with placement agent reputation is estimated.

Standard (size-unadjusted) Bonacich centrality in the private equity co-investment network, used in the dyadic matching models. The size adjustment was unnecessary because the squared terms were not included in these models and there is less variance in the number of investments made over the previous five years for firms that retained placement agents.

Total number of votes a placement agent received from general partners and limited partners in Private Equity International's 2005 surveys, in which each group was asked to identify the top three boutique and bank placement agents; 54 general partners and 50 limited partners offered nominations. Because the correlation between nominations from the two groups was .92, the results were pooled and each nomination counted as a vote, tallied by the two organizational forms (bank and boutique). Placement agents not receiving votes from either group were coded as receiving zero votes.

Content analysis of the LCME annual report on medical education in JAMA. The authors extracted sentences with the keyword 'care' in the JAMA texts and took the six words that most frequently modified care, occurring in 40 percent or more of the JAMA texts: clinical, care, clerkships, family, community, and physicians. They summed the frequencies of these six words in each JAMA text to create a ratio measure and divided the sum frequencies for each year by the number of words in the yearly issue. Together the words have an unstandardized alpha reliability of .7759.

Content analysis of the LCME annual report on medical education in JAMA, replicating the process used for the care logic with the Flexner Report of 1910 as base text. The six most frequent words that modified science, occurring in 40 percent or more of the texts across the years, were science, sciences, basic, research, hospital, and laboratory. The sum of the frequencies of these words in each yearly issue was divided by the number of words in the issue; the scale has an unstandardized alpha of .9410 and a standardized alpha of .7199.

variable_name: ratio of care to science logic
description: To capture the relative attention to care versus science each year, the authors used a ratio of the frequencies of care to science. Positive numbers mean that care occurred more frequently, while negative numbers mean that science occurred more frequently.

variable_name: number of accredited public health schools
description: The authors tracked the number of accredited public health schools in the United States for each year, 1966-2004, gathering the data from the Council on the Education for Public Health. The variable is lagged by one year.

Professional differentiation was assessed by counting the number of medical schools in the United States each year using archival data, especially the JAMA annual issue on medical education that lists the complete universe of medical schools in North America. The number of medical schools in the population was calculated for each year, 1966-2004, and lagged by one year.

variable_name: number of calls for reform of medical education
description: For each year the authors counted the number of calls for reform of medical education in North America in Academic Medicine (the Journal of Medical Education before 1989). They performed an electronic keyword search (curriculum, curricula or curricular, or profession, plus reform, revision, innovation, or change) and a hands-on review of the journal's archives from 1966 to 2004, finding high consistency between the two lists (correlated at .81). They combined both lists and excluded articles about medical schools outside North America or about residencies only; the variable is lagged by one year.

variable_name: volume of discourse about managed care
description: The authors collected articles and abstracts from the New York Times that discussed managed care from 1966 to 2004, extracted using the key terms manage* AND care, resulting in 689 articles. The articles were read and coded by two research assistants unfamiliar with the goals of the study, with an overall agreement of 97.4 percent (Brennan and Prediger's free-marginal kappa). The volume of discourse is used to capture public talk and attention to managed care; the variable is lagged by one year.

Survey scale adapted from scales previously developed and validated by Westphal and Stern (2006, 2007); it gauges the extent to which the top manager engaged in flattery toward the CEO during the prior twelve months. Some items ask directly about intent (e.g., how often the respondent made a complimentary remark mainly to gain the CEO's favor) and others gauge intent indirectly, including whether the respondent expressed confidence in the CEO's strategic judgment in a way that exaggerates actual confidence. Factor analysis with promax rotation showed the items loaded on two factors as expected, with an alpha of .89 for the flattery scale, and factor scores were estimated using the Bartlett method.

Survey scale adapted from scales previously developed and validated by Westphal and Stern (2006, 2007); it gauges the extent to which the top manager expressed agreement with the CEO in an attempt to gain favor during the prior twelve months. Some items ask directly about intent and others ask whether agreement was expressed in ways that somewhat exaggerate or overstate the respondent's opinion. Factor analysis with promax rotation showed the items loaded on two factors as expected, with an alpha of .91 for the opinion conformity scale, and factor scores were estimated using the Bartlett method.

Multi-item survey scales assessing the extent to which the top manager engaged in each of the sophisticated forms of flattery toward the CEO during the prior twelve months. Each scale included a variety of response formats, and some items ask respondents to indicate the number of times a particular behavior occurred. Confirmatory factor analysis showed the items in each scale loaded on the same factor as expected, with alphas ranging from .87 to .95 across the seven scales, and factor scores were estimated using the Bartlett method. Kappa coefficients for the parallel behavior items were in the range of good-to-excellent agreement.

Multi-item survey scales assessing the extent to which the top manager engaged in each of the sophisticated forms of opinion conformity toward the CEO during the prior twelve months. As with the flattery scales, each scale included a variety of response formats and some items ask for a count of occurrences. Confirmatory factor analysis showed the items in each scale loaded on the same factor as expected, with alphas ranging from .87 to .95, and factor scores were estimated using the Bartlett method.

Dichotomous measure indicating whether the focal manager was appointed to a particular board where the CEO served on the nominating committee at the time of the survey. In the primary analysis, board appointments were examined at the 2500 largest U.S. industrial and service firms for which data were available and over the two-year period following the survey.

A set of dichotomous variables operationalizing the top manager's background: one variable coded 1 if the individual had previously held a position in sales, a second coded 1 if the individual had previously been employed as a lawyer, and a third coded 1 if the individual had previously held an elected office at the state or federal levels. The measures were developed from archival data sources, and there was a high level of agreement with responses to survey questions about vocational background.

A dummy variable coded 1 if the individual was listed in the Social Register and/or attended an exclusive preparatory ('prep') school, with exclusivity designations taken from prior research.
