Corporate diversification strategy was measured with Jacquemin and Berry's entropy measure of diversification, which captures both the extent of diversity across a firm's activities and the related versus unrelated elements of diversity. For each firm, line-of-business data at the four-, three-, and two-digit SIC code levels were used to obtain the entropy measure of diversification for 1980 and 1983, and change was taken as the absolute percentage change in a firm's entropy measure from 1980 to 1983. The measure's value could range from 0 for single business firms to 4 for highly diversified firms.

Age was calculated from biographical data for members of the 1980 top management team of each firm. The demographic trait measures for interval scaled data were calculated by aggregating values for a team's members and taking the mean.

Heterogeneity of the top management team on the interval scaled data was measured using the coefficient of variation, defined as the standard deviation divided by the mean. The logarithm of the heterogeneity measure was used to capture the anticipated decreasing rate of the effect of dissimilarity in age on changes in corporate strategy.

Organizational tenure was calculated from biographical data for members of the 1980 top management team. To capture low tenures, consistent with Hypothesis 2a, a dummy variable was created with a cutoff at the sample mean tenure minus one standard deviation, which resulted in 11.5 years. The sample was divided into firms with teams with mean organizational tenures of less than 11.5 years and 11.5 years or more; 11 firms were classified as having top management teams with low average organizational tenures. The text does not state which category is coded 1.

Heterogeneity of the top management team on the interval scaled data was measured using the coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean. The logarithm of the heterogeneity measure was used to capture the anticipated decreasing rate of the effect of dissimilarity in organizational tenure on changes in corporate strategy.

Top management team tenure was calculated from biographical data for members of the 1980 top management team and averaged across the team's members, following the procedure of taking the mean of interval scaled demographic trait values for a team.

Heterogeneity of the top management team on the interval scaled data was measured using the coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean, and the logarithm of the heterogeneity measure was used.
Educational level was measured in terms of the number of years of schooling for members of the 1980 top management team, and the team measure is the mean of the members' values.

The specialization represented by the highest obtained university degree determined the educational specialization measure, and individuals were categorized into five educational specializations: arts, sciences, engineering, business and economics, and law. Each team was categorized on the basis of its members' mode specialization, and a dummy variable was developed to capture top management teams dominated by individuals with educational backgrounds in science and engineering. Individuals with B.S. or M.S. degrees were classified as science specialists; B.S. and M.S. degrees with a listed specialty, such as business, were not coded as science degrees; individuals with Ph.D. degrees in the sciences were classified as science specialists.

For the categorical variable educational specialization, Blau's index of heterogeneity was applied, calculated as 1 minus the sum over categories of the squared proportion of a group's individuals in the ith category.

An entropy measure of diversification that takes into account both the number of industries the venture capitalist is operating in and the importance of each area to total operations. It is calculated at the three-digit Venture Economics industry code (VEIC) level, where the percentage of VC investments made in industry j during an eight-year rolling window is weighted by the log of its inverse. The paper's formula block could not be extracted, so the exact equation is not stated here, though the text states that pIj is the percentage of VC i investments made in industry j during an eight-year rolling window, and ln(1/pIj) is the weight for each segment.

variable_name: Percent of portfolio companies that go public
description: The percentage of investments made by a VC firm in the focal year that ultimately yielded an IPO event. The authors follow Hochberg et al. (2007) and use IPO as the indicator of a successful outcome because an IPO is a liquidity event that allows VC firms to realize returns on their investment and is the ultimate goal for most venture capitalists when they initially invest in a company.

For each investment a venture capitalist makes, the venture capitalist reports the stage of development of the portfolio company. VC firms classify each investment in the VentureXpert database as startup/seed, early stage, expansion, or late stage; the authors treat these values as an ordinal scale and calculate an average. Higher stages are associated with lower levels of uncertainty.
scale: ordinal scale: startup/seed, early stage, expansion, late stage

description: The measure is the average of all coinvestors each VC firm reports for each investment over all the VC firm's investments during an eight-year rolling window.

An index formed from questionnaire items developed from the involvement hypothesis and completed by the CEO or top executive of each organization. The eight culture items were assessed with factor analysis and multidimensional scaling, which showed good convergent and discriminant validity for the four traits, presented in two dimensions as suggested by the theoretical model.

An index formed from questionnaire items developed to measure consistency, or the degree of normative integration, and completed by the CEO or top executive of each organization. The items were assessed together with those of the other traits using factor analysis and multidimensional scaling.

An index formed from questionnaire items developed to measure adaptability and completed by the CEO or top executive of each organization. The items were assessed together with those of the other traits using factor analysis and multidimensional scaling.

An index formed from questionnaire items developed to measure sense of mission or long-term vision and completed by the CEO or top executive of each organization. The items were assessed together with those of the other traits using factor analysis and multidimensional scaling.

A set of five questionnaire items asking respondents to compare their own firm's performance to the performance of similar firms on the dimensions of profitability, quality, sales growth, employee satisfaction, and overall performance. Responses were provided by the CEO or top executive in each organization.

Return on assets for the most recent year (1989) as well as the average for the preceding three years (1987-1989), computed for the firms that reported enough usable financial data. Correlations with the culture traits were reported both for the total sample and for a subsample of larger firms with top executive respondents.
Reported sales growth for the most recent year (1989) and the average growth for the preceding three years (1987-1989), available for nearly half of the firms that reported enough sales data.

A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 beginning when a medical marijuana law became effective in a given state, and 0 for years prior to legalization. Because in some states the enactment date precedes the implementation date, the authors use the implementation date to reflect actual policy on the ground. The yearly enactment of the laws is tracked building on Pacula et al. (2014, 2015) and complemented with the authors' coding of the laws and specialized websites.

State-level sales of alcohol measured in millions of U.S. dollars. The authors prefer sales in dollars to survey-based measures because sales data are directly available from firms and are less exposed to the social-desirability bias associated with reporting the consumption of substances considered vices. To control for inflation, all sales variables were transformed to 2010 U.S. dollars.

State-level sales of tobacco measured in millions of U.S. dollars. As with alcohol, dollar sales are preferred to survey-based consumption measures, which are said to substantially understate actual sales. To control for inflation, all sales variables were transformed to 2010 U.S. dollars.

A 'treatment' dummy variable equal to 1 for states that not only legalized medical marijuana but also implemented a medical registration system, and 0 for states that established a voluntary system or that did not institute one. The authors describe the variable as de facto an interaction of the variable Medical marijuana with a dummy variable coded 1 when a patient registration system has been introduced.
scale: dummy (1 = compulsory registration system, 0 = voluntary or none)

description: The proportion of state residents 12 years or older that made use of marijuana, used to evaluate the consequences of medical marijuana legalization before testing the cross-industry hypotheses. Data were retrieved from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and gathered from the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. The authors note that this survey is only available after 2002.

Three coders independently reviewed case studies for each spin-out and rated the parent firm either as 1 (hostile) if the reports evidenced some form of disapproval, reflected by words such as 'litigation,' 'lawsuit,' or 'turmoil,' or as 0 (friendly or neutral) otherwise. The average agreement rate was 94 percent, with a Fleiss' Kappa of 0.86; remaining discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. The coding-based measure was used in the main analyses.

Measured as the number of full months between the firm's founding (its date of incorporation) and the moment at which its costs equaled its revenues so that it started to make profits, as reported by the respondent.
time_window: from founding until the breakeven moment

description: Respondents rated the extent to which the parent and child firm offered similar products on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very similar, 7 = very dissimilar) three years after founding. High values indicate that the spin-out pursued a product strategy different from the parent's, whereas low values indicate that the two firms' strategies were similar three years after founding.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = very similar, 7 = very dissimilar)

description: Respondents reported the number of partners (suppliers, customers, and competitors) they had in the year of founding, then specified how many of these contacts were newly established after the firm's founding and how many resulted from referrals by the parent firm. The authors calculated the ratios of new post-founding contacts to total contacts separately for suppliers, customers, and competitors, disregarding parent referrals, and summed the three ratios into a composite measure. High values reflect that a spin-out renewed its network by acquiring new partners in the industry; low values show reliance on preexisting contacts or parent referrals.
time_window: year of founding and after founding

description: A weighted-average pairwise similarity between the short-list wine descriptors contained in the Wine Spectator tasting notes of same-quality-band wines within a varietal category in a year. Descriptors come from a short list of 320 elemental, sensory-relevant wine words extracted from the reviews. The Jaccard coefficient counts the short-list words found in both reviews divided by those words plus the short-list words that appear in one review but not the other. The measure is built from all reviews within a varietal category over moving three-year windows; the three-year Jaccard measure ranges from a low of 0.00 to a high of 0.251.

Real list price is the suggested retail price at the time of release divided by the consumer price index normalized to unity in 1983; because real wine prices are highly skewed, the natural log of this real price is used. Real list prices are broken into an expected price function of quality, age, vintage, region, varietal category and other covariates and a variance term. Pricing variance is modeled in the second-moment (variance) function, so that a lower variance means list prices deviate less from expected levels.

Indicator variable set to 1 for observations that represent a producer's first published review; such producers have no reputations and no experience anticipating the reactions of critics to their wines. In the test of H2, the interaction between this indicator and the three-year Jaccard measure is added to the variance function. The authors expected a negative coefficient for this variable in the mean function.

The average of all prior quality scores received by the focal producer, included in the mean function because producers with superior reputations tend to charge higher prices. The reputation score is imputed with the overall sample average for producers that never before received a published review from the Wine Spectator.

Indicator isolating producers that received reviews before the focal year and whose reputations fall inside the lowest two quality bands (i.e., 'Not recommended' and 'Mediocre'). The interaction between this indicator and the three-year Jaccard measure is included in the variance function to test H3.

Simpson's index of diversity measuring the diversity of a distribution over a set of discrete categories, computed over the set of varietal categories in which the producer has had wines reviewed over the past three years using the proportion of the producer's total reviewed wines that came from each varietal. It is included in the mean function as a proxy for the economies of scope available to producers with broader niche widths, for which lower prices are expected.

Indicator isolating a group of generalist producers that fall in the highest 25% of the distribution of the niche width variable. The interaction between this indicator and the three-year Jaccard measure is included in the variance function to test H4.

variable_name: external learning composite versus internal learning composite
description: Employees and executives rated the extent to which their firm used 70 randomly ordered human resources practices by sorting the practices into category ratings placed before them. The survey considered two internal learning items and three external learning items; the composites were then compared, and executives also rated the practices' importance for organizational performance.

variable_name: external learning composite versus internal learning composite
description: Participants rated on a five-point scale whether they disagreed or agreed that the same five organizational practices (two internal learning items and three external learning items) were important for their organization's success. The items were combined into an external composite and an internal composite for comparison.

Respondents rated the effort expended by each of the two managers in the scenario: one who implemented services that another member of the chain had offered to customers and one who implemented services a chief competitor had offered.
level: individual (respondent rating each of two managers)

description: Respondents rated how creative each of the two managers was, where one had implemented services another member of the chain had offered and the other had implemented services a chief competitor had offered.
level: individual (respondent rating each of two managers)

description: Respondents rated how competent each of the two managers was, where one had implemented services another member of the chain had offered and the other had implemented services a chief competitor had offered.
level: individual (respondent rating each of two managers)

description: Respondents rated how each manager's action affected their status, that is, how much status the manager gained by learning the services from another member of the chain versus from a chief competitor.
scale: 1 = Hurts them to 7 = Helps them (4 = Neither)
level: individual (respondent rating each of two managers)

description: Respondents rated how likely they were to promote each of the two managers, one of whom learned from an internal source and one from an external competitor.
level: individual (respondent rating each of two managers)

description: Participants allocated bonuses to the two managers in the scenario, the one who implemented services another member of the chain had offered and the one who implemented services a chief competitor had offered.
level: individual (respondent allocating a bonus to each of two managers)

variable_name: manager learns internally versus manager learns from external competitor
description: Respondents read a scenario in which they assumed that they managed a large hotel chain and had to conduct performance evaluations of two managers in that chain. Those managers had attained similar levels of performance, but differed in that one had implemented services that another member of the chain had offered to customers, whereas the other had implemented services a chief competitor had offered. The survey was a within-subjects design in which participants evaluated two managers and allocated bonuses to them; whether the internal learner or the external learner was rated first was counterbalanced, with no order effect found.
level: individual (respondent rating each of two managers)

description: The level of investment in evaluating new technologies and new ideas, and screening ideas suitable for use by the SBU. The authors report that its internal consistency, as measured by Cronbach's alpha coefficient, was 0.68.

The level of integration of ideas and technologies in new products and processes, and how close the SBU is to the state of the art (SOA) in its main line of activity. The alpha coefficient for this construct was 0.76.

Each of the 76 SBUs was categorized by its manager into one of Miles and Snow's strategic types, forming four strategy groups: 32 analyzers, 24 prospectors, 19 defenders, and one reactor which was omitted from the analysis. The authors state that a self-typing instrument based on textual descriptions of strategy was employed.

Two of the four dimensions used to measure the performance of an SBU in the electronics and computers industry. Profitability level is how well the business unit meets its financial objectives and how well it is doing relative to similar business units; generating orders is how well the business unit is doing in achieving sales objectives and creating future orders, and covers the current backlog and how these orders will influence future cash requirements. These are the short-term dimensions, measuring the results of past activities which do not determine future prospects.

Two of the four dimensions used to measure the performance of an SBU in the electronics and computers industry. Generating new opportunities is how successful the unit is in opening new opportunities for new products and for new markets, and whether customers are satisfied with the quality of products and services and will come back for further purchases; preparing the infrastructure for the future is whether the business unit has the scientific and technological knowledge, equipment and facilities required for the development and production of future products. These are the long-term dimensions which determine the SBU's ability to survive in the long run.

Each member firm's R&D expenditures, used as the dependent variable to measure its R&D search in the tests of H1a, H1c, H2a, and H2c. The authors chose the absolute amount of R&D expenditures rather than R&D intensity because a decline in firm sales can inflate R&D intensity. Raw values of R&D investments were divided by 100,000,000 to report one-digit integer coefficients in the model.

A spline function of the discrepancy between a firm's ROA and its aspiration level, taking the value of the (negative) discrepancy when ROA is below the aspiration level and otherwise accounting for outperforming firms in a separate variable, ROA - Aspiration > 0. The composite aspiration level is the weighted linear combination of the firm's historical aspiration level (a mixture of the past-period historical aspiration level and the previous ROA), the social aspiration level (the average ROA of other firms in the same two-digit KSIC industry) and the group aspiration level (the average ROA of other member firms in the same group). Weights of 0.1, 0.5 and 0.4 were obtained by searching all parameter values by increments of 0.1 and taking the combination giving the highest maximum likelihood.

The ratio of the sales aggregation of underperforming firms (member firms with ROA below their aspiration level) to the entire group sales, computed for each business group and year. A sales-weighted ratio was used rather than a simple count of underperforming firms because the underperformance of firms whose sales account for a higher proportion of the group's sales is likely to be given more weight by group-level managers. The variable serves as a group-level moderator of the effect of a focal firm's performance below the aspiration level on its R&D search.

The frequency of performance-related keywords in a group chairman's letter to all employees of the business group at the beginning of a calendar year, normalized by the total number of words in the letter. Keywords were (financial) performance, profit, profitability, liability, sales, and cash. Keywords were counted with an automated analytic tool in R for the Korean language. The variable is used as a dependent variable for H1b and as a moderator for H1c.

The sales-weighted ratio of R&D intensive firms to all the member firms in a business group, computed per group and year. R&D intensive firms were identified as member firms in R&D intensive industries using the same two-digit KSIC codes used to select the sample. The variable serves as a group-level moderator of the effect of a focal firm's performance below the aspiration level on its R&D search.

The frequency of R&D-related keywords in a group chairman's letter to all employees of the business group at the beginning of a calendar year, normalized by the total number of words in the letter. Keywords were R&D, research, technology development, technology commercialization, technology innovation, and patent. Keywords were counted with an automated analytic tool in R for the Korean language. The variable is used as a dependent variable for H2b and as a moderator for H2c.

A binary measure denoting the presence of a matrix structure in a given organization in a given year, focused on identifying matrix structures with geography as one of the dimensions. It was built in four steps: searching the titles of directors and executive officers in annual reports for evidence of dual reporting lines (geographic versus nongeographic senior managers) and checking whether geography-related titles matched reported geographic segments; validating the categorization with news articles, press releases, and employee testimonials from Factiva, Google, and Glassdoor.com; and validating it through direct phone and email contact with senior executives via business school alumni networks. The final set comprises 29 matrix organizations, contributing 158 firm-year observations, versus 2,944 nonmatrix firm-year observations; the total sample size was 3,102 firm-year observations.

The count of all partnerships a firm entered in a given year that involved more than two partners. Whenever multiple subsidiaries of a parent firm participated in an alliance with one or more partner firms, each of these subsidiaries was counted as a partner in the alliance, and alliances that involved only subsidiaries from a single parent firm were excluded from the data set. A binary counterpart, 'at least one multilateral partnership,' takes the value of 1 if a firm formed at least one multilateral partnership in a given year and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: number of partnerships with new partners
description: The count of all partnerships a firm formed in year t that involve partners with which the firm had no previous partnership history. A corresponding binary measure, 'at least one partnership with a new partner,' takes the value of 1 if the firm formed at least one partnership in a given year with a new partner and 0 otherwise.

Alliance diversity was captured with three outcomes: the number of partners from different industries, counted as the number of unique two-digit SIC codes of partners with which a firm partnered in a given year; the number of countries represented by partners, counted as the number of unique countries of partners with which the focal firm partnered in year t; and the number of functions designated to an average partnership, measuring the average functional scope of the partnerships a firm formed in year t. To compute the latter, the key functional orientations of every partnership a firm formed in year t were captured, differentiating among manufacturing, marketing, R&D, licensing and royalty agreements, and supply agreements, and the average number of functions was then calculated.

Three outcome variables captured firms' tendency to enter into partnerships from a position of power. Size advantage in partnerships is the cumulative difference between a firm's sales volume and the sales volume of partners in partnerships the firm formed in year t; a positive difference indicates that the firm tends to enter into partnerships with smaller, less powerful partners. For equity partnerships formed in year t, the number of partnerships entered as a majority partner and as a minority partner was also computed.

variable_name: number of nonequity partnerships formed in year t
description: A firm's propensity to enter equity and nonequity partnerships was measured by counting the number of equity and nonequity partnerships a firm formed in year t. Equity partnerships include joint ventures, which involve partners taking equity stakes in an independent, newly jointly created entity, and partnerships in which one or more partners can take a (minority) equity stake in another partner.

To estimate differences in cumulative abnormal returns incurred by matrix versus nonmatrix organizations for a particular type of partnership, the sample was first split into subsamples based on type of partnership and propensity score matching was then performed within the relevant subsample. Complex partnerships in Hypothesis 6 comprise those involving multilateral relationships, broad geographic or functional scope, unfamiliar or diverse partners, nonequity governance, or a nondominant power position.

Market-adjusted returns were calculated using the S&P 500 market index model, and cumulative abnormal returns are reported for the most typically used time windows, including [-1;0], [0], and [-1;+1], where day 0 is the day of the partnership announcement. Observations that coincide with acquisitions, executive successions, and earnings announcements were filtered out to eliminate the confounding effect of other events.
time_window: event windows [-1;0], [0], and [-1;+1] around the alliance announcement

description: Coded one if the industry in which founders created a firm was the same as the industry in which they worked prior to becoming unemployed, and zero otherwise. Industry was measured at the one-digit level (the 'letter' level of the classification of economic activities in the European Community, NACE Rev. 2), which corresponds to sectors such as 'C. Manufacturing' and 'F. Construction.' The authors describe this approach as conservative because it connotes a considerable distance in moving from the home industry to an external industry.

Measured from survey respondents' choices among nine unemployment categories that are measured in months, from 'less than 1' to 'more than 36'. Because the categories do not reflect a purely linear measure, the authors created three dummy measures capturing short- (less than 13 months), medium- (13-24 months) and long-term (greater than 24 months) unemployment. The long-term unemployed serve as the reference category in the models.
scale: nine unemployment categories in months, recoded into three dummy measures

description: Measured as the number of years that founders worked in the industry in which they held a job prior to becoming unemployed (i.e., their home industry).

Constructed in two steps. First, the revenue growth rate of the industry in which the founder worked prior to becoming unemployed (home industry) is subtracted from the average of the revenue growth rates of all other industries (external industries); both components are based on the respective four-quarter moving average of revenue growth rates prior to new firm creation. Second, the growth-rate measure is weighted with a skill-relatedness measure adapted from Neffke and Henning (2013): the average of skill relatedness indices for each focal industry to all remaining industries, weighted by the knowledge barriers of the focal industry, which were assessed by two experts of Greek nationality.
time_window: four quarters prior to new firm creation

description: Indicator for a move between different organizations that was not coded as involuntary. All moves between different organizations other than the involuntary ones were coded as external voluntary moves, including the 8% of moves where the reason for moving was missing. Together with the external involuntary indicator it is one of the key independent variables in the models, in which internal moves are the excluded category.

Indicator for a move between different organizations that respondents reported as involuntary. Moves were coded involuntary when respondents said they left because of 'position eliminated,' 'company, office, workplace or plant closed,' 'discharged or fired,' or 'left by mutual agreement'; 25% of external moves met these criteria. It is one of the two key independent variables, with internal moves as the excluded category.

Moves between jobs that take place within the same employer; 65% of the moves in the data take place within an organization. In the multivariate models the key independent variables are the external voluntary and external involuntary indicators, so internal moves form the excluded category against which both are compared.
scale: 0 on the external voluntary and external involuntary indicators (reference category)

description: Involuntariness was coded from a question that asked respondents why they left each employer, with 13 possible options and more than one answer allowed. Moves for which respondents answered 'position eliminated,' 'company, office, workplace or plant closed,' 'discharged or fired,' or 'left by mutual agreement' were coded as external involuntary moves, which was 25% of external moves; all other moves between organizations were coded voluntary.

For each job respondents were asked 'what was the total number of people who worked in units that you managed when you first started this job?' The authors took the log of this value after adding one to each observation because of high skew, and calculated the difference between consecutive jobs as the change in log subordinates. For the cross-equation comparisons of pay against responsibilities, the change measures were standardized by subtracting the global mean and dividing by the global standard deviation.

A hierarchical rank code built from the job titles respondents reported for each job, approximating 1 = specialist, 2 = senior specialist, 3 = manager, 4 = senior manager, 5 = VP/director, 6 = senior VP/director, 7 = C-level officer, and 8 = CEO, and refined to apply differently across industries. The change between the ranks of consecutive jobs is used. The authors report that subordinates and log earnings increase monotonically with rank, except for rank 8 whose earnings effect was slightly lower than rank 7.

Respondents reported their total earnings in their first year in each job; the log of this value was taken because of its high skew and the difference in log earnings between the first year of one job and the first year of the next was calculated for consecutive jobs. For the cross-equation comparisons of pay against responsibilities, the change measures were standardized by subtracting the global mean and dividing by the global standard deviation.

For each job respondents selected what function the job was in from a drop-down menu, initially 34 responses based on the functions students were likely to go into and on standardized occupational categories, later revised to 27 functions after pilot testing and again after the survey. A move is coded as involving a change in function when the function reported in the current job differs from the one worked in in the prior job. Respondents were allowed to select only a single function in the data.

Fortune annually surveys several thousand securities analysts and executives who rate firms in the industries they cover or work in; respondents evaluate the ten largest firms in their industry on eight dimensions, and Fortune averages the eight items into a single reputation score and publishes rankings. The authors used within-industry rankings rather than raw scores, creating inverted ranking scores that range from 10 for the top-ranked firm in the industry in a particular year to 1 for the lowest, so that covariates enhancing reputation have positive signs. Analysts' and executives' rankings were disaggregated and each group's ranking included as a separate observation. The prior year's ranking is included in all models, so coefficients reflect year-to-year reputational change.
level: firm-year within industry, separately for each audience

description: A dichotomous indicator of downsizing. The authors searched full-text articles of the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, and several wire services for announcements of companywide personnel reductions aimed at improving efficiency or effectiveness, requiring that the reductions affect at least 1 percent of employees. After applying this screen they found qualifying downsizing events in 103 firm-years, then dropped 12 events announced in December because they appeared to occur after the late-autumn Fortune survey, leaving 91 firm-years with announced downsizings.

A beta-adjusted measure of excess returns as described by Brown and Warner (1985: 28), using CRSP data and an 11-day event window (day -5 to +5) around a downsizing announcement. It measures the change in a firm's stock price net of broader market movements. Excess returns measured across other windows (3 days and 1 day) produced similar results.
time_window: 11-day window (day -5 to +5) around the downsizing announcement

description: The difference between return on book assets in the downsizing year (t) and in the prior year (t - 1); it also serves as the base term for the downsizing by profitability change interaction testing Hypothesis 3. The variable was not centered, because its values (particularly its zero point) have substantive meaning and because its mean was already close to zero.

The firm's within-industry reputational ranking in the previous year, included in all models so that the model is specified as one of reputational change and used as the base term for the downsizing by prior ranking interaction testing Hypothesis 4. The variable was centered before being multiplied by the downsizing indicator to aid interpretation.

The percentage of firms in the sample that had downsized in prior years, including between 1977 and 1985; the variable was centered. It forms the base term for the downsizing by prevalence interaction (Hypothesis 5) and for the triple interactions testing Hypothesis 6.
time_window: cumulative through each study year, including 1977-85

description: An indicator variable multiplied by the downsizing indicator to form the 'downsizing x analysts' interaction testing Hypothesis 7. Its base term does not vary within a given industry-rater-year group, so it is controlled for by the group structure of the data and cannot be modeled independently; only its interactive effect can be examined.

Ratio of dollar investment in IT to sales. IT investment dollars were obtained from Information Week's IW500 data and sales were obtained from Compustat. The variable was centered before being entered in models with interaction terms.

Computed following Chung and Pruitt (1994) as the ratio of market value to book value of total assets, where market value is the fiscal year-end market value of equity plus the liquidating value of the firm's outstanding preferred stock plus current liabilities minus current assets plus the book value of inventories plus long-term debt. Data for computing Tobin's q were obtained from Compustat.

Entropy measure of diversification computed with data obtained from Compustat. Total diversification measures the extent of a firm's operations in different industries, whether related or unrelated, and is equal to the sum of the related and unrelated diversification measures. Details on the construction of the measure can be found in the study by Dewan et al. (1998).

Entropy measure computed with data obtained from Compustat that measures the extent of a firm's operations in different industries within the same two-digit Standard Industry Classification (SIC) code. The measure was centered before being entered in models with interaction terms. Details on the construction of the measure can be found in the study by Dewan et al. (1998).

Entropy measure computed with data obtained from Compustat that measures the extent of a firm's operations in different two-digit SIC codes. The measure was centered before being entered in models with interaction terms. Details on the construction of the measure can be found in the study by Dewan et al. (1998).

Chief administrators were asked, "Has your hospital implemented the following program or policy?", with descriptions of 12 policies and yes or no responses, and affirmative responses were taken to indicate only adoption. Four policies were retained: preadmission testing, physician ordering of drugs by generic name rather than brand name, a formal policy to require departments not to exceed pre-established budgets, and techniques to forecast nurse staffing requirements. Responses to the four items were summed, ranging from 0, adoption of none of the four policies, to 4, all policies adopted.

Chief administrators estimated the number of person-days that they and people in eight other relevant positions had spent dealing with the state's certificate of need and rate review programs during the most recent fiscal year. Responses for each type of regulation for each person were summed. The figure indicates the extent to which a hospital dealt with these regulatory pressures.
time_window: most recent fiscal year before data collection

description: Chief administrators were asked to indicate whether or not they were currently sharing up to 15 different clinical or administrative services with other hospitals. For each item, 1 = yes and 0 = no, and responses to all 15 items were summed.
A dichotomous variable; hospitals were coded 0 if they were either government-owned or religiously affiliated and 1 if they were private voluntary hospitals.
As in most hospital studies, size was the average number of beds in use or available for use during the year prior to data collection.
The average number of occupied beds as a percentage of total available beds. Hospitals with high rates of occupancy were treated as using their facilities efficiently.

variable_name: Length of stay, adjusted for severity
description: Average length of stay multiplied by the percentage of total inpatient days not spent in intensive care, so that hospitals dealing with many severe illnesses, operations and accidents would have their length-of-stay figure reduced to reflect severity; hospitals with few patients in intensive care experienced little change. Average length of stay was total inpatient days divided by total patients admitted. Adjusting for severity makes the figures easier to compare and permits tentative assessments of relative efficiency in processing patients.

Chief administrators were asked to indicate whether or not they served on their hospital's governing board, with 1 = on the board and 0 = not on board. This differentiated hospitals in which chief administrators served on governing boards from all others, as a measure of their potential influence through involvement in board decisions.

Chief administrators were asked to indicate the number of physicians serving on their hospital's governing board; this figure was then divided by the total number of board members. The percentage of physicians relative to all other board members was used, since larger proportions of physicians were considered more likely to inhibit adoption of cost containment policies than small ones.

Strategic differentiation is calculated by comparing the features of an entrant game and those of the exemplary hit game using a Euclidean distance measure. Following previous research, this distance variable was further adjusted for the changing salience and popularity of certain feature combinations over time. A square term of the strategic differentiation variable was created to test the inverted U-shaped relationship between strategic differentiation and market sales of a new entrant.
Market performance of new product entrants is measured by inflation-adjusted, aggregate U.S. dollar sales (logged) of a console video game.

Critics' rating scores of both the exemplar and new entrants were coded using the MobyGames' MobyRank score, described by MobyGames as a statistically accurate metric of critic success for a game, calculated as a weighted average of normalized rankings from individual critics, where the weight is given to each critic based on their rating history, accuracy, and variance. The difference between the MobyRank score of a new entrant and that of the exemplar is used as a measure of relative improvement of the new release.

A temporal dynamic variable counting the time (number of months) lapsed since the exemplary hit game's release. It is interacted with the strategic differentiation variable and its squared term to test how the effect of differentiation changes as a proto-category evolves.

A second temporal dynamic measure counting the cumulative number of prior entrants (logged), which captures the changing competitive intensity resulting from the increasing number of new entrants into a proto-category. The authors use it to unpack the underlying mechanisms of the temporal dynamic.

Industry-adjusted average performance for the two years prior to a succession event. For a given two-year period the authors compared a firm's two-year sales growth with the average sales growth for the semiconductor industry over the same two years. Sales were used rather than profits because many semiconductor manufacturers are willing to operate at a low level of profitability while building market share. This information was provided by two of the market research firms and the firms themselves.
time_window: two years prior to a succession event

description: Board composition was measured as the proportion of inside members on a board of directors. Information on the board of directors for each firm in the study was compiled by the market research firms, and the focal organizations themselves made additional information available.
Inside ownership was the proportion of total firm shares held by individuals employed by the organization. The market research organizations and the semiconductor firms provided firm ownership data.

Inside ownership concentration was the proportion of total firm shares held by the four largest inside owners. The market research organizations and the semiconductor firms provided firm ownership data.

Whether a chief executive successor came from inside or outside an organization, measured for each firm each time a succession occurred. The variable was coded 1 if the successor was from outside the organization and 0 otherwise. These data were available from the three market research firms and corroborated by the firms themselves.

Dichotomous variable that takes value 1 when the firm buys R&D services from other firms, public administrations, universities, or organizations abroad. It is included in the models with a two-period lag.
Dichotomous variable that takes value 1 when the firm acquires R&D services from an affiliate or captive center abroad. It is included in the models with a two-period lag.

Dichotomous variable that takes value 1 when the firm has achieved a product or process innovation. It is used as an independent variable and as a dependent variable to analyze its mediating role, and is included with a one-period lag.

Continuous variable obtained by dividing the difference between sales figures in year t and year t - 1 by the sales figures in year t - 1. It is the dependent variable in Models 1 and 3. The growth models also include the lagged value of sales growth (previous year's sales growth) as a covariate.
time_window: year t relative to t-1; lagged value t-1 used as covariate

description: To measure the extensiveness of a contract's implementation with respect to emerging expectations, the authors sum the products of dummies for each of the 13 contract provisions and the prior period's eigenvector centrality scores for each provision, where the 13 EC values are eigenvector centralities based on the prior period's contracts and the GP values are dummies indicating the presence (1) or absence (0) of each provision. The equation block itself is not readable in the extracted text, so the measure is recorded here as the prose describes it.

To measure how similar a contract is to those adopted in the previous year, the authors first compute a mean for each contract provision by multiplying the prior year's eigenvector centrality scores for each provision by a dummy for that provision's presence (1) or absence (0), and sum those means to obtain a composite average baseline B for expectations established by the prior year's implementations. They then take the absolute value of the difference between that baseline and the focal contract's extensiveness score; the equation block itself is not readable in the extracted text.
The year of adoption of an individual golden parachute plan, entered as a predictor variable reflecting the gradual field-level effects of diffusion over the analysis period.

variable_name: media coverage (number of articles per year)
description: The number of articles per year that mention the terms 'golden parachutes' or 'employee retention plans,' counted across the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Washington Post, Forbes, Fortune, BusinessWeek, and Newsweek. The measure is lagged by one year to avoid reverse causation, and it is residualized by regressing it on the linear time variable and subtracting the predicted values from the measure's actual values.

A count variable of the number of court cases per year adjusted for a firm's state of incorporation, built from all federal and state court cases in which a challenge to golden parachutes was the central issue. Federal cases affect all firms while state cases are treated as affecting only firms incorporated in that state. Pending cases are included, but cases that were eventually ruled in favor of the golden parachute plan are removed.
level: year, adjusted to the firm by state of incorporation

description: The number of times the firm is mentioned in the news media, based on the New York Times or Wall Street Journal, divided by 100.

A dummy variable coded 1 if the firm was subject to either takeover speculation or an actual tender offer. Takeover activity was identified through news article searches in the ABI/INFORM database using a three-month window on each side of the adoption date.
scale: dummy (1 = takeover speculation or tender offer)
time_window: three months on each side of the adoption date

description: A variable distinguishing CEOs hired from the outside versus the inside. Identification used biographical sources such as the Marquis Who's Who Biographies and searches of newspaper articles in the New York Times, Forbes, and the PRNewswire, as well as the firm's own historical proxy statements and annual reports.

The regression models include a dummy for an outsider CEO, with CEO tenure and the percentage of inside directors on the board controlled for; the paper reports that outsider CEOs tended to have perhaps less extensive parachute plans.

Female was coded 1 if the executive was female and 0 otherwise. The authors hand-coded each executive's demographic attributes, including sex, from company organizational charts and the printed and online sources.

Number of years between the year the executive entered the labor market and the year when she or he was appointed to the focal position. The year of labor market entry was obtained from executive biographies as the starting date of the individual's first job; when this information was not available, the year of graduation from the highest level of education obtained was used. Other things being equal, a smaller number of years indicates faster advancement, so higher values on the measure correspond to lower speed of advancement.

Proportion of an executive's career spent in the focal organization before assuming the current executive position. It is computed as the number of years the executive spent in the current organization before being appointed to the focal position divided by her or his total years of work experience before appointment.
time_window: before appointment to the focal position

description: For companies present in the Fortune 100 list in both 2001 and 2011, the number of female executive incumbents in the year 2001, used as a proxy for whether there were women at the top. H3 is tested without company fixed effects because this variable does not vary across individual executives in the same company; those models use company random effects and company-level controls. The H3 analyses also created an indicator variable for more than one female incumbent and spline terms for numbers below and above one.

Firm-level CSP obtained from ASSET4. Following Ioannou and Serafeim (2012), the CSP composite is the equally weighted average of social (i.e., human rights and labor) and environmental performance for each firm-year observation, on a scale of 0-100, with results also analyzed separately for the two subindexes. ASSET4 scores are based on key performance indicators that evaluate the policies or principles to which the firm subscribes, their implementation through processes or programs, and resulting observable outcomes.

The sum of media mentions (i.e., number of possible media impressions) of both cooperative and conflictual interactions that CSP stakeholders have with sociopolitical actors in the country-year. Relevant sociopolitical actors include individuals or organizations that influence formal rules in a country (e.g., politicians, opposition parties, regulators, or the judiciary) as well as those that can influence informal rules (e.g., media, elites, community organizations, or NGOs specializing in other issues). The sum is normalized by the sum of media mentions of all events in the country.

The raw count of unique stakeholder types in each country-year, where stakeholders are classified by differences in organizational forms and issue interests. A country whose active CSP stakeholders are all of one type receives a heterogeneity score of one, whereas a country whose few stakeholders span different types receives a score equal to the number of types.

The percent of mentions-weighted interactions that are conflictual between stakeholder groups relative to (i.e., divided by) the percent of mentions-weighted interactions that are conflictual within stakeholder groups. The measure uses the degree to which interactions between stakeholders are conflictual as a proxy for the degree to which positions across heterogeneous stakeholder groups disagree.

Proselytizing stakeholders are identified as those that initiate twice as many interactions with other CSP stakeholders (outbound interactions) as are initiated by other CSP stakeholders toward them (inbound interactions); the authors count the number of times these stakeholders engaged in direct conflictual actions against firms (e.g., protests or boycotts). The variable is the sum of media mentions of proselytizer actions against firms in a country-year, normalized by the percent of media mentions of events in the country-year that are conflictual.

The density of media-mentions-weighted cooperative interactions between proselytizing stakeholders, divided by the analogous measure of density among all actors in the country. Because the issue networks are directed, the denominator (the number of possible interactions) is not divided by two. The measure captures the relative cooperation of proselytizing stakeholders in general rather than their cooperation with respect to targeted firms.

Number of articles about the focal drug that the innovating firm published in the top medical journals in that year, for drug-year observations ranging from the year the firm applied for FDA approval to 2004. The top medical journals are those accounting for two-thirds of the total impact factor in their respective ISI category. A publication is assigned to the firm if the title or abstract contains the name of the corresponding chemical entity and at least one author is affiliated with the firm.
time_window: each year from the year the firm applied for FDA approval to 2004

description: Count of FDA-approved drugs applying the same mechanism of action as the focal drug that are available for use in the same therapeutic class in the year preceding the observation year.

Number of distinct mechanisms of action underlying drugs in the focal drug's therapeutic class in the year preceding the observation year, because distinct mechanisms capture different knowledge on pharmacology and human physiology.

variable_name: Top medical publications on similar drugs
description: Average number of publications about drugs other than the focal drug that have the same therapeutic use and build on the same mechanism of action, counted over the two years preceding the observation year. Because publication counts are skewed, the measure is the logarithm of the average publication count.
time_window: two years preceding the observation year

variable_name: Top medical publications on potential substitutes
description: Average number of publications across the mechanisms of action in the therapeutic class other than the mechanism underlying the focal drug, computed analogously to the similar-drugs variable, over the two years preceding the observation year and entered as a logarithm.
time_window: two years preceding the observation year

description: The CMS asked respondents to indicate the percentage of their product and process innovations for which patent protection effectively protected their firm's competitive advantage during the 1991-1993 period. For product and process innovations separately there were five mutually exclusive response categories: < 10 percent, 10-40 percent, 41-60 percent, 61-90 percent, and > 90 percent. A weighted average of the product and process scores using midpoints was computed with the percentage of R&D effort devoted to product and process innovations as weights.

The CMS asked respondents to indicate the percentage of their product and process innovations for which secrecy effectively protected their firm's competitive advantage during the 1991-1993 period. For product and process innovations separately there were five mutually exclusive response categories: < 10 percent, 10-40 percent, 41-60 percent, 61-90 percent, and > 90 percent. A weighted average of the product and process scores using midpoints was computed with the percentage of R&D effort devoted to product and process innovations as weights.

variable_name: Effectiveness of being first to market
description: The CMS asked respondents to indicate the percentage of their product and process innovations for which being first to market effectively protected their firm's competitive advantage during the 1991-1993 period. For product and process innovations separately there were five mutually exclusive response categories: < 10 percent, 10-40 percent, 41-60 percent, 61-90 percent, and > 90 percent. A weighted average of the product and process scores using midpoints was computed with the percentage of R&D effort devoted to product and process innovations as weights.

The CMS provides a measure of specialized complementary assets using information related to the frequency of face-to-face interaction between personnel from R&D and production, and R&D and sales/marketing measured in a four-point Likert scale. The authors constructed a binary variable that takes a value of 1 if R&D and manufacturing or R&D and sales/marketing personnel interact daily; the median value is weekly interaction.

This is the percentage of product and process innovations for which a firm applied for patents in the period 1991-1993 in the United States, available from the CMS. The authors computed a weighted average of product and process patent propensities using the percentage of R&D effort devoted to product and process innovations as weights.

Tobin's q is approximated following Chung and Pruitt as the ratio of a firm's market value, defined as the sum of a firm equity value, the book value of long-term debt, and net current liabilities, and the firm book value of its total assets. The authors use the log of the 1991-1993 average of Tobin's q as the main dependent variable in the market-value equation.

The authors constructed a dummy variable equal to one if a respondent indicated 'the prevention of rivals from patenting related inventions'—sometimes defined as 'blocking'—and not licensing, nor cross-licensing, as reasons to apply for their most recent application for a product or process patent. Missing values for non-patenting firms were substituted with zero.

variable_name: % R&D projects initiated to respond to rivals' R&D
description: The threat of entry is measured using the CMS survey question related to the percentage of R&D projects that the R&D unit initiated 'to respond to specific R&D projects of competitors.' The variable was coded in the survey using five mutually exclusive response categories: < 10 percent, 10-40 percent, 41-60 percent, 61-90 percent, and > 90 percent. To test Hypothesis 2, the authors construct a dummy variable equal to 1 if the respondent indicated a category greater than the lowest (< 10%).

A firm's market share is computed as the fraction of total industry sales captured by the firm in its primary business segment. The overall weighted market share of the firm is measured as 1991-1993 average sales in each business segment of the firm, defined at the four-digit SIC level and available from Compustat, divided by total industry sales, available from the 1992 U.S. Census of Manufacturers.

The authors summarize three CMS variables using common factor analysis: the percentage of R&D projects with the 'key goal of creating new products,' the industry rate of introduction of product innovations in a firm's primary business segment, and the average percentage of R&D effort that firms devote to basic research in the incumbent's primary business segment. The three measures reduce to one factor with a dominant positive eigenvalue, and observations are divided into two subsamples using the median value of the drastic innovation variable.

The R&D stock variable is computed as the cumulated stock of past deflated R&D expenditures, available from Compustat, using a 15 percent depreciation rate. The authors use end of 1992 stock measures to match the CMS period, and divide the R&D stock by the book value of total assets.

Mean ROA for the three years (2000-2002) following the base year (1999) is used to measure post-downsizing firm performance. ROA is measured as operating income before depreciation, interest, and taxes divided by total assets. Because of skewness in this ROA measure among sample firms (as indicated by the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic), the natural logarithm of the mean ROA is used in the analysis.

A dichotomous variable representing firms that reduced their workforce (=1) and those that did not (=0), based on the change in the level of year-end employment between 1998 and 1999. Workforce reductions greater than 5% between 1998 and 1999 were used as the demarcation point, consistent with previous research.
The three-year (1997-1999) mean of the average ratios of R&D expenditures to total sales for all firms belonging to the firm's three-digit SIC industry.
The average three-year annual growth rate in the value of shipments between 1997 and 1999, based on data available in the U.S. Census of Manufactures.
The three-year (1997-1999) average ratio of fixed assets/sales for firms in each industry.

Industry dynamism was assessed using a two-step procedure. First, the natural logarithm of sales for each three-digit industry for the years 1997-1999 was regressed against time. Second, the antilogarithms of the standard errors from these models were calculated and used as an index of dynamism for each industry.

The number of a firm's competitors that had previously entered a particular market. It is a count measure, rather than weighted by the size of each competitor; the authors report that a weighted measure using the logarithm of annual sales yielded highly consistent results. Observations are defined by firms, years, and therapeutic categories.

The number of a firm's competitors that had previously entered a particular market. It is a count measure, rather than weighted by the size of each competitor; the authors report that a weighted measure using the logarithm of annual sales yielded highly consistent results. Observations are defined by firms, quarters, and geographic regions in China.

variable_name: Direct encounters between a firm's competitors
description: The number of occasions that the competitors of the focal firm also encountered each other in at least one common market segment, divided by the maximum number of times they could have encountered each other. In Study 1 a market segment was one of the 22 therapeutic categories. The value ranges from 0 to 1, where a higher number indicates more direct market encounters between a firm's competitors.

variable_name: Direct encounters between a firm's competitors
description: The number of occasions that the competitors of the focal firm also encountered each other in at least one common market segment, divided by the maximum number of times they could have encountered each other. In Study 2 a market segment was identified as one of the 20 SIC categories. The value ranges from 0 to 1, where a higher number indicates more direct market encounters between a firm's competitors.

variable_name: Multimarket contact between a firm's competitors
description: How many of the direct encounters between a firm's competitors consisted of multimarket contacts, expressed as a proportion ranging from 0 (no multimarket encounters between competitors) to 1 (all the competitors that directly encounter each other are engaged in multimarket competition). In Study 1 a market segment was one of the 22 therapeutic categories. When this variable and the symmetry variable are both included, this variable models the effect of asymmetric multimarket contact.

variable_name: Multimarket contact between a firm's competitors
description: How many of the direct encounters between a firm's competitors consisted of multimarket contacts, expressed as a proportion ranging from 0 (no multimarket encounters between competitors) to 1 (all the competitors that directly encounter each other are engaged in multimarket competition). In Study 2 a market segment was identified as one of the 20 SIC categories. When this variable and the symmetry variable are both included, this variable models the effect of asymmetric multimarket contact.

variable_name: Symmetric contact between a firm's competitors
description: Market dependence was assessed as the proportion of a firm's total drug portfolio that it offered in the particular market, because sales per segment were not always available in Study 1. The Euclidean distance between each pair of competitors indicated the extent of symmetric market dependence, and this distance was reverse-coded by subtracting it from the maximum distance score in the sample to give a symmetry score. The firm-level variable is the average of those scores across competitors' multimarket contacts, so a high score indicates a set of multimarket competitors that are highly symmetric in terms of their market dependence.

variable_name: Symmetric contact between a firm's competitors
description: Market dependence was measured as the proportion of a firm's sales generated in a particular market. The Euclidean distance between each pair of competitors indicated the extent of symmetric market dependence, and this distance was reverse-coded by subtracting it from the maximum distance score in the sample to give a symmetry score. The firm-level variable is the average of those scores across competitors' multimarket contacts, so a high score indicates a set of multimarket competitors that are highly symmetric in terms of their market dependence.

The dependent variable in the Cox models is the hazard rate, the instantaneous probability of a firm entering a particular market by a specific point in time; a firm was at risk of entering any market it had not operated in before. In Study 1 a market entry event was a firm starting to produce an active ingredient in a therapeutic category that it had not served before. The baseline hazard was stratified by firm to control for unobserved firm-level effects.

The dependent variable in the Cox models is the hazard rate, the instantaneous probability of a firm entering a particular market by a specific point in time; a firm was at risk of entering any market it had not operated in before. In Study 2 a market entry move was the first direct investment made by a Taiwanese company in a particular geographic market, where a geographic market was a province, municipality, or autonomous region in China. The baseline hazard was stratified by firm.
The dependent variable of the prediction exercise in Sample I, operationalized as a dummy variable that takes the value '1' if the focal deal is of an add-on type and '0' if it is a conventional LBO.

The strain on the 'alliance capacity' of a PE fund is measured as the unique number of co-investors in prior deals until the time of the focal deal, measured at the fund (sector) level. The greater the number of co-investors, the greater is the capacity constraint to add new alliance members to the portfolio.
time_window: cumulative up to the focal deal

variable_name: Rivalry (percentage of unique co-investors that are corporates)
description: The potential of 'rivalry' is measured as the percentage of the unique prior co-investors that are corporates, measured at the fund (sector) level. Corporate firms are assumed to be rivalrous to each other if they compete in the same sector.
time_window: cumulative up to the focal deal

description: Dummy variable that takes the value '1' if the focal deal is an add-on deal and '0' if it is a standalone LBO. It is the dependent variable for the tests of H1 and H2.

Dummy variable that takes the value '1' if the focal deal is made in a sector hitherto unrepresented by the investment portfolio of the PE firm and '0' otherwise. The assumption is that a new sector for investment is akin to a new market segment for a PE firm.

variable_name: Capacity: Unique no. of co-investors used in prior deals (fund level)
description: Measured as the unique number of co-investors that a PE fund has done deals with until the time of the focal deal, analogous to the count of alliance partners. Both the capacity and rivalry effects are measured at the fund (sector) level for testing H1 and H2.
time_window: cumulative up to the focal deal

variable_name: Rivalry: % of unique co-investors that were corporate (fund level)
description: Measured as the proportion of the unique prior co-investors of the PE firm that are corporates. It is measured at the fund (sector) level for testing H1 and H2; for testing H3, rivalry is measured at the overall PE firm level. Two corporate firms are considered potential rivals if they belong to the same sector.
time_window: cumulative up to the focal deal

description: A dummy variable that takes the value '1' if a deal is made after 2008 (i.e., after Lehman Brothers' bankruptcy) and '0' otherwise, operationalizing the post-crisis period of 2009-2016 in which banks were skeptical about lending for large LBOs. The variable acts as a moderator for the relationship between capacity constraint (unique number of co-investors) and the likelihood of add-on deal adoption.

The number of 'new' subclasses in which the inventor filed her patents in the current year t, where 'new' subclasses are ones that are not included in the inventor's domain, that is, subclasses in which the inventor had not previously patented an invention during the previous 3 years, t-1, t-2 and t-3. The definition of the inventor's domains therefore does not include the focal year t.

Measured as the change in the total number of patents in the inventor's domain during the domain period, that is, from t-3 to t-1. Specifically, the total number of patents filed in subclasses included in the focal inventor's domain in year t-3 is subtracted from that in year t-1, which effectively lags the variable by 1 year.

The number of patents filed by each of the firm's inventors for the firm across all classes during the domain period, that is, in years t-1, t-2 and t-3 cumulatively. The measure is then the number of inventors in the firm who are less productive (have fewer patents) over this 3-year window than the focal inventor.

Star is one for the identified stars and zero otherwise. Inventors are identified as stars by the quantity and quality of their cumulative inventive output: the average number of patents produced by the focal inventor throughout her career till t-1 is multiplied by the average quality of the patents, the average number of citations received by these patents within 5 years of the patents' filing year. Inventors whose score is at least more than two standard deviations above the mean across all inventors are defined to be stars.

The number of years the focal inventor has been active in patenting for the focal firm, measured as the number of years from the first year the inventor was present in the firm to t-1. The authors assume the inventor was present in the firm 1 year before the filing of her first patent for the focal firm.
time_window: first firm patent year to t-1

description: Computed as the number of citations made in the focal inventor's patents (till t-1) to the firm's patents, that is, the number of cumulative backward citations to the firm's patents. The authors note that they separately control for the total number of backwards citations the inventor makes rather than scaling Interdependence as a ratio.

Consensus is calculated as the mean of the absolute value of the differences between the marketing and R&D managers' responses to the individual differentiation strategy items, and this value is multiplied by negative one so that higher values indicate greater consensus. The four items ask about the degree to which the SBU emphasizes differentiation activities, scored on a 7-point scale with anchors 1 = not at all and 7 = a great deal, and the items were based on Kim and Lim (1988) and Dess and Davis (1984).
scale: absolute differences on 7-point items (potentially -6 to 6), multiplied by -1

description: Consensus is calculated as the mean of the absolute value of the differences between the marketing and R&D managers' responses to the individual low cost strategy items, and this value is multiplied by negative one so that higher values indicate greater consensus. The three items ask about the degree to which the SBU emphasizes low cost activities, scored on a 7-point scale with anchors 1 = not at all and 7 = a great deal, and the items were based on Kim and Lim (1988) and Dess and Davis (1984).
scale: absolute differences on 7-point items (potentially -6 to 6), multiplied by -1

description: Respondents rated on a 7-point scale (1 = very poor and 7 = excellent) how their business unit had performed relative to competitors over the last three years with respect to three adaptiveness items. The marketing and R&D managers' assessments were averaged and this average was used as a dependent variable in the hypothesis tests.

Respondents rated on a 7-point scale (1 = very poor and 7 = excellent) how their business unit had performed relative to competitors over the last three years with respect to three effectiveness items. The measure is described as achieving nonfinancial goals, and the marketing and R&D managers' assessments were averaged and used as a dependent variable.

Respondents rated on a 7-point scale (1 = very poor and 7 = excellent) how their business unit had performed relative to competitors over the last three years on earning profits, the single efficiency item. Efficiency is described as most closely associated with profitability, and the marketing and R&D managers' assessments were averaged and used as a dependent variable.

Marketing managers were asked to assess, on a 7-point scale with anchors 1 = very few changes and 7 = very frequent changes, the frequency of major changes in market-related aspects of the business environment from which their business unit derived its largest amount of sales. The construct was based only on the responses of the marketing managers, since the authors felt R&D managers would not be knowledgeable about items such as changes in sales strategies or pricing behavior.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = very few changes, 7 = very frequent changes)

description: A four-item scale measuring respondents' assessments of the degree to which they and their partner typically adjust their own behavior to accommodate needs of the other (buyer questionnaire alpha .88; supplier version alpha .88). Items asked about flexibility in response to requests for changes, whether the parties would rather work out a new deal than hold each other to original terms when unexpected situations arise, whether the parties will be open to modifying agreements, and whether changes in fixed prices are not ruled out.
scale: 1 = completely inaccurate description to 7 = completely accurate description

description: A four-item scale measuring respondents' assessments of the degree to which each party discloses information that may facilitate the other party's activities, as opposed to keeping all information proprietary (buyer version alpha .79; supplier version alpha .62). Items concerned frequent and informal exchange of information, providing any information that might help the other party, providing proprietary information if it can help, and keeping each other informed about events or changes that may affect the other party.
scale: 1 = completely inaccurate description to 7 = completely accurate description

description: A four-item scale measuring respondents' assessments of the degree to which the parties share the responsibility for maintaining the relationship itself and for problems that arise as time goes on (buyer version alpha .79; supplier version alpha .74). Items covered joint responsibility for getting things done, treating problems as joint rather than individual responsibilities, shared responsibility for making the relationship work, and not minding owing each other favors.
scale: 1 = completely inaccurate description to 7 = completely accurate description

variable_name: Restraint in the use of power
description: A three-item scale measuring respondents' assessments of the degree to which the parties typically refrain from exploiting each other, given the opportunity to do so (buyer version alpha .68; supplier version alpha .63). The authors expected cooperation to manifest in a partner's willingness to forgo short-term profits gained at severe cost to the other party.
scale: 1 = completely inaccurate description to 7 = completely accurate description

description: A four-item scale measuring respondents' assessments of the open-endedness of future interaction between themselves and their partners, or the degree to which the parties expected the relationship to continue indefinitely (buyer and supplier version alphas .88). The authors intentionally avoided using a formalized measure such as the length of time stated in a formal contract.
scale: 1 = completely inaccurate description to 7 = completely accurate description

description: Respondents' estimates of how many times per quarter buyers received deliveries from suppliers. Only the buyer survey requested this information; the item asked how often deliveries of the components are received from the supplier (per week, per month, or other).

A four-item scale measuring respondents' assessments of the level of effort a buyer must put forth to assess the quality of the product produced by a supplier (buyer and supplier version alphas .66). Items covered the inadequacy of evaluating the supplier on component prices alone, the need for extensive incoming inspection, the need for on-site inspection at the supplier's plant, and the need to make sure the supplier follows approved production and quality control procedures.

Measured as the number of existing designs a firm repeated in year t-1. Exploitation is contextualized as repetition or refinement of a firm's existing form factors, using new form factors as indicators of exploration; this is described as the short-term measure.

Measured as the number of new designs for existing form factors a firm created in year t-1. This counting measure is used together with repetitive exploitation t-1 in the models of the likelihood of exploration and of exploration timing.

Measured as incremental exploitation t-1 divided by the sum of repetitive exploitation t-1 and incremental exploitation t-1. It captures the relative effort distribution between the two types of exploitation in year t-1.

A dummy variable with value 1 indicating the creation of new designs for new form factors that are first introduced by a firm in a focal year, and value 0 indicating the absence of such new designs in that year. The authors adopt 10 time frames to capture the focal year (year t through year t+9), thus forming 10 dependent variables, one for each focal year. The development of each different sized disk (form factor) involved a new performance trajectory, a new market segment, and new routines and values.
time_window: year t through year t+9, one dependent variable per focal year
