description: Measured as the number of years a firm had waited before exploring the emerging new market segment, with the count starting at 1 for a firm that explored the new market segment during the first year. It is used to measure how quickly a firm explores a new market segment.

The total number of patents a focal firm applied for in year t + 1, counting only patent applications that were eventually approved; the year of application is used as the point at which the invention was produced. Patents were extracted from the NBER database of US patents and restricted to those filed between 1986 and 2002 under category no. 2, 'computers & communications'. The authors report that these criteria identified 143,500 patents issued to the 410 firms in the sample.

The extent to which the community comprised distinct firms in year t compared with the previous year, measured as the inverse of community overlap across both years: 1 - (Ci,t-1 intersect Ci,t)/(Ci,t-1 union Ci,t). Linear and squared terms were specified.

The number of distinct communities in which the firm was a member prior to t, excluding the current community. The variable was set to 0 if the firm had no prior community affiliations (e.g., it just entered the network in year t). Linear and squared terms were specified.

Firm-actor-centric measure based on the continuous core/periphery model of Borgatti and Everett (1999), capturing to what extent a firm is positioned closer to the core than to the periphery of its network community. For Hypothesis 3a the firm's coreness in its current network community was captured; for Hypothesis 3b the time-varying average coreness was used, computed by summing the firm's within-community coreness in each year and dividing by the number of years the firm spent in the network until t.
time_window: current year (H3a); averaged over all prior years until t (H3b)

description: Specified as the average network reach between any two firms in a network: 1/Nt(Nt-1) summed over i and j (j not equal i) of 1/dij, where Nt is the size of the network in year t and dij is the shortest network distance between two firms i and j; the measure varies between 0 and 1, with higher values indicating greater global network reach. For Hypothesis 4b the time-varying effect of a firm's average global network reach, measured over the firm's entire history of community affiliations, was captured by summing yearly global network reach over the years the firm was present and dividing by the total number of years the firm spent in the network until t.
time_window: year t (H4a); averaged over the firm's affiliation history until t (H4b)

variable_name: Similarity of patent stocks and patent citations within network communities
description: The composition of patent stocks and patterns of patent citations were analyzed within and across the identified network communities. Any two firms from the same network community were on average twice as likely to cite each other's patents as firms outside the community, and same-community firms' patents were more likely to be distributed across a similar set of three-digit technological classes. A computer simulation randomly redistributed firms over the network communities in each year, keeping the number of communities and the size of each community fixed, repeated 1,000 times per year, to compute the baseline similarity of patent stocks and forward and backward citations using an inverse of Blau's diversity metric; real and baseline similarity scores were compared with a z-score.
time_window: each year of the study period

description: The primary respondent was asked to indicate whether their company had created a dedicated alliance function, defined as a position to manage or coordinate all alliance-related activity in the firm. Firms with a dedicated alliance function were also asked when the function was established, how many people were in the function, and the managerial position of the person who headed the function; this information was cross-checked from public sources such as annual reports and company websites. The existence of a dedicated alliance function was measured by a categorical rather than a metric variable, and almost 64 percent of the companies in the sample had established one.

Count of each firm's alliances over the 10-year period from 1988 to 1997. The raw count came from the SDC Mergers, Acquisitions and Alliances database and was corrected with the primary respondent in each company, because SDC missed some alliances, some announced alliances did not progress, and some announcements carried no strong commitment or intent to proceed. A straightforward technology licensing deal for a fee is not considered an alliance unless it was accompanied by an agreement to access other skills across some part of the value chain. In the alliance-level analysis, cumulative alliance experience is a count of all the alliances formed by the firm up to and including the specific alliance whose abnormal gains are being assessed.

Incremental value creation measured as abnormal stock market gains following alliance announcements. Residuals are extracted from a standard asset-pricing model estimated with daily stock market returns for each publicly listed firm over a 180-day period prior to the event day, against the value-weighted S&P 500; predicted returns are then computed over a 14-day period surrounding the event day (days -10 to +3), and daily firm-specific excess returns are the difference between actual and predicted returns. Two market-based measures were created: percentage abnormal stock gains for each individual alliance formed by each firm during 1993-97 (INDABNORMAL) and, for each firm, an average of the abnormal stock gains across all its alliances formed during 1993-97 (AVGABNORMAL).
time_window: Alliances formed 1993-97; 180-day estimation window; event window days -10 to +3

description: Managerial assessments collected with a survey instrument for every alliance each firm formed during 1993-97, each alliance being evaluated by the manager or executive responsible for managing that alliance on a 7-point Likert type scale on four performance dimensions. Every alliance that received a score of 4 or more on three of the four dimensions was rated 'successful or satisfactory', and the firm's overall alliance success rate is the ratio of its successful/satisfactory alliances to all its alliances during 1993-97. A second firm-level measure, AVGPERF, was created by summing the ratings across the four performance dimensions for each alliance and averaging this score across all the firm's alliances; the two perceptual measures correlated very strongly (0.88).

A firm's market share is calculated as its number of active mobile cellular connections over the total number of active mobile connections in a country. Following Adner and Kapoor (2010) and Ferrier et al. (1999), the market share is introduced into the main estimation after the natural logarithm transformation.

Dummy that takes the value 1 when a demand window is open in country k in that quarter and 0 otherwise. Demand growth in each country is the percentage change in the number of mobile cellular connections from period t-1 to period t; a country is considered to have experienced a demand window when its demand growth in the quarter was higher than the worldwide mean demand growth from 2000 to 2015.

Dummy that takes the value 1 during the first year after the introduction of a technological change in country k and 0 otherwise. Technological changes are the shifts from the 2G to the 3G standard and from the 3G to the 4G standard.
time_window: first year after the introduction of a technological change

description: The cumulative number of quarters in which a firm has been operating in countries with demand windows from January 2000, including the home country. For firms owned by an MNC, the cumulative value of the owner group was allocated to the firm that was majority owned by that group; for purely domestic firms only experience accumulated in the home country is counted. The variable is 0 when the firm has no accumulative experience with demand windows and positive when it has such experience.

The cumulative number of technological windows, beginning in 2000, that the international group owner of the firm experienced in the countries in which it operated; the changes counted are the shifts from 2G to 3G and from 3G to 4G. An MNC was considered as experiencing a technological window in country k if it was operative in that country in the quarter in which the window was open. The cumulative value was allocated to each majority-owned subsidiary, and for purely domestic firms the variable considers only technological discontinuities accumulated in the home country.

Blau's index of the two classes of demand windows a firm has experienced up to time t, calculated by subtracting the sum of the squared shares of each class from one. The classes are DW A, where the market penetration rate is lower than 50% (early adopters), and DW B, where the penetration rate is equal to or higher than 50% (late adopters). For MNC-owned firms the value of the owner group was allocated to the firm owned by that group, and for purely domestic firms only home-country experience is counted. The variable ranges from 0, if the experience is completely homogeneous, to 0.5, if the firm possesses identical amounts of experience with DWs A and B.

Blau's index calculated over the cumulative number of technological windows that each firm experienced from 2000 until t, differentiating between two classes: TW A for technological changes from 2G to 3G and TW B for changes from 3G to 4G. For purely domestic firms only the experience with different classes of technological windows accumulated in the home country is counted. The variable ranges from 0, if the firm does not possess IE or its IE refers to just one class of technological change, to 0.5, if the owner MNC possesses identical amounts of experience with TWs A and B.

The premium paid for the target is calculated by SDC as the percentage difference between the final price per target share paid by the acquiring firm and the target's stock price four weeks before the offer announcement. The authors report four-week premiums in all analyses.
time_window: four weeks before the offer announcement

description: The authors used the SDC database to obtain data on premiums paid by interlock partners. They used the coefficient of variation of the interlock partners' premiums as the measure of partner experience diversity, first calculating the standard deviation of partner premiums divided by the mean partner premium and then calculating a standardized coefficient of variation; they report the standardized measure because partner groups differ in size. Higher values represent more diversity in partner premiums.
time_window: three years prior to the focal firm's acquisition

description: The authors collected data on the acquisition value for all network partner acquisitions in the SDC database and calculated the coefficient of variation across partner acquisition values in the same manner as partner premiums. They report the standardized coefficient of variation.
time_window: three years prior to the focal firm's acquisition

description: To capture information in the focal firm's network, the authors calculated the focal firm's direct and indirect ties. Direct ties are network partners that sit on the focal firm's board; indirect ties are the partners of its network partners. The ratio of indirect to direct ties measures network diversity, with high diversity indicating more unique knowledge per partner tie.
time_window: interlock data from 1985, 1990, and 1993 proxy statements

description: The authors measured the industry heterogeneity of the focal firm's partners using an entropy-based index typical in the treatment of categorical variables. Industry was determined by the organization's two-digit Standard Industrial Classification code, and industry data on the network partners were collected from COMPUSTAT.

The authors calculated the coefficient of variation of the focal firm's network partners' size, measured as number of employees, in the year prior to the focal firm's acquisition. Size data on the network partners were collected from COMPUSTAT.
time_window: year prior to the focal firm's acquisition

description: The authors obtained data on all alliances among publicly held firms from the SDC database and checked each focal-firm-interlock-partner pair to see whether the two firms also shared a strategic alliance, coding multiplexity one if they did. They also checked Business Roundtable and Business Council membership lists and coded one if members of the two firms shared a membership. The multiplexity variable was coded two if the pair shared both an alliance and a Roundtable or Council membership. They then calculated the mean multiplexity of the focal firm's network partners.
time_window: alliances in the study period; membership lists for multiple years between 1986 and 1996

variable_name: partner heterogeneity measures (premiums, acquisition sizes, industries, sizes)
description: Partner diversity was measured with several heterogeneity variables for the focal firm's interlock partners: the coefficient of variation of partners' acquisition premiums and of their acquisition values over the prior three years, an entropy-based index of partner industries, and the coefficient of variation of partner size (employees). Each was entered separately and interacted with tie multiplexity.
scale: coefficients of variation and entropy index

description: R&D project announcements were classified into two groups: preproduct announcements, those made before new product introduction, and new product announcements, those made at the time of introduction or after it. The two groups served as proxies for the innovation and commercialization stages of R&D projects. Two independent coders and one of the authors coded the announcements, with over 95 percent agreement; disagreements were resolved by discussion among them.

Wealth created by the announcements was measured as the excess returns resulting from conventional event study methodology. An ordinary-least-squares market model using the equally weighted CRSP index was estimated for the period from day -1 to day 0, with the estimation period from -120 to -21 days before the announcement date. Excess returns are the difference between actual and predicted returns, and excess returns were averaged to generate a mean excess return.
time_window: two-day announcement period (day -1 to day 0); estimation period day -120 to day -21

description: Measured as the ratio of the three-year average of industry R&D expenditures to average industry sales for the three years prior to the year of an announcement.
time_window: three-year averages prior to the announcement year

description: A firm's R&D intensity scaled by its industry's, operationally defined as the ratio of the three-year average of firm R&D intensity to three-year average industry R&D intensity. It measures the degree to which the firm overspends or underspends its competitors and is sometimes considered a measure of technology leadership.

Operationally defined as the four-firm seller concentration in a firm's dominant industry: the ratio of the three-year average of total sales for the four largest firms in the industry to total industry sales.
Each firm's sales growth was scaled by the dominant industry growth rate, both averaged over three years. Low-growth firms are those that grow more slowly than their industry averages.

Size was measured as the logarithmic transformation of average firm sales over three years, in millions of dollars. To test for a nonlinear firm size effect in the innovation stage, a squared term for firm size was introduced.
scale: logarithm of sales in millions of dollars

description: Founders' expectations of industry growth at the time of the initial survey, obtained by asking respondents to select from a four-point scale whether they perceive market growth to be 'diminishing' (1), 'unchanged' (2), 'expanding' (3), or experiencing 'strong expansion' (4). This variable is time invariant.

Founders' perceptions of market competition, measured at the initial survey by asking respondents to indicate on a four-point scale whether, in the industry where they plan to launch their business, they: 'expect no competition' (0), 'expect low competition' (1), 'expect moderate competition' (2), or 'expect strong competition' (3). The authors describe this variable as time variant.

Founders' perceptions of the expected size of the venture, measured at each wave of the survey by asking them to indicate the number of employees they anticipate will be on the payroll in year five. This variable is time variant.

Perceptions of price competition measured by asking respondents to indicate the importance of offering competitive prices to secure customers on a four-item scale in which '0' equals 'no importance,' '1' equals 'marginal importance,' '2' equals 'importance,' and '3' equals 'critical importance.' This measure is time invariant.

Measured with five questions about activities undertaken by founders when organizing new ventures, asked every six months and coded '1' if the respondent answered 'yes' and '0' if 'no'. The dichotomous measures are totalled to yield a single measure of venture-organizing activities that can be objectively verified by potential investors. The variable is time variant.

Measured by asking the respondents every six months whether they have initiated marketing, and if yes, in which month they initiated marketing. The variable is coded '0' for every month that they have not initiated marketing and '1' thereafter. This variable is time variant.

Measured by asking respondents every six months 'at what stage of development is the product or service this start-up will be selling?' The scale of responses was '1' equals 'no work has been done to develop a product or service,' '2' equals 'work to develop the product or service is still in the idea stage,' '3' equals 'a model or procedure is being developed,' '4' equals 'a prototype or procedure has been tested with customers,' and '5' equals 'the product or service is completed and ready for sales or delivery.' This variable is time variant.

Measured by asking respondents every six months to provide the sales they have earned by month. For every month they recorded sales, the amount of sales is coded as the natural log of sales; otherwise the variable is coded '0'. This variable is time variant.

Stage 1 outcome, measured by asking the respondent every six months whether the venture has sought external funds; if yes, respondents were asked in which month the event first occurred. The variable is coded 1 for each month the event occurred and 0 otherwise, allowing identification by month of when ventures were selected into the first stage.

variable_name: Received funds from an external source
description: Stage 2 outcome, measured by asking the respondent every six months whether the venture had received funds from an external source for the first time; if yes, respondents were asked in which month that event first occurred. The variable is coded 1 for each month the event occurred and 0 otherwise.

The variable capturing environmental performance is binary; it is set to one for lawsuit targets and zero otherwise. Targets are firms named as defendants in environmental lawsuits brought by the EPA or the Department of Justice and settled between 1994 and 1998, identified from the EPA's annual enforcement and compliance report. Only the first time a firm's name appears in the report counts as the event year, so the analysis focuses on firms rather than events. Control firms are non-offenders matched on 4-digit SIC code and sales.

Board size is the sum of all corporate directors at the end of the last fiscal year before the lawsuit settlement. The data are collected from annual proxy statements filed in the SEC's EDGAR database.
time_window: end of the last fiscal year before the lawsuit settlement

variable_name: Fraction of directors in peer firms
description: The sum of all corporate directors who are active executives in other industrial firms. The category excludes consultants, lawyers, financiers, academics, politicians, members of the clergy and the military, and private investors, and includes all inside directors, who are by definition members of an industrial firm. The authors report that the inclusion of insiders in the construction of this variable has no bearing on the results.
time_window: end of the last fiscal year before the lawsuit settlement

description: The average number of directorship posts held by a corporate director, which proxies for director reputation. The data are collected from annual proxy statements filed in the SEC's EDGAR database.
time_window: end of the last fiscal year before the lawsuit settlement

description: The fraction of common stock owned by officers and directors as a group. The data are collected from annual proxy statements filed in the SEC's EDGAR database.
time_window: end of the last fiscal year before the lawsuit settlement

description: The number of paying members of major U.S. environmental and conservation organizations (with an annual budget exceeding $1 million or membership exceeding 2000) per 1000 state residents; it is a measure of revealed preference. A firm-level value is calculated as the average of the proxy for all the states in which the firm has significant operations; where firms specified that they operated in more than 20 states, a nationwide average measure of stakeholder pressure is assumed. Headquarter locations were identified by searching companies' web pages and states of significant operations from items 1 and 2 of the 10-K reports filed in EDGAR. Greater values imply greater amounts of stakeholder pressure facing the firm.

Based on the scorecards of the League of Conservation Voters, which keeps track of roughly 30 pieces of legislation that major U.S. environmental groups consider most important each year and records how senators and representatives voted; the measure captures the percentage of times that members of Congress voted for an environmental measure, with separate records for the House and Senate. The two records are consolidated into a single variable set to one when the majority of proposals received a favorable vote by a firm's 'weighted' average locus of operations in both the Senate and the House, and zero otherwise. A firm-level value is the average across the states where the firm has significant operations, and greater values imply greater stakeholder pressure.
time_window: 1993-1997 (years before the lawsuit was settled and the penalty assessed)

description: A proxy for the pressures exerted on a firm by a state's regulatory environment, based on a state's toxic emissions, that is, the total amount of on- and off-site toxic releases. The amount of toxic emissions is deflated by total employment in each state (to account for differences in the level of economic activity across states), log-transformed, and inverted, so greater emissions correspond to lower regulatory stringency and a lower value of the variable. A firm-level value is calculated as the average across the states in which the firm has significant operations; greater variable values imply greater amounts of stakeholder pressure facing the firm.

variable_name: coded reason theme (authentic motives/inauthentic motives about clinics/patient treatment, 'disinterestedness')
description: Each of the 36 interviewees gave one primary statement of justification for Alpha's failure or Beta's success, and the interviewer hand-coded the quotes into themes. Two main themes emerged, operational differences and the authenticity and commitment of the firms' attempts at diversification, with the authenticity language referring to interest or disinterest in economic gains as the firms' primary motives. The coding was corroborated by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, who agreed on 40 of the 43 coded reasons.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three growth type conditions: No Growth, Within-Category Growth, or Diversification. In the No Growth condition the clinic was described and participants moved on to evaluate it. In the Within-Category Growth condition the program owners had recently begun plans to expand but the treatment focus remained the same, serving patients dealing with substance abuse issues; in the Diversification condition the growth plans also included expanding into two new areas of treatment, process addictions and eating disorders.

Authenticity was signaled by describing whether the clinic was affiliated with outside investors. In the High Organizational Authenticity Signal (no outside investor) conditions participants were told that the clinic 'was started by behavioral health practitioners who still own the facility'; in the Low Organizational Authenticity Signal (outside investor) conditions they were told that the clinic 'was started by behavioral health practitioners and purchased by a group of investors.' In both cases it was made clear that practitioners ran the day-to-day operations. A manipulation check combining the 'authentic' and 'sincere' items (Cronbach's alpha 0.95) showed higher authenticity ratings in the high signal condition (n = 41, mean = 5.20) than in the low signal condition (n = 42, mean = 3.96).

After reading the clinic description or the growth type description, participants were told to assume they had a patient who is dealing with substance abuse and were asked how likely they were to refer the patient to the described clinic. The question was answered on a six-point scale from 1 ('very unlikely') to 6 ('very likely').

Participants were asked about their perceptions of the firm's commitment to patients and rated 'How committed is this firm to its patients' on a seven-point scale (1 = 'not committed at all' to 7 = 'solely and completely committed to patients').
scale: 1-7 (1 = not committed at all, 7 = solely and completely committed to patients)

variable_name: growth condition (Within Category Growth vs. Diversification)
description: The No Growth condition from experiment 1 was dropped, leaving only the Within Category Growth and Diversification conditions. Instead of plans for growth in the future, participants were told that the firm 'has expanded into new locations with the same services' (Within Category Growth) or 'has expanded to provide new services' (Diversification).

The authenticity signal was manipulated more directly through information indicating either interest or disinterest in short-term economic rewards. In the Low Authenticity Signals condition participants were told, 'These owners are excited about the financial opportunities related to running this clinic'; in the High Authenticity Signals (Disinterestedness) condition they were told, 'These owners are known to put patients ahead of short-term rewards.' An attention check asked participants whether the firm had a patient focus or an opportunity focus.
The same set of measures was used as in experiment 1, including the dependent variable of likelihood to refer a patient to the clinic.
The same mediating measure of commitment was used as in experiment 1.

variable_name: growth condition (Within Category Growth vs. Diversification)
description: Participants were randomly assigned to either a Within-Category Growth or a Diversification condition. In all conditions participants were first told that the shop specialized in 'engine and tire repair.' In the Within-Category Growth conditions the service locations had expanded but the actual services remained the same, 'engine and tire service'; in the Diversification condition the shop had expanded into a new line of service, 'aftermarket enhancements and repair body work.'

The authenticity signal manipulation was based on whether the business had a reputation of putting customers ahead of short-term benefits. Participants in the Low Authenticity Signals conditions were told that 'This shop has been known to be focused on its financial success over the past few years'; participants in the High Authenticity Signals conditions were told, 'You were told that this mechanic is willing to do extra work without compensation to make sure the car works.' A manipulation check showed that participants attributed more authenticity in the high signal condition (n = 99, mean = 5.42) than in the low signal condition (n = 101, mean = 4.39).

After reading the growth description, participants were asked to assume that they were in the market for the firm's original service and were asked how likely they were to 'bring your car to this mechanic's shop.' The question was answered on a six-point scale.
Participants rated from 1 (low) to 7 (high) the question, 'How committed is this firm to its customers?'

Following the Granger causality-testing methodology used by Domian (1992), the T-bill rate is regressed onto its own lagged value and onto the lagged value of the average time-to-maturity of a fund's portfolio, and this regression is repeated for each month in the fund's history using data only up to and including that month, yielding fund-specific time-varying coefficients. Because a good forecaster invests in long maturities when rates subsequently fall and short maturities when rates subsequently rise, better forecasting ability produces a more negative Granger-causal impact of current time-to-maturity on subsequent T-bill rates, and the measure of forecasting ability is defined from these coefficients (the estimating equation itself is not readable in the source). Estimation allows for serial correlation in the error term and uses Hatanaka's (1974) estimator. A minimum of eight observations per fund was required to generate stable coefficients, and the average number of months of history on which the measures are based is 65 months.
time_window: all months in a fund's history up to and including the month of observation

description: Gross yield is computed by adding the fund's charged expense ratio back into its net yield. Because the charged expense ratio is unavailable prior to October 1987, this equation can be estimated only on the last 87 months of the data set. The independent variables are the lagged value of the dependent variable (included for Granger causality testing), the lagged value of forecasting ability, and a constant plus a set of fund-specific and time-period-specific fixed effects. The model allows for serial correlation in the error term and is estimated with Hatanaka's (1974) procedure.
time_window: the last 87 months of the data set, beginning October 1987

description: Net yield is the difference between the gross return on an MMMF's portfolio and its expense ratio, i.e., the yield paid to the fund's investors, and it is included for each fund-month in the raw data. It is the dependent variable in an equation containing a lagged dependent variable, the lagged value of forecasting ability, a constant, fund-specific and time-period-specific fixed effects, and a dummy indicating whether the fund's expense ratio was waived or subsidized by the management company; the model is also re-estimated with the subsidization variable omitted so that any impact of forecasting ability on net yield is captured by the forecasting ability coefficient alone. Serial correlation is allowed for via Hatanaka's (1974) estimation procedure.

Each fund's size is its monthly total net assets in millions of U.S. dollars, converted to a constant-dollar figure by dividing by the consumer price index at the time of observation, and used in natural-logarithm form. In the growth model the natural logarithm of deflated fund assets is the dependent variable, with the lagged value of forecasting ability, yield deviation, and deflated category assets among the independent variables. In the capability development model the lagged value of the logarithm of deflated fund assets is the test variable for the effect of growth on subsequent forecasting ability.
time_window: monthly, lagged one month in the regressions

description: Subjects were provided with background financial information that included firm sales and profits over the past ten years and the compensation history of the CEO over that period. In the high-incentive-alignment condition the history showed the CEO's pay was linearly related to the firm's profit performance; in the low-incentive-alignment condition the history showed the CEO's compensation was linearly related to the firm's sales rather than to its profits. The treatment was strengthened with bonus points, traded for cash-prize-drawing tickets if the subject's decisions were consistent with the compensation scheme described in the scenario.
scale: two-level experimental condition (high vs. low incentive alignment)

description: Monitoring was simulated by varying the level and the nature of the board of directors' control over the strategic choices of the CEO and by varying the actions of the experiment's administrator. In the high-monitoring condition subjects were told that there would be additional strategic controls because the board would request more written reports and meet more frequently to evaluate the strategic desirability of the CEO's decisions, more active and direct observation of the CEO's activities, and an internal auditor reporting to the board; subjects also had to prepare written justifications for their decisions, which the administrator read, questioned, and marked as reviewed and approved. In the low-monitoring condition subjects were told that the board was composed of six long-term members who indicated a high level of trust and confidence in the CEO's ability to serve and that the CEO had significant latitude in decision making.
scale: two-level experimental condition (high vs. low monitoring)

description: The term of office treatment was created by assigning subjects to either a long-term-CEO or a short-term-CEO condition. The essential difference between the conditions was the assignment of responsibility for prior decisions: subjects in the long-term condition were in the role of P. Johnson, the CEO of Adams and Smith, throughout the complete experiment and were told that they had made the earlier poor research and development investment decisions. Subjects in the short-term condition began the experiment as chief financial officer, were told that the board designated the CEO to decide which division to invest in, and were then informed that the results were negative, that P. Johnson had retired, and that they had been appointed the new CEO by the board.
scale: two-level experimental condition (long-term vs. short-term CEO)

variable_name: level of investment in the newly created SBUs (profit-maximizing strategy)
description: The first dependent variable, used for all tests of hypotheses, was the level of investment in the newly created SBUs, whose profit growth was predicted to be the result of the research and development expenditure; this was the 'profit-maximizing strategy.' Subjects were to decide how much of a $20 million investment to allocate, facing the alternatives of investment in the previous choice that produced poor results or of allocating the funds to other projects that had different rates of growth and rates of return. Because the profit-maximizing strategy and sales-growth strategy decisions were exact reflections, only the profit-maximizing strategy is reported.
scale: millions of dollars, allocated from a $20 million budget

description: The second dependent variable, used to test Hypothesis 4a, was the investment in the previously poor choices that were made in the earlier periods, the 'escalation-level' decision.
scale: millions of dollars, allocated from a $20 million budget

description: An index based on four variables that have been widely used to indicate CEO power: the tenure of the CEO, the total number of board appointments held by the CEO, the CEO's ownership (the total percentage of shares held by the CEO), and whether the CEO is also the board chair. In the primary analysis these four measures were combined into a single index using discrete principal components analysis; in a separate analysis the sum of standard scores of the four measures was used instead and produced very consistent results.

variable_name: A new director's prior experience with other similar CEOs
description: Each new director's other Fortune board appointments in the previous 3 years were tracked, and the number of tied-to CEOs who were similar to the focal CEO on a given dimension was used to measure the director's prior experience along that dimension. Two CEOs were considered similar in age when their ages differed by less than one standard deviation (9 years), and similar on the other six dimensions when they were the same. The seven measures were combined into a single index by using discrete principal components analysis.

variable_name: A new director's demographic difference from the CEO
description: A new director's difference from the CEO on a given characteristic was coded as 1 if they are different on the characteristic and 0 otherwise, for gender, ethnicity, age, highest degree earned, Ivy League background, functional background, and industry of employment. Following a discrete principal components analysis procedure, the seven measures of difference were combined into a single index.
scale: 0/1 per characteristic; index across seven characteristics

variable_name: New directors' prior experience with other similar CEOs
description: To measure new directors' prior experience with other similar CEOs, the authors first counted the number of new directors who worked with other similar CEOs along each of the seven characteristics, and in the primary analysis combined these seven measures into a single index using discrete principal components analysis. Because the unit of analysis for CEO compensation is the firm-year, these values are aggregated across the new directors appointed to the board in a given year.

variable_name: New directors' demographic difference from the CEO
description: The unit of analysis in analyzing CEO compensation is the firm-year. When a board appointed multiple new directors in a given year, the authors used the mean value of each new director's demographic difference from the CEO to measure new directors' demographic difference from the CEO, based on the same seven demographic characteristics used for individual directors. In a separate analysis the median and the sum of each new director's demographic difference were used as alternatives and produced consistent results.

CEO compensation was measured as the logarithm of the focal CEO's total compensation in the year subsequent to new director appointments (t + 1). Total compensation includes salary, bonus, options, and grants made in a given year; stock option grants were valued using the Black-Scholes method, and other long-term grants (e.g., performance shares and restricted stock) were valued at the market price on the date of grant.

Initial Feedback is the highest payoffs that a participant achieved in the first three trials, representing how successful the participant was initially. It serves as the exclusion restriction for estimating the first stage of the two-step Heckman model. The feedback variables are highly correlated and were orthogonalized in the regressions.
Average Feedback is the average of all payoffs that an individual has received until that trial. The feedback variables are highly correlated and were orthogonalized in the regressions.
time_window: all prior trials up to trial t

description: Immediate Feedback is a binary variable coded 1 if the prior trial improved the status quo and found a better performing alternative, and 0 if the prior trial failed to improve upon the status quo. The feedback variables are highly correlated and were orthogonalized in the regressions.

Active Search is coded as 1 if the subject changes at least one attribute in the present or in a later trial, and zero otherwise; the variable therefore captures not-satisficing. It is the binary dependent variable of the first stage of the two-step Heckman regression, which fits a Probit model.

The authors identify the best-performing alternative found by the subject in any of the prior trials and measure how many attributes are changed relative to it in the current trial. The variable takes a value between 0 and 10. The measure is identical to the Hamming distance. It is the continuous dependent variable of the second stage of the Heckman regression, estimated conditional on Active Search.
time_window: current trial relative to the best prior alternative

description: Trial number controls for the number of used trials to account for the limited resources available for searching, that is, the trials remaining within an assignment. It is interacted with the feedback variables to test whether relationships are stronger or weaker later in the search effort.

A supplier's labor practice improvement between its prior and focal audits, calculated by subtracting the prior audit's labor practices score from the focal audit's score. Each audit results in a labor practice score, a summary score of all code of conduct categories, ranging from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating that labor practices better adhere to the code. Improvement averages 6 and ranges from -62 to 67 in the sample; larger values indicate greater improvement and thus an increase in coupling.
time_window: between the supplier's prior and focal audits (average gap of 9 months)

description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 when the supplier pays its frontline workers on a piece rate, and 0 otherwise. Data were obtained from the audit database, and the lagged value pertaining to the supplier's prior audit is used.

Coded 1 when a supplier is certified to at least one management system standard, such as SA8000, WRAP, ISO 9001, or OHSAS 18001, at the time it is audited, and 0 otherwise. Data were obtained from the audit database and the lagged value pertaining to the prior audit is used.

A dichotomous variable that equals 1 when the supplier is unionized, as recorded by the auditor, and 0 otherwise. Data were obtained from the audit database and the lagged value pertaining to the prior audit is used.

A three-item construct measuring the degree of similarity in economic conditions between the MNC's home and host market environments. The items are the level of industrial development, purchasing power of customers, and communications infrastructure. Responses were given on seven-point rating scales.

A four-item construct describing the extent to which the laws and regulations between home and host markets are similar. The items are technical standards, environmental laws and regulations, and regulations concerning company and customer protection. Responses were given on seven-point rating scales.

A three-item scale assessing the technological intensity and velocity of the industry (the product group identified by the respondent) in which the MNC operates. The items assess the extent to which the MNC competes in a technologically intensive sector, technology is changing rapidly, and technological developments provide significant opportunities. Responses were given on seven-point rating scales.

A three-item scale measuring the extent of similarity in customs and traditions between home and overseas markets. The items are customers' values, beliefs, and attitudes, aesthetic preferences, and level of education. Responses were given on seven-point rating scales.

A four-item construct describing the homogeneity of customers in home and host markets. The items are customer requirements, product evaluation criteria, price sensitivity, and purchasing habits. Responses were given on seven-point rating scales.

A five-item scale assessing the degree of similarity in the MNC's home and host marketing infrastructures. The items are competencies of marketing research agencies and distributors, availability of suitable advertising media, structure of distribution channels, and functions performed by intermediaries. Responses were given on seven-point rating scales.

A single-item construct measuring the degree to which the focal product or product line is in the same life cycle stage in the MNC's home and host markets. The measure is derived from Johnson and Arunthanes (1995) and Kotabe and Omura (1989) and uses a seven-point rating scale.

A three-item construct tapping the degree of similarity in competitive intensity in the MNC's home and host markets. The items are strength of price competition, pace of competitive moves in the product area, and frequency of promotion wars in the industry. Responses were given on seven-point rating scales.

A second-order construct of the degree to which the elements of marketing strategy are standardized in pursuing markets abroad. Respondents were asked to compare their firm's marketing programs in their home and host markets with respect to a set of 22 items representing marketing program elements, covering product, pricing, distribution, and promotion decisions. Responses were given on seven-point rating scales.

A multidimensional, higher-order construct comprising sales performance (sales volume, sales growth, and new product sales), financial performance (profitability as a percentage of sales, return on investment, and profit growth), and customer performance (customer satisfaction and customer retention). Respondents assessed the performance of their subsidiary vis-a-vis that of its main direct local market competitor in each area, using seven-point scales.

Fit was measured with the residual analysis method: the absolute standardized residuals that resulted from the estimation of a regression model based only on the significant contextual factors were regressed onto performance. High levels of such residuals indicate misalignment or misfit between the degree of marketing standardization and contextual factors, which should negatively impact performance, and vice versa. Only those environmental constructs found to be significantly related to international marketing strategy were used for the measurement of coalignment.

A three-day cumulative abnormal return for the innocent firm starting the day prior to the announcement of an RM firm's misconduct accusation. Daily abnormal returns are calculated with the market-adjusted model ARit = Rit - Rmt, where Rit is the return for firm i on day t and Rmt is the return of the Nasdaq Composite index, assuming a market beta of one for all firms. The three-day CAR is the sum over the three-day window of the abnormal daily returns of an innocent firm.
time_window: three-day window comprising the day before, the day of, and the day after the accusation announcement

description: A dummy variable that captures when China was the innocent firm's country of origin. It was included to test whether innocent Chinese RM firms were stronger recipients of negative spillovers independent of the offending firm's country of origin.
scale: dummy (1 = China is the innocent firm's country of origin)

description: A dummy variable that captures when China was the offending firm's country of origin. It was included to test whether spillovers from Chinese offending RM firms to all innocent RM firms were weaker.
scale: dummy (1 = China is the accused firm's country of origin)

description: Using the Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) software and its dictionary, articles on China were classified as positive if the ratio of positive affective content to total affective content was above 0.60 and negative if the ratio of negative content was above 0.60. For each accusation event, the numbers of positive and negative China-related articles published one day prior to the event were counted and combined into the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance. The measure ranges from -1, indicating all media coverage is negative, to +1, indicating all media coverage is positive.
time_window: articles published one day prior to the accusation event

description: A modified Organizational Commitment Questionnaire (Mowday et al., 1979) with items worded to assess the management team's commitment to the IJV rather than the individual's commitment. Each item was assessed on a 5-point Likert-type scale, and individual assessments of organizational commitment were averaged for each IJV. Two items were purged as a result of tests of internal consistency and factor analysis, leaving six items (Cronbach's alpha = 0.81); the interrater reliability estimate for the aggregated measure was 0.98.
scale: 1 = Not at all to 5 = To a very great extent

description: Commitment to the local parent was measured with the same set of eight items used for commitment to the foreign parent; only the name of the parent was changed. Items were assessed on a 5-point Likert-type scale and individual assessments were averaged for each IJV management team (Cronbach's alpha = 0.98).
scale: 1 = Not at all to 5 = To a very great extent

description: Commitment to the foreign parent was measured with the same set of eight items used for commitment to the local parent; only the name of the parent was changed. Items were assessed on a 5-point Likert-type scale and individual assessments were averaged for each IJV management team (Cronbach's alpha = 0.95).
scale: 1 = Not at all to 5 = To a very great extent

description: The target of commitment was a within-team repeated measures factor with three levels, giving three observations of commitment per team, one for each target. As a nominal variable, target was coded into two dummy coded variables: the first comparing the joint venture to the parent companies and the second comparing the foreign parent to the joint venture and local parent.

An instrument adapted from the 6-item procedural justice scale developed by Kim and Mauborgne (1991), which also included two measures of overall perceptions of procedural justice. Instructions preceding the scale referred respondents to the collective (the IJV) and asked them to evaluate strategic decision-making procedures which affect the IJV, though the referent in the items themselves was not altered. Items were assessed on a 5-point Likert-type scale, and individual assessments were averaged for each IJV to provide an index of each IJV management team's perception of procedural justice (Cronbach's alpha = 0.91).
scale: 1 = Not at all to 5 = To a very great extent

description: Three items with responses on a 5-point Likert-type scale assessing the degree to which the parent firms or the IJV management team controlled the strategic decision-making process, focused on the strategy-making process rather than discrete functional decisions. Individual responses were averaged to produce an index of decision control for each IJV (Cronbach's alpha = 0.83). Two of the items attribute control of the strategy-making process to the parent corporations and one item attributing control to the subsidiary was reverse-scored.
scale: 1 = Not at all to 5 = To a very great extent

variable_name: commitment to the IJV, the local parent and the foreign parent
description: Organizational commitment was measured with a modified Organizational Commitment Questionnaire (Mowday et al., 1979) assessing the management team's commitment to three targets: the IJV, the foreign parent and the local parent. Each target was measured with the same items rated on 5-point Likert-type scales, with only the target's name changed.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale, eight items per target

description: Total debt, i.e., bank loans plus bond debt, divided by the market value of the firm (MVF). MVF is computed as the sum of the book value of debt and the market value of equity. When performance is the dependent variable contemporaneous measures of the independent variables are used, whereas when diversification is the dependent variable the independent variables are lagged one year.
time_window: contemporaneous when performance is the dependent variable; lagged one year when diversification is the dependent variable

description: The sum of all bank loans divided by the market value of the firm. It is one of the two debt components, together with bond debt, that make up total debt (leverage).
The sum of all bonds and long-term notes divided by the market value of the firm. It is one of the two debt components, together with bank debt, that make up total debt (leverage).

The ratio of the firm's R&D expenditures to sales. R&D data were not available in PACAP and were imported from the NIKKEI NEEDS database. The variable is used to split the sample into R&D-intensive firms, defined as those with an R&D to sales ratio greater than 5%, and the remaining firms.

The firm's market-to-book ratio, calculated as the market value of the firm (MVF) divided by total assets, where MVF is the sum of the book value of debt and the market value of equity. The measure closely corresponds to Tobin's Q and incorporates both current performance and expectations of future cash flows. As performance was highly skewed by large values, it was transformed by taking the natural log.

Data on Japanese firms' overseas subsidiaries were collected from the publication Japanese Overseas Investments. Following Delios, Xu, and Beamish (2008), an entropy-based measure of diversification was calculated based upon the concentration of the firms' subsidiaries across different geographic markets. The base time series measure was smoothed with a moving average function before change scores were computed.

Data on each firm's product-segment sales, classified using three-digit SIC codes, were collected from the Japan Company Handbook (Delios and Beamish, 1999), and diversification was computed via the entropy measure (Palepu, 1985). The base time series measure was smoothed with a moving average function before change scores were computed.

The year-to-year change for each type of diversification (international and product), computed as the difference between the focal year and the previous year, from the moving-average-smoothed base series. Change measured this way for the two types of diversification.

Following Greve (2003), a spline function in which ↑ diversification represents the positive values of Delta1 diversification with the negative values replaced by zeros. Computed for each type of diversification (international and product).

Following Greve (2003), a spline function in which ↓ diversification is the negative values of Delta1 diversification with the positive values replaced by zeros. Computed for each type of diversification (international and product).

For studies where the original investigators had divided their overall samples into subsamples, coding of high versus low turbulence was based on the original investigators' codings of subsample environmental turbulence or a related variable; samples characterized by high (or low) input uncertainty or high (or low) environmental competitiveness were coded as high (or low) turbulence. Environmental turbulence was coded as mixed for all other samples.

Assessed by examining the average number of employees in the organizations used in each sample; this value was reported in, or could be calculated for, six samples, and organizations with more than 500 employees were coded as large while those with 500 or fewer employees were coded as small, following Miller and Toulouse (1986). Size for 12 additional samples was coded as large or small using the same 500-employee threshold based on descriptions of the organizations in the published studies, and the mean of the binary (1 = large, 0 = small) variable was substituted for the eight samples for which size could not be assessed.

variable_name: Average size of the units of analysis
description: Assessed by examining the average number of employees in each sample's units of analysis; this value was reported in, or could be calculated for, six of the 26 samples and the units in 12 additional samples were coded binarily as large or small using the 500-employee threshold based on descriptions of the sample units. For the remaining eight samples the average size of the units of analysis could not be coded and the mean of the binary unit size variable was substituted. If the level of analysis was the organization, average size of the units of analysis equaled organizational size; if it was the subunit, the average size of the organizations containing the subunits was used as organizational size.

Assessed by examining the effectiveness measure(s) used in each sample; a given measure could reflect the efficiency subconstruct, the productivity subconstruct, or a combination of the two. Three dummy variables were created: use of efficiency measure(s) versus other, use of productivity measure(s) versus other, and use of mixed measure(s) versus other.

Coded as high if greater than 50 percent of a sample's units of analysis were staffed predominantly by professionals (people whose jobs require them to have years of specialized schooling). Samples with less than 50 percent of the units being staffed primarily by professionals were coded low on professionalization; for example, a sample composed entirely of emergency hospital subunits was coded as high.

Assessed by examining the percent of each sample's units of analysis that were manufacturing organizations (or that were within manufacturing organizations for subunit level studies). The resulting variable was labeled 'percent of units in manufacturing'.

Assessed by identifying the source of both centralization and effectiveness data for each sample. If information concerning both variables was collected from either institutional or survey sources, similarity of data sources was coded as high; if information concerning the two variables was collected from different types of sources, it was coded as low.

Assessed by examining how effectiveness was assessed in each sample. Relativity of effectiveness referent was coded as high if effectiveness was assessed relative to the effectiveness of other organizations or subunits in the same industry, if effectiveness data were standardized with respect to industry (or task for subunit level studies), or if a single industry (or task for subunit level studies) was involved; it was coded as low in all other cases.

Centralization was not re-measured; the dependent variable was the correlation between centralization and effectiveness taken from each of the 26 samples in the 16 reviewed studies. Where a sample reported several correlations they were combined into a composite or averaged.

variable_name: centralization-effectiveness correlation per sample; effectiveness subconstruct coding
description: Effectiveness entered through the correlation between centralization and effectiveness reported in each of the 26 samples. The measure of effectiveness used in each sample was coded as efficiency (ratio terms), productivity (nonratio terms) or a mix of the two.

An indicator distinguishing the book in each matched pair that won the award from its matched short-listed counterpart, i.e., the finalist for the same award in the same year with the smallest absolute difference in average rating relative to the winner prior to the announcement of the finalists. The regressions include a dummy variable for each matched pair of books, so the winner indicator captures the within-pair difference between the two books.

Each book rating on Goodreads.com is an integer ranging from one star to five stars, and reviewers can attach written comments to their numeric ratings. Because the authors also gauge expectations from review text, the core analyses are restricted to ratings with accompanying text, which the authors report is the case for approximately 93 percent of the reviews with numeric ratings. The rating is the dependent variable, modelled separately for the period prior to the award announcement and the period after it.
time_window: reviews before and after the award announcement

description: A collaborative-filtering measure of a reader's predicted rating for each winning or short-listed book, built from the reviewer's past evaluations of books carrying the focal book's genre tags and excluding any books in the sample of winners and matched finalists. A reviewer's preference for a genre is the average of his or her ratings of books with that tag, and the predicted rating for the focal book is the average of those genre preferences across the book's tags. If a reviewer has not read any book in one or more genres of the focal book, the prediction aggregates the mean rating for those genres he or she has read before; no prediction is made in the rare case of no genre overlap. It serves as the measure of how predisposed a reader is to viewing a book favorably.

The ratio of the number of reviews a book received in the three months after the winner was announced to the number of reviews it received in the three months before the winner was announced. It is computed per book and captures the rate at which a book's popularity grows following the award announcement.
time_window: three months before to three months after the winner announcement

description: The risk-sharing parameter α is close to 1 when the standard deviation of the supplier's profit is low relative to the standard deviation of the supplier's cost (the buyer absorbs risk) and close to 0 in the opposite case (the buyer shifts risk). Because relation-specific profit and cost data were unavailable, the authors measured α at a more aggregate level, using the supplier's operating income as the profit measure and the supplier's operating costs as the cost measure, instead of other profit or cost measures, because these better capture the nature of the business and allow checks for tax or financial accounting related fluctuations. The estimates are run on the log-odds transform log(1/α − 1), which falls as α rises.
level: supplier (measured at a more aggregate level than the buyer-supplier relation)

description: Following Kawasaki and McMillan (1987) and Asanuma and Kikutani (1992), the variance of the suppliers' operating costs is used as the measure of the suppliers' cost fluctuation. It enters the estimated equation as log(1/VARCOST).

First proxy for suppliers' risk aversion: size. Because of scale economies and risk-pooling effects, a supplier tends to be less risk averse toward any particular relationship the smaller this is relative to its overall operations, so the larger the supplier, the smaller its risk aversion. Each supplier's number of employees (annual average) is used as the measure of the supplier's size, following Asanuma and Kikutani, who used the number of employees rather than total net sales because risk aversion has to be constant and not depend on profit.

Second proxy for suppliers' risk aversion: financial stability, taken as a proxy for the inverse of risk aversion. The more financially stable the supplier, the lower its risk aversion, since it is better able to face unpredictable financial turbulence without support from external entities. The proportion of the supplier's equity to the supplier's total assets is used; the larger this ratio, the more stable the supplier is from a financial standpoint.

Suppliers' technological capability is used as a proxy for suppliers' moral hazard. On the basis of the information gathered during the interviews, each component, and the corresponding supplier, was classified into a typology with an increasing level of the component's technological complexity and the supplier's design responsibility: Drawings Supplied (DS), where the buyer completely designs the component and the supplier just manufactures it; Drawings Approved (DA), where the buyer defines the product concept and functional parameter domains while the supplier works out the design details and manufactures the component; and Marketed Goods (MG), where the buyer purchases a component fully designed and manufactured by the supplier. The variable was transformed into two dummies: DS vendors are coded TEC1 = 0 and TEC2 = 0, DA vendors TEC1 = 1 and TEC2 = 0, and MG vendors TEC1 = 0 and TEC2 = 1, so TEC1 and TEC2 capture the additional effects on the risk-sharing parameter relative to DS as the floor. For suppliers selling more than one component, the most technologically complex one was picked.

variable_name: dummy variable for the status change (DV)
description: A binary dummy variable for the status change entered in the covariance model together with the time trend; the dummy indicates by how much the mean value of the performance ratio changes with the status change. Where an organization experienced two relevant status changes in the period, two binary variables were defined (DV1 for the first status change and DV2 for the second), and an interaction dummy was applied to the time variable where this helped to clarify the direction of change.

Profitability was measured as the percentage return on capital employed (ROCE), one of the six standard financial ratios compiled for each organization. The ratios came from each organization's annual reports and accounts, supplemented where necessary with information from internal accounts and papers.
time_window: four years before and four years after each status change

variable_name: turnover to average net fixed assets employed per annum
description: Turnover to average net fixed assets employed per annum, one of the six financial ratios compiled for each organization from its annual reports and accounts, supplemented where necessary with internal accounts and papers.
time_window: four years before and four years after each status change

description: Stocks (including work in progress) to turnover; the authors state that a decline in the ratios of stocks and debtors to turnover indicates an improvement in performance, but later note that the direction of change in these two ratios signalling improvement or deterioration is not clear.
time_window: four years before and four years after each status change

description: Debtors to turnover; the authors state that a decline in the ratios of stocks and debtors to turnover indicates an improvement in performance, but later note that the direction of change in these two ratios signalling improvement or deterioration is not clear.
time_window: four years before and four years after each status change

description: Labor's share in costs, measured as the wages to expenditure ratio; a fall in the wages to expenditure ratio implies a 'labor shake out' and a movement towards market clearing.
time_window: four years before and four years after each status change

description: Value added per employee, approximated as (P+I+W)/N where P = profit before tax, I = capital charges in the form of interest on long-term loans and W = employees' wages; P, I and W were expressed in real terms deflated by the nonfood RPI. The approximation was used because detailed information on the costs of purchases was lacking.
time_window: four years before and four years after each status change

description: Financial performance was measured with six standard ratios compiled from each organization's annual reports and accounts, supplemented by internal papers: return on capital employed, turnover to average net fixed assets, stocks to turnover, debtors to turnover, wages to expenditure, and value added per employee. Changes in each ratio were tested around the status change.

A department was characterized as mechanistic when managers indicated that all of the following elements were present: hierarchical decision making with three or four levels of management providing close supervision; virtually complete reliance on formal written standard operating procedures and rules; a large set of at least 50 narrow job descriptions; on average one departmental meeting in a month; no job rotation; and specialized or nonoverlapping individual tasks. A department was characterized as organic when managers indicated that all of the following elements were present: two or less levels of management with decision-making authority allocated to the team; discretion to act beyond written standard operating procedures; a small set of fewer than 10 broad job descriptions; high frequency of meetings; job rotation; and team-based tasks. Structural type was treated as a categorical variable (0 = mechanistic; 1 = organic). Each piece of data used was confirmed through at least two managers.

Participants were given identical sets of 40 cards with statements reflecting information elements and were asked to identify and separate out the cards with statements they considered important to successfully accomplishing their own jobs, combine cards believed to be highly related into separate piles, and rank the piles in order of importance. Information gathering was measured as the total number of information elements selected by the individual.

Individuals ranked the relative importance of each information element. The extent to which each individual's interpretation of information overlapped with that of each of the other department members was assessed by calculating the mean Euclidean distance for each individual's rankings, where Si and Sj represent the distance of the ranking of the i-th member from the j-th member and n represents the total number of individuals in the department. This number was then subtracted from 1 to relate greater similarity with larger numbers.

Respondents were asked to put together in one pile all elements they believe are intrinsically linked together. Information synthesis was measured by the number of manufacturing information elements in a pile multiplied by the total number of elements in the pile (to capture linkages), summed for each pile.

A Likert scale from 1 to 7 was used for the items, with larger numbers reflecting higher agreement. The items reflect sense of responsibility for organizational performance, sense of confidence in one's ability to solve problems, and willingness to resolve problems. The Cronbach alpha for these items was 0.7, and a mean-based composite measure was employed for this construct.

BASIC (Behavior Analysis and Safety Improvement Category) score for Hour-of-Service Compliance, capturing the extent to which a carrier's drivers are operating their trucks when ill, fatigued, or noncompliant with legally mandated HOS rules. Each violation is weighted for severity on a 1-10 scale, summed within the category with a maximum of 30, multiplied by a recency weight (three for the last six months, two for six months to a year, one for one to two years), summed across all employee drivers and leased owner-operators, and normalized to control for carrier size and measurement exposure. Higher scores indicate worse safety performance; the authors multiplied the reported scores by 100 to improve estimation of variance components.
time_window: December 2010 to June 2014, semiannual measurement occasions

description: BASIC (Behavior Analysis and Safety Improvement Category) score for Unsafe Driving, capturing the extent to which a carrier's drivers are operating their trucks in a dangerous fashion. Each violation is weighted for severity on a 1-10 scale, summed within the category with a maximum of 30, multiplied by a recency weight (three for the last six months, two for six months to a year, one for one to two years), summed across all drivers and leased owner-operators, and normalized to control for carrier size and measurement exposure. Higher scores indicate worse safety performance; the authors multiplied the reported scores by 100 to improve estimation of variance components.
time_window: December 2010 to June 2014, semiannual measurement occasions

description: Measures the passage of time since the start of the CSA program, where a one-unit increase corresponds to a six-month passage of time. Scores were queried for each carrier on a semiannual basis dating back to the start of the CSA program in December 2010 to June 2014, for a total of eight measurements per carrier.

The natural logarithm of the total power units reported by a motor carrier in its most recent Motor Carrier Census, a biennial survey completed by all carriers operating in the United States. The authors treat this measure as nearly time-invariant and obtained it from the most recent MCS filed in 2012-2014, since the DOT does not have a set schedule for when carriers complete the MCS.

A carrier's safety performance at the start of the CSA program, given by the between-subjects random intercept of the growth model. Positive values indicate that a carrier had worse safety performance than average in December 2010.

The carrier-specific change in its BASIC score for a one-unit (six-month) increase in Occasion immediately after the start of the CSA program and before the estimated transition point, given by the random slope b1i in the Level-1 equation. Because higher BASIC scores indicate worse safety performance, a negative value of this slope indicates improvement.
time_window: from rollout to the estimated transition point

variable_name: b2i (random effect for Occasion minus the transition point)
description: The difference between a carrier's rate of change in its BASIC score after the estimated transition point and its rate of change before that point, given by the random effect b2i. Positive values indicate that a carrier had more pronounced tapering than average over the study's horizon.
time_window: from the estimated transition point to June 2014

description: Goal difficulty was experimentally manipulated between subjects. Teams in the difficult-goal condition were assigned a goal of 75 points for each session, and teams in the easy-goal condition a goal of 10 points per session; goals and scores were not cumulative but were discrete for each session. On the basis of pilot tests, the authors expected 90 percent of teams to achieve the easy goal (83 percent did) and 10 percent to achieve the difficult goal (32 percent did).
time_window: each of the two experimental sessions

description: Monetary incentives were manipulated within subjects: every team was offered a monetary incentive of $15 in one of the two experimental sessions, and receiving the incentive was contingent on the team's achieving its assigned goal for that session. The incentive order condition was nonsignificant and was dropped from the analysis.
time_window: one of the two experimental sessions

description: Prior to each session, members of the team discussed, came to agreement about, and indicated on a single questionnaire the team's level of confidence (0-100 percent) in its ability to achieve each of a series of scores ranging from 0 to 90; a sample question is "How confident are you that your team will be able to achieve a score of 90 (80, 70, 60, etc.) or more?" The efficacy score for each session was calculated as the sum of the percentage confidence ratings for the various performance levels.
scale: sum of 0-100 percent confidence ratings across performance levels

description: Drawing on prior knowledge of the task and on observations of pilot sessions, pillboxes were categorized as low risk, moderate risk, or high risk depending on the likelihood of teams' losing tanks in the process of destroying each target. From the planning maps completed by each team at the beginning of each session, the authors assigned one point for each low-risk pillbox targeted, two points for each moderate-risk pillbox targeted, and three points for each high-risk pillbox targeted, and computed strategic risk as the sum of the risk points for all of the team's targets for a given session. Teams also rated the riskiness of the strategies they had chosen, and objectively scored risk and team-perceived risk were correlated.
scale: sum of risk points (1-3 per targeted pillbox)

description: From previous research with the task, six key tactics important to success were identified. Each attack on a target was rated on these six dimensions on a scale ranging from 1 (the team did not use this tactic in this attack) to 7 (the team consistently used this tactic in this attack), and ratings were averaged for each session. Four researchers rated a random subsample of 61 attacks made by different teams to calculate the intraclass correlation coefficient.
scale: 1 (did not use) to 7 (consistently used) per tactic, averaged

description: Performance was measured using a scoring system derived from analyses of pillbox attacks and tank losses in a previous study and from the analysis of the pilot sessions. Teams received points for each pillbox destroyed and penalties for each tank lost, both scaled according to the difficulty level of the target: low-risk 15 points (-1), medium-risk 25 points (-2), and high-risk 45 points (-3). The penalties were intended to discourage kamikaze-type strategies, to reflect the inherent differences in the risk posed by the pillboxes, and to reflect an environment in which the relationship between risk and expected return was generally positive.
A dichotomous variable set to 1 if the physician graduated from a top-50 American medical school in the year of the physician's graduation from medical school, and 0 otherwise.

The number of quarters the physician practiced medicine after graduating from medical school, used as an indicator of the experience of the physician. The continuous measure is used in the main analysis, and a median level split is used when comparing it to other markers of expertise and when graphically depicting the analysis.

A dichotomous variable set to 1 if the physician is board certified in cardiology, the focal specialization impacted by the new information, and 0 otherwise. The cardiology specialization includes the subspecialties of thoracic surgery, interventional cardiology, pediatric cardiology, nuclear cardiology, cardiovascular disease management, and cardiovascular medicine; a dichotomous measure is used because more than 80% of certified physicians focus on one subspecialty.

The log of the number of stents the physician has performed to date, plus one, capturing task-specific experience gained through repeated performance of specific procedures. A dichotomous measure using a median split is also created and used when comparing this marker with other markers of expertise.

A dichotomous indicator set to 1 if the focal hospital has a higher than median value of any of the four forms of expertise. It is built by aggregating the dichotomous individual-level expertise markers across all physicians within an organization to obtain the proportion of physicians that possess these markers; organizations above the median proportion of expert physicians (18.095%) are coded as having high organizational expertise.

The organizational expertise coding replicated using only physicians possessing markers of deliberate practice, so that hospitals above the median proportion of such physicians (9.78%) are coded as having high organizational deliberate practice expertise.

The dichotomous observed treatment choice for a SCAD patient, coded as 1 if the patient receives a stent and 0 if not; a patient-level indicator is used rather than a physician-level count to avoid aggregation biases and to control for otherwise unobserved patient heterogeneity.
