Change over time is quantified with two linear splines, Period 1 and Period 2, which capture the relationship between stenting and time before and after guideline release; the knot is placed before the first quarter of 2006 to account for the change in behavior expected after the release of the new guideline.

variable_name: Four markers of physician expertise (elite education, tenure, board certification, procedure volume)
description: Expertise was measured through four physician markers: elite education (graduation from a top medical school), tenure (quarters of practice since graduation), cardiology board certification, and procedure volume (log of stents performed to date plus one). Each marker was entered as a predictor of adoption, and hospital-level organizational expertise aggregated these markers.

Indicator variable with a value of one if both the submitter and evaluator of an idea belonged to the same division of the firm (of three) and worked at the same site (of 318), and zero otherwise. The firm organizes itself primarily by broad product divisions and then by geography, so the division-site is treated as the relevant subunit.

Dichotomous variable with a value of one indicating that the initial evaluator decided that the idea merited further consideration, and a value of zero denoting that the evaluator rejected the idea. Evaluators, logging in to the system, saw the ideas assigned to them that had yet to receive an evaluation and either deemed an idea unworthy of further consideration or passed it on to a business unit manager or technical expert for a secondary evaluation. Roughly half (42.3%) of the proposals received favorable evaluations at this first stage.

The logged time, in years (with precision at the level of the number of days), for which the evaluator worked in the division prior to assessing the idea, plus one to avoid logging zeroes. Because Human Resources did not maintain longitudinal data on employees' geographic locations, tenure is measured in the evaluator's current division rather than in his or her division-site or division-country.
time_window: time in the division prior to assessing the idea

description: The logged number of different individuals who submitted an idea and who worked within the same division and site as the evaluator, plus one to avoid logging zeroes. Because the company does not maintain centralized records on the number of coworkers employed at each site in every country, the measure is built from the idea database; an alternative measure based on the subunit memberships of evaluators produced qualitatively and statistically equivalent results.

For each site, the proportion of all submitted ideas classified as R&D related that came from the same site as the submitter; for example, if employees of a subunit forwarded four ideas and the company classified two of them as R&D related, the status measure equals 0.5. The strength of a local subunit's research and development operations serves as a proxy for its standing within the firm.

Each claim of each patent is manually coded as a process claim or a product claim, and for each patent a ratio of the number of product claims over total claims is computed, ranging from 0 (pure process) to 1 (pure product). Process-Product is the mean of this ratio across all patents filed by the firm in a year, and is then transformed as 1 - |0.5 - Process-Product| to give Process-Product Mix, so that higher values indicate a portfolio closer to an even mix of process and product components. Claims coded 'Both' or 'Not sure' were dropped. The variable enters the regressions with a two-year lag.

variable_name: SD of Process-Product (treatment versus control group)
description: The standard deviation of the firm-year level Process-Product, indicating how dispersed the individual patents' product-claim ratio is around the firm-year mean. The sample is split at the median: observations with low SD, where process and product components are more integrated within patents, form the treatment group, and observations with high SD, where the components reside more separately across patents, form the control group. The effect of Process-Product Mix is then compared across the two groups, with the difference isolating the effect of within-patent integration.

The firm's net profits over total revenue, used as the first dependent variable to capture the firm's financial performance; scaling by total revenue also helps account for the influence of firm size. Independent variables enter with a two-year lag.

The natural log of the firm's R&D expenses (scaled in millions) divided by the number of patents the firm files for in the year, used as the dependent variable to capture the cost of innovation per unit of innovation. Higher values therefore represent lower innovative productivity. The independent variables enter with a two-year lag.

The firm's property, plant and equipment, used as a proxy for its production capacity. In the contingency tests each observation is classified as low or high on production capacity relative to its median. The variable is measured with a two-year lag.

The number of countries in which the firm has operations, used as a proxy for its access to markets. In the contingency tests each observation is classified as low or high on access to markets relative to its median. The variable is measured with a two-year lag.

Political risk is measured as 1 - POLCON, so that higher values indicate higher political risk; the same measure is used in both the first and the second stage of the model. POLCON captures the degree of constraints on policy change using data on the number of independent veto points in the political system and the distribution of political preferences both across and within these branches. The independent variables are standardized to facilitate interpretation.

The dependent variable reflects whether a bank has been selected as a lead firm (1) or not (0) for a specific project. The risk set comprises all banks that acted as lead firms in at least one of the syndicates in the sample in the year in which the project was financed, because participation in other projects indicated that banks had the financial and organizational resources to assume lead roles in new projects.
time_window: year in which the project was financed

description: A bank's country knowledge is measured as the count of its projects in the project's host country prior to the year when the project was syndicated. The variable is time-varying and is standardized in the estimation.
time_window: prior to the year of the project's syndication

description: Political influence is measured as bilateral trade between the bank's home country and the project's host country as a share of the host country's total trade: the ratio of the sum of imports and exports from bank i's home country to the project country over the project country's total imports and exports, for the year before the project's syndication. For banks headquartered in the host country, this value is replaced with the mean political influence of all foreign banks. The authors state that the variable is time-varying and is standardized in the estimation.

The dependent variable is a dummy indicating whether a syndicate is realized (1) or is a simulated counterfactual (0). Counterfactual unrealized syndicates were generated for each project by replacing one, two, or three banks, deleting one, two, or three banks, adding one bank, and creating new syndicates of the same size, larger by one bank, and smaller by one bank, with the lead firm remaining the same in the realized and counterfactual syndicates.

Syndicate country knowledge is measured as the sum of bank-level country knowledge, using the same bank-level measure as in the first stage. Knowledge is computed for syndicates excluding the lead firm, and the independent variables are standardized to facilitate interpretation.
time_window: prior to the year of the project's syndication

description: Syndicate political influence is measured as the sum of bank-level political influence, using the same bank-level measure as in the first stage. It is computed for syndicates excluding the lead firm, and the independent variables are standardized to facilitate interpretation.

Diversity is operationalized on four bank-level partner characteristics that create coordination costs: size, measured as a bank's total assets reported in Bankscope; ownership type, using Bankscope's classification into bank-owned, state-owned (including governments, export credit agencies, and development banks), and other ownership types; political risk in the bank's home country, measured as 1 - POLCON; and experience, measured as the total number of projects in which a bank has participated in the past. The authors aggregate these dimensions by calculating the sum of each syndicate member's deviation from the syndicate mean for each dimension, normalizing the underlying size, experience, and home-country political risk variables to range from 0 to 1 and weighting the ownership dummies by 1/sqrt(2); the score is scaled with the number of banks in the syndicate to account for different syndicate sizes.
time_window: at the time of the syndicate's formation

description: Repeat Clients is computed as Transactions minus New Clients, where Transactions is the number of client visits per quarter and New Clients the number of new clients per quarter; Repeat Client Proportion is Repeat Clients divided by Transactions. The authors calculated it from the income-statement information reported by the practices. In the estimated models the proportion shifts the revenue and cost elasticities with respect to transactions.

Total fees for services per quarter divided by transactions. Because both sides are divided by transactions, the estimated relationship is an average revenue curve. The authors take natural logs and estimate ln(Revenue/Transactions) on ln(Transactions), Repeat Client Proportion interacted with ln(Transactions), and the other interaction terms.

Total expense for professional services per quarter divided by transactions. As with revenue, dividing both sides by transactions gives an average cost curve, estimated in natural-log form with ln(Transactions), Repeat Client Proportion interacted with ln(Transactions), and the other interaction terms.

The ratio of total fees for services to total expense for professional services per quarter, obtained by dividing the Revenue/Transaction model by the Expense/Transaction model (Model 3). It is estimated in natural-log form and is the paper's indicator of practice performance and profitability. Its coefficients are differences between the revenue and expense coefficients.

Expenses from outside lab fees and in-house lab supplies divided by transactions, used as an indicator of the degree to which a practice pursues a preventive medicine or early disease detection approach. It enters the models both directly and interacted with Repeat Client Proportion, controlling for its effect on profitability independent of repeat clients.
A dummy variable equal to 1 if the practice includes a facility for boarding animals and 0 otherwise. It enters the models directly and interacted with Repeat Client Proportion.

Transactions per quarter, or client visits, used as the measure of practice scale. It appears in log form in all models, and its coefficient is interpreted as the elasticity of revenue per transaction or expense per transaction with respect to transactions.

A dummy variable that is 1 if the practice is in the Far West region and 0 if it is in any other region, which includes Northwest, Western, Middle West, Northeast, or Southeast. The authors use it to contrast practices facing intense competition from the new chain entrants, who established a presence in the three states comprising the Far West (California, Nevada, and Arizona) before other regions.

Configurational classifications were produced by K-means cluster analysis of the 12 strategy and structure variables, following a series of hierarchical clustering analyses based on subsegments of the data set; five clusters seemed the most common and relevant number. The classifications are labeled Groups 1 through 5, with 272, 199, 233, 241, and 160 organizational members, respectively. Group 1 follows a strategy based on the quality function and represents the preferred configuration type, Group 2 is driven more by efficiency, and Groups 3, 4, and 5 represent a blend of functional orientation and design variation between the extremes.

A mean score for each of the 12 independent variables is taken for the higher-performing configuration group (Group 1) and used to test the summated distance from this mean for each individual organization. The total distance (absolute value difference) represents the extent to which an individual organization deviates from the more ideal type across all independent variables.

Return on sales is one of the four performance variables used in the study. The authors state that ROS, ROE, ROA, and average profitability are each measured using net revenue of the organization prior to disbursement to providers as the denominator, because physician organizations often disperse profits to their owners or partners.

Return on equity is one of the four performance variables used in the study. The authors state that ROS, ROE, ROA, and average profitability are each measured using net revenue of the organization prior to disbursement to providers as the denominator, because physician organizations often disperse profits to their owners or partners.

Return on assets is one of the four performance variables used in the study. The authors state that ROS, ROE, ROA, and average profitability are each measured using net revenue of the organization prior to disbursement to providers as the denominator, because physician organizations often disperse profits to their owners or partners.

Average profitability is one of the four performance variables used in the study. The authors state that ROS, ROE, ROA, and average profitability are each measured using net revenue of the organization prior to disbursement to providers as the denominator, because physician organizations often disperse profits to their owners or partners.

One of the six strategy variables used to derive the organizational configurations, labeled first by the Ketchen et al. (1993) categorization (pricing) and second by operationalization (advertising intensity). It highlights the quality versus efficiency functional demands.

One of the six strategy variables used to derive the organizational configurations, labeled first by the Ketchen et al. (1993) categorization (research and development) and second by operationalization (continuing medical education intensity). It highlights the quality versus efficiency functional demands.

One of the six strategy variables used to derive the organizational configurations, labeled first by the Ketchen et al. (1993) categorization (production and operations capacity) and second by operationalization (procedural efficiency). It highlights the quality versus efficiency functional demands.

One of the six strategy variables used to derive the organizational configurations, labeled first by the Ketchen et al. (1993) categorization (scope of activities) and second by operationalization (practice type). It highlights the quality versus efficiency functional demands.

One of the six strategy variables used to derive the organizational configurations, labeled first by the Ketchen et al. (1993) categorization (distribution) and second by operationalization (fee-for-service ratio). It highlights the quality versus efficiency functional demands.

One of the six strategy variables used to derive the organizational configurations, labeled first by the Ketchen et al. (1993) categorization (production and operations capabilities) and second by operationalization (nonmedical revenue ratio). It highlights the quality versus efficiency functional demands.

Organization size is one of the three expansiveness variables used as a structural design component in deriving the organizational configurations, measured as the number of full-time equivalent (FTE) physicians.
Physical size is one of the three expansiveness variables used as a structural design component in deriving the organizational configurations, measured as the square footage of all buildings.

Geographic dispersion is one of the three expansiveness variables used as a structural design component in deriving the organizational configurations, measured as the total number of separately operating clinics.
One of the three alliance or relational structure components used as a structural design variable in deriving the organizational configurations.

variable_name: Horizontal relationships with other medical practices
description: One of the three alliance or relational structure components used as a structural design variable in deriving the organizational configurations, capturing horizontal relationships with other medical practices.
One of the three alliance or relational structure components used as a structural design variable in deriving the organizational configurations, capturing vertical relationships with hospitals.

A composite score that measures how well each firm's TMT is structured across all five team structure dimensions described above. Firms are decile-ranked on each of the five dimensions using prior literature's expectations (team age, tenure, diversity and ownership positively related to firm performance; team size negatively related), and the average of each firm's decile ranks is a single value that is expected to have a positive relation with firms' operating performance.
time_window: at the firm's initial public offering

description: The average of the firm's quarterly return on assets (net income scaled by the book value of assets) over the twelve fiscal quarters that immediately follow the firm's IPO. For firms that delist before their three-year anniversary, all of the firm's quarterly observations prior to delisting are included.
level: firm (quarterly observations averaged to the firm)
time_window: twelve fiscal quarters (three years) after the IPO

description: Indicator variable that takes the value of one if the firm has a founder-CEO at the time of the IPO, zero otherwise. Founder status is identified from the Management section of each firm's final registration statement: first by searching the statement for the words 'founder', 'founded' and 'founding', then by reading the biographical information for a substitute phrase, and finally, if needed, by checking whether the individual's tenure begins at or prior to the firm's founding year and by searching the firm's name together with the word 'founder'.
time_window: at the firm's initial public offering

description: Indicator variable that takes the value of one if the founder-CEO fails to meet the 5% equity ownership threshold at the time of IPO (i.e., does not hold at least 5% of the firm's equity), zero otherwise. The 5% threshold follows SEC rules that require firms to identify stockholders above it, so ownership below this threshold is not observable.
time_window: at the firm's initial public offering

description: Started from each firm's rating on the Fortune World's Most Admired Companies list (1 to 10 scale, 10 being more favorable). All rated firms were rank-ordered on their ratings such that the highest-rated firm received the largest ranking, and all unranked firms were assigned a zero; the ranking was then logged after adding one. The measure was residualized by running OLS regressions predicting a firm's ranking as a function of logged total assets, logged total revenues, ROA, financial loss, and leverage and taking the residuals, i.e., the component of the Fortune ranking not due to size or profitability. The measure is lagged by one year.

Natural log of the annual audit fees an organization pays its auditor, taken from Audit Analytics. The measure represents the client's total spend rather than hourly rates, so it captures senior staff allocation, hours billed, and any risk premium.

Logged count of news articles in which the client's name appeared at least once in the previous year, tracked with the Factiva news database across a set of especially prominent publications (New York Times, Washington Post, Wall Street Journal, Chicago Tribune, USA Today, and Los Angeles Times).
Count of adverse (income-reducing) restatements caused by a misapplication of GAAP in each two-digit primary SIC code, logged because of skewness; it ranges from zero to almost six.

Binary variable coded as one if the client firm belonged to any of the following primary two-digit SIC codes: alcohol (12), gambling (16), tobacco (20), firearms (21), military (26), or nuclear power (28). These industries are flagged as 'controversial' by MSCI.

Measured at the MSA level as the fees collected by the auditor over the fees collected by all auditors in the focal metropolitan statistical area; results are depicted for each quartile in the market share distribution.

variable_name: Reacting stakeholder prior beliefs (90-day moving average)
description: A daily stakeholder-level measure of beliefs about the target organization constructed as a moving average of all the stakeholder's past actions, weighing more heavily actions that were more frequently reported and more recently reported. Each action is coded on a 20-point conflict-cooperation scale, and the measure combines the level of conflict or cooperation, the number of media-reported events, a moving-average window, and a discount factor; the exact equation is not recoverable from the text provided. A 90-day window and a discount factor of .999 are used, and the measure is lagged by one day so as to capture the value of beliefs just before the critical event.
scale: moving average of conflict-cooperation scores; authors report values from -5.86 to +6.23 with 0 as the neutral point
time_window: 90-day moving average, lagged one day (day before the critical event)

description: The change in a stakeholder's belief about the target firm from the day before the critical event to the day of the reaction, i.e., the difference between the stakeholder's prior belief and the stakeholder's posterior belief. It is measured using only the source-verb-target triplets in which a stakeholder targets the firm, that is, the stakeholder is the subject and the firm is the object of the triplet. Reactions range from very negative to very positive.
time_window: from the day before the critical event to the day of the reaction

variable_name: Prior reactions of peer stakeholders (same type) since critical event
description: The average of all prior reactions of peer stakeholders starting on the day after the critical event and ending on the day before the focal stakeholder's reaction. Two additional variants average these reactions weighted by the peer stakeholders' media visibility and by their status. The reactions of the critical stakeholder are omitted from the construction of these variables.
time_window: from the day after the critical event to the day before the focal stakeholder's reaction

variable_name: Aggregate stakeholder prior beliefs (day before critical event)
description: A firm-level aggregate of the stakeholders' prior beliefs about the target firm, measured on the day before the critical event, which investors use to infer the distribution of stakeholders' beliefs and hence the firm's history of stakeholder relations. It is entered as a predictor of abnormal returns in the days after the critical event.
scale: aggregate of the stakeholder belief measure

variable_name: Aggregate stakeholder reactions to critical event
description: A firm-level aggregate of the stakeholders' reactions (changes in their beliefs) to the critical event, entered as a predictor of abnormal returns in the days after the event. It is also used in versions weighted by the status and by the visibility of the reacting stakeholders.
scale: aggregate of the stakeholder reaction measure (unweighted or weighted)

variable_name: Reacting stakeholder visibility (count of all media mentions)
description: A stakeholder-level measure constructed as a daily count of the stakeholder's previous mentions in the media in articles referencing the mining company and its mine. The measure is standardized to account for variation in the frequency of reporting across mines. It is used as an instrument in the selection equation and to weight peer stakeholders' reactions.

Status is inferred from each stakeholder's position in the stakeholder network constructed from the source-verb-target triplets. It is measured as the Bonacich eigenvector centrality, which captures a stakeholder's status as a function of the status of the other stakeholders to whom that stakeholder is connected through prior events. It is used to weight peer stakeholders' reactions.

The authors first calculated day-to-day changes in stakeholders' prior beliefs about the target organization. Three thresholds, -1.5, -1, and -0.5 times the standard deviation of all changes in stakeholders' beliefs recorded in their panel, capture major, moderate, and minor critical events; the main analyses examine major critical events only. Each critical event was confirmed to have at least 100 days of prior data available, and events occurring within 10 days of an earlier critical event were treated as reactions to the first event.
time_window: day of the event; at least 100 days of prior data required

description: Abnormal returns are calculated using an event study methodology, which assumes that in rational markets investors respond immediately to new information. Normal returns are estimated with a market model using daily stock price data and the daily S&P/TSX 500 market index; the estimation window spans 100 days and ends 10 days before the event to avoid news leakages or anticipation. Abnormal market returns are the difference between the predicted and the observed stock prices for a given firm on a given day, computed for up to 50 days following the event.
time_window: 100-day estimation window ending 10 days before the event; up to 50 days after the event

description: For every directed organizational pair (a focal organization and an assessed organization) the authors compared the focal organization's perception of the ties maintained by the assessed organization with the confirmed ties of that organization in the objective network, coding the four possible combinations of perceived versus actual ties. The measure is the proportion of the actual and absent ties of the assessed organization (from the objective matrix) that the focal organization correctly classified minus the proportion of incorrectly classified ties. The resulting measure ranges between -1 and 1; the formal expression is not readable in the text and was removed from the payload.

The total number of confirmed knowledge exchange relations the focal organization has in the objective network. The measure was calculated for all organizations in the networks and used to create the degree of the focal organization variable.

The total number of confirmed knowledge exchange relations the assessed organization has in the objective network. The measure was calculated for all organizations in the networks and used to create the degree of the assessed organization variable.

Established by whether the focal and the assessed organization were active in the same subfield of the healthcare industry, based on the description of the organizations on their websites. Where a website indicated multiple subfields, the organization was categorized on the primary subfield listed; when both organizations were in the same subfield the variable was coded 1, and all other cases were coded 0.

variable_name: outsourcing rate of upstream activities (rate of patent filing outsourcing)
description: At the patent level, the data allow the authors to distinguish whether the patent was filed by in-house attorneys or whether the applicant was represented by an external patent professional. If European applicants represent themselves before the EPO the 'representative' field remains empty and the case is coded as internally processed; where the database contains a representative's identity, further checks are carried out because an in-house IP department may be listed as the representative. Ambiguous cases are identified by comparing the information in the 'applicant name' and 'representative name' fields, and the classification is cross-checked by searching for strings typically associated with internal patent departments or external law firms. The patent-level observations are finally aggregated to the firm-year level, and the average share of outsourced patent applications is included in the regressions.

The technological similarity of internally and externally processed patent applications is measured by comparing how similarly they are distributed across 30 different technology areas. Two distribution vectors are defined, the elements of which are the shares of patents a firm files in each of the 30 technology classes: one vector contains the internally processed patents and the other the externally filed patents. Proximity is given by the coefficient of uncentered correlation, Upstream Similarity = fifo' / ((fifi')(fofo'))^(1/2); if the distribution of internal and external applications coincides, similarity takes a value of 1, and if there is no overlap in technology areas the value is 0. When firms sourced zero products internally or externally the value of upstream similarity is set to 0, and the measure is susceptible to concentration effects of a firm's patenting across technology areas, for which upstream focus is controlled.

variable_name: downstream performance numerator (firm-year number of oppositions)
description: Within the IP value chain, downstream performance is reflected in the firm's ability to detect targets for proactive litigation, and the ratio of the number of oppositions filed in year t to the number of applications of the focal firm filed in the same year proxies for it. For methodological reasons the actual dependent variable is the firm-year downstream performance numerator, a count variable (firm-year number of patent oppositions), while the logarithm of the firm-year number of patent applications enters as an independent variable in the regressions.

Five-item scale reflecting the overall skill, expertise, and knowledge levels of an organization's employees, based on the original human capital discussions and on contemporary strategic human resource management studies. Informants rated their agreement on a seven-point Likert format. The items were pilot-tested with executive MBA students before being refined.

Five-item scale assessing an organization's overall ability to share and leverage knowledge among and between networks of employees, customers, suppliers, and alliance partners, drawing on the social structure literature and the knowledge management literature. Informants rated their agreement on a seven-point Likert format.

Four-item scale assessing an organization's ability to appropriate and store knowledge in physical organization-level repositories such as databases, manuals, and patents as well as in structures, processes, cultures, and ways of doing business. Informants rated their agreement on a seven-point Likert format.

Three-item scale assessing an organization's capability to reinforce and extend its current expertise and product/service lines, based on discussions provided by Tushman and Anderson (1986) and Henderson and Clark (1990). Respondents rated their organization's capability to generate these types of innovations in the products/services introduced in the last five years.
scale: 1 = weaker than competition; 4 = similar to competition; 7 = stronger than competition
time_window: the last five years, assessed approximately three years after the intellectual capital survey

description: Three-item scale assessing an organization's capability to make current product/service lines obsolete, based on discussions provided by Tushman and Anderson (1986) and Henderson and Clark (1990). Respondents rated their organization's capability to generate these types of innovations in the products/services introduced in the last five years.
scale: 1 = weaker than competition; 4 = similar to competition; 7 = stronger than competition
time_window: the last five years, assessed approximately three years after the intellectual capital survey

description: Using worldwide market research data from Dataquest and ICE as well as the advice of industry executives, the authors first identified six broad markets and segments within them. They then assigned firms to market segments on the basis of their products, and measured the number of competitors in each market segment using worldwide industry data from Dataquest, ICE and, in a very few cases, confidential market research reports from firms in the study. The data were updated annually.

Market stage is a configurational rather than continuous variable; each market segment was categorized as emergent, growth, or mature for each year in the study. Emergent-stage markets were defined as (1) new (less than 7 years old) and (2) small (less than $100 million in sales, adjusted to 1988 dollars). Growth-stage markets were large (more than $100 million in sales, adjusted to 1988 dollars), had high growth (growth rate greater than 20% a year), and followed emergent markets. Mature-stage markets were large, had low growth (less than 20% a year), and followed growth markets. Market stage was updated annually.

Feature size is a physical measurement of the miniaturization of the line widths in the circuit designs used by semiconductor firms; smaller feature sizes mean more innovative technology because packing more circuits into a smaller area is the fundamental technical challenge within the industry. This information was provided by the CEO, chief technical officer, or other key respondent during the structured interviews. Strategy was measured at founding because of the persistence of founding strategy.

Three questions answered by the CEOs or other key respondents during the structured interviews captured innovation through extensions to existing knowledge, innovation that occurs when technologies are combined, and the overall degree of technical innovation. Respondents used a 0 to 10 scale. A three-item index was developed by reverse coding the first question and then computing the mean response to the three questions; the Cronbach alpha is 0.75. Strategy was measured at founding.

Top managers were designated as those people identified as members of top management in the structured interviews, typically the CEO and the people who reported directly to the CEO, all of whom worked full time for the firm in executive positions. Team size was measured as the number of individuals who were designated by the company respondent in the structured interview as members of top management. This measure was updated monthly.

This measure was computed as the number of semiconductor industry firms for which members of the top management team had previously worked. The data on previous employers were obtained from the structured interviews. The measure was updated monthly.

The highest previous job title of each top management team member was recorded, and job titles were coded by hierarchical level, ranging from 7, president or chief executive officer of a firm, to 0, nonmanagerial. The measure is the mean of these codes across the members of the top management team. These data are updated monthly.

variable_name: Rate of product development alliance formation
description: Product development alliances were identified by asking CEOs or key respondents in the structured interviews whether the firm had any formalized alliancing agreements with other companies, and then confirming that the alliance was a product development one, that work was actually done together by the two partners, when the alliance was formed, and the name of the partner. The formation date was defined as the date (month, year) on which both parties agreed to the alliance; almost all alliances involved a formal agreement and an associated press release, so a specific date was available and clear. Firms were tracked from birth until the end of observations in 1988 or, for the few firms that failed, until their deaths.
time_window: from firm birth to 1988 or firm failure; monthly spells

description: Eleven asset strategies (commercial loans, real estate loans, loans to individuals, agriculture loans, other loans and leases, cash, overnight money, securities, trading accounts, fixed assets, other assets) were each measured as a proportion of total assets. In a given year, each asset strategy for each bank was compared to the industry mean for that strategy and expressed as a standard deviation; the absolute values of the standard deviations of all 11 strategy variables were totaled for each bank. The measure includes all numbers greater than or equal to zero and equals zero if and only if all firms have the same strategy. A squared term of strategic deviation is used in the curvilinear model; the algebraic equation in the text is not readable, so the calculation is taken from the prose description.
scale: greater than or equal to zero

description: The performance measure was based on return on average assets (ROA), the ratio of net income to average assets; average assets was used in the denominator, consistent with bank regulatory practice, because banks undertake 'window dressing' of their balance sheets at year-end and assets change over time. Relative ROA is the difference between the bank's ROA and the average ROA of all Twin Cities' banks in a given year, so it indicates how well a bank is doing relative to its competitors. To simplify presentation of the results, relative ROA and its lagged value were multiplied by 100 prior to estimation.
time_window: given year, with the one-year lagged value included as a control

description: Weighted sum of the scores of five stakeholder groups (employees, customers, suppliers, community, and environment), using the corresponding Sustainalytics weights averaged by sector and country. The database translates information from 199 items into a rating grouped into sections, weighting each item by the sector-specific potential negative impact on each stakeholder; the final score is the sum of the scores of the items averaged by their corresponding weight. The index can take any value between zero and 100.

Proxied by dividing the sum of firm equity value, book value of long-term debt, and net current liabilities by the book value of inventories and property, plant and equipment, following Dowell, Hart, and Yeung (2000).

variable_name: R&D expenses to total number of employees
description: Ratio of R&D expenses to a firm's total number of employees. The authors state this ratio is less sensitive to spurious effects of business cycles, accounting manipulations, and asset sales than R&D spending as a proportion of sales, and is positively related to patents and product innovations.

Composite of seven Sustainalytics items that approximate human resource practices contributing to the accumulation of human capital: the measurement of job satisfaction, training programs, profit-sharing programs and employee participation, and the introduction of indicators to seek information about employees. Each item is rated on a five-point Likert scale (0 = non-existent; 1 = below the median; 2 = median level; 3 = above the median; 4 = maximum). Cronbach's alpha for the composite measure is 0.7118.

Reputation is measured with Fortune magazine's 'World's Most Admired Companies' survey, based on responses from executives, directors, and financial analysts, scoring eight attributes on 11-point scales from poor to excellent. Because of the possible halo effect of past financial performance, reputation was regressed on increasingly higher-order lags of CFP until no further significant improvement in R2 was observed; no significant increases in R2 were found beyond two lags. The residual, the difference between reputation and the value predicted from CFP with up to two lags, is the measure of reputation.
scale: eight attributes ranked on 11-point scales from poor to excellent

description: Culture is measured with eight Sustainalytics Platform items covering four dimensions: involvement, consistency, adaptability, and mission. Each item is rated on a five-point scale (0 = nonexistent; 1 = below the median in detail and/or development; 2 = median level; 3 = above the median in detail and/or development; 4 = maximum). Cronbach's alpha for culture is 0.866.

Growth sectors are defined as those two-digit SIC code sectors in which the growth in sales is larger than the yearly mean for all sectors in the corresponding country; the sector split is used to compare growth and nongrowth sectors in the mediation models.

Feature size measures the width of the conducting channels in a semiconductor chip, expressed in microns, and is the most commonly used technological indicator in the industry. Because tacitness varies more than proportionately with feature size and increases as feature size decreases, the authors take the inverse of the feature size of a plant's output so that increases in the measure can be interpreted as increases in tacitness. They label the resulting measure the Feature Size Index. The feature size information is reported in International Fabs on Disk.

Dependent variable coded as 1 for foreign direct investment and 0 for domestic direct investment. The authors apply the standard 10% equity cutoff: domestic investments are instances where a firm held a share of at least 10% in a plant in its home country, and foreign investments those where a firm held a share of at least 10% in a plant in another country. Out of the 386 observations in the sample, 102 are foreign direct investments and 284 are domestic direct investments.
scale: binary (1 = foreign direct investment, 0 = domestic investment)

description: Count of the number of plants previously built by the parent company in its home country using the same generation of technology as the focal investment. It is one of two experience variables computed because domestic and foreign experience may influence foreign expansion differently.

Count of the number of previous investments made by the parent firm abroad using the same generation of technology as the focal investment. It is the second of the two experience variables computed because domestic and foreign experience may influence foreign expansion differently.

Number of years that have elapsed since the parent firm first built a plant using the same generation of technology. For the first plant of a given generation, a value of 0 is assigned. This specification is the same as in Teece (1977) and Galbraith (1990).
time_window: years since first plant of the same technology generation

variable_name: supermajority and classified board antitakeover amendment adoption
description: Indicator of firms proposing corporate charter antitakeover amendments, restricted to supermajority and classified board (staggered board) provisions. The sample comprises 409 firms adopting such amendments for the 1974-88 period; 100 firms were dropped from the initial sample because their stockholders meetings contained matters other than antitakeover charter amendments and another 31 were dropped because of data problems such as insufficient data in the prediction period. The proxy statement mailing date is utilized as the best available estimate of the date of the first public announcement of antitakeover amendment consideration.

Daily abnormal returns are computed from the market model, whose parameters are estimated by ordinary least squares over a period of 110 days (-160 to -51) preceding the event date. Portfolios are formed in event time such that each daily abnormal return is an equally weighted average of individual securities' abnormal returns for that common event date, and cumulative average abnormal returns are the sum of these average residuals over the event window. The event window runs from 50 days before (-50) to 10 days following (+10) the proxy mailing date.
level: firm and portfolio of firms (event time)
time_window: event window -50 to +10; estimation period -160 to -51

description: A five-item survey scale reflecting the primary elements of board decision control described by Fama and Jensen. Items ask the extent to which the board exerted control over strategic decision making by management, requested information from the CEO or another inside director to evaluate progress in implementing strategy, called for revisions to a strategic proposal, constructively criticized a strategic proposal, and sought information to evaluate top management performance. Responses come from outside directors; items loaded on a single factor and interitem reliability was high (alpha = .90), with an average weighted kappa of .83 across raters.

Multiple survey items assessing how strongly each CEO socially identifies with the corporate elite: one set adapted from Mael and Ashforth's group identification scale (e.g., feeling a personal insult when another corporate leader is criticized, saying 'we' rather than 'they'), plus two items adapted from Bergami and Bagozzi's measure, one of which asks respondents to indicate the degree of overlap between their self-definition and the corporate elite using a pictorial display. Confirmatory factor analysis showed the nine items loaded on the same factor as expected; the scale alpha was .85 and factor scores were estimated with the Bartlett method.
scale: five-point agree/disagree scale and pictorial overlap scale

description: A multi-item scale answered by potential help recipients covering the kinds of help in the theoretical argument: provision of advice and counsel on strategic issues, personal referrals to third-party sources of strategic advice not known to the recipient, and information about potential candidates for executive-level management positions and outside directorships. Using the count items, the authors calculated the total number of strategic help-giving episodes between the focal CEO and each potential help recipient in the 12 months prior to the survey; the items loaded on one factor (alpha = .90) and weighted kappas exceeded .75 for all items but one (.71).
time_window: 12 months after CEO identification was measured

variable_name: strategic help solicited but not received
description: Using responses to the help-giving scale items from the survey of potential help givers, the authors counted the number of instances in which a focal CEO solicited help from another CEO in the sample but did not receive it. The items loaded on a single factor with high reliability (alpha = .92), and agreement between potential help givers and focal CEOs was high (weighted kappas exceeded .75 for all items). The measure indicates a focal CEO's difficulty in obtaining strategic help from other CEOs during the prior year.
time_window: the year prior to measurement of CEO identification

description: Respondents listed their personal friends and acquaintances among corporate leaders in the sample frame; the measure was strongly correlated with two other survey items gauging the closeness of personal relationships, and agreement between focal CEOs and potential help recipients about the status of their relationship was 93 percent. For each dyad the authors created a dichotomous variable coded 1 if a focal CEO rated a potential help recipient as a friend; the tables report this variable as 'lack of friendship tie'.

Age similarity was measured as the absolute difference in age between the two CEOs divided by the younger CEO's age; the variable was centered in creating interaction terms to reduce the likelihood of multicollinearity. Higher values indicate greater age dissimilarity.

To measure educational background similarity the authors created a dichotomous variable coded 1 if both individuals held a degree from an Ivy League school (or if both did not have such a degree) and 0 otherwise; the variable is therefore coded 1 for similar educational backgrounds and 0 for dissimilar ones. Separate analyses using alternative criteria for the prestige of educational institutions left the hypothesized results unchanged.

Functional background was categorized into throughput functions (operations, engineering, or research and development), output functions (marketing or sales), and peripheral functions (e.g., law and finance); a dichotomous variable was created coded 1 if both CEOs in a dyad had the same functional background and 0 otherwise, so the variable is coded 1 for similar functional backgrounds.

variable_name: compact, significant changes in R&D expenditure
description: Measured over the 10-year study period as the maximum of the absolute values for all residuals for the firm from a Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedastic (GARCH) time trend of R&D spending. The calculation is performed in a three-step process: first a GARCH model, including a first-order autoregressive term, estimates the R&D expenditure trend; second the residuals around this trend line are studentized by dividing them by the standard deviation of all residuals from the firm-level time series forecast; third the maximum residual is taken when testing Hypotheses 1 and 2 and the maximum absolute residual when testing Hypotheses 3 through 5. Indicator versions of the variable are set to the calculated value in the year the shift occurs and the two years following and to zero in all other years; for Hypotheses 4 and 5 the variable is set to zero in years prior to the most significant shift and to the calculated value in the year of the shift and all years following.

variable_name: technological scope of firm knowledge creation
description: Estimated using a two-step process. First, the amount of knowledge the firm has created in each technological subclass is estimated using the same methodology as firm knowledge creation. Second, the dispersion of this firm-level knowledge creation across technological subclasses is measured using an entropy index (Theil, 1967), computed from PKn, the percentage of firm knowledge granted in USPTO technological subclass n. The formula for the entropy index is not readable in the extracted text.

Citations per patent are estimated by dividing a patent's citation count by the average number of citations per patent in the same industry and the same year; the distribution is right skewed, and an arbitrary cutoff of the 10th percentile is used to distinguish 'highly cited' patents from the rest of the sample. The authors use the natural log of the odds (logit) of the firm creating a patent in the top 10 percent of most cited patents. The indicator dependent variable is set to 1 if the firm generates a highly cited patent in the year that the firm's largest increase in R&D spending occurs, or the two years following, and to 0 otherwise.
time_window: year of the largest R&D increase and the two following years

description: Measured by the number of patents granted to a firm and the number of citations a firm's patents have received from subsequent patents. Because patent grant rates and citation activity differ over time and among industries, the authors adopt Hall et al.'s (2001) 'fixed-effects' approach: each patent's citation count is divided by the average number of citations received for all patents granted in the same industry, during the same year. The equation used to compute firm knowledge creation is not readable in the extracted text; the text states only that f = firm, i = industry, and t = year.

The Lexis-Nexis Academic database was searched for each firm in the sample that reported financial results in Compustat; PR Newswire and Business Wire press releases were searched for new product press releases. A simple count of new product press releases was made for each firm from all press releases issued from 2002 to 2006; if more than one press release was issued for the same product, only the first press release was counted. New product releases are the average value for each firm-year in the year of the largest change in firm-level R&D spending and the two years following the change.

Firm performance is measured using a well-known proxy for Tobin's q (Chung and Pruitt, 1994), defined as the ratio of the market value of a firm to the replacement cost of its assets, with the book value of assets used as an estimate of the replacement costs of assets. Firms with q greater than one are creating economic value. The measure is highly skewed and is log-transformed.

variable_name: firm earnings underperformance relative to industry
description: Operationalized as a lower partial moment (LPM) of the firm's earnings underperformance relative to target, where the target is the average return on assets of the industry within which the firm competes from the previous year. In the general form, m is the number of time periods used in the measure, n is an arbitrary integer greater than or equal to 2, and x = target - actual, with x set to 0 if target < actual; the authors set m equal to 2 and n equal to 2. The formula block is not readable in the extracted text.

Yearly data on the number of antimanagement shareholder resolutions that came to a vote, gathered from the Investor Responsibility Research Center. As the focus was on governance-related investor rights, shareholder-sponsored resolutions asking management to undertake socially responsible activities were not included in the computation of the measure. All of the variables were lagged by a year.

The number of analysts following each firm, obtained from the I/B/E/S database. Because larger organizations may be followed by more analysts than small ones, the number of analysts was divided by the size of the organization to create a standardized measure. All of the variables were lagged by a year.

A time-varying continuous variable consisting of all nonduplicate ties to prior adopters in the sample, computed to test mimetic arguments based on cohesion. All of the variables were lagged by a year. The exact dates of adoption were unavailable for the 80 organizations that had adopted before 1984, so this variable could not be computed for them.

variable_name: No. of adopters in the same industry (SIC) group
description: Competitors were defined as firms sharing the same two-digit SIC code as a focal firm. The number of adopters in a two-digit SIC code was computed as a measure of structural equivalence. All of the variables were lagged by a year.

variable_name: hazard of creating an investor relations department
description: The event of interest was the adoption of an investor relations office, and the dependent variable was the hazard of creating an investor relations department for organization i at time t, where Pr(.) is the probability of an event between times t and t + dt, given that the firm is in the sample at risk at time t. The formula block expressing the dependent variable was not extracted and is unreadable in this payload. Adoption dates were collected by consulting Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporate Affiliations, scanning abstracts from 52 newspapers through the Dow Jones Electronic News Service, and telephoning companies where that information was unavailable. The history of all sample organizations was split into one-year records or spells, with all spells except the year of adoption coded as right-censored.
scale: binary (adoption event in a one-year spell)

description: Binary variable coded 1 when the firm's response on the first day an accusation became public was an accommodation response, and 0 otherwise. Accommodation is where the firm admits that the allegations are true or initiates an action to change some organization-wide policy to assist its overseas workers. Responses were coded by the first author, and a research assistant coded all 44 identified responses with a Cohen's kappa of 0.84. The omitted baseline in the models is no response or no comment.

Binary variable coded 1 when the firm's response on the first day an accusation became public was a denial, where the firm denies the allegation, and 0 otherwise. Responses were coded by the first author, and a research assistant coded all 44 identified responses with a Cohen's kappa of 0.84. The omitted baseline in the models is no response or no comment.

Binary variable coded 1 when the firm's response on the first day an accusation became public was defiance, where the firm challenges its portrayal as an unsympathetic or 'bad' company, and 0 otherwise. Responses were coded by the first author, and a research assistant coded all 44 identified responses with a Cohen's kappa of 0.84. The omitted baseline in the models is no response or no comment.

Binary variable coded 1 when the firm's response on the first day an accusation became public was decoupling, where the firm implements corrective action in response to specific allegations, frequently suspending or terminating a contract with a specific factory, and 0 otherwise. Responses were coded by the first author, and a research assistant coded all 44 identified responses with a Cohen's kappa of 0.84. The omitted baseline in the models is no response or no comment.

Normative legitimacy with the public is measured from the tenor of print media accounts about the firm using the Janis–Fadner coefficient of imbalance. In the measure, p is the number of positive articles that mentioned the firm in the context of the sweatshop labor issue, n is the number of negative articles, and V is the total number of articles that mentioned the firm. The exact formula is not readable in the text. The range of the variable is 1 to -1, where 1 equals all coverage of the firm focused on this issue that was negative and -1 equals all coverage of the firm focused on this issue that was positive. Legitimacy is calculated beginning on the first day an accusation is announced and becomes public (t=0) and continues for two days after the initial accusation.

Investor perceptions of the firm are measured as the market valuation of the firm, operationalized as cumulative abnormal daily stock returns (CAR) observed after an accusation. The normal return is measured with the market model, which estimates the relationship between firm returns and equally weighted market returns for the 200 trading days starting 50 days before the accusation. The abnormal return is the difference between the observed return and the normal return for the same security. CAR is computed over a two-day event window beginning one day after the accusation was first reported (t+1) and continuing for one additional day (t+2).

Number of both executive and non-executive directors with dominant functional background experiences in finance (or accounting and law). Based on individuals' entire pre-CEO career histories, finance background is defined as dominant when the individual has at least five years more experience in finance than in other functions; CEO tenure is not included when determining dominant functional background experience. All models control for the total number of corporate elites, so the measure is a count rather than a proportion. Demographic variables are lagged one year.

Number of executive directors with dominant functional background experience in finance. Created by splitting the number of finance corporate elites into finance executive and finance non-executive subsets. All demographic variables are lagged one year.

Number of non-executive directors with dominant functional background experience in finance, the complement of the finance executive director count within the finance corporate elite total. All demographic variables are lagged one year.
Dummy variable coded one when the CEO has a dominant functional background experience in finance (or accounting and law) and zero otherwise. All demographic variables are lagged one year.

Number of finance corporate elites who are not the CEO, including both executive and non-executive directors with finance backgrounds. Used in the fourth model to distinguish the finance CEO from all other finance corporate elites. All demographic variables are lagged one year.

Dichotomous dependent variable coded one if the firm's degree of related diversification was one standard deviation above the mean level of diversification, and zero otherwise. Related diversification arises from operating in several 4-digit (SIC) segments within a 2-digit segment. Diversification is measured with the entropy measure (Palepu, 1985): the authors state that P is the share of segment i's sales of the firm's total sales (dollar values) and that (1/Pi) is used as a weight to account for the importance of the segment for total sales, but the formula block itself is unreadable in the provided text.

Dichotomous dependent variable coded one if the firm's degree of unrelated diversification was one standard deviation above the mean level of diversification, and zero otherwise. Unrelated diversification arises from operations in several 2-digit segments. Based on the same entropy measure as related diversification, with the entropy formula not readable in the provided text.

Acquisition activity measured in total dollar amounts per year, the sum of all acquisitions per year. Data come from SDC, which includes all acquisitions over $5M. Because most firms in the sample do not acquire businesses in any given year, observed values concentrate at zero, and the authors estimate random-effects tobit models of the propensity or capacity of the firm to acquire businesses.

Three items tapping the extent to which the software and applications used (e.g., billing, inventory management, EDI), the administrative procedures used (e.g., vendor selection, cost accounting procedures), and the operating procedures used (e.g., manufacturing, bar-coding, packaging, shipping procedures) in supplying RetCo are relatively similar to or significantly different from what the supplier uses with other retailers. The items were developed on the lines of prior measures of asset specificity and rated on the same scale as physical-asset specificity.
scale: 7-point scale: 1 = relatively similar as with other retailers, 3 = moderately customized, 7 = significantly customized for RetCo

description: Three items reflecting the level of specialized intangible investment in developing an understanding of the retailer's requirements and the distinct context of the interaction. The items concern the extent to which the knowledge and understanding used in planning for new products, in product conception and design, and in determining product pricing is customized for RetCo or relatively similar to what the supplier uses with other retailers.
scale: 7-point scale: 1 = relatively similar as with other retailers, 3 = moderately customized, 7 = significantly customized for RetCo

description: Single item asking the extent to which the physical assets used (e.g., manufacturing equipment and machinery) in supplying RetCo are relatively similar or are significantly different from what the supplier uses with other retailers.
scale: 7-point scale: 1 = relatively similar as with other retailers, 3 = moderately customized, 7 = significantly customized for RetCo

description: Single item asking the extent to which the location of the distribution facilities used in supplying RetCo receiving points are relatively similar or are significantly different from what the supplier uses with other retailers.
scale: 7-point scale: 1 = relatively similar as with other retailers, 3 = moderately customized, 7 = significantly customized for RetCo

description: Single item measuring the percentage of the supplier's total annual sales made to the specific retailer, asked as what percentage of the supplier's sales in the last year RetCo accounted for. The measure was adapted from Zaheer and Venkatraman (1994) and Walker (1994).

Three items adapted from Heide and John (1990) and Zaheer and Venkatraman (1994) asking the extent to which decisions on key issues are made jointly by the supplier firm and RetCo, rated on a seven-point scale.
scale: 7-point scale: 1 = minimal joint decision making, 3 = moderate, 7 = extensive joint decision making

description: Binary variable equal to one for firms led only by female founders and zero for male founders. Mixed-gender founding teams are not the theoretical focus and are controlled for separately.

variable_name: Number of regular hours per month
description: The number of regular hours worked by the employee at the focal firm per month, extracted from the annual QP data collection. The analyses are limited to full-time employees because hours may otherwise vary with the type of contract.
time_window: monthly, at the time of the annual QP data collection

variable_name: Number of extra hours per month
description: The number of extra hours worked at the focal firm per month, extracted from the annual QP data collection. Because many employees report zero extra hours, patterns in this variable are assessed conditional on having worked at least one extra hour in the reference month.
time_window: monthly, at the time of the annual QP data collection

variable_name: Regular period of work per week
description: The duration, in hours, of the regular weekly work schedule that the employee and the employer agree on when signing the job contract. Higher values indicate that an employee agreed to a longer weekly work schedule.

Experimental manipulation of the apparent gender of the startup's founders. The prompt ended with 'Thank You' followed by 'Matthew & Joe, Co-Founders of Photolytics' in the Male Founders treatment; only the names were changed to 'Amanda & Chloe' in the Female Founders treatment, and no founders were named in the Control condition.
scale: three conditions (Control, Male Founders, Female Founders)

description: Binary variable coded one if the individual agreed to code extra images for the same pay and zero otherwise. The request to code extra photos was identical across conditions and varied only in the names of the founders.
scale: binary (1 = agreed to code extra images)

description: The number of photos the respondent coded without any additional pay. Respondents willing to continue were shown up to five extra photos and could stop at any time.
Random assignment of respondents to either Male or Female Founders, with the same name manipulation as in Study 2 and the neutral condition omitted.
After completing the 12 photos, subjects were asked whether they would be willing to code additional photos without extra pay. The binary outcome records agreement to supply this extra labor.
The volume of extra work supplied by the respondent, measured as the number of additional photos coded for the same pay after the request.

Posttest question asked of respondents after the task: 'We are relatively new to mTurk, was it fair of us to ask if you could do some extra work?', used to capture the perception that the request for extra labor was unfair.

Posttest question assessing whether the respondent's expectations of work demands varied by founder gender: 'Was the HIT harder or easier than you expected?' Higher values, coded on a five-point Likert scale, indicated that subjects considered the work harder than expected.

Indicator that identifies a temporal transition which is a discrete switch between exclusive periods of exploration and exploitation. The authors first identify a temporal transition when the regression coefficient of the firm's innovation focus on year changes sign between year t-1 and t. They consider that a discontinuous jump occurs when the focus ratio is -1 (i.e., all exploitation) in the previous two consecutive years (t-2 and t-1) and turns into 1 (i.e., all exploration) in year t, and vice versa. Among 4,181 firms in the sample, 217 (5.19%) firms conduct discontinuous jumps.
time_window: focus ratios for t-2, t-1 and t

description: Indicator that identifies a temporal transition when the focus ratios for t-2, t-1 and t are greater than -1 and smaller than 1, which indicates that the firm engages in both exploration and exploitation in the given year. It presupposes that a temporal transition occurred between year t-1 and t, identified by the change in sign of the regression coefficient of the firm's innovation focus on year. Among 4,181 firms in the sample, 494 (11.82%) firms conduct incremental transitions.
time_window: focus ratios for t-2, t-1 and t

description: Market-based measure of firm performance used as the dependent variable. The authors compute it using the book value of total assets, share price, the number of common stocks outstanding, the liquidating value of the firm's preferred stock, short-term liabilities and short-term assets, the book value of inventories, and the book value of long-term debt; the equation itself is not readable in the text available here, so only the stated inputs can be recorded. The authors describe a 1-year lagged structure between the explanatory variables and this performance variable.

Firm resources are measured by considering both technological and financial resources. Technological resources are captured with the R&D budget, which is subject to opportunity costs and limited in availability; financial resources are captured with free cash flow calculated following Jensen (1986). Using the R&D budget and free cash flow the authors identify a two-dimensional geometric space and measure the combination of technological and financial resources by computing the Euclidean distance from the origin, where a greater Euclidean distance indicates that the firm has more non-scale-free technological and financial resources. The moderation tests split the sample using the median value of firm resources.

Dependent variable that equals one if a country j was chosen for investment by firm i, and zero for the countries not chosen. Because investment decisions depend only on country characteristics, all investments of an MNE in a given country share the same covariate values and are pooled into a single case with a weight equal to the number of investments the firm has in that country. The pooling weight is also indicative of the magnitude of the MNE's investment in that country.

Computed by aggregating the bilateral distance between countries i and j across all countries, using capital cities as the points of measurement, standardizing these geographic proximity measures, and weighting them by each country's R&D investment (the $ value of R&D investment in a country). The result is transformed into an index ranging from 1 to 100 in which lower values indicate greater proximity, so higher values imply lower proximity and negative coefficients imply positive effects of proximity.

Computed by aggregating the standardized bilateral distance between countries i and j across all countries, using capital cities as the points of measurement, and weighting by the market size of each country, operationalized by PPP per capita GDP. The result is transformed into an index ranging from 1 to 100 in which lower values indicate greater proximity; higher values imply lower proximity.

Computed by aggregating the standardized bilateral distance between countries i and j across all countries, using capital cities as the points of measurement, and weighting by each country's labor resources, operationalized by the potential size of the labor force, i.e., the number of people of working age, 15-64. The result is transformed into an index ranging from 1 to 100 in which lower values indicate greater proximity; higher values imply lower proximity.

The $ value of R&D investment in the focal country (country i), reflecting the argument that a country's own characteristics also affect the likelihood of its choice as a location by MNEs. Highly dispersed and not normally distributed variables such as the focal country measures are introduced in logged form.

PPP per capita GDP of the focal country (country i), reflecting the argument that a country's own characteristics also affect the likelihood of its choice as a location by MNEs. The focal country measures are introduced in logged form.

The potential size of the focal country's labor force, i.e., the number of people of working age, 15-64, reflecting the argument that a country's own characteristics also affect the likelihood of its choice as a location by MNEs. The focal country measures are introduced in logged form.

Firm size is measured by the number of employees of the investing MNE. Because a multinomial choice model does not allow firm main effects, this firm characteristic is entered only through interaction with the country proximity measures.

A broad measure of firms' performance, measured by sales per employee of the investing MNE. Owing to the inability of the choice model to include firm main effects, it is entered only through interaction with the proximity measures; the interactions with sales per employee were later excluded from the analysis because they were not significant.

variable_name: HH, HL, LH, LL dyad indicators
description: Relative collaborative density of a firm is a binary variable equal to one if the firm's collaborative density (number of realized ties divided by the total number of possible ties, computed over a 5-year moving window) was above the median in the corresponding firm-size quartile and zero otherwise. Four categorical variables capture the relative positions of the two firms in the dyad: HH, HL, LH and LL, where the first letter represents the losing firm and the second the hiring firm. The LL dyad is the omitted category in the regressions.
time_window: 5-year moving window for the collaboration ties

description: Count of citations made to any patents belonging to the losing firm within 5 years after the mobility event, summed over all three knowledge types. Citations are counted regardless of when the cited patents were granted, and the past knowledge exchanges between the firms are accounted for.

Count of citations made to any patents belonging to the hiring firm within 5 years after the mobility event, summed over all three knowledge types, capturing knowledge spill-backs to the losing firm. Citations are counted regardless of when the cited patents were granted.

Count of citations made to the losing firm's patents that were developed by the mobile employee's collaborators but not by the focal inventor (Type II) or by other firm members (Types III), i.e., knowledge the mobile employee was not directly involved in developing, within 5 years after the mobility event. It is the sum of the Type II and Type III citation counts for flows from the losing firm to the hiring firm.

Count of citations made to the hiring firm's patents that were developed by the mobile employee's collaborators but not by the focal inventor (Type II) or by other firm members (Type III) within 5 years after the mobility event, capturing spill-backs of broader knowledge to the losing firm. It is the sum of the Type II and Type III citation counts for flows from the hiring firm to the losing firm.

An aggregate scale of five questionnaire items relating to technical features and machine design. The questions were designed to assess the technical novelty of the equipment, its maturity, and its advance relative to existing practice, and most questionnaire items were measured on five-point scales. Cronbach alpha of the aggregate scale was 0.90. Discriminant validity was supported by comparing the median intra-scale item correlation of 0.64 with the median inter-scale item correlation of 0.18.

An aggregate scale of five questionnaire items that investigated the plant's familiarity with the conversion concepts and production approach involved. Most questionnaire items were measured on five-point scales. Cronbach alpha of the aggregate scale was 0.86 and the median intra-scale item correlation was 0.505.
The size of the introduction project was measured by the total capital investment involved, as reported in project documentation. Figures are stated in 1986 U.S. dollars.

An aggregate scale measuring the contribution of factory personnel to the development of new equipment and related systems prior to installation. It comprises two questionnaire items rated on 5-point scales, and two coded interview responses (Cronbach alpha = 0.67).

An aggregate scale based on three items. Two questionnaire items measured the involvement of personnel from other facilities or organizations during installation and optimization of the new process (5-point scales). Interview responses were coded (yes or no) for the existence of a problem solving partnership with outside experts (Cronbach alpha = 0.79).
scale: 5-point scales; interview item coded yes or no

description: Determined by the form of lateral relations between production and engineering personnel involved in the project. Following Galbraith (1973), overlap was coded on a scale from 1 (handoff between functions) to 5 (fully integrated team, no functional distinction between engineering and production personnel). Information was obtained from interviews aided by graphical description of the project organization and the critical event method to elicit reliable recall.
scale: 1 (handoff between functions) to 5 (fully integrated team, no functional distinction between engineering and production personnel)

description: Constructed to capture the fact that the early phases of equipment installation and initial debugging are more disruptive and costly to the factory than the later optimization phase, by taking the sum of two periods. Installation period: the elapsed time in months from delivery of the equipment until parts are being produced. Introduction period: the elapsed time in months from delivery until the introduction is considered complete. Information was obtained from questionnaires supplemented by interviews and project documents.
time_window: from equipment delivery until the introduction is considered complete

description: An aggregate scale of three interview items (Cronbach alpha = 0.86). Ratings by respondents were corroborated by managers at the plant or division level; disagreements among informants were investigated during follow-up interviews, and if disagreement persisted the more conservative (lower) rating was used. In most cases project documentation describing project objectives and post audit reports (where they had been performed) were available.

Technological process change is measured through its two distinct aspects, technical complexity and systemic shift. Technical complexity is a five-item scale on the novelty, maturity and advance of the equipment, and systemic shift is a five-item scale on the plant's familiarity with the conversion concepts and production approach. Hypothesis 1 is tested with both scales as separate predictors of startup time.

Introduction success is measured by two outcomes. Disruption is the startup time in months (installation period plus introduction period), where a shorter time means a more successful introduction. Operating improvement is an aggregate scale of three interview items on the intermediate-term benefits of the new technology. Each is a separate dependent variable in the tests.
