scale: startup time in months; three-item operating improvement scale

description: The aggregate number of entries of commercial television stations in each semester from 1940 to 1960. Entry dates are defined as dates on which a station begins broadcasting. During the period of observation the authors identified 596 commercial television station entries.

A semiannual Hirschman-Herfindahl concentration index (multiplied by 100) of the relative frequency of groups of New York Times articles about television. Articles were counted when the word 'television' was cited in the same paragraph (within approximately 1,000 characters) with 'radio', 'film', or 'newspaper', with articles citing television independently of these domains forming a fourth group. The variable uses cumulative article counts from 1923 to each semester; the exact formula is not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: cumulative from 1923 to each semester in the 1940-1960 window, lagged one period

variable_name: Density of de alio radio stations
description: The number of television stations in operation during each semester that entered from radio broadcasting. Density is measured by the number of stations in operation during each period, and de alio density is a subcount of total density based on the origin of entrants.

The number of television stations in operation during each semester that entered without prior experience in other domains (de novo entrants). It is the density subcount that is compared with the disaggregated de alio densities.

Coded 1 if the feature requested by the customer was fulfilled, and 0 otherwise. The authors describe it as an output-side measure of incremental innovation in that any feature added to the existing product is clearly a new combination. Of the 152 unique customer requests, 120 (79%) were fulfilled and 32 (21%) were not.

A fulfilled request was either standardized into the next release or customized for the customer making the request. The indicator is coded 1 if the customer request was standardized, and 0 otherwise (customization). Of the 120 fulfilled requests, 92 were integrated into the next packaged release and 28 were pursued as customization projects.

For every change request received, the firm sends a survey to all existing customers of the product; they are asked to indicate whether the proposed feature will be useful to them. The variable is measured as the percentage of customers who indicated a new feature would be useful and ranges from 0 to 100.
time_window: at the time the request was received

description: A customer initiating a feature request is required to indicate its importance. The variable is coded on a Likert scale ranging from 1 to 5 and measures perceived importance of the proposed feature; higher values reflect greater importance to the customer. The codes run from 1 (the change is preferred but not essential for day-to-day operations) to 5 (the feature requested is essential and time critical).
time_window: at the time the request was received

description: For each request the vendor firm received, it generated an estimate of the cost of implementing the feature. The estimate includes the direct cost of manpower and the time required to implement the feature and test a new version before rollout.
time_window: at the time the request was received

description: In practice it is extremely difficult to measure the number of interdependencies within a software product, but the number of interdependencies is related to software size. Four measures of software size were collected at the time the request was received - number of lines of code, number of functions, number of objects, and number of classes - all highly correlated, so the authors used the number of classes to estimate the level of interdependencies. A class represents the highest level of aggregation in object-oriented programming.
time_window: at the time the request was received

description: As the code base of software ages, it undergoes iterations that increase its complexity. Product age is measured using the version number of the software (1-28) on the date of the customer request.

Measuretronics characterized the magnitude of change required to the existing code base. A customer request was considered a minor change when only one module was affected, and a major change when modifications affected two or more modules. The variable is coded 1 if the change was major.

For the subset of customer requests that were fulfilled, the authors collected data on the number of objects that were modified to implement the change request. An object is a self-contained functional entity that consists of both data and procedures to manipulate the data. The larger the number of objects modified, the greater the complexity of the request.

For the subset of requests that were fulfilled, the authors obtained the number of internal intermediate releases before the change was finalized. A larger number of intermediate releases reflects greater change complexity.

The analyses use indicator variables of three kinds of format changes: innovative change (entry into Soft Adult Contemporary, New Age, Urban Contemporary, or Soft Urban Contemporary), satellite change (entry into formats programmed by satellite), and other format change (all other changes in format or production). An indicator of any format change is also interacted with multimarket corporation and with lagged share to test hypotheses 2 and 3. Format changes were coded from a weekly newsletter that reports stations judged to have changed their format, with data on origin and destination formats.

The dependent variable is the 12+ Metro audience share (Monday-Sunday, 6 A.M.-midnight). It shows the average proportion of all listeners over 12 tuned in to the focal station during the broadcast week. It is a gross market share that does not take into account which age segment the station targets, which makes it convenient for comparing stations with different formats. Annual performance measures are available for the same period as the format data.

An indicator variable showing whether the station was owned by a multimarket corporation, defined as an entity owning three or more stations. It is interacted with format change to test whether branch stations experience a greater performance loss when changing, and the classification threshold was varied from two to six stations in additional specifications.

The station's market share in the previous period, entered as the lagged dependent variable in the partial adjustment model together with the other covariates. In the interaction with format change the lagged share is expressed as a deviate from the mean share in the market, so the coefficient shows the effect of having pre-change performance different from the market mean; a negative interaction coefficient indicates regression toward the market mean.

Count of how many of the three climate change risks - regulatory, physical, and other - the company discloses in the CDP questionnaire (question CC5.1), ranging from 0 to 3. For each type of risk disclosed, companies are asked to describe the risk and its potential impact, characterize its timeframe, likelihood and magnitude of impact, estimate its financial implications before mitigating actions, and describe how the risk is being managed and the costs of those actions. In auxiliary analysis the three categories are examined separately with individual indicator variables for the disclosure of regulatory, physical, and other climate change risks.

Number of environment-related shareholder proposals a company faces in a given year. The authors consider all shareholder proposals in ISS for which the field 'resolution type' is 'SRI' and read the descriptions to determine which are environment-related. In the baseline sample, 33% of the 1,110 firm-year observations have at least one environment-related shareholder proposal (the maximum is five). The variable enters the regressions lagged by one year.

variable_name: environmental shareholder activism by institutional versus noninstitutional shareholders
description: Environmental shareholder activism is decomposed by sponsor type. Proposal sponsors are coded as noninstitutional if the field 'sponsor type' in ISS is 'individual,' 'union,' 'religious,' or 'other'; all other sponsor types (public pension funds, SRI funds, special interest investors, and asset management funds) are coded as institutional. The counts of proposals by each sponsor type enter the regression separately, both lagged by one year.

variable_name: environmental shareholder activism by institutional shareholders with long-term versus short-term horizon
description: Institutional sponsors are split by time horizon. All SRI investors and special interest investors are categorized as long-term since their mandate is unambiguously long-term; for all other institutional investors the quarterly churn rate is computed from Thomson-Reuters 13F data, and investors above the average churn rate are categorized as short-term and those below as long-term. Institutional investors in ISS that could not be matched to the 13F data form an additional category of institutional shareholders with unknown temporal horizon. Counts of proposals by each group enter the regression separately.

Cumulative abnormal returns computed by summing daily abnormal returns, i.e., stock returns in excess of the 'normal' returns predicted by an asset pricing model, over event windows around the day on which the CDP report is released for S&P 500 companies. Three asset pricing models are used: the market model, the three-factor model of Fama and French (1993), and the four-factor model of Carhart (1997). The main event window is [-10, 10], with [-5, 5] reported as a shorter window, and [-50, -11] and [11, 50] used to assess pre-trends and reversals.
time_window: event windows around Day 0 (CDP report release): [-10, 10], [-5, 5], [-50, -11], [11, 50]

description: Count of patent grants applied for by the firm within the focal technological regime (monoclonal antibodies or gene therapy) during the three-year period before a potential preclinical trial. Patents come from the Derwent World Patents Index, where mAbs and GT received dedicated classes labeled monoclonal antibody, gene therapy, and gene delivery; a senior scientist confirmed the applicability of these classes to the study. It is one of two proxies for internal research investments, because archival data on internal research expenditures for specific technology regimes are not available.

Count of scientific publications by the firm within the focal technological regime during the three-year period before a potential preclinical trial. Publications were identified from the ISI Web of Science based on the authors' affiliation information and classified into mAbs or GT research through a keyword approach: a publication was in the mAbs domain if 'monoclonal antibody' appeared in the title, abstract, or keywords, and in the GT domain if 'gene therapy,' 'gene delivery,' or 'antisense' appeared in those fields. It is the second proxy for internal research investments.

Count of research contracts initiated by the focal incumbent during the three-year period within a specific technological regime. Using ReCap's agreement type, the authors included partnerships with either licensing (ReCap code L) or research contracting (ReCap code R) but no collaborative arrangement, and only agreements identified for the discovery stage. In these agreements incumbents do not share costs or collaborate with the external party.

Count of research alliances formed by the focal incumbent during the three-year period within a specific technological regime. These arrangements are identified in ReCap as either 'Co*' (collaborative agreement) and/or 'JV' (joint venture), go beyond a simple market-based exchange of IP for money and are based on firms sharing organizational and managerial resources; only agreements identified in ReCap for the discovery stage were counted. ReCap's technology field distinguished mAbs-specific from GT-specific alliances.

Count of acquisitions by the incumbent firm during the three-year period within a specific technology. An acquisition was considered to be in a specific technological regime if it was classified by ReCap as either mAbs- or GT-based, if the acquired target (usually a small biotechnology start-up) had applied for either mAbs or GT patents, or if the target had products in development in the respective technological regime.

Takes the value of 1 if a new preclinical trial was initiated by the incumbent firm for mAbs or GT in a given year, and 0 otherwise. Therapeutic solutions in preclinical trials were identified in Pharmaprojects (mAbs within its biotech classification T3, GT within T4); two researchers independently coded the information, and Adis R&D Insights was used to verify the year the preclinical trial was initiated and to fill in missing data, with the earliest reported year used when the databases differed.

The moderator is operationalized by splitting the sample into the two radical technological regimes studied: monoclonal antibodies, a sustaining regime that, like traditional chemistry-based therapies, is prescribed as long-term treatment with recurring costs, and gene therapy, a disruptive regime of one-off or much less frequent customized treatments with unclear pricing and reimbursement. Because a test showed the unexplained variation differed across the regimes, the authors did not pool the data and instead estimated separate models for mAbs and GT, comparing ratios of coefficients across the two models.
Income before extraordinary items divided by total assets. It is the dependent variable in the performance regressions and was standardized along with the other nonbinary variables for the analyses.

Past income stream variability, measured as the standard deviation of firm ROA during the five-year period up to the year in question. When uncertainty is the dependent variable, network measures in the present year are regressed against income variation in the next five years, so the measure reflects the predictability of future performance.

Firm stock price variability (market performance) based on the capital asset pricing model. Firm beta was estimated using a four factor model (market premium, small minus big, high minus low, and momentum); a high beta suggests that the firm's stock price is susceptible to greater variability relative to the overall market.

Variability of financial analysts' expectations of earnings per share one year in advance. A wide range of estimates, i.e., a higher standard deviation in analysts' expectations, indicates greater uncertainty regarding future firm performance; only firms with more than three analyst forecasts were used.

Calculated as the number of interlock ties a firm has with the other firms. Degree centrality was preferred over other centrality measures because it is common in both the networks-as-external-resources and resource dependence literatures, maps onto the information-gathering, knowledge transfer and learning mechanisms, and is complementary to the structural holes measure.

Calculated in two steps: first, lack of access to structural holes is measured with Burt's network constraint measure; the equation is not readable in the supplied text (the text states only that pij represents the strength of tie between firms i and j and the sum of indirect tie strength in the linkage of i and j through firm k). Second, hole access is calculated as one minus the constraint score of the firm where the constraint score was non-zero, and 0 in each of the other cases; a high hole access score represents less redundancy in the firm's network, a low score higher redundancy.

Binary variable created using information provided by the SDC Platinum database, equal to 1 if the target is privately held and 0 if the target is listed. It is the dependent variable of the probit selection model and the key independent variable of the acquirer return model.

Acquirer abnormal returns are estimated using an event study methodology; the cumulative average abnormal return (CAAR) was calculated following the standard approach described by McWilliams and Siegel (1997). The date of announcement of the acquisition was collected through SDC, Reuters, and LexisNexis. The reported event window is [ - 20;10].
time_window: event window [ - 20;10] around the acquisition announcement

description: Binary variable obtained from the survey. The text states that it takes the value of 1 when the acquirer made the acquisition in its core business and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: Acquirer M&A experience in target industry
description: The number of previous acquisitions made by the acquirer within the 5 years prior to the focal transaction in the target's industry. The measure is survey-based.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal transaction

description: A survey-based measure that captures the international scope of the target's activities: domestic (1), regional (2), and global (3).

Binary variable that takes the value of 1 when the target comes from high-tech industries and 0 otherwise. Measuring the degree of intangibility of the target's assets is difficult for private firms, for which there is little firm-level data on R&D spending and for which a Tobin's Q cannot be calculated. Three survey measures of ex post transfer of target resources (redeployment of innovation, engineering, and marketing resources) were also used, but the simpler binary variable is reported.
Target age was a self-reported measure on a 5-point scale collected through the survey.

Variable that captures the fit between an acquirer's actual choice between a public or private firm and what the discrete choice model predicted that it should do. Given that the dependent variable of the discrete choice model is equal to 1 if the target is private and 0 if it is public, the fit variable is equal to p (the probability of choosing a private target predicted by the model) if the target is private and 1 - p if the target is public.

Dummy variable set to one if a focal complementor provided packages on more than one software platform, and zero otherwise. It is a time-invariant variable used to distinguish observations subject to treatment (multihoming complementors) from their counterfactuals (single-home complementors).

The variable contains the logarithm of the number of programs on GitHub that called a complementor's packages in a software platform ecosystem by the focal month. Once a package is called as a function to implement a new software program, the event is documented, specifying that the installation of the focal package becomes a prerequisite for the functioning of that software program. Instances in which a complementor's packages are documented as installation prerequisites capture the extent to which its offerings are used on the software platform. All variables entered as logarithms capture the natural logarithm of the original count added to one.

Time-varying variable containing the number of upstream dependencies that a complementor's packages have built on, by the focal month, on the home platform, irrespective of the extent to which these upstream programs are used in other packages. To account for skewness, the variable contains the logarithm of this count.

Time-varying measure based on the extent to which the upstream packages used by a focal complement by a focal month overlapped with the upstream packages most frequently used by all the other complements in the relevant domains of use. The relevant domains are those among the top five most frequently used keywords on the platform, and within each domain the comparison is to the top 20 most frequently used upstream packages. It ranges from zero to one, with higher values denoting higher levels of similarity, and for complementors offering multiple complements on the focal platform it is the average similarity score across its complements by the focal month. The equation specifying the measure is unreadable in the extracted text.

A 9-point Guttman-type scale was derived from the decision-stage model of three stages and nine substages. Content analyses of the field interview transcripts, inspection of the secondary data, and telephone interviews determined how far each of the 300 assimilation processes had progressed as of March 1981. Scores range from members being aware of the innovation to the equipment being expanded, upgraded, or replaced with a second generation.

An additive scale combining the three environmental measures; the cluster proved amenable to additive scaling and the Cronbach's alpha for the scale was .89. Demographic measures of each hospital's enacted environment were computed from U.S. census data as averages over the census tracts from which its patients came, weighted by the number of patients originating in each tract. The patient-origin survey located by census tract each patient discharged from each hospital between June 1, 1976, and May 31, 1977.
time_window: patient origin survey June 1, 1976 - May 31, 1977; census data 1960-1970

description: Average population density within the hospital's service area, constructed from U.S. census data. Averages were calculated using the numbers of patients originating in different census tracts as weights.

The average increase in median family income between 1960 and 1970 within the hospital's service area, constructed from U.S. census data by calculating averages weighted by the numbers of patients originating in different census tracts.

The average proportion of Medicare and Medicaid recipients within the hospital's service area, calculated from secondary data using the numbers of patients originating in different census tracts as weights.

An additive scale combining hospital size, structural complexity, and market strategy; the cluster proved amenable to additive scaling and the Cronbach's alpha for the scale was .87. The authors note that the items forming the organizational scale indicate that large hospitals display more complex structures and appear more eager to penetrate new markets than others.
The number of patient beds, with a logarithmic transformation to adjust for curvilinearity.
The availability of 24 distinct medical services, taken to reflect horizontal differentiation because those services required either separate structural subunits or specialized staff members.
Pooling of the judgments of experts concerning the aggressiveness with which each hospital pursued new markets, following Meyer (1982).
The tenure of the chief executive officer, measured in years of service.
An index combining years of graduate and undergraduate education and degrees received, following Kimberly and Evanisko (1981).
The median age of the members of each hospital's active medical staff, used to measure how recently the hospital's physicians received their medical training.

An additive scale combining the innovation attributes risk, skill, and observability; the cluster proved amenable to additive scaling and the Cronbach's alpha for the scale was .70. The authors note that the scale reflects the tendency of highly observable diagnostic innovations such as ultrasonic imaging to reduce risks without requiring many new skills for their utilization.

Measured by pooling the judgments of a panel of medical college faculty members on the level of risk of injury or death to which an innovation exposes patients and the concomitant risk of malpractice litigation to which it exposes physicians who use it.
Measured by pooling the judgments of a panel of medical college faculty members on the degree of manual skill or specialized medical training required to use an innovation.

Measured through the visibility of medical equipment, which largely depends on its impact on patient flows. The expert panel used four categories as an ordinal scale on which to classify the 12 innovations: patient specimens, equipment within a hospital, patients within a hospital, and patients between hospitals. The scale assumes that innovations are maximally observable if they affect patient admissions and transfers and minimally observable if they affect only flows of tissue specimens or blood samples.

An index calculated for each innovation in each hospital reflecting the configuration of potential using physicians, referring physicians, and indirect beneficiaries. The primary criterion is the presence on the medical staff of physicians practicing a specialty appropriate for using the equipment, the secondary criterion physicians whose practices regularly generate referrals to those user specialists, and the tertiary criterion physicians who refer patients only occasionally or would enjoy other sorts of indirect benefits.

Measured for each innovation by assessing the extent to which a CEO (1) personally supported acquisition and (2) exerted influence during decision-making processes. The authors defined CEO's advocacy as influential support.

variable_name: compatibility, CEO advocacy and two interaction terms
description: Innovation-decision attributes are measured by four variables defined at the level of the innovation within a hospital. Compatibility is an index of the fit between the equipment and the specialties on the medical staff. CEO advocacy is the CEO's influential support for the adoption. The other two are the interactions skill by recency of medical education and observability by urbanization.
scale: four variables entered as one block

variable_name: environmental, organizational and leadership variable sets
description: Contextual attributes are measured by three sets of predictors. The environmental set covers urbanization, affluence and federal health insurance in the hospital service area. The organizational set covers size (log of beds), complexity and market strategy. The leadership set covers CEO tenure, CEO education and recency of medical education. The sets enter the regression in blocks, with the environmental and organizational variables combined into scales.
scale: sets of variables entered in regression blocks

variable_name: CEO tenure, CEO education and recency of medical education
description: Leadership attributes are measured by three variables. CEO tenure is the CEO's years of service. CEO education is an index combining years of graduate and undergraduate education and degrees received. Recency of medical education is the median age of each hospital's active medical staff.

The reverse of Fleming's (2001) component familiarity measure: the negative of that measure is taken, and the result is divided by 100 to remove leading zeros in coefficient estimates. Component familiarity is computed for each technology subclass in which an invention is classified, from the number and recency of other patents classified under that subclass, with the time constant of knowledge loss set at five years and k indexing all patents granted prior to the application date of the focal invention. As described in Fleming (2001), the average familiarity across all subclasses of an invention is then computed and the square root of this value is taken. Higher values can be interpreted as indicating unfamiliarity; the underlying formulas are not readable in the text.
scale: continuous; higher values indicate greater unfamiliarity
time_window: prior patents granted before the application date of the focal invention

description: A binary variable indicating that a claim was rejected for obviousness based on an examiner citation to a U.S. patent and the applicant argued that this patent teaches away from the invention. Claims were first matched to the prior art citations examiners used specifically to support obviousness rejections, which was possible for 76% of claims rejected for obviousness. The text of applicant response letters was then searched for variants of the phrase 'teach away', including 'teach against', 'teach the opposite', and 'contrary to the teaching of', and each instance was manually read to identify the prior art citation said to teach away from the focal invention.

A binary variable indicating that a claim was ultimately allowed. It includes claims that were initially allowed as well as claims that were initially rejected but eventually allowed. In the model of claim allowance, this indicator is the dependent variable and the regressors include indicators for different types of rejection, including 'Rejected for obviousness, teach away'.

The level of participation present in the planning process of a given organization is represented by an ordered triple of the three participation variables P1, P2 and P3. Each organization was ranked on each of these variables by the researchers on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal, using Likert type scales as an aid.

Ordinal scale recording which interest groups participate in the planning process, ranked for each organization by the researchers. The ranking was made on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal, using Likert type scales as an aid to the ranking process.

Ordinal scale for the degree of communication within the planning process, ranked for each organization by the researchers. The ranking was made on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal, using Likert type scales as an aid to the ranking process.

Ordinal scale for the involvement of groups in strategic decision making, ranked for each organization by the researchers. The ranking was made on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal, using Likert type scales as an aid to the ranking process.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'clear statement of objectives', on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'integration of planning function', on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'catalytic action of planning function', on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'richness of formulation' of plans, on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'depth of evaluation', on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'treatment of uncertainty in evaluation', on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'resources planned', measuring the range of resources considered in plans, on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'data used', on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'iteration in process', on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'assumptions made', on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'quantification of goals', on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'control measures', responsiveness to uncertainty, on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Ordinal scale for the attribute 'feasibility of implementation', testing of short-listed strategies, on which increasing scores were taken to indicate increasing effectiveness. Each organization was ranked on the attribute by the researchers, using Likert type scales as an aid, on the basis of the structured interviews and document appraisal.

Classification of the sample organizations by sector: the public sector, non-profitmaking organizations in the sample are organizations (a) to (c), with the nationalized industry included in the complementary set of organizations. Used to compare the degree of participation across the public and private sectors.

Consolidated R&D expense divided by net sales revenue. A two-year average (1986-87) was taken to dampen any single-year aberrations that might occur. Because it is used as a surrogate for risk aversion, the authors treat lower values as greater risk aversion.

Questionnaire item measuring the emphasis on division performance as a component of division manager rewards. Coded as a dummy variable where unity indicates an emphasis on the control system attribute. The authors state these items were felt to be a reasonable proxy for an emphasis on financial controls because incentives are likely to have the greatest effect on managerial behavior.

variable_name: Emphasis on short-term division financial incentives
description: Questionnaire item measuring the emphasis on annual (short-term) division return on investment performance as a component of division manager rewards. Coded as a dummy variable where unity indicates an emphasis on the control system attribute.

variable_name: Emphasis on long-term division financial incentives
description: Questionnaire item measuring the emphasis on longer-term performance (several years of results) as a component of division manager rewards. Coded as a dummy variable where unity indicates an emphasis on the control system attribute.

variable_name: Constraints on the application of resources
description: Created from 20 survey items related to six topics: (1) aspects of cost and risks, (2) problems with new technologies and organization, (3) lack of qualified human resources, (4) lack of information, (5) barriers to innovation created by the regulatory officials, and (6) tax burden. The items were coded as binary dummy variables indicating the absence or presence of the constraint. Cronbach's alpha is 0.94.
Measured as the industry average of all of the firms' evaluations of the importance of the external technological potential within each industry. The variable therefore varies by industry.
Proxy for innovative performance representing a firm's innovation turnover pertaining to new products. The construct and measures were aligned to those of Laursen and Salter as closely as possible.

Proxy for innovative performance indicating the turnover from incremental innovation, which consists of new modified products or processes from previous innovations. The construct and measures were aligned to those of Laursen and Salter as closely as possible.

Constructed as a combination of the 14 sources of knowledge or information for innovation, ranging from clients to research institutes. Each source is coded as a binary variable in which 0 represents the unused sources and 1 represents the used sources. Firms that do not use any sources have a search breadth equal to 0, whereas those using all of the sources listed in the survey have a search breadth equal to 14. Cronbach's alpha is 0.85.

Measured by combining the sources of information from the survey used to measure breadth. These sources are transformed into a binary variable with a value of 1 when the firm uses the source to a high degree and 0 otherwise. Cronbach's alpha is 0.64.

Board monitoring is measured in two ways. First, the authors examine board characteristics including board independence and size, CEO duality (the absence of a separate non-executive chairperson of the board), directors' ownership in the focal firm, directors' equity-based pay, prior experience with M&As, and how busy directors were with appointments on other boards. Second, to account for board variables acting as a bundle, they conduct a factor analysis and include an aggregate measure of board monitoring.
time_window: end of the year preceding the M&A event

description: Institutional ownership concentration is measured as the percentage of total year-end shares owned by the top five institutional investors. The data came from the Thomson Reuters Institutional Holdings (13F) Database.
time_window: year-end of the year preceding the M&A event

description: Cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) are calculated following the Brown and Warner procedure, aggregating abnormal returns for the 3 days surrounding the announcement of the deal, with parameters estimated by regressing the firm's returns on market returns for the period of 240 to 40 days preceding the announcement. The percentage CARs are weighted with the firm's market value two days prior to the M&A announcement to estimate how much shareholders lose or gain overall. The authors take the absolute values of these dollar-adjusted abnormal returns to measure how extreme the effect of the deal is on shareholder wealth, and take a logarithmic transformation of the dependent variable to correct for skewness and kurtosis.
time_window: 3-day window around the deal announcement; 240 to 40 days preceding the announcement for parameter estimation

description: The ratio of buyer-supplier relationships to the number of potential ties among affiliates in a given year, computed for each group in each of the five BGT periods. The analysis also uses the square of density to test the predicted nonmonotonic impact on innovativeness. The variable is lagged, so that covariates in 1981, for instance, correspond to the dependent variable covering 1982 and 1983.
time_window: one-period lag relative to the patenting during the two-year period

description: Built from four aspects of the national innovation infrastructure in Taiwan: stock market trading volume for capital market development, the number of for-profit organizations operating in the country for commercial intermediaries, the number of university graduates in Taiwan for the external labor market, and the points the Global Competitiveness Report awarded Taiwan for legal protection. The measure records the mean value of the growth multipliers of the four items after the first time period, using 1981 as the base year.

Aggregate new invention patent application counts by all affiliates of each group over a two-year period following each of the five years for which the BGT provided data (1982-1983, 1987-1988, 1991-1992, 1995-1996, and 1999-2000). Patent identification numbers, application and approval dates, and patent types were coded for each affiliate, and only 'New Invention Patents' - innovations involving wholly new products, materials, or manufacturing processes - were counted. Applications were aggregated at the group level because information arising on buyer-supplier ties can flow throughout the group.
time_window: two-year window following each BGT year

description: Change in residential mortgage lending from year to year, computed as (residential mortgage lending t+1 / total assets t+1) minus (residential mortgage lending t / total assets t). The authors illustrate with a hypothetical S&L having 90 percent of its assets in residential mortgages in 1985 and 70 percent in 1986, which would receive a score of -20 (movement away from mortgage lending), while an S&L increasing residential mortgage lending from 70 to 90 percent would receive a score of +20.

A standardized residual obtained from the generalized least-squares model of strategic change for each observation in the data, of which the absolute value is computed. It captures the extent to which the change undertaken by an individual thrift in a given year deviates from the amount of change predicted by the multivariate contingency model, and was used to predict subsequent performance in terms of both ROA and organizational survival chances. Higher values therefore indicate a lower level of dynamic strategic fit.

Return on assets, defined as net income t+1 / total assets t+1. The authors state that ROA is a standard measure of operating performance in organizational research, in banking research, and in prior studies of S&Ls, and is particularly appropriate because the strategy measure captures how S&Ls allocate their assets while ROA measures how these assets perform subsequently. A 1-year time lag is used because the strategic change measure assesses realized changes in asset allocation.

Failure is defined as the point when an S&L was taken into conservatorship by government regulators. The authors argue this is an appropriate measure of failure because the regulatory safety net provided by the government prevents failing S&Ls from closing in a conventional manner; regulators take over failing S&Ls and arrange for their liquidation or subsequent merger with healthy thrifts.
Measured as total interest paid t / total deposits and liabilities t, consistent with prior research.
Measured as total borrowed funds t / total liabilities t.
Measured as total interest received on mortgages t / total mortgage assets t.
Measured as fixed rate mortgages t / total mortgages t.

A dummy variable capturing decline in net worth, coded as 1 when (total assets t - total liabilities t) was less than (total assets t-1 - total liabilities t-1), and 0 otherwise. Higher values therefore indicate a decline in net worth.

variable_name: local competitors' reliance on residential mortgage lending
description: Measured as the percentage of total assets that other S&Ls within a focal thrift's 3-digit zip code had in residential mortgage lending at time t. For S&Ls with no competition within their local area, the mean level of residential mortgage lending within the thrift's home state was used as a proxy measure of its competitor's activities; this substitution was necessary for about 4 percent of all observations.
The macroenvironmental variable interest rates is defined as the average prime rate which banks charged during a particular period.

variable_name: size of the all-White work group
description: We randomly varied the size of the work group so that it included one to eight people: participants in condition 1 saw a work group including one White man, participants in condition 2 saw a work group including two White men, and so on up to participants in condition 8. The manipulation was checked by asking participants to recall the size of the original work group.

variable_name: size two condition versus size eight condition
description: We randomly varied whether participants were shown two (size two condition) or eight (size eight condition) White male speakers who had already been invited to the seminar, so that participants were assigned to see a smaller or a larger homogeneous group. Participants then recalled the size of the original group of included speakers.

variable_name: size of the all-male Innovation Team
description: As in Study 1, we randomly varied the size of the current Innovation Team from having as few as one to having as many as eight (White male) members. The manipulation was checked by asking participants to recall the size of the original Innovation Team.

Our main predictor was the size of the all-male board, measured in year t and used to predict whether the board added a woman in year t+1. Boards ranged in size from 3 to 18, with a median size of 7; we winsorized board size at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles so that the winsorized board size distribution ranged from 4 to 14.
time_window: year t (board size measured one year before the diversification outcome)

description: Boards ranged in size from 3 to 17, with a median size of 8; board size was winsorized at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles so that the winsorized board size distribution ranged from size 5 to 14. All-White board size in year t was the main predictor of whether the board added a non-White director in the following year.
time_window: year t (board size measured one year before the diversification outcome)

description: Boards in 2018 ranged in size from 4 directors to 23 directors, with an average of 89 boards of each board size and a median of nine directors. We winsorized board size at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles so that the winsorized board size distribution ranged from size 5 to 16, and board size was the main predictor in regressions of the difference between the observed and simulated proportions of homogeneous boards.

variable_name: binary indicator for whether participants chose to hire the Black male candidate
description: Our dependent variable of interest was a binary indicator for whether participants chose to hire the Black male candidate. Participants were shown a set of three candidates (two White men and one Black man) and asked to hire one of them to join the all-White work group.

variable_name: binary indicator for whether participants chose to recommend that the female professor be added as a speaker
description: Our dependent variable of interest was a binary indicator for whether participants chose to recommend that the female professor be added as a speaker. Participants chose among three potential speakers (two White male professors and one White female professor) to add to the all-male, all-White seminar series.

variable_name: binary indicator for whether a female candidate was hired
description: The dependent variable was a binary indicator for whether a female candidate was hired. Participants were shown a set of three candidates (two White men and one White woman) and asked to select one of them to join the all-male, all-White Innovation Team.

Our binary dependent measure took on a value of 1 if the all-male board added at least one woman between year t and year t+1, and it took on a value of 0 otherwise. Of the 3,593 all-male board-year observations, 564 (15.7%) involved boards that added at least one woman in the following year.

variable_name: Non-White Director Added to All-White Board
description: The dependent measure captured whether an all-White board added at least one non-White director in the following year. Of the 4,350 all-White board-year observations, 330 (7.6%) involved boards that added at least one non-White director in the following year.

variable_name: perceived fairness of the original group's selection process
description: To measure the perceived fairness of the process used to select the members of the original Innovation Team, we adapted one question from Sweeney and McFarlin's (1997) procedural justice scale. The item was measured on a 7-point Likert scale where 1 was defined as 'Strongly Disagree' and 7 was defined as 'Strongly Agree.'
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree)

variable_name: perceived diversity of the original Innovation Team
description: To measure the perceived diversity of the original Innovation Team, we used a three-item scale adapted from Unzueta and Binning's (2012) perceived diversity scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.88). All items were measured on 7-point Likert scales from 'Strongly Disagree' to 'Strongly Agree,' and multi-item scales were averaged across items.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree)

variable_name: diversity-related impression management concerns faced by the original Innovation Team
description: To measure the diversity-related impression management concerns relating to the original Innovation Team, we used a two-item scale adapted from the Chng et al. (2015) image concerns scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.92). Items were measured on 7-point Likert scales and averaged across items.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree)

variable_name: potential for a new addition to influence the group
description: To measure the perceived influence a woman would wield if she were added to the original Innovation Team, we used a three-item scale adapted from Spreitzer's (1995) impact scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.83). Items were measured on 7-point Likert scales and averaged across items.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree)

variable_name: percent difference between the observed and expected proportions of homogeneous boards
description: Expected proportions of homogeneous boards for each board size were generated with a Monte Carlo simulation in which the existing universe of 2018 S&P 1500 corporate board members was randomly reassigned to new boards 10,000 times, taking as given the number of boards, the size of each board, and the number of board seats held by each individual director. The dependent variable was the percent difference between the observed and expected proportions of homogeneous boards for each board size (computed separately for all-male and all-White boards), which was regressed on board size.
Respondents reported how much (a) a new driver earned per year and (b) a senior driver earned per year. The difference between the two numbers forms the measure.

A list of four types of individual incentives, common in the trucking industry and derived through pilot testing and discussions with industry officials, was used. Respondents reported the extent to which these incentive systems were used, on a scale from 1 (Not at all) to 5 (To a very great extent). The mean of the items forms the measure.
scale: 1 (Not at all) to 5 (To a very great extent)

description: The traditional bellwether safety measure in the industry, operationalized as the number of accidents per million miles driven. Total highway miles driven were reported in the Blue Book for 1994 and 1995 and were summed, and total accidents for 1994 and 1995 combined were reported in SAFER. Total accidents for these years, divided by total highway miles for these years, and multiplied by 1,000,000 yields the measure.

The frequency of violations attributable to driver mistakes, excluding factors beyond the driver's control. It was operationalized as the number of trucks/drivers taken out of service due to driver fault, divided by the total number of inspections, and multiplied by 100.

The extent to which driver performance in the focal company compared to the performance of other drivers in the industry, compared on 14 dimensions concerning controllable aspects of driver performance. Responses were obtained using 7-point response options ranging from 'Ours are much worse' (1) to 'Ours are much better' (7); the mean of the items forms the measure.
scale: 1 ('Ours are much worse') to 7 ('Ours are much better')

description: Three alternative operationalizations of pay dispersion were available and the analyses were repeated using each. Plant managers reported the starting hourly rate, the hourly rate at the middle of the pay range, and the top hourly rate for production employees, plus typical weekly overtime; the pay rates including estimated overtime pay were annualized and respondents also reported the approximate number of production employees earning each of these three rates. The first operationalization (high minus low) is the highest pay level minus the lowest (or starting) pay level; the second is the coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean; the third is an estimated gini coefficient, with 1.0 indicating absolute inequality of pay and zero indicating complete pay compression.

Pilot tests and discussions with industry officials were used to develop a list of individual incentive practices applicable to the sample. The mean of seven items was used, with responses obtained on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (Not at all) to 5 (To a very large extent).
scale: 1 (Not at all) to 5 (To a very large extent)

description: Because sequential interdependence in concrete pipe production (mixing, casting, curing) is constant across the industry, the measure captured interdependence beyond the production sequence by assessing the extent of use of self-managed teams. The item assessed the percent of production employees currently involved in self-managing work teams.

The number of labor hours worked by production employees in the focal year divided by the tons of concrete products produced in the same year. It was derived by multiplying the average number of full-time production employees in the plant by 2008 hours (the number of working hours in a typical year; also adjusted for average overtime hours reported by the respondent) and dividing by the tons of concrete products produced. Fewer labor hours per ton is indicative of high productivity.
Operationalized as the natural log of the number of lost-time accidents in the plant in the last 5 years. Fewer lost-time accidents indicates better workforce performance.

Designed to parallel the Study 1 measure, assessing controllable aspects of production employee performance in the industry. Responses were obtained using 7-point response options ranging from 'Ours are much worse' (1) to 'Ours are much better' (7), and the mean of the items forms the measure; responses were benchmarked against the industry.
scale: 1 ('Ours are much worse') to 7 ('Ours are much better')

description: We use the foreign partner's percentage of ownership in the IJV to test the baseline prediction on which the moderating hypotheses build. Most of the independent and control variables are either factual or derived from data sources other than the survey used to obtain board composition information.

We followed Kumar and Seth (1998) and divided the number of board members appointed by the foreign partner by the total number of members on the IJV board. To adjust for possible nonindependence of observations within the same host country, we report clustered robust standard errors.

Using generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH) models, we collected daily time series data of the primary stock indices of each host country from Datastream and fitted GARCH models to each individual time series to get daily conditional variances for each country. The daily conditional variances of each country were averaged to obtain a one-year average, for the year preceding the year in which the survey was conducted.
time_window: one-year average for the year preceding the survey year

description: A seven-point Likert scale item measuring how much overlap there is in the markets served by both partners, as assessed by our respondent from the foreign IJV partner.

Taken from IMD's World Competitiveness Yearbook (WCY) to measure how effectively boards monitor management within particular countries. The item used is 'Corporate boards do supervise the management of companies effectively.'
scale: index ranging from 0 (low board effectiveness) to 10 (high board effectiveness)

description: A seven-point Likert scale item measuring how much growth there is in the markets served by the IJV, as assessed by our respondent from the foreign IJV partner.

variable_name: CEO pay gap (cash, long-term, and total compensation)
description: Pay gaps were assessed using cash, long-term, and total compensation collected from proxy statements. Cash compensation includes all remuneration in the form of salary and bonus; long-term compensation equals the value of stock options, performance unit or share plans, restricted stock, phantom stock, and long-term management incentive plans; total compensation is the sum of cash and long-term pay. The gap is the natural logarithm of the quantity equal to the CEO's pay minus the average pay of the four non-CEOs listed in a firm's proxy; top management teams were operationally defined to include the CEO and the four other highest-paid managers. Natural logs were used to reduce heteroskedasticity in the regression models.

Annual return on assets, obtained from COMPUSTAT, was the dependent variable in the performance hypotheses; return on equity yielded similar results. ROA was also used as a control in the analyses of CEO pay gaps.

Relatedness was measured using the Jacquemin and Berry (1979) entropy index: Relatedness equals the sum of P_i ln(1/P_i), where P_i equals the percentage of sales a firm received from its ith four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) segment within its primary two-digit industry. Segment sales and primary industry designations were obtained from the COMPUSTAT Business Segment Tapes.
Number of businesses was measured using the count of four-digit SIC codes listed for a firm in Standard & Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors and Executives.
R&D activity was measured as annual R&D expenditures divided by sales, obtained from COMPUSTAT.

Capital investment activity was measured as annual capital equipment expenditures divided by sales, obtained from COMPUSTAT. The authors note that this measure of capital investment is similar to measures of capital intensity such as the net value of property, plant, and equipment divided by number of employees, but that those measures assess accumulations across time; they considered new capital investment instead.
Firm size was measured as the natural logarithm of a firm's number of employees, data that were obtained from COMPUSTAT.
The number of vice presidents was assessed by counting the number of corporate officers in each firm as listed in Standard & Poor's Million Dollar Directory.

Coordination needs are measured by six separate indicators that were not scaled or aggregated: relatedness of the firm's businesses, number of businesses, R&D activity, capital investment activity, firm size (log of employees) and number of vice presidents. Each enters the regressions as its own variable and the paper treats them as the diversification, technology and structure sources of coordination needs.

Year-to-year change in the total cash compensation paid to the CEO, deflated into constant dollars with the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics cost-of-living index (deflated cash compensation in year t = actual cash compensation in year t / cost-of-living index in year t). Used as the dependent variable for the test of the pay-stock returns hypothesis, on the argument that year-to-year fluctuations in compensation are determined by changes in performance. Compensation is overall cash compensation (salary plus bonus); the Forbes data did not allow the two components to be separated, and stock options are excluded because of measurement problems in valuing them.
time_window: one-year change; independent variables lagged one period

description: The absolute level of total cash compensation paid to the CEO, deflated into constant dollars with the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics cost-of-living index. Used as the dependent variable for the tests of the pay-size and pay-risk hypotheses. Compensation is overall cash compensation (salary plus bonus), which could not be split into components with the Forbes data.
time_window: annual; independent variables lagged one period

description: Number of years an individual had been the CEO of a given company; data were from the Forbes study. Used as the moderator of the pay-stock returns, pay-size and pay-risk relationships.

Abnormal returns were calculated from CRSP data using a market model, E(Rit) = a + B(Rmt) + e, where beta is the five-year stock market beta on stock j and Rmt is the market return, in this case the Standard & Poors Composite Index; both beta and market return are based on market-valued returns. Abnormal returns were operationally defined as the difference between actual and expected returns, Rit - E(Rit). Each time period was one year.
time_window: annual; five-year beta; lagged one period

description: The natural logarithm of the number of a firm's employees. The measure of size was lagged one time period.

Calculated risk by one-year stock market betas, where a high beta indicates that changes in underlying economic fundamentals affect the firm's earnings. The measure of risk was lagged one time period.

variable_name: Extent of strategic change (SC1 and SC2)
description: The dependent variable measures the extent of strategic change enacted during a turnaround, based on field data on the actions managers actually took. SC1 and SC2 were calculated as the average of a firm's standardized scores on a business-level change index (B) and either of two domain change indices (D1 or D2), which use different schemes for weighting acquisitions and divestments. The business-level change index is the total number of business-level management actions taken during the turnaround, with a range of possible scores from 0 to 19. The domain change indices capture acquisitions, divestments, joint ventures, internal start-ups and geographic expansions or contractions, weighted for the number of units involved and/or the percentage of firm sales they represented; the subindices were standardized across sample firms. The exact formulas for the subindices and domain change indices are not recoverable from the text.
time_window: actions taken during the firm's turnaround; CEOs surveyed in late 1989 and early 1990

variable_name: Extent of firm decline (lowest annual ROI during downturn)
description: The extent of a firm's decline was measured as the lowest annual return on investment (net income/total investment) achieved by the firm during its downturn. Lower values indicate more extensive decline, revealed in a deeper trough in the turnaround firm's performance pattern. Turnaround firms were those with at least three consecutive years of ROI below the risk-free rate of return, approximated by the 6-month U.S. treasury note rate at auction.
time_window: the firm's downturn (at least three consecutive years of low performance)

description: Industry growth or decline during a firm's downturn was measured as the GNP-deflated annual growth rate in a firm's industry's shipments during the last 3 years of the firm's performance downturn. The growth rate was calculated from U.S. Commerce Department census data, with a firm's industry defined by the 4-digit SIC code assigned by Standard & Poor's in the first year of the decline if at least 50 percent of revenue originated in that code; for more diversified firms the rate was measured at the 3-digit or 2-digit level at which at least 50 percent of revenue was found.
time_window: last 3 years of the firm's performance downturn

description: Respondents were asked to indicate on a 4-point scale ranging from 'turnaround occurred despite industry conditions' to 'favorable conditions essentially caused the turnaround' what effect they felt the industry environment of the corporation's main business had on the turnaround.
scale: 4-point scale ranging from 'turnaround occurred despite industry conditions' to 'favorable conditions essentially caused the turnaround'

description: The survey asked respondents whether a firm's CEO had been 'replaced' as part of the turnaround, coded yes = 1 and no = 0.

variable_name: Slack resource depletion (highest debt to asset percentage during downturn)
description: The extent of slack financial resource depletion was measured as the firm's highest debt to asset percentage ((long-term debt + short-term debt in current liabilities/total assets) x 100) during its downturn, drawn from the COMPUSTAT data base. Firms with lower values on this ratio have relatively greater access to financial resources through further borrowing, while firms with larger values have more depleted debt capacity.

The level of firm diversity was assessed using the entropy measure, a continuous measure which uses SIC classifications to evaluate extent of diversification. Business segment data (sales and SIC codes) were obtained from COMPUSTAT, with manual collection from Annual Reports, Value Line and Moody's Manuals for firms with downturns beginning before 1978. Diversity was measured in the first year of each firm's downturn, to gauge the level of diversity with which each firm entered the turnaround process.
time_window: first year of each firm's downturn

description: Firm size was measured as a firm's sales revenue (in millions of dollars) for the first year of the firm's downturn. Because firms had different first downturn years and size was measured in dollar revenues, a GNP deflator was used to convert all sales figures into 1988 dollars for consistent comparisons of firms.
time_window: first year of the firm's downturn

description: The number of annual antitrust actions-where actions refer to mergers that are monitored, restructured, prevented, or abandoned-taken by an authority, compiled from raw OECD data on annual national merger policies. The variable reflects an annual account of the antitrust actions, or acts of antitrust holdup, taken by a particular jurisdiction. Higher values therefore represent higher degrees of holdup.

Trade balance (exports minus imports) as a percentage of GDP, calculated from the World Bank's World Development Indicators series. It indicates whether a nation is an overall exporter or importer of traded goods and how much weight the trade profile involves with respect to the domestic economy. The authors expect Trade Balance to negatively impact Antitrust Scrutiny.

Average number of pages devoted to each antitrust jurisdiction in the OECD's annual reports over the 1992-2000 period, used as a proxy of a jurisdiction's commitment to antitrust principles and procedures. The reports are completed by individual antitrust jurisdictions that decide upon the amount of effort and substance put into the reports in response to OECD requests regarding changes to competition laws and policies, enforcement of competition laws and policies, mergers and acquisitions, the role of competition authorities in the formulation and implementation of other policies, and resources. An interaction variable was created by multiplying Institutional Competence and Trade Balance (hereafter Interaction).

The paper does not measure capability separately. It uses one proxy, Institutional Competence, the average number of pages devoted to each antitrust jurisdiction in the OECD annual reports for 1992-2000, as an indicator of the overall competence of an agency in terms of mission, capability and autonomy. It enters the tests as a moderator of the effect of trade balance on antitrust scrutiny.

The paper does not measure autonomy separately. It uses one proxy, Institutional Competence, the average number of pages devoted to each antitrust jurisdiction in the OECD annual reports for 1992-2000, as an indicator of the overall competence of an agency in terms of mission, capability and autonomy. It enters the tests as a moderator of the effect of trade balance on antitrust scrutiny.

The paper does not measure mission separately. It uses one proxy, Institutional Competence, the average number of pages devoted to each antitrust jurisdiction in the OECD annual reports for 1992-2000, as an indicator of the overall competence of an agency in terms of mission, capability and autonomy. It enters the tests as a moderator of the effect of trade balance on antitrust scrutiny.

Reverse-coded density of local newspapers, calculated as the number of daily newspapers per 10,000 people in each MSA. The values were reverse-coded so that a higher value indicated a more severe decline of accountability journalism in each MSA. Only daily newspapers were counted because changing from dailies to weeklies generally indicated that local newspapers were already facing substantial financial distress. Due to unavailable data, missing data for the year 2011 were interpolated assuming a linear relationship over the adjacent years.

Proxy measure based on the density of social associations, calculated as the number of particular social associations per 10,000 people in each MSA. Establishments in County Business Patterns are classified by the North American Industry Classification System, which allows distinguishing private firms, public agencies, and the listed social associations. The annual CBP data were obtained directly rather than from the secondary data created by the Northeast Regional Center for Rural Development.

All official penalties imposed on local firms in a given MSA and year were aggregated and then divided by the total number of establishments in each MSA to standardize the variable. The data come from Violation Tracker, which includes criminal and civil cases brought by regulatory agencies and the Department of Justice and excludes cases against individual executives unless their firm is also a defendant. Penalty amounts less than $5,000 and violations without monetary penalties were eliminated, revised penalty amounts are used, and costs of supplementary projects following settlement are included when officially stated. The MSA-level aggregate measure captures the establishments where wrongdoings occurred rather than headquarters locations.

The overall scale of organizational wrongdoing split into two categories, internal and external. Following the classification of Tang et al. (2012), which differentiates internal and external corporate social responsibility on the basis of how visible the practices are to the public, issues related to employee relations, diversity, and corporate governance are defined as internal organizational wrongdoing. These items were matched to the offense type of individual wrongdoings defined by Good Jobs First.

The overall scale of organizational wrongdoing split into two categories, internal and external. External organizational wrongdoing includes environmental, consumer, competition, and product-related issues. These items were matched to the offense type of individual wrongdoings defined by Good Jobs First.

The dependent variable was the log of the average compensation of top management team members, measured in thousands of DM. German company law does not require the reporting of individual compensation packages, so individual-level data are unavailable; average TMT compensation is used as a proxy for CEO compensation and is argued to be highly correlated with it. All independent and control variables in the models were lagged by one year.
scale: log of average compensation in thousands of DM

description: A relative difference score calculated as the simple difference between CEO education and board chair education, measured as five categories: high school degree (Abitur) or less; vocational university degree; university degree equaling a master's degree; doctoral degree; professor or more than one doctoral degree. The score is positive if the CEO's level of education is higher than that of the board chair and negative if it is lower; equal levels of education result in a value of zero. Absolute (unsigned) difference scores are estimated in separate models for contrast.

Relative tenure was calculated as the simple difference between CEO tenure and board chair tenure, measured in years. An absolute (unsigned) difference score is also estimated in a separate model for contrast.

Presence of the same educational specialization for CEO and board chair was measured as a dummy variable. Specialization was assessed for the highest obtained university degree and categorized into five specializations: arts, sciences, engineering, business and economics, and law.

This binary variable was coded as one if the board chair had at any prior time served as the firm's CEO. It captures similar role experiences between the CEO and the board chair and is used as a proxy for role empathy.

A Herfindahl index used as a continuous measure of ownership concentration, calculated by squaring the share each owner has of the total ownership and summing those squares. The authors note that German firms exhibit much higher ownership concentration than U.S. firms, so a continuous measure is used rather than the binary 5 percent cutoff common in U.S. research.

Measured as the average compensation of supervisory board members for each firm, reported in thousands of DM. Supervisory board members are compensated equally in Germany. All independent and control variables in the models were lagged by one year.

variable_name: Entry tenure of foreign firms in an industry
description: The number of years since each foreign firm was founded in China, then averaged across foreign firms in the four-digit SIC code industry, weighted by their asset sizes. The weighted measure was used to take into account that large foreign firms tend to have greater impact on domestic firms than small ones. Entry tenure of individual foreign firms ranged between 1 and 30 years; the weighted industry-level mean ranged between 1 and 24 years. Values are updated yearly and lagged one year in the models.

Firm annual sales for firm output, deflated using the year 2000's constant price to remove the effects of deflation or inflation due to price change over time. Firm inputs included the log of the firm's capital input (its capital stock, deflated by the GDP deflator on the basis of the year 2000's constant price) and the log of its labor input (its number of employees).

Measured as the sum of foreign firms' export sales divided by the sum of their total sales in the industry. Calculated for each four-digit SIC code industry in the sample and updated yearly. Lagged one year in the models.

variable_name: Intangible asset intensity of foreign firms
description: Measured as the sum of foreign firms' intangible assets divided by the sum of their total assets in the industry. In the CNBS survey database, intangible assets included patents, non-patented technologies, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, and other nonphysical assets. Calculated for each four-digit SIC code industry and updated yearly, lagged one year in the models.

variable_name: Rhythm of entry pattern of foreign firms
description: Following Vermeulen and Barkema's measure of the rhythm of a firm's internationalization process, measured by the kurtosis of the distribution of foreign firms' entry tenure in the industry, where n is the number of foreign firms in the industry, xi is the entry tenure of foreign firm i, and s is the standard deviation of the entry tenure of foreign firms in the industry. Values of the kurtosis ranged between -6 and 11, with higher values indicating more irregular entry patterns and lower values indicating more rhythmic entry patterns; for ease of interpretation it was recoded by multiplying (-1) so that higher values indicate more rhythmic entry patterns. Calculated for each four-digit SIC code industry and updated yearly, lagged one year in the models.
scale: kurtosis values originally between -6 and 11, recoded by multiplying by -1

description: Not directly measured; the paper argues that foreign firms' export intensity, intangible asset intensity, and the rhythm of their entry pattern shape the height of the barriers to imitation faced by domestic firms. The text states that barriers to imitation can be created by information asymmetry and causal ambiguity.

Core strategy measured as R&D expenditure divided by sales. R&D expenditure captures an enterprise's endowment of unique knowledge possessed by individuals and teams within organizations, and these investments require periods from 4 to 6 years to provide a return.
Core strategy measured as advertising expenditure divided by sales. Advertising expenditure captures a firm's intangible assets such as brand name and reputation.
Business performance measured as return on assets, constructed by dividing the annual income before extraordinary items by the total assets.

Industry effects are not measured by observed industry characteristics. They are estimated with variance components, as the share of the total variance in R&D intensity, advertising intensity and ROA that comes from a latent factor shared by firms in the same 4-digit SIC industry. The estimate is made over 5-year (1988-92) and 15-year (1978-92) periods.

Firm effects are not measured by observed firm characteristics. They are estimated with variance components, as the share of the total variance in R&D intensity, advertising intensity and ROA that comes from a latent factor specific to each firm. The estimate is made over 5-year (1988-92) and 15-year (1978-92) periods.

The dependent variable is a dyad-level 1-0 dummy variable indicating whether or not a dyad of two firms formed an R&D alliance in a given year. The authors combined the actual R&D alliances that were formed with dyads that were not realized. The dependent variable is measured for year t, and the independent variables are measured at time t-1. The sample was restricted to domestic alliances with an R&D component between firms headquartered in the United States.
time_window: year t, independent variables at t-1

description: The authors obtained data on the zip codes of the firms' headquarters and used them to determine the latitude and longitude of each firm in the dyad. They then applied spherical geometry, specifically the great circle distance formula, to arrive at a distance calculation in miles; the formula block could not be read in this payload, but the prose states that r is the radius of the earth in miles (3,963) and that latitude and longitude were converted into radians by a division by 180/pi. They then transformed the geographic distance measure by means of a natural log.

Prior_ties equals the number of alliances the design firm has formed with a prospective partner, focusing on the previous alliances formed between the design and partner firm in the past five years. Given the skewness evident for this variable and that firms might not have any prior ties, the authors took the natural log of one plus the number of prior ties.

The authors used the two firms' SIC codes to construct an indicator variable denoting whether they operate in the same industry (i.e., Intraindustry_transaction = 1) or different industries (i.e., Intraindustry_transaction = 0) at the four-digit SIC level. They also examined the robustness of the results by constructing the variable at the three-digit SIC level.
