Founding rates are estimated as the realization of an arrival process in which the dependent variable takes on only integer values; because the variance of the founding rate increases faster than its mean, a stochastic component is inserted in a negative binomial model. The data cover 110 years with 53 observation points at intervals of one to five years, and the different length of the intervals is controlled by creating a variable accounting for diverse time spans and using the offset option.

Focal provincial density is entered linearly to estimate the impact of legitimation processes at the province level and as a squared term to estimate competition at that level. The second model in the analysis uses these local legitimation and competition variables in place of the national density terms.

Density-dependence processes measured at the national level are accounted for with a linear term capturing legitimation and a squared term capturing competition. Both terms are included in the first model, which tests the classical population ecology hypothesis at the national level.

The influence of neighboring subpopulations is measured by a variable computed as the sum of the density values of neighboring provinces; the same variable is squared to verify the nonlinear effect of this influence.

A variable that measures the age of the industry at the province level, included in the model to test the effect of temporal heterogeneity among different subpopulations on founding rates. The same variable is used as the local evolutionary time with which each founder-origin category is interacted.
A variable that controls for the age of the entire industry and is compared with the age of the industry at the province level in the test of temporal heterogeneity.

For each year the authors established whether, during the year before the foundation of a new venture, the founder worked in any of the neighboring provinces, or in more distant provinces, or in no province because he or she was new to the industry. The histories of individual organizations were reconstructed and the geographical movements of 4,272 accountants were tracked over the study period; for every province the sum of the values in each category was lagged to avoid using same-year founders.
time_window: one year before the foundation of the new venture

description: For each year the authors established whether, during the year before the foundation of a new venture, the founder worked within the same geographical area. For every province the sum of the values in this category was lagged.
time_window: one year before the foundation of the new venture

description: The seasonally adjusted monthly unemployment rate, used to gauge current economic conditions. It ranged from a low of 3.8% in April of 2000 to a high of 6.3% in June 2003. Higher values indicate worse economic conditions and are reverse-coded relative to current economic conditions.

The annual unemployment rate in the year each CEO earned his or her highest degree, used to gauge economic conditions at workforce entry. The unemployment rate ranged from 2.9% to 9.7% over this period. Higher values indicate worse economic conditions and are reverse-coded relative to workforce entry economic conditions.
time_window: year each CEO earned his or her highest degree

description: Categorical variable equal to 1 if a grant i at time t has a price-date combination that is only likely to have happened randomly 2.5% of the time or less. To identify such grants, the authors simulated 100,000 randomly assigned grants, calculated the mean and standard deviation of the return for each grant over the possible reporting window, and tagged a grant as suspiciously lucky and likely backdated if it fell outside the 95% confidence interval on the tail representing the lowest rather than the highest price. The dependent variable was estimated using linear probability models.

Our variable of MEPs is the sum of five dummy variables, one for each of the following provisions: staggered boards, limitations on amending bylaws or the charter, supermajority to approve a merger, golden parachutes, and poison pills. Each provision is coded one when the corporation has it. The measure adapts the entrenchment index developed by Bebchuk, Cohen, and Ferrell (2009).

The CSR measure is the result of aggregating the pillars of social performance, environmental performance, and economic performance, giving equal weight to each one. ASSET4 provides performance scores for the four pillars and an overall CSR performance score, ranging between 0 and 100.

The index of internal CSR follows Hawn and Ioannou (2016) and is computed by adding, using the same weights, the respective items of internal CSR actions and then standardizing the resulting measure. Internal actions are substantive actions targeting internal stakeholders, reflected in changes in corporate policies and in CSR implementation practices. The Cronbach's alpha is 83.04.

The index of external CSR follows Hawn and Ioannou (2016) and is computed by adding, using the same weights, the respective items of external CSR actions and then standardizing the resulting measure. External actions comprise claims that firms make to show a commitment to socially desirable behaviors as well as reports and other disclosures. The Cronbach's alpha is 88.04.

Tobin's Q is obtained by dividing the sum of the company's market equity value plus book value of debt by the overall amount of assets. Stock market data were collected from Datastream and accounting information from Worldscope.

Countries were classified into LMEs and CMEs following the framework of Hall and Soskice (2001) and its subsequent refinements for assigning countries with ambiguous systems to the two types of capitalism. The analysis also differentiates the 37 countries into developed and nondeveloped countries and distinguishes between LMEs and CMEs in each group using the taxonomy of Fainshmidt et al. (2018).

Performance minus the aspiration for observations where performance is below the aspiration, and set to zero when performance is above the aspiration. Lower (more negative) values indicate poorer performance, and higher (less negative) values indicate an improvement in performance toward the aspiration from below. The aspiration used is a historical aspiration, an exponentially weighted average of the focal organization's past performance values, with the inertia parameter set at 0.21. The formula for the historical aspiration is presented in a display that is not readable in the available text.

A count of the number of lines of service divested by the hospital during the year. A service line is coded as divested if the service was offered by the hospital during the prior year but is abandoned or discontinued in the focal year. Higher values on the resulting sum indicate greater change.

The number of members on the hospital's governing board. This variable was normed (between 0 and 1, using the lowest and highest values in its range) prior to constructing its interaction with performance.

The percent of the board that has turned over since the prior year. This treatment directly scales for differences driven primarily by overall growth or contraction in board size and focuses more directly on new membership. Values range between 0 and 1.

The percent of the hospital's equity that is held, on average, by each board member. This treatment ensures that differences are driven primarily by the amount of equity held rather than by changes in board size. Values range between 0 and 1.

Dichotomous time-varying measure based on the five most widely circulated rankings of firm donations. It is coded 1 if a firm was located in the lower half of the list and 0 otherwise (i.e., coded as 0 if a firm appeared in the upper half of the list or did not appear on the list). The firm stayed as in the previous ranking and was valuated again on the day when a new list was published, and values were coded as 0 before May 14 and lagged for one day.

variable_name: Not recognized as donor on rankings (lagged)
description: Dichotomous time-varying measure coded 1 after the earliest list was published and if a company did not donate and did not appear on the list; it stayed as 1 until it appeared on a later list, on which day it became 0 and stayed 0. Firms that donated but did not show up on the lists were coded as 0, and the value was lagged for one day.

variable_name: Number of Internet articles on corporate donation (lagged)
description: The total number of articles published on the major websites on corporate donation each day, lagged by one day. The nine most widely read websites (based on Alexa) were selected, and variations in Chinese for 'corporate donation' and 'Sichuan (or Wenchuan) earthquake' were used as key terms to identify articles. The measure was obtained from a previous study of multinational firms' donations in the same context.

variable_name: Number of articles on corporate donation in traditional media (lagged)
description: The total number of articles on corporate donation published in the major nationwide newspapers each day during the same observation period, lagged by one day. Information was collected from WiseSearch, a media database that includes 1,300 newspapers in China, using the category 'the most influential comprehensive media,' which includes 19 newspapers such as People's Daily, Guangming Daily, Economic Daily, South Daily, and Wenhui Daily. The same key terms as for online media were used to identify articles.

The dependent variable is the hazard rate of donation, measured as the number of days from May 12, 2008 until the day the firm made a donation (if ever). Firms that did not donate were considered right-censored, and multiple donations were modeled as repeated events.

The variable private is coded as '1' for private firms and '0' for state firms, based on the Sinofin database's information about the characteristics of the dominant shareholder. State-controlled firms are those where the dominant shareholder is the state, while private firms are those where the dominant shareholder is private individuals.

The real estate industry came under attack because of its potential culpability and extraordinary wealth. About 8% of the sample (47 firms) are in the real estate industry and are coded as '1,' and '0' otherwise.

A binary variable indicating whether a firm had received any of eight nationally recognized reputation rankings or awards or been listed in them before the earthquake; those that had were considered to be firms with high reputation, accounting for 8% of the sample. The rankings include, for example, the most respected companies, the best employer award, China's best corporate citizenship award, and the most praised companies.

Measure of the chair's political status coded 1 if the firm's chair was serving or had previously served as a delegate to the national People's Congress (China's legislative body) or to the national Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference. For those who had served at both levels, only the national-level appointment was considered. In 9% of the sampled firms, the chair had been appointed to the national PC or CPPCC.

Measure of the chair's political status coded 1 if he or she was or had been a delegate to the provincial People's Congress or the provincial Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference. Information was collected case by case through company webpages and corporate publications, and companies were called when public sources were not clear. In 8% of the sample, the chair had been appointed to a provincial office.

variable_name: private, real estate, high reputation and political status indicators
description: Corporate image vulnerability is measured by four sets of firm characteristics: private (non-state) control, being a real estate firm, high reputation (listed in nationally recognized rankings or awards before the earthquake), and the chair's political appointment (national or provincial delegate). Each is a 0/1 variable and each is interacted with the online ranking measures to test the vulnerability hypothesis.

Following He and Wong's (2004) treatment, BD is operationalized as the absolute difference between exploration and exploitation; the absolute difference varies from 0 to 3.25 and the authors reverse it by subtracting the difference score from 5 so that a higher value indicates greater BD. It is built from the CTO-reported exploration and exploitation scales.

CD is operationalized as the product of the exploration and exploitation scales; the exploration and exploitation scales were mean-centered before obtaining their product to mitigate the potential for multicollinearity. It is built from the CTO-reported exploration and exploitation scales.

CEOs rated their firm's performance over the last 12 months on a 1-7 Likert scale in terms of six items. The scale was adapted from Gupta and Govindarajan (1986) and has a Cronbach alpha of 0.89. The same measure was collected from CTOs as a validity check and found to be highly correlated with the CEO ratings.

CTOs indicated on a 1-7 Likert scale the extent to which four statements were true regarding product development in their firm over the past three years (or since founding if the firm was younger). The scale is He and Wong's (2004) exploration scale; the Cronbach alpha is 0.82.

CTOs indicated on a 1-7 Likert scale the extent to which four statements were true regarding product development in their firm over the past three years (or since founding if the firm was younger). The scale is He and Wong's (2004) exploitation scale; the Cronbach alpha is 0.79.

Following prior studies, size is measured as the firm's total number of full-time (or equivalent) employees. Because firm size is log-normally distributed, the authors transform it with the natural log.

Consistent with prior studies, environmental munificence is measured as the average sales growth of firms in the same industry for the past three years, which reflects the availability of resources with which to pursue growth opportunities. The data were obtained from the park administrative offices where the firms were sampled, so munificence is calculated out of all the firms in these parks, including the focal firm.

variable_name: volume of the local-knowledge base (local volume)
description: Informants rated the proportion, on a scale from 0% to 100%, of total working hours the employees of the subunit spent on activities related to each of the three knowledge bases. The authors use this proportion of work as a proxy for the volume of the local-knowledge base, arguing that although the relation between work and knowledge volume is not necessarily linear, it is probably positive and monotonic.

Informants compared the focus of operations of their subunit with that of its direct contact peers and assessed 'How many of your direct contact peers have almost identical operations to yours?' Responses were 'None at all' (coded as 5), 'About half' (coded as 3), and 'Almost all' (coded as 1). Higher values therefore indicate operations that are more dissimilar from peers, i.e., more specialized knowledge bases.
scale: 1-5 (1 = almost all peers with identical operations, 5 = none at all)

description: Multi-item instrument that asked informants, for each of the three knowledge bases, to rate how knowledge was stored in three forms of codification. For the analysis, the average level of codification in these three forms was computed for each knowledge area.

Because direct measures of extra-unit knowledge volume are hard to come by, the number of peer units of a subunit was used as a proxy. The authors argue that a large number of peer units presumably holds more knowledge than a small number of peer units, and that the relationship is most likely positive monotonic although not necessarily linear.

Instrument asking informants to assess what portion of their subunit's employees had good informal relations with employees of peer units and what portion had a good understanding of operations performed at peer units. The measure was used in the models of horizontal inflows, and the alpha coefficient for the scale was 0.84.

Instrument asking informants to assess what portion of their subunit's employees had good informal relations with employees of supervising units and what portion had a good understanding of operations performed at supervising units. The measure was used in the models of vertical inflows, and the alpha coefficient for the scale was 0.78.

Multi-item survey instrument capturing the overall volume of knowledge transmitted into each knowledge base, similar to the approach of Gupta and Govindarajan (1993). Informants were instructed to consider various channels through which knowledge might flow, e.g., meetings, telephone conversations, e-mail, regular mail, policy revisions, training of employees, queries about process or product information, and rated how much knowledge their subunit received from other units for a given knowledge base; the question was repeated for each combination of knowledge base and flow direction. Tests of scale qualities of the flow variables yielded a Cronbach alpha for horizontal inflows of knowledge of 0.74.

Multi-item survey instrument capturing the overall volume of knowledge transmitted into each knowledge base; informants rated how much knowledge their subunit received from other units for a given knowledge base. For example, the item for vertical inflows of technology knowledge asked informants to consider the statement 'Our supervisory units provide us with a great deal of knowledge about technology,' where responses ranged from 1 = 'Agree very little' to 5 = 'Agree very much.' Tests of scale qualities of the flow variables yielded a Cronbach alpha for vertical inflows of knowledge of 0.70.

For the test of reciprocation, intensities of knowledge outflows were measured with a multi-item instrument; the authors state that the questions used are analogous to the ones for inflows. Horizontal outflows of knowledge are used in the models of horizontal inflows.

For the test of reciprocation, intensities of knowledge outflows were measured with a multi-item instrument; the authors state that the questions used are analogous to the ones for inflows. Vertical outflows of knowledge are used in the models of vertical inflows.
Measured via a modified version of instruments developed by Prahalad and Doz (1987). The local responsiveness scale included four items (alpha = 0.63).
Measured via a modified version of instruments developed by Prahalad and Doz (1987). The global integration scale included seven items (alpha = 0.72).

Single-item scale based on cross-functional integration concepts, asking what percentage of the design engineering effort was complete when manufacturing engineering started active involvement in the project. The scale is reverse coded so that a greater value represents greater concurrency.
scale: response scale anchored from no completion at all to complete
time_window: Project execution (start of manufacturing engineering involvement)

description: Three-item scale adapted from Oldham and Hackman's formality measure, covering the degree to which project management rules and procedures were formalized through documents such as contract books and sign-off forms, the degree to which formal project management rules and procedures were actually followed, and the degree to which formal progress reviews (design, gate, phase, or stage reviews) were held. The authors report an internal reliability of 0.83.
scale: response scale anchored from not at all to completely

description: Three-item scale adapted from Van de Ven and Ferry's measure of work group discretion, asking how free project management was, with respect to upper management, to determine interim schedule targets, to determine the project management approach, and to choose the format of progress reviews. The authors report an internal reliability of 0.68.
scale: response scale anchored from not free at all to completely free

description: Three-item scale asking, as perceived by the project group at the beginning of the project, how new on average the product modules were, how new the product configuration was, and overall how new the product technologies to be employed in the project were. The authors report an internal reliability of 0.70.
scale: response scale anchored from not new at all to completely new

description: Three-item scale asking how new on average the individual manufacturing stages were, how new the process layout was, and overall how new the manufacturing technologies to be employed in the project were.
scale: response scale anchored from not new at all to completely new

variable_name: Achievement of the product quality objective
description: Single item measuring the degree to which the original product performance objective was met, answered with respect to how the project group perceived this aspect at the end of the project, at the time of first customer shipment. Response options range from significantly worse than expectations through achieved pessimistic estimates, exactly on target and achieved optimistic estimates, to significantly better than expectations.
scale: response scale anchored from significantly worse than expectations to significantly better than expectations
time_window: End of project execution (first customer shipment)

variable_name: Achievement of the unit cost objective
description: Single item measuring the degree to which the original product unit cost objective was met, answered with respect to how the project group perceived this aspect at the end of the project, at the time of first customer shipment. Response options range from significantly worse than expectations to significantly better than expectations.
scale: response scale anchored from significantly worse than expectations to significantly better than expectations
time_window: End of project execution (first customer shipment)

description: Single item measuring the degree to which the original product time-to-market objective was met, answered with respect to how the project group perceived this aspect at the end of the project, at the time of first customer shipment. Response options range from significantly worse than expectations to significantly better than expectations.
scale: response scale anchored from significantly worse than expectations to significantly better than expectations
time_window: End of project execution (first customer shipment)

description: Single item asking the degree to which customers were satisfied with the product that resulted from the development effort. This is the first market outcome item.
scale: response scale anchored from not satisfied at all to completely satisfied
time_window: At the time of the survey

description: Single item asking how the product's actual sales results compare with sales expectations as of today. This is the second market outcome item.
scale: response scale anchored from much lower to much higher
time_window: At the time of the survey

description: Single-item measure adapted from Olson et al., who describe newness as a function of the firm's experience and familiarity, asking how new the target market was for the company.
scale: response scale anchored from not new at all to completely new

description: Single-item measure adapted from Tyre's measure of disruptiveness, asking to what degree events external to the project (such as strikes, company merger, government regulation, major competitive actions, company reorganization, downsizing) impacted the project.
scale: response scale anchored from no impact at all to great impact

variable_name: market newness and environmentally caused disruption
description: External uncertainty is measured by two single-item survey measures. Market newness asks how new the target market was for the company. Environmentally caused disruption asks to what degree events external to the project, such as strikes, mergers, regulation or competitor actions, affected the project. Each moderates the link between operational and market outcomes.

variable_name: achievement of quality, unit cost and time-to-market objectives
description: Operational outcome achievement is measured by three single-item survey measures of how well the original project objectives were met, answered at the time of first customer shipment: product quality (performance), unit cost and time-to-market. Responses run from significantly worse than expectations to significantly better. Each is a separate dependent variable.
scale: three single items, worse than to better than expectations

variable_name: product technology novelty and process technology novelty
description: Technology novelty is measured by two three-item survey scales, product technology novelty and process technology novelty. Product technology novelty covers how new the product modules, the product architecture and the product technologies overall were to the firm. Process technology novelty covers how new the manufacturing stages, the process layout and the manufacturing technologies were.

Market outcomes are measured by two single-item survey measures: the degree to which customers were satisfied with the product, and how the product's actual sales compare with sales expectations as of today. They are the two dependent variables of the market model.

An eight-item scale measuring the extent to which norms of trust existed, operationalized as expectations for the fulfillment of obligations, mutuality, flexibility, and information exchange. Items were adapted from Zaheer et al. (1998) and Noordewier et al. (1990) and query expectations not due to contracts. Higher values indicate more extensive trust-based governance.

A 13-item scale measuring performance on the outsourced R&D task. There are four dimensions: the (ex post) expected contribution of the technology to the client's product performance, a comparison of actual performance to goals and objectives, adherence to timelines, and the creativity and innovativeness of the technology. Items were adapted from Ancona and Caldwell (1992), Andrews and Smith (1996), and Gatignon and Xuereb (1997), and each dimension is equally weighted in the final scale.

An eight-item scale measuring task-related client skills present at the outset of the engagement. The scale consists of two dimensions within a second-order factor structure that incorporates the experiences and competencies of the client organization and those of individual managers, and each dimension is equally weighted for analysis.
time_window: At the outset of the engagement

description: A five-item teachability scale adapted from Kogut and Zander (1993) that focuses on the lack of need for first-hand experience and/or face-to-face communications to learn the skills involved in the work. The authors report that the composite reliability of this scale is the one exception to the 0.6 guideline they use.

A single item asked whether a significant portion of the supplier's R&D work on the project was conducted at the client's physical site. The responses are entered as a dummy variable in the empirical analysis.

A four-item scale addressing the extent to which R&D activities on the project were performed by the client paralleling the activities of the supplier. The items cover dollar expenditures, value added, hours of work, and numbers of workers.

Average of the standardized scores of firm age, number of employees, and total assets. Employee size and total assets were each measured on a 10-point scale and firm age was calculated as the number of years since founding. Because the respondents were owners or founders, firm success was a proxy for entrepreneurial success.
scale: average of standardized scores of three indicators

description: Average of the standardized scores of three financial indices: ROA, calculated as net income divided by total assets; net asset per share, calculated by dividing total net assets by total share; and three-year sales growth, calculated by dividing the current year's sales by sales three years ago. The larger the number, the more successful the firm. The measure is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Average score of two items measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very strongly): the desire to become a member of the PC and the desire to become a member of the PPCC. The internal reliability of the scale in the hypotheses testing sample has a Cronbach's alpha of .91. The items were included in the Time 2 questionnaire.
time_window: Time 2 questionnaire, two months after Time 1

description: Coded '1' if the chair held a PC or PPCC appointment during the year in which the firm was being observed, and '0' otherwise. In cases in which the position of chair passed to another person during the year, the variable was coded according to the status of the previous chair's political appointment. The unit of analysis is the chair-year.

Six-item scale capturing orientations toward achieving financial and competitive success for the company. Using a projective technique with indirect questioning, respondents identified the importance of each statement based on their personal experience or their judgment of the entrepreneurs around them, on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all important, 5 = very important). The reliability of the scale was .92 in the hypotheses testing sample. The items were included in the Time 1 questionnaire.

Six-item scale capturing desires to address social problems and to shape better social policies. Using a projective technique with indirect questioning, respondents identified the importance of each statement based on their personal experience or their judgment of the entrepreneurs around them, on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all important, 5 = very important). The reliability of the scale was .82 in the hypotheses testing sample. The items were included in the Time 1 questionnaire.

The firm's annual cash dividend payout ratio, which measures the percentage of a company's net income given to shareholders in the form of dividends, used as a standardized score for each chair-year observation. Higher DPR indicates that the chair has a stronger proself motive, contrary to prior literature tailored to Western developed economies. The variable is lagged one year.

Dummy variable coded '1' if the focal firm issued its corporate social responsibility report in a given year, indicating a high prosocial motive, and '0' otherwise. A total of 14% of the firms issued CSR reports. The data were obtained from the Runling database between 2006 and 2012.

The variable growth was measured by the increase in the number of an office's lawyers during the years t - 1 and t and was used to predict the adoption of the tracks during times t and t + 1. Offices that are growing and need to hire additional lawyers have more potential to experience a human resource scarcity. Growth is a "flow" variable; growth between t-1 and t predicts the adoption event between t and t+1.
time_window: t-1 to t, predicting adoption during t to t+1

description: The variable prestige assessed the prestige of principal offices through annual data from the American Lawyer on the top 100 most profitable firms. Profits per partner for a firm was used to impute a measure of prestige for the principal office, and a value of 1 was assigned to the principal offices of firms that ranked in the top 50 on profits per partner and a 0 otherwise. The top 50 was chosen because those in the top 50-100 are apt to move in and out of the top 100 from year to year and do not all enjoy the same reputation for prestige.
scale: 1 = top 50 on profits per partner; 0 otherwise

description: Based on the adoption of the senior attorney track for each principal office. Adoption was flagged when a principal office reported the presence of a senior attorney track for the very first time in its history in the NALP; for example, an office was treated as having adopted during the period February 1, 1989, to February 1, 1990, if the office reported its existence as of the second date but had not as of the earlier date. The variable was coded 1 for adoption, 0 otherwise. Offices that did not adopt by 1994 were treated as right-censored.

Based on the adoption of the staff attorney track for each principal office. Adoption was flagged when a principal office reported the presence of a staff attorney track for the very first time in its history in the NALP. The variable was coded 1 for adoption, 0 otherwise. Offices that did not adopt by 1994 were treated as right-censored.

For the senior attorney track, the variable year 1987 was coded a 1 for 1987 and a 0 for 1988-94. The year 1987 was the first in which the NALP provided information on the existence of senior attorney tracks in principal offices. The variable divides the observations into early and late diffusion windows.

For the staff attorney track, we coded a 1 for the year 1989 and a 0 for years 1990-94. The year 1989 was the first in which the NALP provided information on the existence of staff attorney tracks in principal offices. The variable divides the observations into early and late diffusion windows.

variable_name: firm with interim succession × interim period
description: Two indicator variables are used. 'Firm with interim succession' is coded 1 for treatment firms experiencing interim CEO succession and 0 for control firms experiencing normal succession. 'Interim period' is coded 1 for observations within the period starting from the date a CEO was appointed in an interim capacity to the date he or she was either replaced or promoted to permanent CEO, and 0 for noninterim periods, which run up to eight quarters before the interim appointment and up to eight quarters after the replacement or promotion; for each control firm the counterfactual interim and noninterim periods are coded to match its treatment firm. The interaction between the two indicators is the test of Hypothesis 1, capturing changes in earnings management during interim periods relative to noninterim periods that are incremental to the corresponding changes of control firms.
time_window: interim period of one to 11 quarters, with an average of three quarters

description: Discretionary accruals estimated with Dechow et al.'s modification of the Jones model, with parameters estimated by industry quarter. Total accruals are earnings before extraordinary items less operating cash flows, deflated by the firm's total assets at the beginning of the quarter; the nondiscretionary component of total accruals increases with sales growth, assets growth, and depreciation expenses, which depend on the gross value of property, plant, and equipment. Discretionary accruals are the difference between total accruals and nondiscretionary accruals. A positive value suggests that accruals are used to boost earnings and a negative value that they are used to deflate earnings; higher values indicate a greater extent of income-increasing earnings management.

variable_name: earnings management (discretionary accruals) at Q t - 1
description: The independent variable in the event history models is earnings management measured by discretionary accruals at Q t - 1, lagged relative to the promotion outcome. Discretionary accruals are estimated with Dechow et al.'s modification of the Jones model by industry quarter, as the difference between total accruals (earnings before extraordinary items less operating cash flows, deflated by lagged total assets) and the nondiscretionary component that increases with sales growth, assets growth, and depreciation expenses. A positive value suggests that accruals are used to boost accounting earnings; higher values indicate a greater extent of income-increasing earnings management.

Coded 1 if an interim CEO was appointed permanent CEO at Q t and 0 otherwise. The observation window starts from the quarter in which the interim CEO succession was announced and ends in the quarter in which the interim CEO was promoted or was replaced by a permanent one.
time_window: from the quarter of the interim appointment to the quarter of promotion or replacement

description: Measured by the ratio of outside directors on the board. This governance variable is used as a moderator of the relationship between earnings management and interim CEO promotion.
Measured by the percentage of shares held by the board. This governance variable is used as a moderator of the relationship between earnings management and interim CEO promotion.

Measured by the proportion of directors with a finance or accounting background. This governance variable is used as a moderator of the relationship between earnings management and interim CEO promotion.

A director is defined as a 'busy' director if he or she held three or more directorships; nonbusy board is then measured by 1 minus the proportion of busy directors on the board. This governance variable is used as a moderator of the relationship between earnings management and interim CEO promotion.

Measured by the number of analysts covering the firm, obtained from the I/B/E/S database. This external governance variable is used as a moderator of the relationship between earnings management and interim CEO promotion.

Total number of chemicals patents obtained by a firm in the 4 prior years, used as an indicator of cumulated technical capital. A master list of each firm's divisions, subsidiaries and joint ventures was prepared and its history traced through the study period; chemicals patents were separated from the firm's other patents using the technology classes corresponding to chemicals identified in the Patent Manual. Patent data are from the U.S. Patents Database for all firms, including firms headquartered outside the United States. The variable is lagged one year.

The firm's assets in the chemicals business, computed by multiplying the assets owned by the firm by the proportion of its total sales turnover that was drawn from the chemicals business. Financial data were converted to constant (1985) U.S. dollars and the variable is lagged one year.

The firm's degree centrality (number of linkages) in the prior industry network. Industry networks were constructed for each year from 1982 to 1990 using information on all technical linkages maintained by the firm with the other 96 firms in the sample in that year; data on collaboration activity in 1979, 1980 and 1981 were used to construct the 1982 network to include all linkages formed in the previous 3 years that had not yet been dissolved.

The count of new technical collaborative linkages formed by a firm with other firms in the sample in any year. Only collaborations that involved a technical component were included; agreements that entailed only marketing or distribution arrangements were excluded. Both joint ventures, in which the collaborators set up a distinct organizational entity, and joint development and technology-sharing agreements, in which no distinct organization was set up, were included in the count.

For each successful chemical patent application between 1979 and 1990 the number of citations received by the patent was computed after excluding self-citations; patents applied for in each year were sorted on the basis of their citation weights and the top one-half per cent of patents for that year were identified as key patents. The variable is the total number of such key patents for a firm in a given year. The one-, two-, three- and four-period lagged values were included as covariates.

Identifies capital-poor firms in any year as those that were below the median on all three forms of capital (technical, commercial, and social) for that year. The interaction of this variable with the Important Inventions variable is used to test the prediction that important inventions matter most for firms lacking all three forms of capital.

An indicator variable that equals one if a PE firm has an actual equity ownership stake in the acquirer. As the sample contains publicly listed acquirers, PE equity ownership is only partial and never 100 percent. The authors do not study debt investments by PE firms in acquirers or situations where a PE arranged debt financing without an actual equity stake.

The acquirer's cumulative abnormal return around the takeover announcement, estimated from five days before to five days after the announcement. The measure captures the market's confidence about whether a deal creates value.
time_window: five days before to five days after the announcement

description: Time-variant measure of the target's information environment based on data from the World Bank Governance Indicators. It ranges between 0 (good information environment) and 1 (bad environment). The index measures six components that are related to a deal's information environment.

Time-variant measure of the target's information environment based on the International Country Risk Guide (ICRG) Composite Sovereign Risk index. It ranges between 0 (good information environment) and 1 (bad environment). The ICRG index measures financial, economic, and political risk.

The number of prior deals conducted by an acquirer's PE backer in the target country. The variable is not restricted to a recent time window because PE funds often last for 10 years and key personnel, especially general partners, tend to change jobs less frequently.

The average number of M&A deals that the acquirer's advisors took part in over the past three years. A further variable captures the advisors' cross-border deals only ('# cross-border deals fin. advisors'). The authors restrict the advisor variables to three years because an advisory firm's experience from more than three years ago is less relevant for a current deal.

The average number of M&A deals that the acquirer's most experienced advisor took part in over the past three years. A further variable captures this advisor's cross-border deals only ('# cross-border deals most exp. fin. advisor').

Change in the acquirer's earnings before interest and tax (EBIT). The first measure captures the EBIT change from the year of the acquisition to the year after, while the second one captures the EBIT change until three years after the deal. The authors note the limitation that the increase in EBIT of a PE-backed acquirer may also come from sources other than the acquired firm.
time_window: year of the acquisition to one year after; year of the acquisition to three years after

description: Change in the acquirer's earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) from the year of the acquisition to the year after the deal, and the EBIT change until three years after the deal. The authors note the limitation that the increase in EBIT of a PE-backed acquirer may also come from sources other than the acquired firm.
time_window: year of the acquisition to one year after; year of the acquisition to three years after

description: Burt's (1992) network efficiency variable, calculated from the firm's alliance ego network. In the formula, piq is the proportion of firm i's total ties invested in partner q, mjq is the marginal strength of the relationship between firm j and firm q (who are both partners of i), and Cj is the total number of partners in firm i's ego network. The measure captures the extent of nonredundancy in a firm's network, where higher values, ranging from 0 to 1, signify a network high in structural holes. Alliance ties are assumed to have a five-year productive life span, so a firm's network changes from year to year as alliances are formed or expire.

The logged value of Trajtenberg's (1990) citation-weighted patent count formula, where pi is the number of patents granted to firm i and ci represents the number of citations to firm i's patents. Only fuel cell-related patents (USPTO class 429) were used to measure innovativeness. The measure captures both the rate (pi) and the impact (ci) of innovation. Innovativeness is observed over a five-year window following the observation of the alliance network.
time_window: five-year window following the observation of the alliance network (patent data through 2006)

description: A continuous national corporatism score adopted from Hicks and Kenworthy (1998) and Kenworthy (2003), ranging from 0 to 1, which aggregates macro- and micro-level dimensions of collaboration. The country is assigned based on where the firm carried out the bulk of its innovative activity, as indicated by the location of the majority of its patents' inventors. Because this measure is time-invariant and its main effect is averaged out in a fixed effects specification, the authors created an indicator variable coded 1 if a focal firm hailed from a highly corporatist country (above the sample median) and 0 otherwise, and interacted this indicator with network efficiency.
scale: 0 to 1 continuous; indicator coded 1 for high corporatism

description: The average country-level corporatism score for the portfolio of each focal firm's alliance partners, using the same continuous corporatism measure ranging from 0 to 1. Country assignment is based on where each partner carried out the bulk of its innovative activity, as indicated by the location of the majority of its patents' inventors. The measure changes over time because alliance portfolios are modified as partners from various countries are added or removed, and it is entered continuously and interacted with network efficiency.

variable_name: combinations of focal firm and partner corporatism (HH, HL, LH, LL)
description: Broker and partner corporatism were each split at the median to create four categories capturing combinations of focal firm and partner corporatism: both high (HH), both low (LL), high focal firm and low partners' corporatism (HL), and low focal firm and high partners' corporatism (LH). Each of these categories was interacted with the continuous measure of structural holes. Models 5 and 6 convey the same information but use a different combination as the base category against which the other three are compared.

variable_name: percentage of board meeting time spent in discussion of entrepreneurial issues
description: The dependent variable was the percentage of board meeting time, out of the total amount of time a board met in a year, spent in discussion of entrepreneurial issues. The data were collected from transcripts of board meeting minutes and coded by the target firm's auditors. Coders used a list of indicator words and phrases and recorded the number of times each appeared, how many sentences focused on the topic, the total time spent discussing it, and the percentage of the meeting devoted to it; each coder summed the time, measured in minutes, allocated to identifying or evaluating firm product and/or market opportunities, and this was converted into a percentage of annual meeting time.
scale: percentage of annual board meeting time

description: Board tenure variance was measured as the standard deviation of director tenure, following prior upper echelons studies.

Board functional background heterogeneity was operationalized with Blau's (1977) heterogeneity index (1 - sum of squared proportions), where i is the proportion of the group in the ith category. A high score on this index indicates diversity, and a low one represents homogeneity. Director functional background was categorized as production-operations, research and development and engineering, accounting and finance, management and administration, marketing and sales, law, personnel and labor relations, and other.

The percent output function variable was operationalized as the percentage of directors with functional backgrounds related to output. Output-related backgrounds included marketing and sales, and research and development and engineering.

Each director's firm/industry background, defined as the industry in which the director was employed at the time of each board meeting, was classified categorically as 'insider' (1), 'outsider-intraindustry' (2), or 'outsider-interindustry' (3). Board firm/industry heterogeneity was then calculated using the Blau index described above.

Weak faultlines and strong faultlines were operationalized drawing on Lau and Murnighan (1998), using tenure, functional background, and the firm/industry background of directors on a board. The composite measure (latent construct) was created using a latent class-clustering technique specifically developed for mixed-type data, using the program LatentGOLD to cluster board-years into potential subgroups. Following Barkema and Shvyrkov's (2007) methodology, faultlines were identified and classified as weak, strong, or very strong, and separate weak- and strong-faultline variables were entered in the models. Demographic patterns consistent with faultlines (both weak and strong) were found to be present in 39 percent of the board-years.

The formality or informality of a board's meeting was captured by a factor constructed from three variables: the meeting location, the level of board meeting agenda openness, and the annual frequency of board meetings. Location was coded as the percentage of board meetings held off-site for a fiscal year. Agenda openness was coded by the same accountants who coded the company's board minutes as 1, 'dense detail' (the least openness); 2, 'moderate detail'; 3, 'sparse detail'; or 4, 'no detail' (the most openness). Board meeting frequency was a count of the number of meetings per year; all variables used to construct the factor were standardized and centered, and the factor loadings were .83 (meeting location), .76 (agenda openness), and .78 (frequency of board meetings), with a Cronbach's alpha of .70.

Operationalized as the natural log of the number of full-time employees who had quit in the past year divided by the total number of full-time employees, as reported by store managers. The variable is specific to the full-time employee population.

An additive index of direct and indirect HRM investments, operationalized as a formative measure. Each of the six practice measures was standardized before the z-scores were averaged to form the index.

Operationalized as the natural log of sales per employee, that is, total store sales divided by total full-time equivalent employees. The Chain Store Guide provided sales information for the year following the questionnaire data collection.

Operationalized as the number of employee accidents in the past year divided by total employees, as reported in the questionnaire. The distribution of accident rates was not skewed so the raw ratio was used in the analyses.

Operationalized as the number of full-time employees who had quit in 2004 divided by the number of full-time employees in 2004. The HRM manager provided the number of quits and the total number of full-time employees, checking human resource information systems before reporting. The natural log was used to correct for skewness.

An additive index of HRM practices representing direct and indirect investments, formed from HRM key-informant data and aggregated employee questionnaire responses. Each HRM practice measure was standardized before the z-scores were averaged to form the index.

Operationalized as the natural log of sales per employee. The KIS database provided total sales and total number of full-time equivalent employees for the 2005 calendar year. The productivity ratio had a strong skew so the natural log was used.
Return on assets provided by the KIS database for the 2005 calendar year. The distribution of ROA was not skewed so the raw ratio was used in the analyses.
Profit provided by the KIS database for the 2005 calendar year. The variable was logged because of the skewness of its distribution.

The authors read each AAER entry to identify the years when financial fraud actually occurred and matched them to the independent and control variables based on fraud commitment years. They identified a total number of 265 cases of fraud commitment firm years. Fraud commitment receives a value of 1 if a firm commits financial fraud in a year and is later detected by the SEC, and 0 otherwise.

Following Bushee (2001), dedicated institutional investors are identified among all institutional investors reported in Thomson Reuters Institutional (13F) Holdings using a factor and cluster analysis based on portfolio turnover, momentum trading strategies, and portfolio diversification strategies. Dedicated institutional investors are those low on all three factors, and their average holdings are calculated across four quarters for each year. Dedicated institutional ownership is the ratio of total shares held by dedicated institutional investors to total shares outstanding.

Measured as the sum of six indicator variables: staggered board, limitation on amending bylaws, limitation on amending the charter, supermajority to approve a merger, golden parachute, and poison pill. Because the IRRC published takeover defense provision data every other year until 2004, the four years in the sampling window without IRRC coverage were replaced with data from immediately subsequent years.

Measured as the sum of the average percent of sell recommendations and the average percent of buy recommendations issued by securities analysts across different quarters for each year. The authors focus on sell and buy recommendations because these two types of recommendations have important implications on the trading behavior of individual investors and fund managers, while hold recommendations present the least pressure.

A 95-item, 7-point Likert-type, continuous scale used to measure environmental strategies; due to unidimensionality of the items (as indicated by factor analysis), simple averages of the items were used to construct the scale. High scores indicate proactive strategies of environmental responsiveness. The items were based on the 11 dimensions used in the exploratory research. Because no quantitative data bases reliably measure corporate environmental strategies in the Canadian oil and gas industry, perceptual measures with multiple respondents were used.

A measure of the capabilities respondents perceive as emerging within their organization as a consequence of their environmental practices; it measures the extent to which capabilities with listed characteristics emerged. It was based both on the exploratory study, that is, the three capabilities of stakeholder integration, continuous innovation and organizational learning, and on characteristics of organizational capabilities drawn from the resource-based literature, such as causal ambiguity, lack of an identifiable owner in an organization, path dependency and social complexity. Because hypothesis testing was done within the larger context of the entire industry, a more general measure was used to accommodate other capabilities that companies may associate with environmental responsiveness.

A measure intended to capture the competitive outcomes of the capabilities, developed in order to test Hypothesis 2. The items were determined based on competitively beneficial outcomes of the capabilities perceived by managers during the exploratory study.

variable_name: proactive vs. reactive environmental responsiveness classification
description: The seven case companies were rated along 11 dimensions of environmental response determined by the areas in which the oil and gas industry substantially impacts the natural environment and by dimensions used to evaluate environmental performance in the literature. Companies were considered proactive only if they exhibited a consistent pattern of voluntary environmental practices across all dimensions relevant to their range of operations and a consistent pattern of such voluntary actions over time, before the events of 1988 catalyzed environmental action across most of the industry. Based on these criteria two companies were classified as proactive and five as reactive.

Managers in the second phase were asked, after the concept of capabilities was explained to them, whether they perceived any capabilities as having been built up as a result of their environmental responsiveness strategies; examples of capabilities were not suggested to managers. Interview transcripts were analyzed through the categorization and analysis of emergent concepts and constant comparison to identify common themes, and three emergent capabilities were identified: stakeholder integration, higher-order learning, and continuous innovation.
time_window: 18 months of data collection in 1993 and 1993-94

description: Interviews in the second phase sought to ascertain whether managers perceived environmental practices as having had any positive or negative effects on corporate performance and competitiveness. Managers of the proactive companies perceived a number of competitive benefits, while reactive companies were unable to associate their environmental responsiveness with any positive organizational outcomes other than lower liabilities due to reduction in risk of environmental accidents.

Binary measure distinguishing family firms (= 1) from nonfamily firms (= 0) on the basis of ownership and family involvement in governance and management. Specifically, a firm is classified as a family firm when a family owns a minimum of 5 percent of the shares and at least one family member (a person related by blood or by marriage to the owning family) serves as a member of the top management team.

At least one family member (either the founder or a relative) must serve on the top management team and at least 5 percent of the shares must be held by the family. When the family ownership and control conditions are met, family involvement is measured according to the percentage of ownership held by the family. All firms that do not meet this condition are considered nonfamily firms and are coded as 0, making the variable left-censored.
scale: percentage of family ownership, left-censored at 0

description: The ratio of a firm's R&D expenditures to sales in year t adjusted by subtracting median industry-level R&D expenditures to sales in the same year. The authors treat it as an indication of a firm's long term economic orientation because R&D investments generally do not yield payoffs immediately.

variable_name: R&D variability (logged variance in R&D investments)
description: R&D variability is measured with a multiplicative heteroskedasticity approach adapted to a panel data setting. R&D investments over the previous five-year period [(t - 6) to (t-1)] are used to predict the mean and variance of R&D investments in year t, and the y coefficient representing the log of the variance of R&D is calculated for each firm-year. The y coefficient provides a measure of variability that is over and above the mean levels of R&D investments predicted from previous years. The equations specifying the mean and variance models appear in this text only as formula blocks that could not be extracted, so the exact specification cannot be reproduced from the prose.
time_window: previous five-year period [(t - 6) to (t-1)] predicting variance in year t

description: Following Chen (2008), two continuous but censored variables measure negative aspiration gaps: the absolute value of the gap between a firm's performance in year t - 1 and its historical performance in year t - 2, and the absolute value of the gap between performance in year t - 1 and competitors' performance in year t - 2, each used if the gap is negative and coded as zero otherwise, making the variables right-censored. Performance is return on assets (ROA), which the authors describe as an internally oriented measure under greater managerial control, and competitors' performance is the median ROA of firms in the relevant four-digit SIC industry. The interaction terms for the hypotheses multiply the family firm and family involvement variables by these negative aspiration gap variables.
time_window: performance in t - 1 relative to historical and competitor performance in t - 2

description: We gauged CEO pay level as the logged value of total compensation. Total pay is the combined amount of compensation an executive receives.
Long-term pay structure was measured as the ratio of long-term pay to total compensation, an approach commonly used to assess pay structure.

The level of TMT member pay was calculated by logging the average value of total compensation granted each of the top four executives in 1992. The TMT is defined as the four highest paid executives reporting to the CEO.

TMT long-term pay structure was gauged as the proportion of total compensation paid in long-term forms, averaged over the top four executives in 1992. It serves as a proxy for TMT external alignment, the independent variable used to test Hypothesis 2.

The proxies for managerial complexity (i.e., firm size, R&D intensity, and product and geographic diversification) identified by prior research, along with CEO total pay, were regressed on TMT total pay, and the equation was used to generate a residual for every firm. Positive residuals indicate that complexity and CEO pay have a stronger than expected relationship with TMT member pay; negative residuals indicate that such factors have a weaker than expected association.

Spline variable built from the TMT internal alignment residual: set equal to the residual term if it was positive, and zero otherwise. Spline functions incorporate the notion that preferences and behaviors can vary depending upon whether one's position is above or below a certain aspiration level; here the theoretical aspiration level is where the residual equals zero.

Spline variable built from the TMT internal alignment residual: set equal to zero if the residual was positive, and took the actual residual value otherwise. The sign of the underpayment variable was reversed so that larger positive values signified greater underpayment.

We measured performance as average return on assets (ROA) during 1993-95. ROA indicates the efficiency with which a firm employs its current asset base, and the 3-year average ROA was used to smooth any abnormalities associated with a single year's performance.

Net profits over total assets in a given year. Used as the dependent variable in the performance regressions, together with market-to-book. Winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles because the authors winsorized the key variables that vary substantially, chiefly performance and investment variables.

Computed as the total market value of stocks divided by the book value of equity. It is an indicator of future return on equity and hence incorporates future market expectations about firm-level performance.

Ratio of a firm's yearly capital expenditures to its initial stock of fixed capital, observed at the end of the previous year. Used as the dependent variable in the investment regressions. Winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles.
time_window: capital expenditures in year t over initial stock of fixed capital at the end of the previous year

description: Dummy variable set equal to 1 for a company among whose owners is another company in which BNDES has equity, and 0 otherwise. It captures total stakes, direct or indirect, because precise information on the magnitude of indirect BNDES equity holdings in pyramidal chains is not publicly available; the authors focus on at most two layers of ownership.

Continuous variable measuring the percentage of equity held by the bank (from 0 to 100%) through direct equity holdings by the state via BNDESPAR. Used in the regressions with and without the propensity score matching correction.

Two dummy variables indicating whether a BNDES direct stake was more than 0 percent (i.e., there is some stake) or more than 10 percent. The 10 percent cutoff reflects Brazilian legislation under which shareholders with more than 10 percent of a firm's equity can require a seat on its board of directors, an indication of a potential distinctive capacity of the Brazilian government to influence decisions.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if a company belongs to a business group and 0 otherwise; about 45 percent of the observations are from firms belonging to some group. A firm was considered a member of a group when it was controlled by an owner or owners who controlled other firms in the data set; detection of controlling stakes relied on a detailed analysis of shareholder agreements available at the CVM website and on identifying owners with distinctive control rights (more seats on the board of directors). Multinationals with single subsidiaries in Brazil were not treated as groups.

Composite variable coded 1 if both Q and C are equal to 1 and 0 otherwise. Q is a dummy equal to 1 if Tobin's Q exceeds unity and 0 otherwise; Tobin's Q is computed as the market value of stocks plus the book value of debt, divided by the book value of total assets. C (constraint) is a dummy coded 1 if a firm's ratio of net profits to the initial stock of fixed capital was below the sample median and 0 otherwise, so that a firm coded 1 has low cash flow relative to its stock of fixed assets and needs to attract more external capital. Constrained opportunity was interacted with both the minority and the group dummy.
time_window: same year; Tobin's Q and the profit ratio contemporaneous with the observation

variable_name: ease of credit, competition legislation, availability of skilled labor
description: World Competitiveness Report survey items answered by senior and middle managers: ease of credit asks to what extent credit is easily available for business; competition legislation asks whether competition legislation is efficient in preventing unfair competition; availability of skilled labor asks to what extent skilled labor is readily available. Because these measures are highly correlated with time, they are measured as percentage yearly variation using three-year moving average windows, and time and its interactions with the key variables are added as controls.

variable_name: country credit rating and stock market capitalization to GDP
description: Country credit rating is based on a scale from Institutional Investor; stock market capitalization to GDP was obtained from the World Bank's World Development Indicators database. Both are computed as percentage yearly variation using three-year moving average windows to avoid picking up a natural improvement trend in the local environment, and time and its interactions with the key variables are added as controls.

Simple count measure of time beginning with a value of 1 for the first year of the series (1995), whose objective was to assess how the effect of state equity changed over the years. Used both as an interacted institutional variable and, when a specific institutional variable is added, as a control together with its interactions with the key variables of interest.

Management compensation was measured as the salary, bonus, and other miscellaneous earnings of a company's highest-paid director. Information for calculating wider measures of compensation, such as those including the value of stock options held by top managers, are not typically available in the United Kingdom. Current reporting requirements governed by the 1985 U.K. Companies Act do not lead to sufficient information being released regarding exercise price or vesting periods of options. The variable enters the compensation equation in logarithms.

variable_name: Proportion of outsiders on main board
description: The mix of inside and outside directors was measured as the proportion of directors who were not executives of a company on its main board. Both Lambert and colleagues (1993) and Westphal and Zajac (1994) used such a measure. Data on boardroom governance were derived from each company report annually.

Total shareholder return, reflecting share price appreciation and dividend yield and calculated as the proportional change in a company's return index. The performance measure was calculated from Datastream International, an on-line database with accounting and market-based company information.

A dummy variable equal to one if a company reported the existence of a remuneration committee in its annual report and to zero otherwise. Main and Johnston (1993) used this measure. Models using this variable are estimated on all observations.

variable_name: Proportion of outsiders on remuneration committee
description: The proportion of nonexecutive (outside) directors on a company's remuneration committee; a similar measure was used by Daily and colleagues (1996). This estimate had to drop cases in which a remuneration committee did not exist.

A dummy variable equal to one if the posts of chief executive officer and chairperson were combined and to zero otherwise, following Boyd (1994), Daily and Dalton (1994), Main and colleagues (1994) and Zajac and Westphal (1994).

An indicator termed EPS was calculated as a z score for each firm: the numerator was computed by subtracting the average firm EPS over the past three years from the current year's EPS. The denominator consists of the firm's average standard deviation over the four years, where year i = 1 is the current year and i = 4 is the third previous year. Substandard performers have negative scores, while high performing firms have positive scores. The displayed formula could not be extracted from the paper.
time_window: current year relative to the three previous years

description: The decision for a firm to join either the Microelectronics and Computer Corporation (MCC), incorporated in December 1982, the Software Productivity Consortium (SPC), incorporated in December 1984, or the Corporation for Open Systems (COS), incorporated in March 1985, constitutes the dichotomous adoption measure. The three collaboratives were selected because membership constitutes a substantial departure from conventional methods of organizing large R&D projects, and the timing of their incorporation means the decision to join each must be framed as a separate decision. Nonadopters are the remaining firms in the sample which had not joined a collaborative by the time of data analysis; membership was verified using the collaboratives' Articles of Incorporation, the Federal Register and Department of Commerce participant lists.

In addition to measuring adoption as a dichotomous adopt/nonadopt variable, the timing of adoption is measured using a dichotomous early/late variable. Early adopters were identified from the full membership list of each collaborative during the structured interview process; late adopters are the second wave of members, who typically followed the early adopters by 10 to 19 months after formal incorporation. Two firms joined two collaboratives and, being early adopters of each, were coded as early adopters of both. Each set of adopters was verified using participant lists from the U.S. Department of Commerce Office of Productivity and Technological Innovation and the Federal Register.

A binary variable comparing the average patenting rate of the focal firm to the average of all global firms in its technological class. The compound annual patent growth rate (CAPGR) is calculated over three-year moving windows for firm i and separately for firm i's primary technological patent class c, excluding firm i. Quantitative Convergence is coded 1 if firm i exhibits a higher average patent growth rate than that of the corresponding technological class, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: three-year moving windows over the firm's patenting period

description: A count of the focal firm's patents whose forward citations, excluding self-citations, exceed the average number of forward citations received by all patents, excluding the focal firm's patents, in the same issue year in the corresponding technological class. Forward citations are counted over the five-year period after the patent is issued. The greater the number of patents that exceed the technological class average in forward citations, the closer the laggard becomes to the global technological frontier.

A dummy variable coded 1 if the focal firm's patents cite patents that belong to Korean, Taiwanese, and Chinese firms that have realized convergence to the global technological frontier prior to the focal firm and that operate in the same three-digit SIC industry, and 0 otherwise. Firms that do not cite technologically successful peers typically cite the patents of advanced country firms (such as U.S., European, and Japanese firms).

variable_name: Degree of Learning from Technologically Successful Peers
description: The ratio of focal firm citations to technologically successful peer patents as a percentage of its total citations. The larger the ratio, the more the focal firm relies on knowledge developed by technologically successful peers versus that of advanced country firms. A squared term (Degree of Learning from Technologically Successful Peers Squared) is included to test for diminishing marginal returns.

variable_name: Learning from Technologically Proximal Successful Peers
description: Technological distance from successful peers is calculated as the Euclidean distance between the focal firm's patents and those of its technologically successful peers, defined as the square root of the sum over n patent classes of (p_c - p'_c)^2, where p_c is the percentage of the citing firm's patents in technological class c and p'_c is the percentage of the cited firms' patents in patent class c. Because the authors are interested in proximity rather than distance, the measure is the inverse of that Euclidean distance. Increasing values indicate technologically successful peers that are more technologically similar to the focal laggard, and a squared term is also included.

Market expansion is measured as the number of systems added to a cable operator's holdings in a given year. This represents a decision to extend the firm's existing business model to new markets by making a large infrastructure investment in additional headend facilities. The dependent variable is left censored at zero because market expansion is defined as the increase in cable systems, and there is no expansion in about two-thirds of the firm years in the sample. The average firm adds approximately 4.6 systems per year; the number of systems is drawn from archival industry listings.

CEO tenure is measured as the number of years since a founder started a cable operation or an agent was hired into the chief executive position by a specific organization. In the sample, tenure ranges from 0 to a maximum of 44, with a mean value of 8.66. Because the authors predict quadratic effects, the models also include the variable CEO tenure squared. Archival records are the source for all tenure data, primarily the Television and Cable Factbook and the Cable TV Financial Databook, each of which provides an annual listing of the chief executive for each cable operator.

The authors use the average number of potential customers (i.e., total homes in the firm's franchised areas) per system to proxy for firm-specific market complexity in a contextually relevant way. This measure of population density captures variation in the complexity of markets served across firms and over time because denser systems are typically in more populated areas, which, in turn, are frequently more diverse and provide more alternatives and complexity for infrastructure development. The variable is lagged by one year in the models.

Founder is an indicator variable that equals 1 if the CEO has been with the firm since its inception and still retains at least 40 percent ownership in the firm. In this sample most agent CEOs are division heads within larger media, telephony, or equipment manufacturing firms, while founder CEOs are typically either entrepreneurs who started pure-play cable companies or the heads of regional family-owned media companies that diversified into cable. In the estimation, founder status is interacted with CEO tenure and market complexity.

Dummy variable equal to one for acquisitions classified in the early portion of an industry merger wave, zero otherwise. Industry is defined as all firms having the same 2-digit SIC code; merger waves are identified by starting from the peak year of acquisition activity and working backwards until a year in which the number of acquisitions is less than one-third of the peak year's transactions. Acquirers in the first 20 percent of the acquisitions in a merger wave are classified as early movers; 98 acquisitions (18.85 percent of the sample) are so classified.

variable_name: Combined abnormal announcement return of target and acquirer
description: A weighted combination of the target's and the acquirer's industry-adjusted announcement returns, weighted according to the relative sizes of the target and the acquirer. Abnormal returns are obtained by differencing the returns earned by the shareholders of the firms involved in the acquisition and the returns to a value-weighted portfolio of all firms in the same 2-digit SIC industry, so that industry spillover effects are netted out. The window is three days around the announcement (-1 to +1), with an eleven-day window (-5 to +5) used in one model.
time_window: 3-day window (-1 to +1) around the announcement; 11-day window (-5 to +5) in one model

variable_name: Industry-adjusted acquisition announcement return of the acquirer
description: The acquiring firm's announcement period return differenced against the return to a value-weighted portfolio of all firms in the same 2-digit SIC industry. Announcement returns are measured over the interval -1 to +1 in the main models, and over -5 to +5 in a model that accounts for information leakage and subsequent price adjustments. The mean announcement return for acquirers in the sample is negative.
time_window: 3-day window (-1 to +1) around the announcement; 11-day window (-5 to +5) in one model

description: Dummy variable equal to one for early-mover acquisitions in which the target is in the same industry (same 2-digit SIC code as the acquirer), the acquirer's industry was in an expansionary phase, and cash payments exceeded stock payments; zero otherwise. Twenty acquisitions, roughly one-quarter of the early movers and 3.85 percent of all acquirers, fit this profile.

variable_name: Acquirer and target are in the same industry [1,0]
description: Dummy variable equal to one when the acquirer and the acquired firm shared the same 2-digit SIC code, and zero otherwise. Sixty-three percent of the acquisitions in the sample involved firms in the same industry.

variable_name: Acquirer's industry was in an expansionary phase [1,0]
description: Dummy variable equal to one if the industry merger wave was classified as expansionary, zero if contractionary. For each industry and year classified as part of a merger wave the authors identify the total number of companies with Compustat data and determine inflation-adjusted aggregate industry sales and assets; a wave is expansionary if the industry expanded on at least two of three dimensions (number of firms, aggregate sales, aggregate assets) over the period in question. Eighty-six percent of the acquisitions occurred in expansionary industries.

Dummy variable equal to one if the proportion of stock used in the acquisition exceeds the proportion of cash, zero otherwise. Sixty percent of the acquisitions in the sample were stock-dominated, so higher values of the variable indicate less cash financing.
