Indicator variable that took the value of 1 if a parent-spinoff firm pair shared at least one common director, and 0 if not. Data on the directors serving on the boards of the parent and spinoff firms were hand-collected from proxy statements and registration statements. In the treatment effects models, the predicted values of this variable from the first-stage regression were used as the key independent variable in the second-stage regressions.
time_window: year in which the spinoff took place and the three years thereafter

description: The value-weighted, average annual stock market returns of the parent and spinoff firms. Each firm's independent stock market returns are weighted by its relative size: the parent firm's returns are weighted by the parent's end-of-year market capitalization divided by the sum of the parent's and spinoff's end-of-year market capitalizations, and the spinoff firm's returns are weighted by the spinoff's share of that sum. The authors state it is necessary to construct the variable this way because parent firms are typically much larger in size than their spinoff firms.

Annual stock returns of the parent firm, where annual stock returns (Rt) were defined as (Pt + Divt - Pt-1)/Pt-1, with Pt representing the end-of-year stock price in year t and Divt representing dividends in year t. Financial and stock market data for the parent firms were gathered from Compustat and CRSP.

Annual stock returns of the spinoff firm, using the same annual stock return definition as for the parent firm: (Pt + Divt - Pt-1)/Pt-1, with Pt the end-of-year stock price in year t and Divt dividends in year t. Financial and stock market data for the spinoff firms were gathered from Compustat and CRSP.

The spinoff firm's total sales to its parent firm scaled by the spinoff firm's total sales, both measured in the year pre-spinoff, and applied in all of the post-spinoff years. The pre-spinoff financial information on the spinoff firms was collected from the registration statements filed by the spinoff firms upon completion of their spinoffs. The authors note that post-spinoff sales data are not publicly available, so pre-spinoff sales dependence is used as a proxy.
time_window: measured in the year pre-spinoff, applied in all post-spinoff years

description: Indicator variable taking the value of 1 in all post-spinoff years if Share of Sales exceeded the median value of that variable's distribution in the year pre-spinoff. It is used to identify the two spinoff 'types' in the switching regressions and in the interaction terms.
time_window: measured in the year pre-spinoff, applied in all post-spinoff years

description: Indicates whether entrepreneurs were CPC members before founding their enterprise (1 = yes, 0 = no), based on survey items asking whether the focal entrepreneur was a CPC member or cadre or joined the CPC before establishing their venture, as well as the date when the focal entrepreneur joined the CPC. The variable is time-invariant and reflects entrepreneurs' life history; 25 percent of entrepreneurs in the sample have the communist ideological imprint.

A binary variable reflecting whether the firm has foreign investment (1 = yes, 0 = no). It is one of two proxies for inward internationalization, the other being the ratio of foreign investment over total assets, and it serves as the dependent variable in the first stage of the Heckman model.

variable_name: ratio of foreign investment over total assets
description: The ratio of foreign investment over total assets, used as the continuous measure of inward internationalization in the second stage of the Heckman model.

A binary variable reflecting whether the firm has overseas assets (1 = yes, 0 = no), used as the dependent variable in the first stage of the Heckman model for outward internationalization. Information on outward internationalization is available only from 2000, so these analyses cover the last seven waves of the survey.

variable_name: ratio of overseas assets over total assets
description: The ratio of overseas assets over total assets, used as the continuous measure of outward internationalization in the second stage of the Heckman model. Information on outward internationalization is available only from 2000.

Measured by whether the entrepreneur served in a given year as a delegate to the People's Congress (PC) or the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) (1 = yes, 0 = no), legislative bodies the authors describe as the only means for the public to participate in government decisions.
Gauged by the ratio of firms' profits taken by the government in a given year as 'various fees to be shared with the government' - what Li, Meng, and Zhang (2006) termed 'relational fees'.

variable_name: involvement in the government-created industry social network
description: Measured on an annual basis by membership in the Association of Private Entrepreneurs (APE; 1 = yes, 0 = no), a government-created industry social network.

A binary variable indicating whether it was post-2001 (1 = yes, 0 = no), when the '10th Five-Year National Economic and Social Development Plan' was implemented, explicitly encouraging foreign cooperation.
time_window: yearly indicator of the post-2001 period

description: Calculated by the value of total FDI over the local GDP yearly, using data from the China Regional Statistical Yearbook.

The degree of overoptimism in venture operation was determined as the difference between the nascent entrepreneur's likelihood of venture operation and an indicator variable (status) that equals '1' if the venture is operational and '0' otherwise. The likelihood was elicited as the respondent's answer on a scale of zero to one hundred to the question of the likelihood that the business would be operating five years from now. The formula block in the paper was not extracted, so the exact specification is not readable from the text.
time_window: Expectation at first interview; status at follow-up interviews up to 60 months

description: The degree of overoptimism for sales was determined as a function of ex ante expectations and actual realizations, using a deflator to reduce heterogeneity in the measure. Expectations of total sales, revenues, or fees in the first full year of operation were elicited ex ante and compared with the sales or revenue actually achieved in the first full year of operation. The formula block in the paper was not extracted, so the exact specification is not readable from the text.
time_window: Ex ante expectation compared with actual first full year of operation

description: The degree of overoptimism for employment was determined as a function of ex ante expectations and actual realizations, using a deflator to reduce heterogeneity in the measure. Entrepreneurs were asked how many full-time employees, not counting owners, they expected to be working for pay at the new business by the end of the first full year of operation, and this was compared with the number of nonowner employees hired. The formula block in the paper was not extracted, so the exact specification is not readable from the text.
time_window: Ex ante expectation compared with actual first full year of operation

description: Formal business planning was determined to be present when nascent entrepreneurs responded that they had a business plan and that the current form of the plan was 'formally prepared.' Those responding in the affirmative were coded '1' and '0' otherwise.

The undertaking of financial projections was represented by a dichotomous variable based on the question: 'Have projected financial statements, such as income and cash flow statements or break-even analysis, been developed?' Coded '1' for yes and '0' otherwise.

Respondents were asked: 'On a scale of zero to one hundred, what is the likelihood that this business will be operating five years from now, regardless of who owns and operates the firm?' The likelihood obtained is referred to as the nascent entrepreneurs' expectation of operation.

Respondents classified the current status of the start-up effort as an operating business, an active start-up, an inactive start-up, or no longer worked on by anyone. Those who reported an operating business and did not abandon it at a future date were coded as operating; all those who reported the business was no longer worked on by anyone were coded as not operational unless other team members had successfully started the venture. Those reporting active and inactive start-up activity more than five years from the original phone interview were classified as not operational, and remaining start-ups not operational or abandoned without a phone interview at least 60 months after the original interview were classified as missing.
time_window: Up to 60 months after the initial screening interview

description: Nascent entrepreneurs were asked: 'What would you expect the total sales, revenues, or fees to be in the first full year of operation?' Expectations related to fifth-year sales were also elicited, but the PSED did not obtain information regarding actual fifth-year sales.

Entrepreneurs who were involved in a start-up that had completed its first full year of operation were asked what sales or revenue was achieved in the first full year of operation. Validity checks on the timing of the ventures' launch and the timing of the responses were conducted and cases where responses did not represent first-year operations were removed.

For employment expectations, the entrepreneurs were asked: 'By the end of the first full year of operation, about how many full-time employees, not counting owners, do you expect to be working for pay at this new business?'
time_window: End of first full year of operation (expected)

description: Entrepreneurs who were involved in a start-up that employed a nonowner employee were asked to provide the number of nonowner employees hired in full-time and part-time capacities.
time_window: End of first full year of operation (actual)

description: CEO tenure is measured as the total number of years a specific individual had held the chief executive officer position with a company. It is collected for each year from 1992 through 1996 and is entered in the models both as a linear term and as a squared term.

Firm inventiveness is the count of the total number of patents a firm successfully filed (that is, patents that ultimately were granted) in a single year. It is computed for each year from 1993 through 1997 and matched with independent and control variables measured in the prior year, so that the dependent variable is measured one year after the independent variables (t + 1). Patent filing dates rather than the later grant dates are used to eliminate uncontrolled variance from the patent-granting process.

Technological dynamism captures the exogenous uncertainty surrounding a firm's technological endeavors. The authors started with the population of 238 biotechnology firms plus 12 traditional pharmaceutical firms, used Bioscan data to build 'technology profiles' from each firm's self-reported participation in up to 41 possible areas of technology, calculated the technological proximity of every pair of firms from the correspondence of their profiles, grouped firms with highly similar profiles by cluster analysis, and finally computed the variance in monthly stock market returns for each group of technologically similar companies for each year. Because the groupings were based on technological profiles, differences in return variances among the groups are attributed to differences in the rate of change in and the unpredictability of the technologies pursued by each group.

A multi-item online survey administered by the Reputation Institute to members of the general public, who first had to be somewhat or very familiar with a firm to evaluate it. Respondents rated four items on a seven-point scale where 1 indicated 'strongly disagree' and 7 indicated 'strongly agree'. A company's score is the average of the scores of all respondents evaluating that company within a country, converted to a 0-100 scale.
time_window: survey year, 2007-2011 (2006 data used to construct the lag for 2007)

description: Each firm's one-year cumulative total return, which accounts for stock price changes and disbursements to shareholders by assuming that cash dividends are reinvested on the ex-date. It is not normalized by average market returns in each country. The variable is lagged one year.
time_window: one-year cumulative total return, lagged one year

description: The standard deviation of each firm's return on assets (ROA) over the past 10 years, normalized by the average volatility level for each country. The authors describe this as a long-standing and well-accepted proxy for earnings volatility. The variable is lagged one year.

A binary variable that equals 1 if the company participates in the United Nations Global Compact (UNGC) or the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and 0 otherwise. The authors focus on social reporting and participation in voluntary CSR initiatives as visible signals of the firm's espoused commitment to CSR. The variable is lagged one year.

The World Bank Doing Business project's 'Protecting Investors' index, based on a methodology described by Djankov et al. (2008). A country's score can theoretically range from 0 to 10 based on the presence or absence of 10 representative shareholder rights provisions, organized into three categories. The measure is time-varying and lagged one year.

A four-point index built from components of the World Bank Doing Business project's 'Getting Credit' index that Djankov et al. (2007) suggest are directly related to creditor rights. The index counts whether secured creditors are paid first when a debtor is liquidated, are paid first where the debtor is not subject to an insolvency procedure, face an automatic stay from collecting assets during a court-authorized reorganization, and can enforce a security right outside of court following the creation of a security interest. The measure is time-varying and lagged one year.

A scale ranging from 0 to 2 depending on how many of the ILO's two 'core' standards on collective bargaining and freedom of association were ratified and in effect for each country and year. Previously ratified conventions may be denounced by countries. The measure is time-varying and lagged one year.

Binary variable taking the value of 1 if a given firm acquires a given target plant in a given year and 0 if not; all plants existing at time t are considered potential acquisition targets by a given acquiring firm, and an acquiring firm or target plant is dropped from the sample if it dissolves. The unit of analysis is the acquirer-target-year combination, giving 1,229,057 combinations including the 184 actual acquisitions.

Value of the productivity index developed by Caves, Christensen, and Diewert (1982) and later modified by Aw, Chung, and Roberts (2003) for the potential target plant in the previous year. The index measures the proportional difference between the productivity of firm i in year t relative to the hypothetical firm in the base year, using labor input, material input and capital stock as inputs, with input shares used as weights. Acquirer Productivity, measured the same way (aggregated to a sales-weighted average for multi-plant acquirers), is included as a control so that the coefficient of Target Productivity captures the effect of target capability controlling for that of the acquiring firm.

Two-slope decomposition of the main target productivity measure: equal to Target Productivity if Target Productivity is greater than Acquirer Productivity, and 0 otherwise. Included in the regression together with its interaction with the New Region dummy.

Two-slope decomposition of the main target productivity measure: equal to Target Productivity if Target Productivity is less than or equal to Acquirer Productivity, and 0 otherwise. Included in the regression together with its interaction with the New Region dummy.
Binary variable taking the value of 1 if the target operates in a region where the acquirer has no existing presence and 0 otherwise; geographic regions are treated as distinct markets.

Measure of the acquirer's acquisition capability calculated as one minus the Herfindahl index of its sales distribution across regions, on the basis that geographically diversified firms have greater experience coordinating across markets and more generalized capabilities.

Second measure of the acquirer's acquisition capability, measured as the count of acquisitions the firm has undertaken in the past. The authors note that the two measures represent distinct theoretical constructs that are highly related in this empirical context, and therefore use both as measures of general acquisition capabilities.

The style's annual number of granted patents is segmented into four five-year panels; within each panel a trend is estimated by regressing the number of patents granted yearly against a variable denoting the years in that panel. The dependent variable is that regression's standard error, which yields the turbulence of style s at period p. The variable is used logged in the model.

Function turbulence for a utility category u in period p is calculated in the same way as style turbulence, as the standard error of a trend regression over a five-year panel of the category's utility patents. A style is linked to utility subclasses through citations from its design patents to utility patents; the style-period value is the sum of the turbulence of all utility categories referred to by any design patent in the style period, allowing for repeated citations. It enters the model lagged by one period and logged.

An indicator of the five-year period to which a style-period observation belongs, used to capture the time trend in style turbulence. The style's annual patents are segmented into four successive five-year panels.

Cash and cash equivalents scaled by total assets. This ratio is adjusted by subtracting the mean ratio of cash and cash equivalents to total assets for all firms operating in the same four-digit industry and country as the focal firm, so it is a close estimate of excess cash resources compared to industry and country norms. Consistent with the hypothesized quadratic relationship, financial slack squared was also calculated. All ratio variables were truncated at the 0.5 percent tails.

The number of employees, measured in full-time equivalents, scaled by total sales. The ratio is adjusted by subtracting the mean ratio of employees to sales for all firms operating in the same four-digit industry and country as the focal firm; when firms employ more people to generate a specific amount of sales relative to their peers, they are expected to have more HR slack. HR slack squared was also calculated to capture potential quadratic effects. All ratio variables were truncated at the 0.5 percent tails.

Gross profit on total assets. Gross profit is defined as revenue minus the cost of making a product or providing a service before deducting overhead, payroll, tax, and interest payments. Gross profit is scaled by total assets to make performance comparable across firms of different size and to mitigate heteroskedasticity concerns; this measure is not influenced by differences in tax rates across countries or by differences in financial structures across firms. Measured at time t.

The creditor rights index measuring the power of secured lenders in bankruptcy, constructed by La Porta et al. (1997) and updated for a broader set of countries by Djankov et al. (2007). The value of 1 was added to the index when a country's laws and regulations provided each of four powers to secured lenders. The index aggregated the scores on the four items and varied between 0 (poor creditor rights) and 4 (strong creditor rights). Mean-centered creditor rights is used when interacting the variable with financial slack.

The employment law index developed by Botero et al. (2004), which measures the incremental cost to the employer of deviating from a hypothetical rigid contract in which the conditions of a job are specified and a worker cannot be fired. Higher values of this index indicate more extensive legal protection of workers. Mean-centered employee rights is used when interacting the variable with HR slack.

variable_name: Public disclosure of senator stock purchase
description: Event defined by the date the senator's stock purchase disclosure form is made publicly available on the Congressional website, which may be up to 45 days after the actual trade. The disclosure form reveals the name of the company, a range of stock value, and whether the trade was conducted by a member of Congress, jointly with a spouse, or individually by a spouse or child.

Calculated with the Fama-French four-factor model surrounding the public disclosure date of the stock. For Hypothesis 1 the authors implement multiple event windows, as well as both equally and value-weighted indices. For Hypotheses 2, 3a, b, and c they utilize the 2-day event window of (0, +1).
time_window: (0, +1) to (-1, +2) event windows for Hypothesis 1; (0, +1) event window for Hypotheses 2 and 3

description: Dichotomous measure equaling 1 if the senator was on a committee with direct jurisdiction over a firm's primary industry within the past 3 years, and 0 otherwise. The authors first identified the industry of a focal firm as categorized by the CRP and then identified whether a senator's assigned committee had jurisdiction over that industry.

Number of bills that the focal firm lobbied in the past 3 years that were sponsored or co-sponsored by the senator who purchased the stock. For example, the authors state that if a senator sponsored 10 bills in the past 3 years, and the firm listed six of those pieces of legislation in their lobbying reports, the measure of lobbying the senator's legislation would indicate 6.

Number of times a focal firm's representative testified before the senator in a hearing over the last 3 years. The authors collected transcripts of all Congressional testimonies in which a focal firm representative had testified in the past 3 years and noted whether the senator was present and part of the Congressional hearing committee.
Total amount of political contributions made by the focal firm to the investing senator's political action committee in the past 3 years.

variable_name: number of new ties to foundations' boards
description: The count of new independent boards that the focal firm's CEO joins as trustee. This measure takes values of zero or greater and is observed at time (t + 1). Ties were manually coded from the annual reports and 10-K filings of the S&P 500 firms and from the Foundations Directory Online (FDO) database.

Built from all articles published in U.S. newspapers retrieved through Lexis-Nexis, using the dictionary of positive and negative emotion words in the Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) content analysis program. Each article was categorized based on the ratio of positive and negative emotional content to the overall affect in the article; articles were coded as positive if the ratio of positive affective content to total affective content was at least 0.65, and as negative if the ratio of negative affective content was 0.65 or greater. The positive and negative articles were aggregated using the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance, which assesses the relative proportion of positive to negative articles and also accounts for the total volume of articles. The variable is observed at time (t + 2).

An indicator variable coded as '1' for observations if the focal firm had financial restatement in years t or (t-1), with the first year of restatement observation being 2004, and '0' otherwise. The authors state that the first hypothesis will be supported if this variable has a positive significant coefficient. Data on financial restatements were collected from the United States Government Audit Office's Financial Restatement Database, 2006 and Audit Analytics database, for a total of 296 restatement events in S&P 500 firms during the period.

Coded as '1' if the focal firm has a corporate foundation or a giving program, and '0' otherwise. The presence of a corporate foundation or giving program was manually coded from the National Directory of Corporate Giving published by the Foundation Center, collected from 2003 to 2011 for firms in the sample.
Following earlier research, Fortune's annual reputation ranking was used to code the variable as '1' if the focal firm was ranked in the top 50 firms, and '0' otherwise.

Human capital decile of an individual, constructed from the (log) individual's real earnings (in 2008 dollars) in the quarter that he or she left the parent to form the spinout, based on the full distribution of earnings across all individuals in the sample. The lowest decile is the omitted baseline category. Earnings are used as a proxy for differences in human capital because person-specific effects are the most important determinant of earnings, with employer effects and other drivers of earnings absorbed by parent-year-quarter fixed effects and individual controls.
time_window: the quarter the individual left the parent to form the spinout

description: The size of the parent at time t, measured as the (log) number of employees at the parent establishment. It enters the estimation interacted with the human capital deciles so that the coefficients reflect what happens to the various propensities as parent size increases.

Indicator of founding a within-industry spinout. The dependent variable equals 1 if an individual founded a spinout and 0 if the individual did not, and WSO is the omitted spinout-type category, so the reported coefficients measure the average propensity of individuals in each human capital decile to form WSOs relative to those in the lowest decile, controlling for individual characteristics and parent-year-quarter fixed effects. WSOs are identified as spinouts having the same 4-digit NAICS code as their parent.

variable_name: Spinout type by industry distance (OSO-R and OSO-U)
description: Out-of-industry spinouts are spinouts with a 4-digit NAICS code different from their parent's. The distance from industry A to industry B is computed as the negative (log) ratio of the number of firms that had establishments in both industries to the total number of firms in either of these industries, using the universe of establishments in the LBD for 2002 and the baseline NAICS 2002 4-digit industry definition; where no firms have establishments in both industries the maximum available distance is used. OSOs with a distance less than the median are classified as OSO-Rs and those with a larger distance as OSO-Us, while WSOs are uniformly assigned a zero distance.

Distance between individuals i and j computed as the shortest walkable route between each workstation in meters. The bootcamp space was free of obstacles except for a 5-ft boundary wall, which is accounted for by assuming that participants walk around the wall to interact with teams on the other side. Distances range from just under 1 m to just over 26 m.
scale: meters, just under 1 m to just over 26 m

description: Roster survey measure of knowing: participants were provided with a list of every other participant, including name and photo, and asked to 'select the people you know or know of from the list below', clicking 'yes' on the names of peers they knew. Within-team pairs are excluded, and dyads where i knew j pre-camp are dropped.
time_window: end of the bootcamp's first week

description: Roster method asking whether a respondent received 'feedback and advice about [their] ideas and entrepreneurship' from other participants. The measure captures more intensive interactions between focal participants and peers outside their team; within-team pairs are excluded.
time_window: end of the bootcamp's first week

variable_name: Number of messages from i to j
description: Behavioral measure built from digital communication among participants: data captured from the bootcamp's Facebook page and participants' email activity on the bootcamp's platform. The variable counts the number of emails sent, Facebook likes, and comments from person i to j.

Indicator of whether a participant knew anyone at the bootcamp before the camp. It is constructed from participant's responses to the 'knowing' question in the prebootcamp roster-based network survey, prepared before the bootcamp with questions similar to those asked during the camp. 66 participants knew someone and 46 did not.

Continuous measure that counts how many prior ties an individual had before the bootcamp started, taken in logs because the number of prior ties is heavily skewed. It is used to test whether having more connections reduces the effect of proximity.
Team-level measure obtained by aggregating the dyad-level prior ties measure to the team level for all members i of a given team: the total number of prior connections that a team's members have.
Indicator of whether a team's members have an above- or below-median number of prior connections relative to other teams at the bootcamp.

On Saturday morning each participant conducted a double-blind evaluation of five randomly chosen submissions, excluding that of her own team, rating 13 dimensions on a 5-point Likert scale. Each of the 40 submissions received 14 double-blinded evaluations; the measure averages across the 14 evaluations, then across the 13 dimensions, and is standardized to have mean 0 and SD 1. The variation between top, middle, and bottom teams is statistically significant and was used by bootcamp organizers to select prizewinners.
scale: standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 (from 5-point Likert ratings)
time_window: end of the bootcamp's first week

description: Average Team performance of the N most proximate teams to a focal team, where N is 4, 8, and 16. For instance, if the four most proximate teams had project ratings x1, x2, x3, x4, the peer performance measure is (x1 + x2 + x3 + x4)/4.
time_window: end of the bootcamp's first week

description: Freelancers' profile titles are embedded with OpenAI's text embedding model and matched by cosine similarity to the text embeddings of O*NET occupational titles, excluding occupations not present on the platform; the occupation with the highest cosine similarity is treated as the freelancer's occupation, and the AIOE language modeling exposure score of that occupation is assigned to the freelancer. The measure derives solely from the most recent pre-ChatGPT profile, so it is time invariant and fixed at the time of the shock. A manual check of a random sample of 1,000 profile matches found 97% accuracy.

In the coarsened exact matching specification, the independent variable becomes a binary measure of High AI Exposure: freelancers in the top quartile of AI exposure are matched to those in the bottom quartile on pre-period bidding trajectories (bids the month before the shock and three, six, nine, and twelve months prior) and on the total number of jobs completed in the year pre-treatment. After matching, standardized mean differences on the matching variables fall below conventional thresholds.

The number of bids a freelancer makes each month is counted, and because bidding is lumpy the count is summed over a three-month rolling window. The resulting count variable is heavily skewed, so it is log-transformed as ln(x + 1); freelancers who exit the platform remain in the sample with a bid value of zero.

A freelancer's three-month rolling bids are transformed into a vector reflecting the distribution of bids across work categories, normalized by the total number of bids; a referent vector measures the same distribution over the previous three-month rolling period. A cosine similarity compares the current distribution against the referent vector, capturing how similar the distribution of bids across work categories is to the freelancer's distribution in the prior three months. The measure is missing if the freelancer did not apply for any jobs in either the current or prior three-month rolling window, and it is symmetric with respect to direction.
time_window: current three-month rolling window relative to the prior three months

description: High-value contracts are defined as those that pay more than US$1,000, a threshold used internally by Upwork to define the most valuable jobs; the variable measures what percentage of a freelancer's bids were for high-value contracts. The variable is missing if a freelancer did not apply for any jobs in the three-month rolling window.

Freelancer skill-level is measured as the average skill-level for all jobs completed from December 2021 through November 2022. The skill-level field is a client-assigned field ranging from 1 through 3 (1 = 'Entry', 2 = 'Intermediate', and 3 = 'Expert'); because clients may not specify a skill-level, the field is missing for some jobs, and freelancers who did not complete a job with a skill field are excluded from the analysis. The authors use the average rather than the maximum skill-level because it provides greater variation, and the measure is fixed at the time of the shock and thus time invariant.

In the coarsened exact matching specification, the independent variable becomes a binary measure of High Skill Level: high skill-level freelancers (top quartile) are matched to low skill-level freelancers (bottom quartile) based on pre-period bidding trajectories and jobs completed pre-treatment. Because skill-level is structurally linked to prior platform activity and success, treated and control groups still differ in pre-period activity levels even after matching, and CEM restricts estimation to the region of overlapping pre-period trajectories.

Log of shares demanded in Round 1 by funds and individuals as a percentage of total shares available. All shares were offered at a uniform price of 33.33 points in the first round, so the number of shares demanded reflects the value placed on those shares. Only the first round is used, since later rounds set different prices based on prior-round demand.
Log of shares demanded by investment privatization funds in Round 1 as a percentage of total shares available. Demand by investment funds is treated as the valuation made by experts.
Log of shares demanded by individuals in Round 1 as a percentage of total shares available. This measure captures the value assessments made by individuals rather than by investment fund experts.
Log of total dollar book assets for 1991, summing the liabilities and equity values. Throughout the analysis the most recent data available (1991) are used.

Variance of intra-industry rates of return on assets for 1991. The authors estimate intra-industry variance of return on assets for 1991 using all firms within the same 2-digit ISIC code; for nine firms there were not enough firms in the industry (three or more) to calculate intra-industry variance, so the regressions have at most 979 observations.
Percentage of total liabilities to total assets in 1991.
Return on assets for 1991. The authors use ROA rather than return on equity because equity was a fictional notion during the communist regime.
Percentage of sales of the individual firm relative to total sales of all firms in its industry in 1991.
Log of the number of firms in the industry of the firm in 1991.
Dummy variable with a value of one when the revenue per employee in 1991 is above median for firms in the industry; otherwise zero.

Log of insider ownership in 1991 when there is nonzero insider ownership; otherwise zero. Insider holdings arise from direct domestic sales in the approved privatization plan, which represent purchases by managers and related owners.
Log of restituent ownership in 1991 when there is nonzero restituent ownership; otherwise zero.
Log of foreign ownership in 1991 when there is nonzero foreign ownership; otherwise zero.
Log of government ownership in 1991 when there is nonzero government ownership; otherwise zero.
A dummy variable with a value of one if the firm is a piece of a firm broken into multiple firms. It has a value of zero if it is the original unbroken firm.

Indicator variable that takes a value of 1 for employees who participated in a CSI project during our study period and 0 for nonparticipants. It is the key explanatory variable of interest in the retention analysis and is also used as the dependent variable in the logit estimation of the antecedents of CSI participation.

Indicator variable for cases of employee departure where the employee left by choice, observed from the end of the focal CSI project (or the matched date for controls) to June 30, 2013. The authors also record whether an individual left the firm at all (Left Firm) and whether the departure was nonvoluntary (Left Firm Nonvoluntarily), and the involuntary outcome is used as a further category in the multinomial logit analysis with still being with the firm as the reference category.
time_window: from the CSI project end to June 30, 2013

description: Continuous variable defined as the total number of days a CSI participant billed to a CSI project, and set to 0 for nonparticipants. For the relatively rare cases where an individual had more than one CSI project, the variable combines the time spent on all CSI projects because a project-by-project breakup is not available for a given individual. In the hazard rate analysis the variable is transformed into its logarithmic form, adding 1 first to deal with zero values for nonparticipants.

Indicator variable defined as 1 when the CSI participant worked on a project based entirely in an emerging market, and set to 0 for other participants as well as nonparticipants. In the hazard rate analysis it is described as an indicator for whether CSI project work primarily involved working in an emerging market.

Binary variable set to 1 in the year(s) that a firm received venture capital funding and 0 otherwise, with deals taken from Zephyr. A dummy was used because investment size was not available for all deals and because firms may seek different levels of investment. The dependent variable is lagged one year behind the independent variables.
time_window: 1994-2005 (one year ahead of the independent variables)

description: Yearly count of a science start-up's technology patents, i.e., patents that hybridize its product offerings outside its home science category. Patents are classified by StarTechZD from the science areas of the previous patents and publications they cite, with biology, chemistry and medicine, and other sciences coded as science patents and the rest as technology patents. Also measured as a cumulative count (Tech. patents, overall) to account for process effects, and variables are based on patent application dates.

Yearly count of hires at the top two levels of a science start-up's management hierarchy who have technology backgrounds, coded as technology hires when they came from engineering schools, other start-ups, or extant firms. Chief financial officers were excluded because the position is relevant to all start-ups. Also measured as a cumulative count (Tech. TMT, overall).

Yearly count of a science start-up's collaborations with actors holding technology commercialization expertise. Collaborations were inventoried from the organization assignees and inventors listed on a firm's patents, from a firm's academic publications, and from its website or founder interviews, with inventor backgrounds crossmatched against CNT researchers in StarTechZD. Also measured as a cumulative count (Tech. collabs., overall).

Classification of a firm as a science start-up based on its initial patent focus (patents rooted in biology, chemistry and medicine, or other sciences) and the functional background of its founder(s) (a PhD in biology, chemistry, physics, or cognate disciplines). Where patent focus and founder background diverged, website archives or founders were consulted and firms developing general-purpose technologies were considered science start-ups.

Binary variable set to 1 in the year(s) that a firm received venture capital funding and 0 otherwise, with deals taken from Zephyr. A dummy was used because investment size was not available for all deals and because firms may seek different levels of investment. The dependent variable is lagged one year behind the independent variables.
time_window: 1994-2005 (one year ahead of the independent variables)

description: Yearly count of a technology start-up's basic science patents, i.e., patents that hybridize its product offerings outside its home technology category. Patents are classified by StarTechZD from the science areas of the previous patents and publications they cite, with biology, chemistry and medicine, and other sciences coded as science patents. Also measured as a cumulative count (Science patents, overall), and variables are based on patent application dates.

Yearly count of hires at the top two levels of a technology start-up's management hierarchy who have a PhD in a basic science discipline, coded as science hires. Chief financial officers were excluded because the position is relevant to all start-ups. Also measured as a cumulative count (Science TMT, overall).

Yearly count of a technology start-up's collaborations with actors holding basic science expertise. Collaborations were inventoried from the organization assignees and inventors listed on a firm's patents, from a firm's academic publications, and from its website or founder interviews, with inventor backgrounds crossmatched against CNT researchers in StarTechZD. Also measured as a cumulative count (Science collabs., overall).

Classification of a firm as a technology start-up based on its initial patent focus (patents in computing and information technology, semiconductors, circuits and superconductors, or other engineering) and the functional background of its founder(s) (an engineering background or experience in technology commercialization with an extant firm, another start-up, or a VC fund). Where patent focus and founder background diverged, firms developing specific products were classified as technology start-ups.

A 0-1 expansion effect variable was used to distinguish between the 271 incumbents that had not expanded into new subfields by the end of the study and the 100 that did expand. Mean effect dummy variables also distinguished firms that did not expand, expanders that had exited the new subfield by the end of the study, and expanders that continued to participate. Firms that had not expanded by the end of years 4, 8, and 16 were treated as nonexpanding cases for the analyses of the relevant market shares. The variable is defined at the level of the firm's participation in a base subfield following the emergence of a new subfield.
time_window: by the end of the study; by the end of years 4, 8, and 16 for the market share tests

description: Mean effect dummy variables were defined to distinguish between firms that did not expand, expanders that had exited the new subfield by the end of the study, and expanders that continued to participate. In the survival models "expand and survive" took positive mean effects and "expand and exit" took negative mean effects, with no expansion as the remaining category. Exit from the new subfield is the withdrawal of the firm from the new subfield, treated by the authors as failed expansion.
time_window: by the end of the study

variable_name: Number of years of participation in the base subfield
description: The dependent variable for the analyses of survival was defined as the number of years an incumbent participated in its base technical subfield or subfields after the emergence of a new subfield. The count started at 1 for firms that exited a base subfield during the year in which a new subfield emerged, and incumbents remaining in the base subfields at the end of the study were coded as right-censored. In the analyses of incumbents that expanded, the count started at the firm's expansion date rather than the subfield introduction date. Exit by dissolution and exit by acquisition were each treated as a censoring case in the analysis of the other.
time_window: from the emergence of the new subfield (or from the firm's expansion for Hypotheses 5 and 6) until exit or the end of the study

variable_name: Subfield dollar revenue market share at years 4, 8, and 16
description: The authors recorded the subfield dollar revenue market share held by a pre-introduction incumbent during years 4, 8, and 16 after the emergence of the new subfield. The 4- and 8-year measures apply to all base and emerging subfields, while the 16-year market share measure does not apply to base subfield performance following the emergence of the magnetic resonance and digital radiography subfields. For each measure the analyses were limited to pre-introduction incumbents that survived at least 5, 9, and 17 years, respectively, so the market share tests contain a survivor bias. The authors prefer absolute market share over change in market share because their primary interest lies in absolute performance.
scale: market share (percentage of subfield dollar revenue)
time_window: years 4, 8, and 16 after the emergence of the new subfield

description: An incumbent's prior industry-wide market share was calculated as its percentage of overall industry sales during the calendar year before the emergence of the new subfield. The authors note that there is a significant positive correlation between the industry-wide and base subfield market share measures.
time_window: calendar year before the emergence of the new subfield

description: Each incumbent's prior subfield market share was recorded for the year before the emergence of a new subfield. The authors note that there is a significant positive correlation between this measure and prior industry-wide market share, so the influences of the two measures on survival must be interpreted carefully.
time_window: year before the emergence of the new subfield

description: How early a firm expanded into a new subfield was measured by the number of years between the emergence of the subfield and the expansion of the firm, starting at 1 for firms that expanded during a subfield's first year. The count was then squared in order to test for middle-range effects. The waiting period tests required estimation of both a main and a squared effect, so the authors expected positive main effects and negative squared effects.
time_window: years between subfield emergence and the firm's expansion

description: A variable recorded the number of times the firm had expanded in the past. The incidence of sequential expansion in the sample allows the authors to test the hypotheses that address the effects of learning from past expansion; the pool included 151 distinct firms, because many were incumbents of more than one subfield.
time_window: all prior expansions before the focal expansion

description: IT competency is modeled as a second-order factor with three first-order factors: IT knowledge, IT operations, and IT objects. It is a new scale and the theoretical domain for the scale items was drawn from literatures in marketing, IT, and information sciences. Seven-point Likert scales were used to operationalize the three dimensions. The loadings of the first-order factors on the second-order factor were all significant at p < 0.001.

Four items measured on a seven-point Likert scale with 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. The items ask about the firm's computer-based technical expertise, the knowledge of the technical support staff, knowledge about new computer-based innovations, and the knowledge to develop and maintain computer-based communication links with customers. This is a new scale developed for this study.

Six items measured on a seven-point Likert scale with 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. The items cover routine use of computer-based systems to access market information from outside databases, skill at collecting and analyzing market information about customers, set procedures for collecting customer information from online sources, use of decision-support systems, use of computer-based systems to analyze customer and market information, and reliance on computer-based systems to acquire, store, and process customer information. This is a new scale developed for this study.

Five items measured on a seven-point Likert scale with 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. The items cover having a formal MIS department, budgeting significant funds each year for new IT hardware and software, employing a manager whose main duties include IT management, creating customized software applications, and linking firm members by a computer network. This is a new scale developed for this study.

Organizational learning is modeled as a higher-order construct composed of five first-order factors: information acquisition, information dissemination, shared interpretation, declarative memory, and procedural memory. Seven-point Likert scales were used to operationalize the dimensions. The loadings of the first-order factors on the second-order factor were all significant at p < 0.001.

Six items measured on a seven-point Likert scale with 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. The scale was adapted from Baker and Sinkula (1999). The items cover in-house research on customer needs, regular meetings with customers, viewing customers as a source of market information, asking customers what they want or need, collecting industry information from customers by informal means, and regularly collecting information about customers' objectives.

Six items measured on a seven-point Likert scale with 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. Items were adapted from Baker and Sinkula (1999) and Kohli, Jaworski, and Kumar (1993). The scale contains one reversed item, namely that customer information is rarely shared between functional departments.

Five items measured on a seven-point Likert scale with 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree; a new scale was developed for this construct. The items cover managers being on the same page in interpreting customer needs, agreement on how best to serve customers, disagreement about what customers want (reversed), conflicting opinions about how best to satisfy customers (reversed), and agreement on how new customer information will impact the firm.

Seven items measured on a seven-point Likert scale with 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree; a new scale was developed for this construct. The items ask whether the firm retains information about the markets its customers compete in, customers' overall business objectives, customers' strengths and weaknesses, customers' R&D efforts, customers' competitive positions, customers' sales goals, and the marketing strategies customers have used in the past year.

Five items measured on a seven-point Likert scale with 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree; a new scale was developed for this construct. The items cover learning from past experience how best to deal with hard-to-please customers, a set procedure for handling routine purchase orders, standard procedures for determining customer needs, experience about what questions to ask customers, and a standard procedure for dealing with customer complaints.

Instead of objective measures, respondents were asked to report how well their firm performed during the last 3 years relative to all other direct competitors in terms of profitability, return on investment, customer retention, and sales growth. The four performance measures are summated to provide a global indicator of how well a firm is performing relative to direct competitors. This indirect approach was used because respondents are often hesitant to report sensitive performance data such as profitability and ROI.

Respondents indicated the percentage of their product and process innovations for which patent protection had been effective in protecting the firm's competitive advantage during the prior three years, choosing among five mutually exclusive categories (below 10%, 10%-40%, 41%-60%, 61%-90%, above 90%) separately for product and process innovations. The authors computed a weighted average of the product and process scores using midpoints, with the percentage of R&D effort devoted to product and process innovations as weights.

A binary variable constructed from the CMS question on how frequently R&D personnel talk face to face with personnel from the production, marketing or sales, and other R&D units functions, measured on a four-point Likert scale. The variable takes value 1 if R&D and manufacturing personnel interact daily (the median value in the sample is weekly interaction), and 0 otherwise; the authors focus on specialized manufacturing capability.

Respondents stated the percentage of their R&D projects over the last three years that were undertaken with the objective of earning licensing revenues, in five categories (below 10%, 10%-40%, 41%-60%, 61%-90%, above 90%). The authors used the midpoints of each category, assigning all respondents in the first category a zero licensing propensity unless they indicated that the possibility of earning licensing revenue was one of the reasons for patenting. The measure is an ex ante intention to license rather than actual licensing deals, and it is not separately available for products and processes.

Respondents reported the percentage of product and process innovations for which they applied for patents in the period 1991-1993 in the United States. The authors computed a weighted average of product and process patent propensities using the percentage of R&D effort devoted to product and process innovations, respectively, as weights.

variable_name: probability of licensing conditional on patenting
description: The share of patented innovations that are licensed, derived inside the structural model from the patenting and licensing propensities (Y1 and Y2). The authors note that the elasticity of the probability of licensing equals the elasticity of the conditional probability plus the elasticity of patenting, and they report marginal effects and elasticities of this conditional probability with respect to patent effectiveness.

The payoff from patenting and licensing an innovation relative to the payoff from not patenting and not licensing it (keeping it secret). It is made a linear function of observed firm and industry characteristics with an additive stochastic component that is observed by the firm but not by the econometrician, and is estimated in the GMM structural model.

The payoff from patenting but not licensing an innovation relative to the payoff from not patenting and not licensing it. Like the net licensing payoff it is made a linear function of observed firm and industry characteristics with an additive stochastic component, and is estimated in the GMM structural model; the estimates for VL - Vp are obtained as the difference between the estimates of VL - Vs and Vp - Vs.

The number of times each word in the category label appeared in the Factiva database of key general and business news sources was counted with a one-year lag, approximating how common the word was in the English language at that time. The frequencies of the component words are averaged, and the average is divided by the highest frequency found for all labels that year to obtain a scale from 0 to 100. The measure is then logged and enters the regressions in linear and quadratic terms with a one-year lag.

For each word combination in the category labels the authors counted co-occurrence in a random sample of articles from the weekday editions of The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and USA Today. They compute the ratio of the number of co-occurrences of the two words in the label over the number of times the two words are mentioned individually in those paragraphs, and creativity is the difference between one and this co-occurrence ratio. For labels with more than two words the average of each pair combination is taken; single-word labels are assigned a default value of one. The measure enters the regressions in linear and quadratic terms, with a one-year lag and in transformed logarithmic form.
scale: 0 to 1 in theory before log transformation

description: The level of a category label's adoption in a given year is measured by counting the number of press releases that used a given category label at least once. The authors describe this as providing greater granularity than alternative measures such as label survival.

variable_name: frequency of label use in given year
description: Computed as the total number of times a category label was used in all press releases by any smartphone producer in a given year. The authors describe it as measuring the intensity of producers' adoption of a given category label because it discriminates between a press release that contains just one mention of a category label and another that uses the label several times.

Participants were provided with a short definition of familiarity as a construct and then asked to score the familiarity of each of 50 category labels selected randomly from the pool of 400 labels, assigning a value from 1 to 7. The order in which the word combinations appeared on the page was randomized.

Participants were provided with a short definition of creativity as a construct and then asked to assign a value from 1 to 7 for a list of 50 word combinations selected randomly from the pool of 400 labels. The order of the familiarity and creativity pages was randomized across respondents.

After completing the familiarity and creativity pages, subjects were asked: how likely are you to use each of the following word combinations to refer to a new technology you have never heard of before? The authors purposely left a degree of ambiguity and provided little information to avoid cognitive biases toward particular technologies.

Following the procedure of Experiment 1, participants scored the familiarity of each category label, but with an added randomization between subjects: one subset considered a new hypothetical product based on a radical technology and another subset an incremental technology.

Following the procedure of Experiment 1, participants assigned creativity scores to the word combinations, with the same between-subject randomization of the technology scenario (radical versus incremental).

Participants answered the same question about their likelihood of using each word combination, but a random subset was asked to consider a new, hypothetical product based on a radical technology and a second random subset a product based on an incremental technology. A manipulation check eliminated respondents who did not show they understood the assigned technology setting.

Country scores on the Schwartz egalitarianism orientation, taken from the Schwartz value survey conducted largely during the 1990s. The scores are used to construct cultural distance measures for every pair of countries.

Countries' scores on the Schwartz cultural egalitarianism orientation, used as the independent variable in the firm-level analyses of organizational practices. The authors find that firms in more egalitarian countries pay their CEOs a lower multiple of the average worker's pay, are more likely to face objections and outside criticism on employment issues, and adopt employee-favoring policies.

For every pair of countries, the square of the difference between the countries' scores on the egalitarianism orientation. A signed version, signed egalitarianism distance, is the algebraic difference between the score for the investing firm's country of origin minus the score for the host country.

Egalitarianism distance predicted from instrumental variables, namely social fractionalization, dominant religion, 19th-century war experience, and communist-rule history. The authors use these instruments to buttress an argument on culture's causal role; the predicted variable exhibits a significant negative sign.

The natural logarithm of one plus bilateral FDI flows between an origin and a host country in a given year. Data come from UNCTAD and OECD; because both capture data from governments, their data for the years 1985-2004 are consistent, with UNCTAD the source for years prior to 1985, and the authors combined the two sources. The authors rely on inward FDI observations but incorporate outward observations if the former are missing. Because the data are sharply skewed, the natural logarithm of (FDI flows + 1) is used.

The ratio of production worker compensation to subsidiary value-added. Value added is computed by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis from the factor income side as the sum of costs incurred (except inputs) and profits in production. The analysis is restricted to instances of positive value-added. The authors find that subsidiaries pay production workers a greater share of their value-added the more egalitarian the host country.

The ratio of CEO hourly wage to average production worker hourly wage, taken as national averages. Sources are Fernandes et al. (2011) and the Boardex database for CEO compensation, and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics for worker wage. The data are firm-level observations aggregated and averaged to create measures of social norms.

LNSIZE attempts to approximate the own resources of the entity, defined as the natural logarithm of the sum of capital, rotation fund, reserves, subordinated financing, and retained earnings, taken at the end of the previous year. Natural logarithms are used in order to reduce the skewness of the size distribution.

For a given size, the relative magnitude of the position as a net lender in the money market (INTER) is also relevant, as it provides incentives to look for new markets in which to allocate the money in the form of loans at higher rates. It is the net balance (as a lender) of savings banks in the money market, normalized by the average assets of the entity, at the end of the previous year.
Profitability is measured through net profit divided by total assets. The covariate is taken at the beginning of the year under observation in order to avoid endogeneity problems.

A dummy variable that takes a value of one when the objective market under study was geographically adjacent to the core market of the savings bank and zero otherwise. It captures proximity stemming from the firm's original scope of operation.

A dummy variable constructed to take into account the proximity arising as a consequence of diversification; it takes a value of one when the market is adjacent to the new markets entered by the savings banks, and zero otherwise. The authors expect the effect of this variable to be of a lower magnitude than that of PROXIC.
The capacity of a firm to manage operations across markets is measured by the number of markets (provinces) in which the organization was operating at the end of the previous year.

The squared term of the number of markets in which the savings bank operates, included in the estimations together with NMARK to capture the hypothesized quadratic (inverted U-shaped) effect of the degree of diversification on entry timing.

Rivalry in the core geographical markets is measured through a Herfindahl type index. A province Herfindahl index was first developed using the number of branches as a proxy for market share; the core market Herfindahl index was then calculated by multiplying each single Herfindahl index of the provinces in which the entity was operating in 1986 by the relative importance of the province for the entity, again measured by the number of branches. Higher values indicate greater concentration, that is, less rivalry.

Province Herfindahl indexes were used again to proxy for current rivalry in the objective market. In order to take into account the interaction between banks and savings banks, this index has been calculated considering the branches of both types of intermediaries. Higher values indicate greater concentration, that is, less rivalry.

The authors first identified the markets in which the firm was not present and the degree of potential competition associated with any market was then obtained by counting the number of savings banks operating in the provinces adjacent to the objective market (end of previous year).
Intensity of demand in the objective market is measured through two variables. DEPHA accounts for the amount of deposits per habitant in the market (end of previous year).
Density of population is a variable frequently used in the literature on bank branching to proxy for population concentration in the objective market (end of previous year).
Market growth in the objective market is measured as the average relative growth in the deposit market for the 3 years prior to the year under observation.
time_window: 3 years prior to the year under observation

description: The dependent variable takes a value of one for the entity-market-year observation in which an entry is recorded and zero otherwise. An entity is only considered present in a market when it has at least 1 percent of the branches of that market. The number of observations is given by all the possible combinations of savings bank-year-market in which the entity is not present at the beginning of the follow-up.

The proportion of executives in a system's executive team whose roles belong to the revenue functional subgroup. It is calculated as the count of revenue-related roles at the system level divided by the total number of executives at that level.

The proportion of executives in a hospital's executive team whose roles belong to the revenue functional subgroup. It is calculated as the count of revenue-related roles at the hospital level divided by the total number of executives at that level.

The proportion of executives in a system's executive team whose roles belong to the medical mission functional subgroup. It is calculated analogously to the revenue subgroup measure, counting roles associated with the broader medical mission at the system level divided by the total number of executives at that level.

The proportion of executives in a hospital's executive team whose roles belong to the medical mission functional subgroup. It is calculated analogously to the revenue subgroup measure, counting roles associated with the broader medical mission at the hospital level divided by the total number of executives at that level.

The median pricing of a hospital's basket of reported shoppable services by CPT class for commercial payers. For each service, the measure aggregates the median negotiated price across all insurers and related plans and divides it by the hospital-adjusted Medicare reimbursement rate; the median is then taken over CPTs within the CMS-defined CPT class.

Measured as the regional average response to the question 'Generally speaking, would you say that most people can be trusted or that you can't be too careful in dealing with people?'. The answer categories are 'most people can be trusted' (1) or 'can't be too careful' (0). The question was asked in the national language of the country in which the survey was administered. Regions required at least 30 respondents; for the regions in the sample the number of respondents varied between 30 and 598 with an average of 124.

Measured as bought-in materials and services expenses divided by operating expenses. Materials and services expenses are calculated by subtracting labor expenses from operating expenses, and operating expenses are calculated as operating revenue minus earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. The conceptual origin of this measure is the value-added model; the study focuses on bought-in materials and services from suppliers as normalized by operating expenses.
Earnings before interest and taxes divided by total assets. The variables are winsorized at the upper and lower 5% of the distribution to reduce the effect of extreme values.
Earnings before interest and taxes divided by operating revenue. The variables are winsorized at the upper and lower 5% of the distribution to reduce the effect of extreme values.

The years 2008-2010 are coded as 'economic downturn' and the year 2007 as 'transition to downturn'; the year 2006 is the baseline, prior to the economic downturn. The coding is based on the timing of the Great Financial Crisis in Europe: in 2007Q3 BNP Paribas suspended redemptions and in 2008Q2 EU GDP dropped for the first time since the start of the crisis.

Task environment was categorized as simple or complex. A simple task environment (coded 1) is both decomposable, in which the components of the task can be processed independently, and concentrated, in which most problems are of the same type. A complex task environment (coded 2) is either nondecomposable, in which the task components depend on each other, or dispersed, in which problems of differing natures occur with no particular type dominating. The same categories are used for the computational model and for the coding of the real cases.

Organizational form was categorized as simple or complex. A simple organizational form (coded 1) consists of nonoverlapping communication channels such as a team or a simple hierarchy with a segregated resource access structure. A complex form (coded 2) is composed of complex and overlapping communication channels such as a matrix structure with a nonsegregated resource access structure. The usual form is the form of the focal organization prior to the crisis.

The organizational form of the focal organization during the crisis, coded in the same simple (1) and complex (2) categories, based on the during-crisis organizational structure and resource access structure. Among the real organizations, 25 out of 80 altered their organizational forms when confronted with a crisis. Most of those, 23, switched toward more complex, though not necessarily more rigid, designs.

variable_name: CML, level of substandard operating conditions
description: The number of substandard conditions occurring during the crisis, coded 1 = one substandard condition, 2 = two substandard conditions, and 3 = three or more substandard conditions. Within CORP the location of a substandard condition is chosen randomly for each problem, and when there are joint substandard conditions only one type of substandard condition is allowed to occur in each simulation experiment.
scale: 1 = one, 2 = two, 3 = three or more substandard conditions

variable_name: CMT, type of substandard condition during crisis
description: Type of substandard condition during the crisis: 1 = information uncertainty-based substandard conditions, 2 = agent malfunction-based uncertainties, and 3 = joint substandard conditions using aggregations. Information uncertainty covers missing or incorrect information when it is needed, agent malfunction covers members not at post, communication channels down, or fully trained agents having left, and joint substandard conditions are caused by a combination of both.

variable_name: UCM, complexity match during usual conditions
description: Level of complexity match between organizational form and task environment during usual conditions, with 1 = low and 2 = high. The authors create these more general categories because of the scarcity of the real data, noting that other studies included more fine-tuned analyses of complexity match.

Level of complexity match between organizational form and task environment during the crisis, with 1 = low and 2 = high. As with the usual-conditions match variable, the categories are general because of the scarcity of the real data.

Usual performance of the focal organization prior to the incident, coded 1 = low, 2 = moderate, 3 = high. The measurement mainly takes into account the frequency with which substandard internal operating conditions had previously occurred that could have resulted in a crisis and the frequency of similar crises in the past, and the organization's usual reputation in local society when available. For the artificial organizations, performance was measured as decision accuracy across all 19,683 possible events and then recategorized into the same three-point scale; there are 31 low, 39 moderate, and 10 high performers in the real cases.

Performance during the crisis, coded 1 = low, 2 = moderate, 3 = high. The measurement is based on the actual severity of the crisis outcome as well as on the potential for catastrophic escalation of the crisis. For the artificial organizations, crisis performance is measured as decision accuracy across the events defined to be critical and where there are one or more substandard conditions, and recategorized into the same three-point scale; there are 40 low, 22 moderate, and 18 high performers in the real cases.

variable_name: SFT, shift status of organizational form during crisis
description: Shift status of organizational form during crisis as compared with usual organizational form, with 0 = no shift and 1 = shift. Among the real organizations, 25 out of 80 altered their organizational forms when confronted with a crisis. The authors use the computational model to examine the performance of these organizations under the conditions when they did or did not alter their designs.

The dependent variable, patent termination, is binary and is coded as one if a patent got terminated 4 years after grant date and zero otherwise. Termination is measured through a failure to pay renewal fees 4 years after the grant date. Termination data come from the USPTO, which provides detailed information on patents that are terminated due to nonpayment of maintenance fees; the authors focus only on terminations at the 4-year mark in order to capture the early phases of research.

Subclasses assigned to a patent represent the knowledge components comprising the patent, and shared knowledge components between two patents represent their interdependence. The authors create a network of patents within a research program in each firm using subclasses as nodes and common patents as edges, then take the average of the degree centralities of the subclasses underlying a patent. The numerator is the sum of centralities of the subclasses assigned to the patent in the network of patents in the research program, and the denominator is the count of subclasses of the patent. The formula itself is not readable in the payload.

Constructed using the same methodology as interdependence within the research program, except that the patents considered to construct the network are different: it captures the extent to which knowledge components (subclasses) of the patent are combined with subclasses of patents in other research programs. The authors then calculate the average interdependence of all patents within a research program to arrive at the measure. The formula itself is not readable in the payload.

The number of other firms that have at least one patent in the same therapeutic area as the focal patent. The measure is weighted by the number of each firm's patents in the same therapeutic area to account for the size of each competitor, i.e., a weighted sum of the number of sample firms with at least one patent in the focal research program, with weights equal to each firm's patent count in that program. The formula itself is not readable in the payload.

Dummy variable that equals 1 if a company board member holds or held a position in the political establishment (the country's parliament, state legislatures, or a major political party) or has been a close professional associate of a politician (chief of staff, head of campaign committee, etc.). Politically connected board members were identified with standardized and country-specific keywords in the BoardEx data, and the resulting list was manually screened to obtain the final list. Mostly used for robustness checks.

Average score of the political connection dummy variable over the time window under study. It was the main independent variable; for the treatment effect analysis and doubly robust estimation, values of political capital greater than or equal to 0.5 were replaced with 1 and values lower than 0.5 with 0.
time_window: the time window under study (4 to 8 years in 1-year increments)

description: Time-varying, firm-specific transient persistence coefficient predicted in the first stage by random coefficient models estimated on the first-order autoregressive process in firm-specific returns, using forward-rolling time windows of varying lengths for each starting year. Firm-specific returns are the difference between the return on assets of firm i in year t and the average ROA for all firms in the same country and 2-digit SIC industry in that same year. Both the intercept and the transient persistence coefficient were allowed to vary randomly across firms, but only the latter had a significant estimated standard deviation, so only the marginal coefficient was allowed to vary; the analysis was constrained to decay-only observations.
time_window: forward-rolling windows of 4 to 8 years in 1-year increments

description: Standard deviation of ROA for each firm computed on forward-rolling windows of varying lengths, also varying from 4 to 8 years in 1-year increments. All financial information was obtained from the Bureau van Dijk Osiris (Industrials) database.
time_window: forward-rolling windows of 4 to 8 years in 1-year increments

description: The dependent variable is r(t), the instantaneous rate of failure. Each hotel's history is broken into quarterly spells in which the hotel is at risk of failure, and each quarterly spell is treated as right-censored unless the hotel fails, with the time-varying independent variables updated quarterly with each new STR census. Failure follows Baum and Mezias: cessation of hotel services for short-term visitors, with name, brand-affiliation or ownership changes not counted as failures.

Average room-count difference between the focal hotel and all other hotels in the same urban market, using room count to measure the size of each hotel. The sum of the Euclidean distances to all other hotels is divided by the square root of the number of hotels minus one, so the measure reflects the average distance and is independent of the number of hotels. Large values indicate the focal hotel is far, in rooms, from other hotels, i.e., less size-localized competition; room count of other hotels also forms the size competitive window.

Average distance in miles from the focal hotel to all other hotels in the same urban market. Distances between all individual property pairs are calculated with the great circle distance formula from latitudes and longitudes expressed in radians, and the measure is multiplied by 3,956 to approximate the mileage radius of the earth. The sum is divided by the square root of the number of hotels minus one so that the standardized value is the average distance in miles to other hotels in the market.

Average price-point difference between the focal hotel and all other hotels in the same urban market. STR estimates the average price actually received by every hotel and sorts prices into five categories for each market, coded 1 = Luxury, 2 = Upscale, 3 = Mid-price, 4 = Economy, 5 = Budget. The sum of price-point distances is divided by the square root of the number of other hotels, giving the average price-point distance on the five-point scale.

Coded 1 if a new venture received funding from at least one corporate investor and 0 otherwise.
