Whether an investor was a CVC or IVC investor was determined following the VentureXpert classification system, and diversified banks and insurance companies were excluded as CVC investors because the resources they provided do not directly relate to the technology commercialization of new ventures. Because most CVC-funded ventures were also funded by IVC investors, IVC-only funded ventures constitute the control group.

Coded 1 if the new venture operated in the wireless or customized semiconductor industries and 0 if it operated in the computer or standard semiconductor industries, according to VentureXpert classifications. The authors reason that firms in the wireless industry and customized semiconductor developers (code 3111) generally require specialized complementary assets, whereas computer firms and standardized semiconductor developers (3112) generally require generic complementary assets.

An omnibus measure combining two standardized proxies for the same construct. The first is demand uncertainty: trends in total industry demand are estimated over the five years ending in the year of the venture's last funding round using total sales of all firms with the corresponding SIC code, demand for the year following the last round is forecast from that trend, and the difference between actual and predicted industry demand is divided by total industry demand in that year. The second is industry stock market volatility: the yearly standard deviation of the natural log of weekly returns of the NASDAQ Computer index, the NASDAQ Telecommunications index, or the Philadelphia Semiconductor index (SOX), taken for the year following the last round of funding. The two standardized measures are strongly and positively correlated and are added up to obtain the omnibus measure.
time_window: five-year demand trend ending in the last funding round; uncertainty measured at the year following the last funding round

description: Binary variable that took a value of 1 if new ventures went public as of January 1, 2009, and 0 otherwise. The authors chose IPO as the success outcome rather than acquisition because both investors and entrepreneurs generally consider IPO to be the most successful outcome for new ventures.
Binary variable that took a value of 1 if new ventures were defunct and 0 otherwise. VentureXpert classifies new ventures as defunct if they are no longer in operation or have declared bankruptcy.

Dummy variable which is coded as 1 for the app-platform that experiences a GPI in the observation window and 0 for the control group. GPI events are identified from the practice of naming mobile game versions with three digits, where an increment in the first digit involves significant changes in the form of new contents, new functions and features, new game designs, and new gameplay modes; minor and bugfix updates are excluded. The variable enters the models interacted with the post dummy (post coded 1 from day 0 to day 7 and 0 from day -7 to day -1) to form the difference estimator.
time_window: day -7 to day +7 around the focal GPI

description: Customer adoption of a mobile game measured by the number of unique users that engage with the app on a specific day in the focal country market. To normalize its distribution the measure is log-transformed such that customer adoption equals ln(number of daily active users + 1), which captures the within-app percent change in customer adoption as a function of the GPI event and change in covariates. Observations range from day -7 to day +7 around each selected pair, with the focal GPI date treated as day 0.
time_window: day -7 to day +7 around the focal GPI

description: Indicator of market position for the focal app on the focal country-platform, coded as 1 if the focal app has reached top 30 in the local market ranking and 0 otherwise. Most ranking lists only show the top 30 ranked apps in a category list, and the ranking lists aggregate information about the usage decisions of all other app users.

Primary operationalization of technological legacy as an event-based measure of technological distance, capturing a product's cumulative innovation history and demand dynamics. It is operationalized as the number of prior GPIs before the focal day (log-transformed), which captures the temporal/technological distance between the present version and initial product introduction as measured by the number of prior generational innovation events.
time_window: all prior GPIs before the focal day

description: Secondary operationalization of technological legacy as a calendar time-based measure of technological distance, measured as the amount of time in days (log-transformed) since the initial product introduction, that is, the log-transformed number of days since the first day of app release on the platform. The authors view it as a less direct measure based on founding era; it also enters the models as a control variable together with its square term.

Dummy that equals 1 for ventures in the Accounting & Financial market starting March 2014. In difference-in-differences terms it is the interaction between a treatment dummy (equal to 1 if the venture is in the 'Accounting & Financial' market and 0 otherwise) and a post dummy (equal to 1 if the period is March 2014 or after and 0 otherwise). The Accounting & Financial market is the treatment group because it is clearly the outlier in reliance on class 705 patents, and March 2014 is the treatment date because oral arguments were heard on March 31, 2014. Higher values indicate a weaker formal intellectual property protection regime.

Binary variable equal to 1 if the venture is experimenting in the current period and 0 otherwise, coded from evidence of disclosure of a preliminary product ('alpha,' 'beta,' 'pilot,' 'prototype,' 'trial,' etc.). It is an absorbing dummy variable that starts at 0 and shifts to 1 when the venture executes its first experiment, and it is undefined (a missing value) after the company launches because experimentation occurs only prior to launch.

Binary variable equal to 1 if the venture has launched in or prior to the corresponding period and 0 if the venture has not yet launched; it is also an absorbing dummy variable. Launch is coded from evidence of circulation of the final product ('formal launch,' 'official launch,' etc.).

Measured as the inverse of the age of a venture's category vector; the panel version is defined as the natural logarithm of the inverse of the age of the venture's category vector. It is built from the vector of product categories that Crunchbase provides for each venture, using the entire software population of firms founded in 2000-2017. Higher values indicate more novel products, which the authors treat mainly as a proxy for market uncertainty.

Measures the presence of AI-related categories within a venture's category vector, built from the categories that Crunchbase provides for each venture. The authors describe it as a proxy primarily for technical uncertainty, because AI is arguably a novel general-purpose technology and firms may not have the capabilities to utilize it effectively.

The number of firms within the same market with a Jaccard Index greater than 0.5, where the Jaccard Index is used as a measure of similarity between firms. It is computed from the category vectors of ventures in the entire software population, that is, all firms in the software-related macro-categories founded in 2000-2017.

The number of large firms within the same market with a Jaccard Index greater than 0.5, where the Jaccard Index is used as a measure of similarity between firms. It is computed from the category vectors of ventures in the entire software population, that is, all firms in the software-related macro-categories founded in 2000-2017.

CEO succession events were identified from changes in the name of the CEO in Forbes' annual survey of CEOs' compensation, which asked CEOs to identify their functional background as well as their salary level. Forbes used nine categories (technical, production, sales, marketing, finance, operations, medical, journalism, and legal), which the authors collapsed into five: production and technical, marketing and sales, finance, legal, and operations and other. For the multinomial logistic regressions legal was collapsed into operations, so the base category was new CEOs of operations and other backgrounds and the models estimate the likelihood of production and technical, marketing and sales, and finance backgrounds relative to it. Where Forbes information could not be obtained, Who's Who in Finance and Industry and proxy statements were used and the titles of previous executive positions were coded following the Forbes classification system.

Following Fligstein (1987), corporate strategy and structure were identified using information from annual reports and 10-Ks and coded as measures of the strategic contingencies affecting a CEO's functional background. Corporate strategy was coded as product-dominant, related diversification, and unrelated diversification, with product-dominant as the omitted category; a firm was product-dominant when one line of business accounted for more than 70 percent of revenues, related diversification when it had multiple related businesses with no single business accounting for 70 percent of revenue, and unrelated diversification when it was engaged in unrelated businesses with no one business accounting for 70 percent of revenue. For the structure variable the authors compared the effects of a multidivisional structure with all other categories, including functional form and holding company, identified from the titles of top officers and the description of companies' business in annual reports, 10-Ks, and proxy statements. Mergers and divestitures is the three-year average of the number of mergers and divestitures undertaken by the firm, coded from Moody's Manual.
time_window: mergers and divestitures averaged over three years

description: The import variable is simply the amount of imports divided by total output in each industry, by 4-digit SIC code. The import and output variables for each industry were obtained from the U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Economic Analysis. The natural logarithm of the import variable was used in the analysis, and the variable also enters interacted with ROA.

Return on assets (ROA), measured as the return on firm assets and adjusted for the industry average, was used as a measure of firm performance. ROA measures were obtained from COMPUSTAT. The variable enters the model both as a main effect and interacted with the log of imports.

variable_name: proportion of CEOs with each functional background in the industry
description: Following Fligstein (1987), isomorphism in the functional background of new CEOs was captured by calculating the proportion of CEOs with technical and production, sales and marketing, and finance and legal backgrounds within each industry, with the proportion of CEOs with operations and all other backgrounds as the omitted category. Two-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes initially gave 19 industries, which were collapsed to 14 because some industries had too few companies to make the variable reliable. Manufacturing companies listed in the Forbes Sales 500 for each year were used, and the company was left out of the calculation when it was included in the Forbes Sales 500 for that year, so the proportion captures the pure effect of the subunit control that existed in the industry for each year.

variable_name: annual percentage of CEOs with each functional background
description: The effects of annual trends and fluctuations in the functional backgrounds of new CEOs were captured by calculating the proportion of CEOs with technical and production, sales and marketing, and finance backgrounds for each year, with the proportion of CEOs with operations and all other backgrounds as the omitted category. As for the isomorphism variable, the background of the CEO of the particular firm-year being coded was excluded from the total number of CEOs for each functional background. The variable applies to the level of the manufacturing sector rather than to the industry.

The political dynamics of the CEO succession process were captured by the functional backgrounds of the last two CEOs in office; this variable records the background of the immediate predecessor. The functional backgrounds of previous CEOs were collected the same way as functional backgrounds of new CEOs, using Forbes and, where needed, Who's Who in Finance and Industry and proxy statements, with the titles of previous executive positions used to code the background. Operations and all other backgrounds of previous CEOs was the omitted category.

The background of the CEO two successions back measures long-term stability in the power of functional subunits across two generations of predecessor CEOs. It was collected the same way as the other functional backgrounds, and operations and all other backgrounds of previous CEOs was the omitted category. The authors use it to compare the entrenchment of financial CEOs with that of other backgrounds.

The excess return over the (-1, 0) period, i.e., the day before and the day of the announcement. The OLS market model is estimated for each firm/announcement over the estimation period from -120 to -21 days before the announcement using the equally weighted CRSP index. The excess return is the difference between the actual and the predicted return, and excess returns are averaged across the announcements to generate the mean excess return used in the regressions.
time_window: (-1, 0) event window; estimation period -120 to -21 days

description: Presence or absence of voluntarily disclosed information about government approval in the R&D announcement article, coded as a 0/1 variable with 1 signifying the presence of the information and 0 its absence. Two independent coders and one of the authors read each article; agreement among the three coders was over 94 percent and disagreements were resolved by discussion.

Presence or absence in the R&D announcement article of the mention of patents (a patent application being prepared), coded as a 0/1 variable with 1 signifying presence and 0 absence. Coded by two independent coders and one of the authors, with over 94 percent agreement and disagreements resolved by discussion.

Presence or absence in the R&D announcement article of a disclosed goal of product substitution, coded as a 0/1 variable with 1 signifying presence and 0 absence. Coded by two independent coders and one of the authors, with over 94 percent agreement and disagreements resolved by discussion.

Presence or absence in the R&D announcement article of a disclosed intention to increase market share, coded as a 0/1 variable with 1 signifying presence and 0 absence. Coded by two independent coders and one of the authors, with over 94 percent agreement and disagreements resolved by discussion.

Presence or absence in the R&D announcement article of the mention of a growing market, coded as a 0/1 variable with 1 signifying presence and 0 absence. Coded by two independent coders and one of the authors, with over 94 percent agreement and disagreements resolved by discussion.

Presence or absence in the R&D announcement article of a disclosed diversification goal, coded as a 0/1 variable with 1 signifying presence and 0 absence. Coded by two independent coders and one of the authors, with over 94 percent agreement and disagreements resolved by discussion.

The ratio of industry R&D expenditures (the sum of R&D expenditures of firms in the industry) to sales (the sum of firms' sales in the industry), measured over the last 3 years prior to the announcement. Industry is the firm's primary industry as indicated by its dominant SIC code.
The log transformation of the total sales of the firm for the 3 years prior to the announcement.

Actions involving government agencies are captured by two 0/1 variables coded from the Wall Street Journal R&D announcement article: whether government approval is mentioned, and whether patents are mentioned. A value of 1 means the information is present and 0 that it is absent.

Social aspirations are measured by the industry median return on assets (ROA), and PRA is the difference between the firm's performance and the industry median ROA in the prior year (t - 1). Negative PRA is measured as zero if PRA is positive, and equal to PRA if it is negative, so that more negative values indicate performance further below aspirations. The variable is winsorized at the 2% level.

Historical aspirations are measured as the prior year's performance (ROA), and PRA is the difference between the current year's performance and the previous year's performance; because the variables are lagged, historical PRA equals the difference between firm performance in t - 1 and t - 2. Negative PRA is measured as zero if PRA is positive, and equal to PRA if it is negative. The variable is winsorized at the 2% level.

Social aspirations are measured by the industry median return on assets (ROA), and PRA is the difference between the firm's performance and the industry median ROA in the prior year (t - 1). Positive PRA is measured as zero if the PRA is negative, and equal to the PRA if it is positive, so that higher values indicate performance further above aspirations. The variable is winsorized at the 2% level.

Historical aspirations are measured as the prior year's performance (ROA), and PRA is the difference between the current year's performance and the previous year's performance; because the variables are lagged, historical PRA equals the difference between firm performance in t - 1 and t - 2. Positive PRA is measured as zero if the PRA is negative, and equal to the PRA if it is positive. The variable is winsorized at the 2% level.

A binary variable equal to 0 if the bank's total assets exceed $1 billion, and equal to 1 if the bank's total assets do not exceed that amount. Observers often differentiate between community and noncommunity banks, defining community banks as those with less than $1 billion in assets.

A single credit risk score calculated as the standardized factor score for the common factor underlying three indicators: allowance for loan losses/total assets, provision for loan losses/total assets, and net loan charge-offs/total assets. The factor analysis produced a single factor explaining 81.7% of the variance with an eigenvalue of 2.45. A higher score on this variable corresponds to greater risk-taking.

The log of the total dollar amount of small business loans that the bank has outstanding. Small business loans include commercial and industrial loans with principal less than or equal to $1 million, which are typically extended to small firms, and not secured by farm or nonresidential properties. Federal regulations require that banks disclose the number and amount of small business loans in their Call Reports. The log of small loans is taken to reduce skewness and kurtosis.

A country-level index of the propensity of courts to apply enterprise liability and 'pierce the corporate veil' in cases involving group affiliates. Countries were scored on a scale of zero to five according to how inclined their courts are to pierce the corporate veil in cases involving corporate groups, with a higher score implying stronger enterprise liability for corporate headquarters. The overall score is the weighted average of five criteria evaluated by the authors in collaboration with scholars at Duke University School of Law.

The natural logarithm of the number of subsidiaries in a corporate group in a three-digit SIC industry in a country for a year. A subsidiary is identified as a legally independent entity in which the headquarters has more than a 50% ownership stake according to Orbis's direct and total ownership share fields, with headquarters identified through the ultimate owner field.

variable_name: dummy for high industry downside risk
description: Industry downside risk is the share of firms in an industry (three-digit SIC) that experience 'failure', an annual drop of at least 50% in revenues, computed from Standard & Poor's CRSP/Compustat. In the interaction specifications the authors use a dummy variable taking a value of 1 for corporate groups operating in industries in the top quartile of the industry downside risk distribution and 0 otherwise.

An aggregate measure of autonomy in hiring, sales and marketing, and product introduction granted by headquarters to the subsidiary, taken from the World Management Survey. It combines the survey items on the agreement a plant needs from corporate headquarters to hire a full-time permanent shop floor worker, the share of sales and marketing carried out at the plant level, and where decisions on new product introductions are taken.

A WMS survey measure of the largest capital investment the subsidiary could make without prior authorization from corporate headquarters. The authors use the log of the investment amount per employee.

An indirect WMS measure of autonomy: the number of levels in the firm between the shop floor and the CEO, i.e., the number of hierarchical layers between the shop floor workers at a subsidiary and the CEO.

An indirect WMS measure of autonomy, a dummy variable taking a value of 1 if a manager from the corporate headquarters was present at the subsidiary being interviewed (whether CHQ is on the site being interviewed).

The annual change in a corporate group's fixed assets in a given country, averaged over the sample period. Groups operating in low-PCV countries are compared with matched groups in high-PCV countries using propensity score matching.
The percentage change in revenues for a corporate group operating in a country between year t-1 and t, averaged over the sample period. Computed on the propensity-score-matched group-country sample.
A dummy variable taking a value of 1 if a corporate group in a given country experiences a decline in annual revenues of more than 50%. Computed on the propensity-score-matched group-country sample.

The log-transformed number of subsidiaries of a corporate group in an industry, compared between corporate groups in the oil and gas industry and corporate groups in other industries relative to the reference year before the 2010 BP oil spill, separately for countries with strong and weak enterprise liability.

variable_name: dummy for high share of family managers; dummy for high board member interlock; dummy for high share of wholly-owned subsidiaries; dummy for high share of subsidiaries using parent's name
description: Dummy variables taking a value of 1 for corporate groups with more than 50% of subsidiaries managed by a family manager, with more than 50% of subsidiaries with at least one board member who also serves on the board of the corporate parent, with more than 50% of wholly-owned subsidiaries, and with more than 50% of subsidiaries taking the same or partially the same name as the corporate parent, respectively. A family manager is a senior manager or executive sharing the same last name as a shareholder of a corporate group as listed in Orbis.

Calculated by subtracting each firm's return on assets from their aspirational ROA and taking the absolute value of this difference. The variable was set to zero for firms that met or exceeded their aspirational ROA. Aspirational ROA was calculated with a social aspirations measure, the median ROA for all firms in the same two-digit SIC industry as the focal firm. The variable is standardized to facilitate interpretation of coefficients.

An indicator variable that takes a value of one if a firm experienced a new litigation claim in a given year, and zero otherwise. Data were obtained from the AuditAnalytics Legal database, which contains all material federal civil litigation cases that must be disclosed as part of firms' annual SEC filings. Because material claims are at least 10% of assets, the variable captures serious misconduct events with considerable stakeholder impact.

An indicator variable taking the value of one if the firm has a Powerful Chief Legal Officer, defined as being among the company's top five highest-paid executives, and zero otherwise. Executives' relative pay is used as a strong measure of their power in the organization, as well as the relative power of the department they lead. Data on executive pay were obtained from Execucomp.

The percentage of firms in the focal firm's industry that experienced a civil litigation claim in a given year. Each firm's two-digit SIC code was used to define their industry, and industry peers are used as social referents, because prior research has shown that managers pay careful attention to other comparable organizations operating in the same field.

Measured by whether the chair had only government working experience before serving as the chair. For privately controlled firms, such a stint usually occurred before the chair joined the company. The measure is widely used and well established in the existing literature to capture the political connection.

Measured by whether a firm's chair was only serving as a delegate to the People's Congress or the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference. While these bodies exist at five different hierarchical levels, only the higher prestige national- and provincial-level PC/CPPCC memberships were considered.

The likelihood of donation is coded 1 for firms that donated in a given year and 0 for those that did not donate. Donation information is available in the CSMAR database from 2001 to 2006 and was extended to 2012 by collecting donation data from the notes to financial reports in company annual reports.

The logarithm of the total donation for cases with a positive amount of donation, leaving those cases with no donation as 0. Among firms that donated, the average donation amount is approximately ¥1,291,410, accounting for 1.7% of the firms' profit and 5.2% of the firms' cash flow.

Calculated by computing the proportion of SOEs' sales to those of the total industry at the three-digit level for each year, based on well-established calculations of state monopoly across industries in China. A higher score indicates a higher level of state monopoly, i.e., stronger state control of those industries. Examples of highly state-monopolized industries are electricity, finance, telecommunications, and petroleum.

variable_name: quality of regional market development (reverse coded)
description: Captures the quality of market development of the firm's headquarters province using the provincial marketization indices developed by the National Economic Research Institute. The variable is reverse coded by subtracting the value of the marketization index for each province from 12, the maximum possible value, so that a higher value indicates a lower quality of regional market development. The 2009 values were used for 2010 to 2012.

Asymmetric dependence of focal firm i is defined as supplier concentration of focal firm i divided by buyer concentration. The numerator is the ratio of the transaction from supplier N to focal firm i to the sum of all transactions from all suppliers to focal firm i; the denominator considers suppliers' bargaining power, with BWNi being the ratio of transactions from supplier N to focal firm i to the sum of transactions from supplier N to all firms, and the two portals' outflow traffic concentration is weighted by their relative importance to the focal firm and summed. The full formulas are not readable in the text. To ensure enough variance, the authors calculated the percentage change per month.

A dichotomous variable coded 1 at time t when a site failed and 0 otherwise, with a total of 44 failure events. Failure timing was determined by listing disconnected sites as of September 2011, searching newspaper databases and then blogs, internet communities and Web pages, checking the site's status in the Internet Archive, and regarding the first month for at least five consecutive months with a reach rate below one percent as the failure time.

The ratio of a firm's Web traffic from major portals to its total Web traffic in terms of PV. The authors note that because firm-to-firm resource flows were directly available they did not apply the industry-level dependence intensity approach used in prior research.

A dichotomous variable coded 1 when a site belongs to the top three as category market leader at time t and 0 otherwise; the largest firm in terms of PV is the benchmark used to decide whether a focal site belongs to category market leaders.

The number of dependent firms except for the focal firm within a category, where dependent firms are defined as commercial sites reached through portals' searches in the category that the focal site belongs to.

A binary parish-level pre/post scandal variable set to zero in all years before a parish was associated with an accused priest (and for parishes never associated) and one in all years after it became associated with an accused priest. Priests' names from the grand jury report and the Database of Publicly Accused Priests were matched to specific parishes, and the year of the first publication about a priest's alleged abuse was used to date the switch. If the first news was published in the first half of the year, the variable takes a value of one starting that year; if in the second half, it takes a value of one starting the following year.
time_window: year of first public allegation; value switches in that year or the following year

description: The sum of three variables: the number of baptisms, marriages, and funerals at an individual parish each year. All three reflect members' decision to engage and provide for a conspicuous and occasional association with a parish during transitions from one life stage to the next. Because of ambiguity, any activities that had a value of zero were recoded as missing. To compare it with rites of integration, which is measured on a different scale, the variable was standardized by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation.

Average weekend attendance during October masses, an engagement statistic collected by each individual parish each year. No major Catholic holidays take place in October, so average weekend mass attendance in this month provides the best estimate of members' decision to engage in rites of integration at each parish. Because of ambiguity, activities with a value of zero were recoded as missing, and the variable was standardized by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation to allow comparison with rites of passage.

For each parish, the percentage of its polygonal territory perimeter that was shared with other parishes implicated in the scandal in a given year. Parishes' latitude and longitude coordinates based on street address were used to construct Thiessen polygons for each year of the sample, and the share of shared boundary with implicated neighbors gives the variable. Its value ranges from 0% to 100%, with intermediate values determined by the geographic configuration of the parish and its neighbors.

A binary variable equal to one for older parishes and zero for younger parishes. It was calculated by categorizing all parishes in the sample by the median parish founding year, such that parishes founded before 1920 were considered old and parishes founded in or after 1920 were considered young. The authors used a binary variable rather than a count variable to focus on the difference between more historic, older parishes and to avoid the difference that stems from a parish getting one year older.

The number of registered members of each parish in each year, reported in conjunction with the other yearly parish-level statistics. It is also entered as a time-varying control (parish membership) in all analyses.

A composite measure with three components: the quality of law school attended by partners (a proxy for articulable knowledge and prestige), the average firm-specific experience of the partners in a focal firm, and total partner experience in the legal field averaged across the partners in the focal firm. The three components were factor analyzed and loaded on one factor (eigenvalue = 2.07; alpha = .75), and a composite was created from standardized factor scores. Law school quality was based on the Gourman Report ranking, with an average ranking score calculated for each firm using 1991 data; experience data came from a 2000 survey and were adjusted backwards year-by-year for each firm.
scale: factor scores, mean 0 and standard deviation 1
time_window: law school ranking from 1991; experience values adjusted backwards year-by-year to 1999-92

description: A composite of three components: the number of the 250 largest U.S. corporations that were clients of the law firm in a year; the total percentage of these clients' sales that resulted from their foreign operations; and the continuity of the relationships, coded 0 in the first year the firm served a corporation and incremented by one for each consecutive year, log-transformed and aggregated. Internal reliability was alpha = .91; the components loaded on one factor (eigenvalue = 2.54) and standardized factor scores were used.
scale: factor scores, mean 0 and standard deviation 1

description: A composite of three components: the number of foreign governments that were clients of the firm in each year; the total yearly compensation received from these governments; and the number of consecutive years a government had been a client. FARA reports were unavailable for 1992-94, so averages from the previous four years were used, and missing compensation values (about 10 percent of cases) were estimated with the year average. Internal reliability was alpha = .89; the components loaded on one factor (eigenvalue = 2.46) and standardized factor scores were used.
scale: factor scores, mean 0 and standard deviation 1
time_window: 1992-99; 1992-94 values estimated from previous four years

description: An entropy measure based on the number of foreign offices and the number of lawyers in each office; the number of lawyers in each office was used as a proxy for the revenue provided by that office because revenue data were unavailable. The measure captures both the number of foreign markets in which a firm operated and the relative importance of these markets to the firm. Data were obtained from The American Lawyer.
time_window: 1993-99 as dependent variable; 1992-98 as independent variable (one-year lag)

description: The ratio of worldwide net income to total firm revenue, derived from the profitability index reported annually by The American Lawyer (the API, the ratio of profits per partner to revenue per lawyer). The number of partners was removed from the numerator and the number of lawyers from the denominator, so the resulting measure can be interpreted as return on sales.

A firm was designated owner-controlled if at least 5 percent of its outstanding stock was in the hands of one individual or organization that was not involved in actual management of the company, and management-controlled when no individual or organization controlled 5 percent or more of its stock. A dummy variable was used, with owner-controlled firms coded as 1 and management-controlled firms coded as 0. Of the firms, 19 were owner-controlled and 52 were management-controlled, and no firm in the sample was owner-managed, with a dominant stockholder who was also the CEO.

Several average measures were calculated for each firm over the four years from 1979 through 1982 with the goal of developing reasonably independent parameters for scale and performance. The nine measures were factor-analyzed by the principal axis method with the squared multiple correlation as the estimate of communality, and a distinct performance factor emerged composed of the four-year rates of change in profits and sales, return on equity, earnings per share, stock price, dividend yield, and annual percent change in market value. Each factor score was calculated by adding the standardized value of each variable weighted by its factor loading and then standardized, and the resulting two factor scores are not highly correlated.

Scale is one of the two composites that emerged from the principal-axis factor analysis with varimax rotation of the nine averaged financial measures, and it is composed of sales volume and total dollar profits. Using each separate item as an independent variable would have created a severe multicollinearity problem, so the two composite factor scores were used instead. Each factor score was calculated by adding the standardized value of each variable weighted by its factor loading and then standardized.

variable_name: mean absolute dollar amounts of salary, bonuses, and long-term income
description: Three different compensation measures were constructed for each executive in the sample. The level measure is the mean absolute dollar amounts received from 1979 through 1982 for salary, bonuses, and long-term income. Long-term income includes a wide array of deferred compensation benefits like pensions, profit sharing, stock options, IRAs, and bonus deferrals.

variable_name: mean annual percent change in salary, bonuses, and long-term income
description: Of the three compensation measures constructed for each executive, the change measure is the mean annual percent change over the period for each of the compensation components: salary, bonuses, and long-term income. It is used both for the level of each component and for its rate of change over time.

The mix measure is the relative weight of each component in the earnings mix, calculated as an average ratio of the value of a particular component to total compensation received during this period. It covers salary, bonuses and long-term income as fractions of total compensation.

A subsidiary's total exposure to terrorist attacks in a host country in year t (exposure). Whether a subsidiary was considered 'exposed' to a terrorist incident depended on the geographic proximity of the subsidiary to the incident, with the 99th percentile of the distribution of great-circle distances between subsidiaries and incidents (4.26 km) used as the cutoff. The authors then calculated the frequency that a subsidiary encountered terrorist attacks within this distance range in a host country in year t to capture its aggregated exposure in that year. The variable was log-transformed in the analyses due to high skewness.

An MNE's divestment of a subsidiary from a host country from year t to year t + 1, taking the value of 1 when an MNE closed off a subsidiary or sold off all its equity ownership in a subsidiary and 0 otherwise. Divestment was determined by comparing the existence of a subsidiary in an MNE's corporate hierarchy over years and conducting an exhaustive web search of news indicating that a subsidiary ceased to exist or that a parent MNE divested all its ownership in a subsidiary in year t + 1.

One of two proxies used for each of three country dyads: the host country relative to (a) the executive's country of origin, (b) country(ies) of higher education, and (c) country(ies) of main work experience. Institutional distance was calculated as the difference between two countries along nine dimensions of countries' formal and informal institutional environments in the Institutional Profile Database, using the Kogut and Singh (1988) index. For the MNE-level measure, the authors averaged the institutional distance of all executives other than the CEO and then took the average of this mean with the institutional distance of the CEO.

For each executive, a dummy variable (common language executive) captures whether any of the three country dyads (host country relative to the executive's country of origin, country(ies) of higher education, and country(ies) of main work experience) share the same official language; it takes the value of 1 if any of the three country dyads share the same official language. At the MNE level, the common language measure takes the value of 1 if the common language executive variable equals 1 for any of the top executives of the MNE and 0 otherwise. When any of the top executives in an MNE spoke the official language of a given host country, the social distance of the MNE's executives from the host country is smaller.

Firms were assigned to Rumelt's diversification strategy categories using the specialization ratio, the related ratio and the vertical ratio computed from line-of-business data. This study's sample includes the two constrained categories, dominant-constrained and related-constrained, and the other selected categories serve as the comparison group. Classifications for 125 of 128 firms matched Rumelt's.

Firms were assigned to Rumelt's diversification strategy categories using the specialization ratio, the related ratio and the vertical ratio computed from line-of-business data. The low-performing unrelated portfolio category, which had absorbed most of the firms previously designated unrelated-passive, was selected to represent the high end of the diversification continuum.

Weighted market share index for the firm, built from the firm's share in each of the 4-digit S.I.C. markets in which it sells together with the percentage of the firm's total sales in those markets; the formula printed in the appendix is not fully readable in this payload. The market data are those of Economic Information Systems, available through the Lockheed Dialogue System and subdivided by 4-digit S.I.C. category.

Concentration of the markets in which the firm participates, recorded at the four-firm, eight-firm, twenty-firm and fifty-firm concentration levels. The authors note that the four-firm and eight-firm levels behave differently from the twenty-firm and fifty-firm levels, which they read as reflecting differences in the number of firms in a market and the associated size of barriers to entry.

Growth of the firm's markets, measured over 1972-1976 from shipment growth in dollars across the firm's 4-digit markets; the appendix presents it as an annuity measure and the formula is not fully readable in this payload.

Weighted return on assets associated with the firm's markets; the appendix also lists a weighted industry return on equity measure (PROF2). The authors report that PROF1 differed significantly across the strategy categories.
Firm size, measured as log assets averaged over 1975-1977. It is one of the firm-specific variables reported alongside the market variables in the comparison of strategy categories.

Return on invested capital, one of the performance measures used to compare strategy categories. The authors also use it in a risk-adjusted form (ROCRR) that divides average return on invested capital by its standard deviation. The formulas in the appendix are not fully readable in this payload.

Return on assets, one of the return measures used in the category comparisons. The authors note that dominant-constrained firms' higher than average returns on assets suggest that they were better than average performers.
Return on equity, one of the return measures used in the category comparisons. It is reported alongside return on invested capital and return on assets.

Risk adjusted return measure that divides average return on invested capital by its standard deviation. The authors interpret it as an accounting risk measure, so higher values indicate lower accounting risk.

The dependent variable in the time-to-IPO models is the instantaneous rate of going public, estimated from the date of founding onward, with all venture-backed firms in the sample at risk of experiencing an IPO. The authors divided the period during which each organization is observed into quarter-year spells and updated all time-changing covariates every calendar quarter. Each quarterly spell is treated as censored on the right except for spells that terminate in an IPO, and the handful of firms that disbanded or were acquired while still private were also censored. The rate is estimated with a piecewise exponential model with three age periods.

The market value of a firm at IPO was computed from the IPO subscription price: the firm's total market capitalization (the IPO subscription price multiplied by the total number of shares outstanding) with the dollar amount raised in the IPO subtracted. All nominal figures are converted into real dollars, and the value is observed only for the 121 firms that undertook an IPO. The log of market value is the dependent variable in OLS regressions estimated with Lee's (1983) sample selection correction.

Commercial prominence of an organization is its normalized degree score in the network of strategic alliances, defined broadly to include all biotechnology-related partnerships, and is interpreted as the proportion of all biotechnology alliances in which it had participated. The authors organized the alliance data as symmetric organization-to-organization matrices updated quarterly, normalized the elements in each matrix by the total number of alliances formed in the industry prior to that quarter, and summed over each row to produce a vector of prominence scores. A focal biotech venture's score is the sum of the prominence scores of its alliance partners in each period. In the event-history data the variable was updated each quarter, and in the valuation models it assumes its value at the time the firm went public.
level: firm-quarter (firm at IPO in the valuation models)

description: A technologically prominent organization is one with a highly cited portfolio of biotechnology patents, and its technological prominence is its degree score in a network configured from the patent citations between the patent portfolios of all biotechnology innovators. The authors created an organization-to-organization patent citation matrix for each calendar quarter, normalized the elements by the total number of patent citations made during that period, and summed across each row so that each score is the proportion of all biotechnology patent citations flowing to an organization's patent portfolio. A focal venture's variable is the sum of the technological prominence scores of its alliance partners.
level: firm-quarter (firm at IPO in the valuation models)

description: The same measure of commercial prominence—an organization's normalized degree score in the biotechnology alliance network, the proportion of all biotechnology alliances in which it had participated—is summed over the non-venture-capital organizational equity investors of a focal biotech venture in each period. Ownership relationships were updated as they changed, with alliances and patents of subsidiaries and divisions aggregated up to the corporate parent. In the event-history data the variable was updated each quarter, and in the valuation models it assumes its value at the time the firm went public.
level: firm-quarter (firm at IPO in the valuation models)

description: The technological prominence score of an organization—the proportion of all biotechnology patent citations flowing to its patent portfolio, computed from quarterly organization-to-organization patent citation matrices—is summed over a focal biotech venture's non-venture-capital organizational equity investors. Ownership structures were traced and updated, and the patents and alliances of subsidiaries were aggregated to the corporate parent. In the event-history data the variable was updated each quarter, and in the valuation models it assumes its value at the time of the IPO.
level: firm-quarter (firm at IPO in the valuation models)

description: The prestige score of the investment bank that acted as lead manager for a firm's IPO, taken from the scale constructed by Carter and Manaster (1990). Carter and Manaster built the scores from investment banks' positions in the tombstone announcements for new issues, producing a scale of investment bank prestige ranging from 0 (lowest prestige) to 9 (highest prestige). The identity of the lead manager was coded from IPO prospectuses, and the variable was included only in the market valuation models.

Firm age is the time elapsed since incorporation and is used as a measure of the uncertainty about a firm's quality, because very young companies have limited performance histories on which quality can be assessed and uncertainty declines as a venture ages. In the time-to-IPO models age is the duration clock and is represented by three age periods (less than 3 years, 3 to 7 years, and more than 7 years) that allow the baseline hazard to shift. In the market valuation models firm age was entered directly as a regressor and interacted with the prominence measures.

A cumulating sum of the cash raised by each firm in private financing rounds (pre-IPO venture funding). The authors treat the level of funding as a measure of the uncertainty about firm quality and of firm size, because there is more uncertainty about the value of small firms and because the greater the size of venture capitalists' investment the more certain they are of venture quality. In the hazard models the variable was updated quarterly to reflect any changes, and in the market valuation models the total amount of cash raised in all private financing rounds was included.
time_window: updated quarterly (cumulative as of IPO in the valuation models)

variable_name: commercial and technological prominence of alliance partners and equity investors
description: Partner prominence is measured in two areas, commercial and technological, for two kinds of partners, strategic alliance partners and non-venture-capital equity investors. Commercial prominence is the partner's normalized degree score in the biotechnology alliance network, and technological prominence is its score in the patent citation network. For each venture the scores are summed over its affiliates each quarter, which gives four prominence variables.

Firms' reputation was measured with the most visible marker of a VC's prior performance, the IPO event; the authors examined VC reputation by the number of prior exits in China before the focal deal. The number of IPOs has been widely applied in previous studies to assess the reputation of VC firms. A one-year lag was applied to all time-variant independent variables.
time_window: prior to the focal deal (one-year lag)

description: Syndication is the dependent variable used to account for the likelihood of VC investment through alliance formation for each deal. It was coded '1' if the VC firm invested through syndication and '0' in all other situations.

The variable foreign indicates the focal firm's country of origin. It was coded '1' for firms registered or headquartered abroad and '0' for firms registered in China. The data set included VC firms from 16 countries (regions) outside mainland China.

The level of institutional development was assessed using two aspects, business environment and political environment, with institutional data obtained from the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU)'s database. Relevant indicators were factor analyzed for each year using principal components analysis with varimax rotation, which generated two distinct factors; the factor scores were then used to account for the business and political environment in China.

Number of years that the two parties have cooperated through trade or investment before forming a focal IJV, weighted by the quality of previous cooperation. Quality of previous cooperation is the informant's degree of satisfaction, on a 5-point scale, with this previous cooperation.

Mean of responses, on a 5-point Likert scale, assessing the degree to which an IJV contract (original main body and appendices as well as renewal supplements, if any) specifies relevant terms and clauses in four categories. Informants assessed contract completeness benchmarking with the IJV industry's standard regarding the desired level of this completeness. Factor analysis with Varimax rotation condensed the items into this factor, with loadings of 0.82, 0.88, 0.82 and 0.84 and a Cronbach's alpha of 0.71.

Mean of responses to three items on the extent to which term specification is adaptive for issues particularly vulnerable to uncertainty, the contract specifies major principles or guidelines for handling unanticipated contingencies, and the contract provides alternative solutions for likely contingencies. Factor analysis with Varimax rotation condensed the items into this factor, with loadings of 0.95, 0.90 and 0.91 and a Cronbach's alpha of 0.77.

Mean of the responses, on a 5-point Likert scale, to the degree of interparty cooperation in nine areas of IJV decision making and operations. Unidimensionality and reliability were validated by exploratory factor analysis communality estimates of 0.86-0.94 and a Cronbach's alpha of 0.69.

Total domestic and export sales divided by total assets, obtained from the archival database. The average of this measure between 1997 and 1998 is used to test performance implications of the contract and cooperation.
Profit divided by total investment, obtained from the archival database. The average of this measure between 1997 and 1998 is used to test performance implications of the contract and cooperation.

Abnormal returns around the announcement of the joint venture termination, calculated after estimating the market model for each firm over the period -250 to -50, with the announcement date serving as 0. Event study results are presented for days -1, 0 and +1, since longer windows would have been contaminated by confounding events, and the day 0 abnormal returns are used in the regressions. Significance was tested with the Patell test and with two non-parametric tests (the binomial test and the Wilcoxon signed rank test).
level: parent firm around the termination announcement
time_window: days -1, 0 and +1 around the announcement date; market model estimated over -250 to -50

variable_name: venture acquisitions with the objective of growth and expansion in a target market
description: A classification of the 46 venture acquisitions retained in the sample, based on articles discussing the reason for termination. Two independent researchers examined the articles, met and decided whether a particular termination was consistent with the real options view, applying the rule that the article should specifically highlight how the venture acquisition played a role in the parent firm's expansion in a target market. Descriptors such as 'the venture acquisition fits with the company's strategy to grow in the region' were used, and three instances where a parent firm exercised an option to acquire a venture from a partner were also included. Acquisitions for other reasons (more flexibility and control, sole ownership, management conflict) and cases with no reason available were eliminated.

variable_name: venture divestitures to refocus a firm's product-market portfolio
description: A classification of the 39 parent firms whose articles specifically discussed how the venture divestiture helped the parent firm refocus its operations. A procedure parallel to the one used for acquisitions was followed, with the reason for termination identified from articles that quoted executives at the parent firm and analysts tracking the companies. Divestitures for other motives (raising cash and easing liquidity pressures, management conflicts, lack of flexibility as a minority partner) and cases with no reason given were excluded.

Volatility in the value of shipments of the industry in the 10 years prior to termination, constructed at the 4-digit SIC level of the joint venture's industry. The higher the volatility, the higher the degree of uncertainty, and the variable broadly captures demand uncertainty.

A dummy variable based on Scherer's (1982) classification of industries into regimes of technological opportunity, which broadly denotes the opportunities for technological advance and appropriability. It is coded for the top two industry groups with the greatest technological opportunity, electronics and organic chemicals, while the remaining five groups (electrical, mechanical, chemical, traditional, and metal industries) serve as the reference. The greater the technological opportunity, the more the technological uncertainty and the greater the returns to R&D.

The Herfindahl index in 1992, used as an approximation for the extent of rivalry in the joint venture's industry because data on the number of rivals operating in each industry were not available. The higher the Herfindahl index, the lower the degree of rivalry.

The reduction in fixed assets during the decline period, measured as a difference measure of the percent change in average fixed assets between the three-year decline period and the three-year potential recovery period. Average fixed assets were used rather than beginning and end values so as to mitigate any potential temporary wide shifts in asset composition.
time_window: 3-year decline period versus 3-year potential recovery period

description: The firm's sales were averaged over the 3-year decline period and the subsequent potential recovery period, respectively, and the percentage change taken. Percentage differences were employed because they negate the impact of different currencies and firm sizes.
time_window: 3-year decline period versus 3-year potential recovery period

description: The decrease in accounts receivable was measured as a ratio to sales to control for shifts of accounts receivable attributable to changes in sales. That measure was averaged over the decline period and the potential recovery period, respectively, and the percentage change taken.
time_window: 3-year decline period versus 3-year potential recovery period

description: Data were gathered from each firm's annual report on changes in the Chair during the last 2 years of the decline and the first year of the potential recovery period. A dummy variable was used to indicate if the Chair was replaced (1) or was not replaced (0) during this time.
time_window: last 2 years of the decline period and first year of the potential recovery period

description: Adjusted ROI is a firm's ROI for a given year less the risk-free rate of return for that year, produced so that performance improvements were not driven by inflationary gains. The average adjusted ROI of the 3-year decline period was subtracted from the average adjusted ROI of the potential 3-year recovery period to obtain the dependent variable. The difference score was used because the reliability of financial performance measures in proximate time frames and similarity across observations is high, and an index such as ROI negates the impact of size and currency differences.
time_window: 3-year decline period versus 3-year potential recovery period

description: The authors collected all analyst reports released after the announcement for each acquisition using a five-day window (from day 0 to day +5) located via Thomson One. For each report they computed the number of positive and negative emotion words, classified using the positive and negative emotion categories in the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software. They then computed the ratio between the number of positive and negative emotion words for each report, and analyst reaction for an acquisition is the average of these ratios across the reports for that acquisition.
scale: ratio of positive to negative emotion words

description: The authors created dictionaries associated with the core members of the competition, cooperation and interconnection families. For each core member they compiled word lists, validated them, reviewed the transcripts to ascertain whether the words were used metaphorically, and calculated the frequency of each core member's usage in the call transcripts. Metaphorical language for a family is the sum of the values for all its core members, and the total is the sum across families, calculated as its percentage in top management's remarks in the conference calls.
scale: percentage of words in top management's remarks

description: War language is the percentage of words in top management's remarks in the conference calls that are war-related metaphors. The dictionary was compiled from thesauri and related-word services, words with salient nonmilitary meanings were removed and expressions converted to word stems, yielding a list of 190 words, expressions or word stems that was validated by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers; after removing words used nonmetaphorically the final word list has 42 words/expressions. In the relative war language specification, war language is divided by total metaphorical language.
scale: percentage of words in top management's remarks

description: The competition family comprises the source domains war, hand-to-hand combat, predation, racing, team sports and games. The variable is the percentage of top management's words in the call transcripts accounted for by the core members of this family. In specifications that isolate war, the war source domain is excluded from this variable and reported separately.
scale: percentage of words in top management's remarks

description: The cooperation family comprises the source domains family, friends, partners, work crew, community and animal group. The variable is the percentage of top management's words in the call transcripts accounted for by the core members of this family.
scale: percentage of words in top management's remarks

description: The interconnection family comprises the source domains organisms, constructed objects and natural objects. The variable is the percentage of top management's words in the call transcripts accounted for by the core members of this family.
scale: percentage of words in top management's remarks

description: The authors used the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index to capture this variable. They calculated it by summing the squared market shares for all firms in the acquirer's corresponding market, using the four-digit SIC code, in a given fiscal year.
level: market (four-digit SIC industry) per fiscal year

description: The authors calculated this variable by dividing the acquirer's total sales (for each fiscal year) by the entire market sales, using the four-digit SIC code, for that same fiscal year.

Strategy was measured using Rumelt's five-level diversification-type classification scheme, converted into a ranked, ordinal variable: single-business strategies were assigned a value of 1 and vertical, constrained, linked, and unrelated strategies respective values of 2, 3, 4, and 5. In the kinked regression models, model 1 contains only single-business, vertical, and constrained firms with the strategy variable scaled from 1 to 3, and model 2 contains constrained, linked, and unrelated firms with the strategy variable scaled from 3 to 5. In the dummy variable model (model 3), strategy is represented by a four-level dummy variable, with the unrelated strategy category omitted.
time_window: Rumelt's 1974 classification used for 1975-77; Hawks's 1980 update used for 1978-80

description: Estimated from a market model of the form (Rit - Rft) = ai + bi (Rmt - Rft) + eit, where Rit is a firm's return to common stockholders (appreciation plus dividends), Rft is a proxy for the risk-free rate of return, and Rmt is a proxy for the return of all risky assets estimated by returns to an equally weighted CRSP portfolio. Unsystematic risk is the standard deviation of the error term eit over the estimation period of each market cycle. Risk was estimated over the first 150 trading days (about nine months) of each distinct market cycle for each firm between 1968 and 1980, or up to nine times per firm; for the two cycles lasting less than 150 trading days all of their trading days were used.
time_window: first 150 trading days of each distinct market cycle, 1968-1980

description: Estimated from the same market model, as the estimate of bi, or the covariance of the return to a firm with the return to the market portfolio. It was estimated over the first 150 trading days of each distinct market cycle for each firm between 1968 and 1980, following the same estimation procedure used for unsystematic risk.
time_window: first 150 trading days of each distinct market cycle, 1968-1980

description: The time frame associated with each market cycle interval was identified by the direction of movement in the stock market time series presented in Value Line, a composite consisting of approximately 1,700 securities: a bear cycle by a general downward movement lasting at least six months, a bull cycle by a general upward movement of the same duration, and a stable cycle by at least six months showing no discernible movement. Nine market cycles were identified. In the market cycle analysis a dichotomous dummy variable was used (1 = bull market, 0 = bear market), the data from the three stable periods were omitted, and the design included a strategy-by-cycle term.
scale: dummy variable (1 = bull market, 0 = bear market)

description: Retained earnings were measured as a firm's total retained earnings, logged, and lagged one year. In China these funds were equivalent to state funds because they were owned by the state and used to determine remitted profits.

variable_name: capital received from external sources (multicategory dependent variable)
description: The outcome variable was an indicator of whether the firm received capital from any of five common sources of external borrowing: bank loans, interfirm loans, interfirm investment, public debt, and foreign funds. The dependent variable was a single, multicategory variable for each year between 1980 and 1989, indicating whether the firm had capital from any of these five sources; because a firm may have received funds from more than one source in a year, the variable can take more than one category. For example, if the firm had bank loans and issued debt, the variable was coded 10010, and if it received only interfirm loans and interfirm investments, it was coded 01100.

variable_name: bank loans (category of the dependent variable)
description: Bank loans included all loans from domestic banks but excluded direct state transfers. Whether the firm received bank capital is one of the five categories of the multicategory dependent variable recorded for each year between 1980 and 1989.

variable_name: nonstate, nonbank sources (categories of the dependent variable)
description: The nonbank categories of the multicategory dependent variable are interfirm loans, interfirm investment, public debt, and foreign funds, each recorded for every year between 1980 and 1989. Interfirm loans were loans from other Chinese firms; interfirm investment was the sale of partial ownership rights in the company to another Chinese firm; public debt included corporate bonds but excluded equity issues; foreign funds were loans and direct transfers of capital from foreign corporations and banks.

Market development was a dichotomous variable indicating whether managers thought 'poor market development' was an important problem. The value thus indicates the manager's assessment that markets in the firm's area were poorly developed.

Two standard diffusion equations were used to measure exposure of each organization to practices used by all other organizations. Predicted values for each firm (the expected likelihood that the firm borrowed from each source given firm and regional traits) were obtained and, for each firm pair, divided by the geographic distance between the two, using greater circular distance calculated by the author from firm latitude and longitude estimates. The equations as printed in the text are not readable, so the exact functional form cannot be recorded from the prose; the resulting exposure measure was used as a predictor variable in the regression models, lagged one year.

variable_name: exposure weighted by size or profits
description: To test Hypothesis 2B, the exposure was weighed by actual profits or the number of workers, so that the potential influence of other firms was greater when those firms were large or profitable.

Optimal matching was used to group trajectories, or sequences, by determining how difficult it is to transform one into the other, using the multicategory borrowing variable over time; firms with similar trajectories will be in the same group. Substitution costs were set according to the likelihood that firms had encountered the capital source in the past and the degree to which the strategy reflected principles of market organization as opposed to state planning, derived from manager familiarity with and reported risk of each borrowing method. Four distinct financial trajectories emerged from the sequence analysis.

The dependent variable, technological specialization (Tech_Spec), captures the extent to which a firm's inventive effort at a given time is focused on particular types of technologies. The authors traced all patents filed by a firm in a given year that were subsequently granted, identified the technology classes to which these patents are assigned, and then calculated the concentration ratio (Herfindahl index) of these patents across technology classes, which indicates how focused the firm is within certain classes. For example, spreading four patents evenly across two classes gives 0.5, whereas three patents in one class and one in another gives 0.625, reflecting greater specialization. Specialization is measured in the year following the independent variables.

The firm's stock option-implied volatility, backed out from the firm's traded stock option premium after factoring in other parameters such as stock price, strike price, expiration date, and interest rates. The authors use the implied volatility of the firm's one-month-expiration, European-style, at-the-money call option on the first trading day of the calendar year. Implied volatility reflects the market's current expectation of the upcoming uncertainty the firm will face (forward looking) and captures the impact of current information releases (contemporaneous). It encapsulates multiple components of firm-level uncertainty, so in the second stage only the technology-based portion predicted by the policy shock is retained.
time_window: first trading day of the calendar year

description: The predicted change in Uncertainty from the first-stage estimation (Table 3, Model 2), instrumented by the interaction of the policy shock and whether the firm is active in fuel cell technologies. It includes only the technology-based portion of Uncertainty that arises from the policy shock and is used in the second stage to test the authors' propositions.
time_window: one year after the policy shock (2001)

description: The number of patent infringement lawsuits initiated by rival firms within the communications equipment technology classes that firm i patents in. It varies across firms in each year because firms are active in different sets of technology classes and face different rivals; these lawsuits, although requiring infringements to have allegedly occurred, indicate how willing rivals are to proceed with litigation, so rivals who initiate more lawsuits are more litigious.

The number of patents filed, on average, by rivals within the technology classes in which the firm is active in the year. The firm observes rivals' existing innovations to assess rivals' speed or lead-time advantage.

Munificence was measured by the growth in industry sales over a 5-year period, using the regression slope coefficient divided by the mean value. Coefficients are based on a regression of time against value of shipments, and the estimate for any given year is based on the five preceding years. Industries are defined using four-digit SIC codes.
time_window: 5-year period preceding the observation year (e.g. 1976-1980 for 1980)

description: Dynamism was measured as the variability of the industry sales growth rate over the same 5-year period. The measure is the standard error of the regression slope coefficient divided by the mean value, using the same regression model as for munificence.

Complexity is measured by the Herfindahl index, the sum of the squared market shares for all firms in an industry group, which ranges between 0 and 1. A score of zero represents perfect competition and a value of 1 represents a perfect monopoly. H values are published by the Commerce Department starting in 1982; for 1980 the index was estimated from 4, 8, 20, and 50 firm concentration ratios using the MIN approximation suggested by Schmalensee.
Number of directors on the firm's board. These data were collected from 1980 annual reports and proxy statements. Average board size for the sample was 12 directors.

Number of a firm's interlocks with other organizations, where a direct interlock occurs when a director also sits on the board (or is an officer) of a different firm and an indirect interlock occurs when two firms have representatives on the board of a third company. These data were collected from 1980 annual reports and proxy statements; the sample averaged 22 interlocks.
Firm size is a variable in the models; the text does not state how it was operationalized.

A time-variant measure of national institutional environments for each country, using the Index of Governance and Enterprise Restructuring drawn from the EBRD Transition Report. The index is created from measures of soft budget constraints, subsidy policies, bankruptcy legislation, governance efficiency, and the market for corporate control at the enterprise level. Over the sample period the index ranges from 1 to 4.3, with 4.3 representing the greatest level of progress to market institutions and 1 representing little change during the initial institutional transition.

A binary dependent variable indicating whether a firm made a hierarchical entry attempt in a given country-year, where a hierarchical entry attempt is an independent entry made via an acquisition. The variable was developed using the SDC database and includes entry announcements whether or not the transaction was ultimately completed. A firm was considered at risk of entry in a given country in a given year even if it had previously entered that country.
time_window: country-year, from the year of the first foreign acquisition in that country

description: A binary dependent variable indicating whether a firm made a relational entry attempt in a given country-year, where a relational entry attempt occurs when a firm entered a transition economy with one or more partners through a mutual cooperative arrangement such as a joint venture or a strategic alliance. The variable was developed using the SDC database and includes announced entries whether or not they were completed.

A time-varying count of the number of past acquisition entry events made by a firm in a host country. An entry attempt announced but not completed was not counted as previous entry experience. Twenty-five percent of entry attempts had prior hierarchical entry experience.
time_window: time-varying, prior years of the observation period

description: A time-varying count of the number of past relational entry events made by a firm in a host country, measured in the same way as hierarchical entry experience. Fourteen percent of entry attempts had prior relational entry experience.
time_window: time-varying, prior years of the observation period

description: Host-country entry experience is measured as the past involvement of a firm in a given country, using time-varying counts of the firm's past acquisition entry events (hierarchical entry experience) and past relational entry events (relational entry experience) in that host country. Announced but uncompleted entry attempts are not counted. Both counts are interacted with institutional transformation to test the moderation.

Dummy variable that measures the technology switch to DOCSIS 3.0. The switch occurs when the cable incumbent offered DOCSIS 3.0 in 2013 in a local market but had not in 2012. In the estimation, the dependent variable is a dummy that measures the technology differential across the state border: it is 1 if the cable ISP has adopted in market m but not in the neighboring market m0, and 0 otherwise. Twenty-nine percent of observations exhibit technology adoption.

Dummy that takes the value 1 if the market has institutional entry barriers (i.e., entry restrictions or ban) for public firms and 0 otherwise. It captures whether a regime with restriction neighbors a regime with no restrictions. The state laws do not change often and thus do not vary over time.
scale: dummy (1 = market in a state with institutional entry barriers)

description: Dummy that takes the value of 1 when the incumbent is a national cable provider (i.e., Time Warner Cable, Comcast or Charter Communications) and 0 otherwise. These three firms are considered the major incumbents in the U.S. broadband industry. Almost half of observations are national incumbents.

Equal to the number of fiber firms in the market, capturing the intensity of quality competition by incumbent ISPs that offer fiber broadband. Fiber firms are the main high-quality competitors of cable providers when they switch to DOCSIS 3.0. The majority of these firms are private.

Cumulative abnormal returns around the acquisition announcement, cumulated over t = {-5, ..., +5} days around the announcement date. Consistent with the event study methodology, the market model is used to estimate the expected stock market return, with an estimation period of t = {-60, ..., -20} days around the announcement day. The authors note that the average CAR in the sample is one percent.
time_window: -5 to +5 days around the announcement date; estimation window -60 to -20 days

description: Dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if the reputation ranking of the IPO lead underwriter is higher than 7.9 at the time the acquisition deal is announced, and 0 otherwise. The rankings range from a low of 0 to a high of 9 and can change over time; the cut-off follows the classification of an underwriter as 'highly reputable' if its ranking is higher than 7.9.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition deal (ranking at the time of the IPO also used in supplemental models)

description: Dichotomous variable that takes the value of 1 only if the advisor in the acquisition deal is the same as the underwriter of the firm's IPO, and 0 otherwise. It captures whether the newly public firm reactivated its relationship with its IPO lead underwriter by retaining it as acquisition advisor.
Dummy variable which takes the value of 1 only if the IPO is backed by a venture capital firm, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Continuous measure constructed as the natural logarithm of the number of days between the IPO date and the preannounced lockup expiration date. Most IPO firms in the sample declared a lockup period of 180 days (51 percent) or 181 days (22 percent); given the skewness of the variable the natural logarithm was used for scaling and, where necessary, the variable was mean centered to eliminate multicolinearity.
scale: natural logarithm of lockup days (mean centered)
time_window: from the IPO date to the lockup expiration date

description: One-year pre-event Tobin's q is used as an indicator of the firm's intangible assets.
