True Tobin's q is the ratio of the market value of all financial claims on the firm to the replacement value of tangible and intangible assets; in practice it is proxied by dividing the market value of all financial claims against the firm by the book value of total assets. Firms with Tq greater than or equal to 1 are put in the high-intangibles group and firms with Tq below 1 in the low-intangibles group.
time_window: one year prior to the acquisition announcement

description: For each firm, the natural logarithm of the number of days between its IPO date and each acquisition deal announcement. Where necessary because of high multicolinearity, the variable was centered at its mean value. Interaction variables were created by multiplying AFTERIPODAYS by LEADMGR, VCBACK, and ADVISOR.
scale: natural logarithm of elapsed days (mean centered)

description: Political risk ratings for the countries in which sample firms had operations were collected for 1991 and 1994 from the Institutional Investor's Country Credit Ratings, which are based on information provided by over 80 leading international banks. The ratings were reverse-scored so that 0 represented the lowest political risk and 100 the highest. A weighted average of the ratings was developed using the number of employees of the firm in each country as the weight; the printed formula could not be extracted from the text. The measure is the average of the political risk ratings for the countries represented in a firm's portfolio in 1991 and 1994, and the authors report a minimum value of 15.67 and a maximum value of 57.35.

The total number of directors employed by the firm on whose board they sat divided by the total number of directors. The information for all independent variables was from corporate proxy statements for 1991.

The total number of outside directors with an affiliation as specified by SEC regulation 14A, item 6(b), divided by the total number of directors. The information for all independent variables was from corporate proxy statements for 1991.

Coded as 0 when a firm's CEO also served as chairperson of its board and as 1 when different individuals served as CEO and board chair. The information for all independent variables was from corporate proxy statements for 1991. Higher values of this variable therefore denote separation of the CEO and chair roles, the opposite of duality as the construct is named here.

The number of CTO meetings in a given year in which both firms in the dyad participated, computed from meeting attendance rosters that record which individuals represented which firms at which meetings. The variable ranges from a minimum of 0 to a maximum of 46, while the average is .80. The formula defining the variable is not legible in the text.

For each dyad, the percentage of representatives in a given year that have CTO experience from the prior year, constructed by comparing the set of individuals representing both firms in year t with those in the prior year. The formula defining the variable is not legible in the text.

The number of technical alliances formed by the dyad during the previous three years, that is, over the window t-1 through t-3. Its square is also included in the models to control for the inverted U-shaped relationship between previous alliances and subsequent ones.

Yearly counts of all patents in the cellular classes 371, 375, 333, 370, 379, 455, 380, and 273 of the U.S. patent system. For each dyad the patents of both firms were summed and then logged because the variable was highly skewed.

Counts of dyadic alliances formed by any two firms in the sample in a given year, extracted from all cellular alliances listed in the SDC database and restricted to those alliances containing a research and development component. For alliances that involved more than two firms, the alliance was counted as linking every possible dyad in the agreement. Technical alliances formed by dyad ranged from 0 to 5, with a mean of .020.

Scale built from the items composing the internal process value, which centered on the efficient use of scarce resources. The value scales were derived from a 24-item instrument tailored to the sample; respondents rated each item on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from not important to utmost importance. Senior commanders and deputy wing commanders were the best informants on unit values, and their responses were aggregated at the deputate level.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale (not important to utmost importance)

description: Scale built from items tapping the rational goal value, which stressed productivity through technology acquisition and improvement. Items came from a 24-item instrument tailored to the sample and were rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from not important to utmost importance. Responses were aggregated at the deputate level.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale (not important to utmost importance)

description: Scale built from human relations value items that pertained to personnel development. Items came from a 24-item instrument tailored to the sample and were rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from not important to utmost importance. Responses were aggregated at the deputate level.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale (not important to utmost importance)

description: Scale built from open system value items representing change and adaptation concerns. Items came from a 24-item instrument tailored to the sample and were rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from not important to utmost importance. This was the only value scale with a reliability score below 0.70.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale (not important to utmost importance)

description: Respondents identified the major coordination mechanisms used for mission accomplishment in their unit from a list of 18 alternatives; the measure was based on frequency of use of vertical coordination. Available response options included never, quarterly or less, monthly, biweekly, weekly, 2 to 3 times per week, and daily. Squadron commanders, who are close to actual operations, were the best informants on the unit's coordination techniques.

Respondents identified the major coordination mechanisms used for mission accomplishment in their unit from a list of 18 alternatives; the measure was based on frequency of use of horizontal coordination. Available response options included never, quarterly or less, monthly, biweekly, weekly, 2 to 3 times per week, and daily. Responses were aggregated at the deputate level.

Task routineness was measured with 5-point Likert items describing each unit's daily technical or line work, based on task analyzability (TASKANAL) and task variety (TASKVAR). The two indicators were treated as error-laden measures of the latent task routineness construct in the LISREL model. Squadron commanders emerged as the best informants on the unit's technology.

Respondents estimated the relative percentage of each type of workflow (independent, sequential, and reciprocal) between their own unit and others at the same level. Coded percentages were combined into the WKFLOW scale, with high levels of independence corresponding to low scale values and high levels of interdependence corresponding to high scale values. Senior commanders and deputy wing commanders were the best informants on workflow patterns.

Training complexity was measured with 5-point Likert items describing each unit's daily technical or line work, based on training demand (TRDEMAND) and training difficulty (TRDIFFIC). TRDEMAND had a low reliability score but remained a strong factor in the LISREL analysis and could not be eliminated from the model. The two indicators were treated as error-laden measures of the latent training complexity construct.

Scale consisting of items reflecting the unit's ability to acquire resources from the environment. It was one of three environment measures and was used as the latent resource scarcity construct in the LISREL model. Senior commanders and deputy wing commanders were the best informants on the environment and available resources.

Scale indicating the availability of information about each of the four sectors salient to the Air Force: technological, regulatory, resource supply (e.g., government contractors, availability of recruits), and users (groups that expect the Air Force to serve them). The scale had a low reliability score but could not be eliminated from the LISREL model. Responses were aggregated at the deputate level.

A context-specific measure of technological uncertainty that supplemented the measures of information and resource availability to enhance measurement validity. Respondents rated the amount of change in the technological sector, its predictability, its complexity, and information available about events, activities, and trends in technology. Because technology changes faster and more unpredictably for the Air Force than other domains, perceptions about technology measured environmental uncertainty.

Residual from an ordinary least squares regression estimating expected pay. Total pay is the TDC1 variable in Execucomp, reflecting the total ex ante value of all salary, bonuses, restricted stock grants, option grants, performance share grants, and other income, summed over the first two fiscal years in office and natural log transformed. The wage model includes company size, company age, an S&P 500 indicator, R&D intensity, two-year averages of ROA, MTB and total shareholder return, time in office over the first two fiscal years, cost of living index, and industry and year dummies. Positive residuals denote overpayment and negatives denote underpayment.
time_window: first two fiscal years in office

description: Residual from a wage model predicting current pay, defined as salary and bonus, natural log transformed with a small constant added before logging to accommodate zero values. The model uses the same predictors as the total pay model plus the value of the prospective pay component as an additional control. Higher values denote greater overpayment of current pay.
time_window: first two fiscal years in office

description: Residual from a wage model predicting prospective pay, defined as restricted stock, stock options, and any other income included in TDC1 besides salary and bonus, natural log transformed with a small constant added before logging to accommodate zero values. The model uses the same predictors as the total pay model plus the value of the current pay component as an additional control. Higher values denote greater overpayment of prospective pay.
time_window: first two fiscal years in office

description: Computed with the CEO in Context method. Annual company performance, measured as return on assets (net income divided by total assets), is modeled as a function of year dummies, industry performance (industry average ROA excluding the focal firm), inherited firm conditions (company average ROA in the two years before succession and the ratio of company market-to-book value to industry median MTB in the year before succession), and CEO dummies. Residuals after all contextual factors are modeled become the dependent variable in a final model in which CEO dummies are the independent variables; the regression coefficient for each CEO dummy is that CEO's career performance score, interpreted as the amount by which the CEO over- or underperformed expectations across the tenure. Models were estimated on 1992-2017 Execucomp data with generalized estimating equations and an autoregressive correlation structure clustered by firm, and industries were defined with four-digit GICS codes.
scale: ROA percentage points relative to expectations
time_window: entire CEO tenure (or portion observed through 2017)

description: An index of seven indicators of organizational discretion. Company sales, company employees, company age, and capital intensity (assets divided by sales) capture inertial forces and were reverse coded; company slack (current assets divided by current liabilities) and R&D intensity (R&D costs divided by sales) and advertising intensity (advertising costs divided by sales) capture available resources and product differentiability. Each variable was standardized to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 and the seven transformed variables were summed into an index of firm-level discretion.

Count measure ranging from 0 to 6 that represents the range of prior functional experience brought by the founding team at founding. Prior positions from career histories are coded into the six functional areas and a six indicates that all possible functions are represented in the prior experiences of the team. The mean number of prior functional experiences at founding is 1.5.

variable_name: depth of founding team functional experience
description: Number of founding team members who have prior experience in a given functional area, coded at founding from career histories in which up to three prior positions per individual are assigned to one of the six functional areas.

Count measure ranging from 0 to 6 of the number of unique functional categories in which the firm has an executive-level position at founding. Firms with no executive positions are coded 0 and firms with executive positions in all six functions are coded 6; the mean at founding is 1.8, typically a general administrative position such as president or CEO plus a vice president of science or engineering.

Whether the firm has a defined executive-level position in a given functional area at founding and how many executive-level positions in that function simultaneously exist; for example, a firm may be founded with a CTO and a vice president of engineering.

Count measure ranging from 0 to 6 that represents the range of prior functional experience brought by the team in each month, where six indicates that all possible functions are represented in the prior experiences of the team. Updated monthly.

Team-level career-history variable, updated monthly, indicating how many team members have prior experience in a function, capturing the depth of functional experience on the team. Up to three prior positions for every individual are coded into one of the six functional areas.

Count measure ranging from 0 to 6 that represents the number of functional categories covered each month, used to predict the breadth of functional structure. Firms with no executive positions are coded 0 for structure; firms with executive positions for all six functions are coded six.

For each firm the measure records whether the firm has a given functional position, when it is first established, and how many executive-level positions in a given function simultaneously exist in a team for each month of the firm's life. Six functional areas are coded.

Event history measure of the time from founding to first venture capital funding, modeled as the rate of obtaining a first VC round; the authors focus on time to first VC funding rather than cumulative rounds or total funds raised. 118 of the 158 firms at risk (71%) obtain VC funding during the sampling period.
time_window: from founding until event or end of observation

description: Event history measure of the time from founding to initial public offering, modeled as the rate of going public. 87 of the 158 firms at risk (51%) go public during the sampling period.
time_window: from founding until event or end of observation

description: Customer satisfaction is measured using the satisfaction scores reported in the American Customer Satisfaction Index (ACSI) published by the National Quality Research Centre at the University of Michigan. The authors use ACSI as a proxy for the customer satisfaction information used by internal and external stakeholders such as compensation committees, and note that it is an aggregate measure of the firm's overall customer satisfaction rather than an individual's satisfaction with a specific transaction. Firms with multiple ACSI scores are excluded from the sample, as are firms with too few observations to estimate lead indicator strength.

Lead indicator strength is measured as the association between current satisfaction and future profit, measured as one-period-ahead ROA, and is estimated separately for each firm in the sample. It is the coefficient on Customer satisfaction (alpha 1) in a regression of one-period-ahead ROA on Customer satisfaction, current ROA, one-period-lagged ROA, current stock returns, and one-period-lagged stock returns. The authors describe the measure as conservative because, by construction, it excludes any element of customer satisfaction that influences future profit but is also reflected in the current and past series of profit or stock returns.
time_window: estimated separately for each firm over 1994-2005

description: CEO total compensation includes CEO short-term compensation and long-term incentives, which are primarily comprised of restricted stock, stock options, and cash payouts from long-term performance plans. The natural log of the measure is used in the empirical tests to mitigate the potential influence of heteroskedasticity, and the value of CEO stock option awards is estimated using the Black-Scholes valuation model.

CEO short-term compensation captures salary and bonus awarded to the CEO in a given year. The natural log of the measure is used in the empirical tests to mitigate the potential influence of heteroskedasticity.

Compensation relevance is calculated as the sum of two terms: the coefficient on Customer satisfaction from the tests of Hypothesis 1 multiplied by the firm's customer satisfaction score, plus the coefficient on the Customer satisfaction x Lead indicator strength interaction from the same regression multiplied by customer satisfaction and lead indicator strength. Customer satisfaction is the satisfaction score for each firm for 2006-2010 and lead indicator strength is the same firm-level measure used in the tests of Hypothesis 1, estimated for each firm over 1994-2005.
time_window: customer satisfaction 2006-2010; lead indicator strength estimated over 1994-2005

description: Growth in future shareholder value is measured as two-period-ahead percent stock returns, a choice justified by the fact that CEO compensation arrangements usually take some time to impact shareholder value. Any component of the measure that is already impounded in current or past measures of financial performance is excluded, and the influence of current, one-period lagged and two-period lagged profit and shareholder returns is removed using a standard orthogonalization procedure.

Growth in CEO compensation is calculated as the year-on-year percent change in CEO compensation, expressed in equivalent terms to the measure of future firm performance used in the tests of Hypothesis 2.
Board independence is defined as the proportion of nonexecutive board members over the total board size. The measure follows prior audit-fee studies (Carcello et al., 2002; Hay et al., 2006).
This variable takes the value one if the CEO and chairman positions are held by the same person and zero otherwise.

The dependent variable is the natural log of audit fees, following prior studies on the relationship between corporate governance and audit demand. It considers the total fee paid for the audit services to all auditors.

Firms are categorized as having concentrated ownership if an individual, family group, or firm has a total stake of at least 20 percent of the shares. Both direct and indirect ownership are considered to determine the ownership structure, using a threshold level of 20 percent to define control for indirect ownership. Firms without controlling shareholders are classified as firms with dispersed ownership.

Firms are classified into three types of owners: families, corporations, and banks. The controlling owner is defined as the largest shareholder with at least 20 percent of the shares at each step of the ownership chain, taking into account both direct and indirect shareholdings as well as possible family ties. Kinship relationships between individual shareholders are identified in order to fully capture family ownership.

The number (count) of primary patent classes that a patent lists, taken from the United States Patent Classification (USPC). Although patents list both primary and secondary classes, only the primary classes are counted, because those are the most salient categories to both examiners and inventors. The number of patent classes listed reflects the linkages drawn by both inventors and examiners.

The natural log of the number of months elapsed between the filing date of a patent and the date it gets approved. It provides a measure of how recognizable a patent application is to USPTO examiners.

The cumulative number of citations a patent receives in its first three years after approval. To ensure three full years are included, patents granted after 2002 were excluded from the citations analysis.

The number of NSF grants awarded to proposals with multiple principal investigators, computed by year. The measure follows a litmus test for interdisciplinarity identified in interviews with 12 experts involved with NSF or NIH efforts to measure or promote IDR growth: whether grants have only a single principal investigator or multiple investigators. In the approval time analyses the measure is taken for the year in which a patent application is filed; in the forward citation analysis, for the year in which a patent application is approved.
time_window: year of application (approval time analysis); year of grant (citation analysis)

description: Constructed in two steps. First, a proximity index is computed for each pair of classes: it is the average of two proportions, calculated by dividing the number of times the classes are co-mentioned by the total number of times the first and second are mentioned, respectively, using co-mentions in the same patent over the five years prior to the focal patent year. Second, typicality averages the proximity indices for every unordered pair of primary patent classes the focal patent lists; for patents that have only one class the typicality score is 1. Larger scores mean that a patent's listed classes occur together more frequently, whereas smaller scores mean a more unusual or atypical blend of prior art areas. The equations for the proximity index and for typicality are not readable in the text, but their content is described in prose.
time_window: five years prior to the focal patent year (for the proximity index)

description: Dichotomous indicator of whether a worker was a boomerang (coded '1') or a new hire ('0'). Boomerangs are individuals who previously worked full time for Asclepius and returned to work for the organization; new hires are individuals who had not worked for Asclepius prior to their entry into the organization during the study period.

Based on the annual rating each employee receives for each calendar year. Managers first enter ratings for their subordinates; then all managers who supervise workers in similar jobs meet in calibration discussions to ensure consistency across the organization. At the beginning of the observation window all employees received a rating on a scale of 0 to 9 points, with 9 the highest possible rating; the company transitioned to an 8-point rating system with two components over a three-year period. To make the two scales compatible across years, the authors standardized the measures within division, pay grade, and year, transforming the original values to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 among employees in the same division and same pay grade each year.
scale: standardized within division, pay grade, and year (mean 0, SD 1); underlying scales 0-9 and an 8-point system

description: Average of the scores of two of the three items from the role relationships scale in the O*NET work-context domain, excluding the single item assessing whether the job requires dealing with external customers. The two retained items assess whether the work requires an individual to 'work with a group or team' and to 'coordinate with or lead others,' and had an alpha reliability of .84.

Average of the scores for the three items that compose the interpersonal orientation scale in the O*NET work-styles domain, which assesses the extent to which a job requires being pleasant, cooperative, sensitive to others, easy to get along with, and having a preference for associating with other organization members. The three-item scale had an alpha reliability of .88.

Average of the scores for the three items that compose the administering scale in the O*NET work-activities domain, which assesses the level of administering, monitoring, or controlling organizational resources that a job requires. The three-item scale had an alpha reliability of .87.

variable_name: % recent new hires in work unit
description: The number of employees in the unit with fewer than two years of tenure in the firm, divided by the work unit size. Work units are defined by Asclepius's personnel records and consist of employees who report to the same manager. The decision to define recent hires as those with fewer than two years of tenure derives from research suggesting that it takes approximately two years for new hires to fully adjust to an organization.
The number of years the employee's direct manager had been employed at Asclepius.

A designer's popularity index counts the citations received, excluding self-citations, by that designer's patents in the preceding three-year rolling window. An inventor whose popularity index is in the top 2% of all inventors is considered, at the time of measurement, to be a star designer. Star emergence is the event in the designer's career when the popularity index first attains the 2% threshold; a star designer is assumed to remain a star throughout the observation window. The event history models estimate the hazard of this event.

An indicator variable set to one for treated designers (who collaborate with a star designer) and set to zero for control designers (who do not). The two groups are created by coarsened exact matching: each treated designer is matched with exactly one control designer who is statistically similar on six pretreatment observables at the time of the treated designer's first star collaboration (the treatment event).
time_window: at the time of the focal designer's first star collaboration

variable_name: Direct ties to stars and direct ties to nonstars
description: Direct ties to stars is measured as the count of the number of the focal designer's unique star collaborators until time t (|H_it|). Direct ties to nonstars is measured analogously as the count of the focal designer's unique nonstar collaborators until time t (|L_it|).

The average fraction of common third parties within the focal designer's network with respect to the focal designer's star collaborators: the average proportion of the focal designer's past collaborators who also collaborated with the focal designer's star collaborators. The measure equals zero if there are no third parties in common with any star in the focal designer's network and equals one if all the focal designer's past collaborators are also past collaborators of the star collaborators. It is equivalent to the focal actor's local network density; the formal equation is not legible in the source text as provided.

Defined analogously to network cohesion with stars, but computed with respect to the focal designer's nonstar collaborators: the average fraction of the focal designer's past collaborators who also collaborated with the focal designer's nonstar collaborators. The continuous measure ranges from zero (no common third parties) to one (all past collaborators shared).

The average fraction of areas of expertise that are common to both the focal designer and a star collaborator, divided by the number of the focal designer's areas of expertise. Areas of expertise are identified with the USPTO design patent classes and subclasses: each subclass is viewed as a distinct area of expertise in which a designer has been granted patents until time t. The variable ranges from zero (no expertise similarity between the focal designer and all star collaborators) to one (complete overlap); the formal equation is not legible in the source text as provided.

Defined analogously to expertise similarity with stars, but computed with respect to the focal designer's nonstar collaborators: the average fraction of areas of expertise shared between the focal designer and a nonstar collaborator, divided by the number of the focal designer's areas of expertise. It also ranges from zero to one.

A dummy variable created to reflect the experimental level of primary uncertainty in the decision scenario (1 = low, 2 = high). The independent variables were manipulated by inserting in the cases one set of alternative paragraphs describing primary uncertainty (either high or low).

A dummy variable created to reflect the experimental level of competitive uncertainty in the decision scenario (1 = low, 2 = high). The manipulation consisted of one of two alternative paragraphs describing competitive uncertainty (either high or low).

A dummy variable created to reflect the experimental level of supplier uncertainty in the decision scenario (1 = low, 2 = high). The manipulation consisted of one set of alternative paragraphs describing supplier uncertainty (either high or low).

A two-item scale (alpha = 0.94) that asked participants to indicate the extent to which they agreed or disagreed with two statements: 'Vegas Press should outsource its finishing operations' (reverse coded), and 'Vegas Press should expand its in-house finishing operations.' Items were averaged to create a variable score since there was no theoretical grounding for using weighted averages in the calculation.

Measured with five items that were averaged to create a variable score (Cronbach alpha = 0.71). Participants were presented with the information items used to construct the case scenarios and asked to indicate the extent to which they would use each piece of information in making their decision.
Assessed with one item on which participants indicated the degree to which they used information about competitive uncertainty in making their decision.

Measured with three items that were averaged to create a variable score (Cronbach alpha = 0.68). Participants indicated the extent to which they took supplier uncertainty information into account in making their decision.

A formative scale measuring the extent to which the contractor shares in property rights over the technology. Individual items were developed by appeal to the legal and economic literatures and are built on ownership rights, usage rights, and rights to financial returns, and on the ability to exclude others; items focus on both the contractor's rights and the extent to which the client was prohibited from certain actions. Respondents were asked about many of the rights granted to the contractor in terms of their overall significance. All items are preserved in the final measure and the item scores are averaged to get the overall scale score.
A five-item scale adapted from Anderson (1985) measuring the extent to which the client's investments are characterized by limited redeployability and limited salvageability.
A five-item scale adapted from Moorman and Miner (1997) that describes unforeseen changes in the market for the client's product.
A four-item scale developed specifically for this study that assesses changes in the underlying technologies used to perform the contracted tasks.
A five-item scale developed specifically for this study measuring the extent to which the technology has applications beyond those uses targeted by the client.

An eight-item scale adapted from John (1984) measuring strategic self-interest-seeking behavior undertaken in order to redirect profits from vulnerable partners. The items tap a number of opportunistic behaviors that the contractor may exhibit during project execution.

Measured as the number of citations that a firm's patents filed in year t had received in subsequent years up to 2004. The number of citations that a patent receives is generally accepted as a significant predictor of both its value and technological impact. Changes in coupling are expected to affect the quality of inventions that are generated and, thereby, affect the number of citations received.
time_window: patents filed in year t; citations received up to 2004

variable_name: Change in couplings among existing knowledge domains
description: Measured as the change in coupling between domains that were present in both time periods, by comparing each firm's coupling matrix for t-6 to t-4 with that for t-3 to t-1. The coupling between technology classes j and k is based on the number of the firm's patents assigned to class j, to class k, and to both classes (co-listed), so that repeated recombination of two domains implies strong coupling. Change is the weighted number of technology class pairs that had undergone a significant change in coupling, where a significant change was defined as a change that exceeded one quartile, and quartile rankings were estimated from all nonzero couplings as a function of the size of the firm's patent portfolio and time. The weight is (pi + pj)/2 + (p'i + p'j)/2, where pi (resp. pj) and p'i (resp. p'j) are the percentages of patents that belong to class i (resp. j) in the earlier and later periods; the equation block itself was unreadable.
time_window: t-6 to t-4 compared with t-3 to t-1

variable_name: Coupling between new and existing knowledge domains
description: Measured as the changes resulting from the addition of couplings between new and existing knowledge domains, using the same quartile-ranking-based procedure as for changes among existing domains. A significant increase was recorded when a class pair moved from a zero value in the earlier period to the second, third or fourth quartile in the later period, from the first quartile to the third or fourth quartile, or from the second to the fourth quartile. The change measure is the weighted number of technology class pairs that had undergone a significant change in coupling, with the same weights as for changes among existing domains.
time_window: t-6 to t-4 compared with t-3 to t-1

description: A proxy based on the potential for recombination (Etk) of Fleming and Sorenson, calculated for a technology subclass as the number of other subclasses with which it had been combined (co-listed in a patent) in the previous five years divided by the number of patents assigned to that subclass in the same period. Because all patents in the patent database are used, it is an exogenous measure, unlike coupling. Domain complexity for a firm in a year is a weighted measure of the potential for recombination of each of the technological subclasses in which the firm has patents, with weights equal to the fraction of the firm's patents in each subclass, averaged over the previous six years corresponding to the two periods over which change is calculated. The equation blocks were unreadable.
time_window: previous five years, averaged over the previous six years

description: The average of the reciprocal of network distance between the focal fund and all other funds of the same category; the measure increases as a fund is connected to other funds via shorter distances. When a fund is disconnected from the main components, the authors assume that the reciprocal of network distance is zero since 1/∞ approximates to zero. The network is a one-mode projection of a two-mode network linking managers and their employers, built from managers' career biographies, and is time-invariant. The formal specification of closeness is not readable in the supplied text (the formula block was removed).
time_window: career snapshot at the end of October 2008; study period March-October 2008

description: The shortest network distance between two funds, also known as the geodesic, categorized into direct (dij = 1), indirect (dij = 2), distant (dij ≥ 3), and disconnected (dij is undefined). Distant contacts with a network distance of three steps or more are pooled because they are qualitatively similar in being deprived of mutual contacts.
time_window: career snapshot at the end of October 2008

description: The average Pearson correlation of monthly returns between two funds. Because the authors could not observe the specific investment positions each fund took, they assumed that two funds whose investment portfolios were similar would show a greater level of correlation between their monthly returns. It is computed for pairs of funds of the same category, distinguished by the network distance between the two funds.
time_window: before the shock (monthly returns in the pre-shock period)

description: The percentage change in a fund's assets during a given month net of capital invested into or withdrawn from the fund. The fees the fund charged were not subtracted because the authors were interested in returns as a measure of organizational performance rather than the efficacy of hedge funds as investment vehicles. Reported monthly for each fund over the study window.

Funds were identified from the descriptions provided in BarclayHedge: descriptors such as 'long-short equity' and analogous terms (equity long, equity short, equity market neutral) identify long-short hedge funds, and descriptors related to the word 'arbitrage' (fixed income arbitrage, convertible arbitrage, event-driven) identify relative value funds; the categorization was cross-checked with Lipper TASS and fund websites. Long-short funds face an information environment that deeply engages with soft information, whereas relative value funds operate in an environment that draws almost exclusively on hard information.

Dependent variable indicating whether a foreign operation generated new incremental patent applications (ultimately granted) at time t. The authors consider incremental innovation to include those foreign patents that cite similar technology class-subclass combinations in their backward citations to those that already exist in the USPTO data. For every patent in the NBER database the authors created the cited technology combination that exists, and then compared the technology class citation combinations of the foreign patents of the sampled U.S. MNCs to the already cited technology combinations in the pool of all patents in years prior to the focal patent. If the technology class citation combination had already been cited prior to the application year of the granted focal patent, the innovation was categorized as incremental.

Dependent variable indicating whether a foreign operation generated new radical patent applications (ultimately granted) at time t. Radical innovations are new technology class-subclass combinations, which the authors say captures new technology trajectories or frontiers, and this definition means that radical innovations are those that are new to the field (not just new to the firm). If the technology class citation combination had not already been cited prior to the application year of the granted focal patent, the innovation was categorized as radical.

Operationalized as total royalty payments to parent firm operations divided by the total sales of the foreign operation. Royalties and licensing fees are paid to parent firms for the use of intangible property, such as patents, trademarks, copyrights, industrial processes, manufacturing rights, franchises, or other intangible assets or property rights. The authors note that U.S. MNCs report that technology licensing fees account for close to 90% of the royalty payments.

The ratio of backward citations to local host-country generated patents to total citations in the patents generated in the foreign operation over the prior three years. The authors use inventor locations, following majority rule for patents with multiple inventors, to determine the country of origin of each cited patent.

The ratio of backward citations to third-country MNC generated patents to total backward citations in the patents generated in the foreign operation over the prior three years. The country of origin of each cited patent is determined from inventor locations, following majority rule for patents with multiple inventors.

Dummy variable coded one if an analyst is designated a member of the "All-American Research Team" in year t (regardless of whether the analyst is first, second, or third team or honorable mention) by Institutional Investor magazine and zero otherwise. Independent and control variables were measured between April 1 of year t-1 and March 31 of year t, capturing the information available to institutional investors when they cast their ballots.
Dummy variable coded one if the analyst was designated an All-Star analyst in year t-1 and zero otherwise. It is used as an independent variable in Hypotheses 3a and 4a.

A count of the number of All-Star designations an analyst received between the beginning of the study period and year t-2. Because an All-Star designation in year t-1 is coded separately, this measure captures the accumulation of prior certifications beyond the most recent one.
time_window: beginning of study period through year t-2

description: The average difference between the focal analyst's forecast errors and the average forecast error of analysts who follow the same firm during the same period. The focal analyst's absolute forecast error is subtracted from the average absolute forecast error of all analysts covering the same firm, the difference is divided by that average absolute forecast error to reduce heteroskedasticity, and the deflated scores are averaged across the firms for which the analyst issued forecasts. The variable is reverse-coded so that higher values indicate greater accuracy; zero means the analyst's estimates equal the average for all analysts covering the same firms. For Hypotheses 3 and 4 the same operationalization serves as the dependent variable, calculated from forecasts issued between April 1 of year t and March 31 of year t+1.
scale: continuous, reverse-coded; zero equals the average for all analysts covering the same firms
time_window: April 1 of year t-1 to March 31 of year t (independent variable); April 1 of year t to March 31 of year t+1 (dependent variable)

description: The proportion of an analyst's revised estimates that deviate from the consensus forecast, where the consensus forecast is the average forecast made by all other analysts following the firm immediately prior to the analyst's revised forecast. A revised forecast was classified as deviating if it was either above both the analyst's own prior forecast and the consensus forecast or below both, using a 90-day window prior to the issue date of the revised forecast to calculate the consensus. The proportion is the number of deviating estimates between April 1 of year t-1 and March 31 of year t divided by the total number of estimates the analyst made in that period; what is relevant is how often the analyst deviated, not the magnitude or direction of the deviance. For Hypotheses 3 and 4 the same operationalization serves as the dependent variable.
time_window: April 1 of year t-1 to March 31 of year t (independent variable); April 1 of year t to March 31 of year t+1 (dependent variable)

description: Event history analysis of the likelihood of firm mortality given that a firm has not exited yet. Firm age in years is set as the clock and the history of each firm is split into firm-years. Transition rates are assumed constant within each of the following time pieces but vary across them: 0–1 years, 1–3 years, 3–5 years, 5–15 years, and 15 or more years.

Proximity-weighted density at founding, obtained by recording the degree of contemporaneous localized competition faced by the focal firm in the year of its founding; contemporaneous localized competition sums all other firms existing at a given time weighted by their geographical distance to the focal firm, as in the formulation adapted from Sorenson and Audia (2000). A squared term for this density at founding measure is also included.

Proximity-weighted density at founding, obtained by recording the degree of contemporaneous localized competition faced by the focal firm in the year of its founding, applied to the cohort of firms founded in the postshock period. A squared term for this density at founding measure is also included.

variable_name: Competitive experience with Civil War firms
description: Cumulative measure of past contemporaneous competition with firms of the cohort, following Barnett (2008): the sum of contemporaneous competition with firms of the qth cohort in each prior year after the end of the Civil War for the focal firm, up to the current time.
time_window: from the end of the Civil War to the current year

description: Cumulative measure of past contemporaneous competition with firms of the cohort, following Barnett (2008): the sum of contemporaneous competition with firms of the qth cohort in each prior year after the end of the Civil War for the focal firm, up to the current time.
time_window: from the end of the Civil War to the current year

description: Years since the Civil War, used to control for changes in the mortality rates of firms over time and interacted with the density at founding and density at founding squared variables to test Hypotheses 2(a) and 2(b).

Equity tie centralization is operationalized as the average difference between the centrality of the most central affiliate and that of all other affiliates, based on degree centrality. The degree centrality measure was created by counting the number of direct partners with which a focal affiliate has equity ties. The measure ranges from 0 (where all the affiliates have the same degree centrality) to 1 (where one affiliate is connected to all the other affiliates, but those affiliates are only connected to the lead firm). The authors use the overall equity centralization built from both inward and outward ties; the equation itself is not readable in the text.
We use affiliate ROA to capture firm profitability. We measured this as (Net income of the affiliate)/(Total assets of the affiliate).

Period after 2008 is a dummy variable that equals 1 for the period of 2009-2013 and 0 otherwise. The authors use the 2008 financial crisis as an exogenous shock that made the business environment highly turbulent, treating firms in industries affected by the turbulence (electronics and computers, metals and metalworking, chemicals, petrochemicals, pharmaceuticals) as the treatment group and firms in industries largely unaffected (food, beverage, textile, leather) as the control group.
Listed firm is a dummy that equals 1 if an affiliate is listed in the Taiwanese Stock Exchange and 0 otherwise.

Dependent variable coded as the year in which the focal firm adopted a CSR position for the first time. The authors compiled an original database on the creation of CSR executive positions among Fortune 500 companies by identifying common phrases associated with executive job titles, selecting for each firm the most relevant CSR position with the highest rank, and keeping only positions with the title 'Vice President' and above because individuals with these titles are likely to have a direct voice in the firm's overall strategy. Information was triangulated using online sources including executives' LinkedIn profiles, corporate press releases, alumni associations, and media coverage of corporate actions. In the event-history models the variable captures the likelihood and speed (hazard) of adoption.

variable_name: Prior adoptions among industry peer firms
description: Baseline count of prior adoptions of a CSR executive position in the focal firm's industry, entered in the contagiousness vector. For each focal firm, referent firms in the same 4-digit-GICS industry were specified as the relevant reference group in the social proximity vector. The authors report that this count of prior adoptions in the industry was a significant predictor of the focal firm's hazard of adoption, providing evidence of baseline imitation.
time_window: from the start of the study window until year t-1

description: Index built from the focal CEO's political donation records, coded for the 10 years prior to the executive becoming CEO. Four indicators are computed: the number of donations to Republicans divided by the number of donations to recipients of both parties; the dollar amount of donations to Republicans divided by the amount donated to both parties; the number of years the CEO donated to Republicans divided by the number of years the CEO donated to either party; and the number of distinct Republican recipients to which the CEO made donations divided by the total number of distinct recipients of both parties. The composite is a simple average of the four indicators (Cronbach's Alpha = 0.92), with index scores ranging from zero to one, higher scores representing conservatism and lower values liberalism; CEOs who made zero political contributions were imputed a score of 0.50.

Key independent variable computed as a count of prior adoptions in the industry, from the start of the study window until year t-1, where each adoption is first multiplied by the prior adopter CEO's ideological conservatism and the conservatism-weighted adoptions are then aggregated at the level of the focal firm-year observation. It is entered in the contagiousness vector together with a simple count of prior adoptions in the industry, which tests whether the ideology of prior adopters affects the focal firm's imitation decisions above and beyond baseline imitation.
time_window: from the start of the study window until year t-1

description: Measure based on the number of shareholder resolutions urging management to increase their firm's engagement in CSR issues in a given year. Data on shareholder proxy proposals were collected from the Ethvest database and were obtained from the Interfaith Council on Corporate Responsibility (ICCR).

variable_name: Peer CEO conservatism-weighted adoptions (same state) and Peer CEO conservatism-weighted adoptions (other states)
description: Following the approach established by Marquis and Tilcsik (2016), firms that were both industry and community (headquartered in the same state) peers were considered institutionally equivalent. To test the hypothesis, the primary independent variable was split into two parts, Peer CEO conservatism-weighted adoptions (same state) and Peer CEO conservatism-weighted adoptions (other states), each coded as the count of prior adoptions among the relevant group of referent CEOs weighted by their ideological conservatism. The hypothesis was tested by comparing the coefficients of the two variables.
time_window: from the start of the study window until year t-1

description: Dichotomous variable coded 1 if a firm was convicted of a violation and 0 if no convictions existed.

Three-point scale based on Clinard and colleagues' criteria, rating violations from somewhat serious (coded 1) to very serious (coded 3). Two raters independently assessed seriousness with agreement of .84; the authors averaged the two ratings when raters disagreed.

Number of additional convictions a firm received in the same year as its initial conviction, or during the five-year post-conviction period. The sample contained 47 firms with one conviction, 15 firms with one extra, 4 firms with two, and 2 firms with three or more additional convictions.
time_window: same year as initial conviction or five-year post-conviction period

description: Coded 0 for unconvicted firms, 1 for firms with a single conviction (no subsequent illegalities), and 2 for firms convicted of subsequent violations. Subsequent convictions were those occurring after an initial one, either during the five-year post-conviction period or in any year after that period until 1983.

Income before extraordinary items and discontinued operations, plus interest expense, divided by total assets. The authors used ROA in the year after a conviction or target year and computed a five-year average of ROA for analysis.
time_window: one year after conviction or target year; five-year average

description: Income before taxes divided by total sales. The authors calculated one-year and five-year average measures of ROS.
time_window: one year after conviction or target year; five-year average

description: Change in stock price from one year to the next, computed from stock price data in Moody's Common Stocks. The authors computed the change in price over the year following a conviction or target year, and the average change in shareholder returns over a five-year period.
time_window: one year after conviction or target year; five-year average

description: Four dichotomous variables, one for each type of illegality, each coded 1 if a firm was convicted of that type and 0 if the firm was not convicted of that type of illegality. The types are discrimination, per se antitrust, product liability with punitive damages, and other violations.

Estimated number of participants in each pro-LGBTQ protest event, coded from local newspaper reports. The variable has values ranging from 2 to 450,000, with a mean of 900 across all events, and is log-transformed. In the instrumental variable regressions it is the endogenous regressor, instrumented by rainfall on the event date.

Yearly count in each city of LGBTQ-affiliated organizations listed in the Gayellow Pages that have both inside and outside audiences, that is, organizations seeking support from a mix of LGBTQ and non-LGBTQ customers/clients or owners/managers. The counts are log-transformed and are aggregated to the central counties of each city's core-based statistical area. The covariates enter the regressions with a one-year lag.

Yearly count in each city of multiaudience LGBTQ-affiliated businesses listed in the Gayellow Pages, that is, bridging organizations classified in the commercial categories of the directory. Like the other organization counts it is log-transformed and used as a dependent variable in the fixed-effects instrumental variable regression.

Yearly count in each city of LGBTQ-affiliated organizations listed in the Gayellow Pages that are owned or managed by LGBTQ people and serve exclusively or primarily the LGBTQ public. These counts are log-transformed and are the dependent variable in the fixed-effects instrumental variable regression.

Yearly count in each city of LGBTQ social movement organizations listed in the Gayellow Pages, defined by the directory categories the authors use to identify SMOs. This model uses untransformed counts, as the skewness of SMO counts is not significant.

Organizations listed in the Gayellow Pages are classified as businesses by following the list of categories described as commercial organizations in table 3 of Negro et al. (2013). Businesses in the directory include restaurants and cafés, bars and clubs, hotel accommodations, bookstores, food stores, office supplies, and real estate agencies, which comprise an almost 70% share of the listings.

Uniqueness is captured in three items that assess the degree to which the technology in question is uncommon in the industry, or the degree to which competitors had fundamentally similar technology. Items were measured using seven-point Likert scales and each measure included at least one reverse-coded item. Where dual responses were received, the responses from the multiple raters were averaged for each construct.

Barriers to imitation is measured by three items questioning the perceived difficulty of imitating or reverse engineering the technology. Items were measured using seven-point Likert scales and each measure included at least one reverse-coded item. Multiple rater responses were averaged for each construct for the final sample.

Commercial uncertainty is evaluated with five items that assess the degree to which managers were confident the technology would meet technical and/or commercial expectations. Items were measured using seven-point Likert scales and each measure included at least one reverse-coded item; multiple rater responses were averaged for the final sample.

Dynamism is captured in two items that assess the length of time for which the technology was anticipated to be valuable, or the length of its life cycle. Items were measured using seven-point Likert scales and each measure included at least one reverse-coded item; multiple rater responses were averaged for the final sample.

Threat of opportunism includes three items that assess the degree to which managers perceived that there was a risk of being taken advantage of, or the likelihood of partners and suppliers behaving dishonestly if given an opportunity, and the amount of oversight that would be required in the exchange. Items were measured using seven-point Likert scales and each measure included at least one reverse-coded item; multiple rater responses were averaged for the final sample.

Potential for sustainable competitive advantage is measured in three items that capture the degree to which managers felt the technology would differentiate the firm, or the degree to which managers felt that competitors would be able to reap similar strategic benefits within a short period of time. Items were measured using seven-point Likert scales and each measure included at least one reverse-coded item; multiple rater responses were averaged for the final sample.

Governance mode was coded as a dichotomous variable (0 = license agreement, 1 = acquisition). It was first derived from the public announcement of the sourcing arrangement in the newswires, and care was taken to ensure that the motivation of the sourcing arrangement was technology driven rather than marketing or market growth related; a respondent from the acquiring firm subsequently verified the motivation. Each executive was also asked to verify the nature of the agreement (licensing, acquisition) and that the underlying motivation was technology driven.

Uniqueness items were part of the instrument pilot tested on 30 responses from executives who had made recent sourcing decisions; the measures were revised on the basis of the pilot test. Items were measured using seven-point Likert scales.

variable_name: Technological uncertainty (commercial uncertainty and technological dynamism)
description: Technological uncertainty is captured by two survey sub-scales from the executive survey: commercial uncertainty (five items on confidence that the technology would meet technical and commercial expectations) and technological dynamism (two items on how long the technology was expected to be valuable, or its life cycle). The two dimensions are modeled separately in the path model.

Number of a firm's rewarded patents whose value is below the average value of patents in the same technological class, divided by all of a firm's patents. Rewards counted as pay for performance are salary increases or bonus payments accruing when a patent is filed, and patent value is the inventor's self-reported estimate of the monetary value of the patented invention. It is a firm-level variable reflecting the firm's pay system and the degree to which it is affected by false rewards.

Number of a firm's nonrewarded patents whose value is above the average value of patents in the same technological class, divided by all of a firm's patents. Patent value is the inventor's self-reported estimate of the monetary value of the patented invention, compared with the average monetary value of all patents in the same technological class. It is a firm-level variable reflecting the firm's pay system.

Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 for inventors who rated both peer community recognition ('prestige and reputation') and the desire to solve intellectual challenges higher than the sample median (2 and 3, respectively). Motivations were assessed on five-point rating scales ranging from 1 ('not important') to 5 ('very important'). The dummy demarcates corporate scientists from other types of inventors.
Responses to a survey question asking for the number of weekly working hours that the inventor dedicated to creative R&D activities during the project that led to the patented invention.

Constructed as (a - b)/(a + b), where a is the frequency of interactions with colleagues in the R&D department and b is the average frequency of interactions with colleagues in other departments (production, marketing, logistics, human resources). The scales for both a and b range from 1 ('never') to 5 ('daily').
Log of the number of the firm's patents as computed from the survey. Used to split the sample at its median into firms with many and with few patents.

variable_name: three-year index and dividend corrected market value change
description: Excess returns to acquirer shareholders relative to the same-period market index, measured over a three-year period. With respect to dividends, a buy-and-hold strategy was assumed and dividends were added back to the market value of the firm. The capital asset pricing model was not used for determining cumulative abnormal returns because of potential validity problems regarding beta; market valuation data were extracted from CRSP.
scale: excess market return over a three-year period
time_window: three-year periods within the observation window

description: The average number of acquisitions that a firm undertakes during the focal and the preceding two years.
time_window: focal year and the two preceding years

description: The standard deviation of the yearly number of acquisitions across the focal year and the two preceding years. Firms that acquire a large number of targets during a short period of time followed by periods of low activity or even inactivity have a higher variability of the acquisition rate.
scale: standard deviation of yearly acquisition counts
time_window: focal year and the two preceding years

description: The number of acquisitions carried out prior to the window of observation. It is a proxy for a firm's acquisition capability.
The logarithm of the acquirer's total assets at the beginning of the window of observation.
time_window: beginning of the window of observation

description: A change in the acquiring firm's two-digit SIC code portfolio during the period of observation. The more a firm's two-digit SIC code portfolio expands during the period by acquiring firms from unrelated industries, the broader its acquisition program scope.
scale: change in two-digit SIC code portfolio

description: Constructed from the Federal Trade Commission's line-of-business data on the dollar amounts of intracompany transfers between a focal line of business and the other lines held by its parent company. The overall degree of integration, labeled degree of total integration, is the simple average of the degrees of forward and backward integration. The measurement complications associated with these measures tend to lead to underestimation of the degree of integration, providing a conservative test of the hypotheses.

The ratio of the dollar value of internal downstream transfers to total sales, where total sales is external sales plus transfers out of the line of business. Computed for each line of business from the Federal Trade Commission's data on intracompany transfers.

The ratio of the dollar value of internal transfers received by the line of business to the cost of sales. Computed for each line of business from the Federal Trade Commission's data on intracompany transfers.

A line of business's ratio of media advertising expenditures to sales, one of five cost variables used as dependent variables. Sales was the sum of internal downstream transfers and market transactions. The ratio of expenditures to sales was used to control for the obvious influences of size on expenditures.

A line of business's ratio of other selling expenses to sales, one of five cost variables used as dependent variables. Other selling expenses consisted mainly of wages for salespeople and promotional expenditures.
A line of business's ratio of R&D expenditures to sales, one of five cost variables used as dependent variables. The Federal Trade Commission database does not separate process and product R&D.

Production costs were measured using the ratio of cost of sales to sales, one of five cost variables used as dependent variables. Under full absorption accounting, cost of sales includes payroll, raw material, factory depreciation, and rental expenses incurred in the manufacturing of a product; the cost of raw materials was adjusted to market prices using methods similar to those used for adjusting reported operating income, and the reported and market-adjusted ratios were so highly correlated that both yielded substantially the same results.

Overhead expenses were measured as the line of business's ratio of general and administrative expenses to sales, one of five cost variables used as dependent variables. All nontraceable costs, including expenses borne by corporate headquarters and shared facilities, were allocated among each firm's lines of business using the allocations the companies themselves provided to the Federal Trade Commission.

Reported operating income over sales, one of two profit margin variables used as dependent variables. Income was pretax, pre-interest expense income from operations for a line of business. Return on sales was used instead of return on assets because measuring assets requires a lot of common asset allocations among lines of business, increasing the measurement error for return on assets.

The ratio of reported operating income to sales adjusted for transfer prices, one of two profit margin variables used as dependent variables. The Federal Trade Commission allowed companies to set transfer costs using a market, cost, cost-plus, or other valuation method, and only roughly half the firms chose market transfer prices.

Measured as the R-squared derived from regressing industry sales from 1972 through 1976 against a time variable (year 1 through year 5), using data on shipments recorded in the Annual Survey of Manufacturers. A second measure used the R-squared derived from regressing industry sales from 1972 through 1980 against time from year 1 through year 9; both stability measures yielded the same results. The R-squared measures the explained variance in, or the predictability of, demand over time.

Operating costs are measured by five separate cost variables, each a line of business's ratio to sales: media advertising, other selling expenses, R&D, production cost (cost of sales), and general and administrative (overhead) expenses. Each ratio is used as a dependent variable in the regressions on vertical integration.

The dependent variable, calculated as the level of R&D investments divided by the firm's sales, assets, or number of employees. Here, R&D investments are standardized by total assets because some firms do not have sales in the early years of product development.

Calculated as the average number of years managers have spent in a particular firm. The top management team is defined as all inside top-level executives including the chief executive officer, chief operating officer, business unit heads and vice presidents; all inside executives listed in the management section of the prospectus are included.
Calculated as the sum of the shared experiences across all dyads on the team. This measure incorporates the shared team-specific experience of all current executives.

Calculated with a Herfindahl index, where p is the percentage of top management team members in each functional background category. The list of functional categories provided in Michel and Hambrick (1992) is used to code the various functional backgrounds. Managers were coded on their current function (or department) at that time.
Measured with a dummy variable that takes the value of one if the CEO of the firm is not the board chair at the same time.

Calculated as the proportion of outside (i.e., non-executive) directors who were appointed before the current CEO took office. This measure excludes outside directors who may be appointed by the CEO during his/her tenure due to former personal or business ties, but does not exclude affiliated outside directors such as financiers and channel partners.

Created to test Hypothesis 1, it measures a firm's stock of relevant transferable skills and knowledge potentially available for new uses. The authors considered each firm's pool of pre-1966 patents to reflect its level of preadaptation with respect to fiber optics, regardless of whether the sample firms actually leveraged (cited) their prior experience. Patents prior to 1970 are not available in electronic format, so this knowledge was identified through patent backward citations. The variable was entered into the final model after applying a logarithmic transformation; because it equals 0 for several firms, the value 1 was added before taking the log.

Captures the extent to which firms build on their prior experience in a different domain by using backward self-citations that refer to patents filed until 1966, the year chosen as the dividing line. It is the ratio of total backward self-citations until 1966 (the number of citations that all patents filed by firm i in year t made to patents filed by firm i in 1966 or before) to total backward citations (the sum of all backward citations made by the patents firm i filed in year t). The filing year rather than the grant year of the cited patents is used. It takes the value 0 when a preadapted firm did not leverage its prior experience, when a firm in existence before the observation period had no prior relevant knowledge, or when a firm was founded after 1966.
time_window: backward self-citations to patents filed in 1966 or before

description: Following Trajtenberg, the dependent variable estimating the impact of a firm's patenting activity is computed as an index of weighted citation counts. C is the number of future citations that patent j filed by firm i in year t received in subsequent years (until 2004) from patents filed in fiber optics by other firms; citations were collected up to April 2004 net of a firm's self-citations. Because patents filed in earlier years are exposed to the risk of being cited for a longer period, patents are compared only to those filed during the same year. The weights used in the index are given in a formula that is not readable in the text, so the weighting specification cannot be recorded from the paper.
time_window: citations received until April 2004 for patents filed 1970-1995

description: Indicator produced by the first-step probit analysis, in which the TC and non-TC variables were used to separate respondents into Fit and Non-fit firms. Fit firms, those that used the entry mode prescribed by the enhanced TC model (i.e., firms that the model correctly classified), were coded as 1. Non-fit firms, those that chose entry modes inconsistent with the model's prediction, were coded as 0.

Perceptual measure of the performance of the vertical integration mode. Raters were asked how satisfied they were with the performance of the indicated mode with respect to five items. Items were assessed on a 10-point Likert scale where 1 = very dissatisfied and 10 = very satisfied. The five measures were averaged for each firm to form a composite performance index (Cronbach's alpha = 0.88).
scale: 10-point Likert scale, 1 = very dissatisfied to 10 = very satisfied

description: Dependent variable of the probit model, distinguishing between the two modes of entry studied: joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries. The authors studied these two modes because, in Western European firm entry into Central and Eastern Europe, the majority of entries were made using either wholly owned or joint venture modes.

Three attributes of asset specificity were measured using three seven-point Likert-type scales and averaged for each firm to create the composite measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.64). The questions addressed the specificity of investments in the form of training, the proprietary nature of products/services, and transaction-specific general investments.

Behavioral uncertainty was measured with five Likert-type questions, which were averaged for each firm to create a composite measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.83). Three questions addressed the problems associated with monitoring performance related to product/service quality. One question addressed monitoring/safeguarding proprietary knowledge, and one addressed the costs of search, contracting, and enforcement.

Economic uncertainty was measured with three separate, seven-point Likert-type items and averaged for each firm to create the composite measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.67). The items measured the stability of the political, social, and economic conditions, and the risks of adverse political actions.

The extent of app developers' knowledge sharing was captured by the frequency of knowledge sharing, measured as the total number of questions and answers posted by an iOS or Android app developer in a week. It is aggregated to the app developer-week level and serves as the dependent variable in the main difference-in-differences regressions.
time_window: weekly over the 21-week observation window (October 13, 2013 to March 8, 2014)

description: Following the quasi-experimental design, the 'treatment group' variable iOS is a dummy that takes a value of 1 for iOS app developers and 0 for Android app developers, and the 'after' variable After is a dummy that takes a value of 1 for the weeks after the jailbreak event and 0 for the weeks before the event, including the focal week of the jailbreak. The interaction term DD (iOS*After) identifies the treatment effect of the lapse in gatekeeping. A value of 1 therefore indicates an incumbent iOS developer exposed to the weakened gatekeeping after the jailbreak.

Following the literature on knowledge and innovation, the authors used Kauffman's NK framework, in which the complexity of a system is determined by the degree of interdependence among its subcomponents. Tags assigned to each StackOverflow question were used to capture the interdependence among subcomponents of app developers' knowledge. In three steps the authors calculated a tag-level 'ease of recombination' measure for each tag, then a question-level complexity measure for each question, and finally averaged all question-level complexity measures to represent knowledge complexity at the developer level, since developers' knowledge complexity is likely to be relatively stable and time invariant. The equations for the first two steps are not readable in the text, so the exact formulas cannot be stated. Questions to which developers provided answers were included in addition to the questions they posted.

Knowledge routineness relates to the application frequency and functional variability of knowledge and was captured with tag frequency: when a tag is mentioned frequently, the associated knowledge is likely to be routinely and invariably used during app development. In three steps the authors calculated tag-level routineness from overall tag use frequency, then a question-level routineness measure for each question, and finally averaged all question-level routineness values for a developer in the observation window to obtain the individual-level measure. The equations for the first two steps are not readable in the text, so the exact formulas cannot be stated. The measure is distinct from complexity because it is based on tags' application frequency without considering their co-appearance with other tags.

variable_name: TOTAL MODELS, SAME NICHE, and SAME NICHE 2
description: TOTAL MODELS is the number of total models in the desktop laser printer market at the time; SAME NICHE is the number of products competing in the same local PPM-DPI class as the product under consideration, and SAME NICHE 2 is its square. In the exit models these variables enter as multipliers of the hazard rate; in the entry models they enter as multipliers of the rate of product introduction. SAME NICHE 2 is included to capture a nonlinear, concave effect of niche competition.

A product exit is the first year that the product drops out of the dataset, meaning that none of the sources reports that the printer is being shipped to retailers from the manufacturers, although it may still be available in some retail outlets from inventory. If any one of the sources reports the printer is still being shipped, it is recorded as still on the market. The exit analysis models the hazard rate of exit with an exponential specification, and the estimation procedure accounts for right censoring.

variable_name: count of products introduced by the firm in a niche-year
description: Each observation is a firm-niche-year observation and the dependent variable is the count of products introduced by the firm in a given niche-year. Once a firm has entered the market, it becomes at risk for entry into any niche and remains at risk for all time periods that it still has a printer on the market.

A dummy variable indicating whether the vendor was one of the top 10 producers in terms of market share for the given year. The authors use it as a measure of firm market share, and hence of a lower cost position from scale economies, because they do not possess precise data on the number of units sold by product model. They note that market share position could indicate either a lower cost position or market power, so the test can only reject the cost hypothesis rather than distinguish the two explanations.
level: product-year (firm characteristic of the product's vendor)

description: DPI is the log of the printer's resolution measured in dots per inch; PPM is the speed of the printer measured in pages per minute, and PPM 2 is its square. Because innovative products lie on both the high-speed (top) and low-speed (bottom, mass-market) frontiers, the authors expect the relationship between speed and survival to be non-linear and non-monotonic, with PPM raising and PPM-squared lowering the hazard rate.

The number of new patents issued, by application year, in the patent classes most relevant to the industry: 271 (sheet feeding and delivering), 355 (photocopying), 359 (optics), and 399 (electrophotography). The authors use it to measure the innovative activity and innovative capacity of the firm, acknowledging that some firms may hold patents covering products other than laser printers, which would create noise in the measure.

variable_name: HP, IBM, DEC, XEROX, and CANON dummy variables
description: Dummy variables for products made by the firms with the strongest laser printer brands. To assess brand strength the authors conducted phone and in-person interviews with six independent experts and company managers in 1998, asking each to name the five companies with the highest customer recognition of brand in the laser printer industry; all six listed HP, Lexmark/IBM, and Canon, five included Xerox and four included DEC, and all printers of firms with four or more votes were coded as having strong brands. The authors note that the rankings relate specifically to desktop laser printers.
time_window: brand list assessed in 1998 and treated as relatively constant between 1986 and 1997

description: The extent of the buyer's investments that are specific to a given supplier and can be deployed exclusively into that supplier.
