The fieldwork revealed four areas of investment: special tools and dies built or lent specifically for the component delivered by the supplier; tailoring of design work to key components; time and effort spent by purchasing and engineering staff to learn the supplier's business practices; and time spent developing the relationship. The extent of the buyer's specific investments in the supplier is indexed by a four-item scale tapping the extent to which the manufacturer has made major investments in the supplier along these dimensions.
scale: seven-point interval scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree)

description: The extent to which the interface between the supplier's component and the assembled vehicle is critical to the buyer's product performance. Less critical component-vehicle interfaces can be managed with standardized plug-in technical solutions and specifications defined ex ante. Measured as the significance of the interface between this component and the rest of the vehicle.
scale: seven-point interval scale (extremely significant to very insignificant)

description: The complexity and customization of the task of designing and producing the component for the buyer, covering the number of exceptions and unanticipated events that require different methods or procedures. Complex components need to be customized to different model specifications and/or are based on novel technologies which typically require high capital investments and heavy engineering efforts from suppliers. Multiple items tap technical simplicity, customization, engineering effort and capital investment.

Headcount, the number of employees of the component supplier. The authors treat absolute supplier size as reflecting accomplished economies of scale and profit levels which support the firm's investments in a larger labor force, and hence as an indicator of generalized competence.

The supplier's market share as a percentage of the market at the automaker's market level (Japan or North America) for this component only. A high share is treated as a reflection and consequence of the superiority of the supplier's assets, skills and capabilities.

The inability to forecast accurately the volume (quantity) requirements in the relationship. As demand for its own cars fluctuates, the buyer finds it more difficult to plan and schedule its production and subsequently its volume requirements for the components it needs. Two items ask how predictable the volume requirements for this component are and how reliable the buyer's estimates for this component are.
scale: seven-point interval scales (very predictable to very unpredictable; very reliable to very unreliable)

description: Indexed using four indicators of the likelihood of major changes in a component, its performance, and its manufacturing process. Components that exhibit a fast pace of technological change make it difficult for the buyer to forecast the ongoing technical requirements within the relationship. The measure correlates positively with market growth and market instability, which the authors read as evidence of nomological validity.
scale: seven-point interval scales (very unlikely to very likely)

description: Measured following the guidelines of Scherer and Ross. The combined share of the top five suppliers in the relevant market is used as an overall measure of concentration, as the top five suppliers should be salient to the respondent and their combined shares should be small in a fragmented market and large in a concentrated market. In addition, the share of the top firm is used, as this should also be salient and, if large, indicates a situation approaching monopoly. These two estimates are averaged to form a concentration scale.

variable_name: Standard resources required to produce component
description: Whether the production of the component requires capabilities and skills unique to this supplier, or can be produced with standard capabilities and labor skills by any supplier. Where the requisite resources are standard, any supplier may have them; where they are unique, only a few suppliers are real candidates. The items span facilities, knowledge, design, manufacturing and managerial skills.
scale: seven-point interval scales (very standard to very unique to this supplier)

variable_name: Scope of the overall supply relationship
description: The number of distinct components (including this one) that this supplier provides to the buyer's firm. A larger scope means the supply relationship is embedded in a broader business relationship.

variable_name: Age of the overall supply relationship
description: The length of time the buyer's firm has done business with this supplier altogether, not necessarily just for this component.

The supplier's reputation and track record in the industry along three criteria: holding to its commitments, responding to design changes, and being a low cost provider. A strong-form trustworthy supplier acquires such a reputation over time through favorable dealings with business partners.
scale: seven-point scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree)

description: Dummy variable identifying the national institutional environment of the buying firm, Japan versus the United States, capturing the institutional context within which the supply relationship is embedded and which serves as a check on opportunism.

Bid leaders indicated on a 7-point scale, anchored 'no documents consulted' and 'a great number of documents consulted', the extent to which the sales team consulted documents available in Centra's electronic databases for (1) the industry and company background analysis, (2) the qualifications and value statement, (3) the solution description, and (4) the proposal overall. The average of the responses to these questions generated a continuous measure of the amount of knowledge obtained and used from electronic document databases, with a Cronbach alpha of 0.82.
scale: 7-point scale per item, averaged into a continuous measure

description: Each sales team leader recorded the number of Centra partners and consultants who were not working on the bid who assisted the team and broke this number down by the total hours of assistance, i.e., the number of people who provided 1-2 hours, 3-5 hours, 6-10 hours, 11-20 hours, 21-40 hours, and 40-60 hours (anyone who worked more than 60 hours was part of the team). The number of people who assisted the team was multiplied by the mid-value of the hours of assistance they provided and the scores were aggregated into a continuous measure of person-hours of help, emphasizing the actual extent of help from colleagues for a given proposal.

Team leaders answered two questions, 'Prior to the start of this sales proposal, how much experience did the sales team have with the solution [methodologies] described in this proposal?', on 7-point scales with anchors of 'no experience' and 'very extensive experience'. The two items were averaged to create a measure of the aggregate level of team experience with the requirements of the task, with a Cronbach alpha of 0.86.
time_window: prior to the start of the sales proposal

description: The bid leader indicated whether the bid was competitive and, if so, how many other consulting companies were involved in the bid. The number of other competing companies was recorded, with a value of zero entered if the bid was not competitive, creating a continuous measure of the level of task competitiveness.
scale: count (0 if the bid was not competitive)
time_window: at the time of the bid

description: A sales bid was classified as a win when the client signed a letter of intent to hire the firm, or as a loss when the client decided not to hire the firm. The dependent variable is coded 1 if the team was successful in securing the contract or 0 if it was lost; outcomes of bids still active at the time of the survey were determined by a follow-up with the team leaders two months later.

Entertainment and travel expenses disclosed in firms' annual reports. Following Cai et al. (2011), the authors first estimated a model of entertainment and travel expenses as a function of total sales, total assets, marketing expenses divided by total sales, capital intensity, and the average compensation of the three highest-paid executives. The residual from this model, abnormal entertainment expenses, is used as the measure of bribery expenditure and can be attributed to bribery activities. This approach provides a measure of bribery expenditure that does not depend on self-reporting by managers.

Industry-adjusted R&D intensity, calculated as a firm's R&D expenditure divided by its sales minus industry R&D intensity. Industry R&D intensity is the average R&D intensity of all firms in a three-digit China Securities Regulatory Commission industry category.

Equal to firm ROA minus industry average ROA if firm ROA was less than industry average ROA, and 0 if firm ROA was greater than or equal to industry average ROA. ROA is a firm's net income divided by the average of its beginning and ending total assets in a specific fiscal year; the social aspiration level is the average ROA of all listed companies with the same three-digit China Securities Regulatory Commission industry code in a year.

Equal to firm ROA in a year minus firm ROA in the previous year if firm ROA in that year was less than ROA in the previous year, and 0 if firm ROA in that year was greater than or equal to ROA in the previous year. The historical aspiration level is the firm's own ROA in the previous year.

Equal to firm ROA minus the average ROA in the industry if firm ROA was greater than or equal to the industry average ROA, and 0 if firm ROA was less than industry average ROA. ROA is a firm's net income divided by the average of its beginning and ending total assets in a specific fiscal year; the social aspiration level is the average ROA of all listed companies with the same three-digit China Securities Regulatory Commission industry code in a year.

Equal to firm ROA in a year minus firm ROA in the previous year if firm ROA in that year was greater than or equal to ROA in the previous year, and 0 if firm ROA in that year was less than ROA in the previous year. The historical aspiration level is the firm's own ROA in the previous year.

The subdimension of the National Economic Research Institute index on market institutions' development and legal protection, reflecting provincial-level economic, political, and legal development in China. It contains three items: development of market and legal intermediaries, in terms of the shares of lawyers and independent accountants in local population; the legal environment for businesses; and legal protection of intellectual property rights.

Industry concentration measured with the Herfindahl-Hirschman index, which equals the sum of squares of the percentages of sales of individual firms in each industry based on the three-digit standard industry classification code. The index was reverse-coded so that higher scores indicate higher competition levels in an industry.

variable_name: Agglo: Korean, same and related industries
description: Cumulative count of Korean establishments in the same and related industries of a focal firm in each region each year. Relatedness between two industries is the average of a focal industry's input and output ratios computed from input-output data, and an industry is related to the focal industry when its relatedness is above the median value. Agglomeration in related industries is the summation of the number of establishments in all related industries weighted by their relatedness to the focal industry, and the measure is the summation of this part and Korean-firm agglomeration in the same industry (the number of Korean establishments in the focal industry). The four agglomeration measures are standardized in the regression analyses.

Summation of the number of Korean establishments in all unrelated industries in a region in a year. The number is not weighted because conceptually relatedness is not relevant to unrelated industries. The measure is standardized in the regression analyses.

variable_name: Agglo: Non-Korean, same and related industries
description: Same procedure as the Korean-firm measure, applied to non-Korean foreign firms: the cumulative number of establishments of non-Korean (non-Chinese) foreign firms in the same and related industries of the focal firm in each region each year, with related industries weighted by their relatedness to the focal industry. Data on non-Korean firms come from ASIF; because ASIF data are available only until 2008, the 2008 value is used as the proxy for 2013-2018. The measure is standardized in the regression analyses.
time_window: one-year lag (non-Korean firm counts measured in 2008)

description: Summation of the number of non-Korean foreign firm establishments in all unrelated industries in a region in a year, calculated similarly to the Korean-firm unrelated-industry measure and not weighted. Non-Korean firms are non-Korean foreign firms; Chinese firms are excluded. The 2008 value of the ASIF data is used as the proxy for 2013-2018. The measure is standardized in the regression analyses.
time_window: one-year lag (non-Korean firm counts measured in 2008)

description: A dummy variable at the firm level, coded as one if a Korean firm in an industry established a subsidiary in a region in a given year, and zero otherwise. Observations are at the firm-region-year level, and each firm is faced with a set of alternative regions (31 in total) to choose from. If the same firm had multiple establishments in different regions in different years, they are coded as separate observations; if a firm had multiple establishments in the same region in the same year, only one is considered. Data come from KOTRA.

A dummy that takes the value of one if an observation is in the post-THAAD period of 2016-2018 and zero if the observation is in the pre-THAAD period of 2013-2015. The stand-alone dummy is excluded from the estimation because the conditional logit model controls for time-invariant firm fixed effects and including it would cause perfect collinearity; it enters the model through its interaction with the agglomeration measures.

A dummy that equals one if the Korean parent firm is among the top 200 in the Korea Investors Service (KIS) database in terms of market capitalization value and zero otherwise. For each Korean establishment in China reported in KOTRA, the name of the corresponding Korean parent is first identified manually using Qi Cha Cha and the parent's information is then gathered from KIS.
scale: 1 = parent among top 200 in market capitalization, 0 otherwise

description: The average score of the three dimensions of the 'government and market relations' subindex in the Marketization Index for China's Provinces, calculated for each region each year and then reverse coded by multiplying it with -1 so that a higher score indicates weaker institutions. For the split-sample analyses, regions with Korean investments are categorized as having strong or weak institutions based on the median value of subnational institutional weakness in the year before the establishment of new Korean subsidiaries.
scale: continuous score, reverse coded (higher = weaker institutions)
time_window: year before the establishment (for the strong/weak split)

description: A scale developed for this study, since no validated instruments existed, on which IT managers were queried regarding the extent to which redesign strategies were coordinated with IT strategies. Principal components analysis with Varimax rotation generated a two-factor model explaining 74.4% of the variance, with the coupling items loading on one factor and a Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin value of 0.79 indicating internal consistency among the items.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 4 = neutral, 7 = strongly agree)

description: A scale developed for this study on which project managers were queried regarding the novelty of newly implemented process designs. Items asked whether the redesigned process was unique to the company, was a de facto industry standard, was adopted because of its proven usefulness in the industry, was a major departure from previous operations, and was similar to process designs used in other areas of the company; three items were coded in reverse. Principal components analysis produced a separate innovativeness factor distinct from the strategy coupling factor.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 4 = neutral, 7 = strongly agree)

description: The project performance section of Pinto and Slevin's (1986) Project Implementation Profile, used to subjectively measure clients' views of project performance. Principal components analysis showed convergent validity, and a Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin value of 0.80 indicated a high level of internal consistency. A composite satisfaction index was derived for each respondent by summing the scores for the ten items.
Objective measure obtained from the project manager during the initial phone interview: the actual duration of the longest IT-related stoppage experienced by the project.

Objective measure obtained from the project manager during the initial phone interview: overall schedule slippage, based on the project's initial scheduled completion date and its actual completion date.

The number of sell-offs made by each restructuring firm during the 10 years prior to the year of the focal restructuring event, as reported with dates in the SDC Mergers & Acquisitions Database. These counts were summed for several different periods: one year prior to the focal event, two years prior, three and four years prior, five to 10 years prior, and the sum over the entire 10-year period. The window lengths were used to separate immediate, short-term, and long-term counts from one another. The unit of analysis is the restructuring firm and its specific experiences over each of the 10 years prior to the focal event.
time_window: 10 years prior to the year of the focal restructuring event, split into 1 year, 2 years, 3-4 years, 5-10 years, and 10-year sum

description: The number of spin-offs made by each restructuring firm during the 10 years prior to the year of the focal restructuring event, as reported with dates in the SDC Mergers & Acquisitions Database. These counts were summed for several different periods: one year prior to the focal event, two years prior, three and four years prior, five to 10 years prior, and the sum over the entire 10-year period. The window lengths were used to separate immediate, short-term, and long-term counts from one another.
time_window: 10 years prior to the year of the focal restructuring event, split into 1 year, 2 years, 3-4 years, 5-10 years, and 10-year sum

variable_name: Restructuring mode (coded 1 for spin-off, 0 for sell-off), reverse-scored
description: Restructuring mode represented how the focal restructuring event occurred and was coded as 1 when the focal event was a spin-off and as 0 when it was a sell-off, so higher values on this measure indicate spin-offs and lower values sell-offs. The classification of spin-off and sell-off was found in the SDC's Worldwide Merger & Acquisition Database, 2000. No restructuring events were a hybrid of the two alternatives or another type of restructuring.
time_window: year of the focal restructuring event

variable_name: Restructuring mode (coded 1 for spin-off, 0 for sell-off)
description: Restructuring mode represented how the focal restructuring event occurred and was coded as 1 when the focal event was a spin-off and as 0 when it was a sell-off. The classification of spin-off and sell-off was found in the SDC's Worldwide Merger & Acquisition Database, 2000. No restructuring events were a hybrid of the two alternatives or another type of restructuring.
time_window: year of the focal restructuring event

description: Return on assets for each of the five years after the year of the focal restructuring event; an average of the five yearly values was also calculated for the five-year period. ROA is described as one of the most common accounting-based performance measures and as correlating highly with other such proxies, including return on sales and return on equity. Financial variables were normed relative to their industry averages (differences from the mean). Data were found in COMPUSTAT.
time_window: each of the five years after the focal restructuring year (and their average)

description: Mean earnings per share for each of the five years after the year of the focal restructuring event; an average of the five yearly values was also calculated for the five-year period. The authors state that EPS reflects financial performance from the investor's perspective. Data were found in COMPUSTAT.
time_window: each of the five years after the focal restructuring year (and their average)

description: The number of directors who are not and have never been employees of the firm, are not related to any employee of the firm, and do not work for a company with significant business relationships with the firm, divided by the total number of directors. Data are collected from prospectuses, proxy statements, and/or Forms 10-K as close to 1 January of each year as possible.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each fiscal year (as close to 1 January 2000 as possible, updated annually)

description: The count of the members of the board of directors at the beginning of the year. Data are collected from prospectuses, proxy statements, and/or Forms 10-K.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each fiscal year (as close to 1 January 2000 as possible, updated annually)

description: A composite of three indicators of CEO power: duality (the CEO is also the chair of the board), founder status (the CEO is a founder of the firm), and shares owned by the CEO as a percent of total shares outstanding. Each element is standardized and the standardized scores are summed, weighting each indicator equally. Expert power is excluded from Finkelstein's (1992) four elements because it is difficult to obtain for small, young firms and difficult to judge in a newly emerging sector.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each fiscal year (as close to 1 January 2000 as possible, updated annually)

description: The Ohlson bankruptcy prediction index, calculated using financial statement data and the parameter estimates and weights derived from Ohlson's (1980) analysis. Its components address four basic factors derived from financial statement data: size, financial leverage, profitability, and liquidity. Higher values indicate a greater likelihood that the firm will declare bankruptcy during the upcoming year.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each observation year

description: A firm is coded as having failed if it was delisted from the stock exchange on which it was traded for reasons other than acquisition and there is evidence that it has ceased conducting business, verified with company descriptions from Hoover's online. Firms delisted but still operating as independent entities are coded as survivors, and firms acquired during the observation period are right censored at the acquisition date rather than treated as failures.
time_window: observed over the year following each measurement, through the 31 December 2002 cutoff

variable_name: board membership inequality (Gini coefficient of board memberships)
description: The clarity of the informal hierarchy is proxied by the inequality of directors' board memberships, that is, the number of corporate boards on which individual directors serve simultaneously, log-transformed to take into account the diminishing marginal effect of each additional membership. The Gini coefficient is computed over the log-transformed board memberships of the directors on each firm's board, calculated with the Stata user-developed command 'inequal'. The Gini ranges from 0, indicating absolute equality in which all directors have the same value, to 1, indicating absolute inequality in which the value equals 0 for all but one director.

variable_name: return on assets (ROA) with one-year lead
description: ROA was calculated using net income (or loss) and the total assets reported by a firm for each year, with a one-year lead on the dependent variable. Industry effects were corrected for by including industry average ROA as a control in the analyses.

A dummy variable that took the value of 1 when a firm's CEO held more board memberships than any other director, and 0 otherwise. It was used as a moderator of the relationship between board membership inequality and ROA.

The average number of directors' board memberships was computed for each board, and then the sample mean and standard deviation. The dummy variable was coded 1 if the average number of board memberships of a particular board fell within one standard deviation of the mean, and 0 otherwise (signifying a low- or high-ranking board).
Board size was captured by the total number of directors on a board. It was used both as a control and, in interaction with board membership inequality, to test the moderating hypothesis.

Past firm performance was measured by the previous year's ROA (t - 1). Including it also helps address the possibility of reverse causality whereby the clarity of a board's informal hierarchy correlates with financial performance because successful firms attract a few competent directors with many board seats.

A standardized measure of the volatility of the industry sales growth rate over the five preceding years. Net sales for all Compustat firms in each four-digit SIC industry were summed for each year between 1996 and 2006, and five years of four-digit primary SIC industry-level data were used to gauge dynamism for the sixth year; for each year and industry the five previous years' industry sales were regressed against year, and dynamism was quantified as the standard error of the regression's slope coefficient divided by the mean value of industry sales over the five-year period.

All investors' ethnicities were coded from the family names registered to their accounts in the NSE registration database. Eight independent coders, all indigenous Kenyans representing Kenya's six largest ethnic groups, coded the 16,230 most-common family names (capturing 95 percent of all accounts) from Kenya's 12 primary ethnic groups plus South Asian and Anglo, identifying each name with at least 75-percent confidence and allowing multiple ethnic codes, with non-unanimous names passed to a second team of four coders. The 14 ethnic codes were collapsed into four continuous measures-the dominant Kukuyu group, the rival groups (Luo and Kalenjin), non-rival groups, and an ''other'' group (South Asian, Anglo, or indigenous names signaling no identifiable ethnicity)-and the normalization equation is unreadable in the provided text. Because 95 percent of investors scored higher than .5 in only one of the four categories, that value was used as a cutoff to assign each investor to a discrete category used as a subsample, with the rare overlapping cases assigned to ''other''. Foreign investors were excluded from the analysis.
scale: proportional membership in each ethnic category, collapsed to four discrete categories

description: Models use a three-category measure of victimization: clients of the corrupt brokerage with no financial loss (a Nyaga client without an ICF-verified loss), clients of the corrupt brokerage with financial loss (an ICF-verified loss), and the reference group of clients of all other intermediaries. The authors note that they cannot definitively know that all clients who experienced a financial loss filed a claim that was verified, but that assuming no false claims were verified, the potential measurement bias is against finding a result for clients with financial loss.

A linear probability model estimates whether an account became inactive for three years following the fraud, defined as the account neither transferring to another brokerage nor trading any shares. The authors interpret inactivity as avoidance of the market because the investor effectively surrendered his or her assets when the regulator froze all Nyaga accounts. Models include fixed-effect dummies for the investor's district of residence and each stock held.

variable_name: Participation in the post-fraud telecom IPO
description: A second linear probability model estimates the likelihood that the investor invested in the popular telecom IPO three weeks after the scandal. This measure combines the 77,928 Nyaga clients who had participated in at least one IPO before the scandal with the 327,647 Kenyan investors who were clients of other intermediaries. Models include fixed-effect dummies for the investor's district of residence and each stock held.

A modification of the standard measure of trade imbalance: investor i's market participation at six months post-regulatory intervention (t + 6) is measured as the number of shares held by i at the time of intervention t plus shares bought and minus shares sold in that six-month period, normalized by the number of shares held at t. The measure takes a value of 0 if an investor liquidated all shares and exited the market, 1 if the investor's net level of market participation was unchanged, and increasingly positive values if the investor bought more shares after the fraud relative to what he or she held at the time of the fraud. The equation itself is unreadable in the provided text. Models include fixed-effect dummies for the investor's district of residence, the intermediary used, and each stock held.
scale: ratio, 0 = exit, 1 = unchanged, positive values = net buying

description: Each of the 35 intermediaries available during the weeks between regulatory intervention and the telecom IPO was categorized by its social and professional traits as a Kukuyu or non-Kukuyu stockbrokerage or commercial bank, with same versus different defined in relation to the corrupt Kukuyu brokerage. Ethnic identities were measured by surveying three market insiders-two fund managers and a past member of the CMA board of directors-with unique ethnic backgrounds, who unanimously identified the Kukuyu-operated intermediaries and reported that intermediaries' ethnic affiliations were common knowledge in Kenya. An alternative-specific conditional logit estimates the effect of the ethnic match between investors and each type of intermediary on the choice among the four types while holding investor attributes constant; the reference category is choosing another Kukuyu stockbroker.
scale: four alternative categories; odds ratios relative to another Kukuyu stockbroker
time_window: the weeks between regulatory intervention and the telecom IPO

variable_name: Match between victims' ethnic group and the type of new intermediary chosen
description: The Poisson models estimate the level of market participation six months after regulatory intervention predicted by the match between victims' ethnic group and the type of new intermediary chosen, with each intermediary type interacted with client victimization status (client with no financial loss; client with financial loss). Marginal preferences from the alternative-specific choice model indicate each group's integrity-based assessments of each type of intermediary, and matching those preferences to the level of post-fraud investing enacted through that type provides the diagnostic framework. Models include fixed-effect dummies for the investor's district of residence, the intermediary used, and each stock held.

Uncertainty in the regulatory environment, seen as resulting from variation in the way the federal government and other third-party payers influenced the physicians' organizations, was measured with two items; the Appendix gives the complete scales.

Following previous studies, the author assessed two attributes of uncertainty in the physicians' environment: complexity and dynamism. Complexity was assessed by asking the physicians to what extent the types of health-care provider firms with which their practices competed directly had changed during the last six months. The rate of change was measured with two items, one on change in the number of their key competitors and one on change in the number of products and services offered by their competitors.

The physicians were asked to indicate the significance of 12 different activities to the current strategies of their practices; seven items tapped intraorganizational activities, four of which represented managerial responses that used an organization's present resources and were typically boundary spanning. Examples are the importance of designating an individual within the practice to monitor and work with the environment and of attending educational programs that deal with changes in the health care environment.

Five items tapped the significance of interorganizational activities; the two managerial linkages included represented simple exchanges in which an organization attempts integration while preserving autonomy. Through an alliance with an HMO or a preferred provider organization (PPO), for example, physicians might attempt to remove demand uncertainty in terms of both fees and numbers of patients.

Three of the seven intraorganizational items typified technical-level responses involving alterations in actual services provided and representing changes in an organization's technical core designed to retain latitude and flexibility by increasing excess capacity. One item assessed the importance of hiring an M.D. who can offer services the practice doesn't now provide, indicating altering a firm's product line and capabilities, and another asked the importance of performing clinical services within the practice that were previously done by outside firms.

Three items on technical-level interdependencies, which require organizations to forfeit more of their independence, include one on sharing such nonclinical services with other organizations as office personnel, office space, computers, and purchasing.

Environmental uncertainty is operationalized through the two survey measures of uncertainty in the physicians' environment: regulatory uncertainty (two items on how the federal government and other third-party payers influenced the practice) and competitive uncertainty (complexity and dynamism of the competitive niche). The two are entered as separate latent environmental variables in the structural model.

Equals 0 when corporate performance, measured as operating profit margin (the ratio of corporate operating income to corporate sales), is greater than the corporate aspiration level; for all other observations it equals the difference between corporate performance and aspirations. The aspiration is a historical aspiration, an exponentially weighted moving average of past corporate performance, with the adjustment parameter chosen by maximum likelihood. The variable is lagged by four quarters.

Equals 0 when business unit performance, measured as operating profit margin (the ratio of business unit operating income to business unit sales), is greater than the business unit aspiration level; for all other observations it equals the difference between performance and aspirations. The aspiration is a historical aspiration, an exponentially weighted moving average of past business unit performance. The variable is lagged by one quarter.

Equals 0 when corporate performance is below the corporate aspiration level and otherwise equals the performance-aspiration gap, where performance is operating profit margin. Lagged by four quarters, symmetrically with the below-aspirations variable.

Equals 0 when business unit performance is below the business unit aspiration level and otherwise equals the performance-aspiration gap, where performance is operating profit margin. Lagged by one quarter, symmetrically with the below-aspirations variable.
The number of new phones introduced during each quarter in a year. A mobile phone qualifies as new if at least one of its design characteristics differs from those of the firm's previous products.

The ratio of business unit operating income to the firm's overall operating income; it captures the relative importance of the business unit in corporate performance. It is interacted with the corporate performance-aspiration gap to test H3.

The cumulative number of prior mobile phones introduced by the business unit; it reflects the relative experience of the business unit. It is interacted with the corporate performance-aspiration gap to test H4.

The count of the annual number of citations a gene paper had received, beginning in the year the paper was published and continuing until 2006. Author self-citations, defined as citations of papers written by any author of the focal paper, are excluded. It is a highly right-skewed count variable taking nonnegative integer values, with a mean of 13 annual citations and a maximum of 294.

A dummy variable equal to 1 for all years after a patent was granted and 0 prior to patent grant. Its mean of 0.58 indicates citation-year observations were almost equally distributed between years when patents were in operation and those when they were not.

Following Lerner (1994), defined as the number of national classes in which a patent was categorized (mean = 6.20). To enable analysis of the impact of increase in scope from its mean value, the mean number of classes was subtracted from the actual number of classes.

Calculated as the number of claims in the patent (mean = 15.61), a measure of patent strength following Scotchmer (1991). To enable analysis of the impact of increasing strength, the measure used was the actual number of claims minus the mean number of claims.

Defined in the same way as public address, denoting whether at least one assignee was from a public (academic or government) institution (mean = 0.58). All public assignees denotes instances in which all patent assignees were from a public institution (mean = 0.54).

Constructed in the same way as public assignee, denoting a private sector assignee (mean = 0.46). All private assignees denotes instances in which all patent assignees were from a private institution (mean = 0.42).

variable_name: Gene patent categories: gene patent 1; gene patent 2 to 4; gene patent 5 to 7; gene patent 8 to 10; gene patent 11 to 20
description: From the total gene patent population of 4,270 patents, the authors counted the total number of patents eventually associated with each gene in the focal pair and broke the count into five categorical variables. Gene patent 1 equals 1 (otherwise 0) for genes claimed by one patent, including the focal patent (mean = 0.34); gene patent 2 to 4 is for genes claimed by 2 to 4 patents (mean = 0.52); gene patent 5 to 7 (mean = 0.10), gene patent 8 to 10 (mean = 0.03), and gene patent 11 to 20 (mean = 0.02) were similarly calculated.

A measure of gene fragmentation for each gene based on its Herfindahl index (herfgene), the sum of the squares of the shares of a gene held by each individual owner. The patent-gene fragmentation index weights gene fragmentation across all the genes claimed by the patent; the formula itself is not readable in the extracted text. There was more fragmentation as the index approached zero (mean = 0.67; minimum 0.11 was the most fragmentation). To make application more intuitive, the index was subtracted from unity so that 0 denoted no fragmentation and 0.89 the most fragmentation; a further measure subtracted (1-mean fragmentation index) from (1-fragmentation index).

variable_name: OMIM gene; cancer gene; disease gene
description: OMIM gene is a binary variable set to 1 if at least one of the genes in a patent-paper pair was listed in OMIM as expressing a human-disease-related phenotype (mean = 0.25). Cancer gene captured whether a focal gene was listed in the Sanger Institute Cancer Gene Census as a known cancer gene (mean = 0.08). Disease gene is a binary variable capturing whether a focal gene was listed in either of the two databases (mean = 0.27).

Indicator variable for instances in which a unit lost a manager to unexpected death. Deaths are identified from the code specifying the reason for the termination of an employment relationship, and only deaths of managers aged 65 or less who died of non-work-related causes and were not hired in the year of death are counted. Because redeployment is measured as of December year-over-year, the indicator equals 1 if a manager dies in either year t or year t + 1.

Firm-level indicator variable indicating firms that lose a manager to unexpected death in any unit. The same criteria as for Manager death are used to count only unexpected, non-work-related deaths of managers aged 65 or less who were not hired in the year of death.

Indicator variable for workers who switch employment between establishments of the same firm between the end of 1 year and the end of the following year, measured at the worker-year level; a worker leaving an establishment is referred to as outward redeployment. In the small number of cases where workers simultaneously hold more than one position, the highest-paying observation is used. The sample is managers employed in an establishment at year-end.

Indicator variable for workers who switch employment between establishments of the same firm between the end of 1 year and the end of the following year, measured at the worker-year level; a worker joining an establishment is referred to as inward redeployment. Each inward redeployment necessarily has a matching outward redeployment.
Indicator variable for a firm having closed at least one establishment in a year, measured at the firm-year level. An establishment is identified as closed in the last year in which it has employees.

Indicator variable for a firm having opened at least one establishment in a year, measured at the firm-year level. An establishment is identified as new in the first year it appears in RAIS, which is also the first year it has any employees.

Technology intensity was measured as the ratio of annual R&D expenditures to sales. In the models, R&D is the degree of investment in research and development (in millions of dollars) divided by sales in year t.

CEO short-term incentives were measured using the CEO's annual bonus, taken from the firms' proxy statements. Bonus is the CEO's bonus in year t + 1 (1993-95), so the dependent variable is measured one year after the independent variables.

Total incentives were calculated by adding CEO annual bonus and long-term income. Long-term income was estimated as the number of options granted to the CEO multiplied by 25 percent of their exercise price, an approach found to be highly correlated with values derived using the Black-Scholes formula. The measure is the CEO's total variable compensation in year t + 1 (1993-95).
Each firm's financial results were measured using its annual return on equity (ROE), the firm's reported return on equity for that fiscal year in year t (1992-94).

Measured as the number of times a firm's previous five years of patents are cited in the current year. This count was converted to an index by dividing it by the average for all U.S. patents that year from the same International Patent Classification (IPC) 4-digit subclass, so a value of 1.0 represents average citation frequency, 2.0 twice average citation frequency, and 0.25 twenty-five percent of average citation frequency.
scale: index where 1.0 represents average citation frequency
time_window: current year t (1992-95), based on the firm's previous five years of patents

description: Measured by the number of references in the firm's own patent applications to scientific papers, which reveals how closely linked a patent is to cutting-edge scientific research. This count was converted to an index by dividing it by the average number of science references for the IPC subclass, which controls for differences across industries and technologies in the extent to which science is used in innovation.
scale: index relative to the IPC subclass average

description: Firm performance was operationalized as firms' market-to-book ratio for the period 1992-95; the model uses the firm's ratio of market value to book value in year t + 1. Firms with ratios > 1 are judged under-invested, demonstrating the existence of growth opportunities, while firms with ratios < 1 can be judged as over-invested.
scale: ratio of market value to book value

variable_name: Three-way interactions of technology intensity, CEO incentives, and performance indicators
description: CEO incentive alignment is captured by three-way interaction terms between technological intensity (R&D/sales), CEO pay (bonus with return on equity; total incentives with invention resonance and with science harvesting), used to predict the firm's market-to-book ratio.

Following Barnett's measure of local population density, the authors calculated regional community density separately for each community for each year by counting the number of national technology development zones within the focal community's provincial location. The province level was used because zones in the same province are subject to the provincial government's administration and support, and because a province may have multiple zones while a city can have only one at maximum. The values of this variable ranged from 1 to 6 in the data.
time_window: annual; measured one year before the dependent variable

variable_name: Geographic proximity to the nearest community
description: Geographic distance between communities was first measured as the natural log of the distance, in kilometers, between the city where the focal zone is located and the city where the next closest zone is located; distances were derived from China's Railroad Bureau data on railroad transportation distances. The logged values of geographic distance ranged from 3.40 to 7.58. To transform geographic distance into geographic proximity, these values were subtracted from the maximum value of 7.58 in the data, yielding geographic proximity values ranging from 0 to 4.18.
time_window: annual; measured one year before the dependent variable

variable_name: Domain overlap with the nearest community
description: Consistent with Podolny and colleagues' measure of niche overlap, domain overlap was calculated as the percentage of the focal zone's major industries that were also present in its next closest zone in the prior year. A zone's primary industries were identified from the MST Web site, individual zone Web sites, and a publication introducing the zones, and were verified by telephone with each zone's administrators; among the 53 zones, 9 experienced significant changes in major industries, and data were updated to reflect the time-based change in industry mix. The measure varies from 0 (none of the focal zone's major industries present in the next closest zone) to 100 percent (all present).

Community growth is estimated in terms of a zone's annual sales revenues. These data are collected by the zone administrators from the resident firms, aggregated to the zone level and reported annually to the MST, which publishes the data; sales revenue data are in Chinese RMB 1,000 and corrected for inflation using RMB value in 1990. Community growth in sales revenue is modeled as a function of a community's sales revenue and a number of covariates, and the dependent variable is lagged by one year behind the independent and control variables.
scale: RMB 1,000, corrected for inflation to 1990 RMB

description: Locus was measured using the Rotter I-E scale, which contains 29 paired statements (including six dummy pairs which are not used in the scoring) and has received extensive support for its reliability and convergent and discriminant validity. Participants were presented with a series of paired statements and asked to identify which statement of each pair they considered to be more true. Each 'external' response was counted as one point and the points were summed; the measure is represented by a single score.

Calculated as the average of the 15 items of the perceived discretion questionnaire (Cronbach alpha = 0.82), which measured the degree to which participants believed they had discretion over specific strategic organizational issues. The instrument was comprised of 15 items customized for each position based on the industry experts' determinations of high and low discretion situations. Each item was scored on a 7-point Likert-type scale ranging from 'Little/No Discretion' to 'Much Discretion' with 7 indicating much discretion.
time_window: Completed the evening before the simulation and returned the morning of the simulation

description: Calculated as the average of the Likert scale responses to the 10 items over which the participant would have discretion according to the panel of experts (Cronbach alpha of 0.78). It consists of the 10 issues for which industry experts considered the manager in that position to have much discretion.
time_window: Completed the evening before the simulation and returned the morning of the simulation

description: Calculated as the mean response for the five items over which the participant would not have discretion according to the panel of experts (Cronbach alpha of 0.74). It is the average of the remaining five items for which the manager in a particular position would not have discretion.
time_window: Completed the evening before the simulation and returned the morning of the simulation

variable_name: High and low discretion issue designations
description: The industry experts designated for each managerial position 10 issues for which the individual had much objective discretion, and five items for which he or she had little discretion. The experts agreed unanimously in their designations of high or low discretion issues, made for each management position based on the strategic and operational issues facing the firm.

In a post-simulation questionnaire, respondents indicated which of their fellow participants were among the three most influential managers on each committee (mean committee size of six, with participants serving on one to three committees). The effect of unequal committee membership was eliminated by adjusting for the number of committee memberships held by each participant, so that a respondent rated as among the three most influential committee members by four participants for one committee and by six for another received an overall power score equal to the sum divided by the number of committees served.

CEO gender is a dummy variable of 1 if the CEO was female and 0 if male. All predictor variables were lagged 1 year before the dependent variable and standardized before creating interaction terms (dichotomous variables were not standardized).
time_window: lagged 1 year before the dependent variable

description: Number of acquisitions is the annual total number of majority acquisitions announced and completed for deals over $10 million. It is the dependent variable in the negative binomial models; n = 10,351 firm-years.

Acquisition spending is the total annual dollar value (log-transformed) of spending for every majority acquisition announced and completed for deals over $10 million. The SDC database does not report a value for every acquisition, so a within-firm-year mean replace was conducted for acquisition value when it was missing; in firm-years with one or more acquisitions but no reported value, the value was treated as missing, leaving 8,923 observations. It is the dependent variable in the Tobit models.

The authors regressed industry sales (two-digit SIC code) on a year-count variable over a 5-year window. Industry dynamism was captured by taking the standard error of that regression coefficient and dividing it by the mean industry sales.
time_window: 5-year window, lagged 1 year before the dependent variable

description: Media coverage is measured as the number of articles published about the firm each year. Ravenpack News Analytics captures all news reports from Barron's, The Wall Street Journal, and Dow Jones Newswires, tagging each to the firms featured, and assigns a relevance score from 0 to 100 reflecting how central the company is in the article; only articles with a relevance score of 90 or higher were included.
time_window: annual, lagged 1 year before the dependent variable

description: Relative board power was operationalized using three indicators that capture the relative power of the board compared to the CEO: CEO duality, the ratio of CEO ownership to board ownership (number of shares owned by the CEO from Execucomp divided by the sum of shares owned by all directors from ISS), and the ratio of the number of directors appointed after the CEO began their term to the total number of board members. Each indicator was standardized and summed, and the value was reverse-coded so that higher values represent more relative board power.
time_window: lagged 1 year before the dependent variable

description: Equals 1 if the players of directed dyad i faced each other on the field during the 2018 World Cup, and 0 otherwise. It is the treatment variable of the difference-in-differences design and enters the estimation as its interaction with Post World Cup. Because the model includes dyad fixed effects and the treatment is at the dyad level, the variable itself is omitted from the estimated equation.

The number of successful passes from player A to player B in directed dyad i in match t. Passes from player A to player B are distinguished from passes from player B to player A, so that asymmetries within a dyad are captured. The authors argue that the number of times a player passes the ball to a teammate captures well his willingness to collaborate.

A binary variable that equals 1 if the pass giver in the dyad has a strong identification with the extra-organizational affiliation and 0 otherwise. The authors construct it using four proxies: whether the pass giver has a single rather than multiple citizenship, whether he has lived in the country of his national team above the median number of years, whether he tweets about his national team above the median amount, and whether he has at least one child. Each proxy is used in a separate model comparing dyads in which the pass giver scores high on the proxy with dyads in which he does not.

Equals 1 for dyads whose two players directly encountered each other on the field as opponents in a World Cup match (the default treatment group). Equals 0 for the alternative control group of dyads whose national teams played each other in the World Cup although the focal players themselves were not together on the field, for example because one was injured or benched.

A categorical variable between 5 and 1 capturing the government hierarchy. A value of 5 was assigned to firms affiliated with the central government, 4 to firms with a provincial government, 3 to firms with a city government, 2 to firms with a county government, and 1 to firms without government affiliation.

The summation of upstream innovativeness, downstream innovativeness, and horizontal innovativeness in the focal firm's region, measured by regions because of substantial regional differences in China. Upstream innovativeness is the summation of all upstream industries' new product output weighted by the focal industry's input ratios; downstream innovativeness is the summation of the new product output of all downstream industries in a region weighted by the focal industry's output ratios; horizontal innovativeness is the new product output of firms in the same industry and the same region, excluding the focal firm's own new product output. Input and output ratios come from the 2002 and 2007 NBSC input-output tables, with values for other years filled in by extrapolation and interpolation.
time_window: lagged one year; input-output ratios for 2001-2006 interpolated from the 2002 and 2007 tables

description: The log of a firm's yearly output of new products; one was added to all observations with a value of zero before log transforming the variable. New product output is the current market price of the new products a firm produces in a given year, and new products are defined as those new to the Chinese market that either adopt completely new scientific principles, technologies, or designs or are substantially improved relative to existing products.

Binary indicator equal to one for LSPs with an LAA for waste recycling after year 2007, and zero otherwise. It is defined as D = (treatment * d), where treatment is a dichotomous variable equal to one for the treated group (LSPs with a recycling LAA) and zero for the control group (LSPs without an LAA), and d is a time dummy switched on for post-2007 observations, that is, after LAAs came into force.
time_window: post-2007 observations (LAAs came into force in 2008)

description: The dependent variable is the percentage of household waste reused, recycled, or composted in each LSP, and the estimated models use the log of the recycling rate for year t in LSP i. Information on LSPs' waste recycling rate comes from the U.K. Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, which publishes a range of environmental policy statistics; U.K. recycling statistics are verified by government auditors.
scale: percentage of household waste recycled (logged in the models)

description: A Blau index denoting the relative share of organizations from the public, private, and nonprofit sectors represented on the executive board of each LSP. Board composition information was drawn from the Sustainable Community Strategies that LSPs were required to produce in 2008 and from executive board meeting minutes from the same period available online, using a coding frame that assigned board representatives to a particular sector of the economy. The variable is time invariant and therefore cannot be separately estimated in a fixed-effects model.

The years that have passed since either the present LSP itself was set up or a predecessor areawide cross-sector partnership was in place. The variable captures accumulated partnership capabilities and is akin to those used in the strategic alliances literature. Information on the history of cross-sector partnerships in each area served by an LSP was gathered by searching documentary evidence available online, drawing only on information identifying the inauguration date of an area-wide strategic cross-sector partnership.

An index of administrative capacity capturing the resources devoted by local governments (the public organizations principally responsible for leading LSPs) to central services (e.g., finance, internal audit) and management and support services (e.g., human resources, IT). It gauges the volume of administrative support potentially available to LSPs and is constructed by normalizing the expenditure on central administration in a 0,1 range for each year in the sample, with a higher score indicating higher capacity, so that admin capacity = [cs - min(cs)]/[max(cs) - min(cs)], where cs represents expenditure on central administration per capita.

The experience of the senior manager principally responsible for the performance of the CSP, measured as the length of tenure in years of the chief executive of the lead local government for each LSP. According to the related literature, the accumulated experience of a chief executive can be considered a proxy for managerial capability.

Instead of a dummy treatment variable, this variable captures the treatment intensity, TI, that is the LAA target stretch: a variable with different treatment intensity across LSPs, defined as the improvement required from the baseline 2007 recycling figure to hit the 2010 target. The formal definition of the variable is not readable in the available text.
time_window: improvement required from the 2007 baseline to the 2010 target

variable_name: transition rate from representative office to branch office
description: The event analyzed is the issuing of the branch license to a foreign bank in Shanghai. The transition rate is defined as the probability that a foreign bank opens a branch office in Shanghai at (or shortly after) time t, given that it has maintained a representative office in the city up to time t. The event was dated from the exact date on which the license was granted as listed by the central bank.

variable_name: duration of the organizing period (waiting time)
description: The time a bank spends between establishing a representative office and obtaining branch status, measured in years. Because no functional form for the transition rate was chosen in advance, the waiting time entered the piecewise exponential model as period segments in which the rate is constant; the following division appeared to produce the sharpest results: (0, 2], (2, 4], (4, 7], (7, 11], and periods longer than 11 years.

A simple count of foreign bank branch offices, specified as a time-varying covariate at the city level and, in district-level models, for the same district as well as for other districts. All density measures were lagged one year in the modeling. Some density tests were accompanied by a second-order term to capture any nonmonotonic patterns, but density effects were not tested concurrently with other sets of quadratic terms to avoid multicollinearity.

A simple count of representative offices of foreign banks, specified as a time-varying covariate at the city level and at the district level. The effect of the presence of other representative offices in the same district as well as in other districts on the rate of transition to branch office was tested. All density measures were lagged one year in the modeling.

A measure of size localization constructed from the nearness between the size of an organizer's parent bank and the sizes of the organizations already maintaining a branch office anywhere in Shanghai. It is a Gaussian function of the distance in size between the two, developed as an alternative to Banaszak-Holl's (1991) inverse-distance measure so that very small differences in size induce relatively little change in the value of nearness. Parameter delta in this analysis was set equal to 2, because this yields a nearness of almost 0 as the difference in size approaches its maximum.

variable_name: density of bank branches from the same home region
description: The count of branch offices belonging to banks that originate from the same home region as the organizer; home region was defined in terms of Japan, the Middle East, the rest of Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Africa, and Australia. The effect of the density of bank branches from the same home region, as well as from other regions, was evaluated, and all density measures were lagged one year.

The 2005-2011 study period is divided into a period of economic munificence (2005-2007) and a period of global economic recession (2008-2011). Separate models are estimated for each period and the variance partition coefficients of the two periods are compared.

Share of the total variance in ROA attributable to firms within industries, calculated as the level-1 variance component divided by the sum of the firm, industry and country variance components [σ2/(σ2+τπ+τβ)]. The variance components are estimated in a three-level random coefficient model in which firm performance is the average ROA of firm i in industry j in country k. Values are reported for the all-years model, the expansionary period and the recessionary period.
level: firm (nested in industry, nested in country)

description: Share of the total variance in ROA attributable to industries, calculated as the level-2 variance component divided by the sum of the firm, industry and country variance components [τπ/(σ2+τπ+τβ)]. Estimated in the same three-level random coefficient model for the all-years, expansionary and recessionary periods.

Share of the total variance in ROA attributable to countries, calculated as the level-3 variance component divided by the sum of the firm, industry and country variance components [τβ/(σ2+τπ+τβ)]. Estimated in the main effects model and separately for the emerging-economy subsample for the expansionary and recessionary periods.

Indicator explanatory variables are created for each country at level 3 with random intercepts uncorrelated and variances constrained to be equal, and interaction groups are generated by combining the industry with the country of each company, resulting in 760 different groups. An additional nesting level estimates the variance component for the interaction term Country × Industry, which is reported as a share of total ROA variance.

Firm performance is measured as Return-on-Asset (ROA) ratios, averaged for each examined period: mean ROA for the entire period 2005-2011 in the overall model, mean ROA for 2005-2007 in the expansion period and mean ROA for 2008-2011 in the recession. The outcome Performance ijk is the average ROA of firm i in industry j in country k, which the three-level model partitions into firm, industry and country components.

The scope of formal ethics activities was measured with survey items that asked objective questions about a company's ethics structures and activities, including the presence of a code of ethics or other ethics policy documents, the extent of the distribution of those policies to employees, the presence and staff size of special ethics offices and committees, the frequency with which various levels of employees received ethics-oriented communications and training, and the use of dedicated ethics telephone lines. These items were answered in yes/no, percentage, or Likert-scale formats. A composite measure was formed by summing the Z-scores of all the items, so that higher scores reflected the presence of more ethics-oriented structures and activities.

The extent of a program's compliance orientation was measured with six Likert-type items assessing the prominence of (1) discipline for nonconformity, (2) investigation of complaints, and (3) auditing for compliance in the firm's overall effort to foster good ethics (alpha = .84). A sample item is "How prominent is the activity of investigating complaints in the firm's overall effort to foster good ethics?"

The extent of a program's values orientation was measured with four Likert-type items assessing ethics programs' emphases on (1) encouraging shared values, (2) supporting employee aspirations, (3) communicating company values, and (4) building trust and confidence (alpha = .80). A sample item is "How prominent is the activity of encouraging shared values in the firm's overall effort to foster good ethics?"

variable_name: top management's awareness of USSC guidelines
description: Three five-point Likert-type survey items (alpha = .88) measured executives' awareness of the U.S. Sentencing Commission's guidelines. The items queried the extent to which top management meetings and communications addressed the impact of the guidelines and the respondent's knowledge of the guidelines; an example is "High-level managers in this firm have discussed the 1991 U.S. Corporate Sentencing Guidelines."
scale: five-point Likert scale (5 = strongly agree, 1 = strongly disagree)

variable_name: media attention to company's ethical failings
description: Media attention to a firm's ethical failings was measured using the database Newspaper Abstracts, which covers 25 regional and national newspapers. For each responding company, the number of article abstracts in the database that suggested ethical failure at the company was summed. Two trained research assistants counted abstracts indicating violation of the law, harm or threat to the public, allegedly ruthless business practices, or suggestions of undisclosed corporate impropriety; interrater agreement between an author and the assistants was 71 and 70 percent.

variable_name: company's presence at Conference Board meeting
description: Conference registration lists were used to measure a company's representation at the three ethics meetings the Conference Board held prior to administration of the survey (1992, 1993, and 1994). A company was considered to have been represented if one or more of its members appeared on the list for one or more of the three conferences; the total number of conference attendees from a company was not used.

Informants rated "the overall business orientation of your firm's top management by [rating] the extent to which various subjects are a topic of conversation for your firm's top management team (i.e., executive vice presidents and higher)." Eight items suggesting that executives viewed ethics as intrinsically valuable loaded on one factor explaining 55 percent of the variance (alpha = .88); performance-oriented topics served as foils. The more highly a management was rated on items suggesting the intrinsic value of ethics, the more the authors considered that management committed to ethics.
scale: five-point Likert scales ranging from "never" to "very frequently"

description: Binary variable that captures whether the headquarters of a manager's previous employer ('parent firm') was in one of the geographical hubs of the financial services industry, New York or London. It equals 1 if the location of the previous employer is New York City or London and 0 otherwise. Headquarters location is used as a proxy for the location of the manager's job spells.

Abnormal returns are the difference between a fund's actual monthly raw return, net of fees charged to investors, and the fund's expected return estimated from a fund-level longitudinal regression on eight hedge fund specific factors. The fund's information ratio is the fund alpha divided by the standard deviation of the residual; the eight factors are seven from Fung and Hsieh (2004) and a liquidity risk exposure factor from Pastor and Stambaugh (2002). Firm-level information ratios are computed by averaging across all funds in the same firm, weighting each fund's returns by its assets under management, and are windsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

variable_name: Manager's previous job in investment management
description: Dummy variable coded as 1 for any parent-firm job spell in financial securities trading (third party or proprietary trading), mutual fund management, asset management, trust management, wealth management, private banking, pension fund management/institutional investor fund management, and hedge fund/alternative investment management. Other job spells were coded as zero, including any other finance or non-finance related job, most notably corporate finance professionals, brokers, research analysts, commercial bankers, consultants, lawyers, accountants, and academics. It is interacted with parent-firm location to measure the marginal effect of closely related experience on hedge fund performance.

Measured by the ratio of CEO compensation to average employee compensation. CEO compensation is an aggregate of the annual salary, bonus, the value of restricted stock grants, long-term incentive plan payouts, and the value of other option grants. Average employee compensation was measured by dividing the difference between total labor expense and CEO compensation by the number of employees (excluding the CEO). The measure was rescaled by dividing the value by 100.

The ratio of External stakeholder treatment over Employee treatment. Employee treatment was the aggregate of the MSCI KLD strength scores on five 'employee relations' items, excluding the 'health and safety' item. External stakeholder treatment was measured with the same method for community, environment, and customers. To make scores across stakeholder dimensions comparable, each dimension's strength scores were divided by the total number of items in that dimension per year.

Captures the staggered changes in NCA enforcement level across states defined by the location of the establishment, and equals 1 (-1) if the decreases (increases) in the state-level enforceability scores are greater than or equal to 2. The NCA enforcement index ranges from 0 for no enforcement to 9 for extremely strong enforcement.

Measured using the total number of inspections triggered by employees' complaints of firm i in its establishment j during year t. Employees can file complaints with OSHA if they believe their working conditions are unsafe or unhealthy.

Participants were randomly assigned to read a news article depicting either a high or low CEO-employee pay disparity, adapted from a real Business Insider article about the CEO-employee pay gap. Based on data from ExecuComp and Compustat, top and bottom 5% CEO-employee pay gap values were used to manipulate high (756 times) vs. low (14 times) gaps. The condition was coded 0 = low condition, 1 = high condition.

Measured with adapted items from Chen et al. (2002) with the referent of 'supervisor' changed to 'the company'. Three dimensions of the scale suitable for the experimental context were used. A sample item was 'I would support my company under all circumstances.' Respondents answered on a scale from 1 = Strongly disagree to 7 = Strongly agree; alpha = .96.
Measured by the question 'Please indicate your willingness to submit a complaint to OSHA regarding the issue of inadequate ventilation you have observed' (1 = Not willing at all to 7 = Very willing).
scale: 1 = Not willing at all to 7 = Very willing

variable_name: external stakeholder - employee treatment disparity (experimental condition)
description: Participants were randomly assigned to read a news article depicting either a high or low external stakeholder-employee treatment disparity. The article was modeled on a Rockwell Automation (2024) news article and adopted the indicators and related descriptions from MSCI KLD. The condition was coded 0 = low condition, 1 = high condition.

Measured with adapted items from Chen et al. (2002) with the referent of 'supervisor' changed to 'the company'. Three dimensions of the scale suitable for the experimental context were used. A sample item was 'I would support my company under all circumstances.' Respondents answered on a scale from 1 = Strongly disagree to 7 = Strongly agree; alpha = .95.
Measured by the question 'Please indicate your willingness to submit a complaint to OSHA regarding the issue of inadequate ventilation you have observed' (1 = Not willing at all to 7 = Very willing).
scale: 1 = Not willing at all to 7 = Very willing

description: Indicator equal to one if newspaper i is published and distributed in the evening, and zero for a morning newspaper. For newspapers circulated in both the morning and the evening, the circulation share of the morning paper is calculated as morning circulation divided by the sum of morning and evening circulation; the newspaper is considered a morning newspaper if that share is greater than 70% and an evening newspaper otherwise. The morning or evening designation is treated as a fixed trait of a newspaper that does not vary over year t.

Dummy variable that equals one for all years, t, after a TV station enters newspaper i's local market; otherwise it has a value of zero. The information on the dates of TV entry into different markets is obtained from George (2009).
Subscription price of the newspaper, obtained from the Editor & Publisher International Year Book. The regressions use the logarithm of the price because the variable is highly skewed.
Weekly circulation of the newspaper, obtained from the Editor & Publisher International Year Book. The regressions use the logarithm of circulation because the variable is highly skewed.
Advertising rate of the newspaper, obtained from the Editor & Publisher International Year Book. The regressions use the logarithm of the advertising rate because the variable is highly skewed.

variable_name: TV ad rate (log TV Ad rate)
description: The rate a TV station charged for 1 hr of advertising, collected from the Television Factbook for 1949, 1955, 1957 and 1962, the only years when such data were available. The regression uses the logarithm of the TV advertising rate because the variable is highly skewed. Unlike the newspaper-level regressions, this variable is defined at the market level and is undefined until TV enters the market.
The percentage of the newspaper circulation in market m and year t for evening newspapers. The higher this percentage, the higher the percent of the market that single-homes.

Respondents were asked to report the number of prior alliance agreements with the same partner firm. Because an examination of the variable's distribution indicated significant positive skewness, the authors redefined the variable using the natural log transformation ln(1 + variable). In supplemental analyses they also examined whether the presence or absence of prior ties affects the outcomes and found the same results.

Respondents evaluated four statements on 5-point Likert-type scales ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'; the items had a Cronbach alpha of 0.79. The items all query behavior consistent with norms of reciprocity and equity and capture the informal, voluntary nature of this behavior (i.e., not specified by formal agreements), and they can become established, or institutionalized, as normal and expected behavior for a large set of individuals from the two organizations.

Based on the scale of affect-based trust developed by McAllister (1995), respondents evaluated five statements characterizing the personal relationships between the people from their firm and those from the partner firm(s) who worked for the alliance, using 5-point Likert-type scales (alpha = 0.77). Consistent with social exchange theory, the items do not capture just affect, but affect that is reciprocated.

Respondents evaluated four statements on 5-point Likert-type scales (alpha = 0.70); the second item was reverse coded. The measure was operationalized using previous studies that discuss the partner as a source of learning in alliances, knowledge about a partner, or the predictability of its behavior.

Three five-point Likert-type items measuring the extent to which partners were operating in similar markets before the alliance were multiplied: product markets, geographic markets and customer segments. The measure can take on values ranging from 1 to 125. The multiplicative measure reflects the idea that competition might not be relevant if firms that operate in the same country do not also compete in the same product markets (and vice versa), or if they target different customer segments within a given industry.

Three five-point Likert-type items with a Cronbach alpha of 0.84. The first two items were adopted from Kale et al.'s (2000) construct of 'partner fit' because they refer to cultural similarity rather than to similarity in partners' resources and capabilities; respondents rated the extent to which the partners were similar in organizational cultures and management and operating styles at the outset of the collaboration, and a third item capturing similarity in decision-making processes was added to enhance reliability.
time_window: at the outset of the collaboration

description: A studio's capability is measured as the efficiency by which inputs to film projects in a given year (the budget and the talent available to the firm) are turned into outputs (revenue in that genre), estimated with stochastic frontier estimation using maximum likelihood.
