The SFE model builds on a production function with a technical efficiency component and includes gross revenue as output and budget and cumulative awards as inputs; cumulative awards proxy the extent of artistic talent available to the firm. Capability of studio i at time t is calculated using the prediction for u_it and, by definition, the estimates fall between 0 and 1.
time_window: annual, measured for each year t

description: Studio revenue is the sum of the domestic box office grosses of all the movies made by a studio in a given year, in millions of inflation-adjusted dollars. Following prior literature, growth is modeled as the relative size of studio revenue in the current and past time periods, which allows the growth rate to vary with size. A log transformation of the growth equation yields a specification that can be estimated using a linear panel estimator; the dependent variable is thus a log-transformed first-difference measure.
The number of major partners is calculated as the number of major studios with which the firm has a distribution or coproduction deal at a given time.

Market overlap measured at the coarse level of the software product classification system, which consisted of four product classes. It is the ratio of the number of product classes to which both firms introduced software products in the three years preceding the event date, divided by the number of product classes in which the non-accused firm operated during that period. Values range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater overlap.
time_window: three years preceding the event date

description: Market overlap computed at the intermediate level of the classification system, which consisted of 54 product segments. The ratio compares the product segments in which both the non-accused firm and its accused peer introduced products with the segments in which the non-accused firm operated in the three years preceding the event. The values range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater overlap.
time_window: three years preceding the event date

description: Market overlap computed at the fine-grained level of the classification system, which consisted of 464 product functions. The ratio compares the product functions in which both the non-accused firm and its accused peer introduced products with the functions in which the non-accused firm operated in the three years preceding the event. The values range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater overlap.
time_window: three years preceding the event date

description: The level of the product classification system used to measure market overlap: a coarse level of four product classes, an intermediate level of 54 product segments, and a fine-grained level of 464 product functions. The system is nested, and the granularity of the lens is varied across regression models to compare the stigma and competition effects.

A three-day cumulative abnormal return starting the day prior to the announcement, computed as the sum over the three days of the daily abnormal return of the non-accused firm around the accusation event of its industry peer. The daily abnormal return is the difference between the firm's actual return and its expected return on that day, calculated with the market model, where the return of the CRSP value-weighted index and market model parameters estimated over a 255-day window ending 46 days prior to the accusation event are used.

Dummy variable that received a value of 1 for hedge funds and mutual funds and a value of 0 for banks, insurance firms, investment advisors, and other institutional investors. Mutual funds were identified based on the investors' classification in the Thomson Reuters database, and hedge funds based on the listing provided by Griffin and Xu (2009), further elaborated with a manual online search for the identity of the institutional investors.

Calculated by subtracting the percentage of shares of an investor in the non-accused firm in the quarter prior to the accusation from the percentage of shares held in the quarter following the accusation event. The respective percentages were calculated by dividing the number of shares held by the investor by the number of outstanding shares in the corresponding quarters.
time_window: quarter prior to the accusation to the quarter following the accusation event

description: A spline function using the fine-grained level of market overlap for more sophisticated institutional investors and the market overlap at the intermediate level for less sophisticated institutional investors, because the data are limited to institutional investors and these market classifications are correspondingly associated with more and less sophisticated institutional investors.
time_window: three years preceding the event date

description: A firm-year measure set to be the ratio of the top to median benchmark pay within a given firm and year, constructed in two variants, one using geographic benchmarks and one using industry benchmarks. Each division manager's benchmark pay is set at the 75th percentile of pay earned by peers working within the same geography (state) or industry, excluding employees in the focal firm; the top benchmark is defined as the 90th percentile. The two benchmarks are logged and their difference is the measure; the log-distance calculation is used rather than a pure arithmetic ratio to reduce skewness.

Indicator variable that takes the value one for the 278 division-firm-year observations in which divisions exit the sample, that is, the years in which those divisions are divested. It takes the value zero for the 732 division-firm-year observations pertaining to divested divisions in the years prior to their divestitures and for the 3,847 division-firm-year observations pertaining to remaining divisions within divesting firms.
time_window: year t (with divestitures reported during years t to t + 2)

description: The probability that chain j acquires target i, given that chain j made an acquisition in year t. The unit of analysis is the chain-acquisition target dyad: each time a chain acquired a nursing home, observations on all homes at risk of being acquired were pooled, and the set of possible targets includes all homes operating in Ontario at the start of the year in which an acquisition was made. Each observation was treated as right-censored unless the home was acquired. When a chain acquired n nursing homes in a year, each acquisition was given a weight of 1/n in the likelihood calculations.

variable_name: i's distance from j's last acquisition
description: Euclidean distance between target i and the Kth (last) of chain j's K prior acquisitions. Euclidean distances were measured using the latitude and longitude of nursing homes' postal addresses, and smaller values indicate greater proximity. The variable is time varying, measured at the start of the year in which the acquisition occurred.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's distance from j's nearest acquisition
description: Euclidean distance between target i and chain j's prior acquisition closest to target i. Distances were measured using the latitude and longitude of nursing homes' postal addresses, and smaller values indicate greater proximity; the variable is time varying and measured at the start of the acquisition year.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's distance from j's current components
description: Measure of the average Euclidean distance between target i and chain j's current components, where the sum runs over chain j's kth of K total components. Smaller values indicate greater proximity; the variable is time varying and measured at the start of the acquisition year.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's similarity to j's last acquisition
description: Variables capturing the similarity of target i to a chain's most recent acquisition, computed for size, context and compactness. A nursing home's size was measured as its number of beds and its context based on its latitude, which in Ontario differentiates densely populated urban southern regions from mixed and sparsely populated northern areas. Spatial compactness was measured as target i's distance to the acquiring chain's prior acquisition nearest to it, and MinED is the Euclidean distance from chain j's most recent acquisition to its nearest other unit. Smaller values indicate greater similarity.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's similarity to j's nearest acquisition
description: Similarity of target i to chain j's prior acquisition nearest to target i, computed analogously to the most recent acquisition variables for size, context (latitude) and spatial compactness. For compactness, MinED is the Euclidean distance between chain j's prior acquisition nearest to target i and the nearest of chain j's other components. Smaller values indicate greater similarity.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's similarity to j's current components
description: Similarity of target i to chain j's current components, computed for size, context and compactness. AvBed and AvLatitude are the average number of beds and latitude of chain j's current components, and AvMin(EDkk) is chain j's spatial compactness, the average minimum Euclidean distance among its current components. Smaller values indicate greater similarity.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's distance to large chains' last acquisitions
description: The average Euclidean distance from target i to each other chain's most recent acquisition, scaled by each other chain's size. ED is the Euclidean distance between target i and the last acquisition by other chain h, Bed is the sum of beds in all of chain h's components, and H is the total number of other chains; scaling by chain size discounts the distance in proportion to chain h's size, so the larger chain h the greater the discount. Smaller values indicate greater proximity.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's distance to large chains' nearest acquisitions
description: An analogous measure based on other chains' acquisitions nearest to target i, where ED is the Euclidean distance between target i and chain h's nearest acquisition to target i, scaled by chain h's size. Smaller values indicate greater proximity.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's distance to large chains' current components
description: Variable in which AvED is the average Euclidean distance from target i to all of other chain h's current components, scaled by each other chain's size. Smaller values indicate greater proximity.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's distance to similar chains' last acquisitions
description: A set of four variables, one each for chain size, component size, spatial compactness and latitude (context). Each variable takes ED, the Euclidean distance between target i and other chain h's most recent acquisition, and weights it by the magnitude of the difference between acquiring chain j and chain h on that organizational feature; weighting magnifies the distance as the difference between the chains increases. The difference factors use the total beds operated by chains j and h, the average component size of their current components, the average latitude of their current components, and their spatial compactness measured as the average minimum Euclidean distance among their current components.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's distance to similar chains' nearest acquisitions
description: Variables constructed in the same way as the most-recent-acquisition imitation variables, using the same four organizational features, but based on the distance between target i and other chain h's acquisition nearest to target i. Larger values indicate greater dissimilarity/distance.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

variable_name: i's distance to similar chains' current acquisitions
description: Variables constructed in the same way as the other similar-chain imitation measures, using the same four organizational features but based on the average Euclidean distance from target i to all of other chain h's current components. Larger values indicate greater dissimilarity/distance.
time_window: start of the year in which the acquisition occurred

description: Standard setting activities are traced using data on specific SEP disclosures to SSOs, which maps standard setting to particular technology subcategories. Standards Own is constructed by first counting the number of technological subcategories in which the focal firm itself disclosed SEPs in the year, and then scaling this count by the number of subcategories in which the firm files for patents in year t, resulting in a proportion measure.

Standards Non-Own is constructed by counting the subcategories in which the firm patents and in which SEPs were disclosed by other firms, scaled by the focal firm's total number of subcategories. The variable was further orthogonalized against Standards Own to ensure the two main independent variables are picking up different information.

The natural logarithm of the firm's stock option implied volatility at time t, backed out from the firm's stock option premium using the Black and Scholes option pricing model. It is measured using the firm's European-style call stock option with a 1-month (30 days) expiration date, and to avoid potential bias due to illiquidity in December the measure is led by 1 year and calculated as the daily average of implied volatility over the month of January in year t+1.
time_window: daily average over January of year t+1, from the option at time t

description: Complementary technological areas are identified using patent co-citation: a patent filed in year t is deemed complementary to an SEP disclosed in year t if the patent is subsequently co-cited with the SEP within 5 years from t, and patents assigned to the same technology class as the SEP are not considered complementary. For each focal firm in year t all complementary areas in which it is active are compiled, the total complementary patents in each area owned by non-focal firms are counted, and the non-focal firm owning the largest proportion of complementary patents in each area is identified; Strong Rival is the natural log of the largest of these proportions across all of the focal firm's complementary areas in year t.
time_window: year t, with a 5-year co-citation window

description: For each focal firm in year t, the firm's complementary patents filed for in the year are determined following the co-citation-based definition of complementary technological areas and counted.
The natural log of the firm's gross total property, plant, and equipment (PPE).

The initial acquisition premium is measured as the ratio of the initial offer price over the closing stock price 4 weeks before the announcement. The authors follow Haunschild (1994), Dinc and Erel (2013), and Bertrand et al. (2016) and note that Bertrand et al. (2016) recommend using a 4-week period since information could leak earlier and distort the effect.

A continuous variable, built on the measure of Bertrand et al. (2016), determined by the voting behavior between two countries in the UN General Assembly and ranging between zero and one. A value of one represents completely consistent voting behavior between two countries and thus strong political affinity, while zero represents completely opposite voting behavior and thus weak political affinity.

A time-varying dummy which is one if the identical voting behavior of two nations dominates opposite voting behavior (strong political affinity) and zero otherwise (weak political affinity). The authors describe the dummy as a second, more conservative approximation of political affinity that allows them to investigate whether results depend on the variable construction.

Cumulative abnormal returns from 1 day before to 1 day after the announcement, with the announcement day being the focal day. Abnormal returns are determined with all six factors (market, size, book-to-market, momentum, investment, and operating profitability-based factors) from the factor models of Carhart (1997) and Fama and French (2015), with an estimation window that runs from 210 to 11 days before the event.

Cumulative abnormal returns from 1 day before to 1 day after the announcement, with the announcement day being the focal day. Abnormal returns are determined with all six factors (market, size, book-to-market, momentum, investment, and operating profitability-based factors) from the factor models of Carhart (1997) and Fama and French (2015), with an estimation window that runs from 210 to 11 days before the event.

The absolute value of outside director stock options is the product of the number of stock option grants awarded to each outside director during the firm's fiscal year and the Black-Scholes options value at that fiscal year-end. The deviation from prior option grant values is computed by taking the value of each outside director's own stock options received in the prior year at time t - 2 and subtracting it from the actual value of outside director stock options at time t - 1. An indicator variable for negative deviation equals one if an outside director's prior stock option grant value falls below the reference point, so positive deviation is where the option grant value met or exceeded the reference point; the authors also estimate a parallel variable for values below the reference point. The model specification is given as a formula that was not extracted and could not be read; the authors state that pay values are averaged across nonmanagement directors because each outside director was awarded annual grants of an equal number of shares.
time_window: one-year comparison window: t - 1 option value against the t - 2 reference point

description: Following Devers et al. (2008), firm-level strategic risk-taking intensity is proxied with three risk dimensions: R&D investments (a firm's aggregate R&D spending), capital investments (a firm's capital expenditures), and long-term debt (a firm's total long-term debt), all measured in millions of U.S. dollars. A factor analysis of the risk proxies produced a single factor with an eigenvalue of 2.27 that captured 75.80 percent of the variance, and factor loadings were greater than 0.84. The three risk variables were scaled by firm annual sales and then normalized and summed to create the composite strategic risk-taking intensity index.
scale: composite index of normalized sales-scaled risk variables

description: CEO ownership is measured as the ratio of the number of outstanding shares held by the CEO to the firm's total amount of outstanding shares. Raw variables were normalized before the interaction variables were created.
scale: ratio of shares held to total outstanding shares

description: CEO duality is dummy-coded such that the indicator variable is set to one if the CEO also holds the board chair position and zero otherwise. The variable was measured at year t - 1 like the other substantive predictors.

Measured with Bass and Avolio's Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ)-Form 6S, following the methodology of Baum et al. (1998). The instrument includes 21 items measuring only leadership behaviors, divided into seven factors: Idealized Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, Individual Consideration, Contingent Reward, Management-by-Exception, and Laissez-Faire; Laissez-Faire was not included in the strategic leadership behaviors and was used as a control variable instead. Vision development, an additional transformational behavior, was measured by the strategic leader's vision possessing seven attributes: clarity, brevity, challenge, abstractiveness, future orientation, stability, and desirability or ability to inspire. The MLQ items were completed by the subordinate members of the top management teams, not by the titular heads.

The titular heads (presidents, managing directors, or CEOs) of each organizational unit rated the amount of influence (1 = no influence to 5 = a dominant influence) that their TMT had on a list of specific innovations, reflecting the time lag between managerial action and innovation outcomes. The measure follows Jemison's (1981) multi-item approach and uses Hoffman and Hegarty's (1993) measures, conceptually based on the Miles et al. (1978) typology. It comprises three items: new products or services (for existing markets); new markets (for existing products/services); and new products or services for new markets. Cronbach's alpha for the scale was 0.78.
scale: 1 = no influence to 5 = a dominant influence

description: Rated by the titular heads (presidents, managing directors, or CEOs) of each organizational unit, who indicated the amount of influence (1 = no influence to 5 = a dominant influence) that their TMT had on a list of specific innovations in order to capture the lag between action and outcome. The measure follows Jemison's (1981) multi-item approach and uses Hoffman and Hegarty's (1993) measures. It comprises three items: new planning and control system; new department or permanent position; and new system for training, development, or promoting managers. Cronbach's alpha for the scale was 0.80.
scale: 1 = no influence to 5 = a dominant influence

description: Measured using the formula TMT Ten Het = sigma(TMT)/mu(TMT), where sigma(TMT) is the standard deviation of executives' respective job tenures on the top management team and mu(TMT) is the mean of executives' respective tenures on the same top management team. The higher the resulting score, the greater the TMT tenure heterogeneity. The data were obtained from self-reported job tenure information provided by the respondents.

Operationalized as a nominal variable within the three cultural clusters (Anglo, Germanic, and Eastern Slavic), converted into three dichotomous variables through dummy coding of 0 or 1 for use in regression analyses. Anglo culture was represented by a 0 score on the other two cultures. The data were obtained from self-reports by the respondents.

A binary variable equal to 1 if the start-up adapts their product and 0 otherwise. Adaptations are major, observable changes to chemistry or architecture of the solar PV module, such as switching from single-layer to multilayer cells or from flat to textured cells. The variable excludes adaptations peripheral to module technology (such as targeting new downstream applications or adding minor components) and changes to manufacturing processes. The classification was validated by a panel of experts consisting of industry CEOs, executives, and analysts.

The average number of industries in which TMT members have preentry experience, computed as the count of prior industries for each TMT member divided by total TMT members. Industries were defined based on the classifications listed by the 2007 North American Industry Classification System at the five-digit level.

The proportion of the TMT who have the majority of their preentry experience in the solar PV industry, computed as the number of TMT members with majority work experience in solar PV divided by total TMT members.
The proportion of TMT members who have the majority of their preentry experience in an entrepreneurial setting.
The proportion of TMT members who have the majority of their preentry experience in a business context versus a science context (public or private science institutions).

Kirsch et al.'s (2002) outcome control scale, with minor adaptations, measured on a seven-point Likert scale. The scale captures the extent to which the client prespecified desired controllee outputs and the associated evaluation criteria and placed weight on them in the project. Responses were provided by the lead project manager.

Kirsch et al.'s (2002) process control scale (labeled 'behavior control' in their study), with minor adaptations, measured on a seven-point Likert scale. The scale captures the extent to which the client placed weight on an understandable written sequence of steps for accomplishing project goals, meeting client requirements, and ensuring project success. Responses were provided by the lead project manager.

New seven-point Likert scale tapping the extent to which the relationships between the outsourced subsystem and the base system were characterized by high interoperability, stable well-defined interfaces, well-understood interdependencies, and minimal unnecessary interdependencies. The item pool started from Nambisan's (2002) modularity decision scale and Worren et al.'s (2002) modular product scales and was iteratively refined with feedback from seven software industry professionals and five academics. Responses were provided by the lead project manager.

Four items adapted from Faraj and Sproull's (2000) scale, consistent with software alliance performance criteria. The items assess the effectiveness of the development process in successfully fulfilling the client's project needs, quality expectations, functional requirements, and objectives, on a seven-point Likert scale. Responses were provided by the lead project manager.

Multi-item perceptual scale developed from the differentiation scale used by Doty, Glick, and Huber (1993). It measures the degree to which a firm's product-market strategy is based on differentiation. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Multi-item perceptual scale developed from the differentiation scale used by Doty, Glick, and Huber (1993). It measures the degree to which a firm's product-market strategy is based on differentiation. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Multi-item perceptual scale developed from the cost-focus scale used by Doty, Glick, and Huber (1993). It measures the degree to which the firm focuses on cost efficiencies in its product-market strategy. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Multi-item perceptual scale developed from the cost-focus scale used by Doty, Glick, and Huber (1993). It measures the degree to which the firm focuses on cost efficiencies in its product-market strategy. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Multi-item perceptual scale developed from the product-market scope scale used by Doty, Glick, and Huber (1993). It measures the degree to which the firm operates in many (versus few) markets or market segments. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Multi-item perceptual scale developed from the product-market scope scale used by Doty, Glick, and Huber (1993). It measures the degree to which the firm operates in many (versus few) markets or market segments. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Multi-item scale adapted from Vorhies and Morgan (2003, 2005) that measures the degree to which firms engage in specified routine marketing activities. Respondents rated how well their organization performs the marketing activities relative to its closest competitors. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Multi-item scale adapted from Vorhies and Morgan (2003, 2005) that measures the degree to which firms engage in specified routine marketing activities. Respondents rated how well their organization performs the marketing activities relative to its closest competitors. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Multi-item scale adapted from Vorhies and Morgan (2003, 2005) that measures the degree to which firms engage in specified routine marketing activities. Respondents rated how well their organization performs the marketing activities relative to its closest competitors. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Multi-item scale adapted from Vorhies and Morgan (2003, 2005) that measures the degree to which firms engage in specified routine marketing activities. Respondents rated how well their organization performs the marketing activities relative to its closest competitors. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.
Derived by creating an interaction term, multiplying the specialized and architectural marketing capabilities measures.
Derived by creating an interaction term, multiplying the specialized and architectural marketing capabilities measures.

Perceptual measures of attainment of market share growth, sales growth, and desired market position of the firm, with items gauging the degree to which the responding firm achieved its goals in those respective areas. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Perceptual measures of attainment of market share growth, sales growth, and desired market position of the firm, with items gauging the degree to which the responding firm achieved its goals in those respective areas. Reported by a key informant from the top management team of the business.

Firm cash flow return on assets calculated by taking cash flow and dividing by the firm's total assets, using objective published financial data for the subsequent one-year period following survey data collection. Dividing by total assets removes the impact of firm size; the variable was then logarithmically transformed to normalize it. Cash flow is preferred over earnings-based measures because it is less subject to accrual accounting methods and accounting manipulations.

Firm cash flow return on assets calculated by taking cash flow and dividing by the firm's total assets, using objective published financial data for the subsequent one-year period following survey data collection. Dividing by total assets removes the impact of firm size; the variable was then logarithmically transformed to normalize it. Cash flow is preferred over earnings-based measures because it is less subject to accrual accounting methods and accounting manipulations.

Social CSR was measured using Eikon's social pillar, which includes 61 items across four areas: workforce quality, emphasis on human rights, organizational community involvement, and product responsibility. The mean score in the sample was 40.5 on a scale of 0 to 100.

Governance CSR was measured using Eikon's governance pillar based on 50 items across three areas: management quality (compensation, independence, diversity), shareholders' rights, and board composition and strategy. The mean score in the sample was 40.5 on a scale of 0 to 100.

Environmental CSR was measured using Eikon's environmental pillar, based on 61 items across three areas: resource use, harmful gas emissions, and innovation in controlling environmental degradation. The mean score in the sample was 28.7 on a scale of 0 to 100.

Performance was measured as percentage return on assets, computed by dividing earnings before interest, taxes, and depreciation by total assets. Financial data for the sample firms were obtained from the Prowess database. The average ROA in the sample is 15%.

Business group affiliation was measured using a bivariate variable coded as one if a firm was affiliated with a business group and zero otherwise. Following previous studies, the Prowess database was used to identify group affiliation.

The implementation of a policy nudge was measured with the passage of the Companies Act of 2013, whose specific CSR requirements took effect on April 1, 2014. Nudge is a dummy variable that equals one for years after the policy nudge and zero otherwise, splitting the sample into a prenudge period and a postnudge period.

Dichotomous variable that equals 1 if the focal firm is the target of an acquisition in a given year based on the acquisition announcements reported by SDC and 0 otherwise. Acquisition bids with a deal value of less than $500,000 were excluded, as were deals labeled as buybacks, exchange offers, privatizations, spin-offs, carve-outs, self-tenders, and recapitalizations. The approach samples all firms that could become a target and avoids ex post selection bias.

The difference-in-differences treatment is identified by the interaction of two indicators. Michigan equals 1 if a firm was located in Michigan based on the historical location of the firm's corporate headquarters. After is an indicator variable that equals 1 for 1988 or thereafter and 0 otherwise (i.e., 1987 or before); the break between 1987 and 1988 was chosen to allow time for the policy change to be disseminated by law firms and acted upon by potential acquirers. Michigan x After identifies the treatment effect of MARA and is used to test Hypothesis 1.

Measured as the level of knowledge workers employed in a focal firm's three-digit SIC industry as a proportion of the total workforce employed in that industry, using OES occupational codes below 50,000 to define knowledge workers. The proportion calculated for a given three-digit SIC was assigned to each focal firm, weighted by the proportion of the firm's sales in its three-digit SIC industries; sales were extracted by four-digit NAICS from the COMPUSTAT Segments file and converted to three-digit SIC using the U.S. Census Bureau NAICS-to-SIC concordance. Knowledge Workers is a continuous measure from 0 to 1, mean centered at 0 in the models.

Measured as the proportion of total U.S. sales generated by other firms located in the same state and same industry (three-digit SIC) as the focal firm, using data from the COMPUSTAT Segments file, with the focal firm's own sales excluded. The measure was assigned to each firm weighted by the proportion of the firm's sales in its three-digit SIC industries. In-state Competition is a continuous measure from 0 to 1.

Uses the Cohen et al. (2000) industry measure of the mean percentage of product innovations for which patents are an effective mechanism for protecting the underlying knowledge and appropriating the returns, obtained by industry from their Table 1 and assigned to the manufacturing firms in the sample in a way similar to the other explanatory variables. A value of 0 was assigned to nonmanufacturing firms, as the measure is not relevant to those firms, and the measure was rescaled to vary continuously from 0 to 1 to be consistent with the other two moderating variables.

Dummy variable set to one if a firm has at least one tie to the largest weakly connected component of the Boston network in a given year. The measure is calculated independently for the Boston and the Boston + networks; this entry refers to the network that includes only organizations located in the region and the ties among them (58 DBFs, 19 PROs and 37 VC firms).

Dummy variable set to one if a firm has at least one tie to the largest weakly connected component of the Boston + network in a given year. The Boston + network comprises all organizations in any location that have a network tie to a Boston-based organization, excluding the ties that make up the Boston network.

Betweenness centrality score of the firm in the Boston network, based on Freeman's measure, capturing the extent to which firms sit astride network pathways between other organizations. The authors calculate betweenness for both the Boston and the Boston + networks.
Betweenness centrality score computed on a geographically dispersed network that excludes ties among Boston area organizations.

Yearly count of successful patent applications, a count of patents assigned to the firms and developed from the U.S. Patent Office's online database. The authors model counts of patents by application date in an 11-year pooled cross-section for the panel of 58 DBFs, arguing that application date best measures when patentable research was actually completed.

Dummy variable set to one for the period 1993-1998, used to indicate the differential effects of centrality in a network anchored by PROs (time period = 0) and by firms (time period = 1). The authors note that the separation of the 11-year time frame into two periods corresponds with increasing volatility and growth in DBF membership in the local component and a steep decline in the component's reliance on PRO ties.

The variable is the difference between a BU's capital expenditure (CAPEX) and its own after-tax cash flow (ATCF), following Billett and Mauer (2003); the ATCF is calculated from the BU's reported earnings before interest and taxes, depreciation and amortization, imputed interest expense and imputed tax rate. For each treated and control observation the authors compute the difference between the BU's average resource allocation after the treatment minus its average resource allocation before the treatment, and deflate this difference by the total segment assets averaged over the 3 years before the treatment. The equations in the article record are not readable.
time_window: 3 years before to 3 years after the tariff cut

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if either the owning firm (BUs Indirectly Affected Sample) or directly the BU (BUs Directly Affected Sample) experiences a tariff cut, and 0 otherwise. Tariff changes are computed as the ad valorem tariff rate, the ratio between duties collected by U.S. Customs and the free-on-board value of imports; a negative tariff change counts as a cut only if it exceeds three times the average tariff variation for its industry, the tariff rate in the year before the cut is at least 1%, and the cut is not preceded or followed by equivalently large tariff increases.
level: business unit (directly affected sample) or firm (indirectly affected sample)

description: The authors multiply the logarithm of the assets reported by the BU in the year of the shock by Kim and Kung's (2017) redeployability proxy and then reverse-code the measure to obtain an estimate of sunk cost. Kim and Kung's industry-level redeployability score is built from the 1997 Bureau of Economic Analysis capital flow table: each asset class is weighted by the market capitalization of the industries that use it, and industry redeployability is the asset-class scores weighted by the industry's expenditure in each asset category, also taking into account the extent to which firms' output in an industry co-moves.

For each SIC4 industry pair the authors compute a 3-year rolling sum of the total amount of cross-citations between patents granted to companies operating in one sector and patents granted to companies in the other. The relatedness of BU i is calculated as a weighted average, by segment sales, of the cross-citation measure between its operating sector and the firm's other operating sectors, and the authors take the natural logarithm of the resulting measure. Patents are attributed to SIC4 codes using the operating sector of the patent owner as reported in COMPUSTAT.

Organizational performance is measured using the ratio of total operating expense to premium income, the operating cost efficiency ratio. Top performance firms exhibit low operating cost efficiency ratio values, indicating that a greater proportion of each revenue dollar is set aside for policyholder and investor benefits; weak performance firms exhibit high or above average values of the ratio. The numbers for total operating expense and premium income are based on the subtotals for operating expense and premium income by line of business. Operating expenses do not include sales commissions or the payment of policyholder benefits as a part of costs. Premium income is used in the study as the proxy measure for firm output.

Information technology investment intensity is examined using the ratio of information technology expense to total operating expense, the IT expense ratio. Information technology costs include all expenses for information processing in the firm, e.g., hardware, software, personnel, data communications, and miscellaneous in both data processing and line/staff departments, including depreciation. The substitution of information technology costs for noninformation technology costs increases the level of operational dependency on information technology resources and results in higher values of the IT expense ratio. The operating cost efficiency ratio can be computed from the information technology investment ratios by multiplying the IT cost efficiency ratio times the inverse of the IT expense ratio.

Information technology investment intensity is examined using the ratio of information technology expense to premium income, the IT cost efficiency ratio. It is a single-factor expense measure of the cost economies of information technology, and high ratio values reduce the attractiveness of the industry to potential entrants and act as a mobility barrier to industry participants. Information technology costs include all expenses for information processing in the firm, e.g., hardware, software, personnel, data communications, and miscellaneous in both data processing and line/staff departments, including depreciation. Lower IT cost efficiency ratio values are derived from lower information technology costs, or higher premium income revenues, or both.

In the firm size analysis the premium income ranking is used as a proxy measure for firm size. Each factor is measured at four levels, where ranking I represents the lowest 25% of the ratio values, ranking II the next largest 25%, ranking III the third highest 25%, and ranking IV the largest 25%. A two-way table is constructed with the operating cost efficiency ratio as the dependent variable and premium income ranking and the IT expense ratio ranking as factor inputs.
'Age' was a continuous 2-digit number reported by each participant. The average age of the respondents was 49, and the ages ranged from 34 to 69.

'Technical education' was constructed as a dichotomous variable (0 = no, 1 = yes). Participants were assigned a value of 1 if the executive had either an engineering or a physical science degree; otherwise this variable was 0. Respondents were asked to report their undergraduate and graduate degrees.

Respondents were asked to indicate their primary work experience. Those executives who indicated engineering or R&D as their primary work experience were categorized as having principally technical work experience and coded as 1. Executives who reported a primary work experience other than these two (e.g., marketing, production, finance, general management) were coded as 0.
The firm's emphasis on technology was measured using a 3-item 5-point Likert scale (low to high). The coefficient alpha for this scale was 0.91.

To capture the firm's risk orientation, two previously utilized scales were combined: Khandwalla's 6-item scale and a 2-item scale derived from Miller et al. All eight items used a 5-point Likert scale format. After data collection, one item from Khandwalla's scale was found to be deficient and subsequently dropped, leaving a 7-item scale (coefficient alpha = 0.86). The scale was constructed so that the higher the score, the greater the firm's propensity for risk taking.
scale: 7 items, 5-point Likert scale; higher = greater propensity for risk taking

description: Respondents indicated how many collaborative technological relationships their firm had been involved in and the number it was currently participating in; these responses were added to form the measure of total collaborative experience (Experience). A 2-item scale was constructed for success: the overall success rating of previous collaborative technology development activities on a 5-point scale, and the estimated percentage of such relationships that had been successful recoded on a 5-point scale (1 = 0-20% to 5 = 81-100%); the two were added (alpha = 0.83). The success measure was multiplied by total collaborative experience (Experience · Success).

Each respondent evaluated the same set of 30 different scenarios. The dependent variable for each scenario was the executive's rating on two items, each on a 7-point Likert scale: the attractiveness of the proposed relationship and the probability that they would pursue such a relationship. These items were combined to create the dependent variable, 'assessment of the opportunity' (alpha = 0.95).

Twelve of the 17 factors that describe the scenarios can be categorized as factors associated with strategic intent (stretch), relational risk, and performance risk. The opportunity-based attributes concern the commitment of the firm to a technology policy that supports firm strategy, learning from alliance partners, and broad corporate applications of technology and exposure to related markets. Each of the 17 criteria was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high) in each of the 30 scenarios, and each criterion entered the regression as a separate independent variable.

Examples of alliance attributes that top executives may associate with relational risk are the compatibility of management styles (can we work together?), the number of potential cooperative partners (what are my alternatives if this partner acts opportunistically?), and the favorability of a potential partner's cooperative history. Each of the 17 criteria was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high) in each of the 30 scenarios, and each criterion entered the regression as a separate independent variable.

Factors that executives may associate with performance risk are the potential for decreasing development risk by cooperating, the total expected cost for developing the technology, the ability to patent protect the technology once developed, and the availability of technological substitutes. Each of the 17 criteria was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high) in each of the 30 scenarios, and each criterion entered the regression as a separate independent variable.

Threat-based information in the policy-capturing scenarios comprises the attributes associated with relational risk (compatibility of management styles, number of potential cooperative partners, favorability of a potential partner's cooperative history) and those associated with performance risk (potential for decreasing development risk, total expected cost for developing the technology, ability to patent protect the technology, availability of technological substitutes). Each of the 17 criteria was randomly assigned a number on a scale ranging from one (low) to five (high) in each of the 30 scenarios, and each criterion entered the regression as a separate independent variable.

Count of directors who are classified as independent in the firm's proxy statement, have a title of COO and/or president at their place of primary employment, and are not serving as CEO at their place of primary employment. The authors report that 67 percent of boards had no external COO/presidents, 23 percent had one, 7 percent had two, and 3 percent had more than two.

Count of independent directors who served as executive officers (i.e., held titles such as CEO, CFO, or executive vice president) at their primary place of employment and did not also serve as either COO or president at their primary place of employment. This classification allowed the authors to include any directors who might be considered executives at their primary firms.

Firm net income divided by the book value of its assets, minus the average ROA for the firm's industry; industry performance measures were compiled at the three-digit SIC code level. Performance is captured in time t while the operational efficiency measures are captured in time t-1, so performance is future relative to the efficiency variables.
time_window: fiscal year t; efficiency predictors measured at t-1

description: The one-year growth rate in cost of goods sold (COGS) minus the one-year growth rate in revenue, so that higher values indicate costs growing faster than revenue. The authors report a mean value of 0.002, indicating that growth in COGS exceeded growth in revenue by only 0.2 percentage points on average.

The one-year growth rate in selling, general, and administrative expenses (SG&A) minus the one-year growth rate in employment, so that higher values indicate employment-related costs growing faster than actual employment. The authors report a mean value of 0.04, indicating that SG&A outgrows employment by 4 percentage points on average.

Growth in employee productivity over the previous year, calculated as the change in revenue ($1,000s) per employee; because the ratio varies positively with efficiency it is reverse-coded and labeled declining productivity. The authors report a mean value of -12.205 (reverse-coded), indicating that employee productivity grew by an average of $12,205 per employee annually.

The dependent variable is a binary variable taking the value of one if a firm was still operating two years after the date of data collection and zero if it failed. The information regarding the evaluation of possible bankruptcy is lagged by two years. The dichotomous dependent variable and the relatively short time span support the use of logistic regression.
time_window: two years after the date of data collection

description: Sociometric techniques were employed in the Survey of Norwegian Firm and Network Financing 2001 to collect affiliation data of focal firms and their main suppliers and customers; in total 1,498 interfirm dyadic relations and all firm banking affiliations were identified. The number of relations that each bank received was counted, where receipt of a relation is defined as the provision of financial services to the main supplier or customer of a focal firm. The count of relations per bank was divided by the total number of relations reported, resulting in a percentage measure, and this relation ratio was then divided by bank size, measured as the bank's market share.

Bank specialization evident from the distribution of affiliated organizations was measured in terms of bank concentration of activities in a specific industry. Using Statistics Norway's modification of NACE, the sample was divided into 132 different industries and the measure computed as the ratio of the total loans of actors affiliated with bank j and operating in industry i divided by the total number of loans to all industries granted by bank j.
Organization age is measured by the natural log of the number of years since founding date minus two.

Bank loss, the first dependent variable, was measured as the standardized average bank loss per failed customer over the three-year period. All bank assets invested in firms that failed a year before the declared bankruptcy were summed and divided by the number of failed customers.

variable_name: proportion of customer failures within a bank's portfolio of customers
description: The second dependent variable was calculated as the percentage of firms that actually failed out of the total number of firms affiliated with each bank.

The same customer-set connectedness measure used in the firm-level analysis enters the bank-level models: the number of relations a bank receives, defined as the provision of financial services to the main supplier or customer of a focal firm, divided by the total number of relations reported and by bank size measured as market share. Bank size was measured by the sum of the number of customers per bank.

Measured as the natural logarithm of the number of establishments with fewer than 20 employees entering the industry between 1976-78, 1982-84, and 1986-88, for each of the three periods of the study and then averaged to produce the final measure. As defined in the USELM data file, business formation refers to the establishment of new operations in an industry, whether an independent establishment or a dependent establishment of an already existing firm. The 20-employee size cut-off was used to help increase the probability that the new small firm establishments were independent.

Measured in the same manner as small business formation except that only formations with 100 or more employees were included, using the natural logarithm of the number of such establishments entering the industry in each of the three periods and then averaged. A correlation analysis against entirely independent formations gave a value of 0.610, suggesting that the large formations measure is a mix of independent (new) and dependent (diversifying) formations.

Computed similar to Burton, Kasserman, and Mayo (1995) for each study year and then averaged for the years 1977, 1982, and 1987. The measure represents the average establishment asset size adjusted for depreciation and rental payments, using gross value of depreciable assets, number of industry establishments, depreciation charges, and rental payments for buildings and structures and for machinery and equipment.
Measured as the four-firm concentration ratio for each industry and similarly averaged across the three study periods.
Calculated as the industry value added divided by the value of shipments in 1977, 1982, and 1987 and then averaged.

Measured as 100 minus the percentage practical plant capacity utilization averaged for the years 1976/1977, 1981/1982, and 1986/1987, for the three periods of the study, respectively. As with the other variables, the computational results for each time period were averaged to produce the final measure.

Operationalized as the industry price cost margin and averaged across the three study periods, using the formula PCM = (VA - PAY - SUP - KB - KM)/VOS, where VA is value added, PAY is payroll, SUP is supplementary payments to labor, KB is capital costs for buildings and structures, KM is capital costs for machinery and equipment, and VOS is value of shipments.

Computed as the percentage change in the value of shipments for three separate time periods from 1972 to 1978, 1977 to 1983, and 1982 to 1988 for each of the three study periods, respectively, and then averaged. The percentage change for each period was calculated as 100 times the regression coefficient of the trend in the natural logarithm of the industry value of shipments.

Measured for each of the three time periods as the change over time in the value of shipments for the major product class (i.e., the largest 5-digit SIC category) within the industry. To compute the 1977 value, the largest product class in the industry was identified for the preceding 5-year period (1972); the fraction of the industry's sales share accounted for by this product class was computed for 1972 and 1977, and the absolute value of the difference between the current period's sales share and the preceding 5-year period sales share was taken. If the industry had only one product class in the preceding 5-year period, a value of zero was assigned. The results were averaged across the three formation periods.

Calculated as company-sponsored R&D expenditures for the industry divided by industry sales as reported in NSF's report, Research and Development in Industry. Since NSF only reports data aggregated at the 2- and sometimes 3-digit SIC level, 2- or 3-digit aggregated statistics were applied to 4-digit industry categories. The computational result for each of the three study periods was averaged to produce the final measure.

Operationalized as the industry's advertising intensity and calculated as the ratio of industry advertising expenses to sales, averaged for the years 1976 and 1977. Data to compute advertising intensity were not available for later study periods, so no averaging across the three study periods was possible.

Formation size is the size class of new establishments entering an industry. Small formations are establishments with fewer than 20 employees and large formations are those with 100 or more employees, each counted from the USELM file and analyzed in separate regressions.

Industry structure is operationalized as a set of industry-level variables: sunk costs, concentration, vertical integration, excess capacity, past profitability, market growth, niche dynamism, technological development, and product differentiation. Each is computed for 1977, 1982, and 1987 and averaged across the three periods.

The aggregate intensity of multipoint contact between firm i and those multipoint rivals j that operate in market m at time t. The authors count the markets where firm i meets rival j to calculate a proportion (range zero to one) and then condition this proportion on the fact that firm j operates in market m at time t and on the number of markets in which firm i operates; the conditional proportion is summed across all firms j. The variable ranges from zero, when firm i does not meet any multipoint rivals in market m, to industry density minus one; only multimarket firms have non-zero values.
scale: zero to industry density minus one

description: The summed intensity of multipoint contact among incumbents in a focal market, used to test the hypotheses about single-market firms. The authors sum the intensity of multipoint contact among incumbents in a focal market; the formula block is not readable in the text.

The total market share of the four multimarket firms with the largest branch-office networks in the focal market at the start of the focal year. The authors counted the number of branch offices operated by the four largest firms and divided by the total number of branch offices operated by all firms; when there were ties between firms ranked fourth and fifth, only one of the tied firms was included, so market share was always summed for exactly four firms.

An indicator variable equal to one if a firm's branch-office network expanded between a focal year and the next one and zero otherwise; grow equals zero if the focal firm's branch-office network remained the same size or shrank. Growth is treated as a repeated event.
time_window: between a focal year and the next one

description: An indicator variable equal to one if a firm entered a market between a focal year and the next one and zero otherwise; enter equaled zero if the firm did not operate in the market in question in either a focal year or the next one, or if the firm operated in the market in both years. Only entries through the expansion of established firms were studied; entries through the birth of new firms were ignored. Market entry can be a repeated event.
time_window: between a focal year and the next one

description: Advice network density describes the number of manager pairs which form among TMT members to facilitate the exchange of advice and information on international operations divided by the total possible pairs in the TMT network. The network was treated as asymmetrical: a pair formed by team member A seeking advice from member B is different from the pair formed by team member B seeking advice from member A. For the purpose of measuring this variable, each team member was asked how often he/she seeks every other team member's IB advice, and answers rated as 'very often' and 'extremely often' were considered to indicate a primary source of IB advice information. The network analysis program UCINET was used to measure the density of the TMT's IB advice network.

Internationalization extent measures the degree to which the firm has extended its business activities outside its home country. The measure has three items which were reported by the CEO: international sales as a percentage of total sales, international assets as a percentage of total assets, and number of international employees as a percentage of total employees. Because these three items are highly correlated and measure different dimensions of the same construct, factor analysis was used to arrive at a combined measure, and the resulting composite internationalization measure represents the factor scores computed from this procedure, which produced one factor with significant loadings from all three items.

Internal mode was measured as the sum of the percentages of IB activity attributed to doing business through wholly-owned subsidiaries and majority-owned subsidiaries. Majority-owned subsidiaries were included in internal mode because the MNC can be expected to exercise substantial control over most of the activities of such a subsidiary. To measure this variable, the CEO was asked the percentage of the company's IB activity which is conducted through each of seven modes which total 100 percent of the MNC's international activities.

Interdependence was reported by all TMT members, and a summed average score given by the team along eight dimensions had an acceptable reliability (Cronbach alpha = 0.83). A common factor analysis with a subsequent varimax rotation was performed using the eight scale items on the 37 TMT average scores, and a purification procedure led to a two-factor solution. The four items which load significantly on Factor 1 are all related to upstream activities, the remaining two items, Sales and Marketing Activities, load on Factor 2 and are related to downstream activities, and the deleted items are Procurement and Management/Employee Development. The factor scores were saved as values of the two international interdependence variables which were used to test the hypotheses.

Airline deregulation, mandated in the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978, is treated as an abrupt environmental shift. Averages were calculated for the four years preceding (1973-1976) and four years following (1979-1982) deregulation, and every change score brackets 1978.

Automated text analysis of each airline's letter to shareholders for every year in the timeframe. A dictionary was built from Miles and Snow's entrepreneurial problem (e.g., market, innovate, growth) and engineering problem (e.g., efficiency, accounting, productivity) seed words and their synonyms, then rated by three judges on a scale from 1 (definitely engineering) to 7 (definitely entrepreneurial); 75 entrepreneurial words and 69 engineering words were retained. Entrepreneurial attention is the ratio of the number of entrepreneurial words to the sum of entrepreneurial and engineering words in the letter.
time_window: annual, 1973-1986; used as its level in t+6 with its value in t controlled

description: An annual index of four objective indicators of each airline's realized strategy: number of city-pairs served, number of planes, passenger service expenditures (including food and beverages, other onboard amenities, and club lounges), and advertising and sales expenditures. The four variables were standardized over all firm-years and summed to create the index.
time_window: measured in t+8, with its value in t controlled

description: The mean number of years the executives had worked in the airline industry until the focal year, identified from the Dun and Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Management and proxy statements. Change was calculated as the difference between the appropriate post- and prederegulation years (post minus pre), so that positive values indicate increases.

The proportion of executives on the team whose primary experience had been in output-related functions such as marketing, sales, and customer relations, identified from the Dun and Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Management and proxy statements. Change was calculated as post minus pre.
The coefficient of variation of the airline industry tenures of team members. Change was calculated as post minus pre.

Blau's index based on the percentages of TMT members whose experiences were primarily in each functional category, calculated as 1 - sum of the squared category percentages; the higher the score, the greater the TMT's heterogeneity. Change was calculated as post minus pre.

Total compensation minus base salary divided by total compensation; total compensation included salary, bonus, long-term and deferred compensation, stock grants, and option grants (valued by Black-Scholes formula). A high score indicates that pay was largely unguaranteed or tied to performance. Change was calculated as post minus pre.

A summary index constructed to parsimoniously test the interactive and mediating effects of TMT composition: the average of the standardized values for all the TMT composition variables (reverse-scoring Δ industry tenure).

variable_name: Changes in TMT composition and compensation variables
description: TMT characteristics are measured as pre- to post-deregulation changes in TMT composition (industry tenure, output-function experience, industry-tenure heterogeneity, functional heterogeneity) and in performance-based pay. A summary composition index averages the standardized composition variables and is interacted with the pay change.

The within-group (related) component of the Entropy measure of diversification uses only sales from manufacturing lines of business defined at the 3-digit SIC level, and lines of business belonging to the same industry group are given the same industry group identification. The less a firm's sales are dispersed across different industry groups, the higher is the related component of the Entropy measure. RATIO (Physical) is the ratio of related-to-total diversification where related diversification is defined as diversification within 2-digit SIC product groups.

Each industry is characterized by its underlying profile of specialties, defined as the different types and extent of human skills required, as indicated by occupational distributions, and industries with similar skill profiles are grouped by cluster analysis to form skill-related industry groups. The Entropy measure of diversification is then computed on manufacturing sales at the 3-digit SIC level, with industry groups defined by the skill clusters. RATIO (Skill) is the ratio of related-to-total diversification where related diversification is diversification within skill groups revealed by the cluster analyses.

Return on assets, defined as net income divided by total assets, expressed as a percentage, and averaged across 1985-87 so as to reduce the effects of unusually good or bad years. The measure was computed for each firm from the COMPUSTAT files.

Return on sales, defined as net income divided by net sales, expressed as a percentage, and averaged across 1985-87. The measure was computed for each firm from the COMPUSTAT files. Using ROS allows comparison with several other diversification studies, and the measure is less sensitive to firms' capital structure than ROA.

Market to book value of equity, defined as market value of equity at year-end divided by net worth at year-end, averaged for 1985-87. The measure was computed from the COMPUSTAT files and is considered an acceptable proxy to Tobin's Q.

Jensen's alpha measures firm performance relative to the stock market average and is obtained by estimating the intercept in a regression of firm returns on market returns, both computed in excess of the risk-free rate; the regression was estimated using daily stock returns for 1985-87 on the CRSP equally weighted index with distributions. The regression equation itself is not readable in the paper's appendix, which defines the terms as the stock return on day t for firm r, the market portfolio return, the risk-free rate from a 12-month treasury bond, systematic risk, and Jensen's alpha.

Binary classification of strong and weak divisions based on innovation performance. A division is defined as strong if its patents were greater than the mean number of patents in the firm-year. Three-year moving averages of patents were used to overcome idiosyncrasies in a particular year's numbers.

Binary classification of strong and weak divisions based on sales performance. A division is defined as strong if its sales were greater than the mean in the firm-year. Three-year moving averages of sales were used to overcome idiosyncrasies in a particular year's numbers.

Count of the alliances a division formed that involve knowledge sourcing in the discovery, pre-clinical, and formulation stages. Alliances were mapped to stages by the authors and a doctoral student in pharmacy using Recombinant data and Factiva newswires; the Recombinant data clearly stated the stage for most alliances, and alliances with ambiguous information were not included in the sample.

Count of the alliances a division formed that involve knowledge sourcing during and after clinical trials. Stages were coded from the Recombinant data and Factiva newswires, with alliances whose stage could not be determined excluded from the sample.
The number of early-stage alliances aggregated from the division level to the firm level in order to examine differences in knowledge-sourcing strategies across firms.
The number of late-stage alliances aggregated from the division level to the firm level in order to examine differences in knowledge-sourcing strategies across firms.

Gini coefficient used to measure inequality in innovation performance across divisions within a firm, calculated from division-level patents. A value of 0 denotes complete equality across divisions, while a value of 1 denotes complete inequality across divisions.

Gini coefficient used to measure inequality in sales performance across divisions within a firm, calculated from division-level sales. A value of 0 denotes complete equality across divisions, while a value of 1 denotes complete inequality across divisions.

Binary variable for whether a firm had a dedicated function for knowledge sourcing. It was constructed by searching for words such as 'alliance', 'licensing', 'business development', and 'office' in the annual reports and 10K statements of sample firms and coding descriptions of a dedicated function. Coding was cross-verified between two coders, including one of the authors, with an interrater reliability of 89%.

variable_name: Inclusion in II's All-America Research Team
description: The dependent variable is the inclusion of an analyst in Institutional Investor's All-America Research Team (first, second, and third place, plus runner-up), coded as zero or one. The authors used a binary variable rather than the order of the ranking to reflect the views of interviewed analysts and investors, who simply distinguish ''ranked'' from ''unranked'' analysts and pay far less attention to ranking within the team.

How much an analyst's framings correspond to investors' needs, where needs were identified by coding the needs experienced investors articulated in the authors' interviews, the lists published annually by Institutional Investor of what investors expect from analysts' services, and 279 quotes from investors published with the annual All-America Teams since 1987. Across these sources the authors found convergence on three needs: clarity of presentation, technological industry knowledge, and financial orientation. Clarity of presentation was operationalized with the categories ''no clearly stated motivation'' and ''no clearly stated goal'' (both reverse coded), computed as the average percentage of an analyst's reports that had a stated motivation or goal over the prior 12-month period; technological industry knowledge as the percentage of reports with the stated goal of translating scientific discoveries into investment implications and the topic of products or technologies; financial orientation as the percentage of reports that discuss the comparative attractiveness of a company's stock or of an industry and/or include the goal of identifying investment opportunities. The omnibus variable was computed by adding the categories identified as resonating with either of the specific investors' needs, so a report that resonates with all three receives a higher score than one that resonates with only one, and reports were then aggregated to analyst-years.
time_window: 12 months prior to the II ranking

description: A continuous metric of concentration, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index, capturing the consistency of an analyst's framing repertoire in the corpus of his or her reports during the 12 months prior to the II ranking. The index is bounded between 0 and 1, with 0 reflecting an even distribution across categories (variability) and 1 indicating the use of a sole category in all reports (consistency). Separate consistency variables were created for each framing dimension, and overall consistency was computed as a linear combination of the distributions across the categories on all three dimensions.
time_window: 12 months prior to the II ranking

description: A novelty score was created for each report and then aggregated to the analyst-year. The score for a report was computed as 1 minus the aggregate percentage of all reports that used a category in the 90 days prior to the publication of the focal report, using a 90-day moving-average window with linearly decreasing weights. An overall novelty variable was created by averaging the novelty scores on the three dimensions, and the analyst-level novelty score is the average novelty of all reports by the analyst in the 12 months prior to the II survey.
time_window: 90-day window per report; 12 months prior to the II survey at analyst level

description: An analyst's previous II ranking, used as a proxy of visibility and individual status. The variable was coded as 1 if an analyst had been included in the All-America Team in any of the previous years, and 0 otherwise.

The analyst's employer organization status, calculated as the inverse of Institutional Investor's continuous ranking of banks for that year, ranging from -1 (top ranked) to -25 (not ranked). It serves as a proxy for access to other highly qualified analysts and for the resources available to the analyst to promote his or her work.

variable_name: Resonance, consistency, and novelty of framing repertoire
description: The framing repertoire is measured from the categories coded in an analyst's reports over the prior 12 months, summarized as frame resonance with investor needs, repertoire consistency (Herfindahl-Hirschman concentration of categories), and repertoire novelty (one minus the share of other reports using a category).

Indicator variable coded 1 if the distance between a focal store and its nearest rival store is not greater than 10 miles, that is, if a competitor of the focal store appears within the 10-mile circle, and 0 otherwise. The nearest rival is the store of the rival chain with the shortest spherical distance from the focal store, computed from each store's latitude and longitude.

Indicator variable coded 1 if the nearest rival store is within one mile of the focal store, and 0 otherwise. Following Rosenthal and Strange (2003), one mile is used as the collocation cut-off; the measure is applied to the subsample of stores that face competition. COLLOCATE is instrumented with its predicted value from a first-stage probit model.

The logged number of stock-keeping units (SKUs) a store carries in the digital camera product category, retrieved from the chain's website with a Web crawling program. The authors use SKUs as the measure of product variety because consumers typically choose among SKUs on the basis of various product attributes. A log transformation is used because the number of SKUs exhibits approximately log-normal distributions in the data.

The logged number of products carried by both a store and its nearest competitor, less the logged number of randomly drawn common products (the dartboard approach of Ellison and Glaeser). The expected number of overlapping SKUs by chance is ninj/N, where ni is the number of SKUs at the focal store, nj is the number of SKUs at the rival store, and N is the total universe of SKUs in the particular market. The measure is computed only for competitive markets, comparing each pair of rivals.
level: store pair (focal store and nearest rival)

variable_name: large/small categorical measure of organizational size
description: The main measure of organizational size is a categorical measure that distinguishes between large and small firms, defined relatively for each year and updated from year to year. For years prior to 1976, this designation was made by examining historical documents to identify major players in the industry in each year. For observations after 1976, the authors relied on the data source Disk/Trend.
A measure of size in terms of the dollar value of hard disk drive sales. The authors state that this measure was available only for large organizations and only after 1976.

For each organization in each year t, the authors measured the sum of its domestic technology-overlap density score in each previous year from its birth through year t-1. This measure counts only competition experienced at times when the organization was a small organization. Exposure is measured in organization-years, so that an organization that competed with four rivals during each of its first and second years of life would have a value of 8 during its third year of life.

The cumulative prior exposure to competition of the focal organization, counting only competition experienced at times when the organization was a large organization. It is specified separately from the small organization's competitive experience so that the authors can compare the two coefficients.

variable_name: Small domestic rivals' competitive experience (experience-weighted overlap)
description: The prior competitive experience of the focal organization's domestic rivals, distinguishing competition these rivals experienced when they were small organizations. It is the rivals' analog of the organization's own competitive-experience measure: the rivals' prior exposure to competition, weighted by their technology overlap with the focal organization.
time_window: prior exposure accumulated over the rivals' histories

variable_name: Large domestic rivals' competitive experience (experience-weighted overlap)
description: The prior competitive experience of the focal organization's domestic rivals, counting only competition these rivals experienced when they were large organizations. It is specified separately from small rivals' competitive experience so that the strength of rivalry generated by each type of rival can be compared.
time_window: prior exposure accumulated over the rivals' histories

variable_name: Small foreign rivals' competitive experience (experience-weighted overlap)
description: The competition generated by small foreign rivals as a function of their own domestic competitive experience. Foreign rivals are rivals based outside the focal organization's own region of the global economy, and the measure captures the exposure to domestic competition each such rival experienced in its home country.
time_window: prior domestic exposure accumulated over the rivals' histories

variable_name: Large foreign rivals' competitive experience (experience-weighted overlap)
description: The competition generated by large foreign rivals as a function of their own domestic competitive experience in their home countries. It is specified separately from small foreign rivals' competitive experience so that the authors can test whether the effect depends on the size of the foreign rival.
time_window: prior domestic exposure accumulated over the rivals' histories

description: The dependent variable is the organization's failure rate, modeled with a piecewise exponential specification for each organization's market tenure.
