The authors measured t in terms of market tenure rather than organizational age, because firms with operations in other markets may have been born before they entered the hard disk drive market. Separate tenure effects were estimated for large and small organizations, and 157 exits are observed in the data.

Social capital was measured by multi-item, evenly weighted scales whose items were adapted from Shane and Cable (2002) and reformulated for investors; the mean of the items was used as the scale score (Cronbach alpha 0.78). The three items asked whether the venture capitalist had a professional relationship with the entrepreneur prior to seeing the business plan, whether he or she engaged in informal social activities with the entrepreneur prior to seeing the business plan, and whether the entrepreneur was a personal friend prior to seeing the business plan. Responses were on a five-point Likert scale ranging from strongly agree (5) to strongly disagree (1).
scale: five-point Likert scale from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5)
time_window: prior to seeing the business plan

description: Social capital was measured by multi-item, evenly weighted scales whose items were adapted from Shane and Cable (2002); the mean of the items was used as the scale score (Cronbach alpha 0.72). The four items asked whether someone the respondent trusts to discuss important confidential matters knew the entrepreneur, whether a third party whose judgement the respondent trusts provided nonpublic information about the entrepreneur, whether the respondent could obtain information about the entrepreneur from his or her network of contacts faster than other investors, and whether the respondent could obtain such information in a relatively inexpensive manner. Responses were on a five-point Likert scale ranging from strongly agree (5) to strongly disagree (1).
scale: five-point Likert scale from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5)

description: Strong ties was measured by a single friendship item: 'The entrepreneur was a personal friend prior to seeing the business plan.' The item was answered on a five-point Likert scale ranging from strongly agree (5) to strongly disagree (1). The authors also employed this item as a component of the prior-relationship scale, and state that the two independent variables were not used together in any of the analyses.
scale: five-point Likert scale from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5)
time_window: prior to seeing the business plan

description: Technology/product and business plan scale items were adapted from Shane and Cable (2002); the mean of the items was used as the scale score. The technology/products scale is composed of two items (Cronbach alpha 0.72): 'The technology employed or products offered by the venture would provide a significant competitive advantage' and 'The venture's technology had a strong proprietary position.' Responses were on a five-point Likert scale ranging from strongly agree (5) to strongly disagree (1).
scale: five-point Likert scale from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5)

description: The team scale is composed of two items and is an evenly weighted scale whose mean was used as the scale score (Cronbach alpha 0.76): 'At least one member of the venture team had previous startup experience' and 'At least one member of the venture team had experience in the relevant industry.' Responses were on a five-point Likert scale ranging from strongly agree (5) to strongly disagree (1).
scale: five-point Likert scale from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5)

description: The growth potential scale is measured by two items and is an evenly weighted scale whose mean was used as the scale score (Cronbach alpha 0.71): 'The venture is a potentially high growth firm' and 'The venture's competitive strategy is superior than its competitors.' Responses were on a five-point Likert scale ranging from strongly agree (5) to strongly disagree (1).
scale: five-point Likert scale from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5)

description: Technology/product and business plan scale items were adapted from Shane and Cable (2002); the mean of the items was used as the scale score. Two items for the business plan scale were (Cronbach alpha 0.76): 'The business plan was thorough in its coverage of key issues' and 'The business plan did an excellent job of articulating the opportunity.' Responses were on a five-point Likert scale ranging from strongly agree (5) to strongly disagree (1).
scale: five-point Likert scale from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5)

description: A binary variable of one if the venture received an investment, and zero otherwise. Each general partner selected the last two positive investment decisions and the last two negative investment decisions of 2000, so investments were selected randomly within the two groups.
scale: binary (0 = firm decided not to invest, 1 = firm decided to invest)

description: The number of covenants in contracts that protect interests of investors, obtained by asking: 'How many covenants that protect your firm's interests were formalized in the final contract.'

Measured as the number of months from the date of the positive investment decision to the date of the first injection of investment into the venture. The authors note that a previous study indicated that timing is an important variable in venture capital practices.

The difference between the initial value and the final value of the venture, expressed as a percentage of the initial value. The initial value of the venture was calculated from the initial size of the investment offered to the venture team and the initial equity sought in the venture; the final value was calculated from the final investment amount decided and the percentage of equity the firm received. All data in the Chinese currency were deflated by the year 2000's average exchange rate of the Chinese currency and the dollar published in The Economist.
scale: percentage change relative to the initial value

description: Comic values are the collector values reported in the Comicbase data for the year 2003, at least five years after a comic's publication, standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of unity in each publication year. The deviation measure is the absolute deviation of a comic's standardized value from the mean of the standardized variable, which is zero. It is the dependent variable in the models reported for Hypotheses 1 through 5.
time_window: collector values for 2003, at least five years after publication

description: The within-year standardized collector market value of a comic as reported in the Comicbase data for the year 2003, standardized to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of unity in each year, so that it expresses performance relative to other comics in the same year. It is the dependent variable in the models reported for Hypotheses 5 through 8.
scale: standardized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 within year
time_window: collector values for 2003, at least five years after publication

description: A count of the writers and artists involved in a comic. A creator can act as both writer and artist, but typically a team of creators develops a comic, and adding team members on a comic often adds different perspectives to the creative process.

The diversity of creator backgrounds is coded as the number of genres in which creators had worked over the year prior to the publication of a focal comic. It is a count of all genres that the creators on a team had worked with in their careers, omitting double counts of genres that more than one creator had worked with, and it captures a team's range of genre knowledge domains. Comicbase categorized comics into 22 genres but associated some comics with multiple genres.
time_window: one year prior to publication; career data back to 1930

description: The number of times a creative team had worked together previously; the authors kept track of the team's number of collaborations rather than the number of collaborations between the individual members of a team. A measure counting all collaborations between members of a team gave the same findings and correlated nearly perfectly with this one.
The average number of comics that the creators of each comic had produced in the past year.

The number of years elapsed since each team member's first published comic; the authors took the highest value among the team members as the team's tenure. Tenure and genre variables were based on data going back to 1930 to measure experience before 1972.

Organizational resources were measured as the sum of the standardized values of the number of comics published, total circulation, and number of affiliated creators per year for each publisher. The measure was constructed using a data set in which each firm-year contributed one observation in order to avoid overweighting the large firms.

An indicator value for single creator, entered to address the possibility that a creator acting as both writer and artist denotes a special creative process. It is also interacted with genre experience to test whether knowledge diversity has a stronger effect for individual creators than for teams.

Internal rate of return of each buyout, measuring the gross equity return earned by investors from the sale of the company. It is calculated as an annualized effective compounded rate of return using monthly cash flows and annual valuations. The variable was Winsorized at the 95th percentile (i.e., 191%) because the data include significant outliers.
time_window: over the life of the buyout

description: The random intercept variance at the PE firm level (level 4) of the multiple-membership, cross-classified multilevel model of buyout IRR. It captures the share of variance in buyouts' performance attributable to differences between PE firms and accounts for 4.6 percent of that variance in the preferred model. For buyouts executed by more than one PE firm, membership weights are the percentage of capital each PE firm invested in the focal buyout.

The random intercept variance at the PE fund level (level 3), with PE funds nested within PE firms in the multilevel model. It explains 7.3 percent of the variance in buyouts' performance, more than the PE firm effect.

The random intercept variance at the buyout level (level 2) of the multilevel model, corresponding to the business-unit effect in earlier variance decomposition studies. It accounts for 40.2 percent of the variance in buyouts' performance.

The random intercept variance at the industry level (level 3), with each buyout assigned to an industry based on the 48 Fama and French industry classification. It accounts for 1 percent of the variance in buyouts' performance.

The calendar year during which a buyout was acquired. It is added as a continuous random slope in the random part of the model at the PE firm level to test whether the PE firm effect grows over time, and it is centered on its mean to facilitate the models' convergence.

The number of months between acquisition and exit of the buyout, used as a proxy for the degree to which investment performance is influenced by value addition or selection: selection is expected to dominate in shorter buyouts and value addition in longer ones. It is added as a random slope at the PE firm level and is centered on its mean.

A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if the buyout is located in Africa, the Middle East, Asia, Latin America, or Eastern Europe, and 0 otherwise. Of the buyouts in the database, 732 were realized in emerging markets. It is added as a random slope at the PE firm level to compare the PE firm variance in emerging and developed economies.

The average annual percentage GDP growth rate during the duration of the buyout, at market prices based on constant local currencies, according to World Bank data. Aggregates are based on constant 2005 U.S. dollars. It is added as a random slope at the PE firm level as a proxy for economic conditions.
scale: average annual percentage GDP growth rate
time_window: during the duration of the buyout

description: Governance form was measured with an indicator variable coded such that mutual = 1 and stock = 0. This variable was measured in the study's initial year (1980) and did not vary over the subsequent panels used in the analyses. In the core models, mutuals that converted to the stock form during the study period are treated as mutuals throughout.

variable_name: Simple change in the percentage of nonmortgage assets
description: The percentage of total firm assets invested outside of residential mortgage lending was calculated at the end of each year, and a year-to-year measure of change in this variable was then created. It is a 'simple' measure of change in a percentage variable, not a percentage-change measure, and it captures both increases in nonmortgage assets and decreases in mortgage assets. In the between-effects models the measure is averaged to the firm level across all firm-years in which the organization is observed.

The dependent measure is the simple annual change in return on assets, where ROA is calculated by dividing each S&L's net income for the year by its total assets. In the between-effects models the measure is averaged to the firm level, so the coefficients represent effects on an organization's average annual performance change across all time periods in which it is observed.

Objective measure used to capture the economic performance of parent firms in alliances. The authors state that they focused on the economic effect on parent firms and chose an objective measure, return on assets (ROA), because perceptual measures are affected by different characteristics of managers and their positions and are more often subject to inconsistency and ambiguity. ROA is the dependent variable in all regression models.
time_window: annual measure for each year in which firm performance is measured (1988-2000)

description: Based on a comparison between the focal firm's four-digit SIC code and that of its partners in alliance relations. The authors first counted the number of partners that have different SIC codes from the focal firm, and then divided that number by the total number of alliance partners; for example, a firm with three partners among which one has the same SIC code receives a value of 2/3 or 0.667. A five-year moving window was used.

Dummy variable coded 1 for high societal status and 0 for low societal status. All firms listed in a particular year with an overall score of 4.10 or above on Fortune's 'Most Admired Corporations' rankings were treated as high societal status firms, while others, including those in the sample but not listed on Fortune's lists, were considered low societal status firms; a continuous measure of status was not used because of the ambiguous nuances among different levels of status. Fortune's 'America's Most Admired Corporations' was used for U.S.-based firms and Fortune's 'World's Most Admired Companies' for foreign-based firms; because the world ranking was not available before 1997, the 1997 list was used to map out foreign-based firms' status before 1997.
scale: dummy (1 = high societal status, 0 = low societal status)

description: Measured as a focal firm's total number of alliance partners with high societal status divided by the total number of alliance partners allied with the firm. Identification of high-status partners is similar to that of a focal firm using Fortune's 'Most Admired Corporations' rankings, with the 1997 world list used as a proxy for foreign-based partners from 1988 to 1996. A five-year moving window was used to calculate the ratio of high-status alliance partners, together with a one-year lag.
time_window: five-year moving window with a one-year lag

description: A firm is said to have high societal status partners (coded as 1; otherwise as 0) if its partners' average societal status score is at or above 0.50, the midpoint between 0 and 1. Societal status asymmetry was then calculated as the absolute difference between a firm's own societal status and the above averaged partner societal status.

Bonacich's eigenvector centrality in the firm's industry network. Yearly network matrices were constructed for each industry based on the nondirectional alliance ties within each industry; for instance, 1,205 alliances formed by 41 focal firms in the computer industry, involving 583 different alliance partners, produced a yearly network matrix with 583 x 583 dimensions. Following Baum et al. (2005), each firm's eigenvector centrality was computed for each five-year network and assigned to the final year of each five-year period. The centrality calculation was conducted in Ucinet 6.
time_window: five-year networks, value assigned to the final year of each five-year period

description: Calculated by looking at the network status of a firm's alliance partners based on the five-year moving window. Because a firm may have multiple alliances each year, the authors used the summed eigenvector centrality for all alliance partners divided by the total number of alliance partners possessed by the focal firm.

A firm is argued to have partners of high network status (coded as 1; otherwise as 0) if their average network status score is above the midpoint of the full scale. Network status asymmetry was then calculated as the absolute difference between a firm's own network status and the above averaged partner network status; for instance, if the focal firm's own network status is also above the midpoint, the network status asymmetry between the firm and its partners is 0.

Measured as the unpredictability of the net sales of all firms in a four-digit SIC industry, following Bergh and Lawless's (1998) approach. Dynamism was measured as the standard error of the regression slope coefficient divided by the mean of sales to create a standardized index of industry dynamism, calculated by regression analyses in which the variable year was regressed on the net industry sales variable. Five years of data were used for each regression (e.g., net industry sales values for 1983 through 1987 were used to predict volatility in 1988), and larger values of unpredictability indicated greater environmental dynamism.
time_window: five years of data per regression (e.g., 1983-1987 to predict volatility in 1988)

description: Age was measured by subtracting the incorporated year from the alliance event year. It is controlled because age difference will greatly change the ultimate result of the alliance.

Variable capturing the occurrence of employment affiliation-based hiring at the focal firm in year t. The authors track the employment history of every founder and new hire for 10 years prior to joining the focal firm and code the firm as hiring from founders' prior employment affiliations when a hire shares a prior employer with at least one founder.

Coded when the firm hires from founders' proximal employment affiliations: for each hire sharing an employment affiliation with the founder(s), the authors verify whether the hire worked at the same physical unit (workplace) and/or at overlapping time periods as the founder(s).
Coded when (some of) the hires share an employment affiliation with a founder but overlapped with any of the founders neither in time nor in physical workplace.

Variable capturing the occurrence of educational affiliation-based hiring at the focal firm in year t. The authors track the education history of every founder and new hire for 10 years prior to joining the focal firm and code the firm as hiring from founders' prior educational affiliations when a hire shares a prior education institution with at least one founder.

Coded when a new hire overlaps with the founder(s) in educational affiliation, cohort (including adjacent cohorts) and education program, that is, the firm hires from founders' most proximal educational affiliations.
Coded when the firm hires employees who share an educational affiliation with the founder(s) but there is neither overlap in their cohort nor in the program attended.

The firm's yearly profitability, measured in year t + 1. Profits are measured in Danish kroner, adjusted for inflation using the year 2000 as a baseline, and taken in natural logarithm to account for skewness in the data and enhance normality.
scale: natural logarithm of Danish kroner (2000 baseline)

description: The firm's total sales, measured in year t + 1. Sales are measured in Danish kroner, adjusted for inflation using the year 2000 as a baseline, and taken in natural logarithm to account for skewness in the data and enhance normality.
scale: natural logarithm of Danish kroner (2000 baseline)

description: Indicator of firm exit, equal to one if the firm exits in t + 1 and zero for any period prior to that, making the outcome of interest relatively rare and right-censored for firms exiting after 2012.

variable_name: Occurrence of affiliation-based hiring (EMP-ABH and EDU-ABH)
description: Affiliation-based hiring is coded from Danish register data that track the employment and education history of every founder and new hire for 10 years before joining the firm. A firm is coded as making affiliation-based hires in year t when a hire shares a prior employer (EMP-ABH) or education institution (EDU-ABH) with at least one founder.

variable_name: Proximal versus distal affiliations (EMP_proximal/EMP_distal, EDU_most proximal/EDU_most distal)
description: Affiliation proximity is coded from the overlap between hires and founders. For employment, proximal means the same workplace and/or overlapping time at the shared prior employer, distal means neither. For education, most proximal means the same institution, cohort (including adjacent), and program, most distal means neither cohort nor program overlap.

Binary variable taking the value 1 if individual i in year t became a new member in the foundation. Individuals apply to a volunteer membership committee by listing their contributions once they have accomplished a nontrivial contribution, and the committee makes decisions based on membership guidelines set by the board of directors. The authors focused only on new members and dropped observations after an individual was subject to membership renewal. Website data were cross-checked with information from the mailing list and membership applications from 2000 to 2005.

Binary variable taking the value 1 if individual i was elected in year t to the foundation's board of directors. Because only foundation members can be nominated for the annually elected board, the second level of progression is conditioned on the first, so the data set used to predict board directors is smaller. Election data were retrieved from the foundation's creation in 2000 to the year 2005.

Number of code commits submitted by individual i in year t, taken from individual submissions of source code checked in the CVS. Source code that has been checked in CVS has gone through the community's peer review process, where individuals evaluate the code to see whether the contribution constitutes an improvement to the code base. Because the distribution was heavily skewed, the authors took the natural log after adding one to the measure because zeros exist.
scale: count (natural log of count plus one), standardized in the regressions

description: Alternative measure of technical contribution derived by counting the number of resolved bugs submitted by individual i in year t in the Bugzilla database. As with the other skewed measures, the authors added one and took the natural log.
scale: count (natural log of count plus one), standardized in the regressions

variable_name: number of responses to technical discussions
description: Number of responses individual i posted to technical discussion threads in year t. The 137 mailing lists used by the community were content-coded to distinguish different types of project activities and consolidated into technical discussions and coordination work; the bulk of the lists was focused on technical discussions. Because measures of initiation and of responses were highly correlated, the authors selected responses to threads as opposed to initiation.

variable_name: number of responses to coordination discussions
description: Number of responses individual i posted to coordination mailing lists in year t, counted from the threads coded as coordination discussions. Coordination discussions focused on organizing projectwide affairs such as code releases, conferences, the project website, or the foundation's governance, and never reached 3.5% of all communication in any given year.

With mailing list data, the number of mailing lists an individual i posted a message to in year t divided by the overall number of mailing lists in year t. This indicates the proportion of the project's communication venues in which an individual participated.

With CVS data, the number of subprojects to which individual i contributed source code divided by the overall number of subprojects in year t. Those with a higher technical boundary spanning score are more likely to obtain general project knowledge than those specializing in a single technical area; the measure differs from technical contribution, which counts an individual's raw number of contributions.

Respondents to Vault.com's annual survey individually rate firms on a scale of 1-10 based on how prestigious they think it would be to work for the firm, where 1 is least prestigious and 10 is most prestigious. Vault then averages all firm-level responses to create a firm prestige score that is updated annually. Respondents do not rate their own firms and are asked not to rate firms with which they are not familiar, so the ratings reflect the perceptions of those not employed by the focal firm. In the analyses the authors take the log of raw prestige scores to generate a centered and approximately normal distribution.
scale: 1-10 (log of the raw prestige score is used in the analyses)

description: Count of a firm's associates who depart for partner positions at Vault 100 firms, normalized by the total number of lawyers at the focal firm to capture a rate of departure. Departures involving rank promotions are identified as departures by associates to partner positions at other firms, and departures to high-status firms are identified as departures to firms ranked in the Vault 100. The variable is entered at the departure year and at one-, two- and three-year lags.
time_window: year t and lags t-1 to t-3

description: Rate of all employee departures to partner positions at other firms, not distinguishing among different types of departures. The count is normalized by total number of lawyers at the focal firm. This variable is used in the baseline model.

Rate of departures by a firm's partners to partner positions at firms ranked in the Vault 100, that is, moves that are to high-status firms but do not involve a rank promotion. The count is normalized by the total number of lawyers at the focal firm.
time_window: year t and lags t-1 to t-3

description: Rate of departures by a firm's partners to partner positions at firms not ranked in the Vault 100, that is, moves that neither are to high-status firms nor involve a rank promotion. The count is normalized by the total number of lawyers at the focal firm.
time_window: year t and lags t-1 to t-3

description: Rate of departures by a firm's associates to partner positions at firms not ranked in the Vault 100, that is, moves that involve a rank promotion but are not to a high-status firm. The count is normalized by the total number of lawyers at the focal firm.
time_window: year t and lags t-1 to t-3

description: Members of each industry's expert panel—trade association executives, industry consultants, large buyers, and managers in the industry itself—were asked to rate, on a scale of 1 to 7, the importance of each of the following attributes for the profitability of a firm in that industry; attributes were presented alphabetically with definitions accompanying. A total of 150 questionnaires were distributed to the six KSF panels, with an overall response rate of 78 percent, and the lowest single-industry response rate was 70 percent (valves).

variable_name: Strength rating of firm on attribute (strength panel)
description: The second wave of data collection, conducted in 1983, used six new expert panels (one per industry, with no members overlapping the first panels), who were asked how they would rate the five organizations in their industry on each attribute, on a scale of 1 to 7, with attributes presented alphabetically with accompanying definitions. Each questionnaire included only those five attributes judged as most critical by the first panel of that industry, so as to keep the questionnaire short and to keep the number of independent variables small. A total of 146 questionnaires were distributed to the six strength panels, with an overall response rate of 50 percent, the lowest single-industry rate being 42 percent (valves).

Pre-tax return on assets using data from annual reports and 10Ks, computed for the firm as a whole when the entire firm was specialized in the industry of interest or for a reporting unit when the firm was diversified and one of its reporting units specialized in the industry under study. The value of each firm's return on assets was a 5-year average over the period 1978-82. Because data on multiple industries were analyzed together, the difference between each firm's own performance and its industry average was computed, divided by the industry average, and multiplied by 100, giving in percentage terms how much better or worse the firm performed compared to its industry.
scale: percentage difference from the industry average

variable_name: Weighted index of a firm's ratings on its cell's five attributes
description: Because regressing performance on the five attribute ratings would leave too few degrees of freedom with ten observations per cell, an index was computed to represent a firm's ratings on all five attributes of its cell. The index is a weighted sum of the firm's ratings on each attribute, the weights being the ratings given by the first (KSF) panels. Each firm's weighted sum was then taken as its difference from the mean of its industry, and that difference was divided by the industry mean to obtain a standardized score.

Each acquisition was classified as related if the bidding firm and the acquired firm shared at least one of the following characteristics: similar production technologies, similar science-based research, similar products and/or markets; otherwise it was treated as unrelated. The classification used Salter and Weinhold's typology, and the 1975-80 period matches their study. The distinction between related-complementary and related-supplementary acquisitions was not used.

An abnormal return of a firm is the deviation between its realized return and the expected return from the market model estimated for the security. The abnormal change in dollar value of a firm is the abnormal return multiplied by the market value of the firm on the preceding day. The gains of the acquired firm and of the bidding firm are combined to measure the synergistic gains from the transaction. Mean dollar gains are computed for related and unrelated acquisitions, and a version of the gains standardized on the value of acquired assets, ranging from 0 to 1, is also computed.
scale: millions of dollars; the standardized version ranges from 0 to 1
time_window: day -800 to day +400 around the announcement (day 0)

variable_name: cumulative abnormal returns of acquired firms
description: Abnormal returns of the acquired firm are estimated with the market model and aggregated into an equal-weighted portfolio; the portfolio residuals are then cumulated over time to obtain cumulative abnormal returns. The reassessment of target firm returns is reported for period I (from 5 days before to 25 days after the event) and for period II (from 25 days to 100 days after the event), separately for related and unrelated single-bid acquisitions.
time_window: period I: day -5 to day +25; period II: day +25 to day +100

variable_name: cumulative abnormal returns of acquiring firms
description: Cumulative abnormal returns of the bidding firms, estimated with the market model and cumulated over the event window, reported separately for related and unrelated single-bid acquirers. The authors note that an acquisition by a firm affects only part of its businesses, so the announcement effect on the acquirer's returns is less easily detected than for target firms.

Composite of four items developed by Ashford (1986), with minor wording modifications for subsidiary presidents. Respondents were asked how frequently, in order to find out for themselves how well they are performing, they observe rewarded performance behaviors, compare themselves with executives at their level, pay attention to how superiors act toward them, and observe the characteristics of rewarded executives. A 7-point Likert-type response scale ranging from 'very infrequently' to 'very frequently' was used, and the four responses were averaged (mean = 3.75, S.D. = 1.38, Chronbach alpha = 0.83). Confirmatory factor analysis supported the distinctness of the monitoring and inquiry modes.
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale (very infrequently to very frequently)

description: Composite of three items developed by Ashford (1986), with minor wording modifications for subsidiary presidents. Respondents were asked how frequently, in order to find out for themselves how well they are performing, they seek information from colleagues about their work performance, seek feedback from superiors about their work performance, and seek feedback from superiors about their potential for advancement. A 7-point Likert-type response scale ranging from 'very infrequently' to 'very frequently' was used, and the three responses were averaged (mean = 2.92, S.D. = 1.34, Chronbach alpha = 0.76).
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale (very infrequently to very frequently)

description: A composite measure of culture distance between each subsidiary's 'host' country and its particular 'home' country, computed following Kogut and Singh (1988) from Hofstede's (1980) four indices of national culture using an Euclidian distance formula; the formula block is unreadable in the text and is not reproduced here. The authors state that Di,host represents the host country's value on cultural dimension i, Di,home the home country's value on this dimension, and Vi the variance in this dimension across all countries (mean = 1.74, S.D. = 1.47).

Each subsidiary president provided 'yes' or 'no' answers to three questions about whether the subsidiary has one or more research and development facilities, one or more manufacturing facilities, and one or more marketing and sales facilities. The total count of 'yes' responses was treated as the measure of value chain scope (range = 1 to 3; mean = 2.21; S.D. = 0.81). Construct validity was checked against a measure of product flows between the focal subsidiary and the rest of the corporation, which correlated negatively with value chain scope.

A 5-item instrument adapted from Rizzo, House, and Lirtzman (1970). On a 7-point Likert-type scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree', each subsidiary president indicated agreement with five statements; responses were averaged to yield a composite measure (mean = 3.48, S.D. = 1.13, Chronbach alpha = 0.53).
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree)

description: A 4-item instrument adapted from Rizzo, House, and Lirtzman (1970). On a 7-point Likert-type scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree', each subsidiary president indicated agreement with four statements; responses were averaged to yield a composite measure (mean = 2.44, S.D. = 0.96, Chronbach alpha = 0.73). The items as printed are worded in terms of clarity (certainty about authority, clear goals, proper division of time, knowing what is expected), so higher scores on the printed items indicate lower role ambiguity.
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree)

description: Following Vancil (1980), respondents rated the typical influence they had in affecting the outcome of nine strategically relevant decisions on a 5-point Likert scale, where higher values indicate less subsidiary influence and hence higher centralization. Responses on the nine questions were averaged to create an index (Chronbach alpha = 0.86; higher values indicate higher centralization; mean = 1.96, S.D. = 0.74).
scale: 5-point Likert scale of influence over decision outcomes

description: Measure adapted from Van de Ven and Ferry (1979). For each of four modes of communication, respondents indicated the frequency of communication between themselves and executives from the parent corporation on a 7-point scale ranging from '1 = daily' to '7 = less often than once a year'. The responses were reverse scored and averaged across the four items (mean = 4.71, S.D. = 1.02, Chronbach alpha = 0.80).
scale: 7-point frequency scale (1 = daily to 7 = less often than once a year), reverse scored

description: Based on Galbraith (1973), Nadler and Tushman (1987), and Miller, Kets de Vries, and Toulouse (1982), this variable was measured through a 3-item Likert-type 7-point scale ranging from 'used rarely' to 'used very frequently'. Respondents indicated the extent to which their subsidiary used liaison personnel, temporary task forces, and permanent teams to coordinate decisions and actions with sister subsidiaries. The final measure was a weighted average in which permanent teams received a weight of 3, temporary task forces a weight of 2, and liaison personnel a weight of 1 (mean = 2.92, S.D. = 1.53).
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale (used rarely to used very frequently), weighted average

description: Measure adapted from Ghoshal and Bartlett (1988). Respondents provided 'yes' or 'no' answers to four questions about their participation in corporate socialization mechanisms. The total count of 'yes' responses was treated as a measure of participation in corporate socialization mechanisms (mean = 2.07, S.D. = 1.13).

Firm growth was measured as growth in sales. Sales growth was the proportionate increase in revenue over the year prior to which top management change or addition was measured. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Strategic diversification was operationalized as diversification into new product areas. Using data from the market research firms, 20 comprehensive product groups within the semiconductor industry were identified. The measure is any increase in the number of product groups in which the firm competed in the prior year.

An organization-level variable that measured the average amount of time that current top managers had worked in the semiconductor industry. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Top managers were found to come from four types of primary functional experience: research and development; manufacturing and operations; marketing and sales; and finance, accounting, legal, and administrative. The measure is an entropy measure, where Pi is the percentage of top managers in the ith functional area across the four functional areas; the formula itself is not readable in the paper. Higher scores indicate a more diverse set of functional experiences for the top management team.
Top management ownership measured the proportion of total firm ownership held by individuals who were employees of the firm. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.
Chief executive ownership measured the proportion of firm ownership held by the chief executive of the firm. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.
Venture capital ownership measured the proportion of firm ownership held by venture capitalists who were funding the organization. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.
Outside directors measured the proportion of board members who were not employed by the firm. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.
Venture capital directors measured the proportion of board members who were members of venture capital firms. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

The top management team is defined as the chief executive and all top managers reporting to the chief executive. The variable is the sum of the number of additions to the top management team and the number of departures from the top management team. It is a count with a lower boundary of zero, observed annually over the first seven years after founding.
scale: count with a lower boundary of zero
time_window: annual, first seven years after founding

description: Sales and purchasing managers in each subsidiary assessed to what extent the subsidiary has adapted its way of doing business because of the relationships with the most important external customers and suppliers, on a 5-point Likert-type scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very much). They also assessed the number of different functional areas involved in direct contacts with customers and suppliers (chief executives, administration, purchasing department, sales department, production department (technical staff), and R&D department). Scores on adaptation of business conduct in each external relationship were added together and divided by the number of external relationships of the subsidiary to produce an average score, and the score for the number of functional areas was treated in a similar way. The questions refer to the subsidiary's most important product or group of products.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = not at all to 5 = very much) for adaptation; count of functional areas

description: The subsidiary's sales and purchasing managers were asked to assess to what extent a specific relationship with an external customer or supplier had caused the subsidiary's product development and production development to be adapted, each on a 5-point Likert-type scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very much). The subsidiary's average technical embeddedness was calculated by adding the scores of each of the subsidiary's external relationships and dividing this score by the number of external relationships identified for each subsidiary. Questions refer to the subsidiary's most important product or group of products.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = not at all to 5 = very much)

description: Expected market performance is measured by expected profitability, sales volume, and market shares, as perceived by divisional HQ managers. The measure gives the divisional HQ the possibility to make comparisons across subsidiaries and countries. A 5-point Likert-type scale from 1 (very small) to 5 (very high) was used to separate the answers.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = very small to 5 = very high)

variable_name: Subsidiary importance for MNC competence development
description: Indicators reflecting the divisional HQ management's assessment of the subsidiary's importance for technical development in terms of product and production development for other sister units. Using the divisional management's responses separates them from the responses relating to embeddedness and gives the divisional management the possibility to compare the contribution different subsidiaries make to competence development. A 5-point Likert-type scale from 1 (very small) to 5 (very high) was used.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = very small to 5 = very high)

description: Multiple-item scale (six items) on which respondents indicated their agreement with statements about the technological uncertainties of the selected development project, using a 0 to 10 Likert-type scale (0 = strongly disagree, 10 = strongly agree). The first item, which describes the project technology as a well-developed science, is reverse-coded; the other items concern the unpredictability of the rate and direction of change in the technology. The authors report a Cronbach alpha of .87 for the scale and note that, when the data were split at the mean of the composite, 96.2 percent of projects received the same high or low classification as the project managers' own dichotomous self-classification.

Six items asking how well or adequately the firm undertook each marketing activity in the product development process relative to how the respondent thought it should have been done, answered on a 0 to 10 scale (0 = done very poorly or mistakenly omitted altogether, 10 = done excellently). The authors report that the scale is reliable and unidimensional in the confirmatory factor analysis.

Six items asking how well or adequately the firm undertook each technical development activity in the product development process relative to how the respondent thought it should have been done, answered on a 0 to 10 scale (0 = done very poorly or mistakenly omitted altogether, 10 = done excellently). The authors report that the scale is reliable and unidimensional in the confirmatory factor analysis.

Five statements about intelligence activities during the early stages of the development process, rated on a 0 to 10 scale (0 = strongly disagree, 10 = strongly agree). The authors report that the scale is reliable and unidimensional in the confirmatory factor analysis.

Eight items stating that the company's marketing skills and resources were more than adequate for the project, answered on a 0 to 10 scale. Four items refer to marketing research, salesforce, advertising/promotion and distribution skills and four to the corresponding resources.
Four items stating that the company's R&D and engineering skills and resources were more than adequate for the selected project, answered on a 0 to 10 scale.

Three items asking whether the integration between R&D and manufacturing, between marketing and R&D, and between marketing and manufacturing was very good for the selected project, answered on a 0 to 10 scale.

Five items comparing the product with competing products in terms of unique features, meeting customers' needs, permitting the customer to do something not previously possible, quality, and technical performance, answered on a 0 to 10 scale.

The return on investment of the project for the first, second, and third years of the product's introduction. The authors also collected these objective financial performance data in a longitudinal study of the originally surveyed NPD projects.
time_window: first three years of the product introduction

variable_name: Product competitive advantage and product financial performance (ROI)
description: Project outcomes are measured by two variables: product competitive advantage (five survey items comparing the product with competing products) and project financial performance (return on investment for the first three years after introduction).

Skill and resource synergy is measured with two survey scales: marketing synergy (fit of the project with available marketing skills and resources) and technical synergy (fit with R&D, engineering, and production skills and resources), each rated on a 0 to 10 scale.

variable_name: Marketing proficiency, technical proficiency, and competitive and market intelligence
description: Development process proficiency is measured with three survey scales rated by respondents: marketing proficiency (six items), technical proficiency (six items), and competitive and market intelligence (five items), each on how well the firm executed these activities in the project.

The dependent variable is the event of placing an order for an innovative ship type. Shipping firms typically place orders for multiple ships at a time, and all ships ordered by the same shipper in the same month are assumed to be a single order, so there are fewer events than there are ships. Because one hypothesis concerns the effect of having adopted an innovation on subsequent acquisition, firms that have ordered an innovative ship type are retained in the data.

The dependent variable is the event of placing an order for an innovative ship type, here a double-hull oil tanker. Ships ordered by the same shipper in the same month are assumed to be a single order. Firms that have ordered an innovative ship type are retained in the data, so repeated orders are counted as subsequent events.

Indicator variable for prior adoption of a post-Panamax container ship, entered in the propensity part of the diffusion model. It distinguishes firms that have already placed an order for the innovative ship type from firms that have not.

Indicator variable for prior adoption of a double-hull tanker, entered in the propensity part of the tanker diffusion model. It distinguishes firms that have already placed an order for the innovative ship type from firms that have not.

Cluster-theory social proximity variable for whether the firm is in a different nation than past adopters. It enters the diffusion model as a social proximity term, so that past adopters in the same nation are more influential than those in a different nation.
Variable for whether the tanker firm is located in a different nation than past adopters, entered as a social proximity term in the tanker diffusion model.

Variable for whether the firm has connections to the same builders as past adopters, derived from the supplier-buyer network in which a tie is defined between a shipping firm and a shipbuilder if the shipping firm owned a ship constructed by the builder. In the analysis the direct-tie variable affects social proximity, so that directly tied firms are more influential.

Variable for owning ships from the same builder as past adopters, entered as a social proximity term in the tanker diffusion model. It is built from the supplier-buyer network of shipping firms and shipbuilders.

Variable for whether the firm is located in a different network cluster than past adopters. Clusters were computed with a CONCOR partition of depth three (giving a maximum of eight clusters) on the shipping firm network, in which firms that share a shipbuilder are tied to each other, so clusters are created according to the structural equivalence of the nodes. Cluster numbers were compared with the previous analysis and adjusted when the analysis had switched numbers, a cluster had dissolved, or a new cluster had appeared.

Variable for whether the tanker firm is located in a different network cluster than past adopters, where clusters are computed by CONCOR on the network of shipping firms tied through shared shipbuilders. It enters as a social proximity term in the tanker diffusion model.

The number of received ties divided by the total number of received ties in the population, measuring centrality in the network. A share measure rather than a count measure was used because in a time-varying network the density of the networks increased in the neighborhood of the shipbuilders that were building the innovative ship type. In the analysis centrality affects the susceptibility to adopting the innovation.

The number of received ties divided by the total number of received ties in the population, measuring centrality in the time-varying supplier-buyer network. It affects the susceptibility of the focal tanker firm to influence from prior adopters.

A dummy variable that equals 1 if the year t is after target startup firm j is acquired, and 0 otherwise. In the dynamic version each year k around the acquisition between -4 and 5 is separately estimated as a dummy, with the year prior to the acquisition (k = -1) omitted as the reference group.
time_window: -4 to +5 years relative to the acquisition

description: A firm-year-level measure that divides the number of employee entrepreneurship events in a given year by the total number of workers. For each year in the 10-year window around the acquisition ranging from -4 to 5, the total number of workers employed at the sample of high-tech startups is measured (denominator) and those workers are observed in the focal as well as the following year to count the number of workers who become founders of new companies in t or t + 1 (numerator). The measure is scaled by 100 for legibility.
time_window: t and t + 1 within a 10-year window around the acquisition (-4 to 5)

description: Same-industry employee entrepreneurship counts only new firms whose four-digit NAICS industry is the same as that of the target firm; the measure is otherwise constructed as the rate of employee entrepreneurship described above.
time_window: t and t + 1 within a 10-year window around the acquisition (-4 to 5)

description: Outside-industry (different-industry) employee entrepreneurship counts new firms founded by the target firm's workers in an industry other than the target firm's four-digit NAICS industry; the measure is otherwise constructed as the rate of employee entrepreneurship described above.
time_window: t and t + 1 within a 10-year window around the acquisition (-4 to 5)

description: A binary variable equalling 1 if the acquired establishment is moved to the location of, or absorbed by, the acquirer's headquarters within 3 years of the acquisition, and 0 if the acquired establishment remains in its original location in the three-year window. Relocation is measured by tracking the acquired establishment before and after the acquisition using establishment identifiers that do not change after a change in ownership.

The target firm's relocation outcome assigned to the individuals present at the target firm in the year prior to the acquisition: 1 if the acquired establishment is moved to the location of, or absorbed by, the acquirer's headquarters within 3 years of the acquisition, and 0 if it remains in its original location.

A binary variable equalling 1 if the individual is a founder of the target firm, and 0 otherwise. Founders are identified with the approach used to identify founders of new businesses, based on appearing in the new firm at its first quarter of operations and being among the top three earners in the first year.
time_window: pre-acquisition (individuals present in the year prior to the acquisition)

variable_name: Founding within 5 years of the acquisition
description: An individual-level indicator for whether the individual leaves to start a new company within 5 years of the acquisition, estimated on a cross-sectional sample of individuals present at the target firm in the year prior to the acquisition. The measure distinguishes founding in any industry, in the same industry as the target firm, and in a different industry.

For each of the 30 FDI opportunities, executives rated two items on a seven-point Likert scale: (1) the attractiveness of the opportunity as a joint venture and (3) the probability that they would recommend pursuing the opportunity as a joint venture. The two items were summed to create the dependent variable IJV attractiveness; the correlation between the two items is high.
scale: seven-point Likert scale from 1 (very low) to 7 (very high) per item; two items summed

description: For each of the 30 FDI opportunities, executives rated two items on a seven-point Likert scale: (2) the attractiveness of the opportunity as a divestiture and (4) the probability that they would recommend pursuing the opportunity as a divestiture. The two items were summed to create the dependent variable Divestiture attractiveness.
scale: seven-point Likert scale from 1 (very low) to 7 (very high) per item; two items summed

description: The variable Divestiture attractiveness was subtracted from the variable IJV attractiveness to create the dependent variable Preference for IJV versus divestiture.

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: the extent to which the U.S. firm possesses strong technological capabilities. The values of the criterion were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: unique competencies held by the U.S. firm. The values of the criterion were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: financial resources that the U.S. firm is able to provide. The values of the criterion were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: the extent to which the U.S. firm possesses market knowledge in China. The values of the criterion were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: the degree to which the Chinese firm possesses intangible assets that are difficult for the U.S. firm to value. The values of the criterion were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: the degree to which the two businesses' product markets overlap. The authors note that the variable is inversely coded, such that the greater the variable's value, the less the amount of information asymmetry between the firms. Values were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: the U.S. firm's familiarity and knowledge of the Chinese business' resources and capabilities. The values of the criterion were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: the extent to which the U.S. firm would consider the Chinese business' affiliated organizations reputable. The values of the criterion were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: the level of unique asset investments required by the Chinese business. The values of the criterion were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: the number of other U.S. firms interested in this investment opportunity with the Chinese business. The authors state that small numbers bargaining is inversely measured by this variable, so a higher value indicates less small numbers bargaining. Values were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: the level to which the U.S. firm has used detailed contracts with others in the past. The values of the criterion were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

One of the 16 decision criteria summarized in each FDI scenario: favorability of the U.S. firm's cooperative history. The values of the criterion were randomly assigned for each of the 30 scenarios from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

Generic resources are manipulated in the experimental scenarios through two policy criteria describing the U.S. investor: financial resources it can provide and its market knowledge in China, whose values were varied across the 30 FDI scenarios.

Firm-specific resources are manipulated in the experimental scenarios through two policy criteria describing the U.S. investor: technological capabilities and unique competencies, whose values were varied across the 30 FDI scenarios.

Percentage of a company's shares held by foreign institutional investors, taken from annual financial reports. Ownership averaged 12.8 percent in the sample and rose from 10 to 18 percent over the observation period. The variable is lagged by one year.

Percentage of board members whose task areas described in the Handbook of Board Members include either CSR or IR. In most firms in the sample there is only one CSR or IR board member, but their influence can be greater on small boards than on larger ones. The variable is lagged by one year.

Binary variable coded as one for company-years in which a given company appointed one or more new female directors. It was created using information on individual directors from the Handbook of Board Members. Appointment rather than the proportion or number of female directors is used because most Japanese companies still have no female directors on their boards.

Log odds that managers are women. Odds are calculated as the proportion of female managers divided by the proportion of male managers, and the log transformation is used because the raw ratio of female to male managers is highly skewed.

Representation of women in non-managerial, white-collar positions, measured as the log odds that such employees are women. It was added as a lower-rank outcome to test whether the hypothesized effects appear only at upper-rank positions.
Representation of women at the entry level, measured as the log odds that new hires for non-managerial, white-collar jobs are women. For this outcome variable the authors have data for 2001-2008.

A dummy variable coded as 1 if the hospital was involved in a merger, else 0. Merging hospitals were identified using past issues of the publication Modern Healthcare, verified with Ohio State Health Department officials. Twenty-two of the 105 hospitals in the sample merged during 1994-95.

The change in the proportion of patients from DRG i in the total patients of hospital j in the post-merger year relative to the pre-merger year, computed as the log of the ratio of the post-merger proportion to the pre-merger proportion. A logarithmic transformation is used because a simple ratio as a dependent variable is constrained to be positive, while a logarithmic transformation can take both positive and negative values. Computed for the high-profit DRGs, using combined pre-merger and post-merger numbers of patients for the merging hospitals.
time_window: post-merger year (t) relative to pre-merger year (t-1), 1-year post-merger window

description: The change in the proportion of patients from DRG i in the total patients of hospital j in the post-merger year relative to the pre-merger year, computed as the log of the ratio of the post-merger proportion to the pre-merger proportion. A logarithmic transformation is used because a simple ratio as a dependent variable is constrained to be positive, while a logarithmic transformation can take both positive and negative values. Computed for the low-profit DRGs, using combined pre-merger and post-merger numbers of patients for the merging hospitals.
time_window: post-merger year (t) relative to pre-merger year (t-1), 1-year post-merger window

description: The log of the ratio of the market share of hospital j in DRG i in hospital market k in the post-merger year to its market share in the pre-merger year. The authors' example is ln(11/10) = 0.095 when a hospital's market share in DRG112 rises from 10 percent to 11 percent. Market shares of individual hospitals in each DRG were calculated using Health Service Areas as the definition of hospital markets. Computed for the high-profit DRGs.
time_window: post-merger year (t) relative to pre-merger year (t-1), 1-year post-merger window

description: The log of the ratio of the market share of hospital j in DRG i in hospital market k in the post-merger year to its market share in the pre-merger year. The authors' example is ln(11/10) = 0.095 when a hospital's market share in DRG112 rises from 10 percent to 11 percent. Market shares of individual hospitals in each DRG were calculated using Health Service Areas as the definition of hospital markets. Computed for the low-profit DRGs.
time_window: post-merger year (t) relative to pre-merger year (t-1), 1-year post-merger window

description: The HHI of concentration for the hospital market, defined at the DRG level as the sum of squared market shares (proportion) of all the hospitals operating in the hospital market, measured in the pre-merger year. Market share is measured in proportions for easier interpretation of the coefficients. A highly competitive market is one which has low HHI.

variable_name: Low investment relative to rivals in physical capital
description: Ratio of premises and equipment expenses to number of branches, taken to proxy the bank's level of investment in physical capital, compared with the average investment level of the firm's asset-class group ($100M-$300M, $300M-$1B, or $1B-$5B). The spline function splits this continuous relative investment variable at the knot of rivals' norms, and the low investment variable contains only the negative deviations from that norm. Because the variable contains exclusively negative deviations, a positive coefficient indicates that greater deviation leads to poorer performance.
time_window: 1998-2002 (data collected at the end of each year)

variable_name: High investment relative to rivals in physical capital
description: Ratio of premises and equipment expenses to number of branches, taken to proxy the bank's level of investment in physical capital, compared with the average investment level of the firm's asset-class group ($100M-$300M, $300M-$1B, or $1B-$5B). The spline function splits this continuous relative investment variable at the knot of rivals' norms, and the high investment variable contains only the positive deviations from that norm. Because the high investment variable is exclusively positive numbers, the sign of the coefficient directly expresses the relationship.
time_window: 1998-2002 (data collected at the end of each year)

variable_name: Low investment relative to rivals in human capital
description: Ratio of salary and benefit expenses to full-time equivalent employees, taken to reflect the firm's investment in human capital, compared with the average investment level of the firm's asset-class group ($100M-$300M, $300M-$1B, or $1B-$5B). The spline function splits this continuous relative investment variable at the knot of rivals' norms into a below-the-knot variable containing only negative deviations from the norm.
time_window: 1998-2002 (data collected at the end of each year)

variable_name: High investment relative to rivals in human capital
description: Ratio of salary and benefit expenses to full-time equivalent employees, taken to reflect the firm's investment in human capital, compared with the average investment level of the firm's asset-class group ($100M-$300M, $300M-$1B, or $1B-$5B). The spline function splits this continuous relative investment variable at the knot of rivals' norms into an above-the-knot variable containing only positive deviations from the norm.
time_window: 1998-2002 (data collected at the end of each year)

description: Ratio of commercial-related loans (construction, commercial real estate, multifamily housing, farmland, farm operations, and industrial loans) to total loans, used because the distribution of the bank's loan portfolio reflects its position on the simple-to-sophisticated continuum. The continuous variable ranges from zero to one, with banks offering simple services scoring closer to zero and those offering sophisticated services scoring closer to one. The data were collected from the FDIC.

Market-based measure of economic performance, proxied following Kor and Mahoney (2005) by the firm's market value and long-term debt to total book assets. Values below one indicate that the firm is poorly managing its resources, while values surpassing one indicate the extent of the firm's value creation and economic performance via effective use of resources. Because Tobin's q quickly reflects the market's reaction to firm actions, data were collected at the end of each year. The required data were obtained from the FDIC and Research Insight.

Counts of renewable electricity words in the organization's 10-K report in each year. Word counts of relevant renewable electricity technologies - solar, wind, biomass, hydroelectricity (or hydro), and nuclear - were generated with the program Atlas.ti and summed to create the dependent variable. To validate the measure, 20% of the 10-Ks were manually checked by counting the words and confirming that context did not distort meaning (96% accuracy), and an additional 20% was compared with a Microsoft Word search (100% accuracy).

A count of the number of years remaining until an organization must be compliant with its state's RPS; time to compliance may range from 1 - 20 years, and the greater the number of years the greater the level of uncertainty. The variable takes the value of 0 for all observations that do not face an RPS and ranges from 0 to 20.

Equal to 0 if the unit is a subsidiary and 1 if the unit is a headquarters. The 38 headquarters in the sample include 20 organizations that are solo headquarters without subsidiaries and 18 headquarters supervising an average of 1.67 subsidiaries. Separate 10-K filings by headquarters and by subsidiary limited liability corporations allow their agendas to be distinguished.

Identifies whether a single unit - either headquarters or subsidiary - possesses both operating experience and regulatory experience. Operational experience is present if the focal unit generates electricity (production of any type of electricity); regulatory experience is present if the focal unit is in a state that has undergone deregulation. Units that possess both types of experience are coded as 1; units possessing one type or neither type are coded as 0.
Units that possess both renewable operating experience (i.e., production of renewable electricity) and regulatory experience (i.e., deregulation) are coded as 1; 0 otherwise.

A count measure based on shared production of any type of electricity between a focal unit and its alter unit. Coded 0 if neither unit produces electricity, 1 if the alter unit produces electricity, 2 if the focal unit produces electricity, 3 if both units produce electricity. Each headquarters is assumed to be connected to all its subsidiaries, and each subsidiary connected to only its headquarters.

A count measure based on shared production of renewable electricity. Coded 0 if neither unit produces renewable electricity, 1 if the alter unit produces renewable electricity, 2 if the focal unit produces renewable electricity, 3 if both units produce renewable electricity.

A count measure of four successively increasing levels of shared regulatory experience based on whether units are located in a state that has experienced deregulation. Coded 0 if neither a headquarters nor its subsidiaries are located in a deregulated state; 1 if the focal unit has not experienced deregulation but its alter unit has; 2 if only the focal unit has experienced deregulation but the alter unit has not; 3 if both the headquarters and its subsidiary have experienced deregulation.

Dummy variable equal to one if a promotion occurred by the survey date and zero otherwise. It is the dependent variable in the probit models whose marginal effects of interest are those of the worker's performance rating (P) and the typical worker's performance rating (P0). Sampling weights are used so that weighted observations are representative of firms.

Dummy variable equal to one if a promotion was expected to occur within 5 years of the survey date and zero otherwise. It is used as a dependent variable in probit models parallel to those for actual promotions. The expected-promotion models drop workers who had already been promoted by the survey date.

The employer's answer to the question asking, on a scale of 0-100 where 50 is average and 100 is the best score, to rate the most recently hired employee's performance in the job into which he was hired. It is the measure of the worker's own performance in the probit models of promotion and expected promotion.
scale: 0-100, where 50 is average and 100 is the best score

description: Relative performance is not entered as a single variable; the probit models include the worker's own performance rating P and the typical worker's performance rating P0 separately. The authors interpret a positive marginal effect of P together with a negative marginal effect of P0 as evidence that promotions depend on relative performance, and they describe relative performance as the difference P - P0.

Dummy equal to one if a promotion occurred by the survey date and zero otherwise. It is the observed dichotomous promotion variable in the structural model, whose latent counterpart is the performance threshold (the 'bar') that the worker must exceed to be promoted. Only the discrete realization of the promotion variable is observed, so the promotion equation is identified only up to a scalar multiple, with σνν normalized to one.

Employer-reported performance rating of the most recently hired professional worker, on a scale of 0-100 where 50 is average. It is the dependent variable of the performance equation of the structural tournament model, and in the empirical work performance stands in for the theoretical notion of worker effort.

Difference in wages between the post-promotion and pre-promotion jobs. For workers promoted by the survey date it is the current (post-promotion) wage minus the starting wage; for workers not yet promoted it is the wage they expect if promoted minus their current wage. Reported wages were converted to hourly wages measured in 1990 dollars, deflated using the CPI-UX.

Employer-reported rating of the typical employee's performance in the same job, entering the latent promotion threshold (the 'bar') equation. Its coefficient γ3 is the structural test of whether promotions are determined by relative performance; theory predicts γ3 > 0 because higher performance of the worker's competition raises the bar and therefore lowers the probability of promotion.

Estimated covariance between the unobserved determinants of worker performance and of the wage spread in the structural model; it is an estimable parameter of the covariance matrix. The authors use it to test Testable Propositions 2 and 3 jointly, since together they imply σ12 < 0.

The CEO's need for achievement was measured with the Manifest Need Questionnaire developed by Steers and Braunstein (1976), whose predictive, convergent, and discriminant validities and acceptable test-retest reliabilities the authors cite. The scale was completed by each firm's CEO.

Environmental uncertainty was gauged using Miller and Dröge's (1986: 557) scales, which reflected the degree of change and unpredictability in market-related and technological dimensions. The questions on environmental uncertainty were answered by each firm's most senior vice president or general manager rather than by the CEO, in order to reduce common method variance.

Strategy-making rationality was measured using Miller's (1987: 32) analysis (ANALY) scale and Miller and Dröge's (1986: 559-560) process liaison (LIASDMG) scale. Miller and Dröge used the process liaison scale to measure structural integration, but the authors judged it to relate much more closely to the interaction taking place in the strategy-making process. In the LISREL model RATIONALITY was measured by ANALY and LIASDMG.

Formalization comprised codified rules and procedures, role specialization, and the use of formal controls; it was measured with the specialization (SPEC) and formalization (FORMAL) abbreviated scales of the Aston studies (Inkson, Pugh, & Hickson, 1970) and Miller and Dröge's (1986: 560) CONTROL scale. In the LISREL model FORMALIZATION was measured with error by FORMAL, SPEC, and CONTROL.

Centralization, the distribution of power in an organization, was measured using the Aston scales (Inkson et al., 1970). These questions were answered by each firm's most senior vice president or general manager. In the LISREL model CENT was the single indicator of CENTRALIZATION.

Integration, the coordinative and collaborative devices a firm used, was gauged with Miller and Dröge's (1986: 559) structural liaison variable, LIASTRUC. In the LISREL model LIASTRUC was the single indicator of the INTEGRATION construct.

The strategic content dimension, innovation, was measured using five-year average expenditures on R&D as a percentage of sales (R&D) and five-year average expenditures on new product development and commercialization expenses as a percentage of sales (INNCOMM). The innovation scale was completed by the CEO. In the LISREL model INNOVATION was measured by R&D and INNCOMM.
Size was measured as the natural logarithm of the number of full-time employees. It was specified as an exogenous variable in the LISREL model.

The amount of money donated by a corporate foundation to non-U.S. beneficiaries in a host country in a year. Donations were summed at the foundation-country-year level and the logarithm was taken to avoid skewness. General-purpose grants that were not earmarked for a particular country were counted as part of giving elsewhere and excluded from the focal observations. The data come from foundations' tax filings and only grants of $10,000 or more are observable.
scale: log of US dollars (grants of $10,000 or more)

description: Donations that go directly to an agency in the beneficiary country, such as a donation to a charity in Indonesia for its post-tsunami recovery efforts. It is the logarithm of the focal foundation's direct local giving in the focal country-year. Direct local giving and intermediated giving have similar average amounts per donation.

Donations that go indirectly by way of an intermediary outside of the beneficiary country, such as a donation to Doctors Without Borders in New York for malaria treatment in Mali. It is the logarithm of the focal foundation's intermediated giving in the focal country-year.

For all of a firm's donations in a year that marked a country as the final beneficiary, the percentage of donations received by local entities in that country. The measure is a ratio at the firm-country-year level; observations are missing when total giving in that country-year is zero and are dropped when a firm gives exclusively locally or exclusively through intermediaries in the presence of firm fixed effects.

Country-level governance index obtained from the World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators database; higher values indicate stronger rule of law. It is one of the two indices reported, the other being Control of Corruption; the WGI indicators are highly correlated and cannot be used simultaneously.

Country-level governance index obtained from the World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators database; higher values indicate better control of corruption. It is entered in models separately from Rule of Law because the WGI indicators are highly correlated.

A dummy variable indicating whether the funding firm had set up new subsidiaries in the host country within the past 5 years, captured at the firm-country-year level from DCA. In robustness tests the window was shortened to the past 3 years with qualitatively the same results.

The number of externally oriented managers at the firm's local subsidiaries. Job titles of top managers at the local subsidiaries were categorized into two bins: externally oriented managers working in marketing, corporate outreach, or supply chain management, and internally oriented managers working in R&D and production. Internal orientation, the number of internally oriented managers, is controlled for separately.

Indicator for whether the venture was female-led; 26% of the 43 businesses in the final data were female-led.
