The organization matched judges with business plans such that each venture was evaluated by multiple judges, and judges did not necessarily possess prior or outside knowledge of the businesses they evaluated.

Each business plan was independently coded by research assistants blind to the study hypotheses; the coders measured, for each business plan, the raw number of paragraphs in which social impact was explicitly mentioned either as a motivation for starting the business or as an outcome of its operation. The value of the social impact framing variable was calculated as the number of paragraphs that explicitly mentioned social impact divided by the total number of paragraphs in the business plan, and ranged from 0.02 to 0.28. Continuous variables were centered.

For each business plan, judges were asked to assess the business' viability by responding to the question, 'Do you think this is a viable business in its current form?' The outcome variable perceived business viability was measured on a 1 to 5 point scale, where 1 corresponded to 'poor' and 5 corresponded to 'outstanding.'

Gender was manipulated through the recording of a male or female entrepreneur giving an otherwise identical pitch presentation while holding constant other factors that might affect evaluation. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four versions of a pitch.

To manipulate commercial and social impact framing, the pitch presentation evaluated by the social impact framing groups contained additional phrases that emphasized the benefits of venture activities for society and their contribution to general social-environmental welfare. The pitch in the combined commercial and social impact framing condition, in addition to explaining the venture's commercial merits, claimed that it targeted 'poverty reduction and environmental solutions' and 'social and environmental impact.'
scale: binary condition (commercial framing only versus combined commercial and social impact framing)

description: Traits associated with warmth adapted from Fiske et al. (2002); participants were asked to indicate the extent to which they would describe the entrepreneur as 'compassionate,' 'kind,' and 'warm' (alpha = 0.86), and these values were averaged to create a measure of perceived warmth. Responses used a 1 to 5 agree-disagree Likert scale.

Competence traits adapted from Fiske et al. (2002); participants were asked to indicate the extent to which they would describe the entrepreneur as 'competent,' 'proficient,' and 'adept' (alpha = 0.83), and these values were averaged to create a measure of perceived competence. Responses used a 1 to 5 agree-disagree Likert scale.

Following Kerr et al. (2014), the authors used measures of venture growth ('This venture will grow to have 100+ employees at some point in the future') and venture financing ('This venture will be successful in getting the financial investment it needs to grow'), alpha = 0.89, to create an aggregate score for business viability.

We measured a firm's technological know-how in terms of areal density using a two-step procedure. First, the areal density of the best drive produced by firm i of diameter j in year t was divided by the highest areal density available in that diameter in the market that year to obtain the firm's diameter-specific relative technological position. Second, these positions were averaged across all diameters produced by the firm in a year to obtain the firm's average relative technological know-how. A firm at the frontier in all the diameters it produced would have a value of 1, and a firm behind the frontier in any one diameter would score less than 1. The formula blocks in the source are unreadable.
scale: 0 to 1 (1 = at the frontier in all diameters produced)

description: Market pioneering know-how was measured as the number of times a firm introduced drives of new diameters within the first year of their introduction into the industry divided by the total number of new diameter introductions in the industry since the firm's year of entry. Pik is a dummy variable indicating whether the firm was an early mover when a new diameter was introduced, and Dk is a dummy variable indicating whether a diameter was introduced in that year. For each firm operating in the market at the time of a new diameter's introduction the denominator increased by 1, and the numerator increased by 1 only if the firm was an early mover for that diameter. The authors assumed no depreciation of market pioneering know-how. The formula block in the source is unreadable.
time_window: annual, updated at each diameter introduction since the firm's entry

description: This dummy variable took the value of 1 if a spin-out was created in the year following a given year by an employee or employees of a firm founding a new venture, and 0 otherwise. It served as the dependent variable for testing Hypothesis 1.
time_window: one year following the observation year

variable_name: Parent technological know-how in year prior to spin-out inception
description: The parent firm's technological know-how, measured with the same areal-density-based relative measure, in the year preceding the spin-out's entry into the industry. It was an explanatory variable for Hypothesis 2 and was time-invariant in the analyses of the spin-out's know-how over its life span.
time_window: the year preceding the spin-out's entry into the industry

variable_name: Parent market pioneering know-how in year prior to spin-out inception
description: The parent firm's market pioneering know-how, measured with the same measure based on early entry into new diameters, in the year preceding the spin-out's entry into the industry. It was an explanatory variable for Hypothesis 2 and was time-invariant in the analyses.
time_window: the year preceding the spin-out's entry into the industry

description: Computed as a dummy variable with a value of 1 if a firm survived to the year following an observation (with acquisitions being treated as censored observations) and a value of 0 otherwise. It was the dependent variable for Hypothesis 4.
time_window: one year following the observation year

description: Coded 1 if at least one founder of a firm was an ex-employee of an incumbent firm in the year prior to its formation and 0 otherwise. It was an explanatory variable for Hypotheses 3 and 4.

Coded 1 if a firm was affiliated (was a subsidiary or joint venture, or parent-backed) with an incumbent in the disk drive industry and 0 otherwise. It was an explanatory variable for Hypotheses 3 and 4.
Coded 1 if a firm existed in some other industry prior to entering the disk drive industry and 0 otherwise. It was an explanatory variable for Hypotheses 3 and 4.

Number of book titles publisher i releases in category c in the 3-year period p, where each travel destination (country) is treated as a product category. The variable is a non-negative count of titles, spanning the publisher's book releases in the period.

Book density is calculated by dividing a book's weight in ounces by its volume in cubic inches, and the publisher's value is the average over all of the publisher's books in the 1994-2007 period. Physical Differentiationi is coded 1 if the publisher's average book density exceeds the overall average and 0 otherwise. High quality paper, better bindings, and color graphics are the physical attributes that raise density.

Count of the number of hotels detailed in the publisher's last pre-2007 Paris travel guide; Paris was chosen as a common basis to assess as many publishers' positionings as possible. High Content Cost takes a value of 1 if the count exceeds the average across all publishers and 0 otherwise. Hotel coverage is used as the indicator of reliance on primary content.

Total number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites, natural or cultural, counted in each product category (country). Low Demand Diversity takes the value of 1 if the category has a below average number of World Heritage Sites and is 0 otherwise. World Heritage Sites are treated as major tourist destinations that proxy for the potential demand diversity of the category.

Indicator for the post-Kindle period, equal to 1 for the 2011-2013 window and 0 for the pre-Kindle 2005-2007 window. Amazon launched Kindle in November 2007 and a 3-year gap is used before the post-Kindle window to allow the platform to penetrate the consumer market and publishers to adjust their strategies.

The percentage of a firm's total imports that originated from low-wage countries. A country is classified as an LWC if its average annual GDP per capita was less than 5% of the U.S. annual GDP per capita in 1972-1992, using the list of Bernard, Jensen, and Schott (2006). Import transactions carry a firm identifier and a 10-digit Harmonized System product code, which the authors link to 1987 four-digit SICs.
scale: percentage of a firm's total imports

description: The logarithm of the total toxicity-weighted emissions of plant i of parent firm j in year t. Toxic emissions from a plant are its all-media release of designated toxic chemicals multiplied by the RSEI toxicity weight for each chemical; emissions to air are weighted using inhalation toxicity and emissions to other media are weighted using oral toxicity.

County-level demographic measure based on the U.S. Census' American Community Survey, indicating a more educated population in the county where the plant is located. It is entered as a measure of local institutional pressure and interacted with the parent firm's LWC import share.

County-level voter turnout in presidential elections, based on the U.S. Census' American Community Survey. It is entered as a measure of local institutional pressure and interacted with the parent firm's LWC import share.

State-level Sierra Club membership, used as a measure of the presence of environmental nongovernment organizations and of local institutional pressure for environmental performance. It is interacted with the parent firm's LWC import share.
Plant-level productivity derived from the U.S. Census' plant micro data, used as a measure of plant capability. It is entered both directly and interacted with the parent firm's LWC import share.
Productivity of the plant's parent firm, used as a measure of firm capability. It is entered both directly and interacted with the parent firm's LWC import share.

Parent firms that are publicly listed are matched to Compustat to collect information about their R&D and brand equity, i.e., R&D and advertising expenditure. It is entered both directly and interacted with the parent firm's LWC import share.

The toxic content of a firm's imports, computed by summing the firm's import value in each industry weighted by the industry's pollution intensity. Industry pollution intensity is the sum of the RSEI-based toxic emissions of all plants in a four-digit SIC industry in 1992 divided by that industry's total output in 1992.
Toxic imports scaled by the firm's total imports, measuring the pollution intensity of a firm's imports.

The pollution content of a plant's output, computed by summing the plant's output in each industry weighted by the industry's pollution intensity (RSEI-based toxic emissions of all plants in the four-digit SIC industry in 1992 divided by that industry's 1992 total output).
Toxic output scaled by the plant's total shipment value, measuring the pollution intensity of a plant's output.

Total Pollution Abatement Operating Costs, which comprise salaries and wages, parts and materials, fuel and electricity, capital depreciation, contract work, equipment leasing, and additional operating costs associated with the abatement of air and water pollution as well as solid waste reduction or disposal. Because of the significant gaps in time coverage of PACE data, industry x year and plant fixed effects are included separately rather than jointly.
The number of pollution prevention practices adopted by the plant, constructed from the TRI database following Harrington et al. (2014).
The total tonnage of production waste (waste produced before treatment), constructed from the TRI database.
The cost of fuel consumption per unit of output, calculated from the U.S. Census' plant micro data as a measure of energy efficiency, controlling for total output.

Aggregated experience of all project team members in the particular industry domain of the project client. If a project was in the banking domain, the total experience of all team members in previous banking projects was added and divided by team size to arrive at the domain experience measure, in months.
time_window: experience in previous projects before the focal project

description: Composite domain-competence score calculated for each project by adding all the weighted scores (by exam level) for each project team member and then normalizing those with the team size. The firm developed several exams in different industry domains at three levels of increasing difficulty, following the same principles as the technological exams; a higher score indicates greater business-domain expertise for the project team.
scale: weighted certification exam points, averaged by team size
time_window: exams taken by team members before project completion

description: For each project, a technology competence score was developed by adding the exam scores of every employee who worked in the project. An individual's exam score was included if the exam was in the same technology as the project technology and if the employee took the exam at least 90 days before the project completion date. For exams with different levels of difficulty, a simple weighted scoring method was used: the exam score was multiplied by two (for level 2 exams) or three (for level 3 exams), and the final score was divided by team size.
scale: weighted certification exam points, averaged by team size
time_window: exams taken at least 90 days before the project completion date

description: Aggregated experience of all project team members in the particular technology of the project. If a project used Java technology, the total experience of all team members in previous Java projects was added and averaged by team size to arrive at a technological experience measure in months.
time_window: experience in previous projects before the focal project

description: The dependent variable was project gross profit (revenues minus direct costs). Direct costs include the salaries of project team members, related travel costs, and software licenses required for a given project. All revenue numbers are given in USD equivalents adjusted for currency fluctuations and recognized as of the day of project delivery, that is, the project's end date; overhead costs were not included in calculating project gross profit. The dependent variable was logged.
time_window: three-year study period (April 2005 to March 2008), recognized at project end date

description: A firm's degree centrality in the firm-level network of joint committee participation. For each year the authors create a firm-by-meeting affiliation matrix and convert it into a firm-by-firm matrix using the minimums method for valued data, so a cell counts the number of times representatives of two firms encountered each other, limited by the lower number of representatives in each meeting. Centrality scores were normalized by dividing by the largest centrality in that year, and degree centrality was set to 0 for firm-years in which the firm attended no meetings.
scale: degree centrality normalized by the largest centrality in the year
time_window: annual, computed for each year of the panel

description: A count of formal TIA projects that contain protected intellectual property of each firm, taken to represent influence because having a formal project that contains a firm's IPR could be evidence that the firm exerted influence to initiate this project. Because of changes to the TIA's record-keeping, these data are available only for the period 1996 to 2000.

A count of TIA project initiation forms where a firm representative is identified as the document editor; the editor is typically the document's author and also exerts editorial control over the document. The forms were revised in 1998 to capture the name and affiliation of the document's editor, so the data are available for 1998 to 2000.

The aggregated social capital of individual representatives moving into the firm in a given year, representing an individual's social capital with his or her degree centrality in the person-by-person network of joint meeting participation. Person-by-meeting affiliation matrices were converted into person-by-person matrices of joint participation using the same procedure as for firm social capital, and a mover's social capital is this degree centrality for the two years preceding the move, normalized for the number of meetings held in that year. The variable was centered and lagged one year. Mobility events were identified from roster affiliation changes and, where a participant patented for another firm in the set after last attending a meeting, from patent records.
time_window: two years preceding the move, lagged one year

description: The aggregated social capital of individual representatives moving out of the firm in a given year, using the same individual degree centrality in the person-by-person network of joint meeting participation as for inflows. A mover's social capital is his or her degree centrality for the two years preceding the move, normalized for the number of meetings held in that year. The variable was centered and lagged one year.
time_window: two years preceding the move, lagged one year

description: An index of redundant participation that averages the number of participants for each meeting the firm attended in a given year. Because the authors expect the effect of redundancy to decrease with each additional redundant participant, the index is log transformed, and it was set to 0 for firms that failed to participate in any meeting in a given year. The variable was centered before being used in interaction terms.

The natural log of the count of subcommittees that a firm stopped participating in from one year to the next; for example, a firm that stopped participating in one subcommittee in 1997 counts one strategic change in 1997. The variable was centered and lagged one year, and its product with Out-Social Capital forms the interaction term used in hypothesis testing.

Operationalized as the logged sum of: (1) the number of top managers with industry experience, (2) the number of top managers with prior TMT experience, (3) the number of top managers aged 40 or over, and (4) the number of top managers with advanced degrees (Master's or equivalent). TMT members are defined as all executives above vice president. The logged sum is used because legitimacy is treated as a cumulative function of the individual legitimacy of team members, subject to diminishing returns. A principal components analysis of the four variables produced one factor with an eigenvalue greater than one.

The raw stock price change two weeks after the IPO, expressed as a percentage of the initial price, adjusted for the contemporaneous return in the broader stock market: the market return (NYSE, AMEX, and NASDAQ weighted according to the value of each market) is subtracted from the raw return. The authors state that the measure of underpricing is based on Carter and Manaster (1990).

Each of the 200 MNEs was classified according to Rumelt's (1974) nine-category classification schema using the descriptive narrative in Stopford (1983), Annual Financial Reports and 10-Ks, supplemented by reference to periodical business publications. Two of the authors and a research assistant independently classified the companies, and discrepancies were resolved through a joint consultative process, which was required for 18 of the 200 sample firms. For the hypothesis test, firms were assigned to three general classes: high-performing strategies (dominant-constrained and related-constrained), medium-performing strategies (active conglomerates, related-linked, and single business), and low-performing strategies (unrelated-passive and dominant-vertical). Eleven firms whose strategies (dominant-linked, dominant-unrelated) did not cluster into one of the three general classes were excluded from the analysis.
scale: nine-category typology grouped into three performance classes

description: Ratio of net annual profits-to-sales obtained for each company in the list, calculated as the mean after-tax profits-to-sales over the 5-year period 1977-1981. All observations were included regardless of whether the firm registered a profit or loss in a particular year. The measure was highly correlated (r=0.91) with net after-tax profits-to-total assets (return on assets) and was chosen as the preferred performance measure because sales are expressed in more current monetary terms than assets. Results of all analyses are reported for both raw and standardized (z-score) data.

Net after-tax profits-to-total assets employed, described as another customary performance measure. Both this measure and profits-to-sales were calculated from comparative data provided in Stopford (1983). Results of all analyses are reported for both profits-to-sales and profits-to-total assets, using both raw and standardized data.

Ratio of a company's foreign subsidiaries' sales to its total worldwide sales for the period 1977-1981. Because the authors could not obtain reliable data discriminating foreign subsidiary and export sales volumes for a sufficient number of firms, the preferred ratio of foreign subsidiary sales to total MNE sales could not be used. To establish the validity of the ratio, its simple correlation with another surrogate measure of multinationality, the ratio of a firm's non-domestic sales to its total sales, was determined and exceeded 0.8 for each of the European and the U.S. samples. The measure evidenced high inter-period stability, with individual firms' average DOI deviating minimally over 1977-1981. For the analysis, firms were classified into one of five internationalization categories, each representing an interval of 20 percentage points along a scale of 0 to 99 per cent of total sales generated by foreign affiliates.
scale: 0 to 99 per cent of total sales; five categories of 20 percentage points

description: The number of consecutive years (up to five) before the dispute that the firm had lobbied the government agency in which the contract was awarded. It showcases a direct indication of the length of the relationship that a firm has cultivated with a particular government agency in charge of the contract award. Separate measures are created for the firm seeking to maintain the status quo and for firms seeking to alter it.
time_window: up to five consecutive years before the dispute

description: The number of agencies a firm targeted for lobbying divided by the total number of targeted agencies and pieces of legislation each year. Separate measures are created for the maintaining and altering firms. As a firm's administrative focus increases, so too does its alignment with the governmental domain.

The average positivity score of media coverage of the firm in a year when the firm engaged in the contract dispute; specifically, the average Event Sentiment Score from RavenPack for the year of the contract dispute. The variable takes a value between 0 and 100, with lower (higher) scores indicating negativity (positivity) in news coverage about the firm and a score of 50 coded as neutral. Separate measures are created for the maintaining and altering firms.

A binary variable taking on a value of one if the maintaining firm successfully maintained the contract award (zero otherwise). Positive coefficients indicate an increased probability of winning the dispute for firms seeking to maintain the status quo, and negative coefficients indicate an increased probability of winning for firms seeking to alter the status quo.

Correlation coefficient between the marginal profit-to-sales ratio of a firm, the change in its profits relative to the change in its own output, and the change in the sum of the output of all its competitors, measured following Sundaram et al. (1996). Net income measures firm profits and firm sales measure output; competitors are the other firms in the same four-digit NACE industry. The ratio was computed for each firm in the year prior to entry of the sample start-ups and the correlation coefficient was computed across the firms within each four-digit NACE industry, using annual data from 1991. Positive values indicate strategic complements and negative values strategic substitutes.
scale: correlation coefficient (CSM > 0 strategic complements; CSM < 0 strategic substitutes)

description: Concentration ratio that takes the market share of the largest four firms in the industry into account, used as a traditional proxy for the type of strategic interactions within an industry.
Herfindahl-Hirschman concentration index, which considers the market shares of all firms in the industry, used as a traditional proxy for the type of strategic interactions within an industry.

External debt relative to total financing sources in the start-up year. External debt includes long-term debt and current liabilities (including trade credit). Total financing includes equity, external debt and loans provided to the firm by the entrepreneur, and therefore excludes retained earnings, representing the funds available at the time of start-up.

Exit is determined at the time the firm's employment falls to zero and does not become positive again in subsequent years. The hazard rate represents the probability that a start-up firm exits the industry within a particular time interval conditional upon survival until that period. Start-ups that survived the sampling period are treated as censored observations that may still exit later on.

Bankruptcy rate of the entrants that were founded in a particular four-digit NACE industry over 1988-91, which are then tracked over a 3-year period following entry (moving window). It proxies the potential for adverse selection and moral hazard problems: start-ups in industries with a failure rate above the sample median are classified as operating under potentially high adverse selection and moral hazard problems, and firms below the median are classified as facing smaller problems. Results are also reported for the 40th and 60th percentiles of this variable.

The same historical industry failure rate used as the splitting variable for the subsample regressions: firms below the 40th percentile and below the median of the failure rate form the low-problem subsamples, and firms above the median and above the 60th percentile form the high-problem subsamples.

Coded as the estimated percentage of individuals between the ages of 18 and 64 in the general population who have started a venture in the last three years that has at least 25% of its customer base from other countries. It is an estimated proportion of the population rather than the proportion of entrepreneurs, so it captures the country's propensity of individuals to launch born globals. The variable was calibrated into fuzzy-set membership scores using the direct method, with the 75th percentile of the population as full membership, the mean as the crossover point, and the 25th percentile as full nonmembership.
time_window: latest survey year of each country, 2012-2014

description: Composite index taken from the 'trading across borders' component of the Doing Business Survey; it assesses the degree to which a country's regulatory framework supports international business, including observations for the number of days for and costs of engaging in international trade activities. The index was calibrated by using the absolute positions of countries on the scale.
time_window: one year prior to the born global formation rate data (for all but four countries)

description: The IMF Financial Integration Index measures the degree to which the inflow and outflow of equity, debt, money market instruments, and other financial transactions are permitted in countries around the world. The index was calibrated by using the absolute positions of countries on the scale, reverse coded so that higher membership scores represent greater integration into the global financial system.
time_window: one year prior to the born global formation rate data (for all but four countries)

description: Measured as the average of five five-point items in the GEM National Expert Survey that assess the degree to which societal members of a country value individual success, autonomy, risk taking, creativity and innovativeness, and personal responsibility, capturing normative support for entrepreneurship. The items were weighed equally and exhibited acceptable reliability (Cronbach's alpha of 0.944). The measure was calibrated with the 75th percentile as full membership, the midway scale score between the minimum and maximum as the crossover point, and the 25th percentile as full nonmembership.
scale: five-point Likert scale (average of five items)
time_window: one year prior to the born global formation rate data (for all but four countries)

description: Measured by averaging two subindices based on five items on a five-point Likert scale from the GEM National Expert Survey; the items assess the degree to which universities and other parts of countries' education systems prepare societal members for starting and growing new firms. The items were weighed equally and exhibited acceptable reliability (Cronbach's alpha of 0.899). Because the data systematically rate countries low on this feature, calibration used all countries GEM sampled, with the 75th percentile as full membership, the mean as the crossover point, and the 25th percentile as full nonmembership.
scale: five-point Likert scale (average of two subindices of five items)
time_window: one year prior to the born global formation rate data (for all but four countries)

description: Measured as the average of three items from the World Governance Indicators: control of corruption, rule of law in society, and political stability. The items were weighed equally and exhibited high reliability (Cronbach's alpha of 0.976), and higher scores reflect more sound formal institutions governing economic activity. Calibration used the 75th percentile as full membership, the midway scale score between the minimum and maximum as the crossover point, and the 25th percentile as full nonmembership.
time_window: one year prior to the born global formation rate data (for all but four countries)

description: First-generation immigrant population as a percentage of the general population, taken from the World Bank; it is a good indicator of the inflow of this unique form of human capital and its prevalence in society. It was calibrated with the 75th percentile as full membership, the mean as the crossover point, and the 25th percentile as full nonmembership.
time_window: one year prior to the born global formation rate data (for all but four countries)

description: The ratio between the sum of the GDP of all bordering nations, using both land and maritime borders, and the domestic market size; both numerator and denominator use country GDP in constant 2010 dollars from the World Bank. The higher the ratio, the greater the likelihood that an entrepreneur will look abroad rather than within the domestic context for market opportunities. It was calibrated with the 75th percentile as full membership, the mean as the crossover point, and the 25th percentile as full nonmembership.
time_window: one year prior to the born global formation rate data (for all but four countries)

description: The number of stars (out of five) assigned to the restaurant by the reviewer on the focal Yelp review. Each review consists of the reviewer's identification tag, the date of the review, a star rating of the restaurant ranging from one to five, and a commentary review with text of unlimited length. The average rating is 3.7 and the mode is 4.

A set of dummies based on the health grade assigned by the LADPH rather than the underlying numerical score, because the grade is publicly posted and more salient to the consumer. A score of 90-100 points is an A, 80-89 a B, and 70-79 a C; restaurants receiving a score below 70 points are not given a letter grade but are assigned the numerical score, referred to as grade F. Each Yelp review was linked to the most recent health grade in the system; grade A serves as the omitted baseline category.
time_window: most recent health inspection prior to the focal review (inspections July 2004-June 2010)

variable_name: No. of positive hygiene words in review
description: Count of positive hygiene words in the free commentary text of the focal review, obtained by content analyzing the review texts. The keyword list contains the 36 synonyms found in the 2012 Webster's Thesaurus for 'clean' and 'hygienic'. Positive hygiene words preceded by 'not' or 'no' were counted as negative hygiene words.

variable_name: No. of negative hygiene words in review
description: Count of negative hygiene words in the free commentary text of the focal review, obtained by content analyzing the review texts. The keyword list contains the 35 synonyms for 'dirty' and 'unhygienic'. Positive hygiene words preceded by 'not' or 'no' were counted as negative hygiene words.

An authenticity score for each review obtained by content analyzing the free commentary text for authenticity- and inauthenticity-related keywords. The keyword list is the list of 92 authenticity-related keywords of Kovács et al. (2013), each assigned a score from highly inauthentic to highly authentic based on consumer responses. Each review's score is the weighted sum of authenticity-keyword frequencies, which directly captures the focal reviewer's perception of the restaurant's authenticity.

The average authenticity score of all prior reviews of the focal restaurant, excluding the focal review. This measure reduces concerns of endogeneity because reviewers can assign a star rating and offer comments in any order, and it is used to estimate the rating of a given review on the basis of hygiene and authenticity exogenous to that review.
time_window: all prior reviews before the focal review

description: Treat takes one for firms where the country of the largest non-U.S. unit was included in the VWP, and Post takes one for years after the VWP introduction and zero otherwise. The interaction Treat × Post is the posttreatment period indicator for treated firms, i.e., the increased ease in short-term travel between the firm's R&D centers in the United States and in VWP countries. These variables are used to test all four hypotheses.
time_window: T in [-5, 7] relative to the VWP introduction

description: Logged number of patents registered with the United States Patent and Trademark Office at the firm-year level. To determine the timing of invention, the authors look at the initial submission date of patent applications ('date of apply') for granted patents, and a zero was imputed to a firm-year observation where no patent was filed.
time_window: T in [-5, 7] relative to the VWP introduction

description: Logged average number of technology classes of patents, using four-digit Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) codes, at the firm-year level. It is computed as the average across the firm's patents in a firm-year.
time_window: T in [-5, 7] relative to the VWP introduction

description: Proportion of patents in overlapping technology fields at the four-digit CPC level over all patents, using the primary and secondary technology classes; a high degree of overlap signifies a lesser distance. Treated firms are split into three groups: small overlap [0, 0.33] (high knowledge distance), medium overlap (0.33, 0.66], and large overlap (0.66, 1] (low knowledge distance).
level: firm (pair of U.S. and non-U.S. R&D centers)

description: The empirical sample is split based on whether the U.S. and VWP units are in countries with the same spoken language (English). To construct this variable, the authors checked whether English is a de jure or de facto official language of the relevant VWP country; centers in countries with a different language are treated as more culturally distant.
level: firm (pair of U.S. and non-U.S. R&D centers)

description: A dummy variable that has a value of 1 for LBO firms and a value of 0 for control firms. LBOs were identified as delistings on COMPUSTAT and confirmed using the Wall Street Journal Index and/or Predicasts, and are those among the largest 1000 manufacturing firms for which line of business data is available. Each LBO firm was matched with a control public firm on the basis of firm size, the identity of the firm's core business, and total firm diversification.

variable_name: Change in firm sales and employment
description: Firm growth was measured using changes in firm revenues and number of employees during the 3-year postbuyout period. Percent changes in sales and employment are also reported. Changes were measured from the year preceding the LBO to 3 years after the LBO.

Change in total diversification was measured using the Jacquemin-Berry Entropy measure of diversification, estimated as the sum over lines of business of P_i ln(1/P_i), where P_i is the share of total firm sales of the ith line of business. Following Palepu (1985), total diversification is measured using the 4-digit SIC lines of business of the firm to estimate P_i. Change is measured as the absolute change during the 3-year postbuyout period.

Change in unrelated diversification is measured with the same entropy formula, estimated using the 2-digit SIC lines of business of the firm to estimate P_i. Change in unrelated diversification is measured as the absolute change during the 3-year postbuyout period.

variable_name: Change in periphery business sales and employment
description: Changes in sales and employment of the firm's periphery business portfolio were measured for the 3-year postbuyout period. The periphery business portfolio is those 4-digit SIC lines of business that are not in the same 2-digit SIC as the core business, where the core business is the largest 4-digit SIC business in terms of sales. Establishment-level data on sales and employment come from TRINET.

variable_name: Change in core business sales and employment
description: Changes in sales and employment of the firm's core business portfolio were measured for the 3-year postbuyout period. The core business portfolio is all 4-digit SIC activities that share the same 2-digit SIC as the core business, where the core business is the largest 4-digit SIC business in terms of sales. Establishment-level data on sales and employment come from TRINET.

variable_name: Change in number of periphery lines of business, periphery additions and deletions
description: Data on the number of 4-digit SICs in the periphery portfolio were taken from establishment-level TRINET data. The number of lines of business are counted as 4-digit SICs that were added (dropped) during each 3-year postbuyout period. Additions to and deletions from the periphery portfolio are also measured in terms of sales and employment.

variable_name: Change in number of core lines of business, core additions and deletions
description: Data on the number of 4-digit SICs in the core portfolio were taken from establishment-level TRINET data. The number of lines of business are counted as 4-digit SICs that were added (dropped) during each 3-year postbuyout period. Additions to and deletions from the core portfolio are also measured in terms of sales and employment.

Local density measure computed as the number of ties among network actors over the maximum number of possible ties, N(N-1)/2, where N is network size. Ties are defined to exist between all investor pairs that co-invested in a venture in the five years up to and including the month prior to the focal investment, and the measure is calculated on the aggregate ego-level network of the syndicate group, including prior syndication relationships among syndicate members, their additional prior syndication partners, and potential alter-alter ties between these partners. The measure ranges from 0 (fully open network) to 1 (fully closed network); descriptive statistics show non-standardized variables, but variables were standardized before inclusion in the regression models.
time_window: five years up to and including the month prior to the focal investment

description: Obtained from the past investment portfolios of all network actors, based on their investments during the five years preceding the focal investment. The technological specialization of each investor in the network is described by a vector of length 32, where a cell describes which fraction of that investor's investments was in startups in a specific subsector of the IT industry. Actors' knowledge similarity is calculated as the average cross-product of the vectors for each pair of network actors. The measure ranges from 0 (fully diverse network) to 1 (fully specialized network).
time_window: five years preceding the focal investment

description: Whether the venture attracted a second round of funding after its first round. Firms active in high-tech sectors typically require several rounds of funding at comparatively short intervals, so receiving a second round signals that the initial investors are happy with the venture's progress or that new, possibly larger and more experienced investors have been attracted. Second-round funding was observed up to the end of 2013, given an average time of 19 months between first- and second-round funding.
time_window: second-round funding observed up to the end of 2013

description: Dichotomous variable that equals 1 in the month that the developer first released app product(s) in the focal product category. For the same developer-month, all other categories the developer could have entered but did not are coded 0. The realized case group contains all developer-month-categories in which an entry occurred, and control cases are all developer-month-category observations in which an entry did not occur.

Built by counting only acquisitions in which the acquirer and the target have overlapping product category(ies). The authors pooled all user reviews in the time window and applied natural language processing to extract the top 100 unique noun keywords of each category, then counted the total number of occurrences where an acquirer's user reviews comentioned the top keywords of the target's category(ies) (comentioning). That count was expressed as a percentage by dividing by the maximum across all sampled acquisitions, and then averaged across overlapping acquisitions in a 3-month moving time window leading up to and including the focal month in a category.

Built by counting only acquisitions in which the acquirer and the target do not have any overlapping product category. Using the same comentioning procedure as for user-side EOSL, the total number of occurrences where an acquirer's user reviews comentioned the top keywords of the target's category(ies) was divided by the maximum across all sampled acquisitions, and the resulting score was averaged across nonoverlapping acquisitions in a 3-month moving time window leading up to and including the focal month in a category.

Built by counting only acquisitions in which the acquirer and the target have overlapping product category(ies). An SDK-to-category matrix was constructed from all SDKs adopted by all apps in the time window, where each cell is an SDK's percentage of usage in a category; a composite measure combines the acquirer's frequency of usage of an SDK and that SDK's percentage of usage in the target's category, summed across all SDKs of the acquirer and all categories of the target. The measure was aggregated to the category level by averaging across the overlapping acquisitions in the 3-month moving time window, and scaled down by 1000.

Built by counting only acquisitions in which the acquirer and the target have no overlapping product category. Using the same SDK-to-category matrix and composite measure of SDK fungibility (the acquirer's frequency of SDK usage times the SDK's percentage of usage in the target's category, summed across all SDKs and target categories), the measure was aggregated to the category level by averaging across the nonoverlapping acquisitions in the 3-month moving time window, and scaled down by 1000.

Seven items answered by the joint venture CEO on a 7-point scale (1 = not true, 7 = very true), covering acts such as controlling the process of importing material or equipment and exporting outputs without sharing true price information, roping in or lobbying key personnel of the Chinese party, blocking key technologies or knowledge, controlling the joint venture's information systems in accounting, finance, marketing and operations, controlling foreign currency financing and cash flows, seeking solutions in its own best interests when conflicts arise, and giving priority to its unilateral benefits. Communality estimates range from 0.89 to 0.96 and Cronbach's alpha is 0.82.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = not true to 7 = very true)

description: Seven items answered by the joint venture CEO on a 7-point scale (1 = not true, 7 = very true), addressing the extent to which the Chinese party controls local distribution, local marketing and local outsourcing, ropes in or lobbies key personnel of the foreign party, controls relations with local government agencies, controls local currency financing and cash flows, seeks solutions in its own best interests, places its key personnel in key positions, and gives priority to its unilateral benefits. Communality estimates range from 0.89 to 0.93 and Cronbach's alpha is 0.83.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = not true to 7 = very true)

description: Measured from archival data in two steps: first the standard deviation of an industry's sales growth, output growth, and profit growth for 3 years (2000-2002), and then the geometric average of the three standard deviations. Standard deviation is used as a common measure of volatility, and growth ratios rather than absolute values are used because the setting is a fast-growing emerging market.

The inverse average score of information availability, accuracy, comprehensibility, and analyzability, each of which was rated along seven sub-items (economic, regulatory, socio-cultural, technological, customer demand, competition, and supply) on a 7-point scale by the joint venture's deputy general manager. The measure is inversely coded so that higher values indicate greater unverifiability.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = very low to 7 = very high)

description: A multi-item survey construct developed from the authors' own theoretical explanations and prior studies of business law enactment and enforcement in emerging economies. Responses were given by the joint venture's deputy general manager on a 7-point scale, and the measure is inversely coded so that higher values indicate greater law unenforceability.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = very weak to 7 = very strong)

description: The compound growth rate (%) of the respective industry's sales from 2000 to 2002, based on the China Statistical Yearbooks.
A dummy variable coded 1 if the joint venture is local market-focused and 0 otherwise (export-oriented), obtained from the CD-ROM Directory of Foreign-Invested Enterprises.
Average return on investment between 2000 and 2002, based on the survey information received from joint venture CEOs.
Average sales growth (%) over the period 2000 to 2002, based on the survey information received from joint venture CEOs.
The CEO's overall satisfaction with joint venture achievement over the period from 2000 to 2002, measured on a 5-point scale from 1 (very unsatisfied) to 5 (extraordinarily satisfied).
scale: 5-point scale (1 = very unsatisfied to 5 = extraordinarily satisfied)

variable_name: Industry structural instability, information unverifiability, and law unenforceability
description: Environmental volatility is operationalized as three separate variables: industry structural instability (archival standard deviations of industry growth), information unverifiability (inverse average of information availability, accuracy, comprehensibility, and analyzability), and law unenforceability (multi-item survey construct).

The extreme certainty measure was first compared to the achieved success factor measure for each success factor the respondent identified. An individual was overconfident on a given success factor if he or she received an extreme certainty score of 1 but the subsequent achieved success factor score was below 4. The composite overconfidence measure was the percentage of success factors for which each respondent was overconfident.
time_window: certainty at product launch; achieved success 18 months later

description: The response for each success factor was coded either extreme certainty (1) or not (0). Extreme certainty included statements like "I have no doubt," "definitely," "completely sure," and "absolutely positive"; responses indicating some window of doubt, such as "maybe," were coded 0. The final extreme certainty score was the percentage of times a manager was coded 1 for each success factor he or she had identified.

The extent to which each new product was market-pioneering was measured using a coding procedure based on other studies of pioneering, applied to interview statements and all other product documentation. The coding categories covered how the product differed from competitive offerings, what distribution channels the manager planned to use, which customers the product targeted, how those customers currently were meeting their needs, and when other companies introduced products within the same market category. Conflicting evidence was resolved by asking follow-up questions. The final coding ranged from 1, "not at all pioneering," to 4, "very pioneering."
scale: 1 = not at all pioneering to 4 = very pioneering

description: Initial success factors were matched to second-phase survey data on the product introduction's success, captured by six multi-item scales: five two-item scales and one three-item scale. Managers responded to each item on a seven-point Likert-type scale where 1 represented "strongly agree" and 7 represented "strongly disagree"; any score lower than 4, the midpoint, indicated that the firm had to some degree failed to achieve success in that factor. The final measure was the percentage of the success factors originally mentioned by the respondent that were subsequently achieved.
scale: percentage of originally mentioned success factors achieved

description: A cumulative count of a professor's Financial Times 50 (FT50) publications. Since FT50 publications affect overall business school rankings, business schools generally tend to incentivize publications in these outlets and consider them top tier publications. Publication data were collected by querying all publications for each professor and retaining only peer-reviewed publications.

A dummy variable that takes on a value of 1 in any year where the individual served as an associate dean, and a value of 0 otherwise. Data on all ADs were hand-collected from all the schools in the sample and their CVs were used to identify and code their years of service in AD positions.
scale: binary (1 = served as AD in that year, 0 otherwise)

description: The natural log of the professor's annual financial compensation. Salaries were logged to adjust for any skew in the distribution. Most universities reported a nine-month base salary, but a few reported total annual compensation (including summer support), which was addressed through a school fixed effect.

One of two measures of innovative differentiation; it employed scales assessing product innovation, new-product development expenditures, and strategic aggressiveness towards competitors. Each of these three dimensions was scored and weighted equally and then averaged. The strategic composite variables were suggested by Miller (1986, 1987a). The CEOs completed the strategy questions with the help of the interviewers, who explained the strategic scales during the interviews.

The second measure of innovative differentiation used only purely quantitative measures of R & D and new-product commercialization expenses as a percentage of sales. It was used to measure only the most complex type of innovation, that manifested by R & D and product development and commercialization expenses. All analyses were conducted for both kinds of innovative differentiation. In the performance equations only the cost of innovation was used, to avoid multicollinearity between the two measures.

Composite measure of Porter's strategy dimensions in which the set of items gauged advertising intensity, market segmentation, and prestige pricing. The items were those upon which both Hambrick's (1983) and Dess and Davis's (1984) panels of experts agreed, and the composite variables were suggested by Miller (1986, 1987a). The scale was rated by the CEOs during in-person interviews.

Cost leadership was gauged using items assessing cost control, price cutting, minimization of marketing and product development costs, and conservatism in responding to markets. Capacity utilization and indices of production efficiency, integral aspects of Porter's dimension, were not measured because they apply only to manufacturing firms. It is one of the composite measures of Porter's strategy dimensions.

Strategic breadth is one of the composite measures of Porter's strategy dimensions. It is the opposite of Porter's focus strategy, which caters to a circumscribed and specialized segment of a market. A broad strategy requires a firm to confront and acknowledge great heterogeneity, that is, many differences in customer and competitor behavior in its target markets.

Environment was assessed using measures of dynamism, unpredictability, and heterogeneity; dynamism and unpredictability are generally considered the key components of uncertainty and were combined into an overall uncertainty dimension. Because the intercorrelations among all three environmental variables were generally strong, a composite index of uncertainty—unpredictability plus dynamism—was used in all regression equations and the measure of heterogeneity was deleted. Managers select very specific market segments and customers for attention, so the environment was gauged by assessing managers' perceptions of their actual target markets.

One of the environmental scales, taken with all the other environmental variables from Miller (1983). Unpredictability is conceptually distinct from dynamism, though the two are usually correlated. It was assessed through managers' perceptions of their actual target markets.

One of the environmental scales, taken with all the other environmental variables from Miller (1983). Dynamism is conceptually distinct from unpredictability but usually correlated with it; both are generally considered key components of uncertainty. Product innovation is generally more prevalent and useful in dynamic environments, in which products and practices change quickly.

The third environmental dimension assessed alongside dynamism and unpredictability. Heterogeneity refers to many differences in customer and competitor behavior in a firm's target markets. The measure was deleted from the regression equations because of the strong intercorrelations among the environmental variables.

One of four structural variables selected from the four categories of structure—delegation, formalization, specialization, and integration; liaison devices are the measure of integration and, like delegation, were measured broadly. Because strategies were expected to influence actual tasks, the authors were mostly concerned with emergent structure—the procedures that were actually used—rather than with institutional structure, which favored questionnaire over archival research. Structure and environment were reported by general managers and senior vice presidents, not by the CEOs who reported strategy, to avoid spurious correlations from common method variance.

One of the four structural variables measured; according to the hypotheses of this research, technocratization and controls should be the aspects of specialization and formalization most strongly related to strategy. Technocrats are specialized, highly trained professionals such as scientists and engineers. The variable was reported by general managers and senior vice presidents.

The delegation variable was taken from the Aston research (Inkson, Pugh, & Hickson, 1970; Pugh & Hickson, 1976) and was measured broadly. It gauges the distribution of power to make very routine decisions, such as setting delivery dates, overtime hours, and work allocation. The authors note that this dimension had measurement problems and related to no strategy.

One of the four structural variables measured; according to the hypotheses of this research, controls should be the aspect of formalization most strongly related to strategy. Items gauging the use of written policies and organization charts were eschewed, as those aspects of formalization seemed too pervasive and general to relate differentially to Porter's strategies. The variable was reported by general managers and senior vice presidents.

To ensure its unambiguous assessment, performance was measured with three distinct indices: five-year (1978-83) averages of return on investment and growth in net income, obtained from financial statements, and CEOs' comparisons of the profitability of their firms for the last five years to that of their major competitors. The unsuccessful subsample (N = 43) included only firms that scored below the means for each indicator and the successful subsample (N = 37) only firms that scored above the means. Nine firms with mixed high and low performance indicators were deleted from all subgroup and interaction analyses.

variable_name: Liaison devices, technocratization, delegation, and formal controls
description: Organizational structure is measured by four survey-based structural variables, one from each of the categories of delegation, formalization, specialization, and integration: use of liaison devices, technocratization, delegation, and formal controls.

variable_name: Performance subsample split (successful vs unsuccessful firms) and performance-by-predictor interaction terms
description: Strategy-context complementarity is tested by dividing the sample into clearly successful (N=37) and clearly unsuccessful (N=43) firms on ROI, income growth and relative profitability, then comparing the strategy-environment and strategy-structure correlations and regression coefficients across the two groups. Interaction terms formed as the product of each independent variable and a 0/1 performance dummy test whether the associations differ by performance group.
scale: subsample split (0/1 performance dummy) and interaction terms

description: The independent variable organizational status is measured by a dichotomous variable Fortune 500 that equals one if a company is ranked within the Fortune 500 and zero if ranked between the Fortune 501 and 1000. The rank position in the Fortune 1000, Fortune-rank, is the assignment (running) variable of the regression discontinuity design; subtracting the threshold of 500 from the rank positions normalizes it so that the treatment coefficient is the average causal effect. The Fortune ranking in year t is based on the revenues of fiscal year t-1 and is published in the spring of year t.
time_window: ranking year t, based on fiscal year t-1 revenue

description: The baseline dependent variable measures whether the company provides nonpecuniary employment-related benefits with a binary variable indicating if the company has any strength in the pertinent MSCI subcategories. The nonpecuniary subcategories of the employment relations dimension are treated as nonpecuniary, each subcategory being a binary variable indicating if the company has a strength in that area in a given year; the measure equals one if one or more of these subcategories equal one and zero otherwise. The authors treat the ratings as a proxy measure of the amount of effort (and consequently the cost) expended by a company to improve its reputation in nonpecuniary employment-related CSR.
time_window: year t (MSCI score released after the end of year t, about 8 months after the Fortune ranking publication)

description: A measure of the degree to which industry demand diverged from the level of demand that would have been rationally predicted on the basis of historical information. A GARCH model, in which the variance of the error term is a function of the first-order lag of the variance itself and the squared error term, was estimated on the time series of annual industry output for each industry, including the first-order autoregressive term of industry output in the basic regression. The variable is the market forecast error, calculated as the absolute percentage difference between the value of industry output predicted by the model at year t and the observed level of industry output at year t.

Built on patent data and based on the Technology Cycle Time indicator, computed as the median age in years of the U.S. patent references cited on the front page of the patent. Calculated at industry level, it captures the speed of the technology cycle in the industry. For each industry and year the variable is calculated as the inverse of Technology Cycle Time.

variable_name: gamma, the market valuation coefficient of R&D capital (K/A)
description: Estimated within the hedonic model in which the natural log of the ratio of the firm's market value to the book value of tangible assets is regressed on R&D capital over tangible assets, other intangible assets, size and year dummies, and on the cross products between K/A and the measures of market and technological uncertainty (and their squares). The coefficient gamma expresses the market valuation of one currency unit invested in R&D by the firm as compared to one currency unit invested in tangible assets. The estimation of the coefficients on the uncertainty interactions allows the authors to assess how the market valuation of R&D capital varies with market and technological uncertainty.

The R&D capital (K) is computed as a perpetual inventory of the past R&D expenditures, under the standard assumption of a constant annual 15 percent depreciation rate of past R&D expenditures for all firms in the sample. In the regression it is scaled by the book value of the firm's total tangible assets (A).

The level of growth opportunities is measured by the annual growth rate of the industry output, that is the growth rate of the industry output from year t-1 to year t. Data on the aggregate output at industry level were gathered from the STAN database released and maintained by the OECD.

Calculated by recurring to patent self-citations, that is patent citations referring to previous patents owned by the same patentee, considered an indicator of cumulative sequential invention achieved within the same company. The patents selected from the CHI Research database were matched to those of the NBER/Case Western database, in which the percentage of backward citations made to a patent with the same assignee code on the total of the patent backward citations has been calculated. The variable is the average percentage of self-citations at industry level.

Binary measure equal to 1 for observations in the quarters after the policy was introduced in the focal country, and 0 for prior observations. It captures the reduction in customer switching costs brought about by the introduction of mobile number portability.

Binary variable equal to 1 if a firm entered the market up to two years prior to or after the introduction of MNP, and 0 otherwise. The variable includes entry up to two years prior to the regulatory change since regulators typically announce implementation decisions well in advance, allowing entrants to anticipate regulatory changes.

Dichotomous measure equal to 1 if a firm offers both prepaid and postpaid services before MNP, and 0 otherwise. It was constructed based on the average share of a firm's services that were prepaid in all quarters prior to MNP introduction: coded 1 if the average prepaid share was greater than 0% and smaller than 100%, and 0 if the firm offered only prepaid (prepaid share = 100%) or only postpaid (prepaid share = 0%) services.
time_window: all quarters prior to MNP introduction

description: Customer base, measured as the total number of subscribers in quarter t. To reduce the skewness of the outcome variable, the authors computed its natural logarithm.

Revenue, calculated by multiplying a firm's average revenue per user (ARPU) by its total number of subscribers in quarter t. To reduce the skewness of the outcome variable, the authors computed its natural logarithm.

Binary measure equal to 1 if a firm offers both prepaid and postpaid services, and equal to 0 if a firm offers only one of these services in its launch year. It was obtained from the average share of a firm's services that were prepaid during the year it launched its networks, expressed as a percentage; coded 1 if a firm's average prepaid share was any value greater than 0% and smaller than 100% in its launch year.

Each firm's R&D intensity, calculated as R&D expenditure (in dollars) divided by the number of employees, was used as a proxy for innovation strategy. The rate of inflation was adjusted using the Consumer Price Index, and because the distribution is skewed the variable was logarithmically transformed. Firm-level independent variables were taken with a one-year lag.

An indicator variable equal to 1 if an employee holds an R&D job and 0 otherwise. The dataset provides three job family categories: R&D jobs (semiconductor engineers, CAD engineers, development engineers), technical jobs (business systems analysts, data base specialists, application programmers) and administrative jobs (finance, legal, human resources). Job family was controlled for only when testing Hypothesis 1.

Total pay includes virtually all forms of monetary compensation (e.g., base pay, profit sharing awards) and non-monetary compensation (e.g., stock options, employee benefits); monetary values of employee benefit plans represent hypothetical values an employee would need to purchase equivalent plans in the marketplace. The distribution is skewed, so a logarithmic transformation was applied, and the rate of inflation was adjusted using the Consumer Price Index.

Short-term pay includes base pay, profit-sharing award and other short-term incentives (i.e., cash award related to annual corporate, division, unit or individual performance). Base pay is included in short-term pay since it is revised annually or more frequently based on short-term performance and increased skill. The variable was logarithmically transformed because of skewness and adjusted for inflation using the CPI.

Long-term pay includes equity-based compensation (e.g., stock options), and its value was estimated using the Black-Scholes pricing model. The variable was logarithmically transformed because of skewness and adjusted for inflation using the CPI.
The ratio of long-term pay to short-term pay was calculated as the dependent variable to test Hypothesis 2. Because the distribution is skewed, a logarithmic transformation was applied.
Vesting period was measured by number of years. A stock option vesting period is the amount of time it takes for an option to become exercisable.

Four items covering behaviors and actions tied to the modernization program, asked during on-site interviews; responses were limited to 'yes' (the action had been accomplished), 'no', and 'in process', coded 3, 1, and 2 respectively. The items concern the impact of adopting advanced manufacturing technology on business unit or functional strategies, technology agreements with the labor force made in conjunction with the new technology purchase, equality of sacrifice among employee groups in a downturn, and sharing business data directly with blue-collar employees. Cronbach alpha was .66, the average interitem correlation was .32 (n = 30), and the scale mean was 9.2 (s.d. = 2.46).

Five items on behaviors and actions tied to the modernization program, with 'yes', 'no', and 'in process' responses coded 3, 1, and 2. Items cover training in DFA or DFM, a manufacturing representative signing off on design reviews for new products on the system, new structures developed and implemented to coordinate design and manufacturing, job rotation between design and manufacturing engineering, and movement of personnel from design engineering to manufacturing or vice versa. Cronbach alpha was .73, the average interitem correlation was .36 (n = 27), and the scale mean was 9.15 (s.d. = 2.92).

Seven items on procedures and policies introduced for component and material suppliers as part of the modernization program, with 'yes', 'no', and 'in process' responses coded 3, 1, and 2. Items cover just-in-time purchasing or delivery, new purchasing policies, buying integrated components from suppliers, programs to educate suppliers in areas such as statistical process control, contingency supply policies such as identified backup sources, reduced inspection of incoming parts, and supplier award programs. Cronbach alpha was .85, the average interitem correlation was .45 (n = 20), and the mean was 14.6 (s.d. = 4.86).

Eight items developed from the customer section of the interview, asking about behaviors and actions tied to the modernization program, with 'yes', 'no', and 'in process' responses coded 3, 1, and 2. Items cover new contracts with customers, changed net payment periods or terms, changed warranty agreements, including customers in decisions about product development and manufacturing using the new system, joint ventures with customers, sharing the technology of the new system with key customers, changed product standards to benefit customers, and reducing the number of paper forms used for business transactions with customers. The mean of the scale (n = 22) was 13.77 (s.d. = 4.59), the alpha was .79, and the average interitem correlation was .30.

The percentage of target cycle time actually achieved, equivalent to the ratio of actual cycle time in average net parts per hour divided by target cycle time in net parts per hour. The average obtained was 94 percent.

Respondents showed production records indicating two-shift utilization time, that is, time actually producing parts under automated cycle control, on a two-shift (16-hour) basis. The average was 72.3 percent.
A percentage based on comparisons of throughput time intervals before and after a system was installed. The average was 54 percent, and the measure ranged from 0 to 200 percent.

Scrap and rework rates obtained as percentages of total manufacturing costs for the new systems (average 2.91 percent) and for the plants (average 4.26 percent). Higher values indicate worse capacity-related performance, so the measure runs opposite to the construct.

The average time required to change a system over to produce new parts, new part families, or new models, measured in hours. The 19 complete data cases averaged 6.25 hours (s.d. = 22.75 hours); because of the skewed distribution the median of 0.45 hours may be more representative. Higher changeover time indicates less flexibility, so the measure runs opposite to the construct.

The number of part families manufactured with the new system, recorded from production data and validated by examining parts actually being produced in the shops. The average was 40.35 (s.d. = 155.45); the median was 3.5.

variable_name: reduction in service and warranty costs
description: A measure of reduction in service and warranty costs coded 1 for 'yes' and 0 for 'no'. The response was based on warranty cost estimates, service reports filed from the field, and postings of warranty problems, as available.

variable_name: Hierarchical, design-manufacturing, and supplier integration scales
description: Value-added chain integration is measured with three interview-based scales of changes tied to the modernization program: hierarchical integration (four items), design-manufacturing integration (five items), and supplier integration (seven items), with yes/no/in-process responses coded 3, 1, 2.

variable_name: Guttman scale on strategic planning formality
description: Planning formality was measured with a six-statement Guttman scale developed for this purpose by Wood and LaForge (1979), used because it overcomes the irreproducibility weakness often leveled against Likert and Thurstone methods and enables the systematic comparison of firms in terms of the completeness of, commitment to, and utilization of their strategic planning activities. Respondents were asked which of the six statements best described their company's strategic planning activities. The items were numbered 1 through 6, corresponding to an empirically verified natural growth pattern from less to more formality in the planning process.

Respondents were asked to categorize their 'overall grand strategy' in terms of the four generic types developed by Glueck (1980). The scheme was selected because its classifications were sufficiently broad to encompass a wide range of business-specific situations. Operational definitions of the four strategies, based on the work of Hitt, Ireland and Palia (1982), were provided to respondents.

variable_name: firm sales, return on assets (ROA), and return on sales (ROS)
description: Each CEO was asked to provide information on firm sales, return on assets (ROA), and return on sales (ROS) for the beginning and ending years of the 5-year period under study. Forty-two firms provided most or all of this information. These objective figures were correlated with the CEOs' responses on the subjective measurement scales to validate that technique.
time_window: beginning and ending years of the 5-year period under study

variable_name: subjective numerical evaluation of the firm's performance in comparison to its overall industry
description: Each CEO was asked to provide a subjective, numerical evaluation of the firm's performance on four performance dimensions in comparison to its overall industry: after-tax return on total assets, after-tax return on total sales, firm total sales growth over the past 5 years, and overall firm performance/success. The appendix instructs respondents to circle the number from 1 to 5 that best estimates how their firm compares with similar sales volume firms in its industry and region, from the top 20 percent of the industry to the lowest 20 percent. All of the sample firms responded to this question.
time_window: at the present, compared with similar firms in the industry today

description: The unique number of sub-industries invested in by all major corporate shareholders of the focal firm. Only investments where the investors are among the top 10 shareholders with at least 0.5% of the firm's shares are counted. The major investors' investment breadth in year t - 1 is used to predict external cooperation and innovation performance in year t.

The unique number of sub-industries invested in by all major family shareholders of the focal firm. Only investments where the investors are among the top 10 shareholders with at least 0.5% of the firm's shares are counted. The major investors' investment breadth in year t - 1 is used to predict external cooperation and innovation performance in year t.

The number of cooperative projects formed by a firm in each year divided by the average number of cooperative projects in the same sub-industry, so as to measure the intensity of external cooperation relative to the sub-industry. Cooperation data were collected by searching and coding related news in major Taiwanese newspapers and business magazines using the keywords cooperation, alliance, agreement, joint development, and merger and acquisition.

Innovation quantity is measured by the number of patents granted in the United States. To alleviate the truncation bias related to patent counts data, the patent counts are divided by the number of patents applied for in the same technology class, in the same year.

Innovation quality uses forward citations of patents to indicate the technological significance and impact of an invention. To correct for truncation bias related to citation counts data, the citation counts are adjusted by the average citation counts of all patents applied for in the same year and technology class.

An entropy index is used to calculate the product portfolio diversity of app producers, measured with a one-month lag, over the subcategories covered by the producer's apps. Pj(t-1) captures the ratio of the number of apps that belongs to category j to all the apps in the producer's app portfolio at time t-1. The measure captures the extent of product portfolio diversity across a producer's existing product portfolio by considering the number of app categories as well as their relative importance. The full equation is not readable in the extracted text.

Producers generally follow the semantic versioning tradition, which is based on three digits (e.g., Version 3.7.2), in releasing new updates; an increment in the first digit means significant improvements or changes in interface, features and functionalities, an increment in the second digit reflects relatively minor feature changes and/or additions, and an increment in the third digit suggests very marginal changes or bug fixes. To distinguish design iteration from bug fixes, only the number of changes in the first and second digits in month (t) is used as a proxy for design iteration.

The indicator of monthly active user (MAU) measures new product performance. It captures the total number of users who have opened the app within the current month (t), and each individual user is counted once during each month. Log-transformation is used to address the skewness of its distribution.

ATM adoption was modeled with nine indicator variables corresponding to the nine years in which a bank in the sample may have adopted ATMs, from 1971 to 1979. For banks that adopted ATMs between 1971 and 1979, the variable for the year in which the bank first installed ATMs has a value of one and the other adoption variables have a value of zero. Separating ATM adoption by year estimates the incremental average effect of adoption in a given year over that of banks that did not adopt ATMs during the 1971-1979 period.

variable_name: Personal loan market share ratio (M p,i)
description: The dependent variable for market share is a ratio of personal loan market share for bank i in year p to personal loan market share for bank i in 1972, multiplied by 100, where p is the performance measurement year. Market share is measured with statewide data, where the set k comprises all banks in state k and total market share in state k equals 100, and personal loans are loans to individuals for household, family and other personal expenditures, in $ millions. Five observations were obtained for each bank, one for each performance year. The equation as printed in the paper is not readable in the available text.
scale: percentage of 1972 personal loan market share
