time_window: performance years 1979-1983 relative to the 1972 base year

description: The performance measure INC p,i is the change in IBITS (income before income taxes and securities gains or losses) for bank i between 1972 and performance year p, divided by the total assets of bank i in 1972. It represents the change in income per dollar of bank assets. The equation as printed in the paper is not readable in the available text.
time_window: performance years 1979-1983 relative to the 1972 base year

variable_name: Bank size (L i = log10 of total assets in 1972)
description: Bank size is measured by the base 10 logarithm of total assets in 1972, i.e., L i = Log10 (TA 72,i). The authors use the logarithm because bank size spans many orders of magnitude and a change in performance is unlikely to be linearly related to size over so large a range. The same size measure is used to form the interaction terms of ATM adoption and bank size.

The number of female board members at the time of the annual meeting in that calendar year, taken from the board-level data. The authors note that the vast majority of female board members (88% in the sample) are independent directors, and that results were robust to using the percentage of female directors or a categorical variable. The measure is lagged by one year relative to the firm value measure.

A proxy of Tobin's q, a measure of the average value of the firm over the course of the fiscal year, approximated as the sum of market capitalization and total debt over total assets, all annual measures for the fiscal year. The natural log of Tobin's q is used in the analysis because its distribution is closer to normal.

The total score for all KLD STATS strength items in the diversity dimension, with ratings that are binary and give each firm a score of 1 or 0 for any item for which a specific strength was identified. The score for board diversity is excluded from the diversity strengths variable so that board diversity is measured only once. The measure is not lagged because KLD STATS ratings are by design retrospective.

Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which the firm cares about profit goals, measured in the experimental study of investor perceptions. The authors report that firms that appointed a female director were perceived as caring less about profit goals than firms that appointed a male director.

Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which the firm cares about social performance, measured in the experimental study of investor perceptions. Female-appointing firms were perceived as caring more about social performance than firms that appointed a male director, and the effect was strengthened when diversity was made salient.

Calculated as the difference between the consensus of analysts' earnings forecasts and the firm's potential earnings, evaluated at the beginning of the quarter, and standardized by the firm's stock price at the beginning of the quarter. The consensus forecast is the average of the last round of analysts' earnings forecasts prior to the start of the quarter, and potential earnings is estimated with Matsumoto's (2002) method using historical earnings trends and the information contained in stock price returns before the analysts' forecasts. The measure is positive when forecasts are greater than potential earnings and is ex ante, so it is not affected by competitive actions or earnings management during the quarter.

The average ticket price that an airline charges in a city-pair route, divided by the route's distance in miles; a commonly used measure of price or revenue generation in the airline industry that allows comparison of routes of different length. The variable was log-transformed because it was skewed. Higher yield means less aggressive pricing.

The average number of flights per day served by the airline in a city-pair route. If a route comprised two segments or parts of a flight, frequency was calculated as the minimum daily flights of both segments. The variable was log-transformed because it was skewed.

The average percentage of dedicated institutional investor ownership at the beginning and at the end of a quarter, following Bushee's (1998) classification of institutional investors into dedicated, transient and quasi-indexer categories. The authors focused on the dedicated and transient categories, the most differentiated of the three. One-quarter lagged measures were used to avoid reverse causality between competitive behavior and ownership changes.
time_window: one-quarter lagged (average of beginning and end of the quarter)

description: The average percentage of transient institutional investor ownership at the beginning and at the end of a quarter, following Bushee's (1998) classification. Transient institutional investors take small equity positions in many firms and tend to trade frequently. One-quarter lagged measures were used.
time_window: one-quarter lagged (average of beginning and end of the quarter)

description: The dollar value of restricted stocks and unexercisable unexercised stock options owned by the pertinent CEO, following the categorizations proposed by Devers et al. (2008), used to measure long-term, unvested stock-based incentives. Lagged measures were used in the analysis.

The dollar value of stock and exercisable unexercised stock options owned by the pertinent CEO, following Devers et al. (2008), used to measure short-term, vested stock-based incentives. Lagged measures were used in the analysis.

Earnings pressure was dichotomized based on the continuous earnings pressure variable being above zero, that is, forecasts greater than potential earnings. The dummy indicates whether the rival firm in a duopoly market experienced an earnings pressure shock in the subsequent period, for cases where the rival had not experienced earnings pressure in the previous period.
time_window: from period t-1 to the subsequent period

description: The pre-post change in the focal firm's ticket yield in a duopoly market, compared between cases in which the rival experienced an earnings pressure shock (treatment) and cases in which it did not (control). The comparison is made across different airlines, markets and periods in the baseline models and within the same focal firm and period in the matched models.
time_window: pre-post change around the rival's earnings pressure shock

description: The pre-post change in the focal firm's flight frequency in a duopoly market, compared between cases in which the rival experienced an earnings pressure shock (treatment) and cases in which it did not (control).
time_window: pre-post change around the rival's earnings pressure shock

description: Dummy indicating that the rival firm's dedicated institutional investor ownership was higher, that is, above the sample median; used to split the difference-in-differences treatment effect by the rival's ownership composition.
time_window: contemporaneous with the rival's earnings pressure shock

description: Dummy indicating that the rival firm's transient institutional investor ownership was higher, that is, above the sample median; used to split the difference-in-differences treatment effect by the rival's ownership composition.
time_window: contemporaneous with the rival's earnings pressure shock

description: Dummy indicating that the rival firm's CEO held higher unvested stock-based incentives relative to vested incentives; used to split the difference-in-differences treatment effect by the rival's CEO incentive horizon.
time_window: contemporaneous with the rival's earnings pressure shock

description: Dummy indicating that the rival firm's CEO held higher vested stock-based incentives relative to unvested incentives; used to split the difference-in-differences treatment effect by the rival's CEO incentive horizon.
time_window: contemporaneous with the rival's earnings pressure shock

description: The yearly number of subsidiaries that a focal firm has in any given foreign country, used as a proxy for the total equity investment in a host country. The variable is transformed using the natural logarithm to alleviate its skewness. Observations are aggregated at the firm-country-dyad level.

Calculated as the moving standard deviation of absolute voting affinity in the UN General Assembly between two countries for the past 5 years (n = 5). The moving standard deviation is computed from a moving average calculated for each country-to-country dyad. Volatility is lagged by 1 year to limit reverse causality.

Based on UN General Assembly voting: the sum of absolute distances between votes in the voting portfolio for the dyad divided by the maximum distance in voting for the dyad. The value ranges from 0 to 1; 0 indicates that the countries voted opposite each other in a given year, and 1 indicates identical voting patterns. Abstention is counted as half-agreement with a yes or no vote. Level of political affinity is lagged by 1 year.

A time-variant binary variable that equals 1 if a firm has a political connection during an election cycle and 0 if it does not. A firm is politically connected when its political action committee (PAC) donates to a US politician in that election cycle, using campaign finance data on corporate PAC contributions to politicians running for president or for office in the Senate or House of Representatives. PACs are matched with corresponding firms in Compustat and, where firms have multiple PACs, data are aggregated to the firm level.

A dichotomous indicator of whether posting (1) or slotting (0) was used to fill the job. The author was able to unambiguously identify how each job was filled because HealthCo maintains separate systems for posting and slotting. Of internal hires, 3,648 (45 percent) were made through posting and 4,459 (55 percent) through slotting.

A worker's contribution score assesses his or her contribution to the success of the organization, department, or line of business, depending on the job. It is measured on a 1 to 4 scale: 1 = low contribution, 2 = moderate contribution, 3 = full contribution, and 4 = exemplary contribution. The performance measures reflect performance in the first year on the job.
time_window: first year in the new job

description: A worker's competency score assesses his or her skills relative to the job requirements. Each worker receives a score from 1 to 4 (1 = learning, 2 = exhibiting, 3 = demonstrating, 4 = modeling) for each of the eight competencies assigned to the job, which the author averaged to compute a continuous measure of overall competency. The performance measures reflect performance in the first year on the job.
time_window: first year in the new job

description: Managers rank workers in similar jobs as part of an annual calibration process; the ranking is intended to measure overall value to the organization, accounting for previous performance and future potential. The author used these rankings to create two dichotomous measures of relative performance: whether a worker is ranked in the top quartile (top 25 percent) or bottom quartile (bottom 25 percent) of his or her cohort in the first year in the new job.
time_window: first year in the new job

description: A dichotomous measure indicating whether a worker exits the organization within one year of moving to a new job. Voluntary and involuntary turnover were not distinguished, as both are indicators of poor matches.
time_window: one year after the move to a new job

description: A dichotomous measure indicating whether a worker exits the organization within two years of moving to a new job. Voluntary and involuntary turnover were not distinguished, as both are indicators of poor matches.
time_window: two years after the move to a new job

description: A dichotomous measure of whether a worker was promoted within 2 years after being hired into the new job. Time to promotion varies across jobs, so the author created cutoff-based dichotomous measures.

A dichotomous measure of whether a worker was promoted within 3 years after being hired into the new job. Time to promotion varies across jobs, so the author created cutoff-based dichotomous measures.

The natural logarithm of the total annual compensation the employee should expect to receive for the year, as reported in HealthCo's personnel records. Expected compensation includes salary and, for bonus-eligible roles, the expected bonus, so that the expected compensation for a worker with a salary of $60,000 in a role eligible for a 10-percent bonus is recorded as $66,000. The recorded figure reflects the total compensation an individual should expect to earn during the year and is the figure he or she is most likely to negotiate.

The number of female directors in a given firm-year divided by total board size. In robustness tests the authors dummy-coded this variable with a value of 1 if there was at least one female director on the board, generating similar results.

The number of acquisitions in a given firm-year; in the sample this ranged from 0 to 9. Acquisitions counted are those that had been completed, where the acquirer controlled less than 50 percent of the target's shares prior to the announcement and 100 percent after the transaction, and where the deal value exceeded US$1 million.
The total value of all transactions in a given firm-year, scaled by the annual sales of the acquirer.

A dummy variable indicating whether the firm's official language is a strong- or weak-FTR language. It is obtained by manually checking the focal firm's headquarters location and the official language of that region; for countries with multiple official languages the language spoken in the region where the firm is located is used, and if the region is itself multilingual the language use is coded based on characteristics of top management and significant investors. The classification of strong and weak FTR follows the EURORTYP and Chen's (2013) strong-criterion classification.

MSCI's Intangible Value Assessment program measures a corporation's environmental and social risks and opportunities, using raw data from corporate documents, environmental groups and other NGOs, trade groups, government databases, periodical searches, and financial analysts' reports. Companies are rated and ranked against their industry peers from international markets, so the rating does not depend on local CSR situations and rules; the data are converted to a relative rating by giving the best performers within their industry sector on a global scale a AAA (top) rating and the worst a CCC (lowest) rating, with the remaining firms rated pro rata between AAA and CCC. Each rating is then converted to a score from six to zero. MSCI constructs a series of 29 CSR ratings for each company.
scale: score from six to zero (CCC to AAA)

description: A firm's total R&D expenditures over its total assets, winsorized at 95%. Data on R&D investment are obtained from Worldscope and the measure is described as a standard way of measuring corporate R&D engagement that aims to capture the uncertainty in future rewards.

Greenberg's (language) Diversity Index, which measures the probability that two people selected from the population at random will have different mother tongues, obtained from the UNESCO World Report.

The KOF Index of Globalization, which measures the degrees of a country's global connectivity, integration, and interdependence in the economic, social, technological, cultural, political, and ecological spheres and has the broadest coverage on countries.

The sum of the holdings of all institutions domiciled in a country different from the one in which the stock is listed, divided by the firm's market capitalization; the data are obtained from the FactSet (Lionshares) database.

The private negotiations period was established by recording the date on which the target and a potential acquirer initiated conversation about a potential acquisition and the subsequent date of its public announcement. The authors captured special board meetings and regularly scheduled board meetings that occurred during this period and in which, according to the acquisition-related SEC filing, the target board discussed an ongoing acquisition. The variable is the ln-transformed number of target board meetings that occurred during private negotiations; the ln transformation was applied after adding one because for some acquisitions no evidence of any target board meeting during private negotiations was found.

Event study methodology was used to calculate cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) of both the acquirer and the target in response to the acquisition announcement, using the market model with a 250-day estimation window and a 7-day event window centered on the acquisition announcement date. Because CARs are percentages of each firm's total market value, the authors then calculated the absolute amount of value captured by the target as the target preannouncement market value in millions of U.S. dollars multiplied by the target CARs during the event window. The total absolute value created in an acquisition was calculated as the sum of the absolute returns accruing to the acquirer and the target, and was used as a control, whereas target value capture is the dependent variable.
time_window: 7-day event window centered on the acquisition announcement date

description: A target director was classified as overboarded if that director sat on three or more other boards in the year prior to the focal acquisition; the variable is a count of the number of overboarded directors on the target board. Board size and composition were hand coded from annual reports and proxy statements of the sampled firms.
time_window: year prior to the year of the focal deal announcement

description: A director was recognized as having acquisition experience if that director had served as a director for another firm that completed a public firm acquisition during the five years prior to the focal acquisition; the variable is a count of the number of such directors on the target board. Director career backgrounds were hand coded from annual reports and proxy statements of the sampled firms.
time_window: year prior to the year of the focal deal announcement; five-year look-back for the experience criterion

description: The variable is a count of the number of female directors on the target board. Director demographics were hand coded from annual reports and proxy statements of the sampled firms.
time_window: year prior to the year of the focal deal announcement

description: A binary variable coded as one if, according to the acquisition-related SEC filing, the acquisition was initiated by the acquirer and as zero if it was initiated by the target.

A binary variable operationalized with Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code-based dissimilarity; it took a value of one for acquisitions of targets that did not conduct their primary business activity in the same industry as the acquirer based on a two-digit SIC code in the year prior to the acquisition and zero otherwise.
A count of all four-digit SIC codes in which the target was active in the year before the acquisition.

The variable Political embeddedness was created based on a charity's organizational and personal political embeddedness, taking the value of 1 if a charity is embedded in organizational or personal political relations, and 0 otherwise. It was assessed from the background of each charity and its senior leadership team.
time_window: annual, 2005-2012; lagged one year in the analyses

description: Organizational political embeddedness was coded 1 if the charity's founding members involved a political or quasi-political entity such as a Political Consultative Conference, labor union, women's federation, federation of returned overseas Chinese, or any entity under the direct leadership of the Communist Party. If no such entity was involved, the variable was coded 0. The variable was time invariant.
time_window: as of founding; time invariant over 2005-2012

description: A charity's Personal political embeddedness was quantified as a count of positional interlocking ties between the charity and the political entities involving the charity's senior leaders (e.g., Chairman, Vice-chairman, General-secretary) each year. A tie was recorded if a charity's senior leader held or had previously held a senior position in a key unit of the government; definitions of senior political positions are given in Table 2, Note c.
time_window: annual, 2005-2012; lagged one year in the analyses

description: Total donations is the sum of corporate donations received annually by a charity, extracted from the philanthropic foundations' annual reports from 2005 to 2012. The authors took the logarithmic form of the variable to reduce skewness.

To distinguish between foreign and domestic corporate donors, the authors disaggregated Total donations into donations from domestic firms and donations from foreign firms. Donations from domestic firms is the volume of corporate donations received from domestic corporate donors, and the logarithmic form was taken to reduce skewness.

To distinguish between foreign and domestic corporate donors, the authors disaggregated Total donations into donations from domestic firms and donations from foreign firms. Donations from foreign firms is the volume of corporate donations received from foreign corporate donors, and the logarithmic form was taken to reduce skewness.
Donor identity is operationalized by disaggregating total corporate donations to a charity into donations from domestic firms and donations from foreign firms, each logged.

Measured as the difference between an app's topic distribution and the average topic distribution for all apps in the same category. Topic distributions come from applying Latent Dirichlet Allocation to app descriptions, so that each app is characterized by a probabilistic distribution over topics. The measure is computed at each month so that the prototypical representation of a category can change over time and apps can be repositioned. The equation presented for this measure is not readable in the text, so the exact formula is not reproduced.
time_window: computed each month, May 2016 to October 2017

description: App performance is measured as the monthly number of downloads, taken from proprietary data provided by Apptopia. The authors used the natural logarithm of the number of downloads (plus 1) to reduce the skewness in this variable. The measure is described as directly reflecting the app's legitimacy with customers and as applicable consistently to paid and free apps.

Apps are classified by their revenue model as either paid or free; the estimation sample contains 72,017 paid and 196,019 free apps. Separate sets of models are estimated for the paid and the free samples.

Coded as a dummy variable capturing whether the app description contained an explicit privacy notice that elucidates how and why the app uses customer data. Coding was based on searching the app description for key phrases such as 'data privacy', 'data protection', 'privacy policy', 'privacy statement', 'respect your privacy', and 'your privacy is important'. The variable is coded '1' if one or more of those key phrases was present and zero otherwise.

Operationalized as a dummy variable indicating whether a free app uses freemium. Two ways were observed: an app can offer a menu of upgrades available for in-app purchase, or a developer may associate a free app with a premium version made available as a separate paid app, matched by subset detection of shared titles and cosine similarity of descriptions. Coded '1' if a free app had in-app purchases or was associated with a paid app, and zero otherwise.

Market-based performance measure computed as market value divided by total assets. The authors consider it a forward-looking measure since it incorporates investors' expectations about firm performance. It is the dependent variable in all estimated models.

Continuous measure of family influence set equal to the degree of family ownership for firms where the family owns at least five percent of the firm's shares and the ultimate controlling shareholder is a family or an individual directly involved in the firm's executive leadership (CEO, General Manager, Board Chairman, or Vice Board Chairman). All firms that do not meet both conditions are considered non-family firms and have Family Influence equal to zero. Higher values indicate increasing family influence; of the 2,032 firm-year observations, 894 relate to family firms.

Ratio of a province's actual speed of reforms to its fastest speed of reforms. The actual speed of reforms for province j in year t is the difference between the current year's scope of reforms and the 2003 scope of reforms divided by the years elapsed since 2003, so it is calculated for 2004-2009 because the denominator is zero in 2003. The fastest reform speed is the maximum scope of reforms (one) minus the province's 2003 scope of reforms, that is, the speed at which a full market economy could be reached in one year. More positive (negative) values mean the province is implementing faster (slower) reforms.

Performance is measured as ROA, calculated as the net income of the focal subsidiary divided by its total assets in each year. Total assets are controlled for in the regressions to limit the possibility that performance improvements are a function of decreases in assets, given that ROA could vary because either the numerator or the denominator varies.
scale: ratio of net income to total assets

description: Cultural distance between the parent firm's home country and the U.S. is measured using four Hofstede dimensions as per Kogut and Singh (1988); the long-term orientation dimension is excluded because it is available for only a small subset of the countries in the sample. The specification compares each cultural dimension in country i with the same dimension in the U.S., scaled by the variance on that dimension across all countries; the published formula block is unreadable and is not reproduced.

Economic distance is the absolute value of the difference between the foreign firm's home-country financial market orientation and the U.S. orientation. Market orientation is a country-specific ratio of market capitalization (scaled by GDP) divided by bank credits to the private sector (scaled by GDP); a greater value indicates a greater difference between the financial market of the home country and that of the U.S.

Regulatory distance is built from four dimensions of banking regulation (Bank Activity Regulations, Banking/Commerce Mixing Regulations, Competition Regulations, and Capital Regulations) for which public data were available. Each regulatory dimension in country i is compared with the same dimension in the U.S. and scaled by the variance on that dimension across all countries; the published formula block is unreadable and is not reproduced. For all periods from 1978-2000 the 1998-2000 survey measures are applied, and the 2001-2003 survey data are used for 2001-2006.
time_window: 1998-2000 survey measures applied to 1978-2000; 2001-2003 survey data for 2001-2006

description: Political distance is the absolute value of the difference in political volatility, measured by the CHECKS index (the number of veto players in a political system, adjusted for political cohesiveness), between the firm's home country and the U.S. A greater value indicates a greater difference between the political environment of the home country and that of the U.S.

For each foreign bank subsidiary, its asset strategy in each of eight asset classes is computed as a proportion of total assets; the mean asset strategy of all U.S. banks in the same MSA is computed in the same way. The subsidiary's proportions are compared with this MSA mean, divided by the standard deviation of the asset strategy of U.S. banks in the MSA, and multiplied by -1 for ease of interpretability. A larger value reflects greater levels of local isomorphism and a smaller value lower levels. The published formula block is unreadable and is not reproduced.

Host country experience is the cumulative number of bank-years of operation in the U.S. at the parent bank level at time t. It reflects experience with any U.S. banking operations established by the parent bank, not restricted to commercial banking operations and not limited to the focal subsidiary, and it accounts for local experience accumulated prior and subsequent to the opening of the parent bank's full-fledged U.S. subsidiary.

Lagged subsidiary profit-type return, a BEA-calculated measure based on reported net income that is gross of foreign income taxes, excludes capital gains and losses and income from equity investments, and reflects adjustments converting profits from a financial accounting basis to an economic accounting basis. Because profits can fluctuate from year to year, two- and three-year average performance measures were examined, and the two-year results are reported. The two-year average performance variable has been scaled by a two-year average sales variable in all models, and predictors are lagged.

Binary variable that takes a value of 1 when a parent firm divests from a foreign affiliate in year t and 0 otherwise. Divestments that result from parent firm death, such as a merger with another U.S. company, were excluded; parent firms need to be in existence in the year after the divestment. The event of divesting is the discrete event that occurs with a certain hazard rate, and observations that are not divested are censored and remain in the analysis.

Lagged three-year average GDP per-capita growth rate of the country in which the subsidiary is located. The three-year average growth rate was created for each country using information from the annual World Development Indicators from the World Bank.

Lagged political constraint index from Henisz's (2000) POLCONV index for the country in which the subsidiary is located, measured annually. In the index the highest score of 1.0 represents the most constraints in the political system (meaning the most stable) and 0 represents the least constraints in the system (and the most unstable).

Lagged three-year mean volatility in the real exchange rate of the country of the subsidiary operation, calculated as the standard deviations in real exchange rate changes over the prior three-year period. Real exchange rates were created using nominal exchange rates deflated by the price index ratio between the United States and host countries using CPI data.

Dummy variable identifying unrelated product market activities in subsidiaries. A firm's core industry is defined as the largest three-digit SIC business in terms of total firm sales, and unrelated businesses are those business activities that are not in the same three-digit SIC code as the firm's core business. If a subsidiary has the majority of its sales in a different three-digit SIC code it was coded as unrelated; distribution-only subsidiaries of the main industry of the parent were coded as related, so the variable takes the value 1 for unrelated operations.

Subsidiary R&D intensity, used to capture intangible sunk costs; measured as R&D expenditures divided by total subsidiary sales. R&D investments are treated as sunk-cost investments because they create intangible, highly firm-specific knowledge assets that are tightly coupled to a firm. The measure is lagged.
Total investments in plant, property, and equipment divided by total subsidiary assets, used to capture more tangible sunk-cost investments in the subsidiary. The measure is lagged.

Measures the number of licensed plants by firm i, in product j, and geographical area k, over the period 1986-96. Only the small subset of the 153 firms that possesses technological competencies in a given product j is in the risk set for that product, and this subset changes for each product.

Counts the number of firms, excluding firm i, that have licensed a given process technology for producing product j in the period 1980-85 or have built a plant in-house using their own technology. This is used as a proxy for the number of potential licensors of that technology in the period 1986-96, and is estimated with the number of potential licensors varying across j and across jk.

Computed as the ratio between the capacity built by firm i in product j and geographical area k and the total capacity in jk. Because market shares in the mid 1980s were not available, they were reconstructed using the information on capacity investment provided by the database. Installed capacity may not always be a good proxy for sales, although the authors see no reason to believe the difference biases the findings.

A principal component of three proxies for technology-specific product differentiation: the number of different feedstocks that can be used to fabricate a given product standardized by the size of the world market of that product; a Herfindahl index at the sub-sector level computed from plant counts at the product level, taking the value 0 if the sub-sector has homogeneous products and 1 if products are totally differentiated; and the average cost in U.S. dollars per unit of capacity installed in each product. The authors note that the database did not provide a direct measure, forcing them to use proxies.

Computed as the number of downstream chemical producers active in product j and geographical market k prior to 1986. The authors note that this proxy is likely to underestimate the number of potential licensees, as it does not account for entry.

A dichotomous variable indicating whether the firm filed for bankruptcy. Sample 1 bankrupt firms constitute the largest bankruptcy filings during the years 1973-82; the control firms did not file for bankruptcy during that same period.

A dichotomous variable indicating whether the firm filed for bankruptcy. Firms filing for bankruptcy reorganization were identified from Predicast's F&S Index of Companies, and bankrupt and control firms were matched by firm size, industry, and the year in which the bankrupt firm filed.

In any one year for a given company, CEO change is a dichotomous variable: either the CEO was replaced in that year or not. Over the 5-year period of the study the variable has a different nature; for this group of companies firms had a range of no change to three CEO changes over the period.
scale: dichotomous in any one year; count of changes over the 5-year period
time_window: the year the bankruptcy was filed, 2 years, and 4 years prior to filing

description: In any one year for a given company, CEO change is a dichotomous variable: either the CEO was replaced in that year or not. Over the 5-year period of the study the variable has a different nature; for this group of companies firms had a range of no change to three CEO changes over the period.
scale: dichotomous in any one year; count of changes over the 5-year period
time_window: the year the bankruptcy was filed, 2 years, and 4 years prior to filing

description: Board turnover, for any given year, is a continuous variable: the number of board members who left the board over the 1-year period. In the aggregate for the 5-year period the variable is simply the total number of director changes over that period.
scale: count of directors leaving the board
time_window: the year the bankruptcy was filed, 2 years, and 4 years prior to filing

description: Board turnover, for any given year, is a continuous variable: the number of board members who left the board over the 1-year period. In the aggregate for the 5-year period the variable is simply the total number of director changes over that period.
scale: count of directors leaving the board
time_window: the year the bankruptcy was filed, 2 years, and 4 years prior to filing

description: Board composition is traditionally operationalized as the proportion of outside directors to total directors. It is measured on three occasions prior to the bankruptcy filing.
time_window: the year the bankruptcy was filed, 2 years, and 4 years prior to filing

description: Board composition is traditionally operationalized as the proportion of outside directors to total directors. It is measured on three occasions prior to the bankruptcy filing.
time_window: the year the bankruptcy was filed, 2 years, and 4 years prior to filing

description: A finer distinction in which independent directors are outside directors who were appointed prior to the current CEO, while interdependent directors are those outside directors appointed by the current CEO as well as those directors currently serving in the management of the firm. This approach is relied on in subsequent analyses.
time_window: the year the bankruptcy was filed, 2 years, and 4 years prior to filing

description: A finer distinction in which independent directors are outside directors who were appointed prior to the current CEO, while interdependent directors are those outside directors appointed by the current CEO as well as those directors currently serving in the management of the firm. This approach is relied on in subsequent analyses.
time_window: the year the bankruptcy was filed, 2 years, and 4 years prior to filing

description: The duality is binary: either the CEO concurrently serves as board chairperson or not. It is measured at three periods over the course of 5 years.
time_window: the year the bankruptcy was filed, 2 years, and 4 years prior to filing

description: The duality is binary: either the CEO concurrently serves as board chairperson or not. It is measured at three periods over the course of 5 years.
time_window: the year the bankruptcy was filed, 2 years, and 4 years prior to filing

description: The dependent variable is simply the logarithm of the hazard rate, that is, the log of the probability that the firm exits at time t, given that it survived until t-1. Exit is defined as firm closure, and because the data come from an annual survey durations are grouped into yearly intervals. A firm is classified as a closure only if it is absent from the files for at least two years; firms absent for one year were treated as active, with employment imputed as the average of the adjacent years.

Firm size measured by employment, the number of workers, computed for every year the firm appears in the data. In the specification that separates founding from current conditions, the current effect is captured by the change in the variable since birth (the current value minus the founding value).

The firm's employment (number of workers) in its founding year, entered in the model as the founding condition x0. Its regression coefficient is allowed to decay with age, so that the effect of founding size may be transitory rather than permanent.

The proportion of college graduates among each firm's labor force, computed for every year the firm appears in the data. Because there is no information available for the workforce for the 1990 survey, human capital variables were interpolated for that year by taking the average value for 1989 and 1991.
The proportion of college graduates in the firm's labor force in its founding year, entered in the model as the founding condition x0 and allowed to decay with age.
Gross domestic product (GDP) growth, used to characterize the macroeconomic environment at each moment during the firm's life. GDP growth is available from official sources.
GDP growth in the year in which the firm was founded, entered in the model as the founding condition x0 and allowed to decay with age.
The Herfindhal index of concentration computed for the market in which the firm operates, used as a proxy for the competitive conditions of the market.
The Herfindhal index of concentration of the firm's market in its founding year, entered in the model as the founding condition x0 and allowed to decay with age.

The entry rate defined as the total number of entrants divided by the total number of firms in the (five-digit) industry, used as a proxy for the competitive conditions of the market in which the firm operates.
The entry rate of the firm's (five-digit) industry in the year of the firm's founding, entered in the model as the founding condition x0 and allowed to decay with age.

Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity, computed as 1 minus the sum of the squared proportions of group members in each category. The categories are white, black, Hispanic, Asian, and American Indian, reported for 1995 on an EEO-1 Standard Form 100 included in the questionnaire. The index would have a value of .80 under maximum heterogeneity with five groups, as in this study.

Asset growth for fiscal years 1994 and 1995 taken directly from the Sheshunoff Bank Search database. Asset growth for 1994 is the percentage growth in total assets from year-end 1993 through year-end 1994, and asset growth for 1995 covers year-end 1994 through year-end 1995. Higher percentages reflect a growth strategy, and negative percentages reflect asset reduction or a downsizing strategy. A two-year average was used to smooth annual fluctuations produced by the above-normal number of mergers and acquisitions in the banking industry.

Productivity was calculated as the logarithm of net income per employee for year-end 1995. It is described as an intermediate output measure reflecting employee efforts disassociated from variations in product and capital markets, and it follows the labor productivity equation derived by Bartel (1994).

Return on equity for year-end 1996, obtained from the Sheshunoff bank database. The authors describe return on equity as the ultimate measure of the strength of any financial institution and the preferred measure of a bank's financial performance.

A perceptual bottom-line measure in which respondents at year-end 1996 compared their organization's performance over the last 3 years with other organizations that do the same kind of work on four items: marketing, growth in sales, profitability, and market share. Responses were measured on a four-point Likert scale ranging from 1, 'worse,' to 4, 'much better.' The scale alpha was .81, and the measure correlated with return on equity (r = .40) and employee productivity (r = .37).
scale: four-point Likert scale (1 = worse to 4 = much better)

description: Calculated as the difference between two ratios that Trucost developed to assess companies' environmental transparency: absolute disclosure ratio minus weighted disclosure ratio. The absolute disclosure ratio is the proportion of relevant environmental indicators for which a company publicly discloses quantitative worldwide figures, where the denominator is the number of environmental indicators relevant to the company based on its industries. The weighted disclosure ratio incorporates the extent of environmental impact associated with each environmental indicator. Positive values indicate that the company disclosed its less harmful indicators; the measure approaches its maximum value of 1 when a company discloses many less harmful indicators but few if any of its more harmful indicators, and tends toward the minimum value of -1 for a company disclosing just the few indicators that matter most.

Trucost's estimate of environmental impact. The company's annual revenues are allocated to a subset of a standardized set of 464 industries based on data from the FactSet Fundamentals database, corporate annual reports, corporate regulatory filings, and company feedback. Trucost's model then estimates the company's total annual tonnage of pollution emissions (to air, land, and water) and resources consumed based on the company's revenues from each industry, using environmental factors derived from pollution release and transfer registries and economic input-output models. These physical quantities are multiplied by environmental damage cost factors drawn from academic research on the pricing of environmental externalities; the total represents the cost of the environmental damage created by the company in a particular year in millions of U.S. dollars. For the analysis the authors use the log of Trucost's environmental damage cost.
scale: log of millions of U.S. dollars

description: The number of International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) member organizations operating in each company's headquarters country in 2003, the year before the sample period, divided by that country's population in 2004 measured in millions. IUCN is an international environmental organization with more than 1,000 member organizations, including the most significant international environmental NGOs.

Annual national averages of political rights and civil liberties scores from the annual Freedom in the World reports, which assess civil liberties (such as freedom of expression and assembly) and political rights (such as free elections). The authors reverse-coded the results so that higher values reflect more civil liberties and political rights.

The KOF Index of Globalization, calculated annually for 208 countries, which incorporates a country's social, economic, and political integration with other countries. Social integration reflects the flow of international information and norms through measures of personal contacts (such as telephone traffic, international tourism, and the proportion of population that are foreigners), information flows (such as the prevalence of Internet access), and cultural proximity (such as the import and export of books as a percent of GDP). Economic integration is measured by trade flow indicators and trade restrictions; political integration is represented by measures such as the number of foreign embassies in the country and the number of UN peace missions in which the country has participated.

variable_name: listed on a foreign stock exchange
description: A dichotomous variable built from stock exchange listings data, coded 1 for companies that listed their stock on an exchange outside their headquarters country in a given year, and 0 otherwise.

Rumelt's nine sub-categories reduced to the four originally developed by Wrigley: single, dominant, related and unrelated business firms. Firms were classified from Rumelt's (1978) classifications for the 1970-74 period where available, and the remaining firms were classified by the authors using Rumelt's classification procedure. Firms changing strategy classification during the five-year period were eliminated. In the regressions strategy was included as a nominal variable represented by dummy variables.

Owner's equity divided by invested capital (E/C), where invested capital is represented by the book value of total assets less current liabilities; the authors selected it because it measures how the business is financed long-term, without the fluctuations of short-term financing. Values are the arithmetic average of the annual ratios of E/C over the period of the study, a smoothing that the authors say captures the target nature of leverage ratios. The measure is the inverse of what is commonly known as leverage, so a high value indicates low debt levels.

Average return on assets (ROA) over the period of the study. The measure uses earnings before debt charges and the tax-reducing effects of debt charges, so that return is not confounded with the firm's leverage; the authors note that Bettis (1981) supported the use of ROA as a profit measure.
Average total sales over the study period. The authors chose this measure because Ferri and Jones (1979) found it discriminated among leverage classes of firms better than other size measures tested.

Average growth rate calculated using a regression fit to a uniform growth model, rather than a simple arithmetic average of yearly growth rates, which the authors say yields a consistent upward bias. Rumelt (1974) and Toy et al. (1974) also used this measure.

Ratio of the average of net fixed assets to total book assets over the time period of the study. The authors state that averaging is a better indicator of the use of fixed assets than any single-period measure, and that Ferri and Jones (1979) found this measure provided the most reliable and significant discrimination among leverage groups compared with other operating leverage measures.

Coefficient of variation of profit over the study period. The authors chose the coefficient of variation because it allows earnings variation to be de-coupled from the absolute size of earnings, and because it is the variability of earnings which affects the ability of a firm to service debt.

Because the study uses a difference-in-differences design, the explanatory variable of interest is an interaction between the treated group and the posttreatment period. Post-intervention is a binary indicator set to 1 if the year was 2002-2004, and rival complementor is a binary indicator set to 1 if the firm competed in a complementor market in which Microsoft's in-house complementor had high market share. To avoid collinearity with firm and year fixed effects, only the Post-Intervention x Rival Complementor interaction is included in the fixed effects regressions, and its coefficient captures the effect of the antitrust intervention on the treated group of complementors.

Binary indicator set to 1 if the firm competed in a complementor market in which Microsoft's in-house complementor had high market share (developer tools, database management) and 0 otherwise. Microsoft held 16% market share in database management (#3 vendor) and 15% market share in developer tools (#2 vendor), while it held a substantially weaker or even insignificant position in application integration (0.3% market share), network and system management (1.6% market share), and security (less than 1% market share), which form the control group.

Yearly counts of the patents each firm had applied for (and later received). Patent data were collected using the NBER database and the authors added citations from the USPTO. The authors argue that patents are a particularly appropriate measure of innovation because each patent is novel, nonobvious and useful, and that patenting is standard in software during their study period.

Return on sales, measured annually for each firm. The authors state that ROS is more appropriate than alternatives such as return on assets because software firms rely primarily on intangible assets and tend to reinvest their profits to continuously grow the business. Firm data including profits were collected from Compustat, supplemented by SEC filings and CapitalIQ.

Binary indicator set to 1 if the firm had less than 10% market share prior to the intervention and 0 otherwise. To contrast low- versus high-share firms, the authors compared split samples, distinguishing low-market-share (less than 10%) complementors from high-share ones. Pre-intervention market share information came from Gartner market share data.

Spline variable equal to the difference between social performance and the social performance aspiration when performance is below aspiration, and zero otherwise; it is multiplied by negative one so that larger values represent a larger social performance shortfall. Social performance is the Refinitiv ESG Combined Score, derived by discounting the firm's ESG Score with its ESG Controversies Score. The aspiration is a weighted moving function of size-weighted peer performance in the same two-digit SIC industry and the firm's historical aspiration, with weights of 0.6 for social comparison and 0.6 for the historical component. Explanatory variables are lagged by one year.

Spline variable that equals zero for all observations in which performance is below aspiration and equals social performance minus aspiration when performance is at or above aspiration, so higher values indicate better social performance relative to the aspiration. It is built from the same Refinitiv ESG Combined Score and the same weighted aspiration model as the below-aspiration variable, and is lagged by one year.

CSR is measured with the Refinitiv ESG Score, which aggregates over 400 distinct metrics into ten categories and then into three main pillar scores; higher ESG scores indicate greater CSR activities. Change in CSR is defined as the difference between the CSR score at time t + 1 and the score at time t, so a positive value indicates an increase in CSR activities in the following year.

CSI is measured with the Refinitiv ESG Controversies Score, which is derived exclusively from external global media sources and captures the severity and frequency of negative ESG incidents such as lawsuits, fines, and media scandals across 23 controversy categories; lower scores indicate more severe or more frequent negative events. The reported score is reverse-coded by subtracting it from 100 so that higher values represent higher levels of CSI. Change in CSI is the difference between the CSI score at time t + 1 and the score at time t.

Perceptions of the firm's sustainability image were measured with three items from Kissel and Büttgen's (2015) corporate image scale, rated on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). The scale showed a reliability of 0.96.

Charity donations were used to capture CSR. Participants read that Tech Corp had a $10 million discretionary budget for donations to CERES, a sustainability-focused non-profit organization, and that the firm donated $5 million to CERES last year; they then indicated their chosen donation for this year on a $0-$10 million slider and could donate more, less, or the same amount.

A pollution-reduction task adapted from Sachdeva et al. (2009) captured CSI. Participants read that Tech Corp's manufacturing facilities release pollutants through smokestacks and that emissions can be reduced by running air filters at a monetary cost, and that the firm operated the filters 50% of the time at a cost of $5 million last year; they indicated their preferred filtration level for this year on a slider ranging from 0% to 100%, with each 1% increment costing approximately $100,000.

Perceptions of the firm's sustainability image were measured with the same three items as in Study 2A, adapted for the specific company being evaluated. The three-item scale demonstrated good reliability across scenarios (within-person alpha ranged from 0.89 to 0.93; average 0.914).

Moral self-image was measured with three items adapted from moral self-regulation research (Aquino and Reed 2002, Jordan et al. 2015), rated on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). The three-item scale demonstrated good reliability across scenarios (within-person alpha ranged from 0.96 to 0.97; average 0.964).

Participants read that their company could allocate a portion of its earnings to CSR initiatives and that the firm had contributed $5 million to CSR initiatives in the previous year, and they indicated their preferred CSR allocation for the current year on a $0-$10 million slider, choosing to increase, decrease, or maintain this level of spending.

Participants evaluated a sourcing decision involving a new low-cost supplier that offered the same quality materials but faced criticisms for potential CSI activities, including accusations of weak environmental safeguards and poor working conditions. They used a slider from 0% to 100% to indicate how much of the company's materials they would source from this supplier in the upcoming year.
The effectiveness of the moral self-image manipulation was assessed using the same three items that measured moral self-image in Study 2B.
Participants completed the same CSR decision task as in Study 2B, indicating their preferred CSR allocation for the current year on a $0-$10 million slider.

Participants completed the supplier decision task from Study 2B with one modification: the new supplier was again described as facing criticism for not fully meeting global best practices in sustainability, but it was also made explicit that the supplier was fully compliant with local legal standards, to minimize the extent to which the decision was shaped by legality. Participants indicated how much of the company's materials they would source from this supplier on a 0%-100% slider.

Following PHMSA's definition, the authors considered a severe accident to be any accident that involved (1) any human loss or injury, (2) the evacuation of 25 or more people, or (3) gas loss (in dollars) one standard deviation above the mean. They counted the number of severe accidents and took the natural logarithm. To test Hypotheses 1 and 2 they created the interaction terms of the count of severe accidents with capability reputation and character reputation, respectively.

PHMSA categorizes the major causes of gas pipeline accidents; an accident induced by obvious force majeure, such as natural forces or outside forces, was considered an uncontrollable accident because these causes are clearly beyond the control of the pipeline operator, in contrast to causes such as corrosion that could have been prevented with regular maintenance and replacement of pipeline. After categorizing each accident as controllable or uncontrollable, the authors created counts for each of the four categories of severe and controllable accidents (severe-controllable, severe-uncontrollable, nonsevere-controllable and nonsevere-uncontrollable) and used the natural logarithms of each of the counts in their estimations. Interaction terms of the count of severe-controllable accidents and the count of severe-uncontrollable accidents with capability reputation and character reputation were constructed to test Hypotheses 3a and 3b.

Capability reputation was measured using shippers' responses on a 1-10-point scale to the question, '[How well does the operator provide] direct access to ample and diverse gas supply?' The ratings come from Mastio and Company's annual Natural Gas Pipeline Customer Value and Loyalty Study, which scores operators based on responses of approximately 1,100 North American gas shippers. The authors note that although this measure does not cover all aspects of an operator's capability reputation, it corresponds well to the capability most critical to shippers.

Character reputation was measured with one survey item each year; the wording was updated at three points in the observation period: in 2004 the item asked respondents to rate the 'integrity of transportation provider,' from 2005 to 2007 the wording was '[Does the operator] honor contracts and agreements?' and from 2008 it was '[Does the operator] communicate in an honest and forthright manner?' The three items are not combined into an aggregate measure of character reputation in the same year but are used independently across the three time periods, and all models include year fixed effects that control for differences in the survey item wording over time. Responses were given on a 1-10-point scale.

Using the FERC customer index, the authors observed when each interstate gas transmission pipeline operator started and ended its contract with shippers. The count of shipper ties formed is the number of new shippers each pipeline operator gains each year. The dependent variables are overdispersed count data and are used in logged form in the estimations, with all control variables lagged by one year.
time_window: t+1 (dependent variable in the year after the accident)

description: Using the FERC customer index, the authors observed when each interstate gas transmission pipeline operator started and ended its contract with shippers. The count of shipper ties dissolved is the number of current shippers each pipeline operator loses each year. The dependent variables are overdispersed count data and are used in logged form in the estimations, with all control variables lagged by one year.
time_window: t+1 (dependent variable in the year after the accident)

description: The dependent variable is the firm's assessment of its recent, general (nonspecific to any government branch) influence on the laws and regulations that have a substantial impact on the firm's business. It is measured on a five-point Likert scale (0 = no influence, 1 = minor influence, 2 = moderate influence, 3 = major influence, 4 = decisive influence). The authors state that this variable is utilized because influencing public policies is a primary goal of corporate political lobbying.

An indicator that equals 1 if the firm answered affirmatively to the question of whether it had lobbied the government to influence the content of laws or regulations. It serves as the key explanatory variable in the analysis.

The POLCON index is a measure of partisan competition determined by both partisan heterogeneity and government branches with veto power. It is constructed based on spatial modeling techniques by first identifying the independent branches of government (executive, legislative, and judiciary) that have veto power over policy changes at the national level and then calculating the distribution of political preferences of political actors inhabiting these veto positions in terms of political party affiliations. A higher value indicates greater difficulties for any single political actor to unilaterally change a policy because of partisan opposition, and thus stronger checks and balances on political actors.

Defined to be equal to the ACLP competitive democracy indicator initially developed by Alvarez et al. (1996) and Przeworski et al. (2000) and subsequently extended. As a common standard to measure competitive democracy in political science, the indicator captures whether the ruling party of a country is threatened with losing office through electoral means. To construct the indicator, researchers retroactively coded whether a ruling party suffered an electoral defeat in contending for the chief executive position and surrendered power peacefully in each country, and they also made adjustments based on deep contextual knowledge.

The number of government tiers in each country, counted following Fan et al. (2009). Fan et al. (2009) identified a government tier if there was a state executive body that met three conditions: (1) it is funded from the public budget, (2) it has authority to administer a range of public services, and (3) it has territorial jurisdiction.

Used to measure the decentralization of political power across subnational tiers, indicating whether a country has adopted a federalist system. A federalist system allows subnational governments to have greater autonomy and political power compared with a centralized system. In the subsample analyses, nonfederal systems (Model 5) correspond to Federalism equal to 0 and federal systems (Model 6) to Federalism equal to 1.

A composite measure built from two count measures of a firm's FDI activities: the number of overseas subsidiaries in each year, irrespective of entry mode, and the number of countries in which the firm had overseas subsidiaries in a given year. Each count was divided by the sample maximum number of FDIs or FDI countries to change it from a count to a ratio, and the average of the two ratios was computed, so the measure takes values from 0 to 1, with 1 representing the highest level of internationalization in the sample.
The accounting-based financial performance measure, computed as the ratio of net income to total assets. Data for the computation of ROA were obtained from the NEEDS tapes.

The market-based financial performance measure, a ratio defined as the market value of assets divided by the replacement value of assets. The authors used an intricate routine to compute the replacement value of assets rather than using book value, following the procedure of Goyal and Yamada (2004). Data were obtained from the NEEDS tapes and the PACAP database.
R&D expenditures expressed as a percent of sales, used as the measure of technology assets such as technological know-how and patents.
Advertising expenditures expressed as a percent of sales, used as the measure of advertising assets such as brand names and goodwill.

Intangible assets were measured with two intensity ratios: R&D intensity (R&D expenditures as a percent of sales) for technology assets such as know-how and patents, and advertising intensity (advertising expenditures as a percent of sales) for advertising assets such as brand names and goodwill. Each ratio entered the models as its own interaction with internationalization.

The technological strength of a venture's technological alliance partners, measured as the aggregate number of patents obtained by partners during the five years preceding each observation year. Patents are treated as a valid indicator of a firm's technological capabilities, especially for biotechnology firms, and the five-year span follows earlier studies of biotechnology firms. A venture's technological alliances were recognized as those involving a technological component using the ReCap and BioScan categorizations, and the nature of these alliances was verified with SEC filings. Patent data were obtained from the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office Web site.
time_window: five years preceding each observation year

description: A count of the number of marketing alliances with foreign firms that a venture has in each year it is in the sample, used to proxy the foreign marketing knowledge derived from foreign firms. Marketing alliances were defined as interfirm cooperative agreements intended for marketing and distribution purposes. These alliances were identified through ReCap, BioScan, and SEC filings and the same duration-verification process was applied to each marketing alliance. Data about partners' national identity were gathered from COMPUSTAT, Lexis-Nexis, organizational Web sites, and SEC filings; given the limited number of marketing alliances held in any year, analyses used the linear effect.
time_window: each year the venture is in the sample

variable_name: Number of internationally experienced domestic marketing partners
description: A count of the number of internationally experienced domestic marketing partnerships held by the venture in each year of the study. A domestic marketing partner was conceived as internationally experienced if it had engaged in international operations before its alliance with the focal venture. Data from COMPUSTAT, Lexis-Nexis, organizational Web sites, and SEC filings were used to find partner national identity and international activities, with the same data sources and collection procedures applied as for the other alliance measures.

The cohesion of a venture's network, gauged by the sum of the 'constraint' of each of a venture's relations. In the constraint formula, Pij is the proportion of venture i's alliance network represented by its alliance with firm j (for example, 0.33 if venture i has a network of three partners), and PiqPqj accounts for the alliances among venture i's partners; the constraint equation itself is not readable in the available text. Burt's term 'constraint' means a limit on the possibility of finding a structural hole in a network by the existence of an alliance, so a high value of the sum indicates high cohesion and fewer structural holes. The measure was calculated based on relationships present in each year the venture is included in the data, with Lexis-Nexis and SEC filings used to determine ongoing alliances.
time_window: each year the venture is included in the data

description: The dependent variable, calculated as the hazard (the instantaneous rate) of a venture beginning international sales and coded dichotomously with 1 indicating that the venture realizes an initial foreign sale and 0 otherwise. Prob() is the probability of an event (here the initial foreign market sale) between time t and t + Delta t, given that firm i has not generated foreign sales before t; the hazard-rate equation itself is not readable in the available text. Foreign sales were defined as sales revenue derived from exports or other foreign operations, and all ventures that initiated foreign sales continued sales abroad thereafter. Incorporation dates came from COMPUSTAT, Mergent Online, ReCap, BioScan and SEC filings, while the date of first foreign sale was determined from COMPUSTAT and SEC filings.
time_window: from the year of incorporation until the first international sale or the end of the study period

description: Time was modeled through a lagged model structure rather than a single variable: all independent variables were lagged by one year to test for the short-term impact of alliance networks and by five years to test for long-term effects. The five-year lag reflects the biotechnology product life cycle, since it commonly takes five years or more for a firm to fully take advantage of a new idea or technology.

A count of the number of articles run in U.S. newspapers that discuss a particular firm's disaster relief efforts in the first six months following the firm's first announcement of its disaster relief plans. It was constructed by searching for the combination of the company name (along with abbreviations) and the disaster name (along with variants) in the 'U.S. Newspapers' source category of Dow Jones' Factiva database. Hits were then reviewed by hand to count the articles discussing the company's disaster relief efforts and to discard duplicates before being summed to create the count variable.
time_window: first six months following the firm's first announcement of its disaster relief plans

description: A count of newspaper mentions of corporate disaster relief philanthropy, constructed exactly as the six-month measure with the exception that only articles that occurred within the first five days following a firm's first announcement of its disaster relief plans (including the day of the announcement) were counted. This variable was designed to proxy for short-term stakeholder attention.
time_window: first five days following the firm's first announcement, including the announcement day

description: CAMR compares a firm's actual market returns around an event of interest to the firm's expected market returns in the absence of that event; the events of interest were corporate announcements of disaster relief aid. Expected returns were estimated by the market model method, regressing a firm's daily stock return against that of a value-weighted market portfolio made up of all securities in the CRSP database over a 255-day estimation window ending 46 days before the event day, or by the market adjusted method, in which expected market returns are set equal to the market portfolio returns on the days of interest. Daily abnormal returns (actual minus expected) were summed over event windows of four, five, and six days.
time_window: four-, five-, and six-day event windows surrounding the announcement of disaster relief aid; 255-day estimation window ending 46 days before the event day

description: Indicates the magnitude (monetary value) of a firm's disaster relief philanthropy, scaled by firm assets. In the BCLC data, 15 percent of firms that reported contributions to the four disasters did not indicate the value of their contributions; for these firms Disaster CSR value was imputed based on the other independent and control variables.

An indicator variable that took a value of 1 if at least one press release discussing a firm's relief philanthropy was issued by a nongovernmental relief organization that partnered with the firm (within the first six months following the firm's announcement of its relief activities), and a value of 0 otherwise.
time_window: first six months following the firm's announcement of its relief activities

description: Tracked the timing of the firm's first public announcement of its disaster relief aid, taking a value of 1 if the first press release occurred within five days of the disaster, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: within five days of the disaster

description: An indicator variable that took a value of 1 if at least a portion of a firm's relief aid consisted of in-kind donations of goods and/or services, and a value of 0 otherwise, capturing whether relief activities involved concrete goods or services rather than only monetary donations.

variable_name: Disaster relief CSR program and its characteristics (CSR value, NGO partner, CSR urgency, in-kind)
description: Disaster relief CSR is observed as a firm's reported contribution to relief efforts after four large natural disasters, taken from the BCLC data; the sample consists of firms with such programs. In the tests, disaster relief CSR enters through the characteristics of each program: Disaster CSR value (monetary value scaled by firm assets), the NGO partner indicator, the CSR urgency indicator and the in-kind indicator, which are the independent variables predicting cumulative abnormal market returns around the announcement.
scale: sample membership plus program characteristic variables (continuous value and 0/1 indicators)

description: Market-to-book value of equity measured at the end of the year prior to the survey date, adjusted for the average market-to-book value among all firms in the industry over the prior three-year period. The authors describe the continuous variable as effectively indicating the extent to which performance is poor, and it appears in the models as '(Low) market-to-book value'. Interactions between firm performance and advice-seeking interactions were tested with the product-term approach, with component variables centered.
time_window: end of the year prior to the survey date (t-1)

variable_name: advice seeking from managers with similar backgrounds
description: Count of the number of times in the past year that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies who had a similar functional background to the CEO. Functional background was divided into three categories: throughput functions (operations, engineering, or research and development), output functions (marketing or sales), and peripheral functions such as finance and law. Respondents named the managers at other firms from whom they had sought advice and indicated the number of times they had done so.

variable_name: advice seeking from managers with dissimilar backgrounds
description: Count of the number of times in the past year that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies who had a different functional background to the CEO. Functional background categories were throughput, output, and peripheral functions. The count was created from the managers named by the CEO as advice contacts.

variable_name: advice seeking from managers who are friends
description: Count of the number of times in the past year that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies whom the CEO considered to be friends. Respondents were asked to consider their personal relationship with each manager listed as an advice contact and to indicate whether they considered each person to be an acquaintance or a friend.

variable_name: advice seeking from managers who are not friends
description: Count of the number of times in the past year that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies whom the CEO did not consider to be friends. Respondents distinguished acquaintances from friends when assessing each manager listed as an advice contact.

variable_name: advice seeking from managers in the same industry
description: Count of the number of times in the past year that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies who worked as full-time executives in an industry with the same primary, two-digit Standard Industrial Classification code as the CEO's firm.

variable_name: advice seeking from managers in a different industry
description: Count of the number of times in the past year that the focal CEO had sought strategic advice from managers at other companies in an industry with a different primary, two-digit Standard Industrial Classification code from the CEO's firm.
Absolute change in product market diversification over the two-year period following the survey date. Product market diversification was operationalized using the entropy measure.
time_window: two-year period following the survey date (t to t+2)

description: Absolute change in geographic diversification over the two-year period following the survey date. Geographic diversification is a composite measure formed by summing three components: foreign sales as a percentage of total sales, foreign production measured as foreign assets divided by total assets, and geographic dispersion, indicating the number of country subsidiaries calculated as a percentage of the highest value in the sample.
time_window: two-year period following the survey date (t to t+2)

description: Count of the firm's product listings in Data Sources that can be classified as workstations. The authors acknowledge that firms vary in the degree to which they consider different component configurations to be distinct products, but note that observed differences across products typically far exceed the customizations allowed within a product, and that a finer-grained definition might let manufacturers market wares as more closely tailored to consumers' needs. Because firms are assumed to have fixed resources, the count also proxies the average resources allocated to any particular product offering.

Indicator equal to one if the firm exits the workstation market that year. The authors argue exit is attractive because presence in the market is logically prior to making a profit, exit can be observed for all companies (including private ones for which sales, profits and returns are hard to observe), and exit should indicate poor performance; they concede that exit captures performance below a threshold rather than mean performance.

Sum of the number of workstations offered by all rival firms in a given year. The authors state that this measure increases both when new firms enter the market and when existing firms expand their product lines.

The total number of products removed from the market divided by the total number of products introduced by the firm up to that point in time. The specification is intended to capture both the cumulative nature of learning through product line culling and the decreasing returns to that experience. The variable ranges from zero, for a firm that has never culled any products, to one, for a firm that removes all of its products from the market (which cannot occur empirically because it implies firm exit).
time_window: cumulative up to the current year, updated yearly

description: For each year, product sales in year t are correlated with sales of the same product in year t-1 across all products in the market, and the resulting correlation is subtracted from one so that increasing values indicate greater volatility rather than greater stability. The authors reason that products represent relatively stable baskets of attributes, so purchasing the same products from one period to the next indicates stable consumer preferences.
time_window: yearly, comparing year t with year t-1

description: Measured in the year prior to the observation year by dividing a count of shared markets by the sum of each partner's total markets. Contacts are captured with sales data across eight downstream markets in the semiconductor industry. Unlike Ryu and colleagues, the authors did not manually allocate a value of zero to observations when partners had one market contact.
time_window: t-1 (year prior to the observation year)

description: For each shared market the authors determined whether partner i or partner j possessed a larger market share.
