In cases where the number of employees at the year of alliance was not available, the number of employees at the closest available year was used instead.

Firm size measured using the (logged) number of employees in the focal year. The primary data sources are the Directory of Corporate Affiliations and Compustat historical databases. In cases where the number of employees at the year of alliance was not available, the number of employees at the closest available year was used instead.

The (logged) number of a firm's patents in the U.S. patent subclasses related to pharmaceutical and biotechnology (patent classes 514 and 435) in the 10-year window prior to the alliance. A 10 percent depreciation is applied so that more recent patents have greater weights. Data come from the NBER 2006 patent database and account for organizational structure and acquisition history of firms.

The (logged) number of a firm's patents in the U.S. patent subclasses related to pharmaceutical and biotechnology (patent classes 514 and 435) in the 10-year window prior to the alliance. A 10 percent depreciation is applied so that more recent patents have greater weights. Data come from the NBER 2006 patent database and account for organizational structure and acquisition history of firms.

The (logged) number of a firm's FDA-approved drugs that were on the market in the 10-year window prior to the alliance, taken from the drugs@FDA database. As with the patent measures, the variable accounts for the organizational structure and acquisition history of firms and assumes a 10 percent depreciation rate.

The joint value created by a pair is not observed; the maximum score estimator identifies the coefficients of the joint production function from the local production maximization inequalities written for all pairs of observed and counterfactual alliances in the market. Under this specification a positive coefficient on the interaction of two partner attributes suggests that the two attributes are complements (increasing returns in joint value production), while a negative coefficient suggests they are substitutes. The coefficient for technological overlap is set equal to one for scale normalization and the other coefficients are compared to this baseline.

Number of media articles on smartphone patent lawsuits and related developments (such as patent acquisition, M&A, and amount of damages awarded) covered in all major world publications, counted for each quarter using LexisNexis. Articles are identified by the keywords 'smartphone,' 'patents,' and 'litigation' and their uses in other combinations; the frequency of media coverage proxies the level of vendor knowledge about these conflicts and captures the importance of each event.

Number of smartphone units vendor i sells in a given country or region j in each quarter t, divided by the total number of units the vendor sells in that quarter across all countries and regions. The measure is multiplied by 100 to facilitate the presentation of the results, so it is the percentage of the vendor's total quarterly sales attributable to country j.
scale: percentage of vendor's total quarterly unit sales (0-100)

description: Country-level measure of the strength of the IP system based on the Intellectual Property Rights Index (IPRI), published annually since 2008 by the Property Rights Alliance, which combines the Ginarte and Park (1997) index with an opinion-based measure of IP protections from the World Economic Forum's Global Competitiveness Index in which experts rate their nation's IP protection from 'weak and not enforced' to 'strong and enforced'. Higher values reflect increased IP protection; countries with IP indices above (below) the median of all sample countries are considered strong- (weak-)IP countries. For the multicountry regions in the sample, a GDP (PPP)-weighted IP_index is used.
scale: IP index (about 4.0 to 8.5 in the sample)

description: Number of smartphone-related patents obtained by each vendor, counted from the USPTO patent database using patents filed under international patent classification code H04 (electric communication techniques). Patents are counted at the end of 2008 for all firms, including those headquartered outside the United States; the logarithm of one plus the total patent count is used to account for skewness.
scale: log of one plus total patent count

description: Vendor-specific dummy variable that equals 1 if a vendor comes from a country with weak-IP protection and 0 otherwise. A vendor's country of origin is taken to be its headquarters' country, and the dummy is set to 1 when the IP_index of that country is below the median IP_index for all sample countries across the study period.
time_window: time-invariant, based on the median IP_index across the study period

description: Interaction term between the quarterly industry-level measure of patent war intensity and the country-level IP index. The authors expect this interaction to have a negative and statistically significant effect on the vendor's country sales share, and the marginal effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in PatentWarIntensity at the mean of all other variables is reported as a reduction of 1.7 percentage points in the dependent variable.

The net reduction in costs and/or assets between time-2 and time-3; in the first analysis the independent variable was the total net reduction in total assets and total costs. Firms were also assigned to one of four levels of retrenchment: no cost or asset retrenchment, asset but not cost retrenchment, cost but not asset retrenchment, or both cost and asset retrenchment, and were dichotomized into retrenchers versus nonretrenchers, where a retrencher had sustained a net reduction in total costs or total assets for at least one year subsequent to time-2.

The net reduction in total costs (selling, general, and administrative, interest, and miscellaneous) between time-2 and time-3. Negative retrenchment would indicate an increase over the period and thus denoted a cost nonretrencher.

The net reduction in long-term and short-term assets (cash and equivalent, accounts receivable, inventory, plant and equipment) between time-2 and time-3. Negative retrenchment would indicate an increase in assets over the period, i.e. nonretrenchment in assets.

The majority of statistical analyses relied on a continuous measure of turnaround performance, the net change in ROI between time-2 and time-4. For the categorical analyses the sample firms were classified as turnaround (successful) or nonturnaround (unsuccessful): subsequent to the decline, turnaround firms achieved at least two consecutive years of absolute simultaneous increases in ROI and ROS at a rate greater than the industry average and a return to predownturn (time-1) levels of ROI and ROS. Time-4 data were gathered for nonturnaround firms at a point corresponding to the average turnaround period for the successful firms in the industry.
time_window: net change between time-2 and time-4

description: Altman's Z uses five financial ratios and linear discriminant analysis to classify firms as solvent or insolvent and was calculated for each firm at time-2 to measure the severity of the downturn in terms of the threat of insolvency it posed. Firms were dichotomized into high or low severity according to whether they did (low) or did not (high) have a Z value greater than the median Z.

Executives indicated the relative impact of each external problem source by assigning it a value between 1 (completely insignificant) and 7 (greatest significance); the overall impact of the external problems was measured by summing the assigned values for sources 1-4 for each firm, and the mean survey response per firm was computed. A firm was assigned a high external causality classification if the summation of its four external problem ratings exceeded the mean for all respondents.
scale: 1-7 significance ratings summed across four external sources

description: Executives indicated the relative impact of each internal problem source by assigning it a value between 1 (completely insignificant) and 7 (greatest significance); the impact of the internal problems was measured by summing the assigned values for items 5-8 for each firm. A firm was assigned a high internal causality classification if the summation of its four internal problem ratings exceeded the mean for all respondents.
scale: 1-7 significance ratings summed across four internal sources

variable_name: overall nature of the turnaround response
description: The final item of Section 2 asked the respondents to classify the overall nature of their firm's turnaround response by placing it on a continuum between 1 (efficiency) and 7 (entrepreneurial). The item contrasts primarily efficiency-oriented responses, with belt tightening and streamlining of operations, with primarily competitive strategy-oriented responses, with changes in technology, products, or markets.

In Section 2 respondents distributed 100 points across five strategy areas to indicate the relative concentration of the firm's recovery efforts between predownturn and new activities; change in the operating and efficiency components - the manufacturing system and the management and organization system - reflects an efficiency response. In the analysis of the performance implications of matching cause and response, the presence of a sustained net reduction in total assets plus total costs for at least one year subsequent to time-2 was used to represent a more efficient, as opposed to entrepreneurial, response.

Degree of change in the market and product components of the firm's strategy in response to the turnaround situation; respondents distributed 100 points to indicate the relative concentration of recovery efforts on predownturn versus new markets and predownturn versus new products. Firms that rated external sources as more important in contributing to the downturn were expected to exhibit greater change in these strategy components.

Retrenchment focus was examined through the separate relationships of asset retrenchment (net reduction in assets) and cost retrenchment (net reduction in costs) with turnaround performance, compared across high and low severity groups.

variable_name: External and internal problem impact scores and causality classification
description: Executives rated the impact of eight problem sources from 1 (completely insignificant) to 7 (greatest significance); sources 1 to 4 are external and 5 to 8 internal. External impact is the sum of items 1 to 4 and internal impact the sum of items 5 to 8. A causality score was computed as the difference between the two sums, and firms were classified as high or low in external and internal causality relative to the respondent mean for the ANOVA test of hypothesis 3.
scale: sums of 1 to 7 ratings; difference score; high/low classification

variable_name: first-mover, second-mover, third-mover, fourth-mover, and fifth-mover dummy variables
description: A set of five dummy variables indicating, respectively, whether (1) or not (0) the MMMF was the first-mover, second-mover, third-mover, fourth-mover, or fifth-mover in its product category. First-mover status is defined over the 33 product categories introduced between 1972 and 1991; the second-, third-, fourth-, and fifth-movers are treated as separate categories in the empirical model. The reference category is the sixth or later entrant.

The natural logarithm of the total number of months of delay between the MMMF's entry and the entry of the first-mover in the product category. The logarithm was used because each additional month of delayed entry is expected to have a diminishing marginal impact on price and market share.

The fund's market share within its product category, computed as the ratio of fund TNA to product category aggregate TNA. It is the dependent variable of the demand equation and is measured on a scale from 0.0 to 1.0 rather than from 0 to 100 percentage points. Each observation is a fund-month.

The expense ratio charged to the MMMF's shareholders, expressed as a percentage of invested assets per annum. It is the dependent variable of the supply equation and is subtracted from the gross yield on the portfolio to yield the net yield received by investors.
scale: percent per annum of invested assets

description: The natural logarithm of the total number of MMMFs in the product category, included as an independent variable in the supply equation because each additional competitor is expected to have a diminishing marginal impact on prices. In the demand equation the inverse of the number of funds in the product category (1/N) is used instead. The same count also enters as the natural logarithm interacted with each of the five mover dummy variables to measure erosion of entry-order advantages.

Count of the number of events about social causes sponsored by Kiehl's during the month of each product's launch. From the 523 PROMT articles containing the word 'Kiehl's,' a subset of 215 articles referring to an 'event' was read and classified manually; to be included, the event had to prompt a specific reference to a social value (e.g., marathon for water supply, fundraiser for cancer). After checking for double counting, 61 events were identified, related to health-care issues, human rights causes, and the environment. The month in which the article appeared is assumed to be the month of the event.

Price in dollars per ounce at the time of a product's introduction. The variable has significant stickiness, because the entry price did not change for 92 percent of products during the study period. Entry price was entered in both absolute values and relative terms: price in dollars per ounce divided by the average price of all products introduced by Kiehl's in that niche up to time t; the absolute measure accounts for implicit price comparison and the relative measure for explicit comparison.

Time-variant dependent variable equal to 1 if the product is withdrawn from the market and 0 if it persists into the next month. Each product enters the dataset when it appears on the webpage and exits when it disappears from the site. The hazard rate is the probability of product withdrawal at time t, conditional on the product being in the firm's product portfolio at time t-1, estimated with a piecewise exponential model.

A composite institutional variable capturing the confluence of weak and inefficient political, regulatory, and economic institutions at the national level. Data on formal institutions were obtained from Holmes et al. (2013); the data were reduced to 20 variables loading on four factors: political democracy, regulatory control, capital availability, and market liquidity. To measure institutional weakness/inefficiency, the factors of political democracy, capital availability, and market liquidity were reverse-coded, whereas regulatory control institutions stand in contrast because overly bureaucratic rules and procedures can be onerous and inefficient for entrepreneurs; a higher institutional score reflects a greater confluence of weak and inefficient formal institutions. The latent variable institutions was created in the PLS analysis, where the four factors load positively (0.90, 0.99, 0.84, and 0.89) with differential weights.

Using the name generator method, each respondent was asked to name up to five individuals in each of three networks: business advice, business resources, and emotional support; each contact was named only once. For each contact respondents reported how close they felt to the person and reported the relationship between pairs of contacts. Structural holes is measured as 1 minus Burt's (1992) network constraint score, with larger scores denoting more structural holes; the constraint formula, in which pij is the proportion of total relational strength that i directly allocates to j, is not readable in the text provided. Network constraint scores were calculated with UCINET 6 software.

In the interview, entrepreneurs were asked for revenue growth information for the four years prior to the time of the telephone survey. Revenue growth is the difference between sales in two consecutive years divided by sales one year earlier. The variable revenue growth is the sum of revenue growth percentages divided by the number of revenue years.
time_window: four years prior to the telephone survey

description: Residual-based measure derived from a Cobb-Douglas production function for each game. The log ratio of the focal team's points to the opponent's points is regressed on the log of individual player performance and controls, including home-game, attendance, and missing-attendance variables. Annual complementarity for a team is the variance in team performance not explained by individual players, averaged across regular season games.

A player's share of firm surplus is the ratio of his wage to the firm surplus, where firm surplus is the sum of team wages and operating profit. The dependent variable in the regression is the logit transformation of this share. Higher values indicate that the player appropriates a larger share of firm surplus.
Binary variable equal to 1 if a player was selected for the all-star game, lagged by one year. Used as the moderator in H1B.
Votes received by a player for the all-star team, lagged by one year. Used as a control for star effects in the wage-share models.
Binary variable equal to 1 if a player was nominated for the most valuable player award, lagged by one year.
Binary variable equal to 1 if a player was nominated for the best defensive player award, lagged by one year.
Binary variable equal to 1 if a player was nominated for the most improved player award, lagged by one year.
Binary variable equal to 1 if a player was nominated for the best sixth man award, lagged by one year.

For players returning to a team's roster in year t, the measure averages total minutes played in years t-1 and t by each returning player, aggregates the average minutes of all returning players, and divides the sum by the team's roster size in year t. The authors provide an example calculation.

Average amount of shared experience among pairs of team members. It is calculated as the sum over all pairs of the number of games in which players i and j played in year t, divided by N(N-1)/2, where N is roster size, and then divided by a team's regular season games to capture average team familiarity per game.

Ratio of the minutes of the player with the maximum playing time to the aggregate minutes of the five players with the most playing time in the team. Higher values reflect individual dominance; lower scores reflect equality among players on the team.

Team-level measure based on the average of individual assists of players recruited through interteam trades, using the two-year average of their NBA record on assists. Assists are used as a proxy for team orientation.

Team-level measure based on the average of individual assists of players lost/released through interteam trades, using the two-year average of their NBA record on assists. Assists are used as a proxy for team orientation.

Team-level measure based on the average of individual assists of players selected through the annual NBA draft, using the last three years of their collegiate or international league records on assists. Assists are used as a proxy for team orientation.
time_window: last three years of collegiate or international league records

description: Firm surplus is measured as team wages plus operating profits in millions of 1984 dollars. It is used as the dependent variable in a test of whether the one-year lagged value of complementarity increases firm surplus.
Dichotomous indicator of the respondent's gender, coded 1 for female and 0 for male. The authors describe gender as the independent variable of central importance in the analysis.

Respondent coded 1 if she or he reported being actively ''alone or with others, currently trying to start a new business'' (i.e., a nascent entrepreneur) or ''alone or with others, currently the owner of a business'' that she or he helped manage (i.e., an established business owner), and 0 otherwise; nascent entrepreneurs and established business owners are combined in this measure. Nascent entrepreneurs are defined as individuals actively trying to start a business but who have not paid salaries, wages, or payments in kind for more than three months. By this inclusive definition, 13 percent of respondents in the sample were engaged in entrepreneurial activity.

variable_name: Weeks of full-time equivalent (FTE) paid leave for mothers
description: Weeks of full-time equivalent (FTE) paid leave that the state makes available to mothers, where FTE paid leave is calculated as the wage replacement rate multiplied by the duration of leave. Multiple sources were used to create an FTE paid-leave database so that policy changes over time could be incorporated, and policy changes were lagged by one year. A squared term for paid leave is also included in the models because particularly lengthy leaves may decrease women's attachment to the labor market. The authors note the measure cannot capture complexities such as variability in wage replacement rates.
time_window: policy changes lagged by one year

description: Percentage of a country's GDP spent on childcare services, capturing all public financial support (in-cash, in-kind, or through the tax system) for formal daycare services for children under the age of five. Data were published in 2005 and again in 2007, and information for missing years was imputed. The authors note the measure does not capture variability by region in access to or quality of childcare services.
Percentage of women in paid employment who work part time, used as a proxy for the extent to which states facilitate part-time work as a viable work-family strategy for women.

Indicates whether an entrepreneur reports that she or he became an entrepreneur because she or he lacked a more desirable employment option. Those who indicated that they became entrepreneurs because they had ''No better choices for work'' were coded 1; those who did not were coded 0. Thirty-one percent of business owners said this was the case.
scale: 1 = motivated by limited employment options; 0 = otherwise

description: Log of the number of full-time employees. The number of employees was increased by 1 for each business to permit the log transformation and to account for the owner's labor.
scale: log of number of full-time employees

description: Indicator variable for whether or not a respondent expected to hire more than five additional employees in the next five years (1 = yes), following Kelley et al. (2012). Seventeen percent of entrepreneurs expressed high-growth expectations.

Indicator for whether, in the entrepreneur's opinion, the product or service is ''new and unfamiliar to all customers'' (1 = yes). Only 9 percent of entrepreneurs believed they were introducing a brand-new product or service. Data are available only for survey years 2002-2008.

variable_name: Product or service uses new technology
description: Indicator for whether or not the product or service ''requires the use of technologies that are less than five years old'' (1 = yes). Twenty-two percent of entrepreneurs were using new technologies. Data are available only for survey years 2005-2008.

variable_name: Paid leave, childcare spending and women's part-time employment
description: Supportive work-family institutions were measured by three country-level indicators entered separately and not combined into an index: weeks of full-time equivalent paid leave for mothers, state childcare spending as a percent of GDP, and the percentage of employed women working part time. Data came from OECD sources, with policy changes lagged one year.

Computed as the percentage of the difference between the offer price and the first-day closing price. The lower the difference, the more capital the firm is able to raise through the IPO. Lower underpricing is the desirable outcome, indicating superior ability to raise capital and a more successful IPO.
scale: percentage difference between offer price and first-day closing price

variable_name: Directors' cumulative public company board experience
description: Measured as the average number of public company boards the directors served on in the past as reported in the prospectus. Directors include nonexecutive and executive directors and exclude the CEO.
time_window: past board service as reported at the time of the IPO

description: The number of public company boards the CEO served on in the past, as reported in the prospectus.
time_window: past board service as reported at the time of the IPO

description: Measured as the average number of public company boards the directors currently serve on at the time of the IPO. Directors exclude the CEO.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Measured as the number of public company boards the CEO serves on at the time of the IPO.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Measured as the proportion of directors (excluding the CEO) who have a bachelor's or above college degree in science. The paper notes that these metrics have previously been used in upper-echelons and human capital literatures.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: A dummy variable that takes the value of one if the CEO has a bachelor's or above college degree in science.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Measured as the average years of biotech experience of board members, excluding the CEO. The authors argue that the number of valuable links with key industry players rises with the duration of experience in the focal industry.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Measured as the number of years of experience working in the biotech industry. The authors argue that the number of valuable links with key industry players rises with the duration of experience in the focal industry.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: A binary variable for the formation of patent pools in the optical disc area; three patent pools were formed between the years 1997 to 1999. It takes a value of 0 for all observations before 1998 and a value of 1 for all observations after 1998, the year used to differentiate the time period before and after patent pool formation.

A binary variable that takes a value of 1 when a firm was a contributor of essential patents to one or more of the three optical disc industry patent pools, and 0 when it is a noncontributor of such patents. The variable takes a value of 1 or 0 independent of patent pool formation; firms are tagged as licensors in the time period before 1998.

A binary variable that takes a value of 1 when a firm is engaged in the inbound licensing of essential patents from one or more of the three optical disc industry patent pools, and 0 when it is not engaged in such inbound licensing. It likewise takes a value of 1 or 0 independent of the formation of the patent pool; the omitted class is the group of firms classified as nonparticipants.

The number of related patents generated by a given firm in a given year. Related patents are those that have a technology classification corresponding to one of the 10 USPTO technology classes representing optical disc technology. The panel dataset uses the application year to measure the quantity of patenting.

The citation count of related patents generated by a given firm from its grant date to the end of the study period in 2006. Related patents are those that have a technology classification corresponding to one of the 10 classes representing optical disc technology. The offset option of the estimation procedure was used to control for differing citation times.

Estimates were obtained of the proportion (0-100%) of members of each of two groups, 'exempt' and 'nonexempt' employees, who were covered by each of 18 high-performance work system practices. Using the number of employees in each group, the authors computed a weighted average for each practice, and the mean of these 18 weighted averages represented a firm's high-performance work systems score. Cronbach's alpha for the composite scale was .78.

Productivity was measured as the logarithm of the ratio of firm sales to number of employees, drawing on prior research. Data were obtained from COMPUSTAT. The authors note limitations: it does not control for potential increases in costs such as labor costs, and not all elements of the outcome are directly controllable by employees.
The three-year (1997-99) average ratio of fixed assets to sales for firms in each industry defined at the three-digit SIC level.
The average five-year annual growth rate in value of shipments based on data available in the U.S. Census of Manufacturers. The authors note this measure of industry growth has been widely used.
The three-year (1997-99) mean of the average ratios of R&D expenditures to total sales for all firms belonging to the sample firms' three-digit SIC industries.

A two-step procedure following Keats and Hitt (1988): first, the natural logarithm of sales for each three-digit industry for the years 1997-99 was regressed against time, and then the antilogarithms of the standard errors from these models were calculated. These antilogarithms represent an index of volatility or dynamism for each industry.

A personal letter was written to all 450 CEOs requesting their participation and that of the three fellow executive directors who they considered to comprise the caucus of the TMT. Respondents were therefore either the chief executive or an executive director of the same company. 108 CEOs and 310 executive directors returned questionnaires.

Width of functional experience was measured by starting function, predominant career function, and current function; breadth of company experience was related to company tenure, to international postings, to the number of companies worked for and the reasons for moving, and to running their own business; workloads were measured by the hours worked, and by the number of nights spent away from home on company business. Data from this group were essentially factual and reported by the executives themselves. Metric data were analysed with two-tailed t-tests, and non-metric data with the chi-squared test of homogeneity.

Where responses were judgemental, particularly within this group, scales were drawn from the leadership literature referenced in the paper. Variables were operationalized to measure ambition, need for achievement, challenge, career replication and managerial style, in addition to personal habits, political and religious affiliation, and age. Self-perception of managerial style was recorded on a nine-point scale (1 = completely dictatorial; 9 = completely democratic).
scale: nine-point scale for managerial style (1 = completely dictatorial; 9 = completely democratic)

description: Variables were operationalized to measure childhood influences—sibling position, locality, parental guidance and socioeconomic grouping, trauma; current marital situation; and the level and type of educational achievement. Data from this group were essentially factual and reported by the executives themselves. Non-metric data were tested with the chi-squared test of homogeneity.

Indicator variable that identifies whether the specialized ITC tribunal was targeted for patent enforcement by the firm over general-purpose district courts (the reference category). The disputes in the sample were restricted to company-initiated patent infringement suits that cover imported products.

Strategic stakes is measured by the number of patentee self-citations to the focal patent, that is, the extent to which the focal firm has built on the disputed patent in its subsequent patenting activity. Self-citations proxy the firm's resource investments in the domain of the patent and reflect its competitive strength or relative position. Because the forward citation series ends with the last year of available patent data, the measure is adjusted by estimating 'lifetime' citations over 17 years.

Defined as the absolute difference between the values of the cross-national index of patent strength of the plaintiff's and the defendant's countries. The index has a potential range from 0 (weak) to 5 (strong) and is derived from objective features of a country's patent system, which are updated at five-year intervals starting in 1960. Institutional distance is based on the first-listed defendant country.

Measured by the total number of suit-years the firm spent in patent enforcement at the ITC over the previous five years. For example, if a firm had two prior suits lasting six and nine months, respectively, the experience measure would be 1.25 suit-years. Prior patent enforcement data are used beginning from the early 1970s.

Measured by the total number of suit-years the firm spent in patent enforcement at district courts over the previous five years. Prior patent enforcement data are used beginning from the early 1970s, which identify firm names in the district courts but not patent numbers.

The lead patent holder is coded foreign if the headquarters or country of registration of its ultimate parent was foreign, and domestic if the ultimate parent is headquartered in the United States. Foreign-domestic equals one when the lead patent holder is a foreign firm and the lead challenger is a domestic firm (about 20% of the sample). Foreign-foreign equals one when both the lead patent owner and the lead challenger are foreign firms (about 5% of the sample); the omitted category is domestic-domestic (about 56% of the sample).

The lead challenger is coded foreign if the headquarters or country of registration of its ultimate parent was foreign, and domestic if the ultimate parent is headquartered in the United States. Domestic-foreign equals one when the lead patent holder is a domestic firm and the lead challenger is a foreign firm (about 19% of the sample); the omitted category is domestic-domestic (about 56% of the sample). Four participant pairs are coded on the identity of the lead patent owner and challenger: domestic-domestic, domestic-foreign, foreign-domestic and foreign-foreign.
A discrete variable equal to one if the patent holder won the focal dispute. Patent holders won roughly 52% of the disputes in the sample.

Coded as one for judgments that exhibit nationalistic rhetoric, identified through topic modeling that relies on word and phrase patterns (bigrams) to determine clusters in a set of documents. The methodology identified eight distinct topics based on the words and phrases in the judgments; seven of the eight topics mostly comprise legal phrases, while 'topic 3' is associated with terms that potentially signify nationalist rhetoric. The dummy is coded as one if a judgment was classified under 'topic 3' or zero otherwise; about 16.30% of the disputes (9576) exhibited nationalistic rhetoric.

A judge's ideology is scored between +2 (most conservative) and -2 (most liberal) based on his or her federally reported campaign contributions to political candidates and Political Action Committees. Campaign contributions provide a costly and informative signal about a donor's ideology. Conservative scores are computed using a spatial utility model that jointly estimates scores for donors and recipients from a contingency matrix of donation amounts.

Four participant pairs are coded based on the identity of the lead patent owner and challenger: domestic-domestic (about 56% of the sample, omitted category), domestic-foreign (about 19%), foreign-domestic (about 20%) and foreign-foreign (about 5%). A lead patent holder or challenger is foreign if the headquarters or country of registration of the firm's ultimate parent was foreign. Judgments on mixed pairs (domestic-foreign and foreign-domestic) are compared with judgments on same pairs (domestic-domestic and foreign-foreign).

Response to a leaf question that asked how big a competitive threat informal sector firms were for the responding firm, on a stem question asking respondents to describe a few characteristics of their industry and market on a scale from 1 to 5, where 5 represents a specific type of firm as being a big threat and 1 represents that type of firm as being no threat.
time_window: contemporaneous with the dependent variables, referring to the last fiscal year relative to the survey year

description: Response to the leaf question 'How big a competitive threat are foreign firms operating in India?', on a scale from 1 to 5, where 5 represents foreign firms as being a big threat and 1 represents them as being no threat.
time_window: contemporaneous with the dependent variables, referring to the last fiscal year relative to the survey year

description: Built from survey questions on whether an informal gift or payment was expected or requested by government officials to obtain approval on applications for business licenses and/or infrastructure within the last two years, and whether a gift or informal payment was ever expected/requested by government officials from the tax, labor, and safety agencies during inspections and required meetings during the last one year. The main measure first codes 1 for firms that answered 'yes' for at least one of the gift/payment question items, but because that is expansive it uses the question measuring the respondent's perception of corruption as an obstacle: firms that did not perceive corruption as a serious obstacle to doing business but were asked or expected to pay bribes are coded 1 as having engaged in corruption more proactively, and 0 otherwise. Thirteen of the focal firms fall in this 'proactive corruption' group.
time_window: last two years (license/infrastructure payments) and last one year (inspections)

description: Built from two survey questions: whether the firm ran formal in-house training programs for its permanent, full-time employees during the last one year, and whether the firm sent its permanent, full-time employees to formal training run by other organizations during the last one year. The main measure is an ordered three-degree measure that codes 2 for firms that invested in both types of HR training, 1 for firms that invested in only one type, and 0 for firms that did not invest in any HR training.

A diversification index based on the Simpson diversity index, calculated using survey data on firms' sales on their primary product/service (including software products) as a percentage of their total annual sales. The index was calculated as (1 - p^2) where p is the proportion of a firm's primary product/service sales to its total annual sales. Only the proportion of a firm's primary product/service sales to total sales was used due to lack of availability of data in the survey about all of a firm's products and services.

Measured with survey questions on the firm's patent activity, often employed in prior studies as a proxy of technological capability. Coded 1 if the focal firm applied for, or was awarded any patents, in the last three years and 0 otherwise.

The HRC's annual report Corporate Equality Index rates a firm on a scale between 0 and 100 with 100 being the highest equality. The rating indicators include whether a firm includes 'sexual orientation' and 'gender identity' in its equal employment opportunity policy, whether a firm provides diversity training on sexual orientation and gender identity, and whether the firm has supportive gender transition guidelines, domestic partner health insurance, and at least one transgender wellness benefit. Scores for the breakdown sub-indicators are publicly available since 2005, and the number of sub-indicators changed from seven in 2005 to 11 in 2006, a change common to all firms. The authors collected CEI manually from the annual report from 2002 to 2006.

Monthly stock returns in percentage point, obtained from CRSP. The yearly right-hand-side variables, including CEI, are matched with the monthly left-hand-side variable using same-year, cross-year or lagged-year matching, and each of the yearly variables has the same value for a firm across months in the same year. Following Fama and MacBeth (1973), cross-sectional regressions are run for each month and time-series average values of the monthly regression coefficients are obtained with time-series t-statistics calculated using Newey-West standard errors.

The market value of total assets divided by the book value of total assets, measured at the firm-year level. In the estimated model the dependent variable is the natural logarithm of the Q ratio, and industry and year fixed effects are included with standard errors clustered at the firm level.

Firm income per employee, defined as income before extraordinary items divided by the number of employees in a firm, used as a proxy for employee productivity. The dependent variable in the estimated model is the natural logarithm of income per employee, ln(Income/employee), with industry and year fixed effects included and standard errors clustered at the firm level.

A scale measure with seven items adapted from previous studies that assessed constructs such as management's values on HRM and CEO (leadership) support for SHRM. Each item is measured on a five-point Likert-type scale, where 1 meant 'strongly disagree' and 5 meant 'strongly agree'. The internal reliability of the construct is 0.90; item C7 was dropped during inspection of the CFA modification indices to improve final model fit.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Established from commitment-based HR practices used in previous studies, with all survey questions on a five-point Likert-type scale where 1 meant 'strongly disagree' and 5 meant 'strongly agree'. Following a subscale aggregation approach, the mean scores of each subscale of HR practices were calculated and used as indicators of the commitment-based HR system latent variable in the confirmatory factor analysis. The internal reliability of the construct is 0.87; one pay-for-performance item (utilizes a reward system based on seniority) is reverse-coded.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Annual sales for 2006 (in Korean won) divided by the number of employees in the workforce, since sales and firm size are positively correlated. Because both sales and number of employees were nonnormal, the natural logarithm of this productivity measure is used, and the sales number was divided by 1,000 to decrease the difference in the scales of the variables in the analysis.

Return on equity data were taken from a database built by the Korea Information Service, which collaborates with Moody's to provide information on firms operating in South Korea for an international audience. ROE is included as a more distal financial accounting measure of firm performance.

Composed of six items (Delaney and Huselid, 1996), each measured on a five-point Likert-type scale where 1 meant 'strongly disagree' and 5 meant 'strongly agree'. The items compare the firm with its competitors on customer satisfaction, employee commitment, quality of products and services, ability to attract and retain essential employees, employee job satisfaction, and employee work productivity. The internal reliability of this construct is 0.86; in the CFA the items were represented through parceled composite indicators.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

variable_name: Employee productivity, ROE and perceived firm performance
description: Firm performance was measured with three variables: employee productivity (log of sales per employee), ROE from the Korea Information Service database, and a six-item perceived performance scale compared with competitors.

variable_name: market share relative to combined share of three largest competitors
description: Businesses were categorized into the three share/performance groups using their market share relative to the combined share of the three largest competitors together with their ROI. The cutoffs separating low share from high share businesses are given in the criteria for categorization rather than in a prose sentence.

Profitability was measured by return on investment as reported in the PIMS data base. Businesses with ROI above a high cutoff were categorized as effective and those below a low cutoff as ineffective; the cutoffs are given in the criteria for categorization rather than in a prose sentence.

The variables describing product-market choice listed in Table 1 (product, market and industry characteristics) were used in a cluster analysis. Sample businesses were assigned to clusters based on their product, market and industry characteristics, not on their share performance status, and the sample fell into six clusters. The distribution of the three share/performance groups across these clusters was then compared with the goodness-of-fit test.

The 13 competitive strategy variables define the competitive position of a business relative to other sellers, including emphasis given to various functional activities and resource allocation priorities. Linear combinations of these variables (log-odds discriminant functions) were formed to maximize the competitive differences between the two groups under comparison, and each pairwise comparison generated a SEP'N value measuring the strength of the discrimination.

Calculated as the number of governmental levels separating the central government from the level of government that holds the monitoring and/or control rights of a given firm. It was computed differently for state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and non-SOEs: for SOEs it is the number of tiers separating the controlling governmental organ (the ultimate owner) and the central government, with ultimate owner data obtained from annual reports; for non-SOEs an additional step (indicating that they are under the monitoring power of their local governments) was added to the distance score of the geographically nearest and administratively lowest governmental jurisdiction in which they were embedded, taken from the annual report. Larger values represent greater administrative hierarchical distance; the distance variable was calculated according to the scale presented in Table 2.

Based on a content analysis of firms' annual financial reports and CSR reports as obtained from CNINFO and firms' official websites. Coding was done in NVivo 10 in several steps: an open coding process on 10 randomly selected annual reports to note the environmental issues firms focused on, labeling of the aspects identified, and calculation of the total number of words covered by each label. To correct for the fact that some firms' reports are wordier than others, the percentage of words related to corporate environmentalism out of the total words in the relevant reports was calculated. To avoid the inclusion of greenwashing instances, only substantively specified actions were counted; the variable was log-transformed.

Calculated as the percentage of waste gas emission reduction over the past five years by industry to indicate the level of regulatory stringency faced by a firm. Industrial soot and dust emissions by firms during their production processes were used because these emissions are the main regulatory targets to combat air pollution given their high nuisance levels in China. Sectorial emission data was collected from the Environmental Statistics Dataset disclosed annually by the National Bureau of Statistics of the People's Republic of China; the variable was log-transformed.

Measured as the number of staff working in the environmental monitoring stations in the province in which a focal firm is located, to capture monitoring in a local area. The variable was retrieved annually from the China Environment Yearbook and was log-transformed.

Dummy variable identifying firms founded by entrepreneurs who were previously employed in downstream industries that use semiconductors as components in their final products, such as manufacturers of computers and office equipment, consumer electronics, communication equipment and automobiles. Entrants with at least two founders who worked for the semiconductor-related divisions of vertically integrated producers are classified as focal spinouts instead. For teams, firms are classified by the majority rule, and where founders come from different backgrounds by the principle of the most influential founder.

Dummy variable identifying firms founded by entrepreneurs whose last employment was in a semiconductor firm (SIC 367), including firms founded by entrepreneurs with a background in semiconductor software and/or in semiconductor design and production such as electronic design automation. Entrants with at least two founders who worked for the semiconductor-related divisions of vertically integrated producers are also classified here. For teams the majority rule and, for mixed backgrounds, the most influential founder principle were used.

Residual dummy variable identifying firms whose founders come from universities or research institutes or who were previously employed in areas such as finance, venture capital, business software, business and/or engineering consultancy. It serves as the base category in the entry and survival models.

The dependent variable of the survival analysis is the hazard of exit from the industry, modelled in discrete time. Firms that exit the industry are treated as unsuccessful new ventures, and exit by failure and exit by acquisition are modelled separately and jointly. Exit years were recorded for each firm over the observation period.

The main product market of activity at entry was identified from company profiles and divided into generic semiconductors, market-specific semiconductors and other semiconductors. Market-specific semiconductors are chips targeted at specific application markets whose design requires knowledge of the applications or systems in which they are integrated, and may involve a complete platform tailored to a specific submarket or user firm. The market-specific category is further divided into communications, consumer products, computation and storage, industrial, and other submarkets. Category definitions and product lists were cross-checked with industry experts.

A structural change ratio based on senior executive title changes, computed in three steps: the proportion of titles in each horizontal category (business area, geography, function, customers, technology) and each vertical level per firm-year, then the absolute difference of each category from its value in the previous year, then the sum of those differences. Titles were coded to a maximum of four levels, with CEO, president and COO titles coded as general managers, and heir-apparent COOs excluded to avoid inflating the ratio. The ratio was converted into a dummy variable coded 1 above a 0.30 cutoff; the cutoff was guided by interviews and documentary sources, since changes below it often reflected simple reconfigurations or ad hominem changes. In the data set the change ratio varies between 0 and 0.97.
scale: dummy coded 1 above a 0.30 change ratio; raw ratio ranges 0 to 0.97

description: The authors count additions, mergers, transfers, splits, and deletions of organizational units as reconfigurations. Where two or more units are involved, the process is counted as a single reconfiguration. Reconfigurations occurring in the same year as a restructuring are excluded from the analysis because they are parts of discontinuous change.

The annual number of reconfigurations is summed between two occurrences of restructuring, with the cumulative count reset to zero after each new restructuring. The variable is standardized. The smaller number of observations for this variable arises because in some cases the first observed restructuring takes place much later than the start of the time window, so preceding observations cannot be cumulated.
time_window: between two occurrences of restructuring, reset after each restructuring

description: The number of reconfigurations in a single year, used to identify relatively intense bursts of activity (discrete perturbations). Because there is little theoretical guidance on the likely delay between a discrete perturbation and its outcome, a range of lags up to four years before a restructuring was tested. The variable is standardized.
time_window: single year, lagged up to four years before a restructuring

description: The number of declines in ROA, Sales, or Tobin's q between two restructurings, with the clock reset to 0 after each new restructuring; these measures range from 0 to 12. Performance is captured by two accounting-based measures (Return on Assets and Sales) and one stock-market based measure (Tobin's q) using the standard formulae of the strategy literature, computing a moving percentage change between two consecutive years. The models report the cumulated Tobin's q declines since the previous restructuring.
time_window: between two occurrences of restructuring, reset after each restructuring

variable_name: Consecutive number of years of decline
description: The consecutive number of years of decline in ROA, Sales, or Tobin's q over four years; these measures range from 0 to 4. Both decline measures aim to capture the effect of prolonged performance declines, the cumulated count capturing gradual accumulation and the consecutive count capturing the discrete perturbation effect. The models report consecutive sales declines in t-4 to t-7.
time_window: consecutive years of decline over four years

description: Dummy variable coded 1 when the new CEO does not come from the company. To test the accumulation hypothesis a one-year lag of external CEO change is used so that interactions correspond with the last year of accumulated incremental change; for the perturbation hypothesis multiple lags were tried. The data come from annual reports.
time_window: one-year lag for accumulation; multiple lags tried for perturbation

description: Strategic interconnectedness is measured by the extent of related diversification using an entropy index based on a firm's dispersion of sales across four-digit industry SIC codes. The less dispersed a firm's four-digit SIC codes across higher-level two-digit SIC codes, the more related-diversified a firm is held to be, with more interdependence across business divisions. A one-year lag is used for the accumulation test and multiple lags were tried for the perturbation test. The data are from the Compustat Business-Segment Reports.
time_window: one-year lag for accumulation; multiple lags tried for perturbation

description: The level of strategic interconnectedness, based on the related-diversification entropy index, entered as a main term in the models in which its interaction with cumulated reconfigurations or with reconfiguration intensity is tested. Lagged values (t-1 and t-3) are used so that the interactions correspond with the relevant accumulation and perturbation terms.

Measured from the 556 individual project time-to-build observations as product-region averages per unit of output, so that the average time needed to accumulate resources to produce one unit of output in each petrochemical subindustry is captured. The time-to-build of each project was computed by taking the date on which the project was first reported in the OGJ minus 90 days as the official start and the last report plus 90 days (or the expected completion date, when reported) as the official end. All measures were scaled up to 100,000 metric tons per year of equivalent capacity, and resource accumulation lag was standardized to reduce multicollinearity between its main and squared terms.
scale: months per 100,000 metric tons per year of equivalent capacity

description: For a given observation year, investment was equal to 1 for all observations in which a firm expanded either by adding a new 'greenfield' plant or by increasing at least one existing plant's production capacity by more than 10 percent. Otherwise, it was equal to 0. Debottlenecking, representing only 0-10 percent of capacity expansion per year, does not reflect a major capacity expansion decision and was not included in the analysis.

Defined as the standard deviation of four years' worth of industrial production prior to the year under consideration. The four-year period prior to the focal year was chosen to match the operationalization of similar variables in prior empirical work in this industry. Demand uncertainty was computed for each geographic region (U.S., Europe, and Japan) and was standardized.
time_window: four years prior to the focal year

description: Respondents reported their perception of each environmental sector's criticality, deterrence, variability, unpredictability, heterogeneity, and diversity on a 7-point Likert scale. These elements were then converted into one of the three environmental dimensions. Complexity was measured by the mean of heterogeneity and diversity across all eight environmental sectors.

Respondents reported their perception of each of the eight environmental sectors on a 7-point Likert scale. The elements reported were converted into one of the three environmental dimensions. Dynamism was measured as the mean of variability and unpredictability across all these environmental sectors.

Respondents reported their perception of each of the eight environmental sectors on a 7-point Likert scale. Hostility was measured as the mean of criticality of resources controlled by each environmental sector and deterrence, which indicates the extent to which each environmental sector becomes a threat to the growth of a firm.

Strategic orientation is a multidimensional construct measured with nine items, i.e., three sets of three items representing each strategic type. Strategic orientation constitutes the average response across the three items for each orientation, ranging from one to seven. Instead of forcing firms into one of the three strategic types, the authors measured their tendencies toward each strategic orientation.

One of the three strategic orientations measured with three of the nine items that focus mostly on a firm's orientation in reacting to regulatory and competitive changes, pursuing market and product opportunities, monitoring performance, and managing decision making and other internal processes. The score constitutes the average response across the three items, ranging from one to seven.

One of the three strategic orientations measured with three of the nine items that focus mostly on a firm's orientation in reacting to regulatory and competitive changes, pursuing market and product opportunities, monitoring performance, and managing decision making and other internal processes. The score constitutes the average response across the three items, ranging from one to seven.

Subjective assessment of return on assets at the subsidiary level on a 5-point scale that ranges from the lowest 20 percent to the top 20 percent in comparison with close competitors in the industry. It is one of the three performance measures used in the study.
scale: 5-point scale from the lowest 20 percent to the top 20 percent relative to close competitors in the industry

description: Subjective assessment of sales growth at the subsidiary level on a 5-point scale that ranges from the lowest 20 percent to the top 20 percent in comparison with close competitors in the industry. It is one of the three performance measures used in the study.
scale: 5-point scale from the lowest 20 percent to the top 20 percent relative to close competitors in the industry

description: Subjective assessment of competitive position (e.g., market share) at the subsidiary level on a 5-point scale that ranges from the lowest 20 percent to the top 20 percent in comparison with close competitors in the industry. It is one of the three performance measures used in the study.
scale: 5-point scale from the lowest 20 percent to the top 20 percent relative to close competitors in the industry

description: Scale assessing the perceived trustworthiness of the source organizational unit in terms of ability. Four items were derived from Walton (1975) and Mayer et al. (1995): whether superior results of the source were visible and remained stable, whether the source possessed the necessary resources to support the transfer, and whether the source was able to accommodate the needs of the recipient into the practice. Answers used the balanced five-point Likert-type scale (Y! y o n N!) unless otherwise stated, and the construct score was computed by adding up the standardized item scores.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (Y! to N!); sum of standardized item scores
time_window: 3.5-month band starting 5 months after first use by the recipient

description: Eight-item scale. Five items are derived from Lippman and Rumelt's (1982) theory of uncertain imitability and three items infer causal ambiguity from the degree of tacitness of the practice. Items marked (RS) are reverse scored, so that higher scores indicate greater causal ambiguity. Construct scores were computed by adding up the standardized item scores.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (Y! to N!) for most items; sum of standardized item scores
time_window: 3.5-month band starting 5 months after first use by the recipient

description: Eight-item measure of the degree of similarity between the replica and the template. Six items assess general modifications: compared to the source's practice, the recipient's practice is 1 = 'Exactly the same' to 5 = 'Completely different' (RS); whether modifications were introduced to make the practice workable (RS) and to adapt it to different environments (RS); whether unnecessary modifications were performed (RS); whether the practice was modified contrary to expert's advice (RS); and whether altering the practice created further problems (RS). Two items assess specific modifications: the incompleteness of the replication on a five-point scale from 'All modules have been transferred' to 'None of the modules have been transferred' (RS), and whether original modules were replaced by existing ones at the recipient's side (RS). Construct scores were computed by adding up the standardized item scores.
scale: five-point response scales and Likert-type scale; sum of standardized item scores
time_window: 3.5-month band starting 5 months after first use by the recipient

description: Firms' turnover that pertains to new products. The variable contains 2009 sales generated from products introduced between 2007 and 2009, measured in raw values rather than as a ratio of overall sales. Due to the strong skew, the natural logarithm of new product sales is used in the regression models.
time_window: 2009 sales from products introduced between 2007 and 2009

description: The CIS survey asked firms whether they allocate resources to product innovation projects in a single step or across multiple steps, coded as '0' or '1' respectively. A more continuous operationalization using the count of resource allocation steps is used only for robustness checks.

The CIS survey asked firms to what extent they agree with the statement 'not all projects receive the requested resources-projects are meant to compete for resource allocation,' rated on a 1-5 Likert-type scale from not at all to fully. The lower two ratings are treated as relatively higher commitment and assigned the value '0'; the higher two ratings are treated as relatively lower commitment and assigned the value '1.'

The CIS survey asked respondents to state the number of projects discontinued during the observation period. The authors code the firms with 0% projects discontinued as '0' and the firms with discontinuations greater than 0% as '1,' yielding 183 firms coded '0' and 255 firms coded '1.'

A reverse-coded absolute difference measure of the match between the binary low commitment and reallocation measures. The authors subtract the binary measure of reallocation from that of low commitment, use the absolute value of the result, and then code it in the reverse, so that '1' means fit (both or neither) and '0' means lack of fit.

A binary variable taking the value of '1' if the firm displays either low commitment or reallocation, which distinguishes regimes making tentative bets from those making definitive bets. For the test of Hypothesis 3 the information in the tentative variable is combined with the fit and sequencing variables to separate the observations of Type B from those of Type D.

Entry cost reduction is equal to one if an individual is working in a municipality that, at year t, has enacted the On the Spot Firm reform, and zero otherwise. Errors are clustered at the municipality level, the level of the shock, to address potential serial correlation concerns. A value of one therefore denotes a lower cost of entrepreneurship (the reform is in place).

The dependent variable wage is computed as the sum of the following monthly components: (a) base pay, or the gross amount of money paid in the reference month to employees on a regular monthly basis for their normal hours of work; (b) tenure-related payments; and (c) regular payments. The main specification models the logged monthly wage, and the authors also report estimates when the relationship between treatment and outcome is assumed to be linear rather than log-linear, in which case the (monthly) wage of high earners increases by about 156 euros per month.

High earner is a dummy equal to one for employees occupying, in a certain year t, the top tercile in the municipality's wage distribution (and zero otherwise). Middle earner is a dummy equal to one for employees in the middle tercile (and zero otherwise). Low earners, employees in the bottom tercile, are the baseline category omitted from the analysis.

Computed in two steps. First, the probability that an individual is a founder, that is owner and manager of a new venture versus a wage worker, is estimated as a function of standard individual-level attributes: age, age squared, gender, educational credentials, qualification, and occupational status, all measured at time t-1, including year, municipality, industry, and worker fixed effects. Second, the predicted probability of entrepreneurship is computed in each year for every individual in the sample; for individual-year observations after 2005 the predicted probability in 2004, the last year before the enactment of the shock, is used.
time_window: covariates measured at t-1; post-2005 values taken from 2004

description: Outside options was computed as the number of jobs in the same industry-occupation-region of the focal employee (in 2004, i.e., one year before the reform was enacted, to alleviate endogeneity concerns) minus the number of similar jobs in the firm of the focal worker, divided by 1,000.

A dummy variable equal to one for industries with a more decentralized and flexible salary negotiation process and zero otherwise; the measure is time invariant. Industries with such decentralized negotiation processes include financial services; information and communication; and utilities, transport, and logistics, whereas most other Portuguese industries have centralized collective bargaining agreements.

For each firm, annual return on equity (ROE) data were used to calculate the average ROE and the variance of ROE for the relevant five-year period. Within each two-digit industry a rank order of all companies for ROE variance was constructed and then divided at the median, so that each company was deemed High or Low on risk. The authors note that the detail of the calculations for ROE and ROE variance follows exactly from Bowman's (1980) article.
time_window: each of four non-overlapping five-year periods

description: The beta values were calculated by ordinary least squares using the capital asset pricing model for the relevant five-year periods from 60 monthly observations taken from the CRSP tapes. A value-weighted market return, including ordinary dividends, was used as a proxy for the market return. The derived beta measures for each firm and the industry were then used to define 'high' and 'low' on the market-based risk characteristic, defining the HH, HL, LH and LL cells of the risk-return matrix.
time_window: 60 monthly observations for each five-year period

description: The average ROE was calculated from annual data for ROE derived for each firm in each two-digit industry for each of the four non-overlapping five-year periods. Within each industry a rank order of all companies on ROE was constructed and divided at the median, so that each company was deemed High or Low on return.
time_window: each of four non-overlapping five-year periods

description: For each time period each company was placed in one of four quadrants of a two by two contingency table: High ROE, High Variance (HH); High ROE, Low Variance (HL); Low ROE, High Variance (LH); and Low ROE, Low Variance (LL). Negative association ratios (i.e. (HL + LH) divided by (HH + LL)) were calculated for each two-digit industry for each of the four non-overlapping five-year periods. A binomial test similar to Bowman's was used to assess the statistical significance of the proportion of negative associations.

variable_name: negative association ratios using beta to measure risk
description: The negative association ratios were recalculated using the market-based beta measure of risk instead of the variance of ROE, so that the high and low risk cells of the risk-return matrix were defined from beta for each industry and period. Using a binomial statistical test no one of the negative association ratios was significantly different from 0.5 at the chosen 10% significance level, so there is no evidence of negative association in this table.

Separate Bowman-type risk-return analyses were performed for the non-overlapping five-year time periods 1960-64, 1965-69, 1970-74 and 1975-79. The authors interpret the two earlier periods as the more predictable and stable environment of the 1960s and the two later periods as the more uncertain environment of the 1970s.

variable_name: high, medium and low relative ROE industries
description: The research sample of industries was re-worked in order to identify industries in each period as being in one of three categories: High relative ROE (Birth/Growth), Medium ROE (Mature) and Low ROE (Decline). The classifications of High, Medium and Low in each time period were obtained by dividing the overall industry ROE distribution into tertiles corresponding to the upper one-third, middle one-third, and lower one-third of the distribution.
time_window: each of the four five-year periods

variable_name: risk measure (variance of ROE or beta)
description: The risk-return analyses were run with two risk measures: the accounting-based variance of returns and the market-based beta (or systematic risk) derived from application of the capital asset pricing model. The authors note that while market measures focus around a capital market perspective, accounting measures can be particularly useful for managers of diversified firms.

For every structure adopted, the authors code the number of homogeneous and heterogeneous units and then calculate the proportion of the focal structure's homogeneous units by dividing that number by the structure's total units (homogeneous + heterogeneous units). The measure captures the firm's current interaction structure and is lagged relative to the focal reorganization. Because the proportion of heterogeneous units is the exact inverse of this measure, results are reported only for the proportion of homogeneous units. The authors note that it would be preferable to count employees grouped into homogeneous versus heterogeneous units, but unit-level employee data were not available.
time_window: lagged by 1 year relative to the focal reorganization

description: For every structure adopted, the number of heterogeneous units is divided by the structure's total units (homogeneous + heterogeneous units), giving the proportion of the structure made up of heterogeneous units. This measure is the exact inverse of the proportion of homogeneous units, so its regression results are reported as the exact inverse of those for hom/total units and its coefficients are omitted from the tables. The measure is lagged relative to the focal reorganization.
time_window: lagged by 1 year relative to the focal reorganization

description: Dichotomous measure of the probability that a reorganization ran counter to the firm's current structure. A reorganizing firm that increases its number of homogeneous units and/or reduces its number of heterogeneous units is coded as a shift toward greater homogeneity. Four reorganizations left the structural emphasis unchanged (for example, moving from three homogeneous and three heterogeneous units to four and four); for these cases the authors inspected the raw data to discern the relative importance of the changes and coded the reorganizations accordingly.

Dichotomous measure of the probability that a reorganization ran counter to the firm's current structure. A reorganizing firm that increases its number of heterogeneous units and/or reduces its number of homogeneous units is coded as a shift toward greater heterogeneity. Of the sample's 102 reorganizations, 53% shifted the firm's focus toward more heterogeneous units.

Count measure of the number of days between reorganizations, used to test the timing hypotheses. The dependent variable in the fixed-effects Poisson models; a larger value means a longer delay until the next reorganization.

Blockholder equity positions were measured in two different ways: as the number of 5 percent owners who were not directors or employees of the firm, and as the total percentage of equity owned by such 5 percent owners. The 5 percent cutoff was used because it reflects significant ownership and the level of ownership that must be reported in corporate proxy statements.

Representation of outsiders on a board was measured as the number of outsiders divided by total board size. Outsiders were defined as directors with no past or present personal or professional relationship with the firm other than the position of director; insiders were firm employees and affiliated outsiders were retired managers, relatives of current managers, or lawyers serving as firm counsel and were deleted from the analysis.
Outside director equity interests were calculated as the sum of their equity holdings divided by the total equity of common shares outstanding.
Inside director equity interests were calculated as the sum of their equity holdings divided by the total equity of common shares outstanding.

Level of firm diversification was calculated with the entropy measure, the sum over segments of the percentage of firm sales in a segment times the natural log of one over that percentage, which takes into account the number of segments and the relative importance of each segment's sales. The entropy measure was calculated using the COMPUSTAT Business Segment Tapes. Relative product diversification was calculated by subtracting a firm's dominant two-digit industry's average level of diversification from firm diversification, so firms with values greater than 0 are above the industry average.

Firm leverage was calculated using two variables: long-term debt divided by total net sales and long-term debt divided by total assets. To control for industry effects, the dominant two-digit industry's average debt-to-sales and debt-to-total-assets ratios were subtracted from the comparable firm ratios.

Relative R&D investment is a strategy construct stated in terms of firm minus industry levels, following the practice that all strategy and performance hypotheses were stated in terms of firm minus industry levels. The prose of the article does not give the ratio used to construct the measure.

Accounting-based performance was measured using three indicators: return on assets (net income divided by total assets), return on equity (net income divided by total common equity), and return on sales (net income divided by total net sales). To control for industry effects, the dominant two-digit industry's average ROA, ROE, and ROS were subtracted from their firm counterparts.

Market-based performance was measured using three indicators: the Sharpe measure, the Treynor measure, and Jensen's alpha. The Sharpe measure is the firm's average market return minus the average risk-free rate from T-bill auctions, divided by the total variance in the firm's returns for the year prior to restructuring; the Treynor measure uses beta, the firm's stock price variance relative to market variance for all stocks listed on the same exchange, as the denominator. Jensen's alpha is the intercept from a regression of the firm's excess return on the market excess return. Daily stock market returns, market index returns, and the risk-free rate were obtained from the CRSP tapes.

Divestment intensity was defined with three variables measuring different aspects of the construct: number of business units divested, percentage of sales divested, and time required to restructure. Number of divestitures was the total number of business units sold through sell-offs, buyouts, or equity carve-outs, or spun off during restructuring. Percentage of sales divested was the sales price of a sold unit divided by its total sales for the previous year, summed over the years a firm spent restructuring; in the absence of a publicly reported price, the unit's sales for the previous year approximated the price. The time spent restructuring was the number of years between the announcement of restructuring (or the first divestiture) and the announcement that restructuring was completed, with a two-year gap in divestitures taken to mean completion when no announcement was made.
time_window: the restructuring period following the year prior to the restructuring announcement

description: Two 5-point Likert-style indicators for the respondent's estimate of the firm's average revenue and asset growth relative to industry peers over the preceding three years. A higher reported score indicates higher growth.

variable_name: sales growth rate and asset growth rate
description: Financial measures of sales growth rate and of asset growth rate constructed from FAME using sales and asset data from the two full fiscal years preceding data collection. Both growth indicators were winsorized to address skewness and kurtosis, and were entered in the model as observed indicators.
time_window: two full fiscal years preceding data collection

description: Three 7-point Likert-style indicators modified from Jansen, Van Den Bosch, and Volberda (2005). Higher reported scores correspond to higher adaptive capability.

The same indicators for the focal latent constructs were used in Study 2 as in Study 1. A measurement error covariance between two adaptive capability indicators (AC1 and AC2) was freed to improve fit.

Measured with the Covin and Slevin (1989) entrepreneurial orientation scale and the Anderson et al. (2015) measurement model. Four EO indicators (INN1, INN2, PRO7, RISK9) were eliminated because of poor loading on their intended construct and/or cross-loading with other constructs, resulting in three indicators for entrepreneurial behaviors.
