Three items are used to measure the extent of partner experience, reflecting the length of the prior relationship (in years), and the frequency and size of prior transactions. All questions were framed in relation to the time periods that the respective constructs reflect.

variable_name: Supplier search time (log of search time)
description: Supplier search time is the total time spent in persondays on supplier and product comparison and selection, indicating the actual effort exerted by the buyer to find a 'good' supplier. Because its distribution is highly skewed (most buyers spent only a limited amount of time on selection, whereas several spent a substantial number of days), the authors use the log of search time.

Measures the time and effort invested by the buyer in evaluating and comparing suppliers on four selection criteria that the buyer considers important for supplier selection and transaction success. It reflects the buyer's focus in the search process, and a path from search time to supplier evaluation reflects the interrelation of the two search dimensions.

Measured with three items about the extent to which buyers, before making a choice for a supplier, possessed information about cost-benefit analyses of different products offered by different suppliers; publicly available information relating to suppliers' attributes, in particular technology, network, and market positioning; and information about the values, integrity, and ethics of suppliers. Items were measured using a five-point Likert scale, with 1 representing a 'low degree' and 5 a 'high degree'.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = low degree, 5 = high degree)
time_window: before making a choice for a supplier

description: Measured by the extent to which buyers at the moment of contracting possessed information about the supplier's likelihood to continue activities in a similar way in the longer term, reliability to achieve milestones (e.g., cost and quality), ability to adapt technology to the buyer's needs, and technology development plans and prospects. Items were measured using a five-point Likert scale, with 1 representing a 'low degree' and 5 a 'high degree'.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = low degree, 5 = high degree)

description: Measured by the extent to which buyers at the moment of contracting possessed information about expectations about the cooperation, mutual dependencies, and development of scenarios regarding how to cooperate. Items were measured using a five-point Likert scale, with 1 representing a 'low degree' and 5 a 'high degree'.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = low degree, 5 = high degree)

description: Outcome control functions without interference in suppliers' processes and is measured by five items about the extent to which the buyer during transaction management engaged in target setting, evaluation and rewarding of outcomes, and provision of feedback to the supplier. Items were measured using a five-point Likert scale, with 1 representing a 'low degree' and 5 a 'high degree'.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = low degree, 5 = high degree)

description: Measured by six items about the procedures specified and used to achieve certain goals, not necessarily focusing on the extent to which these goals are achieved. The items include the extent to which the buyer monitored the supplier's use of procedures, modified the supplier's procedures, required reports, provided feedback, and shared in costs if guidelines were followed. Items were measured using a five-point Likert scale, with 1 representing a 'low degree' and 5 a 'high degree'.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = low degree, 5 = high degree)

description: Interfirm control mechanisms were measured as two scales: outcome control (five items on target setting, evaluation and rewarding of outcomes, and feedback) and behavior control (six items on monitoring and modifying the supplier's procedures, requiring reports, feedback and cost sharing), on five-point Likert scales.

variable_name: Supplier search time and supplier evaluation
description: Partner search was measured by two dimensions: supplier search time (log of total persondays spent on supplier and product comparison and selection) and supplier evaluation (time and effort spent evaluating and comparing suppliers on price, reliability, service and technological capabilities).

Years of schooling is described as the most common measure of human capital. Average industry education was calculated from U.S. census data and ranges from the high school level (12 years of school) to some graduate school (17 years). The authors note that some firms in each industry are above and some are below the average.

NLSY respondents were asked about the number of hours of training required in the last year to maintain their skills; this number of hours of training was used as an indicator of firm-specific knowledge. The hours of training were then aggregated at the respondent's industry level (three digit). The measure reflects the average hours of informal training required to upgrade or maintain knowledge in each industry.

The extent to which the offer exceeds the target's market value two months before announcement; the variable is log transformed. It was compiled by ADP from SEC filings, news reports and, in some cases, interviews with management.
The portion of the offer that is in cash. It was compiled by ADP from SEC filings, news reports and, in some cases, interviews with management.
The number of days from the announcement of the buyer's interest to the date that the transaction closed. Poisson regression is used because the variable is essentially a count of days.
Indicates whether the transaction was a tender offer. It was compiled by ADP from SEC filings, news reports and, in some cases, interviews with management.

Buyers in unrelated industries are identified by comparing the expertise profiles of the buyer and target industries. The measure draws on Farjoun's expertise-based industry profiles and Klavens' expertise-based relatedness measure, using the percent distribution of employees in 823 five-digit occupational categories from the Occupational Employment Survey. The Euclidean distance between industry expertise profiles ranges from 0 to 1, where higher values indicate less related expertise; the equation itself is not readable in the text.

Information on financials, market, and stage of product prototypes was varied to create strong versus weak business viability conditions. In the strong condition investors read that the product was ''fully functional and operational at the moment''; in the weak condition they learned that the project was ''very rudimentary at the moment, and there is still work to be done.''

variable_name: perceptions of the founding entrepreneur (experimental manipulation)
description: Positive versus negative perceptions of the entrepreneur were elicited with quotations and statements made by the founder during conferences, pitch presentations, and subsequent Q&A sessions, taken verbatim from original sources and presented in the executive summary.
Investors assessed the extent to which they were presented an opportunity in which they would likely invest, using a 1-5 Agree-Disagree Likert scale.
An assessment of probable investment amount based on the current state of the venture, measured with a sliding scale with dollar amounts.
scale: sliding scale of dollar amounts ranging from $0 to over $20,000

description: Investors rated ''the extent to which you have a positive perception about the entrepreneur'' (interrater r = .86) and ''the extent to which you have a negative perception about the entrepreneur'' (interrater r = .85) on a 1-5 Disagree-Agree Likert scale. Each pitch was watched three times by three distinct investors who were blind to the outcome of the pitch.

Business viability data were measured based on coding of ''the extent to which this opportunity has strong business viability'' (interrater r = .71) and coding of ''the extent to which this opportunity has weak business viability'' (interrater r = .75).

Ventures that qualified as homeruns were coded as 1, with the others coded as 0, using the cutoffs of a successful acquisition, an IPO, or a return of 10 times or greater; all coding was completed retrospectively. The authors identified six ventures that qualified as homeruns.
time_window: four years after the funding decision

description: Venture survival was measured as a binary indicator variable as of March 2014, four years after the funding decision from pitch competitions. Survival was determined first by attempting to directly contact the ventures and then by searching each venture's website and cross-checking continuing operations through industry databases, newswires, and early-stage entrepreneurship databases and forums. Evidence was found that 78 out of the 90 ventures had survived, while 12 showed no evidence of having survived.
time_window: as of March 2014, four years after the funding decision

description: Venture growth was measured based on growth of the number of employees from 2011 to 2014, identifying employment levels as an exact figure or, when ranges were given, transforming them into point estimates by assigning the average of the reported range. A binary indicator variable was assigned based on whether the venture had demonstrated growth in the number of employees, with 39 ventures having no evidence of growth and 51 ventures showing growth.

Venture financing was measured as a binary indicator variable based on whether the venture received venture financing, using databases, press reports and media notices from public searches, and direct cross-checking with ventures. Financing included Small Business Innovation Research funding, seed-round funding, or venture capital Series A and Series B funding, but not self-investments or friends and family money; 46 ventures had received some type of financing.
time_window: four years after the funding decision

description: A value of 1 was assigned to all entrepreneurs who received funding from the pitch competition and a value of 0 to all entrepreneurs who did not receive funding from the pitch competition.

Attractiveness of the target country to the observing country, calculated with the Euclidean distance formula from response-bias-corrected GLOBE scores. For each cultural dimension the observer's cultural values ('should be') are matched with the target culture's practices ('as is'), using absolute rather than real value differences; CA for a dimension is six when the congruence between target practices and observer values is largest and zero when it is smallest. All nine GLOBE dimensions are included; the composite formula block printed in the article is not readable.

Attractiveness of the host country to the home (observing) country, calculated with the Euclidean distance formula from response-bias-corrected GLOBE scores. For each cultural dimension the observer's cultural values ('should be') are matched with the target culture's practices ('as is'), using absolute rather than real value differences; CA for a dimension is six when the congruence between target practices and observer values is largest and zero when it is smallest. All nine GLOBE dimensions are included; the composite formula block printed in the article is not readable.

Attractiveness of the target nation to the acquirer's nation, calculated with the Euclidean distance formula from response-bias-corrected GLOBE scores. For each cultural dimension the observer's cultural values ('should be') are matched with the target culture's practices ('as is'), using absolute rather than real value differences; CA for a dimension is six when the congruence between target practices and observer values is largest and zero when it is smallest. All nine GLOBE dimensions are included; the composite formula block printed in the article is not readable.

Country-dyadic annual reputation ratings collected by the Reputation Institute: respondents in the Group of Eight nations were asked to rate the reputation of up to two countries they are familiar with using a four-item measure. The individual ratings are aggregated to obtain annual bilateral reputation scores, that is, the average reputation of a target country ranked by all respondents from one observing country in a given year.

Annual bilateral FDI flows used as the dependent variable to study the scope of MNE investment between two countries. The variable captures the aggregate country-level FDI flow from a home into a host country in a given year. Because the FDI data are skewed, the natural logarithm of (FDI flows + 1) is used.

Cumulative abnormal return of the acquiring firm around the acquisition announcement, capturing whether the event had a positive or negative effect on shareholder wealth. Daily stock prices are collected around the announcement date t0 and a standard market model is used, with the market model parameters estimated over a 200-day window from event day -210 to event day -11 before the announcement; daily abnormal returns are added over the five-day window (-2, +2) surrounding the announcement.
time_window: five-day window (-2, +2) around the acquisition announcement

description: The five-day cumulative abnormal return (-2, +2) is added up from the daily abnormal returns, where the abnormal return is the acquirer's daily stock return minus the market model expectation based on the daily stock market return.

The KLD scale was customized to exclude issues outside of the primary stakeholder domain of corporate social performance, and the items chosen for stakeholder management came from five existing KLD categories: employee relations, diversity issues, product issues, community relations, and environmental issues. Each category is rated on a scale ranging from -2 (major concerns) through 0 (neutral) to +2 (major strength), and each category is given equal weighting. The categories were combined as a gestalt measure using simple summing of the dimensions. The measure is taken for the year 1994 (reported by KLD in 1995).

The SIP variable includes the KLD categories of Other, alcohol/tobacco/gambling exclusionary screens, military exclusionary screens, nuclear power exclusionary screens, and non-U.S. concerns over investment in Burma and Mexico. These are the KLD issues excluded from the stakeholder management measure because they fall outside the primary stakeholder domain. Each category is rated from -2 (major concerns) through 0 (neutral) to +2 (major strength), given equal weighting, and combined as a gestalt measure using simple summing. The measure is taken for the year 1994.

MVA is calculated as market value minus capital, where market value refers to the equity market valuation of the company and capital refers to the debt and equity invested in the company. MVA is the stock market's estimation of net present value. The authors use MVA not cross-sectionally but by examining the change in MVA between one year and the next; the measure of MVA for 1996 represents the change in market value added between 1995 and 1996. The change in MVA between 1995 and 1996 is the dependent variable for Hypotheses 2 and 4, and the change between 1996 and 1995 is used in the correlation tests of Hypotheses 1 and 3. MVA data were taken from the Stern Stewart Performance 1000 data base, in which MVA is calculated based on data available from Compustat.

Calculated as the ratio of the number of exploratory collaborations to the total number of collaborations between the firm and its partner over a 5-year moving window. The nature of each alliance was coded by content analysis of the deal summary from the focal firm's perspective: R&D alliances with the objective of exploring and creating critical new knowledge were coded as exploratory, while co-marketing, manufacturing, and licensing alliances were coded as exploitative; R&D alliances aimed at incremental changes to an existing technology were coded as exploitative. The value of the variable ranges from 0 to 1.

Contains three items: the number of competitive actions (i.e., market entries) that the firm launched against its partner following the alliance announcement, and the width and depth of its competing actions. Width measures the number of different therapeutic areas in which the firm entered that compete against its partner; depth measures the number of destructive competitions (i.e., modified brand-name drugs) launched against its partner. A factor analysis showed all three items loaded high (>0.73) on one latent factor and Cronbach's alpha is .81; the average score of the three items is the dependent variable.
Measured by counting the number of repeated alliance ties between the firm and its partner over the previous 5 years.

Yearly alliance matrices within the pharmaceutical industry were constructed for 1984–2003 using a 5-year moving window, and a symmetric (non-directional) matrix was built for each year in Ucinet 6; the degree centrality of each firm within these matrices was then calculated. Relative centrality is calculated as the firm's degree centrality minus its partner's degree centrality.
Measured by counting the number of common third-party partners that the firm and its partner shared during the previous 5 years.

The absolute value of the difference between the equity stake predicted by a two-tailed Tobit model and the equity stake actually held. The Tobit model calculates the expected equity stake from a host country's uncertainty - political uncertainty, legal/regulatory uncertainty, and economic uncertainty - plus several control variables. Negative raw values mean the parent holds a lower stake than expected and positive values mean a higher stake than expected, so the absolute value is used because the predictions pertain to the degree of misalignment regardless of its direction. It ranges from 0%, perfect correspondence with the predicted stake, to almost 100%.
time_window: predicted for the host country at a particular time

description: The rate of period-to-period change in misaligned equity stakes, which the authors state cannot be directly observed and is inferred from the partial (dynamic) adjustment model as one minus the coefficient of the Lagged Misalignment variable. Smaller coefficients for Lagged Misalignment indicate higher rates of adaptation, that is, a faster decrease in misalignment, while larger coefficients indicate lower rates of adaptation.

The total number of equity stake adaptations the Japanese parent has undertaken before the focal observation in the same host country as the focal subsidiary. The measure focuses on learning about the specific task of equity stake adaptation in the focal host country rather than on less proximate tasks.
The count of the equity stake adaptations that were made by all sample Japanese parent firms that were active in the same host country preceding the focal observation.
The parent firm's fungible slack resources, measured via its cash holdings in absolute currency, here in trillions of Yen, because the flexibility value of cash is subject to economies of scale.

Dummy variable that provides information on whether the transportation of parcels through domestic trucking for the parcel's city pair reflected ownership (coded 1) or contracting (coded 0). An equity stake involved in the governance of the segment for a particular city pair is classified as ownership. In the main analyses the predicted value of this variable, generated from the Nickerson et al. (2001) model of organizational choice, is used instead of the observed value to control for potential endogeneity.

Dummy variable that provides information on whether the transportation of parcels through international air transit for the parcel's city pair reflected ownership (coded 1) or contracting (coded 0). An equity stake involved in the governance of the segment for a particular city pair is classified as ownership. In the main analyses the predicted value of this variable, generated from the Nickerson et al. (2001) model of organizational choice, is used instead of the observed value to control for potential endogeneity.

Dummy variable that provides information on whether the transportation of parcels through foreign trucking for the parcel's city pair reflected ownership (coded 1) or contracting (coded 0). An equity stake involved in the governance of the segment for a particular city pair is classified as ownership. In the main analyses the predicted value of this variable, generated from the Nickerson et al. (2001) model of organizational choice, is used instead of the observed value to control for potential endogeneity.

Dummy variable equaling 1 if ownership is used for all stages of the transportation chain (Own(Dom), Own(Air), and Own(For) are all equal to 1), and 0 otherwise. It captures ownership of multiple sequential activities in the value chain. In the main analyses the predicted value of this variable, generated from the Nickerson et al. (2001) model of organizational choice, is used instead of the observed value to control for potential endogeneity.

LnDaysDev is the deviation from expected delivery time, computed as the residual of an OLS regression of the natural logarithm of delivery time (LnDays) on parcel- and courier-specific control variables. The parametric test compares the residual variance of a linear mixed model (estimated through Bayesian methods) with and without the focal ownership variable in the random-effects matrix Z, using the ratio of the estimated residual variance with and without inclusion of that variable, and assesses significance with an F test.

A Rosenblatt-Parzen kernel density estimator with an Epanechnikov kernel and a bandwidth computed from Fox's (1990) formula is used to estimate the distribution of LnDaysDev for the whole sample and the counterfactual distribution that would have prevailed had all parcels been transported under each ownership pattern. Each observation is weighted by the inverse probability that it would be sampled, computed from probit predictions of organizational choice. Reliability is read from the right-hand portion of the distribution, the mass of shipments that arrive later than expected; compression of that mass indicates higher reliability (lower variability).

A cumulative index of patient encounters at the ED, accumulated over the organization's history and depreciated geometrically by a fixed retention parameter. The retention parameter was chosen by iteratively estimating a base model including the experience measure and the study's controls while varying the depreciation value, and selecting the value that maximized model fit. The resulting experience variable was logged to account for its marginally diminishing impact as experience increases.
time_window: cumulative through year t-1 (lagged one period)

description: The percentage of patients seen by the ED who die within the department, aggregated at the department-year level. The authors limit the focus to mortality within the ED rather than mortality of patients admitted from or discharged home from the ED, since within-department mortality is a more direct indicator of the quality and effectiveness of care received directly within the ED.

Based on the total number of hours that a focal ED actively diverts ambulances away from the facility during each year. The total hours of ambulance diversions were scaled by 10,000s to facilitate interpretation, accumulated across years, and depreciated using the same formula and parameter as the cumulative patient experience variable, so that more recent constraint events are weighted more heavily than more distant ones.

Built from detailed monthly ambulance diversion hours for each ED. An entropy index is used, which takes higher values whenever diversion hours are more evenly distributed across categories, in this case months; P is the proportion of the focal ED's diversion hours that occur during month i, summed across each month within a particular year. The index was then accumulated and depreciated for each ED, similar to the cumulative experience and cumulative diversion hours variables.
time_window: cumulative across study years, depreciated, built from monthly data

description: The capacity utilization rate of a firm in a market and year, calculated as the ratio of its net annual output in the market (in megawatt hours) divided by the number of hours per year (365 x 24) and its total summer capacity (in megawatts). Net generation output equals gross output minus internal electricity use and pumping energy. The measure represents average capacity utilization over the year, although output decisions are made continuously.

The difference between the analysts' EPS forecast consensus for year t, measured at the beginning of the year, minus the potential EPS (Matsumoto's measure at the beginning of the year), standardized by the firm's stock price at the beginning of year t. Potential earnings combines information about trends in a firm's historical performance with recent stock market returns, with the predictive effect calibrated using regression parameters from other industry peers, excluding the focal firm. To limit the impact of extreme observations, earnings pressure was capped to be positive or negative 0.1 if the difference exceeded 10 percent of the stock price. Firms receiving forecasts from at least three different analysts were selected.

A generator's share of summer capacity in its NERC regional market in a prior year. It was calculated on the basis of capacity levels rather than output levels and lagged rather than current levels to reduce concerns about endogeneity and reverse causality.

A Herfindahl market concentration index based on the summer capacity of all other rivals (for-profit and not-for-profit utilities) in the wholesale market in the prior year, excluding the focal firm. Excluding the focal firm reduced collinearity between a firm's dominant share and market concentration.

The total capacity share in the market of all other for-profit firms (publicly traded or privately owned) in the prior year, excluding the focal firm. It measures the market presence of for-profit competitors relative to non-investor-owned generators.

The average capacity utilization level of all other firms in the market (including for-profit and not-for-profit) in the prior year, excluding the focal firm. Higher values indicate rivals with more spare utilization headroom, i.e. looser capacity constraints.

For each firm in each market, the average of the earnings pressure measures of the publicly traded rivals in the focal market (excluding the focal firm), weighted by their respective capacity shares. The variable is computed at the beginning of the year to examine the cross-rival effect of earnings pressure.

Created for all consumer ratings that were lower than those of experts by subtracting the consumers' overall rating of a hotel from the expert rating (indicated as hotel class) for this same hotel, both ratings ranging from one to five. Instances of evaluation equal or superior to those of experts were coded as 0. For example, if TripAdvisor rates a hotel as four stars and a consumer rates it as two stars, Devaluation for this hotel equals 2.
scale: difference between two ratings ranging from one to five; 0 for equal or over-evaluations

description: A dichotomous variable created at the review level of analysis, equal to 1 if an online review is responded to publicly and 0 otherwise.

Organizational reputation is traceable through the TripAdvisor Ranking, obtained from an algorithm that incorporates the quantity, quality and recency of TripAdvisor reviews and aims to represent the beliefs of consumers regarding the likelihood that a hotel will deliver value. Hotels are listed according to their ranking and search results are presented according to the same rationale; the intensity of economic benefits for a hotel is inversely proportional to its positioning in the ranking. Because organizational reputation may decline in a non-linear fashion with the rank, TripAdvisor ranking was log-transformed; smaller values suggest higher ranks and a better organizational reputation.
As the length of the response may also proxy a rationalizing effort, the authors counted the number of words used in the response and log-transformed this count.

The rationalizing efforts of the response were measured as the percentage of words belonging to the cognitive category of cause, computed with the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software, which matches the words contained in texts with predefined dictionaries and computes the percentages of words devoted to validated grammatical and psychological categories. 'Because,' 'justify,' and 'solve' represent exemplary words of this category.
scale: percentage of words in the response

description: The rationalizing efforts of the response were measured as the percentage of words belonging to the cognitive category of insight, computed with the LIWC software. Insight words are indicative of in-depth thinking and reasoning and imply making sense of events, analytical thinking, learning and understanding; words such as 'acknowledge,' 'explain,' 'appreciate,' and 'reconsider' represent prime examples of this category.
scale: percentage of words in the response

description: Attempts at deflecting the pejorative quality of devaluations were captured by counting the percentage of exclusive words used in the public response of hoteliers, computed with the LIWC software. Exclusive words, such as 'either,' 'except,' 'unless,' and 'without,' signify cognitive efforts and reflect complexity of the language being used to maintain a true story.
scale: percentage of words in the response

description: Attempts at deflecting the pejorative quality of devaluations were captured by counting the percentage of motion words used in the public response of hoteliers, computed with the LIWC software. Motion words such as 'run,' 'change,' and 'replace' provide simple, concrete descriptions, serve as a means of averting attention away from the self and are associated with higher degrees of unreliability; the authors therefore expect a negative relation between motion words and devaluation.
scale: percentage of words in the response

description: Variation along market identities is captured by stars ranging from one to five; stars in the article refer to the hotel rating provided by TripAdvisor. Star ratings appear prominently on the TripAdvisor website and critically shape hotels' market identities by providing an effective tool for establishing boundaries of inclusion and exclusion via market segmentation. In the sample, hotels were distributed across star levels from one to five, with TripAdvisor using 0.5 intervals.

The performance gap is operationalized by accumulating the industry-adjusted profitability for 5 years by using industry-level profitability from COMPUSTAT with the firm's sales breakdown into 3-digit SIC industries as a weighting factor. Two profitability measures are used: return on asset (ROA), net income after tax but before extraordinary items deflated by total assets, and operating cash flow (OCF), operating cash flows (sales minus cost of goods sold and selling and administrative expenses, plus depreciation and goodwill expenses) deflated by total assets. The formula by which the gap is computed from these measures is not readable in the text.
time_window: 5 years before the entry or exit event (e.g., 1978-82 for 1983 entries)

description: Dissimilarity is computed from the percentages of four human resource groups (managerial, engineering, scientific and marketing) reported by the OES for each 3-digit SIC industry; the overall distance between an incumbent industry i and a target industry j is the square root of the sum of the four squared differences in human resource percentages. For the extensive search model, the dissimilarity of a target industry is the minimum of the distances from the industries the firm is already in. For the intensive search and exit models, the dissimilarity of a business is the sum of its distances to the firm's other incumbent industries, weighted by the sales of those other businesses.

variable_name: Human resource profile dissimilarity measured from the previous entries
description: Measure of human resource profile dissimilarity of a target industry evaluated from the closest industries that a firm previously entered at time t - 1. It is entered in the yearly logit regressions of sequential extensive search.

In the entry models the observed binomial dependent variable equals one if the ith firm enters industry j at time t and zero otherwise; entry is defined by a number of establishments corresponding to each SIC industry from zero to a positive number. Entry into a new 3-digit SIC industry is extensive search and subsequent entry into a 4-digit SIC industry within an existing 3-digit industry is intensive search. In the corporate-level performance model the magnitude of entry is measured in terms of sales of entered lines of business, deflated by average total sales figures of the firm.

Exit is defined by change in the number of establishments from a positive number to zero, measured at 4-digit SIC, and the analysis is limited to exit from incumbent businesses as of 1981. The dependent variable in the exit models is a hazard rate that denotes the likelihood of a line of business to be divested at each time period. In the corporate-level performance model the magnitude of exit is measured in terms of sales of divested lines of business, deflated by average total sales figures of the firm.

Entry into a new 3-digit SIC industry, i.e., one in which the firm did not previously operate. It is the dependent variable of the pooled logit regressions of extensive search and of the yearly sequential search regressions.
Entry into a 4-digit SIC industry within an existing 3-digit industry. It is the dependent variable of the logit regressions of intensive search.

variable_name: Extensiveness of a firm's previous search activity
description: A ratio of extensive search to the total entry at the previous time period in terms of sales. It measures the momentum of continuing the same type of search and is entered in the yearly regressions of extensive search.

A proportion of sales from businesses that a firm entered through extensive search from 1981 until time t - 1 to total sales of the firm. It captures the threshold effects that contribute to switching into another search mode.

Performance change is measured by subtracting the 3-year average of profitability in 1978-80 from the 3-year average of profitability in 1990-92, using both ROA and OCF. In addition to the absolute level of profitability change, industry-adjusted profitability change is examined, computed in the same way as the performance gap except that a 3-year average is used. The corporate-level regressions are weighted by the number of 4-digit SIC businesses to correct for heteroscedasticity.

Survival is a dichotomous variable that notes survival/exit at time t + 1. Exit occurs when a valid observation at time t does not show up in the database at time t + 1, after it has been matched with various demographic information in several instances. Firms that exited might have closed down or been sold, or their sales might have dipped below 5 million RMB in the case of non-SOEs.

Aggregated share of employment of non-HMT foreign firms in a three-digit Chinese Standard Industry Classification industry at time t, measured at the national level. The employment shares of the four types of firms sum to one, and the national conventional local firms' employment is treated as the base group in all analyses.
time_window: t (one year before the survival outcome)

description: Share of employment of non-HMT foreign firms in an industry within a region at time t. Regions were defined using two-digit area codes for provinces, autonomous regions, and centrally administered cities (Beijing, Chongqing, Shanghai, and Tianjin). The regional conventional local firms' employment is the base group.
time_window: t (one year before the survival outcome)

description: Aggregated share of employment of HMT (Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan) firms in a three-digit Chinese Standard Industry Classification industry at time t, measured at the national level. The employment shares of the four types of firms sum to one, and the national conventional local firms' employment is the base group.
time_window: t (one year before the survival outcome)

description: Share of employment of HMT firms in an industry within a region at time t. Regions were defined using two-digit area codes for provinces, autonomous regions, and centrally administered cities. The regional conventional local firms' employment is the base group.
time_window: t (one year before the survival outcome)

description: Aggregated share of employment of reformed local firms (private, shareholding, and limited liability companies) in a three-digit Chinese Standard Industry Classification industry at time t, measured at the national level. The employment shares of the four types of firms sum to one, and the national conventional local firms' employment is the base group.
time_window: t (one year before the survival outcome)

description: Share of employment of reformed local firms in an industry within a region at time t. Regions were defined using two-digit area codes for provinces, autonomous regions, and centrally administered cities. The regional conventional local firms' employment is the base group.
time_window: t (one year before the survival outcome)

variable_name: National versus regional employment share variables
description: Market commonality was operationalized by the market level at which group presence was measured: national industry employment shares versus regional (province-level) industry shares. Regional shares are expected to show stronger competition effects than national shares.

The presence of each group of firms was measured as its share of employment in a three-digit industry (non-HMT foreign firms, HMT firms, reformed local firms, with conventional local firms as the base group), at the national level and within regions.

variable_name: Ownership group of the focal firm and the present group
description: Resource similarity was operationalized through the pairing of firm groups: for example, HMT firms are treated as more similar to local firms than non-HMT foreign firms, and reformed local firms as more similar to foreign firms than conventional local firms. The effects of each group's employment share on local and foreign firm survival were compared across these pairings.

A seven-item index based on previous research. Respondents indicated the extent to which each statement describes the responsibilities of the subsidiary concerning any one of its dominant product lines, on a five-point scale from 1 = 'to a very little extent' to 5 = 'to a very great extent'. The first item was reverse scored. The coefficient alpha for the scale was 0.87. The correlation between the key informant and secondary respondent was 0.80.

A multi-item scale assessing the extent to which the foreign subsidiary has operational and strategic decision-making authority across its entire product line, with the response scale based on studies by Ghoshal and colleagues and the list of decision items drawn from Egelhoff (1988) and the Aston studies. For the overall business activities of the subsidiary, respondents indicated the extent of headquarters and/or subsidiary influence on each decision, on a four-point scale from 1 = 'headquarters almost always decides' to 4 = 'subsidiary almost always decides'. The coefficient alpha was 0.90.

Respondents were asked to indicate the number of managers comprising the subsidiary top management team and the number of these managers who are from corporate headquarters. The headquarters supervision measure is the percentage of the subsidiary top management team that is from corporate headquarters.

A seven-item scale based on several previous studies. Respondents indicated how frequently information in each subsidiary area is reviewed by headquarters, on a scale of 1 = daily, 2 = weekly, 3 = monthly, 4 = quarterly, 5 = annually, and 9 = never; the responses were recoded such that a higher score indicates a greater level of monitoring. The coefficient alpha was 0.68.
scale: frequency categories (daily to never), recoded so higher scores indicate greater monitoring

description: A five-item scale assessing the degree to which the desired subsidiary outcomes are specifiable and quantifiable. Respondents indicated the extent to which each statement describes the subsidiary, on a five-point scale from 1 = 'to a very little extent' to 5 = 'to a very great extent'. The scale exhibited acceptable internal consistency (alpha = 0.85) and the responses of the primary and secondary respondents were significantly correlated.

Following Buchko (1994) and Wholey and Brittain (1989), industry volatility was assessed as the variance in worldwide industry production over the past ten years for the primary industry of the subsidiary as determined by the four-digit SIC code for the subsidiary. Worldwide industry production figures were collected from the Industrial Commodity Statistics Yearbook, which details country-based and worldwide yearly production figures broken down by international standard industrial classification codes.

Host country volatility was measured by Euromoney's 1996 Country Risk Ratings. The Euromoney country risk assessment uses nine categories that fall into three broad groups: analytical indicators, credit indicators, and market indicators, and calculates a weighted score for each country. The scores are on a scale from 0 through 100 with higher scores indicating less country risk; in this study they were reverse scored so that higher scores indicate greater country risk.

Based on Balkin and Gomez-Mejia (1987) and Galbraith and Merrill (1991). Respondents were asked to indicate the percentage of subsidiary senior management compensation paid through each of: fixed salary, incentives based on short-term performance, and incentives based on long-term performance, with the total of the three components equaling one hundred percent. The sum of the percentages allocated to short-term and long-term performance incentives was used as the measure of monetary incentives.

A multi-item scale measuring the degree to which activities and outcomes at the foreign subsidiary affect or are affected by activities of headquarters, based on Astley and Zajac (1990). Respondents indicated the extent to which each statement describes the subsidiary, on a five-point scale from 1 = 'to a very little extent' to 5 = 'to a very great extent'. The scale exhibited an acceptable coefficient alpha (alpha = 0.63), and the two interdependence measures were hypothesized to have different effects, so they were measured separately.

A multi-item scale measuring the degree to which activities and outcomes at the foreign subsidiary affect or are affected by activities of other foreign subsidiaries, based on Astley and Zajac (1990). Respondents indicated the extent to which each statement describes the subsidiary, on a five-point scale from 1 = 'to a very little extent' to 5 = 'to a very great extent'. The scale exhibited an acceptable coefficient alpha (alpha = 0.88), and the two interdependence measures were hypothesized to have different effects, so they were measured separately.
Measured with four objective items relating to personal interaction between headquarters and subsidiary managers that were averaged to form an index. The coefficient alpha for this measure was 0.53.

A nine-item scale based on Gupta and Govindarajan (1993) and Roth et al. (1991). Respondents indicated the extent to which each activity occurs in the subsidiary, on a five-point scale from 1 = 'very rarely' to 5 = 'very frequently'. The coefficient alpha for this measure was 0.91 and the correlation between the responses of the primary and secondary respondents was 0.75.

Items were developed following Churchill (1979): after specifying the domain of the construct through a literature search, personal and telephone interviews with international compensation and/or human resources managers confirmed the domain and generated survey items, and subsequent interviews were used to confirm and edit the items. A thirteen-item scale was factor analyzed with varimax rotation after dropping two items that loaded on multiple factors; the first factor consists of six items related to the subsidiary manager's career path, and an index was created from these items labeled non-monetary career related rewards (alpha = 0.87). The measure was validated by correlating the key informant's responses with the secondary respondent's (r = 0.57).

The three items that loaded on the second factor of the thirteen-item non-monetary incentives scale were combined in an index for a measure of non-monetary subsidiary-related rewards (alpha = 0.81). The measure was validated by correlating the responses of the key informant with those of the secondary respondent (r = 0.47).

Latent construct represented by four survey items covering effort toward copying the partner's practices exactly: managing the business exactly like the partner, implementing the partner's practices exactly as they existed, copying practices down to the smallest detail, and spending substantial time making sure adopted practices worked just as they did at the partner. Respondents rated each item on a five-point Likert scale (agree/disagree) for the first year of the relationship and for 2001; the structural model uses the initial-year responses. Confirmatory factor analysis shows each item loading significantly on the construct and reliability well above the 0.7 threshold.

Latent construct represented by four survey items covering effort toward modifying or combining the partner's practices: usually modifying practices when implementing them, usually combining the partner's ideas with other ideas, spending substantial time modifying practices to make them work, and carefully selecting practices to adopt. Respondents rated each item on a five-point Likert scale (agree/disagree) for the first year of the relationship and for 2001; the structural model uses the initial-year responses. Each item loads significantly on the construct and reliability is well above the 0.7 threshold.

Latent construct represented by three survey items about what the receiving unit obtained from the partner: the partner provided valuable information for the business, the firm learned a lot from the partner, and the partner provided examples of new ways to manage the business. Respondents rated each item on a five-point Likert scale (agree/disagree) for the first year of the relationship and for 2001; the structural model uses the initial-year responses. Each item loads significantly on the construct and reliability is well above the 0.7 threshold.

The variable cell was coded from survey responses and indicates whether the firm operates only in the cellular telecommunications market. Cellular firms are treated as having fewer links with the environment because regulators do not impose universal service obligations and because the infrastructure does not require installation in every neighborhood.
time_window: 2001 and first year of the relationship

description: The variable new indicates whether the receiving firm was founded at the same time as the transfer relationship; it was coded from survey responses. Firms that pre-date the relationship have historical routines that acquire connections to the environment as they face new contingencies over time, which makes their knowledge less discrete.
time_window: founding of the receiving firm relative to the relationship

description: The variable template indicates whether the source firm had operations in its home country, and was drawn from company reports. Firms without home operations are more likely to transfer knowledge from multiple source locations, introducing connections with multiple source environments; as a result, firms with a home template are treated as possessing more discrete knowledge.

The number of years the knowledge transfer relationship had existed in 2001, taken from survey responses. The authors treat it as representing understanding built through experience in this particular relationship.

The number of countries where the source firm provided telecom services in 2001, taken from company reports. The authors treat it as source-unit understanding of connections built through repeated transfer.

The number of source-firm relationships within the same country as the receiving firm, taken from company reports. The authors treat it as source-unit understanding of the specific country setting built through multiple relationships.
level: source firm in the receiving country

description: Performance of the receiving firm is measured as improvements in efficiency in the year after the knowledge transfer relationship was founded. Efficiency is the number of subscribers per employee, calculated for the end of the first year and the end of the second year of the relationship. The variable edelt12 is defined as the percentage change in this measure between the first year and the second year of the relationship.
time_window: first year to second year of the relationship

variable_name: average share of the dominant firm
description: The first of three measures used to focus on the level and the persistence of market share: the average market share of the dominant firm in each industry during the period from 1987 to 1994. Market shares were gathered for each of the years for the four leading firms in each industry and were determined on the basis of the dollar volume of sales of each firm relative to total industry sales. In cases where full year data were not available, estimates were derived from quarterly or semi-annual data.

variable_name: relative share of dominant firm (relative market share)
description: The extent of dominance assessed by the relative market share of the leading firm during the period from 1987 to 1994, defined as the share of the leading firm relative to the total share of the four leading competitors. It was obtained by expressing the leading firm's average share as a percentage of the average of the total market share for the four leading competitors over the period studied. The level of this share indicates the extent to which the firm held a dominant position among its closest rivals.

variable_name: relative stability (persistence) of dominant firm share
description: The extent of dominance assessed by the persistence of the market share of the dominant firm over the period from 1987 to 1994. Persistence in the annual shares was determined by the coefficient of variation first used by Jacoby (1964) and further developed by Schneider (1966), a measure used because it is more sensitive to large swings in market share than to incremental trends. It is provided by the standard deviation, expressed as a percentage of the mean market share of the dominant firm, so that higher values indicate larger swings and therefore weaker persistence of share.

The significance attached to a product's purchase was determined by the type of retail outlet that accounted for the vast majority of its sales. Products primarily sold through convenience stores, which are typically purchased more frequently and are lower in price, were given a score of 0; products mainly sold through other types of stores, particularly specialty stores, which are purchased less frequently and are higher in price, were given a score of 1. Information on the type of retail outlet used for each product was obtained from a breakdown of sales outlets provided in surveys such as Off-the-Shelf Industry Reports, supplemented by information from the 1987 Census of Retail Trade. This classification was found to correspond quite closely to available information on price range and purchase frequencies of products.

The extent of possible differences in tastes among existing consumers was represented by a composite estimate of the product breadth for each industry studied. Product breadth was defined as the average number of products that were offered by all of the significant competitors for the years covered; all of the products that may be offered as part of a particular line were individually counted, even if certain products could be considered to fall under the banner of a single line or single brand. Information was largely based on brands and models offered by each of the firms, collected from Companies and Their Brands and from surveys such as Off-the-Shelf Industry Reports and verified through annual reports, catalogues, and circulars obtained from the firms studied. Because measures of product breadth showed systematic differences in variance as they increased in value, a log transformation was carried out on these measures.

Salience of information was represented by a measure of advertising intensity in each of the industries, determined by calculating the advertising to sales ratio: the annual advertising expenditures of all of the significant competitors divided by the total annual industry sales. These ratios were calculated for all of the 8 years that were studied, and the annual figures were used to derive a mean value for advertising intensity for each of the industries in the sample. Information on advertising expenditures was obtained most prominently from the Ad $ Summary and verified with information from Off-the-Shelf Industry Reports and issues of Advertising Age and Marketing and Media Decisions.

Respondents indicated the percentage of time the head coach used each of the three strategies (speed, power, finesse) over the past 5 to 10 seasons. A coach's preferred strategy was defined as the strategy used the most; because coaches were asked about past strategy, a coach in his first season at a school based his responses on his strategy at previous schools.

Respondents indicated the percentage of time their teams used each of the three strategy options during the 1991-92 season, and actual strategy was defined as the one emphasized the most. For the analysis, team strategy was dummy-coded as two variables, with use of the speed, finesse, and power strategies respectively coded 1, 0; 0, 1; and 0, 0.
scale: percentage of time; dummy-coded for analysis

description: A new dummy-coded variable computed for the test of Hypothesis 2, where 1 = actual and preferred strategy consistent and 0 = inconsistent.

Six items from the 16 recruit characteristics, each rated by the coach on the importance he placed on the skill when evaluating recruits to play his preferred strategy, using a seven-point scale (1 = one of the least important, 4 = average importance, 7 = one of the most important). The items loaded on the first factor of a principal components analysis with varimax rotation and were summed to create the scale (alpha = .69).
scale: seven-point importance scale (1-7) per item, summed

description: Three attitudinal items from the 16 recruit characteristics, each rated by the coach on the importance he placed on it when evaluating recruits to play his preferred strategy, using a seven-point scale (1 = one of the least important, 4 = average importance, 7 = one of the most important). The items loaded on the second factor of a principal components analysis with varimax rotation and were summed to create the scale (alpha = .83).
scale: seven-point importance scale (1-7) per item, summed

description: Two items from the 16 recruit characteristics, each rated by the coach on the importance he placed on it when evaluating recruits to play his preferred strategy, using a seven-point scale (1 = one of the least important, 4 = average importance, 7 = one of the most important). The items loaded on the third factor of a principal components analysis with varimax rotation and were summed to create the scale (alpha = .58).
scale: seven-point importance scale (1-7) per item, summed

description: The same 16 items that composed recruit skills were used to rate team skills, with each respondent rating his team as a group on the level of skills shown in the previous season (1 = poor, 4 = average, 7 = outstanding). Six items loaded on the first factor of a principal components analysis with varimax rotation and were summed to create the scale (alpha = .91); these items emphasize less glamorous but highly important aspects of basketball.
scale: seven-point rating scale (1-7) per item, summed

description: Items from the 16 team-skill ratings on which respondents rated their team as a group on the level of skills shown in the previous season (1 = poor, 4 = average, 7 = outstanding). Three items referring to generic athletic skills loaded on the second factor of a principal components analysis with varimax rotation and were summed to create the scale (alpha = .78).
scale: seven-point rating scale (1-7) per item, summed

description: Items from the 16 team-skill ratings on which respondents rated their team as a group on the level of skills shown in the previous season (1 = poor, 4 = average, 7 = outstanding). Three shooting items loaded on the third factor of a principal components analysis with varimax rotation and were summed to create the scale (alpha = .76).
scale: seven-point rating scale (1-7) per item, summed

description: Sagarin's final rankings for the 1991-92 season, used as an objective performance assessment over the course of the focal season. The ratings control for the quality of competition and apply a diminishing returns principle so that teams are rewarded for doing well against good opponents; they are inverted, with 1 the highest ranking.

Respondents indicated their agreement with seven statements about the team's day-to-day performance (e.g., 'Our team had an outstanding season'; 'Our players got along well with each other'), on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). One item, 'Our players had problems in their studies,' was reverse-coded; the summed items had a coefficient alpha of .91.
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1-7) per item, summed

variable_name: importance of each sector of the task environment
description: Respondents rated the importance of each sector of the task environment in the firm's planning and goal-setting activities. The sectors rated were raw material suppliers, competitors, customers, suppliers, creditors, and regulatory agencies. The measure was adopted from Dill's (1958) notion of task environment and Miles and Snow's (1978) concept of task contingency.

variable_name: ability to predict changes in a sector
description: Respondents rated their own abilities to predict changes in each sector of the task environment, including regulatory agencies. Predictability was reported per sector of the task environment.

variable_name: ability to control for the effects of a sector
description: Respondents rated their own abilities to control for the effects of each sector of the task environment, including regulatory agencies. Controllability was reported per sector of the task environment.

Respondents rated the frequency with which they applied five types of adjustments in direct response to the actions of each sector of the task environment. Each adjustment type was defined with corresponding examples: procedural, personnel-related, process, structural, and strategic. The answer scale was: never, rarely (once or twice), sometimes (three to five times), frequently (six to ten times), and considerable (more than ten times), constructed within the given time period 1977-1979.
scale: never; rarely (once or twice); sometimes (three to five times); frequently (six to ten times); considerable (more than ten times)

description: Respondents rated characteristics of regulatory agencies in terms of the severity of their effects on organizations. The characteristics were frequency of contact with regulatory agencies, harmful effects on morale, costs of record keeping, noncooperative attitude of regulatory officials and inspectors, and difficulty in obtaining information.
Number of employees was used as the measure of firm size. The data were obtained from questionnaires and then verified from standard corporation directories.
Age was measured by the number of years of operation and was obtained from the questionnaire.

Companies in each industry were selected from the Directory of Oregon Manufacturers using Standard Industrial Classification codes. The two industries were high technology/electronics (producers of electrical and industrial equipment, components, and analytical test instruments) and wood products (producers of hardwood, veneer, plywood, and softwood).

variable_name: Six rated sectors of the task environment
description: Task environment sector was operationalized as the six sectors respondents rated: raw material suppliers, competitors, customers, suppliers, creditors, and regulatory agencies. Importance, predictability, controllability and adjustment ratings were each reported per sector.

variable_name: Ratings of importance, predictability, controllability and adverse practices of regulatory agencies
description: Managerial assessments were measured by respondents' ratings of regulatory agencies' importance in planning, their ability to predict and to control agency actions, the severity of adverse agency characteristics, and the frequency of adjustments, which were then correlated with firm size and age.

Measure adapted from the differential benefits measure developed by Gulati and Wang (2003), with two modifications. Percentage abnormal stock returns were replaced with corresponding dollar returns obtained by multiplying event-window percentage returns by the firms' market capitalization 20 days before the JV announcement. The measure was then revised so that it yields zero when partners obtain dollar returns in parallel to their ownership shares in the JV, with Sharey/Sharex accounting for weighting in the partners' ownership shares. Partner returns (dcarx and dcary) are cumulative abnormal returns in dollars calculated over the event window [-1,+1]. The exact equation is not recoverable from this text: the formula block was not extracted, so the specification is recorded only as the authors describe it in prose.
time_window: cumulative abnormal returns over the event window [-1,+1]; market model estimated over the 50-250 trading days before the announcement date; market capitalization 20 days before the JV announcement

description: Average profitability of the JV's 3-digit SIC industry, measured as the return on equity, during the 3 years before the JV formation. Three-year averages attenuate any potentially confounding effects of transient, atypical industry profitability. Because this measure is defined at the industry-year level, it demonstrated sufficient variance throughout the sample featuring 144 unique industry-year combinations across 178 observations.

Average sales growth in the JV's 3-digit SIC industry during the 3 years before the JV formation. Three-year averages attenuate any potentially confounding effects of transient, atypical industry growth. Together with industry profitability it proxies the perceived common benefit potential of the JV, which partners perceive to be higher when the JV industry is growing or profitable.

Dichotomous variable coded '0' for JVs in which the ownership shares are equally distributed and coded '1' to indicate any distribution imbalance. In the sample, partners have equal ownership shares in 100 JVs while the remaining 78 JVs disclose unbalanced distribution of ownership shares; ownership shares in JVs are used as the indicator of the sharing of common benefits among partners.
scale: dichotomous (0 = equal ownership shares, 1 = any imbalance)

description: Measure developed by Gulati and Singh (1998), which infers the type of task interdependence from the purpose of the alliance formation. Any alliance formed to share complementary technology, reduce the time needed for innovation, or develop new technology was categorized as demonstrating reciprocal interdependence; market-access alliances were labeled as those with sequential interdependence; and alliances formed to share high costs, risks, and financial resources were categorized as those with pooled interdependence.

Dichotomous variable taking the value of '1' if one of the partners appointed the CEO of the JV, and '0' otherwise. The operationalization follows the finding that contracts devote special attention to the CEO appointment and that operational control rights predominantly feature the appointment of top management in the alliance.
scale: dichotomous (0 = no partner appoints the JV CEO, 1 = one partner appoints the JV CEO)

description: The number of years of work experience of the most experienced founder among all the founders of the focal firm. Work experience is measured as the number of years from the year that the founder received his or her last academic degree until the year of founding of the focal start-up, on the assumption that greater work experience is associated with higher potential wage earnings. For firms with multiple founders, the founder with the most work experience was designated as the main founder and his or her characteristics were used to characterize the start-up.

A time-based measure of entrepreneurial opportunity cost, coded one if the focal firm was founded after 2000. The authors argue that entrepreneurs would have low opportunity cost after the bubble, as employment opportunities in IT shrank.

The initial size at entry, measured as the number of employees at the time of entry, used as a proxy for the quality of the start-up. The authors cite the literature showing that more able entrepreneurs start larger firms and that initial firm size is highly correlated with firm performance, typically measured as survival.

The U.S. information security patents (U.S. patent technological class 705, subclass 50-79, 380, and 726) assigned to the start-up at the time of formation, used as a measure of the venture's technical ability. Each patent is weighted by forward citations, adjusting for year of grant.

The number of IT trademarks of the previous employer of the founder at the time of entry, used to proxy the marketing ability of the start-up on the assumption that the founder inherited some of the marketing ability from the earlier employer. Where the start-up had multiple parents, the authors use the number from the parent with the greatest number of IT trademarks. Trademark descriptions were searched in the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office trademarks database.

A start-up is identified as having failed if it either went bankrupt or was acquired on unfavorable terms. An acquisition was classified as unfavorable using three criteria: (i) for VC-funded start-ups, if the transaction value was less than the total capital raised; (ii) if a start-up was not VC funded and reported a loss in the year prior to the acquisition; (iii) if the start-up is not VC-funded and profitability data are lacking, if none of the founders joined the acquiring firm. The year of failure is the year in which the corporate website was last available on archive.org, or the year of the sale in the case of a distress sale.

Cash-out is defined as a favorable acquisition or an IPO, whichever was earlier. A favorable acquisition is an acquisition of a VC-funded start-up whose transaction value exceeded total capital raised, or an acquisition of a non-VC-funded start-up that reported a profit in the year preceding acquisition, or, absent that data, an acquisition of a non-VC-funded start-up that resulted in at least one of the founders joining the acquiring firm. The date of acquisition was identified using the Zephyr database.

The top six officers in the sampled firms rated the strength of the corporate culture of each other sampled firm in their own industry, judging the degree to which managers at a firm were influenced in their decision making by a strong corporate culture in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Respondents rated each firm on a scale of one to five, and an average score across respondents was computed for each firm. Kotter and Heskett's inverse coding was reversed, so higher scores indicate a stronger corporate culture.

Yearly net income divided by invested capital, where invested capital is stockholders' equity minus current liabilities. It is an accounting measure of how profitably the firm's managers put invested capital to use, measured yearly from 1979 to 1984.

Annual sales less the sum of costs of goods sold, selling, general and administrative expenses, and the annual change in working capital, measured in constant 1984 dollars. Measured yearly from 1979 to 1984.

variable_name: Log variance of return on invested capital
description: Variation about a predicted mean performance level, where greater variation means lower reliability. In the multiplicative heteroscedasticity models the residual variance of the performance equation is modeled as a log-linear function of the covariates predicting the mean; the culture-strength coefficient indicates the effect on the log variance of ROI. Factors that increase the reliability of performance should have a negative coefficient.
level: firm-year (variance modeled within the pooled firm-year data)

variable_name: Log variance of operating cash flow
description: Variation about a predicted mean performance level, where greater variation means lower reliability. In the multiplicative heteroscedasticity models the residual variance of the performance equation is modeled as a log-linear function of the covariates predicting the mean; the culture-strength coefficient indicates the effect on the log variance of operating cash flow. Factors that increase the reliability of performance should have a negative coefficient.
level: firm-year (variance modeled within the pooled firm-year data)

description: Yearly beta parameters are estimated separately for each firm in Kotter and Heskett's data using OLS regressions of firm returns on the return of a value-weighted portfolio of securities in the entire market (NYSE/AMEX and NASDAQ). Daily returns over 1979 to 1984 come from the CRSP database. The industry volatility measure is the yearly mean of the betas for all of the sampled firms in an industry.

The measure of market constraint used by Burt et al. (1994). Industries with higher market constraint scores are internally fragmented and face well-organized suppliers and buyers; these markets are more competitive and have lower profit margins.

Factor score for munificence, the slack or scarcity of resources, calculated by Dess and Beard (1984) for each of 52 four-digit SIC industries for the years 1967 to 1977. The values are used as clustering variables in the two-step cluster analysis that produced the four environment types.

Factor score for complexity, the number and variety of organizations with which a firm must interact, calculated by Dess and Beard (1984) for each of 52 four-digit SIC industries for the years 1967 to 1977. The values are used as clustering variables in the two-step cluster analysis that produced the four environment types.

Factor score for dynamism, change that is hard to predict, calculated by Dess and Beard (1984) for each of 52 four-digit SIC industries for the years 1967 to 1977. The values are used as clustering variables in the two-step cluster analysis that produced the four environment types.

Four environment groups derived by two-step cluster analysis of the munificence, complexity and dynamism factor scores: a hierarchical agglomerative method produced centroid estimates that were used to seed an iterative partitioning (K-means) method for the final cluster solution. Ward's method was chosen for the first step. The clusters were interpreted and labelled using Hrebiniak and Joyce's framework as Minimum Choice (I), Differentiated Choice (II), Maximum Choice (III) and Incremental Choice (IV).

Cost leadership or low cost strategies are indicated by measuring direct costs to sales. Cluster interpretations are based on the value of each strategy measure within each cluster group relative to the grand mean and standard deviation for all 146 single-industry firms; negative values of cost of goods sold indicate pursuit of a low cost strategy.

variable_name: R&D expenses to sales and advertising expenditures to sales
description: The ratio of product research and development expenses to sales measures the prevalence of differentiation-innovation strategies, and the advertising expenditures to sales ratio measures the presence of differentiation-marketing strategies. Cluster interpretations are based on values relative to the grand mean for all 146 firms, with positive values of advertising to sales indicating differentiation-marketing and positive values of R&D expenses to sales indicating pursuit of differentiation-innovation.

variable_name: inventory to sales and receivables to sales
description: Inventory to sales and receivables to sales ratios are used to indicate asset parsimony strategies. Cluster interpretations are based on the value of each strategy measure relative to the grand mean and standard deviation for all 146 single-industry firms; negative values of receivables or inventory indicate pursuit of asset parsimony.

Returns are defined broadly to include both accounting and market value performance variables to reflect a full range of possible firm objectives. Accounting variables include return on investment, return on equity, return on assets and sales to total assets. Six variables measure market value performance: earnings per share, cash flow per share, sales per $100 market value of stock, pretax income per $100 market value of stock, net income per $100 market value of stock and dividend yields. One-way ANOVAs compare mean values among strategy types within each environment.

Measured with the World Bank Regulatory Quality indicator, which measures 'perceptions of the ability of the government to formulate and implement sound policies and regulations that permit and promote private sector development'. The authors use the average of the indicator scores for 1998 and 2000, which resulted in scores of -1.975 (Belarus), 0.155 (Bulgaria), 0.755 (Lithuania), and -0.720 (Ukraine). The variable was mean centered to reduce the risk of multicollinearity in interactions.

Dummy variable coded 1 for founding in a Communist institutional environment and 0 for founding in a market institutional environment (before or after the Communist influence). The start of Communist influence was 1920 (Belarus; central/eastern Ukraine), 1940 (Lithuania), 1945 (Bulgaria, western Ukraine), and the end was 1990. The variable was not mean centered, to aid interpretation of interactions.

Respondents indicated the importance of the aspiration 'to increase exports' for implementing changes to each of four functions from 1999 to 2001 on a seven-point Likert scale. The variable averages the responses across the four functions of the firm and the Cronbach alpha exceeded 0.70. The measure was normalized by country standard deviations and mean centered by industry category.

Respondents indicated the importance of the aspiration 'to increase domestic sales' for implementing changes to each of four functions from 1999 to 2001 on a seven-point Likert scale. The variable averages the responses across the four functions of the firm and the Cronbach alpha exceeded 0.70. The measure was normalized by country standard deviations and mean centered by industry category.

Respondents indicated the importance of the aspiration 'to satisfy customer requirements' for implementing changes to each of four functions from 1999 to 2001 on a seven-point Likert scale. The variable averages the responses across the four functions of the firm and the Cronbach alpha exceeded 0.70. The measure was normalized by country standard deviations and mean centered by industry category.

Respondents indicated the importance of the aspiration 'to improve product/service quality' for implementing changes to each of four functions from 1999 to 2001 on a seven-point Likert scale. The variable averages the responses across the four functions of the firm and the Cronbach alpha exceeded 0.70. The measure was normalized by country standard deviations and mean centered by industry category.

The CEO traits of tenacity, proactivity, and passion for work were measured in the 1993 questionnaire; Table 1 reports the number of items, format, composite reliability, and research source for each. An adapted version of the questionnaire was completed separately by employees to test the validity of the CEO self-reports. The three traits served as indicators of the traits domain in the structural equation model.

The CEO's general competency was measured as organizational skill and opportunity recognition skill in the 1993 questionnaire; Table 1 reports the number of items, format, composite reliability, and research source for each measure. The two measures served as indicators of the general competency domain in the structural equation model.

The CEO's specific competency was measured as industry skill and technical skill in the 1993 questionnaire; Table 1 reports the number of items, format, composite reliability, and research source for each measure. The two measures served as indicators of the specific competency domain in the structural equation model.

The CEO's situationally specific motivation was measured with vision, growth goals, and self-efficacy in the 1993 questionnaire; Table 1 reports the number of items, format, composite reliability, and research source for each measure. The three measures served as indicators of the motivation domain in the structural equation model.

Following Porter (1980), the venture's competitive strategy was measured as its emphasis on focus, low cost, and differentiation, with differentiation split into differentiation through innovation and differentiation through quality/service; Table 1 reports the number of items, format, composite reliability, and research source for each measure. These measures were modelled as reflections of the competitive strategy domain.

The environment was measured on three dimensions: dynamism (negative stability, the predictability of the environment), munificence (the environment's support for organizational growth), and complexity (the concentration or dispersion of organizations in the environment); Table 1 reports the number of items, format, composite reliability, and research source for each measure. The authors predicted that complexity would be a negative reflection of the environment domain, but report that this did not hold.

Three measures of venture growth were calculated from the 1993 and 1995 CEO questionnaires: average annual percent sales growth, average annual percent employment growth, and average annual percent profit growth. Sales growth was one-half the difference between 1992 and 1994 sales, divided by the base year (1992), and similar calculations produced the employment and profit growth measures. The three measures formed a composite with a reported reliability of .87 and served as the dependent variable.
