The reciprocal of clinical approval success rate estimates within therapeutic categories. The estimates come from DiMasi et al. (2010), who employed an extensive dataset of 1,738 new drug candidates that entered testing in the period spanning 1993-2004 to derive clinical approval success rates in therapeutic categories based on their classification in the IMS R&D Focus database, which uses the World Health Organization's Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification. These therapeutic areas are matched to the therapeutic areas for individual alliances provided by Recap.

The alliance is classified into one of three types of interdependence (reciprocal, sequential, pooled) using Thompson's (1967) definitions based on input-output relationships and Recap's classification of the partners' division of labor across research, development, manufacturing, and marketing. Reciprocal interdependence equals 1 for agreement types in which both partners participate in activities within the R&D function (Collaboration and Co-Development), and 0 otherwise; the coding is described as conservative because only alliances with shared upstream R&D activity are treated as reciprocal. Sequential interdependence equals 1 for agreements classified as Research, Development, Manufacturing, and Co-Market types, with the omitted category of pooled interdependence comprising licensing, marketing, promotion, and distribution agreements. In the event that an alliance is classified under multiple types, interdependence is coded using the highest level.

The angular measure introduced by Jaffe (1986): the technological position of a firm is determined by the distribution of its patents across patent classes, with each patent represented as a vector with 1 on the dimension of the original three-digit USPTO patent class and 0 for the other patent classes, and these patent vectors are aggregated at the firm level for each of the partners. Technology overlap is bound between 0 and 1, with values closer to 1 indicating greater overlap in partners' technological resources. The authors account for all patents applied for by a partner before signing the alliance agreement.
time_window: all patents applied for by a partner before signing the alliance agreement

description: Indicator identifying female executive directors in the matched sample. Each female executive director in the sample was matched with a male director who performed the same role in an industry and size matched company; the final sample contains 262 firm-year observations for female executives and 262 for male executives. In the Tobit models this variable enters as the main effect of gender, and it is also interacted with the performance measures.

The absolute size of the bonus paid to an executive director, expressed in £ thousands. The variable is left-censored because more than a fifth of the directors in the sample did not receive any bonus in the year analyzed, and it is modelled in a Tobit regression as a function of company performance in the preceding year and the control variables. The Tobit coefficients indicate the effect of a regressor on both the likelihood of receiving a bonus and on the size of this bonus.
time_window: year t; performance lagged by one year

description: The bonus expressed as a percentage of base salary, that is, the relative size of the bonus. It is the dependent variable of the second Tobit model, which relates the relative size of the bonus to company performance in the preceding year and the control variables.
time_window: year t; performance lagged by one year

description: Accounting-based measure of corporate performance, return on assets expressed in percentage terms. Performance indicators were lagged by one year, so the size of directors' bonuses in year t was modelled as a function of corporate performance in year t-1.

Stock performance indicator defined as the ratio of the sum of market capitalization and book value of debt to the book value of total assets. Like the accounting measure, it was lagged by one year in the models of bonus size.

Total pay of the executive director, defined as the sum of base salary, bonus, other direct compensation, and incentive pay, expressed in £ thousands. It is used in the univariate comparison of the remuneration packages of matched female and male executive directors.

Exploratory learning comprises the activities of recognizing and assimilating external knowledge. The five-item scale recognize captures a firm's activities of environmental scanning and monitoring, the examination of industry information, and the observation of external knowledge sources; the four-item scale assimilate addresses absorbing knowledge from external sources, approaching and meeting external knowledge sources, and a firm's competencies of inward knowledge transfer. The items were answered by the first informant (head of R&D), and item rating used anchors of 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree.' In the interaction analyses the construct is used as a mean-centered arithmetic mean; in the structural models the items load on the higher-order factor exploratory learning.

Transformative learning refers to the activities of maintaining and reactivating knowledge. The four-item scale maintain captures a firm's activities of retaining and storing knowledge and addresses knowledge sharing and communication inside the firm; the four-item scale reactivate captures whether a firm can quickly react to opportunities by relying on its existing knowledge and its proficiency in addressing environmental changes by reactivating its knowledge. The items were answered by the first informant and rated from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree.' The construct is used as a mean-centered arithmetic mean in the interaction analyses and as a higher-order factor in the structural models.

Exploitative learning comprises the activities of transmuting and applying knowledge. The four-item scale transmute captures a firm's proficiency in combining new and existing knowledge and addresses the matching of technologies with new product ideas; the four-item scale apply addresses whether firms easily implement technologies in new products, constantly consider how to better exploit technologies, and regularly implement adaptations to their products. Items were answered by the first informant on 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree' anchors. The construct is used as a mean-centered arithmetic mean in the interaction analyses and as a higher-order factor in the structural models.

Absorptive capacity is modeled as a higher-order factor that accounts for the relationships between the three learning processes; the target coefficient showed that absorptive capacity accounted for 94 percent of the relations among the three learning processes. In the regression analyses the effect of absorptive capacity as a higher-order construct is estimated with the constructs' arithmetic means, and complementarity is additionally examined with a three-way interaction of the three learning processes. Four additional two-item constructs were included in the questionnaire to reflect the higher-order constructs.

Technological turbulence is measured with a five-item scale that is based on Jaworski and Kohli (1993), one item of which is reverse-coded. The items were answered by the second informant (head of corporate marketing, innovation management, or business development) on 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree' anchors. In the interaction analyses the variable is mean-centered and treated as a quasi moderator.

Market turbulence is measured with a four-item scale that also draws on Jaworski and Kohli (1993), one item of which is reverse-coded. The scale was answered by the second informant on 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree' anchors. In the interaction analyses the variable is mean-centered and treated as a quasi moderator.

Innovation is measured with a three-item scale used in many prior studies, covering the overall performance of the firm's new product development program. The items were answered by the second informant in each firm and were additionally included in the questionnaire for the first informant; item rating used the anchors 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree.' The intraclass correlation coefficient between the informants is .75 for innovation, and the data of the second informant were used in the analyses.

Performance is measured with a four-item scale for perceptual performance developed by Reinartz et al. (2004), with the stem 'Relative to your competitors, how does your firm perform concerning the following statements.' For this scale the anchor points were 1, 'much worse,' to 7, 'much better.' The items were answered by the second informant and additionally included in the questionnaire for the first informant; the intraclass correlation coefficient between informants is .71, and the data of the second informant were used in the analyses.

Dependent variable equal to 1 when successive patents of an inventor have different assignees, indicating a change of employer; it is associated with the latter patent. Moves are assumed to have occurred at the midpoint between the former and the subsequent patent. Transitions from self-employment to a firm are ignored, while transitions from employment to self-employment are tracked. Because at least two patents are needed to detect a move, inventors with only one patent are excluded from the analysis.

Indicator for inventors active in Michigan following the change in the law, formed by interacting a Michigan residence indicator with a post-MARA time-period indicator. The post-MARA indicator marks a patent application date of 1986 or later; the Michigan indicator marks patents applied for by inventors residing in Michigan. In the models this two-way interaction is further interacted with firm-specificity and technical specialization.

Measured as the proportion of the citations to a given patent that are from internal as opposed to external firms. Hypothesized continuous variables were centered at zero to simplify interpretation of interaction effects.

The (logged) concentration of an inventor's inventions, calculated with a Herfindahl measure based on the patent technology class. Hypothesized continuous variables were centered at zero to simplify interpretation of interaction effects.

Senior IT executives subdivided their firms' total IT budgets across the four asset classes, so this variable captures the IT investment allocated to infrastructure. Infrastructure provides the foundation of shared IT services, both technical and human, used by multiple IT applications, such as servers, networks, laptops, shared customer databases, help desk and application development.

Firms' IT investment allocated to transactional systems, obtained from senior IT executives' subdivision of their total IT budgets. Transactional investments automate processes, cut costs, or increase the volume of business per unit cost, such as order processing, point of sale processing, billing statement production and insurance renewal.

Firms' IT investment allocated to informational systems, obtained from senior IT executives' subdivision of their total IT budgets. Informational investments provide information for managing, accounting, reporting and communicating internally and with customers, suppliers and regulators, and include decision support, sales analysis, planning and six sigma programs.

Firms' IT investment allocated to strategic systems, obtained from senior IT executives' subdivision of their total IT budgets. Strategic investments reposition firms in the marketplace by supporting entry into a new market or the development of new products, services or business processes.

Firms' total IT investment intensity, operationalized as a ratio of IT expenditure to sales. Senior IT executives reported their total IT budgets, which the authors first analyze in the aggregate before disaggregating them by asset class.

A single aggregate measure of organizational IT capabilities built from the six competency and practice metrics, entering the analyses as an interaction term with IT investment intensity by asset class. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to validate the grouping of the 18 indicators of ITC into the six capability variables.

Estimates the human resource competency of firms by assessing the technical and business skills of IT staff, the IT skills of business users, and the relative ability of firms to satisfy their demand for highly skilled IT labor. The authors note that the co-presence of IT and highly skilled labor has rarely been examined for its performance implications.

Assesses both the degree of senior management commitment to IT projects and business unit involvement in IT decisions. The authors justify the measure with prior evidence that senior management championing improves the value created by IT investments and that disconnects between business units and the IT function hinder returns from IT.

Describes the degree to which internal communications and work practices are conducted electronically, measuring the use of electronic communication media such as email, intranets, and wireless devices for internal communications.

Describes the degree to which information exchanges with suppliers are conducted electronically via email, remote wireless connections, the Internet, and non-Internet electronic data interchange (EDI) connections.

Measures the degree to which both internal and external transactions are conducted electronically, and is a linear combination of two ratios: electronic purchase orders to total purchase orders and electronic sales to total sales. The authors argue that more digital transactions with suppliers reduce input, coordination, transaction and agency costs.

Measures the degree to which firms employ Internet architectures in sales force management, employee performance measurement, training, and postsales customer support, activities that prior work and the authors' case studies show benefit from IT adoption.

variable_name: Net margin and return on assets (ROA)
description: Profitability is measured by net margin and return on assets (ROA). Both measures are obtained from Compustat archival data and are used as dependent variables in the asset-class and interaction regressions.

Market valuation is measured by Tobin's q, obtained from Compustat. The authors argue that market value reflects the market's assessment of firms' future value, so infrastructure investments that are transparent to the market should show a positive association.
Operational performance is measured by the cost of goods sold, taken from Compustat. It is the dependent variable on which the cost-reducing effect of transactional investments is assessed.

variable_name: Sales from new products and sales from modified products
description: Product innovation is measured by revenues from new and modified products, collected through the MIT survey as a share of total sales. Because these variables are derived from the survey, the authors do not have lagged measures of them in relation to investments in particular asset classes.

variable_name: Profitability, market valuation, operational performance and product innovation
description: Firm performance was measured along four dimensions: profitability (net margin and ROA), market valuation (Tobin's q), operational performance (cost of goods sold) and product innovation (revenues from new and modified products), from Compustat and the MIT survey.

variable_name: IT intensity by asset class (infrastructure, transactional, informational, strategic)
description: IT assets are measured as IT investment intensity (IT spending relative to sales) disaggregated into four asset classes. Senior IT executives in the MIT survey subdivided their total IT budgets according to descriptions of the four classes, infrastructure, transactional, informational and strategic, which gives the share of IT investment allocated to each strategic purpose.
scale: ratio of IT expenditure to sales, by asset class

description: The share of private debt as a fraction of the sum of interest-bearing debt (including all loans and bonds outstanding) and account payables. In the numerator, public debt and debt by affiliated companies are excluded, but bank debt cannot be distinguished from debt of other institutions that are not affiliated with the firm. All explanatory variables are lagged by one period.

The share of all universal bank owners among the top five investors of the firm, excluding investment banks; universal banks that are large shareholders are known to also have an intense lending history with the firm. To account for the risk aversion of banks, the authors apply the common quadratic transformation to the shareholdings. All explanatory variables are lagged by one period.

The variance of FDI portfolio payoffs, calculated as the weighted sum of the variances of the payoffs of the projects of firm j in countries i to N in year t. The variances are proxied with the political risk of the countries where the projects are located, and the weights are the squared share of the firm's FDI activities in a country in its total activities in the year; risks between countries are assumed to be uncorrelated. FDI activities are captured by affiliate employment multiplied by the share of Japanese firm ownership, aggregated over all subsidiaries in a country of the firm in the year, and total activities include both the foreign and the domestic employment of the firm. The formula block for the specification could not be read.

Dependent variable coded 1 for a syndicate formed in reality and 0 for a hypothetical syndicate that could have been formed but was not. Hypothetical syndicates were generated by randomly selecting VC firms, of the same syndicate size, from a potential pool of U.S. VCs investing in the same industry, state, year, and quarter as the focal venture. Five hypothetical syndicates were matched to each real syndicate.
time_window: at the time of the first-round investment

description: Prior tie density was measured as the ratio of preexisting dyadic ties to the total number of possible dyadic ties within the prospective syndicate. A prior tie was deemed to have been created when two VC firms had co-invested at least once in the same round for the same venture during the five years prior to the new focal investment. It is a continuous variable ranging between 0 and 1; in the example given, if two of three dyads have a prior collaboration, density is 2/3.
time_window: five years prior to the focal investment

description: Measured using the total number of VC firms investing together to form a syndicate. Hypothetical syndicates were generated with sizes equal to that of the real syndicate for the venture, so that syndicate size varies within venture.

Measured as the standard deviation of tie strength among all dyads in a prospective syndicate, with a log transformation to correct for skewness. Because network faultlines has a high correlation with prior tie density and average tie strength, the measure was orthogonalized against prior tie density and average tie strength using the Gram-Schmidt procedure so that it captures faultline risk above and beyond those constructs.

VC status was captured using centrality in the co-investment network, calculated with Bonacich's measure of centrality; the equation for this measure is not readable in the text, which explains that ci is the centrality score of firm i, Rij measures the relationship between firm i and j, a scales the measure, and b weights the centrality of all firm i's alters, with b set to three-quarters of the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue. Status similarity within each pair of VCs was computed by dividing the minimum status by the maximum status within a pair. This was then converted to a group-level measure of status heterogeneity, calculated as 1 minus the average of the pairwise measures of status similarity in the syndicate.

Measured by computing the standard deviation of status similarity among all dyads within the prospective syndicate. Status similarity is based on the same Bonacich centrality-based firm status measure used for status heterogeneity.

Measured as the total number of ventures at the 'Startup/Seed,' 'Early,' or 'Expansion' stage receiving first-time VC funding in the same industry segment as the focal venture in the prior year. Ten industry segments were identified based on the VentureXpert database. A log transformation of the variable was used to adjust for skewness and to capture the nonlinear impact of increasing industry popularity.

A frequency-based measure: the number count of acquisitions conducted by local firms in the same host country, in the same industry, in a three-year period prior to the transaction. The reference group is acquisitions in the same industry in the same host country, and only the most recent cross-border acquisition activities in the host country are counted. These observations were collected from the SDC Platinum database.
time_window: three-year period prior to the transaction

description: A frequency-based measure: the number count of acquisitions conducted by other foreign firms in the same host country, in the same industry, in a three-year period prior to the transaction. The reference group is acquisitions in the same industry in the same host country, and only the most recent cross-border acquisition activities in the host country are counted. These observations were collected from the SDC Platinum database.
time_window: three-year period prior to the transaction

description: A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if the market entry is made via acquisition and 0 if the market entry is made via alliance. Alliances are treated as directional because the authors are interested in the outward strategies of emerging economy firms, and alliances and acquisitions are coded as dyads.

Based on a composite measure of governance indicators established by the World Bank, whose six dimensions address political, civil and human rights, market restrictions, predictability of legal decisions and law in action, and corruption. The World Bank scores cover 209 countries and territories on a biannual basis starting from 1996, and each year's score is used to represent two years in the sample. The formula used to aggregate the home and host country scores into a distance index is not described in the text.
time_window: biannual from 1996; each year's score represents two years

description: Built from indicators largely based on items from the broad category of government efficiency from the World Competitiveness Yearbook; five indicators were introduced and an exploratory factor analysis using principal component analysis with varimax rotation was performed. The adaptability of government policy item was dropped because it did not have clear loadings, and the remaining four items have factor loadings of more than 0.80. Normative distance is then measured using the Euclidean distance index with these four items.

The number of times a firm introduces a drive in a new market within the first year of the market's introduction into the industry, divided by the total number of new markets introduced in the industry since the year of entry for the firm. Firms that entered in the first year of a new market, whether incumbents in the industry or new entrants, are identified as market pioneers in that product generation. For firms that entered between two consecutive market introductions, the variable takes the value of 0 until the year of the next market introduction. The measure varies over both time and firms.

The number of times an incumbent firm entered a market after the first year of the market's introduction into the industry, divided by the total number of new market introductions in the industry since the year of entry for the firm for the time until time t. It captures whether incumbent firms that did not pioneer a market subsequently entered it during their life span. New entrants that entered a market after the first year but did not respond when a new market opportunity was introduced are included in the baseline group.

Built in a two-step procedure from areal density: the areal density of the best drive produced by firm i in diameter j in year t is first divided by the highest areal density in that diameter available in the market that year to obtain the firm's diameter-specific relative technological position; this measure is then averaged over all diameters produced by the firm in year t. Measuring the firm's capabilities against the best drive in that market circumvents problems related to cumulative and absolute increases in technological know-how over time because it is a relative, time-varying measure. The measure is computed on an annual basis.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if a firm survived to the following year and 0 otherwise; acquisitions are treated as censored observations. The dependent variable is observed for all members of the sample that entered new markets.
scale: dummy (1 = survived to the following year, 0 = otherwise)

description: Valuation of unrealized investments reported as a percentage of called capital in a focal year t of the first-time fund, net of fees and carried interest. The value of unrealized investments 'represents an estimate of the amount at which an asset could be acquired or sold in a transaction', i.e., uncertain returns on paper. The authors take the natural logarithm of unrealized performance because of the decreasing value of an additional unit.

Distributions to the LPs up to a focal year t as a percentage of called capital of the first-time fund, net of fees and carried interest. It is 'the income and capital (less expenses and liabilities) realized from exiting investments by way of an initial public offering, acquisition, or another form of exit'. The natural logarithm of realized performance is taken.

Number of citations in ProQuest Global Newsstream of a specific PE firm in t - 1, counted this way to avoid including media coverage that follows from raising a follow-on fund. The natural logarithm of media attention is taken because of the decreasing value of an additional unit. Variables entering interaction terms were mean centered.

Dummy variable that equals 1 when a new PE firm i raises a follow-on fund in a focal year t, and 0 otherwise. The authors state that it 'directly relates to the ability of PE managers to overcome resource mobilization challenges' by raising new financial resources from prospective capital providers.

Realized performance at the end of the fund's economic lifetime, when all funds have been redistributed to the LPs, used as the dependent variable in the signal-strength regressions. Because this dependent variable shows no variation within PE firms, the authors also use an alternative dependent variable, eventual realized performance minus the realized performance already locked in, which does vary within PE firms and allows PE firm fixed effects.
time_window: end of the fund's economic lifetime

description: The primary independent variable is the interaction between two binary indicators. Post equals one for the time periods after (and including) February 2018, when the Airbnb Plus program was launched in Los Angeles but not in San Diego, and zero before the launch; LA (Treated) equals one for listings located in Los Angeles, one of the 13 cities in the initial launch, and zero for listings in San Diego. The interaction captures the certification treatment for non-Plus listings.

Monthly revenue of each Airbnb listing, aggregated from daily data to the monthly level and log transformed to address skewness. Following prior research in the Airbnb and hotel industries, the authors use it as the performance measure for listings in Los Angeles and San Diego, capturing a more direct performance outcome than booking rates alone.

The host-level quality indicator given out by Airbnb: hosts can automatically earn the Superhost badge by meeting a set of quantifiable criteria including the number of nights hosted, high overall rating, and quick response rate, and can retain it if they continue to meet the criteria. The badge is purely based on quantifiable yet basic performance metrics and operates at the host level.

The overall rating of each Airbnb listing, a listing-level quality indicator given by previous customers and one of the most significant reputation signals in online marketplaces. Both the Superhost badge and customer ratings were introduced years before the launch of Airbnb Plus. The variable is also used as a control in the main spillover models.

A binary indicator of whether a listing falls outside the price range of Airbnb Plus listings. A listing is categorized as having Low price similarity if its average daily rate falls below the first percentile average daily rate of all Airbnb Plus listings, that is, it caters to a different customer segment and is less likely to be evaluated as a close alternative to Plus listings.

A binary indicator of listing type; it is coded one if the listing is either a 'private room' or a 'shared room' and zero if the listing is an 'entire place' or a 'hotel room.' Following Cui et al. (2020), the authors treat private and shared rooms as relatively unique accommodations because they offer lower privacy and greater opportunities for social interaction than the accommodations typically found in traditional hotels.
scale: binary (0 = entire place or hotel room, 1 = private or shared room)

description: Respondents assessed the extent to which each of their contacts was instrumental in supporting and developing their own innovativeness with the item 'When I interact with this person it is easy for me to generate new creative solutions and/or ideas', measured on a 5-point Likert scale. The responses were entered into a squared catalyst matrix C. Each respondent's catalyst assessments were weighted by the log-transformation of the number of patents the respondent applied for in a 24-month period, and the dependent variable is the normalized in-degree centrality of the weighted C matrix.
scale: 5-point Likert scale for the underlying item; final variable is normalized in-degree centrality

description: Computed with the algorithm implemented in UCINET 6 on the confirmed exchange of information matrix. For each ego, the measure represents the average within ego-network degree of alters and expresses the extent to which each of ego's alters are tied to ego's other alters; the text writes it as 2t/n, where t is the number of ties in the network (not counting ties to ego) and n is the number of nodes excluding ego. The values were entered into a squared redundancy matrix R.

Built from eight external knowledge source items rated on a 1 to 7 scale, which a principal component factor analysis with varimax rotation reduced to two factors, scientific external knowledge and industrial external knowledge. The diversity of external knowledge between each pair of individuals in the sample is computed in the matrix D from their reliance on scientific and industrial sources of external knowledge; the diversity available in each ego network is the average of alter-alter knowledge differences (matrix K), and the final ego-network measure sums those values and divides by the number of alters. The equations in the text were not legible in the source available here.
scale: items rated on a 1 to 7 scale

description: An element-wise multiplication of the values reported in the dyadic redundancy matrix R and the knowledge diversity matrix K produced a new matrix B, adjusting the redundancy score of each alter in a given ego network by the amount of external knowledge diversity he or she provided to ego. Summing the values of the B matrix across all alters in ego's network gives the R-K Index, describing the extent to which each ego is embedded in a redundant structure that is at the same time rich in diverse external knowledge. The formal equation was not legible in the source available here.

The number of patents the individual applied for in a 24-month period, obtained from company monthly reports of patent applications that the company used to assess and reward individual performance. It is used to weight catalyst assessments through the log-transformation ln(e + p), where e is a constant and p is the number of patent applications.

Dummy variable coded 1 if a firm employs at least one star scientist and 0 otherwise. A star is a scientist whose productivity score is at least two standard deviations above the average of all inventors in the sample; the score divides a scientist's number of patents applied for by year t by the scientist's industry tenure (years since first patent application) and multiplies this by the average forward citations of the scientist's patents received by year t. Scientists' scores are updated annually so that non-stars may become stars over time; 531 star scientists (about 7% of the scientists in the sample) employed by 155 firms were identified. The formula block is unreadable in the available text.

Successful patenting by the firm, used as an indication of a firm's innovative productivity following prior research. Patents are weighted by citations received in the five years after issuance to account for variance in patents' value. The models including star patents count all patents the firm applied for in year t, while models excluding star patents drop patents on which the star was a co-inventor.
time_window: citations received in the five years after patent issuance

description: The number of unique non-star inventors who applied for patents on which a star scientist was not a co-inventor, correcting for the possibility that the number of inventors might bias the measure. The authors focus on identifying the number of unique inventors who patented without a star rather than the number of patents applied for without a star, so that if non-star inventor i applied for three patents without a star and non-star inventor j applied for two, their collective innovative leadership is scored 2 rather than 5. The formula block is unreadable in the available text.

Diversification in the technological classes associated with a star's patents, assessed from all patent applications with which the star was involved. Using Tzabbar's (2009) 22 technological fields, each of the star's patents at time t is assigned to a technological field, and the breadth variable subtracts the resulting concentration value from 1, following Hall (2002) with a nonbiased Herfindahl index for citations. Where a firm has more than one star scientist, the effect of the breadth of expertise of the star with the highest level of expertise breadth is examined. The formula block is unreadable in the available text.
level: star scientist (firm value taken from the star with the highest breadth)

description: The average level of co-invention frequency between star and non-star scientists in firm s, capturing the breadth and frequency of stars' co-inventions with colleagues. In the formula, z (ranging from 0 to 4) is the frequency with which star scientist i co-invents with team members j, max(z) is the largest possible number of collaboration ties that star i could have within the firm, and Ns is the number of members in firm s. Collaborative strength varies from 0 (no co-invention) to 1, which would imply a complete network containing all possible ties among incumbent scientists; the moderating terms and their main effects are mean centered. The formula block is unreadable in the available text.

Performance below the aspiration level equals 0 when performance is above the aspiration level and equals performance minus the aspiration level when performance is below the aspiration level. It was computed for return on equity and return on assets, each evaluated against both historical and social aspiration levels.

Performance above the aspiration level equals 0 when performance is below the aspiration level and equals performance minus the aspiration level when performance is above the aspiration level. It was computed for return on equity and return on assets, each evaluated against both historical and social aspiration levels.

Generated by taking an exponentially weighted average of past values on the performance variable, with the weight given to the most recent aspiration level estimated by fitting the models with different values of the weight; the weight was 0.1 for ROE, 0.3 for ROA and 0.2 for ROS. The formula itself is not readable in the extracted text of the paper and is not reproduced here. The low weights suggest fairly rapid updating of the aspiration level.
The average performance of other firms in the same year, taken as the social aspiration level on the performance variable.

The logged number of employees, which the authors use as a measure of overall firm size in a given industry; in these data it correlates highly with the accounting value of assets. Logging means that a given percentage increase in employees has the same effect regardless of firm size. For the interaction analyses the variable was normalized between 0 and 1 using the lowest and highest values in the data, so that the largest firm had a score of 1 and the smallest a score of 0; the main effect of performance is then the effect for the smallest firm and the main effect plus the interaction is the effect for the largest firm.
scale: normalized between 0 and 1 for the interaction analyses

description: The logged ratio of the year-end to year-start value of the firm's machinery, a long-term investment that cannot easily be disposed of if it turns out not to be needed. Machinery can be purchased and installed quickly and is not autocorrelated across years, making it the most sensitive indicator of investment decisions.

Score of the expansion factor extracted from five variables by a principal factor analysis with varimax rotation. The expansion factor had similar loadings for the value of machinery, the value of nonmachinery real assets and the number of workers, and small loadings of the function add and drop variables. The score of the expansion factor was used as the dependent variable in the analysis.

A 0/1 indicator variable coded 1 if the label is in the first or second year it has ever been used in the entire press release corpus and it is the first year the firm claimed that label. The first or second year is included because 75% of new labels only have one or two members in the first 2 years and do not gain traction until after the second year. There are 787 events of category innovation by 581 firms, and 302 events by 144 patenting firms.

Measures category combination based on the number of market categories a firm is in, taking the natural log as the measure exhibits skew. Firms can score high on this measure with one offering that is in multiple market categories, or with multiple products in different categories. The formula block for this equation is unreadable in the supplied text.

Captures whether the technologies a firm develops draw on elements of different market categories, based on the firm's position in a patent citation network and how close in knowledge space its patents are to market categories it is not in. A knowledge space is created for each year using all Computers & Communications patents in a 5-year moving window; similarity between patents is the number of shared citations divided by the total number of citations made by the focal patent, with second-degree similarity also computed. Areas of knowledge space are mapped to market categories based on the category membership of the firm assigned the patent, weighted by that firm's grade of membership. Patent-level proximities are averaged over the number of patents issued to the firm in the year and the natural log is taken. The formula blocks for these equations are unreadable in the supplied text.

Leniency is built on fuzziness, the inverse of category contrast, and is calculated by multiplying the inverse of the category's contrast by the number of distinct categories with which the focal category overlaps. Following Hannan et al. (2007), contrast is calculated as the average grade of membership of firms in the category. The formula block for this equation is unreadable in the supplied text.

Six-item subscale of the perceived passion scale measuring the perception of affective passion: the presenter had energetic body movements, displayed rich body language, was animated, showed facial emotion, used gestures, and modulated his or her voice. Participants evaluated the presenter on a five-point scale (1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'frequently') after watching the videotaped presentation. The alpha reliability for this six-item subscale is .95, and it reflects the items loading on the first factor of the two-factor solution.

Five-item subscale of the perceived passion scale reflecting the perception of preparedness (cognitive passion): the presentation was thoughtful and reflected depth of understanding, had substance, reflected the broader context, was coherent and logical, and was supported by facts cited. Items were rated on a five-point scale (1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'frequently') and the alpha reliability for this five-item subscale is .87.

After watching the videotaped presentation, participants who were told to role-play VCs made a funding decision for the business plan, answering 'yes' or 'no'. This dichotomous variable was the dependent variable in the logistic hierarchical regression analysis.

Experimental manipulation of business plan quality using two plans from the previous year's business plan competition at the same university: the plan ranked 1st out of the 16 semifinalists (a high-quality biotechnology venture) and the plan ranked 8th (a medium-quality venture proposing a financial magazine for teenagers). Written executive summaries were constructed from these plans, and a professional actor presented the same verbal content for the respective plans in the videos. A manipulation check confirmed that participants in the high-quality condition gave significantly higher preparedness scores than those in the medium-quality condition.

The 11-item perceived passion and preparedness scale from Study 1 was used to measure judges' perception of the presenters' passion; the affective passion subscale consists of the six nonverbal-cue items. Judges filled out the evaluation forms immediately after each presentation. The alpha reliability for the passion scale was .94.

The preparedness subscale of the same 11-item scale used in Study 1 was used to measure the preparedness judges perceived in the presentation, covering the substance and coherence of the presentation content. Judges completed the evaluation form immediately after each presentation. The alpha reliability for the preparedness scale was .90.

As part of the competition evaluation form, each judge indicated whether or not he or she intended to invest in the business plan just presented. Each judge's evaluation of each plan was treated as an independent observation in the logistic hierarchical regression.

A measure derived from World Business Environment Survey questions that ask respondents to rank the corruption they face in their environment on a scale of 1 to 6 according to the extent to which "unofficial payments" are needed to get things done connected with government approvals, permissions, licenses, infrastructure, services, or taxes. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to assess convergent and discriminant validity, and the resulting factor forms the measure of corruption pervasiveness.

A measure derived from World Business Environment Survey questions that ask respondents to rank their environment according to the extent to which the terms of corrupt transactions are predictable and the services or items for which a bribe is paid are usually delivered as agreed. The factor resulting from the authors' confirmatory factor analysis forms the measure of corruption arbitrariness.

A trichotomous dependent variable constructed from variables in the PPI database that indicates the entering firm's choice of entry mode. The three entry-mode choices comprise two equity-mode choices (wholly owned subsidiary and joint venture) and one nonequity mode choice (build-own transfer/turnkey projects). The multinomial logit models compare these alternatives pairwise.

One category of the trichotomous entry-mode variable built from the PPI database: joint venture. The other categories are wholly owned subsidiary, joint venture and nonequity entry, compared pairwise in multinomial logit models.

One category of the trichotomous entry-mode variable built from the PPI database: nonequity mode (management contracts, build-own-transfer or turnkey projects). The other categories are wholly owned subsidiary, joint venture and nonequity entry, compared pairwise in multinomial logit models.

One category of the trichotomous entry-mode variable built from the PPI database: wholly owned subsidiary. The other categories are wholly owned subsidiary, joint venture and nonequity entry, compared pairwise in multinomial logit models.

Third-party ratings combine previous quality ratings from Consumer Reports and J. D. Power and Associates. The Consumer Reports component uses the five-point scale "trouble indexes": the mean of the "overall problem rate" scores of each model for the most recent three years of ownership, then an automaker's overall problem rate score in a year is the average of the overall problem rate scores of all its car models in that year, averaged over the five years prior to the selected year. The J. D. Power component uses "initial ratings", six scores ranging from 2 to 5 from consumer ratings of vehicles purchased after the first few months of ownership; the mean of the six scores is calculated for each model and averaged across the automaker's models in the year, again over the five prior years. The two scores are combined into a single index using principal components analysis, and a separate factor analysis confirms they load on a single factor accounting for 86.6% of their combined variance. The single measure is rescaled so that the highest-reputation automaker in a given year has a score of 1 and the lowest has a score of 0.
time_window: average score over the five years prior to the selected year

description: Depreciation rate is calculated from the Kelley Blue Book: Used Car Guide (Western edition), using the last issue (November-December) of each year for "list prices" (the original suggested retail price) and "suggested retail values" (the Kelley Blue Book's estimated asking price). A car model's depreciation rate of price in selected year T is the depreciation rate of its T-3 year-model price during the three-year period. An automaker's depreciation rate of price in a year is the average of the depreciation rates of all car models' prices of that automaker in that year. The depreciation rate is rescaled such that the automaker with the lowest depreciation rate in any given year has a score of 1 and the automaker with the highest depreciation rate has a score of 0.
time_window: T-3 year-model price over the three-year period

description: The composite measure of reputation is created by combining third-party ratings and depreciation rates into a single variable using principal components analysis. A separate factor analysis confirms that the two scores load on a single factor accounting for 83.3% of the two scores' combined variance. The composite variable is rescaled so that the highest-reputation automaker has a reputation score of 1 and the lowest 0. Models using this combined measure produce the best model fit.

The dependent variable is the rate of change in an automaker's market share over the observation period, modeled with month as the unit of time. Market share is used rather than sales units because market shares are not affected by temporal fluctuations in seasonal demand. Data on automakers' monthly market share come from their reports to Automotive News. The market share of automaker i at month t-1 enters the power function that is transformed to its natural logarithm for estimation.
time_window: monthly, current month (t) relative to month t-1

variable_name: severe and nonsevere product recall dummies
description: Product recalls are taken from NHTSA reports provided to the U.S. Department of Transportation. A dummy variable indicates whether an automaker experienced a severe product recall (1) or not (0) during month t-1, and a second dummy indicates the event of a nonsevere product recall. Severe recalls are those involving significant hazard (NHTSA hazard Types A and B) and nonsevere recalls are Types C and D. The 46 sampled automakers experienced a total of 1,853 recalls over the period studied.

Substitutability is proxied by the extent to which a reputation level is crowded by automakers. It is measured as the total number of other automakers whose reputation scores are within one standard deviation of the focal automaker's reputation score, measured at the industry level in a given year. The greater the number of such automakers, the more substitutable the focal automaker.

Two indicators of generalism/specialism are combined into a single index using principal components analysis; a factor analysis confirms the two scores load on a single factor accounting for 78.7% of their combined variance. The first indicator is the spread of engine capacity (measured in liters) over all car models an automaker produced in a given year, measured as the largest minus the smallest engine capacity, so that lower values indicate greater specialism. The second is the number of car models an automaker produced in a given year, with fewer models being an indicator of specialism. The two components correlate at 0.60.

An indicator variable that equals one if the IC exception is adopted in the state of the firm's headquarters by year t. Labor contracts are governed by state laws, and the state of firm headquarters governs the firm's overall employment contracts. Two-year lags of IC are used to allow sufficient time for IC to affect adjustment activities.

Calculated as the difference between firm performance and the industry benchmark, defined as the median ROA at the four-digit SIC level. The subtraction adjusts for competitive benchmarks and industry-level performance. One-year lags are used to examine how firms respond to performance; in the persistence models both one- and two-year lags are included.
Industry-adjusted ROA is splined into two parts; Positive Performance takes the value of industry-adjusted ROA if firm performance is above the industry benchmark and zero otherwise.

Industry-adjusted ROA is splined into two parts; Negative Performance takes the value of industry-adjusted ROA if firm performance is below the industry benchmark and zero otherwise. It takes a negative value by construction, and the absolute value is taken for the ease of interpretation.
Measured as the positive percentage change in the number of employees based on the log difference from the prior period.
Measured as the negative percentage change in the number of employees based on the log difference from the prior period.

Measured as the difference between total new capital investments and maintenance investments, that is, the amount of investment necessary to simply maintain current assets in place. Maintenance investments are proxied by amortization and depreciation.
Counts of all acquisition transactions reported in SDC Platinum. SDC's coverage during the early years is limited, so 1983-2000 is used for acquisitions.
Sales contributions from the acquisition, tracked with the Compustat item aqs, in addition to the usual acquisition counts.
Counts of all divestiture transactions reported in SDC Platinum, using 1983-2000 because SDC's coverage during the early years is limited.
Identified as a change in the name of the CEO reported in ExecuComp from 1985 to 2000. An indicator equal to one when the CEO changes.
Dispersion in analyst forecasts of firm earnings obtained from Thompson Reuters Institutional Holdings, covering 1976-2000; it proxies for the uncertainty in a firm's future performance.

variable_name: Seven adjustment activities (hiring, firing, net capital investments, acquisitions, joint ventures and alliances, divestitures, CEO turnover)
description: A set of seven corporate activities used to adjust firm resources, each used in turn as the dependent variable: hiring and firing as the positive and negative percentage change in employees, net capital investments as new capital investment minus depreciation and amortization, acquisitions, divestitures and joint ventures and alliances as counts of SDC Platinum transactions, and CEO turnover as a change of CEO in ExecuComp. Dispersion in analyst forecasts is added as a more general measure of the level of adjustment.
scale: mixed: percentages, log amounts, counts, 0/1 indicator
time_window: annual, 1976 to 2000 depending on the activity

description: Indicator variable that switched to 1 if an evaluator evaluated an idea in the blind condition. In the blind condition the innovation manager received no information about the idea proposer, shown as 'Submitted by: N/A', whereas in the non-blind condition the proposer's name, unit, and geographical location were shown.
Main dependent variable, as specified in the pre-analysis plan. For each idea, evaluators were asked: 'On a scale of 1 to 7 (1 lowest to 7 highest), please assess the overall quality of the idea.'

Switched to 1 if an idea was proposed by a woman. Gender was coded based on name matching, and when name matching did not yield a clear match internal documents from the partnering firm were consulted to resolve ambiguity.

Switched to 1 if an idea proposer was part of the same division, function, or geographical market as the innovation manager evaluating the idea. The employee's position was determined based on an internal code retrieved from the company's intranet.
Switched to 1 if an idea proposer was in the same country as the evaluator. Location was coded from the employees' addresses in the internal records.

Condition indicator for the online experiment, which replicated the within design of the field experiment and complemented it with a between design in which evaluators evaluate only blinded or only non-blinded ideas.

Evaluation score used as dependent variable in the online experiment, following the same evaluation setup and experimental conditions as the field experiment and analyzed with the same steps: mean comparisons, distribution graphs, and regression analyses.

In the online experiment, female and male names were randomly assigned to the ideas, so no interaction needed to be specified; the main effects of Female name and Male name give the difference between assigning female and male names and the blind condition, the baseline.

An index constructed of 17 items, each describing some aspect of a firm's CEO pay-setting process and the policies and practices governing it, created from the theoretical bases underlying agency theory. Respondents used five-point Likert-type scales ranging from "strongly agree" to "strongly disagree" to indicate the extent to which an item characterized the CEO pay determination process in their firms; after coding changes so that 5 represents high monitoring and 1 low monitoring, the items correlated positively and were averaged into a single monitoring score. A principal axis factor analysis yielded only one strong factor, and Cronbach alpha was .82.
scale: five-point Likert-type items, averaged into a composite score

description: The same 17-item index, describing aspects of a firm's CEO pay-setting process and the policies and practices governing it, with responses on five-point Likert-type scales ranging from "strongly agree" to "strongly disagree". A principal axis factor analysis of the scale yielded only one strong factor and the items were averaged into a single monitoring score; Cronbach alpha was .89.
scale: five-point Likert-type items, averaged into a composite score

description: Created by adding a CCO's responses to three items (alpha = .84). One item asked CCOs to indicate their firm's level of profitability relative to similar firms in its industry during the previous five years; in the second, the firm's stock performance over the previous five years was ranked relative to the performance of similar firms; in the third, CCOs ranked the trend in the firm's overall performance over the previous five years relative to trends for similar firms.

Four performance indicators common in this type of research were obtained for the years 1982-86: average earnings per share, average return on investment, average return on common stock, and average annual percent change in the firm's market value. A principal axis factor analysis produced only one factor on which all measures loaded highly; standard scores for each of the four indicators were multiplied by the respective factor loading and summed to obtain composite firm performance scores. The 867 firms were ranked on the composite scores and divided into quartiles, and each returned survey was assigned an ordinal performance ranking ranging from 4 (for the quartile performing best) to 1 (for the worst); the mean performance score of responding firms was 2.44.
scale: ordinal ranking from 4 (best quartile) to 1 (worst quartile)

description: Assessed with two items reported by the CCO. The first asked whether there was any single individual or institution outside the firm which owns 5% or more of the company's stock; a firm was classified as owner-controlled (N = 75) when the response was yes and management-controlled (N = 100) when the answer was no. The second item asked whether any individual within the firm (e.g., the CEO) owned 5% or more of the company's stock; in study 1 there were no firms in this owner-managed category.

Assessed with the same two items used in study 1. A firm was classified as owner-controlled (N = 95) when a single individual or institution outside the firm owned 5% or more of the company's stock and management-controlled (N = 148) when the answer was no. There were 12 owner-managed firms (an individual within the firm owning 5% or more of the stock), but because that number was small they were not included in the analysis.

Count of the total number of producers active in a system (platform) in a given month. The paper treats variation in this number as the explanatory variable of interest for platform-level variety and for producer scope, and instruments it with U.S. software employment and wage series interacted with platform dummies in the preferred specifications.
The total number of software varieties in a system, measured as the sum of varieties (or scope) offered by the producers on a platform. The unit of analysis is a platform in a given month.

Count of the number of genres in which a producer has products, i.e., the number of distinct software categories in which the producer offers application software. The unit of analysis is an individual producer in a given month.

Number of months between subsequent releases of new versions developed by a given producer within a given system and genre. Double releases in the same time period are counted as a single incidence of a new release, and the first version is disregarded because the development time before it is not observed. The authors model these nonnegative durations with an IV Tobit framework; a shorter time, all else being equal, implies higher effort and input.

Count of the number of producers on a given platform working in a particular genre (e.g., databases, medical and health, games). Titles for which a genre has not been specified are disregarded in calculating this variable.
Count of the number of producers working on the same platform in a genre other than the focal one. Titles for which a genre has not been specified are disregarded in calculating this variable.

A measure of polarization based on the deviation of the observed distribution of power from the ideal proportion of 0.5, computed for each of three indicators of structural power and combined into a single index across the three. The formula is unreadable in the extracted text, so only this verbal specification is recorded. Higher values indicate lower disparity, or greater structural power equality.

The mean of the regression residual from a Fama-French four-factor model of quarterly stock returns on the market return, the size factor (SMB), the book-to-market factor (HML), and the momentum factor (UMD), with the risk-free rate based on quarterly Treasury bond yields. The unsystematic return is the idiosyncratic component of return driven by the firm's resources and capabilities.

The mean of two indicators, average magnitude of instability and proportional unpredictability, computed from quarterly industry sales of all Compustat firms in the 4-digit SIC code over a rolling 20-quarter window. Instability is the antilog of the standard error from regressing the natural log of industry quarterly sales over 20 quarters; unpredictability is the share of change that is irregular, obtained by regressing sales on sales lagged one quarter and reverse coding the adjusted R-squared by subtracting it from 1. The inter-item correlation between the two indicators is 0.784.

Governance ratings from GovernanceMetrics International (GMI), based on indicators ranging from board accountability to financial disclosure and internal controls, and from shareholder rights to executive compensation and corporate behavior. GMI collects governance information from regulatory filings, press releases, board and executive interviews, company policies, and confidential documents.
scale: 1 (poorest governance) to 10 (best governance) in increments of 0.5

description: Based on information in SEC Compact Disclosure filings and proxy statements, if the founder holds the title of the chief executive officer (CEO) the variable is coded '0,' and a non-founder CEO is coded '1.'

The measure counts the overall number of drug launches reported in the therapeutic areas in which each sample firm was considered active in a given year. Drugs launched by the focal firm itself in a given year are excluded when constructing the variable. A firm is considered active in a therapeutic area if it had drug development projects or drugs launched in the previous five years. A higher value indicates stronger competitive pressure on the focal firm.
level: firm-year (therapeutic areas in which the firm is active)

description: The total number of licensing-in deals that firm i had engaged in in year t. It is a count variable that takes value 0 if a focal firm did no licensing-in in a given year and the corresponding number of deals otherwise. Only licensing deals reported in Recap were counted; other forms of interfirm agreement were not. Deals covering technologies that were ready to commercialize downstream were excluded.

The count of successful patent applications from firm i in year t that were associated with therapeutic areas in which rivals exerted pressure on the firm through product launches. Patents were linked to therapeutic codes by matching Pharmaprojects therapeutic area descriptions to Derwent World Patents Index codes, in particular category B14 'Pharmaceutical Activities'; assignments were checked by two expert medical practitioners. The patent application date was used because it is closely related to the timing of knowledge creation. The measure used in the regressions is the logarithm of Innovation toward competition + 1.
time_window: year t (patent application date); outcome modeled at t+1 to t+3

description: The variable counts the number of ongoing and successfully completed phase 3 trials of drugs that had not yet been approved for launch as reported by Pharmaprojects, in the therapeutic areas in which rivals had launched new products. Late-stage (phase 3) trials are used because drug development proceeds stepwise and phase 3 investments entail validating efficacy in large-scale clinical testing, making them accumulated and path-dependent R&D investments in a therapeutic area.
level: firm-year (therapeutic areas in which rivals launched new products)
time_window: ongoing and successfully completed phase 3 trials reported in a given year

description: Proxy statements provide descriptive information on the structure of managerial compensation contracts, including the performance metrics used for performance-based compensation. The authors manually searched each executive's compensation description for performance metrics linked to social and environmental performance and coded the executive with a dummy variable equal to one for that year if such incentives were provided. To construct a firm-level measure of CSR-based incentives the authors compute the percentage of executives whose compensation includes CSR criteria for that year; the measure is essentially binary, and the authors interpret it as a binary variable that indicates whether the company uses CSR-based incentives.

The LT-index is obtained by conducting a textual analysis of the companies' annual reports, on the rationale that an organization's time orientation is reflected by its discourse. The authors perform a textual analysis of the firms' 10-K filings, obtained from the SEC's EDGAR database, and count the number of keywords referring to the short term and the long term, respectively. The LT-index is computed as the ratio of the number of long-term keywords to the sum of long- and short-term keywords.

Tobin's Q is constructed from Compustat as the ratio of the market value of total assets to the book value of total assets. The market value of total assets is obtained as the book value of total assets plus the market value of common stock minus the sum of the book value of common stock and balance sheet deferred taxes. To mitigate the impact of outliers, Tobin's Q is winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles of its empirical distribution.

The CSR data are obtained from the KLD database, which compiles ratings of how companies address the needs of their stakeholders; for each stakeholder group, strengths and concerns are measured to evaluate positive and negative aspects of corporate actions toward stakeholders. The authors construct a composite KLD-index by summing up the number of CSR strengths with respect to employees, customers, the natural environment, and communities. In the analysis they also consider subindices based on specific stakeholder groups - the less salient stakeholders (the natural environment and communities) and the more salient ones (employees and customers).

To measure emissions the authors use the TRI data, which contain annual data on emissions of over 650 toxic chemicals from thousands of facilities in the United States. Each chemical is weighed by its toxicity by multiplying the quantity of each chemical emitted by the inverse of its reportable quantity, following the method used by King and Lenox (2000). Toxicity-weighted emissions of each chemical are aggregated at the facility level and ultimately the firm level; the dependent variable is the logarithm of one plus the toxicity-weighted emissions at the firm level.

Patent data are obtained from the NBER patent database, which contains annual information on the patent assignee name, the technology class, the number of citations, and the year of patent; the database is extended using the raw files of the USPTO. Green patents are identified using the classification of Amore and Bennedsen (2016). The dependent variable is the ratio of the number of green patents divided by the total number of patents filed by the company that year; since this ratio is only well-defined for patenting companies, the sample used for this analysis is smaller by construction. In auxiliary analyses the authors distinguish between green patents pertaining to pollution and recycling and green patents pertaining to renewable energies.

For the subset of companies that indicate a dollar amount of CSR contracting, the authors compute the share of CSR compensation as the ratio of CSR-based compensation to total compensation; the average of this ratio is 4.2% and the SD is 5.3%. In the regressions, the share of CSR compensation is set to zero if the company does not use CSR contracting, while companies that use CSR contracting but do not specify the amount are excluded from this analysis. The authors then reestimate the baseline regressions using this continuous variable instead of the binary CSR contracting variable.

variable_name: CSR contracting provisions pertaining to the environment and communities
description: In Panel A of Table 5, the authors reestimate the baseline specification replacing CSR contracting with a set of three dummies that indicate whether the CSR contracting provisions are targeted at the dependent stakeholders (i.e., the natural environment and local communities), the key stakeholders (i.e., employees and consumers), or whether no specific stakeholder is mentioned. The measure recorded here is the dummy for the contracting provisions pertaining to the environment and communities. Out of the companies that use CSR contracting, 49% have contracting provisions that are specific to the dependent stakeholders, 37% refer to the salient stakeholders, and 28% do not mention a specific stakeholder group; the percentages add up to more than 100% since some companies target several stakeholder categories.

A dummy variable that equals one if the company is incorporated in a state that has passed a constituency statute by year t, and zero otherwise; information on states of incorporation comes from Compustat. By 2006 a total of 34 states had adopted constituency statutes (Nebraska's 2007 statute is not considered because the sample ends in 2006). The statutes are used as plausibly exogenous variation in a firm's orientation toward stakeholders.
scale: dummy (1 = incorporated in a state that has passed a constituency statute by year t)

description: The patent count for each firm in each year: the number of patent applications filed in a year that are eventually granted, assigned to the application year. The number of patents is subject to a truncation problem because patents appear in the NBER database only after they are granted (about two years on average); the authors correct for this by including year fixed effects. The estimated dependent variable is log(1 + patents).

The number of citations in subsequent years divided by the number of patents for any given firm and year, a measure of innovation quality. To account for truncation, the number of citations is multiplied by the adjustment factor of Hall et al. (2001) provided in the NBER database, and citations are set to zero if the company has no patent. The estimated dependent variable is log(1 + citations/patents).
time_window: subsequent years, up to 2006; sample period 1976-2006

description: The measure of originality constructed by Hall et al. (2001), defined similarly to generality but with respect to the citations given to other patents. Firm-level measures are obtained by averaging across all patents for any given firm and year. The measure is only defined for companies with nonzero patents.
time_window: sample restricted to years prior to 2002

description: One minus the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of the citations that the patent receives over patent classes, so that a patent whose citations are spread over more technology classes is regarded as more general. Firm-level measures are obtained by averaging across all patents for any given firm and year, and the measure is only defined for companies with nonzero patents.
time_window: sample restricted to years prior to 2002

description: Following Azoulay et al. (2011), a patent is coded as a hit (flop) if the number of citations it receives is above (below) the highest (lowest) citation quartile across all patents in the same technology class (using all patents in the NBER database). The firm-level measure divides the number of hits and flops by the number of patents for any given firm and year. The sample is restricted to companies with nonzero patents and to years prior to 2002.
scale: ratio of hits and flops to patents
time_window: sample restricted to years prior to 2002

description: A measure of innovative productivity obtained by dividing the number of patents by the number of employees (from Compustat). It is used as a dependent variable in the auxiliary analysis of employees' innovative productivity, estimated on 148,037 firm-year observations.

A measure of innovative productivity obtained by dividing the number of citations by the number of employees (from Compustat). It is used as a dependent variable in the auxiliary analysis of employees' innovative productivity.

The ratio of operating income before depreciation to the book value of total assets. It is used as a control variable in the baseline innovation regressions and as the accounting-based dependent variable of financial performance, where the authors assess both the average effect and the dynamics of the treatment effect over the years before and after the treatment.

The market-based performance measure used as the second dependent variable of financial performance; the authors describe it as a forward-looking measure that accounts for all future cash flows of the company. In the variable definitions the authors define the market-to-book ratio as the ratio of the market value of total assets (book value of total assets plus the market value of common stock minus the sum of the book value of common stock and balance sheet deferred taxes) to the book value of total assets.

A dummy variable indicating whether the company's institutional ownership is above the median across all companies in the year prior to the treatment. Institutional ownership is computed as the percentage of shares owned by institutional investors using data from the Thomson Reuters institutional holdings database; it is interacted with the treatment dummy.
scale: dummy (1 = institutional ownership above the median in the year prior to treatment)
time_window: the year prior to the treatment

description: A dummy variable indicating whether the company operates in the business-to-consumer sector, based on the partition of Lev et al. (2010) using four-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes. It is interacted with the constituency statute treatment dummy in the tests of Hypothesis 2C.

A dummy variable indicating whether the company operates in a high-polluting industry, i.e., one of the seven industry sectors identified by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency as accounting for 92% of all disposal and other releases of toxic release inventory chemicals, matched to four-digit SIC codes via the Census Bureau's NAICS-SIC bridge. It is interacted with the constituency statute treatment dummy in the tests of Hypothesis 2D.

No direct measure of experimentation is constructed; the authors test the experimentation argument indirectly through the innovation outcomes of originality, generality, and hits and flops, which they describe as consequences of employees experimenting more after the adoption of stakeholder-friendly policies.
The number of years that the director served on the board at the time of the death. The analysis regresses cumulative abnormal returns on director tenure and on the square of director tenure.

Cumulative abnormal returns around the first announcement of the death of a director. A measure of systematic risk is estimated by regressing firm returns on the value-weighted CRSP market index over trading days from t-290 to t-90 (201 days), the abnormal return is the actual return minus the expected return, and abnormal returns are cumulated on the day of the exit and for one and two days following the event, with the '0;2' window used as the primary analysis window.
Dummy variable equal to 1 if the director is a member of at least two of the three key committees (audit, nominating, and compensation).

Firm-year ratio of outside directors in their prime tenure period (7 to 18 years of director tenure) to board size. The measure ranges between 0 and 1, where 0 means no outside directors of the firm were in the prime period and 1 means all directors were in the prime tenure period.
Ratio of cash compensation (salary plus bonus) to total compensation. A shift in the mix of compensation to less cash-based compensation indicates an increased sensitivity of pay to performance.
Ratio of equity-based compensation to total compensation. Equity-based compensation is the value of restricted stock grants in a given year, and option compensation is omitted from this measure.

The dollar change in executive pay for each 1% change in shareholder wealth, estimated as the coefficient on performance in regressions of compensation against performance and other control variables.
Change in total compensation; the authors use it to check whether the overall level of compensation rises with the percentage of directors in the prime tenure period.

Using a 5-point Likert-type scale and a deck of alliance cards, experts evaluated how the alliance has helped the pharmaceutical firm in terms of learning new skills or capabilities and technology or research developments (1 = very poorly; 5 = very well) as well as which partner benefited most from knowledge spillovers (1 = biotechnology firm; 5 = pharmaceutical firm). Interrater reliability for all the experts was high (0.85), so their responses were averaged for each performance measure for each alliance. The three averaged performance measures had a high degree of covariance (Cronbach's alpha = 0.88) and were summed to create the index used as the dependent variable.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale items; index is the sum of three performance measures

description: Participation breadth of knowledge was measured as the percentage of research communities associated with a scientific discipline in which a firm was active, weighted by the square root of the discipline size (the number of research communities) to give a weighted participation rate (WPR) for each of a firm's disciplines. Each WPR was calculated using the 1992 and 1994 data and then averaged. The biotechnology firm's WPRs were standardized (mean = 5, S.D. = 1) to establish the relative importance of each discipline to that firm's research, and multiplied by the pharmaceutical firm's corresponding WPRs to convert them into a knowledge relevance score (KRS). Hypothesis 1 is measured with the KRS for biochemistry for the alliance.

Specialized knowledge relevance was measured by summing all the knowledge relevance scores (KRSs) for all disciplines, except biochemistry, that were used by the alliance partners. The KRSs are built from weighted participation rates calculated with the 1992 and 1994 CRP data and adjusted for each discipline's importance to the biotechnology firm.

Each firm's structure was measured with formalization and centralization scales taken from Galbraith and Merrill (1991), which adapt Miller and associates' scales for R&D-intensive organizations. Formalization uses a 10-item scale (five items for upper management, five for lower management) on a 7-point Likert-type scale.
