Because the full centralization and formalization scales did not demonstrate reliability, the four subscales were used separately; the upper management formalization subscale had an acceptable Cronbach's alpha of 0.74. Partner similarity scores were computed from the subscale scores of each alliance partner following the procedure used by Judge and Ferris (1993).

The lower management formalization subscale consists of five of the 10 formalization items, answered on a 7-point Likert-type scale, taken from the Galbraith and Merrill (1991) adaptation of Miller and associates' scales. The subscale had an acceptable Cronbach's alpha of 0.77 and was used separately because the full scale was not reliable. Partner similarity scores were computed from the subscale scores of each alliance partner following the procedure used by Judge and Ferris (1993).

The centralization scale, taken from Galbraith and Merrill (1991) and adapted from Miller and associates, is a seven-item scale (four items for R&D decisions, three items for management decisions) using 7-point Likert-type items. Because the full scale was not reliable, the business centralization subscale was used separately; its Cronbach's alpha was 0.65. Partner similarity scores were computed from the subscale scores of each alliance partner following the procedure used by Judge and Ferris (1993).

The research centralization subscale consists of four of the seven centralization items concerning R&D decisions, answered on 7-point Likert-type scales, taken from the Galbraith and Merrill (1991) adaptation of Miller and associates' scales. It had an acceptable Cronbach's alpha of 0.76 and was used separately because the full scale was not reliable. Partner similarity scores were computed from the subscale scores of each alliance partner following the procedure used by Judge and Ferris (1993).

The compensation instrument included 10 items from Gomez-Mejia's (1992) basis of pay scale, a modified item on the time horizon of pay reflecting the use of stock options, and two added items on the firm's emphasis on publications and reputation in the outside scientific community in evaluating research staff. All 13 items use 7-point scales; they showed a moderately high level of covariance (Cronbach's alpha of 0.62) and were summed to create a compensation index for each firm. The compensation index scores were converted to similarity measures using the same procedure as the organizational structure variables.
scale: 7-point scales for the 13 items; index is their sum

description: Using company-wide research community lists, the overlap of the student's and teacher's organizational problem sets was measured by counting the number of research communities in which both alliance partners had published during the period covered by the CRP data. The more communities shared by the partners, the greater the overlap of their problem sets should be.
time_window: period covered by the CRP 1992 and 1994 data bases

description: Cumulative abnormal return for U.S. firms computed with standard event study methodology and calculated over a -2, +2 window around the layoff announcement. Announcement dates come from the Wall Street Journal, and stock returns data come from the CRSP tapes of the University of Chicago.

Cumulative abnormal return for Japanese firms computed with standard event study methodology over a -2, +2 window. Weekly Japanese publications are typically published on Wednesday, so day 0 is identified as the middle of the 5-day period covered by the publication. Stock price data come from Datastream International.

Whether the announced layoff is permanent or temporary, identified for both the U.S. and Japanese samples from the news articles reporting the announcement. Permanent layoffs are due to long-term changes in the firm and its competitive environment, while temporary layoffs represent alternatives to inventory accumulation and a convenient way of dealing with seasonal demand shifts.

Whether the announcement is part of a series of layoffs or a single event, identified for both the U.S. and Japanese samples from the news articles; multiple announcements are treated as the higher value of the construct.

variable_name: percentage of the work force laid off
description: The number of employees being laid off, as indicated in the layoff announcements, divided by the firm's total number of employees. Data on the total number of employees in U.S. firms, reported in the previous quarter, come from Compact Disclosure, and data on the number of employees in Japanese firms come from Worldscope. Quintile and quartile break-downs of this variable are used to test Hypothesis 5.
time_window: total employees reported in the previous quarter

description: Coding of whether the announced layoff is proactive or reactive, based on the news articles for both the U.S. and Japanese samples. Proactive announcements are defined as layoffs that are part of a strategy or a restructuring plan which anticipates the direction of the competitive environment; reactive announcements are layoffs that are a direct response to financial distress. A coder reliability check was conducted, and in 82 percent of the cases the secondary coder's data matched the primary coder.

variable_name: first layoff announcement in a given industry
description: Classification of each U.S. layoff announcement as either the first layoff announcement in a given industry or a subsequent announcement; industries are identified by 4-digit SIC codes reported in the CRSP tapes.

Each observation is a layoff announcement by a listed firm, taken from news sources (Wall Street Journal for U.S. firms, Asian Wall Street Journal, Nikkei Weekly and other sources for Japanese firms) over 1990 to 1994. Announcements by government organizations and private companies and those with confounding events are dropped. The announcement date is the event date for the event study.

National institutional context is a group split: the U.S. sample of NYSE, American Stock Exchange and NASDAQ firms versus the Japanese sample of firms listed in Tokyo. Cumulative abnormal returns to layoff announcements are compared between the two samples.

Indicator variable equal to 1 if a firm's founder or a member of his family by blood or marriage is an officer, director, or blockholder of the firm, either individually or as a group, and 0 otherwise. Information on the identity of the founder and family relationships among shareholders was manually gathered for a random subsample of firms from proxy statements filed with the SEC, corporate histories extracted from Hoover's, company websites, and Internet searches.

Indicator variable equal to 1 if a firm's CEO is the founder or a member of the founding family. Within the family-firm subsample, non-family-CEO firms are those that are not managed by the founder or any member of the founding family. The information on family management was manually collected for each firm-year.
Indicator variable equal to 1 if a firm's CEO is its founder, regardless of whether other family members of the same or later generations serve as officers or directors in the firm.
Indicator variable equal to 1 if a firm's CEO is a descendant of the founder.

Indicator variable that takes the value 1 if a firm undertakes at least one divestiture in a given year, and 0 if not; this is the variable used to test a firm's propensity to undertake divestitures. The divestiture data consist of information on every divestiture undertaken by each firm in the sample, the mode of divestiture (sell-off or spinoff), and the dollar value of each transaction.

Our measure of firm value is Tobin's q, the ratio of the firm's market value to the replacement cost of its assets. Market value is the value of common equity plus the book value of preferred stock and debt, and the replacement cost of assets is proxied by their actual book value. In the second-stage coarsened exact matching regressions the dependent variable is the first-differenced value of Tobin's q, defined as Q t - Q t - 1, which soaks up the effects of time-invariant, firm-specific characteristics.
time_window: change from year t-1 to year t

description: Announcement dates of all of the divestitures in our sample were identified using SDC Platinum, and daily stock returns within 250-day estimation windows [ - 800, - 551] before these announcement dates were collected from CRSP. Firms' normal returns were predicted from their daily stock returns and the stock market's returns, and their abnormal returns were computed within three-day event windows [ - 1, + 1] surrounding the announcement dates. CAR is the cumulative sum of these abnormal returns over this three-day window.
time_window: three-day window [ - 1, + 1] around the announcement date

description: Cash flow margin (CFM) was calculated from the ratio printed in the paper as the sum of net income, depreciation and interest expense over the sum of net patient revenue and total other income; the printed formula is broken into fragments and the components of numerator and denominator cannot be read unambiguously from the text. The measure was calculated for each hospital for the years 1996 and 1997 and then averaged to eliminate any single year anomaly.

Industry experts rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale the potential of each hospital service to enhance the reputation or increase the attractiveness of the hospital to physicians, patients and insurance companies, where 5 designates high potential and 1 low potential, and 0 indicates no strategic value whatsoever. The average of the six experts' ratings for each hospital resource was calculated and assigned as weights to each respective hospital service, and an overall measure of the value of each hospital's service bundle was calculated as the weighted value summed over services divided by the total number of services. To reflect each firm's relative position in the market, this measure was standardized relative to the local market by transforming each observation into a Z-score.
scale: 5-point Likert-type rating (0-5) used as weights; standardized Z-score within market

description: Industry experts evaluated on a 5-point Likert-type scale the relative importance of each physician service in building an efficient and effective integrated delivery system, where 5 denotes the service as critical to the effectiveness of an integrated delivery system and 1 designates it as not an important part of an integrated delivery system. The average of the six experts' ratings for each type of physician service was calculated and assigned as weights to each respective physician service, and this weighting factor was applied to the type of physician services each hospital is linked to and summed to derive a measure of the strength of each hospital's physician linkages.

A composite of two determinants of managed care's ability to influence the demand structure in the market: managed care penetration and the percentage of managed care that is Medicaid and Medicare related. Managed care market penetration is the percentage of the MSA population enrolled with an MCS in 1996, calculated as the number of enrollees per MSA divided by the total MSA population. The two measures were factored together, with principal components used to extract the buyer power factor and factor scores generated using the regression methodology.

A modification of the Herfindahl index, a measure of market concentration that considers both the magnitude and the relative differences of market shares of competitors in a market. The measure of rivalry was calculated as 1 minus the calculated Herfindahl index, so that higher values correspond to greater levels of hospital competition in a particular market. Total revenues for each hospital used in the calculation were obtained from the 1998 American Hospital Directory.

Binary variable taking the value 1 if the inventor was listed on patents filed by the company while he or she was CEO and within 2 years of the current year (i.e., t - 2 to t + 2), and 0 otherwise. Involvement is assessed from inventor CEOs' pattern of patenting while in the CEO role, tracked by matching CEOs in Execucomp to a disambiguated list of inventors from the Harvard Patent Network Dataverse. The authors argue that being listed as an inventor legally requires creative contribution, so the indicator reflects direct, hands-on engagement in firm innovation activities. In the sample, about 46% of inventor CEOs were listed on their firms' patents as CEO in at least 1 year and 54% were not.

Proportion of exploitative citations to the total number of exploitative and exploratory citations on patents filed by the firm in year t. A firm's existing knowledge base is operationalized as its own patent portfolio as well as other patents it cited over the previous 5 years (backward citations from t - 6 to t - 1); citations included in that knowledge base are exploitative and citations that are not are exploratory. The variable ranges from 0 to 1, where 0 reflects completely exploratory patenting, .5 reflects an even split, and 1 reflects completely exploitative patenting.
time_window: t, with backward citations from t - 6 to t - 1

description: Binary variable taking the value 1 if the inventor was appointed from within the firm or was an original founder of the company, and 0 otherwise. Coding is based on whether the CEO had verified employment in an outside firm within 2 years of appointment, combined with their listed titles and roles in the focal company. Outsiders are classified as non-founder CEOs who had verified experience in an outside firm within 2 years of their appointment. In the sample, about 65% of inventor CEOs are insiders, with around 30% founders and 35% other insiders, and the remaining 35% are outsiders.

Subsample indicator created by splitting the insider variable into founders and other (non-founder) insiders. Founders are identified from their listed titles and roles in the focal company as a 'founder' or 'cofounder' of the company, and separate models are estimated for founders and for other insiders.

Blau's (1977) index of directors' primary industry backgrounds, calculated as 1 - sum of pi squared, where pi equals the proportion of directors with primary experience in each industry. All non-executive directors on the board in a given year are identified from BoardEx, comprehensive employment histories are compiled, and each director's primary industry background is classified as the industry where they had the most years of experience prior to t based on two-digit Global Industry Classification Standard (GIC) codes.

Exploratory innovation is the same share variable as exploitative innovation, read the other way: the proportion of a firm's patent citations that fall outside its own patents and those it cited in the previous five years is one minus the exploitative share. A value of 0 means completely exploratory patenting and 1 completely exploitative patenting, so low values mean more exploratory innovation.

The independent variable is the post-dismissal period. The 4 years subsequent to witnessing the first CEO dismissal receive a value of '1' and the 4 years prior to witnessing that dismissal (including the year of dismissal) receive a value of '0.' Where a competitor CEO witnessed multiple CEO dismissals, the first dismissal event is used because the authors expect the first would be most impactful.
time_window: 4 years before to 4 years after the first witnessed CEO dismissal

description: Following the summated approach, the authors measure the sum of research and development (R&D), capital expenditures, and acquisitions scaled by total revenues. They use a summated measure because all three individual measures are highly skewed and log transformations do not correct that problem, whereas the log-transformation of the summative measure approximately follows a normal distribution, which their synthetic control method requires.

Following Connelly et al. (2017), the authors use the sum of four constitutional limit provisions that Bebchuk, Cohen, and Ferrell (2009) identify as most critical to managers. In later discussion of the effect they define strong constitutional constraints as having two or more constitutional limit provisions and the rest as weak constitutional constraints.

The authors use the score provided in the TNIC-3 data generated by Hoberg and Phillips (2016), whose firm-by-firm similarity measure is based on firm product descriptions. The moderator uses TNIC-3 to create a similarity score between the two firms under investigation; its operationalization is distinct from the independent variable, which just uses TNIC-3 as a means to identify relevant competitors.

The first dependent variable is job insecurity, measured with a 3-item scale adopted from Hellgren, Sverke, and Isaksson (1999). After each of the first four scenarios respondents were asked to rate their perception of job insecurity. In two further scenarios job insecurity was instead manipulated as low or high, described to respondents as their job being secure or not secure.

Respondents ranked six ways of potentially allocating company financial resources in terms of the likelihood they might take that action in the scenario, with 6 being the most likely action and 1 being the least likely action. One of the six usages is a high-risk investment while the other five are all relatively low risk.
scale: 1 = least likely action to 6 = most likely action (ranking)

description: We measure vertical integration as the log of the total yearly mortgage securitizations issued by the parent firm, that is, the log of residential mortgage-backed securities issued by the firm during year t, used together with firm size controls as a proxy for the degree to which the firm internalizes origination-to-securitization flows.

A firm-year measure of the incremental likelihood that a mortgage defaults if originated by that firm, calculated by extracting the firm fixed effect from a mortgage-level model of the probability of loan default conditional on mortgage attributes, macroeconomic factors, and year and firm fixed effects. Observations above zero represent lower loan quality and observations below zero represent higher loan quality relative to the market average.

A raw count of the standard 24 provisions in corporate charters and bylaws as well as state law that limit shareholder rights, as reported by the Investor Responsibility Research Center. The 24 provisions represent five broad categories thought to increase the discretionary power of top managers, such as delay, voting and protection provisions. A higher score indicates worse governance quality ('Dictatorships'), while low values indicate 'Democracies'.
Institutional ownership ratio, calculated as the ratio of shares outstanding held by institutional owners to total shares outstanding.
The number of unique institutional investors.
IO concentration, measured as the Herfindahl index of all institutional investors.
The percent of institutional owners that are depository banks or insurance companies, traditionally conservative, regulated owners.
The percent of institutional owners that are hedge funds, family offices, or other investment vehicles that are traditionally more aggressive owners.

variable_name: Firm in operation by end of 2010
description: A 0/1 indicator that the lender was still operating at the end of 2010, modeled on a cross-sectional dataset built by collapsing the firm-year panel and demeaning all control variables from 2003 onward, since the dependent variable varies at the firm and not the firm-year level.

A proxy for Tobin's q used as a stock market-based measure of firm-level economic performance. It is calculated as the ratio of the sum of (1) market value of equity and (2) book value of total debt to the book value of total assets. The extent to which q is greater than one indicates how much economic value a firm creates for shareholders. The authors note that more complex measures of Tobin's q may induce sample selection bias as a result of data unavailability.

Calculated as the average percentage increase in R&D investments during the previous 3 years. The measure captures the relative magnitude of changes in the level of dollar investments in R&D over 3 years. The 3-year window reflects the finding from an in-depth examination of prospectuses that, in this industry, R&D investments convert into revenue-generating products typically within a period of 3 years.
time_window: average over the previous 3 years (t-1 to t-3)

description: Calculated as the average percentage increase in marketing investments during the previous 3 years. The measure captures the relative magnitude of changes in the level of dollar investments in marketing over 3 years. The authors project that marketing investments to build a strong brand name and close relationships with customers and distributors have economic performance effects longer than 1 year.
time_window: average over the previous 3 years (t-1 to t-3)

description: Measured as the level of R&D investments standardized by total assets. The authors standardize investments by total assets because some firms do not have sales in the early years of product development. The variable is used both to calculate the interaction terms and as a control variable.

Measured as the level of marketing investments standardized by total assets. The authors standardize investments by total assets because some firms do not have sales in the early years of product development. The variable is used both to calculate the interaction terms and as a control variable.
Measured as average firm tenure, i.e., the number of years that managers spent in a particular firm, of the top managers.

Calculated as the total percentage of ownership by institutional investors. Institutional investors include pension funds, mutual funds, insurance companies, investment firms and venture capital firms.

The CEO's self-reported counts of new opportunities, in terms of new products, services, and markets that the firm had identified during 2007-2009. The questionnaire emphasized that exploitation was not a requirement for opportunities to be reported and that minor modifications to existing products and services should not be considered new opportunities. The variable was constructed as the sum of opportunities of all three types.

Based on the individual educational backgrounds of all non-management employees. In conformity with the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED), education was first decomposed into eight categories based on length and the qualifications provided. Because the complexity of an educational area varies between educational levels, diversity was calculated as the number of different areas of study within the same level of education; the sum of unique educational backgrounds was then summed across levels and divided by the number of employees, so that the measure ranges from 0 to 1.

Respondents were presented with four different entrepreneurial decisions and asked to indicate the hierarchical level at which the authority to make decisions in relation to the activity was vested. The four activities were: (a) developing new products or services, (b) introducing major changes in marketing activities, (c) making significant changes in products and services, and (d) discontinuing a major product or service. Based on Miller and Droge (1986), the lowest level of centralized decision making was coded 0 and denoted 'lower-level management' and the highest level was coded 3 and denoted 'senior management'; an average composite measure was constructed (alpha = 0.7).

Respondents were asked whether 'the identification of new business opportunities primarily happens at the senior-management/corporate level.' The variable was coded 1 if respondents answered 'no' and 0 otherwise. Posing the question in general terms and using binary reporting captures the firm's general acceptance of opportunity formation as a bottom-up process.

The dependent variable, bankrupt firm delisting, was coded '1' in the year of delisting, otherwise coded '0.' COMPUSTAT and CRSP were used for identifying deletion reasons and the Lexis-Nexus and Factiva databases were searched to code the dependent variable. Being acquired by other firms was viewed as a desired outcome rather than corporate failure, so acquired bankrupt firms were coded as '0.'

Using the COMPUSTAT segment database, the authors measured de-diversification as the change in the number of business segments between year t - 1 and year t - 2, namely, a decrease in the number of segments.

variable_name: increase in the number of alliance partners
description: This construct was measured by (the number of alliances in year t - 1) - (the number of alliances in year t - 2), that is an increase in the number of alliances over time. Alliance data were collected from the SDC Alliances database and confirmed through a search of the Factiva and Lexis-Nexus databases.

variable_name: increase in the number of institutional investors
description: Using data from the Thomson-Reuters Institutional (13F) Holdings database, this variable was calculated as (the number of institutional investors in year t - 1) - (the number of institutional investors in year t - 2).
Using the I/B/E/S database, this variable was calculated as (the number of analysts in year t - 1) - (the number of analysts in year t - 2).

Measured by comparing executives ' use of content words between the management discussion (MD) and the Q&A portions of the call. The authors created two vectors of the counts of all content words spoken by executives in the MD and the Q&A, used text-embedding vectors to identify the semantic similarity of the meanings of each pair of content words, calculated the dot product of the two vectors weighted by those semantic similarity scores, and normalized the result by the lengths of the two vectors. This score was reverse-coded to capture the content newness of executive communication and adjusted for document length following Lee (2016). The measure was standardized in the regressions.
time_window: MD and Q&A portions of the conference call

description: Measured by the Fog index of the Q&A portions of the calls; the Fog index captures sentence length (the average length of sentences) and word complexity (the number of words containing three or more syllables) and indicates how many years of formal education a person needs to understand a message. The authors reverse-coded the measure by subtracting it from 24 (which equals the maximum Fog score in the working sample plus one) to capture the composition simplicity of executives ' responses during the Q&As. The measure was standardized in the regressions.
time_window: Q&A portion of the conference call

description: Measured as the dissimilarity in executives ' use of function words between the MD and the Q&A portions of the call. For each call, the authors parsed the transcript into an MD document and a Q&A document, created vectors for the counts of all function words spoken by executives in each document, and computed the cosine similarity between the two vectors. They subtracted this similarity score from 1 to capture the dissimilarity in the use of function words, which they considered evidence of a more unscripted Q&A delivery, and adjusted the measure for document length following Lee (2016). The measure was standardized in the regressions.
time_window: MD and Q&A portions of the conference call

description: Bid–ask spreads are used to capture the differences in investors ' opinions; a reduction in the bid–ask spread indicates that the valuation differences among investors have decreased. The pre-event period spread is the average per-second difference between the highest quoted bid and the highest quoted offer price, divided by the midpoint between those two prices, during the pre-event period (from 90 to 15 minutes before the scheduled start of the call). The event period spread is calculated in the same way for the event period (from 20 minutes after the scheduled start of the call, the typical start of a Q&A session, to 100 minutes later). Investor opinion convergence is the difference between the pre-event period spread and the event period spread; a positive value indicates that differences of opinion have decreased (convergence) and a negative value that they have increased (divergence).
time_window: pre-event period (90 to 15 minutes before the call) and event period (20 to 120 minutes after the scheduled start of the call)

description: Measured by the book-to-market ratio, calculated as the total value of shareholders ' equity (the book value) at the end of the most recent quarter before the conference call divided by the market value of outstanding shares at the end of that quarter. The authors note that firms with a higher book-to-market ratio face greater uncertainty in their future earnings compared with other firms.
time_window: the most recent quarter before the conference call

description: The portion of the firm's stock return around the new CEO appointment that is unanticipated by a model of anticipated, normal returns, expressed as the difference between the observed return and the predicted or normal return. Alpha and beta were estimated over an estimation period of 250 days, from 295 days to 45 days before the event, using returns on stock i for day t and returns on the market portfolio for day t. The dependent variable is the cumulative abnormal return (CAR) over the two-day window (0,1) around the announcement date of the CEO appointment. The equation specifying the return model appears in the text as an unreadable formula block.
time_window: two-day window (0,1) around the announcement; estimation period from day -295 to day -45

description: The percentage of independent board members who were 'CEO directors,' where a CEO director is an independent director who currently was, or previously had been, the CEO of another firm. The authors first identified the name of each independent director's current employer—or most recent employer if the director was retired—and his or her job title(s) with the employer. The variable was created for year t-1, treating the year of the new CEO appointment as t, and measured only for the independent directors of the focal firm, coded from the sample firms' proxy statements.

A dichotomous variable coded 1 if one or more independent directors had current or past work experience in the same industry as the focal firm, and 0 if no independent director had current or past experience in the same industry. The focal firm's industry was defined using four-digit SIC codes based on COMPUSTAT segment data. The variable was created for year t-1 and measured only for the independent directors of the focal firm.

Internal social capital, calculated as the overlap in independent directors' board tenures, following prior research. The formula in the text is an unreadable formula block; the surrounding prose indicates it is based on the board tenure of the i-th director (ui) and the number of pairwise comparisons (n). The variable was created for year t-1 and measured only for the independent directors of the focal firm.

External social capital, measured as the average number of external directorship ties held by the independent directors of the focal firm. The variable was created for year t-1 and measured only for the independent directors of the focal firm.

Coded '1' if the new CEO was an insider and '0' if he or she was an outsider. Characteristics of the arriving/departing CEOs and succession events were coded from the Wall Street Journal, company press releases, and corporate proxy statements.

Following Kogan et al. (2017), the authors first measure the three-day abnormal return following a design patent's grant announcement, which contains both the announcement signal and noise. They remove the noise by measuring the price variance for the firm in the same year and how much more volatile trading becomes on the days when a firm receives a patent (the signal-to-noise ratio). Assuming that a patent's value follows a normal distribution truncated at zero and that the signal-to-noise ratio is a constant, the patent's value is derived from the market capitalization of the firm and the count of patents issued on the same day; the explicit formula is not readable in the text provided. The value enters the models in log form (log-log setting).
time_window: three-day window following the grant announcement

description: The focal design's sum similarity to other designs in the same style whose patents were granted within the last year (rolling 365-day window) of its grant date. Pairwise similarity between two designs uses the Jaccard index: the number of overlaps in the two designs' reference lists divided by the total number of unique references the two designs made, plus one over the size of the citing design's reference list if one design references the other. The sum is entered in log form (log + 1) to reduce the effect of outliers.
time_window: rolling 365-day window before the grant date

description: The focal design's sum similarity to other designs in the same style whose patents were granted within the two years preceding the last year (rolling window of 1,095 to 366 days) of its grant date, using the same Jaccard-based pairwise similarity index computed from reference-list overlaps. The sum is entered in log form (log + 1).
time_window: rolling window of 1,095 to 366 days before the grant date

description: A binary measure at the three-digit Standard Industrial Classification level, set to one if the industry is involved in making visible products and zero otherwise. The classification is based on Heffetz's (2011) survey of U.S. respondents, in which automobiles, clothing, furniture, jewelry, watches, tobacco products, and home recreational products topped the list in terms of visibility.

Following Bilir (2014), the technological lifespan of the designed product is established at the three-digit SIC code level using the average of utility patent citation lags in years in each industry. Longer time lags indicate a long technological life because innovations continue to be reused by innovations far in the future.

Respondents reported their evaluation of the expressive value of the focal product by answering how much they agree that 'the Swift RM18 is unique'. Responses were assessed using a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree), such that higher scores represented a greater perceived value of the focal product.
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: Respondents reported their evaluation of the informational value of the focal product by answering how much they agree that 'the functionality and affordance (i.e., the quality or property of products that defines their possible uses) of the Swift RM18 are easily understood'. Responses used a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree).
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: Respondents saw two reference lawnmower designs that were either similar (designs A and B) or dissimilar (designs C and D) to the focal design. The manipulation was validated with a separate sample of 196 consumer respondents from Prolific who rated on a seven-point scale how much they agreed that the reference design was similar to the focal design, with higher scores representing greater perceived similarity.

Respondents were randomly assigned to a past or a contemporary condition by manipulating the introductory date of the reference designs: the past condition received a gardening magazine cover published in Spring 2018 and was told the products were advertised two years ago, whereas the contemporary condition received a Spring 2020 cover. All respondents then reviewed the focal design in an issue dated Spring 2020.

Revenue per available room was calculated by dividing total room revenue by the number of rooms available for sale. Monthly revenues were summed for a year and divided by the annual number of rooms available, with monthly data aggregated to the annual level as a means to eliminate seasonal fluctuations within clusters.
time_window: year 2000 (monthly data aggregated to the annual level)

variable_name: Proportion of properties in cluster pursuing high differentiation
description: The proportion of lodging properties in a competitive cluster (tract) that were pursuing a higher differentiation (i.e., product-quality) strategic orientation. It is measured at the tract level, where tracts are defined by Smith Travel as a subset of a Metropolitan Statistical Area market defined by counties and/or zip codes. For luxury hotels this variable is 0 by definition, so it was not used in the luxury model.

variable_name: Proportion of properties in cluster pursuing low cost
description: The proportion of lodging properties in a competitive cluster (tract) that were pursuing a lower-cost strategic orientation. It is the opposite way of measuring the same basic phenomenon as the differentiation-based variable, and the two variables are never included in the same model at the same time. It was used to test Hypothesis 1b for luxury firms.

variable_name: Distance between strategic orientation of hotel and central tendency in cluster
description: To measure central tendency, each strategy type was assigned a number from 1 ('economy') to 5 ('luxury'); the average strategic type in the cluster was then calculated. The distance score was the absolute value of a firm's own value minus the cluster's central tendency. A strategic distance variable for the size of the lodging company was also calculated for completeness.

Smith Travel supplied a categorical variable describing the product/service quality segment category of each hotel, adapted from the Bear Stearns U.S. lodging industry categorization scheme. The scheme divides the industry into five segments based upon important differences in product and service offerings: full-service hotels are divided into luxury, upscale, and midscale with food and beverage; limited-service hotels are divided into midscale without food and beverage, and economy.

A time-varying count variable that records the number of foreign firms censored by the government and hence excluded from the sovereign wealth fund's investment universe. The measure is the cumulative count of censorship announcements by the government, used as the operationalization of the government's normative pressure; the first exclusions were announced in 2005, following the formation of the Council on Ethics in 2004.
time_window: cumulative up to the focal year

description: For a focal firm's cross-border investment portfolio in a given year, the proportion of target firms in which the sovereign wealth fund has previously invested. If the focal firm invested in n firms in year t, of which ns firms received prior equity investments from the sovereign wealth fund, the proportion of overlap in year t is calculated as a ratio of ns and n.

A binary measure assigned a value of 1 when the cross-border investments in a given year comprise a responsible investment target that is listed on any one of the following sustainability indices or organizations: the Dow Jones Sustainability Index (DJSI), OMX Ethical Index, FTSE4Good Index Series, UN Global Compact, or UN Principles for Responsible Investment; otherwise it is assigned a value of 0. A listing on one of these recognized sustainability indices or by international organizations is taken as an indicator of commitment to social responsibility criteria.

A dummy variable for majority stakeholding by the government, defined as equity ownership greater than 50%, which accounts for the extent to which firms may be prone to isomorphic behavior as a result of regulative pressure. This ownership data were obtained from the firms' records in the SDC data set; 14% of the 437 firms in the sample are government owned.

Multi-item scale based on a single consensus rating completed by two project team members. The items asked whether the team had to ask a higher manager before it could do almost anything, whether even small matters had to be referred to someone higher up for approval, whether little action could be taken until a higher manager approved, whether any decision had to have a higher manager's approval, and whether a team member who wanted to make his or her own decisions would be quickly discouraged; these items were reverse-coded. One item was deleted. The response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.'

Multi-item scale based on a single consensus rating completed by two project team members, capturing open transfer of information among team members. Items covered whether members hid issues from each other, whether channels of communication were open, whether access to information from members was quick and easy, whether members engaged in open and honest communication, and whether members willingly kept each other informed. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.' Reliability is above the commonly accepted threshold of .70.

Multi-item scale based on a single consensus rating completed by two project team members, focusing narrowly on reaching out to customers. Items covered the effort put into interacting with potential customers, the frequency of interactions with likely customers, collection of information about new market developments affecting customers, and monitoring of new technology developments affecting customer requirements. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.'

Multi-item scale based on a single consensus rating completed by two project team members, capturing the project team's direct contact with other organizational functions. Items covered close personal interactions with other members of the firm regarding the project, frequent consultation with other departments, and effort put into building relationships with other functions. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.' Its reliability is below the commonly accepted threshold of .70, which the authors say calls for cautious interpretation.

Multi-item scale based on a single consensus rating completed by two project team members, capturing the use of a formal, staged procedure for the project. Items covered use of a formal process with frequent reviews of progress, a formal process with different stages for major activities, review of progress towards objectives at specific stages, and a documented process with specific milestones for each activity. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.'

Multi-item scale based on a single consensus rating completed by two project team members. Items covered whether the project leader had experience in both technical and management aspects of product development projects, had diverse technical and management knowledge and experience in the industry, and had significant technical and management skills and knowledge about the team's project. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.'

Multi-item scale based on a single consensus rating completed by two project team members, capturing acceptance of and identification with overall project goals. Items covered commitment of team members to the same project goals, project goals linking members together, members accepting project goals as their own, behaviour supporting overall project goals, and specific objectives felt as personal goals. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.'

Multi-item scale completed by the team leader of each project a few weeks after the team members' ratings. Items asked the extent of agreement that several alternative solutions were identified for each problem the team encountered, that the team seemed always to come up with solutions to problems encountered, and that it was always easy to identify new solutions to the team's problems. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.' Its reliability is below the commonly accepted threshold of .70, which the authors say calls for cautious interpretation.

Multi-item scale completed by the team leader of each project, with items worded in the direction of slowness and then reverse-coded: solutions found for problems faced were not timely, the project team was very slow in finding and implementing solutions to problems encountered, and ideas for solving problems were discovered rather late to be implemented successfully. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree,' so that higher values indicate faster problem solving.

Multi-item scale completed by the team leader of each project. Items asked the extent of agreement that the solutions found generated fresh thinking about product quality in the project team, that the solutions found were very creative, that the solutions found were quality solutions for the problems faced, and that the solutions were exactly what the team needed. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.'

Multi-item measure completed at project completion by the senior manager or CEO with overall responsibility for the project. Items asked how well statements described the project: the project duration met the planned time schedule, the project was completed on time as planned, the length of the project met the planned objectives better than previous projects, and the speed of development was faster than previous projects. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.'

Multi-item measure completed at project completion by the senior manager or CEO with overall responsibility for the project. Items asked how well statements described the project: the product conformed to performance specifications required by customers, the product performance met the requirements of customers, and the design of the product met the quality standards expected by the firm's customers. Response format was 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.'

Data on the exact day, month, and year in which an organization defected from the NASDAQ to the NYSE were obtained from CRSP data tapes. The event of interest was the switching of a firm's listing from NASDAQ to NYSE, and the dependent variable was the continuous hazard rate. Event histories of all sample organizations were split into one-year spells, with all spells except the year of adoption coded as right censored.

An identity-discrepant cue was defined as the defection of a NASDAQ member to the NYSE. The number of identity-discrepant cues facing an organization was the cumulative number of defections on the ending date for each spell. These cumulative defection counts are interacted with the characteristics of at-risk firms in the susceptibility vector.

The sum of all nonduplicated sent and received ties that a firm's board had to boards in the NASDAQ stock market. Sent ties arise when an executive of the focal firm sits on the board of another firm, received ties when an executive of the other firm sits on the focal firm's board. When computing NASDAQ interlocks, a focal organization's ties to all other firms in the sample of 2,020 NASDAQ firms listed in the National Market as of 1987 were considered.
time_window: proxy statement issued closest to January 1, 1987

description: The sum of all nonduplicated sent and received ties that a firm's board had to boards in the NYSE. All interlocks between the focal NASDAQ firm and 1,337 organizations listed on the NYSE as of July 1, 1986 were considered, including large publicly traded American industrial and service enterprises.
time_window: NYSE organizations listed as of July 1, 1986; proxy statement issued closest to January 1, 1987

description: The sum of all nonduplicated sent and received ties that the defecting firm's board had to boards in the NASDAQ market. The measure enters the infectiousness vector as a characteristic of the immediate prior defector.
time_window: proxy statement issued closest to January 1, 1987

description: A focal organization's ties to prior defectors consisted of all nonduplicated ties to prior defectors in the sample, following Davis (1991). The value 1 was used for firms that have a connection, and 0 was used for unconnected firms. If the at-risk organization and the defector had direct ties, the value 1 was used for such proximate observations, and 0 was used for distant observations.

Mean ROS of the foreign affiliates within each parent firm per year over the observation period. ROS is a profit measure defined by the ratio of profit before tax over total sales. This is the dependent variable of the regressions.

Skewness of the performance (ROS) distribution of the foreign affiliates within each parent firm per year. The authors state that it is measured according to a formula, but the equation itself is not readable in the extracted text.
Kurtosis of the performance (ROS) distribution of the foreign affiliates within each parent firm per year. One of the two moderating variables in the regressions.

Standard deviation of the performance (ROS) distribution of the foreign affiliates within each parent firm per year, the measure the authors use for variance. One of the two moderating variables in the regressions.

Mean ROS of the foreign affiliates within each industry per year over the observation period. ROS is a profit measure defined by the ratio of profit before tax over total sales. This is the dependent variable of the regressions.

Skewness of the performance (ROS) distribution of the foreign affiliates within each industry per year. The authors state that it is measured according to a formula, but the equation itself is not readable in the extracted text.
Kurtosis of the performance (ROS) distribution of the foreign affiliates within each industry per year. One of the two moderating variables in the regressions.

Standard deviation of the performance (ROS) distribution of the foreign affiliates within each industry per year, the measure the authors use for variance. One of the two moderating variables in the regressions.

Mean ROS of the foreign affiliates within each host country per year over the observation period. ROS is a profit measure defined by the ratio of profit before tax over total sales. This is the dependent variable of the regressions.

Skewness of the performance (ROS) distribution of the foreign affiliates within each host country per year. The authors state that it is measured according to a formula, but the equation itself is not readable in the extracted text.
Kurtosis of the performance (ROS) distribution of the foreign affiliates within each host country per year. One of the two moderating variables in the regressions.

Standard deviation of the performance (ROS) distribution of the foreign affiliates within each host country per year, the measure the authors use for variance. One of the two moderating variables in the regressions.

Perceived agreement correlates one's own ratings of the importance of the acquisition objectives with one's estimates of the ratings in the other organization. Agreement scores are within-subject correlations of individual ratings of the importance of objectives and mean group ratings of the same objectives.

Actual agreement correlates one's own ratings of the importance of the objectives with the mean ratings of the other organization. Agreement scores are within-subject correlations computed across the objectives.

Accuracy correlates one's estimates of the importance ratings in the other organization with the actual mean scores of that organization. Agreement scores are within-subject correlations computed across the objectives.

Internal agreement correlates one's own ratings of the importance of the objectives with the mean ratings of one's own organization. Agreement scores are within-subject correlations computed across the objectives.

Overall expectations is an estimate of expectations of success, without reference to particular objectives, calculated on a 10-point scale. It is intended to reflect success expectations that are not reducible to individual values on particular objectives. In the analysis it is controlled for aggregate expectations so that the two are independent by construction. Responses were collected 1 year after the acquisition.

Aggregate expectations is the mean likelihood of success across the 14 acquisition objectives. For each objective respondents rated, on 10-point scales, the likelihood of the objective being accomplished in the short term (2 years or less) and the likelihood of it being accomplished in the long term (more than 2 years). Because of their high intercorrelation the short- and long-term expectations were averaged to provide a single measure of expectations for each objective, and these were then aggregated across objectives.

Personal value measures the overall personal importance that respondents attached to acquisition objectives. It is the mean of the ratings of importance that each respondent provided for the 14 objectives. Importance ratings were elicited on 10-point scales.

Organizational affiliation distinguishes respondents from the acquiring hospital from respondents of the acquired hospital. It is listed among the controls and is the grouping variable for the hypotheses about differences by organization. The text does not state which group is coded 1.

Professional background distinguishes respondents who are M.D.s from those who are not. It is listed among the controls and is one of the grouping variables for the hypothesis about professional roles and tasks.

Tasks classify respondents into administrative, clinical, or joint tasks. Joint tasks are those for which the incumbent may have both clinical and administrative duties, the position of clinical chairman being an example. It is listed among the controls and is one of the grouping variables for the hypothesis about professional roles and tasks.
Involvement with integration was assessed for respondents by senior executives of each hospital. The three levels used are high, medium, and low.

Commercial banks' deposit amount is calculated by summing up deposits across branches for a given bank in a given year. Credit unions' deposit amount for a given credit union in a given year is taken from the NCUA call reports. It is the dependent variable in the organizational-level regressions.
A dummy variable that equals 1 for all years after 2007 (inclusive), and 0 otherwise. Because a year in this setting begins on June 30, the dummy covers June 30, 2007 and after.

A dummy variable that is coded 1 for banks with less than $1 billion in assets, and 0 otherwise, consistent with the FDIC definition of community banks. Large commercial banks serve as the omitted category in the bank regressions.

variable_name: Single-bond credit unions; Multibond credit unions; Other credit unions
description: Dummy variables defined from NCUA data on credit unions' fields of membership. Single-bond credit unions have a relatively narrow and well-defined set of customers; multibond credit unions have more diffuse networks of members and are seen as less typical; other credit unions, for which the grade of membership is less clear, serve as the omitted category.

Credit unions' deposit market share for a given market and year is the share of credit-union deposits as a fraction of total deposits (credit-union deposits plus bank deposits). Community banks' and large banks' deposit market shares are computed as a fraction of total deposits measured by credit-union deposits plus bank deposits, and single-bond, multibond, and other credit unions' deposit market shares are computed as a fraction of total deposits measured by credit-union deposits (of all types) plus bank deposits. The variable is bounded between 0 and 1 and is estimated with linear probability models.
A dummy variable that equals 1 for all years after 2007 (inclusive), and 0 otherwise, used in the market-level regressions to compare deposit market shares before and after the financial crisis.

variable_name: Large banks; Community banks; Single-bond credit unions; Multibond credit unions
description: The market-level analysis separates deposit market shares by the same grade-of-membership distinctions used at the organizational level: large banks versus community banks (banks with less than $1 billion in assets), and single-bond versus multibond credit unions based on their fields of membership. Separate regressions are estimated on each group's deposit market share.

Measured by adding the correlations for the years t-3 to t of industry-level sales (the aggregate amount of sales of all publicly traded firms operating in each given two-digit SIC industry) among each pair of two-digit SIC industries in which each sample firm operates for a given year, and dividing the result by the number of its distinctive pairs of two-digit SIC industries to assure comparability across firm/years. The measure captures the extent to which sales' changes in the industries a firm operates mutually compensate each other, i.e., revenue smoothing. To facilitate interpretation, the authors multiplied this measure by -1, so that -1 indicates no financial diversification or revenue smoothing and 1 indicates perfect smoothing among firm businesses.

FCF is defined as operating cash flow minus cash dividends minus capital expenditures. Operating cash flow is defined as the net cash receipts and disbursements resulting from the operations of the firm, and is the sum of funds from operations, funds from/used for other operating activities (which accounts for changes in working capital), and extraordinary items, as per the Thomson database.
The ratio of variable compensation over total CEO compensation for a given year, indicating the extent to which the salary of the CEO is contingent upon some measure of firm performance.
A dichotomous measure for CEO stock options: 1 when the CEO had stock options in a given year and 0 otherwise.
The percentage of the firm's stock held by the CEO in a given year.
The share of stock owned by the largest owner in the given year.

The proportion of independent directors, that is, outside non-CEO directors; outside directors are directors who are not employees of the firm. CEOs in other French companies were excluded from outside directors because, when an outside board director serves concurrently as a CEO for another firm, he or she may be less inclined to intervene independently on behalf of the focal firm's shareholders.
A dummy indicating whether the chairman and CEO positions are split (value of 1) or not (0).

The yearly change in shareholder return, which is measured as the firm's stock price at the end of the year minus the firm's stock price at the beginning of the year plus dividends, divided by the firm's stock price at the beginning of the year.

Excess value compares a firm's value to its imputed value, that is, the sum of the values of the firm's businesses, if each of its businesses operated as a stand-alone, single-business firm. Each business sale is multiplied by the median sales multiplier of all publicly traded single-business firms available in the Thomson database in the corresponding two-digit SIC industry in a given year; the sales multiplier is the median of the ratio of total capital over sales for all single-business firms in the corresponding two-digit SIC industry. Excess value is defined as the log of the ratio of firm value to its imputed value; a negative value implies that the firm destroys value (trades at a discount) and a positive value implies that it creates value (trades at a premium), with values ranging between -2.31 and 2.71.
NOT_A_CONSTRUCT_CONTROL

variable_name: Interest alignment devices (variable pay, options, ownership)
description: Three interest alignment devices are used: CEO variable compensation (ratio of variable compensation to total CEO compensation), a dummy for whether the CEO held stock options in the year, and CEO ownership (percentage of the firm's stock held by the CEO). Each enters the model separately and interacts with free cash flow.

variable_name: Control devices (ownership concentration, independent directors, non-duality)
description: Two control devices are examined: ownership concentration, the share of stock owned by the largest owner in the given year, and board independence, captured by the proportion of independent (outside non-CEO) directors and by a dummy for chairman/CEO non-duality (1 if the positions are split). Each device enters the model separately and interacts with free cash flow.

A survey question asking whether the firm had increased, decreased, or not changed its use of outsourcing since the beginning of the liberalization program 5 years earlier. Responses were coded +1 if outsourcing was increased, -1 if outsourcing was decreased, and 0 if no change. Of the 163 respondents, 46 asserted that they had increased their use of outsourcing, while only 11 claimed that they had decreased it and 106 reported no change.
time_window: since the beginning of the liberalization program, about 5 years before the 1996 survey

description: The dependent variable in the logistic regression, modeled as a binary variable of whether or not the firm had increased its level of outsourcing. The authors coded it as binary because Hypotheses 2-5 do not predict that firms would decrease their level of outsourcing from the previous period.
Respondents were asked to what extent the market reforms had increased the flexibility of their labor policies, responding on a Likert scale. The average response was 4.90.
Respondents were asked whether the reduction of tariffs and other reforms had reduced the cost of importing inputs. Fifty-three of the firms responded in the affirmative.

A 7-point Likert scale question in which individuals were asked to what extent the lowering of inflation had a positive impact on their business; the higher the score, the more positive the impact. The average was 5.66.
Takes on the value of 1 if the firm was selling to MNEs in Argentina in 1995 and 0 if it was not. Forty-three firms met the criteria.

Technological application diversity consists of the number of application domains in which the firm is involved or to which it applies its technological resources in each year, as derived from all the available secondary sources. It distinguishes nine technological application domains: equipment for research, animal health, human food, vegetal production, human health, cosmetics, animal food, environment, and other. Values range theoretically from 1 to 9, with larger (smaller) values indicating greater diversification (specialization) by the firm.
time_window: each year; lagged one year as an independent variable

description: Exploitation alliance is a dichotomous variable that indicates whether the firm has developed an exploitation alliance with at least one of the 10 biggest companies in Europe in its activity domain (e.g., pharmaceutical, veterinary, agrofood). It was coded as 1 when an alliance exploited the biotech firm's resources (clinical tests, commercialization, promotion, distribution) and 0 otherwise.
time_window: each year; lagged one year as an independent variable

description: Articles refers to the yearly number of scientific articles published per firm during the study period and thus represents the production of new ideas and knowledge by firms. Publication data came from the Science Citation Index (SCI) and the Biotech Citation Index (CD-ROM BCI); all publications from the French biotech firms in the SCI database were downloaded and addresses were used to discard homonymous names of firms from other countries. When used as an explanatory variable in the models testing Hypotheses 4 and 5, article t-1 refers to the one-year lagged value of the logged number of articles.

Patent uses data drawn from the OST/OEB database to record the number of new U.S. and European patents owned by a biotech firm in each year. When used as an explanatory variable in the models testing Hypotheses 4 and 5, patent t-1 refers to the one-year lagged value of the logged number of patents.

The authors define performance as the return on sales for each firm averaged over a two-year window. The data were gleaned from firms' compulsory annual tax declarations, collected by the Bank of France and the French Ministry of Industry and accessible via the DIANE database. Traditional firm-specific financial ratios were adopted as performance measures because the vast majority of French biotechnology firms have not gone public, so market value measures could not be used.

Service orientation is one of two binary variables used to characterize a biotech firm's strategic orientation, covering activities such as in vivo and in vitro tests, preclinical and clinical tests, transgenic models, monoclonal antibodies, and consulting activity. To measure this variable the authors relied on the secondary data sources and kept it stable over time, because some observation points were missing.

Research orientation is one of two binary variables used to characterize a biotech firm's strategic orientation, covering producing innovation related to new drugs and production processes. To measure this variable the authors relied on the secondary data sources and kept it stable over time, because some observation points were missing.

An index that encompasses multiple measures of MFO size; the authors generated factor scores that reflect the size of each MFO in the analysis. Exploratory factor analysis verified that the size, financial performance, and transparency indicators load onto three distinct factors, and a confirmatory factor analysis with maximum likelihood estimation confirmed the three-factor solution. The size indicators are the number of employees, total assets, and number of offices.

An index that encompasses multiple measures of MFO financial performance; the authors generated factor scores that reflect the financial performance of each MFO in the analysis, based on exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis showing that the size, performance, and transparency indicators load onto three distinct factors. The financial performance indicators are return on assets, operational self-sufficiency, and the write-off ratio.

The inflation-adjusted logged amount of capital in U.S. dollars acquired by a focal MFO from commercial funders in a specific year, constructed from the MIX funding database. In cases in which an MFO did not receive any loan dollars from a commercial funder, the value was set to '1' prior to logging.

The inflation-adjusted logged amount of capital in U.S. dollars acquired by a focal MFO from public funders in a specific year, constructed from the MIX funding database. In cases in which an MFO did not receive any loan dollars from a public funder, the value was set to '1' prior to logging.

Country-level measure based on data compiled by the PRS Group's International Country Risk Guide, comprising 12 measures that capture the degree of political stability: government stability, socioeconomic conditions, investment profile, internal conflict, external conflict, corruption, military in politics, religious tensions, law and order, ethnic tensions, democratic accountability, and bureaucracy quality. The variable is measured on a 100-point scale with higher values indicating lower uncertainty, and was reverse-coded so higher values denote greater uncertainty. To test the hypotheses, it was interacted with MFO size and financial performance using mean-centered values.

Country-level measure reflecting a country's ability to meet its commercial and trade debt obligations, based on data compiled by the PRS Group's International Country Risk Guide. It is constructed as a 50-point scale and includes five components: foreign debt as a percentage of GDP, foreign debt service as a percentage of exports, current account as a percentage of exports of goods and services, net international liquidity as months of import cover, and exchange rate stability. The variable was reverse-coded, and was interacted with MFO size and financial performance using mean-centered values.

Superficial similarity was manipulated in the 2X2 within-subject design by varying descriptive elements of the technology: where the technology was first developed, who its first users were, what materials its developers worked with, and what object(s)/service(s) its developers produced with the technology, while holding the target market descriptions constant. Each participant evaluated one scenario in each cell of the design, so every participant was exposed to both high and low superficial similarity. The scenarios were built from documented cases of technology transfer.

Structural similarity was operationalized through variations in the capabilities of the technology—what it could and could not do—holding the market descriptions constant. Each participant evaluated one scenario in each cell of the design, so every participant was exposed to both high and low structural similarity. The scenarios were built from documented cases of technology transfer.

A five-item measure capturing participants' level of certainty that a scenario does (or does not) constitute a potential opportunity, with three items capturing fit and two items capturing feasibility. Participants answered on a nine-point scale anchored on the left by "NO, certainly not" and on the right by "YES, certainly," so answers to the left correspond to beliefs that a scenario is not an opportunity and answers to the right to beliefs that it is, while the midpoint indicates uncertainty. Item-total correlations ranged from .73 to .89 and Cronbach's alpha was .94 for sample 1.
scale: nine-point scale anchored by "NO, certainly not" and "YES, certainly"

description: Participants were asked to state their intent to "start another new firm within the next five years," answered on a scale from 1, "I certainly will not," to 9, "I certainly will." A single item was used because the construct is unidimensional, clear to respondents, and sufficiently narrow, and because data from other studies supported the item's validity and reliability.
scale: 1, "I certainly will not," to 9, "I certainly will"

description: Following each opportunity scenario, participants reported their prior knowledge of (1) the technology presented and (2) the scientific and engineering principles underpinning the technology. Participants answered each question on a scale anchored at 1, "minimal knowledge," and 7, "considerable knowledge." Strong correlations between the items targeting the same dimension justified the creation of average scores.

Following each opportunity scenario, participants reported their prior knowledge of (1) the market of interest and (2) the problems affecting this market and current solutions to this problem. Participants answered each question on a scale anchored at 1, "minimal knowledge," and 7, "considerable knowledge." Strong correlations between the items targeting the same dimension justified the creation of average scores.

The same manipulation as in sample 1: superficial similarity was varied through the technology's descriptive elements (where it was developed, its first users, the materials its developers worked with, and the outputs produced) while market descriptions were held constant. Each participant evaluated one scenario per cell of the 2X2 design. Scenarios were built from documented cases of technology transfer.

The same manipulation as in sample 1: structural similarity was varied through the capabilities of the technology—what it could and could not do—holding the market descriptions constant. Each participant evaluated one scenario per cell of the 2X2 design. Scenarios were built from documented cases of technology transfer.

The same five-item measure of certainty that a scenario does (or does not) constitute a potential opportunity, with three items capturing fit and two items capturing feasibility. Participants answered on a nine-point scale anchored on the left by "NO, certainly not" and on the right by "YES, certainly." Cronbach's alpha was .93 for sample 2.
scale: nine-point scale anchored by "NO, certainly not" and "YES, certainly"

description: The same single item asking respondents to state their intent to "start another new firm within the next five years," answered on a scale from 1, "I certainly will not," to 9, "I certainly will."
scale: 1, "I certainly will not," to 9, "I certainly will"

description: Following each scenario, participants reported their prior knowledge of (1) the technology presented and (2) the scientific and engineering principles underpinning the technology, each on a scale anchored at 1, "minimal knowledge," and 7, "considerable knowledge," and average scores were created for the dimension.

Following each scenario, participants reported their prior knowledge of (1) the market of interest and (2) the problems affecting this market and current solutions to this problem, each on a scale anchored at 1, "minimal knowledge," and 7, "considerable knowledge," and average scores were created for the dimension.

A multi-item survey scale measuring the innovation strategy construct of the theoretical model. Items were selected from the review of the manufacturing SME innovation literature and were rated by one respondent per firm on the survey instrument that was designed and pilot tested for this study. A confirmatory factor analysis was conducted to check structural validity, using a factor loading threshold to remove the construct's weak indicators.

A multi-item survey scale measuring the formal structure construct of the theoretical model, drawn from the reviewed manufacturing SME innovation literature and administered to one respondent per firm. Its structural validity was checked with a confirmatory factor analysis in which weak indicators were removed, leaving the retained items with high loadings.

A multi-item survey scale measuring the customer and supplier relationships construct of the theoretical model, administered to one respondent per firm. The construct was validated through content, structural and criterion validity checks, with a confirmatory factor analysis used to remove weak indicators.

A multi-item survey scale measuring the innovation culture construct, which the authors describe as consisting of soft items. Items cover rewards, informal meetings and knowledge sharing, as well as experimentation and teamwork. The scale was administered to one respondent per firm and its indicators were retained in the confirmatory factor analysis.

A multi-item survey scale measuring the technological capabilities construct of the theoretical model, administered to one respondent per firm. The scale's structural validity was checked with a confirmatory factor analysis that removed weak indicators and retained the remaining items.

The dependent construct, developed according to Venkatraman and Ramanujam's (1986) organizational performance framework, consisting of several dimensions of business and operational performance as outlined in Figure 1. It covers product configuration, new product success, speed to market, waste reduction, market opportunities, delivery performance, product innovations, work methods and processes, and quality.

Site specificity was operationalized as the distance in miles between the supplier plant (manufacturing the highest volume component) and the automaker's small and midsize passenger car plants. Greater site specificity is presumed when a supplier plant is located 50 miles from an automaker plant, compared to a supplier plant located 500 miles from an automaker plant. On objective questions such as plant distance, suppliers and purchasing agents were asked the same question, and purchasing agent responses were used only if the supplier did not respond.

Physical asset specificity (PHYSICAL) was operationalized as the percentage of the supplier's total capital investments which would have to be scrapped if the supplier were prohibited from conducting any future business with the automaker, estimated by supplier respondents; specificity was assumed to increase with the percentage of capital investment which could not be redeployed. Because some suppliers sold the majority of their output to the automaker while others sold only a small percentage, an adjusted measure (PHYSICAL/SALES) was created by dividing the percentage of total capital equipment that was nonredeployable by the percentage of the supplier's total sales which went to that particular automaker.
scale: ratio of nonredeployable capital investment to sales share

description: The annual 'man days' that the supplier and automaker spent in face-to-face contact in 1991, covering contact between supplier sales and engineering personnel and automaker purchasing and engineering personnel. Days of contact were calculated by having the supplier's sales VP identify the number of sales people that worked directly with the particular automaker and the average number of days per week that the typical salesperson would spend in a face-to-face meeting with automaker personnel; engineering VPs provided the same information for engineers. Total man days of contact was divided by the supplier's sales (in millions of dollars) to the automaker to normalize for the volume of exchange (FACE/SALES).
scale: man days of contact divided by sales in millions of dollars

description: The average number of colocated or 'guest' engineers; greater human asset specialization is expected when more engineers are colocated and completely dedicated to a particular customer. To normalize for the volume of exchange, the number of guest engineers was divided by the supplier's sales (in millions) to the automaker (GUEST/SALES).
scale: number of guest engineers divided by sales in millions of dollars

description: An overall measure of information sharing was developed by averaging the scores on the five information-sharing questions. Supplier respondents reported the extent to which they shared confidential information (TRUST) and information on their production costs (PCOST), and the extent to which they received information and assistance from the automaker to lower production costs (COSTASST), improve quality (QUALASST), and improve delivery and inventory management (DELASST). Each item was answered on a Likert scale (1 = Not at all, 7 = To a very great extent).
scale: 1 = Not at all to 7 = To a very great extent

description: The 3-year (1990-92) weight average defects (problems) per 100 vehicles as reported in J.D. Power & Associates New Car Initial Quality Studies. Fewer defects indicate higher product quality. The performance measure of quality is for the automaker (production network) as a whole, not for each supplier.

The average number of months between a major model change for each automaker's top selling models (in 1992 units) in five car sizes/classes. Shorter cycle times indicate faster new product development. The performance measure of new model cycle time is for the automaker (production network) as a whole, not for each supplier.

The buffer stock between an upstream supplier and downstream assembler is the sum of the supplier's finished goods and the assembler's raw materials inventory.
