Supplier inventory costs were measured as the ratio of finished goods inventory to sales (average 1982-91) and automaker inventory costs were measured as the ratio of raw materials to sales (average 1982-1991). For U.S. automakers and suppliers, which only report total inventories, the ratio of total inventories to sales was used.

Automaker profitability (AUTOROA) was measured as the 10-year average pretax return on assets from 1982 to 1991. Supplier profitability (SUPPROA) was measured as the 5-year average pretax ROA from 1988 to 1992.

Each supplier was ranked on each of the three specificity measures (site, physical, and human), which were then equally weighted to create an overall specialization rank for each supplier. This overall specificity ranking was then correlated to automaker and supplier profitability using Spearman's r.

'Pioneer' was measured by a dummy variable equal to 1 if the firm was the first entrant to introduce the semi-submersible rig into that national market, 0 otherwise. A firm could be a pioneer in one market and a later-entrant in another. Entry dates, pioneers and later-entrants were identified from annual rig data.

Number of other markets in which entrant had been a pioneer prior to entry in this market. Entry dates and pioneers across national markets in the annual rig data were used to count prior pioneering experience.
time_window: prior to entry in the focal market

description: Entrant's share of the national market in 1984, measured by the number of semi-submersible rigs in a national market owned by an entrant divided by the total number of semi-submersible rigs in that market. The number of rigs was the most relevant measure of economic activity because drilling firm revenue does not have a direct relationship with actual oil found or produced. In the model that includes succumbed entrants, entrants who had withdrawn from the market by 1984 are assigned a 0 for Market Share instead of being treated as missing values.

Measured by the coefficient of variation of the residuals from the regressions used to measure trend growth. Trend growth follows Boyd's (1990) measure of munificence: the regression coefficient from regressing time against industry value added (and separately against industry production) for the 10 years prior to the survey, divided by the mean value of industry value added (respectively production) over those 10 years. The final dimension score was obtained by weighting the indicators with their factor loadings from a principal component analysis and standardizing them.

Computed as the autocorrelation coefficient of the residuals of the regression used to estimate the trend in industry growth, multiplied by -1 so that higher scores reflect higher rates of change. A positive autocorrelation coefficient corresponds to a long and smooth wave (a low rate of change), while a negative coefficient corresponds to a sawtooth series with many changes in direction (a high rate of change). The final dimension score was obtained by weighting the indicators with their factor loadings and standardizing them.

Based on the OECD industry-level input-output tables, input heterogeneity was computed as 1 minus the Herfindahl index of the value of an industry's purchases from all other industries, and output heterogeneity as 1 minus the Herfindahl index of the value of that industry's sales to all other industries. All scores were calculated for 2002 and these were subtracted from the scores for 2006 to capture the relative change in the heterogeneity of inputs and outputs. The final dimension score was obtained by weighting the indicators with their factor loadings and standardizing them.

Combines two Herfindahl indices. The first is the sum of the squared market share of each individual firm in the industry, based on employment figures obtained from the LISA database, ranging between 0 (perfect competition) and 1 (perfect monopoly). The second captures how evenly the economic activities in an industry are distributed over geographical space: establishments and employees per industry were aggregated to the NUTS-2 regional level (40 regions in the Netherlands) and a regional Herfindahl index was calculated. The final dimension score was obtained by weighting the indicators with their factor loadings and standardizing them.

Computed by dividing the number of time-bound alliances by the overall number of alliances in the firm's portfolio, yielding a measure ranging from 0 (all open-ended) to 1 (all time-bound). In the second survey wave respondents were asked whether their firm was currently engaged in a strategic alliance, in how many alliances it was currently participating, whether an ex ante termination date had been agreed upon at the time of alliance formation for any of them, and if so how many were characterized by such a priori time boundaries. By definition the measure could only be calculated for SMEs with at least one alliance, reducing the sample size from 1,137 to 839 SMEs.

The number of current alliances in the firm's portfolio for which an ex ante termination date had been agreed upon at the time of alliance formation, reported in the second survey wave. Analyzed as a count variable in a seemingly unrelated negative binomial regression together with the number of open-ended alliances. This second measure of the dependent variable allows the full sample of 1,137 SMEs, including those without any strategic alliance, to be retained.

The number of current alliances in the firm's portfolio for which no ex ante termination date had been agreed upon at the time of alliance formation, reported in the second survey wave. Analyzed as a count variable in the seemingly unrelated negative binomial model estimated jointly with the number of time-bound alliances on the full sample of 1,137 SMEs.

Dependence was constructed from facility-level toxic chemical release data that were aggregated at the firm-state level. A firm's dependence on a state is its total pounds of toxic chemical releases in that state divided by the firm's total pounds of chemical releases in all states. The measure is intended to reflect enacted dependence, because toxic releases indicate the environmental intensity of the firm's operations in a state and because regulators, the media, and SMOs attend to these data.

Corporate political activity was measured as the total donations to candidates or political parties in a state by a firm. The measure includes contributions made directly by the firm and contributions from its political action committee (PAC).
time_window: same year as the outcome; independent variables lagged by one year (t-1)

description: National media tenor was measured with the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance for each firm in a given year. An article was coded as positive (negative) if 80% or more of its content was positive (negative), with content analysis performed using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count software. The measure was reverse-coded so that higher values reflected more negative tenor. Articles about each firm were searched in The Wall Street Journal using keywords such as 'environment,' 'pollution,' and 'habitat destruction.'
time_window: each firm in a given year; lagged by one year (t-1)

description: Local media tenor was constructed using the same method that was employed for national media tenor. The authors used the NewsBank database to search a major newspaper for each state (e.g., the Tampa Bay Times) that was more state oriented rather than nationally oriented in scope.
time_window: each firm in a given year; lagged by one year (t-1)

description: SMO resources was measured as the income received by environmental SMOs headquartered in a state scaled by the state's population. The authors focused on environmental nonprofits within each state because many SMO effects are inherently local.
time_window: each year; lagged by one year (t-1)

description: TMT turnover was measured as the number of executives who left each year divided by the number of TMT members at the beginning of that year. The authors did not correct for normal retirement, because the theory does not differentiate among types of turnover.
time_window: each year; lagged by one year (t-1)

description: Gubernatorial and legislative turnover were each created by dividing the number of newly elected officials by the total number of each state's offices. Politician turnover was calculated as the simple average of gubernatorial and legislative turnover.
time_window: lagged to the prior election cycle

description: The difference between a fund's achieved risk-adjusted performance and the external social performance aspiration. The aspiration is the mean risk-adjusted return of the external referent group, i.e., other funds outside the firm and within the same fund category, so the measure is the fund's risk-adjusted returns minus its external social aspiration. It is modeled as a single continuous variable and lagged by four months to alleviate simultaneity.

The difference between the fund's achieved risk-adjusted performance and an internal social performance aspiration. The aspiration is the mean monthly risk-adjusted performance of the internal reference group of funds, i.e., other funds inside the same firm and within the same fund category. It is modeled as a single continuous variable and lagged by four months.

Measured as the frequency with which funds trade their stocks, indicating the percentage of a fund's holdings that have changed over the past year, bought and sold by the manager. It is derived from the CRSP database and calculated annually as a ratio of the fund's total sales or purchases (excluding cash) and the fund's average monthly assets during the year, with higher values indicating greater change to a fund's portfolio. The CRSP measure was logged to eliminate outliers.

Computed as the Herfindahl Index of security concentration, defined as the sum of the squared weights of each stock in the fund's portfolio; the index equals 100 if a fund owns only one common stock and an equally weighted portfolio of N securities has an index of 1/N. To the extent that increasing concentration may indicate risk, the measure is the absolute value of changes in the index, using a three-month window.

Measured as the absolute value of changes in a fund's sales loads, the primary one-time fees paid directly by investors, over a three-month window. Because the SEC does not limit the sales load charged by the fund, managers hold considerable discretion over setting the load percentage.

Market beta, a standard indicator of a fund's portfolio systematic risk in relation to the market, derived by estimating the linear regression of the capital asset pricing model of a time series of returns on a given fund and the returns on the market portfolio, typically represented by the return on the S&P 500. Regressions were estimated using rolling windows of the past 12 months of data, and changes in market beta were calculated over a moving three-month window.
time_window: rolling past 12 months; changes over a three-month window

description: Financial risk specific to individual securities held in the fund portfolio and not correlated with overall market risk, measured as the standard deviation of return residuals from the market regression used to estimate market beta. Regressions were estimated using rolling windows of the past 12 months of data, and three-month time spans were used to account for changes in the standard deviation of residuals.
time_window: rolling past 12 months; changes over three-month spans

description: Monthly volatility of historical fund returns, the standard deviation of returns calculated over the 12 months preceding a given month, with higher values indicating greater total risk of the fund's portfolio. Because returns may reflect overall market volatility, risk-adjusted returns were calculated as the difference between the fund's return and the market return (the S&P 500); changes in the standard deviation of risk-adjusted returns were computed in three-month time spans.
time_window: past 12 months; changes over three-month spans

description: Change in the average portfolio stock size quintile over a moving three-month window, following the methodology of past research. Each stock listed on U.S. exchanges was grouped into size quintiles and received a score between 1 and 5, with stocks with the highest market capitalization receiving a score of 1 and stocks with the lowest market capitalization receiving a score of 5. Higher values of the measure indicate greater amounts of risky change taken by fund managers.
scale: 1 to 5 quintile scores (change in average score)

description: Change in the average portfolio stock growth quintile over a moving three-month window. Each stock was grouped into quintiles according to its book-to-market ratio and received a score between 1 and 5, with stocks with the highest book-to-market ratio receiving a score of 1 and stocks with the lowest book-to-market ratio receiving a score of 5. Higher values indicate greater amounts of risky change taken by fund managers.
scale: 1 to 5 quintile scores (change in average score)

description: Patent-based measure of a firm's specialization in certain technical domains. The computer industry covers 16 technical domains classified by the USPTO at the three-digit level. To determine the patent stock of a firm for a certain year, the application date of successful patents is used. Knowledge specialization is calculated by the maximum number of patents in any one technical class weighted by the total number of a firm's patents.
time_window: one-year lag prior to the event year

description: For each pair of firms, patent data from 1984 to 1997 are collected with a five-year moving window, and the patent stock of both firms is compared up to that particular year's alliance or acquisition announcement. Following Ahuja (2000a) and Rosenkopf and Almeida (2003), the distribution of a firm's patents across the 16 technical domains is constructed and the proportion of the firm's patents falling within each technology class is computed. The technical distance is the Euclidean distance between a pair of firms in this technological space. The measure ranges from zero (firms with identical patent profiles) to 1.4 (no overlap in patent activities).
time_window: five-year moving window; measured until the year of the announcement, one-year lag

description: Network status is measured using Bonacich's (1987) eigenvector centrality in firms' industry networks. The status distance is computed as the absolute difference between two firms' eigenvector centrality. Alliance relationships between the 187 firms are constructed for each year from 1985 to 1997, with a five-year moving window used to capture the previous network and minimize left-censoring.
time_window: five-year moving window; one-year lag prior to the event year

description: Measured with Bonacich's (1987) eigenvector centrality in the firm's industry network (Baum et al., 2005; Shipilov and Li, 2008). Alliance relationships between the 187 firms are constructed for each year from 1985 to 1997. A five-year moving window is used to capture the previous network and minimize the potential left-censoring problem.
time_window: five-year moving window; one-year lag prior to the event year

description: The authors adopt Burt's (1992) measure of constraint, which taps the extent to which a firm's network is directly or indirectly concentrated in a single contact; a network concentrated in one contact means fewer structural holes. The index uses p_ij, the proportion of i's relations invested in contact j, and the total in parentheses is the proportion of i's relations that are directly or indirectly invested in the connection with contact j; C_ij is summed across contacts j to obtain the network constraint index C for each focal firm. Following Soda et al. (2004), the value of constraint is multiplied by -1 to capture structural holes.
time_window: five-year moving window; one-year lag prior to the event year

description: Dependent variable for the first condition, a binary decision (1 = partnering, 0 = no partnering). It captures whether a firm seeks external resources through interfirm linkages, given firm-level characteristics, dyadic difference, and network attributes.
Dependent variable for the second condition, a binary decision (1 = acquisition, 0 = alliance). It is used for the choice firms make when they do take actions to build interfirm linkages.

Respondents were asked to report on a scale of one (strongly disagree) to five (strongly agree) the extent to which the company explicitly emphasizes six items of rational decision-making. The scale is adapted from Goll and Zeitz (1991) and Goll and Sambharya (1995) and reflects a conceptualization of rationality that goes beyond formal systematic planning, viewing rationality as a strategy-making mode. Cronbach's alpha is 0.85.

Following Dess and Beard (1984) and Rasheed and Prescott (1992), munificence was measured as the growth rate in the value of shipments, operationalized as the regression slope coefficient of the value of shipments for the period 1975-84. Munificence was calculated using industry-level data since it is an industry-level construct, with the data obtained from the Census of Manufactures.

Dynamism was measured as the variability in the value of shipments and operationalized as the standard error of the regression slope coefficient of the value of shipments divided by the industry mean for the period 1975-84. This operationalization corresponds to Milliken's (1987) notion of state uncertainty. Dynamism was calculated using industry-level data since it is an industry-level construct, with the data obtained from the Census of Manufactures.

Return on assets is net income from continuing operations, excluding extraordinary items, divided by assets. The average ROA was computed for 1985-86 to avoid the possibility of erroneous inferences based on a single year's profit performance. The data were collected from Business Week and Standard and Poor's Stock Reports.

Return on sales is net income from continuing operations, excluding extraordinary items, divided by sales. It is used alongside return on assets as a measure of firm performance. The data were collected from Business Week and Standard and Poor's Stock Reports.

Coded by examining press releases at the time of the acquisition to determine if the acquirer intended to integrate the new unit's R&D activities with the parent's R&D activities. Statements indicating intentions to keep the new R&D units independent, such as 'no plans to integrate R&D operations,' and statements indicating integration, such as 'will involve relocation of the 500 R&D employees,' were clear. The variable was coded one if the acquirer's stated intentions were to integrate the R&D activities of the acquired company.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: Calculated as the pre-minus-post difference between two percentage standings, so that larger scores indicate larger loss of status. Preacquisition status is the percentage of all productive inventors in the acquired firm whose preacquisition productivity (number of patents in t-4 through t) was lower than that of the focal inventor; the inventor's percentage standing was similarly calculated relative to the preacquisition productivity of all inventors in the acquired and acquiring firms combined. For example, an inventor who was most productive among a preacquisition group of ten inventors had a status of 90%; if he sits at the middle of the combined groups, at the 50th percentile, his loss of relative standing is 40.

Built from the USPTO's system of three-digit classes for assigning patents (patents can be assigned to more than one class). The authors first identified, for each acquiring firm, the top three classes in which its inventors had patented over the five years prior to the acquisition. An acquired inventor's divergence score reflects how few of those same classes she had patented in during the same period, ranging from three if the inventor had patented in none of the acquiring firm's top three classes to zero if she had patented in all three.
time_window: five years prior to the acquisition

description: Measured as the average number of coauthors on the inventor's patent applications in the five years prior to being acquired. The greater the inventor's dependence on others, the greater the score on this measure of social embeddedness.
time_window: five years prior to the acquisition

description: Identifies those inventors who continued to patent at all with the newly combined company, as indicated by one or more patent applications in any of the first five years following the acquisition. The variable was coded zero for those who ceased patenting at the firm and one for those who continued patenting. This outcome reflects an unobserved combination of involuntary departure, voluntary departure, and output reduced to zero.
time_window: first five years following the acquisition

description: For each known survivor the authors counted the total number of patent applications over the five years following acquisition. Successful patent applications, not issuances, were examined to indicate inventor productivity.

For each known survivor the authors calculated the sum of citation-weighted patent applications over the five years following acquisition; the weight for each patent was the number of citations it received in the five years following its application date. This measure incorporates an indication of each patent's technical significance.

A residualized measure of press mentions. The authors searched Lexis-Nexis for yearly article counts in which the name of a team appeared in the text and in which either the heading or the leading paragraph contained the term 'Formula One'. Status was measured by the residuals obtained by regressing press mentions on the total points scored by a team for each yearly cross-section, and these residuals were standardized by year to have a mean equal to 5 and a standard deviation equal to 1. To avoid issues of causality, status was lagged by a year when it was included in models.

Team status advantage equaled 0 when team status was lower than engine supplier status and equaled the status difference when team status was higher than engine supplier status. The status difference was computed by subtracting the status of the engine supplier from the status of the race team, and engine supplier status was the average status of all the race teams the engine supplier supplied during the previous racing season. Engine supplier status was normalized by year to have a mean equal to 5 and a standard deviation equal to 1.
time_window: team status lagged one year; engine supplier status from the previous racing season

description: Team status disadvantage equaled 0 when team status was higher than engine supplier status and equaled the status difference when team status was lower than engine supplier status. For ease of interpretation, this last variable was reverse-coded. It is built from the same difference between team status and the year-normalized status of the engine supplier.
time_window: team status lagged one year; engine supplier status from the previous racing season

description: The authors collapsed engine modifications and engine redesigns, considering the occurrence of either as a relevant remedial action, and created a dichotomous variable taking the value 1 if in a given race a team had at least one car with a modified or redesigned engine and 0 otherwise. The time of the event is the date of the race.
Effort was measured as the total number of engine modifications/redesigns a supplier had provided to a team during a season.

The product quality of an F1 racing team was measured as the total points it had earned in the constructor championship at the end of each season. This is the sum of the points earned in each race of a season by a team's two cars.

The number of engine failures a team had experienced in the current racing season up to the present race. This variable not only controlled for current engine quality, but also tested Hypotheses 1 and 2 when interacted with the status variables.
time_window: current racing season up to the present race

description: The total number of retirements a team experienced during a racing season caused by engine failures.

Carburetors were the low-modularity product of the study. Carburetor design and production required customization to and of ignition systems, fuel systems, power trains, and other sections of automobiles, and carburetors were complex, unstandardized goods throughout the study period. The design and manufacturing processes required a considerable degree of give and take between supplier and buyer.

Clutches had achieved high modularity and become relatively standard by the beginning of the period. The relatively simple single-plate clutch quickly became the choice of most automobile manufacturers and required little customization for specific automobile models. Once established by about 1919, the basic principles of the clutch remained unchanged for many years.

We measured the duration of a supplier's relationship with an assembler as the cumulative years it supplied the given component for at least one model produced by that assembler. We reset this count to 0 if there was a span of greater than five consecutive years during which the supplier did not supply a component for at least one model produced by that buyer, which captured the effect of the decay of relation-specific routines and trust. In the case of an acquisition by either a supplier or an assembler, we based our calculations on the acquiring firm. Maximum duration of customer relationship recorded the longest single relationship a supplier had with any current customer.

We measured the duration of a supplier's relationship with an assembler as the cumulative years it supplied the given component for at least one model produced by that assembler. We reset this count to 0 if there was a span of greater than five consecutive years during which the supplier did not supply a component for at least one model produced by that buyer, which captured the effect of the decay of relation-specific routines and trust. In the case of an acquisition by either a supplier or an assembler, we based our calculations on the acquiring firm. Maximum duration of customer relationship recorded the longest single relationship a supplier had with any current customer.

We measured the current autonomy of a supplier as the ratio of the number of assemblers to which it sold to the mean number of suppliers its customers had. The variable captured the relative dependence of the supplier on its current buyers: the more alternatives available to a firm, the less dependent it was on any given partner, and the power of firm A over firm B depended on the difference between A's dependence on B and B's dependence on A. Autonomy was measured using ratios because it is an inherently relative concept.

We measured the current autonomy of a supplier as the ratio of the number of assemblers to which it sold to the mean number of suppliers its customers had. The variable captured the relative dependence of the supplier on its current buyers: the more alternatives available to a firm, the less dependent it was on any given partner, and the power of firm A over firm B depended on the difference between A's dependence on B and B's dependence on A. Autonomy was measured using ratios because it is an inherently relative concept.

We measured the potential autonomy of a supplier as the ratio of the number of existing assemblers to which it did not sell to the mean number of existing suppliers from which its customers did not buy. This variable captured the relative abilities of a supplier and its buyers to create new ties.

We measured the potential autonomy of a supplier as the ratio of the number of existing assemblers to which it did not sell to the mean number of existing suppliers from which its customers did not buy. This variable captured the relative abilities of a supplier and its buyers to create new ties.

The proportion of a focal supplier's customers that were vertically integrated into production of the component the supplier provided. It was included as a complementary measure of autonomy because an assembler can replace a supplier by vertically integrating production of the component the supplier provided; when this value is high, the supplier has less autonomy.

The proportion of a focal supplier's customers that were vertically integrated into production of the component the supplier provided. It was included as a complementary measure of autonomy because an assembler can replace a supplier by vertically integrating production of the component the supplier provided; when this value is high, the supplier has less autonomy.

We measured customer status according to three categories prominent in the automobile industry during the study period: (1) the major assemblers (Ford, General Motors and, following the acquisition of Dodge, Chrysler); (2) the major independents, which were referred to by that term (e.g., Hudson and Packard); and (3) the minor independents (all others, e.g., Dort and Geronimo). We assigned each assembler to one of the three status categories using Kennedy's (1941) year-by-year commentary. Status was denoted with two dummy variables, medium status (major independents) and high status (major assemblers), relative to low status.
scale: two dummy variables (medium, high) relative to low status

description: We measured customer status according to three categories prominent in the automobile industry during the study period: (1) the major assemblers (Ford, General Motors and, following the acquisition of Dodge, Chrysler); (2) the major independents, which were referred to by that term (e.g., Hudson and Packard); and (3) the minor independents (all others, e.g., Dort and Geronimo). We assigned each assembler to one of the three status categories using Kennedy's (1941) year-by-year commentary. Status was denoted with two dummy variables, medium status (major independents) and high status (major assemblers), relative to low status.
scale: two dummy variables (medium, high) relative to low status

description: We defined supplier failure as a supplier shutting down its production in the automotive carburetor market, and estimated the hazard rate (the instantaneous rate of supplier dissolution) using a piecewise exponential model. Our data were annual, so we updated time-varying covariates each year; we treated all annual spells as right-censored except those that ended with dissolution of the supplier, and we treated dissolutions as occurring midway through the year. Divestitures that occurred during the study period were treated as censoring events.

We defined supplier failure as a supplier shutting down its production in the automotive clutch market, and estimated the hazard rate (the instantaneous rate of supplier dissolution) using a piecewise exponential model. Our data were annual, so we updated time-varying covariates each year; we treated all annual spells as right-censored except those that ended with dissolution of the supplier, and we treated dissolutions as occurring midway through the year. Divestitures that occurred during the study period were treated as censoring events.

variable_name: pure strategy and mixed strategy (combinations of strategy intensity)
description: Strategy choice is characterized jointly by the intensity of commitment to cost leadership and to differentiation. In the analysis a pure strategy is represented by setting one of the strategic choices at the maximum, a raw score of 7 on the Likert scale, and the other at one standard deviation below its mean; the high mixed strategy sets both cost leadership and differentiation to the maximum, a raw score of 7. Performance at these strategy intensities is then predicted at various levels of market orientation.

Intensity of commitment to a cost leadership strategy, computed as the average of seven-point Likert scale ratings from each of the four functions. The survey asked the respondent to indicate the importance of 'to reduce costs' for implementing changes to each function from January 1999 to December 2001. In the analysis the variable was transformed using the zeta-squared transformation within each industry category.

Intensity of commitment to a differentiation strategy, computed as the average of seven-point Likert scale ratings from each of the four functions. The survey asked the respondent to indicate the importance of 'to improve product/service quality' and 'to satisfy customer requirements' for implementing changes to each function from January 1999 to December 2001, and the measure averages the two items. Factor analysis confirmed the two items loaded on one latent variable, and the Cronbach alpha is 0.90. In the analysis the variable was transformed using the zeta-squared transformation within each industry category.

Degree of market orientation, measured with the Heritage Foundation Index of Economic Freedom, which provides a measure of nine characteristics that reflect a country's adherence to free-market principles. The authors used the average scores for 1999-2001, with higher numbers indicating greater economic freedom and thus higher market orientation.

The survey question asked the respondent to indicate the success of changes implemented in each function from January 1999 to December 2001. The authors took the average of the scores for the four functions (quality assurance, human resource management, marketing, and technology) to calculate success of change. Cronbach's alpha of 0.83 for the four items exceeds the minimum acceptable level of 0.70.

variable_name: Equity share of the largest shareholder
description: Equity share of the largest shareholder was measured by the percentage of shares held by the largest owner. It is one of the independent variables in the models. All independent and control variables were lagged by one year.

Assessed using the institutional index developed by the NERI (Fan and Wang, 2006). Appraisals of the regional institutions are made along several dimensions, namely, the relationship between the government and the market, the development of the non-state sector, the factor markets, and the product markets, and the development of market intermediaries and legal environment. Along these dimensions, the NERI provided each of the 31 provinces, municipalities, and autonomous regions a score that captured the progress of institutional development, where a higher score means better institutional development.

Assessed using information disclosed in corporate annual reports. Like previous research on the political connections of Chinese listed firms, the CEO's affiliation with the local government was used as an indication of political connections. CEO political connection is a dummy variable coded as '1' if the CEO is a current or former government officer, or a member of People's Congress or Political Consultative Conference, and '0' otherwise.

The dependent variable was the hazard rate of a firm experiencing a takeover in a particular year. A takeover was defined as a change in a firm's controlling shareholder where the new owner was not the state, and uncompensated administrative transfers between government entities were excluded. Firms that were not subjected to a takeover by the end of the study period were considered right-censored, and if a firm had more than one takeover during the study period the first event was used. The dependent variable was coded as '1' if a firm experienced a takeover in a particular year, and as '0' otherwise.
scale: dummy (1 = takeover in that year, 0 otherwise)

description: A dummy variable coded 0 if the firm has executed projects for the client in the past and coded 1 if it is the first project executed for the client. Repeat clients are treated as a proxy for client-specific capabilities developed by the firm, and the authors expect the sign on this coefficient to be negative. It is one of two ways the study measures client-specific capabilities.

Because the dataset contains multiple projects for each client, the authors estimated a client fixed effect by including a dummy variable for each client. This produces a within-sample estimate of the client-specific effect. Since a single parameter cannot be estimated for the client fixed effects, the authors only examine whether they are jointly significant after controlling for input and project characteristics and time.

Project contribution, revenues minus costs, measured in Indian rupees and recognized on the date of project completion. The authors chose the project level because the firm capabilities they study primarily exist and evolve at the project level, while firm profitability is essentially an aggregate of project-level contribution. The variable is logged and year dummies are included, which removes the inflation and INR-USD exchange rate adjustment factor from the estimated parameters.

The number of in-process defects identified during the project execution phase, normalized by a project size measure (function points) because in-process defects can vary with the size of the project. In-process defects measure defects detected in the product and reflect a firm's software development and management capabilities. The authors expect that lower in-process defects will lead to higher project contribution.

The difference between the actual person-months required to complete the project and the person-months that were initially estimated, normalized by budgeted person-months because effort overrun is likely to vary directly with budgeted person-months. It reflects effort estimation and management capability, and the expected sign on its coefficient is negative. It was entered as levels rather than logs since zero or negative values are possible.

The extent of schedule slippage, that is the delay in project completion date, measured in days and normalized by expected project duration (also measured in days) because the magnitude of slippage varies directly with expected duration. It reflects schedule estimation and management capability. Delays can hurt profitability through contractual penalties for late completion and increased labor costs, and the expected sign on its coefficient is negative.

The announcement date of each M&A deal is coded as t0, and abnormal returns are cumulated over the event window from two days before to two days after the announcement date (t - 2 to t + 2). The event window is the unit around which acquiring and rival firms' returns are measured.

Cumulative abnormal returns for rival firms calculated with a standard market model, with the announcement date coded as t0; daily abnormal returns are summed over the five-day window (-2, +2). Because rival firms in the same industry react to an announcement at the same time, the rivals' CARs are grouped into industry portfolios equal to the average CAR of the individual rival firms in the industry, giving 1,074 industry rival firm portfolios. These portfolio CARs are used as the dependent variable in the regression models.
level: industry rival-firm portfolio per acquisition announcement
time_window: five-day event window (-2, +2); market model parameters estimated from day -130 to day -30

description: For each focal firm's acquisition, acquisition performance is measured with abnormal returns on stock prices (CAR [-2, +2]), calculated with the same market model procedure as for the rival firms. In the main analysis the acquirer firms' CARs are categorized as a binary variable, with positive CARs equal to 1 and negative or zero CARs equal to 0.
scale: binary (1 = positive CAR, 0 = negative or zero CAR)

description: A sales-based Herfindahl index (Hp,t) computed for each industry p in year t and normalized so that the normalized index lies between 0 and 1. A high value of the normalized index indicates high concentration (low competition) in the industry.
time_window: year t of the acquisition announcement

description: Industry relatedness of the target and acquiring firms is measured with the firms' four-digit SIC codes, the most detailed industry information available in the SDC Platinum database. A binary variable classifies acquirer and target firms as related if they have the same four-digit SIC code and unrelated otherwise.
scale: binary (1 = same four-digit SIC code, 0 = otherwise)

description: Binary variable that equals 1 if the firm adopts computerized dispatching technology between 1992 and 1997 and 0 otherwise. It is built from two technology surveys, the TCRP survey and the authors' own 2005 mail survey of taxicab operators in the Dun & Bradstreet business register, which asked about current and past dispatching systems (type and year of adoption). The survey observations were matched to the 1997 Economic Census by zip code or county code and firm size.

Change in the share of vehicles owned by fleet i between 1992 and 1997, i.e. the change in the proportion of taxicabs in the fleet owned by the firm. The variable is continuous and bounded between −1 and 1. It is constructed from Economic Census counts of taxicabs by ownership type (fleet owned versus driver owned) in the two census years.
scale: change in a proportion, bounded between −1 and 1

description: Firm-level expenditures on R&D deflated by total sales, averaged for the period 1976-89. The authors use firm-level intensity for the Japanese companies because line-of-business spending on R&D is difficult to gather, assuming that firm-level spending contributes technological knowledge equally to every line of business. The variable was entered directly in models 1 and 2 to test Hypothesis 1.

Firm-level expenditures on advertising deflated by total sales, averaged for the period 1976-89. Advertising efforts are at the firm level, and each line of business is assumed to benefit from the marketing know-how and brand loyalty created by the centralized advertising. The variable was entered directly in models 1 and 2 to test Hypothesis 1.

Competitive advantage in R&D at the line-of-business level, calculated as Japanese firm-level R&D intensity minus industry-level U.S. R&D intensity for each three-digit line of business. Industry-level R&D intensities of U.S. firms were collected from the COMPUSTAT aggregate file. Used in models 3 and 4 to test Hypothesis 2.

Competitive advantage in advertising at the line-of-business level, calculated as Japanese firm-level advertising intensity minus industry-level U.S. advertising intensity for each three-digit line of business. Industry-level advertising intensities of U.S. firms were collected from the COMPUSTAT aggregate file. Used in models 3 and 4 to test Hypothesis 2.

Sales of a line of business as a proportion of total sales, normalized for each firm by dividing it by the average size of the firm's lines of business to control for level of diversification. For instance, a line accounting for 40 percent of total sales deflated by 30 percent, the average size of that firm's businesses, yields 1.33. Sales during 1976-89 were broken down by businesses using U.S. SIC three-digit categories.

The number of a firm's previous entries at the time of a new entry, constructed from the raw entry data; because of multicollinearity with firm size (r = .81) the authors dropped the firm size variable in favor of this accumulated entry variable. Nonmanufacturing entries were included when calculating the accumulated entry variable. It was one of the time-varying covariates, fixed for the duration of each spell.

Dummy variable for association with a horizontal business group, one of the eight horizontally connected groups (Mitsubishi, Mitsui, Sumitomo, Fuyo, DKB, Sanwa, Tokai, and the Industrial Bank of Japan). Since transfer of experience or learning is possible only when other business group members have made prior investments, the variable was assigned a value of 1 only after some other group member had invested in the United States.
time_window: assigned after prior investment by another group member

description: Dummy variable for association with a vertical business group, a structure centered around a big manufacturing firm (31 major groups, e.g., Hitachi, Matsushita Electric Company, with their suppliers and subcontractors). The variable was assigned a value of 1 only after some other group member had invested in the United States.
time_window: assigned after prior investment by another group member

description: The dependent variable is a hazard rate that denotes the likelihood of a firm's investing in a line of business at a given time. For a line of business with several direct investments, the interval (spell) between investments constituted an observation, and the time elapsed from the last investment, or from 1976, constituted an observation. The model ranks events temporally, and hazard rates are presumed to be log-linear functions of the covariates.

Defined as the number of patients enrolled in a study divided by the enrollment goal for that trial. For each protocol the sponsoring firm sets a common enrollment goal across all sites, and normalizing by that goal allows comparison across trials of varying sizes. The authors note that the value may exceed 100 percent and that the log of this variable is used in all multivariate regressions.

An estimate of the enrollment output achieved per unit of labor, measured as the number of full-time-equivalent study coordinators dedicated to the trial. The numerator (enrollment) is available in the Rapidtrials data. The denominator is calculated by first estimating the number of concurrent trials at the site from the number of FDA registrations submitted by all physician-investigators at that site within 1 year before or after the month the site signed the contract for the trial of interest, then dividing the number of study coordinator FTEs at the site by the number of concurrent trials. The authors note this site average is their best estimate of the administrative resources dedicated to a trial.
time_window: 1 year before or after the month the site signed the trial contract

description: Indicator for a site's level of focus, contrasting sites with dedicated or separate trial businesses (dedicated research centers and plant-within-a-plant sites) with sites that integrate trials with traditional patient care. Unfocused sites (integrated with patient care) are the excluded category in the regressions.

Indicator for dedicated research centers, sites that only conduct clinical trials and are therefore focused at both the firm and divisional level. Unfocused sites are the excluded category in the regressions; the authors compare firm-focused sites with plant-within-a-plant sites to test Hypothesis 3.

Indicator for community-based sites that conduct both clinical trials and traditional patient care but have set up organizational (and sometimes legal) partitions creating distinct business units for each function, i.e., a plant within a plant with divisional focus but no firm focus. Unfocused sites are the excluded category in the regressions.

Scale is defined as the number of FTE study coordinators at each site. The authors argue that the larger the number of study coordinators employed, the greater the number of simultaneous protocols the site can perform.

variable_name: Investigator experience, study coordinator experience, organizational experience
description: Learning is measured at three levels based on the cumulative number of trials completed by the investigator, the study coordinator, and the site as a whole, entered as separate variables in the regressions. These data are self-reported in the pretrial site qualification survey conducted by Rapidtrials.

A composite of four indicators of the CEO's political donation behavior, each divided by the total number across both political parties: the number of donations to Republicans, the dollar value of donations to Republicans, the number of donations to distinct Republican candidates or PACs, and the number of donations in different years to Republicans. The four indicators were averaged to generate a composite score ranging from zero to one, where higher values reflect higher degrees of conservatism (a score of one is extremely conservative). CEOs with no donation data were assigned a score of 0.5.

The same four donation indicators computed at the firm level by aggregating employees, but focusing on donations to Democrats rather than Republicans, with each indicator divided by the total number across both parties. The four indicators were averaged to generate a composite score ranging from zero to one, where higher values reflect higher degrees of organizational liberalism (a score of one is extremely liberal).

A binary variable that took a value of one if the CEO endorsed the Human Rights Campaign letter opposing North Carolina's HB2 (74 CEOs) and zero if not (251 CEOs). Signing the letter was treated as a clear example of liberal activism, as protection and advancement of LGBTQ individuals is a core ideal of liberalism.

Indicator set to 1 if there is a listing in a new product category for the firm in a given year, and 0 otherwise. It is measured at the finest degree of characterization in the CorpTech data, covering 2,681 product categories, so there are multiple observations per firm-year. All specifications include firm fixed effects, year fixed effects and dummies at the level of the 18 sectors.

Market relatedness is set to 1 for potential product market entries where the firm has experience (already offers at least one product) within the same industry though not within the product category; to 0.5 if the firm has experience within the sector though not within the same industry; and to zero if the firm has no experience within the sector at all. It uses proximity within the CorpTech product classification, which reflects output characteristics and commonalities in customers rather than inputs.

The technological profile of a product category is the set of the 421 USPTO patent classes in which two or more firms offering that product have patented in the previous three years, identified using small focused firms active in three or fewer product categories. Relatedness between a firm's patent classes and a product's technological profile is computed from the frequency with which patent classes cite each other; TRij is set to 1 if the firm has a patent in any relevant patent class of the product, and otherwise equals the highest relatedness between the firm's patent portfolio and the product's technological profile.
time_window: previous three years for the product-level technological profile

description: Number of joint ventures and alliances formed by the firm, obtained by matching CorpTech to the Securities Data Company (SDC) Platinum database. The variable is regressed on indicators for years t-2, t-1, t, t+1 and t+2 relative to a new product market entry in a linear probability model, with the sample restricted to firms that make at least one entry.
time_window: years t-2 to t+2 relative to entry

description: Technological relatedness between the firm's patent portfolio and the technological profile of the entering product category, estimated at the firm-category-year level with indicators for years t-2, t-1, t, t+1 and t+2 relative to entry; nonentering product categories within the same firm serve as the comparison. The postentry increase reflects firms directly filing for patents in the technology classes relevant to the entered market.
time_window: years t-2 to t+2 relative to entry

variable_name: Subsample splits proxying access to external technological resources
description: Access to external technological resources is not a single variable. It is proxied by cross-sectional splits of the entry model: top versus bottom half by firm sales, public versus private status, and high versus low technological competency (total number of patents, and maximum patent generality as capacity to absorb new technology), plus sector-by-sector estimates ordered against the perceived strength of external markets for technology (discrete versus complex sectors after the Carnegie Mellon Survey). The market relatedness coefficient is compared across subsamples with z-statistics.

Factor score for explorative innovation strategy obtained by factor analysis of eight Likert-scale items on the objectives for undertaking innovation projects in the last three years, with acceptable Cronbach alpha (0.752). The items were rated from 1 = not important to 5 = very important and asked how important it is for the firm to carry out innovation projects to enter new product-market domains. The variable was centered on its mean before the interaction term was created.

Factor score for exploitative innovation strategy obtained by factor analysis of eight Likert-scale items on the objectives for undertaking innovation projects in the last three years, with acceptable Cronbach alpha (0.807). The items were rated from 1 = not important to 5 = very important and asked how important it is for the firm to carry out innovation projects to improve existing product-market efficiency. The variable was centered on its mean before the interaction term was created.

Group classification using the 'median cut-off' criterion: all firms were ranked in descending order of explorative or exploitative innovation strategy factor scores, and firms in the upper half were classified as explorative or exploitative respectively. A firm was then defined as ambidextrous if it belonged to both the explorative and exploitative group.

variable_name: absolute difference between explorative and exploitative innovation strategies
description: The absolute difference between the firm's explorative and exploitative innovation strategy scores, used as the measure of relative imbalance between the two strategies ('fit as matching').

Self-reported compounded average sales growth rate in the last three years (from 1996 to 1999 with 1996 as the base year), used as the measure of firm performance. Sales growth estimates were chosen because they are more easily available and reliable than profitability estimates from a survey and are a proxy indicator of other dimensions of superior firm performance.

variable_name: standard deviation/mean sales growth rate ratio
description: Group-level dispersion of sales growth rate computed as the group's standard deviation divided by its mean sales growth rate for the four innovation strategy groups defined by the median cut-off criterion (ambidextrous, explorative, exploitative, and no-emphasis). To obtain a formal test, the four standard deviation values were regressed against the four mean sales growth values weighted by group size.

Percentage of total annual sales that consist of new/improved products introduced over the last three years, used as an intermediary variable measuring innovation performance. Natural log of product innovation intensity was used to compensate for skewness.

Percentage of annual production volume using new/improved processes introduced over the last three years, used as an intermediary variable measuring innovation performance. Natural log of process innovation intensity was used to compensate for skewness.

The firm's Gini coefficient of employee compensation divided by the average Gini coefficient of other firms in the same state. The Gini coefficient ranges between 0 (absolute equality) and 1 (absolute inequality), measures half the relative mean difference of the pay of any two employees selected at random from a firm's compensation distribution, and is computed with individuals indexed in nondecreasing order of pay. State is used as the comparison unit because state-specific bar examination requirements limit the competition of firms and the mobility of lawyers to within state lines.
scale: Gini coefficient from 0 (absolute equality) to 1 (absolute inequality); the measure is the firm's Gini divided by the average Gini of other firms in the state

description: Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if individual i was identified as a high performer at time t, that is, if the individual is in the top 10 percent of the residual from an ordinary least squares compensation equation estimated for each person year within the individual's current firm. The compensation equation regresses total taxable compensation on individual characteristics and firm-level characteristics, and includes state, MSA and year dummies. The residual approach identifies individuals who are paid more than others in the same firm with the same age, tenure, education, gender, and race.

Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if individual i was identified as a low performer at time t, that is, if the individual is in the bottom 10 percent of the distribution of the residual from the compensation equation within the individual's current firm. The same compensation residual framework is used as for high performers, so that identification is relative to coworkers with similar observable characteristics.

Dummy variable coded 1 if an individual had changed employment since the previous year and 0 otherwise. For individuals who worked at multiple firms in a given year, the dominant employer, defined as the firm at which the employee earned the most during the year, is used. The data do not permit identifying whether exits were voluntary or involuntary.
time_window: change between the previous year and the focal year

description: Among turnover events only, a dummy variable that takes the value 1 if the change in an employee's dominant employer since the previous year was to a new firm in the data (employee entrepreneurship), and the value 0 if the change in dominant employer since the previous year was to an existing firm (employee mobility). The measure includes not just firm founders but also non-founding employees in the first year.
time_window: change between the previous year and the focal year

variable_name: Market performance (log adjusted market value t+1)
description: Market performance captures the annual change in the market value of the focal firm's common shares. Market value is calculated by multiplying the firm's stock price by the number of common shares outstanding, averaged over the 12 end-of-month values of the calendar year, and adjusted by dividing it by the ratio of the compound S&P 500 market value at year t to the compound S&P 500 market value at the year 1990. The annual change divides the adjusted market value at year t+1 by the adjusted market value at year t and is log-transformed, with all independent variables lagged one year relative to the dependent variable. The algebraic form of the adjustment is not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: annual change from t to t+1; 12 end-of-month values of the calendar year

description: Technology network resources were measured as the mean value of R&D investments of partners in the focal firm's alliance portfolio. Financial data were extracted annually from Compustat for the years 1990-2001 and converted to billion U.S. dollar units. The variable was lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.
time_window: t (lagged one year relative to the dependent variable)

description: Marketing network resources were proxied by the mean value of advertising investments of partners in the focal firm's alliance portfolio. The data come from annual Compustat records, and the variable was lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.
time_window: t (lagged one year relative to the dependent variable)

description: Financial network resources were calculated based on the mean value of cash funds available to partners in the focal firm's alliance portfolio. The data come from annual Compustat records, and the variable was lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.
time_window: t (lagged one year relative to the dependent variable)

description: Human network resources indicated the mean number of employees of partner organizations, reported in 100Ks. The data come from annual Compustat records, and the variable was lagged one year relative to the dependent variable. The authors note that the incorporation of the number of employees also controls for the size of partners in the firm's alliance portfolio.
time_window: t (lagged one year relative to the dependent variable)

description: Network prominence is the percentage of publicly traded partners in the focal firm's alliance portfolio. Partner public status was coded from the alliance records compiled from SDC Platinum and corroborated with other archival sources. The authors assume that publicly traded partners typically play the role of prominent endorsers that are well known to, and frequently appreciated by, the investor community, suppliers, and customers.
time_window: t (lagged one year relative to the dependent variable)

description: Relative profitability measures the mean difference between the return on assets (ROA) of partners in the alliance portfolio and the focal firm's ROA in a given year, averaged across the partners in the firm's portfolio. The formula is not readable in the extracted text. Higher values suggest that partners in the firm's alliance portfolio are less dependent on the outcomes of alliances relative to that firm. Partner and focal firm ROA come from annual Compustat data.
time_window: t (lagged one year relative to the dependent variable)

description: Relative alternatives captures the structural dependence of the focal firm on its alliance portfolio, computed as a function of the ratio of each partner's number of alliances with other focal firms to the number of alliances that each focal firm had with other partners, averaged across partners in the firm's alliance portfolio in a given year. Higher values suggest that partners in the alliance portfolio have relatively more alternatives than the focal firm. The formula is not readable in the extracted text; Kj,t is the total number of alliances between partner j and all the focal firms in year t, and Ki,t,j is the number of alliances between focal firm i and partner j in year t.
time_window: t (lagged one year relative to the dependent variable)

description: Bilateral competition is the percentage of matches between the focal firm's primary industry segment (four-digit SIC) and the primary industry segments of its partners. It is computed as the average across partners of a dummy that receives a value of 1 when the SIC of firm i matches that of partner j in year t. Higher values indicate more competition between the focal firm and its partners.
time_window: t (lagged one year relative to the dependent variable)

description: Multilateral competition is the sum of squared proportions of partners' sales in each industry segment, a concentration measure that resembles the inversed Berry-Herfindahl diversification index except that it is based on the sales distributions of partners rather than on those of the focal firm. If all of the firm's partners generate their sales in the same industry the measure takes a value of 1, and if each partner specializes and extracts equivalent revenues from a unique industry it becomes proportional to the inverse of the number of industries in which partners compete. Partner sales by four-digit primary SIC come from annual Compustat data; the formula is not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: t (lagged one year relative to the dependent variable)

description: Length of time it takes a radiologist to read a case. For the first case of a shift, read time equals time out minus time in; for all subsequent shift cases, read time equals time out for the current case minus time out for the prior case. Each radiologist's cases are partitioned into shifts using a 30-minute break window between the time out of consecutive reads. The models use the natural logarithm of READTIME, and shorter read times indicate better performance.
Cumulative number of prior cases read by a radiologist for the customer of the current case. It is entered in the baseline model together with IndvlOtherCustomer.

Cumulative number of prior cases read by a radiologist in the domain, and for the customer, of the current case. It is the key variable of interest in the individual-experience models, entered together with the other three experience segments.
Cumulative number of prior cases, outside the domain of the current case, read by a radiologist for the customer of the current case.
Total cumulative number of prior cases for a given radiologist that match the domain of the current case but not its customer.
Cumulative number of prior cases read by a given radiologist in all domains and for all customers other than those of the current case.

Herfindahl-style index of customer concentration. For each case, the share of the radiologist's prior volume devoted to each customer is measured; these volume shares are then squared and summed. Higher values indicate a greater degree of customer concentration, i.e., less variety.

Total number of prior cases a customer has sent to OutsourceCo less the current reading radiologist's cumulative experience with that customer. It is examined in both linear and discrete forms; the discrete form splits the linear variable into thirds (OrgCustomer1, OrgCustomer2 and OrgCustomer3).

Flow betweenness computed on 130 x 130 symmetric matrices of alliance relationships. The measure assesses the amount of flow (mjk) between firm j and firm k that must pass through firm i; the flow betweenness of firm i is the sum of all mjk where i, j and k are distinctive. It is a measure of the contribution of firm i to all possible maximum flows and depends on the number and intensity of alliances of firm i, each alliance being scored on a continuous 9-point intensity scale with multiple alliances between a pair summed into a composite index.

Operationalized as the average difference between the centrality of the most central firm and that of all other firms. In the reported formula Cmax is the centrality measure of the most central firm and n is the number of firms in the network; the formula itself is not readable in the extracted text. Values are reported as percentages of centralization for each network period.

UCINET IV was used to collapse firms into blocks and map relationships within and between blocks. Relations between or within blocks were considered to exist if the density was at least equal to or greater than the overall network density, where network density is measured as the total value of all ties divided by the number of possible ties. The number and strength of the resulting arcs were compared before and after each event.

Two anchor industry events were selected and classified by the authors. The regulatory shock of 1984 (the Cooperative Research Act, the approval of the National-NKK venture, and the Voluntary Restraints Agreement) was classified as a structure-reinforcing event because it did not change the basis of competition but removed barriers to cooperative activity. The technology shock of 1987 (Nucor's adoption of Compact Strip Production for its Crawfordsville, Indiana plant) was classified as a structure-loosening event because it acted as a competence-destroying discontinuity that radically changed the basis of competition.

The 130 firms were divided into six technology blocks using the criterion of contextual equivalence, i.e., similarity on the attribute of technology (integrated, minimill, specialty). Because contextually equivalent blocks keep block membership constant, the authors could observe how relations within and between those blocks changed over time.

The shortest distance in kilometers between each event of violence and each business is entered into a quadratic distance decay function, with a cutoff point of 0.5 km after which the protest is assumed not to have an effect. The measure of exposure to violent protests is calculated as the sum of all exposures for each entrepreneur over all events of violence over the period of 6 months between survey waves.

Profits during the month prior to the survey, logged. Entrepreneurs' reports of profits over the previous month are described as highly correlated with other long-term measures of performance and as tending to be accurate.

Operationalized as the number of local civic association meetings that entrepreneurs attended per month. Civic associations include non-governmental organizations, neighborhood associations, professional associations, and religious groups; associations were considered local when the majority of their members were residents of the business's neighborhood. The local community was defined as the business's neighborhood.
time_window: baseline, 6 months prior to the survey (t = 0)

description: Entrepreneurs were asked to name individuals whom they trusted and whom they reached out to for help and advice about their business, and were asked about the profession of their contacts and the neighborhood they worked in. The sum of all advice contacts who worked in different neighborhoods from the focal entrepreneur is the measure of non-colocated advice relationships.

Entrepreneurs were asked to name individuals whom they trusted and whom they reached out to for help and advice about their business, and were asked about the profession of their contacts and the neighborhood they worked in. The sum of all advice contacts who worked in the same neighborhood as the focal entrepreneur is the measure of colocated advice relationships.

variable_name: Number of patents filed by individuals in the sample
description: The company made patent data available in the form of monthly R&D reports used to assess and reward individual performance; for each of the 16 labs, 18 monthly reports were made available, 6 before and 12 after the collection of the social network data. Cross-examination of all reports allowed the authors to identify patent applications filed by respondents in the sample. The authors note that granted patents could also be used but are a noisier measure, and that the number of patent applications reported in the monthly report formed the basis for performance review and promotion decisions.
time_window: 18 months (6 before and 12 after the network survey)

description: For each individual the E-I index was constructed by considering the difference between the number of external ties (Ei, ties to/from members of labs other than the individual's own) and the number of internal ties (Ii, ties to/from members of the same lab). The formula defining the index appears in a block that could not be read. The index ranges from -1, when all ties are internal, to +1, when all ties are external, with 0 indicating that bridging ties exactly equal nonbridging ties. It was computed on the set of confirmed knowledge-sharing ties and, in the decomposition models, on subsets of ties (all raw ties, weak ties, strong ties, Simmelian ties, non-Simmelian ties).

variable_name: Strong ties (number of strong ties; bridging strong ties and bridging weak ties)
description: Raw knowledge-sharing ties were measured on a 1-5 scale from two network survey questions about how often the respondent goes to a colleague for information or knowledge and how often the colleague comes to the respondent. Confirmed ties are the average of the two individuals' responses, which produces possible fractional values. Ties were categorized as strong or weak using the dichotomy of 4 and above versus 3.5 and below: strong ties have a confirmed value greater than or equal to 4, weak ties are the remaining ties with values smaller than or equal to 3.5. Bridging strong and bridging weak ties were then computed as the E-I index on each subset of ties, and the number of strong ties was also entered as a count.
scale: 1-5 for raw ties; strong >= 4 versus weak <= 3.5

variable_name: Bridging Simmelian ties / number of Simmelian ties (and bridging non-Simmelian ties)
description: Using the direct formulation provided by Krackhardt (1998), a tie from i to j is Simmelian if and only if it satisfies two stated conditions; the formulas appear in blocks that could not be read. A non-Simmelian tie is any tie that does not satisfy these conditions for being Simmelian. Simmelian ties are based on the Boolean graph of confirmed ties. Bridging Simmelian ties and bridging non-Simmelian ties were measured by computing the E-I index on each subset of ties, and models also used the number of Simmelian ties.

Each outlet's cumulative sales of primary loans since the introduction of the new incentive regime. Used as a proxy for experience and learning under the regime because it reflects both experience and exposure over time as well as learning by doing.
time_window: since introduction of the incentive regime

description: One minus the ratio of value appropriated by outlet employees to the value created by the outlet in a given month. Value appropriated is the sum of outlet employees' monthly bonus from the sale of primary loans. Value created is the outlet's sales performance in primary loans, calculated as the difference between total revenues from primary loans and imputed costs of capital.

Outlet's sales performance in primary loans, calculated as the difference between the outlet's total revenues from primary loans and the corresponding imputed costs of capital. The marginal cost of capital is assumed equal to the interest rate offered on savings deposit accounts and allowed to change in proportion to changes in the central bank's base interest rate.

Sum of outlet employees' monthly bonus from the sale of primary loans, obtained by matching actual sales figures with the structure of the studied incentive regime. Only the bonus, the variable component of pay, is used because fixed wage data were unavailable.

A dummy variable set to 1 when a company's weighted profit gap is at least .20, that is, when the total profit filed with MOST and the profit filed with SAIC differ substantially. The weighted profit gap subtracts the firm's total profit filed with SAIC from the profit filed with MOST and normalizes the difference by the profit reported to MOST, giving a percentage-based measure of misstatement. The 20 percent threshold was chosen to allow for accidental omissions of small earnings or cost items that may occur in good faith. Using this threshold, 55 percent of the sample reported substantively different financial results to MOST and SAIC.
time_window: same fiscal year for both sets of books; the grant application year T0

description: A dummy variable set to 1 if a company received an innovation subsidy grant from the Innofund. Slightly more than half (53.96 percent) of the firms in the sample received grants.

Online recruiting ads were used to measure firms' intentions to expand, giving three counts per company-year: the total number of positions advertised, the number of non-R&D positions, and the count of R&D positions. Ads that gave a range of positions were coded at the mean of the range, and ads for ''multiple openings'' were assigned the average number of jobs posted by all job-posting firms in that year. A position was classified as R&D-related using a list of R&D job titles and the requirement of an advanced STEM degree. The panel structure was collapsed so that there is a single pre- and a single post-grant-application observation per firm.
time_window: annual observations, collapsed into a pre-grant period (T0+1 and the three prior years) and a post-grant period (T0+2 to T0+5)

description: The count of invention patent applications filed by each company, taken from SIPO. Invention patents, which apply to novel products, processes, or their improvements, are much more significant than utility patents and are weighted by the Innofund at six times the value of a utility patent. Design patents were excluded from the analysis.
time_window: pre-grant period (T0+1 and the three prior years) versus post-grant period (T0+2 to T0+5)

description: The count of more marginal new utility patent applications filed by each company, taken from SIPO. Utility patents protect new technical solutions proposed for the shape or structure of a product that are fit for practical use, and they are treated as less important than invention patents. Design patents were excluded from the analysis.
time_window: pre-grant period (T0+1 and the three prior years) versus post-grant period (T0+2 to T0+5)

description: Executives rated 17 normative beliefs, the importance of 17 operative goals from Quinn and Rohrbaugh's competing values model of effectiveness, and 22 cause-effect beliefs, how positively or negatively each of 22 business tactics would influence long-term profitability. The 39 belief variables were factor analyzed and six dimensions were retained: innovation, human resources, quality, efficiency, bottom line, and image. A high score on a dimension indicates high perceived efficacy for the goals/tactics underlying that dimension, while a low score indicates low or negative perceived efficacy. Separate regression analyses were used for each of the six belief dimensions.

Functional background was assessed as the number of years the executive had spent in each of eight major functional areas: general administration, personnel, production and operations, research and development, finance, accounting, marketing, and sales. Eight separate functional background indicators were used in the analyses, each indicator representing the number of years in a functional area.

Current functional position was coded into the same eight categories by two independent raters who coded the job titles of executives using standardized coding instructions. Coefficients were dummy-coded (0 or 1) for each of the eight current position variables. Cohen's kappa for inter-rater reliability between the two coders was 0.79, and disagreements were resolved through discussion between the two coders.
scale: dummy-coded 0 or 1 for each of eight functional categories

variable_name: beliefs of other upper-echelon team members
description: Beliefs of other upper-echelon team members are operationalized as the belief scores of all upper-echelon team members excluding the focal executive's, on the six belief dimensions. Each executive in turn is considered the focal executive while all other upper-echelon team members are considered as nonfocal executives. In estimation the beliefs of all team members were averaged for each belief dimension and the average was entered in the regression, because the focal executive is assumed to be equally influenced by all other executives except as specified by the moderator variables.
level: individual executive (average of other team members)

description: The absolute difference in functional background between the focal executive and each team member, averaging across differences in all functional areas, was averaged across all team members and the multiplicative inverse was taken to arrive at a similarity score for each focal executive. Averaging across functional areas and across team members reduces these effects to a single term for the effects of similarity in team members' functional areas. All variables were standardized before the multiplication of two variables at any stage in the calculations.
