Age similarity was assessed by calculating the absolute difference in age between the focal executive and each team member, averaging across all team members, and taking the multiplicative inverse of this average to get a single score for each focal executive. All variables were standardized before the multiplication of two variables at any stage in the calculations.

Tenure similarity and the interaction of tenure similarity and team member beliefs were calculated in a manner similar to that applied to age: the absolute difference in tenure within the upper-echelon team between the focal executive and each team member was averaged across all team members and the multiplicative inverse taken. All variables were standardized before the multiplication of two variables at any stage in the calculations.

Organizational structure was coded from the 'governance and management' section of Morningstar's one-page fund reports, which describes fund managers and how they manage the portfolio, following four coding rules: N is set to the number of people mentioned as manager or comanager (excluding those with an explicitly secondary role); if the description is explicit about the number of 'sleeves' or subadvisors, N is set to the number of divisions of the portfolio and C is set to 1; if two or more managers are mentioned but nothing is said about how they coordinate, consensus (N = C) is assumed; and funds with no specific manager names, or run by an algorithm, are left unclassified. Funds were then aggregated into three broader categories: 1/1 (managed by an individual), N/1 (decentralized), and N/N (centralized), and funds unclassified or with consensus levels other than 1 or N were eliminated. In the regressions, the decentralized and individual structures are entered as dummies and the centralized structure is the omitted dummy.

The number of stocks bought by a fund per quarter, determined by looking at the stocks added to the portfolio since the last reported quarterly holdings. Because the distribution of the number of stocks bought is highly skewed, its logarithm was used as the dependent variable in the regressions testing Hypothesis 1.

Measured as the total unbought positive returns (TUPR), the sum of the returns of the good assets that belong to the fund's investment universe but were not bought in the current period. An asset is 'good' if its holding period return equals or exceeds the benchmark b, the average return of the assets in the fund's investment universe. A bootstrap creates the population of portfolios of the same size that could have been drawn from the same investment universe (each fund competes against 100,000 simulated portfolios), and the fund's error is reported as a standardized score relative to that population; the higher the score, the higher the error.

Measured as the total negative return (TNR), the negated sum of the returns of the bad assets the fund bought during the period, where an asset is 'bad' if its holding period return falls below the benchmark (the average return of the assets in the fund's investment universe). A bootstrap computes the population of portfolios of the same size that could have been drawn from the same investment universe, and the fund's error is expressed as a standardized score of its deviance from that population; the higher the score, the higher the error.

Based on the Sapir-Whorf notion that language reveals cognitive schemas, the authors collected partners' 'About Us' web pages and developed custom dictionaries for five cognitive frames: time, responsibility, motivation, innovation, and strategy. An organization's frame is reflected in the relative frequency with which words belonging to that frame's dictionary appear in its web pages, so that each organization exhibits a specific pattern within each frame, and organizations are not 'low' or 'high' in any frame. Cosine similarity was used to quantify the textual similarity between partners' web pages for each frame. Cognitive frame similarity is the mean of the five frame-specific cosine similarities of each pair of 'About Us' web pages.
time_window: web pages from 6 months before the focal contract's effective date

description: Count of good faith provisions in each contract. All good faith provisions were manually coded according to a strict coding protocol, and the coding scheme was cross-validated with two legal experts. Every contract was coded independently by the first author and a research assistant who was unaware of the study's purpose and had received extensive training with a sample dataset; discrepancies between the coders occurred in less than 1% of the cases and were resolved through discussion.

Count of genuine good faith provisions in each contract, obtained by distinguishing genuine from guarded good faith provisions during the manual coding of the contracts. Genuine good faith provisions are those used without additional explicit stipulations to address cases in which partners fail to reach an agreement in good faith.

Count of guarded good faith provisions in each contract, obtained by distinguishing guarded from genuine good faith provisions during the manual coding of the contracts. Guarded good faith provisions combine good faith with an explicit provision that takes effect when good faith efforts fail.

A continuous measure reflecting the heterogeneity of the clinical approval success rates of compounds across therapeutic areas. For each alliance the authors extracted information on the therapeutic area and development phase from the contracts and accompanying press releases and matched this information with the average success rates in different therapeutic areas and clinical phases reported by DiMasi et al. (2010). The final measure is the inverse of these success rates.

The total number of alliances into which the client firm had entered before the focal alliance. Data were obtained from Informa Business Intelligence, which has recorded alliances involving firms and research institutes in the biopharmaceutical industry since 1991, and were cross-validated and complemented with press releases and contract data from BioScience Advisors. Because the variable is highly skewed, a natural logarithmic transformation was applied, which also accounts for diminishing marginal gains in experience. The partner that typically provided financial support was identified as the client firm.

The total number of alliances into which the R&D firm had entered before the focal alliance. Data were obtained from Informa Business Intelligence, which has recorded alliances involving firms and research institutes in the biopharmaceutical industry since 1991, and were cross-validated and complemented with press releases and contract data from BioScience Advisors. Because the variable is highly skewed, a natural logarithmic transformation was applied, which also accounts for diminishing marginal gains in experience. The partner that contributed primarily to intangible assets such as R&D knowledge and expertise was denoted as the R&D firm.

The type of partnership used to source the technology was used as a proxy for organizational interdependence. Dummy variables were created for the polar extremes: licensing (loose coupling) and acquisition (tight coupling), with a 1 indicating that the partnership was of the type associated with the particular dummy variable. Joint development (moderate coupling) was indicated when both the licensing and acquisition dummy variables were rated 0.
time_window: at the time of the sourcing decision

description: The uniqueness of the sourced technology was measured at the time of the sourcing decision (phase 1) with four items rated on a seven-point scale from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'; the higher the ratings, the greater the perceived uniqueness of the specific technology. Item Q4 ('Many of our competitors had fundamentally similar technology') and item Q16 ('This specific technology was common within the industry') were reverse-coded. Responses from multiple raters were averaged for the final sample.
time_window: phase 1, at the time of the sourcing decision

description: The difficulty of technical imitation was measured with three items on a seven-point scale from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree', collected during phase 1 of the survey. The higher the ratings, the greater the perceived difficulty of imitating the technology. One item (Q18, 'It would be easy for other firms to imitate this technology') was reverse-coded.
time_window: phase 1, at the time of the sourcing decision

description: The measure of technological uncertainty consisted of six items rated on a seven-point scale from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' that tapped the uncertainty associated with engineering design and commercial success of the technology at the time of the sourcing decision (phase 1). The higher the ratings, the greater the uncertainty. The measure was influenced by the previous efforts of Simonin (1991) and Souder and Shrivastava (1985).
time_window: phase 1, at the time of the sourcing decision

description: A technology's degree of dynamism was measured with two seven-point items about the expected length of the technology's life cycle and the likelihood of future competency-destroying developments. The higher the rating, the more dynamic the technology. The life-cycle item (Q1) was reverse-coded.
time_window: phase 1, at the time of the sourcing decision

description: Sourcing performance was conceptualized as a second-order multidimensional construct consisting of three first-order dimensions: capability development, attainment of objectives, and estimated return on investment, each composed of multiple items. Attainment of objectives was an eight-item weighted aggregate: the importance of each objective at the time of the decision (three-point scale) was used as a weight (1, 2, or 3) for the corresponding fulfillment measure three to four years later (seven-point scale), and the weighted measures were summed. Capability development was measured with three seven-point items, and estimated return on investment with three five-point items comparing outcomes with industry and firm norms. Ratings on the three dimensions were standardized and combined using the weights from the confirmatory factor analysis to create the composite measure.
time_window: attainment of objectives spans phase 1 (importance) and phase 2 (fulfillment); capability development and estimated return on investment in phase 2

description: The dependent variable, measured as the percentage difference between a purchase price and an IPO target's value four weeks prior to the date of the announcement of the acquisition reported in the SDC database. The four-week time lag was used to obtain a scaling factor that is not confounded by the takeover announcement and leakage of information right before the announcement.
time_window: four weeks prior to the acquisition announcement

description: Measured with the ranking index developed by Carter and Manaster (1990), which is constructed from investment banks' positions in 'tombstone' announcements listing members of an underwriting syndicate. Because IPOs are often comanaged by underwriting syndicates, the authors focused on the ranking of the lead underwriter for each IPO, identified through the new issues module of the SDC database. The reputation data were taken from Loughran and Ritter (2004).

A dummy variable equal to 1 if any of the VCs associated with the IPO target was on the list of prominent VCs, and 0 otherwise. The authors identified all VCs that provided financing to a particular IPO firm and examined the number of other IPOs in which those VCs were involved five years prior to the IPO target's issuing date, identifying a VC as prominent if the number of IPOs it backed was above the median number of IPOs for all VCs during that period.
time_window: five years prior to the IPO issuing date

description: The number of an IPO firm's alliance partners that were publicly listed, counted for alliances formed both before and after the IPO but prior to the M&A transaction. Compustat and CRSP were used to verify whether or not alliance partners of an IPO firm were publicly listed. Because of positive skewness, the variable is defined as the log of 1 plus the number of prominent alliance partners.
time_window: alliances formed before and after the IPO but prior to the M&A transaction

description: A continuous measure of knowledge distance between acquirer and target calculated from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Occupational Employment Survey, which offers information on the proportion of employees in each of 823 occupational categories within industries at the three-digit SIC level. The employment distributions are used to calculate the knowledge distance variable; the formula itself is unreadable in the supplied text and is not reconstructed here.
An indicator variable equal to 1 if an acquirer was a foreign (non-U.S.) firm, and 0 otherwise.

Coded as one if the alliance common pool resource units exceeded the threshold of 150 in a particular period, and zero otherwise. The alliance common pool started each period at 100 resource units; each of five alliance members received 20 resource units per period and decided how many units to give to or take from the pool. If the pool had at least 150 resource units the alliance achieved a successful outcome and each alliance member received a bonus representing common benefits.
time_window: each period of the 11-period repeated game

description: Measured as the net amount of resources transferred to the alliance common pool, that is total giving minus total taking by all alliance members in each period.
time_window: each period of the 11-period repeated game

description: The total amount of resources in the alliance pool at the end of each period, which is the sum of the residual resources from the prior period (after depreciation) and the net transfer of resources in the current period.
time_window: each period of the 11-period repeated game

description: Indicator variable equal to one if the observation was drawn from that treatment, and zero otherwise, where treatments differ in the bonus structure implementing the ratio of common to private benefits. In the high common benefit treatment the bonuses were $35,000 for two of the firms and $40,000 for three of the firms, so that it collectively cost the firms $50,000 to contribute to the alliance common pool while they collectively received $190,000 in common benefits. In the low common benefit treatment the bonuses were $4,000 for two firms and $5,000 for three firms, so that contributing cost $50,000 against a collective common benefit of only $23,000.

Indicator variable for the treatment in which three of the firms received high bonuses ($35,000, $35,000, and $40,000) while two firms received low bonuses ($5,000 each), creating heterogeneity among the bonuses received by the alliance members. The bonus values are still consistent with incentive alignment for the strategic alliance to succeed ($120,000 of benefits versus $50,000 of costs), but the heterogeneity in bonuses creates a problem because the low common benefit firms have an incentive to take the resources in the alliance pool.

The two treatments that permitted communication were implemented via a free-form chat box. Strategic alliance members had the ability to chat with all of the other members in their strategic alliance, or send private messages to any one alliance member. The 'chat' feature resembled instant messaging, and a record of all prior messages was available for each member as the strategic alliance progressed across periods.

Composite scale of three items adapted from Jehn et al. (1999) and based on Van de Ven et al. (1976), asking respondents about the extent to which they worked as a team with WFP employees on the project, made decisions concerning the project jointly, and discussed crucial project steps together before carrying them out. Internal consistency is α = 0.87.

Two-item scale adapted from Kraimer et al. (2012) capturing whether employees felt that their MtW experience defined a large part of who they were and distinguished them from others. One further item on whether the MtW experience continued to be a significant part of employees' life was dropped because it loaded only marginally (0.56); the retained measure has α = 0.82.

Survey measure adapted from Bartel et al. (2001) asking employees to assess on a 7-point Likert scale how much they learned about the humanitarian sector, the country, and the problems or challenges targeted by the project. A fourth item on whether their skills had improved was dropped due to a low factor loading of 0.46. The domains were defined by coding verbal cues of learning in the qualitative data; the scale has α = 0.78.

A subset of Kraimer et al.'s (2012) 12 survey items measuring international expatriate job recognition, i.e., how expatriates felt they were treated during the year following their return compared to colleagues who had not completed an international assignment. Eight survey items relevant to corporate volunteering were used based on qualitative data and confirmation from TNT, and six were ultimately retained (α = 0.94).

The scale used by Kraimer et al. (2012) with no revisions beyond exchanging the terms 'my international assignment/role' or 'my overseas experience' with 'my MtW assignment/role/experience' (α = 0.88).

variable_name: dependent variable (U.S. or U.K. exchange listing)
description: The dependent variable is binary: whether a foreign firm makes its IPO on the U.S. or U.K. exchanges between 2002 and 2006. Foreign IPOs listed on U.S. exchanges were coded 1 and U.K. listed foreign IPOs were coded 0. The sample of foreign issuers was identified from the SDC New Issues database.
Founder-CEO was a dummy variable, coded as 1 if one of the original founders of a company was the CEO at the time the company went public. It was collected from the offering firm's prospectus.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Executive stock options was dummy coded as 1 if stock options were offered to the CEO prior to the firm's IPO. It was collected from the offering firm's prospectus.
scale: dummy (1 = CEO stock options offered, 0 otherwise)

description: Board independence was measured as the percentage of independent directors each firm had at IPO, as identified in the offering prospectuses.
Board interlocks was measured as the sum of directorships of all board members. It was collected from the offering firm's prospectus.

Underwriter prestige was measured based on the ratings assigned to the underwriters by Carter and Manaster (1990) and Carter et al. (1998) after the modifications suggested by Loughran and Ritter (2004).

VC syndication was measured as the number of VC firms involved in an IPO. The presence of VC backing was identified by first referencing the 'Principal Stockholders' section of each prospectus and then verifying those VCs against 'The VentureOne Venture Capital Source Book' to ensure the shareholder was indeed a VC firm.

A planning dimension produced by a rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the 40 questionnaire items, with a reliability alpha of 0.94. The exact factor score produced by the factor analysis was used in the regression analyses.
scale: exact factor score derived from 5-point Likert items (1 = strongly agree; 5 = strongly disagree)

description: A planning dimension produced by a rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the questionnaire items, with a reliability alpha of 0.87. The exact factor score produced by the factor analysis was used in the regression analyses.
scale: exact factor score derived from 5-point Likert items (1 = strongly agree; 5 = strongly disagree)

description: A planning dimension produced by a rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the questionnaire items, with a reliability alpha of 0.74. The exact factor score produced by the factor analysis was used in the regression analyses.
scale: exact factor score derived from 5-point Likert items (1 = strongly agree; 5 = strongly disagree)

description: A planning dimension produced by a rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the questionnaire items, with a reliability alpha of 0.68. The exact factor score produced by the factor analysis was used in the regression analyses.
scale: exact factor score derived from 5-point Likert items (1 = strongly agree; 5 = strongly disagree)

description: A planning dimension produced by a rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the questionnaire items, with a reliability alpha of 0.80. The exact factor score produced by the factor analysis was used in the regression analyses.
scale: exact factor score derived from 5-point Likert items (1 = strongly agree; 5 = strongly disagree)

description: A planning dimension produced by a rotated (varimax) principal components factor analysis of the questionnaire items, with a reliability alpha of 0.71. The exact factor score produced by the factor analysis was used in the regression analyses.
scale: exact factor score derived from 5-point Likert items (1 = strongly agree; 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Each CEO indicated the strategic orientation of their bank based on written descriptions of Miles and Snow strategy types developed by McDaniel and Kolari (1987); the strategy descriptions did not reference information-processing abilities. Strategy was operationalized as a binary categorical variable, with Defender coded 0 and Prospector coded 1. The strategy type chosen by responding CEOs was validated by state-appointed bank supervisors, who agreed with the CEOs 86 percent of the time.
scale: binary (0 = Defender, 1 = Prospector). Direction: higher = more prospector (defender to prospector scale)

description: Archival measure of Return on Assets gathered for the time span of 1991 through 1993. An aggregate measure was calculated by averaging the scores of the three years, so that the variable ROA is the average ROA for the period 1991-93.

Archival measure of Return on Equity gathered for the time span of 1991 through 1993. An aggregate measure was calculated by averaging the scores of the three years for the variable, which was then used as a dependent variable in the regressions.

Archival measure of Loan Growth gathered for the time span of 1991 through 1993. An aggregate measure was calculated by averaging the scores of the three years, yielding the variable LOANGROWTH used in the regressions.

The CEO rated 40 five-point Likert items on the strategic planning process. A varimax principal components factor analysis reduced them to six dimensions (Accounting Control, Integration and Coordination, Flexibility, Goals and Plans, Scanning, Broad Analysis), and exact factor scores for each dimension were used in the regressions.
scale: 40 Likert items reduced to six factor scores, alphas 0.68 to 0.94

description: A binary variable distinguishing whether the deal, from the perspective of each focal firm, primarily involves technical capabilities or specialized complementary assets, based on descriptions in SDC and Recap, press releases in LexisNexis, and attributes of partner/target firms. Each alliance or acquisition is classed as sourcing technical capabilities if the focal firm seeks genes, methods of genetic modification, or molecular biology knowledge, or if the partner/target is a biotechnology unit. In collaborations or joint technology developments the authors assume that both partners may obtain technical capabilities, whereas only the licensee in licensing agreements may be the recipient.
time_window: at the time of the focal deal

description: The same binary resource-type variable, read for the specialized complementary assets side of the distinction. A deal is classed as sourcing specialized complementary assets if the focal firm seeks elite varieties or seed breeding knowledge, or if the partner/target is a conventional seed breeder. Coding draws on deal descriptions in SDC and Recap, press releases in LexisNexis, and attributes of partner/target firms.
time_window: at the time of the focal deal

description: The dependent variable is a binary variable equal to one for alliances and zero for acquisitions. Joint ventures and minority equity alliances (less or equal to 50% ownership after the deal) are counted as alliances; majority equity investments (more than 50% ownership after the deal) are counted as acquisitions. The unit of analysis is each external deal, that is, an alliance or acquisition.
time_window: from the firm's first investment until market entry or exit, tracking deals until 2002

description: An indicator variable designating whether a firm had adopted a stock-based incentive plan. Both stock option plans and pseudo stock incentive plans were coded as stock-based incentive plans. If a firm had a stock-based incentive plan during the year, the variable was coded 1 and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: pioneer adopter, momentum adopter, or nonadopter
description: A dependent variable created to indicate whether a firm was a pioneer adopter, momentum adopter, or nonadopter of stock options. Pioneer adopters, defined as firms that adopted stock option pay before it was formally legalized in 1998, were coded 1, late adopters were coded 2, and nonadopters were coded 0.

Indicator variable coded 1 if the firm had American Depositary Receipts and 0 otherwise. An ADR is a receipt for the shares of a foreign-based company held by a U.S. bank that entitles the shareholder to all dividends and capital gains of the underlying stock; by listing ADRs in the United States, foreign firms submit themselves to some scrutiny by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the potential oversight of large U.S. investors.
A measure of the degree to which firms were dependent on the United States for sales, calculated as the natural logarithm of a firm's U.S. sales.

An indicator variable coded 1 if a firm's CEO possessed a graduate business education and 0 otherwise. The authors searched the Munzinger Archiv and company biographies of top executives to determine whether an executive had a graduate degree in business.

A variable indicating whether a firm had abandoned the German method of audited accounting procedures, known as the Handelsgesetzbuch (HGB), and adopted the more transparent U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) or the international accounting standards (IAS). If the firm had adopted GAAP or IAS accounting conventions during a year, the variable was coded 1; it was coded 0 if the firm's convention was HGB. Early adoption and continued use of GAAP or IAS were treated as a successful experience with an institutionally contested practice.

The number of board interlocks involving the focal firm's CEO or board chair being on the supervisory board of another firm that had adopted stock-based pay. Because of the skewed distribution of the number of interlocks by firm, the measure used in the analyses is the natural log of the number of interlocks plus unity.
scale: log of count of interlocks plus unity

description: The number of board interlocks in which the focal firm had outside supervisory board members from firms that had previously adopted stock-based pay. As with sent ties, the measure used in the analyses is the natural log of the number of interlocks plus unity.
scale: log of count of interlocks plus unity

description: The number of firms within the same general industry as a focal firm that had previously adopted stock-based pay. Industry membership was defined using the ten industry groups defined by the Deutsche Boerse.
The number of prior adopters within the DAX 100, used as an indicator of structural equivalence.

A dummy variable coded 1 for a year prior to 1998 and 0 otherwise, used as an indication that the government now sanctioned stock option pay. Prior to 1998, firms used legal maneuvers to circumvent laws prohibiting stock-based pay.

Binary measure of repeat initiative taking, taking a value of 1 if an idea initiator put forth an idea and submitted another idea during the next four years and 0 if he or she did not. It is analysed on data set A, which excludes all ideas submitted in the last four years of the observation period because those initiators would not have the same allocated time frame to submit another idea.
time_window: four years following the last submission

description: Ideas were classified as successful and coded 1 if they passed the second screening, in which a panel of broader experts assessed the potential, viability and impact of the idea and funding was awarded so that the proposal formally became a project. An unsuccessful idea was one that did not get accepted after either the first or second panel and was coded 0.

For the analysis of repeat initiative taking, all successes the initiator had experienced with both the focal initiative and any prior initiative were separately tallied. The variable enters the models regressing on repeat initiative taking estimated on data set A.
time_window: focal initiative and all prior initiatives

description: For the analysis of repeat initiative taking, all failures the initiator had experienced with both the focal initiative and any prior initiative were separately tallied. The variable enters the models regressing on repeat initiative taking estimated on data set A.
time_window: focal initiative and all prior initiatives

description: For the analysis of initiative success, all successes that the focal initiator had experienced in initiating prior initiatives only were separately counted. The variable enters the models regressing on initiative success estimated on data set B, which excludes all first ideas from the dependent variable.

For the analysis of initiative success, all failures that the focal initiator had experienced in initiating prior initiatives only were separately counted. The variable enters the models regressing on initiative success estimated on data set B.

Prior success experiences of initiating ideas were counted for the focal contributor of an initiative, and tallied if there were more than one contributor to an initiative. The variable enters the models regressing on initiative success.

Prior failure experiences of initiating ideas were counted for the focal contributor of an initiative, and tallied if there were more than one contributor to an initiative. The variable enters the models regressing on initiative success.

The HR manager at each participating company rated the extent to which he or she agreed (1 = 'strongly disagree,' 5 = 'strongly agree') that the company used various HR practices to manage knowledge workers similar to those identified by the CEO. Sixteen items represented three subdimensions: internal labor markets and selection based on fit to the company; group- and organization-based incentives; and training programs and performance appraisals based on long-term growth, team building, and development of firm-specific knowledge. A principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation showed all 16 items loading on a single factor, and the scale showed good reliability (.87). A high score reflects a high use of commitment-based HR practices.

Knowledge workers assessed the degree to which they agreed (1 = 'strongly disagree,' 5 = 'strongly agree') with 12 items adapted from Mayer and Davis (1999), including 4 items for each of the three dimensions of trust identified by Mayer et al. (1995): ability (belief that other knowledge workers are capable and skilled), benevolence (wanting to do good toward each other), and integrity (behaving fairly with each other). The 12-item scale showed reliability of .91, and intraclass correlations for the aggregated index exceeded levels suggested by Bliese (1998). Responses for the knowledge workers in each firm were therefore averaged to create an aggregated firm-level measure.
level: firm (averaged across knowledge workers within each firm)

description: Knowledge workers assessed their agreement (1 = 'strongly disagree,' 5 = 'strongly agree') with a six-item scale adapted from Chatman and Flynn (2001). Sample items included 'There is little collaboration between employees at this company' (reverse-scored), 'Employees here are willing to sacrifice their self-interests for the benefit of the group,' and 'There is a high level of sharing between employees in this organization.' The scale demonstrated high reliability (.88) and intraclass correlations exceeding levels suggested by Bliese (1998); responses for knowledge workers within each firm were averaged to estimate cooperation.
level: firm (averaged across knowledge workers within each firm)

description: Knowledge workers rated five items developed based on Nahapiet and Ghoshal (1997) on the same agreement scale (1 = 'strongly disagree,' 5 = 'strongly agree'). Sample items included 'Employees are always on the same page when they talk about work' and 'Employees in this company have trouble understanding each other when working together on a project' (reverse-scored). The scale demonstrated high reliability (.84) and acceptable intraclass correlations; responses across knowledge workers within each firm were averaged.
level: firm (averaged across knowledge workers within each firm)

description: An eight-item scale assessing knowledge workers' beliefs that exchange and combination would yield personal or organizational value (motivation) and the extent to which they believed that employees could exchange and combine information (ability). Knowledge workers assessed the extent to which they agreed with each statement on the same five-point scale (1 = 'strongly disagree,' 5 = 'strongly agree'). Scale reliability (.91) and intraclass correlations for the aggregated index were good; responses for respondents within each firm were averaged.
level: firm (averaged across knowledge workers within each firm)

variable_name: revenue from new products and services
description: Collected through a follow-up survey sent to each CEO one year after the original data collection. Each CEO was asked to identify the percentage of sales for the past year that was driven by the sales of products or services released in that year.
time_window: one year after the original data collection

description: One-year sales growth collected from COMPUSTAT for the year following the date of collection of the HR manager and knowledge worker surveys.
time_window: year following the collection of the HR manager and knowledge worker surveys

description: An index formed from ratings respondents provided on eight 11-point scales (0 = poor, 10 = excellent) in the Fortune survey conducted between September and December of 1985. The survey asked respondents to rate firms relative to their principal competitors. A varimax factor analysis of the eight attributes extracted a single factor, and overall reputation was adjusted for sector differences. Scores for reputations at the end of calendar years 1982, 1983 and 1984 were also used in a cross-sectional time series model.
scale: 0 = poor to 10 = excellent on each of eight 11-point scales
time_window: survey conducted September-December 1985; additional scores for end of 1982, 1983 and 1984

description: The ratio of market to book value for September 27, 1985, capturing market value just prior to the assessments of firms' reputations in fall 1985. It was entered into the reputation models as a standardized residual score created from regressions against profitability, risk, size, and advertising.

Firms' beta coefficients on September 27, 1985, the degree to which movement in a firm's stock is associated with general stock market movements. Beta was entered as a standardized residual score created from regressions against profitability, risk, size, and advertising.

A ratio of the prior four quarters' dividends divided by share price on September 27, 1985. It was entered as a standardized residual score created from regressions against profitability, risk, size, and advertising.

Prior-year accounting profitability measured as return on invested capital (ROIC) at the end of fiscal year 1984, a measure that is independent of capital structure. It was included among the four signals derived from prior-year accounting data in the cross-sectional time series model.
The level of accounting risk in 1984, estimated by the coefficient of variation (the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean) of ROIC in the previous nine years, 1975-83.
The concentration of a firm's stock in institutional hands, representing the percentage of all outstanding shares held on September 27, 1985 by banks, insurance companies, and mutual funds.
A firm's charitable contributions during 1984, adjusted for firm size, taken from corporate giving and philanthropy directories.

A dummy variable distinguishing between firms that had a separately endowed foundation in 1984 through which they funneled charitable contributions and those with no such foundation. Foundation data were coded from The Foundation Directory.
scale: dummy (1 = has a separately endowed foundation, 0 = no such foundation)

description: The total number of articles written about a firm in 1985, the calendar period most closely matching the period during which survey respondents formed their individual judgments of firms. The indicator was adjusted for both sector and size effects. The titles of the 15,400 articles found were content-analyzed by a rater.

A favorability index calculating the degree to which media reports were not negative as the proportion of positive and neutral ratings received. Article titles were classified as indicating either positive or negative news about a firm; three raters independently rated a 10 percent subset of the articles with a .88 coefficient of reliability against the principal rater.
scale: proportion of positive and neutral ratings

description: A logarithmic transformation of total sales in 1984.
A firm's total advertising expenditures in 1984, adjusted for firm size. Advertising expenditures are data not regularly reported to the SEC.

A continuous Herfindahl-type measure of diversification across business segments at the end of fiscal year 1985, calculated as one minus the sum of squared segment sales divided by the square of total sales, where the index runs over the number of segments (the printed formula is partly garbled). Higher scores indicate that firms are more likely to encompass less related businesses under their corporate umbrellas, and segment-level sales were assigned equally to distinct four-digit industries only when they did not fall under the umbrella of the same two-digit sector.

The standardized residual score of the market-book ratio after regressions against profitability, risk, size, and advertising, representing the information remaining in the variable after the influence of readily available accounting information had been removed.

Respondents were asked to assess the degree to which past acquisitions conducted by the firm were successful, coding each acquisition on a scale: -2 for 'many problems,' -1 for 'some problems,' 0 for 'average,' 1 for 'OK,' and 2 for 'great.' Acquisitions that were evaluated as 1 or 2 were considered to be successful. Past Success was then defined to be the proportion of the firm's prior acquisitions deemed to be successful. It is a firm-level attribute measured at the time of the focal acquisition.
scale: proportion of prior acquisitions rated successful
time_window: prior acquisitions up to the focal acquisition

description: Benchmark portfolio-adjusted cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) of the acquiring firm following the acquisition. The variable is computed as the cumulative difference between the acquiring firm's monthly stock return and the return in the equal-weighted size- and market-to-book-ranked portfolio to which the firm belongs, over a period of 36 months. One hundred benchmark portfolios were constructed from the cross-product of 10 size deciles and 10 market-to-book deciles, rebalanced every month and based on all companies traded on the New York Stock Exchange and the American Stock Exchange with accounting data available in Compustat.

Computed simply as the number of acquisitions completed by the acquirer prior to the focal acquisition. It is a firm-level count of prior deals of the same type, measured at the time of the focal acquisition. The variable was z-scored before entering the models, together with past success and experience heterogeneity.
time_window: prior acquisitions before the focal acquisition

description: Defined as the average difference among all past acquisition events of the firm. Prior acquisitions were classified using respondents' judgment of the preacquisition quality of the acquired firm, measured as an assessment of the preacquisition profitability of the target coded on a five-point scale. The written formula is not recoverable from the text. Because the measure compares pairs of prior acquisitions, all acquisitions with fewer than five prior observations by the same acquiring bank had to be excluded from the analysis.
time_window: stock of prior acquisitions (minimum five) before the focal acquisition

description: Measured as the number of tools specific to the management of the acquisition process that the acquirer had developed at the time of the focal transaction. These include documents, models and manuals such as the due diligence checklist, due diligence manual, systems conversion manual, affiliation/integration manual, systems training manual and products training manual, and quantitative models including financial evaluation, staffing models, product mapping, training/self-training packages and project management tools. Since the survey asks for the year of creation of each tool, a stock of existing tools can be computed for each year, so the measure varies not only by firm but also by year.
time_window: stock of tools existing in the year of the focal acquisition

description: Abnormal returns were calculated using residual analysis of the market model, with the event date set at t = 0 at the joint venture announcement. The market model was estimated over the window t = [-250, -10] using the common stock return of firm i and the corresponding daily market return on the equal-weighted S&P 500, and the estimates were used to predict daily returns over the two-day event window [-1, 0]. Daily abnormal returns are the difference between actual and predicted returns, and the cumulative abnormal return of firm i over the event window is the sum of daily abnormal returns for t from -1 to 0.
time_window: estimation window [-250, -10] days around the announcement; two-day event window [-1, 0]

description: For each focal firm, PSE was measured by calculating the accumulated number of all prior joint ventures formed with the same partner beginning in 1975 until the day prior to the recent joint venture announcement. The measure was updated for each new joint venture event between the focal firm and a focal partner.
time_window: 1975 until the day prior to the recent joint venture announcement

description: For each focal firm, GPE was measured by calculating the accumulated number of all prior joint ventures in which the firm participated beginning in 1975 until the day prior to the recent joint venture announcement. This measure was updated for each new joint venture event.
time_window: 1975 until the day prior to the recent joint venture announcement

description: For each focal firm, the measure captures the extent to which the asset value of the firm's recent partner differed from that of the firm's prior partners. The asset distance of the new partner of focal firm i is a function of the absolute value of this partner's assets divided by the average value of assets of all prior partners since 1975; a logarithmic transformation was applied to reduce skewness and eliminate potential outlier problems. The higher this measure's value, the more distinctive the recent partner relative to partners participating in prior joint ventures of the firm.
time_window: partner assets for the year preceding the joint venture event; prior partners since 1975

description: For each joint venture in which a focal firm participated between 1987 and 1996, R&D intensity was calculated as R&D expenses divided by net sales in the year preceding the recent joint venture event. Data on R&D expenses and net sales were extracted from Compustat.
time_window: the year preceding the joint venture event

description: For each joint venture event, a measure of solvency, a function of cash divided by long-term debt, was calculated in the year preceding the recent joint venture event. Because of the skewness of this measure, a natural logarithm was taken from the resulting value.
time_window: the year preceding the joint venture event

description: Firm-specific uncertainty was measured as a function of the volatility in the focal firm's stock price, operationalized as the difference between the standardized monthly volatility of the focal firm's stock price in the year preceding the joint venture announcement and the average standardized monthly volatility in the stock price of the sampled firms in the corresponding year. The standardized volatility was calculated as the standard deviation in monthly closing stock price divided by its mean value during the year preceding the joint venture announcement. By subtracting the market-specific volatility component, only the volatility idiosyncratic to the firm was considered; the higher the variance in the firm's stock price relative to its mean value, the higher the perceived firm-specific uncertainty.
time_window: the year preceding the joint venture announcement (monthly observations, January to December)

description: Dummy for firms that operated both taxicabs and limousines: lateral diversifiers are firms that had SIC code 412100 and no limousines in their fleet in 1992 but had at least one limousine in their fleet by 1997, so that sigma = 1 if the firm is a two-product firm and zero otherwise. In the 1997 cross-sectional regressions scope enters through STATUS dummies that cross firm scope with entry status (single-product incumbent, lateral diversifier, taxicab-only start-up, diversified entrant), with single-product incumbents as the excluded category.

Categorical variable that captures whether the firm diversified during the sample period, used as the explanatory variable in the first-differenced within-firm regressions of changes in taxicab productivity. Firms are classified as lateral diversifiers if they had SIC code 412100 and no limousines in their fleet in 1992 but had at least one limousine in their fleet by 1997.

theta = 1 if the firm is an incumbent and zero otherwise. In the 1997 cross-sectional productivity regressions entry status enters through STATUS dummies that cross entry status with firm scope (single-product incumbent, lateral diversifier, taxicab-only start-up, diversified entrant), with single-product incumbents as the excluded category. Firms that existed in 1992 but were small or reported incomplete data are treated as incumbents rather than start-ups.

The net cost of organizational rigidity, computed as the difference between d1, the gap in relative productivity between taxicab-only start-ups and taxicab-only incumbents [d1 = (beta s | taxicab-only start-up) - (beta s | taxicab-only incumbents)], and d2, the gap between taxicab and limousine start-ups and lateral diversifiers [d2 = (beta s | taxicab and limousine start-ups) - (beta s | lateral diversifiers)], so that C(delta) = d1 - d2. The difference in these two differences recovers the net cost of organizational rigidity, the main test of the second hypothesis; the standard error of C(delta) is computed as the square root of a weighted sum of the squared standard errors of the coefficient estimates, using the lincom command.

Total factor productivity in quantities, computed as the residual of a regression of a time-specific intercept, a market-level fixed effect, and the log of establishment-specific capital on the log of dollar denominated revenue; because the taxicab production function is approximately Leontief, the labor term is dropped in the final specification. TFPQ is interpreted as physical asset utilization relative to other fleets in the same market and is standardized to have mean zero within market (county), and is Winsorized at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles. The cross-sectional tests are performed on 1997 taxicab-only data.
scale: standardized to mean zero within market (county)

description: Change in taxicab productivity at the firm level between 1992 and 1997, obtained by taking differences in TFPQ between the two years to eliminate unobservable time-invariant firm characteristics that influence productivity. It is the dependent variable in the within-firm change regressions.

Coordination costs are not observed directly but estimated as the within-firm change in taxicab productivity (TFPQ, 1992 to 1997) of firms that added limousines (lateral diversifiers) compared with firms that did not, using first differences and a two-stage least squares check with limousine market concentration as the instrument. A negative effect indicates coordination costs.

Dummy variable coding all recordings by firms founded from the birth of the industry in 1887 till 1917 (and that had their first recording before 1920) as recordings by Victorian Era firms, where 1917 is the year when jazz was first commercialized. Of the 12 record companies producing the 1,985 recordings in the sample, four are coded as Victorian Era firms and eight as Jazz Era firms. The variable is used as a main effect and in interaction terms.

Dummy variable assigned the value of 1 each time a group's recording was reissued under a fictitious name. The variable is restricted to equal 1 only when the pseudonym was reissued under the same record company (92.3% of all pseudonyms) and not under a competitor.

Dummy variable for whether the group was a highbrow white orchestra; white nonorchestras are omitted as the reference category. Race was determined from multiple jazz pictorials of groups and musicians in that era, and 'orchestra' was identified by whether the group was identified as an 'orchestra' in its title.

Dummy variable for whether the group was a lowbrow black nonorchestra; black refers to both African-American and Creole, and three mixed-race groups were coded as black. Race was drawn from jazz pictorials and orchestra membership from whether the group was identified as an 'orchestra' in its title.

variable_name: Prop. of white orchestras produced by Jazz Era firms
description: Continuous variable that captures the annual proportion of white orchestra recordings released by Jazz Era firms. It is used to test H3A through its interaction with whether the firm is Victorian Era.

variable_name: Prop. of market represented by Jazz Era firms
description: Continuous variable capturing the annual proportion of the firms in the market that are Jazz Era firms. It is used to test H3B through its interaction with whether the firm is Victorian Era.

Dependent variable in the Heckman probit model, capturing whether the fictitious new name of the group contains the word 'orchestra'. The model is estimated conditional on the selection equation for the likelihood that a song by a black nonorchestra group was first reissued using a pseudonym. The correlation between the error terms in the selection and outcome equations is constrained to zero.

variable_name: Cost of recording: No. of takes
description: The number of takes for jazz recordings in the sample, extracted from catalogue numbers using Phillips and Owens' (2004) coding scheme. Multiple takes were very costly in the 1920s because of musician and equipment fatigue. The variable is examined by type of record company and type of group recorded.

Count of the number of times a song was rerecorded by multiple labels, drawn from Phillips and Owens' (2006) study of recording success. The authors treat the number of reissues as a supply-side indicator of recording success, since the more popular a song, the more companies and labels reissued it.

The authors counted all words belonging to a coherent sentence structure that were necessary to make sense of a metaphorical expression and classified those words as metaphorical communication. The measure divides the total number of words in a CEO's metaphorical communication during a conference call by the total number of words in the CEO's contentual communication during the same call. Coding was manual and context-sensitive, and dead metaphors, idioms, and technical jargon were excluded.

The authors manually coded journalists' statements about each firm in the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal into favorable, ambiguous, and unfavorable categories. The Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance was calculated as the ratio of favorable to unfavorable statements in the period after a focal conference call, controlling for the total number of statements. The dependent variable is the change in this favorability from the period before the focal call to the period after it.
time_window: period before vs. after each focal conference call

variable_name: Favorability of analysts' evaluations (EPS forecast measure)
description: The measure is based on one-year EPS forecasts from the Thomson Reuters I/B/E/S detailed forecast database. It is calculated as the difference between an analyst's first EPS forecast after the focal conference call and that analyst's last EPS forecast before the call, standardized by the share price at the close of the quarter in which the call was held and multiplied by 100. The authors then aggregate forecasts for each call and firm by taking the median change across all analysts.
time_window: last EPS forecast before the focal call to first EPS forecast after the call

description: The authors used individual analyst recommendations from the I/B/E/S detailed database. They classified recommendations as positive (I/B/E/S codes 1 and 2), neutral (code 3), or negative (codes 4 and 5), calculated the Janis-Fadner coefficient before and after the focal conference call, and used the difference between the two scores as the dependent variable.
time_window: period before vs. after each focal conference call

description: The authors computed the difference between a firm's quarterly EPS and the mean of analysts' EPS forecasts for that quarter, scaled by the actual EPS. They splined this variable and included negative earnings surprises, i.e., earnings below the mean of analysts' EPS forecasts, as a moderator.

Multimarket contact between airlines i and j is the sum of centrality-weighted proportions of their jointly occupied routes, where each market contact is weighted by the significance of the route to the firms, measured as the route's centrality (the proportion of an airline's routes that connect with that route) to each airline's network. The measure equals zero for carriers that meet in one or no routes, and higher values indicate a greater potential for mutual forbearance. Because it reflects both the number and the centrality of contacts, a smaller number of contacts in high-centrality markets can yield higher multimarket contact than a larger number of contacts in low-centrality markets. It is computed yearly for each focal airline i and each of its j competitors using the routes the airlines served at the start of each observation year; to test curvilinear effects, linear and squared terms (both multiplied by 100 for rescaling) are included. The equation itself is not legible in the text.
time_window: computed at the start of each observation year

variable_name: MMC ij /Average MMC i with competitors other than j
description: Relative multimarket contact is measured as multimarket contact between airline i and competitor j divided by the average multimarket contact between airline i and all its competitors other than j. Multimarket contact is defined as above and is computed based on the routes airlines i and j flew at the start of each year. The authors describe the variable as a form of competitive asymmetry.
time_window: computed based on routes flown at the start of each year

description: Relative size of airline i to its competitor airline j is measured as the size of competitor j divided by the size of airline i. The size of airline i is defined as the total available seat miles flown by i in the prior year, and the size of competitor j as the total available seat miles flown by j in the prior year. The authors test Hypotheses 3a and 3b by interacting relative size with multimarket contact ij.

variable_name: Airline i's entries into competitor j's routes
description: The dependent variable is the yearly number of entries by firm i into each of its j competitor's routes. Market entries were defined to occur in the first year an airline was reported in the OAG to fly one of a given competitor's incumbent routes. Because the dependent variables are count measures (integers truncated at zero), the number of market entries expected to occur within an interval of time is estimated with a Poisson regression model. During the observation period the 15 carriers entered 138 of each other's California routes, and the entry analysis includes 589 competitor-dyad/year observations.

variable_name: Airline i's exits from competitor j's markets
description: The dependent variable is the yearly number of exits by firm i from each of its j competitor's markets. Market exits were defined to occur in the first year an airline was no longer reported in the OAG to fly one of a given competitor's incumbent routes. As with entry, the count of exits expected within an interval of time is estimated with a Poisson regression model. During the observation period the 15 carriers exited 68 of each other's California routes, and the exit analysis includes 172 competitor-dyad/year observations.

Natural log of the number of years from company inception to the time of the acquisition. Start dates were obtained from the venture capital database, press releases about the acquisition, and news articles profiling the company or its founders; for 47 companies both month and year were available, and for the remaining 138 only the year was available, in which case the beginning of the year was used. The age of the target at the time of acquisition ranged from two months to 61 years with a mean of 8.4 years.

Abnormal return of the acquirer on the acquisition announcement day, computed with the market adjusted return model as the difference between the firm's actual return and the market return. A one-day window (day 0) is used to isolate the effect of the acquisition announcement, and firms with other announcements on the announcement date were dropped. The abnormal return is used as the dependent variable in the regressions.

Indicator variable set to 1 if the target held one or more patents during the three years prior to the acquisition and 0 otherwise. It was built from a data set of 3,858 individual patents held by the potential target firms, including filing date, grant date and a detailed list of citing patents. Only 25% of the targets in the sample had a patent within three years of the acquisition.
time_window: three years prior to the acquisition

description: Indicator of the target's ownership status defined as 1 if the target was private and 0 if it was public. Private targets accounted for 67% of the sample. The variable is entered in the acquirer-profit regressions and interacted with target age.

A normalized measure of the citations received by the patents owned by the target (patent stock), adjusted for the age of the target; it values a patent portfolio from the number of citations a patent received in subsequent years and how recent the patent is, extrapolated to a consistent 30 year lag period following Hall et al. (2005). The metric is divided by the number of employees at the target so that it is uncorrelated with target size. For the hazard analysis the metric is calculated at the end of each focal month.
scale: natural log of citations per employee

description: Total venture capital funding that the target received until the time of acquisition, converted to January 1995 equivalents using the CPI. For the hazard models of acquisition risk the metric is calculated for each month by including all venture funding received up to and including the focal month. At the time of acquisition targets had from US$0 to US$110 million in funding with a mean of US$2.1 million.

In the Cox proportional hazard model the event being explained is the acquisition of the target firm by a buyer, and each potential target contributes a monthly observation of its characteristics until it is acquired or the study period ends. The data set covers 377 potential target firms and 20,057 monthly observations, and firms that were never acquired are retained as non-events. Shared frailty by potential targets is included to incorporate unobserved heterogeneity in target specific risk.

Firm capability is measured using stochastic frontier estimation, a method that measures a firm's efficiency by its ability to turn resources into outputs and incorporates an inefficiency term estimated by maximum likelihood. Inputs to film projects in a given year are the budget and the talent available to the firm (cumulative awards, calculated with a Koyck lag) and the output is gross revenue. The predicted inefficiency term is used to compute technological efficiency for every firm-year; estimates of efficiency range between 0 and 1 and are treated as estimates of firm capability for the corresponding firm-year observation.
time_window: given year; cumulative awards calculated with a Koyck lag

description: The number of major studios with which the focal independent studio has a partnership in a given year. Since there are six majors in the U.S. motion picture industry, this variable ranges from 0 to 6.
Measured as the total number of alliances the focal studio has had with majors in the past.
Measured as the number of majors dropped from the focal studio's alliance portfolio since the last period plus the number of new partners added to the alliance portfolio.

Measured based on the genres of the movies produced by the focal studio in a given year. Six general movie genres that can be clearly distinguished from one another are used, so a studio's movies in a given year can target a maximum of six genres. The level of specialization is defined as 6 minus the number of distinct genres targeted by the studio's movies, so that the higher the number of genres targeted by a studio's movies in a given year, the lower the studio's specialization in that year, and vice versa. A movie's genres were recorded only when listed consistently in both IMDb and Rotten Tomatoes.

Business groups' social endowment of high status measured by the centrality of the owner-manager family in the 1987 intergroup marriage network, using Bonacich's (1987) centrality score. The score considers both the amount of deference received and the extent to which deference is directed, and is calculated with the software program UCINET using the standard setting for the Beta term of 0.995/maxeigen. It is a cross-sectional measure for year 1987 and is therefore absorbed by the group fixed effects.

variable_name: Bonacich Measure of Status by Year
description: Business groups' social endowment of high status in a given year measured by the centrality of the owner-manager family in that year's intergroup marriage network, using Bonacich's (1987) centrality score as described for the 1987 measure. It is the time-varying version of the status measure.

A dummy that takes the value of one if the business group's ROA performance is between the 25th percentile and the 75th percentile of industry-adjusted and industry-weighted ROA performance relative to peers. The authors state that the range for mediocre performance is by far the largest, with low performance by those in the bottom 25th quartile lacking resources to pay a bribe, and that business groups wanted to remain in the top 25% of performance relative to peers.

The interaction term between 'Bonacich Measure of Status in 1987' (high status measured by the Bonacich centrality in the year 1987 marriage network among Korean business groups) and 'Mediocre ROA Performance'. It is a cross-sectional measure for year 1987 and therefore gets automatically absorbed as part of the group fixed effects.

The interaction term between 'Bonacich Measure of Status by Year' (high status measured by the Bonacich centrality in this year's marriage network among Korean business groups) and 'Mediocre ROA Performance'. It replaces the 1987 status term of Definition 1 with the time-varying status measure and is the measure that fully reflects status change over time.

variable_name: Yearly Bribe Paid by Business Group
description: The annual bribe amount (KRW billion) paid by each of the 40 business groups. The annual group bribery amount ranges from zero to 14 billion won with an average of 1.45 billion won, and each business group paid 8.57 billion won on average over the 6 years, ranging from 0.2 billion won to 35 billion won in total.

Dummy variable that is equal to 1 if the patent family filed a priority in the United States. Priority is established in the patent authority that a patent family is filed in first, and it is considered to be the country of invention.

Number of forward citations from outside the USPTO within 5 years of a patent family's publication, excluding firm self-citations. The measure was adjusted by the industry average number of forward citations for the filing year (using four-digit NACE) and citations from patents within the USPTO were excluded.
time_window: within 5 years of patent family publication

description: Count of the number of countries in which the patent family was granted, based on Patstat's DOCDB identifier, measuring the geographic scope of the innovation. The number was weighted by the average number of patent family countries for all firms in the firm's main industry (using four-digit NACE) for the filing year.

Considering four-digit IPC technology classes, the total number of other companies creating patents in the same four-digit IPC technology class as the focal patent family in each country during the filing year of the focal patent family, divided by the total number of companies that create patents in that technology class in the year. It was built from Patstat and geocoded data on inventor locations for patent families not filed in the USPTO.
time_window: filing year of the focal patent family

description: Dummy variable for each patent family that is equal to 1 if an MNC files a case in a US Federal Court alleging infringement (of their patented innovation) over the time-period from 2000 to 2020. Cases filed in court name the specific USPTO granted patent alleged to be infringed, which was matched to the patent family number in Patstat.

Burt's network constraint measure used to capture the cohesion of each firm's exploratory alliance network. For the focal firm i, cohesion Ci is a function of the proportion of the total strength of the alliances that ego firm i devotes to a given alter firm j in proportion to the sum of relational strengths of all other of ego firm's alter ties (0 = no alliance, 1 = non-asset alliances, 2 = asset alliances/joint ventures) and of the degree of triadic closure between i, j and third parties k. The cohesion-squared term for the exploratory network was also calculated. The formula block in the text was not readable, so the exact specification is not recorded.

Burt's network constraint measure used to capture the cohesion of each firm's exploitative alliance network. For the focal firm i, cohesion Ci is a function of the proportion of the total strength of the alliances that ego firm i devotes to a given alter firm j in proportion to the sum of relational strengths of all other of ego firm's alter ties (0 = no alliance, 1 = non-asset alliances, 2 = asset alliances/joint ventures) and of the degree of triadic closure between i, j and third parties k. The cohesion-squared term for the exploitative network was also calculated. The formula block in the text was not readable, so the exact specification is not recorded.

The dependent variable, the addition of new exploratory partners, was evaluated as the number of a firm's exploratory partners at Time t+1 that were in neither its exploratory alliance network nor its exploitative network at any time before. It is a count variable.

The dependent variable, the addition of new exploitative partners, was evaluated as the number of a firm's exploitative partners at Time t+1 that were in neither its exploratory alliance network nor its exploitative network at any time before. It is a count variable.

Coded one if product code x can be traced through corporate ownership change to a producer of x in the year prior to the entry event, that is, the product is acquired from an incumbent; zero otherwise. A firm is identified as entering market x in year t when product code x appears in the firm's portfolio for the first time in year t and remains listed in year t+1. When one of the firm's existing divisions or subsidiaries also adds product code x in the same year as the acquisition, the case is conservatively coded as entry via internal development.
time_window: entry year (acquisition traced in the prior year)

variable_name: Where the new market resides: 1 = inside; 0 = outside a firm's primary business domain
description: Each firm's primary business domain is classified according to the root categories of CorpTech's hierarchical product classification structure; the primary business domain of most firms in the sample is telecommunications. Entries inside the primary business domain are distinguished from those outside by comparing the root category of a product market and the category of the firm's primary business domain. An entry is coded one when the product market shares the same root of the hierarchy as the firm's primary business, and zero otherwise.
scale: 1 = inside; 0 = outside a firm's primary business domain

description: Firm n's proximity toward market x in year t, measured by taking the maximum value of the pairwise similarity index among the firm's products each year with respect to the market entered, i.e., the distance to the closest product in the firm's portfolio. The pairwise similarity index for two products is the normalized count of firms that produce both products, calculated as the angular separation between the two products' presence vectors across a population of firms; it equals one when the two products have identical patterns of joint occurrence and zero when they do not co-occur at all. If a firm in the population is also in the estimation sample, that firm's products are removed when constructing the similarity index for the given firm. The value used in estimating entry mode is the degree of relatedness observed one year prior to market entry.

variable_name: Trajectory of relatedness: amount of change in degree of relatedness
description: Computed by subtracting the initial greater-than-zero value of the degree of relatedness from the value of the degree of relatedness one year prior to entry. A positive difference shows the firm's movement toward market x, a negative difference shows movement away from market x, and a difference of zero shows no change with respect to market x.
time_window: from the initial non-zero value to one year prior to entry

description: The amount of time, in years, that elapsed since the initial observation of a greater-than-zero value of the degree of relatedness until one year before firm n enters market x. The longer the duration, the more time firm n has been in the vicinity of market x, although the degree of relatedness may vary over time. A dummy variable indicates cases of left censoring where the duration is one year but that is the first year of observing the firm in the sample.
time_window: since the first non-zero relatedness value until one year prior to entry

description: The firm's external financial resources, measured as the ratio of its market-to-book value. The authors expect this measure to be positively correlated with the use of acquisition as entry mode, since financial resources in the form of highly valued stock can be readily applied to make acquisitions.

The ratio of R&D expenditures to net sales in the year prior to entry. Because a few firms experienced a sharp decrease in net sales in certain years, the maximum R&D intensity is restricted to 100 percent. The authors expect this measure to be negatively correlated with the use of acquisition as entry mode.

Expected pay mix was measured as the percentage of total pay that employers planned or expected to distribute through the group reward plan. If group plans covered multiple hierarchical levels of employees and the pay mix ratios differed by level, an average weighted by the percentage of participants at each level was calculated. Respondents failed to provide the data necessary to calculate expected pay mix for 139 plans.

Actual pay mix was calculated as the ratio of the incentive payouts from a group incentive plan to the fixed pay (wages and salaries) received by the group. If group plans covered multiple hierarchical levels of employees and the pay mix ratios differed by level, an average weighted by the percentage of participants at each level was calculated. Respondents failed to provide the data necessary to calculate actual pay mix for 114 plans.
scale: ratio of incentive payouts to fixed pay

description: Unit size was the natural log of the number of employees in the organizational unit in which the plan was embedded. For profit-sharing plans, unit size functioned as a precise measure of group size, since all employees in a unit were included in a plan. In other cases, multiple plans might be embedded in a single unit, or only a portion of a unit's employees might be included in a plan; however, for 80 percent of the plans in the sample, more than 70 percent of the employees in a given unit were included in the plans.
Firm size was measured as the natural logarithm of the number of employees in a firm.

Level of measurement was calculated as the organizational level at which a plan measured group performance. For plans that measured performance at multiple levels, the authors used the level of measurement encompassing the smallest group. The measurement levels were coded (1) whole company, (2) group, division, subsidiary, or strategic business unit, (3) facility, (4) department, (5) work group, and (6) small team.
Percent management was the percentage of plan participants who were senior, midlevel, or first-line managers.
Percent professionals was the percentage of plan participants who were nonmanagement professionals.
Quality was a dummy variable coded 1 if a plan used quality as one of its payout-determining measures. About 40 percent of the pay plans used quality as a determinant of payouts.

Number of performance measures was the number of performance measures used in determining payouts. Approximately a third of the pay plans used only a single measure of performance, and about 3 percent used more than ten measures.
Age of plan was the number of years a plan had been in existence.

An indicator equal to one if at least one of the project members involved in the technology selection decisions had spent several years working on a relevant technology in the research organization, and zero otherwise. It is the empirical indicator of the research-based knowledge that revolutionary advances draw on.

The capacity of the experimental fabrication facility dedicated to the development project, expressed in wafers per week. The authors treat it as the indicator of the breadth of experimentation efforts, i.e., of how many different experiments can be performed in a given unit of time.

The minimum time taken to fabricate a test sample at the experimental fabrication facility, that is, the minimum time elapsed between the experimental design and its results. It captures whether the experimentation setup is optimized for rapid, focused feedback.

The fraction of project members participating in technology selection decisions that had not participated in a complete project aimed at developing a major new semiconductor process generation. The authors use this variable in the regressions rather than the correlated measures counting full generations of prior project experience, so higher values indicate less project experience.

The lowest known upper bound model of product performance, an analytical function of fundamental parameters such as the minimum line width and the number of layers of a semiconductor. It represents the maximum achievable performance given the product's base of fundamental technology; in the analysis the residual of technological potential is used, and higher values indicate a greater revolutionary component.

Actual realized performance divided by technological potential; because technological potential is the lowest upper bound, it is always less than one. It captures the impact of the details describing the interaction between the fundamental technologies and the complex context of application, and higher values indicate a greater evolutionary component.

Gate density, the number of transistors per unit of area on the integrated circuit, which is the most critical driver of both manufacturing cost and product performance. Because gate density increases with time on average, the measure of performance is the residual of a regression of the logarithm of gate density against time, or time is included explicitly in the regressions.
scale: transistors per unit of area, in logarithms

description: A count of the number of referrals from the PCP to the specialist in the year preceding the index (first-opinion) consultation between patient and specialist. The authors also report a median split in which a dummy variable takes the value of one if there have been nine or more referrals between the PCP and specialist in the past year, and a binary indicator equal to one if the specialist seen by the patient is the provider with whom the PCP has the strongest tie in that specialty. Because the regressions include PCP-by-specialty fixed effects, the estimates come from variation across patients within a PCP-specialty combination.
time_window: the year preceding the index visit

description: Set equal to one if there was a second opinion and to zero otherwise. Second opinions were identified as all instances in which a patient saw a second specialist in the same specialty following a first-time consultation in that specialty; the second opinion visit had to occur within 180 days of the first consultation, and both appointments had to originate from a PCP's referral. The authors report that under this definition 4 percent of all first-time specialist referrals were followed by a second opinion consultation. A patient who trusts the specialist is expected to be less likely to obtain a second opinion.
time_window: within 180 days of the first consultation

description: Set equal to one if there was a follow-up visit and to zero otherwise.
