description: Four dummy variables describing the type of foreign expansion. An expansion was coded as horizontal if it was within the same three-digit SIC category as the firm's core business activities, as related if it was within the same two-digit SIC category but not the same three-digit category, as vertical if it was within the firm's value-added chain, and as unrelated if none of the above three categories applied.
time_window: at the time of the expansion

description: An index designed to capture goal configuration through the combination of both major and minor goals. It gives additional weight to emphasizing major goals, as compared to minor goals, and provides a deflation factor based on the total number of goals emphasized as a percentage of the total possible. The index is defined as [2 (number of major goals) + (number of minor goals)] x [(number of major goals + number of minor goals)/16]; higher values indicate a more dispersed goal configuration.

The sum of the responses indicating that the goal is a 'major goal.' Respondents were asked to indicate how important each of the listed goals was to their business, using a response scale with three categories: 'major goal,' 'minor goal,' or 'not a goal,' which was used to facilitate translation and to avoid cultural-based acquiescence or extremity bias.
Operationalized as the firm's country-of-origin; the authors state this measure has been widely used in the literature.

A measure adapted from the Roth, Schweiger and Morrison (1991) study, designed to differentiate industry position through determining the extent to which the firm confronts global competitive forces. Respondents were asked to consider the primary sector of the industry in which their business competes and indicate how characteristic six statements were in describing their industry position, with response categories ranging from 1 = 'not at all characteristic' to 5 = 'extremely characteristic.' Based on these variables, firms were partitioned into three groups (multidomestic, global, multifocal) using cluster analysis.

Defined by the percentage of total sales that are earned abroad. The authors state this measure was consistent with the operationalization used by Garnier (1982) and has also been used to indicate foreign commitment, the extent of foreign activity and foreign dependence.

Respondents were provided a list of possible rewards criteria, with the listed criteria paralleling the set of potential firm goals, and were instructed to indicate the criteria for executive compensation in their business, checking each item their firm uses as a criterion; they were also provided the opportunity to indicate other reward criteria that were not listed. A rewards/compensation index was created by summing the number of criteria that were indicated as being used.

A self-reported measure with objective scales, asking respondents to indicate their firm's average annual after-tax return on assets during the past three years using predefined intervals. Response categories were: 1 = 'greater than 25 percent,' 2 = 'between 20 percent and 25 percent,' 3 = 'between 15 percent and 20 percent,' 4 = 'between 10 percent and 15 percent,' 5 = 'between 5 percent and 10 percent,' 6 = 'between 0 percent and 5 percent,' and 7 = 'negative.'
time_window: average annual performance during the past three years

description: A self-reported measure with objective scales, asking respondents to indicate their firm's average annual sales growth rate during the past three years using predefined intervals. Response categories were: 1 = 'greater than 25 percent,' 2 = 'between 20 percent and 25 percent,' 3 = 'between 15 percent and 20 percent,' 4 = 'between 10 percent and 15 percent,' 5 = 'between 5 percent and 10 percent,' 6 = 'between 0 percent and 5 percent,' and 7 = 'negative.'
time_window: average annual performance during the past three years

description: A subjective measure asking respondents to indicate the global performance of their firm over the last 3 years as compared to other (U.K., Japanese, or U.S.) firms in the industry in their country, a country-based reference point used because the pretest indicated that not all companies had the capability to assess accurately their performance as compared to firms in other country locations. Items comprising the scale were the 16 goal items used to operationalize goal configuration, with response categories 1 = 'below average,' 2 = 'average,' and 3 = 'above average.' A 'relative' performance index was created for each firm, where the index was the average reported performance only for goals that were indicated as being major goals.

Records the year in which a college or university initiated intercollegiate basketball, ice hockey, and lacrosse. The variable was coded as one when a college incorporated the activity and zero at other points in the observation period. It was coded from data on when schools began to sponsor football, basketball, ice hockey, and lacrosse programs.

variable_name: prior establishment of a football program
description: Operationalized as the establishment of an intercollegiate football program prior to incorporating one of the emerging sports. Because of the early prominence and prevalence of football, its distinctive resource demands, and the early inclusion of a football program as a 'standard' component of a modern college, the prior establishment of a football program at a school is used as evidence of a dominant logic in the local organization.
time_window: prior to incorporating the emerging sport

description: Operationalized as organizational membership in the NCAA prior to incorporating one of the three emerging sports programs. This variable receives a value of one if a school joined the NCAA prior to incorporating one of the three sports and a value of zero if it joined the NCAA after incorporating one of the three sports, or if a school never joined the NCAA. For lacrosse the variable was not included in the models because its correlation with playing football is 0.95.
time_window: prior to incorporating the emerging sport

description: Fieldwide emulation is operationalized for each emerging sport as the time-varying cumulative count of all schools that have incorporated the sport in prior years. The measure follows diffusion research that uses cumulative counts to proxy generalized legitimacy and contagion pressure.

variable_name: count of prior incorporations in a given region
description: A time-varying, segment-specific count of prior incorporations in a given region, i.e. the number of schools that have previously incorporated a sport in the focal school's region. Region is used to proxy functional considerations and corresponds to the regional classifications used by the NCAA and the NAIA as early as 1910.

variable_name: count of prior public school incorporations
description: Operationalized as counts of prior public school incorporations. This variable receives a value of zero for all nonpublic schools (religious schools and private schools) and a value of the number of the prior public school incorporations for schools that have a public affiliation. It represents the spread of the incorporation of each sport strategy across only public schools.

Interpartner trust was treated as a third-order construct, incorporating affective and calculative beliefs and forbearance and influence acceptance behaviors. Affective trust items reflect partner habitualization and institutionalization aspects and were modified from Nooteboom et al. (1997); the calculative trust scale was developed from Lewicki and Bunker (1996); forbearance items were modified from measures used by Gundlach et al. (1995) and Parkhe (1993a); the influence acceptance measure includes items adapted from Kumar et al. (1992) and work on conformity by Kiesler and Kiesler (1969). For the structural model, the mean scores for the affective and calculative trust dimensions identify the latent construct of trust beliefs and the mean scores for forbearance and influence acceptance identify trust behaviors, which in turn identify interpartner trust. Items were rated on seven-point response scales, one influence acceptance item being reverse-coded.

Alliance performance is viewed as a second-order construct comprising the dimensions effectiveness, efficiency, and responsiveness, each assessed with perceptual performance indicators. Effectiveness uses a three-item scale adapted from Fisher et al. (1997); efficiency uses a three-item scale drawing on Majumdar (1998) and Sarkar et al. (2001); responsiveness uses four items modified from Ayers et al. (1997). Composites for the effectiveness, efficiency, and responsiveness dimensions are posited to identify the latent construct of ISA performance, and one item in each of the effectiveness, efficiency and responsiveness scales is reverse-coded.

Respondents were asked to indicate the number of full-time employees in the alliance. This size measure distinguishes between small/intimate and large/bureaucratic alliances. A natural logarithmic transformation was employed to reduce variance.

A three-item measure adapted from Kumar et al. (1995a). A prompting sentence, 'How fair is your firm's share of alliance outcomes and earnings considering ...', was employed to emphasize the relative nature of the partners' rewards for the ISA's joint work; the items concern the alliance roles and responsibilities assigned, the importance of the firm's contributions to alliance goal achievement, and the overall balance of skills and resources contributed by both sides.

Partner similarity was assessed using an index of items (a formative scale) in which each item reflects a single aspect of the construct, because the fieldwork suggested the construct may be viewed from a formative measurement perspective. The items cover similarities between the partners on aspects such as profit seeking, new product development, technological expertise, organizational culture, and volume of business. Emphasis was placed on ensuring the content validity and theoretical basis of the index; the highest variance inflation factor among the indicators was 2.07.
scale: seven-point scale anchored by 'strongly disagree' and 'strongly agree'

description: The main independent variable is the posttreatment dummy, Treated × Post. Treated takes the value 1 for firms in New Jersey and 0 otherwise, and Post takes the value 1 for observations after the start of the NJ PFL program (i.e., from 2009 onward) and 0 otherwise. Ventures in California are omitted from the main analytical sample.
time_window: 2004-2011, with the posttreatment period from 2009 onward

description: The main dependent variable for evaluating venture performance is whether a business has profits in a given year. The dependent variable, Has Profits, equals 1 if the business has profits of zero or more and equals 0 otherwise. A binary measure is used because profit amounts may be subject to distortions resulting from different accounting procedures.

The main measure of the venture's innovation type is High-Tech, a binary variable indicating whether a firm is in high-tech industries. Whether a firm is in a high-tech industry is based on the Standard Industry Classification code.

Number of Key Employees represents the total number of individuals responsible for key job functions and responsibilities. It allows the author to examine whether employment growth or attrition in these areas occurs posttreatment.

The average number of weekly work hours for active owner-operators essential to business operations, used as a proxy for how much people work in the absence of data on employee work time. Active owner-operators are defined as owners who provide regular assistance or advice regarding the day-to-day operations of the business rather than providing only money or occasional operating assistance.
Total payroll expenses on employee wages and benefits divided by the total number of employees.
Total outputs (revenue from selling goods and services) divided by the total number of employees. This variable proxies for employee-level productivity.

Binary variable indicating whether any of the patents the focal incumbent firm applied for (and were subsequently granted) in observation year t cited the focal new venture patent. A focal incumbent firm may apply for multiple patents in year t; if any of these patents cited the focal new venture patent, the variable was equal to 1. The authors treat the incumbent as having absorbed the focal new venture technology/patent when it used this technology in its own inventive pursuits.

Continuous measure based on the cumulative investment that the focal incumbent firm had made in the focal new venture for each year. Prior CVC research typically used a dichotomous indicator, but the authors' measure also captures the level of managerial commitment to the investee. Because the marginal influence of investment levels was expected to wane as the absolute investment level increased, the values were transformed using a natural logarithm.

Calculated in two steps. First, an individual inventor's clustering coefficient was computed as the proportion of his or her collaborators who were themselves directly linked to each other. The clustering coefficient of the overall network was the average of this measure across all inventors in the network. It can range from 0 (no clustering) to 1 (completely clustered).

Computed on a yearly basis, measuring the proportion of inventor dyads that were connected by a path of any length. Specifically, connectedness is equal to the fraction of all dyads in a network for which there is an undirected path from inventor i to inventor j, and it can range from 0 (completely disconnected) to 1 (completely connected). Unlike density, it also captures the distribution of ties or reachability of inventors in the network.

Each firm's diversity type was classified for the pre-buyout period into single business, related business, unrelated business or conglomerate, using a scheme derived from Rumelt's (1974) typology. The classification started from a listing of the identifiable businesses of the firm and their relative importance to the firm's overall operations, using company descriptions of their business activities and, where available, sales data by line of business. Relatedness was judged by whether the lines of business shared common assets or resources such as distribution channels, purchasing economies of scale and technology, with SIC codes used for assistance and supplemented by the judgement of the researchers; for the statistical tests the single business/related diversification categories and the unrelated/conglomerate categories were combined.
scale: four-category classification (single business, related business, unrelated business, conglomerate)

description: Each firm's diversification type was classified in the post-buyout period using the same four-category scheme as for the pre-buyout period, as of December 1991 or the date the firm returned to public ownership, whichever was earlier. Firms that stayed in the same diversification class, focused their activities (moved from a higher to a lower diversification type), increased the scope of their activities, or were complete bustups are distinguished; 14 firms considerably focused their activities. For the chi-square test the 2 x 2 contingency table combined the single business/related diversity categories and the unrelated diversity/conglomerate categories in both the pre- and post-buyout phases.
scale: four-category classification (single line of business, related diversity, unrelated diversity, conglomerate) plus bustup
time_window: post-buyout period, as of December 1991 or the date of return to public ownership

description: Firms were classified as specialist-associated when the MBO was undertaken with the assistance of a buyout specialist, and as 'independent' MBOs when the firm arranged the financing of the buyout independently. Twenty of the 32 firms in the sample underwent the MBO with the assistance of a buyout specialist and the remaining 12 did not. For the test the firms were cross-tabulated against the combined pre-buyout diversification categories (single line of business/related diversity versus unrelated diversity/conglomerate).
time_window: at the time of the buyout

variable_name: number of months under the MBO organizational form
description: The number of months the buyout entity remained under the MBO organizational form, measured from the initiation of the buyout proposal until the earliest of the date the firm returned to public ownership, the date it ceased to exist, or December 31, 1991. When a division of the post-buyout firm or the remaining assets of the firm as a group were sold, the assets were treated as leaving the firm and the analysis. Sixteen firms remained private for over the median of 45 months; the mean was 55.8 months for the conglomerate and unrelated-diversified firms together and 51.4 months for the single and related-diversified firms as a group.
time_window: from initiation of the buyout proposal to the earliest of return to public ownership, cessation, or December 31, 1991

description: Firms were classified by whether they had no payment difficulties or had payment difficulties in managing and fulfilling their debt obligations at the ending date, the latter indicated by renegotiating the terms of their debt or exchanging debt to obtain more flexibility in making payments, and/or by filing for protection under Chapter 11 of the bankruptcy code. Five of the 32 firms renegotiated or exchanged debt one or more times and four filed for Chapter 11 by December 31, 1991, so that 9 firms (28%) were having difficulties servicing their debt, while 23 firms had no apparent difficulties. Cross-tabulated by post-buyout diversification type, the incidence of financial distress was independent of diversification type.
scale: dichotomous (no payment difficulties vs payment difficulties)

description: Binary variable equal to one for each M&A lawyer dyad assigned to work on a focal M&A mandate and zero if the dyad was unassigned. For each mandate the authors constructed the entire risk set of all possible M&A lawyer dyads potentially available to the advising law firm. A firm with four M&A lawyers has six possible lawyer dyads; the assigned dyad is coded one and the remaining dyads are coded zero.

Binary variable equal to one if a lawyer dyad was assigned on another M&A mandate worked on by the law firm within the prior 24 months and zero otherwise. For a focal M&A deal in May 2002, the 24-month window is computed from June 2000. A positive relationship between prior collaboration and collaboration on the focal project indicates repeat collaboration; a negative relationship indicates new collaboration.

Captures the lawyer dyad's total prior experience working on M&A mandates for the focal client. It is measured as the sum of the number of prior M&A mandates each lawyer in the dyad has worked on for the focal client. For example, if lawyer A worked with the focal client once before and lawyer B twice, the variable equals 1 + 2 = 3.

Captures the firm's prior experience with the focal client, calculated as the number of prior M&A mandates the focal law firm has previously advised the client on, independent of the particular lawyers staffed on the deal.

Binary variable equal to one if the focal client is a FTSE 100 company listed on the London Stock Exchange and zero otherwise. The FTSE 100 is described as the most prominent stock index in the UK, and inclusion in this index bestows firms with reputational capital, market power, and higher status.

Captures the degree to which clients distribute their M&A legal work among many different law firms as opposed to fewer. It is measured as a three-year moving sum of the number of law firms used by the client for its M&A legal work, which indicates the pattern of clients' outsourcing preferences.

Captures the capacity constraint of the lawyers in the dyad because of their workload at the time of the deal. It is computed as the sum of the number of M&A mandates that both M&A lawyers had been staffed on in the 180 days before the focal mandate.

Measured as the size of the focal firm's portfolio of clients. A larger portfolio of clients presents greater resource management complexity and resource constraint. Computed as the number of clients in a law firm's portfolio to which it provided M&A legal services over a three-year window.

Ordered categorical measure of the breadth of contractual tasks that the private actor undertakes, built on the PPP contractual categories reported in the PFI database. Cases coded as zero include PPPs in which the private operator's primary task is to build the asset (which it then leases back from the public actor) and never involve ownership; cases coded as one are those in which the private actor builds and operates the facility but does not design it or typically own it. Cases coded as two are those in which the private operator is responsible for most of the activities of the project (including financing and ownership) but not the design phase; cases coded as three are those in which the private operator designs, builds, operates, and provides capital to invest in the facility as well as assumes full ownership rights for an extended period of time.
scale: ordered categories from zero (lowest) to three (highest)

variable_name: past PPPs executed in the country
description: Count of cumulative public–private collaborations in the particular country and sector of the PPP, based on the year in which the PPP was signed and on the list of PPPs in the database, with 1992 as the first observation year. For instance, if the PPP was in water and sewerage, the authors counted the number of past PPPs in water and sewerage executed in the country in previous years. The sector-specific focus follows the rationale that partnering capabilities are likely to vary across sectors.
time_window: cumulative prior years up to the signing year

description: Number of years since the establishment of a country-level government unit or public agency specialized in the design, governing, and/or monitoring of PPPs, with older units assumed to have more developed routines and governance processes. The existence of such a unit and the year when it was created were researched and recorded for each country in the data set through websites and numerous archival sources.

variable_name: past PPPs executed by the firm
description: Cumulative number of past PPPs engaged in by the private actor in a given sector and country. The authors consider that experience depends on the intersection of country- and sector-specific conditions affecting the ability of private actors to learn about the specific activity of the PPP as well as the specific institutional attributes of the country.
time_window: cumulative prior years up to the signing year

description: Percentage of past PPPs executed by the private actor in the same country that had the presence of state capital through equity-based arrangements and/or public subsidies. The presence of state capital in a special purpose vehicle (SPV) crafted to manage the PPP is interpreted as an indicator of a firm's ability to comanage specialized public–private organizational units with relevant public actors. To compute this ratio, the authors considered at least three instances of past PPPs in the country executed by the private actor.
time_window: past PPPs prior to the observed PPP

description: Index of institutional quality built from variables reported in the IMD World Competitiveness Yearbook. The authors performed a factor analysis based on three institutional features that are expected to affect the perceived quality of the local environment for PPPs and that seem to be highly related: quality of the bureaucracy, absence of bribery or corruption, and perceived transparency. The index is computed as the average of those measures (Cronbach's alpha = 0.808).

A dummy variable coded 1 if one of the original founders of a company was the CEO at the time the company went public. A score of 1 therefore indicates the presence of a founder-CEO at the time of the IPO.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Equals the percentage of shares outstanding that were beneficially owned by an IPO firm's CEO upon completion of the IPO. The measure reflects concentration of stock ownership in the hands of a single individual.

Ownership by multiple venture capitalist entities, which in the sample ranged from one to fourteen VCs per firm. To capture the degree to which a large proportion of an IPO firm's shares were concentrated in the hands of one or a few VCs, the authors constructed a Herfindahl index by squaring and summing the percentage of stock ownership of each venture capitalist that owned stock in the company upon completion of the IPO.

Calculated by summing the tenure with an IPO company of each management team member listed in the prospectus and dividing the sum by the total number of management team members. It captures how much experience a management team's members had working together at the time of the IPO.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The authors identified the lead underwriter for each IPO and the institutional investors that owned stock in each IPO at the end of the quarter in which the company went public, then determined for each underwriter-investor pair how frequently the two actors participated in offerings together, collecting data from IPOs conducted in 1991 on 4,754 such pairs. For each pair they identified the number of offerings in which investment bank i participated as lead manager or comanager and institutional investor j owned shares, and the number of deals bank i participated in as lead or comanager, and calculated a Herfindahl-type concentration ratio for each deal network k as the sum of squared ratios of pair offerings to bank deals.
time_window: end of the quarter in which the company went public; embeddedness based on 1991 IPO transactions

description: Defined as delisting from the primary exchange on which a firm traded with a delisting code between 500 and 585, codes associated with firm bankruptcy and the inability of a firm to maintain the minimum size, shareholder number, and stock price requirements for continued listing. The authors constructed a time-varying dichotomous outcome measure coded 1 during the year a firm was delisted and 0 otherwise. A firm was dropped from the sample after delisting, and the others remained right-censored.
time_window: the five years following the IPO

description: Participants reviewed one of two restaurant menus and were not given category labels. The low-atypicality menu contained eight items, seven of them Chinese and one Thai; the high-atypicality menu also contained eight items, four diagnostic and representative of Chinese cuisine and the remaining items linked to French, Greek, Mexican and Spanish cuisines, with items rated as having a 0% likelihood of cuisine co-occurrence. Menu items were pretested to be diagnostic and representative of a single cuisine.

Role instructions at the onset of the task told participants that the restaurant owners either would (high accountability) or would not (low accountability) monitor and use their evaluations. In the high-accountability condition participants were told they would be interviewed by the restaurant owner at the end of the survey, that they should be ready to justify their opinions, and that the discussion would be taped; in the low-accountability condition they were told they were not selected for this interview, that no one would ever know who they were, and that all information would be discarded after use.

Participants assigned stars to each restaurant on a five-point scale (1 = low and 5 = high) and also reported whether they like the restaurant and its quality on an 11-point scale ranging from 1 (dislike intensely/very low quality) to 11 (like a great deal/very high quality). The three answers were averaged (Cronbach's alpha = 0.84); the stars variable was rescaled (multiplied by 2.2) to be consistent with the other scales. Ratings were entered after each menu, and this is an ex-ante evaluation of the restaurant.

Study 1b used the same atypicality manipulation as Study 1a: participants reviewed one of two restaurant menus with no category labels, a low-atypicality menu drawing on a single dominant cuisine and a high-atypicality menu combining several distinct cuisines whose items had no cuisine co-occurrence.

In the high-accountability condition participants were informed that they were selected to explain their answers at the end of the survey and that they needed to be ready to justify their opinion of the restaurant to other restaurant goers; they were told they would need to draft an email that other restaurant goers would review and evaluate. The accountability manipulation was identical to the manipulation used in Study 1a in all other respects.

Study 1b uses the same dependent variable as Study 1a, combining assigned stars, liking and quality ratings into an averaged index of appeal. The internal consistency of the index in this study was Cronbach's alpha = 0.77.

Instead of a menu, participants reviewed a set list of five items and were not given category labels. The low-atypicality set list contained four items from one genre (jazz) and one from a different genre (rock); the high-atypicality set list contained three items from rock and one each from reggae and jazz, with the musical styles having a low likelihood of co-occurrence (under 20%). Musical styles were used as set items to evoke genres and were pretested to be diagnostic and representative of a single genre.

Study 1c uses the same accountability manipulation as Study 1b, in which participants in the high-accountability condition had to explain and justify their evaluation to their peers, whereas participants in the low-accountability condition had no expectation of justifying their decision.

Study 1c uses the same dependent variable as Studies 1a and 1b, an averaged index of assigned stars, liking and quality ratings of the band. The internal consistency of the index in this study was Cronbach's alpha = 0.84.

Study 2a uses the same stimulus material and atypicality manipulation as Study 1a: participants reviewed one of two restaurant menus with no category labels, a low-atypicality menu drawing on one dominant cuisine and a high-atypicality menu combining several distinct cuisines.

Study 2a uses the same accountability manipulation as Study 1a, in which participants in the high-accountability condition were told they would be interviewed by the restaurant owner and would have to justify their evaluations, whereas those in the low-accountability condition were told their choices would not be monitored.

Study 2a uses the same dependent variable as Study 1a, an averaged index of the stars assigned to the restaurant and the liking and quality ratings. The internal consistency of the index in this study was Cronbach's alpha = 0.87.

At the onset of the task participants were either told that the restaurant owner likes typical restaurants, meaning those that specialize in one cuisine and serve dishes that draw from a single culinary tradition, or atypical restaurants that combine cuisines and serve dishes that draw from multiple culinary traditions. Participants received this information in both the low- and high-accountability conditions, and the labels typical and atypical were not used in the study.

Study 2b uses the same stimulus material and atypicality manipulation as Study 1c: participants reviewed a five-item set list with no category labels, a low-atypicality set list dominated by one genre and a high-atypicality set list spanning genres with a low likelihood of co-occurrence.

Study 2b uses the same accountability manipulation as Study 1c, in which participants in the high-accountability condition had to justify their evaluation to their peers while participants in the low-accountability condition did not.

Study 2b uses the same dependent variable as Study 1c, an averaged index of the stars assigned to the band and the liking and quality ratings. The internal consistency of the index in this study was Cronbach's alpha = 0.85.

At the onset of the task participants were given information on others' preferences and were either told that other festival goers like typical bands or that other festival goers liked atypical bands. To ensure comparability with Study 2a, participants received this information in both the low- and high-accountability conditions.

A scale-based manipulation check comprising three items about respondents' perceptions of the relevance of their audience, for example whether, when evaluating the restaurant menu, they thought about whether the restaurant owner would approve of their evaluation of the restaurant. The three questions were rated on a five-point scale ranging from '1 = not at all' to '5 = very much' and combined into one scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.82). A one-way ANOVA yielded a significant main effect of accountability (F(1,340) = 6.77; p < 0.01); participants in the high-accountability condition (M = 3.11) rated their role as involving the consideration of the restaurant owners' perspective to a greater degree than participants in the low-accountability condition (M = 2.76).

The change in a merged product's price over its premerger level after controlling for the change in the product's market share and the change in its cost, and then netted of its covariance with ex ante (premerger) and postmerger market forces. Price changes were computed for each branded product from a 1983 baseline to 1985 through 1990, giving 2-year through 7-year spans. Cost is proxied by the price of the branded product's private-label counterparts.

The change in a Kraft/General Foods merged product's price over its premerger level, constructed as in the 1984 mergers with the same two control variables (change in market share and change in cost). For this sample the 1-year and 2-year models use 1989 and 1990 as the postmerger years.

A categorical variable coded 1 for specialist-related products and 0 for generalist-related products. A case is specialist related when the product of one of the merging firms is in the same product 'family' or resource space as a product from the other firm; cases involving branded food products from different product families are generalist.
The same specialist (1) versus generalist (0) classification applied to the products of the 1988 Kraft/General Foods merger.
A categorical variable assigned a value of 1 if the product of interest is one of the top two market share leaders (in terms of tons sold) in its niche in 1983 and a value of 0 if not.
A binary variable indicating whether the product was among the two top-selling brands in its niche at the time of the merger, coded 1 if so and 0 if not.
time_window: at the time of the merger

description: A dummy variable capturing the variance associated with idiosyncratic administrative, resource, and cultural differences between the two mergers, coded 0 for the Nestlé/Carnation merger and 1 for the RJR/Nabisco merger.

Sales (in tons) of the top two products in each product category during 1983 (the year before the merger) divided by the total tonnage sold in that market niche in 1983, including tons sold of private-label products.
The same premerger concentration measure (sales of the top two products over total tonnage in the niche) computed for the premerger structure of each Kraft/General Foods product's niche.
A count of the number of different brands listed by SAMI in each product category during 1983.
The same count of the number of brands in each product category, computed for the Kraft/General Foods niches before the merger.
Computed by subtracting the Initial Market Concentration (1983) from the concentration computed in 1985, and likewise for each subsequent postmerger year (1986-90), yielding six measures.
The change in niche concentration for the Kraft/General Foods products over the two postmerger years, formed from the premerger concentration and the concentration observed after the merger.
Six measures computed using Initial Market Density (1983) as the baseline and comparing it with the density observed in each postmerger year (1985-90).
The change in niche density for the Kraft/General Foods products over the two postmerger years, formed from the premerger density and the density observed after the merger.

The authors computed six Market Growth measures by subtracting sales (in tons) observed for each product-market niche for each of the six postmerger years (1985-90) from the sales of that niche in 1983.
The change in sales (in tons) of each Kraft/General Foods product-market niche over the two postmerger years relative to the premerger baseline.
time_window: two postmerger years relative to the premerger baseline

description: Postmerger niche competitiveness is measured by the change in niche concentration and the change in niche density after the merger, each computed relative to the 1983 premerger baseline for each postmerger year (1985 to 1990 for the 1984 mergers; two postmerger years for Kraft/General Foods).

Premerger niche competitiveness is measured by initial market concentration (sales of the top two products over total tonnage in the niche in 1983) and initial market density (the count of brands in each product category in 1983).

Horizontal merger is the event that defines the sample: branded food products involved in the 1984 acquisitions of Nabisco by R. J. Reynolds and of Carnation by Nestle (132 products) and in the 1988 Kraft/General Foods merger (155 products). Premerger levels (1983 baseline) are compared with postmerger years.

A dummy variable coded 1 if the firm appointed at least one female director in the focal year and 0 otherwise. Following Knippen, Shen, and Zhu (2019), the authors used a dummy variable rather than the count of new female directors because only 4.3 percent of observations in the sample included more than one new female director appointment in a given year and because they are interested in the firm's likelihood of response rather than the level of response.

A time-varying measure capturing the annual number of participants in the Women's March protests in the CBSA where a firm is headquartered, as a function of the local population. The authors counted the total number of Women's March protestors from month n-12 to month n-1, where n is the month of the focal firm's annual shareholders meeting, summing the total number of protestors in all events when there were multiple events in a CBSA. They took the natural log of the size of the protest, and to capture protest scale at the community level they divided the natural logarithm of the number of participants in local Women's March protests by the natural logarithm of population in the community; protest size equals 0 if there was no protest event in the local community in the 12-month window. The estimated mean size reported by the CCC was used as the focal measure, and missing protest size values were replaced with zeros.
time_window: 12 months preceding the focal firm's annual shareholders meeting

description: Equals 1 if most voters in the state voted for the Republican presidential candidate, Donald Trump, in the 2016 presidential election and 0 otherwise. The authors use this state-level election result to capture each community's dominant political ideology as conservative or liberal, following the blue/red shorthand for state-level political identity.

An index of each firm's diversity climate generated from textual employee reviews on Glassdoor using the wordscore method, a supervised machine learning model trained on 2021 diversity-and-inclusion (D&I) ratings and the associated textual reviews (263,564 reviews). Punctuation, numbers, stopwords, and low-frequency words were removed, and the model was trained separately for words in the Pros and Cons sections. The trained model was applied to all reviews from 2017-2020 to backfill the predicted D&I rating for each firm-year, with the final predicted rating computed as the average of the scores generated from the Pros and Cons sections. The measure was replaced with the mean value of the sample if the focal firm was not listed on Glassdoor or if the firm received fewer than three reviews per year (21 percent of the total observations).
time_window: reviews from 2017-2020, model trained on 2021 reviews and ratings

description: Media disapproval is measured as the relative prevalence of a negative evaluation over all media evaluations of a firm's CEO pay. The authors first located all Factiva articles covering CEO compensation irrespective of tone, measured in the year following compensation disclosure, and then evaluated the tone of an article using an automatic Python script that identifies negatively connoted keywords within a range of, at most, 32 words between a CEO's name and words related to compensation; an article was classified as having a negative tone if the script detected a negative keyword. The variable is calculated as the sum of all negative articles divided by the total number of articles that covered a CEO's pay in a given year, and takes values between 0 and 1, representing the proportion of negative coverage received yearly by a given firm.

CEO compensation was first calculated as the (logged) total annual value of all salary, bonuses, restricted stock grants, long-term incentive-plan payouts, and option grants valued using the Black-Scholes formula and all other income paid to a CEO. Anticipated CEO compensation was then calculated through annual cross-sectional regressions of the natural logarithm of total pay on an array of well-proven economic determinants of compensation (including industry controls). The residuals of these annual regressions capture CEO overcompensation.
time_window: annual; t+1 in the firm-response models

description: Philanthropy was measured using KLD data, which are collected from annual questionnaires sent to the company's investor relations office, firms' financial statements, annual and quarterly reports, general press releases, government surveys and academic journal publications. A total of eight KLD items are related to philanthropy, each assigned to a binary measure in which firms are awarded a 1 ('strength') if they fulfill specific criteria; the scores are then summed to provide an overall evaluation for the category. The sum of concerns for the same items is included as a control variable.

Total number of directors listed as active members on the board of directors. The measure was built from data on hospital board structure and composition. It is entered as an independent variable in models predicting service additions, divestitures and reorganizations.

Eleven occupational groupings for board members were first created based on previous research (e.g., physicians, hospital administrators, corporate executives), because these groups reflect important constituencies likely to influence hospital operations. A Gibbs-Martin Index of diversity was then computed based on the distribution of board members within these groups, where P(i) represents the proportion of a board accounted for by the ith group. The measure ranges from an index of 0, indicating complete homogeneity with a single group, to an index of 1, reflecting an equal distribution of members across a very large number of groups. The published formula for the index is not readable in the available text.

Proportion of total board membership held by outsiders. Hospital management and physicians are treated as insiders, and all other board members as outsiders. The measure was included so that the effects of board diversity and outsider representation on strategic change could be differentiated.

Additions were noted when a hospital indicated the availability of a service not provided in the previous year. A service addition occurred either by the hospital directly providing the new service or by establishing a contractual relationship with another provider. For each year the number of new services added by the hospital was determined and summed to create the dependent variable.

Divestitures were noted when the survey indicated that a service previously provided (either by the hospital or by an external provider) was no longer provided by the hospital. A summary measure of total service divestitures was computed.

Reorganizations were determined based on changes in the governance of a given service. A reorganization was coded when services previously provided in-house were presently contracted out, or services previously contracted out were currently provided in-house. A summary measure of total service reorganizations was computed.

Respondents were asked to rate on a scale from 1 to 7 (1 being 'not at all' and 7 being 'to a very large extent') the extent to which different sources of external knowledge were important for them in their professional activity. A principal component factor analysis with varimax rotation on the external knowledge items revealed external scientific knowledge as one of two distinct factors (Cronbach's alpha = 0.77 and principal component explaining 63.2% of the variance). The variable is measured as the average of the respective four items.
scale: 7-point Likert scale, 1 'not at all' to 7 'to a very large extent'

description: Respondents were asked to rate on a scale from 1 to 7 (1 being 'not at all' and 7 being 'to a very large extent') the extent to which different sources of external knowledge were important for them in their professional activity. A principal component factor analysis with varimax rotation on the external knowledge items revealed external industrial knowledge as one of two distinct factors (Cronbach's alpha = 0.81 and principal component explaining 58.4% of the variance). The variable is measured as the average of the respective four items.
scale: 7-point Likert scale, 1 'not at all' to 7 'to a very large extent'

description: Network data were collected through a combination of name-generating and name-interpreting questions: respondents checked in a roster of the 276 members of the research division the names of those with whom they had worked in the past two years on one or more projects, and then answered name-interpreting questions about each contact. Structural holes were measured following Burt (1992) using respondents' answers to 'Please indicate how often you generally go to this person for information or knowledge on work-related topics', rated on a one-to-five scale, one being 'seldom' and five being 'very frequently'. Structural holes are expressed as a decreasing function of the extent to which an individual's relationships are embedded in a dense system of common third-party ties; dyadic constraint has a term reflecting the proportion of i's interaction devoted to colleague j and a term measuring indirect dyadic constraint through third-party ties, and when summed over alters gives the extent to which ego's network is concentrated in redundant contacts, ranging from 0 to 1; 1 - constraint indicates network rich in structural holes. The formula blocks for the constraint equations are not readable in the text.
scale: constraint ranges from 0 to 1; 1 - constraint indicates network rich in structural holes
time_window: past two years (roster of project collaborators)

description: Using information obtained from 288 R&D reports compiled monthly by each laboratory after the collection of network data, each patent application filed internally by respondents was tracked down to determine whether or not it was ultimately granted by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). The number of patents generated by respondents and granted by the USPTO represents the study's dependent variable.
time_window: after the collection of network data

description: Department research performance is measured with the UTD research contribution score, which counts and prorates, depending on the number of coauthors, the number of articles published in 24 leading academic business journals. Journals were assigned to individual departments, for example The Accounting Review, the Journal of Accounting and Economics, and the Journal of Accounting Review to the accounting department. Missing research performance observations, typically due to zero publications in the relevant journals, were set to zero.

Department status is measured with the standard network centrality measure (Bonacich, 1987) applied to department-level PhD exchange networks, where cell ij includes the number of PhDs exchanged between department z in school i and department z in school j. Symmetric department networks are used, and five-year rolling hiring and placement data are used to create the PhD exchange matrices; status in 2012 therefore depends on hiring and placement of PhDs between 2008 and 2012. The status of a department depends on the status of the departments with which it exchanges PhD students.

Business school status is measured with the standard network centrality measure (Bonacich, 1987) applied to annual symmetric 109 x 109 PhD exchange matrices, in which cells denote the total number of PhDs exchanged between business schools i and j, calculated by adding the number of PhDs hired by school i from school j to the number hired by school j from school i. Five-year rolling hiring and placement data are used to create the matrices. The status of a business school depends on the status of the schools with which it exchanges PhD students.

Status inconsistency is measured following Lenski (1954) as the extent to which the statuses of the accounting, finance, management, marketing, and operations departments within a business school differ. The authors state that Si is the status of department i and M is the average status of the different departments within a business school; the formula itself is not readable in the supplied text. Because department status and status inconsistency are defined at two different measurement levels (department and business school), status inconsistency is not a linear function of department status.

variable_name: F Joiner & M Founder (FM), M Joiner & F Founder (MF), F Joiner & F Founder (FF)
description: Three dummy variables capture the founder-joiner gender combinations: FM is equal to 1 if the joiner is a woman and the founder is a man, MF is 1 for the opposite gender combination, and FF is 1 if both joiner and founder are female. The coefficients measure the influence of these combinations on the probability of a joiner becoming an entrepreneur relative to the baseline group of male joiners with a male founder.
time_window: measured at the time of the joiner's entry into the firm

variable_name: Joiner's transition to entrepreneurship (broad and strict definition)
description: Joiners are followed from the moment they join the firm until they leave or until the last year of data, and their subsequent occupation is classified as entrepreneurship. The broad definition includes all joiners who become founders of new firms with or without personnel (both self-employed and employer categories), while the strict definition considers only joiners who found a firm with personnel.
time_window: from joining the firm until leaving the firm or until 2012

description: Whether the joiner is a woman or a man, used both as the F/M part of the founder-joiner gender combination dummies and to split the estimations into female and male joiners.
time_window: measured at the time of the joiner's entry into the firm

description: Whether the unique full-time founder of the startup is a woman or a man. The core sample includes startups with a unique full-time founder, 29% of whom are female, and founder gender is time-invariant for most joiners.
time_window: time of startup founding, time-invariant for most joiners

variable_name: Female founder and above/below mean sales; female founder and above/below mean productivity
description: The influence of female founders is estimated separately for founders running firms with sales above versus below the mean and with labor productivity above versus below the mean. Labor productivity is measured as the logged ratio between sales level and total employment. The results are reported as robust when using the median performance as a threshold.
scale: above versus below the industry mean

variable_name: Female founder with same/different status (age rank, education background, birth place, motherhood status)
description: Founder-joiner similarity is captured separately for four attributes: age rank, education background, birth place and motherhood status. Similarity in age rank means an absolute age difference not greater than 5 years; similar education means the same level and field of education; similarity in motherhood status means either that both are mothers or that none of them have children; sharing the same birthplace is used as a further indicator of similarity.

variable_name: Previous firm was young; entrepreneurial mother
description: The joiner's previous exposure to entrepreneurship is captured by whether the previous employer was a young firm (up to 10 years old) rather than a mature firm, and by whether the joiner's mother was ever an entrepreneur. Female founder influence is estimated separately for those with and without each of these sources of exposure.
time_window: previous employment before joining the startup; parental history

description: Firms were allocated to strategy categories following Rumelt's method: the firm was divided into discrete businesses, using the divisional organization of the firm as a useful guide to the boundaries of each business, and the businesses were then judged as related or not on the key issue of whether they drew upon similar management skills, indicated mainly by related technology and related markets. The Wrigley classification rests on the specialization ratio, the firm's sales within its major activity as a proportion of its total sales, and the related ratio, the proportion of the firm's total sales which are related to one another. Rumelt's refinement distinguishes constrained from linked diversification, and vertically integrated firms are classified into a separate dominant-vertical category; in the empirical analysis dominant-linked and dominant-unrelated were combined to form a single category.

Firm size is measured as firm revenue in £ millions, as defined in Table 2. LSIZE is the logarithm of SIZE and is the variable entered in the regression equations. Category averages of size are compared across strategy types using analysis of variance.

Capital intensity is the value of fixed assets per employee in £ thousand, as defined in Table 2. Category averages of fixed assets per employee are compared across strategy types, and CAP is included as a firm-level variable in the profitability regressions.

The debt/equity ratio is total borrowings as a proportion of shareholders' funds, as defined in Table 2. Category averages of the debt/equity ratio are compared across strategy types, and D/E is included as a firm-level variable in the profitability regressions.

Firms are assigned to broad SIC industry groups, which the authors use to represent industry membership and the industry environment. In the cross-tabulation the fixed-strategy sample is tabulated by strategy type and industry group. In the regressions industry effects were estimated by dummy variables for each industry group except the excluded group (food, drink and tobacco), and the industry groups whose coefficients were significantly different from zero are reported.

Return on net assets is profit before tax and interest as a percentage of net tangible assets, as defined in Table 2. Average RONA is reported by strategic category for the fixed-strategy sample for the period as a whole and for the beginning (1972-75) and the end (1980-84) of the period, and RONA is used as a dependent variable in the regression equations.

Return on equity is profit after interest and tax as a percentage of shareholders' funds, as defined in Table 2. Average ROE is reported by strategic category for the fixed-strategy sample over the period and for the two sub-periods, and ROE is used as a dependent variable in the regression equations.

Return on sales is profit before tax and interest as a percentage of sales revenue, as defined in Table 2. Average ROS is reported by strategic category for the fixed-strategy sample, and ROS is used as a dependent variable in the regression equations.

Sales growth of the firms in each strategic category over the period 1972-84. The authors report average sales growth by strategic category and the change in sales growth between the first and the last sub-period, but do not state how the growth variable was computed.

Corporate respondents rated, using a 1-7 Likert scale (1 = much below average, 4 = average, and 7 = much above average), each subsidiary's expertise in collecting market information, distributing market information, and analyzing and acting on market information. The three-item scale had high reliability (alpha = 0.92).

Each respondent unit voted for the most capable subsidiary in collecting market information, distributing market information, and analyzing and acting on market information. The peers' rating variable is the sum of all votes in the three items above received by a focal subsidiary.

The focal subsidiary's self-rating was measured using Jaworski and Kohli's (1993) established index. The scale had high reliability (alpha = 0.81). The bulk of the questions were attitudinal, asking respondents to assess the extent to which they agreed with each question on a 1-7 Likert scale.

Subsidiary managers were asked about the frequency of outflows to the MNC headquarters of (1) know-how about new products and new services and (2) marketing best practices, on a 1-5 Likert scale (1 = never; 2 = less than once a year; 3 = once or twice a year; 4 = around 3-6 times a year; 5 = more than 6 times a year). Responses across the two items were averaged to yield a composite measure.
scale: 1-5 Likert (1 = never to 5 = more than 6 times a year)

description: Subsidiary managers were asked about the frequency of outflows to peer subsidiaries of (1) know-how about new products and new services and (2) marketing best practices, on a 1-5 Likert scale (1 = never; 2 = less than once a year; 3 = once or twice a year; 4 = around 3-6 times a year; 5 = more than 6 times a year). Responses across the two items were averaged to yield a composite measure.
scale: 1-5 Likert (1 = never to 5 = more than 6 times a year)

description: Subsidiary managers were asked about the frequency of inflows from the MNC headquarters of (1) know-how about new products and new services and (2) marketing best practices, on a 1-5 Likert scale (1 = never; 2 = less than once a year; 3 = once or twice a year; 4 = around 3-6 times a year; 5 = more than 6 times a year). Responses across the two items were averaged to yield a composite measure.
scale: 1-5 Likert (1 = never to 5 = more than 6 times a year)

description: Subsidiary managers were asked about the frequency of inflows from peer subsidiaries of (1) know-how about new products and new services and (2) marketing best practices, on a 1-5 Likert scale (1 = never; 2 = less than once a year; 3 = once or twice a year; 4 = around 3-6 times a year; 5 = more than 6 times a year). Responses across the two items were averaged to yield a composite measure.
scale: 1-5 Likert (1 = never to 5 = more than 6 times a year)

description: Based on a simple frequency scale where 1 = daily and 7 = yearly or less, respondents indicated how often they communicated with (a) HQ managers face-to-face to discuss operations, and (b) HQ managers through other means to discuss operations. The responses to these two items were averaged to yield a composite measure (alpha = 0.75). The communication items were reverse coded so that a higher number is associated with more frequent communication.
scale: 1 = daily to 7 = yearly or less, reverse coded

description: The same questions on communication frequency (1 = daily and 7 = yearly or less) were posed in relation to communication with peer subsidiaries. Responses were averaged, and a composite measure of communication with peer subsidiaries was created (alpha = 0.74). The items were reverse coded so that a higher number is associated with more frequent communication.
scale: 1 = daily to 7 = yearly or less, reverse coded

description: A dummy variable that took the value of 1 only when the focal subsidiary met all of the following criteria: it experienced (1) vertical knowledge outflows less than once a year; (2) vertical knowledge inflows less than once a year; (3) horizontal knowledge outflows less than once a year; and (4) horizontal knowledge inflows less than once a year, and the value of 0 otherwise. 'Less than once a year' is a score of 2 on the five-point knowledge-flow scale.

Corporate respondents (i.e., the subsidiary manager's boss) rated the subsidiary's relative financial performance on three dimensions: overall sales revenue, overall market share, and operating profit (1 = much below average, 4 = average, and 7 = much above average). Responses on the three items were averaged to yield a composite measure; reliability was moderate (0.69).
scale: 1-7 (1 = much below average, 4 = average, 7 = much above average)

description: Measured based on the Custódio et al. (2013) CEO General Ability Index, which considers five aspects of the CEO's professional career: the number of past positions held, the number of firms worked for, the number of industries worked in, whether the CEO has held a CEO position at a different firm (dummy), and whether the CEO has worked for a conglomerate (dummy). Principal component analysis combines the five factors into a single measure proxying for the CEO's knowledge and skill set. Like Custódio et al. (2013), the authors created the dummy variable Generalist CEO, coded as 1 if a CEO's general managerial knowledge and skills measure was above the median for all CEOs, and 0 otherwise.
The number of acquisitions a firm engaged in during a given year, counted from the sample of M&A deals.

Constructed using the same methodology as the Generalist CEO measure, based on the average knowledge and skills of independent board members, and is a continuous measure. In the two-sided matching analysis the variable was rescaled from 0 to 1 (from the lowest to the highest generalist board values in the sample).
scale: continuous score (rescaled 0 to 1 in the matching analysis)

description: Measures whether the firm had engaged in any unrelated acquisitions in that year, conditional on the firm engaging in an acquisition in the given year. An unrelated acquisition is one not in the acquirer's primary industry, measured at the SIC 2-digit level.

The number of unrelated acquisitions a firm engaged in, in a given year, conditional on the firm engaging in an acquisition in the given year. An unrelated acquisition is one not in the acquirer's primary industry, measured at the SIC 2-digit level.
A dummy variable coded as 1 if a generalist CEO engaged in an unrelated acquisition or a specialist CEO engaged in a related acquisition, and 0 otherwise.

The cumulative abnormal return measured over day x to day y, where day 0 is the announcement date of the acquisition. The benchmark model is a market model with a value-weighted market index whose parameters are estimated from day -230 to day -30.
time_window: event windows around the acquisition announcement (day 0)

variable_name: Refocusing measured using the Wall Street Journal announcements
description: Firms were classified as refocusing if they publicly announced in the Wall Street Journal their intention to refocus AND actually divested at least 10 percent of their asset base. The number and size of the divestitures undertaken by the sample firms were collected from a variety of merger and acquisition sources because no single source was found to be reliable or complete. The variable distinguishes firms that refocused from those that did not.

variable_name: Refocusing measured using the Rumelt categories
description: The sample firms were classified according to Rumelt's (1974) strategic categories using data from Trinet as well as annual reports, and were placed in their strategic category in both 1981 and 1987. Those firms that moved from a 'broad' strategic category in 1981 to a more 'narrow' one in 1987 were classified as refocused: from Unrelated to Single, Dominant or Related; from Related to Single or Dominant; and from Dominant to Single.

variable_name: Refocusing measured using the entropy index (DT)
description: For each firm the entropy index of diversification (DT) was calculated in the manner shown by Palepu (1985) using data from the Trinet tapes, for all four years 1981, 1983, 1985 and 1987. If a firm's index of diversification decreased in the relevant period, that firm was classified as refocused. The refocusing activity of each firm was measured in three distinct time periods-1981-83, 1983-85 and 1985-87-to allow for the possibility that refocusing's effect takes time to materialize.

variable_name: Change in industry-weighted return on sales (DROS 87-81)
description: Profitability is the firm's ROS minus its industry-weighted ROS. ROS is measured from Compustat as operating income before depreciation and interest as a percent of sales. To calculate the industry-weighted ROS, a Compustat program was used to identify all the firms assigned to each 2-digit SIC and to calculate their ROS; a breakdown of each sample firm's sales by SIC was obtained from the Trinet tapes, the percentage of the firm's sales in each SIC was calculated, and the industry-weighted ROS was estimated by multiplying the share of the firm's sales in each SIC by the corresponding ROS of that SIC and adding the results. The dependent variable is the change in this industry-weighted profitability from 1981 to 1987.

Five different strategies were used to assign firms to the over-diversified group. Strategy 1 ranked the sample firms by their 1981 diversification level (DT) and picked the 70 most-diversified firms. Strategy 2 sorted firms by core industry and placed in the high-diversification group those whose DT was bigger than their industry's median DT. Strategy 3 took the 42 sample firms belonging to the Rumelt 'Unrelated-Business' category in 1981. Strategy 4 grouped firms by diversification strategy and classified as over-diversified those whose DT was greater than the group median. Strategy 5 took the related-linked firms (above-median DR and above-median DU) as the high-diversity group.

For each firm the entropy index of diversification (DT) was calculated in the manner shown by Palepu (1985) using data from the Trinet tapes, and the index was calculated for all four years 1981, 1983, 1985 and 1987. The 200 sample firms were ranked according to their 1981 diversification level, and firms were also sorted by core industry and ranked according to their diversification level within that industry.

Two independent reviewers coded the full sample of 250 acqui-hires using the decision tree in Figure 2, checking whether the target operates in one of the acquirer's main lines of business, addresses a niche customer segment, offers a new set of features and performance attributes, and offers a new value proposition with the potential to disrupt existing solutions. There was 92% agreement between reviewers. If both reviewers coded a target firm's know-how as disruptive then Disruptive Know-how was coded as 1 and 0 otherwise.

Key team members listed on Crunchbase were identified and their LinkedIn accounts checked to identify their new positions and business units; press releases, business press articles and technology blogs were also examined. If there was an explicit mention of moving the acqui-hired team as a whole into a specific business unit immediately after the acquisition and the LinkedIn accounts confirmed this transition, Preserved Integration was coded as 1; if the LinkedIn accounts showed integration into more than one business unit, Dispersed Integration was coded as 1.

The positions held by the co-founder(s) when they joined the acquiring firm were used, obtained from the LinkedIn accounts of the acqui-hired firms' founders. High Status Position was coded as 1 when all co-founders of the target firm were assigned to a high status position following the acquisition and 0 otherwise. High status positions include managerial/executive positions such as Vice President and nonmanagerial senior level positions such as Senior Research Scientist.

Measured by observing acqui-hired firms' founders' employment as listed on their LinkedIn accounts. Premature exit was coded as 1 when one or more co-founders of the target firm exit the acquiring firm within a year after the acquisition and 0 otherwise.
time_window: within a year after the acquisition

description: Following Venkatraman's (1989) fit-as-matching approach and Dewar and Werbel's (1979) operationalization, the authors regressed disruptive know-how on preserved integration, calculated the residuals of that regression, and used the absolute values of the residuals to indicate the lack of fit.

variable_name: Disruptive know-how & High Status Position Misfit
description: Following Venkatraman's (1989) fit-as-matching approach and Dewar and Werbel's (1979) operationalization, the authors regressed disruptive know-how on founder high status position, calculated the residuals of that regression, and used the absolute values of the residuals to indicate the lack of fit.

A binary indicator that takes the value one if a social auditor detected any of the eight socially irresponsible employment practices in the relevant year, and zero otherwise. Audits are aggregated to the annual level; when audits in the same year give different results, a practice is coded as present if any of the audits detected it. The authors assume that auditors are more likely to miss a harmful practice that is present than to report a violation where none occurred.
scale: binary (0 = no practice detected, 1 = any practice detected)
time_window: annual (audits aggregated to the calendar year)

description: The percentage of 'passes' that each factory's products received in quality control inspections. The measure is assessed by the import-export agent's product quality personnel through different processes from the social audit. It ranges from 0% to 100%.

The percentage of orders that the factory fulfilled by the contracted delivery date in that year. It ranges from 0% to 100% and is measured through separate processes from the social audit that detects socially irresponsible employment practices.

The total annual value of orders placed by the import-export agent at each factory, divided by the factory's employees and natural-log transformed. Order value data were shared only in 14 binned categories, and the midpoint of each bin is used as the estimated spend. The log transformation allows the coefficient on the presence of any irresponsible practice to be read as a percent change in the orders per employee placed at the factory.

variable_name: Quality pass rate, on-time delivery, order value
description: Manufacturing outcomes are three separate measures: the quality inspection pass rate, the on-time delivery rate, and the natural log of annual order value per employee placed by the import-export agent at each factory. They come from the agent's records, separate from the social audits.

variable_name: Ratio of corporate giving to sales
description: Corporate giving data were compiled from each firm's annual income statements, on which every publicly listed firm must report the amount of its corporate giving. According to the Corporate Tax Act of South Korea, the income statement item covers only monetary donations, including direct cash contributions and the value of product donations, and excludes nonmonetary charitable activities such as employees' volunteered time or executives' nonprofit board service. The measure is the ratio of corporate giving to sales in a given year, used because giving adjusted for firm size indicates social conformity to what a firm 'ought to be'. Because the sample consists of publicly listed firms, the records were externally audited and confirmed by independent certified public accountants.

variable_name: Positive media coverage of a firm's corporate giving
description: The authors searched 20 major daily newspapers for articles containing a firm's name and any of the keywords 'donation,' 'social contributions,' and 'social responsibility'. Two trained research assistants independently read each identified article and coded whether it reported the firm's philanthropic efforts in a favorable light; the kappa coefficient between the coders was .81 with 99% agreement, and one of the authors assessed each rare case of disagreement. The variable is the natural logarithm of the number of positive media coverage articles, logged because of right skewness.

variable_name: Negative media coverage of lawsuits against family owners
description: The authors first identified a list of family owners based on the shareholders list of each company in the KISLINE database, then searched all articles in 20 daily newspapers containing both the names of the identified family owners and the keyword 'lawsuit'. Two trained research assistants independently verified all the identified articles; the kappa coefficient between the coders was .88 with 97% agreement, and each rare case of disagreement was assessed. The variable counts the number of articles reporting legal actions that different external constituents brought against the family owners of a given firm, and was constructed as the natural logarithm.

Firm profitability is measured as the return on assets (ROA). The authors constructed two interaction terms by multiplying each media coverage independent variable with ROA to test Hypotheses 1b and 2b. The firm performance variable used for the interactions was also controlled in the models.

variable_name: resource complementarity (type of investors; headquarters location; geographical strength; industry strength)
description: Four variables measure complementarity. Complementarity in the type of investors is the absolute difference between the proportion of institutional registered representatives [IRRs/(IRRs+RRRs)] of the lead bank and that of a potential partner. Headquarters location is coded 1 if a bank dyad is headquartered in different states and 0 if in the same state. Geographical strength and industry strength are the summed absolute differences between the two banks' proportions of issuers across 51 states (51st for a foreign client) and across 99 two-digit SIC industries; both range from 0, indicating complete overlap, to 2, indicating no overlap.
time_window: past three years relative to each deal (initial measures from 1980-1982)

description: A bank's status is measured from its bracket positions in tombstone advertisements in Investment Dealer's Digest, adopting Bonacich's (1987) c(a,b) measure for asymmetric relational data. The matrix element r_ij is the number of syndications in which banks i and j jointly participated as non-managing banks and bank i appeared in a higher bracket than bank j, divided by the number of syndications in which banks i and j jointly participated as non-managing banks during 1980-1982; main diagonal elements are set to 0. To measure the status similarity of two banks, the smaller status value is divided by the larger, and if the status of both banks is 0 the value is set to 1, so the largest value of 1 indicates the greatest similarity in status.

The variable direct ties, indicating the level of direct prior alliance experience between a bank dyad, is measured by the number of deals that a lead bank has offered to the potential partner for syndicate participation over the past three years. A squared term for direct ties is also used to assess the possibility of a damper effect resulting from frequent alliances between two firms.

The variable co-participation, indicating the level of indirect prior alliance experience through co-participation, is measured by the number of deals managed by third parties over the past three years in which both the lead bank and the potential partner participated as ordinary syndicate member firms. A squared term for the variable co-participation is also included.

The number of deals given by the potential partner to the lead bank divided by the number of deals given by the lead bank to the potential partner during the past three years. One is added to both the numerator and the denominator to avoid values of infinity. A value of one indicates that the two firms exchanged an equal number of deals over the past three years.

For each deal, the dependent variable records whether the lead bank invited a particular bank to be a syndication member. It is coded 1 if a lead bank chooses a certain bank as a syndicate member for a particular public offering and 0 if it does not. Cases are not broken into dyad-years.

The synergy score directly operationalizes the percentage synergistic gain in an acquisition, defined as (actual post-acquisition value) minus (expected value/no acquisition), divided by (expected value/no acquisition). It is computed for each pair of combining firms and averaged within subsamples. The authors state that it is an unbiased measure but has troublesome statistical properties, so the nonparametric Mann-Whitney U-test and the binomial test were used. The algebraic expression of the measure is not legible in the available text.
time_window: event period days -40 to T (T is the fifth day after the announcement of the ultimately successful bid)

description: The average cumulative abnormal return of a subsample portfolio of pairs of combining firms, used in addition to the synergy score because it has useful statistical properties. The cumulative abnormal return is computed for each pair of combining firms from day -39 to day T and then averaged for the subsample. To ascertain whether value creation measured by ACAR is statistically different from zero, each CAR was first standardized by its estimated standard deviation and the resulting values were transformed by dividing each by its known standard deviation. The authors note that this measure is an approximation relative to the synergy score.
level: pair of combining firms; subsample portfolio

description: Acquisition type classified using the FTC categorization of acquisition types: horizontal, vertical, product extension, market extension and unrelated. Horizontal mergers refer to acquisitions in the same product markets; vertical mergers involve firms which had a potential buyer-seller relationship prior to the merger; market-extension mergers are undertaken by firms which manufacture the same products but sell them in different geographic markets; unrelated mergers involve the consolidation of two essentially unrelated firms.
