Two different subsamples of related acquisitions were formed: one combining horizontal, vertical, product-extension and market-extension acquisitions, and a second excluding vertical acquisitions and following theoretical similarities in technologies, markets and operations of firms operating in upstream versus downstream industries.

Acquisitions are classified as related according to Porter's scheme if both firms were of the same type in Porter's classification of industries. Porter differentiated between industries based on buyer-seller relationships, detecting specific similarities in terms of markets served and distribution systems within three distinct types of industries: producer goods, consumer convenience goods, and consumer non-convenience goods.

variable_name: relative size of the target to the bidder
description: The market value of the target firm relative to the market value of the bidder firm. The size analysis was repeated after eliminating all acquisitions in which the market value of the target was less than 10 percent of the market value of the bidder, producing a reduced sample of 80 acquisitions.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: Binary variable coded one if a buyer and a seller are located in the same village. Villages are small cities and are the boundary most often used to delimit a geographic community; in Champagne, villages map onto specific crus and each has a strong identity rooted in common history.

Binary variable coded one if the buyer and the seller are in the same school district. Using government data for the Region Academique Grand Est, the author created a map of all ecoles primaires (schools for children ages 2 to 11), computed the shortest driving distance between each school and each buyer and each seller, and used this information to assign school districts.

For each transaction, the actual price paid per kilogram of grapes minus the normative price for these grapes according to the echelle des crus (the prix indicatif prorated by cru quality rating). The variable captures the extent to which the final transaction price deviates from established pricing norms; the larger the difference, the greater the deviation. In the sample this difference is always positive because the price paid per kilogram is never lower than the normative price. The data on prix indicatif were obtained through the CIVC.

The final price paid per kilogram of grapes, net of transportation charges, which are always paid by the buyer. Used as the dependent variable in the multiplicative heteroskedastic models; the results do not change if the natural logarithm of final price is used instead.

variable_name: Variance in final paid price (multiplicative heteroskedastic model)
description: In the multiplicative heteroskedastic model, the mean and the variance of the final price paid per kilogram are estimated simultaneously via maximum likelihood as functions of buyer-seller relations, including joint community affiliation. The variance is modeled with dummies for sellers and buyers and a control for the grapes' quality grade on the echelle in place of cru fixed effects.

The cumulative number of years of the exchange relation between a buyer and a seller at the time of the transaction, following previous research. Because the effect of relation duration is rarely linear, the author took the natural logarithm of this measure. The measure is left censored because exchange relations were only observed starting in 2003.

A yearly concentration measure computed from the number of buyers with which a seller works and the percentage of the seller's sales volume sold to each buyer; a score of one indicates that all the seller's grapes go to only one buyer. The specification is reported as an equation that is not readable in the available text.
The same concentration formula applied to each buyer to compute an index of concentration for each buyer, capturing the extent to which a buyer concentrates its purchases with a few sellers.

For each seller's village, the capacity of the salle des fetes (village hall) weighted by population, computed from the Guide Curien. The greater the capacity of this community space, the greater members' engagement in local events, gatherings, and festivities is presumed to be.

The number of restaurants in the seller's village weighted by population, computed from the Guide Curien. Local businesses capture not only the vitality of a community but also the extent to which members informally hang out to share local information.

Annual data from the CIVC extranet on the proportion of grape growers between 25 and 35 years of age in each departement, matched with sellers' school districts. Individuals of this age are most likely to have elementary school-aged children and therefore to attend school-related activities that foster social engagement.

A unit was classified as a center of excellence only if it met all three criteria: strong capabilities, formal recognition by headquarters, and use of its capabilities by other units. Respondents rated competence in research, development, and manufacturing on a 7-point scale from 'weak competence' (1) to 'very strong competence' (7), with 4 as the cut-off for strong competence; they indicated whether 'Our competence is formally recognized by the headquarters' (1 = yes, 0 = no); and they rated the extent to which the subsidiary's distinctive competences in each activity are of use for other units in the corporation on a 7-point scale (1 = 'No use for other units at all' to 7 = 'Very useful for other units'), with a cut-off of 4 out of 7.

A composite index calculated as the sum of the scores across four items assessing the business environment in which the unit competes: availability of supply material; quality of suppliers; demanding customers; level of competition. Each item was rated on a 1-7 scale (1 = very low, 7 = very high). The items were combined because of the high intercorrelation between many of them.

Respondents assessed the impact of four organizations outside the boundaries of the firm on the development of the subsidiary's competencies, where 1 = no impact at all and 7 = very decisive impact. The four external organizations were customers, suppliers, competitors, and external research institutions. The models use a composite measure based on the sum of the responses across the four actors.

Mirroring the external measure, respondents assessed the impact of four specific internal organizations on the development of the subsidiary's competence, where 1 = no impact at all and 7 = very decisive impact. The measure is the sum of the individual scores.

For each of research, development, and manufacturing, respondents were asked to 'describe the level of investment in the Canadian Subsidiary for the past 3 years' on a scale from 1 = very limited to 7 = very large. Missing values were interpreted as indicating little or no investment in that activity, as cross-tabulations showed they were overwhelmingly cases where the respondent also checked 'NA' for any activity in that area, and were recoded as 1. The resulting measure is an activity-specific measure of parent firm investment in the subunit, ranging from 1 to 7.

Based on the scale developed by Roth and Morrison (1992), respondents were asked to identify the level at which certain decisions were made, where 1 = subsidiary level, 2 = subcorporate, 3 = foreign corporate HQ. The measure is based on the average of six items (alpha = 0.63); lower numbers indicate more autonomy.

variable_name: CEO support for police reform (experimental treatment)
description: Randomly assigned treatment condition. Participants in both conditions were told that the killing of several Black men by police has increased debate about police reform; those in the treatment condition were additionally informed that Business Roundtable recently advocated for creating a police misconduct registry and increasing standards for the use of 'no-knock' warrants, and were given information about the companies it represents.

variable_name: CEO activism that constituents find objectionable (experimental treatment)
description: Randomly assigned treatment condition appended to the business relocation vignette: for the treatment group, the CEO of the business has been outspoken on a couple of social issues and taken positions that most people in the community find objectionable. The situation was always framed as the CEO taking positions the policymaker's constituents would find objectionable rather than positions they would support.

Support for creating a national police misconduct registry and support for implementing stricter standards for the use of no-knock warrants, each measured on a 5-point scale ranging from 'strongly oppose' (1) to 'strongly support' (5); the two responses are averaged to create a single measure of support for police reform. This is the prespecified outcome of interest, covering the two policies explicitly endorsed by Business Roundtable.

variable_name: Willingness to privately meet with the CEO
description: Response to the question 'How likely would you be to privately meet with this CEO to encourage the company to locate its new facility in your community?', measured on a 5-point scale from 'not likely at all' (1) to 'extremely likely' (5).

variable_name: Willingness to publicly advocate for the company
description: Response to the question 'How likely would you be to publicly advocate that the company locate its new facility in your community?', measured on a 5-point scale from 'not likely at all' (1) to 'extremely likely' (5).

Regulative activity is measured from information on the passage of country-level Bitcoin regulations collected from various sources and websites. The regulative status variable uses three categories: zero when no clear regulation exists (unregulated), one when Bitcoin trading is legal, and two when Bitcoin trading is illegal. Three of the authors independently coded the categories and obtained consistent results with more than 97% agreement, and remaining cases were resolved by discussion. In the estimations the legal category is compared with the unregulated case.

Regulative activity is measured from information on the passage of country-level Bitcoin regulations collected from various sources and websites. The regulative status variable uses three categories: zero when no clear regulation exists (unregulated), one when Bitcoin trading is legal, and two when Bitcoin trading is illegal. Three of the authors independently coded the categories and obtained consistent results with more than 97% agreement, resolving remaining cases by discussion. In the estimations the illegal category is compared with the unregulated case.

The number of Bitcoin exchange platforms in a particular country and year. The authors compiled the platform data based on the websites coinmarketcap.com and cryptowisser.de, then validated the information provided manually and matched it to the countries in the sample. They note that although Bitcoin operates as a DAO, the vast majority of Bitcoin transactions still take place on centralized exchanges, and that the proliferation of these platforms indicates increasing entrepreneurial activity.

The yearly Bitcoin trading volume (ln) in U.S. dollars. The variable was created by summing the trading volume from the respective exchanges listed on the website bitcoincharts.com and supplemented by data from coin.dance and bitcoinity.org. To account for variations in population density and because a larger population might trigger more trading, the Bitcoin trading volume was divided by population size obtained from the World Bank. Because the dependent variable is nonnormal and skewed, the natural logarithm was used.
scale: natural logarithm of U.S. dollars per capita

description: An alternative measure for petty and grand corruption developed by the authors from data from the World Justice Project (WJP; Rule of Law). The WJP Rule of Law Index calculates scores and rankings for 8 factors and 44 subfactors; a principal components analysis with a varimax rotation and the Kaiser criterion produced a two-component solution. The Cronbach's alpha for grand corruption is 0.97, and the raw data were reverse-coded so that greater grand corruption is indicated by higher scores.

An alternative measure for petty and grand corruption developed by the authors from data from the World Justice Project (WJP; Rule of Law). The WJP Rule of Law Index calculates scores and rankings for 8 factors and 44 subfactors; a principal components analysis with a varimax rotation and the Kaiser criterion produced a two-component solution. The Cronbach's alpha for petty corruption is 0.97, and the raw data were reverse-coded so that greater petty corruption is indicated by higher scores.

Measured as Trajtenberg's weighted patent count: the number of applications by firm i in year t plus the total number of forward citations received by those patents within the 3 years following the year of EPO publication. The authors state that if firm i applied for 10 patents in t and received 15 citations to these patents in the subsequent 3 years, the dependent variable would add to 25. Forward citations are used as the quality dimension because patent counts alone are an imperfect proxy for innovation output.
time_window: year t, with a 3-year forward citation window following the year of EPO publication

description: Share of the firm's R&D workers in year t who were newly hired directly from a university. Hires are defined as workers employed by different employers in t-1 and t; worker shares are formed as the number of R&D workers of the type divided by the total number of R&D workers, and the shares add to one so that stayers form the excluded base category. R&D workers are individuals with a master's or a doctoral degree in the technical, natural, veterinary, agricultural, or health sciences holding a job function requiring high or intermediate skills and aged between 20 and 75.

variable_name: Hires from firms w/ university experience (employment share)
description: Share of the firm's R&D workers in year t who were hired from another (non-affiliated) firm and who were previously employed as university researchers. Hires from firms are split along two dimensions of experience: hires from a patenting versus a non-patenting firm, and workers previously employed as university researchers versus those never employed in a university.

variable_name: Hires from patenting firms w/ university experience (employment share)
description: Share of the firm's R&D workers in year t hired from a firm with patenting experience who also have previous university research experience. This is the group in Figure 1 Panel (4), combining academic and technological experience.

variable_name: Hires from patenting firms w/o university experience (employment share)
description: Share of the firm's R&D workers in year t hired from a firm with patenting experience who have no previous university research experience. This is the group in Figure 1 Panel (3), assumed to add strength in utilizing technological information.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the present top management team (TMT) includes at least one individual with an R&D education and 0 otherwise. The authors use the inclusion of a scientist on the TMT as a proxy for firms with an academic research-friendly organizational culture. The dummy is interacted with the employment shares of hires from firms with and without university experience and with university hires.

An index built from each CEO's personal donations to the two major political parties, obtained from Federal Election Commission filings, which include any gift of $200 or more to a candidate, campaign committee, or political action committee. Following prior research, the CEO's donation records from the prior 10 years were used. Four ratio indicators were coded - count of donations to the Democratic party divided by the count of donations to both parties, amount donated to Democrats divided by the total donated to both parties, number of years the CEO donated to Democrats divided by the number of years the CEO donated to either party, and number of unique Democratic recipients divided by the total number of unique recipients - and averaged into a composite index ranging from 0 (extreme conservatism) to 1 (extreme liberalism). CEOs without political contributions were assigned a score of .50.
time_window: prior 10 years of donations; donations observed over 1992-2012

description: Measured from political donations made by organizational members other than the CEO, recorded in the FEC database, where donors report their employers and titles or positions; a search identified all contributions by donors listing any of the sampled firms as their employers. Over the timespan 1998-2012, an average of 1,881 donation records per firm from non-CEO employees were identified. A four-item index is computed for each two-year election cycle: count of contributions to the Democratic Party divided by count of contributions to both parties; total amount contributed to Democratic recipients divided by total contributions to recipients of both parties; count of unique employees donating to the Democratic Party divided by count of unique employee donations to either party; and count of unique recipients affiliated with the Democratic Party divided by count of all unique recipients. To enhance reliability of the four-item index, the average of the two latest election cycles is used.
time_window: two-year election cycles; average of the two latest election cycles (donations observed over 1998-2012)

description: Coded in two steps. First, unit-level capital allocation is measured as new capital investment to each business segment i belonging to corporate parent j for each year t, scaled by segment assets at the beginning of the year (Capx/Assets), indicating the degree to which the firm allocates new capital to a unit as a proportion of the unit's assets already in place. Second, the coefficient of variation of all such allocations made to the units of a firm in a given year is computed. For ease of interpretation this dispersion measure is multiplied by -1 and then standardized, so that higher values reflect more evenhandedness and lower values more disparate allocations. The variable also serves as the independent variable in the models predicting performance.

Subsequent firm performance is measured as Tobin's q, the ratio of market value (the sum of the book value of debt and the market value of equity) to the replacement cost of assets (book value of total assets). With evenhandedness in year t as the key independent variable, Tobin's q is predicted for year t+1 in a separate set of regressions. The models control for the firm's Tobin's q in year t as a lagged dependent variable as well as for average industry Tobin's q in the same year as the dependent variable.

Computed as the proportion of total CEO compensation comprised of stock options (the ex ante value of stock options granted) and restricted stock. Following Sanders and Hambrick (2007), the variable is measured as a two-year average (t - 1 and t - 2), as companies may not grant options every year.

Measured as the percent of company stock owned by the CEO, following prior research. It is used as a moderator of the association between CEO liberalism and evenhandedness in resource allocation. The authors note that, unlike equity-based pay, which strictly reflects financial incentives, equity ownership reflects both power and financial incentives.

The attainment discrepancy between the franchise's performance during season t-1 and its historic aspiration level during that season, calculated by subtracting the historic aspiration level from achieved performance. Performance is operationalized as team win percentage, the ratio of the franchise's games won to total games played, and this same measure is used in constructing the historic aspiration level. The historic aspiration level follows the specification in Levinthal and March (1981); because the aspiration level might be sensitive to the alpha weighting constant, the variable was modeled at 0.25 increments of alpha and an alpha of 0.25 was selected based on goodness of overall model fit. The aspiration-updating equation itself is not readable in the provided text.
time_window: t-1 (the season preceding the off-season divestment period)

description: The percentage of the franchise's pitching capacity divested during the off-season (time t). It is created by summing the innings pitched during the previous season (t-1) by those pitchers removed from the team during the off-season and dividing this sum by the total number of innings pitched by all pitcher resources used by the team during season t-1. Player departures due to trade, release, or free agency are not differentiated, but any player who retires is excluded. During the sampling frame values ranged from 0 to 66 percent with a mean of 16 percent.

The percentage of the franchise's developed pitching capacity divested during the off-season (time t). A developed resource is defined as any player who had six or more years of MLB tenure. The variable is created by summing the innings pitched during the previous season by those pitchers with six or more years of MLB tenure who were removed from the team during the off-season, and dividing this sum by the total number of innings pitched by all pitchers with six or more years of MLB tenure during the previous season.

The percentage of the franchise's less developed pitching capacity divested, constructed in the same fashion as the other two resource divestment variables but using only those players with fewer than six years of MLB tenure.

Factor market bargaining power is a period split: before the 1976 free agency rule change, the reserve clause made the factor market monopsonistic (firm power); after it, the market was monopolistic for more developed players (player power). Models are run separately on the two 7-year panels.

Strategic similarity between two airlines based on the discrete classification scheme used by the Department of Transportation, which groups airlines by annual operating revenues into majors (over $1 billion), nationals ($100 million to $1 billion), large regionals ($10 million to $100 million) and medium regionals (up to $10 million), with 12, 19, 13 and 4 airlines of the sample in those categories respectively. The pairwise measure is distributed between zero and one, with zero representing the maximum interfirm difference in that dimension and one representing maximum similarity. For each airline-route the measure is aggregated as the average similarity to all other actual and potential competitors in the market; the normalizing formula is unreadable in the text available.

Based on Stinchcombe's hypothesis that firms originating in a given period are imprinted by their founding environment and follow similar strategies, so that date of founding proxies for strategy. The measure is one minus the difference in years of founding, normalized to a zero-to-one range: it takes the value zero (minimum similarity) when the difference in founding dates between two firms equals the maximum difference in the sample (62 years) and one (maximum similarity) when the founding dates are the same. The measure is aggregated as the average over the actual and potential competitors of a firm in a market; the normalizing formula is unreadable in the text available.

Strategic similarity computed from seven standardized variables describing each airline's competitive strategy: (1) passenger-weighted average density of the markets in which the firm competes, (2) passenger-weighted average distance of those markets, (3) percentage of tourist markets among all markets served, (4) passenger-weighted percentage of direct flights over all flights, (5) passenger-weighted average daily frequency, (6) passenger-weighted market share of the firm in its markets, and (7) passenger-weighted average premium over standard industry fare level per mile. The variables were averaged across the multiple markets and time periods so that one seven-dimensional datapoint represents the strategy of each airline over the five-year period. Strategic similarity is one minus the Euclidean distance between the standardized points, normalized to the zero-to-one range: zero when the Euclidean distance is the largest for all pairs in the sample and one when the distance is zero; the effect is aggregated as the average similarity to all actual and potential competitors in the market. The formula is unreadable in the text available.

A count measure that sums the number of markets outside the focal market m in which firms i and j also compete. An instance of multimarket contact is counted when a firm i that is an incumbent in focal market m and another actual or potential competitor j in market m meet in another market n in which competitor j is an incumbent and firm i is an incumbent or potential entrant. The overall measure is the average number of such multimarket contacts with all relevant competitors (actual and potential) in market m, so it includes potential contacts as well as actual ones. The formulas are unreadable in the text available.

The average price charged by a firm to passengers in a city-pair market divided by the distance of the market, an industry practice that reports such data as 'yield' or revenue per passenger-mile. Dividing by distance scales all observations to be comparable across markets and facilitates the use of linear methods. Actual prices were used rather than announced or advertised prices, because airlines can easily change prices by changing the availability of seats to different fare categories. Yield is the dependent variable and is used to capture the intensity of rivalry experienced by the firm in that market, so higher yield corresponds to lower rivalry.

Proportion of outside directors is equal to the number of outside directors divided by the total number of directors, and is based on information provided in Standard & Poor's Register of Corporations. For the companies included in the study, the proportion of outside directors ranged from 0 to 100 percent, with a mean of 65 percent.

Whether the board was sued by shareholders for failure to maintain its fiduciary responsibilities. Instances involving boards of directors and violations of fiduciary responsibilities were identified through the use of LEXIS, yielding 56 cases with final outcomes and board composition that could be accurately determined. A control group of 56 companies incorporated in Delaware, yet not sued by their stockholders, was matched to the original sample.

Whether the court's decision was favorable to the defendant board or indicated a violation of duty by the board. Of the suits, 46 resulted in decisions favorable to the defendant (i.e. the board), while in 10 cases decisions indicated violation of duty by the board.
scale: binary (outcome in favor of board versus outcome in favor of stockholder)

description: The authors split the data into two groups based on the variable CEO duality, separating cases in which the positions of CEO and chairman are held by a single individual from cases in which they are held by two separate individuals. In 72 percent of the companies a single individual served as both CEO and chairman of the board.
scale: binary (single individual versus two separate individuals)

description: Political ideology is measured from political campaign donations made by each director to political campaigns, collected from the Federal Election Commission. A director's political orientation is the net donation made to the Republican Party: total donated to the Republican Party minus total donated to the Democratic Party, divided by the total donated to both parties, with values from -1 (all donations to the Democratic Party) to +1 (all donations to the Republican Party). Board conservatism is a weighted summation of individual ideology values, where the chairperson of the board gets a weight of 1, the audit committee chair 0.5, and other directors 0.3. Donations between 1979 and 2014 were used, and the variable was collected at the misrepresentation announcement. For 326 directors, the measure was correlated (0.802, p < .01) with manually collected political party affiliation data.
scale: -1 to +1 for individual director political orientation
time_window: donations made between 1979 and 2014; variable collected at the misrepresentation announcement

description: A dummy variable indicating CEO dismissal, using the ExecuComp database. The authors first collected all cases of CEO replacement after a misrepresentation announcement, focusing on a 2-year window after the announcement, and identified dismissals using criteria from previous studies: (a) CEOs were fired or forced out; (b) CEOs stepped down for undisclosed personal reasons or resigned to pursue other interests; and (c) CEOs retired before reaching age 65 and also gave up their board seat/advisory or consulting role. These cases were coded as CEO dismissal equal to 1, and 0 otherwise, and the accuracy of the variable was further verified using SEC documents, press releases, and news articles.

Groups were randomly assigned to one of three manipulations: dialectical inquiry, devil's advocacy or consensus. In the dialectical inquiry manipulation the four-person group was divided into two two-person advocate subgroups that developed opposing recommendations and assumptions and debated them. In the devil's advocacy manipulation one subgroup formally critiqued the recommendations of the other subgroup. In the consensus manipulation groups were instructed to discuss recommendations and assumptions openly and constructively without formally structured or encouraged conflict.

Judges computed scores for numbers of assumptions by counting the assumptions that each individual or group provided. The average individual member score was computed by summing the performance measure of interest for all members of a group and then dividing it by the number of members. The best individual member score was that of the highest individual performance score among a group's members.

Judges rated the validity of each assumption on a five-point scale ranging from 1 (low confidence in the validity of the assumption) to 5 (high confidence in the validity of the assumption). Validity was defined for judges as the likelihood that the assumption being rated was accurate (given material contained in the case) and would occur. Final individual and group validity scores were calculated by summing the validity ratings of each individual's or group's assumptions and dividing the sum by the number of assumptions stated by the individual or group.

Judges rated the importance of each assumption on a five-point scale ranging from 1 (not important) to 5 (very important). Importance was defined for judges as the significance of the assumption on the outcome of the case. Importance scores were computed in the same way as validity scores, by summing the ratings and dividing by the number of assumptions stated.

The two judges rated the global quality of each individual's or group's recommendations on a five-point scale ranging from 1 (low quality) to 5 (high quality). Quality was broadly defined for judges as the extent to which the recommendations were consistent with the external environment of the firm and appropriate in light of the firm's resources, the extent to which parts of the recommendations were internally consistent, and the extent to which the recommendations were workable given the firm's situation. The correlation between the judges was 0.68 with full agreement on 60 percent of the judgements, and discrepancies were resolved by discussion.

variable_name: difference between group and average member performance
description: Difference scores were computed between each group's performance and the average of its respective members' performance, and these scores were then compared across group conditions. The average individual member score was computed by summing the performance measure of interest for all members of a group and then dividing it by the number of members.

variable_name: proportion of groups surpassing best member performance
description: The performance score for each group was compared to that of its respective best member, and a proportion of the number of groups that exceeded the best member to the total number of groups for each condition was calculated. Tests of significance of these proportions used 0.33 as the expected value of a group's ability to exceed the performance of its best member, based on data presented by Nemiroff et al. (1976).

Decision making by four-person groups, as opposed to individual members working alone, on the same case. Group performance was scored on the same measures as the written work of each of the 120 individual subjects, and each group was compared with the average and the best of its own members.

Indicator of a realized firm–SMO collaboration on a given environmental issue, coded 1 for actual collaborations (treated rows) and 0 for matched counterfactual collaborations of similar firms on the same issue. In the estimation the treatment variable is instrumented using fitted values from a probit model of collaboration.

variable_name: SMO bilateral collaboration / SMO multilateral collaboration
description: Two dummy variables describing the form of the collaboration. SMO bilateral collaboration is coded 1 for a collaboration involving one firm and one SMO and 0 otherwise; SMO multilateral collaboration is coded 1 if the collaboration involves more than one firm or SMO and 0 otherwise. Each collaboration in the data was coded as bilateral or multilateral when it was identified.

The sum of SMOs operating in a given movement to which the collaborating SMO is connected via a board interlock. Board members' names are taken from each SMO's IRS tax filing, recorded manually and matched computationally on last name and first initial to directors of other SMOs in the same filing year, with matches validated visually and by internet search.

The sum of contentious challenges mounted against any firm on the issue in the previous 3 years by the SMO with which a firm collaborates. It is used to test whether the decrease in contention is larger for partners with a history of contentious tactics.

The sum of contentious challenges against any firm on the issue by the partner SMO that rely on grassroots participation outside institutional channels, including boycotts, protests, civil disobedience, and letter-writing campaigns, computed over the previous 3 years.

The sum of the partner SMO's contentious challenges against any firm on the issue over the previous 3 years that rely on professionals (e.g., lawyers) and institutional arenas (e.g., regulatory hearings), such as lawsuits, regulatory interventions, or shareholder proxy proposals.

The number of times a firm has been contentiously challenged by the 136 SMOs in the sample on an environmental issue. In the matched sample analysis contentious challenges a firm faces on an issue are summed over the 3 years post-collaboration, and the outcome is logged because it suffers from overdispersion and is highly skewed.

Indicator at the firm–movement–year level for whether the firm has a collaboration with an SMO on the movement's environmental issue. Each row in the panel estimations represents a firm's relationships with SMOs in one movement, and variables are calculated on a yearly basis with a one-year lag for independent and control variables.

variable_name: SMO collaboration bilateral / SMO collaboration multilateral
description: Dummy variables distinguishing the form of the firm's collaboration, computed on a yearly basis at the firm–movement level. Bilateral denotes a collaboration involving one firm and one SMO; multilateral denotes a collaboration involving more than one firm or SMO.

The number of board interlocks the firm's partner SMOs have with SMOs in the movement; if a firm collaborates with more than one SMO in an issue-year, the number of board interlocks all of its partner SMOs have is summed.

The contentious repertoire of the firm's partner SMO on the issue; when a firm has more than one partner SMO in an issue-year the authors use the maximum value of partner SMOs' repertoires, which best reflects the theorized signal mechanism.

The portion of the partner SMO's contentious repertoire that relies on grassroots participation outside institutional channels (boycotts, protests, civil disobedience, letter-writing campaigns), computed yearly for the collaboration partner.

The portion of the partner SMO's contentious repertoire that relies on professionals and institutional arenas (lawsuits, regulatory interventions, shareholder proxy proposals), computed yearly for the collaboration partner.
The logged count of one plus the number of contentious challenges a firm received from a movement, computed on a yearly basis at the firm–movement level.

A multidimensional index combining the diversity of the directors' educational, industrial, and organizational experiences. Educational experience diversity is the additive inverse of the Herfindahl concentration index of the alma maters conferring bachelor's degrees to the firm's directors; industrial experience diversity is the additive inverse of the Herfindahl concentration index of the directors' cumulative work experiences across different industries (three-digit SIC); organizational experience diversity is the average number of other boards in the S&P 1500 on which current members serve. Each component is normalized by its mean and SD, and the combined index is standardized.

A focal patent's CD index captures the degree to which the patent increases or decreases the use of prior technological knowledge by subsequent patents, computed from changes in its backward and forward citation networks. Path-breaking patents are those with a positive CD index based on forward citations within 5 years after patent issuance and all backward citations of the focal patent. The variable is the logarithm of one plus the count of all path-breaking patents for which a firm applied in a year.
time_window: forward citations within 5 years after patent issuance

description: The logarithm of one plus the 5-year forward citation count of all path-breaking patents for which a firm applied in a year. Path-breaking patents are those with a positive CD index computed from the focal patent's backward and forward citation networks.

Industrial competition is measured as the reverse of the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, constructed using firm market share in sales. Tercile indicators of competition are created and board experiential diversity is interacted with the second and the third terciles (Mid_Competition and High_Competition).

Following Coles et al. (2008), the complexity score is calculated as the first component of firm revenue, leverage ratio, and firm employment in principal component analysis. Tercile indicators of firm complexity are created and board experiential diversity is interacted with the second and the third terciles (Mid_Complexity and High_Complexity).

Board monitoring is proxied by the share of independent directors, and tercile indicators are created based on its sample distribution. Board experiential diversity is interacted with the first and second terciles of independent director shares (Low_Monitoring and Mid_Monitoring), relative to the third (high monitoring) tercile.

The experiential diversity of a firm's nonlocal director supply is first computed with the board experiential diversity formula over each firm's uniquely defined pool of nonlocal director candidates in a year. Nonlocal candidates live at least 150 miles from the firm's HQ and within 50 miles of an airport serving nonstop flights to the focal firm's HQ. The measure is then weighted by the frequencies of nonstop flights serving between the firm HQ and the nonlocal director domicile airports.

Classification of a venture's entered industry into three levels of concentration following Bain's (1959) first classification system, which is based on the eight-firm concentration ratio. Concentration ratios for each venture's entered industry were obtained from the Census of Manufactures concentration ratios. The authors report that this operationalization provided the strongest support for differences in venture performance and selected it for the pairwise comparisons.

Bain's (1959) second classification system for the level of industry concentration, which consists of six categories and is based on a combination of the eight- and four-firm concentration ratios. Concentration ratios for each venture's entered industry were obtained from the Census of Manufactures concentration ratios. The authors report partial support for differences in venture performance with this operationalization.

Classification system discussed by Caves (1972) that is based on a combination of the 20- and eight-firm concentration ratios and consists of three categories. Concentration ratios for each venture's entered industry were obtained from the Census of Manufactures concentration ratios. The authors report partial support for differences in venture performance with this operationalization.

Three-category classification system based on the four-firm concentration ratio developed by Biggadike (1979), which has also been used in subsequent strategic management studies. The authors report that these cut-points resulted in the classification of 105 of their 115 ventures into the low-concentration industry category and that the operationalization failed to support Hypothesis 1, suggesting that the 55 cut-point is too high for samples such as theirs.

Dichotomous categorization of the degree of product differentiation, as used by Buzzell and Gale (1987), that classifies industries into categories of high versus low degrees of product differentiation using the mean advertising intensity as the cut-point. Advertising intensity data were drawn from the COMPUSTAT data base. The authors report that this operationalization failed to support the hypothesis regarding expected differences in venture performance.

Three-category classification of the degree of product differentiation based on the advertising intensity of the industry, using cut-points based on the recommendations of Bain (1956, 1959) and Caves (1972) regarding whether the industry sold its products primarily to other industrial users or consumers; the cut-point of 0.5 percent for the homogeneous product classification converged with the type of industry characterized by sales to other producers. This operationalization was developed in this study and supported by prior theory in industrial organization. The authors report statistically significant differences in ROA, ROE, and ROS based on this measure.

variable_name: Sandberg's 3-category product differences and change in product technology system
description: Classification of the degree of product differentiation into heterogeneous, partially differentiated, and homogeneous categories, based on evidence of physical differences in products, image differences in products, and rates of changes in product technology. The approach is based on the classification system developed by Sandberg (1984, 1986) and subsequently utilized by Kunkel (1991). Information for classifying this operationalization was obtained from the ventures' IPO prospectuses; the authors report that it did not differentiate performance among the degrees of product differentiation and that 111 of the 115 ventures were classified as entering industries characterized by heterogeneous products.

Revised seven-stage life cycle model based on Hofer's (1977) six-stage model, to which Kunkel (1991) added a seventh stage. In addition to market growth criteria, the seven stages are based on technological change in the product design and technological change in process design. The authors report no support for Hypothesis 3 with this operationalization and note that 80 percent of the ventures were classified as entering industries in the growth stage, leaving small sample sizes in the remaining categories.

Four-stage life cycle model that contains the stages of life cycle suggested by Shepherd (1975) and that the majority of prior strategic management research has followed. The classification criteria described by the authors are: introductory (primary demand just starting; many potential users unfamiliar with products); growth (real growth 10 percent or more; technology and/or competitive structure still changing); maturity (potential users familiar with products; technology and competitive structure stable); and decline (products viewed as commodities; weaker competitors exiting). The authors report that this model produced better differentiation among the industry structures entered by new ventures and stronger statistically significant results than the extended Hofer life cycle model.

Two categories of industry growth rate, high versus low, based on whether or not the venture's industry grows at more than a 10 percent annual rate in real terms, following the approach of Miller and Camp (1985), Hambrick and Lei (1985), Roure and Maidique (1986), and Siegel et al. (1993). Market growth rates were obtained from Industry Norms and Key Business Ratios compiled by Dun & Bradstreet Credit Services. The authors report that the growth rate operationalizations failed to support differences in performance.

Three categories of growth rate following Shepherd's (1975) suggestion: high (market growing at 10 percent or more annually in real terms); slow (market growing between 0 percent and 10 percent annually in real terms); and negative (market growth rate declining in real terms). Market growth rates were obtained from Industry Norms and Key Business Ratios compiled by Dun & Bradstreet Credit Services. The authors report that the growth rate operationalizations failed to support differences in performance.

The average of the first three complete fiscal years following the venture's initial public offering was used for this measure of performance. The use of 3-year averages is common in prior research and smooths out yearly fluctuations in the data, which are likely to be quite extreme with this sample of new ventures, while also providing measures which are more long term in nature. Measures of venture performance were obtained from COMPUSTAT.
time_window: average of the first three complete fiscal years following the IPO

description: The average of the first three complete fiscal years following the venture's initial public offering was used for this measure of performance. The use of 3-year averages is common in prior research and smooths out yearly fluctuations in the data, which are likely to be quite extreme with this sample of new ventures, while also providing measures which are more long term in nature. Measures of venture performance were obtained from COMPUSTAT.
time_window: average of the first three complete fiscal years following the IPO

description: The average of the first three complete fiscal years following the venture's initial public offering was used for this measure of performance. The use of 3-year averages is common in prior research and smooths out yearly fluctuations in the data, which are likely to be quite extreme with this sample of new ventures, while also providing measures which are more long term in nature. Measures of venture performance were obtained from COMPUSTAT.
time_window: average of the first three complete fiscal years following the IPO

description: The average of the first three complete fiscal years following the venture's initial public offering was used for this measure of performance. The use of 3-year averages is common in prior research and smooths out yearly fluctuations in the data, while also providing measures which are more long term in nature. The authors report that most striking was the lack of general support for the sales growth measure in comparison to the three profitability measures.
time_window: average of the first three complete fiscal years following the IPO

description: Trust was measured using a five-item Likert-type scale adapted from Aulakh et al. (1996) and Sako and Helper (1998) that captures fairness, reliability, and goodwill among alliance partners. The measure has high statistical reliability based on Cronbach's alpha (.85). The authors also report that the correlation between trust and performance in their data was .52, within the range reported in prior studies.

Alliance performance was measured using a five-item Likert scale reflecting the extent to which the local partner is satisfied with the overall performance of its alliance, the extent to which the local partner perceives the foreign partner to be satisfied with the overall performance of the alliance, the partners' satisfaction with respect to the attainment of goals, the extent to which the local partner is satisfied with the financial performance of the alliance, and the extent to which the local partner perceives its foreign partner to be satisfied with the financial performance of the alliance. With a Cronbach's alpha of .90, the performance scale demonstrated high reliability.

Nine strategic rationales (the eight identified by Gulati and Singh [1998] plus access to technology) were assigned to one of Thompson's (1967) three classes of interdependence: pooled, sequential, and reciprocal. Interdependence was the average composite score of the strategic rationales present in an alliance, weighted by the type of interdependence each rationale represented; ordinal weights of 3, 2, and 1 were assigned for reciprocal, sequential, and pooled interdependence, respectively, so that higher values indicate higher interdependence. The equation specifying the composite score (CIi) is given in an unreadable formula block; the text states that CIi was the weighted composite interdependence score for alliance i, wi,j the weights reflecting the level of interdependence implied by each strategic rationale j in alliance i, and SRi,j the presence of strategic rationale j in alliance i.

A three-category measure of the degree of competitive overlap between partners. A score of 2 was assigned if an alliance operated in the same four-digit SIC code industry as both partners and neither partner was active in any other four-digit SIC code area; a score of 1 if both partners operated in the same four-digit SIC code area as that of the alliance but one or both partners were active in other four-digit SIC codes as well; and a score of 0 if the partners did not operate in the same industries.

The measure captures instability in the sales of each alliance's industry over the preceding five years, using data from Capitaline, an authoritative database of financial information about India. Industry sales were regressed on year and the standard error of the regression slope coefficient was divided by the mean of industry sales; larger values indicated greater environmental instability.
time_window: five years preceding the survey year

description: The measure used industry sales data spanning five years, obtained from Capitaline, to capture the extent to which alliance partners could predict future trends in product-markets from the recent past. Unpredictability was measured as the coefficient of alienation (1 - R2) of the regression of industry sales in the survey year on the industry sales of the five preceding years.
time_window: five years preceding the survey year

variable_name: number of newly certified B Corps
description: Count of newly certified B Corps in each four-digit NAICS industry per year. To assign industries, the authors scraped firm profile pages on the B Lab website multiple times beginning in 2010 and visited individual firms' websites, then compared each firm's product or service information with detailed U.S. Census Bureau NAICS category descriptions. When multiple NAICS categories were relevant to a firm's main product, they assigned the NAICS code of the public company producing the most similar product or service, categorizing the entire sample of 514 B Corporations into 99 four-digit NAICS industries.

Number of mass layoff events at the industry level, obtained through a special request to the Mass Layoff Statistics program of the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Mass layoffs are treated as a salient manifestation of incumbents' continued pursuit of shareholder value.

Ratio of average executive compensation to average nonsupervisory production worker compensation at the industry level. Executive compensation comes from Compustat Execucomp and worker compensation from the BLS Current Employment Statistics.

Aggregate number of announced stock repurchase plans in the industry-year, counted using the Thompson Financial database (formerly Securities Data Company). Stock repurchase is described as an emblematic corporate policy to appease financial stakeholders.

Based on the CSR strengths in MSCI ESG Stats (formerly known as KLD), which rated the 3,000 largest U.S. corporations on the dimensions of environment, community, human rights, employee relations, diversity, product, and governance. Firm-level scores divide the focal firm's number of strengths by the maximum possible on each dimension and sum the ratios across all dimensions, generating a range of zero to seven; these scores were then averaged at the industry level. The authors use the strength scores because they reflect externally recognized firm reputation rather than actual environmental performance.

The authors built a weighted dictionary of CSR-related one- and two-word phrases by comparing phrase rates in the B Lab corpus describing the 514 B Corps with rates in a corpus of 1,000 Wall Street Journal business-section articles, weighting by frequency in the B Lab corpus; the top 200 phrases were extracted and normalized to range from 1 to 100. Trademarks of large public companies were extracted from the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office dataset, with companies identified using Compustat and matched on firm names. Each dictionary match in a trademark was multiplied by its index score and summed by industry-year.

Completed deals in the United States in the Zephyr acquisitions database in which the acquired firm was not a public company and its description matched the authors' CSR dictionary. The index values of the matched phrases from these deals were summed and tabulated by industry-year using the NAICS codes associated with the acquired firms, yielding a measure of corporate acquisitions of companies specialized in environmental and social responsibility.

Binary coding of whether a firm's stated reason for certification expressed the higher-order reason of opposition to the status quo. The authors separately coded each firm's reasons by assigning short terms summarizing abstract meanings and built a hierarchical structure of 24 first-order codes nested under four higher-order codes, then constructed a binary matrix of the higher-order codes; 57 percent of the 499 firms expressed the opposition reason.

Binary coding of whether a firm's stated reason for certification expressed the higher-order reason of confirming and demonstrating authentic commitment to sustainability. The codes were derived inductively from each firm's stated reasons and tabulated in a binary matrix of higher-order codes; 56 percent of the 499 firms expressed this reason, and it was negatively and significantly correlated with the opposition reason.

The centrality of the inventors on a patent is measured as Bonacich power, computed for all active inventors in the three-year window with UCINET VI. Beta is set equal to three-fourths of the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue of the network matrix, so that inventors linked to influential inventors are themselves more influential by virtue of that linkage. The patent-level independent variable is the maximum of the Bonacich power measure of the associated inventors.
time_window: network of inventors in the three calendar years prior to the start of the spell

description: The constraint measure of structural holes (Burt 1992) is computed from the ties between inventors using UCINET VI. The independent variable is the maximum value of the structural holes spanned by any of the inventors associated with a focal patent.
time_window: network of inventors in the three calendar years prior to the start of the spell

description: The efficiency measure from Burt (1992) uses the ratio of nonredundant contacts to total contacts for a focal inventor. Higher values on this index reflect inventors whose ego networks are rich in structural holes; if all the coinventors of a scientist are unconnected to one another the index takes a value of one. For inventors without any coinventors the index was set to 0.1, and the patent-level independent variable is the maximum value of the structural holes spanned by any of the inventors associated with the focal patent.
time_window: network of inventors in the three calendar years prior to the start of the spell

variable_name: rate of intrafirm citation to a patent by inventors other than those who are involved in its creation
description: The dependent variable is the rate of intrafirm citation to a patent by inventors other than those who created it; self-citations by inventors were excluded, reducing the set of events from 13,729 to 7,571. Spells of up to one year are created for each patent, beginning on the date of issue and ending either at the close of the year (censored) or at the time of citation (event). Observation of citation records stops on December 31, 1998, so the last spell is automatically censored.

variable_name: technological classes of intrafirm citations and patent output
description: The authors examined the patterns of sourcing and patenting in various technological classes by classifying intrafirm citations and granted patents into USPTO technological classes. They report that a small number of classes account for a large share of intrafirm citations and of patent output, and that the top classes appear consistently in the annual top-five rankings, which they treat as evidence of specialization. The authors also computed a Spearman rank order correlation between the citation classes and the output classes.

Dummy variable representing extra-institutional tactics, formed by collapsing boycotts, protests, and letter-writing campaigns. The authors first coded each of the five types of activist actions in the data as dummy variables (lawsuits, protests, boycotts, letter-writing campaigns, and proxy votes) and, given the results of Hypothesis 1, collapsed these into extra-institutional (boycotts, protests, and letter writing) or institutional (civil suits and proxy votes) tactics. Extra-institutional and institutional are coded as the inverse of one another.

Dummy variable representing institutional tactics, formed by collapsing civil suits and proxy votes. The authors first coded each of the five types of activist actions as dummy variables and then collapsed them into extra-institutional (boycotts, protests, and letter writing) or institutional (civil suits and proxy votes) tactics. Extra-institutional and institutional are coded as the inverse of one another.

Count of the newspaper articles mentioning the event in the focal year, gathered using Factiva database searches and excluding the one used to code the event. The authors took the natural log of this variable (plus a constant of one) to address the skew in its distribution and to retain those events with a value of 0. Because the Factiva database goes back to 1980, observations before that year were dropped from these regressions.

KLD negative ratings in the year following the event, used to proxy investor environmental risk reactions. Coded as equal to 1 if the sum of the firm's weaknesses exceeded the sum of its strengths on the rated seven dimensions in a given year, and 0 otherwise. KLD is an investment advisor for socially oriented investors that has historically used the information as a factor in investment decisions, so the authors characterize these data as investor perceptions rather than environmental performance.

variable_name: Activist religious, Activist investors, SMO (set of dummy variables)
description: Each type of activist is coded as a dummy variable consistent with prior research. The sample includes religious groups (Activist religious), activist investors such as pension fund managers and socially responsible investment groups (Activist investors), and nongovernmental organizations such as issue advocacy groups (SMO). Activist individuals serve as the referent group in the data.

Two indicators of the profitability associated with the relationship over a 5-year period, given all costs and revenues: the profitability of the relationship of the supplier firm (PROFITS) and of the customer firm (PROFITC), the latter assessed by the interviewed supplier manager. The question reads: 'Considering all costs and revenues associated with this relationship, how would you assess its profitability for your own company over the last five years'. The authors describe this as a composite measure of the current and historical profitability of the relationship, and conclude that there is one joint profitability associated with the relationship rather than two separate profitabilities.

Two indicators of the potential effect on one party's business of losing its partner, and vice versa: the potential effect on the supplier's business if it were to lose its customer (SLOSEC), a measure of the supplying firm's dependence on the customer, together with the reverse dependence situation (CLOSES). The authors state that, unlike measures based on the share of the supplier's sales and customer's purchases, this measure focuses on the overall importance of the partners to each other as estimated by the respondent.

Two questions about investments in the relationship of the partners, one concerning the supplier's investment in the relationship with the customer (INVESTS) and the other the customer's investment in the relationship with the supplier (INVESTC). The authors interpret mutual commitment as the higher-order theoretical construct affecting both indicators simultaneously, on the basis that the shared domain of two parties' views of their relationship is their mutual view; the questions were preceded by a detailed discussion of aspects of relationship investment. The wording, 'In all, how large is the investment made by your firm in your relationship with this customer?', asks the respondent to condense all specified aspects of investment into one.

Four indicators of the influence that relationships with third parties have upon the focal relationship, concerning the influence of relationships with noncompetitive third party suppliers and customers to both parties in the focal relationship. Two indicators concern the extent to which business in the focal relationship is affected by the relationship with the supplier's suppliers (SS) and the supplier's other customers (SOC); the remaining two reflect the extent to which business in the focal relationship is affected by the customer's relationship with his customers (CC) and with his suppliers of products supplementary to those of the focal supplier (COS). The construct is indicated only by measures of directly connected relationships.

Indicator set to one for the 50 percent of sample companies categorized as first movers within their competitive set. Incorporation dates were used to determine market entry rank within competitive sets, except when a company diversified into its set from another line of business, in which case market entry order was based on website launch dates for all competitors in the set. Competitive sets were defined to include companies selling products or services likely to be viewed as close substitutes.

A composite that sums three categorical variables reflecting winner-take-all structural attributes, assessed for each generic business model: network effects (NETWORK = 1, 2, or 3), static scale economies measured by average variable contribution margins (SCALE = 1, 2, or 3), and customer switching costs (SWITCH = 1, 2, or 3). Managers provided information on contribution margins through field interviews, and the attribute assessments were reviewed by over two dozen scholars and managers with relevant expertise. Because the three components were collinear, it was difficult to test their separate impact. The variable was standardized and logarithmically transformed before estimation.

Marketing spending during the year of the company's IPO, used to measure the intensity of investment in accelerated growth; reliable measures could not be developed for aggressive discounting or mergers. It was estimated as part of a system of simultaneous equations with sales and cash balances, after logarithmic transformation and standardization of the variables. In step two, the residual of this equation (RESMKT) measures the firm's commitment to accelerated growth: a positive residual indicates that a company invested more heavily in customer acquisition efforts than would be predicted, after controlling for firm and market characteristics.

Long-term return on invested capital: the numerator sums the market value of a company's equity and the book value of its debt at year-end 2001; the denominator equals the total amount of equity and debt capital raised, net of any equity repurchases or debt repayments, over a period that includes the last two full fiscal years as a private company plus all periods during which it had publicly traded equity. For the 19 companies that were bankrupt or had been delisted prior to the end of 2001, equity and debt values were assumed to be zero, and for the 16 companies acquired during 2001 market value was assumed to equal the total proceeds received by investors.

The authors identified individual industry experts among the nonexecutive directors on the board. They captured the positions of each director over the past four years in which he/she served as either a nonexecutive or executive director, excluding focal firm positions, and allocated each prior position the firm's primary four-digit SIC code. They identified the maximum number of coinciding, consecutive SIC digits between prior positions and the focal firm, starting from the first SIC digit, and assigned an experience value between zero and four to each director. Industry expertise is the proportion of nonexecutive directors with experience values at a minimum of three.
time_window: positions over the past four years

description: Strategic change is a composite measure built from four ratios: (1) plant and equipment newness (net P&E/gross P&E); (2) nonproductive overhead (selling, general, and administrative expenses/sales); (3) inventory levels (inventories/sales); and (4) financial leverage (total debt/equity). A change in these ratios across years indicates a departure from a firm's prior profile and suggests strategic change. The authors calculated the absolute value of the differences between two subsequent years in these ratios, standardized each resulting value by year across all firms, and calculated the average across the four standardized values to obtain the composite variable.

The paper uses the disclosure requirements index (DRI) of La Porta et al. (2006) as its proxy for institutional information provision. The index is a country-level measure of disclosure requirements, where environments with low institutional information provision are countries with a weak disclosure standard. The authors also used the index of accounting standards (IAS) as an alternative proxy for institutional information provision in their robustness checks.

The paper uses the anti-self-dealing index (ASD) of Djankov et al. (2008) as its proxy for institutional control provision. The ASD is a country-level index that captures the degree of shareholder protection laws against insider expropriation; greater values denote insiders' limited ability to extract private benefits against minority shareholders. The strength of investor protection index (SIP) was used as an alternative proxy for institutional control provision in robustness checks.

A dummy variable that equals one for firms that had misrepresentations and zero for firms that did not. The event year is the first year restated; the authors identified the actual year misrepresented from business press announcements and the EDGAR database, assuming the year immediately preceding the announcement where the actual year could not be identified definitively. Firms that restated multiple years appear only once in the sample.

Total stock option grant value divided by total compensation, where total compensation is the sum of salary, bonus, and options. Options are valued consistently across firms using a 10% growth model, and the values of restricted stock awards are added to the values of stock options granted. The ratio is bounded between zero and one and uses data from the year immediately before the year of misrepresentation.

Bonus divided by total compensation, where total compensation is the sum of salary, bonus, and options. The ratio is bounded between zero and one. Bonuses came directly from Compustat's Execucomp or firm proxy statements and use data from the year immediately before the year of misrepresentation.

The firm's return on assets in the year prior to the misrepresentation minus the mean return on assets for the firm's industry for the same year. The comparison industry is formed from Compustat data on firms in the same four-digit SIC code as the focal firm, excluding the focal firm from the industry calculations. Separate variables are constructed for positive and negative values of social relative performance to allow different slopes on either side of zero.

Net income before extraordinary expenses divided by assets in the year before the restatement year (ROA t-1) minus the return on assets for two years before the restatement year (ROA t-2). Self-relative performance is split into two variables to allow for different slopes for positive and negative values: the positive variable equals zero whenever self-relative performance is negative and equals self-relative performance otherwise, and symmetrically the negative variable equals zero for observations where self-relative performance exceeds zero and equals self-relative performance otherwise.

Dummy variables that equal one when relative performance is greater than zero and equal zero otherwise, permitting a discontinuity in the influence of relative performance at zero. As with self-relative performance, separate variables are constructed for positive and negative values of social relative performance and a dummy variable for positive values of social relative performance; both dummies use data from the year before the misrepresentation.

SIC codes for each firm were collected from the Trinet data base and diversification strategy was classified according to Rumelt's (1974) typology. Three categories of strategy were used: related-constrained, related-linked, and unrelated. Firms with a related ratio of 0.7 or greater (70 percent or more of sales coming from the largest group of related businesses) were classified as related, and the nature of the relatedness was evaluated to determine whether a related strategy was constrained or linked; firms with a related ratio less than 0.7 were classified as unrelated.

The same Rumelt (1974) classification of diversification strategy into related-constrained, related-linked, and unrelated firms, based on SIC codes collected from the Trinet data base, was applied to the second sample. Firms with a related ratio of 0.7 or greater were classified as related and the nature of the relatedness determined whether the strategy was constrained or linked; firms with a related ratio less than 0.7 were classified as unrelated.

Diversification mode was measured according to the relative frequency of acquisition used by the firm when entering new businesses, following the method described fully in Lamont and Anderson (1985). Information about acquisitions was collected from the Mergers and Acquisitions Rosters by MLR, Inc. and the Predicasts F&S Index of Corporate Change; Dun's Million Dollar Directory, Standard and Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors and Executives, and company annual reports provided further information about the acquired firms.

For the second sample the same measure was used: the relative frequency of acquisition used by the firm when entering new businesses, following Lamont and Anderson (1985). Acquisition information came from the Mergers and Acquisitions Rosters by MLR, Inc. and the Predicasts F&S Index of Corporate Change, supplemented by Dun's Million Dollar Directory, Standard and Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors and Executives, and company annual reports.

Four measures were used: return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), return on investment (ROI), and sales growth (GRSALES). Averages were calculated over the 1978-84 time frame for Sample I to provide an overall assessment of the performance effects of strategy and mode.

The same four measures were used: return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), return on investment (ROI), and sales growth (GRSALES). Averages were calculated over the 1983-87 time frame for Sample II to provide an overall assessment of the performance effects of strategy and mode.

variable_name: Optimal match between strategy and mode
description: Firms were classified by whether they exhibited the optimal match between strategy and mode (related-constrained with internal development, related-linked with a mixed mode of development, and unrelated with acquisitive development) or adopted the same strategy via a different mode. Of the 47 firms in Sample I, only 12 firms or 25.5 percent of the sample used optimal modes.

variable_name: Optimal match between strategy and mode
description: Firms were classified by whether they exhibited the optimal match between strategy and mode (related-constrained with internal development, related-linked with a mixed mode of development, and unrelated with acquisitive development) or adopted the same strategy via a different mode. Of the 95 firms in Sample II, 38 firms or 40 percent used optimal modes.

Set to 1 if the new plant was part of a multiunit firm and at the time of startup belonged to a SIC3 industry in which the firm had operated up to that point, and 0 otherwise. Plants that started as a single-plant firm but were acquired by another, multiplant firm were excluded. De novo entrants are the omitted baseline category in the regressions.
time_window: at the time of plant startup

description: Set to 1 if the new plant was part of a multiunit firm and at the time of startup belonged to a SIC3 industry in which the firm had never operated up to that point, and 0 otherwise. All plants not classified as incumbents or diversifying entrants were classified as de novo entrants, the omitted baseline category.
time_window: at the time of plant startup

description: Productivity of a new plant venture in each year of its life, computed as the residual from a production function estimated industry by industry; the equation itself is not reproduced in the extracted text. Value added is the difference between plant output and expenditure on materials, both adjusted for industry-specific inflation; capital stock is the sum of investments in that year and the depreciated capital stock from last year; labor is labor hours in production-worker equivalents. Productivity is therefore the part of value added not explained by the two inputs, and ordinary least squares was used to estimate the industry regressions.
time_window: each year of the plant's life

description: Year-on-year productivity growth, defined by the authors as the change in productivity over the last time period.

The estimated coefficient on log cumulative experience from an augmented production function estimated separately for each SIC3 industry with at least 50 new plants over the sample period. Productivity is decomposed into the industry learning intensity times log cumulative experience, industry-year dummies, and an idiosyncratic error, where cumulative experience is the prior cumulative output of the new plant venture. Ordinary least squares was used to estimate these coefficients.

Measured by the average of the firm's return on assets (ROA) in the two half-year periods subsequent to the half-year during which the succession occurred. For example, a succession occurring between January 1 and June 30 of 2000 uses the firm's ROA in the half-years July 1-December 31, 2000 and January 1-June 30, 2001. This operationalization uses a time horizon of at least 12 months (and up to 18 months, depending upon the succession date).
time_window: the two half-year periods after the succession half-year (12 to 18 months)

description: A successor CEO was considered to have an early departure if s/he was no longer in the CEO position at the end of the second half-year subsequent to the half-year during which the succession occurred; 720 early departures were identified. An early departure was considered an early non-routine departure if it was not retirement, health reason, promotion, position rotation, or change in the controlling owner; examples are termination, resignation, unspecified personal reasons, or unspecified other reasons (395 cases). The variable is a dummy coded '1' for an early non-routine departure and '0' otherwise.
time_window: second half-year after the succession half-year

description: An early departure was considered an early routine departure if the reported reason was retirement, health reason, promotion (e.g., becoming the board chair of the focal firm), position rotation (e.g., taking a position in the parent company, or in a sibling firm), or change in the controlling owner (325 cases). Departures due to a change in the controlling owner were coded as early routine departures. The variable is a dummy coded '1' for an early routine departure and '0' otherwise.
time_window: second half-year after the succession half-year

description: Coded as '1' if the predecessor CEO was a male and the successor was a female, and '0' otherwise. These successions were compared to same-gender successions (i.e., male-to-male or female-to-female successions).

Coded as '1' if the predecessor CEO was a female and the successor was a male, and '0' otherwise. These successions were compared to same-gender successions (i.e., male-to-male or female-to-female successions).
Measured by the proportion of female directors (other than the female CEO successor if the successor was a female) on the firm's board in the year of succession.
Measured by the proportion of females (other than the female CEO successor if the successor was a female) in the top management team as reported in the firm's annual report in the year of succession.
Coded as a dummy variable, '1' if the successor CEO was promoted from within the firm and '0' if hired from outside.
