CEO succession with gender change was captured by two dummy variables: male-to-female succession (predecessor male, successor female) and female-to-male succession (predecessor female, successor male), each compared with same-gender successions. Gender change occurred in 289 of 3,320 successions.

variable_name: mean abnormal return (AR) and cumulative abnormal return (CAR)
description: Using the market-adjusted returns approach, the abnormal or unexpected return for security i on day t is the actual return on the security minus the expected return, where the expected return is estimated as the mean return on the stock market (the Standard and Poor 500) for day t. Mean abnormal returns are averaged across announcements of strategic investment decisions, and cumulative abnormal returns are cumulated over event days. Because most announcements were actually made prior to the close of trading on the previous day, the announcement period is days -1 and 0, and the two-day cumulative abnormal return is used to evaluate the market's reaction; returns were also calculated for the succeeding two trading weeks.
time_window: Days -1 and 0 (announcement period), cumulated through day 10

description: Announcements were identified from the 'What's News' column of the Wall Street Journal and confirmed in the full article. An announcement was excluded if the article included information about the firm's sales or earnings, or if another announcement concerning the firm's sales, earnings, personnel changes, etc. appeared within one day (before or after) of the investment decision announcement, in order to minimize the effect of extraneous influences on stock prices. The final sample contained 767 announcements made by 248 companies in 102 industries.

Each announcement was classified into one of four broad types of strategic investment decision: joint venture formation, research and development project, capital expenditure, and product/market diversification. These broad investment decisions were further classified into appropriate subcategories, such as ongoing versus new research and development projects, capacity expansion, plant modernization and capital budget increases among capital expenditures, and old product/new market, new product/old market, and new product/new market for diversification.

variable_name: investment size (investment dollars relative to total assets)
description: In 365 of the 767 cases the Wall Street Journal article gave information about the dollar size of the investment. The dollar amount of the investment was first divided by the total assets of the firm so that each investment was expressed as a relative percentage, and the subsample of 365 announcements was then dichotomized at the median (5.3 percent) to compare small with large investments, i.e. less than or greater than 5.3 percent of total firm assets. Over 95 percent of the investments in this subsample came from the research and development and capital expenditure categories.
scale: Percentage of total firm assets, dichotomized at the median into small and large

description: The expected life span or duration of a corporate investment was provided in 287 cases. This subsample was divided into two categories, short-term (less than 3 years) and long-term (more than 3 years), and the stock market valuation of each group was calculated. Over 95 percent of the investments in this subsample came from the research and development and capital expenditure categories.
scale: Short-term (less than 3 years) versus long-term (more than 3 years)

description: The personal goal score was based on responses to five questionnaire items; each question was scored dichotomously as indicating either a hard or easy goal and the overall score was the total number of responses rated 'hard', yielding a five-category continuum from a very consistent rating of a hard personal goal to a very consistent rating of an easy personal goal. Two raters scored the open-ended items, with interrater reliability of .97, and differences were discussed and resolved. Because the correlation between the assigned goal and personal goal variables was nonsignificant, indicating that the goal manipulation failed, the personal goal variable was the one actually used.
scale: five-category continuum from very consistent hard to very consistent easy personal goal
time_window: administered at the end of the simulation

description: Strategy was measured from the actual decisions made during each of the ten decision periods of the simulation; the decision variables were converted to z-scores and summed based on three time periods, then factor analyzed for each time period using the principal component method and varimax rotation with variables loading below .30 eliminated. All participants received a score on each strategy based on their factor score for items that loaded on that strategy. The volume strategy was the most effective in terms of predicting performance and was thus the main strategy variable used in subsequent analyses.
time_window: three time periods: decision periods 1-3 (time 1), 4-7 (time 2), and 8-10 (time 3)

description: Like the other behavioral strategies, the quality strategy was derived from participants' actual simulation decisions: decision variables were converted to z-scores, summed over three time periods and factor analyzed with the principal component method and varimax rotation, eliminating loadings below .30. Participants received a score on the strategy based on their factor score for items loading on it. The quality strategy was inversely related to the volume strategy.
time_window: three time periods: decision periods 1-3 (time 1), 4-7 (time 2), and 8-10 (time 3)

description: The scan strategy was derived in the same way as the other behavioral strategies from the actual decisions made during the simulation, using z-scored decision variables summed over three time periods and factor analyzed with principal component analysis and varimax rotation. All participants received a score on the strategy based on their factor score for items loading on it. The authors note that the scan strategy is not a well-developed strategy, since it only entails scanning an environment with any resulting actions unspecified.
time_window: three time periods: decision periods 1-3 (time 1), 4-7 (time 2), and 8-10 (time 3)

description: The focus strategy was derived in the same way as the other behavioral strategies from the actual decisions made during the simulation, with z-scored decision variables summed over three time periods and factor analyzed with principal component analysis and varimax rotation. Participants received a score on the strategy based on their factor score for items loading on it. The focus strategy was inversely related to the volume strategy and was the least successful strategy.
time_window: three time periods: decision periods 1-3 (time 1), 4-7 (time 2), and 8-10 (time 3)

description: The seven performance variables were factor-analyzed for each of the ten decision periods through the principal component method using orthogonal, varimax rotation. Factor 1, sales, consisted of the sales variable alone and had factor loadings of .93 to .99 throughout the ten decision periods. Since all the groups were combined for data analysis, within-group z-scores were used in all cases to provide a common metric across the groups.
time_window: each of the ten decision periods, combined into three time periods

description: Factor 2, income, consisted of the six other financial variables and had factor loadings for all variables equal to or greater than .89 for all ten decision periods. Pearson correlations between the two performance factors ranged from .32 to .44, which the authors attribute to sales affecting the financial variables in factor 2. Within-group z-scores were used to provide a common metric across the groups.
time_window: each of the ten decision periods, combined into three time periods

variable_name: behavioral strategy typology (volume, quality, scan, focus)
description: Task (business) strategy was measured from the participants' actual decisions in each of the ten simulation periods. Decision variables were factor analyzed into four behavioral strategies named volume, quality, scan and focus, and the volume strategy was the main strategy variable in the performance tests.
time_window: three time periods of the ten decision periods

description: Firms are classified by national origin: the firms selected originally included 25 of the world's 33 largest pharmaceutical firms, those with a global market share in ethical pharmaceuticals of greater than 1 percent. Five large generic manufacturers and six smaller U.S. research firms were added to the data base, and Japanese firms that participate in the U.S. market primarily through licensing were excluded. Nine European firms are studied as foreign entrants: Beecham, Boots, Burroughs-Wellcome, Glaxo, Imperial Chemical, Ciba-Geigy, Hoffmann-LaRoche, Sandoz and Hoechst.

Characterized from the historical analysis of the parents' origins and competencies: Ciba, Geigy, Hoechst and Sandoz all began as dye firms that later moved into chemical products and still later into pharmaceutical drugs, and ICI began as a fine chemical firm, then proceeded into dyestuffs and, finally, into pharmaceuticals. Glaxo's historic strength was in children's foodstuffs, Burroughs-Wellcome was known for vaccines, Boots established a retail chemist chain, and Beecham came to prominence as the leading British producer of antibiotics after World War II. Parent global sales positions were also used, with four of the five organic chemistry entrants leading the global pharmaceutical sales table for calendar 1977.

Each firm is assigned to a strategic group within each stable strategic time period. Groups were formed by Ward's minimum variance clustering of the seven strategic variables (ARD, RRD, HRD, HOSP, CHRN, HMK and RELPROD) within each period, and each grouping carries a label that generally describes its members at that time. Groups range from those with less success in bringing a broad scope of new products to market to groups of strong firms with diverse product bases and deep R&D skills.
time_window: five stable strategic time periods spanning 1969-1988

variable_name: expansion path (sequence of strategic group membership)
description: Recorded as the sequence of strategic groups a firm occupied across the stable strategic time periods. The paper outlines this sequence for the four firms that entered groups with lower barriers (Beecham, Glaxo, Boots and Burroughs-Wellcome); the progression is generally from weaker to stronger groups.

Recorded as firms' changes of strategic group membership across the stable strategic time periods. The Appendix maps the movements of all firms, U.S. and European, across strategic space, and the historical analysis compares the movement patterns of U.S. firms with those of the European entrants.

A measure of research activity developed using a logged patent count. Patent data come from the U.S. Patent Office's breakdown of annual patents granted by classes of products, and only those classes related to pharmaceutical products were used. When clustering, firms were only considered in the U.S.A. when they both patented chemical entities and registered products in the U.S.A. in their own name or that of a subsidiary.
Measures the relative acceleration or deceleration of a firm's R&D pace. This allows the R&D level to be assessed relative to the firm's historic allocations.

One of two Herfindahl-type indices developed from the product line data using the 7-year time frames; this one is based on the relatedness across the research classes. Product mix variables were developed to measure how balanced a firm's product line was across both therapeutic and research classes.
A Herfindahl-type index based on the relatedness across the therapeutic classes, developed with the 7-year time frames. Substitution across therapeutic classes is not possible with pharmaceuticals.

A proxy measure that roughly identifies each firm's product mix and research thrusts along the clinical/retail dichotomy, developed by identifying the percentage of new drug approvals for delivery forms that are primarily used in a hospital or other clinical setting. Hospitals and clinics purchase their own drugs and their physicians use formularies for drug dispensing, where inclusion is competitive and often requires firms to compete aggressively on price.

A proxy that attempts to measure the extent to which products approved by the FDA are targeted for long-term patient consumption. Chronic care drugs hold high potential for profits because patients often refill the same prescription, perhaps for life, and physicians are reluctant to change a prescription after the patient begins using a particular product.
A measure of each firm's annual new product production relative to the industry as a whole.

The age of the firm's owner-manager, in years. Firms are treated as owner-managed when the listed CEO is also the majority shareholder, identified with a name-matching algorithm that compares the list of firm managers to the list of firm owners. In separate regressions the continuous age variable is replaced by dummies for the age brackets less than 34, 35-40, 41-46, 47-53, 54-59 and above 59.
Investment is the annual change in log total assets. It is computed for each year from 2003 to 2012 and measures the change in log total assets from the previous year to the focal year.
Sales growth is the annual change in log sales. It is computed for each year from 2003 to 2012 and measures the change in log sales from the previous year to the focal year.
Return on assets is net income over assets, calculated for the focal year. The 3-year differenced result reported for ROA is the log change in ROA between the focal year t and year t-3.

A dummy for firm exit, modelled with a Cox proportional hazards specification whose hazard function is conditional on covariates including firm assets, firm age and a set of dummies for age categories. The estimated hazard ratio compares the likelihood of exit from business for firms with young versus old CEOs, with 1.0 indicating no effect of CEO age on survival.

A dummy for whether the firm changed ownership, estimated in linear probability models as a function of measures of financial development, CEO's age, and other firm and geography controls. The analysis of ownership changes is based on the firms for which the authors have comprehensive ownership coverage.

Information on the number of financial institutions in each region comes from Structural Business Statistics provided by Eurostat. A credit institution is defined as an undertaking whose business is to receive deposits or other repayable funds from the public and to grant credits for its own account; all credit institutions in this measure operate in the 'other monetary institution' (NACE 65.12) and 'other financial intermediation' (NACE 65.2) segments. In all regressions the authors control for a region's geographical size and population and also explore specifications normalizing the number of institutions by region size.

Financial sector productivity is the ratio between total revenues by financial institutions in a region and number of financial sector employees, and is from the European Competitiveness Index 2006-07 report.
Private equity investment data is from the statistical annexes of each country's private equity or venture capital association.

Industries are classified as creative following the detailed classification of creative industries provided by the UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which includes advertising, architecture, art, crafts, design, fashion, film, music, performing arts, publishing, research and development (R&D), software, toys and games, radio, TV, and video games. In the estimations, CEO-age categories are interacted with the creative-industry indicator.

The authors use Eurostat's industry classification to measure technological dynamism and distinguish between manufacturing and service industries. Manufacturing industries are aggregated based on R&D intensity (R&D expenditure to value added) of economic activities and classified as high-technology, medium-high-technology, medium-low-technology or low-technology. Service sectors are aggregated into knowledge-intensive services and less-knowledge-intensive services based on the share of tertiary-educated employees at the two-digit industry level.

Managers in the willingness to accept condition read a scenario in which they were awarded 100 unexercisable stock options in each of six publicly traded businesses and were offered a one-time cash bonus in lieu of the award. They indicated the amount of cash bonus per set of 100 options they would require to convert the options to cash, and this figure was divided by 100 to yield a per-option value. Each manager gave six responses, one for each trend-volatility graph.
time_window: one-year historical weekly stock price performance shown in each graph

description: Managers in the willingness to pay condition read a scenario essentially identical to the willingness to accept scenario except that they had earned a cash bonus, had $10,000 per business to convert into stock options in that business, and indicated how many options per business they required for the conversion. Willingness to pay equals $10,000 divided by the number of options required per business.
time_window: one-year historical weekly stock price performance shown in each graph

variable_name: Willingness to accept/willingness to pay condition
description: A between-individuals experimental manipulation: managers were randomly assigned to either the willingness to accept or the willingness to pay condition and completed the corresponding questionnaire. The condition was coded 0 for willingness to accept and 1 for willingness to pay in the analyses.
scale: dichotomous (0 = willingness to accept, 1 = willingness to pay)

description: A within-individuals manipulation: within each pair of graphs one stock exhibited high volatility (45 percent) and the other exhibited low volatility (5 percent), while the stocks had the same mean market performance. The levels were chosen relative to the prevailing Chicago Board Options Exchange volatility index (VIX), whose average was approximately 25 percent for the nine months preceding the study, by adding 20 points for the high-volatility figure and subtracting 20 points for the low-volatility condition. Coded 1 for high volatility and 0 for low volatility.

A within-subjects manipulation: each participant was presented with two graphs (high and low volatility) within each of three trends, flat (neutral), positive (rising) and negative (declining), for six graphs in total. To capture the effect of positive versus negative trend, the repeated-measures regression was performed on the positive and negative trend conditions only, in which the stocks had identical starting and ending prices and the negative condition was the inverse of the positive condition. Valuations in the two conditions were equated by adding $6.25 to negative trend valuations.

Values were calculated with the Black-Scholes equation for each trend and volatility condition. The inputs are the per-share market price (the ending price from each trend), the per-share exercise or strike price of $45.00, time to expiration of ten years, the estimated stock price volatility, the risk-free interest rate and the cumulative standard normal distribution. The risk-free rate was the approximate average of the ten-year U.S. Treasury bond for the 12 months preceding data collection, which was 3.95 percent. The equation itself is not legible in the text supplied.

Number of joint ventures entered into by the firm prior to and including the joint venture in question, within the time window of the data. The measure has a lower bound of 1 and varies from 1 through 23 deals. It is left-censored, since it only accounts for the deals entered into by the firm since 1990.
time_window: deals prior to and including the focal deal, within 1990-93

description: Number of licensing agreements entered into by the firm prior to and including the current licensing contract, within the time window of the data. The measure has a lower bound of 1 and varies from 1 through 30 deals, and is left-censored at the 1990 cut-off. It equals 1 for deals with no prior experience, 2 for exactly one prior licensing, 3 for two or three prior licensings, and 4 for at least four prior licensing deals.
time_window: deals prior to and including the focal deal, within 1990-93

description: A measure created for each firm that multiplies the abnormal returns measure (defined as the cumulative excess returns in the event window day -10 through day +1) by the market value of equity of the firm on day -10, the first day of the event window. It is described as an approximation to the actual wealth effect based on the product of abnormal returns over the event window.

Daily firm-specific excess returns are the difference between actual daily returns and predicted daily returns from a market model estimated over a 240-day period prior to the event day, where the market return is the value-weighted S&P 500. Returns are predicted over a 14-day period surrounding the event day (event days -10 through +3), and the abnormal returns measure is the cumulative excess returns in the event window day -10 through day +1, expressed in percentages.
time_window: estimation period 240 days prior to the event; event window day -10 through day +1

description: Specifications (iii) and (iv) estimate 147 firm fixed effects in addition to the experience and control variables, thus controlling for unobserved heterogeneity. The firm fixed effects are identified by differences in average performance across firms that have engaged in more than one deal, whereas the experience effect is identified by variation across deals for the same firm over time. Each firm fixed effect is interpreted as a measure of that firm's alliance capability, and the joint hypothesis that the firm fixed effects are zero is rejected.

SDC provides information on various contract-specific characteristics, including contract type (i.e., whether it is a joint venture agreement, licensing agreement, etc.). For joint ventures, SDC provides additional information on whether these are entered into at the R&D stage or marketing stage; these are classified as research joint ventures and marketing joint ventures respectively, and the remaining joint ventures, which mostly involve cooperation exclusively in manufacturing, are classified as production joint ventures. The classification is cross-checked with information from the Nexis-Lexis data base.

Internet measures whether both establishments j and k of a particular firm had adopted basic Internet by time t. Internet technology had not diffused among firms prior to 1995 except in very rare cases, so the value of this variable equals zero prior to this date, and it is set equal to zero for all establishments in 1992 and 1994.

variable_name: Basic Internet adoption at the location
description: In the within-location models, Internet is a binary indicator of whether basic Internet has been adopted at the location. In cases where there are multiple establishments within an MSA, a firm location is calculated as adopting basic Internet when at least one establishment has done so.

A dummy variable for whether there is a patent coinvented by researchers in both locations j and k of a particular firm i at time t, dated by application year. The authors form the complete set of pairwise combinations of firm MSAs within a given organization and, based on coauthorship, identify the incidence of collaborations performed between units in different MSAs.

A binary indicator for the incidence of a patent applied for in year t with at least two inventors in location j of a particular firm i. It is used to measure the impact of basic Internet adoption on within-location collaborations.

The incidence of a patent from a single inventor, obtained by reestimating the within-location equation using only single-authored patents. The variable is a binary indicator of whether a firm location produced a single-inventor patent in a given application year.

The percentage deviation of a car's qualifying time from that of the fastest car during the qualifying session, multiplied by the negative of 1 so that higher values indicate better R&D team performance. Qualifying sessions take place on the day preceding a Grand Prix race, and only the qualifying result of the faster of a constructor's two cars is used because driver errors are independent of an R&D team's accomplishment. The authors argue that a car's qualifying time is a better indication of R&D team performance than the race time because competing cars are not allowed to block each other and qualifying results are not affected by accidents, refueling or tire changes.

A Herfindahl Index constructed over five areas in which R&D team members have gathered task-related experience. The authors define the index as the sum, across experience fields z = 1, ..., N, of the square of the share (s_z) of R&D team members who have experience in a given field z; the corresponding formula block is unreadable in this payload, so only the prose definition is recorded. The authors interpret higher values of the index as higher levels of experience diversity.

Proxied by the annual budget (in constant USD) available to constructors for paying for drivers, engineers, support staff, chassis, tires, fuel, transportation, logistics, and so on; engine expenditures are excluded from the constructor budget for comparability. In the moderation tests the authors flag large constructors with a dummy that takes the value of 1 for constructors above the median of the constructor size distribution and, as a robustness test, above the 75th percentile.

The number of years elapsed from the foundation of the constructor. In the moderation tests the authors use a dummy that takes the value of 1 for constructors above the median of firm age and, as a robustness test, above the 75th percentile of firm age.

The ratio of equity partners to junior lawyers, where junior lawyers include associates and nonequity partners. The authors use it in place of the model's promotion ratio, which the model says is positively proportional to it. It is entered in the regressions in logarithmic form, with effects reported for a 1% change in the ratio.

variable_name: average pro bono hours per lawyer
description: Average pro bono hours per lawyer per year, taken from the American Lawyer's Pro Bono Survey. Pro bono is defined as legal services provided to those who could not otherwise afford them, and reported hours are based on US offices only; work done by paralegals or summer associates, time on bar association work, on boards of nonprofit organizations, and on nonlegal work for charities is not included. The average in the sample was 44 pro bono hours per lawyer per year.

variable_name: percent of lawyers with 20+ hours pro bono
description: Percentage of lawyers in the firm logging at least 20 hr of pro bono per year, from the American Lawyer's Pro Bono Survey. In the sample, 36% of lawyers logged at least 20 hr of pro bono per year.

The average among ranked analysts of the number of years that they have each been ranked in the past. It takes a value of 0 if all analysts who appear in the category ranking at time t were not ranked before, and increases as the analysts who appear at time t are well-known analysts who appeared many times in the past. Two specifications are used in the main models: one considering all ranked positions (runners-up included) and one considering star positions only (the first three analysts in the ranking).
time_window: analysts' ranking history up to time t; outcome measured at t+1

description: A dummy variable coded 1 if the category is changed by II at time t+1, and 0 otherwise. To account for differences among the specific methods in which II expands or retracts its categories, the authors also estimate models with a categorical variable coded 0 if the category remains unchanged, 1 if a category is dropped or merged (a contraction) and 2 if a category is split (an expansion).

A latent threshold on the probability of success: the firm advances a compound into clinical trials if Pg > Pg*. The threshold is assumed to be a function of a set of independent variables X, with ln(Pg*/(1-Pg*)) = Xbeta, and is estimated jointly with the success equation by maximum likelihood. It is not observed directly but recovered as a function of firm, market and technology characteristics.

The firm-specific mean of the distribution from which the log odds ratio ln(Pg/(1-Pg)) is drawn, assumed normal with mean SLmu and unit variance. SLmu is assumed to depend linearly on a set of independent variables Z, i.e., SLmu = Zgamma, and is allowed to differ by therapeutic area (indication).

Scale at the program level, measured as the cumulative number of past projects for that indication, that is, the number of projects already started by the firm for that indication. It is measured at the project level.
Scale at the level of the firm, measured by the total number of ongoing projects in all indications. It varies only across firms.
Scope is measured by the Herfindahl index of diversification of projects across indications, for the firm. It varies only across firms.

Binary indicators for four types of companies. Pioneer Biotech are firms that apply biotechnological methods to the discovery and development of new drugs and were founded before 1988; Other Biotech are all other firms using biotechnology for the discovery of new drugs; Established Pharma are pharmaceutical firms among the top 50 firms worldwide by sales for at least 10 years during the 15-year period 1983-1998; Other Pharma are all other pharmaceutical firms. In the estimations firm-type dummies are used with Established Pharma as the reference group.

Equals one if the compound is licensed, which the authors code only if the licensing agreement was signed in preclinicals. The database records the licensor and licensee(s); where multiple licensees were present, the development of the project was assigned to the largest U.S. firm, and it was manually verified that the firm was in charge of development.

Gini coefficients of the 20-year distribution of annual industry leadership ('firsts') within each industry. Raw data were converted to ranks and the Gini computed by the Lorenz-curve method described in the Appendix as the ratio of Area A to Area (A + B) - 20; the Appendix formulas themselves could not be read from the extracted text. The Gini ranges between 0 (perfect parity) and +1.00 (maximum disparity). Five measures were used (total profit, ROS, ROE, 1-year investor yield, 10-year investor yield), and the overall industry figure is the mean of the five Ginis. z-scores were obtained by comparing each observed Gini with simulated Ginis for the same number of competitors.

Gini coefficients produced by simulation: firms compete for 20 years, each firm having probability 1/n of winning in any year; wins are distributed by a random number generator, counted after 20 periods, and the Gini computed. The simulation is repeated to N = 10,000 trials, a mean and standard deviation are computed for the Gini coefficients, and the simulations are repeated for industries of other sizes.

Theoretical Gini coefficients implied by Pareto's law, in which wins for a firm ranked r are in proportion r - a to those of the leading firm. Finding the Pareto number of wins in an industry requires the constant c that sums all firms' wins to 20. Ginis were computed for two variants of Pareto parity, a = 1.0 and a = 1.5, and the resulting z-scores were compared with the Fortune data.

Gini coefficients computed with the same method applied to the Fortune data for 20-year performance data gathered in a variety of nonindustrial competitive domains, including team sports, individual sports, politics, games and entertainment. The data were drawn from various databases, journals, books, almanacs and web sites, with no systematic sampling pattern aside from an implicit preference for accessible data.

variable_name: Perfect parity benchmark (Gini coefficient of zero)
description: Perfect competitive parity is the null distribution in which every firm in an industry leads the same number of times over the 20 years, which corresponds to a Gini coefficient of zero. The actual 20-year industry Gini coefficients of annual leadership are tested against this zero benchmark; any positive Gini departs from perfect parity.

The number of APIs that were added or modified for the components used by the top five apps by revenue in a category i for the quarter t. APIs are mapped to the underlying component by searching for the focal component name in the APIs' release notes, and the measure is built from all APIs added or modified by Apple between 2010 and 2015 (approximately 87,000 APIs).

The standard deviation in the revenue-based ranks of apps belonging to the category i in the quarter t, used as the measure of uncertainty over the value-generation potential of the product market. Revenue-based ranks proxy for the value generated by apps, and the ranking is done for all apps across product categories, not within category. Actual app revenues are not made available by app developers; the authors argue that volatility in revenue ranking mirrors volatility in actual revenues.
time_window: quarter t, lagged by one quarter in the models

description: A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if the estimated revenues for the category i in a given quarter t is greater than the average revenues across all categories. An app's revenue is first inferred from its revenue-based ranking using the method described in Kapoor and Agarwal (2017), and category revenues are calculated by aggregating the estimated revenues of all apps belonging to the focal category.
time_window: quarter t, lagged by one quarter in the models

description: The percentage of apps in a category i in a given quarter t that multi-home on the Android platform. Multi-homing on the competing platform indicates that the apps are likely to have higher demand by users and hence are more likely to have high revenues.
time_window: quarter t, lagged by one quarter in the models

description: The proportion of apps in a category i in quarter t that generates revenues only from in-app purchases. Revenues from in-app purchases are recurring, as users pay on an ongoing basis to use the app functionality, and therefore capture users' usage behavior more accurately than one-time download purchases; the higher the proportion of apps generating revenues through in-app purchases, the greater the fine-grained information about the future revenue prospect of the product market.
time_window: quarter t, lagged by one quarter in the models

description: The average of the downloadable binary size for the apps in the category i at a given quarter t. An app's binary size is used as a proxy for the associated complexity, as more complex apps tend to have more lines of code, and the complexity of the app obscures the platform owner's learning from observing the app.
time_window: quarter t, lagged by one quarter in the models

description: Placeholder removed.

A search of the business press for the 1980-88 period produced 870 restructuring announcements, of which 81 were refocusing announcements. A story was classified as a refocusing announcement if the term "refocusing" or "concentrate on the core" appeared in it, if the author of the story evaluated and described the action as refocusing, or if the action announced amounted to a return to the firm's core business. To enter the final data an announcement also had to have a date identifiable in the Wall Street Journal Index, no major confounding announcements (earnings, dividends, share repurchases) within five days before or after the announcement day, and stock returns available on the CRSP tapes, and the firm had to have made no other refocusing announcement in the three prior years; these steps eliminated 36 announcements, leaving 45. Day 0 is the day the Wall Street Journal published the news of refocusing and the announcement period is two days, day -1 to day 0.

Market model parameters were calculated for each firm over the period from 270 to 90 days prior to the refocusing announcement using daily company returns and equally weighted market returns from the CRSP tapes, and the market model was used to calculate excess returns over the two-day announcement period. The mean two-day cumulative abnormal rate of return is the sum of all two-day abnormal returns divided by the number of firms, and its t-statistic divides that mean by the standard deviation of the two-day excess returns over the square root of the number of firms. Of the 45 two-day cumulative abnormal returns, 30 are positive and they range from -12.7 percent to +18.9 percent; the average overall two-day CAR is +1.73 percent (t = 2.03, p < .05, two-tailed test).
time_window: market model estimated over days -270 to -90; event window days -1 to 0

description: Because a firm's optimal diversification limit cannot be measured, six strategies were used to classify firms as under- or overdiversified: all 45 refocusers were assumed to be overdiversified; firms above the group median of the entropy index of total diversification; firms in the fourth quartile of that index, with the first quartile designated the not overdiversified group; firms above their core industry's median diversification index; firms above the median diversification index (1.99) of a random sample of 210 Fortune 500 firms; and firms above the group median diversification index whose profitability was below the group median. The index was calculated for the year prior to the refocusing year, or for two years prior if only those data were available, and because of missing information it could only be calculated for 33 of the refocusing firms. The classification was also repeated using the index of unrelated diversification instead of the index of total diversification, and the median diversification and profitability criteria were also applied using core industry median figures as cutoff points.
time_window: year prior to the refocusing year (or two years prior if only those data were available)

variable_name: entropy index of total diversification (DT) and entropy index of unrelated diversification (DU)
description: For each firm an entropy index of total diversification (DT) and an entropy index of unrelated diversification (DU) were calculated in the manner demonstrated by Palepu (1985). The indexes were calculated for the year prior to the refocusing year, or for two years prior if only those data were available, with data from the Trinet Historical Large Establishment tapes; because of missing information the index could only be calculated for 33 of the refocusing firms, and the two indexes are highly collinear (r = .85). To estimate industry median diversification levels, a random sample of 250 Fortune 500 firms was drawn by taking 50 firms at random from each successive group of 100 firms in the list, and after 40 firms were lost to missing Trinet information, 210 firms remained.
time_window: year prior to the refocusing year (or two years prior if only those data were available)

variable_name: return on sales (ROS) minus industry-weighted ROS
description: Profitability was measured as a firm's return on sales (ROS) minus industry-weighted ROS. A COMPUSTAT program identified all the firms assigned to each two-digit SIC code and calculated their ROS, and the average ROS of every two-digit group was estimated using the firms' sales as weights. Using each refocusing firm's breakdown of sales by two-digit SIC code from the Trinet tapes, the industry-weighted ROS was estimated by multiplying the fraction of the firm's sales in each SIC code by the corresponding ROS of that code and adding the results.
time_window: year prior to the refocusing year

description: Firm size was measured with employee information from Dun & Bradstreet and computed as the logarithm of the sum of all employees at all of a firm's facilities. Employee data were chosen because they are the best publicly available data for both public and private firms; for the 343 firms with both asset and employee data, employees and assets were highly correlated at 75.5 percent.

Focus was measured as the log of the total number of employees in facilities within the chemical industry over the log of the number of employees in the total company. The variable thus grew with the degree to which a company was focused on chemicals.

To determine visibility, the authors asked master's of business administration students at the Stern School of Business to indicate if they recognized a company's name or knew any of its brands. Companies were randomly distributed among seven surveys, with between 25 and 35 students responding to each survey. Visibility was the percentage of those who recognized a company's name and/or brand among the number who were asked to respond for that company.

Aggregate releases for a facility in a given year were calculated by summing the weighted releases of the 246 common chemicals in the TRI database, where the toxicity weight for each chemical is the inverse of its reportable quantity. The authors estimated the production function between facility size and aggregate toxic emissions for each four-digit SIC code within each year using ordinary least squares, and the relative environmental performance of a facility is the standardized residual, or deviation, between observed and predicted emissions, so that a facility emitting more than predicted for its size and SIC code has a positive score. Firm-level performance was created as a weighted average of these facility-level scores, weighted by the percentage of total production each facility represented for the company.

The dirtiness of a sector was calculated as the total emissions for the sector divided by the total number of employees in it. A firm-level measure, sector emissions, was created by aggregating the dirtiness of the mix of sectors in which a company owned facilities, using the percentages of the company's total production in each sector as weights.

CMA membership, and thus participation in Responsible Care, was coded as a binary variable. Using data provided by the CMA, a firm and/or its facilities were coded as participating in Responsible Care in each year of membership. The year 1990 was chosen as the base year for participation since Responsible Care was not ratified by CMA members until October 1989. In some rare cases, facilities or business units, but not entire companies, are members, and these were coded accordingly.

Relative improvement measures the change in relative emissions over a one-year period. In the authors' formula it is the negative of the difference between a firm's relative emissions in the following year and its relative emissions in the current year, so that positive values indicate improvement relative to the industry.

Absolute improvement was measured as the percent change in total weighted emissions over a one-year period. It was used to estimate the program's impact on industry-wide rates of improvement, because by definition the mean improvement in relative emissions is zero in any given year for any given sector.

A dummy variable marks the years 1990-96, that is, the period after the inception of Responsible Care, and indicates whether there has been a change in the industry's rate of improvement since the inception of the program. Prior to 1990, the Responsible Care variable indicates that a firm was a member of the U.S. Chemical Manufacturers Association.

The number of houses to which the focal fashion house is connected through outward designer mobility, rather than a simple count of the number of people leaving the focal house; for example, if over the six years preceding a given show seven designers leave the focal house to join five different houses, the out-degree of the focal house for that show is 5, not 7. Out-degree is routinely used in network research as a measure of centrality. To test Hypothesis 1, linear and quadratic specifications were constructed.
time_window: six years preceding the focal fashion show

description: Based on the same principles as the out-degree measure except that it captures the number of fashion houses to which the focal house is connected through hiring designers over a six-year period preceding the focal fashion show.
time_window: six years preceding the focal fashion show

description: At the end of every fashion season, the French Journal du Textile asks 70 industrial buyers (e.g., retailers and wholesalers of high-end clothing) to score the creativity of the fashion houses' collections. Each buyer gives points to fashion houses ranging from 20 (highly creative) to 0 (not creative), and JdT adds up these scores across all buyers, with a theoretical maximum of 1,400 points and a minimum of 0. The actual number of points each house received for the creativity of its collections is used; the scoring is compiled and published after each collection's show, so the dependent variable is captured after the independent variables.
time_window: fall/winter 2000 to fall/winter 2010 seasons; captured after the independent variables

description: Captures the length of experience that a designer had in the focal fashion house as a creative director for a collection evaluated by buyers. If there was more than one creative director in charge of a specific collection, tenures were averaged across individuals. To test Hypothesis 3, this variable was interacted with a linear term of Mobility out-degree.

Measures whether the creative director of the focal house had received at least one of the major international fashion industry awards. In cases where there was more than one award-winning creative director involved with a collection, their number was summed. To test Hypothesis 4, this variable was interacted with a linear term of Mobility out-degree.

To identify the position of a fashion house in the model-sharing networks, a series of sociomatrices was built in which the value of a cell is the number of models shared by houses i and j over two seasons: the focal season and the previous season. Based on this sociomatrix, each fashion house's normalized power centrality in the model-sharing network was computed with UCINET using the approach defined by Bonacich, with a beta value set to 75% of the highest eigenvalue. To test Hypothesis 5, this variable was interacted with a linear term of Mobility out-degree.
time_window: the focal season and the previous season

description: Firms were classified into matched country samples of 100 U.S., 100 German, and 100 Japanese public companies, based on principal location or headquarters. The German sample was generated first from all public German companies in continuous operation from 1988 to 2002, then matched to Japanese and U.S. firms by industry and 1988 revenues.

variable_name: CEO effect (percent of variance attributable to CEOs)
description: The proportion of variance in each firm performance variable that is statistically associated with the presence of individual CEOs in the sample, after partitioning variance attributable to year, industry, and company. Each firm-year was assigned to the CEO in place that year; a CEO effect is observed to the extent that individual CEOs have distinctive and persistent patterns of performance during their tenures. The model was estimated separately for each country sample using maximum likelihood and simultaneous ANOVA, and estimates were corrected for serial correlation in error terms.
Net income divided by total assets, expressed as a percentage, for each firm-year.
Net income divided by sales, expressed as a percentage, for each firm-year.
Sales in year i minus sales in year i-1, divided by sales in year i-1, expressed as a percentage, for each firm-year.
Market value divided by book value of common equity, for each firm-year.

An index built from 23 work-related value items. Each manager answered three questions about every item on five-point scales of perceived importance: 'How do you feel things ought to be?' (OTB), 'How were things at your firm before the merger?' (WAS), and 'How do things appear now at the buying firm?' (IS). A compatibility score was computed for each item from the manager's responses to the three questions and the equation the authors give (their rendering of the equation is only partly legible). The item scores were summed and divided by 23, giving a final index that ranged from -20 to +20, where a negative score signifies the highest degree of unattractiveness, zero signifies neutrality, and a positive score signifies attraction. Responses of multiple managers from one firm were averaged.

Eleven items, drawn from the items used by Chatterjee et al. (1992), assessing the extent to which the buying firm involved itself in the acquired firm's key decisions. A five-point response scale was used, ranging from 'your firm decides' (1) to the 'buying firm decides' (5), with 'consensus' (3) being the midrange choice. A Cronbach test on the responses to the 11 items revealed the construct to be reliable (alpha = 0.89), and each firm's responses were averaged to form an index.

Managers of the acquired firm were asked to indicate the approximate size of the buying firm relative to the acquired firm at the time of the merger. A six-point scale was used, ranging from 'smaller' (0) to '3-5 times the size' (3) to 'more than 10 times the size' (6). The authors note that the scale captures perceptions of relative size rather than a continuous accounting-based interval measure.
time_window: at the time of the merger

description: Acquired managers reported their perceptions of the acquired firm's performance since (and because of) the merger. Three performance appraisal items (earnings, sales, and market share) were used on a five-point scale ranging from 'Greatly deteriorated' (scored 1) to 'Greatly improved' (scored 5). The three items showed a high level of reliability (alpha = 0.70) and were averaged to obtain an index of post-merger performance.

A two-level, categorical variable for the nationality of the acquired firm (0 = British; 1 = French). It was entered in the base model as a control and used as the moderator in the additional moderated regressions in which an interaction term between a relative standing variable and Nationality of the Acquired Firm was added to the seven-variable base model.

variable_name: Merger type (nationality of buying and acquired firms)
description: The sample was built as a 3 x 2 design in which acquired firms were classified by the nationality of the buying firm (British, French, or U.S.) and by their own nationality (British or French), distinguishing domestic mergers (British acquiring British; French acquiring French) from cross-national mergers (U.S. acquiring British or French; British acquiring French; French acquiring British).

Annual firm CVC investment in millions of dollars in ventures within a given sector. Because the ventures are not publicly traded and are typically not associated with a SIC code, the authors manually assigned a sector to more than 2000 entrepreneurial ventures that received CVC backing between 1990 and 1999 using a two-step process based on the venture's Venture Economics Industry Classification. A firm that is not found to have invested in any ventures assigned to a given sector in a given year is assigned a zero. The amounts represent actual dollars disbursed during the year; the dependent variable is adjusted to 1999 dollars and the natural logarithm is employed in the regression analysis.
scale: millions of dollars (log-transformed in the regression)

description: Defined as the average number of citation-weighted patents applied for by firms in a given year in a given sector defined by each 2-digit Standard Industrial Classification; it gauges the level of innovative, or quality, patenting for a given industry in a given year. Because the authors are interested in technological ferment in the focal year, patents are pegged by their application date rather than their grant date. The measure is highly skewed, so the natural logarithm of Tech Opportunity is employed in the regression analysis.
time_window: annual; patents pegged by application date

description: Derived from the Carnegie Mellon Survey measure of the mean percentage of innovations for which patenting was considered an effective mechanism in protecting intellectual property within an industry. The higher the value of IP Regime, the more effective are patents in protecting inventors' profits. For presentation purposes the variable is divided by 100 to create a 0-1 scale. By construction the variable varies across industries but is time-invariant.

Taken directly from the Carnegie Mellon Survey measure of the reported importance of distribution and sales capabilities within an industry, which the authors describe as the relative importance of complementary assets in bringing an innovation to market. For presentation purposes the variable is divided by 100 to create a 0-1 scale. By construction it varies across industries but is time-invariant.

Defined as income before extraordinary items (i.e., income after interest and taxes) plus depreciation and amortization, following Fazzari et al. (1988), Hall (1992), Himmelberg and Petersen (1994) and Gilchrist and Himmelberg (1998). Since firms treat R&D as an expense, some studies add R&D back into the usual accounting definition of cash flow, but the authors do not do so because they control for R&D expenditure separately. Cash Flow is adjusted to 1999 dollars and exhibits a high level of skewness, so the natural logarithm is employed in the regression analysis.

Captures the absolute level of the firm's absorptive capacity as the stock of patents a firm has been granted. Following Blundell et al. (1995), it is calculated as the depreciated sum of all patents applied for from 1963 to the current year; the authors adopted a depreciation rate of 30 percent, so patents granted prior to 1963 have little impact given the 1- to 4-year lag between patent application and granting. Firms are matched to U.S. Patent and Trademark Office assignee codes so that all patenting activity is captured. The paper's exact formula for Patent Stock is not readable in the supplied text; the depreciated-sum definition is stated in prose.
time_window: patents applied for from 1963 to the current year

description: Follows Jaffe (1986) and examines the extent of technological overlap between a firm and a sector in which the firm may potentially invest in entrepreneurial ventures. First, each firm's technological portfolio is determined by measuring the distribution across patent classifications of the patents associated with its businesses using Silverman's (1996) concordance between SIC codes (line of business) and patent classes (domain of expertise). Next, for each sector in which a firm may potentially invest, ventures' domain of expertise is identified using the same methodology. Finally, the overlap in technological portfolios (activity in the same patent classes) is calculated for each firm-venture sector pair; the approach does not rely on the firm having actually invested in ventures within that sector.
The square of the Proximity measure, included in an additional specification to test for a concave relationship between technological proximity and learning.

The measure was created by summing the four champion scores (general management, marketing, production and customer), each coded 1 for presence and 0 for absence. The index has a mean of 1.87, a standard deviation of 1.23 and a range of 1-4. Respondents significantly agreed about the presence of champions in each functional group.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Presence (1) or absence (0) of a champion in general management (CEO and direct subordinates responsible for corporate strategy) for the project. Respondents were given a definition of a champion and coded present only if both respondents indicated presence; disagreement or absence of indication was coded 0. Agreement was 65% between respondents.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Presence (1) or absence (0) of a champion in marketing for the project, based on respondents who were given a definition of a champion. Coded present only if both respondents indicated presence; disagreement or non-indication was coded 0. Agreement was 70% between respondents.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Presence (1) or absence (0) of a champion in production for the project, based on respondents who were given a definition of a champion. Coded present only if both respondents indicated presence; disagreement or non-indication was coded 0. Agreement was 62% between respondents.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Presence (1) or absence (0) of a customer acting as a champion for the project, based on respondents who were given a definition of a champion. Coded present only if both respondents indicated presence; disagreement or non-indication was coded 0. Agreement was 69% between respondents.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: The measure was created by summing the four antagonist scores (general management, marketing, production and customer), each coded 1 for presence and 0 for absence. The index has a mean of 0.51, a standard deviation of 0.75 and a range of 1-3. Respondents significantly agreed about the presence of antagonists in each functional group.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Presence (1) or absence (0) of an antagonist in general management for the project, based on respondents who were given a definition of an antagonist. Coded present only if both respondents indicated presence; disagreement or non-indication was coded 0. Agreement was 74% between respondents.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Presence (1) or absence (0) of an antagonist in marketing for the project, based on respondents who were given a definition of an antagonist. Coded present only if both respondents indicated presence; disagreement or non-indication was coded 0. Agreement was 70% between respondents.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Presence (1) or absence (0) of an antagonist in production for the project, based on respondents who were given a definition of an antagonist. Coded present only if both respondents indicated presence; disagreement or non-indication was coded 0. Agreement was 67% between respondents.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Presence (1) or absence (0) of a customer acting as an antagonist for the project, based on respondents who were given a definition of an antagonist. Coded present only if both respondents indicated presence; disagreement or non-indication was coded 0. Agreement was 71% between respondents.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: From a list of sixteen possible sources (including R&D staff, R&D first-level supervision, R&D management, VP of R&D, general management, marketing/distribution/sales, production, engineering, finance, technical services, customer, government representative, vendor/supplier, university consultant, private consultant, and nonconsulting technical/professional colleague) respondents indicated the original source of suggestion, and could indicate more than one source. Projects described by both respondents as suggested by R&D alone were coded 1 and projects with one or more business sources were coded 2; when respondents disagreed the project was scored 2. The coding yielded 36% R&D alone and 64% business input.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Respondents assessed the firm's prior project experience with four items about using the process, using the process in this line of business, using this particular process, and the extent to which the process fits the established business practices of the firm. Items were answered on a numbered 1 to 7 scale with 1 labeled INCREMENTAL and 7 labeled RADICAL. Coefficient alpha was 0.82 and the intraclass correlation was 0.55.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Participants chose one or more of four categories: establish new product, establish a new process, make recognizable changes to an existing product, and make recognizable changes to an existing process. New and changed products were collapsed into a product code and new and changed processes into a process code, giving a response coded 1 for product, 2 for mixed and 3 for process. Respondents' agreement about PROJECT TYPE was 62% with an intraclass correlation of 0.35.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Respondents indicated how frequently management assigned additional resources to a project in four areas: assignment of additional personnel, increases in the budget, replacement of project members, and changes in the project team leader. Answers used the scale 1 = not to my knowledge, 2 = once, and 3 = more than once, and a higher score indicated the addition of higher levels of resources for a project. Cronbach's alpha was 0.76 and the intraclass correlation was 0.60.
scale: 1 = not to my knowledge, 2 = once, 3 = more than once
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Whether the firm discontinued the project, coded 1 = yes and 0 = no. A project was coded 1 only if both respondents indicated that the firm terminated the project; when respondents disagreed the project was considered not terminated and coded 0. Respondents agreed on project TERMINATION in 91% of cases.

Seven items assessed the project's overall impact on representative business goals: profitability, sales volume, product cost, market position, employee benefits, stockholder benefits, and firm image. Items were assessed on a scale from 1 = strong negative to 7 = strong positive, with a higher score indicating a more positive PERFORMANCE impact (alpha = 0.89; r = 0.67). Missing data were replaced with sample means for 8% of the cases.
time_window: retrospective; data collected at project completion

description: Binary outcome equal to one if the focal team won the focal game and zero if it lost. Match-level fixed effects restrict comparisons to the two randomized teams in the focal game, since each match features a winner and a loser. Observations for the two teams in a match are not independent, so standard errors are clustered at the match level.

For each pair of players on a team the authors identify whether they played together in a tournament game (i.e., as members of the same professional team) within the past 12 months. This binary characterization is summed across all possible dyads on the team to obtain an aggregate measure of prior collaboration at the team level. The measure is analogous to those used in prior research.

For each pair of players who were professional teammates in the past 12 months, the authors distinguish whether they played tightly or loosely coupled roles during that prior collaboration. Two players are classified as tightly coupled if, during the laning phase (the initial 15 minutes of the match), they were located in the same segment of the game map, which indicates task interdependence. The number of such dyads on the team is summed to a team-level measure.

For each pair of players who were professional teammates in the past 12 months, the authors distinguish whether they played tightly or loosely coupled roles during that prior collaboration. Two players are classified as loosely coupled if they were not located in the same segment of the game map during the laning phase. The number of such dyads on the team is summed to a team-level measure.

Equal to one if a game update was released in the two months before the focal match and zero otherwise. Following Clement (2023), the two-month postpatch window is used to capture the period of elevated task uncertainty. The measures of tightly and loosely coupled collaboration are interacted with this variable.
time_window: two months before the focal match

description: Family Firm identifies firms in which the founder, the founder's descendant, or other family member by blood or marriage is listed in that year's proxy as an officer, director and or as a blockholder (with beneficial ownership rights exceeding 5%), either individually or as a group. The identity of each firm's founder or founding family was gathered from company websites, obituaries, Wikipedia, and other Internet searches, and each firm's annual proxy statements were reviewed to determine whether a family member related to the founder was listed as an insider and/or as a blockholder.

Activist Targeted takes the value one if an activist hedge fund initiated a campaign against a firm in a given year, and zero otherwise. Campaign data come from SharkWatch, excluding campaigns that only included social/environmental or political demands and those initiated by pension funds, ex-directors, and unions.
time_window: annual, campaigns announced between January 1, 2010 and December 31, 2018

description: CAR is the cumulative sum of abnormal returns during a three-day event window ([-1, +1]) surrounding the announcement of an activist hedge fund campaign. Abnormal returns are the difference between a firm's expected and actual returns during the event window, with expected returns predicted from the firm's and the stock market's returns during a 250-day estimation window ([-800, -551]) before the announcement date.

variable_name: compound rate of growth of sales revenues
description: The compound annual rate of growth of sales revenues, taken by the authors as their measure of performance. Firms are ranked by the percentage increase in net sales over a 5-year period; growth was calculated for 1981 through 1985 for the 1986 Inc. 100 and for 1975 through 1979 for the 1980 list. High growth firms are those listed by Inc.; low growth firms were retained only if growing at less than 19 percent per year, with 19 percent given as the annual growth rate for SIC 3573.

Founders categorized the degree to which the product/market/technology of their start-up firm was related to that of the last firm they worked for before starting the new firm. Measured categorically as (1) the same, (2) very closely related, (3) somewhat related, and (4) not related, across product, markets, and technologies. Lower values indicate closer relatedness to the incubator organization.
scale: 1 = the same, 2 = very closely related, 3 = somewhat related, 4 = not related

description: The number of individuals included on the initial team of founders, reported categorically as (1) one person, (2) two persons, (3) three persons, (4) four or more persons.
scale: 1 = one person, 2 = two persons, 3 = three persons, 4 = four or more persons

description: Founders indicated the extent to which the initial product/market focus of their firm had changed since founding. Measured categorically as: the initial product focus has changed (1) none, (2) little, (3) lots, (4) entirely. Higher values indicate more change, so the measure runs opposite to stability as the construct is named.
scale: 1 = none, 2 = little, 3 = lots, 4 = entirely (extent of change since founding)

description: Founders described the timing of their entry on a five-point scale: (a) the first firm in the market with your product(s), (b) one of the first few firms in the market, (c) was not one of the first nor close to the last, (d) one of the later firms to enter the market, or (e) one of the last firms to enter the market. Higher values indicate later entry, so the measure runs opposite to early entry as the construct is named.
scale: ordinal from first firm in the market to one of the last firms to enter the market

description: Founders indicated the percentage of their firm's sales revenues derived from foreign sales, measured categorically as (1) none, (2) <10 percent, (3) 10 to 20 percent, (4) 20 to 30 percent, and (5) >30 percent. The authors note that in some cases cells were collapsed to avoid low expected frequencies.
Founders indicated categorically the number of acquisitions their firm had completed during the 5-year period: (1) none, (2) one, (3) two or three, and (4) four or more.
scale: 1 = none, 2 = one, 3 = two or three, 4 = four or more acquisitions

description: A latent variable reflected by counts of repeated equity-based relationships. The counts were derived by coding the partners of a firm's international alliance network and, when a second relationship between these same firms was found, the datum was coded as a repeat partnership. Three indicators are used: repeated relationships with home-country (Japanese) firms, repeated relationships with local (host-country) firms, and the total number of repeated relationships combining the two. Each of these figures was transformed into its natural logarithm, although the authors report that the raw versus transformed values did not create an appreciable difference in the model results.

A latent variable built from several commonly used accounting-based performance measures: operating return on sales, return on assets, and operating return on capital. To avoid the potentially confounding effects of idiosyncratic asset valuation and local tax treatment, the return on sales and return on invested capital figures were based on operational profits rather than net, after-tax profits. The information was collected from Compustat's GlobalVantage database.

Following Luque (2002) and others, technical uncertainty is measured using patent data to derive the percentage change in patenting activity by industry. The raw data are 624,052 patents granted between 1995 and 1999 obtained from the National Bureau of Economic Research, categorized and matched with the corporate-level data using the methods of Hall et al. (2001). The percentage change in the number of patents in industry i between periods t and t-1 signals the rate of technological change; the paper's formula for the measure is not recoverable from the text. For the multigroup analysis, firms were categorized into higher or lower technical uncertainty groups based on whether their environments were above or below the median level of patenting activity within the five-year window of 1995-1999.

Six-item, seven-point scale that assessed the coupling between the outsourced system and the outsourcer's technological portfolio, based on descriptions of the construct in the modularity literature. The items are seven-point semantic differential items asking how the relationship between the outsourced system and the client systems with which it had to interoperate is characterized. Higher values indicate looser coupling and therefore greater modularity.

Measured by reverse scoring four items that assessed the outsourcee's knowledge about the project's application problem domain, that is, the outsourcer's project business objectives, business routines, and business rules implemented in the system. The items ask about the outsourcee firm's knowledge in areas specific to the project. The scale was reverse scored to compute ignorance, so higher values indicate greater ignorance.

Assessed project outcomes in terms of system reliability, functionality, meeting planned objectives and requirements, and overall fit with outsourcer needs. Respondents characterized the project's outcomes compared to other IT projects completed by their company. Anchors run from 1 = Much Worse to 7 = Much Better.

Project managers were asked to indicate whether team members had sought knowledge in any of the other subsidiaries except the focal one; they could answer reliably because they kept detailed logs on how engineers on the project spent their time. The variable is coded 1 if a team had sought knowledge from another subsidiary and 0 otherwise.

Each team member was asked to name persons in the subsidiary from whom they regularly sought information and advice, to whom they would go on a regular basis to get buy-in for their work, and with whom they interacted informally as a friend. Respondents reported how long each relation had existed, and relations that commenced after the start of the focal project were excluded. Density is the number of existing relations divided by the number of possible asymmetric relations, given by N × (N - 1), where N is the number of team members.
scale: 0 ('no relations exist') to 1 ('all possible relations exist')
time_window: relations existing prior to the start of the focal project

description: Team members were asked how frequently they had interacted with each person over the past year (1, 'once a day,' to 7, 'once every 3 months') and how close they were to that person (1, 'very close,' to 7, 'distant'). The two dimensions were reverse-scored and averaged to create average within-team relation strength; the Cronbach alpha for this scale was .81.

Subsidiary R&D managers were asked, 'Over the past two years, are there any units from whom your unit regularly sought technical and/or market-related input?', followed by a list of the 41 subsidiaries in the study that the manager could check. Respondents indicated the age of each relation and relations that had commenced after the start of focal projects were excluded. The variable is the number of established relations with other subsidiaries that existed prior to the start of the focal project, assigned to each focal project.
time_window: past two years; relations existing prior to the start of the focal project

description: For each relation listed on the survey, subsidiary R&D managers answered how frequently people in their subsidiary interact with the other subsidiary (1, 'once a day,' to 7, 'once every 3 months') and how close the working relationship is (1, 'very close, practically like being in the same work group,' to 7, 'distant, like an arm's length delivery of the input'). The items were reverse-scored, averaged (r = .83; alpha = .92), and an average was computed for each team.

Each subsidiary R&D manager indicated, for each relationship listed, 'How would you describe the competitive nature between your [subsidiary] and this [subsidiary]?' (1, 'non-competitive: never compete for markets and technologies,' to 7, 'competitive: frequently compete for markets and technologies'). These perceptions are asymmetric across the two parties. The variable is the average of the responses of all subsidiaries with which a focal team had established relations, measuring how they perceived the subsidiary to which the team belonged.

Computed as how each subsidiary's R&D manager perceived the level of competition with direct contacts, that is, the average of the focal subsidiary manager's responses to the perceived competition question across the relations listed.

Following the same procedures as for direct contacts' average perceived competition but limited to only those subsidiaries that provided knowledge to a focal team. The variable is the average value of the providing subsidiaries' responses to the question about the competitive nature of the relationship.

Limited to subsidiaries that provided knowledge to a focal team and using the scale for intersubsidiary relation strength described above, the measure ranges from 0 ('no established relation') to 7 ('very strong relation'). For this measure the mean was subtracted from the values to reduce the correlation with the interaction effect.
time_window: relations established prior to the transfer effort

description: Project managers indicated, for the knowledge transferred from each providing subsidiary, how well documented the knowledge was (1, 'It was very well documented,' to 7, 'It was not well documented'), whether all of this knowledge was explained to the team in writing (1, 'All of it was,' to 7, 'None of it was'), and the type of knowledge that came from the unit (1, 'mainly reports, manuals, documents, self-explanatory software, etc.,' to 7, 'mainly personal practical know-how, tricks of the trade'). Responses were averaged and the mean was subtracted from the values; the Cronbach alpha was .81.
level: dyad (knowledge transferred from each providing subsidiary)

description: Project managers were asked, 'How many engineering-months did the team spend searching for (looking for, identifying, and evaluating) the technical advice, software and hardware that the team wanted from other subsidiaries?' The company defined an engineering-month as the equivalent of a product developer's full-time work for one month. The variable is the absolute number of engineering-months spent on search.

Project managers were asked, 'How many engineering-months did the team spend modifying, editing and incorporating the technical advice, software and hardware that came from the other subsidiaries?' They kept a close eye on engineering-months spent on this activity. The variable is the absolute number of engineering-months spent on transfer; five projects did not report transfer costs and were dropped from the analysis.

Measured as the logarithm of the 1976 to 1980 count of new, legally independent firms reported in USELM. It is a measure of gross entry since it includes all firms new to an industry rather than the number of new firms net of firms exiting the industry. The logarithmic transformation followed previous research and allowed interpretation of relationships between the variables in percentage terms.

Measured as an industry's 1977 new capital expenditures for pollution abatement divided by the industry's 1977 total new capital expenditures and multiplied by 100. It served as a proxy for pollution regulation compliance requirements, representing the degree to which the studied industries were affected by, and reacted to, pollution abatement compliance requirements. Independent variable measures were lagged one or two years relative to the midpoint of the entry measure (1978).

Discrete ordinal index that ranges from 0 to 2: 0 if the founders control neither the CEO position nor the board of directors, 1 if they control one but not the other, and 2 if they control both the CEO position and the board of directors. Control of the CEO position is whether the founder is still the CEO; control of the board of directors is whether the founders and inside executives have more than half of the seats on the board.

variable_name: Log of valuation (pre-money valuation at most recent round of financing)
description: Calculated as the price per share in the financing round times the number of shares outstanding prior to the round. Because the variable was log-normally distributed, the natural log of the variable is used. Missing data in the survey were handled with multiple-imputation methods.
