variable_name: Log of capital raised (total amount of capital raised)
description: The total amount of capital raised by the startup since founding, including all rounds of financing through the time of the survey. Capital used by the company is included, but capital used to buy existing equity from founders or other insiders is excluded. One was added to the metric before taking its natural logarithm to allow for companies that had not raised any capital.
time_window: since founding through the time of the survey

description: Indicator of whether the core founder had prior founding experience. It is included alongside the core founder's years of prior work experience.

Indicator of whether the core founder tapped social networks to attract executive hires, rather than the hires being attracted by someone else. It is entered in the models together with an indicator for whether an angel or a VC on the board attracted the executive hires.
The size of the startup's founding team, entered in the models in logarithmic form. The dataset has an average of 2.70 founders per team.

variable_name: Cofounders' prior years of work experience (log)
description: The founding team's total years of prior work experience, entered in the models in logarithmic form. It is included as one of the founding-team variables alongside the size of the founding team.

variable_name: Exec hires' prior years of work experience (log)
description: The years of prior work experience of the startup's non-founding executives, entered in the models in logarithmic form. The models also include the number of executives who in prior work were the senior-most executives within their functions and the average compensation of the executives.

variable_name: VCs invested in last round of financing
description: Dummy variable indicating whether the startup's last round of financing included venture capitalists. It is one of three dummies for the source of financing, the other two being the founders themselves and angel investors.

variable_name: Angels invested in last round of financing
description: Dummy variable indicating whether the startup's last round of financing included angel investors. It is one of three dummies for the source of financing, the other two being the founders themselves and venture capitalists.

Each startup's business segment was categorized into the three segments with the highest capital intensity and the three segments with the lowest capital intensity, based on the capital-intensity ratings published in the IBISWorld industry reports. The higher capital intensity segments were Biopharma, CleanTech, and Hardware/Semiconductors/Communications; the lower capital intensity segments were Digital Media/Content, Software, and Medical devices. The remaining segments were categorized as Other.

The age of the startup, entered in the models in logarithmic form. It is used as a control in the control and value models and interacted with the control index to test whether the tradeoff grows stronger as startups age.

Informants reported whether the organization currently belonged to the consortium and, if so, whether it expected to continue its membership (1 = yes; 2 = no). The authors reverse coded the item and used it to separate organizations into stayers (those intending to remain members of the consortium) and leavers (those who had left very recently and those who acknowledged their intent to leave). Validity was checked against Federal Register filings subsequent to the questionnaire response and against consortium membership lists.

Informants rated, on a 7-point Likert-type scale, three statements reflecting the member organization's satisfaction with the consortium: the consortium's overall effectiveness (1 = not at all effective, 7 = extremely effective), the extent to which the consortium had met the member's expectations (1 = not at all, 7 = completely), and the degree to which the manager would like to change the manner in which the consortium conducted its activities (1 = not at all, 7 = completely), which the authors reverse coded. The measures were used as a reflective indicator of performance, corroborated by a Cronbach's alpha of 0.80.

The authors emphasized the criticality component of importance and evaluated whether the consortium's research was similar to the member organization's primary research interests. An informant rated, on a 7-point Likert-type scale, the similarity of the consortium's research efforts to their organization's primary research interests (1 = similar, 7 = dissimilar, which was reverse coded).

Informants rated, on a 7-point Likert-type scale, the member organization's capability for conducting the research being done in the target consortium in three alternative arrangements: internally, externally through grants or contracts, and externally through other consortia or joint ventures (1 = very low, 7 = very high). Collectively these choices create a formative indicator of alternatives.

Knowledge-related involvement consists of personnel and information contributions (researchers, managerial skills, and technical knowledge) together with the two variables of information exchange and influence (communication and influence). Communication frequency was recorded as how often the member received information from the consortium on its performance and how often it communicated with other members (daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, or yearly) and converted into the percentage of days per year; the two items were combined into a single variable labeled communication after a significant correlation. Influence was rated on a 7-point Likert-type scale for the degree of influence over consortium goals, operating decisions, budget allocations and the selection of research projects (1 = no impact, 7 = a great deal of impact). Each of these is a formative indicator.
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale; percentage of days per year for communication

description: Contributing technical equipment and financing comprise nonknowledge-related involvement; informants categorized the assets contributed to the consortium into one of researchers, managerial skills, technical knowledge, technical equipment, or financing. This is a formative indicator.

Three measures representing benefits derived from membership were used to evaluate a firm's level of learning: the consortium's contribution to skills and knowledge of the member organization's researchers, the consortium's contribution to the member's competitive position, and the value of shared information on the internal research of other member organizations. Informants rated the consortium on these items using a scale of 1 = very poor performance, 7 = very good performance, and the items were used aggregately as a reflective indicator (Cronbach's alpha = 0.70).
scale: 1 = very poor performance, 7 = very good performance

description: Informants were asked to specify which of four types of relationships their organization had with at least one other member of the consortium: membership in the same trade association, contracting or licensing agreement, manufacturing or marketing joint venture, or R&D joint venture or consortium. The two joint venture scores were combined into one measure, and the resulting three types of relationships (trade association, contract or licensing, and joint venture) made up a formative indicator of network relations.

variable_name: membership conditions (importance, alternatives, knowledge and nonknowledge involvement, learning, network ties)
description: Membership conditions were treated as the set of six survey-based variables on file for the paper: importance of the research, alternatives, knowledge-related involvement, nonknowledge-related involvement, learning and network relations. They were entered together as predictors of satisfaction with performance, and performance was also tested as a predictor of each of them.

Operationalized as the multiplication of exploration (i, t) and exploitation (i, t) in each period. This yielded a continuous measure of ambidexterity, taking a minimum value of 0 for firms with a one-sided focus on either exploration or exploitation and a maximum value of 0.25 for firms with a balanced allocation. Exploration and exploitation are measured by content analysis of the firms' press releases; a firm's relative degree of exploration in each period is the number of exploration words divided by the sum of the exploration and exploitation words (and accordingly for exploitation).

Operationalized as the difference between a firm's exploitation at t-1 and exploitation at t. In all models predicting a change in firms' exploration-exploitation allocation, the independent and control variables are lagged by one period.

Operationalized by means of the ratio of firms' cash and short-term investments divided by their short-term debt. The control variable and other accounting data were drawn from COMPUSTAT and A.M. BEST.

To measure maintaining high levels of ambidexterity, the authors calculated ambidexterity's arithmetic mean over three periods. Aggregating three periods is described as a standard approach to measuring organizational learning such as exploration and exploitation in complex settings.
Measured in terms of insurance firms' three-period average return on equity (RoE). The RoE was winsorized at the 1% level to ensure that extreme observations would not drive the results.

Measured through content analysis of the firms' press releases using the number of words relating to exploration, which are based on March's (1991) word list. Since differences in firms' communication styles may influence the measure, each firm's total average exploration and exploitation words were subtracted from the exploration-exploitation word count in each specific press release. A company's relative degree of exploration in each period is the number of exploration words divided by the sum of the exploration and exploitation words.

Measured through content analysis of the firms' press releases using the number of words relating to exploitation, based on March's (1991) word list, with each firm's total average exploration and exploitation words subtracted from the word count in each specific press release. The relative degree of exploitation in each period is accordingly computed by dividing the number of exploitation words by the sum of the exploration and exploitation words.

Respondents first described, along a 5-point scale, the extent to which a series of 11 areas of expertise and 15 managerial behaviors accurately depicted their firm's current CEO. They then identified the extent to which these same dimensions were appropriate for the CEO in the year 2000, again using a 5-point scale. Absolute differences in the two scores for each item were calculated and averaged (Cronbach alpha 0.79), creating a measure of the extent to which the respondent believed the current and future leaders should differ along these attributes. A measure of leadership CSQ, or perceived degree to which the current and future CEO should be similar, was derived by subtracting the difference measure from the maximum possible difference score of 4.

Measured in a manner identical to leadership CSQ, but based on respondents' scores gauging the degree to which 11 different types of competitive weaponry and seven modes of growth strategy accurately described the firm at the time of the study (1988) and would be appropriate for the same organization in the year 2000. Absolute differences between the current and future scores were computed and averaged, and the resulting difference measure was subtracted from the maximum possible difference score (Cronbach alpha 0.76).

Respondents were assigned their country's cultural value score for individualism as provided in Hofstede (1980, 1991). Cultural values are treated as group-level (country-level) phenomena and are captured at that level.
Respondents were assigned their country's cultural value score for uncertainty avoidance as provided in Hofstede (1980, 1991). The scores are country-level values applied to individual respondents.
Respondents were assigned their country's cultural value score for masculinity as provided in Hofstede (1980, 1991). The scores are country-level values applied to individual respondents.
Respondents were assigned their country's cultural value score for power distance as provided in Hofstede (1980, 1991). The scores are country-level values applied to individual respondents.

Respondents were assigned their country's cultural value score for long-term vs. short-term orientation as provided in Hofstede (1980, 1991). Because these scores are not available for all sampled countries, this dimension is examined in a model estimated on a reduced sample.

Dummy variable coded 1 for each of the 15 years in the sample involving presidential elections (1952, 1956, 1960, 1964, 1968, 1972, 1976, 1980, 1984, 1988, 1992, 1996, 2000, 2004, and 2008) and 0 otherwise.

Company's reported advertising dollars spent in the year on advertising media (radio, television, newspapers, and periodicals) and promotional expenses. Available Compustat data were collected for each variable in the model for each firm in each year from 1950 to 2011. The model includes one-year and two-year lagged spending values.
time_window: 1950-2011; one- and two-year lags included in the model

description: Coded using the headquarter country code (LOC) in Compustat. Companies with U.S. headquarters were coded 1, and those headquartered outside of the United States were coded 0. The location did not vary over time within firms in the sample, and the main effect dropped out of the fixed-effects model.

Dummy indicating whether the industry was played in a presidential election year (coded 1) or in a nonelection year (coded 0). Three years of simulation data were analyzed, comparing the nonelection years 2002 and 2003 with the election year 2004.

Advertising expenditure for product p of firm f in industry i in period t. At the beginning of each period teams reviewed their prior financial performance and submitted a series of spending decisions for the current period, made at the product level. The model includes one period of lagged advertising spending.
time_window: one-period lag included in the model

description: Training expenditure decisions made at the product level in each period of the simulation. Because the unit root test indicated that training spending level was not stationary, the analysis used a first-difference measure of training spending, that is, the difference between current and prior period training spending.
time_window: first difference between current and prior period

description: Dummy indicating whether the industry was played in the fall term (coded 1) or in the spring or summer terms (coded 0). Since teams played the games in the spring, summer, or fall terms, this variable captures temporal proximity to Election Day.

Randomly assigned condition. In the election condition participants read a newspaper article containing comparative political information about two candidates running for a U.S. Senate seat in the 2018 midterm elections in Tennessee and reported their opinions about the candidates on 11-point scales. In the control condition they read an article about the state of Tennessee's history, geography, economy, and education and evaluated the state along several dimensions.

Percentage of the HR budget participants decided to spend on the chosen training program (Time Management or Effective Communication) and the percentage they would save. In one analysis all participants were included and those choosing neither program were assigned 'zero dollars spent'; in a second analysis only participants who chose one of the training programs were included.

Randomly assigned condition. In the comparative political information condition participants compared three pairs of candidates running for three positions (state senator, state representative, and secretary of state), read the two candidates' biographies, and indicated which candidate they would support on an 11-point scale. In the noncomparative political information condition the biography of one randomly selected candidate from each pair was presented and participants indicated the extent to which they would support that candidate.

Randomly assigned selection versus rejection frame. In the selection frame participants decided among 'Market Model A,' 'Market Model B,' and 'Market neither model and save the budget.' In the rejection frame the options were framed as 'Reject Model A,' 'Reject Model B,' and 'Reject both models and save the budget.'

Percentage of the marketing budget participants decided to spend on the computer model they chose to market and the percentage they would save. Participants who decided to market neither model (selection frame) or to reject both models (rejection frame) did not make this spending-level decision; in one analysis they were included with 'zero dollars spent.'

In the selection frame condition choice was coded as 1 if participants chose either 'Market Model A' or 'Market Model B' and coded as 0 if they decided to 'Market neither model and save the budget.' In the rejection frame condition choice was coded as 1 if participants chose either 'Reject Model A' or 'Reject Model B' and coded as 0 if they decided to 'Reject both models and save the budget.'

Participants rated the importance of 12 product features in making their decisions (0 = Not at all important, 10 = Extremely important). The importance ratings of the four negative attributes (two per each computer model) were averaged to generate one negative attribute importance score, which was used to assess how negativity importance differed as a function of the manipulation of comparative political information and decision frame.

A 36-item instrument covering the seven TQM practices identified in prior research, used to gauge comprehensively the degree to which TQM had been implemented within the organization. A factor analysis confirmed seven factors, with each item loading on the expected scale, and the items were averaged within each scale to construct seven factor scores. A final factor analysis showed that all seven variables loaded on a single factor, so the aggregated average of the seven variables was computed to create the TQM practices variable used in the analysis (alpha = .93).

A five-item perceptual measure adapted from scales used by Powell (1995) and Ramanujam, Venkatraman, and Camillus (1986), obtained directly from respondents in the survey instrument to ensure completeness and timeliness. The coefficient of reliability was .90, and analysis of variance showed significantly greater between-hospital than within-hospital variance. The measure was validated against the two-year average archival return on assets relative to competitors for 57 hospitals (r = .40, p < .01).

Each hospital's overall score from the latest audit conducted by the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations, based on a comprehensive audit of 49 standards related to internal hospital processes conducted once every three years. The authors describe it as an industry-expert-rated measure that is not a direct assessment of competitive advantage but may be an alternative proxy for competitive advantages gained through successful TQM programs.

Three items adapted from the seven-item scale originally developed by Khandwalla (1977) and recently used by Covin, Slevin, and Schultz (1994); the items loaded on a factor measuring the degree to which the organizational structure emphasized the control of procedures, systems, and job descriptions. The reliability associated with this scale was .66. The authors state that the scale should be considered exploratory because this is the first study to use these factors.

Two items from the same adapted Khandwalla (1977) scale measuring the exploration capability of the organizations with respect to allowing the flow of financial and operating information throughout the organization and the freedom to depart from past practices to adapt to a changing environment. The reliability of this scale was .67, and the authors state that it should be considered exploratory.

Initial announcements of heir apparent appointment were collected from the Wall Street Journal Index and News Wires for the period 1988-1997. An heir apparent is an inside or outside executive who is the only person appointed as the president and/or COO of the firm and who is at least 5 years younger than the CEO. Announcements with confounding events during a 21-day window (from day -10 to day 10) around the announcement date were excluded, leaving 114 heir apparent appointments in the final sample. Investor reaction to these announcements is captured by abnormal returns.
time_window: 1988-1997 announcements; event window day -1 to day +1

description: Announcements of heir apparent promotion to the CEO position were collected from the Wall Street Journal Index and News Wires for 1988-1997. Announcements with confounding events during the 21-day window around the announcement date were excluded, leaving 130 heir apparent promotions in the final sample. Investor reaction to these announcements is captured by abnormal returns.
time_window: 1988-1997 announcements; event window day -1 to day +1

description: Announcements of heir apparent exit from the firm before promotion to the CEO position were collected from the Wall Street Journal Index and News Wires for 1988-1997. Announcements with confounding events during the 21-day window around the announcement date were excluded, leaving 31 heir apparent exits in the final sample. Investor reaction to these announcements is captured by abnormal returns.
time_window: 1988-1997 announcements; event window day -1 to day +1

description: Announcements of inside CEO successions in which the new CEO was not an heir apparent were collected from the Wall Street Journal Index and News Wires for 1988-1997, excluding announcements with confounding events during the 21-day window around the announcement date. 29 nonrelay inside successions remained in the final sample. Investor reaction to these announcements is captured by abnormal returns.
time_window: 1988-1997 announcements; event window day -1 to day +1

description: Announcements of CEO successions with a successor of outside firm origin were collected from the Wall Street Journal Index and News Wires for 1988-1997, excluding announcements with confounding events during the 21-day window around the announcement date. 34 outside successions remained in the final sample. Investor reaction to these announcements is captured by abnormal returns.
time_window: 1988-1997 announcements; event window day -1 to day +1

description: Firm performance was measured as the return on assets (ROA) during the fiscal year prior to the year when the event of interest occurred. The performance data were collected from COMPUSTAT. Firm ROA is used as the independent variable predicting the cumulative abnormal returns of the succession events.
time_window: fiscal year prior to the year of the event

description: Change in shareholder wealth was measured by abnormal returns. Using a standard market model, market model parameters were estimated from each firm's daily returns over a 255-day period (from day -300 to day -46) for each event; a firm's daily abnormal return is the difference between its actual daily return and the return predicted by the market model. A 3-day event window (-1, +1) was used to calculate cumulative abnormal returns. All daily stock return data came from the CRSP tapes.
time_window: event window day -1 to day +1; estimation period day -300 to day -46

description: The proportion of outside board members over total board size. Outside directors are directors who have never served as executive director, executive officer, employee of the company or any of its subsidiaries, as reported in the companies' annual report. All explanatory variables are lagged by one period.

The natural log of audit fees, following prior studies on the relationship between corporate governance and audit services. The variable represents the amount paid by the company for the professional examination and verification of the financial statements for the purpose of assessing their consistency, fairness, and conformation to accepted accounting principles.

The percentage of total outstanding shares held by non-Japanese investors, reported by the Tokyo Stock Exchange in four categories: between 0 and 10 percent, between 10 and 20 percent, between 20 and 30 percent, and more than 30 percent. The four categories are used as defined by the TSE, which allows testing for nonlinearity and possible cut-off points, with firms below 10 percent as the reference category. The variable is lagged by one period.

A dummy variable taking the value 1 if foreign ownership is at least 20 percent, and 0 otherwise. The 20 percent cut-off point was established as a critical inflection point after using the four TSE categories. The variable is lagged by one period.

The total stake of the largest domestic owner. The sample is split at the median value of this variable to compare the interaction effect between board independence and foreign ownership across subsamples.

The annualized standard deviation of weekly equity returns, following Zajac and Westphal (1994) and Laeven and Levine (2009). The sample is split at the median value of this variable to compare the interaction effect between board independence and foreign ownership across subsamples.

The deviation from prior performance, captured as the current performance compared with the average of the prior two years' performance, where performance is measured with return on assets. The sample is split at the median value of this variable to compare the interaction effect between board independence and foreign ownership across subsamples.
time_window: current performance relative to the average of the prior two years

description: Number of display-related U.S. patents the supplier applied for in the previous 5 years; the figure is updated annually. Display-related patents are those containing the terms 'liquid crystal display' or 'LCD' or classified in International Patent Classification section G02F 1/-, G09G 31-, G09F 9/3-, or G09F 131-, classifications selected according to Spencer (1997) and confirmed against the 'Liquid Crystal Display' section of Derwent Information's Industry and Technology Patents Profiles. An industry informant confirmed the appropriateness of the measure for the display industry: although decision-makers rarely if ever actually count the number of display-related patents each potential supplier holds at a given time, the number of patents held by a supplier correlates closely with its technical capabilities and with other firms' beliefs about those capabilities.

Number of previous years in which the manufacturer had purchased at least one notebook computer display from the supplier. If a manufacturer and supplier had relationships prior to their entry into the data, the measure is truncated; to control for this, decisions made in the first 3 years of a manufacturer's presence in the data are not modeled, leaving 68 of the original 116 innovations.

Indicator variable set to 1 if the supplier is part of the same company as the computer manufacturer. The author also includes the interaction of INTERNAL SUPPLIER and YEARS, since the value of previous transactions may differ for internal and external suppliers.

Rating of industry perceptions of the advance beyond existing technology that each innovation required, ranging from 1 to 5. A researcher in a leading consulting company, an 18-year industry veteran with experience as both a product engineer and product marketing manager, provided this rating for each innovation observed in the data. Since the measure was constructed after the fact, it may be biased by knowledge of which innovations ultimately proved the most difficult.

Dichotomous variable measuring whether suppliers could produce the display by refining existing techniques or whether new techniques were necessary. A resolution increase was coded as highly uncertain if it required new process technology or breakthroughs in metallurgy rather than executing existing materials and processes better; a size increase was coded as highly uncertain if it required the assembly of an entirely new fabrication line rather than being possible through improvements in an existing fabrication line. A senior industry participant who worked in the display division of a firm that made both displays and notebooks identified for each innovation whether it required a new process.

Indicator variable set to 0 for all suppliers except the one the manufacturer chose and to 1 for that supplier, within the set of observations related to a manufacturer's introduction of a given innovation. The analysis focuses on the single supplier used in a manufacturer's initial introduction of a notebook with a given display type.

The cumulative number of applications filed by a focal start-up at time t that eventually result in the successful award of a U.S. patent. It is a time-varying stock measured at the time of the funding round, or, for the firm-level analysis, at the time of the latest funding round. The authors note that investors tend to respond rapidly to information contained in patent application documents.
time_window: cumulative stock at the focal funding round

description: Outcome variable equal to one if the lead investor is in the upper half of the within-sample distribution of VC network centrality, based on annual VC syndication patterns compiled by Hochberg et al. (2007).

The product of a start-up's share price before the funding round multiplied by the number of shares outstanding; it reflects investors' valuation prior to capital infusion at the focal round. Premoney rather than postmoney valuation is used because the former is less sensitive to the quantity of funds injected. The dependent variable in the across-round analysis is the log of premoney valuation, estimated with firm fixed effects.

variable_name: founding team has no prior IPO experience
description: Dummy variable equal to one if no members of the founding team had prior entrepreneurial IPO experience. The authors compiled the names and biographies of founders through web searches and tracked the outcomes of prior companies they had founded, if any.
Dummy variable that denotes first or second rounds of VC funding.

Indicator variable equal to one if the prominence of the lead VC investor in the focal round is in the lower within-sample distribution of VC network eigenvector centrality, i.e., the start-up is not backed by prominent VC investors. It is one of two indicators the authors use to operationalize a start-up's relative disadvantage in conveying quality at IPO.

variable_name: percentage change in first-day stock price
description: The percentage change from the offering price to the closing price on the first day of public trading, for the subsample of firms with IPO exits. Less change in the first-day stock price (i.e., less underpricing) suggests fewer information asymmetry problems between new listings and public investors.

variable_name: not backed by prominent VC and founding team has no prior IPO experience
description: Low reputation endowment was captured with two dummy variables: the start-up was not backed by a prominent VC (lead investor in the lower half of VC network centrality) and the founding team had no prior entrepreneurial IPO experience. Both were entered as moderators of the patent effect on IPO underpricing.

The proportion of restrictive words to total words in each part of the CFR that corresponds to each firm's six-digit NAICS code. RegData identifies instances of 'prohibited,' 'shall,' 'may not,' 'must,' and 'required' to create a count of restrictive words for each NAICS industry. The measure is log transformed to account for distributional skewness and diminishing effects of large counts, and is lagged by one year to allow firms to adjust their innovation output following regulatory change.
level: firm-year (six-digit NAICS industry matched to firm)

description: The sum of the number of regulatory documents published by the agencies in the three preceding years (i.e., from t-3 to t-1). Only documents that are categorized as 'Science and technology' by the Office of the Federal Register and that are marked significant under Executive Order 12866, meaning the regulation is predicted to have a material economic impact of $100 million or more, are counted. The variable is labeled in log form.

The count of patents applied for by the firm in a year whose CD5 value is less than zero, with one added to the count and the value logged. The CD index characterizes the backward and forward citation network of a focal patent and ranges from -1 to 1, with values between -1 and 0 indicating more consolidating work. The index is measured five years after the grant year, and patents are assigned to years according to their application date.
time_window: patents applied for 1994-2013; CD index measured five years after grant year

description: The count of patents applied for by the firm in a year whose CD5 value is greater than zero, with one added to the count and the value logged. The CD index characterizes the backward and forward citation network of a focal patent: if a focal patent is destabilizing, subsequent patents that cite it are less likely to cite the prior patents cited by the focal patent. The index is measured five years after the grant year (CD5), with values between 0 and 1 indicating more destabilizing work.
time_window: patents applied for 1994-2013; CD index measured five years after grant year

variable_name: Killed in terrorist attacks (KTA), killed in natural disasters (KND), killed in technological disasters (KTD)
description: Disaster severity is operationalized with the number of people killed by the disaster in the host country. The authors tested the number of incidents, the number of people killed, and the duration of the disaster, and report the results from the number of people killed. The measure is the logarithm of 1 plus the number killed. Severity is measured separately for terrorist attacks, natural disasters, and technological disasters, and each type enters the model for its own disaster type.

variable_name: Experience in terrorist attacks (ETA), experience in natural disasters (END), experience in technological disasters (ETD)
description: Experience in disasters counts the number of subsidiaries an MNC has in countries that are affected by each type of disaster in the prior year, and is log-transformed. Experience is always disaster specific: experience with terrorist attacks is used in the terrorism model, experience with natural disasters in the natural disaster model, and experience with technological disasters in the technological disaster model. The authors assume that even a subsidiary not directly affected by a disaster will likely gain indirect experience from partners, suppliers, government and nongovernment agencies, and mass media.

variable_name: Experience in high-impact disasters (EHTA, EHND, EHTD)
description: Experience in high-impact disasters counts the number of subsidiaries in countries that are affected by disasters that killed more people on average than other disasters of the same type, log-transformed. It is measured separately for terrorist attacks, natural disasters, and technological disasters.

variable_name: Experience in low-impact disasters (ELTA, ELND, ELTD)
description: Experience in low-impact disasters counts the number of subsidiaries in countries that are affected by disasters that killed fewer people on average than other disasters of the same type, log-transformed. It is measured separately for terrorist attacks, natural disasters, and technological disasters.

Entry is a binary dependent variable that equals 1 when a firm enters a country for the first time and 0 before the first entry. In the entry model, the firm-country-year data points are excluded from the sample after a given firm has entered a given host country.

NSUB is the number of a firm's subsidiaries in a host country, a count-dependent variable with positive integers, used as the measure of expansion and described by the authors as a measure of the real value of commitments in each country. In the expansion model, the firm-country-year data points before a given firm entered a host country are excluded from the sample.

Dichotomous variable indicating whether a technology was introduced by a startup (Startup = 1) or a diversifying entrant (Startup = 0). Classification used the historical method: for each firm the authors collected data about its founding year and historical records about its product introductions from multiple sources, including news releases, 10-K filings, and the Compustat, Hoover's, and VentureXpert databases, and then classified each firm as a startup or a diversifying entrant. In the sample, 62 technologies were introduced by startups, whose average firm age on entry was 1.92 years, and 72 technologies by diversifying entrants, whose average age on entry was 26.78 years.

Coded as 1 if the firm exited the dominance battle in a given year, and 0 otherwise, based on a triangulation of data collected from firms' news releases, research articles, books, and firms' annual reports. Longitudinal observations were created from the year the firm first introduced its technology to the year the technology exited from the dominance battle; if an exit had not happened by the end of year 2007, the observation was right-censored. The authors observed 99 technology exits during their observation window.
time_window: from the year the firm first introduced its technology to the year it exited; right-censored at the end of 2007

description: Dichotomous variable indicating whether a dominance battle was characterized by platform technologies (Platform technology = 1) or non-platform technologies (Platform technology = 0). Detailed technical descriptions were collected for each technology, and two experts with over 10 years of experience in the IT industry reviewed these descriptions and classified each dominance battle using criteria requiring that platform technologies (a) serve as technological bases that combine a variety of functionalities, (b) allow other technologies to sit on them, and (c) require the inputs of various actors in innovation. A total of 12 dominance battles were coded as platform technology-based.

Indicator variable used to differentiate the years when a DD was not established (DD = 0) from the years when a DD was established (DD = 1) in each dominance battle. Two coders independently coded whether and when a technology emerged as a DD, based on a triangulation of information from at least two archival sources, and the measure was validated against market share data. In the final sample, DDs had not emerged in four dominance battles and 38 DDs had emerged consecutively in 27 dominance battles by the end of year 2007.
scale: dichotomous (1 = a DD has emerged, 0 = no DD yet)
time_window: yearly within each dominance battle, up to 2007

description: The count of material, positive announcements made by the focal firm in a firm-authored press release in the three-day period centered on the announcement of the acquisition (one day before and after). The measure is intended to capture the intentional release of unrelated positive information surrounding an announcement; positive announcements include items such as new product introductions or positive earnings releases.
time_window: three-day window centered on the acquisition announcement

description: The ratio of (1) the options exercised by the CEO in the quarter following the focal acquisition to (2) the number of exercisable options held by the CEO at the end of the prior year, using Thomson Reuters Insider Filing data summarized to quarters. Unexercisable (unvested) options are not included in the denominator. The variable was logged because of its skewed distribution.
time_window: quarter following the focal acquisition, scaled by exercisable options held at the end of the prior year

description: The age reported in ExecuComp for the firm's CEO in the year of the acquisition.

A binary variable with a value of 1 for firms that were included on either Fortune's Most Admired or the Wall Street Journal's Corporate Reputation Survey, and a value of 0 otherwise. A combined list was used to keep roughly equal numbers (20-25) of high-reputation firms per year of the sample.

Industry sales were first regressed on a year counter variable with a five-year window, such that the value for year t is calculated from a regression covering years t-4 through t. The standard error was then divided by the industry's mean sales, generating a variable that scales from 0 (perfect stability) upward (greater dynamism).
time_window: five-year window ending in year t

description: The dependent variable is implicitly the number of quarters the firm is under observation until exit. In the accelerated failure time model the time to failure is measured in quarters since founding or first observation, so positive coefficients indicate later exit.
The running total of cumulative profits for each bank, computed from the latter of entry or 1983Q1 through the current quarter.
time_window: from the latter of entry or 1983Q1 through quarter t

description: The probability of being profitable, calculated as the ratio of surviving firms in 1997Q4 to all firms who participated in market j during the period of observation. It is a market-level, time-invariant measure.
The standard deviation of quarterly firm profits measured while the firm is under observation.
time_window: while the firm is under observation

description: The standard deviation of all banks' relative costs in market j during the period of observation, corresponding to the precision of prior beliefs in models of Bayesian updating.

Imputed cost of entry, calculated as the mean value of financial and physical assets for firms entering market j at time t, as described in Wu and Knott (2006). In Dixit's model k represents a sunk cost of entry; the authors cannot observe sunk costs and posit that across the banking industry they are proportional to the total costs of entry. For markets in which there was no entry the value is imputed from entry activity at t-2, t-1, t+1 and t+2.
time_window: market j at time t, imputed from t-2, t-1, t+1 and t+2 when there is no entry

description: Measured as 100 times exp(beta-hat 1 minus 1), where beta-hat 1 is estimated via market-specific regressions of output growth. The equation specifying these regressions is unreadable in the text provided, so the exact specification is not recorded.
Captured as the root mean squared error of the actual versus predicted values from the same market-specific regressions of output growth used to estimate demand growth.

Indicator variable that takes the value 1 if firm i is organized as a bank holding company at time t and 0 otherwise. BHCs are separate legal entities that own 25 percent or more of a bank and have greater separation of ownership and control than independent banks.

variable_name: net income x profit indicator / net income x loss indicator
description: The magnitude of quarterly net income of firm i in quarter t interacted with a profit indicator that takes the value 1 if net income is positive and 0 otherwise, and separately interacted with a loss indicator that takes the value 1 if net income is negative and 0 otherwise. The two interaction terms separately estimate the impact of positive and negative signals on exit.

Fifteen objective criteria were identified through a survey of the literature and recommendations from five academicians knowledgeable of the strategy and mergers and acquisitions literature. The criteria are level of diversification, market share in the firm's primary industry, annual sales, return on investment, stock price, anticipated discounted cash flow, projected new products/services to be developed over the next 5 years, projected demand for products/services over the next 5 years, level of management talent, capabilities in marketing, capabilities in manufacturing, capabilities in R&D, attractiveness of the firm's primary industry, degree of synergy with the acquiring firm, and acquisition price. The level of each criterion was randomly varied on a scale of one (low) to five (high) across the 30 cases, which controlled for potential collinearity among the independent variables.

Executives examined each case describing a target firm on the basis of the 15 criteria and rated the attractiveness of the target firm as an acquisition candidate on a one to seven scale and the probability that this firm would be acquired on a one to seven scale. The coefficient alpha for the scale combining these two questions was 0.90, and this combined scale represented the dependent variable. Each manager evaluated 30 target firms, yielding a sample size of 30 x 65 or 1950 observations.
scale: 1 to 7 for each of the two questions

description: Respondents were asked to denote the industry representing the greatest percentage of total firm sales, and this information was used to help classify the firm into the correct two-digit SIC code. For analytical purposes the firms were further classified into one of six categories including consumer goods (manufacturers), capital goods, producer goods, financial services, professional services and other. Industry was then coded as a dummy variable.

A block of individual characteristics was entered into the hierarchical regression: age, amount and type of education, total years of work experience, combinations of functional experience, level in the firm, cognitive complexity and risk propensity. Because the study did not hypothesize specific main effects for each separate characteristic, the general main effect of this set was examined.
The respondents' chronological age was requested. The average age of the respondents was 47.

variable_name: type of education (major area of study)
description: Respondents were requested to denote the major area of study if they held a college degree (e.g. accounting, engineering, liberal arts). Type of education (major area of study) was coded as a dummy variable.
Amount of education was measured on a five-point scale ranging from high school to a Ph.D. (high school, some college, bachelors degree, masters degree, Ph.D.).
scale: five-point scale from high school to Ph.D.

variable_name: total years of professional work experience
description: Respondents provided the chronological number of total years of professional work experience. The respondents averaged 24 years of total work experience.

Respondents were asked to denote whether they had work experience in one or more of the functional areas (accounting, engineering, finance, marketing, management, R&D, personnel, production/manufacturing, purchasing) or other areas, each coded as a dummy variable, and also provided the number of years of experience in each function. Because the experiences are interdependent, a clustering technique was used to differentiate executives with similar backgrounds; it produced six distinct clusters, of which two single-respondent technical clusters were dropped from further analysis. For purposes of the moderated regression analyses this variable was coded as a dummy variable.

variable_name: levels between respondent and the CEO
description: In addition to the title of the current position, the respondents provided the number of levels between them and the CEO (0 = CEO). The respondents' position ranged from vice-president to CEO with the mean position one level below the CEO.

Cognitive complexity was measured using an instrument developed by Bieri et al. (1966), modified by Vannoy (1965) and validated by Schneier (1979). The instrument involves a 10 x 10 grid whereby the respondent evaluates 10 specific persons (e.g. boss, person who respondent dislikes) including him/herself on 10 bipolar adjectives using a six-point scale, for a total of 100 ratings. The higher the score, the more cognitively simple the person, because she/he is using similar constructs to describe each person; a person who is more cognitively complex (lower score) uses the constructs differently in discriminating among people.

Executives' propensity to take risks was measured using the Job Preference Inventory (Williams, 1965). The inventory consists of eight pairs of descriptive statements regarding a job, and the respondent is asked to choose the statement which describes the job s/he would most prefer. The statements describing a 'risky' job are scored 1 and statements describing a job with little or no risk are scored as 0. The internal reliability (coefficient alpha) for the scale in this study was 0.66.
scale: eight pairs of statements scored 1 (risky) or 0 (little or no risk)

description: A dummy variable indicating whether the firm is an entrant or an incumbent, entered in the baseline model and interacted with individual firm effects so that separate firm-effect variance components are estimated for entrants and for incumbents.

A dummy variable indicating whether the time period is in the regulated or the deregulated regime, entered in the baseline model of the variance components and OLS analyses. The text does not state in prose which value is coded one.

The main analysis decomposes the variance of firm rates of return into components due to time period, strategic group, entrant/incumbent status, regulation/deregulation regime, and individual firm effects for entrants under deregulation and for incumbents under regulation and under deregulation, plus interactions of these firm effects with strategic group membership. The variance component estimates for the firm-effects variables test the hypotheses. The same decomposition is run separately on ROS and on ROA.

Net Income over Sales, computed for each airline and quarter. Used as the dependent variable of the decompositions and regressions reported for the ROS results. The authors note that studies of the airline industry have generally predicted ROS as the relevant measure of airline performance.

Net Income over Operating Assets, computed for each airline and quarter. The authors note that ROA controls for differences across firms in patterns of asset ownership, but that many airlines lease their planes, so return on owned assets may reflect financial policy as well as economic performance.

The average number of 'concerns' per year per firm reported in the KLD database, cumulated across all seven dimensions, over the 2000-2004 period. A log-transformed measure was used because it most closely approximated the normal distribution in terms of skewness and kurtosis, and was seen as preferable to nontransformed or square root transformations. The longitudinal perspective reflects the view that reputation is constructed over time.

Evidence of a Katrina donation was gathered by searching company Web sites, press release archives, and newswires and major U.S. newspapers via Lexis-Nexis for Katrina donation announcements. Evidence of CPDR was found for 245 of the initial 442 firms; after eliminating oil industry firms and firms with contaminating events, 206 donors remained in the working sample. The outcome is modelled as a dichotomous variable distinguishing donors from nondonors.
time_window: days and weeks following Hurricane Katrina (2005)

description: Daily returns were calculated using the lognormal formula over the interval from 20 August 2004 to 21 August 2005 (254 trading days). Abnormal returns are the differences between the ex post return of a security over the event window and the normal, expected return, with the normal return derived from a market model estimated by ordinary least squares. Individual daily abnormal returns were cumulated over the event window [-1, 0], with Friday 26 August 2005 as day -1 and Monday 29 August 2005 as day 0. The S&P 500 Composite Index is used as the market benchmark.
time_window: event window [-1, 0], 26-29 August 2005; estimation window 20 August 2004 to 21 August 2005

description: The disaster is Hurricane Katrina, treated as the event in an event study. Day 0 is Monday 29 August 2005, the day Katrina hit the Gulf Coast, and day -1 is Friday 26 August 2005. Cumulative abnormal returns are computed over this two-day window.

variable_name: Treated firms' associations with ousted corrupt officials (TACO)
description: The productive term between associations with corrupt officials and a post-anticorruption shock dummy valued 1 after the firm's headquartered province experienced an anticorruption shock for the first time and 0 otherwise. Associations with corrupt officials is the total number of personal ties between a firm's executives/directors and all corrupt officials indicted in the focal year, each weighted by the collective degree centralities of the connected corrupt officials in the political network of all high-level officials. Zero for firms that never experienced a shock.

variable_name: Removing existing political connections with corrupt officials (logged)
description: Count of outgoing upper echelons (individuals listed as executives or directors in the prior year but excluded in the focal year) who had personal ties with any high-level officials removed due to corruption charges in the focal year. Each removed political connection is weighted by the sum of standardized degree centrality of all the connected corrupt officials in the experience-based political network across all high-level government officials. Twenty-one politically connected upper echelons who left the firm to join another public firm within 2 years were excluded to remove voluntary ship-jumpers. The weighted count is log-transformed.

variable_name: Adding new political connections with successors (logged)
description: Count of newly listed upper echelons (executives or directors new to the firm in the focal year who held no such position in the firm in previous years) who had personal ties with the successors of all high-level corrupt officials dismissed in the focal year. Each connection is weighted by the standardized degree centrality of the successor in the experience-based political network of all high-level government officials. The weighted count is log-transformed.

The ratio of the firm's revenue received from the government (including subsidies, tax breaks, government contracts, and government funding) divided by the firm's annual operating income. Extracted from firms' financial reports.

The total sum of the eigenvector centrality of all high-level ousted corrupt officials in the political network in a given year, weighted for each firm by the percentage of ousted high-level corrupt officials who had prior employment experience in the firm's headquarter province.

Membership in a group was operationalized using two dummy variables. 'Group 1' was assigned a value of 1 if a firm belonged to the integrated group and 0 otherwise; 'Group 2' was assigned a value of 1 if a firm belonged to the minimills group and 0 otherwise. Because only two categories exist in the sample, only one dummy variable was included in the regression analysis; the excluded group becomes a reference group and the regression coefficient expresses the difference between the two group means.

Return on sales was assessed as the ratio of operating income to total sales. The authors note that although these measures may be distorted due to aggregations, this is generally acceptable when the firms in the sample are relatively undiversified.
Return on assets was assessed as the ratio of operating income to total assets. The authors note that Japanese firms tend, in general, to understate their asset values.

A producer's shift from a history of exclusive use of botti to some use of barriques, analyzed as the hazard of a first defection. For each producer the guide indicates whether each wine was aged in botti only, barriques only, or a combination of botti and barriques. Given the timing of the modernist reinterpretation, the analysis begins in 1980 and ends with the 2001 vintage.

variable_name: average membership in 'traditionalist' style of partial defectors
description: Computed from producer-level grades of membership: a producer's GoM in the old style in each vintage is the proportion of its Barolo/Barbaresco labels that received only botti aging, and its GoM in the new style is the complement, 1 minus the GoM in the old style. The variable is the average GoM in the 'tradition' of the partial defectors, lagged one vintage.

variable_name: average membership in 'traditionalist' style of de novo spanners
description: Computed from the same producer-level grades of membership as the defector variable, as the average GoM in the 'tradition' of the producers who entered as category straddlers, entered to account for remaining effects of category spanning. The GoMs in 'tradition' are lagged one vintage.

variable_name: average tenure in category spanning of partial defectors
description: The average number of years spent since producers who were 'traditionalist' started using barriques. It is used with an interaction term between the average GoM in 'traditionalist' style of partial defectors and the average tenure of partial producers since defection.

A binary variable that reflects whether (1) or not (0) any given director left that position before or when their term was set to expire, meaning when they were available for re-appointment. The variable takes a value of 1 only when the director ostensibly voluntarily exited, which the authors determined by consulting ISS documents, resignation letters, the requisite 8-K document for mid-term resignations, and corresponding press releases. The authors examined whether a director sought re-election in the year following the CEO succession for most of the directors, and in some instances looked 2 or 3 years out depending on the stage of the election process.
time_window: the year following the CEO succession for most directors; 2 or 3 years out in some instances

variable_name: Curvature of the line of incongruence
description: The authors operationalize political ideology (in)congruence between a director and the incoming CEO with a polynomial quadratic specification, so incongruence is tested through the curvature of the line of incongruence, which is calculated from the polynomial estimates using the formulas in the appendix. The curvature captures how the likelihood of director departure changes as the two individuals start at political neutrality and move in different ideological directions, such that a positive value is interpreted as directors being more likely to depart their positions as they do not share the same political ideology as the incoming CEO.

variable_name: Curvature of the line of congruence
description: The authors operationalize political ideology (in)congruence between a director and the incoming CEO with a polynomial quadratic specification, so congruence is tested through the curvature of the line of congruence, which is calculated from the polynomial estimates using the formulas in the appendix. The curvature captures how the likelihood of director departure changes as the two individuals start at political neutrality and move in the same ideological direction, such that a negative value reflects that directors are less apt to depart when they share the same ideology as the incoming CEO.

A continuous variable that calculates the number of years the focal director has spent at the same organization as the individual selected for the role of CEO, either at the firm in question or in previous organizations. Measuring the variable this way, reflecting different values across all the directors on the same board, is requisite because the authors employ a firm fixed-effects approach; the variable therefore detects variance within the same board.

A continuous donation-based score ranging from 0 to 1, where higher values represent a more liberal executive and lower values represent a more conservative executive. It is the average of four indicators: the number of donations to the Democrat party relative to total donations; the dollar amount of donations to the Democrat party relative to the total dollar value of donations; the number of discrete years in which the executive made donations to the Democrat party relative to total years in which a donation was made; and the number of distinct Democrat recipients relative to total recipients. The authors add a value of 0.1 to the numerator of all the dimensions and 0.2 to the denominator, so individuals with no political donations are assigned a score of 0.5, reflecting a neutral political ideology; the four indicators demonstrate high reliability (alpha = 0.95).

A continuous donation-based score ranging from 0 to 1, where higher values represent a more liberal executive and lower values represent a more conservative executive, measured with an identical procedure to the director score. It is the average of four indicators: the number of donations to the Democrat party relative to total donations; the dollar amount of donations to the Democrat party relative to the total dollar value of donations; the number of discrete years in which the executive made donations to the Democrat party relative to total years in which a donation was made; and the number of distinct Democrat recipients relative to total recipients. The authors add a value of 0.1 to the numerator of all the dimensions and 0.2 to the denominator, so individuals with no political donations are assigned a score of 0.5, reflecting a neutral political ideology; the four indicators demonstrate high reliability (alpha = 0.95).

Fundamental organizational transformations were coded as occurring whenever substantial changes were observed in the strategy, structure, and power distribution domains of organizational activity. No restriction was imposed for the length of time over which substantial changes had to be observed over all three domains. Whenever a transformation was identified in this manner, the count of substantial changes was restarted. Substantial changes were identified both qualitatively from event histories and objectively at four percentage-change criterion levels.
time_window: all years of the organizations' lives except their first years and the last years of acquired or failed firms

description: A revolutionary transformation was coded as occurring whenever changes in all three strategy, structure, and power distributions occurred within any two-year time period. A more stringent criterion would require changes in all three domains in a single year; the majority of revolutionary transformations observed did occur within single years, but the two-year criterion was used because some data were reported for corporate fiscal years and some for calendar years. Transformations not meeting this timing criterion were classified as nonrevolutionary.
time_window: firm years, excluding the first year and the last year of acquired or failed firms

variable_name: Accumulated percentage change in activity domains
description: All objective measures of change for each of the three domains were arrayed over all years of all organizations' lives, and annual percentage changes for each variable were summed over successive years. A nonrevolutionary transformation was coded whenever changes in each of the three activity domains accumulated to 30 percent through the addition of multiple small annual changes and all three domains exhibited this level of change. The count of small annual changes was halted whenever a one-year change of at least 30 percent was encountered and was begun again immediately after the occurrence of a large annual change.
time_window: successive firm years over the organizations' lives

description: Organizational performance was measured as the percentage change in a firm's market share over successive annual periods. Crisis was coded whenever the market share percentage change was -.42 or lower, a level representing the lowest 10th percentile of market share changes over all firms for all years. The data were coded as a dummy variable, with 0 = crisis and 1 = no crisis. Market share was calculated by contrasting each firm's minicomputer sales with the total number of minicomputers sold by all competitors.
time_window: successive annual periods for all years of the firms' lives

description: Major changes in environmental conditions were coded as dummy variables (1 = major change, 0 = no major change) to test the effect of environmental change on the likelihood of organizational transformation. Three major shifts, occurring during 1971, 1976, and 1980, seemed severe enough to pose a crisis for competing organizations, involving a technology shakeout and consolidation, steep increases in failure rates and concentration ratios, slowing demand, and the first absolute decline in minicomputer sales.
scale: dummy (1 = major change, 0 = no major change)

description: Succession of a CEO was coded as a dummy variable (1 = a year in which a CEO was replaced, 0 = otherwise) to test the effect of succession on the likelihood of organizational transformation. CEO successions were deliberately not coded as indicators of major shifts in power distributions, because succession often precedes changes in the composition of the executive team and because major changes in power distributions can occur without a CEO change.
time_window: each year of each firm's life

variable_name: Status accumulation (unranked firms; tier 1 and tier 2 firms)
description: Binary dependent variable derived from the firm's position in the Asia Pacific Legal 500 status ranking, which the authors first reverse coded so that tier 6 represented the highest value of the status distribution and tier 1 the lowest and then averaged proportionally per firm per year and rounded to the nearest whole number, where zero indicates an unranked firm. For unranked firms, a value of one indicates that the firm became ranked in a given year; this risk set left 103 law firms and 344 firm-year observations, and 40 law firms moved into the ranking over the 11-year event window. For low-ranked firms (tier 1 and tier 2), a value of one indicates a positive change in the focal firm's status, or moving up in the rankings; this risk set left 46 firms and 183 firm-year observations, of which 21 accumulated status. Firms were removed from the risk set when they accumulated status.

Binary measure of whether law firms at the top of the status rankings (tier 5 and tier 6) decline in status or move down in the rankings. A value of one indicates a negative change in the status of a tier 5 or tier 6 firm, while zero indicates that the status of the firm did not change. The risk set removed firms ranked lower than tier 5 or 6 and left 31 firms and 115 firm-year observations; 11 of the 31 high-status firms experienced a decline in status over the 11-year event window. Firms were removed from the risk set when they declined in status.

variable_name: Status distance between the firms linked by the mobile partner (tier difference)
description: Status distance is operationalized through the tier difference between the two firms connected by the mobile partner, using separate binary indicators for hiring from a firm one tier above, two tiers above, and three or more tiers above the focal firm, and for exit to a firm one tier below, two tiers below, and three or more tiers below the source firm; mobility between firms occupying the same tier is the reference category. The status ranking underlying these tier differences is the Asia Pacific Legal 500's annual ranking of law firms in 13 practice areas into tiers that range from one (highest) to six (lowest). All variables were lagged by one year.
scale: set of binary indicators by tier difference

description: Binary variable for which a value of one indicates that the mobility event has taken place, namely the entry of a partner from a firm that occupied a higher position in the status ranking than the focal firm. The variable is disambiguated by examining the effect of hiring from a firm one tier higher, two tiers higher, or three or more tiers higher than the focal firm. All variables were lagged by one year. Over the event window, 21 out of 103 unranked firms hired 34 partners from above and 18 out of 46 low-ranked firms hired 30 partners from above. Exit variables were included in the status accumulation models to control for simultaneous mobility.

Binary variable for which a value of one indicates that the mobility event has taken place, namely that a partner had gone to a firm that occupied a lower position in the status ranking than the source firm. The variable is disambiguated by examining the effect of a partner going to a firm one tier below, two tiers below, or three or more tiers below the focal firm. All variables were lagged by one year. Over the event window, 7 out of 31 firms had 16 partners leave for a lower-status firm. Hiring variables were included in the status decline models to control for simultaneous mobility.

variable_name: time from acquisition to CEO's departure
description: The dependent variable was the time that elapsed from an acquisition to a CEO's departure, measured in months. All target firms' CEOs were followed for four years to determine if and when they left, and by the end of the four-year period 161 of the CEOs had left their companies. Departures were dated from public information and, where no public information existed, from telephone calls to the firms; departure dates could be definitively established for the CEOs at 181 of the firms.

CEO age was the age, in years, of the CEO of a target firm at the time of its acquisition, and was included together with CEO age squared to model a curvilinear effect. CEO ages ranged from 33 to 80 and exhibited a normal distribution.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: CEO tenure was the logarithm of the number of years an individual had worked in an acquired firm at the time of its takeover; both years as CEO and years of employment in the firm prior to becoming CEO were examined. The log of tenure was taken because tenure had a right skew and because the effect of tenure was expected to have diminishing returns.
time_window: at the time of the takeover

description: Relatedness was a measure of the extent to which an acquiring firm's primary SIC codes were related to the target firm's primary SIC codes. A coding of 1 represented a perfect four-digit match between acquirer and target, and all other firms were coded 0, for 'unrelated.'

Technological distance between each pair of firms was created from the firms' semiconductor patents during the 1980-1989 period. For each firm with more than 10 patents, 10 of the set were randomly selected; if a firm had fewer than three patents during this period, the earliest possible patent data after 1989 were used. The technological classes of each patent were tabulated and the percentage of assignments in each patent class was aggregated into a patent class vector per firm. Euclidean distances between these patent class vectors were calculated for each pair of firms, ranging from zero for identical patenting profiles to 1.4 where both firms allocate all activity to a different single class; higher values therefore connote lower technological similarity.

A binary variable indicating whether the pair of firms was located in the same geographic region. Regions were defined as states within the United States and countries outside the United States, except that California was split into northern and southern California and New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Pennsylvania were combined into one region. The regions were obtained from the inventor's location listed on the citing and cited patents, so the variable records whether the inventors of each patent belonged to the same region at the time of patenting. It is set to one when the inventors for a pair of firms were in the same region and zero otherwise; 32% of dyads were designated as geographically similar.

The authors compiled the announcements of every alliance formed between firms in their sample between 1980 and 1989 as listed in the weekly publication Electronic News. The complete range of alliances that firms undertook was recorded, including joint ventures (for design or for fabrication), equity arrangements, marketing, design, fabrication, and extended licensing agreements. An alliance reported as being between three firms was coded as three dyadic alliances, one between each pair of firms. A total of 160 alliances were identified.

The authors examined the set of semiconductor patents for each firm in the sample over the full 1980-1995 period and tracked each inventor listed on these patents, looking for instances in which an inventor was employed by more than one firm. For example, if an inventor was listed on patents for Firm A in 1987, Firm B in 1989 and Firm C in 1993, Firm C was determined to have access to the knowledge of Firms B and A, while Firm B had access to the knowledge of Firm A. Only mobility occurring between 1980 and 1989 was tabulated, with dates interpolated to the nearest month to estimate timing. One hundred and twenty-one instances of mobility were identified.

For each focal firm the authors catalogued all semiconductor patents granted to the firm between 1990 and 1995, a total of 992 patents. For each patent, citations made to other patents were tabulated and linked to the firms that owned them, so that each citation is one instance of the focal firm drawing upon the knowledge of the cited firm, whether that firm was another focal firm or an incumbent. Self-citations were excluded from this set, and citations made to non-semiconductor firms are not included in the sample. A total of 4,560 citations were identified; the variable is a count of citations from the focal firm to the cited firm.

Coded 1 when a firm's entry model embodied an Intel microprocessor design (Entered with Intel MP) and 0 when it did not (Entered with Other than Intel MP). The Intel iAPX microprocessors were the 8008, 8088, 8086, 80286, 80386, and 80486. Of the 463 firms, 71 percent entered with the Intel microprocessor and 29 percent entered with an alternate design choice.

Four alternatives accounting for design changes after entry: (0) never chose the Intel microprocessor (Never Chose the Intel MP); (1) chose the Intel microprocessor at entry and never changed (Intel-No Change); (2) chose the Intel microprocessor after first using at least one other microprocessor (Other Design-Change); and (3) chose the Intel microprocessor at entry and changed to a different design later on (Intel-Change). Category 0 was the reference category used to test whether or not choice of the dominant design improved success. For the sample of 463 firms, 18 percent never introduced a model with the Intel microprocessor, 70 percent used the Intel microprocessor design at entry and never changed, 11 percent used the Intel microprocessor design some time after entering with an alternative design, and 1 percent entered with the Intel microprocessor and changed.

Duration was measured as the number of years the firm shipped personal computers. Duration for the 463 firms ranged from 1 to 17 years with an average of 5.30 years (S.D. = 3.10 years), and 40 percent (184/463) were still shipping personal computers in 1991. Because hazard is the opposite of survival, hypotheses were supported when the design choice variable coefficient was significant and in the opposite direction of the stated hypotheses.

Market share was computed as the percent of a firm's annual U.S. personal computer shipments to total U.S. personal computer unit shipments; the natural logarithm of market share was used because high market share outliers severely skewed the distribution. It was examined in four years (1984, 1986, 1988 and 1990), including only firms that were shipping computers at least one full year before and at least one full year after the market share year.

A weighted average of the investment-style profiles of the mutual funds that own the firm's stock. Each fund is assigned a profile score from 1 to 5: mixed funds with a greater focus on bonds (fixed income) are assigned 1 and mixed funds with a greater focus on equity are assigned 2, whereas equity value funds, core funds, and growth funds are assigned 3, 4, and 5 respectively. The weight for a fund is the proportion of the firm's equity held by that fund divided by the total equity of the firm held by all mutual funds in a period. The formula block itself is not readable in the extracted text; the weighting is described in the surrounding prose.
time_window: computed by period; lagged one period when used as an explanatory variable

description: The investor orientation of a firm's shareholders immediately prior to the onset of the industry change, computed using the same weighted-average mutual fund formula as Investor profile and measured at t = 0. It is fixed for a firm, so it does not vary within firms over the study period, and it is used as the pre-change explanatory variable in tests of Hypotheses 3 and 4.
time_window: t = 0, immediately prior to the onset of the industry change

description: The logged value of the firm's capital expenditure, following prior research. The authors note that a breakdown of firms' capital expenditures to assess the nature of the investments is not available, but that their reading of analysts' reports indicates firms from both industries were increasing capital investments specifically to participate in the new triple-play market. The variable is lagged by one period in the models; in fixed-effects models it is the within-firm increases in capital expenditures, not the historical base rate, that drive the results.

The mean recommendation value from the I/B/E/S summary file, which averages recommendations across all analysts that track a firm, every quarter. The variable is coded as 1 = strong buy, 2 = buy, 3 = hold, 4 = underperform, and 5 = sell, so higher values indicate more negative reactions and lower values indicate more positive analyst recommendations. It is reverse coded relative to the favorableness of analysts' reactions.

The number of periods elapsed following the start of the convergence between industries, with greater values corresponding to the later years of the study. It enters as the moderator in the interaction terms used to test Hypotheses 3 and 4, and time period controls are included in all regressions to account for unobserved period effects.

Using the SharkRepellent database, the authors identified the founding date of each activist investor and examined their initial campaigns for up to 3 years, coding the number of proxy fights in the initial 3 years to capture the reputation of the activist. For activists that did not engage in a proxy fight in their early years, activist reputation is coded as a '0'; for activists that engaged in proxy fights, it is measured by the number of proxy fights that they engaged in during their early years.
time_window: initial 3 years of the activist's existence (early campaigns)
