description: The authors verified the activist intentions through SharkRepellent and coded the types of demands the activist puts forward, then evaluated the outcome of each campaign in terms of the settlement the activist reached with the target firm. For total campaign success, they coded how successful the activist is by dividing the number of successful intentions by the total number of intentions stated by the activist. When all intentions are met, campaign success is coded as 100% and when no intentions are met it is coded as 0%, while partial success reflects campaigns where the activist succeeded on some, but not on all of its intentions.

Using the Brav et al. (2008) categorization of activist demands, the authors identified the demand types capital structure, governance, business strategy, and sale of firm. Campaign success by demand type is coded as a '1' when the activist was successful in getting that specific demand met and '0' otherwise. The analysis examines only success for those campaigns with that specific activist demand type, so the size of the sample varies by demand type.
Firm performance is measured as a firm's ROA minus the median firm ROA (excluding the focal firm) in a firm's core industry (2-digit SIC) in the year prior to the activist campaign.
time_window: year prior to the activist campaign

description: A dummy variable which takes on a value of '1' if the campaign involves more than one activist, or a value of '0' if the campaign involves only one activist.

Managers' ambidexterity is assessed by computing the multiplicative interaction between managers' exploration activities and managers' exploitation activities, following prior studies that combine exploration and exploitation measures to assess ambidexterity. The exploration scale measures the extent to which a manager engaged in exploration activities last year and the exploitation scale the extent to which the manager engaged in exploitation activities last year. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses showed that exploration and exploitation are two distinct latent factors of a second order construct, managers' ambidexterity.

Seven items measuring the extent to which a manager engaged in exploration activities last year, developed based on the features by which March characterized exploration and on studies of managers' ambidextrous behavior, and refined through interviews and a test version of the survey. Items are measured on a seven-point scale (1 = to a very small extent to 7 = to a very large extent) and form one summated scale; all items loaded on their appropriate factor at greater than 0.69 and no item cross-loading was greater than 0.18. The scale is reliable with alpha = 0.90.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = to a very small extent to 7 = to a very large extent)

description: Seven items measuring the extent to which a manager engaged in exploitation activities last year, developed based on the features by which March characterized exploitation and on studies of managers' ambidextrous behavior, and refined through interviews and a test version of the survey. Items are measured on a seven-point scale (1 = to a very small extent to 7 = to a very large extent) and form one summated scale; all items loaded on their appropriate factor at greater than 0.69 and no item cross-loading was greater than 0.18. The scale is reliable.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = to a very small extent to 7 = to a very large extent)

description: Four-item scale of Dewar et al. (1980) assessing the extent to which a manager has decision-making authority in the performance of his or her tasks and in his or her ability to set goals. The scale is reliable with alpha = 0.91. The variable was mean centered prior to the creation of the interaction terms.

Four-item scale from Desphande and Zaltman (1982) measuring the extent to which a manager's tasks are defined by rules, procedures, or regulations. The scale is reliable with alpha = 0.89. The variable was mean centered prior to the creation of the interaction terms.

variable_name: participation in cross-functional interfaces by a manager
description: Scale based on Nadler and Tushman (1987) and Gupta and Govindarajan (2000) assessing the extent to which a manager participates in cross-unit and cross-hierarchical integrative mechanisms. Each manager was asked to what extent he or she (1) coordinates work across internal organizational boundaries, (2) works in temporary task forces, and (3) works in permanent teams. The final measure is a weighted average of the three items, where the first item is given a weight of 1, the second item a weight of 2, and the last item a weight of 3. The variable was mean centered prior to the creation of the interaction terms.

variable_name: connectedness of a manager to other organization members
description: Four-item scale based on Jaworski and Kohli (1993) and Jansen et al. (2006) assessing the extent to which a manager is networked or connected to other organization members across hierarchical levels and organizational units in terms of direct personal contacts. The scale is reliable. The variable was mean centered prior to the creation of the interaction terms.

Treatment equals 1 for firms targeted by an activist short seller for performance activism and 0 for propensity-score-matched control firms; post-activism equals 1 for the two years after the activism (matched) year and 0 for the two years prior, enabling difference-in-differences estimation. For the 30% of firms targeted multiple times, only the first activism event was used.
time_window: two years before and two years after the activism year

description: Total number of tactical competitive actions in a year in nine categories, recorded from RavenPack news and press-release coverage. Only the first mention of any specific competitive action was kept, although the same type of action could reoccur over the sample window, and an action was counted only if its relevance score was 100 so that the action was directly launched by the focal firm.

Text-based measure of the CEO's implicit need for achievement obtained by applying the LIWC 2015 achievement dictionary (213 words in total, such as win, success, and better) to the CEO's spoken language in the question-and-answer sessions of quarterly earnings conference calls. Scores were computed as a time-invariant weighted average of the pre-activism transcripts, weighted by the number of words the CEO spoke during the Q&A sessions.

Text-based measure of the CEO's implicit need for power obtained by applying the LIWC 2015 power dictionary (518 words in total, such as control, influence, and superior) to the CEO's spoken language in the question-and-answer sessions of quarterly earnings conference calls. Scores were computed as a time-invariant weighted average of the pre-activism transcripts, weighted by the number of words the CEO spoke during the Q&A sessions.

Text-based measure of the CEO's implicit need for affiliation obtained by applying the LIWC 2015 affiliation dictionary (248 words in total, such as ally, friend, and social) to the CEO's spoken language in the question-and-answer sessions of quarterly earnings conference calls. Scores were computed as a time-invariant weighted average of the pre-activism transcripts, weighted by the number of words the CEO spoke during the Q&A sessions.

Dichotomous variable denoting the presence (one) or absence (zero) of an investment dyad between CVC i and entrepreneurial venture j. It is assessed for the 167 realized investments relative to all investment dyads that could have formed, that is 1,646 ventures by 87 CVC investors. The mean value of the dependent variable is 0.001.

Set to one if both parties (the CVC investor and the entrepreneurial venture) have their primary operations in the same four-digit NAICS code, otherwise zero. Venture industry affiliation comes from Venture Economics Industry Classification (VEIC) codes, which reflect a venture's targeted line of business even at its earliest stages, mapped to NAICS through a two-step procedure: for about 2,000 ventures that went public, VEIC codes were matched to their NAICS codes in Compustat to build an initial concordance, and ventures in the remaining 227 VEIC codes were coded based on common code words in their business, customer, competitor, and product descriptions. Additional databases, including Compustat, Dun & Bradstreet, and Lexis-Nexis, were used in the process.

Built on the Carnegie Mellon Survey of R&D, which reports responses from R&D unit managers regarding the effectiveness of patents and other mechanisms in protecting profits due to inventions in their industry. Following common practice, the authors focus on the efficacy of patents, and consider the intellectual property regime strong if respondents score patents as effective (e.g., pharmaceuticals, biological products, surgical instruments, and electromedical equipment) and weak if respondents score patents to be of limited effectiveness (e.g., telecomm equipment, computer equipment, semiconductors, and software). The difference in patent effectiveness scores is highly statistically significant (Wilcoxon z-stat = 9.4, p < 0.001). The analysis is performed by IPP regime as determined by the venture's industry of operation.

Dependent variable of the founding-rate analysis: the annual count of farm winery foundings in each state. The authors treated the population as the unit of analysis and analyzed an annual time series of the numbers of state-level farm winery foundings. Exposure was set to 1, that is, all states were assumed to have equal exposure. A total of 1,711 farm wineries were founded during the period.

variable_name: brand proliferation among mass production wineries
description: The average number of brands per mass producer winery, an industry-level variable used to capture product differentiation by generalists. The authors argue that the greater the average number of brands available in the market, the more difficult it is for a new brand to establish itself, so brand proliferation should help mass producers achieve a robust identity. All independent variables were lagged by one year.

variable_name: advertising intensity among mass production wineries
description: The average advertising intensity of mass production wineries, an industry-level variable. A generalist winery can achieve a robust identity by increasing advertising spending to create an image of quality, and larger firms' advertising may generate a more favorable sales response because of consumer inertia. All independent variables were lagged by one year.

A firm-specific instantaneous mortality rate that is age-dependent, estimated with an extended log-logistic model. Each organization's life history was broken up into annual spells, with all but the last spell censored on the right, and wineries that survived into 1991 were also treated as right-censored. Wineries were assumed to have died in the first year in which they failed to appear in the directory or in the first year in which they were listed as under new ownership. For organizations that did not survive, the mortality event was assumed to occur at the midpoint of the last annual spell.

The size of each winery, measured as the natural logarithm of its capacity. The covariate is time-varying and was updated at the beginning of each year for each organization. Size is treated as one of the two identity characteristics of the specialist organizational form, and the authors report evidence of nonmonotonic size dependence in the mortality rate.

The extent of vineyard land owned by each farm winery, a time-varying organizational characteristic updated at the beginning of each year. The authors argue that vineyard ownership allows farm wineries to exercise greater control over the quality of wine grapes and to label their wines as estate-bottled.

variable_name: brand proliferation among mass production wineries
description: Average number of brands per mass production winery, entered in the mortality models as an indicator of generalist identity. The authors argue that brand proliferation among mass producers is a strategy for achieving a robust identity that allows them to operate in both the specialist and generalist segments of the industry.

variable_name: advertising intensity among mass production wineries
description: Average advertising intensity of mass production wineries, entered in the mortality models as an indicator of generalist identity. The authors argue that mass producers use higher advertising outlays to create robust identities that allow them to compete effectively in both the generalist and specialist segments of the wine industry.

Dependent variable in the random-effects logit regressions, set to one when a subsidiary's activities in a host country were upgraded in a given year between 1988 and 1994. A case was classified as upgrading only when technologically more advanced products, i.e. products with a higher rank sum score in the technology ladder, were added. The addition of new plants or R&D labs was also counted as upgrading.

Dependent variable in the random-effects logit regressions, set to one when a subsidiary's activities were downgraded or the firm exited a host country in a given year. A case was classified as downgrading only when technologically more advanced products were deleted, and the elimination of a plant or an R&D lab as well as exit from a location were also judged as downgrading.

Share of locally sourced components and materials to total sourcing, employed as a proxy for local capabilities developed in the supply network. Creating such local sourcing capabilities is described as slow and difficult, and local sourcing ratios among Japanese electronics firms in the three countries have varied substantially.
Ratio of locally hired executives to local executives including Japanese expatriates, employed to measure local managerial capabilities.

Total capital per employee, viewed as a proxy measure of local engineering capabilities that are embedded in advanced machinery and skilled workers. The authors base this on arguments about capital-skill and technology-skill complementarities in manufacturing.

Dummy variable noting the adoption of integrated production, treated as an indicator of local engineering capabilities embedded in skilled workers and engineers. The transition from simple assembly to integrated production is argued to require internal development of human and physical capital because manufacturing major components requires technical expertise for precision processing.
Measure for overall local experience computed as model year minus establishment year.
Overseas production divided by total production, multiplied by 100, used as a measure of a firm's global capabilities.
Total number of overseas manufacturing subsidiaries, used as a measure of the extent of a firm's overseas production network and thus of its global capabilities.
R&D divided by sales, multiplied by 100, used as the measure of the technological capabilities of a parent company.
Average annual wage per worker in the manufacturing sector of the host country, expressed in US dollars, used as the measure of the local wage level and of comparative advantage.
Manufacturing value-added per worker in the host country at constant prices in US dollars, used as a proxy variable of local productivity and of the skill level of local workers.

Dummy variables for Korea and Taiwan, with Singapore as the reference category, introduced in the ordered logit regression to control for differences in host country environments, especially in terms of government incentive policies on inward foreign investment.

The number of functional areas to which the members of each patenting team belonged. There were 43 functional areas in TechMNC India, reflecting different technological capabilities, and each team member belonged to only one. Because the lead inventor was also a team member, the diversity measures include the leader's characteristics.

Built from employees' voluntary memberships in TechMNC's worldwide online technical communities. The authors calculated the similarity between the affiliations of every pair of individuals in the R&D center using a cosine index, computed the average of the pairwise similarities for all individuals on each patenting team, and reverse-coded this measure by subtracting it from one. The measure includes the leader's characteristics because the lead inventor was also a team member.

The total number of claims listed on each of the initial patent applications in the data set. Total claims usually include both independent claims, which stand on their own, and dependent claims, which refer back to other claims. The number of claims at application can be established with the release of the Public Pair data set.

The time taken (in years) for each patent that was ultimately granted to move from initial application to approval; the authors added one to this measure and took its inverse. The variable is constructed only for granted patents.
Coded for whether this was the lead inventor's first job out of college (coded as 1) or not (coded as 0).
Coded for whether this was the lead inventor's first patent at TechMNC (coded as 1) or not (coded as 0).

Team diversity was measured with two variables from the firm's internal records: formal team diversity, the number of functional areas to which team members belonged, and informal team diversity, based on the similarity of team members' memberships in the firm's online technical communities.

variable_name: Net present value (NPV) of the larger firm
description: Financial gains/losses to the larger partner firm, computed as the product of the short-term cumulative abnormal return in the three-day event window (-1, +1) around the alliance announcement and the market capitalization of the firm 20 days before the announcement. Daily stock returns were estimated for every firm over a 240-day period prior to the event day using the market model. Total financial gains/losses are used rather than abnormal returns to alleviate the scale problem associated with cumulative abnormal returns.
time_window: three-day event window (-1, +1) around the announcement; market capitalization 20 days before the announcement; 240-day estimation period

variable_name: Net present value (NPV) of the smaller firm
description: Financial gains/losses to the smaller partner firm, computed as the product of the short-term cumulative abnormal return in the three-day event window (-1, +1) around the alliance announcement and the market capitalization of the firm 20 days before the announcement. Daily stock returns were estimated for every firm over a 240-day period prior to the event day using the market model. Total financial gains/losses are used rather than abnormal returns to alleviate the scale problem associated with cumulative abnormal returns.
time_window: three-day event window (-1, +1) around the announcement; market capitalization 20 days before the announcement; 240-day estimation period

description: Number of alliances in which the firm was involved from the beginning of 1993 until and including the focal alliance. The count does not distinguish between different types of alliances or between successful and unsuccessful alliances.
time_window: from the beginning of 1993 through the focal alliance

description: Number of functional activities covered in the alliance. An alliance involving cooperation in a single functional area is coded as one and an alliance involving cooperation in R&D, manufacturing, and marketing is coded as three.

Coded 1 for a scale alliance, in which firms jointly contributed resources to the NPD stage of the value chain, and 0 for a link alliance, in which firms contributed resources to different stages of the value chain. For instance, alliances in which firms jointly developed products were coded as scale alliances and alliances in which one firm contributed all the R&D resources and the other firm contributed all the marketing resources as link alliances.

Cumulative number of alliances entered into by the partner firm including the current alliance. It is constructed as the count of alliances in which the partner was involved from the beginning of 1993 until and including the focal alliance.
time_window: from the beginning of 1993 through the focal alliance

description: Mean value of eight items on Fortune's annual survey of America's most admired companies, rated on an 11-point scale (0 denoting poor and 10 denoting excellent). The measure is obtained for the partner firms during 1993-2004.

Count of the patent citations received by the partner firm in the five years prior to the focal alliance date. Patent data were collected from the United States Patent and Trademark Office database, which provides information on patents filed by information technology and telecommunication firms from the beginning of 1975.
time_window: five years prior to the focal alliance

description: A firm is at risk to diversify into a given target market after it enters its first market in the cardiovascular medical device industry, so the unit of analysis is a firm-target market-year. Over time, as the firm diversifies into a given market, that firm-target market is dropped from the analysis, and a firm is censored if it ceases to exist due to closure or acquisition. The analysis contains 1,591 firm-target market subjects and 77 entry events.

The cumulative count of a firm's internally developed Pre-Market Approvals (PMA), which serves as a consistent proxy of a firm's capabilities to develop new products and deal with FDA regulations. Following the literature on calculating R&D stock, a depreciation rate of 15 percent is used to construct the measure. All explanatory variables are lagged two years.

The relatedness between two markets is defined as a dummy variable that takes the value of one if these two markets belong to the same broad sector and zero if not. The firm-specific relatedness measure is the weighted average of the relatedness between the target market and each of the focal firm's current markets, where the weight is the focal firm's cumulative count of product years in a given market during a given year.

variable_name: Relative demand in the current market(s)
description: The relative demand maturity in the current market as compared to the new market is measured as the difference in growth rate between the new and the current market. The growth rate in the current market(s) is calculated as the weighted average of all markets in which the focal firm currently operates, and growth is a three-year moving average of the yearly growth rate of demand.
time_window: lagged two years; three-year moving average

description: A dummy variable that, for a given individual market in which a firm operates, takes a value of one for the years after the firm adds one more market and zero for the years before such a diversification move occurs. Firm-market combinations in which the firm does not diversify further are not included because no comparison can be made with regard to performance change for the same firm-market before and after the move.

Defined as the number of FDA approvals a given firm obtains in a given individual market in which it operates during a given year. It is an annual flow variable that includes all types of FDA approvals in order to capture overall product performance, and it captures innovation performance.

For acquisition-based diversifications (9 out of 42 events), the event date is the acquisition announcement date. For internal development-based diversifications (33 out of 42 events), the event date is the date on which the firm received its first FDA approval in the newly entered market.

Estimated with the market model, which relates the return of stock i in period t to the market return, using the CRSP value weighted index as the market return and estimating the market model parameters from stock returns from event day -210 to event day -11. Cumulative abnormal returns are examined over the event windows (-1,1), (-2,2) and (-5,5), and a one-tailed test is used to examine the null hypothesis that the cumulative abnormal returns are negative or equal to zero.
time_window: estimation window event day -210 to -11; event windows (-1,1), (-2,2), (-5,5)

description: Manipulated between subjects. We manipulated whether movers acquired specialist or generalist experience: specialist movers worked in a donor group with a specialist work division, and generalist movers worked initially in a donor group with a generalist work division. In the specialist work division condition each group member worked on only one part of the task in an assembly line, whereas in the generalist condition members completed all parts of the task. In the specialist condition, new members occupied the same position in the assembly line as the person being replaced.

Manipulated between subjects. Participants in the specialist group work division condition were instructed to work in an assembly line in which each group member worked on only one part of the task, whereas participants in the generalist group work division condition completed all parts of the task. Recipient groups continued working in their assigned work division after the membership change.

Count of ships made by each group in the two postmove work periods. Products had to meet product specifications, which experimenters assessed based on objective criteria. The two postmove work periods, each four minutes long, were modeled as the within-subjects factor in the repeated-measures ANOVA.

Knowledge transfer occurred when the groups adopted the mover's production routine in either of the postmove work periods. The measure could take the value of zero (no use of mover routine), one (use of mover routine in either postmove work period), or two (use of mover routine in both postmove work periods). Groups were instructed that only one production routine could be used and were not informed that the new member's routine was superior.

Survey question used to assess work division fit experienced by the mover: 'To what extent did you perform different tasks in your first group as you did in your second group?' Participants' answers were reverse coded to capture work division fit. Four mover surveys were excluded from this analysis (one lost and three failing the attention check), reducing the observations from 62 to 58.
time_window: measured after the second postmove work period

description: Measured by the number by which the products increased from the first to the second postmove work period. The average number that products increased by condition can be considered as an indicator of learning, and the pattern in the rate of increase in products across conditions followed the pattern proposed in the hypotheses.
time_window: first to second postmove work period

variable_name: executive came from an A unit(t)
description: Dummy variable identifying whether the mobile executive's source unit at time t was an acquired unit. In each model one source-unit composition dummy is excluded as the comparison category, so the remaining dummies are interpreted relative to the omitted type. All independent variables, unit controls and firm controls are lagged to time t and the dependent variable is observed at time t + 1.
time_window: t (one panel period before the move)

variable_name: executive came from an I unit(t)
description: Dummy variable identifying whether the mobile executive's source unit at time t was an internally developed unit. As with the acquired-unit dummy, this variable is omitted in the models predicting movement to an internally developed unit and is compared against that omitted category in the other models.
time_window: t (one panel period before the move)

variable_name: executive came from a R unit(t)
description: Dummy variable identifying whether the source unit was any form of recombined unit (Models 11-13). In Models 1-5 the recombined category is separated into individual dummies for a source unit that is a combination of acquisitions (A + A), a source unit that is a combination of internally developed units (I + I), and a source unit that is a combination of acquisition and internally developed units (A + I).
time_window: t (one panel period before the move)

description: Dummy dependent variable indicating whether an executive was newly assigned to an acquired unit at time t + 1. The authors test each destination unit separately; this is the dependent variable in Models 1 and 6.
Dummy dependent variable indicating whether an executive was newly assigned to an internally developed unit at time t + 1. This is the dependent variable in Models 2 and 7.

Dummy dependent variable indicating whether an executive was newly assigned to a recombined unit at time t + 1. In Models 3-5 and 8-10 the authors use separate dependent variables for movement to a unit that is a combination of acquisitions (A + A), a combination of internally developed units (I + I), and a combination of acquisition and internally developed units (A + I); Model 13 uses a broad dummy for movement to any recombined unit.

variable_name: total number of executives from all other units(t + 1)
description: Count of the number of executives moving into the unit from all other units, used to capture sheer volume of executives moving into a unit.

variable_name: number of executives from an A unit(t + 1)
description: Count of the executives moving into the unit at time t + 1 from acquired source units, separating the volume of inflow into its structural composition characteristics. The authors also estimate the same relations with ratios, using the percent of executives from an A unit among all the executives who moved into the unit at that time.

variable_name: number of executives from an I unit(t + 1)
description: Count of the executives moving into the unit at time t + 1 from internally developed source units, separating the volume of inflow into its structural composition characteristics. The authors also report the percent of executives from an I unit among all executives moving into the unit at that time.

variable_name: number of executives from an A + A unit(t + 1)
description: Count of the executives moving into the unit from source units that are a combination of acquisitions, together with the count of executives from a source unit that is a combination of acquisition and internally developed units (A + I). The variable for executives from a combination of internally developed units was dropped by STATA from the regressions because there were only two observations of such movement.
Dummy dependent variable coded 1 if the unit was recombined with another unit at time t + 2. It is the dependent variable in Models 14-16.
Dummy dependent variable coded 1 if the unit remains unchanged (versus being recombined or divested/shut) at time t + 2. It is the dependent variable in Models 17-19.

variable_name: executive newly assigned to a unit (move to A, I or recombined unit)
description: A dummy for whether an executive was newly assigned to a particular business unit at time t+1, estimated separately for acquired units, internally developed units and each type of recombined unit.

variable_name: Structural composition of the executive's source unit (came from an A, I or R unit) dummies
description: Structural knowledge is proxied by the executive's experience with the structural composition of the unit he or she came from at time t. Dummy variables identify whether the mobile executive's source unit was acquired (A), internally developed (I) or recombined (R).

variable_name: Indicator variables for core, secondary, and solitary firms
description: Firms were assigned to cognitive strategic groups from managers' categorizations: banks were considered to be in the same strategic group if a majority of respondents who chose to categorize both banks identified them as following the same strategy. Within the 21-bank group, 16 banks that were linked to at least 14 of the other 15 core firms were concluded to be core firms, the five banks linked to between two and eight of the 16 core firms were concluded to be secondary firms, and two banks not linked to any other bank were solitary banks. Three dummy variables indicated core, secondary, and solitary firms, with the indicator for secondary firms excluded from the regression to avoid perfect collinearity.

The bank's income before extraordinary items and adjustments divided by average total assets, calculated as an average value for the years 1995-96. The income figure is before extraordinary items to limit the degree to which accounting manipulations may have entered the calculation. The profitability figures were collected from Sheshunoff publications, which contain data from financial reports that all banks are required to submit to the Federal Regulators. The authors focus on ROA as the primary performance indicator because it is consistently used in banking, is described by Sheshunoff as the best indicator of earnings efficiency, is the most frequently used performance measure in strategic management studies of banking, and controls for differences in capital structure.

Uses the same income value as ROA (income before extraordinary items and adjustments) but divides it by the firm's average total equity, averaged for the years 1995-96. The figures come from Sheshunoff publications, which contain data from financial reports that all banks are required to submit to the Federal Regulators.

The firm's operating profit divided by its average total assets, averaged for the years 1995-96. Operating profit equals the bank's income less gains or losses on held-to-maturity or available-for-sale securities before taxes, extraordinary items, and adjustments. The profitability figures were collected from Sheshunoff publications, which contain data from financial reports that all banks are required to submit to the Federal Regulators.

Ratio between the amount of benzene internalized and the total waste generated. Internalized waste includes amounts internally treated, recycled, or used as fuel; externalized waste includes amounts released to water, injected or released to land, released to air, or transferred to other waste management facilities. The authors present the construction in an equation that is not readable in this payload, and describe its terms in prose: I_i is the amount of benzene waste internalized and E_j is the amount of benzene waste externalized to the environment. Off-site transfer is treated as a form of negative externality.

variable_name: net political contributions to the Republican Party by corporate executives
description: Measures the net political contributions given to the Republican Party by corporate executives in each county for each year. The raw data are obtained from the Center for Responsive Politics' database; individual contributions to different political parties by corporate executives were collected and aggregated by county, and a natural log was taken to correct for skewness. The authors chose this measure over voting patterns because voting patterns were highly correlated with community per-capita income, causing a multicollinearity problem, and because political donations are a more consistent revealed preference.

A composite of five variables: (1) per-capita number of EMOs in a community, (2) per-capita revenues of EMOs in a community, (3) per-capita assets of EMOs in a community, (4) reported activist incidents against a facility, and (5) reported incidents of environment-related civil lawsuits against a facility. The first three variables come from the National Center for Charitable Statistics, and the last two community activism variables were collected from the LexisNexis database of newspaper reports. Principal component analysis was used to capture the common factor underlying all variables.

Count of EPA sanctions targeted at each facility. EPA-initiated sanctions against each sampled facility were gathered for the full 13-year period; the data come from the EPA's electronic record of regulatory actions against violators of environmental law called EDOCKET. The number of EPA actions against each facility in year t-1 was coded to test the lagged effect of the enforcement actions on the facility's environmental behavior in year t.

Estimated total tip fee associated with each facility's benzene waste, constructed by multiplying the total amount of benzene waste transferred by each facility by the regional average tip fee for a given year. The amount of benzene waste transferred by each facility comes from the TRI, and the average tip fee for each year in the region comes from the National Solid Waste Management Association. A logarithmic transformation was applied to the variable to correct for skewness.

variable_name: uncertainty avoidance high vs. low group
description: Hofstede's published country cultural value score for uncertainty avoidance, applied at the societal level rather than the individual level. The sample was dichotomized into high and low groups based on respondents' published country value score. The high UA group (N = 89) had a mean UA score of 77.19, ranging from 53 to 112, and the low UA group (N = 127) had a mean UA score of 43.66, ranging from 29 to 46.
scale: dichotomized high vs. low based on published country value score
level: country score assigned to individual respondents

variable_name: power distance high vs. low group
description: Hofstede's published country cultural value score for power distance, used at the societal level; the sample was divided into high and low groups following Hofstede's criteria.
scale: dichotomized high vs. low based on published country value score
level: country score assigned to individual respondents

description: Hofstede's published country cultural value score for individualism, used at the societal level; the sample was divided into high and low groups following Hofstede's criteria.
scale: dichotomized high vs. low based on published country value score
level: country score assigned to individual respondents

description: Hofstede's published country cultural value score for masculinity, used at the societal level; the sample was divided into high and low groups following Hofstede's criteria.
scale: dichotomized high vs. low based on published country value score
level: country score assigned to individual respondents

description: The seven issue characteristics identified by Jackson and Dutton (1988) as controllability items, numbered 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 in their list. Respondents rated the association of each characteristic separately with threat and with opportunity on a 7-point scale anchored by -3 (discrepant) and +3 (consistent), with a midpoint of 0 (can't tell). Only these seven items were used for the tests of hypotheses.
scale: 7-point scale anchored by -3 (discrepant) and +3 (consistent), midpoint 0 (can't tell)

description: A latent (unobserved) variable in the multi-sample confirmatory factor analysis, predicted from manifest issue-characteristic items rated for their association with threat. In the tests of hypotheses the manifest variables are the seven controllability items. Items qualify as threat-discriminant when the average fit rating is positive (mean > 0.50) for threat and negative (mean > -0.50) for opportunity and the difference between the mean threat and mean opportunity ratings is statistically significant.

A latent (unobserved) variable in the multi-sample confirmatory factor analysis, predicted from manifest issue-characteristic items rated for their association with opportunity. In the tests of hypotheses the manifest variables are the seven controllability items. Items qualify as opportunity-discriminant under the same criteria with the reversal of the fit-rating requirement.

Cumulative abnormal return of the transaction partner's stock around the event date (day 0), the date the IPO firm filed its S-1 with the SEC. Abnormal returns are the actual returns during the event period minus the expected returns estimated with the market-adjusted model, whose parameters are obtained by regressing actual returns on market portfolio returns over 239 daily returns from day -244 to day -6 prior to the event. The event period is a short-horizon window of -5 to +5 days, and the abnormal returns are cumulated over that window.
time_window: event window -5 to +5 days around the S-1 filing date; estimation period -244 to -6 days

description: A dummy variable coding the existence of a long-term contract between the IPO firm and its transaction partner, manually collected from the S-1 documents. The variable is coded as 1 when the IPO firm acknowledged having a long-term contract with a transaction partner, and 0 otherwise. The authors state that a long-term contract signals strong cooperation and collaboration between the IPO firm and the transaction partner.

Built from the business unit composition of the transaction partners: the authors checked the SIC codes of transaction partners, their business units, and the IPO firm. The variable is coded 1 when the three-digit SIC code of the IPO firm was the same as the one from the transaction partner's business lines, and 0 otherwise.

The number of transaction partners on which an IPO firm was dependent, coded from the S-1 disclosures and used as the value for each transaction partner. For example, if an IPO firm was dependent on two different transaction partners, those respective companies were coded with a '2.' The variable was used to predict the size of the CAR for those firms in the sample.

variable_name: IPO firm disclosed dependence in S-1 risk factors
description: A transaction partner was coded as one on which the IPO firm depends when the IPO firm named it in a separate risk factor of its S-1 filing as a key customer or supplier. All such dependencies were identified among the 628 IPO firms.

Adjusted controllable unit profit, computed as (sales minus operating costs) multiplied by a decimal constant specific to this study. Multiplying by the decimal constant masks the organization's true controllable profit numbers but does not affect the shape of the distribution or relationships with the variable because it is a linear transformation. It was calculated on a quarterly basis and followed the predictors by one quarter, that is, predictor and criterion scores were lagged one quarter.
time_window: quarterly, lagged one quarter after the predictors

description: Quarterly voluntary turnover among employees hired within the previous six-month period, divided by the total number of employees hired within the same six months. Precise start and end dates were used to determine whether a person was a new hire and whether he or she left within six months of the start date. Once an employee reached the 180-day tenure point they were removed from the risk pool (the denominator). Only voluntary turnover was counted.

Calculated by subtracting the previous quarter's turnover rate from the subsequent quarter's turnover rate. For example, a current-quarter turnover rate of 25% and a previous-quarter rate of 10% yields a turnover rate change of 15%. The process was repeated across all five quarters, so the index of change is based on differences across the entire range of quarters rather than just two.

The individual service orientation of those who voluntarily left each unit was aggregated per quarter, divided by the number of employees who voluntarily turned over, and multiplied by -1 to give an average quality of turnover score for each unit, for each quarter. Service orientation was measured with the Kenexa Retail Associate Selector, a composite score based on emotional stability, agreeableness, conscientiousness (15 items each), situational judgment (20-item scale), and educational success, with raw scores converted to t scores. Unit-level aggregation was supported by an ICC(2) of .83.

Daily turnover events per unit were fitted to a Poisson distribution within each quarter, generating a rate parameter representing the probability that a specific number of turnover events would happen per day. A goodness-of-fit chi-square test against the rate parameter for each unit's turnover data, for each quarter, produced a statistic used as a measure of how often turnover events deviated from the Poisson distribution. Higher fit statistics represent more days with multiple turnover events outside the expected distribution, that is, less turnover dispersion; the measure was centered and standardized for analysis.

Based on the same service-orientation measure and aggregation procedures as the quality of turnover variable, but calculated for hires rather than leavers: the service orientation of every hired employee was aggregated by unit in each quarter and divided by the number of hires per quarter to give the quarterly average quality of hires. Employees hired and turned over in the same quarter were included in both the replacement hire and turnover calculations.
Created by aggregating the number of hires in each unit, per quarter.

Respondents were classified by the ownership type of the organization in which they worked into three levels: state-owned enterprises, privately owned enterprises, and foreign-controlled business. The sample consisted of 233 SOE managers, 96 POE managers, and 106 FCB managers. Ownership type is the categorical independent variable in the analysis.
scale: three categories: state-owned enterprise, privately owned enterprise, foreign-controlled business

description: Score on the Clan dimension of the Organizational Culture Assessment Instrument (OCAI), which consists of 24 short scenario items asking participants to describe six aspects of culture in their organization, answered on a 9-point Likert-type response scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 9 = strongly agree. Participants' scores for each organizational culture dimension were converted to standardized scores, where the standardized score represents the relative acceptability of an organizational culture dimension for each subject; the standardizing equation itself is not readable in the text provided.
scale: 9-point Likert-type response scale (1 = strongly disagree to 9 = strongly agree), converted to standardized scores

description: Score on the Adhocracy dimension of the Organizational Culture Assessment Instrument (OCAI), which consists of 24 short scenario items asking participants to describe six aspects of culture in their organization, answered on a 9-point Likert-type response scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 9 = strongly agree. Participants' scores for each organizational culture dimension were converted to standardized scores, where the standardized score represents the relative acceptability of an organizational culture dimension for each subject; the standardizing equation itself is not readable in the text provided.
scale: 9-point Likert-type response scale (1 = strongly disagree to 9 = strongly agree), converted to standardized scores

description: Score on the Market dimension of the Organizational Culture Assessment Instrument (OCAI), which consists of 24 short scenario items asking participants to describe six aspects of culture in their organization, answered on a 9-point Likert-type response scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 9 = strongly agree. Participants' scores for each organizational culture dimension were converted to standardized scores, where the standardized score represents the relative acceptability of an organizational culture dimension for each subject; the standardizing equation itself is not readable in the text provided.
scale: 9-point Likert-type response scale (1 = strongly disagree to 9 = strongly agree), converted to standardized scores

description: Score on the Hierarchy dimension of the Organizational Culture Assessment Instrument (OCAI), which consists of 24 short scenario items asking participants to describe six aspects of culture in their organization, answered on a 9-point Likert-type response scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 9 = strongly agree. Participants' scores for each organizational culture dimension were converted to standardized scores, where the standardized score represents the relative acceptability of an organizational culture dimension for each subject; the standardizing equation itself is not readable in the text provided.
scale: 9-point Likert-type response scale (1 = strongly disagree to 9 = strongly agree), converted to standardized scores

description: Indicator equal to 1 if the establishment has any form of performance pay and 0 otherwise, corresponding to the theoretical adoption indicator. The survey allows measurement of four types of performance pay: individual incentive pay such as bonuses, commissions, and piece rates; group or team incentives; firm profit-sharing agreements; and stock-based compensation. The authors use the presence of any form because standard principal-agent analysis characterizes very general state-contingent contracts.

Counts the number of tasks that are carried out by the principal, defined as business owners, or, for multiestablishment firms, corporate headquarters. The survey asks who normally makes decisions on each of 12 operating tasks, with five possible layers: nonmanagerial employees, work supervisors, senior managers, individuals or groups outside the workplace (typically headquarters), and business owners. Higher values indicate more centralization of decision authority.

Counts the number of tasks allocated to managerial employees, one of the three measures of the allocation of decision-making authority at the organizational level. It corresponds to the theoretical number of tasks decided by the managerial layer. Higher values indicate more decision authority held at the managerial employee level.

Counts the number of tasks allocated to nonmanagerial employees, one of the three measures of the allocation of decision-making authority at the organizational level. It corresponds to the theoretical number of tasks decided by the nonmanagerial layer. Higher values indicate more decision authority held by nonmanagerial employees.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the individual task within the establishment is allocated to the principal. The establishment-level task allocation data are disaggregated to the task level, and the measure corresponds to the theoretical task-level indicator for the principal.
Dummy variable equal to 1 if the individual task within the establishment is allocated to a managerial employee, corresponding to the theoretical task-level indicator for the managerial layer.
Dummy variable equal to 1 if the individual task within the establishment is allocated to a nonmanagerial employee, corresponding to the theoretical task-level indicator for the nonmanagerial layer.

Integer value from 1 to 12 assigned to each of the 12 survey tasks, based on the ordering of the average level of the organizational hierarchy to which the task is assigned in the Canadian population of businesses. Greater integer values imply higher average levels of the hierarchy that are assigned the task and greater task complexity. The rank ordering of tasks follows the ordering of average decision layers.

Measure of tax progressivity defined as the marginal income tax rate applicable for the average income level divided by the average income tax rate at the average income level for each province. A value of 1 corresponds to a flat tax system, whereas values below 1 imply that the tax system exhibits progressivity, so higher values imply less progressivity and a higher incentive to adopt performance pay. Annual fluctuations are smoothed by taking the 10-year historical average of provincial tax progressivity, and for firms that operate in multiple provinces the tax progressivity of the province where the firm's headquarters is located is used.
scale: ratio of marginal to average tax rate (1 = flat tax)

description: Squared deviation between the observed task allocation to the principal and the task allocation predicted from the first-stage instrumental variable regression of PrincipalControl on performance pay adoption and the control variables, following the theory-based misalignment measure. The predicted allocation reflects the task allocation predicted by performance pay, and the term is directly proportional to potential misalignment losses. The lowest possible value is zero, i.e. no misalignment of task allocation and performance pay.

Squared deviation between the observed task allocation to nonmanagerial employees and the task allocation predicted from the first-stage instrumental variable regression of NonManagerControl on performance pay adoption and the control variables. The measure maps to the theoretical loss term for the nonmanagerial layer. The lowest possible value is zero, and greater values indicate greater misalignment between task allocation and performance pay.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the organization experiences mortality by the time the WES is administered again, which captures the mortality event in the same year or following year after the survey is conducted. It is based on Statistics Canada's annual follow-up with all survey participants to verify instances where respondents went out of business.
time_window: from one survey wave to the next

description: An additive function of three components of the average transaction between employees and clients: infrequency, duration and specificity. Owners or managers and contact employees were asked how frequently employees deal with the average customer/client, how much time it takes to deal with the needs of the average customer/client, and how specific the work is to each customer. Responses were averaged to the organization, with each owner's or manager's responses weighted equally with the average of the employees' responses.

Responses from employees on a 6-item scale measured performance ambiguity; all items used a 7-point response format ranging from strongly agree to strongly disagree, with some items reverse scored. Employees' evaluations were used as a proxy for clients' evaluations of the level of performance ambiguity present in transactions.

Vertical differentiation was measured as the number of supervisory levels in an organization, and span of control as the number of client-contact employees each manager directly supervised; narrow spans of control represent high vertical differentiation. Information came from organizational charts, when available, and from interviews with the owner or line manager of each organization.

Horizontal differentiation was measured as the number of different departments or functions inside an organization. Structural variables were adapted from the operational definitions suggested by Beyer and Trice (1979), and the information came from organizational charts, when available, and from interviews with the owner or line manager of each organization.

Task interdependence was measured as a categorical variable: owners and line managers were given a graphic representation of forms of task interdependence and, after the diagram was explained, asked to classify the interactions among employees necessary to satisfy clients' demands as pooled, sequential, or reciprocal.

Behavior control was measured following Ouchi (1977) with two 7-point scales asking the extent to which the manager checks to see what employees are doing on the job and how frequently the manager gets involved in helping employees perform their normal work activity. Responses were averaged to the organization.

A dichotomous measure differentiating hourly and salaried pay from pay based at least in part on such outcomes as sales. Following Eisenhardt (1985), any form of sales commission or performance-based compensation was considered evidence of output control.
Formalization was measured using Van de Ven and Ferry's (1980) 4-item scale; the authors report the reliability of the scale. Responses were averaged to the organization.

The degree of employees' personal specialization was used as a proxy for professional control: owners and managers described the level of education and the amount of job-related training needed by client-contact employees on 7-point formats. Responses were averaged to the organization.

Transaction characteristics were measured as two variables from questionnaires: transaction uncertainty, an additive function of infrequency, duration and specificity of transactions, and performance ambiguity, a 6-item employee scale.

Profitability measured by computing the firm's return on assets, calculated as the ratio of net income to total assets in a given year and updated annually for each focal firm. ROA was preferred to alternative measures of profitability such as return on equity and return on sales. The dependent variable is ROA in the year following the explanatory variables, since all explanatory variables and controls were lagged by one year relative to the dependent variable.
time_window: t+1 relative to the explanatory variables

description: Composite measure based on the factor score derived from nine indicators of the cultural, geographical, institutional, and economic national differences between the focal firm and its partners' countries of origin. Principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation produced a single factor score with an eigenvalue of 7.321 and a standardized Cronbach alpha of 0.977; the resultant measure was centered with the mean equal to 0 and standard deviation equal to 1. High values of this variable indicate a high degree of foreignness of partners. A partner's country of origin was defined based on the national location of its corporate headquarters, extracted from Compustat for publicly traded partners and from other sources for privately held partners.

The accumulated number of alliances that firm i formed with foreign partners between 1985 and the year t - 1. The measure counts only alliances with foreign partners, distinguishing such experience from the firm's general partnering experience.

Computed based on a series of dummy indicators that for each foreign partner j in firm i's alliance portfolio received a value of 1 if firm i operated a wholly owned subsidiary in partner j's country of origin during year t and a value of 0 otherwise. The measure was then calculated as the sum of these indicators divided by the total number of foreign partners in firm i's alliance portfolio in year t. High values indicate greater overlap in the locations of the firm's subsidiaries and its partners' countries of origin.

The number of foreign partners in the focal firm's alliance portfolio, included as a control to isolate the contribution of API to firm performance by capturing the firm's tendency to ally with foreign partners.

A dummy variable representing the industry segment in which the Model T was introduced. It takes the value of 1 if a firm was positioned near the Model T at the low end of the market and 0 otherwise; because the price data are not comprehensive, firms competing directly with Ford are identified as those producing a vehicle with horsepower of 25 or less, the cut-off chosen because the Model T's horsepower was 20 or 22 and there is a large, natural break in the distribution of minimum horsepower at 25. The omitted category is the high-end segment of cars with horsepower greater than 50.
time_window: yearly; effects evaluated from 1911 to 1926 (models also estimated from 1909 and 1910)

description: The dependent variable of the exit models: the hazard of a firm leaving the industry (firm mortality), estimated with a Gompertz hazard rate specification, which nonparametric analyses suggest fits better than the Weibull and other specifications. The analysis is conducted at the level of the firm rather than the car model because the theory is about firms.

variable_name: Repositioning out of the low segment
description: The dependent variable of the repositioning models, estimated on the subpopulation of firms that were active in the lowest industry segment between 1906 and 1926 and did not exit the industry. For firms that repositioned from the low segment to some other segment during the period, the authors coded the time at which the repositioning occurred, and used a Gompertz hazard rate model to predict which firms were more or less likely to reposition out of the low segment (but not leave the industry) after the introduction of the Model T.

Firm age in years. It is entered as a control variable in the industry exit models and is the predictor in the repositioning models, where its coefficient estimate is compared between the pre-innovation shock period (Model 6) and the post-innovation shock period (Model 7).

The log of firm size, in number of units sold. It is entered as a control variable in the industry exit models (expected to carry a negative and significant sign) and its coefficient estimate is compared between the pre- and post-innovation shock periods in the repositioning models.

The number of car models produced by the firm in the year in question, meant to capture possible economies of scope that could contribute to survival chances. The authors treat firms producing a larger number of models as having a broader technological base, and therefore expected a (more) positive and significant coefficient on NUMODEL for the post-innovation shock period compared to the pre-innovation shock period.

Coded '1' if the WISE had a social APE code and '0' if it had an industry-specific APE code. APE (Activite Principale de l'Entreprise) codes are assigned by INSEE from the objet social that founders file at incorporation and reflect the set of activities emphasized at the time of founding. The APE codes classified as social were 85.3H (sheltered workshops), 85.3K (other types of social service) and 91.3E (associations); roughly 27% of CNEI members in the sample had a social APE code.

Ratio of total annual sales to the number of employees, including both permanent staff and beneficiaries. To account for productivity differences across sectors, the authors computed standardized economic productivity scores that capture by how many standard deviations the economic productivity of each WISE lies above or below the median score in its sector of activity, and these median-standardized scores are used in all regressions.

The percentage of beneficiaries completing their term at the WISE in a given year who found a regular job with a contract lasting more than six months. This rate, known in the field as the 'positive graduation rate,' is reported yearly by all WISEs to the state.

CEO respondents rated, on 7-point scales, the extent to which aspects of the firm's external environment had changed over the past 5 years. Three dynamism variables were used: the predictability of the market activities of key competitors, the predictability of the tastes and preferences of customers in the principal industry, and the rate of innovation of new operating processes and new products or services in the principal industry. Higher scores indicate more dynamism, and the findings are reported for each variable separately.

CEO respondents rated, on 7-point scales, changes over the past 5 years in aspects of the environment reflecting threats to the firm. The hostility variables cover the predictability of the principal industry's downswings and upswings, the hostility of the market activities of key competitors, and the number of areas in which competitors' market activities affect the firm (pricing, delivery, service, quality, etc.). The findings are reported for each variable separately.

One heterogeneity variable was used in the Canadian sample: the diversity in production methods and marketing tactics needed to cater to different customers, rated by CEOs on a 7-point scale as a change over the past 5 years. Higher scores indicate that diversity increased dramatically.

Five analysis variables were used in the Canadian sample, each rated by CEOs on 7-point scales as changes over the past 5 years. Higher scores indicate more of the attribute, and the findings are reported for each variable separately as correlations with the environmental change variables.

Five innovation variables were used in the Canadian sample, each rated by CEOs on 7-point scales as changes over the past 5 years. Higher scores indicate more innovation, proactiveness or risk taking, and the findings are reported for each variable separately as correlations with the environmental change variables.

The Canadian sample was bifurcated into high and low performance segments. Logarithmic averages of growth in sales (revenues) and growth in R.O.E. were taken for the 5 years of the period plus two subsequent years to capture lagged effects. Firms with a sales growth rate of less than 8 per cent (the average rate of inflation for the period) and an average decrease in R.O.E. were classified as low performers; firms exhibiting real growth in sales and R.O.E. were classified as high performers; firms with conflicting performance or missing data were dropped.
time_window: 5 years of the period plus two subsequent years

description: In the published U.S. data sample, one dynamism variable per environmental category was scored for each period of a firm's history, using the scoring procedure and scales reported by Miller and Friesen (1980). Dynamism is manifested by the amount and unpredictability of change in customer tastes, production or service technologies, and the modes of competition in the firm's principal industries. Variables measured the changes that took place in the environment during the period.

One hostility variable was scored for each period of the published histories. Hostility in the environment is evidenced by price, product, technological and distribution competition, severe regulatory restrictions, shortages of labour or raw materials, and unfavourable demographic trends. The variable measured the change that took place during the period.

One heterogeneity variable was scored for each period of the published histories. Heterogeneity in the environment concerns the differences in competitive tactics, customer tastes, product lines, channels of distribution, etc. across the firm's respective markets, to the extent that these differences require very different marketing, production and administration practices. The variable measured the change that took place during the period.

Six analysis variables were scored for each period of the published histories using the scales reported by Miller and Friesen (1980): futurity, integration, analysis, industry expertise, multiplexity and adaptiveness. Scores were converted to change scores showing the differences in the scores of the variables between periods, and the correlations among these change scores are reported.

Three innovation variables were scored for each period of the published histories: new products, risk taking and proactiveness. Scores were converted to change scores showing the differences in the scores of the variables between periods, and the correlations among these change scores are reported.

Of the 135 periods in the published U.S. sample, 112 yielded reliable performance data but only 88 had unconflicting performance in real growth in sales and R.O.E. (simultaneous increases or decreases). Periods with simultaneous increases were classified as high performers and those with simultaneous decreases as low performers.

The number of hours (with minute precision) spent onsite conducting the focal inspection, recorded on the firm's digital repository and reflecting the time spent exclusively for inspection tasks; lag times such as port congestion, union-mandated breaks, and clearance delays were deducted. Longer inspection times are interpreted as greater stringency and shorter times as a more lenient approach, and effects are estimated within each of the 67 inspection types.

Coded as 1 for all inspections conducted for domestic clients, because all inspectors were domestic individuals, and 0 for foreign client inspections. The authors expected that the match or discrepancy between the inspector's nationality and the client's nationality would determine ingroup versus outgroup in this setting.

Inspectors were classified as having less professionalism when they held only the two nationally accredited inspection credentials the firm required, and as having more professionalism when they voluntarily acquired additional industry credentials beyond the mandatory two, which brought no pecuniary benefits. The number of optional credentials distinguishes inspectors with lower versus higher levels of professionalism, and no inspector moved from the less to the more professionalism category during the study period, making the level time-invariant.
scale: two categories: less professionalism (two credentials) versus more professionalism (more than two credentials)

description: An indicator that takes the value of 1 for all inspections conducted beginning on the day after the maritime accident and 0 otherwise. The accident occurred at roughly the midpoint of the study period.

A firm's stock price at the end of a fiscal year, calculated on a per-share basis (share-deflated) to control for scale effects. It is the dependent variable of the value relevance model, in which the estimated coefficients of the financial information covariates reflect shareholders' reliance on those signals.

The firm's net income before extraordinary items during a fiscal year divided by the number of shares outstanding at the end of the fiscal year, measured on a per-share basis to control for size differences across firms. The authors treat earnings as a 'flow' signal of change over a period that is ordinarily a stronger proxy but more susceptible to errors and manipulations. Shareholders' relative reliance on it is captured by its estimated coefficient in the value relevance regression, including its three-way interactions with the restatement and period dummies.

variable_name: Book value of equity per share
description: Stockholder's equity at the end of a fiscal year divided by the number of shares outstanding at the end of the fiscal year, measured on a per-share basis to control for size differences across firms. The authors treat book value as a cumulative 'stock' signal that is a weaker proxy of recent performance but less susceptible to errors and manipulations. Shareholders' relative reliance on it is captured by its estimated coefficient in the value relevance regression, including its three-way interactions with the restatement and period dummies.

A non-time-varying dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if a firm belongs to a restating firm and 0 if it belongs to a matching firm. It is used in the models that compare restating and nonrestating firms without distinguishing severity.

A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 for downward restatement cases only and 0 for the rest (upward restatement cases and matching firms). It is entered together with a No Restatement dummy (1 for nonrestating firms and 0 otherwise) so that upward restating cases serve as the reference category, allowing the effect of downward restatements to be compared directly with upward restatements while still controlling for matching firms. Downward restatements are treated as the more severe violation because they decrease stakeholders' wealth.

A time-varying dummy that takes the value of 0 if a firm-year observation occurred prior to the incumbent CEO replacement year but after a restatement had occurred, and 1 if the observation occurred after an incumbent CEO replacement following a restatement and up to three years following the restatement announcement, inclusive. For matching firms, the actual incumbent CEO replacement date of the matching firm is used. Only purposeful replacements count: departures due to death, health issues, taking up a CEO position in another firm, interim CEOs, long-term retirement plans, or cases where the CEO stayed on are excluded.
time_window: from the restatement year to three years after the restatement announcement, inclusive

description: In the survey, respondents provided basic information about the parent firms (i.e., their names, countries/regions of origin, and equity ownership stake in the focal joint venture). The authors then counted the total number of partners for the focal joint venture. In the sample the number of parents ranged from two to six.

Respondents rated the degree of specification of each of four joint venture contract dimensions on a five-point scale (1 = not specified, 5 = very high degree of specification). The reliability coefficient was 0.82.
scale: 1 = not specified to 5 = very high degree of specification

description: CEOs rated separately the degree to which nine cooperative situations characterize the relationship among partners, on a four-point scale (1 = not true, 4 = very true). The reliability coefficient was 0.85.

Following Geringer and Hebert (1991), the authors adopted a multidimensional approach to the CEO's satisfaction with joint venture performance. Joint venture CEOs rated their satisfaction regarding fourteen aspects of venture performance on a five-point scale (1 = very low, 5 = very high). The reliability coefficient was 0.89.

The raw count, between zero and six, of treatment processes used in the focal year. A facility can treat its chemical waste using up to three active processes - recycling, energy recovery, and treatment - in addition to disposal, and the active processes can be pursued either on site or off site, giving up to six modes for waste management. Facilities that choose not to manage their toxic waste can dispose of it without further action; 80% of the facilities in the sample actively manage their waste.

The log of cumulative waste emitted for the focal chemical within the facility up until the year t-1. Because learning from experience improves performance, the authors expect the coefficient on ln(cum. experience) to be negative and significant, indicating a year-over-year reduction in waste for more experienced facility-chemical pairs.

The log of the ratio of the pounds of waste generated in a given year to the pounds of waste generated in the previous year. Taking the log of this ratio reduces the effect of extreme changes in the amount of waste generated while still approximating percentage changes for moderate changes (for example, ln(1.1/1.0) equals about 10%). Positive coefficients contribute to an increase in waste production in the focal year, consistent with a decrease in relative performance. The paper's printed equation is unreadable in this source; the definition is taken from the surrounding prose.

variable_name: Facility change in breadth in any chemical
description: A facility-level indicator that parallels the focal-chemical Change in breadth measure: it equals one if any change in the type of waste management processes used occurred for any nonfocal chemical at the facility in that year. It is used to test how waste management actions for a nonfocal chemical affect waste reduction of the focal chemical.

Indicator variable that indicates whether a patent is filed as a utility model patent. It is set to 1 if the firm applies for the utility model patent for a particular technology, and 0 if the firm applies for an invention patent. Each observed SIPO patent is linked through priority right information to its USPTO counterpart covering the same invention.

Indicator variable that equals 1 for all years since the implementation of the major China IPR law change in 2001, and 0 for years prior to the change. The amendment was announced on August 25, 2000 and came into effect on July 1, 2001. The variable is interacted with Chinese firm or Western firm to test the differential impact of the IPR law change.

Indicator variable that captures whether at least one of the patent assignees is a Chinese firm. It denotes whether the firm awarded the patent originates from or is home based in China, and firms from Hong Kong and Macau are excluded from the Chinese firm category. It is used in interaction terms with IPR change in force in the main tests.

Indicator variable that captures whether at least one of the patent assignees is a Western firm. It denotes whether the firm awarded the patent originates from or is home based in a Western country. Western firms include those from the United States, Germany, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, France, Canada, Sweden, Italy, Netherlands, Finland, Denmark, Luxembourg, Liechtenstein, Spain, and Norway.

Captured by the average of the number of patent applications and granted patents (for all firms and organizations) divided by the number of R&D or technical personnel in each provincial-level region in China, from the NERI indices. The authors describe it as a reasonable proxy for the level of IPR protection in each region. A patented technology is considered to be developed in a particular region when 50% or more of the inventors in the patent are based in the region.

An alternative measure of the quality of the IPR legal system, constructed from one of the NERI indices computed from surveys to firms and other corporate entities on the effectiveness of legal enforcement and fairness of legal administrations in each provincial-level region for the protection of firms and their assets. The authors report that de facto IPR quality and de facto legal protection are highly correlated (0.76, p < 0.001).

Defined as the number of years the firm assigned to a particular technology patent has had formal operational facilities in China until the year of observation (i.e., patent application year). The natural log of the number of years plus one is used in the analyses to capture the nonlinear effect associated with operational experience as the marginal learning effect may decrease as experience grows.

The official closing price on the first day of trading minus the offer price, divided by the offer price. The offer price comes from the IPO prospectus and the first day closing price from Datastream.

Dummy variable coded one for firms where 20% or more control rights were held by family members and at least two family members were involved in the firm. Ownership and control chains of all IPO firms were reconstructed from official IPO prospectuses and company websites, and shareholder lists were examined for owners, officers, or directors with the same surname as the company's founder or founding family.

Dummy variable coded one for lone-founder firms, defined as firms where 20% or more control rights were held by the founder and no other person related to the founder was a significant shareholder, director, or officer.
Dummy variable coded one for family firms with a founder family CEO, used together with the later generation family firm dummy to classify family firms by the generation of family leadership.
Dummy variable coded one for family firms with a later generation family CEO.

The ratio of retained shares to the amount of post-IPO shares outstanding. Higher values indicate that family owners keep a larger share of the firm after the IPO and thus expect to enjoy continued control and influence.

The median change from the midpoint of the initial filing range to the final offer price for all IPOs issued in the prior month. The variable captures pre-issue excess demand and distinguishes hot versus cold IPO markets.
