The market share of the lead underwriter in terms of capital raised by the same underwriter in European IPOs during the sample period.

variable_name: Relative R&D intensity (R&D spending per employee relative to industry average)
description: Total R&D dollars spent per employee by each firm relative to its industry average. Relative R&D spending was calculated by subtracting from an individual firm's R&D spending a weighted industry average R&D spending amount, where the weighted average uses the percentage of the firm's total corporate sales in each three-digit SIC industry. R&D spending dollar values and the weighted industry average were converted to 1989 U.S. dollars using the GDP deflator for firms sampled in 1990. R&D spending per employee was used because it is argued to be more stable than R&D spending divided by firm sales.

The number of years since being appointed CEO, drawn from the Business Week Corporate Elite CEO profile for the year the firm was sampled. Firms whose CEO had been in place less than one year were not sampled.
CEO age was measured in years, drawn from the Business Week Corporate Elite CEO profile for the year the firm was sampled.

The number of shares owned by the CEO multiplied by the stock price per share on the last day of the stock market in the year sampled. The closing price was drawn from Standard & Poor's COMPUSTAT and values were converted to 1989 U.S. dollars. A natural logarithm was applied because of a skewed distribution. Stock options were not included in the calculation.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO had career experience in the engineering/R&D function, 0 otherwise. Career experiences were coded by the authors into six categories from each CEO's listed Business Week career path; because the categories are not mutually exclusive, a single dummy was created for each area. For the few CEOs whose listed career paths did not fit the scheme, experience was classified using Dun and Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Managements and Who's Who in Finance and Industry.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO had career experience in the marketing/sales function, 0 otherwise. Career experiences were coded by the authors into six non-mutually-exclusive categories from each CEO's listed Business Week career path, so each dummy is interpreted independently of the others.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO had career experience in the finance/accounting function, 0 otherwise. Career experiences were coded by the authors into six non-mutually-exclusive categories from each CEO's listed Business Week career path.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO had career experience in the legal function, 0 otherwise. Career experiences were coded by the authors into six non-mutually-exclusive categories from each CEO's listed Business Week career path.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO had career experience in the production/operations function, 0 otherwise. Career experiences were coded by the authors into six non-mutually-exclusive categories from each CEO's listed Business Week career path.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO had career experience in the administration function, 0 otherwise. Career experiences were coded by the authors into six non-mutually-exclusive categories from each CEO's listed Business Week career path.
Four-point scale reflecting the highest level of education attained by the CEO: 0 = no college degree, 1 = undergraduate degree, 2 = master's degree or JD, 3 = Ph.D. degree.
The actual number of business or economics college degrees earned by the CEO at any level (undergraduate, master's, or Ph.D.).
Dummy variable coded 1 if the CEO had obtained a JD degree, 0 otherwise.
The number of college degrees earned by the CEO in hard sciences or engineering.

variable_name: number of business degrees, legal degree and number of science/engineering degrees
description: The type of higher education was measured by the number of business or economics degrees, a dummy for holding a JD degree, and the number of science or engineering degrees earned by the CEO.

Each CEO's listed career experiences were coded into six functional categories (finance/accounting, legal, production/operations, administration, marketing/sales, engineering/R&D), each entered as a dummy for whether the CEO had experience in that function.

Binary measure equal to one in the year a firm was targeted by a financial activist, and zero otherwise. Targets were identified from Schedule 13D filings in Audit Analytics, keeping filings by institutional investors (including hedge funds) and excluding those by corporate and individual investors, and retaining only filings whose stated purpose pertained to control, disputes, concerns, or discussion. Firms that made multiple filings in a year are counted once.

Number of Democratic members of Congress with ownership stakes in a firm, counted at the end of each calendar year. Holdings come from politicians' personal financial disclosures collected by the CRP, which reports direct holdings in ranges and calculates the dollar amount of shares owned using the midpoint of a reported asset value range. The count ranges from 0 to 46, with a mean of 1 and a standard deviation of 3, and 28% of firm-years have at least one Democratic politician shareholder. The measure was orthogonalized with the Republican politician shareholder count because the two have a correlation of 0.899.

Number of Democratic politician shareholders whose public prominence score is above the median prominence value among all Democratic politicians. A politician's prominence score sums the number of tweets, retweets, @mentions by other politicians, and quotes by other politicians, using Twitter data from Chamberlain et al. (2021); tweets and retweets capture the politicians' own activity on Twitter and mentions and quotes capture their influence in the political arena. Because the Twitter data begin around 2010, models using this measure rest on fewer observations.

Number of Democratic politician shareholders whose public prominence score is below the median prominence value among all Democratic politicians. Prominence is captured by each Democratic politician's number of tweets, retweets, @mentions by other politicians, and quotes by other politicians from Chamberlain et al. (2021). High- and low-prominence counts were orthogonalized together with the Republican politician shareholder count.

Average of all directors' Democratic partisanship scores on a given board. Director names and occupations were gathered from ISS and each director's political campaign contributions from the CRP, with directors absent from the CRP treated as making no contributions. A director's political orientation is the net donations to the Democratic Party (total donations to the Democratic Party minus total donations to the Republican Party) scaled by the total donations to both parties, ranging between -1 (highly supportive of the Republican Party) and +1 (highly supportive of the Democratic Party), with noncontributors set to zero.

Indicator variable that switches to one if the sample scientist is treated by the return of an American-trained scientist. Treated scientists are those affiliated with the institution the FIC AITRP trainee returns to, publishing at least once in the three years before the trainee graduates with over 75% of those publications recording an affiliation with that African institution, and publishing at least one HIV-related publication in the three years prior. Control scientists are assigned a counterfactual return event, returnee and American training institution. The first year of treatment is used in the main analysis.
time_window: first return event in the scientist's career; annual observations five years before and after

description: Publication rate measures generated from each nonmigrant's publication record: the number of publications each year the scientist is an author on, a version weighting each publication by its source normalized impact per paper (SNIP), the number of publications containing keywords associated with HIV-related research, and the number of first or last authored publications. Outcomes are also converted into dummy variables taking the value of 1 if the outcome occurs in a given year. Where scientists experience more than one returnee in a year, outcomes are measured for each returnee and the maximum value is taken.
time_window: five years before and after the return event

description: Dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if the nonmigrant has a collaborative publication with a scientist from one of the top 25 globally ranked institutions for health and medical training or a FIC AITRP U.S. training institution in the three years prior to the return event (or counterfactual), and 0 otherwise. Those with a connection to a scientist in a top global institution prior to the return event represent 37% of the sample.
time_window: three years prior to the return event

variable_name: Citation of publications authored by the returnee's American training institution
description: Taking the nonmigrant scientist's full list of citations used in their publications, the measure captures the extent to which they cite articles published in the five years prior to the return event authored by the returning trainee, the returning trainee's American institution, as well as any American-based scientist, in each year before and after the return event. Estimates use dummy outcomes in a fixed effects linear probability model.
time_window: annual, before and after the return event; cited articles published in the five years prior to the return event

description: Coauthor names and affiliations are extracted from the nonmigrant's publication record to generate collaboration counts with the returning trainee, with any American-based scientist, and with scientists from the returnee's American training institution. Estimates use dummy outcomes in a fixed effects linear probability model.
time_window: annual, before and after the return event

description: Total number of drug innovations invented by a firm in a given year, where the Chinese SFDA lists the focal firm as the inventor of the drug. Of the 1,516 new drugs approved for sample firms during the period, 861 were classified as imitations of foreign drugs because a drug with the same active ingredient already existed in the United States, leaving 655 innovations introduced by 281 different firms. Lagged by one year.

A firm's annual return on sales, calculated as the ratio of the firm's profit to its product sales that year. For all but one year, data on the value of firms' assets were not available, so annual return on assets could not be computed. For the one year that information on assets was included (2000), RoA was highly correlated with RoS.

The variance in a firm's return on sales, modelled as the range of performance outcomes generated around the mean and estimated simultaneously with the mean equation in the multiplicative heteroskedasticity models.

The total series of scientific and clinical experiments required by the Chinese SFDA for a new drug application. New drug applications are divided into five categories based on how novel a drug is, ranging from an entirely new active compound (type 1), for which 25 series of experiments are required, to an incremental variant of an existing drug (type 5), for which only seven are needed. The log of this measure is used, and for the minority of firms that introduced multiple new drugs in a given year the logged average series of experiments is taken; the measure is lagged by one year.

The duration of the SFDA's approval of the drug, collected as the date the application of the new drug was first submitted to the Chinese SFDA by the firm and the exact date the drug was officially approved for production. The mean approval time was 406 days, and the longest approval time was 2,410 days. For each innovating firm in a given year, the approval years of the new drug are used, lagged by one year; the information is not available for the year 2000.

The yearly change in the percentage of state-owned firms within the pharmaceutical industry of each province, because economic transition in China keeps pace with the rate of privatization of state-owned enterprises. The data cover 30 different Chinese provinces and autonomous regions, which represented distinct submarkets with their own local regulations and administrative bodies.

Two-item measure adapted from Yli-Renko et al. (2001) that reflects the extent to which the major local supplier provides the subsidiary with a network of contacts. Items capture whether the subsidiary has gotten new supplier contacts through this supplier and whether the supplier has 'opened the doors' to other suppliers. Scores are the average of the responses of the two senior managers per subsidiary.
level: subsidiary (relationship dyad with major local supplier)

description: Four-item measure adapted from Tsai and Ghoshal (1998) that considers the level of shared goals in the dyadic relationship. Items cover joint enthusiasm for collective goals, commitment to improvements benefiting the relationship as a whole, sharing the same ambition and vision, and joint responsibility for getting things done. Scores are the average of the two informants' responses.
level: subsidiary (relationship dyad with major local supplier)

description: Four-item measure, consistent with Zaheer et al. (1998), that taps the degree of perceived trust between the subsidiary and its major local supplier. Items cover the supplier's trustworthiness, evenhandedness in negotiations, not profiting at the subsidiary's expense, and the subsidiary's willingness to transact when specifications are vague. Scores are the average of the two informants' responses.
level: subsidiary (relationship dyad with major local supplier)

description: Three-item measure adapted from Cannon and Perreault (1999) describing the extent to which the subsidiary has specific, customized, and detailed contractual agreements with the supplier. Scores are the average of the two informants' responses.
level: subsidiary (relationship dyad with major local supplier)

description: Three-item scale adapted from Dhanaraj et al. (2004) and Tsang (2002) asking to what extent the firm has learned from its relationship with the supplier. The items refer to written knowledge about local technology, about local operating routines and procedures, and about management techniques in the host country. Scores are the average of the two informants' responses.
level: subsidiary (relationship dyad with major local supplier)

description: Three-item scale adapted from Dhanaraj et al. (2004) and Tsang (2002) asking to what extent the firm has learned from its relationship with the supplier. The items refer to local marketing expertise that was difficult to articulate, knowledge about local culture and tastes that were not well documented, and noncodified managerial techniques. Scores are the average of the two informants' responses.
level: subsidiary (relationship dyad with major local supplier)

description: An index consisting of seven indicators that cover two of the most common types of hospital regulatory programs operating at the state level in 1978: rate review and certificate-of-need regulation. The indicators come from Bice and Urban's (1982) report on state regulatory activity, in which states are the units of analysis.

The proportion of all community hospital beds in the state controlled by multihospital systems in 1979, developed from the 1979 American Hospital Association Validation Survey of Multihospital Systems. The authors state that this should provide an approximate measure of prior system-model presence.

A dummy variable, based on items from the 1983 American Hospital Association Validation Survey of Multihospital Systems, reporting whether a hospital was a member of a multihospital system or not, with 1 = member. All dependent variables were measured using 1982 data.

Four dummy variables indicating whether a hospital was a member of a public, government-controlled system; a secular, nonprofit system; a religiously affiliated system; or a for-profit system, constructed from the 1983 American Hospital Association Validation Survey of Multihospital Systems.

variable_name: ratio of administrative employees to total full-time employees
description: The ratio of the number of administrative employees to the total number of full-time employees, taken from the HAES survey. An analysis of skewness revealed a moderate level of skewness, so the natural log of the ratio was used in subsequent analyses. Because total full-time employees is the denominator and correlates highly with beds, hospital size was removed from the regression model for this variable.
The size of the hospital's governing board, measured from the HAES survey as one of three buffering strategies.
The proportion of the board consisting of nonmedical and nonhospital-related individuals, measured from the HAES survey as one of three buffering strategies.

variable_name: proportion of clinical services provided externally
description: The proportion of clinical services that were provided externally by other hospitals or service agencies rather than in-house. The bridging measures came from the 1982 American Hospital Association Annual Survey of Hospitals and the 1982 HAES survey.

variable_name: proportion of nonclinical services provided externally
description: The proportion of nonclinical services provided by external organizations rather than in-house. The bridging measures came from the 1982 American Hospital Association Annual Survey of Hospitals and the 1982 HAES survey.

variable_name: membership in a central planning group
description: A dummy variable for whether or not a hospital is a member of a central planning group for area hospitals, with 1 = yes, taken from the HAES survey.

Coded 1 if a focal vehicle received the APEAL award given by J.D. Power and Associates, and 0 otherwise. The APEAL study examines how gratifying a new vehicle is to own and drive, based on owner evaluations of more than 80 vehicle attributes, from responses gathered yearly from more than 70,000 early purchasers and lessees of new model-year cars and light trucks in the United States. Based on the scores, J.D. Power & Associates acknowledges three top-ranked models in each vehicle segment, naming one as a winner and the other two as nominees, and the authors presume that being recognized by the APEAL awards generates high status for vehicles.

variable_name: product unit sales in a home country
description: The number of units of a focal model sold in the home country in a focal year, with data obtained from Ward's Automotive Yearbook. It is the dependent variable in the models of the impact of outside status on sales performance in home countries.

The suggested retail price of the product model in the United States, measured in thousands of USD for computational efficiency across the three different home countries included in the study. The authors verified the validity of using U.S. price by correlating it with the price in Korea for the same model.
Coded 1 if a vehicle is categorized in a luxury segment by J.D. Power & Associates and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: economic distance between the home country and the United States
description: Calculated as the Euclidean distance between the GDP per capita of the home country and of the United States for each year. The Euclidean method, defined as the geometrically shortest possible distance between two points, is described as the most widely used measure for cross-national distance. The formula block in the text is described as EDij for the distance between the jth home country and the United States in year i, with GDPij the GDP per capita of the jth home country and GDPiu the GDP per capita of the United States; the rendered equation itself is not readable in the text.

Logged number of attorneys hired by company j in a given year from any of the other law firms in the sample, excluding a focal supplier firm i. All of the sample suppliers are treated as competitors because they belong to the same upper echelon of patent law firms that can service the patent prosecution needs of Fortune 500 companies. One was added to the count before taking logs, and the variable is lagged one year.

variable_name: buyer firm attorneys who are alumni of supplier
description: The percentage of patent attorneys employed by buyer firm j in any given year who, in their last job, worked for law firm i. It was coded from the career histories of patent attorneys in the digital USPTO OED roster for 1990-95 plus attorney rosters on microfiche and paper for earlier years, which allowed alumni affiliations to be coded for about 87 percent of the 2,411 attorneys employed by buyer firms over all years in the sample. The variable is lagged one year.

The percentage of patent attorneys who exited company j in a given year (to any destination): the number of patent attorneys exiting the buyer multiplied by 100, divided by the number of patent attorneys employed by the buyer including departing attorneys. New hires were excluded from the denominator in the primary analyses. The variable is lagged one year.

variable_name: geographic proximity in buyer firm hiring from competing suppliers
description: Buyer hiring from proximal competitors of supplier and buyer hiring from distant competitors of supplier are the variables for hiring occurring between company j and the competitors of law firm i. A buyer firm's proximal (or local) region is the Metropolitan Statistical Area in which it is located, and the authors used attorneys' physical addresses (places of employment) from the OED roster to measure their actual moves and to capture their proximity to former colleagues and workplace. A discontinuous measure of geography is preferred because the outsourcing impacts of local moves are theorized to be qualitatively different from nonlocal ones.

variable_name: count of patents outsourced to supplier
description: The count of patents prosecuted by law firm i on behalf of company j in year t, i.e., the amount of patent prosecution work outsourced by a Fortune 500 buyer firm to a given law firm in a given year. The number of patents outsourced to a particular supplier is a good proxy for the business revenue obtained by that supplier, with an average per patent price (including application fees, in 1990s' dollars) of $10,000-$15,000. Because firms in professional services such as patent law have limited capital and material costs, total value added also tends to track with revenue.

Self-reported salary for a nine-month academic appointment, measured in 1988. The authors used the academic-year rather than the calendar-year figure as the dependent variable because the two self-reported salaries were highly correlated (.91) and the nine-month salary is the most standard way of reporting faculty pay.

Average annual percentage raises received during the four years preceding the survey, used as a dependent variable in the first set of regression equations. Only 1984-87 publication counts were used as predictors for this equation, and faculty members who had changed affiliations during the four-year period were excluded.

Count of articles, excluding commentaries, book reviews, and rejoinders, published in the 21 journals rated as top-tier in the authors' survey of department chairpersons. Two counts were made for each person: publications appearing during the four years preceding the survey (1984-87), used to predict average annual raises, and publications over the person's total career, used to predict nine-month salary. No adjustment was made for the number or order of authors.

Count of articles, book chapters, papers in published proceedings, and the like that did not appear in one of the 21 top-tier journals; a fine-grained categorization of these outlets did not affect the interpretation of results. Two counts were made for each person: publications appearing in 1984-87 and publications over the total career.

Count of books published, excluding readers and edited volumes, recorded from the curricula vitae; no subcategories such as textbooks and research volumes were distinguished. Two counts were made for each person: books appearing in 1984-87 and books over the total career.

Number of citations to a person's work obtained from the Social Science Citation Index, an annual publication listing citations to books and articles that have appeared in over 5,000 journals. All citations under a person's name up to the year 1988 were counted, except self-citations.

Average of two self-reported items: the respondent's typical student ratings, indicating students' perceptions of the individual's effectiveness as a teacher, and the administration's assessment of their classroom performance. Each was reported on a scale ranging from 1, 'top quartile of college,' to 4, 'lowest quartile of college'; because the two measures correlated at .86 the authors used an average of the two.
scale: 1 = top quartile of college, 4 = lowest quartile of college

description: Number of permanent changes in school affiliations each respondent had made since obtaining a doctoral degree, obtained from the submitted curricula vitae.
Institutional variable with a value of 1 if the school offered a doctoral degree in management and 0 if it did not.
Institutional dichotomous variable rated 0 if a school was privately funded and 1 if it was publicly funded.

SEP was operationalized as statistically significant above average ROA (relative to other firms in the same industry) over a five-year period, using the iterative Kolmogorov-Smirnov (IKS) approach. Through this procedure performance strata were naturally ordered from high to poor and compressed to three per industry: superior performance firms, a modal stratum, and inferior performance firms. A firm was considered to have PSEP if it presented six consecutive windows (10 years) or more of superior performance. A rolling five-year window created 13 consecutive five-year periods in every industry and 13 distributions of returns for each firm for 17 years of data.

Following Wiggins and Ruefli (2005), exit SEP is equal to 1 when a firm exited the superior stratum and 0 otherwise. It is the dependent variable of the event history analysis of the hazard of exiting the persistent superior performance stratum, estimated with a fully parametric log-normal hazard model.

Independent variable used to examine changes in the rate at which firms exited the SEP stratum over time. It corresponds to the 13 consecutive five-year periods created by the rolling five-year window for the 17 years of data in every industry.

Index created following Chan et al. (2008) from 11 variables chosen to reflect different aspects of economic, political, and social institutional development. The first variable was measured in constant dollars, base year 2000, and obtained from Cepalstat; variables 2 to 10 were measured on a Likert-scale from 0 to 10 from the World Competitiveness Yearbook 1995-2006; civil liberties was measured on a Likert-scale from 1 to 7 from Freedom House. The 11 variables were combined using principal component analysis; the items loaded significantly on one factor that explained around 80 percent of the variance, and its scores were used as the index.

Two dummy variables indicate whether companies are multicountry or MNC subsidiaries. MNC subsidiaries were defined as firms with headquarters outside the region; multicountry firms were defined as those with headquarters in the region and a presence in two or more countries, regardless of the legal form or field of activities. Domestic companies are the comparison category, principally identified using information reported by UNCTAD and the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean.

The binary dependent variable takes the value of 1 if a foreign subsidiary exited during a particular year and 0 otherwise. Exit occurs when a firm no longer exists as a U.S. subsidiary of the same foreign parent. Foreign firms can exit through bankruptcy and liquidation, closure, or divestiture; because the data do not allow the authors to discriminate between these different exit forms, the study focuses on overall exit probabilities.

Dummy variable set to 1 if the product line of a subsidiary differs from its foreign parent's major product areas at the four-digit SIC level, and 0 otherwise. The coding only measures whether the foreign subsidiary is in the major areas of the parent firm, which the authors see as an indication of whether the subsidiary is in the core areas of the parent firm. Twenty-one percent of subsidiaries in the sample diversified into areas that differ from the parent firms' activities.

Two dummy variables compare acquisitions and joint ventures with greenfield investments. The variable Acquisition takes the value of 1 for an acquisition entry and 0 otherwise; the variable Joint venture takes a value of 1 for joint ventures. Among the sample firms, 62 percent entered through acquisitions, 7 percent entered through joint ventures, and the remaining 31 percent entered through greenfield investments.

The variable Experience is 0 if the subsidiary is the first-time investment in the U.S.A. by a foreign parent and 1 otherwise. Thirty percent of the subsidiaries in the sample were the first-time investments in the U.S.A. by their parent firms.

Additional investment measures continued commitment from the parent company in the existing subsidiary. It is measured by the number of investments in addition to the initial investment by the foreign parent in the existing subsidiary over the sample period. The text does not state the data source for this variable.

Two graduate assistants blind to the hypotheses coded each startup's statements in the 'why us', 'the product', and 'the technology' sections displayed on the Angel.co website. Coders rated each vision statement as one (yes) or zero (otherwise) for two items: whether it clearly expresses concern for the well-being of other living creatures and/or for nature and the environment, and whether it paints an ideal future without the implied social problem; a statement was rated social only when the venture's activities appeared central in addressing the issue. The two coders' scores were averaged per item and the resulting averages were summed into a total social vision communication score per statement, and the variable was standardized via z-score transformation.

Dummy manipulation variable in the field experiment: one denotes survey participants exposed to a high social vision communication condition, and zero otherwise. The venture's vision statement was manipulated over the test conditions of the two (low versus high social vision communication) x two (low versus high disruptive vision communication) design while keeping the job description and requirements as similar as possible to the original.

Angel.co reported the number of applications each startup received each week, which the authors assigned as the dependent variable. Because startups with postings on the platform for extended periods tend to yield more applications, the number of applications was averaged over the days each venture had job postings in the timeframe.
Dummy variable where one signals student submission of an email address or uploaded resume, and zero otherwise.

Measured with four items adapted from Jarvenpaa and Staples (2001). Respondents indicated to what extent they agreed with the four items on a five-point Likert scale (one = strongly disagree, five = strongly agree); Cronbach's alpha was 0.69.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: Participants indicated the minimum gross monthly salary in euros that the venture would have to offer for serious consideration in joining the venture. The question was answered using a slider scale ranging from 1,578 euros (the Dutch legal minimum wage at the time of the study) to 10,000 euros.

Vacancies often include equity (e.g., stock options) next to salary and jobseekers tend to evaluate both in a total remuneration package, so the authors combine the two into one remuneration variable. Because salary is in thousand U.S. dollars and equity is denoted in percentages, the variable sums the z-scores of average salary and equity offered across job posts per venture within the timeframe.

KLIPS respondents were asked how useful they think the knowledge or skills they learned from their job would be for other jobs if they moved to another workplace in the same industry and occupation. Responses were measured on a 4-point Likert scale: useful as much as in the current workplace, partly useful, hardly useful, or I did not learn any special knowledge or skills from this job. Respondents who reported that they did not learn any knowledge or skills were excluded, leaving a three-category ordinal variable in which higher values indicate greater perceived firm-specificity.

NLSY79 respondents were first asked whether they were able to perform all of the required job duties when hired; those who could not were asked how they acquired the requisite knowledge and skills, reporting the number of weeks and average hours per week for each learning activity. FSHCPerceived was measured by asking how many of the skills learned doing any of these activities they think would be useful in doing the same kind of work for an employer other than their current employer. The 5-item Likert scale ran from 1 = all or almost all of the skills (low specificity) to 5 = none or almost none of the skills (high specificity).

Organizational tenure is measured as the number of years a respondent was with a firm, calculated by subtracting each person's job start date from the date the survey was administered. The authors took the natural log because the distribution was heavily skewed, particularly in the KLIPS sample.

KLIPS workers were asked whether they participated in vocational/occupational training. Only training meeting three criteria was included: the purpose was to improve job skills, the training was initiated by the employer, and the training took place on-the-job. The measure is the total worker-reported days of training meeting these criteria, logged.

Organizational commitment in the KLIPS is measured with five items adapted from Mowday, Steers, and Porter's (1979) Organizational Commitment Questionnaire. The items are on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree) and were averaged to create a single measure.

Organizational tenure in the NLSY79 is the number of years a respondent was with a firm, calculated by subtracting each person's job start date from the date the survey was administered, and taken as the natural log.

The NLSY79 measure is the sum of the hours of informal training with supervisors, peers, and self-guided learning that the employee required to come up to speed, logged. These sources were selected because they are most likely to involve tacit knowledge and be associated with the development of firm-specific human capital.

The NLSY79 survey does not measure organizational commitment but does report job satisfaction, which the authors use as a proxy. The authors note that while job satisfaction may be empirically indistinguishable from organizational commitment, theoretically the two constructs are distinct, so the proxy should be interpreted with some caution.

Proportion of a VC firm's initial-round investments in portfolio companies at the start-up stage each year. Observations are restricted to a VC firm's initial-round investments in portfolio companies that are also among the first-round investments these portfolio companies received from any VC investors. The databases classify the deal stage into four categories: start-up, growth, expansion, and mature.
scale: proportion bounded between zero and one

description: Calculated as the value of performance minus aspiration for those observations where performance is below aspiration and zero otherwise. Following Baum et al. (2005), the values were multiplied by negative one so that larger values represent increasing shortfalls of actual performance relative to aspiration. Aspiration is the mean ROI of VC firms with the same primary investment industry in the same year, excluding the focal VC firm.
time_window: year t, lagged by one year in the models

description: Equals performance minus aspiration when performance is above or equal to aspiration, and is set to zero otherwise. Higher values indicate better performance. Aspiration is the mean ROI of VC firms with the same primary investment industry in the same year, excluding the focal VC firm; performance is the VC firm's weighted average annual ROI based on the returns from its portfolio companies' IPO exits.
time_window: year t, lagged by one year in the models

description: Structural holes in a VC firm's network, computed as one minus the constraint value in the network matrix; the higher the score, the more structural holes the firm has. The yearly network matrix was constructed using syndicates formed among VC firms in China in the past three years.
time_window: yearly network matrix using syndicates formed in the past three years; lagged by one year in the models

description: Bonacich's (1987) eigenvector centrality of the VC firm in the syndicated network, calculated with the eigenvector centrality command in UCINET based on the yearly network matrix using syndicates formed among VC firms in China in the past three years. It captures affiliation with other high social status actors.
time_window: yearly network matrix using syndicates formed in the past three years; lagged by one year in the models

description: Industry adjusted return on sales, computed as firm ROS minus the industry average ROS at the three-digit SIC code level. Measured three years after the retrenchment event to account for a potential recovery period. Return on assets was not used because it can be directly affected by asset retrenchment.
time_window: three years after the retrenchment event

description: Industry adjusted return on sales, computed as firm ROS minus the industry average ROS at the three-digit SIC code level. Measured three years after the retrenchment event to account for a potential recovery period.
time_window: three years after the retrenchment event

description: Percent reduction in total assets from one year to the next year, consistent with previous studies. A retrenchment event is defined as at least a five percent reduction in assets; the asset-retrenched sample consists of firms that cut total assets by more than 5% over the period 1992-1997.

Percent reduction in total SGA costs from one year to the next year. A retrenchment event is defined as at least a five percent reduction in SGA; the cost-retrenched sample consists of firms that cut SGA costs by more than 5% over the period 1992-1997.

Firm tangible asset intensity divided by industry tangible asset intensity, where tangible asset intensity is the book value of tangible assets divided by total sales. Relative tangible asset intensity is used as a proxy for the Ricardian rent creation focus on the assumption that Ricardian rent creation requires extensive investments in property-based resources.
Industry tangible asset intensity divided by total sample tangible asset intensity. It captures the extent to which an industry's business model is asset dependent and capital intensive.

Firm R&D intensity (R&D expenses divided by total sales) divided by industry R&D intensity. Relative R&D intensity is used as a proxy for the Schumpeterian rent creation focus because it indicates the strategic importance of innovation to the firm relative to its industry rivals.
Industry R&D intensity divided by total sample R&D intensity, described as the extension of the firm-level argument to the industry level.

variable_name: proportion of reviews concerned with stigma
description: For each dispensary, the number of reviews in which users revealed explicit concern about stigma transfer divided by all reviews received by the dispensary in a given year. Reviews expressing concern were identified with the computational approach SenseClusters, which removed stop words, calculated word frequencies and generated a dictionary of words and expressions expressing concern about stigma from the texts of all reviews.

variable_name: exposure to dispensaries with identity names
description: The grade of membership (GoM) of each dispensary was calculated by summing the marijuana-association scores of all words in its name and dividing this sum by the total number of words in the name. The GoMs of all dispensaries located in a given county in a given year were then summed and the sum divided by 100 for scaling. Word scores were obtained from a pairwise-comparison survey on All Our Ideas.

variable_name: exposure to reviews with open attitudes
description: The GoM of each review received by a dispensary was calculated by summing the marijuana-association scores of all words in the review and dividing this sum by the total number of words in the review. The average GoM of all reviews each dispensary received in a given year was then computed, and this measure was aggregated to the county level by averaging the value for all reviews of all dispensaries in a given county in a given year.

Built from the GSS, which asks respondents to place their political views on a seven-point Likert scale ranging from extremely liberal to extremely conservative. The variable is the proportion of respondents in a given county in a given year who self-identified as extremely liberal, liberal, or slightly liberal; on average 32 percent of respondents consider themselves at least slightly liberal. Because there are no data for 2009, 2011 and 2013, linear interpolation was used for those years.
time_window: same year (t), with interpolated values for 2009, 2011 and 2013

description: All name similarity variables were created using a latent semantic analysis through a computational approach developed by Pedersen (2003). Stop words were eliminated, the remaining words represented the meaningful features of names, and the software created feature vectors revealing the presence or absence of a particular word, then identified similar features between each pair of show names. The general name similarity variable measures the number of all shows with a name similar to the focal show's name in a given month-year; for example, in June 1950 Armstrong Circle Theatre shared the feature 'theatre' with eight other shows and had a score of eight.

Measures similarity to names of popular shows, defined as shows that were ranked by the Nielsen Ratings as Top 30 in a given time period. To avoid potential confounding between popularity and high status, cases in which a comparison name belonged to a show that was both popular and high status were excluded.

variable_name: name similarity to high status shows
description: Measures similarity to names of high status shows, defined as shows that had won an Emmy award by a given month-year. To avoid potential confounding between popularity and high status, cases in which a comparison name belonged to a show that was both popular and high status were excluded.

The dependent variable is the show-specific instantaneous rate of withdrawal from prime time plus during the show's first 12 months on the air; a TV show is considered to be withdrawn on the day it was cancelled by the network. Withdrawal rates are assessed using a continuous-time event-history analysis with a piecewise exponential function that breaks the duration scale at one month and older than one month. A split-spell data file breaks observed durations into month-long periods with covariates updated every month-year, and robust standard errors are clustered.

Controls for the past popularity of the genre of a focal show to rule out the concern that the beneficial effect of name similarity exists because shows with similar names are clustered within genres that are more popular with viewers. The variable counts the number of Top 30 series within a focal show's genre in the prior year.

The time that a show has been broadcast during prime time plus. In the piecewise exponential specification the duration scale is broken at one month and older than one month; in the Weibull specification show age is modeled as a continuous variable in months and interacted with the name similarity measures.

A dummy variable for the fall season; industry research on seasonality of the TV series industry separates a year into fall, spring, and summer seasons. Models that test seasonality include season dummies instead of month dummies and interact the fall season dummy with the name similarity variables.

Proportion of blocks in a given census tract where IOF providers offer high quality service. High quality provision is defined as the use of either fiber or fixed wireless technologies, the technologies associated with the highest upload and download speeds in the sample. The measure captures both the quality of service provided by IOFs and their coverage of a given census tract.
Dummy variable indicating whether a cooperative ISP is present in a given census tract or not. It captures whether a community is served by a cooperative at all.
Proportion of census blocks within a given census tract that are served by any cooperative, based on census block level coverage information. It captures the extent of cooperative provision.
A census tract is counted as Rural if it includes an area designated as rural by the US Census. The measure is not time-varying within the sample period.
Log of median household income for a census tract, taken from the census, used to distinguish high-income from low-income communities.

Alternative measure for the income hypothesis. The census defines a county as having persistent poverty if the poverty rate for the county has consistently been above 20% for the prior three decades. The measure takes the value of 1 if a census tract falls within a PPC, and 0 otherwise, and is time invariant.

Ethnic fractionalization index constructed following prior literature as 1 minus the sum of squared population shares across the categories White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, Native American, and Other. Data on population ethnicity is taken from the census.

Percentage of the population in a census tract that has immigrated from outside the United States; the logic is that immigrants will generally have weaker social ties and may have different needs and preferences than other community members. Data on migration rates is taken from the census.

Calculated by first computing the standard deviation of the population density of the census tracts covered by a cooperative, and then classifying cooperatives as either high variety or low variety based on the median value of this variety measure. Population density is used as the focal characteristic to compare across communities because density affects both the costs of internet service provision and the value of externalities generated.
scale: high variety vs low variety (median split)

description: Second measure of cooperative heterogeneity distinguishing between diversified cooperatives, existing cooperatives providing other utilities (mostly electricity), and focused cooperatives, which include both new cooperatives formed to provide internet services and existing cooperatives providing telephone or cable services that are expanding to include internet provision.

Cooperative provision was measured with two dependent variables: a dummy for whether a cooperative ISP is present in a census tract, and the proportion of census blocks in the tract served by any cooperative.

All entries of Japanese firms were coded by assigning a value of 1 to the chosen region and of 0 to all other regions in the choice set of 30 provinces and regions. In case of subsequent entries, the province in which the firm has already entered is omitted from the choice set, as repeat entries in the same province are not examined.

The total number of previous entries by model firms in a region was measured by counting the total number of prior electronics manufacturing establishments of Japanese firms in each region. The count is included in logarithmic form after adding 1, and all time-varying counts are lagged by one year. A square term (all Japanese firms' affiliate count-squared) is included to test for a declining marginal impact.
scale: count, entered in logarithms after adding 1

description: The number of Japanese affiliates in each Chinese region by firms with a similar organizational size as the focal investing firm. Organizational size is measured by total employment of the Japanese parent firm; the size distribution of all investing firms is classified into deciles and each firm that occupies the same or a neighboring size decile is defined as similarly sized.
scale: count, entered in logarithms after adding 1

description: The count of the number of affiliates in a province classified in the same industry segment as the focal affiliate, mostly at the three-digit level and sometimes at the four-digit level of the Japanese standard industry classification, giving 37 industry segments. If the focal affiliate is active in multiple segments, the sum of the prior entries in the province in these multiple segments is taken.
scale: count, entered in logarithms after adding 1

variable_name: same horizontal business group firms' affiliate count
description: The number of existing manufacturing establishments in a Chinese province by Japanese firms that belong to the same horizontal business group as the focal firm. Horizontal group affiliation data classifies Japanese firms as belonging to one of eight horizontal business groups: Mitsubishi, Mitsui, Sumitomo, Fuyo, DKB, Sanwa, Tokai and IBJ.
scale: count, entered in logarithms after adding 1

description: The number of manufacturing establishments in the Chinese province established by high status firms. High status firms were identified as the 10 Japanese firms with the largest number of Asian affiliates in each year of the study, which resulted in the identification of 16 large electronics manufacturers.
scale: count, entered in logarithms after adding 1

description: For each count variable, the paper calculated the average age of the establishments included in that count. Age is measured by the number of years the previously established affiliates had been in operation at the time of entry of the focal affiliate, so that a higher value means less recent model behavior.

variable_name: first versus subsequent entry into China
description: The sample is split into firms' first region entries into China, a decision for which uncertainty levels are highest, and firms' subsequent entries into additional Chinese regions, the latter representing location decision processes where firms have already obtained experience in establishing and operating manufacturing plants in China. Equation (1) is estimated separately for the two groups in a split-sample analysis rather than through an interaction term.
scale: binary group (first entry versus subsequent entry)

description: The dependent variable is coded as 1 if a firm and SMO collaborated in a given year and movement and 0 if they did not. Collaborations were identified from media reports, press releases, and firms' financial filings as cooperative interactions in which organizations work together by committing resources to achieve mutually relevant outcomes, excluding arm's-length transactions such as donations, logo licensing, or employee volunteering.

Measured with the Janis-Fadner (JF) coefficient of imbalance, which assesses the relative proportion of contentious and arm's-length cooperative interactions the SMO had with any sampled firm on a given environmental issue, while accounting for the total volume of interactions. Interactions over the preceding three years are taken into account, and formal collaborations are excluded from the measure. The coefficient ranges from -1, indicating an SMO that relies on contention alone, to 1, indicating a purely cooperative SMO.

Measured using Freeman's (1978) segregation index, in Bojanowski and Corten's (2014) reformulation that allows between-group ties to exceed those expected under random mixing. The index compares the proportion of observed between-group ties with the number expected under random mixing, accounting for the connectedness and size of the underlying network, using the classification of SMOs in each movement as moderate or radical.
scale: negative values = more between-group ties than expected; zero = ties as expected; positive values = fewer between-group ties than expected

description: Calculated as the difference between the focal SMO's JF coefficient and the median JF coefficient of other SMOs in the movement. Specialization in cooperative tactics increases in value the more cooperative the focal SMO's repertoire is in comparison to the movement median, up to a maximum of two.

The sum of all cooperative ties the focal SMO has to any radical SMO in the movement in the preceding year, i.e., when negotiation over collaboration is most likely to occur, scaled by 10 for readability. Ties were captured from manually coded interactions between SMOs reported in news reports, press releases, or other public reports.

The sum of all contentious challenges (e.g., protests, boycotts, lawsuits) a firm received on a given environmental issue from SMOs in the movement in the preceding two years. The two-year window was chosen because collaborations take time to negotiate.

Dyadic geographic distance between a new unit and each incumbent unit. Address information for each hotel in the STR census data was converted into longitude and latitude data through Texas A&M geocoding services, and the shortest line between the two units was computed with the STATA geodist command. For each new unit the authors identified the 15 nearest incumbents, so the distance is computed for each new unit-incumbent pair.

Each incumbent unit is classified as a rival unit, a same-brand (same-market-segment) sister unit, or a different-brand (different-market-segment) sister unit, using information on parent company, chain affiliation, and hotel class (economy, midscale, upper-midscale, upscale, upper-upscale, and luxury) in the STR census data. For the multinomial logit models with the different-brand (different-market-segment) sister unit as the base group, that base group was coded 2, rival units were coded 0, and same-brand (same-market-segment) sister units were coded 1; a parallel model uses the different-market-segment sister unit as the base group.

Number of hotel rooms offered by the new unit, as reported in the STR census data. Because the number of rooms was highly skewed, the variable was log-transformed and centered to compute the interaction term with geographic distance.

The quality of a new unit is coded 1 if its STR class was upscale or above (luxury, upper upscale, and upscale) and zero otherwise (hotels categorized by STR as upper midscale, midscale, and economy). The authors note that units classified as upscale or above are perceived as externality contributors, while lower-quality units are externality beneficiaries.
Each hotel establishment is classified as franchised or company operated using the operation information in the STR census data. Franchised units were coded 0 and company-operated units were coded 1.

Incumbent units were classified by parent company and chain affiliation in the STR census data: a same-brand sister unit shares the chain brand of the new unit, while a different-brand sister unit belongs to the same parent firm under a different chain brand. In the multinomial logit model with the different-brand sister unit as the base group, the different-brand (different-market-segment) sister unit was coded 2 as the base group, rival units were coded 0, and same-brand (same-market-segment) sister units were coded 1.
scale: nominal category (base group coded 2, rival 0, same-brand 1)

description: Incumbent sister units were classified by hotel class in the STR census data, using the six product segments economy, midscale, upper-midscale, upscale, upper-upscale, and luxury. A same-market-segment sister unit belongs to the same hotel class as the new unit, and a different-market-segment sister unit belongs to a different class. For the analysis with the different-market-segment sister unit as the base group, same-market-segment sister units are compared with that base group.
scale: nominal category within the six hotel classes

description: Indicator coded 1 when the acquisition's strategic motive, inferred from managers' public rationales at the time the transaction was announced, is an operating synergy, and 0 when the primary motive is a financial synergy. Motives are categorized from the announcement press release, the conference call transcript, and S-4, 14A, or 14D filings with the SEC, using the process described in Appendix A.
scale: dummy (1 = operating synergy acquisition, 0 = financial synergy acquisition)

description: The complement of the operating synergy indicator: acquisitions whose stated primary motive is a financial synergy rather than an operating synergy. The same public disclosures (press release, conference call transcript, and SEC filings) are used to classify the stated motive at the acquisition announcement.
scale: dummy (0 on the Operating synergy acquisition indicator)

description: Buy-and-hold returns are generated by compounding 24 monthly returns starting in the month following the acquisition announcement. Monthly returns are adjusted for the weighted-average market return, using the CRSP files. The measure captures the extent to which the acquisition is value enhancing or destroying over the 2-year period after the announcement; the authors also report robustness to a 3-year window.
time_window: 24 months (2 years) after the acquisition announcement

description: An assessment of the SBU's output quality made by the management teams of the sample firms, pooled for the years for which data were available.
time_window: pooled for the years for which data were available

description: The SBU's revenue share relative to its three largest competitors, pooled for each firm.
time_window: pooled across the years for which data were available

description: The SBU's cost structure relative to the three leading firms in its industry.

Returns are proxied by the average ratio of cashflow to total investment for the years of the study. Rather than using ROI to proxy returns, this measure is used because it is subject to fewer accounting procedure vagaries.
time_window: average over the years of the study (1970-1986)

description: Year-to-year changes in the business's cashflows relative to total investments are regressed against year-to-year changes in the ratio of cashflows to investments for the market portfolio; the surrogate measure for each firm's systematic variance in returns is the individual regression slope coefficient. A large regression coefficient would tend to indicate that the SBU experiences relatively high levels of systematic variance during the period of the study. Figures reflecting annual changes are employed because estimating systematic variance using actual accounting data tends to result in autocorrelated residuals.

The individual regression residual serves as a proxy for unexplained variance (unsystematic risk), that portion of variance in returns which is not explained by changes in the market portfolio's cashflows-to-investment levels. Large (small) regression residuals would suggest that the SBU is exposed to high (low) levels of unexplained variance.

We measured the number of cross-cutting ties in a given U.S. state as the number of R&D agreements between firms located in the focal state and those in other states. For year t, this variable includes only cross-cutting ties involving incumbent firms, that is, firms founded in or by year t-1. Information on R&D agreements in this industry was obtained from the Recombinant Capital database. The authors did not regard marketing agreements, such as joint promotion campaigns, as cross-cutting ties, and they excluded R&D agreements that targeted markets outside the United States; industry-university linkages and personnel mobility were also not examined.
time_window: year t, counting ties involving firms founded in or by year t-1

description: Organizational density, a proxy for density-dependent legitimation and competition, was measured by the number of firms that operated in a given state. To correct for skewness and mitigate correlations with other control variables, the variable was log-transformed. Information to compute this variable was obtained from LEEM and the Census Business Patterns, both compiled by the U.S. Census Bureau.

The number of new firms was measured by the number of de novo entries into the biotechnology industry in a given state. A de novo entry for year t is defined as an active business entity that hires at least one employee and that did not exist prior to year t. This definition excludes both a new business entity that is a branch of a multiestablishment firm and one that is created by name or location changes. Data on de novo entries were obtained from the Longitudinal Establishment and Enterprise Microdata (LEEM) archive.

Industry capital intensity is defined as the industry capital stock to employment ratio. In the plant-year learning regression it enters interacted with xijt, the plant's cumulative output, so that the coefficient on prior experience, the learning rate, is allowed to vary with industry capital intensity.

Industry R&D intensity is R&D expenditure divided by sales, obtained from Compustat. It enters the plant-year learning regression interacted with prior experience, so that the estimated learning coefficient varies with industry R&D intensity. The authors report that the coefficient on prior experience is significantly higher in industries with greater R&D intensity.

Industry advertising intensity is advertising expenditure divided by sales, obtained from Compustat. It enters the plant-year learning regression interacted with prior experience, so that the estimated learning coefficient varies with industry advertising intensity. High advertising intensity is argued to signal differentiated industries in which firms learn less from competitors.

Industry wages are used as a proxy for complexity because they may reflect the underlying skill requirements of the industry. The variable enters the plant-year learning regression interacted with prior experience. The authors report that the interaction effect of industry wages on prior experience becomes insignificant once industry-year effects are controlled for.

The learning intensity of an industry is the coefficient on prior cumulative output xijt in the logarithmic production function, estimated by ordinary least squares separately for each three-digit SIC industry with more than 50 plants. Prior cumulative output is the sum of real output through the end of the previous period and proxies accumulated operating experience. A higher value of the coefficient implies a greater role for accumulated experience in the production process.

The estimated industry-by-industry learning coefficients from the first-stage plant-level regressions are used as the explanatory variable of interest in the industry-year regressions of firm performance dispersion. Each three-digit SIC industry has a single learning coefficient, treated as an industry characteristic. The variable is the only one in Equation 11 that does not come from Compustat.

Firm profitability is measured as the ratio of operating profits before depreciation to total assets. Firm-year observations in the top and bottom one percent of profitability are eliminated, and the remaining observations are aggregated to the three-digit SIC industry-year level. The baseline measure of heterogeneity is the difference between the 90th and 10th percentiles of firm profitability within an industry during a given year, and this measure is logged in the regressions.

Tobin's q is computed for each firm-year as the ratio of the market value of assets to the book value of assets. Outlying firm-year observations in the top and bottom one percent of q are eliminated, and the data are aggregated to the three-digit SIC industry-year level. Heterogeneity is measured as the difference between the 90th and 10th percentiles of firm q within an industry during a given year, logged in the regressions.

The event date of a firm's public announcement of divestment of a South African subsidiary. For the period January 1, 1984 through December 31, 1990, 116 divestments were identified through a search of the list compiled by the Investor Responsibility Research Center for corporations departing from South Africa; announcements were verified in the Dow Jones News Retrieval and in indexes of the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times and through perusal of annual reports. Firms were excluded if their event dates were not available in these indexes or if they were not publicly traded, and the authors checked that divestments were not forced on management by shareholder resolutions or in response to lawsuits. The final sample consists of 31 firm announcements.

variable_name: excess returns (daily percentage excess rates of return)
description: Observed daily common stock rates of return from the CRSP data base are adjusted for the expected rate of return calculated according to the Capital Asset Pricing Model; subtracting the expected component leaves the excess return attributable to firm-specific activity. The parameters necessary to calculate the expected return are estimated over an estimation window of day -260 to day -11, approximately a year's worth of trading activity. Excess returns are then cross-sectionally averaged across the sample of corporations to obtain a mean excess return for each day in the reporting window, which covers 10 days prior to and 10 days following the announcement.
time_window: 10 days prior to and 10 days following the announcement; estimation window day -260 to day -11

description: Constructed by counting the number of media articles that provide coverage of CSI per firm and per quarter, based on data provided by RepRisk AG. RepRisk screens a broad range of media, stakeholder, and other third-party sources in 15 languages on a daily basis, and trained analysts read and summarize each news item, linking it to the firm being criticized and to the issues to which the criticism pertained. If the same news story appears in multiple sources, the story is taken from the most influential source, and every news story is only entered once unless there is a development in the story, the story reappears in a more influential source, or the same story appears again after 6 weeks.

Financial risk is operationalized by focusing on credit risk, which is observable in the market for credit default swaps (CDS). For each firm and each quarter the authors used the quoted 5-year CDS spread occurring at the end of the quarter, ensuring that the dependent variable was always measured after all articles counted in CSI coverage had been published. As the distribution of CDS spreads has a heavy right-hand tail, the authors took the natural logarithm of CDS spreads, which yielded a normally distributed dependent variable.

RepRisk provides an assessment of the reach of the source for each news item, describing the potential audience that a given media article could reach, based on the reporting medium's circulation and geographic range. Articles are categorized in three levels of reach: high reach includes global news outlets with a strong international presence, medium reach includes print media of national or regional importance with a circulation of at least 150 k, and low reach includes local newspapers with a circulation of less than 150 k. In the main specification the three levels were linearized, assigning the numerical value 1 for the low level, 2 for the medium level, and 3 for the high level, and these numerical values were then averaged over the amount of news per firm-quarter.

The severity of CSI coverage refers to the harshness of the criticism, and the assessment is based exclusively on the text of an article. Every news article is assigned to one of three levels of severity, with assignment based on three equal-weighted subcategories: the extent of negative consequences, the extent of culpability, and the extent of irresponsibility. The three levels were linearized, assigning the numerical value 1 for the low level, 2 for the medium level, and 3 for the high level, and these numerical values were then averaged over the amount of news per firm-quarter.

A factor score combining three measures: a multi-item survey scale that directly measures competitive uncertainty (inter-item reliability α = 0.92), a text-analysis measure based on the percentage of security analyst reports in each year that suggested the focal firm faced at least some competitive uncertainty, and the mean-deviated concentration level of the focal firm's primary industry (inverted so that higher values correspond to medium levels of concentration). All three measures loaded on the same factor with factor loadings above .6, and factor scores were estimated using the regression method.

variable_name: Formation of board-friendship ties to CEOs of competitors
description: Measured as the number of outside directors appointed to the focal board during the subsequent year who were friends with the CEO of a competitor. The survey prompted nominating committee directors to indicate friendships between each outside director on the board and each CEO of competitors, buyer firms, and supplier firms, with directors and firms listed by name. In the main analyses the measure is based on the survey responses of one nominating committee member selected at random.

A board-friendship tie to the CEO of a competitor was coded as broken if an outside director was friends with the CEO at time t−1 and there was turnover of the CEO and/or director during the subsequent 12 months. A broken board-friendship tie between an outside director of the focal firm and the CEO of a competitor firm was coded as reconstituted if a new outside director of the focal firm was friends with the CEO of the competitor at time t+1.

variable_name: Headhunter solicitation of director candidates from a competitor's CEO (tie formation)
description: A dichotomous variable coded '1' if responding directors indicated that the focal firm's headhunter solicited the CEO of a competitor for board candidates on behalf of the focal firm during the current year. It is built from survey questions asking nominating committee members from whom the headhunter solicited candidates for a position on the board during the previous twelve months and approximately when.

variable_name: Headhunter solicitation of director candidates from the CEO of the other firm (tie reconstitution)
description: A dichotomous variable coded '1' if responding directors indicated that the focal firm's headhunter solicited the CEO of the firm to which the tie was broken (Alter) for board candidates on behalf of the focal firm during the year after a board-friendship tie to Alter was broken.
time_window: year after the tie was broken

description: In the primary analyses the focal firm's financial performance is measured as industry-adjusted return on assets (ROA) in year t+1. In separate models the authors used industry-adjusted return on equity (ROE) and Tobin's q, and also estimated net income while controlling for total assets.

Availability captures the degree to which the available cues were known by the team when they made their decision. It is calculated as the number of unique knowledge bits for the issue known within the team divided by the number of knowledge bits available within the simulation for that issue, multiplied by 100. The level of availability is diminished when knowledge embedded in the start-up material goes undetected and/or when the team fails to seek knowledge that was only available from interaction with managers from another division or 'phantom' corporate support staff.

Pervasiveness assesses how widely knowledge is held within the team, that is, to what extent all team members were informed of the available information. The measure, derived from Hollenbeck et al. (1995), is calculated as the sum of the knowledge bits known by all team members divided by the number of team members times the number of knowledge bits available, multiplied by 100. Pervasiveness could be low while availability is high, which would occur if each member held a small, but unique, amount of the overall knowledge.

When the simulation was developed, LGI designers asked a panel of industry and academic experts to rate the quality of each potential alternative, identifying each alternative as good, poor, or indifferent and assigning values ranging from 1 to 10 indicating the extent to which the alternative was 'good' or 'poor,' with 10 representing the best or worst possible score and 0 representing indifference. Summing the number of good and poor points across the alternatives selected for a given decision yields decision quality = (number of good points - number of poor points) / total possible good points, multiplied by 100. For a decision where all good alternatives are selected, quality equals 100, and when poor points exceed good points quality is negative.

The external environments of the LGI SBUs were designed using Duncan's (1972) conceptualization of dynamic vs. static environments, and LGI designers used customers, technology, markets, and competition to differentiate SBU dynamism. Dummy variables were used to denote environments: the dynamic environment of Advanced Products, the moderate environment of Industrial Glass, and, when both the dynamic and moderate environment dummies were zero, the stable environment of Commercial Glass.
CONFLICT is a cumulative count of conflicts since 1816 to t - 1 per dyad, where t = {1988, …, 2000}. The authors state that it was constructed to test Hypothesis 1a.

We coded the aggregated corporate activity as a dummy variable at the dyadic level. This variable has a value of 1 if in a given year, at least one firm-level cross-border deal occurred in a given dyad; otherwise, the value is 0. The panel also includes observations with no corporate deals of any type.
scale: indicator (1 = at least one deal, 0 = none)

description: We used the residuals from a rare-event logistic regression estimated to predict the probability of nation-dyadic conflict as a proxy for the degree to which nation-dyadic conflict is less than predictable. The authors describe the estimated error term as representing the unaccounted for and idiosyncratic nation-dyadic characteristics, an unpredictable portion of the conflict-proneness of the nation-dyad, and use it as a measure of the unpredictability of dyadic conflicts to test for H1b.

To test Hypothesis 2, we constructed a count variable (GENDIST) representing the total number of generations between the first and final conflict between nations i and j in the previous year. We used generations to capture the time frames surrounding the events following Strauss and Howe (1991), who have integrated the impact of global leaders and events into nine distinct cohorts and generations identified with blocks of time, starting with 1822.

To test Hypothesis 3, we used the Global Education Database and constructed a continuous variable, that is, PROFESSIONAL, to represent the combined average percentage of tertiary level social sciences, business and law students in nations i and j in the previous year t - 1. The education data were obtained from the Global Education Database compiled by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics, which reports the percentages of graduates in major fields of study in each country since 1999.

The dependent variable is the hazard of the focal venture being acquired in a given year. M&A Event is denoted as whether or not the venture became the target of an acquisition in each spell. Ventures still operating independently without being acquired at the endpoint of the sample period were treated as right censored, and IPO and becoming 'living dead' (not obtaining additional VC funding for at least 7 years) were treated as competing risks.

variable_name: Number of prior acquisitions within the venture's subfield (log)
description: Measured from M&A announcements in each industry subfield, equal to the number of prior acquisitions targeting the venture's rivals during the past 3 years. Because the variable exhibited positive skewness, the count measure was transformed by taking the log of one plus the number of rivals' acquisitions.
scale: count, log of one plus count

description: The average return on equity of prior acquirers in the venture's subfield, used to operationalize the prominence of prior acquirers in the venture's subfield.
The average total assets of prior acquirers in the venture's subfield, used as an alternative operationalization of the prominence of prior acquirers.

Calculated as the monthly standard deviation of the returns for each biotech industry subfield index composed of publicly traded biotech firms. To capture the returns across subfields, the authors used the concordance table developed by Dushnitsky and Lenox (2005) and mapped the subfields in VentureXpert into SICs. Data on monthly stock prices came from CRSP; in robustness tests the measure was replaced by product market uncertainty.

Calculated based on the venture's and its acquirer's portfolios of patents over the most recent 5 years, and defined as the Euclidean distance between the firms' portfolios of three digit patent classes categorized by the USPTO, weighted by the number of patents in individual patent classes. Before forming the interactions between this variable and the variables related to rivals' M&A activity, the variables were mean centered.

Computed in three steps. First, the direct unit cost of each aircraft k used by a carrier in a market is the total direct cost of aircraft k divided by total output (ASM) produced with that aircraft. Second, the carrier's average direct unit cost in market j is the sum of these direct unit costs weighted by the proportion of instances in which aircraft k was used in market j. Third, the focal carrier's cost efficiency advantage is the average over its rivals in the market of the natural logarithm of the rival's direct unit cost divided by the focal carrier's direct unit cost. A positive value indicates the focal carrier's direct unit costs are lower than a rival's; a negative value indicates a cost disadvantage.

Computed in two steps. First, the focal carrier's horizontal differentiation from each rival in a city pair is one minus the Sohn (2001) cosine metric, a dyadic airport pair overlap metric based on the passengers each carrier transports in each airport pair found in the city pair market; the metric is bounded between zero and one, zero denoting non-overlapping airport pairs and one complete overlap. Second, this value is averaged across all of the carrier's rivals in the city pair market in the quarter.
