A large value (maximum of one) suggests the focal carrier is horizontally differentiated from its rivals.

The natural logarithm of revenues from direct flights divided by the direct cost of direct flights for carrier i in city pair market j in quarter t. The numerator is the carrier's revenues from all airport pairs serviced nonstop in city pair j, computed as itinerary price multiplied by number of passengers at each price, summed over the carrier's serviced routes in that city pair. The denominator is computed by multiplying each aircraft's direct unit cost (total direct cost divided by available-seat-miles produced) with the output generated using that aircraft and the proportion of direct passengers, summed over airport pairs and aircraft in the city pair. Indirect operating costs are excluded because they cannot be allocated to specific passenger traffic.

Three items taken from the scale developed by Zander and Kogut (1995): whether a competitor can easily learn how to manufacture the product by studying the unit's manufacturing employees at work, by taking a tour of the plant, or by examining the machines. Responses were given on a 1 = totally disagree to 7 = totally agree scale. Cronbach's alpha for the scale was 0.86.

Six items built on measures developed by Zander and Kogut (1995), covering the need to combine knowledge about many different technologies, the inability to divide tasks between units because all equipment must be kept in one location or because daily face-to-face communication is needed, the importance of the firm's long experience with the manufacturing technology, the importance of R&D personnel's long experience in the specific R&D unit, and the need for constant contact between workers and engineers. Responses were on a 1 = totally disagree to 7 = totally agree scale. Cronbach's alpha was 0.69.

Based on Lawrence and Lorsch's (1967) definition of integration, integration was measured as the sum of three separate questions about the number of occasions in the last year on which personnel from the unit went to technical meetings organized by the company, visited other R&D units in the company, and received visitors from other R&D units in the company. Each question used a 1 = never, 2 = once, 3 = 2-4 times, 4 = 5-10 times, 5 = more than 10 times scale. Cronbach's alpha was 0.75.
scale: 1 = never, 2 = once, 3 = 2-4 times, 4 = 5-10 times, 5 = more than 10 times

description: The 14-item scale developed by Hedlund (1981) was reduced, following factor analysis, to a 6-item scale with good reliability (alpha = 0.86). Respondents indicated who makes the decisions regarding the R&D budget, the overall direction of the R&D unit's efforts, which new R&D projects to pursue, product design, documentation standards, and the frequency and format of reports for R&D results, where 1 = decided independently by subsidiary, 2 = decided by subsidiary after consultation with HQ, 3 = decided by subsidiary but subject to approval by HQ, 4 = decided by HQ after consultation with subsidiary, 5 = decided by HQ.
scale: 1 = decided independently by subsidiary to 5 = decided by HQ

description: Respondents were asked whether in the last five years the unit had actively transferred locally developed technological know-how to other manufacturing or R&D units in the company, with separate answers for transfers to units in Sweden and to units outside Sweden, each recorded as a number of occasions. The two answers (transfer to Sweden, to other countries) were averaged. Cronbach's alpha was 0.86.

Event history analysis is used to examine how quickly MNC subsidiaries responded to the online campaign with a donation; the dependent variable is the hazard rate of donation, where at any given time each firm in the risk set faces some underlying 'risk' that it will donate. The number of days from May 12, 2008 to when the firm made a donation was measured, in daily spells spanning May 12 to June 30, 2008. Donations were modeled as repeated events, and firms remained in the data set after making a donation because they were still at risk of making another; 295 firms made at least one donation, 53 of them donated more than once, and the other 200 firms did not donate and were treated as right-censored.

The magnitude of firm response was examined through the cash amount of the total donation, which ranged from ¥10,000 (US$1,441) to ¥56,850,000 (US$8,191,643), the average being ¥5,662,657 (US$815,945). The natural logarithm of donation amount was used as the dependent variable. It was estimated with an OLS model for the whole sample, coding no donation as 0, and with a Heckman selection model to correct for potential sample selection bias, with the authors reporting results consistent across the two.

Subsidiaries of MNCs were coded as 1 on the first day they appeared on the 'stingy' list of international iron roosters compiled by online activists, and as 1 thereafter; MNC subsidiaries not on the stingy list were coded as 0. The variable is time varying and was lagged by one day to allow for corporate response. For the analysis of donation amounts, the variable is measured as whether the company ever appeared on the stingy list.

variable_name: number of Internet articles on corporate donation
description: The total number of articles published each day on the nine most widely read news sites related to corporate giving for disaster relief, counted using variations in Chinese for 'corporate donation' and 'Sichuan (or Wenchuan) earthquake' as key terms. The count varied substantially during the campaign and was lagged by one day to allow for firm response.
Coded as 1 if the China subsidiary had a CSR statement (including corporate citizenship and other related material) on its website and 0 otherwise; 57% of firms in the sample had such a statement.

A binary variable indicating whether a firm had received any of eight nationally recognized awards or had been listed in the rankings before 2008, which put them in the 'high-reputation' category; 10% of the firms in the sample are coded as high-reputation firms.

MNC subsidiaries whose home-country origin is the United States were coded as a category under the influence of the institutional logic of discretionary corporate philanthropy, whereas subsidiaries whose home-country origin is not the United States were considered as not under the influence of this institutional logic. In the analysis the country of origin was classified into three categories: the Greater China area (the omitted category), the United States, and European countries, Canada, and other Asian countries; 51% of the firms were in the first category and 10% were headquartered in the second.

The difference between the current year and the time that the firm first entered the industry. For dedicated semiconductor firms, the date of first entry is the firm's incorporation date; for entrants from other industries, the date of entry is the first year that the firm began producing semiconductor devices. Models include both a monotonic and quadratic organizational age term.

Because the biotechnology sample consists of dedicated producers only, the age clock for the firms in this sample always begins at incorporation, and age is the difference between the current year and that date. Models include both a monotonic and quadratic organizational age term.

The instantaneous rate of issuing a patent, estimated with a Cox proportional hazards model in which the hazard is the product of an unspecified baseline rate and a term specifying the influences of covariates. Duration is measured as the time elapsed since the last patent application date or, if the firm has issued no previous patents, the time since the firm was founded; application dates of patents are recorded to the day. The data are left-truncated, not left-censored, so duration for the initial spell of each firm could be measured correctly.

The instantaneous rate of issuing a patent, estimated with a Cox proportional hazards model with an unspecified baseline rate. Duration is the time elapsed since the last patent application date, or the time since the firm was founded if it had no previous patents. For this sample the U.S. patent system was searched for the names of all 237 firms in the sample to compile their patents.

Estimated in a competing-risks event-history model in which the overall patent rate is decomposed into the overall rate of transition times the probability of the destination state, given that the transition has occurred. Self-citing patents are those that include one or more citations to the firm's prior patents, as opposed to non-self-citing patents, which do not build on the firm's earlier patented inventions. Because a firm can only issue a self-citing patent if it already possesses patents, these analyses are restricted to spells occurring after the firm's first patent.

Estimated in a competing-risks event-history model that decomposes the overall patent rate of the dedicated biotechnology firms into self-citing and non-self-citing patents. Self-citing patents include one or more citations to the firm's own prior patents; the analyses are restricted to spells occurring after the firm's first patent.

Constructed by averaging the age of all patent citations (the difference between the current year and the year in which a cited patent was applied for) made in the patents of each firm in each year. The measure is defined for a firm in a year only if the firm had at least one new patent in that year; it is continuous and approximately normally distributed. Estimated with OLS corrected for autocorrelation of the disturbances within firms using a fixed-effects estimator, including firm dummies and annual period effects, and with Lee's (1983) generalization of the Heckman correction for sample selection bias.

The average age of the prior art cited in the patents applied for by a dedicated biotechnology firm in a year, where the age of a citation is the difference between the current year and the year in which the cited patent was applied for. Estimated with fixed-effects OLS including firm dummies and annual period effects, with Lee's (1983) correction for sample selection bias.

Analyzed at the level of the individual patent: each patent is assumed to be at risk of being cited by other firms from the time that it is issued and onward, and citation is treated as a repeatable event. Duration is defined as the time elapsed since the issuance of the patent (if the patent had not been cited) or the time since the last citation, and each time a patent is cited it reenters the risk set with duration reset to zero. Estimated with Cox models using robust variance estimates that adjust for clustering at the firm level; the analyses exclude all citations that a firm makes to its own, previously issued patents.

The rate at which the patents of the dedicated biotechnology firms are cited in subsequently developed inventions, modeled at the patent level as a continuous-time event history with citation treated as a repeatable event and duration reset to zero after each citation. Estimated with Cox models and robust standard errors adjusted for clustering at the firm level, excluding all citations a firm makes to its own previously issued patents.

variable_name: Growth rate (Size in retail sales of electricity to households)
description: The dependent variable is the change in size of each MU. Size is measured using the retail sales of electricity to households in megawatt hours; annual revenues were not feasible because electricity prices were volatile and the number of employees was unsuitable because MUs are involved in other business areas. Growth rates are modelled in the log-linear transformation of Gibrat's growth model, which includes lagged size as a predictor.

Measured as the amount of resources released by near-center producers, represented by the aggregated amount of sales to tariff customers freed by the failed regional utilities in a given year. Tariff customers include household customers and small commercial customers. The unit of measurement used in the construction of this measure is 10 million MWh. All independent variables were lagged by one year.

Measured as the difference in voter turnout between county and national-level elections in each county. Because electoral institutions and party systems are similar across German counties, variation in this difference is taken to capture variation in voters' attachment to their local community. Because elections are held every four or five years, missing years were filled through linear interpolation. All independent variables were lagged by one year.

Measured as the proportion of people in a county voting for the German Green Party in the Bundestag (the lower house of the federal parliament) election. Bundestag elections are held every four years, and linear interpolation was used for the missing years. All independent variables were lagged by one year.

A dummy variable coded 1 if the focal MU engages in any cooperative activity that signals a commitment to localness and/or greenness, and 0 otherwise. Such activities include collective marketing and sales and the building of shared generation capacities. Collective purchasing of electricity was coded 0 because it reflects the willingness to increase collective bargaining power rather than a genuine commitment to the MU identity. All independent variables were lagged by one year.

CEO narcissism was measured with the Narcissistic Personality Inventory through third-party ratings of video samples of CEOs. Videos of CEOs in 2007 were acquired from public internet sources and edited to omit identifying information that could bias evaluations; video samples of 2.5 minutes were used based on a pilot study of acceptable video lengths. Three expert raters, blind to the study hypotheses, rated each focal CEO on the narcissism items using a seven-point Likert scale; the scale demonstrated a coefficient alpha reliability of 0.95 and the raters showed significant agreement, ICC (1, 3) = 0.54, p < 0.001, rwg = 0.85. Narcissism was measured as invariant in line with previous research that has viewed narcissism as a stable disposition.

CSR was measured with KLD ratings, which are based on ratings by independent analysts of a variety of categories of CSR characteristics of firms including community, diversity, employee relations, environment, and human rights. The measure is an aggregate net score at t + 1 of the various dimensions reported in the data, following the most commonly utilized approach in the literature.

Media praise for CEOs following company philanthropic actions was assessed by a content analysis of key publications that cover general and business news through targeted searches in the Factiva database. Articles including the company name for the firm/year were isolated for philanthropic events using the predefined Philanthropy reputation driver of the Factiva Expert Search module. Two independent raters coded the number of articles that positively mention the CEO associated with philanthropic events for each firm year observation, with high interrater agreement (ICC1 = 0.78); disagreements were resolved by an additional independent content analysis. To account for the possibility that certain industries attract more media attention the variable was standardized by industry (two-digit SIC code).
time_window: firm-year; lagged value at t - 1 used as predictor

description: Performance is examined using Return on Assets (ROA), a common measure of firm performance, calculated as net income divided by assets at t.

Analyst i's MPC on firm k is a function of the focal firm's relatedness with other firms m, where relatedness is the number of overlapping analysts between the focal firm and another firm and binary indicators equal to one if the focal analyst covers firm k (m) and zero otherwise. In terms of the two-mode analyst–firm network, this refers to the number of unique 3-step paths separating each analyst from each firm. The measure is updated annually to reflect coverage changes, and is expressed as the analyst's percentile ranking in the distribution of MPC for all analysts covering the focal firm, ranging from zero, when the other firms in the analyst's portfolio had the least relatedness to the focal firm, to one, when they had the greatest relatedness among all analysts.

For the natural experiment, the departed analyst's pre-9/11 MPC, as previously calculated, on each of the firms they covered. It captures the departed analyst's knowledge advantages in the months preceding 9/11 as well as surviving rivals' reliance on this knowledge to guide their forecasts. For treatment firms, Victim's MPC has a mean of 0.13 and a standard deviation of 0.17, and it is zero for firms in the control group.

Accuracy is negative forecasting error for analyst i covering stock k in year t, following Hong and Kubik (2003). The forecast used is the last forecast issued by analyst i for firm k in year t before the firm published its actual earnings; the absolute difference between that forecast and actual earnings is scaled by the firm's lagged stock price and multiplied by 10,000 to express the forecast error in terms of basis points. The authors report results using the log of Accuracy.

Information leadership is calculated as the ratio of the sum of the number of days between each forecast estimate and the dates of the preceding two estimates (X1 and X2) to the sum of the number of days between each estimate and the following two estimates (Y1 and Y2), where n refers to each forecast issued by analyst i on firm k in each year t. Analysts' mechanical year-end forecast revisions following quarterly earnings releases were eliminated by dropping revisions occurring within 5 days of the quarterly earnings report. The authors report results using the log of information leadership.

The difference between a focal analyst's annual forecast on a focal firm and the consensus estimate for all analysts covering that firm, where the consensus estimate is the outstanding consensus estimate of all analysts covering firm k at the time firm k reports its EPS numbers for year t. To reduce skewness, the authors report results using the log of Differentiation.

A measure of firm-level outcome uncertainty used in prior research, entered as a control and as the moderator of the MPC–accuracy relationship. Dispersion reflects the inherent difficulty of deciphering a focal firm's prospects.

The accuracy of EPS forecasts, calculated as in the main analysis, made by 188 surviving analysts on the earnings of 453 firms (173 affected firms and 280 control firms) with a fiscal year ending on December 31, 2001. The pre-9/11 period started in January 2001, when the first annual forecasts were made, and ended September 10, 2001; the post-9/11 period started on September 17, 2001, when the markets re-opened, and ended when the last firms released their actual earnings in February 2002.

Three scales were used to assess how visible each type of attack might be to rivals. Respondents rated on a 5-point scale (1 = very low, 5 = very high) the amount of industry publicity associated with each move and the likelihood that this type of attack would be publicly announced by top management; as a third, objective measure the number of lines of print in Aviation Daily associated with each move was counted and converted to a 5-point scale. The three scales were standardized and then averaged, with a Cronbach alpha of 0.62.
scale: 5-point scales (1 = very low, 5 = very high), standardized and averaged
level: competitive action (action type for the questionnaire scales)

description: Response difficulty was assessed using five scales: the estimated financial expense of making a move, the degree of disruption of staff and systems, the amount of relocation of staff or equipment required, the need for complex coordination among different functional departments, and the overall perceived difficulty of making the move. The first four scales were completed by questionnaire respondents on the 5-point scale and were equal for all actions within a type; all the moves were also assessed along a 5-point scale by both authors, whose scores correlated at r = 0.85 (p = 0.001). The Cronbach alpha for the five-scale response difficulty measure was 0.95.

Airlines affected by each action were first identified as those which provided service to at least one of the sample airports affected by the action; these airports were the 37 major hubs identified by the Department of Transportation. The centrality of an action was taken as the proportion of annual passengers affected, and an aggregate index for each action was obtained by averaging the centrality measures for each affected airline. Centrality varies among actions even for the same airline in the same year when different airports are affected, and among competitors with a different mix of business.

For testing Hypotheses 1 to 4, which are couched at the level of the action/response dyad, the response variable is simply the number of responses evoked by an action. It is defined as the total number of competitors who actually respond to an action, and was determined by counting the number of airlines that responded to an action as reported in Aviation Daily. The total sample consisted of 780 actions and 222 responses in kind.

Because Hypothesis 5 concerns the impact of retaliation on organizational performance, the analysis is at the firm level and financial performance is reported by company and by year. To obtain a matching response ratio, all the competitive responses directed towards the actions of a given firm in a given year were summed and expressed as a proportion of the total number of actions made by that firm in that year.
scale: proportion of the firm's actions responded to

description: Financial performance was assessed using total operating revenue per revenue passenger mile (RPM), operating profit per RPM and profit margin, complemented by Standard and Poor's published stock ratings for each airline for each year; the stock ratings could be obtained only for 112 of the 168 observations. These performance variables were used in lieu of return on assets. A factor analysis of the four performance variables produced a one-factor solution accounting for 57.2 percent of the variance with an eigenvalue of 2.29; the loadings were 0.67 for revenue per RPM, 0.94 for operating profit per RPM, 0.76 for profit margin and 0.61 for the S&P stock rating.

Index of concentration (1 minus the Simpson's index of diversity), calculated as the sum of the squared proportions of the wines in a winery's portfolio made in each style in a vintage. It ranges from 0 to 0.5, where 0.5 means the winery produced wines equally in each of the two styles (maximally spanning) and 0 means it released wines in only one style (not spanning at all). The two styles are botti only and barrique only, distinguished by the aging vessel; the coding of vinification methods culled from the guide was confirmed with a telephone survey of producers.

Rating assigned by the Gambero Rosso guide after blind tastings in which tasters do not know the price category of the wine or the identity of the winery, with different labels sampled uniformly by type and vintage and decisions made collegially by groups of tasters. The guide assigns one black glass, two black glasses, two red glasses, and three red glasses (red ranks higher than black); two red glasses were treated as a value of 3 and three red glasses as a value of 4.

Rating assigned by the Veronelli guide on a four-point scale expressed in stars, ranging from one ('good wine') to three ('excellent wine'), plus an award of distinction ('super three stars') to wines considered outstanding, coded as four stars. The tastings are conducted by Luigi Veronelli and his three collaborators, who know the producer's identity and other information including wine type, the area of production, and the vintage.

CEO power over the board is proxied by a vector of eight variables rather than one variable, reflecting the view that managerial power is multidimensional and not easily observable. The proxies are: number of directors on the board; proportion of outside directors on the board; presence of an outside shareholder who owns at least 10 percent of the firm's shares outstanding; whether the CEO is the chairman of the board; proportion of the firm's shares held by outside directors; average tenure of the CEO divided by average tenure of outside directors; whether the CEO served on the board before taking the CEO office (internality); and the proportion of firm shares held by the CEO, plus its squared value to control for possible nonlinearity. CEO power is expected to be positively related to board size, duality and relative tenure, and negatively related to outside directors, blockholder presence, outside director ownership and CEO internality.

Pension increment represents a present value equivalent of annual SERP compensation and is calculated as the actuarially adjusted difference between the present value of the SERP in year t and the present value of the SERP in year t - 1. It is computed in three steps: the value of the annual pension already accumulated by the CEO according to the terms of his or her SERP is estimated; death probability tables are applied to calculate the present value of accumulated SERP benefits; and the present value of SERP benefits in year t - 1, adjusted for a one-year discount rate, is subtracted from the present value in year t. Where firms voluntarily reported accumulated pension values, estimated rather than reported values are used to keep actuarial assumptions homogeneous.
Annual cash compensation, used as one of three alternative dependent variables in the compensation regressions; it includes base salary and annual bonus.

The value of annual stock option awards, computed using the model proposed by Smith and Zimmerman (1976) for employee stock options: Maximum (0, Stock price at grant date - Present value [Exercise price + Future value {Dividend stream compounded at the risk-free rate until option expiration} ]).
Dichotomous variable equal to one if t is a year in which CEO pensionable earnings are determined (determination year), and zero otherwise.
Dichotomous variable equal to one if CEO pensionable earnings are based on the performance bonus, that is, when SERP benefits are contingent on firm performance, and zero otherwise.

Firm total R&D expenditures deflated by firm revenue and relative to the industry average; industries are defined by Standard Industrial Classification codes at the two-digit level. The relative measure controls for the variation in R&D across industries and firms of different sizes.

Indicator variables for each founder-investor gender combination, crossing firm founder gender (female-founded versus male-founded) with the gender composition of the first round investors (female VC partners only, male VC partners only, or both male and female VC partners). A firm is identified as being backed by a female (or male) VC based on the gender of the investment partner directly involved in the deal.
Indicator identifying firms with at least one female founder as 'female-founded', following prior work; firms with only male founders form the comparison group.

Dichotomous indicator of whether a venture raised a subsequent round of financing on a given day, conditional upon not having already received it. A venture enters the risk set on the date it receives its first funding round and exits the risk set at the time of the second round or at the time of right-censoring.
time_window: from first funding round until second round or right-censoring

description: Manipulated through the name and picture of the venture capital investor from the fictional VC firm 'Pegasus Ventures Fund' said to have already invested in the business (John versus Katherine Clark). The slides and narration script are identical across conditions except for the investor's name and picture; the photographs were pretested for similarity in perceptions of age, attractiveness, and professionalism.

Manipulated through the name of the founder and CEO presenting the pitch (David versus Laura Anderson). The slides and narration script are identical across conditions with the exception of the founder's name; the name pairs had been tested in prior research.

Composite measure of the evaluated quality of the pitch, adapted from prior research as well as scoring criteria from a business school pitch competition. Ratings were given on seven-point Likert scales and aggregated across the set of items to obtain an average measure (Cronbach's alpha of 0.82). The specific items are laid out in the Online Appendix.

Composite measure of the perceived competence of the entrepreneur, adapted from prior research as well as scoring criteria from a business school pitch competition. Ratings were given on seven-point Likert scales and aggregated across the set of items to obtain an average measure (Cronbach's alpha of 0.83). The specific items are laid out in the Online Appendix.

A set of nine Likert-type items with everyday statements presented as proxies for how trusting managers would describe trusted local staff. The statements concern not being let down, sharing objectives, confidently delegating, seldom conflicting, openness, friendship, and good atmosphere. The nine items give a reliable scale with a single dominant factor and a Cronbach alpha of 0.89. The assumption is that a manager who agrees strongly with such descriptions of local staff has positive expectations of their intentions and behavior and would accept vulnerability towards them.
The Hong Kong managers' individual perceptions of the effectiveness of the Chinese legal system for their business, measured with four Likert items. The scale has a Cronbach alpha of 0.86.
Three Likert items presented to the respondents assessing how arbitrary they find the behavior of Chinese officials. The scale has a Cronbach alpha of 0.77.
The Hong Kong managers were asked how satisfied they were with the availability of training, managers, and employees in China. These are three Likert items with a Cronbach alpha of 0.81.
Three Likert items concerning efforts in getting to know Chinese managers personally, shaping positive attitudes, and careful selection. The scale has a Cronbach's alpha of 0.81.

A single item ranging from 'all recruited in mainland China' to 'all recruited from Hong Kong/outside mainland China', presented to find out to what extent the managers for Chinese operations are recruited locally. The text does not state which end of the range is coded high.
scale: single item ranging from 'all recruited in mainland China' to 'all recruited from Hong Kong/outside mainland China'

description: Hong Kong managers were asked to indicate their agreement or disagreement with having succeeded in transferring practices in six areas: accounting, marketing, purchasing, operations, HRM, and technical standards. The scale has a Cronbach's alpha of 0.84.

Respondents were asked to provide a rating on a 1-7 basis for three items concerning satisfaction with activities in China. The items making up the scale were based on the discussion in Venkatraman and Ramanujam (1986). The Cronbach alpha for the scale was 0.86.

variable_name: Growth of sales and profits in Chinese operations
description: Two more objective measures that most companies were willing to provide: the growth of sales and profits in their Chinese operations over the previous two years. These were reported separately, with N = 467 for sales growth and N = 512 for profit growth.

Dichotomous variable indicating the year of retirement and the year before the retirement year. The authors assigned 1's to the retirement year and the year before retirement and 0's to other years, because a CEO's focus on short-term firm performance is expected to be most pronounced in the CEO's last two years with the firm.

variable_name: Firm commitment to corporate social responsibility
description: Following the common practice in the literature, firm commitment to CSR was defined as the sum of all strength items minus the sum of all concern items in the KLD Social Ratings. The KLD ratings have been used by previous studies as a measure of firm commitment or managerial attention to CSR.
time_window: t+1 (one-year lag relative to the predictors)

description: CEO age was measured as of the current year.

A dichotomous variable denoting whether the retired CEO served as a board member of the same firm after having stepped down from the CEO position. Following Brickley et al. (1999) and Evans et al. (2010), a CEO was considered retained as a board member if he or she remained with the firm two years after retirement. Examination of 10-K's and other corporate annual reports showed that the Execucomp database sometimes erroneously reported that a CEO had remained as a director, an error usually corrected after two years, so measuring retention two years after retirement minimizes the impact of possible measurement errors.
A firm's annual return on sales, measured as the ratio of firm profits to product sales in the same year. It is the dependent variable in the firm-level regressions.

For every submarket (province) in a given year, the percentage of all TCM producers within that submarket that began introducing hybrid TCM in Western dosage form by the end of the previous year. Firms were assigned to one of 29 submarkets based on geographic information recorded in the yearbooks; no firm changed location during the study period. The squared term of this measure was also entered in the regressions to capture second-order effects.
time_window: by the end of the previous year

description: The yearly percentage of a province's rural population, mean-centered before entry into the regressions. A rural population is defined in the China Population Statistics Yearbook as all individuals whose livelihood depends on agriculture, hunting, fishing, or forestry.

A binary variable indicating whether a firm owned any exclusive classic TCM formula in a given year, that is, a unique and often newly uncovered ancient formula for which the SFDA granted 3 to 8 years of market exclusivity. It is identified from the SFDA's new drug registration database.
Firm output scale, measured using the logarithm of a firm's annual sales. It is regressed on the linear and squared terms of competitors' new technology adoption and all other control variables.

The firm's published score in the Fortune 'Most Admired Companies' survey in a given year. Fortune sends thousands of securities analysts, executives, and directors the survey each year and asks them to rate the 10 largest companies in their industry on eight attributes using a 0 to 10 scale; the eight item scores are averaged to generate the published overall reputation score. Because ratings reflect surveys completed near the end of the previous calendar year, the independent and control variables are measured in the year prior to the one in which the ratings are published.
scale: 0 to 10 scale per attribute, averaged across eight attributes
time_window: survey year, published in February or March; predictors lagged one year

description: A count of the articles in the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal that met the search parameters during the focal year, which captured only articles in which the CEO was mentioned at least three times in the body text. For the propensity score analysis the continuous measure was converted into a categorical one with three levels: No CEO Media Coverage, Moderate CEO Prominence (one article about the CEO that firm-year), and High CEO Prominence (two or more articles).
time_window: focal year (the year prior to the Fortune survey publication year)

description: The valence of the same articles used to construct the prominence measure, assessed with the Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) program and its dictionary of positive and negative emotion words. Articles were coded as positive if the ratio of positive affective content to total affective content was at least 0.65, and the positive and negative articles were aggregated into an annual CEO Media Tenor measure using the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance; the formula itself is not readable in the source text. The measure was categorized into three levels with a dichotomous variable for each: Negative CEO Media Tenor, Neutral CEO Media Tenor, and Positive CEO Media Tenor.

The unfavorable-valence portion of the CEO media coverage, built from the same articles used for the prominence measure and scored with the LIWC dictionary of positive and negative emotion words. Articles were coded as negative if the ratio of negative affective content to total affective content was 0.65 or greater, and the annual measure was formed with the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance, whose formula is not readable in the source text. Negative CEO Media Tenor is one of three categories (with Neutral and Positive) captured by dichotomous variables in the analysis, defined as a Janis-Fadner coefficient below zero.
scale: Janis-Fadner coefficient ranges from -1 to 1; negative category is below zero

description: A dummy variable coded as 1 if the current CEO was announced as an award winner that year (the announcement was typically in March) and 0 otherwise. The award is a bronze medal in Financial World magazine's 'CEO of the Year' competition, in which a group of securities analysts and CEOs rated other CEOs' managerial expertise and a committee of experienced analysts selected three bronze winners in each of approximately 60 industry categories; following Wade et al. (2006), bronze medals are used to measure CEO awards.

A dichotomous variable set to 1 if the incumbent CEO had fewer than three years of tenure at the focal organization at the time of their appointment as CEO, and 0 otherwise. The three-year pre-appointment window follows prior research and aims to properly categorize cases in which an outsider CEO was initially hired for an executive position other than CEO and groomed for a short period as the successor. If a CEO arrives as an outsider, the variable remains at 1 until the year he or she leaves office.

The size in square feet of incumbent casino i near potential entrant j at monthly lag t relative to the entry date. The specification regresses casino size on the post x nearby interaction with entrant fixed effects, incumbent property fixed effects, year fixed effects and standardized market and incumbent controls. The coefficient of interest estimates the mean difference between how nearby incumbents change capacity and how incumbents farther away change capacity.
time_window: 18 months before to 30 months after the entry plan, excluding the adjustment period from -11 months to +23 months

description: The indicator post equals 1 for observations after the entry plan and 0 otherwise. The indicator nearby equals 1 if the incumbent is within 100 miles of the proposed entry site. Their interaction is the difference-in-differences term capturing the capacity response of nearby incumbents to the entry plan.
time_window: entry plan date with monthly lags from -18 to +30 months

description: A specification perfectly analogous to the entry-plan specification but centered on the date a potential entrant breaks ground on construction; post_const equals 1 after first construction. The specification also includes post_plan and its interaction with nearby, where post_plan equals 1 only if the after-plan date is also prior to the date at first construction.
time_window: event window around the first construction event, excluding the adjustment period

description: The per-capita cash accessed at incumbent casinos by patrons who reside in zip code j within 200 miles of entering casino i, aggregated across all incumbent casinos at lag t relative to the entry date. The sample is restricted to a nine-month window around the month of opening. Controls include an indicator for county population exceeding one million residents and the log of county population.
time_window: May 2010 to June 2012; nine-month window around the month of opening (-4 to +4 months)

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if the entry plan was stalled, that is observed for 48 months in the data without ever being observed as open. A stale record that is no longer updated indicates a failed entry plan. The estimation sample is restricted to observations that could be classified as stalled or not.

The average increase in casino floor space of nearby incumbents (within 100 miles) by one year after the entry plan relative to the baseline of 12 months prior to the entry plan. The variable is standardized to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 to ease interpretation of the marginal effects.
time_window: -12 months to +12 months relative to the entry plan

description: Allocation of attention was measured by the number of times consultants accessed, or hit, a practice group's database in a month; a hit is treated as evidence of time spent searching through and evaluating the content of that database, and access events are assumed to last the same amount of time on average across databases. The dependent variable logs the total number of hits by the firm's consultants on a focal group's database in a month. The measure was also lagged one month and the lagged value was entered as an independent variable.
time_window: monthly, lagged one month when entered as a predictor

description: Crowdedness is the extent of overlap in knowledge content between a focal group and all other groups, computed from the keywords attached to documents using Centra's taxonomy of 101 keywords. For each pair of groups in operation in a month the overlap coefficient is the sum across keyword categories of the smaller of the two groups' numbers of keyword mentions in the category, divided by the focal group's total number of keyword mentions; the crowdedness measure sums these dyadic coefficients for the focal group. The equations are given in formula blocks that are unreadable, but the prose example describes the calculation (a group with 150 keyword mentions and 50 shared SAP mentions has an overlap of .33). The measure was lagged one month, updated monthly, and standardized in the models.

The Herfindahl index computed over the 101 topic areas of the keyword list: the sum of squared fractions of a group's total keyword mentions falling in each topic area. The measure ranges from 1/n to 1, where n is the 101 keyword categories, and equals 1 when a practice group has all its documents in one keyword category. It was standardized in the models.

Practice-group coordinators answered the survey question 'What percentage of documents submitted to your database is typically accepted?', and this proportion was reverse scored to give a rejection rate. Because the reported proportion had not changed much over the study period, one time-invariant value per group was used for the 18 months. Reported rejection rates ranged from 0 to 80 percent.

The cumulative number of documents available in a group's database, obtained from the log files of the 43 databases, lagged one month and updated monthly. It measures the effect of total document supply on the ability to attract attention.

A dummy variable coded 1 if the number of documents released to the database was 10 times larger than the number released in the prior and subsequent months in that database, registered in the two months prior to the observation month, and 0 otherwise; the measure was updated monthly. Avoiding batch releases was one of the practices through which groups were selective, so a value of 1 indicates the less selective case.
time_window: two months prior to the observation month, updated monthly

description: For each alliance, a categorical indicator coded 1 if the alliance involved a knowledge-generating R&D agreement, 0 if it was an agreement based on existing knowledge (joint marketing and service, OEM/VAR, licensing, production, or supply), and 0.5 for a combination of R&D and other agreements. Coding took the perspective of the focal firm, so that marketing a partner's solution without joint R&D was coded as a marketing agreement. The measure is the average value of this indicator across all alliances formed by firm i in year t.

For each alliance formed by firm i, an indicator received a value of 1 if the firm had no joint prior alliances with partner j and 0 if such alliances existed. Structure exploration is the average value of this indicator across all alliances formed by firm i in year t. In order not to classify a firm's first alliance as structure exploration by default, 181 firm-year observations corresponding to years in which firms formed their first and only alliances were excluded.

Built from four indicators of partner attributes in the year of alliance formation: partner size (asset value), propensity to invest in marketing (advertising intensity), financial strength (logarithm of the ratio of cash to long-term debt), and industry focus (four-digit SIC code). For the first three attributes, the absolute difference between the partner's attribute value and the average attribute of the firm's ten prior partners was computed for each alliance; for industry focus, a dummy received a value of 1 when the new partner's primary four-digit SIC code was not on the list of primary SIC codes of the ten prior partners, and 0 otherwise. Each indicator was standardized by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation, the four were aggregated with the Euclidean distance formula, and the resulting variable was normalized by linear transformation to range between 0 and 1.

Computed with the same formula used for constructing the function exploration measure, but instead of incorporating the alliances formed by firm i in year t, it counts all the alliances formed by that firm between 1985 and the preceding year (t-1). It captures the firm's accumulated exploration experience in the function domain.

Computed with the same formula used for constructing the structure exploration measure, but instead of incorporating the alliances formed by firm i in year t, it counts all the alliances formed by that firm between 1985 and the preceding year (t-1). It captures the firm's accumulated exploration experience in the structure domain.

Computed with the same formula used for constructing the attribute exploration measure, but instead of incorporating the alliances formed by firm i in year t, it counts all the alliances formed by that firm between 1985 and the preceding year (t-1). It captures the firm's accumulated exploration experience in the attribute domain.

variable_name: Time clock (year of alliance formation, 1990 = 1 to 2001 = 12)
description: Time is measured by the year in which alliances were formed, as a firm-year clock running from 1 for 1990 to 12 for 2001.

Residuals from a between-effects panel regression (clustered on firms) of CEO total pay on important determinants of CEO total pay. The authors state that the equation included firm size (natural logarithm of sales and of assets), firm performance (ROA and shareholder return), CEO human capital (CEO tenure, number of years in the CEO role, and the square of CEO tenure), and CEO labor market membership (industry group dummy codes based on SIC two-digit codes, S&P large-cap/mid-cap/small-cap index membership, and year); the equation itself is not readable in the text. Negative residuals represented negative relative pay standing: the variable was set at the residual value if negative and to 0 if not, and the negative signs were reversed so that increasing positive values reflected higher underpayment. The values of CEO underpayment were lagged by one year.

The number of acquisitions announced during a year and subsequently completed. The extreme 1 percent of the distribution of the acquisition activity variables was Winsorized to reduce the effects of extreme observations. This count measure was used as the dependent variable in random effects negative binomial regressions.

A separate measure of acquisition activity that included only large acquisitions, calculated as the number of acquisitions whose total deal size was greater than $1 million. The extreme 1 percent of the distribution of the acquisition activity variables was Winsorized.

Following McNamara, Haleblian, and Dykes (2008), the acquirer's 'percentage of the stock used' variable was drawn from the SDC Mergers & Acquisitions Database. This value was averaged on an annual basis based on all acquisitions announced during the year and subsequently completed. When the SDC database did not report a percentage of stock used, the value was recorded as 0.

The total CEO compensation each firm publicly reported during each year of the sample, with the previous year's total compensation simultaneously controlled for so that the influence of previous year total compensation is partialled out of current year total compensation. For years 1996-2005 total compensation is the sum of salary, bonus, total value of restricted stock awards, Black-Scholes value of stock option awards, long-term incentive payouts, and other compensation; for years 2006-2008, following FAS 123(R), it is the sum of salary, bonus, value of stock option awards, value of stock awards including restricted stock and restricted stock units, non-equity incentive plan compensation earned, change in pension value and non-qualified deferred compensation earnings, and other compensation. Due to skewness, the natural logarithm of the compensation variables was used.

Total CEO compensation was separated into change in short-term compensation and change in long-term compensation, and the long-term component served as the dependent variable in three of the compensation models. The text does not state in prose which reported compensation components fall into the long-term part. Due to skewness, the natural logarithm of the compensation variables was used.

Total CEO compensation was separated into change in short-term compensation and change in long-term compensation, and the short-term component served as the dependent variable in three of the compensation models. The text does not state in prose which reported compensation components fall into the short-term part. Due to skewness, the natural logarithm of the compensation variables was used.

For firm i in year t, the number of backward citations to patents in primary U.S. classes that firm i did not patent in during year t divided by the number of backward citations made by firm i in year t. The measure uses primary three-digit patent classes rather than subclasses, and the application year of each patent is used to approximate the time of invention. High values indicate substantial use of technical knowledge originating from outside the firm's own technological base.
time_window: firm-year, measured at the patent application year

description: A stock measure built from the firm-level flow measure: because ongoing firm knowledge brokering is a fraction, it is multiplied by the number of patents awarded to the firm in that year, and, starting from its founding year, each firm's knowledge-brokering stock is the cumulative sum over previous years of this product. An exponential depreciation parameter is included in computing these stocks.

The number of external citations to the focal patent within five years of its issue, a well-established measure of innovative impact. Self-citations are excluded so that citations made across organizational boundaries are counted; the dependent variable is a nonnegative count.
time_window: within five years of patent issue

variable_name: Initial knowledge brokers versus initial nonbrokers
description: Subsample classification of the firms: initial knowledge brokers are entrepreneurial firms that licensed the Cohen-Boyer patent at the time of founding or within two years after founding, and initial nonbrokers are contemporaneously founded firms that did not license the recombinant DNA patent. Only de novo firms (as opposed to established pharmaceutical firms) are included.
time_window: at founding or within two years after founding

variable_name: Hired inventors with different technical knowledge stock
description: For each firm, all inventors new to the firm in each year are identified along with all patents awarded to the inventor throughout her career; among these inventors, the measure counts those who had previously patented in technological classes different from the ones the firm received patents in within the past five years. The flow variable is then transformed into a cumulative stock of new hires with different technical knowledge for each firm-year, and the independent variables are lagged by two years.

For each firm and quarter, the authors determine the set of components that the firm has used and observe the pattern of interdependence that exists among these components in the interdependence matrix calculated on the four quarters. To operationalize it on the firm level, the authors borrow the ego density measure used by network scholars. In the example given, if the website casper.com used three components A, B and C and more than 10% of firms in the ecosystem used A-B and A-C together, Local Component Interdependence takes a value of 2/(0.5[3^2 - 3]) = 0.66. The equation as rendered in the text is not readable.
time_window: firm's components in the quarter; interdependence matrix computed on four quarters

description: Dispersion across Clusters is computed as 1 minus the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index of component use concentration by the focal firm. The authors first decompose the ecosystem's matrix of interdependencies into clusters using a unipartite modularity algorithm, which partitions a network into groups of components with as many internal links and as few external links as possible. The resulting partition of the 15 networks varied from 2 to 4 clusters. The equation as rendered in the text is not readable.
time_window: interdependence matrix computed on four quarters

description: The authors first computed the eigenvector centrality of each component in the ecosystem-level network, and components in the 99th percentile in terms of eigenvector centrality are defined as central components. Central Component Use is defined as the proportion of the firm's components that are central. The equation as rendered in the text is not readable.

Alexa tracks a global representative sample of users in 129 countries through user-installed toolbars and scripts installed by websites, and Alexa's algorithm records the number of page views per million users in this sample over 3-month periods. The authors use the logged value of average page views per million in each quarter as a dependent variable. The web traffic variable is always based on data in the next two quarters following the independent variables.
time_window: next two quarters following the independent variables

description: Treatment Country is a binary variable indicating whether the firm is in the treatment group, and Post-change is a binary variable indicating whether the dependent variable for an observation is recorded after (Post-change = 1) or prior to the enforcement of the regulation in Q2 of 2018 (Post-change = 0). The negative shock to interdependencies is captured by the interaction of these two variables.

We measured acquisition experience as the total number of prior acquisitions that an institution in our sample made between 1988, the year following the last major regulatory change (CEBA) that had significant impact upon bank acquisition strategies, and the year of a focal acquisition. Experience before the regulatory changes was excluded because it might not represent viable resources for future learning.
time_window: 1988 to the year of the focal acquisition

description: Focal acquisition performance was measured using abnormal returns: the difference between the observed return and the predicted, or normal, return for the same security. Rather than comparing a bank's return with a general market index, the normal return was predicted from the return of a banking industry portfolio, giving an industry-specific abnormal return. Abnormal returns were averaged over an event window beginning 5 trading days before and ending 15 trading days after the announcement of an acquisition event (-5, +15). The mean cumulative abnormal return (CAR) was -0.01, and of the 2,523 acquisitions in the sample, 1,410 (56%) had negative CARs, and 1,113 (44%) had positive CARs.
time_window: (-5, +15) trading days around the acquisition announcement

variable_name: Likelihood of making a subsequent acquisition
description: Our dependent variable, the likelihood of making a subsequent acquisition, was estimated as the hazard of a bank in the sample making a subsequent acquisition after a focal acquisition. We used the piecewise exponential model, which splits the time axis into predefined time segments and permits the hazard rate to vary in an unconstrained way across time periods; duration was divided into four-year time periods. Because the survival analysis used the information provided by right-censored cases, it did not require an ad hoc time window to determine whether an acquirer made a subsequent acquisition after a focal acquisition.

Treatment is a binary variable equal to 1 if application i (or developer, at the firm level) is identified as treated by the entry, and 0 otherwise. Post is a binary variable equal to 1 if the observation is in the post-treatment timeline, including and after June 2017, when the entry was announced, and 0 otherwise. Their interaction captures the difference-in-differences effect, while the main effects of treatment and post are absorbed by the application and time fixed effects.

Developers are classified by their positioning prior to the platform owner entry: multihoming developers are those that also had applications on Play Store prior to the entry, and singlehoming developers are those with no prior experience on the competing platform. The authors use this pre-entry positioning to split the sample into SH and MH units rather than to code a continuous variable in the main analyses.
Product innovation measured as the number of updates which application i received in month t on the focal platform. Applications are observed monthly over the 14-month period.

Product maintenance measured as whether application i appears as active in month t on the focal platform. An application marked as active is maintained by the developer and available to all users, whereas an inactive application is not maintained and is no longer accessible for users to view or download. Keeping an application active is treated as requiring effort allocation.

New-application release, measured as the number of new applications released by developers on the focal platform. Given the longer development cycle for releasing new applications relative to updating existing ones, this variable is measured at the developer-quarter level, with each observation covering a developer for three-month intervals over the same 14 months.

Product innovation on the competing platform, measured as the number of updates which application i received in month t. The sample includes all applications that multihoming developers had across the different product categories for which data on the competing platform are available.

Product maintenance on the competing platform, measured as whether application i appears as active in month t; an active application is maintained by the developer and available to users, while an inactive one is not maintained and no longer accessible. The analysis is limited to applications developed by multihoming developers on Play Store.

New-application release on the competing platform, measured as the number of new applications released by developers on Play Store at the developer-quarter level, with each observation covering a developer for three-month intervals over the same 14 months.

For the Microsoft To Do entry the authors follow the same approach as in Analysis 1, forming treated and matched control applications and estimating a Treatment × Post interaction; the same procedure is applied to the SanDisk Cloud entry in the same market as the Files application, with errors clustered at the application level.
time_window: same monthly observation window as Analysis 1

variable_name: Adjusted number of welfare work articles
description: Yearly count of articles on welfare work techniques, summed over the branch headings under the Wilson index root headings "welfare work" (changed to "employees' benefit plans" and then to "fringe benefits"); the procedure resulted in a set of 65 welfare work techniques selected as the top 40 percent of branch headings by number of years they persisted. To adjust for growth in the index, the number of articles in any one year was multiplied by the ratio between the number of index pages in 1953 and the number of index pages for the given year. The series covers 1913 through 1992.

variable_name: Adjusted number of human relations/personnel management articles
description: Yearly count of articles on human relations/personnel management techniques, summed over the branch headings located under the root headings "employment management" and "personnel management" (the root heading changed in the 1967 Business Periodicals Index); a set of 40 such techniques was retained. Counts were adjusted for index growth by multiplying the number of articles in a year by the ratio of index pages in 1953 to index pages in that year. The series covers 1913 through 1992.

variable_name: Adjusted number of scientific management articles
description: Yearly count of articles on scientific management techniques, summed over the branch headings under the root heading "scientific management"; 15 scientific management techniques were retained. Counts were adjusted for index growth using the ratio of index pages in 1953 to index pages in the given year. The emergence of this rhetoric was additionally traced with Litterer's (1959) counts of articles across all U.S. periodicals between 1875 and 1900 (not adjusted for growth in the total number of articles) and with Shenhav's (1995) counts of pages devoted to the rhetoric as a percentage of pages devoted to management issues in American Machinist and Engineering Magazine between 1879 and 1932.
scale: count (and percentage of pages for the Shenhav series)

variable_name: Adjusted number of systems rationalism articles
description: Yearly count of articles on systems rationalism techniques, adjusted by the ratio of index pages in 1953 to index pages in the given year. Because no root heading existed for this rhetoric in the Wilson indexes, the branch headings selected by Barley and Kunda (1992) were used. The series begins with the rhetoric's emergence in 1947 and the regression sample contains 45 observations.

Yearly count of articles on organization culture and quality techniques, adjusted by the ratio of index pages in 1953 to index pages in the given year. Because no root heading existed for this rhetoric in the Wilson indexes, the branch headings selected by Barley and Kunda (1992) were used. Statistical tests were not used on this series because it contained too few data points.

Yearly national voluntary turnover rate per 100 employees, drawn from the U.S. Bureau of the Census Historical Statistics of the United States for the 1914 to 1970 period and from the U.S. Department of Labor's Handbook of Labor Statistics thereafter. The U.S. government ceased reporting turnover rate data in 1986.

The national percentage of employees belonging to labor unions, measured yearly, drawn from the U.S. Bureau of the Census Historical Statistics of the United States for the 1914 to 1970 period and from the U.S. Department of Labor's Handbook of Labor Statistics thereafter.

Yearly number of strikes involving more than six employees nationwide, drawn from the U.S. Bureau of the Census Historical Statistics of the United States for the 1914 to 1970 period and from the U.S. Department of Labor's Handbook of Labor Statistics thereafter; the government ceased reporting data on strikes involving more than six employees in 1981. For the 1982-1992 period the series was estimated from the series for strikes involving more than 1,000 employees, which was reported between 1949 and 1992 and correlates at .65 with the more-than-six series over 1949-1981.

Long wave stages were taken from the estimates averaged across sources by Barley and Kunda (1992), since scholars' estimates of long waves' timing differ slightly. Two long waves overlap with this study's time frame: the third Kondratieff long wave, with a 1894-1921 upswing and a 1921-44 downswing, and the fourth Kondratieff long wave, with a 1944-71 upswing and a downswing between 1971 and the present.
time_window: macroeconomic stages covering the study period

variable_name: Rational rhetoric series (scientific management, systems rationalism): adjusted yearly article counts
description: Rational rhetorics are a class of two rhetorics, each measured by its own yearly count of Wilson index articles adjusted for index growth. For the emergence of scientific management before 1913 the paper also uses Litterer's 1875 to 1900 article counts and Shenhav's 1879 to 1932 page percentages. There is no combined variable; hypotheses on rational rhetorics are tested series by series.

variable_name: Normative rhetoric series (welfare work, human relations/personnel management, culture-quality): adjusted yearly article counts
description: Normative rhetorics are a class of three rhetorics, each measured by its own yearly count of Wilson index articles, adjusted for the growth of the index by multiplying each year's count by the ratio of index pages in 1953 to index pages in that year. There is no combined variable; hypotheses on normative rhetorics are tested series by series.

Indicator variable taking the value 1 if an outside or outside-related director is not the founder of a Fortune 500 company, is not the current or retired CEO or chairman of a Fortune 500 company, is not a director of more than one Fortune 500 company, and owns shareholdings of at least 0.1 percent. Share ownership is measured as the percentage of total shares outstanding beneficially owned by each director.
Indicator variable taking the value 1 if a firm has at least one SOLE Director serving on its board, and 0 otherwise.
Count of the number of SOLE Directors on a firm's board.
scale: count, ranging from zero to five

description: Indicator variables taking the value 1 if a firm has N SOLE Directors, where N is 0, 1, 2, or 3, with the final category representing firms that have three or more SOLE Directors on their boards.
Variable representing the departure of at least one SOLE Director from a firm's board in a given year.
Variable representing the decrease in the number of SOLE Directors on a firm's board in a given year.
Indicator variables representing a decrease by N SOLE Directors from a firm's board in a given year.
Tobin's q, approximated as a firm's current market-to-book ratio.

Cognitive ability is measured by the age-adjusted AFQT score, indicated in percentiles and calculated from the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery. NLSY respondents took the ASVAB in 1980, when they were 16-23 years of age, and scores are age-adjusted using the procedure described in Altonji, Bharadwaj, and Lange (2012).
time_window: ASVAB administered in 1980; score is fixed for each individual

description: Measured on an ordinal scale such that 0 = No formal schooling, 1 = completion of 1st grade, 2 = completion of 2nd grade, ... 12 = completion of 12th grade (high school), 16 = completion of four-year college, and 20 = completion of eight years of college or higher. It serves as the measure of a worker's educational signal, consistent with previous work at least since Spence (1973).

Measured on an ordinal scale which indicates 0 = No formal schooling, 1 = High School Diploma (or equivalent), 2 = Associate/Junior College, 3 = Bachelor of Arts, 4 = Bachelor of Science, 5 = Master's, and 6 = PhD or other advanced professional degrees (MD, JD, LLD, DDS). It is used as an alternative measure of the educational signal, entered as a dummy variable for each possible degree.

Equal to 1 if the NLSY respondent indicated his or her current job as 'self-employed in his or her own business, professional practice, or farm'. NLSY defines an individual as self-employed if he or she owned at least 50 percent of the business, is principal managing partner, or files a form SE for Federal income taxes. Independent contractors, consultants, and freelancers are also classified as self-employed.
time_window: current job in each survey round, 1979-2010

description: Equal to 1 if the self-employed individual reported his or her business as incorporated. Incorporated self-employment is used as a separate occupational state in the multinomial logit models of occupational choice and in the earnings regressions.
time_window: current job in each survey round, 1979-2010

description: Total net family income expressed in 2010$; values are top-coded such that incomes of the top 2 percent of earners are coded as the average value of the top two percent. Annual income is the dependent variable in the earnings regressions, where it is logged.

Created by summing all asset values and subtracting all debts of the respondent's family and expressed in 2010$; net-worth of the top two percent is top-coded as the average of the top two percent. It is used as an outcome in the quantile regressions and is not logged because it can take negative values.

Difference between each individual's AFQT score and the median AFQT score for those sharing the individual's educational qualification. The measure can be positive, indicating that the employer will likely underestimate the worker's ability, or negative, indicating a probable overestimate; a one percentile point increase means the individual's AFQT score is one percentile above the median for his educational qualification.

variable_name: Annual income distribution by degree and occupational status
description: The distributions of income are presented as box plots for entrepreneurs and employees, conditional on the highest academic degree obtained. The boxes span the 25th to 75th percentiles, the horizontal bar in each denotes the median, while the whiskers extend from the 5th to 95th percentiles; panel (b) repeats the same presentation for household net-worth.

Age of respondent in years. It captures the stage of the worker's career over which information imperfection about ability resolves; the authors estimate how the entrepreneurial ability advantage and the returns to ability evolve over workers' careers by interacting ability with age in the self-employment and income regressions.

Time-invariant dummy variable equal to one for all scientists whose primary affiliations were exclusively with U.S.-based institutions during the preshock period and equal to zero for all other scientists in the sample. Because scientist fixed effects are included, no separate independent variable for scientists' country of affiliation is used.

The natural logarithm of one plus the total number of citations to scientist i's publications in the hESC subfield of stem cell research in a given year t. Citation-weighted publications are used because they capture the extent to which a scientist's allocation of research effort to a given area generates scientific impact, covering both the quantity and quality margins of output. In these regressions the sample is restricted to the 1998-2012 period.

The natural logarithm of one plus the total number of citations to scientist i's publications in a non-hESC subfield of stem cell research in a given year t. Publications were categorized into hESC and other non-hESC subfields of stem cell research by trained graduate students in biology, with each paper read by at least two research assistants.

Using the author affiliation information from each publication on Scopus, the authors identify whether an institution with which a scientist is affiliated belongs to one of two categories: academic research, hospitals, and other health service provision; or corporations. A dummy variable indicates whether scientist i was affiliated with an institution in each respective category in year t. Where a scientist does not have an identifiable affiliation because no publication is observed in a given year, the affiliation is interpolated between observed data points using the most proximate observed affiliation.

Dummy variables created from the affiliation information on a publication to indicate whether scientist i's publications in year t involve industry-affiliated coauthors on papers in stem cell subfields, including separate indicators for hESC and non-hESC publications. The dependent variable is only observed if in year t scientist i has a publication.

variable_name: publication involves collaboration with scientists from countries with flexible funding regimes
description: A set of dummy variables indicating whether scientist i's publications in year t involve coauthors from a set of countries with more permissive funding/policy regimes on papers in stem cell subfields (separately for hESC and non-hESC stem cell publications). The authors use these to examine whether U.S. scientists sought collaborations with scientists whose resource access was unaffected by the policy change.

variable_name: scientists' citations in the five years prior to the policy shock relative to their cohort
description: To test the heterogeneity prediction the authors split the sample according to scientists' citations in the five years prior to the policy shock relative to their cohort of scientists whose first publication is observed in the same year. Higher-quality scientists are argued to have, on average, lower effort cost of securing resources if these become more competitive and greater ability to have higher-impact publications in the hESC subfield.

variable_name: count of prior investments (adjusted for recency and credibility)
description: For a given VC owner at the time of a given investment, expertise was measured by the count of prior investments made up to that point by that VC owner across all firms in the VentureXpert dataset, along each of the three dimensions of interest: stage of development, industry domain, and time horizons. The raw counts were then adjusted for recency, by depreciating experience yearly and proportionally to the total vintage of prior experience of all VC owners at each round of investment, and for credibility, by disaggregating the count of prior investments into successful versus unsuccessful prior investments and dividing the former by the latter. The measure captures changes in a VC owner's expertise across rounds of financing as well as the introduction of new expertise by new VC owners investing in the firm.
time_window: updated at each round of financing

description: At each round of financing the authors first assessed the stage of development of the private firm and then transferred to the private firm each VC owner's aggregate number of prior experiences, adjusted for recency and credibility, that matched the stage of development of the focal private firm. The fit index equals the sum of successful matched experience at each round of investment divided by the sum of unsuccessful matched experience at each round, so higher numbers of matches observed at each financing round aggregated across all rounds reflect better fit. The authors note that no double-counting occurs when a VC firm has multiple rounds of investment at the same stage.
time_window: constructed for each round of financing and aggregated across all rounds up to the outcome

description: Industry fit was calculated before each round of financing by measuring, for a focal private firm, the aggregate number of prior investment experiences that its VC owners had had in industries matching the focal firm's SIC1 industry, adjusted for recency and credibility. The SIC1 classification was chosen because it best matches the industry classification of VC owners provided by the VentureXpert database. Higher numbers of matches observed at each financing round, aggregated across all rounds, reflect better fit.
time_window: constructed for each round of financing and aggregated across all rounds up to the outcome

description: Because time horizon is not easily gleaned from archival sources, the authors quantified it through a content analysis of the number of occurrences of the words 'growth' or 'profit' in the S-1 or SB-2 file submitted by focal firms, dividing firms into three groups: firms in the upper third of the relative count of growth were considered growth-oriented, firms in the upper third on the relative count of profit were considered profit-oriented, and the remaining middle third were considered to have taken a blended approach. The prospectuses of all firms in which the VC owners had made previous investments were content coded in the same way. Time-horizon fit is the count of prior experiences a private firm's VC owners have had with firms whose time horizon matched that of the focal private firm at each financing round, adjusted for recency and credibility and aggregated across all financing rounds.
time_window: prior investments up to each round of financing; aggregated across rounds

description: Successful exit was coded 1 when a venture's attempt to go public resulted in an IPO and 0 when the attempt did not result in an IPO. Acquisitions were included in the measure of successful exit; using M&A SDC Platinum the authors identified 65 VC-backed private firms that were acquired within two years after the S-1 or SB-2 filing. Unsuccessful versus successful IPOs were measured at the first attempt.
scale: binary (1 = IPO or acquisition, 0 = no IPO)

description: Short-term post-IPO performance used the natural logarithm of the ventures' percentage change in stock price at 90 days. This outcome was estimated in a two-stage Heckman regression on the sample of VC-backed ventures that attempted to go public.
scale: natural logarithm of percentage change in stock price

description: Equals one for the years in which the home country of a given retail multinational was hit by a systemic banking crisis during the sample period between 1998 and 2010, and zero otherwise. The measure uses the systemic banking crises database that lists the start and end years of banking crises at the country level; the first year in which significant signs of financial distress in the banking system and significant banking policy intervention measures are both present is considered the year in which a crisis becomes systemic.

A subsidiary's store growth is its annual percentage change in number of stores in the host country from the current to the next year: (#Stores t+1 / #Stores t) − 1.
