The dependent variable is then computed in three steps: a subsample of domestic retail chains that operate exclusively in a given country is obtained; the mean store growth of this subsample is computed for a given market and time period (using all domestic retail chains operating in the same world region when the number of domestic chains in a country and year is less than five); and the subsidiary's store growth is adjusted by subtracting the mean store growth of domestic retail chains in the given time period.
time_window: current year t to next year t+1

description: The sales percentage that a parent firm generates in its home country with food (versus nonfood) retail formats in a given year. The variable is standardized to facilitate interpretation of the interaction terms.

The physical geographic proximity between the subsidiary's host country and its parent's home country, based on information on geographic distances (in kilometers) between country pairs obtained from the CEPII's GeoDist database. To make the measure reflect geographic proximity, the distance was multiplied by −1, and the variable was standardized to facilitate interpretation of the interaction terms.

Equals one for the years in which a given retailer did not use the multidivisional form, and zero for the years in which the retailer used the multidivisional form. Almost all non-M-form structures are holdings (H-forms) in the authors' context of retail MNEs. The measure is based on company descriptions from the LSEG Workspace (formerly Refinitiv Workspace) database, which indicates whether the structure is an M-form or not.

Measured as the number of years since a given subsidiary entered the host country, starting in 1998. The sample only includes retail chains that began operations in a foreign country after 1997. The variable is standardized to facilitate interpretation of the interaction terms.

Domestic credit to the private sector as a share of gross domestic product (GDP) in a given host country and year, obtained from the World Bank's global financial development database. Higher values indicate better availability of local capital. The variable is standardized to facilitate interpretation of the interaction terms.

Measured as the percentage difference between the purchase price and the target firm's market value 4 weeks prior to the date of acquisition public announcement. The four-week time lag was used because information leakage right before the public announcement can cause distortions in the stock price, making premiums calculated based on short-term windows smaller than those calculated based on longer-term windows.
time_window: 4 weeks prior to the public announcement of the acquisition

description: A binary measure that took a value of 1 if at least twice during the sample period the acquirer CEO continued to hold stock options with greater than 100% moneyness (the stock price was more than 100% greater than the exercise price) and 0 otherwise. A CEO was classified as overconfident from the year in which that CEO first exhibited this stock option behavior and retained this classification in subsequent years unless that CEO exercises stock options in the future at less than 30% moneyness, treating CEO overconfidence as an attribute that may vary over time.
time_window: from the year the CEO first exhibited the option-holding behavior onward

description: Measured with the number of days between the date on which the acquirer and target signed the nondisclosure agreement, denoting the beginning of the formal predeal process, and the date on which the deal was publicly announced, denoting the commitment to act. The measure was transformed by taking the natural logarithm. High values indicated that the predeal process was slow in pace, whereas low values indicated that the predeal process was fast in pace.
time_window: predeal period from NDA signing to public announcement of the acquisition bid

description: Technological overlap between a spinout and its parent firm, calculated with Jaffe's (1986) measure as the normalized product of the vectors of the number of patents in each patent class for the spinout and for its parent firm. The spinout's patent portfolio uses the patents of the spinout from its founding up until the end of the sample period, and the parent firm's portfolio covers the past 10 years before the founder left. The measure is not sensitive to the absolute number of patents in a class because it is the normalized product of patent distribution vectors. All explanatory variables were mean-centered before creating the interaction terms.
time_window: parent firm: 10 years before the founder left the parent firm; spinout: from founding up until the end of the sample period

variable_name: spinout with high TOSP / spinout with low TOSP
description: Two nested binary variables created by classifying spinouts into two groups based on the mean value of TOSP: spinout with high TOSP and spinout with low TOSP. They are used together with a binary variable (spinout) that takes the value of 1 for ventures founded by former employees of established firms and 0 otherwise, to compare the likelihood that a corporate investor will invest in spinouts with the likelihood that it will invest in nonspinouts.

A binary variable that takes a value of 1 for a realized CVC investment dyad by a corporate investor in a venture in the year t, and 0 otherwise. The sample considers all possible dyads involving a corporate investor and a venture that is at risk of receiving CVC investment in a given year.
time_window: year of the CVC investment dyad

description: A binary variable that takes a value of 1 for a realized CVC investment dyad by a corporate investor in a spinout in the year t, and 0 otherwise. Realized deals are compared with all nonrealized dyads between corporate investors and spinouts.
time_window: year of the CVC investment dyad

description: The number of unique patent infringement lawsuits filed by a parent firm during the five years prior to the year of a given CVC investment dyad. The authors view a firm's litigiousness as a general indicator of its reputation for toughness in enforcing the intellectual property rights associated with patents. The variable was mean-centered before creating the interaction term.
time_window: five years prior to the year of a given CVC investment dyad

description: Technological overlap between the corporate investor and the parent firm, measured using Jaffe's (1986) measure presented in Equation (1) during the five years prior to the year of a given CVC investment dyad. The variable was mean-centered before creating the interaction term.
time_window: five years prior to the year of a given CVC investment dyad

description: The number of medical device products approved by the FDA during the 10 years prior to the year of a given CVC investment dyad. The authors counted the number of products approved through both 510(k) and premarket approval processes, and transformed the value using the natural logarithm function to reduce skewness. The variable was mean-centered before creating the interaction term.
time_window: 10 years prior to the year of a given CVC investment dyad

variable_name: Vertical resource dependence (interaction of concentration of supplier/buyer industries and perceived value of resources provided by exchange partner)
description: Dependence of the focal firm on an exchange partner increases as the value of the resource to the focal firm increases and alternative providers of the resource decrease; it is given by the interaction of two variables. To assess the availability of alternative partners, the survey asked respondents to list the firm's primary inputs and distribution channels and, for each, their primary partners (up to five); NAICS codes were assigned to each partner and four-firm concentration ratios calculated for each partner's industry, with higher concentration ratios indicating fewer alternative sources of supply. A survey scale drawn from Cool and Henderson's (1998) measure asked four questions per input/channel about the impact of the input (or of buyers' services) on differentiation of the focal firm's products and services; items loaded on a single factor (alpha = 0.87) and factor scores were estimated with the regression method. The product term method was used to test the interaction.

Following many prior studies, the debt/equity ratio is used as an indicator of dependence on financial institutions for capital. Retained earnings is included as an additional indicator of financial dependence, divided by total assets to adjust for firm size, and inverted so that higher values signify lower retained earnings.

variable_name: Mean-deviated concentration level of focal firm's industry
description: Competitive uncertainty is operationalized as the mean-deviated concentration level of the focal firm's primary industry, following many prior studies. This variable takes on higher values when industry concentration is neither particularly low nor particularly high.

The CEO survey asked respondents to consider individuals they know personally at buyer firms, supplier firms, financial institutions that provide capital to the focal firm, and competitors, to list their names and primary employers, and to indicate whether each person is a closest friend, a friend but not among their closest friends, less than a friend but more than an acquaintance, or an acquaintance; for each person rated as a friend, respondents also indicated who initiated the relationship and, in the follow-up survey, the year they became friends. A tie is classified as reconstituted if the person identified as a friend at time t leaves their primary employer during the three-year period between surveys or the focal CEO leaves his or her firm during that time, and the focal CEO at time t + 3 has a friendship tie to the CEO of that firm (or to an officer of that firm, for a financial institution) that was initiated by the focal CEO since the tie was broken. Ties initiated by focal CEOs before assuming the CEO position are excluded.
time_window: three-year period between the two surveys

description: The percentage of shares owned collectively by all family members. The family with the most votes was designated the focal family, and in totalling family votes the shares of co-trustees of family trusts who were directly employed by the family were included. Information on vote control and family positions as officers and board members was obtained from at least three sources for each company.

A count of the number of acquisitions made by a given firm in a given year. Only transactions involving at least five percent of the ownership of a target company where the deal was valued at $1 million or more were included, and only transactions labelled as mergers or acquisitions initiated by U.S.-based corporations and completed within a given year.

The average size of the acquisition in terms of purchase price multiplied by the total number of acquisitions, giving an overall estimate of a firm's acquisitions activity. The variable was logged to eliminate skewness and kurtosis.

The ratio of the number of deals that were a standard industrial classification (SIC) code match for the firm to the total number of deals completed by the firm in each year, computed at the three-digit SIC level. As the variable pertains only to firms that actually make acquisitions, analyses incorporating it cover a smaller sample than analyses of the number of acquisitions.

The total number of green investment funds in a country divided by the number of all funds in that country, following Gong (2003). The authors take the natural log of the odds ratio of this percentage (a logistic transformation), which is helpful to correct for skewness in percentage variables. The higher the value of this logistically transformed variable, the more prevalent the environmental logic is in the investment profession relative to the mainstream financial logic. Funds were identified by selecting ''environmentally friendly'' from the ''general attributes'' in the Bloomberg fund screening function.

The environmental score from Thomson Reuters' ASSET4, provided as a z-score for each firm-year. It covers three major sectors, emission reduction, environmental product innovation, and resource deduction. It represents an overall rating based on 136 public and objective data points compiled by trained analysts.

A dummy variable indicating whether an SIF existed in a given country-year. The authors hand-coded these data by first searching for the presence of SIFs online, then consulting internal informants and documents from different SIFs, and finally double checking with historical webpages archived online.

The measure of shareholder protection policy obtained from the IMD World Competitiveness Report. The original item comes from an indicator of ''the extent to which shareholders' rights are sufficiently implemented'' and is determined by a combination of an executive survey and analysis of other objective data conducted by the IMD World Competitiveness Center.

The measure of states' environmental protection policy obtained from the OECD (Botta and Kozluk, 2014). This measure covers a broad range of environmental regulations, such as emission limits for a given substance, the tax rate for emission of NOx, and emission trading schemes for CO2 and SOx.

The dollar amount of charitable giving by a firm in a given year, scaled by the firm's sales in the same period. The dollar amount includes monetary and nonmonetary giving, as well as direct giving and giving through corporate-sponsored foundations, as reported in the Taft Corporate Giving Directories. The scaling was adopted to control for firm size, so the variable measures the relative amount of giving.

Return on assets, an accounting-based measure defined as net income over total assets. Because there is often a lag between corporate giving and its impact on accounting-based performance, the effect of corporate giving was evaluated in terms of subsequent ROA, the average ROA of the three years following the giving year. The second-stage dependent variables were industry mean-adjusted.
time_window: average of the three years following the giving year (t+1, t+2, t+3)

description: Tobin's q approximated as the firm's market-to-book ratio; the numerator is the year-end market value of the firm's common stock plus the book value of preferred stock and debt, and the denominator is year-end total assets. The authors state this approximation explains more than 96% of the variance in a more sophisticated Tobin's q. Like ROA, Tobin's q was calculated by averaging data of the subsequent three years from the year of giving, and the second-stage dependent variables were industry mean-adjusted.
time_window: average of the three years following the giving year (t+1, t+2, t+3)

description: A standardized index of industry dynamism built from industry sales. Following previous studies, industry sales over the five years preceding the giving year (including the giving year) were regressed against time, and the standard error of the regression coefficient related to a time dummy variable divided by the average value of the industry's sales formed the index. For a diversified firm, overall industry sales were first computed as the average of the segment industry-level sales, weighted by segment sales as a proportion of the firm's total sales, and then regressed over the same five-year period.
time_window: five years preceding the giving year, including the giving year

description: RS4, the specification used in the main analyses, sets the number of separate releases in relation to the extent of the global market targeted with those releases; smaller values indicate a more simultaneous feature rollout, larger values a more sequential rollout. As input for the numerator, the authors count releases occurring in the first 12 months of rollouts that began within 3 years of the global pioneering date for a feature, considering releases distinct if they occur by a month or more apart. Single-release rollouts are placed at the sequential end of the dependent variable. For the denominator, the authors use a measure of active postpaid and prepaid sim cards, in 100 m, from the ITU to capture the number of addressable consumers rather than the number of countries.
time_window: first 12 months of rollout, for features launched within 3 years of global pioneering

description: Innovation novelty is captured by the time elapsed since the entry of the global feature pioneer, which ranges between 0 months for pioneers and 35 months for late entrants. The interpretation is that the longer a feature has been on the market somewhere, the more information a focal firm can glean from the pioneer's experience, so higher values of the variable indicate less novel features.

Commission-error experience is a count of all feature innovations launched by the focal firm in the preceding year that did not become commercial successes and also did not become permanent handset fixtures.

Omission-error experience is a count of all the innovations not launched by the focal firm in the preceding year that turned out to become industry successes. These are innovations that generated local peak revenue premiums in excess of €2m per month, comparing average revenues from phones with the focal feature and revenues from otherwise comparable phones without the focal feature; industry practitioners used this threshold for identifying innovative successes.

Innovation competition is a straightforward market-level count of local competitors already offering the focal feature that a firm wants to launch. In the sample this measure ranges from 0 to 16. Feature-specific competition is independent of market size and only mildly correlated with overall competition levels.

Innovation-specific consumer sophistication is rated by the extent to which a market's consumer base buys handsets that are at the technological frontier for the focal innovation. For example, consumer sophistication relevant for the local launch of an 8 mega-pixel camera feature is indicated by the local market share of 5 mega-pixel camera phones; in cases without a generational predecessor, the nearest technology matters, as with the market share of Wi-Fi phones for a putative UMA feature. The higher the market share of handsets with indicator features, the closer the average consumer is to the relevant technological frontier.

The second dependent variable identifies the initial launch country in sequential feature rollouts; simultaneous rollouts have no market-ordering of entry. It is a simple dummy indicating whether or not the country was the market of first introduction, and the analysis is limited to strictly sequenced rollouts, cases where features were launched in no more than one market per month. Because each feature could theoretically have been first launched in any one of the 13 country markets, each firm-feature contributes one observation with the value of 1 and 12 observations with the value of 0.

Subjective assessment of the cost advantage resulting from a firm's environmental strategy, assessed relative to the firm's major domestic and foreign competitors. The measure was chosen over accounting measures of financial performance and over estimates of cost savings because it isolates the effect of the environmental strategy on competitiveness within the industry.

One of the measures for the best practices of environmental management, developed through a factor analysis of eight survey items related to the firms' use of pollution prevention technologies, their innovation of proprietary pollution prevention technologies, and their timing of environmental strategies regarding the issue identified by the respondent.

One of the measures for the best practices of environmental management, developed through a factor analysis of eight survey items related to the firms' use of pollution prevention technologies, their innovation of proprietary pollution prevention technologies, and their timing of environmental strategies regarding the issue identified by the respondent.

One of the measures for the best practices of environmental management, developed through a factor analysis of eight survey items related to the firms' use of pollution prevention technologies, their innovation of proprietary pollution prevention technologies, and their timing of environmental strategies regarding the issue identified by the respondent.

The complementary assets of capabilities for process innovation and implementation were measured by five questionnaire items related to the general innovativeness of a company relative to its major competitors and the propensity of the company to update existing or implement new production technologies and equipment. Continuously updating existing or implementing new technologies and equipment can be expected to lead to the creation of capabilities for process innovation and implementation.

The maximum number of possible outcomes at any stage along equilibrium x's path. A stage is equivalent to an information set facing the player along the path leading to equilibrium x. For example, the (8, 4) equilibrium has a c index of 4 because there are 4 possible outcomes in both Stages I and II, whereas the (7, 5) equilibrium has a c index of 9 because there are 4 possible outcomes in Stage I and 9 in Stage II.

variable_name: Level of iterative knowledge of rationality (r_x)
description: The number of mutual rationality levels needed to reach equilibrium x. A level of mutual rationality is defined as each player knowing the other is an expected-utility maximizer. In an extensive-form game this is equivalent to the number of backward induction steps, and each level requires additional elementary cognitive operations.

variable_name: Level of iterative knowledge of strategies (s_x)
description: The number of levels of mutual knowledge of strategies needed to reach equilibrium x. This knowledge pertains to a player's action choice rather than only to rationality. It is similar to the number of stages along the path leading to the equilibrium, and each level requires additional elementary cognitive operations.
The difference between the payoffs of the two players for equilibrium x. For example, the p of equilibrium (7, 5) is 2.

Outcomes in each round are classified by whether player 1 and player 2 chose the simple equilibrium S or a complex equilibrium C. If both choose the simple equilibrium the outcome is SS; if player 1 chooses a complex equilibrium and player 2 the simple one the outcome is CS; and so on. Tables report frequencies across games and rounds, and the analysis examines the proportion choosing the least task complex equilibrium.

Task complexity of an equilibrium is captured by three metrics manipulated in the games: cardinality of choice space, level of iterative knowledge of rationality and level of iterative knowledge of strategies. In each game only one metric varied between equilibria, and the equilibrium with the smaller metric was labeled simple (S) and the other complex (C).

Counts of all mentions of Kodak's and Polaroid's products by name in the securities analysts' reports, obtained with the Adobe pdf search function on multiple permutations of the product names. Mentions are reported separately for digital products and for film-based or hybrid products and totalled within each category. Broader searches were also run for general mentions of Kodak's participation in digital cameras using the terms 'digital,' 'electronic,' or 'filmless' in reference to Kodak's own camera offerings.

variable_name: Text analysis of analysts' product mentions (positive or negative)
description: The specific texts associated with the product mentions in the analysts' reports were analyzed to determine whether the analysts' reactions were generally positive or negative. The analysis quotes the analysts' statements about Kodak's and Polaroid's hybrid, film, and pure digital products and classifies reactions as positive, critical, or absent.

variable_name: Turning points in analysts' ratings and their justifications
description: Turning points in the analysts' ratings on the incumbents' stock (for example an upgrade from 'Hold' to 'Buy') were noted, and the justifications provided for the rating change in the first paragraph of the reports were analyzed to understand whether and how the incumbents' responses to the technological change affected analysts' recommendations. 'Buy' is used to refer to 'Buy,' 'Overweight,' or 'Accumulate' ratings, 'Hold' to 'Hold,' 'Equal-weight,' or 'Neutral' ratings, and 'Sell' to 'Sell' or 'Underweight' ratings.

Counts of all mentions of the wireline incumbents' products by name in the securities analysts' reports, obtained with the Adobe pdf search function on multiple permutations of the product names. Mentions of the VoIP-based offerings are reported separately from mentions of the wireline (Section 271 or long-distance) offerings; general mentions of the incumbents' VoIP-based offerings were also counted.

variable_name: Text analysis of analysts' product mentions (positive or negative)
description: The content of the texts mentioning the incumbents' strategies was analyzed to determine if analysts were generally positive or negative. The analysis quotes the analysts' brief remarks on VoIP offerings and their extensive, positive, and enthusiastic reactions to the long-distance (Section 271) strategies.

variable_name: Turning points in analysts' ratings and their justifications
description: Turning points in the analysts' ratings on the wireline incumbents' stock were noted, and the justifications provided for the rating change in the first paragraph of the reports were analyzed to understand whether and how the incumbents' responses to the technological change affected analysts' recommendations. 'Buy' is used to refer to 'Buy,' 'Overweight,' or 'Accumulate' ratings, 'Hold' to 'Hold,' 'Equal-weight,' or 'Neutral' ratings, and 'Sell' to 'Sell' or 'Underweight' ratings.

Incumbent products that kept the old technology: in photography, hybrid and film products that preserved a role for film in image capture, and in telecommunications, long distance services based on the existing wireline technology. Products and introduction dates were compiled from the Future Image Report, LexisNexis news and incumbent press releases.

variable_name: Products incorporating the new technology (digital cameras; VoIP phone services)
description: Strategies responding to the new technology are identified by product category: the digital cameras introduced by Kodak and Polaroid in photography, and the VoIP-based phone services introduced by the RBOC incumbents in wireline telecommunications. Products and their introduction dates were compiled from the Future Image Report, LexisNexis English-language news and the incumbents' press releases, and analyst reactions are then counted and coded per product.
scale: product category (set of named product introductions)

description: A composite measure built from two indicators: a count of the number of firms competing in the global landscape (nfirms) and the cumulative global market shares of the four largest mobile phone vendors in terms of units sold (concentration). Following Sanders and Carpenter (1998), the number of firms and the concentration ratio were divided, respectively, by the maximum number of firms and the minimum level of concentration in the sample to obtain two ratios, for which the closer the value is to 1, the more intense the competition. The final measure is the average of the two ratios and takes values ranging from 0 to 1, with 1 representing the highest level of competitive intensity in the sample; the equation itself is unreadable in the supplied text. Competitive intensity increases the higher the number of firms in the industry and the lower the concentration level.
time_window: t (one year before the dependent variable)

description: The firm's product line length was measured with the natural logarithm of the number of models belonging to the firm's product line. Each handset is assumed to be introduced at the beginning of the year t and to remain in the firm's product line only over that year t, so the life cycle of each handset begins on the first day of the year and lasts one year. The dependent variable was computed at time t + 1.

variable_name: Choice of external delivery model when sourcing business services globally
description: Binary variable that takes a value of 1 when a company chooses to source a process from an external service provider and a value of 0 when the firm sources the process internally through a captive services center. Only global (rather than domestic) sourcing projects are included in the sample.

Composite measure that proxies the extent to which the practice of sourcing a particular process has become non-specific to firms from particular industries or home countries. The authors compare the industry and home country distribution of global sourcing projects for each process with the distribution of industries and home countries across all sourcing projects and compute the ratio between the two; the lower the ratio, the more commoditized the process relative to all projects. To capture changes over time, the measure is computed separately for early projects until 2004 and more recent projects after 2004.

For year X, the number of providers offering a particular process-related service at least since year X-1 divided by the total number of providers in the database, including providers that did not yet exist in year X-1 but existed in 2011. The one-year lag accounts for the time it takes for information on the availability of specific service capabilities to spread. The measure captures both the relative availability of a service compared with other services at a point in time and the growth in availability of a service compared with 2011.

variable_name: Prior choice of external delivery model
description: Dummy equal to 1 if the company had, at least in part, chosen external delivery prior to the focal project, and 0 otherwise. Firms that experimented with both governance models have both prior-choice dummies equal to 1.

variable_name: Prior choice of internal delivery model
description: Dummy equal to 1 if the company had, at least in part, chosen internal delivery prior to the focal project, and 0 otherwise. Firms that experimented with both governance models have both prior-choice dummies equal to 1.

Firms are grouped by the year in which they began sourcing services globally: 128 firms (44%) began offshoring before 2004 and 163 firms (56%) started since 2004. Initial projects are those a firm launched in its first year; models are estimated separately on the initial projects of early adopters (M1; n = 202) and of late adopters (M2; n = 266), and on all projects of early (M6; n = 573) and late (M7; n = 331) adopters. Further subsamples use other cut-off points, for example early adopters starting before 2001 (M8; n = 363) and before 2000 (M9; n = 244), and late adopters starting in or after 2005 (M10; n = 235).

Cumulative count of recalls issued by the firm until the prior year (t - 1). Recall counts are accumulated over an equal number of years, 10, for each year in the main models; for example, Accumulated Recalls for a firm for the year 2016 is the sum of all recalls issued by the firm from 2006 to 2015. It is the primary predictor for learning from overall recalls, the base model based on extant research.

Accumulated recalls of a firm that were classified as process-related, accumulated over 10 years up to the prior year. Recalls were classified based on the text of the description for each recall using a combination of manual and automatic text analysis; cross-validating the classification with the self-classification by firms resulted in a 95% match. Process-related recalls represent slip-up failures.

Accumulated recalls of a firm that were classified as design-related, accumulated over 10 years up to the prior year. Recalls were classified based on the text of the description for each recall using a combination of manual and automatic text analysis; cross-validating the classification with the self-classification by firms resulted in a 95% match. Design-related recalls represent knowledge gap failures.

Total number of recalls in a firm-year. Following extant research, the authors use this variable to assess organizational learning from past recall experience. It is the dependent variable in the model of learning from all recalls.
Subsequent Recalls in a firm-year divided into process-related recalls. It is the dependent variable used to test learning from accumulation of process-related recalls.
Subsequent Recalls in a firm-year divided into design-related recalls. It is the dependent variable used to test learning from accumulation of design-related recalls.

Stock of innovations that a firm has accumulated prior to a specific year t starting from the year (t - 10); prior patent counts are accumulated for 10 years. Accumulating prior patent counts for 10 years achieves congruence with the count variables of accumulated recalls, which is helpful because the models estimate interactions of pairs of independent variables. Patents represent the generation of new processes and products.

R&D investment as a percentage of net revenue of the firm for the preceding year (t - 1). It represents firms' strategic decisions to invest in R&D and serves as the moderating variable for the hypotheses on the enhancing effect of R&D efforts.

Respondents characterized the extent to which different elements of systems development knowledge were stored within the CASE repository at their organization. A final set of thirty-two items representing the four different domains of knowledge embeddedness (planning, analysis, design, and construction) was presented, and using a 100 percent scale respondents indicated the proportion of the relevant organizational information stored within the CASE repository. Refinements eliminating items with low loadings or high cross-loadings reduced the final model to twenty-four items for the four dimensions. In the PLS model, knowledge embeddedness was implemented as a formative construct with four indicators: planning, analysis, design, and construction knowledge.

Respondents were asked to identify the types of projects that used CASE in their organization, which focused their attention toward the population of projects that used CASE. They were then asked to indicate the percentage of such projects that had used the CASE technology for at least 25% of the information systems tasks within those projects. Respondents limited their attention to the population of their organizations' systems development projects for just the prior two years.

Respondents named the software development methodology currently implemented at their organization and indicated the extent to which this methodology was in use prior to the implementation of CASE, checking 'not available' if the methodology was implemented during or after the implementation of CASE. The response categories run from not used at all, a few people/projects experimenting with it, a few people/projects regularly use it, a number of people/projects use it, most people/projects regularly use it, to usage has become a standard, with scores from 0 to 5.

Respondents assessed the current use of the software development methodology at their organization on the same set of response categories used for prior methodology use. The categories run from not used at all, a few people/projects experimenting with it, a few people/projects regularly use it, a number of people/projects use it, most people/projects regularly use it, to usage has become a standard, with scores from 0 to 5.

Respondents were asked to indicate the extent to which the methodology is compatible with the implemented CASE technology. The response categories are Highly Compatible, Compatible, Neutral, Slightly Compatible, and Not Compatible.

Management championship was measured through three items adapted from scales developed in earlier research: the amount of IS management support for CASE implementation, the priority placed on CASE implementation relative to other technologies in the IS organization, and the extent to which IS management was convinced about the necessity for implementing CASE technology. Factor analysis showed that the items loaded on a single factor with a high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.90). In the PLS model the aggregate item scores were used for analysis.

SelfRatio_jk is defined as the count of all of firm k's self-citations to patent family j (i.e., forward citations that appear in firm k's patent applications) divided by the count of all forward citations by any firm to that patent family. The authors exclude citations that were added by patent examiners and citations by patent co-authors themselves. Because the measure is at the patent-family level, citations from any patent to any member of its own family are excluded.

Relative giant component size is defined as the number of nodes integrated in the largest component of a network relative to the maximum number that could be integrated. The numerator and denominator are based on all patent applications that firm k submits in year t. Each inventor in the firm is a node and nondirectional ties are recorded each time an inventor collaborates on a patent application with another inventor within the firm.
time_window: firm-year t (patent applications filed in that year)

description: Normalized entropy captures the degree of equality in the size of a network's components, both giant and peripheral. It is computed by first calculating the entropy of the component size distribution and then normalizing it by its maximum value log(C), so that it equals 1 when all components are exactly the same size. Normalized entropy measures the inverse of network integration: higher values of Entropy are associated with lower levels of network integration.
time_window: firm-year t (patent applications filed in that year)

description: SmallWorld is used as a proxy for near decomposability and, following Watts (1999), is calculated from a combination of two measures: the average (characteristic) path length and the clustering coefficient. The characteristic path length is the average number of ties along the shortest path between any two inventors in a firm, and the clustering coefficient is the number of existing connections among a focal firm's inventors divided by the number of possible ties, averaged over all inventors. Small-worldness is determined by comparing these parameters with those of a random network with the same number of nodes and ties, and the authors use the continuous measure rather than assigning a binary type.
Months counts the number of months that have elapsed since the filing of the original priority application. It is introduced as a time-based variable describing patent age at the patent-family level.

The authors content-analyzed the description of each alliance provided in the SDC database. Alliances focused on the discovery and development of new technology were coded as exploration alliances and those focused on marketing and resource utilization as exploitation alliances. A combination of both R&D and other agreements was coded as 0.5 exploration and 0.5 exploitation, and the coding used the perspective of the focal firm.

The dependent variable is a dummy coded 1 for 'partner acquisition' and 0 for 'no partner acquisition'. It captures whether an alliance evolved into an acquisition of an alliance partner, measured at the dyadic level of the alliance partners.
scale: dummy (1 = partner acquisition, 0 = no partner acquisition)

description: For each alliance event the authors recompiled the network matrices by treating the alliance as a node with two partner firms and used Ucinet 6 to compute the constraint score for this alliance node as the value of joint brokerage positions. Following Soda, Usai, and Zaheer (2004), they multiplied the value of constraint by -1 to capture structural holes, the opposite of constraint.

The authors first calculated the degree centrality of each firm in the ego alliance network. They then divided the focal firm's degree centrality by its partner firm's degree centrality to compute the value of relative centrality. A high value indicates that a focal firm has a higher centrality score than its partner firm.

variable_name: Business unit top management overseas (0 = no, 1 = yes)
description: The location of each business unit's top management team was identified by the corporate respondent, to avoid common-method bias. This resulted in a dichotomous variable: 85 business units were located in Sweden (scored 0) and 40 were located overseas (scored 1).

variable_name: Percent business unit HQ functions overseas
description: Business unit respondents indicated the number of business unit HQ functions located outside Sweden, using the same list as for the corporate HQ (investor relations, corporate communications, treasury and group financial management, group tax and legal, group strategic planning, group HR management, group purchasing and logistics, and group R&D). From this the percentage of HQ functions located overseas was calculated. Together with the top management team location this gives one dichotomous and one continuous variable for the business unit HQ.

variable_name: Corporate HQ top management team overseas (0 = no, 1 = yes)
description: Respondents were asked whether the top management teams were located in Sweden or overseas. Of the 35 responding firms, 29 were located in Sweden (scored 0) and 6 were located overseas (scored 1).

Respondents were asked to indicate the number of listed corporate HQ functions that were located outside Sweden: investor relations, corporate communications, treasury and group financial management, group tax and legal, group strategic planning, group HR management, group purchasing and logistics, and group R&D. From this the percentage of corporate HQ functions located overseas was calculated. Legal domicile was deliberately not used because the country is frequently chosen for highly case-specific reasons.

Business unit-level respondents were asked to indicate the percentage of sales units outside Sweden and the percentage of manufacturing units outside Sweden. These two numbers were highly correlated so they were combined to form a single scale.

variable_name: Perceived attractiveness of business climate for business unit HQ location
description: Business unit-level respondents were asked to rate the characteristics of the local business climate on nine specific factors, each on a scale from 1 = very low to 7 = very high. The items were developed from an earlier questionnaire to cover the elements of Porter's diamond model as well as broader attributes of the political and economic environment. The nine items loaded onto a single factor, alpha = 0.75.

Using secondary sources of data (annual reports, Hoovers, analysts reports), the percentage of capital stock owned by non-Swedes was measured as one of two indicators of the influence of international shareholders.

Using secondary sources of data (annual reports, Hoovers, analysts reports), the location of the primary exchange on which the company's shares are traded was coded 0 = Stockholm, 1 = other. This is one of two indicators of the influence of international shareholders.

Using secondary sources of data (annual reports, Hoovers), the percentage of corporate sales outside Sweden and the percentage of corporate competitors located outside Sweden were measured. These two numbers were highly correlated, so they were combined to form a single scale. For competitors, the authors used Hoovers' Directory, which for each corporation lists all major competitors, identified the national home market of each competitor and calculated the percentage that lay outside Sweden.

At the corporate level, interdependence was measured with the entropy index developed by Jacquemin and Berry (1979), which considers the breadth of 3-digit SIC codes in which the MNC competes. The measure includes both the number of 3-digit SIC code businesses in which a firm operates and the proportion of total sales of each of these SIC code segments. The formula is reported in the text as the sum over segments of Pi ln(1/Pi), where Pi is the amount of sales attributed to each 3-digit SIC segment i.

At the business unit level, interdependence was measured in terms of employee flows. Business unit respondents were asked to indicate the number of individuals that had moved from corporate HQ to business unit HQ, and vice versa, over a 3-year period, for each of four categories. An average of all these numbers was used to create an employee flow index.

Using the company's share register for 1999 to identify the name and holding of the largest shareholder, the authors created a single measure of the percentage of voting shares held by this shareholder, ranging from 6 to 100 percent.

Pay premiums were the residuals from a regression of cash compensation on independent variables guided by prior research. The dependent variable was the natural logarithm of CPI-adjusted total cash compensation (salary plus bonus), measured in the last full compensation year before an executive's death; compensation based on long-term performance was not used because it is directly related to prior firm performance. Independent variables were the natural logarithm of CPI-adjusted total assets (firm size), percent change in sales (sales growth), return on assets, market-adjusted stock return, R&D intensity, diversification, foreign market activity, and an indicator for whether the executive of interest received the highest cash compensation at the firm, all reflecting the year prior to the last full compensation year. The regression explained a substantial portion of variance in executive pay (R2 = 62).
time_window: last full compensation year before the executive's death; independent variables in the prior year

description: Executive power was measured with two indicators: board tenure, the number of years a deceased executive had served on the board of her or his firm, and founder status, an indicator variable depicting whether a deceased executive was a founder or founding family member. These measures were standardized and summed to create a single executive power variable; the reliability coefficient for the scale is .74. An executive's percentage of ownership was initially considered but excluded from further analysis because of unacceptably high cross-loadings.

Governance strength was measured with two indicators: board independence, the percentage of independent board members, who were defined as those who were not current or past employees and who did not have substantial business or family ties with the management of the firm whose board they sat on, and an indicator variable depicting whether or not a firm had a nominating committee (1 = "yes," 0 = "no"). These two measures were standardized and summed to create a single governance strength variable; the reliability coefficient for this scale is .64. The presence of an external shareholder with more than 5 percent of a firm's shares was initially considered but excluded from further analysis because of unacceptably high cross-loadings.

Abnormal stock performance was measured as the two-day cumulative prediction error around the executive's sudden death. Normal stock performance was estimated by regressing daily firm returns on daily market returns (the value-weighted index) over 221 trading days, from day -250 to day -30. Daily abnormal returns, called prediction errors, were obtained by subtracting predicted returns from actual returns for each day of the event window, which included the event date (day 0, the date of death or the first trading day thereafter) and one trading day after the date of death (day +1); cumulative prediction errors are the sum of the prediction errors during the event window and represent the stock's two-day abnormal performance.
time_window: event window day 0 to day +1; estimation window day -250 to day -30

description: Composite of the rate and volatility of change in industry variables, created by averaging the z-scores of the rate and volatility measures because the two were highly correlated (ranging from 0.64 to 0.88). Rate of change was measured with three established and validated indicators: number of new products introduced, time span (number of years) between new products introduced, and depreciation rates of capital equipment (coefficient alpha = 0.92). Volatility was calculated from a regression of yearly net industry sales on year, with volatility equal to the standard error of the regression slope coefficient divided by average sales, estimated for each of the 25 years. Industry velocity was measured in the year preceding the year in which the attention focus and causal logic variables were measured.

variable_name: Attention focus on the task sector
description: Measured by network-based measures of centrality of the concepts in the letters to shareholders; centrality reflects the degree to which a concept dominates the causal relationships in a cause map, and the greater the centrality of a concept, the greater the attention focus around that concept. Two centrality measures were used: degree (how well connected a given concept is within a network) and closeness (how close a given concept is to other concepts in the network), computed with Netanalysis software, which uses standard social network algorithms. The centrality of the task sector was represented by the centrality score of the most central concept in that environmental sector. Because the degree and closeness measures were highly correlated, a composite was created by averaging the z-scores of the two measures; observations were gathered from the letters to shareholders for each year from 1970 to 1994 and lagged one year behind the industry velocity measures.

variable_name: Attention focus on the general sector
description: Measured by network-based measures of centrality of the concepts in the letters to shareholders; centrality reflects the degree to which a concept dominates the causal relationships in a cause map, and the greater the centrality of a concept, the greater the attention focus around that concept. Two centrality measures were used: degree (how well connected a given concept is within a network) and closeness (how close a given concept is to other concepts in the network), computed with Netanalysis software, which uses standard social network algorithms. The centrality of the general sector was represented by the centrality score of the most central concept in that environmental sector. Because the degree and closeness measures were highly correlated, a composite was created by averaging the z-scores of the two measures; observations were gathered from the letters to shareholders for each year from 1970 to 1994 and lagged one year behind the industry velocity measures.

Based on in-degree and out-degree analysis of the causal links between environment and strategy in the causal maps: a high number of in-degrees for environmental concepts suggests that strategies influence the environment, and high out-degrees for strategy concepts suggest that strategies can influence the environment, both indicating proactive causal logic. An exploratory factor analysis of the six measures yielded two distinct factors, with in-degree of environment (0.87), out-degree of strategy (0.91), and percentage of strategy → environment links (0.95) loading highly on the proactive factor. The composite measure of proactive causal logic averages the z-scores of these three indicators; observations were gathered yearly from 1970 to 1994 and lagged one year behind the industry velocity measures.

Based on in-degree and out-degree analysis of the causal links between environment and strategy in the causal maps: a high number of in-degrees for strategy concepts suggests that firms consider strategy as primarily an effect of, or response to, environmental concepts, and high out-degrees for environmental concepts suggest that firms perceive the environment as a contingency or a given, both indicating deterministic causal logic. A factor analysis of the six measures yielded two distinct factors, with out-degree of environment (0.93), in-degree of strategy (0.89), and percentage of environment → strategy links (0.88) loading highly on the deterministic factor. The composite measure averages the z-scores of these three indicators; observations were gathered yearly from 1970 to 1994 and lagged one year behind the industry velocity measures.

variable_name: Speed of response to general sector events
description: Measured as the number of days between the occurrence of a general sector event and the initiation of the first strategic response; the fewer the days, the faster the speed of response, so the variable has a reverse interpretation. Strategic actions considered responses to each change were listed from 10-K reports, U.S. Department of Commerce Industry Outlook reports, Wall Street Journal announcements, and published histories of the four industries, and validated with industry analysts. To ascertain the approximate date when each sampled firm initiated the first strategic response action, articles pertaining to each response were content analyzed in the F&S Predicast database, which consists of news article titles and abstracts. Attention focus and causal logic variables were measured in the year preceding the year in which speed of strategic response was measured.

variable_name: Speed of response to task sector events
description: Measured as the number of days between the occurrence of a task sector event and the initiation of the first strategic response; the fewer the days, the faster the speed of response, so the variable has a reverse interpretation. Strategic actions considered responses to each change were listed from 10-K reports, U.S. Department of Commerce Industry Outlook reports, Wall Street Journal announcements, and published histories of the four industries, and validated with industry analysts. To ascertain the approximate date when each sampled firm initiated the first strategic response action, articles pertaining to each response were content analyzed in the F&S Predicast database, which consists of news article titles and abstracts. Attention focus and causal logic variables were measured in the year preceding the year in which speed of strategic response was measured.

Respondents clicked cells of an on-screen matrix that arrayed three clusters of ten job profiles (IP generation, IP protection, IP utilization) against fifteen IP-related activities organized into the same three clusters. The degree of within-unit functional specialization was calculated by counting the number of clicks along the main diagonal of the matrix and dividing it by the total number of clicks. At its upper bound the variable indicates extreme specialization and no cross-functional involvement. A squared term of the measure is also used in the models.
level: firm (largest business line of the corporation)

description: Constructed from a dummy variable capturing whether a patent was granted within the study window. This dummy was divided by the average granting ratio (patents granted/patent applications) for the patent's technological sector and multiplied by the average time between filing and grant in that sector. FGA thus increases with average lag time and decreases with the average granting rate of the technology sector, and is computed so that it can be estimated with ordinary least squares.
time_window: applications filed 2003-2004, observed up to a 40-month window ending April 2006

description: Second version of the dependent variable, used in the survival analysis models: the hazard of patent grant (and, separately, non-grant), estimated from the data on the time between application date and outcome and the nature of the outcome. In the grant model all outcomes other than grant are treated as censored; in the non-grant model all outcomes other than withdrawal or refusal are treated as censored. The authors estimate separate models for the hazards of grant and non-grant to show that the same underlying process generates both outcomes.

A six-item scale capturing information-gathering efforts in supply-side domains external to the organization, answered on seven-point scales anchored at 'strongly disagree' and 'strongly agree'. One item is reverse-scored. Item scores are averaged, so that higher values denote a larger amount of nonlocal supply-side search (a higher exploration orientation).

A six-item scale capturing information-gathering efforts in demand-side domains external to the organization, answered on seven-point scales anchored at 'strongly disagree' and 'strongly agree'. One item is reverse-scored. Item scores are averaged, so that higher values denote a larger amount of nonlocal demand-side search.

A four-item scale capturing information-gathering efforts in geographic domains external to the organization, answered on seven-point scales anchored at 'strongly disagree' and 'strongly agree'. One item is reverse-scored. Item scores are averaged, so that higher values denote a larger amount of boundary-spanning spatial search.

variable_name: Exploration-exploitation orientation (supply-side and demand-side and geographic search)
description: Composite measure formed from the supply-side, demand-side, and geographic search items of the instrument; the firm's exploration-exploitation orientation is given by its average score across the items, with a high average score indicating a more exploration-oriented company and a lower average score a relatively more exploitation-oriented firm.

The percentage of total sales accounted for by new products introduced in the past three years. New products were defined as products that were different from earlier products in terms of technology employed, or component and design changes, or functionality, thereby representing to customers a fresh value proposition compared to products offered earlier by the company.
A three-item instrument (Miller 1987) used to measure the rate and unpredictability of technical change in the firm's industry, with a reliability coefficient of 0.77.

The extent to which firms in a dyad cite each other in their USPTO patent applications in the five years following the observation year, calculated as a proportion of the total citations made by the firms in the same five-year window. The formula combines Firm 1's citations to Firm 2 and Firm 2's citations to Firm 1 in the following five years, each divided by the citing firm's total citations to any firm in the same window. Total citations are used as a base to adjust for relative differences in general propensity to cite across firms.
time_window: five years following the observation year

description: The weighted average of the Hicks-Kenworthy corporatism values for the two firms in a dyad, where the underlying country-level scores range from 0 to 1, with 1 most corporatist. Values for dyads range from less corporatist or more pluralist to more corporatist.

The weighted average of the corporatism values for all firms in the SSO each year, where each firm's country score is weighted by a sociotechnical weighting that gives greater weight to firms with more cumulative patents and greater prominence in the interorganizational network. The weighted corporatism score derived from firms' corporatism and the corporatism scores assigned to the SSO-sponsoring countries (1 = corporatist, 0.5 = mixed, 0 = pluralist) were averaged to create the final measure. Where a dyad simultaneously participated in two SSOs in a given year, the corporatism values corresponding to each SSO were averaged.
scale: from less corporatist (0.01) to more corporatist (0.92)

description: Jaffe's (1986) measure of technological distance, calculated as the correlation between the patent profiles of the two firms in a dyad for each observation year. Each patent profile is a vector of the number of patents in each three-digit patent class; 52 patent classes were identified.
scale: 0 to 1, higher values representing greater technological distance

description: The dependent variable for all hypothesis testing was governance mode, a categorical variable. Licensing was coded as 0 and acquisitions were coded as 1. The mode of each sourcing arrangement was identified in public announcements and executives subsequently verified the nature of the agreement and that the underlying motivation was the pursuit of technology.

Measured with a three-item Likert scale. The items pertain to the threat of being taken advantage of by potential partners, the likelihood of partner dishonesty, and the need for extensive contracts and monitoring. The higher the score, the greater the perceived threat of opportunism; the reliability of the scale is .67.

Measured with five Likert-scale items (1 to 7, strongly disagree/strongly agree) that tap the uncertainty associated with both the engineering and design of a sourced technology and the technology's commercial success. The scale was influenced by the previous efforts of Simonin (1991) and Souder and Shrivastava (1985). The higher the score, the greater the perceived threat of commercial failure; the reliability of the scale is .85.

Measured with a three-item Likert scale. The items pertain to whether the technology would allow the firm to attain benefits that the competition would be unable to match regardless of its efforts, whether the firm would be able to effectively set itself apart from other firms in the industry throughout the life of the technology, and whether the technology would allow the firm to exploit opportunities that the competition would be unable to exploit. The higher the score, the greater the perceived potential for a sustainable advantage; the reliability of the scale is .77.

A firm's propensity for risk taking was measured with a four-item Likert scale (1 to 7, strongly disagree/strongly agree) based on the work of Venkatraman (1989). The higher the scale, the more risk averse the firm is in general; the reliability of the scale is .70.

The percentage of total equity owned by the managers of each firm, collected from Compact Disclosure (1993-94) for the beginning of the year in which the focal licensing agreement or acquisition was announced.
time_window: beginning of the year of the focal announcement (1993-94)

description: Built from the accounts-receivable-to-sales and inventory-to-sales ratios, which loaded on the same factor. Each firm's ratios were indexed against four-digit SIC median ratios, then standardized and added together to represent the level of recoverable slack. Recoverable slack represents the level of discretionary resources absorbed in a firm's operations. Data for each firm came from COMPUSTAT for the fiscal year prior to the year of the focal licensing agreement or acquisition.
time_window: fiscal year prior to the focal agreement

description: Built from the debt-to-equity ratio and the inverse of the interest coverage ratio (interest expense/income before interest and taxes), considered as ratios for the lack of potential slack; these two ratios loaded together. Each firm's ratios were indexed against four-digit SIC median ratios, then standardized and added together to represent potential slack. Potential slack reflects the extent of a firm's debt capacity and represents excess resources not yet absorbed into its operations. Data came from COMPUSTAT for the fiscal year prior to the focal agreement.
time_window: fiscal year prior to the focal agreement

description: The number of LEED registered buildings (logged) in each MSA-year. The authors state that this measure captures adoption in the green building context because registering a building inherently requires the purchase of products and services that the firms in the sample offered.

The number of active peer firms (logged) in the same MSA as the focal firm for each firm-year observation. Industry peers are defined at the granular product category level: for example, a firm producing doors and windows is unlikely to be in direct competition with one selling heating and air conditioning equipment. Restricting the measure to peers in the same product category allows more accurate identification of localized competitive effects.

A factor composed of six items for each MSA-year observation. The first two items capture regional ideologies of an MSA's political leaders and citizens on a liberal-conservative continuum, weighted for each MSA by population; the third is the percentage of voters in a congressional district who voted Republican in national elections; the fourth is the ratio of contributions to Republican candidates relative to all donations; the fifth is the local tax burden for businesses, reverse-coded; and the sixth is labor union density, obtained from the annual number of registered labor unions, aggregated to the MSA, reverse-coded and normalized by population. A principal component analysis loaded these six items onto a single factor with an eigenvalue of 2.25 and an alpha value of 0.66.

A multidimensional factor composed of five items for each MSA-year observation. The first item is the League of Conservation Voters environmental voting record scorecard, which ranges from 0 to 100 and measures how members of Congress vote on environmental issues, averaged across the Congresspeople representing each congressional district and aggregated to the MSA. The second, third, and fourth items are the number, revenue, and assets of environmental nonprofits per capita in an MSA. The fifth item is the number of nonprofit organizations that were members of the USGBC per capita in each MSA. A principal component analysis loaded these five items onto a single factor with an eigenvalue of 2.52 and an alpha value of 0.74.

A dummy variable indicating the absence (zero) or presence (one) of institutional complexity. The authors first generated a two-by-two matrix of market and proenvironmental logics for each year in the sample using a median split, and an MSA-year is coded one when both the market and proenvironmental logic values are above the sample median levels, i.e., the high-high quadrant.

A dummy variable indicating whether the focal firm was de novo (one) or de alio (zero). To be classified as de novo a firm must have been founded after the creation of the USGBC in 1994 (hence less than six years old upon the creation of the GreenSpec directory in 1999), explicitly stated a proenvironmental focus in its mission statement, and only sold products for the green building market. Founding years were identified through a search of company websites and online databases, mission statements were located through the WayBack Machine, and product catalogs were examined in the earliest year available and all years of directory listing. Based on these criteria the authors identified 297 firms as de novo entrants and 936 as diversifying de alio incumbents.

A binary variable that takes the value of zero for all years in which the firm survives (i.e., was listed in the GreenSpec directory) and is set to one for the first year in which a firm is delisted in the GreenSpec directory, other than the final year of the sample window in 2007. The variable is set to missing for all years prior to entry as well as all years subsequent to a firm not appearing in the directory. The authors confirmed that exits of de novo firms reflected failure through web searches and by trying to reach the firms by telephone.
The authors measured the number of female directors on the board as the total number of women serving on the board. Board data were collected from the BOARDEX database.

The authors adopted the measure developed and validated by Eklund and Mannor (2021) and content analyzed the CEOs' presentations at the quarterly conference calls with Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count software using 13 dictionaries of strategic issues. A Herfindahl measure based on the proportion of words/phrases associated with each strategic issue category in a quarterly earnings call was used, and then subtracted from one so that larger values indicate a greater breadth of strategic attention and multiplied by 100 so that it ranges from 0 to 100.
The authors obtained gender information for each CEO through EXECUCOMP and coded gender as a dichotomous variable, with gender equal to 1 if the CEO is a woman.

The authors first obtained information regarding the appointment date of a CEO at a firm from EXECUCOMP and then calculated the CEO's tenure by subtracting the year of appointment from the year of the conference call.

CEO overpayment was operationalized by taking the residuals from the regression of CEO total compensation (TDC1 from EXECUCOMP) on firm size (natural log of firm assets), firm performance (ROA), CEO tenure, whether the CEO is an insider hire, CEO duality, one-digit industry dummies and a year dummy, using random effects with robust standard errors. The authors used the residuals to calculate CEO overpayment, with positive residuals representing CEO overpayment, and coded overpayment as equal to the residual value when it is positive and zero otherwise.

The BHAR measure was obtained through EVENTUS, with an observation window of (0 day, 360 days) starting on the day of the earnings call. It is calculated by comparing the firm's stock returns for the period including the day of the quarterly earnings conference call to 360 days after the call to the returns of a reference portfolio of comparable firms in the same period; BHAR is measured as the difference between the firm's actual stock return and the expected return based on that reference portfolio.
time_window: (0 day, 360 days) starting on the day of the earnings call

description: Indicator that receives the value of 1 for married-owner and nonmarried-owner family firms, and 0 for all other firm types. A firm is classified as family-owned if at least two shareholders have the same last name and hold a majority of the company shares.

Indicator equal to 1 for a family-owned firm whose two leading shareholders have the same last name and are of different gender. Gender is taken from an Amadeus gender variable for shareholders who also appear on manager or director lists, from 'Mr.' or 'Mrs.' prefixes in names, and otherwise from public sources on the most common male and female names for different countries. Misclassification is acknowledged and is said to bias estimates against finding differences between ownership categories.
Sales growth is the annual change in log sales. It is one of the measures of conservatism, where lower sales growth indicates more conservative behavior.

Liquidity is cash over assets. It is one of the measures of conservatism: a greater share of assets held as cash means a firm has a buffer to meet costs or make investments without relying on external credit markets.
Leverage is the sum of current and noncurrent liabilities over assets. It is one of the measures of conservatism: lower leverage indicates more conservative behavior.

Investment is the annual change in log total assets. It is one of the measures of conservatism: a lower rate of investment is associated with a more cautious or conservative management approach and business model.
Return on assets is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) over total assets. The variable is winsorized above 2 and below -2.
Profit margin is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) over sales. The variable is winsorized above 2 and below -2.

Wage costs per employee, entered in logarithmic form as the dependent variable of the wage analysis. The authors report that married-owner family firms have the lowest wages, and that these differences are not driven by very young firms or firms with a very small number of employees.

The annual count of bank entries, sorted into home country subpopulations; each country of origin, ten in all, had a set of annual observations. In line with the conventional approach in organizational ecology, the analysis of entries into subpopulations was based on the founding of the first organization of that subpopulation, and because in a substantial number of cases only the year of a bank's founding was known, event counts were aggregated by year.

Measured as the sum of the grades of membership of all organizations in the total population. In the illustrative year with four British and two Russian banks, traditional density would be six foreign banks, but fuzzy density would be (0.33 x 2) + (0.67 x 4), or 3.33. The measure is defined at the population level.

Calculated as the average grade of membership in the population. The historical trajectory shows contrast was particularly high when a homogeneous set of British banks dominated the industry in the 19th century and lower later, when the population included banks from a variety of nations.
scale: average grade of membership, ranging from zero to one

description: Acceptance by external audiences was measured in terms of media mentions of banking in Shanghai in the New York Times and in the Times of London. For each observation, mentions in the two publications in the two preceding years were added to construct the audience acceptance measure; the nature of the articles was not relevant to these counts.

Calculated as the density of the subpopulation divided by the density of the total population in a particular year. For example, in a year with four British banks and two Russian banks, the grade of membership of each Russian bank would be 0.33 (2 divided by 6) and that of British banks 0.67. The scores were based on an extensive study of background materials describing the institutional context of foreign banking in Shanghai.

Annual volume of beer imports, measured in millions of gallons and obtained from the Brewers Almanac. The authors use it as the indicator of the volume of the new market niche, following Delacroix and Solt's use of wine imports as an indicator of niche volume; imported products come closest to resembling microbrewery and brewpub products.
Annual volume of beer imports, measured in millions of gallons and obtained from the Brewers Almanac, used as the indicator of the volume of the new market niche in which brewpubs are founded.

variable_name: Industry concentration (4-firm ratio as a percentage)
description: Four-firm concentration ratio, calculated as the combined market share of the four largest firms, expressed as a percentage and based on sales data reported in the Modern Brewery Age Bluebooks and the Microbrewery Resource Handbooks. The authors use it as the indicator of resource-partitioning, while noting that market concentration is a weak proxy at best for the degree of resource-partitioning.

variable_name: Industry concentration (4-firm ratio as a percentage)
description: Four-firm concentration ratio, the combined market share of the four largest brewing firms as a percentage, based on sales data reported in the Modern Brewery Age Bluebooks and the Microbrewery Resource Handbooks and used as the indicator of resource-partitioning.

Annual count of microbrewery foundings in a state, calculated from event-history data on the population of U.S. brewing firms. The primary source, American Breweries, was verified against annual lists in the Modern Brewery Age Bluebooks and the Brewers Almanac, and its historical coverage extended to 1995 using Tremblay and Tremblay (1988) and the Microbrewery Resource Handbooks.

Annual count of brewpub foundings in a state, derived from the same event-history data on U.S. brewing firms. Brewpubs are at risk of founding only after the organizational form is legalized in a given state, so the state-year spell is included only once brewpubs are legal; the analysis includes 305 state-year spells.

Organizations' acquisition experience is measured by the number of acquisitions the sample firms made, operationalized as the total number of acquisitions greater than $10 million in asset value made by a firm from 1948 up to the acquisition of interest. Data were collected across three time periods from three data sources: the FTC Large Merger Series (1948-1979), the SDC data base (1980-1983), and the Lexis/Nexus data base (1984-1992).
time_window: from 1948 up to the acquisition of interest

description: The proportion of previous acquisitions made by a firm that shared the same 4-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code as the current acquisition. It compares an acquisition with previous acquisitions made by the same firm.
time_window: prior acquisitions up to the acquisition of interest

description: Acquisition performance is measured as the abnormal return: the difference between the observed return for a security and the predicted or normal return for the same security during a window around the acquisition announcement. The market-adjusted equation, in which the abnormal return is the stock return minus the return on the market portfolio, is the one reported; the authors state that the same results were obtained with the market- and risk-adjusted equation. Betas were estimated over an estimation period of 240 days, from 300 days before to 61 days before the event, and abnormal returns were computed from five trading days before to five trading days after the announcement. The regression equation itself appears in the paper as a formula that is not readable in this text.
time_window: five trading days before to five trading days after the acquisition announcement; estimation period 300 to 61 days before the event

description: Each sukuk's fixed annual interest payment that the bond issuer promises to pay, expressed as a percentage of the bond's face (or par) value. The rate is set when the bond is first issued and does not change; for example, a $1,000 bond with a 5% coupon rate pays the investor $50 in interest every year. Coupon rates are set by issuers with their arrangers, who are cognizant of what consumers are willing to accept, and the observations reflect completed market transactions rather than unsuccessful issuance attempts. The coupon rate is multiplied by 100 to ease interpretation (e.g., a 5% coupon rate is denoted as 5).

The number of 'sheikhs' among the Shariah scholars who approved each sukuk. 'Sheikh' is an honorific title signifying respect, commonly denoting a religious leader, akin to 'Sir/Dame' or 'His/Her Highness' in English, and is usually conferred by community leaders or a council of sheikhs. The names of all the Shariah scholars approving the sukuk appear on the sukuk's prospectus. In the data set there are 64 sheikhs out of 161 Shariah scholars, and the average sukuk includes 3.5 sheikhs on its board, approximately half of the average board size of 6.9 scholars.

Provided by IdealRatings, the rating is based on 21 general and 23 product-specific criteria that comprehensively cover all sukuk standards across different Shariah schools of thought.
