Each criterion is weighted by its importance in Shariah law, so that the total points associated with it can range from one to five points; the criteria range from whether the proceeds of the sukuk will be used in Shariah-compliant investments to more technical aspects such as whether sukuk holders are restricted from their asset disposition rights. All rating criteria are based on objective factors, meaning the sukuk prospectus must explicitly outline the relevant factors to receive a score for that criterion. The theoretical maximum score is 215, and the vast majority of sukuk have compliance scores ranging from 21 to 89.
scale: weighted score (one to five points per criterion; theoretical maximum 215)

description: A composite change variable recording decreased internationalization between successive record years, built from the change in the firm's recorded international strategy categories. Its components are described by the authors as ceasing to operate overseas manufacturing facilities and becoming a U.S.-only participant. The variable is a 0-1 dummy.
level: firm (corporate medical sector and imaging business unit)
time_window: change from period t to period t+1 across the record years 1975, 1978, 1983, 1986 and 1989

description: A composite change variable recording increased internationalization between successive record years, built from the change in the firm's recorded international strategy categories. The authors discuss initiating overseas manufacturing as one of its components. The variable is a 0-1 dummy.
level: firm (corporate medical sector and imaging business unit)
time_window: change from period t to period t+1 across the record years 1975, 1978, 1983, 1986 and 1989

description: A composite change variable recording that a firm starts importing. The authors defined the import category separately because they could not make a strong prior argument for whether it represented increased or decreased international presence. It is a 0-1 dummy.
level: firm (corporate medical sector and imaging business unit)
time_window: change from period t to period t+1 across the record years 1975, 1978, 1983, 1986 and 1989

description: The dependent variable for the market share analysis, defined from the participation and market share data as a firm's average annual change in industry market share between successive record years. The participation and market share data were gathered from an extensive archival search of academic, industry, and government sources, supplemented by interviews with industry and academic participants.
level: firm (corporate medical sector and imaging business unit)
time_window: between successive record years from 1975 to 1989

description: The dependent variable for the survival analysis, defined as the number of years that a corporation continued to participate in the industry after each record year, with a minimum value of one year for firms that exited during the period. A 0-1 right-censor dummy variable recorded firms that continued to participate in the industry at the end of the study.
level: firm (corporate medical sector and imaging business unit)

variable_name: period strategy dummy variables (DOM, IMP, EXP, OVM, MNE)
description: The authors obtained the value of the international strategy variables for each firm in each year that the directory was published and treated the categories as 0-1 dummy variables. The trade guides classify medical sector companies in five relevant categories of international strategy for the record years: domestic-only, importer, exporter, overseas manufacturer, and multinational status. The categories are not mutually exclusive, so a firm might be both an importer and an exporter.
level: firm (corporate medical sector and imaging business unit)

description: The dependent variable, specialization in generality, is the joint occurrence of two events: the focal firm invests in more general upstream resources and it trades in intermediate markets rather than entering downstream markets. It corresponds to the strategy the focal firm pursued in each period among the four possible strategies identified. It takes the value one in firm-years in which investment in general upstream resources = 1 and trading in intermediate markets = 1.

Investment in general upstream resources is a dummy equal to one if the firm increases its average laser generality from year t - 1 to year t and zero otherwise. The degree of the firm's technology generality in each year is the average degree of generality of the lasers in the firm's portfolio. The individual laser's degree of generality is the ratio of the number of uses/markets to which that specific laser type can be applied to the total number of applications/markets across all laser types.
time_window: change from year t - 1 to year t

description: Trading in intermediate markets is a dummy equal to one if in year t the firm exploits any new market in which laser technology could in principle be applied by trading rather than entering. The industry directory indicates whether each firm produces and sells lasers to downstream firms (trades the upstream resource in intermediate markets) versus (also) producing and selling laser systems, the downstream product. The variable takes the value one if the directory indicated that the focal firm was selling lasers to downstream firms and zero if the directory indicated instead that the focal firm entered downstream and also began producing and selling a laser system in a new market.

Downstream production cost is a dummy equal to one for firms operating in a state that introduced the regulation after its enactment and zero otherwise. The state regulations impose obligations on firms manufacturing laser systems inside the state, including registration requirements and fees, injury reporting and regular inspections. In the period considered the new regulations were introduced by the states of New York (1994), Arizona (1996), Florida (1996), Massachusetts (1997), Illinois (1997), and Texas (1999).
time_window: from the year of enactment onward

description: Lack of downstream assets distinguishes between firms that, when deciding to trade versus enter a new downstream market, do not already own downstream assets and capabilities and firms that do. It is a dummy equal to one if a firm, before a certain year t, was not producing and selling laser systems, the downstream product. To alleviate any potential endogeneity between the regulatory change and the decision to vertically integrate, it is measured by looking at the status of the firm in the year immediately before the regulatory change for firms based in states where the regulation is issued and the year of entry into the database for firms based in states in which such regulation was never issued.
time_window: status in the year immediately before the regulatory change, or the year of entry into the database

description: Breadth of demand is calculated by looking at how firms operating in downstream markets are distributed across them for each firm-year. For each focal firm in the sample that supplies lasers, the authors consider the markets in which its lasers are potentially applicable and calculate the variable as one minus the Herfindhal index of concentration of downstream buyers across these markets. Its value is low when potential downstream buyers of the focal firm are mostly concentrated in a few markets and high when potential downstream buyers are instead equally spread across markets.

Coded from synopses of alliance activities provided by the SDC database, the Lexis-Nexis database, and the RDS Business Reference Suite, on a scale ranging from 1 ('very incremental') to 7 ('very radical'). Two independent coders coded the synopses; there was an initial 78 percent agreement between the raters and Cohen's kappa was .83. The raters discussed and resolved disagreements, and the resolved scores were used in the analyses. To eliminate time bias in the coding, the coding of radicality was standardized by year.

The annual measure of intellectual property protection in the market was taken from the World Competitiveness Yearbook, published by the International Institute for Management Development, which conducts executive surveys annually to quantify issues such as intellectual property protection that are not easily measured. The variable was centered to reduce multicollinearity problems.

A categorical variable capturing the relationship between alliance partners, using the number of prior shared alliances as a proxy to categorize friends, acquaintances, and strangers. Partner was set to 1 when alliance partners were strangers (no alliance in the past five years), to 2 when they were acquaintances (one alliance during the past five years), and to 3 when they were friends (two or more alliances in the past five years).
time_window: five years prior to the alliance

description: A dummy variable created for the analysis of the dynamic aspects of alliance formation decisions. Friend equaled 1 when an R&D alliance was formed between friends and 0 otherwise.
time_window: five years prior to the alliance

description: The dependent variable capturing alliance governance mode. Equity was set to 1 when an R&D alliance was organized as an equity-based joint venture and to 0 when it was organized as a non-equity-based contract.

The dependent variable capturing the vertical scope of alliance activities. Scope was set to 1 when an alliance involved R&D activities exclusively; such alliances are more narrow in scope than alliances including manufacturing and/or marketing in addition to collaborative R&D, for which scope equaled 0.
scale: 0/1 (1 = R&D only, 0 = R&D plus manufacturing and/or marketing)

description: The number of successful IPOs in each venture capital firm's Time2 portfolio. A successful IPO is identified using a buy-and-hold strategy as suggested by Ritter (1991): the IPO must have a compounded daily return greater than the return generated by the corresponding daily NASDAQ Composite Index, documented as of the end of each month (where a month is defined as a successive 21-day trading period relative to the IPO offering date), cumulatively, for the IPO's first 12 consecutive months in the aftermarket. The algorithm used is mathematically presented in Appendix 1.

A venture capital firm's product line is defined by the IPOs in which it invests, where an IPO is defined by its primary 3-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code. Any two venture capital firms, if not co-investing, are considered to have competing products if their IPOs are in the same 3-digit SIC code. For each focal firm the authors first calculated the proportion of its IPOs sharing the same 3-digit SIC code with the competing IPOs of every other venture capital firm in the sample, comparing each focal firm with the other 79 firms, and then subtracted each proportion from 1 to arrive at a distinctiveness score (which ranged from 0 to 1.0). These distinctiveness scores were aggregated with every other firm in the sample to give the product niche score. A high product niche score indicates that the firm's product portfolio was relatively distinctive compared to the product portfolios of other firms.
scale: distinctiveness scores ranging from 0 to 1.0, aggregated

description: A process niche captures the extent to which a firm differentiates itself by operating its business using a distinctive process or processes; venture capital firms operate differently in terms of whether they are involved with investments at different stages of a start-up's development, and by being involved in certain stages a venture capital firm creates a profile of its operational knowledge. Using data from Galante's Directories, the authors applied Baum and Oliver's (1996) niche measure to indicate the extent to which a venture capital firm uses a distinctive set of investment stage knowledge. A venture capital firm with a high process niche score used processes that were different compared to the processes used by other firms, and a firm with a low process niche score was very similar to its competitors in terms of its operational processes. Appendix 2 shows the computational detail for the process niche measure; the formula block itself is not readable in this text.

Based on Burt's (1992) network redundancy measure, network embeddedness was operationalized to represent the interconnectedness of each venture capital firm's contacts within the dataset. Each venture capital firm's network is the set of inter-firm relationships defined by the number of times each firm co-invested in IPOs with partner venture capital firms during Time1. Because the redundancy measure can be biased by network size and the two could not be included simultaneously as separate variables, the authors divided the network redundancy measure by network size and then multiplied the result by 100 to adjust it to a scale comparable to that of other variables. The resulting measure reflects the proportional redundancy in a focal firm's network: a high measure indicates that a focal firm's network consists of tightly connected others relative to its network size, and a low measure indicates unconnected or loosely connected others relative to network size.
scale: proportional redundancy (network redundancy divided by network size, multiplied by 100)

description: First-day stock return was the percent change in stock price during the first day of trading for an IPO, computed as ([closing price - offer price] / offer price). First-day trading information for the sample of IPOs was obtained from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) tapes.

R&D intensity was measured as the ratio of R&D expenditures divided by sales in the year prior to the initial public offering. Following Guo et al. (2005), the authors used a log transformation of (R&D/sales x 100 + 1) to account for the skewness in the data. Firm assets, sales, and R&D expenditures in the year prior to the IPO were obtained from Standard & Poor's COMPUSTAT data tapes; in some cases R&D, sales, and asset figures were also obtained from the IPO prospectus.

Patent stock was measured by summing the number of patents that a firm had filed for in the five years prior to its IPO. Following common practice, firm patents were dated according to application (as opposed to granting) date. To account for the skewness in the data, the authors used a log transformation of the number of patents plus one.
time_window: five years prior to the IPO

description: To measure the transparency of the link between patenting and value appropriation, the authors used dummy variables to identify whether an IPO was in a discrete or complex product industry using the classification scheme developed by Cohen et al. (2000). Industries with an ISIC code lower than 2900 (e.g., chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and metals) were coded as discrete, and those with an ISIC code of 2900 or higher (e.g., machinery, computers, and electrical equipment) were coded as complex. If a firm was operating in a discrete product industry, the link was coded as transparent ('high transparency' = 1, 0 otherwise); if in a complex product industry, it was coded as opaque ('low transparency' = 1, 0 otherwise).

Indicator coded as 1 if firm j entered host country i in year t, and 0 otherwise. Following the definition of direct investment of the OECD and the IMF, market entry was ascertained if a firm established a wholly owned facility or acquired at least 10 percent of the ordinary shares of a host country firm. Observed for each firm-country-year of the observation period.

Count of all board ties to experienced partners, regardless of the type of tie. A partner counts only for the specific host countries it had previously entered, so the number of ties depends on partners' prior market entries in that host country; the variable is updated annually for each focal firm-target market combination and lagged one year with respect to the dependent variable. It is used in a baseline model to establish a general effect for interlocks.

Count of ties formed by managers of experienced firms who serve on the focal firm's board, counted on a market-by-market basis so that a tie counts only where the partner had previously entered that host country. The variable is updated annually for each focal firm-target market combination and lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Count of ties created by the focal firm's managers who serve on the board of other experienced firms, counted on a market-by-market basis according to the partner's prior entry into the specific host country. The variable is updated annually for each focal firm-target market combination and lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Count of the focal firm's board members who are directors of another firm with experience in a particular emerging market but play no managerial role in either firm. Counted on a market-by-market basis and lagged one year relative to the dependent variable. These ties are not distinguished as CEO or non-CEO because the individuals creating them have no managerial responsibility in either firm.

Count of outgoing ties created by the focal firm's CEO, that is, ties formed by the manager with formal authority in the focal firm who serves on the board of an experienced firm. Distinguished from outgoing ties created by other members of the top management team to test whether CEOs' ties are more influential than those of non-CEOs.

Count of outgoing ties created by members of the focal firm's top management team who are not CEOs. These managers have similar opportunities as the CEO to learn from other firms but a disadvantage with respect to authority and discretion to use their learning.

Count of incoming ties formed by CEOs of experienced firms who serve on the focal firm's board and are perceived as the architects of their companies' market entry strategies. Distinguished from incoming ties created by non-CEO managers of experienced firms.
Count of incoming ties formed by managers of experienced firms who are not CEOs but serve on the focal firm's board. Distinguished from incoming ties created by CEOs of experienced firms.

Number of years since a firm's first market entry in any of the 21 former Warsaw Pact countries, capturing each firm's general regional experience with running operations in the region. Measured as of year t-1 with respect to the dependent variable. In robustness checks an alternative measure counting the number of countries a firm had entered was used.

variable_name: specific cue for CEO / CFO / CMO / COO position
description: Following the attenuation effect principle, the specific expertise cue was computed from its constitutive competence marker categories as their multiplicative sum; the combinatory formula itself is not legible in the text. The relevant competence markers were revealed by qualitative interviews: the first competence marker is 0.5 for actual prior experience in the respective position (CEO, CFO, CMO, or COO) and 0 for no prior experience in the position, and the second is 0.5 for prior work experience relevant to the position (entrepreneurial experience for CEO, financial experience for CFO, marketing professional experience for CMO, and process or operations management experience for COO) and 0 for no prior relevant experience. A separate cue was computed for each task position.

Computed from two equally weighted competence marker categories: 0.5 for an ethnic majority participant (European American) and 0 for an ethnic minority participant, and 0.5 for a male participant and 0 for a female participant. The authors state that this measure varies from a maximum of 0.75 for a European American male participant to a minimum of 0 for an Asian woman participant.

Computed from two equally weighted competence marker categories: 0.5 for being on the dean's list at the business school where the study was conducted and 0 otherwise, and 0.5 for prior work experience at a prestigious business organization and 0 otherwise. Prestigious organizations were coded using a career intelligence guide (Vault) that students perceive as authoritative and include McKinsey & Company, Boston Consulting Group, Bain & Company, Booz & Company; Goldman Sachs & Co., Morgan Stanley, Blackstone Group, and J.P. Morgan Investment Bank; and Coca-Cola Company, Sony Corporation, Nike Inc., Johnson & Johnson, and Google.

variable_name: CEO position, CFO position, CMO position, COO position, idiosyncratic position
description: A set of dummy variables indicating which founding team member was occupying each task position, used to test the hypotheses on the drivers of task position allocation. At the end of their first decision period teams reported the structures of their organizations, including the specific formal task position of individual founding team members.
time_window: end of the first decision period

description: An ordered dependent variable representing the rank ordering of positions, consistent with the initial priming of participants. CEO position was coded as 4, CFO as 3, CMO or COO as 2, and the idiosyncratic task positions created by each founding team as 1.
time_window: end of the first decision period

description: Coded from individuals' CVs; each participant's previous work experience (from most recent to third most recent) was categorized into one of five functional areas: sales/marketing, finance/accounting, science/engineering/operations, business development/strategic planning, and administrative support/general management. Team functional diversity is the Blau index, one minus the sum over the five areas of the squared percentage of a team whose dominant functional background is in that area. Values range from 0, which represents low diversity, to 1 for high diversity.

variable_name: team fit on diffuse status cue
description: An ordered logit model first predicted the probability of each individual being assigned to one of the four hierarchically ranked positions as a function of his/her diffuse status cue. For each individual, position deviance was calculated as 1 minus the predicted probability of being assigned to that position, then multiplied by minus 1 to obtain a fit index ranging from 0 to minus 1; values closer to 0 indicate a high fit (a typical occupant) and values closer to minus 1 a low fit (an atypical occupant). The team-level measure averages the index scores of the constituent team members.

At the end of the simulation, venture performance was measured as the equity value of the venture using discounted free cash flow techniques. Enterprise value was calculated from each venture's last-period balance sheet and income statement, treating them as representative of the business, rolled forward to estimate free cash flows and discounted to present values; the book value of debt adjusted for excess cash was deducted to arrive at the value of equity. The value of equity was normalized within an industry.

variable_name: option pool (percentage share of the founders' equity pool)
description: At the end of the simulation but before final simulation results were announced, participants anonymously gave themselves and other members of the focal founding team a percentage of the ownership equity such that the total added up to 100% of the founders' pool of equity. The percentages received by the focal team member were averaged after excluding self-ratings, and the averaged percentage was standardized by founding team size to obtain individual performance.
scale: percentage of the founders' equity pool

description: Manipulated by varying founder 1's professional work experience prior to the launch of BronzeStar. In the high specific cue for the CEO position condition, founder 1 was a corporate entrepreneur skilled in business development at a reputable home furnishing company located in the south-west area of the United States; in the high specific cue for the CMO position condition, founder 1 was a marketer with rich marketing skills who worked for a reputable home furnishing company in the same area. Otherwise profiles were equivalent with respect to educational background, age, regional background, and rank in the previous job, and featured the same word count.

Manipulated by varying gender using gender-typical names (e.g., Robert Johnson for the high diffuse cue vs. Julia Johnson for the low diffuse cue) and pronouns (he/his vs. she/her). To minimize subjects guessing the nature of the manipulation, no explicit reference to gender was made; names and pronouns were used when describing demographic, educational, and professional backgrounds in the profile.

Subjects indicated their belief on the extent to which founder 1 should be CEO of BronzeStar ('To what extent do you believe that Robert (Julia) has to be CEO of your venture BronzeStar?') on a 7-point scale where 1 = not at all and 7 = very much. Subjects answered the position questions related to the first founder before knowing anything about the second founder, and could consider a given founder suitable for both positions.

Subjects indicated their belief on the extent to which founder 1 should be CMO of BronzeStar ('To what extent do you believe that Robert (Julia) has to be CMO of your venture BronzeStar?') on a 7-point scale where 1 = not at all and 7 = very much. Subjects answered the position questions related to the first founder before knowing anything about the second founder, and could consider a given founder suitable for both positions.

The authors determined organizations' pay level strategies by averaging wages for the hospitals' job categories. First, the average pay for each job category was standardized, yielding nine standardized variables per hospital; second, a single variable representing pay level strategy was computed as the average of these nine standardized scores. Positive values signified a strategy of leading the market and negative values a strategy of lagging.
time_window: contemporaneous with the dependent variable (time T)

description: Pay dispersion was captured using gini coefficients calculated for each hospital in each year following the subpopulation approach, with average wage values at the job category level. The text gives the gini formula as a function of the average salaries for the job categories of a hospital arranged in decreasing order of size, the mean of those average salaries, and the number of job categories in the hospital. Gini coefficients can theoretically range from 0, indicating a totally egalitarian pay structure, to 1, for a totally hierarchical structure.
time_window: contemporaneous with the dependent variable (time T)

description: The variable is the average number of days patients stay in a particular hospital, calculated by dividing a hospital's total number of patient days by its total number of discharges. Hospitals with shorter lengths of stay are considered to be more efficient in their use of resources.
time_window: contemporaneous with the independent variables (time T)

description: For each hospital, this variable is equal to its risk-adjusted expected heart attack death rate minus its actual heart attack death rate, so positive values represent higher performance. The State of California estimates an expected survival rate for each hospital that is based on each of its heart attack patients' risk factors for a particular year, which allows comparison of patient treatment quality across hospitals while taking case severity into account.
Return on assets (ROA) was used to measure organizational financial performance. The measure captures a hospital's ability to both control its expenses and use its assets to generate income.
time_window: contemporaneous with the independent variables (time T)

variable_name: Resource efficiency, patient care outcomes and financial performance
description: Organizational performance was captured by three outcomes: resource efficiency (average length of stay), patient care outcomes (adjusted coronary survival) and financial performance (return on assets), each analyzed as a separate dependent variable.

Four indices of IT penetration were built from an inventory of computer applications in operation: proportion of control-oriented systems, proportion of coordination-oriented systems, proportion of efficiency-oriented systems, and accessibility. The manager of each IT installation indicated which applications, from an inventory of 539 applications, were in operation; in cities with multiple installations an organization-wide measure was obtained by summing the installation measures. The three application indices were each divided by the total number of applications in operation in the city, and the accessibility index was divided by the total number of employees in the organization.

The city manager or the assistant city manager was asked to calculate the number of managers (staff and line) above first level supervisors and below department heads. The number of middle managers was then divided by the total number of managers in the organization, so that the ratio represented the number of middle managers relative to the organization's managerial workforce. The study included line managers and excluded staff personnel in order to obtain a homogeneous sample of middle managers.

The city manager or equivalent city official indicated the lowest of the seven levels in the organization at which each of 23 key decisions covering the acquisition, allocation, and control of human, financial, and physical resources could be made. The seven levels were given values of 1 for city council to 7 for direct worker and were summed to give an overall score ranging between 23 and 91. Only cities that answered all 23 items of the index were included in the analysis.

The manager of every IT installation indicated who among the IT manager, the department head over IT, the user department heads, the chief administrative officer, or the local legislative body was most influential in each of the major computing decisions. The index included four components: deciding on new applications, approving budgets for major and minor computer purchases, evaluating the services of an installation, and deciding on organizational arrangements. Computing decision authority was considered centralized when authority was concentrated at or above the department head over the IT manager, and decentralized when authority lay at the IT manager level.

For each dyad the technological proximity of the partner firm is calculated following Jaffe (1986) as the uncentered correlation between the two firms' vectors of technological capital, measured as the number of patent applications in technology class k; the proximity measure takes a value between 0 and 1 according to their common technological interests. The variance in relative technological proximity is then calculated as the variance of technological proximity for each firm per year, so that higher values indicate a higher level of variance. A five-year moving window is used to calculate this variable. The equation for the uncentered correlation is not readable in the provided text.

Innovative performance is measured with weighted patent counts, a count variable in which each patent i is weighted according to the subsequent citations it receives, assuming that more important patents receive more citations and vice versa. Attention is centered on patents in USPTO patent classes 424, 435, 436, 514, 530, 536, 800 and 930. Patent citations were collected until 2003 and simulated cumulative distribution lags by Hall, Jaffe, and Trajtenberg (2005) are used to estimate the total number of citations each patent is likely to receive. The formula for the weighted patent counts is not readable in the provided text.
time_window: patents applied for in year t; citations collected until 2003

description: Sourcing mode diversity is calculated using the Herfindahl index as 1-H, where H is the sum of squared shares of each external sourcing partnership in the sourcing portfolio. The external sourcing partnerships under study include CVC investments, strategic alliances, joint ventures, minority holdings, and M&As. A five-year moving window is used for this variable.

variable_name: Industry clockspeed (product, process and organizational clockspeed)
description: Industry clockspeed is measured through three facets. Product clockspeed is the average time span between new products introduced in the industry between 1980 and 1990, and process clockspeed is the average number of years over which firms depreciated capital equipment. Organizational clockspeed is the average time span between new corporate strategic actions introduced by all firms in each industry, tracked through the content of news headlines. The three measures loaded on a single factor and showed high internal consistency.

Complexity is measured with two established measures derived from the CEO's causal map: comprehensiveness, the total number of concepts in a causal map, and connectedness, the total number of linkages in a causal map divided by the total number of concepts in the map. Causal maps were traced from the CEO's letters to shareholders in a five-step procedure and the raw concepts were classified into 35 broad categories. The strategic schema measures for 1990 and 1992 were averaged to reduce potential bias from relying on a single year.

Focus is measured with two established network-based measures: centralization and Bonacich's eigenvector centrality. In centralization, the centrality of each concept in the causal map is computed by adding the total number of concepts to which it is linked directly or indirectly, with a decreasing weight assigned to each successive layer, and the centrality of the map is the sum of the differences between the centrality of the most central concept and all other concepts, scaled by the total number of possible links. Eigenvector centrality is the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue of the network, standardized so that its length equals the eigenvalue. A high value on either measure implies that a few core concepts dominate the causal map.

Strategic flexibility is measured with four measures. Variety in resource deployment is the coefficient of variation across R&D intensity, capital intensity and advertising intensity, where a high coefficient of variation suggests low range flexibility. Shifts in resource deployment is the sum of the absolute differences in the proportions allocated to the three resource types between t1 (1990-93) and t2 (1993-96). Competitive simplicity is a Herfindahl-type index summing the squared proportions of competitive actions in six action categories, where low scores indicate that a firm carries out a broad range of action types. Shifts in competitive action is the sum of the absolute differences in the proportions of actions in each of the six categories across the two periods.

Firm performance is measured with three measures obtained from the COMPUSTAT database over 3 years: sales growth, return on investment, and net income growth. Performance measures are lagged by 1 year. For the year 1990, sales growth and net income growth were the moving averages of changes from 1988 to 1991, 1989 to 1992, and 1990 to 1993, and for 1992 the moving average of changes from 1990 to 1993, 1991 to 1994, and 1992 to 1995; ROI was averaged over 1991-1993 for 1990 and over 1993-1995 for 1992.
time_window: 3-year windows lagged by 1 year from 1990 and 1992

description: The number of grievances filed per 100 workers. One of two variables that capture aspects of the formal conflict resolution systems in these organizations. The data were pooled across the 25 plants and three years, 1978-80.

The number of disciplinary actions involving suspension or some more severe penalty per 100 workers. One of two variables capturing aspects of the formal conflict resolution systems in these organizations.

The absenteeism rate of hourly workers as a percentage of straight time hours, excluding contractual days off. One of three variables measuring aspects of individual attitudes and behavior; higher absenteeism represents a less favorable value of that construct.

A survey asked salaried employees, including first line supervisors, a number of questions regarding compensation and benefit levels, working environment, relationships with supervisors and subordinates, and career progress; low-score responses indicated dissatisfaction. A summary score was derived from these surveys for each plant, and the variable used was the percentage of respondents in each plant that had an overall survey score greater than 3.2 on a 1 to 5 scale, because this was the only measure stored in the information system of each plant.
scale: percentage of respondents; overall survey score on a 1 to 5 scale

description: The percentage of hourly employees that submitted at least one suggestion during the year to a plant's suggestion program. One of three variables measuring aspects of individual attitudes and behavior.

The percentage of hourly employees involved in some form of QWL program in each plant for the years 1978-80, used to measure the extent of QWL programs' development. The QWL activities included quality circles; informal meetings between plant managers, workers, and union officials; and other forms of enhanced communication between labor and management. These figures were annual estimates provided by the personnel director in each plant and were not available for 1978 and 1979 for a few of the plants.

An index that compared actual hours of direct labor input to standardized hours calculated by the company's industrial engineers, with the labor standards adjusted for variations in product attributes. A high direct labor index was associated with relatively high efficiency and low costs.
A quality index derived from a count of the number of faults and demerits that appeared in inspections of the product. A high quality score indicated relatively good product quality.

variable_name: Direct labor efficiency and product quality
description: Organizational effectiveness was captured by economic performance of each plant, measured by direct labor efficiency (index of actual to standardized direct labor hours) and product quality (index from inspection faults and demerits).

Percentage of the studio's total annual output devoted to genres that had recently appeared on its own list of top movies but were not found on the list of top movies for any of its rivals. The lists were compiled from the genres of the 10 movies that had generated the most revenue during a prior two-year period for the studio and for its rivals. Each film was classified by its primary (leading) genre.
time_window: annual output; two-year look-back for the top-film lists

description: Percentage of the studio's total annual output that was devoted to genres that had neither recently appeared on its own list of top films nor on any of its rivals' lists of top films. The top-film lists were compiled from the 10 highest revenue-generating movies of the prior two years. Each film was classified by its primary genre.
time_window: annual output; two-year look-back for the top-film lists

description: Share of the studio's output devoted to genres that had appeared on its own top list as well as on the list for at least one of its competitors. It was used as a reference point alongside the differentiated strategies in the performance models.
time_window: annual output; two-year look-back for the top-film lists

description: Return on sales, the studio's profit on its revenue base, used as the primary indicator of financial performance. The performance measure was limited to sales derived from the production and distribution of films, excluding revenue from theater exhibition until the mid 1950s and from television production after the late 1950s. Data were obtained from annual editions of Moody's Industrial Manuals and from studio financial reports.

Yearly figures on the number of domestic theaters owned or under long-term lease to each studio, expressed in thousands, obtained from Moody's Industrial Manuals. This variable measures the resource that provides a studio with access to major markets and audiences.

Yearly count of stars under contracts of four or more years, obtained from Shipman (1972, 1979), with biographies coded to link each star to a studio; 191 stars held contracts with at least one of the studios during the study period. All had achieved significant recognition for their primary and supporting roles and had won awards from their guilds or film festivals.

Percentage of household recreational spending devoted to movie attendance, used to measure the level of industry demand. The measure could be used across the entire period because it represents the demand for movies relative to all other forms of entertainment and recreation. Data were obtained from the U.S. Department of Commerce, Social and Economic Statistics Administration.

Annual count of the genres on the list of the industry's top 10 films that had not appeared on that list for at least the previous two years, used to assess the stability of consumer tastes. The two-year window was chosen because a genre may drop off the list for a single year. Yearly data on the top 10 films were obtained from Variety.

For each period, the cross-community brokerage of every actor in the network was computed with the Gould and Fernandez (1989) brokerage index, counting a cross-community triad whenever the focal actor occupied an itinerant broker, gatekeeper, representative, or liaison role, and summing these triads. All members of the producer's or creative director's community (excluding the focal executives themselves) were then ranked on this score, and the community member with the maximum number of cross-community triads was used as the hub. The hub's score was attributed to the in-team variable when the hub belonged to the focal show's production team and to the out-of-team variable when the hub did not. The variables were logged.
level: show-year (hub located in the focal executive's community)
time_window: three-year period prior to the focal year

description: The French audience rating agency Mediametrie collects information on shows' audiences and converts it into viewership ''points,'' each representing 600,000 viewers; shows can receive fractions of points. These points determine advertising rates and are the key metric TV channels quote to compare show performance. The number of points was logged to reduce skewness, with 1 added to avoid implausible negative values.
scale: viewership points, each point representing 600,000 viewers
time_window: measured one year later than the theoretical and control variables

description: Communities were identified with a network-partitioning algorithm that accounts for the two-mode network structure arising because each production team yields a fully connected graph. The algorithm yields a modularity value capturing the difference between the ratio of ties within versus between communities and the ratio expected in a random network of the same size, and partitions were obtained for each annual network.
time_window: annual networks aggregated over three-year windows

variable_name: Proportion of departing independent directors (post-boycott turnover and pre-boycott turnover)
description: The dependent variable is the proportion of departing independent directors, naturally bounded between 0 and 1. 'Post-boycott turnover' captures the proportion of directors who were on a board at the time of a boycott but were no longer on the board three years later, while 'pre-boycott turnover' captures the proportion of directors who were on a board three years prior to a boycott but were no longer on the board at the time of the boycott.
time_window: three-year pre-boycott and three-year post-boycott periods

description: A treatment variable coded '1' for boycotted firms and '0' for matched control firms, interacted with a binary period variable coded '0' in the pre-boycott period and '1' in the post-boycott period. The difference estimator is the interaction of the period and treatment variables, testing whether the observed change in turnover differed significantly between treated and control firms.

Computed as (R − D) / T, where R equals the total contributions made to Republicans, D equals the total contributions made to Democrats, and T equals the total contributions to all parties, based on all campaign contributions a director made to any candidate for federal office in the three election cycles prior to the boycott in which the firm was targeted. This produces a scale ranging from −1 (liberal) to 1 (conservative); directors with no observable contributions were omitted unless the Federal Election Commission data indicated they had made at least one contribution to an alternative, nonpartisan vehicle, in which case they were coded 0.
time_window: three election cycles prior to the boycott

description: An ordinal variable coded from −1 to 1, where −1 captures liberal campaigns, 1 captures conservative campaigns, and 0 captures campaigns that were unclassifiable on a political spectrum. Two external experts (both former lobbyists) categorized all boycotts; they agreed on 89% of the ideological classifications and all boycotts about which the coders disagreed were coded as unclassifiable.

The interaction of the director ideology and boycott ideology variables, capturing the degree of an ideological match. Because each of these scales was centered at 0, an ideological match is reflected by a positive interaction value, which occurs when a liberal director meets a liberal boycott or a conservative director meets a conservative boycott.

A binary variable coded '1' if a director left their post at the expiration of their term, and '0' otherwise. The authors searched proxy statements and media articles to code the rationales for departures and excluded the departures they identified as involuntary, including death, explicit ouster, conflict of interest, compliance with tenure or retirement policies, and imprisonment; for employee directors, a departure was also coded as involuntary if the person retained a position at the firm despite exiting the board.

Cumulative abnormal returns surrounding the boycott's announcement, constructed using the market model with a five-day event window (−1, 3) and a 30-day estimation window beginning 30 days prior to the event date. More negative CARs signal that market participants believe a boycott is a greater threat to ongoing performance; the variable also helps control for potential performance-driven departures.

For firm i in a focal market n, the index averages the number of contacts that firm i has with the incumbents in market n in markets different from focal market n. It is built from indicators taking value 1 if firm i (or incumbent j) is established in market m(n) at time t. The measure ranges between zero, when firm i has no contact with incumbents in market n, and the number of markets M in which firm i is established. The exact algebraic rendering of the index is not readable in the text, but the text states its construction and range.
scale: 0 to the number of markets M in which firm i is established
time_window: annual, values taken at the end of the previous year

description: The dependent variable is the hazard that a savings bank enters a certain geographical market, given that it does not have current activities in the market. For an entry to be recorded, the savings bank has to show a certain degree of commitment with the focal market; following Geroski (1991), an entity is considered present in a market when it has at least 1 percent of the total number of savings banks branches in the market. Each potential entrant-focal market pair and its covariates are followed every year until either entry takes place or censoring occurs.

A multidimensional measure of average strategic dissimilarity between potential entrant i and incumbents in market n, built for each year. Six variables capture scope commitments (credits/financial investments; treasury/financial investments; portfolio/financial investments) and resource commitments (personnel expenses/total revenue; net insolvencies/total revenue; (passive-equity)/passive). The dyad measure takes a value of '0' when there is maximum strategic similarity and '1' in the case of maximum dissimilarity; a firm-market specific measure is then obtained by summing and dividing by the number of incumbents in every focal market. The algebraic formulas are not readable in the text.

For every pair of firms with multimarket contact (one potential entrant i and one incumbent j present in the focal market n), the authors build a measure of the importance of the contact from the point of view of both firms; these differences are then averaged for all the multipoint competitors of potential firm i with operations in market n. The index ranges from zero, where for all the incumbents the potential entrant attaches the same importance to the contacts with any incumbent as the incumbent does, to the average number of multimarket contacts. A higher value indicates higher reciprocity between the contacts. The algebraic formula is not readable in the text.
scale: 0 to the average number of multimarket contacts

description: Seller concentration is measured through the use of a province Herfindahl, using the number of branches as a proxy for market share. To take into account the interaction between commercial banks and savings banks, the index has been calculated considering the branches of both types of intermediaries.

Indicator variable that identifies CFO gender. Executives are classified as CFO if the title name contains 'CFO', 'chief finance officer', or 'chief financial officer' and the title is not prefixed by 'Former'; CFO gender is identified using the Execucomp data item GENDER. Female CFOs account for 1,550 firm-year observations and 339 unique firms. Female CFOs represent 8% of the sample.

The Financial Statement Deviation (FSD) Score, computed following Amiram et al.'s (2015) protocol. The authors download the line items reported in the balance sheet, income statement and statement of cash flows in the annual report (form 10-K) and, for all firms with 100 or more line items, generate the frequency distribution of leading digits by recording the percentage of numbers that begin with each digit from 1 to 9. The score compares these actual percentages with the percentages predicted under Benford's Law; the formula block in the paper could not be extracted, so the exact expression is a gap. If the actual distribution equals the predicted distribution the score is 0, and the further the actual is from the predicted the higher the score and the greater the likelihood that numbers in the financial statement contain errors or were manipulated. The authors use the natural log of the FSD Score to mitigate the influence of outliers.
scale: natural log of the FSD Score
time_window: fiscal year covered by the annual report (form 10-K)

description: Institutional ownership is the number of shares held by institutions scaled by total shares outstanding. Because the moderator variables have nonnormal distributions and the multiplicative term is highly correlated with Female CFO, the authors dichotomize the variable, such that those in the lowest quintile are considered 'low' and the rest are considered 'high'.
scale: ratio of shares held by institutions to total shares outstanding; dichotomized into low (lowest quintile) and high

description: Analyst coverage is the total number of analyst estimates of earnings per share (EPS) provided for the fiscal year-end. The variable is dichotomized for the analysis, such that observations in the lowest quintile are considered 'low' and the rest are considered 'high'.
scale: count of analyst EPS estimates; dichotomized into low (lowest quintile) and high

description: Journals were assigned to a three-level hierarchy based on Franke, Edlund, and Oster's (1990) Social Science Citation Index analysis of management journals. The first tier consists of the Strategic Management Journal, Administrative Science Quarterly, and Academy of Management Journal (their number one, two and three listings); the second tier of the Sloan Management Review, Journal of Management Studies, and California Management Review (their number seven, eight and nine listings); the third tier of the Journal of Management, Journal of General Management, and Human Resource Management (their number 13, 16 and 17 entries).

variable_name: replications with extensions as a percentage of empirical studies
description: A randomly selected issue from each of the nine journals was content-analyzed for every year from 1976 through 1995, producing 176 journal issues and some 1373 research articles, notes, and commentaries, of which 701 (51.1%) were empirical. Two of the authors independently classified the 701 empirical papers to ascertain whether they were replications or extensions, and to be accorded replication or extension status an article had to contain a manifest citation of the original work. The variable is the number of replications with extensions divided by the number of empirical studies, expressed as a percentage, reported for each tier and each period.
The study's 20-year window is split into two ten-year periods, 1976-85 and 1986-95, and the publication frequency of replications with extensions is compared between them.

Each replication with extension was classified as supporting, partially supporting, or conflicting with the original findings. The classification is based on the conclusions reached by the replicating author(s); the present authors examined the replication studies, weighed the evidence based on the replicating author's findings (and often those of the original paper), and exercised judgment in interpreting these.
scale: three categories: support, partial support, conflict

description: The time lag in years between the original study and the replication was recorded, and mean lags were compared across tiers: first tier 5.9 years, second tier 9.7 years, third tier 7.3 years.

variable_name: comments and rejoinders as a percentage of all studies
description: The number of comments and rejoinders was counted and divided by the total number of studies published in each tier, expressed as a percentage. First-tier journals devoted 3.0 percent of all studies to commentaries and rejoinders, second-tier journals 1.3 percent, and third-tier journals 4.0 percent; on average across all journal levels only 2.8 percent of the total number of studies are commentaries.

Property rights of the signatory community coded on a 3-point scheme: communities that have only an Aboriginal title coded 0 (weak); communities with a historic treaty coded 1 (moderate); communities with a modern treaty or an interim measure agreement (IMA) with land management rights or institutions coded 2 (strong). A community's strength of property rights is coded over time, and the most recent information is used for the day of the announcement of the CBA. In the sample of 148 events, 31 CBAs were signed with communities with weak property rights, 73 with communities with moderate property rights, and 44 with communities with strong property rights. Data on 637 indigenous communities' property rights were hand-collected from the Aboriginal and Treaty Rights Information System and from the 2015 status report of Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada and validated with an academic expert.
time_window: as of the day of the CBA announcement

description: Sum of all unique extra-institutional mobilization events that the signatory community engaged in prior to the announcement of the CBA, as reported in the media. Events were coded from media reports found by searching the FACTIVA database for articles where the community name (including alternate spellings, historical names, and tribal council names) appears within 10 words of terms typically associated with extra-institutional mobilization such as strike, rally, demonstration, protest, or blockade. Each article satisfying the search criteria was read to ensure that it referred to extra-institutional mobilization by the community, to count only unique mobilization events and to record the date and the entity targeted. Of the 637 indigenous communities, 237 engaged in extra-institutional mobilization, of which 123 had more than one mobilization event, for a total of 569 community events.

Sum of all unique institutional action events that the signatory community engaged in prior to the announcement of the CBA, as reported in the media. Built from FACTIVA searches for media reports where the community name appears within 10 words of terms typically associated with legal action such as petition, grievance, investigation, injunction, lawsuit, legal action, or court; each article was read to confirm that it referred to legal or regulatory action taken by the community, to count only unique events and to record the date of the action and its target. Of the 637 indigenous communities, 318 engaged in institutional action, of which 190 took more than one institutional action, for a total of 872 unique community institutional actions.

Investors' reactions to CBA announcements measured with an event-study measure of short-term cumulative abnormal returns. For firm i and event date t, the abnormal return is ARit = Rit - E(Rit | Rmt), and normal returns are estimated with the market model Rit = αi + βiRmt + εit, estimated over a period of 100 days that ends 10 days before the event. Using the estimated parameters, daily normal returns are predicted for 1 day preceding the event, the event day, and 3 days following the event, abnormal returns are calculated for each of these days, and the CAR is computed for the 5-day event window; the market portfolio is approximated using the S&P/TSX Composite Index because most sample companies are listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
time_window: 5-day event window (-1 to +3 days); market model estimated over 100 days ending 10 days before the event

description: Measured with the videometric approach of Petrenko et al. (2016). Publicly available videos showing the CEO in interview and public speech settings were edited to remove identifying information and to approximately 2.5 min, and discussions of firm performance, reputation, or potentially stigmatic events were removed. Doctoral students in clinical psychology with experience in personality assessment served as coders, and each CEO was independently rated with the items of the Machiavellian Personality Scale (MPS) on a seven-point Likert scale by three expert raters who were blind to the study hypotheses. The instrument showed a coefficient alpha of .93, and expert raters showed significant agreement, ICC(1, 3) = .48.

Market-adjusted premium paid for each transaction. The pre-takeover price is the stock price 30 days prior to the date of announcement; the premium is the purchase price minus the pre-takeover price divided by the pre-takeover price. The premium was then adjusted for market movement within the Standard & Poor 500 Index.
time_window: 30 days prior to the announcement date

description: Ratio of cost of goods sold over sales. This ratio represents the cost component of the gross margin ratio and provides a scaled measure of the direct costs of the organization's goods and services.
Ratio of interest expense to liabilities. It measures what the firm pays to secure and service its debt, based on all financial liabilities.

A more restricted measure of financing costs produced from data in the Capital IQ database. It excludes debt in the form of bonds and notes, providing the interest rate of only the most clearly controllable component of liabilities.

variable_name: Number of school-to-work activities (composite intensity index)
description: The 1997 NES included 20 activities representing linkages between employers and schools, ranging from establishing a formal partnership arrangement to providing internships, youth apprenticeships, student mentoring, participating in school-based enterprises, developing academic curricula, and sponsoring student visits to the workplace and/or employee visits to schools. Employers were asked if they would sponsor or participate in each of these activities, and responses were recoded from 1 = Yes, 2 = No to 1 = Yes, 0 = No. The authors added the number of activities each employer offered to create a composite intensity index; the larger the score, the more STW activities the employer provided that connected work to school.

Mean of the responses to three items assessing the quality of recent high school graduates: 'Based on your experience with hiring their graduates, how would you rate your local high schools' overall performance in preparing students for work in your establishment?', with two further items substituting 'technical institutes' and 'community colleges' for 'high schools'. Responses were made on a five-point scale ranging from 1 = Unacceptable to 5 = Outstanding. Respondents indicating the establishment had not hired any graduates of these institutions, or that no one from these institutions had applied, were eliminated from the analysis.

Mean of the responses to three items assessing the quality of recent high school graduates: 'Based on your experience with hiring their graduates, how would you rate your local high schools' overall performance in preparing students for work in your establishment?', with two further items substituting 'technical institutes' and 'community colleges' for 'high schools'. Responses were made on a five-point scale ranging from 1 = Unacceptable to 5 = Outstanding. Respondents indicating the establishment had not hired any graduates of these institutions, or that no one from these institutions had applied, were eliminated from the analysis.

Ratio of the number of 18- to 25-year-old employees hired over the last 2 years to the total number of employees in the establishment. The total number of employees in the ratio was calculated from the ranges that were used to measure the size of the establishment (fewer than 50 = 25, 50-99 = 75, 100-249 = 175, 250-999 = 650, 1000 or more = 2000).

Average number of weeks the establishment took to fill an entry-level position, based on theories of employer search models found in labor economics, in which employers face uncertainty in the time it takes to find new employees to fill vacancies. The longer it takes to hire entry-level employees, the more uncertain this process would be for the establishment.

An index of the training given to three types of employees - production, office/clerical/sales/customer service, and technical/technical support - was calculated to assess the degree to which the establishment engages in firm-specific training. The index is the mean of the responses (weighted by the percentage of the type of employees in the establishment) to three items, each 1 = Yes, 0 = No multiplied by the percentage of the establishment's employees in the relevant category: sales and customer service; training in the use of computers or new equipment; and training on the safe use of equipment and tools. The composite index is the average percentage of the establishment's employees across each of the three employee categories that receive firm-specific training.

Response to an item assessing the change in the skill level of entry-level positions over the last 3 years: 'During the last 3 years, have the skills required to perform (the position title the respondent had identified) at an acceptable level increased, decreased or remained the same?' A dummy variable was created indicating an increase in skills (1 = increased, 0 = decreased or remained the same).
scale: 1 = increased, 0 = decreased or remained the same

variable_name: Percentage of employees in self-managed teams
description: Response to the question 'What percentage of non-managerial and non-supervisory employees is currently involved in self-managed teams?' The authors use extensive use of self-managed teams as an indication that the establishment is less likely to believe its employees engage in opportunistic behavior, so the variable is an inverse indicator of employee opportunism.

An index of the training given to three types of employees - production, office/clerical/sales/customer service, and technical/technical support - was calculated to assess the degree to which the establishment engages in firm-specific training. The index is the mean of the responses (weighted by the percentage of the type of employees in the establishment) to three items, each 1 = Yes, 0 = No multiplied by the percentage of the establishment's employees in the relevant category: sales and customer service; training in the use of computers or new equipment; and training on the safe use of equipment and tools. The composite index is the average percentage of the establishment's employees across each of the three employee categories that receive firm-specific training.

Response to an item assessing the change in the skill level of entry-level positions over the last 3 years: 'During the last 3 years, have the skills required to perform (the position title the respondent had identified) at an acceptable level increased, decreased or remained the same?' A dummy variable was created indicating an increase in skills (1 = increased, 0 = decreased or remained the same).
scale: 1 = increased, 0 = decreased or remained the same

description: An establishment's investment in new physical assets is used as an indicator of its imitable asset stock. The measure is the log of the establishment's total assets that are less than 4 years old.

Response to the item concerning the establishment's use of benchmarking practices: 'Has your establishment participated in any benchmarking programs that compare your practices and performances with other organizations?' The response was recoded into a dichotomous variable (1 = Yes, 0 = No).

The database contains information about the outcome for every inspection in the form of a district decision variable, consisting of three levels. The most severe level is an 'official action' (OAI), typically accompanied by a publicly available warning letter that threatens seizure, injunction, or recall; the second level is 'voluntary action' (VAI), where some outages have been observed that should be addressed but no formal followup will occur until the next inspection; the third level is 'no action' (NAI), which indicates that violations, if any, were very minor. The district decision variable is generally entered a few weeks after the completion of the plant inspection. In the data, 18% of inspections resulted in official action, 40% in voluntary action, and 41% in no action. Higher values indicate a worse inspection outcome and therefore a higher state of process entropy.
scale: three ordered levels: no action, voluntary action, official action

description: The independent variable to test H1 is the number of days since the last inspection occurred (average of 528). The authors use the natural log of time since the last inspection in the analysis because the time since the last inspection is right-skewed. Larger values mean more time has elapsed since the last renewal.

A dummy variable coded 1 if a merger was completed since the last inspection and 0 otherwise. Mergers are defined as events during which two companies form a new company with a different name, for example Glaxo and Wellcome merging to form GlaxoWellcome in 1995. Mergers were identified via FDA plant ownership information (available for inspections after 2000) as well as Orbis, NETS and ThomsonReuters databases and Google searches.

A dummy variable coded 1 if an acquisition was completed since the last inspection and 0 otherwise. Acquisitions are defined as one company purchasing some or all the assets of another company without a name change, for example Teva buying Novopharm in 2000. The paper considers the effect of an acquisition on the firm being acquired, assuming there is not a substantial shock to the organizational systems of the acquiring firm.

A list of parent banks for each trading room, and up to two 'home' countries for each parent bank, was compiled using the WORLDSCOPE data base and the Bankers Almanac. The first home base was the country from where the largest ownership of the parent bank was derived; in some cases a second home base was created if the parent bank itself was a cross-national joint venture. A trading room was then coded as 'foreign' if its location country was different from all of its parent's home bases. In a couple of cases where a merger or acquisition changed the foreignness of a particular room, those rooms were dropped from the study.

The data used to track entry and exit of market-makers worldwide were taken from the Foreign Exchange and Bullion Dealers Directory published annually by Hambros Bank. Survival is the continued existence of the trading room in the market-making segment, with exit represented by delisting from this directory of market makers. Trading rooms that exited because their parent banks failed for other reasons were treated as censored cases. The continuance of a particular, physical trading room at the same address was the key determinant of continuing survival or exit in the case of bank mergers or name changes.

The models are duration based, in which time represents the duration that a room survives since the time we begin studying it. Exit rates are plotted against tenure in industry (duration time) for foreign and local rooms. A term interacting the foreignness variable and duration time is used to test whether time dependence differs between foreign and local rooms.

variable_name: Period of higher global market integration (H3)
description: We created a variable to break the spells depending on whether the time period in question was prior to or post 1982, to capture the effects of the many financial market deregulations that occurred in the early 1980s. This time-varying variable represents the period of deregulation and higher global market integration.

variable_name: Proportion of foreign competitors in location (H5)
description: The number of foreign competitors in each location was derived from the directories, i.e. the intensity and mix of local versus foreign competition in a location. These time-varying independent variables were collected every year and updated at 3-year intervals using 5-year moving averages to smooth out annual data.

The size of the trading room was measured in terms of number of traders, derived from the directories. Since the directory prints a limit of 12 on the number of traders per room, we decided to classify all rooms that listed 12 traders as 'large' rooms and all rooms that listed fewer than 12 traders as 'not large.'

The parent banks' financial strength was assessed from the tables published every year in the Financial Times publication, The Banker, of the top 200 banks in the world based on assets. A trading room was coded as either affiliated with a 'Top 200' parent or not.

Whether the trading room was part of multinational FX operations, that is, whether it was affiliated to a parent bank that operates more than one trading room worldwide, was derived from the directories.
The number of hierarchical layers in the trading room was derived from the directories and is used as the measure of a hierarchical (bureaucratic) mode of control.

The year the room adopted the electronic dealing technology was taken from the directories, and we created a dichotomous time-varying variable that breaks the spell depending on whether the time period in question was prior to a firm's adoption of the Reuters dealing system or after this adoption. In the case of rooms that, to date, had not adopted this technology, this spell is not broken but we code the variable to indicate that no Reuters dealing system was in place.

Cumulative abnormal returns calculated using the three-day event window of (-1, +1) to account for possible early information regarding the testimony, as well as for reactions following the testimony. Calculated with the Fama-French four-factor model and winsorized at the 0.01 level to account for extreme observations. The event study is conducted through Eventus and results are reported for both equally weighted and value-weighted indices.

Witness status is coded as a 4 if the CEO of the firm testified; executives with the title of vice president or above were coded as 3; witnesses with titles indicating division leadership were coded as 2, and all lower level witnesses were coded as 1. Higher values indicate a higher status witness.
The total number of words that the witness spoke in the testimony. Thus this measure incorporates both witness opening statements, as well as answers to questions posed by committee members.

A dichotomous variable represented as a 1 if the given congressional committee indicated having direct jurisdiction over the focal firm's primary industry and a 0 otherwise. The data on committee jurisdiction was obtained from opensecrets.org.

A measure developed by Hassan et al. (2017), created using pattern-based sequence classification in quarterly earnings calls to determine the proportion of earnings calls the firm devotes to political risks. Calculated as the average risk over the four quarters prior to the congressional testimony.
time_window: average over the four quarters prior to the congressional testimony

description: Created using computer-aided content analysis (CATA) with the Loughran and McDonald's (2011) Financial Sentiment Dictionary, assessing the number of negative words spoken by committee members. The total number of negative words uttered by Congresspersons in their opening statements and in their questions directed toward the focal firm witness was divided by the total number of words spoken in the same statements and questions.

The number of articles focusing on the congressional hearing within our event window (-1,1). To measure the number of media articles, the name of the firm and the witness name were searched along with the words 'testimony,' 'Congress,' and 'Congressional hearing' in leading publications such as The Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg, USA Today, The New York Times, The Washington Post, Los Angeles Times, Thomson Reuters ONE, The New York Post, Daily News (New York) and company press releases in Lexis Nexis Academic database.

Each observation is a Congressional hearing in which a representative of a Fortune 500 firm testified, identified by searching the GPO database for firm names and hand checked, with events with confounding news dropped. The testimony date is the event date for the event study.

Coded when the name of a firm permanently disappeared from the directories without the incidence of an acquisition or name change. Organizations that were alive in 1990 and firms that were acquired by other firms were treated as right-censored. The dependent variable in the discrete-time hazard model is the conditional probability that a firm will die at time t, given that it has not already died.

variable_name: Partners' industry-specific human capital: Graduate education
description: The proportion of partners possessing master's or higher degrees. Graduate education in accounting is taken to develop industry-specific human capital because most C.P.A.s have degrees in accounting and finance. The variable was standardized for each observation period to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one.

variable_name: Partners' industry-specific human capital: Industry tenure
description: Average years of partners' industry experience. Each accountant's career was decomposed into an industry and a firm component, subtracting tenure at the current firm from industry tenure; each partner's industry-specific human capital was proxied by the natural logarithm of tenure in the accounting industry, net of tenure with the current accounting firm, and then averaged to the firm level. One year was added to industry tenure before taking logarithms to avoid logarithms of zero. The variable was standardized for each observation period.
scale: natural logarithm of years of tenure

variable_name: Associates' industry-specific human capital: Graduate school education
description: Measured with the same procedure as partners' industry-specific human capital developed through professional education: the proportion of associates possessing master's or higher degrees, standardized for each observation period. Associates' industry-specific human capital developed through industry experience was not included in the model because associates typically join firms as novices, so their industry tenure net of firm tenure would drop to zero.

Measured as the average of the natural logarithms of partners' tenures (in years) at the firm. One year was added to firm tenure before taking logarithms to avoid logarithms of zero. By taking the natural logarithm the authors assumed that the speed of specific knowledge accumulation decreased over an accountant's tenure. The variable was standardized for each observation period; its squared term was also included in the model.
scale: natural logarithm of years of tenure

description: Associates' firm-specific human capital was measured similarly to partners', as the average of the natural logarithms of associates' tenures (in years) at the firm, with one year added before taking logarithms, and standardized for each observation period. Its squared term was also included in the model.
scale: natural logarithm of years of tenure

description: The proportion of partners who had worked in other industries or in government agencies before joining the accounting firm and were thus likely to have many valuable ties with potential clients. Standardized for each observation period.

The proportion of partners who had left the firm within the previous ten years to work for other industries or government agencies, which gives them strong incentives to take advantage of their social capital when choosing service providers for their new firms. A ten-year span was adopted because the strength of relationships to former firms may decay and because departed partners ultimately retire. Standardized for each observation period.
time_window: previous ten years; lagged by one observation period

description: The proportion of associates who had worked in client environments before joining the accounting firm, measured with the same procedure as the corresponding partners' variable. Standardized for each observation period.

The proportion of associates who had left the firm within the previous ten years to work for other industries or government agencies, measured by applying the same procedure as for partners to client environments. Standardized for each observation period.
time_window: previous ten years; lagged by one observation period

description: Blau's measure of heterogeneity was used to assess the number of partners in each of the three origin categories, reflecting the possibility that the networks of members with similar backgrounds are redundant with respect to client acquisition capabilities. The proportions of partners in each category enter the heterogeneity formula; the specification itself is not readable in the text as extracted. Standardized for each observation period.
