Partners can move to universities, other industries, or government agencies; Blau's measure of heterogeneity was used to quantify the destinations of departed partners. Standardized for each observation period.
Constructed by applying the same procedure as for partners' origins, using Blau's measure of heterogeneity across the three origin categories of associates. Standardized for each observation period.

Constructed by applying the same procedure as for departed partners' destinations, using Blau's measure of heterogeneity across the three destination categories of associates. Standardized for each observation period.

Dummy variable set to 1 if a particular firm was founded by a split and to 0 otherwise. Firms founded de novo were the omitted category. Firms emerging from a split are described as facing unusual challenges because they have to restart the process of accumulating firm-specific human capital, and the owners of such a firm are said to reset the collective firm-specific tenure clock.

When two or more firms joined together and adopted a new name, the event was coded as an acquisition with name change; the largest of the firms involved was classified as a going concern and its smaller counterparts as acquired firms. Firm intervals of firms emerging from such an acquisition were coded 1. The comparison categories were acquisitions without name change (a resulting firm adopted one of the pre-existing names) and name changes without acquisitions; name changes without acquisitions do not change the human and social capital of a firm.

Operationalized by a dummy indicator variable that takes a value of 0 or 1 and reflects the standard practice in the literature on business groups, as typically no affiliate belongs to two different business groups simultaneously. The Prowess database provides ownership details for each firm under categories such as private (Indian), central government, state government, private (foreign) or foreign subsidiary (parent), and Indian business group; all firms in the sample falling under the Indian business group category were identified as being affiliated with a business group.

A dichotomous dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the focal firm in a given year made export sales, and 0 otherwise. When modeling international search propensity, both exporting and nonexporting firms in the sample were taken into account.

Measured by the conventional measure of export intensity, i.e., the ratio of export sales in a year to total sales. The models use only the exporting firms' sample and, following the Heckman (1979) procedure, include the inverse Mills ratio value calculated from the first step of the decision process.

A dichotomous dummy variable that takes a value of 0 for the 1992-1997 period, capturing the broad-scope institutional change, and a value of 1 for the subsequent period of the study, capturing the narrow-scope institutional change (the Drug (Price Control) Order and the TRIPS agreement). The year 1997 was chosen as the cutoff because India had a ten-year window to enact TRIPS and because of political instability during 1996-1999, making 1997 the more conservative midpoint between 1995 and 1999.

Measured by deducting the year of incorporation of the oldest affiliate of the group from the focal year. The oldest affiliate was identified by comparing the year of incorporation of all of the affiliates in a focal business group available in the Prowess database and then eliminating those affiliates that became group affiliates through mergers and acquisitions.
Constructed by simply subtracting the affiliate's age (firm age) from the BG age, so that higher values indicate an affiliate that is younger relative to the founding of the business group.

Created by taking the absolute value of the difference between the 3-digit classification of the founding affiliate of the group and that of the focal affiliate in the pharmaceutical industry, using the National Industrial Classification system available in Prowess.
scale: absolute difference in 3-digit industry classification codes

description: Measured in terms of the liquid assets that are possessed by a firm in the form of cash, bank balances, and marketable securities, normalized with respect to total sales. The measure accounts for only those components of current assets with immediate usability and availability.

Operationalized as the ratio of selling, general, and administrative (SGA) expenses (minus R&D expenses, which were explicitly controlled for in all of the models) to total sales. SGA expenses include overhead costs related to marketing, sales, distribution, managerial, and administrative activities.

Measured in terms of the affiliate's annual contribution to business group revenues, i.e., as a simple ratio of the total sales of the affiliate to that of the entire business group in any given year.

Calculated as the firm's previous relative market share, that is, the one-year lag of the firm's market share relative to the industry leader (the firm's total sales divided by that of the industry leader). The industry leader in a specific year receives a value of 1, and each of the other firms takes values ranging from 0 to less than 1 unless there was more than one industry leader with identical sales figures.

Burt's (1992) constraint measure of structural holes in a bank's ego network, computed from the asymmetric sociomatrix of syndicate co-memberships. The authors state that the lower the values of Constraint (i), the more structural holes the bank is spanning between its direct partners, and they used this measure to test Hypotheses 1 and 2.

A count of the brokerage roles a bank plays across different network neighborhoods, following Gould and Fernandez (1989) and computed after partitioning the network into neighborhoods with the Guimera and Amaral (2005) implementation of Newman's clustering algorithm. Because some brokerage positions might be incidental, brokers were defined as those playing more brokerage roles than the 25th percentile of the index, which was equal to 28 brokerage roles.

The dependent variable of the second-stage analysis, the absolute difference in status between the lead bank and a colead bank; the equation used to compute it is not recoverable from the text. Status is measured with Bonacich's centrality, which is interpreted as a status score when computed using asymmetric network data and is referred to in UCINet as power centrality, with the parameter B set to 75% of the reciprocal of the maximum eigenvalue of the sociomatrix. The variable is continuous and ranges from 0 to 1, with high values indicating higher status dissimilarity, low values similarity, and zero indicating identical status; it is measured at time t+1 and an arcsine root transformation is applied because the variable ranges only from zero to one.
time_window: measured at t+1, predictors at t

description: A bank's social aspiration level based on the market shares of other banks in the network, weighted by market share similarity (the equation itself is not recoverable from the text); the greater the difference between the market shares of banks i and j, the less weight bank i gives to j's market share. For testing Hypotheses 3A and 3B the specification was refined so that firms in brokerage positions compute social aspirations from the similarity-weighted market shares of other firms in brokerage positions and nonbrokers from those of their network neighborhood members.

A bank's historical aspiration level based on its market share, constructed with an anchoring-and-adjustment equation (Equation (1)) whose rendering is not recoverable from the text; alpha is a number between 0 and 1 representing the weight given to the immediate prior performance compared with more distant performances. As a baseline for testing Hypothesis 4, alpha was set to 0.5 for all banks; a grid search assigned nonbrokers a weight of 0.125 to recent performance.

Relative performance defined as the value of the performance metric (market share) at time t minus its social aspiration at time t, split into two spline variables. The value above zero equals zero for observations where relative social performance is less than zero and equals the relative social performance otherwise; symmetrically, the value below zero equals zero for observations where relative social performance is greater than zero and equals the relative social performance otherwise. Variables used in interactions were centered on their means.

Relative performance defined as the value of the performance metric (market share) at time t minus its historical aspiration at time t, split into two spline variables. The value above zero equals zero for observations where relative historical performance is less than zero and equals the relative historical performance otherwise; symmetrically, the value below zero equals zero for observations where relative historical performance is greater than zero and equals the relative historical performance otherwise. Variables used in interactions were centered on their means.
A dummy variable coded 1 if the licensee of a patent was not in existence prior to the license year, and 0 otherwise. Data were gathered from the Technology Licensing Office records.

Annual spells starting when a particular firm licensed an invention and ending when a product using the invention was first sold to a third party. The variable was coded 1 in the year the first dollar of sales was achieved, and 0 otherwise. Data came from the Technology Licensing Office records.
time_window: annual spells from licensing until first sale or censoring

description: Annual spells in which contract records were used to determine if a license to a patent remained in force. License abandonment was coded 1 in the year a patent license was terminated, and 0 otherwise. Records came from the Technology Licensing Office.
time_window: annual spells from licensing until termination or censoring

description: The annual number of firms, both public and private, operating in the industry in which a patented invention was commercialized. Data came from the Census of Manufacturers.

The yearly amount of venture capital funding in an industry, in dollars, created as a time-varying covariate because venture capital funding shifts significantly across industries over time. Data from the Securities Data Corporation's venture capital database were used to calculate the annual dollar value.
The ratio of the dollar value of manufacturing to the dollar value of shipments in each industry annually. Data came from the Census of Manufacturers, and the measure was time varying.
The annual dollar value of shipments in an industry, drawing data from the Census of Manufacturers. The measure was time varying because the sizes of markets change as industries evolve.

Leverage is measured as the ratio of the book value of total debt (long-term and short-term debt) to market value of equity and book value of debt. Because this ratio is bounded at zero and one, the authors also used a logistic transformation, log[Leverage / (1-Leverage)], and report that apart from minor differences in magnitude and significance the results are the same for leverage and its logarithm.

Depreciation, amortization and investment tax credits scaled by earnings before interest, depreciation and taxes, the measure used by Bradley et al. and adopted here as a proxy for redeployable assets. The authors also describe the ratio of depreciation to total assets as an index of the extent to which the assets of the firm are redeployable. Propositions 1 and 2 suggest that depreciation should be positively related to leverage.

Depreciation is proportional to the value of physical assets such as buildings, plant and equipment that act as collateral and provide security for lenders; the same depreciation measure used for redeployability serves as the proxy for investments in tangible assets under Proposition 2.

Ratio of R&D expenses to net sales (R&D intensity), used as a proxy for the firm's intangible assets. To the extent that it is difficult for outsiders to assess the value of these assets, they are interpreted as investments in assets that cannot be readily redeployed, which implies a negative relationship with leverage.

Ratio of advertising expenses to net sales (advertising intensity), interpreted as investment in reputational assets such as brand name. The authors argue that image and brand names may be bought and sold without much transaction cost, and that higher advertising may be seen as a signal that the firm intends to stay in a market and not harvest or liquidate.

Standard deviation of the annual percentage change in cash flows (earnings before interest, depreciation and taxes) for the previous 10 years, the measure used by Bradley et al. The authors also used operating income instead of cash flow in constructing a risk measure and report no qualitative difference in the results.

Ratio of capital expenditures on property, plant and equipment to earnings before interest, depreciation and taxes (EBIT), constructed as a proxy for the firm's future growth prospects. It is used to test the agency theory prediction that growth opportunities will be negatively related to leverage.

Class variable given by the COMPUSTAT identification number for the firm. It is treated as an independent random variable, and its variance component in the leverage decomposition measures the share of total variance in capital structure attributable to unspecified firm-level differences; the components were estimated with the MIQUE method in SAS. The varying intercept of the error components regressions is read as capturing each firm's unique ability to manage its relationships with lenders.

Class variable given by the 3-digit SIC code of the firm's industry, treated as an independent random variable. Its variance component measures the share of total variance in leverage attributable to industry differences.

Class variable for the observation year, treated as an independent random variable. Its variance component measures the share of total variance in leverage attributable to year to year changes in policies and regulations.

A Herfindahl-type measure of product diversity that takes into account both the number of segments in which the firm operates and the relative importance of each segment to the firm's sales; it is similar to measures used by Tallman and Li (1996), Grant et al. (1988) and Itami et al. (1982). A squared term of this measure (Product Diversity squared) was entered in the regressions to test the curvilinear relationship, and the interaction models used centered variables.
time_window: strategic inputs measured one year before performance

description: After-tax return on total sales, treated by the authors as their primary measure of profitability. The rationale given is that sales and profits are both reported at current rates and reflect current operations, avoiding the differential asset valuation effects of measures such as ROA in very international companies. A single-year lag was used from strategic inputs to performance measurement.
time_window: measured one year after the strategic inputs

description: After-tax return on assets, one of the initial performance measures used to facilitate comparison with prior research. The authors report that the results for ROA were very similar to those for ROS, and that they preferred ROS as their measure of profitability.
time_window: measured one year after the strategic inputs

description: Growth in sales, used to test the common perception that Japanese firms emphasize increasing market share over short-term profitability and to provide a measure of operating performance to complement the accounting performance measures.
time_window: measured one year after the strategic inputs

description: Calculated as the ratio of foreign subsidiary sales to total firm sales, a measure used by Grant et al. (1988), Geringer et al. (1989) and Tallman and Li (1996). The authors note that it does not control for intermediate goods exported from the home country and resold by subsidiaries, so it is a relative indicator rather than an absolute measure of international to domestic operations.
time_window: strategic inputs measured one year before performance

description: The ratio of export sales to total firm sales, tested because Japanese firms have been described as focusing on global strategies characterized by large levels of export sales from the home company.
time_window: strategic inputs measured one year before performance

description: Calculated as the ratio of sales by foreign subsidiaries to total international (subsidiary plus export) sales. It differentiates a strictly overseas sales strategy from a multinational operating strategy using internal production; the authors note that intermediate good exports are double counted and therefore absolute effects cannot be stated.
time_window: strategic inputs measured one year before performance

description: A dummy variable representing membership in one of the six major financial or horizontal keiretsu groups, similar to the formulation in Hundley and Jacobson (1998). Positive membership represents only the closest level of affiliation, those companies which are part of the 'president's council' or equivalent; the variable proxies for what are actual continuous variables representing different levels of association.

Years from 1977 through 1993 were grouped into mutually exclusive blocks by LISREL multiple groups analysis, comparing the covariance matrices of a reduced-form regression year by year until a significant difference (better than a 0.05 probability) was found; years within a block were pooled and treated as a single homogeneous sample. The three periods identified were 1977-1986, 1987-1991 and 1992-1993, and regressions were run separately for each.

Response delay is calculated in working days as the difference between the date of the action and the date of the response. Working days were used to assess the number of exchange trading days between two events. Because the response delays were severely skewed, the analysis used the natural logarithm of response delay.
time_window: up to twelve months after the action

description: Stock effects were calculated for the responder at the day of his/her response. A two-day event window was constructed for every action consisting of the day prior to the press release describing the competitive move and the day of the release itself. Actual stock returns in the event window were compared with hypothetical returns calculated from a capital asset pricing model dynamically estimated for each move using the returns of the 120 days prior to the event window, with the market return modeled using S&P 500 index returns. Deviations were standardized using the procedure proposed by Dodd and Warner, representing the stock effect as a deviation from the market-imputed return in standard deviation units of a standard normal distribution. Fourteen responses were excluded because of overlapping events, leaving 91 responses.
scale: standard deviation units of a standard normal distribution
time_window: two-day event window (day before the press release and the day of the release)

description: The wealth effect of the response for the original actor was determined by calculating a stock effect for the first mover on the day of the response, using the same event study procedure as for the responder. Checks against overlapping events for first movers led to the deletion of another 14 responses, resulting in a sample of 77 cases.
scale: standard deviation units of a standard normal distribution
time_window: two-day event window (day before the press release and the day of the release)

description: Average of five separate seven-point Likert-type questions (1 = not at all, 7 = very much) measuring outflow of knowledge from the focal subsidiary to other parts of the MNC. The items ask whether the subsidiary's distinctive competence in each of the following areas/functions is used by other units within the corporation: general management, manufacturing, marketing/sales, service, and R&D. The scale has an alpha of 0.76.

variable_name: GM compensation based on MNC performance
description: The percentage of total compensation for the general manager that is based on overall MNC performance. This measure was calculated by multiplying the percentage of a general manager's total compensation that was bonus compensation by the percentage of bonus compensation based on overall MNC performance.

variable_name: Other top management compensation based on MNC performance
description: The percentage of total compensation for the other top management (excluding the GM) based on overall MNC performance. This measure was calculated by multiplying the percentage of other top managements' total compensation that was bonus compensation by the percentage of bonus compensation based on overall MNC performance. Other top management includes all who report directly to the general manager but not the general manager him/herself.
A scale consisting of two seven-point Likert-type questions measuring the alignment of objectives among different subsidiaries. Cronbach's alpha for the scale is 0.77.
Takes on the value of 0 when the subsidiary is located in Finland and 1 when it is located in China.
Binary variable equaling one for the opposition outcomes 'invalid' and 'valid but in amended form' and zero for 'valid'. The variable has a mean of 0.71 in the sample.

Number of citations received by the focal patent from other patents within the first five years following the opposition outcome, using the earliest filing date of the citing patent as an approximation for the actual invention date. Only citations from patents filed by firms other than the focal patentee are counted. One is added before taking the logarithm to include patents without citations.
time_window: five years following the opposition outcome

description: First principal component based on the number of claims, the number of IPC classes, and the patent family size. The patent value distribution is stratified by year and technology field to account for time- and technology-specific variation of patent indicators.
Citations are split into low- and high-value citations depending on whether the citing patent is of above-average value, based on the principal component of claims, IPC classes, and family size.

variable_name: Same technology class; Same industry; Same country
description: Three binary indicators of product market competition between the focal patentee and the citing firm: (i) the citing patent belongs to the same technology class (same primary IPC4 code) as the opposed patent, (ii) the citing patentee is active in the same industry (same first three digits of NACE Rev. 2) as the opposed patentee, and (iii) the citing patentee resides in the same country (EU, UK, US, JP, RoW) as the opposed patentee. Each indicator is used to split the citation count.

Time-variant density of patent thickets in the focal patent's technology field, measured by counting citation constellations in which three patentees can mutually block each other. The measure is higher in complex technology fields and in recent years.

Dummy variable for whether the patent's granting examiner is part of the opposition division, extracted from documents related to examination and opposition. Participation is due to capacity constraints in the technical art unit at the moment the opposition division is appointed; granting examiners participate in more than 50% of all opposition proceedings.

For each potential director d the authors created a measure of experience in each therapeutic market m in year t by identifying the number of new drugs introduced in year t for market m by each firm j in which director d held a directorship. They then created a dyad-level (focal firm-director) measure by cumulating the experience of director d across all therapeutic markets m in which firm i is considering entering (an indicator equals 1 if firm i is considering entering market m in year t and 0 otherwise). Experience obtained in the most recent three-year window was used with a depreciation factor of 40 percent, because recent experience is more valuable than older experience. The formulas themselves are not readable in the supplied text.
time_window: most recent three-year window; explanatory variables measured in year t-1 for appointment in year t

description: Coded 1 if director d, who was not on the board of company i in year t-1, was appointed to that board in year t, and 0 otherwise. The authors combined the 125 firms that were considering entry into at least one market with a list of 1,810 directors currently serving on the board(s) of other pharmaceutical firms, generating all possible firm-director combinations for the sample period. Appointment data were read from firms' proxy statements.

The number of financial restatement cases in which a focal firm had been involved in the last three years, taken from the Financial Statement Restatement Database, which provides historical information about firms' accounting irregularities.

Each firm's status was calculated by counting the number of alliances the firm had established with other pharmaceutical firms in the last five years; where a potential director served on more than one board, the average of the status scores of all these firms was used. The status score of the incumbent firm where the potential director currently served was then subtracted from the status score of the focal firm, so that higher values imply the focal firm had a higher status than the firm(s) where the potential director currently served.
time_window: alliances in the last five years

description: For each director d of the focal pharmaceutical firm i, the authors created a measure of experience in therapeutic area m in year t by identifying the number of new drugs introduced in year t for market m by each interlocking firm j in which director d also held a directorship. They then created a dyad-level (focal firm-market) measure by cumulating the experience scores for all of the directors who sat on the board of the focal company, capturing the overall experience in market m of all the focal firm's interlocking directors in year t. Experience obtained in the most recent three-year window was used with a depreciation factor (delta) of 40 percent; the formulas themselves are not readable in the supplied text.
time_window: most recent three-year window; explanatory variables measured in year t-2 for entry in year t

description: Coded 1 for those firm-market combinations realized in year t through in-house development, an alliance, or an acquisition, and 0 for those not realized by the end of year t. Potential destinations were therapeutic markets in which the firm had not started to develop a drug before year t through either in-house development or a strategic alliance with an incumbent firm. Entry was identified at the earliest stage at which the intention to enter a new market can be observed, i.e., when a drug candidate targeted at a specific therapeutic market starts pre-clinical trials.

Constructed by counting the number of new drugs the focal firm had developed in the recent three-year window. A depreciation factor of 40 percent was used to calculate this firm-level aggregated measure of experience.

A dyad measure of ex ante overlap between focal firm i and each interlocked firm j created using Sohn's (2001) formula, in which ximt and xjmt are the number of drugs that firms i and j offered in market m in year t respectively. Because a focal firm might be interlocked with more than one incumbent firm, the authors created an overall measure of market overlap at the focal-firm level by averaging all the dyad-level overlap scores between firm i and all the incumbent interlocked firms. The final variable can take a value between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates that the focal firm's drugs are in markets in which the incumbent interlocked firms have no presence, and 1 indicates that the incumbent interlocked firms have as many drugs as the focal firm in the markets in which the focal firm is active.

Each entering operator was associated with the country where it operated, and for every country A the author determined three top international calling partners, B, C and D, using the number of minutes of outgoing publicly switched telecommunications traffic reported in the TeleGeography Annual Traffic Report 2001. For each of a country's three top calling partners, the total number of subscribers using a particular technology was divided by the total number of active subscribers in the partner country in any given quarterly period. The variable is the simple average of the scores of B, C and D.
scale: Share of subscribers (0-1), averaged across the three partner countries
time_window: Two quarters prior to the operator's entry (two-lag specification)

description: The size of the worldwide network for each technology (the 'classical' network effect) was measured by taking the total number of operators worldwide using a particular technology and dividing by the total number of active operators in any given quarterly period. This variable is calculated quarterly for each of the three technologies. Data were compiled from the EMC database.
time_window: Quarterly; captured two quarters prior to entry

description: The dependent variable registers each operator's choice of technology: it takes a value of 1 if CDMA was chosen, 2 if GSM was chosen, and 3 in the case of TDMA. Technologies that had never been implemented worldwide in a frequency allocated to an operator were removed as options for that operator, and cases in which only one option was available were eliminated.

The distribution of a firm's patents across all 64 pharmaceutical patent classes, computed with the inverse of the nonbiased Herfindahl Index proposed by Hall (2002), which adjusts for bias caused by the size of firms' patent portfolios. The index rises with the number of domains (patent classes) a firm invents in and with the equality of its efforts across classes; its value can range from 0 to 1, with a smaller value indicating lower internal knowledge variety. All independent variables are lagged by one year relative to the dependent variable.

The angular separation between a firm's and all of its partners' patent portfolios, which measures the degree to which a firm and its partners patent with the same intensity in the same classes. Each firm's number of patents in a given class is divided by the highest number of patents held by the firm or its partners in that class to adjust for larger partner portfolios. The measure is calculated for each focal firm and partner dyad and then averaged to the firm level; where firms do not patent, the measure is set equal to 1. Values range from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates the greatest possible external knowledge distance and 0 indicates no distance. All independent variables are lagged by one year.

The number of citations that a firm's patents receive, measured as the sum of all citations received in years t+1 to t+3 by all of the firm's patents granted in year t. For patents granted in the final year of the study, 2004, citation data were collected through 2007. The grant date is used rather than the application date because a patent's citation clock does not start until it is issued.

A nine-item scale adopted from prior research, rated on a seven-point scale, asking the three respondents of each initiative to assess the success of the initiative over the last three months on meeting staffing goals, time expectations, quality parameters, reliability parameters, cost parameters, efficiency parameters, user/client satisfaction expectations, service expectations, and objective expectations. Principal component analysis yielded one factor and a scale of nine items with an alpha of .88. Item means were calculated across the three respondents and summed to form the aggregate scale value for each initiative.
time_window: the last three months of the initiative

description: Measured, in congruence with previous studies, as the average of frequency and closeness scores reported on seven-point scales, with an additional box with the value of 0 indicating no contact. Frequency and closeness were each assessed with two questions about interactions with the listed functional units for daily job issues and for social support, and about how close the working and social support relationship was. Based on the validated sociomatrices, an initiative unit's score is the average score for all its ties to other organizational units, using the scores indicated by the organizational units (in-tie-strength) rather than those indicated by the initiative units.
scale: 0 to 7 per item; average of frequency and closeness

description: Degree centrality captures the extent to which each initiative unit had direct relationships and access to other organizational units; a focal unit is more central the larger its number of ties to other units in its network. Because the measure depends on network size, the measure for a given initiative unit was divided by the measure's maximum value, giving the proportion of units out of the total network with which the focal unit had direct relationships. Values for all 76 initiatives were calculated via UCINET 6.0 from validated sociomatrices coded 0 or 1 for the presence or absence of a relationship; the specifications were presented in equations that are not readable in this text.

Burt's measure of indirect constraint was employed to assess the existence or absence of structural holes; the constraint measure is a triadic density measure indicating the presence of strong third-party relationships around a relationship. The indirect constraint measure was calculated for all 76 initiatives via UCINET 6.0 on the validated sociomatrices of tie strength (closeness and frequency); the equations given in the text are not readable. To ease comparability among the hypotheses, all constraint values were subsequently subtracted from 1, so the measure indicates the extent of structural holes for each initiative team.

Two items adopted from Tsai and Ghoshal (1998), assessing the level of shared vision between different organizational units and between a focal unit and its whole organization, rated from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree.' The correlation index between the two items was significant at the .01 level with a Pearson's coefficient of .76, exceeding the threshold for integrating two items into one measure. Item means were calculated across the three respondents and summed to form the aggregate scale.

A six-item measure adapted from McGrath (2001) asking to what extent characteristics or factors of the initiative were new to the company: the systems used; the know-how of the initiative team; the skills of the initiative team; the technology used in the initiative; the products and services; and the informal norms and how things are done. The scale had an alpha of .81. Item means were calculated across the three respondents and summed to form the aggregate scale.

Internal R&D is calculated as in-house R&D spending divided by total sales. It is the independent variable for the outsourcing decision models and is also used as a control variable in the innovation models. Like the other time-varying explanatory variables, it is lagged one year in the outsourcing decision models and three years in the innovation models.
time_window: lagged one year for the outsourcing decision models and three years for the innovation models

description: A dummy variable that takes the value 1 if the firm outsources R&D abroad. Together with the domestic decision dummy it allows for firms that decide not to outsource, to outsource domestically, and/or to outsource abroad.
Represents all spending on transactions with independent R&D suppliers located abroad divided by total sales. It is used as an independent variable in the models of product and process innovation.
time_window: lagged three years in the innovation models

description: A dummy variable that takes the value 1 if the firm decides to outsource domestically. Firms might decide not to outsource, to outsource domestically, and/or to outsource abroad.
Represents all spending on transactions with independent R&D suppliers within France divided by total sales. It is used as an independent variable in the models of product and process innovation.
time_window: lagged three years in the innovation models

description: A dummy variable taking the value 1 if a firm successfully created at least one product innovation in a given year. The survey asks, 'has the firm innovated in terms of its products thanks to its R&D during this year?' Product innovation could consist of improving existing products or introducing new products to the market. The R&D inquiry does not report this variable before 1999.

Constructed in the same way as product innovation, that is as a dummy variable taking the value 1 if the firm successfully created at least one process innovation in a given year. Process is defined as 'the way in which the firm produces its goods.' The R&D inquiry does not report this variable before 1999.

variable_name: Decision to outsource R&D (domestic, foreign) and outsourcing spending
description: R&D outsourcing was measured by two dummies equal to 1 if the firm outsources R&D domestically or abroad, and by spending on transactions with independent R&D suppliers (domestic or abroad) divided by total sales.

The presence or absence of family ties between principal and agent, determined separately for each CEO and editor. For the CEO, the executive's last name was compared with the last name of a newspaper's owners; for the editor, who reports to the CEO, family status was confirmed if both executives had the same last name. Spain legally requires use of the last names of both father and mother, a practice that the authors say makes it easier to trace family ties.

The percent change in the number of newspapers sold from the time the executive took office to the time the executive departed, or to the end of 1993 if the executive was still in office. This measure of the growth (or decline) in newspaper sales during the executive's tenure was calculated separately for each CEO and each editor.
time_window: from the executive's taking office to departure or to the end of 1993

description: The percent change in the average number of newspapers sold between the tenure of a particular executive and the preceding executive. This index was also calculated separately for each CEO and editor.

Business risk during the tenure of each executive was measured as the ratio of the variance in the volume of newspapers sold (circulation) divided by a term consisting of the average circulation minus the minimum circulation squared. The more the average circulation exceeds the minimum circulation, the larger the denominator and the lower business risk; the larger the variance in circulation, the higher business risk. The ratio was subjected to a logarithmic transformation since the distribution that best fitted the data was lognormal, and it was calculated separately for the period corresponding to the tenure of each CEO and each editor.
time_window: the period corresponding to the tenure of each CEO and each editor

description: For each CEO and editor, how much time had transpired between the date of hiring and the date of termination (if the individual had been replaced) or 1993 (if the individual was still on the job). In the latter case the information was treated as censored data.

The degree to which an agency contract is relational, argued to be stronger for a CEO than for an editor: the CEO reports to a firm's board of directors and is responsible for all strategic and financial affairs of the business, whereas the editor is a professional journalist responsible for routine procedural matters, technical issues, implementation of the strategies traced by the CEO and the board, the content of the newspaper, and staff supervision, and is explicitly hired to perform a job for a fee. The analyses of the sensitivity of executive tenure to performance and business risk were conducted separately for CEOs and editors.

Two sets of dummy variables were created to measure the effect of CEO succession on organizational survival, one set for CEOs who had family ties to owners and one set for those who did not. Each dummy variable was coded 1 if a firm had a particular succession and 0 otherwise. Up to four successions were examined for nonfamily CEOs and up to two for family CEOs, since these ranges encompass over 90 percent of the exits during the period.

A measure created to capture how long the newspaper remained in circulation following each CEO succession event up to the next succession event (if any). If the newspaper went out of business after a particular CEO's departure, the chronological difference between the date of succession and the date the paper ceased to be published was used as the measure of survival length; if the newspaper remained in business after a CEO was replaced, survival length was measured as the chronological difference between the two succession events.

Each sampled manager was classified into one of three managerial levels. Top managers were the chief executive officer and his immediate subordinates of at least vice-presidential rank; middle managers were those with at least two levels of supervisors under their responsibility and no more than two reporting levels below top executives; lower-level managers were those reporting to middle-level managers or below. The definitions were closely coordinated with company officials to designate the appropriate managerial level for participants.

variable_name: standardized regression coefficient for each strength and weakness indicator
description: For each manager, stepwise linear regression was used with the effectiveness ratings of 30 simulated firms as the dependent variable and the values of the strength and weakness indicators (randomly assigned across cases) as the independent variables, producing an individual decision model. The standardized regression coefficients represent the decision-influencing cues and their weights. Only models satisfying the heuristic of an R2 greater than 0.40 were retained; one manager's model (R2 = 0.134) failed the heuristic, resulting in a sample of 55 managers and 1650 observations.

Managers were asked to evaluate the predictability of each item of the environment on a seven-point Likert-type scale. The instrument contained six scales, composed of 25 items, covering suppliers of raw materials and parts, competitors' behavior, clients, financial/capital markets, government regulatory agency actions and behavior of labor unions. Means from each of the six scales were obtained and summed for the total PEU scale. Coefficient alphas were calculated for each scale and all were acceptable except for the clients scale, for which elimination of one item resulted in an acceptable coefficient.
scale: seven-point Likert-type items; scale means summed into a total score

description: The managers came from three firms, each in a different industry: oil tools, petrochemical and brewing. Two firms were headquartered in Venezuela and one in Brazil. Firm (company industry) was used as the moderator in the moderated regression analysis of strength and weakness indicator importance, and separate regression models were estimated for each management level within each firm.

The amount of formal governance was measured based on eight mechanisms: business plans, balance sheets, performance indices, profit and loss accounts, internal prices, economic efficiency calculations, reports, and service level agreements. The use of each in the alliance was measured on a five-point scale ranging from 'not at all' to 'to a large extent' and the average was used as the overall measure. The authors describe the measures as formative rather than reflective, so factor analysis was not applied.
scale: five-point scale ranging from 'not at all' to 'to a large extent'

description: To measure the amount of relational governance used, the authors drew on people- and social-based mechanisms that enhance open communication and sharing of information, trust, dependence, and cooperation. These involved six mechanisms: steering committees, project groups, expert committees, a cooperation manager, face-to-face meetings at the top management level, and the filling of key positions. The degree to which each was used in the alliance was measured on a five-point scale ranging from 'not at all' to 'to a large extent' and the average used as the measure.
scale: five-point scale ranging from 'not at all' to 'to a large extent'

description: A list of strategic resources in telecommunications was identified from the literature and reviewed with experts, yielding 14 resources of which five are knowledge-based. Respondents indicated on a scale of one (low) to five (high) the extent to which their own company and the partner transferred these resources into the alliance, and the average score of the five measures was used.

A list of strategic resources in telecommunications was identified from the literature and reviewed with experts, yielding 14 resources of which nine are property-based. Respondents indicated on a scale of one (low) to five (high) the extent to which their own company and the partner transferred these resources into the alliance, and the average score of the nine measures was used.

The measure is based on the degree to which the alliance achieved 13 goals, weighted according to the extent to which each goal was rated as 'relevant to the alliance.' Seven goals came from the prior literature and six were industry specific, confirmed with nine practitioners from the telecommunications industry. The degree to which each goal was reached was rated on a scale of one (not at all) to five (to a high extent), and the final measure is an average of these weighted ratings.
scale: one (not at all) to five (to a high extent)

description: Pilot is an indicator that equals one for establishments affiliated to a pilot firm and zero otherwise. Post is an indicator that equals one for fiscal years 2005 to 2006 and zero for 2002 to 2003. Their interaction identifies the exogenous increase in short-selling pressure for pilot firms during Reg SHO; pilot and post alone are fully absorbed by the fixed effects included.

The sum of injury cases scaled by total working hours of establishment i of firm j in fiscal year t, and the sum is multiplied by 200,000. The injury cases involved general injuries, skin disorders, respiratory conditions, poisonings, all other illnesses, and work-related deaths.

The number of analysts who issue long-term forecasts scaled by the number of analysts who issue short-term forecasts. Analyst data during a three-year period before the Reg SHO pilot program are used to construct the measure. A higher value indicates that the firm confronts more long-term-oriented analysts.
time_window: three-year period before the Reg SHO pilot program

description: Measured based on investors' portfolio churn ratio. Investor-level churn ratio captures how frequently an investor reshuffles its portfolio; the firm-level churn ratio is the share-weighted average of investor-level churn ratios, where the weight is the number of shares held by an investor divided by the number of shares outstanding. The average firm-level churn ratio across eight quarters before the Reg SHO pilot program is then multiplied by -1 to reflect investor long horizon. A higher value indicates that a firm's shares are held by more long-horizon investors.
time_window: eight quarters before the Reg SHO pilot program

description: Labor union status from 2000 to 2004 was constructed from FMCS records of F7 notices. If there are any records indicating a firm or its subsidiaries as affiliated to labor unions, the variable takes one, and zero otherwise.

Based on linguistic analysis of the words in CEO presentation sessions during conference calls. In each transcript the number of long-term keywords (e.g., year or annual, long-term or long-run, look(ing) forward) and short-term keywords (e.g., day(s) or daily, week(s) or weekly) is counted; the number of long-term keywords is divided by the number of short-term keywords. The average value across all transcripts before the Reg SHO pilot program is used. A greater value indicates that a firm's TMT is more long-term-oriented.
time_window: transcripts before the Reg SHO pilot program

description: Discretionary safety expenditures are derived from observable SG&A expenditures, following Caskey and Ozel (2017), estimated by industry-year using SG&A, firm employees and sales; the residuals are taken to capture changes in discretionary safety expenditure. The authors state that safety expenditures are recognized under selling, general, and administrative expenditures under U.S. GAAP.
The sum of the cost of goods sold and inventory divided by total assets. It is used as an outcome of short-selling pressure and as a mediating channel returning to workplace injuries.
The annual sales divided by total assets. It is used as an outcome of short-selling pressure and as a mediating channel returning to workplace injuries.

A two-year average ROA (net income divided by average assets) for 2002 and 2003, computed to guard against any one year outlier performance and to measure ROA later than the independent variables measured in 2001. Net income is revenues minus expenses, calculated as net interest income plus noninterest income minus total noninterest expense; average assets are total assets for the current period plus total assets for the prior year divided by two.

Binary variable capturing a credit union's access to the supplier's technology solutions. It equals 1 for in-sourcing (a client locus of supplier capability deployment), where the credit union procures its supplier's technology as on-site IT platforms and solutions operated by its own staff, and 0 for outsourcing (a supplier locus of capability deployment), where the platforms and solutions reside at the supplier's location and client employees use basic hardware to access and transmit data.

Measured as amount of loans processed divided by loan servicing expenses. Loan servicing expenses comprise recording fees, credit reports to approve loans, loan processing expenses to track payments and refinance, and collection expenses to recoup loans. A natural log transformation is applied given the distributional properties of the ratio.

Average competence scores for each of the top 22 technology solution suppliers in the small credit union market, provided by the Filene Research Institute, where a supplier's score is based on how several credit union clients assess its skill level. The composite score averages five items on a five-point scale from excellent (5) to poor (1) that assess the extent to which a supplier executes its activities well; two items assess proficiency in designing IT systems and platforms and three assess proficiency in technology delivery to clients.
scale: five-point scale from excellent (5) to poor (1)
time_window: survey conducted in the fall of 2001

description: Dichotomous variable equal to 1 if the application received an endorsement, 0 if not. Endorsed applications were tracked by the senior directors of admissions with a prominent, distinctly colored database field containing only the endorser's name; the field was empty for non-endorsed applicants. During the study period 4.8 percent of applicants (1,031 individuals) were endorsed, by university alumni or current students, faculty, admissions staff members, business leaders, university staff members, and persons of interest.

Readers review an application and assign competency scores using an online competency assessment tool, drawing on test scores, academic transcripts, résumés, personal essays, letters of recommendation, and other information about the applicant's career and academic history. The nine competencies are standardized test performance (GMAT or GRE scores), academic excellence (undergraduate GPA), professional accomplishment, social affinity, self-direction, team management, goal attainment, presentation, and creativity. All are scored on a 5-point scale ranging from deficient to exceptional, with the second-to-lowest score reserved for competencies assessed to be average; readers cannot observe which applicants were endorsed.
scale: 5-point scale ranging from deficient to exceptional

description: Interviewers review the readers' competency scores and summary notes before interviews that average 30 to 40 minutes, and during these conversations they use behavioral questions to score applicants along the same set of competency metrics, except standardized test performance and academic excellence, which are assessed only at the reader stage. The scores use the same 5-point scale, and interviewers do not know whether an applicant was endorsed.
scale: 5-point scale ranging from deficient to exceptional

description: Dichotomous outcome equal to 1 if the applicant received an interview invitation. The senior directors of admissions choose applicants with strong competency scores and extend interview invitations; during the study period 36.6 percent of all applicants evaluated by readers were selected for interviews.

Dichotomous outcome equal to 1 if the applicant received an offer of admission. Offers are determined by the senior directors of admissions based primarily on interviewers' competency scores; of all interviewed applicants, 53.4 percent received offers during the study period.

Dichotomous outcome equal to 1 if the student received an academic award. These awards are highly competitive and presented in response to exceptional academic achievement, and just 4.6 percent of admitted students are awardees.
Students' final grade point average, taken from the school's student records for matriculating MBA students.
Students' full-time job salary at the time of graduation, taken from job placement and salary information on matriculating students.
Full-time job signing bonus received at the time of graduation by matriculating MBA students.
Full-time salary increases relative to the student's pre-MBA salary, based on job placement and salary records.
time_window: at the time of graduation, relative to pre-MBA salary

description: Dichotomous outcome equal to 1 if the individual held a student club leadership position while a student; the authors use participation in key student governing activities as a proxy for better citizenship. Records on this variable were available during only three school years.
time_window: as a student (three school years of records)

variable_name: school gift amount in the 5 years after MBA graduation
description: Cumulative monetary donations to the school over the five years after graduating, modeled as the natural log of gift amounts. The distribution of donations is non-normal, with a large number of small donations (54.3 percent of all donations were less than $499) and relevant gift outliers (2 percent of donations were larger than $2,500).

One of two factors obtained from an orthogonal varimax factor solution of eight items on internal manufacturing sources extracted from the literature; it explained part of the 56.03 percent of variance accounted for by the two factors. The five-item factor had an alpha of 0.73 and indicated the existence of strong internal manufacturing-related HR skills among a firm's management and employees.
time_window: the 3 years preceding the dependent variables

description: The second factor from the factor solution of the eight internal manufacturing source items. It had three items and showed the use of external consultants and temporary employees.
time_window: the 3 years preceding the dependent variables

description: The first of three factors obtained from an orthogonal varimax factor analysis of fourteen items on external manufacturing sources. It had five items, an alpha of 0.74, and showed the existence of strong internal manufacturing technological resources and facilities. The authors describe it as the measure of the use of internal technological sources.
time_window: the 3 years preceding the dependent variables

description: The second factor from the orthogonal varimax factor analysis of fourteen items on external manufacturing sources; the three factors together explained 66.11 percent of variance. It had five items and captured the use of joint ventures and alliances in manufacturing.
time_window: the 3 years preceding the dependent variables

description: The third factor from the orthogonal varimax factor analysis of fourteen items on external manufacturing sources. It had four items, an alpha of 0.68, and showed a firm's use of outsourcing and licensing.
time_window: the 3 years preceding the dependent variables

description: The first of three factors obtained from an orthogonal varimax factor analysis of eleven integration items extracted from the literature; the three factors explained 70.21 percent of variance. It had five items, an alpha of 0.82, and captured the formal coordination between manufacturing and other functional units in TC.
time_window: the 3 years preceding the dependent variables

description: The second factor from the factor analysis of eleven integration items. It had three items, an alpha of 0.73, and indicated the involvement of manufacturing in TC.
time_window: the 3 years preceding the dependent variables

description: The third factor from the factor analysis of eleven integration items. It had three items, an alpha of 0.73, and showed the existence of informal manufacturing coordination.
time_window: the 3 years preceding the dependent variables

description: Measured by the number of announcements of new product introductions each firm made over the 1997-99 period. The number of announcements came from Lexis-Nexis. Each product introduction was counted only once, even if it appeared in multiple announcements.

Product announcements were reclassified into radical versus incremental. Following past research, three MBA students independently reviewed all announcements related to a given product introduction and rated it based on its radicalness; 13 announcements with strong disagreements were excluded from the analyses. Radically new products were coded as 1 and incremental products as zero.

The number of a firm's patents, counted using data from the U.S. Patent Office; data were available for 103 firms. The authors note that patent counts did not separate significant from incremental innovations and that some patents did not generate new products.

Data came from the 1999 survey. Managers were asked how long on average it takes their company to introduce a newly developed product to the market, and respondents provided data in months. The measure was validated against references in Lexis-Nexis to the length of time it took some companies to develop and introduce new products and against a survey statement on whether the company has a shorter product development cycle than its key competitors.

Ratio of the mean of TMT pay to the focal executive's pay, where each executive's pay is the sum of short- and long-term pay calculated using the Black-Scholes present value method as listed in ExecuComp. Smaller values indicate that an executive earns relatively more.

Pay dispersion in the new firm's TMT, calculated as the coefficient of variation in pay, where pay includes short- and long-term pay calculated using the Black-Scholes present value method as listed in ExecuComp. Used as a true-value dependent variable with Prior Pay Dispersion included as a control; larger values indicate higher levels of pay dispersion.
Simple difference of pay dispersion from the prior to the new firm (the change score Cx = X2 - X1), capturing the actual amount of dispersion increase or decrease upon moving firms.
Constructed by regressing the simple difference in pay dispersion between the new and prior firms onto the pay dispersion of the prior firm and saving the residuals as the variable of interest.

Pay disparity is the difference between the average total pay of the TMT and the total pay of the focal executive, where each executive's pay is the sum of short- and long-term pay calculated using the Black-Scholes present value method in ExecuComp, such that smaller values indicate an executive was paid more relatively. The true value in the new firm is used as the dependent variable while Prior Pay Disparity is controlled; the authors state that larger values of this dependent variable indicate lower levels of pay disparity.

Simple difference of pay disparity from the prior to the new firm (the change score Cx), capturing the actual amount of disparity increase or decrease when moving firms. Because the variable has positive and negative values as well as a significant skew, the authors take the inverse hyperbolic sinh.
Constructed by regressing the simple difference in pay disparity between the new and prior firms onto the pay disparity of the prior firm and saving the residuals as the variable of interest.
Binary variable equal to 1 if relative pay decreased from the prior firm to the new firm and 0 if not, used as an alternative test of executives improving relative pay when moving to the new firm.
Residualized version of the relative pay advance dummy, created by using a probit model to regress the dummy onto pay disparity in the prior firm and saving the residuals as the variable of interest.
Advertising expenditures collected in the survey and measured at the firm level (i.e., at the Spanish subsidiary level if foreign-owned). Expressed in thousands of pesetas.
R&D expenditures collected in the survey and measured at the firm level (i.e., at the Spanish subsidiary level if foreign-owned). Expressed in thousands of pesetas.
The survey collects total sales and export sales; domestic sales are calculated by subtracting export sales from total sales. Measured in thousands of Spanish pesetas.
Export sales as collected in the survey. Measured in thousands of Spanish pesetas.
Captures the GDP in Spain, calculated from real GDP data published by the U.S. Department of Energy and obtained from Global Insight. Reported in billions of U.S. dollars.
A weighted average of foreign GDP in the three potential destination markets. Reported in billions of U.S. dollars and calculated from the same U.S. Department of Energy GDP data.

Firm-specific real exchange rate index. Destination markets were grouped into three areas: OECD countries in the European Union, non-European OECD destinations, and the rest of the world; a specific exchange rate was applied to each region (peseta/euro, peseta/U.S. dollar, and the IMF effective nominal exchange rate for Spain, respectively). Bilateral rates were converted to a common index using U.S. dollar equivalents and converted into real rates by multiplying nominal rates by the ratio of inflation between each destination region and Spain, using the World Development Indicators. The three destination measures were then combined into a unitary, firm-specific measure weighted by the proportion of firm export sales to each of the three destination regions. For non-exporters, exchange rates were estimated using industry averages for the largest export destination markets. Expressed as pesetas divided by foreign currencies, so increasing values indicate depreciation of the peseta.
time_window: 1990 and 1994 for the breakdown of export markets

description: Dummy variable identifying the name type of the applicant, Male or Female. The gender of the inventor is determined from the given name specified in the application by merging the U.S. Social Security Administration lists of first names differentiated by gender for all years from 1880 to 2015 and calculating the female likelihood, the probability that a given name belongs to a woman. Every name with a female probability of more than 90% is defined as a female name, every name with a female probability of less than 10% is a male name, and all other names are removed from the analysis.

Dummy variable that takes value one if the applicant's application in an art unit and filing year is granted by the examiner over the whole review process, and zero otherwise. Robust standard errors clustered at the examiner level are reported in parentheses.

Dummy variable whether a patent was granted by a first action on the merits, that is, it did not receive a nonfinal rejection. The dependent variable is coded as one if the patent application is granted in this first round; first allowance granted applications are compared with both ultimately successful and unsuccessful applications.

Dummy variable indicating that the examiner's name is a female name. The examiner's gender is identified from the given name in the same way as the inventor's, using the female likelihood derived from U.S. Social Security Administration name lists; ambiguous names, those between 0.1 and 0.9, are excluded from the main analysis.
Measured as the filing year of an application minus the year of the first appearance of the reviewer in the database. The average experience of reviewers is about 9.4 years.

The number of new and ongoing applications (from single inventors and teams) in a given year, divided by 100. Applications are assigned to an examiner's workload from the year of the filing to the year of the issue or final rejection, and the workload of the respective examiner during the filing year is assigned to an application.

For each service market in which a hospital currently operated (and thus was capable of exiting), the average fraction of the services currently offered by the focal hospital that were offered by other hospitals also currently in that service market within a county. It is a service-level construct that differs across hospitals and also within a given hospital, because a hospital's direct competitors in one service market can differ from those in another. The measure ranged from a high of 100%, when each of the other hospitals offering the service also offered every other service that the focal hospital did, to a low of zero when all hospitals offering the service offered no other services in common.

The dependent variable, measured as a dichotomous variable representing the event of withdrawal from a market. An observation was included in the dataset if, for a given service, a hospital offered the service in the prior year (and thus was capable of exiting that market in the current year). Market exit was coded as 1 (a service was offered in the previous period and not offered in the current period) and continued market participation was coded as 0.
time_window: measured from period t to t + 1

description: The way in which a service was provided, measured as a dummy variable denoting whether a hospital contracted for the service or undertook its provision itself.

Chief executive successions were coded for each year of the study. A change was considered to have taken place when the chief executive for a given year was different from the one for the previous year.

The occupancy rate, the average percentage rate of beds occupied in the hospital. It was considered an appropriate performance measure because it indicates how well a hospital's service mix matches demand, and the extent to which beds are filled or empty has a direct link to a hospital's current service offerings.
Financial performance, calculated as the ratio of net income to operating revenues for each year. The authors included it because the sample included for-profit hospitals.
scale: ratio of net income to operating revenues

description: A binary variable coded 1 if a firm was included among the top 50 firms in the previous year's Fortune 'Most Admired Companies' or Wall Street Journal/Harris Interactive 'Reputation Quotient' rankings. The authors state that these rankings are based on industry experts' (peer CEOs and analysts) expectations about firms' future performance and capabilities.

The authors identified each breached firm's 10 nearest competitors in the Text-Based Network Industries database, yielding 1609 firm-years, and combined these with the breached firms to form the pool used to identify celebrity. They collected articles about these firms published by the top 25 US newspapers during the previous year to create two components: volume of public attention (number of articles covering a firm) and positive emotional resonance, computed with LIWC as the ratio of positive emotional words to total emotional words in each article, averaged at the firm level. Scores for both components were standardized, transformed so all values were positive, and multiplied; celebrity firms were those with scores one standard deviation or more above the mean of the pool.
scale: binary, based on scores one standard deviation or more above the pool mean

description: The extent to which the media scandalized a data breach incident, captured as the count of articles covering the focal incident each day during the two weeks following the disclosure date. Only articles about the breach incident, not articles about the firm in general, were counted, and the search was restricted to English-language outlets registered to Factiva. Sixty-four percent of the breaches received no media coverage.

Operationalized as the number of accounts affected by a breach incident, reflecting the quantifiable nature of objective severity. The authors log-transformed the variable because it has a significant rightward skew.

Operationalized using cumulative media coverage about the focal breach, equal to the total number of articles between the breach disclosure date and 1 day before the observation date. Because the variable was significantly right-skewed, the authors transformed it into its natural logarithm after adding a 1 to all observations.
time_window: from the breach disclosure date to 1 day before the observation date

description: Measured as the ratio of a specific subsidiary's sales to the rest of the MNC to which it belongs (including both the parent and other subsidiaries) in a particular year to the total sales of the subsidiary in the same year. Because not all subsidiaries engaged in intrafirm trade, the variable takes a value of zero in a large number of cases.
time_window: same year as the dependent variable

description: Operationalized as the risk of contract repudiation by a subsidiary's host government, using data obtained from the International Country Risk Guide (the IRIS data set). In the IRIS data set higher values imply lower risk, and the authors multiplied the data by -1 before conducting the analyses, so that higher values on the variable used here imply greater country risk. The measure ranges from 0 to 10 and was chosen over risk of expropriation because it has somewhat greater variance.
time_window: 1982-97 data availability; contemporaneous with the dependent variable

description: Measured by counting the lagged number of high-risk subsidiaries in each MNC network by year. High-risk subsidiaries were defined as those falling in the 25th percentile of country risk calculated from the population of subsidiaries, where higher values imply lower risk. The 25th percentile was used rather than the mean or median because so much MNC activity is in 'safe' countries that the mean and median of country risk for the entire population of subsidiaries are very close to the highest possible value of the risk index.

Measured as the lagged total number of international subsidiaries in an MNC network. Together with experience in high-risk countries it constitutes two different levels of granularity of international experience used as a proxy for capabilities in deploying political strategies.

Measured, capturing experience with intrafirm trade, as the lagged sum of the intrafirm sales of all foreign subsidiaries to the U.S. parent and the U.S. parent's sales to all foreign subsidiaries divided by the total sales of the U.S. parent. The same variable is used as a control for MNC strategy in all regression estimates.

Firm risk taking is measured as a multidimensional construct using two risk-taking dimensions: capital expenditure and the firm's long-term debt. All measures were scaled by dividing them with annual sales, and the two variables were weighted by extracting common components using principal component analysis.

Performance is measured as return on assets (ROA), and the aspiration level is a weighted average of the historical and the social aspiration level. The historical aspiration level is an exponentially weighted moving average of the firm's own performance at t-2 and t-3; the social aspiration level is the median ROA of all other firms within the same four-digit SIC industry group. Performance feedback is the difference between the firm's actual performance and its aspiration level, and this variable captures the negative distance from the aspiration level.

Performance is measured as return on assets (ROA), and the aspiration level is a weighted average of the historical and the social aspiration level. The historical aspiration level is an exponentially weighted moving average of the firm's own performance at t-2 and t-3; the social aspiration level is the median ROA of all other firms within the same four-digit SIC industry group. Performance feedback is the difference between the firm's actual performance and its aspiration level, and this variable captures the positive distance from the aspiration level.

The measure first searches for all news articles about a particular CEO that appeared during the first 3 years of their tenure in major media outlets such as Business Week, Financial Times, New York Times, The Economist, and Wall Street Journal. For each CEO the authors determined the number of articles that described the CEO as confident and the number that described the CEO as not confident, counting a term only if it appeared within 10 words of the CEO's name. The difference between the two counts is divided by the total number of articles.
scale: -1 to 1, where higher values indicate higher levels of overconfidence
time_window: first 3 years of the CEO's tenure

description: Following Malmendier and Tate (2005), the measure is based on the premise that CEOs who persistently postpone exercising fully vested in-the-money stock options are overconfident about the future prospects of their firms. The authors analyzed the average moneyness of the CEO's options portfolio for the first 3 years of their tenure and coded a dummy variable that takes a value of one if, at least once during those 3 years, a CEO postponed the exercise of vested options that are at least 67% in the money, and zero otherwise.
time_window: first 3 years of the CEO's tenure

description: The authors employed Altman's (1968) Z-score as an indicator of how close a firm is operating to its survival level. In the split-sample analysis, an Altman Z-score of 1.8 is used as the cutoff point: firms above this score were considered distant from bankruptcy and firms below it were considered close to bankruptcy.

The number of deals that a potential subordinate bank j led for the issuer z in the past four years. The authors note that measures based on the frequency of past interactions between the actors have been shown to be good indicators of the strength of interactor relationships. The variable was logged and lagged one time period relative to the dependent variable.
level: dyad (subordinate bank j and issuer z)
time_window: past four years; period t, with the dependent variable in period t+1

description: The number of times banks i and j together participated in the same underwriting syndicate with either i or j leading that syndicate. The variable was logged and lagged one time period relative to the dependent variable. It is used both as the baseline predictor of future horizontal ties and as one component of the interaction testing Hypothesis 4.
level: dyad (lead bank i and potential subordinate bank j)
time_window: prior four-year periods; period t, with the dependent variable in period t+1

description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if bank i formed a tie with another investment bank j to place an offering for issuer z, and 0 otherwise. Realized dyads in which a bank was a lead manager were combined with a random sample of potential dyads that were not realized, with five times more zeros than ones. The dependent variable is recorded in period t+1 while all independent variables are in period t.
level: dyad (lead bank i, subordinate bank j, issuer z)

description: For each PO that bank j led for the issuer z, the authors compared the midpoint of the offering's filing price range in the primary prospectus with the offering's final price; the formula is not readable in the extracted text and is recorded as a gap. As an example, if the price range in the prospectus was $13-$15 the average filing price was $14, and if the actual launch price was $16 the outcome was 0.143. The outcomes were averaged over the offerings that bank j led for issuer z. A high value signals that offerings were oversubscribed by investors before the launch because they felt the offering was underpriced.

Composite index constructed by adding up the number of CSR strengths with respect to employees, customers, the natural environment, and society at large (community and minorities) in the KLD database. The KLD-index enters the regressions in the preceding year.

Procurement contracts are matched to corporations in Compustat by company names, and the dollar amount of procurement contracts is aggregated for each firm and each year. The dependent variable is the logarithm of one plus the dollar amount of procurement contracts allocated to the company.

The number of years since the company has been receiving procurement contracts. The variable is used as two dummy variables indicating whether relationship length is above and below, respectively, the median across all companies.

Herfindahl-Hirschman index of industry concentration, calculated as the sum of squared market shares of all companies in a given 2-digit SIC industry and year. Market shares are computed from Compustat based on firms' sales; higher values of the index represent lower competition. In the interaction analysis it is used as two dummy variables indicating whether the Herfindahl index lies above or below the median across all industries.

Dependent variable in which multi-year contracts is the dollar amount of multi-year procurement contracts allocated to a given company in a given year; CSRs effect on this variable is compared with its effect on log(1 + single-year contracts).

Dependent variable in which a contract is coded as large if the dollar amount is greater than the average across all contracts awarded in the same year; the dollar amount of large contracts allocated to a firm in a year is used as log(1 + large contracts), and compared with log(1 + small contracts).

Dependent variable using the dollar amount of cost-plus procurement contracts allocated to a company in a given year, compared with log(1 + fixed-price contracts). The FPDS-NG reports the pricing agreement (fixed-cost versus cost-plus) for each contract.
