Dependent variable using the dollar amount of contracts procured by the Department of Defense, identified by department name 'Dept of Defense' in the FPDS-NG database, compared with contracts procured by other government agencies.

The percentage of a focal year that the predecessor was retained as chair, ranging from zero to 100 percent. For models in which the dependent variables could be computed on a pure elapsed-time basis, retention was measured for each 12-month period directly following succession; for instance, a predecessor who remained as chair for 18 months was coded 100 for Year 1, 50 for Year 2, and 0 for years 3, 4, and 5. For models in which the dependent variables were available only on a fiscal year basis, retention was calculated using dates tied to the firm's fiscal year.

A dummy variable, posited as representing a sudden increase in a CEO's discretion, that identifies the first year immediately following the predecessor's departure from the chair position. It was coded one for the first year in which the predecessor was completely gone for at least half the year.
time_window: The first post-succession year in which the predecessor was absent at least half the year

description: A composite of three strategic outlay items readily influenced by the CEO: advertising intensity (advertising/sales), research and development intensity (R&D/sales), and selling, general, and administrative intensity (SG&A/sales). For each item the absolute change (without regard to sign) from the year prior to succession (Year 0) to the focal year (Year t) was taken, standardized across all firm years, and then summed to develop the composite measure. Cronbach's alpha for the three items was 0.79, and the items formed a single factor with loadings of 0.51 or greater.
time_window: Change from Year 0 to focal Year t

description: Counts of acquisition announcements were separately recorded for each focal post-succession year using data from Securities Data Company (SDC) Platinum. Acquisitions were examined separately from divestitures because predecessor retention might affect them differently. The SDC database omits information on the size of many deals, so indicators of acquisition magnitudes could not be developed.

Counts of divestiture announcements were separately recorded for each focal post-succession year using data from Securities Data Company (SDC) Platinum. Divestitures were examined separately from acquisitions because predecessor retention might affect them differently, and information on deal size was often missing in the database.

The number of executives added in a post-succession year who were not on the top management team prior to succession. Executives were defined as those with titles of senior vice president and above, and their names were recorded for the year prior to succession (Year 0) from Standard & Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors and Executives.

The number of executives who were present on the top management team prior to succession but who departed in the focal post-succession year. The names of senior executives with titles of senior vice president and above were recorded from Standard & Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors and Executives. Additions and departures were examined separately because retention might affect them differently.

ROA was net income divided by total assets, recorded for each fiscal year. ROA change was calculated as the absolute difference, without regard to sign, between presuccession ROA and the focal year's ROA, net of median performance change in the three-digit industry (using all Compustat firms in the industry, excluding the focal firm). Because changes in strategy take time to affect performance, a one-year lag was incorporated, so performance change was observed in Year t + 1.

TSR was calculated as share price at the end of the year minus share price at the beginning of the year, plus dividends paid, all divided by beginning share price, and was recorded annually on each anniversary of succession. TSR change was calculated as the absolute difference, without regard to sign, between presuccession TSR and the focal year's TSR, net of median performance change in the three-digit industry.

Managers' assessment of the extent to which business activities in the industry are susceptible to scale economies, obtained from the survey instrument. The item was identified through a principal components factor analysis of the structural and competitive drivers as the economies of scale factor. Indices for the structural and competitive factors were formed by averaging the relevant items identified in the factor analysis.

Managers' assessment of whether factor costs differ significantly from country to country, obtained from the survey instrument. The item was identified through a principal components factor analysis of the structural and competitive drivers as the differences in comparative advantage across countries factor, and was used as an index in the analyses.

Managers' assessments of the standardization of demand in their industry, obtained from the survey instrument on four items. The items were identified through a principal components factor analysis of the structural and competitive drivers as the standardization of market demands factor. An index was formed by averaging the relevant items for the industry-specific regressions.

Managers' assessments of competitive action within their industry, obtained from the survey instrument on items covering the presence of competitors in all key markets and the intensity of international competition. The items were identified through a principal components factor analysis of the structural and competitive drivers as the competitive actions factor.

Managers' assessments of the importance of methods of competing internationally that represent the global integration of business activities, measured with an eight-item scale. A principal components factor analysis indicated a single construct representing the global integration of business activities, and two of the eight items were subsequently dropped in order to improve scale reliability. Assessments of global integration were measured relative to the managers' specific industries; correlations of individual responses with the average of all businesses in the relevant industry ranged from 0.92 to 0.97. The industry-specific analyses used an index based on the six retained measurement items.

Subjective assessments of a business's performance relative to other businesses in the same industry, used because objective data are frequently not available at the business-unit level. Three aspects of performance were assessed: return on assets, return on total investment, and sales growth. By combining financial and competitive performance characteristics in this way the authors sought greater construct validity, and a confirmatory factor analysis conducted on these three measures indicated a single construct.

A six-item scale corresponding to Rich et al.'s (2010) scale measuring the three dimensions (physical, cognitive, and emotional) of engagement, with the referent of the items shifted from one's self to the collective. Rated by individuals at three hierarchical levels on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree). Ratings were averaged over all employees within each credit union to obtain a collective organizational engagement score for each firm. Cronbach's alpha was .82.

The 25 items from Morgeson and Humphrey's (2006) Work Design Questionnaire, covering variety, autonomy, identity, significance, and feedback. Respondents were entry-level employees who indicated the level to which each attribute is present in their jobs on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree). Ratings were averaged within each credit union to obtain an aggregate rating for each characteristic; Cronbach's alphas ranged from .74 to .90 with a composite of .92.

A 10-item measure analyzed as an additive index of HRM investments and expectation-enhancing practices: job security, developmental performance management, performance-based use of incentives, rewards, and promotions, and competitive and fair compensation. Participants rated the extent to which they agreed or disagreed that each practice was being utilized in the organization on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree). Ratings were averaged over all employees within each credit union; Cronbach's alphas ranged from .70 to .81 for the four facets.

Bass and Avolio's (1995) Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire was used to measure the CEO's transformational leadership behaviors. Employees, managers, and executives rated the frequency with which the CEO exhibited the behaviors on a five-point Likert response scale (1 = not at all; 5 = frequently, if not always). Ratings were averaged over all employees within each credit union to obtain an aggregate rating of leadership for each CEO; Cronbach's alpha was .91 for the overall scale and ranged from .79 to .87 for the four facets.
scale: 1 = not at all; 5 = frequently, if not always

description: TMT members rated the extent to which they implemented the firm's strategic objectives using six items based on Mathieu et al.'s (2000) measure of team processes, drawn from the monitoring progress toward goals, goal specification, and monitoring resources facets and revised to focus on the TMT's progress in implementing firm goals and strategies. Responses used a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree). Ratings were averaged over all TMT members within each firm; Cronbach's alpha was .92.

Archival measures of ROA for the six months following the survey were obtained from data collected by the National Credit Union Association. The measure is an accounting-based indicator of business performance; return on assets is viewed as the best indicator of firm performance in the industry.

Change in the logged number of a surviving store's total product variety (SKUs) after the rival chain exits. The authors log-transformed the product variety counts in 2006 and 2010 and defined the dependent variable as their logged ratio (Equation 7), so that it captures relative rather than absolute change. The analysis is in spirit a difference-in-difference comparison: the temporal difference is before versus after the exit, and the second difference is competitive markets versus the baseline monopoly markets.

Coded as equal to 1 if the preexisting nearest rival store is within a half-mile radius of the surviving store, and 0 otherwise. Together with NONCOL it describes one of the two mutually exclusive competitive market structures prior to the exit of Circuit City.

Coded as equal to 1 if the distance between a surviving store and its nearest former rival store was greater than half a mile but no greater than 10 miles, and 0 otherwise. It describes the other of the two mutually exclusive competitive market structures prior to the exit of Circuit City.

Coded as equal to 1 if at least one new Best Buy store opened within the 10-mile radius of a surviving Best Buy store, and 0 otherwise. Because entry decisions are long-term oriented, difficult to reverse and costly, the authors treat ENTRY as potentially endogenous and instrument it with the predicted value from a probit model of new store opening.

Exit of the main rival was the closure of all Circuit City stores in late 2008 to early 2009, treated as an exogenous change for all Best Buy markets. Product variety was compared in 2006 (before) and 2010 (after) the exit.

The total amount of energy sold to a utility's customers each year, measured in megawatt hours. It is constructed from the annual utility sales and customer data reported in Form EIA-861. Customer demand is driven by the population in a company's assigned service territory and by per-capita energy use.

The megawatt hours of electricity generated by the utility itself, i.e., the megawatt hours of energy sourced internally via generation. It is the outcome variable that captures how a utility meets increases in customer demand.

The percentage of total electricity sourced from purchases in the year 1990, used as a proxy for the firm's prior reliance on purchased power to serve demand and hence its contracting experience. A firm with more experience relying on purchased power is assumed to accumulate contracting capabilities and routines for operating under adaptation. It is measured once, in the presample year.
An indicator equal to 1 for firms with ISO membership and 0 otherwise, identified in each year from the control area operator recorded in the utility data.

An indicator equal to 1 for utilities in a state with an interconnection standards policy for each year following the effective date of the policy, and 0 otherwise. State policies took effect between 1998 and 2010.
time_window: annual, following each state policy's effective date (1998-2010)

description: The difference between a utility's operating expenses per megawatt hour of steam power in 1990 and the average value for all utilities in the same region. It proxies for productive capabilities, so higher values indicate higher production cost and therefore inferior capabilities relative to regional peers. It is measured once, in 1990, and is available only for utilities filing FERC Form 1.

Firm environmental performance is the rating assigned by the Green Watch program, which rates firms from best to worst in five colors: green, blue, yellow, red, and black. Firms violating emission and discharge standards are rated red (coded 2), and firms violating standards in more than 60% of inspections are rated black (coded 1, the worst performance), while firms that satisfy the primary benchmarks but violate the secondary load-based standards are rated yellow (coded 3). The rating system also incorporates other performance indicators, such as whether or not the firm received public complaints and whether or not the firm had a China Cleaner Production certificate and/or an ISO14000 certificate.

Market competition is measured by the interaction of a WTO dummy and firm-level output import tariff rates in 1999. The WTO dummy is coded 1 if the year is 2002 and afterward, and otherwise 0, reflecting the fact that China joined the WTO in December 2001. Output import tariff rates in 1999 are used as the pre-sample measure of an industry's exposure to import competition, and because many firms have multiple products, the firm-level rate is constructed using the weights of each of the firm's main products. Tariff data are taken from the WITS database using the rates denoted as 'effectively applied tariffs', merged to the firm data through a concordance between the NBS and WITS industry classifications.
time_window: tariff rates from 1999; WTO dummy from 2002 onward

description: The measure follows Gao et al. (2010) with one modification: while Gao et al. (2010) measured cost strategy by the ratio of production cost to total sales (small values indicating stronger cost leadership), the authors use 'total sales - production cost' as the numerator so that larger values indicate stronger cost leadership. The measure expresses the firm's value relative to the median and range of values, with values between -1 and 1.

Differentiation is proxied by a firm's divergence from the typical level of the ratio of advertising expense to total sales in its three-digit industry, following the Gao et al. (2010) measure. The measure expresses the firm's value relative to the median and range of values, with values between -1 and 1.

variable_name: average of the three industry variety rankings
description: Three related indicators of industry variety were created using cluster analysis. The first ranked the 12 industries qualitatively from lowest to highest variety using spatial plots of the clusters, based on the number of identified strategic groups and the distances between groups on the three competitive strategy dimensions. The second standardized each strategic group's mean on each variable into Z scores, summed the absolute differences between every pair of groups on each variable, and added the three sums into a total variety score. The third added a constant of one to the cluster mean scores and took a natural log transformation before ranking, to reduce the influence of outliers. Because the three measures were so highly correlated (all at or above 0.89), the average of each industry's ranks was used in all subsequent analyses.

The accounting-based measure of industry performance was a 4-year average of return on investment (ROI). The values of this variable for the individual firms in each industry were aggregated to the industry level, and these data were then converted to ranks.

The market-based measure of industry performance was the percent change in stock price (adjusted for stock splits and new issues) over the time period. The values of this variable for the individual firms in each industry were aggregated to the industry level, and these data were then converted to ranks.
scale: percent change; rank (1 = highest performance, 12 = lowest performance)

description: Industries were selected according to 4-digit SIC codes as reported in U.S. Industrial Outlook. Growth industries were defined as those with average annual sales increases (in constant 1982 dollars) above 10 percent over the 6-year period, mature industries as those with sales increases of 1-10 percent, and declining industries as those with negative sales increases, yielding three categories: growth, mature, and decline.

variable_name: ratio of imports to total new shipments
description: The amount of foreign competition in an industry was defined by the ratio of imports to total new shipments (domestic and foreign), and was considered to be substantial if greater than 10 percent. Industries with import ratios below 10 percent were considered to be low in foreign competition.
scale: ratio of imports to total new shipments (percentage)

description: Total number of German news articles mentioning a firm, collected from four daily newspapers: the Handelsblatt, the Süddeutsche Zeitung, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, and the Frankfurter Rundschau. Article counts from these sources were combined into an index of visibility that showed excellent reliability (α = .92), and a principal component factor analysis confirmed that all four items loaded highly and positively on a single factor that accounted for 85 percent of the variance. Data were collected from GENIOS and from the online archive of the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.
time_window: annual, 1990-2000 (three of the four newspapers available only from 1993 onward)

description: Dummy variable coded 1 if the firm's annual report framing of its move toward a shareholder value orientation was classified as a balancing frame, that is, if the report stated that the firm adhered to shareholder value management but qualified this by simultaneously affirming the legitimacy of the claims of other stakeholder groups. Coding followed the frame analysis procedure described by Benford (1993) in three stages and was performed by two independent native German-speaking coders; intercoder reliability for frame choice was high (Cohen's κ = .90) and disagreements were resolved through discussion.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the firm's annual report statement indicated the reporting organization's explicit espousal of a shareholder value orientation without qualification or alteration. Coding was conducted in three stages by two independent native German-speaking coders who classified each statement as indicating either an acquiescence or a balancing framing (Cohen's κ = .90).

Level of ownership by German federal or state government. Data came from Worldscope and were cross-checked with data from Wer gehört zu wem?, a directory of German firms published triennially by the Commerzbank AG. Following prior research, mutually exclusive categories of blockholders were established whose influence was measured on a scale ranging from 0 to 4, with coding tied to the ownership thresholds of 5, 25, 50, and 75 percent.

Level of ownership by German families. Data came from Worldscope and were cross-checked with data from Wer gehört zu wem?. Blockholders were coded into mutually exclusive categories whose influence was measured on a scale ranging from 0 to 4, tied to thresholds of 5, 25, 50, and 75 percent ownership.

Level of ownership by domestic banks that have themselves espoused a shareholder value orientation using a balancing framing. Ownership by German banks was taken from Worldscope and cross-checked with Wer gehört zu wem?, and bank ownership was split according to the framing used by the shareholding bank, with a contrast category for banks using an acquiescence framing. Categories of blockholders were mutually exclusive and measured on a scale ranging from 0 to 4.

Three dummy variables capturing governance practices that demonstrate credible commitment to a shareholder value orientation: value-based management control systems, which tie performance evaluation explicitly to the interests of shareholders and are often linked to profitability goals specified by division or activity; stock option plans for company management; and adoption of internationally accepted accounting standards such as US-GAAP or IAS. Data came from the firms' annual reports and were cross-checked by directly contacting all firms still operating at the time the data were collected.

Total stock market returns, defined as capital gains plus dividends, used as the measure of firm performance regarding shareholder interests. The authors used the total return in the year following the announcement of a shift toward shareholder value management as the dependent variable rather than event-study abnormal returns, because the framing of strategic change is not a single, unanticipated event.

Dummy variable that is 1 if a firm is affiliated with a group and 0 otherwise. Group membership follows the Korean government's annual identification of the 30 largest business groups according to asset size in nonfinancial sectors and its published listing of their affiliates under the Fair Trade Act. Group and firm resource levels are measured with two-year moving averages of time t-1 and time t to predict a firm's innovativeness at time t+1.

Dummy variable that is 1 if a firm is affiliated with a group and 0 otherwise. Group membership comes from the biennial Business Groups in Taiwan (BGT) directory, which constructs the database of business groups by examining the overlaps of shareholders, directors, auditors, or decision makers with the focal firm who have a substantial proportion of shares held by other group members. Because the BGT database is biennial, the preceding even-numbered year's data are used for the odd-numbered years.
time_window: t-1 and t (two-year moving average; closest preceding even-numbered year for group data)

description: Number of successful U.S. patent applications submitted by the sample firms, counting patents applied for in 1992-2000 and granted by 2001, collected from the NBER U.S. patenting databases. The dependent variable is a count with a preponderance of zeros.

Number of successful U.S. patent applications submitted by the sample firms, counting patents applied for in 1992-2000 and granted by 2001, collected from the NBER U.S. patenting databases. The dependent variable is a count with a preponderance of zeros.

Weighted average of return on assets (ROA) for all other affiliates in the same group, using the assets averaged at time t-1 and time t as a weighting factor. It is available only for the group-affiliated subsample, for which group-level variables exist.

Weighted average of return on assets (ROA) for all other affiliates in the same group, using the assets averaged at time t-1 and time t as a weighting factor. It is available only for the group-affiliated subsample, for which group-level variables exist.

Total number of patents owned by all other member firms within a group in the same two-digit standard industrial classification (SIC) industry since 1991. Because economically useful knowledge depreciates, a 20% depreciation rate is applied to calculate the level of technological stock over time, and the number is log-transformed after adding a nominal value of 1 to avoid a log transformation of zeros.

Total number of patents owned by all other member firms within a group in the same two-digit standard industrial classification (SIC) industry since 1991. Because economically useful knowledge depreciates, a 20% depreciation rate is applied to calculate the level of technological stock over time, and the number is log-transformed after adding a nominal value of 1 to avoid a log transformation of zeros.

Entropy measure of group-level unrelated diversification (Palepu 1985), taken as the average of time t-1 and time t. Two-digit SIC codes are used to define industries broadly and to make the classifications comparable between the two countries.

Entropy measure of group-level unrelated diversification (Palepu 1985), taken as the average of time t-1 and time t. Two-digit SIC codes are used to define industries broadly and to make the classifications comparable between the two countries.

variable_name: Country and period split (Korea vs Taiwan; Period 1 vs Period 2)
description: Institutional infrastructure for innovation is not scored as a variable. Taiwan is treated as having stronger infrastructure than Korea, and the late 1990s as stronger than the early 1990s in both countries. Models are estimated separately by country and by period, with 1995 as the cut-off of the 1991 to 1999 sample years (Period 1 = 1991 to 1995, Period 2 = 1996 to 1999, corresponding to patents filed 1992 to 1996 and 1997 to 2000), and the group effects are compared across the splits.

A dummy variable that is equal to 1 if the opera is a robust interpretation, and 0 otherwise. Traditional operas are those characterized by pre-twentieth century music styles and dramatic contents; all operas whose composers were born before 1881 were classified as traditional operas. Robust interpretations were identified in a two-step procedure: the plots of each opera were read in their original formulation of temporal and spatial characteristics, and the visuals of all operas produced by the sampled theaters over the period 1993-2010 were analyzed and hand-coded; robust interpretations transform the original temporal and spatial coordinates of existing operas through modern displacement, while traditional interpretations reproduce them faithfully.
time_window: visuals hand-coded for the artistic seasons 1993-1994 to 2010-2011

description: A dummy variable that is equal to 1 if the opera is a radical interpretation, and 0 otherwise. Radical interpretations are opera productions that not only alter traditional operas' visual dimensions, but also change their established dramaturgic contents, where a dramaturgic change is a change in the storyline or the actions and characterization of the protagonists. Dramaturgic changes were identified by comparing the original stories and characters with those presented on stage after reading the reviews of each opera production. While theoretically possible, the sole change of core features is never present in the population, so the variable captures the simultaneous change of visual and dramaturgic features.

The total number of people attending the opera's opening and any subsequent re-runs, used as an indicator of audience appeal. This is the dependent variable used to test Hypotheses 1 and 2. Since the dependent variable is skewed, it was log-transformed before estimating the models.

The total number of season-ticket holders present at the opera, used to test Hypotheses 3a and 3b. Season-ticket holders purchase a full season package to preempt their seats before the remaining seats are sold to the general public, but their actual attendance varies across productions, so attendance rather than seats sold is measured. The variable is log-transformed because the dependent variables are skewed.

The total number of single-ticket holders present at the opera, used to test Hypotheses 3a and 3b. Single-ticket holders buy tickets for single shows that appeal to them rather than a season package. The variable is log-transformed because the dependent variables are skewed.

In the combined dataset used to test Hypotheses 3a and 3b, a dummy variable that takes the value 1 for the single-ticket segment and 0 for the season-ticket segment, allowing the unobserved heterogeneity to be common to season- and single-ticket holders. It is interacted with robust interpretation and with radical interpretation to test whether the effect of interpreting tradition varies between the two segments.

Degree centrality measured as the count number of direct partners with which a focal affiliate has buyer-supplier relationships, normalized by the number of network member firms, which captures the number of ties a focal firm maintains relative to the maximum number of potential ties it can have. The ties are coded from the figures depicting intragroup buyer-supplier relationships in the BGT directory.
time_window: each two-year period covered by the BGT directory

description: Degree centrality measured as the count number of direct partners with which a focal affiliate has equity ties, normalized by the number of network member firms, capturing the number of ties a focal firm maintains relative to the maximum number of potential ties. Equity ties are coded from the figures depicting intragroup equity cross holdings in the BGT directory.
time_window: each two-year period covered by the BGT directory

description: Degree centrality measured as the count number of direct partners with which a focal affiliate has director ties, normalized by the number of network member firms, capturing the number of ties a focal firm maintains relative to the maximum number of potential ties. Director ties are coded from the lists of names of directors for each affiliate provided by the BGT directory.
time_window: each two-year period covered by the BGT directory

description: Affiliate-level R&D capability is calculated in the way consistent with Dutta, Narasimhan, and Rajiv (2005), using stochastic frontier estimation, which measures the technical efficiency with which a firm employs a given set of resources (inputs) to achieve objectives (outputs). It captures the conversion relationship between R&D inputs and outputs and can differentiate two firms with the same R&D intensity but a different number of patents, and two firms with the same number of patents but a different level of R&D intensity. R&D expenditure is taken from the Taiwan Economic Journal Data Bank and successful patent applications from the Intellectual Property Office of Taiwanese Government database.

Ratio of actual director ties among affiliates within a business group to the total number of potential director ties in that group. It is a group-level property of the intragroup director network in which the focal affiliate is embedded.
time_window: each two-year period covered by the BGT directory

description: Ratio of actual equity ties among affiliates within a business group to the total number of potential equity ties in that group. It is a group-level property of the intragroup equity network in which the focal affiliate is embedded.
time_window: each two-year period covered by the BGT directory

description: Diversification indices are computed for each company for each year using the SIC codes and sales data for each of the principal products of the company, using the Jacquemin-Berry entropy measure of diversification. The measure is a weighted average of the shares of the firm's segments, the weight for each segment being the logarithm of the inverse of its share, so that it reflects both the number of segments and the distribution of sales across them. The formal equation defining the index is given in Appendix 2 but is not readable in the available text.
time_window: computed for each year 1973-1979; the analysis uses 1973 and 1979

description: The related component of the Jacquemin-Berry entropy measure, computed for each company for each year from segment sales data and SIC codes. Related diversification within an industry group is the weighted sum of the shares of each product segment in the firm's sales in that industry, and the firm's net related diversification is the weighted sum of the related diversification within each of the industry groups in which it operates. Products belonging to different four-digit SIC industries within the same two-digit industry group are treated as related.
time_window: computed for each year 1973-1979; the analysis uses 1973 and 1979 levels

description: The unrelated component of the Jacquemin-Berry entropy measure, computed for each company for each year from segment sales data and SIC codes. It arises out of operating across several industry groups and is the weighted average of all the group shares, i.e. the weighted sum of the shares of each of the industries in the firm's total sales. Products from different two-digit SIC industry groups are defined as unrelated.
time_window: computed for each year 1973-1979; the analysis uses 1973 and 1979 levels

description: Net profit after taxes (excluding extraordinary items) as a percentage of net sales, computed for each company for each year during 1969-1979. The profitability index used is the 5-year moving average ROS for 1973 and for 1979 (for example, the average ROS for 1973 is the average of the yearly ROS for 1969 through 1973). The moving average, rather than yearly ROS, is chosen to eliminate some of the noise in the accounting numbers.
time_window: 5-year moving average ending in 1973 and in 1979

description: Profitability growth rate is computed as the percentage change in ROS between the years 1973 and 1979, that is, the change in ROS from the base year to the final year expressed as a percentage.

A binary classification was used to code director type, distinguishing insiders, who are current or former employees of a company, from outsiders. The text does not state which of the two values is coded 1. The information was collected from proxy statements filed with the SEC.

Directors' occupations were identified with 15 separate categories and were later condensed into a binary classification of business versus nonbusiness for the tests of Hypotheses 2 and 5. The text does not state which of the two values is coded 1.
Tenure, the number of years a member has served on the board, was measured on an interval scale. Values were collected from proxy statements filed with the SEC.

A binary classification was used to code gender, distinguishing women from men among board members. The text does not state which of the two values is coded 1. Values were collected from proxy statements filed with the SEC.

Committee names were condensed into a list of 36 groups, and board members were coded either 1 or 0 to reflect membership in a given group. For the tests of Hypotheses 1 through 4, the audit, nominating, compensation, and executive committees were identified as the major committees, and membership on them was compared with nonmembership.

The number of alliances a firm entered into during the first year after its IPO, obtained from the Securities Data Corporation Joint Ventures database. The count includes all forms of strategic alliances represented in the database (e.g., marketing agreements, research and development alliances, product licensing agreements, and equity joint ventures).

Status equals the sum of two high-status affiliation indicators - venture capitalist status and underwriter status - ranging from 0 (no high-status affiliations) to 2 (affiliations with both a high-status underwriter and a high-status VC). Venture capitalist status was based on the lead VC's centrality in syndication networks, coded 1 if the lead VC was in the top quartile of the VC status index the year the firm went public. Underwriter status used Jay Ritter's modified Carter-Manaster index ranging from 0 (low status) to 9 (high status), coded 1 when the value was greater than 8.75. The lead VC is the VC who had the largest percentage equity stake in the company.

A binary indicator coded 1 if firms possessed all three of the following characteristics: (1) high public attention, measured as the count of media articles about a firm in a given year (top quartile dummy); (2) high levels of positive emotional resonance, based on a content analysis of the articles (dummy coded 1 if mean positivity of a firm's coverage was greater than 75% in a given year); and (3) the use of nonconforming language by the media, assessed through a separate dictionary (dummy coded 1 if the firm's nonconforming language exceeded the 25th percentile of the sample). Text was drawn from articles published in Red Herring between 1995 and 2000, retrieved through LexisNexis. Firms were coded as celebrities if they met these criteria in either the year of their IPO or the year prior to their IPO; this resulted in 72 celebrity firms, representing 20% of the sample.
time_window: year of the IPO or the year prior to the IPO

description: Underpricing was measured as the percentage change in stock price on the first day the stock was traded on a national exchange multiplied by 100. The authors used the natural log of this measure to normalize the distribution; because underpricing can take on negative values, they added .01 to the positive counterpart of the lowest underpricing value observed before transforming the measure. Underpricing was mean-centered to reduce nonessential multicollinearity.
time_window: first day the stock was traded

description: Three-item scale that captures employee attitudes regarding knowledge transfer and a firm's past behavior in external knowledge exploitation; a high value on the scale indicates a high degree of NSH. Item 1 states that many employees have negative attitudes to external technology commercialization; item 2 states that employees regard external technology commercialization as an equivalent exploitation mode to the application of technologies in own products and/or services (reverse coded); item 3 states that the firm used external technology commercialization a lot during the past few years (reverse coded). Items were rated on seven-point Likert-type scales anchored 'I strongly disagree' (1) to 'I strongly agree' (7), and Cronbach's alpha is 0.88.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = I strongly disagree, 7 = I strongly agree)

variable_name: time that the company has actively commercialized technologies externally (years)
description: To analyze a firm's prior experience in externally leveraging knowledge, the authors measured the time (in years) that the companies have actively commercialized knowledge assets, following prior measures of experience such as alliance experience. In the exploratory factor analysis this single item did not sufficiently load on any construct and constitutes a separate variable.

Three-item scale on the size and diversity of a firm's product portfolio; the items capture the scope of complementary assets that a firm has in different application areas. The items address the number of different products, the diversity of the product portfolio, and activity in various industrial areas; Cronbach's alpha is 0.93. Items were rated on seven-point Likert-type scales anchored 'I strongly disagree' (1) to 'I strongly agree' (7).
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = I strongly disagree, 7 = I strongly agree)

description: Four-item scale capturing to what degree knowledge transactions are common in a firm's knowledge areas and whether knowledge markets have already existed for a long time, and to what degree the pricing mechanisms for knowledge resemble ideal market conditions. To facilitate the informants' understanding and because of the importance of patents in knowledge transactions, the items focus on the markets for technology; Cronbach's alpha is 0.91. Items were rated on seven-point Likert-type scales anchored 'I strongly disagree' (1) to 'I strongly agree' (7).
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = I strongly disagree, 7 = I strongly agree)

description: Two-item scale adapted from prior work that measured the competitive activity in product markets, adapted to better fit with knowledge markets. The items capture the external knowledge exploitation activities of a firm's competitors and the need for convincing potential knowledge recipients of the superiority of the firm's knowledge; Cronbach's alpha is 0.72. Items were rated on seven-point Likert-type scales anchored 'I strongly disagree' (1) to 'I strongly agree' (7).
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = I strongly disagree, 7 = I strongly agree)

description: A firm's annual revenues from externally commercializing knowledge, that is, the revenues from licensing and selling knowledge. Because of the confidentiality of these revenues in most firms, which had been emphasized in the pretests, they were measured in five categories. In factor analyses this variable formed one factor with the subjective item 'The return on our investments in external technology exploitation is high', so licensing revenues also seem to be a good proxy for profitability in externally commercializing knowledge; the authors focused on revenues as an objective dependent variable to limit common method bias.
scale: ordinal five categories: EUR 0-5 million, EUR 5-20 million, EUR 20-50 million, EUR 50-100 million, and more than EUR 100 million

description: Second dependent variable, measured with three items pertaining to the extent of external knowledge exploitation relative to a firm's direct competitors, thus considering both strategic and monetary aspects; the construct shows that firms that actively commercialize knowledge from a monetary perspective also tend to achieve strategic opportunities, and vice versa. Cronbach's alpha is 0.92; items were rated on seven-point Likert-type scales anchored 'I strongly disagree' (1) to 'I strongly agree' (7).
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = I strongly disagree, 7 = I strongly agree)

description: The main independent variable is measured as the sum, for all new hires, of the average impact factor of the journals in which new hires have published within five years prior to joining the focal department. New hires are the faculty members that joined the department in years t and t-1. The five-year window helps attenuate annual fluctuations and better reflects scientists' propensity to publish in high-impact journals prior to hiring, and the measure varies with both the average research quality of new hires and their number. The paper's printed formula for this variable was unreadable in the text, so the specification is reported from the surrounding prose.
time_window: five years prior to the hiring event

description: Operationalized as the number of publications by incumbent scientists weighted by their respective citations; publications by incumbent scientists only are included, and joint publications between new hires and incumbents are excluded. Incumbents are faculty members that joined the department prior to t-1, while new recruits are those who joined in years t and t-1 (a moving window of two years). A five-year window is used to count citations, which helps eliminate the bias incurred because earlier publications are prone to receive more citations. The variable is computed for each year from 1998 to 2006 with a two-year lag after the independent and control variables, and it is recalculated separately for the subsets of shorter- and longer-tenured incumbents.
time_window: citations counted over a five-year window; dependent variable measured with a two-year lag

variable_name: Shorter versus longer organizational tenure of incumbents
description: Faculty members that joined the department in years t-2, t-3, t-4, and t-5 are classified as incumbents with shorter organizational tenures, whereas those who arrived in year t-6 or earlier are incumbents with longer organizational tenures. The two measures of incumbents' research performance were recalculated for each subset of incumbents, and separate regressions were estimated for each subset.
time_window: entry year relative to year t

description: Measured as one minus the Herfindahl index, constructed using the classification of each publication in subject categories provided by Science Citation Index Expanded; the index is based on the number of publications by department s in subject category k over a five-year window (years t to t-4) relative to the sum of all papers published by the department in all subject categories for the same period. The measure yields values between one and zero, such that larger values correspond to greater diversity. The paper's printed formula for this variable was unreadable in the text, so the specification is reported from the surrounding prose.

Computed as the number of unique ties among department members divided by the total possible number of internal pairwise ties. Department faculty names were matched with the authors of papers that listed the focal department as their affiliation, and all papers coauthored by at least two department faculty members over a five-year window were identified; a unique tie emerges if two department members have coauthored at least one paper during the time window. The total possible number of such ties is n(n-1)/2, where n is the number of professors in the department. The printed formula in the text is partially garbled, but the ratio described in prose is clear.

An indicator that equals 1 if the acquirer's Gompers et al. (2003) GIM index is at least 10, representing a preponderance of antitakeover provisions and entrenchment. The GIM index is constructed by counting the number of 24 key antitakeover provisions that a firm has. IRRC only reports data for every second or third year during the sample period, so for years with missing data the models use data from the most recent prior year.
time_window: pre-acquisition; most recent prior year when the year is missing

description: An indicator that equals 1 if the acquirer satisfies any one of five definitions of being hard to value. The HTV conditions are: the firm is in the software industry; the firm is in the medical industry; the firm's yearly average analyst forecast dispersion is in the top 25% of the IBES population; the standard deviation of analyst forecast errors is in the top 25% of the IBES population for that year; or the firm's analyst forecast error is in the top 25% of the IBES population for that year.

The 5-day cumulative abnormal return accruing to the bidder around the acquisition announcement. Abnormal returns are the difference between actual returns and predicted returns, where the predicted return is based on an estimation of the market model with parameters computed over the period 210 to 11 days before the acquisition announcement.
time_window: five days surrounding the acquisition announcement

description: The acquirer's industry-adjusted Tobin's Q estimated j years after the acquisition announcement. The industry-adjusted Tobin's Q is the firm's Tobin's Q less the average Tobin's Q for all firms in its SIC 4-digit industry and year.
time_window: j years after the acquisition announcement

description: An interaction of an indicator that the CAR is positive with an indicator that the acquisition is of a high-tech target (as defined in Loughran and Ritter, 2004). It captures whether an acquisition of a tech target creates value.

An interaction of an indicator that the CAR is positive with an indicator that the acquirer's R&D in year t + i exceeds its R&D in year t - 1, where year t is the acquisition year. It examines whether an acquisition increases the acquirer's R&D and creates value.
time_window: acquisition year compared with a later year

description: The average premium paid for firms in the target's SIC 2-digit industry in that year, where the takeover premium is variously the transaction value divided by the target's stock price D days before the acquisition announcement. It addresses the fact that takeover premiums are unobserved in acquisitions of unlisted targets and can be endogenous with CARs.

Stock of the firm's patents in the USPTO Class 435, entitled 'Chemistry: Molecular Biology and Microbiology', which the authors assign to core capabilities in the emerging biotechnology. Patent stocks were calculated through the perpetual inventory method: for each firm, all the patents in the class were added up from 1963 to 1988 and depreciated at a yearly rate of 15%, using the application year of the patents instead of the grant year.

Stock of the firm's patents in the USPTO classes from 532 to 570, entitled 'Organic compounds', which signal strength of the firm in organic chemistry. Computed with the perpetual inventory method, adding up for each firm all the patents in the class from 1963 to 1988 and depreciating them at a yearly rate of 15%, using the application year of the patents.

Stock of the firm's patents in the USPTO Class 424, 'Drug, bio-affecting, and body-treating compositions'. This class mainly contains patents on new products (drugs; bio-affecting compositions capable of preventing, alleviating, treating, or curing abnormal and pathological conditions; and antibiotics) and processes for their use or preparation, signaling the ability of the firm to develop new products and processes from its existing core technological capabilities. Computed with the perpetual inventory method, summing patents from 1963 to 1988 and depreciating at a yearly rate of 15%.

Dependent variable of the first equation of the Heckman probit model, set equal to 1 if firm i entered the emerging technological field j between 1989 and 1999 through either alliance or internal development, and 0 otherwise. A firm i is recognized as entering the field j through internal development when, based on BioScan data, the firm was not present in field j in year t−1 and was present in field j in year t; entry through alliance is recognized when BioScan reports an alliance of firm i in the emerging technological field j in year t−1.

Dependent variable of the second equation of the Heckman probit model, coded 1 if firm i entered the emerging technological field j through alliance and 0 if entry occurred through internal development. Entry through alliance and entry through internal development are defined as in the entry equation.

Diversity of the educational backgrounds of TMT members, computed with Teachman's Entropy Index over the nine one-digit educational fields of ISCED97/SUN2000, where TMTEDU i,t,j is the share of the TMT with educational background j of the total TMT managers in firm i in year t. The authors state that the index has a theoretical minimum of 0 if all TMT managers have exactly the same educational background. The equations as printed could not be extracted from the source and are not reproduced here; the authors also report results using the Blau Index, which they describe as similar.

Diversity of the educational backgrounds of MMT members, constructed in the same way as the TMT measure from the shares of MMT members in each of the nine one-digit educational fields. MMT members are identified with occupation codes ISCO 122X and 123X. The equations as printed could not be extracted from the source and are not reproduced here.
scale: 0 to maximum value of the entropy index

description: Dichotomous variable that is equal to 1 if a firm engages in any of five categories of innovation-related activities (expenditures) and 0 otherwise. The five categories are internal R&D, external R&D, the acquisition of machinery as a measure of embodied technological change, the acquisition of other external knowledge, and investment in the market introduction of the innovation.

Binary variable that takes the value of 1 if a firm successfully introduced at least one product innovation within the last three years, and 0 otherwise. It is a direct measure of innovation output, as opposed to an intermediate measure such as patents.

variable_name: Product innovation differentiated by degree of novelty
description: Dependent variable that takes the value 0 if the firm did not introduce any product innovation, 1 if it introduced new-to-firm product innovations, and 2 if it introduced new-to-market product innovations. Since new-to-market innovations are, by definition, also new to the firm, the authors treat the variable as ordered along the dimension of market novelty.

Executives wrote a brief, one-sentence statement of their visions for their firms and then evaluated their own statements by applying 26 items from a list that included risky, action-oriented, inspirational, and bottom-line-oriented. Each item was accompanied by a five-point scale anchored by "very little" (1) and "very much" (5). The 26 items were submitted to factor analysis with varimax rotation, which yielded seven factors with eigenvalues greater than 1.0 accounting for 58 percent of total item variance.

The 26 vision self-description items were submitted to a cluster analysis using the SPSS/PC+ "quick cluster" routine; a four-cluster solution proved simplest but a fourth cluster containing a single member was dropped as uninterpretable, leaving clusters of 22, 97, and 210 executives. Three dummy variables were constructed, each coded 1 for membership in a particular cluster or 0 for membership in all others.
scale: dummy (1 = member of the cluster indicated, 0 = member of any other cluster)

description: Executives stated how far into the future their visions for their firms extended. Executives stated that their visions extended over five years, with a range of 6 months to more than 20 years (x = 64.14 months, s.d. = 63.76 months).

variable_name: speed of change within the firm
description: Respondents evaluated the speed of change within their firms, using a five-point scale. Overall, the speed of change within a firm was evaluated as rapid (x = 3.91, s.d. = .92).

variable_name: speed of change within the industry
description: Respondents separately evaluated the speed of change within their industries, using a five-point scale. Industry changes were likewise seen as occurring rapidly (x = 3.83, s.d. = .98).
Chief executives were asked to provide personal background information that might be of use in understanding their vision, including tenure in their position and tenure in the firm.

Executives were asked how much control they exercised in their organizations, on a five-point bidirectional scale. The respondents agreed that they had a great deal of control (x = 4.29, s.d. = .80), in a test of the difference between the mean and the scale midpoint.
Executives were asked how much control they would like to exercise, on a five-point bidirectional scale. The respondents agreed that they would like to exercise a great deal (x = 4.01, s.d. = 1.00).

Business school deans in the authors' earlier study described their vision for an organization in a single sentence and then used the same 26-item list to evaluate their own vision statements, providing a basis for comparison with the executives.

Measured on a continuous scale from fully Republican (0) to fully Democratic (1), using contributions to political candidates, parties and party-affiliated committees disclosed in FEC reporting, focusing on the firm's PAC. Contributions made in the 10 years prior to the pandemic (since 2010) are used. Four indicators are calculated: the number of contributions to Democratic Party candidates or committees divided by the number given to both parties; the dollar amount given to Democrats divided by the amount given to both parties; the number of years contributions were made to Democrats divided by the number of years contributions were made to either party; and the number of distinct Democratic recipients divided by the number of distinct recipients of both parties. The simple average of the four indicators gives the index; firms that did not contribute are assigned 0.5 (perfectly bipartisan) and flagged with a dummy.

The count of COVID-19 synonyms occurring in conjunction with a risk synonym (within 10 words), multiplied by 1,000, and divided by the total document length (number of words) of the earnings call transcript. Constructed by Hassan et al. from the entire transcript and made publicly available; the authors use it as their main dependent variable.

The frequency with which the disease is mentioned in the presentation statement in conjunction (within 10 words) with a synonym for risk or uncertainty, multiplied by 1,000 and normalized by the length of the presentation section. The authors collected these transcripts themselves and replicated the Hassan et al. measures for the presentation section; their measure correlates at 0.967 with the original measure.

The dependent variable recoded as a binary (0,1) indicator of whether the call mentioned COVID-19-related risk at least once, estimated with linear probability models on the full earnings call transcript.

The presentation-section dependent variable recoded as a binary (0,1) indicator of whether the presentation section mentioned COVID-19-related risk at least once, estimated with a linear probability model.

Pay disparity is operationalized as total CEO compensation divided by the average total compensation of the top four compensated TMT members below the CEO. Total compensation is defined as the sum of short-term and long-term compensation, where short-term compensation includes salary and bonuses and long-term compensation is the sum of restricted stock, stock options, and long-term accounting-based incentive plans. Stock options were valued using the modified Black-Scholes present value method computed by Execucomp.

Performance was measured as the firm's return on assets (ROA) in year t + 1. ROA captures the dimension of performance most closely related to top management team functioning, namely whether management has effectively deployed firm assets, and is independent of market-based or equity-based measures.

Heir Apparent is operationalized as a dichotomous variable with a value of 1 if two criteria are satisfied: (1) a TMT member other than the CEO holds the title of president or COO or both and (2) that person is more than four years younger than the CEO. The value is 1 if both criteria are satisfied and 0 otherwise.

CEO power is operationalized as both Titles and Ownership power, collected as the number of titles of each executive and CEO in each firm year. Titles power is the aggregate distance between the CEO and each executive on number of titles, a variant of the Euclidean distance measure providing a scale invariant indicator of distance between the CEO and TMT members. The measure combines number of CEO titles, which ranges from 1 to 6, and TMT titles, which ranges from 1 to 4.

CEO power is operationalized as both Titles and Ownership power, with overall shares owned by each executive and CEO (excluding options) collected in each firm year. Ownership power is the aggregate distance between the CEO and each executive on ownership level, applying the same Euclidean-distance logic on the traditional notion that shareholdings represent power because they can be either an outcome of power or a source of structural power.

Functional Eligibility was calculated as a variant of Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity, modified following Zajac and Westphal (1996), defined as the sum of (Pi)2, where Pi is the proportion of CEO-TMT member dyads sharing the i th category; it signifies the squared proportion of CEO-TMT member dyads in which both individuals have experience within the same functional area. Functional areas were classified into throughput functions (operations, R&D, and engineering), output functions (marketing and sales), and peripheral functions (such as finance and law).

Eligibility based upon demographic characteristics is constructed using the distance formula previously presented with the alteration of subtracting each value from the highest value in the sample to convert it into a measure of eligibility. CEOs' organizational tenures were measured at the time they took office, and the tenure of TMT members was measured in the focal year t; Tenure Eligibility thus provides a measure of similarity of the TMT to the CEO on tenure at the time the CEO took office.
time_window: CEO tenure at time of taking office; TMT tenure in focal year t

description: Eligibility based upon demographic characteristics is constructed using the distance formula previously presented with the alteration of subtracting each value from the highest value in the sample to convert it into a measure of eligibility. Age Eligibility provides a measure of similarity of the TMT to the CEO on age at the time the CEO took office.
time_window: CEO age at time of taking office; TMT age in focal year

variable_name: repair rate measured during the third year of ownership
description: Consumer Reports frequency-of-repair ratings for four trouble spots that relate closely to manufacturing and assembly: body rust, paint and exterior trim, body integrity, and body hardware. Each rating is converted to the midpoint of the percentage range indicated for that trouble spot, and the four repair rates are averaged into a four-item scale (Cronbach's alpha of 0.70). The scale is used as the dependent variable and is measured in log form in the regression equations. Higher values indicate a worse repair record.
scale: five-point rating scale converted to percentage repair rates
time_window: repair record during the third year of ownership, for cars manufactured 1984-1989

variable_name: repair rate measured during the sixth year of ownership
description: The same Consumer Reports frequency-of-repair data, restricted to three trouble spots - body rust, paint and exterior trim, and body integrity - because the factor analyses did not consistently yield a one-factor solution with all four trouble spots and body hardware was therefore dropped. The three repair rates are converted to the midpoints of the percentage ranges and averaged into a three-item scale with a reliability of 0.75. It is used as a log-transformed dependent variable, where higher values indicate a worse repair record.
scale: five-point rating scale converted to percentage repair rates
time_window: repair record during the sixth year of ownership, for cars manufactured 1981-1989

description: Cumulative production output for a given car model, computed on a model-year basis from Ward's Automotive Yearbook production data and lagged by one year. Typically additional predictor variables are included in the learning curve equation already in log form, so it is entered as a natural logarithm. Because of the one-year lag there is no output value to predict a car model's first-year repair rate.
time_window: cumulative through the previous year (model-year output)

description: Cumulative production output of the car model's narrowly defined platform, i.e., its siblings. For example, GM's narrowly defined 'B' platform included several siblings: the Buick LeSabre, Chevrolet Caprice, Oldsmobile 88, and Pontiac. Platform designations are based on information reported in Ward's, supplemented or confirmed in a handful of cases by checking Consumer Reports and popular-press articles in LEXIS-NEXIS. It is entered as a lagged cumulative production output measure.
time_window: cumulative through the previous year (model-year output, starting 1975)

description: Cumulative production output of the car model's broadly defined platform, i.e., its 'cousins,' models in a related platform built off the same architecture. For example, the slightly larger cousins built off GM's 'D' platform in 1977 were the Buick Electra, Cadillac, and Oldsmobile 98. It is entered as a lagged cumulative production output measure.
time_window: cumulative through the previous year (model-year output, starting 1975)

description: Cumulative production output of the car models of the same division of a Big Three automaker, computed on a model-year basis from Ward's Automotive Yearbook production data. The starting point used for division, company, and industry production output is 1975. It is entered as a lagged cumulative production output measure.
time_window: cumulative from 1975, lagged by one year

description: Cumulative production output of all car models of the same company (Chrysler, Ford, or GM), computed on a model-year basis from Ward's Automotive Yearbook production data. The starting point used for division, company, and industry production output is 1975. It is entered as a lagged cumulative production output measure.
time_window: cumulative from 1975, lagged by one year

description: Industrywide cumulative production output, defined in this study as all United States and Canadian output produced by the Big Three, computed on a model-year basis from Ward's Automotive Yearbook production data. The starting point used for industry production output is 1975. It is entered as a lagged cumulative production output measure.
time_window: cumulative from 1975, lagged by one year

description: The year in which a car model began its production life after a major overhaul or all-new introduction, determined by coding the descriptions in Ward's Automotive Yearbook of each year's car models; typically Ward's described major changes with interchangeable phrases like all-new or debuting or bowing. Coding was done separately by the author and an assistant blind to the hypotheses, with agreement in 93.9% of the cases. In the sample, debut year ranges from 1976 to 1988.
Dummy variables for each year a car model has been in production, up through the 13th year, used as a time trend in the panel regression.

ROA at the corporate level is used as the performance measure, following previous literature on geographic diversification (Hitt et al., 1997; Kim et al., 1988). It is the dependent variable in all of the reported regression models.

An entropy measure based on the firm's foreign sales presence within a region. It is computed in two steps: first the sales within each region (INTRAa), and then the sales in all regions added together (INTRAj), where INTRAa equals the sales within the ath global market region and p a ia is the proportion of sales in the ith country to the total sales of the ath global market region. INTRAj is the weighted average of INTRAaj (a in j), the weight being p j aj. The equation blocks are unreadable in the source text.

An entropy measure based on the firm's subsidiary presence within a region, computed in the same two steps as the sales-based measure. INTRAa equals the number of subsidiaries within the ath global market region and p a ia is defined as the proportion of the number of subsidiaries in the ith country to the total subsidiaries of the ath global market region. INTRAj is the weighted average of INTRAaj (a in j). The equation blocks are unreadable in the source text.

An entropy measure of diversification across different regions based on sales. Here, m is the number of regions in which a firm derives sales, and P i is the proportion of the ith region to a firm's total sales in all regions. The equation block is unreadable in the source text.

An entropy measure of diversification across different regions based on subsidiary presence. Here, m is the number of regions in which a firm has subsidiaries, and P i is the proportion of the ith region to a firm's total number of subsidiaries in all regions. The equation block is unreadable in the source text.

Total geographic diversification consists of the intra-regional (INTRA) and inter-regional (INTER) dimensions, computed as TOTAL = INTRA + INTER. In this measure the sales-based versions of INTRA and INTER are used.

Total geographic diversification consists of the intra-regional (INTRA) and inter-regional (INTER) dimensions, computed as TOTAL = INTRA + INTER. In this measure the subsidiary-based versions of INTRA and INTER are used.

Underpricing is the percentage price change from the offer price to the end of the first trading day, computed as the end of first-day market price minus the initial offering price, divided by the initial offering price. The authors state that IPO underpricing was transformed using square root plus constant to avoid kurtosis and skewness problems; the table note describes it as the square root of underpricing plus one.
time_window: first trading day after the IPO

description: Board knowledge breadth is measured as board experience, the average age of directors on the board at the time of the IPO event.

Board knowledge depth is measured as board technical expertise: the proportion of board members possessing technical expertise relative to the IPO (law, accounting, or finance), computed relative to overall board membership.
External knowledge breadth is measured as educational attainment, a national index comprised of the mean number of years of schooling for adults and children, normalized.
External knowledge depth is measured as IPO activity, the number of IPOs issued during the year of the IPO by economy.

Index built from five vignettes, each derived from a seminal court case and presenting a dilemma between shareholders and one non-shareholder constituency; for each vignette respondents reported their agreement with two propositions on a six-point scale that ranged from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree.' In analyzing the data the authors reversed the scale so that it is more intuitive, and after an exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation they dropped the two creditor items and reversed the pro-stakeholder items, averaging the remaining eight items into an index (alpha = 0.77). Higher values on the index reflect a more pro-shareholder, shareholderist stance.
scale: six-point agreement scale; index is the average of eight items
level: individual (board member, CEO or vice CEO)

description: The full set of 10 personal values was measured with a Swedish version of the standard 40-item Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ) developed by Schwartz, translated into Swedish and back-translated. Standard procedure was followed to control for differences in scale use: when values are correlated with external variables each individual's scores are centered around their own mean. Internal reliabilities (alphas) of nine value indexes ranged from 0.59 to 0.83, which the authors note is well within the range of variation commonly observed for values; they report that the index for tradition exhibited an unacceptable alpha but nonetheless correlated systematically well in further analyses.

Index for the power value computed from the Swedish version of the 40-item Portrait Values Questionnaire; individual scores were centered around each respondent's mean across value items before being related to shareholderism.
Index for the achievement value computed from the Swedish version of the 40-item Portrait Values Questionnaire, with individual scores centered around the respondent's mean across value items.
Index for the universalism value computed from the Swedish version of the 40-item Portrait Values Questionnaire, with individual scores centered around the respondent's mean across value items.
Index for the benevolence value computed from the Swedish version of the 40-item Portrait Values Questionnaire, with individual scores centered around the respondent's mean across value items.

Index for the self-direction value computed from the Swedish version of the 40-item Portrait Values Questionnaire, with individual scores centered around the respondent's mean across value items; self-direction was among the values retained in the stepwise selection for the regressions.
Index for the stimulation value computed from the Swedish version of the 40-item Portrait Values Questionnaire, with individual scores centered around the respondent's mean across value items.

Dummy variable for the employee representative position on the board, coded 1 for employee representative directors and 0 otherwise, taken from firm and board data and entered in the shareholderism regressions to capture role effects.

A count variable of the firm's alliances that focus on the upstream activities of the value chain (basic research, drug discovery and development). Alliances were classified based on the motivation for and activities of the alliance as specified by the alliance partners, following Koza and Lewin's distinction between exploiting an existing capability and exploring for new opportunities. A second researcher coded 10 percent of the sample independently with an inter-rater reliability of 0.94.

A count variable of each firm's biotechnology products in development that have successfully entered clinical trials but have not yet reached the market for pharmaceuticals. The measure is a stock of products in the development and regulatory process.

A count variable of the firm's alliances that focus on the downstream activities of the value chain (clinical trials, FDA regulatory process, and marketing and sales). Alliances were classified by the motivation for and activities of the alliance as specified by the alliance partners.
A count variable of each firm's biotechnology products that successfully completed all stages of the product development process and are now commercialized.

Firm size measured by the number of employees as a proxy. The authors note that firm size is often measured in revenues or market share, but that most biotechnology firms do not have a positive revenue stream at this point, so employees provide a reasonable alternative.

Whether a CEO won a medal in the current year (1 = yes, 0 = no at time t). Financial World medals were announced during the first quarter of every year, and many compensation decisions regarding the CEO and other senior executives are typically made subsequent to the first quarter of the fiscal year.

A count variable summing the number of medals a CEO had won over the five years prior to a current year (i.e., t-1, t-2, t-3, t-4, and t-5). It was used to test H3, H4, and H5 because these hypotheses required a measure of status attained prior to the performance variable used in the models.

The logged difference between the CEO's TDC1 compensation and the average TDC1 of the four other executives listed for the same firm in EXECUCOMP, following previous studies (Carpenter and Sanders 2004). In a few firms this difference was actually negative, and because the measure was logged these negative differences were set to 1.

The natural logarithm of the average TDC1 amounts of the four other executives listed for a focal firm in EXECUCOMP. TDC1 includes salary, bonus, other annual compensation, the total value of restricted stock grants, the total value of stock options granted (using Black-Scholes), long-term incentive payouts, and all other miscellaneous forms of compensation; compensation values were transformed into their natural logarithms so that extreme values would not unduly bias the analyses.

Annual return on equity, which is a measure of how well a company is using the equity provided by stockholders and is often used as a basis for awarding incentive pay. It was obtained from COMPUSTAT and lagged one year in all analyses.

A measure of compounded market returns consisting of the total yearly stock return of the company, assuming reinvestment of dividends. It was obtained from COMPUSTAT and lagged one year in all analyses.

A dummy variable taking the value of 1 when a non-CEO member of a top management team was promoted to CEO of either his or her current firm or another firm within five years after his or her last appearance as a top management team member in the sample, and 0 otherwise. Similar dummy variables were constructed for inside promotion (became CEO of the current firm) and outside promotion (became CEO of a different firm). Only the last year in which an executive appeared in the sample was kept to eliminate redundant data on the same executive.
time_window: five years after last appearance in the sample

description: Composite rating based on respondents' estimate of the probability (0-100%) that the predicted decline in the number of 18-22-year-olds would occur and their rated certainty in that estimate (1 = extremely uncertain, 7 = extremely certain). Adapting Duncan's (1972) scoring system, the author rated responses on a continuum whose low end represented certainty of nonoccurrence and whose high end represented certainty of occurrence, so that a certainty of occurrence and a certainty of nonoccurrence are distinguished rather than collapsed.

Composite rating combining the respondent's estimate of the probability (0-100%) that the decline would affect his or her institution, the certainty of that estimate (1 = extremely uncertain, 7 = extremely certain), and the perceived magnitude of the impact (1 = no impact at all, 7 = extremely significant impact). The effect certainty score was weighted by a factor for perceived magnitude of effect and was taken as a reasonable surrogate for the degree to which administrators saw the trend as a potential strategic issue for their institution.

Six-item scale, based on Conrath's (1967) conceptualization of uncertainty, asking how certain respondents were about their institution's ability to respond effectively to the demographic trend. Responses were on a 5-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 2 = disagree, 3 = somewhat agree, 4 = agree, 5 = strongly agree), with several items written in the reverse direction (for example, that it is hard to decide which alternative is most effective, and that administrators just have to guess which strategy will work). The scale had an acceptable level of reliability (a = .75).

Defined as the ratio of the total number of applicants to the number of accepted applicants. The more selective an institution is, the greater its capacity to attract students relative to less prestigious schools; highly selective colleges have power in the market for students and are less likely to suffer enrollment declines. Data on selectivity were obtained from the College Board's data base on institutions of higher education.

Measured by computing the number of students enrolled in undergraduate and graduate programs and dividing by the number of graduate students, on the rationale that colleges and universities with a large number of graduate students are less dependent on the 18-22-year-old population. The measure was reverse-scored to capture the extent of a college's dependence on its undergraduate programs. Data on the number of undergraduate and graduate students came from the College Board's data base.

Eight-item scale adapted from the Management System Questionnaire (Keller, Slocum, & Susman, 1974) to measure the degree to which an institution's structure supported administrative participation in key decisions. Items included statements such as whether the president or board of trustees usually makes strategic decisions without consultation with other administrators (reverse-scored) and whether administrative task forces are convened for tough problems. The adapted scale had a coefficient alpha of .89 and an average item-total correlation of .67.
