New scale developed for this research to measure the sense of uniqueness characterizing an institution's culture; the scale originally had eight items but two items with low item-total correlations were omitted. For the six-item version, a = .79 and the average r = .55. Items concerned pride in the college's goals and mission among administrators, the view that the college has carved out a unique place in higher education, administrators' knowledge of the institution's history, enthusiasm when talking about the college, and the absence of a well-defined set of goals (reverse-worded). Responses were on the same 5-point scale used for the response certainty items.

Fourteen items taken from Cameron's (1978) more comprehensive measure of effectiveness; the coefficient alpha for the reduced scale was .92. Items asked respondents to estimate the proportions of faculty members who had a national reputation in their field, who had published at least one book or article in a professional journal in the last year, and who were doing active research, and to indicate the estimated proportion of students for whom the school was their first choice, along with other questions assessing the college's academic effectiveness.

Region in which the college is located, dummy-coded as 1 = Southwest and 0 = all other regions, and introduced as a control variable in the regression equations that sought to predict variance in effect certainty. The coding reflects demographic forecasts that the Southwest would experience little or no decline in the number of 18-22-year-olds.

The percentage of employees in an industry exposed to hazardous materials while on the job, taken from the Hickey and Kearney (1978) study. An employee was defined as exposed if he or she came into direct physical contact over a prolonged period with one or more known carcinogenic or co-carcinogenic substances while at work. The variable was logarithmically transformed in the vertical integration model.

The ratio of value added to sales in year i, adjusted for inflation and changes in the tax code over time following Adelman (1955). Value added was computed by summing depreciation, amortization, fixed charges, interest expense, labor and related expense, pension and retirement expense, income taxes, net income after taxes, and rental expenses. The specification of the adjustment is given in a formula block that is not readable in the available text.
The value-added-to-sales ratio measured for 1970 and included as an independent variable; several other years were also included in the model specification without affecting results.
The change in R&D spending in a firm's industry from 1970 to 1976; the greater the change, the greater the technological uncertainty facing the firm. The variable was logarithmically transformed.

A four-firm concentration ratio for each two-digit SIC industry. Four-digit SIC concentration ratios reported in the Census of Manufactures were weighted by the value of shipments in 1976 for all four-digit industries within a two-digit industry, and the weighted average was used as the estimate for the two-digit industry.
The variance in industry sales from 1970 to 1976; the greater this variance in sales, the greater the uncertainty in demand facing a firm. The variable was logarithmically transformed.

variable_name: Percentage change in the number of small firms in an industry
description: The number of firms in an industry with assets of less than $100,000 in 1967 was subtracted from the number of such firms, defined in constant 1967 dollars, in 1980, and the result was expressed as a percentage of these firms in 1967. The $100,000 limit was chosen to ensure that the firms would not have significant assets at risk on liquidation.

The percentage of employees in an industry exposed to hazardous materials while on the job, as measured by the Hickey and Kearney (1978) data, used as the independent variable for the small firm production model.
The percentage difference in value added by industry for each two-digit SIC code included in the Hickey and Kearney study between 1967 and 1978, taken from the 1978 Annual Survey of Manufacturers.

The four-firm concentration ratio of each industry included in the Hickey and Kearney (1978) study, calculated like industry concentration in the vertical integration model but using 1977 data because 1978 concentration data were not available.

The ratio of the cost of fuels and electric energy, expressed as a percentage of the value of industry shipments in 1975, for companies with fewer than 250 employees to these costs for companies with more than 250 employees. The data have only been published once, in Pashigan (1984).

Indicator equal to 1 if the two firms in the dyad jointly invested in their first round via a syndicate during the focal year. Continued coinvestment was explicitly ignored: if the two firms coinvested in a given company in one year and continued in follow-up rounds in later years, only the first year counted as a real coinvestment. A dichotomous indicator was used rather than a count variable because the number of multiple joint investments in the same year was very small.

Number of times firm i withdrew from syndicates in which firm j continued participating in the prior five years to that dyad-year, divided by the overall number of unique syndicates between the two. Because withdrawals are node specific, the two values of the variable associated with both firms in the dyad were summed.

Each VC firm's overall number of withdrawals over the preceding five years divided by the total number of unique syndicates in which it had participated. In the empirical analysis the overall withdrawal rates of the two firms in the dyad were summed, as with the other node-specific variables.

The social overlap of each of the two firms with the abandoned partners of the alter, computed as the count of its ties to the alter's abandoned coinvestors divided by the two firms' combined degree centrality minus that count. Because the measure can differ for the two firms in a dyad, the values were summed as with the other node-specific variables. It is the abandoned-partner counterpart of the overall Social Overlap measure, a Jaccard index that standardizes the number of shared partners by the number of non-shared partners into an index ranging from 0 to 1.

The social overlap of each of the two firms with the non-abandoned partners of the alter, computed as the count of its ties to the alter's non-abandoned coinvestors divided by the two firms' combined degree centrality minus that count. Because the measure can differ for the two firms in a dyad, the values were summed as with the other node-specific variables.

The maximum number of singles released by a rival major in the focal style-year. A higher value of this variable indicates that one of the rivals is pursuing a product proliferation strategy. The variable is lagged by 1 year and standardized before regression.

The degree of heterogeneity in product attributes within a subspace, computed on the basis of nine audio properties that AcousticBrainz showcases to summarize the fingerprint of songs. A product space is defined based on a Mahalanobis metric; the centroid of each style during each year is calculated and the Mahalanobis distance of each product in the style-year from this centroid is computed. The mean distance increases with the degree of heterogeneity in product attributes and constitutes the measure of complexity. Missing values are filled by carrying over the last known value of Complexity from previous style-years, and the variable is lagged by 1 year and standardized before regression.

The number of singles released by a major in a given style-year. Because this is a count variable that violates assumptions of equivariance, it is estimated using a quasi-Poisson generalized linear model. The lagged value of the variable is included among the predictors, and every predictor is lagged by 1 year so that OwnSingles at year t is estimated as a function of independent variables at t-1.
time_window: t (with a t-1 lagged value used as predictor)

description: Buy-outs are split according to whether the transaction value is above or below the median transaction value for each year in the period 1981-1989, and exit rates for the two groups are compared. A further split at transaction values above and below $20m, the cut-off point conventionally used by the U.K. financial community, is also reported. Only buy-outs where the original transaction value is known are included.

variable_name: exit (by flotation, trade sale or secondary buy-out/buy-in)
description: A buy-out is counted as exited if it was floated, sold to a third party or subject to a secondary buy-out/buy-in. By the end of December 1992, 21.4 percent (433 out of 2,023) of buy-outs completed between 1981 and 1990 with a known transaction value had exited, and exit rates are reported as the number exiting as a percentage of all buy-outs in a category.

Buy-outs are grouped by the source from which they arose (divestment from a U.K. parent, divestment from an overseas parent, private/family, privatization, receivership, going private and source not specified), and the exit rate of each group is computed. The authors treat buy-outs of public sector activities and divestments by non-U.K. parents as the sources experiencing the greatest pre-buy-out constraints, and private/family buy-outs as the least constrained, and test differences against the overall exit rate with z-tests.

variable_name: exit timing / longevity of the buy-out
description: Each case is described in terms of how long the buy-out form persisted and how the exit occurred: TIP Europe was divested through a buy-out in 1986 and floated in 1988; Mansfield Shoe arose on receivership in 1981 and remained independently owned after a decade; National Freight was completed in 1982 and floated in 1989. The evidence comes from interviews and desk research rather than from a quantitative measure.
time_window: buy-out to exit or to the early 1990s

description: Case evidence on the share of equity held by the management team and on devices that increase it. At TIP Europe management invested £500,000 for an initial 10 percent stake, with a management ratchet allowing their equity to increase to 15 percent on profit targets; at National Freight the team of directors held 61.6 percent of the shares by 1991; at Mansfield Shoe the buy-out team held shares with the managing director holding the largest stake. The authors read a relatively stronger position of financing institutions relative to management as a driver of earlier exit.

The extent of share ownership by employees beyond the buy-out team. At Mansfield Shoe eighty out of 330 employees purchased ordinary shares amounting to some 24 percent of the total equity, and the venture capitalist's shares were later repurchased; at National Freight 37.5 percent of employees bought shares which held 82.5 percent of the equity, falling to eight shareholders holding 7.3 percent by 1991. The authors read the desire of incumbent employee share owners for risk spreading as pressure for exit.

The existence and liquidity of a market on which employee shareholders can trade their shares. At National Freight shares could be traded on an internal share market four times a year, and the authors report the danger that, with a workforce relatively stable in size and little staff turnover, the internal market would soon run out of sufficient liquidity to operate effectively; auguring the internal share market was one reason for flotation. At Mansfield Shoe the buying in of employee shares removed the need to exit to provide market liquidity.

Case evidence on the sums required for capital expenditure beyond the levels initially envisaged. At TIP Europe the need to allow for the commitment to significant capital expenditure resulted in a debt:equity ratio of slightly over 2:1, and expansion required a heavy capital commitment and associated borrowings; the flotation proceeds were to be used to reduce the buy-out debt and to set the basis for further expenditure on the trailer fleet.

Case evidence on the rate of change of the market. TIP Europe operated in a sector marked by rapid restructuring and merger activity, and the very favourable stock market conditions of the summer of 1987 encouraged management and the institutional advisers to seek an earlier float than originally anticipated; continuing market changes and recessionary conditions later led to further financial and managerial restructuring. Mansfield Shoe's footwear industry had a relatively low level of merger activity and no imperative to merge to attain critical mass.

Case evidence on constraints experienced before the buy-out. At TIP Europe the U.S. parent was not able to finance its future plans because of severe corporate financial troubles and TIP was not receiving adequate support for product development and market expansion programs, and the authors note that management were able to reverse many of the constraints imposed by the former parent. National Freight had been a state owned corporation from 1947 to 1982 and had failed to adapt to a highly competitive market.

Case evidence on difficulties in catching up after release from pre-buy-out constraints. In the TIP Europe case the authors report that, although management were able to reverse many of the constraints imposed by the former parent, there is also some indication that catching-up was a contributory factor to early exit, with pre-buy-out constraints raising catching-up difficulties.

Indicator variable that equals one if the ultimate acquirer is an EMNE and zero otherwise. Acquirers are classified as EMNEs if they come from 'Emerging Market and Developing Economies' according to the IMF's classification. For acquisitions going through tax havens, the ultimate acquirers were traced through internet searches and DCA data and classified depending on their location.

Ratio of the retained target TMT 2 years after the transaction to the pretransaction TMT; for example, if three of five pre-transaction TMT members remained 2 years after the transaction the rate is 0.60. Executives are tracked in DCA with a combination of a fuzzy match program and manual verification that excludes false turnovers due to name changes, misspellings, name prefixes and suffixes, nicknames, and abbreviations.
time_window: 2 years after the transaction, relative to the pretransaction TMT

description: Total number of completed acquisitions, including both domestic and cross-border acquisitions, by the cohort in the last 5 years before the focal deal. The cohort is the set of acquiring firms headquartered within 150 km of the ultimate acquirer's headquarters city. The measure is scaled by 1/1000 in all regression outputs.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal deal

description: Total number of cross-border acquisitions by the cohort in the last 5 years before the focal deal. The cohort is the set of acquiring firms headquartered within 150 km of the ultimate acquirer's headquarters city. The measure is scaled by 1/1000 in all regression outputs.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal deal

variable_name: Cohort L5Y Crossborder Acquisition Experience in Similar Target Countries
description: Total number of completed cross-border deals by the cohort to similar target countries, that is, developed countries, in the last 5 years. The cohort is the set of acquiring firms headquartered within 150 km of the ultimate acquirer's headquarters city. The measure is scaled by 1/1000 in all regression outputs.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal deal

variable_name: Cohort L5Y Crossborder Acquisition Experience in Target Country
description: Total number of completed deals by the cohort in the focal target country in the last 5 years. The cohort is the set of acquiring firms headquartered within 150 km of the ultimate acquirer's headquarters city. The measure is scaled by 1/1000 in all regression outputs.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal deal

description: Total number of completed acquisitions, including both domestic and cross-border acquisitions, by the ultimate acquirer in the last 5 years before the focal deal. The measure is scaled by 1/1000 in all regression outputs.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal deal

description: Total number of cross-border acquisitions by the ultimate acquirer in the last 5 years before the focal deal. The measure is scaled by 1/1000 in all regression outputs.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal deal

variable_name: Firm L5Y Crossborder Acquisition Experience in Similar Target Countries
description: Total number of completed cross-border deals by the ultimate acquirer to similar target countries, that is, developed countries, in the last 5 years. The measure is scaled by 1/1000 in all regression outputs.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal deal

variable_name: Firm L5Y Crossborder Acquisition Experience in Target Country
description: Total number of completed deals by the ultimate acquirer in the focal target country in the last 5 years. The measure is scaled by 1/1000 in all regression outputs.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal deal

description: Count of Chaoxian - those that moved to China pre-1949 and their descendants - by province and year. Data were collected for 2003, 2005, 2007, 2009, 2010, and 2012 from the Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and for 1990, 2000, and 2010 from the Chinese Census; for 2010 the Korean data were primarily used except for a few provinces where the Census offered a more reasonable number. Missing data were replaced with counts from the closest year, and standardized counts were used in the estimation to reduce multicollinearity.
time_window: lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: Indicator coded as 1 if Korean bank i made an investment in province j in year t, and 0 otherwise. For each realized investment the choice set includes 16 location options: the 11 locations that received investments from Korean banks during 1992-2013, plus five provinces (Fujian, Hainan, Shaanxi, Yunnan, and Zhejiang) that received investments from non-Korean foreign banks and have Chaoxian communities. Investments in the same year were placed in the same choice set, so each choice set is defined by a firm-investment year.

Average of the components of the marketization index developed by Fan, Wang, and Zhu (2011) that capture the strength of laws and market intermediaries protecting buyers and sellers; results are the same if the components are summed. Because the index is available for 1997-2009, the 1997 values were used for 1992-1996 and the 2009 values for 2010-2013, an extrapolation justified by the stability of the rank ordering of provinces over time.
time_window: lagged one year relative to the dependent variable; index available 1997-2009 with extrapolation to 1992-1996 and 2010-2013

description: Root mean squared error of a regression of gross regional product (GRP, logged) on its lagged value and on a linear time trend, estimated recursively from 1986-2012. The measure is region-specific and time varying.
time_window: recursive estimation over 1986-2012; lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: Standard deviation of the interest rate paid by all firms in the province in the year before the investment is observed. The interest rate data cover all firms in China with sales of more than 5 million yuan, collected annually by the Chinese National Bureau of Statistics during 1998-2007; values were extrapolated for the pre-1998 and post-2007 years. The authors control for the distribution of industries across provinces and other macroeconomic factors so that the measure captures transaction hazards net of variation in economic fundamentals.
time_window: the year before the investment is observed

description: Subsamples of Chinese provinces created by splitting the sample of 82 investments in two based on the median value of legal during 1992-2013, in order to compare the effect of Chaoxian across provinces with strong versus weak property rights laws.
Subsamples of Chinese provinces created by splitting the sample at the median of macroeconomic uncertainty to compare locations with high and low macroeconomic uncertainty.
Subsamples of Chinese provinces created by splitting the sample according to the median of lending uncertainty to compare regions with high and low lending uncertainty.

Dependent variable capturing the change in the performance gap of the leader (the boat that is first in the race at the start of the upwind leg) over her rivals over the upwind leg. It is the minimum difference between the leader's performance gap at the start of the upwind leg and her performance gap at the leg's end relative to the boats that started second, third, and fourth: if g12, g13 and g14 are the changes in the gap relative to those rivals, the variable equals min(g12, g13, g14). It takes positive values if the extent of the performance gap over the rivals was increased over the upwind and negative values if at least one of the rivals reduced the gap to the leader. The variable was log-transformed before the analysis.
scale: seconds, measured to tenths of a second precision

description: Binary variable that takes on a value of 1 if the leader's imitation of the challenger (the second boat around the mark at the start of the leg) is higher than or equal to the leader's imitation of her neighbor and of the other boat competing in the upwind. The underlying imitation measure combines the lagged correlation between the compass headings of the boats (with a one second lag) and the similarity of their average positions relative to the sides of the course, ranging from 0 (neither actions nor positioning imitated) to 1 (both fully imitated). The leader's imitation efforts are focused on the challenger in around half of the upwind legs in the sample.

The authors consider the leader to be using a neighbor imitation strategy when the converse of the challenger focus coding holds, i.e., when the leader's imitation of the challenger is lower than her imitation of the neighbor (the boat closest to her in terms of position relative to the sides of the course, reflecting strategic similarity), in which case the challenger focus variable takes on a value of 0. The measure is therefore the same binary variable, read on the opposite side.

Variable that takes on the maximum value of the leader's imitation of her rivals, corresponding to the extent to which the leader imitated the rival who was the focus of her imitation efforts during the upwind. It is built from the same imitation measure that combines the lagged correlation between the boats' compass headings and the similarity of their average positions relative to the sides of the course, ranging from 0 (no imitation of actions or positioning) to 1 (full imitation of both).

Measured as the average extent (in degrees) of wind shifts over the course of the upwind, calculated from detailed wind direction data recorded five times per second. The mean magnitude of wind shift is around 4.5 degrees, while the maximum average magnitude of wind shift is 30.6 degrees. The variable was log-transformed by taking the logarithm of the original value plus 1.

Calculated as the number of wind shifts - reversals of changes in wind direction of at least 2 degrees over 15 s - over the upwind, normalized by the upwind's duration. The frequency ranges from 0 to over 3.5 wind shifts per minute of the upwind, with an average value of 1.6. The variable was log-transformed by taking the logarithm of the original value plus 1.
scale: wind shifts per minute of upwind

description: A strategy is effective for the leader when it results in her performance gap over her rival(s) being maintained or extended throughout the course of the competition, where performance is defined as the sum of payoffs generated until the current period. The measure takes the minimum of the (pairwise) changes in the performance gaps between the leader and all other rivals in the system, capturing the largest erosion of these relative performances while removing changes in performance common to all competitors.
level: leader agent in a simulation run
time_window: over the 50 periods of a simulation run

description: The leader takes the prior period configuration of her challenger, the second-placed rival, as a reference point in a distant search process. The number of points in the neighborhood of the rival that the leader can choose from decreases with the number of choices the leader must alter in order to move to the rival's configuration; the leader moves to the best performing of these configurations, even if its performance is inferior to that of her current configuration.
level: leader agent in a simulation run
time_window: prior period configuration, evaluated each period

description: The leader imitates the rival that is closest to her on the landscape (her neighbor), the rival that is most similar to the leader in terms of their configuration. The prior period configuration of this rival is taken as the leader's reference point for a distant search process proceeding in the same manner as in the challenger imitation strategy.
level: leader agent in a simulation run
time_window: prior period configuration, evaluated each period

description: To introduce environmental changes into the simulation, the landscape is altered at regular intervals by generating another landscape with the same N and K parameters and defining the payoffs of the landscape at period t + 1 as the weighted average of the payoffs at time t and those of the newly generated landscape. The weight w used in this updating reflects the magnitude of environmental changes and takes the values 0.1, 0.5, and 0.9, with 1 - w being the weight assigned to the previous landscape.

The frequency f of changes corresponds to the length of intervals between periods in which the landscape is altered and takes the values 10, 5, or 2, corresponding to the landscape changing every f periods. High levels of environmental variation are associated with low values of f and high values of w.

Operationalized as the percentage of business (commercial premiums) directed to the interfaced carrier through the proprietary electronic channel, obtained as a response to the question asking the percentage share of the agency's total annual commercial premiums accounted for by the focal carrier. Convergent validity of this single-item measure was assessed by its negative and significant correlations with the number of carriers accounting for 80% of the agency's business and with the number of carriers that each account for at least 2% of the agency's business.

Measured in terms of the extent to which three facets of the business processes are customized relative to the interfaced insurance carrier: the skill level of the employees working on the interfaced carrier's business, the extent of training needed, and the workflows and routines of the interfaced carrier. For each question the agency indicated its position on a 7-point scale ranging from "Relatively Similar to Other Carriers" to "Significantly Customized for the Focal Interfaced Carrier".

Operationalized as the agency's perception of the level of trust with the interfaced carrier using three indicators: the interfaced carrier and our agency have a high level of mutual trust; the interfaced carrier and our agency work together as partners; and it is assumed that the agreements will be renewed. Each indicator was measured on a 7-point scale from strongly agree to strongly disagree.

Measured in terms of the agency's perception of the degree to which the interfaced carrier has invested resources in three areas: initial training pertaining to the use of the electronic interface, providing customized support, and technical support. Each indicator was measured using a 7-point scale ranging from invested hardly any resources to invested considerable resources.
scale: 7-point scale (hardly any resources to considerable resources)

description: Dummy variable coded 1 if a successor CEO was not an employee of the firm in which he or she took office at the time of succession, and 0 otherwise. It captures CEO origin as an outsider.

Dummy variable coded 1 for the first five years of a CEO's tenure and 0 otherwise. The five-year cutoff draws on Gabarro's (1987) qualitative study, which suggested that establishing authority in office generally takes from 30 to 48 months, and on the authors' preliminary analysis. CEO tenure was divided into fiscal years to permit annual updating of the time-varying covariates.
Calculated as the number of directors who were current executives of a firm, excluding the CEO, divided by the total number of directors.
Calculated as the proportion of a firm's outstanding shares held by all executives other than the CEO who were listed in the company's proxy statement.

Dummy variable set to 1 when a current executive of a firm became CEO after the predecessor's dismissal and 0 otherwise. Dismissals were identified in two approaches: an analysis of news reports that classified a turnover as a dismissal if the CEO was directly reported as fired or forced out, reported as having resigned unexpectedly or immediately, or reported as taking early retirement with discussion of performance problems; and a classification based on CEO age and continuity as a board member, in which a departure was a dismissal when the incumbent terminated service as both CEO and board member before the age of 64 for reasons other than death or health, taking a similar position at another firm, or a merger or acquisition. The two approaches were compared, and a total of 65 CEO dismissals was identified, 38 of them followed by inside succession.

A simple heuristic was used rather than self-typing. Local adaptors were those with 50 percent or greater of their work devoted exclusively to the local market. Of the remainder, units where more than 50 percent of the work fell into basic research or development were called international creators, and those where more than 50 percent fell into product/process improvement or adaptation were called international adaptors. This resulted in 28 local adaptors, 40 international adaptors and 41 international creators.

Hedlund's (1981) measure of subsidiary unit autonomy was used as the basis for this scale, with the wording altered to make it specific to R&D units. A factor analysis identified two subscales: strategic issue centralization (4 items, alpha = 0.84) and operational issue centralization (7 items, alpha = 0.92). Respondents indicated who makes decisions for each listed issue; the scale is coded so that higher values mean more subsidiary autonomy, i.e. reversed with respect to centralization.
scale: 1 = decided by HQ or division; 5 = decided independently by subsidiary

description: Two measures were used: the existence of standardized reports to various other units within the MNC, and the use of technical standards for drawing, testing and measuring for that R&D unit. Neither measure was established in the literature; from pilot study interviews and reference group meetings they were identified as the mechanisms used by parent management to formalize R&D unit activities. All answers were either one or zero and absolute values are reported.

Four measures were used, all tapping different facets of the construct: visits by R&D unit members to other R&D units; visits by other R&D unit managers to this unit; personnel involved in corporate training programs; and personnel involved in long-term job rotation programs. Visits were reported for 1991 on a five-point frequency scale; training and rotation were reported as actual numbers of individuals.
scale: visits: 1 = never to 5 = more than ten times; personnel trained and rotated: actual number of individuals

description: Respondents estimated the frequency of (a) personal face-to-face contacts and (b) other types of contacts (letter, phone, digital) with R&D, manufacturing and marketing units in Sweden, in terms of the average number of contacts per year. Questions that specifically mention Sweden were answered only by the foreign R&D units.
scale: average number of contacts per year, split into seven categories from daily through to never

variable_name: Lateral communication with other R&D units
description: Respondents estimated the frequency of personal face-to-face contacts and of other types of contacts with other R&D units in the local market and with R&D units in other countries, in terms of the average number of contacts per year. The data are reported individually to bring out the subtle differences between communication patterns.
scale: average number of contacts per year, split into seven categories from daily through to never

variable_name: Lateral communication with manufacturing and marketing units
description: Respondents estimated the frequency of personal face-to-face contacts and of other types of contacts with manufacturing and marketing units in the local market and in other countries, in terms of the average number of contacts per year. The data are reported individually rather than aggregated.
scale: average number of contacts per year, split into seven categories from daily through to never

description: Respondents estimated the frequency of personal face-to-face contacts and of other types of contacts with universities and research institutions, customers and suppliers in the local, Swedish and international domains, in terms of the average number of contacts per year. The data are reported individually to bring out the subtle differences between communication patterns.
scale: average number of contacts per year, split into seven categories from daily through to never

description: A binary measure of task- and firm-specific skills derived from the fund-level data set and aggregated to the manager level by averaging each manager's quarterly performance across all sole funds she manages concurrently, then creating a cumulative average measure for each manager along each skill dimension. The variable takes a value of 1 if the manager falls into the top 50% of managers on the task-specific dimension and the bottom 50% on the firm-specific dimension, and 0 if the opposite is true; managers high or low on both skill types are omitted to allow a clean comparison. The authors note that the 50% cutoff is arbitrary and replicate all results with continuous measures in the online supplement.
time_window: cumulative average across the manager's quarters in the sample

description: One of three components into which raw fund performance (quarterly gross return) is decomposed using data on the quarterly buying and selling decisions of fund managers following Daniel et al. (1997), each component measured in relation to its benchmark. It is the ability to select stocks that outperform their benchmarks, i.e., stock selection within the consideration set, which prior research shows determines the bulk of variation in a fund's relative performance within its category. The authors label it manager specific (task specific) and transferable across firm boundaries and retain it as their measure of task-specific skills.

A single component formed by combining Characteristic Timing and Average Style, both measured in relation to their benchmarks. Characteristic Timing is the ability to time investments into particular stock types as described by their benchmarks; Average Style is the skill in holding stocks of particular types as defined by the benchmark portfolios, largely determined at the stage of selecting the pool of stocks. The authors label both as reflecting firm-specific skills, and find in Model (10) that external manager changes affect this combined component negatively and significantly.

A proxy measure of mentoring, because access limitations preclude observing interactions among mutual fund managers in the same firm. It is a binary variable with a value of 1 if an existing manager already managing a solo fund joins a team-managed fund in the firm, and 0 otherwise; the authors argue that managers with task-specific skills are more likely than managers with firm-specific skills to join a team of less-skilled managers who are expected to learn from and be mentored by the employee with task-specific skills.

Risk taking is identified as an act by an existing manager of starting a new solo-managed fund; the binary variable New Fund is coded 1 in the fund's first quarter of existence and 0 otherwise. Launching a new fund is described as a common but risky activity for both the manager and the firm, and the authors note that this firm/career risk of fund failure is distinct from risk as a fund characteristic, which the analyses control for with benchmark adjustment, fund volatility and Lipper categories.

Spillovers are defined as the cash inflows accruing to all the funds offered by the management company, excluding those managed by the focal manager, capturing the effect of a manager's skill in managing a focal fund on her ability to draw in new investments to the firm. The standard finance measure of cash inflows is borrowed from the literature and defined as the change in the fund's total net assets between any two quarters net of growth in value; the formula itself is not legible in the text, and the authors state only that k is the focal manager's funds, f the firm, i the fund and TNA total fund net assets.

Percentage of stakes owned by the government. Because ownership structure does not change often, the authors describe this measure as an enduring, objective indicator. It is used as a continuous variable in the models, with a one-year lag for independent variables.
scale: percentage of stakes owned by the government

description: Dummy variable indicating whether a firm was an SOE, that is, a firm with majority state ownership. The authors report that the continuous and dummy measures produced consistent results, and both are used in the main models.
R&D expenses divided by a firm's total sales. Independent variables are lagged one year in the models.

Ratio of new product output to a firm's total industrial output. In the census, new products are defined by the National Bureau of Statistics as those new to the market that are based on substantially new technologies and designs or make substantial improvements to functionality and performance.
scale: ratio of new product output to total industrial output

description: A composite ''marketization'' index compiled yearly by the National Economic Research Institute (NERI) to indicate institutional development at the provincial level. Because the index is endogenous to regional economic development, the authors instrument it with the shortest physical distance from the capital city of each province to one of the two major seaports, Hong Kong and Shanghai, and substitute the instrumental variable estimate into the models.

Herfindahl index used to measure industrial competition (one minus industry concentration). It was calculated at the three-digit industry level for each year using the sales revenue and market share of each firm.

Dummy variable indicating whether an enterprise was established as a new venture within the previous five years (1 = yes; 0 = no). The authors note that start-ups that have failed to build strong market positions in five years likely go out of business, making the five-year cutoff a reasonable indicator of start-up status.
scale: 1 = established as a new venture within the previous five years; 0 = otherwise

description: State ownership of publicly listed manufacturing firms, measured in the same way as in Study 1, as the percentage of stakes owned by the government. Independent variables are lagged one year in the models.
scale: percentage of stakes owned by the government

description: Firms' cumulative R&D investment, used as the innovation input to capture the effect of past R&D expenditure on the long-term process of fundamental innovation. A declining weight of .4 was adopted for R&D investment from previous years, and the authors report that findings were robust with different declining weights.
time_window: cumulative, declining weight of .4 for prior years

description: Total number of invention patents applied for by a listed firm in a given year of 2007-2010 and granted by the end of 2012. Chinese patent law defines an invention patent as a new technical solution relating to a product, a process, or an improvement, and it can be approved only after substantive examination by patent examiners.
time_window: patents applied for in 2007-2010 and granted by the end of 2012

description: Institutional development measured in the same way as in Study 1, using the NERI ''marketization'' index at the provincial level, with the distance to major seaports used as an instrumental variable.
Industrial competition measured in the same way as in Study 1, with the Herfindahl index (one minus industry concentration) computed at the industry level for each year.

The authors report that because the latest founding year of listed firms in this sample was 1995, they could not test the three-way interactions with the variable of start-ups proposed in hypothesis 4.

Firms are clustered into strategic groups within each stable strategic time period using Ward's hierarchical clustering on the eight key strategic variables. Two criteria are used for each stable strategic time period to set the number of clusters: an additional cluster increases the overall fit by less than 5 percent, and the clusters obtained explain at least 65 percent of the overall variance. Multivariate analysis of variance is used to test the adequacy of the clustering results by comparing between-group and within-group variability for each strategic variable separately (ANOVA) and for all of them simultaneously (MANOVA).
time_window: within each stable strategic time period, 1970-84

description: The combined ratio is a common industry measure used to indicate the overall performance level of an insurance company. It is calculated as incurred losses plus loss adjustment expenses plus underwriting expenses plus dividends divided by net premiums written. Firms with a lower combined ratio than the industry average are described by the authors as enjoying superior returns.
The firm's share of industry volume, computed as the firm's net premium written divided by industry net premium written.

A measure that indicates the firm's dominance of particular lines of insurance. It is a weighted average across lines of insurance, in which the market share of the line in the segment is weighted by the relative share of that line in the firm's total portfolio.

The standard deviation of the combined ratio. Because most of the stable strategic time periods are relatively short (one or two years), a meaningful estimate of the standard deviation could not be obtained within each period. The standard deviation was therefore calculated on a cumulative treatment of stable strategic time periods starting with the third one, so that the risk for the third period covers 1970 to 1973, and the same procedure was adopted for each subsequent period.
time_window: cumulative from 1970, by stable strategic time period

description: The standard deviation of the market share measure, calculated with the same cumulative treatment of stable strategic time periods used for the other risk measures.
time_window: cumulative from 1970, by stable strategic time period

description: The standard deviation of the weighted market share measure, calculated with the same cumulative treatment of stable strategic time periods used for the other risk measures.
time_window: cumulative from 1970, by stable strategic time period

description: The ratio of the combined ratio to its standard deviation (COM/RCOM), i.e. average firm performance divided by the standard deviation for the time period. The authors describe it as return per unit of risk.
The ratio of the market share measure to its standard deviation (MS/RMS).
The ratio of the weighted market share measure to its standard deviation (WMS/RWMS).
The ratio of personal net premiums written to personal plus commercial net premiums written. Personal lines are policies sold to individuals and commercial lines those sold to businesses.

A variable that measures the extent of activity in the property/liability segment relative to property/liability and life insurance combined, constructed to describe the product mix aspect of firm strategy.

A Herfindahl index constructed to measure the extent of a firm's diversification across lines of insurance business. The authors note that there are almost 30 different lines of insurance business that insurance companies are routinely willing to cover.
The logarithm of net premiums written, used to capture the absolute size of insurance firms in terms of premium volume.

The ratio of underwriting expenses to net premiums written. The authors argue that net premiums written is preferred to earned premiums as a measure of output since a major portion of underwriting expenses are incurred at the time of writing new and renewal policies.
The proportion of insurance activity that is reinsurance, measured to capture the firm's use of reinsurance for risk sharing, catastrophe protection and increased underwriting capacity.

The ratio of net premiums earned to policyholders' surplus. Policyholders' surplus is defined as the sum of paid-in capital and net surplus, including voluntary contingency reserves, and is used as a surrogate for equity to provide an equity measure applicable to both stock and mutual companies.

The proportion of stocks in the investment portfolio (stocks divided by stocks plus bonds), used to describe insurance investment strategies. A higher value of PSTOCK is considered to be associated with a higher level of risk taking.

variable_name: Combined ratio, market share, weighted market share and their risk and risk-adjusted forms
description: Firm performance was measured with three sets of measures: combined ratio (COM), market share (MS) and weighted market share (WMS), plus the standard deviation of each as risk and the ratio of each to its standard deviation as risk-adjusted performance.

Firms were assigned to the defined categories on the basis of conformity of their planning systems to the strategic planning models, coupled with the length of their planning horizons. Respondents indicated the emphasis their corporate-level planning placed on 19 items on a five-point scale ranging from 'no emphasis' to 'strong emphasis' with a 'not applicable' alternative; eight items loaded on a single dimension and were used to develop a scale for planning openness with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.75, and the summed scores of the eight items were converted to a five-point scale. The planning horizon was divided into four categories based on the longest period for which a specific plan was prepared.
scale: five-point classification (1 = short-term forecasting to 5 = strategic planning)

description: Respondents were asked to indicate the relative importance of 60 information types in determining the outcome of the firm's planning process on a five-point scale ranging from 'very unimportant' to 'very important' with an alternative of 'not applicable' available. Complexity was divided into internal and external components, depending upon the nature of the information types. The sample distributions of the summed scores for each type of complexity were used to create five-point scales for each variable.

Respondents were requested to indicate the relative volatility of the information types over the last 3 years, taking into consideration both the frequency and the magnitude of fluctuations, on a five-point scale ranging from 'very unstable' to 'very stable'. Volatility also was divided into internal and external categories. The sample distributions of the summed scores for each type of volatility were used to create five-point scales for each variable.

The respondents to the questionnaire were asked to indicate the relative importance and stability of 60 types of information which had been identified by various authors as necessary for effective planning. Three categories of information were defined: internal (operations within the enterprise), environmental (factors outside the enterprise with which the enterprise did not directly interact) and external (factors outside the enterprise with which the enterprise interacted directly on a regular basis). A five-point scale ranging from 'very unimportant' to 'very important' was used with an alternative of 'not applicable' available.

The importance to the planning process of eight sources of information was measured using a five-point scale ranging from 'very unimportant' to 'very important' with the option of 'not applicable' available. The questionnaire included: specific management information systems (MIS) for planning, accounting system, personal contact with superiors, personal contact with subordinates, personal contact with outsiders, outside publications, inside reports and outside studies.

Senior management involvement in the planning process was evaluated using five-point scales to measure the importance of four possible levels of activity: setting goals at the start, mid-way review, review and revision near the end, and review and approval at the end of the planning process.

Dichotomous variable that takes the value of 1 if a property is sold by an agent performing both the seller and buyer side of the same transaction, and 0 otherwise. It is modeled as a linear function of a vector of property type dummies, the natural logarithm of market size, the natural logarithm of market heterogeneity, control variables and fixed effects, and estimated by OLS. Because dual agency is the opposite of the division of labor, a negative coefficient indicates a greater likelihood of the division of labor.

A set of dummies corresponding to quintiles (20%) of the distribution of property prices in a given month and market. The first quintile (Q1) corresponds to low-end properties at the bottom of the distribution, whereas the fifth quintile (Q5) corresponds to top-end properties; Q1 serves as the baseline in the regressions. Property prices are corrected for inflation according to the Consumer Price Index, using 2010 as the base year.
scale: five dummy variables for price quintiles

description: Market size measures the number of listed properties for sale in a given month in a given market. It is log-transformed to correct for the skewness of its distribution.

Market heterogeneity corresponds to the standard deviation of the price of listed properties for sale in a given month in a given market. It is log-transformed to correct for the skewness of its distribution.

Binary variable equal to 1 if the firm exits the solar PV module manufacturing industry during the shakeout period and zero otherwise. In the case of diversifiers, exit events are coded based on the termination of the firm's solar PV manufacturing business and not for the firm as a whole.

Binary variable equal to 1 if the firm exits solar PV module manufacturing via acquisition and zero otherwise. Episodes of dissolution include bankruptcy, wherein the firm's assets are disaggregated and auctioned, and cessation, wherein the firm ceases operations with or without piecemeal liquidation of assets. Pre-shakeout acquisitions are treated as censored observations.

The variable cSi takes a value of 1 if the firm entered with cSi technology and 0 if the firm entered with other competing thin-film technologies. Firms that pursued a second technology after entry were categorized based on the technology that they entered with, because the initial technology choice is more likely to represent a superior match with respect to firms' pre-entry capabilities and founder experience.

A firm is categorized as a diversifying entrant if it was an established firm operating in another industry before entering the solar PV industry, and as a start-up otherwise. In the exit models, firms are represented by categorical variables for the quadrant they occupy (diversifier cSi, start-up cSi, diversifier non-cSi), with start-ups that entered with non-cSi technologies as the omitted category.

Sum of the mean-centered market shares of prior movers in the host country over those domestic market segments in which the focal firm is present, weighted by the focal firm's percentage of telecommunication revenues obtained in each segment. Market shares in each segment (local exchange, long distance, cellular service) were calculated from segment-specific revenues and were centered around the mean market share of all incumbents in that segment during the study period. The formulas given for the aggregation are not readable in the received text. Dyadic mimicry was tested by interacting this variable with the focal firm's domestic market share.

Sum of the focal firm's mean-centered market share in those domestic market segments occupied by prior movers, weighted by the focal firm's percentage of telecommunication revenues obtained in each segment. Market shares were computed from segment-specific revenues and centered around the mean market share of all incumbents in the segment during the study period. The formula for the aggregation is not readable in the received text. In models including the interaction term, the coefficient is interpreted as the conditional relationship when the other interacting market share is at average level.

The dependent variable is the hazard of an international entry move by a firm into a host country, modeled on firm-country event histories. An event history ended with an entry move when a move into that host country was announced; of the 203 firm-country event histories, 30 ended with an entry move and the remaining 173 were right-censored by the end of the observation period or by the disappearance of the firm from the sample. Entry moves were identified from announcements and crosschecked across several sources, and only successful entry moves were included.

Number of prior movers in a host country that were active in the domestic long-distance segment, and zero otherwise. The parallel variable, regional holding company facing regional holding company_ict, counted the prior movers in a host country that were Baby Bells, and was zero otherwise. Both variables shift the hazard rate for the two relevant subgroups and were compared with a Wald test of the equality of their coefficients.
time_window: time-varying, changed at year-end or when a firm entered the host country

description: Assessment of the environmental complexity faced by each national subsidiary, provided by a single senior headquarters respondent for each of the MNC's national subsidiaries. Like all constructs in the headquarters instrument it was operationalized as a single variable measured on a centrally anchored five-point scale, and each case was measured as a standardized deviation (z-score) from the mean conditions of the company of which it was a part.

Rating of the level of local resources of each national subsidiary, provided by a single senior headquarters respondent for each subsidiary of the MNC. Operationalized as a single variable on a centrally anchored five-point scale, and measured as a standardized deviation (z-score) from the mean conditions of the company.

The lack of subsidiary autonomy in decision-making, rated by a single senior headquarters respondent for each national subsidiary. Operationalized as a single variable on a centrally anchored five-point scale, and measured as a standardized deviation (z-score) from the mean conditions of the company.

Extent of formalization of policies and systems in the headquarters-subsidiary relation, rated by a single senior headquarters respondent for each national subsidiary. Operationalized as a single variable on a centrally anchored five-point scale, and measured as a standardized deviation (z-score) from the mean conditions of the company.

Extent to which the national subsidiary is in tune with the overall goals and management values of the parent company, rated by a single senior headquarters respondent. Operationalized as a single variable on a centrally anchored five-point scale, and measured as a standardized deviation (z-score) from the mean conditions of the company.

Subjective assessment of the average overall performance of each national subsidiary by a senior corporate manager responsible for international operations, obtained for every headquarters-subsidiary relation; the paper argues that no comparable objective measure of subsidiary performance was available. Measured on a centrally anchored five-point scale and expressed as a standardized deviation (z-score) from the mean conditions of the company.

Weighted Euclidean distance between the structure of a focal subsidiary and the empirically derived ideal structural profile of its contextual category, the ideal profile being the mean scores of the structural variables for the top-performing subsidiaries in that cluster. Each structural dimension is weighted by its standardized beta, or contribution, in a multiple regression with performance as the dependent variable and all the structural dimensions as the independent variables. The written formula itself is not extractable from the text. Higher values indicate a greater deviation from the ideal profile, i.e. less fit.

Three doctoral students in psychology, blind to the hypotheses, watched edited pitch video clips and rated the focal CEO's behavioral manifestation of narcissism using the Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Questionnaire (NARQ). Admiration is a second-order latent variable consisting of three first-order facets each with three indicators. All items were measured on a six-point scale ranging from 1 = do not agree at all to 6 = agree completely; reliability of the overall admiration measure was alpha = 0.76 and the intraclass correlation coefficient across raters was 0.75.
scale: 1 = do not agree at all to 6 = agree completely

description: Rivalry was rated by the same three doctoral student coders using the NARQ, based on pitch video footage edited to remove confounding content such as prior sales revenues and investor reputations. Rivalry is a second-order latent variable consisting of three first-order facets each with three indicators. Items were measured on a six-point scale ranging from 1 = do not agree at all to 6 = agree completely; reliability of the overall rivalry measure was alpha = 0.64.
scale: 1 = do not agree at all to 6 = agree completely

description: The authors transcribed the video pitches, located where investors asked questions and interacted with CEOs, and counted sentiment terms from Loughran and McDonald's Master Dictionary with Sentiment Word Lists as they appeared in the transcripts after each investor's name. Investor sentiment scores were computed as the difference between the number of positive and negative terms divided by the sum of the two counts for the total number of investors appearing in any given pitch. The aggregation of individual sentiment scores across all investors had a reliability of alpha = 0.72.
scale: continuous, ranging from positive to negative
level: pitch (aggregated across the investors appearing in the pitch)

description: New venture funding is the natural logarithm of the total dollar value of funding received by each CEO who pitched on Shark Tank. The authors triangulated these data with secondary sources, such as Crunchbase.

Indicator variable set to 1 if the focal company adopted a given practice in a particular year, and 0 otherwise. There are 11 practices, concerning board structure, evaluation process, and share and ownership structure, and each practice defined by the BSCI yields its own indicator; the adoptions are pooled in the analysis by stacking the matrices of single-practice diffusion regressions. The firm has an observation on a practice for each year in which it did not yet use the practice, and once an organization has adopted a practice it can no longer generate an observation for that practice, so the data consist of firm-year-practice observations.

The BSCI score, ranging between 0 and 100 points with higher scores indicating better governance, obtained from the Clarkson Centre. Separate aspiration levels (AL) were computed from ROA and BSCI and then subtracted from actual BSCI to yield performance relative to the aspiration level. To enable comparison of slopes above and below aspiration level, this relative performance variable was split by a spline: BSCI below AL equals 0 for observations where relative performance is greater than 0 and equals relative performance otherwise, so it always takes either 0 or negative values; the analogous BSCI above AL variable takes 0 or positive values.
scale: points (0-100 for the BSCI score; relative performance in points)

description: ROA obtained from COMPUSTAT; separate aspiration levels were computed based on ROA and BSCI and then subtracted from actual ROA to yield performance relative to the aspiration level. The relative performance variable was split by a spline: ROA below AL equals 0 for observations where relative performance based on ROA is greater than 0 and equals relative performance otherwise, so it always takes either 0 or negative values, while ROA above AL equals 0 for observations with relative performance below 0 and equals relative performance otherwise.

Historical aspiration levels for ROA and BSCI were computed with the formula the authors label equation (1); the formula block in the text is unreadable and is recorded as a gap. The authors state that Performance t-1 is the ROA (or BSCI) at time t-1 and that a is a number between 0 and 1 representing the weight given to the immediate prior performance. They set a = 0.5, giving equal weight to past performance and aspirations, and because last year's historical aspirations incorporate earlier aspirations and performance, current historical aspirations are recursive.

Social aspirations for each firm were computed as the average ROA and BSCI for all firms in the TSX Index but excluding the focal firm. Each firm's performance was weighted by 1/[1 + w], where w was set to 0 if the two firms were in the same industry and to 1 otherwise.

A dummy variable coded 1 where a firm used a bank on its prior acquisition. Because it is quite correlated with the other bank variables, it is entered in a separate equation for the purposes of data analysis. Company statements, including financial reports, and Securities Data Corporation are the sources of these data.

A count of the number of times banks advised the firm on its prior acquisitions. The variable is left censored in 1985 because the author lacked data on bank usage prior to that date. When the firm only made one acquisition during the sample period (1985-90) the variable is coded 0. To avoid overrepresenting any one acquisition, the maximum count on any one acquisition is 1.

A dummy variable coded 1 where a firm used the same bank on its prior acquisition that it did on its focal acquisition. It is entered together with the other bank-influence variables in separate equations.

variable_name: Performance of prior acquisition with bank
description: The interaction of using a bank on a prior acquisition with the performance of that acquisition, where performance is measured by announcement returns as discussed. This is the variable entered to test whether the success of an engagement on which a bank was hired conditions clients' subsequent hiring of banks.

A count of those acquisitions, between January 1, 1985 and the time of the acquisition, of the times that the acquiror makes a stock-financed acquisition without banks. It captures clients' experience of doing stock-financed deals independently of advisors.

Bank and stock financing is one of four possible outcomes that govern choices about the medium of financing and acquisition advisors; the others are bank and cash financing, no bank and stock, and no bank and cash. Outcomes that involve a combination of stock and cash are coded as stock, an outcome that concerned less than 5 percent of all acquisitions in this sample. Because the acquiring firm uses stock in these cases, the outcome is suited to bank expertise. It is analysed with multinomial logistic regression models that predict the joint outcome of stock and banks against the other categories.

Analogous to bank and stock financing, with the exception that this variable is coded 1 when the bank on the focal acquisition is the same as that on the prior acquisition. It is the dependent variable in the model testing whether a client rehires the bank that worked on its prior acquisition.

Acquisition performance is measured using the event-study methodology that yields cumulative abnormal returns. A market model estimates the relationship between firm returns and equally weighted market returns for the 250 trading days (roughly 1 year of trading) starting from 30 days prior to the announcement of the acquisition, a 30-day cushion that seeks to remove the effect of takeover news that could already be incorporated in the market price of the acquiring firm. Immediate acquisition returns are the abnormal or excess returns of the acquiring firms as measured over a 5-day interval, the day of the acquisition announcement and the 2 days immediately prior to and after the announcement. The Center for Research on Security Prices is the source of data on the excess returns.

The natural log of the value of shares purchased on the open market by all insiders in a given year. The value equals the number of shares purchased multiplied by the average purchase price for all insider purchases in a given year. Following Seyhun (1990), other transactions such as the exercise of options and shares acquired from compensation plans are set aside. The dollar value is log-transformed because of the skewed nature of the variable, especially when comparing large and small firms. Values are computed separately for the year before, the year of, and the year after the firm's top patent application.
time_window: one year before, the year of, and the year after the top patent application date

description: The number of patents a firm applied for in a given year. It is used to test whether the number of patents in a given year influences insider trading.
time_window: one year before, the year of, and the year after the top patent application date

description: A count of the number of citations received by the firm's most heavily cited patent over the 3-year period, using citations to the patent through 1999. It measures the strength of a firm's best patent. The variable is adjusted by subtracting the average citations for a patent in that technology subfield, using the NBER classification of 36 technology subfields.
time_window: citations through 1999; 3-year period around the top patent

description: The number of patents a firm applied for that were ultimately in the top 10 percent most heavily cited in their technology subfield. It is calculated from Cites received and allows recognition of when firms have multiple breakthroughs in the same year. The authors experimented with cut-off points between 10 percent and 0.5 percent and present the 10 percent cutoff.
time_window: one year before, the year of, and the year after the top patent application date

description: The number of claims made for the firm's top patent, reflecting the number of distinct uses specified for the innovation in the patent. It is used as a proxy for how many applications a given innovation may have. The average claims made for the patent's technology subcategory was subtracted to account for different norms for claims by type of technology.
time_window: one year before, the year of, and the year after the top patent application date

description: The citation lag in years for the firm's strongest patent, reflecting the time before the patent is cited. It is used to capture the extent to which trading was driven by the speed with which follow-on work was under way.
time_window: one year before, the year of, and the year after the top patent application date

variable_name: #Patents, Cites received, #Breakthroughs, Claims and Cite lag in each timing window
description: Patent activity is captured by the same patent variables, measured in three timing windows constructed around the firm's top patent application date. The windows are 18 months before to 6 months before the application (t - 1), 6 months before to 6 months after (t), and 6 months after to 18 months after (t + 1). Models A and B use #Breakthroughs and Cites received with #Patents, Models C and D again use them, and Models E and F repeat them for the later window.
time_window: 18 to 6 months before the application; 6 months before to 6 months after; 6 to 18 months after

description: Treatment indicator, coded 1 if firm i engaged in an M&A and 0 if it did not. The estimator imputes the missing potential outcome of treated units by using the outcomes of control units with similar values of pretreatment variables. Matching is applied with replacement and four comparison units, using the Stata routine of Abadie et al. (2001), and the control deals are drawn from the Compustat universe.

The number of patent applications per year. It is calculated with reference to the patents for which firms filed an application two years before and two years after the deal was completed, for the acquiring and target firm taken together as a single entity. The before-after comparison also reports the number of patents normalized for industry average.
time_window: two years before and two years after the deal was completed

description: Impact is the number of forward citations received by a focal patent, which the authors read as the influence of a patent on future inventions, and also as strictly associated with its monetary value. Every citation-based measure is normalized by the average value of the measure itself calculated over all patents belonging to the same technological category whose application was filed in the same year. The measure is computed over the patents of the combined unit filed two years before and two years after the deal.
level: patent, averaged for the combined M&A unit
time_window: two years before and two years after the deal was completed

description: Generality of patent i is measured as 1 minus the sum over patent classes j of s_ij squared, where s_ij indicates the percentage of citations received by patent i that belongs to patent class j, out of n patent classes. The measure is high if the patent is cited by subsequent patents belonging to a wide range of technological fields, and close to zero if most citations are concentrated in a few fields. The measure is normalized by the average value in the same technological category and application year.
level: patent, averaged for the combined M&A unit
time_window: two years before and two years after the deal was completed

description: Originality of patent i is measured as 1 minus the sum over patent classes j of t_ij squared, where t_ij indicates the proportion of the citations made by patent i to patents that belong to patent class j. A patent that cites previous patents belonging to a narrow set of technologies, i.e. the result of 'local' search, receives a low originality score. The measure is normalized by the average value in the same technological category and application year.
level: patent, averaged for the combined M&A unit
time_window: two years before and two years after the deal was completed

description: Second-order construct based on Pehrsson (2006), with wording changed to assess complementarity rather than similarity. It consists of product market-related issues (six items), resource-related issues (six items), and value chain attributes (four items). Items are assessed on a 5-point scale.

Second-order construct using scales developed by Jöns and colleagues. It consists of four dimensions: strategy (four items), structure (two items), leadership (five items), and interrelationship (four items). Items are assessed on a 5-point scale.

Second-order construct adopted from Cording et al. (2008), assessed on different organizational levels. It consists of sociocultural integration (three items), integration of production (two items), marketing integration (three items), and system integration (three items). It is measured on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 = no integration at all to 7 = complete integration.

Assessed following Cording et al. (2008), with the same organizational levels as the degree of integration. The authors assess speed of integration with four items on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 = longer than 24 months to 5 = shorter than 7 months. After the deletion of two items, the measurement model was sufficiently reliable and valid.

Self-reported measure from managers of the acquiring firms, using the measurement model developed by Becker (2005). It consists of two dimensions—objective success and subjective success—each measured with four items. The objective dimension uses a 7-point scale ranging from 1 = strong negative development to 7 = strong positive development; the subjective dimension uses a 7-point scale ranging from 1 = completely disagree to 7 = completely agree.

Respondents reported the number of days per year that personnel from the automaker and supplier met on a face-to-face basis to exchange technical information at the supplier's plant. This was measured by having the plant manager identify the average number of days per year that personnel from this customer visited to exchange technical information and provide assistance. In the tests the supplier's response for the U.S. OEM was subtracted from the supplier's response for Toyota, producing dOEMFaceDays.

Supplier respondents were asked to report on the extent to which they had received quality assistance from each customer, responding to the item: 'To what extent has this customer provided assistance to help you reduce defects and increase the overall reliability and quality of the products you sell?' Responses were given on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = Not at all; 4 = To some extent; 7 = Great extent). In the tests the U.S. OEM response was subtracted from the Toyota response, producing dQualityAssistance.

The extent to which each customer provided inventory assistance was measured by having suppliers respond to the item: 'To what extent has this customer provided assistance to help you develop a more efficient inventory management system (i.e., a just-in-time system) designed to lower inventory costs and/or make delivery more efficient?' Responses were on a 1-7 Likert scale (1 = Not at all; 4 = To some extent; 7 = Very great extent). In the tests the U.S. OEM response was subtracted from the Toyota response, producing dInventoryAssistance.

The plant's number of defective parts per million produced for each customer, based on a statistical sampling of parts at the supplier's plant; defects in parts per million must be provided to the automaker as evidence of the supplier's quality. Performance data were provided for the years 1990, 1992, 1994 and 1996. The rate of improvement is reflected in the change in defects from 1990 to 1996 (DefectsChange), and the tests use the difference between the Toyota and the U.S. OEM rate of improvement (dDefectsChange).
level: supplier plant manufacturing cell for a customer

description: Inventories (raw materials, WIP, and finished goods) directly attributable to each customer as a percent of sales to that customer. Performance data were provided for 1990, 1992, 1994 and 1996, and the rate of improvement is reflected in the Inventory/Sales Change from 1990 to 1996. The tests use the difference between the Toyota and the U.S. OEM rate of improvement (dInventory/SalesChange).
level: supplier plant manufacturing cell for a customer

variable_name: Network constraints reported as a barrier to transfer
description: Coded from the plant manager interviews conducted after the survey: whether the plant manager reported being unable to transfer the knowledge employed in one manufacturing cell to another cell due to 'customer policies' or 'constraints imposed by the customer.' In eight of the 13 interviews the plant managers reported being unable to transfer knowledge for this reason; the authors also note which respondents agreed only after being prompted by the interviewer.

variable_name: Process rigidities reported as a barrier to transfer
description: Coded from the plant manager interviews: whether plant managers reported not transferring the knowledge gained from Toyota because of manufacturing process rigidities in the layout of the manufacturing cells for the U.S. customer, such as high levels of automation or large capital investment in heavy equipment. Suppliers were much less likely to attempt to transfer the knowledge when the U.S. customer's production process involved a high level of automation or large capital investment.

Firms were assigned ratings on a four-point ordinal scale based on increasing interdependence: unrelated = 1, related-linked = 2, related-constrained = 3, and vertically integrated = 4. The underlying classification of each firm's diversification strategy through 1974 came from Rumelt's (1978) Databank, and the study group was further limited to firms that had maintained stable strategies between at least 1971 and 1974.
time_window: strategy classification through 1974, stable between at least 1971 and 1974

description: Tenure was measured as the mean number of years the members of a top management team had spent with a firm. A company's top team was defined as including all officers above the level of vice president and any other officers who were on the board of directors, coded for 1973 from the Dun and Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Management.

Tenure homogeneity was based upon the coefficient of variation for top management team tenure. To convert the measure from a heterogeneity indicator to a homogeneity indicator, each firm's coefficient of variation was subtracted from 1.43, the highest value in the firms studied.

Measured by a variation of the Herfindahl-Hirschman index: H is the sum over i of S-sub-i squared, where S-sub-i is the percentage of a top management team's members with dominant functional career track i. A dominant functional career track was defined as the area in which a manager had spent more time than in any other, and i took on the values 1 to 9; H can take on values from 0 to 1, with high values indicating that a top team is homogeneous, with typically one or two areas dominant.

Interunit moves was coded as the mean number of times team members had moved between distinct lines of business within a company. For example, a move from the General Electric Company's large turbine business to its locomotive business would be counted as an interunit move, whereas a move from the large turbine business to the small turbine business would not.
Core function expertise was measured as the percent of team members whose primary functional careers had been in production-operations, marketing, or R&D.
