Profitability was measured as return on assets (ROA), defined as net income after taxes divided by total assets, and averaged for 1973-76. Financial performance data were taken from the COMPUSTAT tapes.

variable_name: goal condition (stretch versus moderate profit goal)
description: Teams were randomly assigned either a stretch profit goal (n = 25) or a moderate profit goal (n = 25). The stretch goal is based on the 90th percentile and the moderate goal on the 50th percentile of performance levels achieved in pilot tests in which decision makers were instructed to do their best to maximize cumulative net income. Teams in the stretch (moderate) goal group were told that the board of directors had set their cumulative net income target equal to $315 ($60) million by the end of 10 years.

variable_name: goal condition (stretch versus moderate profit goal)
description: Participants were randomly assigned stretch (n = 30) or moderate (n = 29) profit goals. In addition to the goal for year 10, participants were assigned cumulative net income goals for each year starting in year 3, and were told they would be paid performance-based bonuses for each intermediate year in which their cumulative profit met or exceeded the goal for that year and a larger amount if they met or exceeded the final goal.
time_window: annual goals from year 3 plus a year 10 goal

description: Performance is measured by cumulative net income at the end of the third simulation round. For those experiencing bankruptcy (equity falling below zero), cumulative net income when bankruptcy occurs is used, which can be negative or positive.
time_window: end of the third simulation round (year 10)

description: Performance is measured by cumulative net income at the end of the third simulation round. For those experiencing bankruptcy (equity falling below zero), cumulative net income when bankruptcy occurs is used, which can be negative or positive.
time_window: end of the third simulation round (year 10)

description: Assessed with the Levene test for equality of variances between the stretch and moderate goal groups for year 10 of the simulation; the Levene test does not require normality of the underlying data. Those assigned stretch goals exhibited significantly higher performance variance, with a standard deviation of cumulative net income of $219 million versus $113 million under moderate goals.

Assessed with the Levene test for equality of variances between the stretch and moderate goal groups for year 10 of the simulation; the Levene test does not require normality of the underlying data. Participants assigned stretch goals exhibited significantly higher performance variance, with a standard deviation of $526.6 million versus $114.5 million under moderate goals.

Tested with the robust Jarque-Bera test to assess the skewness of the performance distribution in year 10. The performance distribution for stretch goals is right-skewed, whereas the distribution for moderate goals is not skewed.

Tested with the robust Jarque-Bera test to assess the skewness of the performance distribution in year 10. The performance distribution for the stretch goal condition is right-skewed, but is not skewed under moderate goals.

The ratio of mean performance to the standard deviation for all participants in each condition. The null hypothesis that the Sharpe ratios are equal in the two goal conditions is evaluated by estimating the 95% confidence interval of the difference between the two ratios from 5,000 bootstrapping samples. In Study 1 the ratio for the stretch goal condition is 0.66 compared with 1.00 for the moderate goal condition.

The ratio of mean performance to the standard deviation for all participants in each condition, with the 95% confidence interval of the difference between the two ratios estimated from 5,000 bootstrapping samples. In Study 2 the Sharpe ratio for the stretch goal group is 0.67 compared with 1.31 for the moderate goal group.

A six-item, task-specific measure of willingness to take risk in the next decision round, developed from well-established measures of perceived risk taking. Items included, for example, 'How much risk will you take in your aircraft purchasing decisions?' Participants were asked to complete the questionnaire before each simulation round (three times in total).
time_window: before each of the three simulation rounds

description: A five-item measure of goal commitment adapted from prior research. Items included, for example, 'Quite frankly, I don't care if I achieve the annual goals or not.' Participants were asked to complete the questionnaire before each simulation round (three times in total); the reported decrease in goal commitment is expressed on a scale from 0-10.
time_window: before each of the three simulation rounds

description: The exogenous goal for cumulative profit at the end of the round (G) less actual cumulative net income achieved at the end of round 2 (P r=2). Entered as a predictor of commitment to the exogenous goal prior to round 3 together with an intercept and an error term.
time_window: performance at the end of round 2 predicting commitment prior to round 3

description: An indicator distinguishing acquisitions in which the acquired firm had been structurally integrated from those in which it had not. To record the structural integration decision for each acquisition, the authors examined the CORPTECH database in the year after the acquisition; continued appearance of the acquired firm in CORPTECH published in the second year after the acquisition was interpreted to mean that structural integration had not been carried out, whereas disappearance from CORPTECH meant that structural integration had occurred and the firm was no longer traceable as a distinct organizational entity. The validity of this measurement was verified through an examination of press releases and articles.

A count of post-acquisition patents filed by the acquirer-acquired firm combination that both cite a patent previously filed by the acquired firm and include at least one acquired firm inventor as an author (cell A), plus post-acquisition patents that cite a previously filed acquired firm patent but have no acquired firm employee as an author (cell B). A citation is treated as evidence of inventive effort that leverages the acquired firm's existing knowledge codified in the patent and other secondary sources as well as the tacit component resident in the acquired firm's employees. The active knowledge base of the acquired firm prior to acquisition is defined as all patents filed in the three years preceding the acquisition. The results section describes the measure in the reverse way, as all patents in which a target firm inventor appears as an author (cells A and B), which conflicts with the cell labels in the measurement section.

A count of post-acquisition patents filed by the acquirer-acquired firm combination in which at least one inventor previously employed by the acquired firm is among the authors (cells A and C), which the authors argue shows that the acquirer has leveraged the innovative capabilities of the acquired firm, both as an individual and in conjunction with his or her colleagues. Measures of capability leverage were constructed by tracking patents filed by target firm inventors after the acquisition through an exhaustive search and matching on surnames, initials, technology classes and location.

A count of prior acquisitions conducted by the acquirer from the earliest date for which SDC data are available up to the focal acquisition. Although the study window began in 1988, the count starts in 1984 so that acquisitions made before the study window are included.

The treatment indicator Facebook takes the value of one for developers in Facebook projects and zero for developers in GAAT projects, and post scandal is coded as one for months after March 2018 and zero otherwise. The main analyses use the interaction of the two indicators, which varies within developer pairs, projects and months.

Developer engagement is measured with four monthly activity counts and their sum. Commits are the monthly number of approved code changes a developer made to a focal project, pull requests the monthly number of proposed code revisions, issue reports the monthly number of requests for bug fixes or new functions, and comments the monthly number of discussions about commits, pull requests and issue reports. Total activities captures overall engagement as the total monthly number of commits, pull requests, issue reports and comments.

Choice space captures a developer's choice set for alternative projects and is proxied by the number of projects held by other firms with at least five contribution records from the focal developer in the last 12 months. A project counted as an alternative is one the developer had shown interest and ability to contribute to, inferred from past contribution records. Projects of the same firm were not valid alternatives because switching between them could not alleviate the dissonance associated with the firm.

Social embeddedness is constructed in two steps based on the focal developer's social interactions with other project members in the community. Social interactions are proxied by the number of comments made by the developer in the focal project; this project-level measure is then divided by the total number of comments made by the developer across all GitHub projects. The ratio captures the degree of social embeddedness in the focal project, taking into account all of the developer's social activities on GitHub.
scale: ratio of comments in the focal project to all comments

description: The authors identify the technology classes listed in each inventor's prior patents, including single-authored patents, as a proxy for the inventor's knowledge base. Each patent is assigned to its primary U.S. patent class, and aggregating these assignments yields a 37-dimensional knowledge vector for each inventor: the percentage of assignments to each of the 37 technology classes. Team knowledge distance is the angular distance between each inventor's knowledge vector; for a two-inventor team it is the angle measured in radians between the two vectors, and for teams with more than two members it is the average of the pairwise angular distances between all member dyads. Inventor vectors are updated yearly.
time_window: accumulated prior patents; inventor vectors updated yearly

description: Technological impact is operationalized as the number of forward citations received by the focal patent, net of self-citations and inclusive of examiner citations, within five years of issue. The authors define the measure as the number of citations to a focal patent and note that citations to most patents peak within five years.

Density is the completeness of the shared ties between team members. For each pair of scientists on a patent team, a score of one is given to pairs who have collaborated in the past and zero to pairs who have not previously been listed as coinventors on a patent. This variable is summed across pairs of scientists on the team and divided by the total possible number of pairs on the team, N(N-1)/2, where N is the number of inventors on the team. Density ranges from zero to one. For the hypothesis tests, the authors created a dummy variable indicating teams with high versus low density (above the 75th percentile versus below the 25th percentile), omitting teams in the 25th to 75th percentiles.
scale: 0 to 1 continuous; dichotomized high vs. low

description: Centralization is measured as the relative concentration of team members' prior collaborations around one or a few core members, whereas other members remain isolated. The authors calculate degree centrality for each inventor as the number of inventors each inventor has patented with in the past. They sum the difference between each inventor's degree centrality and the degree centrality of the most central inventor, then divide this value by the maximum centralization score given the team size. For the hypothesis tests, the authors created a dummy variable indicating teams with high versus low centralization (above the 75th percentile versus below the 25th percentile), omitting teams in the 25th to 75th percentiles.
scale: continuous concentration score; dichotomized high vs. low

description: Subgrouping is operationalized as the standard deviation of the count of pairwise numbers of collaborations for each possible pair of inventors on the team. First, the authors examine each possible pairwise combination of inventors on the focal patent and count the number of times these inventor pairs were listed as coinventors on prior patents. Second, they calculate the standard deviation of that series of pairwise counts. A higher score reflects a team in which prior collaborations are concentrated in a small subset of team members. For the hypothesis tests, the authors created a dummy variable indicating teams with high versus low subgrouping (above the 75th percentile versus below the 25th percentile), omitting teams in the 25th to 75th percentiles.
scale: standard deviation of pairwise collaboration counts; dichotomized high vs. low

description: The dependent variable is the probability of receiving an inbound tie during a subepisode. It is coded as one when a tie arrival event is observed and zero otherwise. Each guideline version was split into subepisodes of one-fifth of a year and all covariates are time-varying and updated at the beginning of each subepisode.
time_window: subepisodes of one-fifth of a year

description: Measured with the number of guidelines in the CPG collection in a given year. It is a system-level, time-varying covariate updated at the start of each subepisode. It was rescaled by dividing by 100 to obtain coefficients that display more digits.

Constructed by adding the counts of the number of rule birth events and rule revision events in a given year. It is a system-level, time-varying covariate updated at the start of each subepisode. It was rescaled by dividing by 100 to obtain coefficients that display more digits.

Constructed using the information on the research publications cited by CPGs, measured with the number of healthcare publications a guideline version cites. The variable was square-root transformed in the analyses. It is time-varying and updated at the start of each subepisode.

Captured with the number of CPGs that are citing the focal guideline when the current subepisode begins. The variable was square-root transformed in the analyses. It is time-varying and updated at the start of each subepisode.
time_window: at the beginning of the current subepisode

description: Measured with the number of years between the effective date of a guideline version and the beginning of the current subepisode. The variable was square-root transformed in the analyses. Each time a rule is revised, version age is reset to zero.
time_window: at the beginning of the current subepisode

description: Stock repurchase activity was measured as the dollar value of stock repurchase programs announced during a given year. The value of announced repurchase programs ranged from 0 (when no repurchase program was announced) to several billion dollars. The values for stock repurchase programs were highly skewed, so the authors logarithmically transformed them after adding 1 to each value. Only open market purchases were considered.
scale: dollar value of announced programs (log-transformed after adding 1)

description: Using a conventional measure, the authors assessed research intensity as the ratio of research and development expenditures to total sales. It was measured in the year prior to the measurement of stock repurchase announcements.
time_window: year prior to the announcement year

description: CEO stock option pay was measured as the proportion of total annual pay given in stock options. Stock options received during annual compensation grants were valued using the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) present-value method: the authors assumed that a firm's stock price appreciated at 5 percent per year over a ten-year period, subtracted the option price, and then discounted the potential gain at 5 percent per year.
time_window: year prior to the announcement year

description: The measure of performance expectations was the ratio of market value to book value, an accepted indicator of a firm's market-anticipated growth opportunities. This ratio measures how much value the market expects the firm to be able to extract from its pool of assets. Following others, the authors measured it as market value divided by book value at the beginning of a given year.

To gauge unmet performance expectations, the authors used the interaction of performance expectations at the beginning of a year and actual performance for the year. Actual firm stock performance was gauged as total stockholder returns: stock price appreciation plus dividends distributed, divided by beginning stock price. To test Hypotheses 5 and 6, an interaction term composed of these two measures was constructed.
time_window: beginning-of-year expectations and same-year actual performance

description: Dummy variable representing if the focal firm is foreign or domestic. Foreign subsidiaries were coded 1 and U.S. firms were coded 0. Foreign subsidiaries were identified from directories of German, Japanese, and British affiliated companies, and each foreign subsidiary has a matched U.S. firm in the same 4-digit SIC code and the same location.

The count of federal labor lawsuit judgments against a firm in 1995 and 1996. Only labor lawsuit judgments from courts with jurisdiction in the focal firm's specific location (Atlanta, Chicago, New York City, or San Francisco) were counted. Judgments were tracked using the Labor Library of Lexis-Nexis.

The count of state labor lawsuit judgments against a firm in 1995 and 1996. Only labor lawsuit judgments from courts with jurisdiction in the focal firm's specific location (Atlanta, Chicago, New York City, or San Francisco) were counted. Judgments were tracked using the Labor Library of Lexis-Nexis.

Dummy variable representing if the focal subsidiary has an American in charge of HR issues. Those using Americans were coded 1 and those using expatriates were coded 0. The variable was collected through the survey of foreign subsidiaries.

Dummy variable representing if the focal subsidiary's officer in charge of HR issues is an HR professional. If HR or Personnel is part of this officer's title, then the variable was coded 1; if not, the variable was coded 0. The variable was collected through the survey of foreign subsidiaries.

Dummy variable representing if the focal subsidiary has had an American top officer (titles vary from CEO, President, to Chairman). Subsidiaries with American top officers were coded 1 and subsidiaries with expatriate top officers were coded 0. The variable was collected through the survey of foreign subsidiaries.

Dummy variable reflecting the reporting chain of command for the focal subsidiary. Subsidiaries reporting directly to an affiliated U.S. operation were coded 1 and subsidiaries reporting directly to their parent were coded 0. The authors interpret this reporting variable as a measure of autonomy from the parent firm.
The total number of affiliated U.S. operations of the focal subsidiary's parent. Data came from the survey, which supplemented data on the number of affiliated U.S. offices.
The number of years the focal firm has operated in the particular metropolitan location, rounded to the nearest year.

Average annual salary for the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) occupational class 'Managerial Occupations' in the metropolitan area (MA), 1998-2000, in dollars. The authors retrieve the wages of the class 'management occupations' from the Occupational Employment Statistics of the U.S. BLS and assign to each city the 1998-2000 average wage of the U.S. MA where the city is located. The BLS definition of wages includes all the elements of the full compensation of the employee foreseen explicitly by the job contract, including individual bonuses mentioned in the contract and stock options explicitly mentioned in the initial job contract, but not collective bonuses offered on a nonindividual basis or stock options offered outside the contract.

Interquartile range (difference between the 75th and 25th percentiles) of the salary of the occupational class 'Managerial Occupations' in the metropolitan area, 1998-2000, in dollars. The 1998-2000 average of this range is used as a measure of the variability of the managerial salary. Among other things, this limits the potential effect of any dot.com fever bias, because the dot.com bubble occurred during approximately 10 months between June 1999 and March 2000.

Ratio (a/b) between (a) the citations made by the patents of firms in the city to other patents by unaffiliated assignees whose address is in the same city, and (b) the total citations of the patents of firms in the city. A patent is attributed to a city only if at least one of the inventors' addresses is in the same city of the assignee. To obtain the numerator, the citations to firms located outside the assignee's city are first excluded, and the self-citations (assignee's citations to its own patents) are then excluded from that subsample.

Share of scientists and engineers employed in the city who changed employer at least once in the previous year (average 1998-2000). For each city the authors calculate the average turnover experience (i.e., the share of mobile scientists) of all scientists and engineers, based on whether they change employers in the year before the survey and whether they remain in the same city, using the same eight occupation categories for scientists and engineers used by Kim and Marschke (2005).

Ratio between the total number of self-citations (i.e., citations to the same assignee) and the total citations made by the patents in the cities. A larger value denotes that a larger share of the knowledge produced in the city depends on previous knowledge produced within the same organization.

Pearson coefficient of skewness (mean minus median over standard deviation) of the employment distribution of the firms in the city, 1998-2000. It is computed from all the firms in the sample cities selected from the database Icarus of Bureau Van Dijk, which produces 10,662 firm-year observations, and it is an indicator of the skewness of the distribution that does not depend critically on the shape of the distribution itself. A larger value indicates the presence of some very large firms in the city compared to the median firm.
Not applicable.

variable_name: abnormal return on the day of the shareholder meeting
description: Abnormal returns are computed using the four-factor model of Carhart (1997), where the four factors are the market return, the size factor, the book-to-market factor and the momentum factor. The coefficients of the four-factor model are estimated by OLS using an estimation period of 200 trading days that starts 20 trading days prior to the shareholder meeting, and a stock must have at least 15 days with non-missing returns during that period. Abnormal returns provide an estimate of the impact of passing a long-term compensation proposal on shareholder value.

Return on assets is the ratio of operating income before depreciation to the book value of assets, obtained from Standard & Poor's Compustat. To mitigate the impact of outliers the measure is winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles of its empirical distribution. The dynamic RDD specification estimates its change in the year of the vote, the following year, and the average of the subsequent three years relative to the base period.
time_window: year of the vote (t), t+1, and the average of t+2 to t+4

description: Net profit margin is the ratio of operating income before depreciation to sales, obtained from Standard & Poor's Compustat. To mitigate the impact of outliers the measure is winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles of its empirical distribution. The dynamic RDD specification estimates its change in the year of the vote, the following year, and the average of the subsequent three years relative to the base period.
time_window: year of the vote (t), t+1, and the average of t+2 to t+4

description: Sales growth is the growth in sales from one fiscal year to the next, obtained from Standard & Poor's Compustat. To mitigate the impact of outliers the measure is winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles of its empirical distribution. The dynamic RDD specification estimates its change in the year of the vote, the following year, and the average of the subsequent three years relative to the base period.
time_window: year of the vote (t), t+1, and the average of t+2 to t+4

description: Investments in innovation are measured by R&D expenditures, computed as the ratio of R&D expenses to total assets (from Compustat). The ratio is winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles of its empirical distribution. The dynamic RDD specification estimates its change in the year of the vote, the following year, and the average of the subsequent three years relative to the base period.
time_window: year of the vote (t), t+1, and the average of t+2 to t+4

description: Stakeholder relationships are measured with the KLD-index obtained from the Kinder, Lydenberg, and Domini (KLD) database, which relies on independent rating experts to assess how well companies address the needs of their stakeholders. The composite index is constructed by adding up the number of KLD strengths along the dimensions employees, customers, the natural environment, and society at large (community and minorities). The dynamic RDD specification estimates its change in the year of the vote, the following year, and the average of the subsequent three years relative to the base period.
time_window: year of the vote (t), t+1, and the average of t+2 to t+4

description: An index of long-term orientation based on the organization's discourse, constructed through a textual analysis of the firms' 10-K filings obtained from the SEC EDGAR database. The authors count the number of keywords referring to the short term ('short run,' 'short-run,' 'short term,' 'short-term') and long term ('long run,' 'long-run,' 'long term,' 'long-term') and compute the LT-index as the ratio of the number of long-term keywords to the sum of long- and short-term keywords.

variable_name: Passage of a close-call long-term compensation shareholder proposal
description: Exogenous change in long-term incentives was proxied by an indicator for whether a shareholder proposal advocating long-term executive compensation passed the majority vote threshold, in a regression discontinuity around the threshold.

The total amount of funding in U.S. dollars pledged by backers to the project. The authors note that funding amount is a more refined measure of success or failure in fundraising on Kickstarter and has more practical implications for entrepreneurs. Due to skewness and its nonnegative nature, the natural log was taken before entering it into the analyses.

The number of backers who pledge money to the project, which captures the audience's decision to support the project. Due to skewness and its nonnegative nature, the natural log was taken before entering it into the analyses.

Each pitch video was thinsliced into frames lasting approximately one tenth of a second, and FaceReader calculated the intensity of joy for each frame based on the FACS coding rules, giving an objective displayed joy score for each frame with visible facial expressions. The original score ranged from 0 to 1 and was rescaled by multiplying by 10, so the score ranges from 0 to 10. The highest displayed joy score within all frames of a video was taken as the peak displayed joy.

The total length of time in seconds during which the entrepreneur's displayed joy reaches the peak level during the pitch. It was computed by first counting the number of video frames in which the displayed joy level reaches the highest level within a video, and then converting that frame count into seconds based on how long each frame lasts for that particular video.

The intensity of peak displayed joy within the beginning phase, defined as the first third partition of the pitch video. It was identified by partitioning each pitch video into three parts and taking the peak displayed joy score within the first partition.
time_window: first third of the pitch video

description: The intensity of peak displayed joy within the ending phase, defined as the last third partition of the pitch video. It was identified by partitioning each pitch video into three parts and taking the peak displayed joy score within the last partition.
time_window: last third of the pitch video

description: The intensity of peak displayed joy within the middle phase, defined as the remaining partition after the first and last thirds of the pitch video. It was identified by partitioning each pitch video into three parts and taking the peak displayed joy score within the middle partition.
time_window: middle third of the pitch video

description: The total length of time in seconds during which displayed joy reaches its peak level within the beginning phase, defined as the first third partition of the pitch video. A squared term of this variable was also entered in the analyses.
time_window: first third of the pitch video

description: The total length of time in seconds during which displayed joy reaches its peak level within the ending phase, defined as the last third partition of the pitch video. A squared term of this variable was also entered in the analyses.
time_window: last third of the pitch video

description: The total length of time in seconds during which displayed joy reaches its peak level within the middle phase, defined as the remaining partition of the pitch video. A squared term of this variable was also entered in the analyses.
time_window: middle third of the pitch video

variable_name: Novelty of the geographic location of investments
description: Rank-ordered dependent variable with four categories of increasing novelty: value 1 for an investment in the home country (The Netherlands); 2 for an investment in a foreign country where the firm had invested before; 3 for an investment in a new country in a familiar cultural block; and 4 for an investment in a new country and a new cultural block. A positive slope coefficient for an explanatory variable implies a positive effect on the novelty of the geographic location of investments.

TMT tenure is the number of years of membership of an individual in the TMT. Tenure diversity was computed in the conventional way using the coefficient of variation across TMT members. Diminishing returns from tenure diversity due to information overload were modeled by taking the log of this variable.

Measured using Blau's heterogeneity index, calculated as the reverse of the Herfindahl-Hirschman homogeneity index; H is the homogeneity index, S the percentage of TMT members with a dominant educational track i, and n the number of different educational backgrounds. Educational titles used are 'Drs' for university graduates in Economics and Social Sciences, including MBAs, 'Mr' for a university degree in Law, and 'Ir' for a university degree in Engineering; managers without a university degree were categorized as 'no degree'. The log of this variable was taken.

The operationalization of faultlines was based on Lau and Murnighan (1998) and on the age, tenure, and education type and level of team members; level of education was coded 0 for no university degree, 1 for university degree, and 2 for doctorate. A two-step approach was used: an objective procedure (latent cluster analysis, using both ratio- and nominal-scale data) to determine whether or not faultline situations existed in TMTs, i.e., whether subgroups could be identified, and in the second step Lau and Murnighan's qualitative procedure to distinguish between weak and strong faultlines. A dummy captures strong faultline settings.

The measure of common historical experience, TLAP, proposed by Carroll and Harrison (1998) to capture the overlap in tenure of team members as a proxy for their social interaction over time. It averaged pair-wise overlap in tenure for all possible pairs in the TMT, where N is the total number of pair-wise comparisons. The logarithmic transformation of TLAP was used to capture the diminishing effects of interaction between team members over time.

variable_name: TMT tenure diversity and educational diversity
description: TMT demographic diversity was measured by tenure diversity (coefficient of variation of years of TMT membership, logged) and educational diversity (Blau heterogeneity index over educational backgrounds, logged).

An index of corporate social performance constructed from the eight corporate social performance attributes rated consistently across the entire Standard and Poors 500 by KLD. Five attributes emphasizing key stakeholder relations (community relations, employee relations, environment, product characteristics, and treatment of women and minorities) are rated on scales ranging from -2 (major concerns) to neutral to +2 (major strength); three attributes (military contracting, nuclear power, and South Africa) are rated only from -2 (major concern) to 0 (neutral). A panel of three experts in the social issues arena used the simple multiattribute rating technique (SMART) to evaluate and trade off the eight attributes and construct a weighting scale; values from 0 to 100 representing the relative importance of each attribute were normalized and averaged across the panelists, and a weighted average CSP index was computed for each company. Raw CSP data were taken from KLD as of 1990.

variable_name: Return on assets, return on equity, return on sales
description: Firm financial performance (profitability) was measured using three accounting variables: return on assets, return on equity, and return on sales, providing a range of measures used to assess corporate financial performance by the investment community. All financial data were derived from COMPUSTAT tapes. Financial data from 1989 were used in the models that treated CSP as the dependent variable; profitability in 1991 was taken as the dependent variable and 1990 data were used for CSP and control variables in the models that treated profitability as the dependent variable.
time_window: 1989 in the CSP models; 1991 in the profitability models

description: A dummy-coded variable that takes the value of 1 if the venture paid a VDO client fee and 0 otherwise. The authors use the fee as an indicator of affiliation because the VDO scrutinizes new ventures and their founders before accepting them as a client.

A continuous variable that is a count of the number of other businesses in Oklahoma that the founders have owned or principally managed. Founder names and locations in the VDO's records were matched with business owners and principal managers listed in the Oklahoma file of the NETS database. The authors expect in-state experience would be most salient and observable to investors and thus serves as a reasonable proxy for managerial experience.

A single dummy-coded variable, equal to 1 for firms with products on the market and 0 otherwise, defined using information from the VDO's records regarding the active status of the venture and their stage of development.

A single dummy-coded variable, equal to 1 for firms located in commercial / non-residential areas and 0 otherwise. It was defined by matching address information in the VDO's records with publicly available real estate records.

A dichotomous variable equal to 1 if a new venture secured equity investment and 0 otherwise. The external investment it indicates includes venture capital, private equity, and angel investment and does not include founder equity, friends and family investment, debt financing, or government sources such as grants. Investment information was collected from initial contacts with the VDO, the VDO's annual surveys of client and non-client firms, tracking of investments by funding sources to which the VDO referred a client, and validation against major VC databases.

The number of M&As initiated by a focal firm in each year, capturing the firm's overall M&A activities. The acquisitions target both prior alliance partners and non-alliance partners in each electronics industry alliance network. The count is nonnegative and its variance exceeds its mean, which the authors give as the reason for using a negative binomial model rather than a Poisson or standard regression.

Closeness centrality is calculated for each firm from a symmetric (nondirectional) matrix of the yearly industry alliance network constructed with Ucinet 6, using the program's 'closeness centrality' command. The authors state the index with C'c(pk) as the closeness centrality for firm k, d(pi, pk) as the path distance between firm i and k, and n as the total number of firms in the network; the printed equation itself could not be read from the text. A five-year moving window is used to construct the network, so the window for 2001 is based on the cumulative alliances announced from 1997 to 2001.

The authors use Burt's (1992) measure of constraint, which captures the extent to which a firm's network is directly or indirectly concentrated via a single contact; a firm whose alliance partners all have one another as partners is highly constrained and has few structural holes. Following Soda et al. (2004), the value of constraint is multiplied by -1 in order to capture structural holes, the 'opposite' of constraint. A five-year moving window is used to construct the yearly industry alliance network.

The number of exploitation alliances formed by a firm in the five years leading to year t divided by the total number of alliances formed by that firm in the same five years. Alliances are classified by content-analyzing the SDC alliance description and background information: alliances focused on the discovery and development of new technology, such as R&D and technology alliances, are coded as exploration alliances, and alliances dealing with marketing and resource utilization, such as licensing, marketing, and supply alliances, are treated as exploitation alliances; alliances created for both purposes are coded as 0.5 exploration and 0.5 exploitation. For the China sample, alliance descriptions are taken from WIND and firms' Web sites and annual reports. Two Ph.D. students coded all the alliances independently with 95 percent intercoder reliability.
time_window: five years leading to year t

description: A dummy variable representing the degree of institutional development. The United States is treated as a developed institutional setting, coded institutional development = 1, and China as an underdeveloped institutional setting, coded institutional development = 0.

A chair appointment equation is first estimated at the individual outside-director level at IPO with a Tobit estimator, where chair appointment is the fraction of the number of chair positions an individual outside director holds divided by the total number of chair positions on the board. The degree of undervaluation or overvaluation is measured by the residuals from this equation, calculated as the difference between the true value and the predicted value of chair appointment; negative residuals indicate undervaluation and positive residuals indicate overvaluation. Spline functions are used: undervaluation is set as the value of the residuals when they are negative and as zero when they are positive. The individual-level undervaluation is then aggregated to the board level by taking the average of the individual-level undervaluation of undervalued directors.

The count of undervalued directors who were on the board at IPO and exited the focal firm within 3 years post-IPO. Exit dates are determined from proxy statements, annual reports, and the Boardex database and are triangulated across these sources when possible. The assessment of turnover levels does not distinguish between voluntary turnover (quits) and involuntary turnover (discharges).

The average number of board meetings from the IPO year to the third year post-IPO. The authors argue that averaging across 3 years is more appropriate than using the frequency of meetings in a particular year because the IPO year may have unusually frequent meetings and because director turnover is more likely to be a reaction to the board climate over time. The data are collected from firm prospectuses and annual reports.
time_window: IPO year to third year post-IPO

description: Coded as 1 if the CEO is also the founder of the firm; if not, it is coded as 0. The data were collected from the firm prospectuses.

Dichotomous variable distinguishing a lead founder who is an industry generalist from one who is an industry specialist. A lead founder was coded as an industry specialist if he or she always worked in the same industry as the IPO firm; otherwise the founder was coded as an industry generalist. Coding was based on the founder's resume in the IPO prospectus using the ten broad industry classes of the Industry Classification Benchmark, and three researchers coded the information.

Dichotomous variable distinguishing a lead founder who is a functional generalist from one who is a functional specialist. A lead founder was coded as a functional specialist if he or she always worked in the same function as his or her current role in the entrepreneurial venture; otherwise the founder was coded as a functional generalist. Functional categories were based on the Standard Occupational Classification Hierarchy of the Office of National Statistics in the United Kingdom.

Categorical variable classifying lead founders into three groups: full specialists (worked in the same industry and the same function), partial specialists (worked in the same function across industries or different functions in the same industry), and full generalists (worked across functions in various industries). Full specialists are the baseline, and the other two groups are dummy coded.

Offer price multiplied by the number of shares sold in the offering, log-transformed. It is the study's measure of funds raised at IPO and reflects public investors' interest in the venture, and it also indicates the value of the focal firm.
The proportion of a venture's equity held by venture capitalists at IPO. The measure captures the proportion of a venture's equity retained by venture capitalists at the time of the offering.

Randomly assigned experimental condition in which the lead founder presented in the prospectus and video pitch was an industry generalist (Conditions 3 and 4), contrasted with the industry specialist conditions (Conditions 1 and 2). The manipulation was checked with participants' perceptions of the lead founder's industry background on a continuum from 1 = industry generalist to 7 = industry specialist.

Randomly assigned experimental condition in which the lead founder presented in the prospectus and video pitch was a functional generalist (Conditions 2 and 4), contrasted with the functional specialist conditions (Conditions 1 and 3). The manipulation was checked with participants' perceptions of the lead founder's functional background on a continuum from 1 = generalist to 7 = specialist.

Randomly assigned condition manipulating the lead founder's profile: full specialist (Condition 1), industry specialist but functional generalist (Condition 2), functional specialist but industry generalist (Condition 3), or full generalist (Condition 4). Dummy variables for the two partial specialist conditions and for the full generalist condition relative to the full specialist benchmark were used in the regressions.

Five-item scale adapted from Sapienza and Korsgaard (1996), measured on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). Items: 'I trust the lead founder'; 'I believe the lead founder is inconsistent and unreliable' (reverse coded); 'When the main founder makes decisions that are different from decisions that I would make, I trust the lead founder has good reasons for making these decisions'; 'Taking all things into consideration, I'm satisfied with the lead founder'; and 'I believe the lead founder will be honest in dealings with me.' The five items converge with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.826.

variable_name: Funds raised at IPO (proportion of investors' available funds)
description: The proportion of funds available that the investor would recommend investing in the IPO, measured as a percentage. It is the experimental equivalent to funds raised at IPO: a higher proportion of funds from many prospective investors indicates more funds raised by the entrepreneurial venture at IPO.

Randomly assigned experimental condition in which the lead founder was an industry generalist (Conditions 3 and 4), contrasted with the industry specialist conditions (Conditions 1 and 2). A manipulation check at the end of the survey asked investors about their perceptions of the lead founder's breadth of experience on a continuum from 1 = generalist to 7 = specialist.

Randomly assigned experimental condition in which the lead founder was a functional generalist (Conditions 2 and 4), contrasted with the functional specialist conditions (Conditions 1 and 3). The manipulation check asked investors to rate the lead founder's functional breadth from 1 = generalist to 7 = specialist.

Randomly assigned condition manipulating the lead founder's profile into four groups: full specialist (Condition 1), industry specialist and functional generalist (Condition 2), functional specialist and industry generalist (Condition 3), and full generalist (Condition 4). Dummy variables for the partial specialist conditions and the full generalist condition relative to the full specialist benchmark were used in the regressions.

Twelve-item scale measured on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree), comprising the five items from Study 2 plus seven additional items adopted from Connelly et al. (2018): 'With confidence, I can rely on the lead founder to keep the promises he made'; 'I trust that the lead founder will consistently meet expectations'; 'I trust that the lead founder keeps investors' best interest in mind'; 'The lead founder will not use opportunities that arise to profit at my expense'; 'I don't think it is necessary to be cautious with the lead founder'; 'I believe the lead founder will be evenhanded in his dealings with investors'; and 'This is one of the most trustworthy lead founders with whom I could invest.' The Cronbach's alpha for the scale is 0.934.

variable_name: Funds raised at IPO (proportion of investors' available funds)
description: The proportion of available funds the investor would recommend investing in the entrepreneurial venture at IPO, captured as in Study 2.

variable_name: Perceived consistency of the lead founder
description: Three-item measure captured on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). The items are reverse scored: 'I am concerned that the lead founder will pivot the firm in new directions not necessarily desired by investors'; 'I am concerned that the lead founder will exit the business soon to pursue his latest idea'; 'I am concerned that the lead founder appears to have too many diverse business interests.' The Cronbach's alpha is 0.828.

variable_name: Concerns about the lead founder's competence
description: Three-item measure captured on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree): 'I am concerned that the lead founder does not have the domain expertise to grow this business'; 'I am concerned that the lead founder does not have the in-depth knowledge to grow this business'; 'I am concerned about the lead founder's inability to manage the expansion of this business.' The Cronbach's alpha of the scale is 0.893.

The chief executive officer was identified as the Chair of the Board of Directors (unless the Chair was listed as an outsider with other full-time responsibilities), the CEO, or the President in cases where no other individual was listed as Chair or CEO; in firms with both a chairperson and CEO, the chair was considered the more senior executive. CEO succession was coded as 1 for any year in which a new individual was installed in office, and 0 otherwise. Successors were also coded as internal promotions or external recruitment.
scale: 0/1 (1 = new individual installed as CEO that year)
time_window: yearly over each firm's life span

description: For each year of a firm's existence other than the first year, the membership of the executive team (not including the CEO) was compared with membership of the preceding year, with all executives down through the vice-president level counted as team members. Executive-team change was calculated as the percentage of the team to change in the particular year. In Table 4, executive-team change is categorized as either high or low based on a median split.
scale: percentage of the executive team changed
time_window: yearly over each firm's life span

description: Strategy was defined in terms of products and markets, and changed when a company added or deleted a major product line and/or entered or exited a market category. Structure was examined through changes in distributions of executive-team titles coded as functional, product divisional, market divisional or geographical divisional; structure changed for any year during which titles of any one divisional category reached 25% of total titles or dropped below this threshold. Change in formal control practices was coded when two or more of inventory controls, management information systems, manufacturing controls and formal incentives were initiated or changed. Two coders working independently defined a reorientation as having occurred only when strategy, structure and formal control all changed within a two-year period; for nonpublic firms, reorientations were coded 1 where strategy and structure both changed.
time_window: year-by-year over each firm's life span

description: Organization performance was measured by return on assets (ROA), measured yearly for each firm. The percentage change in ROA between the year of succession and two years subsequent to succession was utilized to explore effects of succession and reorientation on organization performance. A two-year interval was employed to provide a time period long enough to permit changes to take place, but short enough not to be confounded by other factors.
time_window: from the year of succession to two years subsequent

variable_name: Historical performance categories (consistently high performing, moderately effective, failing)
description: Organizations were classified into three historical performance categories by comparing firm ROA to industry-average ROA for each year of a company's life. A firm was categorized as consistently high performing if its ROA was greater than industry-average ROA for all years, excluding the firm's startup and allowing for at most one outlier year of low performance later in the company's life; fifteen firms were so categorized. Six failing organizations performed below industry average ROA for the majority of their years of operation, and the remaining seventeen organizations were categorized as moderately effective firms.
scale: three categories (consistently high performing, moderately effective, failing)
time_window: each year of a company's life

variable_name: Internal promotion versus external recruitment of the new CEO
description: Successors were coded as internal promotions or external recruitment. A successor was coded as externally recruited if he or she held a position outside the organization less than one year prior to being appointed CEO; otherwise the new CEO was coded as an insider.
time_window: at the time of CEO appointment

description: A matrix was created with six product performance criteria across the top and a list of the components relevant to a particular technology down the left-hand side. Respondents ranked the components according to their importance for influencing each performance criterion in turn, and components a firm does not use were left blank, so the rankings indicate both the number of components used and the equality of their importance. A concentration ratio was computed for the set of components used to influence each of the six performance criteria, the six ratios were averaged, and the average was subtracted from one to obtain the measure of complexity. Cronbach's alpha is 0.89.

Tacitness was measured as the inverse of a formulator's ability to explain and predict the relationships between components, design choices, and product performance; knowledge that cannot be verbalized remains tacit, and an inability to predict what to do to manipulate performance indicates a lack of causal understanding. Respondents reported their ability to predict which component varieties and which amounts of a component to use, and to explain why particular varieties and amounts produce specific performance characteristics. Cronbach's alpha is 0.93.

Resource specificity captures the extent to which what a firm knows about product components is specific to a customer, application, or component varieties. The items ask whether knowing how the physical properties of a backbone polymer affect adhesive performance helps the formulator manipulate the same properties of other backbone polymers, and whether knowing how one type of component affects performance when combined with that backbone polymer helps determine how to use those components with other polymers. Cronbach's alpha is 0.79.

Design specificity is measured as the extent to which a firm acquires specialized architectural knowledge by tailoring its adhesive formulas for individual customers and applications. The two items ask whether the firm exploits the same physical properties of a backbone polymer and uses the same component varieties to improve adhesive performance regardless of the application, so high agreement indicates low design specificity and the items are reverse-worded relative to the construct. Cronbach's alpha is 0.75.

The number of months it typically takes competitors to replicate major performance improvements. Respondents referred to their three largest application areas by sales revenue for a given technology when providing responses, and the variable can be treated as an event count.

A second measure of persistence for major improvements, created by subtracting Months to Develop from Months to Imitate, so that the measure adjusts Months to Imitate for a firm's own development time in the same way the items for minor improvements do.

Two seven-point Likert scale items asking whether it usually takes competitors longer to replicate a firm's product improvements than it takes the firm to develop them; the second item is worded in the reverse fashion.

Cumulative number of projects involving computer operations, automatic teller machines, bank/smart cards, telecommunication and point of sales, counted from the Predicast Index from 1977 up to the event. Only actual activities and financial commitments, and not intended or surmised trials, were included in the counting. The scores represent the cumulative number of involvements up to the year of innovation, and an innovating firm was deleted from the data set in the year of innovation.

Total dollar investment in systems and equipment divided by company assets, taken as a three-year average from a time series of annual reports. The authors treat increased investment in systems and equipment as signalling cumulative skills and absorptive capacity, i.e. learning by using. The measure captures a broad range of hardware, including not only computers and telecommunication equipment but also office furniture and typewriters.

Cumulative number of interorganizational actions, including licensing and contract agreements, joint ventures, purchases of systems, and mergers and acquisitions, counted from the Predicast Index up to the year of the event. The links were also specified by type of partner, such as computer hardware firms, software houses, telecommunication firms, banks, financial services, news/publishing firms and retail/merchandising firms.

Cumulative number of technological links divided by the total number of exchange relationships, where exchange relationships include licensing and contract agreements, joint ventures, mergers and acquisitions and systems purchases involving computer and telecommunication know-how, counted from the Predicast Index.

The dependent variable is the innovation event and was scored as a zero-one for each firm-year: coded 1 if the organization realized home banking in that year and 0 if it did not. Once home banking had been installed, it contributed no more observations to the data pool. The list of home banking firms was assembled from directories and surveys and verified through telephone calls, Predicast listings and annual reports.

Among innovators the dependent variable flags the form of implementation, internal versus external. Two dichotomous dependent variables were created, one coded 1 for internal implementation and 0 otherwise and one coded 1 for external implementation and 0 otherwise, and the event history analysis was performed separately for the two types of events. Because only six of the 49 banks were involved in a joint venture, they were lumped together with banks that implemented the innovation through licensing agreements or long-term contracts.

variable_name: Investment expenditure, systems and equipment (second information technology variable)
description: Placeholder removed; see m_tech_investment.

The FTC report recorded acquisitions of firms greater than $10 million in assets and characterized them by type; the authors coded product extension and conglomerate acquisitions as diversifying acquisitions. For the count models, each firm-year observation was assigned the number of diversifying acquisitions completed by the firm in that year. For the binary models, each firm-year observation was coded 1 if the firm completed a diversifying acquisition in that year and coded 0 otherwise.

One dummy variable indicates whether CEOs were listed in a social register and/or attended an exclusive secondary school, with exclusive secondary school designations taken from Domhoff (1970). Data on chief executive officers and presidents were updated annually, with the likelihood of acquisition in a particular year considered a function of data collected for the previous year.

One dummy variable indicates whether CEOs were Jewish. CEO data were updated annually, with the likelihood of acquisition in a particular year considered a function of data collected for the previous year.

One dummy variable indicates whether the CEO's firm was headquartered in the South or West. Data on chief executive officers and presidents were updated annually, with the likelihood of acquisition in a particular year considered a function of data collected for the previous year.

One dummy variable indicates whether CEOs were members of at least one of the 40 most exclusive social clubs in America, with exclusive club designations taken from Domhoff (1970). The authors note that an alternative measure that tallied the number of clubs to which CEOs belonged produced substantively identical results.

Count of the sent interlocks each corporation maintained with other firms identified by Fortune magazine as being among the largest 500 industrials in any year between 1962 and 1975. Sent interlocks are created when a corporation's managers sit on another firm's board of directors. Measurements of interlocking directorates were updated biannually at the end of 1962, 1964, and 1966.

Count of the received interlocks each corporation maintained with other firms identified by Fortune magazine as being among the largest 500 industrials in any year between 1962 and 1975. Received interlocks are created by outside directors principally affiliated with other industrial firms. Counts were updated biannually at the end of 1962, 1964, and 1966.

Count of the neutral interlocks each corporation maintained with other firms identified by Fortune magazine as being among the largest 500 industrials in any year between 1962 and 1975. Neutral interlocks are created by outside directors sitting on the boards of firms with which they are not principally affiliated. Counts were updated biannually at the end of 1962, 1964, and 1966.

One dummy variable indicates whether CEOs possessed an undergraduate degree from an elite college or university, with elite designations taken from Useem and Karabel (1986). CEO data were updated annually, with the likelihood of acquisition in a particular year considered a function of data collected for the previous year.

One dummy variable indicates whether CEOs possessed an M.B.A. from an elite graduate school of business, with elite designations taken from Useem and Karabel (1986). Elite business schools included Columbia University, Dartmouth College, Harvard University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Northwestern University, Stanford University, University of California-Berkeley, University of California-Los Angeles, University of Chicago, University of Michigan, and the University of Pennsylvania.

Stock ownership data were collected primarily for 1964; the authors recorded the percentage of outstanding common stock greater than 3 percent held by a group of individuals related by kinship or partnership. Three ownership variables were computed according to whether the owning group was represented in the CEO position, represented in other top management positions, or were outsiders who were typically represented on the board of directors. The authors argue these data provide reliable estimates of ownership concentration throughout the period because major non-institutional stock ownership positions are highly stable over time.

The ownership group variables record the percentage of outstanding common stock greater than 3 percent held by related individuals, distinguished by whether the owners were represented in the CEO position, in other top management positions, or were outsiders. The moderation hypothesis compares the strength of the negative ownership effect between owners represented in top management and other owners.

Percentage of outstanding common stock greater than 3 percent held by related individuals who were outsiders, typically represented on the board of directors rather than in top management. Used as the comparison category for judging whether the negative ownership effect was strongest or weakest when owners were represented in top management.

variable_name: Proportion of TMT upstream employment affiliations
description: Employment affiliations of the TMT were assessed by manually identifying and classifying the last five years of the managing officers' employment and board memberships as listed in the firms' final prospectuses. The proportion was measured as the total number of TMT members with at least one affiliation with a prominent research organization divided by top management team size. An academic institution was classified as prominent if it appeared as one of the top 10 in any of the listed disciplines for that IPO year; nationally based government institutions such as the NIH and non-university research institutions with a high ratio of grant money per employee were added.
time_window: last five years of employment; indices tied as closely as possible to the year the firm went public

variable_name: Proportion of TMT horizontal employment affiliations
description: The number of affiliations that members of a firm's TMT had to prominent biotechnology firms through employment and/or board memberships, divided by TMT size. Prominent biotechnology companies were those on the list of worldwide revenues for the top 30 biotechnology companies in each of the years 1990-96; the 1990 rankings were used to classify affiliations as prominent from 1979 through 1989 and the 1990-96 ranking was used year by year thereafter. A total of 38 companies were coded as prominent.
time_window: last five years of employment; rankings by IPO year

variable_name: Proportion of TMT downstream employment affiliations
description: The number of affiliations that TMT members had to prominent pharmaceutical and/or healthcare institutions through prior employment and/or board memberships, divided by TMT size. Prominence was determined from yearly lists of the top pharmaceutical and healthcare organizations by sales, based on the top 30 U.S. organizations from 1979 to 1987 and the top 30 U.S. and international organizations from 1988 to 1996, supplemented with major private or European/Japanese companies listed in PharmaBusiness. A total of 56 pharmaceutical/healthcare companies were considered prominent.
time_window: last five years of employment; rankings by IPO year

description: Measured two ways. First, a variation of the Herfindahl-Hirschman index in which H is the measure of heterogeneity or range and p is the percentage of individuals who have affiliations with prominent institutions in each of the three categories; the formula itself is not readable in the text as provided. Second, a count, 0 to 3, of the number of affiliation categories (upstream, horizontal, and downstream) covered by the career experiences of each firm's TMT. The count measure is the one reported.
time_window: last five years of employment; tied as closely as possible to the IPO year

description: Set to 1 if the individual holding the position of Chief Scientific Officer (or equivalent, such as VP of Research) had worked as a CSO or equivalent in a healthcare-related (biotechnology or pharmaceutical) company in the past, and 0 otherwise. Prior research positions held in universities or government health institutions were coded 0.
time_window: prior career, evaluated at the time of the IPO

description: Set to 1 if the individual holding the position of Chief Financial Officer (or equivalent) had worked as a CFO or equivalent in a pharmaceutical or biotechnology company in the past, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: prior career, evaluated at the time of the IPO

description: Set to 1 if the CEO had held a CEO position in a pharmaceutical or biotechnology firm in the past, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: prior career, evaluated at the time of the IPO

description: The prestige of the lead underwriter as measured by an index developed by Carter and Manaster (1990) and updated by Carter, Dark, and Singh (1998), based on investment banks' positions in the tombstone announcements of IPOs in Investment Dealer's Digest or the Wall Street Journal. Scores range from 0, indicating lowest prestige, to 9, indicating highest prestige; the mean score in the dataset was 7.63. The name of the lead investment bank was obtained from the front page of the final prospectuses; information was available for all but 25 of the underwriters in the dataset.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Institutional investors were identified from the CDA/Spectrum Institutional Ownership Database, which reverse-compiles the form 13-F filings that institutions must submit quarterly, for the first report after the IPO date; the number of institutional investors investing in the firm was determined, along with the percentage of available shares each held. Investors were then qualified using Bushee's coding scheme, which classifies institutional investors by year into categories based on portfolio turnover and diversification; dedicated institutional investors have low portfolio turnover and low diversification strategies. The total number of dedicated institutional investors was used as the primary dependent measure.
time_window: first report post the IPO date

variable_name: TMT employment affiliations and role backgrounds
description: TMT composition was measured by the proportions of TMT employment affiliations with upstream, horizontal and downstream prominent institutions, diversity of those affiliations, and CSO, CFO and CEO background dummies.

Annual count of nanotechnology patents applied for by the firm. Patent data come from the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). Nanotechnology patents are identified using the USPTO's classification number (977).

Number of new U.S. patent classes that a focal firm entered in the previous three years. A firm enters a new technology class when it applies for a patent in a class in which it has not patented in the previous five years. The square of this variable tests the nonlinear relationship.

Variance of technological distance between a focal firm and all its partners. Technological distance is computed using Jaffe's measure of technological similarity, calculated longitudinally from patent class distributions. The alliance portfolio in year t-1 includes partners from years t-3, t-2 and t-1.
time_window: alliance portfolio year t-1, including partners from t-3 to t-1

description: Number of scientific articles published by the firm along with at least one university scientist in year t-1. Data come from the Thomson Reuters ISI Web of Science. The square of this variable tests diminishing marginal returns.

Number of semiconductor patents citing scientific articles applied for by the focal firm in year t-1, assuming that each such prior patent indicates prior exploration of scientific knowledge. The square of this variable tests diminishing marginal returns.

Forty-eight questions using a 7-point scale asked respondents to assess the level of hostility, dynamism and complexity in each of eight environmental segments rather than for the environment as a whole. The complexity dimension was measured by the heterogeneity and diversity of these elements in the environment. Factor analysis retained two factors per environmental dimension, and the four segments loading on the first factor (regulation, competition, international and technology) were aggregated into the variable COMPLEX.

Dynamism was assessed with the same 7-point questions across the eight environmental segments and measured by the variability and predictability of these elements. Factor analysis retained two factors per environmental dimension, and the four segments loading on the first factor (regulation, competition, international and technology) were aggregated into the variable DYNAMIC.

Hostility was assessed with the same 7-point questions across the eight environmental segments and measured by the importance and availability of resources controlled by different environmental elements. Factor analysis retained two factors per environmental dimension, and the four segments loading on the first factor (regulation, competition, technology and supplier) were aggregated into the variable HOSTILE.

Fifteen questions using a 7-point response format approximated the five dimensions of strategic orientation, namely Analysis, Defensiveness, Futurity, Riskiness and Proactiveness. Exploratory factor analysis using Promax rotation retained three factors, and confirmatory factor analysis showed the Proactiveness, Futurity and Riskiness dimensions had factor loadings of 0.93, 0.94 and 0.91, indicating that these three strategic dimensions are highly convergent. These dimensions were combined into the strategic orientation variable PROSPECT.
From the same fifteen 7-point strategic orientation questions, the Analysis dimension loaded on a factor of its own and was retained as the single-dimension strategic orientation variable ANALYSIS.

From the same fifteen 7-point strategic orientation questions, the Defensiveness dimension loaded on a factor of its own and was retained as the single-dimension strategic orientation variable DEFENSE.

Dependent variable of the first multiple regression equation, described by the authors as overall performance. It comes from the five questions asking managers to estimate how their firm compares to close competitors on after-tax return on total assets, after-tax return on total sales, total sales growth, overall performance and success, and competitive position, using a 5-point scale running from bottom 20 percent to top 20 percent. The text does not state in prose how the five items were combined into PERFORM.

Dependent variable of the second multiple regression equation, which the authors describe as profitability. It is drawn from the five relative-performance questions (after-tax return on total assets, after-tax return on total sales, total sales growth, overall performance and success, and competitive position) answered on a 5-point scale from bottom 20 percent to top 20 percent. The text does not state in prose how the items were combined into PROFIT.

Dependent variable of the third multiple regression equation, which in turn was measured by total sales growth and market share relative to close competitors. These come from the five relative-performance questions answered on a 5-point scale from bottom 20 percent to top 20 percent. The text does not state in prose the exact aggregation rule.

Strategic orientation was measured by fifteen 7-point questions approximating Venkatraman's five dimensions (analysis, defensiveness, futurity, riskiness, proactiveness). Factor analysis retained three orientations used as variables: PROSPECT, ANALYSIS and DEFENSE.

Narrative distinctiveness is built from latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic modeling of each listing's narrative, which comprises the listing's name, a summary of the accommodation offering, and a description of the accommodation space. A separate topic model with 25 topics was estimated for each observation period. A listing's narrative distinctiveness is the sum over all 25 topics of the absolute distance between the weight of a topic in the listing's narrative and the category's average weight for that topic at the time; a value of 0 indicates that the listing's narrative draws on all topics with exactly the same weights as the prototypical narrative in its category at the time. Category averages were calculated based on all available listings in the category, not only those included in the regression sample.

Category distinctiveness is measured from categories' prototypical amenities (56 amenity types observed during the observation period). Each category-period is represented as a probability vector of amenities based on the relative share of listings in that category offering each amenity at the time. The cosine distance between two categories is calculated over all 56 amenities, and a given category's category distinctiveness is the median distance between the focal category and each of the other 44 categories; a high level implies that the prototypical amenities of the category substantially deviate from the prototypical amenities of other categories.

Price premium is calculated by subtracting the average price per night in a listing's neighborhood at a given time from the listing's price per night at that time, and dividing the result by the standard deviation of the price per night in the neighborhood at that time. Prices were standardized within each neighborhood using Airbnb's classification of neighborhoods and within each observation time, which also nets out seasonal price fluctuations. A price premium of 0 indicates a price that aligns with the neighborhood average, and 1 indicates a price one standard deviation above the neighborhood average.
scale: 0 = neighborhood average price at the time; 1 = one standard deviation above the neighborhood average

description: The number of 'backward' citations to prior patents made by the licensed university patent. Following Lanjouw and Schankerman (2001), the authors treat this as a measure of technological maturity: in less developed technological areas, with less prior art to cite, there is likely to be greater uncertainty regarding the commercial potential of patented inventions, whereas a greater number of prior art citations indicates a more derivative invention and less uncertainty.

The mean citation weight of the firm's patents that are in the same primary patent class as the university patent under consideration. Each patent in the firm's portfolio is weighted by the number of forward citations it received, normalized by the mean number of forward citations to all patents issued in the same year and in the same primary (3-digit) USPTO technology class, which controls for right-side truncation bias and for differences in the propensity to patent across fields. A squared term, Expertise squared, is included in the option submodel to allow for decreasing returns.
time_window: patents applied for 1975-1998; forward citations through 1998

description: The citation-weighted share of the firm's patent portfolio at the time of the licensing decision that is assigned to the same primary patent class as the class of the licensed patent. The numerator is the citation-weighted sum of the firm's issued patents applied for within six years at the time of the licensing decision that are in the same primary patent class as the university patent, and the denominator is the citation-weighted sum of all patents issued to the firm applied for by that date. A squared term, Focus squared, is included in both licensing submodels to allow for decreasing returns.
time_window: six years prior to the licensing decision

description: Discrete dependent variable of the nested logit coded 1, 2, 3, or 4, corresponding to the licensing alternative chosen by the firm: secrecy agreement only, secrecy agreement plus exclusive license, secrecy agreement plus option, or secrecy agreement plus option plus exclusive license. Panel A of the model estimates the probability that the firm takes an option prior to making its licensing decision, based on the 457 option outcomes.

Discrete dependent variable of the nested logit for the licensing choice: whether the firm licenses or rejects the technology. Panel B reports the license-or-reject choice for the 400 licensing decisions made when an option was not taken, and Panel C reports the license-or-reject choice for the 57 licensing decisions made after an option was taken.

The binary variable state election takes a value of 1 during election years for state governor and 0 otherwise. The theory suggests that the state (gubernatorial) election is the relevant election because state elections determine the government leaders who oversee the SOEs in question. The models also include a variable for municipal (i.e., local mayoral) election years so that the omitted category represents non-election years. Election years are the years in which the relevant election took place.

Return on sales (ROS), i.e., operating profit margin, calculated as net income before interest and taxes over sales. It is a commonly used measure that reflects contemporaneous performance over the short run. To reduce distortions in the analyses, the dependent variables were trimmed at the 1 and 99 percent regions and the sample was restricted to non-missing observations on both dependent variables.

The workforce at the utility level, defined as the total employment at the utility, measured in logarithmic scale. There is significant precedent for using this measure in research on political cycles and firm behavior.
