The variable was trimmed at the 1 and 99 percent regions together with the other dependent variable, and the sample was restricted to non-missing observations on both dependent variables.

Constructed using micro-level household data from the 2000 Brazilian Population Census: the average income per capita of each municipality, in logarithmic scale, reverse coded to reflect the level of poverty in the municipality. The variable varies across municipalities but is constant over time. Community information collected in 2000, prior to the beginning of the sampling window, was used to avoid the possibility of reverse causality.

Binary variable that takes a value of 1 if water service is provided by a state-owned enterprise that has admitted private investors as minority shareholders, and 0 otherwise. Private investment in SOEs has typically occurred through public listing and, in most cases, conceded the appointment of independent external members to the board of directors. During the sample period, private investors in these SOEs were minority shareholders, and the state remained the controlling shareholder.

Binary variable that takes a value of 1 if water service is provided by a state-owned enterprise and 0 otherwise. The comparison group includes private firms and local waterworks departments, which make a good comparison group because electoral and civil service laws restrict hiring and nominations at departments before elections, the Fiscal Responsibility Law constrained municipal governments' ability to balloon employment and fiscal deficits, and departments are less likely to be influenced by state elections.

Log employment at the organization included as an additional independent variable in the model with return on sales as the dependent variable, following prior mediation work. It is used to assess whether employment mediates the relationship between state elections and financial performance.

Dichotomous variable set to 1 if the client relationship dissolved in that year. A relationship is coded as dissolved the first year the advertising firm no longer lists the client account in its Red Books record. If a relationship did not dissolve in the observation period (2000-2003) or if data were not available, the relationship was considered censored.

Relationship duration is used as the measure of relational embeddedness: the length of the relationship in years from its start year to 2000, the year of the acquisition, or as of the year 2000 for observations in the control sample. The start year was coded as the first year in which the agency listed the client in its Red Books record, gathered by consulting archives of the Red Books for each year dating back to 1980 or the next earliest available year. For relationships for which the start year could not be determined, the start year was set as the first year in which data were available, and an indicator of relationship duration truncation was included as a control variable.

A time-varying measure of the change in the number of client accounts with the same primary (four-digit) U.S. SIC code in each year in the advertising firm's portfolio. It is defined as the count of clients in the same SIC in the current year minus the count of clients in the same SIC in the previous year, with the baselines for the first year being the counts of clients in the acquirer and target separately and, for each subsequent year, the prior year's count for the merged firm. The measure was updated annually and used in lagged form, so that the change in competitive overlap in the current year predicts dissolution in the following year.

The total amount of grants given to charity either through a foundation or directly by the corporation, recorded for each firm-year. The variable was log-transformed to correct for skewed values. Data were collected from the National Directory of Corporate Giving for the years 1981 to 2007, which is available in even-numbered years; because the regression models used lagged independent variables, the first year of usable observations for the dependent variable was 1982.

A firm's institutional equivalents are its community peers that were also simultaneously its industry peers, where community peers are Fortune 1000 firms headquartered in the same core-based statistical area as the focal firm and industry peers are Fortune 1000 firms in the same two-digit SIC code. Firms were classified by whether they had at least one such overlapping peer; the presence versus absence of institutional equivalents defines the two subsamples used to test H1 and H2.

The average corporate philanthropic contributions of the focal firm's institutional equivalents, defined as its community peers that were also simultaneously its industry peers. The values came from the National Directories of Corporate Giving and were log-transformed. This variable was lagged by two years because CPC data were available only in even years.

Data on the average CPC of industry peers in a given year came from the National Directories of Corporate Giving and were log-transformed. Industry peers were defined as Fortune 1000 firms in the same two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code as the focal firm. This variable was lagged by two years because CPC data were available only in even years.

The average corporate philanthropic contributions of community peers, defined as Fortune 1000 firms headquartered in the same core-based statistical area (CBSA) as the focal firm, calculated for each year and log-transformed. This variable was lagged by two years because CPC data were available only in even years.

Defined as the absolute value of the difference between industry peers' giving and community peers' giving, capturing the degree of dissimilarity between industry and community peers' levels of philanthropy. The variable was standardized to ease the interpretation of the regression results involving interaction terms.
time_window: lagged two years (built from the peer giving variables)

description: Firm size measured as sales revenue, obtained from Compustat. The variable was standardized to ease the interpretation of the regression results involving interaction terms.
Financial performance measured as return on assets (ROA), obtained from Compustat. The variable was standardized to ease the interpretation of the regression results involving interaction terms.

A five-item Likert scale adapted from prior studies, including Constant et al. (1996) and Lakhani and von Hippel (2003). The items considered customer perceptions related to providing prompt peer support, being a responsible and contributing community member, offering constructive ideas to peer customers, and interacting in a helpful manner. Items were measured on a five-point Likert scale with 1 = strongly disagree and 5 = strongly agree. Composite reliability is reported as 0.82.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: A two-item scale adapted from Wasko and Faraj (2005) and Lakhani and von Hippel (2003) was used to measure expectations of self-image enhancement. Respondents indicated the extent to which they believe they can derive each benefit from participation in the online forum, on a multi-item five-point Likert scale. Composite reliability is reported as 0.76.

A four-item scale adapted from Dholakia et al. (2004) and Hertel et al. (2003) was used to measure expectations of expertise enhancement. Respondents indicated the extent to which they believe they can derive each benefit from participation in the online forum. Composite reliability is reported as 0.78.

A four-item scale created to measure customers' perceived sense of partnership with the company in product innovation. The scale items, based on prior studies (Bstieler 2006, Jassawalla and Sashittal 1998), reflected the extent of customers' understanding of the innovation goals and outcomes and of how the firm views or uses their contributions. Composite reliability is reported as 0.83.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Customers' identification with the customer community was measured using an existing seven-item scale from Choi (2000) that in turn draws on a scale of McCroskey et al. (1975) on perceived homophily. The items related to how closely the customer perceived other community members to be similar to himself or herself, to think like he or she does, etc., and are presented as bipolar response options. Composite reliability is reported as 0.93.

Customers' identification with the company was measured using an existing scale from Bergami and Bagozzi (2000), which has been used in prior studies (Ahearne et al. 2005). Respondents specified the degree of overlap between their own personal identity (self-image) and the company's identity by marking the appropriate box on an 8-point scale.

Data on customer postings in the online forums obtained through the Netscan database, covering postings made by the respondents in the two weeks following the completion of the survey. Content analysis was performed on all 1,339 postings so identified to determine whether they related to a customer query on product usage or a product-usage suggestion/comment, a product improvement suggestion or new product idea, or other issues. One of the authors and an expert independently coded the postings; the intercoder reliability, evaluated using Cohen's kappa, was 0.86. For each study subject, the number of postings in the first category was adopted as the measure of his or her contribution to the community.
time_window: two weeks following completion of the survey

description: Data on customer postings in the online forums obtained through the Netscan database, covering postings made by the respondents in the two weeks following the completion of the survey. Content analysis classified each posting; the postings coded as a product improvement suggestion or new product idea were used. For each study subject, the number of postings in this category was adopted as the measure of his or her contribution to the company.
time_window: two weeks following completion of the survey

description: An aggregate narcissism score assigned to a CEO following the Chatterjee and Hambrick (2011) method for unobtrusive measures, based on four indicators: the prominence of the CEO's photograph in the company's annual report, the prominence of the CEO's name in press releases relative to the rest of the TMT, the CEO's relative cash pay relative to the next-highest paid TMT member, and the CEO's relative non-cash pay relative to the next-highest paid TMT member. The variable was operationalized as an average score of these indicators from the second and third years of tenure (t + 1 and t + 2) for each CEO.
time_window: second and third years of CEO tenure (t + 1 and t + 2)

description: All board discussion focused on firm risk-taking was isolated using a list of risk-taking words and phrases highlighted with NVivo, and two coders identified how many sentences surrounding these words were relevant to the risk-taking discussion. The risk-taking text was then analyzed with LIWC positive and negative affect libraries by board-year. The variable was computed as the number of positive affect words divided by the sum of the number of positive affect words and the number of negative affect words.
time_window: by board-year over the fiscal year

description: Risk-taking was calculated by collecting data on three forms of spending typically identified as having uncertain returns: R&D, capital expenditures, and acquisitions. Because these indicators are often used as substitutes and using only one paints a partial picture of risky outlays, all three forms of spending were aggregated into one sum, and the natural log of that sum was used to calculate risk-taking for a given firm.
Duality was measured dichotomously. Firms employing CEOs who also chaired the board were coded as 1, and firms separating the responsibilities as 0.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if patent i is added to a pool in year t and 0 otherwise. Its coefficient captures the net effect of inclusion in a pool on the subsequent average yearly citation rate of a typical patent. The variable is used in patent-year estimations that also include patent and year fixed effects.

Dummy equal to 1 if in year t there exists at least one pool patent to which technology subclass c is assigned as its primary technology subclass. It captures when a technology subclass is first affected by a pool. Its coefficient captures the impact of the seven modern pools on the total number of patents in technology subclasses associated with them.

Log-transformed number of citations (plus 1) received by patent i in year t, excluding any self-citations by the owner of patent i to capture the impact of the pool on technological development by other parties. The nonlinear effect of patent age on yearly citation frequency is captured by a set of five dummies from a five-degree polynomial age function.

Log-transformed number of patents (plus 1) in technology subclass c in year t. The total amount of patenting in a technology subclass proxies for the total amount of innovative activity in that technology subclass.

The share of vertically integrated firms that cite patent i in year t. It is the dependent variable in the estimation of whether the share of vertically integrated firms citing a patent declines after the patent is added to a pool. For the MPEG-2 analyses the share is computed only for the entities citing MPEG-2 pool patents and the patents matched to them.

The ratio of startups to diversifying entrants citing patent i in year t. It is the dependent variable used to estimate whether follow-on innovations by new entrants are disproportionately developed by startups after the formation of modern pools.

New entrants in a particular upstream technology market are the firms granted a patent for the first time in any given technology subclass. Startups are new entrants that have never patented before; diversifying entrants are those that have previously patented in other technology subclasses. Upstream technology markets are defined at the level of technological subclasses defined by the USPTO.

A firm is marked as vertically integrated in a given year if there is any indication from publicly available information about its activities and products that it manufactured downstream products in that year. Nonintegrated entities include firms that do not manufacture any downstream products, universities, nonprivate research labs, and independent inventors not associated with any institution. This status was collected only for the entities that cited MPEG-2 pool patents and the matched control patents for MPEG-2, covering 695 entities.

Dummy for the 70 publicly listed firms that had cited the MPEG-2 pool patents before the pool's formation, interacted with a dummy for the years after the formation of the MPEG-2 pool in 1997. The interaction equals 1 for vertically integrated firms after the formation of the MPEG-2 pool and 0 otherwise. The sample comprises 40 vertically integrated firms and 30 nonintegrated, upstream firms.

Log-transformed total number of successful patents (plus 1) applied by firm f in year t, with patents assigned to the firm and its subsidiaries identified using Delphion, the NBER patent database, and other public sources. Firm fixed effects control for time-invariant firm characteristics and year fixed effects control for macro trends affecting all firms similarly. Because the sample is restricted to publicly listed firms, the change in patenting rate can be interpreted as a change in R&D investment direction rather than a decrease or increase in total R&D investment, sales, or size.

Dichotomous indicator of the experimental manipulation of directors' concern. Participants were primed with instructions stating that studies show that when the board votes, an independent director should mainly consider the impact of the vote on his or her public reputation, and should avoid sacrificing his or her public reputation for other purposes. The variable took a value of 1 if the participant was assigned to the public reputation concern condition and a value of 0 if the participant was assigned to the director labor market concern condition.
scale: 1 = public reputation concern condition; 0 = director labor market concern condition

description: Dichotomous indicator of the experimental manipulation of directors' concern. Participants randomized to this condition were primed with instructions stating that studies show that when the board votes, an independent director should mainly consider the impact of the vote on his or her prospects in the director labor market, and should carefully consider whether the vote will increase, maintain, or decrease future opportunities to be reappointed by the current company or appointed by other listed companies. This condition is the reference category of the public reputation concern dummy described above; the two conditions are contrasted in the analyses.

Dichotomous indicator of the experimental manipulation of boardroom transparency. Participants read the statement that each director's vote (including theirs) will [not] be made public, that is, the general public and the public shareholders will [not] know how each director voted. The variable took a value of 1 if the participant was assigned to the transparent condition and a value of 0 if the participant was assigned to the nontransparent condition.

Monitoring behavior operationalized as the independent director's voting choice on each of the two board proposals. It was coded as 1 if the director voted 'against' or 'abstain' and 0 if the director voted 'for'. Voting 'against' and 'abstain' are both considered forms of dissent voting because the disclosure requirement is identical, because the Companies Law of China regards both as nonsupport, and because regulators typically consider the two choices similar and comparable. Proposal 1 involves a principal-agent problem (increasing salary and decreasing incentive compensation of top managers) and Proposal 2 involves a principal-principal problem (acquiring a real estate firm owned by the spouse of the controlling shareholder).

The number of first-generation Indian immigrants to which the focal VC firm became connected through its domestic investments in the focal year. A tie is formed in the year the VC invests in a startup in which the immigrant is a founder or CEO, and each individual immigrant counts as a separate tie. Individuals were identified by a surname most common in India, with surnames most common in Bangladesh, Pakistan, or Sri Lanka also included. Individuals with an Indian last name and an undergraduate degree from an Indian university are categorized as first-generation immigrants.

The number of later-generation Indian immigrants to which the focal VC firm became connected through its domestic investments in the focal year. Individuals with an Indian last name but an undergraduate degree from a U.S. university are considered later-generation immigrants of Indian ethnicity. This variable is used to test Hypothesis 2a and is included as a control in all models.

variable_name: Ties to Indian immigrants (Bangalore), ties to Indian immigrants (Mumbai), ties to Indian immigrants (other regions)
description: Counts of ties to first-generation Indian immigrants from specific regions of India. An individual is classified as having connections to a specific region if either their name or their undergraduate institution is associated with that region, or both. Bangalore is the hub of Southern India and Mumbai is the hub of Western India.

A count of the Indian startups in which the VC firm invested during the 5 years following the focal year. Only the first investment made by the VC in each Indian startup is counted, because the mechanism by which ties to immigrants help VCs applies mainly to the initial opportunity. To test Hypothesis 2b the counts are broken down by subregion within India (Bangalore, Mumbai, and the rest).
time_window: 5 years following the focal year; investments in India observed 2006-2019

description: An indicator coded 1 if the Indian startup experiences any of three possible liquidity events: it is acquired by another firm, it is listed on the stock market (IPO), or the focal VC sells its stake in a secondary sale. It is used as a proxy for the performance of the VC firm's investments in India. In the hazard models exit is coded 1 in the year the liquidity event occurs, with ties measured either as a flow of new ties each year or as a stock of accumulated ties.
level: VC firm-Indian startup dyad (dyad-year in the hazard models)
time_window: 5 years following the focal investment (pre-investment model); from the year of investment until a liquidity event or the end of the sample (hazard models)

variable_name: Total U.S. VC in preferred sector
description: The amount of VC investment (billions of USD) in the focal year that flows into the industry sector in which the focal VC firm made the greatest number of investments in the previous year. It captures how much capital competes in the firm's primary domestic investment segment.

Indicator of whether the worker moved jointly with colleagues. Comobility is defined as two workers moving within the same calendar month from the same establishment within the sending firm to the same establishment at the receiving firm, where both establishments do not have more than 100 employees. Timing of a move is identified from the number of days a person has been employed at the workplace during that calendar year; workers with 365 days are removed together with their co-movers.

variable_name: Change in wage from previous firm to subsequent firm
description: The dependent variable in all wage models: the difference between the mover's final (log) hourly wage at the prior firm and the initial (log) hourly wage at the receiving firm. It is used to estimate the wage premium of comobility among movers.

Worker skill level taken from the International Standard Classification of Occupation (ISCO), distinguishing four categories: 4 = Professionals; 3 = Technicians and Associate Professionals; 2 = Clerical, Service, and Sales Support, Agricultural/Forestry, Plant/Machine Operators/Assemblers; 1 = Elementary Occupations. In the wage models the worker is represented by individual contributor dummies for occupational skill levels 1 through 4, which are also interacted with the co-move indicator.

Indicator that the worker has a managerial occupation, identified in the IDA data. In the wage models the indicator is also interacted with the co-move dummy to test whether managers capture larger wage gains when they co-move.

Presence of related skills among co-movers, computed from the four-digit ISCO occupational code of each co-mover: two co-movers have related skills if they share the same initial digit but the remaining three digits do not match (an electronics engineer 2144 and an electrical engineer 2143 are related, as are a civil engineering technician 3112 and a safety/health/quality inspector 3152). For pairs of co-movers the indicator is binary and the same for each co-mover; for three or more co-movers a worker-specific measure is computed as the share of the focal worker's co-movers whose occupation is related. An analogous indicator records identical skills, where four-digit ISCO codes match, and co-movers with unrelated skills are the omitted category.
scale: absent, identical, or related (proportion for groups of 3+)

description: Binary measure indicating whether or not the paired VC and company both had personnel belonging to any one of the eight ethnic groups with distinct identities in the United States: the variable is set to one if any VC partner and any company executive of the VC–company pair share the same ethnicity other than Anglo-Celtic, West European, or others. Ethnic origins were assigned by Origins Info Ltd. from the family names and given names of VC partners and company executives listed by VentureXpert. According to this measure, 46.6% of the VC–company relationships were based on at least one coethnic partnership.

Continuous measure of ethnic distance between each VC–company pair, computed as the Mahalanobis distance between the pair's ethnicity position vectors, where a firm's vector records the proportion of its top executives or partners belonging to each of the ten ethnic groups plus a miscellaneous 'others' category. The measure accounts for the statistical prevalence of the different ethnicities in the sample as well as their co-occurrence. It is specified in logs in all regressions.

Dependent variable set to one for actual VC–company pairs, i.e., pairs for which the VC invested in the company, and zero for counterfactual pairs representing possible but unrealized matches. Counterfactual pairs were constructed by eliminating pairs in industries the VC never invests in and pairs where the VC was not active in a one-year window on either side of the dates on which the company received funding. Because more than 30 million pairs are theoretically possible, the analysis works with a 10% random sample of 1,300,761 actual and counterfactual pairs, of which 3,520 were actual matches.

Binary dependent variable equal to one if the company went public or was acquired and zero for all other outcomes. Private companies that, as of December 31, 2010, had received no funding in more than four years were eliminated from the analysis. IPO and acquisition events were counted as successful exits only when VentureXpert's indication of the event was also present in the SDC databases. The estimation sample consists of 17,418 actual VC–company pairs.

Ordinary least squares estimates of the relationship between ethnic proximity and post-IPO performance, measured separately by the companies' market capitalization and by their net income one year after IPO. The authors report that an additional coethnic pair is associated with, on average, a $0.1 million higher market capitalization and $0.009 million higher net income one year after IPO.

Gender of the appointed executive, coded 1 for female and 0 for male. A separate interaction variable, female insider, is coded 1 if the individual is a female insider and 0 otherwise. Female and male CEO appointments are compared as subsamples of the announcement data.

variable_name: gender of the CEO in the articles
description: Articles collected about each CEO were separated into two groups, ones about male CEO appointments and the ones about female CEO appointments. Each group was then grouped together into a single document and analyzed jointly, so that how women and men are treated in general could be compared.

Three-day cumulative abnormal returns over the -1, +1 window around the announcement, computed with standard event study methodology using a market model whose parameters require shares to be traded on each of the days in the -240 to -20 day window. Because the subsample of female CEOs is extremely small (17 observations), standard errors are produced from the distribution across 500 bootstrap iterations. Returns are reported in percent.

The number of popular press articles about each CEO within the year of appointment. Searches began with the Wall Street Journal in the ABI-Inform database and were expanded to the New York Times, Fortune, Forbes, Business Week, The Economist, and Financial Times, and then to the company name within a year before and after the announcement. The mean number of articles was 2.77 for women CEOs compared to 2.41 for men CEOs; an independent-sample t-test did not achieve statistical significance.
time_window: year of appointment (with searches one year before and after the announcement when needed)

description: Centering resonance analysis performed with the Crawdad Version 1.1 text analysis system; the influence of a word is determined by its betweenness centrality in the network of words. Article groups were cleaned of extraneous information and words above a 0.015 influence cut-off were ranked, with the top 15 most influential and the last 15 influential words reported. Two of the 10 most influential words in the reports about women CEOs referenced gender or femininity, whereas no references to gender appeared in the top 10 words for male CEOs.

variable_name: CEO appointment vs. top management team (TMT) appointment
description: The sample of top executive appointments (including CEO, CFO, COO, President, and Executive Vice President) is split into CEO appointments and TMT appointments, which are analyzed as separate subsamples. Stock market reactions to female TMT appointments are compared with those to female CEO appointments, and male TMT appointments with female TMT appointments.

Firm insider is coded as 1 if the executive is promoted from within the firm and 0 if the executive comes from another firm. An interaction variable, female insider, is coded 1 if the individual is a female insider and 0 otherwise, and is used to test whether the reaction to female appointments is moderated by insider status.
scale: 1 = promoted from within the firm, 0 = comes from another firm

description: Number of biotechnology patent applications granted to the firm in each year of the 1980-2001 study period, used as the proxy for the firm's innovative output in biotechnology. The authors relied on patent applications granted because this provides a closer link between the timing of the invention and its recording, and obtained the most recent U.S. PTO report including patent data until the end of 2004. The models explicitly control for lagged biotechnology patents and for nonbiotechnology patents.

Total number of a firm's scientists who published in academic journals, used as the proxy for a firm's intellectual human capital. The authors searched the ISI Science Citation Index for academic journal articles published between 1980 and 2004 that had a keyword related to science research and could be unambiguously connected with one of the pharmaceutical firms in the sample, and then tied each author back to the sample firms based on the authors' affiliations as indicated in the journal articles.
time_window: articles published 1980-2004 (three years longer than the study period)

description: Scientists identified from the population of scientists using three increasingly stringent approaches based on the distributions of citations and publications; the measure used is the intersection of publication stars and citation stars. Publication stars are scientists who published, on average, more than 27 papers during 1980-2004 (z-score > 3.0), and citation stars are scientists whose publications had been cited at least 847 times (z-score > 3.0); this intersection yielded 851 star scientists. Because applying both a publication and citation filter is a fairly stringent and thus conservative approach, the authors used it as their proxy for star scientists.

The difference between total scientists and star scientists, inserted in the regression analysis to isolate the effect of star scientists on innovative output more fully. The average pharmaceutical firm employed about 17 star scientists and 197 nonstar scientists in a given year over the study period.

A pharmaceutical firm's R&D capability proxied by its R&D expenditures, while explicitly controlling for firm revenues. Proxying R&D capability by R&D expenditures is preferred over R&D intensity because in the latter measure significant uncertainty exists as to whether any observed effects on innovation are due to the numerator or the denominator. All financial variables are inflation adjusted in constant 2000 U.S. dollars, and R&D expenditures are lagged by one year in the models.

Number of alliances the pharmaceutical firm entered with providers of biotechnology research, tracked as alliances with universities, research institutions, and biotechnology firms. Each alliance description was content analyzed to ensure that the focal alliance indeed pertained to the new biotechnology paradigm. The measure is lagged by one year.

Number of biotechnology acquisitions a pharmaceutical firm had consummated during the study period, identified from SDC Platinum. Each acquisition description was studied in detail to ensure that the focal acquisitions were indeed targeted toward the sourcing of R&D. The measure is lagged by one year.

variable_name: Size / ln Size (annual production of automobiles)
description: Size is measured as the firm's annual production of automobiles. Because precise production figures were unavailable for most short-lived firms, the authors coded firms qualitatively as 'small' (including firms producing only 'a few' automobiles or with no size information), 'middle size', and 'large', and imputed values from the size distributions of firms whose production levels are observed: small firm-years were assigned a value from a uniform distribution ranging from zero to the first quartile of the size distribution for the historical period, medium and large firm-years the second and third quartile values respectively. The counts often come from new vehicle registrations and from counts of surviving automobiles. Main-effect analyses using the three qualitative classes and using the natural logarithm of the quantitative value gave substantively similar results; the constructed metric measure is used in the models.

Relative size is the ratio of each firm's size to the size of the largest firm in the national population of automobile producers at the time. In the full-population analysis it enters through a proportionate specification that adds a squared and a cubic term of size to the baseline; by Hypothesis 1 the first- and third-order terms were expected to be negative. The variable is used only in the test of Hypothesis 1 and not in the test of Hypothesis 2.

variable_name: Aggregate distance from larger competitors (D it)
description: Each firm's position at each point in time is calculated on a downward-sloping curve represented by the inverse quadratic root of the size variable S, after adjusting for minimum size; the text gives the calculation as (Sit - S min) - 1/4. The transformation was chosen because its shape resembles a typical long-run average cost curve, and the authors report that exploratory analyses with transformations using lower- and higher-order roots show consistent patterns. The aggregate distance of each firm from its larger competitors is then computed by summing the differences in scores; the summing formula appears in a block that could not be extracted from the text and is not reconstructed here. The greater the number of larger competitors, the greater the competitive pressure, and a unit size difference creates more pressure when the focal firm is small.

The outcome event of interest is disbanding/exit to another industry, defined to include events of unknown type, since the authors' reading of the historical materials suggests that most exits of unknown type were either disbandings or exits to other industries. Firms known to have ended by other events (merger, acquisition, etc.) were treated as noninformatively censored on the right at the times of these events. Tenures in automobile production are measured in decimal years, with dates known only to the year coded at the midpoint of the year.

The betas used were compiled by Merrill Lynch and are based on 60 months' observations, ending March 1978. Beta is the slope of the linear function relating the return on a security to the general market factor, and it cannot be diversified away by the investor, which is why it is the risk measure of concern.

Each firm is assigned to one of Rumelt's diversification strategy categories using three ratios: the specialization ratio (the proportion of a firm's revenues attributable to its largest single business), the related ratio (the proportion attributable to its largest group of related businesses) and the vertical ratio (the proportion arising from all by-products, intermediate products and end products of a vertically integrated sequence of processing activities). Each firm is thoroughly evaluated from a managerial perspective and classified according to its unique history and patterns of relatedness. Six of Rumelt's nine strategy categories are used, and the categories reported run from single business to the unrelated portfolio category; the strategy classifications are from the same time period as the betas.
time_window: same time period as the beta observations

description: A weighted market share index selected as an indicator of the presence of market power. The text states that MS(i) is the weighted market share of firm i, m(ij) is the percentage of firm i's total sales that are in 4-digit SIC market j, and M(ij) is firm i's share of 4-digit SIC market j; the formula itself is not readable in the supplied text. The denominator appears as an adjustment for firm sales data that do not add to one, which is the case whenever any of a firm's sales are in foreign markets.
Capital structure is measured as leverage, defined as (book value of debt)/(book value of equity).

The depreciation/sales ratio was used as a measure of capital intensity. The authors note that accounting differences across firms and general problems relating to historical cost data complicate the empirical representation of the labour/capital trade-off.

Counts the number of times within the 5-year window after alliance formation that the client firm's patents cite any of the R&D firm's patents that belong to the technology domain of the alliance. Recap's assignment of each alliance to technology areas was matched to technology groups under the Cooperative Patent Classification scheme to identify alliance-related patents and citations. Citations that originated during patent examination are excluded. Partners are distinguished as R&D firm and client firm based on which partner primarily contributes technology to the alliance, as indicated by Recap.

Counts the number of times within the 5-year window after alliance formation that the R&D firm's patents cite any of the client firm's patents that belong to the technology domain of the alliance. Alliance technology areas from Recap were matched to Cooperative Patent Classification technology groups to identify alliance-related patents and citations. Citations that originated during patent examination are excluded. Partners are distinguished as R&D firm and client firm based on which partner primarily contributes technology to the alliance, as indicated by Recap.

A patent vector is derived for each partner from the distribution across CPC technology groups of all patents applied for prior to the alliance formation, following the method Jaffe (1986) proposed. Technology overlap between the partners is the uncentered correlation coefficient of these patent vectors, bounded by 0 and 1, and takes greater values when the technology profiles of the partners become more congruent.
time_window: all patents applied for prior to alliance formation

variable_name: Value of R&D firm knowledge (in scope)
description: Built for the R&D firm's patent portfolio as the number of forward citations received by a patent in the 5-year window after the grant, counting all issued patents applied for in a 10-year window prior to the alliance, and restricted to patents in technological areas that are focal to the alliance. A logarithmic transformation is applied.
time_window: 10-year pre-alliance application window; 5-year post-grant citation window

variable_name: Value of client firm knowledge (in scope)
description: Built for the client firm's patent portfolio as the number of forward citations received by a patent in the 5-year window after the grant, counting all issued patents applied for in a 10-year window prior to the alliance, and restricted to patents in technological areas that are focal to the alliance. A logarithmic transformation is applied.
time_window: 10-year pre-alliance application window; 5-year post-grant citation window

description: A binary variable coded from the alliance contract, which equals one when the partners establish a joint steering committee with oversight responsibilities of alliance activities and zero otherwise. Because the decision to establish a steering committee is unlikely to be random, the probability of establishing a steering committee is estimated and used in the models of knowledge flows.

Following Garg et al., a chair appointment equation is first estimated for individual outside directors and the residual is obtained as the difference between the true value and the predicted value, capturing the part of the chair appointment that cannot be explained by the normatively accepted director characteristics. The degree of undervaluation is assessed by taking the negative residuals and using a spline function so that undervaluation is coded as the value of the residuals when the residuals are negative and zero otherwise, with the absolute value taken so that the higher the value, the higher the undervaluation. Board undervaluation, the independent variable, is constructed by calculating the average director undervaluation of undervalued directors. Director undervaluation is calculated each year by running an updated equation, thus accounting for possible reallocations of chairs.
time_window: measured each year (year t); lagged one year relative to the dependent variable in the models

description: Calculated from a fractional response model predicting chair appointment for individual outside directors. For each right-hand-side variable, the focal director's value has the average value of the rest of the outside directors on the same board subtracted from it, so that the differences capture the director's advantage or disadvantage from peer directors along that dimension. Director undervaluation is the negative residuals from this equation, splined so that undervaluation equals the value of the residual when it is negative and zero otherwise, with the absolute value taken so that higher values mean higher undervaluation.

Following prior studies on director turnover, director turnover is measured with a binary variable, coded as 1 if any outside director exits the firm in a certain year and 0 otherwise. Outside directors are identified from the 'Management' section of the IPO prospectus and their turnover dates from the Boardex database. The authors note that they cannot perfectly distinguish whether the turnover is voluntary or involuntary, although they believe turnover is largely voluntary in nature.
time_window: each post-IPO year (t + 1 in the mediation models)

description: The qualification index is a weighted average of the right-hand-side variables in Equation (1) where coefficients are used as weights. Based on Equation (1), a qualification index is constructed for each director who was on the board in a given year-end, and then the average across all the new directors in that year is used to construct the dependent variable.
time_window: year t + 1 in the mediation models; controls and the independent variable are lagged by one year except for the number of new directors (same year as the dependent variable)

description: ROA is calculated with a one-year lead vis-à-vis the mediators using the net income and total assets reported by the firm each year. The industry-adjusted ROA is calculated by subtracting the industry mean. The higher the ROA, the better the firm performance.
time_window: year t + 2 in the mediation models (one-year lead vis-à-vis the mediators)

description: The cumulative forward citation frequencies to an individual patent. Forward citations count the number of times a patent (the 'cited patent') is included in the prior art of subsequent patents. All forward citations received by each patent are counted as of the end of 1999. The first U.S. patent in the patent family issued during 1992-1995, inclusive, is used.
time_window: citations received through the end of 1999

description: Raw citation counts to each article are normalized by the mean and standard deviation of citations received by all sampled articles in its publication year. Normalized citations are then summed across years for each firm and divided by the number of the firm's publications, yielding an average citation measure for the firm as a whole. In the models, normalized citations are aggregated up to the year the observed patent was filed.
level: firm (cumulated to the patent filing year)
time_window: cumulated from the start of the publication period up to the time of the observed innovation

description: The total number of firm publications, cumulated up to the year in which the observed patent was filed. The variable is specified in log form to take account of the highly skewed distribution of publications.
time_window: cumulated up to the year the observed patent was filed

description: Percentage of all publications by the firm that were collaborative publications with an external organization, cumulated up to the year the observed patent was filed. Collaboration is represented by articles in which both the firm and an outside organization are listed as institutional affiliations of one or more of the authors.
time_window: cumulated up to the year the observed patent was filed

variable_name: Science Intensity of Firm's Patents / Patent Science Intensity
description: Science intensity is a 'backwards' citation count, measured as the number of times a patent references nonpatented literature in its prior art. For the firm, the mean number of citations to nonpatented literature across all of its patents is calculated. The firm-level measure is used when firm-level science indicators are included, and the patent-level measure is used when the cited patent's own prior art is counted.

The percentage of all individuals listed on a patent who are also listed on at least one publication. The variable is calculated first at the patent level and then for the firm as a whole by aggregating all scientists listed on the firm's patents during the sample period. Among inventors, 57% are also publishers (1,170 out of 2,035 inventors); only 6% of publishers are also inventors (1,170 out of 19,638).

Target firm wealth creation measured by cumulative prediction errors (abnormal returns) from a market model. The market model was applied to monthly share price data over a 36-month estimation period to obtain cumulative prediction errors for the subsequent 6-month period, which embraces 3 months prior to the announcement of the bid, the bid month itself and a further 2 months during which the bid was completed. Adjustments for thin trading were made using the procedure suggested by Fowler and Rorke (1983).
time_window: 36-month estimation period; 6-month event window ending 2 months after the bid month

description: A dummy variable indicating whether the bid is friendly or hostile, equal to 1 if hostile and 0 if friendly. A bid is considered hostile if the target company publicly rejects the bid and also engages in a clear defense strategy, such as increasing the dividend pay-out, revaluing company assets, divesting assets or attempting to get the bid referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission. A rigorous search of the financial press resulted in each bid being classified as hostile (= 1) or friendly (= 0).

A dummy indicating relatedness between bidder and target, equal to 1 if both companies were classified in the same Stock Exchange Industrial Classification (SEIC) group and 0 otherwise. The SEIC classifies industries at a level of disaggregation akin to the 2-digit SIC.

The valuation ratio of the target firm, a proxy for Tobin's q ratio, defined as the market value of the company at the end of the fourth month before the bid divided by the book value of equity. It is introduced as a measure of financial performance before the bid and is a proxy for managerial performance.
time_window: end of the fourth month before the bid

description: Measures the difference between VALR of bidding and target companies. It enters the wealth equation in place of VALR in the second estimated equation.

The proportion of shares of the target firm held by its directors. The square of managerial equity (TDIRSHR2) is also included in the wealth equation to capture nonlinearity, with the coefficient of TDIRSHR constrained to be positive and that of TDIRSHR2 negative.
Large shareholdings held by individuals or institutions, i.e., ownership that collectively amounts to at least 5 percent of the total equity.
The percentage of shares of the target company owned by the bidding company management before the bid.
Gearing in the bidding company, expressed as total debt over the book value of total assets. It is used as an alternative to GEARDIF in the mood equation.
The difference in gearing between the bidding and the target company, where gearing is total debt over the book value of total assets. It is used as an alternative to BIDGEAR in the mood equation.

The number of times the focal firm i licenses to a buyer in an application industry k in year t during the study period. The authors identified the technology-based licensing agreements of their sample firms in the SDC Platinum alliances database and selected only those in which the sample firms were the technology suppliers; where the deal description did not specify the supplier, the search was complemented with online archival news sources. They then determined which application industry the licensing targeted using both the SIC industry code of the alliance assigned by SDC and analysis of the synopsis. Each sample firm granted from zero to eight licenses each year to each of its application industries.

A firm i's knowledge transfer capability in year t is measured as the cumulative number of codevelopment deals in which firm i's technologies were used to develop applications for industry k. These deals were identified from the SDC database by reading each deal synopsis and selecting those that involved the transfer of a focal firm's knowledge. The stock was depreciated using a 15 percent discount rate, while the simple cumulative count was used as a robustness check.

The typical level of absorptive capacity of potential buyers from an application industry, measured as the average absorptive capacity of the public firms in that application industry, which were taken as the set of potential buyers. Absorptive capacity itself is measured from the Carnegie Mellon Survey on industrial R&D, which contains a measure of the percentage of R&D effort devoted to gaining novel external knowledge, collected from 1,477 R&D labs across a broad range of industries. Each lab was assigned a primary SIC code and the industry averages of the CMS absorptive capacity measure were matched to each application industry using the USPTO concordance. Since this survey-based measure is time invariant, its main effect is not estimated in the conditional fixed-effect models.

Computed from the Carnegie Mellon Survey as the share of respondents, among the 1,477 R&D labs of the survey, whose R&D and marketing/manufacturing personnel interacted daily, per each application industry k. The possible responses include daily, weekly, monthly, rarely, and never, and the median frequency reported by these labs was weekly. The authors describe the measure as reflecting the degree of bilateral dependence between upstream and downstream activities in the value chain. The measure is not time variant because the CMS was conducted in 1994.
scale: share of respondents reporting daily interaction

description: An entropy measure equal to the sum over products of Pi times the natural log of 1/Pi, where Pi is the percentage of sales in the firm's primary line that the ith product accounted for. A firm's primary line is the one with the highest level of sales in the prior year. The measure accounts for both the number of products and the relative importance of each. It was lagged by a year and updated annually.
time_window: lagged by one year, updated annually

description: The number of new products that a firm introduced within its primary line during the current year. It was determined by the product introduction dates in the IDC data.
The number of new products introduced during the current year that were not members of a firm's primary line.
The natural log of the total number of new products introduced within the industry during the current year, excluding introductions by the focal firm.

A firm was coded as failing in year t if it sold no personal computers in year t + 1, so the year of failure was known but not the precise month or day. Failures included the deaths of entire firms and industry exits by multibusiness corporations. Hazard rates were estimated in discrete time with a complementary log-log function to recover continuous-time hazard rates.
time_window: failure in year t indicated by no sales in year t + 1

description: The ratio of R&D expenditures over sales, one of two frequently used indicators of intangible assets. Midpoint values were allocated to each of five intervals. All ownership measures refer to 1992.
scale: ratio of R&D expenditures to sales

description: The percentage of exports in value that the firm sells in foreign markets without a brand, used as the second indicator of intangible assets. A higher value indicates fewer branding-related intangible assets.

A dummy variable with a value of one if the firm manufactures standardized products in large batches, and zero otherwise. It captures product variability, with the mass producer standing for the standardized, low-variability end.

The log of total firm revenues in billion Spanish pesetas for each firm, used as the measure of resource availability to invest in distribution. Midpoint values were allocated to each of eight intervals.
scale: log of total revenues in billion pesetas

description: The ratio of exports to sales for each firm, used as the measure of commitment to export sales. It refers to 1992.

GNP per capita in 1992 adjusted by purchasing power for the country or trade bloc mentioned by the firm's export manager as the location of the firm's competition in export markets. If two or three country locations were mentioned, the variable equals the mean of GNP per capita for these countries weighted by their population size. The index was divided by the level for the United States and multiplied by 100.

A dummy variable indicating whether a country situated on the Mediterranean Sea was mentioned as being the location of the firm's competition in export markets, because Mediterranean countries have comparative location advantages similar to Spain's and tend to compete with each other in many export markets.
The growth potential of the market abroad, measured by the firm's export intensity growth rate between 1987 and 1992.

A three-point decreasing measure of the perception by the firm's manager responsible for exports that the firm's level of access to foreign markets represents an advantage relative to the competition (value one), neither an advantage nor a disadvantage (two), or a disadvantage (three). It measures institutional entry barriers such as the difficulty in penetrating distribution channels.

A dummy variable given the value of one when the firm's manager responsible for exports perceives lack of knowledge about export markets as a limitation, and zero otherwise; it measures cognitive constraints on the part of the firm.

Binary dependent variable equal to one if the firm has internalized export activities, through either a commercial alliance or proprietary distribution abroad, and zero otherwise. It is built from the 1992 survey of Spanish manufacturing exporters.

Dependent variable for the mode of internalization among the 253 firms that internalized exports. It equals one if the firm internalized through proprietary distribution channels and zero if through a commercial alliance. In the multinomial version firms are coded as no internalization, commercial alliance only, or proprietary distribution.

An indicator variable that takes the value of 1 if, in and after the first year, a firm is targeted by an NPE-initiated lawsuit as a defendant (i.e., for the treatment group) and 0 if otherwise. For the control group of firms, post-NPE always takes on the value of 0. It is the main difference-in-differences variable of interest.
time_window: in and after the year of the first NPE lawsuit

description: The proportion of the total number of self-citations that a firm has cited in all its patent applications filed in a given year (which are eventually granted) to the total number of all citations (self or external) made in the firm's patent applications filed in the same year (which are eventually granted). It captures a firm's tendency to undertake an inward innovation strategy by drawing and building upon its own in-house technologies relative to technologies from other firms.
time_window: patent applications filed in a given year

description: The proportion of the total number of forward non-self-citations to the total number of all forward citations (self or external). A patent's forward non-self-citation refers to the citations made by the applicants who are not the patent holders themselves. A higher value indicates a greater tendency for a nontarget firm to conduct follow-on R&D in a similar technology area as the target firm.

An indicator variable that equals 1 if the average of numbers of inventors per patent for the firm is above the median and 0 if otherwise; the paired less-inventors variable equals 1 when that average is below the median. When more inventors per patent takes on the value of 1, it indicates that the innovation cost of developing a patented technology for a firm is relatively high.

An indicator variable that equals 1 if a firm's total similarity is above median and 0 if otherwise, where total similarity is a score that gauges the product similarity between paired firms based on text-based network industry classification (TNIC) and is negatively related to pricing power in the framework of product differentiation theory. The paired low rival similarity variable equals 1 when total similarity is below the median.

An indicator variable that equals 1 if a firm's number of rivals in the same TNIC industry is above median and 0 if otherwise; the paired fewer-rivals variable equals 1 when that number is below the median. When high rival similarity or more rivals equals 1, it suggests that the firm faces a relatively high level of competition in the product market.

For each firm-country-year and each of the four distance dimensions, the time-weighted average Mahalanobis distance between host country k and the J countries in the firm's home base, i.e. the countries the firm had already entered before year t, including its home country. Each country j in the home base is weighted by A_jt, the number of years the firm had operated in country j until year t, and T_t is the total number of country-years the firm had been in existence before year t. When J = 1 the firm operates only in its home country and the WAD equals the difference between host country k and the home country. The Mahalanobis rather than Euclidean method is used because the dimensions are correlated, have different variances and are measured on different scales; the displayed formula for this variable is unreadable in the available text.
time_window: as of year t, with country weights equal to years of operation until t

description: The static Mahalanobis distance between the firm's home country and the host country, calculated for each firm-country-year observation and separately for each of the four dimensions of distance (cultural, demographic, political and administrative). It is the traditional, home-country-based measure of the liability of foreignness and remains unchanged even as the firm expands internationally.

For each firm-country-year and each distance dimension, the weighted standard deviation of the distance between the firm's home base and host country k at year t, using the same terms and country weights as the weighted average distance. When J = 1, i.e. a firm has no foreign operations, A_jt = T_t and D_jk = WAD_ikt, so that WSD = 0 for purely domestic firms. The displayed formula for this variable is unreadable in the available text.
time_window: as of year t, with country weights equal to years of operation until t

description: Dependent variable taking the values of 0 or 1, indicating whether the firm entered the host country; the value 0 is much more frequent than 1, which is why rare-event logistic regression is used. Foreign subsidiaries are identified from the annual reports of the listed firms, from company websites and through further Internet searches, with the establishment year of each subsidiary as given by the company.

The total count of innovative acts during the previous five years divided by total bank assets. The counts come from the full text of press articles and annual reports, which were searched for discrete modifications to back-office processes, distribution systems, and product/service offerings. All innovation variables are constructed over the previous five years.
The same five-year count of innovations by all other banks in the sample divided by the sum of their bank assets. It captures the cumulative impact of value-chain modifications by competitors.
A count of the number of reported Australian firsts during the previous five years. Firsts were noted when an article indicated that the modification was a first for Australian retail banking.

The five-year counts of product-related, process-related and distribution-related innovative acts are each divided by the five-year count of total innovative acts, and the squares of these three proportions are summed. The variable equals 0.33 when innovative activity is evenly spread across categories and increases toward unity as activity becomes focused on a single category. The formula itself is not readable in the extracted text.

For each of the three categories the squared year-to-year changes in that category's proportion of total innovative activity are summed over the previous four years, and the negative of the sum of these annual changes across the three categories is computed. The maximum value is zero, realized when the distribution of innovative activity across categories is constant over the previous five years; larger negative values indicate greater year-to-year instability. The formula itself is not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: previous five years (annual changes summed over the previous four years)

description: Calculated from the differences between the proportion of a bank's own innovative activity devoted to each category and the corresponding industry averages for product, process and distribution innovations. The variable equals zero when a bank's composition of innovative activity moves in step with the industry average and increases with the degree of dissimilarity. A squared Divergence variable is also generated to capture the hypothesized nonmonotonic effects. The formula itself is not readable in the extracted text.

Bank return on total assets (ROA), an accounting rate of return, used as the financial performance measure. Table 3 summarizes the ROA for each sampled bank over the 1986 to 1995 period and shows considerable dynamic variability.

Executive social capital endowments for year t were measured as the executive's eigenvector centrality (log-transformed) within the board-interlock network across all directors in year t - 1. In this interlocking directorship network, executives connect with other directors by serving on the same board, excluding the tie achieved through their own company. Eigenvector centrality weights ties with well-connected contacts more heavily than degree centrality. The squared term of this variable is also entered in the models, and the calculations were conducted using UCINET 6.

Peer social capital was operationalized as the average of the logged eigenvector centrality of all other executives and directors in the company. Eigenvector centrality was computed within the board-interlock network across all directors in year t - 1. The calculations were conducted using UCINET 6.

The size of a sample firm's alliance network in year t was operationalized as the number of alliances the firm was engaged in during year t - 1, adjusted based on the average number of alliances engaged in by all public firms in the firm's industry.

The dependent variable was coded 1 in the year of exit, and otherwise coded 0. Ship jumpers were defined as executives who took new executive positions within 1 year after they left a sample company, tracked through a database operated by a government-funded human-resource monitoring institute. Reports about top executive turnover in the sample *ST firms were searched in the newspaper database of The National Library of China, and outgoing executives reported as being fired or forced out, resigning unexpectedly due to unspecified reasons, or taking unexpected early retirement were classified as dismissed rather than ship jumpers. Combining the two searches identified 95 of the 278 sample executives as engaging in ship jumping.
scale: binary (1 = ship jumping in the year of exit, 0 otherwise)
time_window: 2 years prior to the *ST announcement (years N - 3 to N - 1)

description: Measured as the total number of years the new CEO served on the focal firm's board during the 10 years prior to becoming the CEO. Using this 10-year window allowed the authors to capture sufficient variation in prior board experience while ensuring the experience was reasonably recent and relevant. Because this experience is time-invariant and potentially endogenous to the succession context and peer practice, the residuals from a first-stage regression of the variable on presuccession firm performance, peer CEOs' prior focal board experience, firm size, and industry and year dummies are used as the proxy of the independent variable in the main analysis.

Measured as the total number of years the new CEO served as a director at other firms during the 10 years prior to becoming the CEO. Among the 429 new insider CEOs, 65 (15.2%) had one or more years of prior other board experience. As with prior focal board experience, the residuals from a first-stage regression on the succession-context and peer-practice variables are used as the proxy of this independent variable in the main analysis.

Changes in six key strategic dimensions were used: advertising intensity (advertising/sales), research and development intensity (R&D/sales), plant and equipment newness (net P&E/gross P&E), nonproduction overhead in selling, general, and administrative (SGA) expenses (SGA expenses/sales), inventory level (inventory/sales), and financial leverage (debt/equity). The absolute change in each dimension was calculated from the end of year t (the year of succession) to the end of year t + 2; because these changes were right-skewed their values were log-transformed, each of the six log-transformed measures was standardized to make them comparable, and the sum of the standardized scores was used as a composite measure of strategic change for each new CEO.
time_window: end of year t (year of succession) to end of year t + 2

description: Eigenvector centrality measure (Bonacich, 1987) of the firm's position in its home country syndication network; we considered a network tie to exist only if two firms invested together in the same U.S. venture and in the same round. For each year t, the centrality score was calculated using information for two (t - 2) and one (t - 1) years earlier and for t itself. The centrality score ranges between 0 (for isolated firms with no contacts) and 1 (for firms that syndicated with other central firms only), and we assigned a 0 to isolated firms with no ties to others. For the interaction terms the continuous main effect was centered by subtracting the mean.

Burt's (1992) reverse-signed index of constraint, calculated using UCINET. In this measure a value of 0, the maximum, is assigned to isolated nodes, and the measure approaches -1 as the node becomes more constrained-that is, as the observed firm loses brokerage advantage; the measure is increasing in brokerage advantage. For the interaction terms the continuous main effect was centered by subtracting the mean.

The dependent variable is an event that equaled 1 if firm i entered country j during year t. The sample consisted of firm-country-year observations, and each venture capital firm was at risk of entering a country during a given year. The first sample excluded firm-country-year observations subsequent to a focal venture capital firm's first entry into each country j. We excluded from all analyses the 17 investments in ventures that had gone public before the U.S. venture capital firm invested.

variable_name: Presence of syndicate partners in country
description: Dummy variable coded 1 if any of firm i's syndicate partners in its home country network had made at least one investment in country j up until year t - 1. It was also multiplied by the social status measure and by the brokerage measure to form the two interaction terms.

Indicator variable taking the value 1 if, in a given year, a firm has an independent director with tenure of 15 years or more. Fifteen years corresponds closely to the mean and median tenure of the director with the longest tenure among the firms in the data. LTID status with respect to firm performance in a given year is determined from board data reported early in the following year.
scale: 1 = has an independent director with tenure of 15 years or more; 0 otherwise
time_window: board data reported early in the following year

description: Tobin's q, calculated as the book value of a firm's assets plus the market value of the firm's common equity minus the book value of common equity, deferred taxes, and investment tax credits, divided by the book value of the firm's assets. It is a forward-looking measure of firm performance reflecting the market's assessment of the value the LTID's presence will add.

Indicator of firm complexity based on Coles et al. (2008), derived from a factor analysis of three observable firm attributes that make firm governance more complicated and thus boards more useful: diversification, size, and leverage. Coles et al. (2008) provide robust evidence that Complex predicts a board will be larger and have more outside directors.

Indicator defined to correspond to the mature stage in the eight-stage firm lifecycle classification system developed by Dickinson (2011). It takes the value 1 if and only if a firm has positive cash flow from operations and negative cash flow from both investing and financing activities.
Count of how many CEOs the firm's longest-tenured director (who may or may not be an LTID) has served with at the firm.
time_window: over the tenure of the longest-serving director

description: Index created for this purpose by Bebchuk et al. (2009), a count of how many of the listed provisions a firm has, where a higher number indicates that the firm's management is more entrenched because the provision makes it harder to replace them.

Capped is an indicator for whether the assignee is subject to the H1B visa cap and Shock is an indicator for years 1999 through 2003; the interaction captures the percent increase in herbal patenting caused by relaxing the H1B visa cap. The authors interpret the shock as an exogenous increase in the supply of first-generation ethnic migrant inventors to capped assignees.

The log number of herbal patents granted to an assignee (a firm or university) in a given year, aggregated into assignee-year observations. For years in which an assignee was in the sample but was not granted any herbal patents, the number of patents is set at zero; because the count is skewed the authors add 1 and take logs.

Indicator for whether all inventors listed on a patent have Chinese/Indian names, derived from inventors identified in PatentsView and classified by the open-source name categorizer 'ethnicityguesser' using names' linguistic cues. The authors also create indicators for uniformly non-Chinese/Indian (Nonethnic) and mixed-ethnicity (Mixed Team) inventor sets.

A patent is coded as Recombined if the patent text refers to synthetic nonherbal formulations in addition to herbs. The authors use the Derwent classification, a manually curated standardized patent classification system, identify three classes that consist of both herbs and synthetic compounds, and code a patent as recombined if it belongs to any of these classes.

The authors do not construct a separate variable for reuse in the main analysis; a patent that is not coded as Recombined is treated as reuse of knowledge transferred from the inventors' home regions. Because Hypothesis 2 states that patents with exclusively ethnic inventors are more likely to involve reuse, the authors expect a negative coefficient on Fully Ethnic in the recombination regression.

Investment is measured as capital expenditures allocated to business units scaled by unit assets. Overinvestment occurs when investment in low-prospect business units exceeds the average scaled investment among all high-prospect business units from all industries each year, where high-prospect units are those with Tobin's q above the median of all business units across all firms excluding the focal firm. Business unit q is approximated by the average q of at least five single-business firms in the same industry, at the narrowest SIC level at which five such firms exist. The measure was multiplied by 100 for easier interpretation of parameter estimates.

Investment is measured as capital expenditures allocated to business units scaled by unit assets. Underinvestment occurs when investment in high-prospect business units is less than the average investment of low-prospect business units from all industries each year. Expectation of unit growth prospects is proxied by Tobin's q estimated at the industry level. The measure was multiplied by 100 for easier interpretation of parameter estimates.

Peer social performance comparison is measured as operating income divided by assets (return on assets) for business unit i in firm j at time t minus average peer business unit ROA at time t. Peer returns were calculated across all business units in the same industry as the focal business unit, including units of diversified firms, and only when at least five rival business units existed in the same industry, using a stepwise procedure that began at the narrowest SIC level possible. All performance comparison measures were reverse-coded when focal performance was below aspirations; the below-aspiration version is used for the overinvestment models and the above-aspiration version for the underinvestment models.

Internal social performance comparison is measured as current focal business unit ROA minus the average ROA of the remaining business units in its firm. All performance comparison measures were reverse-coded when focal performance was below aspirations; the below-aspiration version is used for the overinvestment models and the above-aspiration version for the underinvestment models.

Historical performance comparison is measured as current business unit ROA minus unit historical performance, where historical performance is measured as a two-year moving average of the prior two years of unit performance with both years weighted equally. All performance comparison measures were reverse-coded when focal performance was below aspirations; the below-aspiration version is used for the overinvestment models and the above-aspiration version for the underinvestment models.
time_window: current year minus a two-year moving average of the prior two years

variable_name: variance in business unit performance comparisons (VPC)
description: VPC is the variance of the performance comparison measure, computed separately for each performance comparison (peer social, internal social, and historical) and only for firms with two or more business units. Each focal business unit is included in the calculation of the variance of the choice set it faces.

Slack is measured as cash flow, operating earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization divided by total assets for each firm and year. Changes in inventory, accounts receivable, and accounts payable are not included in this measure because firms are inconsistent in providing these data. In addition to controlling for the amount of free cash flow that may be allocated to businesses, the variable is used to moderate the effect of performance aspirations on over- and underinvestment.

Count of ownership transfers within the same industry that take place in other zip codes in which a multiunit owner has outlets, calculated for the year before each period in which the outlet is at risk. The count includes only nonfranchised outlets whose owners own 20 or fewer outlets. Zip codes contiguous to the zip code of the outlet at risk are excluded. A transfer is identified when an individual with a different surname is listed as an outlet's new owner, with corporate cases checked against the Texas Secretary of State's incorporation database.

variable_name: Transfers with a change of name
description: Variable 1 split into two separate counts, this one counting only ownership transfers in the owner's other zip codes that involved a change of business name.

variable_name: Transfers that keep the same name
description: Variable 1 split into two separate counts, this one counting only ownership transfers in the owner's other zip codes where the business name remained the same after the change of owner.

variable_name: Exit-entry pairs in these other zips
description: Count of pairs of exits and entries in the vicinity of a multiunit owner's other outlets in the previous year. Both the exit and the entry must be of nonfranchised outlets with small owners and both must be in the same market. If one of the owner's other outlets has only exits nearby and another only entries nearby, the exits and entries are not considered a pair and the value of the variable is zero.

The dependent variable for the event history analysis is outlet-level exit. Outlets are at risk of exit until they have permanently closed down. Outlets are not considered to have exited merely due to changes of ownership or business name, as long as someone is operating the same type of business at that location.

Equals 1 if a firm contributed any comment on a draft piece of regulation to the government within the past year and 0 if it did not. More than a fifth of firms in the sample (21.4%) reported doing so. The variable captures the variation in labor contracting associated with unacknowledged participation when the stricter responsiveness variables are also in the model.

Narrows commenting firms down to those whose comment received a formal government acknowledgment. According to firm responses, fully two-thirds of all commenting firms did receive responses (13.6% of the sample). A stricter variant, Effective participation, captures the higher form of government responsiveness in which the firm understands its comment to have contributed to altering the regulation, and more than a third of commenting firms reported this.
