scale: 1 = commented and received a government response, 0 = otherwise

description: Each firm's self-reported share of long-term employees with formal contracts, the authors' main operationalization of regulatory compliance. Article 18 of the Labor Code requires labor contracts to be signed before starting long-term, full-time work, including for seasonal workers for whom contracts were not previously required. Mean compliance across the sample is 72%.
scale: 0-100% of long-term employees under formal contract

description: A three-point scale created to address the heavy skew of the continuous measure toward full compliance, scoring a firm as noncompliant (0) if it had less than 50% of employees under contract, partially compliant (1) if it had between 50 and 99% of employees under contract, and fully compliant (2) if the firm had 100% of employees under contract. It is analyzed with an ordered probit procedure.

A latent variable generated by a factor analysis with varimax rotation on three PCI survey indicators of firm perceptions of government legitimacy; the procedure identified a single factor explaining 56% of the variation, and a simple regression-based prediction generates the variable used in the mediation analysis. In analysis the fairness item's scale was reversed so that a higher score implies a more positive evaluation of the intentions behind government regulation.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions. In the individual condition each participant makes her own decision. In the DDM condition a group of three participants makes a decision based on a majority rule, the final decision being the one with at least two votes. In the CDM condition all three members choose an investment option simultaneously, but the randomly assigned leader's choice becomes the final group decision regardless of what the followers choose. Group size was set to three, the smallest size that can follow a majority rule without a tie.

Weight on performance feedback in the exponential weighted average model, estimated separately for each condition. When an agent holds a belief about the expected payoff of an option and receives a payoff after choosing it, the updated belief is a weighted average of the existing belief and the feedback, with φ as the weight on that feedback; higher φ means a belief is adjusted to new information more quickly and the influence of old experiences fades away more rapidly. Parameters were found by a grid search over 0.01 ≤ φ ≤ 1 with 0.01 increments that maximized the likelihood of the observed choice sequences, averaging over 10,000 randomly generated sets of priors.

Parameter of the soft-max choice rule, estimated separately for each condition; the probability of choosing an option depends on its relative attraction, and τ moderates the effect of that relative attraction. When τ is high, the choice depends less on the subjective valuation of the investment options (more exploration); as τ approaches zero, the choice becomes more consistent with beliefs (less exploration). Estimated with the same grid search over 0.01 ≤ τ ≤ 1 with 0.01 increments.

The proportion of good investment decisions, i.e., choosing the option with the higher success probability, with the 100 rounds grouped into five time blocks for the intertemporal comparison of individuals, groups with DDM and groups with CDM.
level: individual or group, by time block

description: Binary variable coded 1 if one of the firm's large shareholders, board members, or top firm officers was a member of the legislature or the national or provincial executive; a cabinet member or agency chief; or a close relative (such as a sibling or spouse) of a top politician, and 0 otherwise. Thirty-seven ventures had political ties. All political ties were civilian.

Binary variable coded 1 when a high-ranking military officer (such as a colonel, general, or admiral) or a close relative (such as a sibling or spouse) of the high-ranking officer belonged to the airline's founding senior management team or advisory board or was a major investor at founding, and 0 otherwise. Fifty-seven of 282 ventures had military ties, and 37 (65%) of the military officers were retired.

The date of organizational failure is used as the dependent variable. Only airlines that ceased operation were designated as failed; those that were acquired were designated as exited and were dropped from the analysis.

Measured as the average change in imports and exports over a four-year running average. This variable was then reverse coded. A running average was used to capture trends in economic contraction and growth as well as to address any annual data aberrations.
Measured as the highest score for whether state lawmakers have substantial authority over policy, taxation, and disbursement of government funds, as well as the power to override executive vetoes.

Captured the volatility of political institutions by summing the number of revolutions or illegal or forced changes to the top government elite, or any attempt at such a change, in a given year and country.
Measured using the yearly sum of incidents of armed activity and violence that resulted in at least 500 directly related deaths over the course of a year.

The value of all components of the CEO's compensation for a specific year, including salary, bonuses, long-term incentives, and the value of options granted in that year. Higher total compensation is treated by the authors as an indication of less effective monitoring, so the measure is inversely related to the construct.

The ratio of the CEO's base salary to the total compensation he or she earned for the year, used to measure the salary portion of compensation that is not directly linked to organizational outcomes. A greater salary proportion indicates more behavioral-based compensation and hence more effective monitoring.

The ratio of options and bonus to the total compensation the CEO earned during the year, measuring the proportion of compensation contingent on firm-level outcomes both in the short term and in the long term. A higher contingent proportion indicates greater reliance on incentives and hence less effective monitoring.

The sensitivity of the options grant per $1,000 change in shareholder wealth, calculated following Yermack (1995) using the partial derivative of the Black-Scholes value of options grants. A sensitivity value of 1.13 indicates that the value of stock option compensation increased by $1.13 per $1,000 increase in shareholder value. It is described as an ex ante measure of performance sensitivity rather than an ex post measure such as changes in CEO pay; the printed specification of the partial derivative could not be read from the extracted text.
scale: dollars of option value per $1,000 change in shareholder wealth

description: The percentage of shares owned by the largest institutional owner in the focal firm, computed as the top institutional owner's shares divided by the firm's total number of outstanding shares. Data come from the CDA/Spectrum Thomson Financial 13F database. The measure captures the owner's influence at the firm level but, as the authors note, fails to account for owners' incentives to monitor from the portfolio perspective.

The average value of the investments in the institutional owner's portfolio, computed as the sum of portfolio weights (shares held times stock price) in firm k at the end of the year divided by the total number of stocks owned by the institution. It measures the tendency of the top institutional investor to hold large stakes in its portfolio. Because the variable is skewed and kurtotic, the authors apply a natural log transformation; the printed formula could not be read from the extracted text.
scale: average portfolio investment value in dollars (natural log)
time_window: end of year, lagged one year

description: A modified version of Bushee's (1998) measure of the proportion of the actual blockholdings in the institutional owner's portfolio, multiplied by 1 if the institutional owner is a blockholder in the focal firm and 0 otherwise. A portfolio holding counts as a block when the percentage holding in firm k is greater than or equal to 5%, and the focal firm is treated as a target when the percentage holding in it is greater than or equal to 5%. The printed formula could not be read from the extracted text.
scale: proportion of portfolio held in blocks
time_window: end of year, lagged one year

description: The trading behavior of the largest institutional investor, measured following Bushee (1998) as the average absolute change in the institution's ownership position over a quarter. Because increased turnover may be fueled by the fund's growth and availability, the shares traded are scaled by the fund's equity holdings at both the beginning and the end of the quarter. The authors take a natural log transformation to correct for skewness; the printed formula could not be read from the extracted text.
scale: average absolute quarterly change scaled by equity holdings (natural log)

description: The percentile ranking of the focal firm in the portfolio of its largest owner based on the dollar value of the investments, computed as 1 minus (position of the focal firm in the portfolio divided by the number of firms in the portfolio). The measure is inversed, so a higher number indicates that the focal firm is of greater importance to the institutional owner; the 99th percentile means that the investment in the focal firm exceeds in value 99% of the other investments in the portfolio.
scale: proportion (0-1) of the portfolio ranked below the focal holding
time_window: end of year, lagged one year

description: Dichotomous indicator equal to one if a fashion house used fur in a given year and zero otherwise. Whether a fashion house used fur in each year's Fall or Spring collections was determined using Vogue's runway reports, which provide detailed description of the elements used in all collections shown in the major fashion shows. Of the 670 fashion houses in the data set, 389 (about 58%) used fur at some point in the time window of the study.

variable_name: Vogue consideration of contestation over fur
description: Constructed by analyzing the text of Vogue runway collection reports over time; standard text processing was used to measure whether each Vogue review in the database referenced any ethics-related keywords. An initial set of keywords was identified by coding 200 randomly selected reports for terms related to ethical concerns, synonyms were added through several online thesauri, and an additional 100 randomly selected reviews were coded to make sure the expanded keyword list captured references to contestation-related concerns. The final list contained 35 distinct text strings or phrases related to the ethics of fur use and related production concerns, such as 'ethical*', 'cruel*', 'slaughter*', 'vegan*', 'animal free', and 'animal rights'. Figure 1 shows the proportion of runway collection reports that reference contestation each year from 2001 to 2018, with a steady increase starting around 2009 that rises in magnitude around 2014.
time_window: one year prior to each focal season (i.e., two seasons)

description: Counts events targeting the fashion houses in all four countries in the prior year; events covered in multiple newspapers or articles were counted once. Data were collected on all events surrounding the use of fur by fashion houses as reported in selected newspapers in France, Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States, using a mix of global and local online newspaper archives. Search terms for identification were ((antifur or profur) or (fur* and 'animal rights' and fashion) and (boycott* or protest* or campaign* or attack* or demonstrat*)), with similar terms used in French and Italian. For each event, information was collected on date and location, type of claim, form of event, targets of the event, and named associations and/or organizations involved.
time_window: prior year (one year prior to each focal season)

description: A network approach was used: a matrix was constructed in which columns and rows are fashion houses and the cells are the numbers of models the houses have in common. A Bonacich status measure was computed in which the centrality of a fashion house is determined by the centrality of the models to which it is connected. Higher-status houses have higher centrality and overlap in their hiring of higher-status models; examples of higher-status houses in the data set are Chanel, Christian Dior, Dolce & Gabbana, and Hermes, while houses such as Nanette Lepore, Randolph Duke, and Elie Tahari rest in the lower ranges of status.
time_window: one year prior to each focal season (i.e., two seasons)

variable_name: Extent of tacitness in overseas information
description: Measure adapted from Zander and Kogut (1995), covering three dimensions relevant to this context: complexity, codifiability, and observability of information about the differences among countries. When the information about the differences among countries was more complex, less codifiable, and more difficult to observe, that information was considered more tacit and less explicit. Respondents rated the characteristics of the information their project acquired from overseas locations (about differences among overseas markets, manufacturability in overseas plants etc.) on a 1-7 scale, using bipolar items running from simple to complex, easy to document in manuals or reports to difficult to document, easy to understand from written documents to difficult to understand, easy to precisely communicate through written documents to difficult to communicate, obvious to all competitors to subtle nuances known only to a few competitors, and easy to identify without personal experience in overseas locations to difficult to identify without such experience. Cronbach alpha 0.81.

Dummy variable denoting the presence or absence of overseas managers in the project team, used to measure co-location or the existence of cross-national teams. Measured as 1 if there were overseas members in the team, 0 otherwise.

variable_name: Teams with domestic members having prior overseas experience
description: Dummy variable denoting the presence or absence on the project team of domestic managers with prior overseas experience. Measured as 1 if the team had domestic members who were posted in overseas offices for at least a year, 0 otherwise.

Following Ghoshal et al. (1994), communication intensity was measured as the frequency of interactions between project members and overseas managers. Three items cover faxes to and from overseas managers, telephone conversations with overseas managers, and email to and from overseas managers, measured on a 1-7 scale running from 'Very rarely (once a year)' through 'Moderately (monthly)' to 'Very frequently (daily)'. Cronbach alpha 0.86.

Measure developed by integrating key indicators from previous related studies: frequency of new product introductions, order of market entry, simultaneous entry in multiple markets, the ability to be responsive to market requirements, the ability to be competitive in terms of price, and the ability to penetrate new overseas markets. Respondents rated, with respect to their key competitors, how their product category currently fares on these dimensions. Measured on a 1-7 scale from 'Much worse than competition' to 'About the same' to 'Much better than Competition'. Cronbach alpha 0.84.

Measure developed to test the predictive validity of the dependent variable. Following Venkatraman and Ramanujam (1987), it captured multiple dimensions of business performance-namely, how satisfied managers were, vis-à-vis their competitors, with their division's growth in sales, growth in market share, return on investment and return on sales.

Takes the value of '1' if the treatment allows for Firm B to engage in communication in the pre-acquisition stage, and 0 otherwise. It is implemented via a chat box: in treatments without prior communication only the two divisions within Firm A can discuss the situation and their decisions, whereas in treatments with prior communication the manager of Firm B can observe and participate in the discussions.

Implemented based on whether the manager of Firm B is able to make resource allocations in the pre-acquisition quarters. In the communication only and outright acquisition treatments only the two divisional managers of Firm A make resource allocations during the first three quarters, while in the complete alliance and allocation only treatments all three managers make resource allocation decisions.

In the models investigating Hypotheses 2 and 3, indicator variables for the organizational architecture treatments are used, e.g., complete alliance = 1 for observations drawn from that treatment and 0 otherwise. The outright acquisition treatment is the omitted category. The four treatments are complete alliance, allocation only, communication only and outright acquisition.

The dependent variable for H1-H3 and H5, measured as post-acquisition success: success is coded as '1' if the total resource allocations by all divisions meets or exceeds the threshold amount required for synergistic profits from combined activities, and '0' otherwise. Estimated with random effects logistic regression on group-quarters.

Takes the value of '1' if the threshold value was met during the pre-acquisition stage, and 0 otherwise. It is used as the measure of the performance of the pre-acquisition alliance in the analysis of the stickiness of routines.

Calculated based on the benefits received by Firm B relative to Firm A in the successful pre-acquisition rounds. The higher this ratio is, the less equitable the division of value, so a lower ratio indicates more equitable value appropriation. Estimated with random effects regression on the subset of rounds in which value creation succeeded.

Constructed similarly to the post-acquisition contribution ratio, that is, based on the relative resource contributions of the managers in the successful rounds of the pre-acquisition alliance stage. It serves as the independent variable capturing the resource allocation routines established during the alliance.

The dependent variable for H6, calculated as the contribution ratio of the manager of erstwhile Firm B relative to managers in Firm A, based on the contributions of each manager during successful post-acquisition rounds. Estimated with random effects regression.

Signal credibility in a given year is defined as the correlation between quality and warranty coverage for all brands that operated in that year in the U.S. market. It is the dependent variable of the industry-level models and is computed for each year of the sample. Figure 1 graphs, for each year, the correlation coefficient between warranty and quality across all brands.

Accuracy is assessed at the brand-year level through the association between brand quality and the powertrain warranty the brand offers. The authors estimate the warranty model separately for periods of high variance and periods of low variance and read accuracy from the sign and significance of the quality coefficient, with warranty coverage consistent with a signaling logic when quality and warranty are positively correlated.

A dummy variable coded as 1 during periods of high variance in warranty coverage and 0 during periods of low variance. The periods were identified with a discriminant analysis procedure applied to the annual variance of warranty coverage across brands, which yielded three high-variance periods (1962-1969, 1980-1990, and 2000-2008) and two low-variance periods (1970-1979 and 1991-1999). The underlying quantity is the variance of powertrain warranty miles across all brands in the U.S. market in a year.

The primary dependent variable is the number of miles stipulated in the powertrain warranty offered by a brand. Powertrain warranties cover the key components, namely the engine, transmission, and driveshaft, and provide coverage limited by the number of miles and the duration. The authors use the powertrain warranty rather than the basic warranty because it is emphasized more prominently by auto manufacturers, has greater variance across brands, and is modified more frequently.

Brand quality at time t, operationalized as an unweighted average of the quality of the individual models sold by each brand in each year. Model quality scores come from the annual Consumer Reports Buyer's Guide, whose automobile reviews focus strictly and solely on reliability and make no adjustment for price, size, power, mileage, or other attributes. Because Consumer Reports twice changed the format of the information during the sample period, the authors normalized the scale over those periods using simple linear transformations.

Pervasiveness of a particular name attribute within institutional fields, measured for each name attribute separately. For length it is the mean number of letters in organizational names; for ambiguity, the percentage of names coded as 0; and for domain specificity, the percentage of names coded as 0. Two-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes were used to measure institutional frames of reference, and firms were classified into industry groups.

variable_name: Old name's length, ambiguity, and domain specificity
description: Three attributes of the old organizational name, measured in the same manner as for new names. Interrater reliability was satisfactory for ambiguity and for domain specificity. These attributes of the old name were entered as independent variables predicting the corresponding new name attributes.
time_window: old name, prior to the name change

variable_name: New name's length, ambiguity, and domain specificity
description: New name's length was a count of the number of letters in the new organization name; letters rather than words were used in order to increase variance. New name's ambiguity measured the use of ambiguous, coined, or fabricated words, coded by two independent raters on a two-point scale: 0 for ambiguous names and 1 for names composed entirely of real words; interrater agreement was r = .94, and higher values indicated less ambiguous names. New name's domain specificity measured the extent to which names specifically described an organization's business, products, services, or operations, coded 0 for nonspecific names and 1 for specific names; interrater agreement was r = .85, and higher values indicated more domain-specific names. For institutional prevalence, positive values indicated greater name conformity.

Measured as a name's conformity and computed in a way comparable to assessments of strategic conformity for a single asset in previous research. The three name attributes (length, ambiguity, and domain specificity) were compared on institutional prevalence and expressed as standard deviations. Institutional prevalence was measured as in study 1.
scale: expressed as standard deviations from institutional prevalence

description: Assessed as the percentage of responses correctly categorizing an organizational name into an industry, and used as the measure of legitimacy. Respondents were asked to indicate, based only on the name, the industry suggested by each of ten actual organizational names; industry choices were manufacturing, food, chemicals, oil and gas, medical products/health care supplies, and telecommunications, and an industry could be chosen more than once. The percentage of correct responses varied substantially across the ten organizational names.

Dummy variable coded 1 for membership in utilitarian organizations and practices and 0 otherwise. Respondents were drawn according to their membership in utilitarian or ideological settings: M.B.A. students represented extensive employment in, and exposure to, institutionalized business practices and organizations, and adults in the arts or human services and liberal arts undergraduates represented little or no exposure to, or involvement in, utilitarian organizations and practices.

The total number of regulatory sanctions each year involving employees, consumers, environment, community, and others, as compiled by Violation Tracker from the federal, state, and local branches of around 50 regulatory bodies. The authors use a count variable because it is a less skewed measure than the penalties of firms' stakeholder management. Violation Tracker does not include penalty amounts below $5,000. All explanatory variables were lagged by one year.
time_window: annual count, lagged by one year

description: Coded 1 if a CEO is dismissed in a year, 0 otherwise. Dismissal data were compiled from Gentry et al. (2021), which documents the reasons for CEO departure (e.g., voluntary, involuntary) in S&P 1500 firms based on manual coding of news articles.

Language-based measure built on the agency dictionary of Pietraszkiewicz et al. (2019), which comprises 192 words such as 'able,' 'accomplish,' 'ambition,' 'completion,' 'dependable,' 'doable,' and 'mastering'. LIWC counted the total number of agency-related words each CEO spoke in conference calls each year, and the authors computed the proportion of these words to the total number of words spoken in conference calls that year. Only the management discussion sections of quarterly earnings calls with investors and analysts were used, and the annual score is the average across the calls a CEO attended that year.

Language-based measure built on the communion dictionary of Pietraszkiewicz et al. (2019), which comprises 184 words such as 'accord,' 'affinity,' 'care,' 'friend*,' 'kindly,' and 'public'. LIWC counted the total number of communion-related words each CEO spoke in conference calls each year, and the authors computed the proportion of these words to the total number of words spoken in conference calls that year. Only the management discussion sections of quarterly earnings calls with investors and analysts were used, and the annual score is the average across the calls a CEO attended that year.

Net CSR scores calculated by subtracting the 'concerns' scores from the 'strengths' scores in a given year, using the KLD database's ratings of CSR strengths (positive qualities) and concerns (negative issues) across areas such as product quality, employee relations, community relations, diversity, and environment.
time_window: annual (lagged by one year in the models)

description: The mean composite sentiment score (CSS) of a firm's news in a given year, based on RavenPack News Analytics. RavenPack assigns each news event a relevance score indicating the degree to which the firm is the focus of the article (0 = not relevant to 100 = very relevant) and a CSS ranging from 0 to 100 that combines five proprietary sentiment measures. The authors keep only news with a relevance score of 100 and then average the CSS by firm-year.
time_window: annual (lagged by one year in the models)

variable_name: Number of political ties with KMT
description: Count of the business group's political ties with the KMT, the ruling party under the united government of 1998. The authors combined formal position interlocks, obtained by matching the names of group leaders with lists of political actors, with informal ties, and then counted ties with each political party according to the party affiliation of each connected politician.

variable_name: Number of political ties with DPP
description: Count of the business group's political ties with the DPP, the ruling party with executive authority under the divided government after 2000. Ties were obtained by combining formal position interlocks (name matches between group leaders and political actors) with informal ties reported in the data sources, and counting ties per party by the affiliated politician's party.

variable_name: Number of political ties with DPP
description: Count of the business group's political ties with the DPP, the opposition party under the united government of 1998. Ties combine formal position interlocks with informal ties (familial/marital, friendship or same hometown, trade association and social club memberships), counted per party according to the connected politician's party affiliation.

variable_name: Number of political ties with KMT
description: Count of the business group's political ties with the KMT, the opposition party with legislative authority under the divided government after 2000. Ties combine formal position interlocks with informal ties reported in the data sources, counted per party according to the connected politician's party affiliation.

Diversity of portfolios measured with the Blau Index of Variability, computed as one minus the sum of the squared proportions of a focal business group's ties with each of the political parties, where the proportion is a party's share of all the group's political ties. The index ranges from 0 (a completely homogeneous portfolio) to 1 (a perfectly heterogeneous portfolio with political ties evenly distributed among all political parties); the printed equation is not legible in the text and the specification is described only in prose. The measure applies only to politically connected groups.

Count of the group's entries into new 2-digit SIC industries in two two-year periods, 1998 to 2000 and 2004 to 2006. The first author assigned a 4-digit SIC code to each member firm by matching product/service information to the Standard Industrial Classification of the Economic Ministry of Taiwan (2006), and the first two digits denote unrelated industries. Groups entered unrelated industries if 2-digit industries not present at time t appeared at time t + 2 in their industrial profiles, aggregating member firms' industry information to the group level.

The ratio of liability to total assets for the group, described by the authors as indicating the group's dependence on external financial resources. Independent variables were lagged by two years in all models.
time_window: lagged two years relative to the entry windows

description: The total number of market entries conducted by the group since 1990, the onset of large-scale economic liberalization in Taiwan. The authors treat it as the group's internal capability of market entry.

Number of reexamination certificates issued to firms other than firm i in technology class j in year t-1. The measure excludes instances where patents are subjected to but fail the reexamination process, and excludes certificates issued to firm i itself. Reexamination records are classified by USPTO technology class and matched to the NBER database by assigned patent numbers.

Number of patents firm i applied for in class j in year t that are subsequently granted. Counts of granted patents are measured at their application dates rather than grant dates. The variable is not scaled by the firm's inventive effort across all classes; that denominator is included as a control variable instead.

Average 'product, plant, and equipments' (PPE) across the firms other than firm i that are issued the reexamination certificates in class j, measured at year t-1. Fixed production assets like plants and equipment are used as an indication that firms with prior investments in these assets can implement subsequent production at faster speeds and have learned about other production activities.

variable_name: Rivals' downstream capabilities nonit-1 relative to focal firm's Downstream capabilities it-1
description: Comparison used to split the sample into two groups: whether the average downstream capabilities (PPE) of firms other than firm i that were issued reexamination certificates in class j in year t-1 is greater than the focal firm's own downstream capabilities (PPE) in year t-1. Columns report results for the group where rivals' capabilities are less than or equal to the focal firm's and the group where they are higher.

Average number of litigation cases initiated by the firms other than firm i that are issued reexamination certificates in class j, measured over the two years prior to year t-1. Litigation records include filing dates of lawsuits and the identities of plaintiffs and defendants.
time_window: two years prior to year t-1

description: The number of the focal firm's previous alliances that had the same functional type as the current alliance. Total alliance experience was counted as the number of the firm's alliances starting from January 1, 1990 to the event day, not including the new alliance, and the type of each alliance was identified from the activities performed by the alliance as reported by SDC, with major types being licensing services, R&D services, marketing services, manufacturing services, supply services, retail and wholesale services, and computer integration services. When the current alliance included more than one service, the principal service was used.
time_window: from January 1, 1990 to the event day

description: The number of the firm's previous alliances in which the partner(s) had the same four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code as the current partner. Previous multilateral alliances were included in computing this measure as long as at least one of the partners had the same SIC code as the partner in the current alliance.
time_window: from January 1, 1990 to the event day

description: The Blau index of variability (also known as the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of heterogeneity) computed on the number of the firm's previous alliances in each alliance-type category, where the percentage of a given category is denoted p_i. According to the index, a perfectly homogeneous group has an index value of 0, whereas a perfectly heterogeneous group receives a score of 1.
time_window: from January 1, 1990 to the event day

description: The Blau index computed on the number of the firm's previous alliances in each of eight broad industry groups, formed by aggregating the four-digit SIC codes of partners: agriculture; mining and construction; manufacturing; transportation, communications, and utilities; wholesale and retail; financial services; services; and public administration. The eight groups were used as a consistent base of categories across all firms, and the number of alliances in each group was then used to compute the Blau index.
time_window: from January 1, 1990 to the event day

description: Event-study measure of the market's expected value gain from an alliance. Standard event study methodology is described in the paper via a market model, but because the sample includes firms with multiple alliances within the same year the authors used value-weighted market returns as the expected normal returns and computed daily excess returns from that benchmark. The daily excess returns were cumulated over a five-day window from two days before the event day to two days after the event day, i.e., day -2 through day +2.

The extent to which a firm uses IT-based tools to capture and codify knowledge, measured by asking participants in the InformationWeek annual surveys to estimate the percentage of their knowledge assets and intellectual property data that are captured and accessible by current IT-based knowledge management procedures. Survey participants were the firms' senior IT executives such as chief information officers. The percentage reflects the firm's capability in cataloging knowledge formally or informally with the help of technologies such as groupware or teamware, systems for group memory or content management, tools for text/document search, systems for expertise profiling, and expert systems or artificial intelligence tools.

variable_name: Abnormal return on the announcement day (day 0)
description: The average abnormal return on the announcement day (day 0) is 0.26%, with 50.6% of the announcements resulting in positive gains; the authors report this descriptive statistic in prose as a check on the sample's wealth effect.

The proportion of stock options that are canceled, forfeited, expired, or terminated during each year. Its validity rests on the notion that firms typically give stock options only to a subset of key employees whom they particularly want to retain, and on prior research suggesting that a change in stock options is a good proxy for the loss of human capital as it typically occurs upon employee departure from the firm. The information was collected from the Compustat database, which comprises data available after 2004.

Return on assets, that is, net income divided by total assets. To account for potential time lag effects, the authors use the average ROA over 3 years. In robustness checks they also use ROA in year t and the average ROA over 2 years.

Each firm's 'employee relations' score (i.e., total strength score) from the KLD database, which annually compiles information on US firms' employee relationship practices and policies covering union relations, no-layoff policy, employee involvement, retirement benefits strength, and health and safety strength. A firm's EF relationship strength is coded 1 when its adjusted EF relationship score is higher than the industry median in the respective year, and 0 otherwise; a dummy is used rather than a continuous variable because the distribution of the KLD measure is highly skewed.

A dummy variable coded as 1 when a firm belongs to the treatment group, that is, firms identified from Compustat headquarters information as located within 50 miles of any operating nuclear plant, and 0 when it belongs to the control group of matching firms located between 100 and 150 miles away from a nuclear plant. Information about all operating nuclear power plants in the United States was gathered from the Union of Concerned Scientists.

A supplier is identified as novel by capturing when it is used for the first time within the focal technology category in the company's records. Because the authors theorize about the formation of new interorganizational ties, the dependent variable is operationalized with a binary indicator, assessed from the firm's weekly purchase order records that link each supplier choice to a project and a week.
time_window: weekly purchase records, assessed against all prior firm purchases

description: To measure the formal power of the initiator, the authors identify the individual listed as the orderer on a given supplier choice and use a binary measure to capture whether that person is a partner in the firm. Partnership is the clearest manifestation of formal power at Northern Automation: partners have ownership rights, sit on the board of directors, each have an equal vote, receive a portion of profits, participate in firm-level oversight, and have unrestricted access to information on worker performance and supplier histories. Removing a partner requires a 90% vote of partners, and empirically zero partners lost partnership status in the years studied.
time_window: focal week of the supplier choice

description: The authors identify the set of individuals who worked on the project during the week when the supplier choice occurred, excluding the initiator, and calculate the proportion of partners among them. This aggregate captures the formal power of the initiator's teammates on that purchase decision.
time_window: focal week of the supplier choice

description: Measured as the Bonacich (1987) beta measure of power centrality of the purchase orderer in the weekly collaboration network, calculated recursively so that a person's informal power is a function of both whom the individual has worked with and the informal power of those contacts. The networks are constructed from administrative records of weekly project assignments: a tie is assumed to be formed when two people work on the same project in the same week for at least five hours each, and to persist for 40 weeks (the median project duration) after the last time the two worked together. Moving-window networks correspond to week 41 through week 691, each based on dyadic collaborations during the focal week and the preceding 40 weeks, and centrality was computed with the igraph package in R.
time_window: focal week, with the network built from the focal week and the preceding 40 weeks

description: The average Bonacich power centrality of the other team members, that is, of the initiator's teammates in a given week, calculated from the same weekly collaboration networks used to measure initiator informal power. It captures the informal power held by those who respond to the initiator's proposal.
time_window: focal week, with the network built from the focal week and the preceding 40 weeks

description: A continuous variable measuring the natural log of the geographic distance between the customer in a focal contract and the closest Compustar office. During the sample period Compustar had five U.S. offices (including headquarters) staffed with IT professionals and sales personnel.

Captures the cost of measuring quality after project completion and is based primarily on technological aspects. Compustar personnel coded measurement as 1 if quality was difficult to determine and 0 if it was readily apparent, using as criterion whether a brief, inexpensive test or inspection could determine the quality of the work done.
scale: 0 = quality readily apparent, 1 = quality difficult to determine

description: Information on the level of business each customer had completed with Compustar prior to a focal project measured this effect. Compustar developed a Likert-type variable for relationship breadth capturing the extent of non-IT services provided by Compustar for each customer.
scale: 1 (no prior ties in other lines of business) to 7 (one of the largest customers outside of IT services)

description: Coded 1 if a project had the potential to produce knowledge that Compustar could reuse for projects with other customers and 0 otherwise. Compustar engineers coded reuse on the basis of examination of the contract for a project, not project execution.

Coded 1 if an IT services contract allowed the buyer the unilateral right to extend the project and 0 otherwise. If a provision was included, rights were granted to the buyer but not to the supplier (Compustar). Of the 385 contracts in the sample, 55 included an extendibility provision.

Coded 1 if a contract allowed the buyer the unilateral right to terminate the project prior to completion and 0 otherwise. If a provision was included, rights were granted to the buyer but not to the supplier (Compustar). Of the 385 contracts in the sample, 51 included an early termination provision.

A count measure, firm-specific and time invariant, of the number of distributors that a firm had in the predisruption period 1975-1980. The information was collected from the secondary directories, especially the AMTDA directory. The analysis is restricted to firms that had at least two distributors.

A firm-specific, time-variant measure built in several steps. First, the four most significant performance features affecting machine tool flexibility were identified: spindle rotation per minute, rapid traverse in inches per minute, the number of axes, and the number of spindles. Second, a hedonic OLS regression of the log of a machine tool's price on its performance features was estimated for products introduced from 1981 through 1987 and its coefficients used to weight the four performance dimensions. Third, the most flexible disruptive product in each of eight lathe-based product classes was taken as the product farthest from the origin in the four-dimensional weighted space. Fourth, the measure is the angle between the vector describing the product a U.S. incumbent introduced in a product class and the vector of the most flexible disruptive product in that same product class, so a smaller angle means a greater match.
scale: angle in degrees between product vectors

description: Each partner's technological portfolio is generated by measuring the distribution of its patents across patent classifications, year by year, captured by a multidimensional vector whose elements are the number of patents assigned to the partner in each patent class. Diversity between a pair of partners is computed from these vectors; the exact specification is given in a formula block that is unreadable in the available text, and the text states only that the measure varies from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating the greatest possible technological diversity between partner firms. The measure is not sensitive to the number of patents in a class and captures differences between partners based on diversity rather than volume. For an alliance involving more than two firms, the measure is calculated for every combinatorial pair of firms in the alliance and averaged. The square of the measure, technological diversity squared, is also included to capture the expected nonlinear relationship.
level: alliance (pair of firms, averaged over pairs for multilateral alliances)
time_window: four years prior to alliance commencement

description: Count of citation-weighted firm patents in a four-year postalliance window: each patent is assigned a weight based on citations made by later patents, since ex post citations are correlated with the estimated value of the underlying invention. A one-year lag is imposed between alliance commencement and firm patenting, and the patent application date is used, so that an alliance commencing in 1993 is measured from weighted patents applied for in 1994-97. Patent portfolios are constructed for each firm at the corporate level, aggregating patents assigned to the parent firm and to all of its subsidiaries.
time_window: four years following a one-year lag after alliance commencement

description: Dummy variable created from information provided by SDC that equals 1 when an alliance is organized by equity joint venture and 0 when it is organized by bilateral contract.

Sum of the number of protests against wood pellet resource suppliers by state and year of the focal firm, logged to normalize the distribution. The data were obtained by searching and coding more than 73,650 local newspaper articles from Access World News. The variable is lagged by one year.

Total number of lawsuits filed in a state and year of the focal firm that sought to prevent timber harvesting and wood processing, summed and logged. The state is used as a natural boundary because forestry lawsuits are generally bounded by state lines. The variable is lagged by one year.

Sum of the number of protests against individual wood pellet producers, obtained by searching newspaper articles from Access World News, matching the protest to the pellet producer's name and address, and eliminating duplicate articles from the count. The variable is lagged by one year. None of the pellet producers were sued by forest-conservation activists in the study period.

Full-text searches of each article with a dictionary of renewable-biomass-energy keywords generated an overall frequency score per article, represented as the frequency of words from the dictionary per 1,000 words in the article. The words-per-thousand scores were then summed by firm and year. A total of 829 articles comprising 196 press releases and 633 news pieces were identified; each article was matched to the specific pellet venture that either issued a statement or was interviewed. Coding reliability against manual coders was substantial.
scale: words from the dictionary per 1,000 words, summed by firm and year

description: Averaging the renewable-biomass-energy frame score of all other pellet firms within the focal pellet firm's state and year. The variable is lagged by one year.
The number of pellet-venture new entrants and firm exits divided by the total number of pellet firms operating in a given state and year. The variable is lagged by one year.

A binary measure capturing whether and when a state's Renewables Portfolio Standard (RPS) included wood pellets on its list of renewable-energy sources. Inclusion in an RPS is a signal that the state's government recognizes the ventures' renewable-energy identity claims as legitimate.

Yearly operating costs (XOPR in Compustat) are deflated by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Producer Price Index by stage of processing for intermediate materials, supplies, and components. Deflated IT labor and non-IT labor are subtracted from the operating costs, and the result is subtracted from yearly sales (SALE in Compustat), which are deflated by the BEA Gross Domestic Product Price Index for gross output for private industries. All monetary values are converted to 2013 dollars and reported in millions of dollars.

Built from the number and type of operating systems used at the firm as reported in the Harte Hanks survey. For each site the number of server operating systems is evenly split over the total number of servers at the site, and the same is done for PCs, yielding an estimate of how many instances of a given type of operating system exist at the site; this is aggregated to the firm level, divided by the number of sites at the firm in the Harte Hanks database, and multiplied by the total number of sites in the firm to impute firm-wide values. One is added before taking the natural log because the number of operating systems in a category can be zero.

Constructed by calculating the total number of noncommercial open source operating systems at the firm, following the same site-level splitting, firm-level aggregation and firm-wide imputation used for the overall OSS measure. One is added before taking the natural log because the number of operating systems in a category can be zero.

Constructed by calculating the total number of commercial open source operating systems at the firm, following the same site-level splitting, firm-level aggregation and firm-wide imputation used for the overall OSS measure. One is added before taking the natural log because the number of operating systems in a category can be zero.

Binary variable that is 1 if the firm has ever contributed to Linux and 0 otherwise. It is constructed from Linux Foundation contribution records, in which each contribution is linked to a firm when the contributor was paid by the firm to contribute, and it is used to separate contributing firms from matched noncontributing firms.

The number of individual contributors at the firm in a given year, regardless of the type of contribution they make, constructed from the unique email address attributed to each contribution. Because of the high skew in the measure, the natural log is taken after adding one to each observation.

The number of changesets written by individuals at the firm in a given year, that is, the number of changes to the Linux code the firm made. Because of the high skew in the measure, the natural log is taken after adding one to each observation.

The number of sign-offs made by individuals at the firm in a given year; every code change requires at least one experienced contributor to sign off on the code, and these sign-offs are marked with email addresses, allowing them to be counted and attributed to firms. Because of the high skew in the measure, the natural log is taken after adding one to each observation.

variable_name: OSS output elasticity and its interactions with contribution
description: Returns to OSS use are the output elasticity of OSS in a log-linear production function with value added as output. They are estimated as the coefficient on ln(OSS) and, for contributors, as the additional elasticity from its interactions with the contribution measures (Contrib, NumCont, NumChng, NumSign).

variable_name: Prior plant locations by other firms (log)
description: Calculated as the log of the count of prior plant locations by all the Japanese firms in the sample in a given country in each year. A plant location in 1990 would not appear in the data until 1991, and years of operational experience receive a diminishing weight as they recede into the past. The count includes all prior plant locations on which the authors had data, including those before 1990.
time_window: annual, lagged (a 1990 entry first appears in 1991)

variable_name: Prior plant locations by firms in the same industry (log)
description: Calculated as the log of the count of prior plant locations in a given country by all Japanese firms in the same industry group prior to the establishment of a focal firm's foreign subsidiary. Industry is defined using a Japanese analogue to the 2-3-digit Standard Industrial Classification level, as categorized in the Nikkei NEEDS tapes.
time_window: annual, lagged (prior to the focal firm's subsidiary)

variable_name: Prior plant locations by firms in the same business group (log)
description: Measured as the log of the count of prior plant locations in a given country by all firms in the same horizontal keiretsu. Membership in one of the six main horizontal keiretsu was identified using the classification in Industrial Groupings in Japan, with membership in the President's Council as the criterion.

Taken from Henisz (2000a), it measures the extent to which a change in the preferences of any one actor may lead to a change in government policy, based on the number of independent branches of government with veto power and on the alignment and preference heterogeneity across branches. Possible scores for a given country in a given year range from 0 (minimal hazards) to 1 (extremely hazardous).

An indicator variable equal to one when the measure of firm-specific experience in the prospective host country was non-zero. The authors used coefficient estimates obtained by interacting this indicator variable with other independent variables to test hypotheses 3a-3d.

Computed as the log of the sum of subsidiary years of manufacturing experience in a prospective host country. It is the measure of firm-specific uncertainty whose direct effect the authors control for but do not hypothesize about.

variable_name: International experience of investing firm (log years)
description: Based on a firm's investment history internationally. Computed as the log of the sum of subsidiary years of international (outside the prospective host country) experience.

Dummy variable that equals 1 if firm x locates a manufacturing plant in country i at time t, and 0 otherwise. There were 2,123 firm-country-years in which a plant location occurred. The sample includes both joint ventures and wholly owned manufacturing plants.

A cumulative count of diversifying strategic changes over the observed history of a firm. Each firm began with a value of 0; after the first change of this type the counter was set at 1, after the second at 2, and so on. Only diversifying changes were counted, because too few instances of changes involving decreased diversification existed to be used in the analyses.

A cumulative count of decentralizing structural changes over the observed history of a firm. Each firm began with a value of 0; the counter was incremented by one after each change of this type. Only decentralizing changes were counted, because too few instances of increased centralization existed to be used in the analyses.

An elapsed time clock that began with a value of 0 and, after the occurrence of the first diversifying change, recorded the number of years, in monthly increments, since that change. After each subsequent change the clock was reset to 0 and again recorded the years since the most recent change until the end of the observation period.

An elapsed time clock that began with a value of 0 and, after the occurrence of the first decentralizing change, recorded the number of years, in monthly increments, since that change. After each subsequent change the clock was reset to 0 and again recorded the years since the most recent change until the end of the observation period.

A variable recording the number of categories moved in the most recent change of strategy; it took a value of 0 until the first change. After the first change it recorded the difference between the starting category and the ending category and kept this value until another change of the same type occurred, when it was updated.

A variable recording the number of categories moved in the most recent change of structure; it took a value of 0 until the first change. After the first change it recorded the difference between the starting category and the ending category and kept this value until another change of the same type occurred, when it was updated. For example, a move from the functional category to the holding company category produced a magnitude-of-change value of 3.

variable_name: acquiring firm's industry seller concentration ratio
description: Four-firm seller concentration ratio of the acquiring firm's industry, the proportion of industry sales accounted for by the four largest sellers, taken at the four-digit SIC level from the Census of Manufacturers published in the year closest to an announcement. The study group was expanded by 18 more bidder firms by obtaining data at the three-digit SIC level, on the assumption that concentration levels at the three- and four-digit levels are similar.
time_window: Census of Manufacturers year closest to the merger announcement

variable_name: target firm's industry seller concentration ratio
description: Four-firm seller concentration ratio of the target firm's industry, the proportion of industry sales accounted for by the four largest sellers, taken at the four-digit SIC level from the Census of Manufacturers published in the year closest to an announcement. The study group was expanded by 1 more target firm by obtaining data at the three-digit SIC level.
time_window: Census of Manufacturers year closest to the merger announcement

description: Computed by combining buyer and seller concentration ratios: it equals the target firm's seller concentration ratio over its buyer concentration ratio if the acquiring firm is downstream, and the acquiring firm's buyer concentration ratio over its seller concentration ratio if the target firm is downstream. The buyer concentration ratio of an upstream industry weights the seller concentration ratios of the downstream industries by the proportion of the upstream industry's output that each of them uses, so that the relative market power of the two stages, not just the concentration of one of them, is captured.

The cumulative abnormal return for the acquiring firm over a prediction period starting 50 trading days before the first announcement of a merger (day 0) and ending 5 days after it, standardized by the estimated variance of the abnormal returns to correct for heteroscedasticity. Abnormal returns are generated by a market model that regresses the firm's daily returns on the daily returns of the market portfolio, estimated over the period from 200 to 51 trading days before the announcement, with the parameters estimated using CRSP return data. The standardized cumulative abnormal return has an asymptotically normal distribution.
time_window: -50 to +5 trading days relative to the first announcement

description: The cumulative abnormal return for the target firm over a prediction period starting 50 trading days before the first announcement of a merger (day 0) and ending 5 days after it, standardized by the estimated variance of the abnormal returns. Abnormal returns are generated by a market model estimated by regressing the firm's daily returns on the daily returns of the market portfolio over the period from 200 to 51 trading days before the announcement.
time_window: -50 to +5 trading days relative to the first announcement

description: The average cumulative abnormal return for the rivals of each acquiring firm over the same prediction period, standardized. Rivals were identified from the CRSP tapes as firms whose primary four-digit SIC codes were the same as those of the acquiring firms at the times of the merger announcements.
time_window: -50 to +5 trading days relative to the first announcement

description: Percentage change in a company's car sales revenues from the beginning of one 3-year period to the end of the same period. Revenues were determined by multiplying the total unit production for each product by an average sales price. Average sales prices were those in the U.S. market, adjusted to 1991 prices, and prices for products not available for purchase in the U.S. market were estimated from equivalent U.S. products with respect to size and equipment levels.

Number of new product introductions divided by the number of product offerings in the base year, calculated for each manufacturer in each 3-year period. A new product is a car newly introduced with mostly new interior and exterior styling, as opposed to a product with a minor facelift or a variation consisting of minor cosmetic modifications. Variations designed within a single project or within a multibrand project were counted as only one new product.

variable_name: usage of the rapid design transfer strategy (%)
description: Percentage of the new car products introduced by a firm during a 3-year period that followed the rapid design transfer strategy. Rapid design transfers are projects where the transfer from a base project occurred within 2.0 years of the introduction of the base design. Strategy classification used a point scheme based on changes in platform technology and design, primarily changes in wheelbase and tracks and in the suspension.

variable_name: usage of the sequential design transfer strategy (%)
description: Percentage of the new car products introduced by a firm during a 3-year period that followed the sequential design transfer strategy. Sequential transfers are projects that shared platform designs with preceding projects for other product lines with a transfer time lag of more than 2.0 years. Strategy classification used the same point scheme based on platform changes.

variable_name: usage of the new design strategy (%)
description: Percentage of the new car products introduced by a firm during a 3-year period that followed the new design strategy. Projects were categorized as new design when they developed new platform designs without any preceding base design.

variable_name: usage of the design modification strategy (%)
description: Percentage of the new car products introduced by a firm during a 3-year period that followed the design modification strategy. Among projects derived from an existing platform, those which developed a new product based on the platform design of the predecessor model were categorized as design modifications.

An index built from CEOs' language patterns in the question-and-answer portions of quarterly conference calls. Three component indicators were computed for each call: the number of differentiation words divided by all of the CEO's Q&A words; the number of weak modal words divided by the sum of weak and strong modal words; and the number of comparative words divided by all words spoken by the CEO. The three items were standardized and averaged to compute a CEO's cognitive complexity score for each quarter t.
Measured as the number of quarters that the CEO had been in office as of quarter t. The data came from ExecuComp and BoardEx.

Built from the long-term volatility of stock returns in each industry. The standard deviation of daily returns was first calculated for each firm covered by CRSP over the entire sampling timeframe, then aggregated to the industry level (two-digit SIC codes) by taking the median size-weighted value of the firms' volatilities, and finally standardized. Size weighting was based on firms' average market capitalizations over the sampling timeframe.

A dummy variable coded to indicate whenever an industry's dynamism in the 45 days before a focal conference call was more than three times its level of systemic dynamism. With this coding threshold, which the authors deemed as indicating an extraordinary burst of dynamism relative to the industry's baseline tendency, there were 67 industry jolts in the sample.
time_window: 45 days before the focal conference call

description: An index consisting of three standardized indicators: duality, coded to one when the CEO was also board chair; percentage of company shares owned by the CEO; and percentage of directors who were appointed after the start of the CEO's tenure. These data came from ExecuComp, ISS RiskMetrics, and BoardEx.

Executive informants were asked to identify and rank each airline's (including their own) top five competitors by standing in the shoes of each airline. Rankings were converted to scores in which the airline rated as the top-ranked competitor received 5, the second 4, and so forth, while airlines not included in the ranking received 0. The focal firm's ranking of a target rival's competitors was compared with the rival's own ranking by a measure of dissimilarity (Euclidean distance) between the two vectors of scores. The dissimilarity score was then reversed and rescaled by a linear transformation so that the acumen score ranged between 0 and 1, approaching unity as the distance approaches zero; the formula blocks in the payload are unreadable, so the exact equation is a gap.

Following Chen (1996), the authors calculated for each pair of airlines an index of airline i's direct market engagement with another airline j, summed over the routes k served by both i and j. The index combines the relative importance of route k to airline i (i's passengers in route k divided by i's passengers across all routes) with airline j's market share in route k (j's passengers in route k divided by all airlines' passengers in route k). To take competitive relativity into account, the raw engagement value was normalized by the total engagements of i, so that the sum of the market engagement indexes across a firm's rivals equals 1; the formula block in the payload is unreadable, so the exact equation is a gap.

The authors first created a network of market-engagement relationships among all possible pairs of firms in the sample, then followed Burt (1987, 1992) and used UCINET to calculate, for each rival firm j that has direct contact with focal firm i, how many of i's other rivals are also tied to j. The measure combines the proportion of i's direct contact invested in the relationship with another airline q and the marginal strength of j's direct contact with q (j's direct contact with q divided by the strongest of j's direct contacts with any firm). The value is large when the proportion of i's network that connects to j is substantial.

Measured at the dyad-market level following Ferrier et al. (1999), the variable captures the change in the market share gap between focal firm i and a given rival j in a route. The logarithm of the ratio of the target rival's market share to the focal firm's market share indicates the gap between their market shares in a particular year, and the formula reflects the difference between the market share gap in 1990 and the market share gap in 1991; the formula block in the payload is unreadable, so the exact equation is a gap. A positive value indicates that the focal firm was able to gain more market share relative to the rival, while a negative value represents the opposite situation.

The authors examined an airline's resource deployment capability by looking at how dominant or active the airline is relative to a given rival at both endpoints (original and destination airports) of a route, on the reasoning that an airline with significant market share at both endpoints has many flights to various destinations and can quickly redeploy fleets and staff. The measure is the logarithm of the ratio between the focal firm's average endpoint market share and a rival's average endpoint market share.

variable_name: CEO - HPE pay disparity (unscaled components and CEO - HPE pay ratio)
description: ExecuComp total direct compensation (TDC1) for the incumbent CEO (CEO pay) and for the highest paid non-CEO executive (HPE pay), each measured for the fiscal year ending before the succession announcement date; TDC1 contains salary, bonuses, and the value of stock awards. Outliers were systematically reviewed: pay that changed by a factor of two or more year-over-year was deemed an outlier, and each outlier was reviewed to adjust for abnormal pay such as hiring bonuses and severance payments. The hypotheses are tested twice, first with each component as an unscaled predictor and second with the ratio of CEO pay to HPE pay while controlling for each component.
scale: US dollars; ratio of CEO pay to HPE pay
level: individual executive (firm fiscal year before the event)
time_window: fiscal year ending before the succession announcement date

description: Dichotomous variable: 1 = outside succession; 0 = inside succession. Successors were coded as inside if they joined the focal firm at least 6 months before the official announcement date that the incumbent CEO would be exiting, to limit changes in compensation that may have been related to the announcement of a succession plan. 285 of 830 (34.34%) events were classified as outside successions.

Count of succession committee members also serving on the compensation committee (range = 0-10; mean = 2.44). The most recent proxy filing before the announcement date determined the succession committee and the directors who served on each committee. If the compensation committee had succession responsibility, or if the full board was responsible, CS linking pin directors equals the number of compensation committee members; when no committee was specified as responsible for CEO succession planning, or no compensation committee members had succession planning responsibilities, the observation was coded zero.
time_window: most recent proxy filing before the announcement date

description: Computed as the mean of the sum of the number of times each player has played against each of their teammates in the past. Complete familiarity measures are computed for all focal players (egos) from their full match histories, while measures for nonfocal players (alters) are incomplete; mean levels of prior interaction are used rather than totals to account for anonymous players with unknown familiarity. The measure is entered in logs in the regressions so the coefficient can be interpreted as a marginal effect/elasticity.
time_window: full careers from the inception of the game in 2011 through the end of 2016

description: Following previous studies (Reagans et al. 2005), computed as the mean of the sum of the number of times each player has played on the same team with each of their teammates in the past. Complete measures are computed for focal players from their full match histories, including matches in which teams were endogenously formed, and averaged at the team level. The measure is entered in logs in the regressions.
time_window: full careers from the inception of the game in 2011 through the end of 2016

description: Indicator set equal to one if the focal team wins the match and zero otherwise. Using victory to measure the outcome of team efforts follows common practice among scholars studying the organizational performance of traditional sports teams and is particularly germane because a player's ranking (MMR), and hence status and tournament eligibility, is completely determined by team outcomes. One team is selected from each match to avoid double counting, with all information about their opponents included as control variables.

Constructed in three steps: the presumed home server (the server closest to the player) is identified for each player, and then the team indicator is set equal to one if at least one team member is playing on a nonhome server and no players on the opponent team are playing on a nonhome server, and zero otherwise. The opponent version is constructed in parallel. Approximately 34% of all matches feature such mismatches, 17% in each direction.

CEO agentic value display equals the total number of agentic words used by a CEO during the presentation sections of all earnings calls in a year, scaled by the total number of words spoken by the CEO in the presentations of these same calls. The dictionary is the customized agentic value dictionary of Pietraszkiewicz et al. (2019), which contains 192 distinct adjectives and verbs; only the presentation section of calls, not the Q&A period, is analyzed. CEO relative agentic value display is the difference between a CEO's agentic value display and the average agentic value display of all other CEOs belonging to the same Fama-French 17 industry group, after excluding the focal CEO.
scale: share of words spoken; relative measure in deviation units

description: A dummy equal to one in the year a firm is targeted by an activist shareholder and zero otherwise. Targets were identified from Schedule 13D and 13D/A filings by shareholders who acquired more than 5% of a class of security with the intent to influence or control management, restricted to institutional investors (hedge funds and non-hedge fund institutional investors) and to filings whose stated purpose pertained to control, disputes, concerns, or discussion.

variable_name: Categorical activism variable (value of one for control activism)
description: A categorical dependent variable assigned a value of one if a firm-year was associated with 'control' activism and zero if the firm-year was associated with no shareholder activism; the zero case serves as the baseline in the multinomial logit model. 'Control' includes intent to acquire control of the company, intent to change or nominate individuals to the board of directors, and intent to replace management.
scale: categorical (0 = no activism, 1 = control activism, 2 = noncontrol activism)

variable_name: Categorical activism variable (value of two for noncontrol activism)
description: A categorical dependent variable assigned a value of two if a firm-year was associated with 'noncontrol' activism, that is, filings whose stated purpose pertained to disputes, concerns, or discussion, and zero if the firm-year was associated with no shareholder activism. 'Disputes' consist of allegations about misleading management, disagreements with management actions, disputes with management, and litigation; 'concerns' include concerns about stock price performance, opposition to a future acquisition, demands for information, and suggestions about strategy; 'discussion' includes holding or requesting discussions with management.
scale: categorical (0 = no activism, 1 = control activism, 2 = noncontrol activism)

description: Measured as the natural logarithm of the total spending on R&D, acquisitions, and new capital, as reported in Compustat. The three components are treated as one category of difficult-to-reverse, long-term outlays of resources.

Data came from the environment, community, product, employee, and diversity dimensions of the MSCI KLD database, which covers both strengths and concerns of each stakeholder dimension. For each dimension, a company's total number of strengths (concerns) is first divided by the respective number of strength (concern) indicators in a given year, and the difference between the adjusted strength and concern values is taken to measure investment in that stakeholder group. Stakeholder investment is then calculated as the sum of each score for the five dimensions in a year.
scale: sum of adjusted strength-minus-concern dimension scores

description: The total number of times task i is performed by physicians belonging to a given specialty s in quarter t. It comes from the Canadian Institute for Health Information's proprietary National Physician Database and is based on physicians reporting the tasks they perform to the MOHLTC to ensure they get paid for their work. The average task volume for a task–physician specialty pair is 1,625, though the median is 1, indicating the data are right-skewed; the log-transformed task volumes have a mean of 1.7 and standard deviation of 2.41.

The dollar amount paid to a physician, by the MOHLTC, when the physician performs a particular task. In this sample, the average task fee is $193 CDN (with a standard deviation of $270 CDN); the log-transformed fees have a mean of 4.52, and there is considerably more variation in fees across tasks than within. In the regressions the task fee variable is centered at its mean to aid in interpretation of the interaction effects and intercept.

For each task–physician specialty combination, the share of the task's total volume that is provided by that specialty for a given quarter t. The formula for the measure is not readable in the text supplied, so the specification is taken from the authors' prose description. The measure has an average value of 17.5%, meaning that on average a given physician specialty performs 17.5% of a given task; the variable is bimodal, with many zeros and many one hundreds. The log-transformed variable has a mean of 1.25 and a standard deviation of 1.74.
scale: share of a task's total volume, 0 to 100% (log-transformed)

description: For each task–physician specialty combination, the share of the specialty's total volume that is represented by task i in a given quarter t. The formula for the measure is not readable in the text supplied, so the specification is taken from the authors' prose description. On average, the jurisdictional prominence of a task is 0.08%, meaning that on average a task represents 0.08% of a specialty's total task volume; the maximum is 43%. The log-transformed measure has a mean of 0.03 and a standard deviation of 0.19.
scale: share of a specialty's total volume, 0 to 100% (log-transformed)

description: The firm-level stock of overdue wages, reported by a top manager of each sampled firm in each year from 1991 to 1998. Managers usually expressed this stock in terms of monthly wage bills, so the variable is measured in months of wage arrears. The standard measure of the amount of wage arrears in Russia in balance sheets, official statistics, and the minds of workers is this stock of overdue wages.
scale: months of the monthly wage bill

description: A dummy variable for whether the firm had any wage arrears in a particular year, constructed from the reported stock of monthly wage arrears. It captures any use of the wage arrears practice, in contrast to the continuous months measure.

The average stock of wage arrears among the sampled agricultural and industrial firms in the firm's raion. The variable refers to a firm's raion in the previous year. Russian raions are distinct administrative units below oblast governments, similar in size to U.S. counties, and are the unit used to bound the communities around which the hypotheses were developed.
scale: months of the monthly wage bill

description: The share (proportion) of organizations in the firm's raion using wage arrears. In both cases the variable refers to a firm's raion in the previous year. It is the frequency-based counterpart to the intensity-based months measure of the community norm.

Quit rates for each year are calculated by dividing total voluntary separations by average employment for the corresponding year. The data are obtained from the survey with reference to annual employment reports to Goskomstat (the P-4 form).

A dummy variable for the incidence of strikes, measured through survey questions to top managers on whether work protests had occurred at their firms. Conventional work stoppages and, in a few cases, hunger strikes, demonstrations, and slowdowns were reported. The survey asks for the main motivation for each protest, and more than 90 percent of the responses report wage arrears as the cause.
