Indicates how much the SBU's planning process is formalized, is strictly implemented, and is explicit in terms of defining long-term objectives, generating alternatives, and monitoring results. The measure is a five-item scale from Armstrong (1982). The variable was centered at the middle of the scale for the estimation of interaction effects; item details are in Appendix S1.

The number of NPD projects initiated during the previous 12 months at the SBU level; it captures the firm's innovative activity (as defined by Mellahi and Wilkinson, 2008). Respondents referred only to the NPD projects of the NPD teams within their own SBU.
The SBU's ROI as a percentage one year following the first survey; it measures the firm's financial performance.
time_window: one year following the first survey

description: The number of years from the SBU's establishment to the year of the survey. The variable was centered at its mean for the estimation of interaction effects.

Measured with a three-item scale adopted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993), indicating the degree to which a firm makes decisions with uncertain expected outcomes, with hard-to-achieve decision goals, and with potential outcomes that include some extreme consequences. The variable was centered at the middle of the scale for the estimation of interaction effects.

Measured with a three-item scale also adopted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993), capturing the extent to which evaluations and rewards of employees are based on the accumulation of new knowledge and its use in idea generation. The variable was centered at the middle of the scale for the estimation of interaction effects.

Corporate strategy was classified into four categories according to the share of turnover contributed by the core business: single business, dominant business, related diversification and unrelated diversification. The category was reported by the CEO in the questionnaire for each of the two years, 1993 and 2003. For the analysis, single business and dominant business were grouped as nondiversified firms, and related and unrelated diversification as diversified firms.

A firm's structure was classified into four categories following Rumelt (1974): functional, functional-with-subsidiaries, holding and multidivisional. The structure was reported by the CEO in the questionnaire for 1993 and 2003. In the analysis, functional includes functional-with-subsidiaries and is treated as non-divisionalized, while holding and multidivisional are treated as divisionalized; the holding structure is not included among non-divisionalized firms.

Middle managers rated their immediate superior's (i.e., a top executive's) humility with Ou et al.'s (2014) 19-item humility measure (alpha = .93). Items were answered with Likert-type scales ranging from 'Strongly disagree' (1) to 'Strongly agree' (6). Because there were insufficient MMs sampled per top executive, the authors did not aggregate MM perceptions by top executive, so the measure stays at the individual MM level.
level: individual (MM rating of a top executive)

description: Job satisfaction was evaluated with three items (alpha = .89) from Bono and Judge (2003), answered on Likert-type scales ranging from 'Strongly disagree' (1) to 'Strongly agree' (6). One item is reverse coded. MMs reported their own job satisfaction at Time 2.

HR managers reported each incidence of turnover, whether it was voluntary or not, and provided specific turnover reasons; the authors verified HR managers' designation of turnover voluntariness with their own coding based on turnover reasons, following Campion's (1991) classification system. The turnover index coded voluntary turnover as 1 if employees quit due to dissatisfaction with the company, pay, or supervisors; better career opportunities elsewhere; further education; health issues or pregnancy; or family migration, and coded turnover as 0 when employees left due to retirement or layoffs, or when employees remained employed.

TMT faultlines were computed as a multiplicative product of faultline strength and faultline distance. Faultline strength was measured using Thatcher, Jehn, and Zanutto's (2003) algorithm, based on multivariate clustering analysis, and captures the percentage of total variation in overall group characteristics accounted for by the strongest group split; faultline distance was calculated as the Euclidean distance between vectors of attribute means for two subgroups. Faultlines were operationalized with six commonly used demographic attributes: age, gender, education level, education specialization, company tenure, and team tenure; functional background, ethnicity, and nationality were omitted because they showed no variance in the sampled companies.

The natural logarithm of the number of outlets in the franchise system in the year of observation. The authors state that the number of outlets in the system is a good measure of size and that changes in this variable represent system size. In the fixed-effects model the dependent variable is the log of the total number of outlets in the franchise system.

The percentage of sales that franchisees must pay to the franchisor in the year of observation. Following Shane and Foo (1999), if the franchise system reported a range of royalty rates the average rate is calculated, and if a flat dollar amount of royalty was reported this amount is divided by the industry average level of sales for an outlet to normalize the variable. Entered in the model as the log of one plus the royalty rate.

The dollar amount of the up-front franchise fee in the year of observation; if the franchisor reported a range of fees, the mean of those values is used. Measured in inflation-adjusted dollars and entered in the model as the log of the franchise fee in thousands of dollars.

The dollar value of the franchisee's initial investment to open an outlet in the system in the year of observation, measured in inflation-adjusted dollars. Entered in the model as the log of the initial investment by the franchisee.
The ratio of company-owned outlets to the total number of outlets in the system. Entered in the model as the log of one plus the proportion of company-owned franchise outlets.
A dummy variable equal to one if Entrepreneur Magazine reports that the franchisor finances the franchisees' purchase of outlets in the year of observation, and zero otherwise.
The number of years since the franchise system was established, measured for each year of observation. Entered in the model as the log of the number of years in franchising.

The dependent variable is the portion of a firm's value attributable to growth options, calculated from the Stern Stewart data set. The authors solve their valuation identity for the present value of EVA growth (the value of growth options) and scale it by firm value; the present value of current-level EVA is calculated by treating the firm's current EVA as a perpetuity discounted by the firm's weighted average cost of capital. The equation itself is rendered unreadable in the text. Firm-specific discount rates and value-based measures such as EVA, capital invested, and market value added are available from the Stern Stewart data set.

Using the SDC database, the authors tracked a firm's joint ventures and counted the number of international JVs the firm had during a five-year rolling window, following the approach of Barkema and colleagues (1997). The five-year window was chosen as a compromise between longer windows that might count terminated or less relevant JVs and shorter intervals that might miss important investments. The resulting count is a firm-level measure used to test Hypothesis 1.

Each IJV was classified as either a minority IJV (less than 50%) or a nonminority IJV (50% and above). The authors then counted the number of minority IJVs a firm had over the five-year rolling window and entered this count in the regressions.

Each IJV was classified as either a minority IJV (less than 50%) or a nonminority IJV (50% and above). The authors then counted the number of nonminority IJVs a firm had over the five-year rolling window and entered this count in the regressions.

Each IJV was classified as either a core or a noncore IJV, depending on whether or not it operated in the firm's primary business at the four-digit SIC level. The authors then counted the number of core IJVs a firm had over the five-year rolling window and entered this count in the regressions.

Each IJV was classified as either a core or a noncore IJV, depending on whether or not it operated in the firm's primary business at the four-digit SIC level. The authors then counted the number of noncore IJVs a firm had over the five-year rolling window and entered this count in the regressions.

Each IJV was classified as located either in an emerging/developing economy or in a developed economy, as defined by the United Nations on the basis of the World Bank's World Development Indicators 2004, where all countries other than 24 high-income OECD members were considered emerging/developing economies. The authors then counted the number of a firm's IJVs in emerging/developing economies over the five-year rolling window and entered this count in the regressions.

Each IJV was classified as located either in an emerging/developing economy or in a developed economy, as defined by the United Nations on the basis of the World Bank's World Development Indicators 2004, with developed economies being 24 high-income OECD members. The authors then counted the number of a firm's IJVs in developed economies over the five-year rolling window and entered this count in the regressions.

The sum of all bank loans divided by total debt, where total debt is the sum of all bank loans and all bonds outstanding. Because a dependent variable bounded between 0 and 1 is problematic, it was transformed by taking the natural logarithm of relational debt divided by one minus relational debt, with values of 0 and 1 replaced by 0.001 and 0.999 before the transformation. Results were qualitatively identical if the variable was not transformed or if the arcsine transformation was used.
Total research and development expenditures divided by total assets. R&D and advertising expenses were obtained from the Nikkei NEEDS database while the other variables came from the PACAP database.

The market-to-book ratio, calculated as the sum of total debt and the market value of equity divided by total assets; this measure closely corresponds to Tobin's Q and incorporates current and expected future performance. Because the distribution was highly skewed, the natural log of the market-to-book ratio was used, and results were similar if performance was not logged.

Inside and outside respondents were asked to identify and rank, from each airline's viewpoint, its top 5 rivals from a list of all 12 other competitors. In the scoring scheme, the airline rated as the top-ranked rival of a focal airline received a score of 5; the second, a score of 4, and so forth, and those not included in the ranking received a score of 0. Scores were then averaged over all responses, so each score reflected the degree of competitive tension a focal airline experienced from a given competitor in the eyes of managers and industry stakeholders. Separate measures were constructed for insiders (airline executives assessing their own companies) and outsiders (security analysts, consultants, and travel agents), and a combined measure was also analyzed.
Measured as a rival airline's scale divided by a focal airline's scale during the same period. Scale was 'available seat-miles', a common measure for airline capacity.

The volume of a rival's attack on a focal firm's market was measured as the number of the rival's entries into the firm's routes from 1989 to 1990. An airline was considered an incumbent if it had at least a 1 percent share of a route.

Similarity captured the extent to which two airlines had the same profile in terms of fleet structure. The authors first calculated the Euclidean distance between two airlines based on the distribution of different types of aircraft; a zero distance indicated that two airlines had exactly the same distribution of aircraft types, and a high degree of distance indicated very different fleet structures. They then reverse-coded the distance to arrive at a measure of similarity. The distance formula itself is not readable in the extracted text; the prose defines the terms as the number of type m aircraft operated by an airline, the airline's total number of aircraft overall, the equivalent quantities for the rival, and m as a type of aircraft operated by both airlines.

Salience captured the extent to which a rival was a dominant player flying the aircraft that were vital to a focal firm's operations. In the calculation of the salience index, the first term captured the strategic importance of a given type of aircraft to the focal firm and the second term reflected the share of this type of aircraft owned by the rival. The results were normalized so that the sum of the salience indexes for all of a given firm's competitors was equal to 1. The formula itself is not readable in the extracted text.

variable_name: volume of a focal firm's attack
description: The volume of a focal firm's attack on a given rival's markets was measured as the firm's number of entries, among the 10,000 sample routes, into the rival's routes from 1991 to 1992. An airline was considered an incumbent in a route if it had at least a 1 percent share in the route.

Count of firms that have multimarket contact with the focal firm in a given market. The authors interpret it as the number of firms that monitor the focal firm in a given market and might discover a defection, computed from the markets in which the firm and its competitors jointly participate. It is measured at the firm-in-market level and is lagged.
time_window: lagged (first year of the data omitted to construct lagged measures)

description: Count of firms that have one or more multimarket competitors present in the market. The authors interpret it as the number of firms monitoring the market and as indicating the overall level of mutual forbearance in that market. It is measured at the market level and is lagged.
time_window: lagged (first year of the data omitted to construct lagged measures)

description: Difference between the focal firm's growth rate in the market and the median growth rate of all firms in the market, left censored at zero so that only positive differences are modeled. Sales are defined as revenue from own premiums, which equals premiums sold minus premiums reinsured. A positive difference is interpreted as a defection from the mutual-forbearance equilibrium.

The principal champion's hierarchical level measured for five levels, from the CEO scored a 5 to four levels down scored a 1. The identification of the principal champion was based on a consensus of the venture team's responses. The variable was normally distributed encompassing the entire range from 5 to 1, with a mean of 3.04 and a standard deviation of 1.29, and CEOs came not only from corporate headquarters but also from subsidiaries or divisions of the corporation.

A dummy variable for the principal champion's organizational location, scored 1 if the champion was from corporate headquarters and 0 otherwise. Of the 136 ventures, 40 were championed by someone from corporate headquarters.

Ventures whose principal champion's level and organizational sponsor's level were equal were assumed to have one champion playing both roles, a dual-role champion. The venture's reporting level was used as a proxy for the level of the organizational sponsor on the argument that the sponsor's primary functions of mentoring and monitoring are tied to the venture's reporting activities.

An index built from three measures of innovativeness: the timing of entry of the venture, the life-cycle stage of the market at the time of entry, and the technological newness of the offering. Timing of entry scored first entrants 3, pioneers 2, early followers 1, and later entrants 0; life-cycle stage scored introductory 3, growth 2, mature 1, and declining 0; technological newness scored new-to-the-world 3, an established product based on new technology 2, and imitative 1. The scores were summed to form an index with a range of 9 (the most innovative) to 1 (the least innovative), with all measures weighted equally.
We measure Science park by whether the focal venture is located in and a member of a science park (1), otherwise 0.

Consistent with prior research (Li et al., 2012), the authors measure Returnee by whether the respondent received an educational degree outside of China. The returnees in the sample received degrees from 34 different universities abroad, and the authors confirmed that each returnee had received a degree from abroad and worked abroad, including starting firms, working for new firms, and working for multinational corporations such as GE and Microsoft in their North American or European offices.

The authors measure Local elites by whether the respondent received a degree from Tsinghua University, Peking University, or a Chinese Academy of Sciences university or institute, the leading institutions in China (Zhou, 2008).

The variable is measured by whether the focal firm participated in the two major government programs that provide public resources to technology-based ventures: the High-Tech Enterprise Certification Program and the Innovation Fund for Small and Medium High-Tech Enterprises (InnoFund). Because funding amount by firm is unavailable, the authors use a count, measuring Public policy resource access by the number of these sources from which a venture received funding, from 0 (none) to 3 (obtained high-tech certification, and local and national InnoFund grants). Information was accessed from the complete directories of all firms that received high-tech enterprise certification and InnoFund grants at the national and municipal (Beijing) levels.

The dependent variable is a start-up's international alliance-formation rate, with q representing the discrete probability of forming another international alliance between time t and (t + Δt), conditional on the history of the process up to time t; the rate provides information on the time span between successive events, and higher values correspond to shorter times between events. All contract-based marketing and distribution and R&D alliance events between 1996 and 2015 were identified, and all alliances with partners located in a foreign country were coded as international alliances, excluding those with foreign MNCs located in Germany. If no international alliance events occurred during a certain quarter, the international alliance event variable was coded as zero.

A network was constructed using all the alliances in a region over a five-year window prior to year t, identifying all direct cooperative agreements between the MNCs and their alliance partners in a particular region; observed alliances were considered active network links for five years unless information on a prior termination or an extension was available. Using UCINET 6, degree centralities were calculated for all actors with Freeman's measure of degree centrality, and the MNC's average network centrality was calculated as the ratio of the cumulative degree centrality of all the MNCs in the region divided by the number of MNCs active within this region in that period. Higher values suggest greater MNC regional network activity.
time_window: five-year window prior to year t

description: The MNCs were divided into foreign and domestic categories and separate average network centrality scores were calculated. The foreign score uses the degree centrality of the foreign MNCs in the region, averaged over the number of foreign MNCs active in the region in that period.
time_window: five-year window prior to year t

description: The MNCs were divided into foreign and domestic categories and separate average network centrality scores were calculated. The domestic score uses the degree centrality of the domestic MNCs in the region, averaged over the number of domestic MNCs active in the region in that period.
time_window: five-year window prior to year t

description: A count of the number of alliances with MNCs in the region prior to the time of the international alliance event, using a five-year window prior to the year of the event. Because the impact of an additional tie may have diminishing returns, a natural log of the counts was used.
time_window: five-year window prior to the year of the event

variable_name: Alliances with foreign MNCs in region
description: A count of the number of alliances a start-up had with foreign MNCs in the region prior to the international alliance event, over a five-year window prior to the year of the event, with a natural log of the counts.
time_window: five-year window prior to the year of the event

variable_name: Alliances with domestic MNCs in region
description: A count of the number of alliances a start-up had with domestic MNCs in the region prior to the international alliance event, over a five-year window prior to the year of the event, with a natural log of the counts.
time_window: five-year window prior to the year of the event

description: Before versus after percentage changes in the acquiring firm CEO's salary, bonus, and value of stock options. Salary and bonus changes are percentage changes from the year prior to an acquisition announcement to the year of the announcement, adjusted for inflation. Option values are estimated for the year prior to the announcement and for the year of the announcement, and the percent change is calculated using the lower-bound valuation method of Agrawal and Mandelker (1987) and Kerr and Kern (1992) rather than Black-Scholes.
time_window: year prior to the acquisition announcement to the year of the acquisition announcement

description: Returns were assessed with event study methodology, estimating cumulative abnormal returns for two event windows: -1 to 0 days and -3 to +3 days. The event date (day 0) is defined as the day an announcement was carried on the Dow Jones wire for the first time.
time_window: -1 to 0 days and -3 to +3 days around the acquisition announcement

description: Returns were also assessed by measuring the year-over-year percentage change in an acquiring firm's return on equity (ROE). These values reflect the sample firms' changes in ROE from the year of the acquisition to the year following the acquisition.
time_window: year of the acquisition to the year following the acquisition

description: Pre- and postacquisition changes in firm size were measured as percentage changes in sales. These values indicate the percentage changes in the acquiring firms' sales in the year following the merger versus the year of the merger announcement, adjusted for inflation.
time_window: year following the merger versus the year of the merger announcement

description: Firms were categorized into vigilantly and weakly monitored groups using the median values of three monitoring mechanisms (median residual value of 1.04 analysts following, median value of 4.4 percent ownership by activist institutions, and median value of 40 percent independent board members), and 11 firms with a mixture of lax and active monitoring were eliminated. Analyst following was adjusted for firm size by regressing the number of analysts following a firm on sales and using the residual values. Activist institutional ownership is the percentage of each firm's stock held by activist institutional investors (public pension funds, mutual funds, endowment funds, and foundations unaffiliated with the firms in which they invest); independent board members are nonemployee or nonformer-employee board members (managers of publicly traded firms with no business links to the organization, executives of nonprofit organizations, directors with no primary employer, venture capitalists, military officers, government officials, or academicians) relative to total board membership.

Takes a value of one if a director departs the board by the time he or she would next come up for reelection following the fraud announcement, and zero if the director remains on the board beyond this point in time. Departures are examined at the director's first reelection opportunity rather than the conventional three-year window. Using this approach, the data show that 22 percent of outside directors exit the board.
time_window: from the fraud announcement to the director's first reelection opportunity

description: An individual's normalized eigenvector centrality (logged) within the director network in the year preceding the revelation of fraud. Directors are connected to one another by virtue of serving on the same boards, and the database contains information on board membership for over 3,200 North American companies. This measure accounts for the number of ties that a director maintains but gives greater weight to ties with well-connected individuals. Calculations were implemented using Pajek and UCINET 6.
time_window: the year preceding the revelation of fraud

description: Dichotomous variable equal to one if a given director is an active or former CEO of another firm, and zero otherwise. Data on directors' backgrounds was gathered from the biographical information provided in firms' proxy statements.

Dummy variable equal to one if a director has worked as an accountant, banker, CFO, lawyer or public relations professional during their careers, or if their background otherwise provides evidence that they possess industry-specific technical expertise (e.g., Ph.D. in a related field, employed by a niche consulting firm), and zero otherwise. Built from the biographical information provided in firms' proxy statements.

variable_name: Director capital (relational capital and human capital)
description: Director capital is disaggregated into relational capital and human capital, and measured by the set of three director-level variables: relational capital from the director's network position (Board Analyst data), and two human capital variables, business expert and professional specialist. They enter the exit model together as the independent variables.
Simple count of commercial banks in Singapore in a calendar year, taken from Carroll and Teo's bank density variable. All independent covariates are lagged by one calendar year.

Simple count of financial cooperatives in Singapore in a calendar year. The linear term captures emergent (prepopulation) proliferation and the squared term captures proliferation beyond the density threshold at which categorical distinctions cohere.

variable_name: Categorical name change (CNC); Cumulative CNC in population (C_c)
description: Categorical name changes were first coded at the organization level and then aggregated to create a cumulative time-varying variable updated annually. A categorical name change is one that replaces the phrase thrift and loan with credit co-op; name changes reflecting transitions in agency sponsorship or institutional affiliation are not categorical.
time_window: annual, cumulative, lagged one calendar year

description: The hazard that a co-op disbands, estimated with organizational age as the clock variable; a co-op becomes at risk once founded, and the authors coded exact founding and disbanding dates converted to decimal numbers. Variation in organizational age is modeled as a stochastic piecewise-exponential function with breakpoints at 2, 5, 10 and 25 years.

Entropy measure of the diversity of FDI country origins in a four-digit SIC code manufacturing industry sector in a year, adapted from previous studies' measurements of the diversification of a firm's business portfolio. S_i is the number of foreign firms with country origin i as a percentage of the total number of foreign firms in the industry sector in a year, and N is the total number of country origins of foreign firms present in the sector in a specific year. Entropy equals zero if all foreign firms in an industry sector in a year have the same country origin and it rises with the extent of the diversity in FDI country origins. The entropy formula itself was not readable in the text provided. The variable was calculated for each four-digit SIC code manufacturing industry in the sample and was updated yearly.

Domestic firm output measured as the log of firm annual sales. Firm sales were deflated using 1990's constant price to remove the effects of deflation or inflation due to price change over time. It is the dependent variable of the log-linear Cobb-Douglas production function; the estimated equation itself was not readable in the text provided.

Log of the firm's capital input, its capital stock, entered as a firm input in the production function and used as the measure of domestic firm size in the interaction with the diversity of FDI country origins. The capital stock was deflated by the gross domestic product deflator on the basis of 1990's constant price.

Log of the firm's labor input, its number of employees, entered as a firm input in the production function and used as a second measure of domestic firm size in the interaction with the diversity of FDI country origins.

Difference between the average productivity of foreign firms in a four-digit SIC code manufacturing industry sector and the productivity of a domestic firm in the same sector, where productivity is firm annual value added (in RMB10 million) divided by the number of employees and the foreign firm average is weighted by firm asset size. The higher the value of this variable, the more technologically advanced FDI is relative to the focal domestic firm. The measure was calculated for each domestic firm in the sample and was updated yearly.

An index created as the simple mean, after standardization, of four unobtrusive indicators: the prominence of the CEO's photograph in the annual report, the CEO's prominence in company press releases, the CEO's relative cash pay, and the CEO's relative non-cash pay. In the primary analysis the authors used the two-year moving average value of each indicator, excluding the starting and ending year of each CEO's tenure when applicable. Photograph prominence was coded from one point (no photograph of the CEO) to five points (photo of the CEO alone occupying more than half a page), press-release prominence as the number of times the CEO was mentioned by name divided by the total number of company press releases, relative cash pay as the CEO's salary and bonus divided by that of the second-highest-paid executive, and relative non-cash pay as the CEO's non-cash compensation divided by that of the second-highest-paid executive.
time_window: two-year moving average of each indicator; prior-year annual reports, press releases and compensation

description: The log-transformed mean of the adjusted prior decisions (acquisition emphasis or international diversification) of all firms where the CEO held a board position in the previous three years. Prior decisions in years t-1, t-2 and t-3 were multiplied by factors of 1, 2/3 and 1/3 respectively to account for recency, and prior decisions of an individual's employer firm were multiplied by two. Board membership was identified using a director's name and birth year.

Calculated similarly to the CEO's prior experience: the log-transformed average value of prior decisions experienced by other directors of the focal board in the previous three years, after adjusting for the recency effect and the employer-firm effect.

The total value of all acquisitions conducted by a firm in a given year divided by the firm's total sales in the same year. Because the dependent variable was not distributed normally, its logarithm value was used in the analysis. Acquisition data were collected from SDC Platinum.

The ratio of a firm's international sales over its total sales. Because the dependent variable was not distributed normally, its logarithm value was used in the analysis. Data on international diversification were collected from COMPUSTAT.

A single index of CEO power created by summing the standard scores of seven indicators: CEO tenure, the CEO's total number of other board appointments at other Fortune 500 companies, percentage of inside directors, percentage of outside directors appointed after the CEO, outside directors' ownership, the CEO's stock ownership, and CEO duality. CEO duality is a dummy variable equal to one if the CEO was also the board chairman.

variable_name: Status of firms tied to the CEO
description: The average status of the other firms tied to the CEO, where each firm's status is the sum of standard scores of firm size (the logarithm of total sales), performance (the firm's return on assets minus the industry average return on assets), and whether the firm was ranked as one of the top 50 America's Most Admired Companies by Fortune magazine in each year.

Respondents rated the level of autonomy at the time of the surveyed invention on a Likert scale (1 = no autonomy to 6 = very high autonomy) on two items: selection of the tasks or projects (AUT1) and allocation of their working time (AUT2). Because exploratory factor analysis reveals unidimensionality of the two autonomy variables, the authors simply sum the responses over these items to build the aggregate measure AUTONOMY. The aggregate is used as the dependent variable alongside the two component measures in the autonomy models.
scale: 1 = no autonomy to 6 = very high autonomy for each item; the aggregate sums the two items
time_window: at the time of the surveyed invention (reported retrospectively)

description: Inventors were asked the extent to which they agreed or disagreed, on a 1-5 Likert scale, with two statements about the organization's instruments and complementary resources for the invention. The scores for the two statements each highlight an aspect of PRC; given their unidimensionality, the authors construct the PRC measure by summing them up. They also generate the square term of this variable (PRC_sq) to check for nonlinear effects in the specification.
scale: 1-5 agreement scale for each statement; summed into PRC, with a squared term PRC_sq
time_window: at the time of the surveyed invention (reported retrospectively)

description: Number of references to nonpatent literature (typically scientific journals) for the surveyed invention, listed by the patent examiners when evaluating the patent application. The authors use it as a proxy for the scientific output of the project and for the strength of the patent's scientific linkage, and they take it from the patent examiner's search report obtained by matching the survey inventions to PATSTAT identifiers.

Index of the commercial value of the project output built from survey information about whether the firm uses the patented invention commercially (i.e., in a product, service, or manufacturing process); 0 indicates noncommercialized patented inventions and 1 represents commercialized patent inventions. The authors interpret this index as the observed outcome of an unobserved continuous measure of the project's commercial value, where the firm undertakes commercialization when that value exceeds a threshold.
time_window: responses collected a couple of years after the patent application

description: The measure is based on product self-fluidity in Hoberg et al. (2014), which captures how a firm changes its own product words in its business description from year t - 1 to t. A unique product-word vector is generated for each firm-year from text analysis, populated by 1 if the firm uses the given word and 0 otherwise and normalized to unit length. Product self-similarity is the cosine similarity between the firm's normalized product vectors in year t - 1 and year t, and subtracting that score from one gives the firm's repositioning score from t - 1 to t, so that the more similar a firm's own product words are between the two years, the less it has shifted. The reported measure is the 3-year moving average of these repositioning scores.
time_window: year t - 1 to t, aggregated as a 3-year moving average

description: Based on IBES, all coverage analysts of each firm each year are identified, where an analyst is a firm's coverage analyst if he/she makes any earnings estimates of the firm in a given year. Analyst churn is the logged number of analysts who either initiate or stop covering the firm in year t + 1. Because these numbers can be related to the total number of coverage analysts at year t, the proportion of churn is also used as an alternative measure, winsorized by 1% and 99%.
time_window: coverage changes measured in year t + 1 relative to repositioning at year t

description: A firm's abandoned coverage analysts are those who cover the firm at year t but stop the coverage from year t + 1. Analyst termination is the logged number of analysts stopping coverage of the firm in year t + 1; its proportion relative to the total number of coverage analysts at year t is used as an alternative measure.

A firm's newly initiated coverage analysts are those who do not cover the firm at year t but initiate their coverage at year t + 1. Analyst initiation is the logged number of analysts initiating coverage of the firm in year t + 1; its proportion relative to the total number of coverage analysts at year t is used as an alternative measure.

Relative accuracy is calculated as the absolute differences between forecasting and actual earnings per share divided by the absolute value of actual earnings, multiplied by -1, so that a forecast is more accurate if it is closer toward the firm's actual earnings. Only the last earnings forecast made by each analyst before a firm's release of its financials for a given period (quarters or years) is estimated. The variable is winsorized.
time_window: last forecast before the firm's earnings release for a given quarter or year

description: An alternative measure of accuracy created to enhance comparability. All forecasts for the same firm and time period are first ranked based on their absolute forecast errors, with the least accurate forecast receiving a rank of 1. Accuracy rankings are then calculated from the rank of an analyst's relative forecast errors and the number of forecasts provided for the firm and period, so that the most accurate forecast gains a score of 1, while the least receives 0.
time_window: last forecast before the firm's earnings release for a given quarter or year

description: An aggregate measure of CSP built from the KLD data covering the community relations, diversity, employee relations, environment, and product dimensions. Each dimension was standardized to make the scores directly comparable across dimensions and over time, and weaknesses were subtracted from strengths to arrive at a net score for each dimension. CSP was measured at the end of the prior year and entered the valuation model as this lagged value.

Firm value was measured as price of the firm's equity. In the empirical model Pit is the equity value (per share) of firm i at the end of fiscal year t. Valuation effects were expressed as a percentage of the mean (or median) share price of the relevant group.

A dummy variable set to 1 if a firm's primary industry belonged to one of the industries characterized by a high level of litigation risk, and 0 otherwise. The high litigation risk industries were SIC codes 2833-2836 (biotechnology), 3570-3577 and 7370-7374 (computers), 3600-3674 (electronics), and 5200-5961 (retailing), selected following prior studies based on their actual incidences of securities litigation.

Altman's Z-score was used to measure the likelihood of a firm experiencing financial distress or bankruptcy, where a higher Z-score means better financial health. A firm was classified as having a high distress risk if its Z-score was lower than 2.7 (or 3.0); high distress risk took a value of 1 for such firms and 0 otherwise. The main tests partitioned the sample at the 2.7 and at the 3.0 cutoffs.
scale: dummy (1 = high distress risk, i.e., Z-score below 2.7 or 3.0)

description: A dummy variable indicating firms in the alcoholic beverage, firearms, defense, gambling, forestry, mining, or tobacco industries. Such firms were coded 1 with all others coded 0. This variable was used to quantify moral legitimacy.

The event is the announcement that a firm has received a Training Top 125 award for its excellence in training and human capital management. The award is granted for superior training programs by Training magazine on the basis of a questionnaire that is 75% quantitative and 25% qualitative, without distinguishing between general and firm-specific training.

Cumulative abnormal returns generated through event study analysis using a market model, a value-weighted index, and a 200 trading day estimation window preceding the event window. The event window of (-15, +1) was used for the analyses; the specific event day each year is the first trading day following the announcement of awards.
Measured as R&D investment (labeled annual 'Research and Development Expense' in Compustat) divided by sales. Measured in the year before the award, so data for a February 2006 award come from 2005.
Measured as physical capital investment ('Property, Plant, and Equipment - Total (Net)' in Compustat) divided by sales. Measured in the year before the award.
Measured as advertising expenditures (labeled 'Advertising Expense' in Compustat) divided by sales. Measured in the year before the award.

variable_name: R&D intensity x physical capital intensity (RDINT x PCINT)
description: Product of the firm's R&D intensity (R&D expense over sales) and physical capital intensity (net property, plant and equipment over sales), both from Compustat for the year before the award, entered as an interaction term in the regression of cumulative abnormal returns.

The number of alliances completed by the acquiring firm with other banks prior to the focal acquisition. Data on alliances formed by responding firms were obtained from SDC data files; the measure counts alliances from 1986 onward because SDC data are not available in a reliable fashion for preceding years.
time_window: prior to the focal acquisition, from 1986 onward

description: The difference between the return on assets (ROA) of the acquiring bank three years after the acquisition relative to one year prior to the acquisition. To control for market conditions, the acquiring bank's ROA is first adjusted based on the performance of its rivals in the same geographic market of its headquarters, using the universe of banks in Compustat for which performance data were available. Accounting data were obtained from Compustat, Compact Disclosure, and Moody's.
time_window: three years after the acquisition relative to one year prior to the acquisition

description: The acquiring firm's cumulative abnormal returns three years following the acquisition, calculated relative to a size and market-to-book (MTB) based benchmark. Acquisition financial performance is the difference between the acquiring firm's stock return and the return in the equal-weighted size- and MTB-ranked portfolio to which the firm belongs; 100 benchmark portfolios were constructed from the cross-product of ten size deciles and ten MTB deciles and the classification is reevaluated each month. Stock return data came from CRSP and accounting data from Compustat.

Measured on a single 0-3 scale, where 0 corresponds to no integration, 1 to a minor degree of integration, 2 to a major degree of integration, and 3 to complete integration of the acquired firm. The scale was the answer to a question on the degree to which procedures were aligned, information systems were converted, and products were standardized. Validity was examined in a second-round survey of 57 observations using 15 items on structural integration and process alignment of major functions.

Proxied by the degree to which the management of the acquired bank was replaced after the acquisition, measured on a four-point scale: 0 = retention of the entire management team of the acquired bank, 1 = minor top management changes, 2 = many changes in top management personnel, and 3 = complete replacement of the acquired bank's top management team. Negative values were assigned for these four categories to interpret the variable as a proxy for relationship quality, so higher values indicate higher relational quality.

Counts the total stock of patents held by the firm up to a given firm year, generated from all patents granted to the sample firms in USPTO data, the NBER patent database, and a proprietary patent database updated through 2004. It is used as a proxy for the degree of firm-level spillovers that exist as a result of deal-level choices to manage the threat of expropriation, assuming that the more patents held by the firm, the more likely its R&D deals are to include its own patents. Like the other continuous variables, the variable is entered with one added and in natural log form.
time_window: cumulative to the current firm year

description: The number of alliance events by a focal firm in the current year with firms partnered with in the past. The variable proxies for the extent to which past bilateral collaborations may lower expropriation hazards due to reputation and/or trust effects and the potential for future deals in enforcing discipline on opportunism threats between parties in the current period.

The total number of equity R&D deals the focal firm has been involved with (up to the given year) since the firm's inception. Such experience captures governance capability components ranging from recruiting collaborative partners to negotiating and structuring agreements of a particular type, and proxies for the interlocking activity system of organizational knowledge, routines, and design that collectively comprise governance capability.

The total number of pure licensing R&D deals the focal firm has been involved with (up to the given year) since the firm's inception. It represents the firm's accumulated experience in structuring arm's-length licensing relationships and thereby proxies for its licensing governance capability.

The numerator is the total number of alliances during the given firm year in which equity is a component of the deal; the denominator is the total number of alliance events in a given firm year where the focal firm is the R&D partner. The numerator excludes any non-equity form of R&D collaboration, so the variable is not simply the mirror image of license-only intensity.

The numerator is the number of pure licensing alliances during the given firm year; the denominator is the total number of alliance events in a given firm year where the focal firm is the R&D partner. The numerator excludes deals with any component other than a pure licensing agreement.

The difference between the percentage of all prior cooperation events utilizing equity (based on the stock of such experience) and the percentage of all current year cooperation events utilizing equity. Positive values suggest that historic use of the mode exceeds current usage. Because the deviation terms are potentially nonlinear, the square of the term is also included in the valuation regressions.
time_window: current firm year relative to the firm's history to date

description: The difference between the percentage of all prior cooperation events utilizing arm's-length licensing (based on the stock of such experience) and the percentage of all current year cooperation events utilizing licensing. Positive values suggest that historic use of the mode exceeds current usage. The square of the term is also included in the valuation regressions.
time_window: current firm year relative to the firm's history to date

description: For firms' private years, the valuation at the most recent round of venture funding; for public years, market capitalization, the product of publicly traded share price and number of shares outstanding. The variable is meant to capture the overall value of the firm as assessed by its shareholders, and is transformed by taking the natural log to address its skewed distribution.

The average level of the Lerner Biotechnology Index for the current year, an index tracking the munificence of external funding from VCs, corporations, and the public markets available to biotechnology firms. The index is available through 1999; for 2000-2005 the authors use estimates constructed by regressing the Lerner index on the Nasdaq Biotechnology Index for the overlapping 1993-1999 years and applying the estimated coefficients to actual values of the NBI.

Respondents were asked to indicate the extent to which they search unfamiliar information (information to which they have never been exposed, information that is different from other information used in the past) as opposed to familiar information (information used in the past, or information that was once known) by assigning 100 points to both these categories. The extent of the team's terrain unfamiliarity was calculated as the average of the point allocation to unfamiliar information for all TMT members. Higher values indicate more unfamiliar information searched by the team.
level: TMT (individual responses averaged to the team level)
time_window: at the time of the search survey

description: Respondents allocated a total of 100 points to three different types of information sources: inside (within organization), intraindustry, and outside industry. Terrain distance was then calculated as the average number of points allocated by the members of a TMT to intraindustry and outside industry information sources. Higher values of this variable indicate more distant information sources utilized by the TMT.
level: TMT (individual responses averaged to the team level)
time_window: at the time of the search survey

description: Terrain source diversity refers to the range of sources utilized by a TMT to acquire information and is broken down into 12 categories. It is calculated using the formula 1 - Sigma_b (Sigma_n S_bn / n)^2, where S_bn is the share or proportion of search conducted in the bth information source category by the nth member and n is the number of TMT members. A higher value indicates greater diversity in the information sources different TMT members use.
time_window: at the time of the search survey

description: Search effort, the extent to which the members of a TMT devote time and energy to search rather than to other activities, was assessed with four items on a scale ranging from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree' (alpha = .81). Because items were assessed at the individual level, the variable was aggregated to the team level by calculating the average value of each variable across TMT members. Higher values of search effort reflect more effortful search.
level: TMT (individual responses averaged to the team level)
time_window: at the time of the search survey

description: Search persistence is defined as the extent to which, on average, members of a TMT continue to gather information despite the number of alternatives that have been found, in order to be exhaustive in determining optimal outcome. A four-item scale (alpha = .75) was used, with higher values reflecting greater TMT search persistence, and items were aggregated to the team level by averaging across TMT members.
level: TMT (individual responses averaged to the team level)
time_window: at the time of the search survey

description: Data on the dependent variable were collected through a content analysis of articles in the public press: relevant articles were searched with keywords (e.g., 'new product,' 'new service,' 'introduce,' 'announce,' 'launch,' 'offer,' 'debut,' 'roll out,' 'unveil') combined with the name of each sample firm in Lexis-Nexis, and each article was read to eliminate duplicates. A second author independently coded 10 percent of the firms with 97.21 percent interrater reliability. The variable is the total number of new product introductions for each firm in 2006 and, in separate models, the average number of new product introductions for each firm in 2006-08.

Calculated as the difference between acquirer country shareholder rights and target country shareholder rights; a positive value means that the target was acquired by a firm from a country that was more protective of shareholder rights. It uses the time-varying country shareholder rights index developed by Schneper and Guillén (2004), which builds on the La Porta et al. (1998) index that adds one point for each of six provisions protecting shareholder rights in a country's commercial code or company law. For Hungary, indexes developed by Pistor (2004) were used.

Measured with the OECD time-varying Employment Protection Legislation (EPL) strictness index. For each country, employment protection legislation is described along 18 basic items that can be classified under three main areas: employment protection of regular workers against individual dismissal, specific requirements for collective dismissals, and regulation of temporary forms of employment; a four-step procedure produced cardinal summary indicators. The strictness index varies from zero to six, with zero for countries with very low employment protection and six for countries with very strict employment protection legislation; version 1 of the index was used in the study.

Adapted from the instrument developed by Datta (1991), it measures the extent to which the operations of the target firm were restructured along three main functions: R&D, manufacturing, and sales networks. For each function the degree of restructuring is the mean value of three questions pertaining to the degree of capacity disposed of (closed or resold), the degree of capacity restructured, and the degree of personnel layoffs, measured on a seven-point continuous scale (1 = 0% restructured, 7 = 91-100% restructured). Cronbach's alpha on the three-item scale ranged between 0.80 and 0.90.

variable_name: Redeployment of acquirer resources to target
description: Three types of resource-redeployment variables measure the extent to which the acquirer redeployed its own resources to the target firm: technology, marketing, and management resources. The redeployment of acquirer technical resources to the target is the average of two five-point scale items measuring the extent to which the acquirer redeployed its own researchers and engineers to the target; the redeployment of acquirer commercial resources is measured with two five-point scale items on the redeployment of commercial and administrative staff from acquirer to target; the redeployment of acquirer managerial resources is a five-point scale item on the redeployment of acquirer senior executives to the target firm. Cronbach's alpha varied between 0.74 and 0.77.

variable_name: Redeployment of target resources to acquirer
description: The same type of technology, marketing, and management variables were used to measure the extent to which the target redeployed its resources to the acquirer. Cronbach's alpha varied between 0.82 and 0.90.

A self-reported measure of the number of acquisitions made by the acquirer within the five years preceding the acquisition of the specific target. To reduce the level of correlation between the interaction term and target country labor rights, the variables measuring target country labor rights and acquirer M&A experience were mean-centered before the interaction term was calculated.

The major certifications accumulated by MLB players: Most Valuable Player (MVP), World Series MVP, Rookie of the Year, All-Star, and Gold Glove. The number of each type of award won was standardized and these standardized scores were summed into one variable, so that awards with only one or two winners a year and awards with many winners have a similar impact.

A statistic developed by Bill James to assess the overall level of a player's technical performance; James states that a perfect player would score 100, that those who score 60 or higher are exceptional and likely seen as clearly exceeding the standard of desirability, and that players become viable candidates for the Hall at 35. The statistic was centered before the squared value and the interactions with certifications were generated.
Dummy variable used as the variable of interest for Hypothesis 1: it equals one if the player is inducted into the Hall as a result of voting by the BBWAA and zero if a player is not.

The percentage of votes a player received in each round of voting, used to capture the iterative assessments of actors for Hypothesis 2. In rounds subsequent to round one, the voting percentage received in the previous round of voting is also included as a control variable.

Factor score from an exploratory common factor analysis with oblique rotation of three CEO ratings of the importance of the market environment, the technological environment, and the competitive environment. Each item asked the CEO to rate the importance of the sector on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (very important) to 7 (not at all important). The three items loaded on the second factor, named 'scanning emphasis on the task environment'; the external environment items were factor analyzed separately from the internal items.
scale: 7-point importance scale (1 = very important, 7 = not at all important) for each item

description: Factor score from an exploratory common factor analysis with oblique rotation of three CEO ratings of the importance of the sociocultural environment, the economic environment, and the political/legal environment. Each item asked the CEO to rate the importance of the sector on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (very important) to 7 (not at all important). The three items loaded on the first factor, labelled 'scanning emphasis on the general environment'.
scale: 7-point importance scale (1 = very important, 7 = not at all important) for each item

description: Factor score from an exploratory common factor analysis with oblique rotation of three CEO ratings of the importance of internal value-chain activities. Product R&D, market research, and basic engineering loaded on the second internal factor, labelled 'scanning emphasis on innovation'. Each item was rated on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (very important) to 7 (not at all important).
scale: 7-point importance scale (1 = very important, 7 = not at all important) for each item

description: Factor score from an exploratory common factor analysis with oblique rotation of three CEO ratings of the importance of internal value-chain activities. Cost control and operating efficiency loaded on the first internal factor, labelled 'scanning emphasis on efficiency'; financial management did not exhibit a simple structure and was dropped from further analyses. Each item was rated on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (very important) to 7 (not at all important).
scale: 7-point importance scale (1 = very important, 7 = not at all important) for each item

description: Miller and Droge's (1986) multi-item, Likert-type scale, on which CEOs rate the rate of change in their firm's environment on a 1-7 scale. The questions contrast rarely changing marketing practices with extremely frequent change, a very slow rate of product/service obsolescence with a very high rate, and production/service technology not subject to much change with modes of production/service that change often and in a major way. The authors use CEO perceptions because executives act on their perceptions.

The CEOs reported their best subjective estimates of performance compared to similar firms in their industry on a 5-point scale for after tax return on total assets and after tax return on total sales. Because the two items correlated highly, they were combined into an 'accounting return' measure of performance. Five-year average estimates were elicited.

The CEO reported a subjective estimate of the firm's sales growth compared to similar firms in its industry, on a 5-point scale. Five-year average estimates were elicited to minimize the influence of short-term performance variations.

The CEO reported a subjective estimate of the firm's overall performance/success compared to similar firms in its industry, on a 5-point scale. Five-year average estimates were elicited to minimize the influence of short-term performance variations.

Continuous variable constructed as the cumulative change in the share of the firm's R&D budget that is allocated to corporate headquarters in year t. It can take values between -1 and 1, so a firm that goes from 100% centralized to 100% decentralized has a value of -1 and a firm that moves from 100% decentralized to 100% centralized takes a value of 1, capturing the direction as well as the extent of cumulative change. Firm fixed effects are included in all estimations, so the coefficient is interpreted as the within-firm effect of changes in this share.

Spline variable that equals the value of BudgetCentralization for observations in which that variable is positive (increases in centralization), and is set to zero otherwise. It is used to unpack whether relationships between budget control and the dependent variables are driven by firms that are centralizing, separately from those that are decentralizing.

Spline variable that equals the value of BudgetCentralization for observations in which that variable is negative (decreases in centralization), and is set to zero otherwise. It is used together with IncreasedBudgetCentralization in the spline estimations.

Categorical variable set equal to 1 if the firm ever substantially centralized its R&D budget during the observation period, and 0 otherwise, where a substantial change is defined as one that increases the corporate share of the firm's R&D by more than 40 percentage points. Seven firms are centralizers under this definition.

Categorical variable constructed analogously to Centralizer, set equal to 1 if the firm ever substantially decentralized its R&D budget during the observation period and 0 otherwise, using the same more-than-40-percentage-point threshold. Nine firms are decentralizers, and no firm both substantially centralized and decentralized its R&D during the sample period.

Categorical variable set equal to 0 until the year that the focal firm changed its R&D budget structure and 1 thereafter; for a nonchanging peer firm it is set to 0 until the year that the matched 'changer' firm changed and 1 thereafter. It is interacted with Centralizer and with Decentralizer.
time_window: year t relative to the year of change

description: Proportion of the firm's inventors who are connected within the largest component of the firm's coinvention network in a year. Each inventor is a node and a tie is recorded whenever an inventor collaborates on a patent application with another inventor within the firm; ties are non-directional and networks are mapped for each firm-year. The numerator is the number of inventors in the largest cluster of the firm's network in year t and the denominator is the total number of inventors at the firm in year t, based on all patent applications submitted in that year regardless of whether or when they were granted.

Normalized entropy of the network captures heterogeneity in the size of the network components. It equals 1 when all components have the exact same size, and the more asymmetric the distribution of component sizes, the lower the entropy value; the value is normalized between 0 and 1. The authors use it as a complementary whole-network measure of connectedness, with lower entropy indicating greater connectedness: as isolated components connect, the relative giant component increases while entropy decreases.

Patent-level measure calculated as one minus the Herfindahl index of the primary U.S. patent classes of the patents cited by patent j. For firm-level estimations the authors average the patent-level measure across all patents by firm k in year t to construct Originality.

Patent-level measure of the breadth of innovation impact calculated as one minus the Herfindahl index of the primary U.S. patent classes of the patents that cite patent j. For firm-level estimations the authors average the patent-level measure across all patents by firm k in year t to construct Generality.

Unit managers reported their unit's exploratory innovation on a six-item scale adapted from Jansen, Van den Bosch, and Volberda (2006) and its exploitative innovation on a six-item scale adapted from Jansen et al. (2006). Unit ambidexterity is then measured as the multiplicative interaction of exploratory and exploitative innovation, consistent with conceptualizing ambidexterity as the non-substitutable combination of the two. Responses of up to two additional senior employees per unit were used to assess reliability; the median interrater agreements were 0.75 for exploratory innovation and 0.79 for exploitative innovation.

A unit's financial performance was measured as its profitability-achieved rate, that is, actual profitability divided by target profitability, where targets for units are set by branch management. Actual and target profitability were collected through internal corporate records and the achieved rate was averaged for 2004 and 2005, up to one year after the measurement of ambidexterity.

Following Dewar and Hage (1978), structural differentiation was based on the division in the organizational chart and was captured by the number of units in each branch, where these units serve distinct product-market segments. It is measured at the branch level.

Centralization was measured with the hierarchy of authority sub-construct of Hage and Aiken (1967), a five-item scale reflecting the extent to which decision making is concentrated in a branch. The items were answered by the executive director and additional senior team members of the branch (alpha = 0.78), with adequate interrater agreement.

Resource munificence was measured with accounting-based measures as the average branch's level of cash reserves divided by total expenses in 2003 and 2004 (Voss et al., 2008). Cash reserves and total expenses for each branch were ascertained through internal corporate records.

Resource interdependency was measured with a five-item measure adapted from Van der Vegt and Janssen (2003), referring to the extent to which units must exchange information and resources or work together to complete their tasks and activities. It was answered by the executive director and a second senior team member of the branch, with adequate interrater agreement.

Return on assets, used together with ROE to measure firm performance. The data were obtained from the Worldscope and PacificBasin Capital Markets (PACAP) Research Center databases. It is an accounting return measure used because the study compares a firm's sequence of acquisitions over different periods.

Return on equity, used together with ROA to measure firm performance. The data were obtained from the Worldscope and PacificBasin Capital Markets (PACAP) Research Center databases. It is an accounting return measure used because the study compares a firm's sequence of acquisitions over different periods.

A total count of acquisitions that the firm had pursued each year. The data were collected from SDC Platinum and Lexis-Nexis. Because acquisitions are less prevalent in the region, the firm's acquisitions were tracked on a yearly basis within each period and the data were collapsed into three periods. Number of acquisitions and size of acquisitions were tested in separate analyses.
time_window: each year, collapsed into three periods (1994-1996, 1997-1999, 2000-2002)

description: Sums the dollar amount of the acquisitions the firm had pursued. It is scaled by firm size (total sales) and expressed in percentage. The data were collected from SDC Platinum and Lexis-Nexis. Number of acquisitions and size of acquisitions were tested in separate analyses.
time_window: each year, collapsed into three periods (1994-1996, 1997-1999, 2000-2002)

description: A composite measure of organizational slack formed using the factor scores from equity to debt ratio and cash flow divided by sales. The study focused on unabsorbed slack because acquisitions require discretionary resources that are easily redeployable. The data were obtained from Worldscope, PACAP, and various years of Moody's International Manual and Mergent International Manual.

Annual firm expenditures for each R&D activity divided by annual sales revenue for the entire firm. Computed separately for each of the five R&D activities examined. Serve as dependent variables in the regressions and are also averaged per firm over 1974-81 and per year across firms to produce the firm-level and industry-level averages used to compare variation between firms and through time.

Annual dummy variable coded 1 if the firm had positive R&D expenditures in a given activity and 0 if not. Reported for each of the five R&D activities and for total firm R&D, and used with lags of one to seven years in the correlation analysis.
scale: 1 = positive R&D expenditures, 0 = zero R&D expenditures

description: R&D intensity for an activity with observations lagged one, two, three, four, five, six or seven years, paired by firm with the current observations in the correlation analysis. In the regressions the one-year lagged dependent variable is included among the independent variables, and the higher its estimated coefficient the greater the path dependence.

The firm's annual share of industry (FRS company) annual R&D activity expenditures divided by the firm's share of industry annual sales revenue. Each firm's annual share variables are averaged over 1974-81, giving each firm five average share variables, one per R&D activity; the coefficients of variation of these share variables are compared across R&D activities.

R&D activity is the type of business application of R&D, split into five categories: oil and gas recovery, refining, coal gasification/liquefaction, oil shale, and tar sands. Separate R&D intensity and share variables are built for each activity from firm R&D expenditures reported in the FRS data.

variable_name: Firm identity: between-firm variation in firm-level average R&D intensity
description: Firms are the 26 major U.S. energy companies in the DOE Financial Reporting System. Each firm's annual R&D intensity in an activity is averaged over 1974 to 1981, and between-firm differences are assessed by the mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation of these firm-level averages across firms. Firm fixed effects are also used in the persistence regressions.
scale: coefficient of variation of firm-level averages

description: Participants were randomly assigned to one of five performance shortfall conditions in a between-subject design: $15K, $100K, $300K, $500K, or $585K below the aspirational level, which was $600K. The remaining resource stocks in each condition were $585K, $500K, $300K, $100K, and $15K, respectively.

variable_name: proportion of resource stock allocated to the risky option
description: A firm's motivation to take risks was operationalized in relative terms as the proportion of a firm's resource stock allocated to the risky option versus the conservative option. The risky option was entering a new market with a 50% chance of decreasing the resource stock by the bet size and a 50% chance of increasing the resource stock by the bet size; the conservative option was saving the money in the bank with an annual interest rate of 2%. This proportion allowed the authors to control for a firm's ability to take risk (i.e., resource stock) and to isolate the motivation to take risk from the ability to do so.

variable_name: weight given to concern for firm survival
description: After the allocation decision, participants indicated the weight they gave to the concern for firm survival in their investment decisions on a six-point scale. The scale ran from 1 = significantly more weight to preserving the aspiration level to 6 = significantly more weight to avoiding bankruptcy.
scale: 1 = significantly more weight to preserving the aspiration level; 6 = significantly more weight to avoiding bankruptcy

description: Performance shortfall was manipulated orthogonally to concern for firm survival in a 2 x 3 between-participant design with three levels: $100K, $300K, or $500K below aspiration. Participants were randomly assigned to one of the six conditions.

variable_name: proportion of resource stock allocated to the risky option
description: A firm's motivation to take risks was calculated the same as in Experiment 1: the proportion of the firm's resource stock allocated to the risky option rather than the conservative option.

variable_name: concern for firm survival (low versus high)
description: Concern for firm survival was manipulated orthogonally to performance shortfall, yielding low versus high concern conditions. In the low concern condition participants were told that their goal was to preserve cash reserves at $600K, diverting their attention away from the firm's survival; in the high concern condition they were instructed that their goal was to prevent bankruptcy, centering their focus on the firm's survival. At debriefing, participants rated the importance of both goals on a seven-point scale (1 = not at all and 7 = very much) as a manipulation check.

Participants were presented with all three scenarios of firms' performance shortfall: $100K, $300K, and $500K below aspiration, manipulated within participants. Each scenario was presented in a different trial and referred to three different firms, and the order of the scenarios was counterbalanced across participants.

Performance momentum was manipulated between participants by framing the scenario as: 'For the past several years, your firm has failed (succeeded) to meet cash reserve targets.' This created underperformance versus outperformance momentum relative to aspiration.

Participants rated their confidence in the firm's ability to achieve its targets in the current year on a seven-point scale (1 = extremely low and 7 = extremely high). Confidence was modeled at the scenario level (subject-centered) and at the subject level (averaged across the scenarios).
level: scenario within participant and individual participant (subject level)

description: Participants rated their concern that their firm might go bankrupt, that is, concern for firm survival, on a seven-point scale (1 = not at all to 7 = very much).
scale: 1 = not at all to 7 = very much

description: Performance below aspiration at t-1 equals performance minus aspiration for those observations where performance was below aspiration, and is set to zero otherwise. Performance was measured as return on assets (net income divided by total assets) in the base year (t-1), and the aspiration level was measured as historical performance one year prior to the base year (t-2). The more negative the value, the larger the performance shortfall, and a quadratic term for performance below aspiration was included in the estimations.
scale: difference in return on assets (zero when at or above aspiration, negative below aspiration)

description: New foreign market entry is a binary indicator coded as one if the focal firm entered at least one new foreign market within the given period of time and zero otherwise. Because there were relatively few new foreign market entries in a given two-year period, one or more entries into foreign markets within a period was considered an event.

Earnings per share growth, measured as the five-year average of annual EPS growth adjusted for stock splits from the I/B/E/S-adjusted summary details file, scaled by the firm's stock price. For each month in which an analyst gave a rating, the EPS growth/price of the other stocks the analyst was actively covering at that time was gathered, the portfolio was rank ordered on EPS growth/price, and the focal stock's position in this ranking was recorded. The ranking was scaled by the number of stocks the analyst covered to create a percentage and reverse coded so that a higher percentage indicates superior relative performance.
time_window: five-year average of annual EPS growth; rank computed in the month of the rating within the analyst's portfolio

description: Computed in a two-step process following Zuckerman (2004). First, for each quarter, the proximity of each pair of stocks was calculated as the minimum overlap of each pair of analysts for all earnings forecasts issued in the prior 12 months; the first quarter of 1995 contained all analyst forecasts from January 1, 1994 to December 31, 1994. Coverage coherence was then calculated from these proximities together with indicator variables for whether each analyst follows a given firm; the equation for this second step is not readable in the text. The measure lets industry groupings be defined solely by the coverage patterns of individual analysts.
time_window: prior 12 months of earnings forecasts, computed quarterly

description: Analyst recommendations were coded using the translation ratings supplied by I/B/E/S, which run from 1 to 5, with 1 a positive recommendation, 3 a neutral recommendation and 5 a negative recommendation. Because brokerages may not use all five categories and a rating of 2 can have a different qualitative meaning across brokerages, the focal variable is coded 1 for stocks that receive the brokerage's highest rating as determined by its own rating system and 0 otherwise.

Dichotomous patent-level measure equal to one where the DISTANT score of the patent is above the 90th percentile in any given year, and zero otherwise, capturing whether the patent represents a potentially radical opportunity. DISTANT is calculated as 1 minus the lowest (rarest) LINK score for all of the citations made by the focal patent, and is normalized by subtracting the average DISTANT score for all patents filed in the same technological class in the prior year. For a citation made by a patent in class i to a patent in class j, LINK is the percentage of backward citations of all other patents in class i in the prior five years that were to class j. The authors dichotomize the measure because they are only interested in patents at the highest end of the DISTANT spectrum.
time_window: prior five years (t-5 to t-1) for LINK; prior year (t-1) for normalization

description: The (log-transformed) count of forward citations received by the patent, used as the primary measure of the success of potentially radical inventions. The authors note that the correlation between citations received and economic value at the patent level is relatively weak but consider the measure consistent with their focus on invention.

Alternate binary measure of success, equal to one if the patent's citations are in the highest 5% of all patents from the same class in the same year, and zero otherwise. It is analyzed with a probit model with firm fixed effects within the sub-set of potentially radical patents.

Spline variable that takes the value of zero if the firm is actually below aspirations and the value of aspirations-normalized productivity otherwise. Aspirations are a blend of social aspirations, measured as the average citations per patent received by all other patents in the technological class in the previous year, and historical aspirations, a moving average of the firm's own performance, with a weighting of 70% social and 30% historical aspirations.
