Performance versus aspirations subtracts the firm's category-specific aspiration level from its own measure of citations per patent in the prior year in that category.

Spline variable that takes the value of zero if the firm is actually above aspirations and the absolute value of aspirations-normalized productivity otherwise, so that higher values represent performance further below aspirations. Aspirations are a blend of social aspirations (average citations per patent of other patents in the technological class in the previous year) and historical aspirations (a moving average of the firm's own performance). Performance versus aspirations subtracts the firm's category-specific aspiration level from its own measure of citations per patent in the prior year in that category.

Dummy variable that takes the value of 1 when the firm is above aspirations and zero otherwise, included alongside the spline variables in order to test the prediction (Hypothesis 1a) that the pursuit of radical invention will be less likely when performance is above aspirations.

The firm's productivity in a patent class, measured as the average number of citations received by the firm's patents that were filed in the previous year in the focal technological category ('nclass' in the NBER data). It is used unadjusted (not aspiration-adjusted) to assess the effect of firm technological performance on the success of radical inventions.

A patent-based Herfindahl measure based on the patent classes in which the firm patented, with higher levels representing firms that are concentrated in fewer classes. The sample is split at the median into technologically focused and diversified firms to test Hypothesis 3, and the variable is also included as a control in the main analysis.

The firm's general technological performance, calculated analogously to local productivity, aggregated to the firm-year level using the share of the firm's patents in each category as weights. The sample is split into high performing and low performing firms on this measure to test Hypothesis 4, and it is also included as a control in the main analysis.

Indicator variable coded '1' when the CEO was classified as an agent (18.6 percent of observations). In companies with a single class of equity, CEOs owning more than 20 percent of their company's equity were defined as owner-managers; companies with multiple classes of equity were categorized as owner-managed when their CEOs' shareholdings entitled them to more than 5 percent of dividends and the right to elect a majority of the board; and all limited partnerships were categorized as owner-managed. Ownership status could not be coded as a continuous variable for the full sample because data on CEO equity ownership were unavailable for some privately held companies.

Continuous variable reflecting the company's number of business segments outside of the cable industry; vertical integration into cable programming services was not included. Diversified companies (SEGMENTS > 0) accounted for 47 percent of observations. Standard measures of diversification such as entropy and Herfindahl indices or Rumelt's taxonomy could not be employed because data on revenue by line of business were not available for many of the privately held companies in the sample.

Composite ('TURB') of three measures of environmental turbulence: retrospective assessments by a panel of six industry experts on a 5-point scale; a count of the annual number of Wall Street Journal article abstracts containing the term 'cable television', used as a proxy for information load; and an estimate of cable companies' stock return volatility. To form the composite, the three measures were standardized, then averaged, then transformed by adding an arbitrary constant. Stock return volatility was computed from daily total returns for nine relatively 'pure play' cable companies and adjusted in two steps: divided by the standard deviation of total returns for the overall NASDAQ index, then used as the dependent variable in an OLS regression with company indicator variables, debt-to-total-capital ratio and log total capital, with the coefficients on year interpreted as industry-level turbulence. TURB and its square (TURB2) were lagged by one year in the model.

Outcome category of the dependent variable, formed from PERCENT, which measures the net number of subscribers acquired or divested during each year from 1986 through 1995 as a percentage of the company's total number of subscribers at the beginning of the year and reflects only the purchase and sale of entire cable franchises. EXPAND includes any positive value for PERCENT (15.8 percent of observations) and is the reference category (h = 4) in the multinomial logistic regression.

Outcome category of the dependent variable that includes all values of -100 percent for PERCENT, representing full exit from the cable business. EXIT accounts for 7.4 percent of the 1,327 total observations.

Outcome category of the dependent variable that includes all negative values of PERCENT, provided they are greater than -100 (8.4 percent of the cases). Contracting involves divesting some cable assets without exiting the cable business altogether.

variable_name: Prospector and Defender orientation dummy variables
description: Strategic orientations were assessed through a survey questionnaire administered to senior executives in November 1987, using 20 items (7-point Likert-type scales) representing five aspects of utility strategy during 1983-87. A composite measure was obtained for each scale by averaging the individual item raw scores, and a K-means clustering algorithm was used to identify each firm's overall strategic orientation. Two dummy variables were created to represent the Prospector and Defender strategic orientations, with Reactors serving as the base case; clusters derived from perceptual data were validated with 1983-87 archival data and cluster membership was identical for 47 out of 50 firms.
scale: 7-point Likert-type scales for the underlying items
time_window: strategies during 1983-87; stability of orientations assessed over 1988-92

description: Accounting performance was defined as the annual return on capital employed, a measure considered quite appropriate for assessing electric utility financial performance. Annual data for this measure for 1988-92 were obtained from Moody's Public Utility Manuals. Two other accounting measures, return on total assets and return on stockholders' equity, were also obtained and were highly correlated with return on capital employed, and the results held across all three measures, so only return on capital employed is discussed.

Market-based performance was defined as total market return to shareholders and operationalized as the capital gain (i.e., gain in share price) in a firm's share over a year plus the value of dividends paid during the year, divided by the value of the share at the beginning of the year, all multiplied by 100. Annual data for this measure for 1988-92 were obtained from Standard & Poor's Compustat.

Coded 1 if the firm had an annual bonus plan for executives/managers based on the financial performance of the past year and 0 otherwise. Information provided in annual corporate proxy statements was used to code incentive plan characteristics for each firm for each of the 5 years (1987-91). Most adopting firms linked the bonus to accounting measures such as return on equity, return on capital employed and earnings per share, and most offered only cash bonuses.

Combined measure coded 1 if the firm had a cash-based long-term incentive plan for executives/managers and/or had a long-term incentive plan that used accounting measures such as return on equity, return on capital employed and earnings per share to evaluate performance, and 0 otherwise; the performance evaluation period for such plans ranged between 3 and 6 years. Because the use of cash incentives and accounting measures was very highly correlated in the sample, the two measures were combined into a single measure defined as long-term plan (cash/accounting). A firm without any long-term plan scores 0 on this measure.

Combined measure coded 1 if the firm had a stock-based long-term incentive plan (e.g., performance shares, performance units and restricted stock awards) and/or had a long-term incentive plan that used market measures such as share price growth/appreciation and market return to evaluate performance, and 0 otherwise. Because the use of stock incentives and market measures was very highly correlated in the sample, the two measures were combined into a single measure defined as long-term plan (stock/market). A firm without any long-term plan scores 0 on this measure.

Coded 1 if the firm had a stock option plan for executives/managers and 0 otherwise, based on annual corporate proxy statements. Consistent with the description of stock option plans as discretionary incentive plans, none of the stock option plans specified any specific performance criteria or any time period for evaluation of performance, and in all cases the timing and size of option grants was solely determined by a compensation committee of the board of directors.

Each firm's yearly R&D expenditure scaled by the firm's total assets, used as an innovation-input proxy for the level of a firm's innovative knowledge assets. The authors expected investment in R&D to positively contribute to the output or stock of a firm's innovative knowledge assets. The variable is lagged one year relative to the performance measure.

A patent-citation-based measure of innovative knowledge output: the total citations of the cumulative numbers of patents that a firm possessed. Because the unit of analysis was the firm, patents and their citation counts were aggregated to the firm level. Patent citations are argued to be a better measure of the level of a firm's innovative knowledge assets than a simple patent count.
time_window: patents granted 1963-1999 and citations 1975-1999; lagged one year (t - 1)

description: A patent-citation-based proxy for the level of firm-specific innovative knowledge, computed as the focal firm's self-citations as a percentage of all its patent citations multiplied by the focal firm's citations of prior self-citations as a percentage of all the citations of the focal firm's self-citations, based on patent citation data from 1975 to 1999. The text states that a third factor was added, specifying the extent to which a firm subsequently self-cites its previously self-cited patents, so that specificity is discounted when the prior patents are also widely cited by other firms; the factor is described in prose rather than printed in the formula.
time_window: patent citation data 1975-1999; lagged one year (t - 1)

description: The market-to-book ratio is used as the proxy for economic performance: the numerator is the year-end market value of a firm's common stock plus the book value of its preferred stock and debt, and the denominator is year-end total assets. A logarithm transformation of the market-to-book value was conducted, one rationale being that intangible capital is likely to have multiplicative rather than additive effects on value. It is measured at time t.

Outsider representation on the board of directors is measured by the percentage of independent outside directors. Nonexecutive outsider representation is generally considered a key force for effective monitoring, so a higher percentage indicates more monitoring.

The presence of large outsider blockholders is measured by the percentage of shares held by outside shareholders with greater than 5 percent shareholding. Large outside shareholders are conventionally considered guardians of firm resources and thus a monitoring mechanism.

A dummy variable set equal to 1 when a firm's CEO also chaired the board of directors. If a CEO is also chairperson, a board's monitoring role will be compromised, so duality indicates less monitoring and is reverse coded relative to the monitoring construct.

CEO equity ownership is measured as the shares of a company's common stock held by its CEO. Equity ownership rights are treated as residual rights of control that link managerial financial gain to firm performance.

CEO contingency pay is measured as the proportion of bonuses, long-term incentive payments, and stock options in the CEO's total compensation, capturing the components of CEO compensation that are directly related to firm value.

Coded as 1 if the dominant shareholder of a firm was linked to the central government or its agencies and 0 otherwise. The CSMAR database provided detailed information on the dominant shareholder (as well as the other nine largest shareholders). For these central government-owned firms, the average percentage of shares owned by the central government was 42%, while the second largest owner held an average of 9%.

Coded as 1 if a firm's top executive (Chair or CEO) served as a delegate to the National People's Congress (NPC) or the National Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), which are the two most important national political councils. In China the most powerful executive position in many firms is the chairman of the board, equivalent to the combined chairman/CEO position in the United States.
scale: 1 = top executive holds a national political appointment; 0 = otherwise

description: Measured by the number of employees (natural logged). In the interaction terms the continuous variables (size and provincial government priority) were standardized following Aiken and West (1991).

variable_name: priority given by the provincial governments to GDP growth
description: A composite score created out of two measures based on content analysis of provincial governments' 11th Five-Year Plans, coded by two independent native-speaker researchers. The first measure is the proportion of GDP growth-related economic objectives out of all objectives, obtained by dividing the number of paragraphs that are primarily GDP growth related by the total number of paragraphs on government objectives. The second measure codes whether a provincial government's approach is fixated on GDP growth targets (coded 1) based on the first itemized objective about overall economic development. The alpha coefficient for the two measures was 0.7, and a high score indicated high GDP priority. The value for the province where a firm was headquartered was used as a proxy for local institutional pressure on the firm.
scale: composite score; higher = higher GDP priority
level: province (assigned to firms by headquarters location)

variable_name: hazard rate of issuing a report
description: The dependent variable for the speed of adoption is the hazard rate of issuing a report, estimated with discrete-time event history analysis; in any given year each firm in the risk set faces some 'risk' that it will issue a report. Issuance of reports was modeled as repeated events since 2007, and firms remained in the data set after issuing a report, since they were still 'at risk' of issuing another. Firms that had not issued any reports by the end of 2011 were considered to be right-censored.

Quality of CSR reports was gauged with the ratings published by RKS (Rankins CSR Ratings), created from a rating system based on the Global Reporting Initiative (3.0) adapted to the Chinese context. All CSR reports were rated based on three dimensions - overall evaluation, content evaluation, and technical evaluation - with over 70 subdimensions that consider the range of CSR activities and the extent of engagement in each, including disclosure of metrics and third-party auditing of reports. The final score was a weighted average ranging from 0 to 100. The correlation between the RKS score and the authors' own measure of pages per item was 0.87.

Coded as 1 if a firm issued its first report early (i.e., in 2008 or 2009 - within the first two years after the announcement of the guidelines at the end of 2007) and its report quality was below the average of all firms in the observation year, and 0 otherwise. Early issuance with high-quality reports, as well as late issuance with high- or low-quality reports, were not considered as decoupling.

Decision speed was measured as the average of three items, one for each of three strategic decision scenarios (acquisition, new product introduction, and technology adoption). Each item asked the respondent to circle the approximate number of days it would take their organization to decide, using the response set 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, more. Higher values therefore indicate a slower decision.

Growth was measured with two items: the percentage change in annual sales from 1996 to 2000 and the percentage change in year-end employment from 1996 to 2000. Self-reported objective measures were used rather than subjective measures.
Profit was measured with one item, the average annual pretax net profit percentage of assets for 1998, 1999, and 2000.

Subjective measure of the environment based on CEO perceptions, using items in Likert response format. Items were selected from the questionnaire with a statistical routine that maximized Cronbach's alpha, and the measurement item reflections of the latent variable were weighted as part of the SEM optimizing process.
scale: 5-point Likert response format (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Subjective measure based on CEO perceptions, using items in Likert response format selected from the questionnaire with a statistical routine that maximized Cronbach's alpha. CEO reports of munificence were compared with an objective index built from Standard & Poor's category sales growth.
scale: 5-point Likert response format (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Subjective CEO perception measure using items in Likert response format, selected to maximize Cronbach's alpha. Respondents were asked to consider the difference between operational and strategic decisions, and the concept concerns the concentration of authority over strategic management in the firm.
scale: 5-point Likert response format (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Subjective CEO perception measure using items in Likert response format, selected to maximize Cronbach's alpha. The concept concerns the dispersion of authority over day-to-day operations management in the firm.
scale: 5-point Likert response format (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Subjective CEO perception measure using items in Likert response format, selected to maximize Cronbach's alpha. Respondents were asked to consider the difference between routine and non-routine tasks; the concept covers formalization of routine organization policies, processes and networks.
scale: 5-point Likert response format (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Subjective CEO perception measure using items in Likert response format, selected to maximize Cronbach's alpha. The concept covers the absence of formalization for non-routine organization policies, processes and networks.
scale: 5-point Likert response format (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Measured as of founding, ignoring subsequent reincorporations or changes in ownership, and updated at the end of each year. The authors report that age in the sample ranged from 2 to 99 years, with several firms founded before World War II and one before the Japanese occupation.
time_window: updated at the end of each year, 1987-1995

description: A time-varying dummy indicating whether a firm in the same business group had previously established a plant in China. It was coded as 0 until the first event occurred and as 1 thereafter for all of the firms associated with the group. For firms that were the first in their group to establish a plant, the dummy was not coded as 1 until a second firm in the same group set up a plant, so as to avoid double counting of establishments by the firm and by other firms in the same group.

Measured as the proportion of firms in each of 19 industries that had previously established a plant in China. The value was updated at the end of each calendar year, and all spells were split at the end of each year between 1987 and 1995 in order to update it.
time_window: annual, updated at the end of each year, 1987-1995

description: A dummy variable for previous entry by the same firm, coded as 0 before the firm's first entry and as 1 thereafter. The authors chose the dummy over the count of previous establishments by the same firm, with which it is highly correlated, in order to be able to test Hypotheses 4 and 5.

variable_name: Rate of establishment of new plants in China
description: The rate at which firms established new manufacturing plants in China, modeled as a repeated hazard with spells that start at the beginning of January 1987 or at the firm's founding date, whichever came last, and are right-censored just after the end of December 1995. The month and year in which the Bank of Korea authorized an investment was considered to be the time at which a plant was established; cases in which authorization was obtained but no plant was established were deleted, additions to a preexisting plant were treated as enlargements rather than new entries, and indirect investments through a Korean subsidiary in a third country were attributed to the ultimate Korean owner.

The focus of a firm's CSR efforts, measured using the index of KLD strengths. The authors summed the total number of strengths KLD awarded the firm in each of the four domains and divided this sum by the maximum number of strength points that KLD can allocate to each domain. Because CSR strengths may vary by industry, the measure was adjusted for a given firm based on the average CSR strength for its industry (SIC2); the resulting standardized CSR strengths score is the independent variable.

Dummy variable that takes the value of one if a CEO of any of the S&P 500 firms is listed for the first time on the board of trustees of any foundation during the time frame, and the value of zero if the CEO was a trustee of the foundation previously or is not part of any foundation board of trustees during the focal period. Of the 1,109 CEOs in the database, 233 joined a foundation for the first time during 2003-2011. Accounting for a one-year lag structure, the cross-sectional panel yielded 3,576 CEO-year links.

Dummy variable of the creation of a tie for a corporation-foundation dyad via the CEO, used as the substantive independent variable in the risk-set of all possible annual corporation-foundation dyads. The data set includes all possible CEO-foundation dyads for each year in the sample.

A measure of similarity in social cause priorities at foundation selection, calculated as the inverse Mahalanobis distance between the corporate CSR strengths and foundation allocations across the four social domains. The distance measure is standardized by year, reflecting the relevant risk-set of foundations at that point. The data set includes all possible CEO-foundation dyads for each year, for a total of 954,276 annual dyadic observations.

The independent time variable in the growth curve model of similarity, observed starting the year a CEO joined a foundation's board for as long as the CEO remained on that board. The panel for this test consists of the 244 CEOs that became foundation directors, yielding 780 CEO-foundation-year observations.

The CSR emphases of the firm and the social cause priorities of the foundation were first transformed using z-scores, a synthetic average between the two was taken, and two separate dependent variables were created. The corporation changes variable reflects whether the corporation deviates away from or gets closer to the middle point; if the corporation moves away from the middle point, the value is negative, reflecting divergence.

The CSR emphases of the firm and the social cause priorities of the foundation were first transformed using z-scores, a synthetic average between the two was taken, and two separate dependent variables were created. The foundation changes variable reflects whether the foundation deviates away from or gets closer to the middle point; if the foundation moves away from the middle point, the value is negative, reflecting divergence.

Employee-related KLD index, obtained from the KLD database, constructed by summing up all KLD strengths pertaining to employee relations (e.g., employee involvement, health and safety policies) and diversity (e.g., promotion of women and minorities, work-life benefit programs such as childcare, elder care, or flextime). The authors rely on the index of KLD strengths rather than netting out KLD concerns. It is the dependent variable in all main and auxiliary regressions.

Natural logarithm of the UI benefits in the state where the firm is located in the preceding year. Following Agrawal and Matsa (2013), a state's UI benefit is computed as the product of the maximum benefit amount and the maximum duration allowed, using the U.S. Department of Labor's 'Significant Provisions of State UI Laws'.

Dummy variable indicating whether the company operates in an industry whose labor intensity lies above the median across all industries. Following Agrawal and Matsa (2013), labor intensity is defined as the ratio of labor and pension expenses to sales (from Compustat) and computed as the average across all companies in the same 2-digit SIC industry. It is interacted with log(UI benefits).

Dummy variable indicating whether the company operates in an industry in which product market competition is above the median across all industries. Competition is measured by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) of industry concentration at the 2-digit SIC level, defined as the sum of the squared market shares of all companies in the same industry using sales data from Compustat; HHI is an inverse measure of competition. It is interacted with log(UI benefits).

Dummy variable indicating whether the company operates in a high-polluting industry, identified using the classification of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which identifies seven industry sectors that account for 92 percent of all disposal and other releases of toxic release inventory chemicals. High pollution is a fixed industry characteristic and is therefore absorbed by the firm fixed effects when entered alone; it is interacted with log(UI benefits).

Ratio of the firm's external technology sourcing over its total technology sourcing, the sum of its internal and external technology sourcing, bound between 0 and 1. Data were obtained from the survey respondents, who indicated what percentage of technology the firm sourced internally versus externally.

Ratio of the firm's external sourcing of known technologies over its total sourcing of known technologies, the sum of its internal and external sourcing of known technologies, bound between 0 and 1. Known technologies were defined for respondents as technologies that are being used by the firm for some time, not new to the firm or the industry.

Ratio of the firm's external sourcing of new technologies over its total sourcing of new technologies, the sum of its internal and external sourcing of new technologies, bound between 0 and 1. New technologies are defined as the inverse of known technologies.

Proxied by the firm's R&D expenditures in millions of dollars, considered a reflection of the firm's willingness to invest in absorptive capacity. Annual R&D expenditure data were collected for the five-year period between 1995 and 1999 and averaged into an R&D index to compensate for annual fluctuations.

Ratio of a firm's R&D activity dedicated to the acquisition and further development of externally sourced technologies over its total R&D activity, the sum of its R&D activity dedicated to internally and externally sourced technologies, bound between 0 and 1. Obtained from survey respondents.

Firm financial performance was proxied by return on equity, which assesses how efficiently a firm uses its resources. Annual data were collected for each firm during the four-year period 2000 to 2003 and averaged to create a performance index; a logarithmic transformation was applied. All financial data were obtained from Compustat.

Firm innovativeness was proxied by the total number of patents assigned to the firm by the U.S. PTO during the four-year time period between 2000 and 2003. The 141 sample firms obtained a total of 1,679 patents, or close to 12 patents per firm on average.
Constructed in the same fashion as the dependent variable but for the five-year time period between 1995 and 1999, to control for specification bias arising from unobserved heterogeneity.
Constructed in the same fashion as the dependent variable but for the five-year time period between 1995 and 1999, to control for specification bias arising from unobserved heterogeneity.

Respondents were asked about specific events that cause a household's social structure to change, namely changes in the composition of its working and adult members. They were asked whether the household head had suffered a chronic/severe illness, death in the family, break-up with a spouse or partner, incarceration of a household member, contracted HIV/AIDS, or fought with neighbors in the previous three years. The positive responses to these questions were counted; the variable has a mean of 1.61 and a standard deviation of 1.27, and the highest count is 7.

variable_name: Initiating action to start a business
description: The dependent variable is a multi-category variable with three categories: baseline (heads who had not started work on a new business and had not expressed an intention to start one in the next three years), intention (expressed an intention to start a business in the next three years but had not started work), and initiating action (expressed interest in starting a business in the next three years and had already started work on a new business). The analysis compares the baseline category with initiating action, while accounting for the presence of the third category using a multiple logistic regression.
scale: three nominal categories (baseline, intention, initiating action)

description: Total income lost by the household due to all types of shocks over the three years before the focal year (t = -1, -2, -3), compared with the income earned in the focal year (t = 0) as a reference point. When the variable is positive and increases, the household lost more in notional income than the income it earned in the focal year; as the variable turns negative, the household earned more in the focal year than the notional income it lost in the preceding three years; when the variable is 0, focal year income equals the notional income lost. The average household lost approximately US$1,862 from all the shocks it experienced over the three-year period, about 30 percent of total household income.
time_window: three years before the focal year (t = -1, -2, -3) relative to the focal year (t = 0)

description: Male household heads were coded with a value of 1, and female household heads were coded with a value of 0. Consistent with the social norm, 90 percent of the male household heads had a spouse, whereas only 7 percent of the female household heads had a spouse.
scale: binary (1 = male household head, 0 = female household head)

description: An indicator variable that took a value of 1 if household members belonged to a community group used for raising loans, and was coded as 0 otherwise. Nearly 35 percent of the households had members who belonged to such community institutions.
scale: binary (1 = member of a loan-raising community group, 0 = otherwise)

description: A dummy variable coded as '1' if the CEO also served as board chair, and '0' otherwise. Data were collected from proxy statements and annual reports for 1980.

Average return on investment (ROI) over the 5-year period 1980-84. Because policy decisions made by the CEO and board are not likely to be reflected in the balance sheet for several years, performance was averaged over five years. Data were collected from Compustat and supplemented by annual reports as needed.

Munificence was operationalized using a standardized measure of industry sales growth over a 5-year period. The measure is taken at the level of the industry group. Firms were classified into low and high groups based on the sample mean for the dimension.

Dynamism was operationalized using a standardized measure of the volatility of the industry sales growth rate over the same 5-year period used for munificence. The measure is taken at the level of the industry group. Firms were classified into low and high groups based on the sample mean for the dimension.

Complexity was operationalized using the Herfindahl index, the sum of the squared market shares for all firms in an industry group, which ranges between 0 and 1. A score approaching 1 implies only a few competitors in an industry, or a few firms which have a dominant market share (monopolistic or oligopolistic structures), which are considered less complex than industries approaching more perfect competition. Because the index is negatively associated with complexity, a low Herfindahl score indicates a more complex environment.
placeholder

For the inventor's patent portfolio in year t, the numerator is the number of cites to patents (applied between years t-6 and t) created by other Indian inventors, regardless of technology or location; the denominator is the total number of patents cited by that portfolio in the six years prior to year t. Cited inventors are classified as ethnic community members when the cited inventor had an Indian name. The variable therefore reflects the proportion of the inventor's knowledge sourcing attributable to the ethnic community; self-citations by the inventor are not included in the cited patents.
time_window: citations to patents applied between t-6 and t

description: A count of the distinct Indian copatenters indicated on the inventor's patent portfolio in year t. The authors determined patents with multiple inventor assignees in the portfolio and scrutinized the names of the other inventor assignees to identify Indian collaborators, following the same procedure used to build the sample of Indian inventor patents. Ethnic collaborators could be listed in any order of authorship, and repeated collaboration with the same Indian inventor on multiple patents results in a count of 1.

The total number of citations received within six years of year t by the inventor's patent portfolio, defined as all semiconductor patents filed by the inventor as first author in year t. This operationalization excludes self-citations by the inventor, self-citations by the assignee firm, and citations by other Indian inventors, providing an assessment of inventor quality external to, and independent of, the inventor, the inventor's assignee firm, and the ethnic network.

The total number of citations received within six years of year t by the inventor's patent portfolio (all semiconductor patents filed by the inventor as first author in year t). This operationalization excludes self-citations by the inventor and self-citations by the assignee firm, but includes citations by the ethnic network.

A three-item survey scale following Schulz (2001) assessing the amount of technological, market, and business-model knowledge that boundary spanners transferred from external knowledge sources that were part of the program to the home organization at each measurement occasion (Cronbach's alpha of 0.80). An introductory sentence specifies that the questions concern knowledge accessed from external sources, that is, other firms in the program, and the items re-emphasize transfer from the external innovation program to the home organization; a sample item is 'I have been providing a great deal of knowledge about technologies developed in [the collaborative innovation program] to individuals inside [my organization].'
level: individual boundary spanner in each survey wave
time_window: each measurement occasion, referring to the period since the end of the previous module

description: External and internal engagement were measured in each survey wave with scales adopted from prior studies: respondents selected, from lists of external parties (other firms in the program) and internal parties (functions within their own firm), those they had engaged with during the specified time period and then rated the intensity of engagement with each on a seven-point Likert scale; the number of external (internal) parties an individual engaged with intensively (moderately high, high, or very high) forms the External (Internal) engagement count. The degree of switching subtracts the number of internal engagement parties from the number of external engagement parties at each point in time (the focus on external versus internal engagement) and then takes the within-person absolute change between two consecutive time periods, divided by the total number of external and internal engagement parties.
level: individual boundary spanner in each survey wave
time_window: change between two consecutive survey waves (t to t + 1)

description: Built from two inputs. First, an eight-item survey question asked each individual whether they were comfortable addressing technical aspects associated with eight knowledge areas (yes/no). Second, a proxy of the areas of expertise that a particular external knowledge source (firm) in the program represents was created by aggregating individuals' measures to the firm level, using the average expertise of all individual participants belonging to that firm. For each individual at each point in time, the variable accumulates the number of expertise areas of a boundary spanner's engagement parties that did not overlap with their own expertise, divided by the total number of external engagement parties; because the information exists at each point in time, the variable is time-varying.
level: individual boundary spanner in each survey wave, with firm-level expertise aggregated from participants

description: The authors presume that startups are more distant from utilities (and closer to other startups) and that utilities are more distant from startups (and closer to other utilities), and that the more time an individual spends engaging with the other organizational type (startup-utility) relative to the same organizational type (startup-startup; utility-utility), the more they attempt to transfer knowledge from that other type of organization. At each measurement point respondents reported how many hours they allocated to engaging with startups and utilities, and the time-varying variable was constructed as the ratio of hours spent with external parties of the other organizational type. A value of 70, for example, implies that an individual on average spent 70% of their time engaging with external parties of the other organizational type and 30% with the same organizational type. The equation for this variable is not readable in the available text.
level: individual boundary spanner in each survey wave

description: Time is exploited to proxy the varying importance of boundary-spanning activities across the process, assuming a gradual and continuous shift in the relevance of these activities. Measurement occasions are coded as a linear time trend (-4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3); the coding with zero at the center follows best practice in longitudinal research and allows easier interpretation of interaction coefficients.
time_window: eight measurement occasions across the program

variable_name: Publications in 2 years prior to survey
description: The number of publications by faculty member i in the 2 years prior to each survey, as reported in the survey administered in year t. It is the main indicator of faculty research output and the dependent variable in the regressions. The level of analysis is the faculty-year.
time_window: 2 years prior to each survey wave

variable_name: Hours per week advising and/or counseling students
description: The average number of hours per week that faculty member i allocated to advising and/or counseling students, reported in year t. The authors note that the survey does not include the time each faculty member spends supervising research staff and that they expect a positive correlation between the two variables.

variable_name: Received funding in 2 years prior to survey
description: Funded is equal to 1 if faculty member i indicated that she had received funding in year t, and 0 otherwise. The authors note that they do not observe the amount of funding received and instead rely on whether the faculty member received any research funding in the 2 years prior to each survey wave.
time_window: 2 years prior to each survey wave

description: Faculty were grouped into seven major areas, following NSF reporting practice: engineering, life sciences, physical sciences, psychology, social sciences (other than psychology), humanities, and management. The interaction model is estimated separately for each major area. Engineering, life sciences, physical sciences, and psychology largely use the funded research model, while (other) social sciences, humanities, and management largely use the hands-on research model.

For each faculty member who reported at least one unexpected absence, all of that person's publications were collected from the Scopus database and the number of citations each publication had received was used to weight it, following previous research that uses the citation impact of each publication to adjust for its quality. The variable is the citation-weighted publication output per scientist-year; the sample includes 1,752 scientist-year observations.
time_window: scientist-year observations with incidents occurring between 1996 and 2016

description: Each absence incident is coded based on its length, ranging from 0 to 1: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1 for the absence lengths of 2-4 months, 5-8 months, 9-12 months, and more than 12 months, respectively. Based on the authors' interviews with faculty, the effect on research output is estimated with about a 2-year lag between the incident and its effect on publication output.
time_window: about 2 years lag between the incident and its effect

description: For each scientist, the research model was coded as either hands-on or funded based on department affiliation. Fifty-four faculty were flagged as affiliated with the funded research model and 17 with the hands-on research model. The median scientist assigned to the hands-on model reported having below $50,000 in annual funding and fewer than three team members at the time of the absence incident, while the median scientist assigned to the funded model reported having between $200,000 and $500,000 in funding and six to eight team members.

Let Complaint Rate denote the number of consumer complaints per 100,000 passengers against airline i in quarter t. The data are quarterly consumer complaints filed with DOT from the fourth quarter of 1987 through the fourth quarter of 1998. During this period consumers could only file complaints with DOT in writing, by telephone, or in person, and airlines were not involved in collecting and reporting these complaints.
time_window: quarterly, fourth quarter of 1987 through fourth quarter of 1998

description: Experience t-1 denotes the cumulative number of flights operated by airline i from October 1987 until the previous quarter (t-1). It is constructed from flight data obtained from Form 41, which airlines must file with DOT.
time_window: cumulative from October 1987 until the previous quarter (t-1)

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if i is a full-service airline (American, Continental, Delta, Northwest, TWA, United, or US Airways), and 0 otherwise. The three focused airlines in the data are Alaska, America West, and Southwest, which focused on routes in North America only.

Dummy variables for individual airlines (Dij = 1 if i = j, 0 otherwise). Because the intercept is a linear combination of all ten airline dummy variables, one airline dummy must be dropped; the authors do not include a dummy variable for Southwest, so Southwest serves as the reference airline.

Annual count of new GBEL certifications in a city, hand collected and translated from MOHURD data. Continuous variables are transformed as ln(1 + X) because of the highly skewed distribution of city size. Because both LEED and GBEL enter in logs, the estimated spillover coefficient is an elasticity.

Annual count of new LEED certifications in a city, collected from the USGBC at the city-year level. The authors use certification instead of registration data in the analysis because certification is viewed as a better measure of actual investments. The variable enters the regressions as ln(1 + LEED).

Number of LEED Accredited Professionals in a local market year, collected from the USGBC and used as a measure of supplier adoption; the authors describe it as reflecting the supply of professional services for the nonsubsidized label. It replaces the outcome variable in the spillover regression and enters as ln(1 + LEEDAP).

Indicator variable that equals one for all years following the adoption of a local financial subsidy for GBEL certification. The information was hand collected from MOHURD and local government websites and reflects staggered adoption of subsidies across provinces and cities.

A time-trend that equals zero prior to the adoption of any GBEL subsidy, and equals y - t_i after adoption, where y is the calendar year and t_i the year when a subsidy was introduced in city i. Together with SUBSIDY it forms the vector of instruments Z.

A city's score on the 'China Green Low-Carbon City Index', used as a variable that captures local taste for green products and as a proxy for the local demand for green amenities. The measure is available for a subset of 115 cities and enters the interaction model as lnGRINDEX after centering at its sample mean.

Building-level measure obtained by matching MOHURD and USGBC data and calculating the number of certified projects that use both labels. The authors compare the probability of multi-labeling versus single-labeling conditional on adopting either GBEL or LEED, and report how few certified buildings adopt both labels.

Membership in one of five strategic scope groups, obtained from a cluster analysis performed on the factor scores of the scope/scale factor (factor 1). SSG1 consisted of two breweries, Alken-Maes and Interbrew, the two largest breweries in Belgium; SSG2 contains 11 firms; SSG3 consisted of 7 firms, SSG4 consisted of 9 firms, while SSG5 consisted of 7 firms. Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA revealed that the SSGs differ statistically significantly at the 0.05 level on the first factor, scale/scope, but do not differ statistically significantly on any of the other factors.

Membership in one of five strategic groups identified by a cluster analysis on the factor scores of the second, third and fourth factors within SSG2. The five groups can be defined and described as differentiators, specialist, defensive marketing differentiators, reactors and prospector. These five strategic groups differ statistically significantly on the third (marketing differentiation) and fourth factors (innovative differentiation), not on the second factor (corporate identity).

The average ROA is computed by dividing the (average) gross operating profit in the numerator by the (average) amount of non-financial assets. ROA is taken before taxes and before debt charges to cope with differences in capital structure. The risk-adjusted ROA measure is computed by dividing the 4-year average ROA by the variability of ROA during the period of investigation (1985-88); unstable results are deflated while stable results are augmented.

Volume is a measure of firm size and used as a proxy for the geographical reach of the firm. Instead of working with three categories (e.g., national, regional and local), the brewers were asked for the average output level, and the natural logarithm of (average) output volume was used, as the brewers themselves commonly use output volume to compare their firm sizes. The natural logarithm was taken as an attempt to normalize the size variable.

The number of product types was asked for in the questionnaire and is in the first place used as a measure of competitive scope, but as with the variable volume it also has implications for the potentiality of arriving at competitive advantages.

Rather than using a categorization into 'mainly pils brewers' and 'mainly non-pils brewers,' the type of firm is operationalized as the percentage of pils brewed relative to the total volume of beer produced of whatever type.

Channel control is a measure of the resources committed to gain control over the distribution channels, operationalized as the number of cafés owned by the brewery or privately owned by the top management team. The number of tied outlets via subtenancy, financial support, etc., has not been incorporated. It is a measure of forward vertical integration, but a measure (of one source) of seller power as well.

Factor score per firm on the second factor of the principal components factor analysis of the strategic variables, considered as a differentiation dimension. The higher the importance of self-made output, the more important is the capital intensity and the investment intensity, and the end result is a slow asset turnover.

Factor score per firm on the third factor, labeled marketing differentiation in light of the high loading of the advertising intensity. The positive loading of the volume variable indicates that larger firms spend more on advertising, and the positive loadings of working capital intensity and variable costs are in line with firms seeking a marketing differentiation advantage.

Factor score per firm on the fourth factor, which is aimed at creating new product-market combinations and resembles the prospector strategy of Miles and Snow. The positive loading of channel control indicates that a strong home market supports innovation (e.g., new brands or exports), innovation also goes hand in hand with more investment intensity, and the negative loading of the type of firm (percentage of pils production) indicates that an emphasis on pils does not stimulate exports or the creation of new beers.

Burt's constraint is computed over banks' ego networks: the dependence level of bank i on each contact j is cij = pij + sum over q of piq*pqj, and the constraint measure Ci is the sum of the dependence levels over all contacts of i. To facilitate comparisons the authors convert constraint into a measure of structural holes, creating the variable brokerage by taking 1 - Ci, so that high values mean the bank occupies a brokerage position. For social isolates and dense networks of fewer than four contacts, Ci is set to 1 and brokerage correspondingly to 0.

Computed on binary ego networks as the proportion of the shortest paths between two contacts j and k in i's ego network that pass through i, summed over all pairs of contacts, following Freeman. It is a continuous rather than discrete variable, reflecting the continuity of the exclusive brokerage concept.

An index adapted to weighted networks by Burt, in which the proportion of shortest paths passing through the ego is replaced by the extent to which communication between j and k through ego is strong and exclusive. The formula as it appears in the supplied text is garbled and cannot be read reliably. The index is a continuous measure and is closer to the brokerage measure, thus serving as a better basis for comparison.

A dummy variable set to 1 if a bank was exposed to the dot-com bubble in the period 1999-2000, that is, did at least one public offering in the Internet sector in the period 1999-2000, and 0 otherwise.

The total dollar value, adjusted for inflation, that the bank receives from all of its deals during a particular time period. The dollar value banks receive from each deal is calculated following Jensen, assigning the proceeds of each offering to syndicate members so that the leads receive two shares of the deal value and the co-leads receive a single share. The authors label this variable Revenue and take its natural log plus unity to correct for its highly skewed distribution.
The authors simply count the numbers of new partners in the period {t+1, t+2} compared with the period {t-1, t} and take the natural log to reduce skewness in the distribution.

The authors count the numbers of new clients in the period {t+1, t+2} compared with the period {t-1, t} and take the natural log to reduce skewness. The variable is operationalized only over lead deals of the focal bank due to the passive roles of co-lead banks in finding and working with clients.

The degree of similarity between two sets of sectors in which the focal bank does business: a time-fixed set measured over the pre-crisis period 1994-1998 and a time-varying set measured over the period {t+1, t+2}. Each deal is first classified into 10 sector categories based on its SIC code. In the index, a represents the number of sectors in which the focal bank worked both pre-crisis and in {t+1, t+2}; b represents the number of sectors in which it participated pre-crisis but not in {t+1, t+2}; and c represents the number of sectors in which it worked in {t+1, t+2} but not pre-crisis. The metric, known as Jaccard's similarity coefficient, varies from 0 to 1 and captures the extent to which the focal bank pursued a persevering strategy in terms of sectoral scope.

variable_name: New partners, new clients and sector similarity (joint pattern)
description: Ambidextrous response is operationalized with three outcomes taken together: number of new partners and number of new clients (innovating or exploration) and sector similarity (persevering in existing sectors). A positive effect of exclusive brokerage on all three is read as an ambidextrous response.

Customer perceptions of MARTA's service quality, evaluated with five items on five-point, Likert-type scales anchored with 'excellent' at the extreme positive end and 'poor' at the opposite end. Items were based on existing measures and conceptual definitions in the services literature but adapted to the partnered service experience. They focused on the overall service quality delivered by MARTA as well as the quality of key processes in the experience. Construct reliability was 0.93.

Customer perceptions of the service quality offered by Delta, measured with an adapted scale of four items on the same five-point, Likert-type format anchored 'excellent' to 'poor'. The items assessed the overall quality of the check-in experience, the quality of interactions with the Delta service agents, and customers' perceptions of the excellence of service with respect to waiting time. Construct reliability was 0.88.

The waiting time experienced by each respondent was timed and recorded by the interviewer without the respondents' knowledge, with all time measurements recorded to the second. The interviewer disqualified any potential response for which there was not an accurate waiting time measurement, so the measures are treated as objective and assumed to be without measurement error. The length of time in line was recorded after the respondent exited the MARTA train and joined the Delta check-in queue.

A single-item indicator of the perceived value of the check-in experience. Consumers were asked their perceptions of the value of the partnered service on a four-point scale anchored on the positive end by 'much more value' and by 'no value' on the opposite pole. No items pertaining to a price component were used because the value-added check-in station did not incur additional fees or discounts.
scale: four-point scale anchored 'much more value' to 'no value'

description: Reuse intentions were measured with a single question asking respondents how likely they would be to reuse this service in the future. The item was measured on a scale anchored at the extremes by 'very likely' and 'very unlikely'.
scale: single item anchored 'very likely' to 'very unlikely'

description: Sampled companies were dummy coded as being included in Easton and Jarrell's TQM sample or not. Easton and Jarrell built their sample from computerized searches of annual reports, Standard and Poor's Register of Directors and Executives, Businesswire references to quality awards, and Baldridge Award lists, then conducted semistructured interviews with a top manager to develop a time-line of TQM efforts and assess deployment; firms whose efforts were judged inadequate were eliminated. Of the 100 companies in this Fortune sample, 36 were determined to have implemented TQM programs, and the authors interpret the coding as a conservative measure of implementation.
time_window: implementation dated mostly to the late 1980s, latest starting date 1991

description: Number of articles retrieved on both the company name and the descriptors of quality, teams, and empowerment, divided by firm size measured as the average of normalized sales and assets. Searches coupled the technique terms with work-related adjectives to avoid false hits. Because the number of citations depended highly on firm size, the division reduces multicollinearity; the measure can be interpreted as the amount of attention paid to a firm's popular management techniques relative to other firms of its size.

For each corporation, the number of articles linking the firm with the three popular management techniques was divided by the total number of citations received by that firm during a given year. The resulting measure taps the proportion of each firm's citations devoted to these procedures and is considered less subject to corporate impression management than the exposure measure.

Return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), and return on sales (ROS) recorded from COMPUSTAT; the intercorrelation of the three indicators averaged .80. Each financial indicator was first normalized and then the scores were aggregated into an overall financial performance measure. Regression equations predict 1995 performance and, in the longitudinal equations, changes in performance over three-, four-, and five-year periods.

Ratings recorded from the Fortune "Most Admired" survey, using Fortune's web site for 1995 and the magazine's archives for previous years. Fortune sends surveys to executives and outside directors asking them to rank companies in their own industries and to financial analysts asking them to rank companies within the industries they cover; approximately 11,000 people receive the survey and the response rate is between 45 and 50 percent. The authors recorded ratings from both sampled executives and financial analysts on overall admiration (alpha = .97 for 1995 data).

One of the eight individual ratings Fortune reported for aspects of corporate reputation, recorded for the sampled companies included in the Fortune "Most Admired" data base. Used as a dependent variable in regressions holding constant prior performance and size.

One of the eight individual ratings Fortune reported for aspects of corporate reputation, recorded for the sampled companies included in the Fortune "Most Admired" data base. It is used both as a dependent variable in regressions holding constant prior performance and size and as a mediator in the CEO pay analyses, using 1993 data that were published during 1994.

Data on CEO salary and bonuses came from the "Executive Pay Scoreboard" published by Business Week for the years 1990 through 1995. Salary and bonus is the short-term compensation measure used as the dependent variable in the compensation regressions, which control for prior pay and other determinants of executive pay.

Long-term compensation data were drawn from COMPUSTAT's Execucomp data base for the years 1992 (the first year available) through 1995. Long-term compensation includes the value of restricted stock grants, long-term incentive payouts, the value of stock options granted (using the Black-Scholes formula), and all other long-term compensation for the year; the value of stock options exercised during the year was not included. Regression equations on long-term pay were constructed as in the salary and bonus analyses.

Built from a code that operationalizes cognitive flexibility in its two main analytical categories: identification of key problem elements and reflective perspective. Each time a protocol from Task 2 contained a statement relating to any one of the specific codes, it was interpreted as an instance of the corresponding category and the participant's cognitive flexibility score was altered accordingly: items 1-6, 9, and 10 were positively associated with cognitive flexibility and added points, while items 7 and 8 subtracted points. The unit of analysis was the meaningful phrase, and protocols were coded by three of four trained coders, with acceptable levels of agreement.
Performance in Task 1 was measured with each participant's total cumulative score, in a task whose objective was defined as 'score as many points as you can'.

Two research assistants with experience in content analysis independently scored Task 2 performance from 1 to 10, based on how likely it was that the participant's stated solution would fulfill the problem's objective ('keep your tribe safe'). Each protocol's performance measure is the mean score given by the two research assistants.

To allow for a comparison across the two tasks the authors standardized each score, rescaling each to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, and added the two scores to create a unique performance measure summarizing how well a participant performed in solving both problems.

The time it took participants to solve the well-structured four-armed bandit task, used as a proxy for the type of process they were using: Type 1 processes are fast while Type 2 processes are slow. It is treated as a continuum variable, so no arbitrary threshold between fast and slow responses is imposed.

The time it took participants to solve the ill-structured think-aloud task, used as a proxy for the type of process they were using: Type 1 processes are fast while Type 2 processes are slow. It is treated as a continuum variable, so no arbitrary threshold between fast and slow responses is imposed.

A variable identifying the type of problem a performance observation belongs to: the well-structured four-armed bandit task (Task 1) or the ill-structured think-aloud task (Task 2). It enters the models as the 'task' term in the task x response time moderation and in the three-way interaction with cognitive flexibility.

The count of corporations that are headquartered in a CBSA in a given year, logged to correct for a skewed distribution. The corporate sampling frame includes all U.S.-based corporations listed on the two major U.S. stock markets, the New York Stock Exchange and NASDAQ, that were covered by disclosure in each of the four panel years.

Count of elite-oriented 501(c)(3) operating nonprofits headquartered in a CBSA in the year following each panel year, collected from NCCS SOI data based on annual filings of IRS Form 990. Elite-oriented nonprofits include the NTEE categories of arts, culture and humanities, and philanthropy, as well as recreation and sports subcategories that would benefit the elite. The model includes the t-period count as a lagged dependent variable so that the equation measures change in the dependent variable from t to t+1.
time_window: t+1 relative to the panel year

description: Count of social welfare-oriented 501(c)(3) operating nonprofits headquartered in a CBSA in the year following each panel year, collected from NCCS SOI data based on annual filings of IRS Form 990. Social welfare-oriented nonprofits include the NTEE categories of mental health, employment, housing, health care, public safety, youth development, human services, civil rights, public benefit, food and nutrition subcategories that relate to providing meals for homeless or homebound populations, and broadly oriented recreation and community improvement subcategories. The model includes the t-period count as a lagged dependent variable so that the equation measures change in the dependent variable from t to t+1.
time_window: t+1 relative to the panel year

description: Mean local degree, that is, the average number of network ties each firm in a CBSA maintained with other firms in its CBSA, constructed from shared directors among the boards of all firms in the corporate sampling frame for each panel year. This number is high to the extent that local companies recruit directors that also serve on the boards of other local companies.
The presence of upper-class clubs in each CBSA, determined from the upper-class club list established by Domhoff (1967).
A dummy variable used to assess a community's regional culture, indicating whether the region is the Northeast.
The number of incorporated firms in each city in 1905, taken from the Census of Manufactures. Because of extreme values, this variable was logged.

The number of outside directors as a percentage of all directors. Full-time or retired employees of the BHC (or of subsidiary banks controlled by the BHC) and individuals with family relationships to these employees were classified as inside directors; all other directors were classified as outsiders. The authors note that the measure assumes directors classified as outsiders operate truly independently of managerial influence and is therefore an approximation.
Percentage of the total outstanding common stock of the BHC controlled by the five largest nonmanager shareholders.
Percentage of the total outstanding common stock of the BHC held by the largest nonmanager shareholder.

Percentage stock ownership of the top executive. One of the alternative definitions of the top management team used to measure the incentive effects of managerial share ownership; percentages are of total outstanding common stock of the firm.
Percentage stock ownership of the Chairman, CEO and President, used as one of the alternative definitions of the top management team. Percentages are of total outstanding common stock of the firm.
Percentage stock ownership of all inside directors, used as one of the alternative definitions of the top management team. Percentages are of total outstanding common stock of the firm.
Percentage stock ownership of all inside directors and managers, used as one of the alternative definitions of the top management team. Percentages are of total outstanding common stock of the firm.

MMID1 = 1 - TOPTOID, where TOPTOID is the shareholdings of the top executive as a percentage of the shareholdings of all inside directors. The authors state that this measures the potential for monitoring the top manager's activities by other inside directors.

MMID2 = 1 - HHID, where HHID is the sum over inside directors of (shares held by each inside director divided by shares held by all inside directors) squared. This Herfindahl-type index of the dispersion of inside director shareholdings measures the potential for mutual monitoring of inside directors.

Equals 1 when the top executive holds all of the positions of Chairman, CEO or President that exist in the firm, and 0 when these positions are shared between two or three individuals. Dominance is measured by the number of titles held by the top executive.

Downside risk is specified as a function of a firm's annual return on assets relative to a target level that changes over time, in the form of a second-order root lower partial moment; the equation itself is not readable in the text. The target performance level is the average return on assets for the firm's two-digit industry in the preceding year, calculated based on the full population in the Development Bank of Japan database. The difference between the industry's average ROA and the firm's ROA, conditional on this difference being positive, is squared and summed over a five-year period from the focal year to four years back. Hence, downside risk is positive in the case of below-target performance and zero in the case where the firm performs better than the target; the dependent variable is censored at zero and is multiplied by 100 in the tables.
time_window: five years, from the focal year (t = 0) to four years back (t = -4)

description: Measured as the number of countries in which the Japanese firm operates manufacturing affiliates, averaged for the same five years as the dependent variable. The authors use it as a measure of the switching options embedded in multinational investment, reflecting the idea that operating subsidiaries located in separate countries can provide the valuable option to shift production.

Calculated based on correlations in labor costs, adjusted for exchange rates, among all of the host countries in which the firm has established manufacturing activities; the equation itself is not readable in the text. The labor cost correlation is first calculated for any pair of host countries in the firm's portfolio, these correlations are summed and the summed value is divided by the total number of possible host country pairs, and the resulting value is averaged for the five years including the focal year, in order to avoid larger multinational operations displaying higher cost subadditivity simply because they operate in a larger number of countries. A high correlation indicates high-cost subadditivity, whereas a low or negative correlation indicates that production switching opportunities are more abundant and more valuable; labor cost data are converted into dollar terms using exchange rate information.
time_window: five years including the focal year

description: Calculated as the Japanese firm's average equity stake in its portfolio of foreign manufacturing affiliates; the equation itself is not readable in the text. The authors interpret this variable as capturing the control the firm has over its affiliates and as facilitating the coordination of cross-border activities among the portfolio of affiliates. It is averaged for the same five years as the other time-varying variables.

Calculated as the unweighted average of the ratio of expatriate employees over total employees over all foreign manufacturing affiliates that the firm operates. A ratio rather than a count measure is used to account for affiliate size and the associated coordination challenges. The measure reflects the extent to which expatriates have managerial influences in the affiliates and the degree to which the affiliates can be managed in close coordination with corporate headquarters; the authors note as a limitation that they cannot fully identify the roles of all expatriates. Averaged for the same five years as the other time-varying variables.

Coverage mismatch is the sum over the firm's segments of the weighted score of the segment's size (its proportion of total sales or assets) multiplied by one minus the number of firm coverages divided by the maximum coverage number in that segment. Its range is zero (all securities analysts who specialize in the firm's segments cover it) to one (none of them do). Analysts are identified as industry specialists if they follow either 40% of the firms in the industry or at least five firms in the industry.

The log-transformed number of unique words used in the firm's 10-K business description, taken as a measure of the spanning width of the firm's own self-description. A high number of unique words indicates that the firm's self-described business spans a wider set of activities.

The imputed value of each segment is the median ratio of total capital to sales for single-segment firms in the same industry multiplied by the segment's sales, and the imputed value of the firm is the sum across its reported segments; the measure compares the firm's value with this imputed value. Industry median ratios use the most detailed SIC group that includes at least five single-business firms with at least $20 million of sales. A positive excess value indicates that diversification enhances the value of segments beyond that of their stand-alone counterparts, and negative implies that diversification reduces value. Firms with a sales-based discrepancy greater than 1% between summed segment data and firm-level data were given missing values, and the rest were proportionally rescaled.

The assets-based analogue of excess value, in which the imputed value of each segment is the median ratio of total capital to assets for single-segment firms in the same industry multiplied by the segment's assets, summed across the firm's segments and compared with the firm's value. Firms with an assets-based discrepancy between summed segment data and firm-level data greater than 25% were given missing values, and the rest were proportionally rescaled.

The cosine similarity score for each firm and year between the 10-K-based document embedding space (doc2vec, 300 dimensions) and the analyst coverage network embedding space (iterative random projection network embedding, 300 dimensions) after the two spaces are aligned with an orthogonal Procrustes transformation. The score ranges from -1 to 1 by definition, although most values fall between zero and one. A firm that submits a 10-K report but receives no coverage from financial analysts is assigned zero as its cosine similarity score.

Computed by fixing the organizational position in one space and calculating the cosine similarities between the organizational positions in the other space for the current and next years, then subtracting the next-year cosine similarity score from the current-year cosine similarity. This version holds the audience expectation space fixed and captures change attributable to the firm's own movement in its 10-K self-description.

Computed by fixing the organizational position in one space and calculating the cosine similarities between the organizational positions in the other space for the current and next years, then subtracting the next-year cosine similarity score from the current-year cosine similarity. This version captures change attributable to the audience's changed expectations while the firm's self-description is held fixed.

variable_name: membership on a particular organization's TMT
description: Each informant was coded by the organization (business segment) in which he or she was employed. The CEO of each participating firm completed a form identifying the members of the top management team, and questionnaires were sent to those managers; only firms with data from multiple informants could be used to test the hypotheses. Membership in the same organization was used to predict the similarity or dissimilarity of the views of TMT members.

Each firm, and thus each TMT member, was categorized by industry at the level of the 4-digit SIC using the Compustat-II data base. Because informants from a particular organization could be assigned only to the industry of their organization, industry membership is nested within organization membership.

Assessed originally with nine Likert-type questionnaire items on 7-point scales based on the work of Duncan (1973) and Bourgeois (1985). Four items were eliminated after factor analysis revealed low loadings, and the coefficient alpha for the resulting scale was 0.71.

Assessed originally through seven questionnaire items developed by the author based on the work of Glick et al. (1990). One item was eliminated after factor analysis revealed a low loading, and the alpha for the scale was 0.88. Respondents reported how accurate each statement was.

Assessed originally with five items based on the work of Dess and Beard (1984). One item was eliminated because of a low factor loading, and the alpha for the scale was 0.60. Respondents indicated how strongly they agreed or disagreed with each statement.

Assessed with five questionnaire items adapted from Thomas and McDaniel (1990); the alpha for the scale was 0.84. Respondents indicated how strongly they agreed or disagreed with each statement about the situations their firm encounters.

Assessed with five questionnaire items based on the work of Thomas and McDaniel (1990); the alpha for the scale was 0.84. Respondents indicated how strongly they agreed or disagreed with each statement about the firm's ability to control situations.

variable_name: Variance in perceptions explained by organization and industry membership
description: Homogeneity of perceptions is assessed with a nested random-effects ANOVA of the 307 executives' perceptions of five environmental attributes. It is read from the significance and the proportion of variance explained by organizational membership and by industry membership.
level: individual executive nested in organization and industry

variable_name: Strength of Community Consensus Around a Resource Conservation Logic
description: Measured with the voting patterns of U.S. congressional representatives with respect to the environment, taken from the League of Conservation Voters' National Environmental Scorecard, which reports the votes of members of Congress on bills selected for having proenvironmental and antienvironmental dimensions; an absence counts as an antienvironmental vote. The LCV score for each representative and senator runs from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating a higher percentage of proenvironmental votes. To represent the core of an MSA, the House of Representatives districts that comprise an MSA are used to create an average LCV score. The variable is lagged one year.

variable_name: Strength of Community Consensus Around a Resource Conservation Logic (state level)
description: The average of the annual LCV scores for each state's two U.S. senators was used for the models with dependent variables of the change in wind and solar incentives that occurred at the state level. The score runs from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating a higher percentage of proenvironmental votes. The variable is lagged one year.

variable_name: Number of Wind Energy Equipment Manufacturers in MSA
description: Derived from the Thomas Register of American Manufacturers for the years 1978-2006. Essential components of wind energy systems were first identified from industry reports, Renewable Energy Policy Project reports, and interviews with public service commissioners and renewable energy professionals; the Thomas Register was then used to create a database of firms manufacturing components and systems. For each year, an MSA has a different number of manufacturers for solar and for wind. The analysis ends in 2006 because the Thomas Register moved from compact discs to an online rolling directory in 2007.

variable_name: Number of Solar Energy Equipment Manufacturers in MSA
description: Derived from the Thomas Register of American Manufacturers for the years 1978-2006 using the same procedure as for wind, based on the essential components of solar energy systems identified from industry reports and interviews. For each year, an MSA has a different number of manufacturers for solar and for wind. The analysis ends in 2006 because the Thomas Register moved from compact discs to an online rolling directory in 2007.

Knowledge spillovers are represented by the underlying science developed in related university departments, proxied by total annual research spending by all universities in each MSA in the relevant engineering disciplines.
