Only universities located in MSAs were considered, because knowledge spillovers fall sharply beyond a 100-mile radius. Relevant engineering disciplines for wind energy are aerospace, electrical, and mechanical. The variable is logged after adding 1 to avoid logging a value of 0.

Knowledge spillovers are represented by the underlying science developed in related university departments, proxied by total annual research spending by all universities in each MSA in the relevant engineering disciplines. Only universities located in MSAs were considered, because knowledge spillovers fall sharply beyond a 100-mile radius. Relevant engineering disciplines for solar are chemical, electrical, and mechanical. The variable is logged after adding 1 to avoid logging a value of 0.

Technological uncertainty is not measured directly; the authors test for differences in relevant coefficients between models estimating wind and solar equipment manufacturers. The samples of wind and solar energy equipment manufacturers represent two separate populations that differed dramatically in the technological uncertainty associated with the two technologies: wind energy technology embodied less technological uncertainty than solar, as evidenced by the establishment of a dominant design for wind turbines and the far greater number of cumulative wind installations. Variation on technological uncertainty is therefore measured by comparing outcomes for wind energy equipment manufacturers with outcomes for their solar counterparts.

variable_name: Technological Uncertainty (wind vs. solar incentives comparison)
description: For the state-level test, technological uncertainty is represented by comparing the relevant coefficients between the models predicting wind incentives and the models predicting solar incentives, because the two technologies differ in technological uncertainty.

The count of state wind incentives is used as the dependent variable, because states adopted different policies toward the two technologies. State incentives were identified through listings in the Database of State Incentives for Renewable Energy (DSIRE); for years prior to the founding of DSIRE in 1995, incentives were identified and confirmed across multiple legal and association publications. This measure is similar to that used by Lee and Sine (2005) and Sine and Lee (2009).

The count of state solar incentives is used as the dependent variable, because states adopted different policies toward the two technologies. State incentives were identified through listings in the Database of State Incentives for Renewable Energy (DSIRE); for years prior to the founding of DSIRE in 1995, incentives were identified and confirmed across multiple legal and association publications.

The hypotheses about temporal decline are tested with an interaction term consisting of the resource conservation logic variable and a time trend; because the models include fixed effects for years, the direct effect of the time trend is not included in the specifications.

Coded as a dichotomous dummy variable set equal to 1 if the organization switched its structure to become a division of an M-form and set equal to 0 if it did not. The coding follows the organization structure codes used by Fligstein (1985), who drew upon the studies of Chandler (1962) and Rumelt (1974).
scale: 1 = became a division of an M-form, 0 = did not

description: Computed as the natural logarithm of the number of publishing imprints per firm. It is described as a measure of personal imprint publishing and author-editor relational networks.

Set equal to 1 if a publishing organization (supplier) had a contract for distribution of its books by another separately owned distributor or publisher and set equal to 0 if it did not. It is described as a measure of publisher-distributor relational networks.
scale: 1 = had a distribution contract, 0 = did not

description: Set equal to 1 if a firm acquired another firm and set equal to 0 if it did not. The business press articles referenced by the LMP were reviewed to distinguish the acquired from the acquiring firms.

A ratio measure of the annual count of potential competitors (all publishing organizations) relative to available resources (the number of students enrolled in colleges and universities). College and university student enrollment data came from the Digest of Education Statistics.

Observations for the hazard rate models were divided into two historical periods, 1958-74 and 1975-90, which correspond with the respective prevalence of the editorial and the market ideal types of institutional logic. The periodization was based on the in-depth interviews and historical research, and validation was the fact that the ideal types are used at a well-known university publisher's college in its executive education program.

Experimental condition. In the reputation condition, before deciding each trial subjects saw four items about the newly paired partner on their decision screen: the partner's cooperation history (number of times the partner cooperated in alliances prior to those alliances ending), the partner's defection history (number of times the partner competed in alliances prior to those alliances ending), the partner's exit history (number of times the partner opted out in alliances), and the historic alliance stage completion ratio (the number of alliance stages the partner was able to play in the past relative to the maximum number of stages the partner could have played). In the no-reputation condition none of this information was provided. The information was updated at the start of each trial.
time_window: updated at the start of each trial

description: The proportion of cooperative play in all stages of alliances played pre-exit. A separate initial-stage measure is the choice of cooperation in the initial stage of any alliance, expressed as the percentage of initial-stage cooperative choices. Means are compared across the reputation and no-reputation experiments with two-tailed t-tests.
time_window: all stages of alliances played pre-exit

description: The proportion of alliance stages played pre-exit relative to the possible alliance stages, averaged across the experiments and compared between the reputation and no-reputation conditions.

Overall welfare measured as the average alliance stage payoff of players, in experimental currency (francs), computed from the payoffs of the cooperate, compete and opt-out decisions in each alliance stage.

At the beginning of each trial, prior to making a strategy decision, the computer required subjects to estimate the probability that their partner would cooperate in that trial by moving a slider button. The measure was collected prior to every played alliance stage and averaged for comparison across conditions.
time_window: prior to every played alliance stage

description: Systematic (beta) risk is the amount of price variation in an organization's stock returns that can be explained by changes in the overall markets of firms. It was computed following the capital asset pricing model from monthly stock data for t - 1 through t - 10, with a value-weighted market portfolio of all stocks in the CRSP database as the market index and the U.S. government Treasury Bill rate at time t as the risk-free return. A separate beta was calculated for each year, and the lagged measure of risk at t - 1 was used in the analyses.
time_window: monthly data from t - 1 through t - 10; lagged at t - 1

description: Unsystematic (epsilon) risk measures variation in an organization's stock returns that is due to factors specific to the organization itself, such as managerial decisions. It was computed following the capital asset pricing model from monthly stock data for t - 1 through t - 10, using a value-weighted market portfolio of all stocks in the CRSP database as the market index and the U.S. government Treasury Bill rate at time t as the risk-free return. A separate epsilon was calculated for each year, and the lagged measure at t - 1 was used in the analyses.
time_window: monthly data from t - 1 through t - 10; lagged at t - 1

description: Systematic (beta) income stream risk is the amount of price variation in an organization's income stream (return on assets) that can be explained by changes in the overall markets of firms. It was computed following the capital asset pricing model from annual accounting data from the previous ten-year period, with a value-weighted average of all companies in the COMPUSTAT primary, secondary, tertiary, full, and research databases for each year as the market index. The lagged measure at t - 1 was used in the analyses.
time_window: annual accounting data from the previous ten-year period; lagged at t - 1

description: Unsystematic (epsilon) income stream risk measures variation in an organization's return on assets that is due to factors specific to the organization itself, such as managerial decisions. It was computed following the capital asset pricing model from annual accounting data from the previous ten-year period, using a value-weighted average of all companies in the COMPUSTAT databases as the market index. The lagged measure at t - 1 was used in the analyses.
time_window: annual accounting data from the previous ten-year period; lagged at t - 1

description: The measure of incentive pay was based on the ratio of bonus to base pay, derived by dividing a manager's annual bonus by the manager's annual base. Because agency theory predictions are framed in terms of contracts with single agents, individual managers' pay data were used in the incentive pay equation.
scale: ratio of bonus to base pay

description: Because the performance analysis involved firm-level outcomes, a proxy of firm compensation policies was computed by using the average pay of all the managers reported by a firm in a single year. This firm-level incentive pay measure was used in the firm performance equation.

Base pay was measured by the natural logarithm of annual base pay. Individual managers' base pay data were used in the base pay equation, consistent with agency theory's individual-level framing of compensation contracts.

A proxy of firm compensation policies was computed by using the average pay of all the managers reported by a firm in a single year. This firm-level base pay measure was used in the firm performance equation.

Total shareholder return consists of the year-end closing price of a firm's stock plus adjusted dividends divided by the stock return from the previous year. It reflects the one-year total gain (loss) a shareholder received for holding the firm's common shares, and it was chosen because the principals of the sampled firms were the owners of their common stock. The measure is short-term, just as bonuses are typically tied to short-term measures of firm performance.

An indicator variable was created for each firm that had at least one major nonmanagerial shareholder who held 5 percent or more of the firm's stock and retained voting rights to those shares. The 5 percent rule is a common cutoff used in research on managerialism. A value of 1 therefore indicates an owner-controlled firm with a strong outside principal, rather than a manager-controlled firm.

variable_name: Low earnings relative to consensus forecasts (negative earnings surprise) at alter's firm
description: In the primary analyses, negative earnings surprises were measured as the difference between the firm's most recently reported quarterly earnings and the median forecasted earnings for the same period among all analysts who covered the firm, adjusted by the firm's stock price at the end of the most recent quarter. The variable was inverted so that higher values indicate more negative earnings relative to consensus forecasts and was set to zero when earnings were above forecasts. In the models of IM support it is the moderator of the prior-support variables.

variable_name: (Low) reported corporate earnings vs. forecasts at focal CEO's firm
description: Same construction as for alter's firm: the difference between the focal firm's most recently reported quarterly earnings and the median analyst forecast for the same period, adjusted by the firm's stock price at the end of the most recent quarter, inverted so that higher values indicate more negative earnings and set to zero when earnings were above forecasts. In the models of journalists' reports it moderates the effect of IM support and is also a control.

For H1, the independent variable is the number of instances of IM support provided by alter to the focal CEO, as reported by alter, following a negative earnings surprise at the focal CEO's firm during the prior two-year period (t-2 to t0). IM support was measured with a multi-item count scale, and for the CEO-dyad models the counts for each question were aggregated across journalists. IM support provided by alter during the previous three-year period (t-5 to t-2) was also measured separately.
time_window: prior two-year period (t-2 to t0); separately t-5 to t-2

variable_name: Prior IM support by other CEOs
description: For H2, the independent variable is the number of instances of IM support provided by all other CEOs except alter to the focal CEO following a negative earnings surprise at the focal CEO's firm during the prior two-year period. The same multi-item IM support scale was used, with counts aggregated across journalists for each CEO dyad. Awareness of IM support by alter during the previous three-year period was also measured separately.

In the primary models, journalists' responses measure the number of instances in which other CEOs made positive statements about the focal CEO's leadership or external attributions for low performance at the focal CEO's firm in conversations with the focal journalist during the two-week period subsequent to an earnings disclosure. The survey items directly parallel the IM support items answered by CEOs, and for the firm-journalist dyad models the counts were aggregated across potential support providers.
time_window: two-week period subsequent to an earnings disclosure

description: The dependent variable in the models of IM support: the number of instances of IM support provided by the focal CEO for another CEO (alter) following the disclosure of quarterly earnings at alter's firm, as reported by the focal CEO. It is the average of seven count items; respondents answered these questions separately for each CEO in their industry with whom they were familiar, and in the CEO-dyad models the counts for each question were aggregated across journalists. IM support was measured for the two-week period following earnings disclosures while controlling for support in the prior period.
time_window: two-week period following each earnings disclosure

variable_name: Awareness of prior IM support by alter for other CEOs
description: For H3, the independent variable is the number of instances of IM support provided by alter for other CEOs during the prior two-year period of which the focal CEO is aware, based on survey responses from the focal CEO just prior to the earnings disclosure at alter's firm. The six-item scale directly parallels the IM support items, for example awareness of instances in which alter made positive remarks about another CEO's leadership or strategy to a journalist. The scale alpha was .91, and the correlation between the focal CEO's perception of IM support by alter and alter's self-reported IM support was high (ICC = .88).
time_window: prior two-year period (also the previous three-year period)

variable_name: Negative statements about firm's leadership by journalist
description: Three coders independently assessed each article written by journalists in the sample during the four-month period following the period in which IM support was measured that mentioned a firm or CEO in the sample. In the primary analysis the recording unit was the sentence: each sentence referring to a company or CEO in the sample was coded positive, negative, or neutral, and coders then determined whether each negative statement referred to the leadership or strategy of the firm. The number of such statements in articles by the focal journalist was summed over a two-month window in the primary analyses. The intraclass correlation coefficient across coders was .92.
time_window: two-month window after the period in which IM support was measured

variable_name: External attributions for low performance by journalist
description: Coders judged whether each statement represented an external attribution for low firm performance, using coding instructions based on Staw, McKechnie, and Puffer's (1983) procedure for identifying external attributions in annual reports. The number of external attributions in articles by the focal journalist was summed over the specified time period (a two-month window in the primary analyses). Interrater reliability was high (ICC = .93).
time_window: two-month window after the period in which IM support was measured

variable_name: IM in conference calls by executives at focal firm
description: An archival measure based on a content analysis of archived conference calls that occurred at the time of earnings announcements by firms in the sample, conducted by the three coders. Coders looked for positive statements by executives about firm leadership, strategy, or performance prospects, and external attributions by executives for low performance, following Staw, McKechnie, and Puffer's (1983) procedure. Positive statements and external attributions accounted for approximately 94 percent of all statements made by executives in conference calls.

variable_name: IM in letters to shareholders at focal firm
description: A content analysis of letters to shareholders in the firms' most recent annual report prior to the period for which journalist reports were measured. The three coders searched these documents for positive statements about firm leadership, strategy, or performance prospects, as well as external attributions for low performance. Interrater reliability for annual reports was adequate (ICCs from .87 to .91 across press releases and annual reports).
time_window: most recent annual report prior to the measurement period

variable_name: IM in press releases at focal firm
description: A content analysis of press releases in the PR Newswire issued by the focal firm at the time of the earnings announcement and over the period for which IM support is measured. The three coders searched for positive statements about firm leadership, strategy, or performance prospects and external attributions for low performance. Interrater reliability was adequate (ICCs from .87 to .91 across press releases and annual reports).
time_window: earnings announcement and the period for which IM support is measured

variable_name: IM by focal CEO in comm. with journalist outside conference call
description: A survey scale that directly parallels the measures of IM support, with separate questions for IM by the CEO (for example whether the CEO suggested that low firm performance could be attributed to uncontrollable factors in the industry and whether the CEO made positive remarks about his or her leadership). Respondents answered these questions separately for each journalist with whom they had communicated during the period for which IM support was measured, and journalists' responses were used in the primary models of journalists' reports. Alphas ranged from .87 to .93 and ICCs from .89 to .94.
time_window: the period for which IM support was measured

variable_name: IM by CFO of focal firm in comm. with journalist outside conference call
description: A survey scale paralleling the IM support measures, with separate questions for IM by the CFO of the focal firm in communications with journalists. Respondents answered separately for each journalist with whom they had communicated during the period for which IM support was measured, and the primary models used journalists' responses. Our survey data indicated that it was rare for executives other than the CEO or CFO to communicate regularly with journalists about the firm.
time_window: the period for which IM support was measured

variable_name: IM by other staff of focal firm in comm. with journalist outside conference call
description: A survey scale paralleling the IM support measures, with separate questions for IM by public relations staff of the focal firm in communications with journalists. Respondents answered separately for each journalist with whom they had communicated during the period for which IM support was measured, and the primary models used journalists' responses.
time_window: the period for which IM support was measured

description: Respondents identified and briefly described the most significant strategic decision made by their firm in the last 2 years and reported the month and year of two events: when the firm began to actively consider alternative courses of action, and when a commitment to a specific choice was made. Decision duration was the number of months during which the decision was considered. The duration measure was logged in order to normalize its distribution and then multiplied by (-1) in order to provide an intuitive measure of speed, for which higher values represented faster decisions.

Entrepreneurs were asked to report their age, measured in years. Background data were gathered in the second stage of the survey and combined with archival data on managers' backgrounds obtained from website biographies.

Entrepreneurs were asked to report the number of times they had previously been involved in founding or managing a new venture. Because the task-relevant human capital conferred by an initial new venture experience is likely to be considerably greater than the impact of each subsequent experience, prior experience was coded as a dummy variable for which '0' represented no prior new venture experiences and '1' represented one or more such experiences.

Absolute values of industry-adjusted year-to-year changes in six key strategic ratios were standardized within the sample and averaged into a composite index. Industry adjustment subtracted the industry median change in each ratio, with the focal firm excluded from the industry median; the six standardized absolute values were then averaged.
time_window: annual change from t-1 to t, updated yearly

description: The focal firm's annual ROA minus the industry median ROA of its primary four-digit industry, with the focal firm excluded from the industry median. ROA and industry median ROA data were collected from COMPUSTAT and updated yearly.

Coded one if the CEO was an outside CEO who had firm tenure of less than two years when he or she assumed the CEO position, and zero otherwise. Data on CEO origin came from the Dun & Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Management and from firm proxy statements.

Dummy variable capturing whether or not there was one or more foreign investment projects announced in a given industry and year. Foreign investment projects were identified from CapEx, a database of all investment projects announced since 1988, with most companies making regular announcements about their capital investment projects. The announcement date of the project reflects the initial stage of investment, when promoters announce their intention to invest.

Binary indicator capturing whether or not the firm announced one or more projects in a given industry and year. Observations in which an MNE and a local firm both announced a new project in the same industry on the same day, which could reflect a strategic alliance or other coordinated action, were dropped (0.5% of all observations in the sample). In years in which there were announcements by both MNEs and local firms in a particular industry, the variable takes the value of 1 only when the local announcement occurred at least one day after the first MNE investment of that calendar year; 12% of all local announcements were treated as 0 because they occurred before an MNE investment in that year.

Dummy indicator that takes the value of 1 when the firm belongs to a group and 0 when the firm does not belong to a group. Group membership was based on CMIE's classification of firms into business groups, which has been used in other studies.

The percentage of firms in the group in which family members occupy no executive positions in the firm (i.e., the member firm uses only professional managers). A given firm was considered to be professionally managed if neither the promoter nor any individuals sharing the promoter's family name were part of the firm's management, including the board of directors, chief executive officer, managing director, chairperson, vice chairperson, executive director, or president.
scale: percentage of firms in the group

description: The total number of instances in which two member firms employed the same director on their board, divided by the total number of potential overlaps in the group. It is a group-level measure of the extent of interlocking directorates within the business group.

The percentage of the firm's equity that was held by the promoter or family members. A 'promoter' refers to the founder, who maintains effective control of the business, and the term generally encompasses those who have a controlling interest in the firm with a 20% or more equity holding.

The difference between control rights and cash flow rights of promoters. The control rights measure reflects the sum of the equity holdings by promoters and holdings by Persons Acting in Concert (PACs, where PAC are affiliates and their holding companies or subsidiary companies); cash flow rights are defined as the aggregate equity holdings by promoters. The ownership information in Prowess is provided only from 2001 onwards, so the wedge in each of the years from 1995 to 2000 is assumed to be the same as its 2001 values.
scale: difference between equity-based control rights and cash flow rights
time_window: 2001 ownership data; 1995-2000 values assumed equal to the 2001 values

description: Degree centrality of a firm within its business group, calculated using UCINET 6.0, capturing the number of other firms in the network with which a given member firm shares directors. The 2008 network was used for measurement purposes and these values were not varied over time.
scale: number of other firms with which the member firm shares directors

description: Count of SOKIs operating in country i in year t−1. A SOKI was defined as an organization operating in both country i and at least one primary country in year t−1. The first year in which a SOKI was counted as operating in a country was determined by its appearance in the Alliance's partner directory.

Number of domestic clean cookstove companies entering country i in year t. Organizations were included if listed in the Alliance partner directory as a 'small or medium enterprise' or 'national or multinational company,' indicated cookstove or fuel 'work' on their profile, only operated the focal country, and were founded in or after 2013. Founding year was determined by incorporation year according to Orbis or Open Corporates, domain name registration date from WHOXML or WHOXY, self-reported founding year on social media or website, or the year the organization joined the Alliance partner directory.

Absolute value of the difference between the number of company SOKIs and nonprofit SOKIs operating in country i in year t−1. Organization types were based on self-reported classifications: 'small or medium enterprise' or 'national or multinational company' for company SOKIs and 'nongovernmental organization' for nonprofit SOKIs.
Average number of countries in which SOKIs operating in country i were active in year t−1. This variable captures the geographic dispersion of the SOKI population in a country-year.

Percentage of domestic industry actors with clean cookstove knowledge, calculated as the number of domestic organizations in country i in year t−1 reporting work as 'cookstove design/manufacture/assembly' or 'cookstove distribution/retail/consumer finance' divided by the total number of domestic industry actors in the country in year t−1 multiplied by 100. If no domestic industry actors were present, a value of zero was imputed to reflect the absence of local cookstove-related knowledge.

Takes the value of 1 for scientists belonging to academic units with a rotator. In the difference in differences specification it is interacted with Ex Post, which takes the value of 1 for observations corresponding to the ex post period and 0 otherwise. The treatment group is composed of faculty members in the academic unit with a rotator who had no NSF funding in the ex ante period.

The dependent variable is the inflation-adjusted sum of funds raised by each scientist before and after having a rotator as a colleague. It does not include grant extensions or continuations. The ex post period is the five years after the rotator returns to her academic unit and the ex ante period is the five years before the rotator started her tenure at NSF.
time_window: five years ex ante and five years ex post

description: Measured as the number of years the rotator has been employed at the focal university. For scientists in the control groups the authors used the values of the moderators corresponding to academics estimated to be similar to the rotators.
time_window: measured at the time of rotation

description: Captured by the number of top-10 keywords of the rotator's ex ante articles that are also among the top-10 keywords of her focal colleague's ex ante articles. The ex ante period is used under the expectation that the relationships that strengthen knowledge transfer take time to develop. For scientists in the control groups the authors used the values of the moderators corresponding to academics estimated to be similar to the rotators.

Measured as the absolute value of the difference between the H5 index of the rotator and the H5 index of the focal colleague, multiplied by -1 so that increasing values correspond to higher productivity similarity. The H5 index is a measure of scientific productivity: in the last five years, a scientist with an index of h has published h papers, each of which has been cited in other articles h times or more. For scientists in the control groups the authors used the values of the moderators corresponding to academics estimated to be similar to the rotators.

Percentage of total loans produced through a bank's own retail branches, as opposed to those purchased from brokers or correspondents, measured in dollar value. Most banks in the sample use the mixed mode, so the degree of integration varies continuously from 0 percent to 100 percent specialized in origination. In the logit analysis the same variable is coded 0 if a bank makes less than 10 percent and 1 if it makes more than 90 percent of its loans in-house, with observations in between dropped.

Transaction costs are measured as the composition of a bank's loan portfolio in terms of the percentages of three loan types: government-sponsored FHA/VA loans (highest risk), fixed-rate conventional mortgages (FRMs, intermediate risk) and adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs, lowest risk). Firms with a larger proportion of 'dangerous' loans should be more integrated in order to mitigate such risks (Hypothesis 1). The loan categories are treated as a direct measure of the transactional hazards of misrepresentation and measurement.

Labor productivity is defined as the number of loans processed (originated by the origination segment) per full-time equivalent employee (FTE) in that segment. Lower FTE per loan indicates greater productive capability. The authors use the natural logarithm of the FTE-per-loan metric in their regressions, and note that results are similar whether the number of loans or the dollar volume of loans is used.

Operating margin (revenue less total cost) in the origination segment, obtained through the MBFRF income breakdown which isolates segment-specific cost and revenue. The authors use the natural logarithm of this margin measure in the regressions and treat it as a corroborating capability metric alongside the FTE-based efficiency measure.

Labor productivity in the warehousing segment, defined as the number of loans serviced in that segment per full-time equivalent employee (FTE). Lower FTE per loan indicates greater productive capability. The authors use the natural logarithm of this FTE-per-loan metric in the regressions.

Operating margin (revenue less total cost) in the warehousing segment, obtained through the MBFRF income breakdown which isolates segment-specific cost and revenue. The authors use the natural logarithm of this margin measure in the regressions and treat it as a corroborating capability metric alongside the FTE-based efficiency measure.

Binary variable equal to one if the firm is included in the Vault Law 100 in the previous year (t - 1) and zero otherwise. Rank position, rather than the raw prestige score, is used as the running variable, with the inclusion threshold at the 100th rank position; rank volatility for high- and low-volatility subsamples was computed from published and unpublished Vault data covering the five prior years.

variable_name: Number of pro bono support policies
description: The number of formal policies a firm offers that encourage pro bono work, counting paid pro bono (giving billable hour credit for pro bono work), pro bono bonus consideration, and public fellowships. This variable ranges from 0 to 3, sampled law firms have 1.75 pro bono support policies on average, and 9.7% of these firms increased their support policies in any given year. The policies are compiled from the NALP Directory.

The typicality of a firm's pro bono support portfolio, estimated as its similarity to the average profile of peer firms in the prior year. Peer firms are those previously listed in the Vault Law 100, and for each pro bono policy the authors calculated the proportion of these peer firms that had adopted it. Similarity between the focal firm's portfolio vector at time t and the average peer vector at t - 1 is represented by the Jaccard similarity index; the equation itself is not readable in the provided text. The measure takes a greater value when a firm's set of support policies becomes more similar to the average portfolio of its peer firms.

Captured using the 5-year moving standard deviation of each firm's Vault rank; for 2007, the authors tracked 5 years of historical rank positions from 2002 to 2006. For the moderating tests, the sample of marginal firms was split into two based on the median of the rank standard deviation, with a 10% gap in the middle range (one sample at least 5% above the median and the other at least 5% below the median).

For the RD validity checks, the authors computed the difference-in-means across proximate firms on pre-treatment characteristics with two optimal bandwidths and a full-sample parametric estimate controlling for distance from the threshold, finding no significant differences.
time_window: year preceding the Vault Law 100 publication

description: Three items measured the degree to which the human and physical assets used to produce an information service were custom-tailored to the firm: the degree to which individuals must acquire company- or division-specific information, the degree to which the approach to the function is custom-tailored to the company, and how costly in time and resources it would be to switch to outsourcing or switch outsourcing vendors. Items were measured on a 7-point scale ('1' represented 'low degree' and '7' represented 'high degree') and combined into one construct because interitem reliability was quite high (Cronbach alpha = 0.82).

A single indicator measured the level of difficulty in measuring worker performance: 'To what degree is it difficult to measure the collective performance of those individuals who perform this function?' The item was measured on a 7-point scale ('1' represented 'low degree' and '7' represented 'high degree').

Two items measured the degree of change in both skills and technology: the degree to which the underlying skills associated with the IS function are rapidly changing, and the degree to which the optimal configuration of hardware and software required to perform the function is rapidly changing. The items had a high level of interitem reliability (correlation = 0.83) and were combined to form a single construct, measured on a 7-point scale ('1' represented 'low degree' and '7' represented 'high degree').

A single item measured the degree to which a firm had scale sufficient to support the efficient production of a service: 'To what degree do you have sufficient scale in your operations to perform this function efficiently in-house?' It was measured on a 7-point scale ('1' represented 'low degree' and '7' represented 'high degree').

One item measured the magnitude of the skill set required to perform the activity: 'To what degree does performing this function require personnel with extensive knowledge and skills?' It was measured on a 7-point scale ('1' represented 'low degree' and '7' represented 'high degree').

Respondents rated their satisfaction with the outsourced service on three performance goals central to exchange performance: the overall cost, the quality of the output or service, and responsiveness to problems or inquiries. Each was measured on a 7-point scale in which '1' represented 'dissatisfied' and '7' represented 'satisfied'. The three measures were averaged into a composite performance measure, and the authors generally interpreted the models for the composite performance measure.

Respondents rated their satisfaction with the internally sourced service on three performance goals central to exchange performance: the overall cost, the quality of the output or service, and responsiveness to problems or inquiries. Each was measured on a 7-point scale in which '1' represented 'dissatisfied' and '7' represented 'satisfied'. The three measures were averaged into a composite performance measure, and the authors generally interpreted the models for the composite performance measure.

The boundary choice was measured in three ways for each information service: the percentage of the service that was outsourced, so that a functionally similar set of activities could be wholly or partially outsourced; a dichotomous make-or-buy measure, in which above 75 percent outsourced was coded as wholly outsourced; and a decision-process measure distinguishing companies that had rejected the possibility of outsourcing a service from those that either currently outsourced or planned to consider outsourcing. The authors used the decision-process measure because boundary choices were unlikely to be optimally defined at any point in time.
scale: percentage outsourced (0-100%); make-or-buy and rejection-of-outsourcing measures are dichotomous

description: Ratio computed for each quarterly earnings conference call transcript as the number of long time horizon words divided by the number of short plus long time horizon words; a higher ratio indicates a longer time horizon. The word list was inductively compiled from corporate documents and supplemented with preestablished dictionaries on 'time' from WordStat, Diction, and Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count, inflected to identify 166 unique synonyms, and divided by three raters into short term, long term, and unclear so that only agreed words remained. Counting rules excluded certain phrase combinations, a keyword repeated within two words of itself, and words preceded by negation words. Six raters' gestalt assessments of 60 transcripts matched the ratio for 54 transcripts, an interrater reliability score of 90%.
Total number of downward recommendations issued in a quarter for each firm divided by the total number of analysts covering the stock, computed from analyst recommendations data.
Total number of upward recommendations issued in a given quarter for each firm divided by the total number of covering analysts, computed from analyst recommendations data.

Percentage of a firm's shares held by transient investors minus the percentage held by dedicated investors; the higher the value, the greater the ownership by short-term investors. Built by manually merging institutional holdings (13F) data with Bushee's (1998) institutional investor classification data, which classifies investors as transient, dedicated, or quasi-indexers; this accounts for shares not held by either transient or dedicated investors, such as quasi-index investors.

Souder and Bromiley's (2012) calculation of asset durability, which measures, in a given year, the average annual expected life of a firm's property, plant, and equipment (PP&E). Gross PP&E represents the total value of all PP&E a company owns without any accumulated depreciation, and capital expenditures represent the funds a company uses each year for new additions to gross PP&E; higher depreciation rates and expenses and lower CAPEX decrease asset durability. A lower value for asset durability signals that a firm is making fewer investments in long-term capital; only firms that use straight-line depreciation were included. The formula itself is unreadable in the text available to us.

variable_name: Quarter dummies and their interactions with downgrades
description: A set of dummy variables for each quarter of the year, interacted with downgrades, in which the first quarter is the reference point; the fourth-quarter interaction tests whether downgrades shorten time horizons more at the end of the information cycle.

Upgrades received in the previous quarter, entered in the model as a lagged count of upward recommendations in the preceding quarter, used to contrast downgrades that follow upgrades with downgrades that follow downgrades.

Downgrades received in the previous quarter, entered in the model as a lagged count of downward recommendations in the preceding quarter, used as the comparison sequence for downgrades that follow upgrades.

Analyst recommendations are captured by two quarterly variables from I/B/E/S: Downgrades, the number of downward recommendations in the quarter divided by the number of covering analysts, and Upgrades, the same for upward recommendations.

A bank's performance level was measured by its CAMEL rating, a composite index that assesses capital risk, asset quality, margins, earnings, and leverage, computed by IDC and ranging from 1 (the lowest) to 300 (the highest). A bank was defined as being successful when it obtained a CAMEL rating of 200 or higher in a given quarter. Success experience of a bank at time t was operationalized as the discounted sum of the total number of quarters in which the bank recorded a CAMEL rating of 200 or higher since its charter, with each experience discounted by the age of the experience. The formula itself was not readable in the text.
time_window: since the bank's charter, discounted by age of the experience

description: Each recovery experience was operationalized as occurring when a bank's CAMEL rating drops below 125 for at least two consecutive quarters and then moves up to a rating higher than 125. A bank with a CAMEL rating below 125 is considered to be under severe financial strain and at high risk of failure, corresponding to 4 or 5 on the FDIC's official CAMEL rating scale. Recovery experience for bank i at time t was operationalized as the discounted sum of the total number of individual recovery experiences that a bank has accumulated since its charter. The formula itself was not readable in the text.
time_window: since the bank's charter, discounted by age of the experience

description: The dependent variable is the unobserved hazard rate of failure of banks in the sample. Banks were considered to have failed if they were (1) liquidated or (2) merged with another bank with FDIC financial assistance. Failure was recorded quarterly at the end of each quarter. Voluntary, non-FDIC-assisted mergers and acquisitions that were not associated with failure were not treated as failures but as being right-censored.

For each firm i at year t, sales growth was measured using a logarithmic power function: ln(Sales i,t+1) = alpha ln(Sales i,t) + pi'x i,t + e i,t. This model is said to yield unbiased and efficient estimates under the linearity, homoscedasticity, and independence assumptions of OLS regression. All independent variables and controls (denoted by x i,t) were lagged by one year relative to the dependent variable.
time_window: annual; dependent variable at t+1 with predictors lagged one year

description: The Herfindahl diversity measure was calculated at the second level of the product typology using the proportion of active products of firm i in market segment j in year t, that is, the number of products the firm has in a particular market segment divided by the total number of products it has in all market segments in a given year. Its stated advantage is the ability to capture the relative importance of market segments by considering the proportion of products introduced in each segment. The formula for the measure appears in a block whose OCR rendering is unreadable in the available text, so the exact specification is a gap; weights are based on counts of products offering a particular function or classified to a certain market segment.

Diversity C,it = sum over j and k of m ijt m ikt r ikjt, where j, k = 1 ... n, with N it being the number of third-level product functions firm i has offered in year t and m ijt the proportion of product category j in firm i's products in year t. The term r ikjt receives a value of 0 if j and k share the same third-level product function, a value of 1 if they have different product functions but share the same second-level market segment, and a value of 2 if they reflect different market segments. Its stated advantage is that it takes into account the relatedness of product categories by considering the distance between different product functions.

Technology intensity was measured as the firm's R&D investment divided by its sales during the year in question. R&D expenses were extracted from Compustat as part of the annual financial data on the sampled firms.

Intra-industry product diversification experience was measured by calculating a weighted average of product diversity during the period from 1985 to t-1, with the experience decay function assigning higher weight to more recent years while avoiding left censoring bias. The weights are given by 1/(t-k) summed over the same period, and the diversity term is either the Herfindahl or the Concentric measure of intra-industry product diversity of firm i at year t corresponding to the independent variable used.

Dichotomous variable designating each film as belonging to a unique type of coproduction; a hybrid coproduction is a film coproduced by a mixture of at least one generalist and at least one specialist production company. Films are defined as coproductions when they are made by two or more distinct production companies, which are responsible for the development, funding, and producing of the project. Combined categories of solo productions are the baseline in the film-level innovation models.

Dichotomous variable designating a film as a central coproduction, that is, a film coproduced by at least two generalists and no specialists. It is entered alongside the other coproduction types, with solo productions as the reference category.

Dichotomous variable designating a film as a peripheral coproduction, that is, a film coproduced by at least two specialists and no generalists. It is entered alongside the other coproduction types, with solo productions as the reference category.

Count of a production company's cumulative hybrid coproduction films in its production history, measured up to the previous year. Generalists have participated in 16 hybrid coproductions on average and specialists have participated in 1.

Count of new keywords introduced in a film. A keyword is considered new if it is less than three years old, accounting for the delay between when a creative feature is generated and when it is released in a film; there are 57,000 unique keywords in the data and a film is comprised of 110 creative features on average. Keywords are submitted by users but are reviewed and published by IMDb in-house staff.
time_window: three-year window for newness; estimations begin in 1990 after a five-year learning period

description: Count of new combinations of keywords introduced in a film in a given year. Each keyword was used in films prior to that year but together they represent never-before-seen combinations. It is a distinct, nonnested measure from new creative features.
time_window: three-year window for newness; estimations begin in 1990 after a five-year learning period

description: The average pairwise Jaccard distance (one minus Jaccard similarity) of keywords in the films a company produces from the keywords in all films released by other companies within the same market segment in a year. Higher values represent that the creative content in a company's films is more differentiated from the creative content of its within-segment competitors.

variable_name: Competitive differentiation from prior own products
description: The average pairwise Jaccard distance of keywords in the films a company makes from the keywords it has used in its films in prior years. Higher values indicate that the creative content in a company's current films is more differentiated from its prior films.
time_window: current films relative to prior years' films

description: Takes on a value of one in the final observation in which a company releases a film if the company does not release another film within the 95th percentile of interarrival times - five years - and does not release a subsequent film during the sample period, and zero otherwise. The interarrival distribution measures how much time passes between each production company's prior film and its current film.

A production company is defined as a generalist if it is in the top quartile of niche width in terms of the genres it releases films in a given year of production; other companies are specialists. Niche width is measured by taking the Jaccard distance of all film genres in each year based on their co-occurrence in all companies' productions. Companies coded as generalists include the traditional 'major' studios and other companies that became significant players during the study period; in the data, being a generalist represents spanning 10 genres per year and being a specialist represents spanning 3 genres per year.

The number of options held by a CEO that had nonpositive value with respect to the spread between strike price and market price as reported in Execucomp. The authors used number of options rather than spread or Black-Scholes value because it was necessary to differentiate between options that were in the money and out of the money.

The number of options held by a CEO that had positive market value, as reported in Execucomp. The authors report that the average correlation of this measure with spread value was .58 and with Black-Scholes value .47.
For compatibility with the option measures, stock ownership was measured as the number of shares of stock owned by a CEO.

A dichotomous variable coded 1 if a firm manipulated its earnings and 0 otherwise. The behavior was coded for the year in which the manipulation occurred. Cases were identified from the GAO restatement database and confirmed through media and filing searches.
time_window: year in which the manipulation occurred

description: Firm performance was measured as sales change in a given year. This measure was chosen because it represents a useful gauge of the extent to which pressure due to low revenue recognition might induce CEOs to manipulate earnings.
The number of years that an individual had served as CEO of his or her present company.

For each four-digit SIC industry and year, a polynomial of facility size was regressed on total waste generated. Performance is estimated as the deviation of a facility's actual performance relative to the prediction of the model for a facility of identical size, year, and industry, so facilities with a positive score produced more waste than comparable facilities in the same year and sector. Scores are normalized using the standard deviation of the error, and a corporate level score is created by summing the scores for all facilities owned by the firm, weighted by facility size.

Set equal to one for the 2 years following an acquisition of a target bought by a relatively less wasteful firm, and zero otherwise. The two-year window is chosen to allow time for the treatment to take effect without other events confounding the results. The classification of the acquirer as less wasteful is based on the comparison of the corporate performance scores of the acquiring and selling firms.

Set equal to one for the 2 years following an acquisition of a target by a relatively more wasteful firm, and zero otherwise. The authors state that they did not develop a hypothesis about targets bought by a lower performing (more wasteful) firm but estimate the effect for consistency.

Set equal to one for the 2 years for all incumbent facilities in an acquiring firm that is more wasteful than the target's previous owner, and zero otherwise. Incumbent facilities are the facilities already owned by the acquiring firm at the time of the asset sale.

Set equal to one for the 2 years for all incumbent facilities in an acquiring firm in which the firm is less wasteful than the selling firm, and zero otherwise. It is the comparison category used when incumbent facilities are separated by the relative environmental performance of the firms engaged in the asset sale.

variable_name: Incumbent Same Industry More Wasteful Acquirer
description: Captures whether incumbents of an acquiring firm share the industry affiliation (two-digit SIC code) of the newly acquired target, given the relative corporate environmental performance; it is set for incumbents of an acquirer that is more wasteful than the seller and that operate in the same industry as the acquired facility. The parallel variable Incumbent Same Industry Less Wasteful Acquirer identifies incumbents sharing the target's industry when the acquirer is less wasteful.

Built from Waste Generation, measured as the pounds of waste for chemical c in facility i in year t, including all waste generated by a chemical regardless of how it is disposed (for example releases, recycling, treatment, or energy reconversion). The change is calculated as the log change in waste for a given chemical c for a given facility i from year t to year t+1, multiplied by 100 so that coefficients can be interpreted as percentage changes. Positive values correspond to an increase in waste generation in year t+1 relative to the previous year for a given chemical, that is, a worsening of the facility's environmental capabilities. The equation for the log difference is not legible in the source text.
time_window: from year t to year t+1

description: Respondents rated on a seven-point scale their involvement in five aspects of the strategic process: identifying problems and proposing objectives, generating options, evaluating options, developing details about options, and taking the necessary actions to put changes into place. The scale anchors ranged from 'fully involved' to 'not at all involved.' The mean scores of respondents in each organization for each of the five scaled items constituted the measures of middle management involvement.
scale: seven-point scale from 'fully involved' to 'not at all involved'

description: Nine seven-point, Likert-type items, modified from previously developed instruments, were used to measure strategic commitment. A principal-components factor analysis yielded a single-factor solution, and the scale was defined as the sum of the nine items (alpha = 0.92). The mean of this index among respondents in each organization constituted the measure of middle management commitment.

Each CEO described the organization's most important strategic priority and a content analysis revealed five recurring themes, which were included on the questionnaire. CEOs and middle management respondents were asked to allocate 10 points, based on relative importance, among the five priorities. The absolute differences between the weights assigned by each middle manager and the CEO's weights were computed and summed for each organization; this total difference score was divided by the number of respondents and subtracted from a constant to produce a measure of how well middle-level managers understood the organization's strategic priorities as articulated by the CEO.

Strategic consensus was defined as the product of middle management commitment to, and understanding of, strategy; the measure combines the organization-level understanding and commitment measures multiplicatively.

Company CEOs rated on a seven-point scale their organization's recent performance in five areas. The correlations between published ROA and subjectively reported ROA and overall financial performance were used as a partial validation of the subjective measures.

Director deaths were treated as a quasi-randomly assigned treatment. Death Group is a binary one/zero dummy coded as one if there was a death event in a firm, and Postdeath is a binary one/zero dummy coded as one in firm-years after the death of a director and coded as zero otherwise. The coefficient on their interaction captures the treatment effect on the treated, and the main effect of Death Group is absorbed by firm fixed effects.

CSR is an aggregate measure composed of six dimensions from the KLD Social Ratings database: community relations, diversity, employee relations, environment, human rights, and product quality. Within each dimension there are individual items relating to CSR strengths and concerns, and only the CSR strengths were used because strengths and weaknesses lack convergent validity and should not be combined as a net score. The overall CSR measure is the sum of the CSR strengths scores for each of the six dimensions in a given firm-year.

A one/zero binary variable reflecting the relational connection between the CEO and the deceased director, coded as one if the deceased director had been appointed within the CEO's tenure. For control firms, the variable was coded as zero.

A one/zero binary variable reflecting death immediacy, operationalized following Nguyen and Nielsen (2010): a death was characterized as sudden if it was unexpected and occurred instantaneously or within a few hours of an abrupt change in the person's previous clinical state. Sudden deaths were coded based on an assessment of the circumstances surrounding each death taken from relevant news articles, obituaries, and company reports; of the 89 death events in the final sample, 12 (13.5%) were coded as sudden.

Indicator variable taking the value 1 if patent j cites paper i of set of paper twins k, and 0 otherwise. The authors tracked references in the patent literature to the 90 publications making up the 39 sets of paper twins by searching each paper in the Dataverse patent database using the first author's last name, journal name, publication year, and the paper's first page number. All self-citations were excluded by screening out instances in which inventors of patent j work in an organization in which one or more of paper i's authors were also based. Only patents awarded within five years of the discovery's publication were considered, because older sets of paper twins have had more time to be referenced.
time_window: patents awarded within five years of the discovery's publication

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 if the paper i corresponding author is based in academia; 0 if he/she is based in a firm. The authors collected the addresses of corresponding authors for each paper and coded them as academic or industrial, and details about the corresponding author as well as each author's address come from an analysis of the text of the publications.
level: scientific publication (within a set of paper twins)

description: Respondents were asked to 'assess the performance of your project over the last 2 months' on 10 generic kinds of business objectives, where a score of 1 indicates that results were far worse than expected and a score of 5 indicates that results were far better than expected. Each team's average response for each item was first calculated, and these average scores were then totalled to provide the overall score for the construct. Subjective ratings were used following the logic that such ratings are the ones used for budget and promotion decisions.
scale: 1-5 (1 = results far worse than expected, 5 = results far better than expected)

description: To measure the extent to which members of a project team feel they understand cause/effect relations on the most significant drivers for their projects, respondents scored 16 items on a scale in which a 1 is equivalent to 'we have no idea at this stage' and a 5 is equivalent to 'we know exactly'. Two sets of items are used: one tailored toward projects intended to generate revenues directly and one tailored toward projects not intended to generate revenues directly. Each team's average response for each item was calculated and totalled to provide the overall construct score.
scale: 1-5 (1 = we have no idea at this stage, 5 = we know exactly)

description: Project group members are asked to position their projects on a five-point scale between two semantic differentials. A score of 1 implies processes which are clumsy or unresponsive, requiring substantial expenditures of resources to coordinate tasks and solve problems, while a score of 5 indicates maximum effortlessness of task coordination and problem solving. A higher score is always associated with greater process deftness for a team; team member responses were averaged per item and totalled to give the construct score.
scale: five-point semantic differential (1 = clumsy or unresponsive processes, 5 = maximum effortlessness of task coordination and problem solving)

description: Dummy variable indicating that the head coach of the opposing team has experience with the advantageous set of routines that make up the West Coast Offense. It is equal to one if the head coach is either a first- or second-generation assistant to Bill Walsh, i.e., the coach either worked directly for Bill Walsh or was an assistant to a coach who previously worked under Walsh, and zero otherwise. A total of 56 (13.6 percent) of the 49er games were against these coaches.

The number of times that the opposing team's head coach has competed against a first- or second-generation Walsh assistant. It captures the rival's accumulated competitive exposure, through other organizations, to the advantageous set of routines.

The number of games in the current season scheduled against first- or second-generation Walsh assistants. It captures the rival's expected exposure to the advantageous set of routines in upcoming contests.

The number of points scored in a game by the 49ers minus the points scored by their opponents. A positive value indicates a San Francisco victory; a negative value indicates a loss. The authors describe the margin of victory as the best measure of the relative strength of the two teams in the context of this study, and it is the dependent variable in the main model.

The dependent variable is the discrete time hazard rate, the conditional probability that a biotechnology firm exits at time t. Year was used as the discrete unit of time and each time unit was viewed as an independent trial: a firm that exited in its kth year was treated as having experienced k trials, with success indicators coded 1 if an exit occurred during a trial and 0 otherwise. Each trial carries a vector of annually updated independent and control variables. Left-censored firms were handled with a conditional likelihood approach that conditions their estimates on having survived to 1991, and parameters were estimated by logistic regression using TDA 5.7.

Set of time-varying, firm-specific variables that separately count the aggregate number of alliances a focal firm's rivals had at the start of each year with each of nine types of organizations. Given the form in which alliance data appear, each member of an alliance was counted as a full-fledged partner, so a firm can be assigned more than one partner for a single alliance. Rivals were those companies operating in one or more of the same biotechnology sectors as the focal firm and not its partners.

variable_name: rivals' alliances with other biotechnology firms
description: Time-varying, firm-specific count of the aggregate number of alliances a focal firm's rivals had at the start of each year with other biotechnology firms, defined as companies operating in one or more of the same biotechnology sectors as the focal firm and not its partners. Because each horizontal alliance involves two firms of the same partner type, each alliance consumes two links.

Time-varying, firm-specific counts of the aggregate number of alliances a focal firm's rivals had at the start of each year with upstream partners; alliances with each of the upstream partner types were counted separately. Rivals were those companies operating in one or more of the same biotechnology sectors as the focal firm and not its partners.

Time-varying, firm-specific counts of the aggregate number of alliances a focal firm's rivals had at the start of each year with downstream partners; alliances with each of the downstream partner types were counted separately. Rivals were those companies operating in one or more of the same biotechnology sectors as the focal firm and not its partners.

Set of time-varying, firm-specific variables counting the aggregate number of alliances a focal firm's rival partners, firms that are simultaneously its rivals and its partners, had at the start of each year with each of the nine partner types. The variables were constructed in the same manner as the rivals' alliance measures, counting each member of an alliance as a full-fledged partner.

Following prior studies (Devers et al., 2008; Larraza-Kintana et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2013), current wealth is calculated as the number of options from each option grant, multiplied by their corresponding spread (for in-the-money options) on the final day of the fiscal year. Data come from Execucomp.

Following Martin et al. (2013), prospective wealth is computed from the number of options held by the CEO, the total number of years remaining before the CEO's stock options expire, and the present-day stock price measured at the end of the year. The value of stock options is compounded by the average annual increase in the Dow Jones Industrial Average over the study period to estimate how CEOs might forecast the future value of the options they hold. The average time to expiry of CEOs' options was estimated using the Core and Guay (2002) estimation technique, since actual time to expiry was unavailable for the full sample period.

The language used by CEOs during quarterly earnings conference calls was analyzed to measure their temporal focus. Consistent with Nadkarni and Chen (2014), the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) text analysis software and its separate dictionaries for the dimensions of temporal focus were used; the improved LIWC 2015 dictionaries provide more inclusive dictionaries consisting of hundreds of words that reflect the various temporal foci. Words spoken only by the CEO were included in the main analysis.

The language used by CEOs during quarterly earnings conference calls was analyzed to measure their temporal focus. Consistent with Nadkarni and Chen (2014), the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) text analysis software and three of its dictionaries that separately measure the dimensions of temporal focus were used, with the improved LIWC 2015 dictionaries consisting of hundreds of words that reflect the various temporal foci. Words spoken only by the CEO were included.

Following prior research (Gamache & McNamara, 2019), acquisition spending is measured as the natural logarithm of a firm's total expenditures on acquisitions in a given year. This variable represents the cash outflow of funds related to the acquisition of a company in the current year and the effects of an acquisition in a prior year carried over to the current year. Because about half of the deals reported by SDC have missing values on transaction value, acquisition spending data from financial statements were used instead.

Seven-point, ten-item semantic differential scale adapted from Andrews and Smith's measure of marketing program distinctiveness, chosen because it captures distinctiveness at one end and similarity at the other. Key informants rated their firm's new products compared to competing alternatives along a battery of bipolar adjectives, such as conventional versus unconventional, ordinary versus unique, and revolutionary versus average. Respondents focused on all the new products introduced by their firm in the previous year. Scale scores are calculated by simple summation of item scores.
time_window: products introduced in the previous year

description: An abbreviated version of the Chandy and Tellis (1998) scale. A seven-point, five-item Likert-type scale; the reliability of this scale is acceptable. Scale scores are calculated by simple summation of item scores.

Newly developed for this study to assess the extent to which the firm accesses and takes into account information regarding trends in the customer and competitive environments. Items were developed based on the literature that focuses on paying attention to future markets and environments. A seven-point, four-item Likert-type scale. Scale scores are calculated by simple summation of item scores.

A mix of existing and new items was used to measure environmental turbulence in three domains of the organization's environment. The scale for customer turbulence is similar to the one used by Atuahene-Gima and Li (2004) and Jaworski and Kohli (1993), and it is a seven-point, four-item Likert-type scale. Scale scores are calculated by simple summation of item scores.

A new measure developed to assess changes in competitors and their strategies. The competitive turbulence scale is a seven-point, three-item scale. Scale scores are calculated by simple summation of item scores.

The measure is similar to the one used by Atuahene-Gima and Li (2004) and Jaworski and Kohli (1993). The scale for technological turbulence is a seven-point, four-item scale. Scale scores are calculated by simple summation of item scores.
A dummy with value 1 if the firm being evaluated is headquartered in a different country than the stakeholder, and 0 if both are headquartered in the same country.

The cultural distance between the MNC's home country and the host country, using Kogut and Singh's (1988) index based on Hofstede's four cultural dimensions. The printed formula could not be extracted from the text; the authors describe I as the index for cultural dimension i and host country j, V as the variance of the index of cultural dimension i, and k as the headquarter country.

The difference between the quality of regulation in the MNC's home country and the host country on the dimensions of credit, labor, and business regulation, based on the Economic Freedom Network. A positive score means that the MNC's home country has more sophisticated regulation than the stakeholder's country.

variable_name: Stakeholder rating of firm's social performance
description: Solicited directly from stakeholders in the interviews. Stakeholders were asked first to define firms' responsibilities toward society and then 'Where would you position the firm in honoring its responsibilities?'; they answered on a ten-point Likert scale (1 = very poorly; 10 = very highly). The authors deliberately did not impose their own definition of social responsibility on interviewees.
scale: ten-point Likert scale (1 = very poorly; 10 = very highly)

variable_name: Do good CSR in country / Do no harm CSR in country
description: For foreign firm-stakeholder dyads, the authors collected sustainability reports for 2006 and identified whether each report mentioned one or more CSR initiatives in the country where the stakeholder was based. Binary variables then code whether the initiative(s) corresponded to do-good or do-no-harm CSR; a dyad could score 1 for both. Two researchers independently coded the data using a coding scheme based on Baron (1996), with a Cohen's kappa of 0.602.

To manipulate the foreignness of the company, participants were told that the company planning a new manufacturing center in their local community was either from the United States or from Canada. Canada was selected because it has a similar culture and regulatory regime to the United States.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of 2 (CSR type: do-no-harm vs. do-good) x 2 (firm foreignness: domestic vs. foreign) between-subjects conditions. In the do-good CSR condition the company was described as undertaking initiatives to support the local environment, to invest in employee training and development and to contribute positively to the local community; in the do-no-harm condition it was described as undertaking initiatives to limit the negative effects of its activities on the environment, to restrict unsafe treatment of its workers and to reduce disruption to the local community.
After reading the scenario, participants indicated their impression of the company on three nine-point scales (1 = bad/unfavorable/negative, 9 = good/favorable/positive; alpha = 0.98).

Participants assigned 100 points among six constituencies to represent their perceived influence on the plan to establish the manufacturing center. The authors treated the interests of managers and shareholders (those with an ownership stake or direct influence on resource allocation) as internal to the firm, and used the points assigned to these internal stakeholders as an index of internal attribution.
scale: points out of 100 assigned among six constituencies

description: The authors summed the scores attributed to the four remaining stakeholder groups to create a measure of external attribution. Because points were assigned among six constituencies, this measure is the complement of the points assigned to managers and shareholders.

Dummy variable used to indicate whether the acquisition was completed (1) or remained incomplete (0). The sample included 1,603 acquisition announcements, and 17.3 percent of acquisitions in the sample remained incomplete.

Calculated as the log of the miles between coordinates for the zip codes of acquirer and target firm headquarters. The distance between two points equals C[arccos[sin(lat a)sin(lat b) + cos(lat a)cos(lat b)cos(|lon a - lon b|)]], where lat and lon refer to the latitude and longitude of the two locations and C is a constant that converts the result to miles on the surface of the earth; the authors used C = 3,437. The SDC database contained many typological errors and missing data in the zip code and city information, which the authors corrected by referring to company websites, directories and real estate websites.

0-1 variable equalling 1 when the target operated in the same four-digit NAIC as the acquirer and 0 when the target operated in another four-digit NAIC segment. In the sample, 876 of 1,603 cases were related (54.6%). This formulation treats acquisitions across the basic chemicals, synthetic fibers, agriculture, paints & adhesives, cosmetics, ink & explosives, and pharmaceutical sectors as unrelated.
Counts the number of related acquisitions implemented prior to the focal acquisitions.

Calculated as the average distance, in miles, for all acquisitions announced prior to the focal acquisition. To test the hypothesis the sample was split into sets of firms with high or low distance experience; the authors examined alternative formulations of the splits, including splitting at the mean, median, and across alternative values of centiles.
0-1 dummy variable that was 1 when the acquirer had previously acquired in the same state (other than the firm's headquarters state) as the focal acquisition.

variable_name: Acquirer is multiunit; State-level completion; Acquisition involved intermediary
description: Three variables measured the flow of information from secondary sources. Acquirer is multiunit is a 0-1 indicator of whether the acquiring firm was a multiunit firm or a single unit firm; in the sample of 724 acquirers, 497 were single units, 125 were parents with subsidiaries, 122 firms were subsidiaries themselves, and 20 firms were both parents and subsidiaries. State-level completion counts the number of successfully completed acquisitions in the focal state over three years before the announcement. Acquisition involved intermediary is a 0-1 indicator of whether the acquiring or target firm used an intermediary-such as accountancy or consultancy firms-to aid in the process of the acquisition.
time_window: three years before the announcement for the state-level completion count

variable_name: percentage of sequential FDI entries in the same industry in the same province
description: Computed by dividing the number of sequential investments by the total number of investments by all other U.S. firms in the same industry in the province or municipality. It captures learning from experienced reference firms, that is, the proportion of experienced entrants among prior entrants in the location. Both the linear term and its squared term were entered in the models.
A dummy variable coded as '1' if a foreign investment was located in a particular province and as '0' otherwise. It is the dependent variable in the nested logit models of location choice.

An investing firm's experience in China was represented by a count of the number of previous investments by the parent firm in China. The variable was centered before the interaction terms between learning from others and firm-level FDI experience were formed.

variable_name: firm's prior investments in the province
description: The firm's experience in the particular province, quantified using a count of its previous investments there. This was used to disaggregate the firm's experience in China as a whole. It was entered in interaction with the percentage of sequential FDI entries in the same industry in the same province, and both variables were centered.

variable_name: firm's prior investments in other provinces
description: The firm's experience in other Chinese provinces, quantified using a count of its previous investments there. This was used to disaggregate the firm's experience in China as a whole. It was entered in interaction with the percentage of sequential FDI entries in the same industry in the same province, and both variables were centered.

Failures of compounds undergoing phase III clinical trials, identified from the ADIS database, with the date of the failure and the associated indication. The study restricts attention to failures that originated at publicly traded firms with common stock listed on any U.S. market at the time of the failure. Each failure is the event around which the abnormal return is measured.
