The abnormal return is the component of the return that cannot be explained by the return-generating models, the difference between the actual return and the expected return, attributed to the failure event. The abnormal returns for each day in the event window are aggregated to obtain the cumulative abnormal return, the main dependent variable. Three return-generating models are used: the comparison period model, the market model, and the Fama-French three-factor model, estimated for each event over the window (-255, -10).
time_window: (-2, +4) days relative to the failure; also (-3, +3) and (-4, +4)

description: The change in the time-adjusted probability of indication success when the failed phase III compound is removed from the portfolio. It is a function of the number of compounds at each stage of development for the market in question and of the probabilities of success of each compound. The indication- and phase-specific probabilities are estimated from all clinical trials in the ADIS database at the level of an indication, assuming all drugs for an indication at the same stage have the same odds of failure; an annual discount rate of 12% is used for the discount factors applied to phase I and phase II compounds. For compounds failing for more than one indication at the same time, an aggregated UPDelta TAPIS is computed as the sum of the multiple values.

The recent phase II success rate minus the long-run phase II success rate for the firm in question. Success rates are computed as the number of phase II successes divided by the total number of phase II trials (successes plus failures) across all indications. The recent success rate uses successes and failures in the 300-day period preceding the day of the failure announcement; the expected (long-run) success rate uses the successes and failures for the firm over all periods of the data set, 1994 to 2004.
time_window: 300 days before the failure announcement; long-run rate over 1994-2004

description: Market model parameters were estimated for each firm by ordinary least squares using 200-day returns beginning with event day t = -270 and ending with event day t = -71, with the firm's daily common stock return regressed on the return of the CRSP value-weighted index. The impact of the announcement was measured over the two-day trading period consisting of t = -1 and t = 0, referred to as the announcement period, with a minimum of 100 days of returns required for a firm to be included. Firms with confounding announcements about earnings, dividends, mergers, or other important firm-specific information during the announcement period were eliminated.
time_window: event days t = -1 and t = 0; parameters estimated over 200 days from t = -270 to t = -71

description: Joint ventures were classified along the two dimensions of adding new products and serving new customers. To distinguish truly new products from similar products, the authors determined whether the parent firms or their divisions involved in the formation already had operations in businesses with the same four-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes as the businesses of the newly created joint ventures; to distinguish market expansion, they assessed whether the joint ventures allowed parents to expand into new geographic markets of the parents' existing businesses or to serve customers in new industries. Classification was based on data obtained from published announcements of joint venture activities.

The joint ventures for which both or all parents were included in the full data set were identified and then split into two subgroups using data from COMPUSTAT segment tapes and 10-K reports. The parent with the higher sales portion of businesses related to the joint venture business was categorized as the parent with opportunity and the other firm as the parent without opportunity. Two businesses were classified as related if they shared at least one of the following characteristics: similar products, markets, or both; similar production technologies; and similar science-based research. For joint ventures involving more than two parents, parents with similar sales levels were put into the same subgroup.
level: parent firm within a joint venture

description: Parents were categorized into a related partner subgroup if they had partners with operations in related businesses, so that the unrelated-partner subgroup consisted of parents with partners having operations in unrelated businesses. Relatedness was measured as in the test of the relation between a joint venture and a focal parent's portfolio. In joint ventures involving multiple partners, parents with at least one related partner were put into the related partner subgroup.
level: parent firm within a joint venture

description: Starting with all joint ventures for which both or all parent firms appeared in the full data set, the authors split the data in terms of size. The parent having the larger common stock market value three trading days before the announcement of joint venture formation was categorized as the larger partner and the other as the smaller partner. For joint ventures involving more than two parents, parents more or less similar in size were put into the same category.
level: parent firm within a joint venture
time_window: three trading days before the announcement

variable_name: managerial assessments of joint venture performance
description: Letters were sent to the CEOs of every parent firm studied with a two-page questionnaire and a request to forward it to the manager most knowledgeable about the status and benefits of each joint venture; usable data were received from 56 parents, nearly 25 percent of the study group. Each manager assessed the joint ventures in relation to five key objectives on a response scale ranging from 5, 'much better than expectations,' to 1, 'much worse than expectations.' A summated index was calculated because the indicators covaried consistently, as a Cronbach alpha of .71 indicated.
scale: 5 = much better than expectations to 1 = much worse than expectations

description: Dummy variable indicating whether an operator had prior experience with 2G in other countries at the time of original market entry; it tags operators that have prior experience in rolling out 2G service in another market. Experience was tracked at the date of entry even if it occurred before 1998, and was collected from company histories, news reports, and prior research; where there were multiple investors, an investor's prior experience was counted if the investor owned 25% or more of the firm.
time_window: at the time of original market entry

description: Dummy variable indicating whether the operator was a fixed-line incumbent in the focal country at the time of original market entry. It was constructed alongside the prior 2G experience dummy from data on firm structure, ownership, and mobile and fixed brands, drawn from company histories, news reports, and prior research, with an investor's experience counted at a 25% ownership threshold.
time_window: at the time of original market entry

description: Dummy variable tagging a firm as an early entrant if it entered a country in the first quarter in which 2G was originally offered, including firms that entered before the first quarter of the data. Entry timing was tracked together with the type of experience held at the date of entry.
time_window: at the time of original market entry

description: Average monthly minutes of use per subscriber on an operator's 2G network. It is built from Merrill Lynch data on the total number of minutes called per operator, which are used to construct the average usage per consumer. The second-step regressions use the operator-specific persistent usage effect recovered from the first-step model rather than the quarterly value.

Number of 2G subscribers to a given operator expressed as a share of the country's population, in percent. Subscriber counts come from Informa T&M and population from the World Bank's World Development Indicators. The second-step regressions use the operator-specific persistent subscription effect recovered from the first-step model.

Managers were asked to identify a set of 'general strategies' used by banks to compete in their metropolitan area, after being given a brief definition of the term 'firm strategy'; the survey instructions told them they could list as few or as many strategies as they thought were necessary. The individual-level count of strategies listed was aggregated to the team level as a weighted average, where the weight was each respondent's proportion of decision-making influence within the TMT, calculated from a four-item, seven-point Likert scale on influence over strategic decisions. The resulting team-level variable was standardized with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

Managers were given a list of the banks in their metropolitan area (banks with assets of at least $80 million) and asked to identify which of their self-generated strategies each bank followed, with the option not to categorize any banks with which they were not familiar. The variable is the number of firms contained in the questionnaire for which a respondent felt comfortable identifying a generic strategy, aggregated to the team level as a weighted average using each respondent's proportion of decision-making influence within the TMT. The team-level variable was standardized with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

Calculated by dividing the number of firms categorized by the number of strategies listed, initially at the individual level and then aggregated to the team level using the same weighted-average approach based on each respondent's proportional decision-making influence. The variable focuses on the average number of firms perceived to be following a similar strategy rather than other barometers of size such as revenues or employees. Because it is a ratio of the two base complexity variables, it was treated similarly to an interaction variable in the analyses, and it was standardized with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

Average Return on Average Assets (ROA) for the years 1995 and 1996. The profitability figures were collected from three annual volumes published by Sheshunoff: Banks of Colorado, Banks of Minnesota, and Banks of Wisconsin, whose information is taken from financial reports that all banks are required to submit to the Federal Reserve.

Accounting performance measured as return on assets (ROA), downloaded from the NEEDS database. Performance was adjusted by a firm's aspiration level, computed as a mixture of social and historical aspiration levels. To test for different effects above and below aspiration level, performance was specified as a spline function with separate variables for performance above and below aspiration level.

Computed as a mixture of social and historical aspiration levels. The social aspiration level is the average of other firms' performance, calculated as the mean ROA of all large shipbuilders except the focal firm. The historical aspiration level is a mixture of the past-period historical aspiration level and the previous performance of the focal firm. The weights were estimated by searching parameter values by increments of 0.1; the resulting weights were 0.8 for industry-average performance and 0.2 for the historical aspiration level.
time_window: previous period for firm performance and historical aspiration

description: The ratio of selling, general, and administrative expenses (SGAE) to sales. In the analyses of R&D intensity the slack variables were lagged by one year; in the analysis of innovations they were calculated as five-year moving averages.
time_window: one-year lag for R&D intensity; five-year moving average for innovation launches

description: The ratio of quick assets (cash and marketable securities) to liabilities. In the analyses of R&D intensity the slack variables were lagged by one year; in the analysis of innovations they were calculated as five-year moving averages.
time_window: one-year lag for R&D intensity; five-year moving average for innovation launches

description: The ratio of debt to equity. Since greater debt gives lower borrowing ability, the prediction for this measure is a negative coefficient. In the analyses of R&D intensity the slack variables were lagged by one year; in the analysis of innovations they were calculated as five-year moving averages.
time_window: one-year lag for R&D intensity; five-year moving average for innovation launches

description: Research and development expenditures divided by sales. Data were downloaded from the Nikkei NEEDS database, which takes its data from corporate accounts. R&D is treated as an important form of organizational search.

The number of innovations made by a firm as reported by the monthly journals New Technology Japan and Techno Japan from 1971 to 1996. Reports on the initiation or progress of R&D projects were omitted to preserve the focus on innovation launches. The journals nearly exclusively report innovations that are ready for market launch; most were product innovations, with process innovations underrepresented.

Stock concentration was measured by the total percentage of common voting stock held in blocks of 0.2 percent or greater in 1980. Information for this measure was taken from the 1981 Corporate Data Exchange publication, Stock Ownership Directory: Fortune 500.

Management stockholdings were measured by the natural log of the percentage of common voting stock held by management. Data on management stockholdings were collected from the December 1980 Computer Directions Advisors publication, Spectrum 6: Insider Holdings.

The measure of board composition used in the analysis was the proportion of inside to outside directors on the board. Details of board composition were collected from Dun and Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management for 1980. Higher values of the ratio indicate a greater proportion of insiders relative to outsiders.

Firm emphasis upon innovation was measured by research and development expenditure per employee. The deviation of a firm's R&D expenditure from mean R&D expenditure per employee in its industry was computed, and the resultant deviations were expressed as standardized Z-scores to factor out the effects of industry differences in R&D intensity. The R&D data came from COMPUSTAT.

Diversification was also measured by the number of two-digit SIC industries that a firm was involved in for the year 1980. The source for this information was Dun and Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management. The authors note that such industry counts tell nothing about the extent to which a firm's activities are concentrated in major business areas.

To identify diversification strategy, a variant of the scheme developed by Rumelt was used and the sample firms were classified into four main categories: single and dominant businesses, related constrained businesses, related linked businesses, and unrelated businesses. Source information was drawn from 1980/81 company annual reports. The categories were used as dummy variables in the profitability regressions, with the single and dominant dummy kept out of the equations to avoid a singular matrix so that the remaining coefficients are interpreted with reference to it.

The specialization ratio was developed by Rumelt to assist in the classification exercise and was also used as an important strategic variable in its own right in the analysis. It tells how concentrated a firm's activities are in its major business area, so a higher value indicates a lower emphasis upon diversification.

The related ratio was developed by Rumelt to assist in the classification exercise and was also used as an important strategic variable in its own right in the analysis. It tells to what extent a firm's diversified activities are related to each other, so a higher value indicates a lower emphasis upon extensive, unrelated diversification.

Using COMPUSTAT data, the return on assets of all firms in the sample was calculated. This measure was averaged over the 3-year period 1979-81. Each firm's return on assets was adjusted for industry means to factor out industry effects and expressed as a positive or negative deviation from its industry mean.

The time-varying ''capacity1'' measure in the State Capacity Dataset version 0.9. It is a normalized index focusing on core functions of the state, calculated by Hanson and Sigman using latent-variable analysis on 24 indicators related to the state's ability to reach their populations and collect and manage information, preserve borders and maintain internal order, develop policy and deliver public goods and services, enforce policy, and regulate commercial activity.

The same time-varying ''capacity1'' measure from the State Capacity Dataset version 0.9, entered as a main effect and interacted with minority shareholder rights in the analysis of stock market development.

The normative influence of the professions was measured by counting the number of economics articles authored by residents of each country in each year, as reflected in the Web of Science database, and dividing it by each country's population in millions. The authors argue the measure is continuous, less skewed than alternatives, and based on the actual production of knowledge by economists.

A time-varying count indicating how many countries within the same geographical region as the focal country increased their degree of protection of minority shareholder rights during the previous year, meant to capture frequency-based imitation. Countries were grouped into seven regions and Australia, Canada, Mauritius, New Zealand, and the United States were left as the baseline category.

Trait-based imitation was measured by calculating the year-on-year change in the degree of protection of shareholder rights in the United States, which has been generally proposed as the leader in terms of the development of shareholder capitalism. Similar measures were also calculated for Japan and Germany as the emulated countries.

The coercive effect of having entered into an agreement with the IMF was measured with the amount of IMF credit as of the end of the year divided by the country's gross domestic product, as reported in the World Development Indicators database.

The dependent variable is the sum of the scores for each of ten legal provisions, coded between 0 and 1 depending on the nature and strength of the specific legal provisions contemplated in national legislation; intermediate scores between 0 and 1 are possible. A team of 52 legal scholars, each with a J.D. degree from his or her home country and able to read the legal material in the original language, coded the country-years, and disagreements (about 20 percent of cases) were scrutinized and resolved. A legal scholar with knowledge of multiple countries then ensured that the data were coded according to uniform criteria across countries and over time. The index ranges from 0 to 10.

The sum of the scores for each of the ten legal provisions protecting minority shareholder rights, ranging from 0 to 10, treated as an endogenous independent variable in the analysis of stock market development. The authors correct for its endogeneity using the two-stage residual inclusion method, entering the residuals from the first-stage adoption model as a separate regressor.

Predicted factor scores from a principal-component factor analysis of three World Bank variables: stock market capitalization as a percentage of GDP, the value of stocks traded as a percentage of GDP, and stock turnover ratio. Principal-component factor analysis revealed that the three variables loaded onto a single factor of stock market development, with rotated-factor loadings of .79, .96, and .71, respectively, and Cronbach's alpha of .75; the predicted factor scores are used as the dependent variable, and results for each of the three indicators separately are also reported.

Stock market capitalization as a percentage of GDP, obtained from the World Bank, used as a dependent variable in a fully specified model predicting each of the three indicators of stock market development separately.

The value of stocks traded as a percentage of GDP, obtained from the World Bank, used as a dependent variable in a fully specified model predicting each of the three indicators of stock market development separately.
The stock turnover ratio, obtained from the World Bank, used as a dependent variable in a fully specified model predicting each of the three indicators of stock market development separately.

The value score for uncertainty avoidance for each country, reported by Hofstede (1980a, 2001). The authors use the four Hofstede dimensions as the independent variables in their models of CEO compensation. The measures have been criticized on the use of surveys, the single company from which the data were collected, the age of the data, and the number of cultural dimensions, but replication studies support Hofstede's work.

The value score for power distance for each country, reported by Hofstede (1980a, 2001). It is one of the four dimensions of national culture used as an independent variable in the compensation models.

The value score for individualism-collectivism for each country, reported by Hofstede (1980a, 2001). It is one of the four dimensions of national culture used as an independent variable in the compensation models.

The value score for masculinity-femininity for each country, reported by Hofstede (1980a, 2001). It is one of the four dimensions of national culture used as an independent variable in the compensation models.

Measured by the total compensation estimates reported by Towers Perrin. It includes one or more of the following components: basic compensation, long-term incentives, variable bonus, compulsory company contributions to social security and benefit programs, voluntary company contributions to social security and benefit programs, perquisites, and variable compensation. The data are average compensation levels for the CEO position in industrial companies in each country.

variable_name: proportion of variable compensation to total CEO compensation (VC/TC)
description: The ratio of the sum of annual bonus plus long-term incentives to total compensation. It is computed from the Towers Perrin compensation data for the CEO position in each country and year.

variable_name: ratio of CEO pay to the lowest level employees (CEO/Worker)
description: Measured by the ratio of CEO total compensation to total compensation of manufacturing workers in the respective country. It is computed from the Towers Perrin compensation data for the CEO and manufacturing employee positions in each country and year.
Net income before extraordinary items divided by total assets, obtained from Compustat.

Dummy variable for each firm within its four-digit SIC primary industry. A value of one indicates that the firm has its ROA below the industry median for the given year. The authors reverse code it as HighPerformance in some analyses.
time_window: given year; lagged one year in models

description: Standard deviation of the firm’s ROA for the subsequent five years.
Standard deviation of analysts’ earnings per share forecasts made one year in advance, divided by share price to make the variable comparable across firms.
Dummy for when the annual percentage growth of GDP is negative for the year.
Dummy for when annual GDP growth exceeds 4%.
ROA in 2007, the pre-crisis performance measure for each firm.
Standard deviation of ROA for the five-year period 2008–2012.
Standard deviation of analysts’ earnings per share forecasts for 2008, and also measured over the five-year period 2008–2012 as AnalystDisp08-12.

Dichotomous outcome obtained from a content analysis of letters to shareholders included in Clarion's annual reports. It takes a value of 1 if the subsidiary was mentioned in a given year and 0 otherwise. Because less than 4 percent of subsidiaries were mentioned more than once in the same letter to shareholders, the outcome was treated as dichotomous, which focuses on the capture of attention rather than its quantification.

Number of expatriates in a subsidiary, measured with data from the Kaigai Shinshutsu Kigyou Souran dataset. In the estimated attention model the variable is instrumented with host country political stability and host country education level.

Growth in the subsidiary's size, based on the total number of employees. It is computed as the difference in value between the year of the observation and the previous year, divided by the previous year's value.

Growth in subsidiary sales, which are based on the log of the value of sales in U.S. dollars for each year. The measure is the difference in value between the year of the observation and the previous year, divided by the previous year's value.

Growth of the market in which the subsidiary operates, measured as the difference in the number of cars sold in the host country between the year of the observation and the previous year, divided by the previous year's value. The number of cars sold is used on the assumption that the number of car radios sold is correlated with the number of cars sold in a country; the number of cars sold per country comes from multiple editions of the Ward's Automotive Yearbook.

variable_name: Two locations; three or more locations
description: The authors formed two binary indicators, one indicating whether a firm had two R&D locations within Finland and another indicating whether it had three or more locations; the reference case (and omitted variable) is one location. R&D locations are identified as separate counties where R&D activity took place within Finland. Firms with one location include 57 companies that did not report formal R&D units but conducted innovation activities, coded as having one location.

Summary variable counting the seven external sources of information for innovation activity the survey asked about: customers, suppliers, competitors, universities, nonprofit research institutes, professional meetings and publications, and trade fairs/exhibitions. For each source a survey response of two (important) or three (very important) was assigned a binary value of one, and a response of zero (not important at all/not used) or one (some importance) a value of zero; the binary values were then summed.

variable_name: Any innovation; product innovation; log(product innovation sales revenue)
description: Binary (0/1) variables indicate whether a firm introduced any technological innovations during 1998-2000 and whether it introduced any product innovations. A continuous variable measures total firm sales revenues in 2000 from technologically new products introduced during 1998-2000, expressed in natural logarithmic terms. The binary variables record whether a firm introduced any innovations and whether it introduced any product innovations.
scale: binary (0, 1); natural logarithm of sales revenue

description: A binary (0/1) variable indicates whether the firm had any new-to-the-market product innovations. A second variable measures sales revenues from new-to-the-market product innovations, expressed in natural logarithmic terms.
scale: binary (0, 1); natural logarithm of sales revenue

variable_name: Product and process innovation; range of important innovation effects
description: A binary (0/1) variable indicates whether the firm had both product and process innovations, as opposed to only one or neither type of innovation. A second variable reflects the number of different innovation effects that firms viewed as important or very important: each of nine innovation effects was assigned a binary value of one if it received a value of two (substantial impact) or three (a very substantial impact) and a zero otherwise, and the binary values were summed.

The total number of scientists and engineers hired to do pharmaceutical R&D at a particular point in time, taken at firm level from the National Research Council survey reports. For the input-side analysis the authors work with successive differences of this count between adjacent observation years, transform the square root of the dependent variable, and estimate the change parameters with a robust (iteratively reweighted least squares) procedure. Each change parameter divided by the length of the time interval gives an average annual growth rate.

The number of biologists hired to do a firm's pharmaceutical R&D at a particular point in time, taken at firm level from the National Research Council survey reports. An increase in the number of biologists is treated as indicating commitment to be in the forefront of innovation during the antibiotic revolution. Successive differences of this count are used as the dependent variable in the SD regression, with the same square-root transformation and robust estimation as for scientists.

Firms are classified into two groups: a firm is an antibiotic innovator if it generated at least one new antibiotic by 1960, otherwise it is an imitator. This group variable defines the two groups whose change parameters are compared in the successive difference regressions. In the Poisson regression the dummy variable INNOVATORS takes the value one when firm i generated one or more new antibiotics before 1960 and is zero otherwise.

The dependent variable is the number of new chemical entities for firm i in time interval t, which measures innovative performance. New antibiotics are excluded from the count to avoid informational redundancy with the innovator dummy. The counts come from Review of Drugs, 1941-1961 and are modeled as a random-effects Poisson process in which the length of the period is a scale factor and the rate parameter depends on firm characteristics.

variable_name: concurrent entry by other firms from the same prior industry
description: Count of the number of other firms with the same prior industry affiliation that introduced a particular feature in year t. The authors compare its effect with concurrent entry by firms from a different prior industry: if firms from the same prior industry have similar beliefs about what features to incorporate, they should be more likely to introduce a feature at the same time.

variable_name: concurrent entry by firms from a different prior industry
description: Count of the number of other firms with a different prior industry affiliation that introduced a particular feature in year t. It is the comparison term for concurrent entry by firms from the same prior industry.

variable_name: cumulative previous entry by firms from the same prior industry
description: Cumulative count of the number of other firms with the same prior industry affiliation that had introduced a particular feature as of year t-1. For example, for photography firms such as Nikon or Kodak, the cumulative number of other photography firms that had introduced a camera with a feature in prior years.

variable_name: cumulative previous entry by firms from a different prior industry
description: Cumulative count of the number of other firms with a different prior industry affiliation that had introduced a particular feature as of year t-1. It is the comparison term for cumulative previous entry by firms from the same prior industry.

variable_name: firms from same prior industry present in feature
description: Count of the number of firms from the same prior industry that are currently in the market with a camera that has the feature. The variable is mean centered, and mean-centered values are used to compute the interaction with the firm's own experience.

variable_name: firm experience in feature (cumulative models t-1)
description: Cumulative number of models with the feature that the firm has introduced as of year t-1, measured for all features other than resolution. The variable is mean centered, with mean-centered values used to compute the interaction with the presence of firms from the same prior industry.

variable_name: firm experience (previous entry into a megapixel generation)
description: For the resolution analysis, firm experience is measured as a firm having previously entered a megapixel generation. This experience measure enters the interaction with the presence of firms from the same prior industry in a megapixel generation.

Binary dependent variable that has a value of 1 in the first year that a firm introduces a model with a given product feature (e.g., LCD). A firm is at risk of introducing a feature starting the year after a digital camera with that product feature was first introduced into the industry and ending once the firm introduces a model, the firm exits the digital camera industry, or the period under consideration ends. Since the choice of features for a firm's initial digital camera reflects its framing of the opportunity, the first model introduced by a firm is included in the analysis.

variable_name: annual count of firm new models with feature
description: For all features other than resolution, a firm's ongoing commitment to a feature is measured as the number of digital cameras introduced by firm i in year t that had a particular feature. The data for these analyses began in the year following the firm's initial year of entry into the feature.

For the resolution feature, ongoing commitment is measured by the timing of a firm's entry into each subsequent megapixel generation from 2 megapixels to 6 megapixels, since an ongoing commitment to high resolution is indicated by a firm continuing to introduce increasingly higher resolution cameras rather than more cameras with greater than VGA up to 1 megapixel resolution.

The dependent variable is calculated as the number of checks a single player delivered against a single opposing player in one game. A check is the action in which an opposing player rams a player who is in possession of the puck to separate them from the puck; checks are the most commonly used defensive technique and are directed at specific individuals. Because checks can be traced back to an individual's effort rather than to an overall team effort, the authors use them to proxy a player's actions toward a competitor.
A dummy variable that equals one if a player has ever played for the opposing player's current team, and zero otherwise. It is one of the two indicator variables used to test the hypotheses.
A dummy variable equal to one if a pair of players has ever played together in a team, and zero otherwise. It is one of the two indicator variables used to test the hypotheses.

A binary indicator of transfer mode. The authors measured the mean affordance for tacit knowledge exchange of the methods used at transfer initiation and at transfer implementation. Transfers with higher initiation than implementation affordance were coded as front-loading (1); transfers with lower or equal initiation affordance were coded as back-loading (0). The coding yielded 98 back-loading and 18 front-loading transfers.
time_window: initiation and implementation phases of the transfer

description: A multi-item scale measuring the experienced difficulty of a transfer in terms of its eventfulness. Each item measures the eventfulness of a specific transfer-related problem using a five-point Likert scale. The measure spans both the initiation and the implementation phases of a transfer. The full set of items is reported in Online Appendix 1.
A multi-item scale capturing gaps in understanding the causes of success and failure of a practice. The scale and its items as well as its reliability are fully detailed in Online Appendix 1.

A multi-item scale measuring the arduousness of the relationship between the source and recipient of knowledge in terms of the strength of the tie between them, detectable in the ease of communication and in the intimacy of their relationship. The scale was developed by Szulanski (2003); its items and reliability are fully detailed in Online Appendix 1.

The average level of affordance for tacit knowledge exchange of the methods deployed during a transfer. Each method's affordance was scored by mapping independent raters' evaluations on four criteria—affords interaction, personalized communication, observation of the practice, and recipient practice—onto a one-dimensional Euclidian space using multidimensional scaling. Higher scores signify higher levels of affordance for tacit knowledge exchange.

Three-item instrument based on the scale developed and validated by Heide and Miner (1992). It captures the degree to which exchange partners share the responsibility for resolving problems as they arise, asked about the firm's main supplier. Respondents rated the items on an agreement scale.
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Parallel three-item instrument based on the scale developed and validated by Heide and Miner (1992), capturing the degree to which exchange partners share the responsibility for resolving problems as they arise, asked about the firm's main customer. Respondents rated the items on an agreement scale.
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Modified version of the instrument developed and validated by Heide and Miner (1992). It captures the degree to which parties actively exchange information beyond the letter of the contract - information that can facilitate the other party's activities - asked about the firm's main supplier.
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Parallel modified version of the instrument developed and validated by Heide and Miner (1992), capturing the degree to which parties actively exchange information beyond the letter of the contract, asked about the firm's main customer.
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Three-item scale based on a shortened version of the scale developed and validated by Cummings and Bromiley (1996). It reflects the degree to which the exchange partner is fair in its dealing and does not try to take advantage of the focal firm, asked about the firm's main supplier.
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Parallel three-item scale based on a shortened version of the scale developed and validated by Cummings and Bromiley (1996), reflecting the degree to which the exchange partner is fair in its dealing and does not try to take advantage of the focal firm, asked about the firm's main customer.
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: A seven-point scale that captures three primary stages associated with the acquisition of capabilities: knowledge-awareness, evaluation-choice, and adoption-implementation. It is operationalized with three items measuring various product and process changes, adapted from a national survey of pollution prevention conducted in one of the job shop industries selected for the study (Cushnie, 1994).
scale: seven-point acquisition scale (1 = we know little about this practice, 7 = we do this all of the time)

description: Measured with the same seven-point, three-stage acquisition scale (knowledge-awareness, evaluation-choice, adoption-implementation). TQM is measured with three items capturing the use of statistical process control charts to provide operators with feedback, based on the measurement instrument developed by Flynn, Sakakibara, and Schroeder (1995).
scale: seven-point acquisition scale (1 = we know little about this practice, 7 = we do this all of the time)

description: An indicator that equals one if supplier i and buyer j share at least one common director in year t and zero otherwise. The authors use the terms board tie, shared director, and common director interchangeably to refer to a common director serving on both the supplier's and the buyer's boards.

An indicator that equals one if supplier i and buyer j share at least one common director in year t and zero otherwise. It enters the investment-Q sensitivity regressions on its own and interacted with Buyer Tobin's Q, and enters the longevity regression as the key explanatory variable.

The number of the supplier's patents containing buyer-specific words divided by the total number of the supplier's and buyer's patents. Buyer-specific words are words that appear in the principal claims of the buyer's patents but are not present in those of the supplier's other buyers. The measure is set to zero if either the supplier or the buyer of a dyad-year did not file any patent in the last five years. Reassigned patents are excluded and generic words appearing in the patents of at least 50% of sample firms are removed.
time_window: supplier patents filed in the most recent 2 years and buyer patents filed in the most recent 5 years

description: The number of buyer-specific words divided by the total number of words in the supplier's and buyer's patents. Buyer-specific words are words that appear in the principal claims of the buyer's patents but are not present in those of the supplier's other buyers. Stop words, numbers, words with only one character, and generic words appearing in the patents of at least 50% of sample firms are eliminated. The measure is set to zero if either the supplier or the buyer of a dyad-year did not file any patent in the last five years.
time_window: supplier patents filed in the most recent 2 years and buyer patents filed in the most recent 5 years

description: An indicator that equals one if the number of alternative suppliers that are product market rivals of the focal supplier is greater than the 75th percentile of the sample (i.e., 5), and zero otherwise. Product market rivals are identified based on the similarity of the two firms' products using the 10-K text-based network industry classification data of Hoberg and Phillips. The indicator is interacted with the buyer-specific innovation measures in the moderation test.

The supplier's total research and development expenditures in year t. R&D investment is measured at the firm level rather than the pair level because the supplier's investment specific to a given buyer is not observed; the analysis assumes that the sensitivity of firm-level R&D to the buyer's Tobin's Q captures the degree to which the supplier takes the buyer's growth opportunities into account.

The buyer's Tobin's Q in year t-1, measured as the market value of equity plus the book value of assets minus the book value of equity, divided by the book value of assets. It enters the regressions of supplier R&D on its own and interacted with the board tie indicator and other dyad characteristics.

The natural logarithm of the number of years from the year in which a supply chain relationship was first established between firms i and j until the end of the sample period or the last year of the relationship, whichever is earlier. To identify the first year of a relationship the pair is required to have no supply chain relationship over the three years before a given year, so the sample is restricted to relationships that began in 2006, with 2013 as the last formation year.
time_window: from relationship formation to the end of the sample period or the last year of the relationship

description: The period of economic shock was identified as the years 1997 and 1998, following the clear identification in prior studies. The phenomena of sudden stop and recession were captured using the aggregate market capitalization growth and per capita GDP growth, respectively, and all economies in the sample experienced sudden and negative GDP growth rates between 1997 and 1998. Because per capita GDP growth was highly correlated with the economic shock dummy variable and its inclusion or exclusion did not influence the results, the economic shock dummy variable was retained instead of the per capita GDP growth rate.

Growth was calculated using the change in a firm's total assets over time: total assets at t equals total assets at t-1 plus acquisition at t plus organic growth at t minus divestiture at t. Divestiture was calculated as the sum of the reported disposal of fixed assets, the absolute value of the reported negative net assets from acquisition, and the absolute value of the negative growth in total assets. Growth reconfiguration was recorded using a 0-1 dummy variable when acquisitions or organic growth increased in size by more than 10 percent of prior size, with zero or limited concurrent retrenchment during the period.

variable_name: Firm performance (next period return on assets)
description: Firm performance was measured as the next period return on assets (ROA), which records the extent to which a firm is able to profit on its invested resources. As a measure of performance, ROA was examined at the next point in time relative to the period in which growth occurred. Stock market measures of firm performance were not used because they are often distorted in emerging markets and may not reflect the firm's underlying asset-based performance.

The ending event of firm failure was recorded when a firm exited by means of acquisition, bankruptcy, or dissolution. Bankruptcy and asset sales are not mutually exclusive and both are retained as indicators of firm failure, with separate sensitivity tests for each of these modes of exit. Overall, 307 firms in the sample exited during the observation period.

Financial slack was measured as an indicator of whether a firm has low financial risk, using the Altman Z score. The score was calculated as the sum of five financial ratios: earnings before interest and taxes per unit of total assets, sales per unit of total assets, equity by debt, working capital per unit of total assets, and retained earnings per unit of total assets, with 3.3, 0.999, 0.6, 1.2, and 1.4 as respective weights. A score greater than 2.99 is considered safe, a score less than 2.7 is considered risky, and a score of less than 1.8 implies a high risk of impending bankruptcy.

Product diversification was recorded using the entropy measure, calculated as E equals the sum over segments of Pi times ln(1/Pi), where Pi is the share of the ith segment in the firm's total sales. Since the Worldscope database did not report annual product segment sales, and instead reported only segment data for 1994, entropy is not time varying for the analysis, and refers to the level of diversification before the economic shock.

Institutional development was calculated as an average of seven EIU ratings: overall business environment, infrastructure, labor market, political environment, policy towards private enterprise, financing, and political environment for foreign investment. This recorded a time-varying measure of market orientation on a scale of 1 (low) to 10 (high).

The dependent variable, measured at the patent level, represents the extent of knowledge sourced from the hired engineer's previous firm. It is operationalized as the number of citations each hiring firm patent makes to any patent from the mobile engineer's previous firm. An increase in this measure indicates an increase in the degree to which a patent builds upon knowledge from the mobile engineer's previous firm.

Path dependence of the hiring firm is measured with self-citations, which occur when a patent filed by a firm cites another patent from the same firm. It is operationalized as the ratio of the number of self-citations to the number of total citations made by a hiring firm in each patent technology class to which a hiring firm patent belongs.
time_window: five-year window preceding the specific patent's application date

description: A dummy variable that takes on a value of one if the mobile engineer's prior area of expertise and the hiring firm's core technology are identical, and a value of zero otherwise. An engineer's key area of expertise is assessed by the technology class of the highest percentage of the engineer's total patents filed at the previous firm; a firm's core technology area is assessed through the technology classes that account for the highest percentage of the firm's patents. Core technology classes are identified as those with a more than 10% patent share in the five-year window and in which the hiring firm has filed patents for the five consecutive years preceding the specific hiring firm patent's date of application.
time_window: five-year window preceding the specific hiring firm patent's application date

description: A dummy variable indicating whether the mobile engineer filed a hiring firm patent in a technology class included in the core technology area or not. The variable takes on a value of one if the technology class of the specific hiring firm patent is identical to the firm's core technology areas and a value of zero otherwise.
time_window: five-year window preceding the specific hiring firm patent's application date

description: A dummy variable for domestic mobility. Mobility from a U.S. firm to a U.S.-based R&D lab of a non-U.S. firm is coded as one and mobility to a non-U.S.-based operation of a non-U.S. firm is coded as zero.

A count of the number of years for which an analyst forecasts annual EPS for the parent company. The variable is expected to be negatively associated with Parent EPS forecast error, that is, more forecasts indicate more accurate forecasts.
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: An indicator variable taking the value '1' if an analyst forecasts the expected growth in the parent company's EPS, and zero otherwise. It is expected to be negatively associated with Parent EPS forecast error.
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: A count (zero, one, two, or three) of the number of pro forma financial statements produced for the parent company by the analyst. It is expected to be negatively associated with Parent EPS forecast error.
scale: count of zero to three statements
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: A count of the number of years for which an analyst forecasts annual EPS for the spun-off subsidiary. It is expected to be negatively associated with Subsidiary EPS forecast error.
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: An indicator variable taking the value '1' if an analyst forecasts the expected growth in the spun-off subsidiary's EPS, and zero otherwise. It is expected to be negatively associated with Subsidiary EPS forecast error.
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: A count (zero, one, two, or three) of the number of pro forma financial statements produced for the spun-off subsidiary by the analyst. It is expected to be negatively associated with Subsidiary EPS forecast error.
scale: count of zero to three statements
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: An indicator variable taking the value '1' if an analyst describes the rationale for an upcoming spin-off, and zero otherwise. It is expected to be negatively associated with Parent EPS forecast error because it reflects situations in which analysts put more effort into understanding diversified companies.
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: An indicator variable taking the value '1' if an analyst discusses the conglomerate discount in his/her report, and zero otherwise. It is expected to be negatively associated with Parent EPS forecast error.
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: An indicator variable taking the value '1' if an analyst includes segment-level financial information in his/her reports, and zero otherwise. It should be negatively associated with Subsidiary EPS forecast error.
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: The absolute value of the difference between forecasted earnings per share (EPS) and actual EPS on the forecast date, scaled by the company's stock price; the parent company's stock price is measured at the end of the fiscal year prior to the forecast period. Higher values indicate that a forecast is less accurate. Observations in which the relevant stock price is less than $1 and those for which EPS forecast error is greater than or equal to two are eliminated as outliers.
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: The absolute value of the difference between forecasted earnings per share (EPS) and actual EPS on the forecast date, scaled by the company's stock price. Because spun-off subsidiaries do not have a stock price in the year prior to the forecast, the subsidiary's stock price at the end of the first fiscal year in which the stock trades is used. Higher values indicate that a forecast is less accurate.
time_window: reports issued from one month prior to the spin-off announcement date to one month after the effective date

description: The sum of the squared shares of a firm's total sales provided by each of its segments, representing the level of diversification within the firm. It is also used to construct the indicator variable Diversified firm.

An indicator variable taking the value '1' if the Herfindahl Index exceeds the mean value in its distribution, and zero otherwise. It is interacted with the variables representing analysts' research about parent firms.
The total assets of the spun-off subsidiary divided by the total assets of its parent company. It is used to construct the indicator variables Large spin-off and Small spin-off.

An indicator variable taking the value '1' if Relative size exceeds the mean value in its distribution, and zero otherwise. It is interacted with the variables representing analysts' research about parent firms.

An indicator variable taking the value '1' if Relative size is less than the mean value in its distribution, and zero otherwise. It is interacted with the variables representing analysts' research about spun-off subsidiaries.

An indicator variable taking the value '1' if a firm undertakes multiple spin-offs simultaneously, and zero otherwise. Two or more spin-offs by the same parent are defined as a multiple divestiture when either the announcement or the effective dates of the transactions occur within a week of each other.

An indicator variable taking the value '1' if a spun-off subsidiary did not previously have a tracking stock, and zero otherwise. It identifies spun-off subsidiaries that have no stock price history as independent companies.

An indicator variable taking the value '1' if the parent company and its spun-off subsidiary do not share a four-digit SIC code, and zero otherwise. It is interacted with the variables representing analysts' research about spun-off subsidiaries.

Analysts' research about spun-off subsidiaries is measured by a set of report-level variables: number of annual EPS forecasts, an EPS growth forecast indicator, a financial statement index (count of pro forma statements, 0 to 3) for the subsidiary, and an indicator for analysis of segments within the parent. Each enters the subsidiary forecast error regressions separately.

Analysts' research about parent companies is measured by a set of report-level variables: number of annual EPS forecasts, an EPS growth forecast indicator, a financial statement index (count of pro forma statements, 0 to 3), and indicators for analysis of the spin-off rationale, the conglomerate discount, and segments. Each enters the parent forecast error regressions separately.

Shared procedural justice was measured as the average of the two individual parties' perceived procedural justice, multiplied by the interparty agreement index ([procedural justice 1 + procedural justice 2]/2 × rwg), where rwg is James, Demaree, and Wolf's within-group interrater reliability. Each party's procedural justice score is the average of eight items addressing the fairness of alliance procedures over the three years prior to survey administration, rated from 1 ('not true at all') to 7 ('very true'). 'Fair' was defined as referring to whether the procedures and criteria were unbiased, representative, and transparent and whether they conformed to the specifications described in the alliance agreement.
scale: 1 = 'not true at all' to 7 = 'very true' on the component items
time_window: three years prior to survey administration

description: The foreign party's boundary spanner's average score on the eight procedural justice items, rated from 1 ('not true at all') to 7 ('very true'), addressing the fairness of alliance procedures over the three years prior to survey administration. Internal consistency and item appropriateness were respectively validated by a Cronbach's alpha of .79 and communality loadings of .76 to .92.
time_window: three years prior to survey administration

description: The Chinese party's boundary spanner's average score on the eight procedural justice items, rated from 1 ('not true at all') to 7 ('very true'), addressing the fairness of alliance procedures over the three years prior to survey administration. Internal consistency and item appropriateness were confirmed by a Cronbach's alpha of .74 and communality loadings of .79 to .90.
time_window: three years prior to survey administration

description: An alliance's profitability was measured by averaging return on investment (ROI; net profit/total investment) over the period 2000-02. The ROI data came from the Jiangsu Provincial Commission of Foreign Trade and Economic Relations.

Cultural distance was measured via Kogut and Singh's composite index (1988) and Hofstede's latest data set (2001), which contains five cultural dimensions (power distance, uncertainty avoidance, individuality, masculinity, and long-term orientation).

Structural uncertainty was defined as the geometric average of standard deviations in the output, sales, and profits of the industry in which an alliance participated ([s.d. output × s.d. sales × s.d. net profit]1/3). All information was obtained from the China Statistical Yearbook for 1998 to 2000.

variable_name: Focal CEO's compensation relative to market
description: Measured as the percentage difference between the focal CEO's annual total compensation and the median total compensation of CEOs at peer companies in the previous year. Annual total compensation is the annual total direct compensation, including salary, short-term bonus, the total value of restricted stock granted, the total value of stock options granted, long-term incentive payouts, and all other annual total compensation. Peer companies are identified based on industry (i.e., the same two-digit SIC code) and firm size (i.e., larger or smaller than the industry median sales level). All CEOs' annual total compensation was adjusted for annual inflation.
time_window: peer compensation measured in the previous year

variable_name: Average prior CEO compensation (relative to market) experienced by directors
description: The median CEO compensation level (relative to market) witnessed by each outside director in the previous three years across all public boards, including the focal board, was calculated first. The measure is then the mean value of this variable among all outside directors. It captures the average extent to which the prior CEO compensation level experienced by directors exceeded or fell below the market level.

Measured as the total asset difference between the focal firm and the average firm previously served by the majorities (measured as the number of standard deviations in total assets) divided by the size difference between the focal firm and the average firm previously served by the minorities. For example, a value of 2 indicates that minorities served at firms that are twice as similar to the focal firm in terms of size as the majorities.

The industry similarity between the focal firm and another firm was measured as k if they share the same k-digit SIC code and 0 if they are in totally different industries. Relative similarity in industry (minority versus majority) was calculated as the average industry similarity between the focal firm and firms previously served by the minorities divided by the average industry similarity between the focal firm and firms previously served by the majorities.

Measured according to functional background, industry of employment, highest degree obtained (i.e., Ph.D., master's, bachelor's, or associate's degree), and gender. Functional backgrounds were categorized into three categories: throughput functions, output functions, and peripheral functions. Homogeneity on each characteristic was calculated using a variant of the Blau's index. The four measures were combined, after standardization, into a single index using principal components analysis without rotations.

An index based on four measures of outsiders' power widely used in prior research. The four measures are the average tenure of outside directors on the focal board relative to the average tenure of inside directors, the total number of board appointments held by all outside directors divided by the total number of board appointments held by all insiders, the proportion of outside directors on the board, and whether the board chair position is also occupied by the CEO. The four measures were combined into a single index using principal component analysis.

Return on assets, calculated as the ratio of the firm's net income to its total assets, with net income defined as income minus costs and expenses, which includes income taxes. Used as the primary dependent variable in the replication, consistent with the accounting-based measure used by L&B and with the nature of a sample that includes both public and private firms.

Composite index built by dividing the number of foreign countries in which the firm operates in a given year by the maximum number of countries in which any firm in the sample operates in that year, doing the same calculation for the number of foreign subsidiaries, and then averaging the two scaled variables. The index ranges between 0 and 1. The squared and cubed terms of Internationalization are included to test the S-curve hypothesis, and the interaction between Internationalization and R&D intensity to test the moderating hypothesis.

The parent firm's R&D spending as a percentage of its sales, constructed to capture the level of a firm's intangible assets and used to replicate the test of L&B's second hypothesis. Advertising intensity, L&B's second measure of intangible assets, could not be replicated because the BEA does not capture advertising spending.

A firm's reported spending on research and development per $1,000 of sales. The authors note that R&D intensity is not a perfect measure of innovation, that it is likely to be lower in large firms, and that low ratios may in some settings indicate skillfully leveraged R&D or diversification into areas requiring little R&D. The variable is meant to reflect the intensity of investment in the inputs supporting the innovation process rather than innovation itself.

The entropy measure of diversification, defined as the sum over segments of P ln(1/P), where P is the sales (dollar value) attributed to segment i and ln(1/P) is the weight for each segment. The measure thus takes into account both the number of segments in which a firm operated and the relative importance of each segment in total firm sales. It was calculated from Standard and Poor's COMPUSTAT segment file for 1980-82.

A simple K-means clustering algorithm was used to identify corporate strategy types from the related (DR) and unrelated (DU) components of the entropy measure, forming four categories: dominant-business, related-constrained-business, related-linked-business, and unrelated-business. In the dummy variable regression each strategic category was assigned a value of unity if the firm was included in the category and a value of zero otherwise, with related-linked as the omitted category.

The relatedness component of the entropy measure of diversification, defined as the related diversification arising out of operating in several segments within an industry group. Four-digit SIC industries were treated as the industry segments, and two-digit SIC industries as the industry groups, and the component was calculated from the COMPUSTAT segment file for 1980-82.

The unrelatedness component of the entropy measure of diversification, defined as unrelated diversification between industry groups, with two-digit SIC industries treated as the industry groups. It was calculated from the COMPUSTAT segment file for 1980-82.

variable_name: Analysts' reservations about stock repurchase plans
description: Multi-item survey scale measuring analysts' reservations about stock repurchase plans. Respondents assessed four items on a five-point scale ranging from 1 ('not at all') to 5 ('very much so'); responses were inverted so that higher values indicate greater reservations. Cronbach's alpha was 0.92 and the test-retest kappa was 0.90.
scale: five-point scale (1 = 'not at all', 5 = 'very much so')

description: Multi-item survey scale asking how confident the respondent believes other analysts are that stock repurchase plans reflect well on adopting firms' performance prospects, reflect well on a firm's corporate governance, will be implemented, and enhance economic efficiency. Items were assessed on a five-point scale and responses were inverted so that higher values indicate greater perceived reservations of others (Cronbach's alpha 0.87, test-retest kappa 0.93). In the models of earnings forecasts and upgrades the variable is inverted so that higher values indicate lower perceived concern of other analysts.
scale: five-point scale (1 = 'not at all', 5 = 'very much so')

description: Respondents listed the names of other security analysts with whom they had communicated during the prior 12 months and specified how many times they had communicated with each analyst and the approximate amount of time they had spent communicating with each analyst over the past year. In the primary analysis communication ties is measured as the total amount of time spent communicating with other analysts during the prior year (in minutes). Interrater reliability was assessed with a separate survey of listed contacts and the intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.92.

The focal analyst's subsequent earnings forecast following the focal repurchase plan adoption, expressed in dollars per share of common equity. A static dependent variable was used for earnings, estimated in the second-stage Heckman regression for the sample of analyst-firm dyads.
scale: dollars per share of common equity
time_window: subsequent to the focal repurchase plan adoption

description: Dichotomous measure that indicates whether the focal analyst's subsequent report following the focal adoption included an upgrade (i.e., a more positive stock recommendation) for the adopting firm, coded 1 if the analyst issued an upgrade and 0 otherwise. A dynamic dependent variable was used for recommendations.
time_window: subsequent to the focal repurchase plan adoption

variable_name: Difference between analysts' own reservations and perceived reservations of others
description: Operationalized in an analysis of covariance on a data set with two records per analyst, in which a dummy variable is coded 1 for respondents' own reservations and 0 for perceived reservations of others while the dependent measure is set equal to own reservations in one record and perceived reservations in the other. The analysis is equivalent to regressing the difference between the respondents' own reservations and the perceived reservations of others on the independent variables.

Informants evaluated how well or poorly the joint venture performs specific activities or possesses specific capabilities relative to its major competitors, on an 11-point scale. The three indicators are customer-linking capabilities, market-sensing capabilities, and channel-bonding capabilities, which form a latent construct. The items were adapted from Day (1994). Factor loadings were constrained equal across the high and low turbulence groups.
scale: 11-point scale, 0 = Much worse than your major competitors to 10 = Much better than your major competitors

description: Informants evaluated how well or poorly the joint venture performs specific activities or possesses specific capabilities relative to its major competitors, on an 11-point scale. The three indicators are technology development capabilities, manufacturing processes, and new product development capabilities, which form a latent construct. The items were drawn from Day (1994). Factor loadings were constrained equal across the high and low turbulence groups.
scale: 11-point scale, 0 = Much worse than your major competitors to 10 = Much better than your major competitors

description: Respondents rated the extent to which the joint venture had achieved three outcomes relative to its objectives: overall profit margin, overall sales, and overall ROI. Ratings used an 11-point scale anchored 'low'/'high'. Subjective performance scales relative to objectives were used so that comparisons could be made across firms and contexts; the case-study managers preferred subjective to objective measures because the latter are often confidential.

Respondents indicated the degree to which they agreed or disagreed with statements about the joint venture's industry on an 11-point scale. The items cover rapid change of industry technology, big opportunities from technological changes, difficulty of forecasting where the technology will be in the next 2-3 years, and technological developments being rather minor (reverse-worded). A composite score was computed, and joint ventures were sorted into high or low turbulence by comparison with the sample mean, combined with a researcher classification of the industry environment.
scale: 11-point scale, 0 = strongly disagree to 10 = strongly agree

description: Six-item scale derived from the task-related hurry subscales of a measure developed by Landy and colleagues (1991). CEOs rated the six items on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). Examples of items are ''people that know me well agree that I tend to do most things in a hurry'' and ''I often feel very pressed for time.'' Cronbach's alpha was .72.
scale: 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: A behaviorally anchored rating scale (BARS) consisting of five graphs, each with a written description below it. Respondents read the descriptions and selected the graph that best captured how they pace their work when performing a task. The first graph reflected an early-action style and the last depicted a deadline-action style, while the midpoint showed a steady-action style; the second and fourth intermediate graphs reflected moderate tendencies toward early- and deadline-action styles. Because the graphs were ordered continuously, a lower score indicates an early-action style and a higher score represents a deadline-action style.
scale: five ordered graphs (continuous ordering from early-action to deadline-action)

description: Seven-item temporal leadership scale adapted from Mohammed and Nadkarni (2011), with the referent changed from ''your project leader'' to ''the CEO of your firm.'' At least three TMT members (excluding CEOs) in each firm rated the seven items on a 5-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = a great deal). Cronbach's alpha was .78 at the individual level and .80 at the team level; checks for aggregation revealed ICC(1) = .56, ICC(2) = .83, mean rwg(j) = .96. Responses of TMT members were averaged to derive the CEO temporal leadership scores.
scale: 5-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = a great deal)

description: An established 16-item scale that broadly measures a firm's actual (rather than preferred) entrepreneurial activities on innovation (five items), corporate venturing (five items), and strategic renewal (six items). At least three TMT members (including CEOs) in each firm filled out the scale (individual-level alpha = .90, team-level alpha = .92). A second-order factor model indicated by the three first-order factors fit the data, confirming a three-dimensional structure. Checks for within-group agreement revealed ICC(1) = .54, ICC(2) = .79, mean rwg(j) = .97, and an aggregated corporate entrepreneurship score was computed by averaging individual responses of TMT members.

Market share performance was measured by the Hunter and Coggin (1983) growth statistic, MSP = B/MS (x 100), where MS is the firm's average market share during the 1978-87 period and B is the raw-score regression coefficient of the market share trend regression. The authors chose market share rather than profit data because, in the global setting, market share data for different firms are more nearly equivalent.

The authors counted the number of alliance agreements that a firm had with its competitors during the 1978-87 period. They note that the approach is objective but can only give an indication of intensity of cooperation, since the degree of cooperation established in different alliances will vary a great deal.

The number of competitors with whom the firm entered into one or more alliance agreements during the 1978-87 period. Only one alliance with a given competitor is required to reduce competitive uncertainty, which is why this variable is used instead of the number of agreements.

variable_name: Absolute deviation of size from intermediate firm size (SIZEDEV)
description: Mean firm size, the natural log of average annual production, served as the benchmark for intermediate firm size. Firm size deviation was calculated as the absolute deviation of actual firm size from mean firm size, where firm size is the firm's average annual production during 1978-87.

Average annual unit production by the firm (AAPf) was used to assess firm size, based on production data obtained from World Motor Vehicle Data. Because the distribution of firm size was skewed by a proportionally larger number of smaller firms, the authors used the natural log of size to compress the large firm tail of the size distribution.

variable_name: Highest proportion of linkages within a single subnetwork (HPLWSS-N)
description: For each firm the authors identified the number of its partners found in that subnetwork in which most of its partners were based (NoPm), and divided this by the firm's total number of partners (NoP). Subnetworks were first identified by computing Euclidean distances between firms from their geodesic distances and applying multidimensional scaling and cluster analysis; BMW, which formed a cluster on its own, was dropped from the analysis.

variable_name: Difference between average actual and average potential partner size (DPAPS)
description: The authors computed the average size of each firm's potential partners during the 1978-87 period based on the size distribution of the other firms in the industry, and the average size of its actual partners. DPAPS, the difference between average actual and average potential partner size, indicates a firm's preference for larger or smaller partners relative to what random choice among potential partners would produce. The formula blocks for these averages are not readable in the retrieved text.

Coded 1 if the respondent reported denying at least one request for information, data, or materials related to his or her published research in the last three years, and 0 otherwise. The sample was restricted to the 1,251 respondents who reported having received at least one such request.

Average number of times that the members of each reference group reported withholding information from another scientist who requested it. Computed separately for reference groups defined by field, specialty, and status (same rank, experience, productivity, or budget as the focal scientist).

Standard deviation in the number of times that the members of each reference group reported withholding information. Computed for status-based reference groups defined by same rank, experience, productivity, or budget as the focal scientist.

Average of the reference group members' responses to the statement 'Academic scientists should freely share information, data, or materials with all academic scientists'. The response scale is 1 = 'completely agree', 2 = 'somewhat agree', 3 = 'somewhat disagree', or 4 = 'completely disagree', and a higher score indicates more favorable attitudes to withholding in the group.

Reference groups were constructed at three levels of increasing professional similarity to the focal scientist. The first level was professional field: geneticist versus non-geneticist. The second was specialty within genetics, based on the model organism studied. The third was status within specialty, using academic rank, research experience, research productivity, and research budget to identify status-equals and status-superiors.

Scanning is one of the managerial activity variables and is part of information gathering within planning. The measures of scanning, futurity, analysis, and interaction were adopted from Miller (1987a, 1987b) and Miller and Dröge (1986), and were operationalized using definitions in Miller (1987a, 1987b).
Futurity is the second information gathering variable within planning. Along with scanning, analysis and interaction it was adopted from Miller (1987a, 1987b) and Miller and Dröge (1986).

Analysis is one of the managerial activity variables and is part of information processing within planning. The measures of scanning, futurity, analysis, and interaction were adopted from Miller (1987a, 1987b) and Miller and Dröge (1986).

Interaction is the second information processing variable within planning, defined in terms of interaction with others. Together with scanning, futurity and analysis it was adopted from Miller (1987a, 1987b) and Miller and Dröge (1986).

Decentralization is one of the two variables representing organizing within managerial activities. The measures of decentralization, specialization, formality, and control were modeled after similar scales in Miller and Dröge (1986).

Specialization is the second variable representing organizing within managerial activities. Together with decentralization, formality and control it was modeled after similar scales in Miller and Dröge (1986).

Formality is one of the two variables representing control within managerial activities. The measures of decentralization, specialization, formality, and control were modeled after similar scales in Miller and Dröge (1986).

Cost control is the second variable representing control within managerial activities. Miller and Dröge (1986) and Miller et al. (1988) found these variables explanatory in the cost control mechanisms of small firms.
