Proactiveness is one of the two entrepreneurial orientation variables. The measures of proactiveness and innovativeness used in the present study were taken from Miller (1983) and Miller and Friesen (1982).

Innovativeness is the second entrepreneurial orientation variable. The measures of proactiveness and innovativeness used in the present study were taken from Miller (1983) and Miller and Friesen (1982).

Dynamism is one of the three environmental turbulence variables, referring to unpredictable environmental changes. Dynamism, hostility, and heterogeneity were measured in this study using scales from Miller (1983) and Miller and Friesen (1982).

Hostility is one of the three environmental turbulence variables, referring to environmental threats to the firm's vitality. Dynamism, hostility, and heterogeneity were measured in this study using scales from Miller (1983) and Miller and Friesen (1982).

Heterogeneity is one of the three environmental turbulence variables, referring to diversity of the firm's environments. Dynamism, hostility, and heterogeneity were measured in this study using scales from Miller (1983) and Miller and Friesen (1982).

Growth was measured by using the actual change in the number of employees over a 5-year period and the dollar sales volume over a 4-year span. Absolute changes in employment and sales volume were deemed to be better indicators of growth than relative measures (percentages) since proportions exhibit deceptively large amount of increases relative to low magnitudes of change among very small firms. Employment and sales were chosen over profit measures because of the nonuniformity of accounting procedures, heavy reinvestment, and the pay-scale of owner-managers in privately held, small firms.
time_window: 5-year period for employment; 4-year span for sales

description: Managerial activities are measured by eight survey-based variables: scanning, futurity, analysis, interaction (planning), and decentralization, specialization, formality, and cost control (structure and control). They are the variables used to cluster the small firms into four profiles.

Mean number of innovation-related sentences in the résumés of a firm's employees that contained at least one quantitative word. Résumé text was first filtered to sentences containing at least one word related to the product-innovation process; quantitative terms include analytics, statistics, and data science. The measure is obtained for each firm in each year and lagged one year because about one year typically elapses between committing to a product launch and the launch itself.
scale: proportion of innovation-related sentences containing a quantitative term

description: Mean number of innovation-related sentences in the résumés of a firm's employees that contained at least one qualitative word. Résumé text was first filtered to sentences containing at least one word related to the product-innovation process; qualitative terms include focus groups, customer interviews, and user stories. The measure is obtained for each firm in each year and lagged one year.
scale: proportion of innovation-related sentences containing a qualitative term

description: Sum of dollar sales of a product in the two quarters that conclude the two-year post-launch period; the launch is the first quarter in which the product has observable sales in the NielsenIQ data. Sales in the final two quarters of the two-year post-launch period are used to mitigate confounding signals from the initial size of the launch. In the firm-year panel data the variable is aggregated by summing the new-product sales of all products launched each year. Its mean at the product level was about $1.2 million.

Product classified as a hit, coded 1 when the product reached the top 5 percent of new-product sales in its product group. In the firm-year panel dataset the classifications are tallied by summing them at the firm level for all products launched each year, and hit rate is the proportion of products launched that were hits.

Product classified as a flop, coded 1 when the product fell in the bottom 50 percent of new-product sales in its product group. In the firm-year panel dataset the classifications are tallied by summing them at the firm level for all products launched each year, and flop rate is the proportion of products launched that were failures.

Interaction term multiplying the firm-year measures of quantitative and qualitative analysis, entered in the sales regressions to test complementarity. Both variables are normalized and mean-centered at 0, so a statistically significant positive coefficient on the interaction is interpreted as evidence that the marginal effect of one type of analysis is stronger in the presence of the other.

Organization size was measured by the natural log of the number of year-round employees. It is one of the two contextual variables in the study and enters the causal model as one of the four exogenous variables of context.

Perceived environmental uncertainty was measured with a modified version of the Downey, Hellriegel, and Slocum (1975) adaptation of the Duncan (1972) instrument, which asks for only 3 external environmental factors from a list of 14. Respondents ranked the three most important factors that can cause uncertainty in decision making in their food processing supply company. The three factors were scaled separately for each of the three information uncertainty questions; the Cronbach alpha for Factor 1 was .87, for Factor 2 .82, and for Factor 3 .77, and the total summed scale coefficient alpha was .86. Decomposition of this scale by environmental priority is a key feature of its application in this study.

Technology policy was measured by an 8-item, 5-choice Likert scale adapted from Ettlie and Bridges (1982). Five of these items survived the factor and item analysis, with a Cronbach alpha of .78. They included questions on a tradition of being first with new methods and equipment, recruiting technical and marketing personnel, money spent on new product development, and commitment to technological forecasting.

Three items were used to measure performance gap, two of which make a scale with Cronbach alpha of .62. Both are questions involving comparison of performance with expectations and previous levels in the short term (one year) and long term (five years). The question that did not make the scale was the percent of plant production capacity utilization. Because performance gap was hypothesized to be a function of contextual variables, it was included with the intervening policy variables of the study.

The market policy variable was ultimately decomposed into two scales; the first scale was called direct market policy. The three questions used to probe this variable make a scale that just meets minimal reliability requirements with a Cronbach alpha of .56. The first question asks if sales personnel are employed that are involved in direct customer contact; the second two questions involve top management: do top managers get involved in selling and/or other customer-related activities?

The second variable was constructed from the responses to an open-ended question concerning the circumstances under which top managers become involved in customer sales. Firms were coded according to the extent to which a special priority system was used by top managers for becoming involved with customers: high scores were assigned for specific priority systems, lower scores for vague priority systems, and lowest scores for no priority system. Scores were assigned as follows: a score of 5 was assigned to the response category 'most important projects, customers, new projects, problems'; a score of 4 to 'special occasions (trade shows, seminars, etc.)'; a score of 3 to 'final contract negotiations, closing, or at customer request'; a score of 2 to 'as needed'; and a score of 1 to 'primary job of management' or 'rarely'. This variable was called top management customer relations and is a variant on the management by exception principle.
The rate of product innovation is the number of new products introduced during the last three years. It is one of four measures of innovation used in the study.

To measure whether or not a supplier was currently offering or considering manufacture of this technology, a scale of four items was developed with a Cronbach alpha of .86. The questions ask if the firm is manufacturing the retortable pouch or tray, or equipment to form, fill, and seal the pack, and if the firm plans to introduce or has a long range strategy for marketing the components of this innovation. The technology is a flexible or semirigid package that is thermostabilized like a metal can and is shelf-stable.

The second category of dependent variables is the rate of process innovation, decomposed into two types; the first is the number of major or radical process innovations incorporating technology new to the industry. This covered the past three years and was indicated with examples by respondents.
The second type of process innovation is the number of minor or incremental process innovations. This covered the past three years and was indicated with examples by respondents.

variable_name: Rate of product and process innovation
description: Innovation is the set of dependent variables for rate of product and process innovation: rate of new product introduction, introduction of retortable packaging technology (radical product), and rates of radical and incremental process adoption, from the supplier survey.

Ownership concentration measured as the percentage of shares outstanding held by the largest shareholder. The authors chose this continuous measure because it is among the most widely employed in the literature and is the most widely available and accurate measure to obtain across countries. Because ownership information is available for only 1 year, the 1991 level of ownership concentration is taken as the best available estimate for all years.
time_window: 1991 level applied to all years of the 1986-91 panel

description: The square of OWN, the percentage of shares outstanding held by the largest shareholder, used to allow for a nonlinear relationship between ownership concentration and profitability. For each country the model was run with and without the squared term and an F-test was used to decide its inclusion; the nonlinear specification was confirmed for the United States, Germany and France, while the linear (OWN only) specification was confirmed for the United Kingdom and Canada.
time_window: 1991 level applied to all years of the 1986-91 panel

description: Return on assets, measured as the ratio of net income to total assets. This is the dependent variable in all equations.

Diversification measured with the weighting method proposed by Caves (1975). Worldscope lists the 4-digit SIC industries in which the firm operates and lists them in order of importance but does not list the revenues generated within each industry, so industry weights are imputed from a geometric series (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) rather than taken from actual line-of-business data. Relatedness is incorporated through classification of secondary segments as being in the same 3-digit industry, the same 2-digit industry, or a different 2-digit industry from the primary segment. The variable could only be calculated for 1 year, 1991, and is therefore assumed constant over the relevant period.

The national governance context is operationalized by splitting the sample into the five countries and estimating a separate equation for each, after Chow tests indicated that pooling was not appropriate. The countries are characterized in the paper as relying on internal constraints (France and Germany), on external constraints (the United States and the United Kingdom), or on both (Canada).

Data on brand name reputation was culled through four items on the expert panel survey, each answered on a seven-point Likert scale. Each chain's brand name reputation was calculated by summing responses to the four questions and dividing by the number of expert raters, so values could range from 4 (all raters gave the chain the lowest possible score on all four questions) to a high of 28.

To measure TMT experience, the authors compiled (1) the total number of years of executive-level food service experience and (2) the total number of years in the firm for all inside directors in each restaurant chain as of 1992. These measures were standardized and then summed to create a unit-weighted scale.

Slack measures previously used by Singh (1986) and Hambrick and D'Aveni (1988) were used. Each chain's equity-to-debt ratio in 1992 assessed its amount of unused borrowing capacity, or potential slack. Available slack, representing highly liquid, existing capital available for immediate investment, was measured for 1992 as cash and marketable securities divided by the number of outlets in the chain. These measures were standardized and then summed to create a unit-weighted scale.
Outlet-level asset specificity was assessed through four survey items answered on seven-point Likert scales, comparing the company to all other food service operations.
Specific knowledge was assessed through four survey items answered on seven-point Likert scales, comparing the company to all other food service operations.

Two measures that reflect a chain's geographic dispersion were examined: the number of states and number of countries with operations in 1992. The measures were standardized and then summed to create a unit-weighted scale.

Measured as the percent of growth accomplished through interfirm cooperation during 1992 and 1993: the number of new restaurants built with cooperative partners divided by the total added to the chain (cooperative ventures plus wholly-owned facilities) in those years. Outlets structured as management contracts were eliminated from the calculation.

Return on assets was used to measure financial performance, a measure of the efficiency of business operations. Performance measures were averaged over 1994 and 1995, the 2 years immediately following the last year of the interfirm cooperation measure, to guard against any 1-year outlier performance.

Market-to-book value approximates the stock market's perception of the value of the firm's present and future income and growth potential. Because it measures performance at the corporate level, only single and dominant chain firms (those with over 70% of revenues derived from a single chain) were included in this part of the analysis, and the measure was available for 77 of the 94 chains. Performance measures were averaged over 1994 and 1995.

For the test of Hypothesis 3 the authors placed firms into the four cells portrayed in Figure 1 based on resource and exchange condition variable medians and created two groups: those firms expected to prefer full ownership according to Hypothesis 3 (the top left cell of Figure 1) versus those expected to prefer interfirm cooperation (all firms in the other three cells).

For the test of Hypothesis 3 the authors placed firms into the four cells portrayed in Figure 1 based on resource and exchange condition variable medians. Exchange conditions that facilitate full ownership are low outlet-level asset specificity, high specific knowledge, and low geographic dispersion.

Likert-type items adapted from the work of Hill (1983), Perrow (1967), and Hickson et al. (1969), each measured on a seven-point scale. Items capture the changeability and multi-usability of the primary process and equipment and the breadth of employees' methods and know-how. Item selection was based on exploratory factor analysis with principal component procedures and varimax rotation; the scale's reliability is 0.67 and its composite reliability is 0.80.

Indicators adapted from Burns and Stalker (1961), Pugh et al. (1963), Lawrence and Lorsch (1967), Mintzberg (1979), and Hrebiniak and Joyce (1985), each measured on a seven-point scale. All four items are reversed items, so higher values indicate a more organic structure. The scale's reliability is 0.75 and its composite reliability is 0.84.

Items based on the work of Ouchi (1979), Camerer and Vepsalainen (1988), and Hofstede et al. (1990), each measured on a seven-point scale. Three of the four items are reversed, so higher values indicate a more innovative culture. The scale's reliability is 0.70.

Items reflecting environmental turbulence were adapted from Dill (1958), Duncan (1972), Lawrence and Lorsch (1967), and Thompson (1967) and measured on a seven-point scale. The variable is formed as the product of the level of dynamism within the market environment and the degree to which changes are unpredictable. The two underlying dimensions are market dynamism (reliability 0.84) and unpredictability of changes (reliability 0.75).

A scale with three survey items adopted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993), each measured on a seven-point scale. The authors compared the survey data of the performance scale with the available accounting performance data and report that the survey measure appears to correlate highly with return on assets; both the interrater agreement score and the interrater reliability score for this scale are adequate. The scale's reliability is 0.83 and its composite reliability is 0.89.

Computed in two steps: first, the approximate fit line is established as a line in which the level of the organization design variable equals that of the contingency variable (environmental turbulence); second, misfit is the deviation of a response variable from this particular fit line. Contingency misfit is the sum of the deviations of the response variables technology, structure, and culture.

The average values of the organizational design variables (technology, structure, and culture) were calculated for a subsample of high-performing firms (high Z-score for firm performance) for each of four industry categories (industrial, trade, service, and nonprofit). For the remaining firms, institutional misfit is the sum of the absolute deviations of the three organization design variables from those high-performer values in the firm's industry category.

variable_name: Contingency misfit x institutional misfit interaction
description: Metafit is tested through the interaction term between contingency misfit and institutional misfit in the firm performance regression (Model 5). Contingency misfit is the sum of deviations of technology, structure and culture from the fit line with environmental turbulence, and institutional misfit is the sum of absolute deviations from high-performer values in the firm's industry.

Industry concentration measured as the 10-firm concentration ratio. For Hypothesis 1 the yearly concentration ratio is used. For Hypothesis 2 a two-year running average of the 10-firm concentration ratio is used because exits are counted between each two years.

A measure of innovation implementation constructed from hedonic prices of personal computers and from the number of related patents recorded by the U.S. patent office. The former estimates implemented technology while the latter estimates the possible available scope of innovation, and their ratio provides a measure of how much of the possible innovations were implemented in the industry in a given year.
The yearly number of firms exiting from incumbency as a top-10 net profit-maker, counted between each two years. The data are treated as count data.

variable_name: Average appellation status over prior 3 years
description: For each year, appellation status scores are computed from a square, asymmetric relational matrix counting the number of wineries located in region i that use the appellation of region j, with the main diagonal set to 0; Bonacich's c(a, B) measure is applied, with B set at its upper bound (the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue of the R matrix) and a scaled so that the highest-status region in that year has a status score of 1. A winery's status is then summarized with a three-year moving window, averaging the status of all appellation affiliations across all bottles produced by the winery over the three prior years. The authors illustrate that a winery producing bottles with status scores of .023 and .05 in 1982, .10 in 1983, and .08 in 1984 has a status of .0633 in 1985.
time_window: three prior years (moving window); status scores compiled for 1981, 1984, 1987, and 1990

description: Each bottle is assigned the most recently measured status score of the appellation with which it is affiliated; for example, a bottle produced in 1982 is given the status of its appellation in 1981, since 1981 is the most recent year for which appellation status information exists.
time_window: most recently measured year of the appellation status scores

variable_name: Average quality of wine over prior 3 years
description: The average of the Connoisseur's Guide ratings of all bottles of wine reported for the winery over the three prior years, a moving three-year window. The Guide rates wine on a four-point rating scale under peer group, single-blind conditions, so that all wines of a similar type are rated together and raters are blind with respect to the wine's producer and its price.
scale: average of a four-point rating scale

description: The price at which a winery sells a given bottle of wine, in dollars, as reported for that bottle by the Connoisseur's Guide to California Wine. The guide consistently reports retail price and quality data in conjunction with a wine's appellation affiliation.

The average price per ton of the primary grape used in a given wine, indicated by the varietal, appellation, and year listed on its label, for all years and varietals for which data were available; grape price data were available for approximately one-third of the bottles in the sample. For the remaining observations, cost was set equal to 0 and an indicator variable coded 1 for missing cost information was constructed. The authors treat this variable as the quality of the raw material used in production.

The rating reported in the Connoisseur's Guide for a given bottle of wine, on a four-point rating scale under peer group, single-blind conditions (raters blind to producer and price). It is used as the dependent measure of the quality a winery subsequently produces and as a control for the quality of the bottle itself in the price models.

Measures the performance of a firm's previous alliance NPIs relative to the firm's aspiration levels, blending social and historical comparisons. For a product introduced in year T, its sales are divided by its industry benchmark, the average sales of all products launched in the same business domain in the same year and the previous 3 years, giving the product's deviation from the benchmark. The average deviation of all prior products the firm introduced through the alliance mode before T is then divided by the average deviation of all of the firm's prior products; the equation blocks in the paper are not readable, so the formulas are reconstructed only from the prose description of this three-step procedure. A higher value indicates better performance of prior alliance NPIs, and the average deviation of all prior products is used as the denominator so that the denominator is not zero.
level: product (new product introduction of a firm)
time_window: all prior products introduced before the focal product's introduction year; industry benchmark based on the introduction year and the previous 3 years

description: Binary dependent variable used to test Hypotheses H1 and H2, taking the value of 1 if an aircraft model was brought to market through an independent NPI and 0 if it was an alliance NPI. The governance mode of each project is captured from the Contractor and Licensees headings of the aircraft reports: an independent project lists a single firm while joint developments list all primary contractors.
level: product (new product introduction of a firm)

description: Measured as the number of firms that produced and sold aircraft models of the considered type (fighter, turboprop, helicopter, and jet) in a given year. It accounts for the intensity of competition in each area of business at the time of product introduction.

Binary independent variable used to test Hypotheses H3a and H3b, taking the value of 1 if a former alliance partner undertakes its next NPI through independent development and 0 otherwise. For instance, Saab (Sweden), which had allied with Fairchild for a turboprop regional aircraft and then unveiled its own Saab 2000, was coded 1 for the Saab 2000; Fokker, which never independently developed a fighter, was coded 0.
level: product (new product introduction of a firm)

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 if an alliance partner's prior alliance performance is less than 1, meaning its past alliance NPIs performed below aspirations in that they were worse than its past independent NPIs relative to their respective benchmarks, and 0 otherwise. It is interacted with Alliance to Independence to test Hypothesis H3a.
level: product (new product introduction of a firm)

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 if an alliance partner's prior alliance performance is greater than 1, and 0 otherwise; it takes the value of 1 if the firm's past alliance NPIs performed above aspirations in that they deviated to a lesser extent from their industry benchmark than did the firm's past independent NPIs. It is interacted with Alliance to Independence to test Hypothesis H3b.
level: product (new product introduction of a firm)

description: Measured by the cumulative number of units sold over the lifecycle of the firm's next product; sales volume is the traditional measure of product performance in studies of the aircraft industry, and the measure refers to the firm's immediate next product. An NPI is considered to have achieved breakthrough performance when its performance falls in the 85th, 90th, or 95th percentile of all products' performance, and the hypotheses are tested with quantile regressions at these quantiles.
level: product (new product introduction of a firm)
time_window: lifecycle of the firm's next product

description: The independent variables are China, an indicator equal to one for those patents developed by inventors residing in China, and blockade of Google, an indicator equal to one for patents whose priority dates were after June 1, 2014. The main variable of interest is their interaction term, China X blockade of Google; its coefficients indicate the changes in the dependent variables for inventors in China compared to those in the control regions after the blockade.
time_window: patents with priority dates between June 1, 2013 and June 1, 2015

description: Constructed from the backward citations of a focal patent, using only applicant-added citations. First, the pairwise knowledge distance between two fields (IPC subclasses) was computed from a cross-citation matrix based on patents from the past 5 years, giving the proportion of citations made by patents in one subclass to those in another, adjusted by the base rate of the cited subclass being cited in a random search; knowledge distance is one minus this knowledge proximity. Second, for each backward citation the citation-dyad level distance from the focal patent's field to the cited patent's field was calculated and aggregated across all backward citations to derive the technological search distance of the focal patent. The authors used the natural log of this variable to account for its skewness; the equations for knowledge proximity, knowledge distance and the aggregation are not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: cross-citation matrix based on patents from the past 5 years

description: Constructed from the backward citations of a focal patent, using only applicant-added citations. Knowledge visibility of each cited patent was measured as temporal visibility (the time lag from the cited patent's last use to the time point when the focal search took place) and assignee visibility (one divided by the ranking of the cited patent's assignee in the cited patent's field based on patent count in the past 5 years); the two were standardized and summed to derive overall visibility, and cognitive distance was the reciprocal of that visibility. The citation-dyad cognitive distance was then aggregated across all backward citations to derive the cognitive search distance of the focal patent; the aggregation equation is not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: assignee ranking based on patent counts in the past 5 years

description: The size of the social collaboration network accessible to the inventor team, considering both direct and indirect ties. It was calculated as the number of direct collaborators with the focal team members within the past 5 years plus the number of second-degree ties to the team members, with a 0.5 discount assigned to the indirect ties because they are relatively remote and weaker information channels. The natural log transformation was used to account for the skewness of the network size; the calculation equation is not readable in the extracted text.

Citations from patents to non-patent scientific publications were identified using the dataset constructed by Marx and Fuegi (2019). A citation network using all patent citations, including patent-to-patent and patent-to-paper citations, was constructed; each patent's distance to science was the minimum degree of ties that can connect the patent with a scientific publication, coded iteratively up to the 10th degree with a distance of 10 assigned to all remaining patents. A field's proximity to science is 10 minus the field's average distance to science, so that a higher value represents a closer link to science.
scale: proximity to science, with 10 minus average distance to science; in the sample values ranged from 4.837 to 8.635

description: The percentage of managers in the TMT belonging to each of four functional areas (marketing, operations, finance and general management) was first calculated for the acquiring firm and, similarly, for the acquired firm. A difference score was calculated by subtracting the percentages for each function in the acquiring firm and acquired firm. The absolute value of the differences in the four functional areas was summed to derive the independent variable, complementarity. Managers were categorized into one of the four major functional areas if they had spent more than half of their career in that function.

The names of the TMT in the acquired firm were obtained for two time periods: the TMT during the time of the acquisition, and the TMT 3 years after the acquisition. The TMT turnover was measured as the proportion of change in the TMT between the two time periods. This information was collected from the Dun & Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Management.

Postacquisition performance of the consolidated organization was measured using accounting measures, specifically the ROA averaged for a period of 3 years immediately following the acquisition, with information collected from Moody's Industrial Manual. In the analyses, the dependent variable was measured as the residuals from a regression of the control variables (industry profitability, prior performance and relative size) on the accounting measure of postacquisition performance.

Firms were classified as related if the two firms belonged to the same dominant 2-digit SIC groups at the time of the acquisition, and classified as unrelated otherwise. Data required to make the distinction between related and unrelated acquisitions were collected from the quarterly reports of Mergers and Acquisitions and from Mergers Statistical Review.

CEOs were asked to list up to 10 of the most significant client bases of their firm, a client base being described as a set of unique customers who essentially buy the same set of goods and services, and to indicate in a matrix which businesses of the firm sold services to each client base. Client-related businesses were identified as those that served some common client bases of a firm. Searches of computerized news and business data bases identified the first reports of firms' intentions to enter these client-related businesses, and entries accompanied by other published information about the firm within one day were excluded, leaving 84 related diversification moves by 71 service firms.

CEOs identified up to 10 of the most significant firm-level resource bases used in the businesses of their firm, describing them as physical plant or equipment, personnel's specialized knowledge or skills, or special routines or repertoires, and entered in a matrix in which businesses each resource was used. Resource-related businesses were identified as those that used some common significant resources of a firm; use in multiple businesses implied resource-relatedness, which served as a surrogate for economies of scope. First reports of firms' intentions to enter these resource-related businesses were located in computerized data bases, and entries with other published information within one day were excluded, leaving 79 related diversification moves by 68 service firms.

Two independent expert raters familiar with the literature on information economics categorized all services listed in the 4-digit SIC classification into either the search or the experience category, using criteria suggested in the literature; agreement between the two raters exceeded 95 percent and disagreements were resolved by reference to the services marketing and management literature. A primary SIC code was identified for all businesses of each sample firm by comparing the businesses listed on the questionnaires with firms' 10-K reports and segment data in COMPUSTAT, and each of the 163 entries was classified as primarily involving either search or experience services.

Cumulative abnormal returns over the 3-day announcement period Day -1, Day 0 and Day +1, where Day 0 is the day on which a report of the diversification move appeared in one of the publications covered in the computerized data bases searched. The abnormal return is the difference between the actual return on a security and the return on the Standard and Poor's 500 index for that day; average abnormal returns and cumulative abnormal returns are computed for a portfolio of events, and a test statistic based on the cross-sectional portfolio standard deviation of the CAR is used to assess whether cumulative abnormal returns differ from zero.
time_window: Day -1 to Day +1 relative to the first report of the move (Day 0)

description: All applicants were asked to state their gender in their applications, which was used to construct a dummy variable for the gender of the founder. Female gender was coded as 1 for applicants self-identifying as female and 0 for male. The variable appears as female founder in the models.

Our dependent variable, commercial activity, is a five-point scale that measures the degree to which a venture uses commercial activity. A score was assigned to each venture based on in-depth coding of rich text descriptions of that venture, generated by the founders and collected via the fellowship application process. We developed a five-point scale of commercialization, ranging from 1 for projects that relied exclusively on noncommercial sources of revenue to 5 for projects that relied exclusively on commercial sources of revenue. Two external coders used this scale to assess the level of commercialization of each of the social ventures; intercoder reliability using Krippendorff's alpha was 0.92, and differences in coding were resolved by discussing the application essays until a consensus was reached.

variable_name: female business owners (prop; CBSA; mean centered)
description: We constructed a measure of community female business ownership by counting the proportion of businesses with a payroll, located in the corresponding CBSA, that were majority-owned by women. This measure was mean centered. These data were collected from the U.S. Census Bureau's (2007) Survey of Business Owners and Self-Employed Persons (SBO), a national establishment-level survey of 2.3 million randomly selected businesses conducted every five years.

A binary variable for female leader took the value 1 if a woman occupied at least one of the leadership titles 'founder,' 'executive director,' or 'chief executive officer' among the top five ranking officers of each organization. To identify the gender composition of leadership, we matched each first name to statistics on the use of that name by each gender in the U.S. population. We assigned a gender to a name if 95% or more of occurrences in the census and Social Security Administration data were associated with that gender.

To measure the use of commercial activity, we relied on additional financial information from tax filings. Nonprofit accounting divides revenues into program services and dues received in exchange for the provision of programs, and those from public and charitable donations. Following prior studies of nonprofits, we measured commercialization as the percentage of total revenues from program revenues and dues.

variable_name: female business owners (prop; CBSA; mean centered)
description: Consistent with our main analysis, we measured the proportion of female business owners in the local community using the U.S. Survey of Business Owners. For the replication analyses, we used the 2002 edition of the survey, which was closest to the date of the nonprofit leadership data for 2003.

The dummy variable for serial sales system is obtained from the survey of dealership management practices. It marks dealerships that use a liner/closer process, in which a less experienced salesperson begins the negotiation and can turn the customer over to a more experienced closer, as opposed to a parallel ('straight sell') process in which one randomly assigned salesperson handles the entire transaction.

Price is obtained from the DSA data, which include features of each vehicle sold, the census block of the buyer's home, the cost of the car to the dealership, and the price paid by the buyer. To restrict variation to the phenomena of interest, the data are restricted to cash transactions on new cars, where a cash transaction is one in which the dealer does not provide financing and does not receive a trade-in.

The competitor measure 'has competitor' is computed at the transaction level; it is a dummy for whether the focal car was for sale at another dealership within a 20-mile radius at any point in the data window. Competition is the feature the authors state drives down the transaction cost for customers.

The competition measure is a dummy for whether or not there is another dealership within 20 miles selling a car that the focal dealer sells. Distance is defined as the Vincenty distance from latitude and longitude coordinates for the focal dealership. The authors state that competition drives down the transaction cost for customers.

Focal car inventory at the time of sale is defined for a focal car and focal dealer as how many of that same car the dealer has on the lot at the time of the sale. This value is computed using the day of the sale for every car and imputing, for each car sold, the day of its delivery to the dealership from the number of days it spent on the lot before being sold; a value of 0 indicates that this was the only car of its type on the lot at the time of the sale. A larger inventory of the vehicle in question reduces the dealer's opportunity cost of selling the vehicle.

Average total inventory is the average number of vehicles that the dealership has on hand at any given time, calculated with Little's law for regenerative processes from data on the number of days that each sold car spent on the lot. The model suggests that average total inventory raises the marginal value of improved bargaining ability by lowering the average outside option of selling a vehicle.

The proportion of the customer's census block group without a college education, included as a proxy for the customer's tendency not to use the Internet for price research and the implied decrease in bargaining ability. At the transaction level, an individual's demographics are proxied with the demographics of his or her census block group, which generally contains between 600 and 3,000 residents.

The proportion of local residents who are themselves employed in sales, calculated at the dealership level by averaging the demographics of all customers for whom the focal dealer is the closest dealer that sells vehicles of the nameplate that the customer eventually bought. The authors state that the number of local residents involved in sales careers affects both the relative costs of the serial sales process and the average bargaining ability of a prospective customer, and that features reducing the supplier power of labor, and hence the idling cost of closers, increase the likelihood that the serial system is preferred.

variable_name: Customer demographics: No college (proxy for customer bargaining ability, hence dealer appropriation factor)
description: The appropriation factor is a model parameter. Proposition 6 is tested with the proportion of the customer's census block group without a college education, used as a proxy for customers who do not use the Internet for price research and so have lower bargaining ability; under the assumption that appropriation factors add to a fixed value, this implies a higher dealer appropriation factor. The variable is entered alone and interacted with the serial sales system dummy in the price regression.

variable_name: R&D Contract, Sales Contract, Service Contract
description: Dichotomous variables indicating whether contracting for a function was an important organizational arrangement employed by the firm. Data on the use of external contracts in R&D, Sales and Service were collected from the SEC documents, where firms disclose information about significant contracts; the discussion of a contract was taken as evidence that the contract was an important organizational boundary choice. When a contract spanned multiple functional areas it was assigned to a functional area based on the primary objective of the contract. Coding: '1' = the firm uses contracts for that function.
time_window: measured at t1, 1 year after the IPO

variable_name: Average sales performance and average net income performance
description: Two accounting-based measures of performance: Sales, the revenues generated from the sales of a firm's products and services, and Net Income, the firm's revenues minus its costs, including taxes as costs. Performance measures were averaged over 3 years (t1 through t3) to increase the reliability of annual accounting measures. Annual figures were standardized to represent a 12-month period; for example, if Sales and Net Income were reported for a 9-month period, these numbers were divided by 9 and multiplied by 12.
time_window: averaged over the 3 consecutive years following the IPO (t1-t3)

description: A firm's annual spending on R&D, coded from a firm's income statement. If a firm capitalized R&D, the amount spent in any given year was adjusted to reflect the firm's annual expenditures on R&D.
time_window: measured at t1, 1 year after the IPO

description: A dichotomous variable coded from the description of a firm's business, which indicates whether a firm sells products to at least one vertical market ('1' = vertical markets strategy).
time_window: measured at t1, 1 year after the IPO

description: A dichotomous variable created based on the description of whether a firm offered customized programming and product design ('1' = customized service strategy).
time_window: measured at t1, 1 year after the IPO

description: A two-item scale combining (1) the number of yearly changes in administrative titles net of any additions or deletions in positions, to indicate duty changes, and (2) the absolute value of yearly changes in the number of administrative positions (deletions and additions). Each reorganization indicator covered five years of data, from 1974 through 1978, and responses on the variables were summed to create the scale. Cronbach's alpha for the two-variable scale was 0.81.

Age was computed by subtracting each school's founding date from 1969, the starting date of the study. A log-base-ten transformation of age was used in the analyses, because a comparison of the basic model with and without logarithmically transformed age and size showed a significant 5 percent increment in explained variance for the model with the transformed variables.

Size was operationally defined as the number of students each school had in 1969. A log-base-ten transformation of size was used in further analyses in place of the nontransformed contextual variable.

Proportional change in the number of full-time equivalent students between 1969 and 1974. To compute proportional change in size, the logarithm to the base ten of 1969 enrollment was subtracted from the log base ten of 1974 enrollment.

variable_name: age x size x change in size
description: Configurational context was modeled as the three-way multiplicative interaction of change in size (growth or decline), age, and level of size, all logarithmically transformed. Reorganization was regressed in steps on the control and main effects variables, all two-way interactions, and then the three-way interaction. Significant multiplicative terms were illustrated by substituting selected values of the other variables into the product terms, showing the effect of one variable given different combinations of the other variables.
time_window: age and size measured in 1969; change in size 1969-1974; reorganization 1974-1978

description: Matched responses from both a VC and a CEO were used to measure the frequency of their interaction. Each member of the dyad indicated, on a seven-point Likert-type scale, the frequency of his or her interaction with the other member face to face, by telephone, and through writing. The six responses were reverse-coded and combined to yield a composite measure of the frequency of VC-CEO interaction (alpha = .86). The measure correlated positively and significantly with the VCs' reports of the number of hours devoted to the ventures over the previous year.
scale: 1 = every day to 7 = less than once a quarter, reverse-coded

description: CEOs provided data on venture ownership. Management's ownership level was the sum of the percentages of a venture's ownership held by the CEO and all other managers.

Congruence in goals was measured via the responses of the VC and the CEO on the relative importance of 15 objectives, 6 financial and 9 nonfinancial. Respondents allocated 100 points across the financial criteria and 100 points across the nonfinancial criteria to indicate each one's importance, and also used 100 points to indicate the percentages of emphasis they believed should be given to financial goals and to nonfinancial goals. These percentages were multiplied times the point allocations to derive a weighted score for each criterion, and for each dyad the sum of the absolute differences in the two ratings yielded a composite measure of goal differences. This variable was multiplied by -1 to obtain a measure of VC-CEO goal congruence in which high values indicate greater agreement.

CEOs provided information on their new venture experience by indicating whether they had had no prior new venture experience (coded 1), worked in start-ups before but not founded one (coded 2), or previously founded or co-founded a venture (coded 3).
scale: 1 = no prior new venture experience, 2 = worked in start-ups but did not found one, 3 = previously founded or co-founded a venture

description: VCs were asked to identify each venture's financing stage using a scale running from seed financing to bridge-acquisition. The measure correlates as expected with other measures of venture development provided by the CEOs: number of employees, time since founding, time since initial venture capital investment, and sales revenue.
scale: 1 = seed financing, 2 = start-up, 3 = first stage, 4 = restart-up, 5 = expansion, 6 = bridge-acquisition

description: Data on the levels of the ventures' technical innovation were obtained from the CEOs only. On a five-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1, 'to no degree,' to 5, 'to a great degree,' CEOs rated the extent to which they were attempting innovation relative to competitors in terms of product design and process technology. Similarly, on a five-point scale from 1, 'significantly lower,' to 5, 'significantly higher,' they rated their positions relative to competitors' in terms of R&D spending and process technology. Responses to these four items were averaged (alpha = .70).

Venture-level uncertainty is measured with the VentureXpert classification of the maturity of the venture at the time of the focal investment. Following Dushnitsky and Shapira (2010), the value is set to 4 for 'Startup/Seed' investments, 3 for 'Early Stage' investments, 2 for 'Expansion'-stage investments, and 1 for 'Later Stage' investments, so that higher values indicate greater venture-level uncertainty.
scale: 1-4 (4 = Startup/Seed, 3 = Early Stage, 2 = Expansion, 1 = Later Stage)
time_window: at the time of the focal investment

description: Country-level uncertainty is operationalized using a reverse scale of the PRS Group's International Country Risk Guide law and order index, which assesses the strength and impartiality of a legal system as well as the popular observance of the law on an annual basis. The index was reverse-coded to represent country-level uncertainty intuitively; the measure ranges from 0 to 6, with higher values indicating greater country-level uncertainty.

variable_name: international experience in managing venture-level uncertainty (ln)
description: Measured as the cumulative number of early-stage ventures that each VC firm had invested in abroad prior to the year in which the focal investment was made, where early-stage ventures are those recorded as 'Startup/Seed' or 'Early Stage' at the time of the transaction. The weight of experience is decreased depending on its recency using an annual depreciation rate of 30%, and a natural logarithm is used.
time_window: cumulative prior to the focal year, with a 30% annual depreciation rate

variable_name: international experience in managing country-level uncertainty (ln)
description: Measured as the cumulative number of ventures located in foreign countries with high country-level uncertainty that each VC firm had invested in prior to the year when the focal investment was made. Country-level uncertainty was considered high in countries with a value on the reverse law and order index over 1, which is in the top 75th percentile of all host countries in the sample. An annual depreciation rate of 30% was employed, and a natural logarithm is used.
time_window: cumulative prior to the focal year, with a 30% annual depreciation rate

variable_name: international experience in the host country (ln)
description: Measured as the total number of previous ventures in which a foreign VC firm invested in a host country up to the year of the focal transaction. An annual 30% depreciation rate was applied to account for decay in the effect of the experience over time, and a natural logarithm is used.
time_window: cumulative up to the focal year, with a 30% annual depreciation rate

variable_name: whether to partner (or not) with a local VC firm
description: The dependent variable classifies each VC investment into one of four categories: investing in a venture in the home country ('0'), investing in a venture in a foreign country alone ('1'), investing in a foreign venture with other foreign VC firm(s) ('2'), or investing in a foreign venture with at least one local VC firm ('3'). A case is considered 'foreign' if the focal VC firm was investing in a non-home country, and 'syndicated' if at least two VC firms had invested in the venture together in the first round; the nominal taxonomy allows the multilayered decision to be modeled as sequential or as unordered.

Entropy measure of international diversification, adopted to measure an MNC's level of international dispersion and embeddedness and following Hitt et al. (1997). It is computed as the sum over foreign regions of the region's sales share multiplied by the natural log of the inverse of that share, where the weight given to each foreign region is based on sales in 2001.

An abnormal return is calculated as the difference between the observed return for a security and the predicted or normal return for the same security, so the impact of an exogenous event is measured by the part of the return that violates pre-event expectations. The market model relates the return on stock i for day t (September 11, 2001) to the return on the market portfolio for day t, a constant and the stock's beta, with an independent disturbance term; the mathematical expression as given in the paper could not be read from the text. Parameters were estimated with 251 daily return observations from September 11, 2000 to September 10, 2001.
time_window: event day September 11, 2001; estimation window September 11, 2000 to September 10, 2001

description: Long-term MNC performance after the September 11 attacks measured as the firm's q-ratio for 2002, calculated following Chung and Pruitt's (1994) method. Tobin's q reflects current and anticipated profitability and requires no risk adjustment or normalization to compare q across firms.

variable_name: Speed of absorption of externally acquired knowledge
description: The time it takes firms to absorb a licensed technology, calculated using the number of months between the licensing date and the first time the licensee incorporated the licensed technology as a backward citation in a new patent. The patent application date is used as the reference rather than the patent granting date. To model this dependent variable the authors use a dummy variable that takes the value 1 if the licensed technology has been cited in a new patent, and 0 otherwise, in an event history structure, with the licensing date as the onset of risk.
time_window: patenting tracked up to December 2006; censored at the latest dates available in the patent citations data

description: Measured using the 'focal index' proposed by Ziedonis (2007): the technology distance between a licensed technology and the firm's knowledge base is measured by the patent class connected to the licensed technology and the technology classes in which the licensee was active prior to the licensing event. In prose, the numerator is the citation-weighted sum of the firm's patents applied for within five years of the license agreement that belong to the same primary patent class as the licensed patent, and the denominator is the sum of all citation-weighted patents issued to the firm that were applied for by that date in the same five-year window, with a correction term applied to counter the downward bias of patent-class distance indexes. The equation itself was not extractable from the supplied text.
time_window: five years prior to the license agreement

description: Captures the distribution of technical knowledge across patent classes by inventors in the co-invention network of the focal firm. Active inventors are those with at least one patent application during the five years prior to the focal year; inventors' mobility is taken into account, so knowledge accumulated by an inventor at another firm before moving to the focal firm counts, while knowledge of inventors who left does not. Diversity is examined only among inventors with at least one active intrafirm tie. The authors define N_it as the total number of patents produced by the active inventors within firm i in the previous five years and N_jit as the number of patents assigned to technology class j among them; the equation itself was not extractable from the supplied text.
time_window: five years prior to the licensing contract

description: Measured by calculating the overall density of the intrafirm network, that is, the extent to which potential linkages within a network are realized. Observed ties are defined as the number of unique ties existing between two inventors that co-patent, and the number of possible ties as N(N-1)/2 for the total number of inventors listed in the firm's patents. The density equation itself was not extractable from the supplied text.
time_window: five years prior to the licensing contract

description: For each firm-year, the number of patents applied by the firm in that year in technological subclasses identified by Popp (2002, 2006) as involving alternative sources of energy, i.e. research pertaining to alternative sources for energy. These subclasses represent efforts toward paradigm-changing technologies.

For each firm-year, the number of patents applied by the firm in that year in technological subclasses identified by Popp (2002, 2006) as reducing demand for energy, i.e. research to improve the energy efficiency of current processes and products. These subclasses represent efforts toward paradigm-deepening technologies.

Constructed in three steps. First, for each SIC industry an input vector is built from the IO table capturing the inputs directly required to produce one dollar's worth of output, and the dyadic relatedness between industries i and j is the angular distance between the two vectors. Second, for each manufacturing industry i of a firm, relatedness to all other industries of the firm is the weighted average of dyadic relatedness using the sales of the other industries as weights. Third, firmwide input-relatedness is the weighted average of that measure across all industries of the firm, using the sales of each industry as weights. The measure is mean-deviated to reduce collinearity; parts of the formula are unreadable in the text.

Using the IO tables, the amount of oil used, both directly and indirectly, in producing one dollar's worth of output is obtained for each industry at the SIC level and multiplied by the oil prices prevailing in that year to give an industry-specific oil-dependence measure. For each firm, the industry-specific oil-dependence values of the four-digit industries it operates in are weighted by the percentage of firm sales in each industry and summed. The measure is mean-deviated to reduce collinearity; the formula block in the text is unreadable.
time_window: 1982 IO tables; oil prices of the prevailing year

description: The event year, year t, is defined as the year of formal ISO 9000 certification, and the authors focused on the first ISO 9000 certification because a company could have multiple plants/sites certified. Because the average preparation time to pass the ISO 9000 audit is between 9 and 18 months before certification, year t-2 was taken as the initiating time of ISO 9000 implementation. Certification and certification-year data were collected through two online databases of ISO 9000 certified firms.

CEO total cash compensation, i.e., salaries and bonuses, collected from EXECUCOMP. The distributions of the compensation data were highly skewed, so a natural logarithmic transformation was used to control for skewness in total cash compensation. Total cash compensation is treated as an ex post measure that rewards a CEO for his current performance.
time_window: one year before ISO 9000 implementation through three years after certification

description: Value of stock options granted to the CEO, collected from EXECUCOMP, and estimated using the Black-Scholes formula, which is commonly adopted in the financial literature. A natural logarithmic transformation was used to control for skewness in stock options.
time_window: one year before ISO 9000 implementation through three years after certification

description: Return on assets, measured as operating income (before depreciation, interest, and taxes) divided by total assets. Financial performance data for both the sample and the control firms were obtained from COMPUSTAT.
time_window: one year before ISO 9000 implementation through three years after certification

description: A six-item, multiple-item measure centered on the prevalence of and the degree to which firms engage in bribery activity. Items evaluate the extent to which firms 'pay some irregular 'additional payments' to get things done' and whether 'firms like yours typically make extra, unofficial payments to public officials.' The response scale ranged from 1, 'always true,' to 6, 'never true,' and the items were reverse-coded so that higher scores represented greater bribery activity. The measure is reliable at an alpha of .86; construct validity was verified through high positive correlations with corruption indexes such as the Transparency International CPI.

Measured with the performance orientation items from the GLOBE study, which measure the extent to which a society 'encourages and rewards group members for performance improvement and excellence.' The final measure comprised four items, for which the GLOBE scholars reported an alpha coefficient of .72. The authors used the 'should be' GLOBE judgments and the adjusted GLOBE country scores.

The GLOBE study assessed the in-group collectivism component of culture with four items loosely based on Hofstede (1980), restructuring the earlier work and focusing on collective beliefs that a group's members should take pride in one another's work and accomplishments; respondents were queried on the extent to which such accomplishments were considered honorable for the group as a whole. The measure tapped the values of group cohesiveness and loyalty and was reliable at an alpha level of .77. The 'should be' judgments and adjusted GLOBE scores were used.

The GLOBE measure for humane orientation contained five items; the central concepts measured were sensitivity, friendliness, generosity, other regarding, and tolerance despite mistakes. The measure is derived from managers' ideas of compassion theoretically characteristic of a humane orientation and was reliable at an alpha level of .88; the 'should be' measures and adjusted scores were used.

A three-item index derived from the extant literature on welfare socialism, whose data came from the International Labour Organization's 2000 World Labor Report and the United Nations Development Program's 2002 Human Development Report. The index infers institutional safeguards through welfare safety nets and other redistributive services resulting from increasing levels of government intervention, and is reliable at an alpha level of .78.

A commonly accepted measure, the Political Constraint Index developed by Henisz (2000, 2002), a structurally derived and internationally comparable assessment of constraints on policy formulation and adaptation in a majority of the world's countries. It focuses on critical attributes of a polity grounded in notions of checks and balances for national political institutions: the existence and strength of veto power in a nation's political system and the distribution of office holders with various political preferences over and within government branches. The measure has been used extensively in international business research.

A seven-item measure derived from WBES items characterizing the extent to which the respondents believed financial issues obstructed firm growth and development. Firm managers assessed the extent to which they believed various financial blocks limited performance, including collateral requirements, unfavorable interest rates, lack of firm-retained earnings, local banks' lack of resources, and access to nonbank equity investors. The measure retained desirable measurement properties and was reliable at an alpha level of .76.

A measure designed to assess the relevant number of competitors in a firm's primary strategic group. The WBES instrument asked managers to evaluate the number of significant rivals their firms regarded as viable competitive threats in their major product categories; responses to the item were categorical. The authors argue that the perceived number of significant competitors in a strategic group is an appropriate indicator of the rivalry firms encounter.

CEO prevention focus was measured through a content analysis of CEOs' annual letters to shareholders using dictionaries previously developed and validated for content, convergent, and discriminant validity. The text was coded with the Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) software to ensure high coding reliability. The measure is the percentage of prevention-related words within each letter. Predictor variables were lagged one year.

CEO promotion focus was measured through a content analysis of CEOs' annual letters to shareholders using dictionaries previously developed and validated for content, convergent, and discriminant validity. The text was coded with the Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) software to ensure high coding reliability. The measure is the percentage of promotion-related words within each letter. Predictor variables were lagged one year.

CEO prevention focus was measured through a content analysis of CEOs' annual letters to shareholders using previously developed and validated dictionaries, coded with the Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) software. The measure is the percentage of prevention-related words within each letter. Predictor variables were lagged one year.

CEO promotion focus was measured through a content analysis of CEOs' annual letters to shareholders using previously developed and validated dictionaries, coded with the Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) software. The measure is the percentage of promotion-related words within each letter. Predictor variables were lagged one year.

Engagement in governance-oriented initiatives was the total number of strengths a firm scored in KLD's corporate governance category, which is calculated based on eight different components. The total strengths score was adjusted by subtracting the mean number of strengths for all firms available in each given year. Only strengths, not concerns, were used because strengths capture purposeful actions designed to create positive stakeholder benefit.
time_window: focal year (t + 1 outcome with 1-year lagged predictors)

description: Engagement in socially-oriented initiatives was measured as the sum of the total strengths KLD reports across the following categories: community, diversity, employee relations, environment, and human rights. Following prior research, the KLD category ' Products ' was excluded because these actions are tied more directly to economic value than other issue areas. The total strengths score was adjusted by subtracting the mean number of strengths for all firms available in each given year.
time_window: focal year (t + 1 outcome with 1-year lagged predictors)

description: Receptivity to governance-oriented activism was captured using the voting status of governance-oriented shareholder proxy proposals, identified by the ISS database classification 'GOV'. Following McDonnell et al. (2015), the measure is the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance, where P is the number of positive response outcomes to proxy proposals, N is the number of negative responses, and V is the total number of proxy proposals submitted to the firm in a given year; the underlying formula is not readable in the supplied text. Outcomes are classified as negative (omit), neutral (vote), or positive (withdrawn). The continuous variable ranges from -1 to 1, and firms not receiving a proposal in a given year were scored as missing values and dropped.

Receptivity to socially-oriented activism was captured using the voting status of socially-oriented shareholder proxy proposals, identified by the ISS database classification 'SRI' (Socially Responsible Investing). Following McDonnell et al. (2015), the measure is the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance, where P is the number of positive response outcomes to proxy proposals, N is the number of negative responses, and V is the total number of proxy proposals submitted to the firm in a given year; the underlying formula is not readable in the supplied text. Outcomes are classified as negative (omit), neutral (vote), or positive (withdrawn). The continuous variable ranges from -1 to 1, and firms not receiving a proposal in a given year were scored as missing values and dropped.

Following Servén's (1998) methodology for measuring unexpected changes in the rate of growth of the economy, the variable is the natural logarithm of the conditional variance of nominal GDP growth in a given year, fitted by using the information on GDP growth until that year that is known to executives. The conditional variance is estimated separately for each country with a GARCH(1,1) model. The variable is lagged one year in all analyses.

Henisz's (2000) POLCON V index of political constraints, which ranges between 0 (no constraints on the executive branch's power to introduce policy changes) and 1 (full constraints), subtracted from unity so that higher values indicate policy instability or governmental policymaking discretion free from institutional constraints. The variable is lagged one year in all analyses.
scale: 0 to 1 constraints index, subtracted from unity

description: A dummy variable taking a value of 1 if the state held a stake in the equity of the company as of the end of the previous year, and 0 otherwise. The information to build this variable was obtained from Vergés (1999).

variable_name: Previous firm entries in Latin America
description: A counter for the number of previous entries into Latin American countries made by the company as of the end of the previous year. Entries were identified from press databases and from the companies' annual reports and Web pages.
time_window: as of the end of the previous year

description: The dependent variable is the count of entries in each unique firm-country-year combination. If no entry occurred in a given firm-country-year the variable is coded 0; otherwise it is coded as a nonnegative integer depending on the number of investments that took place. Following the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, a foreign direct investment is any acquisition of 10 percent or more of a foreign business enterprise, and only entries entailing effective involvement of the firm in the management of a regulated service in a Latin American country were considered. Marketing agreements, unsuccessful bidding attempts, financial investments without management involvement and, for banks, investment banking branches or representative offices were excluded.

Coded 1 when a focal firm compared itself with a particular target firm but consumers did not compare the focal firm with the target firm when making a purchase decision, and 0 otherwise. The variable was constructed by juxtaposing the automaker Web site comparison data with the consumer data. When a focal automaker had multiple models, all product comparisons were aggregated to construct the focal automaker's competitive comparison.

Coded 1 if a focal firm did not compare itself with a particular target firm even though consumers compared the two firms when making a purchase decision, and 0 otherwise. It was generated through the same procedure as self-asserted comparison, juxtaposing firm and consumer comparison data.

Reputation was measured by third-party evaluations of an automaker's product quality collected from the December 2004 Consumer Guide; industry experts test drove vehicles and rated them on 10 categories. The average of the quality ratings of models was taken for automakers with more than one mid-size sedan model. Relative reputation was created by subtracting a focal firm's reputation from a target firm's reputation, so a positive score indicates the target firm is more reputable than the focal firm and a negative score indicates the target firm is less reputable.

Data were gathered from Automotive News through content analysis. All articles in 2005 and 2006 containing at least one of the specified keywords were searched, and each article was checked to identify dyad-level competitive actions; a total of 159 dyad-level competitive actions among automakers in the sample were identified. The variable was operationalized by subtracting the target firm's volume of competitive actions from the focal firm's volume of competitive actions.

variable_name: focal firm's sales growth relative to that of a target firm
description: Sales growth for each firm was first calculated using the logarithm of the firm's sales change between 2005 and 2006: sales growth i = log(sales i, 2006 / sales i, 2005), where sales refers to the number of total cars sold. After each firm's sales growth was acquired, the target firm's sales growth was subtracted from the focal firm's to obtain relative sales growth.

Measured by the total number of letters of environment-related complaints/reporting received by local environmental protection bureaus, aggregated at the provincial level, as recorded in the China Environment Yearbooks published by the Ministry of Environmental Protection of China and China Environment Yearbook Press. The count is standardized by provincial total population and then log transformed to reduce skew. During the period of the study there was an average of 4.58 petition letters per 10,000 people per province year.
scale: count per 10,000 people, log transformed and standardized
time_window: one-year lag before the dependent variable

description: Measured by counting and aggregating, at the provincial level, the total number of reports of environmental protests in approximately 50 leading media outlets with wide readership, under the assumption that bigger events draw attention from more media outlets. The authors systematically searched five leading international media outlets, five key social media and news sites covering environmental issues, ten leading domestic Chinese social media sites and newspapers, and the largest newspaper in each of the 31 Chinese provinces based on readership. The aggregate was log transformed to reduce skew.
scale: count of reports, log transformed and standardized
time_window: one-year lag before the dependent variable

description: Measured with the legal framework development measure of the NERI Index of Marketization of China's Provinces, which assesses the protection of property rights, the effectiveness of judicial systems, and the efficiency of public administration. Because the NERI has updated the index only up to the year 2009, the authors extrapolated data for 2010. The variable is standardized in the models.
time_window: one-year lag before the dependent variable

description: Measured with the Media Marketization Index developed by Stockmann (2013), which assesses the marketization of traditional media and new media by incorporating media income from advertising (instead of government funding) and the penetration of the internet (percentage of internet users). The index ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating the highest level of media development in China. A second measurement, the China Media Development Index published by People's Daily Press, yields largely similar results; the authors report regression results using the first measurement. The variable is standardized in the models.
time_window: one-year lag before the dependent variable

description: A categorical variable coding the level of severity of the administrative sanctions local environmental protection bureaus imposed on firms: 0 indicates no penalties, 1 indicates a warning (mandatory treatment), 2 indicates a fine, and 3 indicates an operation suspension for rectification. The authors manually coded these penalty records for each firm-year from 2007 to 2011 from the IPE website; all environmental penalties in the sample fell into the first three categories. For firms subjected to multiple penalties within a given year, the highest-level penalty that occurred was coded. The authors focused on environmental penalties that occurred in a firm's headquarter province.

Civic activism is captured by two provincial-level variables used together: the number of environmental complaint letters received by local environmental protection bureaus (within-the-system) and the number of reported environmental protests (outside-the-system). Both enter the penalty models as the paper's indicators of vibrant environmental activism.

For a given firm/quarter, interpersonal heterogeneity is the mean Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between the LDA topic probability distributions for all unordered pairs of reviews in that firm/quarter. Each review was represented as a vector of unigram counts and assigned by the LDA model to a probabilistic mixture of 500 cultural topics. JS divergence is a symmetric measure of the dissimilarity of two probability distributions. The measure was standardized and lagged by one quarter in the models.

Each review is represented as a probability distribution over cultural topics; the Herfindahl index of concentration was applied to these distributions and the mean Herfindahl score was calculated across all reviews for a given firm/quarter. The inverse was taken so that higher values indicate that employees discuss a broader range of cultural topics. The natural log of the mean Herfindahl index was taken because the measure has a highly skewed distribution. The measure was standardized and lagged by one quarter in the models.

Income before extraordinary items over total assets. The authors describe ROA as a commonly understood measure of profitability that indicates a firm's ability to effectively capitalize on its assets, used as a reflection of a firm's capacity for efficient execution.

The market value of a firm's assets relative to their book value, used as the market's expectation of a firm's growth potential and as an indicator of intangible capabilities and assets. The paper presents the definition of market value of assets in a formula that was not extracted.

The total number of patents a firm applies for in a given quarter that are later approved, used as a measure of a firm's ability to successfully produce patents. The raw patent count was modeled in a negative binomial specification and the logged count in OLS specifications.

The mean number of backward citations made by the patents in a firm's portfolio in a given quarter, described as a common indicator of the technological importance and market value of the patents. The mean backward citations measure was logged to account for skew.

A time-invariant measure of the total number of citations that the given patent received from subsequent patents from patent issue until 1997. The authors argue that a time-invariant measure captures the underlying economic value of the invention at the time of invention. An alternative specification divides this count by the number of citations received by an average university patent of that age and in that technology field.

A time-invariant count of the number of three-digit patent classes in which previous patents cited by the given patent are found, but the patent itself is not classified. Patents are divided into about 600 three-digit classes representing distinct technical areas, so citing patents in classes other than the ones the patent is in suggests that the invention builds upon different technical paradigms.
