To control for collinearity between the amount of long-term income and total compensation level, the authors calculated a residual score for LTI, 'partialing out' the common scale effect it shared with total compensation; as a result, the residualized LTI had a correlation of zero with total compensation.
LTI as a proportion of total compensation for the 1995-98 period, that is, the share of the total compensation package that is long-term income.

The percentage of stock owned by family members (excluding the CEO), measured from firms' proxy statements. Owing to limitations in the information available, the authors could only identify shareholders that owned 5 percent or more of a company's stock.

The percentage of stock owned by institutional investors, measured from firms' proxy statements. Institutional investors included public pension funds, mutual funds, insurance companies, banks, nonbank trusts, and corporate pension funds; family trusts and/or foundations were not considered as institutional investors. Only shareholders that owned 5 percent or more of a company's stock could be identified.
The ratio of R&D expenditures during the 1995-98 period divided by the natural logarithm of sales.

The part of the variance in a firm's returns that can be explained by changes in the market, calculated from monthly adjusted stock data from 1995 through 1998. Monthly stock prices gathered from COMPUSTAT were used to calculate a firm's monthly stock returns, and the Standard & Poor's 500 index was used to approach the market portfolio return; beta was calculated as the correlation coefficient between a firm's monthly adjusted returns and market portfolio monthly returns.
The variations in firm returns that are the result of factors specific to an organization itself, calculated from monthly adjusted stock data from 1995 through 1998.

Business risk is the variability in a firm's stock market returns, measured in two ways: systematic risk (the part of return variance explained by the market) and unsystematic risk (firm-specific variance). Both are computed from monthly adjusted stock returns against the S&P 500 and entered separately.

Operationalized by subtracting the average predicted rating of all analysts from the average predicted rating of analysts who are likely to cover a firm based on its position. The probability of receiving coverage from each analyst is estimated from the similarity between the firm and the other firms in that analyst's coverage portfolio, where similarity is measured with LDA topic modeling of firms' business description sections in their 10-K reports and Jensen-Shannon divergence. The predicted ratings come from the FunkSVD collaborative filtering model; the exact formula is not readable in the extracted text.

Within the IBES dataset, only an analyst's latest investment recommendation on a firm in each calendar year is kept. The IBES standardized recommendations were reverse scored by subtracting them from 6 so that a higher score corresponds with a more favorable investment recommendation, 5 being the most favorable and 1 being the least. The dependent variable is the aggregate investment recommendation that a firm receives from the analysts who follow it in a given year.

To measure this construct, the authors took the standard deviation of all analysts' predicted investment recommendations for a given firm in a given year. A high value indicates that security analysts would come to highly divergent investment recommendations for the firm if they were to evaluate it, whereas a low number indicates a higher level of convergence in analysts' predicted recommendations.

variable_name: Heterogeneity in the evaluative schemas of the audiences a firm engages with
description: Measured by investigating the heterogeneity in broad conceptual concerns raised in the questions the firm decided to engage with during its earnings calls. Questions asked during all events within a year are combined for each firm and LDA topic modeling is applied to the corpus of all asked questions, with the number of topics set at 30. Following the formula used by Haans (2019), a heterogeneity metric was constructed from the topic weights; the exact formula is not readable in the extracted text. Earnings call data are only available from 2008.

The difference between the date that the focal job began and the date that the worker's first regular postcollege job began, minus any time that the worker spent out of the labor market. Reported in years.

Respondents were asked, 'How many employees worked/work for your employer at your primary job site?' The measure refers to establishment size rather than firm size. Consistent with standard practice, the natural logarithm of workplace size is used as the dependent variable to minimize the skewness of residuals.

variable_name: Dummy for organizations in occupationally intensive industries
description: Respondents reported their employer's industry, and about 70% of those who answered the industry question gave a verbal description that the authors coded into industry categories. Occupational intensity was measured as the percentage of the overall industry workforce in the computer specialist occupation (Code 15-1000) using the Bureau of Labor Statistics' National Employment Matrix. The dummy takes a value of 1 for industries in which 24% or more of the workforce were computer specialists: software, IT consulting, computer hardware, and Internet services, plus jobs in the general IT industry; all other organizations are referred to as generalist.

Job spells were assigned to metropolitan statistical areas using zip codes from respondent addresses provided by the universities taking part in the study, assuming respondents had lived at the same address throughout their careers; 115 MSAs were represented. For each MSA, the authors used the Census Bureau's 2002 County Business Patterns survey to calculate total employment in the three industries with the highest numbers of technology workers and divided this by total employment within the MSA.

Turnover is analyzed from the reported end dates of jobs. Job spells still ongoing at the time of the survey were treated as censored, as were job spells that ended due to involuntary turnover. The 14% of job spell terminations that were due to being fired, laid off, or the company going bankrupt were treated as involuntary, and the 1.3% of job spells described as ending due to transfers within the same company were also treated as censored.

variable_name: prior experience in small related acquisitions
description: Following previous studies, acquisition experience was considered in the four years prior to a focal acquisition. Prior experience in small, related acquisitions was calculated as the natural log of the total number of prior deals that were less than US$100 million and in the same two-digit primary SIC code as the focal target. Natural log transformations were used to better capture the declining marginal returns associated with experiential learning.
time_window: four years prior to the focal acquisition

variable_name: prior experience in large related acquisitions
description: Prior experience in large related acquisitions was measured as the natural log of the total number of prior deals that were at least US$100 million and in the same two-digit primary SIC code as the focal target, counted over the four years prior to the focal acquisition. Natural log transformations were used to better capture the declining marginal returns associated with experiential learning.
time_window: four years prior to the focal acquisition

description: We measured the difference in the acquiring firm's ROA three years after the acquisition in relation to one year prior to the acquisition. ROA was chosen because it is less sensitive to estimation bias due to changes in leverage or bargaining power following M&As. The variable is labelled 'Change in ROA' in the descriptive statistics.
time_window: from one year prior to the acquisition to three years after the acquisition

description: A factor that emerged from an exploratory factor analysis (principal factors extraction with varimax rotation) of seven survey items asking executives to assess the extent to which bidders and targets differed prior to an acquisition; each item used a five-point Likert scale with ratings ranging from 'very similar' to 'very dissimilar.' The factor captured the predeal product-market domains of both firms and comprised three items (alpha = .80).
scale: five-point Likert scale from 'very similar' to 'very dissimilar' (factor score)

description: A single survey item (geographic markets served) from the seven bidder-to-target dissimilarity items, on which respondents rated the extent to which bidders and targets differed on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 'very similar' to 'very dissimilar.' It formed the third factor in the exploratory factor analysis.
scale: five-point Likert scale from 'very similar' to 'very dissimilar'

description: A factor capturing perceptions of both firms' predeal organizational cultures, based on three survey items on which executives rated how dissimilar bidders and targets were on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 'very similar' to 'very dissimilar' (alpha = .77).
scale: five-point Likert scale from 'very similar' to 'very dissimilar' (factor score)

description: Two individuals content-analyzed target firms' predeal proxy statements and 10-Ks as well as the postdeal proxy statements and 10-Ks of the combined firms to determine if top managers of the targets continued to serve in a similar capacity after the deals (interrater reliability was 0.93). Target management retention was calculated as the number of target top managers retained as executive officers divided by the number of target top managers before the deal.

Level of integration was assessed by a survey item asking respondents to indicate how operations of the two firms changed following the deal. The resulting variable had three values: 0, 'neither firm changed significantly'; 1, 'one firm changed significantly'; and 2, 'both firms changed significantly.'
scale: 0 = neither firm changed significantly; 1 = one firm changed significantly; 2 = both firms changed significantly

description: Both upper-management and lower-management racial diversity were calculated using Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity at time t, one minus the sum of the squared proportions of each racial category. Five categories of race were used (White, African American, Hispanic, Asian, and Native American). The theoretical range of Blau's index, based on five categories, is from 0 to 0.8, and all interpretations are limited to the range of the data. The authors report an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.346 for upper-management racial diversity, indicating that aggregating racial diversity according to firms produces important similarity.

Lower-management racial diversity was calculated using Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity at time t, one minus the sum of the squared proportions of each racial category. Five categories of race were used (White, African American, Hispanic, Asian, and Native American). The theoretical range of Blau's index, based on five categories, is from 0 to 0.8, and all interpretations are limited to the range of the data. The authors report an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.229 for lower-management racial diversity.

variable_name: Racial diversity congruence (UMRD-LMRD polynomial terms and response surface)
description: Congruence was examined with polynomial regression in which mean-centered upper-management racial diversity (UMRD) and lower-management racial diversity (LMRD), their squared terms, and their interaction were entered stepwise; a positive UMRD x LMRD interaction together with two negative squared terms indicates congruence. Surface analyses assessed the slope and curvature along the congruence line (UMRD = LMRD), the slope and curvature along the incongruence line (UMRD = -LMRD), and whether the ridge of the response surface (first principal axis) had a slope of 1 and an intercept of 0, with 95% confidence intervals based on 10,000 bootstrapped iterations. For the initial descriptive comparison, firms whose upper- and lower-management racial diversity scores differed by within a radius of 0.04 (within 0.5 SD of upper-management racial diversity) were viewed as congruence examples.
time_window: t (independent variables); dependent variable at t+1

description: Productivity at time t+1, an intermediate measure of organizational effectiveness, was measured as revenue divided by number of employees in thousands of dollars per employee, consistent with previous racial diversity effects research. Since productivity is skewed, the authors used a log transformation of productivity; the authors report that results remain unchanged using the untransformed productivity measure. The dependent variable was lagged so that, for example, 2011 racial diversity data were matched with 2012 firm productivity data.
scale: thousands of dollars per employee, log-transformed

description: Respondents were asked to specify the proportion of their annual disposable income they would be willing to invest in QKD: 'As an early-stage R&D investment decision for the organization, please specify the percentage of your disposable income that you would be willing to commercially invest in bringing QKD to market.' Because the variable was highly right-skewed with some zero values, the authors applied a log transformation, adding 1 to all observations with a value of zero prior to transforming the variable.
scale: percentage of annual disposable income (bounded by 100%)

description: The authors adapted the seven-point scale used by Jeppesen and Lakhani (2010) and asked decision-makers: 'To what degree is QKD as a new technological cybersecurity solution: [1] inside your field of expertise; or [7] outside your field of expertise.' Higher scores indicated a higher degree of expertise distance.
scale: 1 = inside field of expertise to 7 = outside field of expertise

description: Three questions measured the degree to which respondents engaged a high-level construal when evaluating QKD. Decision-makers specified their degree of agreement with the stem 'When considering QKD as a new cybersecurity solution for investment, I think about the technology in terms of:' followed by three items. Cronbach's alpha for this three-item measure is .875.

Three questions measured the degree to which respondents engaged a low-level construal when evaluating QKD. Decision-makers responded to the stem 'When considering QKD as a new cybersecurity solution for investment, I think about the technology in terms of:' followed by three items. Cronbach's alpha for this three-item measure is .766.

Three items used in prior studies measured perceived novelty. Decision-makers were asked 'To what extent do you consider QKD as a new technological cybersecurity solution to be:' followed by three items. Cronbach's alpha for this three-item measure is .901.

Three items used in prior studies measured perceived usefulness. Decision-makers were asked 'To what extent do you consider QKD as a new technological cybersecurity solution to be:' followed by three items. Cronbach's alpha for this three-item measure is .872.

Participants were asked to specify their likelihood of investing in self-driving cars from [1] extremely unlikely to [7] extremely likely, using a measure of investment likelihood that has been used in prior experimental studies rather than asking participants to specify proportions of disposable income.
level: individual participant (assumed role of Senior Executive)

description: Participants in both conditions were told they had prepared notes based on their personal expertise: in the low expertise distance condition notes related to self-driving cars, in the high expertise distance condition generic notes about the taxi industry. They then rated the extent that self-driving cars were 'inside their field of expertise as a Senior Executive' or 'outside their field of expertise as a Senior Executive' on the same seven-point measure used in Study 1. Because levels of reported distance in the high condition fell below the midpoint, the authors collapsed conditions and used the continuous measure of expertise distance in their empirical analyses.
scale: seven-point scale from inside to outside the field of expertise

description: Participants were randomly assigned to a why (high-level) or how (low-level) condition and answered priming questions adapted from Freitas et al. (2004). Participants in the high-level construal condition were asked why they would improve their physical health, go to work, and go on holiday, and provided two additional 'whys' to each response; participants answered a total of nine why or how questions. In the analyses construal level was coded 0 = low-level construal and 1 = high-level construal.

Participants were randomly assigned to a how (low-level) condition in which they were asked how they would perform each of three activities and provided two additional 'hows' to each prior response, answering nine questions in total. The same binary construal level variable was used in the analyses, coded 0 = low-level construal and 1 = high-level construal, so higher values indicate a lower level of low-level construal.

Two items akin to those used in Study 1 measured perceived novelty. Depending on the construal condition, participants were asked 'Thinking about the whys (hows) of self-driving cars, to what extent do you as a Senior Executive view self-driving cars as:' followed by the two items. Cronbach's alpha for this two-item measure is .709.

Two items used in Study 1 measured perceived usefulness. Depending on the construal condition, participants were asked 'Thinking about the whys (hows) of self-driving cars, to what extent do you as a Senior Executive view self-driving cars as:' followed by the two items. Cronbach's alpha for this two-item measure is .811.

A continuous measure of the extent of diversification in four-digit SIC markets, computed from four-digit SIC revenues. The market power and market structure estimates are weighted sum measures: the percentage of a firm's total sales that occurred in each of its individual four-digit markets is multiplied by the value of the variable in that market, and these products are summed over all SIC markets in which the firm participates. The sample was split at the median of this measure because no a priori reasoning pointed to a specific dividing point.

A weighted sum measure of a firm's market power: the firm's share in each four-digit market is weighted by the percentage of the firm's total sales that are in that market, and the products are summed over all SIC markets in which the firm participates. Market indices were weighted averages of the corresponding variables in each of the firm's individual markets, with weights being the fractions of the firm's total sales attributable to each SIC market. The sales data for these measures came from the Establishment Database.

A weighted sum measure of the average profitability of the markets in which a firm competes. The industry profitability data were at the three-digit level and were weighted by the fraction of the firm's total sales in each SIC market, then summed over all markets in which the firm participates. The industry profitability data came from 30,000 Leading U.S. Corporations.

Concentration in a firm's markets, aggregated across the individual markets in which the firm participates as a sales-weighted sum in the same manner as the other market power and market structure estimates. The univariate comparison reported differences in market concentration at the twenty-firm and fifty-firm levels, and concentration also entered the multiple regression. Concentration data came from the Census of Manufacturers, 1972.

Overall firm performance measured as return on invested capital, computed as net income after tax plus interest divided by shareholders' equity plus long-term debt, averaged for each firm. The measure is widely used in strategy and economics research and controls for differences in financial structures across firms. Firm-level measures were taken from annual reports.

Average total firm assets, used as a firm-level control for firm size in the multiple regression model. The measure was taken from annual reports and computed as average total assets across the years covered by the study.

Executive turnover is coded as a dummy variable equal to '1' for a firm where at least one executive or director was fired or resigned in connection with the firm's backdating investigation and '0' otherwise. For each of the firms in the sample, the authors identified executive resignations or firings due to backdating in the firm. In the sample of 141 firms, 44 firms had one or more executive and/or director turnovers in connection with backdating, typically for positions such as chief financial officer, general counsel, vice president, president, chief operating officer, and CEO.

variable_name: firm position in the backdating wave
description: A cumulative count measure created by counting the number of firms that had news of scrutiny for backdating prior to the focal firm's backdating news, based on the date when each firm was first identified in the news as being under scrutiny for backdating. To address endogeneity, the authors estimate a model for firm position in the backdating wave and use the residuals from that model as proxies for firm position in the backdating wave.
scale: count (residual values used in hypothesis tests)
time_window: count of prior firms up to the focal firm's first news date

description: The authors identified 1,300 articles published in nine prominent media outlets during the 2005-2007 period. They counted the number of articles over a 31 day period surrounding the date when each firm was first identified in the news as being under scrutiny (+15, -15 days). This variable ranges between 0 and 151 with a mean of 75 and a standard deviation of 32.
time_window: +15/-15 days around the firm's first news date

description: The amount of additional compensation expense (in millions of U.S. dollars) that the firm should have recorded in prior years in connection with its historical stock option grants, i.e., the pretax additional compensation expense of a firm's backdating. For firms where it was concluded that no backdating actually transpired, or where the amount was not material and therefore did not require a disclosure, the variable has a value of '0'. The measure was log transformed.
time_window: prior years' historical stock option grants

description: A dummy variable coded as '1' if a firm restates its previous financial statements as a result of backdating and '0' otherwise. For the sample, 94 firms (66.7% of the sample) had financial restatements associated with backdating. Data on whether a firm had a financial restatement was gathered from Glass, Lewis & Co.'s (2007) report and confirmed with SEC releases on restatements.

A dummy variable coded as '1' if a firm is under investigation for backdating by the SEC and '0' otherwise. Information on this variable was gathered from the Wall Street Journal options scorecard and Glass, Lewis & Co.'s (2007) report and was confirmed with news releases. For the sample, 112 firms (79.4% of the sample) were under SEC investigation.

A dummy variable coded as '1' if a firm is under investigation for backdating by the DOJ and '0' otherwise. Information on this variable was gathered from the Wall Street Journal options scorecard and Glass, Lewis & Co.'s (2007) report and was confirmed with news releases. For the sample, 63 firms (44.7% of the sample) were under DOJ investigation.

A count of the number of multiplayer modes a game offers at launch, based on whether the game includes local cooperative play, online cooperative play, local competitive play, online competitive play, and cross-platform multiplayer. The count is not weighted because the exact number of players a multiplayer game can accommodate is not observed. The assumption is that games offer greater network functionality when they provide more ways for users to play together via different multiplayer modes.

For each year, a genre's market share is calculated by dividing the sum of downloads for all games released in that genre by the sum of downloads for all games released that year. These market shares are multiplied by the number of yearly new Steam adopters (in millions). The measure is lagged by one year to avoid issues of reverse causality.

A dummy that takes the value of 1 if a game's z-score of standardized download performance is equal to or greater than 1 and 0 otherwise. The z-score is the difference between a game's own cumulative downloads and the mean cumulative downloads of games released in the same year, divided by the standard deviation of downloads of all games released in that year; each year is treated as a separate market. The authors note that 3.58% of all games are coded superstars.
time_window: cumulative downloads, with at least one year to accumulate downloads

description: A dummy variable indicating whether a game operates the freemium business model (1) or is a paid game (0), collected from Steam Spy. In the treatment effects model this variable is the endogenous treatment condition.

Computed with Geographic Information System (ArcGIS) by measuring the shortest Euclidean distance from a mining site's location to the nearest water source (either river or lake) based on GLWD and by extracting the indices of physical water risk in terms of water quantity and water quality, both of which range from 0 to 5, from Aqueduct. Water risk-adjusted proximity is measured as the sum of the two Aqueduct indices of water quantity and water quality divided by the log of Euclidean distance and is standardized. It is an inverse measure of distance, so higher values mean the mine is closer to the water source.

CAR is calculated by summing the abnormal returns (ARs) during an event window. ARs are obtained by subtracting the predicted return from the actual return of a mining company, where normal returns are estimated using stock prices within an estimation window of between 150 days before an event date and 31 days before an event date ([-150, -31]). CAR was computed for 6-day ([-1, +4]) and 2-day ([0, +1]) windows.
A dummy variable indicating whether a mining site is a gold mine based on the primary mineral commodity extracted during mining operations as reported in the SNL Metals & Mining Database.

A dummy variable indicating whether the nearest water source to a mining site is a river (including freshwater marsh, where drinking water is accessible) as opposed to other types of water source, such as lakes and reservoirs, categorized in GLWD.

Measured as the sum of three standardized variables: WGI's Voice and Accountability, Reporters Without Borders' WPFI, which is reverse coded because the raw value of WPFI denotes 0 as the freest and 100 as the least free, and GCI's Judicial Independence. Voice and Accountability is a proxy for mobilizing structure, Judicial Independence is a proxy for political opportunities, and WPFI is a proxy for framing structures.

Log (plus one) of total pounds of the 243 toxic chemicals added to the TRI list in 1995 that the establishment reported as production waste, transfers offsite, and emissions to air, land, water, and underground injection. Lower values represent better environmental performance, so a more negative trend coefficient indicates greater improvement. Values are left-censored when emissions fall below TRI reporting thresholds.

Dichotomous establishment-level variable coded 1 for establishments located in the same city as their headquarters and 0 otherwise. Establishment addresses came from TRI and headquarters addresses from NETS; the variable was fixed at its 1994 value, or its 1993 value if 1994 was missing.

Dichotomous, establishment-level, time-invariant variable coded 1 for establishments with at least one TRI-reporting sibling in the same city in 1994 and 0 otherwise. Sibling identities and addresses came from the NETS database.

variable_name: proximate same-industry sibling / proximate different-industry sibling
description: Two dichotomous establishment-level variables. Proximate same-industry sibling is coded 1 if at least one same-city sibling operated in the same two-digit SIC industry and 0 otherwise. Proximate different-industry sibling is coded 1 if at least one same-city sibling operated in a different two-digit SIC industry and 0 otherwise.

Dichotomous, time-invariant, establishment-level variable coded 1 if the establishment's 1994 employment exceeded the median employment of all TRI-reporting establishments in the same state that year and 0 otherwise. Employment levels came from NETS.

Dichotomous classification of the establishment's city based on the number of TRI-reporting establishments there in 1994. A sparse city had no more TRI-reporting establishments in 1994 than the median number of 10.5 for all U.S. cities that year; a dense city had more TRI-reporting establishments in 1994 than the median city.

Continuous measure defined as the log of the number of TRI-reporting establishments in the focal establishment's city in 1994. It was interacted with the annual counter and large establishment in the full-sample model.

Dichotomous, time-invariant, establishment-level variable coded 1 if, in 1994, an establishment was owned by a publicly traded firm and 0 if owned by a privately owned firm, based on data from the NETS database.

Negative tone scored with the Loughran-McDonald measures of negative tone in the LIWC text analysis software and applied to the top executive's prepared remarks on the earnings call. Where both a CEO and a chair were present (4.5% of cases), their scores were averaged to reflect coordination.

A material positive earnings surprise. Raw earnings surprise was calculated as the percentage increase of actual earnings per share over the mean analyst EPS forecast. Following Pfarrer et al. (2010), 'material' surprises are those in the extreme industry quartile in the past 365 days (the top 25% of all positive surprises) in the same SIC-4 industry.
time_window: past 365 days for the materiality threshold

description: Fiscal quarter split into three levels: a base case of Q2 and Q3 combined, Q1, and Q4. The authors treat the turn of the fiscal year as the expectation-updating occasion, with Q1 and Q4 as the periods in which stakeholders take stock and update expectations and Q2/Q3 as the mid-year comparison.

variable_name: Total on- and off-site TRI releases
description: The total on- and off-site TRI releases reported for a plant by EPA, used as the dependent variable of the model. All TRI values were logged to tone down the effect of extreme observations. The authors used 1997 TRI data since the most recent census data they utilized to construct stakeholder measures were for that year.

Per capita income in the county where a plant was located, used as a proxy for community income and for the heterogeneous capacity of this stakeholder group to influence organizational outcomes. Information on county per capita income was collected from the U.S. Census Bureau's USA Counties 1998 database.

Population density in the county where a plant was located, measured as the number of county inhabitants per square mile. Information on county population density was collected from USA Counties 1998.

Community pressures associated with community environmental preferences were measured as the number of paying members of major, national U.S. environmental and conservation organizations (organizations with annual budgets exceeding $1 million or memberships exceeding 2,000) per 1,000 state residents. Andrews (1994) provided this information.

This variable captures the percentage of times a member of the U.S. House of Representatives voted for an environmental measure, taken from the scorecards of the League of Conservation Voters. Congressional district boundaries were obtained from the National Atlas of the United States and the Web site of the U.S. House of Representatives, and each district and representative's voting record were matched to the counties they represented and the plants located in those counties. Where counties were split between congressional districts, the average voting record was used.

Calculated as the ratio of total state environmental budget relative to total state budget, in order to capture the priority assigned to environmental issues. Data on environmental and total state budgets were obtained from the Council of State Governments.

Measured as the ratio of state environmental agency employment to the total number of state employees, intended to capture a state's long-term commitment to environmental protection and its institutional capacity. Data on state environmental agency employees were obtained from the Environmental Council of the States, and state government employment data from the U.S. Census Bureau's annual survey of government employment.

variable_name: Plurality group (hats held and hats added)
description: Announcements are grouped by the number of top titles the executive held before the announcement and the number of titles added: have one title and add one, have one and add two, have two and add one, and have no hats and add two or three. Only the first Wall Street Journal announcement in which an executive assumed more than one title is considered; announcements in which an executive assumed only one hat, or received a new hat but dropped the old one, are excluded. Binary variables represent each plurality group in the cross-sectional regressions, where they are also multiplied by each control variable to form interaction terms.

Market model parameters are estimated over the interval -121 to -21 days relative to the announcement day (day 0) and applied to actual returns around day 0 to obtain normal returns; the difference between actual and normal returns is the prediction error, and prediction errors are summed and averaged across sample firms for various event intervals to produce the MCPE. The cross-sectional regressions use each firm's MCPE for the interval -5 to +1 as the dependent variable, regressed against the plurality group indicators and their interactions with the control variables, with t-tests for the significance of each coefficient.
time_window: event windows around day 0 (e.g., -5 to +1 and -5 to +5 days); estimation period -121 to -21 days

description: For each contact in their network, respondents evaluated four items capturing different aspects of successful knowledge acquisition on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Factor analysis revealed that the items loaded on a single factor, and Cronbach's alpha for the four items was 0.85. The authors calculated the mean of the four items to define the level of successful knowledge acquisition, measured from the point of view of the knowledge recipient.
scale: five-point Likert scale, 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree

description: Each team, laboratory, and technological road map was assumed to represent a distinct stock of knowledge and expertise, and a cross-unit transfer was defined in terms of the number of organizational units it spanned. The authors created indicator variables for the three types of knowledge transfer relationships that cut across at least one organizational unit; if the relationship spanned one boundary the one unit indicator was set equal to 1, if it spanned two boundaries the two units indicator was set equal to 1, and if it spanned all three boundaries the three units indicator was set equal to 1, each remaining 0 otherwise. Within-unit transfers, in which the two individuals shared membership in all three types of units, were the reference category.

Each respondent described the strength of his or her relationship with each cited contact; tie strength was measured in terms of communication frequency, which ranged from 1 (rarely) to 5 (very frequently), and the qualitative response categories were given quantitative values using log-linear multiplicative models, with no communication assigned a value of 0 and very frequent communication assigned a value of 1. Following prior research, the authors measured tie strength as the proportion of available network time and energy a respondent allocated to a focal contact: every relationship in a respondent's network was first divided by 2, the strongest relationship a respondent could have had, and the marginal strength relationships were then divided by the total amount of network time available to the individual. The formulas for these transformations are not readable in the available text.
scale: communication frequency from 1 (rarely) to 5 (very frequently), transformed into network proportions

description: To capture the extent to which a knowledge sharing relationship was embedded in a dense web of third-party ties, the authors used Burt's measure of indirect structural constraint, which assigns higher scores to interactions that were surrounded by strong third-party ties. In the specification, p_iq reflects the proportion of i's network time devoted to colleague q and p_qj reflects the proportion of q's network time allocated to contact j; the resulting term c_ij indicates the extent to which i and j's relationship was surrounded by relatively strong third-party ties. The formula itself is not readable in the available text.

Network range was measured with information centrality, computed using UCINET VI. Like closeness centrality, information centrality is a function of the path distance (i.e., geodesic) between any two actors; unlike closeness centrality, however, which gives maximum weight to the shortest path between two actors, information centrality considers all paths and assigns greater weights to shorter paths. Individuals who were high on information centrality were connected to nonequivalent contacts in the knowledge transfer network and were therefore more likely to be exposed to nonredundant knowledge and information.

Degree of reorganization counts the number of unit boundary changes that occur in a firm within a time period. If two units are combined, both are reorganized in some way and this is counted as two reorganization events; if a unit is split into two newly created units and loses its original identity, this also counts as two; if a unit loses part of itself to another existing unit, both units are changed and this counts as two. The authors describe the operationalization as charting all units across time with arrows indicating unit changes and counting the number of arrows within a period. No arrows are drawn for a unit acquisition or divestiture at time t, but if an acquired unit is structurally changed in a subsequent period, arrows are drawn and this is measured as reorganization.
time_window: lagged one time period (t - 1) and two time periods (t - 2)

description: Degree of innovation is a count variable calculated as the number of entries (via internal innovation, not acquisition) into new product markets by the firm within a time period. Innovations are observed at the product level and are radical, i.e., internal entry into new product markets; incremental innovations, changes within existing product lines, are not addressed.
time_window: period t (the period following the lagged reorganization measures)

description: Cluster membership derived from Ward's minimum-variance cluster analysis of the four standardized strategy variables. The cluster consists of brands demonstrating low-end product position, low prices, limited product range, but broad market focus.

Cluster membership derived from Ward's minimum-variance cluster analysis of the four standardized strategy variables. The pattern of scores shows these brands pursuing a broad market focus with a wide range of products, differentiating with high-end brand appeal at medium prices.

Cluster membership derived from Ward's minimum-variance cluster analysis of the four standardized strategy variables. The emphasis for this cluster is on a narrow product range and narrow market focus, while offering high-end, high-price specialty products.

Target focus was measured by three items centering on the number of potential customers, the spectrum of customers, and the degree to which a niche strategy was pursued. Coefficient alpha was 0.73 for the scale. One target focus item was removed following exploratory factor analysis.

Product range was measured by an index rather than a scale. Respondents were asked to indicate which of eight speaker categories were sold by their firms; a high number of product subcategories indicated a manufacturer's effort to serve a wide range of customer segments.
Four items comprised the scale, centering on relative level of technology, design advantages, and performance of the brand from low-end to high-end. Coefficient alpha was 0.88.
Product pricing, i.e., the brand's pricing strategy relative to its competitors, was measured by a single item.

The three items comprising the scale focused on the level of effort by the manufacturer in monitoring distributors' conformance to specific behavioral standards. One of the items was reverse coded. Coefficient alpha for this scale was 0.65, exceeding the acceptable level of 0.60.

Contractual restrictions were measured with a six-item index. Manufacturers first indicated whether or not they had a formal agreement with distributors. They then identified which distribution activities were addressed in the agreement.

A six-item index was used to measure manufacturer coordination effort. Manufacturers were asked to indicate the extent to which they attempted to coordinate five distributor activities (e.g., implementation of sales promotions, dealer service standards). Higher scores on the index indicated greater effort to coordinate across the six activities.

Manufacturer support was measured by a five-item index. Managers were first asked to indicate if each type of assistance was provided; if so, they rated the assistance on its relative importance in contributing to dealer satisfaction.

Three items were used to measure this construct. Two items related directly to the number of distributors used per trade area. The third asked about the firm's distribution pattern relative to competitors, ranging from exclusive to intensive. Coefficient alpha for the scale was 0.79.

Formative construct computed as the weighted sum of two component variables, reaching out to new alters and establishing interpersonal knowledge of new alters, with weights of 30% and 70% respectively identified through a grid search over parameter values. The component variables were measured with validated scales developed using established techniques and administered to the panel of entrepreneurs during the initial face-to-face meetings. Respondents rated how frequently they engaged in the itemized actions during the previous 12 months on a response scale of 1 to 7; for these two variables respondents were asked to think about new people not yet part of their personal network.
time_window: previous 12 months, reported at the initial face-to-face meeting

description: Formative construct computed as the weighted sum of three component variables, time-based interaction pacing, relational embedding, and network preserving, with weights of 30%, 50%, and 20% respectively identified through a grid search over parameter values. The component variables were measured with validated scales administered to the panel of entrepreneurs during the initial face-to-face meetings. Respondents rated how frequently they engaged in the itemized actions during the previous 12 months on a response scale of 1 to 7; for these variables respondents were asked to think about people who were already part of their personal network.
time_window: previous 12 months, reported at the initial face-to-face meeting

description: Coded in three steps. First, from the business cards (or Excel files) of new interpersonal contacts a list of the organizations they represented was drawn up, merging organizations identified as different business units of the same parent organization. Second, from the Web survey, organizations that did not have an existing relationship with the focal venture yet were reported as a potential exchange partner (a potential customer, alliance partner, or supplier) were coded as 'new' organizations. Third, a focal new organization was coded as accessed through a referral if at least one of the new contacts representing it was accessed through a referral and the referee was an existing network contact not employed by the focal venture. The variable was then calculated as the ratio of potential exchange partner organizations accessed through a referral to the total number of potential exchange partner organizations accessed during the two-month period.

The initiation (or not) of an economic exchange relationship between the focal entrepreneur's venture and the organizations targeted in Phase I, collected during a face-to-face meeting 12 months after Phase I ended. Coded as the count of new interfirm exchange ties initiated between the focal venture and the target organizations (potential customers, alliance partners, and/or suppliers). In all cases the relevant documents providing objective evidence of an interfirm exchange relationship were physically inspected.
time_window: 12 months following the end of Phase I

description: Networking actions are measured as two formative constructs, each a weighted sum of component networking variables from validated scales: network-broadening (reaching out to new alters, establishing interpersonal knowledge, weights 30% and 70%) and network-deepening (three further variables). Both are entered as separate predictors.

One of three between-subjects priming conditions (control, prototype-based, goal-based). In the goal-based group participants were asked, 'How do you think a financial product could help an entrepreneur achieve his/her strategic goals?', which focused them on a goal instead of on fit with a prototype.

One of three between-subjects priming conditions (control, prototype-based, goal-based) applied immediately before evaluation. In the goal-based group participants were asked, 'How do you think a mobile device could help you watching movies on the go?', focusing them on a goal rather than on a prototype.

One of three between-subjects priming conditions. In the prototype-based group participants were asked, 'Could you describe what you would expect from a traditional loan?', which ensured they focused on fit with a prototype; the control group evaluated the loan without any priming.

One of three between-subjects priming conditions. In the prototype-based group participants were asked, 'Could you describe what you would expect from a traditional mobile phone?', focusing them on fit with a prototype; the control group received no priming.

The loan was described along five attributes, consistent with the description used by Public Bank. In the high-ambiguity condition ambiguity was increased by connecting unrelated specificities with the operators 'and' and 'or' (for example 'fixed or floating rate' versus 'fixed rate'), which decreased the typicality of the offering. Both descriptions were similar in size by number of lines and word count.

variable_name: level of ambiguity (low versus high) via one unclear attribute
description: Each offering presented five product attributes and only one attribute was manipulated, holding the other attributes constant. In the low-ambiguity condition the offering had '4G surfing speed (6 GHz), perfect for optimal web browsing'; in the high-ambiguity condition it had '4G surfing speed with floating capacity of plus or minus 3 to 9 GHz'. The manipulated attribute was chosen so that it was at least minimally relevant to the primed goal.

Participants were asked to evaluate the loan on a 10-point scale from 'I do not like it at all' (0) to 'I like it very much' (9). Across conditions evaluation had a mean of 5.92 (SD = 1.93), and this evaluation score was the dependent variable in the ANOVAs.

variable_name: evaluation (combined likability and perceived market success)
description: Participants evaluated the offering on a 10-point scale from 'I do not like it at all' (0) to 'I like it very much' (9) and also rated whether they thought the offering would be successful, from 'not at all' (0) to 'absolutely' (9). Evaluation is the average of the likability score and the perceived market success score (r = 0.80, p < 0.01), with a mean of 6.83 (SD = 1.56).

variable_name: perceived utility of the unclear attribute
description: After evaluating the offering, participants rated the utility of each attribute presented ('How would you rate the utility of the following feature?') on a 10-point scale from 'not useful at all' (0) to 'very useful' (9). The perceived utility of the unclear attribute is the rating of the manipulated attribute ('4G surfing speed with floating capacity of plus or minus 3 to 9 GHz'); a separate score averages the four clear attributes held constant across ambiguity conditions.

Following factor analysis, items with low loadings or high cross-loadings were dropped, leaving two items asking whether IT had enhanced (1) existing products or services and (2) existing business processes between 2001 and 2003. Responses were measured on a seven-point Likert scale in which 1 represents that the firm never uses IT in this manner and 7 that it frequently uses IT in this manner. The measure is the arithmetic average of the two items, with a Cronbach alpha of 0.897.

Four survey items measuring the respondent's perception of how the firm used IT to enable new capabilities between 2001 and 2003: to develop new products or services; to implement new business processes; to create new customer relationships; and to change ways of doing business. Responses were measured on a seven-point Likert scale in which 1 represents that the firm never uses IT in this manner and 7 that it frequently uses IT in this manner. The measure is the arithmetic average of the four items, with a Cronbach alpha of 0.893.

A survey question asking respondents to evaluate how the firm expected its competitive environment to change over the next five years, with response options (1) less competitive, (2) similar level of competitiveness, or (3) more competitive. The measure compares the firm's response to its industry group's average response for this item, so that it represents the ratio of the firm to its industry group average. This measures whether the firm expects its operating environment to be more or less dynamic.
scale: 3 response options (1 = less competitive, 2 = similar, 3 = more competitive)

description: Heterogeneity is observed through greater levels of capability efficiency: the greater the efficiency of the capability, the greater the expected heterogeneity of the capability relative to capabilities in other firms. The measure takes the extent of change in each of four business processes (product and service quality assurance, human resources system, technological base, and marketing program) divided by the firm's level of ordinary capability usage, and compares this ratio to the industry group average for each process. A large ratio indicates that the firm achieved more change than its industry group given the level of capability usage; a small ratio indicates it achieved less. The formulas stated for these calculations are not readable in the available text.
time_window: change over the prior three years (2001-2003)

description: Built in the same way as ordinary capability heterogeneity, the measure takes the extent of change in each of the four business processes of the firm divided by the level of dynamic capability usage in the firm, and compares this ratio to the industry group average for each of the four process areas. A large ratio indicates that the firm achieved more change than its industry group given its level of dynamic capability usage, indicating a higher degree of heterogeneity. The formulas stated for these calculations are not readable in the available text.
time_window: change over the prior three years (2001-2003)

description: Respondents were asked how 'the use of IT and its related organizational changes in the last three years has impacted' productivity, business process performance, and quality of products or services. Responses were measured on a seven-point Likert scale in which a low score (1) represents a significant decrease, a moderate score (4) no impact, and a high score (7) a significant increase in performance across the items, and the three items have a Cronbach alpha of 0.897. The measure is the arithmetic average of the three items, divided by the industry average (manufacturing, service, or other) for that firm from within the sample.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = significant decrease, 4 = no impact, 7 = significant increase)

description: Respondents indicated their firm's profits as a percentage of sales for 2003 by choosing one of five profitability/sales ranges (< 0%, 0%, 0 to 5%, 5 to 15%, and > 15%); ranges rather than actual numbers were requested because fieldwork indicated managers did not want to provide specific numbers. Responses were coded using the mid-point of each range (-5%, 0%, 2.5%, 10%, and 20%), with the open-ended extremes set at -5 percent and 20 percent, so raw responses ranged from -5 percent to +20 percent, with a mean of 8.59 percent. The measure was divided by the firm's dominant industry group (manufacturing, service, or other) average for this measure to calculate a measure of relative firm performance.

Hospitals were grouped along three form measures using a two-stage cluster analysis (Ward's minimum variance method followed by an iterative partitioning procedure) that classified the sample into Prospectors, Defenders, Analyzers, and Reactors. Costs (COSTS) is a composite of three standardized cost measures: total expenses divided by the average number of occupied beds, cost per adjusted patient day, and salary per adjusted patient day. Services offered (SO) is the average number of services offered, divided by the log of organizational size measured by total revenues. Operating slack (OS) is the ratio of employees per adjusted patient day. The classification was performed on form measures averaged over 1981-83 and repeated to determine each hospital's form after the environmental shift.
time_window: 1981-83 averaged for the pre-shift classification; repeated after the environmental shift

description: A composite performance measure was generated with five indicators: total margin (TM), operating margin (OM), total revenue relative to adjusted patient days (TR), the ratio of net operating revenue to the total number of beds (NOR), and percent occupancy (OCC). The five measures were standardized (mean = 0, standard deviation = 1) and summed to yield a composite measure of prior performance (PERFB4) and outcome performance (PERFAFT). Average values of each performance measure over the years 1981-83 and 1988-90 were used, and each organization's scores were adjusted for time trends by subtracting the sample mean for each measure.

Each hospital's strategic form before the environmental shift was compared with its strategic form after the shift to identify which hospitals changed form and the alternative form to which they changed. For example, a hospital classified as a Defender before the environmental shift and an Analyzer afterwards was considered as changing its form, a between-form response. Hospitals classified in the same form in both periods were treated as making within-form responses instead.
time_window: form before the 1983 environmental shift versus form after the shift

description: Within-form organizational responses were examined as changes in the same three variables used to classify organizational form: costs (CHGCOSTS), services offered (CHGSO), and operating slack (CHGOS). Changes for each organization were measured in the years 1984 and 1988, so difference scores could be used to measure organizational responses to the environmental event. Each variable was adjusted for time trends by subtracting the sample mean for each year from each organization's score in that year, and response scores were derived by subtracting the adjusted 1984 values from the adjusted 1988 values.

variable_name: form change patterns (movements between strategic forms)
description: The movements between strategic forms over the time of the environmental shift were tabulated, showing for each hospital its form before the shift and its form after the shift. The tabulation reports how many Analyzers, Prospectors, Defenders, and Reactors were present before and after the environmental shift.
time_window: before versus after the 1983 environmental shift

description: Plant capacity measured relative to the owning firm's average plant capacity. Capacity is used because direct efficiency measures are not available and because larger plants have cost advantages and are relatively young. The variable is observed at the beginning of year t, except for plants commissioned or acquired during the period, for which it is defined at the time of commissioning or acquisition.

Plant capacity measured relative to the average of all plants of a corresponding clay type (fletton or non-fletton) operating within the region. Using CAP FIRM and CAP IND the authors define a closure program as efficient at the industry level if the closures involve plants that are small relative to the industry average.

Dummy variable indicating whether the aesthetic appearance of the brick is of low quality. Plant output was graded for aesthetic quality (A for bricks with an inherent beauty in terms of colour and texture, B for less handsome bricks, C for more utilitarian bricks, with the final classifications shown to production directors for corroboration).
Dummy variable indicating whether the aesthetic appearance of the brick is of high quality, defined alongside ASTHLOW to test the role of quality in determining the closure programs.

The regional Herfindahl index, used as the measure of the level of competition. When a plant is located adjacent to an efficient road network giving easy access to the major metropolises of neighbouring regions, the plant is classified as competing in each of those regions.

The log absolute value of any decrease in capacity undertaken by rival firms in the same region during the previous year. The authors treat the positive coefficient on this variable as evidence that closures follow a reduction in capacity by local rivals, i.e. a relaxation of competitive pressure.

The firm's regional operational capacity at the beginning of the period as a proportion of the total capacity of plants within range of that region. Plants located adjacent to an efficient road network may be treated as players in each of the neighbouring regions they can easily supply. The shares are computed among firms included in the sample, which excludes a number of very small firms supplying specialist markets.

Dummy variable that signifies whether the plant is owned by a firm involved in an acquisition; it combines plants owned by the acquiring firm prior to the acquisition and plants acquired in the acquisition. It is used both on its own and interacted with SHARE.
Time dummies for each year in which a major acquisition took place (1992, 1995 and 1996), included to test for a general industry-wide effect of acquisitions on plant closures.

Dummy variable that takes the value one during the year of acquisition for plants owned by an acquiring firm prior to the acquisition. A positive coefficient for this dummy would indicate that the acquiring firm carries out a disproportionate number of plant closures.

Dummy variable that takes the value one during the year of acquisition for plants newly acquired in that acquisition. A positive coefficient for this dummy would indicate that the acquiring firm carries out a disproportionate number of plant closures.

Dummy variable that takes the value one if the plant is located in a rural or village setting, used to test the employee loyalty hypothesis about the reluctance of firms to close geographically isolated plants because of poor alternative job opportunities.

Dummy variable that takes the value one if the plant is located near (within travel to work distance) plants owned by the same firm, because staff can then be relocated or offered employment at the remaining site, which makes employee loyalty less of an obstacle to closure.

Dummy variable that takes the value of one for plants owned by a diversified firm that does not manufacture bricks as its core business. The variable is not included in the logit regressions to avoid perfect colinearity with firm fixed effects.

Dichotomous dependent variable for each plant-year that is zero if the plant is open throughout the year and one if it is closed during the year; otherwise the plant does not appear in the dataset. The independent variables are observed at the beginning of year t.

Based on the number of patent attorneys that left the law firms used by buyer firm i in year t - 1. Because the focal buyer's supplier portfolio as a whole is examined, a weighted average is calculated based on the strength of the relationship with each law firm in the portfolio. The weights are the average share of the focal buyer's outsourced patents prosecuted by each law firm over the past 3 years, t - 1 to t - 3.
time_window: t - 1 (weights based on t - 1 to t - 3)

description: The percentage of patent applications filed using an in-house attorney by buyer i in year t. It is based on the 'Attorney/Agent' field of the application document, and for cases where this was missing the granted patent was relied upon. Roughly 1% of patents did not list attorney information in both documents and were excluded; where an individual attorney was listed, the attorney's address was checked against corporate addresses to distinguish in-house lawyers.
Calculated as the natural log of one plus the average number of patent attorneys working at buyer firm i in years t - 1 and t - 2.

All patents filed in year t - 1 on behalf of buyer firm i by law firms that suffered employee losses in year t - 1 are isolated and a list of all primary patent classes is created. The variable is the percentage of those classes that were also listed as primary patent class in patents prosecuted by in-house attorneys during years t - 1 to t - 3. It is set to missing when there are no supplier employee losses.

The weighted average of the within-portfolio supplier employee losses - patent attorneys that left the law firms used by buyer firm i to join other competing law firms also used by buyer firm i in year t - 1 - divided by the weighted average of all supplier employee losses, using the same weights as for Supplier employee losses. It is set to missing when there are no supplier employee losses.

The list of primary patent classes is generated for patents filed by law firms with employee losses in year t - 1, and the variable is the percentage of those patent classes that were also listed as primary patent classes in patents prosecuted by the remaining law firms used in the same year (those not experiencing employee losses) during years t - 1 to t - 3. It is set to missing when there are no supplier employee losses.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two pitch decks that differed only in the content of the product slide. In the concrete condition the wearable sensor was described in terms of how to use it (for example, 'Select your TrackMee model and buy it on its website'); in the abstract condition it was described in terms of why to consider it (for example, 'To train like an elite professional and maximize your training effectiveness').

The same material and procedure as in Study 1 was used: participants were randomly assigned to one of two pitch decks whose product slide framed the wearable sensor in concrete how terms or in abstract why terms.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two short narratives of the lamp idea (SunLamp). The concrete framing explained how to use SunLamp (for example, 'Place the lamp on a table or nightstand, and connect it to a plug'), while the abstract framing focused on why to use SunLamp (for example, 'Natural light improves productivity and concentration during the day').
The same manipulation of the short narrative was used as in Study 3: the concrete framing explained how to use SunLamp, while the abstract framing focused on why to use SunLamp.

Novices were participants recruited via the online platform Prolific; prior research on entrepreneurial pitching treats such participants as representative of everyday citizens. They are audience members who have not developed domain-relevant expertise in evaluating novel ideas.

Experts were professional investors recruited by email through the network of three centers for entrepreneurship; 61% identified themselves as angel investors, 27.1% as venture capitalists and 11.9% as angel investors and venture capitalists. They had an average work experience of 23.81 years and had made, on average, 31 investments.

Novices were participants recruited online through Amazon's Mechanical Turk, a group used in entrepreneurial research as 'amateur crowds'; they are audience members who are not used to the novel idea evaluative task.

Experts were current and former students of an Executive MBA program in innovation management; given their occupational position, all participants had a high level of expertise in idea evaluation across a variety of industries, with roles ranging from head of innovation to chief innovation officer to innovation portfolio manager.

The attractiveness of the idea was measured by asking participants how much they liked the idea on a 7-point scale (1 = 'I liked it very much', 7 = 'I disliked it very much'), with the coding reversed so that higher values correspond to greater liking, and by their likelihood to further consider the business opportunity, captured with three items on a 7-point scale (1 = 'Not at all', 7 = 'Extremely'). The three items were averaged into a single score and combined with the idea liking measure into a summative indicator.
scale: summative indicator combining a reverse-coded 7-point liking item and the average of three 7-point items

description: The dependent variable was measured in the same way as in Study 1: idea liking on a reverse-coded 7-point scale combined with the average of three 7-point items on the likelihood of further considering the business opportunity, into a summative indicator of the attractiveness of the idea.
scale: summative indicator combining a reverse-coded 7-point liking item and the average of three 7-point items

description: To capture actual support for the entrepreneurial idea, participants were given a bonus payment of 10 cents and asked how much of it they would like to donate to support the development of SunLamp. Participants reported their choice on a sliding scale ranging from 0 to 10 cents.

Willingness to invest in the idea was measured by asking participants to imagine they were an investor with 20,000 euros that they could invest in SunLamp and to indicate how much of the 20,000 euros they would invest in the idea. Participants answered using a sliding scale ranging from 0 to 20,000 euros.

Participants rated the usefulness of the idea on a 7-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely) using four items adapted from the Creative Product Semantic Scale. The items were averaged into a single index.

As in Study 3, participants rated the usefulness of the idea on a 7-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely) using four items adapted from the Creative Product Semantic Scale. The items were averaged into a single index.

Probability that an individual in a given three-digit census occupation and two-digit NAICS industry cell stays in the same industry over a four-month period, multiplied by 100. It is estimated from the longitudinal structure of the merged monthly CPS, and only occupation-industry combinations with at least 500 observations in the underlying CPS data are included. The authors interpret a higher probability of staying in the industry as indicating more limited transferability of skills across industries.
level: three-digit census occupation by two-digit NAICS industry cell

description: Measure of the strength of state noncompete enforceability taken from Starr (2018), which refines the measure used by Bishara (2011) by using factor analysis on seven scores to generate less subjective weights. The scores are standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one in a sample where each state has the same weight. The 1991 scores are associated with the SIPP data from 1996 and 2001, and the 2009 scores with the SIPP data from 2004 and 2008.
The employee's reported tenure, in months, with the employer, constructed from the individual-level data in the SIPP.
The number of months between when the individual reports finishing his or her highest degree of education and when being hired into the job, calculated from SIPP individual-level data.

Indicator equal to one if the respondent reports that the firm paid for the most recent training event, among the SIPP training questions asked of those who received skill-improving training in the last year.

Indicator variables equal to one if the respondent indicated that the most recent training event included training in new skills or training that upgraded existing skills; the combined indicator equals one if either type was included. Examples given by the SIPP for new specific work skills are how to use equipment, machinery, or technical procedures, and no examples are provided for upgrading skills.

Indicator variables equal to one if the respondent indicated that the most recent training event included basic skills training or training in company policies; the combined indicator equals one if either type was included. The SIPP examples for basic skills are office software, work habits, or management practices, and for company policies guidelines or requirements.
The log of hourly wages, obtained by dividing the respondent's reported monthly earnings by the product of reported hours worked per week and 4.33 (since there are 4.33 weeks in a month).

A count of the unique occupations in an organization, used to measure the knowledge scope of an organization. Occupations are identified from Brazil's occupational code system. The authors note it is the first use of the count of occupations as a measure of knowledge scope. The variable is lagged by one quarter in the survival model.

Binary variable capturing the addition of a management layer, defined as hiring at least one employee from the manager level. Employees at the executive or manager level employed on the firm's first day ('founder-managers') are excluded from the measure. The authors assume all firms have at least one top manager from birth.

The extent to which two occupations require similar tasks, calculated as the cosine similarity of their tasks using O*NET task data at the level of intermediate work activities; it equals 1 when two occupations have identical tasks and 0 when they have no common tasks. The firm-level measure is the mean task similarity across all possible pairs of employees. Brazilian occupations are matched to O*NET using a crosswalk.

The size of the largest, multi-employee connected component of employees in the shared experience network divided by team size. Connections are identified from all instances in which employees previously worked for another firm in the same establishment, occupation, and year; the connected component is the largest set of employees who can be linked by shared work experience at one or more firms.
time_window: lagged one quarter; employment history back to 1992

description: Alternative knowledge scope measure using the coarser 4-digit occupational families instead of 6-digit occupation codes. Reported in Online Appendix B as a robustness check.

Constructed from the cost efficiencies calculated in the Stage 1 model: the average log cost of firms in state s other than firm i, multiplied by -1, so that a larger value represents more external knowledge. Cost is used as a proxy for knowledge itself, viewing cost as an outcome of employing knowledge in production, C = f1(K), so that knowledge is the functional inverse K = f1^-1(C).
The cumulative number of quarters in which a bank has competed in the market. A firm's experience is represented as x i1 t = ln(t + 1) so that at time 0 a firm has no experience.

A problem is defined as occurring if loan output dropped for two consecutive quarters. This measure reflects a problem that arises when performance is assessed relative to a firm's own past performance.

A dummy indicating whether the bank is a new commercial banking institution. Banks that entered within the years 1984-1997 are considered entrants; incumbents are those firms founded prior to 1975. The data are split into entrant and incumbent subsamples.

The expected value of firm-quarter cost efficiency from the Stage 1 stochastic cost frontier, E[uit | eit], reflecting the log of firm i's costs relative to a firm on the cost frontier. Lower values correspond to increased efficiency. It is used as the Stage 2 dependent variable after transformation with the monotonic function g(ui1t) = ln(e^ui1t - 1).

variable_name: k i1 t (external knowledge) term in Equation (8)
description: The coefficient of vicarious learning unaided by experiential learning, k, estimated from the external knowledge term ki1t in the cost model of Equation (8), which controls for time-varying firm- and market-level attributes.

The dependent variable is the logarithm of the net flow of money to a fund at time t. The net flow of money is calculated for each mutual fund for each three-month period using data on net asset values and return at fund level from MoneyMate (Sweden). The specification involves the fund's total net assets at time t and at time t-1 and the fund's rate of return at time t, but the equation itself is not readable in the text.

Total fee was constructed using data on management, entry, and exit fees. One-sixth of the entry fee and one-sixth of the exit fee were added to the management fee, based on the assumption that a consumer on average holds a fund for six years. The variable was mean-centered before the interaction with negative fee articles was constructed, because of near multicollinearity.

The authors constructed a variable of the quarterly count of articles with negative coverage of mutual fund fees. Articles were content coded from a data set of business press articles on mutual funds; coverage was considered negative if the articles reported that mutual fund fees are too high or explicitly told the reader to consider mutual funds with lower fees. In the models the variable enters lagged, referred to as the lagged logarithm of the negative media articles about mutual fund fees, and it was mean-centered before the interaction was constructed.
time_window: quarterly, lagged one period, 1992-2005 article set

description: The authors split the sample of funds into those sponsored by banks and those that are not, and estimated separate models for each group. In the Swedish market the four nationwide retail banks controlled close to 90% of the assets under management at the outset. The authors report that a comparison of the standard deviations of the total fees for bank and non-bank funds shows no discernible difference between the two groups.

Measured by reverse coding firm performance at Year 0, the year when the firm entered its turnaround situation. The worse the ROE (or market-to-book ratio, to correspond to the measures of subsequent performance), the more severe the performance crisis. The variable also served to control for regression to the mean.

An industry was identified as struggling if its median ROE-COE spread was negative during all the Years -2, -1, and 0, a three-year period used to ensure that industry problems were not temporary. Among struggling industries, industry median performance at Year 0 was reverse coded to measure severity. Firms in nonstruggling industries were given industry performance severity scores of 0. All indicators of industry performance were based on all the firms in the three-digit industry in COMPUSTAT, not just those in the sample.

Dummy variable coded as 1 if the firm replaced its CEO in Years 0 and +1, and 0 otherwise. Replacements were identified using the Execucomp and Factiva databases. In the sample of 223 firms, 98 replacements occurred during Years 0 and +1, an annual rate of 22%.
scale: 1 = CEO replaced in Year 0 or Year +1; 0 otherwise

description: The number of years the incumbent had been CEO in the focal firm. Data on employment histories were drawn from proxy statements, Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management, Capital IQ, and Standard and Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors, and Executives.
The number of years the incumbent CEO had worked in the focal firm's primary industry (three-digit SIC). Based on executive employment history data.

Dummy variable coded as 1 if the incumbent's primary function was not throughput oriented, and 0 otherwise. A CEO's primary functional background was that in which he or she had the longest employment history, categorized as output (marketing, sales, and product development), throughput (operations, engineering, and accounting), or other (law, consulting, finance, general management).
scale: 1 = primary function not throughput oriented; 0 otherwise

description: Dummy variable coded as 1 if the new CEO had less than two years' tenure in the firm, and 0 otherwise.
scale: 1 = less than two years' tenure in the firm; 0 otherwise

description: Dummy variable coded as 1 if the successor CEO's primary function was throughput-oriented, and 0 otherwise. Primary functional background is the function in which the executive had the longest employment history, categorized as output (marketing, sales, product development), throughput (operations, engineering, accounting), or other (law, consulting, finance, general management).
scale: 1 = successor's primary function throughput oriented; 0 otherwise

description: Dummy variable coded as 1 if the new CEO was hired from a different industry (three-digit SIC), and 0 otherwise.
scale: 1 = hired from a different three-digit SIC industry; 0 otherwise

description: Accounting-based indicator of subsequent performance: operating return on equity before extraordinary items, examined at Years +2, +3, and +4, where Year 0 is the year of initial losses. Each firm contributes three observations.
Market-based indicator of subsequent performance, measured at Years +2, +3, and +4, where Year 0 is the year of initial losses.

Policy risk for host country j in year t, defined in the main specification as POLRISKjt = 1 - POLCONjt.
