POLCON reflects the extent to which the formal relationships among a country's branches of government (executive, legislative, and judicial) and the partisan composition of the individual actors inhabiting these branches constrain any one institutional actor from unilaterally effecting a change in policy. A POLCON value of 0 reflects the absence of effective veto players and thus a complete concentration of policy-making authority; each additional institutional veto player has a positive but diminishing effect on POLCON's value, whose theoretical maximum is 1.

Binary measure that takes a value of 1 if firm k from home country i invested in a new generation facility (i.e., a facility in which it had not previously invested) in country j in year t, and 0 otherwise. Each firm investment year consists of multiple records, each representing a potential investment choice, that is, a host country that was open to FDI in electricity generation that year.

For a firm from home country i as of year t, defined as POLRISKit = 1 - POLCONit, and included both by itself and in a multiplicative interaction term with host-country policy risk. A three-year moving average was used to reflect a firm's recent home-country experience. Higher values indicate weaker home-country institutional constraints.
time_window: three-year moving average ending in year t

description: A firm's time-varying home-country Gini coefficient, a commonly used measure of income dispersion that ranges from a theoretical minimum of 0, indicating perfect income equality among the residents of a country, to a theoretical maximum of 1, indicating the possession of all national wealth by a single individual. Coefficients come from the World Bank's 'World Development Indicators' database; because they are reported at irregular intervals that vary by country, missing annual values were interpolated, and in the main specification the annual home-country Gini coefficients were averaged over a three-year moving window.
time_window: three-year moving average ending in year t

description: A measure of a firm's home-country ethnolinguistic fractionalization level. The ELF index measures the probability that two randomly selected people from a given country do not belong to the same ethnolinguistic group. It was originally developed by a team of researchers at the Miklukho-Maklai Ethnological Institute in the Soviet Union and subsequently adopted by Easterly and Levine (1997) and others.

Total number of new product technologies (belonging to a specific technological system) imitated by the focal firm within the year t. A product technology is coded as imitated when the firm adopts for the first time, in one of its new handset models, a technology previously introduced by the pioneer, and only technologies not yet installed in more than 50% of all products launched in the market are counted.

variable_name: Focal firm's average speed of imitation
description: Time to imitation in months was first computed for each technology imitated by the firm in year t, then normalized by dividing it by the maximum imitation time for that technology in the sample, transforming the variable from a count to a ratio; finally the mean of the firm's normalized imitation timing of technologies belonging to the technological system was computed. The resulting measure ranges from 0 to 1, and the closer to 1 the higher the focal firm's imitation speed.

The total number of imitations realized by the focal firm at time t+1 was subtracted from the total number of imitative actions taken by all competitors at the same time, t+1, in a focal technological system. Only imitative actions subsequent to the focal firm's imitative actions are thus accounted for.

Computed by taking the mean of the average speed of imitation of all of the focal firm's rivals at a certain time, t+1, following the procedure outlined by Derfus et al. (2008). The resulting measure ranges from 0 to 1, with higher imitation speed for values closer to 1.

Number of handsets sold on a yearly basis (sales performance) in the U.K., a measure widely used by mobile phone industry specialists such as Gartner Dataquest and Mintel International Group Limited. Data on handsets sold per vendor were collected from Mintel International Group Limited, Euromonitor International, and firms' archival data.

Measured with the Shannon entropy index computed for each technological system i at year t. In the formula, p is the percentage of products introduced in year t equipped with technology k and S is the number of technologies introduced and related to technological system i. The index equals zero when all products introduced at time t are equipped with the same set of technologies related to the system (a dominant design), and larger values indicate greater variety in the population, i.e., more technologies in the system and lower diffusion of these technologies among existing products.
scale: entropy index (zero when all products carry the same set of technologies; larger values indicate more variety)

description: Firm-level weighted average of top executives' personal political orientation. Each executive's score equals the dollar value of his/her contributions to the Republican Party minus the dollar value of contributions to the Democratic Party, divided by the total dollar value of contributions to both parties, averaged across the election cycles in which the manager contributed, bounded between +1 (all contributions Republican) and -1 (all Democratic). In the firm-level aggregate each executive is weighted by the inverse of his/her compensation-based rank at the firm (highest paid gets 1, second highest 1/2, third 1/3).
time_window: contributions from 1991-2008; scores averaged across election cycles

description: The personal political orientation score of the firm's chief executive officer, computed from the manager's personal political contributions as the dollar value of contributions to the Republican Party minus the dollar value of contributions to the Democratic Party, divided by total contributions to both parties, and averaged across election cycles.
time_window: contributions from 1991-2008; scores averaged across election cycles

description: The personal political orientation score of the firm's chief financial officer, computed from the manager's personal political contributions as the dollar value of contributions to the Republican Party minus the dollar value of contributions to the Democratic Party, divided by total contributions to both parties, and averaged across election cycles.
time_window: contributions from 1991-2008; scores averaged across election cycles

description: The personal political orientation score of the departing CEO, computed from the manager's personal political contributions in the same way as the other executives' scores. It is used as the independent variable in the regression of the incoming CEO's political orientation.
time_window: contributions from 1991-2008; scores averaged across election cycles

description: A dummy variable identifying the change in the firm's CEO political orientation around a CEO turnover: it equals 1 if a Republican replaced a Democrat as CEO, -1 if a Democrat replaced a Republican, and 0 if the political orientation was unchanged. A dummy rather than a continuous change is used to make the measure insensitive to changes in the firm's political environment.

The firm's cash effective tax rate, calculated using worldwide cash taxes paid divided by worldwide total pretax accounting income. The results reported use a one-year measure; a higher effective tax rate indicates less tax avoidance. Firm-years with a rate below 0 or above 1 were excluded.

The firm's financial accounting effective tax rate, calculated using worldwide total income tax expense divided by worldwide total pretax accounting income. A higher effective tax rate indicates less tax avoidance. Firm-years with a rate below 0 or above 1 were excluded.

Change in the firm's Cash ETR around a CEO turnover: the average value over the three full fiscal years after the CEO took office (t+1, t+2, t+3) minus the average over the last three full fiscal years before the turnover (t-1, t-2, t-3). Each three-year average is demeaned by its industry average over those three years to control for time and industry trends, and the resulting change variable is transformed by decile ranking because of outliers after winsorization.
time_window: three years before versus three years after CEO turnover

description: Change in the firm's GAAP ETR around a CEO turnover: the average value over the three full fiscal years after the CEO took office (t+1, t+2, t+3) minus the average over the last three full fiscal years before the turnover (t-1, t-2, t-3). Each three-year average is demeaned by its industry average over those three years, and the change variable is transformed by decile ranking.
time_window: three years before versus three years after CEO turnover

description: Entrenchment score ranging from 0 to 6 based on the presence of staggered boards, poison pills, golden parachutes, limits to shareholder bylaw amendments, and supermajority requirements for mergers and for charter amendments, following Bebchuk, Cohen, and Ferrell (2009). Firms with scores at or above the sample median were considered entrenched, and the sample was partitioned at that median.

The personal political orientation score of a newly hired top management team member, constructed from the manager's personal political contributions in the same way as the other executives' scores. It is the dependent variable in the regression of new executives' political orientation on the current TMT's political orientation.

The personal political orientation score of the incoming CEO, constructed from the manager's personal political contributions in the same way as the other executives' scores. It is the dependent variable in the regression of the new CEO's political orientation on the departing CEO's political orientation.

variable_name: NTVL, normalized total value created by the merger
description: The sum of the value created for target and bidder shareholders divided by the sum of target equity and bidder equity. Abnormal changes in equity value were obtained with the market model: parameters were estimated for both the acquiring and acquired firms over a period of 250 trading days ending approximately 3 months before the merger press date, a prediction error was calculated for each firm for each day around the first public announcement, and the prediction errors were cumulated over the 3-day period around the merger press date. The formulas for the prediction error and for NTVL are not readable in the text as provided.
time_window: 3-day period around the merger press date (t = -1 to 1); estimation period of 250 trading days ending about 3 months before the press date

description: The percentage of an acquisition's target-bidder business combinations classified as identical fits. Each target business and each bidder business is weighted by its share of corporate revenue and the products sold and customers served are compared for every target-bidder pair; a pair is identical when the bidder and target are in the same business.
time_window: line-of-business data for the year prior to the acquisition

description: The percentage of an acquisition's target-bidder business combinations classified as related-supplementary fits. Each target business and each bidder business is weighted by its share of corporate revenue, relatedness is judged with the four criteria in Table 1 (similar customer type, similar product type, similar technology in production, similar purpose or function served in use), and a related pair is related-supplementary when the target business permits entry into a new but related industry.
time_window: line-of-business data for the year prior to the acquisition

description: The percentage of an acquisition's target-bidder business combinations classified as related-complementary fits. Each target business and each bidder business is weighted by its share of corporate revenue, relatedness is judged with the four criteria in Table 1, and a related pair is related-complementary when the target unit permits the bidder to expand its product line, strengthen its competitive position in a given market, or integrate forward or backwards.
time_window: line-of-business data for the year prior to the acquisition

description: The percentage of an acquisition's target-bidder business combinations classified as unrelated fits. Each target business and each bidder business is weighted by its share of corporate revenue, and businesses are unrelated when affirmative answers to fewer than three of the four relatedness questions in Table 1 are met.
time_window: line-of-business data for the year prior to the acquisition

description: Our main independent variable identifies a CEO as having been appointed either following an interim period or in a direct succession. The measure takes the value of one if a CEO had directly succeeded an interim CEO and zero if a CEO directly succeeded a normal CEO. Interim CEOs were identified by manually inspecting the titles of all executives of a firm as reported by BoardEx; a CEO was designated as an interim CEO if the CEO's title was interim CEO, acting CEO, or temporary CEO.

Return on assets, calculated as a firm's annual net income divided by its total book value of assets. One-year ROA is calculated as the firm's ROA in the year following the succession. Two-year ROA is calculated as the average ROA over the two years following the succession, and three-year ROA is calculated as the average ROA over the three years following the succession.
time_window: one, two, and three years following the succession

description: A composite index that considers environmental dynamism, strategic differentiation of peer firms, and industry R&D intensity. Environmental dynamism uses the Bergh and Lawless (1998) measure of the volatility of net sales in an industry (four-digit SIC), computed as the regression slope coefficient divided by the mean of sales. Strategic differentiation among peer firms is the inverse of Finkelstein and Hambrick's (1990) measure of strategic conformity, computed from six ratios and averaged per four-digit SIC industry. Industry R&D intensity is the median R&D/sales in year t - 1 of companies within the same four-digit SIC industry. These three measures were standardized and summed to create the composite measure, captured in the year prior to the succession.

A composite index that considers the firm's size, its degree of diversification, and its acquisition activity. Firm size is the number of a firm's employees in the focal year, collected from Compustat. Diversification is Palepu's (1985) entropy measure calculated for business segments, collected from Compustat. Acquisition activity is the number of acquisitions in the focal year that were at least 2% the size of the focal firm, collected from the SDC Mergers & Acquisitions database. These three variables were standardized and summed to create the composite index, captured in the year prior to the succession.

The number of executives holding a title of executive vice president (EVP) or higher who were in a firm in the focal firm's industry (four-digit SIC) that was a maximum of 25% larger or smaller than the focal firm by sales. Titles considered higher than EVP were limited to chief financial officer and chief operations officer. The variable was captured in the year prior to the succession.

Measured as the logarithmic difference between the waste produced by chemical c in facility i in year t as compared to year t-1, multiplied by 100 to facilitate interpretation of the coefficients, which can be interpreted as percentage change for a unit change of the covariates. Increases in waste indicate lower operational performance while decreases indicate higher operational performance, so higher values of this variable mean worse performance. The authors state that the formula for the calculation is given in a block whose rendering is unreadable in this payload.
time_window: year t relative to year t-1

description: Captures the number of knowledge sources a firm looks to, using the section of the TRI form in which managers specify the methods used to identify possible solutions to reduce waste. For instance, a manager who used both an employee recommendation under a formal company program and an independent employee recommendation would count two knowledge sources. The variable can potentially range from zero to nine, and the observed maximum is eight.

Alternative measure that counts only sources that are distinctive as independent knowledge sources, built from the four clusters of knowledge sources: assistance programs, audits, employee programs, and others. A facility that used both informal and formal employee recommendation methods would have a value of 1 because the two types of knowledge sources are similar in terms of screening and implementation costs.
Counts the total number of different knowledge sources used in the periods prior to the current year t.
time_window: all periods prior to year t

description: Takes into account only the cumulative number of unique clusters of knowledge sources over time.
time_window: all periods prior to year t

variable_name: diversity of the business portfolio of a firm in the industry
description: The diversity of the business portfolio of a firm in the industry was evaluated by the number of products x markets, in terms of three categories: focus on one business, a few businesses, or most of the businesses of the industry. Data on the scope of the company were collected from documentary sources (annual reports, industry studies and the business press).
scale: three categories: focus on one business / a few businesses / most of the businesses of the industry

description: The geographic scope of a firm was evaluated by the geographical limits of its targeted markets in the industry, according to three categories: national, national and a few foreign countries, or international (several major foreign countries). Data came from documentary sources (annual reports, industry studies and the business press).
scale: three categories: national / national and a few foreign countries / international (several major foreign countries)

description: The interactions with a parent company were evaluated according to three categories: independent company, belongs to a group from the same country, or belongs to a multinational group from a foreign country. Data came from documentary sources (annual reports, industry studies and the business press).
scale: three categories: independent company / belongs to a group from the same country / belongs to a multinational group from a foreign country

description: The comprehensiveness of a manager's cognitive map was measured by the number of concepts (elements) in the map, computed separately for the map of the structure of the industry and for the map of the dynamics of the industry. Because the managers belonged to companies in four industries, the values were standardized by dividing the original value by the average for the corresponding industry, and standardized measures were used in all further analyses. The authors report that the CEOs' maps of the structure contained from 9 (minimum) to 34 (maximum) concepts with an average of 17.9, and that the maps of the dynamics contained from 6 to 16 concepts with an average of 9.9.

The connectedness of a manager's map of the structure of the industry was measured by the number of links between concepts divided by the total number of concepts in the map. The connectedness of a manager's map of the dynamics of the industry was measured by the number of concepts in the largest submap divided by the total number of concepts in the map; a submap is a subset of elements (concepts) linked together directly or indirectly, and the largest submap is the one which includes the most elements linked together. Values were standardized by dividing by the average for the corresponding industry.

variable_name: standardized complexity (combined measure of comprehensiveness and connectedness)
description: The complexity of a CEO's cognitive map of the structure of the industry is the combined measure of comprehensiveness and connectedness, namely the number of links between concepts in the map (the score of comprehensiveness multiplied by the score of connectedness). The complexity of a manager's map of the dynamics of the industry is the number of concepts in the largest submap, again the score of comprehensiveness multiplied by the score of connectedness. Values were standardized by dividing by the average for the corresponding industry.

Employees reported the stretchiness of the idea generation goal of their unit on four items adopted from Zhang and Jia (2013): 'I find that the goal in my unit is too high'; 'From the beginning, I think the work goal is too high to be achieved for my unit'; 'Within the extant resource and condition, I don't think we can accomplish the goal for my unit'; and 'According to the knowledge and expertise that I have, it's impossible for us to achieve this goal for my unit.' The mean is 3.70, the standard deviation is 1.40, and alpha equals 0.86. Individual responses were aggregated to the unit level after interrater agreement and intraclass correlations were examined (average rwg(j) equals 0.72, median equals 0.76, ICC(1) equals 0.24, ICC(2) equals 0.58).
time_window: measured at the beginning of the 12-month study period

description: A binary variable coded as one if the employee registered at least one new business opportunity during the 12-month period and zero otherwise. It was built from the firm's system used for registering and evaluating new business ideas.

The number of ideas an employee submitted during the 12-month period, counted for those employees who submitted at least one idea. It was built from the firm's system for registering and evaluating new business ideas.
The count of ideas submitted by an employee that were subsequently accepted and sold to customers. It was built from the firm's system for registering and evaluating new business ideas.

The count of ideas submitted by an employee that were ultimately rejected by the organization. Rejections were typically based on technical feasibility, (technical) misalignment with the firm's strategy, issues with implementation in the market (i.e., regulatory issues), or lack of demand.
A binary variable coded as one if the employee had registered at least one fruitful idea in the year previous to the study period (before stretch goals were implemented) and zero otherwise.
time_window: the year previous to the study period

description: The number of years the specific person had served at the firm.
The number of layers below that individual in the hierarchy of the service unit. The higher the number of layers below, the higher the employee was ranked in the hierarchy.

Three-level ordered dependent variable. If the model and a banker's assessment agreed, the rating was assumed correct; where they differed, the banker was defined as in error when the banker's assessment moved toward the model's assessment within the next two years. Observations were classified as overrated (coded 1), other (coded 0), and underrated (coded -1). Only firm-years with two subsequent years of assessments were classified; each firm-year combination was one observation.
time_window: assessment in year t, with movement checked in t+1 and t+2

description: For Hypothesis 6, overrated and underrated loans were combined in order to test the hypothesis that the number of misrated loans decreased as standardization increased. Binomial logistic regression was used with the standardization variable as the only independent variable.
The number of years the bank had loaned to a given customer measured the duration of the relationship. The beginning date of the lending relationship was collected in the annual loan review data.
The outstanding amount of a loan in millions of dollars measured its size. The amount of existing loans was collected in the annual loan review data.

Three banking industry experts rated the interest/excitement of all industries represented in the sample on a scale of 1 to 5, with 5 being high excitement. Because the bank questioned the accuracy of its four-digit SIC categorization, each rater's responses were averaged to obtain estimates at the two-digit SIC code level, and the ratings of the three experts were then averaged for each two-digit SIC code industry.

Measured as the profitability of a branch in the prior year. Since the bank changed its profitability measures during the span of the study, an ordinal variable was used that reflected the relative profitability of each branch in each year.

Because the degree of standardization could not be measured objectively, three senior managers who had been in management roles throughout the study completed a short questionnaire assessing the degree of standardization by year using four questions rated on a seven-point Likert scale. Three questions were modified versions of questions used by Van de Ven and Ferry (1980) for measuring unit standardization, and a fourth question measured the degree of standardization across units (branches). Responses were averaged across questions and respondents to get an overall indication of the degree of standardization by year.
time_window: by year over the study period

description: Each crowdsourcing event was assigned one of three sets of governance instructions. Instruction Set 1 asked crowd participants to post solutions, tweak others' solutions, and provide feedback; Instruction Set 2 additionally asked them to offer their problem frames in terms of facts, tradeoffs, and examples; Instruction Set 3 additionally asked them to integrate knowledge of the problem offered by others when offering solutions. In the analysis, Instruction Sets 2 and 3 were compared against the baseline Instruction Set 1, and each was then multiplied with the dummy for unconstrained problems to create the interaction terms.

A dummy variable for the problem posed to the crowd by the firm, coded 0 for a constrained problem (12 events) and 1 for an unconstrained problem (8 events). Problem statements expecting solutions that simultaneously embody new products and new markets are unconstrained because they neither restrict the solver to a market nor products.

The executive who had developed the problem statement evaluated each solution idea's implementability on a 7-point scale from 'not at all implementable' to 'extremely implementable'; the evaluations were then standardized. Only the temporally first solution idea among semantically similar ones was included in the spreadsheet, and in events that received more than 20 semantically different solution ideas executives were shown 20 randomly selected ideas, leading to 297 evaluated solution ideas in total. The executives were blind to the instructions their crowd had received.

The executive who had developed the problem statement evaluated each solution idea's novelty on a 7-point scale from 'not at all novel' to 'extremely novel'; the evaluations were then standardized. Only the temporally first solution idea among semantically similar ones was included, and in events that received more than 20 semantically different solution ideas executives were shown 20 randomly selected ideas, leading to 297 evaluated solution ideas in total. The executives were blind to the instructions their crowd had received.

variable_name: number of problem framing elements in trace
description: To identify framing elements, coders manually coded all 2428 postings for the presence of any of three problem framing elements (facts, tradeoffs, and examples), and each post was given a score for the number of different problem-framing elements it included. The number of prior problem frame elements was calculated as the sum in the trace (the five posts immediately preceding the focal posting) before the focal post; the variable varied from 0 to 8. Because it exhibited right-skewness and possibly scored zero, Yeo and Johnson's (2000) transformation (i.e., ln[x + 1]) was applied.

The text of all postings was cleaned by stemming all words to their stem form and removing punctuation, numerical values, and stop words. Event-specific matrices were created with each posting as a column and each word that occurs in any posting as a row, the intersections showing the number of occurrences of the words in the postings. The cosine similarity between the solution idea and each of the five preceding postings (its trace) was measured, and the five cosine values were summed to determine the overall similarity between the solution and the postings in its preceding trace, for all 1198 solutions.

Obtained through structured content analysis of 37,149 articles published by Aviation Daily from 1991 to 2010. The term alliance is interpreted broadly, ranging from point-specific code sharing to marketing alliances to extensive equity-based strategic alliances involving joint operations, sharing of facilities, and revenue pooling; only alliance arrangements that had been confirmed or would go into effect shortly after the announcement were coded. For each quarter, the authors summed the total number of alliance relationships among all incumbent dyads in a market and scaled this number by the total number of rival pairs in that market.

Measured as the average overlap in institutional investors among incumbent airlines in a market. The percentage of common ownership between a given pair of rivals is the minimum level of ownership percentages among all common investors when a pair has more than one common investor. The overlap in common investors is summed across all rival dyads and divided by the total number of dyads in a market. The measure ranges between 0 and 1, where 0 means there are no common ownership ties between any pair of rivals in a market, and 1 means complete overlap between rivals' investors. The printed equation could not be read from the text.

Measured as the average number of financial analysts in common among incumbent airlines in a market, where an analyst is defined as following a firm if the analyst had issued at least one earnings forecast for the firm in the previous 12 months. The authors first counted the number of unique analysts following each firm, then calculated the number of analysts in common for each quarter and each pair of rivals, scaled this number by the mean number of analysts covering each pair of rivals, and finally averaged the dyadic measure across all pairs of rivals in a market.

variable_name: incumbents at war in other markets
description: Captures the percentage of incumbent dyads in a market that were at war in other markets in the previous period. For each pair of incumbents in the focal market a dummy variable was created indicating whether the rivals were at war in other markets; a pair is considered to be at war in other markets only when price wars occurred in at least 5% of their shared markets. At the market level the variable is the percentage of incumbent dyads in the focal market that were at war in other markets in the previous period.

A dichotomous variable that takes the value of 1 if a market hits the 20% price drop threshold in a given period and 0 otherwise. A market is considered to be at war when actual prices are more than 20% lower than expected prices, with actual prices captured by passenger yield and expected prices predicted by autoregressive models using lagged pricing data from the previous eight quarters. Only the first period of a war's commencement in a market is coded as 1; subsequent observations representing the continuation of a war are coded as 0.

A dummy variable assuming one if the school is public and zero otherwise. Public schools in Brazil have weak incentives, bureaucratic rules, and restrained managerial autonomy; the baseline case is private schools, which can be either for-profit or nonprofit, and which the database cannot distinguish.

variable_name: Proportion of teachers with graduate certificate
description: The proportion of teachers within a given high school holding a graduate certificate, taken from the Brazilian School Census for 2007 and 2008. Past research has found that teachers with a higher educational background and qualifications are strongly correlated with student achievement.

The number of computers for administrative use divided by the number of employees. The variable represents the extent to which school staff had access to technological resources to run their day-to-day operations, such as keeping track of students' records, absences, and class schedules.

A single index representing a school's adherence to internal operational and external engagement management practices, built from a set of questions answered by ENEM test takers from 2005-2008 about their perception of several practices adopted by their schools. Most questions measure student perceptions (such as planning and conflict management) on a 0-2 Likert scale or use binary questions on the existence of certain practices (such as the organization of lectures with visiting speakers); the index was constructed following a five-step procedure. The main specifications use the management variables for 2007 and 2008; two subindices for internal operational practices and external engagement practices were also computed.

Firms with high SEPs are those that were part of the KLD Domini 400 Social Index for all three consecutive years, 1991-1993, and that belonged to sectors represented by at least 10 companies, yielding a sample of 195 companies. To determine the firms comprising the KLD 400, the KLD Committee selects companies whose positive social and environmental records are based on community relations, diversity, employee relations, human rights, product quality and safety, and environment and corporate governance. For the analyses, treated firms are assigned the value of 1 and the propensity-score matched control firms the value of 0.
scale: dichotomous (1 = high SEP firm, 0 = matched control firm)

description: The authors collected the month-end changes in stock price indices (monthly returns) for each company, covering the 180 months from January 1994 to December 2008. For each year they calculated the standard deviation of monthly returns, described as one of the most commonly used measures of volatility, which resulted in 15 observations for each company. Market data for 22 pairs were unavailable, so these analyses were performed with only 99 pairs (198 firms).
scale: standard deviation of monthly stock returns

description: Growth over the long term was measured as the accumulation of net sales growth from 1994 to 2008. The authors argue that accumulated growth is a better measure for capturing the differences between treated firms and control firms than year-over-year growth because growth occurs continuously and incrementally over time.

Event is a dichotomous variable that takes the value of 1 if the firm fails during the 15-year period and 0 if it does not; reasons for failure include acquisition or merger, liquidation, and bankruptcy, all of which the authors believe are linked to a lack of resilience. The variable time shows the number of years that firms survive from the initial point (t0 = 1994) to the final period of observation (t15 = 2008), so firms that survive the whole period are right-censored at 15 years. Firms that disappear from the database when the cause is neither specified nor easily linked with resilience are not included.

Short-term profitability is measured by the change in ROA between two consecutive years. ROA is described as one of the most commonly used financial measures to assess the financial performance of a firm's operations.

A list of items describing corporate sustainable development was grounded in literature and in interviews, then generated independently from a sample of annual reports by the author and a researcher not familiar with the hypotheses. The items were pared down on generality, discriminability, readability, and non-redundancy, and six researchers coded each item into one of the three principles (environmental integrity, economic prosperity, social equity); all items met the condition of substantive validity. For a firm to have a score greater than zero, at least one item in each of the three principles had to be identified in the company's annual report. The number of items mentioned in each principle was divided by the total number of possible items for that principle, and the three proportions were summed. Each item was coded as 0 (no indication) or 1 (some presence) from the annual reports in the target year, with satisfactory interrater reliability (Cohen's kappa 0.79).

Two measures were used for each panel: the number of countries in which the firm operates and the percentage of foreign sales relative to total sales. The data on countries were right censored at 10 countries because the reliability of the data for larger numbers was questionable. Foreign sales were calculated as the percentage of sales outside of Canada divided by total sales as reported in the segment data of the financial statements. Following Sanders and Carpenter (1998), each variable was normalized to a value between zero and one and summed to derive a single variable with a theoretical maximum value of two.

Capital management capabilities were proxied by capital intensity, measured by the value of property, plant and equipment after depreciation divided by sales. This mirrors the choice of capital intensity measures used by Sharma and Kesner (1996), Lubatkin and Chatterjee (1994), and D'Aveni and Ilinitch (1992). The fourth root of capital intensity was taken to generate a normal distribution.

Current assets over current liabilities was used in the analysis for each panel, a measure also used by Schuler (1996), to recognize extra liquidity that could be invested in sustainable development activities. The inverse of organizational slack was used because it yielded the most normal distribution.

The variable included two components that were summed. The first component was the number of times that the firm incurred a fine or penalty under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act (CEPA) and the Canadian Fisheries Act (CFA), counting fines imposed in year t-1 and year t because both would likely influence corporate sustainable development in year t. The second component was the number of fines or penalties disclosed in the annual report that were not covered under CEPA and CFA.
time_window: year t-1 and year t of each panel

description: The variable was coded 1 if three conditions were met: the firm conducted an environmental audit in that year; the firm had not been assigned a 1 in the past; and over 20 percent of firms in the prior panel for the industry conducted an environmental audit. An environmental audit could include a formal or informal audit, conducted by an internal audit group or a consultant. Data were extracted from annual reports.

Media attention incorporated two measures: the total number of articles that included a statement about the company and their environmental issues, labeled 'total media', and the number of articles about the company with a negative aspect of their environmental practices, labeled 'negative media'. The articles were extracted from the computerized databases of two of Canada's national newspapers, the Globe and Mail and the Financial Post, using keywords that included the company name and signals for sustainable development (sustainable development, environmental, pollution, and toxic) for articles in the year prior to and the year of the panel. As the distributions of both measures were highly skewed, with many firms with no articles, 1 was added to both measures, the natural log of each was taken, and then summed to produce the final variable.
time_window: year prior to and year of the panel

description: A linear trend variable with values from one to four was introduced to represent each contiguous panel, in order to test Hypotheses 7a, 7b, and 7c. The hypotheses were tested by evaluating the coefficients of the interaction between the hypothesized variable and the linear trend variable.

Manipulated treatment describing the restaurant in the scenario as having either a fictional 'Zagalin' cuisine rating of 28 with comments 'creative,' 'innovative,' 'unique style' (high reputation) or a rating of 20 with comments 'lacks imagination,' 'unoriginal,' 'ordinary style' (low reputation). The Zagalin rating was explained as equivalent to a Zagat rating from 0 to 30. Coded Excellent = 1, Average = -1. A manipulation check asking how prestigious the chef would be considered by colleagues was successful.

Manipulated treatment describing the restaurant in the scenario as either 'geographically very close to your restaurant' (high proximity) or 'geographically very distant from your restaurant' (low proximity). On the advice of informants no reference point was inserted, to avoid subjectivity in interpretation. Coded Close = 1, Far = -1; no manipulation check was needed because the treatment is a concrete statement of fact.

Manipulated treatment describing the restaurant in the scenario as having 'cuisine style and ambience similar to your restaurant' (similar positioning) or 'cuisine style and ambience very different from your restaurant' (different positioning). Coded Similar = 1, Different = -1. A manipulation check asking how comparable the restaurant was in terms of positioning was successful.

Manipulated treatment describing the restaurant in the scenario as either 'frequently reviewed by local media and customers (among the restaurants with more reviews)' (high review) or 'rarely reviewed by local media and customers (among the restaurants with fewer reviews)' (low review). No reference point was inserted, on the advice of the chefs with whom the design was piloted. Coded Frequently = 1, Infrequently = -1; no manipulation check was needed because the treatment is a concrete statement of fact.

Reported likelihood that the chef described in the scenario would conform to the three social norms regulating the use of transferred knowledge: modify the knowledge rather than copy it exactly, credit the respondent as its creator, and ask permission before passing it to others. Measured on a 7-point Likert scale for each of the three knowledge types after each scenario. The three norms' measures were combined into a single measure for a given knowledge type.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely)

description: Reported likelihood that the respondent, if asked, would provide the requested knowledge to the chef described in the scenario, asked separately for the recipe for a dish, the recipe for one of the respondent's signature dishes, and information about a cooking technique. Measured after each of the two scenarios on a 7-point Likert scale. Responses for the three types of knowledge were not aggregated; they were marked with dummy variables to isolate the effect of knowledge type.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 4 = neutral, 7 = very likely)

description: During each fortnight of phase I, entrepreneurs provided the business cards of new people with whom they had interacted and indicated which of those new people they wanted to stay in touch with. After at least one interaction, the entrepreneur evaluated whether he/she intended to follow up with subsequent interactions and thereby attempt to build a relationship. Tie formation intention was coded 1 for an entrepreneur-new person dyad if the entrepreneur wanted to remain in touch with the new person and 0 otherwise.
scale: 1 = wanted to remain in touch; 0 = otherwise
time_window: during each fortnight of phase I

description: From the web survey the authors identified entrepreneur-new person dyads for which no exchange relationship existed between the venture and the organization with which the new person was affiliated. For those dyads, interfirm tie formation was coded 1 if the entrepreneur reported that meeting the focal new person led to the establishment of an interfirm relationship between their respective organizations during the 12 months subsequent to phase I, and 0 otherwise. The authors physically inspected relevant documents providing objective evidence of an interfirm exchange relationship. 1,082 of the 1,437 dyads exhibited a one-to-one mapping between the entrepreneur-new person interpersonal tie and the venture-organization interfirm tie.

The similarity in caste between entrepreneurs and the new people they met was calculated as the joint probability of the entrepreneur and new person belonging to the same caste. Entrepreneurs self-reported their caste and were placed into Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra, or Dalit categories. Because the author could not directly interact with the new people, their caste was probabilistically inferred from last names using data from two large Indian online matrimonial agencies. Caste homophily ranges from 0 to 1 inclusive and was set to 0 for the 14 percent of new people who were not of Indian ethnicity. To test interaction effects, indicator variables high caste homophily and low caste homophily coded observations one standard deviation above and below the mean.

The similarity in language between entrepreneurs and the new people they met was calculated as the joint probability of the entrepreneur and new person being proficient in the same Indian language. Entrepreneurs reported the Indian languages in which they could carry on a business conversation in addition to English. The new person's language was probabilistically inferred from his/her last name using the matrimonial database. Language homophily ranges from 0 to 1 inclusive and was set to 0 for the 14 percent of new people who were not of Indian ethnicity. Indicator variables high language homophily and low language homophily coded observations one standard deviation above and below the mean for interaction tests.

Entrepreneur homophily was coded as 1 whenever the focal respondent and the new person met were both business founders and as 0 otherwise. In some cases the formal title of the new person indicated that he/she was a founder or cofounder. In other cases, the author examined the web site of the new person's organization and web sites that track individuals' career histories to code whether a new person was a business founder.

During the initial face-to-face meeting, entrepreneurs reported their best estimate of the percentage of working time they intended to allocate in the subsequent three months to ten activities such as working with existing customers, seeking new customers, working with existing alliance partners, seeking new alliance partners, working with existing investors, seeking new investors, working with existing suppliers, seeking new suppliers, interacting with competitors, and other activities. During phase I, entrepreneurs categorized the organizations represented by the new people they met as existing or potential alliance partner, customer, investor, supplier, competitor, or none of these. Task complementarity was defined as the product of these indicator variables and the proportion of time the focal entrepreneur intended to spend on the ten activities. The measure ranged from 0 to 1 inclusive depending on the extent of overlap between the entrepreneur's task priority areas and the new person's organization. Indicator variables high task complementarity and low task complementarity coded observations one standard deviation above and below the mean for interaction tests.
time_window: task priorities: subsequent three months from initial meeting; organization categorizations: during phase I

variable_name: Social similarity (caste, language and founder homophily)
description: Social similarity is measured by a set of three dyadic homophily variables: caste homophily, language homophily, and founder (entrepreneur) homophily, each comparing the focal entrepreneur and the new person met. They are entered together in the logit models.

variable_name: Fit on match criteria (caste, language, founder homophily, task complementarity)
description: Match quality is tested through the set of match criteria entered jointly in the full model of exchange formation: caste homophily, language homophily, founder homophily and task complementarity between the entrepreneur and the new person. Greater fit on these criteria is read as better match.

Firm performance is measured by a firm's Tobin's q, defined as the ratio of the market value of the firm to the replacement cost of its tangible assets, using Chung and Pruitt's approximation for q. For publicly traded firms, market value is the market value of outstanding common shares plus estimates of the market value of the firm's debt, and tangible assets are an estimate of the replacement value of the firm's tangible assets. All scaled variables in the specification have been transformed by adding a constant and taking the natural log of this sum, and the models use the first difference of Q (Delta1Q) as the dependent variable.

The number of new foreign subsidiaries in developing countries by each firm in each year, coded from each volume of the Directory of Corporate Affiliates for 1981 through 2000. Each foreign subsidiary was coded as coming from an advanced or a developing country, with all countries other than the United States, Canada, Western Europe, Japan, Australia and New Zealand classified as developing. To control for serial correlation, the first differences of all variables were used and for the FDI variables the analysis focused on new subsidiaries in the prior year.
time_window: annual, 1981-2000; new subsidiaries in the prior year

description: The number of new foreign subsidiaries in advanced countries by each firm in each year, coded from each volume of the Directory of Corporate Affiliates for 1981 through 2000. Advanced countries include the United States, Canada, Western European countries, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand. To control for serial correlation, the first differences of all variables were used and for the FDI variables the analysis focused on new subsidiaries in the prior year.
time_window: annual, 1981-2000; new subsidiaries in the prior year

description: The sample was divided into subsamples based on quartile differences for the total number of nations in which a firm has subsidiaries, with a 1-year lag in the information on the number of nations. For high knowledge-intensive industries, a low level of multinational operations is assigned to firms with subsidiaries in one to three foreign countries, a medium level to four to fifteen foreign countries, and a high level to sixteen or more foreign countries; for low knowledge-intensive industries the cut-offs are one to two, three to five, and six or more foreign countries respectively. About 25 percent of the observations are for firms with no foreign operations (domestic-only firms), and these firms are included in each of the other three subsamples to provide a base case for analysis.
time_window: annual, 1981-2000; number of nations lagged one year

variable_name: High vs. low knowledge-intensive industry groupings
description: The larger and more internationally integrated industries were run separately where possible and then grouped into what the author calls the high knowledge-intensive industry grouping, comprising the chemical, electric equipment, industrial machinery, transportation equipment, and precision instrument industries. The remaining industries make up the low knowledge-intensive group, including textiles, food, paper and paper products, rubber products, and fabricated metals. The high group corresponds well with what the OECD calls 'high R&D intensive industries,' based on R&D spending as a percentage of sales ratios.

variable_name: ratio of time- to ego-moving language
description: Two researchers, one of whom was blind to the purpose of the study, independently read the fourth-quarter earnings call transcriptions, tagging all references to the future and isolating those that also involved spatial language, noting whether the reference involved ego-motion or time-motion; this left 674 ego- or time-moving mentions of the future. The firm-level variable is the ratio of time-moving to ego-moving language. References to periods below one year (e.g., 'month,' 'quarter') were flagged as short-term and mentions of periods of one year or longer (e.g., 'years ahead,' 'next decade') as long-term.

Subjects answered the question: 'A meeting arranged for next Wednesday has been moved forward two days. What day is the meeting now that it has been rescheduled?' 'Monday' responses reflect a time-moving frame (the meeting is moved closer) and 'Friday' responses reflect an ego-moving frame (the self moves forward and the meeting is displaced further ahead). The authors created a dummy variable with 1 = ego-moving frame and 0 = time-moving frame.

Subjects were randomly assigned to two groups. Subjects in Group 1 (ego-moving condition) were presented with the information: 'The company moved its annual shareholder meeting forward from March 11 to March 18.' Subjects in Group 2 (time-moving condition) were presented with: 'The company moved its annual shareholder meeting forward from March 18 to March 11.' Subjects also rescheduled identical events variously described as being moved forward or backward. The treatment variable indicates the time-moving condition.

Subjects' locus of control was measured using Rotter's (1966) scale as well as Hodgkinson's (1992) strategic locus of control scale; the reported analysis uses Rotter's scale. The variable enters the discount-rate regressions as an individual characteristic.

Subjects completed Rotter's (1966) locus of control scale. Internal locus of control is operationalized as having an internal score on the Rotter scale one or more standard deviations above the mean, and external locus by a score at least one standard deviation below the mean. The scale has 23 levels.

In the matching task, subjects indicated how much money they would need to receive after 1, 5, 10, and 20 years instead of receiving $1,000 tomorrow. The points of indifference were converted into annual discount rates over each of the four intervals. Participants who indicated that they preferred to receive less than $1,000 in the future were excluded, and the data were winsorized at the 97th percentile to exclude outlier influence.

After the framing manipulation, subjects read a scenario about a pharmaceutical firm's potential acquisition of a biotechnology firm and were asked to advise the CEO. The scenario stated that if they advised in favor of the acquisition, the firm would probably miss its short-term earnings forecast even if the acquisition led to earnings increasing in subsequent years. Subjects indicated whether they believed the acquisition would create economic value for the acquirer on a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 9 (strongly agree).

variable_name: Treatment indicator (formed an alliance for new resources, 1996-2000)
description: A dummy variable reporting if a firm formed an alliance for new resources between 1996 and 2000, used to distinguish firms that reacted to the technological discontinuity from those that did not. Firms that formed at least one such alliance were assigned to the treatment group and all others to the control group. The treatment and control groups comprised 82 (28.8%) and 203 (71.2%) firms.

variable_name: Number of alliances for new resources formed
description: The dependent variable for Hypothesis 1 and the explanatory variable for Hypotheses 2a and 2b: the number of alliances for new resources formed in a year, computed by counting the number of alliances formed within the new-resource category for each year. Alliances were classified using Recap's primary technological resources exchanged, with combinatorial chemistry and high-throughput screening treated as requiring new resources.
time_window: annual, 1990-2000; lagged by one year in the two-stage least squares models

variable_name: Number of alliances for reinforced resources formed
description: The dependent variable for Hypothesis 1a and explanatory variable for Hypothesis 3a: the number of alliances for reinforced resources formed in a year. Alliances are classified according to how the discontinuity affected the value of the resources exchanged, based on Recap's 53 technology areas and expert classification. Some alliances exchange more than one type of resource and were recorded as separate alliances for each type exchanged.
time_window: annual, 1990-2000; lagged by one year in the two-stage least squares models

variable_name: Number of alliances for challenged resources formed
description: The dependent variable for Hypothesis 1b and explanatory variable for Hypothesis 3b: the number of alliances for challenged resources formed in a year. Alliances are classified according to how the discontinuity affected the value of the resources exchanged, based on Recap's 53 technology areas and expert classification. Multi-resource alliances were recorded as separate alliances for each type exchanged.
time_window: annual, 1990-2000; lagged by one year in the two-stage least squares models

variable_name: Number of alliances for reinforced resources terminated
description: The number of alliances for reinforced resources terminated in a year. Recap reported termination dates for only a small share of alliances, so termination dates were established by searching Factiva for press releases using partners' names and other alliance characteristics, and for the remaining alliances by recording the last year in which a press release referred to an alliance. Multi-resource alliances were recorded as separate alliances for each type exchanged.
time_window: annual, 1990-2000; lagged by one year in the two-stage least squares models

variable_name: Number of alliances for challenged resources terminated
description: The number of alliances for challenged resources terminated in a year. Termination dates came from Recap where reported and were otherwise estimated from Factiva press releases and from the last year in which a press release referred to an alliance. Multi-resource alliances were recorded as separate alliances for each type exchanged.
time_window: annual, 1990-2000; lagged by one year in the two-stage least squares models

variable_name: Number of alliances for unaffected resources terminated
description: The dependent variable for Hypotheses 2b, 3a and 3b: the number of alliances for unaffected resources terminated in a year. Termination dates were established from Recap, from Factiva press releases and, for the remaining alliances, from the last year in which a press release referred to an alliance. Multi-resource alliances were recorded as separate alliances for each type exchanged.
time_window: annual, 1990-2000; lagged by one year in the two-stage least squares models

description: One of two spline variables created from the degree of perceived inequity computed with the four-item Walster Global Equity Measure. Informants rated their firm's contributions, the supplier's contributions, their firm's outcomes, and the supplier's outcomes on seven-point scales (1 = 'extremely low', 7 = 'extremely high'), and inequity was calculated from these ratings. When inequity exists, the appropriate spline variable reflects the nature and degree of that inequity and the other spline variable equals zero; when equity is reported, both spline variables equal zero.
scale: Computed from seven-point ratings of the four equity components

scale: Computed from seven-point ratings of the four equity components

description: Four items assessing hostility, anger, frustration, and resentment toward the principal supplier of the informant (a dealer). Informants reported how their firm feels when reflecting on the relationship with the supplier on a five-point scale (1 = 'strongly feels this way', 5 = 'does not feel this way'); codings were reversed.

Ten items, five assessing the supplier's honesty and five measuring the supplier's benevolence, rated on a seven-point agreement scale (1 = 'strongly disagree', 7 = 'strongly agree'). One honesty item is negatively worded and reversed.
scale: 7-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Three-item scale addressing the dealer's confidence that the relationship would continue, rated on a seven-point agreement scale (1 = 'strongly disagree', 7 = 'strongly agree'). One item, stating that it is unlikely the firm will still be doing business with this supplier in two years, is reversed.
scale: 7-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: A single item asking whether the firm feels guilt when reflecting on the relationship with the supplier, answered on a five-point scale (1 = 'strongly feels this way', 5 = 'does not feel this way'); codings were reversed.
