description: A single item asking whether the firm feels guilt when reflecting on the relationship with the supplier, answered on a five-point scale (1 = 'strongly feels this way', 5 = 'does not feel this way'); codings were reversed.

Three items adapted from the first three of Jaworski and Macinnis's four-item measure; respondents indicated on a seven-point Likert scale how strongly they agreed with statements about top management monitoring the extent to which growth initiatives followed established procedures, evaluating the procedures used to accomplish a given task, and modifying the initiatives' procedures when desired results were not obtained. Items were worded in the past tense. Cronbach's alpha was 0.77.
level: strategic initiative (reported by a senior executive)

description: Three items based on LaBahn, Ali, and Krapfel plus a fourth item based on Jaworski, Stathakopoulos, and Krishnan to account for the degree to which evaluations are based on results. Respondents answered on a seven-point Likert scale about establishing and monitoring specific dates for milestones, specific performance goals, and critical cost budgets for growth initiatives, and about performance evaluations placing primary weight on results. Cronbach's alpha was 0.86.
level: strategic initiative (reported by a senior executive)

description: Three reverse-coded items retained from the supervisor political behavior factor of the Perceptions of Organizational Politics Scale, measuring the extent to which employees were encouraged to speak out frankly even when critical of well-established ideas, and to challenge or refute the strategic views of top management team members. A factor analysis showed the three items load on a common factor; Cronbach's alpha was 0.71.
scale: Seven-point scales (item 1: 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree; items 2 and 3: 1 = not at all to 7 = to a very great extent)
level: strategic initiative (reported by a senior executive)

description: Two items retained from the coworker and clique political behavior factor of Ferris and Kacmar's Perceptions of Organizational Politics Scale. Respondents rated on a seven-point Likert scale whether there were cliques or 'in groups' that hindered the effectiveness of their growth initiatives and whether informal networks rather than merit determined who got ahead. The two items loaded on a common factor; Cronbach's alpha was 0.70.
level: strategic initiative (reported by a senior executive)

description: An 11-item self-reported scale adapted from prior research, asking respondents to assess the performance of their growth initiatives up to now on criteria such as meeting budget, staffing, deadline, quality, reliability, cost, efficiency, user/client satisfaction, service, and revenue objectives, plus meeting objective overall. Items were answered on a seven-point scale ranging from very unsuccessful to very successful. The scale had an alpha of 0.88.
level: strategic initiative (reported by a senior executive)

description: For a focal actor, the attention-share of each alter is multiplied by the inverse of that alter's network constraint and these values are averaged over all of the actor's alters. The attention share is the proportion of the actor's attention to that alter's information relative to the sum of the actor's attention to all of his or her alters; attention to an alter is the average of four survey items, each on a 7-point scale, covering noticing, encoding, interpreting, and focusing of time and effort. The alter's network constraint is the whole-network constraint score of that communication partner. Proportions rather than absolute amounts of attention are used because they capture the opportunity cost of attention allocation. A high ATB score indicates that the actor pays more attention to alters with low network constraint (brokers) than to alters with high network constraint (non-brokers); the displayed equation for the variable is not legible in the text.

The R&D director and four chief engineers identified 37 innovations as significant changes to existing software products or processes or introductions of new products or processes, and rated every engineer's contribution to each innovation on a 10-point scale. Engineers received the highest scores (9 and 10) if they proposed the initial idea and led the whole development process, and the lowest scores (1 and 2) if they were not involved in any stage of the innovation. Each engineer's score is the highest score received across all 37 innovations, based on agreement among the R&D director and four chief engineers.

Network constraint was calculated following the routine in UCINet, which assumes that an actor spends more time and energy on an alter if the alter also cites the actor; ego's network was input as raw network data including anyone the ego nominated and anyone who listed the ego as an alter. The whole-network constraint score was used for each communication partner and for the focal actor's own network structure. Low scores indicate brokers who span structural holes, high scores indicate non-brokers.

variable_name: First-time order for a fast ferry
description: The dependent variable in the main analysis is the event of placing a first-time order for a fast ferry. Order and building dates are reported to the nearest month and the event times in the analysis are given with a month's precision. Firm observations are split annually to update covariates and split again within the year whenever needed to update the diffusion covariates. A firm remains at risk of adoption until it orders a fast ferry or no longer owns other passenger ships.

A cumulative count of fast ferry orders placed by firms headquartered in the focal firm's nation, used to capture the information from the adoption decisions of proximate firms. The diffusion variables are restricted to the focal nation and are cumulative counts of orders and deliveries within each nation, with the nation based on the firm headquarter. In Models 5, 9, 12 and 13 the counts are weighted by a decay factor of 0.9 per year so that temporally distant adoptions are treated as less salient.

A cumulative count of deliveries of newly built fast ferries to firms in the focal firm's nation. Delivery is separated from order because the time lag between ordering and finishing a ship allows the adopter to operate the ship and learn its true value, information that may leak to other firms. Because the sum of proximate and non-proximate adoptions is controlled through the time dependence, the coefficient shows how much greater the effect of a proximate delivery is than that of a non-proximate one.

A cumulative count of secondhand fast ferries received into the focal firm's nation, examined as an alternative specification of the effect of deliveries. Although such sales are less common than new sales and are likely to be at a price discount, they may also prove informative for other shipping firms.

A cumulative count of fast ferries sold by their original buyer among firms headquartered in the focal firm's nation. Sales by the original buyer are examined because such sales are likely to involve the greatest economic losses, and a sale is treated as a noisy negative signal of the innovation's value. The coefficient shows how much greater the effect of a proximate sale is than that of a non-proximate one.

Recorded when a firm sells its last fast ferry. Abandonments are less common than sales but may be a stronger signal of disappointment and hence have greater influence over other firms. When a firm is recorded as selling its last fast ferry and not owning any other vessel subsequently, no abandonment event is recorded because the firm may have failed rather than voluntarily sold the vessel.

A count of the number of firms at which more than one member of the founding team had worked, constructed from the career histories of individual team members. The most recent three firms for which each founder had worked were used. The measure was calculated at founding and is not time-varying. For the firm growth analysis a median split was used, coding common prior company affiliation as 1 if any of the founders had worked at the same prior company.

A count of the number of discrete prior firms reported by all the members of a given founding team, constructed from the career histories of individual team members. All discrete firms were included, even those where founders' experience overlapped, because ideas come from the full range of prior companies in which founders have worked. For the firm growth analysis a median split was used, coding diverse prior company affiliation as 1 if the founding team had worked at three or more unique prior companies.

The strategic behaviors and intentions that comprised firm strategy were examined, with founders reconstructing early firm actions in the interviews. A firm was coded as having an exploration strategy (exploration = 1, otherwise = 0) if it had a technical innovator strategy; innovators seek to gain first-mover advantages by winning technology races. Coding was done by two people in an iterative fashion using a list of phrases and words and supplemented by early press reports, product announcements, business plans, and prospectuses; disagreements were reconciled with a third person.

Two independent coders examined the interview transcripts to measure whether a firm's founding idea changed. The coding scheme for the founding idea included 'stable,' 'elaborated,' 'one major restart,' 'multiple ideas pursued,' and 'multiple ideas considered.' The variable was coded 1 if an initial idea changed and 0 if the idea was stable or elaborated. The interviews did not contain enough information to adequately code this variable for a sizeable number of firms, leaving only 68 observations in the relevant model.

An exploitation strategy was coded as present (exploitation = 1, otherwise = 0) if a firm had an enhancer or low-cost strategy. Enhancer firms seek to produce products similar to those of other companies but develop general modifications or enhancements to gain competitive advantage, and low-cost producers seek cost advantages through efficient production techniques, relationships with low-cost suppliers, or economies of scale. Because the enhancer and cost strategies both revolve around extending existing products or services, they were grouped together; the remaining firms had marketing or hybrid strategies.

Firms with exploitation strategies are likely to ship products more quickly, and time to first product shipment was used as an additional measure of exploitation. The dates of product shipment came from a founder survey; not all founders completed the survey, but interviews and other company data were used to supplement when possible. Event history analysis was used to examine time to first product.

Firm growth was measured as growth in employees, and a proportional firm growth measure was created; the formula block for this measure is not readable in the text provided. Number of employees was collected at the end of each year from survey and archival sources. Growth was examined with a panel random-effects regression in which teams with high common and high diverse prior affiliations were compared with other teams.

variable_name: Common and diverse prior company affiliations both high
description: Dummy variable identifying founding teams whose common and diverse prior company affiliations were both high: common prior company affiliation was coded 1 if any of the founders had worked at the same prior company, and diverse prior company affiliation was coded 1 if the founding team had worked at three or more unique prior companies. Twenty-two percent of the firms were coded into this category. In the firm growth models this category was included alone (model 2) or with the low diverse/low common category as the omitted category (model 3).

Total pounds of toxic chemical emissions each firm reported to the EPA's Toxic Release Inventory as production waste, transfers, and releases. To reduce the impact of outliers on the results, the authors take the log after adding 1. The TRI data were obtained from the Corporate Environmental Profiles Directory, which aggregates facility-level data from a variety of EPA databases.

Dummy variable coded 1 for firms whose initial KLD environmental ratings consisted only of concerns (no strengths), and 0 otherwise. A second dummy, initial rating mixed or good, was created to identify firms whose initial environmental ratings consisted only of strengths, of both strengths and concerns, or of neither strengths nor concerns. In the empirical analysis these firm-level variables are interacted with KLD rated, a time-varying dummy coded 1 in years in which firms were rated by KLD and 0 otherwise.
time_window: year in which the firm was first rated by KLD

description: Dichotomous variable coded 1 for companies with a primary standard industrial classification (SIC) code of mining (SIC 10), oil exploration (13), paper (26), chemical and allied products (28), petroleum refining (29), metals (33), or utilities (49), and 0 otherwise. A second dichotomous variable, low environmentally regulated, applies the inverse of this coding scheme.

Environmental efficiency is operationalized as the ratio of each firm's toxic chemical emissions to revenues. Each firm's average ratio during 1999-2000, the two-year period immediately before any of the firms in the sample were rated by KLD, was compared with the corresponding industry median value during that period. Less environmentally efficient was coded 1 for firms with a ratio that exceeded the industry median, and more environmentally efficient was coded 1 for firms with ratios below the industry median.

Constructed to capture firms' inadequate experience in dealing with the CP program. A plant that was the first to become certified in the CP program within the company was coded as 1; otherwise it was coded as 0. 99 firms had more than one plant join the program; 319 sampled plants were owned by these companies.

For each power plant, the number of environmental violations detected through online monitoring and regular on-site inspections in the three years before joining the CP program. These data were collected from local EPBs and a leading environmental NGO.
time_window: three years before joining the CP program

description: Plants using novel technologies (i.e., those that use relatively clean fuel sources, such as natural gas, biomass, and biogas) were coded as 1, while plants using established technologies (i.e., coal-fired plants burning 'brown' coal) were coded as 0. Classification followed the literature and the technology classifications within China's power sector.
A continuous variable based on the proportion of majority shareholders that are SOEs or directly owned by the government.

A dummy coded as 1 if a power plant hired a public intermediary (e.g., local EPB-affiliated service center and government-sponsored environmental associations) to audit its CP program implementation and 0 if it hired a private intermediary (e.g., university lab, industrial association, or private consulting firm). This is a one-time measure for each plant since there is no mandate on certification renewal. Among the 530 plants, 196 selected public intermediaries and 334 chose private ones.
time_window: at the time of CP program participation

description: Coded as 1 if a power plant filed a CP application within the three years from early 2005 to 2007, when the State Environmental Protection Administration initiated three campaigns to target major polluting industries including the power sector, and 0 otherwise. The author focuses on regulatory changes that always happen to tighten requirements.

Deemed equal to 1 if a sampled plant was located in a so-called National Environmental Model City (NEMC) or an NEMC-to-be within two years of joining the CP program, and 0 otherwise. The NEMC policy was initiated in 1996 to encourage local political leaders to address pollution and aim for sustainable urban development.
time_window: within two years of joining the CP program

description: The National Economic Research Institute (NERI) index of marketization is used, specifically its first dimension, government and market relations. This dimension captures the business costs of dealing with governmental control, the proportion of resource allocation by the market, and reduction in government interference in the business sector. The higher the index, the more noninterventionist the government is.

Organizational structure was measured by presenting respondents with descriptions and simplified organization charts of the various types of structure and asking them to select that which best described their organization. This variable represents the operating structure, which can be different from the legal structure of MNCs. Ten different types of structure were identified in the sample.

A grouping formed by combining structures into categories that contain or exclude a given structural dimension. The structures containing the PD dimension are the PD structure, the FD × PD matrix, the PD × GR matrix, and the Tensor structure; the remaining structures lack this dimension.

A grouping formed by combining structures into categories that contain or exclude a given structural dimension. It distinguishes firms whose structures contain an international division dimension from firms with other structures.

A grouping formed by combining structures into categories that contain or exclude a given structural dimension. The structures containing the GR dimension are the GR structure, the FD × GR matrix, the PD × GR matrix, and the Tensor structure; the remaining structures lack this dimension.

variable_name: Worldwide functional division or worldwide product division dimension (FD/PD)
description: A grouping formed by combining structures into categories that contain or exclude a given structural dimension. It distinguishes firms whose structures contain a worldwide functional division dimension or a worldwide product division dimension from firms without such dimensions.

Foreign product diversity was measured by the number of 5-digit product classes associated with the company (taken from the Hoppenstedt classification system). This measure of total company product diversity was used, because there is no official data available on a firm's foreign product diversity. The authors argue it is reasonable to believe that foreign product diversity and total company product diversity are highly correlated in most German firms with foreign sales.
Size of foreign operations was measured by the percentage of a company's sales occurring outside of the parent country.
Size of foreign manufacturing was measured by the percentage of a company's manufacturing occurring outside of the parent country.

Intracompany transfers was measured by adding the percentage of the parent company's procurement of final and intermediate products that are sourced from the company's foreign operations to the percentage of the parent company's sales which are transfers to the company's foreign operations. It measures total intracompany transfers into and out of the parent company rather than transfers at the subsidiary level.
Size of foreign R&D was measured by the percentage of the company's R&D employees working outside of the parent country.

The roles of executives responsible for decision making were coded from the client firms' annual reports (10-K/20-F) and archival webpages for the year prior to the formation of the alliance. The authors identified whether multiple therapeutic area leads reported to separate heads on the top management team, or whether the firm's R&D or research groups reported to a single head on the top management team. The variable took a value of one when there was a single R&D head on the top management team overseeing all the R&D-related activities of the firm, and zero otherwise. Coding was replicated by an independent research associate and discrepancies were resolved by discussion among the research team.
time_window: year prior to the formation of the alliance

description: The authors counted the client's IP rights rather than downstream rights or those of the R&D startup, focusing on eight distinct IP rights commonly outlined in such contracts. Using contract data available from Cortellis, they manually coded the proportion of control rights allocated to the client firms, i.e., the sum of the coded rights divided by eight, without assigning specific weights to individual rights.

The count measure for Vertical Alliance Scope captured the number of different functional activities that an alliance performed. The authors also calculated the vertical scope of an alliance as a categorical variable.

The authors calculated the horizontal scope of an alliance by counting the number of therapeutic areas involved in the deal. In the biopharmaceutical industry each therapeutic area is considered a different product market, and firms ally with each other in one or more product markets; the number of therapeutic areas involved in a particular deal was therefore used as the measure.

The authors examined the contracts signed by the partners and identified deals in which the partners were jointly working on R&D, identifying terms such as 'codevelopment' and 'collaboration for research'. They complemented this classification with Recap's classification of the types of activities performed in each deal (codevelopment, copromotion, comarketing, codistribution, and collaboration). Technology interdependence is a binary variable taking the value of one if the partners were jointly involved in collaboration on research and codevelopment, and zero otherwise.
Knowledge breadth was calculated as the number of distinct technological classes represented in a firm's patent portfolio, reflecting the diversity of knowledge areas leveraged by the client firm.

Patent originality is calculated as a function of the technological knowledge referenced in a patent, using the formula Originality_i = 1 - sum over j of t_ij squared, where t_ij represents the proportion of citations made by patent i to patents that belong to patent class j. A lower originality score indicates that a patent cites a concentrated set of technological domains, reflecting a narrower, more localized search approach, whereas a higher score signifies that the patent draws on a broader array of technological fields.

Patent generality was calculated with the formula Generality_i = 1 - sum over j of s_ij squared, where s_ij represents the proportion of citations made to patent i that belong to patent class j. A high generality score indicates that a patent is cited across a broad range of technological domains, suggesting its widespread applicability.

variable_name: Innovative search magnitude at time t
description: Calculated as the change in R&D expenditures between time t and time t-1, divided by R&D expenditures at time t-1. The authors state that the measure captures a firm's R&D spending compared to its standard allocations to R&D, thereby reflecting search efforts that deviate from routines. The higher the value, the higher the magnitude of the firm's overall search efforts.

variable_name: Innovative search scope at time t
description: Following Katila and Ahuja (2002), measured by assessing the share of citations in a focal year's citations that could not be found in the previous five years' list of patents and citations by that firm. For example, if a firm applies for five patents in a given year and each cites five additional patents, the total citation number is 25; if 5 of these 25 citations are new, the search scope is 5 divided by 25, or 0.2. Values range from 0 to 1.
time_window: previous five years relative to the focal year

variable_name: Innovative search depth at time t
description: Following Katila and Ahuja (2002), measured by calculating the number of times that, on the average, each citation in year t was repeatedly used during the past five years. For example, if five citations used at time t had been previously used and had appeared a total of 2, 1, 2, 2, and 2 times in the five years preceding the focal year, then the total repetition count is 9 and the search depth for the focal year is 9 divided by 25, or 0.36. Values cannot be negative.
time_window: previous five years relative to the focal year

description: A firm was coded as 0 if its performance was above or equal to aspiration, and the length of the underperforming period was used for underperforming firms. For example, a firm would be coded as 1 if it had been underperforming for 1 year, 2 if it had been underperforming for 2 consecutive years, and so on. The variable is measured at t-1.

Return on assets (ROA), used as a measure of performance, capturing efficiency. This variable is lagged 1 year relative to the dependent variable. Together with aspiration it is used to determine whether and for how long a firm is underperforming.

Industry aspiration at t-1 is measured as the median performance of firms in the same industry as the focal firm at t-2. The comparison industry was identified from COMPUSTAT data using firms in the same 4-digit SIC code as the focal firm. The paper focuses only on the firm's social aspiration.

A composite index for each firm, constructed by multiplying the usage score for each strategic action by its risk score and averaging these products across all nine items. CEOs rated each of nine strategic actions on the extent of risk the firm faces from increasing investment in it (1 = very low risk; 7 = very high risk) and on the extent to which the firm engages in it (1 = never used; 7 = frequently used). The mathematical specification is given in a formula block that was not extracted from the paper; the text states that greater usage of high-risk actions produces a higher value, while greater usage of lower-risk actions or minimal usage of high-risk actions produces a lower value. The authors report an inter-rater correlation of 0.91 across two random subsamples and a Cronbach's alpha of 0.51 for the nine items.
scale: seven-point response scales for usage and perceived risk; composite index
time_window: survey administered in the third and fourth quarters of 1998

description: CEOs indicated for each of five forms of compensation the extent to which this pay item has varied over the years since the IPO, on a six-point scale (1 = does not vary from year to year; 6 = is extremely variable over time; almost unpredictable). The variability scores were weighted by the percentage of each form of pay CEOs allocate to essential expenses and summed across the five forms of pay. A high score corresponds to high variability in those elements of compensation that are largely devoted to essential expenses. The authors write the formula as the sum over the five pay forms of (allocation to essential pay times variability of pay).
scale: six-point scale (1 = does not vary from year to year; 6 = extremely variable over time; almost unpredictable)

description: CEOs indicated for each of five forms of compensation the extent to which each type of pay has faced a chance of loss since the IPO, on a six-point scale (1 = no downside risk to my pay; 6 = extremely high downside risk to my pay). The downside risk ratings were multiplied by the percentage of each form of pay allocated to essential expenses and summed across the five types of pay. The higher the value of this index, the greater the risk to pay that is largely devoted to essential expenses. The authors write the formula as the sum over the five pay forms of (allocation to essential pay times downside risk of pay).
scale: six-point scale (1 = no downside risk to my pay; 6 = extremely high downside risk to my pay)

description: A single survey item asked CEOs about threats to their employment in recent years, with agreement indicated on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree) to the statement 'There were years when I believed my employment security was at risk.' Answers were recoded into a dummy variable where one indicates CEOs who responded with 'strongly agree' and zero represents those who selected answers 1 through 6 on the scale. The authors concentrated on the extreme case to ensure they captured those for whom termination was most likely. External validation showed the item correlated with prior CEO departures, with failure to satisfy performance targets, and negatively with average ROA.
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree), recoded to a dummy
time_window: recent years, reported in the 1998 survey

description: The value of stock options held by CEOs, taken as the average value of options held as reported in the firm's proxy statement over three years (1995-97). The value of stock options was calculated by multiplying the number of stock options held against the difference between the stock price and the exercise price of the options at year-end. For firms with less than three years of data the average was based on available data, so some values are based on one or two years of data.

variable_name: Current capability relevance (composite degree of relevance, CDR)
description: The CDR of a firm is the normalized sum of the similarity indices across all the firm's products in each year. Each product's similarity index is the cosine of the angle between the vector indicating the presence of that product across a sample of entrants and the vector indicating the presence of the focal product, networking switches; it is the normalized count of the entrants that produce both products. The similarity indices are sorted in descending order and the dot product with the firm's product-presence vector is rescaled by K so that the maximum attainable value of the CDR is 1 and the minimum is 0.

The composite degree of relevance of a firm as measured at the time of market emergence, using the same index of similarity and aggregation as for current capability relevance. It is set at the time of market emergence and distinguishes the firm's initial condition from its later, annually measured capability relevance.

Estimated under a duration model in a hazard-rate framework. The entry event takes the value of 1 if the firm becomes an entrant, and for the years prior to the entry event the state variable stays constant at 0. The duration variable is the number of years elapsed since market emergence before a firm's entry event or censoring at the end of the study. The entry rate at time t is the derivative of the entry probability by time t, so earlier entry corresponds to a higher entry rate.

Time since market emergence, in years, entered as t in the model predicting a firm's current capability relevance and in the hazard model of entry. In the current capability relevance model it also enters as an interaction with initial capability relevance.

The number of new drugs with NCEs that appeared in the firm's current drug portfolio, as reported in the Pharmaprojects database. Counted using a 3-year moving average (t, t+1, t+2) to smooth out annual fluctuations. An NCE is a completely new chemical entity whose medical effects were previously unknown, so NCE-based products represent the exploration of novel knowledge.

A drug was recognized as a failure if its final recorded status in the Pharmaprojects database indicated that the firm permanently discontinued the drug development; the reason for failure was checked in Pharmaprojects and Trialtrove so that drugs strategically discontinued by the firm were not counted. Failure is the number of drug discontinuations during the development stage (preclinical, Phase 1, Phase 2, and Phase 3 testing) for the focal firm, measured as a 3-year moving average (t-3, t-2, t-1) to smooth out annual fluctuations.

Inventors were first scored on patent productivity using a function of the number of patents for which the scientist applied by year t, the inventor's tenure in the industry (total years since first patent application in the sample), and the average forward citations of the inventor's patents by year t. Inventors whose individual productivity was greater than two SDs above the mean were categorized as prolific. This yielded 294 prolific inventors out of 18,041 inventors (about 2%), employed by 96 of the 457 firms. The published formula for the productivity function is unreadable in the text as provided.

Using co-invention patent data, collaborative strength is the level of co-invention frequency between a prolific inventor and his or her colleagues in the firm in a prior 5-year window, computed as the average level of co-invention frequency between prolific inventors and their colleagues in the firm. The frequency with which prolific inventor i co-invents with inventor j is coded from 0 to 4. The prolific inventor's collaborative strength is aggregated to the firm level by averaging the collaborative strength of all prolific inventors at a focal firm in a specific year. The published formula is unreadable in the text as provided.

A prolific inventor's tenure is inventor i's organizational tenure in the firm, defined as the total number of years since inventor i's first patent application in the firm. It is computed at the firm level as the average tenure of all prolific inventors at a focal firm in a specific year t.

The intangible asset stock at the beginning of a period is built as the eroded asset stock from the prior period plus current period investments conditioned by time compression diseconomy and asset mass efficiency. The accumulation expression is expanded over one through ten years of prior R&D investment (T1-T10) and substituted into the firm's final goods-production function so that the accumulation coefficients and the stock's contribution to output are estimated simultaneously. Because the coefficients generating the stock cannot be distinguished econometrically from the contribution of the stock to output, the estimated accumulation vector represents the true accumulation vector inclusive of output elasticity. The estimated coefficients are also applied to firms' actual R&D expenditures over time to compute each firm's asset stock.
time_window: one to ten years of prior R&D investment

description: Current year spending on R&D, entering the accumulation function as the flow that combines with the existing asset stock to create additional intangible assets. It is the flow counterpart of the knowledge stock in the comparison between stock and flow models.

Total firm sales in the observation year, used as the dependent variable of the firm's final goods-production function. Output in a given year is a function of the current knowledge stock, physical capital, labor and industry spillovers.

Annual erosion of the intangible asset stock in the accumulation function, estimated jointly with the production function in each of the ten accumulation models. The estimate is 0.88, a very high level of asset erosion corresponding to complete write-off of new investments within three years, which indicates that the restriction on allowed years of accumulation is nonbinding beyond the T3 model.

Coefficient on current period investment in the accumulation function, modeled as a concave function of current period investment so that increases in investment raise the asset stock at a decreasing rate; it is bounded between zero and one in estimation. The estimate is 0.095, above the coefficient in the flow model but within normal ranges for R&D elasticity.

Coefficient capturing economies of scale in producing intangible asset stock from existing asset stock, modeled as an accelerator of current period investment by the prior period's asset stock and bounded between zero and one in estimation. The coefficient on asset mass is zero across all ten models, which the authors treat as compelling evidence that there are no asset mass efficiencies.

The accumulation process is characterized by three parameters of the intangible asset accumulation function, estimated jointly with the production function: asset erosion, time compression diseconomy and asset mass efficiency. Their sign and significance are used to judge the process.

Commitment was measured with a 3-item scale. Items asked whether the dealer would like to discontinue carrying the manufacturer's product, whether the dealer is very committed to carrying the manufacturer's products, and whether the dealer has a minimal commitment to the manufacturer. The first and third items are reverse scored, and all items use a 5-point strongly disagree/strongly agree scale.

Coordination was measured with a 3-item scale; one item had a low item-to-total correlation and was dropped from the analysis, leaving two items. Responses use a 5-point strongly disagree/strongly agree scale.

Trust was measured with a 3-item scale using a 5-point strongly disagree/strongly agree response format. The items cover the belief that the manufacturer's decisions will benefit the dealer's business, the feeling of getting a fair deal, and the degree of harmony in the relationship.

Interdependence was measured with a two-item scale that examined the ease with which each party could switch to a new trading partner. Both items are reverse scored, so that as the sum of the two items increases, interdependence in the relationship increases. Items use a 5-point strongly disagree/strongly agree scale.

Communication quality was assessed with a 5-item scale asking dealers to what extent they feel their communication with the manufacturer is timely, accurate, adequate, complete, and credible. Each item is a 5-point semantic differential with the unfavorable pole at one end and the favorable pole at the other.

Participation was measured with a 4-item scale that tapped the extent to which the dealer's input was solicited by the manufacturer for planning purposes. Items use a 5-point strongly disagree/strongly agree format.

Information sharing tapped the extent to which partners kept each other informed about important issues on a voluntary basis and was initially assessed with an 8-item scale. Two items were dropped during initial reliability assessment: the two items assessing the manufacturer's sharing of information with the dealer did not exhibit clean loadings and loaded more strongly on the other communication behavior measures. Four items were retained for the dealer's information sharing with the manufacturer (coefficient alpha = 0.68), using a 5-point strongly disagree/strongly agree format.

Joint problem solving was measured as a single composite indicator. Respondents were asked, assuming that some conflict exists over program and policy issues, how frequently joint problem solving is used to resolve such conflict, on a 5-point very infrequently/very frequently scale. Because these items cover a spectrum of conflict resolution modes, traditional reliability analysis was not appropriate.

Persuasion was measured as a single composite indicator asking how frequently persuasive attempts by either party are used to resolve conflict. Responses use a 5-point very infrequently/very frequently scale.

Two conflict resolution items, harsh words and manufacturer-imposed domination, exhibited a relatively high intercorrelation and were summed and labeled Severe Conflict Resolution. Each item asked how frequently the method is used to resolve conflict over program and policy issues, on a 5-point very infrequently/very frequently scale.
scale: 5-point (very infrequently to very frequently), items summed

description: Arbitration was measured as a single composite indicator asking how frequently outside arbitration is used to resolve conflict over program and policy issues. Responses use a 5-point very infrequently/very frequently scale.

Smoothing over the problem was measured as a single composite indicator asking how frequently the method is used to resolve conflict over program and policy issues. Responses use a 5-point very infrequently/very frequently scale.

Two objective measures of sales volume were taken; one was a direct measure and one was indirectly computed from two other items. The direct measure asked the dealer for the approximate volume of sales of this manufacturer's product on a monthly basis (seven categories); the indirect measure multiplied the dealer's total monthly sales (seven categories) by the percent of total dealership sales coming from this manufacturer's product. The sales measures were adjusted for the size of the dealer in terms of number of employees, log-transformed to account for the increasing size of the categories, and summed to form one measure, Dyadic Sales.
scale: seven categories for sales items; percent in 10% increments; measure is a logged scale

description: A factor analysis of the satisfaction items resulted in a two-factor solution. The larger factor, comprised of the satisfaction items other than profit and margins, was termed Satisfaction with Manufacturer Support. Dealers rated how satisfied they are with aspects of the relationship with the manufacturer on a 5-point very dissatisfied/very satisfied scale.

The second satisfaction factor was comprised of the two items tapping satisfaction with profit and margins and was termed 'Satisfaction and Profit'. One item asks how satisfied the dealer is with profit on sales of the manufacturer's product on a 5-point very dissatisfied/very satisfied scale; the other asks how the manufacturer's product stacks up to its closest competitors on reseller margins, on a lower/higher scale.

The average proportion of inpatient care paid for by non-Medicare/Medicaid (private) sources, compared for hospitals that survived and hospitals that closed. In 1986 Medicare inpatient days as a proportion of total inpatient days was 47 percent nationally while Medicaid accounted for an average 5.8 percent of all inpatient days nationally. The closed hospitals averaged 34 percent non-Medicare/Medicaid inpatient days versus 48 percent for survivors.

The 1986 occupancy rate of each hospital, averaged separately for hospitals that remained open through 1991 and those that closed. The national average for 1986 was 60.67 percent; the average occupancy rate for survivors was 65 percent and the average for closed hospitals was 48 percent.

Whether or not the hospital offers obstetric services, used as the indicator of the range of services in the test of Hypothesis 3. Hospitals were categorized along two dimensions: whether or not they offer obstetric services and whether they remained open through 1991.

Indicates whether the hospital closed in the Chicago metropolitan area between 1986 and 1991 rather than remaining open through 1991. To identify the hospitals that had failed, closures in the Chicago metropolitan area from 1986 through 1991 were examined; of the closures recorded between 1985 and 1991, 14 are used for the hypothesis tests and one closed hospital outside the city limits was added, while hospitals that closed in 1985 (before the operating period used in the cost estimation) were excluded.

Overall short-run economies of scale are measured as the reciprocal of the sum of the cost elasticities with respect to each output, evaluated at the mean of the data. Values greater than one indicate increasing returns and values less than one decreasing returns. The estimated value was 1.19, implying increasing short-run returns to scale near the average level of outputs and input prices.

Local economies of scope are tested at the point of approximation (the mean levels of input and output variables); Denny and Pinto showed that the sign of the scope expression is determined by a combination of the second-order and first-order output parameters, and local economies of scope are indicated when that expression is less than zero. The computation is carried out for all pairs of the five output variables, and only the pair of medical and obstetric services is statistically significant.

The dependent variable for the consumer non-durable sample is the relative market share of business i, used instead of market share because the PIMS database pools cross-sectional data from businesses across different industries. The authors state that the PIMS study defines relative market share for business 'i' from the market share of business 'i' and the market shares of its three largest competitors; the printed formula itself is not readable in the available text. A Goldfeld and Quandt test of homoscedasticity made a log transformation of the dependent variable necessary.

Relative level of effort on the breadth of product line dimension, where the level of effort of the business is assessed as relatively more, comparable or less than the average for leading competitors (the three largest competitors). These categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables, with competitive parity as the reference level.

Relative product quality was originally operationalized as an index measure with the average for leading competitors set at 100, and was transformed for this study into three broad categories: superior, comparable and inferior. Cut points were set at levels such that approximately a third of the observations were assigned to each category. The categories correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage and enter the regression through two dummy variables with parity as the reference level.

variable_name: relative level of new product activity
description: Originally an index measure with the average for leading competitors equal to 100, transformed for this study into three categories of relative new product activity: higher, comparable and lower. Cut points were set so that roughly a third of the observations fell into each category. The categories enter the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

Relative level of customer service quality, assessed as relatively more, comparable or less than the average for leading competitors. The categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

Relative level of sales force expenditure, assessed as relatively more, comparable or less than the average for the three largest competitors. The categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

Relative level of advertising expenditure, assessed as relatively more, comparable or less than the average for the three largest competitors. The categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

Relative level of sales promotion expenditure, assessed as relatively more, comparable or less than the average for the three largest competitors. The categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

Relative price was originally an index measure with the average for leading competitors equal to 100 and was transformed for this study into three broad categories: lower, comparable and higher. Cut points were set so that approximately a third of the observations were assigned to each category. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables, and the authors state that no attempt is made to label the price variable as either a success producer or a failure preventer.

variable_name: relative degree of forward vertical integration
description: Relative degree of forward vertical integration, assessed as relatively more, comparable or less than the average for the three largest competitors, the only variable representing the distribution component of the marketing mix in the model. The categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

The dependent variable for the capital goods sample is the relative market share of business i, defined by the PIMS study from the market share of business 'i' and the market shares of its three largest competitors. The relative rather than absolute measure is used because the PIMS database pools cross-sectional data from businesses across different industries. The dependent variable was log-transformed because a test of homoscedasticity required it.

Relative level of effort on the breadth of product line dimension for the capital goods sample, assessed as relatively more, comparable or less than the average for leading competitors (the three largest competitors). The categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

Cut points were set so that roughly a third of the observations fell into each category. The categories enter the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

description: Relative level of new product activity, originally an index measure with the average for leading competitors equal to 100 and transformed into three categories: higher, comparable and lower. Cut points were set so that approximately a third of the observations were assigned to each category. The categories enter the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

The categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

The categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

Relative level of sales promotion expenditure, assessed as relatively more, comparable or less than the average for the three largest competitors. The categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage. The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

The variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level, and the authors do not classify price as either a success producer or a failure preventer.

variable_name: relative degree of forward vertical integration
description: Relative degree of forward vertical integration, assessed as relatively more, comparable or less than the average for the three largest competitors; it is the only variable representing the distribution component of the marketing mix in the model. The categories roughly correspond to competitive advantage, parity and disadvantage, and the variable enters the regression through two dummy variables with competitive parity as the reference level.

A binary coach-year variable coded 1 for a particular coach-year if the individual had worked with a high-reputation leader for a year and was no longer working on the same staff, and 0 otherwise. High-reputation leaders were head coaches coded annually as having reached at least one of five reputational milestones: winning one or more Super Bowls; appearing in two or more Super Bowls; winning five or more playoff games; appearing in 10 or more playoff games; winning 100 or more regular season games. If an acolyte later returned to work with the same high-reputation leader, the variable was coded 0 for the years in which the two individuals remained on the same staff.

Each coach's degree centrality within the network of NFL coaches in a particular year. The network nodes comprised all coaches named on NFL start-of-season rosters for that year. A tie existed between two nodes if the two coaches had worked together for at least one year.

The number of years of NFL coaching experience prior to the start of the focal year. It is used as a second measure of evaluative certainty, on the reasoning that the more years an individual has worked in the industry, the more information there is concerning performance.
time_window: prior to the start of the focal year

description: The number of different teams that an individual had coached for prior to the focal year. It is used as a third measure of evaluative certainty, on the reasoning that the greater the number of different organizations within the industry an individual has worked for, the more sources of information there are likely to be concerning performance.

A binary coach-year variable coded 1 for a given coach-year if the acolyte was coded as 1 and the high-reputation leader's experience matched the acolyte's experience up to that point in time. High-reputation leaders were first coded as having knowledge in one or more of offense, defense, or special teams based on their prior coordinator or position-coach work, and the same procedure was repeated for each acolyte. The three binary variables (acolyte: knowledge match, acolyte: no knowledge match, non-acolyte) are mutually exclusive, and non-acolytes were treated as the reference category and omitted from the analyses.
time_window: experience up to that point in time

description: All coaching positions were coded according to a five-level hierarchical scale reflective of coaching tiers that are well established in the NFL: head coach (level 1), assistant head coach (level 2), coordinator (level 3), position coach (level 4), and assistant position coach or other (level 5). An overall binary coach-year promotion variable was coded as 1 in a particular year if an individual worked at a level higher than that of the previous year, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: coach-year, compared to the previous year

description: For every promotion in the data the authors determined the eventual result. A promoted individual was treated as remaining in the same role for as long as he remained with the same team and at the same coaching level; when at least one of these criteria changed, the role was treated as concluded and the individual's next NFL coaching role was coded. A positive outcome was coded as being a further promotion or lateral move, and a negative outcome as being a demotion (taking a lower-level position at the same or another team).
scale: binary: positive (further promotion or lateral move) vs. negative (demotion)
time_window: from the promotion until the role concluded

description: Each first partner's reputation was calculated by dividing the number of IPOs achieved in year t by the number of all companies that were added to the VC portfolio over the five years preceding time t; the scores were then summed across the partners in the newcomer's first syndicate. First partners are the coinvestor(s) in the first recorded syndicated investment in which the newcomer took part, identified by sorting all the newcomer's investments by date. The variable enters the analyses as a time invariant covariate because it is observed at the time of the newcomer's entry into the network.
time_window: Observed at the time of the newcomer's entry into the network (t entry); IPO counts in year t scaled by portfolio additions over t-5

description: After identifying all the members of the newcomer's first syndicate, the authors traced their co-investments in the five-year window preceding the formation of the syndicate with the newcomer. They then calculated the valued density of relations among the first partners, excluding the newcomer: this measure sums all the first partners' past relationships in the respective period and divides this number by the number of possible dyads between these partners (n(n-1)/2, where n represents the number of the newcomer's first partners). The variable is observed at the time of the newcomer's entry into the network.
time_window: Five-year window preceding the formation of the syndicate with the newcomer

description: Bonacich's (1987) centrality measure of a VC firm's network status, in which a firm's status depends on the number of other VC firms with which it syndicated and on the status of those firms, which is in turn contingent on the status of their partners, and so on. The parameter alpha is an arbitrary scaling coefficient and beta, the degree to which the centrality of a firm is a function of the centralities of other firms, was set as the reciprocal (inverse) of the largest eigenvalue of the relational matrix. Scores were calculated for each VC firm in the network and normalized by the maximum status score in the sample for the respective year, so that the highest status firm in the sample for any given year has a score equal to one. The dependent variable is measured at t + 1 in each column.
scale: normalized so that the highest status score in a year equals one (limited between zero and one)

description: A weighted average of the LBD rates of all of firm i's 4-digit SIC code industries reported in the Historical Segments data of Compustat. The weight for each industry is the ratio of sales from that industry to total sales. The industry LBD rates are the 'Learning Coefficients' that Balasubramanian and Lieberman (2011) calculated for the U.S. manufacturing industries using plant-level data from the Censuses of Manufacturing and the Annual Surveys of Manufactures over 1972-1996, estimated with the Olley-Pakes method rather than ordinary least squares. Higher learning coefficients mean higher sensitivity of value added in manufacturing to prior cumulative output, that is, higher intensity of LBD in manufacturing in the industry.
time_window: LBD rates estimated from 1972-1996 data and treated as fixed over the 1997-2001 observation window

description: Measured by the absolute difference between LBD Ratei and the LBD rate in target industry j. It is constructed for each firm-target industry dyad, considering each firm at risk of entering each of the 357 manufacturing industries for which LBD rates were available if it is not already present in the industry.

Coded as one if firm i is reported as being involved in at least one new industry in year t where it was not in year t-1 and zero otherwise. Entries by the sample firms are captured following prior research on diversifying entries by using the changes in the 4-digit SIC codes reported in the Historical Segments data in Compustat.

Coded as one if firm i is reported as being involved in target industry j in year t while it was not in year t-1 and zero otherwise. Entries are captured with the changes in the 4-digit SIC codes reported in the Historical Segments data in Compustat; only manufacturing industries were considered as target industries because LBD rates were available only for them.

Measured on a scale of 1 to 10 as the average of recruiters' ratings of a school on 13 attributes related to student quality. The Cronbach's alpha for the measure was .98. Because the unit of analysis was the organization, the score for each school was calculated as the average of the individual scores of all recruiters who rated that school; 92 schools were ranked by more than one recruiter and the mean interrater agreement (rwg) across those schools was .95.

Measured by the number of recruiters that nominated a given school. Recruiters were invited to select three schools they would like to rate, and the authors reasoned that recruiters would choose to rate the schools most prominent in their minds; across the 1,600 recruiters this nomination procedure captures the relative prominence of business schools among corporate recruiters as a stakeholder group.

Measured by the mean starting base salary, not including bonuses or other benefits, received by each school's MBA graduates in 2000, as reported in U.S. News & World Report (2001). This objective measure of recruiters' economic choices was adjusted for cost-of-living differences among geographic regions by multiplying each school's mean starting base salary by the cost-of-living index score for that school's geographic region.

Measured as the average GMAT scores of students entering MBA programs in 1998 and 1999, as reported in U.S. News & World Report. Incoming students constitute the major resource input in the educational process of an MBA program, and one of the main admission criteria is applicants' scores on standardized scholastic aptitude tests such as the GMAT.

Measured as the average number of years of academic experience possessed by a business school's faculty. The authors generated a data set of over 9,000 full-time faculty in the 107 sample schools and calculated the average level of academic experience for each school as the average number of years prior to 2000 that had elapsed since the members of the full-time faculty had received their Ph.D. degrees.

Measured by a business school's rank in BusinessWeek's 1998 rankings, used because it is the oldest and best-established ranking of U.S. business schools and was the most recent listing at the time recruiters completed the survey. For the ranked schools the actual position was used (e.g., first, second, third), and a constant was assigned to the unranked schools.
scale: rank position first, second, third, ... plus a constant for unranked schools

description: Measured as faculty publications in premier journals, computed as the sum of the total number of publications of the faculty of a business school over the five years (1996-2000) prior to the survey. Two forms were captured: research publications in premier research journals and publications in well-established practitioner journals; the number of publications was calculated for each school by adding all publications authored by the faculty members at that school.

Measured by faculties' doctorates from prestigious universities, which provide business schools with an indirect affiliation with these universities. The Gourman Report (1997) was used to assign a Ph.D. degree-prestige score to each professor employed by a given school, and a school score was created by averaging the individual faculty scores, producing a single continuous score for each school.

Average of three seven-point Likert items: 'At the outset, to what extent did you plan: (a) a course of action on how to develop the product/technology, (b) a course of action on how to build a customer base, and (c) for each round of financing?' (from 'not at all' to 'very detailed'). The authors used Likert items rather than zero-one variables because each approach may be pursued with varying degrees.
scale: average of three seven-point Likert items
time_window: at the outset of the venture

description: Seven-point Likert item: 'You spent a lot of time and resources to discover influence factors not initially known' (from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'). The authors state the question focuses on active learning of unknown factors rather than flexibility to adjust to these unknowns, because in the sample all startups claimed to be very flexible.

Maximum of three seven-point Likert items: 'If you pursued multiple alternatives (sequentially or in parallel), to what extent did you eliminate these alternatives (a) during concept testing, (b) during technical development/implementation, and (c) during market testing of the finished product/technology?' (from 'none' to 'all'). The maximum rather than the average was used because unknown unknowns or complexity on the technology side normally require selectionism in an earlier phase than on the market side.
scale: maximum of three seven-point Likert items

description: Item asking: 'Of those alternatives you eliminated, what proportion did you eliminate based on direct feedback from customers, representative of the real target market?' (from < 5% to > 95%). The authors state that incorporating customer feedback results in tests that mirror the true market conditions of the startup more closely, albeit still not perfectly.

Seven-point Likert item: 'What is your qualitative evaluation of the success of the startup (considering all aspects of performance)?' (from 'major failure' to 'major success'). Quantitative measures (retained earnings, profits, current valuation, return on investment) and partial qualitative measures (profitability, liquidity, return on investment) were also collected, but the authors used the overall qualitative measure, which they say is formed in the context of, and thus accounts for, the venture's age and industry.
Seven-point Likert item: 'In retrospect, how many factors ended up influencing your startup that were not included in your plan?' (from 'very few' to 'very many').

Seven-point Likert item: 'The number of influence factors and interactions among them increase the complexity of a startup project. In retrospect, what was the level of complexity of your startup?' (from 'very low' to 'very high').

Similarity in domain knowledge is measured with Jaffe's angular proximity measure. The technological position of a firm at year t is a vector whose elements are the fraction of the firm's patents that are in each patent class during the years t-3 to t-1, and similarity between two firms is the angular proximity between their vectors. The equations for the vector and for the proximity measure were not extractable from the paper text. The two independent variables and the moderating variable were standardized.

The coupling between two technology classes for a firm is computed from the number of the firm's patents assigned to one class but not the other and to both classes; the formula was not extractable from the paper text. Because firms with larger knowledge bases tend to have weaker couplings as an artifact of the measurement process, the authors computed percentile values of couplings for every knowledge base size and year and estimated percentile values of coupling as a function of knowledge base size and year using a power-law relationship, then computed a percentile score for each firm's couplings. Dissimilarity in architectural knowledge is the weighted sum of the absolute difference in percentile scores between the two firms for all technology class pairs common to them, the weight being based on the fractions of patents of each firm in the two classes; it is set to 0 when the two firms have no common domain pairs.

Coded as 1 if the two firms formed an alliance in year t, and 0 otherwise. Alliances were identified from the SDC database and, because SDC records announcements rather than actual formation, the existence of announced alliances was traced and verified using Factiva.

variable_name: Firm degree of knowledge base decomposability
description: Measured following Yayavaram and Ahuja's (2008) procedure, with details provided in the Appendix in File S1. The measure indicates the extent to which the firm's knowledge base, represented by its couplings between knowledge domains, can be divided into clusters of tightly coupled domains. The written-out procedure and formula were not extractable from the paper text.

Percentage of foreign equity held in the subsidiary. In a two-party joint venture with one Japanese partner and one local partner, foreign equity is the equity percentage held by the Japanese partner; in cases with multiple Japanese partners, the equity of the Japanese partner having the largest equity share was considered. The equity variable was log transformed to test the hypothesized diminishing, nonlinear function. Subsidiaries with Japanese equity of less than 5 percent were removed from the directory sample as they were considered portfolio investments.

A subsidiary that ceases to be listed in a particular year's directory, after appearing consistently for one or more years, was deemed as terminated; the process considers terminations as exits by either divestiture or dissolution, both of which suggest a cessation of operations in that subsidiary from the foreign partner's point of view. The data provide for each subsidiary the status at the end of the observation period and its longevity at the time of exit if it was terminated during the observation period. Subsidiaries that continue to survive at the end of the observation period are treated as censored cases.

Knowledge creation was measured by counting the nanotechnology publications associated with each research program. The lead scientists were designated as authors in all publications resulting from their research programs, so their journal articles published since the initiation of the current research program until January 2009 were extracted from Thomson's ISI Web of Knowledge database, considering name variations of authors and verifying university affiliations by matching publication records to employment history. Following an established algorithm that isolates publications in the field of nanotechnology, the titles, keywords, and abstracts of publications were searched for relevant nanotechnology keywords. Books were excluded and only scientific journal articles subject to peer review were counted.
time_window: since the initiation of the current research program until January 2009

description: Respondents were asked to indicate the current progress of their research programs as of May 2008 using one of the following values: 1 for preliminary studies, 2 for prototype, 3 for testing, and 4 for commercialization. Preliminary studies involve initial exploration of ideas to determine the viability of technological concepts and to identify probable solutions to a scientific problem; prototypes are then constructed for selected solutions; at the testing stage prototypes are subject to a range of conditions to verify robustness and finalize the product design; and commercialization entails engineering, large-scale manufacturing, and marketing. When the research program involved multiple projects at different stages, the most advanced stage of knowledge application was coded.

Academic collaboration was measured with the cumulative number of all collaborators ever associated with each research program, as reported by the lead scientist. Any nonmember university scientist who had been working with members of the nanotechnology research program to produce new knowledge was considered a collaborator. To enhance the accuracy of this measure, respondents were prompted to list the names and affiliations of their collaborators.
time_window: cumulative, since the initiation of the research program

description: Industry collaboration was measured with the cumulative number of industry partners ever involved in the nanotechnology research program as reported by the lead scientist. Industry partners included start-up firms and established corporations, and domestic as well as international firms. To enhance the accuracy of this measure, respondents were asked to identify their industry partners.
time_window: cumulative, since the initiation of the research program

description: Respondents were asked to indicate the cumulative funding available for their nanotechnology research programs. Given the sensitivity of this information, a categorical variable was used indicating the range of available funding: 0 for no funding, 1 for less than $100,000, 2 for $100,000-$500,000, 3 for $500,000-$1 million, 4 for $1 million-$5 million, and 5 for funds larger than $5 million. Respondents were also asked to identify their funding sources, which included the host institution, Israeli/international scientific funds, Israeli/international government programs, independent funds/donors, Israeli/foreign corporations, and venture capital investors.

A dummy variable set to one if there are multiple R&D groups reporting to separate members within the top management team and zero if the firm has a single centralized R&D group reporting to a TMT member. It is determined by examining whether firms' R&D is organized into a single centralized unit or into multiple units, evaluated through a careful examination of firms' annual reports, 10-Ks, 20-Fs, and DEF 14As. These sources are used to develop a database of 15,129 executive roles for the sample of 49 firms over the period 1995-2015.

The proportion of inventions entering a firm's innovation pipeline that are sourced externally in a focal year. Whether a drug candidate is internally created or externally sourced is assessed by first examining the originators and licensees of each drug candidate in Pharmaprojects, then cross-checking other drug candidate transactions using the Recap database and the overview section of Pharmaprojects; if no evidence of external sourcing is found, the candidate is designated as internally created.

The proportion of externally sourced drug candidates of low novelty, calculated for each firm-year by dividing the number of drug candidates of low novelty entering a firm's pipeline through external sourcing by the total number of drug candidates of low novelty entering the pipeline (via external sourcing and internal creation). A drug candidate is of low novelty if neither its mechanism of action nor the origin of material in the broad therapeutic domain is new to the firm.

The proportion of externally sourced drug candidates of moderate novelty, calculated for each firm-year by dividing the number of drug candidates of moderate novelty entering a firm's pipeline through external sourcing by the total number of drug candidates of that novelty level entering the pipeline. A drug candidate is of moderate novelty if one of the two features, the mechanism of action or the origin of material in the broad therapeutic domain, is new to the firm.

The proportion of externally sourced drug candidates of high novelty, calculated for each firm-year by dividing the number of drug candidates of high novelty entering a firm's pipeline through external sourcing by the total number of drug candidates of that novelty level entering the pipeline. A drug candidate is of high novelty if both its mechanism of action and the origin of material in the broad therapeutic domain are new to the firm.

The proportion of drug candidates sourced via licensing, estimated by dividing the number of drug candidates entering a firm's pipeline in a focal year via licensing by the total number of drug candidates entering a firm's pipeline.

The proportion of drug candidates sourced via acquisitions, estimated by dividing the number of drug candidates entering a firm's pipeline in a focal year via acquisitions by the total number of drug candidates entering a firm's pipeline.

The proportion of drug candidates sourced via alliances, estimated by dividing the number of drug candidates entering a firm's pipeline in a focal year via alliances by the total number of drug candidates entering a firm's pipeline.

variable_name: degree of novelty of a drug candidate
description: A classification of each drug candidate's novelty to the focal firm based on two features of innovation in the pharmaceutical industry: the mechanism of action and the origin of material within the broad therapeutic domain (e.g., oncology, diabetes, cardiovascular). If both the mechanism of action and the origin of material are new to the firm, the drug candidate is considered to be of high novelty; if one of these is new, it is of moderate novelty; and if neither is new, it is of low novelty.

Our main independent variable, corporate lobbying, is measured as a binary variable set to 1 if a firm reported any lobbying activity targeting the FDA in the year prior to a device application, and 0 if it did not. Lobbying Disclosure Act filings identify the agencies targeted by a firm's lobbying activity and total lobbying expenditures, but do not report spending amounts allocated to specific agencies or regulatory targets. Lobbying activity is captured in the year prior to the application quarter, i.e., in the year prior to the device application.
time_window: the year prior to the device application

description: Our dependent variable is the number of calendar days from the date FDA acknowledges receipt of a 510(k) application to the date of FDA's approval decision. This measure captures the full duration over which discretionary review decisions accumulate, including any AI request periods; we do not adjust for AI hold periods. To address the variation in approval times, these long periods were divided into shorter, quarterly intervals, so the expected approval time ranges from 0 to 10 quarters after submission. The device application is the unit of analysis.
time_window: from FDA acknowledgement of receipt to the approval decision, in quarters after submission

description: We construct a binary indicator equal to 1 if the firm experienced at least one product recall within 180 days prior to a device application submission date, and 0 otherwise. This window is designed to capture recent recall activity that is most likely to be salient to regulators during the application review process. All types of recalls are included in this measure.
time_window: 180 days prior to the device application submission date

description: This variable captures a firm's innovation reputation as perceived by external audiences, measured as the number of breakthrough patents by each firm in the previous year. Following prior work we use USPTO citation data and identify breakthrough patents as those whose forward citations from external firms rank in the top 1 percent of the industry, based on the number of citations received within five years of the patent grant. Breakthrough patents are drawn from the previous year in which a firm had patent applications.

Number of breakthrough patents by each firm in the previous year, where breakthrough patents are those whose forward citations from external firms rank in the top 1 percent of the industry based on citations received within five years of the patent grant. Citation counts capture externally recognized technological impact and generate a reputational signal that circulates beyond the focal firm.

An alternative coding of the same firm-level measure, using breakthrough patents identified by the top 3 percent and top 5 percent of industry forward citations rather than the top 1 percent. As a further alternative measure of innovation leadership, the authors code the number of Prix Galien Product Awards that a focal device firm has received prior to the submission.
time_window: prior to the submission; previous year for patents

description: Value is measured using three items on seven-point semantic differential scales: the extent to which an IS process is considered valuable, the extent to which it permits a firm to differentiate its activities, and the extent to which it is strategically important. The three items load on a unique factor with a reliability of alpha = 0.78.

Rarity consists of four items that load onto a unique factor with a reliability of alpha = 0.77. Capabilities related to an IS process are rare when suppliers in factor markets, relative to the focal firm, do not possess knowledge and skills, do not possess equipment and machinery, or do not have sufficient productive capacity.
