Inimitability is operationalized using four items resulting in one factor with a reliability of alpha = 0.70. IS processes are more inimitable when they draw upon several different technologies, are not easily reverse engineered, are associated with tacit knowledge, and are complex.

Respondents provided information on the extent to which a given firm IS process had been outsourced, ranging from 0 to 100. The authors transformed this variable into a binary dependent variable that takes the value of 0 when a process was completely in-sourced, and one when it was partially or completely outsourced. Forty-three percent of the processes are completely in-sourced and 57 percent are partially or completely outsourced.

Measured as the percentage of shares outstanding owned by the CEO. The authors use a percentage stake because the credibility of a signal is related to its cost, and a percentage stake in a diversified firm is likely to be more costly than in a focused firm. Ownership data come from ExecuComp; years 1992 and 1993 were excluded because a substantial portion of the data are missing.

Diversification measured with both the Berry-Herfindahl and entropy diversification indices, calculated using the reported company's sales in the Compustat Business Segment database. Total diversification is regressed in time period 1 and time period 2 in separate models.

Related diversification computed as one component when total diversification (entropy) is separated into related and unrelated parts, based on sales reported in the Compustat Business Segment database. It is used as a dependent variable in the ownership models and as an independent variable in the ownership-change models.

Unrelated diversification computed as one component when total diversification (entropy) is separated into related and unrelated parts, based on sales reported in the Compustat Business Segment database. It is used as a dependent variable in the ownership models and as an independent variable in the ownership-change models.

Probability that a start-up supported by a focal syndicate will undergo an initial public offering. The authors model a binary outcome variable, the IPO event of a start-up company, in fixed-effect weighted logistic regressions.
level: start-up supported by a focal syndicate

description: Count of concurrent investments by syndicate members in the industry segment of a focal syndicate, adjusted by a measure of concentration captured by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index. In the formula, m is the number of start-ups in which a syndicate member invests in an industry segment during the time period between the first and last round of investment in the focal syndicate, and p is the firm's share in the total number of start-ups supported by all syndicate members in that industry segment. The authors state that for a given number of concurrent investments, the value is higher if more syndicate members make these investments, capturing multilateral competition; the formula as printed in the text is partly garbled by OCR.
time_window: period between the first and last round of investment in a focal syndicate

description: Firm i's ratio of the number of IPOs to dollar amount invested in the 4 years prior to a focal syndicate minus its ratio of the number of IPOs to dollar amount invested since the firm's founding and before the current period, divided by M, the number of firms in the alliance. The variable captures deviation in performance and was adjusted for possible regression to the mean.
time_window: 4 years prior to a focal syndicate; since firm founding

description: Firm i's ratio of the number of IPOs to dollar amount invested in the 4 years prior to a focal alliance minus the average number of IPOs to dollar amount invested in the 4 years prior to a focal alliance achieved by all firms in the industry segments in which the focal firm operated in the 5 years prior to the focal alliance, divided by M, the number of firms in the alliance. The variable captures deviation in performance and was adjusted for possible regression to the mean.
time_window: 4 years prior to a focal alliance; 5 years prior to a focal alliance for the reference group

description: Within-syndicate variance in the performance relative to historical aspirations variable, used to capture partners' goal asymmetry. The authors operationalize dispersion with the coefficient of variance, a scale invariant measure of dispersion, and weight the variance variable by syndicate members' equity shares in the syndicate.

Within-syndicate variance in the performance relative to social aspirations variable, used to capture partners' goal asymmetry. The authors operationalize dispersion with the coefficient of variance, a scale invariant measure of dispersion, and weight the variance variable by syndicate members' equity shares in the syndicate.

Dummy variable coded 1 if a pair of firms I and J had formed an alliance in that year, 0 if the pair of firms had not formed an alliance in that year. The data are organized as dyads: for each year the dependent variable covers the 595 potential alliances that could be formed among the 35 firms, giving 5950 observations over the 10-year period.
scale: 1 = alliance formed in the year, 0 = no alliance

description: The total density of alliances formed in each period, computed in any year T as the sum of alliances formed until period T divided by T times the number of possible dyads N(N-1)/2, where N is the number of firms in the industry. A quadratic term of the measure was included in the analysis to capture the postulated nonmonotonic effect.

For any two firms I and J who are members of strategic groups SGI (with NI total members) and SGJ (with NJ total members), the cumulative density of ties until the prior year across the strategic groups to which the two firms belong. In any period T it is computed as the sum of alliances formed between any two firms from strategic groups SGI and SGJ until period T divided by T times (NI(NJ-1)/2). When SGI = SGJ the measure captures the density of alliances within a strategic group. A square term of this measure was included to test whether the strength of the relationship is nonmonotonic.

Each firm was assigned to one of the discrete strategic groups identified by Nohria and Garcia-Pont's (1991) strategic group analysis of the same set of firms. The classification was based on variables previously used to define strategic groups and organizational niches, including size, breadth of product line, geographical location, technological and organizational competencies, and cost structure, and was recognized by industry experts as a meaningful basis for differentiation within the industry.

Computed as the logarithmic transformation of a Herfindahl measure of stock concentration, where S_i is the share of the ith stockholder and n is the number of stockholders with holdings of 0.2 percent or greater. The data set details the percentage of common voting stock held in blocks of 0.2 percent and more for the Fortune 500 in 1980, and the measure is identical to that used by Demsetz and Lehn (1985).
The natural logarithm of the percentage of common voting stock held by management in 1980. Data were collected from the 1980 Computer Directions Advisors publication Spectrum 6: Insider Holdings.

Following the product count method used in the industrial organization literature, the number of two-digit SIC industries outside a firm's primary two-digit industry that the firm was active in during 1980. Data were collected from Dun and Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management.

The number of four-digit SIC industries within a firm's main two-digit industry that the firm was active in during 1980, measured with the product count method. Data were collected from Dun and Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management.

R&D expenditure per employee for 1979-81, drawn from the COMPUSTAT tapes. The measure was adjusted for industry differences by standardizing it for each industry: (RD_ij - RD_j)/SD_j, where RD_ij was the expenditure per employee for firm i in industry j and SD_j was the standard deviation for all firms in industry j. R&D data were available for only 81 of the 122 firms studied.

The ratio of capital to labor in a firm, computed on the basis of COMPUSTAT data for 1980. The raw capital-to-labor ratio was adjusted for industry differences by standardizing the measure for each industry: (CL_ij - CL_j)/SD_j, where CL_ij was the capital-to-labor ratio for firm i in industry j and SD_j was the standard deviation for the firms in industry j.

Value added per employee, where value added = (pretax income + capital costs + employment costs)/number of employees, using Athanasopoulos's estimates for 1980. Firms were grouped into industries according to Fortune's criterion, membership in a two-digit SIC, with each firm classified into its most important industry on the basis of 1980 revenues; each firm's productivity was expressed as an index number with a score of 100 as the industry mean.
scale: index number with a score of 100 as the industry mean

description: Operationalized as market thinness, since goods requiring highly specific assets often result in a small number of willing suppliers, so that switching is difficult and costly. Three items relating to this concept were adapted from prior work and included in the survey. A composite score was computed using the confirmatory factor analysis loadings as item weights.

Measured by asking respondents about forecast inaccuracies and unpredictability in volume patterns. Two items adapted from prior work were included on the survey to measure this attribute. A composite score was computed using the confirmatory factor analysis loadings as item weights.

Measures the likelihood that technological change will occur, referring to the innovation potential for either the good or the processes used in its production; in this mature industry the likelihood rather than the magnitude of change was measured. Three items from prior work were adapted to measure this variable, and a composite score was computed using the confirmatory factor analysis loadings.

Operationalized as information asymmetry rather than complexity, such as when simple inspection techniques are not adequate to evaluate quality, when production problems occur that cannot be traced to a specific cause, and when it is difficult to compare goods from different suppliers. Five items were developed to measure this attribute, some of them adapted from prior work, and a composite score was computed using the confirmatory factor analysis loadings.

Measures reflected the extent to which the firm's overall costs were reduced by producing the good along with its other products. Firm scope economies were measured by two items, and a composite score was computed using the confirmatory factor analysis loadings.

A separate variable from firm scope economies because each party has its own established product mix and resource base. It reflects the extent to which suppliers can reduce their overall production costs by making the good for the firm, and was measured by one item; a composite score was computed using the confirmatory factor analysis loadings.

Reflects the extent to which the firm has considerable skills and capabilities for producing the good and an understanding of the underlying technology. Four items were used for firm expertise, some borrowed or adapted from prior work and others original, and a composite score was computed using the confirmatory factor analysis loadings.

Reflects the extent to which suppliers have considerable skills and capabilities for producing the good and an understanding of the underlying technology. Five items were used, some borrowed or adapted from prior work and others original; reliability for this variable was the only one not above 0.60. A composite score was computed using the confirmatory factor analysis loadings.

Derived from one survey item that asked whether the firm sourced the item internally, externally, or concurrently; for the concurrent option the percentage of internal production was obtained using six provided choices rather than relying on the respondent's recall, and where a good was not used the observation was dropped. To test the continuum view, each of the eight options was placed in order from 0 to 100 percent produced internally and an ordered logit model was used.
scale: eight ordered options from 0 to 100 percent produced internally

description: Three categories were created for goods that were made, bought, and concurrently sourced. A 10 percent cutoff was used such that items produced internally 90 percent or more often were considered 'made', those outsourced 90 percent or more often were considered 'bought', with the rest considered concurrently sourced; this reclassified 82 of 805 observations. A multinomial logit model compared the three modes.
scale: three categories: make, bought, concurrently sourced

description: The number of years that elapsed between the initiation and completion of M-form adoption, measured in years as the data did not always permit a more precise determination. The transition period was identified by (1) the formation of a corporate office with an associated staff, (2) decentralization and the formation of semiautonomous units, and (3) the creation of appropriate M-form controls, such as cash flow allocation. Estimates of the length of each firm's implementation period came from telephone interviews with a company archivist and from corporate histories compiled from books, annual reports, periodicals, and press releases, after which company officials were contacted again to reconcile differences. The authors cross-checked their estimates against Harris's independent identification of transition periods.

The difference between the average annual industry-adjusted ROA during the transition period and prior performance, the latter calculated as the average industry-adjusted ROA for the five years prior to reorganization. Each firm's annual ROA was divided by the corresponding annual ROA for the firm's dominant industry; dominant industry was defined using the Internal Revenue Service industry classification system, equivalent to the three-digit Standard Industrial Classification system. ROA was chosen because it is robust to changes in firm size and allows comparisons with previous work. Data were obtained from annual reports, Moody's Industrial Manuals, Fortune 500 lists, and Internal Revenue Service Statistics of Income.
time_window: the transition period and the five years prior to reorganization

description: The number of years, after the reorganization was completed, it took each firm's industry-adjusted ROA to reach or exceed its prior performance. An upper limit of ten years was set on the estimate of recovery time because some firms may never recover or may take decades to do so. The 15 firms that did not recover within ten years were retained in the analyses and treated as right-censored observations.
time_window: after completion of the M-form reorganization, up to ten years

description: Classification of each firm as an unrelated, vertically integrated, or related diversifier. Earlier studies had identified the strategies of 62 of the 76 firms; two researchers experienced in diversity classification independently determined the strategies of the remaining 14 firms, and only firms for which both raters agreed were included. Classifications were based on data from annual reports and Moody's Industrial Manuals, and the firms' strategies primarily corresponded to the dominant-vertical, related-constrained, and acquisitive conglomerate strategies in the Rumelt (1974) typology. Reflecting the ordinal nature of the hypotheses, the variable was coded unrelated = 1, vertically integrated = 2, related = 3, but it was treated as a classification variable in the analyses to detect departures from the ordinal predictions.

A time-invariant dummy that takes the value of one if the name of a beer contains an anti-mass-production reference. The authors settled on a list of 23 oppositional words after a four-step selection procedure.

For each review, the mean of the reviewer's four scores on look, smell, taste, and feel, each given on a one-to-five scale in increments of 0.25. All reviews that a beer received in a given year were then aggregated into the beer's average review score for that year. The resulting measure is a time-varying continuous variable ranging from one to five.

A time-invariant dummy that takes the value of one if the style of a given beer is in the American lager category. This category includes American adjunct lager, American red lager, American imperial pilsner, American pale lager, California common/steam beer, and American light lager.

A time-variant count of the cumulative number of unique beer styles for which the brewery has received at least one review on BeerAdvocate in a given year. Recognized styles include American ales, Belgian/French ales, English ales, Finnish ales, German ales, Irish ales, Russian ales, Scottish ales, American lagers, Czech lagers, European lagers, German lagers, Japanese lagers, and hybrid styles. The measure was lagged by one year.

At the level of each focal biotech firm alliance, the authors determine whether the particular alliance involves the R&D function and code a binary variable as 1 if it does (0 if R&D is not associated with the alliance). For the pharma partner associated with that alliance they determine the percent of other alliances in the partner's portfolio where the R&D function is present. The overlap value at the alliance activity level is the product of the binary variable and the percentage variable, and since the measure is at the focal biotech firm-year level these values are averaged over the biotech's portfolio of alliances within a 5-year rolling window.
level: focal biotechnology firm-year (alliance activity values averaged)

description: Total forward citations within a 4-year window following the current firm-year to current firm-year patents. All patents associated with the sampled firms are identified in the IQSS Patent Network database by extracting all patents where the assignee name matches current or former names of the focal firm, and cross-checks are conducted with Google Patents.
A count of products in the focal firm's product pipeline that have entered preclinical trials, that is, before human trials begin. It is constructed at the focal biotechnology firm-year level.

In any given firm-year, the average share of the focal firm's partners' portfolios involving alliances with firms in the same industry as the focal firm, as defined by their 4-digit SIC code. It is constructed at the focal biotechnology firm-year level.

Contract framing was measured at the buyer-supplier dyadic level by verifying the presence of promotion-framed clauses in the subject's contracts across five dimensions: payments for performance, payments for products, mutual activities, guidelines for exchange parties, and contract period. A clause's presence was scored as 1 and its absence as 0, with the total for each contract type indicating the extent of promotion framing. Buyers provided the information about contracts.

Contract framing was measured at the buyer-supplier dyadic level by verifying the presence of prevention-framed clauses in the subject's contracts across five dimensions: payments for performance, payments for products, mutual activities, guidelines for exchange parties, and contract period. A clause's presence was scored as 1 and its absence as 0, with the total for each contract type indicating the extent of prevention framing. Buyers provided the information about contracts.

Exploration was measured with three items adapted from Jansen et al. (2006) and Nijssen et al. (2012). The items were answered by the supplier, which provided information about its learning activities within the buyer-supplier relationship.

Exploitation was measured with three items adapted from Azadegan and Dooley (2010) and Jansen et al. (2006). The items were answered by the supplier, which provided information about its learning activities within the buyer-supplier relationship.

Difference in R&D expenditure intensities between the host and the home country, where R&D intensity is R&D expenditures divided by industry size. Positive values indicate that the host country's technology in the entered industry is greater than that of the home country. Results are reported for the continuous difference and for a dummy version that marks whether host country R&D intensity exceeds home country R&D intensity.

Binary responses for individual entries (acquisition or greenfield) grouped by the 4-digit SIC industry of entry, year of entry, and home country of the entrant, giving the proportion of investments made by acquisition within each industry-country-year group. Proportions that equal 0 or 1 were rescored as 0.001 and 0.999 to avoid problems in maximum likelihood estimation.

Advertising expenses in the entered U.S. industry measured relative to industry sales, used as a measure of brand equity in the entered industry. Industry-level data were used because the hypotheses concern the capabilities a foreign firm needs to acquire to compete as a typical firm within the U.S. industry that it entered.

Number of salesforce employees in an industry (persons selling goods and services and others directly related to sales) divided by the total number of employees in that industry. It is the second measure of the intensity of distribution, alongside selling expenses scaled by sales. The advertising and selling expenditure terms could not be included in the same model because of their high collinearity.

Amplitude was measured as the difference between the minimum and maximum values in the seasonal adjustment indexes computed with the SAS implementation of the X-11 procedure of the Bureau of the Census. The seasonal adjustment index is the ratio of an observed value over the point-specific moving average, all multiplied by 100, so it is the percentage deviation from a moving average. The authors' amplitude measure is the difference between the largest and smallest seasonal adjustment factor in a given year divided by 100, yielding an indicator of the magnitude of variation that ranges between 0 and 1 and is the total percentage deviation from average sales.

Frequency was measured as the number of slope reversals in a time series divided by the total number of observations. This gives the probability of a reversal in any period; the measure can also be computed with the seasonal adjustment figures, and the two measures are equivalent.
Predictability was measured with the R-squared for sales (or other resources) regressed on sales lagged one year. A high R-squared indicates that a prior year's sales predicts current year's sales.

Hypothesis 2 was examined with Dess and Beard's (1984) instability measure: the standard error of the coefficient of the time trend of monthly shipments divided by mean industry shipments. This measure was multiplied by 100 to ensure consistency of scales.

Measures for frequency, amplitude, and predictability were calculated for each city using quarterly restaurant sales data deflated to constant dollars and published by the California State Board of Equalization. The proposed measures are calculated with constant dollars and data from which growth has been factored out, and are unit-independent so that they can be compared across industries.

Measures for frequency, amplitude, and predictability were calculated for each city using quarterly restaurant sales data deflated to constant dollars and published by the California State Board of Equalization, using the same proposed measures as for the manufacturing data.

Measures for frequency, amplitude, and predictability were calculated for each city using quarterly restaurant sales data deflated to constant dollars and published by the California State Board of Equalization, using the same proposed measures as for the manufacturing data.

Respondents were asked whether their restaurant had an off-season and other questions about employee characteristics, menus, and the division of labor. Because the managerial report of seasonality was a binary variable, the analysis estimated the model of the probability that managers reported restaurant sales as varying seasonally. Overall, 31 percent of all respondents reported having an off-season.

The difference between the number of civil lawsuit judgments involving the target firm in the five-year postacquisition period and in the five-year preacquisition period. The counts cover six types of civil action that most directly capture the possibility that a firm is not acting prudently. Judgments are included whether the focal firm is a defendant or a plaintiff. Windows of five years are used because lawsuits brought to judgment are relatively rare events and because the median time from civil lawsuit filing to judgment was 14 months.

The number of the six focal categories of civil lawsuit judgments involving the target firm in the five years before the acquisition. It is included as an independent variable to capture whether the change in lawsuits is affected by the level of lawsuits in the preperiod, for instance because firms with zero lawsuits in the preperiod cannot realize a decline.

The revenues of the target firm in millions of dollars at the time of the acquisition, taken from the periodical Mergers & Acquisitions (1987). Target revenue data are available for 196 of the 576 acquisitions. Target firm size is operationalized by revenues because it is the most comprehensive measure of size the authors can access from a source where they believe the data are comparable.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: A dummy variable coded one if the acquiring firm is foreign owned and zero if it is U.S. owned. Because all targets are U.S.-owned firms and foreign acquirers change control to foreign owned, the variable is equivalent to the change in the nationality of control.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: Acquisition status is operationalized by comparing each target firm's civil lawsuit judgments in the period after acquisition, when the firms are combined, with the period before, when they are independent. The post-minus-pre difference is the outcome.
time_window: 5 years before and after the 1987 acquisition

description: The distance between a potential new model i and the nearest existing model j of the introducing firm f. Distances are obtained in a product attribute space built from a single quality measure estimated with a discrete choice model on observable product attributes. The authors use it to measure the first indirect effect of a new model on the firm's own variable profits.

The distance between a potential new model i and the closest product of any rival r of firm f. It is computed from the same product space distance measure and is used to measure the second indirect effect of a new model (total industry profit).

The market share of firm f during period t. It is entered in the logit models on its own and interacted with the distance to the firm's own nearest model and with the distance to the nearest rival model.

A dummy set equal to one if firm f, or a division of f, did not manufacture a model in the United States prior to 1980, and zero otherwise. The entrant models are those introduced by Hyundai, Lexus, Infiniti, and Acura; there were a total of 56 new models by these entrants.
A dummy set equal to one if firm f is a foreign manufacturer during period t and zero otherwise.
A dummy variable equal to one if firm f introduces new model i and zero otherwise. It is the dependent variable of the logit models of product introduction.

The dependent variable was measured by calculating the cumulative abnormal return using the event study methodology with a market model. The abnormal return for stock i at time t is the actual return minus the calculated expected return, where the expected return depends on beta for systematic risk relative to the average daily return of the market portfolio over an inspection period running from 270 trading days before to 20 trading days after the acquisition announcement, and on the firm-specific parameter alpha. The market return was estimated from a market value-weighted return index of the combined major stock exchanges (New York Stock Exchange, American Stock Exchange, and NASDAQ). The CAR to the acquiring firm was computed for five trading days before to five trading days after the announcement of an acquisition event.
level: acquisition event of the acquiring firm
time_window: five trading days before to five trading days after the acquisition announcement

description: This variable measured the degree to which the product strategy of a target complements the product strategy of an acquirer, and was operationalized as the Mahalanobis distance in the loan portfolio between the acquirer and the target. The loan portfolio composition of a bank is captured in a column vector of the eight loan categories as percentages of total loans. The Mahalanobis distance between the acquirer vector and the target vector is computed using the inverse of the pooled covariance matrix, and therefore takes into account the correlation-covariance matrix among the eight loan categories as well as the mean difference between acquirer and target.

This variable was operationalized as the Mahalanobis distance between the loan portfolio of the acquirer's markets and the loan portfolio of the target's markets, where the market-level loan portfolio aggregates the amount of each of the eight types of loans for all commercial banking institutions operating in the market in a given year. A bank's geographic market was defined at the state level, and for banks operating in more than one state the total value of the eight loan types in those states was aggregated to create the market-level loan portfolio.

Acquirer strategic focus was operationalized as the log of the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of the loan portfolio of an acquirer, specifically as a sum of the square of the amount of each loan type as a percent of the sum of all loans on the books of an acquirer. High scores signify a business portfolio heavily concentrated on a small number of loan types, while lower scores indicate a more balanced portfolio across different types of loans.

Operationalized as the sum of the total number of acquisitions from 1988 to the year of the focal acquisition that a bank made outside the state in which its primary operations were located. The value of each experience was discounted by age and weighted by the geographic distance between the buyer and the target, the geographic distance being calculated as the spherical distance between the two zip codes that define the physical location of the headquarters of the merging partners. The experience of acquiring a distant target is weighted more heavily than the experience of acquiring a proximate target.
time_window: from 1988 to the year of the focal acquisition

description: The four weights on the reference points prior aspiration (A), prior performance (P), performance of the external reference group (E), and performance of the internal reference group (S) in the aspiration adaptation equation, estimated for each magazine and period by a grid search in 0.025 increments. Values between 0 and 1 were given to the weights under the constraint that all weights add up to 1.0, and the solution minimized the root mean square percentage error between observed and estimated aspiration levels. Estimation used 21 quarterly observations, and the quarterly weight series were collapsed into yearly averages for hypothesis testing.
time_window: quarterly, lagged one quarter; averaged into yearly values for the hypothesis tests

description: Weight allocated to the magazine's own prior aspiration level in the aspiration adaptation equation, estimated by the same grid search as the other three weights, with values between 0 and 1 and all four weights constrained to sum to 1.0. Quarterly estimates were collapsed into yearly averages for the hypothesis tests.
time_window: quarterly estimates averaged into yearly values

description: Weight allocated to the magazine's own prior performance in the aspiration adaptation equation, estimated by the same grid search as the other three weights, with values between 0 and 1 and all four weights constrained to sum to 1.0. Quarterly estimates were collapsed into yearly averages for the hypothesis tests.
time_window: quarterly estimates averaged into yearly values

variable_name: a3 (weight on competitors within the same content category)
description: Weight allocated to the prior performance of the external reference group, the average performance of magazines competing in the same content category, estimated by the same grid search as the other three weights. Values lie between 0 and 1 and the four weights sum to 1.0; quarterly estimates were collapsed into yearly averages for the hypothesis tests.
time_window: quarterly estimates averaged into yearly values

variable_name: a4 (weight on sister magazines within the same publisher)
description: Weight allocated to the prior performance of the internal reference group, the average performance of magazines published by the same publisher, estimated by the same grid search as the other three weights. Values lie between 0 and 1 and the four weights sum to 1.0; quarterly estimates were collapsed into yearly averages for the hypothesis tests.
time_window: quarterly estimates averaged into yearly values

variable_name: early stage of the organizational life cycle (1 = yes)
description: Dummy variable specifying whether a given magazine was within six years of its founding and therefore in the early stage of the organizational life cycle. The six-year period is consistent with the entrepreneurship literature defining new ventures as companies six years old or younger and also guaranteed the reliability of the grid search procedure.
Dummy variable marking whether a given year was the last full year a magazine was in business, thus signaling the approaching end of the organizational life cycle.

Years since a magazine started its first issue; for magazines of foreign origin, years since the foreign origin magazine started its first issue in Germany. The variable had to be left out of the within estimation model because the magazine fixed effects account for age differences across magazines in the initial period.

Years since the publisher (parent organization) was founded. As with organizational age, the variable had to be left out of the within estimation model because the magazine fixed effects interfere with the age variables.

Aspirations were measured as the number of magazine copies printed. The authors argue the measure is more direct than unobserved measures such as an exponentially weighted average of past performance values because it is observable, verifiable, and decided by magazine managers; interviews confirmed that printed copies constitute a representative measure of their aspirations.

variable_name: organizational performance (number of magazine copies sold)
description: Organizational performance was measured as the number of magazine copies sold.

variable_name: performance of the external reference group (E)
description: Calculated as the average performance of magazines in the same content category, capturing the performance of competing organizations in the same product market. For comparisons within the reference groups, the respective group's average performance excludes the focal organization.

variable_name: performance of the internal reference group (S)
description: Calculated as the average performance of magazines that are published by the same publisher, capturing the performance of sister organizations under the same parent organization. For comparisons within the reference groups, the respective group's average performance excludes the focal organization.

Categorical variable coded 1 if firm i enters industry j between 1981 and 1985 and 0 otherwise. Entry is read from the Trinet database, which was compiled every other year between 1979 and 1989 and covers corporate ownership and four-digit SIC scope of operations for every establishment with twenty or more employees in the United States. Any industry in which firm i did not participate in 1981 is a potential destination industry; those potential destinations in which firm i participates in 1985 are entries. Entry can occur through either acquisition or internal expansion and the study does not distinguish between the two modes.

Probability-weighted count of the patents in firm i's portfolio that are applicable to industry j. Each patent is assigned to four-digit SICs using a U.S. Patent Class-U.S. SIC concordance that uses the frequency with which Canadian patents in each patent class are assigned to each SIC to create a probability distribution relating U.S. patent classes to U.S. SIC codes. These probability-weighted SIC assignments are then aggregated over the firm's entire patent portfolio, where N_ic equals the number of patents in firm i's portfolio assigned to U.S. Patent Class c. The explicit formula is not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: patents with applications filed before December 31, 1981

description: Applicability of firm i's patent portfolio to industry j relative to the applicability of that portfolio to other industries, derived from AbsTech_ij. The authors state that it is derived from AbsTech as follows but the formula itself is not readable in the extracted text, so the exact form of the relative measure cannot be recovered from the payload.
time_window: patents with applications filed before December 31, 1981

description: Industry-level rating of the importance of license royalties as a method of appropriating returns to innovation in industry j. Senior R&D executives in several hundred large U.S. firms rated, on a seven-point scale for their line of business, the importance of several mechanisms for appropriating returns to innovation, including licensing royalties. Higher values indicate that licensing is a more feasible and lower-hazard way of contracting for technology in the industry.

Industry-level rating of the importance of secrecy to appropriating returns to innovation in industry j, taken from the same Yale survey question in which senior R&D executives rated mechanisms for appropriating returns to innovation on a seven-point scale for their line of business. Higher values indicate that contracting for technology in the industry is subject to hazards associated with concern about information leakage.

Industry-level rating of the importance of learning curve advantages to appropriating returns to innovation in industry j, taken from the same Yale survey question in which senior R&D executives rated mechanisms for appropriating returns to innovation on a seven-point scale for their line of business. The authors assume that in industries where learning curve advantages are efficacious, knowledge is sufficiently tacit that it does not leak out of the learning firm.

The percentage of licensing and manufacturing agreements within the biotechnology field entered into by the pharmaceutical firm up to, but not including, the year of the focal project. The measure is based on all such alliances the pharmaceutical firms and their biotechnology subsidiaries entered into within biotechnology and is not limited to the sample of collaborative R&D projects. It also controls for the cumulative total number of alliances formed prior to the year of the focal project.
time_window: cumulative, up to but not including the year of the focal project

description: The percentage of R&D alliances entered into by the pharmaceutical firm in the biotechnology field up to, but not including, the year of the focal project. The measure is based on all such alliances the pharmaceutical firms and their biotechnology subsidiaries entered into within biotechnology and is not limited to the sample of collaborative R&D projects. It also controls for the cumulative total number of alliances formed prior to the year of the focal project.
time_window: cumulative, up to but not including the year of the focal project

description: The lagged, cumulative number of R&D projects that a firm had initiated in a particular therapeutic domain, characterized at the therapeutic class level using 15 therapeutic classes from the Anatomical Therapeutic Classification. Projects count if the focal firm is listed as the lead firm, and a project is excluded if it belongs to the focal sample of biotechnology-based R&D projects to avoid double counting with solo biotech experience. The average sample firm accumulated experience by engaging in 10 internal R&D projects within a given therapeutic area.
time_window: lagged, cumulative up to the focal project

description: The cumulative percentage of a firm's pharmaceutical sales derived from the therapeutic class of the focal project, based on historical global sales data for the firms in the sample. The measure is intended to capture the extent of a firm's regulatory, marketing and sales expertise, key downstream competencies that may be leveraged in a biotechnology-based R&D project.
time_window: cumulative up to the focal project

description: The hazard rate for drug approval, incorporating information on whether the event occurred and project duration. Duration is proxied by the number of months from initiation of the project to market approval by either the FDA in the United States or the EMEA in Europe. About 80 percent of the marketed drugs were introduced in the United States before or simultaneously with their introduction in Europe.
time_window: from project initiation to approval, observed through 2000

description: The hazard rate for project termination, that is, when a project is discontinued. Project termination is a more common occurrence in this context and allows the authors to apply a competing hazard rate model that leverages all the available data. In this sample, 139 projects were terminated before the end of the study period.
time_window: from project initiation to termination, observed through 2000

description: Worker tenure is measured in years and is based on responses to the various tenure questions in the different supplements: the job mobility supplement asked workers, 'How long have you been working CONTINUOUSLY for your present employer?'; the benefits supplements asked, 'How many years have you been working for [employer's name]?'; and the contingent work supplements asked, 'How long have you been working for [employer's name]?' Because people round their responses, giving disproportionate peaks at one, two, five and ten years, a random amount was added to exact-year responses following Farber's (2008a) approach; the printed range of that random amount is garbled in the text ('0 0 5 to C 0 0 5').

Unionization is measured at the industry level. The earnings supplement of the CPS asks workers whether or not they are members of a union; because this supplement is only implemented in the fourth and eighth month a household is interviewed, answers for the other workers were matched into the data from earnings supplements in subsequent months. For each year and for each three-digit industry as defined by the census for that year, the percentage of all workers in that industry (including women and those outside the age range of the primary sample) who were members of a union was calculated, using the CPS weights to adjust for sampling differences.
scale: percentage of workers who are union members

description: Import penetration was calculated using industry-level data on the gross value of imports from 1979 to 2006, identified by Standard Industrial Classification and NAICS codes and aggregated into U.S. Census Bureau industries using crosswalks. Import penetration rates divide total industry imports by gross industry output, taken from the National Income and Product Accounts. These import data are only reported for commodity and manufacturing industries, so analyses using them are restricted to those industries.
scale: ratio of imports to gross industry output

description: Industry-level spending on information technology was calculated from the input-output tables of the National Income and Product Accounts, which are released every five years (data for 1977, 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997, and 2002); employment data were matched with the most recent data on IT spending. IT intensity divides each industry's total purchases of IT-specific goods and services by the total purchases of those industries in that year. Because the input-output tables aggregate all of wholesale and retail into just two categories, wholesale and retail industries are omitted from analyses using these data.
scale: share of total industry purchases devoted to IT goods and services

description: The 1979, 1983, 1988, and 1993 benefits supplements contained data on both tenure and organizational size; organizational size data for other years were gathered by matching in size data from responses to the March supplement of the CPS, which respondents answered in a different month. Workers reported the total number of persons working for the employer at all locations, and the different response categories were consolidated into three: under 25 workers, 25-999 workers, and 1,000 workers or over.
scale: three categories: under 25 workers, 25-999 workers, 1,000 workers or over

description: Changes in tenure over time are assessed with a linear year variable. A significant negative effect of year on tenure indicates that tenure declined over time, holding worker demographics, occupation, and local unemployment constant.

A dummy variable set to 1 if a firm experienced one of the serious safety-related events in a given year and to 0 otherwise. The events comprise safety-based drug withdrawals, nonapproval of a new drug by the FDA, and boxed warnings and contraindications added to a drug's label. Because serious drug errors are a rather discrete outcome, the authors argue that the relevant variation is between observations with no serious drug error and those affected by such errors.
time_window: observation year; lagged by one year in the models

description: The number of clinical trials that a firm started in that year. The variable considers trials about any of a firm's drugs, capturing the firm's generalized concern with safety-related issues rather than a focused response to errors affecting any particular drug. The authors control for a firm's number of new drug applications to account for the possibility that a firm with more drugs in the pipeline conducts more trials.

The number of scientific articles whose references mentioned clinical trials in the title or abstract fields and which were published by authors affiliated with the focal firm in the observation year. The authors argue that publicly disclosing information about the safety of a drug in scientific journals, as opposed to privately communicating it, likely reflects the extent to which the firm emphasizes drug safety.

The number of a firm's successful patent applications in the observation year, following prior research that uses patent counts as an indicator of innovation output. Using this measure allows the authors to observe safety and innovation foci independently and to examine the dual effect that errors exert on them.

variable_name: time elapsed since last serious drug error
description: A variable capturing the time that has elapsed since the last serious drug error, entered as a control to ensure that the reported results are net of the main effect of time elapsed. The moderating role of time elapsed is tested by plotting predicted values of the dependent variables against serious drug error with separately fitted least-square lines for low (below the mean) and high (equal to or above the mean) values of this variable, and by t-tests comparing marginal effects across subsamples.

variable_name: time elapsed since last serious drug error
description: The same time-elapsed variable is used in the models predicting innovation focus, where predicted values of innovation focus are plotted against serious drug error separately for low and high values of time elapsed since the error. The marginal effect of serious drug error on innovation focus is then compared across subsamples using t-tests.

Count of the number of functional roles on the founding team. The survey asked respondents for the role at founding for themselves and for each cofounder; these roles were coded according to whether they fell under technology roles (chief technology officer, chief scientist, etc.), finance, sales and marketing, or other, so the number of roles ranges from 1 to 4.

Dichotomous variable equal to 1 if the founding team was entirely composed of individuals who indicated that their role at founding was focused on the development of the technology, as opposed to other roles including marketing, sales, finance, and management.

Composite index of the extent to which a firm innovates as the basis of its strategy, ranging from 0 to 3. A firm receives a 3 if it indicated that innovation was critical for its success, it held at least one patent at the time of the survey, and the idea for the venture came from a research lab (corporate or university); a 2 if two of these conditions hold, a 1 if only one holds, and a 0 if none holds.

Firms' industry sectors were matched to the Carnegie Mellon University industry R&D survey. The importance of complementary assets in the sector averages the importance of complementary manufacturing and sales or services, and IPR strength averages the importance of patents for protecting products and processes; both were logged to account for skewed distributions. The median values of these two measures split the sample into firms in an environment where complementary assets are important and patent protection is strong versus firms in an environment where complementary assets are less important and patent protection is weak.

Equals 1 if the venture experienced an IPO or an acquisition that met either of two criteria: it made money for the investors (the valuation was higher than the capital raised), or the acquired firm was older than five years and had positive revenues. Acquisition and IPO events were self-reports in the MIT survey, and their accuracy was confirmed with the Compustat and SDC Platinum databases.

The number of monthly visits to the target firm's platform. Quantcast and Compete report TVisits, and for target firms with multiple platforms TVisits includes the monthly visits for all platforms. Continuous variables, including TVisits, are log transformed in the analysis.
The price paid for the target firm. The SDC database, news reports in Factiva, and Crunchbase report TValue. TValue is log transformed in the analysis.

FGC, UCC, and IGC are set to one for firm-generated content, user-contributed content, and interaction platforms, respectively. The coding was based on the primary value proposition of the platform, determined through news articles, acquisition announcements, descriptions on Crunchbase, and an evaluation of platform content at the time of acquisition; subcategories were identified first and mapped to the three categories. UCC is the base case in the reported models.

For many platforms, Alexa provides a list of other platforms that provide similar functionality and a percentage overlap with each such platform. Overlap is defined as the maximum percentage overlap with another platform for each of our focal platforms. As Overlap increases, switching cost for the user decreases because there is an alternative platform available with similar functionality.

An indicator coded for each target platform based on whether the feature is present. IntTools is coded as one for all interaction platforms and only for those firm-generated content platforms that allow participants to interact with each other (beyond simple commenting), such as by enabling reservations, payments, or sales. The authors completed the coding by visiting the platform at the time of acquisition through the Wayback Machine.

An indicator coded as one for all user-contributed content platforms; for many interaction platforms that have user content (e.g., social networks, dating platforms, and some online communities); and for a few firm-generated content platforms that have user content (beyond simple commenting or posts), such as reviews or user-written articles in addition to editorial content. The authors completed the coding by visiting the platform at the time of acquisition through the Wayback Machine.

An indicator that captures whether the platform fosters a sense of community among users. It is coded as one for those interaction platforms that enable interactions within defined groups (messaging platforms and social networking sites) or have a niche topical focus (online communities), for blog-hosting sites (within the user-contributed content platform category) because they foster a sense of community among followers, and for some firm-generated content platforms that are targeted toward niche groups, such as students, kids, or teachers.

A modified version of the 12-item measure developed and validated by Judge and colleagues (2003). Because an executive population is more apt to have a stronger predisposition toward the higher end of the measure, the authors used a seven-point scale ranging from 1 ('very strongly disagree') to 7 ('very strongly agree') to more precisely assess higher core self-evaluations. The final measure demonstrated acceptable internal consistency with a coefficient alpha of 0.80.
time_window: first survey wave, one year before the entrepreneurial orientation assessment

description: A nine-item, semantic differential scale developed and validated by Covin and Slevin (1986) to measure a firm's entrepreneurial orientation, with a coefficient alpha of 0.87. Because it was measured using the responses of TMT members, the agreement index R wg (j) was used to justify aggregating individual responses to the team level (median R wg = 0.93), with acceptable intraclass correlations (ICC1 = 0.30; ICC2 = 0.66) and an aggregate-level coefficient alpha of 0.87.
level: team level (aggregated from individual TMT members to the firm)
time_window: second survey wave, one year after the CEO survey

description: Assessed using Miller and Friesen's (1983) six-item measure. Using a scale ranging from 1 ('not at all') to 7 ('a great extent'), both CEOs and TMT members were asked to assess the extent to which changes occurred in various aspects of their primary industry. An acceptable level of agreement among CEOs and top managers warranted aggregating responses to the TMT level, and the aggregate-level coefficient alpha for the environmental dynamism scale is 0.76.
level: team level (aggregated from CEOs and TMT members)

description: The dependent variable is whether or not product j of firm i was manufactured in the United States at the end of 1986. INV is equal to 1 if this is the case, and 0 otherwise. In 343 cases (or 19.1% of the sample), a Japanese firm was manufacturing one of its products in the United States.
scale: dummy: 1 = manufactured in the U.S., 0 = no

description: Plant-level MES was measured by the sum of the shipments of plants in the median and all higher classes divided by the number of plants in these classes at the 4-digit SIC level, over total industry shipments. Shipments in classes below the median are typically very small, hence the calculation starts at the median class. Industry shipments data were taken from the Census of Manufactures (1982).

The transportation cost of a given product was measured by the radius within which 80 percent of its total tonnage is shipped. Data on tons shipped by distance of shipment was taken from the 1977 Census of Transportation. The higher transportation cost, the smaller the radius, so transportation cost is inversely related to TRANS.

U.S. trade barriers are represented by a dummy equal to 1 if a product category is subject to a high tariff rate or export restraints, and zero otherwise. Data was taken from the U.S. International Trade Commission (1989).
scale: dummy: 1 = high tariff rate or export restraints, 0 = otherwise

description: A product's natural resource intensity is described by a dummy variable equal to 1 if it is natural resource intensive and zero otherwise. SIC 20 (food and beverages), 24 (wood except furniture), 26 (pulp and paper), 29 (petroleum), 30 (rubber), 32 (stone and glass), and 33 (primary metals) are classified as resource-intensive industries.

A dummy variable equal to one for all second-tier firms within a Keiretsu if their first-tier firm manufactured any product in the U.S. at the end of 1984, and to zero for first-tier firms, for second-tier firms within a Keiretsu if their first-tier firm had not invested by 1984, and for firms which are not part of Keiretsu groups. First entries of first-tier Keiretsu firms made in 1985 and 1986 are not counted because it was assumed that it takes at least two years for this 'follow-the-customer' pattern to take effect.
scale: dummy: 1 = second-tier member whose first-tier customer invested in the U.S. by 1984, 0 = otherwise
time_window: first-tier investment by the end of 1984

description: The amount of technological know-how held by a Japanese firm was measured by its R&D expenses divided by its total sales, normalized by the industry's average R&D intensity. Data for R&D intensity were taken at the firm rather than the product level due to the unavailability of product-level data. Sources were Yukashoken Hokokusho, Japan Company Handbook, and Toyo Keizai (1991).

The Japanese parent's endowment of goodwill or reputation was measured by its domestic media advertising expenses divided by its domestic sales, normalized by the industry's average advertising intensity. Sources were Yukashoken Hokokusho or Toyo Keizai (1991).

A dummy variable equal to 1 if a Japanese firm previously produced any product in the U.S., and to zero otherwise. Firms which entered the U.S. for the first time in 1985 and 1986 are coded as inexperienced.
scale: dummy: 1 = already manufacturing any other product in the U.S., 0 = otherwise

description: The concentration ratio of the target U.S. industry was measured by the Herfindhal-Hirschman index for the 50 largest companies at the 4-digit SIC level, as listed in the Census of Manufactures (1982).

Following Flowers (1976), exchange-of-threat is measured by the number of U.S. firms which had invested in the Japanese firm's industry three years before a Japanese firm's reverse investment in the U.S. (or 1986 in the case of noninvestment). Only U.S. entries are counted if the Japanese industry is loosely oligopolistic.
time_window: three years before the Japanese firm's U.S. investment (or 1986 for noninvestment)

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if the Japanese firm is in a loose oligopolistic industry and if its domestic rivals have already made previous investments in the U.S., and zero otherwise. The authors first checked whether a Japanese firm was in a loose oligopolistic industry and then ascertained whether any other Japanese firm in the same industry had previously invested in the U.S. First entries made in 1985 and 1986 are not counted, since the lag would be too short to observe subsequent 'follow-the-leader' investments.
scale: dummy: 1 = loose oligopolistic industry and rivals already invested in the U.S., 0 = otherwise
time_window: prior U.S. entries up to 1986, excluding 1985 and 1986 first entries

description: A Japanese firm's domestic market share was calculated as the ratio of its sales to the total sales of its industry. Because a medium SHARE should lead to a greater propensity to manufacture in the U.S. than a very high or a very low SHARE, the quadratic form is used, so SHARE should enter with a positive sign and SHARE squared with a negative one.

GROWTH is the average 10-year growth rate of industry shipments in the 4-digit SIC U.S. target industry, as listed in the 1982 Census of Manufactures. It was used as a control variable, on the argument that Japanese investors should have greater incentives to manufacture products in the U.S. when the demand for these products is growing rapidly.

Domestic industry concentration is used to classify a Japanese firm's industry as a loose oligopoly, defined by a Herfindahl-Hirschman index between 1000 and 1800 (8-firm concentration ratio 50 to 70). The classification enters the follow-the-leader dummy.

The proportion of shares held by CVC firms, calculated as the percentage of the total number of the venture's shares. The information comes from the principal stockholders reported in Form S-1, which includes investors who retain their shares when the venture goes public. Consistent with prior CVC studies, diversified banks and insurance companies are excluded because the resources they provide do not directly relate to the technology commercialization or R&D of new ventures.
time_window: at the time of the IPO, reflecting the last year the venture was a private firm

description: Takes a value of 1 if the founder is a CEO or a technology-related executive, such as a CTO or chief scientist, and 0 otherwise. In cases with more than one founder, the venture is labelled as having a founder as an incumbent manager if any of the cofounders is a CEO or a technology-related executive. In the sample, the founder is the CEO in 141 ventures and the CTO in 52 ventures, and the founder is not present at the time of the IPO in 126 ventures.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The ratio of R&D expenditures to total assets, taken from the last year that the venture was a private firm before eventually going public. The authors normalize R&D expenditures by firm assets rather than by sales because young ventures often have very low and unstable sales, while the total assets of young entrepreneurial ventures are relatively stable and serve as a reasonable measure of firm size.
time_window: the last year the venture was a private firm before the IPO

description: Count of a firm's number of product categories in each year within its core six-digit NAICS industry. The number of product categories in 2000 was tracked from firms' financial and/or own reports, and entries into new product categories were identified from press announcements of new and existing product categories; withdrawals from product categories were used to correct each firm's yearly count. Whether an announcement constituted a new product category rather than a new model of an existing product was determined by a panel of high technology industry experts. The resulting counts were triangulated with the number of product categories reported by the firms themselves. The linear term was used to test Hypothesis 1, the squared term to test Hypothesis 2 and the cubed term to test Hypothesis 3.
time_window: one year lagged relative to the dependent variable

description: The annual increase in the number of new product categories of a given firm divided by the total number of product categories in the preceding year. The measure was used for testing Hypothesis 4 and is included as an independent variable in the second-stage models. It is built from the same product category entry data used for the within-industry diversification measure.
time_window: annual change (year t relative to year t-1), lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: Returns on sales, computed using firm earnings before interest, tax and depreciation rather than net earnings, in order to avoid problems arising from different financing strategies, tax treatments and depreciation rules across industries. It is the dependent variable of the second-stage regression models.

The number of technology domains to which the firm's patents are classified in each year; the front page of each patent provides information on the main three-digit technology domain to which the USPTO has assigned the invention. The linear, squared and cubed terms of technological diversity and its annual rate of change are used as instrumental variables for the within-industry diversification terms in the 2SLS models.

Abnormal returns are the prediction errors of a market model whose parameters were estimated using the 200 trading days ending 10 days before an announcement. The event window was a period of up to seven days centered around the event day, including the three days before and the three days after the event day. Abnormal returns were also cumulated over several alternative intervals within the seven-day window surrounding the announcement.
time_window: seven-day window around the announcement day; market model estimated over the 200 trading days ending 10 days before the announcement

description: A dummy variable that takes on a value of one if it is a technological alliance and zero otherwise (that is, a marketing alliance). Technological alliances involve cooperation in upstream value chain activities such as R&D, engineering, and manufacturing, while marketing alliances involve cooperation in downstream activities such as sales, distribution, and customer service.

Profitability measured as the accounting rate of return, the ratio of net income to the book value of the firm. Data for the fiscal year-end immediately preceding an alliance announcement were obtained from the annual COMPUSTAT files.
time_window: fiscal year-end immediately preceding the alliance announcement

variable_name: Firm size (total assets, net sales, number of employees)
description: Three alternative measures of size obtained from the COMPUSTAT database: total assets, net sales, and total number of employees, taken at the fiscal year-end immediately preceding an alliance announcement. For the tests of the resource dependence hypothesis, each firm in an alliance pair was classified as the small partner or the large partner under each size metric.
level: firm (and alliance pair for the partner size tests)
time_window: fiscal year-end immediately preceding the alliance announcement

description: Return variances were computed over a symmetric window of 50 trading days surrounding the announcements, before and after. Following standard practice, a 10-day period immediately adjacent to each event date was excluded from these windows to allow for increased volatility in returns due to the announcement itself. The percentage change in return variance was also computed.
time_window: 50 trading days before and 50 trading days after the announcement, excluding the 10 days adjacent to the event date

description: The number of publications in top medical journals that scientists affiliated with a pioneering firm authored in the three years preceding an observation year. Premier journals were those accounting for two-thirds of the total impact factor in three Web of Science subject areas relevant to pharmaceutical drugs: general and internal medicine, research and experimental medicine, and pharmacy and pharmacology. Any top medical articles that the pioneer published about the focal drug were subtracted from that total.
time_window: three years preceding an observation year

description: The number of new drugs of the firm pioneering a new mechanism that the FDA approved in the three years preceding the observation year. The measure follows prior work that measured certifications as approvals of applications submitted to a regulatory agency.
time_window: three years preceding the observation year

variable_name: Pioneer's advantage in premier scientific publications
description: The difference between a pioneer's and a rival's publications in top medical journals in the previous three years. Greater scores indicate greater certification advantage of a pioneer over a rival, and the variable takes a negative value when a rival has a stronger history of certifications than a pioneer.
The difference between a pioneer and a rival in FDA new drug approvals in the previous three years.

variable_name: Premier scientific publications on pioneering drug
description: The count of publications about the pioneering drug in top medical journals in the previous three years. It is used as the contingency variable indicating scientific certifications of a pioneering innovation.
A dummy variable set to 1 in the years following the pioneering drug's FDA approval and to 0 otherwise.
time_window: years following the pioneering drug's FDA approval

variable_name: Rival's entry into a new mechanism
description: The dependent variable takes the value of 1 if the focal rival entered the new mechanism in the observation year and 0 otherwise. Yearly observations run for each rival in the risk set until the year in which a rival entered a focal mechanism or until 2004, whichever occurred first. The year of discovery of a drug was based on the year in which the innovating firm filed the application of the earliest patent protecting that drug.

The three guides adopt an ordered scale from 1 to n bands, with 1 representing the highest rank, and both the number of bands and the number of firms covered vary across practices and years, so the band figure alone is not meaningful. For each guide the authors compute a rating from the band in which a firm–location is ranked (the formula given in the paper is not readable in this text), then average the ratings within each practice area across the guides that cover it, and finally average over all practice areas in which the firm is covered. The resulting rating decreases from 1 (firms in the first band) to a value close to 0 for firms at the bottom. Example given: a firm with ratings 1 and .8 in tax and .5, .2, and .2 in real estate receives an average rating of .9 for tax and .3 for real estate, hence a final evaluation of .6.

Performance is based on the revenue per lawyer (RPL) at the law firm's branch office. RPL is worldwide revenues divided by the worldwide number of lawyers; the authors multiplied it by the branch office's number of lawyers, so that performance estimates the portion of total revenue generated by a branch office as a function of its number of lawyers. In the models it is expressed in hundreds of millions of dollars, using international dollars adjusted for purchasing power parity with World Bank estimates.
scale: hundreds of millions of international dollars (PPP-adjusted)

description: Category spanning is computed as 1 minus Simpson's (1949) index of diversity; that is, 1 minus the sum of the squared grades of membership of the firm–location across the practice areas in which it operates. Grades of membership in each of the eight practice areas are taken from the guides' coverage. The minimum value is 0 for specialists engaged in only one practice area and the maximum is .875 for generalist law firms covering the eight practice areas.

For each firm–location the authors use a set of eight dummy variables flagging coverage in the eight practice categories in at least one guide (1 = presence, 0 = absence), concatenated into an octuple reflecting the firm's category combination. The variable corresponds, for each year and location, to the logged sum of the frequencies of all the existing lower-degree n-tuples (septuplets, sextuples, quintuples, quartets, trios, and pairs) that are included in the octuple. The vector with all eight categories present is the most inclusive configuration, while the least inclusive is a pair present only once; specialists who do not combine categories get a value of 0.
scale: logged sum of frequencies of included lower-degree category combinations; 0 for specialists

description: Respondents were asked how many independent directors were jointly appointed by the parent companies and served on the JV board at the time of its formation. To estimate the likelihood of independent directors being selected, the authors created a dummy variable that took the value of one if an outsider was appointed to the JV board and zero otherwise.
time_window: at the time of joint venture formation

description: Respondents rated the degree to which the parent firms are similar in terms of (i) the products and services that they offer, (ii) the geographic markets they serve, and (iii) the customer segments they serve. The summed measure had a Cronbach's alpha of 0.70 and all items loaded on a single factor explaining 60.2% of the variance. Market overlap was measured as a multiplicative measure of the three individual items, and given the high skewness the measure was log-transformed.

Respondents indicated which functional activities were performed in the joint venture. The measure of JV scope represents the total number of activities performed by the JV. An exploratory factor analysis showed that all items loaded on a single factor that explained 87.3% of the variance.

Respondents rated the extent to which each of five external environmental factors were predictable: technological trends, competitive culture, raw material and equipment supply, customer demand, and government policies and regulations. To weight each factor, respondents in a separate question allocated a total of 100 points to these five factors based on how important they are to the ultimate success of the joint venture. Each five-point Likert-scale item was then reverse coded (i.e., 'unpredictability') and multiplied by the weight given by the respondent; the exact formula is not readable in this payload.
scale: five-point Likert items multiplied by a 100-point allocation weight

description: Respondents indicated which of eight types of contractual provisions were specified by the parents in their contracts. The provisions were ranked in terms of stringency to calculate a weighted measure of contractual complexity, where Di equals one if the first provision was instituted and zero otherwise, two if the second provision was instituted and zero otherwise, and so forth. The exact formula is not readable in this payload.

Respondents were asked how many collaborations they had undertaken with the current JV partner(s) prior to the formation of the focal JV. Given the positive skewness of this measure, a logarithmic transformation was performed by taking the log of one plus the number of prior ties.
time_window: prior to the formation of the focal JV

description: Number of years that a firm had participated in the personal computer industry.

A dummy variable coded 1 if a firm derived at least 50 percent of its sales from proprietary technology in the year it was founded, and 0 otherwise. The percentages of sales from proprietary and standards-based technology had a marked bimodal distribution, and about 90 percent of the firms maintained the same strategy throughout their lives.

variable_name: Square root of deflated annual sales
description: Sales growth was assessed by modeling how the square root of a firm's annual sales of personal computers, in thousands of dollars, varied across time. A GNP-based deflator was used to make sales figures comparable from year to year, and the square root was examined to reduce heteroscedasticity in the regression models.

A firm was coded as failing in year t if it sold no personal computers in year t+1. Failures included the deaths of entire firms and industry exits by multibusiness companies, and eight acquisitions were treated as continued survival of separate organizations.

The authors first identified the demographic dimension(s) along which a new director was similar to 50 percent or more of incumbents. Similarity along each similar dimension was measured by the proportion of incumbents who were similar to the new director on that dimension, and the final measure is the average of these per-dimension proportions. The measure thus captures the average degree to which the new director is similar to incumbents along shared dimensions.
scale: proportion (average of proportions of similar incumbents)
time_window: at the time of the new director's appointment

description: The authors identified the demographic dimensions along which a new director differed from more than 50 percent of incumbents (dissimilar dimensions). Dissimilarity along each dissimilar dimension is the percentage of incumbents who differed from the new director along that dimension, and the final measure is the sum of these dissimilarity measures. It can be viewed as an aggregated measure that uses the degree of difference along each dissimilar dimension as a weighting factor; for the illustrative case of Thomas W. Jones this sum was 1.00 + 0.64 + 0.73 = 2.37. Two directors were coded as similar in age when their ages differed by less than one standard deviation of age among all Fortune directors (eight years), and functional background was classified into throughput, output, and peripheral functions.
scale: continuous sum of per-dimension dissimilarity percentages
time_window: at the time of the new director's appointment

description: Prior common board appointment between a new director and incumbents was measured as the total number of incumbents who had prior common board appointments with the new director. In a separate analysis the total number of other boards on which the new director had prior common board appointments with incumbents was used as an alternative measure.

Director tenure was measured as the number of years that a demographically different director served on the focal board. Tenure of a director who stayed until the end of the study period was right censored. In a separate analysis a dummy variable indicating whether a new director's tenure was longer than three years was used.

Committee appointment was measured as 1 if a new director who has different demographic characteristics from incumbents served on the focal board's major committees (i.e., the compensation, audit, nomination, and corporate governance committees) within three years after the initial appointment and 0 otherwise.
time_window: within three years after the initial appointment

description: Committee chair appointment was measured as 1 if a director who had different demographic characteristics from incumbents served as a major board committee chair on the focal board within three years after the initial appointment and 0 otherwise.
time_window: within three years after the initial appointment

description: A binary variable coded as one when the CEO appeared in a CNBC interview in year t and zero otherwise. The authors obtained 6,567 CNBC interviews by CEOs of Execucomp firms over 1997-2009: 4,757 interviews for 1997-2006 collected from Factiva using the key words 'CEO interview' and 'CNBC', and 1,810 interviews for 2007-2009 identified from the CNBC website after the transcripts were no longer available in Factiva.

The number of news articles naming the CEO in the corresponding fiscal year, downloaded from Factiva for Execucomp firms when the company name appeared in the first paragraph or the title. Java codes classified an article as about the CEO when the CEO's name or title was found, and a second round matched nicknames and middle names using lists of English nicknames. One was added to the number of news articles with CEO names and the natural log was taken.
