description: Measured as an index based on five commonly used formative indicators of CEO power: CEO duality, CEO tenure relative to directors, CEO ownership relative to directors, proportion of inside directors, and institutional ownership. CEO duality is a binary variable set to 1 when the CEO was also the board chair in the same year and 0 otherwise; CEO tenure relative to directors is the CEO's tenure divided by the average tenure of independent directors; CEO ownership relative to directors is the percentage of common shares owned by the CEO divided by the average percentage owned by independent directors; proportion of inside directors is the proportion of directors who are also top executives of the firm; institutional ownership is the percentage of outstanding shares held by the largest institutional block holder. The authors used the sum of standardized scores of these five indicators to create the index, reversely coding institutional ownership so that greater values reflect greater CEO power.
time_window: 1 year prior to the dependent variable

description: Following Keats and Hitt (1988), the authors regressed industry sales against year from year t - 4 to year t and then used the regression coefficient as the measure of environmental munificence.

The highest degree of presence that any competitor manifests in markets in which it overlaps with a focal firm; the competitor with the highest market commonality was used rather than an average among all competitors. It was built from a matrix of market commonalities between every pair of firms in the sample, based on sales in each product-market, normalized so that the sum of the market commonality indexes for all of a given firm's competitors equaled 1, and repeated for all eight quarters of analysis. For a given foothold, the authors extracted the market commonalities between the firm with the foothold and every other firm with sales in that product-market and quarter and took the highest of these scores. The equation printed for the market commonality index is not readable in the text.
time_window: eight quarters of analysis; predictors precede the dependent variables by one time interval

description: The greatest extent to which any multimarket competitor possessed strategic endowments comparable in type and amount to those of a focal firm, using the most similar competitor. Each firm's resource portfolio was dimensionalized each quarter from publicly available data along four dimensions, transformed to standardized scores for comparison between firms. Pairwise resource distance was calculated as the Euclidean distance between the resource profiles of the two firms; for a given foothold the authors took the smallest of these distances (the distance to the most similar market participant) and reverse-coded it to create a similarity score. The equation printed for the resource distance measure is not readable in the text.
time_window: each quarter of the eight-quarter sampling frame

description: Dichotomous variable indicating that a firm launched a foothold attack, which the authors treated as having occurred when the firm announced a price action on products in the foothold market, launched a new promotional campaign oriented toward that market, signaled intent to grow its presence there, increased its share of the market via an acquisition, or introduced a new product there. Potential actions were identified by searching LexisNexis press releases for keyword lists covering new product introductions, price actions, promotional campaigns and signaling actions, and the lead author read each article to discern whether it recorded an attack; an independent rater coded a 10 percent random sample with intraclass correlation agreement of 95.8 percent. Acquisitions were identified from SDC Platinum.
Dichotomous variable coded as a withdrawal when sales for the foothold's market dropped to zero for two consecutive quarters.

A market position was counted as a foothold only if the firm that owned it recorded quarterly sales in a product-market representing less than 3 percent total market share. Positions that declined into small market shares were not considered footholds because they were not intentionally established, and new positions established in markets a firm already competed in (such as fighting brands) were not included. Given the focus on competitor analysis, only footholds belonging to a firm competing head-to-head with a rival in both the foothold market and at least one other market were examined.

The highest degree of presence that any competitor manifests in markets in which it overlaps with a focal firm; the competitor with the highest market commonality was used rather than an average among all competitors. It was built from a matrix of market commonalities between every pair of firms in the sample, based on sales in each product-market, normalized so that the sum of the market commonality indexes for all of a given firm's competitors equaled 1, and repeated for all eight quarters of analysis. For a given foothold, the authors extracted the market commonalities between the firm with the foothold and every other firm with sales in that product-market and quarter and took the highest of these scores. The equation printed for the market commonality index is not readable in the text.
time_window: eight quarters of analysis; predictors precede the dependent variables by one time interval

description: The greatest extent to which any multimarket competitor possessed strategic endowments comparable in type and amount to those of a focal firm, using the most similar competitor. Each firm's resource portfolio was dimensionalized each quarter from publicly available data along four dimensions, transformed to standardized scores for comparison between firms. Pairwise resource distance was calculated as the Euclidean distance between the resource profiles of the two firms; for a given foothold the authors took the smallest of these distances and reverse-coded it to create a similarity score. The equation printed for the resource distance measure is not readable in the text.
time_window: each quarter of the eight-quarter sampling frame

description: Dichotomous variable indicating that a firm launched a foothold attack, treated as having occurred when the firm announced a price action on products in the foothold market, launched a new promotional campaign oriented toward that market, signaled intent to grow its presence there, increased its share of the market via an acquisition, or introduced a new product there. Actions were identified by keyword searches of LexisNexis press releases with 95.8 percent rater agreement on a 10 percent random sample, and acquisitions from SDC Platinum.
Dichotomous variable coded as a withdrawal when sales for the foothold's market dropped to zero for two consecutive quarters.

CEO career horizon is measured using the CEO's expected tenure with the firm, based on a combination of CEO tenure and age relative to the industry average CEO tenure and age. The measure compares CEOs in the same four-digit SIC industry along two dimensions: current age and the length of tenure. The formula itself could not be extracted from the text. Higher values of the variable correspond to longer career horizons.

Real option intensity is the sensitivity of firm value to changes in firm-level uncertainty, computed in two stages. First, firm volatility is calculated on a weekly basis as the standard deviation of daily stock returns for year y, month m and week w, and the change in volatility is the difference from the prior week. Second, the weekly data for each firm within a year are used to regress the firm's excess return (return minus the risk-free rate) on the change in volatility, a market factor loading, and control variables including the log of one plus the book-to-market equity ratio, the log of one plus the equity market value, the six-week lagged return for weeks w-7 to w-2, and the weekly trading volume divided by the number of outstanding shares; the regression specification itself could not be extracted from the text. A total of 15,970 separate firm-year regressions are run, and the estimated coefficient is used as the firm-year dependent variable in the main equation.
CEO long-term incentives are approximated with unexercised options (exercisable + unexercisable) and restricted stock holdings scaled by total compensation, as reported in ExecuComp.
Institutional ownership is calculated as the ratio of stock owned by institutions.

Mean of the extent to which the MNE parent has exploited distinctive resources that are (1) rare and firm-specific, (2) inimitable, and (3) rent-generating for operations in China. Each of these three dimensions was computed as the average of the responses about three strategic resources: product and process technology, industrial or intellectual property rights, and managerial and organizational skills. Internal consistency and dimensionality were confirmed by a Cronbach's alpha of 0.76 and communality estimates of 0.80 obtained from a factor analysis. Respondents assessed capability exploitation for the past three years.

Mean of the extent to which the MNE parent has committed and dedicated itself to (1) learning and absorbing the critical capabilities needed for local operations from other organizations, (2) developing and creating the new skills needed for local operations through learning and innovation, and (3) revitalizing and applying current competencies to new situations in the host country. Each dimension was the average of responses to multiple questions, and the construct was assessed on a seven-point Likert scale over the past three years. Internal consistency and dimensionality were confirmed by a Cronbach's alpha of 0.76 and communality estimates of 0.80 from a factor analysis.

Multidimensional construct consisting of diversity and heterogeneity, each of which contains macroeconomic, political/legal, and sociocultural segments. The variable is measured as the average of the two dimensions, each of which is calculated as the mean of the three segments, using a seven-point Likert scale. Respondents were asked to assess environmental variables based on the past three years as the time frame.

Measured as the geometric average of the standard deviations of sales growth and net profit growth in the industry in which a subunit operated during 1994 to 1996. Industrial data were collected from three consecutive annual editions of the China Statistical Yearbook.

Defined as the mean of a pair of questions involving how the commercial practices and business culture differ from commonly accepted international standards and how location specific they are, as perceived by foreign managers on a seven-point Likert scale. Respondents assessed environmental variables for the past three years. The authors report Cronbach's alphas of at least 0.74 and communality estimates of at least 0.83 for these multidimensional constructs, indicating high reliability.

Dummy variable defined as one if the subsidiary is wholly owned and zero otherwise (joint venture). The information for entry mode was obtained from the Directory of Foreign-Invested Industrial Enterprises and the Almanac of China's Foreign Economic Relations and Trade (1993-1996).

Dummy variable defined as one if the subsidiary is local market oriented and zero otherwise (export oriented). A firm is defined as export oriented if it exports more than 70% of its total outputs, the criterion regulated by MOFTEC; the information about market orientation is from the survey.
scale: dummy (1 = local market orientation, 0 = export market orientation)

description: Return on investment measured as net return divided by total investment in 1997. The ROI of the sample firms was obtained from a CDROM produced by the Computer Center in China's MOFTEC, and ROI was missing for 14 sample firms. The total sample was separated into a high-performance group (n = 70) and a low-performance group (n = 83) based on the mean score of subsidiary performance.

The dependent variable equals 1 if the hiring firm was ranked below Brobeck in the Vault 100 in 2002 and equals 0 otherwise. Because Brobeck was ranked 26th in the 2002 Vault 100, any employer ranked 27th or worse or unranked is coded as status loss and any firm ranked 25th or better as status gain. The employer status measure is based on the rank of each lawyer's first post-Brobeck employer in the Vault 100.

The number of years that a lawyer was a member of the Brobeck partnership as of 2003. The authors state that this variable measures the strength of each partner's association with failure, accounting for the extent to which a partner's labor market identity is intertwined with Brobeck.

The law school attended by each lawyer was identified from website biographies, and ranks were obtained from the 2003 U.S. News and World Report 'Best Law School' list. Actual U.S. News ranks were assigned for schools ranked between 1 and 100, and a rank of 152 was assigned to all Tier Two and unranked law schools. Educational prestige is reverse coded so that more prestigious schools are assigned lower numeric ranks.

A binary indicator that equals 1 if the lawyer graduated from Berkeley, Columbia, Chicago, Georgetown, Harvard, Michigan, New York University, Stanford, Virginia, or Yale law schools, and otherwise equals 0. The coding follows Phillips and Zuckerman (2001).

The average reputation of the firms in the focal firm's network, measured with the partner's Fortune reputation rankings in a given year, taken from Fortune's annual listing of the 'Most Admired Companies'. Because the Fortune list includes different numbers of companies each year and sometimes modifies its evaluation scales, the authors used yearly standardized rankings. The average value of the network partners' reputation is used as the dependent variable.

The average profitability of the focal firm's network partners, measured with return on assets (ROA) in a given year. Because profitability varies substantially by industry, the variable was normalized across industries by subtracting out the average profitability of all firms in the same two-digit SIC industry code before entering it into the analysis. The average value of the network partners' profitability is used as the dependent variable.
scale: ROA, normalized within two-digit SIC industry

description: The average size of the focal firm's network partners, measured with sales obtained from COMPUSTAT. The size variable was highly skewed, so it was normalized by log transformation prior to entering it into the analyses; because size varies substantially by industry, it was also normalized across industries by subtracting out the average size of all firms in the same two-digit SIC industry code. The average value of the network partners' size is used as the dependent variable.
scale: log of sales, normalized within two-digit SIC industry

variable_name: Added partners are lower quality than lost ties
description: A dichotomous dependent variable indicating if a firm has a lower average reputation, sales, ROA, and network prominence for any new ties relative to ties that were lost. If a firm had a lower average quality of added ties, the authors coded it as '1'; otherwise, they coded it as '0'.
scale: dichotomous (1 = lower average quality of added ties, 0 = otherwise)

description: Bonacich eigenvector centrality, which weights focal firm centrality by the centrality of its interlock partners and gives a firm a higher prominence score if its connected ties are more central players in the network. It was computed with UCINET v.6.118 from an adjacency matrix representing the interlocks among all Fortune 300 firms, coded '1' when two firms were tied through an interlock and '0' when they were not.

Structural cohesion for the focal firm, measured with the 'indirect structural constraint' outlined by Burt (1992) and Reagans and McEvily (2003). The formula for the indirect structural constraint is not readable in the available text; the text states that the term Piq Pqj' indicates the proportional strength of i's indirect connection with j through the third-party actor q.

variable_name: Number of unethical acts (prior three years)
description: The total number of unethical acts committed by the focal firm in the preceding three years. Acts were coded by searching articles published in the Wall Street Journal, Business Week, Fortune, Forbes, and the New York Times for the 1987-1993 period, with an extended search in Lexis Nexis when no acts were found. The preceding three years were used because the time for director changes to take effect can be as short as one year or as long as three years. Because the number of acts was highly skewed, the variable was log transformed prior to entering it into the analysis.

variable_name: Average illegitimacy of acts (prior three years)
description: The average illegitimacy ratings for all unethical acts committed by the focal firm in the preceding three years, used as a continuous variable to capture the effects of degree of illegitimacy independent of the number of acts. The ratings were obtained by asking 34 individuals to indicate the degree of illegitimacy on a five-point scale for each of the 18 categories of acts.

variable_name: Added partners are lower quality than lost ties (dummy)
description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 when the firm's newly added ties have a lower average reputation, sales, ROA and network prominence than the ties it lost, and 0 otherwise.

Count of positive, material press releases issued by the acquiring firm within the event window, which is day -1 to day +1. Clearly positive events (e.g., new product releases, social good efforts like donations) were coded as impression offsetting; for event types that may or may not be positive the coders looked for additional information, comparing announced earnings to consensus expectations for earnings releases and requiring an unambiguously positive characterization of the event for other events. In total 415 events were categorized as positive, 49 as neutral, and 56 as negative. A primary coder coded all 4,969 press releases and inter-rater reliability with a secondary coder on 100 press releases was Cohen's kappa of 0.99.
Count of acquisitions fitting the sample specification that the acquirer made in the three years immediately prior to the announcement date (i.e., day -[365 * 3] to day -1).
time_window: three years immediately prior to the announcement date

description: Coded 1 when the acquiring organization was within the top 25 of either Fortune's Most Admired list or the Wall Street Journal and Harris Interactive's corporate reputation rankings in a particular year and as 0 otherwise; the variable was lagged in all analyses.
Coded 1 for acquisitions in which the acquirer and target have different two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes, and 0 otherwise.

Coded 1 if the target organization in an acquisition has a zero or negative net income in its annual report in the year prior to acquisition announcement and as 0 otherwise. To create the variable the authors flagged all acquisitions where the offer price-to-earnings-per-share ratio was missing in SDC Platinum and, once they manually verified that this missing data indicated negative earnings, coded it as unprofitable.

Sum of daily abnormal returns for a security over the event window, where abnormal returns are the part of the return on a security unanticipated by an economic model of expected returns and are assessed against the return of the value-weighted market portfolio. Estimates of the model's constant and beta were calculated during a 250-day window that falls between 295 and 45 days before the focal acquisition, and the reported event window is the three-day window centered on the acquisition (day -1 to day +1); the CAR variable is the average of the abnormal returns for the event window. The formula for the abnormal returns is not readable in the text.
time_window: three-day event window (day -1 to day +1); estimation window of 250 days between 295 and 45 days before the acquisition

description: Composite index of the internal resource munificence of a firm, combining financial and managerial resources. Financial resources were measured with equity divided by total debt, the inverse of the leverage ratio and thus a reflection of unused borrowing capacity; managerial resources were measured with a prestige scale composed of the sum of five standardized items capturing top managers' educational and professional affiliations. Both variables were standardized and were not correlated in any of the five years preceding bankruptcy, and the empirically derived discriminant function D-score = (1.84 x equity/debt) + (0.528 x prestige) + 0.11 was used as the index. A low D-score indicates a high probability of a firm's being a bankrupt, so as a firm's D-score decreases over time the firm declines.
time_window: T-5 to T-1 (the five years preceding bankruptcy)

description: Bankrupt firms were classified into patterns of decline by cluster-analyzing each firm's profile of D-scores from the fifth to the last year before bankruptcy, using Ward's minimum variance hierarchical clustering algorithm and the squared Euclidean distance between firms. The three-cluster solution was the best statistically; clusters were labeled on the basis of the level of each cluster's D-score and the significance of changes in those levels. Cluster 1 (postdecline lingerers) firms appeared to linger in a postdecline state from at least T-5 to T-1, cluster 2 (gradual decliners) had high D-scores five years before bankruptcy but had completed their decline in T-1, and cluster 3 (sudden decliners) declined rapidly.

The number of wholly owned subunits acquired by or merged into a firm, taken from published financial statements. Variables were calculated as two-year averages to smooth out momentary fluctuations, based on the periods T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The number of new lines of business added to a firm's portfolio. Variables were calculated as two-year averages to smooth out momentary fluctuations, based on the periods T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The number of wholly owned subunits liquidated or disposed of by a firm, taken from published financial statements. Variables were calculated as two-year averages to smooth out momentary fluctuations, based on the periods T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The number of lines of business dropped from a firm's portfolio. Variables were calculated as two-year averages to smooth out momentary fluctuations, based on the periods T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The percentage of members of the top management team whose formal titles indicated that they reported directly to the CEO, that is, were on the hierarchical layer immediately below the CEO. Variables were calculated as two-year averages based on T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The percentage of top team members whose dominant career background was in the financial or accounting functions. Variables were calculated as two-year averages based on T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The percentage of top team members whose dominant career background was as an attorney or as an employee in a corporate counsel's office. Variables were calculated as two-year averages based on T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The percentage of top team members whose dominant career background was in sales or marketing. Variables were calculated as two-year averages based on T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The percentage of top team members whose dominant career background was in R&D. Variables were calculated as two-year averages based on T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The percentage of top team members whose dominant career background was in production or internal operations; for retailers, operations included store management and warehousing and purchasing functions, and for transportation firms, operations included maintenance, scheduling, and other operations. Variables were calculated as two-year averages based on T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The annual percentage growth rate in total industry revenues in real dollars for the firm's primary line of business. Variables were calculated as two-year averages, based on T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: The variability in annual industry demand growth rates, calculated as the mean percentage deviation of the actual demand growth rate from the five-year average demand growth rate for the firm's primary line of business over the five years leading up to the year in question. Variables were calculated as two-year averages based on T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: A firm's net fixed assets in millions of dollars, taken from published financial statements and used as a proxy for its ability to downsize by liquidating fixed assets. A measure of saleable assets was unavailable, so net fixed assets was used as a proxy; it includes assets that may not be saleable.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

description: A firm's long-term debt in millions of dollars, taken from published financial statements and used as a proxy for creditors' commitment because it is a measure of aggregate losses suffered by creditors of a bankrupt firm. Better measures, such as the average loss suffered by individual creditors or the ratio of the average loss to the average creditor's total assets, were unavailable.
time_window: two-year averages, T-5 to T-4 and T-2 to T-1

variable_name: Strategic and managerial characteristics of postdecline firms
description: Consequences of decline are measured through a set of strategic and managerial variables compared between postdecline lingerers and matched survivors: mergers and acquisitions, entries, liquidations, exits, CEO span of control, and top team functional backgrounds. Differences are tested with t-tests and logistic regressions.

Directed 78 x 78 matrix of reported social ties. Each informant was given the full list of 125 drug development companies in the region and asked to indicate those in which he or she had ties; 1 was entered in the matrix cell at the intersection of the ego's row and the alter's column if the informant reported a tie, and 0 otherwise. Acquaintance is one of the two tie types modeled, distinguished from friendship by tie strength; the questionnaire instructed informants to consider the two types of ties as the same, except that friends 'regularly spend time together for other reasons than work.'
level: directed dyad (informant's row to company column)
time_window: as of the time of the interview

description: Directed 78 x 78 matrix of reported friendship ties, recorded in the same way as acquaintance (1 in the cell at the intersection of the ego's row and the alter's column if reported, 0 otherwise). Friendship is the stronger of the two types of ties: the questionnaire instructed informants to treat the two types as the same except that friends 'regularly spend time together for other reasons than work.'
level: directed dyad (informant's row to company column)
time_window: as of the time of the interview

description: Nonsymmetric 78 x 78 matrix coded 1 if the row company entered a drug development area earlier than the column company (and 0 otherwise), and transposed relative to the dependent matrices so that the analysis captures the effect of exposure to signals rather than sending them. It captures the collegial aspect of competition that joint area membership affirms when it is not coupled with a perception of challenge by a newcomer. Its ties are not mutually exclusive with those of initiated area contact because a dyad member may initiate contact in one area and have the other member initiate contact in another.

Symmetric matrix coded 1 for pairs of companies that have been simultaneously developing a drug for the same indication and 0 otherwise; only drugs that entered clinical trials were considered. Indication contact does not count as area contact, so two companies may have both types of contact only if they have worked on the same indication and on another project in the same area. In models that include the interaction with status competition, the main effect of indication contact captures the effect of indication contact in the absence of status competition.

Nonsymmetric 78 x 78 matrix where initiation of area contact, i.e., entering the area later than the other company, is coded as 1 and 0 otherwise; it captures the goal conflict signal that incumbents perceive when a newcomer enters their area. The matrix is transposed relative to the dependent matrices so that the analysis captures the effect of exposure to signals rather than sending them.

variable_name: Status competition reported by informant in signal origin company
description: Indicator combining two items measured on a five-point Likert scale (Cronbach's alpha 0.76); the informants evaluated the applicability of each statement to every competitor they had identified. The 1-to-5 scale was converted into a 0-to-4 scale to ensure that the lowest score ('strongly disagree') is equivalent to the absence of status competition, and the sum of the two item scores was entered in the adjacency matrix at the intersection of the informants' rows and the competitors' columns, with zeroes for all companies not named as competitors. The scores were summed rather than averaged because the analysis software allows only integers in network matrices. The matrices were transposed so that the analysis examines the effect of status competition reported by an informant in one company on reactions of informants in a different company.
level: dyad (informant's company row to competitor company column)

description: Interaction between the matrix of indication contact and the matrix of reported status competition, capturing the extent to which a company competes for status with its indication competitors. Its negative effect shows that the positive effect of indication contact on social ties significantly decreases as status competition intensifies.

A three-item measure of the stakeholder's trust in the organization, created without referencing specific trustworthiness dimensions. The first item asked whether the respondent trusted the organization ('I trust the organization'). The second and third items proxied the respondent's willingness to be vulnerable by evaluating their willingness to recommend the organization to others: one general recommendation item ('I would recommend the organization because I predict a good future for the organization') and one targeted, stakeholder-specific recommendation item asking whether they would recommend to friends that they buy, invest, work for, or work with the organization. The alpha for the three items was 0.84.

Three survey items, all beginning with 'The organization ...', measuring attributions of integrity ('does not try to deceive', 'has high moral standards', 'treats its stakeholder with respect'). Responses were marked using a five-point scale with endpoints labeled 'strongly disagree' (1) and 'strongly agree' (5). Items were selected from a larger set based on high convergent and discriminant validity in pretest samples using exploratory factor analysis; coefficient alpha for the scale was between 0.85 and 0.93.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: Three survey items, all beginning with 'The organization ...', measuring attributions of benevolence ('is caring', 'listens to my needs', 'does not abuse stakeholders'). Responses were marked using a five-point scale with endpoints labeled 'strongly disagree' (1) and 'strongly agree' (5). Items were selected from a larger set based on high convergent and discriminant validity in pretest samples using exploratory factor analysis; coefficient alpha for the scale was between 0.85 and 0.93.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: Four survey items, all beginning with 'The organization ...', measuring perceptions of transparency ('explains its decisions', 'says if something goes wrong', 'is transparent', 'openly shares all relevant information'). Responses were marked using a five-point scale with endpoints labeled 'strongly disagree' (1) and 'strongly agree' (5). Items were selected from a larger set based on high convergent and discriminant validity in pretest samples using exploratory factor analysis; coefficient alpha for the scale was between 0.85 and 0.93.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: Three survey items measuring identification with the organization ('I can identify with the organization', 'My personal values match the values of the organization', 'I feel connected with the organization'). Responses were marked using a five-point scale with endpoints labeled 'strongly disagree' (1) and 'strongly agree' (5). Items were selected from a larger set based on high convergent and discriminant validity in pretest samples using exploratory factor analysis; coefficient alpha for the scale was between 0.85 and 0.93.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: Two survey items, beginning with 'The organization ...', measuring perceived managerial competence ('can successfully adapt to changing demands', 'is able to reach set goals'). Responses were marked using a five-point scale with endpoints labeled 'strongly disagree' (1) and 'strongly agree' (5). Items were selected from a larger set based on high convergent and discriminant validity in pretest samples using exploratory factor analysis; coefficient alpha for the scale was between 0.85 and 0.93.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: Two survey items, beginning with 'The organization ...', measuring perceived technical competence ('is very competent in its area', 'generally has high standards'). Responses were marked using a five-point scale with endpoints labeled 'strongly disagree' (1) and 'strongly agree' (5). Items were selected from a larger set based on high convergent and discriminant validity in pretest samples using exploratory factor analysis; coefficient alpha for the scale was between 0.85 and 0.93.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: Depth was operationalized from respondents' reported prior interactions and length of contact with the organization. Stakeholders who reported more than 100 interactions and more than three years of contact with the organization were classified as having a deep relationship; stakeholders with fewer than 100 interactions or less than three years of contact were classified as low-depth stakeholders. This classification resulted in relatively equal sample sizes between the shallow (665 stakeholders) and deep (633 stakeholders) categories.

Stakeholders were classified by their position relative to the organization: employees and investors were classified as internal stakeholders because they represent the organization (they work for it or own it), whereas customers and suppliers were classified as external stakeholders because they neither work for nor own the organization. This resulted in 556 stakeholders classified as internal and 742 as external.

Number of banks that suffered depositors' runs in a city during the Panic of 1893. It is the first independent variable and measures the severity of bank runs in the community's prior crisis experience.

Dummy variable of whether community collective action, the issuing of currency substitutes, was organized during the Panic of 1907. Currency substitutes were small denomination notes in convenient denominations of $5, $10, and $20, in some places as low as 25 cents, issued by banks for public circulation. The authors report that Andrew (1908) provided the exact dates when banks in a city first issued the small denomination currency substitutes.

Dummy variable of whether organizational collective action, mutual lending through clearinghouse loan certificates, was organized during the Panic of 1907. Financially stressed members of a clearing house could borrow loan certificates by collateralizing their assets and paying interest and use them in place of currency in the interbank clearing process. The authors report that Andrew (1908) provided the exact dates when banks in a city first issued the clearinghouse loan certificates.

Hazard rates of a bank run for each city during the time period of the 1893 bank run, obtained from Greve et al. (2016). Their model shows that banks are more at risk of a run when there are bank runs in nearby communities, in banks of the same form (national, state, savings, or commercial), and in communities with similar demographic characteristics. The authors calculated the mean hazard of bank runs across banks in the community.

variable_name: percentage of banks in 1907 that were founded before 1893
description: Percentage of banks in the city in 1907 that were founded before 1893, i.e., that existed at the time of the Panic of 1893. In the results the authors refer to this variable as the percentage of banks that survived the Panic of 1893 in a city.

Dummy variable indicating that a clearinghouse was built by local banks after the Panic of 1893. The authors control separately for the existence of a clearinghouse in a community at the time of the 1907 estimation.

variable_name: percentage of sales going through all direct channels
description: Respondents indicated the percentage of the product line's sales that each of a number of alternative channels accounted for during the past year. Following John and Weitz (1988), the channel integration construct was operationalized by the percentage of sales going through all direct channels. A five-point semantic differential item ('Channels mostly third party' vs. 'Channels mostly company-owned') served as a check for convergent validity and correlated 0.63 with the percentage measure.

Four items, taken from scales developed by Anderson (1985), John and Weitz (1988) and Klein et al. (1990), assessing the extent to which specialized knowledge of the firm's products and procedures is required by salespeople. The items were measured on a seven-point Likert scale ranging from 'Strongly disagree' to 'Strongly agree'; coefficient alpha for the scale is 0.76.
scale: seven-point Likert (Strongly disagree to Strongly agree)

description: A scale developed by John and Weitz (1988) whose four items primarily relate to the level of volatility in the environment. The items were measured with five-point semantic differential scales; the scale has an alpha of 0.86.

Three items from Anderson (1985) and John and Weitz (1988) reflecting the extent to which it is difficult to assess selling performance in the distribution channel. These items were measured using seven-point scales ranging from 'Strongly disagree' to 'Strongly agree'; the scale has an alpha of 0.63. One item, stating that it is always easy to assess how well each salesperson is doing, is reverse scaled.
scale: seven-point scales (Strongly disagree to Strongly agree)

description: An index of firm market power was created for each product-market from responses of the senior executive and the product/market/sales manager. The senior executive indicated the firm's overall market power in the selected product-market on a scale ranging from 'Low' to 'High' with 'Moderate-Low' and 'Moderate-High' as the intermediate scale points. The product/market/sales manager provided two market share items and two product differentiation items on seven-point 'Strongly disagree' to 'Strongly agree' scales. A factor analysis of these five items produced two factors; the five items are combined and treated as an index.
scale: index combining one four-point item and four seven-point items

description: In the second base model and the interaction model, the firm's market power was included as an independent variable, entered as the five-item index of firm market power described above. The variable was mean-centered before the interaction terms were formed, as recommended by Aiken and West (1992), to minimize multicollinearity between the main effect and interaction terms.

The main predictor is the interaction of two dummy variables. The first dummy receives a value of '1' for NYSE adopters and '0' for NASDAQ adopters. The second is a postadoption dummy that is '1' for the 5 years subsequent to (including) lead director adoption or until the end of the sampling window and '0' for the 5 years prior to adoption. Because the specification includes year and firm fixed effects, the noninteracted NYSE and postadoption period dummy variables are not included.
time_window: 5 years prior to and 5 years subsequent to lead director adoption

description: A binary indicator of CEO dismissal. The authors classify dismissals based on firm press releases and news reports to identify forced turnovers from the larger set of all CEO turnovers. It is modelled with firm fixed-effects logistic regressions.
time_window: dependent variable measured at time t

description: Receives a value of '1' if a CEO is also Chair of the Board and '0' otherwise in a year. It is modelled with firm fixed-effects logistic regressions.
time_window: dependent variable measured at time t

description: The difference between a CEO's actual pay and predicted pay, with larger residuals reflecting higher excess CEO compensation. Predicted pay is obtained from an ordinary least squares regression of CEO total compensation on the natural logarithm of total assets, the percent of CEO equity ownership, CEO age, CEO tenure, return on assets, two-digit SIC industry dummy variables, and year dummy variables.
time_window: dependent variable measured at time t

description: Operating performance measured as ROA, used instead of market performance because market performance can be influenced by managers' impression management. It is modelled with firm fixed-effects OLS regressions.
time_window: dependent variable measured at time t

description: The average quarterly level of dedicated institutional investor ownership percentage for each year in the panel. Institutional investors are classified as DII, TII, or quasi-indexer following Bushee (2001), who used factor and cluster analysis to classify institutional investors based on portfolio diversification (breadth), portfolio turnover, and momentum trading (earnings sensitivity). The ownership data end in 2013, the final year for which the data were available.

Firms that adopted a lead director in 2003 and 2004 are defined as early adopters, because the NYSE required its listed companies to disclose the lead directors' names in 2003 and NYSE adoption is especially concentrated in 2003 and 2004. The first 2 years are used as the cutoff because they capture an early minority of adopting firms but not so many that the practice had become entirely commonplace. About one third of the final sample of firms are early adopters.

An index built from three standardized components. The first component is social capital, measured by the number of board directorships that the CEO and the lead director hold. The second component is human capital, measured by educational level. The third component is their relative tenure on the board, because a CEO that originally appointed a director to the board has more power over them than if they were not part of the group that originally appointed them.

A total of 11 items were used to capture the extent of synergy realization, including realized benefits from purchasing, production, marketing, market power, administration, vertical economies, new market access, cross-selling, transfer of current know-how, creation of new know-how, and other substantial synergy sources that may be described in a case. Each of the items was coded as low (0), moderate (1), or high (2), and then summed to create an overall measure of synergy realization (Cronbach alpha = 0.68).
scale: sum of eleven items, each coded 0 (low), 1 (moderate), 2 (high)
time_window: the integration period described in the case

description: Combination potential was measured as the sum of four items: similarity of marketing operations (e.g., geographic markets, customer groups, and industries); similarity of production operations (e.g., types of input, process, and product); complementarity of marketing operations (e.g., possible transfer of marketing capabilities to new markets or new products); and complementarity of production operations (e.g., possible vertical economies by transferring production capabilities) (Cronbach alpha = 0.66).
scale: sum of four items coded on 5-point scales

description: Organizational integration was computed as the sum of the extent of operational interaction and the employment of coordinating mechanisms and structures during the post-combination integration period (Cronbach alpha = 0.78). The degree of integration can be divided conceptually into the degree of interaction between the joining firms (through, for instance, restructuring and material flows) and the extent of coordinative effort to improve the quality of that interaction.
scale: sum of two items coded on 5-point scales

description: Employee resistance was measured as the active and passive opposition of acquired company employees to the acquisition. To assess whether employee resistance varied over time, resistance was measured separately for the first and second halves of the integration process described in each case, and the resulting measure was computed by taking the mean score across those stages (Cronbach alpha = 0.60).
scale: mean of two items coded on 5-point scales
time_window: first and second halves of the integration process described in the case

description: Management style similarity was measured by comparing the degrees of formality and participation across merging organizations, coded from very low to very high on a 5-point scale.
time_window: at the beginning of the integration phase

description: Cross-border mergers were coded as one (1) if the bidder and target were headquartered in different countries and as zero (0) otherwise.
scale: binary: 0 = same home country, 1 = different home countries

description: Relative company size was coded simply as the ratio of target to bidder size.

For a given county/quarter, the logged sum of the production capacity of all corporate plants operating in that county and the counties adjacent to it. Adjacent counties are included because the impact of a mid-sized cooperative ethanol plant on corn prices and supplies is felt up to 70 miles from the plant. The authors examine production capacity rather than density because capacity matters more in terms of its effect on the process of competition. Explanatory variables were lagged by six quarters.

A dummy coded '1' if, in a given quarter/county, a cooperative plant officially commenced production. The clock variable in each county starts in January 1978 and ends when a founding event takes place in that county, which then resets the county clock. Because of the large number of counties, quarterly spells were constructed; no two cooperative plants were founded in the same quarter/county. Entry is dated at the time the plant officially began production.

A dummy that indicates whether the county permits corporate farming ('1' = yes) or not ('0' = otherwise). The authors list the states and counties with laws prohibiting corporate farming; counties in which corporations have the potential to enter farming are coded as facing a vertical integration threat.

The absence of right-to-work (RTW) laws serves as a general indicator of anti-corporate climate, with the dummy coded '1' if a RTW law is absent. RTW laws are considered a good proxy because, to opponents of corporations, they signify a general threat posed by corporations to local autonomy, commonwealth, and self-sustainment, and they were accompanied by other corporate-friendly policies such as low capital taxes and lax environmental regulations. By June 2013, 24 states were RTW states.

The history of the Farm Bureau in a given county, measured by the logged number of quarters. Founding dates of Farm Bureaus were obtained from states' business entity filings. Nearly 2,600 counties had active bureaus in 1978, and by June 2013 this number had risen to 2,772.

variable_name: local corporate ethanol production capacity owned by oil and agribusiness companies
description: Local corporate ethanol production capacity split into two components based on ownership; one component represents the production capacity of 46 commercial plants owned by agribusiness and oil companies, and the other captures the capacity of the remaining commercial plants not owned by agribusiness or oil companies. Plants owned by agribusiness and oil companies entered with an average capacity of 70 mgy, whereas other plants began production with 40 mgy capacity on average. In 1990 agribusiness- and oil-owned plants accounted for 59% of total U.S. production capacity; by June 2013 their share had declined to 21%.

Experimental manipulation of compensation scheme: participants were randomly assigned to either incentive compensation or fixed salary compensation. Under incentive compensation they were told the company's executive compensation was performance based (base salary plus performance bonuses of up to 100% of the base salary) and that their participation fee depended on how well they performed (a 100 yuan base fee plus an additional 50 to 100 yuan). Under fixed salary compensation they were told compensation was an annually negotiated fixed salary that does not change regardless of firm performance and that their participation fee was fixed at 150 yuan.

A 12-item measure developed by Judge and his colleagues (2003) using a seven-point scale, as suggested by Hiller and Hambrick (2005), to account for the higher range that is likely for executives. Subjects completed this survey as part of a scale validation exercise at least 12 days before the simulation. The scale had a reported alpha of 0.822. Example items included: 'I am confident I can get the success I deserve in life,' and 'there are times when things look pretty bleak and hopeless to me.'
time_window: at least 12 days before the simulation

description: Two versions of the simulation, representing either organizational growth or organizational decline, were implemented; both focused on a medical equipment company but presented different firm performance contexts. In the organizational growth context the company was growing and enjoying good performance, with performance goals of capturing at least 40 percent market share (starting from 23%) and increasing net profits above $25 million (starting from $13.6 million net profits). In the organizational decline context the company was declining and suffering poor performance, with goals of recapturing at least 40 percent market share (starting from 23% after a peak of 58%) and returning the company to profitability (starting from $13.6 million net losses).

A single-item measure of the intention of participants to continue playing the simulation in order to achieve the stated performance goals. After receiving feedback that they were making little progress toward their performance goals, subjects were asked after Q5 to indicate on a seven-point scale their intention to persevere beyond the last quarter: 'If you had more funds and time, how much would you want to continue playing the simulation beyond the six quarters to improve the company's performance?' From the subjects' perspective, the possibility of playing additional decision rounds was entirely possible.

A second measure of perseverance, the total time participants spent making allocation decisions in the sixth and final quarter, included consistent with psychological studies that used time-on-task to assess perseverance.

The authors summed the total budget allocation of each participant over the five competitive strategies in Q3 to Q5. Competitive strategies sought to improve the company's competitive position relative to that of competitors and are inherently more risky than public relations strategies, which sought to favorably present the company and its executives to key stakeholders. Participants allocated budgets between $0 and $2 million (in increments of $50,000) to each strategy each quarter.
scale: budget allocation in dollars ($0 to $2 million per strategy per quarter)

description: Participants were informed that fraudulent reporting of revenues and expenses by the company's chief financial officer had been uncovered and that, given the manner of reporting, it was unlikely that anyone outside the company would discover this in the near term. Participants were then given the option to restate as many of the previous fraudulent reports as they desired, or none at all (between 0 to six reports); they were told that the more reports they restated, the closer they would be to fulfilling government regulations and professional expectations, but that restating more reports would increase financial losses and decrease their performance relative to other students. Participants were assessed to be more ethical if they restated more reports.

Measured as the diversity of participants' strategic allocations to competitive strategies, using an entropy-based score commonly used to measure heterogeneity: -[Σ P_i (ln P_i)], for i = 1...5, where P is the proportion of the budget allocated to each of the five competitive strategies in Q3 to Q5. The score was reversed so that higher scores indicated greater strategic risk taking.

Firms' annual production of solar PV cells in megawatts (MW) in each country, as listed in the PV News archive, used as the dependent variable of the growth model. The dependent variable is measured one year after the predictor variables. To verify the reliability of this production information the authors consulted industry professionals, interviewed the current and former editor of PV News, and cross-checked the data against a survey by another industry journal, Photon International.
time_window: year t, measured one year after the predictor variables

description: The number of publication issues in each year that mention Greenpeace divided by the total number of issues published that year, based on all monthly issues of PV News available from the beginning of the observation period complemented with the full archive of Photon International. It captures industry-level attention to the SMO. Continuous predictor variables were standardized before running the models.
time_window: yearly, one year before the dependent variable

description: Number of paying Greenpeace members in a country per year, used as a proxy for the strength of environmental movement support in that country. It was constructed by combining information coded from the Greenpeace International archive at the International Institute of Social History, data on Greenpeace supporters published in a study of the ratification of the Kyoto protocol, and data from annual reports issued by Greenpeace national branches. A few missing values were imputed using linear interpolation.

A firm's share of production over total European PV production for that year, reported by PV News, capturing its past commitment relative to competitors. Two further operationalizations were created: a firm's prior production as a proxy for its absolute commitment, and a variable accounting for firms' cumulative commitments over time with a decay factor for more recent investments; because the magnitude of production share is easier to interpret, the results are reported using the production share.
scale: share of total European PV production
time_window: yearly, lagged relative to the dependent variable

description: The number of articles that indicate an adversarial relationship between the focal firm and environmental groups through protests, boycotts, demonstrations, or lawsuits, gathered from media reports in the LexisNexis Academic database with searches repeated in six languages (English, Spanish, French, German, Dutch, and Italian). The measure at time t covers the previous three years. Because the variable was highly skewed, it was transformed to its natural logarithm after adding 1.
scale: count of articles, logged after adding 1

variable_name: SMO prominence based on articles reflecting support for solar PV
description: A content-coded version of the prominence measure that counts only industry press articles mentioning Greenpeace that reflect a supportive stance toward the solar PV industry, coded from all industry press articles mentioning Greenpeace. This operationalization was used in additional analyses of the content of industry press coverage.
scale: proportion of issues mentioning Greenpeace in support of PV

description: Respondents reported the total number of persons who worked for their employer during the preceding calendar year, counting all locations where the employer operated. Responses were grouped into four categories: fewer than 100 employees, 100-499 employees, 500-999 employees, and 1,000 or more employees.
Inflation-adjusted (to 2014 dollars) annual wage and salary earnings divided by annual work hours, logged. Earnings include overtime pay, tips, bonuses, and commissions.

Estimated as the logged wage difference between each larger firm-size group (100-499, 500-999, 1,000+) and the reference group (fewer than 100 employees) at the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of the wage distribution, using RIF regression coefficients.
The analysis estimates effects at the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of the logged wage distribution.

Observed and counterfactual logged wage gaps between the 90th and 10th percentiles and between the 90th and 50th percentiles of the wage distribution. Counterfactuals remove the firm-size wage premium or hold it at its 1989 level.
Year of observation, with analyses conducted for each year between 1989 and 2014 and year-centered exponentially weighted models used to detect trends.

After reading the alliance scenario, which featured the hypothetical partner name ABC Company, respondents rated how critical trust was for selecting a partner in that alliance. The scale asks directly how critical trust is for partner selection and covers benevolence (goodwill and honesty between partners) and competence (confidence that partners will carry out their roles in a competent and dependable manner). The coefficient alpha is 0.80.

After the real partner name was divulged, respondents indicated their perceptions of trust in that partner on a scale focused on benevolence and competence. The coefficient alpha for the trust perception scale is 0.73.

Respondents rated how critical complementarity was for selecting a partner in the alliance scenario, independent of the chosen partner. Complementarity refers to the degree to which one partner's marketing operations complement the other's operations. The three-item image complementarity scale has a coefficient alpha of 0.83.
Perceptions of the partner's complementarity, measured after a real partner name was divulged. The three-item image complementarity scale has a coefficient alpha of 0.88.

Respondents rated how critical commitment was for partner selection under the alliance scenario. Commitment is operationalized as the willingness of partners to supply tangible resources such as money, people, skills, and time to an alliance relationship. The reliability coefficient for commitment criticality is 0.86.

Perceptions of the partner's resource commitment, that is, its willingness to supply tangible resources such as money, people, skills, and time to the alliance relationship, measured after a real partner name was divulged. The reliability coefficient is 0.89.

Respondents rated how critical financial payoff was for partner selection in the alliance scenario. The three-item scale captures the perceived financial payoffs associated with entering into partnership with a specific partner and has a coefficient alpha of 0.91.

Perceptions of the financial payoff associated with entering into partnership with the specific partner, measured after a real partner name was divulged. The three-item scale has a coefficient alpha of 0.91.

Partner attractiveness was operationalized with a three-item scale, assessed after the real partner name was divulged, that measures how attractive and valuable the choice of a particular partner will be for the alliance-initiating firm for a given alliance project type. The coefficient alpha for this three-item scale is 0.92.

Five items tapping the amount of management time, energy, and emotional stress required for alliance initiation and implementation, the number of organizational departments and people involved, and the intensity of interaction and communication required. Due to high reliability (alpha = 0.97) the items were averaged to assess the success of the manipulation. Low scores are indicative of a more difficult process to manage.

Five items, e.g., measurability, quantifiability, ambiguity, and equivocality of various alliance outcomes, were averaged (alpha = 0.92) to assess the success of the outcome interpretability manipulation. Lower agreement scores on the seven-point Likert scales were indicative of high (or easier) outcome interpretability.

The same criticality scale as in Study 1, asking respondents how critical trust is for selecting a partner given the alliance scenario. In Study 2 the scenarios contained only process manageability and outcome interpretability information and the same partner name was used across all four scenarios.
The same perception scale as in Study 1, measuring perceptions of the partner's trustworthiness after the partner name (Boeing, followed by Airbus as a replication) was divulged.
The same criticality scale as in Study 1, asking respondents how critical complementarity is for selecting a partner given the alliance scenario.
The same perception scale as in Study 1, measuring perceptions of the partner's complementarity after the partner name was divulged.
The same criticality scale as in Study 1, asking respondents how critical commitment is for selecting a partner given the alliance scenario.
The same perception scale as in Study 1, measuring perceptions of the partner's willingness to supply tangible resources after the partner name was divulged.
The same criticality scale as in Study 1, asking respondents how critical financial payoff is for selecting a partner given the alliance scenario.
The same perception scale as in Study 1, measuring the perceived financial payoff associated with partnering with the specific partner after the partner name was divulged.

The partner attractiveness scale was modified so that its items do not measure overall alliance attractiveness; the items ask whether the partner is appealing, attractive, and a valuable partner for the airline. The items were averaged because of high reliability (reported as 0.90 in the text).

The same manipulation-check measure as in Study 1, used with the revised scenarios that contained only process manageability and outcome interpretability information. Planned contrasts showed that respondents in the high process manageability scenarios had higher means than respondents in the low process manageability scenarios.

The same manipulation-check measure as in Study 1. Lower agreement scores on the seven-point Likert scales were indicative of high (or easier) outcome interpretability, and respondents given low outcome interpretability scenarios found outcome interpretability to be more difficult than respondents given high outcome interpretability scenarios.

A newly developed five-item scale measuring the extent to which individuals engage in bootlegging, built on interview material and prior studies, with all items measured on a seven-point scale ranging from 1 for strongly disagree to 7 for strongly agree. Exploratory factor analysis of the five items using the principal factor method produced a one-factor solution explaining 98% of the variance. One item with a factor loading below 0.4 was excluded, and the resulting bootlegging scale shows strong internal reliability with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.80; factor scores are used in the regressions.
scale: seven-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Respondents were asked how much of a typical work week during the previous 12 months had been devoted to unofficial side projects, outside of formal work plans, and to provide the same information for the three years prior to the survey. The time devoted to bootlegging in 2007 is used as the past bootlegging time measure. Standardized by subtracting the mean from the value and dividing by the standard deviation.
scale: percentage of a typical work week

description: Calculated as the difference in the log of the percentage of time allocated to bootlegging in 2010 minus the log transformation of the percentage in 2007. The authors note the possibility of recall bias in the calculation for 2007 based on inaccurate recollection of the time dedicated to this activity three years earlier.

Neptune conducts an annual evaluation involving a committee of line managers from the different business divisions who assess the performance of individual technologists relative to peers, based on specific contributions to new products, processes, features, business development, technologies, or designs that create value for the organization. The appraisal system classifies individuals into two bands with a forced distribution across the three seniority levels, and the authors use the innovation rating as their measure of individual innovative performance. Individuals were asked to declare their innovation rating for each of the last three years; the rating is self-reported in the survey but is not a self-assessed measure since the evaluation was made by others. In the sample, 24% of individuals received the highest rating.
time_window: current rating and the three prior years (2008-2010)

description: Measured as the share of technologists with the highest innovation rating in 2009, exploiting Neptune's archival data on the distribution of ratings across the entire population of technologists, across all of its R&D sites. Neptune has over 20 units, each having between 5 and 80 R&D staff members. Standardized by subtracting the mean from the value and dividing by the standard deviation.

Measured as the average bootlegging time of researchers in 2007 for each R&D unit, using all the survey responses (N = 405). Individuals in R&D units where fewer than three employees had responded to the survey were dropped, and the focal individual was excluded when calculating the unit average. Standardized by subtracting the mean from the value and dividing by the standard deviation.

A dummy variable indicating whether a focal VC firm participates in a syndicate in a given round. A focal VC firm refers to a prospective newcomer VC firm at risk of joining a syndicate. The realized newcomer is compared with matched hypothetical newcomers that could have joined the focal syndicate but did not.

Depth of embeddedness captures the maximum tie strength between a prospective newcomer VC and incumbent syndicate members. Dyadic tie strength is the number of good-quality co-investments between two firms in the same round for the same company in the past five years, excluding those in which either VC one-sidedly withdrew from the syndicate. The maximum of these dyadic tie strength values between the newcomer and the syndicate members is taken.

The number of syndicate members with whom the focal newcomer has had at least one good-quality co-investment tie in the past five years, divided by the total number of syndicate members. The prospective newcomer's strongest tie, used to measure depth, is excluded from both the numerator and the denominator to avoid double-counting. The measure ranges from zero to one and was orthogonalized against the newcomer average tie strength of relevant ties using the Gram-Schmidt procedure.

The standard deviation of the tie strength between each dyad of members within the syndicate, using good-quality ties for the past five years. The variable was orthogonalized relative to the average tie strength of incumbent members. Because it is invariant in syndicates at each round, its main effect dropped out of the regressions and the hypotheses were tested through its interactions with the other independent variables.

The status of each incumbent member was measured with Bonacich's eigenvector centrality in the co-investment network of all VC firms. A prospective newcomer's strongest tie with the syndicate is the member with the highest number of good-quality ties to the newcomer, and that member's centrality is used; when two or more VC firms were equally identified as strongest ties, the one with the highest centrality was used. When the newcomer's maximum tie strength with syndicate members is zero, the status of the strongest tie was assigned to be zero.
The total number of companies the newcomer invested in prior to the focal investment year.
time_window: prior to the focal investment year

description: Purity is operationalized as the angular measure θ of a firm's polar coordinate in the two-dimensional strategy space formed by operating excellence and product leadership, where θ is the ratio of the subset of strategic activities consistent with one strategy to the subset consistent with the other. A firm with a very high or very low value for θ occupies a position of relative purity in the P-O space, while firms close to the 45° slope line occupy the middle ground in strategic space. The authors also calculated a purity ratio anchored on the product leadership axis (ϕ = arctan(O/P)) and the absolute deviation from the mean purity slope line (ψ). The equations specifying these measures are not readable in the available text.
time_window: 1999 panel (predictors measured one year before the outcome)

description: Summed score (maximum 20) of four survey items on which respondents rated the relative importance of each item for their workplace's general business strategy, on a scale from 1 (not important) to 5 (crucial). The items are reducing operating costs, improving coordination with customers and suppliers, reorganizing the work process, and improving measures of performance. The factor emerged from exploratory factor analysis on half the sample and has an alpha coefficient of 0.70; using the simple sum of the items did not give qualitatively different results from factor scores.
scale: 1 (not important) to 5 (crucial) per item; summed score with maximum 20

description: Summed score (maximum 20) of four survey items on which respondents rated the relative importance of each item for their workplace's general business strategy, on a scale from 1 (not important) to 5 (crucial). The items are developing new products and services, undertaking R&D, total quality management, and developing new operating techniques. The factor has an alpha coefficient of 0.76, and confirmatory factor analysis on the other half of the dataset supported the two-factor measurement model.
scale: 1 (not important) to 5 (crucial) per item; summed score with maximum 20

description: Gross revenues minus gross expenses, expressed as a percentage of revenues, drawn from the second panel of the survey. It was selected over alternative measures such as revenue growth or growth in size because it measures value creation and capture.
time_window: 2000 panel (the year subsequent to the predictor variables)

description: Measure of pure-financial diversification based on the proportion of total profits made by businesses with the same combination of economic sector and business cycle indicator. Each segment is assigned to one of the combinations formed by broad economic sectors and by whether the segment leads, lags or is coincidental with the business cycle, and segments with the same combination are treated as one industry. The index is computed from the proportion of total profits made by businesses with the same combination. The authors argue the index captures the firm's operating risk more accurately than SIC-based measures.
time_window: computed annually for 1977-83; results reported for 1980

description: Berry-Herfindahl type measure of total diversification computed from the proportion of total profits in each four-digit SIC industry. Because the study focuses on pure-financial diversification, the operating income of each segment rather than sales is used in the computation. The measure equals zero for a firm operating in a single four-digit SIC industry and approaches one for highly diversified firms.
time_window: computed annually for 1977-83; results reported for 1980

description: Measure of total diversification based on the entropy concept (Palepu, 1985), defined as DT = DR + DU, where DR is diversification within two-digit SIC industries and DU is diversification across two-digit SIC industries. It is used to identify firms with above-mean total diversification for the analysis of relative related diversification; results for DT itself are not reported in the study.

Entropy-based measure of related diversification computed in two stages: DR_k is first computed for each two-digit SIC industry from the proportion of total profits in that industry made by each four-digit segment, and DR is then the weighted average of DR_k using the proportion of consolidated profits made in the two-digit SIC industry. It measures diversification of related businesses within the same two-digit SIC industry but not diversification across two-digit SIC industries.
time_window: computed annually for 1977-83; results reported for 1980

description: Relative related diversification, computed as DR divided by DT; it measures the proportion of total diversification attained through diversification into different four-digit SIC industries within the same two-digit SIC industry. Firms with an above-mean DT in 1980 were classified into a high-NDR group (above-mean DT and above-mean NDR) and a low-NDR group (above-mean DT but below-mean NDR).

Funds from operations in 1980 divided by total assets in 1980. Funds from operations are computed by adding back to net income all expenses that do not affect current assets and liabilities, such as depreciation, so the measure is free from the effects of differential accounting methods relating to non-current assets and liabilities.

Return on assets in 1980, used as an additional profitability measure to facilitate comparisons with previous studies. The authors state only that NITA is the return on assets in 1980; its formula appears in a formula block that is unreadable in the available text.
Standard deviation of the funds from operations divided by total assets, computed over the period 1974-83. It approximates the variability of operating cash flows.
Standard deviation of the return on assets, computed over the period 1974-83. It measures the variability of accounting profits.
Financial leverage measured as the total debt to total assets in 1980.

The number of articles that referenced #MeToo from the onset of coverage to the present. Coverage was examined using Factiva for major news outlets including CNN, The Financial Times, Fox News, The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Washington Post, the outlets most followed by participating directors.
time_window: from onset of coverage to the present

variable_name: Media coverage of #MeToo in prior week
description: The count of articles that referred to #MeToo in the previous week (week t - 1) in the same major news outlets. Coverage was examined using Factiva for CNN, The Financial Times, Fox News, The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Washington Post.

variable_name: Gender difference between incumbent and candidate
description: A dichotomous variable indicating whether or not an incumbent director and the potential board candidate possess the same gender category. It is part of the set of dichotomous indicators of whether incumbent and candidate share a demographic category.

A single index combining the dichotomous measures of similarity beyond gender, built with discrete principal components analysis. The component indicators are whether the incumbent and candidate share functional background (Hambrick and Mason classification), race (African American, Arab, Asian, Hispanic, White), and educational background, with educational background operationalized as the highest degree earned and possession of an elite (Ivy League) degree; age similarity is coded as one if the two individuals differed by less than one standard deviation.

The number of other boards on which the incumbent director and the board candidate both held an appointment, based on actual board ties between the incumbent and the candidate. Board appointments at both nonprofit organizations and for-profit companies were included.
An indirect board tie exists between an incumbent director A and a potential board candidate B when A sits on another board with a third director C, who also sits on a different board with B.

A nine-item survey measure developed and validated for samples of top executives, adapted from survey scales developed by Mael and Ashforth and by Bergami and Bagozzi, answered by participants monthly throughout the study period. Factor analysis indicated that the items loaded onto a single factor (all loadings > .5) without loading onto other factors in the model, and inter-item reliability was high (alpha = .88); factor scores were estimated using the regression method.

A multi-item survey scale measuring the perceived attractiveness of an individual as a potential board candidate, with item wording based on the language used by directors and headhunters in the preliminary interviews and on Lorsch and colleagues' qualitative research. Respondents were asked to imagine that the search firm hired by their company had identified the individual as a possible candidate for an open board position and to assess the individual as they would if they served on the nominating committee. The scale included different response formats and reverse-scored items; factor analysis indicated the items loaded onto a single factor with all loadings > .5 and did not load onto other factors in the model, and inter-item reliability was high (alpha = .87).

Respondents were randomly assigned to one of four possible conditions (control, close, moderate, distant) and one of five songs.
