Respondents in the three treatment conditions were shown a prime indicating that the artist was initially signed as a musician of another genre and then decided to record the song they heard; the prime genres were the ones ranked first (close), fourth (moderate), and ninth (distant) in relatedness to the focal song's genre. The prime was designed to vary the background information provided to indicate that the performer was trying to bridge genres that were different distances apart.

The space between any two genres is calculated as Ljk = 1 - Fjk, where Fjk equals Yk / Xj, Xj is the number of people who like genre j 'best' and Yk is the number of those people who also 'like' genre k; the value is constrained between zero and one, where one indicates complete disparity and zero perfect overlap. The distance an artist moves is then a function of the artist's genre membership and the song's genre membership in the set of musical genres, multiplied by the distance between each genre pair; artists who only use elements from within their genre score zero and the measure is constrained between zero and one. A square of the distance term is also included in the models. The equation for the artist-movement distance is not readable in the text as provided.

Respondents were asked how they would describe the song they just heard using five preset choices and one option for 'other.' The choices were displayed in random order but ranged from the most abstract (e.g., 'sound') to that song's specific subgenre (e.g., 'outlaw country'), with a lower number indicating a higher-order category. For example, a person hearing the country song had the choices (1) sound, (2) a song, (3) a country song, (4) a country rock song, (5) an outlaw country song, or other. The variable was estimated with an ordered logistic regression.

After being required to listen to the clip at least once, respondents were asked to evaluate the quality of the song they heard on a seven-point scale. This is the outcome used for the principal experimental test of the second hypothesis, estimated with an ordinary least squares regression that controls for respondent-level differences and song indicators.

Success was measured using the log of sales for each performance. All sales were made through iTunes only, and data were provided by Nielsen Soundscan for Canada; U.S. sales data were only available for the first two seasons but produced similar results. Any duets or multivocalist performances were not included in the measure of sales, and because most auditions were not available for purchase only artists who were selected to participate, and therefore performed at least two televised songs, were included.

The firm's name was entered as a key word into the Factiva database and all articles mentioning the firm were retrieved, then restricted to seven business publications. Repeated reports were counted once, excluding duplications. Two of the authors developed a coding scheme for counting positive media stories by reading 50 randomly generated articles and then independently coded 200 randomly generated articles, reaching an interrater reliability of 0.93. One author coded all remaining articles to identify the total number of positive stories for each firm in each focal year; the logged value of this variable was used.
time_window: focal year, lagged one year behind the dependent variable

description: The entropy measure of diversification was chosen as a valid and widely used indicator; it was calculated from the proportion of revenues collected by the firm in each of the four lines of service. The formula itself is not readable in the text. The entropy measure reaches its maximum value when there are equal sales in all service lines, so a positive and significant coefficient supports the hypothesis of a positive relationship between balanced diversification and performance.
time_window: lagged one year behind the dependent variable

variable_name: Centered leverage and centered leverage squared
description: The leverage ratio is the number of professionals (including partners and nonpartners) divided by the number of partners. To lessen multicollinearity between leverage and its squared term, the leverage measure was centered on its mean and labelled Centered Leverage, and the squared term was created and named Centered Leverage Squared (the squared term itself was not centered). Hypothesis 3 would be supported if the coefficient of Centered Leverage Squared is significantly positive and the trough point of Centered Leverage lies within its range.
time_window: lagged one year behind the dependent variable

description: Performance is measured by revenues per professional (R/P), computed from the statistics published in the Public Accounting Report. Previous researchers have reported high correlations between this measure and accounting measures of profitability; a study of U.S. law firms reports a correlation of 0.71 between revenues per professional and 'profits per partner' and of 0.89 between revenues per professional and 'relative profitability.'

variable_name: Patenting performance (count of successful patents filed)
description: Count of all (granted) U.S. patents filed by the firm in a given year. For each firm the entire corporate family (including subsidiaries, divisions, and affiliates) was compiled each year using the Directory of Corporate Affiliates, and patents were matched to each firm-year with codes assigned by the USPTO to patenting entities within the corporate family. The methodology is similar to the NBER patent database, except that corporate families are tracked over time rather than aggregated in a single year.

Total number of U.S. patent attorneys and agents employed within the firm's corporate family in a given year. Employer was determined from the official addresses in the USPTO patent attorney database, whose currency the Office of Enrollment and Discipline aggressively enforces. The approach was validated on a sample of 100 patent attorneys listed on patents from the data set, correctly coding the employer in all 98 cases for which the employer could be independently identified. The variable is transformed by logs after adding 1.

Total R&D financial expenditures reported for each firm in a given year, gathered using the Research Insight database and converted into year 2000 dollars with the GDP deflator. Based on prior literature and on insignificant and poorly identified lagged effects in the data, same-period R&D is used to measure the impact of knowledge resources on firm patenting. The variable is transformed by logs.
time_window: same period as the dependent variable

description: Coded 1 if at least one member of the firm's top management team was a patent attorney, and 0 if not. TMT members were compiled from Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management, which also contains their professional biographies, and both these biographies and the USPTO patent attorney database were used to determine whether a TMT member had ever been a patent attorney, with 100% agreement between the two sources. To minimize noise, coding was restricted to the CEO, President, Chairman of the Board, and the top legal position in the firm.
scale: 1 if at least one TMT member was a patent attorney, 0 otherwise

description: Using U.S. patent classes, the authors measured the fraction of patents filed by the focal firm in two key technology groups, assigning the fraction in 'electronics, computers/communication, optical and nuclear' to the systems-hi-tech variable and the fraction in 'mechanical' to the systems-mature variable. The fraction of patents in 'drugs and medical' and 'chemicals' jointly formed the reference materials-based industry category, and patents in the 'other' group were excluded. The industry variables do not vary within firm and, because fixed-effects panel techniques are used, they were entered only as interactions with patent law expertise.
scale: fraction of the firm's patents in each technology group

description: Degree to which decisions with long-term consequences are made by top management or taken by the workforce itself. Survey participants were told that strategic decisions have to do with purchases of stand-alone machinery and large-scale capital equipment, introduction of new technologies, hiring and dismissal of plants' employees, individual and collective incentives, and career paths. The initial answers were grouped and recoded into an ordinal variable.

Degree to which decisions with short-term consequences are made by top management or delegated fully to workers. Participants were told that operating decisions include the daily and weekly production plan, the definition of employees' tasks, the control of results, and the modification of the production plan and processes in the face of unexpected shocks. The answers were grouped and recoded into an ordinal variable.
Share of operators, among the total workers on the shop floor, who are normally involved in work teams of a permanent or temporary nature, as reported by the production manager.

Share of operators, among shop floor workers, who normally perform the same task. Specialization was transformed by introducing its quadratic to fulfil the parametric assumptions inherent to an OLS estimation.

Construct built up with principal component analysis from indicators of the number and predictability of environmental eventualities that affect labor transactions, originally based on the contribution of Lawrence and Lorsch (1967). The indicators were generally valued on a five-point Likert-type scale, those providing the highest reliability were retained, principal component analysis was applied to obtain a single value for every case, and the latent variable was transformed to make it start with one.

Construct built up with principal component analysis from indicators of worker behaviour that consciously reduces the quantity and quality of output, using the work of John (1984) and Anderson (1985) on sales force as a starting point. The retained indicators were valued on a five-point Likert-type scale, a single value per case was obtained by principal component analysis, and the latent variable was transformed to make it start with one.

Construct built up with principal component analysis from indicators of the propensity of a principal to impose orders exceeding the previously agreed limits on other agents who do not have to be consulted, with items inspired by Willman (1983), Dow (1987), and Grimshaw and Rubery (1998). A single value per case was obtained by principal component analysis and the latent variable was transformed to make it start with one.

Construct built up with principal component analysis from indicators of investments in a specific design of the production process that cause lock-in effects among different work stations, with items inspired by Williamson (1985) on technological separabilities and by Masten et al. (1991). A single value per case was obtained by principal component analysis and the latent variable was transformed to make it start with one.

Ordinal variable recording the mean time that most of the operators spend carrying out their main task, ordered so that higher levels denote shorter task durations and hence more recurrent transactions.

Ordinal variable based on the difference between the time that a new worker with no experience in the industry spends until he or she reaches the normal productivity of his or her mates and the time that a new worker who already has experience in the industry spends until he or she reaches that normal productivity.

Competitors who hold the highest score of the three players before the Final Jeopardy! clue. The authors estimate models separately for the 48 leader decisions and the 64 follower decisions rather than entering a position indicator in a pooled model.

Competitors in second or third place before the Final Jeopardy! clue. Followers with scores below 4,000 were excluded from the data set because even if they risked all of their points they were not likely to advance as a wild card.

For leaders, operationalized as their own score minus the second-place follower's score, that is, the level of risk needed to maintain the lead. For followers it equals the amount by which the follower trails the leader (the leader's score minus his or her own score). It is measured in points before the final clue.

Operationalized as the absolute difference between a competitor's score and 8,000. The 8,000 score was identified from the cumulative probability of advancing as a wild card because the probability of qualifying falls from 80% to 50% with a 500-point decrease from 8,000 to 7,500.

The number of points a competitor places at risk on the last clue of his or her first-round game. Competitors can risk any amount between zero and their entire score, and this is the dependent variable in the regressions.
time_window: Final Jeopardy! of the first-round game

description: For leaders, an indicator for choosing the shutout bet when it was larger than the bet needed to reach 9,300; the shutout bet doubles the nearest follower's score, adds one point, and subtracts the leader's own score. Leaders choosing the shutout bet are considered focused on maintaining their leading position and to be taking the riskier strategy. For followers the analogous indicator is choosing a bet to take the lead when that bet was larger than the bet needed to reach 9,300.
time_window: Final Jeopardy! of the first-round game

description: Based on Parkhe's (1993) set of eight contract provisions, the measure counts the number of provisions represented in the contract signed by the firms, ranging from zero to eight, with higher scores representing greater reliance on contractual governance. The level of contractual detail governing the relationship was measured at the time the dispute arose, by examining the actual formal contracts. An unweighted composite index is used, following Deeds and Hill (1999) and Reuer and Ariño (2007).
time_window: at the time the dispute arose

description: Measured as the ratio of coordination-related clauses included in the contract, that is, clause 1 and/or 2 from Parkhe's (1993) index, to the total number of clauses in the contract. Controlling for the total number of clauses mitigates the concern that coordination provisions were included incidentally because of institutional factors promoting greater contractual detail. Appendix clause category 3 (audit rights) was excluded because it may relate more to enforcement than to coordination.
time_window: at the time the dispute arose

description: Every document exchanged between the disputing firms during the entire resolution process was analyzed; each communication by one firm to the other was counted as a message and a choice not to reply was also coded as a ('no reply') message. In total 2,293 messages were studied, of which only 132 were coded as 'no reply.' Each message could be coded as pursuing neither, one, or both approaches, and the ratio of rights-based messages to total messages served as the measure of the degree to which the rights-based approach was pursued. Two researchers coded the messages following Weber's (1990) protocol and the response categories in the Appendix, with 98% agreement and a rating correlation of 0.969.

Every document exchanged between the disputing firms during the entire resolution process was analyzed; each communication by one firm to the other was counted as a message and a choice not to reply was also coded as a ('no reply') message. In total 2,293 messages were studied, of which only 132 were coded as 'no reply.' Each message could be coded as pursuing neither, one, or both approaches, and the ratio of interest-based messages to total messages served as the measure of the degree to which the interest-based approach was pursued. Two researchers coded the messages following Weber's (1990) protocol and the response categories in the Appendix, with 97% agreement and a rating correlation of 0.928.

Dispute resolution costs were estimated using legal fees, that is, the (log) amount of money paid by the client to the law firm, in thousands of inflation-adjusted Euros. The figures underestimate total costs because only fees paid by one disputant and no non-legal costs are observed, but the authors argue that unbiased underestimation is not problematic for comparing costs across cases. All data come from the same law firm, which maintained one uniform invoicing process throughout the period examined.
scale: log of thousands of inflation-adjusted Euros

description: Measured as the log of the absolute difference between the revenue of Firm A and the revenue of Firm B. Revenue was measured in thousands of inflation-adjusted Euros for the year when the contract was signed, and the data were obtained from the Bureau van Dijk's ORBIS database. The authors report that they found no effects of power asymmetry using their measure of alternatives and focus on the revenue-based measure.
scale: log of absolute difference in revenues
time_window: year when the contract was signed

description: A content analysis of the communications between the parties identified mentions of alternative options and/or alternative partners. Because the text did not allow calculation of the precise number of alternatives that each party had, the strength of a party's alternatives was estimated from the frequency with which the party mentioned alternatives. Asymmetry of alternatives is the absolute difference between the number of references to alternatives by Firm A and the number of references by Firm B.
scale: absolute difference in counts of references

description: Four-item scale based on questions originally developed by Martinez and Jarillo (1991), with wording slightly adjusted to fit the R&D context. Managers indicated the degree of local autonomy, the degree of direct supervision, the existence of integrated planning systems, and the utilization of reporting systems. The items were subjected to a principal component factor analysis with oblimin rotation, which produced three stable factors representing centralization, formalization and socialization.

Two-item scale assessing the emphasis placed on standardized processes and procedures and the degree to which formalized rules and policies were enforced. Items were based on questions originally developed by Martinez and Jarillo (1991) and slightly adjusted for the R&D context. The factor analysis produced a stable formalization factor.

Five-item scale measuring the degree of shared values, the use of expatriates, the frequency of R&D personnel exchange between units, the degree to which local managers participated in international trainings, and local management's involvement in joint teams and taskforces. Two items measuring international trainings and participation in task forces did not consistently discriminate between the three factors and were dropped, leaving three items for socialization.

Following Harzing (1999) and Conger (1992), the construct was operationalized on a three-item scale asking for the percentage of work that was received from other units, the percentage of work that was passed forward to other units, and the percentage of projects developed jointly. A Chronbach's alpha of 0.72 was obtained for this measure.

variable_name: Mandates of R&D units (international adaptors, international creators)
description: Units that direct their effort exclusively to the local market are classified as local adaptors. The remaining units were divided into two groups depending on the primary nature of their work, assessed by the percentage of work devoted to capability-exploiting versus capability-augmenting activities, with a split at the 50 percent mark: more than 50 percent capability augmenting yields international creators, otherwise international adaptors. In the regression models the mandate enters as two dummy variables (international adaptors and international creators) with local adaptors serving as the baseline.

Measured at the firm level as a value-weighted invention count of patents. Patent counts were aggregated to the firm-year level, and invention performance was calculated as the sum of a firm's value-weighted patents over the alliance's duration, assumed to be a 4-year window with a 1-year lag after alliance announcement (years t+1 to t+4). Patents were weighted following Cirillo (2019) using a weighted index of the number of claims awarded to a patent, the forward citations a patent received within 5 years of application, and the backward citations a patent made to prior patents.
time_window: t+1 to t+4, where t is the alliance announcement year

description: Assessed as the similarity of the firms' technological profiles in year t. Following Jaffe (1986), the technological profile of each firm is the distribution of all its patents across technology classes applied for until the year of alliance formation. Technological overlap was then calculated as the uncentered correlation coefficient of the firms' technological profiles. The measure is bounded between 0 and 1, with 1 indicating complete technological overlap.

Built from data on the zip code of the firms' headquarters in year t. On the basis of this information the latitudes and longitudes of the locations were calculated and the great circle distance formula was applied; the specification of the formula is not readable in the text. Geographical distance was log-transformed to account for distance decay. Finally, geographical distance was reverse-coded to obtain the measure of geographical overlap, ranging between 0 and 1, where 1 indicates the highest possible geographical overlap.

Uses the measure established by Hoberg and Phillips (2010), which captures the extent to which the firms had overlapping product markets in year t. Computer-aided text analysis of firms' product descriptions in SEC 10-K filings is used: a main dictionary of unique words used in all product descriptions is built each year, each firm is characterized by a binary N-vector normalized to unit length, and product market overlap is the multiplicative product of the two firms' normalized N-vectors (cosine similarity). The measure is time-variant and continuous, bounded between 0 and 1, with a higher score indicating a higher product market overlap in year t.

The authors used Burt's (1992) constraint measure of structural holes and reverse-coded it by multiplying by negative one in order to examine the effects of less constrained positions, that is, spanning structural holes. Constraint is measured as Ci equals the sum over j of (pij plus the sum over q of piq pjq) squared, where pij is the proportion of firm i's total ties invested in competitor j. The measure is built from the competitors a firm lists in its 10-K in a given year.

The measure examines whether the competitor listed in the focal firm's 10-K was also listed by other firms in the focal firm's market(s) and uses lack of listing by other firms to construct the measure. It is calculated as the sum of 1/dj where dj is the number of firms in the focal firm's markets that listed competitor j in their 10-K, aggregated across all competitors listed by the focal firm. Peripherality is limited to competitors in the focal firm's markets.

The number of newly listed competitors (competitors listed in year t that were not listed in year t-1) is added to the number of dropped competitors (competitors listed in year t-1 but not listed in year t), and the sum is divided by the total number of competitors listed in years t-1 and t. It therefore captures the proportion of the focal firm's listed competitors that are added or dropped from the previous year.

Count of new infrastructure software products introduced and subsequently shipped by each firm yearly, collected by content analysis of company press releases. To qualify as new, a product had to be brand-new only (version 1.0); extensions of existing products (e.g., 1.1 or 2.0) and ports of existing products to new operating systems were excluded, and only products confirmed to have shipped were included. Product descriptions were cross-referenced with keywords from the Gartner IT Glossary to retain infrastructure products and exclude consumer, enterprise application, and server operating-system products.

variable_name: CEO's social status in the corporate elite
description: Five indicators of social status in the corporate elite were used: the number of corporate board appointments held, the number of nonprofit board appointments held, elite education, the average stock rating of firms where the individual served as outside director, and memberships in prestigious social clubs. Elite education follows Finkelstein's (1992) measure, and prestigious social club memberships follow Palmer and Barber's (2001) listing. Each variable was measured in the year prior to the period for which flattery and opinion conformity were measured; in the primary analysis CEO status was standardized for the population of CEOs.
time_window: year prior to the period for which flattery and opinion conformity were measured

variable_name: average, standardized status of potential ingratiators
description: The same five indicators of social status in the corporate elite used for CEOs were measured for potential ingratiators and averaged. The average status of potential ingratiators was standardized and interacted with CEO status to assess the effect of relative status, while the absolute status of both CEOs and potential ingratiators was controlled.
time_window: year prior to the period for which flattery and opinion conformity were measured

variable_name: flattery and opinion conformity directed at the CEO
description: In the primary analyses, measured as the average number of instances of each ingratiatory behavior toward the focal CEO in the prior 12 months, i.e., the average response to a particular survey item among potential ingratiators, which essentially estimates the level of flattery and opinion conformity 'per interlocutor'. The scale items, adapted from Westphal and Stern (2006), prompt respondents to indicate the number of times a particular type of behavior occurred and gauge the extent to which flattery and opinion conformity involve exaggerated praise or agreement. Confirmatory factor analysis showed the items loaded on a single factor, with acceptable interitem reliability (alpha = .91).
scale: number of times a behavior occurred

variable_name: CEO self-enhancement in regard to strategic judgment and leadership capability
description: Operationalized as a positive difference between self-assessed abilities and the assessment of one's abilities by others. The CEO survey included a five-item scale that prompted CEOs to assess their strategic judgment and leadership capability compared to other CEOs of large U.S. companies, and the survey of potential ingratiators included a parallel set of questions about the CEO. The difference between the CEO's self-assessment and the average assessment of potential ingratiators was calculated for each question, and these difference scores were specified as measures of self-enhancement in the structural equation model; the measures loaded on one factor (alpha = .87).
scale: difference score on a six-point response scale running from 'well below average' to 'perhaps the best'

description: A composite of change in business strategy and corporate strategy. Business strategy was operationalized according to resource allocations across the primary functional areas of the firm; the five indicators were standardized and summed into a composite measure of change in business strategy. Corporate strategy was captured by change in product market diversification, measured with the entropy measure of diversification. In the structural equation model, change in business strategy and change in corporate diversification were specified as formative indicators of change in overall firm strategy.
time_window: two-year period after the CEO survey

description: Three measures of firm performance were used: market-to-book value of equity and total stock returns (market-based measures) and return on assets (an accounting-based measure). Each measure was adjusted for industry differences by subtracting the average value for the firm's primary industry, defined at the two-digit SIC code level. Confirmatory factor analysis showed the three measures loaded on a single factor. To test the effect of flattery and opinion conformity on strategic persistence in response to low firm performance, performance relative to competitors was measured in the year prior to the period for which strategic change was measured.
time_window: year prior to the period for which strategic change was measured

description: This variable takes the value of 1 for all Indian firms and 0 for all U.S. firms. It is interacted with the lagged performance measure to test for differences in persistence between Indian and U.S. firms.

This variable takes the value of 1 for all Indian firms that are neither subsidiaries of foreign multinational corporations nor part of a business group and 0 for all other firms. It is interacted with lagged performance on the subsample of poor performers in India to compare the persistence of unaffiliated firms with that of affiliated firms.

This variable takes the value of 1 for all Indian firms that are part of a business group and 0 for all others. The classification of firms into groups available in the database used is adopted. It is interacted with lagged performance to test whether the difference between affiliated and unaffiliated poor performers is driven by business group affiliates alone.

variable_name: Subsidiary of a foreign MNC dummy
description: This variable takes the value of 1 for all firms that are affiliated with an MNC and 0 for all others. The classification made in PROWESS is followed to identify MNC subsidiaries. It is interacted with lagged performance to test whether the difference between affiliated and unaffiliated poor performers is driven by MNC subsidiaries alone.

Persistence is the percentage of a firm's performance from previous periods that still remains in the current period and is captured by the coefficient of the lagged performance variable in a fixed-effects dynamic panel data model. The model is estimated on the subsample of superior performers, and the Indian firm dummy interacted with lagged performance tests whether persistence differs between India and the United States. Results are reported separately with NROA and FSR as the measures of performance.

Persistence is the percentage of a firm's performance from previous periods that still remains in the current period and is captured by the coefficient of the lagged performance variable in a fixed-effects dynamic panel data model. The model is estimated on the subsample of poor performers, and interactions of the Indian firm dummy (or the unaffiliated, business group and MNC dummies) with lagged performance test group differences in persistence. Results are reported separately with NROA and FSR as the measures of performance.

Performance is the relative profitability advantage enjoyed by a firm in period t. NROA normalizes a firm's returns when compared to the economy as a whole by removing the cyclical component of economy-wide profitability changes but retaining industry-level differences. It is computed using post-tax ROA as the measure of firm profitability.

Firm-specific rent normalizes a firm's return compared to its industry at the 3-digit SIC code and thus corrects for fixed industry effects, following Waring (1996). It is computed using post-tax ROA as the measure of firm profitability.

Redundancy (R), the number of patents in the intersection of the acquirer's and target's knowledge bases, divided by the number of unique patents in the target's knowledge base (Kt). A firm's knowledge base consists of the firm's own patents and the patents cited by those patents with an application date in the seven years prior to the acquisition announcement, after eliminating duplication. The variable ranges from 0 to 1.
time_window: seven years prior to the acquisition announcement

description: Redundancy (R), the number of patents in the intersection of the acquirer's and target's knowledge bases, divided by the number of unique patents in the acquirer's knowledge base (Ka). A firm's knowledge base consists of the firm's own patents and the patents cited by those patents with an application date in the seven years prior to the acquisition announcement, after eliminating duplication. The variable ranges from 0 to 1.
time_window: seven years prior to the acquisition announcement

description: A count of the target's patents, each weighted by the number of forward citations it has received to control for quality differences. Patent counts are dated by application date and patents with an application date in the seven years prior to the acquisition announcement are counted.
time_window: seven years prior to the acquisition announcement

description: A count of the acquirer's patents, each weighted by the number of forward citations it has received to control for quality differences. Patent counts are dated by application date and patents with an application date in the seven years prior to the acquisition announcement are counted.
time_window: seven years prior to the acquisition announcement

description: Cumulative abnormal returns of the acquirer, constructed with the event study method, over a three-day event window from one day prior to the announcement to one day after. Daily acquirer returns and equally weighted market returns come from CRSP, with an estimation window of 250 days from 300 to 51 days prior to the announcement; Scholes-Williams coefficients are used to calculate the CARs. Acquisitions with a confounding event within a five-day window were eliminated after a LexisNexis search.

The dependent variable is the logarithm of wine price, adjusted on constant 1995 dollars. Prices reflect the suggested retail price; when the suggested retail price is not available, the prevailing wholesale price with a standard markup added is published.

Tasting score rated by Wine Spectator (ranging from 50 to 100) is used as the indicator of an individual wine's evaluated status. It represents the taster's evaluation of the wine's quality relative to other wines based on blind tasting, i.e., the wine label and winery name are neither revealed nor taken into account in scoring. The variable is centered on its mean in the interaction models.

Dummy variables distinguish appellation status, a low-status California or county appellation versus a high-status AVA appellation; a wine affiliated with a California or county appellation is distinguished from a wine affiliated with an AVA appellation (the reference category). Appellation labels follow government regulations: an AVA appellation requires that at least 85% of the grapes in the bottle come from that AVA, whereas a state or county appellation requires only 75% from that state or county.

Dummy variables distinguish the status on extra designation inscribed on the wine label, 'no special designation' indicating a low status versus a special designation of a vineyard or a wine characteristic as a high-status marker (the reference category). A vineyard designation requires that at least 95% of the wine be derived from grapes grown in that vineyard.

variable_name: winery avg. wine score over past 3 years
description: A winery's organizational status is measured by the average tasting score of all wine products for a winery in the previous three years before the focal wine's release (a three-year window in the time lag). The measure is validated by the practice that tasting scores of a wine's recent siblings from the same winery are often shown on the price tag. The variable is centered on its mean in the interaction models.
time_window: previous three years before the focal wine's release

description: Home rule is the key independent variable and is operationalized as an indicator variable equal to 1 if a municipality has home rule status either due to population or through a special referendum, and 0 if a municipality does not have home rule status. In the fuzzy RDD, home rule is instrumented by an indicator variable specifying whether a municipality achieved home rule status by crossing the population threshold of 25,000.

Following Vieregger et al. (2017), capital reallocation is measured by the change in capital expenditures in any given year as compared to the allocation in the previous year. In the first step, capital reallocation is calculated for each of the 13 functions of a municipality; in the second step, values of reallocation for all functions are added to calculate capital reallocation for a municipality. The authors illustrate the construction with a stylized example in which a three-function organization attains a total value of capital reallocation of 110%. The formula block is not readable in the payload, so the specification is not reproduced here.
scale: percentage (allocations and changes expressed in percent of total capital expenditures)
time_window: year t compared with year t-1

description: The authors use the survey of the Census of Governments to obtain the number of governments by type - both general-purpose and special-purpose governmental units - which provides the count of special districts per county, and they use the surveys from 2007, 2012, and 2017 to track changes in the number of special districts. Because special district boundaries are not conterminous with municipal boundaries, the variables of interest are aggregated at the county level. The number of special districts per capita is calculated by dividing the number of special districts by county population, scaled for 1000 inhabitants of a county. Cook County, including Chicago, is excluded as a population outlier.
scale: number of special districts per 1000 county inhabitants

variable_name: proportion of outsiders on the board
description: Board composition variables are independently coded by four Chinese-speaking graduate assistants, who are able to reach a 99 percent agreement, with remaining disagreements resolved by consulting directly with the companies. A total of 52.1 percent directors are identified as insiders currently employed by the focal firm and its subsidiaries, and the remaining non-management directors are classified as representing the state (6.2 percent), institutional (legal person) investors (30.9 percent), or individual investors (10.8 percent). State directors are regarded as quasi-inside directors, and only directors representing institutional and individual interests meet the criteria of 'outside directors.' The proportion of outsiders on the board is computed for each year.

Institutional directors are those representing domestic entities, called 'legal persons' by Chinese terminology, other than the state, the focal firm, and its subsidiaries, and they represent 30.9 percent of all directors. The authors find that 92 percent of institutional directors represent entities which have some identifiable professional relationships with the firm, thus becoming affiliated directors, and conclude that institutional directors are in general affiliated outside directors. In the performance models the proportion of affiliated (mostly institutional) directors is entered separately from the proportion of non-affiliated directors.

Individual directors, representing 10.8 percent of the directors, are those not related to the focal firm, government entities, or institutional investors. The authors find only two cases of disclosed family relationships among individual directors and that almost all individual directors do not have professional relationships with the firm, and conclude that individual directors are in general non-affiliated outside directors. Their proportion on the board is entered separately from the proportion of affiliated directors in the performance models.

Operationally, the authors obtain ROE by using net income divided by the average of owners' equity during a given year. It is one of two widely used accounting-based performance measures, chosen because capital markets in China are not well developed so volatile market-based measures may not reflect firms' true performance, and because Chinese practitioners and officials attach great importance to ROE.

Since a single measure such as ROE may be inadequate, sales growth (annual growth of total revenue) is used as a second measure to triangulate the construct of firm performance. The authors note that sales growth represents resource inflows closer to the spirit of resource dependence theory.
Prior performance is measured by all previous years' ROE and sales growth. It is used as a predictor of the appointment of outside directors in the proportional hazards models.
Firm size is measured by the logarithm of total assets.
Firm age is based on the founding year of the listed firm.

To test Hypotheses 2-5, the authors record the appointment of new outside directors for each year. In the proportional hazards model the dependent variable is the hazard function, that is, the rate of moving from having no outside directors (0) to having some outsiders on the board (1).
scale: 0 = no outside directors, 1 = some outsiders on the board

description: The degree of expertise overlap was measured with the Teachman's Index applied to the concentration of hired individuals with respect to their areas of expertise, using each partner's practice area in the cluster hire as a proxy for his or her areas of expertise. Biemann and Kearney's (2010) bias-corrected formula was used to account for the potential influence of group size on the Teachman's Index, and the values were reverse coded so that higher values indicated less variety or more concentration. Partners with more than one practice area had the weight attributed to each practice area reduced by dividing 1 by the partner's total number of practice areas. The equation itself is unreadable in the text; the text states the specification only in prose.

The degree of co-mobility was assessed with the Teachman's Index, using the prior employers of the individuals in the cluster hire. Larger values in the co-mobility variable indicate greater concentration and lower values indicate more diversity. The equation itself is unreadable in the text; the text states the specification only in prose.

variable_name: Strategic human capital depth at hiring firm
description: This variable was calculated in two steps. First, the number of partners at the hiring firm in each of the cluster hire's practice areas was counted; if a partner at the hiring firm had more than one practice area, the weight attributed to each practice area was reduced by dividing 1 by the partner's total number of practice areas. Second, the number of partners at the hiring firm was averaged across all of the practice areas associated with the cluster hire.

Change in firm profitability was calculated as the difference in profit per partner between 2010 and 2011, expressed in thousands of dollars per partner. The profit per partner data were obtained from The American Lawyer's Top 200 Law Firm Report. The prior year's change in firm profitability, calculated as the difference between profits per partner in 2009 and 2010, was used as a control.

Multiple-item scale adapted from Eggleston et al. (2000) and Luo (2002) that captures the degree to which clauses contain contingencies for different situations. It is in line with prior research that examines complexity as the scope of clauses found in exchange agreements. Responses were given on a seven-point scale. In the buyer perspective model the buyer manager provided the contractual information, and the reverse holds for the supplier perspective model.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Multiple-item scale adapted from Heide and Miner (1992) that assesses one party's expected continuity in its future exchanges with its partners. The measure reflects the expectation of future business that casts a shadow of the future over the present. Responses were given on a seven-point scale.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Scale developed using Nobel and Birkinshaw (1998) with three items describing social interactions between the two partners. It captures the deliberate attempts of organizational members to interact through social activities and personal relationships. Responses were given on a seven-point scale.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Scale adapted from Currall and Judge (1995) with four items examining how a firm watches and checks on various aspects of its partner's activities. Monitoring allows one party to observe and measure another party's behavior or processes. Responses were given on a seven-point scale.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Scale adapted from Blader (2007) and Luo (2007) that captures exchange parties' perceptions of outcome distribution, that is, the evaluation of an outcome related to an allocation decision such as the compensation a party receives. Perceptions of equity are intrinsic to the measure. In the buyer perspective model the supplier manager provided this information, and the reverse holds for the supplier perspective model.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Scale adapted from Schulz (2001) to assess consistency in exchange procedures and processes, that is, the process by which allocation decisions are made. It rests on perceptions of accurate and consistent procedures and of granting voice to those subject to them. In the buyer perspective model the supplier manager provided the fairness information, and the reverse holds for the supplier perspective model.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Perceptual measure adapted from Bercovitz et al. (2006) that includes two aspects: one partner's assessment of the other party's task performance and satisfaction with the relational quality. The authors note that objective performance indicators in buyer-supplier exchanges are difficult to specify and obtain, so most studies employ perceptual measures. Responses were given on a seven-point scale.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: The modified Jones (1991) model divides current accruals into discretionary and nondiscretionary parts. Nondiscretionary current accruals are estimated by regressing the current accruals of firms that were not in the sample, matched by two-digit SIC code, on their changes in sales, with all variables deflated by the lagged value of total assets. The resulting regression parameters are applied to the change in sales less the change in accounts receivable of the sample firms to predict the level of nondiscretionary current accruals normal in each industry; the difference between the predicted nondiscretionary current accruals and the actual reported accruals is discretionary current accruals. When its value is significantly different from zero, the discretionary current accruals are considered to be evidence of earnings management.

Each succession announcement was categorized as indicating either duality or nonduality. The variable is dichotomous (0, 1), where 1 represents a succession announcement that put one individual into a dual leadership role and 0 otherwise.

Cumulative abnormal returns, the summed daily abnormal returns, over a 200-trading-day period extending from 350 days prior to an announcement date to 150 days prior to the announcement date. The authors used standard event study methodology and the market model, whose parameters come from the period -600 to -351 days, which adjusts stock returns for overall market movement and individual firm risk. A positive (negative) value means the firm's stock performed well (poorly) relative to the stock market.
time_window: from 350 days to 150 days prior to the announcement date

description: For each year, the number of open triads in the focal firm's ego network in which the broker and both of its disconnected partners are located in the same institutional setting as the broker (the same country). Counts were generated with NetworkX in Python and verified using Ucinet 6, and the measure used in the models is the log of one plus the number of triads.
time_window: focal year (t), with alliance ties counted from their announcement year

description: For each year, the number of open triads in the focal firm's ego network in which the broker has one partner from a different institutional setting (a different country) and one from the same setting as the broker. Counts were generated with NetworkX in Python and verified using Ucinet 6, and the measure used in the models is the log of one plus the number of triads.
time_window: focal year (t), with alliance ties counted from their announcement year

description: For each year, the number of open triads in the focal firm's ego network in which both of the broker's disconnected partners are embedded in an institutional setting different from that of the broker (different countries from the broker). Counts were generated with NetworkX in Python and verified using Ucinet 6, and the measure used in the models is the log of one plus the number of triads.
time_window: focal year (t), with alliance ties counted from their announcement year

description: Patent counts, calculated as the log of one plus the number of patents granted to firm i during a five-year window. The dependent variables are captured during the five-year window following the year of observation (t+1 to t+5); the application date determines the period of innovation, but only patents that were eventually granted are included.
time_window: t+1 to t+5 (five-year window following the observation year)

description: The patent-level measure developed by Funk and Owen-Smith (2016), which captures the extent to which patents amplify the use of prior art or diminish it by enhancing use of the focal patent's ideas without reference to prior ideas. The paper's equation for the measure could not be extracted from the text. The authors aggregate the measure to the firm level by taking its average value across all of the firm's patents during a five-year window; radicalness cannot be calculated for firms without any patents, and the variable takes negative values.
time_window: t+1 to t+5 (five-year window following the observation year)

description: Return on assets, the ratio of net earnings available to common stockholders divided by average annual assets. It is one of two bank performance measures used in the compensation regressions.

Stock market return, the change in year-end stock prices plus annual dividends, divided by the prior year-end stock price. It is one of two bank performance measures used in the compensation regressions.

Data on CEO compensation were extracted from each bank's annual proxy statements. Total compensation comprises annual salary, short- and long-term bonuses, and stock and stock option grants, with stock and stock option grants evaluated using Smith and Zimmerman's (1976) model. Compensation is measured as the natural logarithm of compensation, as a means of attenuating potential heteroscedasticity problems.

A single composite measure inferred from five distinct dimensions, each captured through a binary variable (1 or 0). The value is computed for each bank by adding up the individual scores from each respective dimension, so the resulting value ranges from zero (lowest managerial discretion) to five (highest managerial discretion). Strategic domain and geographical span cut-offs are selected in order to effectively discriminate among subgroups while approximating the sample's limit for the top quartile.
scale: zero (lowest managerial discretion) to five (highest managerial discretion)

description: Coded 1 for boycotted firms and 0 for the matched firms, with a period dummy coded 0 before the boycott announcement and 1 after it; the interaction of the two is the difference estimator. Boycott events were identified from reports in six national newspapers and matched with company-specific financial data.
time_window: six months before and six months after the boycott announcement

description: Count of the prosocial claims a firm issued in a period, where a claim is a press release associating the company with a prosocial activity. The data form a firm-event-period panel in which each firm-event is observed twice, once in the six months before the boycott announcement and once in the six months after. Claims were located by searching Factiva's two largest press release outlets, PR Newswire and Business Wire, for social-action-related press releases issued by each boycotted company in the year surrounding the announcement.
time_window: six months before and six months after the boycott announcement

description: Number of times each targeted company issued a press release associating itself with a prosocial activity in the six months after the boycott's announcement. Constructed through a manual content analysis of each firm's press releases, searching Factiva's PR Newswire and Business Wire for social-action-related releases; items not sent out directly by the company, such as award announcements, were excluded. No press release issued in the post-boycott period mentions the boycott explicitly.
time_window: six months after the boycott announcement

description: Count of the number of times each targeted company issued a press release associating itself with a prosocial activity in the six months before the boycott's announcement, collected with the same manual content analysis of PR Newswire and Business Wire described for the dependent variable.
time_window: six months before the boycott announcement

description: Count of the number of newspaper articles that discuss a boycott in the six-month period following the announcement of the boycott, searched across the six national newspapers in the sample. Articles dealing with the initial announcement of the boycott, meaning those on the day the boycott was first mentioned, and articles dealing with a concession resulting from the boycott were excluded.
time_window: six months following the boycott announcement

description: Ordinal transformation of a firm's raw score on Fortune magazine's annual 'Most Admired Companies' index, which is based on surveys of peer-firm executives and industry analysts and ranges from 0 to 10. The raw scores were divided each year into three quantiles: companies in the lowest third received a 1, those in the middle third a 2, and those in the top third a 3. Unranked firms were assigned a value of zero to reflect their peripheral field position.
time_window: year prior to the boycott announcement

description: An annual measure based on CEOs' portrayal in the media. The authors searched for all news articles referring to each CEO in a range of major publications, and for each CEO and year determined the number of articles that referred to the CEO in 'confident' terms ('confident,' 'confidence,' 'optimism,' or 'optimistic') and the number that referred to the CEO in 'nonconfident' terms ('reliable,' 'cautious,' 'conservative,' 'practical,' 'frugal,' 'steady,' 'not confident,' or 'not optimistic'). Following Hribar and Yang's (2013) modification, overconfidence is the difference between confident articles and nonconfident articles, divided by the total number of articles; it is continuous, with a higher value indicating greater overconfidence, and CEOs without media coverage are assigned a zero value.

A binary measure based on CEOs' personal portfolio decisions. A CEO was coded as being overconfident if, at least twice during the sample period, he or she continued to hold stock options that were more than 100 percent in-the-money (the stock price was greater than the exercise price by more than 100%). As in Campbell et al. (2011), a CEO was classified as being overconfident from the year when he or she first exhibited the behavior.
time_window: from the year the CEO first exhibited the behavior onward

description: A continuous annual measure based on an index of three antecedent variables that might influence a CEO's overconfidence: recent firm performance, media praise for the CEO, and CEO relative compensation, measured following Hayward and Hambrick (1997). The overall measure was created using the sum of the standardized values of the three variables. Pairwise correlations among the three indicators were all positive and significant and an exploratory factor analysis indicated that the three items loaded onto a single factor.

The dependent variable for all hypotheses. Management forecast error was operationalized as the absolute difference between the management-forecasted earnings and actual earnings, scaled by the share price at the beginning of the year. Improvement of management forecasting accuracy was calculated as error at time t minus error at time t - 1, multiplied by minus one, so a positive value indicates improvement in forecast accuracy while a negative value indicates deteriorating accuracy. Improvement was measured across two successive forecasts in the same CEO's tenure.
time_window: from time t - 1 to time t

description: Prior forecast optimism was coded as 1 if the prior forecast (at time t - 1) was greater than the actual earnings for the year, and 0 otherwise.

Time horizon of the prior management forecast (at time t - 1) was calculated as the log of the number of days between the management forecast date and the fiscal year-end date. The earlier a forecast was issued, the greater the time horizon.

An index comprised of four variables, each measured with annual data at the two-digit SIC industry level. Capital intensity is the industry average of net value of property, plant, and equipment divided by the number of employees, reverse coded because greater capital intensity reflects lower managerial discretion. Product differentiability is the industry average of research and development intensity, calculated as total research and development expenses divided by total sales at the industry level. Market munificence is the average growth in industry sales over the previous five years. Market concentration is the Herfindahl index of industry concentration, reverse coded so that higher values reflect higher discretion. The overall index was created by standardizing and summing the four component measures.
time_window: annual; five-year window for market munificence

description: The differences between the proportions of expertise on the board and the corresponding proportions of risks faced by the firm in the same year were calculated, and board misalignment is the sum of the differences in which the firm does not have sufficient expertise to address the risks (the cases in which the percentage of expertise on the board is smaller than the percentage of risks in the same category). The lower the score, the better aligned are the boards' expertise relative to the firms' risks. Misalignment in year 0 uses expertise and risks in year 0; misalignment in year 3 uses expertise in year 3 and risk factors in year 0.
time_window: year 0 and year 3, with risk factors measured in year 0

description: Strategic board reconfiguration captures the degree to which the board adjusted expertise based on risks over a 3-year window; it was created by subtracting the board misalignment in year 3 variable from the board misalignment in year 0 variable. A positive measure means the board improved its expertise composition and is better aligned relative to the firm's risks; a negative number means the board's expertise composition is even more misaligned relative to firm risks.

Following prior research, CRSP data were used and a market-adjusted model employed to calculate the daily difference between returns for the market (using a value weighted index) and the individual firm to ascertain the abnormal return. Daily abnormal returns were then summed over the fiscal year to ascertain the annual CAR.

Director expertise data was collected from Morningstar, which captures directors' biographies from proxy statements. SAS 9.4 automatically parsed the biographies and searched for keywords in the expertise dictionary; director expertise was coded as 1 if their bio keywords suggested they had a specific type of expertise and 0 otherwise, giving each director a vector of eight potential types of expertise. Individual vectors were aggregated to the board level and the number of each type of expertise present on the board was divided by the sum of total types of expertise to obtain the relative proportions of each type of expertise for the board as a whole.

Links to 10-Ks were collected in SEC's EDGAR database and Python was used to extract the text from the 'ITEM 1A-Risk Factors' section, specifically the headings in the Risk Factors section. The total number of times the search words and phrases appeared in the risk factor dictionary was divided by the total number of words in the risk headings for each firm per year to calculate the relative frequency of key words and phrases. Because the risk factors are compared with the boards' collective expertise, the risk factor score was scaled to have the same range as the boards' expertise categories.

Binary variable that receives the value 1 if there existed a ratified BIT between the home country and the potential host country in year t-1, and 0 otherwise. The authors focus on ratified BITs because signed but not ratified BITs do not create a sufficiently credible commitment. Data are sourced from UNCTAD.

Calculated as the sum of the products of each foreign investment a firm has made prior to the focal investment and the recipient host country's inverted rule of law score from the World Bank's World Governance Indicators. The inverted rule of law score varies from 0 to 5, with lower scores denoting greater rule of law. Because fDiMarkets starts in 2003, only investments from 2003 onward enter the score, so firms investing in 2003 are treated as having no political competence. The variable is used to split the sample into investments by firms in the top decile in a given year and investments by other firms.
time_window: lagged one year (t-1), accumulating investments from 2003 onward

description: Binary variable that equals 1 if the firm is politically connected in its home country, and 0 otherwise. The authors start from Faccio's (2006) list of politically connected firms, defined as firms in which at least one large shareholder or one top officer is a member of parliament, a minister, or is closely related to a top politician or party, and add firms in which at least one board member or top manager previously held a high-level political office in the firm's home country, identified from biographies in the Orbis historical database. The final sample of 101 politically connected firms includes 24 firms from Faccio's original list and 77 additional firms.

Binary variable equal to 1 if the firm invests in the host country in the year, and 0 otherwise. For each investment observation the authors build an industry-specific choice set of potential countries in which the focal firm could enter, treating a country as a potential target if it received at least one foreign investment in the same two-digit SIC industry during the same year. Choice sets range from 99 to 107 countries depending on the industry, the value 1 is assigned to the country the firm actually entered and 0 to the others, and the final sample for analysis comprises 258,974 data points.

The dependent variable is a firm's tendency to undertake new strategic actions in a certain location despite its poor performance there. The authors focused on scenarios in which a firm had been operating at a loss ever since its initial entry into a location and estimated its hazard rate of undertaking at least one new action at a given point in time, measured in quarters, using the Cox semiparametric model. In gap time models a spell is the time duration since the last event in the location; a spell ended in an event when a firm undertook at least one new action while it was still operating at a loss, and was otherwise right censored because the firm turned profitable, exited the location, or reached the end of the observation period. The 680 actions taken while operations in a location remained loss-incurring spanned six types: inbound logistics, product, capacity, outbound logistics, technology, and partner actions.
time_window: quarterly observations, 1998-2011 (records traced back to 1992 to determine gap times)

description: Larger competitors of a firm were other Taiwanese companies belonging to the same product segment and generating comparatively higher average revenues over the past two years. The authors identified all the actions carried out by the focal firm's larger competitors in a given location in China and captured each competitor's action volume as the total number of actions taken by that competitor in the target location over the past two years. Each competitor's action volume was then divided by its overall size, the logarithm of revenues in TWD (million), to adjust for the general correlation between resource endowment and activeness. The variable was computed as the average of larger competitors' size-adjusted action volume in a given location during the two-year moving window.

A firm's smaller competitors were other Taiwanese companies belonging to the same industry segment and generating comparatively lower revenues. Each smaller competitor's performance was captured as the rate of return on its invested capital in a given location in China over the past two years. The variable was computed as the average rate of positive return by those smaller competitors that were operating with profit; where no smaller competitor of a firm was able to profit from the target location, zeros were assigned to indicate the non-existence of supportive cues.

Some of a firm's larger competitors might profit from a given location in China while others might operate at a loss there. The authors first computed the average rate of negative return by those larger competitors that were operating at a loss, then removed negative signs from the average figures so that competitors' larger losses corresponded to higher positive values of the resulting measure. Where no larger competitor of a firm was operating at a loss, zeros were assigned to indicate the non-existence of unsupportive cues.

Two-step measure. In the first step, the similarity (structural equivalence) of a given pair of OS platforms was computed from production-side data: for each product (application), the proportion of independent software firms that offered the product to both OS platforms simultaneously was computed, and the results were averaged over all products in year t. In the second step, the platform relatedness of a firm's product portfolio was computed by weighting the similarity of each pair of OS platforms that the firm's products supported by the proportion of product sales generated from that pair, and normalizing the resulting value to remove double-counting bias. The similarity of OS platforms is high when their API sets overlap.

Two-step measure. In the first step, the structural equivalence (similarity) of all pairs of product-market categories was inferred from the consumption side, from product sales distribution patterns, by building a matrix of firms by product-markets whose elements capture the total sales of a firm's offerings in a product-market category; a pair of product-markets is structurally equivalent to the extent that the profiles of product sales within those markets are similar. In the second step, the product-market relatedness of a firm's product portfolio was computed by taking a sales-weighted average of the similarity metrics across pairs of product-markets supported by the firm's products, weighting each pair by the proportion of product sales generated from it and normalizing to remove double-counting bias.

Firm i's sales growth was computed as the logarithm of the firm's total revenues in year t + 1 divided by its total revenues in year t. A one-year lag was introduced into the performance measures to assess how the independent variables and controls in year t impacted firm performance in year t + 1. The corresponding formula block is unreadable in the supplied text, so the measure is recorded from the prose.

Firm i's market share in year t + 1 is computed as the sum, over all product-markets, of the sales-weighted shares of each product-market, where pij,t+1 is the proportion of firm i's revenues from product-market j in year t + 1. The formula block is unreadable in the supplied text, so the measure is recorded from the prose. A one-year lag was introduced into the performance measures.

Aggregate measure of a country's commercial institutions, calculated as the standardized mean of the Labor, Capital, and Legal dimensions. Each dimension is a rank-order composite of two items whose rank order in the full list of 183 countries was converted into a percentile range and averaged over the available years prior to 2006; Labor Markets combines 'Ease of Employing Workers' and 'Percentage of Labor Force That Has a Tertiary Education,' Capital Markets combines 'Ease of Protecting Investors' and 'Ease of Getting Credit,' and Legal Transparency combines 'Ease of Registering Property' and 'Ease of Enforcing Contracts.' Higher values indicate higher market development and less severe voids in commercial institutions.
scale: 0 to near 1 for the dimensions; aggregate is the standardized mean of the three dimensions

description: Dependent variable calculated as the proportion of the 12 MID and BCD service categories offered by an incubator that fell into either of the two BCD categories. Values range from 0 to 1, and larger values mean that an incubator placed greater emphasis on BCD relative to MID.

Dependent variable formed as the ratio of the MID-Finance services an incubator offers to the 12 MID and BCD service categories. MID-Finance is one of the two factors into which MID services split in the confirmatory factor analysis, and counts for services within the subcategory range from 0 to 3.

Dependent variable formed as the ratio of the MID-Space services an incubator offers to the 12 MID and BCD service categories. MID-Space is one of the two factors into which MID services split in the confirmatory factor analysis, and counts for services within the subcategory range from 0 to 3.

Dependent variable formed as the ratio of the BCD-Training services an incubator offers to the 12 MID and BCD service categories. BCD-Training is one of the two factors into which BCD services separated in the confirmatory factor analysis, and counts for services within the subcategory range from 0 to 3.

Dependent variable formed as the ratio of the BCD-Consulting services an incubator offers to the 12 MID and BCD service categories. BCD-Consulting is one of the two factors into which BCD services separated in the confirmatory factor analysis, and counts for services within the subcategory range from 0 to 3.
Dummy variable identifying incubators with private sponsors as reported in the infoDev data. For the analysis the sponsor measures used mean-effects coding, with the omitted categories coded as -1.
Dummy variable identifying incubators with academic sponsors as reported in the infoDev data. For the analysis the sponsor measures used mean-effects coding, with the omitted categories coded as -1.

Dummy variable identifying incubators with government sponsors as reported in the infoDev data. For the analysis the sponsor measures used mean-effects coding, with the omitted categories coded as -1.

Dummy variable identifying incubators with non-governmental organization sponsors as reported in the infoDev data. For the analysis the sponsor measures used mean-effects coding, with the omitted categories coded as -1.

Measured using the percentage of banking organizations that were not affiliated with the NYCHA in a year, as the extent to which the market was beyond the control of the NYCHA. The authors note that about 80 percent of the banking organizations that remained outside of the NYCHA were excluded for reasons unrelated to the functionality of the institution: 43 percent were trust companies prohibited from becoming NYCHA members and 36 percent were banks too small to meet the minimum size requirements.

A dichotomous variable coded 1 for banking organizations that were affiliated with the NYCHA in a given year. Because only two banks relinquished their NYCHA memberships before they failed, the authors assumed that a bank remained a member once it joined and defined the treatment as a regime shift.
scale: dichotomous (1 = affiliated with the NYCHA in a given year)

description: The dependent variable is a banking organization's hazard of failure in a year. Out of the 240 banking organizations in Manhattan during this period, 129 failed: 65 ended in liquidation, 63 were absorbed by another banking organization, and one bank moved out of Manhattan. Because voluntary mergers may occur for different reasons than failures, banking organizations that ended with a voluntary merger were treated as right censored; a merger was coded as an absorption or as being voluntary if historical documents clearly state which type of event occurred, and otherwise a voluntary merger was coded using Banaszak-Holl's (1991) criteria.
Measured as the number of non-NYCHA member banks that failed in the previous year.

The interlock network density among NYCHA member banking organizations, measured as the ratio of the number of existent interlock ties between any pair of banking organizations to the total number of all possible ties between them, i.e., the sum of existing ties divided by [n × (n - 1)/2]. Two banking organizations were coded as sharing an interlock tie if they had at least one common executive or board director. Data were collected on banking organizations' executives and directors from 1885 onward because one source did not start to list the names of executives and directors of state banks until 1885.

The social-club network density among NYCHA bankers, calculated in the same way as the interlock network density from NYCHA banking organization presidents' affiliations with social clubs in New York City. Two banking organization presidents were coded as having a tie if they had at least one common social club affiliation; the ten most central clubs among the bankers were identified and their membership rosters were manually checked to verify each banker's affiliation, and affiliations with two elite cultural organizations, the Sustaining Members of the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Board of Directors of the Metropolitan Opera House, were also considered.

Network centrality of each individual banking organization, measured as the eigenvector centrality of a banking organization in the interlock network; interlock ties are shared executives or board directors.

Network centrality of each individual banking organization, measured as the eigenvector centrality of a banking organization in the social club network; presidents were coded as having a tie if they shared at least one social club affiliation.

The share of the MNE's affiliates in the affected country in the year of the disruption, where each affiliate is weighted by the MNE's ownership percentage, expressed relative to the same ownership-weighted affiliate count worldwide. For countries where the MNE has no operations, economic importance equals zero. It ranges from zero (low) to one (high). The authors present the specification as the ratio of ownership-weighted affiliates in country c to ownership-weighted affiliates in the world in the year of the disruption.

A continuous variable of the total U.S. dollar amount donated by the MNE to the relief and recovery of the affected country, logged for the analyses. Values are recorded for MNEs for each country-event, including nondonors.

A Herfindahl-Hirschman index calculated at the country level as the sum of squares of the proportion of revenues of the largest five firms in the focal country in the year of the institutional disruption. It provides a normalized value of firms with large shares of the country market and ranges from zero to one, with larger values indicating more dominant MNEs in the country market. The raw data source is Orbis.

The average value of gross national expenditure in current U.S. dollars in the previous two years divided by the disaster's economic damage. Data from the two years before the event are used to capture the information available when the donation decision is made and to avoid reverse causality.

The average of net official development assistance and of official aid received for disasters in the two years preceding the disruption. Data from the two years before the event are used to capture the information available when the donation decision is made and to avoid reverse causality.

Regulatory quality from the World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators. The variable ranges from -2.5 to 2.5 and captures perceptions of the ability of the government to formulate and implement sound policies and regulations that permit and promote private sector development.

Shocks are identified as sudden and unpredictable using the 30-day criterion between start and end dates for sudden shocks, and as severe by selecting shocks that rank at the 99th percentile in the affected country in any of three impact areas: deaths, affected people, or economic damage. The percentile distribution of each variable is calculated by country for all shocks reported in EM-DAT. Terrorist attacks, natural disasters, and epidemics qualify.

The measure is based on an algorithm using multivariate clustering analysis that assesses the extent to which the alignment of individual characteristics divides a group into two subgroups. Based on the strongest group split, the algorithm calculates the ratio of the between-group sum of squares to the total sum of squares; the higher the ratio, the stronger the faultline. The algorithm is operationalized on the attributes of education, functional background, and tenure. Educational background is one of five areas (arts, sciences, engineering, law, and business and economics), functional background is classified into eight tracks, and tenure is measured as years in the firm.

variable_name: industry-adjusted ROA and industry-adjusted Tobin's Q
description: Firm performance is measured with industry-adjusted ROA and industry-adjusted Tobin's Q. ROA is income before interest and taxes divided by the book value of assets, and Tobin's Q is the ratio of the market value of assets to the replacement costs of assets. For both measures the median ROA and median Tobin's Q were subtracted from firm ROA and firm Tobin's Q, respectively, to control for potential industry effects. Control and explanatory variables are modeled at time t-1, and ROA and Tobin's Q are averaged over three periods of time: t, t+1, and t+2.
time_window: averaged over t, t+1 and t+2; explanatory variables at t-1
