description: Environmental dynamism is represented by instability and unpredictability. Instability is measured with three indicators: amplitude of change, average magnitude of instability, and frequency of changes in fortune; unpredictability is measured with two indicators: magnitude of unpredictability and proportional unpredictability. The indicators are computed from quarterly industry sales of all Compustat firms listed by four-digit SIC codes, using a rolling five-year (20-quarter) window and the X11 procedure in SAS 9.2. The second-order factor of the five indicators showed a better fit than a measurement model with the individual constructs of instability and unpredictability.

Environmental complexity is proxied through the concentration of competitors using a four-dimensional measure of component heterogeneity: the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI), the four-firm concentration index (Firm-4), the eight-firm concentration index (Firm-8), and establishment diversity, i.e., the number and distribution of small, medium, and large organizations. The HHI, Firm-4, and Firm-8 measures are created from the 2002 U.S. economic census and assess the degree to which an industry departs from pure competition. The HHI is 1 minus the sum of the squared market shares for all firms in a four-digit SIC code and ranges between 0 and 1, where higher values indicate more competitors; Firm-4 and Firm-8 are the market shares held by the four largest and eight largest competitors subtracted from 100, with higher values indicating greater complexity. The reliability of the four-item measure was 0.86.

Environmental munificence is measured using information on four-digit SIC codes from Compustat. The authors ran regressions of the natural log of industry net sales and the natural log of operating income over a five-year period. Munificence is the average of the antilog of the betas of the two regressions.

Categorical dependent variable equal to zero if the nationality of the partnering firm is Japanese, one if American, and two if a non-U.S. foreign country. It is estimated with multinomial logit, sequentially comparing Japanese domestic relationships first with U.S.-Japan relationships and second with Japanese relationships with firms of other countries.

Firm size is measured by the level of employment (number of employees) of the firm. Employment level is used rather than average sales because sales may fluctuate widely in any given period and because Japanese firms are known to have a relatively stable employment policy.
A count of the number of four-digit level industries, by the two-digit SIC code, in which the sampled firm conducts business, constructed to measure the effect of related diversification.

A count of the number of industries, as defined by the two-digit SIC code, in which the sampled firm operates. Because of its broad scope, the two-digit level really measures unrelated diversification, more likely to be beyond what is meaningful for commercializing biotechnology.

A dummy variable equal to one if the Japanese parent firm's business includes either or both of the sectors indicated by the three-digit SIC codes 283 and 512, and zero otherwise. These sectors are the manufacturing and the wholesale business of pharmaceutical products.

A dummy variable equal to one if the cooperative relationship involves the commercialization of a pharmaceutical product, and zero if otherwise. The predicted sign for this variable is positive when comparing Japanese partners with American partners; the variable is expected to be significant for American partners but not for partners of other countries.
A dummy variable equal to one if the cooperative relationship entails technology transfer or licensing, and zero otherwise.

One of four dummy variables indicating if a particular function is governed by the sample cooperative relationship. The dummy variables are not mutually exclusive, so multiple functions are possible for a relationship. Research and development agreements commonly involve exchange of technical data and information.

One of four dummy variables indicating if a particular function is governed by the sample cooperative relationship. The dummy variables are not mutually exclusive, so multiple functions are possible for a relationship.

One of four dummy variables indicating if a particular function is governed by the sample cooperative relationship. The dummy variables are not mutually exclusive, so multiple functions are possible for a relationship. There are relatively few cooperative relationships which cover the function of manufacturing.

One of four dummy variables indicating if a particular function is governed by the sample cooperative relationship. The dummy variables are not mutually exclusive, so multiple functions are possible for a relationship. Marketing is a major obstacle for a foreign firm to enter and compete in the Japanese market.
The year of formation of the cooperative relationship. Extensive data were compiled on 264 Japanese cooperative relationships, but the time of formation was available on only 173 of these.

Continuous variable capturing the extent to which a firm relies on external vendors to adopt a set of eight online service areas. Informants reported their bank's percentage of in-house development versus outsourcing for each service area at the time each service was adopted. Degree of outsourcing was calculated by summing the percentages of outsourcing across all service areas offered and dividing the sum by the total number of online service areas offered; it includes service areas adopted completely in-house.
time_window: at the time of adoption of each online service (first survey)

description: A latent construct based on three seven-point Likert scale items on which informants rated the degree to which their bank is capable of customizing standardized off-the-shelf technology to its Internet applications, is capable of developing future applications of Internet banking services, and has adequate IT skills to operate Internet banking in-house. The standardized Cronbach coefficient alpha for the three items was 0.85 and a factor analysis ensured the items loaded on one factor; the three items were combined and averaged.

The percentage of a bank's total customer base (demand-deposit households) that regularly checks balances online, reported by respondents as of the spring 2003, the time of the second survey. The authors argue this is a suitable performance measure because online banking is a lower-cost channel and because customer adoption and usage of a new technology are viewed as measures of new technology acceptance and success.

A binary variable of one for banks that had at any point in time a PC direct-dial program for their retail customers and of zero otherwise. PC direct-dial programs require client software installed on customers' PCs with a direct modem connection either to the bank or to an Internet service provider supporting the service on behalf of the bank.
time_window: at any point in time (first survey)

description: Percentage of founders in the founding team who had some experience in the financial sector. Prior banking experience was excluded because it could be influenced by both financial and community logics. Financial professionals covered under financial logics included investors, investment bankers, accountants, and insurance providers. The composition of the founding board was captured as of the initial charter request to regulators, before the bank had been established and before investor capital had been gathered.
time_window: as of the initial charter request to regulators

description: Degree of personal community involvement, measured as the number of volunteer community associations (Boy Scouts, Red Cross, local Chamber of Commerce, country club, etc.) that members of the founding team had listed in their biographical statements. A total count of voluntary associations was used rather than the percentage of founders with community involvement because it captures better the community-oriented cognitive and motivational predispositions of a team; being involved in one and only one community board is a weak measure.
time_window: as of the initial charter request to regulators

description: Number of members of the founding board of directors, which is the proxy used for the founding team. Board membership captures both the stature and degree of involvement of the key participants, who fund and drive the founding effort and determine its orientation. The founding board always includes the CEO and, in 30 percent of the teams, other members of the management team.
time_window: as of the initial charter request to regulators

description: Percentage of bank deposits that were mediated by a broker. It captures risky behavior adopted, or at least tolerated, by the founding team and is aligned with the financial logic and misaligned with the community logic. The measure was assessed early, in the first quarter after opening, to best reflect the founding team's influence before other contingencies and considerations intervened. Using such deposits exposes banks to funding shortages if the market turned less liquid, as happened in 2008.

The ratio of equity analysts and fund managers to the number of equity funds marketed by a firm at a given point in time. It approximates adoption resistance by the strength of the financial professional collective of the focal firm, relative to other firms in the industry. The absolute number of finance professionals is not used because some small investment boutiques are analyst powerhouses. Data were coded from the annual member directory of the SSFA, supplemented where necessary by annual reports and interviews.

The propensity component of the heterogeneous diffusion model, estimated in the propensity vector with its own intercept, capturing the firm's rate of adoption not from contagion. Variables assigned to the propensity vector on a theoretical basis, otherwise following Greve et al. (1995) with test runs to determine best model fit. Time-varying covariates are updated annually unless specified otherwise.

variable_name: Average fund size (averages of fund size within each product category)
description: The observable adoption performance of earlier adoptions proxied as the average fund size within each product category, rather than the average annual growth in fund size for the category, because fund attractiveness to potential adopters is a threshold-like value. Fund size is an easily observable fund feature reported daily in the media, and industry experts claimed an industry rule of thumb indicated attractiveness if a fund could be expected to reach a size of about SEK 300 million. Fund size data were coded from annual reports and from Morningstar's (Sweden) database.

The susceptibility component of the heterogeneous diffusion model, estimated in the susceptibility vector with its own intercept, capturing the focal firm's susceptibility to influence from earlier adopters. The average fund size variable and its interaction with analyst intensity are placed in this vector.

variable_name: Analyst intensity (t-1) x average fund size (t-1)
description: An interaction variable between analyst intensity and average fund size added to the susceptibility vector to test Hypothesis 3, capturing whether the contagion effect of prior adoption performance is weaker in organizations with stronger internal resistance.

variable_name: Hazard of adoption of mixed asset, index, and SRI funds
description: The dependent variable is the day, month, year, and category of product adoptions per firm, collected from The Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority, which registers all new products. Adoption is modeled as a competing risks hazard rate for the nth case entry into the jth product category, allowing simultaneous analysis of the diffusion of mixed asset, index, and SRI funds.

Artists are coded as high-status when they appear in the 2005 edition of The Rolling Stone Encyclopedia of Rock and Roll, a volume reporting information about approximately 1,800 artists considered of particular significance to 20th-century music and selected by veteran music journalists. The variable is a cumulative count of a focal band's coappearances with high-status alters up to time t. Because none of the sample bands appears in the volume, only alter status is captured. The measure was orthogonalized against the count of past alters with Billboard Hot 100 hits to avoid multicollinearity.

Bands enter the observation window when they first appear in a concert and are assumed to exit when they fail to appear in any concert for three consecutive years, so that occasional breaks from touring are not inadvertently coded as exits. The dependent variable is modelled as the hazard of failure in Cox proportional-hazard models. The models do not include fixed effects because the necessary time-invariant dummy variables cause estimation to fail.

The logged dollar amount of revenues attributable to each individual artist or group. Because concert lineups are typically structured so that the most popular and highly paid artists perform last, total concert revenues are allocated so that the headliner receives twice as much revenue as the second artist, who in turn receives twice as much as the third, and so forth. The models are first-differenced and include a lagged dependent variable (revenues allocated to the artist in year t-1).
A simple count of the years elapsed since the first appearance of the entrant in the data. It is included as a moderator of the effect of high-status affiliations.

The change in the three-month average spatial distance between CCTV1 and satellite channel i in time slot s, taken between the period immediately before and the period immediately after the CCTV1 shift. The variable is defined as -1 times the distance shift when CCTV1 moves closer to a satellite channel and is zero otherwise, so larger values indicate that CCTV1 moved closer. Values range from 0 to 1.57 radians.
time_window: Periods 2 to 3 (three-month averages before and after the May 2003 shift)

description: The change in the three-month average spatial distance between CCTV1 and satellite channel i in time slot s, taken between the period immediately before and the period immediately after the CCTV1 shift. The variable takes the value of the distance shift when CCTV1 moves away from a satellite channel and is zero otherwise, so larger values indicate that CCTV1 moved further away. Values range from 0 to 1.57 radians.
time_window: Periods 2 to 3 (three-month averages before and after the May 2003 shift)

description: The change in product spatial distance between satellite channel i and CCTV1 in time slot s subsequent to the CCTV1 programming shift. The 12-month sample period was grouped into four three-month periods; the three-month average distance in Period 3 (immediately after the overhaul) was subtracted from that in Period 4 (the last three months). A positive value indicates that the channel repositioned away from CCTV1 and a negative value that it repositioned closer. Distance is the angle between the channels' 87-element programming vectors, calculated using vector dot products.
scale: difference in radians (each distance measure ranges from 0 to 1.57 radians)

description: Audience rating share of satellite channel i in each time slot in Period 2. A greater value indicates that the satellite channel possesses greater competitive strength in the time slot. This is the firm-market level measure of competitive strength.

The proportion of a satellite channel's audience generated from its top four program categories across all time slots in Period 2. A greater value indicates that the satellite channel possesses greater competitive strength. This is the firm-level measure of competitive strength.

A dummy variable that takes the value one during evening prime time, 7:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., and zero otherwise. During prime time viewers in a family tend to watch television together, so customer preferences are concentrated in common-denominator programming categories, leaving little demand for shows of other categories.

The extent of channel i's own programming change between consecutive months in Period 2, first averaged and then divided by CCTV1's programming change in time slot s in order to control for seasonal or current events at the time slot level. A large value indicates that the channel has shown a low level of commitment to a product space in the time slot market.

A continuous index tapping three dimensions: the firm's emphasis on product development, its emphasis on market development, and its willingness to take a risky position in the capital markets. These are measured by the firm's consolidated allocations to R&D as a percentage of sales, its consolidated allocations to market development (advertising) as a percentage of sales, and its debt/equity ratio. The index was computed as a standardized score with respect to the means and standard deviations of the original sample. Factor analysis loaded the components on a single factor, and all variables were standardized with respect to sector means and standard deviations.

Corporate aggressiveness in the second four-year period, 1981-1984, modelled with corporate aggressiveness in period 1 included as a separate regressor. The residual effects of the other variables on aggressiveness in the current period are interpreted as change that departs from the trend line.

Corporate aggressiveness in the first four-year period, 1977-1980, which provides an estimate of the inertia arising from prior resource commitments that carry the organization forward. It is also entered as the lagged regressor in the equations predicting aggressiveness in the second period.

Firm size was computed as the logarithm of total employees, chosen because measures based on numbers of employees and total revenues were highly correlated in this sample. Size provides a gross estimate of the contextual forces that inhibit change.

Performance was measured by return on assets, calculated as the ratio of operating income to total assets. The authors used this measure because they were interested in performance viewed as resource availability rather than market assessments.

A measure of sector volatility was calculated by aggregating the sale volatility coefficients of individual firms within a sector. The resulting coefficient correlates highly with industry expert ratings of environmental turbulence and gauges the uncertainty faced by the corporate enterprise as a whole.

The size of ego's potential loss was measured on a two-item scale. Items were answered on five-point response scales and were added to yield a measure of the latent variable. Factor analysis showed the items of size of loss formed a dimension separate from the probability of loss, which warranted a separate regression equation.

The probability of loss was measured on only a one-item scale. Adding the single probability item to the size-of-loss items deteriorated the alpha coefficient drastically, and the item loaded only just above the cut-off point, which the authors take as evidence that size and probability of loss represent separate dimensions.
scale: single item on a five-point response scale

description: For the relative value that a partner offered the authors had two measures, one of which was the partner's share of the total sales of ego. This measure was used alongside the other value measure rather than combined with it, because joining them into one scale of partner value greatly reduced the alpha coefficient.

The second measure of the relative value that a partner offered was a scale of four other items, the remaining indicators of the value of alter. It was used alongside alter's share of sales because combining the two measures into one scale of partner value greatly reduced the alpha coefficient.
scale: four items on five-point response scales

description: Ego's asset specificity was the aggregate of four variables, one for each dimension of asset specificity specified by Williamson, with a total of ten items. It measures the switching costs ego would incur in moving to an alternative partner.

variable_name: Restriction of room for alter's opportunism
description: Restriction of room for alter's opportunism was the aggregate of two scales, one for legal ordering and one for private ordering, with a total of seven items. The two component scales had alphas above the .70 cut-off.
One of the two scales aggregated into restriction of room for alter's opportunism, measuring legal ordering in the relationship. Its scale had an alpha above the .70 cut-off.
One of the two scales aggregated into restriction of room for alter's opportunism, measuring private ordering in the relationship. Its scale had an alpha above the .70 cut-off.

Trust was the aggregate of two dimensions, habitualization and institutionalization, with a total of six items. The overall trust variable includes one item more than the total of its components; this item was kept separate because it could with equal justification be added to either dimension.
A multi-item scale for the trust dimension of the partners' shared norms and values. Its alpha was above the .70 cut-off and it was also combined with habitualization into an overall trust variable.

A multi-item scale for the trust dimension covering partners' having established habits, bonds, good communication, and empathy. Its alpha was above the .70 cut-off and it was also combined with institutionalization into an overall trust variable.
The relative value offered by ego to alter was an aggregate of six items. Its alpha was above the .70 cut-off.

Continuity of the relationship was an aggregate of two scales, past growth of the relationship and future perspective, with a total of five items. All multi-item scales had alphas above .70 except growth of business between the partners, whose alpha was .68.
Limitation of alter's inclination toward opportunism, or restraint of alter, was composed of five items. Its alpha was above the .70 cut-off.

Uncertainty avoidance of ego had seven items and its alpha was above the .70 cut-off. Respondents answered on five-point response scales, and the items were added to yield the measure of the latent variable.
scale: seven items on five-point response scales, items added

description: Firm size of ego was naturally a cardinal measure, in contrast to the five-point response scales used for the other items; it is a property of the supplier firm rather than of the individual relationship.

Three perceptual indicators of alliance performance were used to gauge the implications of alliances for partnering firms. Respondents indicated on a five-point Likert scale their satisfaction with the knowledge accumulated from participating in the collaborative agreement, the extent to which the alliance created new opportunities for the firm, and the degree to which the alliance satisfied the partnering firm's initial objectives. The three indicators were standardized and summed to construct a global measure of alliance performance, which had a Cronbach alpha of 0.83.
scale: five-point Likert scale for each indicator; indicators standardized and summed

description: Respondents were asked to report the number of prior agreements with any partner on any subject. Because examination of the variable's distribution indicated significant positive skewness, the variable was redefined using the natural log transformation 'new variable' = ln(1 + 'old variable').

Respondents were asked to report the number of prior agreements with any partner in product areas similar to the one of the focal agreement. Because the variable's distribution showed significant positive skewness, it was redefined using the natural log transformation 'new variable' = ln(1 + 'old variable').

Respondents were asked to report the number of prior agreements with the same partner. Because the variable's distribution showed significant positive skewness, it was redefined using the natural log transformation 'new variable' = ln(1 + 'old variable').

A dummy variable indicated whether or not the collaborative agreement was an equity alliance. Equity-based alliances can involve one partner owning a minority stake in the other partnering firm, or the two firms creating a new entity whose ownership is shared among them.

Industry return on equity (ROE) and return on assets (ROA) are used as measures of overall industry performance in each of the four industries and are examined as time series, using quarterly data to ensure sufficient observations. Because a quarterly ROA time series was not available in the telecommunications industry, annual ROA data were used there. Separate models are estimated for ROE and ROA, with the break date captured by an indicator variable.

Incumbent firm performance is measured as firm ROE and firm ROA obtained as annual observations, setting up pooled time-series, cross-sectional panels of data. In parallel to the industry analysis, both ROE and ROA are applied as dependent variables, with ROE used in Models 1 and 2 and ROA in Models 3 and 4.

Measured by the sum of a firm's cash and all securities readily convertible to cash as listed in the current assets section of the balance sheet, a measure the authors interpret as a firm's free cash flow and hence a proxy for financial strength. The variable is lagged by one year to compensate for a potential simultaneity bias. It is split into prediscontinuity and postdiscontinuity time series, with the postdiscontinuity series used to test the hypotheses.
time_window: lagged by one year; prediscontinuity and postdiscontinuity series

description: Proxied by an incumbent firm's R&D expenditures, the outlays for R&D as listed in the annual income statements. As with financial strength, the variable is lagged by one year to compensate for a potential simultaneity bias and is split into prediscontinuity and postdiscontinuity time series, with the postdiscontinuity series used to test the hypotheses.
time_window: lagged by one year; prediscontinuity and postdiscontinuity series

variable_name: Type of complementary assets needed to commercialize the new technology (generic vs. specialized)
description: A qualitative, industry-level categorization of the complementary assets required to commercialize each new technology, based on the discontinuity's impact on incumbents' downstream competencies. The computer and steel industries were classified as generic because the new technologies were commercialized through devalued downstream assets, while the pharmaceutical and telecommunications industries were classified as specialized because regulatory, sales, and switching-network assets were enhanced and could be applied without significant additional investments.

variable_name: Technological discontinuity (identified event and structural break date)
description: In each of the four industries one technological discontinuity was identified from industry accounts using the Tushman and Anderson price-performance criterion and classified as competence-destroying: the PC, the electric arc furnace, biotechnology and wireless telephony. In the industry-level test its timing is the statistically estimated structural break date in the quarterly industry ROE and ROA time series, entered as a break-date indicator variable. The same break dates split the firm-level explanatory variables into pre- and post-discontinuity periods.
scale: Qualitative identification of the event; break-date indicator variable in the time-series models
level: Industry (break dates also applied at firm level)

description: Multi-item perceptual scale measuring the degree to which respondents agree that the firm aggressively pursues technological change. The items cover exploring the most up-to-date production-operations technology, moving ahead with plans to evaluate new processing equipment, having a reputation for being first in trying out new methods and equipment, planning to increase R&D spending over the next five years, spending more than most firms in the industry on new product development, recruiting the best qualified technical and marketing personnel, and doing technological forecasting for products and for production processes.
Factual measure computed as the number of scientists, engineers, programmers, and technicians divided by the total number of employees.

Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales using opposite anchor phrases, capturing the degree to which the firm has complete job descriptions for all jobs, employees must strictly abide by company rules, and there are no arguments about job overlap among managers.
Scale measured on 7-point scales corresponding to managerial levels, capturing the level of management responsible for making each type of decision.

Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales ranging from "never used" to "used extremely frequently", capturing the extent to which the firm uses each scanning method to gather information about its environment.
scale: 7-point scale from "never used" to "used extremely frequently"

description: Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree", capturing the extent to which the firm sacrifices profitability and cuts prices to gain market share.

Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree", capturing the extent of formal planning, coordination and evaluation activities with respect to strategic alternatives.
Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree", capturing the emphasis on performance monitoring and enhancement of core manufacturing competencies.

Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree", capturing the presence of a long-term view and of activities designed to provide longer-term benefits.
Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree", capturing opportunity seeking, first-to-market innovativeness and strategic acquisitions.

Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree", capturing risk management in terms of resource allocation decisions, operations and choice of projects.
Factual measure of research and development investments expressed as a percentage of annual sales.

Composite measure of the level of process innovativeness using data on computer-based administrative and manufacturing applications, inspired by the Khandwalla Score. For each application, an indicator takes the value 0 or 1 depending on adoption of the innovation, and it is multiplied by the degree of radicalness of that application as established by a panel of experts who ranked each innovation on 7-point Likert scales, thus providing for each firm a total weighted score of process innovativeness. Computer-based administrative and manufacturing applications are not distinguished.
Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales ranging from "very minimal" to "very maximal", capturing the extent of the firm's technological awareness and knowledge.

Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales ranging from "not a substantial threat" to "a very substantial threat", capturing the extent to which the external environment and specific challenges are considered a threat to the survival of the firm.
scale: 7-point scale from "not a substantial threat" to "a very substantial threat"

description: Perceptual scale measured on 7-point scales using opposite anchor phrases, capturing the perceived unpredictability and rate of change of the external environment.

Perceptual measure on 7-point scales ranging from "below industry average" to "above industry average", capturing respondents' performance evaluation compared to the industry average. Subjective measures were used because CEOs of small firms are often reluctant to provide hard financial data.
scale: 7-point scale from "below industry average" to "above industry average"

description: Factual measure computed as export sales divided by total sales. Factual measures were used because the CEOs surveyed did not consider these measures to be sensitive information.
scale: ratio of export sales to total sales

description: Strategic orientation was measured with Venkatraman's STROBE instrument, with separate multi-item scales on 7-point agree-disagree anchors for aggressiveness (4 items), analysis (6), defensiveness (4), futurity (5), proactiveness (5) and riskiness (5). Reliabilities in this study ranged from about 0.51 to 0.71.

variable_name: Realized innovative efforts (R&D %, process innovativeness, external technological experience)
description: Realized innovative efforts were measured by three separate dependent variables: R&D investments as a percentage of annual sales, the degree of process innovativeness of computer-based administrative and manufacturing technologies (composite score weighted by expert-rated radicalness), and the extent of external technological experience (perceptual scale).

variable_name: Determinants of technology policy (predictor set: structural characteristics, scanning, STROBE)
description: The determinants are the set of ten predictor variables entered in blocks in the hierarchical regression of technology policy: three structural characteristics (technocratization, formalization, centralization), scanning mechanisms, and the six STROBE dimensions (aggressiveness, analysis, defensiveness, futurity, proactiveness, riskiness). Each has its own scale or factual ratio from the CEO interviews. The moderation hypotheses compare the form and the predictive validity of this set across subgroups split at the median of perceived hostility and dynamism.
scale: Set of ten predictors (7-point perceptual scales and one factual ratio)

variable_name: Initial financial contribution by the lead entrepreneur
description: The amount of initial financial resources contributed by the lead entrepreneur in the first year, taken from the PSEDII question in every wave about the amount of financial resources invested each year by an owner-founder. It is the lead entrepreneur's contribution used to predict members' contributions in ensuing years.

variable_name: The lead entrepreneur has worked full time for the start-up (0/1)
description: Whether the lead entrepreneur worked more than 35 hours per week for the start-up, built from the PSEDII question asking in what months an owner-founder was working for the start-up for more than 35 hours per week. The indicator is time varying and used to predict whether team members work full time.

The financial contributions by a co-owner-founder to the venture, in individual-year units, from the PSEDII question in every wave about the amount of financial resources invested each year by an owner-founder. When there is more than one co-owner-founder, separate observations are created for each co-owner.
time_window: yearly, in the years following the initial interview

variable_name: Whether a co-owner-founder works full time
description: Whether a co-owner-founder worked more than 35 hours per week for the start-up, in individual-month units, based on the PSEDII question asking in what months an owner-founder was working for the start-up for more than 35 hours per week; team members' work status was coded at a weekly basis. Separate observations are created for each co-owner.

A time-varying binary indicator of whether the team had signed a formal contract regarding ownership shares by the current month in which an investment by a cofounder is made. Respondents were asked what proportion of ownership they would have and whether and when the team had signed an agreement regarding this ownership share.
time_window: time-varying, by the current month of an investment

description: Constructed from CMS items asking respondents to report the percentage of their product innovations, and separately of their process innovations, for which the competitive advantage from those innovations had been protected by product complexity. Responses were given on a five-point Likert scale signifying below 10 percent, 10-40 percent, 41-60 percent, 61-90 percent, and over 90 percent, which the authors transform to a measure ranging from zero to one. The converted product and process complexity values are averaged across all respondents in the same four-digit SIC code to create an industry-level score, which is time invariant because the survey was conducted once in 1994.

Following Chung and Pruitt (1994) and DaDalt et al. (2003), FirmQ is calculated as the sum of firm market value (share price multiplied by outstanding shares) and the book value of long-term debt, preferred stock, and net current liabilities, all divided by the total asset value of the firm, for each firm in each year of the sample. LogQ is the natural log of FirmQ, created to be consistent with the derived estimation equations. All data for these calculations are taken from Compustat.

A measure of the natural log of the average FirmQ within each four-digit SIC code industry. The industry-level derivation calculates the mean of firm values within an industry for market value, tangible assets, and intangible assets before making the same transformations made in the firm-level derivation.

The second (variance) moment of q for all firms within the same four-digit SIC industry for each year in the panel. VarQ is calculated as the standard deviation of FirmQ, that is, the square root of the variance of FirmQ. Because some industries have too few participants in a given year, observations are lost relative to the profitability models.
The third (skew) moment of q for all firms within the same four-digit SIC industry for each year in the panel. Together with VarQ it represents the two higher moments of q at the industry level.

Buyer trustworthiness measured as the sum of three submeasures: the extent to which the supplier trusts the manufacturer to treat the supplier fairly; the extent to which the supplier perceives that the automaker will take unfair advantage of the supplier if given the chance (reverse scored); and the extent to which the automaker has a reputation for trustworthiness (following through on promises and commitments) in the general supplier community. Each scale item was measured on a seven-point Likert scale (1 = not at all; 7 = to a very great extent). Cronbach's alpha for the construct was 0.84.
scale: seven-point Likert (1 = not at all; 7 = to a very great extent)

description: Buyer trustworthiness is the mean trust score for all the suppliers who are associated with the particular automaker. It is used in the automaker-level model of buyer transaction costs.

Computed as total annual person-days of face-to-face time spent multiplied by the percent of time spent on price negotiation/contracting, divided by the supplier's sales to the buyer, so the measure represents transaction cost per dollar of sales. Suppliers estimated the number of person-days of contact between their organization and the automaker during the previous year and the percentage of their face-to-face communication time with automakers that involved negotiating a price or contract.

Computed as total annual person-days of face-to-face time spent multiplied by the percent of time spent haggling and assigning blame for problems, divided by the supplier's sales to the buyer, so the measure represents transaction cost per dollar of sales. The percentage of face-to-face communication time involving ex post haggling in the form of assigning blame for problems was estimated by suppliers.

Information sharing was operationalized as the extent to which the supplier shares confidential/proprietary information with automaker buyers and engineers, measured on a seven-point Likert scale. The authors note that this was a single-item measure.

The proxy for buyer transaction cost is the average procurement dollars per person in the purchasing department of the automaker; automakers incur lower transaction costs as they increase the dollars of goods procured per person. It is built from the total number of individuals employed in procurement for production parts (including management, purchasing agents/buyers, lawyers, and support staff) and the total value of goods they procured, both provided by the procurement head of each automaker.
The automaker's average profitability is measured as ROA, or pretax profits divided by assets, over the period 1985-1995.

The number of HTF product introductions by a firm in a given year. For each year, HTF and LTF products were identified by independent latent class cluster analysis on the pixel density of the digital cameras introduced that year, and the consistent Akaike's information criterion was used to check that the two-cluster solution was better than a single-cluster solution (in 1991 and 1992 K-means was used because too few products were introduced). There were 76 HTF products, varying from 1 to 27 per year.

The number of LTF product introductions by a firm in a given year. For each year, HTF and LTF products were identified by independent latent class cluster analysis on the pixel density of the digital cameras introduced that year, with K-means used for 1991 and 1992 because too few products were introduced. There were 353 LTF products, varying from 3 to 89 per year.

variable_name: HTF product introductions of similarly sized firms
description: The number of HTF product introductions in the previous year by firms with the same size code as the focal firm. Size was measured by firm sales lagged one year; for publicly traded firms sales information was obtained from the COMPUSTAT and WORLDSCOPE databases, a quartile split was created, and size was coded as ranging from 1 to 4.

variable_name: HTF product introductions of successful firms
description: The previous year's number of HTF product introductions by highly profitable firms, that is, firms in the top quartile of firms on return on assets (ROA), the authors' indicator of a firm's success.

variable_name: HTF product introductions of firms from the same origin industry
description: The number of new HTF product introductions in the previous year by all firms from the focal firm's origin industry. Origin industry was measured by whether the firm entered the digital camera market from photography, consumer electronics, or computing.

variable_name: HTF product introductions of firms from outside the origin industry
description: The number of new HTF product introductions in the previous year by all firms outside the focal firm's origin industry. Origin industry was measured by whether the firm entered the digital camera market from photography, consumer electronics, or computing.

variable_name: LTF product introductions of firms from the same origin industry
description: The number of new LTF product introductions in the previous year by all firms from the focal firm's origin industry. Origin industry was measured by whether the firm entered the digital camera market from photography, consumer electronics, or computing.

variable_name: LTF product introductions of firms from outside the origin industry
description: The number of new LTF product introductions in the previous year by all firms outside the focal firm's origin industry. Origin industry was measured by whether the firm entered the digital camera market from photography, consumer electronics, or computing.

The amount of money a campaign received as a percentage of the amount requested. The authors used the funding percentage because it provides a fine-grained measure of how much appeal a project had for external resource contributors, while controlling for achievement of the funding goal. Resource contributions ranged from 0% to 358.5% in the data.
time_window: cumulative during each campaign at each point of observation

description: Availability of technical demonstrators (game walk-throughs provided by the developer as videos consisting of actual in-game, non-interactive footage) and game demos (playable pieces of the game) in the project pitch. Coded '0' when the pitch offered neither a technical demonstrator nor a game demo, '1' when it provided a technical demonstrator, and '2' when it provided a game demo, because game demos are interactive and provide a stronger signal of product attributes than technical demonstrators do.
time_window: three times a week during the campaign (Monday, Wednesday, Friday)

description: Rating of the degree to which the project pitch at each point of observation referred to external press coverage in expert outlets, on a seven-point Likert scale. Two independent coders, blind to the hypotheses, read all 2,702 pitch observations, watched embedded images and videos, and assigned ratings; inter-coder agreement was excellent (ICC = 0.76) and their ratings were averaged.
time_window: three times a week during the campaign (Monday, Wednesday, Friday)

description: Coder rating of how strongly pathos-based signals (appeals to emotion) were perceived in a pitch at each observation, coded separately from logos and ethos following the coding manual. Each of two coders independently read the 2,702 pitch observations, watched embedded videos and images, and assigned a rating on a seven-point Likert scale; inter-coder agreement was good (ICC = 0.66) and the coders' ratings were averaged.
time_window: three times a week during the campaign (Monday, Wednesday, Friday)

description: Coder rating of how strongly logos-based signals (rational and neutral information about the product to be developed) were perceived in a pitch at each observation. Each of two coders independently read the 2,702 pitch observations, watched embedded videos and images, and assigned a rating on a seven-point Likert scale; inter-coder agreement was excellent (ICC = 0.76) and the coders' ratings were averaged.
time_window: three times a week during the campaign (Monday, Wednesday, Friday)

description: Coder rating of how strongly ethos-based signals (information on the qualifications of the developer) were perceived in a pitch at each observation. Each of two coders independently read the 2,702 pitch observations, watched embedded videos and images, and assigned a rating on a seven-point Likert scale; inter-coder agreement was excellent (ICC = 0.79) and the coders' ratings were averaged.
time_window: three times a week during the campaign (Monday, Wednesday, Friday)

description: Respondents who confirmed that their businesses were selected are coded as treated if they reported that their companies were incubated (120 respondents) and as control if their businesses were not incubated despite having been selected (30 respondents). The treated and control groups had similar baseline performance in sales revenue, operating costs, employment, and business registration status at the time of selection. The effect of being incubated is estimated by an inverse-probability-weighted average treatment effect, where the weight is the probability of being incubated (treated) estimated with a logistic link function on the residual of the applicant's commuting distance to the incubator.
scale: binary (incubated versus selected but not incubated)
time_window: T0 to T1 (six months after applying)

description: The survey asked applicants about their monthly sales revenues, prompting respondents to report their average, high, low, and typical sales revenue in Rand, both at the time of applying (T0) and six months after applying (T1). The change measure is constructed as a log ratio of performance at T1 relative to T0, written in the paper as Log(1 + xT1/xT0), where the text's labelling of the two periods appears reversed; endnote 4 states the formula is mathematically equivalent to the difference in log-adjusted performance, log(xT1) - log(xT0).
time_window: T0 to T1 (six months after applying)

description: Applicants reported the total headcount of their employees, including both full-time and part-time employees, at the time of applying (T0) and six months after applying (T1). The change measure is computed with the same log-ratio procedure used for sales revenue and operating costs.
time_window: T0 to T1 (six months after applying)

description: Mentors' ability is operationalized as the lagged average score improvement of participants paired with each mentor in prior cohorts. The measure is built from the mentors' track records of working with mentees from previous cohorts, that is, from the score improvements of past mentees, comprising the average difference between the baseline and exit exam scores of these mentees. Mentor assignment (as captured by this measure) serves as the instrument for entrepreneurial learning in the 2SLS IV models.

Each participant's final exam score (on a scale of 0-100), measured their knowledge of the same material after completing the 24-week incubation program, and the measure of learning is the difference between the final score and the baseline score (Score Improvement = Final Score - Baseline Score), with the natural log of the result taken to adjust for skew. The exams test core knowledge and skills required for business scaling.
time_window: during the 24-week incubation program (final relative to baseline)

description: Monthly business revenue in Rand, logged, collected over 12 consecutive months after participants graduated from the incubator. It is the dependent variable in the second-stage IV models of post-incubation performance.

Monthly business profits in Rand, logged, collected over 12 consecutive months after participants graduated from the incubator. It is the dependent variable in the second-stage IV models of post-incubation performance.

Each participant's baseline exam performance on a scale of 0-100, measuring their understanding of basic business operations and management concepts such as bookkeeping, operations, strategic planning, and sales and marketing; the score proxies for a participant's human capital based on prior education and work experience. The models control for baseline exam scores as pre-entry knowledge, and the measure is interacted with mentors' ability when testing whether the benefits of mentoring decrease with pre-entry knowledge.

Participants' age in years at the time of entering the incubator, which the authors use to capture entrepreneurs' prior work experience. The models include age among the controls, and the interaction of mentors' ability with age is interpreted as the moderating role of experience.

variable_name: Social capital from top managers at other firms
description: Respondents assessed the extent to which top management had used personal and social networking relationships (USED) and how such relationships had benefited their company through access to information (INFO), access to valuable resources (RES), and acquisition and exploitation of knowledge (KNOW), from 1998 to 2000, on a seven-point scale. The measure was developed as the average of the products of use and benefits: [(USED x INFO) + (USED x RES) + (USED x KNOW)] / 3. It was measured using three items: relationship with suppliers, buyers, and competitors.

Respondents assessed the extent to which top management had used personal and social networking relationships (USED) and how such relationships had benefited their company through access to information (INFO), access to valuable resources (RES), and acquisition and exploitation of knowledge (KNOW), from 1998 to 2000, on a seven-point scale. The measure was developed as the average of the products of use and benefits: [(USED x INFO) + (USED x RES) + (USED x KNOW)] / 3, computed over six items.

Respondents assessed the extent to which top management had used personal and social networking relationships (USED) and how such relationships had benefited their company through access to information (INFO), access to valuable resources (RES), and acquisition and exploitation of knowledge (KNOW), from 1998 to 2000, on a seven-point scale. The measure was developed as the average of the products of use and benefits: [(USED x INFO) + (USED x RES) + (USED x KNOW)] / 3, computed over two items.

Respondents rated their firms on five measures of performance - growth of sales and revenue, growth of net income or profits, growth in productivity, return on assets, and return on sales - relative to the major competitors in their industry in the years 2001 and 2002. Items were measured on a scale ranging from 1 'much worse' to 7 'much better'. The five measures were highly correlated, with bivariate correlation coefficients all greater than 0.60, and their ratings were averaged to obtain a composite but global measure of firm performance.

Respondents assessed the extent to which their organizations had placed emphasis on 16 competitive methods from 1998 to 2000 on a seven-point scale. A factor analysis of the competitive methods produced two factors, low cost and differentiation, and the low-cost strategy was operationalized with six items.

Respondents assessed the extent to which their organizations had placed emphasis on 16 competitive methods from 1998 to 2000 on a seven-point scale. A factor analysis of the competitive methods produced two factors, low cost and differentiation, and the differentiation strategy was measured with seven items.

A categorical variable created from the composite values of the low-cost strategy and the differentiation strategy: firms whose composite values for both the low-cost strategy and differentiation strategy were greater than the mean of each respective strategy were considered to be pursuing an integrated strategy and were coded 1, while all others were coded 0.

For each firm unit-university-year observation, the number of scientific articles published in that year that listed at least one co-author affiliated with that firm and at least one co-author affiliated with that university. To account for skewness, models enter the natural logarithm of these linkages added by one unit.
scale: count, entered as natural logarithm plus one

description: For each firm unit-university-year observation, the authors identified all successful patent applications of that firm in the previous year listing at least one co-inventor in the same location as the focal university and then counted the number of distinct locations of the co-inventors that these patents listed. Location of residence of co-inventors was mapped at the state level for addresses in the U.S. and at the country level for non-U.S. addresses. Higher scores correspond to higher levels of collaboration between the focal R&D unit and other units of the focal firm.

For each firm unit-university-year observation, the number of scientific articles published in that year that listed at least one co-author affiliated with any of the nonfocal sample firms and at least one co-author affiliated with that university. The procedure followed is analogous to the one used for the dependent variable.

Using the mine-community dyad as the unit of analysis, the dependent variable is a dyad-level dummy, coded one if a mine-community dyad has signed a CBA and zero otherwise. Dyads were formed by mapping each mine's coordinates onto the coordinates of all indigenous communities in Canada within 500 km.

A dummy variable coded one for communities with use rights over the land where the mine is located and zero otherwise. Using the coordinates for each mine and drawing a 1-km radius around each coordinate, the authors identified whether the land was on historic treaty lands with use rights; they relied on archival sources, including the original texts of historic treaties, to determine which of 70 historic treaties included rights to hunt and fish on the lands covered by the treaty.

Coded one when the mine and community are located in the same watershed subdrainage area, and zero otherwise. Each community's land boundaries and each mine's geographic coordinates were mapped on the Watersheds in Canada map, which is based on Water Survey of Canada data and includes main drainage and subdrainage areas.

Coded one when the community is within a 50-km drive on the National Road Network from the mine's point on the NRN, and zero otherwise. Community and mine geographic coordinates were mapped on the Canadian National Road Network map, 10-km buffers were drawn around mine coordinates because the NRN does not always contain industrial roads, and the point on the NRN geodesically closest to the mine was identified.

A count of the number of times that a community mobilized through institutional channels - the judicial system or the regulatory process - in the preceding 10 years. It was built from Factiva searches for reports in which the community name appears within 10 words of terms associated with institutional mobilization (petition, grievance, investigation, injunction, lawsuit, legal action, and court); each article was read and coded for the date, the type of mobilization, and its target.

A count of the number of times that a community mobilized via extrainstitutional tactics, such as protests or blockades, in the preceding 10 years. The measure is restricted to communities located within 100 km of the mine, as those communities are likely to use extrainstitutional mobilization to deny a firm physical access to the mine site. It was built from Factiva searches using terms such as strike, rally, demonstration, protest, and blockade.

Each of the three companies was classified as a prospector, an analyzer or a defender on the basis of Miles' (1982) study of the adaptive modes of the companies to the crises they faced between 1950 and 1975. Philip Morris was labeled a prospector, R. J. Reynolds an analyzer and American Brands a defender. Miles confirmed that the orientation of each firm remained the same throughout the 25-year period, so the labels are treated as valid for the full period.

variable_name: proportion of outsiders in the upper echelon
description: An executive was categorized as an outsider to the company if his tenure there was shorter than five years, even if he had worked for another firm in the same industry or in another industry, and as an insider after his fifth year in office in the company. For each company a yearly roster of upper echelon executives (rank of vice-president and above) was compiled and the proportion of outsiders was computed. In the pair-wise analyses the proportion of outsiders in the upper echelon was treated as the dependent variable, strategic orientation as a two-level factor and firm size as the covariate.

variable_name: proportion of executives in each functional track
description: The functional responsibility of each upper echelon executive, as indicated by the title of his vice-presidential office, defined his functional orientation; where an executive worked in more than one functional track, the track in which he spent the most years was used. The variable is the proportion of a firm's upper echelon executives falling in each functional area (marketing, research and development, production, finance), reported as percentages for the firms. A series of pair-wise t-tests compared the proportions of executives in each functional track between pairs of firms.

variable_name: proportion of production and finance executives in the upper echelon
description: Each upper echelon executive was assigned a functional orientation from the title of his vice-presidential office, or the track with the most years if he worked in several. The variable is the percentage of a firm's upper echelon executives in the production and in the finance tracks, reported for each firm and compared across firms with t-tests.

variable_name: proportion of marketing and R&D executives in the upper echelon
description: Each upper echelon executive (vice-president and above) was assigned a functional orientation from the title of his vice-presidential office, or the track with the most years if he worked in several. The variable is the percentage of a firm's upper echelon executives in the marketing and in the research and development tracks, reported for each firm and compared across firms with t-tests.

Organizations at the strategic extremes within each industry were identified by combining published quantified data on product market additions, expert panel assessments, and assessment by the chief executives. Interviews with chief executives were then used to confirm that the organizations were pursuing strategies in line with the external measures. Only organizations judged to be relatively 'pure' Prospectors or Defenders were retained for the study; the three organizations judged to be Analysers were not considered.

Respondents were asked how frequently they learned of events or trends in twenty subsectors of the environment, five subsectors for each of the four broad environmental sectors. For each respondent an average score of between 1 and 7 was calculated for each of the four environmental sectors and for the overall environment. Items that did not contribute significantly to their scales were dropped after internal reliability analysis; revised scales consisted of four or five items with Cronbach alphas of 0.64 to 0.88.

Executives rated the extent to which they made a point of staying abreast of the same twenty subsectors used in the frequency method, using an ordinal scale running from 1 ('I generally do not try to stay abreast of this type of information') to 5 ('I try to know all there is to know about this type of information'). An average interest score of between 1 and 5 was calculated for each respondent for the four sectors and for the overall environment.

Executives were asked what percent of their scanning time was directed at each of the environmental sectors and, in turn, how many total hours they spent scanning in an average week. The authors express the results in terms of hours to allow comparison with earlier findings, and note that the percentage figures may be more reliable than the hours figures. Results did not differ appreciably between the percentage and hours figures.
scale: percentage of scanning time and hours per week

description: Average of the frequency scores for the five subsectors classified as belonging to the entrepreneurial sector, calculated for each respondent on the same 1 to 7 scale as the overall frequency score.

Average of the interest ratings for the five subsectors classified as belonging to the entrepreneurial sector, calculated for each respondent on the same 1 to 5 ordinal scale as the overall interest score.
The share of an executive's scanning time allocated to the entrepreneurial sector, converted into hours per average week.
scale: percentage of scanning time and hours per week

description: Average of the frequency scores for the five subsectors classified as belonging to the engineering sector, calculated for each respondent on the same 1 to 7 scale as the overall frequency score.

Average of the interest ratings for the five subsectors classified as belonging to the engineering sector, calculated for each respondent on the same 1 to 5 ordinal scale as the overall interest score.
The share of an executive's scanning time allocated to the engineering sector, converted into hours per average week.
scale: percentage of scanning time and hours per week

description: Average of the frequency scores for the five subsectors classified as belonging to the administrative sector, calculated for each respondent on the same 1 to 7 scale as the overall frequency score.

Average of the interest ratings for the five subsectors classified as belonging to the administrative sector, calculated for each respondent on the same 1 to 5 ordinal scale as the overall interest score.
The share of an executive's scanning time allocated to the administrative sector, converted into hours per average week.
scale: percentage of scanning time and hours per week

description: Average of the frequency scores for the five subsectors classified as belonging to the regulatory sector, calculated for each respondent on the same 1 to 7 scale as the overall frequency score.

Average of the interest ratings for the five subsectors classified as belonging to the regulatory sector, calculated for each respondent on the same 1 to 5 ordinal scale as the overall interest score.
The share of an executive's scanning time allocated to the regulatory sector, converted into hours per average week.
scale: percentage of scanning time and hours per week

description: Respondents reported the percent of the trucks in their fleets with on-board computers, satellite tracking, and truck diagnostic or performance monitoring systems. Since companies are unlikely to have all three types of computer monitoring systems and since some technologies encompass others, the variable was operationalized as the maximum use of any of the monitoring systems. Higher scores on this index indicate greater monitoring.

Respondents reported the percent of trucks with on-board systems to communicate with dispatchers, and cellular telephones. The maximum use of either of these practices constituted the measure. Unlike computer monitoring, these systems allow two-way communication between drivers and dispatchers.

Span of control was measured as the reverse of the number of drivers reporting to each dispatcher, and was logged for analysis. Higher values indicate a lower span of control, i.e., higher levels of monitoring. The variable was reverse coded to ensure consistency with predictions.

In a relay system, a driver delivers the truck and the shipment to a designated point where another driver continues the trip in the same cab, necessitating that drivers adhere to strict schedules and patterns. The use of relays was measured as the percent of drivers typically driving in relays. Higher scores on this variable reflect higher levels of agent monitoring.

This variable was measured as the frequency with which schedule changes for drivers occurred at the last minute, with responses ranging from (1) Never to (5) Almost Always, and was reverse coded for analysis. Higher scores reflect greater schedule stability and thus higher levels of monitoring.

This variable was operationalized as the percent of drivers who had worked for the company for more than 24 months. The 24-month cutoff was used since industry experts indicated that drivers usually quit within the first two years of employment.

Outcome-based pay was measured as the mean of four items assessing the extent to which differences in pay rates across drivers were based on driver performance, i.e., on driver performance, driver accident rates, traffic violations, and driver fuel mileage. Each item had five response options ranging from (1) Not at All to (5) To a Very Great Extent.
scale: (1) Not at All to (5) To a Very Great Extent

description: Pay for number of miles driven is common in the trucking industry and was used as an intuitively obvious indicator of performance-based pay. The variable was strongly skewed and was transformed using the arcsine transformation (specifically A = 2*arcsine*sqrt(p)) for proportions. Thus, the variable was operationalized as the arcsine of the percent of drivers paid by the mile.
scale: arcsine of the percent of drivers paid by the mile

description: Close supervision was the mean of three items with seven response options, with high scores reflecting higher levels of monitoring. A sample item is 'Managers and supervisors work closely with their subordinates.'

Narrow supervisory span was operationalized as the reverse of the number of employees reporting to each first-line supervisor. Higher values indicate a lower span of control. The variable was logged for analysis.

Programmability was operationalized as routine work and assessed the extent to which the work of operating employees was routine as the mean of six items with seven response options. A sample item is 'In general, our employees have very routine jobs.'
Agent tenure was measured as the average length of service (in years) of direct production/service employees at the facility.

Outcome-based pay for production or operating employees was measured as the mean of three items with seven response options. The items assessed the extent to which differences in pay across employees doing the same job were based on quantity of performance, quality of performance, and safety records.

Set to 1 if the focal firm had a Medicaid business in the focal state in the previous year, and 0 otherwise. Medicaid is the segment that shares significant resources with the ACA market, while employer-based group plans and non-Medicaid government plans are the less related segments.

Dummy variable that turns to 1 if the focal firm offered an ACA plan for the first time, and 0 otherwise. The authors first identified all non-Individual insurers in a given state and year and then manually searched on the internet to identify those that offered ACA plans in the given state and year. For every firm-state pair, observations were kept from 2013 until the year the focal firm entered the state's ACA market or until the end of the sample period.

Firms were categorized into low and high capability using unit cost, that is, total claims and medical expenses paid out by the firm to the insured divided by total enrollment across all insurance segments in a given state before ACA entry. The firm's average unit cost was compared with the median unit cost of benchmark firms in the same state and over the same time period. If the focal firm's average pre-ACA unit cost was higher than that of the benchmark, the firm was categorized as a Low Capability firm; otherwise it was categorized as a High Capability firm. For the entry sample, all firms in the focal state served as benchmarks.

The same unit-cost categorization of capability was applied in the exit sample: total claims and medical expenses paid out by the firm to the insured divided by total enrollment across all insurance segments in a given state before ACA entry, compared with the median unit cost of benchmark firms in the same state and over the same time period. A firm above the benchmark median was categorized as a Low Capability firm, otherwise as a High Capability firm. For the exit sample, all firms that entered the ACA market in the focal state served as benchmarks.

Measured based on a cost ratio (total medical reimbursement paid to the insured divided by premium revenue), which is similar to the industry standard measure of cost, Medical Loss Ratio. Cost Shock was calculated by taking the difference between the diversifying entrant's lagged cost ratio (after entering the ACA market) and the average cost ratio across all health insurance firms in the target state in the year before the focal firm entered the ACA market.
time_window: lagged (after entry, benchmarked to the year before the focal firm's entry)

description: Dummy variable that turns to 1 if the focal firm stopped offering ACA plans, and 0 otherwise. For every firm-state pair, observations were included from the year when the firm entered the state's ACA market until the year the firm exited or until the end of the sample period, whichever was earlier.

Set to 1 if the focal firm had a Medicaid business in the focal state in the previous year, and 0 otherwise. Medicaid is the segment that shares significant resources with the ACA market, whereas employer-based group plans and non-Medicaid government plans are less related to ACA.

Seven items assessing the extent to which the outsourcing firm understood specific aspects of the outsourced project. The unit of analysis was the outsourced project, and the scale was answered on a seven-point response format with anchors running from not at all to a great extent. The measure exhibited convergent validity, with scale alphas of 0.71 and higher across the construct measures.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (Not at all – To a great extent)

description: Four items adapted from Kirsch et al.'s (2002) scale that assessed the extent to which the outsourcing firm, in assessing the outsourcee firm, placed significant weight on various output-related criteria. The items were answered on the study's seven-point Likert-type scales. The construct measure exhibited discriminant validity (verified through factor analysis) as well as convergent validity.

Three items adapted from Kirsch et al.'s (2002) scale that assessed the extent to which the outsourcing firm expected the outsourcee firm to follow an understandable written sequence of steps specified by the outsourcing firm during the development process. The items were answered on the study's seven-point Likert-type scales.

A nine-item performance scale developed by Faraj and Sproull (2000) in the software project context, on which the outsourcing firm assessed the outsourcee firm's performance on the outsourced project relative to other IT projects. Assessments from a second respondent in 42 firms were cross-validated with an interclass coefficient of 0.783.

CEO personality was measured via the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory, with 12 items for each of the five factors. All items were scored on a scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'). In the structural model, one manifest variable based on the participants' average of the mean-centered scale scores was assigned to each of the five personality factors, with error variances fixed using the alpha coefficients.
time_window: first survey wave, preceding the strategic flexibility survey

description: Conscientiousness was measured with 12 items of the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory; an example item is 'I am pretty good about pacing myself so as to get things done on time.' All items were scored on a scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'). Coefficient alpha reliability was .81.
time_window: first survey wave, preceding the strategic flexibility survey

description: Emotional stability was measured with 12 items of the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory; an example item is 'I often feel inferior to others.' All items were scored on a scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'), and the ratings on emotional stability were reverse-coded to improve the interpretation of results. Coefficient alpha reliability was .79.
time_window: first survey wave, preceding the strategic flexibility survey

description: Agreeableness was measured with 12 items of the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory; an example item is 'I am interested in people.' All items were scored on a scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'). Coefficient alpha reliability was .74. In the nonlinear structural model a squared agreeableness term was computed from the mean-centered agreeableness variable and included alongside the linear term.
time_window: first survey wave, preceding the strategic flexibility survey

description: Extraversion was measured with 12 items of the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory; an example item is 'I like to have a lot of people around me.' All items were scored on a scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'). Coefficient alpha reliability was .70.
time_window: first survey wave, preceding the strategic flexibility survey

description: Openness to experience was measured with 12 items of the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory; an example item is 'I spend time reflecting on things.' All items were scored on a scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'). Coefficient alpha reliability was .72.
time_window: first survey wave, preceding the strategic flexibility survey

description: Strategic flexibility was measured by adapting Grewal and Tansuhaj's (2001) five-item scale assessing a firm's ability to respond to environmental variations. The five items were retained after a pilot test with 30 middle-level Indian business process outsourcing managers who were not in the final sample. All items were scored on a scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'); coefficient alpha reliability for the scale was .84. The surveys were filled out by at least two top managers reporting directly to their firm's CEO.
time_window: one month after receipt of the completed CEO surveys

description: Three established accounting-based measures of firm performance were taken from the financial records provided by the sampled firms: return on assets (ROA), return on sales (ROS), and return on investment (ROI). Because the sampled firms were proprietary or partnership firms, market-based measures such as the ratio of book value to market value or stock price could not be included. Performance was lagged by one year after the survey date. In the structural model the three measures were represented by one manifest variable based on the average of the mean-centered scale scores.
time_window: one year after the survey date

variable_name: Degree of internationalization into a country
description: The number of foreign subsidiaries created (inflows) by the MNE in country c over the period 1996-2001 multiplied by their relative importance over the period 1996-2001. Relative importance for a country is the ratio of the total number of employees in new foreign subsidiaries created in that country (1996-2001) to the total number of employees in all of the firm's foreign subsidiaries (1996-2001). The MNE receives a score on this variable for each one of the 45 countries in the sample, and a high score indicates a strong level of internationalization into that specific country. The measure combines the breadth of internationalization into a country (number of foreign subsidiaries) and its depth (relative number of employees).

The number of the MNE's prior foreign subsidiaries established in a region (1990-1995) multiplied by their relative importance (1990-1995). The same computation as for the dependent variable is applied at the region level and over the period 1990-1995.

The weighted average regulatory control institutional score of all countries in a region, weighting the institutional scores of countries by their GDP (the ratio of a country's GDP to the sum of the GDPs of countries in the same region). The underlying factor measures the degree of government involvement in business through a country's regulatory burden, trade policy, foreign investment restrictions, contract and property rights, government intervention in banking, informal markets, and monetary policy, all loading positively (factor loadings > 0.50). A high score suggests that the country operates with broader and more restrictive regulatory oversight and involvement.

The country's original regulatory control institutional score minus its respective region-level (GDP-weighted average) institutional score. It captures a country's score on regulatory control relative to the countries in the same region, not relative to all other countries.

The weighted average political democracy institutional score of all countries in a region, weighting country institutional scores by their GDP share within the region.
