The underlying factor refers to the level of discretion and power a government maintains over its citizenry, measured through civil liberties, political rights, executive political restrictions, and political constraints; civil liberties and political rights are reverse coded in the data (higher scores indicate fewer rights) and loaded negatively (-0.76 and -0.87), while executive political restrictions and political constraints loaded positively (0.96 and 0.68). A high score suggests that the government is democratic, granting more rights and liberties to its citizens.

The country's original political democracy institutional score minus its respective region-level (GDP-weighted average) institutional score, capturing a country's score relative to the countries in the same region rather than to all other countries.

The weighted average capital availability institutional score of all countries in a region, weighting country scores by their GDP share within the region. Capital Availability captures the availability of capital for domestic entities, with items indicating increased capital in an economy - capital investments, money supply, net reserves, nominal GDP, and total foreign debt - loading positively (loadings > 0.70) and budget balance loading negatively (-0.73), since balancing a country's budget reduces the government's ability to reinvest capital. A higher score implies a greater availability of capital for commerce in the country.

The weighted average market liquidity institutional score of all countries in a region, weighting country scores by their GDP share within the region. Market Liquidity indicates the lack of market liquidity and capital investments: liabilities loaded positively (0.78) because higher debt lowers liquidity in domestic firms, exchange rate loaded positively (0.64) because depreciation reduces cash flow and liquidity, and liquidity loaded negatively (-0.72). Higher scores indicate lower capital investments because of the lack of assets available in the market for reinvestment.

The country's original capital availability institutional score minus its respective region-level (GDP-weighted average) institutional score, capturing its position relative to the countries in the same region.

The country's original market liquidity institutional score minus its respective region-level (GDP-weighted average) institutional score, capturing its position relative to the countries in the same region. Higher scores indicate lower capital investments.

variable_name: completed the entry-level general skills training
description: Dummy variable with a value of one if an entry-level contract worker completed the entry-level general skills training and zero otherwise. The training was non-mandatory and consisted of three one-on-one, in-person mentoring sessions with managers and two online training sessions, totaling 6 h, and focused on developing knowledge about tracking performance indicators and general interpersonal communication skills. In the difference-in-differences test of the baseline hypothesis it is interacted with a dummy for periods after the treated worker of a matched pair concluded the training; in the retention models it is the main explanatory variable.

variable_name: standardized sales and standardized individual gains
description: Two performance measures available at the level of the contract worker per sales campaign. Standardized sales is the total value of sales orders across all direct representatives managed by the worker. Standardized individual gains is the contract worker's compensation, the sum of commissions and bonuses for achieving specific short-term targets that SalesNow defines (e.g., recruitment of new sales representatives or the spot sale of specific products). Both variables are standardized so that their means equal zero and their standard deviations equal one within each sales campaign.

variable_name: retention in sales campaigns after training (3, 6, 12, and 18 months)
description: Four dummy variables used to test the retention hypothesis; each represents retention in sales campaigns occurring 3, 6, 12, and 18 months after training. Specifically, each dummy receives a value of one if the contract worker continues in the work arrangement after concluding the general skills training, and zero otherwise. By design of SalesNow's program and dataset, any contract worker who reported no sales in a particular sales campaign had their arrangement with SalesNow terminated, and the data do not allow a discrimination of voluntary and involuntary turnover.

Dummy variable indicating that the sales zone received the version of the communication package that framed the expected benefits of the new training as the strengthening of the partnership between the firm and the contract worker. Each of the three versions of the package contained the same four communications (two targeting contract workers and two targeting their managers) and differed only in the framing of the expected benefit of undertaking the training. All specifications use the internal productivity framing as the comparison group.

Dummy variable equal to one if the manager downloaded and sent the online phone banner promoting the training to contract workers, and zero otherwise. It measures whether the firm's managers decided to promote the training. Measurements were collected at the end of the experiment.
time_window: by the 8th week after the communication policy started

variable_name: contract worker started the training and contract worker concluded the training
description: Two dummy variables that are equal to one for the respective events and zero otherwise. They measure engagement with the general skills training from the workers' perspective: whether the contract worker started the training and whether the contract worker concluded the training. Measurements were collected at the end of the experiment.
time_window: by the 8th week after the communication policy started

description: Respondents were asked to indicate the maximum price they would be willing to pay to buy a call option on an investment that has a 50% chance to be worth $x1 and a 50% chance to be worth $x2. Three items used (x1, x2) values of (1000, 500), (1000, 0), and (1000, -1000). Reported prices were compared with each option's risk-neutral expected pay-off using one-tailed t-tests.

Respondents who owned the investment indicated the minimum price they would be willing to receive to sell a call option on it to someone else. The items were identical to the call buying items except that the respondent occupied the seller position, using the same outcomes (1000, 500), (1000, 0), and (1000, -1000). Selling prices were also compared with buying prices for the corresponding options.

Respondents who owned an investment that has a 50% chance to lose $x1 and a 50% chance to lose $x2 indicated what they would be willing to pay for the option to transfer the outcome of the investment to someone else. The three items used the outcomes (1000, 500), (1000, 0), and (1000, -1000); for the item corresponding to x2 = -1000 the wording was changed from 'lose' to 'gain'.

Respondents were asked what they would have to receive to sell to someone the option to transfer to them the outcome associated with an investment that has a 50% chance to lose $x1 and a 50% chance to lose $x2. The three items used the outcomes (1000, 500), (1000, 0), and (1000, -1000).

variable_name: Option values with positive exercise prices (call items)
description: The 12 items in Part III differed from those in Part I only in that they involved positive exercise prices. The call items were valued with a $750 exercise price (items 1 and 4) and with a $500 exercise price (items 2, 3, 5, and 6). The within-respondent differences in option values without and with the exercise price were compared with the probability-weighted exercise price using one-tailed t-tests.

variable_name: Option values with positive exercise prices (put items)
description: The 12 items in Part III differed from those in Part I only in that they involved positive exercise prices. The put items were valued with a $750 exercise price (items 7 and 10) and with a $500 exercise price (items 8, 9, 11, and 12). The within-respondent differences in option values without and with the exercise price were compared with the probability-weighted exercise price using one-tailed t-tests.

Computed from the Part II items in combination with four items from Part I, giving implicit discount rates for the periods ending at 6, 12, and 48 months. For the first two 6-month periods the rate was computed as the ratio of the value of an option with an outcome realized in period t to the value of one realized in period t+1, minus one; the rate from month 12 to month 48 assumed compounding every 6 months. Within-respondent mean values for each period were used as the basis for comparing across individuals, and computations involving division by zero were treated as missing data.

Part III of the questionnaire differed from Part I only in that the options involved positive exercise prices. Options were valued with a $750 exercise price (items 1, 4, 7, and 10) and with a lower $500 exercise price for the remaining items.

Part II items were comparable to the Part I items using (x1, x2) = (1000, 0), but involved waiting until a specific future time to resolve the value of the investment before the option could be exercised. The 12 items considered 6-month, 1-year, and 4-year time horizons, so that all of the discounting problems involved European options.

The put seller position was a within-subject condition created by the wording of three questionnaire items (items 10-12) that placed the respondent as the party who would receive a price for taking on the outcome of someone else's investment.

The call seller position was a within-subject condition created by the wording of three questionnaire items (items 4-6) that placed the respondent as owner of the investment selling a call option on it, with the same outcomes as the buying items.

The call buyer position was a within-subject condition created by the wording of three questionnaire items (items 1-3) that placed the respondent as a prospective purchaser of a call option with no preexisting exposure, with outcomes (1000, 500), (1000, 0) and (1000, -1000).

The put buyer position was a within-subject condition created by the wording of three questionnaire items (items 7-9) that placed the respondent as owner of a risky investment paying to transfer its outcome to someone else.

Extraversion scores were computed by applying the support vector machine algorithm of Mairesse et al. (2007) to text spoken by the CEO in the Q&A segment of quarterly earnings conference calls. The Q&A segment was used because text in the presentation segment is likely to be scripted by others, and text spoken during difficult and unanticipated questioning reveals variation in extraversion more readily. All texts spoken by the CEO between 2002 and 2012 were aggregated, and only CEOs with at least 500 spoken words were included; the average word count was 23,088 words. The authors validated the scores against analyst and psychologist ratings and against binary classification tasks performed by raters.

A binary variable that equals 1 if the firm completed at least one deal in a particular year and 0 otherwise. Deals were counted only if they were worth at least 5 percent of the acquirer's value, to ensure the deals required CEOs' attention. M&A data were aggregated by calendar year and merged with CEO-firm data, excluding firm-years in which there was a change of CEO.
time_window: M&A deals completed 2002-2013, aggregated by calendar year

description: The total number of M&As made by each firm in a given year. The count was built from the same completed M&A data aggregated by calendar year and matched to CEO-firm observations.
time_window: M&A deals completed 2002-2013, aggregated by calendar year

description: The transaction values of all completed M&As made by firm i in year t were summed and then standardized by dividing by firm i's total assets in year t. The measure was also divided by the number of M&As in the year to estimate the average transaction value of the deals, giving a continuous measure of M&A size.
time_window: M&A deals completed 2002-2013, aggregated by calendar year

description: Information on CEOs' outside board memberships was collected from BoardEx. In each fiscal year, the authors counted the number of boards on which a CEO served, excluding the focal firm's board. This count was used to run the mediation analysis.

Industry competitiveness was determined by calculating the reversed Herfindahl-Hirschman index, which is based on the market share of all firms in each industry defined by four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes. Market share was calculated based on sales data from Compustat. The measure was reversed so that a higher number reflects higher industry competitiveness. The formula itself was not readable in the text supplied.

The E-index developed by Bebchuk, Cohen, and Ferrell (2009), which measures the number of antitakeover provisions in a firm's charter and in the legal code of the state in which the firm is incorporated. It is based on six provisions: staggered board, limits to shareholder amendments of the bylaws, supermajority requirements for charter amendments, supermajority requirements for mergers, golden parachutes, and poison pills. The number of provisions a company had in a given year was counted and each firm was assigned a score from zero to six; a higher score signals weaker corporate governance and stronger managerial entrenchment.

The daily stock price of each acquirer around the deal announcement period and the corresponding stock market index were collected. Standard market-adjusted models were used to calculate daily abnormal stock returns for each acquirer around the M&A announcement date, and daily abnormal returns were added to measure the cumulative abnormal return over the five-day period (-2, +2 days) around the announcement. The CAR of each deal was regressed on the CEO extraversion score and control variables.
time_window: five-day window (-2, +2 days) around the M&A announcement

description: Price varies by system, service tier, and year, and is logged following other research on pricing. Price data come from Warren Communications' Cable TV Factbook. Evidence of limit pricing is inferred when the log of price is a nonmonotonic U-shaped function of the log of distance to the closest potential entrant, i.e., a negative coefficient on log distance and a positive coefficient on its square.
Dummy variable indicating whether the incumbent system is owned by one of the firms that is a member of CableLabs. It is constructed using data on membership for 2003 and 2006-2009.

Log of the distance in miles from the city of the incumbent system to the city in which the closest potential telecom entrant is located; a squared term is included to capture nonmonotonicity. Distances between zip codes were calculated with zip code distance software. Telecom entrants are subsidiaries of large telecom firms and come from outside the cable industry.

Log of the distance in miles from the city of the incumbent system to the city in which the closest potential cable entrant is located; a squared term is included to capture nonmonotonicity. Distances between zip codes were calculated with zip code distance software. Cable entrants come from within the cable industry, and many were started by veterans of the cable TV industry using technology similar to incumbent cable TV systems.

Log of the distance in miles from the city in which the incumbent system is located to the city in which the closest potential cable or telecom entrant is located, with a squared term included to capture nonmonotonicity. Logs of these distances are used in all regressions to correct for skewness in the data.

Natural log of the total number of active learning-oriented IGOs worldwide that a country is a member of in a given year. IGO memberships were drawn from the COW-2 International Governmental Organizations Dataset, and each IGO's principal objectives/aims were collected from the Yearbook of International Organizations and reviewed; IGOs were classified as learning-oriented if they had a specific mandate for knowledge sharing and transfer, facilitating economic transactions, or enhancing information access among members. Two independent coders classified each IGO under one of the categories, with an interrater reliability of about 0.75, and then discussed differences to reach consensus. The variable was measured in year t-1.

Count of the number of patents with the first-inventor location in the country in a given year, t, based on successful patent applications under the USPTO. Patents were assigned to country-year combinations using the first inventor's location and the application year. The analysis was restricted to patents filed under the U.S. patent system because patents from different patent offices are not comparable with each other, which gives a standardized measure of novel innovations at or near the global technology frontier.

Time-varying country-level measure constructed as a combination of a country's export advantages and the product spaces complementary to those in which the country has an export advantage, based on the methodology and intuition developed by Hausmann and Klinger (2006). Export advantages are revealed comparative advantages computed for each product-country-year from bilateral exports data across 786 four-digit Standard International Trade Classification (SITC Rev.2) categories; a product is revealed as an advantage if its share of the country's exports is equal to or larger than its average share of world exports. Complementarity between product pairs is determined by the conditional probability that countries have revealed comparative advantages in both products of the pair. The measure captures the complementary weighted value of all new product spaces a country could potentially expand into, conditional on its current export advantages; the specification is presented as a formula block in the paper.

The Regulations subindex of the Economic Freedom of the World data developed by the Fraser Institute, which explicitly measures labor-market regulations, credit-market regulations, and business regulations on their effectiveness in promoting economic freedom. Economic freedom is considered present when individuals have the freedom to enter and compete in markets, market forces coordinate voluntary transactions, and strong market-supporting institutions like property rights protection and legal enforcement exist. A higher value on this measure indicates greater reliance on market mechanisms for coordination. The components mirror the financial and labor-market regulations used by Hall and Soskice (2001) in classifying countries into liberal and coordinated market economies.

variable_name: Change in allowed rate of return (ΔROR)
description: The change in the allowed rate of return on equity that had occurred since a utility's previous rate review. The allowed rate of return is the financial rate of return on equity that a state public utility commission determines in its final rate review ruling and that determines allowed rate levels; utilities prefer higher rates of return. The authors used the change rather than the absolute level so as to control for constant firm-level factors that might influence the absolute rate. Rate review data were obtained from Regulatory Research Associates, and a sample of rate review results was cross-checked against NARUC annual volumes.
time_window: since the utility's previous rate review

description: A dichotomous variable for the implementation of a utility's nonmarket strategy, equal to 1 if the expected change in utility profits from an implemented rate review (Δπ) is greater than 0 and 0 otherwise. Δπ is a latent variable, since a utility's decision rule is to initiate rate reviews only when Δπ is greater than 0. The variable is modeled in the selection equation of the Heckman model.
scale: dummy (1 = utility initiated a rate review)

description: A measure of the degree to which residential utility consumers in a state were organized, equal to 1 if a consumer advocacy office existed in a given state in a particular year and 0 otherwise. Thirty states have created consumer advocacy offices charged with representing residential utility consumer interests before state regulatory agencies and courts. Consumer advocates have public funding and statutory power to participate in rate review procedures and can provide strong opposition to utility requests for rate increases.

A time-varying variable equal to the industrial percentage share of electricity consumption in a given state, capturing potential demand-side competition from industrial consumers, who have higher average consumption and thus stronger incentives to organize. Data on electricity consumption by consumer sector were obtained from the Energy Information Administration.

A measure of the extent to which a state population participated in environmental and other activist nongovernmental organizations. It was calculated as the total number of Sierra Club members divided by a state's population (in thousands). Annual information on state membership was provided directly to the authors by the Sierra Club.

A dummy variable for the executive branch, coded 1 if the margin of electoral victory between the winning and second-place candidates in the most recent state gubernatorial election was less than 5 percent and 0 otherwise. The authors used a dummy rather than a continuous variable because the underlying distributions of governor vote margins were not normal but highly skewed. Information was collected from annual volumes of The Book of the States.

A dummy variable for the legislative branch, coded 1 if the margin of control by the majority party (measured by the number of seats in the combined upper and lower chambers) was less than 5 percent and 0 otherwise. A dummy rather than a continuous variable was used because the underlying distributions of legislature party majorities were not normal but highly skewed. Information was collected from annual volumes of The Book of the States.

The public utility commission's budget per capita in a state, used as a measure of the agency's financial resources, on the argument that agencies with larger budgets and greater expertise are better positioned to obtain their own information. Annual information on PUC budgets and commissioner identities was obtained from NARUC annual reports, annual volumes of The Book of the States, and the web sites of individual PUCs.

A measure constructed because experience may partially substitute for financial resources, equal to the sum of each commissioner's tenure in years divided by the total number of commissioners on a focal PUC. The authors expected that more experienced commissioners would have better information and insights regarding utility rate review requests. Commissioner identities were obtained from NARUC annual reports, The Book of the States, and PUC web sites.

A measure allowing PUC resources to vary relative to individual utilities as well as in an absolute sense, equal to the dollar value of utility electricity revenues within a state divided by the PUC budget in each year. The logic is that a PUC with a small budget is less dependent on the utility if the utility itself has minimal resources. Information on utility revenues was gathered from federal utility filings available through the Energy Information Administration.

A measure used in the selection equation, equal to the total number of rate reviews a utility has experienced at a given time. The authors differentiated between the initiation of a rate review and performance in the review since they anticipated that total experience in a variety of regulatory settings would affect a utility's decision to initiate.

A dummy variable used in the regression equation, set equal to 1 if a utility had experienced a rate review in the previous three years and 0 otherwise. The authors argued that a utility's performance in the rate review would be more closely related to its recent experience, since the characteristics of the regulatory environment change over time.
scale: dummy (1 = rate review in previous three years)

description: A dummy variable set equal to 1 if other utilities in the state initiated rate reviews with their PUC in the previous year and 0 otherwise. The variable captured potential utility learning from observing other utilities' experience with the commission.
scale: dummy (1 = other utilities initiated reviews in the previous year)

description: Operationalized using three indicators: number of business units divested, percentage divested, and divestiture period. The number of units divested includes those sold through sell-offs, leveraged or management buyouts, equity carve-outs, or spin-offs during restructuring. Percentage divested measures the net sales or sale price of a unit divided by the parent firm's total sales or assets for the previous year, summed over the refocusing years. Divestiture period is the number of months between the announcement of refocusing (or the first divestiture) and the announcement of the completion of refocusing. The analysis used the standardized average of these three measures added together.
time_window: years a firm spent in refocusing

description: Total compensation (TDC1) from Execucomp, which includes the executive's salary, bonus, restricted stock grants, long-term incentive payouts, option grants (using the Black-Scholes value), and other income. Total compensation was averaged over two years post-refocusing, with pre-refocusing total compensation as a control. The natural log of the total compensation value was used to reduce skewness.
Return on assets, calculated as net income divided by total assets and averaged for the two years pre-refocusing.

The ratio of independent outside directors to board size. Affiliated outside directors are defined as relatives of employees, customers, suppliers, former employees, lawyers, and bankers; the remaining outside directors were classified as independent outside directors. The ratio was averaged for the two years post-refocusing.

Operationalized using Compustat data at the four-digit SIC level, by regressing time on total industry sales for the last five years, then dividing the standard error of the regression slope coefficient by the mean of the industry sales for the five-year period. The average industry dynamism levels for the two years post-refocusing were used.
time_window: five-year regression; averaged over two years post-refocusing

description: Binary event with values equaling one for the month in which an organization released a GPI and zero otherwise. Between 1994 and 1998, 69 GPI events occurred across the 35 software business lines. To identify GPIs, the authors determined whether an innovation release represented a significant advance in technical performance relative to the existing product and within a technological regime, using a triangulating, multiple-indicator approach focused on the number of feature additions and enhancements, the numbering convention for the release, and the pricing schedule for the release.

Elapsed calendar time since the prior innovation release for the product line, where the prior release can be either the initial release of the product or the prior GPI release. TimeSinceInnov starts at one for the first month following an innovation release and increments by one for each month until a subsequent innovation release, its removal from the market, or the end of the data panel. A squared term, TimeSinceInnov squared, is included in the models to test the inverse-U relationship.
Hirschman-Herfindhal Index capturing dispersion in unit market share among competing organizations. The index was calculated as the sum of the squared values of products' market share.

Binary variable indicating whether any competing organizations released a GPI in the prior month. The authors employed the binary form because there were only three instances in which more than one competitor released a GPI in the same market segment and month.

Binary technological opportunity event variable indicating whether a new class of microprocessor was released during the month. To identify new classes of microprocessors, the authors focused on increases in the number of transistors and clock speed, and identified two new microprocessor classes for the IBM-compatible and three new classes for the Macintosh between 1994 and 1998.

Binary technological opportunity event variable indicating whether a major operating system innovation was released during the month. Based on trade press accounts, the authors identified three GPIs for the Macintosh operating system, and for the IBM-compatible they identified four GPIs: two focused on corporate and end consumers (Windows 95, Windows 98) and two focused on corporate customers (Windows NT 3.5, Windows NT 4.0).

Firm-level variable measuring the extent to which a firm expands the scope of its operation, or products or services, beyond its core business, market, or industry. Equation (1) is not readable in the available text; the prose states that G_st is the group of firms in the s-th space to which the competitors of firm i belong in time t, and n_st is the number of other firms in the s-th space in time t. The authors state that this firm-level diversification measure captures dependence upon the competition network structure, creating a foundational awareness cue that reflects the interdependence among arena spaces.

Operationalized as the absolute difference in the competitive pressures of firms i and j in period t in an undirected network; the equation itself is not readable in the available text. Competitive pressure is based on Bonacich's (1987) centrality measure and captures the degree to which a firm is exposed to competitive pressure, considering the influence of not only its direct rivals but their rivals, and so on, cumulatively. The scaling parameter a can be computed implicitly, and the decay parameter b controls the type and distance of the pressure effect; negative values represent the competition or bargaining of adversarial networks, and the primary results use a distant network effect setting of b = -0.4.

A network statistic capturing the endogenous dependence of the competition network on the frequency of transitive competitive encounters; the equation is not readable in the available text. The authors state that the measure adds 1 whenever all three encounters are present together, forming a three-cycle rivalry.

The degree of separation between firms expands on the convergence measure by counting higher degree k-cycles for k >= 4. The authors operationalize the substructures of a competitive landscape using counts of network subgraphs (cyclic tetrads, pentads, etc.) by adding k-cycle predictors in a range of values for k, so that the pattern of coefficients represents the association between network-level rivalry configurations and the likelihood of individual competitive encounters. The authors state that decreasing coefficients that eventually become negative for larger significant k values indicate a negative association between degree of separation and competitive encounters. Three degrees of separation are captured by four cycles and four degrees of separation by five cycles.

The dependent variable y_ijt measures whether a competitive encounter occurred, taking the value of 1 if firms i and j had a competitive encounter in period t, and 0 otherwise. Competitive relations are defined when firms were seen as rivals by news articles, customers, analysts, and other firm outsiders. The authors analyzed 15,824,693 dyad-year observations with 142,446 competitive encounters related to 25 focal firms and their respective 10,232 direct rivals and indirect competitors (2,920 unique firms); Qualtrics, one of the 25 focal firms, faced a total of 7,489 competitive encounters with 531 direct rivals and indirect competitors representing 29 distinct four-digit SIC codes.

Second-order factor formed by the four-item scale internal identification (Cronbach's alpha = 0.87), which captures a firm's proficiency in discovering internal exploitation opportunities, and the four-item scale internal commercialization (Cronbach's alpha = 0.85), which addresses whether firms easily implement technologies and constantly consider how to better exploit them. Items were answered on a seven-point scale and the scales were aggregated by calculating the means of the second-order construct.

Second-order factor formed by the five-item scale external identification (Cronbach's alpha = 0.89), which captures proficiency in identifying external exploitation opportunities such as scanning the environment for licensing opportunities, and the four-item scale external commercialization (Cronbach's alpha = 0.90), which captures whether firms often transfer technologies and whether transfer activities are well organized. Items were answered on a seven-point scale and the scales were aggregated by calculating the means of the second-order construct.

Informants indicated the percentage of revenues from new products introduced during the previous three years relative to all revenues, reported in seven categories: zero-five percent, five-10 percent, 10-20 percent, 20-30 percent, 30-40 percent, 40-50 percent, and over 50 percent. The measure served as the dependent variable in the OLS analyses.
scale: seven categories: zero-five percent, five-10 percent, 10-20 percent, 20-30 percent, 30-40 percent, 40-50 percent, and over 50 percent
time_window: new products introduced during the previous three years

description: A firm's technology licensing revenues, reported in seven categories: EUR 0 million, EUR 0-1 million, EUR 1-3 million, EUR 3-10 million, EUR 10-30 million, EUR 30-100 million, and over EUR 100 million. The dependent variable was calculated as the percentage of licensing revenues relative to a firm's overall annual revenues, using the means of the categories for the first six categories, with the seventh category set to EUR 250 million. Eighteen firms did not report their licensing revenues, reducing the sample to 210 firms in these analyses.
scale: seven revenue categories (EUR 0 million to over EUR 100 million), expressed as a percentage of overall annual revenues

description: Return on sales data were collected from financial databases and annual reports for the year of the survey and for the subsequent year. To give stability to this variable, the mean of ROS in these two years was used. This yielded data for 197 firms in the year of the survey and 188 firms in the subsequent year.
time_window: year of the survey and the subsequent year (one-year lag); mean of the two years

description: Corporate ROA equals operating income before depreciation (COMPUSTAT entry 13, Net Income plus taxes, interest and depreciation) divided by total assets for the corporation. The measure is calculated from observations on the Annual COMPUSTAT data tape.

Following Roquebert et al., business segment ROA is the business segment's operating income divided by business segment assets. The business segment subscript represents the order of the segment within the corporation as it appeared in the original data.

To remove any possibility of simultaneity between business segment ROA and industry ROA, the Industry ROA used for a given corporation's business segment is calculated by removing that segment from the relevant industry operating income and industry total assets. If there are K firms in the industry, the Industry ROA used for business unit m equals 1/(K - 1) times the sum of the other firms' ROA.

Corporate Debt to Total Assets equals Long-Term Debt/(Long-Term Debt + Common Equity), that is, COMPUSTAT entry 12 divided by the sum of entry 60 and entry 12. The authors use debt to total assets as a proxy for financial leverage following Hoskisson et al. (1993b) and Lubatkin and Chatterjee (1991).

Corporate ROA equals operating income before depreciation (COMPUSTAT entry 13, Net Income plus taxes, interest and depreciation) divided by total assets for the corporation. The measure is calculated from observations on the Annual COMPUSTAT data tape.

Following Roquebert et al., business segment ROA is the business segment's operating income divided by business segment assets. The business segment subscript represents the order of the segment within the corporation as it appeared in the original data.

To remove any possibility of simultaneity between business segment ROA and industry ROA, the Industry ROA used for a given corporation's business segment is calculated by removing that segment from the relevant industry operating income and industry total assets. If there are K firms in the industry, the Industry ROA used for business unit m equals 1/(K - 1) times the sum of the other firms' ROA.

Corporate Debt to Total Assets equals Long-Term Debt/(Long-Term Debt + Common Equity), that is, COMPUSTAT entry 12 divided by the sum of entry 60 and entry 12. The authors use debt to total assets as a proxy for financial leverage following Hoskisson et al. (1993b) and Lubatkin and Chatterjee (1991).

A 27-item scale derived from Sun et al. (2007) and based on prior research to measure integrated high-performance HR practices. The index is based on eight unique domains, and the pilot study, exploratory factor analysis and confirmatory factor analysis supported the eight-factor structure. Items are answered on a scale from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.' Following the traditional approach for operationalizing the HPWS measure, the authors used an additive index to reflect a single comprehensive measure of a firm's HR system, where a high score indicates a relatively intensive investment in high-performance work practices.

Ambidexterity was assessed by using measures of both exploration and exploitation, based on an established 12-item scale published by Lubatkin et al. (2006). The 12 items asked the CEO to assess exploration and exploitation during the past three years on a Likert-type scale (1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree'). The congruence between exploration and exploitation was measured using latent congruence modeling (LCM) to incorporate measurement error and model covariance among individual items under exploration and exploitation; the authors refer to this outcome variable as 'ambidexterity congruence.'

Six items from the Lubatkin et al. (2006) scale used to measure exploration, including 'the venture . . . bases its success on its ability to explore new technologies.' The CEO assessed exploration during the past three years on a Likert-type scale from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree' (alpha = .87).

Six items from the Lubatkin et al. (2006) scale used to measure exploitation, focused on issues such as 'the venture . . . commits to improve quality and lower cost.' The CEO assessed exploitation during the past three years on a Likert-type scale from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree' (alpha = .86).

The average of sales and employee growth for the years 2008, 2009, and 2010. To achieve triangulation, multisource sales and employee data were used from Corptech, the Dun and Bradstreet Million Dollar Directory, and the Ward's Directory; all 215 ventures were matched from at least two sources. The authors take the mean of reported sales and employees during 2008-10, for which sales growth is measured as the compounded annual growth rate (CAGR); the CAGR formula itself is not readable in the text. Employee growth is likewise measured as a CAGR of employees during 2008-10.

variable_name: Business similarity between the firm and the partner's acquisition target
description: Calculated based on the primary SIC codes of the firm and the target. When at least one of the parties did not operate in the software industry the measure took decreasing values depending on how many leading SIC digits matched (four digits, then three, then two, then one) and 0 otherwise; the printed fractions are garbled in the source text. For a firm and a target both operating in the software industry, business descriptions in their 10-K SEC forms were used to classify software products into 54 product segments in four product classes, and the variable combined the number of product classes and product segments in which both operate relative to the parties' total number of product segments. The variable ranged between 0 and 1, with a higher value indicating greater similarity.

variable_name: Business complementarity between the firm and the partner's acquisition target
description: Based on the entire Compustat database, a complementarity score for any pair of four-digit SIC codes i and j was first computed as Comp(ij) = (J(ij) - mu(ij))/delta(ij), where J(ij) is the number of times that two SIC codes appear in a firm, mu(ij) = (N(i) x N(j))/K with N(i) and N(j) the number of firms in each SIC code and K the total number of firms, and delta(ij) a standard-deviation term. The business complementarity between a firm and a target was measured as the sum over pairs of SIC codes of Comp(ij) x p(i) x p(j), where p(i) and p(j) are weights of the codes calculated as 1 divided by the number of SIC codes that the firm and the target have, respectively. When both the firm and the target operated in the software industry, the score was supplemented with a term capturing the proportion of the parties' distinct product segments within the same product class. A high value indicates greater complementarity.

Proxied by the joint partnering experience of the firm and its partner, measured as the accumulated number of alliances between them prior to the acquisition announcement. Each prior alliance was weighted by its intensity, which implies greater resource commitment and interdependence between the firm and the partner. The intensity of the alliance relationship was captured by the standardized number of different types of alliance agreements signed between the parties.

The firm's cumulative abnormal return (CAR) around the announcement of the partner's acquisition, computed with residual analysis of the market model. The market model was estimated over a period of 250 days during t = [-260, -11] using the daily market return on the equal-weighted S&P 500, and the resulting estimates were used to predict daily abnormal returns in percentage, which were summed over a two-day event window [-1, 0], with the date of the partner's acquisition announcement set to t = 0. The measure reflects investors' expectations about the value the alliance will potentially create for the firm following the acquisition.
time_window: two-day event window [-1,0]; estimation window t = [-260,-11]

description: Indicator coded as zero if the contract in question contained no contingency planning and one if contingency planning was included; the engineers agreed to code the variable on a binary basis because they had limited time. A lagged version, prior contingency planning, equals zero if the previous contract that Compustar signed with the customer in question did not contain contingency planning and one otherwise, and is coded as missing and excluded from models for the first contract between the two firms.

Coded by two Compustar engineers on a 1-7 Likert-type scale, where 1 represents contracts containing very little detail in the description of the task to be accomplished and 7 represents contracts containing very extensive technical description. Examples of technical detail include references to particular types of databases or other software systems on which Compustar would work, or specific responsibilities the customer must fulfill. A lagged version, prior task description, measures the level of task description (1 to 7) in the previous contract between Compustar and the customer.

Measures the amount of time in weeks that Compustar had worked with a particular business unit of a partner company prior to signing the contract in question. The variable is aimed at capturing effects of partner-specific learning (or trust) over time; alternative measures based on the number of contracts entered into by the parties in the past were assembled but the reported results use the time-worked-together measure.
time_window: prior to signing the contract in question

variable_name: New CEO hired in turnaround situations
description: Dummy variable that equals 1 if new CEOs were hired in turnaround situations (98 cases of treatment group), and 0 if they were hired in non-turnaround situations (a matching 98 cases of 'comparison' group). Turnaround situations were identified among established companies whose operating returns on equity before extraordinary items were greater than their cost of equity for at least two consecutive years, immediately followed by a year of operating loss before extraordinary items; the cost of equity uses a firm beta estimated from prior five-year monthly return data.
time_window: succession year, with the turnaround criterion based on the two prior years

description: The first year's total remuneration, including all forms of compensation received in the succession year (Year 0): fixed salary, performance bonus, life insurance, options, and restricted stocks. The authors checked ExecuComp's database and the new CEO's initial employment agreement disclosed in proxy statements to correct any discrepancies, and they excluded the value of special items such as relocation subsidies and forfeited-benefit replacement grants.

The value of options, restricted stocks, and bonuses; the value of options, based on Black and Scholes' (1973) option-pricing model, is an ex ante valuation measure calculated in the succession year when the options are granted to the new CEOs. The proportion of performance-based pay is the ratio of its value to the total pay.

Dummy variable, coded 1 if the new CEO had 0 tenure before he/she was hired by the focal firm. The interaction term between outsider CEOs and firms in turnaround situations was mean-centered and used to test Hypothesis 2.

A new CEO was regarded as possessing prestigious working credentials if he or she had been employed by a prominent firm at the level of vice president or higher, or had sat or was currently sitting on the most prominent firm's board; a firm was considered prominent if it was a member of the S&P 100 Index. A new CEO was coded as possessing prestigious educational credentials if he or she had received an undergraduate or graduate degree from an elite institution, identified using the list provided by Finkelstein (1992). The variable is coded 1 if the new CEO had either prestigious working credentials or prestigious educational credentials, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: prior career through the succession year

description: Measured by the sum of company tenure and industry tenure beyond the focal firm. Company tenure was the number of years that a new CEO had been employed in the focal company before he or she was promoted to the chief executive position (company tenure equaled 0 if the new CEO was appointed externally); industry tenure beyond the focal firm was the number of years that a new CEO was employed outside the company but within the same industry as the focal firm.
time_window: prior career through the succession year

description: Pay premium defined as the extra pay in addition to the amount a CEO would expect to receive after considering firm characteristics (e.g., size, profitability), industry conditions, and personal characteristics. Expected total pay was estimated from the results of Model 1 of Table 2 in Empirical Analysis I, and the difference between the new CEO's actual total pay and the estimated pay is the pay premium measure.

Pay premium of performance-based pay defined as the extra pay in addition to the amount a CEO would expect to receive after considering firm characteristics, industry conditions, and personal characteristics. Expected performance-based pay was estimated from the results of Model 1' of Table 2 in Empirical Analysis I, and the difference between the new CEO's actual performance-based pay and the estimated pay is the pay premium measure.

An index built from three indicators, each created by adding standardized scores. Downsizing combines fixed assets and employment size reduction measured as the change from the succession year (Year 0) to three years after succession (Year +3), reverse coded so that a greater value means greater downsizing. Cost cutting combines reverse-coded differences between Year +3 and Year 0 in R&D intensity, advertising intensity, and SGA expenses over sales. Product/market refocusing combines reverse-coded changes in entropy-based product and geographic diversification between Year +3 and Year 0. The three indicators are highly correlated and were combined into a single index using the sum of their standard scores.

Cases of complete IJV termination are classified into two groups: intended termination and unintended termination. Intended termination includes IJVs that were terminated because the initial purposes were fulfilled, as reported by the Japanese parent firms in the database. Cases of IJVs that were terminated for reasons that are either unreported or unclassified in the database are not included in the analyses. The variable is used in the chi-square comparison of the relative proportions of intended and unintended termination cases.

Unintended termination includes IJVs that were terminated because of unanticipated contingencies, as reported by the Japanese parent firms in the database. The eight major factors listed in the original dataset are classified into three types of unanticipated contingencies: changes in external conditions, changes in the inter-partner relationship, and changes in the parent firm conditions. Cases terminated for reasons that are unreported or unclassified are not included in the analyses.

Longevity is used in the analyses as a proxy for the likelihood of survival. It is measured by the year count between the year of establishment and the year of termination of the IJV. All variables except cultural distance and the fixed effects variables are specified as time-varying and are measured at each year point in the observation.
time_window: from year of establishment to year of termination

description: The original dataset lists seven major objectives for the establishment of a subsidiary; these are classified into four key purposes of IJV formation. Strategic asset seeking corresponds to research and development. As the original questionnaire allows for the choice of more than one investment purpose, each purpose variable is separately defined by four dummy variables.

variable_name: changes in the parent firm conditions
description: The eight major termination factors listed in the original dataset are classified into three types of unanticipated contingencies. Changes in the parent firm conditions comprise the restructuring of the parent firm businesses and the death or retirement of the Japanese CEO. These variables enter the longevity models as dummies, with completion of the initial purposes of formation used as the baseline.

The eight major termination factors listed in the original dataset are classified into three types of unanticipated contingencies. Changes in external conditions comprise misleading demand, competition with local firms, competition with Japanese firms, competition with third-country firms, and changes in exchange rate.

The eight major termination factors listed in the original dataset are classified into three types of unanticipated contingencies. Changes in the inter-partner relationship comprise conflicts with local partners. This variable enters the longevity models as a dummy, with completion of the initial purposes of formation used as the baseline.

Cases are classified as either IJVs or WOSs using equity ownership: an IJV shares 20 percent or more and less than 95 percent of its equity ownership with a foreign firm or firms, and a WOS shares 95 percent or more of its equity ownership with a foreign firm or firms. The proportional difference in intended versus unintended termination between the two groups is examined by chi-square analysis.

The cultural distance between IJV partners is measured by the cultural distance index of Kogut and Singh (1988). Together with the fixed effects variables, it is one of the variables that are not specified as time-varying.

variable_name: ownership structure of the parent firms
description: The ownership structure of the parent firms is measured by the percentage of equity of an IJV that is owned by the largest Japanese parent firm. A quadratic term is added to the analyses to examine the curvilinear effect of this variable.
IJV size is measured by the total amount of capital investment that is put into an IJV.
The international experience of the parent firm is measured by the number of subsidiaries that are owned by the parent firm.

Each executive's cash compensation, which comprises both salary and bonus, in thousands of dollars. The dependent variable was not transformed because it was normally distributed. Auxiliary models used a salary-only dependent variable.

A dummy variable was used to indicate whether an executive was a founder of a company. It was also multiplied by a company's number of employees and by the number of rounds raised to form interaction variables.

variable_name: Percentage of company equity held by the executive
description: The percentage of company equity held by the executive was used to assess the impact of equity holdings. The authors note that the percentage of equity owned by an executive is the best variable to use in studies focused on the compensation implications of equity ownership.

For the hypotheses regarding company size and changes in the founder discount, company size was estimated using the number of employees, and an interaction variable was computed by multiplying the founder dummy by a company's number of employees.

A variable indicated the number of rounds (i.e., separate private placements) completed, and an interaction variable, computed by multiplying the founder dummy by the number of rounds raised, was used.

The ratio of the entrant's to the incumbent's platform quality on the consumer side, Q = QE/QI. The authors estimate βQ, the coefficient of the console dummy in the log-difference adoption regression, and obtain the quality ratio as exp(βQ). Because Q and F are ratios, console dummies are used in the regressions instead of explicitly measuring the actual quality levels.

The coefficient on the log difference in discounted game variety between the two consoles, ln NEt − ln NIt, in the console adoption regression. It measures the extent to which consumers care about application variety, that is, the strength of indirect network effects, and is estimated by nonlinear least squares because the discount factor enters the same equation nonlinearly.

The discount factor of consumers' future utility from applications, which enters the adoption equation nonlinearly. Model I assumes myopic consumers (φ = 0); Model II relaxes the myopia assumption and estimates φ by nonlinear least squares. A larger value means consumers are more patient and value future applications more.

The percentage of new consumers who choose console j in a month; the authors compute market shares by dividing the number for each console by the sum of the two consoles. The dependent variable of the adoption regression is the log difference between the entrant's and the incumbent's shares, which can be written as ln sEt − ln sIt = ln Q + e(ln NEt − ln NIt).

The discounted total number of applications on platform j in period t, written in the model as exp(ln njt + Σ from s = t+1 to T of φ^(s−t) ln Δnjs), that is, currently available games plus games from future releases discounted by φ. Consumer expectations are assumed fulfilled, so the authors use actual future game release data and express Njt as a function of φ, an errors-in-variables approach. It enters the consumer equation as the log difference ln NEt − ln NIt.

The installed base of console j by month, obtained from cumulative console sales up to the current month subject to a constant rate of decay. The authors experimented with different decay rates and compared console market shares with survey results, choosing an annual decay rate of 10 percent, which corresponds to a monthly decay rate of 0.87 percent. Its logarithm is the main regressor of the game supply equation.

The logarithm of the number of new games released for console j in period t, the dependent variable of the game supply equation; because each developer supplies one application, this measures developer entry on the platform.

The ratio of the two platforms' fixed costs of supporting developers, F = FIt/FEt, obtained as exp(β2) where β2 is the coefficient of the console dummy in the game supply equation; it measures the entrant's cost advantage on the developer side. The authors find that the difference in development costs between the two consoles is statistically indistinguishable from zero.

Because financial performance data were not available at the business level, classification rules based upon market share and survival or non-survival in the given industry were developed. High performers were the three highest-ranked established domestic firms in terms of market share at the end of the growth stage. Low performers were selected first from established domestic firms that had been visible in the industry and then withdrew, and otherwise from the bottom third of the industry's visible domestic firms in terms of market share at the end of the growth stage. Three high-performing and three low-performing firms were tentatively selected from each industry, and corroborative information from secondary sources was sought in every case.

Respondents rated the 'profitability' of the microwave oven business of the given firms on a five-point scale, from 'significantly above average' to 'significantly below average', for each time period. For both periods Kendall's coefficient of concordance indicated a high degree of agreement among the panelists.
scale: five-point scale from 'significantly above average' to 'significantly below average'
time_window: two sub-periods of the growth stage (1972-77 and 1978-83)

description: Degree of diversification was measured with a modified Rumelt (1974) methodology; firms were assigned values from 1 to 5. The same measure was used in the single-industry study, where data for these variables were gathered from secondary sources.

Firm size was measured by net sales and total assets, adjusted for inflation. The same measure was used in the single-industry study, where data for these variables were gathered from secondary sources.

Financial strength was measured with stock ratings from the S&P Stock Guide and bond ratings from Moody's. The S&P stock ratings measure the 'quality' of the given firm's common stock and are not a forecast of future market price performance. The same measure was used in the single-industry study, where data for these variables were gathered from secondary sources.

Two measures were used. Order of entry: firms were assigned an entry rank based on their year of entry into the given industry. Life cycle stage: based on decision rules which classified entry as having occurred during the introduction, 'early growth' or 'late growth' stages, with values from 1 to 3 assigned to these categories. The same measures were used in the single-industry study.
scale: entry rank; life cycle stage values from 1 to 3

description: The percentage of the firm's existing revenues threatened by the young industry. The same measure was used in the single-industry study, where data for these variables were gathered from secondary sources.
The real weighted average growth rate of the Standard Industrial Classification industries that a firm participated in. The same measure was used in the single-industry study.

An SIC measure based on decision rules which compared the four-digit SIC codes of a firm to that of the young industry. Four categories, from 'unrelated' to 'closely related', were defined with values from 0 to 3 assigned to them. The hypothesis was tested for three sets of firms: all firms, non-threatened firms only, and 'less mature' firms only.

Company-initiated R&D expenditures as a percentage of net sales. In the multi-industry study, 11 firms were not considered in the test for R&D emphasis since sufficient R&D data were not available. The same measure was used in the single-industry study.
Considered in the single-industry study. For two time periods, industry executives rated the importance of the microwave oven business to parent companies on a 1 to 7 scale.
time_window: two sub-periods of the growth stage (1972-77 and 1978-83)

description: In the single-industry study, industry executives also assessed the relatedness between the microwave oven business and the parent's other lines of business. Three types of relatedness were individually rated on a seven-point scale: distribution systems, brand names and product R&D skills. This measure was used in the single-industry study in place of the SIC measure; the tests for relatedness considering only non-threatened and less mature firms were not performed there because of the small sample size.
time_window: two sub-periods of the growth stage (1972-77 and 1978-83)

description: Considered in the single-industry study. For each firm, industry executives rated the unit responsible for business in the MOI on a 1 to 7 scale for two time periods.
time_window: two sub-periods of the growth stage (1972-77 and 1978-83)

description: Considered in the single-industry study. For each firm, industry executives rated the unit responsible for business in the MOI on a 1 to 7 scale for two time periods.
time_window: two sub-periods of the growth stage (1972-77 and 1978-83)

description: Composite measure formed by summing four dimensions of internationalization, three of which were drawn from Sullivan (1994): foreign sales to total sales (FSTS), foreign assets to total assets (FATA), and the number of overseas subsidiaries to total number of subsidiaries (OSTS), plus a fourth dimension named Scope. Scope was expressed as a proportion of the highest number of countries with subsidiaries represented in the sample in a given year. The theoretical range for each dimension was from 0 to 1, and the composite measure had a theoretical range of 0 to 4.
Measured as the logarithm of the total of all forms of compensation granted to the CEO during the year. The compensation total includes salary, perquisites, bonus, provident fund, and commission.
Measured as the proportion of outside directors on the board. Outsiders were board members who were not otherwise employed by the firm.
A dummy variable coded '1' if the CEO also occupied the position of the chairperson of the board; otherwise it was coded '0'.

A firm was coded as a family controlled firm if any two of three criteria were met: the founding family had a stake of 20 percent or greater in the firm; a member of the founding family was on the board; and/or a member of the founding family was the chairperson of the board. A firm was coded as a family managed firm if any two of three criteria were met: a founding family member was the CEO; a member of the founding family was an executive director; and/or more than one member of the founding family were executive directors. FCFM was coded '1' when both the family controlled firm variable and the family managed firm variable had values equal to 1, else '0'.

FCNFM firm was coded '1' when the family controlled firm variable had a value equal to 1 and the family managed firm variable had a value equal to 0. All FCNFM firms in the sample had nonfamily CEOs. Data for constructing these variables were manually extracted from firm annual reports, leading business magazines, and corporate history reports in the CAPITALINE database.

The number of adoptions of innovative formats in the local market, measured as a sum over the year before the current period. Local innovations are counted for the focal market only. The total is used together with the count of innovations to model the influence of local innovative activity.
time_window: one year before the focal quarter

description: The number of adoptions of innovative formats in other markets, summed over the year before the current period. The nonlocal variables do not include events in the local market, so each innovation is only counted once.
time_window: one year before the focal quarter

description: The number of nonlocal innovations in the same region of the country, using regions similar to those of Walker (1969), summed over the year before the current period. Events in the local market are excluded.
time_window: one year before the focal quarter

description: The number of innovations in the 10 largest markets, ranked by population, summed over the year before the current period. It is a nonlocal variable, so local events are excluded.
time_window: one year before the focal quarter

variable_name: Innovations weighted by size of corporation
description: The sum of the corporate sizes, measured as the number of stations, of the corporations owning the stations making the changes, summed over the year before the current period. This weighted sum lets the influence of an innovation depend on the size of the corporation that made it.
time_window: one year before the focal quarter

description: The sum of market shares, measured after the change, of the stations making the innovative format adoptions, summed over the year before the current period. This weighted sum lets the influence of an innovation depend on the market share of the innovating station.
time_window: one year before the focal quarter

description: The dependent variable is the quarterly count of format changes of each market. The most inclusive event consists of all changes in format or production, effectively counting all entries in the M Street Journal. Dependent variables are measured at 3-month intervals.

Entry into one of the innovative formats, which is treated as mimetic behavior. Because it omits the most common formats and many less common but older formats, it has substantially fewer events. The change categories are mutually exclusive, so each event occurs only in one subanalysis.
All format changes except entry into innovative or satellite formats, and thus a nonmimetic change of format. The categories are mutually exclusive, so each event occurs only in one subanalysis.

All format changes in which the destination format is a satellite format. Satellite formats are provided by programming services that sell, for money or for a portion of the advertising time, ready-made programming in a number of different formats. Satellite entry is both an operational and a format change.

An operational change that consists of all changes among the production modes of live, simulcast, or satellite that do not also change the format. The categories are mutually exclusive, so each event occurs only in one subanalysis.

The proportion of a supplier's business portfolio that comes from buyers with whom it shares long-term (relational) ties, essentially a weighted average (weighted by business share) of the buyer relationships that are long-term. For each supplier in a year it is the fraction of patent prosecution services provided for buyers that have outsourced to the same supplier in each of the prior four years, so that, including the focal year, these relationships have lasted continuously for at least five years.
time_window: prior four years plus the focal year (at least five continuous years)

description: The one-year logged growth rate in the number of patents prosecuted by patent law firm i. The logged difference formulation, log[number of patents(i,t)] - log[number of patents(i,t-1)], is equivalent to log(number of patents(i,t)/number of patents(i,t-1)). Patent prosecution projects are typically similar in scope, so the measure is also a good proxy for growth in the revenues generated from performing that outsourced work.
time_window: one-year growth rate (t relative to t-1)

description: The weighted-average spread of a supplier's patent legal work for existing buyers across different technology markets, measured using four-digit International Patent Classes (IPC4). Using the fractions of patents in each IPC4, the authors computed a Hirschman-Herfindahl Index, which was then averaged across buyers with weights equal to the fraction of the supplier's business accruing from that buyer over the prior three years, and finally subtracted this weighted-average HHI from one. The measure varies between zero and one, where a higher number indicates greater cross-servicing experience in the recent past and thus greater demonstrated capability to cross-service buyers.

For each buyer, the percentage of outsourced patents that were outsourced to the focal supplier over the prior three years; a higher share of outsourced patent work received from a buyer indicates that the buyer has made a greater relational commitment to the focal law supplier. The authors then computed an aggregate supplier firm-level measure by summing these buyer business shares, using the same weighting procedure based on the fraction of the supplier's business from each buyer.

The weighted average share of patents prosecuted internally (instead of being outsourced) by the focal supplier's portfolio of buyers. For each buyer in the supplier's portfolio, the authors obtained all patents filed at the USPTO over the prior three years and calculated the fraction of those patents prosecuted inhouse by the buyer, then averaged this variable across buyers using the business-share weights.

The weighted average (across buyers) fraction of backward self-citations in patents filed over the prior three years by a supplier for all its buyers. Backward self-citations are the citing of relevant prior patents of the same buyer in a supplier's patent applications; the more extensive a patent's self-citations, the greater the buyer-specificity of knowledge required to write the patent. To mitigate knowledge obsolescence, only backward citations to patents granted over a prior five-year window were used.
time_window: prior three years (backward citations to patents granted in the prior five years)

description: The quantity of a firm's small failures was measured as the number of patents that were discontinued due to non-payment of maintenance fees by the firm each year between 1985 and 2002. Patent expirations are observed at the legally determined deadlines of 4, 8, and 12 years after the application date, and the variable aggregates the number of discontinued patents at the firm-year level. The variable enters the models lagged by one period.
time_window: measured each year between 1985 and 2002; entered in the models as t-1

description: In order to measure the importance of a discontinued patent, the authors calculated the citations to the patent up until the year of expiration, aggregated to the firm-year level. The number of forward citations is used as a commonly used measure of a patent's value and its impact on future inventions and is taken to capture the expectations of decision makers about the potential of a given patent before expiration.
time_window: citations counted up until the year of expiration; entered in the models as t-1

variable_name: Failures after 4 years, 8 years, and 12 years
description: To test the arguments related to the timing of failures, the authors calculated the number of discontinued patents at each stage of patent discontinuation, that is, at 4, 8, and 12 years after the application date, at the firm-year level. A patent discontinued at 4 years is assumed to have elicited feedback earlier than a patent discontinued at 12 years. Because the total expired patents equals the sum of expired patents after 4, 8, and 12 years, the total was excluded from the models when testing the separate effects of the stage variables.
time_window: measured each year; entered in the models as t-1

description: The dependent variable is R&D output, measured as the number of successful patent applications by a firm in a given year, counting only the patents that did not get prematurely discontinued. Because the count is skewed, the measure was log-transformed, and the lagged value of R&D output is included on the right-hand side of the model.

The quality of R&D output was measured for each firm as the total number of citations to all successful patents, that is, patents that did not get discontinued prematurely. Citations are used as a proxy for the quality of innovative or inventive performance. The measure was log-transformed due to skewness and its lagged value is included in the model.

variable_name: Percentage of family ties in the inner circle
description: Family presence is measured as the percentage of family ties in the inner circle. Because the inner circle is organized around the key leader, only the dyadic ties between the key leader and other top executives are counted, and members from both immediate and extended family are included as family members. The percentage is calculated as the number of family ties divided by the size of the inner circle minus one.

A dummy variable with one assigned to second-generation key leaders and zero to first-generation key leaders. The variable was coded from the BGT directory and other biographical sources. Modern Taiwanese business groups emerged only in the 1950s to the 1960s, and the majority of groups are still in the hands of either the founders or the second-generation successors.

A dummy variable coded for key leaders with a management educational background from the United States (including the United Kingdom). In most cases such education was at the graduate level (e.g., MBA). The variable was coded from the BGT directory and other biographical sources.

Because 1987 marked the beginning of large-scale economic liberalization and political democratization in Taiwan, the period 1977-1986 is considered the pretransition era and 1988-1998 the posttransition era. The environmental contingency of second-generation key leaders was examined through the interaction between second-generation key leaders and the posttransition period and through the difference in coefficients of second-generation key leaders in the two periods.

The number of two-digit SIC codes in the group; industry was hand coded for each member firm according to its products using the Taiwanese government's 1996 SIC scheme, with two coders coding independently at a consistency rate of 0.83 and business histories consulted to resolve differences. In creating the interaction terms, groups with above-median diversification were coded as highly diversified and those below the median as low-diversification groups, and the original variable of diversification was included as the base term.

A dummy variable equal to 1 if the board has a finance committee and 0 otherwise. Finance committees are identified by examining proxy statements and classifying committees with the term 'finance' in the title (such as finance and investment committees) as finance committees; joint committees are coded as finance committees if the duties listed in the proxy statement include oversight of the firm's financial transactions and policies. A total of 256 (21.0%) firms have a finance committee.

A dummy variable equal to 1 if the CEO has a financial background and 0 otherwise. CEO backgrounds are hand collected by reviewing the proxy statements, 10-K filings, and Who's Who in Finance and Industry for information on the CEO's work experience. A total of 197 (16.1%) firms have a CEO with a financial background.

The natural log of 1 plus Equity, where Equity is the change in dollar value (in thousands of 2001 dollars) of the CFO's portfolio of options, restricted stock, and common shares owned at the end of year t for a one percent increase in the firm's market value (the portfolio delta). The delta of the CFO's equity portfolio is estimated using ExecuComp data following the procedure outlined in Core and Guay (1999): option portfolio data are used to estimate the average exercise price and time to expiration, which are combined with the firm's disclosed option valuation assumptions to estimate the Black-Scholes sensitivity of the option portfolio to stock price, and the change in value of restricted stock held and common shares owned per one percent increase in market value is added to the option portfolio delta.

The natural log of 1 plus Equity grant, where Equity grant is the change in dollar value (in thousands of 2001 dollars) of the CFO's grants of options and restricted stock during year t for a one percent increase in the firm's market value, following Hartzell and Starks (2003).

variable_name: proportion of total compensation that is equity-based
description: Following Barron and Waddell (2003), the value of annual equity compensation scaled by annual total compensation. Equity incentives are restricted stock and option grants; total annual compensation is restricted stock, option grants, cash compensation, and other long-term package payouts.

Following Jensen and Murphy (1990), the authors regress the change in CFO total compensation against the change in the firm's market value to estimate the CFO's pay-for-performance relation; the coefficient on the change in market value represents the dollar gain per $1,000 increase in firm market value. CFO pay includes equity, cash, and other long-term annual compensation. Because the specification requires the change in total CFO compensation, one annual observation is lost for each CFO, reducing the sample to 2,147 observations.
time_window: change from year t-1 to year t

description: Measured annually over the years from an acquisition to a divestiture. To incorporate the effects of a reference point, it is the percentage of ROA (return on assets) of an acquired unit minus the mean ROA of the unit's industry, with industry defined by two-digit Standard Industrial Classification code. COMPUSTAT Segment Tapes were the main source of performance data.

The dependent variable was dummy-coded in each spell so that it indicated whether the divestiture had occurred or not at the last date of each spell ('divested' = 1, 'not divested' = 0). Announcement dates of each acquisition and divestiture were used to measure the time between the two events. The data were obtained from the SDC database.
time_window: each spell, split on the basis of the fiscal year of each sample or control firm

description: Measured as acquisition frequency, or the number of acquisitions within the same industry as a focal acquired unit, with industry defined by two-digit SIC code. When acquisitions are frequently observed in the industry of a poorly performing unit, the high frequency can be interpreted both as a sign of the attractiveness and of the unattractiveness of the business.
Dummy-coded as a decline in unit performance since a previous year ('decline' = 1, 'no decline' = 0).
