The quick ratio, calculated as cash and short-term investments plus receivables, divided by current liabilities; it indicates uncommitted resource availability in the parent firm of a focal acquired unit. Similar measures have often been used in other research on risk, divestiture, and organizational reactions to poor performance.
The debt-to-equity ratio, which indicates an organization's potentially available level of resources, or borrowing capacity, in the parent firm of a focal acquired unit.
The number of divestitures in the three years before a focal year were counted and accumulated as a running average for each year.
time_window: three-year window before a focal year

description: The size of an acquired unit relative to the acquiring firm was measured as the ratio between the unit's annual sales and its parent firm's sales.

Managers rated each of 34 competitive actions on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (not a part of our strategy at all) to 5 (a key part of our strategy). The index was developed by counting the number of items (out of the 34) that the respondent scored 3 or higher on the scale, so a higher score indicated higher strategic variety and vice versa. A score of 3 was chosen as a threshold because it indicated that a given competitive action was a key part of a firm's strategy. The measure was validated against the ratings of 14 industry experts on 42 new ventures.
scale: count of items scored 3 or higher (out of 34)

description: Information about venture origin was collected by asking respondents directly, following the literature. Corporate ventures were coded 0 and independent ventures were coded 1.

Dynamism of each of the seven industries was gauged using industry experts' responses to Baum and Wally's (2003) 5-item scale, a refinement of prior established measures of the construct. The panel of 14 industry experts rated the seven industries they followed on a 5-point scale; the responses of the two experts for each industry were averaged and that value was used for every venture in that industry.

Sales growth figures averaged over the two-year (2006 and 2007) period following the survey data collection, which avoids the reverse causality problem. The sales growth data were obtained from the SABI/AMADEUS database.

Categorical variable denoting the differences among the 34 states in the United States in which the foreign affiliates are located. It is entered as a random effect variable in the variance component model estimated with the MIXED procedure in SAS. States with 30 or more foreign affiliates throughout the observation period were selected.

Categorical variable denoting the differences among the 21 major cities and provinces in China in which the foreign affiliates are located. It is entered as a random effect variable in the variance component model estimated with the MIXED procedure in SAS. Cities and provinces with 30 or more foreign affiliates throughout the observation period were selected.

Net profit over total sales of the i-th foreign affiliate in the t-th year. The authors use ROS because foreign affiliates, especially strategic alliances, focus on ongoing business activities, and sales can better reflect performance in a dynamic business climate than fixed assets; they also regard ROS as superior to return on assets in the global environment because asset turnover may vary significantly among host countries. ROS is the dependent variable of the variance component model for the United States.

The absolute value of the deviation between the ROS of the i-th foreign affiliate in the t-th year and the mean ROS of foreign affiliates in the r-th subnational region in the t-th year. A low value indicates that the foreign affiliate's performance is close to the regional ROS mean, whereas a high value indicates that it has deviated from that mean, whether negatively or positively. The authors interpret it as the variation in performance, representing the risk of foreign investment, and use it as a dependent variable of the variance component model for the United States.

Net profit over total sales of the i-th foreign affiliate in the t-th year. The authors use ROS because foreign affiliates, especially strategic alliances, focus on ongoing business activities, and sales can better reflect performance in a dynamic business climate than fixed assets; they also regard ROS as superior to return on assets in the global environment because asset turnover may vary significantly among host countries. ROS is the dependent variable of the variance component model for China.

The absolute value of the deviation between the ROS of the i-th foreign affiliate in the t-th year and the mean ROS of foreign affiliates in the r-th subnational region in the t-th year. A low value indicates that the foreign affiliate's performance is close to the regional ROS mean, whereas a high value indicates that it has deviated from that mean, whether negatively or positively. The authors interpret it as the variation in performance, representing the risk of foreign investment, and use it as a dependent variable of the variance component model for China.

variable_name: Host country (United States = advanced, China = emerging)
description: Host economy type was operationalized as a two-country comparison. The United States stands for an advanced economy (study s1, 34 states) and China for an emerging economy (study s2, 21 cities and provinces), and the variance in affiliate performance attributable to region is estimated separately in each and compared.

TRANS refers to the speed and reliability with which alliance partners learn about each other's actions (or moves). It is modeled as the product of three components: the time lag with which a given choice by the other player is detected, the source of information regarding the partner's behavior, and the accuracy of that information. The authors postulate a multiplicative rather than additive model, arguing that summing the responses may overlook revealing off-diagonal cases such as respondents high on speed and low on reliability, or low on speed and high on reliability.

Measured as the product of two items: how many times senior executives from the respondent's firm and the partner firm typically meet per year, and how frequently communication takes place at lower (operational) levels by any means. The second item uses a 4-point scale from 'never' to 'frequently'. The two components are weighted equally.

Attempts to measure the expected durability of the SA as the product of two items, intended duration and perceived likelihood. Intended duration asks what the intended duration of the SA was at the time it was launched (3-point scale from 'short term' (1-3 years) to 'long term' (over 5 years)); perceived likelihood asks how likely it is that the SA will actually last for the intended duration (3-point scale from 'low' to 'high').

variable_name: payoff from unilateral defection minus mutual cooperation (UD-MC)
description: Respondents estimated their own payoffs under four behavioral combinations using a four-cell matrix in which one cell (mutual cooperation) served as the anchor at MC = $1.00; only relative rather than absolute amounts were requested. The residual (UD - MC) captures the joint product lost to unilateral defection and is computed from the respondent's payoff estimates. The payoff structure measure has a test-retest reliability of 0.91.

variable_name: payoff from mutual cooperation minus mutual defection (MC-MD)
description: Computed from the same four-cell payoff matrix in which the mutual cooperation cell was anchored at MC = $1.00 and respondents estimated their own payoffs under unilateral defection, mutual defection, and unilateral cooperation relative to that anchor. The residual (MC - MD) captures the loss to complete breakup of the SA.

variable_name: payoff from unilateral defection minus unilateral cooperation (UD-UC)
description: Computed from the same four-cell payoff matrix in which the mutual cooperation cell was anchored at MC = $1.00 and respondents estimated their own payoffs under unilateral defection, mutual defection, and unilateral cooperation relative to that anchor. The residual (UD - UC) captures the cost of unrequited cooperation.

A composite of the importance and the fulfillment of the firm's strategic needs, based on a 16-item inventory of the strategic contributions of SAs adapted from Contractor and Lorange (1988); sample items include risk reduction through product portfolio diversification, lower average cost from larger volume, and utilization of the partner's special skills in R&D. Importance is rated on a 3-point Likert scale ranging from 'not important' to 'very important' and fulfillment on a 5-point scale ranging from 'very poorly' to 'very well'. Factor analysis of the items yields one factor with an eigenvalue greater than one, and the items were summed to form an index (Cronbach alpha = 0.94).

A single-item measure asking respondents to rate the net spillover effects of the SA for their firm on a 5-point scale from 'strongly negative' to 'strongly positive'. Positive spillover effects may occur when knowhow gained from SA activities can be applied profitably to non-SA operations, while negative spillover effects may occur from competition between the SA and other parent firm operations. Test-retest reliability was 0.79.

A single item reading 'In your overall assessment, how has the SA performed as compared to your expectations?', measured on a 5-point scale from 'very poorly' to 'very well'. Test-retest reliability was 0.92.

The nationality of the partner firm was recorded for each alliance; because of the sample selection criteria all respondent firms were U.S. firms, while the nationalities of the partner firms varied widely. The total sample was disaggregated into U.S.-U.S., U.S.-European, and U.S.-Japanese alliances, with non-U.S. partners also taken as a group, in order to retest the structure-performance relationship.

variable_name: Alliance structure (payoff residuals and shadow of the future variables)
description: Game-theoretic alliance structure is operationalized as the independent variable set in the canonical correlation analysis, made of six survey variables on two of its three dimensions. The pattern of payoffs is captured by three residuals (UD-MC, MC-MD, UD-UC) computed from respondents' estimates in a four-cell payoff matrix anchored at MC = $1.00, and the shadow of the future by behavior transparency (TRANS), frequency of interaction (FROINT) and length of time horizon (HORIZON). The third dimension, number of players, is held constant at N = 2 by the sample selection criteria.
scale: Set of six variables (three payoff residuals, three multi-item survey measures)

description: The CIS survey asked respondents to identify the importance of each of 10 objectives on a Likert scale from zero (not important at all/not used) to three (very important). For each objective the authors first assigned a binary value based on whether the survey response indicated that the item was important to the firm: a response of two (important) or three (very important) received a binary value of one, while responses of zero or one (some importance) received a binary value of zero. The binary values for the different objectives were summed, giving a maximum value of 10.

The CIS survey asked respondents to identify the importance of each of 12 sources of information used in innovation activities on a Likert scale from zero (not important at all/not used) to three (very important). A survey response of two (important) or three (very important) received a binary value of one, while responses of zero or one (some importance) received a binary value of zero. To construct the variable indicating breadth of important knowledge sources, the authors summed the binary values for the 12 sources, giving a maximum value of 12.

A binary (0,1) variable indicating whether the firm introduced any technological innovations (product as well as process) during 1996-1998. These innovations were new to the firm, and may or may not have been new to the market.

variable_name: Percent of product sales revenues from innovation
description: The percent of total firm sales revenues in 1998 that derived from the sale of technologically new products introduced during 1996-1998. The variable is censored because sales of new products can only be zero or positive, and was estimated with Tobit maximum likelihood.

variable_name: uncertainty in the business unit's environment
description: Following Folta and O'Brien (2004) and Carruth et al. (2000), GARCH models were used because they produce a time-varying estimate of the conditional variance of a time series; GARCH-M (1,1) models with ARMA(1,1) in the mean equation were run on value-weighted industry portfolio returns built from monthly stock returns (adjusted for dividends and splits) for all firms in the CRSP database from 1950 to 2004. Industry groupings are based on the classification of Robins and Wiersema (1995). The monthly conditional variances were averaged to obtain annual figures, and the variable is the square root of the average yearly conditional variance. The lagged variable on uncertainty was used, taking uncertainty in the year preceding the closest financial year to the event date.
level: industry-year measure applied to firm-segment observations
time_window: lagged; the year preceding the closest financial year to the event date (returns series 1950-2004)

description: A trichotomous dependent variable where non-divestment is represented by 1, staged/partial divestment (spin-off/equity carve-outs) by 2, and complete divestment by 3. Deals were obtained from SDC and verified against other sources such as Lexis-Nexis, then matched with COMPUSTAT and the COMPUSTAT segment database. The sample of sell-offs was obtained by identifying segments that got dropped from year t to year t + 1 from COMPUSTAT segment data and mapping back to SDC and Lexis-Nexis to ensure they were indeed sold off. Non-divesting firm-segments were obtained through the matched sampling procedure.

A firm was evaluated as having a dominant strategy if its rating for initial strategy was at least 50 points out of 100 points in any one of the four strategy categories; on this basis 38 firms in the study were categorized as having a dominant strategy. Firms with a dominant strategy received 1 in that strategy type and 0 in the three other categories. Firms without a dominant strategy received a 0 in all four categories.
scale: 1 = the strategy type is dominant (at least 50 of 100 points at founding), 0 otherwise

description: The absolute value of the difference between each firm's measure of initial strategy and current strategy for each of the four strategic types, representing the amount of change in that strategy. For example, a firm whose first-mover measure was 70 points at founding and 50 points currently had a difference score of 20. Four separate difference scores, one each for the first-mover, low-cost producer, second-mover and niche strategies, were estimated for each firm and each was regressed on the predictors.

Measured as the proportion of founding group members, excluding the initial entrepreneur, who were engaged in each of three functional areas. The functional areas regarded as most important within an organization are likely to receive a disproportionate share of employees. Information on the functional backgrounds of members of the founding group of each firm was available from two of the semiconductor market research firms.
The proportion of firm ownership that members of the founding group initially controlled. Ownership data were unavailable from two firms.

For each year of operation a firm was categorized as a poor performer if its rate of increase in sales was more than one standard deviation below the average rate of sales increase for the group as a whole in that year. The number of years of poor performance was summed over the number of years the organization had been operating and the sum divided by the number of years of operation. That measure is reversed-coded in the reported results so that higher performance scores represent better performance. Two firms did not provide sales data and were eliminated from this portion of the analysis.
Measured as the number of years since a firm was incorporated. Age was treated as a surrogate measure of an organization's exposure to environmental change and was accounted for in the analysis.
The number of years the founding entrepreneur had remained with a firm after its founding, divided by the age of the firm.
scale: ratio of years with the firm to firm age

description: Negative affect is built from the emotion AI estimates of the seven basic emotions detected in photos of the sample CEOs. A principal component analysis of the seven basic affects yields two dominant components; anger, fear, sadness, and surprise have strong primary loadings on the first component (negative affect) and relatively low secondary loadings on the second. The factor scoring weights are used to construct the measure, which is mean-centered and expressed in standard deviations.

Positive affect is built from the emotion AI estimates of the seven basic emotions detected in photos of the sample CEOs. In the principal component analysis of the seven basic affects, happiness loads strongly on the second component (positive affect) and less so on the first component. The factor scoring weights are used to construct the measure, which is mean-centered and expressed in standard deviations.

Underpricing conformity is the absolute-value deviation from the market's average underpricing level, multiplied by negative one so that higher values indicate greater conformity. Deal data are retrieved from ICObench and trading data used to construct the underpricing measures are obtained from CoinMarketCap.

Underpricing level is the difference between the closing and opening price divided by the opening price on the first day of trading. The measure assumes that the full extent of underpricing is realized at the end of the first trading day. Trading data are obtained from CoinMarketCap.

Asymmetric information is proxied by the word count of each ICO's whitepaper. The variable is scaled so that the natural logarithm of word count is divided by its maximum value and multiplied by negative one, so that the shortest whitepaper has the highest value, consistent with stronger informational asymmetry.

Multimarket contact counts the number of markets in which a firm meets its competitor outside the focal market. Since the firm may have multiple competitors in the focal market, the authors follow Gimeno and Woo (1996, 1999) and Prince and Simon (2009) and calculate the average number of multimarket contacts with these rivals.

On-time performance as a product quality variable is measured as the average number of minutes delay relative to the scheduled arrival time. The sample is truncated by dropping observations with arrival (and departure) delays of more than three hours.

Airline size in terms of the number of routes the airline operates, i.e., the number of markets in which the airline is active. It enters the estimations as a moderating term with multimarket contact, normalized to the smallest airline, which has 172 routes in both subsamples.

variable_name: Share of interlining transfer passengers on route
description: The share of passengers on the route that make a transfer between airlines. The authors use interlining as a proxy for cooperation between airlines in improving the compatibility between flights.

Extent to which the acquiring firm divested its own assets across five main functions: R&D, manufacturing, logistics, sales network, and administrative services. The degree of divestiture for each function was assessed by taking the mean value of two questions concerning, respectively, the degree of capacity disposed of (closed or resold) and the proportion of the workforce cut, measured on a seven-point scale. Preliminary factor analyses showed that the items pertaining to R&D divestiture loaded on a separate construct and, to keep the model parsimonious, these items were dropped, leaving a four-item construct.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = 0% of assets divested over total assets; 7 = 91-100% of assets divested)

description: Extent to which the acquired firm divested its assets across five main functions: R&D, manufacturing, logistics, sales network, and administrative services. The degree of divestiture for each function was assessed by taking the mean value of two questions concerning, respectively, the degree of capacity disposed of (closed or resold) and the proportion of the workforce cut, measured on a seven-point scale. Items pertaining to R&D divestiture were dropped, leaving a four-item construct.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = 0% of assets divested over total assets; 7 = 91-100% of assets divested)

description: Respondents' assessment of the extent to which the acquisition had a positive impact on product costs and input prices. The two indicators are reflective and based on a five-point scale, with one for negative impact and five for positive impact.
scale: five-point scale (1 = negative impact, 5 = positive impact)

description: Revenue enhancement potential captured through two indicators: extension of product lines and broadening of geographical coverage. These items are reflective and based on a five-point scale, with one for negative impact and five for positive impact.
scale: five-point scale (1 = negative impact, 5 = positive impact)

description: Revenue enhancement potential captured through two indicators: improvement of product innovation capabilities and improvement of development design cycle (time to market). These items are reflective and based on a five-point scale, with one for negative impact and five for positive impact.
scale: five-point scale (1 = negative impact, 5 = positive impact)

description: Self-reported measures of changes in market shares, sales, intrinsic profitability, and relative profitability compared to industry average since the acquisition. These indicators, based on a five-point scale, are measured from a consolidated standpoint, with one indicating significant decline and five significant increase, and from a separate standpoint for the target and the acquirer, respectively; the retained measure of acquisition performance used the average of these three values. The four-item construct is reflective.
scale: five-point scale (1 = significant decline, 5 = significant increase)

description: Extent to which the acquirer redeployed its resources to the target after the acquisition, captured through five types of intangible resources. Each indicator measures the magnitude of resource redeployment following the acquisition with a range from 1 to 5, with 1 = not transferred at all and 5 = transferred to a very large extent. The five indicators are reflective.
scale: 1 = not transferred at all; 5 = transferred to a very large extent

description: Extent to which the target redeployed its resources to the acquirer after the acquisition, captured through five types of intangible resources. Each indicator measures the magnitude of resource redeployment following the acquisition with a range from 1 to 5, with 1 = not transferred at all and 5 = transferred to a very large extent. The five indicators are reflective.
scale: 1 = not transferred at all; 5 = transferred to a very large extent

description: Each informant was asked to categorize the price terms of their BCC into one of four ordered categories representing an increasing level of incompleteness in the price structure paid for the procured component. Category 1 (fixed prices) is the most complete because no allowance is made for adjusting the initial price; category 2 uses predetermined formulae based on exogenous indicators (e.g., producer price indices or commodity price indices) or predetermined gain-sharing formulaic adjustments; category 3 adjusts the initial price through negotiated adjustments rather than predetermined formulae; category 4 is the most incomplete because neither the initial anchor point nor the adjustment formulae are fixed, including cases in which price is not explicitly included in the initial contract. The measure is derived from the one used in Crocker and Reynolds (1993).

Interface complexity is measured by a one-item scale derived from Bensaou and Anderson (1999) that captures the extent to which the interface between the branded component and other components in the end product is intricate.

Technological uncertainty is measured by a three-item scale derived from Heide and John (1990) that captures the extent to which the technical aspects related to design and development of the focal branded component are unpredictable.

variable_name: Preexisting differentiation of the vendor brand
description: The measure is the residual from an ordinary least squares regression of realized differentiation on variables that generate differentiation gains during the ex post contract execution stage: the vendor's specific investments, the OEM's specific investments, coordination norms, flexibility norms, and relative size of the parties. Following the approach used to decompose the capitalized value of the firm into tangible and intangible factors, realized differentiation is assumed to be the sum of preexisting differentiation and ex post differentiation, so the expected value of the regression proxies the within-contract portion and the residual measures the differentiation gains not correlated with relationship-specific investments undertaken during contract execution. The residual is denoted as the measure of the preexisting capability that the vendor brings to the table at the contract-writing stage.

OEM's brand strength is a four-item, semantic differential scale that captures the OEM's strength in its own customer market for its most important product line in which the branded component is incorporated.

Realized differentiation is a four-item scale used by Ghosh and John (2005) that captures the extent to which the branded component improves the customer's perceptions of the OEM's product. The measure captures both the preexisting differentiation of the vendor brand and the differentiation provided by the within-contract customization activities.

A rural hospital changed to provide other types of health care services, including outpatient facilities and specialized inpatient facilities (long-term care, substance abuse). Community hospitals that closed but reopened as health care providers within one year of closure were classified as conversions; if the time span from closure to reopening exceeded one year, the event was classified as a closure. An initial inventory of conversion events was compiled by comparing annual changes in hospital status in the AHA annual surveys and then reviewed and modified by representatives in all 50 state hospital associations.

variable_name: Demand (total population; percent of population age 65 or older; per capita income)
description: Demand for hospital services was measured by three variables: population and percent of population age 65 or older are measures of general demand for hospital services (i.e., potential patients), and per capita income reflects the general munificence of the market and the ability of the population to afford hospital services. These demand measures were constructed by averaging the values of the focal and contiguous counties to account for services provided for patients from neighboring counties.

Straight-line distance from the focal rural hospital to the nearest hospital provider (rural or urban), computed from a latitude and longitude listing of all community hospital addresses. The authors considered proximity a better measure of the potential for competition than more traditional measures such as market density or concentration, because of sparse populations and the small number of competitors in most rural markets.

Relative competitive position on size, calculated with a variant of the Euclidean distance that indicates how much an individual hospital differed from other hospitals in its market. The focal hospital's value on size is compared with the value of each other hospital in the market, so the measure reflects the direction of the difference and whether the focal hospital was positioned above or below the market average. The specification equation itself is not readable in the available text.

Scales measuring the relative number of services that hospitals provide in three areas: diagnostic, inpatient, and outpatient services. The authors began with the list of services that appeared consistently in the AHA survey for each year, asked several health care experts to group these services into common domains, used multidimensional scaling because the service items are binary, and used confirmatory factor analysis and Cronbach alpha tests to check the resulting scales. Relative competitive advantage due to service mix was then calculated with a variant of the Euclidean distance comparing the focal hospital with other hospitals in its market; the specification equation itself is not readable in the available text.

Whether each rural hospital held an accreditation from the Joint Commission on Health Care Organizations (JCAHO). This accreditation is the field's primary regulatory approach to increase reliability in the production of hospital services and was used to test H5 on the effects of conformity to regulations.

Pro-competition legislation that focused on rural hospitals in the 1980s, intended to promote competition by reducing or eliminating regulatory barriers to entry into new markets. Several states encouraged hospitals to diversify into nontraditional services (e.g., nursing homes), assuming that diversification would enable rural hospitals to convert to provide more financially viable services.

Strength of states' anti-competition regulation, assessed with a five-item index of Certificate of Need laws that measures variance in both breadth and stringency. Three of the five dimensions measure the breadth of Certificate of Need laws (what services or capital expenditures are covered); each of the five dimensions is rated on a scale from 0 to 3, on which 0 indicates that the law did not cover a dimension and 3 indicates that the law was most stringent. Values for the five dimensions were summed to create an index that ranges from 0 to 15. The measure was available only for one year of the study period, but these regulations changed very little in the study period.
time_window: available only for one year of the study period

variable_name: Capital funds for rural hospitals; reduction in regulation to reduce operating expenses
description: Two types of state legislation used to test the effects of state intervention to support current templates. Capital fund laws provided low-interest loans for rural hospitals to purchase capital equipment (e.g., advanced diagnostic technology) that might attract patients, seeking to inhibit divergent change by providing funds needed to maintain current work. Other legislation reduced the regulatory burden on rural hospitals (for example, allowing continuous physician coverage through on-call physicians rather than on-site), thereby indirectly improving their financial status.

State legislation that provided rural hospitals with capital enabling them to move from providing acute inpatient care to sub-acute care exclusively, i.e., only outpatient care or long-term care (e.g., nursing homes). This measure was used to test H7b on the effects of state intervention in promoting divergent change.

Hospital ownership measured by a series of dummy variables representing private for-profit, public (state or local government), and private not-for-profit ownership; private non-profit is the omitted category. Ownership is treated as a dimension of institutional norms about property rights that specify who owns organizational assets and shape whether owners will use them for divergent change.

Membership in a multihospital system, used as a measure of norms specifying system-level, centralized governance versus local governance of a hospital. Measured with a dummy variable, where membership is indicated and non-membership is not.

The rate of rural hospital conversion in each state, used to measure the availability of nonlocal models of divergent change for a focal hospital to imitate. Rural hospitals that have converted in a given state provide an especially likely role model for other hospitals in that state because so much health care regulation is state-specific.

Measured by content analysis of media coverage about the firm: newspaper articles identified from the China Core Newspapers Full-text Database covering the focal firms over the period of 1 year before the date the crises occurred. Each article was coded as favorable, neutral, or unfavorable from the numbers of positive, negative, and neutral phrases concerning the focal firm; if positive phrases were at least two-thirds of the total phrases the article was coded as positive, if negative phrases were at least two-thirds it was coded as negative, otherwise neutral. The overall rating of media coverage was then estimated using the Janis-Fader coefficient of imbalance, whose range is -1 to 1, where -1 indicates all unfavorable coverage and 1 indicates all favorable coverage.

Measured from the investors' perspective as the number of posts concerning a firm in an online stock forum, Guba, over a 1-year period before the crises. The natural logarithm transformation of this variable was taken to achieve a univariate normal distribution.

Cumulative abnormal adjusted return (CAR) associated with a crisis over a 3-day (-1, 1) time window. Abnormal returns refer to unexpected percentage differences between the normal expected return and the actual return, with the normal expected return captured by the market model (the specification is not readable in the extracted text); in that model the intercept and systematic risk are ordinary least squares parameter estimates and the market portfolio return is the independent variable. The 3-day CAR is the cumulative daily abnormal return over the 3-day event window. Expected returns were calculated for a period of 128 to 8 trading days prior to the crisis event (a total of 120 trading days), and daily market return volatility was calculated using the Shanghai Stock Exchange Composite Index and the Shenzhen Stock Exchange Component Index with the equal weight average method.
time_window: 3-day event window (-1, 1); estimation window 128 to 8 trading days prior to the crisis

description: Measured by reviewing news articles of each crisis on the day of the crisis and coding each crisis with Coombs' (2004) coding scheme into types including product harms, product defects, product tampering, malicious rumors, technical accidents, organizational misdeeds, environment spill, stealth pollution, and financial fraud. The different types of crises were then classified into three clusters: the victim cluster (coded as 1), the accidental cluster (coded as 2), and the intentional cluster (coded as 3), so the higher the score, the more the attribution of crisis responsibility to the focal firm.

A firm was identified as employing a CEO/COO duo when an executive other than the CEO held the COO/president title and served primarily as a COO rather than an heir apparent. The 'four-year age rule' distinguished the two: a COO/president who was older than the CEO, or no more than four years younger than the CEO, was designated as a COO, whereas a COO/president more than four years younger than the CEO was coded as an heir apparent. Firms were classified using 1998 data; 15 percent of sample firms employed a COO.
Average return on assets for the period between 1999 and 2001, following Hambrick and Cannella (2004). The average ROA for firms in this sample was 5.4 percent.

Average market-to-book ratio for the period between 1999 and 2001. The MTB ratio is defined as the market value of the firm's common equity divided by the book value of equity, and captures the premium that stockholders place on the firm's equity. The average MTB ratio in the sample was 4.8.

Measured with Blau's (1977) heterogeneity index and the categorization criteria outlined in Wiersema and Bantel (1992). It captures the extent to which TMT members possess a variety of functional backgrounds, and was coded using 1998 data.

Captures the extent to which executives share common organizational experiences, and was calculated as the standard deviation of the TMT's organizational tenure divided by the mean. It is one of two items used to capture the overarching concept of TMT tenure heterogeneity.

The extent to which executives have shared common experiences as members of the TMT, calculated as the standard deviation of the TMT's team tenure divided by the mean. It is one of two items used to capture the overarching concept of TMT tenure heterogeneity.
Measured as the average age of TMT members, coded using 1998 data.

Indicator variable that takes a value of one if the household welcomed a new son, and zero if there was no newborn during the three-year interval between two consecutive survey waves. New family members were identified from the household roster: a new male member aged three years or younger recorded in a later wave was inferred to have been born between the two waves.
time_window: three-year interval between two consecutive survey waves

description: Indicator variable that takes a value of one if the household welcomed a new daughter, and zero if there was no newborn during the three-year interval between two consecutive survey waves. Like the male indicator, it is built from the household roster by identifying new female members aged three years or younger in the later wave.
time_window: three-year interval between two consecutive survey waves

description: Binary variable that takes a value of one if the household reported implementing any new technology concerning new crop varieties and types, the construction of water-harvesting infrastructures, or implementations of soil and water conservation strategies, and zero otherwise. It is built from the survey question asking what respondents did to protect themselves, their family, or their community from climate change, and it is designed to capture decisions requiring a longer-term horizon. Changing planting dates, also listed among the survey adjustments, is treated as a management decision rather than technology adoption and is excluded from the indicator.
time_window: three-year interval between two consecutive survey waves

description: Built with the morphing technology from standard frontal pictures of all sample car models. Each car's frontal image was normalized by setting the width of the car as one unit without changing the relative height-to-width ratio, and 50 design points were extracted and represented by coordinate values. The automaker morph was the mean position of each of the 50 design points across all car models of the same automaker in each year; within-organization distinctiveness is the Euclidean distance between a car model's design points and the corresponding points of its automaker's morph.

Calculated as the Euclidean distance between an automaker's morph and the car morph, where the automaker morph is the average design of all car models produced by the automaker in a year and the car morph is the average design of all car models in the automotive industry in that year. Both morphs are defined by the mean positions of the 50 design points.

The number of units (in thousands of units) of each car model sold in the U.S. market in each year of the sample period. Market share and sales revenue were used as two alternative variables of market performance in robustness checks.
time_window: each year of the sample period

description: Dummy variable with 1 indicating that one or more evaluators in the focal evaluator's group were working at the two top universities and that one or more members of the focal venture founding team graduated from the two top universities. The value is 1 for both similar (top-university) and dissimilar (non-top-university) evaluators in such a group, whereas the dyad-level evaluator-venture similarity equals 1 only for the similar evaluators. Similarity is constructed on evaluators who were working at, rather than graduated from, the two top universities, and Tsinghua and Peking University are treated as one status group.

Continuous variable measured by the total score that a venture received from each evaluator as an overall assessment. Each evaluator individually evaluated the venture and gave a score after the presentation and the group discussion; the score of each evaluator was not visible to other evaluators and could not be changed later.

Count of instances in which the focal evaluator group asks a substantial number of questions in a row with a negative tone, constructed from transcripts of video recordings. Transcripts were partitioned into paragraphs with natural language processing algorithms developed by iFlytek; conversational paragraphs containing questions were identified; a paragraph was marked as containing challenging questions when there were four or more questions in a row and at least one negative assertion, with negative assertions identified by negation words (no, not, are not; 'bu', 'bushi', 'nandao' in Chinese). The variable counts the conversational paragraphs satisfying this criterion.

Focal firm and rival actions were measured across five types: pricing, capacity, geographic, marketing, and product introductions. Firm total actions or activity was calculated by simply summing the number of all five actions for a focal firm in a given year. Actions were identified and coded by structured content analysis of newspaper and trade magazine articles, and only the earliest report of an action was entered into the database.
time_window: same year as the performance measure

description: Rival total actions or competitive activity was operationalized by subtracting a focal firm's total number of actions in a given year from the total number of actions taken by all competitors in a focal industry. The rival set was officially defined as all the other firms competing in the focal firm's industry for the year under consideration.
time_window: same year as the performance measure

description: Rival firm action speed quantified the average length of time it took rivals to act after a focal firm acted. The authors determined the number of days between each firm action and the first rival action and then averaged those scores for each focal firm for each year. Finally, the reciprocal of this value was taken so that high values equate to fast rival action speed and low values to slow rival action speed.
time_window: same year as the performance measure

description: Focal firm performance was operationalized with accounting measures of return on sales (ROS) and return on assets (ROA) in the same year as the action measure. Financial data were collected from Standard & Poor's Compustat and, where necessary, adjusted to remove contributions from non-U.S. operations so that the financial figures matched the actions accounted for in the study.
time_window: same year as the action measure

description: Focal firm performance was operationalized with accounting measures of return on sales (ROS) and return on assets (ROA) in the same year as the action measure. Financial data were collected from Standard & Poor's Compustat and, where necessary, adjusted to remove contributions from non-U.S. operations so that the financial figures matched the actions accounted for in the study.
time_window: same year as the action measure

description: Industry concentration was calculated as the Herfindahl measure of the market shares of the firms in each industry for each year. This measure served as an independent or control variable in all regressions and was also interacted with firm actions, rival actions, and rival action speed in tests of Hypotheses 2a-2c.

Industry demand was measured as industry growth, defined as the percent change in sales from the previous year to a focal year. It served as an independent or control variable in all regressions and was also interacted with firm actions, rival actions, and rival action speed in tests of Hypotheses 3a-3c.

Relative market position was measured as rank order based on market share for each firm in each industry for each year. This variable was used as an independent or a control variable in all regressions and was also interacted with firm actions, rival actions, and rival action speed in testing Hypotheses 4a-4c.

The risk-adjusted financial performance of a given SRI fund in a given month. RAP is the average monthly return, measured as the percentage change in a fund's market value from the beginning to the end of a month, adjusted by the fund's specific beta. The authors use the CAPM with the S&P 500 as the market index to compute beta from monthly returns, and RAP is the difference between the fund's risk premium and its expected return given its beta and the market's risk premium. The appendix states that RAP captures the fund's return over and above what is expected based upon its beta, and the authors note that returns compiled by CRSP and used in the analyses do not factor in expense ratios.

The fund's choice of number of social screens applied to its investment portfolio, drawn from the 12 types of screens listed by the Social Investment Forum. A value of 12 indicates that the fund employs all 12 screens, whereas a value of 1 indicates that it uses only one of the 12 available screens. The number of screens employed proxies for the extent of diversification of the fund: a large value indicates an increasingly narrow SRI portfolio, while a small value reflects a more diversified portfolio. The authors acknowledge that the additive variable is a coarse proxy because each screen may not contribute equally to the ability to diversify.

Dichotomous variable created to test Hypothesis 2; it equals one if the fund screened out firms based on labor relations criteria and zero otherwise. It is one of the variables entered in the regressions on screening strategies.

Dichotomous variable defined along with labor relations as the two workforce-related screening variables used to test Hypothesis 2; it takes a value of one if the fund screened out firms on equal employment criteria and zero otherwise.

Dichotomous variable created as a test of Hypothesis 3; it received a value of one if the fund screened out firms based on what it deemed as a poor community record, and zero otherwise. It is entered in the regressions on screening strategies.

Dichotomous variable created as a test of Hypothesis 3; it received a value of one if the fund screened out firms based on what it deemed as a poor community record, and zero otherwise. The authors report no systematic relationship between this variable and performance.
Dichotomous variable defined in order to test Hypothesis 4; the authors assigned a value of one if a fund screened out firms based on environmental performance, and zero otherwise.

Return on investment is one of the four retained measures of IJV performance. The performance figures were obtained from the balance sheets and income statements that IJVs submitted to the Provincial Commission of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade, which had been audited by independent certified public accountants. With the exception of operational risk, this measure is entered in SAS after being averaged over multiple years.

Local market expansion is measured by local sales revenue over investment, one of the four retained measures of IJV performance. The figures come from the audited balance sheets and income statements that IJVs submitted to the Provincial Commission of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade. The measure is averaged over multiple years before being entered in SAS.

Export is measured by export revenue over investment, one of the four retained measures of IJV performance. The figures come from the audited balance sheets and income statements that IJVs submitted to the Provincial Commission of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade. The measure is averaged over multiple years before being entered in SAS.

Operational risk facing IJVs is measured by computing the geometric average of the standard deviations of venture performance measures; the authors state that this index is equivalent to the accountingbased risk calculation used in the strategic management literature. A geometric average is used instead of simple multiplication of performance variations because the latter could produce extreme scores in a highly dynamic environment. Unlike the other three performance measures, it is not averaged over multiple years in the same way.

A local firm's absorptive ability is measured by the percentage of professional and technological personnel among the total number of employees, following the findings of Jia (1991) and Kumar (1995) that this percentage mirrors a firm's ability to learn technological and organizational skills.

A categorical (dummy) measure indicating whether the IJV is related (vertical or horizontal) to its local parent firm, coded 1 if related and 0 otherwise. This information is obtained from the Directory of Foreign-Invested Enterprises in Jiangsu Province.
The local partner's market power was its firm sales divided by total industry sales (scaled by 1/10,000) in the year before the IJV was formed.
A dummy variable for the local partner's ownership form, coded 1 if state-owned and 0 if privately or collectively owned.
The local partner's international experience was the number of years it had been involved, directly or indirectly, in international trading or investment before the IJV was formed.
The local partner's market experience was the number of years it had operated in the market before the IJV was formed.

Organizational size is the local partner's total number of employees, expressed in hundreds. Local partner attributes were obtained from the Directory of Foreign-Invested Enterprises in Jiangsu Province and related documents from the Provincial Commission of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade.

Organizational collaboration is the number of years for which the local and foreign partners had cooperated before the IJV was formed. Local partner attributes were obtained from the Directory of Foreign-Invested Enterprises in Jiangsu Province and related documents from the Provincial Commission of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade.
level: Partner dyad (local partner and its foreign partner)
time_window: Before IJV formation (IJVs formed as of end of 1986)

description: The natural log of the cumulative amount of public resources received by a firm under the GPS scheme as of the end of the preceding year; counting started in 1994 to estimate the full amounts each firm was eligible for. A quadratic term, sponsorship squared, was added to test a curvilinear effect. Alternative specifications using mean-centered variables suggested that collinearity was not a concern.
time_window: cumulative, as of the end of the preceding year (counted from 1994)

description: The firm's annual return on investment, computed as a ratio of theatrical revenues (box office) over production costs. Production costs were obtained by summing up production budgets, capturing all the direct expenses required to produce a film as well as the overhead costs allocated by the firm to the films it produces. Because box office numbers are skewed, the natural log of the variable was taken and standardized.

A Herfindahl-Hirschman index used to capture scope, where si is the share of a firm's production allocated to a given genre in the focal year. The variable is equal to 0 when a firm is a specialist (si = 1) and tends to 1 as a firm becomes more generalist (si tends to 0). The specific expression was not readable in the text.

Average consumer ratings, used to capture where firms stood on a continuum ranging from pure mainstream players with a strong market orientation to art-house producers for whom films are cultural pieces. Following McPhee's theory of exposure, market-oriented firms will receive, on average, higher ratings than other firms.

The average number of cast members among the five highest-grossing actors in the three preceding years; for a given level of budget, the higher the number of stars, the more the firm relies on externally engaged rather than internal idiosyncratic resources. The three-year window is typical in film studies due to the relatively short-lived status of film stars.

variable_name: initial filing of an anti-dumping petition
description: An event date: the date the anti-dumping petition was initially filed with the Department of Commerce by a company or group of companies on behalf of the domestic industry. Petition events were identified from the 626 filings reported in the USITC Annual Reports for fiscal years 1980 through 1992 and cross-referenced with those recorded by the International Trade Administration of the Department of Commerce; petitioner names were retrieved from Federal Register notices. Publicly held companies (or their majority-owned subsidiaries) trading on the New York, American, or NASDAQ exchanges accounted for 147 filing events; after eliminating nine filing events for missing financial return data and four for confounding events, 134 filing events by 88 companies remained.

The International Trade Commission's ruling on the petition, coded as affirmative or negative, at each of the two decision stages. At the preliminary determination an affirmative ruling results in the imposition of an anti-dumping duty and a negative ruling terminates the process; at the final determination an affirmative ruling results in a long-term anti-dumping duty and a negative ruling eliminates the earlier duty and terminates the process. Subsamples of petitioners based on these decisions are labelled 'winners' (affirmative) and 'losers' (negative).

The unanticipated change in a petitioning firm's security price around an event, isolated with the market model: the actual return for the security minus the market-adjusted, or normal, return over the event period. Market model parameters are estimated with ordinary least squares over the period from 250 trading days prior to the event to 50 trading days prior to the event, and the error term is assumed to capture the price change associated with the event. The main analysis uses a 3-day event period extending from 2 days prior to the event until the day of the event. Significance tests are based on standardized abnormal returns aggregated across firms into an average standardized cumulative abnormal return and tested with a Z-statistic. The formula blocks in the extracted text are unreadable.
time_window: 3-day event period (2 days prior to the event through the day of the event)

description: The change in market valuation associated with an event, calculated using the current shares outstanding, the closing security price on the day prior to the event window, and the change in security price over the event window; the average of the changes in market capitalization across firms was then computed. The appendix adds that the change in market valuation can also be estimated by multiplying the firm's market capitalization on the day preceding the event window by the cumulative standardized abnormal return over the event period.

Dispositional optimism is measured with the revised Life Orientation Test (LOT-R) developed by Scheier et al. (1994), a self-report questionnaire whose 10 items include three that measure optimism (questions 1, 4, and 10), three that measure pessimism (questions 3, 7, and 9), and four fillers (questions 2, 5, 6, and 8). Respondents rate each item on a five-point scale: 'strongly disagree' (zero points), 'disagree' (one point), 'neutral' (two points), 'agree' (three points), or 'strongly agree' (four points). The final measure is computed by summing the scores of the optimism and pessimism questions, with the latter reverse-coded.

Negative feedback is operationalized as an indicator set to one if the player received negative feedback on the previous round's task performance, and is set to zero if the player was in the no-feedback treatment. Negative feedback consists of communicating that a player lost the immediately preceding round of competition.

A continuous measure of the difference between the expected number of correct answers in the next round and the expected number of correct answers in the previous round. The variable is coded such that greater values correspond to larger downward adjustments in expected task performance.

Ln R&D inputs is computed as the logarithm of one plus the amount of a firm's R&D expenditures. The addition of one prevents losing, when taking the log, those observations with zero R&D expenditures.
An indicator set equal to one if the firm has been granted any patents and set to zero otherwise.

An alternative measure of innovation output that indicates whether the company has introduced any product or process innovations. It is used to capture innovation output even among companies that do not file patents on their innovation.

Shortest path, that is, the minimum number of edges in the collaboration network, between any of the academic authors of the paper and any of the company inventors of the patent at the patent filing year. In a small percentage of the paper-patent dyads (1.7%) there is no connection between any of the inventors and authors and social_dist is assigned a value of nine because eight is the maximum observed value in the data set. To avoid imposing a linear functional-form assumption the authors also use a series of binary indicators from social_dist_0 to social_dist_5_or_more, with social_dist_0 as the reference category in the main specification. No logarithmic transformation is applied to social_dist to maintain ease of interpretation.

Dummy equal to one if paper i is cited by patent k and zero if the patent instead cites another paper from the same twin. Each citing patent is paired with both the cited and the uncited twin paper, so that the uncited twin serves as a counterfactual or pseudocitation. Because twin papers report essentially the same scientific discovery, and U.S. patent law requires disclosure of all relevant prior art, the authors argue it is unlikely that inventors were aware of the uncited twin and deliberately chose not to cite it.

Binary variable equal to one if any coinventor of a patent has published a scientific paper in the year preceding the patent's filing. The authors use this variable to assess whether corporate inventors listed on a patent are actively engaged in scientific research at the time of patent filing.

SPECTER embeddings are computed for each paper based on its title and abstract, and the cosine similarity between corporate inventors' prior publications and the academic twin papers is calculated. At the twin-patent level the maximum of these pairwise similarity scores is taken as a proxy for the extent to which the inventor team possesses scientific expertise closely related to the focal twin discovery. A binary variable, close_paper, is set to one if this similarity measure exceeds the median value in the data set.
time_window: inventor papers published before the patent filing year

description: The dependent variable is the abnormal return to the acquirer around the acquisition announcement, calculated as the difference between the acquirer's actual return and the return that would have been expected had the acquisition not taken place; expected return is estimated over a 250-day period prior to the event (the estimation equation itself is not readable in the text). The abnormal return is aggregated over a two-day window consisting of the day prior to and the day of the acquisition announcement; the authors report similar results with a three-day window. The market reaction is interpreted as the market's expectation of the performance of the acquisition.

The authors state that the measure captures the ratio of external corporate venture investing to total (both internal R&D and external CVC) investing in the year the technology startup is acquired; the equation block itself is not readable in the text. CVC_it is the amount of money firm i invests in startups in the year of the focal acquisition as reported in VentureOne, and R&D_it is the amount of R&D spending of firm i in the focal acquisition year as reported in Compustat. By construction, the measure can vary from 0 to 1.

Measures the number of years that a firm invests in startups (beginning with the first year of CVC investments through the year of the acquisition) divided by the total number of years since the firm's initial CVC investment. By construction, the measure ranges from zero to one; a firm investing in every year since its initial investment scores 1.0 whereas a firm that stopped investing scores lower over time.
time_window: first CVC investment through focal acquisition year

description: Coders rated whether the act described in the story was intended to benefit (1) an isolated individual or individuals personally, (2) the individual who engaged in the unethical act, (3) the focal organization as a whole, and (4) the company where the event occurred. The first two items represent the proself unethical behavior measure and the last two items represent the pro-organizational unethical behavior measure; because the two measures were strongly inversely correlated (r = −0.80), the first measure was reverse-coded and the two measures were averaged. Lower scores indicate that the unethical act was perceived as more proself and higher scores as more pro-organizational. Coders' ratings were aggregated to the event level after establishing interrater reliability.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Coders rated how strongly they agreed or disagreed that (1) the goal of the focal organization is a moral one, (2) the work that the focal organization does has a positive social impact, and (3) the work that the focal organization does impacts people's lives in a positive way. Ratings were made on a seven-point scale and aggregated to the event level.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

variable_name: Moral judgments of the unethical behavior
description: Coders rated how strongly they agreed or disagreed that the act was (1) wrong, (2) immoral, and (3) unethical. Ratings were made on a seven-point scale, and higher values indicate an act being evaluated as more immoral. Ratings were aggregated to the event level.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Eventus was used to estimate abnormal returns following each of the 158 events using the market-adjusted model based on an equally weighted index. The baseline period against which an abnormal return is compared was −254 to −21 days before the event, and the event window was the three trading days −1, 0, +1, where 0 is the date of the published story, −1 the day before, and +1 the day after. Patell z values were significant only for this window.
time_window: event window of three trading days (−1, 0, +1); baseline period −254 to −21 days

description: For the manipulation, participants read real newspaper articles: employee theft in the proself conditions and the focal firm overcharging customers in the pro-organizational conditions. Participants then rated how strongly they agreed or disagreed that the act was intended to benefit (1) an isolated individual or individuals personally, (2) the individual who engaged in the unethical act, (3) the focal organization as a whole, and (4) the company where the event occurred. The first two items represent the proself measure and the last two the pro-organizational measure; the measures were inversely correlated (r = −0.84, p < 0.001) and the first measure was reverse-coded and averaged with the second. The continuous version of the measure was used in the main analysis.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

variable_name: Perceived morality of the organization's goals (continuous)
description: Participants rated how strongly they agreed or disagreed that (1) the goal of the focal organization is a moral one, (2) the work that the focal organization does has a positive social impact, and (3) the work that the focal organization does impacts people's lives in a positive way. For the manipulation, both low-morality conditions described an oil company (Exxon) and both high-morality conditions described a supermarket featuring organic foods (Whole Foods); the actual firm name was replaced with a short firm biography. The continuous version of the measure was used in the main analysis.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

variable_name: Moral judgments of the unethical behavior
description: Participants rated how strongly they agreed or disagreed that the act was (1) wrong, (2) immoral, and (3) unethical. Higher values indicate an act being evaluated as more immoral.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Participants anticipated what they thought the closing value of the stock for the focal firm would be the day after the newspaper story was published, predicting the percentage gain or loss in the value of the stock compared with the expected value had the news story never been published. Participants were provided with the actual expected return for the focal company the day after each story and asked to anticipate the relative return, that is, the extent to which the return would deviate in response to the event; the measure ranged from −10% to +10%. Participants were incentivized for accuracy, receiving a bonus depending on how accurate their estimate was.

The dependent variable, number of services, was obtained by counting the number of different services provided by each firm. The list of 15 business advisory services was developed together with a group of seven experienced authorized accountants and was broadly similar to the list developed by Bagchi-Sen and Kuechler (2000), except that it was somewhat more exhaustive. The variable ranges from 0 to 15; most practices (55%) supplied 5-9 services, 24% supplied fewer than this, four practices did not provide any business advisory services at all, and three practices provided all 15 services.

variable_name: percentage of staff with an accounting diploma
description: The first of two operationalizations of the heterogeneity of human capital is the percentage of front-line staff with an accounting diploma, capturing the degree to which front-line staff are authorized accountants. The authors reasoned that the greater the degree to which a practice comprises authorized accountants the narrower the scope of business advisory services.

variable_name: percentage of staff with a bachelor's degree
description: The second operationalization is the percentage of front-line staff who have a bachelor's degree level of education. A bachelor's degree is treated as a source of heterogeneity indicative of an ability to handle complex information, engage in boundary-spanning activities, and be more receptive to the adoption of innovations, so that greater proportions of degree-level staff are expected to broaden the scope of business advisory services.

Respondents to the questionnaire were asked to indicate if their practice had devised a skills development plan. Responses to this question were coded as 0 for 'no' and 1 for 'yes' in order to form a dummy variable. Forty-five percent of the practices confirmed that they had implemented such a plan.

Respondents were asked to indicate the degree to which their practices cooperate with external service providers within seven specified industries: lawyers, external auditors, consultancies, software providers, IT-firms, banks, and insurance companies. Based on responses to this seven-fold list, the authors counted the number of industries in which the practice had alliance partners to create a measure for the range of external alliances. The variable ranges from zero, where 14% of the practices do not have any alliances at all, to seven, where 6% have alliances in all of the seven industries; on average the practices in the dataset have alliances in 2.8 of these industries.

The practice's client composition is measured by the proportion of gross income obtained from relatively large client firms, large clients being defined as those having more than 20 employees. In the present sample, 35 percent of the practices report that they serve clients with more than 20 employees, and on average practices obtain 20 percent of gross income from clients with more than 20 employees.

variable_name: intention of seeking out new markets or launching new services
description: Strategic intent was measured in part by using an item that maps the absence of intent and an item that measures its presence, both on a four-point scale. Practices responded to the statements 'We will not seek out new markets or launch new services unless forced to do so' and 'We want to strengthen our market position and search for new market opportunities through the continuous development of our services'. Scores for the first item were subtracted from the second to form an index (Cronbach's alpha = 0.68).
scale: four-point scale items combined into an index

description: The foreign sales ratio, defined as a firm's foreign sales divided by its total sales, used to capture the degree of a firm's international diversification. Annual data on firms' foreign sales were taken from COMPUSTAT's geographic segment database, where export sales are not consistently reported separately from sales made by a firm's foreign-based subsidiaries, so the ratio includes both types of foreign sales activity.

An entropy measure of a firm's sales shares in different geographic areas, following Hitt et al. (1997), used to capture the scope of a firm's international diversification. Four comparable geographic areas are identified: Domestic (United States), Asia and Pacific, Europe, and a residual 'other' region, since the COMPUSTAT database limits the total number of geographic regions a firm can report.

Import competition is measured by the ratio of imports to total domestic consumption in the four-digit SIC core industry of the firm. Annual data on import competition by four-digit SIC were provided by Peter Schott (Bernard et al., 2006). A lack of detailed industry data after 1994 on foreign domestic production in the United States constrained the authors to capture foreign competition solely in terms of import competition.
level: industry-year (four-digit SIC core industry of the firm)

description: A world measure of industry trade volume used to capture the extent of an industry's international trade linkages, calculated using values of world trade and world production; since world imports equal world exports, the measure is equivalent to world exports plus world imports divided by world industry sales. Annual data on world industry sales and world industry imports were derived from the World Bank's Trade and Production database (Nicita and Olarreaga, 2001).
level: industry-year (four-digit SIC core industry of the firm)

description: The index of intra-industry trade first developed by Grubel and Lloyd (1975), which indicates the fraction of total trade volume in an industry that is 'matching' or two-way trade and thus captures the two-way exchange of goods within an industry category. Values of the index range from zero to one, with higher values indicative of industries having greater global integration of value-added activities across national boundaries. Values were calculated for each four-digit SIC industry using annual data on U.S. exports and U.S. imports taken from the United Nations Trade Data Bank; the algebraic specification of the index is printed as a formula block that is unreadable in the available text.
level: industry-year (four-digit SIC core industry of the firm)

description: Jacquemin and Berry's (1979) entropy measure of diversification was used to measure the extent of diversity in a firm's lines of business. It was computed using data on the firm's sales in each of 10 possible four-digit SIC businesses as reported by the COMPUSTAT Line of Business database, and is lagged one period in the models.

Sample incumbent carriers are grouped by market position into six FSCs (American, Continental, Delta, Northwest, United, and US Airways) and five LCCs (JetBlue, AirTran, ExpressJet, Midwest, and Alaska). The authors state that in the airline industry there is a clear mapping between market positions and airlines and that Federal Aviation Administration statistics are broken down by the categories of FSCs and LCCs. Hypothesis tests are run on the FSC and LCC subsamples separately.

variable_name: SW threat and SW entry time dummies
description: A set of mutually exclusive time dummies for periods including and surrounding the quarter when Southwest threatened a route and for periods including and after Southwest entered the route. The dummies are collapsed into 1–10 Q before SW threat, 0–12 Q after SW threat, and 0–12 Q after SW entry. Coefficients reflect the relative size of the dependent variable in each dummy period relative to its average value in the excluded period, that is, the 12th and 11th quarters before the quarter of Southwest's threat.
time_window: carrier-route-month; up to 10 quarters before and 12 quarters after the threat

description: The total number of installed seats on flights flown by carrier i on route r (a directional origin–destination pair) at time t. Because carriers had different baseline values, the variable is log-transformed to reduce value dispersion; the log transformation also makes coefficients interpretable as percentage changes in the dependent variable with a unit change in the independent variable. Estimated at the carrier-route-month level on Sample 3, which is based on the OAG dataset.

FSCs' threatened routes were separated into those expected to have a large number of business travelers and those expected to have a large number of leisure travelers, using Bureau of Economic Analysis and Census Bureau information about total personal income, total personal income coming from lodging and food services, and total number of business establishments in the county where an airport is located. Threatened routes expected to have a large number of non-business travelers are routes that either originated from or arrived at a county with an above-median percentage of personal income coming from lodging and food services but a below-median number of business establishments; other routes are more likely to attract business travelers.

For the complementarity test the sample of FSCs' threatened routes was separated into routes that connect to hubs with a large number of international flights, routes that connect to hubs with few international flights, and non-hub routes. Domestic routes connecting to the incumbent's international hubs are those arriving at domestic airports with a large number of international flights operated by the FSC incumbent; entry by an LCC there is expected to increase passengers connecting to the incumbent's international flights (which LCCs do not serve).

Implementation in 2013 in each MNE subunit of actions related to three CSR practices (safety management, employment of female managers, preservation of environmental biodiversity). Among 25 actions, 8 relate to occupational health and safety management, 8 to the employment of female managers and 9 to environmental biodiversity; respondents assessed the level of their unit's implementation of each action on a 7-point Likert scale from 0 'not at all' to 6 'to a very great extent'. For a subunit with k respondents, the unique yearly action implementation level was generated for each action by averaging the responses to the corresponding questionnaire item. A confirmatory factor analysis among the eight or nine actions of each practice yielded factors used to weight the actions into the practice-level variable.
scale: 0 to 6 (7-point Likert: 0 = not at all, 6 = to a very great extent)

description: Derived from six items in the 2012 survey (two per CSR practice). Respondents graded the influence of the corporate and branch headquarters' demands on their performance regarding each practice on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 0 'no influence' to 6 'very strong influence'. The two items per CSR practice (branch and corporate headquarters) reflect the same construct (Cronbach alpha of 0.94); for each observation the responses given by the managers of the corresponding subunit about the two items were averaged.
scale: 0 to 6 (7-point Likert: 0 = no influence, 6 = very strong influence)

description: The average level of implementation by the subunit's peers during 2012 for each of the 25 actions. Subunits were considered peers if they belonged to the same operating branch of the MNE. The variable was moved from the action level to the practice level by weighting the actions according to the loadings obtained in the confirmatory factor analysis.

Generated from six items in the 2012 survey, with two questions for each of the three CSR practices (safety management, employment of female managers, preservation of environmental biodiversity). The items, adapted from Choi and Price (2005), were answered on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 'strongly disagree' to 7 'strongly agree', with 4 being 'neutral'. A principal component analysis confirmed that the two items reflective of each of the three practices loaded onto one factor, and observations were generated at the subunit x practice level by averaging the responses given by the subunit's managers on each practice.
scale: 1 to 7 (7-point Likert: 1 = strongly disagree, 4 = neutral, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Organizational distance is measured by the subsidiary's ownership level in the group pyramid, where apex firms are at level 1 and affiliates controlled directly by level 1 firms are at level 2, and so on. In the World Management Survey regressions the variable enters as ln(ownership level).

The affiliate's ownership level in the group, where the apex firm is at level one; organizational distance is ownership level minus one. Levels are assigned by the algorithm that builds parent-subsidiary control chains from raw ownership data.

The aggregate survey response to the World Management Survey autonomy questions, with higher values indicating greater subsidiary autonomy. The disaggregated questions cover hiring, investment, sales and marketing, and new product introduction decisions.

variable_name: Hierarchy levels to CEO (WMS label: level2ceo)
description: The number of hierarchical layers that separate a subsidiary manager from central headquarters, which the authors assume is located in the apex firm (WMS question: number of levels in the firm between the shopfloor and the CEO). Higher scores imply greater autonomy for the subsidiary.

variable_name: Share HQ managers on site (WMS label: onsite)
