description: The share of headquarters managers that are at the subsidiary site (WMS question: is CHQ on the site being interviewed?). Lower scores imply greater autonomy for the subsidiary.
The largest capital investment the plant could make without prior authorization from central headquarters, entered in logs. Higher values indicate greater investment autonomy.

World Management Survey questions on goal setting: the motivation behind goals and how they are cascaded down to individual workers, and what staff would say if asked about individual targets. Higher values indicate goals that are more clearly specified and measurable.

variable_name: Performance review (WMS labels: perf2, perf3, perf4, perf5)
description: World Management Survey questions on internal performance review: the indicators used for performance tracking, how frequently performance indicators are reviewed, how performance review meetings are structured, and what would happen if a follow-up plan agreed in a meeting were not enacted. Higher values indicate more measurable indicators and more frequent, better structured and more consequential reviews.

variable_name: group affiliate (relative to matched standalone control)
description: Firms in the sample are affiliates of West European corporate groups; each affiliate is matched with a comparable standalone firm based on exact match on three-digit SIC industry code, year of incorporation and country and a continuous match on sales. The dependent variable is the difference in 3-year growth rate between an affiliated firm and its standalone control.

variable_name: sales growth affiliate - sales growth standalone
description: The difference in 3-year sales growth rates between a focal affiliate and its matched standalone control. Relative responsiveness to industry conditions is estimated from the interaction between ownership level and the 3-year industry sales growth rate of the industry in which the focal firm and its matched standalone operate.
A dummy variable that receives the value of one for affiliates that are in the same 3-digit SIC code as the apex firms, and zero for all the other affiliates.

A dummy variable that receives the value of one for affiliates with managers that have the same last name as at least one shareholder that owns at least 5% of the total group assets, and zero for all the other affiliates.

A dummy variable that receives the value of one for affiliates with a manager's ethnicity that is the same as the ethnicity of at least one manager of the apex firm, and zero for all the other affiliates. Manager ethnicity is inferred from last names using the OriginsInfo database.
A dummy variable that receives the value of one for affiliates with at least one board member who is also a board member of the apex firm, and zero for all the other affiliates.
A dummy variable that receives the value of one for affiliates with a common name as the apex firm, and zero for all the other affiliates.
A dummy variable that receives the value of one for affiliates that are in the same 4-digit Nomenclature of Territorial Units (NUTS) code as the apex firm, and zero for all the other affiliates.

variable_name: Compact, significant increases in R&D expenditure
description: Computed in four steps. First, a GARCH model estimates the firm-level R&D expenditure trend over time and its residuals. Second, the residuals are normalized into studentized residuals. Third, the maximum of the absolute values of the firm's residuals is taken. Fourth, if the residual with the largest absolute value is positive, the variable equals the absolute value of that increase, and the decreases variable is set to 0. The measure is log-transformed.

variable_name: Compact, significant decreases in R&D expenditure
description: Built from the same maximum studentized residual from the GARCH time trend of firm R&D spending. If the residual with the largest absolute value is negative, the variable equals the absolute value of that decrease, and the increases variable is set to 0. The measure is log-transformed.

R&D expenditure divided by firm sales, following prior research that operationalizes absorptive capacity with R&D intensity because sustained investment in R&D increases the firm's absorptive capacity. The measure is log-transformed because it is heavily skewed. The same variable is also included as a control variable.

Dependent variable. Set to 1 if the firm is de-listed from Compustat due to bankruptcy or liquidation within the three years following its largest increase (or decrease) in R&D expenditure, and 0 otherwise. Estimated as the natural log of the odds (logit) of firm failure; de-listings for reasons unrelated to organizational failure are not treated as failure.
time_window: three years following the largest annual change in R&D spending

description: A lower partial moment of the firm's earnings underperformance relative to target, where the benchmark is the average return on assets of the industry within which the firm competes from the previous year. In the formula, x equals target minus actual, and x is set to 0 if target is less than actual. Following Mudambi and Swift (2014), m equals 2 time periods and n equals 2. The formula block itself is unreadable in the extracted text.

The scenario was administered in one of two versions. In the actor version the introductory description of the fictitious auto supplier Clark, Inc. was written from the point of view of a manager-actor making sense of his or her own organization's outcomes; in the observer version it was written from the perspective of a manager-observer making sense of another manager's organization's outcomes. Paired phrases (e.g., 'your company Clark, Inc.' versus 'the Clark, Inc. Company') signalled which perspective applied, although neither parentheses nor italics appeared in the distributed scenarios. One-fourth of the sample responded to each of the four scenario versions.

The four equivocal statements about outcomes experienced by Clark were worded to suggest either negative outcomes and failure or positive outcomes and success. In the success version competitors are failing to introduce more efficient production technologies, suppliers are becoming more reliable, the relative quality and performance of substitute products is declining, and buyers are more willing to pay a premium price; in the failure version the same statements were reworded in the opposite direction. The four statements were selected from 40 statements drawn from prior research on business performance because a pilot sample rated them as important but equally reflective of internal or external circumstances.

Four bipolar items asking about perceptions of Clark's strengths and weaknesses (internal factors), answered on a scale running from +4 to -4 that was rescaled to 1 to 9. Two items were written to produce conspicuous face validity (an evaluation of Clark's management and an assessment of Clark's organizational strength or weakness) and the other two were selected because of their pilot ratings. For each respondent the rescaled responses were averaged across the four items to produce an internal scale score; coefficient alpha was 0.74 in the primary sample and 0.92 in the pilot sample.

Four bipolar items asking about perceptions of opportunities and threats in Clark's environment (external factors), answered on the same +4 to -4 scale rescaled to 1 to 9. One item asked for an appraisal of Clark's industry and another for an evaluation of the opportunity or threat present in the firm's environment; the remaining two were selected on the basis of pilot responses. Rescaled responses were averaged across the four items for each respondent; coefficient alpha was 0.71 in the primary sample and 0.75 in the pilot sample, and the two scales were significantly intercorrelated.

Hypothesis testing was performed using difference scores computed from the internal and external scale scores; the authors state that internal scale scores were subtracted from external scale scores, and they interpret positive means as instances of respondent sensemaking dominated by internal, organizational attributions and negative means as sensemaking dominated by external, environmental attributions. Each of the three types of measure (difference, internal, external) was averaged for each of the four groups of respondents, and a priori comparisons were then conducted among group averages.
scale: difference between two 1 to 9 scale scores

description: A binary indicator equal to 1 if a CEO was either a female or an ethnic minority and 0 if the CEO was a white male. Gender and ethnicity of CEOs were identified in RiskMetrics and merged with ExecuComp files, which identified the CEO of a firm in a given year.
scale: binary (1 = female or ethnic minority, 0 = white male)

description: A binary indicator variable that took a value of 1 if a firm reported having a female CEO and a value of 0 for a male. The authors assessed whether results were consistent for the two types of minority CEOs, females and ethnic minorities, using this variable.

A binary indicator variable that took a value of 1 for an ethnic minority CEO and 0 otherwise. Ethnic minority status was defined as belonging to African-American, Asian, Caucasian, Hispanic, and Native American ethnicities, as recorded in RiskMetrics.

Total annual compensation paid by a firm to its CEO, combining short-term and long-term components. The measure includes the CEO's annual salary, bonus, other annual compensation, restricted stock grants, long-term incentive plan (LTIP) payouts, and the value of options granted using the Black-Scholes valuation methodology. The natural log of this total was taken.
A binary indicator that took a value of 1 if a firm reported a change in its CEO position in a given year and 0 otherwise. In the sample there were 1,261 CEO job exits.
scale: binary (1 = CEO job exit, 0 = no exit)

description: Production yield is the operational performance variable, measured in kilograms of sucrose produced per ton of sugarcane harvested. The quality of the sugarcane grown and the effectiveness of industrial processing determine the amount of sucrose produced; lower values mean the unit produces less output per ton of sugarcane harvested. The variable is entered as ln(Production yield) in the regression models to facilitate interpretation of the results using percentages. Because operational performance can only be measured during harvest months, the data set has a monthly structure and the first and last month of each harvest were dropped.
scale: kilograms of sucrose produced per ton of sugarcane harvested

description: Proximity measures the overall geographic proximity between an existing unit and all the units acquired by the company during a time period. It is operationalized as the sum of all the dyadic proximities between a focal existing unit and each of the units acquired during a time period, where dyadic proximity is defined as the inverse of the geographic distance between two units; driving distance is used. The higher the number of units acquired during a time period and the higher the geographical closeness of those acquired units to the focal existing unit, the higher the value of Proximity. The values change at the start of the next harvest season following an acquisition and remain constant until the end of the harvest, and are 0 during a harvest if no acquisitions occurred in the previous harvest or interharvest period.
time_window: harvest following an acquisition (0 if no acquisition in the previous harvest or interharvest)

description: Similarity measures the overall operational similarity between an existing unit and all the units acquired by the company during a time period. It is defined as the sum of all the dyadic attribute similarities between a focal existing unit and each of the units acquired during a time period, where dyadic attribute similarity is the inverse of the attribute distance between two units for a particular attribute. The dyadic attribute similarities are standardized before adding them, and the scores for the different attributes are combined into a single similarity score. The higher the number of units acquired during a time period and the higher the operational similarity of those acquired units to the focal unit, the higher the value of Similarity.
time_window: harvest following an acquisition (0 if no acquisition in the previous harvest or interharvest)

variable_name: Number of harvests since the last geographically close acquisition indicators
description: Five binary variables indicate the number of harvests that have taken place since the last geographically close acquisition, where a geographically close acquisition is assumed when the proximity between the acquiree and the focal unit is in the 85th percentile (approximately 80 km). The five categories are the first, second, third, fourth, and five or more harvests since the last geographically close acquisition. The base case in the regressions is the indicator for five or more harvests since the last geographically close acquisition.
time_window: harvests following the last geographically close acquisition (up to five or more)

variable_name: Number of harvests since the last similar acquisition indicators
description: Five binary variables indicate the number of harvests that have taken place since the last similar acquisition, where a similar acquisition is assumed when the similarity between the acquiree and the focal unit is in the 85th percentile. The five categories are the first, second, third, fourth, and five or more harvests since the last similar acquisition. The base case in the regressions is the indicator for five or more harvests since the last similar acquisition.
time_window: harvests following the last similar acquisition (up to five or more)

description: Relatedness is measured across four strategic dimensions for an individual director and aggregated across all directors for board-level tests. Product-market relatedness is the number of a director's appointments to the boards of companies in a primary business similar (same four-digit SIC code) to the focal firm divided by the director's total number of appointments. Foreign market relatedness counts appointments to the boards of companies with the same primary foreign market as the focal firm, normalized by the number of appointments. Diversification relatedness uses the entropy measure: the absolute difference between the focal firm's diversification and that of each connected firm is summed and normalized by the total number of appointments, and the figure is subtracted from the highest value of diversification dissimilarity in the sample so that higher values indicate greater relatedness. Internationalization relatedness applies the same difference-score procedure to Sullivan's degree-of-internationalization composite (foreign sales, foreign production and geographic dispersion). For board-level models the relatedness of individual director appointments across all directors on a board was aggregated.

The absolute value of the difference between the director's relatedness score on a given strategic dimension and the average relatedness scores of the other directors on the board, using the relatedness measure defined above. High values indicate that a director's appointments differed from the appointments of other board members on that dimension of relatedness; the measure is computed on each of the four strategic dimensions.

The extent to which a board's portfolio of director appointments is heterogeneous in its relatedness on a given strategic dimension, computed from each director's relatedness score, the average relatedness for the board, and the number of board members; the formula as printed is garbled in the text. Higher values indicated greater heterogeneity in strategic relatedness, whereas smaller values indicated that a firm's appointments were concentrated among firms that were either relatively similar or relatively dissimilar to the focal firm on that dimension. The board-level measure excludes duplicate ties to the same firm.

variable_name: director's perceived ability to contribute to board discussions
description: A multi-item scale in the director survey. Specific items assess the degree to which directors perceive that they have sufficient knowledge on relevant strategic issues to contribute to board discussions and the degree to which they feel adequately prepared to contribute, answered on five-point response scales. Cronbach's alpha for this scale was .88; after an iterated principal factors analysis a scree test indicated one common factor, all items loaded on that factor with loadings greater than .5, and factor scores were estimated using the Bartlett method.

A multi-item scale assessing the extent to which the board monitors strategic decision making or evaluates CEO performance, measured at the board level. The response scale for the monitoring items was 'minimally' (1), 'moderately' (3), 'very much so' (5). Cronbach's alpha was .92; after an iterated principal factors analysis and promax rotation the monitoring items loaded on one factor above .5 and below .2 on the other, and factor scores were estimated with the Bartlett method.

A multi-item scale assessing the extent to which the CEO solicits board input on corporate strategy and the frequency of advice and counsel discussions with board members, measured at the board level. Except for the last item, the response scale was 'minimally' (1), 'moderately' (3), 'very much so' (5). Cronbach's alpha was .89; the advice items loaded on a separate factor from the monitoring items and factor scores were estimated with the Bartlett method.

Measured as changes in the industry concentration ratio, the percentage of an industry's sales, at the four-digit SIC level, accounted for by the four largest firms; large absolute changes in the concentration ratio indicate high environmental instability and reflect shifts in market share due to new entrants, exits, consolidations, and erosion of market share. Change was observed over the three-year period prior to the survey date (1992-94). The entire sample was dichotomized at the median of the environmental stability measure, with firms below the median classified as in relatively stable industries and those above it as in relatively unstable industries.

The total number of other firms in the sample with which the firm shared at least one director. It is computed for each firm in each of the four panel years from the basic board and interlock data. This is the centrality measure used in the analyses of appointments of CEOs to bank boards.

Weights interlock ties according to the interlock partner's number of ties, such that sharing a director with a firm whose other directors serve on many boards is weighted more heavily than sharing a director with a firm with few ties. The measure also controls for the size of bank boards. It is used to identify the most central firms in 1982 and 1994.

Indicates the extent to which a node in a network is on the shortest path between many pairs of nodes, and it most closely identifies informational gatekeepers. It is used together with the other centrality measures to identify the most central firms in 1982 and 1994.

The number of Fortune-firm executives who sat on the bank's board, determined for each bank from the board and interlock data. It is one of the two components of a bank's interlocks, the other being bank sent ties (the number of Fortune boards on which the bank's executives sat).
The number of directors on the firm's board, determined from the board data for each panel year. The authors report that the median bank board size fell from 22 in 1982 to 17 in 1994.

The z-score of a firm's return on assets relative to Fortune firms in the corporation's primary 2-digit SIC category, averaged over three years. This is the performance measure for which the reported results are given.
Corporate size measured as total assets. This is the size measure for which the reported results are given.

The firm's debt-to-equity ratio, used as the measure of capital structure. It is one of the financial predictors in the models of appointments of bank executives to nonfinancial boards and of CEOs to bank boards.

Defined as [total current assets minus inventories] divided by [total current liabilities], used as the measure of solvency. Higher values indicate greater solvency and therefore lower indebtedness; the authors treat low solvency as the evidence bearing on the indebtedness hypothesis.

variable_name: appointment of a banker to the board
description: Indicator of whether an industrial firm that did not have a banker on its board at the start of a panel period appointed one by the next panel period. Risk sets of firms that were "at risk" of appointing bankers were defined for 1982-1986 and for 1990-1994. Executives who moved from one bank board to another following a bank merger were not included in the risk set.

variable_name: appointment of a CEO to a bank board
description: Indicator of whether the CEO of an industrial firm that was not on a bank board in the first year of a panel period joined a major bank board by the next panel period. Risk sets were defined for 1982-1986 and 1990-1994.

variable_name: change in domestic commercial and industrial lending
description: The change between 1986 and 1994 in the bank's level of domestic commercial and industrial lending. It is the principal independent variable in each of the three regressions of change in board size, change in received ties, and change in number of interlocks.

Time period was operationalized as the four panel years in which the board and interlock network was observed, 1982, 1986, 1990 and 1994. Centrality and bank received ties were computed in each panel year and compared across years to test the decline.

Binary dependent variable in an observation predicting diffusion of a second-wave practice, set to 1 if the organization adopted the focal practice (board evaluation or director evaluation) in year t and 0 otherwise. Once the organization had adopted a given practice, it no longer generated an observation for that practice, so the data consist of organization-year observations for organizations at risk of adopting.

A variable equal to the cumulative adoption of the same practice among the interlock ties of a focal organization. It uses the set of interlock ties of the focal organization and an indicator variable capturing whether an interlock tie has adopted the same second-wave practice (1) or has not (0), and its value increases with the number of interlock ties that have adopted the same second-wave governance practice. The equation itself is not readable in the available text.

A count of how many first-wave board reform practices out of the set of four an organization had already adopted; a positive coefficient would support Hypothesis 2a, and because a lower value implies retention of management-controlled-board practices, a positive coefficient would also imply support for Hypothesis 2b.

A count of the two other practices consistent with the management-controlled logic - interest-free director loans and director pensions - if they were present in the organization at the time of the observation, used as a separate test for Hypothesis 2b.

A variable that has the value 1 if an organization has previously adopted the other of the two focal practices (board evaluation or director evaluation). When an organization has adopted both, it is no longer at risk of adopting either and is no longer in the data set, so the variable has only 0 and 1 as possible values.

Computed with the interlock-adoption formula to count how many (out of the possible set of four) first-wave practices each of an organization's interlocks had adopted, and then adding up these adoptions for all of the organization's interlocks.

variable_name: exit from the superior performance stratum
description: We examine the sustainability of superior performance for app developers by observing whether their apps continue to be among the Top 500 apps by revenue in the iOS or the Android ecosystem. A firm is assumed to sustain its superior performance if its app continues to be in the Top 500 list in at least one of the following three months; a firm's superior performance is considered eroded if it exits the superior performance stratum, recorded with a three-month window (the app is not present in the Top 500 list for three consecutive months after being in that list in the previous month). If a firm had more than one app in the Top 500 list in the same month, those cases were treated as a single firm-level observation. The model estimates the hazard rate that a firm exits the superior performance stratum and hence its inability to sustain its superior performance.

Since ecosystem complexity faced by app developers is rooted in the diversity in the operating system and handset combinations offered by OEMs, the measure is a Simpson index-based diversity measure: the sum of the squares of the monthly shares of the U.S.-installed base for smartphone OEMs in an ecosystem. It takes a value of 1 for the iOS ecosystem and ranges from 0.28 to 0.40 for the more complex Android ecosystem. The measure was multiplied by -1 so that higher values indicate higher ecosystem complexity.
scale: Simpson index (sum of squared OEM installed-base shares), multiplied by -1

description: We measured ecosystem experience as the total number of months that a firm gained experience in a given ecosystem. To obtain this measure, the authors first identified the month in which the firm introduced its first app in the ecosystem (i.e., month of entry) and then computed the number of months between the observation month and the month of entry.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if a new generation of the smartphone operating system was introduced within the prior three months. The three-month window reflects that it often takes users several weeks to adopt the new generation of the operating system and a similar time frame for app developers to adapt and reconfigure their apps. New generations of smartphone operating system were identified based on change in the code name, and minor 'bug fix' updates were not considered platform-level generational transitions. During the period of study there were two major platform transitions in the iOS ecosystem and one major transition in the Android ecosystem.

Respondents in the two primed conditions first evaluated an Associated Press article describing Starbucks' provision of racial bias training to its employees, initiated in response to a nationally publicized incident in a Philadelphia branch, whereas control respondents read an article about a spring snowstorm affecting the Midwestern United States. The prime raises the salience of racial divisions without suggesting anything pertinent about the ability of African Americans as economic actors. The article prime is coded relative to the response of a respondent receiving a neutral article.

Experiment 2 used the same experimental design and protocol as experiment 1, so respondents again read either a neutral article or the article about the racial incident before evaluating the crowdfunding project. The only stated change was the use of a racially balanced sample of respondents.

An indicator comparing campaigns that ended in the 30 days following peak media coverage of a racially salient event with campaigns that ended in the 30 days prior to the event. Peak media coverage was determined from an analysis of Google Trends, and projects that ended between the event and its media peak were dropped from the analysis so that the comparison is between the pre-event window and the post-peak window.
time_window: 30 days before the event versus 30 days after the media coverage peak

description: Instead of a neutral article, all respondents received a version of the racial incident. The control condition received the same Associated Press article used in the prior two experiments; the procustomer condition received a modified version describing the police as at fault and the customers as innocent; and the propolice condition received a modified version describing the customers as at fault and the police as not responsible. The two accounts were chosen from seven pretested versions that did not differ in awe, utility, interest, complexity or length.

In the unprimed-Black and primed-Black conditions the photograph and name of the founder of the crowdfunding project were changed to a Black man named Malik M.; in the other conditions the founder was a white man named Joe M. The project content was held constant, so the treatment was variation in the signalled race of the founder.

Experiment 2 returned to the same experimental design and protocol described for experiment 1, so the signalled race of the founder again varied across respondents, with the addition of a racially balanced sample.
The design was identical to the first two experiments except for the article assigned in the first experimental task, so the signalled race of the founder evaluated by respondents continued to vary.

Projects were restricted to those including a visible photograph of the founder or founding team, which were processed with the Kairos facial recognition application programming interface to label the race and gender of each founder. Solo Black founder is coded one when the solo founder appeared to be African American based on the profile photo and zero when the founder was of some other race; entrepreneurial teams were omitted. The Kairos output was compared with two independently trained human coders and found to be nearly identical.

variable_name: perceived quality; likelihood you would support the project; likelihood others would support the project
description: Three attitudinal measures of quality borrowed from prior research on bias in crowdfunding, so that results could be interpreted and compared easily. Each measure was estimated in a separate ordinary least squares model, with the article prime, the founder's race and their interaction as predictors.

variable_name: quality; recommendation; interest in seeing more projects from the founder
description: Experiment 2 considered the same set of outcomes measured in the first experiment: three measures of overall preference for or assessment of the project. Results are reported as comparisons of mean responses between primed and unprimed, and between Black and white, respondents.

variable_name: perceived quality; likelihood of recommending; likelihood of success
description: Diagnostics of project quality estimated in ordinary least squares regressions of the article prime and party identification, with each measure estimated separately. The models also include respondent characteristics and, for party identification and its interactions with each prime, tests of moderation.

Respondents rated the skill of the founder along four dimensions, each estimated in separate ordinary least squares models with the prime, the founder's race and their interaction. The questions address the respondent's own assessment of the individual founder's ability rather than expectations about other consumers' behavior.

The same four measures of founder aptitudes used in experiment 1 were collected in experiment 2, including the question of whether the founder is unlikely to deliver the finished product. Responses are compared across primed and unprimed Black and white respondents.

Evaluations of the founder specifically, estimated in ordinary least squares regressions of the article prime and party identification. The procustomer account significantly increased the perception that a founder will fail to deliver and that they will receive complaints, and the effects on delivering on time and at advertised quality were negative but below conventional levels of significance.

Binary indicator of whether the project succeeded in reaching its fundraising goal, modeled with logistic regression on the indicator for a solo Black founder, the post-event dummy and their interaction, together with project-level controls. The sample is U.S.-based projects proposed by solo entrepreneurs that ended during the six observation windows linked to the events.
time_window: six observation windows of 30 days before the event and 30 days after the media peak

description: Binary variable that takes the value of 1 for a team that does not hold a leadership position in any given round but has held one in the past, and 0 otherwise. Each round the highest-ranking team on the composite performance metric in a given business simulation game is coded as the leader. The variable is split into recent former leader (led in the two rounds preceding the observation) and old former leader (last leadership more than 2 rounds in the past).

Binary variable equal to 1 if an outlet does not currently hold one of the prize-eligible positions but has done so in the past, and 0 otherwise. Leading outlets are those occupying one of the prize-eligible positions in their respective tournament group, where the number of identical prizes varies from 1 to 4 across groups. As in Study 1, the variable is refined into old former leader and recent former leader, with 'recent' defined as leadership within the past 14 days.

Calculated as the number of minutes from the beginning of the round until the team closed its decision-making panel, thus sending its final set of decisions to the central system; a commonly used proxy for cognitive effort. Most rounds lasted for 90 minutes, but participants had an option to finish the round earlier or later. On average, teams used 86 minutes to complete each round.

Binary variable denoting whether a team decided to extend its decision-making period into its free time (break), treated as a strong proxy for effort because it denotes 'overtime' work that is particularly costly. Some teams, with a frequency of 20%, chose this option. In 85 cases the timestamp did not allow the variable to be determined unambiguously and those observations were dropped.

Number of loans sold divided by the outlet-specific benchmark, where the benchmark is the outlet's monthly average in the 4 months preceding the contest. The tournament objective function was to maximize sales of personal loans relative to that benchmark, and outlets were ranked each day according to the cumulative number of 'primary' personal loans sold, which had to be sold to a first-time customer to count.
time_window: daily over the 2-month contest; benchmark over the preceding 4 months

description: Sales of primary loans belonging to size Group 4 or 5. Every loan is categorized by the bank's risk department as belonging to one of five size categories, from 1 (largest) to 5 (smallest), and small loans are defined as Categories 4 and 5. Small loans contribute more to the tournament goal, which counted the number of loans sold, and less to the alternative piece-rate bonus goal, which was based on the dollar volume of loans sold.

Sales of primary loans above the small-loan threshold, reported by the authors separately from small primary loans in the substitution analysis. The bank categorized loans into five size categories, from 1 (largest) to 5 (smallest), and small loans are Categories 4 and 5; the paper does not give a separate definition of the large-loan variable in the prose.

Loans to customers who have already been granted a primary loan in the past. They were incentivized with a separate piece-rate plan, but their sales did not contribute to the tournament goal, and the piece rate for these loans was much weaker than that for primary loans, reflecting the bank's focus on extending the consumer base. At the time of the study, primary loans accounted for over 50% of total sales but over 70% of pretax profits from personal loans.

Measured as the average Yelp review ratings the focal restaurant received in a given week. Each review rates a restaurant on a scale of 1 to 5 stars, where 1 star signifies low satisfaction and 5 stars signifies high satisfaction. Restaurant-week spells with no ratings were coded as missing rather than zero, and the potential selection bias was corrected with a Heckman selection model. The review ratings have a J-shaped distribution, suggesting reviewers generally tend to have a positive bias in their ratings.
time_window: weekly; 24-week observation window (8 weeks before, 8 weeks during, and 8 weeks after the outbreak)

description: Measured as a count of news articles published in the 26 major newspapers tracked in the ABI/INFORM database for each of the weeks in the observation window. To be included, an article had to contain the words 'Seattle,' 'Chipotle,' and 'E. coli.' The higher the count, the more salient Chipotle's capability failure and the ensuing crisis were likely to be. The number of articles ranged from 0 to 43 in a given week.
scale: count; ranged from 0 to 43 in a given week

description: Dichotomous variable where all Mexican restaurants in the sample were coded one and all other restaurants were coded zero, because Chipotle sells Mexican cuisine. Cuisine type is one of the restaurant attributes Yelp provides for each restaurant.

Dichotomous variable coded one if the focal restaurant is proximal to a Chipotle restaurant based on sharing the same zip code, and zero otherwise. Restaurant addresses provided by Yelp were used to determine zip code.

variable_name: hazard rate of adopting an ICGC
description: The dependent variable in the event history analysis, defined as the hazard rate of adopting an ICGC: the probability of adoption between times t and t+dt, given that the firm is at risk of adoption at time t. For each firm the event of adoption or censoring and the date of adoption or censoring (liquidation date or the end of the observation period) are recorded. Data on adoption were obtained from quarterly reports filed with the FCSM, firms' websites, and direct requests to firms.

Based on the degree of details provided in a firm's code and captures whether the code mainly consists of general statements or describes in detail specific corporate governance procedures and practices. All ICGCs have been coded into four categories: many details, substantial details, few details, and no details, and code ceremoniality increases as ICGCs become less detailed. All internal codes adopted by firms in the sample were coded by two independent raters (both native Russian speakers) with 91% agreement; in cases of disagreement, raters reviewed their ratings and reached a consensus.
scale: four categories: many details, substantial details, few details, no details

description: Identifies companies with shares traded at major Russian stock exchanges, RTS and/or MICEX. The variable takes a value of 1 for traded firms and a value of 0 otherwise. Data on all companies that were traded at RTS and MICEX were obtained from their websites, and the variable was updated on a monthly basis.
time_window: updated monthly over the observation period

description: Identifies all companies that went through the listing procedure and were included on quotation lists of the RTS and MICEX. The variable takes a value of 1 for listed firms and a value of 0 otherwise. Data on companies included in quotation lists at these stock exchanges were obtained from their websites.
time_window: updated monthly over the observation period

description: Constructed to identify firms that issued ADRs or GDRs, using information about the date of issuing ADRs/GDRs with a one-year lag to account for the fact that firms usually make preparations before they issue ADRs/GDRs. The variable equals 1 if a firm has ADR and/or GDR programs, and 0 otherwise; dates of ADR/GDR issues were obtained from the Bank of New York directory.
scale: 1 = has ADR and/or GDR programs, 0 = otherwise

description: Regional proximity is operationalized as a location in the same region, and for each firm the number of prior adopters in the same federal region is calculated. Russia consists of 83 federal regions, and firms located in the same federal region have executives who spend time in the same administrative center and communicate with the same regional administrators.
time_window: updated monthly over the observation period

description: For each firm, the proportion of prior adopters in the firm's industry. The primary industry for each firm was identified using information from the database of the Expert Rating Agency; 15 industries are represented in the sample.
time_window: updated monthly over the observation period

description: Constructed from data on directors of all firms in the sample obtained from quarterly reports, identifying both 'primary' interlocks created by executives of one firm sitting on the board of another firm and 'secondary' interlocks created by outside directors who sit on boards of two firms without holding executive positions in any of them. For each firm, the variable takes the value of a count of all its interlocks to prior adopters, and when firms in the sample adopted an ICGC the data were updated for all other firms.
time_window: updated as adoptions occurred over the observation period

description: Measured as the proportion of shares controlled by the largest owner. Ownership concentration in Russia is very high compared with the United States or Britain, and it is common for large Russian firms to have a single shareholder with a block of shares that significantly exceeds blocks owned by other shareholders.

Captures deviations of actual returns on sales from the average for the corresponding industry. There is significant variation across industries in average profitability, and shareholders usually evaluate performance of the focal firm in comparison with performance of its industry peers.

Respondents identified whether each of five practices existed on a formal basis in their workplace: flexible job design, information sharing with employees, problem-solving teams, self-directed work groups, and gainsharing. In addition, respondents indicated whether or not formal training had been used in the prior 12-month period. All six practices were dichotomous (1 = yes, 0 = no) and were combined into bundles for 1999 and 2001. The mean number of practices was 1.73 in 1999 and 1.44 in 2001, ranging from 0 to 6 in both years.

Respondents reported the number of employees laid off during a year, with the survey distinguishing layoffs from resignations, retirements, and firings. The layoff rate over the two-year period was calculated as 2000 layoffs plus 2001 layoffs divided by total employees in 1999, and was then transformed using the logarithm of the layoff rate plus 1. Two dummy variables indicating whether or not a workplace conducted layoffs in 2000 and 2001 were also created.

Productivity was measured as the logarithm of revenues minus expenditures per employee. Respondents provided exact gross operating revenue from the sale or rental of all products and services and gross operating expenditures, including payroll and non-wage expenses and the purchase of goods, for their location. Three measures were created: 1999 productivity as a baseline control, and 2001 and 2002 productivity as dependent variables.

variable_name: 1999 and 2001 high-involvement work practices and their interaction
description: To avoid the problems of difference scores, the authors entered the two components of a difference score, 1999 and 2001 high-involvement work practices, into the regression model together with the interaction between them, rather than computing a change score. Continued investment was defined as high levels of these practices in both 1999 and 2001, and discontinued investment as high levels in 1999 but low levels in 2001. The three-way interaction of 1999 practices, layoff rate, and 2001 practices tests whether continued investments mitigate the negative effects of higher layoff rates.

variable_name: Cumulative Go games at time t-1
description: The natural log of the cumulative number of Go games played by team i from the beginning of the first hour through the end of hour t-1, regressed on the natural log of the team's average Go score in hour t. In the final model the cumulative production variable is multiplied by the condition dummies so that a different learning rate (the coefficient on cumulative games) is estimated for teams in each condition. Data were aggregated to the hour level, giving 10 observations per team.
time_window: cumulative from the first hour through the end of hour t-1, over 10 hours

description: Dummy variable (0, 1) coded 1 for teams in the specialization condition, in which the teams played only Go for the entire experimental period. It enters the model directly to capture the condition's impact on the intercept and, multiplied by the cumulative number of games, to estimate the learning rate for that condition.
time_window: hourly over the 10 hours of play

description: Dummy variable (0, 1) coded 1 for teams in the related variation condition, in which teams played alternating blocks of 4 games of Go (the core game) and 4 games of the alternate game Reversi. Reversi was chosen because it is considered highly related to Go in appearance, objectives, and ancestry.
time_window: hourly over the 10 hours of play

description: Dummy variable (0, 1) coded 1 for teams in the unrelated variation condition, in which teams played alternating blocks of 4 games of Go and 4 games of the alternate game Cribbage. Cribbage is a card game relying predominantly on math skills and probabilities and is vastly different from Go or Reversi. The unrelated variation dummy must be omitted from the final model to avoid overspecification.
time_window: hourly over the 10 hours of play

description: The affiliate's R&D expenditure divided by the affiliate's sales, the dependent variable of the analysis. R&D expenditure covers personnel and nonpersonnel expenses for testing and research, including depreciation of R&D-related tangible fixed investments, shared joint research expenses and research consignment fees, but the survey does not allow decomposition over basic and applied research versus development and design. The variable is censored on the left-hand side at zero; 215 of the 420 affiliates reported zero R&D expenditure.

Log of the number of years since the Japanese parent firm established its first manufacturing affiliate abroad, defined for firms that have not expanded abroad through majority acquisitions (a nonacquisitive firm is defined as a firm that has no majority acquired foreign affiliates). The variable takes the value 0 for acquisitive firms, and the value 1 was added before taking the natural logarithm.

Log of the number of years since the Japanese parent firm established its first manufacturing affiliate abroad, defined for firms that have followed an acquisitive foreign entry strategy. An acquisitive firm is defined as a firm that expanded abroad through at least one majority acquisition; the value 1 was added before taking the natural logarithm.
Log of the number of years since the start-up year for greenfield affiliates.
Log of the number of years since acquisition of the affiliate.

Dummy variable equal to one for minority owned or balanced stake joint ventures, that is, ventures in which a local partner had an equity stake of 50 percent or more in 1993. The reference case is a wholly owned greenfield affiliate.
Dummy variable taking the value 1 if the affiliate came under the control of the Japanese parent through an acquisition and if the affiliate was majority owned in 1993.
Dummy variable taking the value 1 if the Japanese firm acquired a stake in an existing foreign firm but did not have majority control in 1993; balanced stakes are included.

The parent firm's R&D ratio, used as a measure of the parent firm's R&D capabilities. It is entered in the model both on its own and, interacted with the minority joint venture dummy, in the test of Hypothesis 3; the authors note that a 1 percent point increase in the parent's R&D ratio leads to a 0.08 percent point increase in affiliate R&D intensity.

variable_name: Parent R&D intensity × minority joint venture
description: Interaction term of the Japanese parent firm's R&D intensity and the minority joint venture dummy. The model includes it to test whether the difference in R&D intensity between minority joint ventures and wholly owned greenfield affiliates depends on the parent firm's R&D capabilities.

The main independent variable denotes the escalation of the U.S.-China conflict after 2016. It is the interaction term Ethnic Chinese x After 2016 and takes a value of one only for the treatment group after 2016; its coefficient quantifies the treatment effect of how the workplace efforts of Chinese-descent inventors change relative to their Korean and Japanese counterparts.
time_window: turns from zero to one after 2016

description: The number of patent applications per year is used to measure inventors' workplace efforts, counting only patent applications with U.S. addresses to avoid the impact of cross-country relocation. It is a skewed, nonnegative count, which is why a conditional fixed-effects Poisson model is used.

Reported working hours of college-educated Chinese-descent workers compared with their East Asian counterparts, using data from the CPS. The analysis is restricted to individuals with at least a college degree, and the reported effect increases with educational attainment.

A dummy variable indicating whether an inventor's first patenting activity occurred in the United States or abroad. It captures whether the inventor started his or her career in the United States rather than immigrating midcareer.

A binary variable indicating whether an inventor's legal first name aligns with Anglo-Saxon, Western European, or Nordic naming conventions (e.g., Ken Liu). Names classified within these categories receive a value of one; otherwise, it is coded as zero.

A binary variable coded as one if the inventor is affiliated with an academic institution (e.g., university or nonprofit research organization) and zero if affiliated with a for-profit corporate organization. It captures the lower dependence of academic inventors on employer sponsorship for immigration processes such as H-1B visas, visa renewals, and green card applications.

The proportion of votes cast for Republicans relative to Democratic candidates in the 2016 presidential election at the county level in which the inventors reside, used as an indicator of the local anti-immigration sentiment immigrant inventors may encounter.

variable_name: Moderating conditions for identity-based career concerns (Career Debut in the US, Western First Name, Academic Inventors, Trump Vote Share)
description: Identity-based career concerns are not measured directly. They are proxied by four inventor or county conditions that the authors argue intensify such concerns after the conflict: whether the inventor's first patent was filed in the United States (career debut in the US, versus midcareer immigration), whether the legal first name is Western, whether the inventor is academic rather than corporate (sponsorship dependence), and the county-level 2016 Trump vote share (local anti-immigrant sentiment). Each is interacted with After Conflict in separate models, and the treatment effect is compared across the conditions.
scale: Three binary indicators and one continuous share, each interacted with After Conflict
time_window: Inventor attributes as of 2016 baseline; effects estimated for 2017 onward

description: Measured using a logarithmic transformation of the number of years of international investment history a firm had accumulated (Delios and Beamish, 2001). Japanese Overseas Investments was the source for data on foreign subsidiaries including host country and international experience. The measure refers to the corporate parent of each subsidiary.

Measured using a logarithmic transformation of the number of years of investment history the parent firm had in the host country (Delios and Beamish, 2001). Japanese Overseas Investments was the source for data on foreign subsidiaries including host country experience. The measure refers to the corporate parent of each subsidiary.

Technological knowledge is measured using a parent firm's R&D intensity, which is a key component and widely used proxy for technological knowledge. The authors used a 5-year average of R&D intensity, lagged by the 5 years preceding the year in which a subsidiary's performance was measured. The measure is at the level of the corporate parent.
time_window: 5-year average lagged by the 5 years preceding the performance year

description: Marketing knowledge is measured using a parent firm's advertising intensity, a common measure of a firm's brand equity and marketing knowledge. The same operationalization as for R&D intensity was used: a 5-year average lagged by the 5 years preceding the year in which subsidiary performance was measured. The measure is at the level of the corporate parent.
time_window: 5-year average lagged by the 5 years preceding the performance year

description: A subjective measure of subsidiary performance drawn from Japanese Overseas Investments. Toyo Keizai developed this measure by surveying a subsidiary's general manager to classify the financial performance of their subsidiary into one of three categories: loss, breakeven, or gain. The authors used profitability in 1994 as the short-term measure of performance because subsidiary performance is unstable for the first 2 years following inception.
scale: three ordered categories: loss, breakeven, gain

description: A subjective measure of subsidiary performance drawn from Japanese Overseas Investments, developed by Toyo Keizai by surveying a subsidiary's general manager to classify the financial performance of their subsidiary into one of three categories: loss, breakeven, or gain. Long-term performance was measured using subsidiary profitability in 1999, 2001, and 2003.
scale: three ordered categories: loss, breakeven, gain

description: The dependent variable is the proportion of total codes that reference the medical-use theme in a dispensary's self-description. Codes were produced by a software program that applied a context-specific coding scheme of identity-related features to each dispensary's self-description in each bimonthly download. Using the count of total identity-related codes as the denominator captures the extent to which a dispensary's claims emphasize the medical orientation of its identity versus other potential identity dimensions. For example, a self-description with three medical-use codes out of nine total codes is measured as 0.33.
time_window: Bimonthly downloads from July 2014 to July 2015

description: A one-month lagged count of recreational dispensaries listed on Weedmaps as operating in the same county as the focal medical dispensary. To isolate the impact of recreational dispensary competition, a one-month lagged count of medical dispensaries operating in the same county is also included as a control.

The percentage of voters in the county who voted in support of the state ballots legalizing recreational cannabis use and sales. Because there is only one observation of voter support per county, the measure is time invariant. In some models counties are split into high versus low recreational dispensary voter support, based on whether their vote supporting recreational legalization was above or below the statewide level of support for both the Colorado and Washington ballot measures.

A time-varying measure of each dispensary's reviewers' focus on products in their review text, constructed with the same 16-theme-based coding process used for dispensary self-descriptions. A review is treated as demonstrating a recreational orientation if it includes references to cannabis products, and the recreational orientation of a dispensary's customer base is the proportion of its total reviews that demonstrate a recreational orientation. This cumulative proportion is lagged by one month in the models.
time_window: Cumulative through the study period, lagged by one month

description: Two indicators on a 7-point interval scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree': whether the partner's technology/process know-how is easily transferable back to the company, and whether the association between causes and effects, inputs and outputs, and actions and outcomes related to that know-how is clear. The items are worded toward transferability and clarity, and the authors state that the scales were reverse-coded where appropriate.

Three indicators on a 7-point interval scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' covering what the company has learned about the partner's know-how, the reduction of its initial technological reliance on the partner, and the assimilation of that know-how into other projects.

Two indicators on a 7-point interval scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree': whether the partner's know-how is easily codifiable and whether it is more explicit than tacit. The items are worded toward codifiability and explicitness, and the authors state that the scales were reverse-coded where appropriate.

Two indicators on a 7-point interval scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' measuring whether, to develop its know-how, the partner had to invest significantly in specialized equipment and facilities and in skilled human resources.

Self-reported latent construct measured by multiple indicators on a 7-point interval scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. The authors state that the wording of the measurement items is given in the Appendix, but the items for this construct are not recoverable from the available text.

Self-reported latent construct measured by multiple indicators on a 7-point interval scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. The authors state that the wording of the measurement items is given in the Appendix, but the items for this construct are not recoverable from the available text.

Self-reported latent construct measured by multiple indicators on a 7-point interval scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. The authors state that the wording of the measurement items is given in the Appendix, but the items for this construct are not recoverable from the available text.

Self-reported latent construct measured by multiple indicators on a 7-point interval scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. The authors state that the wording of the measurement items is given in the Appendix, but the items for this construct are not recoverable from the available text.

Self-reported latent construct measured by multiple indicators on a 7-point interval scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. The authors state that the wording of the measurement items is given in the Appendix, but the items for this construct are not recoverable from the available text.

A 20-item additive index derived from previous research on strategic alliances, in which respondents rate their company's know-how in a list of areas of interfirm cooperation on a scale running from 'no know-how' to 'extensive know-how'. The index ranges from 0 to 140 and is used to split the sample into high and low collaborative know-how groups.

A two-item scale aimed at measuring resource deployment: personnel committed to the alliance, and physical, financial, organizational, and logistical resources committed to support the seeking, diffusion and sharing of information originating from the alliance. Items are rated on a 7-point scale from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree', and the scale is used to split the sample into high and low learning capacity groups.

Computed from the date of inception of the alliance as reported in the questionnaire; the questionnaire asks for the year in which the alliance was formed. The variable is used to split the sample into 'older' and 'younger' alliance groups.

The influencing group was classified into one of three sectors: societal interest groups, industry and business groups, and nonlegislative government bodies. The frequency of reported strategy use was tabulated separately for each sector.

The survey examined directly the usage of 12 influence techniques, which were grouped into four strategy types: information, public exposure/appeal, direct pressure, and political. Frequencies of observations for the four strategy types were tabulated by influence sector together with expected cell values.

Individuals were asked to rate each of the 12 techniques on a scale ranging from a very negative impact (scale value = -10) to a very positive impact (scale value = +10); the middle point (scale value = 0) was described as having little or no impact. Negative values were included because the interviews indicated that some influence methods may produce an effect opposite to that intended. Averages were reported for the four strategy groupings.

Influence mode was operationalized by grouping the four strategy types: information-based and political strategies were treated as positive modes, and direct pressure and public exposure/appeal strategies as negative modes. The perceived impact ratings of these strategy groups (-10 to +10) were then compared across groups.
scale: Grouping of 4 strategy types into 2 modes

description: The ith scientist's specialization in a 4-digit USPTO technology T of his kth patent is the experience the scientist has in that technology prior to the application of the patent divided by the experience the scientist has in all n technologies he has worked with in the past. It is a proportional, Herfindahl-type measure of knowledge concentration in a technology, and values range from 0 to 1.
time_window: experience accumulated prior to the patent application date

description: A chronological list of the scientist's patents is built from application dates, and the set of scientists listed on a patent is treated as the team that worked together on that innovation. Comparing the scientists listed on two sequential patents X and Y, collaborator change takes a value of 1 if the lists differ and 0 otherwise.
time_window: between a scientist's patent and the prior patent

description: Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the scientist works with a new collaborator who had not worked on the prior patent, and 0 otherwise. Entry is a disaggregation of collaborator change.
time_window: between a scientist's patent and the prior patent

description: Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the scientist no longer works with a scientist who had worked on the prior patent, and 0 otherwise. Exit is a disaggregation of collaborator change.
time_window: between a scientist's patent and the prior patent

description: Event history analysis is used to predict the likelihood that a scientist successfully develops a new patent at any given point in time. In a chronologically ordered list of a scientist's patents, an event [E] takes place when a scientist [S] successfully files a new patent; the time in days is determined from the day, month and year the scientist filed the patent. The greater the hazard rate, the greater the scientist's R&D productivity.

Count of the total number of forward citations received by a focal scientist's patent from the patent's year of application until 2017, less the number of self-citations made by the focal scientist to it. Because it is a highly right-skewed count variable that takes non-negative integer values, it is estimated with a Poisson estimator with firm fixed effects.
time_window: from the patent's application year until 2017

description: All scientist-level variables, including specialization, were aggregated and averaged at the firm level to test whether the predicted results apply at the firm level of analysis.
The scientist-level collaborator change variable was aggregated and averaged at the firm level, and its interaction with firm-level specialization was used in the firm-level regressions.
Firm-level regressions for R&D productivity were run using the aggregated and averaged scientist-level variables and firm fixed effects.
Firm-level regressions for citation count were run using the aggregated and averaged scientist-level variables and firm fixed effects.

The Berry Index (Berry, 1975) of firm diversification was computed for the sample retained to reflect the degree of technologically related diversification. The evaluation of technologically related diversification strategies was based on a method described by Pearce (1983) defining five categories of industrial diversification: technological spillover, exploration spillover, vertical integration, product complementarity, and conglomerate diversification; the first four categories are taken to reflect technological relatedness. The variable is built from annual reports.

Market to book value of the firm, taken from Compustat for 1980-1983. It is one of the three measures of the multidimensional dependent variable, firm performance, and is described as a value-based measure that assesses the firm's future risk-return trade-off as perceived by the market.

Relative excess valuation of the firm (Thomadakis, 1977), the ratio of the difference between market and book value to firm sales, taken from Compustat for 1980-1983. It is described as a value-based measure that assesses the firm's future risk-return trade-off as perceived by the market.
Ratio of profits to firm equity, taken from Compustat for 1980-1983. It serves as the accounting-based measure of firm profitability among the three measures of firm performance.

For each establishment the authors counted the number of subsidiary layers existing between the establishment and its parent headquarters. The variable takes the value '0' for the parent headquarters and parent establishments operating under the direct authority of the parent headquarters, '1' for first-level subsidiary headquarters and their establishments, '2' for second-level subsidiary headquarters and establishments, and so on. A higher value means the establishment occupies a lower level in the corporate hierarchy.

A longitudinal version of the level of subsidiary layers, created by supplementing the EPA's TRI program data with the NETS Database's TRI Establishments Database. It records, for each TRI facility-year, the number of subsidiary layers between the facility and its parent headquarters.

A dichotomous indicator of whether a business establishment performs pollution-intensive activities, created by manually comparing the 2013 Dun and Bradstreet's Corporate Family Tree Data and the EPA's 2013 TRI program. It has a value of one if the business establishment in the Dun and Bradstreet data was also listed in the TRI program, and zero otherwise.

State environmental stringency was assessed by the average z-score of two measures: per capita state-level government expenditures on the environment, measured with the US Census Bureau's Census of Governments, and state-level government inspection activities, measured by counting the state-level number of inspections standardized by the number of manufacturing establishments operating in the state, drawn from the US EPA's ECHO. The average z-score of these two measures was calculated for the home states where the parent headquarters are located.
level: state of the parent headquarters (corporate group)

description: The average z-score of per capita state-level government environmental expenditures (US Census Bureau's Census of Governments) and state-level inspection activities standardized by the number of manufacturing establishments operating in the state (US EPA's ECHO), calculated for the host states where the business establishments are located.

The pounds of toxic emissions to the air, water, and land were multiplied by chemical-specific toxicity weights obtained from the EPA's Risk Screening Environmental Indicators. The toxicity-weighted amounts of chemical emissions were then aggregated at the level of facilities and the natural logarithm was taken to address right-skewness in the distribution.

Time-variant count of unique coauthors working at external organizations relative to the university of affiliation of the focal individual over the preceding five years. All unique coauthors and their affiliations are identified from publication data, in which every author has a unique personal identifier and every publication lists affiliations; all affiliations in the publication sample were manually checked and Scopus identifiers pertaining to the same institution were aggregated. A coauthor was considered affiliated with the same institution as the focal individual by comparing their affiliation to the focal individual's affiliation in that year as identified in their CV. Only papers with fewer than 20 coauthors were considered.

Tracks the mobility events and affiliations of every researcher in each period. When an individual changes affiliation, the individual-year observation corresponding to the year of the move is coded 1 if the individual moves to an institution where no coauthors are employed, 2 if the individual moves to an institution where at least one coauthor is employed, and 0 if the individual did not move. A coauthor is defined as an individual who appears as a collaborator in any publication with the focal individual within the previous five years.
time_window: previous five years for coauthor identification; 1995-2009 observation window

description: Dichotomous variable that takes the value of 1 if a researcher moves to a university where one of their previous coauthors is affiliated (in a five-year rolling time window), and 0 otherwise. The pool of coauthors comes from the authors list of each focal researcher's publication history and their related affiliations. It distinguishes the 66 movers to a coauthor's institution from the 90 movers to an institution where none of their coauthors are employed.

Cumulative count of journal articles published by each individual up to each point of time, adjusted by academic tenure, computed within a five-year rolling window (for each year t, data between year t-1 and year t-5 are used). Publication data were downloaded from Scopus and cross-checked manually; in case of discordance between the automated and manual counts, the manual number of publications was kept.

The number of unique new coauthors that are also colleagues of the focal individual in the current employer in every period. For each publication of each focal individual, each coauthor was classified as a previous colleague, a current colleague, or neither depending on the focal individual's affiliation at the time of the publication, and as an old or a new coauthor depending on whether the focal individual had collaborated in the past with that coauthor or whether the coauthor appeared in the five-year rolling window for the first time. Rules were developed to deal with authors who possessed double affiliations.

Used as the independent variable in the hypothesis 3b tests, constructed as the number of unique new coauthors that are also colleagues of the focal individual in the current employer in every period, log-transformed in the difference-in-differences specification. Separate models are estimated for the premove period (After Mobility = 0) and the postmove period (After Mobility = 1).
time_window: premove and postmove periods around the mobility event

variable_name: Type of identity constructed for an entrepreneurial firm
description: One of the authors read the business section of each prospectus in its entirety and noted the essence of the narrative's story line and underlying pitch; the other two authors examined these notes and six latent identity constructions emerged. Each narrative was then classified into one of seven categories using a forced-choice method completed by two independent coders (initial interrater agreement was 79 percent). The categories were dummy-coded, combining the potential contender and potential noncontender categories as the omitted baseline in the analyses.

variable_name: Elaboration (degree of elaboration evident in the rationales for intended initiatives)
description: Each firm's story map, an array of the risks and intended strategic actions listed in its prospectus, was transformed into a 93 x 93 symmetric matrix containing values of 1 or 0 depending on whether or not a link existed between a particular risk-strategy pair. Two coders identified the links among the risk-strategy nodes and consensus was reached before the map was constructed. Ignoring directionality, all links in the lower half of the matrix, excluding the diagonal, were summed to create an overall measure of elaboration.

The measure focuses on the intended strategic actions articulated in a firm's prospectus that other IPO firms in the same industry commonly mentioned. P is the proportion of IPO firms in the same industry that had mentioned the same strategy (s) as focal firm f in their prospectuses during the previous year, and n is the number of strategies listed by more than 50 percent of the prior year's IPO firms in the industry. IPO prospectuses from the year prior to a focal firm's initial filing date were the referent; the formula block in the article text could not be read.
time_window: the year prior to a focal firm's initial filing date

description: The measure focuses on the intended strategic actions articulated in a firm's prospectus that other IPO firms in the same industry infrequently mentioned. P is the proportion of IPO firms in the same industry that had listed the same strategy (s) as focal firm f in their prospectuses during the previous year, and n is the number of strategies listed by 50 percent or less of the prior year's IPO firms in that industry. IPO prospectuses from the year prior to a focal firm's initial filing date were the referent; the formula block in the article text could not be read.
time_window: the year prior to a focal firm's initial filing date

description: Calculated as the difference between the pre-IPO book value per share and the IPO issue price, multiplied by the number of shares issued to subscribers, all transformed to logarithms. This variable captured the net dollars raised by an IPO firm that it could directly use as its own capital. Data on pre-IPO book value, issue pricing, and shares issued were obtained from the Securities Data Corporation database and verified by the 424B filing on EDGAR.

Calculated as the difference between the first-day market closing price and the IPO issue price, multiplied by the number of shares outstanding, all logged. It captured the net change in a firm's valuation at the end of first-day trading relative to its IPO issue price.

Calculated as the difference between a firm's first-day stock closing price and its book value prior to its IPO, multiplied by the total number of shares outstanding, all logged. It captured the total change in stock value from the time of the road show through the end of the first day of market trading.
time_window: from the road show through the end of the first day of market trading

description: Board capital breadth is indicated by functional, occupational, and relational heterogeneity and was calculated using Blau's heterogeneity index. Functional background was captured by the refined taxonomy of Hillman, Cannella, and Paetzold, who categorize directors into one of three board functional roles: business experts, support specialists, and community influentials. Occupational background was coded as one of the following categories: general management, finance/accounting, sales/marketing, legal, information systems, operations, engineering, human resources, military/government, and real estate. Heterogeneity of interorganizational linkages was captured by four-digit SIC codes of the directors' interlocked industries. The measures were indexed by summing the individual measures, so the range of values is between 0 and 3, with values close to 3 indicating higher heterogeneity; Cronbach's alpha was 0.649.

Board capital depth measures industry embeddedness, depth of linkages to, and expertise in industry. Its indicators are the ratio of industry interlocks to total interlocks, and industry occupation. Total interlocks were calculated by summing the numbers of board directorships board members hold at other for-profit corporations, and industry interlocks were determined by first establishing the focal firm's main industry from COMPUSTAT's business segment data and then using two- and four-digit SIC codes to determine which interlocks were from within the same industry. The second indicator is the ratio of directors who have current or past experience in the focal firm's main industry to board size, and the CEO was excluded from both measures. The two ratios were summed to create an index with values from 0 to 2 indicating the board's embeddedness in the focal industry, with higher values indicating higher embeddedness; Cronbach's alpha was 0.752.

Indicators of CEO structural and ownership power are captured: duality (whether the CEO is also board chair), the ratio of nonaffiliated to total number of directors, the ratio of CEO to board equity holdings of the focal firm, and the ratio of directors who were appointed after the CEO began his or her tenure to the number of total directors. These variables were standardized and summed to create an index of CEO power, and Cronbach's alpha between these measures was 0.58.

Strategic variation is a composite measure of six resource allocation ratios: advertising intensity (advertising/sales), R&D intensity (R&D/sales), plant and equipment upgrades (new plant and equipment/gross plant and equipment), nonproduction overhead (SG&A expenses/sales), inventory levels (inventory/sales), and financial leverage (debt/equity). With 2002 as the focal year, exponential smoothing was applied to the actual resource allocation figures for each year and each company to calculate the baseline for 1998-2002, and composite forecasted figures were obtained for 2003 and repeated for 2004. Absolute values of simple differences between the exponentially smoothed forecasted amounts and the actual ratios were calculated, summed, and the natural log of the differences was used to normalize the dependent variable. Because some COMPUSTAT data were missing, the ratios were calculated twice: once with a zero value for missing data for all six ratios, and once excluding the most common missing variables (R&D, advertising, and inventory) and using only the remaining three ratios.

Strategic deviation (departure from industry norms) is calculated as the absolute value of the difference between the value of the industry norm and the firm's actual resource allocation ratios, using the same six resource allocation ratios. The industry norm was obtained by collapsing the 97 industries represented in the sample, based on the focal firm's four-digit SIC code, into French's 49 industries, and by identifying the top four firms in each industry to calculate a composite measure of industry resource allocation norms.
