The top four firms were selected using the commonly used C4 measure of industry concentration, calculated as the average of the top four firms' six sales-weighted resource allocation indicators in the focal firm's primary four-digit SIC industry; the six ratios for each industry were summed to obtain the composite industry norm. Normality assumptions necessitated the use of the natural log of the difference values.

Ambivalence is calculated as A = (D + C)/2 - (D - C), where D is the dominant evaluation and C is the competing evaluation. The degree of positive and negative evaluations of EU enlargement was measured with two items each, adopted from the work of Thomas and McDaniel (1990); the inter-item reliability (Cronbach's alpha) was 0.90 for the positiveness scale and 0.79 for the negativeness scale. Raw scores on each dimension were standardized prior to creating the measure to correct for different means due to the social desirability of positive evaluations. The measure is greater when positive and negative evaluations are about the same and when these evaluations are stronger, discriminating ambivalence from both univalent and weak or indifferent evaluations.
scale: continuous index computed from two seven-point Likert scales

description: Six items measuring firm strategy were adapted from the work of Thomas and McDaniel (1990), based on the strategy framework of Miles (1982), and were reworded to apply to companies of the various industries in the sample. Higher scores indicate a more domain-offensive strategy, and one item was eliminated due to its low factor loading. The scale has a coefficient alpha of 0.88.
scale: seven-point Likert. Direction: higher = more prospector (defender to prospector scale)

description: Three items measuring a firm's international experience were based on the work of Sullivan (1994) and Zou and Cavusgil (2002). The items were coded such that higher scores indicate greater international experience for the organization. The scale has a coefficient alpha of 0.88.

Three items were used to measure the extent to which CEOs thought the strategic issue was under the control of their firm, adapted from the work of Thomas and McDaniel (1990). The coefficient alpha for the scale is 0.89.

Information about the functional responsibilities of TMT members was collected for members of the 2004 TMT of each firm as listed in the Hoppenstedt 2004 database, and validated by telephone with a random subset of firms. Executives were classified into functional background categories used in previous research, and the top manager was classified by functional background where possible and otherwise as general manager. The degree of heterogeneity was calculated using Blau's (1977) index, where p_i is the proportion of the total team that each functional category represents; the higher the resulting score, the greater the TMT's functional heterogeneity. The published formula is not legible in the provided text.

The size of the TMT was measured by using the total number of members of a TMT (Barkema and Shvyrkov, 2007) as listed in the Hoppenstedt 2004 database, and the logarithmic transformation of TMT size was used in the analyses.

The measure is based on the number of different industries in which a company operates, obtained from the Hoppenstedt database, which used the European Classification of Economic Activities (NACE) system. A count variable of the number of five-digit industry groups in which the firm reported activities was created; because almost half of the sampled firms operated in a single industry, a binary variable was created taking the value 0 for single industry firms and 1 for diversified firms.

A variable resulting from two steps of analysis. First, the Compustar engineers coded projects for the extent to which they required innovation, from 1, 'requires no innovation to complete,' to 7, 'cannot be completed without a technological breakthrough.' The engineers then went back and assessed whether the newly created knowledge was likely to be reusable, drawing upon their expertise and records in the contract file. Reuse was coded only from the contract and did not involve seeking to discover what happened during the project.

Dummy variable coded 1 if one or more of Compustar's proprietary technologies was required for a project and 0 otherwise. Projects that require Compustar's proprietary technologies generally make such technology the center of the project. The Compustar engineers coded the variable drawing upon their expertise and the records in the contract files.

Dummy variable indicating whether a project had the potential to create reputational spillovers. It was coded 1 if a project had the potential to shut down a 'significant portion' of a customer's data center, and 0 otherwise. The Compustar engineers and managers agreed that data center incidents had the greatest potential to influence its reputation in the industry, and the engineers coded the variable.

Captures the amount of detail in the Compustar-customer contract that went into describing the task, ranging from 1, 'virtually no description of task (open-ended),' to 7, 'great detail used to describe the task and roles and responsibilities of both parties.' It was correlated at 0.9 with the number of sentences used to describe the task, which the author counted to correct for differences in how various authors of contracts wrote task descriptions. The coders for the description variable were the Compustar engineers, who were experts on information technology.

Dummy variable coded 1 if a subcontractor was involved in a project and 0 if the project was completed using only in-house personnel. It was coded from the records in each project file. Data limitations precluded the use of any finer-grained dependent variable capturing level of subcontractor involvement, and the invoices indicated that subcontractors were rarely involved in only a peripheral manner; Compustar served as project manager for all projects.

Social evaluations by the academic community, taken from a 1988 survey of academics conducted by Kirkpatrick and Locke (1989), in which faculty rated the quality of faculty at each school. The favorability of each school's reputation among academics was measured by aggregating the reputations of each school's faculty members.

A scale composed of three standardized variables (mean 0, S.D. 1) that were highly correlated and loaded onto the same dimension, with a Cronbach alpha of 0.814. The three variables are the school's reputation among recruiters for large companies, among top executives, and among business school deans.

Students' satisfaction with and admiration for their own school, measured by the average response of recent MBA graduates to a questionnaire item in a 1988 Business Week survey sent to a random sample of almost half of the 1988 graduates from each school.
Percentage of all applicants to the MBA program who were offered admission in fall 1988. A low rate of acceptance indicates selectivity, that is, creaming of the applicant pool.

variable_name: Yield rate of the MBA program
description: Percentage of all accepted applicants who decided to attend the MBA program in fall 1988. A high yield indicates attractiveness of the school to accepted MBA applicants.

variable_name: Median salary of executives in flagship executive program
description: Median salary, in thousands, of executives participating in the longest, most expensive general management executive education program offered by the school in 1988.
Average GMAT score for the MBA graduating class of 1988, used as evidence of the quality of students attending the school.
Average GMAT score for the last three years of entering Ph.D. students (1986 to 1988), used as evidence of the quality of students attending the school.

variable_name: Percent foreign students in MBA program
description: Percentage of the MBA class of 1988 who were not U.S. citizens, used as evidence of scrambling for student inputs not sought by schools favored by the national business community.

Mean number of full-time students in the school's MBA program, taken from the annual reports of the schools in the sample. The mean was 387 at the four student-oriented schools and 1152 at the five national-business-oriented schools.

variable_name: Percent MBAs with undergraduate business major
description: Percentage of MBAs entering in fall 1988 who had an undergraduate business major, used as evidence of input avoidance.

variable_name: Average starting salary of MBA graduates
description: Average starting salary, excluding bonuses, of graduates of the MBA class of 1988, used as evidence of streaming MBA outputs to desirable jobs.

variable_name: Percent MBA graduates going into consulting jobs
description: School-reported percentage of the MBA graduating class of 1988 going into consulting jobs, a desirable placement field.

variable_name: Number of MBA graduates who are CEOs of a Business Week 1,000 firm
description: Number of Business Week 1,000 firms in 1988 with CEOs who graduated from the school, used as evidence of the visibility of a school's outputs.

variable_name: Number of Ph.D. graduates on faculties of top business schools
description: Number of tenure-track faculty in 1988 at a top business school (the 23 in the Business Week survey) who held a Ph.D. from the school, used as evidence of Ph.D. output streaming.

variable_name: Percent senior faculty trained at Cluster 1 schools
description: Number of tenure-track associate and full professors who held a Ph.D. from a school in Cluster 1 (schools ranked high by the academic community) divided by the number of tenure-track associate and full professors at the school, based on fall 1988.

variable_name: Percent senior faculty trained at Cluster 3 schools
description: Number of tenure-track associate and full professors who held a Ph.D. from a school in Cluster 3 (schools ranked high by the national business community) divided by the number of tenure-track associate and full professors at the school, based on fall 1988.

variable_name: Percent senior faculty trained at Cluster 4 schools
description: Number of tenure-track associate and full professors who held a Ph.D. from a school in Cluster 4 (schools ranked high by MBA students) divided by the number of tenure-track associate and full professors at the school, based on fall 1988.

variable_name: Percent senior faculty trained at Cluster 2 schools
description: Number of tenure-track associate and full professors who held a Ph.D. from a school in Cluster 2 (schools ranked unfavorably by all three constituencies) divided by the number of tenure-track associate and full professors at the school, based on fall 1988.

variable_name: Percent junior faculty trained at Cluster 1 schools
description: Number of tenure-track assistant professors who held a Ph.D. from a school in Cluster 1 (schools ranked high by the academic community) divided by the number of tenure-track assistant professors at the school, based on fall 1988.

variable_name: Percent junior faculty trained at Cluster 3 schools
description: Number of tenure-track assistant professors who held a Ph.D. from a school in Cluster 3 (schools ranked high by the national business community) divided by the number of tenure-track assistant professors at the school, based on fall 1988.

variable_name: Percent junior faculty trained at Cluster 4 schools
description: Number of tenure-track assistant professors who held a Ph.D. from a school in Cluster 4 (schools ranked high by MBA students) divided by the number of tenure-track assistant professors at the school, based on fall 1988.

variable_name: Percent junior faculty trained at Cluster 2 schools
description: Number of tenure-track assistant professors who held a Ph.D. from a school in Cluster 2 (schools ranked unfavorably by all three constituencies) divided by the number of tenure-track assistant professors at the school, based on fall 1988.

variable_name: Constituency status rankings (academic, national business, student) and status clusters
description: Constituency-based status is measured by three separate, orthogonal rankings, each standardized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1: academia's ranking from the 1988 Kirkpatrick and Locke survey of faculty, the national business community ranking (a three-item scale of reputation among recruiters, top executives and deans, alpha 0.814), and the student ranking from the 1988 Business Week graduate survey. For H1 to H7 the three rankings are regressed on the dependent variables. K-means clustering on the three rankings also sorts the 20 schools into four clusters, each favorably ranked by a specific subset of constituencies or by none.
scale: Three standardized rankings (mean 0, SD 1); four-cluster classification

description: A binary treatment variable built from a continuous measure of utilization: the cumulated number of investment rounds each CVC unit made up to, but excluding, each year t. It is converted into a discrete treatment coded 1 if firm i's cumulated investment exceeded the median across all firms for that year, and 0 otherwise. Investment data come from the VentureXpert database.
time_window: cumulated up to, but excluding, year t

description: A treatment indicator equal to 1 if at least 50 percent of the CVC team was composed of individuals with firm-specific experience, and 0 otherwise. CVC managers whose job immediately preceding their first CVC job was in the adopting firm were coded as internal hires. The composition of managers in each CVC unit was reconstructed for each year, so the variable changes as managers enter and leave the unit. Work histories were reconstructed from biographies of CVC unit personnel found through internet searches.
time_window: reconstructed for each year of the sample; prior career experience

description: A treatment indicator equal to 1 if there was at least one person with independent venture capital experience on the CVC team, and 0 otherwise. IVC experience was identified by examining job titles and employers for prior jobs. Internal and practice experience are treated as independent, such that managers can have either, neither, or both types of experience.
time_window: reconstructed for each year of the sample; prior career experience

description: Takes a value of 1 in the year of abandonment and 0 otherwise. CVC units classified by VentureXpert as 'Defunct' or 'Inactive' were coded as abandoned, and the date of the unit's last investment was used to identify the year of abandonment. Units that made no CVC investments for at least four years were recoded as abandoned, with the first year in that interval coded as the abandonment year.

The number of CVC exits in the same four-digit industry and geographic state as the focal firm, used to capture abandonment pressure from the industry reference group. The measure is confined to similar and proximate others, and it is lagged by one year.
The number of IVC exits from the IVC industry per year, used to capture abandonment pressure from the practice reference group. The measure is lagged by one year.

The range or 'R' index merely counts the number of different types of actions used by an airline in a given year out of the possible 21 types. Range is an inverse indicator of competitive simplicity, so the signs of its betas were reversed in the tables to be consistent with the C and D indexes.

The C index is based on the standard deviation of the standardized (z) scores across the 21 types of actions for an airline in a given year, divided by the total number of actions for that airline in that year in order to adjust for differences in the number of decisions made by large vs. small companies. The standardized scores weight rarer decisions, such as route entries, more heavily than common decisions such as price cuts. The natural log of this quotient was taken to transform the index so that it would conform to the normality assumptions required for OLS regression analysis. The index increases as discrepancies in the standardized scores grow between a given airline's most and least common types of actions for that year, that is, with increasing concentration on the most numerous actions.

The D index is based only on the number of actions, again as measured by standardized scores, in an airline's most emphasized action category. It is the number of actions in the category with the highest number of actions for an airline in a given year divided by the total number of actions for that airline in that year, and the natural log was taken to normalize the quotient for OLS analysis. It is a narrower index of simplicity than the C index.

Market performance was gauged by passenger operating revenues per available seat mile flown. This indicator reflects not only the load factor of the airline, that is, the percentage of seats it fills, but also the revenue produced thereby given an airline's capacity. Return on assets and profit margins were deemed unsuitable because they are influenced by internal operating decisions and by factors with no clear relationship to the market-oriented actions studied.

Breadth of experiences was measured by the number of types of decisions reported in the preceding year; this lagged 'range' variable was used in the regressions incorporating the C and D indexes of simplicity. The regressions of the R index instead employ as an historical experience surrogate the total number of decisions made in the previous year, because the lagged range variable would have been a lagged version of the dependent variable in models predicting range.
Firm age was measured in years since founding.
The size of the organization was measured as the number of employees. The natural logarithm was taken to normalize the variable, which correlated at 0.86 with the log of sales revenues.

Market diversity was assessed by the number of segments and actors in an airline's market environment. It was measured by a composite index gauging (a) the number of different airports served by each airline and (b) the number of competitors faced by each airline (interitem correlation = 0.70).
Market growth was measured by the level of growth in total industry volume as reflected by annual change in total revenue passenger miles for the entire domestic airline passenger business.

The uncertainty index comprised three components: the annual number of route entries by new carriers, route exits, and bankruptcies (Cronbach alpha = 0.88). Each of these components was standardized before summation to ensure equal weighting.

Whether the suit experiences adjudication by the court, coded one if the suit is disposed from the court process by adjudication as against a settlement. It is one of two alternate formulations of the nonsettlement outcome in the second stage of the model, used because the theoretical arguments for nonsettlement suggest that when stake asymmetries in a patent suit are high the parties prefer to obtain a decision from the court rather than reach a settlement.

Whether the suit survives until summary judgment motions are completed, coded one if the suit remained unsettled until that stage. The authors use it because the costs of patent litigation begin to increase substantially at the summary judgment stage, suggesting a significant hurdle that should induce settlement before this stage.

The patentee's self-citations to the litigated patent, transformed into a ratio to all citations to the patent so as to orthogonalize the variable to the overall citation count (CITVAL), and used in log form because the distribution of citation counts is skew. The authors use self-citations because they reflect the extent to which the patentee has built on its own technology and indicate the related technological assets that may be isolated by the litigated patent.

The nonpatentee's citations to the litigated patent, transformed into a ratio to all citations to the patent so as to orthogonalize the variable to the overall citation count, and used in log form. It measures the strategic stakes of the nonpatentee in the technological domain of the litigated patent.
The time lag in years between the issue date of the litigated patent and the date on which the suit is filed. It is used as the measure of how early in the patent's lifetime the patent is sued.

The number of citations from the patentee's patents to the patents in the nonpatentee's portfolio. The authors use it as a measure of the potential for mutual hold-up, because the in-citations by the suing firm's other patents to its rival's portfolio capture the extent to which its need for reciprocal access can encourage settlement of the suit.
A dummy variable for whether a counter-suit is filed against the patentee, used to measure the potential for mutual hold-up and as the indicator of counter-suiting in the industry comparison.

Dummy variable identifying suits in the computer industry within the pooled sample; the models were also estimated separately for the two industries. The two industry samples are computers, which exhibits strong systems products features, and research medicines, which combines pharmaceuticals and medical biotechnology.

A theater's cash reserves at the end of FY 2003. To control for organization size, the authors divided cash reserves by the organization's total expenses in FY 2003. These unabsorbed resources are described as available for immediate deployment for virtually any purpose.
scale: ratio of cash reserves to total expenses

description: The level of subscription revenue for FY 2003 divided by the organization's total expenses in that year. Subscription revenues flowing from rare, relational customers are described as fungible and unabsorbed, and as representing excess resources in the same manner as waiting lists or oversubscriptions for capacity-limited organizations.
scale: ratio of subscription revenue to total expenses

description: Unutilized seating capacity: the total number of empty seats divided by total seating capacity at all performances during FY 2003. The authors state that this measure is closely aligned with conceptual and operational examples of generic, absorbed slack in the literature.
scale: ratio of empty seats to total seating capacity

description: The number of full-time directors, designers, and actors on a theater's staff divided by the total number of directors, designers, and actors it had employed during the year. Most theaters have one full-time artist on staff and hire additional artists as needed; having these resources on staff full-time rather than hiring each resource for a single show represents slack.
scale: ratio of full-time to total directors, designers, and actors

description: Three items asking the extent to which the current season's artistic decisions emphasize creating revolutionary new conceptual approaches, experimenting with radical new works, and challenging traditional artistic boundaries. Responses were given on a 7-point scale anchored 'weak emphasis' (1) to 'strong emphasis' (7). The three items loaded together on a single factor, and the authors averaged the responses for the three scale items to create construct scores.

Three items asking the extent to which the current season's artistic decisions emphasize maximizing the contribution of in-house artistic/production skills, offering shows that stay close to known strengths, and producing shows similar to those that have done well in the past. Responses were given on a 7-point scale anchored 'weak emphasis' (1) to 'strong emphasis' (7). The three items loaded together on a single factor, and responses were averaged into construct scores.

Three items on which respondents indicated agreement or disagreement on a 7-point scale ('strongly disagree,' 1, to 'strongly agree,' 7): whether the theater's economic future is promising (reverse-coded), whether the current overall situation is perceived as an opportunity (reverse-coded), and whether the current operating environment is felt to be particularly hostile. The three items loaded together on a single factor and were averaged into a construct score; the authors note that the reliability of this scale (.66) was slightly below recommended levels.

Following Deephouse (1996) and Miller and Chen (1996), strategic conformity was measured with absolute deviations of a firm's scores from industry medians, assessed against industry medians at the three-digit SIC level. The individual variables consist of six distinct subcategories of business-level strategy: capital intensity, R&D to sales, advertising to sales, financial leverage, dividend policy, and unsystematic (idiosyncratic) risk. Deviation scores were computed as the absolute value of the number of standard deviations from the median, and to derive the composite nonconformity index the six deviation scores were standardized and summed, so that lower values represent greater conformity. Missing values for R&D and advertising were coded as 0 because firms were required by law to report those expenditures on their 10-K filings whenever they were significant.

A dummy variable indicating the presence of one or more family officers, directors, or large (5%) owners was used to test H1. Data on vote control and family positions as founders, executive officers, and board members were obtained from at least three sources for each company: individual proxies, which were the primary and definitive source of data, Hoover's, and company websites. Data on individuals were aggregated to the firm level, at which information on strategy, governance, and market performance could also be collected.

Family control was assessed by the percentage of voting shares controlled by the family, for H2A. Consistent with prior work, the focal family was designated as the one with the most votes, and in totalling family votes the shares of co-trustees of family trusts who were directly employed by the family were included.

The presence of a family CEO was measured by a dummy variable, for H2B. Coefficients for predictor dummies reflect comparisons with the complement of Fortune 1000 firms that do not share the attribute, and separate models were run for predictors that intercorrelated highly.

The presence and generational status of family owners and officer categories (CEOs, chairmen) were determined, for H2C. Family CEOs in the second or later generations and family chairmen in the second or later generations were coded and compared with founder-generation family executives; in the models testing whether later generations are more associated with conformity than first generations, the comparison was only within the sample of family firms.

The presence and generational status of family owners and officer categories (CEOs, chairmen) were determined, for H2C, so that founder-generation family executives could be distinguished from later-generation ones. Family CEOs and chairmen of the founder generation were coded and their association with conformity assessed separately.

Involvement of the family in the business was assessed according to the number of family officers, the number of family directors, and family generations, for H2D. Data on family positions as founders, executive officers, and board members were obtained from individual proxies, Hoover's, and company websites. The authors did not combine the different aspects of family governance because these were expected to have different effects.

Involvement of the family in the business was assessed according to the number of family officers, the number of family directors, and family generations, for H2D. Data on family positions as founders, executive officers, and board members were obtained from individual proxies, Hoover's, and company websites.

Involvement of the family in the business was assessed according to the number of family officers, the number of family directors, and family generations, for H2D. Generational status of family owners and officers was determined from the proxies and corroborating sources.

Performance was assessed as return on assets and Tobin's q, with accounting data drawn from Compustat. In the models of performance on conformity, conformity index variables were lagged one year in predicting performance, and a family dummy conformity product interaction term was used to test whether family firms benefit more from conformity.

Performance was assessed as return on assets and Tobin's q, with market performance data obtained from the Center for Research on Security Prices. Conformity index variables were lagged one year in predicting performance, and a family dummy conformity product interaction term tested whether family firms benefit more from conformity.

The below-aspiration component of innovative performance. Performance below the aspiration level equals 0 when performance is above the aspiration level, and equals performance minus aspiration level when performance is below the aspiration level. Historical aspiration levels are generated by a rule whose input is the firm's historical patent performance and whose weight on the most recent aspiration level is 0.6 in the model predicting diversification and 0.9 in the model predicting dissimilarity.

The below-aspiration component of innovative performance measured against social aspiration levels, which are defined as a firm's patent counts averaged across all firms in the panel in a given year. Performance below the aspiration level equals 0 when performance is above the aspiration level, and equals performance minus aspiration level when performance is below the aspiration level.
The number of patents granted to a firm or its subsidiaries in a given year, used to construct the firm's historical and social innovative performance aspirations.

Potential slack, calculated as the ratio of income before taxes and interest charges to interest charges; a higher ratio reflects a higher ability of the firm to take on further debt. Because the raw measure takes negative values and is highly skewed, a constant is added to the data before applying the log transform, such that the transformation equals log(Y + a) with min(Y + a) = 1, where Y is the raw measure and a is the constant.

A portfolio's diversification measured with the entropy measure, where P is the percentage of R&D investment in a particular strategic vehicle. The measure accounts for two elements of diversification: the number of vehicles used and the relative importance of each, given by the investment amount. The formula block in the text is not readable in the extracted text.

The extent to which a firm changes the composition of its portfolio of technology-sourcing vehicles across years, measured as the sum of the absolute differences between the weights of each sourcing vehicle in the portfolio at year t versus year t-1; weights are based on the resources allocated to each vehicle. The higher the sum of the absolute differences in weights, the greater the dissimilarity of the composition of the firm's portfolio between two consecutive years. The formula block in the text is not readable in the extracted text.

A dummy variable set to 1 if a constructor uses a different engine supplier in the following season than in the current season. The variable therefore measures dissolution between year t and year t + 1 at the constructor-supplier-year level of analysis. The authors report that interviews indicate the decision to terminate the collaboration is generally made by the constructor, not the supplier.
time_window: between year t and year t + 1

description: A constructor's performance is its total number of points scored in the World Championship in the focal year divided by the total points awarded to all teams. The performance-aspiration gap subtracts the constructor's weighted average of its social aspiration level (the mean performance level) and its historic aspiration level from performance. A spline specification separates performance below aspirations from performance exceeding aspirations, and the negative part of the spline is reverse-coded so that the baseline hypothesis corresponds to a positive coefficient. The exponential updating function used to build the historic aspiration level is stated in a formula block that is not readable in the provided text.
time_window: performance in focal year t; historic aspiration updated from past performance (t - 1)

description: For each joint component user, the variable is that user's performance minus its own historic aspiration level, where the historic aspiration level is an exponential updating function of the user's past performance. When there is more than one joint component user, these values are aggregated by taking the mean. For constructors with no joint component users the variable is coded as zero. The aggregate is subjected to a spline transformation about zero and the negative component of the spline is reverse-coded. The aggregation formula is stated in a formula block that is not readable in the provided text.
time_window: focal year t; users' historic aspirations updated from past performance

description: A count of the number of structurally equivalent constructors who use engines from the same supplier as the focal firm. For a constructor of type X the variable counts other type X firms with the same supplier, and for a constructor of type Z it counts other type Z firms with the same supplier, excluding the vertically integrated constructor that supplies them. The variable is standardized in the interaction terms.

The geographic distance between the focal firm and its engine supplier in units of 1,000 km, calculated from the latitude and longitude associated with the organizations' addresses. The authors took the log of this variable to reduce skewness and standardized it in the interaction terms.

Negotiator's individual profits were taken directly from the bargaining solution agreed to by the negotiators in the simulation. Profits attained by bargainers in negotiation simulations are described by the authors as a commonly used measure of negotiation outcomes. The authors' view is that individuals try to maximize their own economic rewards while attempting to keep partners satisfied.

Partner's satisfaction with the negotiation was measured using a four-item scale included in the partners' post-game questionnaires. All scales were developed specifically for this research program. Satisfaction is one of the two negotiation outcome variables included in the study.
level: individual negotiator (as rated by the partner)

description: Two process-related measures were derived from the post-game questionnaires. Participants each rated their own personal bargaining strategy and that of their partner on several items. The scale for problem-solving bargaining strategies combines three items from the negotiator's questionnaire and three items from his or her partner's questionnaire, for a total of six items.

The partner's problem-solving bargaining strategy was measured from the post-game questionnaires, on which each participant rated his or her own bargaining strategy and that of the other party. As with the negotiator's strategy scale, the measure combines three items from the party's own questionnaire and three items rated by the other party, for a total of six items.
level: individual negotiator (strategy of the partner in the dyad)

description: Partners rated the interpersonal attractiveness of negotiators on the post-game questionnaires. The measure is a three-item scale developed specifically for this research program.
level: individual negotiator (as rated by the partner)

description: Each participant was assigned the role of either buyer or seller for the simulated negotiation and received the corresponding position sheet and payoff matrix. Role is treated as a situational constraint in the authors' model, is controlled for in the tests of Hypotheses 1 through 5, and is the effect variable in the test of Hypothesis 6.

Market model abnormal returns calculated with the Eventus software of WRDS using an estimation model period of 255 trading days ending 46 days prior to the event date; Eventus generates a CAR for each event by subtracting the calculated return from the actual return of each stock. The primary window is the six weeks (30 trading days) prior to the grant, and results are also reported for 45, 35, 25, 20 and 15 trading days before the grant. The average CAR across all option grants was used to test Hypothesis 1, and the individual CARs associated with each grant were the dependent variable in the tests of Hypotheses 3, 4, and 5.
time_window: 30 trading days (six weeks) prior to the grant, with alternative windows from 15 to 45 trading days

variable_name: Option grant at end of period
description: A dummy variable taking the value of 1 for the six-week period that ended with an option grant for a given CEO, and 0 for all other periods. Six-week (30-trading-day) periods were created starting from the option grant date and working backward, typically resulting in a panel of eight six-week periods per grant.
time_window: six-week (30 trading day) periods ending with the grant, up to a maximum of one year

description: The count of negative press releases issued by the firm in a given period. Press releases were collected for each firm using Business Wire and PR Newswire through LexisNexis covering one year before each grant, and each release was reviewed to ensure it was released by the firm; a total of 49,436 press releases were collected. Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count software counted the total positive and total negative affective words for each release and the tenor of each release was calculated (the printed formula is not readable in the text provided); a release was categorized as negative if its tenor fell in the bottom quartile of all releases. The variable is measured as 0 when no press releases were issued in a given period.
time_window: six-week (30 trading day) periods covering one year before each grant

description: Press release tenor calculated in the same way as for individual releases but combining all releases in a period together for the calculation. Higher values indicate a more positive tone (the mean tenor was 80.9%, indicating that eight out of 10 affective words were positive), so lower values indicate a more negative period. Unlike the count of negative releases, the overall affective tone takes a missing value for periods without press releases and those periods are excluded from the analyses. The printed formula for press release tenor is not readable in the text provided.
time_window: six-week (30 trading day) periods covering one year before each grant

description: The difference between a CEO's actual and expected pay. Expected pay was estimated with a generalized estimating equations wage model predicting the natural log of total direct compensation (TDC1 in Execucomp, the sum of salary, bonuses, restricted stock grants, option grants, performance share grants, and other income) from sales, R&D intensity (R&D expenses divided by sales), return on assets, market-to-book ratio, total shareholder returns, the natural log of firm age, presence on the S&P 500 index, CEO tenure, a cost of living adjustment for the company's headquarters location, four-digit GICS industry code, and year; sales, R&D intensity, return on assets, market-to-book ratio and total shareholder returns were averaged over the prior two years. The estimated pay was subtracted from actual total direct compensation and the result multiplied by -1, so positive numbers indicate greater underpayment relative to a given CEO's peers; the variable was winsorized at the first and 99th percentile.
time_window: firm performance indicators averaged over the prior two years

description: An industry-level (two-digit SIC) measure of the latitude CEOs have to consider multiple courses of action, built from multiple indicators following Chen, Crossland, and Luo (2015): R&D intensity (industry mean R&D expense divided by total revenue), industry munificence (average market growth over the previous five years), industry concentration ratio (Herfindahl index, reverse coded), and average capital intensity (industry mean net property, plant and equipment divided by the number of employees, reverse coded).
time_window: five years for munificence (average market growth over the previous five years)

description: A count variable of the changes between a team's current initial lineup of players and the players that played in the previous match; it is the number of new players a given team uses in the current match. Only the number of new players in the initial lineup who did not enter the match as a substitute in the previous match are counted, and players entering the lineup because of a red card or accumulated yellow cards are excluded from the calculation. It is measured prior to the start of each round of a season, and all first round observations were dropped from the data set.
time_window: measured before each round, relative to the previous match

description: A dummy variable that captures when a team replaced its coach. When the coach differed from the coach in the previous match, coach change was coded as 1; otherwise it was coded as 0. The authors observed 90 coach changes during their sampling frame.
time_window: measured before each round, relative to the previous match

description: The difference in points between the focal team and the team that occupied the reference group threshold rank, calculated after each round in the season. The reference group threshold is the 15th rank in the overall standings of the German Bundesliga, because this is the last rank that allows a team to remain in the Bundesliga. Small values of the variable indicate performance more proximal to an undesirable threshold.
time_window: after each round within the season

description: The difference in points between the focal team and the team that occupied the top performance threshold rank, calculated after each round in the season using expression (1). The rank needed to participate in the UEFA Cup is used as the contextually relevant operationalization of the top performance threshold. A team's performance above the top performance threshold is an increasingly positive number, whereas the distance below that threshold is increasingly negative.
time_window: after each round within the season

description: Constructed in three steps. The team's historic aspiration level (HAL) is based on the final rank of a team at the end of a season using an exponential weighted moving average; rank and not points is used because rank is the end-of-season performance outcome that becomes the basis for interseason aspiration setting. The absolute difference between the team's HAL rank and the reference group and top performance thresholds is then calculated, and the threshold with the smallest absolute difference to the HAL rank is considered the HiBSAT of a team for a given season, so teams could have 'HiBSAT top performance' or 'HiBSAT avoid relegation'. The HiBSAT is maintained as the performance benchmark for the whole season.
time_window: updated once per season, in the interseason break

description: For each round of a season the difference between a focal team's point total and the points of the team that currently occupies its respective HiBSAT rank was calculated, and a spline function of this variable was constructed for performance below the HiBSAT. The variable measures the distance in points to the HiBSAT for all Bundesliga teams at each round during a given season.
time_window: after each round within the season

description: For each round of a season the difference between a focal team's point total and the points of the team that currently occupies its respective HiBSAT rank was calculated, and a spline function of this variable was constructed for performance above the HiBSAT. The variable measures the distance in points to the HiBSAT for all Bundesliga teams at each round during a given season.
time_window: after each round within the season

description: Appointment announcement events at female-led Fortune 1000 and Fortune Global 500 firms, identified through the COMPUSTAT Executive Compensation Database and LexisNexis searches that included newspapers, magazine articles, industry newsletters, press releases, and news wires. Announcements involving founder CEOs and announcements with confounding events within three days were deleted. The final sample contained 33 unique female CEO appointment announcements.

Dismissal events at female-led firms, identified with LexisNexis searches of the same sources used for appointment announcements, with appointment and dismissal dates recorded for each female CEO. All dismissals in the sample appeared to be nonvoluntary terminations as opposed to planned retirements. The final sample contained 11 CEO departures at female-led firms.

variable_name: cumulative average abnormal returns (CAAR) of female-led peer portfolios
description: A peer female-led firm portfolio was formed for each announcement or dismissal, consisting of all other female-led firms in the sample on that event date, and the peer portfolios were pooled to test abnormal returns. Abnormal returns are the difference between the actual return and the expected return generated by the market model estimated from 255 to 46 days before the announcement date. CAAR is the sum of the average abnormal returns of the peer portfolios over a three-day window, with standardized returns reported using the Patell test and the CRSP equally weighted index as the market proxy.

variable_name: cumulative abnormal returns of male-led peer portfolios
description: The same pooling procedure was completed for each male appointment announcement, with male-led firm portfolios formed for each event. This resulted in 424 usable firms in the portfolio for appointment events at male-led firms, which serve as the comparison sample.

The announcement samples were split by the gender of the appointed CEO: the text analysis used 33 female CEO appointments and 12 male CEO appointments. The male comparison sample consisted of all male-led Fortune 50 firms from 2003 through 2006.

variable_name: mention of other executives of the same gender in appointment announcements
description: The authors reviewed the announcement articles for female CEO appointments to determine whether any additional female executives were mentioned, and completed the same text review for the male announcements. Where other executives were mentioned, linkages between the CEOs (i.e., gender) were recorded, and a t-test compared the female and male announcements.

Long-run averages of past self-employment rates in the parental country of origin, following the OECD definition of self-employment. The measure is constructed from ILOSTAT data and international census microdata and, due to data limitations, averaged over the period 1980-1993, i.e., before the first Current Population Survey wave. It is adjusted for differences in the level of economic development and institutional quality in the country of ancestry (averaged over the same period) so that it captures variation in entrepreneurial culture net of the level of self-employment that can be expected for a given level of economic and institutional development. For ease of interpretation the independent variables are standardized; results are presented as odds ratios.

Long-run averages of past self-employment rates in the parental country of origin, following the OECD definition of self-employment, built from ILOSTAT data and international census microdata and averaged over the period 1980-1993. The measure is adjusted for differences in the level of economic development and institutional quality in the country of ancestry over the same period, so that it captures variation in entrepreneurial culture net of the level of self-employment expected for a given level of economic and institutional development. The independent variables are standardized and results are presented as odds ratios.

variable_name: Entrepreneurial culture observed amongst second-generation immigrants in Europe (hypothetical 'cousins')
description: Ancestral group-level differences in revealed preferences for entrepreneurship among second-generation immigrants in Europe, obtained by estimating country of ancestry fixed effects while controlling for individual-level controls, ancestral human capital and network effects, as well as destination and year fixed effects. The average marginal effects of these country of ancestry fixed effects capture the actual entrepreneurial behavior of second-generation immigrants in Europe and are used as an alternative measure of revealed entrepreneurial culture to predict the likelihood that second-generation immigrant 'cousins' in the U.S. are self-employed. This cross-sample measure is not directly influenced by the economic or institutional conditions in the country of ancestry.

variable_name: Entrepreneurial culture observed amongst second-generation immigrants in the U.S. (hypothetical 'cousins')
description: Ancestral group-level differences in revealed preferences for entrepreneurship among second-generation immigrants in the U.S., obtained by estimating country of ancestry fixed effects while controlling for individual-level controls, ancestral human capital and network effects, as well as destination and year fixed effects. The average marginal effects of these country of ancestry fixed effects capture the actual entrepreneurial behavior of second-generation immigrants in the U.S. and are used as an alternative measure of revealed entrepreneurial culture to predict the likelihood that second-generation immigrant 'cousins' in Europe are self-employed.

Dichotomous indicator capturing whether or not individuals report being self-employed or family workers, following the OECD definition of entrepreneurship. Individuals who actively participate in the labor market are compared, i.e., individuals in self-employment versus wage employment. Individuals younger than 18 years or older than 65 years, full-time students, those taking care of the home, in the military, unemployed, or retired, individuals reporting a disability, and those working in the agricultural sector are not considered.

Individuals' self-employment status, operationalized just like in the U.S. case as a dichotomous indicator of whether the individual reports being self-employed. The same sample criteria as in the U.S. case (such as age thresholds, exclusion of retired individuals and agriculture) are applied.

Binary measure that takes the value 1 if the SIC code of the divested business differs from the parent's primary industry at the two-digit SIC code level, and 0 otherwise. The authors note that results using three-digit or four-digit SIC comparisons are similar.

variable_name: Rival R&D Intensity Higher than Parent
description: Binary variable that takes a value of 1 if the average R&D intensity, that is the ratio of R&D spending to sales, of firms in the divested unit's industry (defined at the two-digit SIC level) is greater than the parent firm's R&D intensity, and 0 otherwise. The measure captures the level of R&D spending by the divested business's rivals relative to its parent. A binary form is used because the hypothesis concerns whether the business's optimal R&D intensity exceeds its parent's, not by how much; results using a continuous measure are similar.

variable_name: Rival New Asset Durability Higher than Parent
description: Binary measure comparing the new asset durability of the divested business's rivals to that of its parent. New asset durability is calculated as the average expected life of new capital assets by dividing capital expenditure in a year by the portion of the depreciation expense attributable to this capital expenditure. Results are similar with a continuous measure of new asset durability difference.

The ratio of the long-term elements of executive compensation, specifically stock options plus long-term incentive plans, to total executive compensation. The measure is calculated for each member of the top management team listed in Execucomp and averaged across the team using individual compensation as weights, excluding the CEO's compensation. It is industry-adjusted by subtracting the average long-term compensation of executives in the same primary industry as the parent (two-digit SIC level).

variable_name: Parent Corporate vs. Divisional Executive Long-term Compensation Difference
description: The gap between the average long-term compensation of executives listed as 'C-level' (such as CEO, CFO, CIO, corporate counsel, or similar positions) and that of executives who do not possess corporate-level titles, such as divisional or executive managers in Execucomp. To reduce correlation with the overall executive compensation measure, the difference between corporate and divisional long-term compensation is divided by the level of corporate long-term compensation, so that higher values imply weaker long-term incentives for divisional executives relative to corporate executives.

Binary measure that takes the value 1 if the acquirer of the divested business was a private equity firm, and 0 otherwise. An acquirer is considered a private equity firm if it is so classified by SDC, and the authors confirm each buyer's identity using Internet searches.

Closeness centrality computed from geodesics (the shortest path length, i.e., the one with fewest intermediaries) between the focal division and another division in a knowledge network, summing over all reachable related divisions excluding the focal one. The measure is standardized so that a division has the shortest path length to related divisions when the index is one and the longest path length when the index is near zero. The measures were computed in UCINET IV. The formula is not readable in the text, so the specification is recorded from the authors' prose description.
scale: standardized index from near zero to one
time_window: network relations measured by only assigning ties that existed prior to the start of the project

description: Project managers allocated 100 points across six categories of ware: already developed ware from own division, new ware developed in own division, already developed ware from other divisions, new ware developed in other divisions, already developed ware from outside the company, and new ware developed outside the company. The project manager also indicated the project's percentage split between software and hardware, and the authors took a weighted sum of already developed ware from other divisions and new ware developed in other divisions, which they divided by 100. The resulting fraction of ware that came from other divisions ranges from zero to one.

The number of months from the start of concept development to the time of market introduction for a given project (or time to the end of the study period or cancellation for ongoing and canceled projects, respectively). Starting time was defined as the month when a dedicated person started working part or full time on the project, and the end date as the date on which the product was released to shipment. Completion times were 14.8 months on average for completed projects.
time_window: from start of concept development to market introduction, end of study period, or cancellation

description: The number of direct advice-seeking relations to related divisions, coded by counting the number of preexisting divisional ties to divisions that had related knowledge for a project and then assigning that value to the focal project. Advice-seeking relations are those in which the focal team went to other divisions for advice; they need to be maintained, unlike advice-giving relations, which require time helping others.
time_window: preexisting ties, assigned only if they existed prior to the start of the project

description: A three-item scale on which project managers rated the level of codification of the knowledge the project team received from other divisions: how well documented the knowledge was, whether all of it was sufficiently explained in writing, and whether it was mainly reports, manuals and self-explanatory software or mainly personal practical know-how and tricks of the trade. The items used seven-point scales and the average of the three scores represents noncodified knowledge (Cronbach's alpha 0.81).

The number of divisions with a competence that matched the requirements listed by the project manager for a given project. It was built from a list of 22 technical competencies developed with three corporate R&D managers, on which divisional R&D managers indicated up to four specific competencies of their divisions and project managers indicated the technical competencies their project required.

Self-reported answer to the survey question, 'In which year did your organization first create a position to deal with ethics and compliance issues?' The variable was coded as 0 in the years prior to adoption and 1 in the year of adoption, after which time the firm was excluded from the data set as no longer at risk of adoption.

variable_name: Fieldwide critical ethics events (1991, 1996, 2001, 2004 step functions)
description: Four variables, one for each event year (the creation of the sentencing guidelines in 1991, the court rulings in 1996, the Enron scandal in 2001, and the guideline revision in 2004), each formed as a step function coded as 0 in the years leading up to the event and 1 in the year of the event, with the coding of 1 retained in later years to test continued influence over time. A resetting clock variable, coded as 1 in the year of an event and increasing incrementally until the next event when it resets to 1, together with its square, models the effect of each event over time. The event years were identified in preliminary interviews with ECOs and in the extant literature.

One of two factors derived from five survey questions identifying the ECO's total annual budget, the number of full-time employees and the number of part-time employees that work for the ECO, the number of times a year the ECO meets formally with the CEO, and the number of times a year the ECO meets formally with the board of directors or one of its subcommittees. The five measures loaded cleanly onto two factors with eigenvalues greater than 1, labeled financial support and TMT support, which together represent the extent of implementation of the ECO position. Financial support captures the budgetary and staffing resources available to the ECO. The survey asked for this information for the current year (2008) and, where different, for each of the first three years following adoption of the ECO position; missing values were imputed with SIC one-digit means.
time_window: First three years following adoption and 2008

description: One of two factors derived from five survey questions identifying the ECO's total annual budget, the number of full-time employees and the number of part-time employees that work for the ECO, the number of times a year the ECO meets formally with the CEO, and the number of times a year the ECO meets formally with the board of directors or one of its subcommittees. The five measures loaded cleanly onto two factors with eigenvalues greater than 1, labeled financial support and TMT support, which together represent the extent of implementation of the ECO position. TMT support captures the ECO's formal access to the CEO and to the board of directors or one of its subcommittees. The survey asked for this information for the current year (2008) and, where different, for each of the first three years following adoption of the ECO position; missing values were imputed with SIC one-digit means.
time_window: First three years following adoption and 2008

description: The number of ethics transgression events reported about the firm in five national business publications (the Wall Street Journal, Financial Times, BusinessWeek, Fortune, and Forbes) in the three years prior to its adoption of the ECO position, based on articles drawn from the Factiva database in which the firm was mentioned in the headline or first paragraph. Articles were searched with a keyword list built from an expert-compiled list of organizational actions considered unethical; two articles containing the same search term within 14 days were coded as covering the same firm event. The number of events was weighted according to the average severity of each action, as rated by 40 ECOs on a 1 to 5 scale, and discounted to allow for the diminishing effects of events over time. Because of their exponential distribution these variables were logged.
time_window: Three years prior to ECO adoption

description: Respondents indicated what percentage of each of the production, R&D, and engineering functions was offshored during the past three years. Each function is a continuous variable ranging between zero percent (the function is fully performed at the domestic location) and 100 percent (the function is fully performed at offshore locations). The extent of offshoring primary functions is calculated by summing the percentage offshored of the three functions and dividing it by three.
scale: percentage offshored per function, zero to 100 percent

description: Measured as the percentage of revenues over the past three years that is attributable to new products and services. The measure shows the actual level of firm innovativeness as it assesses the end result of the innovation process. It was validated with a separate four-item scale adapted from Li and Atuahene-Gima (2002).
scale: percentage of revenues attributable to new products and services

description: A five-item measure adapted from Campion, Medsker, and Higgs (1993) representing the degree of variation in the TMT members' educational background and work experience. Respondents indicated their degree of agreement with the items on a seven-point scale where 1 = 'strongly disagree' and 7 = 'strongly agree'.

A five-item scale adapted from Sinkula et al. (1997) representing the degree of consensus among the TMT members regarding the future strategic direction of the firm. TMT members indicated their degree of agreement on a seven-point scale where 1 = 'strongly disagree' and 7 = 'strongly agree'.

The number of years of CEO experience in the position. The authors state that CEO tenure acts as a proxy for a CEO's knowledge and influences within the firm and outside the firm. In the estimated system of equations CEO tenure is lagged t-1.

Built from KLD data on the strength and quality of corporate actions in building long-term relations with internal stakeholders-employees. The KLD index has 14 dimensions of corporate actions for building relations with employees, such as union relations, a no-layoff policy, retirement benefits, cash profit sharing, employee involvement, health and safety, and workforce reductions. Because each KLD dimension should be standardized to make the scores across dimensions directly comparable, the final measure is the average of the standardized KLD strength scores.

Built from KLD data on the strength and quality of corporate actions in building long-term relationships with external stakeholders-customers, based on 10 separate dimensions. As with employee relations, the final measure is the average of the standardized KLD strength scores.

Measured with the standard deviation of five-year sales growth rates across firms in an industry. The authors state that the larger the standard deviation of industry sales growth, the more turbulent and uncertain the industry environment would be.

Derived from stock price data. Expected return from the broad financial markets is estimated with the Fama-French-Carhart model at the firm level, using market returns, the risk-free rate, size effects (SMB), value effects (HML), and Carhart's momentum effects (MOM). Firm performance magnitude or abnormal stock return is then the difference between observed returns and expected returns. The equations themselves are not readable in the supplied text.

The conditional standard deviation of the model residuals from the Fama-French-Carhart regression of firm returns on market returns, the risk-free rate, size effects, value effects, and momentum effects. It captures the firm's idiosyncratic vulnerability or risk of financial performance after accounting for broad market fluctuations.

Measured with 14 items (alpha = 0.88) based on Zahra (1996). CE was modeled as a meta-construct consisting of the sum of a firm's innovation, venturing, and strategic renewal activities. Confirmatory factor analysis was employed to test the validity of the second-order model; dropping two items produced good fit. The significant correlations of CE with R&D investments as a percentage of sales, percentage of revenue in the last three years due to new products and services, and sales growth further demonstrate the construct validity of CE.

Measured with a six-item scale (alpha = 0.78) from Jansen et al. (2009). The items captured the extent to which organizations separate entrepreneurial and efficiency activities in separate organizational units.
A five-item scale (alpha = 0.87) based on Sinkula et al. (1997). The scale taps into the extent to which there is a common purpose and organizational members' agreement and commitment to it.

Measured by five items (alpha = 0.85) adapted from Smith et al. (1994). The items reflect the attraction to the top management team, satisfaction with other top management team members, and the social interaction among team members.

Measured with a five-item scale (alpha = 0.74) appearing in Jansen et al. (2009). The variable gauges the extent to which firms use formal boundary-spanning integration mechanisms such as task forces, cross-departmental teams, and coordination of knowledge flows.
Captured by a four-item measure (alpha = 0.80) from Jansen et al. (2006), pertaining to the rate of change of the competitive environment.

Measured by the number of employees, log transformed for normality. The data for number of employees was gathered from the Reach database rather than from self-reported measures. Its highly significant correlation with annual revenue (r = 0.92, p < 0.001) suggests convergent validity.

variable_name: Propensity to take out a new option (second patent in a new subclass)
description: The dependent variable is the propensity of a firm to take out a new option, operationalized as the instantaneous probability or hazard rate of taking out a second patent in a patent subclass that is new to the firm, i.e., a subclass in which it has only one previous patent. Investment in an option is operationalized as the granting of a second patent to a firm in a technological area that was previously new to it. A second patent in a new area is taken as evidence of the initiation of a pattern of investment in that area and of a firm-level commitment to it.
level: patent event; level of analysis is the firm
time_window: duration since the grant of the first patent in the new area

description: The number of claims granted in the first patent in the new technical area. A claim is the actual contribution made by the invention, and the number of claims made by a patent indicates the areas of impact. More claims increase the potential application areas for a patent, increasing variance in performance outcomes and hence the option value of pursuing a second patent.
time_window: measured at the time of the first patent in the new area

description: Following prior work suggesting that patents classified in more technological areas are broader in scope, the scope of a patent was operationalized by measuring the number of technological classes into which it is categorized. This measures the potential of the opportunity presented by the first patent for a firm; the greater its scope, the more likely that it has applications in multiple technological areas.
time_window: measured at the time of the first patent in the new area

variable_name: Cumulative number of new areas entered
description: Extensiveness of previous commitments was measured by counting the cumulative number of new areas entered by the firm: the total number of all new technical areas (new subclasses) that the firm has entered in the past. It is measured at the time that the first patent in the current new technical area was granted. The more options the firm has taken out in the past, the more it needs to be concerned with expiration of those options.
time_window: measured at the time the first patent in the current new technical area was granted

description: The cumulative number of patents the firm has been granted in the pharmaceutical sector, calculated at the time when the first patent in a new technical area was granted. It is a measure of the degree to which the firm may be concerned with exploitation of existing options.
time_window: measured at the time the first patent in the new technical area was granted

description: The cumulative number of patents that the firm has been granted in other sectors, calculated at the time when the first patent in a new technical area was granted. It is another, even broader measure of the degree to which the firm may be concerned with the exploitation of existing options.
time_window: measured at the time the first patent in the new technical area was granted

description: The average number of patents granted per competitor in the new technical area for the firm, measured at the time the first patent was granted to the firm in that new technical area. Very low commitment by competitors indicates limited opportunity for firms seeking patents, signaling a sparse environment unattractive to potential new entrants; a large number of patents per competitor signals a hotly contested environment, also unattractive to new entrants.
time_window: measured at the time the first patent was granted to the firm in that new technical area

description: The number of competitors in the technical area at the time the first patent in the new technical area was granted to the firm. Competitors were defined as any other organization with patents in the technical area of concern, which might include not-for-profit organizations such as universities.
time_window: measured at the time the first patent in the new technical area was granted

description: The authors rely on acquirers' and targets' origin countries to measure PDV with Hofstede's (1980) PDV index, which they say remains the most widely used in cross-cultural studies. The index supplies a PDV value for each firm's country of origin.

Constructed for each acquisition by deducting the target's PDV from the acquirer's PDV (acquirer - target). The effect is modeled as piecewise with its slope changing at the theoretically defined breaking point of zero difference: D1 is the section of PDV difference for acquirer PDV < target PDV and D2 for the section of PDV difference for acquirer PDV > target PDV. A larger value of D2 means greater PDV difference whereas a smaller value of D1 means greater PDV difference (equivalent to reverse-coding).

The post-acquisition performance of an acquirer is measured using Tobin's q three years after a given acquisition. Tobin's q is proxied by the ratio of a firm's market value and long-term debt to total book assets. Market-based measures were chosen because accounting measures were not feasible given inconsistent accounting practices across countries.

A dummy variable with 1 for developed-developing cases and 0 for developed-developed cases, based on the long established classification of countries as 'developed' vs. 'developing'. Status inequality is expected to be greater between developed-country acquirers and developing-country targets than between developed-country acquirers and developed-country targets; all acquirers in the sample were from developed countries.

A variable constructed from the colonial history of the countries, with -1 for colony-colonizer cases, 0 for no colonial history cases, and 1 for colonizer-colony cases. An acquirer is expected to have higher status than a target when the acquirer's country is a former colonizer of the target's country.

Following prior studies, coded as 4 if an acquirer and a target overlapped in at least one business at the level of the four-digit SIC code, 3 at the level of the three-digit SIC code, 2 at the level of the two-digit SIC code, and 1 at the level of the one-digit SIC code.
The number of acquisitions that an acquirer made in the current target's country in the past, tracing back to 1980, the earliest data the authors could access.

A categorical measure of structure used to define U-form and M-form organizations along divisional lines, based on a scheme that includes functional (major subunits represent different functional areas), functional (with one or more subsidiaries reporting to top management), product divisions, geographic divisions and holding company. In order to form two distinct categories, the first two categories were classified as U-form firms and the three product divisional categories were classified as M-form firms. There were 43 U-form and 81 M-form firms in the sample. Structural data came from questionnaires completed by each firm's chief executive officer and another senior-level executive.

A categorical measure of diversification strategy with four classifications, each representing an increasing degree of diversification, used originally by Wrigley (1970) and later by Grinyer et al. (1980): single business, dominant business, related business and unrelated business. Because these are all very large firms, the single-product and dominant-product firms were combined. The resulting sample included 30 dominant businesses, 63 related diversified and 31 unrelated diversified firms. Diversification data came from questionnaires completed by each firm's chief executive officer and another senior-level executive.
scale: categorical (single business, dominant business, related business, unrelated business)

description: R&D intensity is research and development expenditures as a percentage of sales. Relative R&D investment was obtained by dividing firm R&D intensity by industry R&D intensity (firm R&D expenditure divided by firm sales, over industry R&D expenditure divided by industry sales). For related and unrelated diversifiers, R&D intensity was divided by the industry R&D intensity represented by the most dominant product within the firm. Both firm- and industry-level R&D expenditure and sales were obtained from the annual Business Week Corporate R&D Scoreboard.

The financial performance measure used to test the tradeoff effects was the Treynor Index. The prose defines MR = market return, GMR = geometric mean annual stock return for firm i, RFR = geometric mean annual riskless rate, and B = beta measure of systematic risk; the algebraic statement of the index itself was not readable in the text. Daily market returns for firms' securities came from the CRSP tapes and a maximum of 5 years (1975-79) of data were used to calculate the geometric mean annual return. The geometric annual risk-free rate was computed from the average selling price at the weekly 3-month treasury bill auction, obtained from the Federal Reserve Bulletin, and beta measures of systematic risk were taken from the Value Line Investment Survey.

An accounting-based profitability ratio which reflects the efficiency of operations and the productivity of the firm's asset base, used extensively as a performance indicator in strategic management research. Values were computed for each spin-off unit for the period before and the period after the spin-off event; the detailed definition given in the variable-definition table could not be read from the text.
time_window: up to 2 years prior to 3 years after the spin-off

description: A market-based measure reflecting the shareholder value of the firm, incorporated as the ratio of market value to book value. The authors note that the difference between market value and book value is an appropriate indicator of the perceived ability of the firm's strategy to achieve the required returns of investors. Pre- and post-spin-off values were computed for each unit; the text does not give the formula used to calculate the ratio.
time_window: up to 2 years prior to 3 years after the spin-off

description: The alpha coefficient from the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where significant alpha coefficients indicate deviations from the risk-adjusted expected market values of the firm and in some sense reflect the average extent to which the firm has created or destroyed value during the period of estimation. Because stock price data are not available for the spin-off unit prior to the spin-off event, changes in alpha brought about by divestiture cannot be determined and only post-divestiture alpha values are used.

Growth in sales, adjusted for inflation, used as a measure of performance in strategic management research. In this study sales growth is seen as an indication of the degree to which management was able to exploit the autonomy provided through the spin-off event to expand its operations. Pre- and post-spin-off values were computed for each unit.
time_window: up to 2 years prior to 3 years after the spin-off

description: Each parent-subsidiary pair was classified as related or unrelated by three judges, who were presented with descriptions of the activities of each parent firm and spin-off subsidiary and were instructed to score cases that were neither clearly related nor clearly unrelated into the most appropriate of the two categories. Agreement among the judges was tested and the degree of concurrence was significant at p < 0.002.

Level of CEO organizational identification measured with nine survey items adapted from Mael and Ashforth (1992) and Bergami and Bagozzi (2000). One question asks respondents to assess the degree of overlap between their self-definition and that of the firm, represented pictorially by a series of Venn diagram-type circles ranging from far apart to complete overlap. A confirmatory factor analysis on the nine survey items showed adequate model fit and inter-item reliability was high (coefficient alpha = 0.87), and the lambdas were highly significant for all nine items. The measure was normally distributed, and data for the dependent variable were collected for year t and year t + 1.
scale: eight-point scale; a five-point scale for the pictorial self-image overlap question
time_window: year t and year t + 1, one and two years after the independent variables measured at t - 1

description: Coefficient of imbalance calculated with the content analysis procedure described by Pollock and Rindova (2003). The prose states that the formula uses P, the number of positive articles about a firm, N, the number of negative articles, and V, the volume of articles about the firm including neutral ones; the OCR rendering of the formula itself was removed from this payload and is not reproduced here. The variable can range from negative one to one, where negative one indicates that all articles are negative and one indicates all positive coverage. Articles about the focal firm were collected from major news and business publications in the U.S. listed in Factiva and LexisNexis, plus daily newspapers in cities where the firm is headquartered or has significant operations.
