The authors know, for example, which of the patents Merck filed in 1983 led to the successful launch of a drug; the observation period for successful launches ends in 2007, when all patents filed between 1981 and 1990 would typically have expired.
time_window: patents filed in year t (1981-1990); launches observed through 2007

description: Dummy coded 1 if the CEO was a member of the controlling family and 0 otherwise. The familial nature of the CEO was determined by surname affinity with that of the controlling family, as recorded in Chamber of Commerce filings. Only firms led by a single CEO were selected for the main analysis.

Return on assets, computed as net operating income before extraordinary items divided by total assets. Financial information was obtained from AIDA. The lagged value of ROA is included as a control in all regressions.

Measured as yearly revenues. Yearly revenues were median-centred to identify the four quadrants, so that smaller firms range between 50 and 90.5 million euros and larger firms from 90.5 million euros upward.

Herfindahl concentration index calculated as the sum of squares of each family shareholder's percentage of shares held, following Schulze et al. (2003a). Shares were recorded for the seven largest family shareholders, since almost 90 percent of the firms had seven shareholders or less. A concentration index close to 1 indicates strong concentration; the index was median-centred to classify concentrated versus dispersed ownership.

variable_name: influence of environmental components on freedom of decision
description: Two sets of questions were presented to the general managers concerning the effects of environmental dependencies on their freedom of decision making. In the first set they ranked environmental factors and conditions, and in the second set environmental entities, according to the amount of influence they exercise on the manager's freedom of decision. The responses produced the 23 variables that entered the matrix of weak monotonicity correlations.

variable_name: Weak monotonicity correlations between perceived dependencies
description: Similarity of perceived effects on autonomy was read from Guttman's coefficients of weak monotonicity computed between managers' perceived-dependency ratings for the components within a segment (23 variables in all). Positive, high coefficients indicate components affecting autonomy in a similar way, and negative coefficients indicate differential effects.

variable_name: Author classification of environmental segments as homogeneous or heterogeneous
description: Segment homogeneity is not scored with a variable. The authors classify the segments a priori by how similar the interests of their components are and whether the components affect the firm's autonomy through the same means: the workers and owners segments are treated as completely uniform (affecting autonomy through costs and through long range plans respectively), the government as the most heterogeneous segment (its agencies were shown in an earlier study to have different interests), and the market segment as mixed because clients and the Common Market affect autonomy through different means. The hypothesis is then checked by comparing the weak monotonicity correlations within and between these segments.
scale: Qualitative classification of segments (uniform, mixed, heterogeneous)

description: Indigent patient days as a percentage of total patient days. It is the percentage of indigent patients for whose treatment the hospital received no compensation to the hospital's total patient population, measured in patient days, and is one of the two measures of beneficence used as a predictor of regulatory leniency.
The number of residents trained per inpatient bed. It is the measure of medical education, one of the two measures of beneficence used as a predictor of regulatory leniency.

Indicator variable equal to 1 in the years a prosecuted hospital engaged in upcoding, that is, the violation period as documented in the FCA settlements, and 0 otherwise. It is a proxy for the rigor of enforcement: a regulator that does not initiate a prosecution or does not join a whistleblower produces a value of 0, so higher values imply less leniency.

The natural logarithm of the settlement amount per hospital as reported in the settlements for upcoding under the FCA. Under the FCA the regulator has three ways of being lenient: do not initiate a prosecution, do not join a whistleblower, or join a whistleblower but make sure that the settlement amount is low; a value of zero reflects the first two, while a positive amount is informative about the third, so more leniency implies a move toward zero.

Indigent patient days as a percentage of total patient days, the share of indigent patients for whose treatment the hospital received no compensation. It is one of the two measures of beneficence used as a predictor of the DRG-specific upcoding ratios.
The number of residents trained per inpatient bed, the measure of medical education, used as a predictor of the DRG-specific upcoding ratios.

Continuous variable between 0 and 1, calculated as the number of patients in the TOP DRG divided by the total number of patients in the DRG group. Three such ratios are estimated, one for each DRG family: DRG79 (high incentives), DRG144 (medium incentives), and DRG296 (low incentives).

SI is a latent construct formed by practical, analytical, and creative intelligence and calculated through LISREL confirmatory factor analysis. The coefficients of the paths to SI are PI = 0.30, AI = 0.16, and CI = 0.21, and SI is composed approximately of 47% PI, 33% CI, and 19% AI. The authors note that interpretation of the composition of SI should be guarded because PI was measured situationally specifically while AI and CI were measured generally.

Responses to three scenarios that followed design suggestions by Sternberg et al. (1995b); each scenario presents a situation and a list of 10 actions that respondents rank-order according to their best sequential plan of action. A standard best-practice ranking of the alternative actions was developed from the average ranking used by respondents from the top 50 companies in sales and employment growth, selected from the 746 initial respondents less the 143 HGEs studied. Total ranking variances from the best practices standards were computed for each scenario for each respondent, then the three total variances were averaged and reversed to measure practical intelligence.

Measured with a Bieri et al. (1966) cognitive complexity grid. Respondents evaluate six people they knew (e.g., closest friend, person to avoid, father) on a five-point scale ((1) extremely low, (5) extremely high) over six characteristics (e.g., responsible, excitable, dull). Differences between the ratings are summed to indicate the test-taker's range of evaluation, and the sum of the differences across the ratings is the single measure of AI, with a high total score indicating an ability to analyze (i.e., differentiate) a situation into many constituent elements.

Measured with 30 associative word problems from Mednick's (1968) Remote Word Association Test (RAT), as extended by Bowden and Jung-Beeman (2003). RAT tests individuals' ability to see associative concepts among 30 sets of three words. The authors selected 30 items that demonstrated high reliability in a questionnaire setting and used the number answered correctly as the single indicator of creative intelligence.

The 22-item scale developed by Chen et al. (1998). The 22 items refer to an individual's ability to perform entrepreneurial tasks (e.g., marketing, innovation, management, risk taking, and financial control). Each item was measured on a five-point Likert scale ranging from (1) completely unsure to (5) completely sure, and the ESE score is the average response for the 22 items.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = completely unsure to 5 = completely sure)

description: Measured with responses to three scenarios (technology adoption, new product development, and market development). Participants were asked to circle the approximate number of days (2, 5, 10, ..., 180 more) it would take to choose from an array of possible improvement actions and to begin trial or revision improvement actions. Responses were reversed and mapped to a 10-point log scale (1 = 180 days to begin and 10 = 1 day to begin).
scale: 10-point log scale (1 = 180 days to begin, 10 = 1 day to begin)

description: Measured with eight Likert-type response scales based on Miner et al. (2001) and discussions of change behaviors with 10 founders. Typical statements were: 'We frequently experiment with product and process improvements.' 'Continuous improvement of our products and processes is a priority.' Each item was measured on a five-point Likert scale ranging from (1) strongly disagree to (5) strongly agree, and scoring was the average response.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Measured with two items: (1) the compound annual sales growth rate from year-end 2001 to year-end 2005, and (2) the compound annual employment growth rate from year-end 2001 to year-end 2005. Nine cases of incomplete performance data were completed with data from Dun and Bradstreet Inc. (2002-2006).

The extent to which the outsourced patent prosecution work of a focal client company is concentrated within a few suppliers (law firms), as opposed to being distributed among a large number of suppliers. It is measured with a Herfindahl-type index (HHI) of outsourced patents computed across different suppliers, using firm-supplier frequency counts, with a bias correction for HHI measures based on count shares. The supplier responsible for each outsourced patent was coded from the 'Attorney or Agent' field on the patent, and where law firm names were absent the listed attorney names were cross-referenced with the USPTO's yearly rosters of registered patent attorneys to identify the law firms that employed them. The variable ranges between 0 and 1, where a larger number implies higher supply portfolio concentration; observations with fewer than three outsourced patents are excluded because the unbiased estimate is undefined or noisy for small counts.

Measured as the percentage of patent citations to the firm's own prior patents (self-citations) averaged over all the firm's outsourced patents in each year. A higher percentage of backward self-citations implies that the firm's outsourced patents build to a greater extent on its own inventions than on technologies invented more broadly in the economy, and because patent legal work requires detailed knowledge about the technological background of the patent, the variable directly measures the firm specificity of the outsourced knowledge work.

Measured by the extent to which a firm's outsourced patents are in connected (versus disconnected) subsets, where any two patents that share common backward citations are assumed to be connected. Components of the resulting graph are identified with UCINET, and interrelatedness is computed as a (nonbiased) HHI of the distribution of patent shares into such subsets; if all the firm's outsourced patents are connected they form one giant component and interrelatedness is 1.0, whereas two equal-sized components give 0.25. Two alternative measures, density and weighted density of the patent graph, were also used.

Measured by the percentage of patents that are outsourced each year by the firm—that is, the number of patents outsourced divided by the total number of patents applied for. The total volume of outsourcing is employed separately as a control variable.

Measured using the technology classes of the firm's outsourced patents: a (nonbiased) HHI of the shares of a firm's outsourced patents across different four-digit IPCs in a given year, subtracted from 1, and adjusted for the relatedness among IPCs. Relatedness is measured by the extent to which suppliers' volumes of patent prosecution work in any two IPCs are correlated, based on 163,524 patents handled by the 100 largest supplier law firms; when all IPCs are unrelated the correlations evaluate to 0 and the measure behaves like a conventional HHI, after which the HHI bias correction is applied.

Measured as the weighted average of the growth rate of patenting across the technological domains (four-digit IPCs) associated with the firm's outsourced projects, weighting each IPC growth rate by the share of the firm's outsourced patents in that IPC in that year. Growth rates were computed from the universe of patents issued by the USPTO from 1986 to 1995, using a three-year moving average of the number of patents in each IPC; only IPCs with at least 10 issued patents during the 10-year observation window were included.

Centralization was measured for each specific headquarters-subunit dyad, accessing the headquarters' influence on each subunit's decisions. Three statements regarding interunit activities measured centralization, assessed on a 7-point Likert scale. The Cronbach's coefficient alpha for this composite measure was 0.83. To transform the measure for analysis, the authors created a new 24x24 matrix reflecting the sum of centralization ratings for each pair of units in the company.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: The pattern of interunit social interaction was assessed through a sociometric question asking respondents to indicate the units with which their own unit interacted frequently during social occasions (such as company picnics or sports clubs). Respondents received a list of all 24 units in the company. A 24x24 matrix was created based on data collected from this sociometric question.

Each respondent was asked to indicate the units from which they received technology or know-how, using a roster and free-choice question format with a list of all 24 units in the company and no constraint on the maximum number of selections. To validate the data, the opposite question was also asked, that is, who came to them for new knowledge or expertise. The relationship was treated as asymmetric, and the data were collected in the 1998 survey.

Internal resource competition was measured by the extent to which organizational units were structurally equivalent based on internal resource flows within the company. Respondents indicated from which units they acquired resources (such as input materials, components, or semiproducts), and a matrix of interunit resource flows was constructed. Structural equivalence was determined using CONCOR, an iterated correlation algorithm, applied to the resource matrix to identify groups of actors with similar relationships; this resulted in four blocks. A new 24x24 matrix was created in which a cell equaled 1 if two units were structurally equivalent and 0 if they were not.

External market competition was measured by asking respondents to indicate which units compete with them in the marketplace. As with the other sociometric questions, the item was followed by a list of all 24 units from which respondents could select their answers. A 24x24 matrix was created based on data collected from this questionnaire item.

The number of occupations represented in a job seeker's network; more occupations in the network are taken to indicate lower occupational focus of the contacts. For each contact entered, the respondent indicated the contact's occupation in open-ended responses; these responses were coded into the same 19 job types used to classify the job options pursued (intercoder reliability was 0.90) and subsequently reduced to 11 categories.
time_window: eight months into the program (job search process survey)

description: An alternative measure of the contacts' occupational focus, described as a measure of the concentration of social contacts. The formula as printed in the paper could not be read from the text; the text states that n is the total number of occupations represented in the job seeker's network.
time_window: eight months into the program (job search process survey)

description: Operationalized as the average level of emotional closeness the job seeker feels with his or her contacts. For each contact, respondents answered the question, 'How close do you feel to this person?' on an answer scale of 1 to 5, where 1 was 'very distant' and 5 was 'very close.' The responses to this question were averaged across all the contacts in the job seeker's network.
level: contact, averaged to the job seeker
time_window: eight months into the program (job search process survey)

description: Measured as the average frequency of interaction with the contacts in one's network. To construct this measure, the authors used answers to the question, 'How frequently have you interacted with this person since you started the MBA program?' Possible responses ranged from 1 to 5, where 1 was 'once' and 5 was 'daily.' The responses were averaged across all the contacts in the job seeker's network.
level: contact, averaged to the job seeker
time_window: eight months into the program (job search process survey)

description: The number of different job types the job seeker applied for. To describe the types of jobs they had pursued, students were asked to provide the industry and functional role of each in an open-ended format and could enter up to three different job types. The open descriptions were coded into a list of 19 job types, condensed into 11 categories used in the analyses.

The total number of interviews obtained by the job seeker. Once a job type description was entered, a follow-up question asked for the number of interviews received in the respective job type; the question was repeated for each type of job pursued and the numbers of interviews in each were recorded separately.

Captures the extent to which the interviews obtained are concentrated in one or more job types, computed from the number of interviews in each job type relative to the total number of interviews obtained; n is the total number of job types applied for by the job seeker. The formula as printed in the text could not be read reliably.

The number of job offers obtained by the job seeker. Once a job type description was entered, a follow-up question asked for the number of offers received in the respective job type; the question was repeated for each type of job pursued and the numbers of offers in each were recorded separately.

An indicator for specialist form identity, accomplished through an interpretive categorical distinction. The criteria were public perceptions of market dominance (reflected in a widely disseminated annual list of the 'top ten firms' in the industry) and an affiliation with a large parent conglomerate, since all but one of the firms coded as generalists had originally been founded as in-house agencies for major Korean corporations. Three researchers coded organizational forms and reached full agreement on all members of the categories, and the industry experts agreed with the coding and did not recommend any corrections.

Individual voluntary turnover (or external mobility), coded 1 when an individual moved from one firm to another within the advertising industry in Korea, and 0 otherwise. The directories do not identify job transitions between agencies, so turnover was coded by comparing each individual's position between two consecutive years and identifying cases in which a job change involving a transition between agencies had occurred. Cases in which an individual did not appear in the directories for at least a year were not marked up as turnover because dismissals likely result in at least a brief period of unemployment.

A duration variable counting the waiting time (in years) until promotion in the current firm. The clock started with an individual's entry in the firm and was reset to zero each time he experienced a promotion or transitioned to a job with a new agency.

Industry experience was first measured as a continuous measure of the years an employee had worked in the industry. The distribution of this variable was then used to mark up cases in the top quintile to denote high industry tenure, a cutoff corresponding to employees with eight or more years of industry experience.

Employee rank was measured with the conventional seven-level position system in Korea: (7) CEO, chairperson, or president, (6) vice president, (5) executive director (Jeon-Mu), (4) managing director (Sangmu), (3) director (Isa), (2) general manager (Bujang), and (1) deputy general manager (Chajang) and manager (Gwajang). To create the measure of high rank position, the top quintile in the distribution was marked up, corresponding to those in positions of managing directors (level 4) or higher. In roughly 5% of the cases employees were listed as directors instead of managers; such cases were recoded conservatively to an equivalent of the seven ranks.

The reputation of an employee's educational institution measured contemporaneously: the universities where the managers were schooled were first identified, annual reputation scores were computed for each university, and the score was matched to each employee-year observation. University reputation scores were constructed from the average national college entrance examination scores (equivalent to the SAT in the United States) of all students matriculated in the department of business administration in the focal university. For specialized universities lacking a business department, the average scores of students in the university's most highly ranked department were used instead. As with the position rank and industry experience variables, the distribution of the continuous status measure was used to mark up cases in the top quintile.

Two independent German-native coders read the firms' annual reports and coded for statements indicating the company's espousal of a shareholder value orientation. Coders were instructed to consider only statements that included either the English term 'shareholder value' or its German translation of 'increasing firm value' ('Unternehmenswertsteigerung'); interrater agreement was 0.916. Adoption was treated as an absorbing event, so firms were removed from the risk set upon adoption.

Adoption of three governance practices considered consistent with a shareholder value orientation: 'value-based' management control systems, stock option plans for management, and internationally accepted accounting standards (IAS or US-GAAP). Implementation was coded both individually, i.e., whether the firm adopted any of these practices, and grouped, i.e., as the number of adopted practices. Data on value-based incentive systems and stock option plans came from annual reports and were verified with the firms; accounting standards were coded zero for local standards and one for internationally accepted standards, and were cross-checked with the annual reports.

A categorical measure of ownership level for the group of German banks that have themselves espoused a shareholder value orientation, with cutoffs tied to substantively significant levels of stock ownership. It was coded zero if the owner category controlled less than 5 percent of a firm's voting shares, 1 for at least 5 but less than 25 percent, 2 for at least 25 but less than 50 percent, 3 for at least 50 but less than 75 percent, and 4 for 75 percent or more of voting shares. Data are corrected for super-voting shares to reflect the voting rights of blockholders, and a matching group was created for non-espousing banks.

The same categorical ownership-level measure was coded for ownership by German non-financial firms that have themselves espoused a shareholder value orientation, using cutoffs at 5, 25, 50 and 75 percent of voting shares. A matching non-espousing group was also created to contrast differences between these groups.

The categorical ownership-level measure was coded for shareholdings controlled by federal and state government entities, split into pro-business and pro-labor governments. Data were collected on whether these governments were controlled by the German conservative or social-democratic party or party-led coalitions.

variable_name: Family ownership level (3rd or later generation)
description: The categorical ownership-level measure was coded for family blockholdings classified by generation using the firm's age: family holdings were treated as controlled by the founder or the founder's generation if the firm's age was less than 30 years, by the second generation if the firm was more than 30 but less than 60 years old, and by the third or later generation if the firm was more than 60 years old.

A variable indicating whether the firm's chief executive officer has a background in economics or law, coded from a directory of German executives and supplemented with other sources and the firms' annual reports. Executives with training in economics or law are treated as more predisposed toward a shareholder value orientation than those trained in other areas.
The age of the firm's chief executive officer, taken from a directory of German executives and supplemented with other sources and the firms' annual reports.

Shareholdings by espousing corporate owners, operationalized in the analyses through the categorical ownership levels of German banks that espouse a shareholder value orientation and of German non-financial firms that espouse a shareholder value orientation, in contrast to non-corporate owners (governments and families).

Managerial predisposition is indicated by the CEO's age and educational background, operationalized through the CEO age variable and the indicator for a CEO degree in economics or law, together with their interaction.

An aggregate measure of stakeholder relations computed from five KLD dimensions. Each of the five dimensions is tabulated in terms of several strengths and concerns in the KLD index; to arrive at a net score for each dimension the total number of concerns was subtracted from the total number of strengths, and each dimension was standardized to make the scores across dimensions directly comparable. The average of the standardized scores on the five dimensions with equal weight was then used to obtain an aggregate stakeholder relations score. The lagged value of stakeholder relations for firm i is used in the persistence models.

variable_name: Persistence rate of industry-adjusted ROA and Tobin's q (superior performance sample)
description: Corporate financial performance was measured in two ways, return on assets (ROA) and Tobin's q, and each measure was adjusted by its industry average calculated at the four-digit Standard Industrial Classification code level. Persistence is estimated with a first-order autoregressive model in which β0 is the persistence rate when there is no influence from other factors, and the interaction of stakeholder relations with lagged financial performance indicates whether firms with good stakeholder relations have a greater persistence rate. The above average group was composed of firms with both lagged ROA and lagged Tobin's q greater than zero.

variable_name: Persistence rate of industry-adjusted ROA and Tobin's q (inferior performance sample)
description: Corporate financial performance was measured in two ways, return on assets (ROA) and Tobin's q, and each measure was adjusted by its industry average calculated at the four-digit Standard Industrial Classification code level. Persistence is estimated with a first-order autoregressive model in which β0 is the persistence rate when there is no influence from other factors, and the interaction of stakeholder relations with lagged financial performance indicates whether firms with good stakeholder relations have a lower persistence rate. The below average group comprised firms with both lagged ROA and lagged Tobin's q less than or equal to zero.

Modeled as an event count: the number of newly started SRI funds per country year. Funds are those that Bloomberg explicitly categorizes as ''socially responsible''; only primary share classes were selected to avoid double or multiple counting because a fund can have multiple share classes managed by the same organization. Each fund's country is identified by its legal domicile, and funds domiciled in known offshore sites were excluded. Inception dates from Bloomberg were used to determine the founding year of the funds.

The proportion of the workforce employed in the financial sector, based on International Labor Organization data, following the definition of the financial sector from prior studies—employment in finance, insurance, and real estate, the FIRE sector. The authors argue the proportion both captures the means the financial logic provides and indicates how legitimate or normative its profit-maximizing ends are. The variable is centered in the models, and its squared term (reported as Finance 2) is used to estimate the curvilinear effect.

Measured as the percentage of employees who are unionized in a country. Obtained from the OECD, which calculated the value using survey and administrative data adjusted for nonactive and self-employed members.
The logged number of Christians in the population, used as a measure of the religious logic. Data for this variable came from the Association of Religion Data Archives.

The share of seats in parliament held by green parties, used as a measure of the extent to which the state is geared toward environmental causes. A country might have one or more green parties, so all green seats were aggregated. The share of seats in a given parliament, instead of the vote share, was used to indicate the power of the green parties. The measure was taken from the Comparative Political Dataset.

This variable is coded 0, which turns to 1 after a firm experiences a lost patent race. The coefficient indicates the primary impact of losing a patent race on a firm's innovation, relative to winning a race. Treatment time is set at the competitor's priority date, the earliest time at which firms can become aware of their status in the innovation race.

Firms' technological innovation is measured as the number of patent applications in a given year. The measure allows evaluation of both public and private firms, and it allows the authors to observe whether an application is granted or abandoned, which is richer than focusing only on granted applications.

The variable for firm ownership type is coded as 1 for public firms and 0 for private firms 1 year before the treatment, as a baseline year. Using IPO and delisting years, the authors distinguish between privately and publicly owned firms and then match to the patent assignee data.

Following a standard approach, the authors measure the ratio of transient institutional ownership out of all institutional ownership, computed as the number of shares held by 'transient' institutional investors divided by the total number of shares held by institutional investors, in US public firms 1 year before the treatment.

The authors used the BoardEx database to create a binary variable that measures CEO duality in US public firms. If a firm's CEO also holds the position of chairman 1 year before the treatment, the CEO duality variable is assigned a value of 1, otherwise 0.

Each consortium member was asked to rate each of the other members' potential performance and then the level of performance those same members actually realized, both on seven-point scales (from 1 = Extremely Poor to 7 = Extremely Good). Free-riding was calculated as the difference between a partner's potential and realized performance, as evaluated by its partners (alters), so that higher scores identify network members withholding more effort from the joint endeavor. Partners were only asked to rate other members they worked or were familiar with, and each partner received ratings from an average of about 8.5 other network members, making the measure perceptual but based on multiple raters rather than a single rater.

Partners were asked to rate the whole consortium's potential and realized performance on seven-point scales (from 1 = Extremely Poor to 7 = Extremely Good). Each actor's perception of consortium effectiveness was calculated as the difference between these two values, and the measure was then reverse-coded so that higher values indicate higher perceived effectiveness. Using the rating of potential network effectiveness as a baseline also controls for variation in organizations' opinions of how well the overall consortium could fare if working at maximum potential. In the models the variable and its mean-centered squared term are included.

Informants were shown a picture of three blocks, one for each institutional type, and asked to draw lines indicating their perceptions of existing collaboration within and between each institutional type, rating the intensity of each line on a seven-point scale (from 1 = Very Low Collaboration to 7 = Very High Collaboration); collaboration among the same types of organizations was indicated with a loop line. Each actor's perceived peers' collaboration was calculated as the average strength of the collaboration ties it reported for the type of organization to which it belonged, that is, the sum of the strengths of the collaboration ties for its own institutional type divided by the number of possible ties.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = Very Low Collaboration to 7 = Very High Collaboration)

description: Binary variable equaling 1 beginning in the year in which migrating inventors are observed to begin patenting at the destination firm and for the subsequent years of observation for the focal-alter dyad pair. A shared tie occurs when individuals from the two firms are listed as inventors on patents filed with a common incumbent organization as the assignee, prior to the founding of their new ventures. The definition of migration cohort ecosystem ties was restricted to a plus or minus five years' window around the founding of the focal venture. Technology links to incumbent organizations that occurred ten years or more prior to the founding of the new venture are excluded.
time_window: from the year migrating inventors begin patenting at the destination firm onward; ties restricted to a plus or minus five years' window around the focal venture's founding

variable_name: Number of Shared Ecosystem Migration Ties
description: Total count of shared ecosystem ties, used in the firm-year panel data structure to provide a sense of the degree of common links to knowledge management practices of the incumbent, with the premise that greater linkages would further enhance the quality of knowledge developed by the new venture.

Extent to which the two firms in the dyad build on common technology areas in their patented inventions, captured as the U.S. patent classification (USPC) codes that appear on successful patent applications of the focal firm in the observation year. The knowledge base of each firm is recorded as a mathematical vector whose dimensions are the unique USPC codes listed on the firm's patents and whose magnitude for each dimension is the count of patents using the USPC code, based on a three-year rolling aggregation of knowledge base patents. The Euclidean distance between the knowledge base vectors of the two dyad firms is calculated and then linearly transformed into a knowledge overlap measure ranging from 0 to 1.
time_window: three-year rolling aggregation of knowledge base patents

description: Count measure reflecting the number of dyad firm licensing agreements with third parties that matched both the same disease category and the same technology category. Data cover all licensing agreements pursued by the sampled firms over the period of the study, with each entry including classifications of the disease category and the technology category. Licensing agreements directly between sample firms were omitted, given that they are more indicative of a direct engagement between dyad firms.
time_window: over the period of the study

description: Count measure reflecting the number of alliances announced by dyad pairs in the year of observation. The measure is limited to alliances categorized as focusing on research and development, more directly reflecting cooperative engagements that have the goal of knowledge sharing and exchange.

Total count of inventor moves between the focal and alter firm in each observation year, captured by identifying scientists originally listed as inventors on patents of counterpart ventures and then later having patents listed under the focal venture. In practice, no more than one such event occurred between sample firms in any given year of observation, resulting in an outcome variable of binary distribution.
scale: binary outcome (count of at most one per dyad-year)

description: Number of patent forward citations by external organizations within five years after the patent application. The measure is aggregated as the sum of external citations across all focal firm patents with application dates in the year of observation. Given the time lag in observations of forward cites, this field-level assessment was not immediately observable to sample firms.

Count of prior collaborations directly connecting inventors of the two firms, demonstrated through the concurrent listing of one or more individuals from each of the two firms as inventors on parent firm patents (patents listing the incumbent firm as assignee, with application dates prior to the founding of the new venture). The measure is distinct from shared ecosystem migration ties: while individuals may forge an ecosystem tie through their patenting history at a common parent organization, this measure demonstrates that the individuals from the new ventures collaborated directly on projects while working for the incumbent.
time_window: application dates prior to the founding of the new venture

description: Total number of teams of two or more inventors who were observed to migrate from an incumbent to the new venture in the year of observation. In the data this was somewhat rare, with no more than a single team observed to migrate to a given new venture in any given year, and team size was relatively small, with teams of three being the largest observed to concurrently migrate.

A five-quarters' rolling correlation between the focal firm's performance relative to historical aspirations (Pit minus HAit) and its performance relative to social aspirations (Pit minus SAit), where performance relative to an aspiration is the difference between current performance and that aspiration level. Historical aspirations are an exponentially weighted moving average of the firm's past market share with an adjustment parameter of 0.6; social aspirations are the simple average of the market share of every other firm in the industry. In some specifications the correlation is splined at zero into Performance-aspirations correlation (positive) and Performance-aspirations correlation (negative), and a dummy coded 1 when both performance-aspirations measures are increasing is interacted with the positive correlation.

The number of new phones introduced during each quarter of a year. The authors report that the mean value for new product introductions is 12.75 and the variance is 217.1, which indicates overdispersion in the data. All main independent and control variables are lagged by one quarter.

Firms were identified as having undergone the transition to an M-form through previous published research and through independent historical research, and the historical evidence on each firm was cross-checked to ensure the accuracy of the transition year. To measure the effect of the change to an M-form structure, performance before and after the change was analyzed, with the year of the reorganization excluded to avoid confounding the performance measures with outcomes during the transition. In the analyses the before/after coding serves as a categorical variable.
scale: categorical: before M-form implementation vs. after M-form implementation
time_window: 10 years before and 10 years after the reorganization year, excluding the reorganization year

description: The central performance measure was a time series of return on assets over 21 years, including the 10 years before and the 10 years after the year of reorganization. All series excluded the year of the reorganization. For firms for which data were not available for the full 21 years, the same number of years before and after the change was obtained. For the purposes of the analysis, the performance data were pooled by diversification-strategy types.
time_window: 21 years (10 years before and 10 years after the reorganization year)

variable_name: Total firm risk (variance in the ROA time series)
description: Risk was measured as the variance in the ROA time series, or the standard deviation, in the 10 years before and the 10 years after implementation. To test the risk hypotheses, an F-test for the difference between two variances was used after controlling for the effects of size, asset growth, and percentage change in GNP.
time_window: 10 years before and 10 years after implementation

description: The firms were classified into three major strategic types using Rumelt's (1974) methodology: 24 vertically integrated, 22 related-diversified, and 16 unrelated-diversified firms. The firms fit the following types in Rumelt's categorization: primarily dominant vertical, related constrained, and unrelated acquisitive.

Following Zatzick and Iverson (2006), six HRM practices commonly used by organizations to involve employees were each coded 1 = yes, 0 = no, based on employees' own reports in the Employee Survey rather than managers' reports. Employee ratings of their individual HIWS experiences were aggregated to the workplace level; the aggregation formula is reported in a formula block that is not readable in the extracted text. A one-factor categorical indicator-based confirmatory factor analysis showed a good fit (Cronbach's alpha = .71), and aggregation was supported by a mean rWG(J) of .57, ICC(1) = .24 and ICC(2) = .61.
scale: dichotomous (1 = yes, 0 = no) for each of six practices

description: Derived from employee responses to the HIWS using a dispersion model, homogeneity was assessed either by the within-workplace standard deviation or by rWG(J) statistics. When the standard deviation was used, it was multiplied by -1 so that higher values represent higher levels of homogeneity, and the authors report that results were virtually the same for the two measures, presenting findings using the standard deviation measure. The employee-experienced HIWS and the homogeneity of HIWS experiences were modeled simultaneously to address the range-restriction issue.

Managers in the Workplace Survey rated the importance of innovative activities to the general business strategy of their workplaces from 1, of no importance, to 6, crucial. The three rated activities were undertaking research and development, developing new products/services, and developing new production/operating techniques. Cronbach's alpha for the scale was .81.

Measured as the total number of joiners (workers who were not employed at the workplace at time t-1 and joined at time t) and leavers (workers who were employed at the workplace at time t-1 and left at time t), scaled by the total number of employees in the workplace. The measure captures the total quantitative flow of human resources into and out of the workplace, regardless of quality.

Two items from the 2006 Workplace Survey were used: product innovation, whether the workplace introduced new products or services that differ significantly from previously produced goods or services, and process innovation, whether the workplace introduced new processes including the adoption of new methods of goods production or service delivery. Workplaces reporting no product or process innovation were coded 0, workplaces reporting either product or process innovation were coded 1, and workplaces reporting both were coded 2.

Employees of the nine restaurants completed a survey measuring trust for the GM, using the measures developed by Schoorman, Mayer and Davis (1996) and adapted by Mayer and Davis (1999). Responses to the five-point, Likert-type agree/disagree formatted items were averaged for each employee to form scores for trust. The employees' scores in each restaurant were averaged to form restaurant composites.
level: individual, aggregated to the restaurant level

description: Total sales for each restaurant, one of the two measures of financial performance used in the analysis. Unit financial data for the quarter following the survey were obtained from the corporate office; sales and profit were selected because they are most clearly indicative of financial performance in this context and are used by the corporation in assessing individual restaurant and GM performance.

Measure of operating profitability calculated by subtracting total operating expenses (direct and indirect) from gross revenue. It reflects the efficiency of the restaurant and the manager's ability to increase sales while controlling variable costs. Obtained from the corporate office for the quarter following the survey.
Turnover data supplied by the corporation, consisting of the percentage of employees who left each restaurant during the quarter. Collected for the quarter following the survey.

Employees' perceptions of the general manager's ability, measured with the same survey instrument and five-point, Likert-type agree/disagree formatted items as trust. Responses were averaged for each employee to form scores for each of the antecedents of trust.

Employees' perceptions of the general manager's benevolence, measured with the same survey instrument and five-point, Likert-type agree/disagree formatted items as trust. Responses were averaged for each employee to form scores for each of the antecedents of trust.

Employees' perceptions of the general manager's integrity, measured with the same survey instrument and five-point, Likert-type agree/disagree formatted items as trust. Responses were averaged for each employee to form scores for each of the antecedents of trust.

Trust for the general manager measured with the same data collection procedure and instruments as Study 1: five-point, Likert-type agree/disagree items averaged for each employee, then aggregated to the restaurant level to test the performance hypotheses. Data collection occurred on site, across all shifts.
level: individual, aggregated to the restaurant level

description: Total sales for each restaurant, one of the three performance variables measured in Study 2 with the same instruments and procedures as Study 1. Performance measures were collected at the end of the quarter following the survey; measures were not available for one restaurant that closed shortly after data collection.

Net profit of each restaurant, measured with the same procedure as in Study 1: operating profitability calculated by subtracting total operating expenses (direct and indirect) from gross revenue. Collected at the end of the quarter following the survey.
Percentage of employees who left each restaurant during the quarter, measured with the same procedure as in Study 1 and collected at the end of the quarter following the survey.

The leverage ratio indicates the number of associates a firm employs per partner at a certain point in time. Previous research has consistently measured partner human-capital leveraging with this ratio. We gathered data for this variable from American Lawyer.

The measure takes into account the numbers of employees in various legal practice areas. Twenty-three legal practice areas are identified in the National Directory of Legal Employers and are grouped into eight areas using the classification scheme of Sherer (1995). The Herfindahl measure of diversification H = 1 - Sigma p-squared is then calculated, where p is the percentage of professionals in each group of legal practice area; higher values of the Herfindahl index indicate higher levels of diversification.

Geographical diversification is measured by the Herfindahl index as well, where p is the percentage of professionals in each local office. Higher values of the Herfindahl index indicate higher levels of diversification.

This measure indicates the degree to which a firm hired associates laterally instead of directly from law schools. It is calculated as the ratio of associates hired laterally to the number of total associates hired during a particular year. We collected data for this measure from the National Directory of Legal Employers.

Firm profitability as the dependent variable is measured by annual profit dollars per partner. Because partners are residual claimants in the law firm, this measure of performance is similar to the return on equity ratio. Profit per partner is in millions of U.S. dollars.

Unsystematic risk was measured as the standard deviation of the error term (that is, the residual) of the capital asset pricing model (CAPM). Unsystematic risk for each corporation was calculated over a 160-day period beginning 20 days after the public release of the TRI data (that is, TRI release day + 21 to TRI release day + 180), and the 20 days surrounding the announcement were deliberately excluded. The unsystematic risk measures for the years 1990 to 1994 were averaged to calculate the final measure. A market index for each of the five industries (each two-digit SIC category) was derived from all firms trading on the NYSE and AMSE exchanges.
time_window: 160-day windows in each of the years 1990-1994, averaged

description: Media accounts in the Wall Street Journal were used to assess corporate environmental legitimacy. Full-text articles were extracted electronically using the company's name and one or more of the modifiers 'environmental,' 'toxic,' 'pollution,' and 'Superfund' for the second and third quarters (April to September) of each calendar year from 1990 to 1994. Each article was coded for whether its impact on the firm's environmental legitimacy was neutral, negative, or positive (0 = 'neutral,' 1 = 'negative,' and 2 = 'positive'); neutral articles and summaries of press releases were dropped, leaving 658 articles. The measure follows Deephouse's application of the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance, which ranges from -1.0 to +1.0, where a high presence of favorable articles yields a value closer to +1.0 and a high presence of unfavorable articles yields a value closer to -1.0; the formula itself was not extractable from the text.
time_window: second and third quarters (April to September) of 1990-1994

description: Articles from the Press Release Newswire were searched with the same environmental keywords and time frame used for the legitimacy measure, and a research assistant counted the number of articles that exhibited disclosure of environmental liabilities, representing a defensive tactic; only press releases issued by the firms under analysis were included. The variable was divided by total assets averaged over 1990-94 to account for the effect of firm size on generation of press releases. Within the sample, 13 firms disclosed information regarding their environmental liabilities in a total of 23 articles.
time_window: same time frame as the legitimacy search (1990-1994)

description: Using the same Press Release Newswire search, a research assistant counted the number of articles that expressed commitment to the environment, representing an accommodative tactic; only press releases issued by the firms under analysis were included. The variable was divided by total assets averaged over 1990-94 to account for the effect of firm size on generation of press releases. Forty-three firms disclosed information about their commitment to the environment in a total of 191 articles.
time_window: same time frame as the legitimacy search (1990-1994)

description: Product diversification growth was calculated as noncore business sales in year t+4 minus noncore business sales in year t, divided by total sales in year t. Normalizing by size in year t captures relative growth over the four-year period. Segment data was taken from Worldscope and annual reports.
scale: ratio (change in sales divided by total sales in year t)
time_window: four years (t to t+4), normalized by total sales in year t

description: International diversification growth was calculated as foreign sales in year t+4 minus foreign sales in year t, divided by total sales in year t. The measure reflects growth along the international dimension over a four-year period, which is in line with previous studies. Segment data was taken from Worldscope and annual reports.
scale: ratio (change in sales divided by total sales in year t)
time_window: four years (t to t+4), normalized by total sales in year t

variable_name: initial product and international diversification levels
description: Firms were assigned to four subsamples based on their levels of product and international diversification in the first year they entered the sample. Firms with both initial product and international diversification levels below the sample median form the low/low experience sample (235 firms, 1,634 observations), and those with both above the sample median form the high/high experience sample (212 firms, 1,572 observations). Firms with above median product and below median international diversification experience (114 firms, 814 observations) and firms with below median product and above median international diversification experience (114 firms, 798 observations) were compared to test whether the impact of product or international diversification experience is greater.
scale: four subsample categories (low/low, high/high, high/low, low/high)
time_window: first year the firm enters the sample

description: The initial level of product diversification is the entropy index of a firm's sales attributed to its four-digit SIC segments, normalized by its theoretical maximum value to obtain a comparable measure. It is included in the product equation in year t to capture a firm's prior experience with diversification, and was measured in the first year the firm entered the sample. Data was obtained from Worldscope and annual reports.
time_window: year t, first year the firm enters the sample

description: The initial level of international diversification is the entropy index of a firm's sales attributed to five geographic regions—home market (U.K., Germany, France or U.S.), Europe, Americas, Asia/Pacific and Other—normalized by its theoretical maximum value. It is included in the international equation in year t to capture a firm's prior experience with diversification, and was measured in the first year the firm entered the sample. Data was obtained from Worldscope and annual reports.
time_window: year t, first year the firm enters the sample

description: Estimated for each magazine and each quarter by a grid search that minimizes the root mean square percentage error between the observed aspiration level (the number of magazine copies printed for that quarter) and the aspiration level predicted by the full adaptive aspiration model containing prior own aspiration, prior own performance, the political reference point and the economic reference point. The attention weight to own experience is w1it = γ1 + γ2, where the weights are non-negative and must sum to one. The grid search is run in 0.025 increments over a rolling window of 21 quarterly observations for each magazine, so the weights vary across magazines and over time within magazines.

variable_name: relative attention to the political reference point (w2it)
description: Estimated for each magazine and each quarter by the same grid search over the full adaptive aspiration model, the attention weight to the political reference point is w2it = γ3, with weights constrained to be non-negative and to sum to one. It captures how much relative attention the magazine allocates to the prior performance of sister magazines under the same publisher when forming the future aspiration.

variable_name: relative attention to the economic reference point (w3it)
description: Estimated for each magazine and each quarter by the same grid search over the full adaptive aspiration model, the attention weight to the economic reference point is w3it = γ4, with weights constrained to be non-negative and to sum to one. It captures how much relative attention the magazine allocates to the prior performance of other magazines in the same content category when forming the future aspiration.

Calculated as the average number of copies sold of magazines under the same publisher, excluding the focal magazine. It is the performance of the sister magazines that form the political reference group.

Calculated as the average number of copies sold of magazines in the same content category, excluding the focal magazine. It is the performance of the external market rivals that form the economic reference group.

variable_name: Cell 1: Consistent feedback above both social reference points
description: Indicator equal to 1 if the magazine's performance in quarter t−1 is above or equal to both publisher average performance (the political reference point) and category average performance (the economic reference point) in quarter t−2, and 0 otherwise. Independent variables are lagged by one period, and because this coding scheme fully specifies all four possible situations, no intercept is included in the regression.
time_window: performance t−1 compared with reference points t−2

variable_name: Cell 4: Consistent feedback below both social reference points
description: Indicator equal to 1 if the magazine's performance in quarter t−1 is below both publisher average performance and category average performance in quarter t−2, and 0 otherwise. Independent variables are lagged by one period, and because this coding scheme fully specifies all four possible situations, no intercept is included in the regression.
time_window: performance t−1 compared with reference points t−2

variable_name: Cell 2: Below political reference point (publisher average)
description: Indicator equal to 1 if the magazine's performance in quarter t−1 is below publisher average performance but above or equal to category average performance in quarter t−2, and 0 otherwise. This is the case of inconsistent feedback in which the magazine underperforms the political reference point and outperforms the economic reference point.
time_window: performance t−1 compared with reference points t−2

variable_name: Cell 3: Below economic reference point (category average)
description: Indicator equal to 1 if the magazine's performance in quarter t−1 is below category average performance but above or equal to publisher average performance in quarter t−2, and 0 otherwise. This is the case of inconsistent feedback in which the magazine underperforms the economic reference point and outperforms the political reference point.
time_window: performance t−1 compared with reference points t−2

description: Count of a firm's strategic alliances that are classified as strong ties: equity alliances, joint ventures, and non-equity cooperative (R&D) ventures. These alliance types require 'up front' resources, a substantially higher level of resource commitment and significantly more frequent interactions between partners. Tie counts are computed for each industry network from the relational data collected over the study period.

Count of a firm's strategic alliances that are classified as weak ties: marketing agreements, and licensing and patent agreements. The alliances in this category require a substantially smaller resource commitment, resemble an arm's length transaction with an instant exchange of value, and require less coordination and interaction across firms. Tie counts are computed for each industry network from the relational data collected over the study period.

A firm's density was measured as the number of existing ties in the ego network (other than those involving the focal organization), divided by the total possible number of ties among its partners if each partner were tied to every other partner. The focal firm and its relationships were excluded from the local density calculations, and local densities were measured using the aggregate network of both strong and weak ties. Density is undefined for firms connected to isolates, which were dropped from the analyses.

Firm performance was operationalized as return on assets (ROA). ROA is reported for the steel and semiconductor subsamples and is the dependent variable in all regression models. The text does not state the source or time window of the financial data.

A dummy variable utilized to capture differences between industries, with steel firms assigned a value of 1 and semiconductor firms a value of 0. The steel industry is treated as the exploitation environment, characterized by a relatively fixed product/market mix, few product innovations, few new entrants and mainly process-oriented R&D. The semiconductor industry is treated as the exploration environment, characterized by rapid technological change, product obsolescence, new markets and product-oriented R&D.

Dichotomous dependent variable coding exit from the market, without distinguishing between bankruptcy and merger or acquisition. It covers the case in which a firm disappears because its owners are no longer listed in the Certified Professional Accountant (CPA) directories as well as dissolution by acquisition or merger. In all such cases the variable was coded one and the firm was removed from the risk set. The founding year is the year in which the organization appeared for the first time on the Register of Accountants and the last year of appearance is the year of dissolution.

Dummy variable flagging whether the event under study involved collective interfirm mobility. A group is defined as consisting of two or more partners who leave their employer and wind up working together for another firm, whether an incumbent or a start-up. A parallel dummy (Individual-exit) flags cases in which the event involved individual mobility. All independent variables were lagged by one observation period.

The logged average number of years that the departing members spent together before their exit, counted across group departures irrespective of destination. Because the variable can take on the value of zero, one was added to its base value before the log transformation, and the variable was lagged by one observation period. The authors also ran the analysis using the minimum number of years that organizational members spent together before leaving as a group, and report that the results do not depend on whether the average or the minimum number of years is used.

The average joint experience of departing members, logged after adding one, disaggregated by the nature of the recipient firm: the experience of departing members founding a new venture versus the experience of departing members joining an existing firm. The sum of these two variables is Group-average-joint-experience-to-any. All variables were lagged by one observation period.

The average joint experience of departing members, logged after adding one, disaggregated by the geographic location of the destination: partners moving to a firm located within the same province as the source firm versus partners moving to a firm located in a different province. All variables were lagged by one observation period.

An indicator for the periods after the imitation event. An indicator for imitated products was not included separately because of product fixed effects. Its coefficient is interpreted as the relative change of demand or interest for the treatment group compared to the control group caused by the release of an imitative product.

Two separate human coders identified whether the imitative products were horizontal or vertically differentiated with respect to the original products. The coders did not agree on 28 of the 855 treated products, discussed these products again, and seven products for which the coders did not agree on the final classification were dropped. The analysis was run on the sample of originals whose imitative products were classified as horizontally differentiated (729 products before matching, 384 treated products after matching).

Two separate human coders identified whether the imitative products were horizontal or vertically differentiated with respect to the original products. The coders did not agree on 28 of the 855 treated products, discussed these products again, and seven products were dropped for unresolved disagreement. The analysis was run on the sample of originals whose imitative products were classified as vertically differentiated (119 products before matching, 104 treated products after matching).

variable_name: Product Awareness (Number of Weekly Product Page Views)
description: The number of views that a product page received in each week, calculated at the weekly level. Product views are counted when a user navigates to the page of a particular product.
time_window: weekly, January 2015 to the end of 2016

variable_name: Product Demand (Number of Weekly Product Prints)
description: The total number of prints that a product received in a given week, calculated at the weekly level. Printing a product means that a user downloaded the design file and printed it, which is costly because consumers incur material and electricity costs or the cost of paying someone else to print, so the number of prints is an indicator of product demand.
time_window: weekly, January 2015 to the end of 2016

description: Equals one if a product's average weekly page views is higher than the median value of the distribution of page views in a given month and category, and zero otherwise. It is used to test Hypotheses H1b and H2b.

Indicator variable that equals zero for taxicab fleets with no limousines and one for taxicab fleets with one or more limousines in their fleet. In the first-difference specification it identifies fleets that moved from focused to diversified between 1992 and 1997.

The share of all taxicabs owned by the fleet, equal to the number of taxicabs owned by the fleet divided by the total number of taxicabs operated by the fleet. The analysis uses the change in this share between 1992 and 1997, so a decline indicates more outsourcing to owner-operator drivers; the authors report that the mean fleet-ownership rate fell from 86% in 1992 to 63% in 1997.
scale: share of taxicabs owned by the fleet

description: The log of 1992 county population per square mile, used as a continuous proxy for task differentiation between the taxicab and limousine segments in a diversified fleet: in dense urban markets street-hails account for a substantial share of taxi revenue while limousines only serve prearranged rides. It enters the model both as a main effect and interacted with DIVERSIFY.
scale: log of people per square mile

description: Indicator variable that equals one for fleets located in counties with population density above 4,000 people per square mile, used as an easy-to-interpret binary proxy for task differentiation; the threshold is based on the average population density of the 1,000 largest U.S. cities by population. It is interacted with DIVERSIFY in the alternative specification.

Ratio in which the numerator is the sum of an institutional investor's fractional holdings in two firms operating in the same industry (common fractional holdings) and the denominator is the sum of the fractional holdings of the pair's non-common institutional investors plus the numerator, aggregated across all of the pair's common institutional investors. The firm-pair measure is aggregated across all of a firm's same-industry peers to form a firm-level continuous measure. A common owner is required to have a blockholding (more than 1% ownership) stake in each firm.

The sum of a dedicated institutional investor's fractional holdings in two firms operating in the same industry (the numerator), divided by the numerator plus the sum of the fractional holdings of the pair's non-common institutional investors (the denominator), aggregated across all of the pair's dedicated common institutional investors. The firm-pair measure is then aggregated across all of a firm's same-industry peers.

Computed in the same way as dedicated CIO, but using the fractional holdings of quasi-index institutional investors, aggregated across all of the pair's quasi-index common institutional investors and then across all of a firm's same-industry peers. Dedicated and quasi-index investors are both classified as long-term investors.
Measured in the same way as dedicated CIO but using the holdings of transient institutional investors, which the authors classify as short-term investors.

KLD assesses firms on strength and concern topics using a binary system, with one indicating the presence of a criterion and zero its absence. The number of strengths (or concerns) a firm has in a given category is divided by the maximum possible number of strengths (or concerns) in that category-year, giving indices with a range of zero to one for each category-year. A net CSR index for each category-year subtracts the concern index from the strength index and thus ranges from -1 to +1; the net indices are summed across the six categories to calculate CSR performance.
The sum of the strength indices across the six KLD categories (environment, community, employee relations, diversity, product, and human rights).
The sum of the concern indices across the six KLD categories (environment, community, employee relations, diversity, product, and human rights).

For each firm-year, material CSR performance is measured by subtracting an index of material concerns from an index of material strengths, using the same process as the main CSR measure. SASB's industry-specific standards are used to map the 53 KLD subcategories as material or immaterial for the 11 sectors (representing 77 industries) covered by SASB.

For each firm-year, immaterial CSR performance is measured by subtracting an index of immaterial concerns from an index of immaterial strengths, using the same method as the material measure and SASB's industry-specific mapping of the 53 KLD subcategories.

Indicator variable that equals one for firms belonging to industries that bear high financial impact from regulatory or reputational attributions and zero otherwise. It follows Brammer and Millington (2004), who identify 41 industries with a high risk of regulatory interference and 21 industries for which reputation is most valuable; the authors validate these lists against environmental and social penalties in Violation Tracker and the RepRisk Index. Firms are coded one in SIC codes 1000-1499, 2600-2699, 2800-2899, 4400-4499 and 1781, 2900-2999, 4600-4699 and 4900-4939, 2100-2199, and 5181-5182, 5813, 2084 and 2085.

Breadth was measured by the number of content categories elicited from the CEO's letter to shareholders. Two raters first divided the assertions in the letters into information units and a second pair of raters categorized the 240 information units into 35 broad content categories in six strategic domains. Breadth was measured separately for each strategic domain (environment, corporate strategy, competitive actions, resources and capabilities, organizational routines, and performance) and then averaged to create a composite measure.

Depth was measured by the average detail or richness of the content categories—the average number of information units (out of 240) in the content categories. Depth was measured separately for each strategic domain and then averaged to create a composite measure across the six strategic domains.
scale: average number of information units per content category

description: A composite measure formed by averaging the z scores of four measures: foreign sales growth, foreign operating profit goals, foreign asset turnover (foreign sales/foreign assets), and operational risk. Operational risk was computed as the geometric average of the standard deviations of foreign operating profit growth, foreign sales growth, and asset turnover and was reverse coded. The four measures yielded a single factor, and each measure was the three-year average of international performance measures immediately following the first international activities.
time_window: three-year average immediately following the first international activities

description: A continuous composite measure of global integration derived by triangulating quantitative and qualitative data sources. The two quantitative measures were industry trade flow level (imports plus exports as a percentage of U.S. consumption) and a dummy variable representing the presence of at least one firm in the industry competing in global markets. The qualitative measure was a six-item subjective scale of global-integration-local adaptation rated by industry analysts, professors, and managers on a 1-5 scale. The z scores of industry trade flow, global competitors, and the subjective scale were averaged into the composite; industries were also classified into global, multidomestic, and transnational for the subgroup analyses.
scale: z-score composite; subjective items rated on a 1-5 scale

description: The dependent variable, the source's assessment of the ease of knowledge transfer to a recipient. It was measured with the items listed in table 1, each item on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree; the items define a single knowledge transfer variable. The indicator is the mean of the items.

Each respondent described the codifiability of knowledge in his or her primary area of expertise using five items adapted from an instrument developed and validated by Zander and Kogut (1995). Items were measured with a 7-point Likert scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree; the items define a single codifiability measure. Cronbach's alpha for the five items is .75 and the first principal component explains 43.4 percent of the variance. The indicator is the mean of the five items.

A tie exists from the respondent to the contact if the respondent reports a relationship; corroboration by the contact was not required. The intensity of a network connection was measured as the product of emotional closeness and communication frequency. Tie intensity was then transformed into tie strength using network proportions, which define the strength of a tie within the context of the aggregate level of affect across a person's network.

Following Burt (1992: 54-56), social cohesion is measured by indirect structural constraint. It is a triadic density measure that indicates the presence of strong third-party connections around a relationship: where the strength of the connection from person i to person q is multiplied by the strength of the connection from person q to person j, the product is summed across all contacts q to measure the overall strength of the third-party connections around the focal relationship. The equation as printed in the paper was not legible in the available text.

Indicator of network range at the level of expertise areas, following Burt (1983). It has two components: a function of how an individual allocates his or her network connections across expertise areas, and a function of the strength of the connections within those areas. Each contact was assigned to one of six primary areas of expertise as designated by the executive in charge of knowledge management. Network diversity increases as an individual's connections are distributed more evenly across multiple areas of expertise and ties among people in the same area are weak. The equation as printed in the paper was not legible in the available text.

Indicator variable based on social similarity with respect to race. Equals one if the respondent and the contact share the same racial heritage. Data from the human resource management department allowed the authors to measure how similar individuals were with respect to race.
Indicator variable based on social similarity with respect to sex. Equals one if the respondent and the contact are the same sex.

Measured as the absolute difference in educational level between a respondent and a contact. Level of education is an ordinal variable that takes on one of four values (1 = high school, 2 = bachelor's, 3 = master's, 4 = doctorate). The variable measures the absence of social similarity and therefore the absence of common knowledge.
scale: absolute difference on a 1-4 ordinal scale

description: Measured as the absolute difference in tenure between a respondent and a contact, where tenure is the length of time (in years and months) that the firm had employed an individual. The variable measures the absence of social similarity and therefore the absence of common knowledge.
scale: absolute difference in years and months

description: Constructed from the expertise data: a term equals one if person i is an expert in area k and a term equals one if person j is an expert in area k, so the product of the two equals one when the two individuals are experts in the same area. Summing the product across all areas of expertise and dividing by the number of areas for the focal individual defines the level of expertise overlap. Expertise overlap ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating more knowledge overlap. Areas of expertise were defined and assigned by the executive in charge of knowledge management from respondents' self-described primary and secondary areas.

A dummy variable set equal to one if the focal contact worked in the same functional area as the respondent and zero otherwise. The functional areas are analytical services, applied science, business services, delivery, engineering, materials, and product-life prediction.

Another indicator of common knowledge, defined from the network data as the extent to which two individuals occupy the same network position. The measure is the Euclidean distance between the network pattern surrounding the respondent and the pattern surrounding the focal contact; the distance is high when two individuals interact with different colleagues in the organization.

Each director's conservatism was coded as the average of four ratio-based indicators of political donations, multiplied by 100, and board conservatism was calculated by averaging the individual conservatism scores across the directors on the board for each firm year, excluding the CEO. Directors for whom no donation data were found were assigned a score of 50, indicating a moderate orientation, and director conservatism was treated as time-invariant. The variable was lagged one year (measured as of t-1).

To test hypotheses 3a and 3b the overall board conservatism measure was replaced with two distinct measures, one of which was compensation committee conservatism; data on compensation committee membership came from RiskMetrics. Like overall conservatism, this variable was lagged one year.

The second of the two distinct measures used to test hypotheses 3a and 3b, capturing the conservatism of the board members other than those serving on the compensation committee. As with overall conservatism, this variable was lagged one year.

The TDC1 variable in Execucomp was used as the measure of CEO annual pay, reflecting the total value of all salary, bonus, restricted stock grants, option grants, performance share grants, and other income paid to a CEO in a given year t.
