The measure was natural log transformed to correct for skew, and all financial and pay variables were inflation-adjusted to 2010 dollars using the U.S. Consumer Price Index. Pre-2006 CEO pay values were adjusted to reflect TDC1 as reported, minus long-term incentive plan payouts, plus ex ante performance share values.

The accounting measure of recent financial performance was return on assets (ROA), calculated as net income divided by year-end total assets. This variable was lagged one year and was standardized when included in interaction terms.

The market measure of recent financial performance was equivalent to total shareholder return (TSR), calculated as the compounded return to shareholders (assuming continuous reinvestment of dividends) for a given fiscal year. This variable was lagged one year and was standardized when included in interaction terms.

Dependent variable is the instantaneous risk of failing, defined as the limiting probability of a failure between t and t + Δt given that the coop was operating at t. A coop is treated as having failed in the year it dissolved; coops that ended with a merger (43 in total) were treated not as failures but as right-censored, and coops still operating in 1992 are right-censored.
Dichotomous variable coded 1 for years after 1948, when the Israeli state existed, and 0 before.
Dichotomous variable coded 1 for coops that were affiliated with the Merkaz and therefore the Histadrut, and 0 otherwise.
Bank density is the number of commercial banks that existed in a year. Bank density excluded the Bank Hapoalim, which is a commercial bank affiliated with the Histadrut.

Density of the credit cooperative population, used to test hypothesis 5a. The authors do not describe in the prose how this density was constructed beyond its use as the measure of the growth of the credit cooperative population.

Density of the kibbutz population, used to test hypothesis 5b. The authors do not describe in the prose how this density was constructed beyond its use as the measure of the growth of the kibbutz population.

variable_name: Fleet accident rate (hull loss relative to aspiration level)
description: The fleet safety variable is airline specific and is constructed from the existing fleet of aircraft models and the hull-loss rate of each aircraft model. The hull-loss rate of a model is the sum of hull-loss accidents divided by the total aircraft-years of operation since that model's first flight, an all-industry cumulative measure updated annually. The airline's fleet accident rate is a weighted average of the model hull-loss rates, with weights equal to the proportion of aircraft of each model in the airline's fleet, and represents the average hull-loss risk of all aircraft in the focal airline's fleet that year. Only hull-loss accidents are coded, i.e., accidents after which the aircraft cannot be repaired.

variable_name: Net media tenor relative to aspiration level
description: Subjective safety indicator built from articles in general and airline industry publications, downloaded by searching for each aircraft model together with the keywords 'accident,' 'damage,' 'fatalities,' and 'incident' for the study period. All downloaded articles were coded for negative and positive tenor with the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count text analysis software, aggregated to annual values by taking the mean across publications, and net tenor was calculated by subtracting negative from positive tenor. The media tenor of each aircraft model is an all-industry single-year measure mapped to the airline level by multiplying each model's average media tenor by the proportion of that model in the airline's fleet. The variable is expressed relative to a social aspiration level defined as the industry mean and is split at zero (spline).

variable_name: ROA relative to aspirations (ROA - AL) and the ROA below aspiration-level indicator
description: Return on assets relative to an aspiration level calculated as the weighted average of a social aspiration level (industry mean) and a historical aspiration level (exponentially discounted past ROA). By iterating through the different possible parameters at 0.1 intervals, the authors assigned a weight of 0.3 to the social aspiration level and a discount factor of 0.6 to the historical aspiration level. The variable is expressed relative to aspirations and is split (using a spline specification) at 0 so that effects below and above the aspiration level are estimated separately. To test Hypotheses 2a and 2b, an indicator variable set to 1 if the airline's ROA is below aspirations and to 0 otherwise is interacted with the splined fleet accident rate and media tenor variables.

Count of the aircraft sold by the airline in the focal year. It is one of the two measures of airline fleet changes, the other being airplane buys; bought aircraft can be purchased either new directly from the manufacturer or used on the preowned aircraft market. Airplanes can be leased, but regular leases are uneconomical and rarely used by the established airlines in the data.

Count of the aircraft bought by the airline in the focal year. It is one of the two measures of airline fleet changes, the other being airplane sales; the bought aircraft can be purchased either new directly from the manufacturer or used on the preowned aircraft market. Airplanes can be leased, but regular leases are uneconomical and rarely used by the established airlines in the data.

Total entropy captures the extent of diversity across a firm's activities. It is calculated from the share of a firm's total sales in 4-digit SIC industry i and the number of 4-digit SIC industries in which the firm operates; the formula itself is unreadable in the supplied text. Total entropy equals zero for a single business firm and rises with the extent of diversity. It is calculated using annual data on a firm's sales in each of its 4-digit SIC business segments.
scale: lower bound of zero for a single business firm; rises with the extent of diversity

description: The Herfindahl index of diversity is calculated from the share of a firm's total sales in each 4-digit SIC segment and the number of 4-digit SIC industries in which the firm operates; the formula itself is unreadable in the supplied text. Since lower values of the Herfindahl index indicate higher levels of diversification, the authors instead use the inverse measure (1/H - 1) for consistency with the other diversification measures. This inverse measure equals zero for a single business firm and rises with the level of diversification.
scale: lower bound of zero for a single business firm; rises with the level of diversification

description: A product-count measure calculated as the number of 4-digit SIC business segments in which the firm participates minus one, so that this measure equals zero for a single business firm. Sales data by 4-digit SIC business segment come from Compustat's Line of Business database.
scale: zero for a single business firm; increases by one with each additional 4-digit SIC segment

description: The authors adopt the technology relatedness measure developed by Robins and Wiersema (1995), which captures portfolio relatedness based on patterns of technology flows among manufacturing industries. Firm-level resource-based relatedness is measured by aggregating over all combinations of two industries in a firm's business portfolio, where r_ij is the relatedness coefficient of similarity between any two different industries i and j in terms of their pattern of inflows of technology and P_i and P_j are the percentage of the firm's sales in industries i and j; the aggregation formula is unreadable in the supplied text. After an adjustment for the number of industries in which the firm is active, the measure has a range from -1.0 to +1.0, with a positive score indicating that the firm has a positively interrelated portfolio of businesses. Data on the r_ij were taken from Robins and Wiersema (1995) and data on a firm's sales in each of its 4-digit SIC business segments from Compustat's Line of Business database.

Foreign-based competition is measured by the ratio of imports to total domestic purchases (i.e., import penetration) in the 4-digit SIC core industry of the firm, lagged one year. No data exist on total domestic purchases at the 4-digit SIC level, so the denominator is commonly measured by apparent consumption, defined as total sales (value of shipments) plus imports minus exports in a given 4-digit SIC industry. The lagged value is used because the authors expect a firm's current strategic decision to be influenced by competitive conditions in a prior period.
level: 4-digit SIC core industry of the firm

description: Foreign-based competition is measured by the ratio of imports to total domestic purchases (i.e., import penetration) in the 4-digit SIC core industry of the firm, lagged one year. No data exist on total domestic purchases at the 4-digit SIC level, so the denominator is commonly measured by apparent consumption, defined as total sales (value of shipments) plus imports minus exports in a given 4-digit SIC industry. The lagged value is used because the authors expect a firm's current strategic decision to be influenced by competitive conditions in a prior period.
level: 4-digit SIC core industry of the firm

description: Core industry growth is measured by the annual growth in the real (constant dollar) value of shipments of the 4-digit SIC core industry of the firm. Data at the 4-digit SIC level on industry value of shipments measured in constant 1987 U.S. dollars were taken from the NBER's Productivity Database. It is one of two measures of the economic attractiveness of the firm's core industry.

Core industry growth is measured by the annual growth in the real (constant dollar) value of shipments of the 4-digit SIC core industry of the firm. Data at the 4-digit SIC level on industry value of shipments measured in constant 1987 U.S. dollars were taken from the NBER's Productivity Database. It is one of two measures of the economic attractiveness of the firm's core industry.

Core industry profitability is measured by the average return on assets (ROA) in the 4-digit SIC core industry of the firm. Annual data on industry assets and industry profit by 4-digit SIC were derived from Industry Norms and Key Business Ratios published by Dun & Bradstreet; industry ROA was then calculated by dividing industry profits by industry assets. It is one of two measures of the economic attractiveness of the firm's core industry.

Core industry profitability is measured by the average return on assets (ROA) in the 4-digit SIC core industry of the firm. Annual data on industry assets and industry profit by 4-digit SIC were derived from Industry Norms and Key Business Ratios published by Dun & Bradstreet; industry ROA was then calculated by dividing industry profits by industry assets. It is one of two measures of the economic attractiveness of the firm's core industry.

Core business profitability reflects the financial profitability of the firm's core business and is measured as the ratio of operating profit to revenues in the firm's 4-digit SIC core business. Annual data on firms' operating profit and revenues were taken from Compustat's line of business segment database.

Core business profitability reflects the financial profitability of the firm's core business and is measured as the ratio of operating profit to revenues in the firm's 4-digit SIC core business. Annual data on firms' operating profit and revenues were taken from Compustat's line of business segment database.

Firm performance is measured as the firm's return on assets (ROA), a widely employed measure of performance that has been shown to be related to a variety of other indicators of a firm's financial performance. Annual data on firm ROA were taken from the Compustat line of business database.

Firm performance is measured as the firm's return on assets (ROA), a widely employed measure of performance that has been shown to be related to a variety of other indicators of a firm's financial performance. Annual data on firm ROA were taken from the Compustat line of business database.

Computed as the standard deviation of employee income growth in the previous 3 years. Changes in a bank's aggregate expenditure on employee compensation are used to derive employee income growth, assuming that changes in total compensation expenses reflect changes in income of the managers involved in resource allocation.

variable_name: Travel time between bank headquarters and branches
description: The average time taken to travel from a bank's headquarters to its branches. Headquarters locations and branch locations were matched to railway stations, and travel times were estimated from the Indian Railways' rail timetable; a larger distance (and hence longer travel time) makes inspections by headquarters more difficult and therefore implies a lower degree of monitoring.

variable_name: Allocation of resources with high middle manager involvement (off-site ATMs)
description: The number of off-site ATMs deployed in a year, computed as the increase in the total number of ATMs from 1 year to the next. Off-site ATMs are used because middle managers have greater control over off-site than on-site ATMs. The variable is a count taking non-negative integer values.
time_window: change from 1 year to the next

variable_name: Allocation of resources with low middle manager involvement (branches)
description: Computed as the increase in the total number of bank branches from 1 year to the next; branch deployment depends more on central managers. The variable is a count taking non-negative integer values and there were no cases of year-on-year reductions in branches.
time_window: change from 1 year to the next

description: Combinations of income growth uncertainty and degree of monitoring that the authors classify as highly favorable, moderately favorable, or unfavorable conditions for increasing allocation. Highly favorable conditions combine high uncertainty with low monitoring; moderately favorable conditions combine either high uncertainty with high monitoring or low uncertainty with low monitoring.

The CAR reflects the amount of capital banks possess to absorb losses before turning insolvent; higher CAR implies that a bank has more slack. Banks are categorized as having high and low slack resources depending on their capital adequacy ratio.

variable_name: Resource type: off-site ATMs (high involvement) vs branches (low involvement)
description: Middle manager involvement was operationalized through the type of resource allocated. Off-site ATM deployments, over which middle managers have greater control, stood for high involvement, and new branch deployments, which depend more on central managers, stood for low involvement. The two allocation counts were modeled as separate dependent variables and the effects compared.

Survival time is measured as the age of the firm at failure or at the end of the sample (or observation) window, with right censoring accounted for by the survival analysis estimation strategy. Using data on the individual income and wealth of all founders, the authors identified exits that were successful rather than failures and reclassified 27 firms that had ceased to exist as successful exits rather than failures; competing hazard models account for the differences between exits due to 'flaming out' (failures) and 'cashing out' (successful exits).
time_window: from founding until failure or the end of the observation window

description: Total sales generated in the observation window, following Dencker and Gruber (2015). The authors assumed that firms that failed before the end of the observation window had zero sales in the year(s) in which the firms no longer existed, and they also tested all of their hypotheses using the natural logarithm of sales as an additional dependent variable.

Continuous measure of the prevalence of kin ties between initial employees of the new firm, calculated as the ratio of the number of horizontal employee kin ties to the number of employees. Kin ties are identified for the firm's first year of operation among the listed categories of relatives (grandparents, parents, parents' siblings, children, siblings, spouse, spouse's parents, spouse's siblings, spouse's grandparents, and spouse's parents' siblings).
time_window: first year of the firm's operations

description: Continuous measure of the prevalence of kin ties between founders and initial employees, calculated as the ratio of the number of such kin ties to the number of all initial members (founders and employees) of the new firm. Kin ties are identified among initial members in the first year of the firm's operations.
time_window: first year of the firm's operations

description: Continuous measure of the prevalence of kin ties between founders, calculated as the ratio of the number of such kin ties to the number of founders of the new firm. The authors formulated no prediction for this variable, but report its estimated relationship with survival and sales.
time_window: first year of the firm's operations

description: A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if newcomer i posts a second idea in calendar month t, where t is any calendar month following the period of the newcomer's first entry. For this analysis, all newcomers who have posted ideas in the past are considered to be at risk for posting second ideas.
time_window: calendar months following the newcomer's first entry (the first observed calendar month is set as month zero)

description: A variable representing a rejection in which the organization simply changes the idea's status to rejected and the newcomer is merely notified that his or her idea has been rejected. The dummy switches from a value of 0 to a value of 1 during the month in which a newcomer's first idea is rejected and then maintains its value of one thereafter.
time_window: monthly, from the month of the rejection onward

description: A dummy variable used to examine whether a newcomer's idea is rejected with an explanation. Like the other decision variables, the dummy switches from 0 to 1 during the month in which the organization rejects the newcomer's first idea and maintains its value of one thereafter.
time_window: monthly, from the month of the rejection with explanation onward

variable_name: First idea rejected - explanation matches idea content
description: Measures whether an organization's explanation matches the newcomer's submission in terms of discussed issues, using large-scale quantitative text analysis. Nonalphabetical characters are removed, all words are converted to lowercase, each word is stemmed to its root form, and stop words with little information content are removed. The remaining texts of the idea and the explanation are treated as bags of words and transformed into binary vectors, which are compared to one another; the match is computed as the cosine similarity of the two binary vectors representing the unique terms occurring in the idea and the response, so responses and ideas with more cooccurring words relative to the total number of unique words used have a stronger match.
scale: cosine similarity of two binary word vectors

variable_name: First idea rejected - explanation matches idea style
description: Measures whether a newcomer's idea and an organization's explanation of a rejection use the same linguistic style, following the approach specified by Goldberg et al. (2016). Nonalphabetical characters are removed and all words are converted to lowercase; the remaining texts are treated as bags of words and classified according to the subcategories captured in the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) 2015 dictionary, counting for each category how many words in the text relative to the total number of words belong to that category. For each text a vector is created capturing the relative share of words in each LIWC category, and the match is computed as the cosine similarity between the idea vector and the explanation vector; an idea and a rejection explanation may therefore be similar in style even if they do not share specific individual words.
scale: cosine similarity between vectors of relative LIWC category shares

description: An indicator that identifies high asset specificity conditions as those where the exchange involves analog, memory, or customized ASIC products, and zero otherwise. The authors argue that analog and customized ASIC production requires a very flexible process with a high degree of coordination between design and production engineers, while digital memory devices require entirely new, state-of-the-art processes.

Demand uncertainty is measured as the sum of squared errors from a regression of the relevant product-market's historical unit demand for the five years preceding the integration decision (1991 through 1995). The units data are indexed based on the starting value and regressed on a quadratic time trend, controlling for seasonality. The segment-level data are quarterly reports of units delivered.

The natural log of the cumulative number of similar products manufactured by the firm. The cumulative number of similar products manufactured is estimated as the firm's cumulative production capacity in the relevant process technology for the prior five years (1991-95).

The number of unique sourcing relationships over the last five years, outside the current observation, with firms that have the ability to produce at the relevant process. The measure assumes that hazard-mitigating sourcing capabilities are primarily determined by experience with similar contracting situations.
time_window: last 5 years, outside the current observation

description: The number of product-market subfields in which the firm sells semiconductor devices. The authors argue that any material presence in a market can provide the firm with a preferential claim (or toe-hold) to switch its technology into that market. The data for this measure are obtained from the 1996 ICE Profiles report. The estimated model also includes a squared term for this variable.

The dependent variable is coded one when the focal process technology-product-market combination is fabricated internally and zero when it is obtained through an external production-sourcing relationship. A separate observation is recorded for each process technology-product-market combination.

The authors summed the shares owned by government agencies and those owned by large SOEs to obtain state shares, categorizing any state-owned shareholder as part of the coalition advocating the logic of state socialism. Use of state-initiated M&As as an outcome was excluded from the main dependent variable, and the ownership variables are scaled as fractions so that coefficients are comparable.

To identify shareholders that are part of a coalition advocating the logic of market capitalism, the authors summed the shares owned by private legal persons - that is, private-sector firms, non-bank financial institutions, and investment funds. The variable is scaled as a fraction so that coefficients are comparable with those of the other power variables.

variable_name: Proportion of directors with state experience
description: The proportion of directors with state experience was found via electronic search of board member résumé data from CSMAR, which indicated the agency at which the individual in question worked previously or currently. An indicator was denoted for whether or not the individual had worked for the state in any capacity, and the sum of these indicators is divided by the number of board members.

Based on CSMAR data, the variable is calculated as the sum of indicators for whether or not an individual director holds any stock in the firm, divided by the number of board members. The proportion of actual shares owned was also available and was tested in preliminary runs, but the results were no different than when the proportion of directors owning any shares was used.

The dependent variable was defined as deals that WIND classified as mergers or acquisitions through obtaining a controlling stake of more than 50% equity ownership. Announcements of M&As initiated and administered by the state were excluded to restrict the sample to market-oriented transactions. The announcement of one or multiple M&As at one time was coded as an event irrespective of whether the announced acquisition was completed (95% of them were).

Using the event study methodology, the authors computed the cumulative abnormal return for each M&A announcement using various time windows around the announcement day. The CAR for each firm in the event window around its M&A announcement is calculated using the CAPM method, which accounts for the market movement as well as the focal stock's movement relative to the market - that is, its b coefficient.
time_window: windows [-1,1], [-1,2], [-1,5], [0,1] and [0,2] around the announcement day

description: The analysis splits the sample period into an 'early' and a 'later' time period and estimates separate coefficients for each, letting the last year of the early period vary from 2006 to 2008. The authors argue that a split at 2007 is the most appropriate because 2007 saw an increase in M&A activity but not to the stable high level of subsequent years.
time_window: early vs. late period split at 2006, 2007 or 2008

variable_name: Legal-person ownership and proportion of directors owning stock
description: The power of the market capitalism coalition was captured by two indicators: external power as the share of equity held by private legal persons (private firms, non-bank financial institutions and investment funds), and internal power as the proportion of board members holding any stock in the firm. Each entered the regressions separately, interacted with time period.

variable_name: State ownership and proportion of directors with state experience
description: The power of the state socialism coalition was captured by two indicators: external power as the summed share of equity held by government agencies and large state-owned enterprises, and internal power as the proportion of board members who had worked for the state in any capacity, from board résumé data. Each entered the regressions separately, interacted with time period.

Replicating the measure of narcissism in Chatterjee and Hambrick (2007), five indicators are compiled from 2006: prominence of the CEO photograph in the annual report (four points if the CEO's picture alone occupies more than half a page, three points if alone and less than half a page, two points if photographed with one or more executives, one point if no picture was available), prominence of the CEO in press releases (ratio of the number of times the CEO's name is used to the total number of words), use of first-person pronouns in CEO interviews (ratio of first-person pronouns to total pronouns), ratio of CEO cash compensation to the second highest paid executive, and ratio of CEO bonus compensation to the second highest paid executive. The CFA indicated adequate fit and acceptable internal consistency, and the final measure is a standardized mean of all the five indicators.

Buy-and-hold abnormal return over the one year from the start of the crisis (from the start of the July 2007 to the end of the June 2008 fiscal quarters), computed as the product over trading days of one plus the abnormal return. Abnormal returns are based on the market model regressing daily stock returns on the return of the S&P 1500 market portfolio, where the abnormal return is the actual return minus the fitted value from that model. All variables are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentile and financial data are adjusted to year 2000 dollars.
time_window: July 2007 to June 2008 (one year after the crisis start)

description: Unsystematic (idiosyncratic) return is the residual from a regression of firm-specific daily stock returns on the industry median daily return, using daily stock returns from CRSP based on stock prices for at least 100 days of 252 trading days in each calendar year. The cumulative effect of CEO actions is assessed on yearly unsystematic returns from the start of the June 2005 quarter to the end of the June 2010 quarter (8 quarters before and 12 quarters after the start of the crisis).

Responses were identified as (1) do nothing (no price change), (2) defend (decrease price in the entered market), (3) counterattack (enter one of the entrant's markets with a lower price), (4) total war (defend and counterattack simultaneously), (5) price leadership in market 1 (increase price in the entered market), and (6) price leadership in market 2 (enter one of the entrant's markets with a higher price). The do nothing, defend and PL1 responses were measured as the difference between the entrant's price at the date of entry and the respondent's price from one month before the date of entry up to 2 months after entry; for the other three responses, which require entry into an entrant's route, no time limit was imposed. The coach fare was selected for the study. Because of the small number of price leadership in market 2 and total war responses, they were dropped from further analysis.
scale: six response categories, four of which were used in the logistic regression analysis
time_window: from one month before the entry date up to 2 months after entry; no time limit for responses requiring entry into an entrant's route

description: Market dependency is measured by three ratios: revenue passenger miles per airline per route divided by the airline's revenue passenger miles for the year on all routes (DEP1); an airline's number of passengers on a route divided by the number of passengers on the airline's top-ranked route (DEP2); and the airline's number of passengers on a route divided by the number of passengers on the airline's top five routes (DEP3). DEP1 was the dependency variable used as a potential response predictor in the multinomial logistic regression.

Barriers to entry are measured by the overall load factor for 1984 for each airline, which represents the percentage of paying passengers filling the available seat capacity, and by customer loyalty, the number of customers preferring a particular domestic airline in a 1984 survey administered by the International Airline Passengers Association. The load factor measure loads almost equally between the sustainable capacity factor and the synergy factor. The customer loyalty measure was not different from sustainable capacity measures.

Synergy is measured as the number of flight departures and arrivals at each city on a city-pair route for each airline. A hub airport for an airline represents many opportunities for keeping passengers on the airline's planes, regardless of the passenger's destination.

Sustainable capacity is measured as the physical and financial capacity of an airline. Two physical capacity measures are total available seat miles in 1984 and available ton miles in 1984; three financial capacity measures are revenue passenger miles in 1984, cash flow for 1984, and the debt-to-asset ratio for 1984. Available seat miles and available ton miles are the units of production for an airline and are most closely related to costs, while revenue passenger miles represent its ability to generate revenues with that physical capacity. ASMTOT84 (physical capacity) and RATIO (financial capacity) were used as potential response predictors in the multinomial logistic regression.

Value Line's stock beta for 1984, employed to measure the stock market's perception of riskiness for each firm. It was included as an additional factor in the study beyond the four dimensions of the Karnani and Wernerfelt model. The market riskiness measure does not fit any of the factors very well and the dependency scale's alpha improves when the beta variable is deleted from the scale.

One of the five dimensions of procedural justice, measured on a 7-point Likert-type scale with scale anchors labeled (1) not at all and (7) great. Head office and subsidiary top managers reflected on the last annual strategic planning/strategy making process between the head office and a given national unit and evaluated this dimension. The dimension's meaning was derived from an open-ended questionnaire to 63 subsidiary presidents and a Q-sort process. Decision unit scores were calculated by averaging the scores of member respondents from each decision unit, with equal weight given to each unit member.
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale (1 = not at all, 7 = great)
time_window: last annual strategic planning/strategy making process

Head office and subsidiary top managers reflected on the last annual strategic planning/strategy making process between the head office and a given national unit and evaluated this dimension. The dimension's meaning was derived from an open-ended questionnaire to 63 subsidiary presidents and a Q-sort process. Decision unit scores were calculated by averaging the scores of member respondents from each decision unit, with equal weight given to each unit member.
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale (1 = not at all, 7 = great)
time_window: last annual strategic planning/strategy making process

Head office and subsidiary top managers reflected on the last annual strategic planning/strategy making process between the head office and a given national unit and evaluated this dimension. The dimension's meaning was derived from an open-ended questionnaire to 63 subsidiary presidents and a Q-sort process. scale: 7-point Likert-type scale (1 = not at all, 7 = great)
time_window: last annual strategic planning/strategy making process

description: One of the five dimensions of procedural justice, measured on a 7-point Likert-type scale with scale anchors labeled (1) not at all and (7) great. Head office and subsidiary top managers reflected on the last annual strategic planning/strategy making process between the head office and a given national unit and evaluated this dimension. The dimension's meaning was derived from an open-ended questionnaire to 63 subsidiary presidents and a Q-sort process. Decision unit scores were calculated by averaging the scores of member respondents from each decision unit, with equal weight given to each unit member.
scale: 7-point Likert-type scale (1 = not at all, 7 = great)
time_window: last annual strategic planning/strategy making process

description: Three items measured this construct using a 7-point Likert response format, coded so high scores indicated effective achievement of the objective. The items were: (1) the extent to which the distinctive knowledge and insight of the head office and the national unit were effectively transferred to and shared with the opposite party; (2) the extent to which new ideas and joint innovations were successfully created through the exchange of the unique expertise residing in the head office and the subsidiary unit; and (3) the extent to which both head office and subsidiary executives gained new knowledge, an increased appreciation and awareness of the opposite party's distinctive expertise, and/or an expanded view of how your organization can compete successfully in the global arena. The Cronbach's coefficient alpha for this three-item measure was 0.82. Decision unit scores were calculated by averaging member responses, with equal weight given to each unit member.
time_window: last annual strategic planning/strategy making process

variable_name: Balancing Global Efficiency and Local Responsiveness
description: Three items measured this construct using a 7-point Likert response format, coded so high scores indicated effective achievement of the objective. The items were: (1) the extent to which the concern for global economies of scale and scope as well as the concern for adaptation to national markets were well represented and given due consideration in the decision process; (2) the extent to which the strategic decisions resulting from this process effectively balanced the need for global efficiency and local responsiveness across all major activities; and (3) the extent to which neither concerns for global efficiency nor concerns for local responsiveness over-dominated all critical aspects of resulting strategic decisions to the virtual exclusion of the other. The Cronbach's coefficient alpha for this three-item measure was 0.93. Decision unit scores were calculated by averaging member responses, with equal weight given to each unit member.
time_window: last annual strategic planning/strategy making process

description: Three items measured this construct using a 7-point Likert response format, coded so high scores indicated effective achievement of the objective. The items were: (1) the extent to which your organization's existing global strategic logic was carefully scrutinized and reexamined in the decision process; (2) the extent to which the assumptions underlying the viewpoints of decision participants were rigorously evaluated in the decision process; and (3) the extent to which the strategic decisions resulting from that process were not mere replications of past successful strategic moves but reflected instead new and updated thinking which was finely attuned to recent changes in the global business environment. The Cronbach's coefficient alpha for this three-item measure was 0.88. Decision unit scores were calculated by averaging member responses, with equal weight given to each unit member.
time_window: last annual strategic planning/strategy making process

description: Two items measured this construct using a 7-point Likert response format, coded so high scores indicated effective achievement of the objective. The items were: (1) given your experience in other decision making processes of similar importance, to what extent was your past global strategic decision making process efficient and quick in reaching final decisions; and (2) given the importance of the decision, to what extent was your just past strategic decision making process unnecessarily lengthy and drawn out (this item was reversely scored). The Cronbach's coefficient alpha for this two-item measure was 0.95. Decision unit scores were calculated by averaging member responses, with equal weight given to each unit member.
time_window: last annual strategic planning/strategy making process

description: The dependent variable takes on the value of one if a focal firm i donates to a major issue j in year t + 1, and zero otherwise. The authors use a dummy variable as the main outcome because of the high occurrence of no annual donation in each issue. Issues are classified using the NTEE major codes.

Tracks donations that a focal firm's competitors in the same industry made to an issue in a year, restricted to competitors that are the focal firm's ideological opponents. Industry competitors are firms in the same NAICS two-digit industry, and opponents are identified from the firm-level ideological position of each competitor: giving by ideological opponents is red competitors' giving for a focal blue firm and blue competitors' giving for a focal red firm. The authors describe the regressors as binary.

Tracks donations to an issue in year t made by the focal firm's industry competitors that are not its ideological opponents, using the same industry (NAICS two-digit) definition of competitors. It is the empirical counterpart against which the effect of giving by ideological opponents is evaluated. The authors describe the regressors as binary.

Measured as the inverse of the standard deviation of ideological preferences among a focal firm's employees who made campaign contributions during the study period. Because a standard deviation gives more weight to large deviations, the ideological positions of firm employees who are extreme outliers are winsorized at the top and bottom 1% before the variable is calculated.

Measured as the absolute difference between the ideology of a focal firm's employees and the average ideology of all other corporate donors that gave to that nonprofit throughout the study period. The higher the ideological gap between the firm and the nonprofit's other corporate donors, the less likely the firm is to fund the given nonprofit.

variable_name: A focal firm's giving to a given nonprofit each year
description: The dependent variable in the firm-nonprofit dyad analysis is whether a focal firm donates to a nonprofit each year. It is coded as one if a focal firm gives to a given nonprofit in a year, and zero otherwise.

Calculated as the average ideological score of the firm's employees (CFScore in Bonica's DIME database) who made campaign contributions during the study period. Firms with positive ideological scores are categorized as conservative (red firms), whereas those with negative scores are categorized as liberal (blue firms). The firm-level ideological position used to classify competitors is time-invariant to maintain the stability of each group's composition.

Using the ReCap data, alliances were coded on an ordered basis along a market-hierarchy continuum. Licensing involves arm's-length transactions and is closest to the market end of the continuum; non-equity governance forms involve less interdependence than equity forms; minority equity arrangements provide less mutual control over a specific investment than equity joint ventures, but by virtue of ownership provide greater control than non-equity arrangements. The coding is one-way licensing (non-equity) = 1, bilateral cross licensing (non-equity) = 2, bilateral not licensing (non-equity) = 3, minority equity = 4, and equity joint ventures = 5.

We used ReCap descriptors identifying alliances as co-development, co-manufacturing, co-marketing, or co-promotion. To reflect increasing levels of scope and complexity in these collaborations, we created an ordinal variable, coding co-marketing alliances as 1, co-promotion alliances as 2, co-manufacturing alliances as 3, and co-development alliances as 4. Alliances without such co-arrangements were coded as 0.

Partner uncertainty was measured as the focal firm's absence of prior ties with its alliance partner. Based on ReCap data availability we created a fixed rule for counting prior ties with one's alliance partner as the 5-year period prior to 2000 (January 1995 to December 1999). We coded the absence of any prior ties during that period with a 1 and the existence of prior ties with a 0.

Input we received from five biotech and pharmaceutical industry experts validated a four-stage technology development model, with Discovery, Early Clinical comprising phase 1 and phase 2 clinical trials, Late Clinical comprising phase 3 clinical trials and approved clinical trials, and Launch. Using ReCap data, we created an ordinal measure where Discovery alliances were coded 4 (reflecting the highest level of uncertainty), Early Clinical alliances were coded 3, Late Clinical alliances were coded 2, and Launch alliances were coded 1 (reflecting the lowest level of uncertainty).

This measure is based on the technological subfield of the alliance. Human therapeutics are less routine than diagnostics because of continuing shifts in targeting technologies and the complexity of in vivo testing, and diagnostics involves technologies that are relatively more recent and dynamic than those involved in chemical compound research. Based on prior work showing systematic differences in volatility among these three sub-fields we examined each alliance for its technology focus, coding technological uncertainty as chemical compound (1), diagnostics (2), and therapeutics (3).

A composite measure of strategic change built from six strategic allocation dimensions: advertising intensity (advertising/sales), R&D intensity (R&D/sales), plant and equipment upgrades (new plant and equipment/gross plant and equipment), nonproduction overhead (selling, general, and administration expenses/sales), inventory levels (inventory/sales), and financial leverage (debt/equity). For each dimension the authors calculated the absolute value of the difference between the ratio in the prior year (t-1) and the ratio in the current year (t), standardized these values by industry by subtracting the industry average and dividing by the standard deviation, and then averaged the six standardized values to obtain the overall composite measure.
time_window: change from year t-1 to year t; in the regressions the dependent variable is measured at t+1

description: A faultline-strength index computed for each TMT based on gender as the focal attribute, using categorical indicators of gender (male or female). The score accounts for the degree of similarity of TMT members' other attributes within each gender-based subgroup and the degree of dissimilarity of members' other attributes between subgroups. Faultline strength is computed as the product of internal subgroup alignment (calculated as an alignment index across each of the other attributes) and the reciprocal of cross-subgroup alignment; the values are distributed between zero and one.
time_window: year t (entered lagged one year behind strategic change)

description: A faultline-strength index computed for each TMT based on age as the focal attribute. Age was classified into four groups: individuals born from 1928 to 1945 (Traditionalists), 1946 to 1960 (Boomers), Generation X (1961 to 1979), and Generation Y (1980 to 1995). The score combines internal subgroup alignment across the other attributes with the reciprocal of cross-subgroup alignment, and the values are distributed between zero and one.
time_window: year t (entered lagged one year behind strategic change)

description: A faultline-strength index computed for each TMT based on educational level as the focal attribute, with members classified into five categories: high school or below, college, university, master's degree, and Ph.D. The score combines internal subgroup alignment across the other attributes with the reciprocal of cross-subgroup alignment; the values are distributed between zero and one. The authors categorized educational level as a relationship-related attribute because it is a strong determinant of subjective social status.
time_window: year t (entered lagged one year behind strategic change)

description: A faultline-strength index computed for each TMT based on functional background as the focal attribute, with members classified into service roles (sales, marketing, and customer service jobs), production roles (manufacturing, supply chain, and production jobs), and support roles (human resources, finance, and law). The score combines internal subgroup alignment across the other attributes with the reciprocal of cross-subgroup alignment; the values are distributed between zero and one.
time_window: year t (entered lagged one year behind strategic change)

description: A faultline-strength index computed for each TMT based on TMT tenure as the focal attribute, with members classified into three categories: less than 3 years, 3 years but less than 6 years, and more than 6 years. The score combines internal subgroup alignment across the other attributes with the reciprocal of cross-subgroup alignment; the values are distributed between zero and one.
time_window: year t (entered lagged one year behind strategic change)

description: Environmental dynamism was computed using industry gross revenues. The authors regressed log-transformed industry gross revenues in a focal year on industry gross revenues of the previous five consecutive years and used the standard error of the regression slope as environmental dynamism. For example, environmental dynamism in 2003 was obtained by regressing industry gross revenues in 2003 on the previous five years (1998-2002).
time_window: five-year rolling window preceding the focal year

description: Single scale item measuring managers' perception that pioneers have higher levels of return on investment. Respondents answered on an eleven-point Likert-type scale from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree), centered for analysis so that -5 represents strongly disagree and 5 represents strongly agree. The authors did not combine this item with the market share item into one multiple-item construct; perceived pioneering performance was measured separately for each.

Single scale item measuring managers' perception that pioneers have higher levels of market share. Responses were given on an eleven-point Likert-type scale from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree), centered for analysis so that -5 represents strongly disagree and 5 represents strongly agree. It is kept separate from the ROI item rather than combined into one multiple-item construct.

variable_name: Pioneering risks after market entry (multi-item scale)
description: Multiple-item scale obtained by adding the individual scale items and then dividing by the number of items in the scale, based on the major categories of post-market-entry pioneering risks. Items were answered on an eleven-point Likert-type scale from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree), centered for analysis so that -5 represents strongly disagree and 5 represents strongly agree. Construct reliabilities for the three multi-item scales exceed the 0.70 level in all nine countries and both industry sectors.

Multiple-item scale obtained by adding the individual scale items and then dividing by the number of items in the scale. The items capture competitor-centered advantages of lower production costs, better access to labor and to experienced managers, better access to raw material supplies, and better choice of equipment and location. Items were answered on an eleven-point Likert-type scale from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree), centered for analysis so that -5 represents strongly disagree and 5 represents strongly agree.

Multiple-item scale obtained by adding the individual scale items and then dividing by the number of items in the scale. The items measure managers' perceptions of the pioneer's advantage in brand image, product quality, and ability to charge a premium price. Items were answered on an eleven-point Likert-type scale from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree), centered for analysis so that -5 represents strongly disagree and 5 represents strongly agree.

Group split of respondent firms into manufacturing firms and service providers. The sample was drawn as half manufacturing and half service firms in each country, and perceptions were compared between the two sectors (1,437 manufacturing and 982 service firms).

variable_name: Western versus Asian Pacific country group
description: Group split of respondents by country into Western (United States, United Kingdom, Germany) and Asian Pacific (Japan, China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore). Differences in perceived advantages across countries were tested with MANOVA and Duncan multiple-range tests.

The questionnaire defined a pioneer as a firm that is the first to introduce a new product or brand into its primary markets. Managers rated, on eleven-point agree-disagree items, whether pioneers compared with later entrants have higher ROI and market share, more post-entry risk, and cost and differentiation advantages.

Indicator of whether the LP-VC tie was realized and the LP invested in the new fund being raised by the VC firm. It is observed for each LP-VC evaluatee dyad appearing in a choice set that contains the factual match and the counterfactual VCs that raised a fund of the same type in the same calendar year and were open to new investors. Dyads in which the LP and the VC already had a prior investment tie, and first-time funds, were excluded.
level: LP-VC dyad within a choice set

description: Count of indirect ties that resulted in a success, defined as an IPO or an acquisition of the portfolio company in which the VC pair co-invested, and did not experience any failure, defined as a bankruptcy or a liquidation of the portfolio company. A single mediating VC counts as one indirect tie even if it had multiple syndications with the focal VC. The count was logged to reduce overdispersion.

Count of indirect ties between the focal LP and VC that resulted in at least one failure, defined as a bankruptcy or a liquidation of the portfolio company in which the VC pair co-invested, and zero successes. Only discrete mediating paths are counted, so a single mediating VC counts as one indirect tie. The count was logged to reduce overdispersion.

An industry specialization overlap index in which the proportion of VC firm i's investments in industry k over the prior five years enters a dyadic overlap formula; the exact formula is not readable in the supplied text. The resulting dyadic industry overlap measure between two VC firms ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating identical distribution of investments across industries. The average industry overlap for each evaluatee-intermediary pair was then dichotomized using the 75th percentile in the distribution of overlap between any two collaborating VCs as a cut-off, separating indirect ties into high industry overlap and low industry overlap counts.

Constructed using the methodology proposed by Lee, Pollock, and Jin (2001): equal-weighted z-standardized scores of a VC firm relative to all firms existing in the industry in the focal year along six dimensions. Based on the calculated reputations of the intermediary and the evaluatee, the overall indirect tie count was divided into a subcount of ties mediated by intermediaries with a higher reputation than the evaluatee and a subcount of ties mediated by intermediaries with a lower reputation than the evaluatee.
level: VC firm-year; used to split intermediary-evaluatee ties
time_window: five years for the performance and activity dimensions; age measured in the focal year

description: Longevity was defined as the number of years that the venture persisted, as evidenced by the firm's annual reports. If a venture was dropped from the list of ventures in the annual report, this was considered to be a termination. If a JV changed into an acquisition, the venture was considered to be terminated as a JV, and this termination was not coded as an acquisition.

One measure for the cultural distance between the host country and the home country (i.e., the Netherlands) is the Kogut and Singh index. The index is based on the four cultural dimensions in Hofstede's (1980) large-scale study, and scores on the four dimensions for the countries in the study were obtained from Hofstede (1980, 1991).

A second measure for cultural distance is based on Ronen and Shenkar's (1985) classification. This measure has a lower score if the cultural block to which the host country belonged was closer to the Netherlands, ranging from 1, when the host country belonged to the Nordic block, to 8, in the case of Africa. While cruder than the Kogut and Singh index, this measure does not implicitly assume that the four factors identified in Hofstede (1980) are the 'true and only' factors capturing national culture, nor does it assume linearity, additivity, and normal distributions of the scores on these factors.

A third measure of cultural distance uses dummy variables for the cultural blocks of Ronen and Shenkar (1985), where the eight cultural blocks are used to form seven block dummies, omitting one extreme block dummy (e.g., Nordic) to serve as a benchmark in the analysis. The dummy measure does not implicitly assume that the persistence of ventures is linear in the cultural distance to the Netherlands. It also provides complementary empirical information on the significance of differences between the persistence of ventures in the benchmark cultural block on the one hand, and in other cultural blocks on the other hand.

The level of foreign experience was operationalized by LEXPERIENCE, the log of all foreign expansions that the firm had undertaken, as available in the data set from 1966 onwards. Using the log of the number of previous ventures reflects the assumption that firms learn from their previous experiences at a decreasing rate.
time_window: prior to the venture; data from 1966 onwards

description: LHOSTEXP is the log of the number of previous expansions of the firm in the same host country.
time_window: prior to the venture; data from 1966 onwards

description: LHOSTBLOCK is the log of the number of previous expansions of the firm in other countries in the same cultural block as the host country. Cultural blocks of countries were coded based on clusters identified by Ronen and Shenkar (1985).
time_window: prior to the venture; data from 1966 onwards

description: LNEARBLOCK is the log of the number of previous expansions of the firm in cultural blocks that, according to Ronen and Shenkar (1985), were closer to the home country than the cultural block to which the host country belongs.
time_window: prior to the venture; data from 1966 onwards

variable_name: Mode and ownership structure of the venture
description: A venture was called an acquisition if the expansion entailed the takeover of an existing firm or one of its business units, and a start-up if it was a newly established subsidiary. The expansion was called a WOS if the expansion was 100 percent controlled by the Dutch firm; a majority JV if the Dutch firm owned less than 100 percent and more than 50 percent of the equity; a 50/50 JV if both firms had a 50 percent stake; and a minority JV if the Dutch firm owned less than 50 percent.

The total number of patents generated by firms in a given year, counted from invention patents filed with the SIPO and eventually granted. Following prior practice, the year of application is regarded as the time when a patent was produced.
time_window: year of patent application; observation year

description: The number of novel patents divided by the total number of patents produced by the firm in the given year, taking a value between 0 and 1. Following Fleming, Mingo, and Chen (2007), a patent is regarded as novel if it involves the first occurrence of a new combination of patent classes compared with all the patents that have ever been granted by the SIPO until the observation year.

The percentage of firm shares owned by board members, used to measure the degree of alignment between agents' private interests and firm value. The authors note that the private incentives of board members shape how they monitor firm management and make important decisions, and that many top managers also sit on boards.

The proportion of firm shares owned by the state, used to proxy for the degree of monitoring exercised by the state principal on SOEs. The authors draw on the blockholder literature, in which larger blockholders tend to exert extra effort in monitoring management because they have further interests at stake, so the higher the shares the state owns, the greater its incentive to monitor the value of the SOE.

The first component from a principal component analysis, conducted each year, of four subindices published by the NERI that proxy for outcomes of government quality. Across all years the average eigenvalue of the first component is 1.72, explaining 43% of the variance.

An SOE is regarded as treated if its SIC 3 industry classification belongs to the industrial categories that produced one or more products designated in the government procurement catalogs. For a treated SOE, post-policy is defined as 1 for the observation years that fall after 2006, the year of the policy issuance (i.e., equal to or later than 2007), and 0 otherwise; for a nontreated SOE, post-policy is always defined as 0. This variable is not lagged.

Three items measuring the extent to which the theater's artistic decisions emphasize product exploration, developed from focus group discussions with performing arts leaders and pilot tested with five managing directors. Managing directors rated the items on a seven-point emphasis scale in the strategic emphasis survey administered at the end of FY 2003. Factor and reliability analyses generally supported the validity of the measure, and the analyses use the orthogonal factor score.

Three items measuring the extent to which artistic decisions emphasize product exploitation; in focus groups this was discussed in terms of incremental departure from tradition, with season selections from the existing canon of plays and conventional conceptualization and interpretation of the stories. Items were rated by managing directors on a seven-point emphasis scale at the end of FY 2003. Factor and reliability analyses generally supported the validity of the measure, and the analyses use the orthogonal factor score.

Three items measuring marketing decisions that emphasize market exploration; focus group participants described it as a commitment to finding new audiences who might best respond to a particular work. Items were rated by managing directors on a seven-point emphasis scale at the end of FY 2003. The reliability score for market exploration (α = 0.65) was slightly below the generally accepted standard of 0.70, and the analyses use the orthogonal factor score.

Three items measuring marketing decisions that emphasize market exploitation; focus group participants represented it through subscription campaigns and efforts to persuade single-ticket buyers to repurchase. Items were rated by managing directors on a seven-point emphasis scale at the end of FY 2003. Factor and reliability analyses generally supported the validity of the measure, and the analyses use the orthogonal factor score.

Total ticket revenue reported to TCG for FYs 2003-2005 divided by the theater's annual seating capacity, the total number of seats available at all performances during the year. The measure controls for heterogeneity in operational capacity and is the dependent variable in all models.

Operationalized as the organization's lagged budget size using the total expense figure reported in the TCG database for FYs 2002-2004. Because the lagged total expense figure was missing for 14% of cases, the total expense figure reported to the IRS on Form 990 (compiled in the Unified Database of Arts Organizations) was used for the missing information. Lagging the measure mitigates endogeneity bias concerns.

Computed as FYs 2003-2005 minus the theater's founding date, so that age varies across the three-year time frame. The founding date was collected from each theater's website, or by contacting the theater directly when the date was not listed.

Interaction term formed from the product exploitation and product exploration factor scores; orthogonal factor scores were used for the strategic emphases and other lower-order terms were standardized before creating interaction terms. It is entered in three-way interactions with firm size and with firm age to capture within-function product ambidexterity.

Interaction term formed from the market exploitation and market exploration factor scores; orthogonal factor scores were used for the strategic emphases and other lower-order terms were standardized before creating interaction terms. It is entered in three-way interactions with firm size and with firm age to capture within-function market ambidexterity.

Entropy index of the dispersion of a firm's operations across six relatively homogeneous global market areas, computed from the relative size distribution of the firm's operations across industry segments and geographic market areas. Size of operations is measured by the number of employees. Firms with above-mean GMD scores were classified as high global market diversifiers and firms with below-mean GMD scores as low global market diversifiers.

Entropy index of the extent of global diversification across business segments (four-digit SIC codes) within the industry segments (two-digit SIC codes) of a firm. Sample means were computed for both UD and GRD; firms with above-mean GRD scores and below-mean UD scores were designated global related diversifiers, and firms with above-mean UD scores and below-mean GRD scores were designated global unrelated diversifiers. Nondiversifiers and dual-strategy diversifiers were omitted from the final analysis.

Growth index of operating profit margin and of return on assets, computed from the raw-score regression coefficient of a simple linear trend regression of semi-annual OPM (ROA) on time, divided by the arithmetic mean of the OPM(ROA) time-series; multiplied by 100 it gives an estimate of the average percent growth in OPM(ROA) per unit of time. The growth measure is unaffected by negative or zero values in the OPM(ROA) time-series. Based on eight data points, representing semi-annual OPM(ROA) for 1982 through 1985. The exact formula as printed in the paper is not recoverable from the text.

Instability index of OPM (ROA) based on the standard deviation of the OPM(ROA) time-series and the coefficient of determination from the simple linear OPM(ROA) trend regression; the measure is divided by the mean OPM(ROA) so that it assesses instability independent of the absolute level of OPM(ROA). It does not confound stable growth or stable decline with variability. Based on eight data points, representing semi-annual OPM(ROA) for 1982 through 1985. The exact formula as printed in the paper is not recoverable from the text.

The authors developed dummy variables, indexed by t, measuring whether a suggestion received attention from an organization in calendar week t. An organization's assignment of the status 'selected' to a suggestion was treated as attention from the organization. A suggestion left the risk set once it received a status of 'selected'. The variables are time variant and traced on a weekly basis after the initial suggestion.
scale: dummy: 1 = implemented (selected) by the organization at time t

description: Crowding was measured by recording how many suggestions were at risk (i.e., had not yet experienced a status change) in calendar week t. The degree of crowding varied with the number of new suggestions being posted (more suggestions increased crowding) and with an organization's completion and rejection of suggestions (more completions or rejections decreased crowding).

Suggestion content was processed by converting all words to lowercase, removing punctuation, white space and non-alphabetic characters, removing stop words, and stemming words to their root form. Each suggestion was represented as a bag-of-words vector in which each cell is the log of the frequency of each word in the suggestion multiplied by the inverse frequency of the word in the organization's corpus, so that words less frequently used in the corpus receive greater weight. Cosine similarities between suggestion vectors in week t were combined into a suggestion-by-suggestion matrix, and the row sum of that matrix in week t was used as a measure of content similarity. Because the theorizing is about content distance, this value was multiplied by negative one.
scale: row sum of cosine similarities (0 to 1), multiplied by -1

description: Measures of the relationships among suggestions were constructed from whether the same external contributors voted on multiple suggestions; the two-mode data were converted to one-mode data to build a network of how suggestions were related via votes in an organization's community. Ties were weighted following Newman's projection, which discounts external contributors who voted for many different suggestions because they contribute less to the weight of the tie linking two suggestions. Structural distance was measured as the weighted degree centrality of a given suggestion in week t in the one-mode projection of the suggestion network, normalized by the size of the community, multiplied by negative one.
The number of implemented suggestions that an external contributor contributed to the focal organization before submitting a focal suggestion, multiplied by negative one.
time_window: before submission of the focal suggestion

description: A depreciating stock of R&D expenditures by the firm, using a 15 percent depreciation rate. To account for high correlations between R&D spending and other firm variables, the main models use the residuals from a fixed-effects panel ordinary least squares model predicting R&D spending as a function of firm size, performance, and debt ratio.

The citation-weighted stock of the firm's patents (also depreciated at 15 percent) divided by R&D spending, yielding a measure of citations per unit spending. Forward citation measures are adjusted by dividing the citations received by each patent by the average citations received in its patent class and application year. A three-part split is also reported, splitting R&D productivity into patents per unit spending and citations per patent.
The average R&D spending for all firms (excluding the focal firm) in the focal firm's primary four-digit SIC industry.

The average R&D productivity for all firms (excluding the focal firm) in the focal firm's primary four-digit SIC industry. A three-part split of rival innovation into rival patents per unit spending and rival citations per patent is also reported.

A count of acquisitions undertaken by a firm in a given year, with data on transactions taken from SDC. Noncore acquisitions are identified by comparing the primary four-digit SIC code of the acquirer and the target as given in SDC; an acquisition is deemed noncore if the target is in a different SIC code from the acquirer.
time_window: focal year (dependent variable measured in year t+1)

description: A count of divestments undertaken by a firm in a given year, with data on transactions taken from SDC. The same procedure as for acquisitions is followed for noncore divestments, comparing the primary four-digit SIC codes of the parties to the transaction.
time_window: focal year (dependent variable measured in year t+1)

description: Long-term debt by total assets. A high debt ratio would mean both a lower capacity for the firm to take on additional debt, which may be particularly salient in the case of acquisitions, as well as lower levels of free cash flow for the same level of operating performance, so that the firm would have less internal funds to invest. To account for firm-level differences in debt preference and to make interactions easier to interpret, the study uses a standardized within-firm measure of debt ratio.
The past correlation between changes in firm profitability and changes in rival sales. The measure ranges from -1 to 1, with -1 being a perfect substitute and 1 being a perfect complement.

Data were collected at two points in time. The 1987 data come from the firms on the 1988 Fortune 500 list and the 1996 data from the firms on the 1997 Fortune 500 list, giving a 10-year interval between observations.

variable_name: number of women serving on the board of directors
description: For each Fortune 500 firm the number of women serving on the board of directors was noted at both time periods, from corporate proxy reports. Results are reported as the percentage of Fortune 500 companies that had women on their board of directors and as the average number of women on a board.

variable_name: number of women serving as CEO
description: For each Fortune 500 firm the number of women serving as CEO of the firm was noted at both time periods, from corporate proxy reports.

variable_name: number of women serving as inside director
description: An inside director is a member of firm management who also serves on the board of directors. The number of women serving in this capacity was noted at both time periods from corporate proxy reports; the 1996 figures are also expressed as a share of the 1251 inside board member positions in the Fortune 500.

variable_name: women outside directors with corporate backgrounds
description: Women serving on the board were classified as having corporate professional backgrounds as compared to noncorporate backgrounds. A female director who serves as chief financial officer of another Fortune 500 firm, for example, would be a director with a corporate background, whereas directors employed in the nonprofit sector or public service and academicians are examples of board members with noncorporate backgrounds. Results are reported as the percentage of female outside directors with this profile.

Women directors with professional ties to the firm or firm management were identified. Relying on the SEC 6(b) guidelines, the classification includes those directors employed by firms providing services to the focal firm (e.g., legal counsel, consultant, accountant). Results are reported as the percentage of women on the board who were affiliated directors.

variable_name: Foreign ownership (treatment group in the matched sample)
description: Companies in which a single foreign corporation holds more than 50 percent of the stock are treated as foreign-owned; all other companies in the register are domestically owned. Each foreign-owned company was matched with a domestic twin in the same four-digit industry category that came closest to it by assets, with share capital used as a secondary criterion. Ownership enters the survival model as the comparison between the foreign member and the domestic member of each matched pair.

Survival time is measured from the year a company enters the study until exit or until the 2005 follow-up. Exit includes merger into a larger entity, liquidation, bankruptcy, and cases recorded as empty or unknown, and is not synonymous with liquidation or death. Observations are left truncated at entry into the study and right censored at the follow-up, and results are reported as hazard ratios of domestic relative to foreign companies within matched pairs, where a relative risk larger than one means a higher exit risk for domestic companies.

variable_name: Number of foreign companies operating at time of entry
description: The variable describes the number of foreign companies operating at the time of entry for the foreign company of each pair. The authors also computed the number of foreign companies within the individual industry sectors active in the calendar year of entry; both measures were entered into the model of relative exit risk, and the industry measure becomes insignificant once the overall measure is controlled for.

Cumulative count of ISO 9000 quality program certifications for a business unit by year; the number for 1996 is the sum of the certifications through 1995 plus the new certifications for 1996. Certifications were selected for business units in SIC code 3861, representing photography and imaging equipment and supplies; where the 4-digit code was 3800 or missing, the certification's scope text was checked for mentions of photography or imaging. The measures were constructed as the extent of process management activities undertaken within a business unit.

Counts of patents in each firm-year that are anchored in existing firm knowledge, built from USPTO patents awarded from 1980 through 1999 and recorded by filing date. Prior patents cited by a patent were coded as existing firm knowledge if they were repeat citations (patents the firm had previously cited) or self-citations (the firm's own previous patents). The extreme measure counts patents with 100 percent of their citations to familiar patents, and further measures count patents with at least 80, 90, 60, and 40 percent of their citations to existing firm knowledge. The measures use a one-year lead on exploitation and exploration.

Counts of patents in each firm-year that depart from existing firm knowledge, built from USPTO patents awarded from 1980 through 1999 and recorded by filing date. The most exploratory category comprises patents having no repeat or self-citations, and measures were also constructed at the 10, 20, and 40 percent levels, i.e., patents constituting 10 percent or less, 20 percent or less, and 40 percent or less of the citations to prior knowledge of the focal firm. The measures use a one-year lead on exploitation and exploration.

The ratio of exploitative innovation to total innovation for a firm, used as the dependent variable to test Hypothesis 3. Because this ratio is constrained between 0 and 1, the authors report results using the exploitation/total patents ratio in cross-sectional, time-series (panel) OLS regressions that incorporate the same panel data designs and controls, including firm fixed effects. The ratio was calculated with three measures of exploitation: patents based more than 60 percent, more than 80 percent, and 100 percent on existing firm knowledge.

Cumulative count of ISO 9000 quality program certifications for a business unit by year; the number for 1996 is the sum of the certifications through 1995 plus the new certifications for 1996. Certifications were selected for business units in SIC code 2851; where only SIC code 2800 was listed or the code was missing, the text describing the scope of the certification was cross-checked for mentions of paint or coatings. The measures were constructed as the extent of process management activities undertaken within a business unit.

Counts of patents in each firm-year that are anchored in existing firm knowledge, drawn from patent class 106, representing coating compositions, and recorded by filing date. Prior patents cited by a patent were coded as existing firm knowledge if they were repeat citations or the firm's own previous patents. Measures count patents with at least 60, 80, and 100 percent of their citations to existing firm knowledge. The measures use a one-year lead on exploitation and exploration.

Counts of patents in each firm-year that depart from existing firm knowledge, drawn from patent class 106, representing coating compositions, and recorded by filing date. The most exploratory category comprises patents having no repeat or self-citations, and measures were also constructed at the 20 and 40 percent levels, i.e., patents constituting 20 percent or less and 40 percent or less of the citations to prior knowledge of the focal firm. The measures use a one-year lead on exploitation and exploration.

The ratio of exploitative innovation to total innovation for a firm, used as the dependent variable to test Hypothesis 3. Because this ratio is constrained between 0 and 1, the authors report results using the exploitation/total patents ratio in cross-sectional, time-series (panel) OLS regressions that incorporate the same panel data designs and controls, including firm fixed effects. The ratio was calculated with three measures of exploitation: patents based more than 60 percent, more than 80 percent, and 100 percent on existing firm knowledge.

A dummy variable equal to 1 if the focal firm has issued a CSR report in a given year, and 0 otherwise. The authors state that there is a one-year lag between all independent and dependent variables. The number of CSR reports issued by Chinese public firms increased year after year in the sample.

A dummy variable equal to 1 if the firm was owned by dispersed private shareholders and 0 if the ultimate owner was the Chinese government and its agencies. It is used as a main effect and in the interaction terms that test the moderation hypotheses. The authors state that there is a one-year lag between all independent and dependent variables.
time_window: lagged one year relative to the dependent variable
