description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if the CEO was a member of the CPCC (as written in the text), and 0 otherwise; elsewhere the text describes this connection as membership in the National People's Congress (NPC) or the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC). Information on the CEO comes from corporate annual reports, which provide a biographical sketch of the CEO, including his or her previous experience in industry and government. The authors state that there is a one-year lag between all independent and dependent variables.
time_window: lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: Firm age is the number of years since the firm was established. The authors treat age as reflecting a firm's founding era and the political legacy carried from it. The authors state that there is a one-year lag between all independent and dependent variables.
time_window: lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: Firm ROA is the return on assets, calculated as net income over total assets. The authors describe it as a common accounting-based measure of financial performance and note that ROA is seen as the best performance measure to use in China. It is one of two variables capturing a firm's financial resources.
time_window: lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: Slack resources are calculated as the sum of cash flow from a firm's operating, financing, and investing activities. To control for firm size, the authors scaled slack resources by total assets. The authors note that cash flow better captures the notion of available resources for discretionary purposes. It is the second variable capturing a firm's financial resources.
time_window: lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: An overall rating of CSR activities as portrayed in the report, obtained from the CSR rating agency RKS (Runling) and covering 2008 and 2009. Firms' CSR activities are rated along three dimensions—overall evaluation (CSR strategy, stakeholder participation, comparability over time, innovativeness, external auditing), content evaluation (leadership and organizational systems and specific metrics for economic, environmental, and social responsibilities), and technical evaluation (transparency, regularity, and availability of CSR information)—which together include over 70 subdimensions. The rating ranges from 0 to 100 and the evaluation system is based on the GRI 3.0 guidelines adapted for China. Each CSR report is evaluated by at least three RKS experts.

A dummy variable used to measure bureaucratic embeddedness; it equals 1 when the CEO is or has been an officer of the central or regional governments, and it is 0 otherwise. Information on the CEO's government experience comes from the biographical sketch in corporate annual reports.

A province's gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, i.e., the province's GDP divided by its population. The authors obtained this measure from the Chinese Statistics Bureau and note that it is consistent with prior research showing that economic development is highly related to government development in China. It varies across the provinces in which firms are headquartered.

The Navy Industrial Fund procedures imposed on the NARDACs starting in 1984, under which all nontactical information system support became reimbursable and customers were billed for services. The authors compare the percentages of information services customers received from each source in 1983, prior to the introduction of NIF, with those reported for 1989.

Secretary of Navy Notice 5236, issued at the end of 1988, requiring Navy customers to first approach the NARDAC for projects exceeding $150,000 life cycle costs, with a waiver provided if the NARDAC could not perform the service. The authors compare the post-NIF/pre-LC-order environment with the customers' expected expenditures for the future five years.

variable_name: percentage of information services received from civilian providers
description: Customers reported the percentage of information services received from four sources: NARDACs, civilian providers, other Navy providers, and in-house operations. These data were collected for 1983, for 1989, and as expected expenditures for the future five years. A Navy customer was classified as a mixed provider user if over 25 percent of its nontactical information requirements were met by the private-sector.

variable_name: percentage of information services done in-house
description: Customers reported the percentage of their information services performed by in-house operations, one of the four sources of information services. A customer was considered to be vertically integrated if over 75 percent of its nontactical information requirements were done in-house.
A size variable based on the customer's response to the question of whether their projects are typically under or over $150,000. The variable was coded 1 = small customer, 0 = large customer.

One of nine strategic dimensions on which customers evaluated their principal NARDAC, both relative to civilian providers and in terms of their degree of satisfaction with the NARDAC; both types of questions were rated using a 7-point scale. NARDAC managers and private-sector providers evaluated their own strategies along the same dimensions relative to their main competitor in the other sector. In the logistic regressions the strategy variables were measured as 'NARDAC relative to the private sector' and the satisfaction variables as the 'degree of satisfaction' with NARDAC along those dimensions.

IJV performance was measured as the level of satisfaction with venture performance in four areas, as perceived by IJV top managers, using a 7-point Likert scale. The four areas are profitability, sales level, competitive position, and overall performance. The factor loadings from the exploratory factor analysis were used as weights in calculating the average score of this construct.

Product relatedness was defined as an index adding the related product linkages of both foreign and Chinese parents and the IJV. Each respondent assessed whether an IJV's primary product or business is related (horizontally or vertically) or unrelated to its foreign and Chinese parents, with the definition of each diversification type provided in the questionnaire. The index equals 2 when the product is related with both parents, 1 if related to only one parent, and 0 if unrelated to both.

Resource complementarity was measured by an average of a respondent's assessment, on a 7-point Likert scale, of the extent to which one parent's contributed resources are complementary to those contributed by the other parent. Factor loadings were used as weights in computing the average scores of this construct.

Goal incongruity (reverse coded) was defined as a multi-item construct asking each respondent to assess, on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 not congruent at all to 7 extremely congruent, the extent to which foreign and Chinese parents are congruent with respect to strategic goals set for their IJV. Factor loadings were used as weights in calculating the average of this variable.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 not congruent at all to 7 extremely congruent)

description: Industrial growth was defined as the average compound growth (%) of an industry's sales, profit, and outputs during 1995-97. The data were obtained from the 3-year editions of the China Statistical Yearbook compiled and published by the State Statistical Bureau.

Institutional deterrence is a categorical construct, defined as 5 if an IJV's industry lies in Restricted Category B, 4 if in Restricted Category A, 3 if in the Newly Opened Category, 2 if in the Encouraged Non-Technological Category, and 1 if in the Encouraged Technological Category. The full list of projects and industries under each of these categories was obtained from The Orientation Directory of Industries for FDI; the higher the number, the greater the institutional deterrence.

variable_name: authority split between FAH and RAH
description: Binary variable with a value of 1 when the task assignments of being responsible and having to execute the task are assigned to two different individuals. The FAH maps the actor from the responsibility chart with the task assignment of being responsible, and the RAH maps the actor with the task assignment to execute.

Counts the number of hierarchical levels separating the FAH and the RAH on the organizational charts. A delegation span of 0 means that the FAH and RAH are located at the same hierarchy level, and a code of 1 means that the RAH is at least one level lower than the FAH, with increasing values signifying greater distance. It is observed only for tasks where formal and real authority are split.

The number of decisions under the responsibility of an FAH, obtained by identifying the job title of a task's FAH and counting for that job title the number of tasks in the responsibility chart that carry the task assignment of being responsible.

Binary variable obtained by content analysis of the task descriptions that equals 1 when the task decision making requires specialized knowledge, such as tasks related to engineering expertise or tax or export regulations, and 0 when task decision making relies on general knowledge, such as tasks related to coordination or administrative assignments.

Binary variable built from content analysis of both task descriptions and job descriptions of job titles. It is set to 1 when the FAH's knowledge domain required for her task decision making matches the expertise domain of her job description and to 0 otherwise.

Underpricing, or first-day return, is calculated as the first-day closing price minus the offer price, divided by the offer price. The authors assume that the full extent of underpricing is already given at the end of the first trading day because the Frankfurt Stock Exchange has no restrictions on daily price fluctuations.

Family firm status is treated as a dummy variable by assigning a value of 1 to family firms and a value of 0 to nonfamily firms. Family firms are those in which the person who established or acquired the firm or their families or descendants possess 25 percent of the decision-making rights; this information was collected from each company's emission prospectus.

Categorical dependent variable indicating whether the focal firm chose to create a fresh alliance with an existing partner, a new close partner, or a new distant partner. Existing partners are coded as 1 if the alliance partner was already in the alliance portfolio at alliance formation; new close partners are coded as 2 when the distance of the new partner is 2 (there is a mutual partner between the focal firm and the new partner); and new distant partners are coded as 3 when the distance of the new partner is 3 and beyond (there is no mutual partner between the focal firm and the new partner). Distance is the shortest alternative path to a partner firm at the time period prior to alliance formation, measured with a four-year moving window, and cases where there was no firm between the focal firm and the partner were treated as infinite distance (distance 6), while the very first alliance partner for firms was treated as 0.
scale: 1 = existing partner, 2 = new close partner, 3 = new distant partner
time_window: four-year moving window, measured prior to alliance formation

description: Measured as the percentage of equity holdings of top executives to the total outstanding common shares of the company. It is the explanatory variable for Hypotheses 1a, 1b, and 1c and one term of the interaction for Hypotheses 3a and 3b.

Measured as the percentage of shares held by all nonexecutive directors to the total number of outstanding shares. Directors were coded as 'insider,' 'affiliated - family or former employee,' 'affiliated - professional relationship with firm' (coded as 0) or 'outsider' (coded as 1). It is the explanatory variable for Hypotheses 2a and 2b and the moderator in Hypotheses 3a and 3b, operationalized as an interaction with managers' stock ownership.

Count of branded upscale hotels in each zip code, computed 2 years before the opening of the new hotel. Upscale brands were split from economy brands based on a brand's average AAA rating in Texas of 2.5 stars in the 1998 guidebook; Comfort Inn was the lowest ranked upscale brand. The count enters the conditional logit as a market-level attribute.
time_window: 2 years prior to the new hotel's opening

description: Count of branded economy hotels in each zip code, computed 2 years before the opening of the new hotel. Economy brands are those below the 2.5-star AAA threshold, with Ramada the highest ranked economy brand. The count enters the conditional logit as a market-level attribute.
time_window: 2 years prior to the new hotel's opening

description: Count of hotels in each zip code that are not affiliated with a nationally known brand, computed 2 years before the opening of the new hotel. The count enters the conditional logit as a market-level attribute.
time_window: 2 years prior to the new hotel's opening

variable_name: Choice of market by branded upscale hotels
description: The dependent variable of the conditional logit: which zip-code market was chosen by each of the 296 new branded upscale hotels, compared against all other markets that could have been chosen for that entrant. Markets with higher values of a variable receiving a positive coefficient have a higher probability of being chosen.

variable_name: Choice of market by branded economy hotels
description: The dependent variable of the conditional logit: which zip-code market was chosen by each of the 161 new branded economy hotels, compared against all other markets that could have been chosen for that entrant. Estimated in a separate model from the unbranded entrants.

variable_name: Choice of market by unbranded hotels
description: The dependent variable of the conditional logit: which zip-code market was chosen by each of the 113 new unbranded hotels, compared against all other markets that could have been chosen for that entrant. Estimated in a separate model from the branded economy entrants.

Dummy variable equal to one if managerial positions are reported as usually being filled 'from outside the company' as opposed to within the firm, with the added condition that at least one manager is hired in the same year if the practice changed from the prior year. The survey asks how vacant positions are usually filled, checking only the most frequently used method. Managers are defined in the survey to include the most senior manager in the workplace and other senior managers whose responsibilities would normally span more than one internal department, or who generally report to senior management and are responsible for a single domain or department.

Dummy variable created by the same procedure as external managerial hiring, applied to the filling of vacant high-skilled nonmanagerial positions, which the survey defines as 'professionals.' It equals one if professional positions are reported as usually being filled from outside the company as opposed to within the firm, with the added condition that at least one professional is hired in the same year if the practice changed from the prior year.

Fraction of 12 operating tasks allocated to either work supervisors or senior managers within the organization. The survey asks 'who normally makes decisions with respect to the following activities?' with five possible responses: nonmanagerial employees, work supervisors, senior managers, individuals or groups outside the workplace, and business owners. The authors calculate the fraction of tasks allocated to either work supervisors or senior managers.

Fraction of the 12 operating tasks for which decisions are normally made by nonmanagerial employees within the organization. It uses the same survey question on who normally makes decisions about the listed activities and the same five possible responses, with the authors calculating the nonmanagerial employees' fraction of allocated tasks.

Respondents rate the factor 'reorganizing the work process' with respect to its relative importance in the workplace general business strategy, choosing from (1) Not applicable, (2) Not important, (3) Slightly important, (4) Important, (5) Very important and (6) Crucial. The authors redefine values of (2) to be equal to (1) and reset the scale to be ascending from 1 to 5, because an increase from the original (1) to (2) and vice versa does not clearly capture changes in strategic priority.

Respondents rate the factor 'developing new products/services' with respect to its relative importance in the workplace general business strategy, using the same six-point Likert scale. As with workplace reorganization, the authors redefine values of (2) to be equal to (1) and reset the scale to be ascending from 1 to 5.

Dummy variable equal to one if the organization reports any of the following organizational changes occurring during the year of the survey: greater integration among different functional areas, downsizing, reengineering, greater reliance on job rotation and multiskilling, and implementation of total quality management. The survey asks whether the workplace experienced any organizational changes during the year, where organizational change is defined as 'a change in the way in which work is organized within your workplace.'

Total number of novel innovations developed during the 4 years after external hiring of professionals has occurred, defined as being first in the local market, in Canada, or in the world. The survey asks whether new products or services were developed during the year of the survey and whether the innovation is the first in its local market, in Canada, or in the world. In creating the innovation measures the authors consider only industries identified as having product development cycles of 4 years or less.
time_window: 4 years after external hiring of professionals has occurred

description: Total number of nonnovel innovations during the 4 years after external hiring of professionals has occurred, that is, innovations that are not the first in the local market, in Canada or in the world. It is built from the same survey questions on whether new products or services were developed and on the novelty of the innovation, and is restricted to the same industries with product development cycles of 4 years or less.
time_window: 4 years after external hiring of professionals has occurred

description: The total number of managerial and professional new hires during 2003, 2004, and 2005 divided by the total number of managers and professionals in the organization at the beginning of each year, respectively; for example, 20 hires on a base of 100 managers and professionals is a 20% hiring rate for that year. Hiring rates were winsorized by specifying 1% of observations in each tail. Because the observation window is 2003-2005, the average of the three years' hiring rates is used in all analyses.

Calculated as the differences in hiring rates for managers and professionals between 2003 and 2004 and between 2004 and 2005; for example, hiring rates of 10% in 2003 and 20% in 2004 give a hiring rate change of 10% over 2003-2004. Because the observation window is 2003-2005, the average of the two hiring rate changes is used in all analyses.

Calculated for the three-year window (2003-2005) with a refined entropy index. Pi is the ratio of hiring rate for managers and professionals in each year over the total hiring rates for these positions during 2003-2005; for organizations that did not hire in a year (Pi = 0), Pi was replaced with 0.0001. The entropy index ranges from zero to one, and the higher it is, the more evenly an organization hired during the three years. The equation itself is not readable in the available text.

An additive index of six yes-no items assessing work practices designed to increase employee participation and collaboration, with adequate reliability (Cronbach's alpha = 0.73). The additive index was divided by six to capture the ratio of CWPs in place for 2003 and 2005, and the average ratio of the two years is used in all analyses; for example, two CWPs in 2003 and four in 2005 gives a score of 0.50.

The 2006 workplace survey asked whether the organization had improved processes, improved goods or services, new processes, or new goods or services. The index ranges between 0 and 4: 0 indicates no innovation; 1 means the organization improved processes or products or services; 2 denotes that it improved processes and products or services; 3 reflects that it developed new processes or products or services; and 4 specifies that it developed new processes and products or services. The index is ordinal and is based on self-reported data.

The natural logarithm of (1 + ) the number of new mods generated for a given platform in a given month. The authors use this variable to infer variation in the intensity of complementor incentives to invest in development. Taking logarithms re-scales variation to reduce skew and allows coefficients to be interpreted as elasticities.

The natural logarithm of the total number of minutes played for all mods for a given game engine platform in a given month. The variable was publicly reported by C-Sport.net and was observable by all platform participants at the time. It is lagged three months in the development-rate expression and one month in the usage expression.

The cumulative release of mods over time, logged, used as the measure of the size of the complementor side of the platform. The authors use mod counts because the number of complementors is almost precisely the same as the number of complementary mods generated, as most individual complementors developed only one mod during the sample period. It is lagged three months in the development-rate expression and one month in the usage expression.

Mergers were taken from the FTC large merger series and classified by the FTC as vertical, meaning that the two firms had a clear buyer-seller relationship before the merger. The population was limited to mergers of at least $10 million in asset value and to full ownership, excluding mergers in which ownership of the target was less than 50%. Firms also had to have CRSP daily returns for a full 200 trading days before the announcement day and after the legal transaction day.

variable_name: DSYS (difference in the bidder's systematic risk)
description: Each firm's pre-merger beta was subtracted from its post-merger beta: pre-merger betas were estimated over a 150-day period beginning 200 days before the announcement day, and post-merger betas over a 150-day period beginning 50 days after the legal transaction day. For the matched sample a second difference score was computed by subtracting the market-value-weighted portfolio beta of the integrator and target (the hypothesized, investor-made merger beta) from the integrator's post-merger consolidated beta. Each difference score was averaged with those computed for other vertically merging bidder firms.
time_window: about two years surrounding the merger event day

description: The 4-firm concentration ratio of the integrator's primary 4-digit SIC industry, obtained from the U.S. Census of Manufacturers. The authors preferred the 4-digit to the broader 2-digit ratio because it is expected to be more sensitive in capturing the power relationships between buyer and seller, and they discarded observations whose CRSP 4-digit SIC codes did not correspond to those published in the Census. Concentration ratios were identified for 42 of the 72 integrating firms.

The difference between the integrator's and the target's 4-firm concentration ratios, expressed as a percentage (ICR/TCR), intended to capture asymmetries in the market structures of the two adjacent industries. The authors note that by construction the measure assumes that upstream assets are fully specific, and that this assumption is unlikely to hold. The asymmetric variable did not appear to be a good predictor in the regressions.
level: industry pair (integrator and target 4-digit SIC industries)

description: The 4-firm concentration ratio of the target firm's 4-digit SIC industry, obtained from the U.S. Census of Manufacturers using the same 4-digit industry matching rule as for the integrator. It was dropped from the subsample regressions of the growth analysis because it did not demonstrate much explanatory power in previous regression runs.

The growth rate in sales of the integrator firm's primary 4-digit SIC industry, obtained from the U.S. Census of Manufacturers; growth data were available for 48 integrating firms. The authors first entered growth as a continuously scaled independent variable in a regression with the integrator and target concentration ratios, and then split the sample into a growth-stage subgroup (industry sales growth between 5% and 10%) and a subgroup of mergers completed in an embryonic stage (sales growth in excess of 10%) or a maturity stage (sales growth less than 5%).

The number of times buyer and supplier had done business prior to the focal transaction. Respondents indicated the number of times they interacted with the supplier in the past on a six-point scale ranging from 'never' to 'many times'. The response was corroborated with another survey item in which respondents indicated the volume of business in prior interactions with the supplier; the correlation between these items was 0.92. The variable is centered when constructing interaction terms with IT expertise.
scale: six-point scale ranging from 'never' to 'many times'

description: The extent to which technical specifications of the product or service being procured are specified in the contract. Respondents indicated the degree of specification on four items, each on a five-point answer scale ranging from 'very broadly' to 'very detailed'. If an item did not apply, respondents were asked to indicate 'not applicable'; the authors coded 'not applicable' as zero and included those items in the analysis. Technical detail is the standardized sum of responses to the four items.
scale: five-point item scale from 'very broadly' to 'very detailed'; standardized sum

description: Measured through 10 items describing legal clauses of the transaction. For each item, the respondent indicated whether it was 'not arranged', 'only orally arranged', or 'arranged in writing'; the authors coded 'not arranged' as zero, 'oral agreement' as one, and 'written agreement' as two. Legal detail is the standardized average of the scores on the 10 items.
scale: three-point item coding (not arranged = 0, oral = 1, written = 2); standardized average

description: A dummy variable coding whether the procuring firm had any employees with expertise in IT. Almost all SMEs indicated that they were unable to produce the product they were procuring in house, yet 56% of them had employees with IT expertise, so the variable captures related but distinct knowledge in the technical domain. The suppliers were IT vendors and were expected to be competent in the technical domain.

Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 for the scenarios where the firm chooses an outside CEO successor and 0 otherwise. An outside successor was described in the scenario as the appointment of an executive from another firm. The dummy takes a value of 0 in the scenario that provides no information about the fate of the incumbent CEO, which is the excluded referent category.

Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 for the scenarios where the firm chooses an inside CEO successor and 0 otherwise. An inside successor was described as succession by another LuxCo executive. The dummy takes a value of 0 in the scenario that provides no information about the fate of the incumbent CEO, which is the excluded referent category.

Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 for the scenarios where the firm appoints an interim CEO and 0 otherwise. The interim referred to appointment of a temporary CEO 'while the firm searches for a permanent replacement,' and the scenario stated that the interim CEO 'used to be CEO of LuxCo but is now retired,' so the interim is neither an insider nor an outsider. The dummy takes a value of 0 in the scenario that provides no information about the fate of the incumbent CEO, which is the excluded referent category.

variable_name: likelihood of buying, selling, or holding the firm's stock
description: Participants selected their responses on seven-point Likert scales that asked them what they would do 'based solely on the limited information provided here,' ranging from 'definitely sell LuxCo stock' to 'definitely buy LuxCo stock.' Each respondent provided one such rating for each of the scenarios presented.

Scenario in which the competence failure involved 'a household item that was not properly tested and could lead to a home fire' wherein LuxCo 'executives did not know, but should have known, that the product needed specific tests that were not completed before it went to market.' Each respondent evaluated four scenarios framed around this failure: replacement of the CEO by an insider, an outsider, an interim, or no information about the current CEO's fate.

Scenario in which the integrity failure was that 'company executives designed a complex web of imaginary holding firms that solely did business with LuxCo with the purpose of hiding losses in LuxCo's quarterly balance sheets.' Each respondent evaluated four scenarios framed around this failure: replacement of the CEO by an insider, an outsider, an interim, or no information about the current CEO's fate.

A proxy for the changing composition of a console's user base, defined as the ratio of platform j's installed base at the time t of the focal game's release to the installed base of platform j at the end of its life cycle. The resulting variable ranges from 0 to 1 and allows for a straightforward interpretation of the effect of a platform's diffusion on game sales within and across platforms. Higher values indicate a platform whose potential adopter pool is more heavily weighted toward later adopters.
time_window: at the time of the focal game's release

description: The size of the next-generation installed base at the time of the focal game's release, used as a second proxy for the changing composition of the platform's user base. Each platform is linked to its same-brand successor (e.g., Sony PS3 for PS2) and the number of next-generation consoles sold up to the time of the focal game's release is counted. The variable is log-transformed to account for its skewness.
time_window: up to the time of the focal game's release

description: The video game's platform-specific lifetime unit sales, log-transformed because unit sales are highly skewed. The sell-through data were collected in the last week of 2011 and include over 90% of all brick-and-mortar and online transactions in the United Kingdom. Video games have very short life cycles, with most releases generating the bulk of their sales within the first few months.
time_window: lifetime sales, collected in the last week of 2011

description: A binary variable that takes the value of 1 if a video game is based on a new, original IP and 0 otherwise. Games based on existing video game properties (sequels, prequels, or spin-offs), sports licenses, or non-video game media tie-ins (movies, TV series, and books) are coded 0. Two graduate students and an industry expert consulted games' box covers and other online sources; 29% of all video games in the sample are based on new IP.

Indicator variable set equal to 1 for actual matches and to 0 for alternative alliances. A probit model analyzed how the actual and alternative alliances differed. For alliances with more members, the characteristics of each focal firm were compared with the average characteristics of the other firms in the alliance.
time_window: new alliances during the study period; independent variables lagged by one year

description: Based on the International Transportation Handbook classification of routes into 16 regions. Set to 0 for firms that did not meet in at least one market because their route networks had to connect in order to obtain complementarity benefits. For firms that met in at least one market, defined as the count of the complement of the markets the firms were represented in divided by the union of the markets the firms were in. The average complementarity of each firm and its alliance partners was calculated.

Absolute difference between a focal firm's average ship size and the average ship size of its alliance partners, calculated using data on container ships owned by each firm; the analysis uses the log of this difference. Greater difference indicated poorer match.

Absolute difference between a focal firm's average ship speed and the average ship speed of its alliance partners, calculated using data on container ships owned by each firm. Greater difference indicated poorer match.

Absolute difference between a focal firm's average ship age and the average ship age of its alliance partners, calculated using data on container ships owned by each firm. Greater difference indicated poorer match.

Isolate firms are firms that have not entered any shipping alliance. Already-networked firms have entered one or more alliances. Separate models were estimated for isolates and for networked firms; variables measuring network position were dropped for isolates because those variables have equal values for all isolate firms.

variable_name: Owned shipping capacity in container units
description: Firm size specified as owned shipping capacity in container units. Estimated with linear regression with random effects and autocorrelated disturbances because capacity in a given year was highly correlated with that of the previous year.

A firm was coded as having exited when it was no longer seen in any liner market and thus had failed, been acquired, or exited liner shipping. There were 40 exited firms in the sample, of which 17 terminated shipping operations in the liner shipping markets studied but continued other shipping services, 7 were acquired, and 16 failed. Mergers were not counted as exits. Analyzed with discrete-time event history analysis using the conditional log-log model.

Return on assets, estimated with linear regression with random effects. There were missing data on ROA because many firms had a legal form or place of incorporation that allowed them not to publicly disclose accounting statements; the selectivity control usually prevents a bias, but the data loss was sufficiently high that the results should be interpreted with caution.

Alliance-level market complementarity was aggregated to the firm-year by taking the mean over all alliances. The measure is based on the classification of routes into 16 regions and captures the complement of markets in which the firm and its alliance partners were represented divided by the union of those markets.

Absolute difference between a focal firm's average ship size and the average ship size of its alliance partners, calculated using data on container ships owned by each firm and aggregated to the firm-year by taking the mean over all alliances. Greater difference indicated poorer match.

Absolute difference between a focal firm's average ship speed and the average ship speed of its alliance partners, calculated using data on container ships owned by each firm and aggregated to the firm-year by taking the mean over all alliances. Greater difference indicated poorer match.

Absolute difference between a focal firm's average ship age and the average ship age of its alliance partners, calculated using data on container ships owned by each firm and aggregated to the firm-year by taking the mean over all alliances. Greater difference indicated poorer match.

Annual data for each automaker on the number of cars produced since they began production, constructed as a count and lagged one year. Because the variable was highly skewed, the authors also took the logarithm, which is standard in learning-curve studies.

Prior automaker experience with recalls, separated into voluntary recalls; the variable counts the number of voluntary recalls experienced during the three years prior to the current year. Whether a recall is voluntary is coded by NHTSA according to the original source of the recall. Recalls that NHTSA initiated and that the company subsequently took over are coded as involuntary.

Prior automaker experience with recalls initiated by NHTSA, counted over the three years prior to the current year. Recalls that the agency initiated and that the company later took over are still coded as involuntary, because the authors expect shallow, rule-bound responses to arise at the time of the original involuntary recall and not to change later.

Cumulative voluntary recalls divided by cumulative total recalls over the prior three years. Because the proportion could not be calculated for automakers with no recalls during the prior three years, these cases were coded zero and a dummy variable was coded one to separate their unique effects from those with prior recalls.

variable_name: level of generalism (spread of engine capacity)
description: Technological niche measured as the spread of engine capacity, in liters, across all models an automaker produces in a given year. The spread is the largest minus the smallest engine capacity, so higher values indicate a higher level of generalism; the variable is continuous and is measured in the prior year.

The dependent variable is the annual number of severe recalls for each automaker, taken from NHTSA recall reports. The NHTSA hazard levels are type 'a' (significant hazard without the automaker's warning), type 'b' (significant hazard with the automaker's warning), type 'c' (a potential safety hazard) and type 'd' (a low risk of significant harm); the authors count recalls of types 'a' and 'b' as severe.

The annual number of severe recalls (hazard types 'a' and 'b') that were initiated voluntarily by the automaker. The authors separate severe voluntary from severe involuntary recalls in some models because preliminary analyses show that the factors affecting these types of recalls differ significantly.

The annual number of severe recalls (hazard types 'a' and 'b') that were mandated by NHTSA rather than initiated by the automaker. This is one of the two types of severe recalls into which the authors separate their dependent variable, since the determinants of the two types differ substantially.

variable_name: number of pages in recall technical reports
description: The number of pages in the technical report issued by the company for each recall campaign, used as an indicator of the depth of analysis and the willingness of the organization to change, and of the knowledge retained in the organization. The authors also compare whether each recall problem was eventually solved, treating unsolved problems as reflecting a shallower or more unsuccessful learning process.

variable_name: Cumulative prior recall experience (voluntary and involuntary)
description: Automaker's prior recall experience, entered as cumulative counts of voluntary and involuntary recalls, each over the three years before the current year, with a proportion-of-voluntary alternative. Recalls come from NHTSA recall reports.

Count of the firm's C-level executive positions (e.g., CEO, COO, CFO), which the authors classified as managerial. All C-level positions were combined into one group. The number of such positions is used as an indicator of the degree to which managerial capabilities are present within the firm.

variable_name: No. of managerial EVP, SVP, VP positions
description: Count of executive positions at the executive vice president, senior vice president and vice president level that the authors classified as managerial because they carry general management duties. This group is the second of the three position levels used to group the capability measures.

variable_name: No. of managerial positions below VP
description: Count of managerial executive positions below the vice president level, the 'below VP' group. The authors state that the below VP group included directors and lower-level executive positions.

variable_name: No. of functional EVP, SVP, VP positions
description: Count of executive positions at the executive vice president, senior vice president and vice president level that the authors classified as functional, that is, positions with specific operational duties rather than general management duties. The existence of a larger number of functional executive positions indicates a firm with more established functional processes or routines.

variable_name: No. of functional positions below VP
description: Count of functional executive positions below the vice president level, the 'below VP' group. This group included directors and lower-level executive positions.

variable_name: Dependent variable: exit by acquisition versus dissolution
description: Dichotomous variable recording whether each sample firm exited by acquisition or by dissolution during 2001. Each of the 172 firms in the sample was either acquired or dissolved: 90 exited by dissolution and 82 exited by acquisition during 2001. Higher values correspond to exit by acquisition rather than by dissolution, so positive coefficients indicate a greater likelihood of an acquisition exit.
Number of years that a firm existed, beginning with the year of founding and ending in the year the firm exited, whether by dissolution or acquisition. The median age in the sample is three years.

Annual firm revenue in millions of dollars, used as the measure of firm size. The authors state that annual sales represented the more relevant measure of capabilities because the presence of organizational processes that help produce revenue was their central concern. The median annual sales revenue in the sample is $10 million.

variable_name: NC AD, CNC AD, CCT AD, MIC AD
description: Indicator variables marking whether a firm adopted each of the four radical manufacturing technologies (coated carbide tools and tips, numerically controlled machine tools, computerized numerically controlled machine tools, and microprocessors for production), regardless of what other technologies it may also have adopted. Adoption dates for the four technologies come from the 1981 and 1986 industry surveys. Table 2 reports the impact of adopting each technology in isolation, when it was the only technology adopted by a firm.

The duration time for firm i is viewed as a random variable with probability density f(t) and cumulative distribution function F(t); the hazard rate h(t) = f(t)/(1 - F(t)) is the conditional probability of the event of interest (mortality). The establishment date of each firm, including firms established prior to 1900, and the closure date, if the event occurred between 1981 and 1986, provide the survival times.

variable_name: NC t, CNC t, CCT t, MIC t
description: For each of the four technologies, the number of years elapsed since the technology was first adopted. The variables therefore indicate the time elapsed since first adoption of the respective technology, so that a larger value reflects an earlier adoption.

variable_name: NC t*, CNC t*, CCT t*, MIC t*
description: Indicator variables for whether or not the firm adopted the technology prior to t*, the inflection point (point of maximum penetration) of that technology's estimated Bass diffusion curve. The inflection points were obtained by calibrating the Bass model to each of the four technologies using adoption data from the inception of each technology.

Magnitude refers to the variety of technologies in the manufacturing technology portfolio of each firm and is captured by whether a firm had adopted any one kind of technology (NC or CNC or CCT or MIC, referred to as T1), any two (NC and CNC or NC and MIC etc., referred to as T2), any three (T3), or any four (T4).

Indicator variables were constructed for all possible combinations of bundling the four technologies: six bundles of two technologies, four bundles of three technologies and one bundle of all four technologies (which corresponds exactly to T4). This approach is described as a search for underlying 'technology ladders' without an a priori assumed hierarchy.

Counting all citations made in a firm's new patents in a certain year that cited the firm's previous patents, then dividing this by the total number of citations made in all of the firm's new patents in that year. Because the unit of analysis was the firm, the patents and their citation counts were aggregated to the firm level. The higher the percentage of such internal accumulation, the more likely the firm's innovative knowledge is firm-specific.
time_window: patent citation data for 1975 to 2002; firm-year

description: A weighted count measure equal to the number of prior self-citations made (adjusted by firm size) multiplied by the extent to which the prior self-cited patents are subsequently cited by the focal firm. The weight takes into account the firm-specificity of the firm's prior patented knowledge: if the firm's prior patents are also widely cited by other firms, the weight is rather small and the count of self-citations made is discounted. The weight is added to take into account the firm-specificity of the firm's prior patented knowledge.
time_window: patent citation data for 1975 to 2002; firm-year

description: Measured in terms of the percentage of beneficial ownership of the firm's common stock held by employees as a collective. Data were extracted from the EDGAR database; the SEC requires every registered firm to file a definitive proxy statement (DEF14-A) annually, which discloses the beneficial ownership of common stock holdings in excess of five percent. For firms in which employees do not hold at least five percent collectively, this information is not reported and was thus coded as zero.

Based on the 'employee relations' dimension of the KLD data, which rates each company's strengths and concerns. A firm's total number of 'concerns' was subtracted from its number of 'strengths' to arrive at a net score. The 'cash profit-sharing' item was excluded from the list, as it is a financial-based governance mechanism; the remaining items take into consideration long-term employee well-being.

Tobin's Q was employed to capture each firm's economic performance, as it reflects the market's expectations of the firm's future growth and profit potential. It was approximated using the market-to-book ratio, where the market value numerator was the year-end market value of the firm's common stock plus the book value of its preferred stock and debt, and the book value denominator was the year-end total assets figure. A log transformation of the proxy of Tobin's Q was conducted so as to be consistent with the statistical model.

Firm size was proxied by the natural logarithm of the total number of employees in a firm. It was controlled for in the equations with employee stock ownership and firm-employee relationships as dependent variables, and entered the performance equation also as a three-way interaction with employee stock ownership and firm-specific knowledge.

Negative news is measured with answers to several multiple-choice questions of the CDP survey, coded to capture the degree to which the firm fails to implement the governance mechanisms and actions that the CDP desires. NoProcess equals 1 when the firm reports that it does not integrate climate change into its business strategy; NoTarget equals 1 when the firm reports not having an emissions reduction target; NoIncentives equals 1 for firms that indicate they do not have incentives for managers to reduce environmental impact; No/LowerResponsible equals 1 when no one or a lower-level manager is responsible for climate change, the latter two standardized options being grouped together. Governance is an aggregate count from 0 to 4 of the governance mechanisms the firm does have in place (coded on the opposite scale of the lack indicators), and #Actions is the number of GHG emissions-reducing actions the firm reports.

The fog index is computed from the raw text of the firm's free-text answer to the CDP survey follow-up question on how (or why not) climate change is integrated into its business strategy, using the Lingua::EN:Fathom package of the Perl language. It captures text complexity as a function of syllables per word and words per sentence, and its value indicates the number of years of formal education a reader of average intelligence would need to read the text once and understand the meaning; complex words are defined as words with three or more syllables. The formula itself is not recoverable from the extractable text of the paper. The dependent variable in the obfuscation analysis is the natural log of the fog index, and the number of words in the response is controlled for to separate obfuscation from text length.

The CDP disclosure score is a rating between 0 and 100 assessing the completeness of each survey response. Points are awarded for the comprehensiveness of the respondent's answers to each survey question, between zero and the maximum possible for that question, with the maximum varying by question importance; for text-based responses the answer is judged by how many topics from a predetermined set are discussed. Points are assessed based on whether the firm answered the question or provided a specific piece of information, not on the content of the response. The total number of points awarded for all questions is divided by the maximum total points possible and multiplied by 100.

CDP summarizes the survey responses of each firm with a performance score, a letter grade from A to E, which the authors code from 5 to 1 (A equals 5). The score assesses the level of action, as reported by the company, on climate change mitigation, adaptation and transparency, awarding performance points for evidence of actions considered to contribute to climate change mitigation, adaptation and transparency. The level of GHG emissions reported in the survey response is not taken into account in the assessment.

The firm's domain-specific reputation is measured with the prior year performance score rating of the firm, which is based entirely on the performance criteria dictated by the CDP and thus captures the firm's reputation vis-a-vis the CDP. The sample is split according to this prior year performance score to compare high and low reputation firms.

Manipulated in the vignette at a high or low level of support by parents for the law. The manipulation contained information indicating the support or opposition of the law by both the parent advisory committee at the specific childcare center and by Boink, the national parent association for the Dutch childcare field. In the high support condition parents considered the new law appropriate and acceptable; in the low support condition they considered it inappropriate and unacceptable.

Manipulated in the vignette at a high or low level of support by organization members for the mandated practice. The vignette described the former way of working as either similar to or radically different from the way of working required by the new law, the norms and interests of the employees, and the degree to which childcare workers are able to acquire the requested skills (quite easily vs. with much difficulty).

Measured directly by asking respondents to mark on a five-year time scale when they would comply with the new law, changing their practices and installing the technology, given that inspection and enforcement would begin in five years. A five-year transition period was used to allow for variation in response.

The combination of the two manipulated variables (support of a powerful external constituent and support of organization members) yields four conditions, grouped into three levels of institutional complexity: low complexity (both supportive), moderate complexity (either powerful external constituents or organization members oppose the practice), and high complexity (both oppose the practice).

Interview data segments referring to anticipated actions were marked with a master 'response' code and then coded for particular actions and, where possible, their targets. Active responses were separated into accommodative responses (including neutralizing and partial compliance) and resistant responses (including stimulating opposition, fighting, and exiting), and a delaying category (waiting to see how the situation unfolded). The number and proportion of responses of each type were counted per condition.
time_window: responses up to and including compliance

variable_name: Frequency of R&D investments (never, start, stop, vary, or always invest)
description: Firms are classified into five mutually exclusive types by their R&D expenditures over the period 1990-2002. Firms are classified as never investing when they do not have positive R&D expenditures in the period, and as always investing when they have positive R&D expenditures for every year in the period. Firms that sometimes invest have positive expenditures in some years and zero in others; start investing means zero expenditures at the beginning of the period followed by positive expenditures continuously until the end; stop investing means positive expenditures continuously at the beginning followed by zero until the end; vary investing means positive expenditures in some years, zero in others, and positive again.
scale: five mutually exclusive categories: never, always, start, stop, vary

description: Measured as the percentage of employees with more than a secondary education. It is one of the two internal knowledge resources in the model. All independent variables are lagged one year relative to the frequency of R&D investments.
Measured by the natural logarithm of free cash flow. It is the second internal knowledge resource in the model, and is lagged one year relative to the frequency of R&D investments.
Measured by the percentage of sales sold to the top three customers. It is one of three external knowledge resources in the model, and is lagged one year relative to the frequency of R&D investments.

Measured by the percentage of inputs purchased from the top three suppliers. It is one of three external knowledge resources in the model, and is lagged one year relative to the frequency of R&D investments.

variable_name: Tight relationship with a parent firm
description: Measured by the percentage of a firm's capital that is owned by another local or foreign company. It is one of three external knowledge resources in the model, and is lagged one year relative to the frequency of R&D investments.

Binary indicator that takes the value of one if a respondent was in a country where the central bank implemented regulatory reforms allowing nonbanks to launch mobile money platforms in 2015 or 2016, and zero otherwise. The authors chose these reforms because they would be expected to increase mobile money platform penetration, and hand-collected the reform data from GSMA Mobile Money Regulatory Index Reports and central bank websites.

variable_name: Borrowed from a formal financial institution
description: Binary variable coded as one if a respondent borrowed money from a formal financial institution (e.g., commercial bank, credit union, MFI) in the past year and zero otherwise, as applicable in the country where the survey was conducted. It enables comparison of rates of financial inclusion prereform and postreform.
time_window: past year before the 2014 and 2017 survey waves

description: Binary indicator of whether respondents reported having a mobile money account. The authors report that respondents were more likely to have mobile money accounts after the reforms compared with before.

Glassdoor.com has direct evaluations of CEOs into three categories: approval, indifferent, and disapproval. The authors coded disapproval as 1, indifferent as 2, and approval as 3, so that a higher value indicates a higher level of approval, and then calculated employee approval of the CEO in each firm-year as the mean of current employees' evaluations of the firm's CEO during the year. Only data provided by current employees were kept, and only firm-years with inputs from at least 60 current employees were retained. Firm-years in which CEO succession occurred were dropped so that the data were about the current CEO.

A dummy variable coded as 1 if the CEO was dismissed during the year, and 0 otherwise. Information on CEO dismissals from 2011 to 2016 was obtained from the extended dataset originally compiled by Peters and Wagner (2014), and dismissals in 2017 and 2018 were identified following the same procedure by searching Factiva news announcements of each CEO turnover. A turnover instance was classified as dismissal when the news reported the departing CEO was fired, forced out, or resigned under pressure, or under specified conditions of age and early retirement. Turnover caused by mergers and acquisitions was excluded.

A composite of two variables. The first is industry adjusted return on assets (ROA), calculated as firm ROA (net income divided by total assets) minus the median ROA of all the other firms in the firm's primary industry at the two-digit SIC level. The second is industry adjusted returns to shareholders, calculated as the firm's annual returns to shareholders minus the median annual returns of all the other firms in the firm's primary industry at the two-digit SIC level. These two variables were standardized and then added together to create the composite measure of firm performance.

Analysts' recommendations of a firm's stock are recorded on a 5-point scale: 1 = 'Strong Buy,' 2 = 'Buy,' 3 = 'Hold,' 4 = 'Underperform,' and 5 = 'Sell.' Because 'underperform' and 'sell' are considered negative recommendations, the number of 'underperform' and 'sell' recommendations was used to calculate negative recommendations as a percentage of the total number of recommendations made by all analysts who covered the firm in each month, and the monthly percentages were then averaged for each year. The average was weighted by the number of analysts who made monthly recommendations for each firm, so a higher value indicates more negative analyst recommendations.
time_window: year t-1; monthly recommendations averaged for each year

description: A composite of six standardized variables: (a) CEO duality, coded 1 if the CEO was also the chairperson of the board and 0 otherwise; (b) the number of outside boards on which the CEO serves relative to the average number of outside boards on which each director serves; (c) the number of titles that the CEO holds within the firm; (d) CEO ownership relative to directors, calculated as the percentage of common shares owned by the CEO divided by the average percentage of shares owned by independent directors; (e) board independence, calculated as the number of directors who are full-time employees of the firm divided by the total number of directors on the board; and (f) the percentage of outsiders appointed after the CEO, calculated by the number of outside directors appointed during the focal CEO's tenure divided by the total number of outside directors. The sum of these six variables' standardized scores forms the composite measure of CEO power.

Number of VC firms that exited at time t−1, were located in the same geographical state as the focal VC firm, and had the same investment focus as given by VentureXpert (early-stage, late-stage, or balanced). Prior exits are counted in one-year windows.
Count of all VC firms that entered the VC market at time t−1 and shared the geographical state and investment focus of the focal firm. Prior entries are counted in one-year windows.

Last-five-year rolling standard deviation in firm performance, where firm performance is measured by the annual cumulated number of the firm's ventures that ended in an IPO divided by the cumulated number of ventures in its portfolio. Firm volatility is lagged by one year.
time_window: last five years; lagged one year

description: Annual standard deviation in the daily value-weighted excess return on the NASDAQ market portfolio. Excess return is calculated relative to the daily risk-free rate. Market volatility is lagged by one year.

Constructed as the absolute difference between exits and entries divided by the sum of exits and entries; the absolute difference in the numerator captures the magnitude of inconsistency and the sum in the denominator accounts for the amount of available information. The term is multiplied by −1 so that values of the variable increase as information inconsistency increases.

Dummy variable that takes on the value of 1 if the focal VC firm exits at time t (the exit year) and 0 prior to that date. Firms classified as defunct or inactive at the end of the observation window were coded as exits, and firms classified as actively seeking new investments were coded as active. The exit year was coded as the year following the firm's year of last investment.
Percentage of the SBU manager's total pay that comes from fixed salary, self-reported by the manager.
Percentage of incentive pay (non-salary) based upon standards relative to prior-year performance, versus future performance.
Percentage of incentive pay based upon growth standards, versus profitability standards.
Percentage of incentive pay based upon long-term performance, versus short-term performance.

Managers evaluated their SBU's overall marketing expenditures relative to competitors and the industry average on a seven-point scale whose mid-point represents the industry average. The variable served as a dependent variable in the log-linear regressions pooled across industry sectors.
scale: seven-point scale with mid-point representing the industry average

description: Managers evaluated their SBU's advertising expenditures relative to competitors and the industry average on a seven-point scale whose mid-point represents the industry average. It was used as a dependent variable in the log-linear regressions.
scale: seven-point scale with mid-point representing the industry average

description: Managers evaluated their SBU's expenditures on sales personnel relative to competitors and the industry average on a seven-point scale whose mid-point represents the industry average. It was used as a dependent variable in the log-linear regressions.
scale: seven-point scale with mid-point representing the industry average

description: Managers evaluated their SBU's product R&D expenditures relative to competitors and the industry average on a seven-point scale whose mid-point represents the industry average. It was used as a dependent variable in the log-linear regressions.
scale: seven-point scale with mid-point representing the industry average

description: Managers evaluated their SBU's process R&D expenditures relative to competitors and the industry average on a seven-point scale whose mid-point represents the industry average. It was used as a dependent variable in the log-linear regressions.
scale: seven-point scale with mid-point representing the industry average

description: Created by the ratio of the responses on two questions: the number of products introduced by the firm over the past three years, and how many products were introduced by the industry over the past three years.

Created by the ratio of the responses on two questions: the respondent's evaluation of the frequency in the previous three years of 'major' technological advances for the firm and for the industry, respectively.

Managers' assessment of the product's or technology's overall quality relative to competitors and the industry average on a seven-point scale whose mid-point represents the industry average. It was used as a dependent variable in the log-linear regressions.
scale: seven-point scale with mid-point representing the industry average

description: Managers' rating of the degree of product line diversification of their SBU relative to competitors and the industry average on a seven-point scale whose mid-point represents the industry average. It was used as a dependent variable in the log-linear regressions.
scale: seven-point scale with mid-point representing the industry average

description: Managers' rating of capital equipment expenditures relative to competitors and the industry average on a seven-point scale whose mid-point represents the industry average. It was used as a dependent variable in the log-linear regressions.
scale: seven-point scale with mid-point representing the industry average

description: Managers' rating of employee training expenditures relative to competitors and the industry average on a seven-point scale whose mid-point represents the industry average. It was used as a dependent variable in the log-linear regressions.
scale: seven-point scale with mid-point representing the industry average

description: Factor score from a nine-item centralization scale on which respondents evaluated the degree that various decisions were delegated to lower levels in the organization, measured with a seven-point Likert scale. Principal-components factor analysis with varimax rotation produced two factors with eigenvalues above 1.0; the first combined the centralization of capital investment, budgeting, management personnel, and pricing/marketing decisions.
scale: seven-point Likert items combined into a factor score

description: Second factor from the same nine-item centralization scale, combining the centralization of R&D-related decisions; items were measured on a seven-point Likert scale and factor-analyzed with SPSS principal-components and varimax rotation.
scale: seven-point Likert items combined into a factor score

description: Factor 1 from a 10-item formality scale on which respondents evaluated how formalized certain descriptions and procedures were, for top management activities and lower management activities separately, using a seven-point Likert scale. Factor analysis with varimax rotation produced two factors with eigenvalues above 1.0; PROC FORM combined elements of procedural formality and was the formality measure used in this study, while a document description formality factor was not used.
scale: seven-point Likert items combined into a factor score

description: SBU size, in terms of employees, obtained from the respondent. The median SBU in the sample had 675 employees, ranging from a low of 125 to a high of 7000.

Indicates a firm's governance choice for feedstock procurement, technology development, bioethanol marketing and distribution, or coproduct marketing and distribution (1 = internalization; 0 = external development). Information on boundary choices at founding was collected from a firm's first filed 10-K (or 10-KSB), which has required sections for each of the four complementary activities, and was checked against the firms' websites and industry publications to outline whether these activities were conducted in-house or externally sourced.

Captures transaction hazards for each activity that endure throughout the industry's life, based on six industry experts' responses to survey questions about perceived frequency and uncertainty for a typical bioethanol producer. Each expert assigned a value from 1 (low) to 5 (high) for each activity, the responses were averaged for frequency and for uncertainty separately, and the measure for enduring transaction hazards is the sum of these two averages for each value chain activity.
scale: 1 (low) to 5 (high) for each of frequency and uncertainty; the measure is the sum of the two averages

description: The year in which a firm started bioethanol production; for a firm with more than one plant, the founding year of its first operating plant, or the earliest available year was used. The authors subtracted 1977 from the chronological year of entry so that 1 represents the earliest entry year in the sample. The measure captures the effect of transient transaction hazards, because industry experts agreed asset specificity had reduced over time.

Indicates whether a firm or its founder had pre-entry experience related to a given ethanol value chain activity (1 = related pre-entry experience; 0 = no related experience). Coding relied on detailed information about whether a firm or founder had prior experience in handling grains (e.g., grain transportation, merchandizing, or trading), in research and development activities related to ethanol production, in fuel sales, transportation, or storage, and in storage and transportation of agricultural processed goods. For diversifying entrants the authors checked what businesses they had operated in prior to entry; for start-ups they ascertained the pre-entry work experience of the primary founders and accounted for all founders' experience.
scale: 1 = related pre-entry experience; 0 = no related experience

description: A dichotomous measure (1 = firm was in another industry prior to bioethanol industry entry; 0 = firm was founded as a bioethanol start-up). Joint ventures, which represent a hybrid organization structure between diversifying entrants and start-ups, were classified as diversifying entrants, given that they could benefit from their parents' firm-level experience and transfer of routines.

A count variable capturing the number of autonomous subsidiary names a focal fashion house possesses in a given year. Semantic autonomy is instantiated when there is not a single word overlapping between the names of the parent and its subsidiary. Coding is cumulative and sticky: a fashion house founded in 2000 that launched its first two autonomous subsidiaries in 2003 and a third in 2007 shows 0 for 2000-2003, 2 for 2004-2007 and 3 for 2008 and beyond, unless a subsidiary was discontinued.
scale: count; highest number in the dataset is 3 and the lowest 0

description: A count variable capturing the number of seeded subsidiary names a focal fashion house possesses in a given year. Semantic seeding occurs when there is at least one word shared between the names of the parent and its subsidiary; the authors did not differentiate by the number or proportion of words shared, treating, for example, Class Roberto Cavalli and Just Cavalli equally. A fashion house with one seeding move in 1985 and two in 2000 would show 1 for 1998-2000 and 3 for 2001 and beyond.
scale: count; highest number in the dataset is 8 and the lowest 0

description: At the end of each fashion season Journal du Textile asks about 70 industrial buyers from world-renowned fashion retailers and distributors to evaluate the season's Fashion Week participants based on their showcased main collections. Buyers are instructed to assign creativity points independently, using the collection's originality and salability as two evaluation criteria, with points ranging from 0 to 20. Journal du Textile compiles the total points in descending order and publishes the season's creativity rankings; the authors averaged the creativity points received by each fashion house, giving a theoretical range of 0 to 20.
time_window: captured after the independent variables to account for the time lag between the Fashion Weeks and the assignment of creativity points

description: The extent of media coverage the focal parent had received in the year leading up to each Fashion Week. Using Factiva, the authors gathered data on the number of articles that referred to the parent in each single year, in 25 languages. The variable was log-transformed to test the interaction effects.
time_window: the year leading up to each Fashion Week

description: Across major fashion trade magazines and newspapers, the authors averaged the number of articles in which the parent's name co-appeared with its autonomous subsidiary name or names, averaging at the level of the fashion house when there was more than one autonomous subsidiary. Two counting approaches were tried: co-appearance within a five-word window or anywhere within the article; the authors chose the less restrictive one for a more conservative test, with results unchanged. Factiva was used to gather the data in 25 languages, and the variable was log-transformed because the data were highly skewed.

Whenever a new semantic move was made, the authors computed the number of years that had passed since the parent's last adoption of the same name choice (autonomy or seeding). For autonomy, this is the number of years since the parent's last autonomy move; if it was the first time such a move was made, the time elapsed since the founding year of the fashion house.

Whenever a new semantic move was made, the authors computed the number of years that had passed since the parent's last adoption of the same name choice (autonomy or seeding). For seeding, this is the number of years since the parent's last seeding move; if it was the first time such a move was made, the time elapsed since the founding year of the fashion house.

Coded 1 when participant i posted one or more reply messages to participant j's question k, and 0 otherwise. The authors consider knowledge shared if the provider posted at least one reply to the seeker's question, so the variable captures actual knowledge-sharing actions. To verify that reply messages were answers, 200 questions were randomly sampled and the replies examined; among the 367 answers to these questions only a very small number (1%) were follow-up questions.
time_window: constructed using data available only after the focal question was posted

description: Coded as 1 if knowledge provider i's office is located in the same city as the corresponding seeker j's office and 0 otherwise. It is built from the office location disclosed in the publicly available user profile. Participants were located in 73 cities in five countries and about 35% of the dyads were colocated.
time_window: constructed based on data available before a focal question was posted

description: Measured based on job titles and coded as 1 if knowledge provider i and seeker j are in the same hierarchical level and 0 otherwise. Because the organization's hierarchy is structured approximately in three levels, participants were categorized into three groups (high, middle, and low): job titles containing words such as chief, manager, senior, principal, chairman, or director were categorized as high; titles with assistant, junior, or trainee as low; and remaining job titles as middle.
time_window: constructed based on data available before a focal question was posted

description: Each participant's expertise profile is a 114-dimensional vector whose elements are the numbers of answers the participant offered in each of the 114 prespecified topic areas up to the point question k is posted. ExpertiseSim_ijk is computed as the cosine similarity of the expertise profile vectors of provider i and seeker j, which determines whether the two vectors point in the same direction by calculating the cosine angle of the two vectors. The resulting similarity ranges from 0 to 1: a value of 0 means the two participants do not have any common expertise and 1 means they have exactly the same expertise sets. The formal equation for the measure is not readable in the available text.
time_window: profiles accumulated up to the point question k is posted

description: Measured by counting knowledge provider i's total number of answer-posting and question-posting activities until question k is posted, which captures the provider's cumulative opportunities to observe other participants' knowledge-sharing activities in the online knowledge community. The variable is log-transformed to adjust for a skewed distribution.
time_window: cumulative up to the point question k is posted

description: Measured by counting the number of answers provided by knowledge seeker j until the knowledge seeker posts question k, capturing how actively the seeker was sharing knowledge in the online knowledge community. The variable is log-transformed to adjust for a skewed distribution.
time_window: cumulative up to the point question k is posted

description: Dummy indicating whether a given firm launching a new aircraft is doing so as the single prime contractor (alliance = 0) or by sharing the prime contractorship with one or several other industry incumbents (alliance = 1). Project classification is based on whether the aircraft project was listed under one or more prime contractors in Jane's reports.

Estimated from product functional attributes as the logarithm of the aircraft's maximum speed (in km/h) multiplied by its range (in km) and takeoff weight (in kg), as reported by Jane's and DMS Forecast. Such indicators have been frequently used in other studies on the aircraft industry.

Captured with the number of aircraft that the firm had previously developed as a prime contractor in the same product domain as the focal project, the domains being fighter aircraft, jet transport aircraft, propeller aircraft, or helicopters.
Measured by the number of past horizontal alliances in the same product domain prior to the focal prototype first flight.
time_window: prior to the focal prototype first flight

description: Inertia was measured as the number of previous relationships between bank i and bank j, using two variables: N_i-j is the number of times in the past bank i was the lead manager for an IPO for which bank j was a co-lead manager, and N_j-i is the number of times in the past bank j was the lead manager for an IPO for which bank i was a co-lead manager. The inertia variables were weighted so that more recent past partnerships had more influence than partnerships occurring farther back in time.
time_window: January 1, 1994, to one day before the IPO event under observation

description: The interaction between N_i-j and N_j-i was employed to operationalize the reciprocity hypothesis, capturing the conditional nature of reciprocity as well as the magnitude of the two parties' past exchanges. The product grows larger as the number of exchanges between i and j increases, and the interaction captures the notion that, given a fixed level of N_i-j, bank i is more likely to choose bank j when the level of N_j-i is high.
time_window: January 1, 1994, to one day before the IPO event under observation

description: The measure compared the midpoint of the filing price range in the primary prospectus with the final offer price: partnership outcome was calculated as the IPO price less the average filing price divided by the average filing price. Because each partner could have been either lead or co-lead manager in past ties, two indexes were used: partnership outcome_i-j was the average partnership outcome of all the IPO deals in which bank i was the lead manager and bank j was a co-lead manager, and partnership outcome_j-i was the average partnership outcome of the IPO deals in which bank j was the lead manager and bank i was a co-lead manager.
time_window: past IPO deals within the observation window (January 1, 1994, to one day before the IPO event)

description: For a given IPO event under observation, bank j's experience in the context of this IPO event was measured by counting the number of previous IPO events in the same industry for which bank j was a member of the underwriting syndicate. Industries were categorized according to each stock exchange's classification scheme, as required by the SEC.
time_window: within the observation window preceding the IPO event
