description: A dichotomous measure recording whether bank i entered into an alliance with bank j for an IPO event. The risk set included only partners with whom bank i had formed an alliance before the observation date, either as lead or co-lead manager, and excluded previously unconnected banks.

An accounting beta estimated for each business unit from an operational definition of the CAPM expressed in terms of risk premium. The regression relates a business unit's annual ROI to the long-term U.S. government bond rate and to the average ROI of all PIMS business units for the year; the formula block for this equation is not readable, but the authors list its terms in prose. Least-squares estimates are then adjusted with empirical Bayes (Stein) procedures that shrink each estimate toward the weighted sample mean, which the authors expected to lower mean square error.
time_window: annual observations, 1970-83; 5 to 13 annual observations per business

description: The standard error of the residual from the equation used to estimate accounting beta, that is, the part of a business unit's ROI variation not explained by the average ROI of all PIMS business units. It serves as the estimate of the unsystematic risk of the SBU.
time_window: annual observations, 1970-83; 5 to 13 annual observations per business

description: Annual return on investment of a business unit, reported by businesses on a standardized form along with items from annual balance sheets and income statements. It is measured as the deviation of ROI from the long-term U.S. government bond rate for that year, a transformation the authors used to induce stationarity in the series and justify pooling the time series and cross-sectional data.

A constructed scale measuring the opinion of the buyer about the supplier compared with the best alternative supplier for this commodity, based on three items that reflect the three elements that define interorganizational trust. Each question used a seven-point Likert scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree. Constructed variables were calculated by standardizing the items and calculating the average of the items; the Cronbach's alpha coefficient for the three-item battery was 0.80.
scale: three seven-point Likert items, averaged after standardizing

description: Identifies how an exchange to procure a component was organized, using a definition of each category provided to respondents. Make comprises exchanges with a division of the respondent's own company, ally exchanges characterized by long-term complex contracts, and buy exchanges characterized by short-term (a year or less) contracts and competitive bidding. MODE was an ordered categorical variable, coded zero for buy, one for ally, and two for make.

A constructed scale measuring the opinion of the buyer about the supplier compared with the best alternative supplier for this commodity. Exploratory factor analysis of 13 performance questions produced a first factor onto which the first 10 variables loaded; the first 10 questions reflected the respondent's view of how attractive a supplier was compared with the best alternative supplier for the commodity (1, much less attractive; 7, much more attractive). Constructed variables were calculated by standardizing the items and calculating the average of the items; Cronbach's alpha for the battery of 10 items was 0.93.
scale: ten seven-point items, averaged after standardizing

description: A constructed scale of three questions about the frequency of buyer-supplier disagreement and the difficulty of negotiations over sharing the financial burden of engineering change requests and raw material cost increases (1, fairly easy, to 7, very difficult). Higher levels of this construct equate to higher levels of conflict; Cronbach's alpha for the battery was 0.78.
scale: three seven-point items, averaged after standardizing

description: A single item measuring a buyer's agreement that the supplier has made significant investments in terms of equipment, facilities, and engineering designed specifically to meet the buyer's supply requirement for the commodity. Responses were on a seven-point scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1, strongly disagree, to 7, strongly agree)

description: A single item measuring the buyer's agreement that the buyer's company has made significant investments in tooling and equipment that are specific to its relationship with the supplier. Responses were on a seven-point scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree. It was not combined with Supplier Asset Specificity because it may signal a credible commitment in response to a supplier's specific investments.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1, strongly disagree, to 7, strongly agree)

description: An ordered categorical measure of the extent to which an assembler used a focal component, coded companywide (0), in more than one platform (1), in one platform (2), in one model (3), or in one trim line (4). Components used over multiple platforms are likely to be standardized, whereas components with a single use are more likely to require cospecialization, so higher levels corresponded to higher degrees of cospecialization.

The formalization of faculty councils and their integration into the universities' structures were used to measure the degree of formal power possessed by challengers whose interest was to preserve the direct voting system. If a university lacked a faculty council, this was coded as 0. If a university had a faculty council that was not a formal part of the university despite its fully legitimized standing after it had adopted a direct voting system, this was coded as 1. If the faculty council was partially formalized as a formal member of the 'assessment committee' in a university, this was coded as 2. Finally, if the faculty council was fully formalized as an official entity called a 'decision committee' in a university, this was coded as 3.

Measured by considering whether those incumbents who were committed to protecting their interests against challengers persisted after the initial replacement of the traditional appointment system in a university. The degree of role commitment on the incumbents' side was largely determined by the university's ownership structure, classified into four categories: government owned, religious group owned, corporation owned, and family owned. Among these, family-owned universities are expected to have stronger commitment to the political role of incumbents; thus, a family-owned university was coded as 1, and otherwise as 0.

Measured in terms of whether or not incumbents employed contentious repression tactics as a form of countermovement that brought about open confrontation with challengers. Content analyses of major nationwide daily Korean newspapers were used to identify open confrontations initiated by incumbents, typically taking the form of public announcements of a university president's appointment without the agreement of professors, refusal to recognize a university president elected by professors, changes in presidential selection systems without the consent of professors, or closing the offices of faculty councils by force. If a university with a direct voting system experienced conflicts resulting from incumbents' contentious countermovement tactics the year before or during a presidential selection year, this was coded as 1 and otherwise as 0.
time_window: the year before or during a presidential selection year

description: The dependent variable was whether a given university that had initially replaced its appointment system with direct voting subsequently replaced its direct voting system with a hybrid system. The dependent variable had three possible outcomes: the maintenance of the newly adopted direct voting system (equivalent to 'no change' as a reference category), return to the traditional appointment system, or transition to a hybrid system. If a university changed its system from the direct voting system to an appointment or a hybrid system in a particular year, this was coded as 1 or 2, respectively, and otherwise as 0 for the multinomial logit analyses.

Syndicate-level measure computed as the average score of dyadic power source match, where dyadic power source match refers to power source match between any two VC firms in a syndicate. A pair counts as a match when the party with the greater ownership score (i) also has the greater status score (Sj > Si does not hold); k is the number of such pairs, divided by the number of all possible dyadic pairs in the round. The formula itself is not readable in the text.
time_window: Each investment round; time-varying, updated each calendar quarter

description: Syndicate-level measure computed as the average of dyadic ownership-dominated power source mismatch. k is the number of dyadic pairs in which a party's ownership advantage (Oi - Oj) is greater than the other's status advantage (Sj - Si), divided by the number of all possible dyadic pairs in the round. The formula itself is not readable in the text.
time_window: Each investment round; time-varying, updated each calendar quarter

description: Syndicate-level measure computed as the average of dyadic status-dominated power source mismatch. k is the number of dyadic pairs in which a party's ownership advantage (Oi - Oj) is less than the other's status advantage (Sj - Si), divided by the number of all possible dyadic pairs in the round. The formula itself is not readable in the text.
time_window: Each investment round; time-varying, updated each calendar quarter

description: Because no exiting datasets provide historical return information, the authors used time-to-IPO or mergers and acquisitions (M&A) as a proxy for the effectiveness of VC syndication. The hazard rate of a portfolio company's exit is modeled over company-quarter spells; each quarterly spell is treated as right-censored except the spell in which the company went to IPO or was acquired, and the remaining companies were treated as right-censored as of December 31, 2005. Among the 1,096 biotech companies, 256 made it to IPO and 74 were acquired by the end of 2005.
time_window: Company-quarter spells from 1976 to the end of 2005

description: Operationalized as the total number of dyadic ties among participating VC firms in the previous five years. The five-year window was used because, as Sorenson and Stuart noted, if two firms have not coinvested within a five-year period it seems unlikely that their members remain close confidants. Consistent with the status measure, familiarity was based on prior collaborations in all industries.

The count of patents that each portfolio company had prior to an investment round, used as a proxy measure of entrepreneurial performance. Patent data were obtained for 236 portfolio companies and missing values were replaced with zero because it was likely that those companies did not have a patent; a binary variable indicating the zero replacement was included. In a separate analysis using the count of patents without zero replacement the results were similar.

A participating VC firm's equity share based on its cumulative investment, ranging from 0 to 1. Following Hochberg et al. (2007), the authors used VentureXpert's estimated amount for the missing equity data and obtained 94 percent of the equity information for all the financing rounds in the sample. Other investors (e.g., banks, insurance companies, endowments) were included in computing ownership, and a dichotomous variable indicated whether the syndicate had investors that were not private VC firms.
time_window: At each investment round (cumulative investment to that round)

description: Bonacich's centrality is used to measure a VC firm's status from network matrices in which each participating VC firm is a node and coparticipation in a prior round is a tie; only private VC firms were included in the matrices and co-investment in all industries was used. To obtain the centrality score the weighting parameter beta was set equal to zero, which essentially computes degree centrality, and the venture capitalists interviewed considered the scores based on the zero value of beta more appropriate. Each VC firm's status score was divided by the sum of the status scores of all VC firms, so that it ranges from 0 to 1.
time_window: Five-year window (t - 5) for the current year t

description: Coded 1 for dyads in which both parties are located in the same one of the 10 identified regional semiconductor clusters, and 0 otherwise. Locations are taken from the city, state and zip code of each firm's headquarters reported in SDC, and the clusters were defined from Almeida and Kogut (1999) and the 1997 Economic Census. The dummy is relative to transactions where the parties do not share a cluster.

Specifies whether the particular transaction was structured as an acquisition (coded 1) or an alliance (coded 0). For alliances with more than two parties, all possible two-way combinations of the transaction partners were included.

Calculated as the Euclidean distance between the two parties' portfolios of three-digit technology classes, weighted by the number of patents in each of the technology classes, based on their patent portfolios over the most recent five-year period.

A logged sum of the two parties' citation-weighted patents over the most recent five years, used to measure the amount of the firms' knowledge-based resources. Patents are treated as a good proxy for levels of information asymmetry in opaque industries such as semiconductors.

The logged geographic distance between the firms, calculated from firm zip codes, the finest level of geographic detail available, and then multiplied by -1 so that the measure represents proximity rather than distance. Including this variable ensures that shared cluster location is not just capturing a proximity effect between the specific exchange partners.

Problem structure is a measure of the degree to which clinical knowledge and information of a particular drug compound is disseminated across firms in the industry, coded by PJB Publishers for each drug compound relative to the number of other drug compounds under development or approved within the same drug indication. It is coded 2 if there are no other drug compounds under development or approved in the same drug indication, 1 if there are one to three, and 0 if there are four or more. Higher values therefore indicate less preexisting industry knowledge about the relevant knowledge sets and their interactions, i.e., more ill-structured problems.

TA experience represents the cumulative success of prior drug development efforts by pharmaceutical firm i in therapeutic area j at time t, built from TA activity, a count of successful drug development projects for firm i in therapeutic area j in time t. The stock is depreciated by 20 percent per period so that recent experience is weighed more heavily than past experience, consistent with organizational forgetting. The specification is given in a formula that is not readable in the text.
time_window: cumulative, depreciated at 20 percent per period

description: internal development indicates whether the drug compound was insourced (coded 1) by the pharmaceutical firm or outsourced (coded 0) in part or in total to CROs. Outsourced development serves as the comparison group in the probit estimation of the organizational decision.

IND time is the logged calendar time between IND submission and NDA submission, based on the exact calendar dates when the IND application was submitted by the pharmaceutical firm to the FDA and when the corresponding NDA was submitted. The authors use this window because it is under the direct control of pharmaceutical firms, whereas the time between NDA submission and NDA approval is determined mainly by internal FDA actions. Variables that lead to shorter (longer) drug development completion times have negative (positive) coefficients in the estimation.
time_window: from IND submission to NDA submission

description: Year-specific merger or acquisition dummy variables enter the earnings equation to parameterize the relationship to an M&A, and the plant- and firm-level equations likewise include year-specific M&A dummies. The reported coefficients are those for the seven years preceding and following a transaction, and they estimate the difference between plants involved in an M&A and establishments in the same industry not involved in an M&A. 'No-data' dummies accompany them to control for measurement error and sample selection biases.
level: plant-year (also entered at the employee and firm level)
time_window: seven years before to seven years after the transaction

description: The dependent variable is the logarithm of annual earnings of individual i working in establishment e of firm f in year t. The equation also contains individual-specific factors, establishment-specific characteristics, firm-specific characteristics, and a year-specific fixed effect, and the reported coefficients are those on the M&A dummy variables in the seven years preceding and following a transaction.
time_window: annual earnings, seven years before to seven years after a transaction

description: Employment is one of the dependent variables of the plant- and firm-level equations, denoted as yijt for plant or firm i in industry j at year t. The equations relate it to labor, capital, and materials, to year-specific M&A dummies, and to 'no-data' dummies.

Mean earnings growth of employees measured from year T - 1 to T, reported separately for employees whose plants were and were not involved in an M&A during year T and by the employees' employment location afterwards.

Employee destinations and earnings growth from year T - 1 to T for employees whose plants were or were not involved in an M&A during year T. Employees are distinguished by whether they stayed in the same plant, moved elsewhere, or were no longer employed; of employees present the year before an M&A, 37.3 percent left their establishment, including 15.2 percent who were no longer employed.

variable_name: mean experience, percentage of employees with a college education, and earnings
description: Plant-level human capital outcomes are mean experience, the percentage of employees with a college education, and earnings, estimated in the plant-level equations together with 'no-data', industry, plant location, plant age, and year dummies. The authors report pre- and post-merger averages of these variables and a test of the change between the five years before and the five years after the transaction.
time_window: five years before to five years after the transaction

description: Total factor productivity is assessed from data on output and inputs, that is, labor, capital, and materials. The estimated equation uses year-specific M&A dummy variables for the years surrounding a transaction; the specification itself is not available in readable form in the text.
time_window: seven years before to seven years after the transaction

variable_name: firm profit per employee and firm market share
description: Two proxies for firm performance of acquiring firms: profit, measured as value-added per employee, and market share. The firm-level regressions include controls for firm size (total firm employment), risk (the debt/asset ratio of the firm), and R&D investment, plus 'no-data', industry, location, and year dummies.
time_window: seven years before to seven years after the transaction

description: Ownership changes are classified as full acquisitions, in which the acquirer purchases a firm consisting of multiple divisions and numerous establishments, and partial acquisitions, in which the acquirer purchases one or several plants from another company. Plant-level productivity, output, and employment results are computed separately for the two types of ownership change.
time_window: five years before to five years after the transaction

description: Number of new entrants in market j in year t, defined as a new commercial banking institution that comes into existence by way of a new charter. This definition restricts the sample to de novo entry by entrepreneurs, excluding conversions, recharters, and the addition of new banks to existing bank holding companies. The model is written with entry counts on the left-hand side and the number of incumbents on the right-hand side to allow the rate to vary with the number of incumbents.

Root mean squared error from the regression ln[(market demand t / market demand t-1) - 1] = a0 + a1 * (trend) estimated over a moving 10-year window, following the conventional approach in which risk is approximated by variability in demand. Demand is measured primarily by state personal income, used as a proxy for demand because gross state product is not available for all years; the correlation between the two for the years both were available was 99.7%. An alternative measure sums the output of all firms in a market year to capture demand directly.

Dispersion of the ex ante cost distribution of independent banks in market j in year t. Firm-year cost inefficiency estimates from the Stage 1 frontier analysis are transformed by taking their natural log and then pooled by market year to form the cost distribution for each market in each year. Potential entrants are assumed to compare themselves to other independent entrepreneurs rather than to large bank holding companies, and the cost dispersion of bank holding companies is examined as an alternative reference set.

Mean of the transformed cost inefficiency of the survivor pool in market j in year t, where the survivor pool is defined as firms that have remained in the industry for three years. Three years is used as the cutoff because it matches expert opinion about the time to reach profitability as well as results in past studies regarding the time to fail. The baseline uses the set of independent banks to construct the cost distribution, and the cost distribution of bank holding companies is examined separately.

Ratio of the number of failures to the number of incumbents in market j in year t. Failure follows the FDIC definition as the sum of 'forced mergers' and FDIC 'paid outs'; forced mergers between a failed institution and a healthier bank are the dominant form of FDIC resolution, while paid outs occur where the FDIC pays depositors for their lost deposits under FDIC insurance provisions.

Mean value of the labor price w1 for all firms in market j in year t, constructed from the input data used in the Stage 1 model. Labor price is salary divided by the number of full-time equivalent employees.

Time-varying entry cost for each market in each year. Data are pooled across all firms to define an asset growth path by regressing firm assets (physical plus financial) on age, year, and market dummies; the coefficients for the age dummies controlling for year and market are then used to de-age the assets of all firms in market j in year t.

Each firm's position in the aggregate network of joint ventures among the set of partnering firms was measured with Bonacich's eigenvector centrality scores. The combined centrality of the two firms in a dyad is the geometric mean of the two firms' scores in a given joint venture founding year, each firm's score being normalized relative to the most central firm in that year. Centrality scores were computed using UCINET 5, and the findings are robust to using the arithmetic mean. To test Hypothesis 1b, observations were split into two groups, one with and the other without prior direct ties.

Cumulative number of prior joint ventures formed between two partners until the year preceding a focal joint venture's founding. For the test of Hypothesis 1b the observations were split into two groups, one with and the other without prior direct ties at founding.
time_window: until the year preceding the focal joint venture's founding

description: Dummy variable coded 1 if one firm in the dyad had a centrality score lower than the mean and the other had centrality equal to or greater than the mean observed in the founding year, and coded 0 otherwise. Similar results were obtained when central firms were defined as those with centrality scores in the top quartile.

Number of common partners two firms shared in the evolving alliance network, measured as the number of common partners they had in the year before the observation year. This variable was interacted with the measure of positionally asymmetric dyads at founding and with competitive overlap to test Hypotheses 4 and 5.

Dummy variable set to 1 if the firms in the dyad had high technical resource overlap and high market overlap, and to 0 otherwise; overlap along each dimension was considered high if the respective score for firms in the dyad was above the sample mean. Overlap along each dimension was measured with the Euclidean distance between the firms' resource positions. Technical resource overlap used the proportion of firms' patent applications in each of 80 technological classes; market overlap was the average of geographic overlap (proportion of subsidiaries owned in each of 156 countries) and product-market overlap (proportion of sales in each of 120 market segments defined at the level of four-digit SIC codes). These measures vary between 0 (complete overlap) and the square root of 2 (no overlap) and were linearly transformed and subtracted from the square root of 2.

Dummy variable created for each dyad in each year until the year of dissolution or until 1992, whichever occurred first; it was coded 1 if the firms dissolved the joint venture in that year and 0 otherwise. Dissolutions were classified as unplanned only when the news stories indicated partners' difficulty in collaborating or an attempt by one partner to exploit a business opportunity alone; cases reflecting goal attainment or unrelated changes in the business landscape were not considered unplanned dissolution.
time_window: each year until dissolution or until 1992

description: Regional similarity is measured through language similarity because Indian regions are delineated by specific regional languages. Data on the last name, caste, religion, and regional language of about six million individuals were coded to the relative frequencies with which a particular last name mapped onto 14 regional languages. For every deal the Mahalanobis distance between the entrepreneurs' and VCs' inferred languages was computed using the 14 languages as axes in a 14-dimensional space, and the minimum distance among all entrepreneur-VC dyads was used; this distance was multiplied by minus one to generate an increasing measure of regional similarity, and winsorized beyond the extreme 1%.
time_window: the focal financing round; regional similarity at the moment of first investment for the financial returns test

description: Caste similarity was computed in the same two-step method as for regional similarity, but in a five-dimensional space made of the priest, warrior, merchant, peasant, and untouchable castes. Individuals of Christian or Muslim religion were set to missing on caste. For each deal the minimum Mahalanobis distance among all entrepreneur-VC dyads was used and multiplied by minus one to obtain an increasing measure of caste similarity, and the variable was winsorized beyond the extreme 1%.
time_window: the focal financing round; caste similarity at the moment of first investment for the financial returns test

description: Venture valuation is defined as the premoney valuation of a portfolio company at the focal round of funding and was computed in three steps. From the PAS3 form filed with the MCA the authors calculated the deal amount as the number of new shares multiplied by the price of the new share (face value plus possible premiums or discounts), and postmoney valuation as the [number of outstanding shares + the number of new shares] multiplied by the new share price. Premoney valuation is postmoney valuation minus the deal amount, and outliers were accounted for by winsorizing the variable beyond the extreme 1%.

Drawing on Bengtsson and Sensoy's (2011) conceptualization, the authors used forms MGT14 and GNL to identify changes in a focal company's Articles of Association and created three broad risk categories based on the type of financial instrument used to structure the deal (100% equity through ordinary shares; a mix of debt and equity through preference shares and convertible debt instruments; 100% debt through optionally convertible debt instruments). Each category was subdivided into four subcategories in increasing order of additional contingent cash flow rights the VC could exercise: no extra rights; one of cumulative dividend rights, redemption rights, or liquidation preferences; any two of those rights; and all three. The measure is therefore subdivided into 12 ordered categories of increasing VC protection, ranging from a low of 1 to a high of 12.

The authors identified the total amount invested by a focal VC firm into a focal company and the companies that experienced an exit event such as an IPO, trade sale, or dissolution. Using the exit valuation and the equity structure at exit (from the same PAS3 form), they computed the payoff received by each VC firm that invested in that company, and then calculated the annualized financial return, where T is the time expressed in years between the payoff and the investment date; the formula block in the text is unreadable in this payload. IRR can theoretically range from -100% to infinity. Since the variable was heavily skewed, it was shifted by 101% (to make it positive) so that its logarithm could be computed.
scale: IRR from -100% to infinity, shifted by 101% and logged
time_window: exit up to December 2016; T is the time in years between payoff and investment date

description: Deals were classified as early stage if the company is raising its first round of institutional financing, if the company is less than 5 years old, and if the capital it raised is less than USD 20 million. Deals were classified as late stage if the company is raising subsequent rounds of institutional financing and is less than 10 years old while raising capital. The dummy variable early stage is assigned the value 1 if the deal is an early-stage deal, and 0 otherwise.

The variable counts the number of VC firms in the deal that are first-time investors in the industry of the portfolio company. Venture Intelligence classifies companies into industry categories using a classification scheme that maps start-up companies into 24 fine-grained industries, and entering new industry can range from 0 to the total number of VC firms in the focal deal.
scale: count from 0 to the number of VC firms in the deal

description: Burt's (1992, p. 52) effective size measure, which represents the difference between the number of a bank's partners and the average number of ties among them, not counting their ties to the investment advisor itself. High effective size means the bank's partners have few ties to one another, so its network contains multiple structural holes. Network positions are computed from sociomatrices whose entries are the number of times two banks worked on a deal together over a two-year period, and are read for the second year of each period.
time_window: two-year moving period, position measured in the second year

description: A combined scope measure computed as a variant of the Herfindahl index over the economic sectors and the acquirer nationalities of the deals in which a bank participated. When this index approaches 1 a particular bank has a narrow scope, whereas when it approaches 0 the bank has a wide scope. Because Hypothesis 1 implies that banks develop routines over time, the measure also incorporates the bank's past experience through a discount factor, and the reported results use a discount set to the age of the experience.
time_window: from 1992 up to year t, with experience discounted by age

description: A modification of the measure of Boeker et al. (1997): dyadic multimarket contact between the focal bank and each other bank is computed from the banks' joint presence in markets, then aggregated across all of the focal bank's partners. Markets are defined both by the primary SIC codes of the targets and by the nationality of the acquirers, and the two resulting measures are averaged. Historic MMC applies a discount factor to the yearly values of multimarket contact, and the reported results use a discount set to the age of the experience.
time_window: from 1992 up to year t, with experience discounted by age

description: Freeman's (1979) betweenness measure, which captures the degree to which a bank falls between the pairs of other banks on the shortest path connecting them. The choice of betweenness centrality is predicated on the assumption that greater betweenness will be associated with greater control over information and resources and the placement of an investment bank at the core of its industry.
time_window: two-year moving period, position measured in the second year

description: The dollar value of each offering is allocated among the members of the advisory team: a deal involving only one investment bank gives that bank 100% of the offering's dollar value, and deals involving multiple banks split the value of the transaction equally among team members. Within each period the value of each bank's M&A deals is divided by the total value of M&A deals completed during this period, which provides the market share measure for each investment bank.

Using the New York Times articles collected from ProQuest, stigma intensity is modeled for every year as the ratio of negative articles to the total number of articles about nuclear power. Articles were classified as positive, negative, or neutral; all were manually coded by the first author, and two additional coders reclassified a random subsample so that a Fleiss kappa could be computed. For each year the ratio is calculated based on articles published in the previous three years; a one-year moving window was used for robustness. Media exposure and stigma intensity were made orthogonal, and the variable was lagged by one year.
time_window: three-year moving window, lagged one year

description: Following Fombrun and Shanley (1990), media exposure is a simple count variable of articles published on nuclear power within a specified time frame, built from the New York Times articles retrieved from ProQuest. Three-year moving windows were used, and the results were largely robust to using a one-year interval. Because media exposure and stigma intensity were highly correlated, the two were made orthogonal by a modified Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization procedure; the variable was lagged by one year.
time_window: three-year moving window, lagged one year

description: The extent of membership in the nuclear power generation category is defined as the ratio between the number of nuclear generating units operated by a utility and the total number of generating units (coal-, oil-, and gas-fired units, as well as nuclear units) operated by the same utility. If a unit is jointly owned by more than one electric utility, only its majority owner is considered. For each year the authors calculated the number of nuclear and nonnuclear generating units controlled by each utility and holding company.
time_window: annual, lagged one year unless otherwise specified

description: The main dependent variable is binary, taking a value of 1 if the proposed reactor project was ultimately cancelled and 0 if it was completed. Only nuclear reactor units completed or cancelled between 1970 and 2000 are included; units whose construction was completed prior to 1970 and units whose cancellation was decided by state governments or courts of law were eliminated from the sample. The last unit to be cancelled was Perry-2 in 1994 and the last completed was Watts Bar-1 in 1996.

Count of outside noncore directors serving on the focal firm's board. Outside noncore directors are defined as independent directors that do not have any business ties to the focal firm, are not former executives of the focal firm, and are not currently holding any executive titles (CEO or otherwise) at other publicly held corporations or the 500 largest private firms published by Forbes. The independent and moderating variables are computed using data extracted from Compustat, the Corporate Library, or proxy statements of the firms.
time_window: t (predictors lagged one year before the dependent variable)

description: Executive entrenchment is measured with the entrenchment index (E-index) score computed from the RiskMetrics database. One point is added for each of six takeover-defense governance provisions adopted: staggered boards, poison pills, golden parachutes, restrictions on bylaws, restrictions on charter amendments, and supermajority requirements for mergers. Hence, higher E-index scores reflect greater executive entrenchment. The E-index score of each firm is adjusted by the industry mean to control for industry effects on the dependent variable.

Mean number of ties the outside noncore directors of each firm have with other directors in the network of interlocking directorates among S&P 500 firms. A tie between two directors exists when both directors are present on the same corporate board of an S&P 500 firm. The more ties that directors have with other directors in the same network, the more embedded the directors are in the corporate elite network. UCINET 6 was used to generate the number of director ties.
time_window: t (predictors lagged one year before the dependent variable)

description: The tenure of outside noncore directors for each firm is computed as the mean tenure among outside noncore directors that serve on a firm's board.
time_window: t (predictors lagged one year before the dependent variable)

variable_name: Outside noncore director equity ownership value
description: The equity ownership of outside noncore directors is measured by first extracting the number of shares owned by these directors and then multiplying these values by the year-end stock price. The authors use the dollar value of a firm's equity instead of the more traditional measure of equity ownership percentage since they are concerned with how much wealth these directors have committed to the firm. The natural log of this variable was entered into the regression model to reduce the influence of extreme values.
time_window: t (predictors lagged one year before the dependent variable)

variable_name: Independent CEO director equity ownership value
description: The equity ownership of independent CEO directors is measured by first extracting the number of shares owned by these directors and then multiplying these values by the year-end stock price. The dollar value of a firm's equity is used rather than an ownership percentage. The natural log of this variable was entered into the regression model to reduce the influence of extreme values.
time_window: t (predictors lagged one year before the dependent variable)

description: Firm performance is computed as a firm's industry-adjusted return on equity. A firm's ROE is first expressed as net income over shareholders' equity, and the industry ROE is then deducted to arrive at a firm's performance relative to its rivals. Industry ROE is computed using two-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes.
time_window: t (predictors lagged one year before the dependent variable)

description: A nine-item survey measure of organizational identification. Six items come from Mael and Ashforth's (1992) measure of organizational identification and two items from Bergami and Bagozzi's (2000) measure, with one additional survey item added on the basis of pretest interviews; the wording of the questions was modified slightly in view of the pretest interviews. A factor analysis on the nine survey items showed that they loaded on one factor, the coefficient alpha for the scale was .87, and factor scores were estimated with the Bartlett method. The correlation between organizational identification in year t and in year t + 1 was .91.
time_window: measured in the January 2004 and January 2005 CEO surveys

description: An index combining four indicators of board independence from management via principal components analysis, justified because the indicators are causal (formative) rather than reflective. The four indicators are the portion of a firm's board composed of outside directors divided by the total number of board members, separation of the CEO and board chair positions, the portion of a firm's outside directors who were personal friends of the CEO, and the percentage of total common equity held by outside directors. Friendship ties were measured with a validated survey scale; in the primary analyses director responses were used. All four indicators loaded on the same factor with an eigenvalue greater than one.

A single construct estimated as factor scores (Bartlett method) from three indicators of firm performance: return on assets, an accounting-based measure, and the market-to-book value of equity and total stock returns, two market-based measures, all measured in year t - 1. The variable is called 'low firm performance' because it is reverse-coded, so its value increases as firm performance worsens.

CEO cash compensation comprises annual salary and bonus, and the natural log transformation of total cash compensation is used in the analyses because the distribution of this variable was skewed. Decoupling of firm performance from cash compensation is tested through the interaction between CEO organizational identification (and board independence) and low firm performance in an OLS regression predicting this outcome; the decoupling outcome of interest is not simply the level of cash compensation.
scale: natural log of total cash compensation
time_window: year t, with firm performance measured in year t-1

variable_name: CEO personal use of corporate aircraft
description: The incremental (annual) cost of a CEO's personal use of a corporate jet disclosed in the firm's proxy statement, following prior research. The variable is estimated with a two-step sample selection model that first estimates whether a firm disclosed any personal aircraft use for its CEO using binary probit analysis and then, for the subset of firms that disclosed some level of use, includes the inverse Mills ratio in a second equation estimating the cost of aircraft use. The decoupling of this perquisite from firm performance is tested through its interaction with low firm performance and CEO organizational identification.
time_window: year t, with firm performance measured in year t-1

description: A 'self-reported' objective measure of economic performance: the average 'after tax return on total assets' for the years 1975-1979. It was one of three items in the last questionnaire, which was directed only to the CEO and administered in the third phase of the research, separately from the TMT questionnaire.

A 'self-reported' objective measure of economic performance: 'total sales' at two points in time, 1975 and 1979. It came from the one-page questionnaire directed only to the CEO in the third phase of the research.

An item on the TMT questionnaire asking members to compare their firm's after tax return on total assets to 'firms of similar sales volume in your industry and region', over a time frame of 'average over the past five years'. The five-point, interval scale ranged from 5 (top 20 per cent) to 1 (lowest 20 per cent). The value of the measure for a given firm was the sum of the responses of the members of the TMT divided by the number of respondents comprising the TMT.
scale: five-point interval scale: 1 = lowest 20 per cent to 5 = top 20 per cent
time_window: average over the past five years

description: An item on the TMT questionnaire asking members to compare their firm's total sales growth to 'firms of similar sales volume in your industry and region', over a time frame of 'average over the past five years'. The five-point, interval scale ranged from 5 (top 20 per cent) to 1 (lowest 20 per cent). The value of the measure for a given firm was the sum of the responses of the members of the TMT divided by the number of respondents comprising the TMT.
scale: five-point interval scale: 1 = lowest 20 per cent to 5 = top 20 per cent
time_window: average over the past five years

description: An item on the TMT questionnaire in which members assessed their firm's overall performance/success against 'firms of similar sales volume in your industry and region', over a time frame of 'average over the past five years'. The five-point, interval scale ranged from 5 (top 20 per cent) to 1 (lowest 20 per cent). The value of the measure for a given firm was the sum of the responses of the members of the TMT divided by the number of respondents comprising the TMT.
scale: five-point interval scale: 1 = lowest 20 per cent to 5 = top 20 per cent
time_window: average over the past five years

description: An item adapted from Lawrence and Lorsch (1967) representing an overall or 'global' assessment of firm performance, asked only of the CEO in the third phase. The CEO was asked '... compared to your competitors, what per cent of ideal or optimal performance do you personally feel that your firm is achieving in your industry?'. The measure is described as implicitly incorporating aspiration levels, allowing the CEO to compare desired to actual (or perceived) results.
scale: percentage of ideal or optimal performance

variable_name: Economic performance (return on assets and sales growth)
description: Economic performance was operationalized with two indicators, return on assets and growth in sales, each measured both objectively (CEO self-reported 1975-1979 figures) and subjectively (top management team comparisons with similar firms).

Cumulative abnormal returns estimated with the event study method served as the dependent variable. The authors estimated CARs for two event windows: the three days prior to and following the acquisition announcement, and the five days prior to and following the announcement. Daily abnormal returns were computed as the portion of each acquiring firm's stock return that could not be anticipated given the return on the market and the firm's beta, with alpha and beta estimated over the period from 300 days to 61 days prior to the announcement. The daily abnormal returns were summed across the event window to arrive at individual CAR values. The text does not name the source of the stock return data.
time_window: three days prior to and following the acquisition announcement; five days prior to and following the announcement

description: The number of independent outside board members on the board. To qualify, board members may have been managers of publicly traded firms with no business links to the organization, executives of nonprofit organizations, directors serving on multiple boards with no primary employer, venture capitalists, former military officers, government officials, or academicians. The number of such board members was used in the analysis.

The percentages of the acquiring firm's shares held by outside board members who either directly owned 5 percent or more of the acquiring firm's shares or represented an organization that did so were summed to reflect the total ownership percentages held by blockholder board members.

The log form of the dollar value of outside board member ownership, exclusive of blockholder board member ownership. The dollar value was estimated by multiplying the number of shares the outside board members collectively owned by the acquiring firm's share price on the day prior to the acquisition announcement. The data were taken from individual proxy statements.
time_window: day prior to the acquisition announcement

variable_name: Outside board members with target industry experience
description: The number of acquiring firm board members who had expertise related to the industry of the target firm. A board member qualified if he or she had been a manager or board member of a firm in the same industry, defined by the target firm's primary three-digit SIC code, within the 5 years prior to the focal acquisition announcement.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal acquisition announcement

variable_name: Outside CEO board members with acquisition experience
description: A dummy variable coded 1 if the acquiring firm had a board member who had been the CEO of a publicly traded firm that completed an acquisition representing at least 10 percent of the acquiring firm's market capitalization within the 5 years preceding the focal acquisition, and 0 if not.

variable_name: Outside board members with acquisition experience
description: The number of directors on the acquiring firm's board who had been members of another board that presided over a major acquisition representing at least 10% of the acquiring firm's market capitalization during the 5 years prior to the focal acquisition.
time_window: 5 years prior to the focal acquisition

description: Binary variable equal to 1 if a firm commercialized a transgenic crop for the first time in a given year. The measure is created by confirming sales of transgenic crops that are approved for commercial release based on the USDA coordinated framework for regulation of plant biotechnology.
time_window: yearly observations from initial investment onward

description: The level of integrative capabilities is measured using the (logged) number of business segments (3-digit SIC) in which a firm was active at the time of its investment, as reported in SEC filings, firms' reports, Compustat, and LexisNexis. The number of parallel value chains that a firm has integrated may indicate its accumulated experience and ability to engage in a consistent and repeatable pattern of integration. The authors state this is an extension to the binary measure separating diversifying and de novo firms.
time_window: at the time of first technological investment (t0)

description: Related technical capabilities are measured using the (logged) number of patents applied for by a firm during the 4 years prior to its investment in related technical fields. Related technical fields are identified as the most frequent international patent classes of all non-agricultural-biotechnology backward citations of the universe of agricultural biotechnology patents; the four classes A01H, C12N, C12P, and C12Q, to which the top 75th percentile of these backward citations belong, are considered to be related fields.

A firm's core technical capabilities are measured using the (logged) number of agricultural biotechnology patents applied for by a firm during the past 4 years. Agricultural biotechnology patents are identified through content analysis of patent documents using the keywords recommended by the USDA Economic Research Services; the USDA Agricultural Biotechnology Intellectual Property project identified such patents prior to 2000 and this database was extended for the firm sample to 2010.

The study uses the (logged) number of protected plant varieties granted to a firm in the preceding 4 years to measure complementary assets. High-quality crop varieties, referred to as elite varieties or germplasm, are considered specialized complementary assets that are used as platforms for genetic modification, and access to elite varieties is also a proxy for downstream activities in seed production, marketing, and distribution. Under the Plant Variety Protection Act, plant breeders are conferred exclusive rights to their plant varieties for 20 years.
time_window: preceding 4 years (measured at t0 and at t)

description: An indicator variable that takes the value 1 if the firm about which an analyst writes a report undertakes a legacy spinoff, and 0 if the firm undertakes a non-legacy spinoff. Legacy businesses were identified using the International Directory of Company Histories and corporate annual reports and then hand-matched to the spinoff data. Of the 62 spinoffs in the sample, 11 were legacy spinoffs.

Takes the value 1 for all reports written in Period 1 by analysts who terminate coverage of a firm once it announces a spinoff (the subset of A analysts who become A2 analysts), and 0 for reports written in Period 1 by analysts who continue covering a firm after it announces a spinoff (the subset of A analysts who become A1 analysts). Period 1 is the year prior to the spinoff announcement.
time_window: Period 1 (the year prior to the spinoff announcement)

description: Takes the value 1 for all reports written in Period 2 by analysts who initiate coverage of a firm after it announces a spinoff (a B analyst), and 0 for reports written by analysts who continue their coverage of that firm from Period 1 into Period 2 (an A1 analyst). Period 2 is the period between the announcement and effective dates of the spinoff.
time_window: Period 2 (between the announcement and effective dates of the spinoff)

description: The absolute value of the difference between forecasted and actual earnings-per-share (EPS), scaled by the end-of-year stock price in which the EPS figure was realized. Higher EPS Forecast Errors indicate that an analyst is less accurate in his forecast, as the gap between forecasted and actual earnings is larger.
time_window: Period 1 for pre-spinoff forecasts and Period 2 for post-spinoff forecasts

description: Dummy that takes a value of 1 if Amazon itself offers the product in the second round, and 0 otherwise. It is the dependent variable in the logit regressions of Amazon's entry pattern, estimated on all products that were offered only by third-party sellers in the first round.

Amazon does not publish sales data for each product but provides sales ranking data for products in each category, and the authors use the logarithm of the product's sales ranking. Rankings are negatively correlated with sales, a lower ranking indicating higher sales, so a lower value of this variable indicates greater demand. Rankings for products Amazon entered in the second round are compared with those of matched control products.
time_window: first round (June 2013); compared again in the second round

description: Average customer rating of the product, computed only for products with at least one review, ranging from 1 to 5. In the regressions, instead of average product ratings the authors include dummy variables for different product rating levels, and the benchmark group consists of products with no ratings. In the impact analysis, average product ratings of affected and unaffected products are compared.
time_window: first round (June 2013); compared again in the second round

description: Price of the product, obtained from the default page Amazon displays when users search for a product, with the authors taking its logarithm. Prices are used as a predictor in the entry regressions and are also compared between treated and matched control products in the second round, where the prices of products Amazon has entered are determined by Amazon.
time_window: first round (June 2013); compared again in the second round

description: Shipping cost of the product, obtained from the default product page shown when users search for a product and logged by the authors. When Amazon offers products, their shipping fees become zero because of Amazon's free shipping programs, and second-round shipping fees are compared between affected and matched control products.
time_window: first round (June 2013); compared again in the second round

description: Dummy coded 1 if third-party product distribution is handled by Amazon (the seller uses Amazon's fulfillment service), and 0 otherwise. It is used as a predictor in the entry regressions, and, for products that continue to be offered in the second round, as the dependent variable in product-level fixed-effects models of whether affected sellers change their use of Amazon's distribution channel.

The total number of sellers that offer the product in new condition, with the authors taking its logarithm to address the skewed distribution. It is used in the entry regressions to capture both the intensity of competition and the ease of sourcing.
scale: logarithm of a count of sellers

description: Rating of the default third-party seller, typically the seller that offers the product at the lowest cost (price plus shipping cost), computed as the average of all ratings received for past transactions. Dummy variables are used for different seller rating levels, with sellers with no ratings as the benchmark group; products of sellers with ratings between 1 and 3 are dropped from estimation because no entry is observed there.

Logarithm of the total number of products offered on Amazon by each third-party seller, gathered in both rounds; for sellers with large catalogs the authors gather information on up to 40 products listed on the seller's store page. It is used in the entry regressions to capture seller size and as the dependent variable in the seller-level difference-in-differences models that examine changes in the number of products offered over the two periods.
scale: logarithm of a count of products

description: Number of answers provided by sellers per month, used to assess sellers' Amazon-specific investment. The authors count the total number of answers provided by sellers in the product page's customer question section and divide it by the number of months since the first question was posted, to account for the fact that products launched earlier are more likely to have received more answers.

Dummy assigned a value of 1 if the seller ceases to offer a product in the second round, and 0 otherwise. It is used to compare, between products affected and unaffected by Amazon's entry, the likelihood that the products are no longer offered by the same third-party sellers in the second round.
time_window: between the first and second rounds

description: 1 - Herfindahl index for company i at time t in country j, calculated as the sum of the square of the shares of the company's sales in all its portfolio niches k at time t in country j. The authors also replicate the analysis using a dummy variable equal to 1 if a firm operates in multiple niches and 0 otherwise, but prefer to maintain the continuous measure to support a full-fledged marginal effect analysis.

An increase or decrease in sales at time t + 1 in country j in niche k for a particular brand z, computed as Sales Growtht+1 = Salest+1/Salest. It is used as the dependent variable in all regressions.

For each country and year, sales by all companies classified under European Classification of Economic Activities code 4711, 'Retail sale in non-specialized stores with food and beverages', are downloaded from Bureau van Dijk Orbis. Concentration is calculated as a Herfindahl index that varies for each country and year, then transformed into a dummy variable by splitting the sample at the median value.

1 - Herfindahl index for niche k in country j at time t, generated as the sum of the squares of the market shares of all active single-niche competitors. It is transformed into a dummy by splitting the sample at the median value for each country j at time t.

Dummy variable that equals 1 if there has been a tax-rate increase in a specific alcoholic niche in a country-year, and 0 otherwise. Taxes do not necessarily affect all alcoholic beverages in a given country at the same time. All data about tax variations for alcoholic-beverage niches in the sample countries and years come from the Excise Duty Tables created by the European General Directorate of Taxation and Customs.

To gauge shelf-space reallocation decisions by a diversifier i, the authors adopt a double-proof test that determines (1) the effect of Diversification × Tax Alcohol on Sales Growth in niches affected by the tax change for a particular brand owned by a diversifier i and (2) the effect on Sales Growth for the same firm i in all other niches in its portfolio not affected by the tax change. If the diversifier experiences relatively less sales growth than single-niche companies in the affected niche and relatively more sales growth than single-niche companies in the other niches, the authors conclude that it redeployed its shelf-space resources productively.

An indicator included in the regressions of revenue expansion and retrenchment, set to 1 for segments of multi-business firms and 0 for single-business firms. It is used to compare how aggressively the two groups expand and retrench revenues.

Revenue Expansion equals Revenue Growth if Revenue Growth is positive, where Revenue Growth for segment j in year t is the change in the segment's revenues between t-1 and t divided by the segment's assets at the beginning of the period. An industry- and firm-adjusted variant, Relative Revenue Expansion, is defined the same way from Relative Revenue Growth, which subtracts the average revenue growth of single-segment firms in the same industry and then the firm's asset-weighted segment growth.

Revenue Retrenchment equals Revenue Growth if Revenue Growth is negative, where Revenue Growth for segment j in year t is the change in the segment's revenues divided by the segment's assets at the beginning of the period. Because the variable is coded as a negative growth value, more aggressive retrenchment appears as a lower (more negative) value. A relative variant is defined analogously from Relative Revenue Growth.

The descriptive comparison of revenue growth variance uses the standard deviation of revenue growth computed for multi-business firm segments and for single-business firms. Revenue growth for segment j in year t is the change in segment revenues divided by the segment's assets at the beginning of the period.

A segment-level index ranging between 0 and 1 that captures how useful a segment's human and tangible resources are in the firm's other segments: 0 indicates that a segment has no common resources with the firm's other segments and 1 implies that a segment uses the same resources as all other segments in the firm's portfolio. It is derived from federal government databases, using the 1997 BEA capital flow table on capital expenditures for 180 different asset categories to calculate similarities in the use of tangible assets across industries and BLS data on 900 different occupational profiles to calculate similarities in the use of types of human capital across industries. The value is calculated by looking within a firm at how similar a segment's tangible and human capital are to the firm's other segments and is adjusted annually as the portfolio changes.

The measure follows Rajan et al. (2000), where opportunities are approximated by the average Tobin's q ratio among single-business firms in the segment's industry. The numerator is the standard deviation of segment asset-weighted qs within a firm, so that a segment's asset endowment conditions its ability to capitalize on an opportunity and more diversity emerges when the larger segments have the better opportunities in the portfolio. The denominator standardizes diversity across firms with different mean opportunities; the underlying formula is not readable in the provided text, so the measure is described from the authors' prose.

A segment's illiquidity is approximated as the inverse of total industry long-term debt divided by total industry assets, following prior work. The logic is that industries whose resources have low salvage value have to rely on equity financing instead of debt, whereas more liquid industries can support a higher level of debt. It is measured for segments of both single- and multi-business firms and is interacted with the multi-business dummy.

VAD is essentially the extent to which firms over- or under-pursue revenues relative to investment opportunities in their segments' industries and also to the firm's own investment opportunities, where qj is industry j's median Tobin's q among single-business firms and q-bar is a firm's average q among its segments. Firms that expand into more attractive segments (qj greater than q-bar) and retrench from less attractive segments (qj less than q-bar) create more value-added with their redeployment activities. A second measure, VAD2, has similar advantages but uses the minimum q in the firm as the comparison benchmark.

variable_name: number of new OSS products announced
description: Count of new OSS products, or new versions of already launched OSS products, announced by a firm from the date of its first OSS product release until December 2003. Built from press articles reporting a product announcement, a new software release, or a software evaluation in the software sector that contain the words 'open source' or 'Linux'. Products are divided into two niches, operating systems (OPSYS) and applications (APP), and separate estimations are run for each. Used as the dependent variable in a count data model.
time_window: from the firm's first OSS product release until December 2003

description: Number of unexpired software patents granted to a given firm up to the month of the announcement of its first OSS product. Software patents are identified by applying search algorithms to the front page of the patent, searching the abstract for the strings 'computer software', 'operating system', 'computer program', 'software algorithm', 'data processing', or 'software application'. Patents data are downloaded from the USPTO database.
time_window: up to the month of the announcement of the firm's first OSS product

description: Number of unexpired hardware patents granted to a given firm up to the month of the announcement of its first OSS product. Hardware patents are identified by applying search algorithms to the front page of the patent, searching for the strings 'computer server', 'computer hardware', 'motherboard', 'peripherals', 'workstation', 'mainframe', 'disk driver', or 'area network'. Patents data are downloaded from the USPTO database.
time_window: up to the month of the announcement of the firm's first OSS product

description: Preentry number of live USPTO trademarks in software filed by a firm up to the month before its first OSS product announcement. Software trademarks are distinguished by applying to the text of the trademark description of goods and services the same search algorithms and word strings used for patents. Trademarks data are downloaded from the USPTO database.
time_window: up to the month before the firm's first OSS product announcement

description: Preentry number of live USPTO trademarks in hardware filed by a firm up to the month before its first OSS product announcement. Hardware trademarks are distinguished by applying to the text of the trademark description of goods and services the same search algorithms and word strings used for patents. Trademarks data are downloaded from the USPTO database.
time_window: up to the month before the firm's first OSS product announcement

description: Binary indicator set to 1 if only one firm in the dyad listed the other as a competitor in year t; which of the two firms perceives the other is not distinguished. The case of no perceived competition (both firms do not list each other) is the excluded category. Independent variables and controls are lagged by one year.
time_window: year t (lagged one year in the models)

description: Binary indicator set to 1 if both firms in the dyad listed each other as competitors in year t. This is one of the two types of perceptual alignment, entered as a separate variable so that no perceived competition becomes the baseline.
time_window: year t (lagged one year in the models)

description: Binary indicator set to 1 for any announced collaboration between two sample firms in year t that had also collaborated in year t-1. Measuring collaboration renewal yearly is appropriate because software R&D collaborations often focus on developing new products and software development lifecycles are typically one to two years. For triads, the focal dyad between ego and alter is considered renewed if there was any collaboration between them in the following year, with or without the third party.
time_window: year t, relative to a collaboration in year t-1

variable_name: Misaligned perceived competition with third party perceived competitor
description: Binary indicator set to 1 if (a) the dyad had misaligned perceived competition, (b) the dyad was part of a triadic collaboration, and (c) ego perceived the third party as a competitor. Its counterpart, misaligned perceived competition without third party perceived competitor, is set to 1 for misaligned dyads that did not meet these criteria; misaligned dyads not part of a triadic collaboration are necessarily coded in this counterpart category.
time_window: year t (lagged one year in the models)

variable_name: Misaligned perceived competition with third party alter experience
description: Binary indicator set to 1 if (a) the dyad had misaligned perceived competition, (b) the dyad was part of a triadic collaboration, and (c) the third party was previously part of a misaligned collaboration with alter, in which alter perceived the third party as a competitor but the third party did not perceive alter as a competitor. Its counterpart, misaligned perceived competition without third party alter experience, is set to 1 for misaligned dyads that did not meet these criteria.
time_window: year t (lagged one year in the models)

description: The proportion of jointly announced products that were launched by the following year. Jointly announced products were collected through manual inspection of press releases related to the collaboration announcement, and actual releases through product press releases; the measure is computed for the subset of collaborations that announced at least one future product.

Litigation between collaborating firms, used as a proxy for a partner's failure to meet behavior expectations. Data on litigation were collected from Bloomberg Law; 43 cases were filed between firms that had collaborated during the study time period, 35 of which were filed between partner firms within two years of an announced collaboration. The authors note that lawsuits are infrequent in this setting and that litigation does not mediate the relationship between misalignment and renewal.

Year t CEO equity compensation, expressed in 1993 dollars and entered in natural log. It includes all equity-based awards such as restricted stocks, stock options and stock appreciation rights, with option values computed using the Black-Scholes approach adjusted for early exercise. Because equity compensation is not awarded in 49.4% of sample firm-years, the equation is estimated with Heckman's two-step procedure.

Year t CEO discretionary compensation, expressed in 1993 dollars and entered in natural log. It includes not only equity-based compensation but also bonuses and other compensation, and is estimated with Heckman's two-step procedure.
Year t CEO base salary expressed in 1993 dollars and entered in natural log. Mean base salary in the sample is $366,000, almost 36% of mean total compensation.

Ownership of the largest stockholder, expressed in percent of total outstanding shares and entered in natural log; the variable equals zero if the largest holder is the CEO. Share ownership includes beneficially owned shares and options exercisable within 60 days. Mean ownership of the largest non-CEO equity holder is about 17.2%.
scale: natural log of percent of outstanding shares

description: Ownership of the largest stockholder, expressed in percent of total outstanding shares, if the largest holder is the CEO, and zero otherwise. The largest shareholder is the CEO in 26.2% of the sample.

0.01 plus the compensation committee's stock holdings expressed in percent of total outstanding shares, entered in natural log. The committee's holdings exclude those of the CEO if the CEO is on the committee. Mean committee ownership is about 4.6% and median ownership about 0.48%.
scale: natural log of percent of outstanding shares

description: A principal component of three variables: the ratio of interest expense to pretax operating income, an indicator variable denoting a 'loser' firm (its three-year cumulative equity rate of return in the bottom 5% of all NYSE/AMEX stocks during any of the prior three calendar years), and the negative of lagged log market value of equity. The three variables are collapsed into a single factor using principal component analysis.
time_window: year t; loser status over the prior three calendar years

description: Beginning net total assets of year t expressed in 1993 dollars and entered in natural log. The authors use total assets to measure the predicted impact of the number of shares outstanding. Firm size in the sample ranges from $4.2 million to $184 billion in total assets.

Indicator variable equal to one if the CEO is also the chairman of the board, and zero otherwise. The authors treat duality as a proxy for high costs of displacing the CEO. About 70% of the sample CEOs are also board chairperson.

0.01 plus the stock ownership of the CEO expressed in percent of total outstanding shares, entered in natural log. On average a typical CEO beneficially holds about 8% of the firm's equity, while the median stock ownership is about 2.3%.
scale: natural log of percent of outstanding shares

description: Log of a principal component of four measures: the sum of capital expenditures, R&D and acquisitions scaled by the sum of depreciation expense over the three years t-2 through t; the geometric growth rate of the change in the market value of assets from t-2 to t; the year t ratio of R&D to the book value of assets; and the end-of-year t ratio of market value to the book value of assets. The authors use the factor score measure developed by Baber et al. (1996) as a proxy for future growth opportunities.
scale: natural log of a principal component

description: 0.01 plus long-term debt divided by the sum of long-term debt and book value of equity, expressed in percent and entered in natural log.
One plus the year t common stock return, adjusted for inflation, entered in natural log.
One plus the year t income before extraordinary items divided by the book value of equity, adjusted for inflation, entered in natural log.

Binary variable that equals one if any of the startup's founders is an academic founder, with a founder classified as an academic founder if their former employer was a university. University employers are identified using text keywords for university, college, school, and institute, followed by manual inspection; fine-grained position data help discern academic employment from medical practice in hospitals affiliated with universities, so that an associate professor of cardiology counts as academic whereas a cardiac surgeon in a university medical center does not. Patent disclosure in technology transfer systems, residing in a university location, or joining scientific boards do not per se count as academic startup formation.

Binary variable that equals one if any of the startup's founders is a within-industry employee founder, classified as such if their former employer was a medical device firm. The first step matches employer names with publicly listed firms in SIC 3841, 3842, 3843, 3844, 3845, and 5047; for remaining employers, whether an employer operated as a medical device firm is assessed using business descriptions from Crunchbase, Medtrack, PitchBook, company websites and related industry sources, together with product and technology descriptions from FDA and USPTO records.

Binary variable that equals one if a startup reassigned rights to any of its patents to another firm during the 10-year window after a startup's founding; reassignment is the legal transfer of rights, title, and interest in a patent and serves as a proxy for activity in markets for technology. Patents granted to a startup are identified by matching original patent assignees with startup names, using IPC A61 (medical or veterinary sciences) classes. Reassignment records from the USPTO patent assignment database are used, excluding within-firm transfers from inventors to firms, name-change registrations, temporary transfers as security pledges, confirmatory transfers of joint rights, and reassignments where the assignor is not the original startup patent owner or that occur materially after a startup's acquisition or dissolution. The authors note that the measure provides a conservative view of markets for technology.

Binary variable that equals one if a startup received approval for any of its medical devices from the Food and Drug Administration during the 10-year window after a startup's founding. The list of approved devices comes from appending FDA databases covering pre-market approvals, pre-market 510(k) notifications, and humanitarian device exemptions, which provides complete coverage of class 2 and 3 devices. The original FDA applicants in this list are then matched with startup names.

Binary variable that equals one if any of a startup's FDA-approved medical devices during the 10-year window after a startup's founding was the first-ever device in its corresponding product code. Each medical device is evaluated by one of 16 FDA advisory panels, each targeting a medical specialty such as cardiovascular or neurology, and within these advisory panels fine-grained product codes separate various devices, their intended use, safety risk profiles, and other attributes.

Binary variable that equals one if an academic founder was listed as an inventor of a patent filed by their university before the founding year of a startup. Patents' assignee names are first matched with universities previously employing founders and then patents' inventor names with the last names of founders, with manual confirmation of first and familiar names. There are 65 startups whose academic founders invented university-owned patents. The complementary binary variable equals one if an academic founder had no past patents.

Binary variable that equals one if an academic founder was employed at a university that had above median licensing activity in the founding year of the startup, where activity is the number of active licenses and options administered by the technology transfer office or its equivalent. Licensing data come from the AUTM licensing activity survey, accessible through the AUTM STATT database; in each year the number of active licenses and options is compared across all participating universities and those with above median activity are designated as strong technology transfer offices. There are 84 startups whose academic founders were employed in such universities, and the complementary binary variable equals one if an academic founder was employed at a university with below median licensing activity.

Binary variable that equals one if a founder's past employment is listed as 'scientist', 'chief scientist', 'science officer', 'technology officer', and so forth, based on the job function in their past employment as reported in the Venture Source database. There are 34 within-industry employee startups whose founders occupied these positions. The complementary binary variable equals one if a within-industry employee founder did not have these positions.

Binary variable that equals one if a founder was listed as an inventor of a patent in IPC A61 filed by their former employer during the five years before the founding year of a startup.
