These data come from first matching patents' assignee names with firm names previously employing founders and then matching those patents' inventor names with the last names of founders, with manual confirmation of first and familiar names. There are 153 startups whose employee founders are listed as inventors, and the complementary binary variable equals one if an employee founder had no past patents.
time_window: five years before the founding year

description: Binary variable that equals one if the number of IPC A61 patents of the former employer is 45 or less at the time of a within-industry employee startup's founding, including 514 startups. The threshold reflects that in the population of patents filed during the time window of the study in IPC A61, each corporate patent assignee has a cumulative average of 45 patents in each five-year window, so a small technology former employer is a firm with 45 or fewer patents in IPC A61 during the five years prior to the employee startup's founding year. The complementary binary variable equals one if the number of patents is over 45.
time_window: five years prior to the employee startup's founding year

description: Binary variable that equals one if the age of the former employer, that is, the number of years between the founding year of the former employer and the founding year of the startup, is 15 or less at the time of a startup's founding. There are 390 startups whose founders were formerly employed in a young firm. The complementary binary variable equals one if the age of the former employer is above 15.
time_window: at the time of the startup's founding

description: Operationalized in the policy capturing scenarios at two levels, weak and strong, consistent with the literature and the interview data. The interview data showed that scientists described strong social relationships in terms of time (the amount of time they had known an individual, their frequency of interaction) and affect (feelings of friendship, closeness, and trust) and whether the individual belonged to their social network. Manipulation checks asked respondents to classify descriptions of strong and weak relationships on a scale of 1 (low/weak) to 6 (high/strong); respondents classified descriptions correctly more than 85 percent of the time in both the intergroup and interfirm samples.

Operationalized in the policy capturing scenarios at two levels, high and low, at both the interfirm and intergroup level. Interviews with R&D scientists confirmed that they think about interfirm competition primarily as competition for the same market, a similar customer base, and the development of substitute products, and that R&D scientists from different project-groups compete for seed money, investment dollars, and budget allocations. Manipulation checks asked respondents to classify descriptions of high and low levels of competition on a scale of 1 (low/weak) to 6 (high/strong), with correct classification more than 85 percent of the time.

Manipulated between respondents through random assignment to two plots, the most workable grouping being firm boundaries. Of the 79 scientists, 41 responded only to scenarios in which the prospective recipient was from the source's own firm (the intergroup plot) and the remaining 38 responded only to scenarios in which the prospective recipient was from another firm (the interfirm plot). Within their plot, subjects responded to four scenarios that differed in social relationships and competition but did not differ in respect to firm boundary.

A four-item scale developed from the interview data, in which R&D scientists reported considering the number of details, the kind of information, the amount of time, and how completely to fulfill a request. The effort related to know-how transfer was measured on an ascending scale of 1 to 6. Chronbach's alpha was 0.935 based on the four-item scale, all inter-item correlations were greater than 0.83 and significant at p < 0.001, and principal components analysis confirmed a one-factor solution that captured 87.8 percent of the variance in the items.

The resource nonoverlap of the dyad's partners, operationalized as the Euclidean distance between them in the space of the 47 technical resources monitored by the IASPC. To make partnerships between small and large firms comparable, this figure was divided by the average endowments of technical resources of the two actors in the dyad. The theoretical value ranges from 0, corresponding to complete resource overlap, to 2, corresponding to no overlap; the observed range was 0 to 1.58. All variables except binary ones were standardized.

Calculated as the absolute value of the sum over the 47 monitored technical resources of the difference between the two partners' endowments, abs[sum_i (RA_i - RB_i)]. Based on the degree to which these differences offset each other, the measure indicates the extent to which the resource endowments of the partners were in balance.

An aggregate measure computed as the mean value of the resource-level depth complementarity values DC_i over the set I of task resources required by the project. Resource i's depth complementarity, DC_i, was set to 0 if either the task did not require the resource or either of the partners could have singlehandedly fulfilled the need for i; it was set to 1 when the partners' joint resources exceeded the task requirements; and for values in between the degree to which the partners fulfilled the task requirement TRQ_i was calculated. Using the mean is equivalent to using a unit weight, assuming all resources are equally important.

The authors first identified the subsets H and K of task resources that either party possessed in sufficient amounts, then identified the resources in H and K that did not overlap (the set complements H not in K and K not in H), and finally defined scope complementarity as the count of resources in the two set complements as a proportion of the count of resources in I, the set of task resources required by the project.

Defined as the inequality in resource endowments of depth complementary resources held by two partners, over the set J of resources where DC_i is greater than 0. The depth imbalance DI_i of resource i ranges between 0 and 1 and increases with the difference between the parties' endowments of resource i. To allow an imbalance in favor of one partner in one resource to offset an imbalance in favor of the other in another resource, the DI_i's were averaged across the resources in J after their direction was assessed through the sign function, and the absolute value of the resulting indicator was then taken.

The imbalance in scope of complementary task resources, calculated in two steps: the subsets H and K of task resources each party possessed in sufficient amounts and their set complements H not in K and K not in H were identified and counted, and scope imbalance was then set equal to 0 if the maximum of the two counts equals 0, and otherwise to 1 minus the ratio of the minimum to the maximum of those counts.

Binary dependent variable taking the value 1 when a tie was realized (an alliance was formed between the lead firm and the partner firm for the project) and 0 when it was simulated. Cases were obtained by disaggregating each of the 474 contract-winning ATIs into dyads formed by their lead firms and the other ATI members, which yielded 749 dyads of which 316 related to 189 projects were useable; each case was matched by controls sharing the same lead firm and task at a 4:1 ratio, giving 316 realized ties and 1,264 simulated ties.
level: dyad-project (triangular configuration of lead firm, partner firm and task)

description: Pattern 1 comprises venture recipients with multiple Phase I awards and no Phase II awards over their first four years of activity with the program (0 <= t <= 3). The variable is coded 1 for ventures with this certification portfolio and for the time following the venture's first award (t >= 0); the reference group is the Referent group (only one Phase I and no Phase II), coded 0. In the estimated model the pattern enters interacted with State Match.
time_window: first four years active in SBIR/STTR (0 <= t <= 3)

description: Pattern 2 comprises venture recipients with only one Phase I and one follow-on Phase II award over their first four years of activity with the program (0 <= t <= 3). The variable is coded 1 for ventures with this certification portfolio in the time following the venture's first award (t >= 0), and 0 for the Referent group. In the estimated model the pattern enters interacted with State Match.
time_window: first four years active in SBIR/STTR (0 <= t <= 3)

description: Pattern 3 comprises venture recipients with multiple Phase I awards and any Phase II award over their first four years of activity with the program, which the authors argue represents broad experimentation that has yielded proof of a potential breakthrough. The variable is coded 1 for ventures with this certification portfolio and for the time following the venture's first award (t >= 0). For Hypothesis 3 the reference group is Pattern 2 (targeted experimentation), coded 0.
time_window: first four years active in SBIR/STTR (0 <= t <= 3)

description: Annual sales is the dependent variable and a standard measure of market-based venture performance. Values are adjusted for inflation, increased by 1, and the natural logarithm is computed to estimate a normal distribution. The authors exclude early-stage investor activity (e.g., VCs and angels) because investors are not buying the venture's outputs, and they control for federal procurement activity as a separate regressor.
time_window: annual, spanning three years before to three years after the first award (-3 <= t <= 3)

description: State Match is coded 1 if the venture is located in a state that administers the noncompetitive Phase I matching program, so the metric reflects variation in state administration of the program. Twenty-three states adopted the State Match as of 2019, 10 of which actively administered the program during the time frame of the study (2001-2011). The authors leverage the exogeneity of the State Match to separate audience-related effects of certification from venture-related effects.

International diversification was measured by combining three widely used measures: (1) firm sales from foreign operations divided by total firm sales, (2) foreign assets divided by total assets, and (3) the number of foreign subsidiaries divided by the total number of subsidiaries. Results of a factor analysis indicated that these three individual variables loaded on the same factor, with factor loadings of .85 (foreign sales per total sales), .85 (foreign assets per total assets), and .67 (foreign subsidiaries per total subsidiaries), and a Cronbach alpha of .73. Because the items used to create the variable are expressed in different units, the authors centered the items prior to combining them. Foreign sales and asset figures and subsidiary data were obtained for 1997, and total sales and assets data for the same year.

Ownership by professional investment management funds was measured as their percentage of equity ownership. Owners were classified as mutual funds if they appeared in the Investment Company Institute's Directory of Mutual Funds for 1993-94; securities brokers and investment banks were those firms operating in the securities industry (SIC codes 60-62). A 1 percent equity ownership cutoff was imposed to remove institutional owners with marginal equity positions and to include only funds with ownership adequate to promote interest and activism. Institutional ownership data were collected for 1996.

Pension fund ownership was operationally defined as the percentage of equity ownership. Public pension funds were identified from the 1994 Pensions and Investments: Directory of the 1000 Largest Pension Funds. A 1 percent equity ownership cutoff was imposed to remove institutional owners with marginal equity positions. Institutional ownership data were collected for 1996.

The presence of outside directors was assessed as the ratio of independent outside directors on a board. Drawing on prior research and SEC regulation 14A, item 6(b), affiliated outside directors were defined as relatives, customers, suppliers, former employees, lawyers, and bankers, and were removed from the sample; the remaining outside directors were classified as independent outsiders with no affiliation with a firm except as directors. The outside director ratio is the number of independent outside directors divided by board size. Board data were collected from proxy statements for 1996.

Inside directors were defined as members of a firm's board of directors who were current firm employees. The variable, a measure of the incentives of the inside directors on a board, consisted of two indicators: (1) inside director equity as a percentage of total equity and (2) the value of inside directors' stock options, expressed as its logarithm. Inside directors' stock options were valued using the Black-Scholes method provided by Standard & Poor's ExecuComp data. The factor loadings were .83 (inside director equity) and .85 (inside director stock options), and the interitem correlation between the two measures was .62. Because the components are expressed in different units, the items were centered prior to combining them.
Technological opportunity was defined as average industry R&D divided by average industry sales at the two-digit SIC level. COMPUSTAT data used for the independent variables were collected for 1996.

The level of geographic diversification into R-P host countries is measured as the number of host countries that were resource-poorer than South Korea in which the MNE had foreign operations. It is one of two conceptually distinct geographic diversification variables used as independent variables. If an MNE had not entered any R-P host countries, the variable was coded 0.

variable_name: index of geographic diversification into R-P host countries
description: An index that takes into account both the number of host countries in which the MNE operated and the extent to which country-level strategic factor markets varied among host countries. ISK represents the FMEI of South Korea, Ii represents the FMEI of a host country in which a Korean MNE has at least one foreign subsidiary, and n is the number of R-P host countries; a firm that had not entered any R-P host country was coded 0. The formula itself was printed as an unreadable block in the extracted text.

The level of geographic diversification into R-R host countries is measured as the number of host countries that were resource-richer than South Korea in which the MNE had foreign operations. It is one of two conceptually distinct geographic diversification variables used as independent variables. If an MNE had not entered any R-R host countries, the variable was coded 0.

variable_name: index of geographic diversification into R-R host countries
description: An index that takes into account both the number of host countries in which the MNE operated and the extent to which country-level strategic factor markets varied among host countries. ISK represents the FMEI of South Korea, Ii represents the FMEI of a host country in which a Korean MNE has at least one foreign subsidiary, and n is the number of R-R host countries; a firm that had not entered any R-R host country was coded 0. The formula itself was printed as an unreadable block in the extracted text.

Firm profitability is measured as the principal component of return on assets (ROA), return on sales (ROS), and return on invested capital (ROIC). ROA was captured as the ratio of net income to total assets, ROS as the ratio of net income to total sales, and ROIC as the ratio of net income before tax plus interest payments to total assets. A three-year moving average of ROA, ROS and ROIC was calculated to smooth out fluctuations, and a time-lag structure was used: when the independent and control variables covered 1993, the dependent variable covered 1994-1996. The factor loadings for the three measures were 0.97, 0.84, and 0.93, and the factor's eigenvalue was 2.51 with a Cronbach alpha of 0.90.
time_window: three-year moving average, lagged relative to the independent variables

variable_name: Influence of corporate legal affairs department (ξ5)
description: Survey respondents were asked: 'To what extent have the following corporate departments influenced your facility to improve its environmental performance?' for the corporate legal affairs department. The five-point scale ranged from 'no influence' (coded 0.2) to 'very strong influence' (coded 1). Respondents could indicate that their corporation did not have either department, and the department influence variables were coded as 'no influence' in such cases.

Survey respondents were asked: 'To what extent have the following corporate departments influenced your facility to improve its environmental performance?' for the corporate marketing department. The five-point scale ranged from 'no influence' (coded 0.2) to 'very strong influence' (coded 1). Respondents could indicate that their corporation did not have either department, and the department influence variables were coded as 'no influence' in such cases.

Respondents indicated the extent to which various external groups influenced their facilities to improve environmental performance, ranking each stakeholder on a five-point scale from 'no influence' (coded 0.2) to 'very strong influence' (coded 1). The latent variable represents receptivity to nonmarket pressure exerted by local communities, environmental organizations, regulators, and the media. An exploratory principal components factor analysis of the stakeholder items produced two factors, with these four items loading on the nonmarket factor. Shareholders, trade associations, and SRI funds were removed because they loaded fairly evenly across both factors.

Respondents indicated the extent to which various external groups influenced their facilities to improve environmental performance, ranking each stakeholder on a five-point scale from 'no influence' (coded 0.2) to 'very strong influence' (coded 1). The latent variable represents receptivity to market pressure exerted by customers, suppliers, and competitors. An exploratory principal components factor analysis of the stakeholder items produced two factors, with these three items loading on the market factor. Shareholders, trade associations, and SRI funds were removed because they loaded fairly evenly across both factors.

Respondents were asked: 'What is the status of the certification of ISO 14001 at your facility?' The five-point scale was 'not being considered' (coded 1), 'future consideration' (2), 'planning to implement' (3), 'currently implementing' (4), and 'successfully implemented' (5). Providing intermediate values gave a more nuanced measure than a simple dichotomous response as to whether or not the facility had already adopted the standard. In the model, the variable was rescaled to have a maximum of one.
scale: 1 to 5 (five-point scale), rescaled to a maximum of one

description: The survey asked: 'What is the status of your participation in voluntary U.S. EPA or state programs such as Energy Star, WasteWise, Environmental Performance Track, etc.?' The four-point scale was 'not being considered' (coded 1), 'future consideration' (2), 'planning to participate' (3), and 'currently participating' (4). In the model, the variable was rescaled to have a maximum of one.
scale: 1 to 4 (four-point scale), rescaled to a maximum of one

description: Five-year estimates of median household income, in tens of thousands of dollars, of each city between 2008 and 2012. Information on city-level characteristics was collected from the 2008-2012 American Community Survey to avoid reverse causality and endogeneity issues.
The proportion of the population aged over 25 who have at least a bachelor's degree, averaged across 2008 through 2012.

All restaurants listed on Yelp are classified into one or more of 108 categories, and these categories as they are shown on the website are used to measure restaurants' degree of variety-enhancing spanning. The measure takes into account the distance between the categories a restaurant spans: numcate denotes the number of categories the organization has membership in and dx denotes the average distance between the categories spanned; the average distance between the categories was calculated using the cosine distance between each pair of categories on a co-occurrence matrix showing what categories are claimed together by restaurants in the sample. The equation itself is not readable in the text available.

The typicality of each word used in dish names and dish descriptions in each of the 108 categories is computed as the Jaccard similarity of the word to the category, excluding all prepositions, conjunctions, and interjections. Dish typicality in the claimed category is the average word typicality of the words used to describe the dish, and in cases of restaurants claiming multiple categories the highest score among dish typicalities in the claimed categories is chosen for each dish; these scores are then averaged to obtain the average dish typicality of a restaurant. Because typicality and category spanning are inversely related, the average dish typicality of a restaurant is subtracted from 1, and the values are rescaled so that the maximum observed value is 1 and the minimum is 0.
time_window: menus and restaurant information downloaded on February 27, 2014

description: Participants in the variety scenario were asked, on a seven-point Likert scale (1: 'Very unlikely'; 7: 'Very likely'), how likely they would try a restaurant that offers one, two, three, and four or more categories of food. The two items on restaurants offering three categories and four or more categories were combined into the two-item measure VARIETY, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.90.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = Very unlikely; 7 = Very likely)

description: Participants in the atypicality scenario were asked, on a seven-point Likert scale (1: 'Very unlikely'; 7: 'Very likely'), how likely they would try a restaurant that offers atypical dishes from the category it belongs to.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = Very unlikely; 7 = Very likely)

description: Participants' annual household income in 2019, in $1,000.
A dummy variable for participants who received a bachelor's or higher degree.

All participants were asked to answer questions about their attributes on a seven-point scale, and the responses were classified into four groups that represent the various attributes of cultural omnivores and used as potential mediators; DIVERSITY is one of these four mediator variables. All participants were asked to answer questions about their attributes on a seven-point scale, and the responses were classified into four groups that represent the various attributes of cultural omnivores and used as potential mediators; NOVELTY is one of these four mediator variables. All participants were asked to answer questions about their attributes on a seven-point scale, and the responses were classified into four groups that represent the various attributes of cultural omnivores and used as potential mediators; RISK is one of these four mediator variables. The specific questions asked are listed in Table 4.

Managers were presented with the statement 'Relationships typically evolve through a number of phases over time. Which of the following best describes your firm's current relationship with (named supplier)?' and checked the description that best applied. The instrument, based on Jap (2001) and Jap and Ganesan (2000), describes each phase parsimoniously and was positioned late in the survey, after the measures of the relationship properties. Relationships in deterioration were pooled with those in decline, and no relationship could fall in the awareness stage.
scale: categorical phase descriptions (exploration, build-up, maturity, decline/deterioration pooled)

description: Within each phase, overall performance evaluation is regressed on dummy variables indicating the relationship's movement through phases over the preceding five years, with the intercept containing all relationships that followed the expected DSO pattern (stability or progression). In the all-phases equation a single aberrant-movement dummy contrasts regression with the expected pattern; within phases the dummies separate forms of regression such as save, renewal, reconsideration, and restart.

Multiple-item scale measured on a seven-point response format where 1 = strongly disagree and 7 = strongly agree. All items for each construct were separated and mixed throughout the survey, and the scale items and their sources are listed in the online appendix.

Operationalized as the sum of the reseller's dependence on the supplier and the supplier's dependence on the reseller. Each component scale runs from 1 to 7 on the same disagree-agree response format used for the other relationship properties.
scale: sum of two scales each ranging from 1 to 7

variable_name: Outcomes given comparison level of alternatives
description: Multiple-item scale measured on a seven-point response format where 1 = strongly disagree and 7 = strongly agree. All items for each construct were separated and mixed throughout the survey, and the scale items and their sources are listed in the online appendix.
The number of alternative partners the reseller has seriously considered. The hypothesis is stated for the inverse of this number.

The reseller's overall evaluation of the supplier's performance, measured with multiple items on the same seven-point disagree-agree format. The items are listed in the online appendix together with the means, standard deviations, and correlation with reseller trust in the sales representative; a confirmatory factor analysis of the two constructs indicates convergent and discriminant validity.

variable_name: Reseller trust in the sales representative
description: Multiple-item scale measuring the reseller's trust in the individual sales representative rather than the role. It is the only set of items in the questionnaire not completed with respect to the relationship with the manufacturer organization. The items are listed in the online appendix and the factor loadings from the confirmatory factor analysis are significant.

Categorical variable set equal to 1 if printer firm j exits the laser printer industry during year t, and 0 otherwise. A firm exits when it ceases to ship all products in the industry; if it withdraws some products but continues to sell at least one other product it does not exit. If the firm is acquired, the observation is right censored rather than coded as an exit.

Count of the number of laser engine firms operating at the beginning of year t. It includes independent laser engine firms that sell all of their products on the open market, fully vertically integrated producers, and partially integrated firms that both sell on the market and sell to a downstream division.

Count of the number of laser engine firms that sell only on the open market at the beginning of year t. It is obtained by disaggregating EngineSellSomeDensity into EngineSellAllDensity and EngineSell&UseDensity.
Count of the number of laser engine firms that both use engines in-house and sell on the open market at the beginning of year t. It is one of the two components of EngineSellSomeDensity.
Count of the number of laser engine firms whose engine production is entirely consumed by a downstream laser printer division at the beginning of year t.

Count of the number of laser printer firms operating at the beginning of year t. The square of this count, PrinterDensity2, is entered in the models to capture the U-shaped density dependence found in organizational ecology.

Count of the number of laser printer firms that use only in-house engines at the beginning of year t. It is obtained by disaggregating PrinterMakeSomeDensity into PrinterMakeAllDensity and PrinterMake&BuyDensity.
Count of the number of laser printer firms that use both in-house and purchased engines at the beginning of year t. It is one of the two components of PrinterMakeSomeDensity.
Count of the number of laser printer firms that buy all of their laser engines at the beginning of year t.

Set equal to 1 if firm j buys all of its engines (i.e., does not produce any engines in-house) during year t and 0 otherwise. The authors use the firm's level of integration to split the sample into nonintegrated focal firms and focal firms with any positive level of integration, cautioning that there are no exits among partially integrated firms and only three among fully integrated firms.

Following standard practice for patent data, the variable is calculated as the nonbiased Herfindahl index of the distribution of the outsourced patents across different law firms. The nonbiased measure corrects for the bias introduced when focal firms outsource few patents; the authors present the formula, which is not legible in the text. The terms are the number of patent applications outsourced by the focal firm in the year and the number outsourced to each outside lawyer at each law firm.

The natural log of the annual number of law firms doing significant legal work for a focal firm in a given practice area, averaged across all practice areas. The data come from ALM's annual survey, which asks General Counsel to identify law firms doing significant legal work on their behalf in given practice areas. The authors state that they take the reverse of this measure for hypothesis testing purposes, so that a high value indicates high concentration.

For the law firms used by a focal firm in a given year, the authors calculate the number of years each law firm was used during the previous three years, then average this number and take the natural logarithm. The measure captures the degree of stability in the focal firm's contracting history with its suppliers.

Each law firm-practice area dyad is treated as a distinct relationship. A relationship is characterized as stable when the law firm was used in the same practice area, or when no other law firm was used in the same practice area, during the previous year. The measure is the natural log of the annual count of such stable relationships.

For each law firm the authors calculate a nonbiased Herfindahl index of patent concentration across technology classes at the 1-digit level of the international patent classification, where high concentration indicates narrow capability breadth. They average this value for the law firms used by a focal firm in a given year and subtract it from one to generate a measure of breadth; the formula is presented but is not legible in the text.

The breadth of supplier capabilities is proxied by the number of practice areas provided by law firms to their clients. For each law firm the authors first calculate the annual average number of practice areas per client firm, then average this number across all law firms providing services to the focal firm and take the natural logarithm. A small number of practice areas per client indicates a specialist, narrow-scope law firm.

The ratio of patent applications insourced to the total patents applied by the focal firm, where insourced means filed using an in-house lawyer as opposed to a lawyer at an outside law firm. The lawyer responsible for the filing is listed in the Attorney or Agent field of the granted patent document, and USPTO PAIR data are the primary source because they list the patent lawyer's address, are recorded at application and have fewer missing values. Patents with no lawyer listed in both application and granted patent files are dropped.

The annual count of focal firm in-house lawyers reported by ALM, used as the dependent variable because detailed data on the total amount of legal work undertaken by law firms on behalf of focal firms are not publicly available. Changes in the count can reflect either the make-and-buy balance or the overall amount of legal work, so the authors control for several focal firm characteristics related to overall demand for legal services.

The number of 4-digit SIC segments in which a firm operates, calculated with 1991 data from the Worldscope database. It approximates an aggregate level of diversification without making a distinction between one closely related to the firm's core business and one less related to it.

The number of 2-digit SIC segments in which a firm operates, calculated with 1991 data from the Worldscope database. It is viewed as an indicator of diversification unrelated to the firm's core business.

The number of countries in which a firm has foreign subsidiaries, calculated with 1991 data from Kaigai Shinshutsu Kigyo Soran. It estimates an aggregate level of international diversification without distinguishing diversification within relatively homogeneous geographic regions from diversification across heterogeneous regions.

The number of regions in which a firm has foreign subsidiaries, calculated with 1991 data from Kaigai Shinshutsu Kigyo Soran. Foreign countries were categorized into regions on the basis of geographic proximity.

Return on assets, an accounting-based indicator of firm profitability chosen over ROE, which is affected by capital structure as well as operational efficiency. To smooth out annual fluctuations in accounting data, 3-year averages from the 1990-92 period were used.
Annual percentage change in sales. To smooth out annual fluctuations in accounting data, 3-year averages from the 1990-92 period were used.

variable_name: keiretsu member firms with strong power (D1) and keiretsu member firms with weak power (D2)
description: Keiretsu membership was taken from the 1992 issue of Dodwell's Industrial Groupings in Japan; keiretsu member firms were then cluster analyzed with Ward's method using four standardized variables characterizing keiretsu ties, of which debt holding structure did not distinguish among clusters and was dropped. Three clusters were obtained; the cluster with tenuous ties was consolidated with independent firms, leaving one cluster of keiretsu member firms with strong power and one of keiretsu member firms with weak power. Dummy D1 equals 1 for keiretsu member firms with strong power and 0 otherwise; D2 equals 1 for keiretsu member firms with weak power and 0 otherwise.
time_window: 1991 (1992 issue of Dodwell's Industrial Groupings in Japan)

description: Activist investors were identified as all investors that had, within the past year, filed a Schedule 13D (or 13D/A) related to concerns, dispute, or control at any firm; filings were taken from the Audit Analytics Investor Activism database. Activist ownership for a focal firm was calculated as the ratio of shares held by activist investors to total shares outstanding for each year in the sample. Of the over 5,000 institutional investors that owned shares of firms in the sample, only 119 were activist investors. In the sample the variable has a mean of 2%, a standard deviation of 3%, and a maximum of 15%.
scale: ratio of shares held by activist investors to total shares outstanding

description: Measured as the summated number of announcements about businesses seeking to sell or divest a business unit, spin-offs or split-offs, discontinued operations or downsizings, and reorganizations for each firm in a given year. Announcements were collected from the Capital IQ Key Development database. Around 16% of observations had one restructuring action announcement and another 16% had more than one. A binary alternative coding (32% coded ' 1 ' for ' restructuring occurred ') yielded substantively the same results.

Measured as the summated number of announcements about mergers and acquisitions, new product introductions, business expansions, and new strategic alliances for each firm in a given year. Announcements were collected from the Capital IQ Key Development database, which collects information on events that can affect securities' market value from over 20,000 news sources as well as regulatory filings and company websites. Around 17% of observations had one growth action and over 57% had more than one.

Following Connelly, Shi, and Zyung (2017), the variable is the sum of four constitutional limit provisions that Bebchuk, Cohen, and Ferrell (2009) identified as most critical to executives: staggered boards, a supermajority requirement to amend the charter, a supermajority requirement to approve a merger, and a supermajority requirement to amend a bylaw. Each observation therefore received a score ranging from 0 to 4. Data on takeover defense provisions were obtained from Institutional Shareholder Services' Governance. Because the variance over time is small (only 25% of observations experienced a change), Hypotheses 3a and 3b were tested with subgroup analyses using a median split on the number of provisions at the beginning of the sample period (median 2.0; mean 1.5).

Following Bushee (1998, 2001), institutional investors were first classified by their ownership stability (quarterly portfolio turnover, i.e., the total market value of sales during the quarter divided by the total market value of the portfolio at the beginning of the quarter, and the percentage of portfolio stocks held continuously for the past two years) and stake size (the percentage of portfolio stocks in large block holdings). Cluster analyses formed three groups of institutions; dedicated institutions have highly stable ownership and large stakes, and investors that do not meet these criteria are ' transactional ' (transient and quasi-indexer investors). The variable was then calculated as a percent, measured as transactional investor shareholdings divided by total shares outstanding.

The average installed base of an incumbent over population in the three years immediately prior to its entry into digital mobile technology. The installed base of fixed lines is taken as a proxy of the stock of complementary assets because it is proportional to the spread of marketing, sales and aftersales systems, the number of links with users, and other intangible resources such as reputation, brand value, and market knowledge. For markets with only one operator providing fixed services, this variable is equal to the penetration rate. For foreign incumbents, which enter by greenfields or by acquiring mobile newcomers, the variable takes the value zero.
time_window: the three years immediately prior to the incumbent's entry into digital mobile technology

description: EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization) divided by the total revenues of the firm in its market. This is a country-specific profitability measure.

An index built from the yearly Index of Economic Freedom provided by The Heritage Foundation. Five dimensions that best fit the concept of market-supporting institutions were selected: trade freedom, business freedom, investment freedom, financial freedom, and property rights protection. The index ranges from 0 (no freedom) to 100 (full freedom).

The Index of Political Constraints developed by Henisz (2000) subtracted from unity, so that the variable takes the value 1 in a scenario of full political instability and 0 in the case of full political stability. The original index ranges from 0 (no constraints on the executive branch's power to introduce policy changes) to 1 (full constraints on political decisions).

Natural logarithm of total CEO compensation reported in the annual report, which includes salary, bonus, commission and all other benefits. Stock options are rare in this context and are excluded because the authors lack data on accumulated option holdings; about 3.8% of observations report stock option grants. It is the dependent variable in all estimated models.

Indicator variable set to 1 when the CEO is drawn from the controlling family (termed promoter in Indian parlance) and 0 otherwise (i.e., a professional CEO). Family CEOs were coded based on documentary evidence of a kin relationship between the CEO and the controlling family, identified from company annual reports and filings with SEBI. For testing H2 it was entered as two splined variables that take the value of family CEO for above-median industry ROA firms and for below-median industry ROA firms respectively.

Financial return on assets (ROA) adjusted by industry median ROA. Industry boundaries were defined with the National Industrial Classification at the three-digit level, and the industry median ROA for each year was identified from the full sample of BSE-500 firms. ROA is taken in the same year as CEO compensation; firms with ROA at or above the industry median are treated as superior performers and firms below it as poor performers.

Burt's (1992) constraint measure computed on the entrepreneurial team's external advice network. To draw up individual members' external networks, respondents were asked to name a maximum of five of the most important people, not employed by their company, whom they rely on for valuable advice, guidance, or information relevant to the company; the team's external network was constructed by adding the network ties of all team members and counting an external contact only once, even if named by several team members. The constraint score captures the extent to which an alter j constrains entrepreneurial team i as a multiplication of the team's investment of time and energy in the relationship with j and the lack of structural holes around j; summed over all alters it is the network constraint measure. Network constraint is lowest when an entrepreneurial team spans many structural holes and is highest when the team spans few structural holes.

The percentage change in sales revenues in the previous year. The CEOs of all 84 ventures were independently contacted by a networking association representative to obtain revenue growth, so the dependent measure was collected independently of the survey.

A three-item scale (alpha = 0.91) on which respondents rated the extent of agreement within the team on each item using a five-point Likert scale anchored from 'strong disagreement' to 'strong agreement'. Each team member's responses to the three items were averaged to obtain a composite score, and this score was then averaged within the entrepreneurial team to compute strategic consensus within the team. The average James, Demaree, and Wolf's (1984) interrater reliability coefficient Rwg(3) statistic for this scale was 0.9, indicating a high level of interrater agreement.

A modified Carless and De Paola (2000) three-item scale (alpha = 0.91) on which team members rated statements using a five-point Likert scale anchored from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. Each team member's responses to the three items were averaged to obtain a composite score for cohesion, and this score was then averaged within the entrepreneurial team to compute team cohesion. The average interrater reliability coefficient Rwg(3) statistic for this scale was 0.9, indicating a high level of interrater agreement.
The Blau (1977) index of functional diversity within the team, computed using self-reported functional areas of expertise by individual team members in the survey.

Skill relatedness is defined as the relative excess labor flow, that is, the ratio of observed to predicted cross-industry labor flows. Predicted flows are obtained from a zero-inflated negative binomial regression of labor flows on the total employment, growth rates and average wage levels of the industries of origin and destination. To reduce noise, employees in the lowest paid half of each industry and those occupying management positions are dropped. The index is calculated for each of the 415 x 414 = 171,810 combinations of 415 industries at the four-digit level of the European NACE classification; a value of one means the industries are unrelated, values over one indicate skill relatedness and values under one relative skill dissimilarity.

The observed labor flow from an industry of origin to a destination industry, cumulative from 2004 to 2007. Job changes are defined as moves to another plant in another firm, so the flows reflect neither reassignments within a firm nor changes in plant ownership. Only employees from plants that already existed in 2004 are used, which reduces the number of job switchers to approximately 280,000 per year, of whom 77.2 percent moved to another industry.

A dummy that tags the diversification moves that have taken place with a one while containing zeros elsewhere. Each of the 649 diversification moves is characterized by an industry pair consisting of the firm's core industry and a diversification target industry; the database stacks these moves together with all of the alternative diversification options that existed but did not take place. Because of a lack of sales data, the core activity of each firm is defined as the industry in which the firm employs the largest portion of its labor force.

Classification-based relatedness, defined as the number of initial digits that two industries have in common. Unlike skill relatedness, which is continuous, it can assume only four different values in a four-digit classification system, and it is entered in the logit regressions as a categorical variable.

The value of the inputs that were sourced by industry i from industry j, divided by industry i's total inputs, giving the relative importance of industry j as a supplier of industry i's goods and services. It is based on the Swedish input-output table for 2005 and, because input-output tables are only available at the two-digit level, the values at that level are assumed to be representative of the four-digit level. The values are transformed into categorical variables using a procedure analogous to the one used for skill relatedness.

The value of the outputs that were sold by industry i to industry j, divided by industry i's total outputs, giving the relative importance of industry j as a buyer of industry i's goods and services. It is based on the Swedish input-output table for 2005, with two-digit values assumed representative of the four-digit level, and is transformed into categorical variables analogous to those for skill relatedness.

The number of industries in a firm's portfolio that are related to each target industry, where industries are regarded as skill related if their skill-relatedness index does not fall into the lowest relatedness category; that lowest category contains 85.7 percent of all industry combinations. The variable indicates the extent to which a potential target industry is related not just to the firm's core activity but to the firm's full range of activities.

Skill vectors are constructed that reflect the relative importance of eight broadly defined skills in each industry, based on employees' answers about the tasks and skills involved in their jobs. Based on these vectors a skill distance is calculated for each industry pair, reflecting the degree of dissimilarity between the skill sets of the two industries. Because the employment survey provides industry information only at the two-digit level, the Swedish data are aggregated to that level and the skill-relatedness index is recalculated.

Total count of new bridging ties formed by the focal firm at time t + 1. Bridging ties are ties that run between network communities, identified by partitioning the semiannual network with a community-detection algorithm using modularity (Girvan and Newman 2002); local ties run within a community. Because the initiating firm in a partnership cannot be identified, the design captures the variance attributed to the focal firm's characteristics and is described by the authors as a more conservative test. Models 8 and 9 use the ratio of newly formed bridging ties to all newly formed ties as the dependent variable.

Count of bridging ties that the firm currently maintains, reflecting the logged count of the firm's existing between-community ties. The count was centered around the mean and logged to reduce multicollinearity and distributional skewness; the authors verified that the log transformation significantly improved model fit.

Count of local (within-community) ties that the firm currently maintains, reflecting the logged count of the firm's existing within-community ties. Like the count of current bridging ties, it was centered around the mean and logged to reduce multicollinearity and skewness.

Log-transformed count of new bridging ties formed by the firm's partners at time t; the authors specify it as the log of the total number of new bridging ties formed by the firm's partners at time t. Alternatively, the authors used the net change in the counts of partners' bridging ties (controlling for decay) and the count of partners that formed at least one bridging tie.

Logged ratio of potential partners outside the firm's community to potential partners inside the firm's community. It takes, for each firm, the ratio of firms outside the firm's network community (excluding firms to which the focal firm was already connected at time t through a bridging tie) to firms inside the firm's network community (excluding firms to which the focal firm was connected at t through a local tie), counting only firms that actually formed at least one new network tie at t + 1. The printed formula is partly garbled in the text; the variable is described as reflecting the changing size of the network, the relative distribution of firms across communities, and the comparative tendency of firms to enter into partnerships.
time_window: t (with firms restricted to those forming a new tie at t + 1)

variable_name: Prior CEO was a star CEO
description: The degree to which the prior CEO was a star CEO, measured using wins in CEO-of-the-year contests. The authors count the total number of wins in CEO-of-the-year contests during the final five years of the prior CEO's tenure in office as a gauge of his or her cumulative standing as a star CEO. Contests included are those from Business Week, Chief Executive Magazine, Financial World, Industry Week, and Worth.
time_window: final five years of the prior CEO's tenure

description: A dummy variable that takes on a value of 1 if the prior CEO founded the company and 0 otherwise. It was coded by reading the press release announcing the new CEO appointment, which typically offers a detailed biography of the departing CEO, and by searching Zoominfo.com for executive work histories when no biography was included. If no information was found indicating that the prior CEO was the founder of the company, the individual was coded as 0.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the newly appointed CEO had previously served as a CEO and 0 otherwise. The authors first read the press release announcing the CEO appointment, then searched the Execucomp database for executive work histories, and finally searched Zoominfo.com. If no information was found indicating this individual had previously served as CEO, the individual was coded as 0.

variable_name: Stock market reaction to CEO appointment
description: An event study measure of the abnormal stock returns associated with the appointment of the new CEO. Using the market model, the authors regress each firm's daily returns on the S&P 500 market portfolio over an estimation period ending 46 days before the event and extending back 255 days prior to the event, and then use the resulting coefficients and the firm's actual daily returns to compute abnormal returns. Abnormal returns are cumulated over a three-day window from one day before the announcement to one day after the announcement.
time_window: three-day window (-1 to +1 day around the first press release announcing the appointment)

description: CEO compensation measured using Execucomp's total direct compensation, which includes salary, bonus, long-term incentive payouts that year, restricted stock grants, options granted during the year valued by the Black-Scholes method, and all other types of cash compensation paid that year. The variable is transformed into its natural logarithm so that extreme values would not unduly bias the analysis. The dependent variable is compensation in the CEO's second year, and compensation in his or her first year is included as a control variable in that equation, which the authors state is equivalent to testing for a change in compensation.
scale: natural logarithm of total direct compensation (US$)
time_window: second year of CEO tenure, controlling for first-year pay

description: A CEO dismissal was coded as an early CEO dismissal if it occurred within 730 days of his or her tenure. In every instance in which a CEO turned within 730 days, two coders read the press release announcing the dismissal as well as all media reports within one week of the CEO succession, and the case was coded as a dismissal when the two coders agreed the CEO was involuntarily dismissed from the firm.
time_window: within 730 days of the CEO's tenure

description: The nature of executive succession was coded by what happens to the departing president. An executive succession is coded as routine when the departing president is appointed as kaicho or vice-kaicho, since this is the normal course of events; it is coded as non-routine when the departing president is not appointed as the kaicho or vice-kaicho, in which case the company lacks a kaicho and the president acts as the informal board chair. The kaicho is listed at the top of the company's directory of executives in the Yuka Shoken Hokokusho filings, and the president's name is listed below that of the kaicho. The models include a dummy for non-routine succession; of the 214 executive succession events for multibusiness firms, 61 (28.5%) were coded as routine and 153 (71.5%) as non-routine.

The absolute percentage change in the size of the company's core business, where the core business is the largest business in terms of the company's sales, used to capture changes in the firm's strategic scope. A three-year period was used to measure post-succession strategic change, and the measure captures both growth and decline in the importance of the firm's core business. Change in the core business size ranges in value from 0 to 62.5 percent and has a mean of 8.3 percent; because the measure was not normally distributed, the square-root transformation of the measure was taken.

variable_name: Firm performance (industry-adjusted ROA, change in ROA, stock return)
description: Firm performance was measured using three different measures of performance: industry adjusted return on assets (ROA), change in ROA, and stock return. All three measures were examined in the interaction with non-routine executive succession and the results were the same. All of these variables were measured for the year prior to executive succession. In the main models change in ROA is the performance measure entering the interaction term.

A dummy variable with a value of 1 when there is no kaicho and the prior president also served as the informal board chair. In Japanese companies without a kaicho the president holds the informal position of board chair, so this variable captures whether the prior president retained that powerful position. The variable was measured for the year prior to executive succession.

Referral network closure is measured using Burt's formula for calculating structural hole constraint applied to the pre-acquisition network. The measure captures the extent to which the focal partner is connected via referral inflows to partners who are also connected to each other. To create the referral network, ties are defined by a focal partner's project billings to other partners' clients; ties are directional and weighted by the total amount billed to each alter partner's clients during the period. High values indicate few structural holes and greater closure; low values indicate less closure.
time_window: three years prior to the acquisitions

description: Interunit client sharing is the count of unique partners in the other legacy firm with whom the focal partner has shared clients during the three years after the acquisition. The measure is based on billings by other partners to the focal partner's clients. Sharing events of any size are counted as evidence of client sharing. Interunit sharing is observed when the sharing partner is in a different legacy firm.

Intraunit client sharing is the count of unique partners in the focal partner's legacy firm with whom he or she shared clients in the three years after the acquisition. It is observed when the sharing partners are in the same legacy firm. This measure is also used as an independent variable in models predicting revenue generation and human capital outcomes.

Intraunit tie cutting is the count of former unique partners in the focal partner's own legacy firm with whom he or she no longer shares clients during the three years following the acquisition. It captures reduction in existing intraunit client-sharing ties, whether or not accompanied by new client-sharing ties to other partners.

Workplace change is a binary indicator of whether partners were in units experiencing major workplace change. Major workplace change was identified using adoption of new information technology, billing, and accounting systems; change in headquarters location; change in the dominant coalition; and change in the organization's name. In this context, members of Alpha experienced no change, while members of both Gamma and Lambda experienced all of those changes.
time_window: at the time of the acquisitions

description: Revenue generation is measured as the total number of billable hours charged to clients for which the focal partner has responsibility, measured over the three years after the acquisition. To model change, post-acquisition revenue levels are predicted while controlling for pre-acquisition revenue levels associated with each partner's clients. The focal partner's own billings to his or her clients are excluded from the post-acquisition revenue variable.

Perceived human capital development is based on upward-feedback evaluations of partners by associates who worked with them. One item asked how the associate rated the partner on associate training and development (1-5 scale), and a second asked whether the associate would like to work with the partner again (yes or no). The firm averaged all associates' ratings for each partner, and records were missing when fewer than three associates evaluated a partner. Both items were rescaled to the same 0 to 100 range and then averaged to create the human capital development index.
Human capital retention is based on subordinate retention. It is calculated as the percentage of associates with whom each partner worked who remained in the firm during the subsequent three years.

The hazard that a VC withdraws its investment in a venture in the current round, conditional on the VC having invested in the previous round. A VC's investment in a venture is coded as withdrawn if the VC does not invest in any of the subsequent rounds, with withdrawal assumed to occur at the earliest round date when the VC no longer appears as an investor. If the VC invested until an exit event (IPO, acquisition, or bankruptcy) the case is not a withdrawal and is censored; cases with no exit event by June 30, 2009 are treated as withdrawals if 549 days have passed since the last reported round.
time_window: from the first financing round to withdrawal, an exit event, or June 30, 2009, whichever is sooner

description: An industry-specific, time-varying measure of industry-level uncertainty. It is the annualized squared standard error (root mean squared error) from a regression of monthly excess market returns in an industry on the three Fama-French factors (market excess return, SMB, and HML). Industries are the 49 Fama-French industries, reclassified from the Venture Economics Industry Classification in VentureXpert.

An entropy-type measure of a VC's portfolio focus in a given industry, constructed following the corporate diversification literature. It is the weighted average of the shares of each project the VC has funded in a given industry in a five-year period (current year included), the weight for each project being the logarithm of the inverse of its share in the portfolio. The measure is time varying, VC specific, and venture-industry specific.

An entropy-type measure of a VC's portfolio diversity across industries, constructed following the corporate diversification literature. It is the weighted average of the shares of the industries in which the VC has invested in a five-year period (current year included), the weight for each industry being the logarithm of the inverse of its share in the portfolio. The measure is VC specific and time varying.

Consistent with the authors' conceptualization, exchange hazards are operationalized in terms of the interaction of asset specificity and uncertainty. Asset specificity was measured with three items reflecting the extent to which specialized investments were made in the production system, tools, and equipment, using a measure adapted from Heide and John (1990). Uncertainty was measured with a four-item measure developed by Noordewier et al. (1990); the uncertainty measure solicits information about the buyer's sourcing market rather than each firm's own sourcing market. Item wordings and scales are provided in an online appendix.

Consistent with the authors' conceptualization, exchange hazards are operationalized in terms of the interaction of asset specificity and uncertainty. Asset specificity was measured with three items reflecting the extent to which specialized investments were made in the production system, tools, and equipment, using a measure adapted from Heide and John (1990). Uncertainty was measured with a four-item measure developed by Noordewier et al. (1990), soliciting information about the buyer's sourcing market. Item wordings and scales are provided in an online appendix.

The five-item measure reported in Zaheer et al. (1998) was used to operationalize the supplier representative's trust in the buyer organization. The measure has been replicated in several studies of interorganizational trust and consistently shown to have strong construct validity. The wording of the buyer and supplier versions of the questionnaire is identical except for the referent firm identified (Customer X versus Supplier X). Item wordings and scales are provided in an online appendix.

The five-item measure reported in Zaheer et al. (1998) was used to operationalize the purchasing manager's trust in the supplier organization. The measure has been replicated in several studies of interorganizational trust and consistently shown to have strong construct validity. The wording of the buyer and supplier versions of the questionnaire is identical except for the referent firm identified (Customer X versus Supplier X). Item wordings and scales are provided in an online appendix.

Power imbalance is operationalized as the ratio of relationship-specific assets of each partner, which is the inverse of the dependence of one exchange partner on the other, following Emerson (1962); the authors state that Pab, the power of a over b, is the inverse of Dba, the dependence of b on a. The measure is the ratio of supplier to buyer asset specificity (AS supplier / AS buyer); the formal equations are rendered in the paper but could not be read in this text. The authors note that while power imbalance and exchange hazards share the element of asset specificity, power imbalance is based solely on asset specificity and captures the relative difference between partners in relationship-specific investments.

The Analyst move variable is one if a ranked analyst switched to another sell-side research department, and zero if a ranked analyst did not move during the year. Analysts' affiliations in the year subsequent to being ranked, and the specific dates of their moves, were identified using analyst directories and news databases; the sample contains 500 moves from one firm to another, of which 366 were switches to competitors' research departments.
time_window: measured in the ranking year t = 0, with performance outcomes observed in t+1 through t+5

description: The dependent variable is the analyst's rank in the Institutional Investor All-America Research Team poll. Voters are asked to evaluate analysts using six criteria: earnings estimates, servicing initiatives, accessibility and responsiveness, stock selection, industry knowledge, and written reports; respondents award a single overall numerical score to each analyst in each industry sector, and votes are cumulated using weights based on the size of the voting institution. In each sector there are five levels of the dependent variable, which is categorical and ordinal: the first, second, third, and runner-up ranks and unranked.
scale: five levels: first, second, third, runner-up, unranked
time_window: t+1 through t+5 after the ranking year

description: The Firm capability direction categorical variable takes the value 'no move' if a ranked analyst does not move during the year, 'moving to a weaker firm' if the move is from a bulge to a nonbulge firm, 'moving to a better firm' if the move is from a nonbulge to a bulge firm, and 'moving to a comparable firm' if the move is from bulge to bulge or nonbulge to nonbulge. Bulge-bracket investment banks are those responsible for the bulk of securities underwritten in the United States; historically the six bulge firms are CS First Boston, Goldman Sachs, Lehman Brothers, Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley, and Salomon Brothers.
scale: four categories: no move, moving to a weaker firm, moving to a better firm, moving to a comparable firm

description: The Coworker move categorical variable takes the value of 'no move' if a ranked analyst does not move in a given year, 'moving solo' if the analyst switches to another sell-side research department solo, and 'moving in teams' if he or she makes such a move with other professionals (junior and senior research analysts, institutional salespeople, or traders who specialize in the same sector). News announcements on the hiring of ranked analysts indicated that ranked analysts occasionally moved in teams; of the 366 analyst-moves, 100 involved such colleagues.
scale: three categories: no move, moving solo, moving in teams

description: The dates on which analyst departures or hirings are first announced were chosen as the event dates. The data set consists of 228 observations of analysts joining publicly quoted firms; subsidiaries of larger diversified firms that generated less than 50% of those companies' revenues were excluded, observations were then checked for confounding announcements in the event period, and overlapping observations involving identical companies were dropped, leaving a final data set of 101 hiring announcements.
time_window: event date plus one day before and one day after

description: A short window study of daily excess returns over the event period of -1 to +1 days (the actual announcement date plus the days prior to and after the announcement date) is used to determine how the stock market reacts to the unexpected news of the departure or hiring of a star analyst. Stock-returns data were provided by the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP).
time_window: event window of -1 to +1 days around the announcement

description: Executives' educational backgrounds were coded as categorical variables following the criteria and procedures outlined in Wiersema and Bantel (1992). The degree of heterogeneity was then calculated using Blau's (1977) index, 1 - sum(Pi squared), where Pi is the percentage of individuals in the ith category. The higher the resulting score, the greater the TMT's heterogeneity on that dimension.

Executives' functional backgrounds were coded as categorical variables following the criteria and procedures outlined in Wiersema and Bantel (1992). The degree of heterogeneity was then calculated using Blau's (1977) index, 1 - sum(Pi squared), where Pi is the percentage of individuals in the ith category. The higher the resulting score, the greater the TMT's heterogeneity on that dimension.

Team tenure heterogeneity was gauged using the coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided by the mean) of executives' respective tenures on the top management team. Allison (1978) is cited as noting that the coefficient of variation is preferable when interval-level data such as time frames are used. High values indicate greater diversity.

Subsequent firm performance was measured as return on assets (ROA), averaged over time t+1 and t+2; averaging served to smooth any potential aberrations associated with a single year's performance. The authors state that ROA is a widely used measure of accounting performance and is relevant here because firm internationalization is theoretically associated with the search for economies of scope and scale.

Internationalization was calculated using a variation of Sullivan's (1994) multi-item measure of firm internationalization developed by Sanders and Carpenter (1998). It gauges internationalization on three theoretically distinct dimensions, each ranging from 0 to 1: foreign sales to total sales, foreign assets to total assets, and geographic dispersion of foreign sales, which are summed to form a composite with a theoretical range of 0 to 3. The three variables loaded on one factor with a high eigenvalue and explained variance and demonstrated high inter-item reliability (alpha = 0.84).

TMT average tenure was calculated using the median of the executives' respective tenures on the top management team. The authors note this variable is analogous to the one used by Harrison et al. (1998) and takes into account the likely skewness in the individual (within-team) distribution of tenure.

Four items from Carter and West (1998), rated by team members on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree) and aggregated to the team. Measured twice, at T1 (alpha team = .93) and T2 (alpha team = .86), with respondents asked to focus on the previous three months of the project.
time_window: T1 (month 3) and T2 (month 7), previous three months

description: Five items from Bresman's (2010) scale, rated by team members on a 7-point Likert scale and aggregated to the team (T2, alpha team = .87), referring to the previous three months of the project.
Four items from Bresman's (2010) scale, rated by team members on a 7-point Likert scale and aggregated to the team (T2, alpha team = .85), referring to the previous three months of the project.

The sponsor of each project rated team performance at T3 on three items used by Bresman (2010) (alpha = .85). Sponsors were fairly high in the organizational hierarchy and had extensive experience evaluating projects within the company.

Four items from Carter and West (1998) that were not modified for this study, rated by team members on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree) and aggregated to the team. Measured at the end of each episode (T1 alpha team = .88; T2 alpha team = .84; T3 alpha team = .84), with respondents focusing on the previous two weeks.
time_window: T1, T2, T3 (end of each two-week episode)

description: The first three items from Bresman (2010), modified to fit the context of MBA project teams, rated on a 7-point Likert scale and aggregated to the team (T1 alpha team = .85; T2 alpha team = .90; T3 alpha team = .88).
time_window: T1, T2, T3 (end of each two-week episode)

description: Four items from Bresman (2010) modified for this study, rated on a 7-point Likert scale and aggregated to the team (T1 alpha team = .88; T2 alpha team = .86; T3 alpha team = .86).
time_window: T1, T2, T3 (end of each two-week episode)

description: New items drawn from team behavior measures that include experimentation-focused items and generated following a scale-development procedure that involved seven cognitive interviews and exploratory factor analysis; rated on a 7-point Likert scale and aggregated to the team (T1 alpha team = .84; T2 alpha team = .82; T3 alpha team = .86).
time_window: T1, T2, T3 (end of each two-week episode)

description: Five items from Hoegl and Gemuenden (2001), rated by team members on a 7-point Likert scale and aggregated to the team, measured at T2 (alpha team = .87).

Two professional management consultants, external to the research team and MBA program, watched and rated each team's recorded 15-minute final presentation on three items adapted from Weiss, Hoegl, and Gibbert (2013) using a 10-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 10 = strongly agree). Interrater reliability was .80 and alpha was .97; the rating correlated with the team's grade for the assignment.

Cumulative number of attention allocation events connecting a participant to a specific problem before the current time, downweighted by elapsed time. A positive effect indicates that the greater the number of attention allocation events connecting a participant to a specific problem, the higher the likelihood of observing additional events reinforcing this connection. Past events are downweighted with a time-weighting function whose half-life is set to 10 days.
time_window: history of events before the current time

description: Current number of attention allocation events performed on a problem by all participants, downweighted by elapsed time. A positive effect indicates that higher levels of attention received by a problem in the past lead to a higher likelihood of receiving even more attention in the future, a 'popular for being popular' effect.
time_window: history of events on the problem before the current time

description: Baseline attention allocation mechanism capturing participants' average propensity to change their current level of attention to the project as a function of their history of participation; it is the cumulative number of a participant's past attention allocation events, downweighted by elapsed time. A positive effect provides evidence of a self-reinforcing motivation to contribute attention.
time_window: history of events before the current time

description: Interaction between cumulative attention (participant activity) and attention reinforcing (problem popularity). A negative effect of Attention mixing implies disassortativity, according to which active participants are less likely to allocate attention to more popular problems.

Number of bipartite four-cycles, defined as the number of three-paths indirectly connecting the participant of the focal dyad to its problem via another participant and another problem that are then closed by an event on the focal dyad. A positive effect implies that participants tend to cluster their attention around shared problems over time and captures the local character of search.
time_window: history of events before the current time

description: Dependent variable is the instantaneous probability of observing an attention allocation event linking a participant to a problem, conditional on characteristics of the participant, characteristics of the problem, and the history of interaction between participants and problems within the project. An attention allocation event occurs whenever a participant modifies a field in (touches) the bug report associated with a problem.
time_window: event times during the observation period

description: Dummy variable coded as 1 for firms that announced layoffs associated with the mergers and 0 for firms that did not announce a merger-induced layoff. Whether a firm announced a layoff was determined by first reading Wall Street Journal abstracts for each firm involved for the year following the transaction; if no layoff announcement was found, the business journal file was searched for layoff news for the companies involved in the year following the acquisition, and if no layoff was found after this second screen it was assumed that no layoff was announced.

Dummy variable coded as 1 if the firms operated in the same 4-digit SIC code prior to the merger, using the set of SICs listed in Compact Disclosure for the year prior to the transaction. All SICs reported for the firms were considered rather than simply the primary ones, because in looking for potential labor redundancy it is only important that firms operate in the same industry, not that the industry be their primary focus.

Two raters independently assessed the degree of overlap between the activities of the merging firms on a scale of 1 to 10, using SIC code data as well as the descriptions of the companies involved in the transaction from Mergers and Acquisitions Magazine. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient; the value of ICC (3,1) was 0.79. The average of the two raters' assessments for each combination was used as an independent variable.

Coded as 1 if the acquiring and acquired firms listed different countries as their headquarters. Since the acquired firms are all domestic, this measure is 1 if the acquiring firm is non-U.S. and 0 if it is headquartered in the United States.

Acquired firm financial performance was measured as return on invested capital the year before the M&A. The data are available on Compact Disclosure. ROIC is described as an improved returns measure that removes some of the inconsistencies across industries included in measures such as ROA.

Operational efficiency of the target firm prior to the transaction was measured as revenue per employee. Industry revenue per employee was included as a control for the operational efficiency intrinsic to the industry.
Variable taken from the SDC (Security Data Corp) data base of mergers and acquisitions, used to test Hypothesis 5. It is coded as 1 if the transaction is financed with borrowing.

Index computed as the sum of the standardized scores of five indicators of power. CEO duality is a binary variable set to 1 if the CEO was also the chairman of the board. The percentage of outsiders appointed after the CEO is the number of outside directors appointed during the focal CEO's tenure divided by the total number of outside directors. CEO long tenure is a binary variable set to 1 if the CEO's tenure was longer than three years. CEO stock ownership is the percentage of the focal firm's stocks owned by the CEO. Institutional ownership is the percentage of shares owned by institutional investors, and its value was reversed in creating the index measure.

All new directors who were CEOs of other Fortune 500 companies were identified and their narcissism was measured the same way as the focal CEO's. A new director's difference from the focal CEO in narcissism was calculated as the absolute difference in their narcissism score divided by the standard deviation of narcissism among all sampled CEOs; because the variable is highly skewed it was transformed with the lnskew0 function in STATA. Similarity in narcissism was then calculated as the opposite of the transformed measure of difference.
time_window: two-year average of each narcissism indicator, excluding CEO succession years

variable_name: New director's prior experience with other similarly narcissistic CEOs
