description: The new director's board appointments at other Fortune companies three years prior to the focal appointment (t-3 to t-1) were identified, and the narcissistic tendency of the CEOs of those tied-to companies was measured. Those CEOs were coded as similar CEOs if they differed from the focal CEO in narcissistic tendency by less than one standard deviation. The measure is the percentage of similar CEOs among all CEOs who worked with the new director on other boards in the previous three years.

variable_name: New director's demographic difference from CEO
description: Measured according to five background characteristics: gender, ethnicity, age, elite education, and functional background. Ethnicity was coded into White, African American, Asian, or Hispanics; elite educational background was set to 1 if a degree was obtained from an Ivy League elite school and 0 otherwise; functional background was coded into throughput, output, and peripheral functions. A new director's age difference from the focal CEO was coded as 1 if their ages differed by more than one standard deviation of age among all directors in the sample and 0 otherwise, and difference along the four other dimensions was coded as 1 if the director and the CEO differ and 0 otherwise. The primary measure is the sum of the standard scores of the five measures.

Index created from four unobtrusive indicators that are under the CEO's control. Prominence of the CEO's photograph in the annual report was coded on a five-point scale from no photograph of the CEO to the CEO photographed alone occupying more than half a page. CEO prominence in company press releases was measured by the average number of times the CEO's name was mentioned in each press release, and its logarithm was used because the measure was highly skewed. CEO's relative cash pay was the CEO's cash compensation (salary and bonus) divided by the second-highest-paid executive's cash compensation. CEO's relative non-cash pay was the sum of the CEO's deferred income, stock grants, and stock options divided by that of the second-highest-paid executive; logarithms were used for both pay measures. CEO succession years were excluded, the two-year average value of each indicator was calculated, and the simple mean of the standardized indicators was used as the primary measure.
time_window: two-year average, excluding CEO succession years

description: The sum of three major forms of risk-taking expenditures, in $billion, namely research and development, capital expenditures, and acquisitions. To account for the potential influence of industry affiliations, each firm's risk-taking spending was further subtracted from the corresponding industry average value in the same year. The primary measure is the average risk-taking expenditure of a firm in the two years following new director selection (year t+1 and year t+2, inclusive).

The same measure as the new director's similarity in narcissism, calculated as the opposite of the transformed absolute difference in narcissism between a new director and the focal CEO. Because the unit of analysis in testing Hypothesis 3 is firm-year, this director-level variable was averaged across multiple new directors when a given board selected more than one new director in a given year.
time_window: two-year average of each narcissism indicator, excluding CEO succession years

variable_name: New directors' prior experience with other similarly narcissistic CEOs
description: The same measure as the new director's prior experience with other similarly narcissistic CEOs, the percentage of similar CEOs among all CEOs who worked with the new director on other boards in the previous three years. Because the unit of analysis in testing Hypothesis 3 is firm-year, this director-level variable was averaged across multiple new directors if there were multiple new directors selected by a given board in a given year.

Materials variety is measured by the number of basic materials in a product line. Basic materials include steel, aluminum, titanium, and carbon fiber. The measure is built from the industry buyers' guide listing of bicycle products and specifications.

Geometry/size variety is measured by the number of different geometries in a product line multiplied by the average number of sizes per geometry. Frame geometries are computed as a function of three variables: the type of bicycle (road, mountain, bmx, tandem), whether or not the bicycle has rear suspension, and differences in the frame angles/tube length. Bicycles sharing the same value of each of these characteristics were coded as having the same frame.

Color and component variety are measured on a per model and per frame basis rather than on an aggregate basis, because once a frame is constructed colors and components may be shared across any frame. Color variety is represented by the average number of colors per model.

Component variety is measured on a per model and per frame basis rather than on an aggregate basis. Because of the high number of components used on a bicycle, the number of derailleurs is used as a proxy for component variety per model.

A firm is classified as being scale efficient if production volume at the production facilities exceeds 600,000 units and classified as scale inefficient otherwise. Independent studies of scale in the industry suggest plants reach minimum efficient scale between 150,000-200,000 units of annual production for one basic frame material, so that being scale efficient in multiple materials requires an additional 150,000-200,000 units of production volume per material. Production volumes associated with Asian facilities typically run in the millions of units per year, while U.S. plants do not produce enough units annually to reach minimum efficient scale in multiple materials.

A firm is classified as distant from the target market if over 50% of production for a given process (frame fabrication, frame painting, and assembly) is located outside North America, and local if production for a given process is located within North America. The authors justify the dichotomous variable because firms report that they do not split production evenly between the U.S. and Asia; on average, 90% of production occurs in one location or the other.

Matching of variety and location decisions is coded by placing firms into a four-quadrant matrix for each product attribute based on supply chain structure (scale-efficient/distant vs. scale-inefficient/local) and variety (high vs. low); a firm is classified in the high variety category if its level of variety with respect to a particular attribute exceeds the sample median. MATCH = materials match + geometry/size match + colors match + components match, where an attribute match = 1 if the firm matches the attribute to the supply chain structure according to the theory and 0 otherwise. For production-dominant variety (materials), a firm matches by offering high variety from a scale-efficient/distant plant or low variety from a scale-inefficient/local plant; for mediation-dominant variety (geometry/size, components, colors), a firm matches by offering high variety from a scale-inefficient/local plant or low variety from a scale-efficient/distant plant.

A perceived performance measure obtained by asking presidents, vice presidents, or marketing managers of firms to rate their overall performance with respect to industry competition on a 1-7 scale. The authors use perceived measures because public financial data is not available for many firms in the industry, and because firms were more willing to provide perceived financial performance data than actual financial data.

A perceived performance measure obtained by asking presidents, vice presidents, or marketing managers of firms to rate their overall performance with respect to industry competition on a 1-7 scale. The authors use perceived measures because public financial data is not available for many firms in the industry, and because firms were more willing to provide perceived financial performance data than actual financial data.

The proportion of directors, at the start of year t, whose biographical records indicated banking experience before joining the board. Such experience tended to be included in biographical records only if the person in question had previously reached at least the rank of Executive Vice President in a bank, so the variable captures the proportion of directors with substantial experience in the banking domain. The variable was time-variant and measured annually.
time_window: start of year t, updated annually

description: The proportion of directors whose biographical records indicated a background in the real estate domain (e.g., in real estate development and construction). Typical profiles included owners or top executives of real estate development and real estate investment companies. The variable was time-variant and measured annually.

A bank failure occurs when the FDIC intervenes in response to a bank's inability to satisfy its depository obligations. Intervention involves either liquidating the bank or acting as a broker between the focal bank and an acquiring bank that assumes its depository liability; if the FDIC cannot find a buyer, it may retain the bank's assets for later disposition and liquidate the failed bank after paying the required insurance amount directly to depositors. Information about bank failures was obtained from SNL Financial. All these outcomes occurred at the bank (rather than branch) level.
A bank's rate of asset growth, taken from financial data on the bank. The variable is lagged by one year in the models.

The amount of non-standard real estate loans, in millions of dollars, taken from financial data on the bank and lagged by one year. Non-standard real estate loans include land, construction and development loans, farm loans, large multifamily residential loans, and other non-residential or farming commercial real estate loans. Standard real estate loans involve smaller family residential properties (with one to four units).

The time-variant count of banks based in the focal bank's county. This measure is consistent with interviewees' accounts that emphasized locally-based banks as the primary direct competitors. To account for variation in the size of the market for banking services across counties, all regression models controlled for the dollar value of total deposits in the county, so the variable captures how many locally-based banks were competing with the focal bank for a given deposit base.

Composite index following Lee et al. (2011), calculated over a 5-year rolling window from six track-record components: the total number of portfolio companies a VC invested in, the total funds invested in portfolio firms, the average dollar amount of the total funds under management, the average number of individual funds raised, the number of portfolio firms taken public, and VC age in the focal year. Each component was z-score standardized before all the variables were added together. The resulting index was scaled so that the maximum value was 100.0 and the minimum value was 0.01 in any given year. The measure is lagged.

Measured based on the number of VC funds raised from LPs. Because market heat is a relative construct, the measure uses a lagged ratio of the number of VC funds raised each year at the industry level among US VC firms to the average number of VC funds raised in the antecedent 3 years. The natural log of the ratio is taken for symmetry and to ease understanding, as values above zero represent a 'hot' market while values below zero represent a 'cold' market. The formula block in the paper is unreadable in the extracted text.
scale: natural log of a ratio (above zero = hot, below zero = cold)

description: A VC's recent successes are measured by the number of portfolio companies that have gone public (had an IPO) in the last year. The authors chose IPOs over acquisitions because acquisitions have a heavy left tail of unprofitable exits and a lower correlation with fund performance than IPOs. The measure focuses on IPOs in the 1-year window immediately preceding the focal year, and the natural log of one plus all IPOs is taken to correct for skewness.
scale: natural log of one plus count
time_window: 1-year window immediately preceding the focal year

description: Binary dependent variable capturing whether a VC firm raises one or more new funds in a particular year. A value of one indicates that a VC both sought to raise a fund and completed raising it ('closed' it) in that year.

Continuous measure of the total capital raised in a given year for a VC's investment funds, measured in millions of dollars. Given the use of a zero-inflated negative binomial estimation approach, the measure was rounded to the nearest whole number in millions and assigned a value of zero in years that a VC firm did not raise any new capital for its funds. Eighteen fundraising events were for amounts less than 500k and were consequently rounded down to zero; these were not included in the second-stage ZINB regression analysis.

Whether or not an electric utility adopted new wind power in a state, coded as 1 if the utility either built a new wind farm or committed to buying wind power from a new wind farm, and 0 otherwise. The authors constructed it from American Wind Energy Association data on all wind farms built across the United States, manually mapped to firm-level FERC data. It was coded for every utility, state, and year combination.

A count of the number of clean energy social movement organizations registered in the category 'Renewable Energy and Energy Conservation' within a given state and year, built from National Center for Charitable Statistics data. The authors describe it as capturing the size of the population of these SMOs and therefore the visibility of the movement towards energy concerns. The measure was subjected to a natural log transformation due to a pronounced positive skew in its distribution.

The annual total dollar spending on lobbying efforts by environmental SMOs in a state, created from National Center for Charitable Statistics data. The authors describe it as a proxy for the efforts of SMOs to bring about regulatory changes that could have important repercussions for local firms. The measure was subjected to a natural log transformation due to a pronounced positive skew in its distribution.

The cumulative number of megawatts (MW) of wind power that a utility's competitors (all other utilities that operate in a focal utility's state) have committed to in prior years (t - 1). The authors built this measure from American Wind Energy Association data on wind energy projects. The measure was subjected to a natural log transformation due to a pronounced positive skew in its distribution.

The proportion of a firm's total revenue obtained from a focal market, in this case from a particular state; it takes a value of 1 for utilities that have 100 percent of their sales in the focal state. The authors used utility sales data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration to construct this measure.

Dummy variable that takes the value 1 if any of the managers reported in ExecuComp for a given firm in a given year is female, and 0 if none is. The authors adopt this operationalization because the fraction of firms with a single woman on the top management team never reaches a third in any year and the number of firms with more than one woman never exceeds 8.5 percent. The managers reported in ExecuComp are taken to be a firm's top management team.

Ratio of the market value of a firm's assets to their replacement value, calculated following Bertrand and Schoar (2003): market value is the book value of a firm's assets plus the market value of the firm's common equity minus the book value of common equity and deferred taxes, and replacement value is the book value of the firm's assets. The authors use a log transformation of Tobin's q in the analysis to reduce skewness.

Ratio of research and development (R&D) expense to assets from the prior year. The variable is log transformed to reduce skewness, and a value of 0 is imputed when R&D expense is not separately disclosed. It is included as a control and interacted with female representation to test Hypothesis 2.

Firm performance is measured as the firm's return on assets (ROA). The authors argue this measure is appropriate because stakeholder attacks may affect both firm revenues (e.g., lower sales owing to boycotts or a lower reputation) and firm costs (e.g., lawsuits or more stringent regulatory requirements). An alternative variable, return on sales, provided very similar results (available on request).

The TRI database documents facility-level emissions for each regulated chemical, and facilities are matched to firms through the parent company identifier. A firm's annual emissions of a given chemical are calculated by aggregating the emissions of the facilities associated with its parent company. Change in chemical use is the difference in the amount of chemical emissions by a firm's facilities from year t to year t + 1, and only observations in which the firm had the exact same facilities in year t and year t + 1 are retained.

At the firm level, chemical stigma is calculated as the average stigma on all the chemicals used by a firm in a given year. The list of chemicals used by a firm is derived from the product markets in which the firm is active: for each product market, the chemicals used by all TRI facilities belonging to that same four-digit SIC product market, including facilities with missing parent company identifiers, are identified. Each chemical's stigma is the natural logarithm of the number of negative articles published in the previous three years on that chemical.

At the chemical level, chemical stigma is the natural logarithm of the number of negative articles published in the previous three years on the given chemical. Using the Factiva search engine, the authors identified full-text articles in the five top-selling U.S. newspapers in which the name of each toxic chemical appeared in the headline and/or the first paragraph. Each article was coded as neutral, positive, or negative; of the 2,909 articles, 75.5% were coded as negative and used to generate the measure.

For each product market, the aggregated annual emissions by all facilities belonging to that four-digit SIC product market are calculated for each of the 347 regulated toxic chemicals, giving a 347-dimension vector per product market and year. Those vectors are used to create a pairwise overlap score between two product markets; the authors state that this score varied between 0 and 1, with 1 representing the greatest overlap. A sales-weighted firm-level measure of chemical overlap is then calculated from the overlap scores of all possible combinations of two product-market categories in a firm's portfolio and the percentage of firm sales in each product market. The equation specifications are not readable in the payload.

For each product market, the aggregated annual emissions by all facilities belonging to that four-digit SIC product market are calculated for each of the 347 regulated toxic chemicals, giving a 347-dimension vector per product market and year. Those vectors are used to create a pairwise overlap score between two product markets; the authors state that this score varied between 0 and 1, with 1 representing the greatest overlap. A sales-weighted firm-level measure of chemical overlap is then calculated from the overlap scores of all possible combinations of two product-market categories in a firm's portfolio and the percentage of firm sales in each product market. The equation specifications are not readable in the payload.

Assessed by identifying and manually coding the last five years of managing officers' and board members' employment and board memberships listed in the firms' final prospectuses. A tie counted when an upper echelon member had at least one affiliation with a prominent research organization during the year the company went public; prominence was coded from the Gourman Report's top-10 rankings in microbiology/bacteriology, biochemistry, biology, biomedical engineering, molecular biology, cellular biology, molecular genetics, chemistry, and medicine, plus national government institutions such as the NIH and nonuniversity research institutions with a high ratio of grant money per employee. The measure was the total number of upper echelon members with at least one such affiliation; the tie measures were divided by upper echelon size to account for team size.
time_window: last five years before the IPO; coded for the year the company went public

description: Assessed by coding the last five years of managing officers' and board members' employment and board memberships from the final prospectuses. A tie counted when an upper echelon member had at least one affiliation with a prominent biotechnology company during the year the company went public; prominent biotechnology companies were the top 30 worldwide by revenues in each year from 1990 to 1996, yielding 38 companies. The measure was the total number of upper echelon members with at least one such affiliation, divided by upper echelon size.
time_window: last five years before the IPO; coded for the year the company went public

description: Assessed by coding the last five years of managing officers' and board members' employment and board memberships from the final prospectuses. A tie counted when an upper echelon member had at least one affiliation with a prominent pharmaceutical and/or healthcare organization during the year the company went public; prominence was based on the top 30 organizations by sales in each IPO year from COMPUSTAT, supplemented with private or European and Japanese companies with comparable sales listed in PharmaBusiness. The measure was the total number of upper echelon members with at least one such affiliation, divided by upper echelon size.
time_window: last five years before the IPO; coded for the year the company went public

description: Measured two ways. First, a variation of the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (equivalent to Blau's index of heterogeneity) in which p is the percentage of individuals with affiliations with prominent institutions in each of the three categories; the variable was set to zero when the upper echelon had no relevant affiliations. Second, as the count, from 0 to 3, of the number of affiliation categories (upstream, horizontal, and downstream) covered by the career experiences of the firm's upper echelon; the heterogeneity and count measures correlated above 0.90, and the count measure is the one reported in the tables.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Investment bank prestige was measured using the Carter and Manaster (1990) index updated by Carter et al. (1998), built from investment banks' positions in tombstone announcements for IPOs. In brief, the authors assigned the highest integer rank (9) to the first-listed underwriter, the second-highest rank (8) to the next-listed underwriter(s), and so on, shifting underwriters down as new banks superseded them, with decimal increments when more than 10 categories were needed; scores range from 0 (lowest prestige) to 9 (highest prestige). The name of the lead investment bank was obtained from the front page of the final prospectuses.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The company sections of the prospectuses were reviewed to determine how advanced the firm's technology was, coding the product at the latest stage into nine categories (discovery stage, research and development, preclinical indication, Phases I-III clinical trials, new drug approval filing/FDA approval pending, final market approval, and revenue generating). The authors then used a three-category classification of the lead product: preclinical stages (coded 1), clinical stages (coded 2), or postclinical stages (coded 3); lower numbers (earlier stages of development) indicate higher technological uncertainty. The use-of-proceeds section was examined to confirm the lead product was designated to receive the most significant funding.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

variable_name: Upper echelon upstream, horizontal and downstream affiliations
description: Affiliations of managing officers and board members with prominent organizations, coded from final prospectuses into three types: upstream (research institutions), horizontal (biotechnology firms) and downstream (pharmaceutical and healthcare organizations). Each is the number of upper echelon members with at least one such affiliation divided by upper echelon size.

Five-item scale adapted from Miller et al. (1998), rated on a five-point response scale from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.' A sample item is 'The new product project members developed many alternative courses of action to achieve intended objectives.' Coefficient alpha was .82 and composite reliability was reported in the correlation table.

Four-item subjective measure for new product performance (alpha = .79) rated on a format ranging from 1, 'low,' to 5, 'high.' Informants rated a new product's degree of success relative to those of competitors' products on sales growth, market share growth, growth in profit, and return on investment.

Key informants reported the sales growth rate for the new product in each of the last three years, and the average of these rates was calculated as the measure of performance. Sales growth had a positive correlation with the subjective new product performance measure (r = .28, p < .01), indicating the validity of the subjective measure.

Five-item scale (alpha = .81) asking informants to assess the degree to which they agreed with questions about the new product's quality, rated on a five-point response scale from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.' A sample item is 'The product was perceived by customers as more reliable than competitors' products.'

Four-item scale (alpha = .80) tapping the perceived speed and magnitude of change and uncertainty in technology and the variety of new product introductions afforded by changing technology in the industry. Measures were adapted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993) and rated on the five-point response scale used for the other noncontrol variables.
level: industry as perceived by the project team

description: Three-item scale (alpha = .64) reflecting the speed of change in customer demand, product preferences and emergence of new customer segments in the industry. Measures were adapted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993) and rated on the same five-point response scale as the other noncontrol variables.
level: industry as perceived by the project team

description: Announcements of product introduction delays identified from the Wall Street Journal and Dow Jones News Service from 1987 to 2003 using key words such as 'product and introduction' together with words such as 'delay, reschedule, and postpone'. Follow-up announcements about a previously announced delay are not treated as separate events because the earlier announcement and its date are kept. If a firm made multiple delay announcements involving different products within three years of each other, the more recent announcements are excluded to avoid overlapping time periods.
time_window: 1987-2003; fiscal year of the announcement is event year 0

variable_name: Abnormal change in the level of ROA
description: Abnormal operating performance is the sample firm's actual performance minus its expected performance if the delay had not happened. Expected performance is the sample firm's performance in the base year (year -2) plus the change in the median performance of the comparison group over the period of interest. Performance is measured over the three-year period from year -2 to year 1 and abnormal performance is estimated with three comparison groups: performance-industry-matched, performance-industry-size-matched, and performance-size-matched. Results are reported after symmetrically capping the data at the 2.5% level in each tail.

variable_name: Abnormal change in the level of SOA
description: Abnormal change in sales over assets, computed as the sample firm's actual SOA minus its expected SOA, where expected SOA is the base-year (year -2) SOA plus the change in the median SOA of the comparison group over the three-year period. Estimated with the performance-industry-matched, performance-industry-size-matched, and performance-size-matched comparison groups. Results are reported after symmetrically capping the data at the 2.5% level in each tail.

variable_name: Abnormal change in the level of ROS
description: Abnormal change in return on sales, computed as the sample firm's actual ROS minus its expected ROS, where expected ROS is the base-year (year -2) ROS plus the change in the median ROS of the comparison group over the three-year period. Estimated with the performance-industry-matched, performance-industry-size-matched, and performance-size-matched comparison groups. Results are reported after symmetrically capping the data at the 2.5% level in each tail.
Firm size is measured as the natural logarithm of sales in year -2 (the base year). It is entered in the cross-sectional regressions of abnormal ROA over the three-year period.

Industry financial attractiveness is measured with two variables. Industry size is measured as the natural log of industry sales in year -2, and industry median ROA is measured as the median ROA of the industry in year -2. A sample firm's industry is defined as all firms that have the same three-digit SIC code as the sample firm.

The sample firm's industry-adjusted performance, measured as its ROA in year -2 minus the median ROA of its industry in year -2. It is entered in the cross-sectional regressions of abnormal ROA, separately for profit-making and loss-making firms through interactions with the PROA and NROA indicators.

Indicator variables with value equal to 1 if the sample firm's ROA in year -2 is positive (PROA) or negative (NROA), and 0 otherwise. The variable for profit-making firms is defined as IADPER * PROA and the variable for loss-making firms as IADPER * NROA, allowing the response coefficients of profit- and loss-making firms to differ.

Score equals 0 when no goal-compliant disclosure appears in the firm's annual report, 1 when environmental issues are tackled in vague and broad terms, 2 when the information is specific to the firm and gives precise information about the environmental dimension at stake, and 3 when the information is firm specific and illustrated by qualitative or quantitative examples, or both. The score was built at the level of the communication medium, taking into account potentially varied or diverging disclosures within a single report; when disclosures of different quality levels appear within one report, the highest score is retained.

Score for goal-compliant disclosures located in stand-alone reports. Equals 0 when there is no such disclosure in the firm's stand-alone report and 1 when the environmental information disclosed consists of qualitative data with few metrics; equals 2 when the stand-alone report contains metrics that track multiyear trends and either provide background information or use a Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) disclosing procedure; equals 3 if the metrics track multiyear trends and provide background information and the firm either discloses its environmental information following the GRI procedure or discusses its listing in the Dow Jones Sustainability Index.

Coded from the least preferred option (0) to the most desirable option (3). Equals 0 when a simple mention is made of an environmental incident, notice of violation, or fine without any other contextual element; 1 when the incident is qualitatively described but without mention of corrective actions; 2 when the report includes qualitative mentions of the incident and a detailed discussion of corrective actions; and 3 when the absence of disclosures mentioning environmental damages is coded, because the highest preference is for a firm not to increase its ecological footprint.

Binary variable for goal-noncompliant disclosures located in annual reports, which were systematically located in financial statements or 10-K reports and took the form of short mentions of environmental fines and penalties for failing to conform to environmental regulations. Equals 0 when no such disclosures are made and 1 when such disclosures are present; an ordinal measure could not be derived from these data.

Raw score of reputation, i.e., the score averaged across the eight dimensions of Fortune magazine's reputation survey, which is based on the answers of some 10,000 executives, directors, and financial analysts asked to rate Fortune 1000 firms in their industry. Each dimension is rated on an 11-point scale (0 = poor, 10 = excellent) and the averaged aggregation of the eight scores determines the firm's overall reputation score, similarly ranging from 0 to 10. The prior year's reputation score is included in the models so that the coefficients of the independent variables indicate year-to-year effects on reputational change.

Intra-industry relative positioning measure based on Fortune magazine's published ranking of firms within each industry. The authors created an inverted ranking ranging from 10 for the top-ranked firm in a given industry to 0 for the lowest-ranked, so that covariates that enhance reputation have positive signs for both dependent measures. The prior year's rank is included in the models.

The firm's reputation score or ranking in the previous year, included in the models following prior studies that investigate changes in reputation, so that the coefficients of the independent variables indicate their year-to-year effects on reputational change. It is used both as a covariate capturing the path-dependent effect between prior and current reputation and, mean-centered, in interaction terms with the four conforming behaviors.

The authors identify all clients of a law firm during the 3 years prior to the application of the focal patent and merge on the firm-to-firm product similarities, derived from textual product descriptions in 10-K filings, for each focal firm–client pair; the similarity measure is the pairwise cosine similarity of the texts, ranging from 0 to 1. Firms similar to the focal patent's assigning firm receive more weight through the Shepard transformation, which has properties similar to an exponential decay curve; the specification itself is given in an equation that is not readable in this text. The authors set gamma = 7 in their preferred operationalization. They sum the transformed similarities, take the natural log, and divide the measure by its standard deviation; high values indicate law firms that have worked with many of the focal firm's competitors as well as with its closest competitors.
time_window: 3 years prior to the focal patent application

description: Law firm choice is binary, denoting whether or not the client–patent-law firm pair has been observed, thereby indicating a realized choice. For each patent, the variable takes on the value one when the law firm was chosen to work on the patent and zero for the matched law firm that was not chosen. Each patent i appears in two observations: one paired with a hypothetical law firm and the other with the actual law firm that handled the patent.

To test how prior interactions moderate the effect of competitive overlap on law firm choice, the authors identify whether a prior relationship exists between the patenting firm and the law firm. The variable takes the value one if a client's prior patent was handled by the law firm. It distinguishes initial interactions from those in which the client has first-hand, prior experience with the law firm.

To test the effect of industry maturity, the authors interact their main predictors with technology age, measured as the average age of patents in the same two-digit USPC category. The variable varies at the level of the patent.

To test the effect of the relatedness of the patenting firm's prior technology, the authors interact their main predictors with technology similarity, a measure of a patent's proximity to a client's prior work. They calculate the Jensen–Shannon distance to the 10 closest patent applications of the same client over the past 3 years, accounting for large clients' diverse expertise, and normalize this measure (0–1) within each client. Values closer to 0 represent distant technologies, while values closer to 1 represent similar patents.

Dependent variable coded 1 if the organization failed during the time period studied and 0 otherwise. Failures included completed bankruptcies, completed liquidations, closures based on company request, and merger or acquisition of organizations at risk of bankruptcy. For mergers, the authors used the Z-score multivariate financial model; if an organization that entered a merger had a Z-score indicating a high probability of bankruptcy (Z < 1.81) it was coded as a failure, and mergers that did not have a high probability of bankruptcy were treated as right censored after the merger date.

Organizations were dummy coded 0 if independent and 1 if a subsidiary organization. Consistent with Swedish law, subsidiaries indicated their parent corporations' name and identifying number in audited statements submitted to the Swedish government.

Following prior work, financial slack is measured as the difference between current assets and current liabilities. It describes short-term resource accessibility, indicating whether a firm is keeping excess resources that are not put into productive use (positive financial slack) or fueling growth that may include short-term deficits (negative financial slack). The authors note this measure is highly correlated (alpha = 0.99) with George's (2005) 'transient slack' measure.

Number of employees, used as one of the organizational resource measures. The authors experimented with using both the absolute number of employees and the logarithm of employees; the resulting models did not differ in fit, and results are reported based on number of employees for ease of interpretation.
Nonliquid assets required for operations, including facilities, equipment, and real property.
Equity was the owner's reported equity in the business, calculated as total assets minus total liabilities.

Dummy variable coded 1 for the economic downturn years of 2001 and 2002 and 0 otherwise. The authors describe the global economic downturn as beginning toward the end of 2000 and continuing through early 2003, with the drop in stock prices mirrored by a decline in production and in new orders across the studied industries. Additional analysis based on defining the jolt period as 2001 through 2003 did not substantially alter the results.

The total number of nominations a theater obtains in the annual Golden Mask festival. The festival program includes productions selected by two boards of experts (one for drama and one for musical theater) as nominations for the award. The number of nominations indicates the extent of a theater's recognition by its peers, that is, the amount of symbolic capital peers are willing to grant.

variable_name: Salience of the stakeholder relationship (number of corporate donors)
description: The total number of corporate donors a theater has in a given year, used to capture the salience of the ties with negatively perceived stakeholders outside the field. Information on corporate partners is public and displayed on a theater's official website and in social media. The variable is continuous and endogenous, and is predicted in a first stage using the percentage of profitable firms and the density of theaters in a region as instruments.

variable_name: Breadth of the relationship (type of collaboration)
description: An independent dichotomous variable capturing the breadth of the stakeholder relationship through the type of pursued collaboration: project-centric collaboration is coded as 0 and institution-centric collaboration is coded as 1. Theaters make discrete either/or choices over the type of collaboration, to save possible transaction and legal costs of a hybrid strategy. The variable is interacted with the number of donors a theater has in a given year.

variable_name: Depth of the relationship (longevity of support)
description: The longest tie with a corporate donor in a theater's portfolio, measured in years of collaboration. Most durable corporate donors usually obtain the status of general partners or general donors and their relationship with a theater is publicized more persistently, creating lasting associations in the public sphere and among peers. The variable is interacted with the number of donors.

variable_name: Valence of the relationship (donors from tainted industries)
description: The number of corporate donors a theater has from mining and extraction (predominantly oil and gas) industries in a given period, capturing the adverse valence of the relationship with the extraneous stakeholder group. The count variable is interacted with the number of corporate donors.

A firm-level classification of a courier's market position: a courier is a document specialist when 90 percent or more of the parcels it carries are documents and a package specialist when 90 percent or more are packages; couriers with between 10 percent and 90 percent documents are full service, the omitted category. DocSpec is coded 1 when a courier is a document specialist and 0 otherwise; PackSpec is coded 1 when a courier is a package specialist and 0 otherwise. Because the authors were unable to ascertain each firm's annual document-package mix, these percentages were calculated from their database of 995 parcels.

Count indices, one per transportation segment, that count the pieces of parcel-level data available from a courier's information network for domestic trucking, international air, and foreign trucking, built from a package-level survey developed with the IPTP for each segment and each route. The indices increase by one for each piece of parcel-level data collected and range from 0, indicating no data are available from the courier's information network, to 7, 8, or 7 for domestic trucking, international air, and foreign trucking respectively. The authors assume that the level of idiosyncratic IT is positively correlated with the amount of real-time information collected in each transportation segment, since financial data on idiosyncratic IT per segment were unavailable.

Organizational choice for each of the three transportation segments (domestic trucking, international air transit, foreign trucking), collected by interviewing each participating courier and then mapping onto each parcel the courier's organizational structure according to origination and destination cities. The existence of any equity relationship between the freight forwarder and the transportation segment is classified as vertically integrated and coded 1; the absence of an equity relation is classified as contracting out and coded 0.
level: parcel (courier transportation segment for a city pair)

description: Net delivery time in days, computed from the parcel pick-up time at the place of origin and the parcel drop-off time at the destination. Because of kurtosis in the data, the authors took the natural logarithm of net delivery time to form lnDays.

Five-item measure adapted from Kale et al.'s (2000) relational capital scale, assessing the extent of close personal interaction at multiple levels, mutual reciprocity, mutual trust, mutual respect, and personal friendship among members of the project team. Items use five-point Likert scales (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree). Individual responses were aggregated to project-level construct scores as simple averages, justified by within-project interrater agreement.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Three-item scale adapted from Campion, Medsker, and Higgs (1993) tapping the degree to which the tie portfolio spans structural holes, i.e., the diversity of experiences, backgrounds, skills, and expertise among members of each project alliance. Items use five-point Likert scales (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree). Individual responses were aggregated to project-level scores as simple averages.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: New scale developed through an iterative, multistep procedure drawing on tacit knowledge inventories, conceptual descriptions of knowledge integration, and qualitative case descriptions. Three retained items measure individual perceptions of knowledge integration at the project level by assessing the extent to which participants synthesized their knowledge and skills in a coherent project-level design. Items use five-point Likert scales (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree) and individual responses were aggregated to project-level scores.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Computed as the product of alignment with project alliance objectives and adaptation to new information that emerged over the course of the project, following Gibson and Birkinshaw's (2004) operationalization. The alignment dimension was measured with five items, of which three were retained after exploratory factor analysis; the adaptation dimension used three items. Items use five-point Likert scales (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree), and data were collected from the senior managers responsible for each project.
scale: product of two five-point Likert-based dimension scores
time_window: over the course of the project

description: The authors identify and count all institutional investors who have a blockholding stake (more than 5 percent of outstanding shares) in both an industry rival and the media company owning the outlet; investors that simultaneously own the focal firm, its rivals, and a media company are excluded. The authors state that the variable multiplies common owners' total ownership stakes in rival firms by their ownership stake in the media company; the equation itself is not readable in the text. Ownership-related variables are averaged over the year.

Annual average of the Event Sentiment Score (ESS) of all news articles about the firm reported by the outlet in the year, retaining only articles with a RavenPack relevance score of 100 so that the firm is the central focus of the article. The ESS ranges from 0 to 100 and is generated by RavenPack through traditional language analysis, expert consensus and market response analysis. The authors subtracted the annual ESS average from 100 and scaled by 100, so the measure ranges from 0 to 1, where higher values indicate more negative media coverage.

Calculated with the TNIC-3 as the average product similarity score between a firm and its rivals with Media-rival CIO. TNIC-3 identifies pairs of competitors from the text of firms' product descriptions in their 10-K filings by comparing binary vectors of word usage, and the reported score indicates the amount by which a pair's pairwise similarity exceeds the 21.32 percent threshold used to classify rivals.

Geographic operations were obtained by using a computer algorithm to extract state names from firms' 10-K filings in EDGAR. The geographic market overlap ratio between a focal firm and each rival with Media-rival CIO is the number of states where both firms compete divided by the total number of states where the focal firm competes; the measure is the average of these ratios between a firm and its rivals with Media-rival CIO.

Media-rival common blockholders are classified by their portfolio churn ratios, which capture the frequency of trading in their portfolios. The quarterly churn ratio is calculated for each common blockholder and averaged annually; owners with a churn ratio below the sample median are classified as long-term. Media-rival CIO is then calculated for this group of investors as Media-rival long-term CIO.

Media-rival common blockholders are classified by their portfolio churn ratios, which capture the frequency of trading in their portfolios; owners with a churn ratio above the sample median are classified as short-term. Media-rival CIO is then calculated for this group of investors as Media-rival short-term CIO, and its coefficient is compared with that of Media-rival long-term CIO.

Measured as the ratio of the value of a media company CEO's annual awarded stocks and options to their total annual compensation, obtained from ExecuComp. The authors focus on the compensation of media CEOs because CEOs are the most important decision makers in companies.

Indicator variable equal to 1 if the firm includes TVRs in the corporate charter in year t and 0 otherwise. Data on the adoption of TVRs were hand-collected from the CONSOB website. TVRs grant double voting rights to shares held by the same shareholder for at least 2 years after registration, and adoption requires a modification of the corporate charter by shareholder agreement.

Family control indicator equal to 1 if one or more family members hold 25% or more of issued equity and 0 otherwise, in line with Leitterstorf and Rau (2014). The authors start from the European Central Bank definition of family enterprise and exclude cases of lone-founded firms from the family group, treating them as nonfamily firms in the main tests. Family ownership data are drawn from Orbis, CONSOB and individual firms' annual reports, and the authors state that an indicator variable facilitates economic interpretation.

Aggregate measure of investment equal to the sum of capital expenditure, R&D expenditure, and acquisitions, scaled by lagged total assets. It is the dependent variable in the empirical tests. Financial and market data used to build it are collected from the Refinitiv Eikon database.

variable_name: Fragile family firm / Dominant family firm
description: Two indicator variables replace Family firm in the heterogeneity tests: Fragile family firm, equal to 1 when family ownership is lower than 50% (family control is fragile), and Dominant family firm, equal to 1 when family ownership is greater than or equal to 50% (family control is dominant). Both are interacted with TVR in the regressions for family firms.

Dummy variable that measures whether the idea for the invention occurred during the employee's leisure time or work time. It is based on the PatVal survey question asking which scenario describes best the creative process that led to the invention, where the answer 'I got the idea underlying this invention during my leisure time' defines a leisure time invention. Of the inventions in the sample, 6% were the result of a leisure time insight.

Dummy variable taking the value of 1 if the patent was classified as being in the chemicals/pharmaceuticals industry and 0 otherwise, used as a proxy for the nature of the technical problem to be solved (science-based or conceptually based). The measure is based on the technical class to which the European Patent Office assigns an invention, using the six main technical areas proposed by the German Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research (FhG-ISI) and the French Intellectual Property Institute (INPI). Inventions in chemicals and pharmaceuticals (also including biotechnology) are assumed to be more science dependent than inventions in other technical fields.

Dummy variable taking the value of 1 where the respondent regarded interactions with people who work in the same organization (apart from the coinventors listed on the patent) as important for making the invention and 0 if not. Importance was measured on a six-point Likert scale, and the intervals 1 'not important at all' and 2 'not important' were sorted into the category 0. This is the first of two categories of meetings or discussions with others distinguished in the survey.
scale: dummy (0/1) derived from a six-point Likert scale

description: Dummy variable taking the value of 1 where the respondent regarded interactions with people from outside the organization as important for getting the main insight underlying the invention and 0 if not. The second of the two categories of interactions distinguished in the survey, it serves as a proxy for weak ties. Importance was measured on a six-point Likert scale, and the intervals 1 'not important at all' and 2 'not important' were sorted into the category 0.
scale: dummy (0/1) derived from a six-point Likert scale

description: Ordinal-scaled variable generated from the total labor input needed for the project, taking values between 1 and 7 according to the intervals less than 1 man-month, 1-3 man-months, 4-6 man-months, 7-12 man-months, 13-24 man-months, 25-48 man-months, and more than 48 man-months. In the survey, the size of the project was requested ex post, so ideas not further developed in an R&D project and projects stopped very early are characterized by a lower labor input.

Dummy variable taking the value of 1 in cases where coinventors from organizations other than the respondent's organization were involved in the project leading to the invention. It forms a proxy for weak ties and was included because such coinventors were explicitly excluded from the two variables describing interactions with other people.

Built from the text of job descriptions' duties and responsibilities sections. The text is preprocessed by converting words to lowercase and stripping endings, punctuation and nonalphabetic characters; each description in year t is a bag-of-words vector weighted by corpus frequency times inverse job frequency, with words occurring fewer than three times excluded. Cosine similarities between all pairs of jobs are computed for each year (25 job matrices), and for each job the measure sums the five largest similarity values, i.e., how much the job's tasks overlap with those of the five most related jobs. The score is approximately normally distributed with a mean of 2.85 and a standard deviation of 1.04.

A word-count measure built by scanning the full corpus of words from the job description data. The authors manually built a shorter list of explicit coordination words focusing on variants of 'collaborate,' 'coordinate,' 'interact,' 'liaise,' and 'team'; job descriptions with more such words entail more coordination with other jobs. Both the complete and the shorter word lists are reproduced in the online appendix.

A dichotomous indicator of whether a job dies in a given year. A job is coded as dead when the formal position is no longer occupied in any future period; for example, 'Apprentice Sign Painter,' first appearing in 1990, has no employees in 1993 or any following year through 2004 and is coded as having died at the end of 1992. The personnel data were used to double-check that the job was not simply renamed, so the measure excludes specious deaths such as a change from 'supervisor' to 'coordinator.'
For each job, the number of its five nearest neighbors, based on the task similarity measure, that died in the previous year.

Each employee's record lists the subunit of the university in which he or she works in a given year, and the authors coded when a subunit closed, visible by the disappearance of any employees in that subunit in later years. For each job-year they counted how many unique subunits where the job was performed closed. To test Hypotheses 5 and 6, this count is interacted with the measures of task overlap and task coordination.

Two items rated by the expatriates on a seven-point scale. The expatriates were asked to rate the extent to which the items accurately described expatriates as a whole in the subsidiary: (a) "Possess superior managerial (people) competencies (knowledge, skills, and experience) to solve difficulties in the knowledge transfer process" and (b) "Possess superior functional competencies (knowledge, skills, and experience) to solve difficulties in the knowledge transfer process" (alpha = .79). The mean within-group agreement (rwg) was .80, higher than the .70 level, so the expatriates' ratings were aggregated.

Five items rated by the expatriates on a seven-point scale, asking them to rate the extent to which the items accurately described expatriates as a whole in the subsidiary (alpha = .86). The statements captured the key components of motivation (direction, intensity, and persistence) while reflecting the expatriate knowledge transfer context. The mean rwg was .83, so the expatriates' ratings were aggregated.

Two items rated by the expatriates on a seven-point scale, asking them to rate the extent to which the items accurately described expatriates as a whole in the subsidiary (alpha = 0.81). The mean rwg exceeded .70, so the expatriates' ratings were aggregated.

Seven items rated by local managers on a seven-point scale (alpha = .87), taken from prior research and modified in light of the interview findings. Local managers indicated the amount of knowledge their subsidiaries received from expatriates in each of seven areas. The mean rwg was .78, so the local managers' ratings were aggregated.

Six items adapted from Jansen, Van Den Bosch, and Volberda (2005), rated by local managers on a seven-point scale (alpha = .87); local managers indicated the extent to which the statements accurately described their subsidiary's employees (excluding expatriates). Exploratory factor analysis indicated a one-factor solution with all loadings at .85 or higher, and the one-factor CFA fit the data well. The mean rwg was .82, so the local managers' ratings were aggregated.

Objective subsidiary return on investment for fiscal year 2009-10 obtained from the FAME and TEJ databases, giving a one-year time lag with the survey measures of expatriate competencies, subsidiary absorptive capacity, and knowledge received by subsidiary.

Objective subsidiary return on equity for fiscal year 2009-10 obtained from the FAME and TEJ databases, giving a one-year time lag with the survey measures of expatriate competencies, subsidiary absorptive capacity, and knowledge received by subsidiary.

Before the survey data collection, one author interviewed 60 expatriates and coded the interview data into categories guided by the ability-motivation-opportunity framework and prior research; three major categories emerged: expatriate ability, motivation, and opportunity seeking to solve difficulties in the knowledge transfer process. Intercoder agreement was .86. On this basis one of the authors developed survey items for expatriate competencies in knowledge transfer.

Interaction between a dummy indicating the periods after the introduction of Game Center and a dummy indicating games categories. Game Center let developers allow users to interact through multiplayer features and to share accomplishments on leaderboards, which the authors treat as increasing the strength of network effects, whereas before it Apple restricted developers' ability to facilitate user interaction. The coefficient on this interaction is the parameter that tests Hypothesis (H1).
time_window: 70 days before and 70 days after the introduction of Game Center

description: Indicator variable that reflects whether the market leader in a particular niche in that particular period uses freemium strategies. Freemium products are released for free (the price of the product is zero) but use in-app purchases to sell premium features, whereas paid-only products are sold for a fee. In the regressions the freemium indicator is interacted with Post GC and Games.
time_window: 70 days before and 70 days after the introduction of Game Center

variable_name: ln ( Total Daily Revenues of leader / Total Daily Revenues of follower )
description: The difference between the log-transformed daily revenues of the market leader (rank 1) and of the follower (rank 2) within a category. The authors use this relative performance measure to estimate the hypothesized relation between leaders and followers directly, noting that it has been used in previous studies.
time_window: 70 days before and 70 days after the introduction of Game Center

description: Daily product revenues of the market leader and the follower in each category-day, log-transformed with 1 added to the base of the logarithm to account for values close to zero. Revenues are imputed from Apple's revenue rankings, download rankings and daily pricing data using a method developed by Garg and Telang (2013), which estimates the relationship between revenue ranking, prices and download ranking and transforms the coefficient estimates into estimates of market share and revenues. Only ranking data from the United States are used.
time_window: 70 days before and 70 days after the introduction of Game Center

description: Products are ranked by daily revenue within a narrowly defined market category; the market leader is the product with the highest daily revenue (first ranked) and the follower is the second-ranked product. The regressions are estimated separately for leaders and followers, and the market categorization used for these rankings comes from an analytics company that classified apps using topic modeling and human inspection.
time_window: 70 days before and 70 days after the introduction of Game Center

description: Eight international equity mutual fund managers were each asked to rate, on a seven-point scale, the extent to which CEOs of public firms headquartered in each of 15 countries possess managerial discretion, with a 'not sure' option. The rubric defined discretion as 'latitude of managerial action,' or the extent to which CEOs are able to influence the actions and outcomes of their firm. The eight panelists provided 97 country ratings, with each country receiving between four and eight ratings, and the measure is the mean rating per country; the intraclass coefficient ICC(3,k) was 0.93.

The independent variable was the expert panelists' country-level rating of managerial discretion, as reported in the national-level discretion scores. Each panelist was treated as a single fixed effect to control for potential unobserved heterogeneity between panelists.

Hofstede's (2001) score for individualism, generated through ecological factor analysis, so that the scores are reflections of national-level values rather than the values of the average member in a society.
Created as the reverse of Hofstede's (2001) uncertainty avoidance score, i.e., the negative value of the raw score.
Hofstede's (2001) score for power distance, generated through ecological factor analysis of national-level values.

Operationalized as the reverse of Gelfand and colleagues' national-level scores for cultural tightness, whose sample item is 'People agree upon what behaviors are appropriate vs. inappropriate in most situations in this country.' For three countries the original research did not collect scores, so looseness was imputed based on geographical-historical proximity: Canada received the same score as the United States, Sweden the same score as Norway, and Switzerland the mean of France, Germany, and Italy.

Built from La Porta et al.'s (1999) proportions of firms that were widely held, where a firm was considered widely held if no shareholder's direct and indirect control rights exceeded a threshold. These authors generated the proportion four ways: for two control thresholds, 10 percent and 20 percent, and two groups of firms, medium-sized and large firms. The ownership dispersion measure is the mean of these four proportions.
La Porta et al.'s (1999) common-law vs. civil-law dichotomy. Each country was designated as having either a common-law legal tradition (coded as 1) or a civil-law legal tradition (coded as 0).

Operationalized from Estevez-Abe et al.'s (2001) index of employment protection, which was constructed using three factors: employment protection legislation, collective dismissals protection, and company-based protection. That data provide the index for 12 of the 15 countries; scores for Korea, Singapore, and Spain were imputed based on their raw scores on Botero et al.'s (2004) 'employment laws index.' Because the source index measures employment protection, higher values represent less protection and thus greater employer flexibility.

Estimated with a four-level nested HLM model of years (level 1) within CEOs (level 2) within firms (level 3) within industries (level 4) run for each of four performance measures in each of the 15 countries. The 'CEO effect' for a given performance indicator is the variance of the CEO-level term divided by total firm variance in a country. Because each performance measure is only a partial indicator of overall performance, the overall index of CEO effects is the sum of standardized z-scores of the four narrower measures.

Measured as an ordinal variable with three categories based on the unit to which the manager belongs. Managers belonging to the gas unit were assigned to category 0 (low distance), managers belonging to the oil unit were assigned to category 1 (intermediate distance), and managers belonging to corporate headquarters were assigned to category 2 (high distance). Thus a higher value of the variable indicates higher shock distance.

Measured using two seven-point Likert items to capture how strongly each participant perceived the firm as having the resources and capabilities, respectively, required to deal with the coming natural gas deregulation. Cronbach alpha for this scale was 0.73. Because moderating effects are tested, the capability perception variable was mean-centered.

Measured using three items related to 'gain (loss) implications,' 'positive (negative) event,' and 'opportunity (threat).' Participants responded to a seven-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (completely disagree) to 7 (completely agree). Cronbach alpha reliability was 0.86 for the opportunity scale.

Measured using three items related to 'gain (loss) implications,' 'positive (negative) event,' and 'opportunity (threat).' Participants responded to a seven-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (completely disagree) to 7 (completely agree). Cronbach alpha reliability was 0.76 for the threat scale.

A dummy variable was created for domain-specific experience (1 if the manager has experience in the gas business, and 0 otherwise). The variable refers to a manager having versus not having experience in the domain (industry) associated with the focal shock, natural gas. The variable does not address in any way the valence of the experience.

Our main predictor captures the depth and breadth of a director's prior experiences with different firms, industries, and dominant strategies. Depth is assessed by first examining the number of years of experience a director has had in each of these different domains, with a three-year minimum threshold applied to ensure the temporal depth required to translate experience to expertise. The number of in-depth experiences is then summed across the three domains (firms, industries, and strategies) for each director. Director strategy scores are generated from 10-K reports of the firms where the director had worked.
time_window: Director's prior career up to appointment

description: This indicator is operationalized as the sum of the absolute differences between a firm's strategic emphases scores on each of the seven generic strategies at t+1 and t0. Strategic emphases scores are seven-point Likert scores produced by automated coding of 10-K reports against a dictionary of terms reflecting each business-level tactic, aggregated to the level of the seven generic strategies.
scale: sum of absolute differences in seven-point Likert scores
time_window: t0 to t+1 (year after a new outside director is appointed)

description: This indicator is operationalized as the difference between (a) the squared root of the squared difference between the firm's Likert score on strategy Si at t0 and the director's Likert score on strategy Si at t0 and (b) the squared root of the squared difference between the firm's Likert score on strategy Si at t1 and the director's Likert score on strategy Si at t0, where strategy Si denotes the strategy in the director's portfolio that has the highest Likert score. A higher positive value means that the firm shifts its strategic emphasis at t+1 in a direction closer to the director's strategic emphasis at t0.
time_window: t0 to t+1 (year after a new outside director is appointed)

description: Board turnover is defined as the number of directors leaving the board during the year divided by the total number of board members at the beginning of the year. The natural logarithm of this indicator is used.
Board tenure heterogeneity is calculated as the variance of member tenures on the board, divided by the mean of tenures. The natural logarithm of this indicator is used.

We measure a firm's time to market for a given DRAM generation as 1 plus the difference in the number of quarters (three-month periods) between the first shipment by the firm and first shipment in the industry. Hence, the first firm that commercializes the new generation takes the value of 1, and a firm that commercializes the generation three quarters after the first firm takes a value of 4.
scale: quarters since first industry shipment, plus 1

description: The binary choice variable outsource mask takes a value of 1 if the DRAM firm outsourced the production of mask technology and a value of 0 if the firm is vertically integrated into mask technology in the year prior to its commercialization of the new DRAM generation.

The variables mask knowledge and resist knowledge are operationalized as the number of successful mask- and resist-related patent applications, respectively, filed by a DRAM firm in the three years preceding the firm's commercialization of a new DRAM generation. Patent subclass 430/5 was identified as the key technology subclass for mask technology.

Number of successful resist-related patent applications filed by a DRAM firm in the three years preceding the firm's commercialization of a new DRAM generation. Patent subclasses 430/270.1, 430/191a, 430/192a, 430/326, 430/325, 430/281.1, 430/190, and 430/311 were identified as key technology subclasses for resist technology.
We defined the variable architectural innovation as taking a value of 1 if the new DRAM generation is enabled by an architectural change and 0 if it is enabled by component change.

Middle managers' facilitating adaptability was measured with three items using a seven-point Likert scale adapted from Floyd and Wooldridge (1992a), anchored by 1 = strongly disagree and 7 = strongly agree. The data are self-reported by the middle managers.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Middle managers' championing alternatives was measured with two items using a seven-point Likert scale adapted from Floyd and Wooldridge (1992a), anchored by 1 = strongly disagree and 7 = strongly agree. The data are self-reported by the middle managers.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Business unit performance is operationalized as a formative construct by averaging the z-scores of (1) sales as a percentage of quota; (2) year-over-year growth percentage of total sales; and (3) a new customer productivity ratio, which measures the percentage of one's customer base that consists of newly acquired customers. These objective performance measures were attained from the company's records and aggregated to the sales district level.

Middle managers were asked to identify at least three sales directors and three peer middle managers whom they go to for advice; these names were double-checked against the company roster for accuracy and coded with unique identification numbers. Middle managers' network centrality was then calculated in the management network, which includes senior managers and middle managers. Reputational social capital is operationalized as in-degree centrality, i.e., how many people named a sales manager as a go-to person in their advice network.

The E-I index is calculated for each manager in each regional network as (E - I)/(E + I), where E denotes the number of ties with people external to the region and I denotes the number of ties with people internal to the sales region. It is a measure of the dominance of external over internal ties, not simply a measure of external links, and thus captures the informational value of external ties relative to that of internal ties.

Network size is the number of subordinates who report directly to a leader, who is either a sales director or a sales manager. For a middle manager this is the number of sales representatives who directly report to him or her, i.e., the size of the business unit network; the size of the sales districts ranges from 3 to 12 salespeople.

Network size is the number of subordinates who report directly to a leader, who is either a sales director or a sales manager. Each regional network includes a sales director who managed from 3 to 16 middle managers, who in turn were in charge of their own sales territories.

Firm-year proxy for intrinsic speed capabilities built from oil and gas construction projects unrelated to LNG. The time-to-build of each project is decomposed into a systematic component (project capacity, local demand growth, and industry, region and year dummies) and an idiosyncratic residual, and time-to-build is discounted with an industry discount rate proxied by the average WACC of oil and gas companies. The residual is standardized within each industry-region-year subgroup using the subgroup mean and standard deviation, then reverse coded so that positive values indicate a faster firm, and averaged over the projects the firm completes in the year. Speed Capability is the moving average of this firm speed measure over the current and prior two years, carried forward when no new information is available, and set to neutral (zero) before any speed information exists for the firm.
scale: standardized project speed residuals averaged by firm (unitless)
time_window: current year and the prior two years (moving average); project data 1995-2007

description: Entry decision dependent variable equal to '1' if a firm begins an LNG facility in a given year and '0' otherwise. Entry is defined as the initiation of a liquefaction or gasification project, and the variable is further differentiated into GAS | Entry (gasification) and LIQ | Entry (liquefaction) projects. The entry queue is partitioned by a pre-2000 highly uncertain regime (Phase I) and a post-2000 regime following uncertainty reduction (Phase II), so that the models estimate entry before and after the end of 2000.

Usage specificity is operationalized by partitioning the sample by facility type. Gasification facilities are usage specific because if the chosen import market does not become economically viable the built facility has little residual value, whereas liquefaction facilities are usage flexible because the LNG output can be diverted and sold in other markets. The empirical hypotheses apply to gasification investments due to their high level of usage specificity.

Cumulative abnormal stock market return over a three-day event window [-1, +1] around the announcement that a firm enters with an LNG facility. For each project the announcement date is identified with Factiva and Lexis-Nexis and merged with stock market return data from CRSP; expected returns are estimated by OLS of the firm's daily return on the CRSP value-weighted market index over a 200-day window 50 days before the announcement, and CAR is the sum of actual minus predicted returns over the event window. Duplicate observations for firms entering more than one project on a given day are dropped.

Binary variable that takes on a value of '1' if the organization certifies with ISO 9000 anytime between 1988 and 2000. Certification occurs at the facility level. Once a facility adopts, it is no longer at risk for adoption and is removed from the sample.

Binary variable that captures for each facility whether a smaller facility in the industry (four-digit SIC code) adopted ISO 9000 in the first year of adoption. It captures the pattern of adoption in the first year of adoption in each industry, so the variables only capture adopters whose adoption decisions were driven by private information and decision making.
time_window: first year of adoption in each industry

description: Logged number of adopters in the facility's industry (four-digit SIC code) that are smaller than the focal facility, computed for each facility and year. A logged count is used because previous research has shown that inference processes often follow a log form.

Bayesian inference analysis estimating precisely what inferences an uninformed but rational manager could make by observing previous adopters. The model assumes that all managers expect the value of adoption to increase with size, but only some managers have private information about the size necessary to make adoption profitable; uninformed managers with diffuse priors attempt to infer the threshold value by observing previous adopters and using Bayes' rule. Programs written in the C programming language estimated the probability for each facility, industry and year, discretizing each industry into 40 size levels.

Binary variable created by the equivalent procedure to Smaller Adopter, capturing for each facility whether a larger facility in the industry (four-digit SIC code) adopted ISO 9000 in the first year of adoption. It is used to compare the influence of smaller and larger initial adopters.
time_window: first year of adoption in each industry

description: Logged number of adopters in the facility's industry (four-digit SIC code) that are larger than the focal facility, computed for each facility and year.

Binary variable that captures whether there is any adopter in the industry (four-digit SIC code) and local area, with local area measured by Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA). The variable is updated for each year. MSAs are defined by the U.S. Census and represent a large population nucleus with adjacent communities that have a high degree of economic and social integration.

Logged number of adopters located in the focal facility's industry (four-digit SIC code) and MSA, updated for each year. Only facilities in the MSA that are also in the focal facility's industry are captured, because the exact relationship between size and value of adoption may be industry specific.

Number of facilities belonging to a corporation in each year. The authors chose this measure over the logged sum of total employees of all facilities belonging to a corporation because the variability of labor intensity across industries may confound use of total corporate employees as an accurate measure of relative corporate size.

The degree to which a platform's MOOC portfolio deviates from the average MOOC portfolio in the market in a given month, in terms of subject genres. The authors state that the measure is built from the proportion of MOOCs in subject genre j among all MOOCs launched on platform i in period t and the proportion of MOOCs in subject genre j among all MOOCs delivered in period t; the formula itself is removed from the available text and is not reported here.
