The market average is calculated on all MOOCs delivered in a given period, including those offered on platforms excluded from the analysis, and the genre classification follows Class Central's 12 subject genres (e.g., business, natural sciences, and computer sciences). Low values indicate a portfolio that closely mimics the market's average (prototypical) portfolio and high values indicate substantial deviation from the average portfolio.

The share of each platform's complementors that are classified as high status in a given month. Universities are classified as high status if they are among the top 25 of the Times Higher Education university ranking, which corresponds to around 3% of all MOOC-providing universities; non-universities are classified as high status when listed in the top 100 of the Brand Finance Global Brand ranking (e.g., Google, Microsoft), a benchmark that equally classified 3% of the non-universities as high status. The distinction between universities and non-universities follows the classification of complementors on Class Central. The authors preferred this relative measure over an absolute measure because an absolute measure would confound the effect of high-status complementors with general network effects, and lagged the measure by 1 month.

Platforms' number of users in a given month is inferred from the number of monthly unique visitors of platform providers' websites, obtained from Mattermark, which provides weekly data points for this metric via an application programming interface. The dependent variable Users is constructed as the natural logarithm of the number of monthly unique visitors; the authors state that the metric is skewed. They eliminated the first observation month for platforms that entered the market during the observation period.

The ratio of the percentage of board seats held by the ultimate controller to ownership is used as the primary proxy of excess control. Board control rights are the percentage of board seats held by the ultimate controllers. For group-level excess control, the equity proportions of each affiliated firm were first weighted to the firm level and then aggregated to the group level.

Measured as the percentage of board seats held by the ultimate controllers divided by ownership. This longitudinal variable was separately averaged across time for each affiliated firm as the measure of firm-level excess control. To reduce multicollinearity, the firm-level excess control predictors were centered with the grand mean.

ROE measures the rate of returns that a company earns for its shareholders. To derive group-level ROE, the average firm-level ROE was first calculated across observation periods for each affiliated firm; group-level ROE was then calculated as the average ROE across all affiliated firms weighted by the proportion of equity of each firm to the total equity of its corresponding group to eliminate the size effect. ROA was used as the secondary proxy, computed in a similar manner with asset proportions as the weighting factor.

ROE is the primary proxy for shareholder wealth and measures the rate of returns that a company earns for its shareholders. ROA was used as the secondary proxy of the overall efficiency of asset allocations, calculated in a similar manner using asset proportions for aggregation at the group level.
A dummy variable used to represent the forms of ownership within business groups. It assumes a value of one for family-based groups and zero for other groups.
A dummy variable used to represent the forms of ownership within business groups. It assumes a value of one for professional management-based groups and zero for other groups.

Share of the served market accounted for by the business. The four-year average of the variable from 1976 to 1979 served as input to the path analysis. Market share is one of the two endogenous variables in the model.

The sum of the absolute deviations around the average return on investment over the time period incorporated in the study, which parallels the conventional representation of risk. ROI itself is net pretax income divided by average investment including both fixed and working capital.

Calculated from the fluctuations of the business around its market share trend. It is the average percentage difference from the exponential trend fitted on the market share points over the four years of the observation period.

The change in prices relative to the change in costs. The authors note that this index does not measure uncertainty in the sense that variations do; what it reflects is the degree of control businesses enjoy in passing their cost increases on to buyers.
The percentage of sales accounted for by products assessed as superior to competitors minus the percentage of sales accounted for by products assessed as inferior to competitors.
Product line breadth relative to the weighted average of the product lines of the three largest competitors.
Average price of this business' products relative to the average price of its three largest competitors.
All expenses for media advertising, catalogues, exhibits, displays, premiums, coupons, samples and price reductions, expressed relative to net revenues.
Sales force compensation and expenses, commissions to brokers and agents, and sales force administration, expressed relative to net revenues.
Percentage of total sales accounted for by products introduced in the past three years.
Expenses incurred to improve existing products or to develop new products, expressed relative to net revenues.
Expenses to improve efficiency of manufacturing and distribution processes, expressed relative to net revenues.

Book value of land, buildings and equipment net of depreciation, expressed relative to net revenues. The authors also report that this variable was positively correlated with the newness of plant and equipment.
Degree of forward integration of this business relative to its three largest competitors.
Degree of backward integration of this business relative to its three largest competitors.

Listed among the manufacturing conduct variables. The study's variable table relates value added to total manufacturing and distribution expenses and cost of goods sold; the exact formula is not stated unambiguously in the text.
Average receivables net of allowances for bad debt, expressed relative to net revenues. Higher levels may represent a strategy of providing customers access to financing and quick delivery.

Average finished goods inventory net of reserves for losses, expressed relative to revenues. Higher levels may represent a strategy of providing customers quick delivery or may be the outcome of poor management practices.

Set of exogenous conduct variables from the PIMS data, covering relative product position (quality, breadth, price), marketing (advertising, sales force, new product emphasis), R&D (product, process), production (asset intensity, integration, value added) and financial management (receivables, inventory). They enter the path model as predictors of market share and risk.

The dependent variable was defined according to whether a position offered an "explicit or implicit contract for long-term employment." Positions the respondents labeled as limited-duration direct hires, as hires from temporary help services, or as contract work hires were categorized as external labor arrangements, while hires of full- and part-time permanent employees were not. The dependent variable was coded 0 for permanent employees and 1 for external workers, so positive coefficients correspond with an increased likelihood that a position will be filled using an external labor arrangement.

Respondents assessed their certainty that they would need at least the current number of employees (full-time equivalents) in the job described at six points in the future: one week, one month, three months, six months, one year, and five years. They assessed their level of certainty on a seven-point Likert scale (1 = "very uncertain," 7 = "very certain"). The items were added, resulting in a range of from 6 to 42, and the reliability of the scale proved acceptable.
scale: sum of six seven-point items, range 6-42
time_window: one week, one month, three months, six months, one year, and five years into the future

description: Respondents estimated, for each worker in the positions they had described, the number of hours of training in four categories: formal training by managers, formal training by coworkers, informal training by managers, and informal training by coworkers. Factor analysis showed three of these four items to load well on a single factor; the fourth item, formal training by coworkers, did not load conclusively on any one factor and was dropped from the scale. The remaining three numbers were added to obtain a score for the amount of training each firm provided each worker.
scale: hours of training (sum of three items)

description: The primary measure of uncertainty was a six-item scale adapted from Jones (1987). Using a seven-point Likert scale, the respondents indicated the extent to which they agreed or disagreed with six statements concerning the ability of supervisors to assess performance in the focal job. On the basis of a factor analysis, the items with the strongest factor loadings were retained and added to create the final measure, and the data were then reverse-coded in such a way that higher scores indicated performance that was difficult to assess.
scale: sum of six seven-point Likert items

variable_name: Core position in the informal knowledge-sharing network (coreness informal)
description: Knowledge-sharing relations were collected with a name-generating/name-interpreting technique: respondents indicated all colleagues with whom they regularly collaborated from a list of all R&D division members and then reported how often they go to each person for information or knowledge on work-related topics. All responses were compiled into a single informal knowledge-sharing network. Core/periphery membership was computed with the core/periphery bipartition algorithm for discrete data (Borgatti and Everett 1999) using UCINET. The indicator variable takes a value of 1 if the focal individual is structurally located at the core of the informal knowledge-sharing network and 0 if located in the periphery.

variable_name: Affiliation with a core organizational unit (coreness formal)
description: To identify the formal core/periphery structure of the R&D division the authors used a blended approach of objective indicators and interviews with company informants. The objective indicators included the age of the laboratory, the number of employees assigned to it, its technological breadth, authority structure and reporting lines, the location of the control system of the budgeting process, and the physical proximity to headquarters; two of the 16 laboratories stood out clearly and were corroborated by qualitative evidence from the corporate VP of R&D, the head of HR, the financial controller and laboratory heads. A dummy variable takes a value of 1 if the focal individual is affiliated with a core laboratory and 0 if affiliated with a peripheral laboratory.

The E-I index (Krackhardt and Stern 1988) is used as an indicator of each individual's knowledge-sharing tie distribution across the core and the periphery of the network and measures the extent to which an individual's ties span different organizational subgroups. For each respondent the authors considered the distribution of network ties within and across the informal intraorganizational knowledge-sharing network core and periphery and calculated the index as the difference between the number of ties that were external and internal to the informal network core. The index ranges from -1 (all ties are internal) to +1 (all ties are external); a value of 0 indicates that the numbers of external and internal ties are equal for the individual.

The number of technological improvements to products contributed by each individual, hand-coded from the internal monthly R&D reports that the company used to monitor and assess employees' performance and justify resource allocations for each budgetary round. The authors hand-coded all available reports to identify instances of a product's technological improvement; a count of all the improvements, regardless of the number of products improved upon, associated with each individual provides the dependent variable. The variable was logged in the main models.
time_window: 6 months before and 12 months after the administration of the network survey

description: A dummy variable that takes a value of one if a firm was identified in the KLD data as exhibiting strengths in generous giving and zero when the firm only engaged in nongenerous giving. The underlying KLD item captures firms that have 'consistently given over 1.5% of trailing three-year net earnings before taxes (NEBT) to charity, or [have] otherwise been notably generous in [their] giving.' The variable is lagged and measured in the previous year.

A dummy variable that takes a value of one if a firm was identified in the KLD data as exhibiting strengths in innovative giving and zero when the firm only engaged in noninnovative giving. The underlying KLD item captures firms that have 'a notably innovative giving program that supports nonprofit organizations, particularly those promoting self-sufficiency among the economically disadvantaged.' The variable is lagged and measured in the previous year.
Measured as the firm's share price obtained from Compustat, expressed on a per share basis at the end of fiscal year t.

A dummy variable that takes the value one if a firm operates in one of the three businesses of alcohol, tobacco, and gaming, and zero otherwise. It is interacted with Generous Giving and Innovative Giving.

Firm life-cycle stages are classified following Dickinson's (2011) method using the patterns of firms' net cash flows from operations, financing and investing. Firms are initially classified into five stages (Introduction, Growth, Mature, Shakeout, Decline); the introduction and growth stages are combined as Growth stage and the shakeout and decline stages as Shakeout stage. Two indicator variables, Growth and Shakeout, are used, with the Mature stage as the base category.

variable_name: previous sale price above a $10,000 threshold
description: Indicator variables for the previous sale price being above each $10,000 threshold, whose coefficients estimate separate discontinuities at each threshold. The key statistical test is whether these coefficients are jointly statistically different from zero. The analysis is restricted to previous sale prices in the $90,000 to $310,000 range.
time_window: previous sale of the same home

description: The original list price set by the seller and listing agent for the current listing, one of the three primary dependent variables in the archival models.
The eventual sales price negotiated in the market for the current sale of the home, one of the three primary dependent variables.
The final sales price less concessions, such as money given toward closing costs, which the authors label the net price and use as an additional dependent variable.

Agent experience levels were measured using agent identifiers in the MLS data. The main model is rerun on listing agent experience subsamples, with listing agent experience cut at the median to form low and high experience groups.

Agent experience levels were measured using agent identifiers in the MLS data and split at the median into low and high experience buyer agents. Only sales price and net price models are presented for buyer agents, as buyer agents have little influence over listing prices.

Each house was shown with a manipulated previous sales price. Conditions were well above (more than $1,500 greater than the round number), just above (up to $1,500 above the round number), just below (as low as $1,500 below the round number) and well below (more than $1,500 below the round number).

Participants estimated the most appropriate listing price for each of the five houses. To account for between-property variance in housing prices, estimated list prices were standardized (z scores) within each house, and the standardized value was preregistered as the primary dependent variable; nonstandardized estimates are also reported.

There were six price conditions: the original house was priced at $397,000, $399,000, $401,000 or $403,000 and participants estimated characteristics for a house $2,000 higher or lower, so that the change either crossed the $400,000 benchmark ($399,000 to/from $401,000) or did not ($397,000 to/from $399,000 and $401,000 to/from $403,000).

Participants used sliding scales (0: extremely unlikely to 100: extremely likely) to indicate how likely each listed characteristic would be present at houses at the new price point. Per the preregistration, changes in likelihood for each attribute were standardized, the sign was reversed for conditions in which the price decreased, and an index was created across all seven characteristics.

A dummy for whether the manufacturer's suggested retail price presented for the vehicle was over or below a relevant round number threshold. MSRPs were manipulated using a normal distribution, with a standard deviation of $700 for all cars, and were rounded to the nearest $100.

For each vehicle, participants answered the question 'What price would you ask for this vehicle?'. Estimated prices were standardized within vehicle and the standardized value was preregistered as the primary dependent variable; an alternate dependent variable, the residual percentage of the MSRP, is also reported.

Self-reported answer to the question 'How familiar were you with used car prices before today's survey?'. The mixed models are split by the median of reported participant familiarity with used car prices.

After seeing the last vehicle, participants reported how many cars they had purchased and how many cars they had sold. The authors note that the number of cars purchased or sold previously did not meaningfully moderate the effects.

Number of R&D alliances the pharmaceutical firm in a dyad had entered up to the year prior to the start of the focal biotechnology collaboration, drawn from the alliance database. Alliances counted as partner-specific alliance experience were excluded to keep the two experience measures independent. The variable was centered, and the centered variable was then squared (alliance experience, pharmaceutical, squared) to test diminishing marginal returns.
time_window: up to the year prior to the start of the focal collaboration

description: Number of R&D alliances the biotechnology partner in a dyad had entered up to the year prior to the start of the focal biotechnology collaboration, drawn from the alliance database. Alliances counted as partner-specific alliance experience were excluded to keep the two experience measures independent. The variable was centered, and the centered variable was then squared (alliance experience, biotechnology, squared) to test diminishing marginal returns.
time_window: up to the year prior to the start of the focal collaboration

description: Number of prior R&D alliances between the pair of firms in a focal dyad. Those alliances were excluded from the general alliance experience measure, and the resulting variable was centered; the centered variable was then squared to test diminishing marginal returns.

Binary indicator coded 1 when a new drug development project was successfully completed, resulting in an FDA- and/or EMEA-approved, marketable new drug; 0 indicates that the project was discontinued. The variable captured both the research and the development activities necessary to commercialize a new drug and was treated as the dependent variable in a logistic regression. Projects still in a preclinical stage or in phase I, II or III clinical trials as of 2000 were not included in the final analysis.

Ratio of the book value of total debt with explicit cost-long-term and short-term debt-to the book value of total debt plus the book value of total equity. The accounting data of sales, total assets, debt, and equity in books were extracted from the annual reports sent to the CNMV.

Analogous ratio to LEVB when using the market value of total equity instead of the book value of total equity. The market value of equity was computed from data collected in the annual 'Boletín de Cotizaciones'.

Ratio of internally expended R&D to total sales. The authors use it to approximate the specificity and opacity level of R&D investment; internally developed technological knowledge is likely to be highly firm specific and opaque. The raw data on total expenses per year of R&D internally developed came from a postal survey.

Ratio of internally expended R&D to total sales. The authors use it to approximate the specificity and opacity level of R&D investment; internally developed technological knowledge is likely to be highly firm specific and opaque. The raw data on total expenses per year of R&D internally developed came from a postal survey.

Ratio of externally bought or subcontracted R&D expenditures to total sales. This category includes R&D acquired by contracting with other parties: firms, universities, or research institutions. Such investments are less specific and/or more transparent due to outsiders' collaboration.

Ratio of advertising expenses to net sales. The authors consider advertising expenses a transparent investment that may represent reputational assets, transmitting information about the firm and its products to current and potential customers. Because it is transparent it could facilitate access to external funding.

A factor extracted after varimax rotation of the correlation matrix, positively correlated with the proportion of personnel with college studies (COLL), technical staff (TECH), and training expenses per employee (TRE), and negatively correlated with the proportion of clerical staff (CLER) and the proportion of temporary (TEMP) over total number of employees. Cronbach's alpha is 0.62.
Dummy variable indicating whether a funding request included documents. It is used to test whether submission of any planning document is associated with VC funding.
Dummy variable taking the value one if a business plan or private placement memorandum was included in the request and zero otherwise. It is one of three mutually exclusive document categories.

Dummy variable taking the value one if an executive summary was submitted but a business plan or private placement memorandum was not submitted and zero otherwise. It is one of three mutually exclusive document categories.

Number of standard sections identifiable in the plan. The sections are product/process description, target market/industry analysis, value proposition, competitive advantage, business stage, team description, marketing plan, and financials and revenue model. Coding used only business plans, private placement memoranda, or executive summaries.
Dummy variable taking the value one if a non-VC round is reported in the funding request and zero otherwise.

Prior private equity investment amount reported in the funding request. The variable is highly skewed, so the natural log of the amount measured in thousands of dollars is used in the regression analysis.
Dummy variable taking the value one if the planning document contained a specific financing request and zero otherwise.

Amount requested, extracted either from the planning documents or from communications between the focal venture capitalist and the requesting firm. The variable is highly skewed, so the natural log of the amount measured in thousands of dollars is used in the regression analysis.
Dummy variable indicating whether management team information was included. It also distinguishes between zero and ln(1) team size.
Natural log of one plus the total number of named executives listed in the business planning documents. Individuals associated solely with the board of directors or other advisory roles are excluded.
Number of managerial roles reported in the planning documents out of 17. A higher score reflects higher team completeness.

Number of management team members divided by the number of roles filled. A low number indicates less specialization; for example, a score below one indicates that a single individual is filling multiple roles.
Dummy variable indicating whether educational attainment was reported in the solicitation. Educational attainment was not generally disclosed in the documents.

variable_name: D BACH / D MBA / D MASTTECH
description: Dummy variables indicating whether any management team member was reported as having a bachelor's degree, an MBA, or an advanced technological degree.

Dummy variable for reporting prior start-up experience in the planning documents. The authors state that 36 percent of solicitations that included team information failed to report any start-up experience.
Total number of past claimed start-up experiences, averaged over all management team members per solicitation.

Indicator for prior company experience in the planning documents. The authors state that, of solicitations that included team information, only 18 percent failed to report any prior company experience.

Total reported number of companies at which management team members worked prior to the venture described in the request. The average number of prior companies reported by team members in each solicitation was 2.26.

Relative frequency that a former employer appears in the dataset. All former employers referenced in the planning documents are listed and the number of times each appears is counted; each individual receives a score equal to that frequency, averaged over management team members.

Dependent variable taking the value one if a funding round was identified in the VentureXpert database after the solicitation date and that round was classified as a PWC deal or readily identifiable as an angel deal. Otherwise it took the value zero.

Measured as the difference between reported earnings and the median forecasted earnings for the same period among all analysts who cover the focal firm. The variable is inverted so that higher values indicate lower earnings relative to forecasts. Earnings are measured for the first quarter of 2005 in hypothesis tests that use 2005 survey data and for the first quarter of 2006 in tests that use 2006 survey data.
time_window: first quarter of 2005 (2005 surveys); first quarter of 2006 (2006 surveys)

description: A nine-item survey scale measuring ingratiation according to the extent to which CEOs engage in a pattern of behavior that includes other enhancement, opinion conformity, and favor rendering. Respondents answered separately for each journalist with whom they had communicated; for each question the responses were summed across alters and a factor analysis was run on the survey items using the principal factor method with promax rotation, with ingratiation items loading on one factor and acceptable interitem reliability. In the primary analyses ingratiation was measured for the seven-day period subsequent to the earnings announcement, controlling for ingratiation prior to the announcement.
time_window: seven-day period subsequent to the earnings announcement

variable_name: Ingratiatory behavior of top executives toward the responding journalist
description: The journalist survey included a parallel set of questions about the ingratiatory behavior of top executives toward the responding journalist, used to provide an additional test of the relationship between CEO ingratiation and subsequent journalist reports. Journalist and CEO responses regarding ingratiatory behavior were compared using the intraclass correlation coefficient, with coefficients ranging from 0.87 to 0.94. Journalists answered the questions separately for each CEO of a company in the sample frame on which they had reported during the prior year.
time_window: period subsequent to the earnings announcement

description: Content analysis of all articles authored by journalists in the sample frame that mention a firm or CEO in the sample, identified for a period subsequent to the period for which ingratiation is measured. Three coders independently read and assessed each article; the recording unit was the sentence, and each sentence referring to a company or CEO in the sample was coded as positive, negative, or neutral. Coders then determined whether each negative statement referred to firm performance, the firm's leadership, or the firm's strategy, and the number of statements in each category was summed and compared across coders.
time_window: three-month period subsequent to the period for which ingratiation is measured

variable_name: Journalist's ability to communicate with the CEO
description: A multi-item survey measure gauging a journalist's ability to communicate with the CEO since the date of the journalist's most recent statements regarding the firm, with the date specified in the survey. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated that the items loaded on one factor as expected, with loadings above 0.5 and high interitem reliability. Respondents answered the survey questions at weekly intervals for four weeks; in the primary analysis journalists' ability to communicate was measured over the two-week period subsequent to issuing statements about the firm.
time_window: two-week period subsequent to issuing statements about the firm

variable_name: Awareness of another journalist's inability to communicate with the CEO
description: A survey scale assessing whether journalists were aware of an instance in which another journalist had lost the ability to communicate with a CEO after issuing negative statements about the CEO's firm. Confirmatory factor analysis showed that the survey items loaded on one factor with high interitem reliability. Respondents were also asked to name the journalists who they believed had difficulty communicating with a CEO; the correlation between this measure and journalists' self-reports of their inability to communicate with a CEO was 0.74, substantiating the construct validity of the awareness measure.

The number of patient deaths experienced by a surgeon in a focal hospital up to period t. All accumulated experience variables were discounted using a discount factor between 0 and 1 to take into account potential knowledge depreciation and changes in the intensity of negative emotions toward failures; for surgeon's own accumulated failures the discount factor was .90. The variable was measured at each hospital rather than across all affiliated hospitals because task experiences were suggested to be hospital-specific in this context. A squared term of the variable, termed 'surgeon's own accumulated failures sq', was also included to test the inverted-U-shaped relationship.

Learning from failures was measured as an increase in a surgeon's performance in the period after experiencing patient deaths. Patient risk-adjusted mortality rate, one of the most commonly used surgical performance measures, was reverse coded into patient risk-adjusted survival rate (RASR) by subtracting patient risk-adjusted mortality rate from 1, so that RASR = 1 means a patient survival rate of 100%. To mitigate the risk of reverse causality, surgeons' patient RASR was measured at period t + 1 while independent and control variables were measured at period t.

Coded as 1 if a surgeon completed a cardiothoracic surgery residency or fellowship at the top 30 best hospitals for cardiology and heart surgery according to the U.S. News & World Report ranking, and 0 otherwise. The ranking was determined based on objective and quantifiable data on hospitals' patient care quality. The measure is time-invariant, so its single term is dropped in models with fixed effects.

Coded as 1 if surgeons had a Fellow of the American College of Surgeons (FACS) designation in period t, and 0 otherwise. FACS designation was given only to surgeons who met exceptional qualification standards set by the College.

Coded as 1 if surgeons spent most time on patient care among their tasks (patient care, research, teaching, administration, and telemedicine), and 0 otherwise. The surgeons in the data mandatorily reported to the Medical Board of California every 2 years how much time they spent on each task. Responses from 2010 to 2016 were used as 2010 was the earliest available data, and 2010 survey values were imputed for periods before 2010.
time_window: 2010-2016 survey responses, imputed for earlier periods

description: An index combining departmental power determinants and consequences. Paradigm strength was measured as the mean page length of 20 doctoral dissertations randomly selected each year from Dissertation Abstracts, subtracted from a constant because shorter dissertations indicate stronger paradigms. Mean staff grade, maximum staff grade, and the staff/instructional unit ratio were the other components that loaded on the departmental power factor; committee representation failed to load and was dropped from the analyses. The index standardizes each of the four contributing variables, weights each according to its loading, and adds the scores together (alpha = .83).

Position power was measured as the pay grade associated with each position; the university's highly formalized pay grade system for nonacademic staff positions essentially equated grade with hierarchical position and, given the hierarchy-based definition of the construct, with position power. Because the dependent variables were yearly counts per department, a position power main effect and interaction term could not simply be entered for each department-by-year observation. Instead, the job evaluation data were split at the median, and also into three parts at the mean and plus or minus one standard deviation, to compare departmental power effects at low and high position power.

Count of a department's yearly successes in obtaining new positions through job evaluation. A new position resulted from the HRM department's authorization to add a nonacademic staff position to a department at the requested pay grade, based on job evaluation. Documentation on new positions was provided to the authors by the HRM department.

Count of a department's yearly successes in obtaining position upgrades through job evaluation. A position upgrade resulted when, for an existing position, job evaluation indicated that the submitting department's suggested pay grade increase accurately reflected the position's evolving responsibilities and worth to the university. Documentation on position upgrades was provided to the authors by the HRM department.

Visibility was operationalized using size, measured as the log of system-wide sales. Size provides greater visibility for restaurants, given that larger organizations have a greater scope of operations and are more likely to be the targets of institutional forces. Size data was drawn from the Directory.

Visibility was also operationalized with a dummy for publicly traded status, coded 1 for public firms and 0 for private firms. Publicly traded firms must communicate with corporate stockholders as well as federally mandated regulatory entities, so greater attention is likely to be paid to them, other things being equal.

Vulnerability was operationalized with a dummy variable, fast food, coded 1 for fast food restaurants and 0 for restaurants that were not fast food. Although NHSA's campaign could ultimately be seen as seeking fat reduction in all restaurants, it was specifically focused on fast food organizations, whose menu items are generally viewed by the consuming public as less healthy and higher in fat. This measure was also drawn from the Directory.

A self-report questionnaire measure of the degree to which respondents thought their firms' technological capabilities represented strengths or weaknesses in the spring of 1990. Technological strength is treated as the dynamic capability of restaurant firms because important advances in food technology made a dynamic capability in relation to it a critically important consideration in restaurant success and in responding to NHSA pressures. The authors state that all survey items are listed in the Appendix.

A self-report questionnaire measure of the degree to which respondents thought their firms' organizational capabilities represented strengths or weaknesses in the spring of 1990. Well-established organizational routines and processes are treated as nondynamic capability, which would have remained important for normal restaurant operations in stable environments.

Urgency was measured using eight items. The data collection instrument instructed respondents to rate all cognition items in relation to the NHSA pressure campaign as of the spring of 1990. Where more than one usable response was received from a firm, the responses were averaged.

Issue manageability was measured using seven items. The data collection instrument instructed respondents to rate all cognition items in relation to the NHSA pressure campaign as of the spring of 1990. Where more than one usable response was received from a firm, the responses were averaged.

A final list of 33 possible restaurant responses to the nutrition issue was constructed from the literature and reviewed by industry and academic experts, and a Delphi panel rated each response's public perceptibility and activeness. Respondents in the mail-out sample were asked to identify every one of the 33 response alternatives that their organization had implemented in response to the NHSA ad campaign. Each response was assigned a number: a response not taken was assigned a 0, a response taken that was neither publicly perceptible nor active was assigned a 1, a response taken that was either publicly perceptible or active was assigned a 2, and a response taken that was both publicly perceptible and active was assigned a 3. For each firm the responses were summed, so higher scores represented greater accommodation and acquiescence.
scale: 0, 1, 2 or 3 per response, summed across responses
time_window: responses to the spring 1990 NHSA campaign, reported in 1994

description: Each TMT's strategic consensus was measured as the sum of the dispersion scores (standard deviations) for each Goals and Means questionnaire item. Consensus on organizational goals was determined using 13 scale items drawn from a synthesis of items utilized in earlier studies. Consistent with Dess (1987), each firm's aggregate dispersion scores were subtracted from positive constants, so that consensus rather than dissensus yielded the higher overall scores. Because TMT members were not asked to indicate the content of their business's objectives and strategies, low strategic consensus reflects differing TMT views as to preferable rather than actual objectives and strategies.

Each TMT's strategic consensus was measured as the sum of the dispersion scores (standard deviations) for each Goals and Means questionnaire item. Consensus on means was determined using 23 scale items drawn from a synthesis of items utilized in earlier studies. Each firm's aggregate dispersion scores were subtracted from positive constants so that consensus rather than dissensus yielded the higher overall scores. Low strategic consensus reflects differing TMT views as to preferable rather than actual objectives and strategies.

An aggregate measure of demographic homogeneity was developed, drawing upon Bantel and Jackson (1989). Blau's index of heterogeneity was used as the basis for this measure, where p is the proportion of TMT members in a category and i is the number of different categories represented on the team; the formula is garbled in the text. The measure is the sum of a TMT's heterogeneity index scores across 12 demographic variables (e.g., gender, education), subtracted from a positive constant. Published data on team members came from the archival list of firm executives.

The machine tools (354-SIC) and electronic components (367-SIC) industries were classified as stable and dynamic, respectively. The classification combined analysis of data on sales and net profits in a manner similar to Keats and Hitt (1988), a survey of a panel of academics, and comparison of the overlap of 'polar' cases. The industry variable enters the regressions both as a main effect and in interaction terms with the consensus and homogeneity variables.

Firm performance was assessed with a three-item, subjective, self-report measure. Published financial data were available for only five of the 65 firms in the sample, so the subjective, self-report performance measures utilized by Dess and Robinson (1984) and Dess (1987) were the default option for this study. In the absence of outside, objective measures of performance to verify each TMT's subjective assessment, an index of item-by-item agreement was adapted from Tinsley and Weiss (1975) and used as an indicator of aggregate TMT performance agreement.

A dummy variable constructed from expert coding of the text of press releases and articles about the acquisition that appeared in a time window spanning one month before and after the announcement date. The coders assessed whether the target's technology was 'to be used as a technological component of a larger product system' (COMPONENT = 1) or 'to be used for creating a standalone product' (COMPONENT = 0). Three expert coders with prior software and hardware systems development experience were used; two coded the entire sample and a third coded only the discrepancies so that the majority value could be used. There was 92% agreement between coders, and disputed cases were resolved through the third coder.
time_window: one month before and after the date of the acquisition announcement

description: The number of technology subclasses in common between the acquirer and target, normalized by the total number of subclasses in which the target firm patented. Patenting by the target in the same technology subclass as the acquirer in the three years prior to the acquisition is taken as evidence that common ground existed between the technical personnel of the acquirer and acquired firms, because both possess similar basic technological knowledge and the act of patenting is in the public record. The continuous measure ranged from 0 to 1.
time_window: three years prior to the acquisition

description: Coded 1 if the target firm disappeared from the CORPTECH database the year after the acquisition, interpreted as structural integration, so that it was no longer traceable as a distinct organizational entity nor maintained separate profit and loss accounts. The continued appearance of the target firm in CORPTECH after the acquisition was interpreted to mean that structural integration had not been carried out (Structural Integration = 0). CORPTECH conducts an annual survey of technology firms and of units within firms that maintain independent profit and loss accounts or are reported as operating entities.

A dummy variable that equals 1 if the product line exception has been adopted by year t-1 in state k, and 0 otherwise. The adoption dates are California in 1977, Mississippi in 2001, New Jersey in 1981, New Mexico in 1997, Pennsylvania in 1981, and Washington in 1984. The variable is lagged one year relative to the outcomes.

A dummy defined at the establishment level, equal to 1 when the firm identifier of an establishment in the current year is different from that in the preceding year. Because information from the preceding year is needed, the variable is not defined for the first year, 1976.

A closure dummy defined at the establishment level, equal to 1 in a given year when the establishment identifier exists in the current year but does not appear in any future year, and 0 otherwise. Because information from subsequent years is needed, the variable is not defined for the last year, 2014.
time_window: current year versus all future years

description: Computed by dividing the number of new establishments for each state-industry-year cell by the total number of establishments for that cell in the previous period. Establishment information is aggregated to the state-industry-year level for this analysis; the log of the total number of new establishments is used as an alternative dependent variable.
time_window: current year relative to previous period

description: FERC kept records of all applications for commission certification and the date of certification. With the exception of 10 firms that proposed plants that did not meet PURPA guidelines, which were dropped from the sample, all firms that paid the fee and applied for certification were certified. This is a dichotomous variable, where a value of 1 indicates that an organization requested and received a commission certification and 0 that it did not; about 38% of the firms in the sample opted for commission certification.
time_window: at the venture's registration with FERC

description: The dependent variable is the hazard of reaching operational start-up, and the risk set includes all ventures that have registered with FERC their intention to build an independent power generator. Although the organizations at risk come from FERC, data on operational start-up were gathered in California from individual utilities that were required by the California Public Utility Commission to maintain records on electricity purchased from QFs, and in New York from the Public Service Commission. The mean time between registering with FERC and becoming operational was approximately 2 years. Time was split into annual spells to update time-varying covariates.
time_window: from FERC registration to operational start-up, observed 1978-1992

description: This variable captures the effect of the Supreme Court decision of May 16, 1983, which upheld PURPA's mandatory-interconnection and avoided-cost provisions and removed much of the legal uncertainty surrounding the implementation of PURPA and legitimated the activities of entrepreneurs in the nascent sector. This variable was set to 1 after the Supreme Court decision and 0 before.

Media coverage was assessed by searching the LexisNexis online database for articles that discussed the emerging independent power sector, using search terms including independent power, qualifying facility, QF, PURPA, cogeneration, cogenerator, solar, wind, biomass, biogas, and Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act. Including only articles that directly discussed the emerging sector, the authors assessed the overall tone of each article, with positive articles emphasizing opportunities and growth within the new sector. The measure counts all articles coded as positive in a given year; each article was coded by two different people, and a Cohen's Kappa of 0.82 indicated high interrater agreement.

Media coverage was assessed by searching the LexisNexis online database for articles that discussed the emerging independent power sector. Including only those articles that directly discussed the emerging sector, the authors assessed the overall tone of each article, with negative articles focusing on the problems associated with the sector and spending relatively little time reviewing its positive aspects. The measure counts all articles coded as negative in a given year; each article was coded by two different people, and a Cohen's Kappa of 0.82 indicated high interrater agreement.
This measure sums the number of ventures that have become operational within the last 2 years in a given state.

This measure captures the recent amount of unsuccessful entrepreneurial activity in the new sector in a given state, created by counting the total number of ventures that had registered but had not yet started operations between 2 and 7 years prior to the focal firm's application for qualifying status, updated yearly. Ventures that applied for QF status but had not reached operational start-up within the 2 years preceding the focal firm's application were not counted, because 2 years was the average time required to reach operational start-up.
time_window: 2 to 7 years prior to the focal venture's application, updated yearly

description: Sector legitimacy was captured by several indicators interacted with certification: a Supreme Court ruling dummy (1 after May 1983), counts of positive and negative press articles, number of recent operational start-ups, and number of recent unsuccessful entrepreneurs in the state.

A dummy variable coded 1 if the company had received venture financing prior to the IPO and 0 otherwise. Data for this measure were collected from the offering prospectuses. Seventy-seven percent of the companies in the sample received venture backing.

Ownership by top managers was operationalized as the log of the percentage of the company owned by the top managers before the IPO, consistent with Beatty and Zajac (1994). Data were collected from the offering prospectuses.

Internationalization was calculated as the ratio of foreign sales to total sales. For Hypotheses 1a through 2d the ratio was calculated for the fiscal year ending prior to the IPO year using data drawn from the offering prospectuses. Estimation of composite, multi-item indicators of global strategy produced statistically unreliable measures, so foreign sales is retained as the primary measure of international strategy.
time_window: fiscal year ending prior to the IPO year

description: The ratio of foreign sales to total sales, calculated for the first full fiscal year after the IPO. The data used to calculate this measure were gathered using COMPUSTAT and firm annual reports. Internationalization at the time of the IPO was also included as a control measure when testing these hypotheses.
time_window: first full fiscal year after the IPO

description: Total TMT international experience was calculated by summing the number of individuals with international work experience and international education for the TMT. An individual was considered to have international work experience if they reported having a year or more of international work experience in the offering prospectus. International education was defined as having received a degree from a school domiciled outside the United States. Actual values ranged from 0 to 4 for TMT international work experience and 0 to 5 for TMT international education.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Total board international experience was calculated by summing the number of individuals with international work experience and international education for the board. To eliminate the possibility of double-counting the international orientation of inside board members, the board international experience and education data reflect the backgrounds of outside board members only. Actual values ranged from 0 to 3 for both board international work experience and education.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Coded 1 if a board member with international experience represented the firm's venture capitalist and 0 otherwise. Using a dummy variable to operationalize this measure is reasonable, since there was only one case where a board contained more than one VC board member who had international experience.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The log of the percentage of the company owned by the top managers before the IPO, entered in the regressions predicting internationalization 1 year after the IPO.

The summed number of TMT members with international work experience (a year or more) and international education (a degree from a school domiciled outside the United States), used as the moderator of the TMT ownership effect on subsequent internationalization.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The summed number of outside board members with international work experience (a year or more) and international education (a degree from a school domiciled outside the United States), used as the moderator of the TMT ownership effect on subsequent internationalization.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

variable_name: Proportion of affiliated directors on committee
description: The proportion of nonmanagement compensation committee members who maintained some form of personal and/or professional relationship with the firm, its subsidiaries, or its management; only nonmanagement committee members were used because only directors who do not also serve as firm managers are permitted to vote on matters of executive compensation. The specific guidelines follow SEC regulation 14A, item 6b. All board composition variables are proportions and represent the year 1991, collected from firms' proxy statements.

variable_name: Proportion of interdependent directors on committee
description: The proportion of nonmanagement compensation committee members who had been appointed during the tenure of the focal firm's incumbent CEO. The variable is a proportion for the year 1991 and was collected from firms' proxy statements.
The proportion of compensation committee members who are CEOs, excluding the focal firm's CEO. The variable is a proportion for the year 1991 and was collected from firms' proxy statements.

Salary and other annual cash compensation, one of the three measures of CEO compensation. All compensation variables are based on logarithmic transformations, since skewed distributions can weaken statistical relationships and lead to heteroscedasticity. Compensation data reflect the 1991 through 1994 fiscal years as reported in firms' proxy statements; years 1992 through 1994 are reflected in the absolute compensation measures.

Stock options, bonuses, and long-term incentive plans, one of the three measures of CEO compensation, based on logarithmic transformations. Stock options were standardized using the Black-Scholes method, with exercise prices, dates, and the number of options granted taken from proxy statements, monthly stock returns and yearly opening and closing prices from CRSP tapes, government treasury bond information from CRSP government securities files and Moody's Manual of Governmental Securities, and dividend information from COMPUSTAT.

The combination of noncontingent and contingent pay, one of the three measures of CEO compensation, based on logarithmic transformations. Measured for the 1992 through 1994 fiscal years as reported in firms' proxy statements.

Change in compensation from one year to the next, computed as the difference in the logarithmic values for the two years involved. Change measures cover the three one-year intervals between 1991 and 1994; change in compensation includes 1991 compensation to allow calculation of the change in pay from 1991 to 1992. Both noncontingent, contingent, and total pay changes were modelled.

variable_name: Ratio of contingent to total pay
description: The pay mix measure, the ratio of contingent pay to total pay, based on logarithmic transformations of the compensation variables. The authors report only this ratio since one ratio is the complement of the other. Measured for 1992, 1993, and 1994 from firms' proxy statements.

variable_name: Number of foundings per community year
description: Count of new banks founded in a community in a given year. Foundings are modeled as an event count rather than a dichotomous entry indicator. Newly founded banks must file with multiple state and federal agencies before opening, and the same sources track them from that point forward.
Count of acquisitions in the MSA, measured as the sum of the numbers of acquisitions in the prior two years. Mergers that occurred within the same holding company were excluded.

variable_name: Acquisitions in MSA by local banks
description: Count of acquisitions in the MSA made by firms local to the MSA, firms that would likely adhere to the same community logic as the firms they were acquiring. Measured as the sum of the numbers of acquisitions in the prior two years.

variable_name: Acquisitions in MSA by out-of-town banks
description: Count of acquisitions in the MSA made by out-of-town firms, firms that represent a more national logic of geographic diversification. Measured as the sum of the numbers of acquisitions in the prior two years.
Percentage of bank deposits in each MSA held by the four largest firms in the MSA.

Count of organizations within a community-year that had a significant presence in all of the major types of banking: individual, commercial, and real estate loans. Banks above the 25th percentile in individual loans were considered to have at least a foothold in their local retail market, and the same 25th-percentile cutoff was applied to commercial and real estate loans.

The authors identified approximately 2,500 banks that existed during the period in the COMPUSTAT database and totaled the number headquartered in each community each year; they then summed these firms' total employees to gauge the number of bank professionals in a community's population in a given year. Values were averaged over the two years prior to a focal year. The database likely underestimates the number of local banking professionals.

The position of each firm in the network measured with Bonacich's (1987) eigenvector measure, computed for each year from a network constructed out of the alliances the firms formed in the previous four years. The centrality score of a firm in a given year is taken relative to the most central firm in that year, and the combined centrality of a dyad is computed as the geometric mean of the centrality scores of the two members of the dyad. Higher centrality scores correspond to higher levels of embeddedness.
time_window: network built on alliances in the previous four years; independent variables lagged

description: Dummy variable equal to one if one of the firms in the dyad had a centrality score lower than the mean while the other had a centrality score equal to or greater than the mean observed in a given year, and zero otherwise. It is paired with the dummy low centrality dyad, which equals one if both firms in the dyad had centrality scores lower than the mean score in the observation year. The two dummies are entered together, leaving dyads between two high-centrality firms as the omitted category, and their coefficients are compared with a Wald test for difference of coefficients.

variable_name: proportion of minority positions - peripheral firm
description: For cases in which the less embedded firm in a dyad was poorly embedded, the proportion of minority positions that the firm with the lowest centrality score in a dyad formed with a partner with higher centrality relative to all alliances formed by that firm. A parallel variable, proportion of minority positions - central firm, controls for the effect of minority positions on the formation of new alliances by central firms.

For each dyad-year observation, a dichotomous dependent variable indicating whether that pair of firms formed a technology-related alliance during that year. The unit of analysis is the dyad; all possible dyads were considered, excluding reverse-ordered pairs, and the dataset was adjusted to account for mergers and acquisitions that occurred during the study period. Observations cover alliances formed from 1983 to 1991, and all dyadic observations were included for alliances involving more than two partners.
scale: dichotomous (1 = formed a technology-related alliance in that year; 0 = did not)

description: A dummy variable with value set to one if the firm with the highest level of embeddedness in a dyad held a majority ownership position, that is, if its share in the equity of the joint venture was greater than 50 percent. Data on the ownership structure were gathered at the time of creation for each joint venture. An alternative measure was calculated as the ratio between the share owned by the partner with the highest centrality score and the share of the partner with the lowest centrality score.
scale: dichotomous (1 = more than 50 percent of the equity)
time_window: at the time of creation of the joint venture

description: The difference in the level of embeddedness between two partners in a joint venture, measured by subtracting the centrality score of the firm with lower centrality from the centrality score of the other firm in the dyad. It is built from the eigenvector centrality score of each firm's position in the alliance network.

Each participant was randomly assigned to one of three treatment groups: overconfident, underconfident, and neutral. Participants in the overconfident group received feedback displaying a high percentage of their correct answers (first round: four correct and one wrong answer; second round: five correct answers), while participants in the underconfident group received feedback displaying a low percentage (first round: one correct and four wrong answers; second round: five wrong answers). Participants in the neutral condition did not receive any feedback during the test.
time_window: During the Raven's matrices test (two feedback rounds)

description: Within the neutral group, participants who estimated their rank as better than their achieved rank are categorized as intrinsically overconfident and those who estimated it as worse are categorized as intrinsically underconfident. This classification uses the participants' own stated beliefs about their rank in the skill-based task rather than the exogenous feedback treatment.

variable_name: willingness to bet (WTB) on skill-based games based on rank (Task B1)
description: Using a bisection method, the authors elicited the amount of money that made the participant indifferent between entering a skill-based game and receiving that amount for sure. Skill-based games SG_i = (500, r_i; 0) pay €500 to the top r_i participants out of 100, and the capacities used are the same as those of the equivalent chance-based games. Games were constructed so that the capacity of a skill-based game SGi in task B1 was the same as the capacity of the equivalent chance-based game CGi in task A1.

variable_name: willingness to bet (WTB) on chance-based games (Task A1)
description: Using a bisection method, the authors elicited the amount of money that made the decision maker indifferent between entering the game and receiving this amount for sure. Chance-based games CG_i = (X, p_i; 0) give the participant a probability p_i of winning €X and a probability 1 - p_i of winning €0, with market capacities of 12.5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 87.5%.

variable_name: willingness to bet (WTB) on skill-based games based on beliefs about one's own rank (Task B3)
description: After eliciting beliefs about their rank in task B2, participants' WTBs were measured on skill-based games that rewarded the rank a given participant believed he or she had a given probability of attaining (12.5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 87.5%), using the same elicitation method as in tasks A1 and B1. For example, if a participant assigned a probability of 25% of being ranked among the top 41 out of 100, the authors measured his or her WTB on a game that paid €500 if he or she was ranked among the top 41 and €0 otherwise.

variable_name: premium paid to enter a skill-based game over a comparable chance-based game
description: The measure compares, for each participant, the willingness to bet on a skill-based game whose subjective probability of success (elicited in task B2) equals the objective probability of success of a chance-based game in task A1. Any difference in WTB between such equivalent games cannot be due to a different perception of the likelihood of success and therefore reflects only a difference in attitude toward the source of uncertainty. A positive premium indicates ambiguity seeking.

Chance-based games CG_i = (X, p_i; 0) give a probability p_i of winning €X and a probability 1 - p_i of winning €0, with outcomes independent of the skills or effort exerted by the subject. Skill-based games SG_i = (X, r_i; 0) pay €X to the top r_i participants out of 100 based on performance on the Raven's matrices task, so that the participant's rank determines the payoff. The authors varied p_i and r_i and refer to these values as market capacities.

Distance-weighted count of collectively owned bicycle manufacturers that were active in the prior month within a five-kilometer radius of the center of a 1-km2 cell. Each manufacturer j is weighted inversely by its distance dij from the center of cell i and the weights are summed (Cit = sum over j of 1/(1+dij)). The count is computed for every cell-month.

Distance-weighted count of state-owned bicycle manufacturers that were active in the prior month within a five-kilometer radius of the center of a 1-km2 cell. Each manufacturer j is weighted inversely by its distance dij from the center of cell i and the weights are summed (Cit = sum over j of 1/(1+dij)).

Distance-weighted count of private bicycle manufacturers that were active in the prior month within a five-kilometer radius of the center of a 1-km2 cell. Each manufacturer j is weighted inversely by its distance dij from the center of cell i and the weights are summed (Cit = sum over j of 1/(1+dij)).

variable_name: Likelihood of a private bicycle manufacturer being founded
description: Indicator for whether at least one private bicycle manufacturer was founded in a given cell-month; when founding events occur, the mean number of foundings in a cell-month is 1.3 and the median and mode are both 1, so the variation is primarily binary. The models are logit models of the likelihood of a founding, with the unit of observation a cell-month and fixed effects and clustered errors at the district level.

Private startups are split into large, medium, and small sizes based on terciles of registered capital, where registered capital consists of all assets at startup, including property and cash. In inflation-adjusted year 2000 values, the average registered capital is ¥3,418,749 for large startups, ¥187,558 for medium-size startups, and ¥25,726 for small startups.

A dummy variable that takes on a value of one when one or more backward citations are outside the primary class of the focal patent, and zero otherwise. Backward citations are used as a proxy for knowledge recombination, and the focal patent's primary USPC class defines the focal domain.

A dummy variable that takes on a value of one when one or more backward citations are within the focal patent's primary class, and zero otherwise. It is modeled as a separate dimension rather than as the opposite end of one continuum, and is included alongside the distant recombination dummy in the regressions.

The logged value of the market-based measure developed by Kogan et al. (2017). The measure is derived from an event study analyzing abnormal stock returns over a three-day window following patent grant announcements and quantifies the short-term financial return following the patent grant announcement. The logged version is used because it is more robust to the influence of outliers.
time_window: three-day window following patent grant announcements

description: The proportion of within-class backward citations of all the patents in a class over the previous five years. A domain with high insularity is one in which knowledge recombination is largely confined to the focal domain, whereas domains that frequently draw knowledge from outside the focal domain are considered less insular. It enters the model as a continuous variable and as part of an interaction with distant recombination. Domain measures are built with the universe of patents.

The generality of patent class k during year t, extending the generality measure proposed by Trajtenberg et al. (1997) to the domain level; h(j,k,t-5 to t-1) is the fraction of the citations to patents in class k from the previous five years that were made by patents from class j. The exact equation was removed from the text and is not readable. Distant domains are classified as general or specific based on whether the generality of the patent class is greater or less than the median generality score of cited classes of all patents in a year; at the patent level two dummies indicate whether any backward citation is in a general domain and whether any is in a specific domain.

A Jaccard-coefficient-based measure that quantifies the underlying dependence of a focal domain on a source domain. For cited class c and focal class f in year t, the authors calculated the frequency with which the patents in class c were cited by the patents in class f over the previous five years and normalized this count by the total number of citations made by patents in class f and the total number of citations received by patents in class c during the same period; the exact equation was removed from the text and is not readable. Strongly connected domains are those above the median connection strength across all focal-cited class pairs observed in the backward citations of all patents in a given year, and weakly connected domains are those below the median; at the patent level two dummies indicate whether any backward citation originates from a strongly connected and from a weakly connected domain.

Technological domains are identified with the U.S. Patent Classification (USPC) system, whose classes delineate groups of technologies that share a common subject matter. The primary ('original') classification of a patent is used because administrative rules and legal considerations ensure it is superior to secondary classifications in representing the core technological knowledge embodied in a patent; it determines whether a cited patent is in the same class as the focal patent.

Amplitude is measured by dividing the difference between the maximum and minimum total annual minutes of IMT service between a market and the United States over the preceding five years by the average traffic over the same window (a four-year window in 1985, because aggregate market traffic data are available only from 1981 onward). The dimension is measured annually for each market and lagged one year so that entry in a given year relates to variability observed in prior years. For newly created markets the measures of resource variation are created using traffic data in the first three years that the market appears.
time_window: preceding five years, lagged one year

description: The measure counts the number of times that the trend of market-U.S. traffic minutes reverses course (changing from increasing traffic to decreasing or vice versa) over the previous five years and divides by four, the maximum number of changes possible over the period. The dimension is measured annually for each market and lagged one year. For newly created markets the measure is created using traffic data in the first three years that the market appears.
time_window: preceding five years, lagged one year

description: Traffic in year t is first regressed on traffic in year t-1 over a five-year time series for each country; unpredictability of resource variation is then equal to (1 - R2) for that regression. The dimension is measured annually for each market and lagged one year. For newly created markets the measure is created using traffic data in the first three years that the market appears.
time_window: preceding five years, lagged one year

description: Entry is recorded as having occurred in the year in which a firm first reports facilities-based traffic between the United States and the foreign market; after that the firm is no longer at risk of entry to that market but remains at risk of entering any markets to which it does not provide service. A firm formed through the combination of two firms is treated as a new entity and any market in which either predecessor firm operated is removed from the new firm's risk set. Entries in 1985 are treated as left-censored because these firms provided service prior to the Modified Final Judgment.

Firm entry experience is measured by the count of the number of other markets a firm has previously entered, and the count is updated annually. To test Hypothesis 2 this measure is interacted with each of the three market resource variation dimensions. The continuous variables firm entry experience and the three resource variability measures are mean-centered in the models.

Market familiarity is measured with a dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if the firm provides pure-resale service to a market in the prior year and zero otherwise. Pure resale allows a firm to provide service to a market without the investment costs of dedicated physical transmission facilities or long-term operating agreements with market carriers. To test whether the moderating effect of firm entry experience on resource variation differs by firm market familiarity, three three-way interaction terms of resource variation dimension x firm entry experience x firm market familiarity are created.
scale: binary (1 = pure resale in prior year)

description: For each customer, the measure is the average pairwise similarity between the 1-by-16 vectors of the self-descriptions of all the dispensaries they have reviewed prior to the focal review, with each pairwise similarity calculated as the correlation between the dispensaries' self-description vectors taken at the time the customer reviewed them. The average correlation is reverse coded to convert it from a similarity into a diversity measure. The dispensary-level variable is lagged by one month, and all time-variant variables are lagged by 1 month.

For each month, a 1-by-16 vector was calculated of the proportion of customers that focused on each of the coded preference dimensions within a dispensary's geographical market, reflecting the market's preference-ordering profile. This vector was compared with the preference-order profile within the dispensary's market 3 months prior by correlating the two vectors, and the correlation was reverse coded to assess the extent of change in market preferences. The measure was updated on a monthly basis and lagged by one month.

Each dispensary's self-description in each month was coded into a 1-by-16 preference vector, and each customer review in the same geographical market (posted by customers of the focal and other dispensaries located within 30 miles) was also coded into a preference vector. Congruence is the average Jaccard similarity between the dispensary's preference vector and the vector of each customer in its market. A higher congruence score indicates that a dispensary's self-description mentions dimensions that customers reflect on more in their review text, irrespective of whether customers mention them in positive or negative ways.

Survival was proxied by a dispensary's continued listing on Weedmaps. Dispensaries were tracked until they ceased to list on Weedmaps; a dispensary's exit time was set to the month in which it was last listed, and all surviving histories are right-censored at the end of the study period in June 2016.
The monthly count of Weedmaps users who post a review of each focal dispensary for the first time. This outcome is lagged by one month relative to congruence in the reported models.
The average rating submitted by Weedmaps users evaluating a focal dispensary for the first time, calculated on a monthly basis, on a scale of one to five stars.

The treatment variable is a dummy variable coded 1 for treated firms - firms that appointed an immigrant CEO to replace a nonimmigrant CEO in a given year - and 0 for control firms. The period variable is a dummy variable coded 1 for the 4 years after the appointment of an immigrant CEO and 0 for the 4 years prior to the appointment. The independent variable is measured as the interaction of treatment and post-appointment period.
time_window: 4 years before to 4 years after the appointment

variable_name: CSI incidents in the homeland country
description: The number of a focal firm's adverse ESG incidents publicly disclosed in the homeland country in a given year, weighted by the severity of the incidents. RepRisk classifies the severity of incidents into three levels - high, medium, and low - and reports the number of incidents at each level; the authors set the numeric values for the high-, medium-, and low-severity levels as 3, 2, and 1 and calculated the score as the sum of the number of incidents at each severity level multiplied by its corresponding numeric value. For a treatment firm, the homeland country is its immigrant CEO's homeland country; for a control firm, it is its matched treatment firm's immigrant CEO's homeland country.
scale: severity-weighted count (0 to 10 in the reported summary statistics)

description: A dummy variable coded 1 if an immigrant CEO moved to the United States after the age of 18 and 0 otherwise. According to family law in the United States, a person is generally considered a legal adult at the age of 18. The authors searched for CEO biographies from a variety of sources, including company websites, company announcements, media interviews, Wikipedia, and other websites, and calculated the age when an immigrant CEO moved to the United States; typically a CEO is considered an adult immigrant if they moved to the United States after getting a bachelor's degree in a foreign country.
scale: dummy (1 = moved to the United States after age 18)

description: Measured using a global ESG dataset from Thomson Reuters ASSET4 as the average of the social and environmental sustainability scores developed by ASSET4 for a focal MNE in a given year. The social score reflects an MNE's social rating in employment quality, human rights, community, and product responsibility; the environmental score captures an MNE's environmental performance in terms of resource reduction, emission reduction, and product development.

The country-level press freedom index derived from annual data produced by Reporters without Borders, compiled from data on abuses and acts of violence against journalists to reflect a country's press freedom level. The index was scaled by dividing it by 100 so the final measure ranges from 0 to 1, with a larger score indicating greater freedom of the press. A treated firm's homeland-country press freedom refers to the press freedom in its immigrant CEO's homeland country, and a control firm's refers to the press freedom in its matched treated firm's immigrant CEO's homeland country.

Count of restructuring actions for the firm, following Kang and Shivdasani (1997) and Sengupta and Faccio (2011). The authors content analyzed media reports for each sample firm and counted all reported financial, portfolio, and organizational restructuring actions; no weights were applied to different actions. Reliability of the coding scheme was tested with eight coders, yielding a Cronbach's alpha of 0.82 for the classification of actions into categories and 0.76 for the assignment of individual reports.

Count of restructuring actions classified as financial restructuring, the category referring to changes in the firm's capital structure. Actions were identified and classified through manual content analysis of media reports, using the broad categories of Bowman and Singh (1990, 1993) as the initial guide for event identification. The count of financial restructuring actions is used as a dependent variable.

Count of restructuring actions classified as portfolio restructuring, the category referring to significant changes in the firm's mix of assets or its scope of business. Actions were identified and classified through manual content analysis of media reports, using the broad categories of Bowman and Singh (1990, 1993) as the initial guide.
