The count of portfolio restructuring actions is used as a dependent variable.

Count of restructuring actions classified as organizational restructuring, the category referring to changes in structure, ownership, management, and employment. Actions were identified and classified through manual content analysis of media reports, using the broad categories of Bowman and Singh (1990, 1993) as the initial guide. The count of organizational restructuring actions is used as a dependent variable.

Composite measure combining governance and access to capital. Governance is a consolidated measure built from four dimensions of the World Bank's Governance Indicators: government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law, and control of corruption. Access to capital is computed as the sum of the standardized annual percentages of stock market capitalization to gross domestic product, total stock market value traded to gross domestic product, and the stock market turnover ratio. The two components were then combined into a single composite measure.
time_window: 1996-1999; governance indicators available for 1996, 1998 and 2000 were interpolated for 1997 and 1999

description: Binary variable indicating the economic shock, equal to 1 for 1998 and 1999 and 0 for 1996 and 1997. Restructuring in 1998 and 1999 is treated as restructuring during the shock, and restructuring in 1996 and 1997 as preshock restructuring.

Binary variable distinguishing firms belonging to business groups (equal to 1) from independent firms (equal to 0). Group affiliation was established by referring to stock exchange handbooks and to self-reported associations on company websites, and was confirmed by referring to data on South Korean and Singaporean groups provided by authors of published studies.

Measured by calculating the number of years between the firm's founding year and the year of its entry into the generic market. Both a linear and a quadratic (age square) term are included in the models. Founding dates were gathered from company databases.

The dependent variable for entries that build on existing technology knowledge. It is measured as the weighted number of prior products with the same technology as the new entry, using drug market size (in million dollars) as the weight to count for the variance of different drugs' impact on knowledge accumulation. A firm can choose among six major technology forms (for example, oral solid, oral liquid, topical, injection, otic/ocular, and others).

The dependent variable for entries that build on existing market knowledge. It is measured as the weighted number of prior products in the same therapeutic (disease) area as the new entry, using drug market size (in million dollars) as the weight. A firm can choose from 19 major therapeutic areas, classified by the FDA.

The score on the 'managerial quality' item of the Fortune survey of America's Most Admired Companies, as rated by executive respondents (including board members). Fortune annually asks respondents to rate the overall quality of the 10 largest firms in their industry along eight dimensions, one of which is management quality. To remove the performance component, the authors regressed this score on several measures of firm performance (log of sales, profitability, change in sales, change in market value, and lagged change in sales and market value) and used the regression residuals as the dependent variable.
time_window: annual; the survey is mailed in October or November and results are published early the next year

description: The same 'managerial quality' item of the Fortune survey of America's Most Admired Companies, as rated by stock analyst respondents. Like the executive measure, it was transformed by regressing the score on several measures of firm performance (log of sales, profitability, change in sales, change in market value, and lagged change in sales and market value) and using the residuals as the dependent variable.
time_window: annual; the survey is mailed in October or November and results are published early the next year

description: Created by taking the managerial reputation item score for executives and subtracting the score for analysts, in order to assess differences in reputational evaluations between audiences. Significant coefficients on the independent variables and hypothesized interactions in this difference model indicate that analysts and executives differ in their evaluations of managers.

A dichotomous, annual measure set to one if a firm had a poison pill announced or in force during the relevant year, and zero otherwise. For example, a firm adopting a poison pill in June 1987 would be coded zero for 1985 and 1986 and one for 1987, 1988, and 1989, assuming the pill remained in force. A firm was considered to have a poison pill for a given year if the pill was in force or had been publicly reported by the end of November of that year.
scale: dichotomous (0 = no poison pill; 1 = poison pill announced or in force)

description: The number of articles in which a firm was mentioned along with the term 'poison pill' in a given year in the Wall Street Journal. A trained coder read each article to ensure that the poison pill reference was actually about the focal firm.

Return on book assets in the relevant year, centered by subtracting its mean value across the full sample to facilitate interpretation of the poison pill x profitability interaction. Financial performance measures were constructed using the four quarters prior to the Fortune survey process rather than calendar- or fiscal-year boundaries.
time_window: the four quarters prior to the survey process

description: The cumulative total of firms in the sample that had adopted a poison pill, centered to facilitate interpretation of the interaction term. The interaction term poison pill x prior adoptions assesses differences in poison pills' reputational impact as the practice spread.

Audience was defined by who rated the firm in the Fortune Most Admired Companies survey: managerial quality as rated by executives (including board members) versus by stock analysts, giving two separate reputation measures.

Dichotomous firm-level dependent variable drawn directly from ownership questions in the World Bank Enterprise Survey. It indicates that the firm is a sole proprietorship, that is, wholly owned by one individual; 57% of the sample are sole proprietorships.

Dichotomous firm-level dependent variable drawn directly from ownership questions in the World Bank Enterprise Survey. It indicates that the firm has a majority owner; because this includes sole proprietorships, it represents 85% of the sample.

Country-level measure of the logged number of slaves exported from a country divided by the country's geographic area in square kilometers. Nunn (2008) estimated the total number of slaves captured from each African country in the four major slave routes by combining historical slave ethnicity data based on records of 80,656 slaves of 229 ethnic designations from 54 separate samples with shipping data from African ports and regions, then aggregating the data to modern countries.

Country-level measure of historical government centralization derived by Gennaioli and Rainer (2007) from Murdock's (1967) ethnicity-level measures of government hierarchy before colonialism but after the slave trade. Murdock's original measure ranged from 0 to 4 and indicated the number of tiers above the village level for each ethnicity, with high values indicating a multilevel institutional hierarchy; Gennaioli and Rainer dichotomized and aggregated this measure to the country level using each country's modern ethnic composition.
scale: original index from 0 to 4, dichotomized and aggregated to the country level
time_window: precolonial (after the slave trade, before colonialism)

description: Transparency International's 2015 Corruption Perceptions Index, which reverse-scores countries on perceived levels of public sector corruption from experts and businesspeople and is used as the authors' modern measure of institutional strength.

Historical country-level measure of ethnic fractionalization from the Historical Index of Ethnic Fractionalization Dataset on the Harvard Dataverse, which lists country-level data as far back as 1945; the authors use the first year for which a given country has data, which ranges from 1945 to 1970. Fractionalization is used as an (inverse) indicator of social capital.

Modern country-level measure of ethnic fractionalization using the most recent measure from the Historical Index of Ethnic Fractionalization Dataset. Fractionalization is used as an (inverse) indicator of social capital.
Dummy variable indicating that the firm operates in the manufacturing sector, drawn from the firm's industry classification among the 28 industry sector indicators used as firm-level controls.

Quiet giving equals one if the firm does not include giving information in its CSR report in a certain year and zero otherwise. The measure is constructed on the sample of firms that donate and issue CSR reports; firms that engage in giving and issue CSR reports but omit their giving information in the CSR report are quiet givers.
scale: dummy (1 = no giving information in the CSR report; 0 otherwise)

variable_name: Mistreatment of employees (compared with industry average wage)
description: Mistreatment of employees is the ratio of average employee wage for the industry (based on three-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes) to average employee wage for the focal firm. A high value suggests that the firm offers less competitive compensation.

variable_name: Mistreatment of investors (compared with industry average dividend yield)
description: Mistreatment of investors is the difference between the average industry-level dividend yield and the dividend yield for the focal firm, where dividend yield equals the ratio of cash dividend payments during a fiscal year to the stock price at the end of that year. Three-digit SIC codes are used to identify firms in the same industry as the focal firm, and a larger value shows that the firm pays below-average dividends among industry peers.
R&D expenditure is the ratio of a firm's R&D expenditures to total income during a fiscal year. The authors use R&D expenditure as a proxy for employee long-term orientation.

Institutional shareholding equals the percentage of a firm's total shares that institutional investors hold divided by total shares outstanding at the end of each fiscal year. The authors use it as an indicator of the long-term orientation of investors.

Funds are represented by 33-element vectors where elements correspond to each trading (18) and asset focus (15). Atypicality amounts to the vector dissimilarity between a given fund and the average of all funds in a given style at a given time. The authors use dice coefficients to calculate vector similarity for measuring fund typicality and multiply the value by negative one to convert it to the measure of atypicality. In models assessing the likelihood of having a deliberate name, atypicality is assigned at market entry; in the models assessing growth and liquidation it can change over time as the composition of funds around a focal fund changes.
time_window: assigned at market entry in naming models; time varying in growth and liquidation models

description: Binary indicator equal to 1 when a hedge fund is coded to have a deliberate name and 0 otherwise. Because all funds are forced to self-identify with only one primary style, deliberate names are defined as those that include either the whole or part of a primary style moniker in the name of the fund itself; in some cases additional words not included in a style designation, such as 'Special Situations' for the Event Driven category, were identified as reliably indicating a primary style category. Because fund names do not change over time, funds are observed only at the time of their entry into the market.

variable_name: Total assets (fund size, assets under management)
description: Fund growth is modeled with fund size, measured as assets under management, as the dependent variable and lagged fund size as an independent variable, so coefficient estimates on all additional covariates amount to predictors of change in fund size. Lagged fund size is measured as the natural log of a fund's total assets. By controlling for prior fund returns the model captures the effects of naming and typicality on investor-driven, as opposed to returns-driven, growth.

The likelihood that a fund was liquidated, analyzed with the recent financial crisis as an empirical backdrop and estimated for 2008 and 2009. Focusing on those years helps ensure that many of the liquidation events present in the data were the result of investor flight as opposed to manager choice or fund performance, which is also employed as a set of control variables.

Captures whether the fund's manager has personal capital invested in the fund. Investing personal capital into one's own fund serves as a signal of fund quality, so the association between atypicality and deliberate naming is expected to be greater in cases where a fund does not receive significant amounts of self-investment.

Captures whether the fund is domiciled offshore rather than onshore. Being nondomestically versus domestically located may make it more costly for current and potential investors to evaluate a given fund's quality, so the association between atypicality and deliberate naming is expected to be greater for funds domiciled offshore.

From the fifth trial of each session onwards, participants' response to each trial was classified as an exploitative or an exploratory choice. Choosing the same machine as in the previous trial was classified as an exploitation choice. The first four trials of each session were eliminated from the analyses so that participants could start with a minimum amount of information.
scale: binary classification of each trial (choosing the same machine as in the previous trial)
time_window: during the 300 trials of the task, from the fifth trial of each session

description: Choosing a different machine from the one chosen in the previous trial was classified as exploration; in this simple definition, any change is exploration. The options were known and the uncertainty was over outcomes, so exploration is measured as switching away from the previous choice.
scale: binary classification of each trial (choosing a different machine than in the previous trial)
time_window: during the 300 trials of the task, from the fifth trial of each session

variable_name: activation of reward-related brain regions (BOLD signal)
description: Neural activation indexed by the blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signal, an indirect measure of the neural activity underlying cognitive processing, recorded while participants played the task inside the scanner. The measure contrasts exploitative with explorative choices: exploitative choices elicited significantly stronger activation than explorative ones in dopaminergic mesocorticolimbic regions associated with reward anticipation, namely the medial prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus bilaterally. Regions-of-interest analyses confirmed that the vmPFC region previously associated with tracking the value of the current choice was more strongly activated by exploitation than by exploration.

Neural activation indexed by the BOLD signal acquired while participants played the task. The measure contrasts exploration with exploitation choices: exploration elicited significantly stronger activation of the attention-control regions, the circuitry composed of bilateral parietal and frontal regions (temporo-parietal junction, intraparietal sulcus, superior parietal lobule, frontal eye fields, middle frontal gyrus and frontopolar cortex), together with the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, pre-supplementary motor area, locus coeruleus and ventral frontoinsular cortex. Because of limitations in the evaluation of BOLD responses in the brainstem, the involvement of the locus coeruleus was also assessed in areas defined on the basis of functional and anatomical criteria.

variable_name: decision-making performance (total number of points accumulated)
description: Decision-making performance was measured by the total number of points accumulated over the 300 trials of the four-armed bandit task. Participants were told that they would be playing a game with the aim of accumulating as many points as possible and that points could be exchanged for money at the end of the game.
time_window: over the 300 trials of the task

description: Munificence is operationalized in terms of the industry's growth rate, using change in gross national product (GNP) to measure it. The measure the authors adopt accounts for the magnitude of changes in resource availability between periods.

Since concentration describes the number and size distribution of firms in the industry, the authors operationalize this construct using the Herfindahl index, which is based on the market share of the top four firms.
Technological change is measured by calculating the ratio of CNC machines produced to the total units produced for each year.

To model the 'voluntary restraint' agreement between Japan and the U.S.A. as an additional environmental variable, the authors include a dummy variable coded '0' from 1979 to 1986 and '1' from 1986 onwards.

Competitive interdependence (as opposed to mutualistic interdependence) is measured using import statistics for the JMTI derived from published reports of the JMTBA. The degree of competitive interdependence from 1979 through 1992 is scaled between zero and one depending on the observed level of import penetration, with a value of zero assigned to the year with the highest number of machine tool imports, so that the greater the observed level of import penetration, the lower the value of the variable; in reporting results the authors describe it as a zero/one variable.

Cost efficiency is assessed by calculating the ratio of cost of goods sold to total sales. The smaller this ratio, the greater is the firm's efficiency, so that the negative signs in the models are as expected.

Asset parsimony is operationalized using capital expenditures and capital intensity measures from the data base. Capital expenditures are assessed as net expenditures for plant and equipment, and capital intensity is assessed as the ratio of assets to the number of employees. Because capital intensity was highly correlated with capital expenditures and with size, the authors dropped the capital intensity and size variables and reestimated their models, leaving capital expenditures as the asset parsimony variable in the reported models.

The differentiation strategy pursued by firms in the industry is operationalized by examining the advertising expenditures for each firm. Using advertising expenditures, the authors estimate each firm's advertising intensity as the ratio of advertising expenses to total sales and express it as a percentage; advertising intensity is an indicator of the importance of market responsiveness.
Exports are assessed as the percentage of foreign sales to total sales. Export sales and market share within an industry are used to capture realized scale/scope dimensions of competitive strategy.

Market share is calculated as the ratio of a firm's sales to total industry sales. The market share variable was not included in the growth models because it was found to be highly correlated with size, the control variable.

Profitability is assessed with return on sales, operationalized as the ratio of operating income to total sales. Although the ROS measure may be distorted due to aggregateness, the authors argue it is acceptable when firms are relatively undiversified, noting that the average degree of diversification in their sample in 1991 was less than 14 percent.
Firm growth is assessed as the change in sales, where the change in sales for firm i in year t equals that firm's sales in year t minus its sales in year t-1.

Firms were treated as silent when they did not express support for BLM on any of three channels. Starting from 312 major national fashion-related firms with accounts on both Instagram and Twitter, 124 participated in Blackout Tuesday, two further firms posted BLM-related content on Twitter and eight supported BLM on their website during the event date, leaving 178 firms that stayed silent on all three channels; these 178 firms form the sample for the main DID analysis.

Indicator variable that is 1 for the focal firm on the treatment platform (Instagram), where Blackout Tuesday occurred and the racial justice issue was highly salient, and 0 otherwise (Twitter). Its interaction with the After indicator is the DID coefficient of interest for H1, giving the causal incremental impact of staying silent on a highly salient social issue.
time_window: study window (4 weeks before and after the event)

description: Defined as the weekly change in a focal firm's number of followers, built from daily total follower counts collected for each firm on each platform. The change in the number of followers is used rather than the absolute count because the parallel trend assumption does not apply to the latter, and the variable was 90% winsorized to reduce the effect of possibly spurious outliers.
time_window: weekly, 4 weeks before and after the event

description: Defined as the weekly number of likes (log-transformed) received by a firm for its posts, aggregated from the like counts collected on each post. The authors describe it as a more direct measure of customer attitudes and agreement with a firm's posts than follower growth. If a firm does not have any new posts in a week, Consumer Liking for that week is not available, so it has fewer observations.
time_window: weekly, 4 weeks before and after the event

description: Captures the proportion of the firm's top 10 closest competitors that posted BLM support on Instagram during the Blackout Tuesday event. A higher score indicates that close competitors of the focal firm supported BLM in the Blackout Tuesday event and thus likely aggravates negative customer responses to staying silent. The relative closeness of rival firms was assessed with the 'People Also Search For' section and the relative rankings of firms from Google search results.

Defined as the average of the Jaccard similarity indexes between the focal firm's follower set and the follower sets of other firms; a smaller value suggests a narrower market niche. To test H3 the sample is split at the median of this measure, with firms classified as 'niche market' or 'mass market' when their average follower overlap is below or above the sample median (0.002).

Operationalized as the directional difference between a firm's engagement scores in material and immaterial social issues, reflecting how the firm allocates resources and attention between these categories. Materiality of social issues was determined using SASB's Sustainable Industry Classification System, and material and immaterial issues within each industry were identified based on SASB standards and linked to corresponding items in the KLD database using the sector-level materiality designation proposed by Khan et al. (2016). Unlike previous studies that scaled this difference by total assets, the primary measure is not scaled by the total social issue engagement score; the paper presents an equation to calculate the difference measure that is not readable in the available text.

Count of investor filings classified within four categories of the Audit Analytic Investor Activism database: concern, dispute, control, and discussion. The database records information disclosed in firms' Schedule 13D and 13D/A filings. Previous research has established that these four categories are associated with shareholder interventions aimed at changing management efforts and seeking significant changes within target firms.

RepRisk index based on a proprietary algorithm that assesses social-based adverse news toward firms from media and other public sources and quantifies a firm's exposure to social reputational risks. The index ranges from 0 to 100, with higher values indicating a greater degree of social disapproval. For ease of interpretation, the authors scaled the index by dividing it by 100, resulting in a variable that ranges from 0 to 1.

Measured by IR officer attendance, that is, the number of times IR officers participate in earnings conference calls in a fiscal year. Participant lists were extracted from conference call transcripts to identify whether a dedicated IR officer, who had been appointed by the focal firm, attended the conference. IR officers were identified by examining participant job titles and including those with keywords such as 'IR,' 'head of IR,' or 'IR'; following the precedent set by Chapman et al. (2019), the first year of an IR officer's tenure was excluded.

Number of social welfare nonprofits in the state where the firm headquarters is located in a given year. Data were obtained from the National Center for Charitable Statistics (NCCS) database, which compiles data from annual IRS Form 990 filings by nonprofit entities. Following previous research, the authors focus on social welfare-oriented nonprofits involved in areas such as mental health, employment, housing, healthcare, public safety, youth development, human services, civil rights, public benefits, food and nutrition initiatives for the homeless or homebound, and recreation and community enhancement efforts.

Dummy variable that differentiates between the period before and after the promulgation of SASB standards. The SASB guidelines were rolled out in a staggered manner across different industries between 2013 and 2016. The dummy variable takes a value of one during the post-promulgation phase of the guidelines and zero during the pre-promulgation phase.

Estimated from a four-level nested HLM model in which years are nested within board chairs and CEOs, which are nested within firms, which are nested within industries. The board chair effect is calculated as the between-board-chair variance estimated in the conditional model (which incorporates year effects) divided by the total variance from the unconditional model. Board chair and CEO identities are coded from the database IDs rather than from names.

Return on assets, taken from Datastream (code WC08326) to keep the ROA measurement consistent across the four countries, following prior research on the CEO effect and board chair effect. Board chair and CEO data were matched to ROA by ISIN code for firms covered by BoardEx and by stock code for Chinese firms; CSMAR's own ROA data were not used.

Latitude of objectives is operationalized at the country level from formal and informal governance institutions. The United States and the United Kingdom are treated as relatively low latitude of objectives because shareholder value maximization is the dominant objective for boards; Germany is treated as higher because formal institutions require supervisory boards to balance often competing stakeholder groups; China is treated as higher because of lax enforcement of formal institutions and the informal institution of power distance afforded to board chairs.

The number of terms the incumbent mayor had been elected to at the time of Uber's entry, used to capture the degree of political competition in a given city. Less political competition implies that a dominant candidate wins multiple elections, allowing the incumbent mayor to stay in office longer and become progressively less sensitive to local constituents' broader preferences. The variable was coded primarily using the municipal governments' official website, complemented with Ballotpedia.org and the media search results from the Factiva, NewsBank, and LexisNexis databases. Higher values therefore represent less political competition.
time_window: at the time of Uber's entry

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if the city officially or unofficially (but de facto) banned ridesharing platforms, and 0 otherwise. Official bans typically involved cease-and-desist letters to Uber, Lyft, and other ridesharing companies and the arrest or fining of ridesharing drivers; lawsuits were identified using public litigation records from Westlaw, Bloomberg Law, and LexisNexis Advance. Cities were also coded as effectively banning when they announced new regulations closely resembling existing taxi regulations and one or more ridesharing platforms exited after claiming the new regulation was too onerous. Bans were identified using media search and archives of Uber's official Twitter and Newsroom blog announcements, and the dependent variable was independently coded three times with a Cohen's kappa of 0.84.

Using data from the American Community Survey (ACS) provided by the U.S. Census Bureau, the population size of each city in the year prior to Uber's entry. To facilitate the interpretation of this variable in the regression models, the raw data were divided by 1,000.
Using the Current Population Survey (CPS), the unemployment rate of each city in the year prior to Uber's entry.

Entry is categorized into three time periods: those that started production prior to 1988; those that started in 1988, 1989 and 1990; and those that started in 1991, 1992 and 1993. The 1988-90 period is the benchmark against which the prior-to-1988 period and the after-1990 period are compared. Firms in the last category had probably not reached a stable level of operation.

Mode of entry was in wholly foreign-owned operations, EJVs, and cooperative operations. The authors also recorded in the case of EJVs and cooperative operations whether state vs. nonstate-owned local firms were involved, but did not find significant differences.
The proportion of sales of the MNC in the local Chinese market in its overall sales. A high proportion of sales in China vis-a-vis that of export indicates a local market focus.
Whether the MNCs used the Chinese sales channels in the local market. Coded 1 if sales in China were channeled through the Chinese sales organizations, and 0 otherwise.
A set of dummy variables was used for the city location of MNC operations: SEZs, national municipality, open coastal city, provincial capital, or other cities.
Whether the MNC operation received preferential income tax treatment. A dummy variable coded 1 if the foreign MNC received preferential income tax treatment, and 0 otherwise.
The ease of transportation of that location, measured by the city's annual railroad shipping capacity in million tons.

An ordinal measure of net profit of MNC operations in China, offered as brackets so that respondents were not compelled to reveal the exact figure: higher than 15 percent of revenues; above 8 percent but less than or equal to 15 percent; above or equal to 3 percent but less than or equal to 8 percent; less than 3 percent; had not made a profit; had incurred a slight loss; and had incurred a heavy loss. In the ordered logistic regression the categories are coded 0 for incurred a heavy loss through 6 for profit greater than 15 percent.

Binary dependent variable coded 1 if the MNC operation continued its business in 1993 and 0 if it had closed down. The independent measures were survey information for the previous year, i.e. 1992. 122 foreign MNCs in the sample had been closed down by 1993.

A dummy variable capturing whether firm i has adopted the worker cooperative structure in year t, coded one for worker cooperatives and zero otherwise. Cooperatives are identified from the government tax records and from the list provided by the French National Confederation of Worker Cooperatives.

A dummy variable capturing whether firm i has adopted the worker cooperative structure in year t, coded one for worker cooperatives and zero otherwise. Cooperatives are identified from the government tax records and from the list provided by the French National Confederation of Worker Cooperatives.

A binary variable coded one if the firm is in an industry categorized as knowledge intensive, based on the education level of workers, and zero otherwise. It relies on the Eurostat classification, in which an industry is defined as high knowledge intensity if one third or more of its employees hold tertiary degrees.

A binary variable coded one if the firm is in an industry categorized as knowledge intensive, based on the education level of workers, and zero otherwise. It relies on the Eurostat classification, in which an industry is defined as high knowledge intensity if one third or more of its employees hold tertiary degrees.

Value added (VA) is total revenue minus intermediary consumption of firm i in year t, entered in logarithms as the dependent variable. It is estimated with a translog production function that also includes the firm's capital and labor inputs, together with the organizational structure and knowledge intensity terms.

Value added (VA) is total revenue minus intermediary consumption of firm i in year t, entered in logarithms as the dependent variable. It is estimated with a translog production function that also includes the firm's capital and labor inputs, together with the organizational structure and knowledge intensity terms.

The standard deviation of logged daily pay within the workplace, used as the primary measure of intraorganizational wage inequality following recent work on intraorganizational pay dispersion. It is the continuous and normally distributed dependent variable of the wage inequality models.

The standard deviation of logged daily pay within the workplace, used as the primary measure of intraorganizational wage inequality following recent work on intraorganizational pay dispersion. It is the continuous and normally distributed dependent variable of the wage inequality models.

Firm performance was measured by return on assets (ROA). The aspiration level was specified as a weighted average of historical aspiration, social aspiration (average ROA of other public firms in the same industry), and group aspiration (average ROA of other affiliated firms in the group). Perf < Asp captures the difference between performance and aspiration when performance is below aspiration, and 0 otherwise. All independent variables were lagged by one year.

Firm performance was measured by return on assets (ROA). The aspiration level was specified as a weighted average of historical aspiration, social aspiration (average ROA of other public firms in the same industry), and group aspiration (average ROA of other affiliated firms in the group). Perf > Asp captures the difference between performance and aspiration when performance is above aspiration, and 0 otherwise. All independent variables were lagged by one year.

This variable measures the cumulative amount of firm value created (or destroyed) while the CEO position was held by a family member. The first part of the equation calculates the difference between the sum of the average annual market value changes for all previous family CEOs of the focal firm and the same value for all previous outsider CEOs. The equivalent measure for peer firms, other family-controlled firms in the same industry, was similarly calculated and subtracted.
time_window: during the tenure of previous family and outsider CEOs

description: CEO succession is a multicategory variable with four mutually exclusive categories. family succession equals 3 if the incumbent was replaced by a member of the family.
CEO succession is a multicategory variable with four mutually exclusive categories. retention equals 0 if the firm's incumbent CEO was retained in the focal year.

CEO succession is a multicategory variable with four mutually exclusive categories. insider succession equals 1 if the incumbent was replaced by an insider who was not a member of the controlling family. An incoming CEO was identified as an insider if he or she had been with the group firms for more than three years.

CEO succession is a multicategory variable with four mutually exclusive categories. outsider succession equals 2 if the incumbent was replaced by a professional, nonfamily manager who did not meet the insider criterion.

Family succession was divided into transgenerational family succession and other types of family succession. The transgenerational family succession variable has five mutually exclusive categories: retention (coded 0), insider succession (coded 1), outsider succession (coded 2), other types of family succession (coded 3), and transgenerational family succession (coded 4). Transgenerational family succession indicates that the incoming family CEO was from a younger family generation than the most recent family CEO.

Models are divided by the origin of the incumbent CEOs: observations in which the incumbent CEOs were outsiders and observations in which they were family members. A firm's CEO was defined as the executive designated as the representative executive in the firm's annual report.

US Census data on shipment sales and value-added for four-digit SIC codes from 2000 to 3999 were used, and volatility was derived from the value-added measure. Following Dess and Beard (1984) and Nadkarni and Barr (2008), industry value-added was first regressed against its four preceding years at the four-digit level to capture volatility for a given year. The standard error of the regression slope coefficient was then divided by the average industry value-added for that industry to obtain environmental volatility.
time_window: four preceding years of industry value-added (US Census data 1987 to 2011)

description: The title of the officer certifying the TRI report indicates the locus of attention. Titles were classified as top-level manager (e.g., CEO, VP, Director, General Counsel) or lower level manager (e.g., manager, plant supervisor, controller), and the data were aggregated at the firm-year level by choosing the most common title by firm and year. The top-manager dummy variable equals 1 when reports were signed by a top manager, and zero otherwise.

Weight assigned to social aspirations in the aspiration equation, calculated with a two-step approach. In the first step, aspirations were log-transformed and matrix columns comprising social aspirations, prior historical aspirations, and past performance were constructed at the chemical level for each firm and year and multiplied by α1 and α2 combinations formed in 0.025 increments, pooling all chemicals by aggregating them from the chemical to the firm level. In the second step, α1 and α2 were re-computed to minimize the discrepancy between actual aspiration levels and those estimated in the first step, using the average of Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (sMAPE) and Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE); panel data of the attention rules were then created for each firm in a given year from the grid search results that provided the best fit.

Weight assigned to prior historical aspirations in the aspiration equation, calculated with the same two-step approach used for α1. Matrix columns of social aspirations, prior historical aspirations, and past performance were built at the chemical level for each firm and year and multiplied by α1 and α2 combinations formed in 0.025 increments, with chemicals aggregated to the firm level. α1 and α2 were then re-computed to minimize the discrepancy between actual and estimated aspiration levels using the average of sMAPE and MASE, yielding panel data of the attention rules per firm-year from the best-fitting grid search results.

Following common practice in prior research, social aspirations were computed as the mean waste level across firms in the same industry (four-digit SIC code) using the same chemicals that same year. This reference group choice reflects interviews in which firms reported assessing how they are doing compared to other companies in their same industry.
Prior historical aspirations denote waste levels set as goals for a given chemical in the previous year, that is, the targets firms report to the EPA for the subsequent year.
Past performance represents actual prior-year waste levels for the same chemical.

A computer program summed the number of times each word appearing in the president's letters was used across all letters, and two coders noted every word that might denote a negative organizational outcome and appeared at least 30 times (Cohen's kappa = .77). Two coders then read every paragraph containing such words and verified whether each word denoted a negative organizational outcome (intercoder reliability = .74), and a third program summed the number of negative words in each letter. Controlling for the number of words in a letter, the authors considered it more negative the more negative words it contained. In model 3 the percentage of negative words was used as an independent variable.
Net income divided by total assets. It is the measure of a corporation's absolute financial performance (absolute organizational performance).
Return on assets in year t-1 subtracted from return on assets in year t. It is the measure of the change in a corporation's financial performance.
time_window: year t relative to year t-1

description: Number of directors who are not corporate officers divided by the total number of directors. Measured as the percentage of outsiders on the corporation's board.

variable_name: Percentage of shares held by outsiders
description: Number of shares held by directors who are not corporate officers divided by the total number of shares. Measured as the percentage of shares held by outsiders.

variable_name: Percentage of shares held by officers
description: Number of shares held by corporate officers as listed in 10-K forms divided by the total number of shares. Organizations' lists of their corporate officers in 10-K forms filed with the SEC were used to define who was a corporate officer.

Dummy variable coded 1 for organizations in which at least one shareholder, neither an institution nor an officer, owns 5 percent or more of shares, and 0 for other organizations. This variable distinguishes owner-controlled firms from management-controlled firms that have no dominant shareholders.

variable_name: Percentage of shares held by institutional shareholders
description: Number of shares held by institutional shareholders divided by the total number of shares. Measured as the percentage of shares held by institutions.

Dummy variable coded 1 for organizations in which at least one institutional shareholder, not an officer, owns 5 percent or more of shares, and 0 for other organizations. This variable identifies institutional investor-controlled corporations.

variable_name: Percentage of shares held by nondominant institutional shareholders
description: Number of shares held by institutional investors, each of which holds less than 5 percent of shares, divided by the total number of shares. Nondominant institutional shareholders are those owning less than 5 percent of a company's shares.

Dummy variable coded 1 for a qualified auditor's report and 0 for an unqualified auditor's report. Accountants issue a qualified opinion when they find that they must discuss nonadherence to accounting standards in certain aspects of a company's financial statements.

Number of officers who sold shares of the organization they manage in the quarter after its president's letter was disclosed (model 3a). A parallel model (model 3b) uses the value of shares sold by officers in the quarter after letter disclosure as the dependent variable. In both models the controls were the number (or value) of shares officers held and change in return on assets.
time_window: quarter after the president's letter was disclosed

description: Indicator variable that assumes a value of 1 when the focal firm received funding from a VC during its first 10 years of existence, and 0 otherwise; the source of these data is the Venture Xpert module of SDC. Only VC capital is counted, excluding equity purchases by banks, corporate VCs, endowments, foundations, pension funds, government-affiliated programs, insurance company affiliates and universities. The search is narrowed to firms coded as 'early stage,' 'startup/seed,' 'expansion,' and 'later stage' by SDC, and both the VC and the focal firm must be headquartered in the United States with their identities fully disclosed.

Indicator variable that takes the value of 1 if the firm entered into at least one alliance during the first 10 years since founding, and 0 otherwise. Alliance activity is tracked for a fixed 10-year window from founding, and only alliances formed after the investment of a VC are counted for VC-backed firms. Because the variable is dichotomous, the models are estimated as logistic regressions.

Computed in two steps: first, the number of entrepreneurial firms in which each VC invested over five-year intervals is counted; second, prominence is coded as 1 if the count of a given VC's five-year investments is greater than the count of the VC sitting at the 75th percentile of the overall distribution during the same period.

Coded as 1 if the number of three-digit SIC codes in which the VC has invested is greater than the 75th percentile of the distribution of all VCs for this variable, and 0 otherwise. The variable is built from data provided in SDC.

Coded as 1 if the number of ZIP codes in which the VC has invested is greater than the 75th percentile of the distribution of all VCs for this variable, and 0 otherwise. The variable is built from data provided in SDC.

Coded as 1 if the number of firms the VC has taken public is greater than the 75th percentile of the distribution of all VCs for this variable, and 0 otherwise. The variable is built from data provided in SDC.

Binary variable set to 1 if the founding CEO graduated from one of the top 10 Japanese universities and 0 otherwise. The top 10 universities are the 7 former imperial universities, Tokyo Institute of Technology (top engineering university), and 2 leading private universities.

Dichotomous variable set to 0 for years 1998 to 2002 and 1 for each year after 2002, because the bankruptcy law reform was fully effective in 2003. Later legislation consolidated these laws but did not add new provisions.
Data are organized into a panel of annual observations; for each firm-year the dichotomous variable is coded 1 in the year that a firm declares bankruptcy and 0 otherwise.
Data are organized into a panel of annual observations; for each firm-year the dichotomous variable is coded 1 in the founding year and 0 otherwise.

Compound annual sales growth rate since founding, calculated as the nth root of the total percentage growth rate, where n is the number of years in the period considered, using a beginning value of ¥1. It is computed for 2007 or, in the case of a bankrupt firm, for the bankruptcy year.
time_window: since founding to 2007 or the bankruptcy year

description: A dummy variable that receives a value of 1 three years subsequent to hedge fund activism (attack years coded as 1), and a value of 0 three years prior to such activism. Only the first instance of hedge fund activism in a firm during the sample period is considered. Because the specification includes year and firm fixed effects, the non-interacted treatment and post-attack period dummies are not included; the influence of hedge fund investor activism is captured by the interaction term.
time_window: three years before and three years after the attack year

description: Dummy variable that receives a value of 1 if a firm was attacked by an activist hedge fund, and 0 otherwise. Treatment firms are matched with control firms in the same two-digit SIC industry through nearest-neighbor logistic propensity score matching on the firm-level controls measured in the year prior to hedge fund activism.
time_window: year prior to hedge fund activism (matching variables)

description: The ratio of employee stock option cancellations to the number of nonexecutive stock options outstanding. Forfeited options are often included with canceled and expired options in financial disclosures, so the sum of cancellations, forfeitures, and expirations is used in the numerator. The number of nonexecutive stock options is measured as the total number of all stock options outstanding minus the sum of the number of exercisable and nonexercisable executive stock options outstanding. Because options are typically canceled upon employee separation from the firm and are awarded mainly to key employees, the measure captures the loss of valuable employees rather than rank-and-file employees.

The average of employee departure in the post-attack period, used as the moderator in the test of H2. Because post-attack employee departure is time invariant, its main effect and its interaction with the time-invariant treatment dummy cannot be included in the regression. Firms are split into high and low subgroups at the median value of this variable.

Measured as total assets less the book value of common equity, plus the market value of common equity, scaled by total assets. It is chosen because it reflects the market value of a firm relative to its total assets and is more objective than accounting-based measures such as ROE or ROA.

Computed from pairwise comparisons of hospital service portfolios using a pairwise asymmetric similarity coefficient operationalized as the ratio of an organization's service niche to the total service niche occupied by it and its competitor. The competition metric is computed from the 51 possible revenue-producing service centers indicated in the OSHPD facility reports, ranging from basic surgical acute treatment to specialty services such as nuclear medicine and cardiac catheterization. An aggregate metric is created by considering the mean level of competition that a hospital experiences with respect to other hospitals in its geographic niche; like the basic Jaccard coefficient, the aggregated measure varies from 0 (indicating no service niche overlap) to 1 (indicating full service competition).

variable_name: adaptation (market differentiation net of ecological drift)
description: Models were estimated for three dependent variables: overall market differentiation, market differentiation due to ecological drift, and differentiation accounted for by organizational adaptation alone. The adaptation variable was detrended by computing 1-year lagged difference scores. It is obtained as the difference of the aggregate competition and ecological drift measures, with a correction for mutual absences; negative scores indicate improvements in a hospital's competitive position, while positive scores indicate a worsening competitive stance.

Exit from the population was analyzed as an event history process with a semiparametric Cox specification, r(t) = h(t) exp(X(t)B), where the unspecified baseline rate controls for temporal variation. Exit events included bankruptcies and acquisitions by other hospitals, but excluded entry into multihospital systems. Conditional partial likelihood estimation was used to accommodate the left-censored nature of the data.

A simple count variable which indicates the number of hospital service additions and deletions during the current year. It is entered into the survivor model testing the disruptive effects of change processes on hospital exits.

In calculating local population densities, a variable-radius approach was used which scales market regions based on consumer concentration: a 35-mile radius for rural areas, and 10- and 15-mile radii for urban and suburban areas. Density reflects the number of other organizations occupying a focal organization's competitive niche.
Organizational size was measured as the number of patient beds, which the authors describe as the most common measure used in hospital economies-of-scale studies.

Service scope was measured in terms of the number of services offered by a hospital from a standardized OSHPD list. It proxies the scope of an organization's operations, with a large scope indicating a generalist and a small scope a specialist.

Age was operationalized as the number of years since hospital founding. For those organizations undergoing equal-status mergers, the time clock of the new (merged) organization was set to zero in order to reflect a potential 'liability of newness.'

An organizational-level indicator distinguishing for-profit (investor-owned) facilities from nonprofit and government-owned hospitals, entered among the organization-level variables analyzed in conjunction with hospital mortality and adaptation. The authors note that investor-owned facilities lack community embeddedness or an eleemosynary orientation.

Share of article abstracts published in the previous 2 years in the leading journals of the grant's field whose similarity to the focal grant abstract is below 0.05. Similarity is computed by a text algorithm that yields a score from 0 (no similarity, i.e., high novelty) to 1 (high similarity, i.e., low novelty), and each grant abstract was compared with, on average, 524 article abstracts. Increasing values of the dependent variable correspond to higher levels of novelty.
time_window: comparison articles published in the previous 2 years

description: Share of grant abstracts funded by the same NSF program in the previous 2 years whose similarity to the focal grant abstract is below 0.05, using the same text algorithm with scores from 0 (no similarity, i.e., high novelty) to 1 (high similarity). Each grant abstract was compared with, on average, 150 grant abstracts funded by the same program in the preceding 2 years. Increasing values correspond to higher levels of novelty.
time_window: grants funded in the previous 2 years

description: Equals 1 if a seconded employee handled the grant and 0 otherwise. It identifies grants in the treatment group, which comprises all grants awarded by seconded employees.

Equals 1 if the grant was awarded in a year when the permanent employee's program had at least one seconded employee and 0 otherwise. It identifies grants handled by permanent employees during the years their program hosted a seconded employee.

Based on sentiment scores of news articles for sample firms relative to their industries, obtained from TRMI. These scores stem from textual analysis identifying the valence of references to a company, ranging from positive to negative, and are adjusted for the media's overall tone within the focal firm's industry and for firms similar to the focal firm. Using a spline function, the authors divided the average of daily sentiment scores for a focal firm in each year into two variables where values less than zero were considered negative media sentiment and values greater than or equal to zero were positive or neutral. To aid interpretation, they created the final measure by taking the reverse-score of the daily average negative sentiment variable. The final variable takes values from 0 to 1, not including zero, where larger numbers indicate more negative sentiment.

The proportion of downgrades of a given firm's stock made by star analysts relative to the sum of revisions made by star analysts each year. The authors categorized recommendations on a scale from 1 to 3: (1) buy, (2) hold, and (3) sell, collapsing strong buy into buy and strong sell into sell. They defined downgrades as any lowering of a rating (buy to hold, buy to sell, or hold to sell) and upgrades as any increase in a rating. Star analysts were identified as analysts named to Institutional Investor magazine's All-America analyst team in the preceding year. The final variable sums all downgrades made by star analysts and divides this number by the total number of revisions (upgrades plus downgrades) made by star analysts in each firm-year.

A binary variable coded 1 if the director left the focal firm within three years of the year the independent variables were measured and 0 if the director did not leave the firm during the three-year period. The authors employed a three-year window because directors typically serve three-year terms, so the measure ensures that a director can avoid reelection at least once.
time_window: three years after the year independent variables were measured

description: Calculated as the sum of standard scores of: (a) a dummy indicating whether the director had a degree from an elite institution; (b) a dummy indicating whether the director was an executive of an S&P 500 firm at the level of vice president or above; and (c) the number of other board appointments the director had on S&P 500 firms outside of the focal firm. The authors describe it as a continuous measure reflecting nuance in directors' relative status.
A binary variable taking the value 1 if the director was identified as serving as the chair of the board in a given year and 0 otherwise.
Measured as the total number of years a director had served on a given board by a given year.

Measured as the time, in years, between a firm's founding and its first international sales. Using first foreign sales as a criterion was appropriate since this is the most common form the first cross-border act takes for growing firms. The mean, median, and range of age at entry were 5.4 years, 4 years, and 0 to 22 years, respectively, and just over 20 percent of the sample firms went international within their first years of operation.
time_window: from founding to first international sales

description: Executives' ratings, on seven-point scales, of three statements about the extent to which knowledge intensity characterized their firms. One item reflected the reputation of a firm for technological excellence; one, the knowledge embedded in products and services; and one was a global rating of knowledge intensity. The scale mean was 5.78 and Cronbach's alpha was .85.

Four items on a seven-point scale focused on how easily outsiders could copy a firm's technology. One item assessed the time it takes outsiders to learn the technology and was reverse-coded; the others assessed the ease of copying the technology, learning it by observation, and learning it via normal operations. The scale mean was 3.15 and Cronbach's alpha was .72. The closest English equivalent to what was implied by 'core technology' in the original Finnish version is the tacit know-how involved in the development and application of a technology.

International sales in 1997 was used as the dependent variable, with international sales in 1992 included as an independent variable to correct for serial correlation. International sales was defined as all sales revenue derived from exports and from other international operations. The sales data were obtained from respondent firms, as no public databases of the sales of privately held firms were available in Finland.

Measured as the percentage of international sales in 1997, with the percentage of international sales in 1992 controlled for. International sales as a percentage of total sales is the authors' proxy for degree of internationalization, and change in it indicates how rapidly a firm internationalizes once the process has been started.
Measured as total sales in 1997, with total sales in 1992 controlled for.

Dummy coded 1 if the target firm had disappeared from CORPTECH the year after acquisition, interpreted to mean that structural integration had occurred so that it was no longer traceable as a distinct organizational entity, and 0 if the target firm continued to appear in CORPTECH after its acquisition, interpreted to mean that structural integration had not been carried out. CORPTECH annually surveys technology firms and units within firms that maintain independent P&L accounts, or distinct status as operating entities. To check validity, press releases from around the announcement dates were coded for the proposed organizational status of the target, yielding 90 percent agreement with the CORPTECH measure.

The hazard (instantaneous probability) of an acquirer launching a new product after an acquisition that incorporated the acquired firm's technology; the hazard incorporates both the number and timing of new-product launches. Counts and dates of new products introduced by an acquirer were obtained through searches of three databases that aggregate news and press releases, for new-product announcements by only the acquirers that mentioned their target firms as the sources of the technologies or products. Each acquisition was tracked from the date of announcement until the first of January 2001, leading to right-censored observations.

Dummy variable recording whether a target firm had introduced at least one product prior to acquisition (prior product = 1). The information was obtained from CORPTECH, which records annual numbers of products and sales, and was supplemented and cross-checked with information from press releases at the time of the acquisition.
Dummy variable distinguishing the initial innovation after acquisition (subsequent product = 0) from subsequent innovation (subsequent product = 1).

Measured as the average number of times a firm repeatedly used the citations in the patents it applied for, calculated as the number of times that, on average, each citation in year t-1 was repeatedly used during the past five years. Patenting activity was used to measure depth of search because a patent by definition includes a description of a technical problem and a solution to that problem. The formula reported in the paper is unreadable in the supplied text.

The proportion of previously unused citations (new citations) in a firm's focal year's list of citations. The share of citations in a focal year's citations that could not be found in the previous five years' list of patents and citations by that firm was assessed. Values for this variable range from 0 to 1. The formula reported in the paper is unreadable in the supplied text.

Count of new products introduced by a firm in a year, following Martin and Mitchell's (1998) definition of a new product as change in design characteristics. A robot was defined as new if one or more of its design characteristics differed from those of the producing firm's previous products. An existing design introduced into a new geographical area, for example, did not qualify as a new product.

Percentage of vague language in incumbent firms' annual reports. A word-count approach counted vague words and expressions, normalized by the total number of words in each document. Vague words and phrases were identified using Hiller's communication vagueness dictionary, which contains 362 vague words and expressions on 10 dimensions. The measure covers the four annual report sections considered most relevant to competition: Business, Properties, Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A), and Financials.

Measured as the average profitability over a firm's portfolio of markets. The profitability of a market was calculated as the ratio between average ticket prices and the Standard Industry Fare Level (SIFL), a measure of cost of production.
Counted the number of potential entrants in each market, averaged over an incumbent firm's portfolio of markets, as an indicator of the prevalence of potential entrants faced by incumbents.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if a potential entrant enters a market in the quarter following the release of incumbent firms' annual reports and 0 otherwise. The analysis modeled the hazard of a potential entrant entering a given market.
time_window: quarter following the release of incumbent firms' annual reports

description: Captured the size of all incumbent firms in a given market by taking the average of all incumbents' total number of employees, weighted by the market share of each incumbent in a market.
Measured the concentration rate by using the Herfindahl index to calculate the sum of the square of the market shares of incumbent firms in a market.

Participants were randomly assigned to a weak or strong organizational identification condition using a variant of the minimal group paradigm, in which they were categorized into an ostensible group of 'inductive thinkers.' In the strong identification condition, participants were asked whether they would agree to stay in their assigned group and performed an intergroup reward allocation task before the main task; in the weak identification condition, they were simply informed that they would stay in their group and performed the same reward allocation task only after the main task. Strong identification was coded as 1, and weak organizational identification was coded as 0.

Measured at the participant level in the post-task questionnaire with three items, on an answer scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'). The measure demonstrated good psychometric properties (alpha = 0.82).

Attention was proxied at the trial level using the behavioral measure of reaction time for the second-stage decision in the individual trials of the main task, indicating the degree to which the participant paid attention to the competing group's choices, with greater attention reflected by longer reaction times. Because reaction times (measured in seconds) were highly skewed, the variable was redefined using a logarithmic transformation, and an average across the 20 trials was created for each participant.
time_window: second-stage decision in each of 20 trials

description: In each trial participants could either resist the influence attempt (1 = stay with the initial choice) or conform to the influence attempt and imitate others (0 = change the initial choice). Focusing on the 20 trials in which self and alter initially disagreed, staying with one's original choice was used as the measure of resistance, and an average proportion of stay decisions across these trials was computed.

After the practice trial, participants were told their flower shop needed a mission statement and that they would be the last group member to contribute one sentence. Participants in the normative identity condition were shown statements emphasizing superior quality, doing what they themselves consider right, and being motivated to do what they believe is right; participants in the utilitarian identity condition were shown statements emphasizing superior competitive performance, the values and rewards of the competitive market, and high profitability. Participants then chose between a normative and a utilitarian completion of the sentence 'When we make decisions, we primarily take into consideration ...'. Normative identity was coded as 1 and utilitarian identity as 0.
Measured with the same 3-item measure used in Study 1 (alpha = 0.84).
Attention was gauged again by the natural logarithm of reaction time, following the procedure of Study 1.
Resistance was measured as in Study 1, using the average proportion of trials in which participants stayed with their initial choice rather than conforming to the competing group's response.
time_window: disagreement trials of the main task

description: Study 3 used the identity type manipulation employed in Study 2 while adding a third control condition in which no identity manipulation took place; in the control condition, participants completed the association test and reward allocation task without any reference to group formation and did not contribute to or learn about a mission statement. Participants were randomly assigned to a control condition, a utilitarian identity condition, or a normative identity condition; in the binary contrast used for the mediation analysis, normative identity was coded as 1 and utilitarian identity as 0.
Certainty was measured using the 3-item scale employed previously (alpha = 0.90).
Similar to the previous studies, attention was captured by the natural logarithm of the time spent reading about the ISO standard.
time_window: time spent reading the ISO standard vignette

description: Participants responded to two items asking them to indicate their support for adopting ISO 31000 for their flower shop, anchored on a 9-point scale ranging from 1 ('totally disagree') to 9 ('totally agree'). The two items were reverse-coded and averaged to capture participants' resistance to normative pressures.

Percentage of surcharges paid in contract value. The median bribe is about 1.3 percent of contract value and the maximum about 4.8 percent; one-third of the bribe values in the sample are 0, which motivates a censored regression model. Surcharge requests were fixed per barrel exported and due 30 days after loading oil for export.

Gap between the phase-average market price and the OFFP contract price. The OFFP price was calculated by dividing contract value by contract size measured by barrels lifted, and the market price is the phase-average daily market price of Arab Gulf Dubai crude oil, used as a substitute for Iraqi oil. Rent by definition should be at least 0, but the use of phase-average prices produces negative values in a number of cases.

variable_name: Ownership dummies (Private, Public, Partial state, State, Unknown)
description: Ownership is categorized by private, public, state, partial-state, and unknown dummy variables. Each dummy takes the value 1 if a firm is privately held, listed on a stock exchange, state owned, or listed while being partially state owned at the time of the contract, respectively, and 0 otherwise. Private is the baseline category in the regressions.
time_window: at the time of the contract

description: The OECD Anti-Bribery dummy takes the value 1 if a home country implemented the Convention on Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business Transactions during OFFP phases 8-12, and 0 otherwise.

A dummy variable for legal origin. It equals 1 if a contract is associated with a country whose legal origin is English common law or a former British colony, and 0 otherwise. The authors use it as a proxy for the effectiveness of legal systems because existing measures of civil dispute resolution and of protection from the state are not conceptually similar to enforcement of criminal law.

Transparency International's Corruption Perception Index, used as a summary measure capturing social norms related to corruption. The index is rescaled so that 1 indicates countries perceived as the least corrupt and 10 as the most corrupt, consistent with the rescaling of all explanatory variables so that higher values indicate a weaker institutional environment.

In the questionnaire a name generator technique was used; each respondent's network was created from the contacts the respondent identified, and the CBU network was constructed by combining the networks of the members of the management team. If no similar contacts appeared, the individual networks were simply combined; if several respondents named the same contact, that contact was listed only once and all connections to it were maintained; where two contacts from different individual networks worked for the same company, a relationship between them was assumed. Ego density was calculated for the combined CBU network using UCINet as the number of links among the contacts as a proportion of the maximum possible number of connections, not including the links with the ego.
scale: 0 (no links among contacts) to 1 (all contacts linked to each other)

description: Data were gathered from The Global Competitiveness Report (Porter and Schwab, 2003), similar to the approach of Wan and Hoskisson (2003), to identify measures of two key aspects of institutional development: certainty and stability of the country governance structures and the degree of trust within the country. The appendix lists the items contributing to the measure; a confirmatory factor analysis was performed and the resulting Cronbach alpha of this factor was 0.982. For the moderation analysis an institutional development dummy variable was created with a value of +1 for more developed institutional environments (scores above the mean) and -1 for less developed institutional environments (scores below the mean).

Performance was defined as the operating margin at the CBU level of analysis for the financial year that ended six months prior to data collection. This was the best match between the data available from the company and the period during which network data were gathered. The data for the dependent variable were provided by company headquarters based on internal financial reports.
time_window: financial year ending six months before data collection

description: Respondents identified the category of each of their contacts (client, supplier, competitor, industry association, consultant, bank, broker, legal advisor, government organization, regulatory agency, chamber of commerce, university/academic, other ServCo division, or other). DPG percentage categories were different for the two business units due to different marketing systems: DPG contact types for Global Commodities were clients, suppliers, banks, and brokers, and for International Standards they were clients, suppliers, and consultants. The percentage of DPG contacts was the total number of contacts from each of these types divided by the total number of contacts in the CBU network.

One survey question (Q2) asked respondents to rate the level of customization that their primary customers currently expect, expected five years ago, and will expect in five years. The three time frames yield three separate variables that were entered in the logistic regression. The survey drew on previously tested scales and questions from the operations management and marketing literature.
time_window: currently, 5 years ago, and 5 years from now

description: Five survey variables (Q3-Q7) capture indirectly the tacit contents of the tasks related to a service offering and their analyzability and interdependence. In the hierarchical logistic regression two of these variables (Q4 and Q6) showed statistically significant differences between processes that kept back-office operations in-house and those that outsourced them. The authors note that the small marginal effect of these variables is due to their correlations with variables already in the model.

One survey question (Q8) asked respondents to rate the demand volume for their process, using three time frames: 'currently,' '5 years ago,' and '5 years from now,' which yield three separate variables entered in the logistic regression.
time_window: currently, 5 years ago, and 5 years from now

description: A single survey question (Q1) asks respondents whether the primary supplier of information, services, and/or materials is internal or external to the company. In the sample, 61 processes outsourced their primary back-office activities and 47 kept them in-house. This binary variable is the dependent variable in the logistic regression that separates processes relying on in-house back-office operations from those using outsourced back-office operations.
time_window: at the time of the survey

description: An index of CSP constructed from the KLD CSP attributes ratings, following Ullmann (1985) and Waddock and Graves (1997), who constructed an aggregate measure of CSP, an index of the eight categories of CSP rated by KLD. The aggregate takes each item of potential social concern into account, so categories with many distinct subcategories receive proportionally greater weight than those with only one subcategory, giving a numerical score rather than a dummy variable. For each company the measure is a weighted average over the three years 1998 through 2000 with a cumulative weight of 0.5.

Operationalized as the weighted three-year average of the company's research and development spending. The weighted average covers 1998 through 2000 with a cumulative weight of 0.5, so that the independent measures are lagged relative to the 2001 performance measure.
Operationalized as the weighted three-year average of the average advertising intensity in each firm's industry. The weighted average covers 1998 through 2000 with a cumulative weight of 0.5.

Performance measured as return on assets (ROA) in the year 2001, after the three-year period over which the independent measures and control variables were averaged, to assess the impact of the independent variables on future performance. The authors state that this measure represents the profitability of the firm with respect to the total set of resources, or assets, under its control.

Because opportunistic behavior is almost impossible to observe firsthand, the heads of each dealership were asked directly, using a 9-item scale based on the work of John (1984), with several items added to conform to the present research setting. Dealers were asked the extent to which they agreed or disagreed with each statement, on a response range of 1 = definitely agree to 6 = definitely disagree, and eight of the nine items are reverse-coded. As responses to the individual items were highly intercorrelated, they were summed to arrive at an opportunism scale (a = .82).
scale: 1 = definitely agree to 6 = definitely disagree; 9 items summed

description: Services critical to the dealers' operations were selected through interviews with a preliminary group of dealers in one locale, and these items were combined to form a 16-item service-dependence scale. Dealers were asked to indicate the extent to which they depended on their primary equipment supplier for each service, on a scale from 1 = no extent to 6 = great extent. The reliability of the combined scale was .88.
scale: 1 = no extent to 6 = great extent; 16 items combined

description: To obtain a more objective measure of dependence, dealers were asked to report the total number of suppliers with which they were engaged, only one of which was the primary supplier. In contrast to the measure of service dependence, high scores on this measure reflected low dependence on any one supplier.

Following Emerson (1962) and Blau (1964), the availability of alternative suppliers was measured by asking dealers to report the likelihood that another supplier could provide the same support in accomplishing their goals as their primary supplier, using a 10-point scale. The scale runs from 1, not as likely as present supplier, to 10, more likely than present supplier, so high scores reflect low dependence on any one supplier.
scale: 1 = not as likely as present supplier to 10 = more likely than present supplier

description: Control over dealer decisions by a supplier was measured using scales that separately assessed formalization, or control through rules and procedures, and centralization. Formalization was measured by five items on a 1 = definitely agree to 6 = definitely disagree response range, with some items reverse-coded; the scale's reliability was .65.

Control over dealer decisions by a supplier was measured using scales that separately assessed formalization and centralization, or control through direct involvement by a supplier's management. Centralization was measured by seven items on a 1 = definitely agree to 6 = definitely disagree response range, with most items reverse-coded; the scale's reliability was .76.

A firm was evaluated for whether it reduced assets or costs within three years of its year of steepest performance decline (SPD). For example, if 1977 was the year of SPD, a firm was required to reduce the absolute value of its assets at some point in the ensuing 1977-79 period to be considered an asset retrenching firm; if a firm's assets remained the same or increased in the three years following the year of SPD, it was classified as an asset nonretrencher.
