Analogous cost retrencher and cost nonretrencher groups were formed using total costs, and a third set of groups distinguished firms that were both asset and cost retrenchers from those that were not; all 32 firms were placed into each set of groups.
time_window: within three years after the year of steepest performance decline (1976-85)

description: ROI is the standard measure used by Standard & Poor's on the Compustat data base, comprised of income before extraordinary items divided by total invested capital. The analysis compares the mean actual performance (ROI) of retrenching and nonretrenching firms for the year of SPD, the 2 years prior to the year of SPD (SPD-2 and SPD-1), and each year for the subsequent 5 years (SPD + 1 through SPD + 5).
Mirroring Robbins and Pearce's methods, ROI change was measured as the difference between a firm's ROI in a given year (SPD + 1 through SPD + 5) and its year of steepest performance decline (SPD).
time_window: SPD + 1 through SPD + 5 relative to the SPD year (1976-85)

variable_name: degree of relatedness as regards the 16 business attributes
description: Each respondent was asked to rate the 16 attributes in terms of degree of relatedness between the two business units that most clearly manifested the main core competence of the firm. The ratings were made on five-point Likert scales, on which scale point 1 represented 'Very different' and point 5 represented 'Very similar.' The 16 attributes were defined as product-market, resource and value chain variables.

Dummy variable indicating that a firm belongs to the High relatedness cluster (1) or not (0). Cluster membership was assigned by K-means cluster analysis of the relatedness ratings, and each of the four clusters was represented by an individual dummy variable in the regression of ROA.

Dummy variable indicating that a firm belongs to the Technology relatedness cluster (1) or not (0). Cluster membership was assigned by K-means cluster analysis of the relatedness ratings, and each of the four clusters was represented by an individual dummy variable in the regression of ROA.

Dummy variable indicating that a firm belongs to the Customer relatedness cluster (1) or not (0). Cluster membership was assigned by K-means cluster analysis of the relatedness ratings, and each of the four clusters was represented by an individual dummy variable in the regression of ROA.

Dummy variable indicating that a firm belongs to the Low relatedness cluster (1) or not (0). Cluster membership was assigned by K-means cluster analysis of the relatedness ratings, and each of the four clusters was represented by an individual dummy variable in the regression of ROA.

ROA is an accounting-based indicator of corporate profitability, chosen as the dependent variable because it is generally considered superior to return on equity, which is affected by capital structure as well as operational efficiency. It was calculated for all firms by dividing profit before depreciation in 2002 by total assets in 2002. Because objective ROA statistics at the business level were not available from most firms, the measure is at the firm level.

Binary variable equal to one if the birth occurred in a hospital after OB nurses were introduced and zero otherwise. Adoption is classified when a hospital has at least six quarters without any OB nurse presence before the adoption quarter, followed by at least six quarters with OB nurses, and when OB nurses are present in at least 25% of all quarters following adoption. OB nurse presence is defined as at least one recorded birth attended by an OB nurse in that quarter.

Binary variable equal to one when a patient's complexity category aligns with the provider's specialization category and zero otherwise; matches occur when low-complexity patients are treated by low-risk specialists or high-complexity patients by high-risk specialists, while all other combinations, including cases involving generalists, are mismatches. The measure is built in three steps: patients are classified into terciles of Client Complexity (low, moderate, high), providers are classified each quarter into terciles of Provider's Risk Specialization (low-risk specialists, generalists, high-risk specialists), and the two categories are compared. The measure is agnostic to provider type (OB nurse or physician) and focuses on whether a provider's prior experience aligns with the patient's clinical risk.

The predicted probability of a C-section estimated from a logistic model fit on a training sample consisting of a random draw of 40% of births from hospitals that never adopted OB nurses, using maternal and pregnancy characteristics such as maternal age, prior pregnancies, history of C-sections, multiple gestation, fetal position, and indicators of pregnancy complications. The estimated coefficients are applied to the testing sample to generate a complexity score for each patient, and scores range from 0.03 to 1. For classification, the national distribution of client complexity is divided into terciles, with the bottom tercile defined as low complexity, the middle as moderate, and the top as high complexity.

The cumulative average Client Complexity of all patients previously attended by the provider; higher values indicate a historical focus on more complex cases and lower values a focus on less complex cases. Providers are classified in each quarter by dividing the national distribution into terciles: the bottom tercile are low-risk specialists, the middle tercile generalists, and the top tercile high-risk specialists. OB nurses' scores concentrate in the low-risk range, whereas physicians' scores vary more widely.
time_window: cumulative up to the focal quarter, classified each quarter

description: Client demand is measured using hospital-level patient volume in the preadoption quarter, and hospitals are classified as having High Client Demand if their volume exceeds the sample median. Hospitals classified as having High Client Demand handled more than 282 births per quarter. For adopting hospitals the moderator is measured in the quarter preceding adoption; for nonadopting hospitals, in the quarter preceding the first observed adoption in the sample.
time_window: quarter preceding adoption (or preceding the first adoption in the sample for nonadopting hospitals)

description: Workflow predictability is measured using the share of planned C-sections in the preadoption quarter, since planned C-sections are scheduled in advance and allow hospitals to better anticipate and manage workflows. Hospitals with above-median planned C-section rates are classified as having High Workflow Predictability, reflecting greater scope for advance planning. Hospitals classified as having High Workflow Predictability scheduled C-sections for more than 16% of births.

Organizational experience is proxied by the average number of deliveries performed per provider in the preadoption quarter, capturing whether a hospital relies on a small number of providers who do many births or a larger number of providers who oversee fewer births. Hospitals with above-median values are classified as having High Organizational Experience, indicating more sustained provider involvement within the same organizational setting. Hospitals classified as having High Organizational Experience are those in which providers average more than 30 deliveries per quarter.

variable_name: Apgar, Low Apgar, Complications, Length of Stay, Log Cost, C-Section
description: Outcome variables used to examine whether improved matching is associated with better maternal and newborn outcomes. Newborn outcomes are the baby's one-minute Apgar score (0-10) and Low Apgar, an indicator equal to one if the score is below seven. Maternal outcomes are Complications (one if medical records indicate delivery or postdelivery complications), Length of Stay (days from admission to discharge), Log Cost (log of total hospitalization cost in BRL), and C-Section (one if delivery was via C-section). Each outcome is regressed on Professional-Client Matching together with maternal and pregnancy characteristics and hospital and time fixed effects.

The percentage of shares held by foreign investors in a firm's total outstanding shares. Firms do not disclose the identity of these foreign owners, so the aggregated shares are used. All independent variables, including this one, are lagged by one year to account for reversed causality.

The proportion of executives or directors (top managers in Japan) who graduated from prestigious Japanese universities. The elite universities are seven former imperial universities (Tokyo, Kyoto, Tohoku, Osaka, Kyushu, Hokkaido, Nagoya) and two other elite universities (Hitotsubashi and Kobe). Admission to these universities is merit-based and very competitive, and a top management team with more graduates from them indicates higher human capital.

The ratio of average compensation to executives over the average compensation to nonexecutive employees. Average executive compensation is the compensation to the entire top management team divided by the number of managers; average nonexecutive compensation is the compensation to all employees (less top management) divided by the total number of employees (less the top management team). The ratio is then divided by the three-digit industry average pay inequality, so a higher value indicates executive pay more deviant from the industry norm.
The annual growth rate in total sales. High sales growth indicates promising market demand and future growth opportunities.

variable_name: Adoption of stock option pay for executives
description: A dummy variable denoting the announcement of a stock option plan by a firm in a year. The firm was removed from the sample after its initial adoption of the stock option plan, and observations were updated annually. The adoption rate of 37.8 percent (584/1,547) in the sample is almost identical to the figure reported by Daiwa Securities SMBC for all Japanese public firms as of March 2005.

Measured as a coach's winning percentage in the season before the NCAA investigated a violation minus the team's previous ten-year average winning percentage. Positive values represent coaches performing relatively better in the season leading up to a violation, whereas negative values reflect coaches performing relatively worse than expected.
time_window: season before the NCAA investigated a violation; ten-year referent

description: Measured as the difference between the perceived and objective severity of a violation. Perceived violation severity is measured as the extent to which the media uses negative or unfavorable tenor in articles about the violations, captured with the negative affective language dictionary in the LIWC software. Objective violation severity is measured with a coding scheme the NCAA uses to characterize the scope and scale of a violation. Because each of the two dimensions features a different scale, each variable was standardized by taking a z-score, and the variable is calculated as standardized perceived severity minus standardized objective severity.
time_window: media coverage gathered for a year before and after the infraction date

description: A categorical variable that takes the value of 0 if there was no head coach turnover following a violation, 1 if the head coach left the institution voluntarily, and 2 if the head coach was dismissed from the institution. Turnover was examined for the period that began after the violation was revealed and ended one year after the NCAA's written assessment of the infraction. Voluntary versus involuntary turnover was identified by examining press releases, monitoring for subsequent positions, and determining whether the coach was nearing retirement.
time_window: after the violation was revealed through one year after the NCAA's written assessment

description: Takes the value of 1 if a coach who departed his job accepted a head coach position at a team of similar or higher caliber (or accepted a job as an athletic director), and 0 if the coach accepted a lesser position (or as an assistant coach) or did not find employment. The new position was classified as equivalent or better if the conference of the new team was of similar or better size and caliber, following the classifications NCAA and rankings officials provide of conferences as major, mid-major, or nonmajor. Four coders, including one former NCAA coach, manually examined all previous and future employment circumstances for each coach.
scale: 0 = lesser position or no employment, 1 = equivalent or better position

description: Yearly natural log of R&D investments, included as an input in the production function and in the risk abatement function. In the risk abatement function the R&D variable also enters as an interaction with the family ownership variable. Unless otherwise stated, there is a one-year lag between the dependent variable and all independent variables.

A continuous measure based on the percentage of ownership of the family when it owns 5% or more of the firm and has members on the top management team (TMT) or board. Firms with less than 5% ownership and/or no involvement on the TMT or board are considered to be nonfamily firms and are coded as zero, making the variable left censored. Family founders, their families, and the role of those families were identified using the Hoover's, IRRC, and ExecuComp databases as well as company proxy statements.
scale: percentage of family ownership, left censored

description: The risk abatement function of the model estimates the influence of its components on the variance (and conversely the reliability) of the dependent variable rather than its mean, using the family ownership variable, the natural log of R&D investments, and the interaction of the R&D and family ownership variables. The model accounts for the effects of inputs on intrafirm variability in sales over the period of observation.

The natural logarithm of yearly sales at time t, used as the dependent variable of the model. The production function, specified as a traditional Cobb-Douglas function, models mean intrafirm sales as a function of the yearly natural logs of R&D investments, capital investments, advertising investments, and total number of employees. Unless otherwise stated, there is a one-year lag between the dependent variable and all independent and control variables.

Firm-year observations are split based on whether firm performance is above or below historic aspirations, measured by subtracting a firm's return on assets (ROA) in time t-2 from its ROA in time t-1. Negative (positive) discrepancies are taken to indicate that decision makers believe current performance is below (above) aspirations, and pooled cross-sections of above-aspiration and below-aspiration firm-years are used in the estimations.

Proportion of words in the opening prepared remarks of a firm's quarterly earnings call transcripts that match a dictionary of terms associated with the distributed electricity generation model, counted with LIWC software. The proportion is averaged across the four quarterly earnings calls in a year to create an average proportion of words per year; the mean proportion for each firm-year observation is then normalized by subtracting the mean proportion for all firms in the sample and dividing by the standard deviation of the word count across the entire sample.
time_window: annual average of the four quarterly calls; lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: Proportion of words in the opening prepared remarks of a firm's quarterly earnings call transcripts that match a dictionary of terms associated with the traditional centralized electricity generation model, counted with LIWC software. As with Distributed Attention, the annual average proportion is normalized by subtracting the mean proportion for all firms in the sample and dividing by the standard deviation of the word count across the entire sample. The dictionary builds on keywords validated by Eklund and Kapoor (2019) and was supplemented and iteratively revised by the authors.
time_window: annual average of the four quarterly calls; lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: A Herfindahl-based measure developed by Eklund and Mannor (2021), computed from the proportions of words in the annual earnings call text consistent with each of the 13 strategic issues identified in the study. A lower value indicates that attention is spread more equally across the many strategic issues, whereas a higher value indicates that attention is concentrated on fewer issues.
time_window: annual average of the four quarterly calls; lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: The natural log of the number of employees within a firm, based on data from Compustat. The authors use employee counts because they better capture the ability of firms to segment their activities in different business models or strategic issues to unique employee groups. The sample is split around the median value of Size-Employees into above-median (large) and below-median (small) firm subsamples.

The natural log of the count of investment announcements in the relevant year plus one, where an announcement is defined as an investment in the distributed electricity generation model if it relates to some form of distributed rooftop solar electricity generation or distributed smart grid and the firm was undertaking activity that would facilitate customer adoption. Each announcement from the Key Developments portion of Capital IQ was read and coded as one (associated with the distributed model) or zero by a research assistant and validated by a member of the research team; in 95% of cases no changes were made, and remaining differences were resolved as not pertaining to the distributed model.

Family ownership at the group level was calculated using a weighted average (weighted by member-firm sales as a percentage of total group sales) of family ownership in all member firms. Family ownership in a member firm was the percentage of shares owned by individual family members and other member firms controlled by family members. The median for group-level family ownership was 31%.
time_window: beginning year of the four-year window

description: Family control was measured by a factor score from two variables. The first was the percentage of board chairs who were family members of the founder of the group; chairs with the same family name as the founder were considered family members, including members from both immediate and extended family. The second was chair overlap, measured by the Herfindahl index, reflecting the extent to which there was a single person (usually the founder of the group or his son) who controlled all the member firms. The two variables were correlated at 0.57.
time_window: beginning year of the four-year window

description: The number of distinct two-digit industries present in a business group's industrial portfolio at t+1 but not at t, counted over a four-year window. Two coders assigned each member firm a four-digit and a two-digit industrial code (1996 version of the Standard Industrial Classification published by the Taiwanese government) according to its products, with an intercoder reliability rate of 0.95, and the industry information of all member firms was aggregated to the group level. Industries with different two-digit industry codes were considered unrelated industries.

The number of distinct two-digit industries present in a business group's industrial portfolio at t but not at t+1, counted over a four-year window. Industry membership was hand-coded for each member firm at the four-digit and two-digit level and aggregated to the group level; industries with different two-digit codes were treated as unrelated industries.

A weighted average (weighted by member-firm sales as a percentage of group sales) of percentages of shares owned by U.S. and U.K. investors in the member firms of a business group. These investors included only industrial firms, as institutional investors were rare in the research period. U.S. and U.K. direct investment in the business groups ranged from 0% to 31.95%, and 83% of the cases had no investment from these countries.
time_window: beginning year of the four-year window

description: A weighted average (weighted by member-firm sales as a percentage of group sales) of percentages of shares owned by Japanese investors in the member firms of a business group. These investors included only industrial firms. Japanese investment ranged from 0% to 40.28%, and 60% of the cases had no Japanese investment.
time_window: beginning year of the four-year window

description: The political connections were measured as a ratio of outside directors who were formerly government officials to the total number of board directors. Whether an outside director was a government official before joining the listed firm was identified from the 'Profile of Directors and Senior Managers' section of the company's annual reports.
Top executive pay was measured by salaries and bonuses and was calculated as the logarithm of average cash pay for the three highest-paid executives at year 2000 prices.
scale: logarithm of average cash pay at year 2000 prices

description: To capture pay compression in a firm, the authors followed Bloom (1999) by using the ratio of the average employee's pay to the average of top three executive pays. A larger ratio indicates greater pay compression and, therefore, less pay dispersion between average employees and top executives.

ROS is used to measure firm performance and is included in the estimation equations to test the moderating effect of political connections on the relationship between executive pay and firm performance.

Total CSR strengths (totstr it) is the equally weighted sum of KLD's positive screens, classified as 'strengths', for firm i in year t, adjusted by the mean of strengths averaged across all firms in the sample in year t to take into account firm entry into the KLD panel. Following the convention established by prior work, equal weights are assigned to the different issue areas of the KLD database. KLD uses a binary system, including a 1 to indicate the presence of a screen/criterion and a 0 to indicate its absence.
time_window: firm-year t (KLD ratings at calendar year end, released around January; recommendations taken in March of the following year)

description: Consensus (mean) investment recommendation for each firm in the month of March of year t, constructed by I/B/E/S and reported in the consensus files. I/B/E/S records analysts' investment recommendations on a five-point scale with 1 indicating a strong buy recommendation and 5 indicating a sell recommendation, and the authors invert this scale so that more favorable recommendations take a higher value. For a given firm in the focal year, I/B/E/S collects all published analyst recommendations (in this case for the month of March) and constructs an equally weighted average. March is selected so that analysts have had time to obtain and analyze the firm-level CSR scores.
scale: five-point recommendation scale, inverted so that higher values indicate more favorable recommendations

description: Based on the full sample, analyst experience is calculated as the total number of years that the focal analyst has followed the focal firm. The hypothesis tests re-estimate the models after confining the sample to the top two quartiles and to the bottom two quartiles of analyst experience.

Brokerage house status is approximated, following Hong and Kubik (2003), by the mean House size, constructed as the average number of analysts working at the focal brokerage house in any given year; elsewhere the text describes mean house size as the average number of employees for all the brokerage houses that employ an investment analyst who follows the focal firm. It is also used as a control variable in the main specifications. The hypothesis tests confine the sample to the top two and bottom two quartiles of mean House size and re-estimate the models.
level: brokerage house-year (aggregated to the focal firm's covering analysts)

description: The relation between CSR strengths and recommendations is traced by estimating the equation on expanding bundles of years beginning with 1993-1996; each subsequent specification adds an additional year to the data, so that the last column presents results for the entire period 1993-2007. The authors estimate the model on these different bundles of years to detect how the relation changes over time.

Constructed by counting the number of state nondiscrimination laws in year t - 1. Information on the year a state enacted a law forbidding discrimination based on sexual orientation was obtained from the HRC WorkNet database; the first state to enact such a law was the District of Columbia in 1977, and by the end of 2002 fourteen states had enacted such laws.

variable_name: Cumulative number of adoptions in the same industry
description: Constructed by counting the number of corporations in the industry of sampled corporations that provided same-sex partner health benefits from 1990 up to and including year t - 1. Adoption information was compiled from the HRC WorkNet database and the Factiva media database.

variable_name: Cumulative number of adoptions in the same state
description: Constructed by counting the number of sampled corporations' headquarters in the same state that provided same-sex partner health benefits from 1990 up to and including year t - 1. Adoption information was compiled from the HRC WorkNet database and the Factiva media database.

Based on content analysis of 1,517 relevant, nonduplicated articles drawn from the top five U.S. newspapers and major U.S. business magazines, retrieved in full text from Factiva and LexisNexis. The article was the unit of analysis; each article was coded as containing only positive tenors, only negative tenors, both positive and negative (balanced) tenors, or neutral tenors. The Janis-Fader coefficient of imbalance was applied to measure the overall tenor in each year; the text states that it ranges from -1 to 1, is zero when positive and negative accounts are equal, and uses the numbers of positive articles (P), negative articles (N), and all articles (Total), but the formula itself is not readable in the provided text.

variable_name: Adoption of same-sex partner health benefits
description: Coded 1 for the year when a corporation started to offer the benefits to its same-sex employees' partners, and 0 otherwise. Adoption data were compiled from the HRC WorkNet database for 1999-2003 and from Factiva searches for adoptions prior to 1999; the remaining 941 corporations were transformed into annual spells.

Natural log of the 'checks and balances' score published in the World Bank's DPI for each host country in the year of an investment project announcement. The score ranges from 1 (no/minimal checks) to 18 (substantial checks) and reflects the number of relevant veto holders in a state's national polity; higher values indicate more veto holders and thus greater policy stability.
scale: natural log of a 1-18 'checks and balances' score
time_window: year of the investment project announcement

description: Percentage of equity funding the investment project, computed as initial equity divided by the sum of equity plus debt multiplied by 100. Measured at the date of a project's initial announcement and used as a forward-looking indicator of the likelihood of loss from project term renegotiation, holdup, or expropriation. Higher values indicate higher investment risk.
time_window: at the date of the project's initial announcement

description: 0-1 dummy that takes a value of 1 when the state owns equity greater than 0% and less than 50% (effectively 1%-49%) of an investment project, and 0 otherwise.

Continuous percentage measure of project state ownership spanning 0%-100%, used in place of the categorical 0-1 minority ownership dummy in the abbreviated specification reported in column (2) of the core regression results.

A scale comprising six highly correlated survey items (Cronbach's alpha = 0.71), constructed by taking the mean of its component variables. The items capture respondents' assessments of the degree to which their organizations attempted to increase job security, increase survivors' marketability, preserve the dignity of downsized employees, carefully explain the reasons behind downsizing decisions, communicate more extensively with employees, and counsel survivors.

A scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.74) indicating the extent to which the organization provided advance notice as a downsizing practice, constructed as the mean of two survey questions. One question asked about the amount of time between the general announcement of downsizing and the notice given about which specific employees would be downsized; the other asked about the amount of time between notice being given to specific employees of their termination and the date these employees actually separated from the organization.

A binary variable indicating whether or not the hospital extended severance pay to laid-off employees. The survey did not identify the actual costs of the practice, so a value of 1 was assigned if the hospital offered the benefit and 0 if it did not.

A binary variable indicating whether or not the hospital extended laid-off employees' insurance benefits beyond the legally required period. A value of 1 was assigned if the hospital offered the benefit and 0 if it did not.

Human resource managers' perceptions of the overall success of their hospitals' downsizing efforts, used as a dependent variable in ordered logit models. The survey asked for an assessment of the success of the downsizing itself rather than for a more comprehensive performance assessment, and the variable takes only the values 1 to 5.

A bottom-line measure of organizational effectiveness: the ratio of free cash available for a hospital's use to the total hospital net revenues, indicating the amount of cash retained after payment of principal and other cash expenses as a percentage of total revenue. It was examined in the year of downsizing and in the three years following downsizing. Measures for cash margin in the relevant years were available only for a subset of respondents, limited to not-for-profit and government affiliated hospitals.
time_window: year of downsizing and 1, 2, and 3 years following the downsizing

description: Mean of two survey questions on the degree to which a detailed plan existed for downsizing and the extent to which a systematic job analysis was performed before downsizing, answered by hospital human resource managers. Cronbach's alpha was 0.58.

A dichotomous variable that equals one when the investor firm receives board membership on the investee firm's board and zero otherwise. The board membership data for each transaction are obtained from Recap. Because this dependent variable is dichotomous, a probit model is specified to test the hypotheses.

Measured using six-digit patent classifications of the USPTO; each patent is classified under a primary three-digit class and a secondary six-digit class. The measure is the proportion of the investee partner's patents with a six-digit classification that also occurs in the investor firm's patent portfolio. The variable ranges between zero and one, and higher values correspond to greater overlap of the investee partner's portfolio with that of the investor. The formula the paper gives for this measure is not readable in the available text, so the exact specification is a gap.

The logarithm of the number of both equity and nonequity R&D collaborations formed by the investor in the same therapeutic area as the focal alliance. Therapeutic categories refer to the organ or system in the human body that is the target of the drug. The collaborations formed by the partner in the five-year window before the focal deal are used to quantify the measure.
time_window: five-year window before the focal deal

description: The six-digit patent classes common to both partners are first identified. A subset of patents applied for by the investee firm in a 10-year window before the focal alliance, ultimately issued by the USPTO and classified in any of the common six-digit patent classes, is then constructed. For each patent in this overlapping set, the number of forward citations received in the five-year window after the grant is counted, and the variable is the average number of citations received by the patents in the overlap set. Higher values correspond to greater value of the knowledge of the investee firm in the overlapping technologies.
time_window: 10-year window before the focal alliance for applications; five-year window after grant for forward citations

description: Dichotomous variable reflecting whether or not a firm announced at least one majority (51 percent or greater) acquisition investment worth at least $1 million in value (if reported) in that quarter (0 = 'no,' 1 = 'yes'). Only announcements of acquisitions that were subsequently completed (at any future time) were included in the sample. The variable was lagged one quarter to ensure that announcements preceded CEO equity-based holdings changes; for example, acquisition announcements in the first quarter of 2006 were used to predict holdings changes in the second quarter of that year.

Two variables were used. The first is a dichotomous variable reflecting whether or not CEOs exercised options during a given quarter (0 = 'no,' 1 = 'yes'). The second is a continuous variable calculated as the ratio of the number of options exercised during a quarter divided by the number of total options held at the start of the same year. Daily insider transaction data reported on SEC forms were collapsed into quarterly data.

A dichotomous variable reflecting whether or not CEOs sold stock during a quarter (0 = 'no,' 1 = 'yes'), plus a ratio of the number of shares of stock sold during a quarter divided by the number of shares of stock owned at the start of the year containing the quarter. To avoid double-counting, stock sold as a result of option exercise was excluded from this variable.

A dichotomous variable reflecting whether or not CEOs received a stock option grant during a given quarter (0 = 'no,' 1 = 'yes'), plus a continuous measure calculated as the number of options granted in a quarter divided by the number of options held at the start of the year containing the quarter.

Cumulative abnormal returns three days prior to and three days following acquisition announcements. Announcement CARs reflect investors' present expectations about the future value of the combined firms (bidders plus targets), and short windows allow stock price changes to be attributed to the announcement with relative confidence. For firms that undertook multiple acquisitions in a quarter, the CAR values for all completed acquisitions in that quarter were averaged.
time_window: three days prior to and three days following the announcement

description: The dependent variable is the price paid by the acquirer for the target firm, which approximates the value of the target when combined with the bidding firm and reflects the acquirer's expectations of resource complementarity. Since the variable is highly skewed, the authors take its natural logarithm.

The stock of XY-type citations that the target's patent portfolio receives as a share of the total citation stock. XY-type references in EPO search reports mark prior art that threatens the novelty or inventive step of a patent application, i.e., conflicting prior art, whereas A-type references indicate relevant noninfringing prior art. Citation stocks are calculated in analogy to the patent stock, and only citations received in a five-year window after the patent has been granted are considered; patent equivalents are taken into account.

The patent stock PS of the acquiring firm is computed with a constant knowledge depreciation rate of 15 percent to weight the importance of older patents, referring to the year prior to the acquisition. The patent stock is then divided by the firm's total assets in millions of Euros. An interaction term between the target's preemptive power and the acquirer's technology intensity is used to test Hypothesis 2.

Relatedness is based on the proximity measure introduced to the patent literature by Jaffe (1986) and captures the extent to which two firms develop technology in the same classes, using the three-digit IPC level. It is defined as the angular separation of the patent class distribution vectors of the acquirer and the target, used as a percentage of the total patent stock; the measure equals the scalar product of these vectors normalized by their scalar products with themselves, so that it takes the value of one for any two identical technology vectors. For Hypothesis 3 the measure is applied to the target's patents cited as preemptive (XY-type) and to the acquirer's patents cited as contributing to the state of the art (A-type), with fractional counting if a patent is cited as both; a linear and a squared term are used and only the linear term is expected to become significant.

Relative attention was measured by asking respondents to answer three questions on a scale ranging from 1 ('much lower') through 4 ('about the same') to 7 ('much higher') about the amount of attention paid to the focal subsidiary relative to key Asian markets, relative to comparatively sized markets in the region, and relative to comparatively sized markets in other parts of the world. Supportive attention used three items on a scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 7 ('strongly agree') about cash bonuses and career opportunities for subsidiary people, parent companies wanting to learn more about the local market and products, and the head office helping diffuse best practices across the firm's global network. Visible attention was assessed from the content of an MNE's annual report as three ratios averaged over two years (2003-04): mentions of the subsidiary country location divided by total words, divided by references to the parent company's nationality, and divided by references to China; all three were converted to logarithms. The three dimensions form an aggregate multidimensional construct that the authors modeled as a second-order factor represented by nine items loading on three first-order dimensions.
scale: 7-point scales (1-7) for relative and supportive items; logged ratios for visible items

variable_name: Strategic significance of a local market
description: The construct was measured with two separate indicators, both computed at the North American Industry Classification Index (NAICS) three-digit-industry level of analysis. Local market size was calculated as the proportion of worldwide industry sales realized in a given subsidiary's host country, using data reported in Compustat Global Vantage. Presence of multinationals in a local subsidiary market was calculated as the ratio of foreign direct investment inflows to foreign direct investment outflows over the most recent previous ten years, using data from the United Nations 2005 World Investment Report.
time_window: Most recent previous ten years (FDI ratio)

description: Measured with a four-item scale adapted from O'Donnell (2000) that asked respondents to indicate, from 1 ('to a very little extent') to 7 ('to a great extent'), whether the activities of this subsidiary influence the outcomes of other subsidiaries, whether work in this subsidiary is connected to the work of other subsidiaries, whether the activities of other subsidiaries influence the outcomes of this subsidiary, and whether this subsidiary depends on the effective functioning of other subsidiaries to keep performing its own tasks effectively. The authors state that the final measure was calculated from these items; the formula itself is not readable in the text.
scale: 1-7 (to a very little extent to a great extent)

description: Measured with a four-item scale from Birkinshaw et al. (1998) tapping various aspects of subsidiary initiatives. The items were all preceded by the stem, 'How often have any of the following activities occurred over the previous five years?' and were answered from 1 ('never') to 7 ('plentifully').

A composite measure capturing track record, commitment to the parent company, and impression management, assessed by confirmatory factor analysis as a second-order construct. Track record items covered the subsidiary's history of delivering what it promised to the parent company, its history of strong internationally-respected leaders, and the credibility of subsidiary top management; commitment items covered whether subsidiary managers care about the fate of the parent company and whether what the parent company stands for is important to them, plus an item on a strong sense of affiliation with the multinational corporation as a whole; impression management items covered working with head-office managers to focus efforts towards corporate goals and values, involving the parent company in the business and welcoming their input, and spending time developing connections with people in positions of authority at corporate headquarters. The sense-of-affiliation item was dropped from the measurement model because of high cross-loadings on other constructs, and the reduced set of items was retained for all subsequent tests.

Computed by applying the great-circle distance formula to the latitude and longitude coordinates of the city locations of both subsidiary and corporate headquarters to precisely calculate physical distance in kilometers. All distances were computed with a calculator available at a public map-crow website.

Each subsidiary's downstream competence was assessed by asking respondents to indicate which value-added activities it performed from a list of eight activities, four downstream and four upstream. The measure of a downstream competence was the number of downstream activities divided by the total number of subsidiary activities.
scale: ratio of downstream activities to total activities

description: The authors counted all alliances and joint ventures of a focal firm with all other firms in the sample within the same three-digit industry while excluding direct competitors with a four-digit SIC code match. The choice of size and industry to capture partner homophily is justified because size and industry boundaries shape the mental models and the resources of a firm and its top management.

The measure counts coinvestment ties with VC firms. The idea behind the measure is that by establishing a CVC unit that coinvests with private VC firms, an incumbent firm could connect to the networks of start-ups and VCs; the connections were operationalized through syndicated investments alongside VCs, i.e., the CVC fund in which an incumbent is the sole limited partner coinvesting with private VCs, thereby creating links between the corporation and VC companies and start-ups.

variable_name: status of partners in homophilous ties
description: Following Podolny, partner status in alliance networks was measured with Bonacich's centrality measure, with beta set to three-quarters of the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue of the relational matrix; the element of the relational matrix is the number of alliances between the companies. Centrality was calculated using the position of every alliance partner in the full network formed by all alliances established in the specified moving window, and the partner measures for focal firms were aggregated by averaging across all partners with which the focal firm had formed alliances or joint ventures in a given year.

variable_name: status of partners in heterophilous ties
description: For CVC coinvestments with VCs, the authors calculated the Bonacich centrality of all VCs with which a focal firm had coinvested in the given moving window using the full VC syndication networks, with beta set to three-quarters of the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue of the relational matrix, in which each element is the number of companies in which firms i and j have invested together. These values were then averaged to arrive at an aggregate value.

variable_name: time of first mention of the Internet in 10-K filings
description: The authors searched the annual 10-K filings of all sample companies over the entire sample period for occurrences of the phrase 'the Internet' within the Business section (Item 1) and recorded the year of the first mention of the discontinuity. The variable is the time between January 1989 and the time of a company's first mention, estimated with a hazard model in which positive coefficients indicate greater hazard, i.e., earlier attention; firms that never mentioned the discontinuity are right censored.

variable_name: time of first mention of wireless technologies in 10-K filings
description: Following the same logic used for the Internet, the authors identified the first mention of variations of the term 'wireless' in the 10-K filings and measured the time between January 1989 and that first mention to test the hypotheses. Other terms such as 'mobile' and 'cellular' were considered, but the word 'wireless' was judged the best choice for the analysis.

The dependent variable is the log of the per-issue price for a 1-year subscription. The per-issue price is the listed price for a 1-year subscription divided by the number of issues. The authors use the per-issue price rather than the total subscription price to allow comparison across magazines with different numbers of issues, and log price because of skewness in price.

A dummy variable that takes a value of one for a particular incumbent magazine if at least one new rival magazine enters the market during the current year, and zero otherwise. All new magazines listed in Samir Husni's annual Guides to New Consumer Magazines published at least four times per year in that year are included, except magazines also listed as entrants in a prior year and new magazines introduced by the incumbent's own publisher, which are not treated as rivals.

The logarithm of the number of years since the incumbent magazine was founded (since it entered the market). The authors use the log of age because the effect of age is likely to diminish at higher levels.
The logarithm of the number of markets in which the publisher sells magazines, used to measure the publisher's corporate scope.
A Herfindahl index measuring market structure, defined on a 0-1 scale.

For each supplier i in year t, the fractions of the firm's patents across 1806 4-digit IPC technology classes are used to compute a Herfindahl-Hirschman index, which is corrected for bias in HHI measures from count data following Hall (2002); the corrected HHI index is subtracted from one to obtain a diversification measure. Because the resulting variable is highly skewed, it is log transformed, specifically as [1 - ln(HHI*10000)/ln(10000)], where multiplying by 10,000 yields an HHI computed with percentages.

First, the fraction of outsourced patents in each 4-digit IPC is calculated for each client in each year; each client's fraction of outsourced business in each IPC is then multiplied by that client's share of the focal supplier's total business over the prior 3 years. These weighted fractions are aggregated across the supplier's entire portfolio of clients for each IPC and used to compute a 'Client HHI' in the same way as the dependent variable. The extent to which clients diversified 'away' from the supplier's business is captured by the Mahalanobis Distance between the weighted, aggregated client scope and the supplier's own scope in the prior year, divided by 100 so that the measure varies between zero and one; the variable is the product of 1-clients' HHI and the MD, using the same log transformation as the dependent variable.
time_window: client shares weighted over the prior 3 years; supplier scope in the prior year

description: Computed for each supplier as the average percentage of backward self-citations relative to all citations in the law firm's patent prosecution work in the prior 3 years, which is equivalent to a weighted average measure of client-level self-citation percentages. High client-specificity in technical knowledge is argued also to mirror client-specificity in other types of knowledge such as clients' strategies, processes, and ways of doing business.

For all clients, the patents outsourced to all U.S. patent law firms were identified and the percentage of those patents outsourced to the focal supplier in the prior 3 years was calculated, giving the share of patent work a supplier captures from each client. The aggregate supplier-level measure sums these client business shares weighted by the fraction of the supplier's business from each client over the prior 3 years.

Measured as the difference between growth in the market segments (IPCs) that a supplier's clients are active in and growth in the market segments that the supplier itself operates in, using the universe of patents granted by the USPTO. Running 3-year log growth in the number of patents applied for in each 4-digit IPC is computed and used to construct IPC-weighted measures of client market growth and supplier market growth.

Performance is calculated as return on assets (ROA). A historical aspiration level is the weighted average of the firm's past performance with most of the weight (0.9) assigned to the most recent ROA; a social aspiration level is the average ROA of all other firms in the same industry, as defined by the three-digit industry code. The historical aspiration level weight was chosen by comparing weights in intervals of 0.1 and choosing the one with best fit to the data. Each performance relative to the aspiration level is divided into performance above and below each aspiration level and interacted with the variables indicating board member experience.

Made by conducting a principal factor analysis of all boards using the proportions of board members with two sources of state experience, one source of state experience, both state and market experience, and market experience. The first factor has positive loading of two and one sources of state experience and both experiences, and negative loading of market experience, so boards can be ordered by their potential for forming a coalition of members with state experience. To take board member status into account, each board member is weighted linearly by age, setting the zero point to the youngest board member age.

Based on faultline theory, market and state experience are defined as binary characteristics that a board member could have either none, one, or both of, and the board is reduced to two groups using the Average Silhouette Weight procedure. The largest of these groups, which always had a majority of members with either state, market, or no experience, is selected as the dominant coalition. The stateness ASW is the proportion of board members in this group multiplied with their average state experience, set to -1 for members with market experience and 0 for members with both experiences.

variable_name: proportion of board members with state experience
description: The proportion of board members with work experience in a state agency or in a state-owned bank. The variable serves as an indicator of experience and comfort with the state and is used as a component of the measure on coalition formation.

variable_name: proportion of board members with market experience
description: The proportion of board members owning shares in the company or having education or work experience in an Anglo-Saxon nation. Board members owning shares are invested in the market economy, which produces greater attention and experience tracking market economy outcomes. The variable serves as an indicator of experience and comfort with the market and is used as a component of the measure on coalition formation.

The choice of what target to acquire among the options of internal, state-bridged, and market-oriented acquisitions. Type of acquisition is 0 for an internal acquisition, 1 for a state-bridged acquisition, and 2 for a market-oriented acquisition, so higher values mean greater distance from state-related actions. The choice is analyzed as an ordered logit, with robust standard errors clustered on the firm.

Analyzed the nature of market-oriented acquisitions by distinguishing asset transactions, minority share acquisitions, and majority control acquisitions, ranked by level of market orientation. Nature of acquisition is 0 for acquisition of assets without any equity stake, 1 for acquisition of minority equity, and 2 for acquisition of a controlling equity stake.

Takes the value of 1 when the loan is taken from a state-owned bank or a policy bank, and 0 for loans taken from a commercial bank, either Chinese or foreign. It is thus a measure of the selection of source of loan, not of whether or not a loan is taken. Only loans of a size exceeding 1% of firm assets are analyzed.

The number of days in which the acquirer's or the target's employees visited the other company's headquarters between 7:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m. of a business day in the 8 months preceding the acquisition announcement. A smartphone is assumed to belong to an employee of the company if it appeared in the company's location during a business day in that window; if a person appeared in both companies' locations, he or she is assigned to the company where he or she appeared on most business days. The variable is winsorized at the 2nd and 98th percentiles.

Percentage cumulative abnormal return on the acquirer's stock over a 3-day window centered on the deal announcement (date t = 0). Abnormal returns are the residuals from a market model estimated on the period from 260 to 20 trading days before the announcement, where the market return is the daily return on the CRSP value-weighted index; daily abnormal returns are summed over the 3-trading-day window surrounding the announcement date [-1, 1]. CAR is winsorized at the 2nd and 98th percentiles.
time_window: 3-day event window [-1, 1] around the announcement; market model estimated 260 to 20 trading days before the announcement

description: The number of bids the target receives from other bidders up to 2 years after the announcement of the focal acquisition. The measure allows some lag between the target's solicitation and the announcement of later bids, because the timing of the solicitation is not observable in the data.
time_window: up to 2 years after the announcement of the focal acquisition

description: The difference in weighted abnormal gains between the two merging companies, computed following Ahern (2012) as ΔCAR = (MVALt × CARt - MVALa × CARa)/(MVALt + MVALa), where CARt (CARa) is the percentage CAR of the target (acquirer) and MVALt (MVALa) is the market value of equity of the target (acquirer) 50 trading days before the announcement. Scaling CARs by each firm's market value accounts for differences in size between merging firms. Defined for the subset of deals with a public target and winsorized at the 2nd and 98th percentiles.
time_window: market values of equity 50 trading days before the announcement; CARs over the 3-day window around the announcement

description: The total abnormal gains of the two merging companies, defined as total CAR = (MVALt × CARt + MVALa × CARa)/(MVALt + MVALa), where CARt (CARa) and MVALt (MVALa) are the target's (acquirer's) percentage CAR and pre-announcement market value of equity. Winsorized at the 2nd and 98th percentiles and estimated on the subset of deals with a public target.
time_window: market values of equity 50 trading days before the announcement; CARs over the 3-day window around the announcement

description: The percentage of the target that is collectively owned by the target's management, broadly defined as executives and directors, collected from the last proxy statement before the deal. The variable is defined for public targets.
time_window: last proxy statement before the deal

description: The extent to which the firm has utilized guanxi connections with buyers, suppliers, and competitors. Responses were based on a 7-point Likert scale, and the authors used the mean of these items for this application of networking.

The extent to which the firm and its managers have utilized guanxi connections with government bodies. Responses were based on a 7-point Likert scale, and the authors used the mean of these items for this application of networking.

Ownership was defined by three groups - state-owned, collectively owned, and privately owned - according to the official classification by the Chinese government, and private and collective-owned firms were combined into one group. A dummy variable represented ownership structure, coded 1 for nonstate-owned firms (collective and private) and 0 for state-owned firms.

A dummy variable was created with 1 for nonopen cities and 0 for open cities, where open regions are those areas the central government has opened to the outside world. Open cities in the sample include Nanjing, Suzhou, Wuxi, Changzhou, Nantong, Lianyuangan, and Shanghai. Higher values therefore denote less open locations, the reverse of the construct as named.

Strategic orientation represents the mean of a multidimensional construct that includes questions of innovativeness, adaptability, and proactiveness, reflecting the level of market effectiveness. Responses for these items were on a 7-point Likert scale.
Firm size was measured by total assets.

Measured by managers' perception of the firm's technological skills and abilities vis-a-vis its major competitors in the industry. The authors note that previous studies show a strong correlation between subjective assessment vis-a-vis competitors and objective measures of firm resource strength.

Measured by managers' perception of the firm's managerial and organizational skills vis-a-vis its major competitors in the industry. Resource strength was measured by managers' perception of these skills relative to their major competitors.
Organizational age was measured as the number of years the firm has been operating in China.

Performance was defined according to financial measures during the most recent 3 years, one of which is sales growth, described by the authors as market expansion; the measure is widely used in studies of Chinese businesses.
Performance was defined according to financial measures during the most recent 3 years, one of which is net profit growth; the measure is widely used in studies of Chinese businesses.

CEO tenure was measured by counting the years a chief executive had been in office. Tenures were identified from public sources and company filings for food companies listed on the New York or American Stock Exchange; tenures continuing beyond 1994 were treated as right-censored, and the food sample's tenures ranged from 1 to 36 years. The predictor was updated annually and lagged by one year, and the square of tenure was also calculated and included where it was significant.

CEO tenure was measured by counting the years a chief executive had been in office. Tenures were identified from public sources and company filings for computer companies with primary SIC codes 3570, 3571 or 3572; tenures continuing beyond 1994 were treated as right-censored, and the computer sample's tenures ranged from 1 to 36 years. The predictor was updated annually and lagged by one year, and the square of tenure was also calculated and included where it was significant.

variable_name: profitability (factor index of return on sales, return on assets, return on invested capital)
description: Firm performance was assessed with three annual measures of profitability: return on sales = net income t / sales t; return on assets = net income t / net assets t; and return on invested capital = net income t / (shareholders equity t + debt t). All financial data were taken from COMPUSTAT. Within each industry the measures were highly correlated, so weights from factor analyses were used to extract a unified construct; in the food industry the analysis yielded a one-factor solution with an eigenvalue of 2.52 that explained 84.1 percent of total variance.

variable_name: profitability (factor index of return on sales, return on assets, return on invested capital)
description: Firm performance was assessed with three annual measures of profitability: return on sales = net income t / sales t; return on assets = net income t / net assets t; and return on invested capital = net income t / (shareholders equity t + debt t). All financial data were taken from COMPUSTAT. Within each industry the measures were highly correlated, so weights from factor analyses were used to extract a unified construct; in the computer sector the analysis yielded a one-factor weighted average of profitability with an eigenvalue of 2.28 that explained 76.1 percent of total variance.

variable_name: Industry contrast (stable branded foods versus dynamic computers)
description: Industry dynamism was operationalized by choosing two industries with contrasting dynamism, stable branded foods and dynamic computers, and estimating separate models for each. No continuous dynamism score was computed.

Technology resource breadth was calculated using a Herfindahl-type index analogous to Hall et al.'s (2001) approach, where S_i is the proportion of n patents in USPTO patent class i; the equation itself is unreadable in the available text. Patent data came from a Delphion search, were matched to NBER patent data using organization numbers, and were supplemented by direct USPTO searches; patents granted prior to 1975 were deleted. The patents were assigned to 67 distinct USPTO patent classes with an average of nine patent classes per firm. Technology resource breadth within the sample ranged from 0 to 0.91.

News articles pertaining to each sample firm for a given year were searched in LexisNexis and categorized into pre-established competitive action categories using N*UDIST NVIVO structured content analysis software; two coders worked independently (intercoder reliability 0.74) and a third coder resolved disagreements. Deviance is calculated as the sum of squared difference in proportions of categories of competitive action between the focal firm and the industry mean, where P_i is the proportion of the ith category for the focal firm and the industry mean proportion excludes the focal firm; the equation itself is unreadable in the available text.

Heterogeneity in age was measured using the coefficient of variation, defined as the standard deviation divided by the mean. TMT demographics data were collected from proxy statements filed with the Security Exchange Commission, and officers of the firm listed in proxy statements were identified as TMT members.

TMT tenure heterogeneity measures both TMT organizational tenure and team tenure heterogeneity, where team tenure heterogeneity might indicate the extent of sharing experiences among TMT members within the team and organizational tenure heterogeneity the extent of sharing experiences within the firm. Both were calculated in the same way as age heterogeneity, i.e., as the coefficient of variation.

Each top management team member was categorized into one of eight functional backgrounds. TMT functional heterogeneity was then measured with Blau's (1977) Herfindal-Hirschman index, calculated as 1 - sum of S_i squared, where S_i is the proportion of a TMT in the ith category.

Following Thatcher et al. (2003), faultline strength was operationalized as the percentage of total variation in group attributes accounted for by the strongest group split, computed as the ratio of the between-group sum of squares to the total sum of squares over all two-subgroup splits; the equations are unreadable in the available text. The same attributes used in the heterogeneity measure were used, and because of the small size of top management teams (4-6 members) only splits into two subgroups were considered. Faultline strength values can range from 0 to 1 (0.10-0.99 in the sample), with higher values indicating stronger faultlines.

Following Lee and Tompkins (1999), Tobin's q was calculated as the sum of market value of equity, preferred stock value, and debt scaled by total assets. To ensure causality, Tobin's q is calculated for the subsequent year of competitive actions and TMT. Data for the Tobin's q calculation were collected from Compustat from 1996 to 2000.
time_window: subsequent year of competitive actions and TMT (data 1996-2000)

description: Set to 1 if the first four digits of the two firms' NAICS codes are the same, 0.75 if the first three digits of the two firms' NAICS codes are the same, 0.5 if the first two digits are the same, 0.25 if the first digit is the same, and 0 if the first digit of the two firms' NAICS codes is different. The authors follow the common SIC-based tradition for measuring business relatedness but use NAICS.

Adapted from the survivor measure of relatedness by Teece et al. (1994), which assumes that activities that are more frequently combined within the same corporation are more related; here the assumption is that activities that are more frequently combined are more complementary, so the degree of complementarity between two NAICS codes proxies business complementarity between two firms with those primary NAICS codes. All firms with more than one NAICS code are selected from COMPUSTAT together with their NAICS codes, and firms with only one NAICS code are excluded. The complementarity score of a NAICS code with itself is coded 0. The formula for the complementarity score between any pair of NAICS codes is not readable in the text provided.

variable_name: Combined alliance capabilities of two firms
description: The total number of alliances formed by both firms with all other firms (including those outside the sample) in the previous 5 years.

variable_name: Combined acquisition capabilities of two firms
description: The total number of acquisitions conducted by the two firms with all other firms (including those outside the sample) in the previous 5 years. The variable is an aggregation of the capabilities of acquiring and target firms.
The total number of alliances formed between the two firms in the previous 5 years.
The total number of acquisitions conducted between the two firms in the previous 5 years. This number could be more than one since many acquisitions are partial instead of complete acquisitions.

variable_name: Occurrence of an alliance or an acquisition
description: A variable with three possible values: 0 (there was no resource combination between two firms); 1 (an alliance was formed between two firms); and 2 (an acquisition occurred between two firms). The transactions of alliances and acquisitions were recorded on the dates when firms announced these deals. The alliance outcome is modeled against the no-resource-combination baseline.

variable_name: Occurrence of an alliance or an acquisition
description: A variable with three possible values: 0 (there was no resource combination between two firms); 1 (an alliance was formed between two firms); and 2 (an acquisition occurred between two firms). The transactions of alliances and acquisitions were recorded on the dates when firms announced these deals. The acquisition outcome is modeled against the no-resource-combination baseline in the same multinomial logit model.

Indicator variable equal to ' 1 ' if a disaster event occurred at least once in the county where the CEO lived between the ages of 5 and 15 years and ' 0 ' otherwise. Disaster events included earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis, hurricanes, tornadoes, wildfires, and other miscellaneous accidents (e.g., airplane crashes) that had 10 or more fatalities. The place where each CEO grew up was retrieved from biographical sources; for 24% of the sample the CEO's birth place was taken as the place where they grew up.

Corporate social performance measured as CSR minus CsiR, where CSR is the sum of the strengths indices in the six KLD categories and CsiR is the sum of the concerns indices in those categories. The KLD dataset is designed as a binary system in which a '1' indicates the presence of a strength (positive screen) or concern (negative screen) and a '0' otherwise. For each year, the number of strengths (concerns) for each firm within each category was divided by the maximum possible number of strengths (concerns) in that category, giving a strengths index and a concerns index for each category.

Corporate social responsibility measured as the sum of the strengths indices in the six KLD categories. The strengths indices were built from the binary KLD screens by dividing, for each year, the number of strengths for each firm within each category by the maximum possible number of strengths in that category.

Corporate social irresponsibility measured as the sum of the concerns indices in the six KLD categories. The concerns indices were built from the binary KLD screens by dividing, for each year, the number of concerns for each firm within each category by the maximum possible number of concerns in that category.

Indicator variable equal to ' 1 ' if a firm is led by a CEO with disaster experience at age 5 to 10 and ' 0 ' otherwise. This period was selected as the younger half of the authors' 5 to 15 year age range.

Disaster severity measured as the (log-transformed) number of fatalities in the disaster. The authors use death toll because, in contrast to event type-specific measures of disaster severity such as seismic intensity, sea swells, and wind speeds, it can be uniformly applied across different types of disaster events.
The number of common shares owned by a CEO divided by total common stock outstanding, measured for fiscal year 1997, the year prior to the year for which advice seeking was measured.

The proportion of a CEO's total direct compensation comprised of long-term incentive pay; total direct compensation was comprised of annual salary, short-term bonuses, and the value of long-term incentive grants made to the CEO in the prior year. Stock options were valued using the Black-Scholes method and other long-term grants, such as performance shares and restricted stock, were valued at the market price on the date of grant. Measured for fiscal year 1997.

A five-item scale in the director survey assessing board monitoring of the focal CEO for the prior calendar year (1997). The five items loaded on a single factor in a principal factor analysis with promax rotation, and factor scores were generated using the Bartlett method. Interrater agreement, assessed with the weighted kappa coefficient, exceeded .75 for all five survey items.
scale: 1-5 response scale for the Likert-type items; number of times for the remaining items

description: The average number of years all focal-firm outside directors had served as executives at other firms, where executives were defined as managers at the rank of senior vice president or above. Measured for fiscal year 1997, the prior year.

variable_name: seeking of advice from executives who are not friends
description: Count of the number of times during the prior calendar year (1998) that the focal CEO solicited strategic advice from managers at other companies who were not friends of the CEO. Friendship was coded from the CEO's indication, for each person from whom advice had been sought, of whether that person was an acquaintance or a friend.

variable_name: seeking of advice from executives with different functional background
description: Count of the number of times during the prior calendar year (1998) that the focal CEO solicited strategic advice from managers at other companies whose functional background differed from the CEO's. Functional background was coded from archival sources into output-related functions, throughput-related functions, and peripheral functions, and was coded as the area in which an executive had spent more time than any other.

Accounting-based measure of focal firm performance, adjusted for industry differences by subtracting the average value for the firm's primary industry defined at the two-digit SIC code level. Measured two years after the survey date.

Market-based measure of focal firm performance, adjusted for industry differences by subtracting the average value for the firm's primary industry defined at the two-digit SIC code level. Measured two years after the survey date.

One-period change in R&D investment for each firm-year observation. R&D investment data were collected for each firm-year observation from COMPUSTAT. The authors argue that change in the level of R&D, rather than change in R&D/sales, is appropriate because R&D is a decision variable while the firm's sales are determined by the market.

Count of new product awards for each firm-year observation, collected from eight widely cited trade publications. The publications screened as many new products shipped within the year as possible and disqualified only those that had low performance specifications or little difference relative to previous generations of products. The independent variables were lagged relative to the change in R&D investment.
time_window: one-year lag (year t) relative to R&D; awards 1991-2000

description: Eigenvector of the largest positive eigenvalue of a relationship matrix, following Bonacich (1972). The measure was generated from each firm's yearly alliances with UCINET IV, a software program for social network analysis. Normalized values were used for each network measure for each firm based on yearly alliances, which meant the measures were not sensitive to changes in network sizes.
time_window: yearly alliances; lagged one year relative to R&D expenditure

description: Count of the number of awards that a firm's partners received in a given year. The impact of the partners' awards variable on R&D expenditure was lagged by one year.

Built from an n x n matrix of yearly patent citations for all listed firms, in which each cell indicated the number of times firm i's patents cited firm j's patents in the last ten years, using a moving window of ten years for each patent citation matrix. Technical proximity is the number of cross citations between firm i and firm j divided by total citations made by all firms in the industry, excluding self-citations.

variable_name: Ratio of partners' awards to a focal firm's awards
description: Ratio of partners' awards to a focal firm's awards, cumulated over the last three years. The higher the ratio, the greater the focal firm's loss of attractiveness relative to other firms with which its partners might form alliances.
time_window: cumulated over the last three years

description: The measure was calculated based upon four different financial measures: net proceeds from the first page of the final prospectus (cash the firm receives as a result of the offering less costs incurred during the IPO process); pre-money market valuation; 90-day market valuation; and 180-day market valuation after the IPO. The pre-money market value uses the final IPO subscription price, the number of shares outstanding, and the number of shares offered in the IPO, and equals the firm's market valuation less the proceeds to the firm; the same formula is used for the 90-day and 180-day valuations with the post-IPO price substituted. Since the four financial measures were highly correlated with one another, these measures were standardized and the mean was taken to create one financial indicator; the estimates were transformed into constant 1996 dollars and logged.
time_window: at the IPO; 90 days and 180 days after the IPO

description: A financial index developed by Lerner (1994) that gauges the receptivity of the equity markets to biotechnology offerings, constructed based on an equal amount of dollar shares of 13 publicly traded, dedicated biotechnology firms. The value of Lerner's equity index at the end of the month prior to the IPO date was used as the indicator of industry uncertainty at the time of the IPO. The measure ranges from low to high or from cold to hot (unfavorable to favorable).
level: firm (dated by month prior to the offering)
time_window: end of the month prior to the IPO date

description: An indicator of whether a firm's VC partnerships were prominent. Lists of prominent VCs were created for each IPO year from VentureXpert rankings based on total dollars invested by each VC in each of the 18 years of the dataset. Firms were coded as 1 if any of the biotechnology firm's VCs with a minimum of a 5 percent stake were listed among the top 30 on the list of prominent VCs for the year prior to the firm's IPO date, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: year prior to the firm's IPO date

description: Measured using an index developed by Carter and Manaster (1990) and updated by Carter, Dark, and Singh (1998), based on analyses of investment banks' positions in the tombstone announcements for IPOs. The authors assigned the highest integer rank (9) to the first-listed underwriter, the second highest rank (8) to the next-listed underwriter(s) and so on, resolving inconsistencies across successive announcements; the final scale is incremented in units of 0.125 and scores range from 0 (lowest prestige) to 9 (highest prestige). The name of the lead investment bank came from the front page of the final prospectuses; information was available for all but 25 of the underwriters, yielding rankings for 244 firms.

The total number of alliances the firm had to prominent pharmaceutical/health care organizations, measured as the number of alliances with prominent pharmaceutical and/or health care companies the year prior to the offering. Prominence was determined by generating 18 yearly lists of the top 30 pharmaceutical and health care organizations by sales since 1979 using COMPUSTAT (top 30 U.S. organizations from 1979 to 1987, top 30 U.S. and international organizations from 1988 to 1996), supplemented with major private or European/Japanese companies listed in PharmaBusiness with comparable sales.

Dummy variable indicating whether an inventor is involved in a knowledge-sharing clique. It was built from the raw scientific knowledge-sharing network matrix by first identifying Simmelian ties with Krackhardt's formulation, that is, ties in which both parties are reciprocally tied to each other and both are reciprocally tied to a common third party; starting from the network of Simmelian ties only, the authors identified for each inventor whether he or she belonged or not to a clique.
time_window: at the time of the network survey

description: Dummy variable indicating whether an inventor is involved in a friendship clique. It was built from the raw friendship network matrix by first identifying Simmelian ties, that is, ties in which both parties are reciprocally tied to each other and both are reciprocally tied to a common third party; starting from the network of Simmelian ties only, the authors identified for each inventor whether he or she belonged or not to a clique.
time_window: at the time of the network survey

description: Count of patent applications filed by respondents in the United States Patent and Trademark Office and the European Patent Office.
