The authors started from the archival data provided by the company, updated and reviewed patent applications, and tracked down patents filed by respondents during an 18-month period: 6 months before and 12 months after the collection of network data. This count represents the study's dependent variable.
time_window: 18-month period: 6 months before and 12 months after the collection of network data

description: Perceptions of authenticity were measured by combining three measures (Cronbach's alpha equals 0.95), adapted from previous work on authenticity. Participants were asked to rate on a one (low) to seven (high) Likert scale the question 'How [authentic, real, genuine] is this Cuban cigar based on the information above?'

For the ultimate dependent variable, participants were asked: 'Based on the information provided to you, rate the above-described cigar on how pleased you would expect that a cigar aficionado would be to receive this type of cigar?' answered from 1 (not at all pleased) to 7 (extremely pleased). The question is phrased in a third-order way in order to reduce the effects of individual differences.

All participants were told that Cuban-style cigars are produced all over the region but originated in Cuba, establishing Cuba as the provenance-based claim. Participants randomly assigned to the provenance-based claim condition were told that the cigar they would view was made in Cuba and sourced by materials and methods from Cuba, whereas those in the nonprovenance-based claim condition were told the cigar was made using materials and methods from Cuba but produced completely in Nicaragua. In all conditions participants were given the same objective quality information and were told that the materials and methods of production came from Cuba.

Participants randomly assigned to the expand within-country condition were told that because the cigar is in high demand, 'the producers have decided to expand production by locating a new factory in [Country Name],' with the provenance-based claim condition listing Cuba and the nonprovenance-based claim condition listing Nicaragua. Participants assigned to the geographical expansion condition were told the same thing except that the location of the new factory would be in Guatemala.
Study 2 used the same composite authenticity measure as Study 1, the three-item scale combining perceptions of how authentic, real, and genuine the cigar was on seven-point scales.
Study 2 used the same single-item appreciation measure as Study 1, asking participants to rate on a one to seven scale how pleased a cigar aficionado would be to receive the described cigar.

Participants randomly assigned to the provenance-based claim condition were informed about the role of location as an important authenticity claim for Cuban cigars in two locations. First, in the description of the history of Cuban cigars, participants were told that Cuban cigars are made from materials in Cuba and rolled using traditional methods, and they were then told the same information as used in the provenance-based claim manipulation used in Study 1.

Participants randomly assigned to the symbolism-based claim conditions were informed about the role of Fidel Castro as a representative of Cuba along with his connection to Cuban cigars, with the emphasis on Fidel's role as a representative of Cuba, a symbol of its history and revolution. After the objective quality information, they were told that Fidel was often seen with cigars and that he was a champion of the brand they were to evaluate.

Participants randomly assigned to the transference-based claim conditions were told the same things about Fidel Castro as the symbolism conditions and also that Fidel 'cultivated [this brand] on his own estates.' Those in the transference conditions were additionally told about how Fidel made physical contact with the land on which these cigars were made ('even rolling a few of these cigars himself') in order to reemphasize the transference mechanism.

After the claim vignettes, participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions describing the expansion of the firm because of increased demand, using the same language as in Study 1. Those in the within-country expansion condition were told that the new factory would be in Cuba, and those in the geographic expansion condition were told that the new factory would be in Nicaragua.
R&D expenditures divided by sales, used as a proxy for the magnitude of the firm's technological search effort. Higher values indicate a larger search effort relative to the firm's sales.

Following prior classifications, the author used current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities) to represent available slack, working capital-to-sales ratio to measure recoverable slack, and equity-to-debt ratio to proxy potential slack. The three proxies were standardized and summed up to obtain a general slack index. Slack is measured at the end of the prior year.

I1 is an indicator variable equal to 1 if firm i's past performance falls below aspiration, either firm specific or industry specific; the variable is this indicator combined with the performance-aspiration gap, so it takes negative values that grow in magnitude the further past performance falls below aspiration. Past performance is return on assets lagged one year relative to the dependent search variable. Aspiration follows an exponentially weighted moving average of past performance; with a weight of 0.4, the firm aspiration at t-1 is a weighted combination of the focal firm's performance at t-2 (weight of 0.6) and at t-3 (weight of 0.4), and the industry aspiration is the weighted median performance of firms in the same four-digit SIC industry. Two aspiration proxies, own-firm and industry median, were run in separate models.
time_window: t-1 (aspiration built from t-2 and t-3)

description: I2 is an indicator variable for firms unlikely to achieve their target performance, equal to 1 if firm i's performance expectation is lower than its targets; the variable is this indicator combined with the difference between expected performance and target, so it takes negative values that grow in magnitude the further expected performance falls below target. Performance expectation is one-year forecasting ROA(t+1), computed by multiplying the median estimate of earnings per share among all analysts obtained from I/B/E/S by the total number of shares and then dividing by total assets. The performance target is the predicted value of ROA(t) from regressing on the firm's (or the industry's median) ROA from time t-1 to t-3.
time_window: expectation for t+1; target from t-1 to t-3

description: (1 - I2) refers to firms whose performance expectation exceeds targets; the variable is the difference between expected performance and target for these firms, so higher values mean expected performance lies further above target. Performance expectation is one-year forecasting ROA(t+1), computed by multiplying the median estimate of earnings per share among all analysts obtained from I/B/E/S by the total number of shares and then dividing by total assets. The performance target is the predicted value of ROA(t) from regressing on the firm's (or the industry's median) ROA from time t-1 to t-3.
time_window: expectation for t+1; target from t-1 to t-3

description: Survey question asking how often the key or most important client obtains the control rights to intellectual output—design, process plan, or technology—created in joint projects. Response categories are never, sometimes, often, or always. Higher values mean more client control and thus less retention by the service supplier.

Survey question asking how often the service firm agrees with key clients that it will not supply similar services to the clients' competitors. Response categories are never, sometimes, often, or always. Higher values mean stronger constraints on the service supplier and thus less retention of control over its intellectual assets.

The sum of output control rights to client and partial exclusivity, ranging from 0 to 6. The two contractual arrangements are assumed to measure the same underlying concept: the degree to which clients can control the service firm's use of its intellectual assets. Higher values mean more client control and thus less retention.

Survey question asking how often the service firm carries out service projects independently from the client, that is, in relatively infrequent interaction with the client. Response categories are never, sometimes, often, or always; operating independently is assumed to indicate greater indispensability.

Survey question asking how often the service provider designs projects for clients. Response categories range from 0 (never) to 3 (always); providing project planning and design is assumed to indicate greater indispensability in client projects.
Binary indicator for whether the firm has a permanent service development team or department. Twenty percent of the surveyed firms report having a permanent development team or department.
Service development investments as a share of sales. The mean of service development expenditures in the sample is 6.3 percent of sales.
Binary indicator for whether the firm made any R&D investments in 1999. Sixty percent of firms report having invested in the development of their services.
Share of employees with higher education (college or university) degrees. In an average firm, one-third of employees have higher education degrees, the median being 25 percent.
Share of employees with postgraduate (licentiate or Ph.D.) degrees. Almost three percent of employees in the firms surveyed have such degrees.
Natural logarithm of the firm's number of employees in 1999, used to reduce skewness. Firm size is treated as a proxy for the firm's established position and reputation in the industry.

Binary indicator for firms that are subsidiaries of a service group, wholly or majority owned by other service firms or holding companies. Ownership structure is treated as a proxy for bargaining power.
Binary indicator for whether the firm had any export sales, treated as a proxy for the firm's position in the industry and thus its bargaining power.
Export sales per sales in 1999, used as a measure of export activity and a proxy for bargaining power.

Sales per employee, used as a proxy for profitability and market power. The ability to price above marginal cost reflects market power and translates into higher profits, and absence of liquidity constraints may improve the firm's bargaining position.

Age of the firm in years in 1999. Newly founded business service providers are less likely to have built solid reputations than more established counterparts, so age is assumed to be associated with bargaining power with clients.

Binary indicator for firms that introduced significantly improved services in the previous three years. The survey question asked whether the firm had introduced significantly improved services during that period.
Binary indicator for firms that introduced completely new services in the previous three years. The services are new to the firm itself, not necessarily to the market.

variable_name: New service and improved service launched
description: Two binary indicators from the survey: whether the firm introduced completely new services (new to the firm) and whether it introduced significantly improved services in the previous three years.

Binary variable equal to 1 if a CEO served in any of the branches of the U.S. military (Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, Navy, and Coast Guard), including the reserves, and 0 otherwise. Built from hand-collected biographical information from Marquis Who's Who, BoardEx, and the Notable Names Database, supplemented with corporate filings, press releases, interviews, speeches and biographies for details on rank, length of service, branch and participation in conflicts. In the fraud sample, 32 (15.53%) of the CEOs have a military background and the average service in the military is 4.07 years (minimum 1 year, maximum 10 years).

Binary variable equal to 1 if a CEO served in any of the branches of the U.S. military (Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, Navy, and Coast Guard), including the reserves, and 0 otherwise. Built from hand-collected biographical information from Marquis Who's Who, BoardEx, and the Notable Names Database, supplemented with corporate filings, press releases, interviews, speeches and biographies. In the lucky grant sample, 213 (16.84%) of the 1,265 CEOs have served in the military and the average service is 6.38 years (minimum 1 year, maximum 38 years).

Binary variable equal to 1 for all fraudulent firms and to 0 for all matched control firms. Fraud cases are firms subject to SEC enforcement actions for allegedly misstating their quarterly or annual financial statements, and the firm is coded as fraudulent in the year when it first engaged in fraudulent reporting, with subsequent fraud years excluded.
time_window: year in which the firm first engaged in fraudulent reporting

description: Binary variable with a value of 1 when at least one option grant to the CEO during year t was given on a day which had the lowest stock price of the month, and 0 otherwise. The measure captures instances of backdating with the greatest economic significance to CEOs and shareholders and is a proxy for opportunistic timing rather than direct evidence that the CEO backdated a grant.

The Gini coefficient computed across hierarchical groups within each firm, implemented to be consistent with the measure of horizontal dispersion. The authors begin by using individual data to compute mean wages at each hierarchical level in the firm and then use these grouped data (wage averages reported by group) as an input into computing the Gini coefficient across hierarchical groups within each firm. Four hierarchical levels are used, because these levels demarcate vertical wage differences in the data. The specification formula is unreadable in the source.

The Gini coefficient computed for each level of firm-hierarchy-year, where wi is the raw wage of the ith ranked individual in a given hierarchy within a firm and is indexed in nondecreasing order, and m is the number of workers within a given organizational rank. The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (absolute equality) to 1 (absolute dispersion). The specification formula is unreadable in the source.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 when an employee switches to another employer in a subsequent year and 0 otherwise. Employees who exit current employment but do not take another job are censored, because such exits may reflect other life-cycle processes, including retirement or death.

Indicator for a top wage earner in the vertical (firm-wide) wage distribution: equal to 1 when the employee ranks above the 90th percentile of the distribution of the absolute wage within their firm in a given year, and 0 otherwise. This measure is interacted with vertical wage dispersion.

Indicator for a bottom wage earner in the vertical (firm-wide) wage distribution: equal to 1 when the employee ranks below the 10th percentile of the distribution of the absolute wage within their firm in a given year, and 0 otherwise. This measure is interacted with vertical wage dispersion.

Indicator for a top wage earner in the horizontal (within-level) wage distribution: equal to 1 when the employee ranks above the 90th percentile of the distribution of the absolute wage within their firm-hierarchy in a given year, and 0 otherwise. This measure is interacted with horizontal wage dispersion.

Indicator for a bottom wage earner in the horizontal (within-level) wage distribution: equal to 1 when the employee ranks below the 10th percentile of the distribution of the absolute wage within their firm-hierarchy in a given year, and 0 otherwise. This measure is interacted with horizontal wage dispersion.

Ratio of the market value of a firm's equity and debt to the replacement cost of the firm's assets, where the replacement value of the firm's assets is as reported on its 10-K form. The estimates of q for 1976 were prepared by Stephen Ross from an initially random sample of 246 firms, and the mean value of q in the sample is close to unity, as theory suggests.

The standard deviation of the residual term in the market model, in which a security's daily return is regressed on the corresponding return of an equally weighted market portfolio. It was computed from daily data for 1976; for the return test, business risk was estimated on odd dates and Jensen's alpha on even dates so as to obtain independent estimates.

Returns in excess of those predicted by the CAPM, estimated with Jensen's performance evaluation model using daily returns and the return on a portfolio of treasury bills; the expected value of alpha is zero if stockholders value only systematic risk. The alpha was estimated on the even dates and the business risk with which it was correlated on the odd dates.

The R&D intensity of a focal firm's industry in year t, used to estimate the technological dynamism of each industry. The index was specified as firms' aggregate R&D spending per year divided by firms' total assets. Data on firms' R&D spending were obtained from COMPUSTAT and Orbis.

The focal firm's ego-network constraint in year t minus its constraint in year t + 1, where constraint is Burt's index ci = Pj (eij + Pk eik ekj)2, which increases as ego's contacts become more connected to one another. A positive value indicated the pursuit of a more-open ego network, whereas a negative value indicated the pursuit of a more-closed ego network. Constraint was computed on the industry-wide partnership networks reconstructed annually, with partnerships assumed to last an average of five years, and only firms that formed at least one new partnership in a given year were included. For the correlation analysis the authors also estimated each firm's probability of forming a more-open ego network in any year (pi), summarized by the fraction of firms with zero probability (frac p = 0) and the average propensity of the remaining firms (p).

variable_name: p (propensity to pursue an open ego network)
description: A probabilistic parameter defined as ego's probability of pursuing an alter associated with the greatest decrease in ego's network constraint; ego's probability of pursuing an alter associated with the greatest increase in constraint was thus 1 - p. The same level of p was set for all firms in an industry, while the fraction of firms with zero probability of forming an open ego network was captured by a separate parameter, frac p = 0. In the model, ego rank-ordered potential alters by the expected change in network constraint and, to ensure matching between ego and alter, only ties that reflected alter's expectations as well were allowed.

Defined formally as an index in which nk is the size of the kth network component and N is the size of the entire network; the index captures how many components are in the network and how they vary in terms of sizes. The possible values range from close to 0 for a highly disconnected network that contains many small components to 1 for a fully connected network that contains one large component. The equation itself is unreadable in the available text, and the description here follows the authors' prose.

Measured with the method of Girvan and Newman (2002), which detects communities by computing the network's modularity index; e is the total number of ties in the network, ekk is the number of ties in the kth community, and the expected number of ties within communities is estimated from a baseline network that connects firms at random while preserving the same distribution of ties as in the observed network. The method effectively evaluates to what extent the observed network differs from a fully random network in terms of its community structure, and the best split was found with the simulated annealing algorithm of Guimera and Amaral (2005). The equation itself is unreadable in the available text, and the description here follows the authors' prose.

A management representative in each establishment completed a comprehensive checklist of HR practices, from which 16 practices that could be mapped onto the AMO model of HRM were selected. Because the items had different scale formats, all HR practices were standardized using industry means to assess an establishment's intensity of use for each practice relative to other establishments in its industry. Ability-, motivation-, and opportunity-enhancing domain scores were created by averaging the standardized scores of the practices within each AMO domain, and the overall HPWS index is the mean across the three AMO domain scores.
scale: index of industry-mean standardized HR practice scores
time_window: measured at t (baseline) for outcomes at t+1

description: Internal consistency of an establishment's implementation of an HPWS was measured as the SD among the three AMO domain scores, where each domain score represents the mean level of intensity with which an establishment employed the practices within that domain. The authors took the reciprocal of this value so that higher scores represent higher internal consistency. Given the use of industry-adjusted A, M, and O scores, the measure concerns the extent to which an establishment's relative intensities of use for the A, M, and O HR domains in its industry are similar across the three domains.

A management representative in each establishment selected one of four descriptions of his or her establishment's entry timing modes for its main products or services: first mover, fast follower, fence sitter, or none of the above. The first mover was defined as one in which the establishment quickly responds to customers' unmet needs and early market signals and tries to pioneer offering new products to the market; the fast follower as one in which the establishment carefully researches first-movers' activities and tries to catch up with first movers in a more efficient and planned way; and the fence sitter as one in which the establishment occupies stable markets with existing products and does not try to develop new products or enter new markets. Four dummy variables were created that correspond to these four choices.
scale: four categories (first mover, fast follower, fence sitter, none of the above)

description: The KLI provided the WPS data along with a financial information set, from which product sales were divided by the total number of employees to account for establishment heterogeneity in terms of size. Given the potential for reciprocal relationships between an HPWS and establishment performance, and the time it takes for an HPWS to affect performance, the authors used a two-year subsequent product sales (t+1) model as a proximal outcome while controlling for current sales (t).
time_window: t+1 (with current sales at t controlled)

description: Financial performance was measured as a ratio of operating profit to average total assets (ROA). Because the distribution of financial performance had high skewness and kurtosis, the variable was winsorized at the 1% level at both tails to reduce the influence of extreme values. As with product sales, subsequent financial performance (t+1) was used as a dependent variable with current financial performance (t) controlled for.
time_window: t+1 (with current financial performance at t controlled)

description: The share of total power sold by IOU i in year t from wind, solar, hydroelectric, biomass, and geothermal generating sources. It examines the total renewable power distributed to the end consumer, which includes power generated by IOUs and power purchased from independent power producers. The authors favor measuring total power distributed because their predictions concern firms' environmental performance, which is a function of both what an IOU generates and what it sources from IPPs.

The average RPS faced by all other IOUs that operate in the same state(s) as a focal firm but excluding the RPS that they commonly face. Peers are firms that operate in common output markets but face differing policy obligations. When a peer is a multistate utility, its RPS objective is measured as the most stringent policy that it faces across its multiple states, not the RPS shared with the focal utility. The average of the RPS for all peers is then assigned to the focal IOU.

The average RPS objective of the contiguous states where the focal firm does not have any operations. The average number of contiguous states for multistate utilities is 6.6 with a maximum of 11 states, and for single-state utilities 3.9 states with a maximum of 7.

The authors used Fine's (1998) notion of industry clockspeed, which treats velocity as the result of the aggregate actions of incumbent firms and is made up of product, process, and organizational clockspeeds. They selected seven high-clockspeed industries (personal computers, computer software, toys and games, athletic footwear, semiconductors, movie, and cosmetics) and five low-clockspeed industries (aircraft, steel, ship-building, petrochemicals, and paper), then matched each high-clockspeed industry with every low-clockspeed industry on 14 aggregate action variables; the semiconductor-aircraft pair had the minimum Euclidean distance. They also used Mendelson and Pillai's (1999) measures to confirm differences in product, process, and organizational clockspeeds of the sampled firms for the study period.

Network homogeneity was identified by two key elements of networks, membership and resource access. Membership homogeneity was measured by the coefficient of variation (sigma/mean) across the frequency of alliances entered into by the sampled firms in each constituent category (seven network members in the semiconductor industry and six in the aircraft industry). Resource access homogeneity was measured by the same coefficient of variation across the frequency of alliances in each of five resource-sharing domains: technology, production, international, marketing, and environmental. A high coefficient of variation reflects high network homogeneity, and a low coefficient of variation represents low network homogeneity.

Two established measures of network strength were used: the average age of networks developed by the sampled firms and the average frequency of networks with the same members. The higher the average network age and frequency of networks with the same member firms, the stronger the network.

Adaptive environmental assumptions were defined as environment → strategy links in the causal maps. The authors used the number and frequency of adaptive links (environment → strategy links divided by total links in the map) to assess the relative importance of these links, scaling the number of distinct adaptive links and the frequency of adaptive links by the total number of links in the map. Because of strong intercorrelations among the measures, they averaged the z-scores of number and frequency of links to develop a composite measure.

Enactive environmental assumptions were defined as strategy → environment links in the causal maps. The authors used the number and frequency of enactive links (strategy → environment links divided by total links in the map) to assess the relative importance of these links, scaling the number of distinct enactive links and the frequency of enactive links by the total number of links in the map. Because of strong intercorrelations among the measures, they averaged the z-scores of number and frequency of links to develop a composite measure.

Complexity was measured by two measures, comprehensiveness and connectedness. Comprehensiveness was measured as the total number of concepts in the aggregated causal map, and connectedness as the ratio of the total number of linkages between concepts in the aggregated map to the number of concepts.
Consensus was defined as the percentage of concepts and links between concepts that were present in the strategy frames of all the member firms in the core group.

variable_name: pattern of changes in the average centrality of concepts
description: The pattern of change was read from the year-to-year changes in the average centrality of concepts in the collective strategy frames over the 20-year period. For the aircraft group changes were quite low for 16 out of 19 one-year changes, with major changes in only 3 periods, whereas for the semiconductor group the average change ranged from 29% to 39% for the 19 periods. An autocorrelation function (ACF) plot was used to test whether these changes represented unpredictable values in the time series of changes in the centrality of concepts.

variable_name: magnitude of changes in collective strategy frames
description: The magnitude of changes in the causal maps is represented by the level of change in the core concepts in the maps, where coreness of each concept was measured by the network-based measure of centrality (the weighted average length of all the total paths that link a concept to other concepts, with each successive layer of concepts given a diminishing weight). The distance between the coreness of concepts in the causal map in year t and t - 1 was totalled across all concepts and divided by the size of the original causal map. The higher the value of the distance measure, the higher the magnitude of changes in the collective frames.

An autocorrelation function (ACF) plot was used to identify significant negative yearly changes in three performance variables—sales, operating profits, and return on investment. Negative yearly changes in these three performance variables in which the standard error values were outside the 95% confidence interval, as assessed by ACF, were classified as performance decline periods; other years were classified as stable performance periods.

variable_name: frequency of changes in aggregate actions
description: The frequency of aggregate product changes (new products introduced), process changes (new processes introduced), and organizational changes (e.g., mergers, acquisitions, divestiture, capital expansions in the form of new machinery, and factories) undertaken by the aircraft and semiconductor groups from 1977 to 1997.

The partner's number of certified products listed on the Wi-Fi Web site in June 2003, standardized by the duration of the partner's membership in the Wi-Fi Alliance; the product count was divided by the number of days (reported in year units) in which a partner was a member prior to June 2003. Duration of alliance membership was also incorporated in the negative binomial regression model as the offset when productivity served as the dependent variable.

In September 2004 a panel of industry experts rated each of the 250 partners on the market success gained with the development, introduction, and marketing of products based on the IEEE 802.11 standard. The four experts independently rated each partner that they recognized on a 1-10 scale, with 10 representing the highest level of success, and partners not recognized by any expert were assigned a 0; the measure is the average score the partner received from the four experts.
scale: 1-10 rating scale (0 assigned to unrecognized partners)

description: The number of relevant press items (reported in thousands) mentioning a partner in connection with the Wi-Fi Alliance, counted from Factiva full-article searches between August 1999 and September 2004 using a search string that combined the partner name with Wi-Fi, WECA, wireless LAN, WLAN, or IEEE 802 terms plus product, technology, offering, market, or develop terms.

Dummy variable coded 1 if a partner was listed as a board member on the Wi-Fi Alliance Web site and 0 otherwise. Board membership entailed a larger financial investment in the alliance as well as stronger voting power and ability to influence resource allocation decisions and set the agenda for alliance committees.

Dummy variable coded 1 if a partner had certified products listed on the Wi-Fi Web site, distinguishing partners that actively engaged in the certification of Wi-Fi products from noncertifiers that did not develop Wi-Fi products. Products certified between March 2000, when certification began, and September 2004 were considered; of the 250 partners, 137 were active certifiers and 113 were noncertifiers.

A count variable indicating the number of competing multipartner alliances in the WLAN industry (HiperLAN, HomeRF, or Bluetooth) in which a partner participated at any time between August 1999 and June 2003. Membership lists came from the HiperLAN and Bluetooth Web sites and from the former marketing chairman of HomeRF, corroborated with Factiva searches for announcements of membership in the three competing alliances.

Partners were sorted by their date of entry into the Wi-Fi Alliance and their order of entry was then calculated; partners with the same recorded entry date received identical scores, so the variable had only 38 unique levels, and it was treated as continuous in the analysis. The approximate date of entry was based on Factiva press items and the Wi-Fi Alliance Web site's press release section, corroborated with periodically issued partner lists, and missing dates were obtained from partners' representatives; entry dates were available for 227 of the 250 partners.

variable_name: Productivity, market success and market exposure
description: Alliance benefits were captured by three dependent variables: certified products per year of membership, expert-rated market success (1-10), and number of press items mentioning the partner with the Wi-Fi Alliance.

Based on total accruals, computed following the procedure that Dechow et al. (1995) designed to measure earnings management. The variable captures the change in noncash working capital before income taxes payable less total depreciation expense. The authors used the absolute value of total accruals because it captures the total amount of earnings transfer regardless of its direction, and they state that the greater the total accruals, the greater the odds that earnings quality is poor.

Dummy coded as one for firms reporting quarterly earnings per share that are the same as or above the consensus analyst forecast. The consensus forecast is the mean of forecasts made by analysts just before quarterly earnings' actual announcement. The information is from the I/B/E/S database.

Binary variable coded as one if a firm's reported quarterly earnings per share are below the consensus forecast, used to construct the interaction terms with the consecutive number of times a firm previously met analyst expectations and with the density of other firms in the focal firm's industry. Because the divestiture dependent variables were updated annually, the authors used annual earnings forecasts to measure whether a firm met analyst forecasts for the divestiture analysis.
level: firm-quarter; firm-year for the divestiture analysis
time_window: quarterly; annual for the divestiture analysis

description: The percentage change in the consensus analyst forecast from the same fiscal quarter in the previous year. The consensus forecast is the mean of forecasts made by analysts just before quarterly earnings' actual announcement.
time_window: next quarter relative to the same fiscal quarter in the previous year

description: A variable capturing the consecutive number of times a firm previously met analyst expectations until the prior quarter (t - 1). It is used as a predictor of future analyst expectations and interacted with failure to meet analyst expectations in the market-reaction and divestiture models.

The percentage of other firms within a focal firm's primary industry, defined by two-digit SIC codes and excluding the focal firm, that met analyst forecasts in the previous quarter. It is used as a predictor of future analyst expectations and interacted with failure to meet analyst expectations in the market-reaction and divestiture models.

Stock market reactions to earnings announcements calculated with an event-study design using the CRSP database. The authors estimated cumulative excess returns over a 3-day period, that is, from day - 1 to day + 1 relative to the date of the earnings report, and report that other event periods such as +/- 3 days or +/- 5 days yielded substantively the same results.
time_window: day - 1 to day + 1 relative to the earnings report

description: The count of the number of divestiture announcements by a firm during a given year, using data from SDC Platinum's Mergers & Acquisition. Divested assets were considered noncore if they were not in the same four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code of the focal firm; those in the same four-digit SIC code were considered core. The authors analyzed divestiture announcements rather than completed deals.

variable_name: announcement of Exemplary Voluntary Efforts Award
description: The event of interest is the U.S. Department of Labor's presentation of its annual Exemplary Voluntary Efforts Award, chosen as the appropriate event to indicate that a firm had a high-quality affirmative action program. The exact dates of the award announcements were available from copies of the Department of Labor's news releases; the award was established in 1983 but winners from before 1986 are not documented, so the list covers 1986-92 winners. For a firm to be included in the sample, it had to have been listed on either the New York or American stock exchange during the investigation period, because only stocks traded on these exchanges are traded frequently enough for reliable estimation and their return history is available on CRSP tapes. Firms reporting other economically relevant events in the 90 days before and after each event were dropped from the sample.

variable_name: announcement of a firm's settlement of a discrimination suit
description: The second event consisted of announcements, found in the Wall Street Journal Index and the Dow Jones News Retrieval Service, of major settlements by firms found to be guilty of discrimination. The event date was the first public announcement of a firm's settlement in response to having been found guilty of discriminatory practices. For a firm to be included, it had to have been traded on the New York or the American stock exchange during the period of the study, and firms reporting other economically relevant events around the announcement were dropped.

variable_name: daily and cumulative percentage residual (excess) rates of return
description: The actual daily rate of return on a firm's stock is adjusted for the expected rate of return estimated through the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the expected daily return equals the risk-free return plus beta times the market return minus the risk-free return. The expected return is subtracted from the actual return to obtain the excess return. For each day in the event window a firm-specific excess return was calculated, and excess returns were averaged across the firms in the sample to obtain mean daily excess returns, reported on both a daily and a cumulative basis. The expected return is subtracted from the actual return to obtain the excess return. Returns are taken from the CRSP data tapes.

variable_name: daily and cumulative percentage residual (excess) rates of return
description: The actual daily rate of return on a firm's stock is adjusted for the expected rate of return estimated through the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the expected daily return equals the risk-free return plus beta times the market return minus the risk-free return. The expected return is subtracted from the actual return to obtain the excess return. For each day in the event window a firm-specific excess return was calculated, and excess returns were averaged across the firms in the sample to obtain mean daily excess returns, reported on both a daily and a cumulative basis. Returns are taken from the CRSP data tapes.

The spousal team variable refers to a firm that is owned and managed by a spousal couple, where a spousal couple is a couple that is married, has a registered partnership, or lives together with children. The variable takes the value 1 when both spouses obtained their main income from the firm while also taking an ownership and management position in that firm, and sibling teams served as the reference group coded 0. Sibling teams refer to the situation when at least two siblings obtained their main income from the firm while also taking an ownership and management position in that firm. Firms including both family constellations (siblings and spousal teams present within one firm) were excluded.

We calculated the growth rate for each firm i in point t as the logarithmic difference in employees from the previous year, following the calculation of logarithmic returns, which assumes that the growth rate is consistent over time. The logarithm of the growth variable corrects for the skewed distribution, resulting in a normal distribution, which is especially important for relatively short time periods. The dependent variable was measured at time t, and these growth measures were recorded for the period between 2005 and 2007.

Firm age was measured as the number of years a firm existed since its inception, and the natural logarithm of this variable was taken to correct for its skewness. The variable was truncated over 20 years because the exact founding year could only be determined from 1987 onward; for firms founded in 1986 or before the database reports a constant firm age of 21 years, and these firms were excluded from the main analysis. Only 5.5% of the firms in the propensity score-matched sample were older than 20 years.
We calculated this variable as the total number of owners for each firm in each year.

Measured by computing the coefficient of variation for the number of years of industry experience within the entrepreneurial team. The coefficient of variation is operationalized as the standard deviation of the number of years of industry experience within an entrepreneurial team divided by the team's average number of years of industry experience, and it captures diversity as disparity rather than as team members' standard deviation in years. Years of industry experience denotes the number of years of work experience a team member has gained in the same industry as the firm he or she is currently involved in.

The measure reflects the median age of the knowledge inputs of a firm's new innovations for a given year, i.e., the median difference between the patent application date and the dates of the patents cited as prior art. For each year the firm's patents are divided into technological areas using patent class codes and the average median input age for all patents within a technology area is computed; the average median age of the firm's patent inputs is compared with the average median age of the inputs to all other patents in the same technology class-year and divided by the variance of the median patent age, producing a z-score. To aggregate across patent classes to the firm level, a weighted average of these z-scores is constructed using the proportion of firm patents in a class as the weight. Firms whose new patents make use of relatively young technological inputs have higher positive scores; firms making use of relatively older inputs have larger negative scores.
scale: z-score (standard deviations from the technology class-year average)
time_window: year t (patents dated by application date)

description: Annual stock return, i.e., the percent change in stock price including dividends, formed from the market value of the firm's stock and its dividends relative to prior-year market value. Compustat provided the annual accounting information used to construct the measure. Because anticipated information is already reflected in the price of the stock, it is only the unanticipated components of a metric that lead market participants to update their expectations and induce a change in share price.
time_window: annual (year t), relative to prior-year market value

description: Technological recency also serves as the threshold variable that sorts observations into regimes. The indicator function takes the value 1 if recency is in regime j and 0 otherwise, so that observations are divided into regimes according to whether recency falls within a given region, and the regimes are distinguished by differing slope coefficients. Testing determines how many thresholds are present and where they occur.

Yearly counts of product approvals received by each sample firm. Both types of FDA device approvals that a firm received in a given year are included: 510(k) (premarket notification) and PMA (premarket approval); radically novel devices require a PMA approval, but these are relatively rare (about 3% in the data). The two types were analyzed in aggregate as well as with 510(k) approvals separately. A new product introduction typically closely follows approval.

The yearly percentage of inventors listed on a firm's patents who were board-certified physicians. Inventors are the individuals listed on each patent, taken from patents applied for (and subsequently approved) in a particular year; a matching algorithm was used to arrive at a unique list of inventors yearly for each sample firm. Individuals were cross-referenced against the AMA Physician Masterfile on first and last names and middle initials, and, if a middle initial was unavailable, additionally on geographical location, to flag board-certified physicians as users.
scale: proportion of inventors on the firm's patents

description: The yearly percentage of a firm's senior executives who were board-certified physicians. Executives encompassed typical executive positions in a surgical instrument venture, including general business functions (finance, e.g., chief financial officer; marketing, e.g., vice president of marketing; CEO; and R&D, e.g., chief technology officer) and roles specific to biopharma firms, such as chief medical officer and vice president of clinical and regulatory affairs. Board certification was identified by matching individuals against the AMA Physician Masterfile.

A binary variable set to 1 if the firm's CEO in a particular year was a board-certified physician and 0 otherwise. The authors checked and found no co-CEO pattern in their data. Board certification was identified by matching individuals against the AMA Physician Masterfile.

The yearly percentage of a firm's board members who were board-certified physicians. The use of proportions to measure user influence follows prior work that typically measures board composition as the percentage of total directors with a particular attribute. Board certification was identified by matching individuals against the AMA Physician Masterfile.

Measured as the share of the network's largest component: the number of inventors in the largest component divided by the total number of inventors, where a component is a subgraph wherein everyone is directly or indirectly connected with everybody else. The internal network of each firm is reconstructed from copatenting ties using three-year moving windows, treating patent data as a two-mode patent-by-inventor affiliation network projected onto a one-mode nonvalued, nondirectional inventor-by-inventor network in which a tie exists if a pair of inventors coauthored at least one patent. Network measures were computed using R Igraph. The variable values range from 0 to 1, with larger values indicating higher levels of integration, and it is lagged by one year.
time_window: three-year moving windows (1986-1988, 1987-1989, ..., 2000-2002), lagged one year (t-1)

description: Measured using Teachman's entropy index: the sum over the total number of technology classes (N) of Pj times the natural log of 1/Pj, where Pj is the share of the firm's inventors who filed at least one patent in technology class j during the previous three years. The index is a direct measure of diversity and ranges from 0 to ln(N): it assumes a value of 0 when all inventors in a firm specialize in the same technological area and approaches ln(N) when the inventors are all specialized in distinct technological areas. The variable is lagged by one year.
time_window: previous three years, lagged one year (t-1)

description: The interaction of collaborative integration and knowledge diversity is the mean-centered multiplication of collaborative integration and knowledge diversity.

Counts the number of times each pair of subclasses cooccurring in a firm's patents within a given year had already been used by the firm during the previous five years, normalized by the total number of combinations created by that firm in that year. Subclass coassignments determine the technological combinations that led to a patented innovation; a value of zero indicates that the firm's current patents are entirely based on combinations the firm has not used in the previous five years, and larger values indicate more innovation by reusing the existing portfolio of combinations. The measure can take values higher than one because the same technological combination can be used more than once in a firm's patents.
scale: greater than or equal to zero (can exceed 1)

description: Computed as the share of subclass coassignments that had not been used by the firm in the prior five years: new combinations divided by total combinations. The variable's range is between 0 and 1; a value of zero implies that none of the technological combinations used by a firm to create its current patents is new to the firm, whereas a value of one indicates that no subclass combination used to generate a firm's current patents had been used by the firm in the past five years. Subclass assignments are decided by the USPTO and are therefore not biased by firms' strategic considerations.

Operationalizes expressive voting dissent as the percentage of shareholder votes opposing the executive board discharge proposal. Shareholders can vote for, against, or abstain; all votes not cast in favor of the proposal are considered shareholder dissent, hence including both against and abstain votes. Because of the skewed distribution of the variable, a log (x + 1) transformation is applied.
time_window: annual shareholder meetings in the sample years

description: For each firm the annual composition of the executive board is checked; whenever the CEO's name changes from one year to the next, the exact dates of the announcement and of the effective departure are traced back. Company press releases, business press coverage and CEO and supervisory board chair interviews up to one year before and closely around the dismissal date are used to assess whether the departure was voluntary or forced. Turnovers coded as dismissals are coded 1 and the remaining CEO turnovers are coded as nondismissals (i.e., 0); interim CEO turnovers and turnovers due to retirement, health, or death are excluded.
time_window: one year before and closely around the dismissal date

description: Categorical variable identifying three main types of supervisory board chairs: family chair (coded 1), independent chair (coded 2), and other chair (nonfamily and nonindependent), the latter serving as the reference category. The variable is coded 1 whenever the supervisory board chair is a member of the family with an ownership stake in the firm; for every firm with an observable level of family ownership the founder is identified and all family names, including in-law family members, are traced up to the latest generation, after which the chair's name is checked against these names. Coding was done manually by two people with an overall interrater reliability (Cohen's kappa) of 0.93.
scale: categorical (1 = family chair, 2 = independent chair, other chair = reference)

description: Category of the supervisory board chair variable, coded 2 for a board chair who is independent from the company and its management board or any controlling shareholder, with family chair coded 1 and other chair as the reference category. Information on each chair's personal and professional relationships was collected by reading firm disclosures regarding conflicts of interest, corporate governance reports, and press articles related to the chair's name. A chair is considered independent when there is no personal (family ties or close associates) or professional (employment or advisory) relationship with a company stakeholder, and any chair appointed within two years after stepping down from the management board was coded as nonindependent.
scale: categorical (2 = independent chair, 1 = family chair, other chair = reference)

description: Percentage of a firm's shares owned by institutional investors (i.e., investors that invest on behalf of other investors), aggregated in a firm-year. Data were extracted from Refinitiv Eikon and checked against firms' annual reports. Eikon's ownertype classification is used to identify shares held by institutional investors, i.e., investment advisors, hedge funds, sovereign wealth funds, endowment funds, banks, insurance companies, and pension funds.

Sum of all ownership percentages held by the founding family or individual family members in a firm-year. The ownership percentage is calculated using the percentage of voting shares of total shares outstanding.

Count of accidents experienced by an operator in the focal year, regardless of cause. Operators involved in an accident must report it and specify on the accident report form the single primary cause of the accident; an operator can experience multiple accidents in a given year.

variable_name: Ct. of total accidents from t-3 to t-1 (log)
description: Cumulative count of all accidents an operator experienced in the three years prior to the focal year. Logged values were used because of the skewness of the counts of accidents.

variable_name: Ct. of accidents by human error (focal year)
description: Count of accidents experienced by an operator in the focal year for which the primary cause specified on the accident report form was human error. Accidents were coded as resulting from human error if the primary cause was 'incorrect operation,' which PHMSA defines as a release or failure resulting from operating, maintenance, repair, or other errors by facility personnel; operators must identify a single cause of each accident.

variable_name: Ct. of accidents by other causes (focal year)
description: Count of accidents experienced by an operator in the focal year for which the primary cause was not incorrect operation. PHMSA provides seven other possible primary causes; some of these designations could arguably be conceived as related to human error to varying degrees, but incorrect operation is the only causal category directly and clearly linked to human error.

variable_name: Ct. of accidents by human error from t-3 to t-1 (log)
description: Cumulative count of accidents resulting from human error in the three years prior to the focal year; logged values were used because of the skewness of the counts of accidents. A three-year observation window was used because of the relative rarity of accidents resulting from human error.

variable_name: Ct. of accidents by other causes from t-3 to t-1 (log)
description: Cumulative count of accidents resulting from causes other than human error in the three years prior to the focal year; logged values were used because of the skewness of the counts of accidents.

A code-preserving change was defined as a dish change of the same nature, i.e., either a replacement of a dish from classical cuisine by another classical cuisine dish or a replacement of a nouvelle cuisine dish by another nouvelle cuisine dish. Chefs nominate three signature dishes per year, so the maximum of preserving changes per year relative to the prior year is three and the minimum is zero. Dishes were coded into classical and nouvelle cuisine by a computer program based on the rules of both cuisines stated in Fischler (1993) and Neirinck and Poulain (1988); a random sample of 400 dishes was also coded by two independent raters with an inter-rater reliability of 95 percent, and the match between raters and the program was 95 percent. The variable measures the number of such changes at t - 1.

A code-violating change was a replacement of a classical cuisine dish by a nouvelle cuisine dish or vice versa. Because chefs nominate three signature dishes, the maximum of transforming changes per year relative to the prior year is three and the minimum is zero. The number of such changes at t - 1 is the variable used to test Hypotheses 2, 4, 6 and 8/8alt.

Every year the authors calculated the difference between a chef's number of code-preserving changes and the average of competitors' changes. Competitors were defined as the chefs belonging to the same region with the same number of stars. Cuisine was treated as a regional phenomenon because ingredients differ by geography, starred chefs are unevenly dispersed, and clients compare only nearby restaurants.
time_window: annual, relative to peers in the same year

description: Every year the authors calculated the difference between a chef's number of code-violating changes and the average of competitors' changes. Competitors were the chefs belonging to the same region with the same number of stars. This variable was used to test Hypotheses 3 and 4.
time_window: annual, relative to peers in the same year

description: The number of stars received by a chef in the Guide Michelin each year, with three possible values: 1, 2, or 3. Michelin inspectors reserve a table, choose their menu from a set of specialties, consume and pay, and rate restaurants only on the quality of the dish, independently of the trio of specialties the guide lists. The specialty dishes that chefs list through the guide's questionnaire are chosen in a process independent from anonymous visits.

Lagged evaluation is the number of stars obtained by the restaurant at t - 1. It is included both as a control and, interacted with the numbers of code changes, to test Hypotheses 7 and 8 and their alternatives.

Restaurant age is the logged number of years the organization was in existence after being given a star. It is used as a moderator of the effects of code-preserving and code-violating changes on external evaluations.

A dichotomous variable measured at the firm-year level indicating whether the firm voluntarily restated its earnings in a given year. Restatement events come from the 2002 U.S. GAO report, and three coders independently labeled each restatement as voluntary or forced after reading announcements via media wires and company reports, conferring until they agreed. Voluntary restatements were those a firm proactively announced without prodding from the SEC.

A dichotomous variable that labels a firm '1' if it was in the industry's seventy fifth percentile or greater in return on assets (ROA) and also voluntarily restated its earnings in the prior year. The variable is lagged to rule out reverse causality.

A dichotomous variable that labels a firm '1' if it was in the industry's seventy fifth percentile or greater in assets and also voluntarily restated its earnings in the prior year. The variable is lagged to rule out reverse causality.
The count of voluntary restaters in a given industry in the prior year. Count variables have been used as a measure of mimetic behavior in prior organizational studies.

A dichotomous variable that returns '1' if another firm in the industry voluntarily restated its earnings previously and shared the same auditor with the firm in the prior year. The measure links behavioral similarities among firms to behavior expectations transferred by an indirect, third-party tie.

The count of firms in a given industry that were previously forced to restate by the SEC in the prior year. It measures the regulatory force that may have the opposite of its intended effect on voluntary behavior.

The rank of the number of the firm's employees vis-à-vis other industry members. The firm with the fewest employees in the industry is ranked 1 and the firm with the most employees is ranked n, with n equal to the total number of firms in the industry. Size and rank have been used as measures of status or prestige in institutional studies.

variable_name: Informal leader and peer forces (performance leader, size leader, peer restaters, shared auditor)
description: Informal social forces were measured by four industry-level variables: performance leader and size leader dummies, count of voluntary restaters in the industry in the prior year, and a shared-auditor dummy with a prior voluntary restater. All are lagged one year and built at the four-digit SIC level.

Dummy variable indicating whether the policy was implemented in the respondent's municipality in a given quarter. It is 0 for all quarters before the municipality's implementation and remains 1 for the duration of the time frame after implementation.

Municipality-level measure of the intensity of the patriarchy logic adapted from Zhao and Wry (2016), focused on the religious and family dimensions most closely related to the normative and cognitive institutions central to the theory. It includes indicators for legal restrictions on remarriage and abortion among women, legislation on marital rape, family violence interventions, divorce laws, protections against sexual harassment, and socioeconomic indicators such as men-to-women's labor participation, households headed by women, and average number of children per woman. Each measure was coded so that higher values indicate greater levels of patriarchy and standardized to a mean of 0, and the first principal component of the measures was used as the index.

Equals one if the individual was a registered business owner in one of the industries affected by the SARE policy's reduction in entry barriers. Multiple individuals, including household members, can indicate ownership of the same business. Industry eligibility was determined by following earlier studies of SARE's impact on entrepreneurship.

The gender gap is estimated with a difference-in-difference-in-differences model in which the coefficient on the interaction between the SARE and Woman dummies measures the differential effect of the SARE policy on women versus men. A negative interaction term indicates a relative decrease in the probability of women engaging in entrepreneurship as owners or founders, compared to men.

variable_name: Unpaid work in a family member's business
description: Indicates that an individual was working for a family member's business without pay in a given quarter. It specifically measures unpaid work in a family member's business and does not include other forms of family labor such as housework or childcare.
Dummy variable indicating whether an individual stated that they were a woman.

Market share data were collected for the years 1990-91 primarily from Yano Keizai Kenkyujo. Firms were classified into four groups: market shares smaller than 5 percent, 5-10 percent, 10-20 percent, and greater than 20 percent. The latter group are considered dominant firms; firms with 10-20 percent are considered competitive but non-dominant firms.

Japanese industry's share of the world market in 1990-92, collected from various sources. Calculated by adding data on overseas production by Japanese firms to figures on domestic production in Japan and dividing this sum by the figure for world market volume. Classified as low (<25 percent), intermediate (25-75 percent), or dominant (>75 percent).

Dummy variable that takes the value 1 for industries with a Herfindahl index greater than 1000 and smaller than 1800, following Shepherd (1997). The Herfindahl index was calculated from the market share data of individual firms in Japan for each product.
Number of patents in the 5-year period 1989-93 granted to the firm or its subsidiaries by the U.S. patent office, per 1 billion yen of turnover.
scale: patents per 1 billion yen of turnover

description: Foreign manufacturing investment in all regions, that is, in the United States and/or the European Union and in Asia. Created by determining whether firms had set up manufacturing plants for each product, counting plants in operation in 1992.

Foreign manufacturing investment in the United States and/or the European Union but not in Asia. Created by determining whether firms had set up manufacturing plants for each product, counting plants in operation in 1992.
Foreign manufacturing investment in Asia only. Created by determining whether firms had set up manufacturing plants for each product, counting plants in operation in 1992.

Dependent variable indicating whether the firm had set up manufacturing plants for the product in the European Union or United States, and in Asia, counting plants in operation in 1992. In 266 out of 519 cases foreign investment occurred.

Count of the number of organizational dimensions that changed in the same time period that business strategy changed. A company was coded as having changed strategies when it either did not mention in 1986 a strategy it had indicated in 1984 or mentioned a new strategy that had not been indicated in 1984. Change in organizational structure was coded when there was evidence of a major change in structure, such as a change from a functional to a divisional organization; change in control systems was coded when new control systems were put into place or old systems were changed; change in power distribution was recoded to a dummy variable, with a cutoff of 25 percent or more change in the representation of functional backgrounds on the top management team. For Hypotheses 1 and 2, a company was coded as having reoriented if a change in strategy was accompanied by changes in at least two out of three supporting organizational dimensions: structure, power systems, or control systems.

Return on assets was collected for the five-year period from 1980 through 1984. Each firm's deviation from the median return on assets in its industry was assessed in each of the five years, and a weighted average of these deviations over time was taken, with recent periods weighted more heavily.

An indication of whether or not a firm mentioned environmental contingencies, coded from the 1986 10K and annual reports. A firm's managers were coded as being aware of environmental contingencies if they indicated explicitly that they had observed or were predicting a specific change in their organization's environment.

Obtained from content analysis of the management discussion in the 10K reports and the president's letter in the annual reports in 1986. Each mention of a performance outcome was coded as positive or negative, and the reason given for that outcome was coded as internal or external. The external attribution bias was coded as present when a company made external attributions rather than internal attributions for poor performance outcomes.

The heterogeneity of the top management team across functional areas was measured using Blau's (1977) formula, calculated as 1 minus the sum of the squared proportions of the top management team in each functional area.
A change in the CEO was coded when the CEO or President changed within the given time period.
Individuals were considered members of the top management team when they were listed as an executive officer. Change in the top management team was measured as a percentage variable.

Firms were chosen from two industries that differed significantly in their degree of turbulence: the furniture industry represents a stable environment and computer software represents a turbulent environment. Firms were chosen based on their SIC code classification, which was verified by both the COMPUSTAT Industrial Data Base and Securities and Exchange Commission records, and the difference in the degree of turbulence was verified using the coefficient of variation on sales.

Experimental condition to which each cooperative was randomly assigned. In the hierarchy condition the four cooperative tasks (membership, finance, production, and planning and marketing) were overseen by a secretary, a treasurer, an organizer, and a vice chairperson, who all reported to a chairperson elected annually by the membership. In the flat condition individuals were organized into committees around the same four tasks, with one individual per committee randomly assigned as a rotating 'liaison' whose job was only to act as a point of contact for intercommittee communication. Formal hierarchy is coded 1 and flat is coded 0.
time_window: intervention in June 2015 and training implemented in September 2015

description: The salience of informal hierarchy was measured by examining the extent of age heterogeneity in a group. Members were asked whether 'most people in their group were around the same age,' coded as 1 = 'Different ages' and 0 = 'Same age.' Rather than using individual age data, the measure gauges the extent to which group members perceive the presence of age similarities or differences within the group. Aggregation to the group level was supported, with a mean interrater agreement Rwg(j) of 0.95.
level: individual responses aggregated to cooperative group

description: A 3-item scale combining distinct attributes of CPO. Items asked about the frequency with which group members 'behave as though they are truly owners of the group,' the frequency with which they 'behave as though they are responsible for the success of the group,' and 'How often do group members behave as though they can have a positive influence on the outcomes of the group?' (1 = 'Never,' 7 = 'Always'). Principal component analysis with orthogonal rotation was used, all items loaded into one factor over .60, the reliability of the scale was .87, and factor scores were used as the final measure. Aggregation to the group level was supported (Rwg(j) of 0.86, ICC(1) of 0.53, ICC(2) of 0.92).
level: individual responses aggregated to cooperative group

description: A four-item scale capturing conflict-related behavior among group members during decision-making and operational activities. Items asked about the frequency with which 'disagreements among group members' were prevalent 'at meetings,' 'while making or delivering products,' and 'about how the group's shared resources should be used,' together with the frequency with which people would 'get angry while working in this group' (1 = 'Never,' 7 = 'Always'). Principal component analysis with orthogonal rotation was used, all items had a single factor loading over .60, and factor scores were used to arrive at the final measure. Aggregation to the group level was supported (mean Rwg(j) of 0.91, ICC(1) of 0.49, ICC(2) of 0.91).
level: individual responses aggregated to cooperative group

description: The export sales of a company in millions of yen in year t. In Model 1 the natural logarithm of export sales (Log(EXPORTt)) is regressed on 1983 R&D expenditures, assets, market leadership, and industry R&D intensity, and the regression is repeated using 1984, 1985, and 1986 data for the dependent variable while holding the independent variables the same. The authors report that the elasticity of exports with respect to R&D is less than one.
(Export sales)/(Total sales) in percent in year t. Used as the dependent variable in Model 3 for 1986 (EXPORT%86), together with versions using shorter lags in Appendix 2.

R&D spending of a company in millions of yen in 1983, entered in logarithmic form (Log(R&D83)) as a key independent variable in Models 1 and 2. Model 4 instead uses the yearly change in R&D expenditures, R&D84-83 = (R&D84) - (R&D83).
R&D intensity of a firm, computed as R&D83 divided by total sales in 1983 (R&D%83). Used as an independent variable in Model 3 to explain the export ratio.
scale: R&D as a share of total sales

description: Industry average R&D percentage in 1983 compiled by the Statistics Bureau, Management and Coordination Agency, Japan. Included in Models 1 and 2 in logarithmic form (Log(INDR&D83)) to control industry characteristics such as the speed of technological innovation and the importance of R&D activities.
Total assets value of a company in millions of yen in 1983, entered in logarithmic form (Log(ASSETS83)) in the models.

Dummy variable that equals 1 if the company is a leading firm in its industry and 0 otherwise. A LEADER is identified on the basis of the firm's relative size in the industry, and the industry categories are taken from MITI's classification; a diversified company is classified into the industry of its largest segment of business.
The domestic sales of a company in millions of yen in year t. Used as the dependent variable in the parallel Model 2 (Log(DOMESTIC86)) to contrast with the results for export sales.

Measured as the total number of foreign subsidiaries established in a specific industry in China by firms from different home countries other than Japan each year. Subsidiaries created by firms from the same home country in the same industry are excluded from this measure but are included in the model analysis as a control variable. The variable is lagged by 1 year relative to the entry year. In Models 1-5 this variable is orthogonalized together with the three control variables that are highly correlated with it.
time_window: t-1 (all independent variables lagged by 1 year)

description: A composite measure jointly considering a Japanese firm's FDIs in a specific industry across different countries and the number of FDI entries outflowed from those countries into the specific industry in China. Firm-country cohesion is quantified by a focal firm i's FDIs in another country j in industry k, further multiplied by the number of FDI entries into China by firms from country j in industry k at year t-1. The equation as printed is not readable in the text; the measure is described from the prose and the definitions of the symbols, and it is lagged by 1 year.
time_window: t-1 (all independent variables lagged by 1 year)

description: A dummy variable that equals 1 if Japanese firm i invested in China in relevant industry j in year t, and 0 otherwise. An industry is defined as relevant for a focal firm when it is one of the listed industries of the firm, or one in which the firm had previously invested in other countries.

A dummy indicator built from China's Guiding Catalogue for Foreign Investment in Industry, which classifies FDI by industry as encouraged, permitted, restricted, or prohibited. Because the Catalogue does not specify industry classification codes, the authors use the 2-digit manufacturing industries identified as restricted for foreign investments by prior work. Japanese firms' primary industries are coded as either restricted or unrestricted, with 1 indicating the restricted industries and 0 the unrestricted industries, including permitted and encouraged industries.

A weighted bank presence computed from the establishment of all Chinese commercial banks and their branches since 1948 in each city. The weight is computed as a ratio of the number of provinces where commercial banks or branches are established by year to 30, the total number of provinces in China. The weight in each year is multiplied by the total number of banks and their bank branches in the same year to indicate bank presence, so that the weighted indicator varies by year.

variable_name: performance index (self-reported performance relative to competitors)
description: Respondents were asked to compare the development of their own firm over the past 3 years relative to their two most important competitors for 10 different dimensions of performance. Five-point scales ranging from 'much lower' to 'much higher' were used, and the items form an index with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.82. The index was collected in the 2000 mail survey; a parallel measure collected in the telephone interview correlated 0.53 (p < 0.01) with it.
scale: 5-point scales ranging from 'much lower' to 'much higher'

description: Following Gupta and Govindarajan (2000), CEOs evaluated the firm's knowledge position on 7-point scales in order to measure procedural knowledge; the scales measure the firm's knowledge position vis-à-vis competitors. Eleven items pertaining to market and technological knowledge were combined (Cronbach's alpha = 0.84) and loaded on one common factor.
The authors used Covin and Slevin's (1989) version of the instrument, consisting of nine items (Cronbach's alpha = 0.75). The items themselves are not reported in the text.

Records the number of alternative market opportunities entrepreneurs considered prior to the first market entry. Through a multistage question, respondents were asked to indicate whether, prior to first market entry, they had considered commercializing their technological resources in market domains different from the market they eventually entered. The authors counted the number of additional market opportunities.

Respondents who indicated that they had considered additional markets prior to entry described those markets with a few keywords, and each market opportunity was categorized according to the SIC system (interrater agreement 0.93). Pairwise comparisons of the SIC codes of all opportunities in the firm's opportunity set were assigned a distance score of 1 to a pair sharing the same three-digit code, 2 to a pair sharing the same two-digit code, and 3 to a pair sharing just the one-digit code. Following the logic of variety measures such as the Blau index, the squared pairwise distance scores were summed into a variety score for the firm's market opportunity set, with larger values indicating greater variety.

variable_name: Diversification after the initial market entry
description: Dummy variable indicating firm diversification (0 = no; 1 = yes) during the venture's early-stage development, that is, within five years after the initial entry. It was created using information on the time of the venture's initial market entry (year and month) and the time (year and month) of entry into any other market domains.
time_window: within five years after the initial entry

description: Using five-point Likert-type scales (from 1 = 'not used' to 5 = 'very high use'), respondents reported the knowledge they obtained prior to their firm's first market entry from five main types of external actors. Each of the knowledge sources was coded as a binary variable, with 0 indicating no use of a particular source and 1 indicating the use of a particular source, and the linear sum of all external knowledge sources used per firm was created, so that a value of 5 indicates that all five knowledge sources were used and 0 that none were used. The variable has a high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.83) and was mean centered.

Respondents indicated in which industries each member of the founding team had gathered prior work experience. The authors created the sum of all the individual industries represented in the founding team and mean centered the variable.

Respondents rated the level of technological experience that their founding team possessed at founding using a five-point Likert-type scale (1 = 'very low' to 5 = 'very high'). The measure assesses the average level of technological experience in the founding team because it represents the group's overall characterization.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = 'very low' to 5 = 'very high')

description: Strategic Asset Ownership is a binary indicator equal to one if the subsidiary holds ownership rights to any MNE strategic assets, and zero otherwise.
