This measure is coded based on information contained in the transfer pricing reports, which explicitly state which MNE entities hold economic ownership rights to the MNE's intangible assets. The author carefully reviewed all reports for each MNE and coded as one each subsidiary that owns any strategic asset.

Innovation Quantity is measured as the total number of successful patent applications associated with the subsidiary's inventors in each year. Patents are matched to years based on the filing date since it is closer to the time of invention than the patent grant date. The natural log of innovation quantity plus one is taken in the analyses.
time_window: each year of the sample period

description: Forward patent citations are used as a measure of Innovation Quality. The variable is calculated as the total number of citations from other firms (excluding examiner citations) received within 5 years on the patents filed in the given year. Citation data were collected through 2014, and because the measure would be truncated for years after 2009, 2009 is the last sample year for the innovation quality analyses. The natural log of innovation quality plus one is taken in the analyses.
time_window: five years after patent filing; citations collected through 2014

description: R&D Tax Subsidies is measured as the proportion of one U.S. dollar of R&D expense funded by the host government through tax relief. It is used as a measure of innovation opportunity. In the DDD analysis the authors use a binary indicator for post-change in R&D tax subsidy, based on a threshold of a 0.01 point increase in R&D tax subsidy, with countries increasing subsidies at varying points in time over the sample.

Host-country RTA is operationalized using the revealed technological advantage index from the OECD, which represents the country-industry's technological specialization. For each subsidiary, host-country RTA is measured as the host country-industry revealed technological advantage index minus the average value of the MNE's locations. The measure reflects the extent to which the focal subsidiary is in a region of greater technological advantage than its MNE counterparts.

Income shielding potential is operationalized using a binary indicator for whether the subsidiary is located in a Tax Haven as classified by Dharmapala and Hines (2009). Tax Haven is used as the instrumental variable for strategic asset ownership in the first stage of the TSLS analysis.

Factor score of three survey items: bilateral communications between members of both firms, disclosure of details related to decision making to members of the acquired firm, and consistency in procedures applied when making decisions. Each item was measured on a five-point scale where 1 indicated the characteristic did not exist at all and 5 signified the feature existed to a very large extent. The three items loaded on a factor labeled informational justice with loadings of 0.79 or greater; Cronbach's alpha was 0.79, and factor scores were used in the regression models.
scale: five-point scale (1 = not at all to 5 = to a very large extent); factor scores
time_window: during the period leading up to and including the integration process

description: Factor score of two survey items: the ability of the acquired firm to challenge or refute decisions of the acquiring firm, and autonomy maintained by the acquired firm in strategic and operational decision making. Each item was measured on a five-point scale where 1 indicated the characteristic did not exist at all and 5 signified the feature existed to a very large extent. Loadings were 0.79 or greater and Cronbach's alpha was 0.70; factor scores were used in the regression models.
scale: five-point scale (1 = not at all to 5 = to a very large extent); factor scores
time_window: during the period leading up to and including the integration process

description: Factor score of respondents' assessments of changes in the combined firm's profitability and stock price one year after finalizing the deal. Each indicator was rated on a five-point scale ranging from significant decrease (= 1) to significant increase (= 5). The two items loaded on a factor labeled financial return, and the resulting factor scores were used as dependent variables in the regression analyses.
scale: five-point scale (1 = significant decrease to 5 = significant increase); factor scores
time_window: one year after finalizing the deal

description: Factor score of respondents' assessments of changes in the combined firm's sales growth, market share, and innovation/research and development one year after finalizing the deal. Each indicator was rated on a five-point scale ranging from significant decrease (= 1) to significant increase (= 5). The three items loaded on a factor labeled market position, and the resulting factor scores were used as dependent variables in the regression analyses.
scale: five-point scale (1 = significant decrease to 5 = significant increase); factor scores
time_window: one year after finalizing the deal

description: Factor score of respondents' assessments of changes in the combined firm's profitability and stock price one year after completing the integration process. Each indicator was rated on a five-point scale ranging from significant decrease (= 1) to significant increase (= 5). The two items loaded on a factor labeled financial return, and the resulting factor scores were used as dependent variables in the regression analyses.
scale: five-point scale (1 = significant decrease to 5 = significant increase); factor scores
time_window: one year after completing the integration process

description: Factor score of respondents' assessments of changes in the combined firm's sales growth, market share, and innovation/research and development one year after completing the integration process. Each indicator was rated on a five-point scale ranging from significant decrease (= 1) to significant increase (= 5). The three items loaded on a factor labeled market position, and the resulting factor scores were used as dependent variables in the regression analyses.
scale: five-point scale (1 = significant decrease to 5 = significant increase); factor scores
time_window: one year after completing the integration process

description: Cumulative abnormal return over the five-day event window t = -2 to t = +2 around the JV internalization announcement (the earliest announcement is used for t = 0 when several appear). Abnormal returns are forecast errors from the Sharpe-Lintner market model, whose firm-specific OLS parameters were estimated over trading days t = -250 to t = -50; the total firm valuation effect is the sum of abnormal returns within the event window. Abnormal returns were standardized using the standard error of the forecast following Patell (1976). The model equations appear in the paper as formula blocks that are not readable in this payload.
time_window: five-day window around the announcement; estimation interval t = -250 to t = -50

description: R&D expense-to-sales ratio for the year prior to the JV termination announcement, constructed from Compustat data. The authors use it as the proxy for the parent firm's intangible resources relating to technological know-how, following previous transaction cost research.
time_window: year prior to the JV termination announcement

description: Advertising expense-to-sales ratio for the year prior to the JV termination announcement, constructed from Compustat data. The authors use it as the proxy for the parent firm's intangible resources relating to marketing know-how and goodwill.
time_window: year prior to the JV termination announcement

description: A weighted index of the cultural distance between the United States and the JV's host country, built from Hofstede's (1980) scales for uncertainty avoidance, individuality, tolerance of power distance, and masculinity following Kogut and Singh (1988); each country's deviation from the U.S. score on a scale is divided by the sample variance of that scale and the terms are combined. The paper also estimated Equation 6 with a categorical approach that classifies JVs into national culture clusters from Ronen and Shenkar (1985) using six binary variables indicating a Far East, Germanic, Latin American, Latin European, Japanese, or other non-Anglo host country, with all six equal to zero for an Anglo nation.
level: country pair (parent home country and JV host country)

description: Measured with proxies for multinational and country-specific experience. Multinationality equals the number of countries in which the firm has direct investments upon the JV partner buyout. A binary variable for prior entry denotes whether or not the firm had entered the JV's host country with a direct investment prior to the JV's termination. Subsidiary data used to construct both proxies were obtained from the Directory of International Affiliations.
time_window: at the time of the JV partner buyout for multinationality; before the JV's termination for prior entry

description: Three host-country variables capturing political change and policy restrictions, obtained from 18-month Political Risk Service forecasts reported in Planning Review for the year preceding the JV internalization announcement. Following Fladmoe-Lindquist and Jacque (1995), political turmoil risk forecasts, reported on a scale from 'low' to 'very high', were converted to numerical scores on a 1-4 scale, and financial transfer and investment restriction risk forecasts, reported on a scale from A+ to D-, were converted to numerical scores on 0-4 scales.
scale: 1-4 for political turmoil risk; 0-4 for financial transfer and investment restriction risk
time_window: year preceding the JV internalization announcement (18-month forecasts)

description: The authors counted the number of times per month that actions continued or changed and computed the difference between continued minus changed actions as a rough approximation of the propensity or disposition of entrepreneurs to act in alternative ways. The propensity to continue actions is indicated when this monthly measure is increasingly positive, while the propensity to change action is indicated when it is increasingly negative. Each event's action was first coded as expansion, contraction, modification, or continuation, then grouped into continue prior action (continuation and expansion) or change prior action (contraction and modification).

Monthly count of positive minus negative outcomes. Events that provided evidence of results were coded as positive (good news or successful accomplishment), negative (bad news or instances of failure or mistakes), or mixed (neutral or ambiguous news or results indicating elements of both success and failure). To minimize classification error, events coded as mixed outcomes were not included in developing the dichotomous variable.
scale: count of positive minus negative outcomes

description: Monthly count of the number of interventions by resource controllers, coded when a resource controller was behaviorally involved in an event. Resource controllers were classified as all executives in the reporting hierarchies from CEO to the top managers to whom SBU members reported in their respective parent companies, in contrast to the innovation's internal management team of SBU members.

Monthly count of the number of shifts in goals or outcome criteria, coded when a resource controller or TAP SBU manager stated a goal or an outcome criterion for judging TAP's success that was different from the past. Interview respondents were asked what current criteria they were using to judge the success of the innovation, whether changes had occurred in the criteria used in the past six months, and what grade they would give TAP's performance.

Monthly count of the number of external context events, coded when an event involved a change in technology, structure, or activity occurring external (but reported as relevant) to the TAP SBU. Context thus includes events that occurred in the larger environment, such as events in other organizations, the industry, or the FDA regulatory agency.

Firm growth is modeled as the first difference of log sales, where Si,t is the sales of firm i at time t and Xit is a covariate matrix. The equation itself is not readable in the extracted text, so the exact specification beyond the first difference of log sales is not recoverable from this payload. The first difference of log sales is estimated using ordinary least squares regression for the tests on firm growth.

The number count of collaboration agreements established by a firm in each year is used as the measure. Collaboration is defined as voluntary cooperation between firms involving exchange, sharing, or codevelopment of products, technologies, or services. The counts come from content analysis of business newspaper articles reporting collaborations for the sample firms.

For each business line in which a firm engages, data on the product market size (in terms of sales) and the number of competing firms within the product market are tracked. The average competition faced by each firm in each of its participating product markets is calculated by dividing the product market size by the number of competing firms. Competitive intensity that a firm faces is the log of the total sum of average competition it faces in all its participating product markets.

The OECD (1997) classification of industries as high, medium-high, medium-low, and low technology intensive is adopted, based on the ratio of R&D expenditure and embodied technology to output. Embodied technology refers to the indirect technology flows during the R&D processes, beyond the direct amount of R&D conducted. Using this criterion, 'paints, pharmaceuticals and other chemical products,' 'petroleum products,' and 'electronic products' are classified as high technology intensive; 'machinery except electrical and electronic,' 'electrical machinery, apparatus and appliances,' and 'industrial chemicals and gases' as medium-high; 'plastic products,' 'fabricated metal products,' and 'transport equipment' as medium-low; and 'printing and publishing' and 'food' as low.

Group assignment in the field test: one computing centre formed the test group and used ZBB as an integral part of its planning process, while the other two centres continued to use only incremental budget planning. ZBB was executed by the planning committee on an annual basis for two planning cycles, after which the committee unanimously adopted it as the ongoing approach to budget planning.

Group assignment in the field test: the two computing centres in the control groups continued to use only incremental budget planning during the field test. All three centres used an integrated planning framework, so the main difference among them was the budgeting model used.

For each of the 14 services, correlation analyses were performed between the importance of the service and the level of service provided, at the then-test and the posttest periods; respondents encoded their assessments of importance and of service level on seven point Likert type scales. The correlation coefficients were transformed using Fisher's Z transformation. Net improvement scores for the test and control groups were computed by subtracting then-test Z values from posttest Z values, used for individual services and totalled for all services combined. In a second, indexed analysis the Z values were multiplied by a relative importance index computed as the mean importance score for a service divided by the total of all mean importance scores.
time_window: then-test and posttest, two years apart

variable_name: attitude toward computing support for instructional activities
description: Users were asked to evaluate the computing services available to support their instructional activities, using the then-posttest methodology. The item was administered to faculty users before and after the two year period, and mean before and after scores and the net improvement (after minus before) were computed for the test group and the two control groups.
time_window: before and after a two year period

variable_name: attitude toward computing support for research activities
description: Users were asked the same question as for instructional activities, this time regarding the computing services available to support their research activities. The item was administered to faculty users before and after the two year period, and mean before and after scores and the net improvement (after minus before) were computed for the test group and the two control groups.
time_window: before and after a two year period

description: Respondents were asked to rate on a seven-point Likert-type scale three statements reflecting the partners' ability to adjust and modify the agreement as needed. These measures were a reliable indicator of the first type of flexibility and were collapsed to form one measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.81) to be included in the analysis.

Respondents were asked to rate on a seven-point Likert-type scale the probability of their organization terminating the alliance relationship within the next year; where an organization had already terminated the relationship it was assigned a "seven." Respondents also rated any unanticipated positive or negative outcomes and two statements reflecting the alliance's performance, and these measures were collapsed (Cronbach's alpha = 0.74) to get one overall assessment of performance. Only those respondents that rated their company's satisfaction below the mean (41 firms) were included in the analysis.

Informants were asked to categorize the assets their organization contributed to the alliance into intangible (administrative personnel and technical personnel) and tangible (technical equipment, facilities, and financing) assets, and to indicate for all types of assets contributed the percentage of those assets that could easily be transferred for use elsewhere. The two sets of measures were collapsed into one measure of the degree of asset specificity in the alliance, with intangible asset specificity reported separately in the structural models.

Informants categorized the tangible assets their organization contributed to the alliance (technical equipment, facilities, and financing) and indicated the percentage of those assets that could be transferred for use elsewhere if the alliance were to dissolve. This set of measures was collapsed with the intangible measures into one degree of asset specificity, with tangible asset specificity reported separately in the structural models.

Respondents were asked to indicate the reciprocal intangible assets invested by their partner in the same manner as their own assets. A calculation was made to compare the balance of asset specificity for intangible investments by taking the absolute difference of the partners' specific assets invested, where a "zero" indicated a perfectly balanced set of investments.

Respondents were asked to indicate the reciprocal tangible assets invested by their partner in the same manner as their own assets. A calculation was made to compare the balance of asset specificity for tangible investments by taking the absolute difference of the partners' specific assets invested, where a "zero" indicated a perfectly balanced set of investments.

Similar to Kogut (1989), hostages was operationalized as concurrent relationships that an organization has, in addition to the focal alliance, with its partner organization. Informants were asked to specify which of five types of relationships their organization concurrently had with their partner company; if any concurrent relationship existed between the partners then a hostage arrangement was considered to exist and was coded as a "one," and when no hostage arrangement existed a code of "zero" was used.

Measures of trust were drawn from the literature on both interpersonal trust and interorganizational trust. After modifying the statements to reflect the nature of the alliance activity, respondents were asked to rate, on a seven-point Likert-type scale, four statements reflecting their organization's trust in their partner organization, reflecting the three components of trust used in much of the interpersonal trust literature (dependability, predictability, and faith). The measures were collapsed to reflect one overall measure of trust (Cronbach's alpha = 0.86).

To measure influence, respondents were asked to rate on a seven-point Likert-type scale four statements concerning their organization's influence over the alliance's goals, operating decisions, budget allocations, and selection of research projects. These measures were collapsed into one measure of influence (Cronbach's alpha = 0.82).

To measure the absence of alternatives, respondents were asked whether their organization was currently able to conduct the alliance activities in any of four alternative arrangements, and they were asked to rate on a seven-point Likert-type scale their organization's potential for conducting these activities if they were not already doing so.

Importance of the resource being obtained was conceptualized in terms of the criticality of the resource; a resource is considered critical when it is a key part of the focal organization's operations or function or to the extent to which the organization requires it for operation or continued survival. Thus the alliance is more critical, and therefore more important, to the organization when the alliance is conducting research that is directly related to the organization's primary research interests.

Consistent with Gulati (1995) and Anderson and Weitz (1989), respondents were asked whether or not their organization had previously partnered with their current partner. This study included another element by asking how long the previous relationship(s) lasted, because a previous short-lived alliance may not increase trust and may actually act to decrease it if the alliance was dissolved prematurely.
Using the same operationalization of attachment as Seabright et al. (1992), respondents were asked to indicate how long (in months) their organization had been involved in the focal alliance.

Respondents were asked to rate on a seven-point Likert-type scale four statements reflecting the quality of communication between the organizations, consistent with measures used by marketing channels researchers. Preliminary analyses indicated that these four measures of communication quality were highly related (Cronbach's alpha = 0.89); hence they were collapsed into one variable: communication.

Two separate aspects of this construct were measured. Consistent with Gulati (1995), the alliance was categorized as either multinational or domestic (1 = all partners from the U.S., 0 = multinational alliance). Respondents also rated on a seven-point Likert-type scale two statements reflecting the degree to which the partners have a common understanding of the motives for joining and the goals and objectives of the alliance; these two statements were highly correlated (Cronbach's alpha = 0.91) and were combined into one variable, shared goals. Consequently, the construct shared values is composed of both shared nationality and shared goals.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (shared goals); binary (shared nationality)

description: One of four policy criteria selected from the literature as determinants of adverse selection risk; measured by the degree to which the product markets of the foreign firm and the Chinese firm overlap. The value of this criterion was experimentally manipulated randomly for each of the 30 scenarios.

One of four policy criteria selected from the literature as determinants of adverse selection risk; measured by the degree to which the Chinese firm possesses intangible assets that are difficult for the foreign firm to value. The value of this criterion was experimentally manipulated randomly for each of the 30 scenarios.

Executives rated each of the 30 investment opportunities using two items: the attractiveness of a joint venture and the probability that they would recommend pursuing a joint venture. Both items were measured on a seven-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (very low) to 7 (very high), and the two items were summed to create the dependent variable. The scale has high internal reliability, as reflected in a correlation of 0.91 between the two items.

Executives rated each of the 30 investment opportunities using two items: the attractiveness of an acquisition and the probability that they would recommend pursuing an acquisition. Both items were measured on a seven-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (very low) to 7 (very high), and the two items were summed to create the dependent variable. The correlation between the two items is 0.91.

Executives' preference for an investment opportunity as a joint venture relative to an acquisition. To understand the factors shaping executives' preferences for IJVs or acquisitions, the authors examined differences in covariate effects across the IJV and acquisition attractiveness equations.

One of four policy criteria capturing other possible sources of information and signals of quality that reduce the risk of adverse selection; measured by the foreign firm's familiarity and knowledge of the Chinese firm's resources and capabilities. The value of this criterion was experimentally manipulated randomly for each of the 30 scenarios.

One of four policy criteria capturing other possible sources of information and signals of quality that reduce the risk of adverse selection; measured by the extent to which the foreign firm would consider the Chinese firm's affiliated organizations reputable. The value of this criterion was experimentally manipulated randomly for each of the 30 scenarios.

A binary indicator variable set to one in years when an executive or director of the focal firm had served as the chief officer or deputy chief officer at the division (chu) level or above in the official hierarchy, and zero otherwise. The resumes of each listed firm's CEO, all other top executives with 'Chief' in their titles, and all directors were hand-collected from the Sina website for every year each firm was listed. This threshold is commonly used in studies of Chinese bureaucrats and indicates membership in the political elite.
time_window: measured each firm-year; lagged one year in the models

description: The logged percentage of the labor force working in non-state-owned firms each year, measured for the nation as a whole because many listed firms operate in multiple locations. State-owned firms follow the National Bureau of Statistics definition. The variable was logged because it was right-skewed.

The logged percentage of fixed-asset investments in non-state-owned firms each year, measured for the nation as a whole. State-owned firms follow the National Bureau of Statistics definition. The variable was logged because it was right-skewed.

Net return on net assets (ROA), used as the primary measure of firm performance because it is comparable across industries and across firms operating on different scales. The authors also calculated net return on equity (ROE) for robustness checks.

The Herfindahl-Hirschman index of concentration, calculated using the market share, based on sales, of all listed firms in each industry each year. Industry was defined using two-digit Chinese Standard Industrial Classification codes. Higher values indicate lower levels of competition.
Firm size was measured using assets, logged to normalize the distribution. The authors also used an alternative measure of size based on sales in robustness checks.

Access to bank loans was assessed by calculating each firm's borrowing ratio, the ratio of bank borrowing to total assets. Scaling by assets makes this variable comparable across firms of different sizes.
scale: ratio of bank borrowing to total assets

description: For each year, the total value of loans and loan guarantees provided by the listed firm to the controlling shareholder or to other firms controlled by that shareholder, minus the value of loans repaid to those entities and loans or loan guarantees provided to the listed firm by those entities. The value was scaled by the listed firm's total assets to make it comparable across firms of different sizes. Data on related-party loans became available only in 1998, when a new reporting requirement was put in place.
scale: ratio of net related-party loans to total assets

description: The main analysis focuses on the direct measure of short-termism, a two-item instrument developed as a direct attempt to capture intertemporal tradeoff. The questions ask whether the respondent focuses on actions to improve long-run financial effectiveness rather than actions that produce good short-term budget performance, and whether the respondent expects subordinates to focus on action that will produce good short-term budget performance rather than actions to improve long-term financial effectiveness. Each item was measured on a five-point scale, with 1 representing strong agreement and 5 strong disagreement with the statement presented; questions 1 and 3 were reverse-scored. Factor analysis showed the direct items loading on one factor (Factor 2), which the authors call the direct measure of short-termism, with a reliability measure above 0.70.
scale: five-point scale per item (1 = strong agreement, 5 = strong disagreement)

description: The short-term bias exhibited by the immediate superior (as established by the direct two-item instrument) was included as the independent variable to predict each manager's short-term bias. A listing of line relationships was obtained from the Human Resources Management department and the manager's status was confirmed by the questionnaire survey. Each questionnaire was coded by reference to the organization chart in order to identify respondents.

Hierarchical level was measured on a scale of 1 to 4, with 1 representing membership of the senior management team, while 2 represented managers who reported to a level-1 manager. Respondents were asked to circle the appropriate number on the questionnaire, and this self-reporting exercise was confirmed by reference to the organization chart.

Each manager at Comserve was supplied with documented information relating to short-term budgetary and nonfinancial performance measures as two among several communication channels that supported performance measurement within the company. The questionnaire asked respondents to rate the importance of the formal channels available to managers using a five-point Likert scale. Principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation produced three factors interpreted in terms of media richness theory, with factor 2 representing lean media and including the items relating to budgetary and nonfinancial measures. The two-item measure representing budgetary and nonfinancial measures was used in the analysis, with Cronbach alphas exceeding 0.60.

Role ambiguity was measured with Kahn et al.'s (1964) 15-item instrument, which was initially developed to measure role ambiguity and role conflict but was used in full given the exploratory nature of the study. Principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation showed all questions loading above 0.50 onto one of three factors, with loadings consistent with separate constructs for role ambiguity, role conflict, and role overload, and Cronbach alphas for each factor exceeding 0.70. The measure of role ambiguity includes three items that are common with the Rizzo et al. (1970) instrument and three items that address the adequacy of information and its associated construct, knowledge; this measure was used in the analysis.

An independent variable was adopted that measured the median short-term behavior for the group as calculated from the scores obtained from all other group members, interpreted as a measure of conformity to the extent that the focal manager's behavior reflects the views of other group members. Managers who shared a hierarchical superior were defined formally as members of a given work group, and managerial work groups ranged in size from five to twelve persons. Groups comprising fewer than three responses were discarded, and groups comprising level 3 managers but without a superior (level 2 manager) were discarded to comply with the measure of contagion. Median rather than mean scores were used because the median gives less weight to extreme cases.

Analysis at the level of business unit affiliation was represented as three separate dummy coded (0 or 1) current position variables. For example, in the first variable, members of business unit one (network infrastructure) were coded 1 and the remainder 0. SBU 1 represents network infrastructure, SBU 2 represents product development, and SBU 3 sales and marketing.

The extent of recombination captures the degree to which, in a given year, incumbent record labels recombine in their releases the elements of a focal style's offering with those of products in other styles. It relies on the releases' grade of membership into a focal style to proxy the extent of recombination: if a release was listed as 'techno,' 'trance,' and 'tribal,' its grade of membership in each style would be equal to one-third. The average grade of membership of the total number of releases associated to each style i in year t was computed, and the extent of recombination was obtained by subtracting the average grade of membership from 1. The measure ranges between 0 (low extent of recombination, crisp boundaries) and 1 (high extent of recombination, fuzzy boundaries).

The mode of recombination captures how much the incumbent record labels experiment with different combinations rather than reproducing them. Every possible pairwise combination observed within each style i in year t was calculated; the count of original combinations observed in style i during year t was then divided by the number of times each combination was reproduced in that style/year; last, the average of the values regarding each original combination was computed. The resulting measure ranges between 0 and 1, with larger values pointing to a style in which a diverse mode of recombination is observed and smaller values to a recurrent mode.

To capture deference, self-citations were first removed from the sample; the total number of citations that, by means of remixes, each style i received in year t was then counted, so that a 'progressive house' remix of a 'synth-pop' track gives the style 'synth-pop' one citation in that year. The status of each style i in year t was calculated based on the Bonacich (1987) centrality score, which attributes more weight to those styles that outrank more prestigious counterparts. To smoothen out short-term fluctuations, a moving average filter was applied.

The volume of investments measures the volume of investments that a category attracts, i.e., the total count of releases issued by record labels in a focal style i during year t. The dependent variables take the form of nonnegative integers.

Organizational entries capture the count of the record labels entered in a focal style i during year t. The variable was then split into the number of entrants that are new to the market, i.e., record labels appearing for the first time in the data set by entering a style i, and the number of lateral entrants, i.e., record labels established in a style j at year t-1, but entered in style i in year t. While this distinction is not aimed at hypotheses testing, it acknowledges the existence of different types of entrants and allows benchmarking with the recent literature.

variable_name: Target company top management turnover rate
description: Members of the target's top management team at the time of the merger were identified in its 10-K or annual report and listed by name, age and position. Parent company human resources officers reported whether each executive was still employed by what was the target company and, if not, the date of departure. The cumulative percentage of the team that turned over was computed at each of 5 years after the merger, and differences between cumulative yearly percentages yielded annual turnover rates. The mean number of executives comprising the top management team was 8.19.
time_window: 5 years after the merger or acquisition

description: The Federal Trade Commission's five-fold typology was used. Horizontal, vertical, product extension, and market extension mergers and acquisitions were coded as related; unrelated conglomerate mergers and acquisitions were coded as unrelated. The sample is composed of 64 percent related and 36 percent unrelated mergers and acquisitions.

The logarithms (base 10) of both the parents' and targets' assets were computed. The difference between the logarithm of the parent's assets and the target's assets at the time of the merger or acquisition established the asset size difference between the two companies.
time_window: at the time of the merger or acquisition

description: If any mention was made in the Wall Street Journal during the course of the merger or acquisition negotiations that the target company had received previous takeover interest from another company, it was recorded. Twenty-three percent of the sample was found to have been subject to such interest.
time_window: during the merger or acquisition negotiations

description: Wall Street Journal articles were coded to portray whether the buyer approached the target's managers with a merger proposal or bypassed these managers and approached the target's shareholders directly with a tender offer. The sample is composed of 63 percent mergers and 37 percent tender offers.
time_window: during the merger or acquisition negotiations

description: The Wall Street Journal recorded the progress of the merger and acquisition negotiations. In 78 percent of the cases the buyer made one offer for the target company, and it was accepted; in 22 percent of the negotiations the future parent company was forced to make one or more counter-offers before the final price was agreed upon.
time_window: during the merger or acquisition negotiations

description: For each merger and acquisition the number of days was recorded between the time the names of the buyer and the target company were first linked in the Wall Street Journal, and the time the formal agreement of the merger or acquisition was established. The mean number of days to settlement was 116.91, with a standard deviation of 99.74 days.
time_window: from the first press link to the formal agreement

description: In 81 percent of the merger and acquisition negotiations the buyer made no mention in the Wall Street Journal of retaining the target company's managers; however, in 19 percent of the negotiations the future parent company did make such assurances.
time_window: during the merger or acquisition negotiations

description: The negotiations were coded as friendly, neutral, or hostile based upon the characterization of the negotiations in the Wall Street Journal. Friendly negotiations were either explicitly labeled as such or reported as unambiguously positive; neutral negotiations were neither friendly nor hostile; hostile negotiations were coded from a direct reference to hostility or unambiguously negative comments. The sample is composed of 42 percent friendly, 46 percent neutral, and 12 percent hostile merger and acquisition negotiations.
time_window: during the merger or acquisition negotiations

description: The method of payment was reported in the Statistical Report on Mergers and Acquisitions, 1979 for each of the mergers and acquisitions. Fifty-three percent of the companies were paid for in cash; 35 percent were paid for in stock; and the remaining 12 percent were paid for in a combination of cash and stock.
time_window: at the time of the merger or acquisition

description: The target company's stock price was compiled for each day in the fourth week prior to the buyer's first public interest in the target company. The mean of these five observations was computed and divided by the final settlement price of the target company's stock. In all cases the premium paid was positive; it ranged from 0.19 percent to 493.14 percent, with a mean of 62.37 percent and a standard deviation of 60.28 percent.
time_window: fourth week prior to first public interest; final settlement price

description: Dichotomous dependent variable indicating whether a target firm resisted a takeover attempt. Values were obtained from Mergerstat's coding of contested takeover bids. Firms that contested takeovers were followed for a minimum of one year to determine whether their opposition generated an auction, and only firms that contested without generating auctions were included as resisting. By this definition, 65 of the 406 target firms resisted.

Dichotomous variable measuring whether or not a CEO had been awarded a golden parachute, coded 0 = no parachute, 1 = parachute. Values were obtained from the proxy statements for the fiscal years prior to the takeover bids to ensure that the parachute was in place prior to the offers.
time_window: fiscal year prior to the takeover bid

description: Percentage of total outstanding shares owned by the CEO of a target firm. The variable was obtained from the proxy statements for the fiscal years prior to the takeover bids to ensure that the holdings were in place prior to the offers.
time_window: fiscal year prior to the takeover bid

description: The age of a firm's CEO at the time of a takeover attempt. CEO age squared was included in the analysis to model a curvilinear effect for CEO age.
time_window: at the time of the takeover attempt

description: The number of years a CEO had held the top position in a firm.
time_window: at the time of the takeover attempt

description: Following the videometric approach of Petrenko et al. (2016), videos showcasing focal CEOs were obtained from public internet sources and edited to omit identifying information that could bias evaluations by coders. Recruited raters were trained to assess and rate CEO humility using a third-person adaptation of the HEXACO-60 scale. The measure combines the values of the four humility items from the Honesty-Humility scale, combining the modesty and greed-avoidance facets in order to avoid conflating honesty and humility. The measurement demonstrated high coefficient alpha reliability (alpha = 0.74), a confirmatory factor analysis produced a CFI of 0.99, and raters demonstrated significant agreement, ICC (1, 3) = 0.37, p < .001, rwg = 0.99.

Operationalized as the I/B/E/S last analysts' consensus forecast for the focal firm's EPS for the year (t), scaled by the year-end firm's stock price for a given year. The authors note that since analysts set market expectations for firms, the finance and accounting literatures typically capture market performance expectations by aggregating all analysts' ratings following a given firm.

variable_name: Actual EPS relative to analysts' expectations
description: Measured following prior research in finance and accounting as the difference between a firm's reported EPS for a fiscal period and the I/B/E/S last consensus forecast for the period issued for the firm, scaled by the end of period stock price for the firm. The authors describe it as the difference between the firm's actual and forecasted EPS, scaled by the firm's stock price.

Calculated as the average of the abnormal returns over a seven-day window (-3, +3 days) on either side of the actual earnings announcement date, reflecting market performance around the announcement of actual earnings. Abnormal returns reflect the part of the return that is unanticipated by a statistical or economic model of anticipated returns and were calculated by subtracting estimated return from the firm's actual market return, then taking the average of that value for the days within the designated window.
time_window: seven-day window (-3, +3 days) around the earnings announcement date

description: Measured as the ratio of the market value of a firm's assets, the combined market value of a firm's debt and equity, to their replacement value. Because the comparison of actual EPS with analysts' expectations is typically announced after the end of the year, TQ is measured for time t + 1.

Calculated by taking the difference in stock price over the year (end of year stock price minus beginning of year stock price) plus dividends and dividing it by the beginning of year stock price. TSR reflects the compounded returns to shareholders for a given fiscal year and is measured for time t + 1.

Investor reaction to a restatement at time t is the CAR of the restating firm in the five-day window [t-2, t+2]. The CAR of firm i is the accumulation of abnormal daily returns (ARit) over that event window, and the abnormal daily return is the difference between the firm's actual return on a day and its expected return on that day. Expected returns were calculated over the estimation window [t-256, t-23], and the authors used the Eventus program (CRSP database) and the market-adjusted model based on an equally weighted index with dividends to estimate the CAR around each financial event. The values were multiplied by 100 to yield percentages; negative CAR indicate the penalty imposed by investors.
time_window: five-day event window [t-2, t+2]; estimation window [t-256, t-23]

description: The salience of alliance announcements was conceptualized as being related to the number of alliance announcements in the recent past, and the variable is the number of alliance announcements that a firm made discounted by the time (in months) between the alliance announcement and the restatement. All alliances announced during the 36-month period before the financial restatement were considered. Information on the alliances formed by restating firms came from Thompson's SDC Platinum database on alliances, complemented with information from the Recombinant alliance database.

The extremity of alliance announcements is measured as the sum of the CARs in the five-day period around a firm's alliance announcements, discounted by the time (in months) between the alliance announcement and the restatement. The greater the magnitude of investor reaction to an alliance at the time of its announcement, the more extreme it is as a signal. As with the frequency measure, all alliances in the 36-month period before the restatement were considered, and the discounting specification is given as an equation in the paper.
time_window: 36-month period before the financial restatement; five-day window around each alliance announcement

description: Firm size was operationalized as the log-transformed total assets of the firm as reported in the quarter before the financial restatement. The variable was log-transformed to correct the skewness of the distribution, and the information was collected from the quarterly financial data of the Compustat database.
The level of a firm's diversification was captured by the count of different industry segments in which a firm had a presence. The information was collected from the Compustat Segment database.

A dummy variable that equals one if the product carries a private label and zero if it bears a manufacturer brand. It was built by surveying all products stocked by the retailer and recording their brand names.

The media expenditures used by the retailer to advertise a product the year before the survey, taken from Ad $ Summary, which outlines the total dollar amounts that companies spend annually on advertising across 10 media. Because retailers often put a basket of products in a single campaign, the information was lumped into 51 categories (e.g., carpet cleaner, car batteries, power tools, home appliances, tires, men's apparel, women's footwear), which is tantamount to the use of a 51-point scale.

The space devoted by the retailer to promoting a product, measured from all promotional flyers inserted by the retailer into a major local newspaper over the six-month period covered by the survey (October 1995 to March 1996), used as a proxy for the intensity of store promotion. Higher values indicate more aggressive store promotion, which the authors treat as a less optimized marketing commitment because it damages the product's brand image.

The total number of pages devoted by the monthly publication Consumer Reports to evaluating a product over a 10-year period, on the reasoning that the magazine usually uses more space to evaluate a product that is still novel to buyers or more complex in its attributes. It serves as a proxy for the barriers to private branding.

Two consumer judges ranked the 197 five-digit SIC items in the sample on the psychological satisfaction that end-users can potentially receive from each of them; the ranking was then matched with a seven-point scale. Products rated purely utilitarian score 1, extremely symbolic items score 7, and moderately symbolic items score 3, 4 or 5.
scale: 7-point scale (1 purely utilitarian to 7 extremely symbolic)

description: The total expenditures used by all manufacturers in each industry to advertise their products through mass media, collected from Ad $ Summary. It is a proxy for the barriers to private branding, since retailers must make comparable marketing efforts to compete with heavily advertised manufacturer brands.

The portion of output sent by a four-digit SIC industry to business buyers, taken from the U.S. Commerce Department's census of manufactures. It proxies for the barrier to private branding, on the reasoning that the retailer faces a lower barrier in industries where manufacturers ship a larger portion of output through non-retail channels to business buyers.

Measured as the percentage of a firm's employees that are announced to be laid off in a given firm-year t. The number of employees laid off is divided by a firm's total number of employees. Downsizing announcements of considerable size, at least 1% of employees, are identified. The final panel dataset of 653 firm-years consists of 167 firm-years with downsizing and 486 firm-years with no downsizing announcements.

Earnings pressure is calculated using a measure developed by Matsumoto (2002). The measure is defined as the difference between the analyst consensus estimate for the earnings per share (EPS) of the firm in year t, measured at the beginning of year t, and the potential EPS for the firm in year t. The difference is then divided by the stock price for the firm at the end of year t-1. The variable is winsorized at the 10% level.
time_window: analyst estimate at the beginning of year t; stock price at the end of year t-1

description: Measured as the percentage of a firm's shareholdings owned by institutional investors in year t-1.
One of three measures used for CEO power, measured in year t-1. The authors analyze CEO tenure and CEO stock ownership separately since these measures are highly correlated.
One of three measures used for CEO power, measured in year t-1. The text does not describe how the variable is coded.

One of three measures used for CEO power, measured in year t-1. Data were collected from the Edgar database and were only available for 535 firm-years. The authors examined both CEO shareholdings of common stock as well as their beneficial ownership, which includes stock options exercisable within 60 days. The values of the variable are in percentage.
Measured as a dummy variable with a value of '1' if the firm is covered by at least 30 analysts (mean of the sample plus one standard deviation) and a value of '0' otherwise.
One of three measures used for a firm's financial condition, measured in year t-1. The text does not describe how the variable is computed.
One of three measures used for a firm's financial condition, measured in year t-1. It is the change in industry-adjusted return on assets.
One of three measures used for a firm's financial condition, measured in year t-1. It is the change in the firm's sales.

The amount of bribes a firm paid to home country government officials, scaled by the firm's total sales, used to reduce the potential size effect. It was derived from a BEEPS question asking managers to indicate the ratio of the amount of bribes paid to home country government officials over firm sales to 'get things done with regard to customs, taxes, licenses, regulations, services, etc.' Bribes used for obtaining operating licenses and acquiring business permits (grease money) were summed, scaled by firm sales, and subtracted from total bribery to isolate bribery in the home country.

Export intensity, or the ratio of a firm's foreign sales over total sales. It was constructed from a BEEPS questionnaire item surveying the proportion of foreign sales over total sales. This variable ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater export intensities.

Three items measured on a seven-point Likert-type scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (to a very large extent). Managers were asked to what extent they were (1) involving customers in close collaboration on development projects and (2) communicating intensively with customers; the third item asked to what extent the overall strategy of the firm emphasizes close collaboration and dialogue with customers. Together the responses indicate the degree of involvement of customers in innovation activities.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale, 1 (not at all) to 7 (to a very large extent)

description: Two items. The first item asks to what extent employees can influence their own job, measured on a seven-point Likert-type scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (to a very large extent). The second item measures the number of employees engaged in teams with a high degree of autonomy (1, 0%; 2, 1%-25%; 3, 26%-50%; 4, 51%-75%; 5, 76%-99%; 6, 100%). The first item captures delegation toward the individual, the second delegation at team/group level; together they form the level of delegation in the firm.
scale: first item 1-7; second item 1-6 categories of percentage of employees

description: Two items on a seven-point Likert-type scale (1, not at all; 7, to a very large extent). Managers indicated the extent to which (1) an employee's salary is linked to the ability and willingness to share knowledge and (2) the salary is linked to the willingness to improve skills and upgrade knowledge. The latter concerns searching for rather than sharing knowledge.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale, 1 (not at all) to 7 (to a very large extent)

description: Two items asking respondents to indicate the extent to which (1) employees exchange information between different functional departments and (2) there is communication between management and employees. Both items were measured on a seven-point scale, ranging from 1 for 'not at all' to 7 for 'to a very large extent'.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 (not at all) to 7 (to a very large extent)

description: Two items in which managers were asked to indicate the performance of the focal firm compared with competitors on (1) innovation capacity and (2) profitability, both measured on a seven-point scale ranging from 1 for far below average to 7 for far above average.
scale: seven-point scale, 1 (far below average) to 7 (far above average)

description: A dummy variable capturing the mode by which the operation was established. It takes the value of 1 when the Japanese parent made a greenfield investment and takes the value of 0 when the Japanese parent acquired an existing company.
The total number of employees of the subsidiary divided by the total workforce of the parent, capturing the size of the new investment relative to the size of the firm.
The ratio of research and development expenditures to total sales of the Japanese parent.
The export ratio of each Japanese parent, used as a proxy for multinational experience. The authors note that the use of export percentage as a proxy may account for differences with earlier studies.
Two five year growth averages (1983-1987 and 1988-1992) for each industry.

A measure developed by Kogut and Singh (1988) indicating the differences in culture between the source country (Japan) and each individual target country. It was computed using the four dimensions of Hofstede (1980): power distance, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity/femininity and individuality.
A measure of a firm's willingness to accept managerial or organizational uncertainty, taken from Hofstede (1980), reflecting the uncertainty avoidance of the host country entered.
Determined by means of the Kompass UCS codes; the more codes a company had, the more diversified a company was assumed to be.
Determined by comparing the product codes of the subsidiary with those of the parent, distinguishing related from unrelated product codes.

Dummy equal to one if the founders had only STEM degrees or a combination of STEM and nonbusiness degrees, where STEM covers natural sciences, mathematics and statistics, information and communication technologies, and engineering, manufacturing and construction. It is one of two classifications of the founding team's knowledge base, the other relying on self-reported skills. In the two-sided matching model the variable enters through its interaction with Accelerator.
time_window: at the time of the first funding round

description: Dummy equal to one if at least one founder holds a STEM degree or specializes in technology skills, provided that no founder possesses a business education or a specialization in business skills. Technological specialization is derived from a relative specialization index computed on the founders' self-reported LinkedIn skills grouped into twelve clusters, with software, engineering, life sciences and cybersecurity counted as technology skills; the index exceeds one when the founder's share of skills in a field is above that field's share in the population of founders (the formula itself is not legible in the text provided). The variable enters the matching model through its interaction with Accelerator.
time_window: at the time of the first funding round

description: Dummy equal to one if at least one founder has a business educational background, business qualifications being degrees in the fields of business administration and law. The category includes teams with only business degrees, teams with business and STEM degrees, and teams with business and other degrees. In the matching model it enters through its interaction with Accelerator.
time_window: at the time of the first funding round

description: Dummy equal to one when any founder possesses a business education or specializes in business skills; business skills are the business, finance and law clusters of the founders' self-reported LinkedIn skills. It enters the matching model through its interaction with Accelerator.
time_window: at the time of the first funding round

description: Dummy equal to one for the actual startup-investor matches and zero for the counterfactual pairings, in which each startup is paired with every seed investor that made a first-round investment in the same year. Each startup appears once, in the year of its first funding round, whereas an investor can appear multiple times when it made multiple investments in the same year.
time_window: year of the first funding round

description: Dummy identifying seed investors that Crunchbase classifies as accelerators. In the two-sided matching model the accelerator attribute enters only through interactions with startup attributes (Accelerator x Pure tech education, Accelerator x Business education, Accelerator x Pure tech skill and Accelerator x Business skill), because the maximum score estimator identifies bilateral preferences only and all predictors must come from interactions between attributes of startups and seed investors.
time_window: year of the first funding round

description: Dummy equal to one for startups whose initial seed investment came from an accelerator and zero for startups financed by a primarily financial seed investor, such as a (micro)venture capitalist, business angel, government program or crowdfunding platform. It is the key independent variable in the matched-sample regressions on subsequent funding.

Dummy equal to one if the founders had only STEM degrees or a combination of STEM and nonbusiness degrees. In the matched-sample regressions it is entered directly and in interaction with Accelerator to test whether accelerators create more value for pure tech teams.

Dummy equal to one if at least one founder holds a STEM degree or specializes in technology skills and no founder possesses a business education or a business skill specialization. It is used as the skill-based alternative to Pure tech education when moderating the accelerator effect in the matched sample.

Dummy equal to one if at least one founder has a business educational background (business administration and law). The baseline group consists of ventures with teams lacking any business background, and the variable is entered directly and in interaction with Accelerator in the matched-sample regressions.

Dummy equal to one when any founder possesses a business education or specializes in business skills. It is used as the skill-based alternative to Business education when moderating the accelerator effect in the matched sample.

The total funding in U.S. dollars raised by the company in all funding rounds, excluding the first round provided by the focal investor. The variable is logged so that coefficients approximate percentage changes, and it serves as the dependent variable in the matched-sample regressions.
time_window: all rounds after the first funding round

description: Discrete variables capturing whether the company collected enough funding to be in the top 50%, top 25% or top 10% of the distribution of total funding. They are used as alternative dependent variables in the matched-sample OLS regressions.

Each product technology was classified using the authors' definition: an evolved technology has a new artifact based on advances in existing knowledge, while a novel technology has a new artifact based on a new knowledge base that represents a completely new way of meeting a functional need. Videotape was based on an evolved technology that used existing knowledge from film technology, and videodisc relied on a novel technology requiring knowledge not previously available about storing video signals on vinyl discs. The CT scanner used existing knowledge about X-rays and computers, whereas MR imaging combined new knowledge about excitation and relaxation times of hydrogen atoms with computers.

Markets were classified as dispersed when they have a large number of potential buyers with access to many information sources and individuals evaluate products on well-established criteria, and as concentrated when a small set of purchasing agents negotiates the evaluation criteria used to assess a product. The videoplayer was selected as a product sold to dispersed markets, while diagnostic imaging equipment was selected because it was sold to concentrated markets.

A technical strategy was indicated by two-event sequences consisting of an event that related to the technical features of a product followed or preceded by an event comparing the product's performance with those of competitors. For each firm the authors computed p(t), the proportion of technical sequences in the two-event sequences for that firm.
time_window: two-event sequences within each firm's event series

description: An institutional strategy was indicated by two-event sequences consisting of an event about evaluation criteria to assess the product followed or preceded by an event comparing the product's performance. For each firm the authors computed p(i), the proportion of institutional sequences in the two-event sequences for that firm.
time_window: two-event sequences within each firm's event series

description: Success is measured by the acceptance of a firm's product technology in the market relative to all other competing product technologies. The market accepted SONY's videotape technology over RCA's videodisc technology, and GE's MR imagers displaced CT scanners in medical diagnostic imaging, while FONAR's variant of the MR imager was not accepted by the market. The market acceptance of each technology is described with sales and market-share figures for the competing technologies.

variable_name: functional importance scores (relative strategic importance of functional areas)
description: Executives were asked to rate a normative list of 55 key result areas on a seven-point, Likert-type response mode ranging from 'completely strategically insignificant' to 'of the greatest strategic significance'. To obtain the relative strategic importance for each function, these ratings were grouped by function and summed, yielding seven functional importance scores. In the original study the senior executive knowledgeable of the firm's overall operations answered the questions relating to these variables.

variable_name: average yearly percentage change in PE, ROE, ROC, SALES and EPS
description: Five financial performance variables were chosen as company performance measures: the price earnings ratio (PE), return on equity (ROE), return on capital (ROC), sales volumes (SALES), and earnings per share (EPS). Yearly percentage change in each of the five financial measures was calculated for a five-year period, adjusted for inflation using the implicit price deflator for 1972, and the yearly percentage changes were then averaged to control for unusual effects in any one year. Thus the performance variables used represent the average yearly percentage change in each of the five financial measures.

Grand strategy was measured on a nominal scale using four strategy classifications derived from Glueck (1976; 1980): Stability Strategy (similar operating levels), Internal Growth Strategy (internal development), External Acquisitive Growth Strategy (acquisitions, mergers, or joint ventures), and Retrenchment Strategy (reduction of operations). Each CEO was requested to complete the questionnaire identifying the firm's grand strategy. None of the 93 firms in the sample listed retrenchment as a grand strategy, so the analysis is based on the remaining three grand strategies.

The senior executive was asked to select the category that most accurately represented the firm's principal industry type (representing the largest percentage of company sales) from four normative classifications of industrial firms. In the sample, 28 firms were in a consumer non-durable goods industry, 12 in a consumer durable goods industry, 19 in a capital goods industry and 34 in a producer goods industry.

variable_name: transaction dependence of the bidder industry
description: The key independent variable in the replication is the proportion of industry i's total transactions that were with industry j. Transactions data for 1947 were taken directly from the input-output table reported in Leontief (1966). Although total transactions can be broken out into sales and purchases, total transactions were used because Pfeffer's results were virtually identical regardless of whether sales, purchases or total transactions were used.

A network-based measure of transaction dependence computed as Cij, where Pij is the proportion of market i transactions with suppliers and buyers that directly or indirectly involve market j, and Oj is the concentration ratio in market j. Cij ranges from 0 to 1 and increases to the extent that industry i transacts primarily with industry j and industry j is highly concentrated. It was computed with the general network analysis program STRUCTURE.

The proportion of the total number of mergers of industry i that were with industry j, after coding mergers listed in the FTC large merger series into different industry categories. Because proportions produce heteroskedastic error terms, the analysis used a transformed version of the dependent variable defined as 2 x arcsine (square root (p)), where p = the proportion.

The transaction dependence of the bidder industry on the target industry was operationalized as industry constraint (Cij) in each of the eight panel years for each of the 51 industries studied. The measure combines the pattern of interindustry transactions with target industry concentration and was computed using the network analysis program STRUCTURE. Input-output transactions between industries came from Department of Commerce tables and the Survey of Current Business, and concentration data from the Census of Manufactures.

The number of mergers between an acquiring industry and each acquired industry was converted into a proportion of all mergers by the acquiring industry in the panel period, and then transformed with the arcsine transformation. The dependent variable consisted of interindustry merger patterns beginning in each of the eight panel years and ending the year prior to the next panel period, with the 1987 period ending in 1992.
time_window: panel periods covering mergers from 1948 to 1992

variable_name: strength of the resource dependence effect in panel period t - 1
description: A measure of the strength of the resource dependence effect in an industry was developed by computing the standardized coefficient for transaction dependence (industry constraint) in a regression of interindustry mergers by bidder industry, controlling for the number of large firms in the target industry and target industry profitability. There were 51 such regressions, one for each industry, in each panel period, each with a sample size equal to 50.

The concentration of the bidder industry itself, entered in the GLS regression together with the interaction of bidder industry concentration with transaction dependence. Data on industry concentration were obtained from the Census of Manufactures.

variable_name: periods of strict Celler-Kefauver Act enforcement
description: Panel periods falling within the years of most intense Celler-Kefauver enforcement were identified following Fligstein (1990), who dated that period from 1962 to 1974. This interval overlaps with four of the time periods studied (1958-62, 1963-66, 1967-71 and 1972-76), with 1963-66 and 1967-71 fully inside the enforcement period; the relationship between transaction dependence and merger was expected to be weaker in those periods.

The extension was investigated across eight different time periods that cover virtually the entire post-World War II era (1948-92). Transaction data were collected for each of eight points in time (1947, 1958, 1963, 1967, 1972, 1977, 1982 and 1987) and used to compute industry constraint scores. These eight years were chosen because they were the only years for which transactions data were published.

Annual corporate IT investment, including hardware, software, and costs concerning maintenance, personnel, and training. Following previous research, a firm's IT investment is divided by its total assets for size adjustment.
ROA is the ratio of net income to the year-end book value of total assets. The authors examine both current period ROA and future ROA, defined as the two-year average ROA subsequent to IT investment.
time_window: current period and two-year average subsequent to IT investment

description: The proportion of outside directors on the corporate board. Outside directors include affiliated directors (past managers, relatives of current managers, affiliated attorneys, and consultants to the firm) and nonaffiliated directors (those without such affiliations).
The percentage of common stock owned by foreign investors. This measure has been used in the literature to study the spillover of technological knowledge associated with foreign ownership.

The four-firm concentration ratio for each firm, which equals the percentage of total sales in the firm's industry sector accounted for by the four largest firms in the same sector. CR4 is negatively related to industry competitiveness; the sample is divided at the median CR4 into less competitive (above median) and more competitive (below median) industries.
Total assets used to measure firm size. The sample is classified into small and large companies by splitting at the sample median of total assets (below median = small, above median = large).

A CEO human capital index comprised of five dimensions. Three dimensions are associated with CEO experience: whether or not the CEO had a prior IPO experience as an executive or a director, a prior experience as CEO, and a prior experience in a public-listed company on the S&P 500 list, the Fortune 500 list or a similar foreign stock market index. Two dimensions are associated with CEO education: whether or not the CEO possesses an MBA or another graduate-level management degree, and whether or not the CEO has an undergraduate degree in finance and/or accounting. The index ranges from zero to five and refers to the CEO at the time of receiving the first round of VC investment.
time_window: at the time the firm receives its first round of VC investment

description: Calculated using the natural logarithm of the shortest travel time in minutes between the headquarters of the IPO firm and the lead VC. The average distance in the sample, measured as the shortest travel time in minutes, is 166.5 min.

Set to '1' if a firm changed CEO between receiving the first round of VC investment and IPO, and '0' otherwise. In the sample of 1,156 IPO companies, 472 firms changed their CEOs between the first round VC financing and IPO, and others did not.
time_window: between the first round of VC investment and IPO

description: Equal to the market value of the assets over its book value, and captures investors' perception of the IPO firm's current and expected profitability. To account for the entire pricing discovery process, the market value of the assets is calculated at the closing price of the first day of trading.
time_window: closing price of the first day of trading

description: Strategic uncertainty was measured as a combination of perceived environmental uncertainty and perceived sector importance. It is assumed to be a multiplicative rather than a linear function of the two components, with SU = EU × I, where SU = perceived strategic uncertainty, EU = perceived environmental uncertainty, and I = perceived sector importance. The measure was computed for each of the seven environmental sectors, yielding the sector-level unit of analysis.

The seven environmental sectors were classified into two layers. The task environment (competitor/industry, customer/market, supplier, and technological sectors) consists of sectors that have direct transactions with the organization. The general environment (political/legal, economic, and sociocultural sectors) is made up of factors external to the organization that exert great influence on its operations but on which the organization has little or no control.

Perceived environmental uncertainty was measured using a 27-item scale adapted from Miles and Snow (1978). The scale included seven subscales containing from three to five items each, corresponding to the key sectors of the external environment. Respondents rated the degree of predictability for various characteristics of the environmental sectors on 7-point Likert scales, with 1 indicating that the environmental element was predictable and 7 indicating that the feature was unpredictable. The adapted scale had a coefficient alpha of 0.78 and an average item-total correlation of 0.64.

Perceived importance of each environmental sector was measured with a new scale that originally had 21 items; two items with low item-total correlations were omitted, leaving 19 items. Respondents indicated the extent to which they perceived the various items as important on a 7-point Likert scale. Cronbach alpha for the 19-item version was 0.76, with an average item-total correlation of 0.55.

Scanning was measured with frequency questions similar to those developed by Hambrick (1982) and Culnan (1983), and validated by Farh, Hoffman, and Hegarty (1984). Respondents indicated the frequency of receiving useful information from various sources on a 7-point ordinal scale, where 1 meant 'once a year or less' and 7 meant 'once a day or more'. The questions distinguished between internal vs. external and personal vs. impersonal sources, producing four source variables: personal external (PE), personal internal (PI), impersonal external (IE), and impersonal internal (II). Following Daft et al. (1988), five additional variables were created to test the hypotheses about personal, impersonal, external, internal, and total scanning; the 'all modes' variable was (PE + PI + IE + II)/4.

Personal scanning was computed as the average of personal external and personal internal scanning sources: (PE + PI)/2. The underlying source variables were measured on a 7-point ordinal frequency scale where 1 meant 'once a year or less' and 7 meant 'once a day or more'.

Impersonal scanning was computed as the average of impersonal external and impersonal internal scanning sources: (IE + II)/2. The underlying source variables were measured on a 7-point ordinal frequency scale where 1 meant 'once a year or less' and 7 meant 'once a day or more'.

External scanning was computed as the average of personal external and impersonal external scanning sources: (PE + IE)/2. The underlying source variables were measured on a 7-point ordinal frequency scale where 1 meant 'once a year or less' and 7 meant 'once a day or more'.

Internal scanning was computed as the average of personal internal and impersonal internal scanning sources: (PI + II)/2. The underlying source variables were measured on a 7-point ordinal frequency scale where 1 meant 'once a year or less' and 7 meant 'once a day or more'.

The log of the number of years of the longest relationship in the firm's network of banking ties. The authors followed theory and focused on the length of the main relationship as an indicator of embeddedness, and logged the measure to capture diminishing returns in the duration of the relationship. They note that the mean duration of all ties is highly correlated with the longest tie.

The number of business and personal bank services used by the entrepreneur at the bank. Personal bank services include exchanges that focus on the banking and financial planning of the entrepreneur's personal finances; relationship managers noted that personal services deepen social relationships and reinforce multiplexity.

The log of the count of the number of banks a firm uses. The measure follows prior studies that used network size to operationalize the network embeddedness of a firm's banking relationships, and logging captures diminishing returns in the number of banks to which the firm is linked.

variable_name: the percentage of early-payment discounts on trade credit taken by the firm
description: The survey item asks for the percent of cash discounts offered for the payment of trade credit before the due date that were taken by the firm, reported in 1 percent increments from zero to 100 percent. Because continuous percentages create statistical problems for ordinary regression techniques, the authors transformed the dependent variable into an ordered categorical variable based on trade-credit theory. The six categories were 0 percent of the available discounts, 1-5 percent, 6-15 percent, 16-50 percent, 51-75 percent, and 76-100 percent.
