scale: six ordered categories: 0 percent, 1-5 percent, 6-15 percent, 16-50 percent, 51-75 percent, 76-100 percent

variable_name: the percentage of late-payment penalties on trade credit incurred by the firm
description: The survey item asks for the percentage of case penalties incurred for the payment of trade credit made after the due date, reported in 1 percent increments from zero to 100 percent. The authors transformed this continuous percentage into an ordered categorical variable with the same six categories used for early payments, based on trade-credit theory and the distribution of the variable.
scale: six ordered categories: 0 percent, 1-5 percent, 6-15 percent, 16-50 percent, 51-75 percent, 76-100 percent

description: Senior subsidiary managers were asked to what extent they agree or disagree, focusing on the end result, with three statements on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = totally disagree to 7 = totally agree: the solution found was adequate to resolve the initial problem; the solution found achieved its intended outcome; and the solution found was not fit for purpose (reverse coded; alpha = 0.78). All items loaded on one factor. The dependent variable is the factor score generated from the three items measured on the 7-point scale, which can take 31 real values.
scale: factor score from three 7-point Likert items
time_window: at the end of the problem-solving project

variable_name: Involvement of senior managers from headquarters
description: Count of headquarters managers listed in the project leader's name generator who were higher in the hierarchy than the project leader, that is, senior. The name generator focused on supportive exchanges in the problem-solving project and allowed respondents to name up to 10 people; if 10 people were named, respondents were asked how many people were important in addressing the problem. The comparative hierarchical level does not imply that individuals are in the same reporting line.

variable_name: Involvement of senior managers from the subsidiary
description: The involvement of senior subsidiary managers was measured using the same procedure as the one with senior headquarters managers: the number of managers from the focal subsidiary listed in the name generator who were higher in the hierarchy than the project leader.

Assessment of whether the problem related primarily to the firm's products and services (external locus) or primarily to the processes through which the firm conducts its activities (internal locus). The variable equals 0 if the locus is external and 1 if the problem has an internal locus.
The natural logarithm of one plus the cumulative number of contests won by a car manufacturer from 1895 up to a given year. This measure was lagged by 1 year, as in the original study.
time_window: lagged by 1 year; cumulative from 1895 to a given year

description: Measured as cessation of operations; mergers were not defined as exits. The authors relied on Smith (1968) for a record of mergers and acquisitions and supplemented this information with descriptions in the Standard Catalogue where necessary; if there was no record of an acquisition in either source, cessation of operations described in the Standard Catalogue was recorded as an exit.

A variable to account for de novo organizations, which were expected to have a higher exit rate. It was coded from the origin stories in the Standard Catalogue and cross-referenced with the Ioannou dataset. The variable is always equal to one if the firm was originally a startup, even several years after the firm was founded.
scale: binary (1 = firm was originally a startup)

description: Firms were classified by direct classification into one of four categories: structured strategic planners, structured operational planners, intuitive planners and unstructured planners. A multiple cut-off classification system similar to Lindsay et al. (1982) and Rue (1973) was used to operationalize planning sophistication, based on the 23-question survey instrument built around the eight planning process components. Structured strategic plans are formalized, written, long-range plans typically 3-15 years in nature; unstructured plans mean no measurable structured planning in the firm. The distribution of firms across the four levels was 38 structured strategic planners, 39 structured operational planners, 42 intuitive planners and 69 unstructured planners.
scale: four ordered categories (structured strategic, structured operational, intuitive, unstructured)

description: Financial performance data that served as dependent variables were revenue growth, entrepreneurial compensation growth and labor expense/revenue ratio growth. Revenue growth and entrepreneurial compensation growth were the absolute annual percentage growth rates during the time-frame examined; entrepreneurial compensation was determined by summing the firm's net profit before taxes and owner/manager compensation. The labor expense/revenue ratio growth was calculated as the absolute annual labor expense as a percentage of sales during the time-frame examined. The variables were developed from performance criteria recommended by the SEFA board, accountants in the dry cleaning field and published industry data sources.

Firms were classified by age, with young firms defined as established less than or equal to 9 years ago and older firms as more than 9 years old; the cut-off was based on SEFA board member recommendations. Usable participants had been in business at least 5 years. The average age of subjects' firms was 15.2 years.
scale: dichotomous (young: established 9 years or less; older: more than 9 years)

description: Firms were classified as small if annual revenue was less than or equal to $400,000 and as large if gross revenue exceeded $400,000; the selection of the cut-off was based on SEFA board member recommendations. Seventy-nine individuals reported more than $400,000 a year in gross firm revenue.
scale: dichotomous (small: revenue of $400,000 or less; large: revenue above $400,000)

description: Firms were classified by the length of time a strategic planning system had been in place, with long planning histories defined as more than 5 years and short planning histories as 5 years or less. Firms with long planning histories had gone through at least two iterations of the planning process.
scale: dichotomous (long: more than 5 years; short: 5 years or less)

description: Respondents were classified as opportunistic or craftsman entrepreneurs using McCain's (1982) scoring guide, which contains 14 questions in four major areas: breadth of education, social awareness and involvement, ability to deal with economic and social environment, and time orientation. Each response is scored 1, 0 or -1 depending on whether it indicates a positive, neutral or negative orientation towards the questions; a positive or negative response is indicative of the opportunistic and craftsman entrepreneurs, respectively. Owners/managers who failed to conform to the opportunistic orientation were excluded from the usable sample.

Letters to shareholders were content analyzed with Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software using a dictionary developed to track regulatory focus through the number of promotion-oriented words (e.g., gain, growth). The dictionary was built from words used in survey measures and word fragment completion tests and reduced to words with the greatest theoretical alignment with promotion focus, producing 27 promotion words; content validity was verified by 25 subject matter experts. The value used in the analysis is the percentage of words within each letter to shareholders found in the respective dictionary, and alternative tenses of the words are captured as well.
time_window: fiscal years 1997-2006; lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: Letters to shareholders were content analyzed with Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software using a dictionary developed to track regulatory focus through the number of prevention-oriented words (e.g., loss, stability). The initial dictionary contained 25 prevention words, validated by expert ratings of content validity. The value used in the analysis is the percentage of words within each letter to shareholders found in the respective dictionary, and alternative tenses of the words are captured as well.
time_window: fiscal years 1997-2006; lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: Options granted is measured based on the Black-Scholes value of individual stock options granted to the CEO, as reported in the Execucomp database in each year. This form of valuation has been widely accepted and validated in prior research. The variable is standardized along with the other predictor and control variables before the interaction term is computed.
time_window: each year; lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: Acquisition data were collected from the SDC mergers and acquisitions database, covering all majority, completed acquisitions during the sample period. Number of acquisitions was calculated as the sum total number of acquisitions completed in a given year, as reported to the SDC.
time_window: annual, measured in the year following the lagged predictors

description: Value of acquisitions was measured based on the total annual value of all majority completed acquisitions as reported in the SDC mergers and acquisitions database. The total value was log transformed because it was highly skewed. Because not all acquisitions report a total value, a within-firm-year mean replacement was used to account for the value of acquisitions with missing data.
time_window: annual, measured in the year following the lagged predictors

description: Firm investment horizon is estimated by dividing a firm's gross property, plant, and equipment (reported net PPE plus accumulated depreciation) by its reported depreciation expense in a given year, which yields the weighted-average estimated life in years of the firm's fixed assets. Accounting standards require expected useful lives between 1 and 40 years, and observations are limited to this range. Because the interpretation of horizon varies by industry, the analyses use relative horizon, calculated as the difference between the firm's horizon in year t and the median horizon for its industry, based on two-digit SIC codes, excluding the focal firm, in the same year. Relative horizon is used in all regression analyses; its squared value is also included to test the quadratic relation.

Firm performance is measured as return on assets (ROA). Extreme values of ROA often occur under extraordinary circumstances, so ROA is winsorized at the 10% level while the other variables are winsorized at the 1% level. After winsorization, the authors report a mean ROA of 3.0% and a median of 4.9%. The primary results use performance in year t+1, with replications using average ROA over two-, three-, four-, and five-year intervals.

Capital patience is measured from stock trading frequency: the volume of shares traded in year t for each firm is divided by its total number of shares outstanding, and each firm's trading intensity is then subtracted from the median value for its industry, which both accounts for industry effects in trading intensity and reverse-codes the variable to yield the patient capital interpretation (the opposite of trading frequency). Values below 0 indicate low patience (high trading activity) relative to the industry average that year, and values above 0 indicate higher patience (lower trading frequency). The variable is lagged by one year to mitigate reverse-causality concerns and create temporal separation from the firm's ROA.

Related diversification is one component of the entropy measure of total diversification, defined as related diversification arising out of operating segments within an industry group. Four-digit SIC industries were treated as the industry segments and two-digit SIC industries as the industry groups, and the measure takes into account the number of segments in which a firm operates and the relative importance of each segment in total firm revenues. Data were taken from Standard and Poor's COMPUSTAT business segment file for 1985 to 1987 and the three-year average index was computed. These variables could only be identified for 138 of the 184 firms in the sample.

Unrelated diversification is the second component of the entropy measure of total diversification, defined as diversification between industry groups. Two-digit SIC industries were treated as industry groups and four-digit SIC industries as segments; the entropy index weights each segment by the logarithm of the inverse of its share. The three-year average index over 1985 to 1987 was computed from Standard and Poor's COMPUSTAT business segment file data.

Average return on assets for the 1986 to 1988 period inclusive was used as the dependent variable in the regressions. ROE was ruled out because its value is as much a function of the capital structure of the firm as of efficiency, and ROA was chosen over ROI because it displayed greater year on year stability, the two being highly correlated. The three-year average smooths out annual fluctuations in the accounting data, and the performance data lag the organizational (1986) and strategic (1985-87) data.

Standardized factor score based on the factor score coefficient matrix, from a second-stage factor analysis of 10 scales; this factor loaded high on the two scales that summarized the degree to which operating and strategic decisions were decentralized to operating divisions. The underlying survey items (14 items on decentralization) each used a seven-point response scale, and items loading 0.4 or greater were assigned to a factor. A high negative score on the dimension indicates that responsibility for operating and strategic decisions was relatively centralized.

Standardized factor score from the second-stage factor analysis of 10 scales; this factor loaded highly on both scales that summarized the importance of integration between divisions and also loaded high on the remaining control scale. A high negative score on the dimension indicated that a high importance was attached to interdivisional integration, so the sign of the factor score is reversed relative to the construct as named. The scale was built from six survey items on interdivisional integration answered on a seven-point response scale.

Respondents were asked whether they used program or project managers, temporary task forces or committees, permanent teams or committees, and formal group structures to achieve integration between divisions. The responses were then transformed into a 5-point scale where 1 signified that a firm used no integrating mechanisms, and a score of between 2 and 5 indicated the number of different integrating mechanisms used. A firm that used all four mechanisms received a score of 5.

Standardized factor score labelled the breadth of control dimension, loading high on five of the six scales describing the extent to which the corporate office used subjective and objective nonfinancial criteria when assessing divisional performance and deciding how to allocate capital within the firm. A high negative score on the dimension indicated that the corporate office relied heavily on subjective and objective nonfinancial criteria, so the sign of the factor score is reversed relative to the construct as named. The scales were built from 13 control items and 10 cash flow allocation items answered on a seven-point response scale.

A dummy variable was calculated to indicate a firm's incentive system. The variable scored 1 if the firm based its incentive systems for divisional managers, at least in part, on corporate profitability, and 0 if incentives for divisional managers exclusively emphasized divisional profitability.

Customers rated their own level of engagement in the volunteering experience with four task absorption items adapted from Schaufeli et al. (2002), which the authors chose as the facet that best fit the one-time, on-site activity. Example items are 'I was immersed in the activity itself when I was volunteering' and 'When I was involved in the volunteering activity, I forgot everything else around me.' Two items from the original measure were not relevant to a one-time, on-site activity and were dropped. The coefficient alpha was .81.
time_window: Time 1 survey, during the volunteering program

description: Volunteering customers assessed their perception of the brewery's reputation using four items from Hochwarter et al. (2007). Example items are 'I think Creature Comforts has a good reputation' and 'I respect Creature Comforts as a company.' Because the scale was initially developed to assess individual reputation, several items were not applicable once the referent was shifted to company reputation. The coefficient alpha was .96.
time_window: Time 2 survey, about one month after the Time 1 survey

description: Friends of the volunteering customers assessed their perception of the brewery's reputation using the same four items from Hochwarter et al. (2007) that the customers answered. Example items are 'I think Creature Comforts has a good reputation' and 'I respect Creature Comforts as a company.' The coefficient alpha was .97.
time_window: Time 2 friend survey, sent when the corresponding customer received the Time 2 survey

description: Friends of the volunteering customers rated their perceived contagion from talking with the volunteering customer using three ad hoc items after the stem 'When my friend talks about Creature Comforts' corporate volunteering program . . .'. The three items were 'I can't help but 'catch' the emotions he or she conveys,' 'I tend to feel his or her emotions as if they are my own' and 'It feels like his or her emotions are contagious.' The coefficient alpha was .95.

Volunteering customers reported their patronage at the brewery using two items. The first was 'How often have you gone to Creature Comforts over the past two years?' with a response scale of 1 = almost never to 5 = very often, and the second was 'Please rate the frequency with which you visited Creature Comforts in the past two years?' with a response scale of 1 = once a year to 5 = once a week. The inter-item correlation was .90.
scale: 1 = almost never to 5 = very often; 1 = once a year to 5 = once a week
time_window: Time 3 survey, two years after the volunteering event

description: Friends of the volunteering customers reported their patronage at the brewery using two items: 'How often have you gone to Creature Comforts over the past two years?' (1 = almost never to 5 = very often) and 'Please rate the frequency with which you have visited Creature Comforts in the past two years?' (1 = once a year to 5 = once a week). The inter-item correlation was .91.
scale: 1 = almost never to 5 = very often; 1 = once a year to 5 = once a week
time_window: Time 3 friend survey, two years after the volunteering event

description: Volunteering customers reported the extent to which they purchased the brewery's products in that time period using two items: 'How often have you purchased [the brewery's] beer (at a bar, restaurant, or store) in the past two years?' (1 = almost never to 5 = very often) and 'Please rate the frequency with which you purchased [the brewery's] beer (at a bar, restaurant, or store) in the past two years?' (1 = once a year to 5 = once a week). The inter-item correlation was .88.
scale: 1 = almost never to 5 = very often; 1 = once a year to 5 = once a week
time_window: Time 3 survey, two years after the volunteering event

description: Friends of the volunteering customers reported the extent to which they purchased the brewery's products in that time period using two items: 'How often have you purchased Creature Comforts beer (at a bar, restaurant, or store) in the past two years?' (1 = almost never to 5 = very often) and 'Please rate the frequency with which you purchased Creature Comforts beer (at a bar, restaurant, or store) in the past two years?' (1 = once a year to 5 = once a week). The inter-item correlation was .86.
scale: 1 = almost never to 5 = very often; 1 = once a year to 5 = once a week
time_window: Time 3 friend survey, two years after the volunteering event

description: Measured with a 15-item scale developed by Lewis (2003); a TMS composite score was computed for each member by summing scores on the 15 items (SLalpha = 0.83). Members' scores were aggregated to the group level on the basis of the r wg statistic, with an average r wg on the learning task of 0.97.
time_window: after the learning task in Session 2

description: The number of task steps recalled, measured in half of the sample (34 intact groups and 32 reassigned groups); recall should be higher in groups with a TMS. The bivariate correlation between TMS and recall is 0.28.

Assembly accuracy-the number of assembly operations done correctly on the telephone assembly. Distinct operations were defined according to steps in the printed instructions; pretesting confirmed 38 distinct operations. A trained experimenter examined each group's completed telephone and counted misplaced or misconnected components, and one point was deducted from the group's score for each inaccurate operation, such that higher scores indicate higher learning-task performance.

The number of assembly operations done correctly for the personal stereo assembly kit, with pretests indicating 34 distinct operations. Points were deducted from a group's score for each inaccurate operation, such that higher scores indicate higher learning transfer to the stereo task.

Groups were asked to articulate a strategy for assembling a third electronics kit (electronic stapler) in the same domain as the learning and transfer tasks, in response to the question 'What sort of strategy would your group develop and utilize if you wanted to conduct the assembly of this kit efficiently and accurately? (How would you go about doing it?)'. Two coauthors blind to condition rated each group's written strategy description on a five-point scale anchored at 1 = trivial and 5 = integrative, where trivial entailed superficial surface elements and integrative transcended surface elements to underlying principles. Interrater reliability was high (ICC(2) = 0.98); the average score of the raters was used for the first 20 groups. A higher score indicates a greater degree of abstract knowledge.

Derived from the number of times members agreed about each member's expertise, both within and between tasks; individual responses were coded into nine expertise categories and agreement was based on consensus categorizations. Scores for each focal member range from 0 to 9, and a group-level score was computed as the sum of focal member scores, with a possible range of 0 to 27. Because the distribution was significantly skewed, the scores were transformed (natural log).
time_window: across the learning and transfer tasks

description: The number of priced technologies in month m in market category c, computed as the total number of MobileApps that exist in a given month in the same market as the focal MobileApp that can be downloaded only if a fee is paid and that have been downloaded at least once in the prior 12 months. All right-hand variables except for the age and time variables are lagged one month.
time_window: prior 12 months for the download condition; lagged one month

description: The total count of MobileApps in the same software market as the focal MobileApp that can be downloaded for free and that have been downloaded at least once in the prior 12 months. The measure includes free MobileApps in which the underlying source code is available for download as well as MobileApps in which only the binary is provided. Shareware MobileApps that users may download for free on a trial basis but must later remunerate a fee to continue to use are counted as free MobileApps.
time_window: prior 12 months for the download condition; lagged one month

description: Computed as the natural log of revenue for each priced MobileApp per month. Priced MobileApps are those that require a payment for users to download and use. Trial versions of priced MobileApps with limited functionality that users can download without paying a fee are excluded from this measure, as these downloads do not generate revenue for the seller; if a user downloads a trial version and subsequently pays to upgrade to the full MobileApp, the transaction is counted as a commercial sale when the fee is paid.

Computed as the natural log of downloads for each free MobileApp per month. Free MobileApps are defined as those that can be downloaded and are fully functional without a requirement that a fee be paid. Trial versions of commercial MobileApps with limited functionality that users can download without paying a fee are included in this measure, as these applications are available to users without paying a fee.

The number of unique competitors with which a firm shared a VC investor in a given year. Yearly bipartite networks of firms and VC investors were created in which a tie indicated that the firm received funding from that VC, and ties between firms and investors persisted for three years. Because the variable was highly positively skewed, the authors took the natural logarithm before inclusion, adding a constant of 0.01 prior to logging to account for situations with 0 indirect ties to competitors.
time_window: three-year tie decay window; current year excluded

description: A yearly count of FDA approvals of devices received by each MIS firm. All approvals in the sample were for devices categorized by the FDA as 'class III' devices. FDA approval is the authors' measure of commercialization, since medical devices cannot be sold in the United States without it; the authors identified 734 approvals in their sample.

A dummy variable for whether the focal firm was ever the first to receive investment out of its competitors from any of the shared VCs. For a given year the authors considered the set of all of a focal firm's VC investors that had also invested in its competitor firms. The variable equals 1 if the focal firm was the first to receive investment from any of those shared VCs, and 0 if it was not the first from at least one such VC, or if none of the firm's VC investors invested in any competitors.

A continuous measure that averaged the relative commitment across each focal firm - VC - competitor triad. Commitment of a VC to a given firm was operationalized as the number of rounds a VC has funded the focal firm. Positive values mean F has more committed ties to shared investors on average than its competitors; negative values mean less committed ties; zero means a balanced level of commitment. The formula is not readable in the extracted text.

Calculated first as the distance between the center of each firm's zip code and that of each of its investors, following Sorenson and Stuart's (2001) approach. In a firm-investor-competitor triad, the value is -1 if focal firm F is geographically closer to a shared investor than competitor Ci, 1 if F is farther, and 0 if the distance is identical; the measure is the mean across triads. Positive mean values indicate that F is on average farther from shared investors than its competitors.

A dummy variable indicating whether a firm received an investment from a high-status venture capital investor. Status was assessed as the VC's eigenvector centrality within investment syndication networks in high-technology industries; the dummy covers the top 30 VCs in the sample in terms of centrality score, with 30 chosen as the cutoff to include VCs central in geographies outside Silicon Valley and Boston.

The average reputation score of the VC investors that a focal firm shares with its competitors, constructed from Lee et al.'s (2011) yearly index of VC reputations. That index assigned yearly reputation scores ranging from 0 to 100 based on VCs' investment histories.

A roster of the entire community was developed from government registries, with possible family members being adults including parents, grandparents, in-laws, siblings, siblings' spouses and siblings' children. During the structured interviews each participant reported the degree of communication she had with each member, with response options from 1 to 5 (1 = less than monthly, 2 = monthly, 3 = weekly, 4 = daily, 5 = multiple times a day) and a 0 entered if she did not communicate with the individual. UCINET 6.29 was used to calculate centrality scores weighted by tie strength; family members were excluded from the other two networks.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each year

description: The community roster included all adult women in the village, excluding family members. Each woman reported her degree of communication with each member on a scale from 1 to 5 (1 = less than monthly, 2 = monthly, 3 = weekly, 4 = daily, 5 = multiple times a day), with a 0 entered for no communication. Centrality scores weighted by tie strength were calculated in UCINET 6.29.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each year

description: The roster of men in power comprised members of the local government, i.e., the Panchayat; all members of the local government in the study villages were men. Communication with each of these men was rated from 1 to 5 (1 = less than monthly, 2 = monthly, 3 = weekly, 4 = daily, 5 = multiple times a day), with 0 for no communication, and UCINET 6.29 was used to calculate centrality scores weighted by tie strength. Ties to family members were excluded even if they were men in power.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each year

description: For women in the 10 intervention villages, ICT use was assessed as the total number of hours each participant used the ICT kiosks in each year of the study. Kiosk attendants maintained a physical ledger of visitors to the kiosk, and these logs were matched with Internet logs recorded by the computers. ICT use was set to zero for participants in the control group villages.
time_window: aggregated over the course of each year

description: Entrepreneurial activity was coded 1 if a woman started a new business venture in a particular year, and 0 otherwise; a 1 was entered if a woman had an operational business. Detailed information about the entrepreneurial activity was gathered during the annual interviews to ensure accuracy and completeness, including informal businesses such as food delivery or milk delivery that were created by women and served the village.
time_window: captured at the end of each year

description: Data on the revenue generated in a specific year from entrepreneurial ventures were collected from government filings in the villages, and the personal interviews conducted each year served to cross-validate the profit data, which was important because some entrepreneurial activities were informal and did not report income. The correlation between the interview-based profit measure and the archival measure was greater than .80 for each year. Because the businesses were small and the women kept their own books, the entrepreneurs were considered best positioned to report their profits.
Time was coded from 1 to 7, in keeping with the year of data collection. Most variables were measured each year, with the exception of ICT use, which was aggregated each year.

The paper uses the model of Carroll (1979) as a proxy for measuring the attention to social and economic goals of the firm. Respondents were asked to allocate 10 points among four items representing the four areas of responsibility; the instrument was shortened to four sets of four items. Two summarized scales were made: the economic and legal perspective on the one hand and the ethical and philanthropic perspective on the other hand. This variable ranges between 0 and 40 with 0 being full attention to economic goals and 40 being full attention to social goals.

Agle et al. (1999) constructed a measure capturing the level of other-regarding values, where values are expected to vary from profit maximization firm-centered values to other-system-centered values. Three items measuring the other-regarding values construct were included (e.g., 'helpful - working for the welfare of others' and 'loving - being affectionate, tender'). Respondents rate each item on a seven-point scale.

To measure the adherence to a utilitarian identity, the operationalization of Foreman and Whetten (2002) is used. Four items that represent the utilitarian identity were included (e.g., value of products or services). Respondents indicate the importance of the items on a seven-point scale.

A debt-to-equity method was used to measure slack resources in the firm as financial data provide verifiable indicators of managerial behavior. This variable can be characterized as a long-term resource and reflects the firm's borrowing capacity. A firm with a low debt-to-equity ratio has a relatively high ability to obtain additional funds, which increases the freedom to reallocate resources.

variable_name: Firm performance (return on total assets, ROA)
description: Firm performance is operationalized as the return on total assets (ROA). ROA is widely used in the strategic management literature as an accounting-based measure of firm performance because it is not affected by the firm's financial leverage and better reflects the influence of internal management than market-based measures.

Yearly count of media attacks against the focal firm, collected from 12 high-circulation, independent and authoritative daily newspapers based across five continents. Keywords such as complain*, blame*, critic*, unethical, corrupt* and violat* were combined with the sampled firms' names and their variants, and article content was matched with the four most common negative stereotypes identified in the industry. For every media attack on a given firm regarding its alleged activities, values, or behavior, 1 was added in the year the article was published. Of the roughly 3,000 articles extracted, 1,166 represented attacks on one of the firms, and the variable was lagged by one year in all models.

Computed by first summing media attacks on focal firms across all firms and then subtracting the total number of attacks targeting the focal firm, so that it represents the total number of articles attacking any firm in the industry but the focal firm. More than 85 percent of the coded material concerns firms' military activities. The variable was lagged by one year in all models, and weighting each coded unit by the readership size of the newspaper did not change the results.

variable_name: media attacks on similar peers and media attacks on distant peers
description: Media attacks on peers were split using a consensual segmentation of the global arms industry along eight subcategories (electronic warfare; artillery and missile; military aircraft; military ground vehicles; military space technology; military ships and submarines; military-grade propulsion systems; combat training, simulation, logistics, and services). Media attacks on similar peers is the sum of all media attacks on proximate peers, i.e., firms with at least one overlapping segment with the focal firm; media attacks on distant peers is the sum of all attacks on distant peers, i.e., firms with no direct product category overlap. The two sum to media attacks on peers, and they were entered separately so that the moderation could be tested without relying on multiplicative interaction effects in a logistic model.

variable_name: asset divestment from the arms industry
description: Binary variable coded 1 when an arms producer divested an arms business unit in a given year (0 otherwise). Divestitures accounting for 5 percent or more of firm revenues were considered significant; data on acquisitions and divestitures were sourced mainly from Information Base and annual company reports, and divergences between the two sources were resolved with press articles. Because divestment remained a rare event, the variable was kept binary and was also coded 1 when divestment of more than one business occurred; when the number of divested businesses exceeded that of acquired businesses, the variable was coded 1. No arms producer exited the contested industry altogether in the data.

Extent to which a parent firm influenced or was involved in three outcome-related activities: overall goal setting, venture performance evaluation, and executive rewards and recognition. Respondents evaluated the intensity of influence or involvement on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high). The three items were aggregated into a single score, computed separately for the foreign parent and for the Chinese parent; all Cronbach's alpha values were well above 0.70.

Extent to which a parent firm influenced or was involved in five behavior- and process-related activities: functional control, rules and regulations, organizational structure, job description, and reporting systems. Respondents evaluated the intensity of influence or involvement on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high). The items were aggregated into a single score for the foreign parent and for the Chinese parent; all Cronbach's alpha values were well above 0.70.

Extent to which a parent firm influenced or was involved in three social-interaction activities: training and seminars, collaborative task forces, and socialization with IJV managers. Respondents evaluated the intensity of influence or involvement on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high). The items were aggregated into a single score for the foreign parent and for the Chinese parent; all Cronbach's alpha values were well above 0.70.

Weighted contribution of property-based resources. Respondents rated the importance of each resource to IJV operations on a five-point scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very important) and rated the extent to which each parent firm contributed that resource on a five-point scale from 1 (none or almost none) to 5 (very much). Each contribution rating was weighted by the importance rating of the item and the weighted values were combined over the items of the resource type; the printed formula could not be read from the extracted text.
scale: importance 1 (not at all) to 5 (very important); contribution 1 (none or almost none) to 5 (very much)

description: Weighted contribution of knowledge-based resources. Respondents rated the importance of each resource to IJV operations on a five-point scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very important) and rated the extent to which each parent firm contributed that resource on a five-point scale from 1 (none or almost none) to 5 (very much). Each contribution rating was weighted by the importance rating of the item and the weighted values were combined over the items of the resource type; the printed formula could not be read from the extracted text.
scale: importance 1 (not at all) to 5 (very important); contribution 1 (none or almost none) to 5 (very much)

description: Respondents assessed the significance of the IJV to each parent firm in terms of overall income, business operation, and global expansion, on a five-point scale ranging from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high). Cronbach's alpha confirmed the internal consistency of the items (0.89 for foreign parent firms and 0.91 for Chinese parent firms).

Composite index of differences between foreign and local parent objectives, measured on a five-point Likert scale for ten objective items. The index combines the foreign parent's and the Chinese parent's responses to each item, weighted by the variance of the item; the printed formula could not be read from the extracted text, and the text states that GI is the goal incongruence between foreign and local parents, Qif and Qic are the Likert scale responses to item i for the foreign and Chinese parent, and Vi is the variance of item i.

Parent resource contribution is measured by two weighted contribution scores from the survey: property-based resource contribution and knowledge-based resource contribution. Respondents rated how important each resource was to IJV operations and how much each parent contributed it, and the contribution ratings were weighted by importance. The two scores are separate predictors in the regressions, computed for the foreign and the Chinese parent.

variable_name: output, process and social control (by parent)
description: Parent control is measured as the extent of influence or involvement of each parent firm in IJV operations, split into three control types: output control (goal setting, performance evaluation, executive rewards), process control (functional control, rules, structure, job description, reporting systems) and social control (training and seminars, task forces, socialization with IJV managers). Each type is a separate five-point Likert score, computed for the foreign parent and for the Chinese parent, and each is used as a dependent variable in the regressions.

The dependent variable is the absolute percentage of annual change in the degree of diversification across the 20 product-markets of the semiconductor industry. Diversification is measured with the Jacquemin and Berry (1979) entropy measure: letting P_i be the percentage of total firm sales in the ith business and n the number of a firm's businesses, entropy equals the sum of P_i ln(1/P_i). Changes in strategy were measured by taking the absolute percentage of change in a firm's entropy measure each year, for the period t to t + 1.
time_window: annual change from period t to t + 1

description: Performance was measured as industry-adjusted average growth for two years: the year prior to the one in which strategic change was measured and the year the strategic change was measured. Average firm growth was measured as two-year revenue growth and compared with average revenue growth for the semiconductor industry for the same two years. Two-year average growth was used because organizations may not ordinarily react to poor performance by making important organizational changes in the same year that poor performance occurs.
time_window: two years: the year prior to and the year of the strategic change

description: Chief executive succession was measured from t - 1 to t and was dummy-coded as 1 when a succession event occurred.
Chief executive tenure was measured as the number of years a firm's current chief executive had held the job at time t.

Top management team members were defined as those individuals reporting directly to a firm's chief executive. The organizational tenure of each top manager was calculated using biographical data available from the market companies and the firms themselves. Team tenure was measured by taking the average of the aggregate tenure of all top managers.

variable_name: top management tenure diversity / top management team homogeneity
description: Top management tenure diversity was measured using the coefficient of variation, defined as the standard deviation divided by the mean. Following Wiersema and Bantel (1992), the logarithm of the heterogeneity measure was taken to capture the decreasing rate of the effect of dissimilarity of team tenure on strategic change. To measure top management team homogeneity, the heterogeneity measure was reverse-coded.

A formative index created by standardizing and then averaging five HRM practice measures, on the assumption that the practices within the index are substitutable. Pay level is the average annual pay for drivers; benefits level is the percentage of health insurance premiums for drivers paid by the company; job security is the average of two seven-point Likert-type items; training is the mean number of hours per year that drivers received formal training in computer, maintenance, and interpersonal skills; procedural justice is a five-item seven-point scale from Shaw et al. (1998).
time_window: time 1 (one year before the quit-rate measures)

description: A formative index created by standardizing and then averaging three HRM practice measures. Pay-for-performance is the percentage of annual driver pay that was variable and based on individual incentives and individual bonuses; performance appraisal is the number of times per year that the company conducted formal performance appraisals for drivers; monitoring is a five-item scale (response options from 1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'to a very great extent') covering the use of computer technologies to monitor driver location, driving hours, contact with dispatchers, driver decisions, and performance measurement.
time_window: time 1 (one year before the quit-rate measures)

description: Key informants reported first how many quits had occurred in the past year and then how many good performers were among those quits. That reported number was divided by the total number of drivers and multiplied by 100 to obtain the good-performer quit rate. No absolute standard of performance was set, because criteria for good performance vary in the industry.

Key informants reported first how many quits had occurred in the past year and then how many poor performers were among those quits. That reported number was divided by the total number of drivers and multiplied by 100 to obtain the poor-performer quit rate. No absolute standard of performance was set, because criteria for good performance vary in the industry.

A formative index created by averaging the standardized scores of the individual practice measures. Pay level is the average hourly pay rate for full-time employees; benefits level is the percentage of full-time employee health insurance premiums paid by the company; training is the total hours of training that a typical full-time employee received each year; job security is a two-item scale (1, strongly disagree, to 7, strongly agree) adapted from Shaw et al. (1998); procedural justice is a five-item scale from Colquitt (2001) with response options from 1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'to a very great extent.'
time_window: time 1 (two years before the quit-rate measures)

description: A formative index created by averaging the standardized scores of three practice measures. Pay-for-performance is a four-item scale from Colquitt (2001) asking the extent to which rewards reflect effort, contributions, are appropriate given the work completed, and are justified given performance; performance appraisal is the number of times per year that the company conducted formal performance appraisals for employees; monitoring is a three-item scale on the use of video cameras, one-way mirrors, or other monitoring devices to prevent stealing, collect appraisal information more accurately, and prevent loafing, with response options from 1, 'not at all,' to 5, 'to a very great extent.'
time_window: time 1 (two years before the quit-rate measures)

description: Informants reported the number of full-time employees who had quit in the last year and then the number of good performers among the total quits, where good performers were those whose job performance was in the highest 20 percent for full-time employees. That number was divided by the total number of full-time employees and multiplied by 100. The performance band was intended to ensure that informants used the same criteria for quits of good and poor performers.
scale: percentage of full-time employees who quit

description: Informants reported the number of full-time employees who had quit in the last year and then the number of poor performers among the total quits, where poor performers were those whose job performance was in the lowest 20 percent for full-time employees. That number was divided by the total number of full-time employees and multiplied by 100. The performance band was intended to ensure that informants used the same criteria for quits of good and poor performers.
scale: percentage of full-time employees who quit

description: The number of times climate change activists served as witnesses in U.S. Senate or House of Representatives hearings on climate change in a given year. Witnesses were identified as climate change activists based on their affiliation with climate change advocacy organizations, and the number of these witnesses was summed per hearing. The predictor is lagged by one year.
The sum of protests related to climate change against oil and gas companies reported in local and national U.S. newspapers. The predictor is lagged by one year.
The number of CO2-injection projects a company pursued in a given year. Data on EOR projects and oil and gas companies came from biennial surveys from the Oil and Gas Journal.

The number of climate change associations a firm joined in a given year. Seventeen climate change associations had accepted petroleum companies as members. Data on membership came from oil and gas companies and from the associations' membership lists.

The annual number of press releases in which oil and gas firms addressed climate change and sought to protect their image. The relevant press releases were extracted from PR Newswire and Business Wire in LexisNexis using search terms such as 'climate change,' 'greenhouse gas,' 'global warming,' and 'carbon capture' by firm-year.

Total number of announced deals that the CDE has done in prior jobs in corporate development or M&A functions before starting the current job. The author assumes that the CDE was involved in all deals done by prior employers during their time in those functions. The measure is scaled by 1/100 in all regression tables. The author notes it likely underestimates actual M&A experience because unannounced deals are not observed.

Number of announced deals the CEO has done before starting their current job, either in corporate development, prior CEO roles, or as specifically stated in their job descriptions. The measure is scaled by 1/100 in all regression tables for ease of display. An alternative measure including all announced deals before joining the current firm is tested in robustness checks.

Log of the total announced deals prior to the current year. Alternative measures using the count of prior deals, binary indicators, and log and count of recent deals are also tested. In some models firm M&A experience is instead measured as a count scaled by 1/100.

Binary indicator that equals one when the CDE joins a firm with fewer than 18 deals (40th percentile of the sample). Alternative cutoff points ranging from the 25th to the 40th percentiles are also tested. Firms are classified based on deals announced before the current CDE began their role.
time_window: before the current CDE began their role

description: Binary indicator that equals one when CEO M&A Experience is greater than CDE M&A Experience. It is used in subsample and full sample tests of H2.

Continuous variable capturing the difference in deal counts when the CEO has more experience than the CDE. The authors describe it as capturing the effects of each additional deal of experience the CEO has over the CDE.

Cumulative abnormal returns to the acquirer's stock price over a 3-day window around the deal announcement, used as the dependent variable measuring M&A performance. The 5-, 6-, and 7-day CAR windows are used in robustness checks.

Count of the CDE's prior deals sharing a given characteristic with the focal deal, defined using observable deal dimensions: same target industry (SIC3); same deal size (above or below $100MM); same control structure (majority or minority); same target public status; same industry and size; same industry and control structure; same industry and public status. Analogous similar-experience measures are constructed for the CEO and the firm.

One minus the Herfindahl index based on the proportion of years the CDE spent in different firms (Models 1-3) or in different job functions (Models 4-6) before starting the current role. It is used both as a subsample split and as an interaction with CDE M&A experience and its square.

variable_name: Log of number of products in line (length)
description: Product line length is calculated by counting the different products that a firm offers in a given year. In the reported models the authors use the natural logarithm of the product count, assuming that additional products have a diminishing marginal impact on firm performance. The count is constructed from Bike'alog's annual model specifications.

variable_name: Segments and materials in product line (complexity)
description: To construct a measure of product line complexity, each bicycle is classified according to its segment and frame material. The complexity measure is the number of cells in the 17 x 5 segment-material matrix that the firm's products occupy in a given year. Thus, a firm that offers only steel mountain bikes would have complexity equal to 1. The data come from Bike'alog's annual model specifications.

Following Sohn's (2001) method, each product class is a segment-material combination, and overlap between two firms is built from the proportion of the focal firm's products that are of that combination multiplied by the minimum count of that combination across the pair. Pairwise overlap values are asymmetric and vary between 0 (no overlap at all) and 1 (complete overlap). The overall measure for firm i is the mean of its pairwise values with all other firms in the industry in a given year, also ranging from 0 to 1. The measure is constructed from Bike'alog's annual model specifications.

variable_name: Failure / exit from the bicycle industry
description: The dependent variable is the firm's exit from the bicycle industry. For those firms that cease to be listed in Bike'alog, trade publications describe the reason for exit. Acquisitions, which occur very rarely in this sample, are treated as right censored.

We use the average number of visits per month before March 2013 (avgVisits_i) as the measure for outlet scale. Like the dependent variable, the measure is highly skewed, so its logarithm is used in the analysis. Since all outlets in the sample were listed by news aggregators before March 2013, the measure incorporates not only direct visits but also visits generated through the news aggregators.

To measure outlet scope, that is, the extent to which outlets are present in different content categories (e.g., news or sports), the authors use the outlet's mean monthly number of page impressions before March 2013 by category, a valid proxy because a relatively large number of page impressions in a category indicates that the outlet concentrates more on that category. For each outlet, the relative number of page impressions for each of the eight main categories is computed as fractions c_i,j summing to one, and an Inverse Herfindahl diversity measure based on a well-known measure of within-firm diversity is computed from these fractions. Higher values indicate broader scope.

The treated variable VGM_i is a dummy equal to one for all VGM members, generated from a list of all VGM members retrieved from the association's website vg-media.de. VGM members were the outlets whose content was removed from several German news aggregators in August 2014. The analysis includes 57 members and 83 nonmembers.

Dependent variable: an outlet's number of visits per month, where a visit is defined as an entire user session; if a user accesses three articles of one outlet, IVW counts one visit, and if a user leaves the domain for at least 30 min and returns, IVW counts two visits. The numbers refer to visits of the outlet's own web page, not the outlet's content on the news aggregator. Because few outlets attract the lion's share of user attention, the logarithm of visits is used as the dependent variable.
time_window: monthly; 18 months before March 2013 and 18 months after August 2014

description: Monthly page impressions as an alternative dependent variable: if a user accesses three articles of one outlet, IVW counts this as three page impressions but only one visit. The logarithm of page impressions is employed. This is reported only as a robustness check and is not part of the main analysis.

The number of forum messages the focal individual's colleagues have sent to the forums of SF.net projects in which individual i is not involved, at time t. Colleagues are the individuals who are members of the same projects as the focal individual; messages sent to projects the focal individual is also a member of are discarded so that only communication the focal individual is exposed to in the community context is counted. The variable is aggregated by month and entered in the regressions lagged one 30-day period.
time_window: monthly (30-day periods); lagged one period in the regressions

description: The number of artifacts (i.e., bug reports, patches, feature or support requests) the focal individual's colleagues have submitted to the tracker system of SF.net projects in which individual i is not involved, at time t. Submissions to projects the focal individual is also a member of are discarded. The variable is aggregated by month and entered in the regressions lagged one 30-day period.
time_window: monthly (30-day periods); lagged one period in the regressions

description: The number of new projects launched by individual i in period t on SF.net. The authors treat launching a project as the behavior in which an individual formulates a new overarching problem and designs the problem architecture. It is a count outcome aggregated by month.

The number of existing projects joined by individual i in period t on SF.net. Joining indicates that the individual takes a second-tier role in an existing team and typically works on a more or less well-defined subproblem within the existing architecture. It is a count outcome aggregated by month.

For each time period the authors calculated the variance of each firm's return on equity as an accounting-based measure of firm risk. Total risk, or variance of returns, was used rather than systematic risk (beta) because managers are responsible to a wider set of stakeholders than shareholders and because beta is both empirically and theoretically related to total risk.

For each time period the authors calculated the average return on equity for each firm as an accounting-based measure of firm return. This return measure was rank ordered and used in the risk-return association analyses.

Two target return levels were used. For firms within the same industry, the industry's median ROE was the target measure; across industries, the overall median ROE was used. Firms were ranked on average ROE within an industry or across all industries and divided at the median, and firms with values below the median were considered below target and vice versa. The median was chosen because it is the middle point of the return distribution and is unaffected by extreme outliers.

A four-item survey measure modified from the six-item short form of Spielberger's anxiety measure, adapted to assess job anxiety in the context of top executives. The items assess the extent to which the executive's friends and family perceived that the executive (1) often worried about making major mistakes in his or her job; (2) appeared concerned that he or she was not the best person for the job; (3) appeared apprehensive about the threats and challenges he or she faced in the job; and (4) appeared nervous making tough decisions in the job. Each item ranged from one to seven, the scale alpha was 0.84, and job anxiety was calculated as the mean of the four items aggregated across an average of 1.7 evaluators per executive; a natural log transformation was then performed to account for positive skew.

A four-item measure assessed by each top executive during the interview, during which they described for each major decision the degree to which their team members (1) knew each other before the decision; (2) were friends before the decision; (3) were loyal to each other; and (4) were loyal to the executive personally. Items were rated on a scale of 1 (not at all) to 7 (to a very great extent) and the alpha for the four items was 0.91. The measure pertains to the specific team involved in each decision and could therefore vary across the decisions of a given executive.
scale: 1 (not at all) to 7 (to a very great extent)

description: During each interview the executive was asked to reflect upon the degree to which the final decision exposed the firm to strategic risk, rated on a scale ranging from 1 (decreased firm risk substantially) to 7 (increased firm risk substantially). Decision-making team members made the same assessment in a separate online survey, with an ICC(1) between evaluators of 0.48 and an ICC(1,k) of 0.65. Because principal component analysis confirmed that the two assessments were largely driven by a single factor, the average value of leader and team perceptions was used as the measure of strategic decision risk.
scale: 1 (decreased firm risk substantially) to 7 (increased firm risk substantially)

description: A psycholinguistic measure built from the transcripts of the executives' in-person interviews, with each discussion of a strategic decision treated as a discrete body of text and all passages not spoken by the executive deleted. LIWC was used to compute the relative percentage of words spoken by the executive in a gain context dictionary (positive emotion language including assent and words associated with achievement, 622 words) and in a loss context dictionary (negative affective language and words associated with inhibition, 610 words). The gain and loss scores were standardized and a net perceived gain/loss context score was calculated as gain minus loss, so that positive scores indicate a gain context and negative scores a loss context.

All prior IVF cases that occurred since clinic i started offering IVF treatment, cumulated until but not including the focal year. The natural log of the cumulated count is used in the regressions, in keeping with the learning-curve literature.
scale: count, natural log used in regressions
time_window: from clinic start of IVF treatment until but not including the focal year (t-1)

description: The number of years since clinic i started offering IVF treatment, as reported to HFEA, until but not including the focal year. It is used as the measure of the time taken to accumulate the clinic's experience.

The number of live-birth events (successful treatments) at a clinic in a given year. The natural log of this count is the dependent variable in the regressions. The natural log of the total number of treatments administered in that clinic-year is controlled for on the right-hand side.
scale: count, natural log used in regressions

description: The proportion of female patients above age 35 whom the clinic treated during the focal year. Treating older women represents a challenge for clinics because the chance of success through IVF decreases sharply after the age of 35.

Dummy variable for the availability of integrators at each clinic: 0 if the clinic had no integrator role, representing a low level of coordination effort, and 1 if the clinic had an integrator. This feature of organizational design displays very low within-clinic variation.
time_window: time invariant within clinics over the observation window

description: The level of generativity in an ecosystem is measured as the number of game titles of diverse types within a given game genre in the console at the month of the individual title's launch. It captures the variants of newly launched game titles within a given genre, that is, the range of different console-game consumption possibilities for each gaming genre. Because a game title's rating does not change across time in the database, only the month each title was launched on each console enters the estimation models.

Gamer evaluations of each game title, collected from IGN.com, which offers historical reviews of games. Each game is rated on a scale of 1 to 10 (10 being the highest) based on consumer feedback. Each game-console combination is assigned a unique rating, so a game sold on multiple consoles may receive a different user satisfaction rating for its performance on each console.

Cross-platform competition is the inverse of the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) computed on the basis of unit sales of competing platforms in a given time period. Because the HHI measures concentration in a market, such that a higher index value denotes lower competition, the authors take its inverse. The variable takes a minimum of 0 for no competition (HHI = 1) and positive values for increasing levels of competition.
time_window: given time period at the title's launch

description: A dummy variable that takes the value 1 for observations in the late maturity stage, defined as game titles launched from the end of the fourth year of a console's life on, and 0 for observations in the early maturity stage, which considers only game titles launched during the first year of a console's life. For most platforms the authors are essentially considering the first and final years of the life cycle.

variable_name: No. of low-rated games/No. of high-rated games
description: Variance in user satisfaction is computed as the ratio of the number of titles with a user satisfaction rating below the mean (at the console-genre-quarter level), the low-rated games, over the number of titles with a rating above the mean, the high-rated games. The measure is intended to capture whether higher generativity increases the mean-adjusted variance of user satisfaction through the proportion of developers producing low- versus high-rated titles. The level of analysis is the console-genre-quarter and all variables are averages at that level.

Indicator variable equal to one if individual i is Black and equal to zero otherwise, as used in the logistic regressions of joint appointment. Race was coded by an ethnically diverse group of human observers: two independent raters manually coded race and gender using information made public on individuals' personal and department websites, relying predominantly on photos while also referring to names and relevant diversity experiences, and a third independent rater coded when the first two disagreed. The main observer-selected measure is based on majority agreement when at least two rounds reflected agreement; the final analysis sample consists of 258 Black and 3,544 White faculty, including 155 Black and 1,780 White faculty at the assistant professor level.

Binary variable equal to one if an individual has salary shared by two or more academic departments in the same year, and as zero otherwise, taken from administrative records at the individual level. The authors took additional steps to verify that only formal joint appointments are identified: interviews with senior faculty confirmed that courtesy, or dry, appointments do not involve shared salary, and for all cases identified as formal joint appointments in the administrative record the authors manually coded how individuals report their appointment status in their CVs and web pages, finding no courtesy appointments.

For all individuals who first appeared in the data as assistant professors, the authors used administrative personnel records to code whether they were retained with promotion to the level of associate professor. Because the administrative data do not have a direct measure indicating whether an exit was voluntary or involuntary, all exits recorded in the administrative record were measured as indicating lack of retention in the main analyses. To account for right censoring, the retention sample was restricted to observations of individuals who were hired as assistant professors prior to the year 2010.

Derived from the MAG database by counting the total number of all research outputs that individuals had accumulated per year, which included journal articles, books, book chapters, and conference proceedings, and separately by counting the total number of journal articles and books that individuals produce every year. The analysis uses author-year panel data on both jointly and singly appointed assistant professors and includes a binary variable Post_joint_appointment equal to one if the author-year observation is subject to joint appointment and zero otherwise, controlling for author fixed effect and year fixed effect.

For each winery and each vintage, this variable was set to 1 if a wine was made with the help of winemaking consultants and 0 otherwise. The data were originally derived from the BordOverview online database and then extensively cross-checked and refined using the four wine guides and an extensive search of the Internet.

'En primeur' tasting scores were extracted from the Bordeaux Primeur online database; there were 1,861 tasting scores from Robert Parker. Both publications use a 100-point scale to rate wines, and because a range is reported for 'en primeur' wines (e.g., 92-94) the low and high values were averaged. A blind tasting process ensured that critics did not know the name of the winery and the price of the wine when they assigned quality ratings.

'En primeur' tasting scores were extracted from the Bordeaux Primeur online database; there were 2,008 tasting scores from the critics of the Wine Spectator. Both publications use a 100-point scale to rate wines, and because a range is reported for 'en primeur' wines (e.g., 92-94) the low and high values were averaged. A blind tasting process ensured that critics did not know the name of the winery and the price of the wine when they assigned quality ratings.

For each year, the average tasting score across all wines in the sample was computed, and a wine's absolute deviation from the mean was calculated. A dummy variable was then set to 1 if a wine was in the top five percent in terms of absolute deviation from the mean, and 0 otherwise.

For each year, the average tasting score across all wines in the sample was computed, and a wine's absolute deviation from the mean was calculated. A dummy variable was then set to 1 if a wine was in the top five percent in terms of absolute deviation from the mean, and 0 otherwise.

For each Bordeaux winery, the quality of the terroir relative to other Bordeaux wineries was assessed using a three-star scale developed by the experts of the Revue du Vin de France. Because the star categories could not be assumed to be equally spaced, three dummy variables were used: one-star terroir, two-star terroir, and three-star terroir, with one-star terroir as the reference. The measure was taken at the winery level and reflects the 'average quality of the terroir' rather than the quality of a particular plot of land.

Prior alliance experience is measured as a count of alliances that a firm has been involved in from 1985 up to, but not including, the year of the focal alliance. These alliances can be of any type, such as marketing, manufacturing, supply, or R&D, because the authors argue that firms learn to manage the coordination difficulties inherent in R&D alliances from any type of prior alliance experience. To take the hypothesized non-linear relationship into account, the natural log of this count is used as the independent variable.
time_window: 1985 up to, but not including, the year of the focal alliance

description: Firm innovative performance is measured as citation-weighted firm patenting in a 4-year, post-alliance window, beginning with a 1-year lag between alliance commencement and patenting (for an alliance commencing in 1991, the sum of citation-weighted patents applied for 1992-95). Each patent is weighted by the citations made to it by later patents, and the application date is used. Patents assigned to the parent firm and to all of its subsidiaries are aggregated at the corporate level to capture the firm's entire patent portfolio.
time_window: 4-year post-alliance window starting one year after alliance commencement

description: A composite measure of the complexity or uncertainty of alliance activities: the estimated probability that allying firms choose an equity joint venture (versus a more contractual form) for alliance organizational form, given alliance characteristics. The probability of choosing an equity joint venture is treated as a signal of the underlying complexity of alliance activities, since equity joint ventures are chosen when specifying partner rights and obligations is difficult and monitoring and enforcement are imperfect. Observations are split into low-uncertainty and high-uncertainty subsamples according to this probability estimate.

Service climate was measured using a scale adapted from the instrument developed by Schneider et al. (1992, 1998), completed by the customer service manager in each of the firms in the sample. The authors collected data on both dimensions of service climate but present only the scale and analysis of the facilitators of service climate, because sample size limitations precluded including both dimensions in one model; analysis with the motivators led to the same results. The authors report that the reliability of this measure is above the generally accepted level of 0.70.

Managerial IT knowledge was measured using an instrument adapted from Boynton et al. (1994), consisting of two parts, one completed by the manager responsible for customer service and the other by the chief information officer in each firm. The customer service manager answered questions regarding the IT manager's knowledge of the operations of the customer service unit and about the level of shared understanding with the IT manager regarding how IT can be used to improve customer service quality; the IT manager answered questions regarding his or her assessment of the customer service manager's understanding of IT and how IT can improve the performance of the customer service process, and about their level of shared understanding. The authors report that the reliability of this measure is above the generally accepted level of 0.70.

A new scale was developed to measure the range and scope of the technology resources used to support the customer service process. Interviews with managers were used to identify the technologies used in the customer service process, and the scope of the implementation of each was assessed using a six-point scale with four anchors (don't intend to implement, not yet begun, standard implementation, highly advanced implementation). This scale is in the spirit of the scale used by Powell and Dent-Micallef (1997) to measure technology resources, and it was completed by the IT manager of each firm. The authors report an alpha coefficient of 0.65 for this scale, close to the widely accepted cutoff of 0.70 and greater than the minimum recommended for newly developed scales.
scale: six-point implementation scale with anchors: don't intend to implement; not yet begun; standard implementation; highly advanced implementation

description: The annual customer service budget and the annual IT budget were used to assess the investment in the customer service process, collected from the customer service and IT managers of each firm. The authors report that the reliability of this measure is above the generally accepted level of 0.70.

A modified version of the customer service quality instrument developed by Parasuraman, Zeithaml, and Berry (1985, 1988, 1991, 1994) from the marketing literature. The original instrument is intended to be administered to an organization's customers, but because the design required the measurement of customer service performance for a large number of companies it was not possible to administer it directly to customers; therefore a modified version was developed and completed by a firm's customer service manager. This measure of customer service performance is referred to as 'PZB'.

An organization's own assessment of the quality of the customer service provided by its customer service unit. Because customer service is regarded as an important activity in the insurance industry, insurance companies conduct periodic surveys to measure the quality of service provided by their customer service unit, and the overall result of that quality assessment was used as the second measure of customer service performance.

The retention ratio weighted by the volume of business in different lines of insurance (life/health), for the policies sold in the previous calendar year. The authors argue that customer service performance is reflected in the ability of firms to retain policy holders, since a company that provides superior customer service is able to retain policy holders over a period of time.

The complaints ratio of a company is defined as the ratio of premiums written to the number of complaints received by the company, classified by the type of insurance activity (life/health), as aggregated by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC). The complaints ratio has been found to be correlated with direct measures of customer service quality as assessed using the instrument developed by Parasuraman et al. (1985). One limitation is that only 28 states collect complaint statistics, so the statistic is not available for a company that operates only in the other states.

Firm performance measured in terms of return on assets, entered as the dependent variable in a model that examines the relationship between the four independent variables (service climate, managerial IT knowledge, technology resources in customer service, and investment in customer service) and firm performance. The authors note that no specific hypotheses were made with respect to the relationship between the four independent variables and firm performance.

Count of patents assigned to the firm that are coinvented with a physician in a firm-year observation, where the year is the application year. If at least one inventor on a firm's patent is a physician, the patent is counted as a physician coinvented patent; 83 percent of these patents also include nonphysician inventors. Concurrent and one-year-lagged values are included in the estimation, and the natural log of the variable is used.

Physician-firm coinvented patents assigned to technology classes that are nascent (class age less than zero), aggregated to a firm-year count of coinventions in nascent technology classes. The variable is included in concurrent and lagged form and entered in natural logs.

Physician-firm coinvented patents assigned to technology classes that are new (0-5 years old), aggregated to a firm-year count of coinventions in new technology classes. The variable is included in concurrent and lagged form and entered in natural logs.

Physician-firm coinvented patents assigned to technology classes that are established (5 or more years old), aggregated to a firm-year count of coinventions in established technology classes. The variable is included in concurrent and lagged form and entered in natural logs.

Firm-year count of the number of FDA approvals of medical device products via the 510(k) and PMA processes, including all classes of products. Innovations are dated by the year the application was received by the FDA.

Firm-year count of product approvals granted through the premarket approval (PMA) process, used as the measure of radical innovations. The PMA process is reserved for the most novel devices, for which no equivalent device exists, and involves animal testing and human clinical trials.
