Firm-year count of product approvals granted through the premarket notification (510(k)) process, used as the measure of incremental innovations. The 510(k) process requires demonstration of substantial equivalence to a device currently on the market and is intended for less risky devices that are often modifications of existing products.

Application year of the patent less the establishment date of the class to which the patent is currently assigned, using USPTO establishment dates at the primary and subclass level. Because patents are reclassified as technology classes are established, class age may be negative. Each coinvented patent is categorized as belonging to a nascent (less than 0), new (0-5 years), or established (5 or more years) technology class.
time_window: patent application year relative to class establishment date

description: An index built from two count measures derived from Japanese Overseas Investments: the total number of overseas subsidiaries a firm had in a given year, and the total number of countries in which it had overseas subsidiaries. Each count measure was divided by the maximum value for that variable to convert it into a ratio, and the index is the average of these two ratios. The measure ranges from 0 to 1, with larger values representing higher diversification.
time_window: same year as reported; independent variables lagged one year

description: The total number of shares owned by foreigners divided by total shares outstanding. Ownership types were assessed as the total percentages of all outstanding shares held by the respective types of owner, so larger values represented more power for an owner type and consequently more influence over the outcomes of strategic decisions.
time_window: end of the previous year (lagged one year)

description: The total number of shares owned by Japanese financial institutions and other Japanese business corporations divided by total shares outstanding. Ownership types were assessed as the total percentages of all outstanding shares held by the respective types of owner, so larger values represented more power for an owner type and consequently more influence over the outcomes of strategic decisions.
time_window: end of the previous year (lagged one year)

description: The ratio of a firm's market value to the replacement cost of its assets. Market value was computed as the sum of the book value of its debt and the market value of its equity, and the replacement cost of assets was computed as the book value of total assets. The authors note it is less susceptible to accounting-based distortions than measures such as return on assets and is forward looking, incorporating expected future cash flows as gauged by the stock market.

The natural logarithm of the year-over-year change in sales, specified as ln(sales t / sales t - 1), following Brush et al. (2000). The variable was winsorized at the 99th and 1st percentiles of its distribution.

Using data drawn from NEEDS, the authors measured employment growth as the natural log of the year-over-year change in the number of total employees: ln(employees t / employees t - 1). The variable was winsorized at the 99th and 1st percentiles of its distribution.

A proxy for managerial compensation using NEEDS data on total director compensation, which includes base salary plus bonuses; Japanese companies report the total pay of all directors, including salaries, bonuses, fees, and other perks and benefits. Because Japanese companies have few and often no outside directors, and the president and top executives comprise most or all of the board, director pay is used as a reasonable proxy for executive pay.

Percentage of applicants to a specific restaurant who had scored at the top of the distribution on a validated selection test and were hired. The test measures basic cognitive ability (e.g., basic math skills) and personality traits linked to service provision, and was designed to predict performance in customer service occupations rather than to be firm-specific. Test scores were broken into three groups, with the 'definitely hire' group scoring at the 66th percentile and above, the 'potentially hire' group in the middle, and the 'definitely reject' group below the 33rd percentile. The authors state this is not a 'selection use' measure but an assessment of generic human capital quality.
scale: percentage of hired applicants scoring at the 66th percentile or above

description: Percentage of employees who completed advanced levels of optional training; because eligibility required a minimum period of work at the unit, the measure contains two sources of variance, on-the-job training and on-the-job experience. Basic training was required of all employees, whereas advanced training consisted of additional modules on customer service and product preparation, each requiring roughly seven hours of on-the-job training. Employees who completed all modules in at least one of the two areas and passed the end-of-training tests were considered to have reached advanced training status. The authors note the measure captures variance in on-the-job experience as well as training.

Customers who called a toll-free number on their printed receipts directly rated the unit's service performance. Using a 100-point scale for each dimension, customers rated the unit's hospitability, order accuracy, product quality, and speed. The dimensions were highly correlated and were combined into a composite. All restaurants had at least 36 calls per quarter, and an outside vendor captured the phone calls and customer responses.
scale: 100-point scale per dimension; composite across dimensions

description: An assessment of restaurant productivity, calculated by dividing unit-level sales by the number of labor hours required to generate those sales. Quarterly sales per labor hour was calculated by taking a restaurant's quarterly sales and dividing it by the unit's number of labor hours for that quarter. The authors note this measure is similar to sales per employee but may be a better measure of profit because it is unaffected by turnover and number of part-time versus full-time employees.

A ratio of each restaurant's controllable profit divided by its projected profit based on its sales from the prior year. Controllable profits are unit sales less variable costs; projected profits are based on sales compared to sales from the same quarter the prior year and adjusted for restaurant size, age, location, and competitive density. Because it compares actual to expected profit, restaurants generating profits higher than expected show values over 100 and those generating profits lower than expected show values under 100.
scale: ratio, with 100 as the expected-profit benchmark

description: Count of reported protest events within the geographic vicinity of a firm's nuclear power plant generating unit(s). The authors count the number of protests that occurred each year, and in the preceding year, within 100 miles of a firm's nuclear unit(s), matching a protest to each nuclear firm within that radius. Protest information was drawn from the Dynamics of Collective Action Project database on antinuclear protest events reported in the New York Times. In the main models the variable is instrumented with the count of nonnuclear protests occurring in the same vicinity.

The percentage financial return a firm is permitted to earn on its assets as determined by the state PUC during a regulatory rate review. RORs vary both within the industry over time and between firms in the same state and year. Over the entire sample the average Rate of Return was 9.89% with a standard deviation of 1.59%.

Binary variable equal to one if the state executive (Governor's office), House, and Senate were all controlled by the Democratic Party and zero otherwise. A comparable variable, Republican Governor and Legislature, measures unified Republican state government.

Measured as the percentage of PUC commissioners who were members of the Democratic Party. Party affiliation information was collected from individual PUC websites, the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, local newspaper reports, and directly from PUC offices.

A firm's reputation is gauged as the residual from a regression model that estimates the firm's ROR in its previous rate review, where the independent variables are the same as the ones used to test the hypotheses. The residuals, which are the differences between the actual ROR allowed in the prior rate review and that predicted by the regression model, are interpreted as the effect of the firm's reputation with the regulator, all else equal. Constructing this variable reduces the observations for estimation of the rate of return from 1,886 rate reviews to 1,680.

A count of the number of nuclear generating units that a firm had cancelled in the previous year, used to measure firm accommodation of activist demands. The variable is constructed using cancellation data from electric utility reports to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's Agency-Wide Documents Access and Management System.

A paper-level measure borrowed from Porter and colleagues, a particular parameterization of the Sterling Index. As input, all subject categories (SCs) from the focal paper's set of references are pooled, rather than the SCs of the focal paper itself or of papers that cite it; the index combines the variety and balance of the referenced SCs with their pairwise similarity taken from an SC x SC co-citation matrix converted to cosines. The score ranges from 0 to 1, with scores closer to 1 indicating greater interdisciplinarity; for person and person-year analyses the authors aggregate by taking the mean IDR score across each scientist's papers, and observations with zero scores are excluded.

variable_name: Number of subject categories (N of SCs)
description: An alternate, less-refined measure of interdisciplinary research that does not incorporate distance: the total number of unique subject categories referenced by a scientist across all of his or her papers, with no regard for their similarity (range 1-107, mean = 32). It is used in place of the IDR measure to assess whether distance matters above and beyond sheer variety.

The total number of articles a scholar published in WoS journals from the beginning of his or her career-the year he or she first published-until 2005; this is a conservative measure that excludes book chapters and articles published in less internationally recognized journals. The authors examined the number of articles at the person and person-year level, taking the natural log at the person level and using a negative binomial specification, with publications summed per year, in the person-year fixed-effects model.

The forward citations that had accrued to each published article indexed in WoS as of 2010, a paper-level measure that the authors aggregate by taking the mean to obtain person- and person-year-level measures of visibility; the person-level outcome was logged.

To test hypothesis 3 about variability in citations, the authors calculated the standard deviation of each scientist's citations. When modeling the standard deviation in citations rather than mean citations, they also controlled for the standard deviation rather than the mean of journal impact factor.

Field-level interdisciplinary research measured both continuously and categorically. Continuous measures are the average IDR score for each field and the trend in IDR for each field, calculated as the slope from a field-specific regression of IDR on publication year. Categorical measures indicate whether the scholar is in the life sciences (the highest IDR field in the sample) or in electrical engineering (one of the lowest IDR fields). Field classification is based on current field as determined by scholars' CVs and department faculty listings, covering nine broad fields.

The variable measures the number of supportive community policing procedures in place at the focal agency - geographic patrols, formal encouragement of collaboration, and supportive incentive structures. It could take a value from 0 (reflecting no supportive procedures) to 3 (reflecting the full mix of supportive procedures). It is used as a dependent variable when examining the antecedents of collaborative engagement and as a predictor variable when examining its outcome.
time_window: one survey period lag as a predictor; contemporaneous as an outcome

description: The volume of calls received by the agency through its 9-1-1 system, in thousands. Members of the general public provide information about crime events, emergencies, and other service issues directly to law enforcement agencies through these 9-1-1 call systems, and the measure is bounded on its lower end by 0. It is used as an unlagged outcome variable in the first analysis and as a logged control in the analyses of community policing practices.
time_window: contemporaneous as an outcome; lagged one period as a control

description: Tracks the rate of reportable crime events per person within the reporting agency's jurisdiction. Reportable crime events refer to the specific criminal offenses tracked by the Uniform Crime Reporting program, chosen because of their severity, because they occur with regularity in all areas of the country, and because they are most likely to be reported to police. The variable is missing for a small number of observations in respect of which the presiding agency could not be uniquely identified, and the data are collected for the year just prior to each focal observation.
time_window: year just prior to each focal observation

description: A dichotomous indicator (civilian oversight board) that is set to 1 if this form of external oversight exists at the focal law enforcement agency, and set to 0 if an external review board does not exist. Civilian complaint review boards are typically tasked with reviewing complaints against the police regarding use of force, misconduct, or other procedural lapses. The relevant moderating hypothesis is tested through an interaction between this variable and the crime rate measure.

Measures the number of nonlethal and less-than-lethal technologies available for routine use at the focal agency, ranging from 0 (no nonlethal equipment available for routine patrols) to 7 (all equipment categories available). The variable tracks whether the agency formally allows patrol officers to use conductive energy devices (stun guns or Tasers), rubber bullets, neck restraints (carotid holds or choke holds), tear gas, pepper spray, soft projectiles (e.g., bean bag rounds), or requires that they wear body armor or other tactical gear on routine patrols. The respective hypothesis was tested through an interaction between this variable and the crime rate variable.

Tracks the number of complaints about excessive force involving an agency's officers that are received by the agency during the year; complaints can be initiated by citizens or on their behalf and are typically investigated by the law enforcement agency or by the civilian review board if one exists. The measure does not track legal actions against departments and likely underreports the true rate of excessive force incidents, but it is treated as an appropriate reflection of the visible public concern surrounding an agency's policing practices. The information was requested for two survey administration periods, each asking for the prior year's force complaints, and the moderating hypothesis was tested through an interaction between this variable and the crime rate variable.
time_window: year immediately preceding each available observation

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if the observation year is between 2011 and 2014, namely after Kinect's launch, and 0 otherwise. As a consequence of including individual and time fixed effects, this term drops out of the estimating equation; the main coefficient of interest is its interaction with the treated-researcher dummy.

The number of academic publications of researcher i at time t, counted at the individual level per year from the IEEE Xplore publication data. The data set is a balanced panel in which nonpublishing years are taken into account as years with zero publications.
The number of academic publications of researcher i at time t weighted by the number of cumulative citations received until 2014.

An intensive measure of diversification equal to the sum of the number of topics where the focal researcher has his or her papers assigned by the HDP in the focal year. Topics are generated by running the hierarchical Dirichlet process algorithm per year on the abstracts of the publications in the data set.
An extensive measure of diversification equal to a count of unique topics where the focal researcher has his or her papers assigned by the HDP in the focal year.

A yearly reversed Euclidean distance in the space of 51 IEEE categories in computer science, electrical engineering, and electronics, applied to yearly publication data over 2007-2014. IEEE assigns each publication to 1 of the 51 main categories listed in its taxonomy, and the distance is calculated based on the squared percentage of keywords from each category that a researcher collects in his or her publication portfolio. The authors note that the formal equation is not readable in the provided text; by construction the measure is less than or equal to 1 and never 0, and it increases with higher levels of keywords spread across IEEE categories.

variable_name: Yearly new HDP topics by distance
description: The distance between topics in consecutive years is calculated as one minus the similarity index between all such topic pairs. For each researcher, the distance between all pairs of topics in year t - 1 and t is summed and then divided by the number of unique topics covered in year t - 1. The measure captures the average number of new topics for researcher i in year t relative to year t - 1, weighted by the distance between the topics.

The number of new coauthors that the focal author has in the observation year relative to previous years. To count the number of new coauthors the authors use the full data set going back to 2001, because the count of new coauthors requires several years of reference data.
The number of new publication outlets in which a researcher publishes each year, relative to each prior year, going back to 2001.

A dummy variable equal to 1 if researcher i is a treated unit and 0 otherwise. Treated researchers are defined as individuals who were publishing in motion-sensing before the launch of Kinect or academics who started to publish in motion-sensing only after the launch of Kinect. Motion-sensing publications were identified by searching the full text and metadata of IEEE Xplore publications using carefully identified keywords.
time_window: treated status based on publishing before and after the launch of Kinect

description: A continuous measure of involvement in motion-sensing before Kinect, calculated as the sum of motion-sensing publications over the period before the launch of Kinect (2007-2010) divided by the total publication output of researcher i over the same period. It replaces the treated dummy in estimations of specialization within the group of within-area researchers.

The composition of a researcher's portfolio of project types is measured with two sets of variables built from the researcher's IEEE Xplore publications: diversification (breadth of topics at time t, from HDP topic counts and a Euclidean distance over 51 IEEE categories) and trajectory (distance in topic space between the portfolio at t-1 and t, from new HDP topics, new coauthors and new publication outlets). Each is used as a separate dependent variable.

Racial heterogeneity of each bank's management group, built from data provided by senior HR executives using the 'officials and managers' job category of the 1998 EEO-1 Standard Form 100. Computed with Blau's index of heterogeneity, 1 - sum of squared proportions, where the proportion is that of individuals in a racial category (white, black, Hispanic, Asian, and Native American) and i is the number of categories; index values theoretically range from 0 to .80 and ranged from 0 to .61 in the sample. The logarithm of the racial diversity measure was used to reduce kurtosis and skewness, and the quadratic term of the measure was used to test the curvilinear relationship.

Gender heterogeneity of each bank's management group, built from data provided by senior HR executives using the 'officials and managers' job category of the 1998 EEO-1 Standard Form 100. Computed with Blau's index of heterogeneity, a continuous measure whose observed values ranged from 0 to .50, reflecting the entire feasible range; values greater than .25 reflect relatively high levels of heterogeneity. The test for normality appeared sufficient, so no transformation was used, and the quadratic term of the measure was used to test the curvilinear relationship.
Productivity, an intermediate output measure and an important performance indicator in a bank, was calculated as the logarithm of net income per employee for year-end 1998.
Return on equity, the bottom-line measure of a bank's financial performance and overall viability, averaged for the years 1997 and 1998 to account for volatility.

Formed from the two items of Covin and Slevin's (1989) nine-item entrepreneurial orientation scale that loaded on an innovativeness factor; the items concerned the number of new or changed service and product lines a financial institution had introduced in the previous five years. The items comprising the factor were summed and divided by the number of items, giving scores ranging from 1 to 7, with higher scores indicating a stronger propensity to engage in firm-level innovative behaviors; the Cronbach alpha was .80.

Formed from the five items of Covin and Slevin's (1989) nine-item entrepreneurial orientation scale that loaded on a risk-taking factor, addressing risk propensity, environmental boldness (competitive aggressiveness), aggressiveness of decision making, competitive posture, and the degree to which a firm was first to market with new services, techniques, and/or technologies. The items were summed and divided by the number of items, giving scores ranging from 1 to 7, with higher scores indicating a stronger propensity to engage in firm-level risk-taking behaviors; the Cronbach alpha was .78.

Governance structure measured at the store level in terms of whether the store is franchised (coded 1) or company-owned (coded 0). The variable does not vary across time: at the beginning of the time series all stores in the sample had pre-established governance structures, and none of them changed over the period studied.

Strategic choice distinguishing the more complex mixed strategy (restaurant-based delivery, or RBD, coded 1) from the simple pure strategy (dine-in only or delivery only, coded 0). RBD combines elements of both traditional dine-in and delivery services in the same store and is the most complex of the three strategic choices available to stores in this setting. In the performance models the variable enters lagged at time t - 1.

Percent change in store sales from time t - 1 to t. Interviews indicated that store sales is regarded as the most important indicator of success in the industry and that profit is highly correlated with store sales, with profit data unavailable to the authors.

To construct this variable, the authors looked at how long each team member had been on the TMT and how many acquisitions had been made during that period. Subsequently, they added the acquisition experience of each team member and divided that by the team size. A natural logarithm was taken to take into account the decreasing marginal returns to which experiential learning is subject. In the models the variable is lagged by two years.

Acquisition success is defined by whether the acquisition was subsequently retained, i.e., successful (coded as '0'), or divested, i.e., unsuccessful (coded as '1'). For each acquisition an event is registered upon divestment; the dependent variable in the survival analysis is the instantaneous rate of subsidiary dissolution and a positive parameter estimate means the variable is positively related to acquisition divestment.

The frequency of acquisitions was measured by the number of acquisitions made by each company in each year. An acquisition is defined as the takeover of an existing company or of any of its business units.

TMT tenure is the number of years an individual has served on the top executive team. Tenure diversity was computed in the conventional way using the coefficient of variation. This information was gathered for each company for each year from annual reports.

Diversity in the type of education was computed in a conventional fashion using Blau's heterogeneity index, calculated as the reverse of the Herfindahl-Hirshman homogeneity index; the formula as printed in the article is not readable in the extracted text. The managers' dominant educational tracks were identified from their titles: 'Drs.' indicates a university graduate with degrees in economics or social sciences (including MBAs), 'Mr.' is the designation for a degree in law, and 'Ir.' indicates a university degree in engineering. The variable was computed for each company for each year from annual reports.

Firm strategic risk is produced by taking a factor analysis of three strategic risks: R&D spending, capital expenditures, and long-term debt. R&D spending is measured by total research and development expenses in millions of dollars, capital expenditures by the firm's capital spending in millions of dollars, and long-term debt as the total amount of long-term debt held by the firm in millions of dollars. The factor analysis revealed a single factor capturing 69% of the variance; all factor loadings exceeded 0.82 with an eigenvalue greater than 2.0. The variables are left unscaled and firm size is instead controlled in the model directly, and increases in the resulting variable are interpreted as increasing firm strategic risk.

Measured by the accumulated cash value of exercisable stock options as reported in the firm's proxy statement. This value is calculated by multiplying the number of options of each option grant against the corresponding spread for that grant as determined on the last day of the fiscal year. The spread is calculated as the difference between the exercise price of an option and the actual stock price at the close of business on that day. The variable is lagged one year.

Measured by the accumulated cash value of unexercisable stock options as reported in the firm's proxy statement. This value is calculated by multiplying the number of options of each option grant against the corresponding spread for that grant as determined on the last day of the fiscal year. The spread is calculated as the difference between the exercise price of an option and the actual stock price at the close of business on that day. The variable is lagged one year.

The value of restricted stock held by the CEO, included as one of the three equity-based variables in the model. The authors state that all compensation and stock measures were taken from the Execucomp database and that all compensation variables are lagged one year; the text does not describe a separate formula for the value of restricted stock.

Base salary and annual cash bonus awards are combined into a measure of total cash compensation that is then divided by total compensation. Total compensation is the sum of the CEO's annual salary, cash bonus, other annual compensation, value of restricted stock granted, value of stock options granted, long-term incentive payouts, and all other compensation not already included in the six categories of pay reported in each firm's annual proxy statement. Combining cash bonus awards with base salary overcomes the range restriction caused by punitive taxes on annual base salaries above a million dollars and is justified because annual cash bonus awards reward annual CEO performance and tend to covary with base salary. The variable is lagged one year.

A dummy-coded variable that is coded one if the board reloads or reprices a CEO's options during the year. Reloading is the replacement of expired or exercised options with new stock options and repricing is the lowering of the exercise price of underwater stock options. The variable is lagged one year.
The variance in firm stock price calculated over the prior 60-month period using daily closing prices. The variable is lagged one year.

A summated index of culture of competitiveness based on the three dimensions of learning, innovativeness, and entrepreneurial orientations, with each construct weighted at one-third. In the higher-order assessment, learning, innovativeness, and entrepreneurship function as first-order indicators of the higher-order construct of culture of competitiveness, and the items of those orientations are their reflective indicators. Residents answered seven-point Likert-type scales ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' in relation to the last order fulfillment process in their supply chain.

An index composed of knowledge acquisition, information distribution, shared meaning, and achieved memory weighted equally, based on both empirical and theoretical rationale. The four dimensions function as first-order indicators of the higher-order construct of knowledge development in the higher-order assessment, with each dimension made up of reflective items. All items were answered on seven-point Likert-type scales.

A summated index created from five items measuring the rate of change in the composition of customers and their preferences, adapted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993). Items cover customers' product preferences changing over time, customers looking for new products, demand from customers who never bought before, new customers having different product needs, and continuously catering to many new customers. Items were answered on seven-point Likert-type scales ranging from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'.

A perceptual scale of cycle time performance of the last order fulfillment process (Hult, Ketchen, and Nichols, 2002; Hult, Ketchen, and Slater, 2004); two of its original items were deleted during the measurement purification process. Retained items cover the length of the supply management process getting shorter every time, satisfaction with the speediness of the process, involving participants in decision making shortening the process, and the process being short and efficient based on respondents' knowledge. Items were answered on seven-point Likert-type scales.

Members' values associated with the generation of new insights, measured with items from Hult (1998) asking whether the ability to learn is the key to improvement in the supply management process, whether the basic values of the process include learning as a key to improvement, and whether employee learning is seen as an investment rather than an expense. One item was deleted after the measurement purification process. Items were answered on seven-point Likert-type scales.

Members' openness to new ideas, measured with items from Hurley and Hult (1998) covering whether technical innovation based on research results is readily accepted in supply management, whether innovative supply management ideas are actively sought, whether innovation is readily accepted in the supply management process, and whether innovation in the process is encouraged. One item was deleted after the measurement purification process. Items were answered on seven-point Likert-type scales.

Chain members' values associated with the pursuit of new market opportunities and renewal, measured with items from Naman and Slevin (1993) covering initiating actions to which other organizations respond, being fast to introduce new administrative techniques and operating technologies, having a strong proclivity for high-risk projects, and being bold in efforts to maximize the probability of exploiting opportunities. One item was deleted after the measurement purification process. Items were answered on seven-point Likert-type scales.

The process by which the supply chain obtains wisdom, measured with items from Kohli, Jaworski, and Kumar (1993) covering meeting regularly to find out what products will be needed in the future, doing in-house research on products that may be needed, being fast to detect changes in product preferences, and being fast to detect fundamental shifts in the supply management environment. Two items were deleted after the measurement purification process. Items were answered on seven-point Likert-type scales.

The sharing of information from different sources throughout the chain, measured with items from Kohli, Jaworski, and Kumar (1993) covering spending time discussing future supply management needs, immediately knowing when something important happens in the supply management process, and alerting participants when something important happens. Two items were deleted after the measurement purification process. Items were answered on seven-point Likert-type scales.

Members' common understandings about data and events, measured with items from Hult, Ketchen, and Slater (2004) covering sharing supply management information effectively between supply management participants, sharing it effectively in the supply management process, developing a shared understanding of the available supply management information, and developing a shared understanding of the implications of a supply management activity. All four items were retained. Items were answered on seven-point Likert-type scales.

The amount of knowledge, experience, and familiarity with the supply chain process, measured with items from Moorman and Miner (1997) covering having a great deal of knowledge about, experience with, and familiarity with the supply management process. One item was deleted after the measurement purification process. Items were answered on seven-point Likert-type scales.

Frequency of street protest events, measured as the total counts of environmental protection and human rights protests in a city at time t - 1. The authors summed, across the five media sources, the verified protests over noneconomic issues that occurred in a focal city, counting only new events that had never occurred before the focal year, and verified events by triangulating with sina.com and the WiseSearch database. After eliminating unsubstantiated reports and duplicates, the final data set comprises 2,202 street protests for the period from 2008 to 2019.

Count of newly founded ventures within a city at time t. TianYanCha.com provides a variable indicating whether a newly founded venture is registered as a small and micro domestic firm; using this variable, the authors aggregated the count of newly founded ventures within a city as the proxy for the founding of new ventures at time t.

Difference in city-level loans of balance from financial institutions at year end between time t and time t - 1, according to the CCSY. The more substantial the change in business loan policies, the greater the increase in business loans. To facilitate the interpretation of coefficients, the authors divided business loan increase by 1,000,000 in the regression models.

Newly announced policies at time t in a given city, taken from the CnOpenData database that spans city policies and regulations newly announced during 2008 to 2019. The first author and a well-trained research assistant independently scrutinized and coded the content of these newly announced policies to identify relevant instances, with any disparities reconciled through discussion and a high interrater reliability of 99%.

Categorical variable at time t - 1 based on a city mayor's highest obtained education level (0 = high school or below, 1 = bachelor's, 2 = master's, 3 = PhD). The authors operationalize a city mayor's political position prospects with this variable, arguing that when street protests arise, highly educated mayors are more likely to respond by enacting economic policies.

variable_name: business loan increase and regulatory reforms
description: Middle-ground approaches are measured by two city-level policy variables used as mediators: the yearly increase in business loans (change in year-end loan balance of financial institutions) and the count of newly announced regulatory reform policies in the city.

Dummy variables were created assigning each unit a 1 or 0 value for membership in each of the three groups. These dummy variables were used as predictors in testing Hypotheses 1 through 3; in the probit analyses the dummy variable for hybrid units was excluded, so coefficients for drug abuse and mental health units are comparisons to hybrid units.

Based on clinical supervisors' indication of how much they relied on professional degrees or credentials as a criterion in hiring staff members. Respondents used a five-point Likert scale ranging from not at all (1) to a great deal (5). Used as a dependent variable in testing Hypotheses 1-4 and as a predictor variable in testing Hypotheses 5-8.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = a great deal)

description: Based on clinical supervisors' indication of how much they relied on a personal history of substance abuse problems as a criterion in hiring staff members. Respondents used a five-point Likert scale ranging from not at all (1) to a great deal (5). Used as a dependent variable in testing Hypotheses 1-4 and as a predictor variable in testing Hypotheses 5-8.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = a great deal)

description: The telephone survey asked clinical supervisors how important in treatment plans for clients is sobriety or complete abstinence from drug use, with response options 1 = not important to 4 = very important. Used as a dependent variable in testing Hypotheses 1-4 and as a predictor variable in testing Hypotheses 5-8.

The survey asked clinical service supervisors whether they used DSM-III routinely (1) or only sometimes (2). This dichotomous dummy variable was labeled use of DSMIII. Used as a dependent variable in testing Hypotheses 1-4 and as a predictor variable in testing Hypotheses 5-8.

The percentage of clients served by a unit in the last 12 months whose primary problem was labeled as drug abuse. Used as a control variable in testing Hypotheses 1-4 and as a predictor variable in testing Hypotheses 5-8; the greater the percentage of drug abuse clients a hybrid serves, the less isomorphic it is with mental health treatment organizations.

Data from the unit directors established hybrids' unit age. Old units may receive more external support than young units because relationships with sources of support become institutionalized over time. Used as a predictor variable in testing Hypothesis 4 and as a control variable in testing Hypotheses 5-8.

Measured as the total number of full-time employee equivalents in 1984, with data from the clinical service supervisor interview. Used as a predictor variable in testing Hypothesis 4 and as a control variable in testing Hypotheses 5-8.

Assessed with 10 yes or no questions about whether the unit receives funds for operating expenses and for payroll from its parent organization, support from clerical, administrative, clinical, maintenance or custodial, or any other staff, and supplies, equipment, and office space. Affirmative responses were scored 1 and negative responses 0; the affirmative responses were then summed.

The extent of a parent's social-psychological support for a hybrid and its staff members was measured by asking to what extent the organization and its staff are accepted by the community mental health center, with responses from 1, not at all accepted, to 3, completely accepted.
scale: 1-3 (1 = not at all accepted, 3 = completely accepted)

description: Unit directors indicated how many of three primary licenses their units held: a license from a state mental health department, from a county or regional mental health department, and from the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Health Care Organizations. Each license or accreditation emphasizes different mental health sector practices, so the extent of a hybrid's licenses or accreditations legitimizes it in the mental health sector.

variable_name: number of mental health financial sources
description: Unit directors indicated whether they had received money in fiscal year 1984 from each of three central sources in the mental health sector: federal agencies (e.g., the National Institute of Mental Health), state mental health departments, and private insurance firms (e.g., Blue Cross).

Unit directors were asked what percent of their units' total operating budgets for fiscal year 1984 came from each central mental health source; these percentages were then used to compute the amounts received. Data were missing for 13 cases on this variable, resulting in a regression analysis with 77 rather than 90 cases.

variable_name: Isomorphism indicators (percentage of drug abuse clients, use of DSM-III, sobriety goal, reliance on professionals, reliance on ex-addicts)
description: Isomorphism of a hybrid unit with the mental health sector is captured by a set of unit-level practices from the 1984 telephone surveys, entered as separate predictors in the regressions for H5 to H8: the percentage of clients whose primary problem was drug abuse (more means less isomorphic), routine use of DSM-III, the importance of sobriety or complete abstinence as a treatment goal (more emphasis means less isomorphic), reliance on professional credentials in hiring, and reliance on ex-addicts in hiring (more means less isomorphic). No single index is formed.
scale: Set of survey items: percentage, dichotomous dummy, 4-point and 5-point Likert items

description: Public offerings completed subsequent to firms' initial public offerings. They were identified by searching the BIOSCAN directory, the Actions database and Standard & Poor's NetAdvantage, and announcement dates and other equity-financing events were recovered through news searches by company name and the words 'equity', 'placement', 'offering' and 'financing' preceded by 'public' or 'private'. Of the public offerings identified, abnormal returns could be calculated for fewer due to stock delistings and insufficient stock returns.

Prediction errors for each firm and day around the announcement are computed from a two-factor model estimated by ordinary least squares over an estimation period of 221 days (250 days prior to 30 days prior to the event); the factors are a value-weighted market portfolio (the NASDAQ Composite Index) and a value-weighted biotechnology index. An average prediction error is calculated for each day, and cumulative abnormal returns aggregate these over windows from period t1 to t2. The specification of the prediction-error and aggregation formulas is not readable in the extracted text. t-statistics are used to determine whether the average daily prediction errors and CARs are significantly different from zero.
time_window: estimation period 250 to 30 days prior to the event; event windows including (-10, 10), (-3, 3), (-2, 1), (-1, 1) and (-1, 0)

description: Indicator variable equal to 1 if firm j initiated a private placement prior to the event and subsequent to the firm's IPO, and 0 otherwise. It is a time-varying variable measured prior to each event, and is used to test whether the existence of a prior private placement affects the rate at which the issuing firm can attract resources.
The cumulative count of all firm j's prior private equity placements. It is a time-varying variable measured prior to each event.
The elapsed time since firm j's last private equity placement, measured in days/365.25. It is a time-varying variable measured prior to each event.

The cumulative abnormal return over the (-2, 1) window for firm j's most recently observed private placement; this 4-day window was chosen because, on average, most of the information is conveyed during this period. If abnormal returns on the firm's most recent private placement could not be observed, a dummy variable, the missing CAR dummy, was coded 1 and 0 otherwise.
time_window: (-2, 1) window around the firm's most recent private placement

variable_name: rate of financing through private equity placements or (seasoned) public offerings
description: The first dependent variable is the rate at which firm j initiates a financing event between two discrete time points, summarizing the intervals of time between successive financing events, with higher values corresponding to shorter times between events. From the date of IPO onward the firms were 'at risk' of attracting resources. The rate is specified as an exponential function of the independent variables and estimated by maximum likelihood; the final sample contains 981 capital-raising events for 259 publicly traded firms.
time_window: from IPO onward, measured continuously between events

description: The second dependent variable is the rate at which firm j initiates a research alliance event between two discrete time points, summarizing the intervals of time between successive research alliance events, with higher values corresponding to shorter times between events. Events were identified primarily from the BIOSCAN directory and the Actions database, and the final sample contains 1476 research partnerships for 259 publicly traded firms.
time_window: from IPO onward, measured continuously between events

description: The third dependent variable is the rate at which firm j initiates a commercial alliance event between two discrete time points, summarizing the intervals of time between successive commercial alliance events, with higher values corresponding to shorter times between events. Events were identified primarily from the BIOSCAN directory and the Actions database, and the final sample contains 1969 commercial partnerships for 259 publicly traded firms.
time_window: from IPO onward, measured continuously between events

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if the paper that reports a simultaneous discovery is a collaborative work between academia and industry, and 0 otherwise. Each simultaneous discovery is disclosed by two or three papers, one of which involves industry collaborators. The variable is the main predictor in all models.

Number of papers by the main (corresponding) scientists of a simultaneous discovery that cite the original paper that reports the discovery, counted after its publication. Only papers listing the scientist as an author are counted.

Citation-weighted number of papers by the main scientists of a simultaneous discovery citing the original paper that reports the discovery. The number of citations that an academic publication received is used as a proxy for its quality, so this is the quality-adjusted version of the follow-on publication count.

Number of patents by the main scientists of a simultaneous discovery that cite the original paper reporting the discovery. The patent set is the intersection of patents that cite either of the twin papers and all U.S. patents awarded to each corresponding author, identified by searching the USPTO website and assessing each patent separately for inventor identity. Follow-on patents are not necessarily patents granted on the original discovery but generally patents filed on subsequent commercial developments informed by the discovery.

Citation-weighted number of patents by the main scientists of a simultaneous discovery citing the original paper that reports the discovery. The number of citations received by the patent is used to adjust the count for quality.

The total number of patents that cite any of the twin papers reporting a simultaneous discovery, used as a proxy for the commercial potential of that discovery. Discoveries above the median are categorized as having high commercial potential. The variable is entered only in interaction form because its direct effect is captured by the discovery fixed effects.

Variable identifying whether the industry partner on the discovery was an established company, based on the age of the company partner at the time of each discovery. Companies with more than 10 years of experience at the time of collaboration are categorized as established; startup firms are those 10 years old or younger. Only the interaction form is included because the direct effect is captured by the discovery fixed effect.

A dummy variable equal to 1 if the paper that reports a simultaneous discovery is a collaborative work between academia and industry, and 0 otherwise. Here it is used as the dependent variable in logit and OLS estimations of the likelihood of collaborating with industry based on the main author's past performance, with twin fixed effects ensuring comparison is between scientists reporting the same discovery, and a limited set of controls.

Cumulative difference between a company's observed return and its expected return during a specific period surrounding the announcement. The estimation window is 250 trading days (one year), measured from 295 to 45 days before each event, and the market portfolio is represented by the NASDAQ Composite Index. Returns are reported for the five-day window around the announcement, CAR(-2, +2).
time_window: 250-day estimation window (from 295 to 45 days before each event); event window CAR(-2, +2)

description: Dummy based on the divesture flag in the SDC Platinum database, which allows distinctions to be drawn between acquisitions of divested assets and stand-alone firms. Acquisitions of divested assets were assigned a value of 1 and acquisitions of stand-alone firms a value of 0; 1,023 out of a total of 5,079 transactions were classified as acquisitions of divested assets.

Separate scores for acquirer-to-target and seller-to-target relatedness were calculated by assigning 6, 4, or 2 points based on the 4-, 3-, and 2-digit primary SIC codes; for secondary SIC codes the points allocated were scaled down to half, and the final similarity score was the maximum value of the point allocation. Seller-to-target relatedness scores were then subtracted from the acquirer-to-target relatedness scores, resulting in a final score ranging between -6 and 6, with a positive score denoting an increase in asset relatedness.
Measured by a firm's debt-to-total assets ratio. To deal with the skewness of the measure, quartiles were used to distinguish the sellers most affected by their leverage.
scale: debt-to-total assets ratio, grouped into quartiles

description: The number of times the inventor's patents are classified as XY-type references in the search reports of the patent applications citing them, computed over the inventor's portfolio of patents filed with the participating firm up to the alliance announcement year and used in logarithmic form. XY-type references are conflicting prior art: an X reference indicates that the invention might not be considered novel on its own, and a Y reference that it might not involve an inventive step when combined with other Y-type documents. The more often a patent is an XY-type reference, the broader it is likely to be, which confers stronger protection to the patented knowledge.
time_window: up to the alliance announcement year

description: The share of XY-type citations relative to the total number of classified citations received by the inventor's portfolio of patents filed with the participating firm up to the alliance announcement year.
time_window: up to the alliance announcement year

description: Indicator of whether an inventor is allocated to a collaboration in which her firm participates, coded one for the actual inventor identified as participating in the alliance and zero for the counterfactual inventors. Participation is identified from the partners' patent application portfolios in the 5 years after the alliance announcement, through applications filed by the joint venture, applications co-assigned between the two partner firms, or post-alliance single-assigned applications listing inventors from both firms. Counterfactual inventors are those employed by the same firm who filed their last application prior to the alliance in the same year and patented in the same combination of IPC four-digit technology classes in the last 5 years, and up to five of them are randomly drawn per actual inventor-alliance pair.
A dummy variable capturing whether the allied firms are direct product-market competitors; firms are considered competitors if they share the same four-digit SIC code.

Overlap in the partners' technology portfolios based on the distribution of the firms' patent applications across IPC four-digit technology classes during the 5 years prior to alliance formation. A multidimensional vector records the number of patent applications assigned to each partner in each technology class, and the overlap between the two partners takes values from zero to one, a higher value indicating a higher degree of overlap. Based on its median value a categorical variable captures low or high technology overlap between the partners.
scale: index from 0 to 1; categorical (low/high based on the median)

description: A dummy variable capturing the vertical scope of an alliance: it distinguishes whether an alliance involves R&D activities exclusively (narrow scope) or includes manufacturing and/or marketing in addition to collaborative R&D (broad scope).

The acquisition's ordinal position within its industry acquisition wave divided by the number of acquisitions that occurred in the overall wave. The variable was centered, and its square was used to test for a curvilinear relationship. Wave position was not standardized, unlike the other variables.
scale: ratio of ordinal position to total number of acquisitions in the wave

description: Abnormal returns are the difference between the observed return for a security and its predicted normal return; alpha and beta are estimated over a 250-day estimation period measured from 295 days before each event to 45 days before it. Abnormal returns were cumulated from 5 trading days before to 15 trading days after the announcement of an acquisition event. The mathematical specification of the return-generating model is not readable in the provided text (the formula block was removed), though the text describes it as an economic model of anticipated, or normal, returns with a constant, a market return term, and a beta.
time_window: event window day -5 to day +15; estimation period from day -295 to day -45

description: Industry sales were regressed on a year-counter variable using five-year windows, with the year of the current acquisition observation as the last year in the panel. Munificence is the regression coefficient from that regression divided by the mean value of industry sales. The variable was standardized with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
time_window: five-year windows ending in the year of the focal acquisition

description: From a regression of industry sales on a year-counter variable using five-year windows, the standard error of the regression coefficient for each industry was divided by the mean value of industry sales. This value was subtracted from 1 so that a high score indicates stability. The variable was standardized with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
time_window: five-year windows ending in the year of the focal acquisition

description: The number of acquisitions a firm participated in throughout an acquisition wave divided by the total number of acquisitions within that wave, giving the frequency of a firm's acquisitions scaled by the overall number of acquisitions in the industry. The variable was standardized with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

The form of consideration offered, measured as the percentage of the acquisition price paid in the acquirer's common stock. The variable was standardized with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

Dichotomous variable with 1 signifying that a firm switched from a combined leadership structure in the previous year to a separate leadership structure in the present year, and 0 signifying no such change. Firms that maintained a separate board leadership structure throughout the period of analysis were excluded, so that only firms that could possibly have separated are compared.
time_window: year of separation relative to the previous year

description: Dichotomous variable taking a value of 1 if the sitting CEO-board chair in the previous year remained board chair in the year of separation, and 0 otherwise. It is one of the three types into which separations were divided.
time_window: year of separation relative to the previous year

description: Dichotomous variable taking a value of 1 if the sitting CEO in the previous year was neither CEO nor board chair in the year of separation, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: year of separation relative to the previous year

description: Dichotomous variable taking a value of 1 if the sitting CEO in the previous year remained CEO in the year of separation, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: year of separation relative to the previous year

description: Holding period return on a company's stock from beginning to end of a calendar year, measured at the time of the separation and entered as firm performance in the separation by firm performance interaction. In the stock return models all performance metrics are stock returns.

Holding period return on a company's stock from beginning to end of a calendar year, measured for the year following the separation and used as the dependent variable of the fixed-effects models. Separations that were followed by a recombination in the next year were excluded so that each separation influenced at least a full year of firm performance.

Mean composite analyst rating of the company's stock in a given year, obtained from IBES. Analyst ratings can take one of five categorical values; the data were coded from 1, 'strong buy,' to 5, 'strong sell,' and the variable was reverse-coded to make the results more intuitive. Due to concerns over multicollinearity the analyst ratings were standardized in the models.
scale: five categorical values from 'strong buy' to 'strong sell'

description: Mean composite analyst rating of the company's stock measured for the year following the separation, used as a dependent variable. Ratings were coded from 1, 'strong buy,' to 5, 'strong sell,' reverse-coded, and standardized in the models because of multicollinearity concerns.
scale: five categorical values from 'strong buy' to 'strong sell'

description: Dichotomous variable with 1 signifying that a firm switched from a separate leadership structure in the previous year to a combined leadership structure in the present year, and 0 signifying no such change. The sample consists of firms with separate leadership structures, the only firms that could potentially combine their leadership positions.
time_window: year following a separate structure year

description: Dichotomous variable taking a value of 1 if the sitting CEO-board chair in the previous year remained board chair in the year of separation, and 0 otherwise; used in the logistic models of recombination.
time_window: year of separation relative to the previous year

description: Dichotomous variable taking a value of 1 if the sitting CEO in the previous year was neither CEO nor board chair in the year of separation, and 0 otherwise; used in the logistic models of recombination.
time_window: year of separation relative to the previous year

description: Dichotomous variable taking a value of 1 if the sitting CEO in the previous year remained CEO in the year of separation, and 0 otherwise; used in the logistic models of recombination.
time_window: year of separation relative to the previous year

description: Holding period return on the company's stock over a calendar year, measured in each focal year of the recombination analysis and used as postseparation firm performance. It is interacted with departure separation to predict the likelihood of recombination, and the analysis was also conducted at above-mean and below-mean levels of firm performance.

Mean composite analyst rating of the company's stock in a given year, measured in each focal year of the recombination analysis and used as postseparation firm performance, interacted with departure separation to predict recombination. Effects were also examined at above-mean and below-mean levels of analyst ratings.
scale: five categorical values from 'strong buy' to 'strong sell'

description: Index measure based on political donations by organizational members, coded as an average of the two most recent election cycles. Four items were coded from employee donations: the dollar amount donated to the Democratic Party divided by the total amount donated to both parties; the count of donations to the Democratic Party divided by the count of donations to both parties; the count of unique employee donors to the Democratic Party divided by the count of donors to both parties; and the count of unique Democratic donation recipients divided by the count of all recipients. The items had similar means and dispersions, so they were averaged to create a composite index of organizational liberalism, with lower values representing conservatism. Donations from CEOs were excluded and used to construct the CEO ideology control.

Computed using the average Euclidean distance in miles between the headquarters and each employee donor. Donor zip codes from the donations database were matched with census data to assign geographic coordinates to each employee donor and headquarters, and Vincenty's formula was applied to calculate geodesic distances between each donor's zip code and the headquarters' zip code. For each firm-year observation the average of distances between headquarters and each unique employee who donated in the two most recent election cycles was computed, and the measure was inverted so that higher values reflect employees' spatial proximity and lower values represent greater distance.

Coded using political contributions made by members of the communities (at the level of U.S. postal zip codes) where the firm had one or more employee donors in the FEC database during the two most recent election cycles. A community liberalism measure was coded for each zip code using the partisan leanings of all donors reported in the FEC database except the firm's own employees, following the same approach as the measure of organizational liberalism. Zip-code-level community liberalism was aggregated for each firm-year observation as a weighted average, using the proportion of the company's employee donors located in a given zip code in the two most recent election cycles as weights.

Operationalized as the average organizational liberalism of all the peer firms in a focal firm's industry. To avoid mechanical overlap among independent variables, the ideology of the focal firm was excluded in computing its industry's ideology.

Coded by searching all media articles in the ProQuest and LexisNexis databases that mention the corporation targeted by the protesters during the six months following the protest event. Trained graduate students looked through the articles to ascertain the corporate response; if an article clearly mentioning corporate agreement to activists' demands was found, the event was coded as a concession. The coding premise is that only announcements made in the same public domain should be deemed as concessions.
time_window: six months following the protest event

description: The dependent variables are the yearly number of DCC foundings at four levels of disaggregation: Metropolitan Toronto (total population), Metropolitan Toronto by organizational niche (10 niches), Metropolitan Toronto by constituent city (six local populations), and Metropolitan Toronto by constituent city by organizational niche (60 local organizational niches). The date of founding was defined as the year in which the original operating license was issued by the Ministry and/or the year of first appearance in the Directory. Because the dependent variables are count measures (real integers truncated at zero), the expected number of foundings within an interval of time is estimated.
level: organizational niche-year, city-year and local organizational niche-year

description: The overlap density of an organizational niche is equal to population density weighted by the overlaps of the focal organizational niche with all other organizational niches. Values were computed by summing the yearly organizational niche densities (the number of organizations in a specific organizational niche) multiplied by the appropriate organizational niche overlap weights. Overlap density differs by organizational niche and is time variant. The equation specifying the measure is not readable in the text provided.
level: organizational niche-year; also computed in local and diffuse form for each constituent city

description: Nonoverlap density is equal to population density weighted by the absence of overlaps of a focal organizational niche with all other organizational niches. Values for nonoverlap density are equal to the differences between population density and the overlap densities of each organizational niche. It gives information about the effective number of organizations whose resource requirements do not overlap with those in the focal organizational niche.
level: organizational niche-year; also computed in local and diffuse form for each constituent city

description: The number of DCCs that occupy the same organizational niche as the focal organizational niche. It is one of the two components into which overlap density is disaggregated.

The aggregate of the organizational niche overlaps with DCCs that occupy different organizational niches from the focal one. It is the second of the two components into which overlap density is disaggregated.
The number of DCCs occupying organizational niches that do not overlap with the focal organizational niche. It is one of the two components into which nonoverlap density is disaggregated.

The aggregate of the organizational niche nonoverlaps with DCCs that occupy different, but partially overlapped, organizational niches. It is the second of the two components into which nonoverlap density is disaggregated.

The organizational niches of DCCs are operationalized using a critical resource dimension, the age ranges of children DCCs are licensed to enroll. DCCs are licensed to provide full-time (more than six consecutive hours) collective care to five or more children in one or more of the age ranges Infant (birth to 18 months), Toddler (19 to 30 months), Preschool (31 to 60 months) and Schoolage (61 to 120 months); the license specifies which ranges may be served. Using this approach the authors identified ten different fundamental organizational niches occupied by DCCs. Organizational niches are characterized in fundamental rather than realized terms, i.e., in terms of the resources DCCs have the capacity to procure rather than the children actually enrolled.

The author represents each film as a vector of the tropes identified within it and determines the similarity between two films by taking the cosine similarity between their vector representations. For a given film released in year y, genre-based typicality is calculated as the cosine similarity of tropes between the film and all other films sharing at least one genre label with it that were released in y and y-1. This is summarized into a single measure by averaging across all relevant pairwise similarity scores.
time_window: two-year period (release year and preceding year)

description: Trope frequencies are determined at the genre/time-period level, and tropes occurring less than the mean frequency for a specific genre/time-period are treated as differentiating features for films released during that genre/time period. For every film, the conspicuousness of its differentiating features is computed for each nonlabel genre by averaging the typicality of those tropes to that genre. The film's conspicuous differentiation score is the maximum value among the nonlabel genre scores.
A score from 1 to 10 (including decimal values) that is the average rating across all IMDb raters at a given date.

The differentiation-evoked genre is the nonlabel genre whose typicality score achieved the maximum (argmax). Evoked-genre density is then computed as the proportion of films in the sample belonging to the differentiation-evoked genre, within the time period that the focal film was released.

Incentive payments as a percentage of the total compensation package, measured as the average ratio of incentive payments over total compensation for each firm or business unit. Salary and fringe benefits percentages were computed in the same way. The pay policies refer to the pay of scientists and engineers in research and development units.

Base salary as a percentage of the total compensation package, measured as the average ratio of salary over total compensation for each firm or business unit. The pay policies refer to the pay of scientists and engineers in research and development units.

Fringe benefits as a percentage of the total compensation package, measured as the average ratio of fringe benefits over total compensation for each firm or business unit. The pay policies refer to the pay of scientists and engineers in research and development units.

A company or business unit's stage was coded into a dummy variable according to the category designated by respondents: the mature stage (products or services familiar to the vast majority of prospective users; technology and competitive structure reasonably stable) or the growth stage (sales growing at 20 percent or more annually in real terms; technology and competitive structure still changing).
Company or business unit size, measured as annual sales revenues. For diversified companies with multiple business units the measure refers to the participating business unit.

A 0/1 dummy variable that defines a company or business unit as high tech if its annual research and development budget is 5 percent or more of its sales revenues, following the Massachusetts High Technology Council definition. The resulting sample consists of 33 high tech and 72 traditional (non-high tech) firms or business units.

A factor score derived from 23 items on which managers responsible for compensation policies rated how satisfied they are with the way current pay practices in their company contribute to the attainment of organizational objectives, using the 1-5 Likert response format of the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire ranging from extremely dissatisfied to extremely satisfied. The factor is a global measure of the extent to which current compensation practices contribute to organizational goals; factor scores were computed by multiplying the salient factor loadings by the standardized item responses and summing the weighted responses. Coefficient alpha is 0.95.

A specific factor score measuring the extent to which current compensation practices contribute to the attraction of a sufficient number of top-quality employees. It is built from the same 23 pay-dimension items rated on the 1-5 Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire response format, with factor scores computed by weighting the standardized item responses by the salient factor loadings and summing them. Coefficient alpha is 0.76.

A factor score measuring the extent to which pay practices reward and induce higher productivity. It is built from the same 23 pay-dimension items rated on the 1-5 Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire response format, with factor scores computed by weighting the standardized item responses by the salient factor loadings and summing them. Coefficient alpha is 0.83.

Actual attrition data, used as a fourth effectiveness measure because retention is an important criterion of success of a compensation system, particularly for high tech firms. The information came directly from company records, and because attrition may have a curvilinear relationship with performance a logarithmic transformation of this measure was used as a dependent variable.

It is easy to measure law changes (as a dummy). Years in which a change in the size of the audit market would be expected because of the 1970 and 1983 changes in legislation are classified as regulatory years, and four variant groupings (A-D) of regulatory and nonregulatory years were distinguished because it is difficult to predict precisely which years will be affected by the regulations.

The number of annual accounts disclosed by public companies, private companies and cooperative societies, taken as a first estimate of the change in demand for audit services; from 1973 the Chamber of Commerce reported the number of firms that meet the disclosure requirement. Estimates for 1971-80 and 1981-90 are reported in Figures 4a and 4b, and the annual accounts for fiscal year 1970 are disclosed in 1971.

variable_name: number of professional employees in public practice
description: The second proxy of the demand for audit services is the number of professional employees in public practice, NIvRA students plus RA licensees, on the expectation that changes in the number of chargeable hours traded in the audit market would be reflected in that number; the number of NIvRA students working in public practice is proxied by the number of part-time NIvRA students. Annual changes in this number (aggregated and per category) were compared for regulatory and nonregulatory years.
scale: count and annual change in counts

description: The C4 ratio of the Dutch audit market; the C4 ratio and the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of the Dutch audit market have very similar patterns. Audit firm size is measured by the number of RAs, which correlates above 0.97 with both total fee income and audit fee income; the calculation of the C4 ratio is standard and the data make it possible to measure firm size for all audit firms.

variable_name: ratio of RA employees plus independent RAs to RA partners
description: The figures are expressed as the ratio (average annual change in the number of RA employees)/(average annual change in the number of RA partners), computed separately for the nonregulatory (1946-70) and regulatory (1971-89) periods; Panel B of Table 3 additionally reports the annual changes for cooperating and independent partners. The number of RAs in audit practice in any year is derived from the membership lists, which cover the whole practising RA population.

Reliable figures on RA income are only available for RA partners in the years 1961, 1966 and 1972; from these the authors construct income change figures for the 1961-66 and 1966-72 periods, where the first period does not and the second period does include a demand-enhancing change in regulation. Panel B of Table 4 reports the income growth of other occupations as a benchmark.

The rankings of the top firms for 14 years in the 1964-90 period are used to provide evidence on whether the audit market has a stable two-tier group structure. In the 1967-90 period a small and relatively constant group of five firms were able to dominate the market and the Big Five succeeded in increasing their joint market share; although the Big Five firms regularly change position, newcomers rarely intrude, and the four major mutations can be explained by mergers.

Respondents described their environmental practices using six items; positive responses indicated that a company (1) had an environmental plan, (2) had a written plan, (3) had communicated this plan to employees, (4) had communicated this plan to shareholders and/or stakeholders, (5) had an EHS unit, and (6) had a board or management environment committee. The six items were subjected to a cluster analysis using the SPSS/PC+ Quick Cluster routine, which assigns a company to its nearest cluster using a squared Euclidean distance measure. Four cluster profiles are defined and described using the terms defined in Table 1: reactive, defensive, accommodative, and proactive. Positive cluster means suggest practices that a profile has, and negative cluster means suggest the reverse.

A factor score capturing respondents' general perceptions of regulatory stakeholders, derived from a common factor analysis with varimax rotation of the 15 retained stakeholder influence items; the four factors together accounted for 66.1 percent of the total variance. Included in this factor are government information and pressures, information from trade associations, information from informal networks, and competitor information.

A factor score gauging respondents' perceptions of community stakeholders, derived from the common factor analysis with varimax rotation of the retained stakeholder influence items. Included in this factor are pressures and information from environmental organizations, community pressure, and other lobby group pressures.

A factor score tapping respondents' perceptions of organizational stakeholders, derived from the common factor analysis with varimax rotation of the retained stakeholder influence items. These include customer, supplier, shareholder, and employee pressures; these stakeholders can directly impact a firm's bottom line if they choose to exert their influence.

A factor score representing respondents' perceptions about media information regarding environmental issues, derived from the common factor analysis with varimax rotation of the retained stakeholder influence items. It comprises information from newspapers and information from television and radio; although these two had a high correlation, both were retained because they reflect different broadcasting mediums.

The number of exploratory patents filed by firm i in year t, that is, patents situated in a technology domain in which the firm has not patented before. A patent is considered exploratory when it contains at least one four-digit IPC class under which a firm has not filed for a patent previously; the EPO classifies all patents into at least one of 628 IPC four-digit classes. The count outcome is modeled with firm and year fixed effects.

The share of newly hired foreign R&D workers in a firm's R&D workforce. Foreign workers are those who immigrated to Denmark when they were at least 21 years old, and R&D workers count as new hires only in their first year of employment at the firm. The stock of a firm's R&D workers is split into native R&D hires, foreign R&D hires, and R&D incumbents.

The share of newly hired native R&D workers in a firm's R&D workforce. R&D workers are separated by mobility status, with R&D workers considered new hires only in their first year of employment at the firm.

The firm's R&D workers after their first year of employment, i.e., those who are neither newly hired foreign nor newly hired native R&D workers. In the estimation the effect of incumbent R&D workers is set as the reference category and normalized to the value of one, so that the estimated coefficients of the other worker types express their contribution relative to incumbents.

The natural logarithm of one plus the total number of EPO patents applied for by firm i over the five years prior to year t that were developed with the involvement of coinventors residing in distinct foreign countries. Countries and regions of all patent applicants and inventors are merged in from their addresses.
