time_window: five years prior to year t

description: The natural logarithm of the median tenure of all incumbent R&D workers, both Danish and non-Danish, employed at firm i in year t. The log-transformation is applied because the untransformed value of the variable is strongly skewed to the right.

For each year t, the number of newly hired foreign R&D workers present in firm i whose home countries are specialized in the respective technology class j. A country is considered specialized in a technology class j in year t if its revealed technology advantage (RTA) value is larger than one.

A dummy variable taking the value of one if firm i explores technology class j in year t and zero otherwise. Exploration at the firm-technology level is obtained by counting the number of patents firm i applied for in technology class j in year t and dichotomizing this variable, and all technology-year pairs after a firm applied for a patent in the respective class for the first time are excluded.

For each year t, the number of newly hired foreign R&D workers present in firm i originating from country c. The number of incumbent foreign R&D workers present in firm i in year t originating from country c is controlled for.

A dummy variable taking the value of one if firm i has filed a patent in year t that cites country c and zero otherwise; equivalently, the variable is built by counting for each year the number of patents filed by firm i with at least one backward citation to country c. The total number of patents filed by firm i in year t that cite country c is used as the count alternative.

variable_name: cumulative abnormal returns over the three-day event window (-1, +1)
description: Daily returns for each company were collected over a 255-day window ending on day -50 (i.e., 50 days prior to the actual filing date of CEO certification) from the CRSP tapes. Normal or expected returns around the filing date were calculated using the rate of return on the CRSP equally weighted market index; abnormal returns represent returns earned after the market has adjusted for the 'normal' return process and were cumulated over the number of days in the event window. The dependent variable is the cumulative abnormal return over a three-day window (-1, +1), with the actual filing date of CEO certification as day 0.
time_window: 255-day estimation window ending on day -50; three-day event window (-1, +1) around the filing date; prior year for controls

description: Measured by the proportion of a firm's outstanding shares owned by the CEO. Data were collected from company proxy statements at the end of the prior year (i.e., year 2001).

The number of external boards of directors (other than the focal firm's board) on which the CEO is serving. Data were collected from company proxy statements at the end of the prior year (i.e., year 2001).
Measured as the number of years a CEO had been in office. Data were collected from company proxy statements at the end of the prior year (i.e., year 2001).

variable_name: CEO associated with the firm's prior restatement
description: Coded as '1' if a company filed at least one financial restatement from 1 January 1999 to mid-2002 (10 days prior to filing CEO certifications) and the restatement announcement was within the CEO's tenure (so the CEO is viewed as being 'associated' with the restatement). Firms that had no financial restatements, as well as firms with restatements that preceded the CEO's tenure, were coded as '0'. Restatements were identified from the Financial Statement Restatement Database and restatement announcement dates from LexisNexis.
scale: dummy (1 = associated with the prior restatement, 0 = otherwise)
time_window: 1 January 1999 to mid-2002 (10 days prior to filing CEO certifications)

variable_name: CEO not associated with the firm's prior restatement
description: Coded as '1' if a company filed at least one financial restatement from 1 January 1999 to mid-2002 (10 days prior to filing CEO certifications) and the CEO was appointed after the restatement (so the CEO is viewed as being 'not associated' with the restatement). Firms that had no financial restatements, as well as firms with restatements that occurred within the CEO's tenure, were coded as '0'. Restatements were identified from the Financial Statement Restatement Database and restatement announcement dates from LexisNexis.
scale: dummy (1 = not associated with the prior restatement, 0 = otherwise)
time_window: 1 January 1999 to mid-2002 (10 days prior to filing CEO certifications)

description: Value of the firm's German FPD patents commencing during a given year, estimated with the patent renewal methodology, which assumes that firms renew patents as long as they are useful and allow unproductive patents to lapse. Relative patent values were calculated following Lanjouw's findings on relative differences in the value of German computer patents renewed in any given year, and the longer a firm chose to protect a patent the greater the commercial value it is estimated to hold. Patents were identified from International Patent Classes G02F, G09G and G09F and assigned to known FPD firms, explicitly excluding traditional display technologies such as cathode ray tubes. Firms based in Germany were eliminated from the analysis.
time_window: patents commencing during a single year, with value traced through renewal decisions into the commercial phase

description: The quantity of knowledge the firm shared with its national innovation system, captured by the number of the firm's researchers' articles and presentations in outlets in the firm's home country. Sharing with the NIS takes place through local and regional technical conferences, publications in domestic outlets, and distribution of papers to domestic colleagues.

The quantity of knowledge the firm shared with its global innovation system, captured by the number of the firm's researchers' articles and presentations in foreign outlets. Sharing with the GIS takes place by attending foreign conferences, publishing papers in foreign scientific journals, publishing papers in foreign languages, and publishing in outlets that are widely read internationally.

The total quantity of knowledge the firm shared with its innovation system, calculated as the sum of the quantity shared with the national innovation system and the quantity shared with the global innovation system (QuantityTOTAL = QuantityNIS + QuantityGIS).

The relevance of the knowledge the firm shared with its national innovation system, reflected in citations of the firm's publications and conference papers by scientists in other domestic organizations. This dimension was standardized to account for variations in the size of firms' NIS and GIS and the data were centered around zero. Citations were entered manually from the physical articles and aggregated to the firm level.

The relevance of the knowledge the firm shared with its global innovation system, reflected in citations of the firm's publications and conference papers by scientists in foreign organizations. This dimension was standardized to account for variations in the size of firms' NIS and GIS and the data were centered around zero. Citations were entered manually from the physical articles and aggregated to the firm level.

The total relevance of the knowledge the firm shared with its innovation system, calculated as the sum of the relevance of knowledge shared with the national innovation system and with the global innovation system (RelevanceTOTAL = RelevanceNIS + RelevanceGIS).

variable_name: Negative and positive legal shocks on JY
description: Dummy indicators marking the direction of each legal event's shock to JY's political standing, equal to one on the event day. Of the first six legal events examined between January 2017 and February 2018, four are negative shocks to JY (the first and second petitions for an arrest warrant, the issuance of the arrest warrant, and the first sentencing) and two are positive shocks (the denial of the first warrant and the appeals court ruling that reduced and suspended the sentence). For the three events that took place while the market was open, the shocks are identified sentence by sentence from the judge's opinion as it was read out and reported as breaking news, and are timed to three-minute intervals. The direction of the ruling is the coding rule for the shock.

One-day abnormal return for Samsung Electronics, following the standard procedure of adjusting the nominal return on the event day by the relevant market or industry benchmark return. The authors report nominal, market-adjusted, and industry-adjusted versions, and note that the pooled OLS regression on these adjusted returns provides a difference-in-differences estimation. In the minute-level analysis they track shifts in the share price over three-minute intervals in response to each judicial development.

One-day abnormal return for Hotel Shilla, computed by adjusting the nominal return on the event day by the relevant market or industry benchmark return. The authors also use Samsung Electronics as the benchmark in one specification to control for any systematic correlation in the share prices of the two firms, and report nominal, market-adjusted, and industry-adjusted versions. Minute-level share price movements are tracked over three-minute intervals around each judicial development.

Yearly and quarterly growth rates of Hotel Shilla's revenue from Samsung affiliates, compared with its growth in revenue from non-affiliates, read from the Notes section of the quarterly 10Q and annual 10K filings. The authors also examine the ratio of affiliate revenue to payments, akin to the export-import ratio used to track trade flows, as a measure of the trade terms obtained in inter-affiliate transactions. The analysis is a forensic reading of disclosed inter-affiliate transactions timed around JY's trial dates.

The dependent variable is the count of TMT members at employer i who came directly from source j, that is, the sources of an employer's TMT hires in 1990-94. It is a count variable with evidence of overdispersion. The data are employer-source dyads.

Network ties were represented as the number of individuals from source j that sat on employer i's board of directors or vice versa in 1989. Board interlock data were compiled from company proxy statements.
Frequency imitation was measured as the number of TMT executives supplied by a given source to other Fortune 500 firms in the sample frame between 1987 and 1989.

The authors first determined the number of employees employed by each firm in the sample in 1989, then, for each given source, averaged the sizes of all the firms that hired from it between 1987 and 1989.

The authors first calculated the average 1987-89 return on assets (ROA, net income divided by average total assets) of each firm in the sample, adjusted for industry by subtracting the median ROA in the firm's primary four-digit SIC category, and then averaged the ROA of all the firms that hired from each source between 1987 and 1989. Three years of ROA were averaged to protect against year-to-year variation.

One of the three composite environmental variables generated for the study, measured with the questionnaire used in the Tan and Litschert (1994) study. The 2002 scores from the survey are compared with the 1990 scores transferred from Tan and Litschert (1994). The text does not report the items or the response scale.

One of the three composite environmental variables generated for the study, measured with the questionnaire used in the Tan and Litschert (1994) study. The 2002 scores from the survey are compared with the 1990 scores transferred from Tan and Litschert (1994). The text does not report the items or the response scale.

One of the three composite environmental variables generated for the study, measured with the questionnaire used in the Tan and Litschert (1994) study. The 2002 scores from the survey are compared with the 1990 scores transferred from Tan and Litschert (1994). The text does not report the items or the response scale.

One of the five composite strategic orientation variables generated for the study, measuring the willingness to sacrifice short-term gain and to commit resources for long-term growth. Measured with the same questionnaire in the 2002 survey and compared with the 1990 value transferred from Tan and Litschert (1994). The text does not report the items or the response scale.

One of the five composite strategic orientation variables generated for the study, measured by the willingness to make aggressive, proactive, and innovative strategic moves. Measured with the same questionnaire in the 2002 survey and compared with the 1990 value transferred from Tan and Litschert (1994). The text does not report the items or the response scale.

One of the five composite strategic orientation variables generated for the study, reflecting the respondents' willingness to take risk. Measured with the same questionnaire in the 2002 survey and compared with the 1990 value transferred from Tan and Litschert (1994). The text does not report the items or the response scale.

One of the five composite strategic orientation variables generated for the study; one of the two relatively conservative orientations. Measured with the same questionnaire in the 2002 survey and compared with the 1990 value transferred from Tan and Litschert (1994). The text does not report the items or the response scale.

One of the five composite strategic orientation variables generated for the study; one of the two relatively conservative orientations. Measured with the same questionnaire in the 2002 survey and compared with the 1990 value transferred from Tan and Litschert (1994). The text does not report the items or the response scale.

Firm performance as reported by the CEO or general manager responding to the survey; performance was one of the three broad categories of the questionnaire, alongside organizational environment and firm strategic orientations. The text does not describe the items or the response scale.

A dummy variable based on the grouping of firms. Those founded before 1990 were coded as 0, and those founded after 1990 were coded 1. It is used as a control variable and as the moderator of the strategy-performance relationship, with five interaction terms added to test that moderation.

Firm strategic adaptation is measured by five composite strategic orientation variables from the CEO and general manager questionnaire: futurity, proactiveness, risk affinity, analysis and defensiveness. Proactiveness and innovation is the orientation used to test the difference between new and older firms.

Transition stage is operationalized as the survey period. The 2002 survey of SOE managers (T3) used the same questionnaire and data collection procedure as the 1990 Tan and Litschert survey (T2), and the environmental and strategic orientation scores from the two waves are compared to test H1 to H7.

A single year (2002) Corruption Perceptions Index was used because CPIs tend to remain relatively constant over time. The original CPI 0 to 10 scale (0 for very corrupt countries) was inverted by subtracting each country's score from 10, making 10 the most corrupt country and 0 the least corrupt. The measure was centered for the regression analyses.

FDI disaggregated following UNCTAD industry-level classifications into market-seeking activities: wholesaling, retailing, transportation, storage, communications, real estate, and financial services. Measured as the average of multilateral FDI flows from 1996-2002. The log of market-seeking FDI was used in its analysis to achieve normality and homoscedasticity; reported values are standardized betas.

One of the two types of resource-seeking FDI, covering textiles, machinery and equipment manufacturing, and clothing. Measured as the average of multilateral FDI flows from 1996-2002. The log of labor-seeking FDI was used in its analysis to achieve normality and homoscedasticity; reported values are standardized betas.
One of the two types of resource-seeking FDI, covering mining, quarries, and petroleum. Measured as the average of multilateral FDI flows from 1996-2002. Reported values are standardized betas.

Following Loree and Guisinger (1995), market attractiveness for market-seeking investment was measured as gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, a proxy for personal wealth in the host market. Data were obtained from World Development Indicators, 1996-2002. The measure was centered for the regression analyses.

For labor-seeking FDI, market attractiveness is likely to be determined by the cost of labor, so it was measured as the average monthly wage in manufacturing. Data were acquired from LABORSTA, a database operated by the International Labor Organization, Bureau of Statistics. Low attractiveness corresponds to high wages; the measure was centered for the regression analyses.

For raw materials-seeking investment, market attractiveness is likely to be determined by the level of domestic energy production. The authors follow the World Bank's definition: the amount of primary energy - petroleum (crude oil, natural gas liquids, and oil from nonconventional sources), natural gas, solid fuels (coal, lignite, and other derived fuels), and combustible renewables and waste - and primary electricity, all converted into oil equivalents. Data came from World Development Indicators, 1996-2002; the log of energy production was used in the analysis and the measure was centered.

Percentage synergistic gain for the ith pair of combining firms, defined as the difference between the actual value of the combined firm and the hypothetical combined value had there been no acquisition, divided by the expected combined value. It is estimated by constructing a time-series of combined daily returns for each pair of combining firms, estimating the ex post capital asset pricing model for each pair, and comparing actual returns with expected returns over the event period. The authors state that the synergy score is a direct operationalization of the definition of the percentage synergistic gain in an acquisition.
time_window: event period of days -40 through day T around the acquisition

description: Cumulative abnormal return to the combined entity, used as the dependent variable in the cross-sectional analysis because of its useful statistical properties, which ensure that the assumptions of the classical linear regression model are met. The authors report that the correlation coefficient between CAR and the synergy score is 0.98.

Each acquisition in the sample is classified as related or unrelated using the FTC typology: nonconglomerate horizontal and vertical acquisitions and conglomerate product extension and market extension acquisitions are classified as related, and 'pure' conglomerates as unrelated. Of the 102 tender offers, 50 are classified as unrelated and 52 as related.

Relative size, measured as the pre-acquisition market value of the target divided by the pre-acquisition market value of the bidder. The authors treat acquisitions with targets that are significant in size relative to the acquirer as having greater potential for creating synergy via increased market power, managerial economies, and economies of scope and scale, and describe the variable as a proxy for sources associated with important potential changes in operating decisions.

Binary variable set equal to 1 if both bidder and target firms are of the same type in a typology of producer-goods, consumer:convenience-goods and consumer:non-convenience-goods firms, and 0 otherwise. The authors present it as a proxy for marketing relatedness, which may also imply other forms of relatedness, particularly technological.

Change in production costs, measured as the difference between the post-acquisition and the pre-acquisition annual average ratio of the production cost of goods sold to net sales for the combined entity. The ratio is computed for each of the two years preceding and following the acquisition, and the simple averages before and after are differenced.
time_window: two years before and two years after the acquisition

description: Change in total debt, measured as the difference between the post-acquisition and the pre-acquisition averages of the ratio of the book value of total debt to the book value of assets of the combined entity. The ratios are calculated for each of the two years immediately preceding and immediately following the year of acquisition, and the difference between the post- and pre-acquisition averages represents the change in the financing decision.
time_window: two years before and two years after the acquisition

description: Change in long-term debt, measured as the difference between the post-acquisition and the pre-acquisition averages of the ratio of the book value of long term debt to the book value of assets of the combined entity. The ratios are calculated for each of the two years immediately preceding and immediately following the year of acquisition, and different ratios are used to ensure that the results are not specific to any one measure.
time_window: two years before and two years after the acquisition

description: Average difference between the post-acquisition and the pre-acquisition systematic risk of the pair of combining firms. Beta is estimated from the ex post capital asset pricing model regression using combined return data from day -140 to day -41 for the pre-acquisition period and from day C to day C+100 for the post-acquisition period.
time_window: day -140 to day -41 before the acquisition and day C to day C+100 after consummation

description: Average difference between the post-acquisition and the pre-acquisition required return of the pair of combining firms. The required return on any day depends on the systematic risk of the pair and on common estimators of the market and risk-free returns computed as averages over the entire time horizon covered by the study.
time_window: day -140 to day -41 before the acquisition and day C to day C+100 after consummation

description: Difference in cumulative abnormal returns between the firm with less valuable resources (identified as the firm with the lower Tobin's q in the dyad) and the firm with more valuable resources (the firm with the higher Tobin's q), computed as LO minus HI. For each partner the market model was estimated over the -250 to -50 period with the announcement date as day 0, and the prediction errors for days -1 and 0 were cumulated.
time_window: two-day window [-1, 0] around the JV announcement; market model estimation window -250 to -50

description: Tobin's q of each partner, computed with the simple measure of q proposed by Perfect and Wiles: the sum of the market value of equity, short- and long-term debt, preferred stock at liquidating value, and the book value of convertible debt, normalized by the book value of total assets. These data items were retrieved for each parent from Compustat for the year end preceding the formation of the JV. The firm with the higher q in the dyad is the firm with more valuable resources (HIQ) and the other is the firm with less valuable resources (LOQ).
time_window: year end preceding the formation of the JV

description: Size of the firm with less valuable resources, measured as sales in the year end prior to the formation of the JV; both partners' sizes were measured as sales in the year end prior to the formation of the JV. For the subsample test, the dummy variable D1 was assigned a value of 1 for the JV when the low-Tobin's q firm had greater sales in the year prior to the formation of the JV than the high-Tobin's q firm, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: year end prior to the formation of the JV

variable_name: D2 (product diversity of the low-q firm)
description: D2 equals 1 when the firm with less valuable resources is more diverse than the median, and 0 otherwise. Diversity in the knowledge base was measured with the Herfindahl index of product diversity calculated using business segment data from Compustat, weighted by the inverse of the 'distance' between the core business of the firm and the JV. The distance was calculated as the absolute value of the difference between the SIC code of the firm's core business (from Compustat) and the SIC code of the JV (from the SDC database).

variable_name: D3 (JV capabilities of the high-q firm)
description: D3 is assigned a value of one for a JV when the firm with more valuable resources had formed more prior JVs than the median number of JVs for all high q firms, and 0 otherwise. JV capabilities were measured as a count measure of all prior JVs undertaken by a firm as listed in the SDC database, the assumption being that the greater the number of prior JVs, the greater the accumulated JV capabilities.
time_window: all prior JVs up to the focal JV

description: Three items adapted from Heil and Walters (1993), Hultink and Langerak (2002), and Robertson et al. (1995), assessed on seven-point Likert-type rating scales with anchors 1 = strongly disagree and 7 = strongly agree. The items refer to Beta's market entry being very aggressive, Beta's primary goal being to acquire a large share of the market, and Beta's entry being aimed to gain sales at the incumbent's expense. Scale items, factor loadings and item reliabilities appear in Table 1, and the measure shows convergent and discriminant validity.
scale: seven-point Likert-type rating scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Two items from Hultink and Langerak (2002), assessed on seven-point Likert-type rating scales with anchors 1 = strongly disagree and 7 = strongly agree. The items concern the incumbent manager's belief that Beta has invested a lot of time and energy in their market entry and that managers at Beta have high expectations toward their product.
scale: seven-point Likert-type rating scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: The consequence of entry for the incumbent was measured in terms of the potential loss in market share, revenue and sales with three items adapted from Heil and Walters (1993) and Hultink and Langerak (2002), assessed on seven-point Likert-type rating scales with anchors 1 = strongly disagree and 7 = strongly agree. Each item asks what Alpha would lose if it did not react at all.
scale: seven-point Likert-type rating scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Participants were asked to indicate a price response in terms of the new price for a box of two screws (in €) in an open question for their brand Alpha. Lower (higher) prices indicate stronger (weaker) incumbent firm responses, so the values are reverse coded relative to the strength of the price response.
scale: price in euros for a box of two screws

description: Manipulated as a dummy variable for the entrant's relative product innovativeness, where 0 = similar (the competitor's product did not offer more benefits than the incumbent's product) and 1 = superior (the entrant's product offered an improved screwing mechanism and slipping protection as additional benefits). The manipulation was checked with the item 'The competitive product is a substantial innovation compared to my product Alpha'.

Manipulated as a dummy variable for customers' price sensitivity, where 0 = low ('Based on prior market research you know that price is a minor determinant for consumers when buying a specialized screw') and 1 = high ('Based on prior market research you know that price is a major determinant for consumers when buying a specialized screw'). The manipulation was checked with the item 'Price is an important decision criterion for customers in the market for specialized screws'.

Manipulated as a dummy variable for Alpha's market share before market entry, where 0 = small and 1 = large, conveyed by the statement 'Your company currently has a small [large] share of the market for specialized screws'. The manipulation was checked with the item 'Alpha currently has a small share in the market for specialized screws'.

In the binomial logit model the dependent variable equals one for equity joint ventures and zero for contractual (i.e., non-equity) collaborations. The multinomial logit model distinguishes three categories of alliances: equity joint ventures, non-equity bilateral forms and non-equity unilateral forms, with the non-equity bilateral category taken as the baseline of the estimates. Non-equity bilateral agreements comprise joint R&D agreements, technology sharing agreements, cross-licenses, arrangements aimed at sharing production facilities, logistics resources and/or distribution networks, and co-marketing agreements; non-equity unilateral agreements comprise R&D contracts, technology transfer agreements, licenses, customer-supplier relations, franchising agreements and other unilateral commercial agreements. Acquisitions of a minority interest were excluded from the empirical analysis because of a small numbers problem.
scale: three categories: equity joint venture, non-equity bilateral, non-equity unilateral

description: For each firm, the revealed technological advantage in a technological field is calculated from the number of U.S. patents granted to the firm in that field over the period 1969-95 as the ratio of the share of the field in the firm's U.S. patents in IT to the share of the same field in the total number of U.S. patents in IT granted to all sample firms, considering 31 technological fields associated with IT sectors. Pearson's correlation coefficient is then calculated between the revealed technological advantage distributions of any pair-wise combination of partner firms across the 31 technological fields. The value of SIMILAR CAPABILITIES for a given alliance is the average value of this coefficient across all pairs of firms involved in the alliance, so that the more technologically related are partner firms the greater the value of the variable.

Dummy variable that equals 1 for alliances that involve R&D and/or design and/or engineering and/or technology transfer; otherwise it equals 0, denoting alliances that concentrate on production and/or commercial activities.

Indicator of whether executive redeployment occurs, coded one for the realized case, that is, the destination affiliate to which a focal executive is redeployed, and zero for unrealized cases, that is, the potential destination affiliates in the executive's choice set that were not chosen. The models estimate the likelihood of a specific affiliate being chosen among all potential destinations in the group in a given year.

Return on assets, defined by net income to total assets, measured for the potential destination affiliate. Because the argument concerns affiliate performance relative to the group, the variable is group-adjusted by subtracting the group average from the focal affiliate's ROA.

Count of the number of turnaround cases an executive experienced. A turnaround is operationalized as an affiliate's ROA turning from negative to positive one year to the next; an executive is credited with the experience when she worked in the affiliate at the time of the turnaround.

Residuals from regressions of affiliate performance on six affiliate-specific characteristics, including affiliate size, market share, cash availability, life cycle, operational complexity, and foreign operations, with clustering standard errors by affiliate and year; separate regressions are run by industry based on the two-digit Korean standard industry classification. The residuals are then used to measure the competitive experience of executives who worked for these affiliates.
Logged number of foreign direct investments (FDIs) made by affiliates during an executive's career in the business group. A logged value is taken in order to control for skewness.
time_window: during the executive's career in the business group

description: Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI), calculated as the sum of squared individual affiliates' market shares in the industry, defined at the two-digit industry level based on the Korean SIC each year. HHI is calculated using all the firms in a given industry included in the KIS database.
Logged number of foreign direct investments by the potential destination affiliate.
Number of years since the affiliate's founding.

Dichotomous variable capturing whether an executive has worked in an affiliate that functions as a de facto holding company, often the peak of a pyramidal ownership structure. These de facto holding companies are identified based on historical descriptions of Korean business groups.
Number of group affiliates in which an executive serves as an intragroup director, based on information on executives' directorate affiliations.

A dummy variable set equal to 1 for the hierarchy of authority condition and 0 for the no hierarchy of authority condition. Participants in the hierarchy condition were informed that they were a junior manager working with one vice president, two senior managers, two other junior managers, and two entry-level analysts; a vertical organizational chart was displayed and they were told the vice president would monitor progress and assess performance. Participants in the no hierarchy condition were told they were a junior manager working with other junior managers, an organizational chart comprised of peers at the same level was displayed, and output would be sent to the team for evaluation.

For the idea generation task, the total number of ideas (defined as the number of nonredundant ideas) was counted for each participant. The dependent variable is a count variable and was modelled with a negative binomial specification.

For the selection task, the five final selected ideas were coded for their respective rank ordering and source (own idea versus coworker idea). Two measures captured the quality of the selected ideas: participants' own evaluations of each selected idea in terms of originality and feasibility on a five-point scale, and evaluations by two independent raters blind to condition, with intraclass correlations of 0.78 for originality and 0.69 for feasibility.
scale: five-point scale for originality and feasibility

description: An indicator variable set equal to one if an idea is external (i.e., a coworker idea rather than the participant's own idea). It enters a logistic regression of the binary dependent variable Selected, set equal to one if an idea is selected, together with Hierarchy and the interaction Source x Hierarchy. A negative and significant coefficient for Source indicates self-promotion bias, specifically that participants favor selecting their own ideas over others' ideas, and a significant coefficient for Source x Hierarchy indicates that the tendency to favor one's own ideas differs by condition.

Hierarchy of authority within each brand was assessed by surveying 13 designers using a subset of validated items from Hage and Aiken (1969), with each respondent rating hierarchy of authority within each brand with the option to not answer for brands they were unfamiliar with, providing from 5 to 12 responses for each brand. Items were answered on a five-point response scale and averaged into one measure, where a higher number indicates a greater degree of hierarchy of authority.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

description: Sales normalized by sales target, calculated as quantity sold over quantity produced, where quantity produced is an exogenous sales target set by the planning function (merchandisers) prior to the development of designs. The measure is applied to the trendy category within the regular planning cycle, where the relative importance of idea generation is greatest because most items are new designs with limited repeats from previous seasons and a large majority of new designs generated are also selected.
scale: ratio of quantity sold to quantity produced

description: Sales normalized by sales target, calculated as quantity sold over quantity produced, where quantity produced is an exogenous sales target set by the planning function (merchandisers) prior to the development of designs. The measure is applied to the basic category within the regular planning cycle and to the trendy category within the quick response planning cycle, categories in which the relative emphasis is on selection among existing or already-observed designs.
scale: ratio of quantity sold to quantity produced

description: Operationalized according to semiconductor product type. The variable equals one if the process manufactures analog or memory products, and is zero otherwise. The authors argue that development of analog and memory products presents ill-structured problems, described as activities based more on art than on science because of incomplete understanding of parameter interdependencies, whereas digital logic products make extensive use of EDA tools and have benefited from standardization around CMOS.

Calculated as the leading-edge process linewidth divided by the linewidth for each new manufacturing process, adjusted according to products manufactured. Process linewidth is the minimum size of the smallest circuit on a device, a well-accepted measure of technological sophistication; because leading-edge linewidths vary over time and by product type, a scaling procedure adjusts each sample process linewidth using industry sources documenting where the leading edge was at the start of technological development. The variable ranges from near zero (mature process technologies) to one (leading-edge process technologies).
time_window: at the start of technological development

description: The number of photolithography machines in the manufacturing facility. Photolithography represents the 'bottleneck' stage, so more machines increase experimentation and problem-solving capacity, allow the examination of multiple technological options in parallel, and support more diverse problem-solving approaches. The estimation also includes a squared Scale term to test for diseconomies of scale.

The number of major process groups in the manufacturing facility. Each process group represents specific sets of procedures, operations, and equipment sets used to manufacture particular products, and economies of scope exist if the technological development activities and problem-solving approaches of one process group improve the performance of other process groups. The estimation also includes a squared Scope term to test for diseconomies of scope.

The time from the earliest stage of process development in a manufacturing facility to achievement of the first functional (or working) product. It captures efficiencies in solving technological development problems. Shorter times represent superior performance, and the performance equations are estimated separately for specialized and integrated manufacturers with a correction for selection.
time_window: from the start of process development

description: The initial yield of the semiconductor manufacturing process, representing the quality of technological development problem solutions. Yield is expressed as line yield (the proportion of wafers not scrapped) and die yield (the proportion of die on a successfully processed wafer that pass functionality tests); the paper compares die yield, which is normalized into a defect-density measure of fatal defects per square centimeter using the Murphy model to control for average die size. Only initial defect density is examined in the empirical analysis, and superior problem-solving performance is represented in lower initial values; the Murphy model equation itself is not readable in the text.

Organizational mode is coded by whether the manufacturing facility belongs to a specialized (market mode, foundry-type) manufacturer or an integrated manufacturer (hierarchy). The two groups are estimated separately in a Heckman selection model, with a selection equation that differentiates the two.

Diversification is measured with the widely used entropy measure, in which Pi is the share of the ith segment of the firm's total sales, with segments operationalized in Osiris at the four-digit SIC level. The authors used the quadratic measure of entropy to test for nonlinear relationships, and report only entropy results because the Herfindahl index alternative was highly correlated with entropy. The formula itself was not readable in the text provided, so the exact specification is not recorded.
Return on assets with a 1-year lag is used as the measure of firm performance for the test of Hypothesis 1.

For Hypotheses 2 and 3 the dependent variable is the log transformation of next period ROA, used as the measure of change in performance. The authors state that using change in ROA as the dependent variable is subject to problems of reliability associated with change scores, and that the log of next period ROA coefficient represents the proportional change in the outcome for an infinitesimally small change in the predictor.

Because there are no theoretically established empirical measures of institutions, the authors adopt a comparative approach, testing hypotheses by estimating country-level models and treating differences across countries as indicative of institutional differences. Table 1 summarizes three measures of institutional development (the EIU indicator, Euromoney country creditworthiness and the composite ICRG risk rating) and one measure of economic development, per capita GNI, and countries are presented in order of institutional development.

Business group affiliation was identified by complementing the Osiris database with several different sources, relying primarily on published papers, researchers, industry and market publications, and firm websites. For Japanese business groups the authors also distinguished horizontal from vertical business groups, and following Chang and Hong (2002) they distinguished the 30 largest business groups in Korea from other business groups. Country samples were split into group-affiliated and independent firm samples to test group affiliation effects.

variable_name: economy-wide shock (industry market capitalization, industry average ROA, and per capita GNI)
description: Three complementary measures of the shock are used: industry market capitalization, computed by summing the market capitalization of all firms in the dataset in each industry, within each country, for each year; industry average ROA; and per capita GNI as a broad indicator of the economic environment. These measures also control for variation in the economy-wide shock in each country, as the shock affected firms most directly through changes in industry-level opportunities and profitability. For the tests of Hypotheses 2 and 3 the authors use 1-year changes in these values to detect the impact of the shock.

Counts of instances in which the plaintiff's lawyers share an educational or professional affiliation with any of the judges of a given court, captured in five variables: potential BA and potential JD contemporaneous affiliations (same institution with at least a one-year overlap during their training), potential BA and potential JD asynchronous affiliations (same institution but non-overlapping training periods), and potential clerkship affiliations (the lawyer previously clerked for one of the given court's judges). Judges' educational information came from the Federal Judicial Center's Biographical Directory of Federal Judges; lawyers' educational attainment records and clerkship data came from their resumes. About 23 percent (clerkship) to 98 percent (asynchronous JD affiliations) of the cases in the data had potential affiliations.

Affiliation counts using the same criteria as potential affiliations, but capturing the affiliations between plaintiff-side lawyers and the presiding judge only, in five variables (realized BA and JD contemporaneous and asynchronous affiliations and realized clerkship affiliations). These affiliations were realized in 2 percent of the cases in the data.

Affiliation counts measuring the affiliations between the plaintiff-side lawyers and all the court's non-presiding judges, in five variables (unrealized BA and JD contemporaneous and asynchronous affiliations and unrealized clerkship affiliations). These are potential affiliations that remain unrealized because the desired presiding judge is not assigned to the case.

The binary dependent variable took the value of 1 if the plaintiff chose a specific court and 0 otherwise, estimated at the level of the plaintiff-defendant-case-court tetrad. Estimated with conditional logistic regression with dyadic fixed effects for plaintiff-defendant pairings, which controls for any time-invariant, unobserved dyadic effects, and with robust standard errors clustered at the plaintiff-defendant level.

A binary variable that took the value of 1 if at least one of a plaintiff's claims was supported in the court via judgment or trial and 0 otherwise. Case outcomes were obtained by manually reviewing the dockets of each terminated case. In the sample, 11.5 percent of cases resulted in judgments for the plaintiff, 6.7 percent favored the defendant, and 81.8 percent were either settled out of court or terminated on procedural grounds.

Count of revised complaints the plaintiff submitted after the presiding judge was assigned to the case (in the data, the judge was assigned after an average of 14 days). Complaint documents were obtained from PACER and Lex Machina and analyzed with text analysis to establish whether the revised complaints differed from the original complaints in length, content, tone, and emotion; the authors anticipated that lawyers with common contemporaneous affiliations with the presiding judge would be more likely to revise complaints following the assignment of that judge.
time_window: after the assignment of the presiding judge

description: The cosine distance between the four-dimensional vectors representing the presiding judge's and the lawyers' linguistic styles, scaled by 100 so that the variable ranges between 0 and 100. Judges' opinions and findings of fact and conclusions of law for the five most recent patent cases decided before the focal case were collected from PACER or Lex Machina, and the full text of original and revised complaints was obtained for all cases in the study. JD-institution-specific variance was removed from this measure using the presiding judge's JD-institution fixed effects to account for cognitive homophily.
time_window: five most recent patent cases decided before the focal case

description: The proportion of plaintiff-side lawyers who (1) have potential social affiliations (with any judge on the bench of the focal court) and (2) studied at a non-elite law school, defined as law schools outside the top 14 U.S. News & World Report ranking. The authors created the measure to capture the degree to which teams emphasize social capital over human capital in selecting teammates. They note that the measure uses the proportion of teammates with advanced degrees from elite institutions to proxy general human capital as opposed to the specialized human capital required for a specific task.

A binary variable computed as 1 if a firm had at least one activist director in the focal year and 0 otherwise. Boards can be subject to more than one activist director appointment, but the authors are conceptually interested in comparing any board presence to no board presence for activist investors. The analyses examine change in the independent variable, which considers the influence of the appointment of an activist director on the dependent variable.

KLD rates companies on activities reflecting their relationships with stakeholder topics and groups, counting the number of strengths and concerns a company has toward each stakeholder category. Rater-reported stakeholder harm is measured as a firm's sum of the total concerns in KLD's community, diversity, employees, product, environment, and human rights categories in the focal year. The corporate governance category is excluded because it is aimed at shareholders.
time_window: focal year (dependent variable measured at t + 1)

description: RepRisk screens media, regulatory, stakeholder, and other third-party sources daily for negative ESG events, and its analysts filter media coverage to remove duplicate reports of the same incident. Media-reported stakeholder harm is calculated as the number of distinct incidents of stakeholder harm reported about a firm in the focal year. Governance-related incidents are excluded because they are aimed at shareholders.
time_window: focal year (dependent variable measured at t + 1)

description: Data on stakeholder regulatory violations come from the Violation Tracker dataset compiled by the Corporate Research Project, which identifies such violations by compiling information from federal agencies (e.g., the EPA and the OSHA) as well as state and local agencies such as state attorneys general and local branches of the Department of Justice. Regulator-reported stakeholder harm is a count of the number of fines a firm incurs for violating the interests of stakeholders in the focal year.
time_window: focal year (dependent variable measured at t + 1)

description: The authors used the Department of Transportation's dichotomous classification, which has been widely used as a key demarcation in airline industry research. Large airlines, or majors, were carriers with annual operating revenues of $1 billion or more, and small airlines, or nationals, were those with annual operating revenues of between $100 million and $1 billion. The sample contained 16 small airlines and 12 large ones. The mean operating revenues in 1985-86 for the 16 small airlines was $333 million (s.d. = 204), and it was $2,591 million (s.d. = 1,705) for the 12 large airlines.

This variable was calculated by dividing the total number of actions an airline initiated in a given year by its total number of routes in the same year. The control for scale of operation was necessary because airlines with many routes have more fronts on which to undertake actions. After all data transformations, the variable was standardized for the two-year averages to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

This was the average amount of time that a firm spent to execute an announced action, first measured as the time difference between the date the firm publicly announced or acknowledged the intended action, as reported in Aviation Daily, and the date that action began to be executed. An action was excluded if its execution was later reported to have been canceled. For each of the 17 types of moves, execution time scores were standardized over all years and airlines to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, and to indicate speed rather than time lag the signs were reversed so that a large value implies great speed. The average standardized score across all the actions taken by an airline in a given year is its action execution speed for that year.
scale: standardized within type of move; signs reversed so large values imply greater speed

description: This variable was defined as the average amount of information available about a competitive action that a firm initiated, measured by counting the number of lines Aviation Daily devoted to reporting an action when the firm first made it public. Because the number of lines reporting an action differs for different types of moves, the same standardization by type of move and averaging process as for action execution speed was used. The variable was then standardized across the two-year averages to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
scale: standardized within type of move; standardized score (mean 0, standard deviation 1)

description: A firm's relative tendency to respond when attacked, determined through a comparison of the difference between the actual response behavior of a firm under attack and the firm's predicted tendency to respond. The predicted likelihood of response came from a logistic regression of response (coded 1 if the action provoked at least one response, 0 otherwise) on the type of action, the visibility of the action, and the degree to which the affected competitor depends for revenues on the markets under attack. A firm's responsiveness rating for an action was the difference between the actual value of response (1 if the firm did respond, 0 otherwise) and the firm's predicted likelihood of response, so a large positive rating indicated higher responsiveness. The ratings for all the incidents in which a firm was under attack in a given year were averaged to calculate its overall responsiveness score for that year.
scale: difference between actual response (0/1) and predicted likelihood of response

description: This variable was defined as the average amount of time it took a firm—relative to other responding competitors—to announce an intended response to an action. It was first measured as the number of days between the action's announcement date and the date the responding airline publicly announced or acknowledged its intended response, as reported in Aviation Daily; a response was excluded if its execution was later reported to have been canceled. To construct a measure of relative speed, each firm's response announcement time was divided by the response announcement time of the fastest other competitor responding to the same action, so only cases with more than one response were used. The average of all the responses taken by an airline in a given year was used and the scores were inverted so that large values implied greater speed.
scale: ratio of a firm's response announcement time to the fastest other responder's time, inverted to indicate speed

description: This variable, defined as the average amount of time that a firm spent to execute a response, was measured the same way as action execution time. Because response execution time not only varies with the type of initial action but also with its execution time, response execution time was first regressed on type of action and action execution time for all years and airlines. The resulting residual indicated how much an airline's rating differed from the value predicted on the basis of the action's type and execution time, and the average residual of all an airline's responses in a given year was used as that airline's response execution time for that year, with the signs reversed so that a large value implied greater speed. In constructing this variable the authors used the full sample of 418 responses from the eight-year database.
scale: average residual; signs reversed so large values imply greater speed

description: This variable was defined as the average amount of information available about a response and was measured by the number of lines Aviation Daily devoted to reporting this response. Because the visibility of a response is affected by both the type and the visibility of the initial action, the same residual process as for response execution speed was used to capture the extent to which a firm's rating differed from the value predicted on the basis of the action's type and visibility. In constructing this variable the authors used the full sample of 418 responses from the eight-year database.

An index composed of two market-related and two profit-related performance measures. Net market share change (in share points) and percentage market share change (net market share change/initial market share) were measured for the airports an airline served, not for the whole U.S. industry, for each year. Profit margin (operating profit/operating revenue) and total operating profit per revenue passenger mile were also assessed. A factor analysis of these four measures yielded a one-factor solution, which accounted for 55.9 percent of the variance and had an eigenvalue of 2.24, and the factor scores were used as airlines' performance indexes in the final analysis; the Cronbach's alpha for the four measures was .79, with no difference between large and small airlines.

Mergers in the FTC large merger series were classified by the FTC as concentric or conglomerate, and only those two categories were selected. Concentric mergers were treated as strategically analogous to related mergers and conglomerate mergers as strategically analogous to unrelated mergers. Very few market concentric mergers passed through the sample screens, so they were deleted from the related merger category.

variable_name: systematic risk difference score (consolidated minus bidder)
description: Systematic risk is estimated by the market model, in which the firm's return is regressed on a value-weighted CRSP portfolio to yield an estimate of beta. Merger event-induced changes were computed by subtracting each bidding firm's pre-merger beta estimate from its post-merger estimate, with pre-merger betas estimated over a 60-month (150-day) period beginning 3 months (150 days) before the first public announcement and post-merger betas over a comparable period beginning after the legal transaction. For the parametric test the pre- and post-merger betas were standardized by their respective standard errors before the difference score was computed, and each difference score was averaged with those of other bidders of the same merger type.
time_window: 60 months (monthly returns) or 150 days (daily returns) before the announcement and after the legal transaction

variable_name: systematic risk difference score (consolidated minus hypothesized)
description: Computed a second way by subtracting a hypothesized systematic risk level from the bidder's post-merger beta. The hypothesized level was determined by forming a market value weighted portfolio of the bidder's and target firm's common stock, with weights computed on a monthly (daily) basis from the value of total outstanding common stock at the end of each trading month (day) during the pre-announcement estimation period; it represents the risk investors would face from an 'investor-made' merger of the two firms' securities. Each difference score was averaged with those computed for other merging firms of the same merger type.
time_window: estimation periods on a monthly (daily) basis before the announcement and after the legal transaction

description: The independent variable is the level of short interest, measured as a percentage of the firm's total shareholdings. The Compustat Short Interest database provides monthly short interest information; the authors first calculate the ratio of the number of short shares to the total number of shares outstanding for each month, and then use this to obtain the firm's average level of short interest for the year.

The number of growth actions is measured at the end of the year, counting the total number of actions a firm announced throughout the year. Growth actions include all new product introductions, mergers and acquisitions (M&As), strategic alliances, plus actions included in the category of business expansion, obtained from company announcements in the Capital IQ Key Development database. The authors take the natural logarithm of the number of growth actions to address skewness.

The authors calculate a Herfindahl index of action types to measure the extent to which firms are engaging in a broad range of actions. This diversity index accounts for how many different types of growth actions a particular firm uses and how (un)evenly that firm uses those types. One minus the Herfindahl index is used so that higher values indicate a complex mix of growth actions and lower values indicate a simpler mix.
Absorptive capacity is captured by research and development (R&D) intensity. R&D intensity is the ratio of R&D expenditure to annual sales revenues.

BoardEx provides information about each director's connections with other firms' directors through directorship interlock, employment, education, and social activities. To measure the degree of centrality, the authors count the number of directors' total connections, normalized by the number of directors on the board.

The authors use Kaplan and Zingales' (1997) prescribed regression coefficients to calculate the KZ index for each firm in every year of the sample, and use the additive inverse of the KZ index to measure financial slack. The KZ index encompasses a combination of: (1) cash flow-to-capital, (2) Tobin's Q, (3) debt-to-capital, (4) dividends-to-capital, and (5) cash holdings-to-capital. The paper presents the specification as a formula that is not readable in the extracted text.

RavenPack scans for action-level data in the Dow Jones Financial Wires, Wall Street Journal, Barron's, and MarketWatch, plus all the daily press releases and regulatory disclosures from 22 different newswires. They use a proprietary algorithm, which they refer to as their Expert Consensus Methodology, that ascribes a news sentiment score, which the authors scale so that the mean is 0 (neutral), positive numbers reflect positive sentiment, and negative numbers reflect negative sentiment. The score is based on language used in the news reports and incorporates commentaries and editorials about firms surrounding their action announcements. The authors use the average tone of all news about a firm that appears throughout a year to measure news sentiment annually.
scale: mean 0 (neutral), positive = positive sentiment, negative = negative sentiment

description: Built in two steps. First, a patent-level recombinativeness score measures the proportion of technological subclasses assigned to a patent that do not belong to the primary class within which the patent is classified, ranging from 1/n to 1 where n is the number of classes the patent is assigned to. Second, class contrast is one minus the average recombinativeness of the patents assigned to the focal class in a given year, so that a class has a contrast of one when all patents classified therein are exclusively classified in that class. The measure is updated yearly and lagged by one year in the models.

Patent impact is measured yearly as the total citations the patent receives from patents applied for in a given year, regardless of whether the citations were added by patent applicants or by patent examiners. The count is used as the dependent variable in log-linear (logged count plus one), Poisson and negative binomial specifications.

The contrast of the primary class to which the patent is assigned at the USPTO, calculated as in Study 1 (one minus the average recombinativeness of the patents assigned to the focal class in a given year). It enters the patent-twin models together with the twin's EPO-side class characteristics.

variable_name: Yearly forward citations added by examiners at the USPTO
description: The dependent variable is the yearly count of citations the USPTO patent receives that were added by patent examiners; applicant-added citations are disregarded so that the USPTO measure is comparable to the EPO, where only examiners add citations. Models use the logged count plus one, Poisson and negative binomial specifications.
The contrast of the primary class to which the patent application is assigned, calculated in the same way as in Studies 1 and 2. Values are lagged to the year before the search sessions.

The count of prior art citations that examiners add during a search session, modeled as the logged count plus one in OLS regressions. The authors note that this is the same dependent variable as used in Study 2.

A binary 0/1 variable that captures whether examiners use classification-based searches in any of the search queries within a particular search session. It is coded from the 'Search query' column of the search logs, where a query such as '235/375.ccls' is a classification-based search.

variable_name: First searched class is same as patent's primary class
description: A binary measure indicating whether, upon receiving a patent application, examiners start by searching for prior art within the patent's primary class itself. It takes the value 1 when the first classification-based prior art search query is executed within the patent's own primary class; it is only defined for the subsample of search sessions with at least one classification-based query.

variable_name: Proportion of classes searched that are the same as the patent's primary class
description: Measures the extent to which an examiner focuses her search within the boundaries of the patent's primary class rather than broadening the scope of her search across patent classes. Like the previous measure, it is only defined on the subset of search sessions that contain at least one classification-based search.
The logged count of search queries that examiners execute in a particular search session, used as the dependent variable in an OLS model.
The logged average number of 'hits' generated by a search query, used as the dependent variable in an OLS model. A smaller number of hits means the query is more on target.

Firm-level categorization of a revealed extension strategy: incumbents that invested most of their product portfolio (more than 90%) in standard carburetors at the end of the emergence period (1982) were categorized as having chosen an extension strategy. Because stated strategies or R&D expenditures are not available, the strategy is measured as revealed in the firm's product portfolio, that is, the proportions of standard carburetor, hybrid carburetor, and EFI products by year based on the unique count of carburetor-car models.
time_window: end of the emergence period (1982) and the threat period (1984-1986)

description: Firms whose revealed product portfolio did not devote more than 90% of their carburetor-car model counts to standard carburetors at the end of the emergence period (1982) were categorized as having a bridging strategy. During the threat period bridging firms pursued a greater proportion of hybrid carburetors with a complement of EFI and fewer standard carburetors.
time_window: end of the emergence period (1982) and the threat period (1984-1986)

description: The dependent variable is the combined city/highway miles per gallon reported by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for each car model. Annual performance improvement is estimated by regressing a car model's MPG on its model year (YEAR) and an interaction of YEAR with a dummy indicating the model was produced after the arrival of EFI (POST), restricting the sample to car models with standard carburetors. PRE covers car model years through 1983 and POST the years after 1983.

Annual performance improvement of hybrid carburetors is estimated with the same MPG regression on model year and its interaction with the post-EFI period, using a sample that includes only standard carburetors in the preperiod and only hybrid carburetors in the postperiod, and by interacting YEAR with technology and strategy variables in the firm-level models.

A Fisher-Pry logistical diffusion function is fitted to counts of annual EFI models, modeling the market share of EFI as a function of its final market share and the crossover year in which EFI achieves a majority of market share. The curve is fitted to EFI counts only through 1982 and its prediction is compared with realized EFI penetration, and with a delay-adjusted count series, to estimate the delay in substitution.
Binary variable indicating whether a particular car has a standard carburetor, based on the presence (or absence) of EFI-derived controls in a car's carburetor.
Binary variable indicating whether a particular car has a hybrid carburetor, based on the presence of EFI-derived controls in a car's carburetor.

Firm outcomes after substitution are examined in terms of survival and failure and then expanded to include acquisition, niche continuance, late adoption, and bankruptcy. Firms pursuing a bridging strategy largely survived in terms of the traditional classification, with two firms transitioning to EFI and then being acquired and the other four transitioning to EFI and remaining major suppliers.

Firms choosing an extension strategy predominantly failed in the classical schema through niche retreat, continuing to make carburetors for many years at reduced scale for niches such as low-cost cars, motorcycles, and lawnmowers, with one of them acquired in a discounted acquisition and one re-emerging later with high-end aftermarket EFI products.

Each TMT member indicated how important each of 15 company objective items was to the firm on 5-point scales ranging from '1 = Not at All Important' to '5 = Extremely Important'. For each item the mean standard deviation of responses among TMT members in a given firm was calculated, and the standard deviations for all items were summed to yield an aggregate firm score. The TMT score was then subtracted from a constant number so that the lower the dispersion of responses within a TMT, the higher the level of consensus.
scale: 5-point importance scale per item; firm-level aggregate consensus score (higher = more consensus)
level: firm (aggregated from top management team members)

description: Each TMT member indicated how important each of 21 competitive method items was to the firm on 5-point scales ranging from '1 = Not at All Important' to '5 = Extremely Important'. For each item the mean standard deviation of responses among TMT members in a given firm was calculated, and the standard deviations for all items were summed to yield an aggregate firm score. The TMT score was then subtracted from a constant number so that the lower the dispersion of responses within a TMT, the higher the level of consensus.
scale: 5-point importance scale per item; firm-level aggregate consensus score (higher = more consensus)
level: firm (aggregated from top management team members)

description: All TMT members rated their firm against 'firms of similar sales volume in your industry and region' on firm total sales growth, with a time frame of 'average over the past 5 years'. The five-point interval scale ranged from 5 ('Top 20 percent') to 1 ('Lowest 20 percent'). The value for a given firm was the sum of the responses of the members of the TMT divided by the number of respondents comprising the TMT.
scale: 5-point interval scale (5 = Top 20 percent to 1 = Lowest 20 percent)

description: All TMT members rated their firm against 'firms of similar sales volume in your industry and region' on after-tax return on total assets, with a time frame of 'average over the past 5 years'. The five-point interval scale ranged from 5 ('Top 20 percent') to 1 ('Lowest 20 percent'). The value for a given firm was the sum of the responses of the members of the TMT divided by the number of respondents comprising the TMT.
scale: 5-point interval scale (5 = Top 20 percent to 1 = Lowest 20 percent)

description: All TMT members rated their firm's overall firm performance/success against 'firms of similar sales volume in your industry and region', with a time frame of 'average over the past 5 years'. The five-point interval scale ranged from 5 ('Top 20 percent') to 1 ('Lowest 20 percent'). The value for a given firm was the sum of the responses of the members of the TMT divided by the number of respondents comprising the TMT.
scale: 5-point interval scale (5 = Top 20 percent to 1 = Lowest 20 percent)

description: The researcher requested total firm sales figures at two points in time, 1976 and 1980, from which annual sales growth from 1976 to 1980 was calculated. The authors describe the measure as 'self-reported objective' performance and note that primary consideration had to be given to brevity and to the confidential nature of the information requested from the CEOs of privately held firms.

The measure is the average after-tax return on total assets from 1976 to 1980, obtained from the CEO. The authors describe it as a 'self-reported objective' measure of organizational performance and note that the brevity of the requested data was a primary consideration given the confidential nature of information from privately held firms.

A single item adapted from Lawrence and Lorsch (1967) that represents an overall or 'global' assessment of firm performance. The CEO was asked: 'compared to your competitors, what percent of ideal or optimal performance do you personally feel that your firm is achieving in your industry?'. The subjective overall or global measures were used to determine the extent to which such measures are correlated with economic performance and to allow respondents to incorporate implicitly non-economic considerations and aspiration levels.
scale: percent of ideal or optimal performance

description: Performance below aspirations equals zero for all observations in which the performance of the focal fund is greater than its aspirations; for all other observations, it equals the difference between the fund's performance and its aspirations. Performance is the fund's one-year risk-adjusted return (the Morningstar risk-adjusted return) in the 12 months before its annual report month. Aspiration level is a weighted average of social and historical aspirations, with the adjustment parameter for historical aspiration set at α equals 0.1 and the weight on social aspiration set at β equals 0.3. The variable is lagged by one year relative to the dependent variable.
time_window: 12 months before the annual report month, lagged one year

description: Calculated by taking the lesser of purchases or sales in securities by the mutual fund in the past year leading up to the annual report month and dividing it by average monthly net assets of the mutual fund. The resulting measure represents the percentage of the portfolio's holdings that has changed over the past year preceding the annual report month. The top 1% of data points were winsorized to minimize the influence of outliers, and the variable is expressed in percentage terms. It is reported every year in the annual report required by the SEC.
time_window: one year preceding the annual report month

description: Prior work experience of all fund managers in a mutual fund, averaged across all managers. For each manager, the start of their fund manager career is the month-year they were first seen working in any fund in Morningstar's career history record, and their prior work experience is the difference in months between when they started their career and the focal fund's annual report month in a given year. The measure captures work experience across all the mutual funds the managers have worked for in their current and previous roles as fund managers. The variable is measured at the annual report month and lagged by one year relative to the dependent variable.
time_window: measured at the annual report month, lagged one year

description: Herfindahl index of all managers' prior work experience across different U.S. equity mutual fund categories at the fund level. Prior work experience (in months) is aggregated for all managers of the focal fund in each of the nine categories, divided by all managers' total prior work experience to find the experience share for each category, and these shares are then used to calculate the fund-level Herfindahl index. The higher the measure, the greater the degree of experience specialization at the fund level. The variable is measured at the annual report month and lagged by one year relative to the dependent variable.
time_window: measured at the annual report month, lagged one year

description: An indicator variable that takes the value of 1 if the firm is the top corporate owner within the business group, and 0 otherwise. The authors manually identified a unique apex firm for each BG: whenever the ultimate owner was a corporation it was identified as an apex firm, while when the ultimate owner was a government, individual, or family the corporate subsidiary immediately following down the ownership hierarchy was selected as the top corporate owner. Any corporations placed lower in the chain of ownership were coded as non-apex firms.
scale: 1 = top corporate owner within the BG; 0 otherwise

description: An index of CSR reporting, claims, and disclosures, including best practices such as Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) guidelines. It is based on a validated scale by Hawn and Ioannou (2016) and comprises 24 performance measures from the ASSET4 database. Each performance measure was first normalized, and the index is the equal-weighted average of the performance measures; the index was then divided by the natural logarithm of total assets and normalized. It is computed annually at the firm level and ranges from 0 to 1.

An index of substantive actions related to socially responsible corporate policies and programs, such as the use of renewable energy and investment in employee training and career development. It is based on a validated scale by Hawn and Ioannou (2016) and comprises 21 performance measures from the ASSET4 database. Each performance measure was first normalized, and the index is the equal-weighted average of the performance measures; the index was then divided by the natural logarithm of total assets and normalized. It is computed annually at the firm level and ranges from 0 to 1.

The natural logarithm of the total (direct and indirect) ultimate ownership percentage of the apex firm over its subsidiaries and the total (direct and indirect) ownership percentage of the ultimate controlling shareholder of the non-apex firms. Total equity ownership of each apex firm was determined using the total (direct and indirect) ultimate shareholding percentage of the apex firm over its subsidiaries (all listed and non-listed non-apex firms within the BG); whenever the total shareholding in subsidiaries was missing, only direct shareholding was considered. For non-apex firms, the reverse logic was used, replacing a missing value with the direct controlling shareholding.

Coded at the apex-non-apex pair level as 1 whenever there was an identifiable overlap between the names of the individual, family, or corporate controlling shareholders and each of the names of the non-apex BG affiliates in the sample, which served as a signal of a strengthened social relationship. The names of the ultimate controlling shareholders within each BG were identified in the BvD Orbis database and, in the case of governments, the name of the corporate subsidiary immediately following in the ownership hierarchy was selected. Two members of the team manually and independently coded all observations.

The absolute value of the difference between Symbolic_CSR and lagged Substantive_CSR. Because a firm would naturally report on its CSR investment with a 1-year lag, the variable ultimately captures the magnitude of the gap between the level of current-year firm disclosures regarding CSR and the actual CSR investments made in the previous year.
time_window: current-year symbolic CSR less lagged substantive CSR

description: Calculated as the ratio of the sum of market capitalization and total liabilities to total assets, for each firm in each year in the sample.

Measured by the acquirer's dividends per share (DPS) paid in the year prior to a focal acquisition. The authors state that DPS provides the clearest indication to investors about a firm's commitment to dividend payments.
time_window: year prior to the focal acquisition

description: Measured by the acquirer's sales growth over the 3 years preceding the year of a focal acquisition.
time_window: 3 years preceding the year of the focal acquisition
