For each SBU, the total number of drug enhancements was calculated for the 1984-1993 time period from innovation data drawn from The FDC Reports. Following FDA criteria, drugs involving combinations of existing drugs, new dosage forms, new indications, and formula changes were coded as drug enhancements.

For each SBU, the total number of new drugs was calculated for the 1984-1993 time period from innovation data drawn from The FDC Reports. New chemical entities (NCEs) were coded as new drugs by FDA criteria, defined as products representing new chemical structures never previously available to treat a particular disease.

variable_name: goal specificity, emphasis on output, professional output, rewards and recognition
description: Output control is measured by four sets of control mechanism scales: goal specificity, emphasis on output (general and professional output) and rewards and recognition, all from 7-point items in the R&D director questionnaire.
Input control is measured by two control mechanism scales: scientific diversity (number of scientific specialties in the R&D laboratory) and professionalization (four 7-point items).
Behavior control is measured by three control mechanism scales from the R&D director questionnaire: centralization, formalization, and frequency of performance appraisals.

Coded 1 for a firm-year if there was an officer other than the CEO who held the title of president or COO or both, and 0 otherwise. The authors note that in this sample there was not a single firm that had more than one person holding the title of president and/or COO at any time. The primary data sources for this variable were the Dun & Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Management and annual corporate proxy statements.

A composite of six strategy dimensions: advertising intensity (advertising/sales), research and development intensity (R&D/sales), plant and equipment newness (net P&E/gross P&E), non-production overhead (SGA expenses/sales), inventory levels (inventories/sales), and financial leverage (debt/equity). The absolute value of the difference between the prior and current year was calculated for each ratio, these absolute values were standardized within the sample, and the average of the six standardized values yielded the overall measure.
scale: average of six standardized values (mean 0, standard deviation 1)

description: Operationalized as return on assets (ROA), adjusted for industry differences by subtracting the industry median ROA (excluding the focal firm). Data on firm ROA and industry median ROA were collected from COMPUSTAT. In all models the predictor variables and controls lagged the dependent variables by one year.
time_window: one year before the dependent variable

description: A categorical variable with 0 representing the occasion in which a CEO remained in the position, 1 representing CEO dismissal, and 2 representing CEO voluntary turnover. Dismissals were identified by combining a news-report analysis of the Dow Jones databases and a classification based on CEO age and continuity as a board member at the time of succession; in total, 46 CEO dismissals were identified among the 207 CEOs.
scale: categorical: 0 = CEO continuation, 1 = CEO dismissal, 2 = CEO voluntary turnover

description: Firms in which the CEO was also the chairperson of the board were coded 1 and other firms were coded 0. Data on managerial titles were obtained from Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management.

Firms in which the CEO was also the chairperson of the board were coded 1 and other firms were coded 0. Data on managerial titles were obtained from Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management.

The authors standardized and summed (mean 0, s.d. 1) the proportion of outside directors on a board and the proportion of firm shares owned by outside board members. Affiliated board members, defined as directors who conducted business with a firm either for themselves or through organizations they represented, were not counted as outside board members because they were not independent of management. Data on boards and stock ownership were collected from corporate proxies.

The authors standardized and summed (mean 0, s.d. 1) the proportion of outside directors on a board and the proportion of firm shares owned by outside board members. Affiliated board members, defined as directors who conducted business with a firm either for themselves or through organizations they represented, were not counted as outside board members because they were not independent of management. Data on boards and stock ownership were collected from corporate proxies.

An objective index formed by normalizing (mean 0, s.d. 1) and summing seven indicators of informal CEO power: expertise, tenure, for-profit board directorships held, nonprofit directorships held, relative compensation, experience, and elite education. The authors state that the indicators can substitute for each other and are complementary but not necessarily correlated, so Cronbach alphas are not meaningful. All data were obtained from Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management unless another source is noted.

An objective index formed by normalizing (mean 0, s.d. 1) and summing seven indicators of informal CEO power: expertise, tenure, for-profit board directorships held, nonprofit directorships held, relative compensation, experience, and elite education. The authors state that the indicators can substitute for each other and are complementary but not necessarily correlated, so Cronbach alphas are not meaningful. All data were obtained from Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management unless another source is noted.

Firm performance was measured by return on assets (ROA), calculated as net income divided by total assets. To rule out reverse causal associations, ROA was lagged by one year in all analyses. Data for this variable were available from COMPUSTAT.

Firm performance was measured by return on assets (ROA), calculated as net income divided by total assets. To rule out reverse causal associations, ROA was lagged by one year in all analyses. Data for this variable were available from COMPUSTAT.

An eight-item construct developed from the authors' definition, measured on a seven-point Likert scale. The eight questions addressed the levels of resource combination and structural integration and tackled integration in both primary and support value chain activities, including what each party would lose if the other withdrew; respondents referred to the past three years. Cronbach's alpha (0.83) confirms the internal consistency of this multi-item construct. The authors report that the path loadings of the eight question items in relation to overall economic integration were statistically significant, and that the overall content validity was also evidenced in significant magnitudes for Bentler and Bonett's Normed Fit Index and Bentler's Comparative Fit Index.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = not true at all to 7 = very true)

description: A multi-item construct measured on a seven-point Likert scale, referencing previous research by Inkpen and Currall (1997) and Zaheer et al. (1998). Some items are reverse coded, for example the item on the partner firm gaining advantage by deceiving the party and the item on reluctance to make resource commitments when contractual specifications are ambiguous. The authors report that Cronbach's alpha and factor loadings suggest reasonable internal consistency and clear factor patterns; one item was omitted due to its low loading score.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = not true at all to 7 = very true)

description: A construct of eight items developed after extensively reviewing the literature on managerial control in joint ventures, measured on a seven-point Likert scale with reference to the past three years. The items cover joint work on policies and procedures, budget and investment control, information control systems, corporate culture, goals and plans, contractual terms and their renewal, and contract enforcement. The authors report reasonable internal consistency and clear factor patterns for the construct.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = not true at all to 7 = very true)

description: A construct of eight items developed after referencing several studies on justice, measured on a seven-point Likert scale with reference to the past three years. The items ask whether the procedures used by the board, in contracting, structuring, managing and sharing, and in decision and contract execution and monitoring are fair, where fair means transparent, adjustable and correctable, representative and nondiscriminatory to each party, and accordant with contractual specifications. The authors report reasonable internal consistency and clear factor patterns for the construct.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = not true at all to 7 = very true)

description: Measured using archival data collected from the Jiangsu Commission of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation. Profitability was defined as an average of ROI over the three-year period (2000-2002) examined, an overlapped yet lagged period relative to the survey period chosen to better capture causality.

Measured by an inverse of a geometric average of the standard deviations of four growth rates, weighted by the n-rooted mean of these growth rates; the equation printed in the paper is unreadable in the available text. Using growth rates rather than absolute amounts in the standard deviation removes constant growth-inflated variations, while the n-rooted mean distinguishes between good and poor performers and better captures stability-related efficiency. The authors note that this measurement has limitations, for example it may not be able to reflect developmental processes.

The authors measured shared team experience by assessing how many years of experience each player had on a specific team at the end of a season. Years of player-team experience was weighted by the minutes played in games in that season by that player, and an average was then calculated for each team-year. An average was appropriate because the number of players on each team varies from season to season owing to trades and injuries.

variable_name: Shared team experience as a proxy for the stock of collectively held tacit knowledge
description: Because tacit knowledge is by definition unobservable, the authors used data from the NBA to construct a measure that taps into team-based tacit knowledge. They argue that this measure, the cumulative experience that members of a team have playing with each other, is a reasonable proxy for the value of the stock of tacit knowledge held in the collective mind of a team. The proxy is built by assessing how many years of experience each player had on a specific team at the end of a season, weighting those years by minutes played that season, and averaging for each team-year.

The number of regular season wins for each team, in each year, was used as a measure of performance. The authors describe this measure as probably the simplest way to establish the presence of a competitive advantage; although the correlation between wins and the shared team experience measure may be mitigated by many other factors, significant results would point to the importance of playing together in building a winning team.

Total regular season team assists for each team, in each year, was also used as a performance measure. A basketball player is credited with an assist when he or she passes to a teammate who scores without dribbling first. The authors argue that since the number of assists is clearly related to the ability of a team to play well together, it may be a purer measure of the outcome of tacit knowledge or organizational learning accumulated by the players on a given team, although it may also be influenced by team strategy, a variable not included in the study.

A variable that captured how long a coach had been with the team at the end of the season. This variable represents years of coaching experience with the team. Although it does not measure coaching quality per se, including it allowed the authors to examine the possibility that the same sorts of tacit knowledge and learning effects might be manifest in the relationship established between the players and the coach, and to investigate the predicted declining performance effects of increasing coaching experience where shared team experience is high.

variable_name: Standard deviation of shared team experience (experience heterogeneity)
description: To calculate a measure of team experience heterogeneity, the authors simply calculated the standard deviation of the shared experience variable for each team-year. That is, this variable is the standard deviation of the experience measures for all players who played for a team in a given year. The authors state that this calculation follows the method used to calculate tenure heterogeneity in previous studies.

Dummy variable set equal to 1 for female directors and those who belonged to an ethnic minority, and 0 for White male directors. African Americans, Arabs, Asians, and Hispanics were categorized as ethnic minorities. Directors' gender and ethnicity were first identified from their last and first names, and, for those who could not be categorized from names, through online sources such as annual reports, corporate proxy statements, LinkedIn profiles, biographical databases, and news outlets; membership in minority clubs and ethnicity information in ISS were also checked. Two external coders agreed in 97% of a randomly drawn subsample of 500 directors.

The number of outside directorships that a fraud-tainted director lost minus the number of outside directorships he or she gained in the three years after the fraud was initially made public. Measured at the level of the fraud-tainted director for the tests of Hypotheses 1 and 2.
time_window: three years after the fraud was initially made public

variable_name: loss of a specific outside directorship
description: Dummy that equals 1 if a minority director lost his or her directorship on the board of another, nonfraudulent firm that he or she was serving on as outside director within three years after the misconduct was revealed. Measured at the level of the pairing between a fraud-tainted minority director and a specific nonfraudulent firm; the sample contained 356 such pairings.
time_window: three years after the misconduct was revealed

description: The sum of articles that appeared in leading business media on the topic of board diversity in the 12 months prior to and the 36 months after the public revelation of the fraud (including the event month). Following Fiss, Kennedy, and Davis (2012), articles were taken from the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Washington Post, Forbes, Fortune Magazine, Business Week, and Newsweek. The variable was included in logarithmic form in the models.
time_window: 12 months before to 36 months after the public revelation of the fraud

variable_name: no. of minority directors at nonfraudulent firm
description: The number of female and ethnic minority directors who served on the nonfraudulent firm's board; this was the independent variable used to test Hypothesis 3. In a robustness test, using the proportion of minority directors instead of their number yielded similar results.

Career winning percentage multiplied by (1 - (1/total number of years as a head coach)). The first part of the equation is a career winning percentage, the proportion of regular season games a manager's teams have won to the total number of games played over his career as a head coach, adjusted for the manager's total number of years as a head coach. We computed this measure at the end of the previous season.
time_window: computed at the end of the previous season

description: Composite measure formed by analyzing dimensions that proxy the accumulation of managerial knowledge and skills, gathered for each head coach for each year beginning with the 1980-1981 season through the 2000-2001 season. A principal components factor analysis extracted one factor with an eigenvalue greater than one; the authors report the factor demonstrated internal consistency and explained 81.2 percent of the total item variance. The scale was constructed by summing the standardized values of each item.

Net productive output per dollar spent on player salaries for the team's offensive resource combination. Net productive output is the sum of standardized team-level scores for total rushing yards gained, total passing yards gained, and total points scored by the offense for games played during the regular season. Payroll dollars sum base salary earned, incentive bonus payments received, and an annual allocation of any signing bonus, for players meeting a minimum-use criterion (eligible for regular season games, designated task assignment on offense, participated in one or more plays). The measure is the ratio of net productive output for the offense to payroll dollars for players assigned to the offensive bundle.

Net productive output per dollar spent on player salaries for the team's defensive resource combination. Net productive output is the sum of standardized team-level scores for total yards (rushing and passing) allowed and total points allowed from touchdowns scored by an opponent's offense during the regular season. Payroll dollars use the same salary components and minimum-use criterion as for the offense. The measure is the ratio of net productive output for the defense to payroll dollars for players assigned to the defensive bundle.

Number of MVPs, all-pro and all-conference players on the team's offensive roster divided by the total number of players named to each status in the league, to account for year-to-year variation in the number of players selected. Players selected in more than one category are included only in the category representing the highest status. Standardized scores for each status category are multiplied by its inverse ratio, using values of 1.0, 0.66 and 0.33 for MVP, all-pro and all-conference, respectively. Honors are those at the conclusion of the previous year applied to the team's roster of players at the beginning of the current season.
time_window: honors at the conclusion of the previous year; roster at the beginning of the current season

description: Number of MVPs, all-pro and all-conference players on the team's defensive roster divided by the total number of players named to each status in the league, to account for year-to-year variation in the number of players selected. Players selected in more than one category are included only in the category representing the highest status. Standardized scores for each status category are multiplied by its inverse ratio, using values of 1.0, 0.66 and 0.33 for MVP, all-pro and all-conference, respectively. Honors are those at the conclusion of the previous year applied to the team's roster of players at the beginning of the current season.
time_window: honors at the conclusion of the previous year; roster at the beginning of the current season

description: Ratio of net combined productive resource output for the team to the total payroll dollars spent on all player salaries with specialized offensive or defensive roles on the team. The sign of the resource combination score for the defensive combination was first reversed; the standardized net productive output scores during the regular season for the offensive combination and defensive combination were then summed, with larger positive scores associated with higher levels of net productive output. Payroll uses the same salary components described for resource productivity.

Ratio of games won to total games played during the regular season, measured for each season. The measure has a mean value of 0.500 (or 50%) for all teams in a given year and is easily comparable across teams and periods.
scale: ratio of games won to games played (0 to 1)

description: We calculate status inconsistency of a firm as the sales-weighted standard deviation of segment status. We use sale percentage to weight the status of segment because the extent to which segment status affects the perceived identity ambiguity of a firm may depend on its size. The formula for the sales-weighted standard deviation is not extractable from the text provided.

Firm status is measured as the sales-weighted average of segment status. Segment status is the sum of the expertise scores of the analysts covering the firm that specialize in that industry segment, divided by the maximum such sum among all firms in the industry at year t. Following Zuckerman (2000), segment status is computed for statistical analysis as its deviation from firm status.

Segment status inconsistency is constructed as the amount of weight a segment adds to the status inconsistency of its firm. The denominator is the variance of all segment status in the firm and the numerator captures the extent to which the segment's status deviates from the firm's status. It ranges from zero to one, with larger values indicating that the segment adds more to firm-level status inconsistency.

Firm prevalence measures firm-level relatedness as the sales-weighted average of segment relatedness. Segment relatedness uses prevalence scores based on the Teece et al. (1994) asymmetric interindustry relatedness matrix. The measure reflects the extent to which a firm's segments are interrelated with each other.

Segment relatedness is measured with prevalence scores. A segment's prevalence score in a firm is its mean relatedness to all other segments in the firm. For the segment-level relatedness measure, the firm-level relatedness is subtracted from a segment's prevalence score.

The dependent variable is an ordinal variable of four divestiture types. Status inconsistency decreasing divestitures are coded 4, status inconsistency neutral divestitures 3, no divestitures 2, and status inconsistency increasing divestitures 1. Higher values indicate that firms are less tolerant of status inconsistency.

The dependent variable is the hazard rate of divestiture, expressed as the divestiture likelihood of a segment occurring at year t conditional on the segment not having been divested prior to year t-1. The model examines the effect of covariates on the log-odds that the segment would be divested in the subsequent year, using a one-year time lag. A segment enters the risk set when it first appears in Historical Segments.

Dichotomous variable equal to 1 if news reports at dismissal indicate the executive was involved in an ethical or legal violation relating to the firm's operations or for personal conduct related transgressions or scandals, and 0 otherwise. Two coders examined the Factiva database for news articles using the executive's name near the dismissal date as well as other media sources discussing the departure, and only attempted to understand how media accounts portrayed the reasons the executive was removed. Examples include fraudulent behavior, stock option backdating, an affair with a company employee, or falsification of resumes. The coders agreed on 97.5% of all observations (Cohen's Kappa = 0.918) and identified 52 character questioning causal accounts.

Binary measure of whether the dismissed executive regained employment as a CEO of any firm. Executives were considered rehired as a CEO in a given year if they were listed as CEO on a publicly traded firm's SEC filings or were named CEO by an existing privately held company. The measure was captured dichotomously for each year for an executive until the point where the executive regained a CEO position or 5 years passed after dismissal. Executives who founded their own firm and named themselves as CEO following dismissal were excluded.
time_window: annual spells up to 5 years after dismissal

description: Dichotomous variable based on whether the CEO has been named the top CEO in his or her industry as reported by Institutional Investor in any year prior to the observation year. Institutional Investor asks buy- and sell-side analysts to identify the best executives from the companies they follow, reflecting the opinions of more than 1,300 analysts across 550 investment firms, and names a top CEO for each industry. The use of the Institutional Investor list to indicate CEO reputation is consistent with prior research using similar lists.
time_window: any year prior to the observation year

description: Dichotomous variable equal to 1 if the CEO attended either an Ivy League institution or one of the US News and World Report top 25 institutions as designated in 2011 for either undergraduate or graduate education, and 0 otherwise. These institutions represent those with national recognition for prestige. Elite education allows individuals to access a network of corporate elites with whom they share a common background.

Separate variable created in additional analyses to distinguish character questioning causal accounts relating to fiduciary duty from those relating to personal conduct. Of the 52 character questioning accounts, 41 suggested fiduciary duty violations and 11 were related to personal conduct violations.

The questionnaire asked "Are you self-employed?", coded 1 for working as self-employed. This dichotomous measure of current self-employment is the dependent variable of the main genetic model, and the authors describe it as their measure of self-employment. It is analyzed with a liability threshold model in which the presence or absence of entrepreneurship is based on the assumption of an underlying continuous liability.

The questionnaire asked "In your working life, how long have you been self employed?" The reported response format in the text is not specified; it is one of the additional operationalizations analyzed with a polychoric model based on asymptotically distribution free weighted least squares.

The questionnaire asked "Have you ever been an owner-operator of a company?" This dichotomous measure of ever having been an owner-operator of a company is one of the additional operationalizations, analyzed with a liability threshold model.
scale: 0/1 (1 = has been an owner-operator of a company)

description: The questionnaire asked "In your working life, how many companies have you been an owner-operator of?" This latter question is measured on the following scale: "one"; "two"; "three"; "four or more". It is one of the additional operationalizations, analyzed with a polychoric model.

The questionnaire asked "Have you ever started a new business?" This dichotomous measure of having started a new business is one of the additional operationalizations, analyzed with a liability threshold model.

The questionnaire asked "In your working life, how many new businesses have you started?" This latter question is measured on the following scale: "one"; "two"; "three"; "four or more". It is one of the additional operationalizations, analyzed with a polychoric model.

The questionnaire asked "Have you taken any actions toward the creation of a new business?" This dichotomous measure of ever having engaged in the business start-up process is one of the additional operationalizations, analyzed with a liability threshold model.
scale: 0/1 (1 = has taken actions toward the creation of a new business)

description: The questionnaire asked "In your working life, for how many new business ideas have you taken any actions toward the creation of a new business?" This latter question is measured on the following scale: "one"; "two"; "three"; "four or more". It is one of the additional operationalizations, analyzed with a polychoric model.

A single Likert scale item that asked respondents to indicate, on a scale from one (a very good career) to five (a very bad career), their view of entrepreneurship as a career. It was examined to identify the mechanism through which genetic factors operate.
scale: 1 (a very good career) to 5 (a very bad career)

description: The regression coefficient of the observed entrepreneurship variable on the latent additive genetic factor in the ACE structural equation model, estimated by maximum likelihood and interpreted as the proportion of variance in entrepreneurship attributable to additive genetic effects. If entrepreneurship is completely genetically determined the estimate would be 1.00, and if it is completely environmentally determined it would be zero. The latent additive genetic factors are correlated 1.0 for monozygotic and 0.5 for dizygotic twins. The coefficient estimated for the model serves as the key coefficient of interest.

The regression coefficient of the observed entrepreneurship variable on the latent common environmental factor in the ACE model, estimated by maximum likelihood and interpreted as the proportion of variance attributable to the environmental factors that people in the same family have in common. The latent common environmental factors are correlated 1.0 for both monozygotic and dizygotic twins.

The regression coefficient of the observed entrepreneurship variable on the latent unique (nonshared) environmental factor in the ACE model, estimated by maximum likelihood and interpreted as the proportion of variance attributable to environmental influences unique to an individual; the coefficient for nonshared environmental effects includes measurement error.

Measured as the difference between the cost savings expected from the offshoring project and the achieved cost savings. Both expected and achieved savings are measured as a share of total costs, so the value can vary from zero percent (when achieved savings equal expectations) to 100 percent (when expected savings are very high but no savings are actually achieved). Cases in which achieved savings are above expectations ('hidden benefits') are deleted from the sample.

A composite measure consisting of three dimensions capturing structural, operational, and social complexity: global diversity of offshore operations, disaggregation of activities, and spread of employees. After each dimension is measured, they are standardized and mean-centered around zero, and the measure is constructed as the product of these dimensions, all of which have equal weight in the composite measure.

Measured as the degree to which service providers view a particular task or process as complex. Data are collected in the service provider survey by asking service providers to rank the complexity of different types of tasks on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not complex at all; 5 = very complex); the variable is the average of these service-level scores.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not complex at all; 5 = very complex)
level: service level, aggregated to the offshoring implementation

description: A simple measure made for each implementation, measured as the time in years between the launch of the first offshoring project by the focal firm and the initiation of the focal implementation. The assumption is that the longer the firm has been engaged in offshoring projects, the more experience it has accumulated.

Respondents indicate the extent to which 'business process redesign' is a driver for offshoring particular services on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not important at all; 5 = very important). The measure captures the extent to which offshoring projects related to particular services have been implemented in conjunction with optimizing the entire work process, and is used as a proxy for the level of managerial attention given to the orchestration of globally distributed processes.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not important at all; 5 = very important)

description: Offshoring complexity is measured along two dimensions: configuration complexity (composite of number of countries, number of services offshored and number of employees in offshore projects) and task complexity (service provider rating of how complex a task is). Both enter the models as separate variables.

Board leadership structure is binary for purposes of analysis. CEO duality is evident if and only if the CEO also served as board chairperson; if different individuals served in these capacities, the roles are independent. These data were derived from Standard and Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors, and Executives. The analysis is restricted to firms that experienced no change in their governance structure over the period.

Return on investment is one of the three accounting return indices used as dependent variables. All performance data were derived from COMPUSTAT sources and Standard and Poor's Stock Reports. The authors report that ROI is correlated with ROE (0.60, p < 0.001) and with profit margin (0.51, p < 0.001), which motivated the multivariate analysis of variance. Mean ROI by year is compared across the two governance groups.

Return on equity is one of the three accounting return indices used as dependent variables. All performance data were derived from COMPUSTAT sources and Standard and Poor's Stock Reports. The authors report that ROE is correlated with ROI (0.60, p < 0.001) and with profit margin (0.46, p < 0.001). Mean ROE by year is compared across the two governance groups.

Profit margin is one of the three accounting return indices used as dependent variables. All performance data were derived from COMPUSTAT sources and Standard and Poor's Stock Reports. The authors report that profit margin is correlated with ROI (0.51, p < 0.001) and with ROE (0.46, p < 0.001). Mean profit margin by year is compared across the two governance groups.

Respondents (first respondents) indicate the extent to which they perceive that their partners' knowledge inputs along eight specific knowledge domains overlap with or are complementary to their own knowledge, on a seven-point semantic scale anchored 'overlapping' to 'complementary'. The measure is new to this study, based on a review of relevant literature and interviews. Cronbach's alpha is 0.88. To verify the measure, the authors also gathered the same measure from second respondents and used it to calculate interrater reliability, which supports the measure's validity.

Measured with data collected from second respondents, using a six-item, seven-point semantic differential scale adapted from Rindfleisch and Moorman (2001); one item was dropped because of its low factor loading. The scale items ask respondents about the extent to which the developed product is novel and offers new ideas to the industry. Cronbach's alpha is 0.91.
time_window: product on the market at least six months; average 11 months since product development completion

description: A newly developed, five-item, seven-point Likert scale. Respondents indicate the extent to which completing each stage of the new product development process depends on input and frequent collaboration by both partners. Cronbach's alpha is 0.86.

Three items adapted from Griffin (1997). On a seven-point semantic scale, respondents evaluate the extent to which the development process is complex and technical and spans a wide range of functions. Cronbach's alpha is 0.74.

The measure comes from Jaworski and Kohli (1993): five seven-point Likert scale items evaluating the extent to which customer preferences, technology, and competitors' actions change rapidly and are unpredictable. Perceptions of environmental dynamism were measured by both the first and second respondents; Cronbach's alpha is 0.78 for first respondents and 0.78 for second respondents.

Four seven-point Likert scale items adapted from Li and Atuahene-Gima (2001). Respondents evaluate the extent to which the alliance has experienced more unfair competitive practices by other firms in the industry and indicate the effectiveness of laws designed to protect the alliance's intellectual property. Measured with both first and second respondents; Cronbach's alpha is 0.82 for first respondents and 0.76 for second respondents.

A firm's market share in a given technology generation in a given year, consistent with prior research on firm performance in new technology generations. The main analysis uses a semi-log specification in which the logarithm of generation share is the dependent variable. As a robustness check the authors also consider a firm's cumulative market share over the entire life of the technology generation.
time_window: given year within a technology generation

description: Entry timing for the firm in the new technology generation, where entry is defined as the first occurrence of revenue for a firm in a given generation. The first firm to enter the generation was assigned a value of one and subsequent firms were assigned values with reference to the years elapsed since the first entrant (a firm entering a generation three years after the leader was assigned a value of four). Lower values therefore indicate earlier entry timing, i.e., greater leadership.

A count of Solid State Technology articles that discuss ecosystem innovation challenges, formed as the sum of the number of articles that discussed innovation challenges in the lens and the source for a technology generation. Articles were matched to a generation and ecosystem element using titles, with abstracts and conclusions consulted when titles were insufficient, and only articles published no later than five years after the commercialization of the first tool in a generation were included. Component challenge for generation g is computed as innov lg + innov sg.
time_window: articles published no later than five years after the commercialization of the first tool in a generation (1961-2001 search)

description: A count of Solid State Technology articles that discuss ecosystem innovation challenges, formed as the sum of the number of articles that discussed innovation challenges in the resist and the mask for a technology generation. Articles were matched to a generation and ecosystem element using titles, with abstracts and conclusions consulted when titles were insufficient, and only articles published no later than five years after the commercialization of the first tool in a generation were included. Complement challenge for generation g is computed as innov rg + innov mg.
time_window: articles published no later than five years after the commercialization of the first tool in a generation (1961-2001 search)

description: The variable takes a value of one if the firm produced its own lens component in a given technology generation and zero otherwise. During the history of the industry no tool manufacturer produced its own energy source.
The number of years that have lapsed since the first commercial sale of a tool in the given technology generation, where the first year of commercial sales is coded as one.

A dummy variable taking a value of 1 for inventors from the acquired firms and 0 otherwise. It was used in the multivariate test of Hypotheses 1, 2a, and 2b, where inventors from nonacquired firms (Table 4a) or inventors from acquiring firms (Table 4b) were the comparison group.
scale: 1 = inventor from an acquired firm; 0 otherwise

description: The total number of granted patents filed by an inventor with a focal firm in a given year after a relevant acquisition; for acquired inventors the focal firm is the acquiring firm. Each inventor's postacquisition innovation productivity was observed for five years after an acquisition, and patents were counted by the year in which the successful application was filed.

A dummy coded 1 if an acquired firm and its acquiring firm participated in similar activities in the semiconductor industry, that is, fell into the same activity category of the authors' classification scheme (integrated device manufacturer, fabless semiconductor, semiconductor system manufacturer, semiconductor manufacturing equipment supplier, semiconductor materials supplier, contract design services provider, software developer); 0 otherwise. The authors assumed that each category was equally different from the others. The classification was informed by interviews with industry participants and industry reports.

The number of patents and backward patent citations common to an acquiring and acquired firm prior to acquisition, divided by the number of patents and backward citations of the acquired firm prior to acquisition. A firm's knowledge base was defined as the list of patents obtained by that firm's inventors five years prior to acquisition plus all backward citations made in those patents. For example, a value of one-quarter results when patent C is common to both knowledge bases.
time_window: five years prior to the acquisition

description: The number of employees in the target firm in the year the acquisition took place divided by the number of employees in the acquiring firm in that year.

Respondents selected the degree of contract specificity by choosing the likelihood that they would use highly detailed and specific contracts to govern the new Web development work. A contract was defined for respondents as 'the written arrangement between the respondent's firm and the partner firm.'

Dichotomous scenario manipulation reflecting the partner's performance within the context of Web development. In the high condition respondents read 'your partner has provided high-quality Web development work,' and in the low condition they read 'your partner has provided some substandard Web development work.'

Dichotomous scenario manipulation reflecting the extent to which the partner had performed reliably in another context (database management). High: 'your partner has reliably maintained your database in the past; there have been no problems with the database crashing.' Low: 'your partner has not reliably maintained your database in the past; there have been some issues with the database crashing.'

Dichotomous scenario manipulation describing the extent to which the partner had intentionally abused the Web development relationship for his or her own gain. High: 'you suspect your partner has inappropriately used processes/programs developed for your Web site for personal gain.' Low: 'you have no reason to suspect your partner has used processes/programs developed for your Web site in an inappropriate manner.'

Dichotomous scenario manipulation describing the extent to which the partner had intentionally abused the relationship in another context for his or her own gain. High: 'you suspect your partner has inappropriately used information from your database for personal gain.' Low: 'you have no reason to suspect your partner has used information from your database in an inappropriate manner.'

All firms founded in the sample were tabulated for each province-year and the natural logarithm was then taken, adding one to handle province-years with no founding. To test Hypothesis 2, founding was split based on whether the firm entered a science park based on its reported address.
The reform variable was one for years after 1998 (the year KIP was initiated) and zero for any year before 1998.

CAS is the total number of CAS research institutes in a given province for a given year. The founding year and province of each research institute were collected from the CAS website, and CAS was recoded based on directories from the CAS Statistical Yearbooks during the time period, yielding consistent results.

Founding was split based on whether the firm entered a science park based on its reported address. As multiple terms are used to signify science parks in China, several keywords were used to capture this variable. Because data were collected from multiple registration sites, this measure also accounts for the possibility that a firm moved locations and thus has multiple reported addresses within its lifetime.
scale: binary (inside vs. outside a science park)

description: Provinces were split into quartiles based on their share of invention patents, or alternatively based on their high-tech founding share, to measure technological development. A higher share indicates greater technological development.

Market development is defined in terms of the first four NERI indicators: government-market relationship, private (nonstate) economic development, product market development, and factor market development. For each indicator, the sample was median split on whether the province was on or above versus below the median for the majority of years in which the analysis was undertaken; a higher score indicates greater marketization.
scale: median split into high and low

description: Legal development is defined in terms of the fifth and final NERI indicator, market intermediaries and legal environment development. The sample was median split on whether the province was on or above versus below the median for the majority of years in which the analysis was undertaken; a higher score indicates greater formal legalization and a lower score indicates less.
scale: median split into high and low

description: A growth-based measure: growth in total industry sales, calculated by dividing the regression slope coefficient by the mean value for shipments (1977-80) for the four-digit SIC codes of the firm's three largest lines of business, which on average represent 76 percent of the firm's total sales. For each firm a weighted industry portfolio measure was calculated by multiplying the firm's relative sales for each industry by that industry's data and aggregating the results. Data are from the U.S. Statistical Abstract for 1977 to 1980.

Measured by changes in the number and size of competitors within the industry, using absolute changes in the four-firm sales concentration ratio (the percentage of total industry sales originated by the leading four firms) for each business in the firm's portfolio, weighted by that business's relative sales revenue and aggregated for the firm. Large absolute changes in the firm's weighted concentration ratio indicate high degrees of environmental instability. Data were gathered from the FTC Line of Business data base.

Measured using product specialization ratios; the value of a plant's primary products in comparison to the value of its total production is its degree of specialization, so high specialization represents homogeneity of operating requirements. The specialization ratio for each line of business was subtracted from one so that increasing environmental complexity is indicated by larger values of the variable, multiplied by its relative firm sales, and aggregated for each firm into a weighted average specialization ratio. Industry specialization ratios at the four-digit SIC code level were gathered from the U.S. Census of Manufacturers.

variable_name: firm performance (ROA relative to the industry)
description: A three-year average of the firm's Return on Assets divided by the three-year average industry ROA, for the time period 1977-80, which immediately precedes the turnover period being studied. All data on firm and industry performance were gathered from the COMPUSTAT data base.

Change in the firm's diversification strategy from 1977 to 1980, based on line of business data from TrInet, where the diversification strategy of the organization was measured using the entropy measure (Jacquemin and Berry, 1979). The entropy formula itself is not readable in the supplied text, so the exact specification of the index cannot be recorded.

The coefficient of variation of team tenure, calculated by dividing the standard deviation by the mean, measured for the 1980 period. The coefficient of variation was preferred over the standard deviation or variance because of its scale invariant properties. Team tenure heterogeneity was selected as the most relevant cohort-related trait because age, organizational tenure and team tenure measures tend to be highly correlated.

Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity applied to education curriculum, measured using the specialization of the highest obtained university degree, measured for the 1980 period. The index is calculated as one minus the sum of the squared proportions of the group's individuals in each of the five educational curriculum categories.

The proportion of team members in 1980 who were no longer with the firm in 1983 and were less than 65 years of age in 1983. Managers equal to or greater than 65 years of age in 1983 were eliminated to control for the effects of normal retirements. The absence or presence of individuals in the top management team was ascertained by the executive listings in the Reference Book of Corporate Managements for 1980 and 1983. The three-year window was chosen as long enough for sufficient turnover to occur yet short enough to observe the effects of demographic heterogeneity measured in 1980.

The dependent variable is a firm's R&D lab investment in a given year in crore (1 crore is equivalent to 10,000,000 rupees) as reported in DSIR's Annual Report. For firms with a single R&D lab this is the investment in their specific R&D laboratory, while for firms with multiple R&D labs it is their investment across all R&D facilities, and the amount reported is assigned to each R&D lab of a multilab firm. The dependent variable is measured in year t + 1 while all independent and control variables are measured at year t. Standard errors are clustered by firm to account for the assignment of the firm amount to each lab.

Based on the number of domestic R&D labs in the same industry in the same metropolitan area, taken from the Directory of Recognized In-House R&D Units. It is defined as the share of the total number of domestic labs in a metropolitan area accounted for by the industry number of labs in the metropolitan area, divided by the share of the total number of labs in India accounted for by the number of labs in that particular industry. The paper's rendering of the equation could not be read. A higher value indicates a higher degree of industry agglomeration in a metropolitan area than a random distribution across the country would predict.

A measure analogous to domestic intra-industry specialization but computed for foreign-owned R&D labs in a metropolitan area. Foreign firms are identified using Prowess and Internet searches. The paper's rendering of the equation could not be read.

Accounts for the presence of domestic R&D labs from industries other than the focal industry of an R&D lab in a metropolitan area. It is nearly identical to domestic intra-industry specialization, but it accounts for the number of R&D labs from other industries (−s) in a metropolitan area (r). A higher value indicates a greater diversity of domestic labs across industries in a particular metropolitan area. The paper's rendering of the equation could not be read.
Accounts for the effect of the presence of foreign R&D labs from other industries in a metropolitan area. The paper's rendering of the equation could not be read.

The standard deviation of return on assets (ROA) based on quarterly data over a two-year period, following the common proxy of the standard deviation of returns. Realized risk can deviate from managers' intended risk because of momentum in firms' strategies and uncontrollable environmental influences, which is why past risk is controlled for. The dependent risk variables were measured in 1995-96, 1997-98, and 1999-2000.

Altman's (1983) discriminant function to identify firms threatened by bankruptcy, computed as (1.2 x working capital divided by total assets) + (1.4 x retained earnings divided by total assets) + (3.3 x income before interest expense and taxes divided by total assets) + (0.6 x market value of equity divided by total liability) + (1.0 x sales divided by total assets). The lower the Z, the higher the likelihood of bankruptcy. The Z-scores for the regression models corresponded to the year prior to the two-year period of the dependent risk variable; firms with Z-scores in the lowest 10 percent of the sample were selected as the low performers.
time_window: year prior to the two-year period of the dependent risk variable

description: Model 1 assumes firm j formulated aspirations in terms of its own two-period-lagged performance (Pj,t-2), which is compared with its previous-period performance (Pj,t-1). Two alternative performance indicators were used: return on assets (net income divided by total assets) and the equity market-to-book ratio (market value of common equity divided by its book value). Annually reported financial ratios were averaged over the two years in each period.

Model 2 assumes the relevant comparison affecting risk was previous-period performance (Pj,t-1) relative to the previous-period industry median performance (Ij,t-2). The same alternative performance indicators were used, return on assets and the market-to-book ratio, and industry medians were computed for four-digit SIC categories.

The treatment effect was tested using the interaction of two dummy variables. Treatment was coded one for observations of a firm's individuals who experienced the treatment and zero otherwise; Post was coded one for observations in the posttreatment period and 0 for those in the pretreatment period.
scale: two 0/1 dummy variables and their interaction

description: To test H1, the authors used the adjacency matrices and computed Burt's measures of network constraints in R-3.6, which is an inverse measure of structural holes. Network constraints capture the extent to which the focal individual concentrates resources within an interconnected group.

The authors created a vector of expertise for the focal individual and for each alter in the ego-centric network, regarding individuals who filed patent applications for a subclass between t-3 and t-1 as having expertise in that subclass at time t, and used Sampson's (2007) measure of alter dissimilarity. Because Sampson's measure assesses dyad-level knowledge dissimilarity and does not capture differences in network size, they made size-adjustments by multiplying the dissimilarity measure with the log of the number of alters. The equation itself is not readable in the supplied text.
level: individual-alter dyad aggregated to the ego network
time_window: expertise vectors from t-3 to t-1; dissimilarity measured at t

description: To test the effects of incentive redesign on the development of small networks (H3), the authors measured the degree of centrality of, or the number of unique alters in, the ego-centric networks at time t.

A firm's investment in knowledge assets was measured in terms of R&D investment, normalized as a firm's R&D expenditures divided by its total assets. Information about firms' R&D investments comes primarily from company annual reports, which disclose R&D spending following China's Accounting Standard for Business Enterprises (No. 6-Intangible assets).

Firm value was computed by dividing the market value of a firm's equity by the book value of its total assets, which was provided by the CSMAR database. It is a market-based measure of financial performance.
Return on assets (ROA) was calculated by dividing reported net income in a fiscal year by the balance sheet value of total assets. It is an accounting-based measure of financial performance.

Ownership concentration was represented by a dummy variable set equal to '1' when the percentage of shares held by the three largest shareholders is above the sample median. The three largest shareholders usually were institutional owners (called legal person shares in Chinese) for these listed companies.

Top management team equity ownership was represented by a dummy variable set equal to '1' when the percentage of each company's shares held by the managers is above the sample median. The managers were identified by their names in the company's annual reports, which were collected by the CSMAR database.
CEO duality was represented by a dummy variable set equal to '1' when a CEO also chaired the board of directors and '0' otherwise.

The sample was split based on the level of regional institutional development, captured by the NERI indices. Among the five subindices of marketization, the credit market index and the legal environment index are most pertinent for the study; the credit market index is the percentage of deposits taken by nonstate financial institutions and the percentage of bank loans credited to nonstate enterprises for each province or provincial level region, and the legal environment index captures the number of independent accountants, lawyers, consultants and chambers of commerce, the legal environment for business, and the protection of intellectual property rights. The two subindices were then combined into a composite index, Regional institutional development, and a firm is in a high institutional development region if it is headquartered in a region where the composite index is above the sample median, and in a low institutional development region otherwise.

The focal firm's shortest (geodesic) distance to all other firms within the network. Six N x N binary matrices are based on the accumulated alliance data for 49 firms from 1989 to the year of observation, between 1991 and 1996, each representing the absence or presence of a nondirectional tie between two firms. UCINET 6 generates the firm-year closeness centrality index, normalized by dividing the firm's index by the maximum possible closeness centrality index in the network. The index ranges from zero percent, where the firm is not reachable, to 100 percent, where the firm is closest to all other firms.
time_window: 1989 to the year of observation (1991-1996); lagged one year in the estimations

description: The number of actual ties among the focal firm's partners, divided by the total number of potential ties among partners. The measure provides an indication of the cohesiveness of subgroups that enables information flows and mutual influence through direct and indirect ties in the ego networks. It is computed for each firm-year observation from the accumulated alliance data.
time_window: accumulated alliance data from 1989 to the year of observation; lagged one year in the estimations

variable_name: Number of partners with repeated ties
description: Equals the number of direct partners with which a firm had established more than one technology alliance, derived for each firm-year observation from the accumulated alliance data. Only one third of the sample firms have established ties with former partners, and the count of these partners is relatively small. The simple count is used rather than a proportion measure because it better reflects a firm's decision to select a few trusted partners for repeated collaborations.
time_window: accumulated alliance data from 1989 to the year of observation; lagged one year in the estimations

description: The count of product awards conferred by trade publishers on new products in each observation year, used as the proxy for innovation performance. Awards come from trade publications that company executives strongly agreed were most highly regarded for new product awards between 1991 and 1996. Products are evaluated through technical benchmarking tests in labs or through polling of editors and lead users. The authors note that award count is a relatively good alternative proxy because patent data tend to reflect outcomes of R&D performed at least 18 months in the past.

A firm's annual R&D expenses, used as a proxy for the extent of resources committed to maintain and develop new and existing products and for the firm's resource position. Competing firms keep track of R&D-related announcements by others, the details of which may include plans for next-generation technology, joint product development, or technology acquisitions. The financial data, including R&D investment and sales revenue, come from Compustat and company-specific 10K reports.
time_window: annual; lagged one year in the estimations

description: Residuals from the regression of the natural log of total CEO pay on a set of theoretically relevant human capital, organizational, and industry factors held to be determinants of CEO pay (a 'CEO wage equation'). A negative residual suggests underpayment because the CEO's actual total pay was less than his or her predicted total pay. CEO underpayment is coded as equal to 1 when the CEO's residual wage score was in the lowest quartile of all CEO residual scores in the sample, and 0 otherwise. The omitted reference group comprises CEOs paid more closely to the executive labor market rate, whose residuals were in the second and third quartiles. Under- and overpayment are entered in the models lagged one year (year t - 1).
scale: binary (1 = lowest quartile of residual wage scores)
time_window: year t - 1 (one year before the outcome)

description: Residuals from the regression of the natural log of total CEO pay on a set of theoretically relevant human capital, organizational, and industry factors held to be determinants of CEO pay (a 'CEO wage equation'). A positive residual represents a condition in which the CEO was overpaid because the CEO's actual total pay was greater than his or her predicted total pay. CEO overpayment is coded as equal to 1 when the CEO's residual wage score was in the highest quartile in the sample, and 0 otherwise, with CEOs paid more closely to the market rate (second and third quartiles) as the reference group. The variable is entered in the models lagged one year (year t - 1).
scale: binary (1 = highest quartile of residual wage scores)
time_window: year t - 1 (one year before the outcome)

description: Calculated as (size t - size t - 1)/size t - 1, where size t represents firm size in any given year t and size t - 1 represents firm size in the previous year; this relative measure helps to control for the fact that larger organizations have greater resources to put forth to growth. Firm size itself is measured as a composite index represented by the single factor resulting from a principal components analysis of two indicators: the natural log of firm sales and the natural log of the number of employees.
time_window: change from year t - 1 to year t

description: Categorical variable such that situations in which the CEO left the position and either became a director or retained a previously held directorship were coded as equal to 1, and 0 otherwise. Firm proxy statements around a CEO's departure were examined to determine the cause for departure. The initial number of observations of CEO turnover was 259, from which six observations were removed where turnover was caused by death or where the cause of turnover was clearly labeled as a dismissal; of the 253 remaining turnover observations, 155 involved the CEO becoming a director, or retaining a directorship, after the turnover event.

Firm profitability is measured using return on assets (ROA), calculated as the firm's net income divided by total assets for each year. Change in firm profitability is calculated as (ROA t - ROA t - 1)/ROA t - 1, where ROA t represents firm profitability in any given year t and ROA t - 1 represents firm profitability in the previous year.
time_window: change from year t - 1 to year t

description: Ownership structure of the firm was measured using a five percent equity-holding threshold to sort organizations into three categories. Manager-controlled (MC) is a dummy variable equal to 1 in which no single equity holder owns five percent or more of the organization's common stock, 0 otherwise. Owner-managed (OM) is a dummy variable equal to 1 in which the CEO owns five percent or more of the common stock, 0 otherwise. Owner-controlled (OC) is a dummy variable equal to 1 in which at least one equity holder, who is not the CEO, owns five percent or more of the common stock, and 0 otherwise. OC firms are the omitted reference category in the tests for voluntary CEO withdrawal and firm size, and MC firms are the omitted reference category in the tests pertaining to firm profitability.

The CEO evaluated each of six capabilities against his/her firm's major competitors' functionally similar capabilities, on a scale from weaker position (-2) to among the strongest positions (2), with 0 as an average position. Each capability score above parity (zero) was coded as a capability strength; scores of zero contribute to neither set. The strength set score was computed with Deephouse's (1999) approach, standardizing the strength score of each capability by its three-digit industry average and standard deviation (the exact equation is unreadable in the text).
scale: -2 (weaker position) to 2 (among the strongest positions) per capability item

description: Each capability score below parity (zero) was coded as a capability weakness, and the absolute value of the raw weakness scores was obtained before computing the variable. The weakness set score was then computed with the corresponding Deephouse (1999) industry-standardized equation (the exact equation is unreadable in the text).
scale: -2 (weaker position) to 2 (among the strongest positions) per capability item

description: An accounting-based measure of firm value-added, calculated by subtracting from the firm's total revenue any intermediate consumption (raw materials, semifinished products, external services used to manufacture finished products, energy consumption, etc.); it approximates the full value actually created by the firm through its operations before distribution to stakeholders. Value-added was used because many firms in the sample are private and because it is less likely to reflect owners' tax strategies. To calculate the relative performance measure, value-added was industry centered on three-digit industry classifications and lagged to correspond to firm performance two years after the year the survey was completed.
time_window: two years after the year the survey was completed

description: Following Sutcliffe's (1994) approach, industry sales were used to create a time trend regression analysis; munificence is the unstandardized regression coefficient in the regression model divided by the mean of industry sales, so a greater value indicates a higher industry munificence score. The data were not obtained through the Sesame surveys but were independently collected by the Banque de France as part of its population-level data collection effort, reflecting the entire population of firms in the focal industry.
Prior performance is proxied by the firm's return on assets for the year of the first survey. These data were gathered independently of the survey, so common method variance is not a concern.
time_window: the year of the first survey

description: The difference between the strength set at the time of the second survey and the strength set at the time of the first survey. The variable was computed for the 1,578 firms that were surveyed twice.
time_window: between the first survey (2001-2003) and the second survey (2004-2006)

description: The difference between the weakness set at the time of the second survey and the weakness set at the time of the first survey. The variable was computed for the 1,578 firms that were surveyed twice.
time_window: between the first survey (2001-2003) and the second survey (2004-2006)

description: Experimental treatment taking a value of 1 for the groups shown CEO compensation that increased by 20 percent over the previous year, from about $9 million to $11 million, and 0 for the groups shown compensation that decreased by 20 percent, from $13 million to $11 million. $11 million was roughly the median pay for a Fortune 500 CEO in 2010, and current pay served as the reference point against which the change was evaluated. Assignment was random.
time_window: current year relative to previous year

description: Experimental treatment taking a value of 1 for the groups whose scenario described CEO compensation at the 95th percentile for Fortune 500 CEOs and 0 for those shown CEO compensation at the 5th percentile. In both cases pay increased year-over-year by only 5 percent. Assignment was random.
time_window: current year relative to previous year

description: Experimental treatment taking a value of 1 for the groups shown a firm whose shareholder return lagged behind the average S&P 500 shareholder return, and 0 for the groups shown a firm whose shareholder return exceeded the average. Participants read a proxy statement in which the firm either grew shareholder value by 35 percent or saw shareholder value decline by 5 percent, contrasted with an average S&P 500 shareholder return of 15 percent, giving a 20 percentage point gain or loss.

Experimental treatment taking a value of 1 for the groups shown a scenario about a firm whose shareholder return lagged behind the industry average, and 0 for groups shown a firm with shareholder return leading the industry average. Instead of the S&P 500 used in Study 1, shareholder return was benchmarked to the industry average, with the relative numbers held at 20 percent above or below.

The participant's vote in the simulated say-on-pay vote, coded 1 if the shareholder voted to approve the CEO's compensation and 0 if he or she voted to reject. The vote outcome was modeled using logistic regression, and the marginal effects of the independent variables on the predicted probability of a vote for approval are presented.

The same outcome variable as in Study 1: the probability that a shareholder chooses to approve, rather than reject, CEO compensation, taking a value of 1 for a vote to approve the pay and 0 for a vote to reject. Logistic regression was used and marginal effects are reported.

Single-item measure reflecting the authors' definition, answered on a 7-point scale from 'strongly disagree' (1) to 'strongly agree' (7). Raw scores were standardized so that marginal effects are shown in terms of standard deviations rather than Likert scale points.

Three-item measure used instead of the single item of Study 1 to reduce potential measurement error. All three items were measured on a scale ranging from 'strongly disagree' (1) to 'strongly agree' (7); the three items were averaged and the average standardized to produce the final measure.

A dummy that takes the value 1 if the firm exits in that year, and 0 otherwise. The data are transformed so that the unit of observation is the firm in each year of activity, each observation being identified by the age of the firm in that year. To be classified as a closure, a firm must be absent from the file for at least two years.
A dummy variable taking the value 1 for firms in which all owners are immigrants, and 0 otherwise. The omitted category is firms created by native entrepreneurs with Portuguese nationality.
scale: dummy (1 = all owners are immigrants, 0 = otherwise)

description: The immigrant dummy is decomposed into two dummies. Immigrant-Distant takes the value 1 if the firm was created by immigrants from institutionally distant countries (countries that are neither Portuguese-speaking nor EU countries), and 0 otherwise. Immigrant-Close takes the value 1 if the firm was created by immigrants from institutionally close countries (Portuguese-speaking or EU countries), and 0 otherwise. The omitted category is firms created by native entrepreneurs.
scale: two dummies (1 = firm created by immigrants of that group, 0 = otherwise)

description: Local labor market experience is measured by the years that an individual was in the host country labor market before creating a particular firm. The proxy is a lower bound to the actual experience in the host country, traced from 1985 and accurately measurable up to 17 years. The measure is entered in logarithms.

The absolute number of people sharing the same nationality that works in firms located in the same county (concelho) as the firm. In the regressions the variable is entered scaled by 10 to the power of 6 (Community size/10^6).
scale: count of persons of the same nationality

description: The dependent variable was coded 1 if a firm's board of directors included at least one woman and 0 otherwise. Director gender was identified in four steps: a national KLD survey of women on boards was checked against the authors' database, press reports about female executives and board members were consulted, gender-specific names were identified, and any remaining gender-ambiguous names were searched online.
Organizational size was measured as the logarithm of sales, a metric commonly used in studies of firm size.

The percentage of employees who were women in each two-digit SIC industry category. The measure reflects annual Bureau of Labor Statistics statistics from the 1994-2004 editions of Employment and Earnings.

Palepu's (1985) entropy measure was used to gauge diversification. The entropy measure for related diversification captures the extent to which a company's sales are represented by similar industry segments and related industry groups; the measure for unrelated diversification gauges the extent to which the firm's sales are derived from different two-digit SIC industries.

The total number of women directors to whom a focal firm was linked through its outside directors. The variable is a count of female directors on the boards of the other firms where the focal firm's directors served on either the top management team or the board.

variable_name: Responsiveness to the change in AACSB accreditation standards
description: Ordinal scale based on a brief semistructured telephone interview with the head of the business program at each institution, typically the dean of the business school or the chair of the business department, conducted during the 1993-94 academic year. A code of 3 indicated that a school had taken active steps to become accredited, at a minimum completing accreditation fact finding by forming a committee charged with determining what it would have to do to become accredited, and possibly entering precandidacy or candidacy; a code of 2 indicated that the school had investigated accreditation by attending a workshop on the new AACSB standards; a code of 1 indicated that the school intended to seek accreditation sometime during the next five years although no other steps had been taken; and a code of 0 indicated that the school had no intention to seek accreditation in the next five years. Each school was assigned to only one point on the scale, the highest-coded activity completed.

Percentage of the school's students majoring in business, taken from Lovejoy's College Guide. It measures the potential economic value of accreditation, which the authors argue is higher for schools with a large proportion of business students. This variable had a nontrivial amount of missing data; for cases in which it was missing the mean was substituted, and a binary variable coded 1 if the mean value was substituted and 0 otherwise was included in all regression models.

Percentage of students whose permanent address is in a different state than the school, taken from Peterson's Guide to Four-Year Colleges. The authors treat it as an indicator of a school's dependence on a geographically broad, national pool of prospective students who are likely to use accreditation in their decision making.

Annual tuition in thousands of dollars, taken from Peterson's Guide to Four-Year Colleges. Higher values indicate the high-cost, high-prestige market niche that the authors argue is associated with stronger pressure to seek accreditation.

Percentage of applicants for admission who are rejected, taken from Peterson's Guide to Four-Year Colleges and used as an assessment of selectivity. In a footnote the authors report that the rejection rate had a significant positive correlation with the proportion of applicants with high SAT math scores, with high SAT verbal scores, and with applicants in the top 10 percent of their high school classes, which they present as evidence that the rejection rate does assess selectivity.

Binary variable indicating whether the dean or head of the business program was ever previously employed by an AACSB-accredited institution, as either a faculty member or an administrator; 1 = "yes," 0 = "no." It was collected in the telephone interview with the head of the business program.
Binary variable indicating whether the school is currently a member of the AACSB; 1 = "yes," 0 = "no." Taken from the 1991 AACSB membership directory.

Total number of accreditations held by all units in the university, taken from Lovejoy's College Guide. It is used as an indicator of local norms about accreditation and of possible coercive pressure from the central administration to become accredited.

Binary variable coded 1 = "public" and 0 = "private," taken from Peterson's Guide to Four-Year Colleges. It distinguishes nonmarket-like public schools from market-like private schools in the analysis.

Firms invest in lobbying, PAC contributions, soft money contributions (legal until 2003), and contributions to 527 groups. Exploratory factor analysis validated that these four measures constituted one factor, which the authors call 'corporate political investments,' regardless of the rotation method used. Data sources reflect federal-level data. In the second-stage regressions the authors use the residual values of CPI from the first-stage regression as the instrument.

Cumulative CPI is the firm's cumulative spending on PAC, lobbying, soft money, and 527 groups across sample years. The measure reflects the current year's CPI plus the previous years' CPI. As with CPI, the residual values from the first-stage regression are used as the instrument in the second-stage regression.

For each firm, a dummy variable representing the existence of directors with prior public service. Any political service tie between directors and federal or state institutions is included, including federal public service as members of the U.S. Congress, ambassadors, ministers, secretaries, and undersecretaries, as well as service in state government such as governors and legislators. Directors' personal biographies and firms' 10-K reports were examined.
scale: dummy (1 = existence of such directors; 0 otherwise)

description: A dummy measure of regulation that differentiates between regulated and nonregulated industries based on Grier, Munger, and Roberts (1994). For example, regulated industries include utilities, telecommunications, transportation, energy, banking, oil, and insurance.

Dollar value of firms' equity at the end of the firm's calendar year. It is one of two complementary measures of firm performance used as dependent variable; the number of firm-year observations for this dependent variable is 8,410.
time_window: end of the firm's calendar year

description: Net income before extraordinary items to total revenue. It is the second complementary measure of firm performance used as dependent variable; the number of firm-year observations for this dependent variable is 10,204.

Country of the responding executive, coded as a dummy variable (0 = U.S., 1 = Korean). It was used as the moderator in moderated regression analysis of the criteria used in strategic decisions and to split respondents into separate U.S. and Korean policy-capturing models.

variable_name: standardized regression coefficients for the decision criteria
description: The instrument contained 30 acquisition cases in which each of the 15 target-firm criteria was randomly varied on a 1 (low) to 5 (high) scale, and executives rated each target's attractiveness as an acquisition candidate and the probability of acquisition on 1-7 scales that were combined into a single dependent variable (coefficient alpha 0.90).
