Policy-capturing models regress these ratings on the 15 criteria, and the standardized coefficients represent the weight placed on each criterion; separate models were developed for the U.S. and Korean executives. A moderated regression analysis with country as a moderator tested whether the criteria used vary by an executive's home country.

Standardized regression coefficient for the industry attractiveness criterion in the policy-capturing model of executives' ratings of acquisition candidates, estimated separately for the U.S. and Korean samples.
level: criterion weight in country-level regression model

description: Standardized regression coefficients for the sales and the market share criteria in the policy-capturing models of executives' ratings of acquisition candidates, estimated separately for the U.S. and Korean samples.
level: criterion weight in country-level regression model

description: Standardized regression coefficients for ROI, stock price, discounted cash flow and projected demand in the policy-capturing models of executives' ratings of acquisition candidates, estimated separately for the U.S. and Korean samples.
level: criterion weight in country-level regression model

variable_name: manufacturing ability and R&D ability criteria
description: Standardized regression coefficients for the manufacturing ability and the R&D ability criteria in the policy-capturing models of executives' ratings of acquisition candidates, estimated separately for the U.S. and Korean samples.
level: criterion weight in country-level regression model

description: Standardized regression coefficient for the management talent criterion in the policy-capturing models of executives' ratings of acquisition candidates, estimated separately for the U.S. and Korean samples.
level: criterion weight in country-level regression model

description: An option-based indicator following Malmendier and Tate (2005). The average realizable value per option is computed as the total realizable value of exercisable options divided by the number of exercisable options; the average exercise price is the fiscal year-end stock price minus the average realizable value per option; average moneyness is the average realizable value per option divided by the estimated average exercise price. The indicator takes a value of 1 for CEOs who do not exercise their exercisable options although they are at least 67% in the money, and 0 otherwise; CEOs had to exhibit this option-holding behavior at least twice during the sample period and were treated as overconfident for the rest of the sample period.

Directors' expertise with breakthrough innovations is captured through their board appointments at other firms that successfully produced breakthrough innovations while the focal director served on those boards; the director had to be appointed at least 1 year prior to the development of the breakthrough innovations and remain on the board for the subsequent year. The heterogeneity of these inter-organizational linkages is measured with the Blau (1977) heterogeneity index, 1 - sum p_i^2, where p_i is the proportion of interlocks within the ith three-digit SIC code category, over a five-year period from t - 4 to t. Multiple interlocks within the same three-digit SIC industry are aggregated so that the index is computed based on 10 distinct industry categories; higher values indicate a more diverse set of experiences and knowledge related to breakthrough innovations.

An index of board power relative to the CEO comprising four indicators: board independence (the ratio of outside directors to the total number of directors), CEO non-duality (coded one if the CEO did not serve as chairman of the board and zero otherwise), relative CEO-board tenure (the average board tenure of the directors divided by the CEO's tenure) and relative CEO-board ownership (the ratio of outside directors' to CEO stock ownership). The index is the sum of the standard scores of these four variables.

The number of a firm's top-cited patents divided by the total number of patents of the firm in a given year. Top-cited patents are the top 1% of cited patents, identified using the number of forward citations a patent receives; following Hall et al. (2001) the number of a patent's forward citations is divided by the mean value of forward citations based on all patents in the same application year and technological subcategory. Breakthrough innovation is measured at t + 1 while predictors and controls are measured at t.

Number of new firms (founded in 1994 or later) listed in the GreenSpec directory for each state-year. Founding dates were obtained through a manual search of the firms listed in the directory, which located founding dates for 1,065 of the 2,604 unique U.S. firms listed. The measure was de-duplicated to show only the first listing of each firm, so it measures entry rather than a cumulative count.

Number of firms founded prior to 1994 listed in the GreenSpec directory for each state-year; these are diversifying incumbents that already existed before entering the focal industry, for which listing in the directory is taken as entry into the green building sector. The measure was de-duplicated to show only the first listing of each firm.

Number of new commercial building permits issued in a state during a given year, used to measure the overall rate of construction in a region as an indicator of economic conditions surrounding the emergent green building supply industry.

Count of LEED-certified projects in a state during a given year, used to measure economic opportunity specifically in green building. The US Green Building Council provided these data directly to the authors.

Cumulative count of state-level policies in place that provide regulatory requirements for LEED certification in a state-year. The authors gathered data on 38 state-level policies supporting green building and coded each policy into one of two categories, of which this is the regulatory category.

Cumulative count of state-level policies in place that provide economic incentives for LEED certification in a state-year. Coded from the 38 state-level green building policies gathered by the authors alongside the regulatory category.

Number of USGBC members in a given state-year, coded as a count variable, used to operationalize the state-level presence of collective action supporting the green building supply industry. The data were provided by the USGBC; membership is not necessary for LEED certification.

State-level measure of the social norm of environmentalism built from the General Social Survey question asking whether the country is spending too much, too little, or about the right amount on 'improving and protecting the environment'; responses of 'spending too little' were coded as environmentalism. Responses were collapsed by the median response for the state for each year, and scores for missing years were linearly interpolated using the ipolate command in Stata. GSS data from the years 2000, 2002, 2004 and 2006 were used.

Informants answered a series of 12 yes/no questions about their firms' actions taken in direct response to the loss of employees; nine of the 12 items were derived from a previously generated list of 16 possible responses, one item concerned requiring remaining employees to sign noncompete agreements, and two items asked about additional defensive and retaliatory actions. Each of the ten specific reactions was a priori classified as defensive or retaliatory, and the classification was validated in a content-validation study. Companies were classified as initiating a defensive response when they reported one or more defensive actions only; 62 firms (45.9 percent) fell in this category.

Firms reporting some type of retaliatory action among the 12 yes/no response items were classified as initiating a defensive-retaliatory response. All 32 retaliating companies had also taken some sort of defensive action, as expected; 32 companies (23.7 percent) were classified as defensive-retaliatory.

Three survey questions were treated as formative indicators of an index and averaged to create the observed variable. The questions asked whether sales of software and/or computer programming services are a significant source of revenues for the hiring company, how similar the products and services of the hiring company are to the target's, and how much overlap there is between the two firms' pools of current and potential customers. Because the variable was used in an interaction term, it was centered by subtracting the mean from each of its elements.
scale: similarity item: 1 = very different to 4 = highly similar; customer overlap item: 1 = no overlap at all to 4 = a great deal of overlap

description: A dichotomous indicator of whether the hiring firm is located outside the target firm's local labor market. Informants reported the driving time from where the former employees worked to the offices of the hiring company; a screening question about whether the hiring company was within one day's driving distance determined whether the driving-time question was asked. Nonlocal labor market competitors were defined as firms more than 90 minutes away by car from the focal firm.

Informants were asked to estimate the impact on firm financial performance of two levels of improvement in the performance of a person in the job from which the employees were hired: from low to average and from average to high. Each item used a four-point scale. The two items were averaged and centered.
scale: 1 = no impact at all to 4 = a great deal of impact

description: A two-item measure of how transferable the human capital developed by workers hired away from a target firm was. Informants indicated how much of the knowledge and skills employees learned in their jobs at the target company could be used at similar jobs in the high-tech industry, and whether the skills learned on their jobs increased their ability to move from one job to another in the high-tech industry. The items were averaged and centered.
scale: item 1: 1 = none to 5 = a great deal; item 2: 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree

description: Appendix A lists the six defensive action items used to classify a company's response set. Each item began 'In direct response to this loss of employees...' and was answered yes or no.

Coded from the job titles of inside directors other than the CEO in Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors. A formal ILM was recorded when a president, chief operating officer, or vice chairman (other than the CEO) was listed as both an officer of the company and a member of the board; such titles coupled with designation as inside directors signal that the occupants are potential contenders for the chief executive position. Formal ILMs for insider succession were in place in 65.4 percent of the CEO-years in the sample.

Constructed by taking the past history of formal designation of internal labor markets and calculating the number of years that a firm had an ILM for CEOs as a proportion of total years the firm had been in the sample, up to and including the current year. The authors note it is subject to some error in measurement because years prior to 1960 or when the firm was privately held are not included in the proportion.
time_window: up to and including the current year

description: CEO succession events were coded from Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors based on changes in the names of the relevant officers. CEOs were coded as insiders if they had been employees of the company for at least two years prior to becoming CEO; otherwise they were classified as outsiders. Data were supplemented by proxy statements, 10Ks, annual reports, and information from Who's Who in Industry and Finance to verify prior employment history.

CEO succession events were coded from Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors based on changes in the names of the relevant officers. CEOs were classified as outsiders if they had not been employees of the company for at least two years prior to becoming CEO; outside members of the board of directors who were appointed as CEOs were classified as outsiders.

One of four mutually exclusive categories of past succession experience, coded founder when the current CEO is the founder. The history of all CEOs in the company since 1950 was recorded from Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors; CEOs of new companies were classified as founders. In the sample 20.1 percent of the company-years were classified as founders.

One of four mutually exclusive categories of past succession experience, coded when all CEOs since 1950, other than the founder, were insiders. The history of all CEOs in the company since 1950 was recorded from Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors. In the sample 52.0 percent of the company-years were classified as past insiders.

One of four mutually exclusive categories of past succession experience, coded when all CEOs since 1950, other than the founder, were outsiders. The history of all CEOs in the company since 1950 was recorded from Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors. In the sample 12.6 percent of the company-years were classified as past outsiders.
Calculated from the date given in Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors of the year of the firm's initial founding or incorporation.

Measured the year the CEO was hired (minus 1900) and was intended to capture historical trends in the rate of CEO succession. It was also used to measure the effects of changing rules of insider succession in the industrial sector, assuming that CEOs are affected by the rules and expectations about CEO succession prevalent during the beginning of their tenure and that these rules were set for the remainder of their tenure. The variable was included in the b vector to account for the possibility that its effect on the rate of succession varies according to the length of tenure of the CEO.

Return on assets (ROA) adjusted for industry average, obtained from COMPUSTAT, used as an economic performance measure given past studies of CEO succession and selection. Data on ROA were lagged one year, and the correlation between adjusted and unadjusted ROA was .94.

Captured through the interaction of the founder category with the duration clock of the model, CEO tenure, which measures the number of years the incumbent has served as CEO and serves as the duration measure in all models estimated. Model 10 presents the interaction effects of founders and tenure, as captured in the b vector of the model.

Following Puffer and Weintrop (1991), retirement age was classified as 64 years old or over. Data on the CEO's age came from Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors, proxy statements, 10Ks, Who's Who in Industry and Finance, and the Wall Street Journal. In models distinguishing early CEO departures the variable is labelled late departure.
scale: dichotomous (1 = CEO is 64 years or older)

description: Estimated as the number of outside board members divided by the total number of directors. The number and affiliation of board members was determined from Standard and Poor's Directory of Corporations, Officers, and Directors, proxy statements, 10Ks, and Who's Who in Industry and Finance.

The eight sample firms are classified into the two groups of the Japanese carbon steel sector according to the technology and critical inputs they employ. The integrated mills produce steel by first converting iron ore into pig-iron in blast furnaces and subsequently reducing the pig-iron into steel in a basic oxygen furnace (BOF); the minimills produce steel by melting ferrous scrap in an electric arc furnace (EAF). The four integrated mills in the sample were Nippon, NKK, Kawasaki, and Sumitomo; the four minimills were Godo, Tokyo Steel, Tokyo Tekko, and Yamato Kogyo.

variable_name: cointegration tests (lambda Max and Trace statistics)
description: For each strategy variable, the Johansen (1988) procedure tests the number of cointegrating vectors among the strategy series of the firms in a group. Each row of the table tests the null hypothesis of rank = k using the lambda Max and Trace statistics. The finite sample critical values at 95 percent reported in Osterwald-Lenum (1992) are used, and the model is run with one lag of the endogenous variables.

An error correction process is added to the vector autoregression so that cointegration between strategies is not misspecified. Estimates of the short-run parameters along with estimates of the 'error correction term' (ECT) are obtained through maximum likelihood estimation, and the ECT consists of the speed of adjustment parameter and the parameters of the equilibrium long-run relationship. The firm reacts to its current departure from the group equilibrium in the subsequent periods.

The speed of adjustment parameter is the coefficient on the error correction term estimated for each firm and each nonstationary strategy in the vector error correction model. A negative estimate indicates that the firm reduces its deviation from the equilibrium in the following periods (converging behavior), while a positive estimate indicates divergence from the reference. Significance is judged with the traditional t-test with n = 18, with critical values of 1.330 at 10%, 1.734 at 5%, and 2.552 at 1%, using an estimation sample from 1980 to 1999 and one lag of the endogenous variables.
Cost efficiency was assessed by calculating the ratio of cost of goods sold to total sales. The variable was calculated for all eight firms in the sample for the period 1980-99.
Capital expenditures were assessed as net expenditures for plant and equipment. The variable was calculated for all eight firms in the sample for the period 1980-99.
Capital intensity was assessed as the ratio of total assets to the number of employees. The variable was calculated for all eight firms in the sample for the period 1980-99.
Exports is operationalized as the percentage of foreign sales to total sales for the firm. The variable was calculated for all eight firms in the sample for the period 1980-99.
Size was assessed as the number of employees on the firm's payroll for each year. The variable was calculated for all eight firms in the sample for the period 1980-99.

Between-subjects manipulation implemented in two phases. In the contract-writing instructions, participants in the letter condition were prompted about the depth of the house so that they would include it as a contract term, while the spirit condition omitted this prompt and participants naturally excluded the term. The assessment e-mail then described the violated expectation as documented in the contract (letter) or as something that was 'clearly not what was intended' (spirit). Letter violations represent the higher value of the variable and spirit violations the lower value.

Three items assessed the perceived intentionality of the subcontractor's violation: (1) whether the subcontractor was fully aware that the submitted house would result in a major flaw (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree); (2) whether the major flaw was based on an act (1 = very unintentional, 7 = very intentional); and (3) whether the subcontractor's actions were very unintentional to very intentional. Reliability was 0.91.

Five items adapted from Mayer and Davis (1999) assessed participants' trusting intentions, including comfort working with the subcontractor again, comfort having the subcontractor work without oversight, keeping an eye on the subcontractor (reverse-scored), not letting the subcontractor have influence over important issues (reverse-scored), and giving the subcontractor a critical task without monitoring. Responses used a seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree); reliability was 0.88.

Shortly after the experiment began but before the violation occurred, participants responded to three statements: (1) I trust my subcontractor to follow the instructions of our contract, (2) I can count on my subcontractor, and (3) my subcontractor will make a good effort to live up to the terms of our agreement (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). Reliability was 0.77.

One item asked participants how many lottery tickets they would like to allocate to their subcontractor, out of the 10 lottery tickets they had received. Participants could enter any whole number between 0 and 10; a smaller allocation indicates a greater willingness to punish, since all condition means fell below the 50 percent allocation described as typical.

Participants read a rental contract containing the term 'The maximum occupancy is 8. No additional persons are permitted to spend the night. Persons on the property are the sole responsibility of the Tenant.' In the letter condition they were told the tenant violated that explicitly documented contract term by having more than 30 people at the home; in the spirit condition they were told the tenant violated the intent of the term. Participants in the letter condition rated the violated expectation as significantly more explicit than those in the spirit condition.
The perceived intentionality measure used in Study 1 was adapted to the vacation-rental context. Reliability was 0.89.
The trusting intentions measure used in Study 1 was adapted to the vacation-rental context. Reliability was 0.90.
Initial trust in the tenant was assessed using the same three measures as in Study 1. Reliability was 0.86.

A context-dependent single item gauged willingness to punish the violator: 'If you could bring legal action against this tenant, how likely is it that you would do so?' (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely).

Contract complexity was manipulated: the high complexity contract was three pages long and contained 24 detailed terms, whereas the low complexity contract was one page long and contained six detailed terms identical to six of the terms in the high complexity version. A manipulation check showed that the high complexity contract was perceived as significantly more complex than the low complexity contract.

The dependent variable represents events in which an alliance did not exist between two airlines one year (l_ijt = 0) but existed the following year (l_ij,t+1 = 1). Since the dependent variable is symmetric for each pair of firms, the unit of analysis is the nondirectional dyad (either dyad ij or dyad ji was in the sample, not both). The year 1994 was taken as the initial network condition and models evaluated alliance formation from 1995 to 1998; alliances that had not formed by 1998 were right-censored. There were 144 new alliances formed between 1994 and 1998.
time_window: formation from 1995 to 1998, with 1994 as the initial network condition

description: Matrix L was divided to capture differences between cospecialized and nonspecialized alliances, defined as mutually exclusive categories. Cospecialized alliances (s_ijt = 1) were extended alliances including a broad set of code-sharing routes (typically alliances to provide connections to a region or a continent) together with a broad range of cooperative activities; nonspecialized alliances (ns_ijt = 1) were those including a few code-sharing routes that did not comprise a regional or global feeding network. Two raters knowledgeable about airline alliances rated all the alliances using the short descriptions of alliance activities provided by Airline Business, reaching an initial interrater agreement of .82 and attaining consensus after discussion with the author.
time_window: alliances active up to the previous month in each survey year, 1994-1998

description: Indicator coded 1 when the alliance formed in the following year was cospecialized (s_ij,t+1 = 1) and 0 otherwise. It is one of the three possible outcomes in the competing-risks model, where each pair-year spell is either no alliance yet, a nonspecialized alliance formed, or a cospecialized alliance formed, with 'no alliance yet' as the baseline outcome. 32 of the 144 new alliances formed between 1994 and 1998 were cospecialized.

Indicator coded 1 when the alliance formed in the following year was nonspecialized (ns_ij,t+1 = 1) and 0 otherwise; it is one of the competing-risks outcomes in the multinomial logit model. 112 of the 144 new alliances formed between 1994 and 1998 were nonspecialized.

Measures whether a potential partner already had cospecialized alliance relations with the rivals of the other potential partner. Because unordered pairs were examined, both situations (firm i as a partner of firm j's rivals and firm j as a partner of firm i's rivals) were equally relevant and were aggregated in the measure. To aggregate among all possible third parties, a weight was calculated for each third party equal to the percentage it accounted for of total revenues for all airlines in the sample except firms i and j, so that the weights summed to one for each dyad. The algebraic formula is not readable in the text supplied.

Measures whether a potential partner already had nonspecialized alliance relations with the rivals of the other potential partner, using the same aggregation as the cospecialized counterpart: both directions of the unordered pair were aggregated, and each third party was weighted by the percentage it accounted for of total revenues for all airlines in the sample except the two dyad members. The algebraic formula is not readable in the text supplied.

Evaluates whether the respective rivals of two potential partners maintained cospecialized alliances; the measure is the sum of the number of such cospecialized alliances, weighted by the competitive relations of those rival firms with the potential partners and aggregated using weights reflecting the combined revenues of both members of the rival alliances. The countervailing logic requires that the competitive relations of potential partners with the members of rival alliances be stronger than those with each other. The algebraic formula is not readable in the text supplied.

Evaluates whether the respective rivals of two potential partners maintained nonspecialized alliances; the measure is the sum of the number of such nonspecialized alliances, weighted by the competitive relations of those rival firms with the potential partners and aggregated with weights reflecting the combined revenues of both members of the rival alliances. The variables looped through all the alliances in the industry involving different firms and aggregated those that involved rivals of the potential partners. The algebraic formula is not readable in the text supplied.

Measured whether potential partners had competitive relations with third-party rivals that were more intense than the competitive relations with each other; the variable is the sum of the combined competitive ties to common rivals, provided that those ties were greater than those linking the pair to each other, weighted by the revenues of those common rivals. A unit scale of the rival alliances and common rivals variables was chosen to facilitate comparison of coefficients. The algebraic formula is not readable in the text supplied.

The total number of unique nonprofit board interlocks held by all directors on each corporate board in each year, divided by the total number of directors on the board in that year. The measure was assessed in the same year as intangible asset investment. The measure is focused on the average number of nonprofit interlocks per director rather than the percentage of board members with any nonprofit interlocks.
time_window: same year as intangible asset investment

description: The average number of unique nonprofit interlocks held by each high-power director at each firm in each year. High-power directors are those with the title of CEO, board chair, or lead director, or those who owned at least 1% of the firm's stock.
time_window: same year as intangible asset investment

description: The average number of unique nonprofit interlocks held by each low-power director at each firm in each year. Low-power directors are those who are not designated as high power, i.e., who do not hold the title of CEO, board chair, or lead director and who do not own at least 1% of the firm's stock.
time_window: same year as intangible asset investment

description: Directors were identified as having high power if they had the title of CEO, board chair, or lead director, or if they owned at least 1% of the firm's stock. Both structural and ownership sources of director power were included in the designation. Dichotomizing power was necessary so that interlocks could be distinguished based on the individual directors holding them; separate interlock measures were created for high-power and low-power directors.

A summative index of investment in intangible assets incorporating R&D intensity and advertising intensity. R&D intensity was calculated as total R&D expenditure divided by revenue and advertising intensity as total advertising expenditure divided by revenue; the two ratios were then added together for each observation and standardized prior to analysis. Missing values of R&D and advertising spending were replaced with 0 following prior studies.
time_window: same calendar year as the nonprofit interlock measure

description: The mean prior year intangible asset investment across all firms in the Compustat database in the same two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) category as the focal firm with revenues above $20 million. The variable was standardized prior to analysis, like the firm-level measure.

The percentage of a firm's basic subscribers who choose to receive expanded basic service, which increases the number of channels from around 13 to over 50. Because customers cannot purchase expanded basic cable service if their cable operator does not make it available, the authors use this percentage as a proxy for new technology adoption. In the sample the average was 21.5 percent, and the value can exceed 100 percent (to a maximum value of 103.9%) when a cable operator allowed subscribers to purchase 'expanded basic' service without first purchasing 'basic' service; the minimum value equals zero percent.
scale: percentage of a firm's basic subscribers

description: A single measure that combines the family ownership categories, i.e., all firms with at least 5% family ownership, so that family firms can be compared directly to non-family firms. It is constructed from the annual ownership data reported for each firm.

A dummy variable that equals 1 if the largest family ownership position in a firm is at least 5 percent and no more than 50 percent. This designation applies to 21 percent of the firm-years in our sample.

A dummy variable that equals 1 if the largest family ownership position in a firm is 50 percent or higher. An additional 42 percent of the firm-years in our sample meet this qualification. The remaining 36 percent of observations, which have less than 5 percent family ownership, are labelled non-family.

The year-to-year change in revenue for each firm. Because of the possibility for extreme changes in performance that might distort results, the variable is winsorized at the one percent level. After winsorizing, firms ranged from a 9 percent decrease in revenue to a 15 percent increase in revenue, and the mean performance improvement for a firm in the sample was 1.5 percent.

A firm-specific measure of population density used as a proxy for the threat of competition, calculated by dividing the total number of homes in the firm's franchised areas (whether or not they subscribe to cable) by its total number of systems. Table 1 presents this data in thousands; firms range from 370 homes per system to 260,000 homes per system, with a mean value of 33,790 homes per system.

Calculated as the sum of all sensegiving activities used by the focal start-up divided by the months from founding until one month before VC funding. The set of communication activities was compiled from prior research and validated with public relations experts and experienced entrepreneurs.
time_window: from founding until one month before VC funding

description: Calculated using Blau's (1977) heterogeneity index, which captures the relative proportion of each communication type in the total: D = 1 - sum p_i^2, where p_i equals the percentage of communication activities that fall in the i-th category. This measure varies from 0 (no) to 1 (high) diversity, with numbers close to 0 reflecting a larger proportion of a single type of communication.
time_window: from founding until one month before VC funding

description: Operationalized as the number (count) of prior start-ups by all of the founders of a focal start-up. Biographical data were collected on all founders in the sample—a total of 675 individuals—from the start-ups' archival websites.

Measured at the organization level as the total number of TMT members who had worked for at least one major firm in the IT industry before joining the focal start-up. Major firms were defined as IT firms listed in the Fortune 500 largest U.S. corporations for the year preceding the startup year. Data were collected on all team members who joined at founding or during the observation period—a total of 1,450 individuals.

Number of articles mentioning a focal startup, collected from the LexisNexis and ABI/Inform databases from founding until one month before the first round of VC funding. Articles that appeared under 'Industry News' were categorized as industry media. For each start-up, the number of industry media articles was divided by its age in months one month before VC funding, obtaining the monthly rate of industry media attention.
time_window: from founding until one month before first VC funding

description: Number of articles mentioning a focal startup, collected from the LexisNexis and ABI/Inform databases from founding until one month before the first round of VC funding. Articles that appeared under 'Magazines and Journals' and 'Newspapers' were categorized as general media. For each start-up, the number of general media articles was divided by its age in months one month before VC funding, obtaining the monthly rate of general media attention.
time_window: from founding until one month before first VC funding

description: Measured at the time of the first round of VC investment as the total amount of investments made by all VCs participating in the first round of a focal start-up's funding, as reported in the VentureXpert database. The amount received was divided by the average investment in all first-round IT deals in the respective funding year to account for fluctuations in the annual supply and demand of venture capital.

variable_name: diversification rate (instantaneous rate of new business starts)
description: The dependent variable is the instantaneous rate of new business starts within existing firms, modelled in an event history framework in which time is the duration a firm spends in the spell of "time since last business entered." Firm activities were coded as distinct businesses on the basis of distinct external markets and distinct internal resources, the market criterion being low cross-elasticities of demand and the resource criterion being that different production facilities and separate distribution channels would be needed. The date of entering a new business was coded as the date product sales in that business first commenced, and coding was conservative: natural product extensions and products running on multiple hardware platforms were not coded as new businesses, and an activity was coded as a separate business only when both coders agreed.
time_window: annual observations from the IPO to 1987

description: A firm's available financial resources were measured with a firm's quick ratio: the ratio of a firm's cash and marketable securities to its current liabilities. The authors state that the quick ratio effectively indicates short-run liquidity and is less susceptible to managerial manipulation than other indicators, such as the current ratio, and that it reflects the extent to which the sum of cash and marketable securities for the year covers current liability obligations.
time_window: value measured in the prior 12 months, updated annually

description: Causal ambiguity was measured with a monotonically decreasing function of a firm's age, the natural logarithm of firm age in months, so that causal understanding increases over time at a decreasing rate. The date of a firm's inception was drawn from the SEC documents, which reported either the month and year in which the firm was founded or the date of firm incorporation; if the former date was provided, age was calculated from this time, otherwise the firm incorporation date was used. The authors state that low levels of firm age (firm youth) are positively associated with causal ambiguity, so that the direction of the predictions regarding causal ambiguity is reversed when age is substituted for causal ambiguity.
time_window: value measured in the prior 12 months, updated annually

variable_name: sales revenue, net income, change in sales revenue, change in net income
description: Four measures of firm performance were collected from the accounting income statements: sales revenue, annual change in sales revenue, net income, and annual change in net income. These four variables shed light on two types of performance (revenues and net income) in two forms (absolute levels and annual fluctuations). Each performance measure is entered separately in the estimated equation, first as a main effect together with financial resources and age, and then interacted with the logarithm of firm age.
time_window: value measured in the prior 12 months, updated annually

variable_name: Strategic planning (GOALS, ANALYS, SCANNG; overall planning)
description: Respondents were asked to indicate, on a scale of 0-5, the accuracy of 11 statements concerning their firms' strategy-making activities, anchored at either extreme with the words 'Very Accurate' or 'Not at all Accurate'. The statements were grouped into goal-setting (GOALS), analysis (ANALYS) and scanning (SCANNG) scales, and an overall planning variable was used in the analysis. The scales were tested for reliability using Cronbach's alpha, with coefficients between 0.77 and 0.79.

Profitability over a 3 year period, measured subjectively; the authors state that the convergent validity between subjective and objective measures was established. It is the dependent variable in the partial correlations with the strategic planning scales.

The study focuses on single-business firms in two U.S. four-digit SIC-code industries. Wooden upholstered furniture (SIC 2512) was chosen for testing H1 because the industry demonstrated market and competitive stability and because formal planning was widely disseminated, according to assessments provided in interviews with industry participants, consultants, and experts. Women's dresses (SIC 2335) was chosen for testing H2 because formal strategic planning was not yet widely disseminated due to a long-standing entrepreneurial tradition.

variable_name: Commitment of the agent to the insurer
description: This is measured via eight items put to the agent on a seven-point, Likert type scale. The scale reflects desire, belief, and action towards the solidarity of the relationship with the named insurer, including willingness to exert effort for the organization and desire to maintain a stable and long-term relationship. Comparing it to Allen and Meyer's scale, the questions focus mostly on normative and affective commitment, not on continuance commitment. Factor analysis indicated only one factor was present, with a high coefficient alpha (0.91).

variable_name: agent's idiosyncratic investments in the insurer
description: The agent reports his or her level of idiosyncratic investments in the insurer; these investments are tailored to the insurer and hence difficult to redeploy to another insurer. They include dedicated personnel, investment in acquiring knowledge that is particular to the insurer, aligning the agent and insurer in presentations to policyholders and prospects, and adopting forms and procedures similar to the insurer's. Several summary statements underscore the idiosyncratic nature of these varied investments.

variable_name: insurer's idiosyncratic investment in the relationship with this agent
description: The insurer reports its level of idiosyncratic investment in the relationship with this agent. Such investments take the form of personnel dedicated to this agent, acquiring knowledge particular to the agent's operations, and aligning the underwriter with the agent in presenting the underwriter to policyholders.

variable_name: general investments the insurer has made in the agency
description: The agent reports the level of general investments the insurer has made in the agency on a nine-item scale tapping several facets of investment. The underlying factor is that the agent can use them in the service of another insurer, both across space and time. The items run a gamut of redeployable investments: advice and assistance about managing the agent's business in general, advice about how to grow a business, and the possibility of subsidies to help the agent acquire or upgrade computing capabilities (automation).

variable_name: insurer's level of satisfaction with the relationship
description: Insurer-reported scale measuring the insurer's level of satisfaction with the relationship with the agent, with a coefficient alpha of 0.93. The authors viewed these subjective assessments by the insurer as a suitable way to make fair comparisons between agents given the different regions and/or products the agents may carry.

variable_name: insurer's expected future benefits from the relationship
description: Insurer-reported scale measuring the insurer's expected future benefits from the relationship with the agent, with a coefficient alpha of 0.83. Like the satisfaction scale, it is a subjective assessment made by the insurer.

Electronic SEC documents for each company and year were imported into a qualitative data analysis package and searched for references to the firm's accounting system; retrieved text was read and scored from 1 (weak, few controls or crosschecks, little top management attention beyond formal signing off) to 7 (strong, controls that are reviewed and changed, top management attention and interest). References that were not relevant or belonged to another variable were deleted. Each company was awarded the highest score it obtained from any one document rather than an average or total. Coding was done without knowledge of the company name or its crime status.
time_window: the year prior to the announcement of the crime

description: References to written policies, procedures, job descriptions, training and process in the firm's SEC documents were retrieved and scored on a 1 to 7 scale based on the context and detail of the references, so that higher values represent clearer policies and procedures (clear divisions of responsibility, communication of policies throughout the organization, manager training, formalization). The company's highest score across documents was used. Coding was blind to the firm's crime status.
time_window: the year prior to the announcement of the crime

description: Firms' SEC documents were searched for text about the code of conduct and ethics, and the retrieved text was scored on a 1 to 7 scale reflecting how specific the code is and how consistently it is enforced, including a clearly articulated code, management training in following the code supplemented by an annual review, and communication of the code to all employees. The highest score obtained from any one document was used for each company. Coding was blind to the firm's crime status.
time_window: the year prior to the announcement of the crime

description: Text referring to formal, organization-arranged communication such as meetings, conferences, retreats, contact, feedback, rotation and interaction was retrieved from each firm's SEC documents and scored on a 1 to 7 scale, where higher numbers represent greater company-wide interaction among employees (e.g., training events involving geographically dispersed employees, job rotation programs, or employees who compare divisions and transfer practices). The company's highest score from any one document was used. Coding was blind to the firm's crime status.
time_window: the year prior to the announcement of the crime

description: References to teams and other informal, ad hoc communication outside the company's express purpose were retrieved from each firm's SEC documents by the content analysis software and scored on a 1 to 7 scale based on the context of the references. Each company received the highest score it obtained from any one document. Coding was blind to the firm's crime status.
time_window: the year prior to the announcement of the crime

description: Text about hiring, selecting, recruiting, applicant testing and employee screening was retrieved from each firm's SEC documents and scored on a 1 to 7 scale based on the context and detail of the references, so that higher values represent more attention to checking qualifications, interviewing and recruiting. The company's highest score from any one document was used. Coding was blind to the firm's crime status.
time_window: the year prior to the announcement of the crime

description: Each firm's SEC documents were searched for references to contingent pay for employees such as performance-based bonuses, profit sharing, options or stock, and the retrieved text was scored on a 1 to 7 scale based on the context of the references. The variable focuses on all employees rather than the CEO or top management team alone. The highest score obtained from any one document was used for each company, and coding was blind to the firm's crime status.
time_window: the year prior to the announcement of the crime

description: Crime is coded 0 for the matched firms without an announced crime and 1 if there is any announced white-collar crime; the number of crimes committed (0 to 6) is used as the dependent variable in the ordered logit models. Firms with crimes were identified through a Lexis-Nexis search of The Wall Street Journal from January 1, 1988 to December 31, 1998, and the SEC documents were gathered for the year before the crime announcement.

Firm performance was modeled using a logarithmic growth function, ln(MVi,t+1) = alpha ln(MVi,t) + pi'xi,t + ei,t, controlling for market value at the prior year. Annual market value is computed by multiplying the firm's stock price by its number of common shares outstanding, and because of its volatility it is calculated by averaging the 12 end-of-month values of the relevant year. All independent variables and controls were lagged by one year relative to the dependent variable.

For each of the firm's products, an indicator received a value of 1 if the firm had not previously released a prior version of that product using similar knowledge, and 0 if a prior version of that product existed; a product that draws on established knowledge and competencies is indicative of exploitation. Exploration via internal organization was calculated as the value of that indicator averaged across all products introduced by the firm in a given year, and the measure was transformed to range between 0 and 1 with high values indicating exploration.

For each alliance, an indicator denoted whether it involved knowledge-generating upstream activities such as joint R&D, coded 1; knowledge-leveraging downstream activities such as joint marketing, resale, production, or supply, coded 0; or a combination of both activities, coded 0.5. Alliance exploration was calculated as the average value of this indicator across all alliances formed by the firm in a given year, and the measure was transformed to range between 0 and 1 with high values indicating exploration.

Based on the business descriptions of acquired firms and a product function typology, each acquisition within SIC 7372 received a value of 0 if the acquiring firm had previously offered a similar product function, 1 if that function was not offered but the firm had prior products in the same market segment, and 2 if that function was not offered but the firm had prior products in the same application class. For targets outside SIC 7372 the indicator ranged from 3 to 6 according to how remote the target's industry was from the acquirer's. Acquisition exploration was calculated as the value of this indicator averaged across all acquisitions in a given year, transformed to range between 0 and 1 with high values indicating exploration.

variable_name: Balance point versus focus point (quadratic exploration specification)
description: Balance within a mode is assessed with a performance function that introduces the linear and quadratic terms of exploration in that mode. Maximum performance is typically reached when focusing on exploitation or on exploration, and a two-sided t-test compares performance at the focus point with the highest performance (exploration value of 0 or 1) with performance at the balance point, taken as an exploration value of 0.5.

variable_name: Exploration in mode A, exploration in mode B, and their interaction
description: Balance across modes is assessed with a performance function that includes the exploration variables of the two modes and their interaction. The performance function is maximized at a balance point (Point E) that corresponds to exploring in one mode while exploiting in the other, and two-sided t-tests compare that balance point with the focus points of exploration in both modes (Point C) and exploitation in both modes (Point B).

Dummy variable indicating the presence at the firm of a biomedical academic entrepreneur, identified as an NIH SBIR principal investigator who had also received one or more NIH research grants while working at a university or nonprofit research institution prior to his or her first SBIR award. The variable is zero before the academic entrepreneur enters the firm and takes the value one afterwards. The authors note that interpreting the significance of this dummy by itself is meaningless because it imposes the counterfactual of zero research and patent productivity.

Cumulative value of the scientist's NIH research awards divided by the number of years he or she was active in the NIH grant system, measured prior to the first SBIR award. Because the variable is interacted with the academic entrepreneur dummy, it is zero before the academic entrepreneur enters the firm and takes the scientist's value afterwards. For firms linked to more than one academic entrepreneur it is calculated as the sum of the scientists' NIH grants divided by the sum of the number of years each was active in the NIH grant system with an academic affiliation.

Total number of U.S. patents, assigned to nonprofit institutions, on which the scientist is listed as an inventor, divided by the number of years he or she was active in the NIH grant system, measured prior to the first SBIR award. Patents invented by the scientists but assigned to firms are excluded. For firms linked to more than one academic entrepreneur it is the sum of the scientists' academic patents divided by the sum of the number of years each was active in the NIH grant system with an academic affiliation; approximately 31% of the SBIR academic entrepreneurs have at least one patent assigned to a nonprofit research institution.

Dichotomous indicator that takes the value of one for those firms that successfully win a Phase II SBIR award and zero otherwise, estimated with a heteroskedastic Probit model. Winning a Phase II award shows that the firm is good at completing academic-style proof-of-concept studies in the judgment of NIH SBIR review committees.

Dollar amount of the firm's Phase II awards, a continuous variable capturing the magnitude of success at Phase II. It is analyzed with a Tobit model, which accounts for the censoring at zero occurring when firms fail to win a Phase II award.

Indicator of whether the firm applied for a patent (that is eventually granted) in a given year; because there are many firms that never patent, this captures the probability of patenting. It is estimated with a heteroskedastic Probit model including 11 time dummies and 17 technology field dummies in the heteroskedasticity term.

Count of the U.S. patents granted (by application date) to the firm, identified in the NBER patent database. It is analyzed with a negative binomial model because equidispersion is clearly rejected, with standard errors calculated heteroskedastic-consistently.

Exit is a variable, Ext, that takes on a value of 1 if MNE x exits in year t, and 0 otherwise. Observations started in 1987 and continued until an exit occurred or was right-censored in 2006. Closures and sell-offs of all Japanese equity ownership were treated as exits; there were 146 exits in total, consisting of 135 closures and 13 sell-offs.

The address of each subsidiary was geocoded with annually varying latitude and longitude coordinates, and war zones were geocoded using their center and radius as the smallest circles containing violence. The great-circle distance formula was applied to the latitude and longitude of the subsidiary and the center of the nearest war zone, from which the war zone radius was subtracted. The final variable was coded as 1 when the calculated distance was negative, and as 0 otherwise.

At-risk resources were assessed by measuring the nonredundancy of a focal subsidiary, or its difficulty of being replaced by other subsidiaries in the MNE's network. To determine the number of possible replacements, the authors counted the subsidiaries in the parent's portfolio in the same industry and at the same value chain stage (upstream or downstream), and then divided the employee count in the focal subsidiary by the employee count in its replacements. A lower denominator translates into a higher value on this variable and greater at-risk resources; the equation itself is not readable in the text.

A proxy for resilience was created by performing a principal component analysis with varimax rotation on the values of four variables, which yielded a principal component explaining 90.0 percent of the variance, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.95. The four variables are: the Political Risk Services scores (reverse coded so that greater values reflect higher risk) of the countries in an MNE's portfolio, weighted by a ratio of the MNE's subsidiary count in a given country to its subsidiary count in the full portfolio, summed over all countries; the number of war-afflicted countries in the MNE's portfolio; the number of subsidiaries an MNE has in war-afflicted countries; and logged MNE sales. The first three variables capture an MNE's experience dealing with and attitude toward political risk, while the fourth is a proxy for MNE size.

The ratio of foreign sales to total sales, described by the authors as the most common measure of internationalization. They choose this ratio over other possible measures, such as international geographic spread, growth in foreign sales, or foreign direct investment, because a majority of firms from emerging economies remain in the early stages of the internationalization process and use exporting as the dominant mode of international expansion. The focal independent variables are lagged by one year relative to this dependent variable.
Profit before interest and tax divided by total sales. Used as one of two commonly used financial measures of firm performance, adjusted for nonrecurring transactions.
Profit before interest and tax divided by average total assets. Used as one of two commonly used financial measures of firm performance, adjusted for nonrecurring transactions.

The sum total of annual foreign exchange spending on capital goods, royalty and know-how, and raw materials, as a percentage of total annual sales. All Indian companies registered under the Indian Companies Act must record and disclose detailed accounts of their foreign exchange spending, which yields three specific categories of annual foreign exchange spending related to inflows of international technology resources. Capital goods represent a tangible side and royalty and know-how represent intangible technological assets; spending on raw materials is included because imports of raw materials likely occur only in areas in which firms are technologically deficient. The variable is lagged by one year in the estimations.

Inflow of international financial resources into firms in India can occur through the issue of new equity shares on international stock exchanges or through raising foreign exchange debt via the issue of debt securities and/or foreign exchange loans. The authors state that a year-wise, firm-wise listing of all such foreign exchange equity and debt issues by Indian firms is available in CMIE Prowess, and introduce the measure with 'the measure of international financial resources is calculated as follows:'. The equation itself is not readable in the text supplied, so the exact specification is a gap. The variable is lagged by one year in the estimations.

A dummy variable that takes the value of one if the firm is affiliated with a business group and zero if not. To identify group affiliation the authors adopt the CMIE Prowess classification of firms into groups.

A time-clock variable created to capture the dynamic effects of international technology and financial resource inputs on product market internationalization over the 10-year study period. Liberalization in the Indian pharmaceutical industry kicked off with India agreeing to introduce product patents in late 1994, and the time-clock variable assumes positive integer values of 1 to 10 corresponding to the 10 years of the data used in this study.

Firms reported the number of innovation projects pursued during 2006-2008. The reported count was divided by firm size, because bigger firms have more projects, to normalize the measure for comparisons across firms. The variable enters the models in lognormal form.

Constructed from the survey question on the number of innovation projects discontinued during 2006-2008. Two categories are formed: a firm that completes all its projects is not selective; a firm that completes only a subset is selective. Thirty-six percent of sample firms were selective.

A composite score of two stated innovation objectives: 'Expand into new product category' and 'Enter new markets,' each rated on a Likert scale from 0 (not important at all/not used) to 3 (very important). Firms with the maximum sum score of 6 are designated as having more ambitious innovative intent and those with a score of 4 or less as having less ambitious innovative intent; observations with a composite of 5 are omitted.
Revenue from all new and improved products in 2008. The measure contains raw values in € million rather than ratios, and all models use a logarithmic transformation of the dependent variable.
Revenue in 2008 from products that are new to the firm's product portfolio, measured as raw values in € million and used in logarithmic form in the models.
Revenue in 2008 from products that are new to the market, measured as raw values in € million and used in logarithmic form in the models.

Firm strategic orientation was determined with the 14 items of Rajagopalan's (1997) measure, based on the Miles and Snow typology. Respondents answered the question 'To what extent does your firm emphasize the following in your strategies?' on a five-point Likert scale from 1 = least emphasized to 5 = most emphasized. Factor analysis (maximum likelihood extraction, varimax rotation) yielded five factors that explained 51% of the variance: efficiency-oriented, domain expansion, market innovation, technological innovation, and market penetration strategies; the factor scores were entered into a K-means clustering algorithm to identify strategic orientations, producing prospector, defender and analyzer clusters. In the regressions, prospector and defender dummy variables are entered and the analyzer strategy serves as the base category for comparison.

A five-item index depicting the extent to which pay is administered flexibly to reward individual differences in the performance and qualifications of employees. Respondents considered 'employees who perform tasks at the core of your organization's business' and indicated on a five-point scale the extent to which the pay system emphasized individual qualifications of the employee (versus task of the employee), individual performance (versus organizational membership), managers' discretion in pay decisions (versus organizational framework for pay levels), and flexibility (versus bureaucracy). The authors chose to measure the pay system design elements that indicate a higher level of horizontal pay dispersion instead of their exact magnitudes, consistent with Rajagopalan (1997).

Respondents were asked: 'How do your (a) entry-level and (b) average salary rates compare with those of other employers in the same geographical area doing similar work?', considering 'employees who perform tasks at the core of your organization's business.' Responses were given on a scale from 1 (considerably lower than others) to 5 (considerably higher than others), and the mean value of the two responses was used.
scale: 1 = considerably lower than others to 5 = considerably higher than others

description: Operationalized as a pay range (Gupta et al., 2012; Kepes, Delery, & Gupta, 2009). Respondents reported the total compensation (base pay and incentives) of the lowest-paid employee and of the highest-paid executive. Consistent with prior research, employee earnings were subtracted from executive earnings and the resulting score was log-transformed to form a relative measure of pay variation, where low values indicate vertical pay compression and high values indicate vertical pay dispersion.

Branch-specific percentile comparisons were used to categorize the profit margins of companies with data retrieved from an archival company database; because the companies were randomly selected from various industries, the percentile comparison is branch-specific.

Respondents assessed the productivity of their firm relative to other firms in the same industry on a five-point scale. The scale also included an 'I don't know' option, which the authors treated as missing data.

Measured using Lewis's (2003) 15-item scale. TMT member ratings (excluding CEO) were used; the coefficient alpha for the entire 15-item scale was 0.86. A confirmatory factor analysis supported a higher-order factor with subdimensions of specialization, credibility, and coordination, and aggregation to the team level was justified by a median rwg(i) of 0.94 and intraclass correlations.

Adapted version of Stam and Elfring's (2008) eight-item measure: sales growth, employment growth, market share, profit, innovation in products and services, quality of products and services, cost control, and customer satisfaction. CEOs rated their firm's performance over the past year on each item relative to competitors on a seven-point scale (much worse, about same, or much better). Internal consistency alpha was 0.78.
scale: seven-point scale from much worse to much better

description: CEOs provided a precise estimate of the firm's sales growth over the past year during on-site interviews; most consulted financial documents and used a calculator. Outliers were adjusted by winsorizing extreme values to the outer tail of the distribution. The median sales growth in the sample was 2.5%.

variable_name: TMT average strength of external ties
description: Following Collins and Clark (2003), respondents indicated the number of individual contacts they had in each of nine external categories: board members, suppliers, customers, financial institutions, competitors, alliance partners, governmental agencies, trade associations, and other. Frequency of communication was the number interacted with once a month; duration was how long on average they had known the contacts; emotional intensity was closeness of the relationship measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all close, 5 = extremely close). The measure was the linear combination of the standardized scores of the three components, aggregated across team members; ICC1 and ICC2 were 0.11 and 0.58.
scale: linear combination of standardized frequency, duration, and emotional intensity; emotional intensity on a five-point Likert scale

description: Seven-item Likert scale developed and validated by Atuahene-Gima and Li (2004). The first four items capture technological dynamism, and three items reflect market dynamism. Alpha was 0.88, median rwg was 0.95, and ICC1 and ICC2 were 0.42 and 0.70.

Dummy variable equal to one for all participants in the Choose team treatment, in which students could choose their own team members but were randomly assigned a predefined idea. The omitted baseline is the Choose neither treatment, in which both team members and ideas were assigned. The team-choice dimension is also present in the Choose both treatment.

Dummy variable equal to one for all participants in the Choose idea treatment, in which students could choose their own idea but were randomly assigned to a team. The omitted baseline is the Choose neither treatment, in which both team members and ideas were assigned. The idea-choice dimension is also present in the Choose both treatment.

Evaluators rated each pitch deck on six criteria: Novelty, Feasibility, and Market Potential on seven-point Likert scales; Success Potential and Invitation Probability as percentages; and Investment as a share of a fictional $1 million budget. The latter three variables are log-transformed and all six are standardized as z-scores using the baseline Choose neither group mean and standard deviation. The performance index is an equally weighted average of the six z-scores; separate regressions also use each indicator.

A company's use of new knowledge based on citations to new patents as a percentage of the total number of distinct citations it made. New knowledge was assessed in relation to the company's total stock of existing patent citations, and repeat citations and self-citations were excluded. Knowledge developed over a two-year period was considered: the company's average number of new citations (not previously cited by the focal company) made during the previous two years as a percentage of the average number of distinct patent citations made by the focal company during that period.

For each medical device company-brokerage firm-year observation, a dichotomous variable set to 1 if the brokerage firm covered the medical device company in the observation year and to 0 if it did not. Coverage was assessed using brokerage firms' buy/sell recommendations and earnings forecasts. All independent and control variables correspond to the preceding year.

variable_name: Share of the company's new knowledge that is new to the brokerage firm
description: The percentage of the company's new knowledge (based on the two-year time window) that has not previously been used by one of the other companies that the brokerage firm is covering, excluding the focal company.

The yearly percentage of the common FDA product codes in which both the focal medical device company and the other medical device companies covered by the brokerage firm, excluding the focal company, had medical devices approved by the FDA.

variable_name: Brokerage firm's coverage of companies that use existing knowledge
description: The average percentage of the distinct repeat citations used during the previous two years as a percentage of the total number of distinct patent citations made by other companies covered by the brokerage firm, excluding the focal company. In the case of missing values, when a brokerage firm covered companies that didn't build on knowledge in the past two years, models assumed that the brokerage firm's experience was entirely with existing knowledge.
Assessed based on the number of four-digit SIC codes associated with the medical device companies covered by the brokerage firm.

variable_name: Alliance network at founding (alliance counts by partner type)
description: A set of firm-specific variables that counted, separately, the number of alliances a BF had at the time of its founding with each of several types of partner. Potential rival BFs are defined as those operating in one or more of the same biotechnology sectors as the startup BF; the authors found no alliances between startups and other BFs in nonoverlapping sectors, so nonrival BF alliance effects could not be estimated. Each partner-type count was entered separately, and the authors expected all counts except potential rival BF alliances to have a positive effect on performance.

Diversity of a startup's alliance partner types at founding, computed as one minus the sum of the squared proportions of a BF's alliances with each of the nine partner types, divided by the startup's total number of alliances at founding. The measure is based on the Hirschman-Herfindahl index and assumes that alliance partners of a given type are roughly structurally equivalent; scaling by total network size lets the variable capture the extent to which the alliances comprising the network are, on average, redundant. A startup with six alliances split evenly across three partner types scores 0.111, while one with five alliances with pharmaceutical firms and one marketing alliance scores 0.046. Network efficiency was coded zero for 13 startups with no alliances at founding.

variable_name: Potential rival BF alliances at founding
description: The number of alliances a startup BF had at the time of its founding with potential rival BFs, defined as BFs operating in one or more of the same biotechnology sectors as the startup BF. The authors describe this disaggregation as somewhat crude but sufficient to distinguish among BFs more or less likely to be potential competitors. Hypothesis 3 proposes, in contrast to Hypothesis 1, that these alliances should on average adversely affect a startup's early performance, so the expected coefficient is negative.

The number of biotechnology sectors in which a focal BF participates divided by the average number of biotechnology sectors in which its potential rival BF partners participate, where the partners are all potential rival BFs allied with the focal BF at the time of its founding. Because the authors lack firm-level data for foreign BFs, partners' relative scope was computed only for Canadian partner BFs, which accounted for more than 90% of all Canadian startups' alliances with other BFs.

variable_name: Partner BFs' patents w/in 5 years (t found)
description: The number of patents granted to BFs allied with each startup BF in the five years prior to the startup's founding, determined from the Micropatent data base using the same measurement procedure as the dependent patent variable. Patents are not weighted by citations because the patent approval process creates a three (or more) year lag between a patent's granting and its citation in later patents. Like relative scope, this variable was computed only for Canadian partner BFs.

Year-over-year revenue growth in 1991 constant dollars; the authors use absolute growth rather than percentage growth because many firms' values on these variables are zero initially and in subsequent years. In the growth models the variable is logged and its own lagged value (t-1) is included as a predictor, with lagged values of the other performance variables also controlled.
time_window: yearly, up to the end of the fifth year

description: Year-over-year growth in the number of non-R&D employees. It is entered in logged form in the growth models together with its lagged value (t-1) and lagged values of the other performance variables.
time_window: yearly, up to the end of the fifth year

description: Year-over-year growth in the number of dedicated R&D employees. It is entered in logged form in the growth models together with its lagged value (t-1) and lagged values of the other performance variables.
time_window: yearly, up to the end of the fifth year

description: Year-over-year growth in R&D spending in 1991 constant dollars; absolute growth is used rather than percentage growth because many firms' initial values are zero. It is entered in logged form in the growth models together with its lagged value (t-1) and lagged values of the other performance variables.
time_window: yearly, up to the end of the fifth year

description: The yearly number of patents granted to a startup BF, identified in the Micropatent data base using U.S. patent data because most Canadian BFs file in the U.S. first. A patent is assigned to a BF at the date of application rather than the date of granting, and for subsidiaries only patents assigned to the subsidiary are included. Although the observation period ends December 31, 1996, patents granted up to May 31, 1999 are included to limit truncation of the count; the variable is a count and is estimated with Poisson regression.
time_window: yearly, with patent grants followed through May 31, 1999

description: A dummy variable denoting the period following deregulation in the airline industry, coded 1 for the years 1979-84 and 0 for the years 1973-78, and interacted with the AIRLINE industry dummy in the regressions.

The average total compensation each of the top five highest paid TMT members received, including base salary in cash, cash bonus, and long-term or deferred income such as stock options, performance unit or share plans and long-term management incentive plans. The Black-Scholes model was used to estimate the value of stock options, and the measure was then converted to natural log.

The average of the proportion of outcome-based compensation received by the top five highest paid TMT members. Each member's proportion of outcome-based compensation was calculated as (total compensation - base salary)/total compensation.

The level of TMT compensation measured in the focal year t, where TMT turnover was measured by the changes occurring between the focal year (t) and two years prior (t-2). The dependent variable of interest is the level of TMT compensation, entered in the change-score panel analysis.
time_window: t, with turnover measured from t-2 to t

description: The proportion of performance-based pay measured in the focal year t, where TMT turnover was measured by the changes occurring between the focal year (t) and two years prior (t-2). This is one of the two dependent variables of interest in the change-score panel analysis.
time_window: t, with turnover measured from t-2 to t

description: The sum of the number of departed executives and the number of newly hired executives during each observation period, expressed as a percentage of the number of executives on the TMT at the beginning of that period. Turnover was measured by considering the changes that occurred between the focal year (t) and two years prior (t-2), a two-year lag being used to capture dynamic changes while minimizing confounding factors.
scale: percentage of TMT at the beginning of the period

description: The environment variables were first standardized, then summed and averaged within six groupings representing the three components of factors (endowed, advanced, and human factors) and the three components of institutions (political, legal, and societal institutions), and an average value for each set of components was taken to obtain one value for factors and one for institutions. Countries were grouped with a split half (and median split) criterion; the more munificent group was Denmark, France, Germany, The Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, and the less munificent group was Austria, Belgium, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Portugal, Spain, and Turkey. To obtain more accurate data on international diversification the sample was reduced to three countries per group: Sweden, France, and the United Kingdom (more munificent) and Ireland, Italy, and Portugal (less munificent).
time_window: early 1990s; 1980s data averaged with 1990s data when available

variable_name: Imputed weighted diversification measure (degree of diversification)
description: Because many firms do not have segment revenues consistently reported in Worldscope, no entropy measure of diversification could be calculated. Worldscope lists each firm's four-digit SIC codes in order of revenues, with a maximum of five codes; following Gedajlovic and Shapiro (1998) the authors used the imputed weighted diversification measure to calculate a firm's level of product diversification. In words, the measure sums over a firm's secondary market segments the product of a weight imputed to each industry, assumed to decline geometrically, and an indicator that equals 0 if the firm operates in only one four-digit industry, 1 if the secondary segment is in the same three-digit industry as the primary segment, 2 if it is in the same two-digit industry, and 3 if it is in a different two-digit industry. The printed formula in the text is partly garbled.

Because many firms do not have country or regional segment revenues consistently reported in Worldscope, an entropy measure could not be calculated. The authors used the number of foreign countries where a firm had subsidiaries or cooperative ventures as the proxy for the level of outbound international diversification, because joint ventures and strategic alliances have become increasingly prevalent. The data were collected from Moody's International Manual and LexisNexis.

To create this measure the authors recorded the number of countries represented by a domestic firm's foreign partners in cooperative ventures with the focal domestic firm. They used LexisNexis and Moody's International Manual to search for cooperative ventures for each firm in the sample. A correlation test between a country count measure and a cooperative venture count measure for Sweden (.895) and Ireland (.90) indicated strong reliability.

ROA was the authors' measure of performance; the use of accounting-based performance measures facilitates comparing results with most previous diversification studies. Although market-based performance measures may indicate the stock market's perception of future performance, their use is premised on the assumption of stock market efficiency, which is likely to differ between more munificent and less munificent environments, so market-based measures were less appropriate. Financial statement data were collected from Worldscope's November CDs for 1996 to 1999, a three-year average was used to avoid annual fluctuations, and a one-year lag was imposed between independent and control variables and the dependent variable.
time_window: 1996-1999; three-year average; one-year lag between independent/control variables and the dependent variable

variable_name: Earnings before interest and taxes divided by assets (EBITOA)
description: EBITOA was used as an additional indicator of firm performance. Because taxation rules as well as capital structure are likely to differ among countries, EBITOA is a useful performance measure in cross-country studies.
