It was computed from the same Worldscope data, using a three-year average and a one-year lag between independent and control variables and the dependent variable.
time_window: 1996-1999; three-year average; one-year lag between independent/control variables and the dependent variable

description: Occupational employment ratios from the OES: the percentage distribution of 480 occupations in all U.S. industries at the three-digit SIC code level of detail. The number of occupational measures was reduced to 41 occupations at the Major Group level of the OES classification, whose distributions add up to 100 percent to allow comparability of profiles. The raw ratio scores were standardized and normalized (square-root transformation, recommended because of the Poisson-like distribution of the original variables) and each variable was given equal weight. The ratios refer to the occupations in which employees are working rather than the occupation for which they may have been trained.

Resource-RIGs were constructed by first building an industry expertise profile from the occupational measures, then computing a summary distance measure (the squared Euclidean distance measure) for each pair of industries, and finally clustering industries by their profile similarity using Ward's method. Agreement on both the CCC criterion and the pseudo F statistic indicated the 11-cluster solution. Each three-digit industry is a member of one Resource-RIG.

Entropy measure of within-group diversification, following the definitions and details in Palepu (1985). For each firm, every line of business (three-digit industry) is assigned to the Resource-RIG to which it belongs; the less dispersed the firm's lines of business are across different Resource-Related Industry Groups, the higher is the related component of the entropy measure. The measure is an analysis-of-variance-like measure that provides indices for both within- and between-group diversification.

Ratio of related (within-group) diversification to total diversification, computed for each of the 12,781 diversified firms. As indicated by this measure, firms pursue on average 43.4% related diversification (within Human Resource-RIGs) out of their total diversity. The measure was compared with the mean RATIO obtained from randomly generated industry groups.

Total diversification of the firm, built from the related (within-group) and between-group components of the entropy measure and serving as the denominator of the ratio of related to total diversification. The authors note that the RIG-generated and the randomly generated measures for a firm's total diversity remain the same in the test.

Entropy-based measure of the firm's diversification across different Resource-Related Industry Groups. The authors caution that between-industry groups diversification is not identical to unrelated diversification because some of it may be related diversification not captured by similarity in human expertise, for example vertical integration to the trade sector, similarity in raw materials, or same distribution channels.

Using the information about natural disaster incidents in EM-DAT, the authors calculated the total number of natural disasters in the country during a firm's tenure in their location; they then took the log transformation. Using this measure based on secondary data lowers the statistical concerns of common method bias.
time_window: during a firm's tenure in their location

description: Respondents rated on a 7-point Likert scale, where 1 indicates 'Not risky at all' and 7 indicates 'Extremely risky', the risk of each of a list of natural disasters in the location (city or town) where they are working. The question was followed by 11 response choices and 'other'. The measure is treated as formative, and the authors calculated the average scores of all items.

variable_name: Organizational learning from others for natural disasters
description: Respondents rated on a 7-point Likert scale, where 1 indicates 'Not at all important' and 7 indicates 'Very important', how important each listed organization is as a source of learning for their company about how to prepare for a natural disaster. The question was followed by 13 response choices. The measure is treated as reflective; in the factor analysis five items were dropped because they did not load onto the construct of interest in the international survey.

Respondents indicated their level of agreement on a 7-point Likert scale with a series of statements about actions their company had taken to prepare for natural disasters. The authors began with a 15-item measure that they treat as reflective; after factor analysis four items were dropped because they did not load onto the construct of interest for the international survey. The Cronbach's alpha for the resulting measure was 0.966.

Using the information about natural disaster incidents in EM-DAT, the authors calculated the total number of natural disasters during a firm's tenure in their location and took the log transformation; the same archival measure was used in both surveys.
time_window: during a firm's tenure in their location

description: Respondents rated on a 7-point Likert scale, where 1 indicates 'Not risky at all' and 7 indicates 'Extremely risky', the risk of each of a list of natural disasters in the location (city or town) where they are working. The measure is treated as formative and computed as the average of all items, as in the international survey.

variable_name: Organizational learning from others for natural disasters
description: Respondents rated on a 7-point Likert scale, where 1 indicates 'Not at all important' and 7 indicates 'Very important', how important each listed organization is as a source of learning for their company about how to prepare for a natural disaster. The question was followed by 13 response choices; the measure is reflective and no items were dropped in the U.S. survey.

Respondents indicated their level of agreement on a 7-point Likert scale with a series of statements about actions their company had taken to prepare for natural disasters. In the U.S. survey all items loaded onto the construct of interest; the Cronbach's alpha for the resulting measure was 0.953.

variable_name: Newly hired refugees (in % of total employment)
description: The share of newly hired refugees in the focal firm's total workforce in year t. Refugees are explicitly identified by Statistics Denmark together with the issuance date of their residence permits, so they cannot be confused with regular immigrants or temporary asylum seekers. Status as a refugee allows individuals to live and work in Denmark. The authors focused on the hiring of refugees aged 18-45 years.

Firm profitability equals the gross profits in year t+1, that is, the difference between a firm's total revenue and the total costs arising from the consumption of goods, energy, wages, and subcontracting. Profits are measured in Danish kroner and adjusted for inflation based on the Consumer Price Index (using 2000 as a base year). The authors take the natural logarithm to account for skewness and exclude the top and bottom 1% of the distribution to eliminate outliers.

variable_name: Job insecurity (% workers in t -> unemployed in t+1)
description: The share of workers in the firm who become unemployed in the following year, i.e., the share of involuntary staff attrition or turnover. Higher values indicate greater job insecurity at the firm.

variable_name: Hours worked (total hours paid, total normal hours, total extra hours, hours per week)
description: Individual-level statistics on hours worked: total hours paid, total normal hours, total extra hours, and hours per week. The upper panel of the comparison includes all foreign employees (both full-time and part-time), while the bottom panel restricts the comparison to refugees and nonrefugees with full-time employment in the focal firm. Newly hired refugees are compared with newly hired foreigners (nonrefugees) using two-sided t-tests.

Hourly wages of refugees and other foreign employees recruited by the firms in the sample, measured in the hiring year, when information asymmetries about these employees' productivity or quality are higher (i.e., entry wages). The comparison reports the average hourly wage of each group of new hires, both overall and across occupations, firm sizes, regions and industries.

Effort of individual i to resolve maintenance task j in module k, computed with the Graves and Mockus (1998) algorithm: each individual is assumed to devote one unit of effort per day, daily effort is divided across all open tasks, and the estimates are iteratively rescaled until the log-likelihood fails to improve. The resulting effort is log-transformed as the dependent variable. The final model is estimated on the subset of tasks for which lines of code modified is available.

Number of MTs assigned to individual i on module k prior to the current assignment j in that module. A log transform of this variable is used to capture diminishing returns to specialization, and the variable is mean centered in the models.
time_window: cumulative experience prior to the current task assignment

description: Total number of unique modules that have been allocated to individual i prior to the point when MT j is allocated. It is entered with both linear and quadratic forms; the authors do not log transform it because they wish to capture not just diminishing but negative returns to increasing exposure to task variety beyond a particular level.
time_window: cumulative experience prior to the current task assignment

description: An adaptation of the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index: HHEI_ij is the sum over modules k of the squared proportion P_ijk, where P_ijk = C_ijk / D_ij, C_ijk is the total number of tasks handled by individual i on module k up to but not including task j, and D_ij is the total number of tasks handled by that individual across all modules. A value of one indicates that the individual has resolved tasks on just one module; the minimum value of 1/N indicates experience equally dispersed across the modules worked on. The HHEI is recalculated at every MT assignment, is not log transformed because its magnitude between 0 and 1 is meaningful, and is entered with both linear and quadratic components.
time_window: recalculated at every task assignment, based on tasks until but not including task j

description: Categorical variable to indicate whether the MT j in module k being assigned to individual i represents the first MT ever assigned from that module to that individual.
The number of individuals who enter the workgroup of individual i when MT j is being worked on.
time_window: during the open period of task j

description: The number of individuals who leave the workgroup of individual i when MT j is being worked on.
time_window: during the open period of task j

description: The degree of variety experience lost from the workgroup of individual i when MT j was being worked on, computed by dividing the variety experience of the exiting individual by the combined variety experience of all the individuals in the workgroup corresponding to individual i when MT j is being worked on. If more than one individual leaves when a specific MT is open, the ratio is added across the exiting individuals.
time_window: during the open period of task j

description: The degree of specialized experience related to module k that is lost from the workgroup of individual i when he or she was working on MT j in module k, computed by dividing the experience of the exiting individual on module k by the combined experience of all individuals in the workgroup on module k. If more than one individual exits when MT j in module k is open, the ratio is added across the exiting individuals. The paper lists this variable among the control variables.
time_window: during the open period of task j

description: Market share data were gathered for each firm in the Canadian mutual fund industry as of December 31, 1998 from the Investment Funds Institute of Canada. Surveying industry experts during January 1998 while measuring market share at the end of December 1998 provided nearly a year's lag for the hypothesized relationships to influence market share.

Firm innovativeness was assessed by industry experts who rated, on a 5-point Likert scale, the extent to which each fund company tends to lead the industry in introducing products and services and adopting new technology. The score for each of the three measures (new products, new services, and new technology) was determined by averaging the responses each firm received from all the experts rating it, and the three average scores were summed for each fund company to create Overall Firm Innovativeness. Because Overall Firm Innovativeness also reflects network position, the authors regressed it on Hole Access and used the residuals to create Ego Innovativeness.

The variable is the average of the Overall Firm Innovativeness scores for all alters with which a focal firm is tied. For the interaction with structural holes the authors used a weighted average measure of alter innovativeness, where the weights were the reciprocals of each alter's redundancy, multiplying the inverse of each alter firm's redundancy score times its innovativeness score for each alter with which the focal firm is tied.

Structural holes were measured as constraint using the 'Network...Ego Network...Structural Holes' routine in UCINET, since network constraint effectively measures a firm's lack of access to structural holes. In the formula, pij equals the strength of direct ties from i to j, and the sum of piq pjq is the sum of the indirect tie strength from i to j via all q; the formula block itself is unreadable in the provided text. Hole Access was calculated as one minus the firm's constraint score (in cases where constraint was non-zero) and zero for all other cases, because a score of zero in the network arose only when the firm was unconnected to others and so had no access to structural holes.
time_window: ties in existence at the end of 1997

description: Created to examine the effect of highly innovative firms bridging structural holes in their network. To overcome potential collinearity between the main effects and the interaction term, the Hole Access variable was centered by subtracting the mean score from each individual value and a constant was added to Ego Innovativeness; the two variables were then multiplied to create the interaction term.

Network closure is the opposite of access to structural holes. Structural holes are measured as one minus the firm's network constraint, so low Hole Access means a constrained, dense, closed network. Support for closure is read from the sign of this variable.

A five-item measure covering knowledge obtained from consultants, commercial laboratories, or public R&D units that provide assistance in the R&D process; conferences, trade fairs, or exhibitions; scientific journals or trade/technical publications; industry associations; and online communities. Respondents used a four-point scale ('not used,' 'low,' 'medium,' and 'high') to indicate the extent to which they had searched for knowledge and information from each knowledge source over the three previous years. Cronbach's alpha was 0.63, and the authors report that confirmatory factor analysis suggested acceptable reliability. The measure was based on items found in the Eurostat Community Innovation Survey and was collected in the questionnaire addressed to the firm's most senior executive.

A self-reported count variable in which respondents reported the number of new business opportunities their firms had successfully realized in the previous three years. Respondents reported on three different types of opportunities: new products and/or services, production technology, and markets, and an overall measure was constructed as the sum of the number of opportunities exploited. Successful exploitation was defined in the survey as those opportunities that had 'contributed to improve financial performance.' The variable was measured in the questionnaire addressed to the firms' senior-most executive manager.

Respondents were given a list of ten tasks and asked to indicate the organizational level at which decision authority for each task was vested. The highest level of decentralization was coded 4 and denoted 'lower level management (e.g., functional managers, plant managers, regional managers, division managers)'; the lowest level of decentralization (i.e., high centralization) was coded 1 and denoted 'top management (e.g., executive director, deputy director).' An average composite measure of the ten items was created (α = 0.83), so that the higher the value, the more decentralized the firm's decision making authority was on average. The measure was constructed from data obtained from the senior HR manager questionnaire.

Seven items derived from O'Donnell (2000) were rated on a seven-point scale indicating how often each item was used, from 'never or very rarely' (coded 1) to 'very often' (coded 7). A higher value indicated that the firm relied more on a certain coordination mechanism, and responses to the seven items were averaged to produce a firm-wide average measure of coordination (α = 0.77). The items sought to capture formal/informal and permanent/temporary coordination mechanisms, and the measure was constructed from data obtained from the senior HR manager questionnaire.
scale: seven-point scale from 'never or very rarely' (1) to 'very often' (7)

description: Each reported case was classified as one of the two intervention options: taking a position, in which the manager took a position on the alternatives being considered, or resisting a decision, in which the manager resisted a decision after it had already been made. Respondents were asked to provide short written descriptions of the most recent cases, if any, in which they took a position on a decision issue and in which they resisted a decision.

Each intervention was classified according to whether the issue over which the manager intervened had an impact confined to the manager's department or an impact going beyond the departmental level (organizational). A decision was classified as organizational if it had an impact on members of the organization outside the authority of the respondent's immediate superior, or on members of other organizations. In a follow-up subsample of 25 percent of respondents the researchers' categories were compared with the respondents' own categorizations, giving a coefficient of association of 0.75.
scale: dichotomous: departmental level impact vs. organizational level impact

description: Each reported action was classified according to whether the intervention was perceived as successful or not, since respondents had been asked to report whether they had been successful or not. The analysis compares the proportion of successful interventions reported at the organizational level across the two intervention options.

Total number of citations received by the environment-related patents granted to a focal firm in a given year, computed over the years following the granting date (year fixed effects partially control for truncation problems). The environment-related patents are the 3,235 green chemistry patents identified by Nameroff et al. (2004), who searched the CHI's Patent Citation Indicators database using examiner-assigned patent classifications plus keywords and phrases in utility patent titles, abstracts, and exemplary claims. Environmental patents were associated to parent companies using the Mergent manuals, COMPUSTAT and, in a few remaining cases, companies' Web sites.
time_window: Citations computed over the years following the granting date; patents granted 1997-2001

description: Ratio of the total number of state on-site inspections to the total number of regulated entities (divided by one thousand) in a state-year, taken from the ECOS report. For firms with subsidiaries in several states, a weighted average was computed using the proportion of the firm's subsidiaries in each state as weights; the variable was log-transformed before entering the models. The assumption is that firms located in a state with more inspections per thousand regulated entities face greater regulatory pressures.

Total number of environmental NGOs divided by the total number of regulated entities (divided by one thousand) per year at the state level, from the NCCS. For firms with subsidiaries spread across states, a weighted average was computed using the proportion of the firm's subsidiaries in each state as weights; the variable was log-transformed before entering the models. The level of normative pressures a firm faces is assumed to increase with the number of NGOs in a given year and state.

Facility emissions weighted by toxicity through the Human Toxicity Potential factor, aggregated across chemicals and to the facility level, then subtracted from the facility's industry average at the four-digit SIC code for every facility-year, so positive values indicate emissions higher than the corresponding industry. Facility-level deviations were averaged by parent company (aggregated with DUNS numbers at the parent level) to yield an annual observation per company; the variable was rescaled by adding a constant so that its minimum value became 1 and then log-transformed.

Ratio of working capital to sales, obtained from COMPUSTAT, logged because of the non-normality of its distribution. The paper also describes a second measure of slack, the ratio between net income and revenues (profit margin), logged; the reported specifications use the working capital to sales measure.

Logarithm of the ratio of the book value of a firm's machinery and equipment to the number of employees, from COMPUSTAT, following Ziedonis (2004) as a proxy for asset specificity. Investments in production plants, machinery and equipment are large and not easy to redeploy and are less likely to be valuable in other firms should the company fail and its assets be liquidated.

Survey items for the HERI data are designed to measure ranges of variables vs. specific values—e.g., the item categories for publications were none, 1-2 articles, etc. Three research norms are compared across areas: total articles published, articles published in the last 2 years, and hours per week spent on research and scholarly writing.

Count of publications in MacMillan's (1989) 14 strategy-oriented journals for the years 1970-93 inclusive for each of the 945 faculty, yielding approximately 13,000 person-years. The measure is a cumulative count modelled as years relative to degree date.
A cumulative count of citations accrued by an individual, collected from the Social Science Citation Index and modelled as years relative to degree date.
The ratio of a person's cumulative citations to their total number of published articles, constructed from the citation data and the publication counts and modelled as years relative to degree date.

Particularism was measured as the prestige of a faculty member's degree-granting institution using three indicators: the average GMAT score of incoming students, the number of editorial board seats held by a department (coded for each journal in MacMillan's 'outstanding quality' pool by institution, excluding Harvard Business Review), and departmental ratings in the Gourman report. The three-indicator prestige model produced highly significant loadings in the expected direction.

Measured as the count of articles published within 1 year of degree completion, to allow for lags in publication time. Precocity was retained as a dimension measured with a single indicator after factor analysis.

The ability dimension was modeled with two indicators: whether or not the subject was the lead author on an early publication, and whether or not that article was A-tier quality, defined as membership in MacMillan's (1989) set of 'outstanding quality' journals.
Universalism is measured by two universalistic predictors: precocity (articles published within one year of degree) and ability (lead authorship on an early publication and a second indicator).

Research outcomes are measured by the faculty member's cumulative publications in 14 strategy journals and cumulative citations from the Social Science Citation Index, modeled as the primary outcomes.
Management faculty are identified in the HERI survey by discipline and compared on research norms with other business faculty and with faculty from all disciplines.

Calculated by counting the total number of articles about each IPO firm. The articles were drawn from all newspaper and print magazine articles available about an IPO firm in the 'Major Newspapers,' 'Journals and Magazines,' and 'Trade Magazines' databases of Lexis-Nexis during the pre-IPO period; 514 pre-IPO media articles were collected and content-analyzed. The measure is used both in its raw form and as a squared term to test the hypothesized nonlinear relationship.
time_window: one year prior to the registration of the offering with the SEC

description: Measured using the Janis-Fader coefficient of imbalance. The text states that the formula uses P, the number of positive articles about a firm, N, the number of negative articles about it, and V, the total volume of articles about it, including articles that are neutral in tenor; the printed formula itself was not readable in this text. The range of the variable is -1 to 1, where -1 equals 'all negative coverage' and 1 equals 'all positive coverage,' and the score was multiplied by 100 to allow for nonlinear transformations. Each paragraph of an article containing a reference to the firm was coded as positive, negative, or neutral in tenor by a trained coder, and an article with relatively equal instances of positive and negative references was coded as neutral.
time_window: one year prior to the registration of the offering with the SEC

description: Equal to the percent change in stock price on the first day a stock traded on a national exchange, computed as (price end - price initial) / price initial x 100. The data used to calculate this measure were drawn from IPO prospectuses and the Center for Research on Securities Pricing (CRSP) database. Turnover was also used as a control variable when predicting underpricing.

Equal to the percentage of shares offered that were traded, computed as (shares traded / shares offered) x 100, on the day of the IPO. The data used to calculate this measure were drawn from IPO prospectuses and the Center for Research on Securities Pricing (CRSP) database.

The KLD-index is constructed by summing up the number of KLD strengths with respect to employees, customers, the natural environment, and communities. KLD ratings are compiled from multiple data sources, including annual questionnaires sent to companies' investor relations offices, firms' financial statements, annual and quarterly reports, general press releases, government surveys, and academic publications. In the analysis the authors also consider subindices based on specific stakeholder groups.

Treatment dummy that equals one if the company is located in a state that has rejected the inevitable disclosure doctrine by year t. The doctrine prevents employees with valuable know-how from working for a competitor in the immediate future, and its rejection by a state court removes this mobility restriction. The state of location is proxied by the state of headquarters' location recorded in Compustat.

variable_name: ... improves the firm's ability to retain knowledge workers
description: Survey item asking respondents to agree or disagree, on a 6-point Likert scale from Strongly Disagree (= 1) to Strongly Agree (= 6), with the statement that CSR improves the firm's ability to retain knowledge workers. 93% of respondents agreed, with a mean response of 4.9 out of 6. The authors also report the related item that socially responsible practices can enhance knowledge workers' appreciation of their current employment (95% agreement, mean 5.0 out of 6).
scale: 6-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 6 = Strongly Agree)

variable_name: ... decreases the risk that knowledge workers disclose a firm's unique and valuable knowledge even if they choose to leave the company to work for a rival firm
description: Survey item asking respondents to agree or disagree, on a 6-point Likert scale from Strongly Disagree (= 1) to Strongly Agree (= 6), with the statement that CSR practices decrease the risk that knowledge workers disclose a firm's unique and valuable knowledge such as trade secrets even if they choose to leave the company to work for a rival firm. 64% of respondents agreed, with a mean response of 3.9 out of 6, significantly above the neutral mid-point.
scale: 6-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 6 = Strongly Agree)

description: Participants were randomly assigned to one of four variations of the description of their current employer: a baseline control with no reference to CSR, a length-matched control that supplemented the baseline with additional generic company information, a treatment describing CSR engagement in terms of employees, and a treatment describing CSR engagement in terms of the environment and communities.

variable_name: Client List B (no disclosure of proprietary info)
description: Participants chose to launch a marketing campaign by emailing (1) Client List A (the previous employer's valuable client list, a well-kept trade secret), (2) Client List B (the new employer's shorter client list), or (3) both lists. Participants who selected Client List B were choosing not to disclose their previous employer's trade secret, whereas those who selected either of the other two options were choosing to disclose it. The reported outcome is the share of participants choosing Client List B.

The same script as the laboratory experiment was used: participants were randomly assigned to one of four variations of the description of their current employer - a baseline control with no reference to CSR, a length-matched control with additional generic company information, a treatment describing CSR engagement in terms of employees, and a treatment describing CSR engagement in terms of the environment and communities.

variable_name: Client List B (no disclosure of proprietary info)
description: Participants chose to launch a marketing campaign by emailing Client List A (the previous employer's valuable client list, a well-kept trade secret), Client List B (the new employer's shorter client list), or both lists. Choosing Client List B meant not disclosing the previous employer's trade secret, whereas choosing either of the other options meant disclosing it. The reported outcome is the share of participants choosing Client List B.

Poor firm performance was measured by reverse-coding return on assets, calculated as annual net income divided by firm assets, so that higher values indicate poorer performance. The measure is lagged one year relative to the separation event. The authors chose this measure because it is widely understood and commonly used in CEO succession research.
Board independence was measured as the percentage of board members who were neither inside directors nor affiliated directors. The variable is lagged one year relative to the separation event.

CEO career horizon was measured as the number of years remaining before the CEO reached the assumed retirement age of 70 (Matta and Beamish, 2008). All available CEO ages were included, including those above 70, as the career horizon continues to decline with age even after reaching the typical retirement point. The variable is lagged one year relative to the separation event.

A categorical dependent variable consisting of the three types of CEO-board chair separation. If the sitting CEO in the previous year remained CEO in the year of separation, the separation was labeled a Demotion; if the sitting CEO in the previous year was neither CEO nor board chair in the year of separation, it was labeled a Departure; if the sitting CEO in the previous year remained board chair in the year of separation, it was labeled an Apprentice separation. The categorization is consistent with Krause and Semadeni (2013), and apprentice separations serve as the base case in the models.

Industry foresight is operationalized as a forecaster's accuracy relative to all forecasters on a specific question. It has three components: the extent of error in the individual's forecast, based on the difference between the forecaster's probability of an outcome occurring and the actual outcome; the extent of forecasted accuracy observed across all forecasters on the question, which keeps a forecaster who simply follows the average forecast of the crowd from scoring high; and the time between when the forecast was made and when the question was closed, so that an earlier accurate forecast is rewarded with higher accuracy. For unordered questions the forecasting error is the sum of squared errors, commonly called the probability or Brier score; for ordered questions partial credit is assigned for answer options close to the resolved answer. The measure can range from -2 to +2, with lower values indicating greater accuracy; the algebraic formula as printed is not readable in the available text.
time_window: each day beginning with the forecaster's initial forecast of the question and over all days until the question closes

description: A simple dichotomous (1/0) variable equaling one if an individual updates their forecast on the focal question during the question window and zero if not. Of the 3,585 forecasters in the sample, 875 updated their forecast on at least one question.

Following Augenblick and Rabin (2021), the extent of Bayesian belief updating is assessed from the weakness of the initial forecast and the magnitude of change in the subsequent forecast, with a value of zero indicating perfect Bayesian belief updating and larger deviations indicating underreaction (negative values) or overreaction (positive values); the algebraic formula as printed is not readable in the available text. The dichotomous variable takes a value of 1 for observations between the 25th and 75th percentile of the distribution for each question, which has a median very close to zero, and 0 for observations that deviate significantly from the median (less than the 25th percentile and greater than the 75th percentile). Observations below the 25th percentile are likely to correspond to underreaction and those above the 75th percentile to overreaction.
time_window: each day beginning with the forecaster's initial forecast of the question and over all days until the question closes

description: Measured based on the forecasting error of the daily consensus forecast of all forecasters on the question, which is calculated by Good Judgment Inc. For each forecaster, uncertainty for a given question is calculated on the day they make their first forecast on that question. To avoid idiosyncratic daily variations, a three-day window between one day before and one day after the initial forecast is used. The variable is operationalized as the mean of the forecasting error of the consensus forecast for each of the three days for a given question.
time_window: three-day window [-1, +1] around the forecaster's initial forecast

description: Cosine similarity of two industry vectors in terms of human capital, comparing the parent's and the unit's industries in terms of the education of their employees and thus comparing workforces based on specialization and entry requirements. It is computed from the number of employees per education category (educational specialization × obtained level) in every industry, normalized by industry size, as yearly values.

Natural logarithm of the number of employees who switch their formal employer from the parent to the unit. It measures the total stock of employees that switch firms rather than the flow, so that employees who quit after transferring are no longer counted and the variable reflects employees de facto employed at the unit in each year.

Natural logarithm of the number of employees who switch their formal employer from the unit to the parent. Like P→U redeployment, it is measured as the stock of employees who switched and remained, not as the flow of transfers.

The P→U redeployment variable divided into two categories depending on the employees' formal education, here the redeployment of generalists, defined as employees without higher education. Measured as the natural logarithm of the stock of such employees who switched from the parent to the unit.

The P→U redeployment variable divided into two categories depending on the employees' formal education, here the redeployment of specialists, defined as employees who have obtained a university degree. Measured as the natural logarithm of the stock of such employees who switched from the parent to the unit.

The U→P redeployment variable divided into two categories depending on the employees' formal education, here the redeployment of generalists, defined as employees without higher education. Measured as the natural logarithm of the stock of such employees who switched from the unit to the parent.

The U→P redeployment variable divided into two categories depending on the employees' formal education, here the redeployment of specialists, defined as employees who have obtained a university degree. Measured as the natural logarithm of the stock of such employees who switched from the unit to the parent.

Generalists are defined as employees without higher education and specialists as employees who have obtained a university degree. The authors describe this as a prudent distinction in their context, as employees in Norway largely obtain on-the-job training rather than higher education, and undergraduate degrees in Norway are specialized and associated with a fixed discipline.

Binary variable set to 1 for closure, that is, the unit is officially closed, has filed for bankruptcy, dismisses all employees, or ceases to exist in the firm register, and 0 otherwise. Exit from the sample due to a merger is not treated as closure; such observations are right-censored and set to 0 for the last year in which the parent company still holds ownership shares in the spinout.

Natural logarithm of unit revenues in thousands of Norwegian kroner. Performance is forwarded by 1 year to lessen concerns of reverse causality and to account for training and socialization in employee mobility.
scale: log of revenues in thousands of Norwegian kroner

description: A dummy with a value of one if the firm-headquartered county has experienced any of the forms of local newspaper decline by year t, and zero otherwise. The decline data were originally compiled by Gao et al. (2020) from the United States Newspaper Panel and the Editor and Publisher Yearbook.

The number of MSCI CSR strengths net of the number of CSR concerns across the six aspects excluding governance (community, diversity, environment, employee relations, human rights, and product). A higher CSR score corresponds to greater socially responsible engagement by the firm.

The log-transformed number of news articles produced by The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, The Washington Post, USA Today, and The Los Angeles Times that cover a given firm in a given year. The variable is lagged by one year in the regressions.
The log-transformed number of forecasts a firm receives in a given year. The variable is lagged by one year in the regressions.
The log-transformed number of ratings a firm receives in a given year. The variable is lagged by one year in the regressions.

For each firm the authors first calculated the standard deviation of the number of years the partners had spent within a focal province. They then captured change in local tenure heterogeneity with a time-varying variable that measures the change in the value of that standard deviation attributable to partner mobility (i.e., new hires or departures). They chose the standard deviation rather than the coefficient of variation because the standard deviation overcomes aggregation bias by computing the distance between individuals, irrespective of the mean. Covariates were lagged by one period.
time_window: one period lag (intervals of one to five years)

description: Team age measures the average overlap in tenure among all the possible pairwise combinations of team members at time t - 1, that is, before the mobility event. It is used as a proxy for the members' social interaction over time. The authors also squared this value, team age squared, to capture the nonlinear returns of interaction between members over time, and tested Hypothesis 1B by interacting membership duration with demographic heterogeneity flow.

The variable measures changes in the overlap computed from the average stock of provincial experience between the focal firm and its competitors located within the same province. For each firm the authors computed maximum and minimum values by adding and subtracting one standard deviation to (from) the mean value of firm tenure and counted the number of firms falling within that band in a given year. To measure changes in overlap they calculated the difference between the numbers of firms in two consecutive time periods. The variation of this variable was restricted to cases in which at least one mobility event (a new hire or a departure) was observed in a given year.
time_window: difference between two consecutive time periods; one period lag

description: Dichotomous dependent variable coded 0 if a firm was still in existence in a given year and 1 once it exited the risk set. The year in which an organization appeared for the first time on the Register of Accountants was treated as its founding year and the last year of appearance as its year of dissolution. Single proprietorships were eliminated from the risk set.

The authors proxied the severity of competition by mapping the strength of local competition on the geographical dimension and counting the number of firms dissolved within a given province in a given year. They opted for this variable and not density because the current number of firms exiting an industry is a more straightforward measure of the realized level of competition. It was interacted with demographic overlap flow to test Hypothesis 2B.

Indicator equal to 1 for patents containing at least one physician inventor, and 0 otherwise. Physicians are identified by matching the names, middle initials and locations of inventors listed on medical device patents to the AMA Physician Masterfile, with flagged cases evaluated manually. Physicians whose 'major professional activity' in the AMA data is recorded as 'inactive' are excluded from the main analyses. The authors also define Some physicians (at least one physician and at least one nonphysician inventor) and Only physicians (only physician inventors) indicators for additional tests.

The number of citations made to the focal patent by future follow-on patents (forward citations), used as the measure of invention importance. Estimated in a count model with technology-class and application-year fixed effects.

The concentration of forward citations across patent technology classes, measured with the generality index as described by Trajtenberg et al. (1997) and adjusted for bias at low numbers of forward citations following Hall et al. (2001). The generality index is equal to 1 minus the Herfindahl index of the concentration of citing patents across technology categories, where s_ij is the percentage of citations received by patent i that are in class j out of n_i citing patent classes. The adjusted index is undefined when one or zero citations are received, so it is set equal to 0 in these cases and a dummy variable equal to 1 when one citation or zero citations are received is added.

A count of citing patents from outside of the focal patent's own technology class, used as a second measure of breadth of impact. The approach is similar to the measure of radical exploration based on a count of citations outside of the disk drive technology classes employed by Rosenkopf and Nerkar (2001).

The number of prior art (backward) citations made by the focal patent, an indication of the amount of prior art related to the invention; an invention near the beginning of the life cycle is expected not to build on much prior art.

The average age of the cited prior art, measured as the average number of years between the grant date of the cited patents and the application date of the focal patent; it indicates the recentness of the prior art being built on.

The age of the technology class, measured as the number of years between the formation of the technology class and subclass at the United States Patent and Trademark Office and the patent application year (Shane 2001).
The number of citations received from follow-on inventions in the medical device industry, indicating the degree to which the invention is utilized in subsequent industry developments.

The measure is intended to capture the extent to which a product is based on third-party development tools, which fell into two categories: game engines (comprising game engines, graphics engines, and 3D engines, which are mutually exclusively used with each other) and physics engines. Middleware use is measured by the number of toolkit types used in a given game, with the value being either zero (no third-party toolkit used), one (only game engine or physics engine used), or two (both game engine and physics engine used). This reflects the extent to which the code within the game was created using these middleware components rather than being hand-coded.

Built from game descriptions (short textual summaries): punctuation was removed, the data were tokenized, only nouns and verbs were selected, and descriptions were converted into term frequency vectors (a 'bag of words' approach). For each title, the algorithm was fitted on all previously released titles to fit a contour (the 'novelty frontier') using a one-class support vector machine with a radial base function kernel; each focal title was then compared with this frontier. Distances from the frontier provide a granular measure of the degree of novelty, where positive values indicate greater novelty and negative values indicate lower novelty.
time_window: comparison against titles previously released (data collected 1990-2012, with 'slack' observations before and after the 2000-2007 analysis window)

description: Commercial success of an individual title-platform (e.g., FIFA 2002 for PlayStation 2) is measured by the total sales (in USD) that the title-platform had in the U.S. market during its lifetime. Since data were collected until 2012 and the sample ends in 2007, these values did not suffer from truncation. In the regressions the outcome variable is the log-transformed product (title-platform) revenues.
time_window: lifetime sales, data collected up to 2012

description: Percentage change in annual net generation for each electric utility relative to year t-1. The authors prefer this measure to sales revenue because it is not confounded by changes in price in measuring growth over time.

Continuous net income variable used as the measure of firm profits. Net income is described as representing managers' primary fiscal responsibility and as reflecting bottom-line performance; it is used instead of rate of return on assets because Hypothesis 2A focuses on deregulated markets, where investors are free to pursue profit maximization directly.

Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the state enacted retail deregulation legislation or issued a regulatory order that year or in prior years and 0 otherwise. For each firm the dummy is weighted by the share of the firm's electricity sales in each state, so a firm selling half of its electricity in a deregulated state receives a value of 0.5.

Average of the League of Conservation Voters scores for the U.S. Senate and House in the firm's state. The LCV scores are based on the voting records of representatives and senators in favor of an environmental agenda, ranging from 0 to 100, with 100 being the highest score; they are taken to measure the preferences of a state's elected representatives and, to the extent legislators represent their constituents, general citizen sentiment toward environmental issues.

Sierra Club membership per thousand people at the state level, obtained directly from the Sierra Club. It measures the extent of NGO pressure and may also represent the environmental preferences of the population of the state in which a firm operates.

Number of state-level formal enforcement actions associated with environmental issues in the last five years, normalized by the number of EPA-regulated major facilities in the state. It measures the extent to which a state inspects polluting facilities and takes enforcement actions against violators, indicating the intensity of regulatory scrutiny to which facilities are actually subjected.

variable_name: Deviation between reported and actual emissions reductions
description: Difference between reported and actual emissions reductions, normalized by the firm's level of reported reductions (the difference between reported and actual reductions divided by reported reductions). The measure is normalized by reported rather than actual reductions because actual reductions can be negative if net emissions increased over time. Positive values indicate overstating of emissions reductions (greenwashing) and negative values indicate understating (brownwashing).

Investor pressure is operationalized as low profits in a deregulated environment: the continuous net income variable interacted with the sales-weighted deregulation dummy, with lower net income under deregulation meaning higher pressure. H2B is tested by further interacting this term with each of the three external scrutiny measures.

Five indicators were factor-analyzed and reduced to a single performance index with a weighted linear combination, the factor scores yielding an economic performance value used as the criterion variable. The one-factor solution accounted for 65.9 percent of total variance; given the low factor loading on return on total assets, the extracted factor is essentially a growth performance indicator. The indicators were averaged over the five years preceding data collection.

Four volatility coefficients were computed over the five years preceding data collection (1971-76): coefficients of variation of first differences for industry sales and for industry earnings, Tosi and colleagues' technological volatility measure, and the Department of Commerce's changing annual projections of industry output computed with the first-differences method. The first factor explained only 38.6 percent of the variance and the second an additional 24.5 percent, so a two-factor solution explaining 63.2 percent of total variance was accepted, the factors being named commercial volatility and technological volatility.

Perceived environmental uncertainty was obtained with a version of Duncan's (1972) instrument, referenced to strategic decisions, restricted to the external task environment, and using one question for each of Duncan's three dimensions on each of five environmental components. Perceived uncertainty on each component was calculated for each individual team member; member scores were pooled to get the team mean on each component, and the mean of the five components served as the overall PEU score for a top management team.
level: individual managers aggregated to top management team (firm)

description: A PEU diversity index was computed by summing the standard deviations of team members' scores on each of the five environmental components, so that a higher value indicates greater within-team disagreement in perceived environmental uncertainty.

Respondents rated the importance of 12 possible corporate objectives to their firm on a 1 to 5 scale. A goals diversity score was calculated by summing a team's standard deviation on each goal item; a firm's score was the mean score for its whole top management team.

Number of goals was calculated in two ways: from the sum of the responses to all 12 goal items for each manager (total goals score), and from the sum of all the managers' responses of 5 ('extremely important to the firm') (number scoring 5). In both cases a firm's score was the mean score for its whole top management team.

A continuous measure of fit was derived by standardizing all firm-level perceived environmental uncertainty scores to z-scores and subtracting this standardized score from each of the two already standardized volatility factors; the absolute value of the result gave a measure of a firm's perceptual divergence from its true relative position. The two divergence scores, one each for commercial and technological volatility, were then summed to yield an overall divergence score, so that the higher the score the higher the divergence of perceived environmental uncertainty from objective volatility.

An index created from proxies based on both structural and ownership power. The indicators are the number of CEO titles as indicated by official company reports, which varies between one and three; the percentage of voting shares owned by the CEO as reported in the ExecuComp database; CEO duality coded as a binary variable that equals one if the CEO is the chairman of the board; whether the CEO is the founder; and the CEO's tenure at the focal firm. These variables were standardized and summed to create the CEO power index.
time_window: lagged one period relative to the dependent variable

variable_name: Nonconforming peer group selection (custom peer group)
description: A binary variable that equals one when the organization includes a peer group in the performance comparisons of its 10-K filing and zero otherwise. The variable was coded by manually coding the stock performance graphs reported in 10-K filings, for the years 2009 to 2012. A graph that includes a newly composed peer group is coded as a one, and a graph that does not include a custom peer group is coded as a zero.

The number of governance shareholder resolutions for the year before the disclosure of the 10-K filing. It represents the total number of shareholder resolutions on governance-related issues, including topics such as CEO pay and board independence. Data on shareholder resolutions for the period under study were obtained from RiskMetrics, a widely used database for the study of shareholder proposals.
time_window: year before the disclosure of the 10-K filing

description: The mean of the I/B/E/S recommendations made by analysts following a firm, computed for the year before the disclosure of the 10-K filing and obtained from Thomson's Historical Earnings Estimate Database. I/B/E/S codes recommendations as follows: 1 = strong buy, 2 = buy, 3 = hold, 4 = underperform, and 5 = sell, so an increase in this variable indicates a more negative assessment of the stock by the analysts following the firm. Because three firms lacked recommendations for specific years, 12 observations were dropped from the final sample.
time_window: year before the disclosure of the 10-K filing

description: Expected performance was coded using net income (in thousands) of the following year (t + 1). The authors chose net income given its relation to shareholder returns and because managers pay attention to this metric when defining performance outcomes. It is used to examine whether high-power CEOs who anticipate poor performance in the following year may pick a custom peer group the year before, because poor performance makes rewards tied to positive performance evaluations more salient.

The difference between the mean industry pay and that of the CEO from the focal firm, measured at t + 1. It is used to examine whether CEOs who anticipate receiving higher compensation relative to their industry peers may use a custom peer group for the evaluation of performance to provide additional justification for the change in salary. The authors note that this is distinct from the reference groups used to justify CEO compensation.

Two types of decisions were identified as characteristically involving high uncertainty and unpredictability and a possibility of large losses: R&D expenditures and diversification. R&D expenses were scaled by firm sales in order to control for firm size. One diversification indicator counted the five-year average number of four-digit industries in which the sampled firms compete; a second diversification indicator was Jacquemin and Berry's (1979) entropy measure, which also takes into consideration the relative importance of each four-digit segment to firm total sales.

Consistent with past risk research, income stream uncertainty was measured using the variance in ROA. This measure was complemented with the five-year variance in price earnings ratio (stock price/earnings per share), chosen because it captures an element of risk relevant to stockholders but also corresponds to income stream uncertainty.

Following prior research, complexity was measured as industry concentration. One indicator is the inverse of the four-firm concentration ratio, calculated by dividing the combined sales of the four largest firms in Compustat (ranked by sales) within each industry by the total sales of that industry, where the industry is defined by three-digit SIC. The second indicator counts the number of industry competitors identified by Compustat within each industry by year and averages the number over the five-year period; it is inversely related to the four-firm concentration ratio. Low concentration corresponds to higher complexity.

Average growth in industry sales and employment over the years 1984-1988. Using all firms not already included in the sample, total sales and employment were acquired for each industry by year; the natural logarithms of these totals were entered into quasi-time series regressions with time serving as the independent variable, and the antilogs of the resulting regression slope coefficients were used to capture industry growth. Growth in total employment identifies growth in resource commitments while growth in net industry sales captures growth in outputs.

The same procedure used in generating the munificence indicators was used, but in this case the antilogs of the standard errors of industry sales and industry income regressions were used to capture differences in the variability of industry growth rates. Both industry sales and industry operating income were used because variability in these measures is most likely to be associated with an organization's income stream variability.

Aspirations for each year were identified by comparing each firm's performance from the previous year (both ROA and ROE) with their respective industry average for that year. When performance exceeded the industry average, aspirations were determined by multiplying prior year performance by 1.05 (effectively adding a growth factor); aspirations were coded as industry average performance from the previous year when the firm's performance was below that average. Attainment discrepancy was calculated by taking the difference between aspirations and the firm's actual performance, repeated for each year and then averaged across years for each firm.

Heterogeneity in upper echelon membership was assessed using Blau's (1977) categorical index of heterogeneity. The first measure captured the mix of education curriculums represented in the TMT, measuring dispersion of the highest obtained university degree as defined by six educational specializations: science, art, business, engineering, medicine, and law. The second measure identified the team's functional heterogeneity. TMT membership was defined as the two highest executive levels: the chairman, chief executive officer, president, and chief operating officer, the next highest tier, and any other officers who are on the board of directors.

Two measures of managerial ownership were used. One captured the proportion of equity ownership held by all officers and directors as a group, an aggregate percentage based on the number of common shares outstanding on the date of record as reported in annual proxy statements. The second summed the proportional equity holding of each reported top management team member, identified from proxy statements, form 10-Ks, or annual reports. Equity was defined as common stock held directly or indirectly for the executives' benefit, excluding options to purchase additional shares.

Three types of slack were included in the study: available, recoverable, and potential. Available slack is measured as the firm's quick ratio and addresses the firm's liquidity, including assets such as idle working capital, marketable securities, accounts receivable, or funding in reserve. Recoverable slack identifies excess administrative and operational expenses and was measured as the ratio of general and administrative expenses to sales. Potential slack identifies a firm's unused borrowing capacity and was measured as debt/equity.

Because complexity and munificence failed to discriminate in the measurement model, the final measurement model collapses them into a single construct named industry rivalry. The two original concentration measures of complexity and the sales growth indicator were retained for this construct; the authors note that high levels of rivalry are common in fragmented industries characterized by rapid growth in sales.

variable_name: long-run virtual resource and scope commitments
description: Panel data DEA maximizes, for each bank, the ratio of aggregate weighted scope outputs to aggregate weighted resource inputs across all periods, yielding a single long-run efficiency index and a common set of long-run weights for the commitments. The products of these weights with the corresponding commitments - the long-run virtual outputs and inputs - quantify the contribution of each variable to long-run efficiency and identify the strategic priorities of the bank's CEO; cognitive groups are formed on these long-run virtual scope and resource commitments.

Banks were assigned to cognitive groups by a two-stage clustering procedure applied to the long-run virtual resource and scope commitments: Ward's hierarchical algorithm defined the number of clusters and the k-means algorithm assigned banks to them, producing three groups. The authors characterize the groups as CEOs who focus their attention on investment banking activities, on commercial banking activities, and on traditional banking activities, respectively.

variable_name: cognitive groups based on CEOs' demographic characteristics
description: CEO profiles in the savings bank industry were identified by conducting a cluster analysis of CEOs' demographic characteristics using the two-step approach. The three resulting groups were labelled as CEOs with positive attitudes toward risk taking, neutral attitudes, and negative attitudes toward risk taking.

variable_name: cognitive groups based on CEOs' letters to shareholders
description: A computer-aided text analysis of the CEOs' letters, obtained from their banks' annual reports for each savings bank and year, was conducted with the DICTION 6.0 software program, which uses predefined dictionaries to characterize five constructs: activity, certainty, commonality, optimism, and realism. CEOs with similar scores on these constructs were clustered with the two-step procedure into three groups, labelled as focused entrepreneurial orientation, broad entrepreneurial orientation, and resistant-to-change orientation.
Performance is the ratio of accounting profits to total assets, expressed as a percentage. Long-run performance is measured as the average ROA between t and t + 5.
time_window: same year, and t to t + 5

description: All IEEE-assigned keywords per author are collected for the four years before Kinect's launch (2007-2010), and each keyword is mapped to its main research area out of the 51 IEEE top categories. The authors count the total number of keywords assigned to each of the 51 categories across the author's papers, convert the counts to percentages, and calculate the Euclidian distance in the multidimensional space of the 51 research areas; the diversification measure equals one minus the calculated Euclidian length, so higher values indicate higher diversity of research areas. By construction the measure is less than or equal to 1 and is never 0; percentages rather than counts are used so that the measure captures knowledge breadth while controlling for knowledge depth. The authors also construct a dummy equal to 1 for researchers above the median of the index (0.646) and quartile dummies with the bottom quartile (index below 0.596) omitted; the text presents the specification as an equation that is not reproduced here in readable form.

Indicator variable equal to 1 for an author who publishes at least one paper referencing Kinect during the four-year period after Kinect's launch (2011-2014), and 0 otherwise. Kinect publications are identified by searching the full text and metadata of all publications in the IEEE Xplore database for the keyword 'Kinect'; authors of at least one such publication are labelled Kinect authors and all other researchers non-Kinect authors.

variable_name: Kinect paper in the top 10th percentile of citations
description: Indicator variable equal to 1 for Kinect authors who published at least one Kinect paper ranking in the top 10% of papers in IEEE Xplore by citation count, and 0 otherwise. Highly cited papers are identified relative to the entire population of publications, that is, all papers published in computer science, electrical engineering and electronics between 2011 and 2014, not only relative to work referencing Kinect; the authors also consider a top 5% threshold.

variable_name: Above median number of IEEE domains
description: Indicator variable equal to 1 if the author published Kinect papers that list a combination of keywords indicating an above the sample median number of IEEE domains, and 0 otherwise. The number of knowledge categories the paper combines is evidenced by the above median number of IEEE domains that characterize the paper, based on the keywords used in each paper.

Indicator of whether a researcher's affiliation is academic rather than in the private sector, collected from the affiliation listed in the IEEE profile of researchers in the period before Kinect's launch. The authors locate and confirm the affiliation of 83,983 individuals in the sample, distinguishing 18,669 researchers with an industry affiliation and 65,314 academic researchers, and include a dummy variable to account for the remaining cases where affiliation could not be verified.

Number of years of active publication since 2001, computed as the number of years since the researcher's first observed publication in the large dataset going back to 2001. Because data on time since degree completion are unavailable, this serves as a proxy for research age, allowing the authors to distinguish a researcher who started publishing at the beginning of the sample window (research age = 1) from one who has been research-active for 10 or more years (research age = 10). The authors note this likely underestimates the true research age of researchers who published before 2001.

Numerical values of the six Hofstede national culture dimensions for the country of origin assigned to each researcher. Country of origin is inferred from the researcher's name with NamSor, a Naive Bayes classification algorithm that outputs a score capturing the probability that a name reflects a certain country of origin; such a score is obtained for 98,277 of the 104,587 researchers in the main CEM sample. The six culture measures are then regressed on the continuous measure of diversification.

A composite measure developed from three indicators of prominence in the alliance network. The eigenvector-based measure of centrality (CENTRAL) is a status measure calculated as the weighted sum of the centralities of the firm's partners from the network adjacency matrix using UCINET V. PARTNER is a count of the number of partners with whom the firm had at least one tie, and TIES is a count of the number of direct ties the firm had with all its partners. The three measures loaded onto one factor in a principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation, and the factor scores were used as the composite measure and to develop the interaction variables.
time_window: calculated for each firm for every year it was in the network

description: A composite measure developed from structural holes and two measures of partner diversity. The constraint measure for structural holes (HOLES) was calculated with UCINET V; high constraint indicates that the firm's partners are densely connected with high redundancy, whereas low constraint indicates a sparsely connected network. The nationality heterogeneity index (COUNTRY) and the technology heterogeneity index (TECH) were computed with Blau's heterogeneity index, where a high value indicates high diversity in the nationality or technology group of the partners. The measures loaded onto one factor and the factor scores were used as the composite measure and to develop the interaction variables.
time_window: calculated for each firm for every year it was in the network

description: Sales per employee in constant US dollars. Figures were converted into U.S. dollars using the exchange rate between the U.S. dollar and the foreign currency prevailing as of 30 June each year, and adjusted for inflation by developing constant price measures with the year 1991 as a base. The performance variable was lagged by one year in the analysis.

Two dummy variables created from an events-based classification of environmental change, each covering a three-year window after the event. The legislative event dummy (SRYEAR) takes the value of 1 for the years 1984, 1985, and 1986 and 0 otherwise; the technology event dummy (SLYEAR) takes the value of 1 for the years 1987, 1988, and 1989 and 0 otherwise. Interaction variables (PROM8486, PROM8789, ENTR8486, ENTR8789) were formed as the product of these dummies and the two network position variables, so that Hypotheses 1 and 2 were tested twice.

A continuous composite measure of firm strategy formed from two ratios: the proportion of sales in the steel industry to total sales and the proportion of domestic sales to total sales. The two measures were reversed and then multiplied to arrive at a composite measure of firm strategy that ranged between 0 and 0.67, with a mean of 0.05; firms with scores closer to 1 indicate that they are pursuing an analyzer strategy. Each measure was calculated using data from Worldscope, supplemented by annual reports when the information was not available from Worldscope.
time_window: calculated for each firm for every year

description: A keyword search for 'restructuring' was run in Lexis/Nexis and Dow Jones News Retrieval coupled with the firm name of the target for the 4 years following the initial takeover attempt. If a clear story about refocusing did not emerge, the remaining firms were searched with no keywords for the 4 years following the takeover attempt. All stories whose headline suggested a possible description of refocusing activities such as spin-offs or sales of plants or divisions were read. A dummy variable was coded as 1 if evidence of refocusing was found and 0 if it was not.
time_window: 4 years following the initial takeover attempt

description: Measured by the proportion of board members who are outsiders without current or past employment contracts with the firm. Higher values indicate greater board independence.
Measured as the number of shares held by inside directors (including the CEO) divided by the total number of outstanding shares. Higher values indicate lower board independence.
Measured as the number of shares held by outside directors divided by the total number of outstanding shares. Higher values indicate greater board independence.
Coded 1 if the CEO also chaired the board (0 otherwise). The presence of CEO duality indicates lower board independence.

variable_name: precision of firms ' annual earnings guidance
description: We measure precision as the range in which guidance is expressed (in cents). Because this range will depend in part on the size of the guidance, we combine this dependent variable with a control variable for the midpoint of the guidance range. Larger guidance ranges represent lower precision, so we create the measurement of precision by multiplying this variable by - 1, meaning higher coefficients connote higher precision.
time_window: annual guidance issued at least one month before the end of the fiscal year

description: This variable measures whether a firm missed its earnings guidance in the prior year, coded 1 if the guidance was missed and 0 otherwise.

This variable captures whether a firm underperformed its industry peers (based on three-digit SIC) in the quarter before earnings guidance was given, coded 1 if a firm was underperforming and 0 otherwise. The choice of measure follows evidence that professional investors examine the performance of focal firms in an industry relative to peers, and that security analysts are usually assigned to industry groups.

This measures whether there was a negative reaction (abnormal return, see above) to an M&A announcement made by the focal firm in the quarter before the focal earnings guidance (if no M&A announcement was made, the variable is set to 0).
time_window: quarter before the focal earnings guidance

description: This measures the degree (as a proportion) to which the focal guidance is higher than the previous year ' s EPS.
time_window: relative to previous year ' s EPS

description: Cumulative abnormal market adjusted returns of a firm ' s share price based on a window of one day before the announcement until one day after the announcement. The expected return (in percent) is calculated from a market model that assumes a stable linear relation between the market return (value weighted, based on CRSP) and return of the shares of the focal firm; the market model is estimated over a window of one year ending a week before the earnings guidance announcement. RavenPack is used to exclude observations with confounding announcements during the announcement window.
time_window: one day before to one day after the announcement

description: Indicator that equals one if the firm's founder (or at least half of the founders if there is more than one) is from an EU country, interacted with a post-Brexit indicator that equals one from the second quarter of 2016 onward. EU nationals are treated as exposed to the immigration uncertainty generated by the referendum, whereas immigrants from outside the EU form the control group and are assumed not to face a change in immigration policy.

variable_name: Growth in the number of new firms
description: Year-to-year growth rate of the number of incorporations, measured as the change in the inverse hyperbolic sine transformation (arcsin) of the new number of businesses in sector s and travel-to-work area r created by founders from country c, between quarters t and t-4. Triplets for which the number of new firms is always zero between 2013 and 2018 are dropped.

Whether the founding team has at least one founder with previous entrepreneurial experience in Great Britain, identified by tracking the complete founding history of entrepreneurs in the data back to 1995. Because experienced entrepreneurs can exploit a wider and more diverse network than non-experienced ones, firms whose founding teams have no previous entrepreneurial experience are treated as more reliant on immigrant actors; the negative entry effect is concentrated in this group.

Number of pages of the incorporation documents filed within one year of the firm's incorporation, used as a proxy for venture quality at founding on the argument that higher-quality start-ups write longer, more complete incorporation documents. Firms are split into low-quality firms (below the 20th percentile of the length distribution, 1-7 pages), medium-quality firms (8-26 pages, between the 20th and 80th percentiles) and high-quality firms (at least 27 pages, above the 80th percentile).
time_window: within one year of the incorporation date

description: Indicator that equals one if the individual's country of origin belongs to the European Union and zero if it belongs to the rest of Europe; interacted with the post-Brexit indicator it captures exposure to the immigration uncertainty generated by the referendum.

variable_name: Low-skilled seeking a job as employees
description: Share of low-skilled people from country c in the United Kingdom who are looking for a job in quarter t out of all low-skilled people from c. Low-skilled workers are those who have not earned at least a bachelor's degree or equivalent.

variable_name: Low-skilled seeking a job as self-employed
description: Share of low-skilled people from country c in the United Kingdom who are looking to be self-employed in quarter t out of all low-skilled people from c, where low-skilled workers are those who have not earned at least a bachelor's degree or equivalent.

Indicator that equals one if the country belongs to the European Union and zero otherwise (EU27 countries are the treatment group and non-EU27 European countries the control group), interacted with a post-Brexit indicator that equals one for 2016, 2017 and 2018.

Inverse hyperbolic sine of the number of high-quality businesses in country c in year t, where high-quality (high-growth) ventures are those with an average annualized employment growth greater than 10% per year over a three-year period. The authors also estimate the same equation using the share of high-growth firms in each country as the dependent variable.

The fractional number of months from the date a given drug development project was initiated by a CRO to its completion date. The authors state that drug development projects take on average slightly more than 29 months to complete in the dataset. Time to complete is considered one of the most important performance measures for CROs. As the measure represents the hazard of a project being completed, variables that lead to shorter (longer) development times have positive (negative) coefficients.

The logged number of full-time employees within the focal CRO at the time the focal drug development project was undertaken. It is one of two scale-related measures examined in the econometric analysis. The authors use a single measure of scale economies in separate models of the baseline analysis because the scale measures are highly correlated with each other.
level: focal CRO at the time of the focal project
time_window: at the time the focal drug development project was undertaken

description: The number of functional areas in which the focal CRO has at least 20 full-time employees (FTEs), measuring whether development performance advantages exist from a more functionally related size measure. The classification scheme creates the following functional areas: clinical; data management; laboratory; medical; quality assurance; and regulatory.

A count of the number of technological areas (therapeutic areas) in which the focal CRO is active.
