It is the authors' measure of scope economies, intended to capture knowledge spillovers from operating in several therapeutic areas. Firms that are active in several therapeutic areas may develop knowledge that is transferable to other therapeutic areas with little cost but with potentially significant performance benefits.

The summation of prior drug development projects completed by CRO i in therapeutic category j at time t, where the count of completed projects in that category is discounted by a depreciation factor so that recent experience is weighted more heavily than past experience, consistent with organizational forgetting. The authors depreciate therapeutic area experience by 20 percent per period in the econometric analysis. The exact specification is given only in an unreadable formula; the prose describes the summation and depreciation given above.

An interaction term of therapeutic area experience and therapeutic area scope, created because the authors examine the compounding effect of scope economies and experience. The constituent variables are mean-centered in this interaction term to minimize multicollinearity concerns and to facilitate interpretation of the results by linking individual coefficient estimates to specific hypotheses.

variable_name: strategy cluster membership (K means cluster analysis)
description: Railroad shippers rated the principal railroads providing them service on nine strategy indicators, on a scale of 1 to 5 (from poor to excellent), both prior to and after deregulation. The judges' evaluations for each railroad were averaged to create organizational scores, and the K means clustering algorithm with squared Euclidean distance measures classified the 54 observations (27 railroads considered as if they were two firms) into clusters representing different strategies. Four clusters - leadership, innovation, quality differentiation and contingency - are focused strategies, while the fifth cluster, the unfocused follower, is unfocused.
time_window: pre-deregulation and post-deregulation ratings (survey administered August 1984)

description: A railroad was classified as having changed its strategy when it was found in two different clusters in the pre- and post-deregulation data, and as not having changed when it clustered into the same strategic group in both periods. Fifteen of the 27 railroads changed their strategies.

Return on investment was obtained from the Interstate Commerce Commission; ROI, ROTC and ROE were defined and computed in accordance with the Bureau of Accounts, Section of Financial Analysis, from the railroads' Annual Report Forms (R-1). The pre-deregulation measure of performance was the average for 1979 and 1980 and the post-deregulation measure was 1983, and the analysis compares the change in performance. These data were not available for seven railroads.

Return on total capitalization was obtained from the Interstate Commerce Commission and defined and computed in accordance with the Bureau of Accounts, Section of Financial Analysis, from the railroads' Annual Report Forms (R-1). The pre-deregulation measure was the average for 1979 and 1980 and the post-deregulation measure was 1983, and the analysis compares the change in performance.

Return on equity was obtained from the Interstate Commerce Commission and defined and computed in accordance with the Bureau of Accounts, Section of Financial Analysis, from the railroads' Annual Report Forms (R-1). The pre-deregulation measure was the average for 1979 and 1980 and the post-deregulation measure was 1983, and the analysis compares the change in performance.

Government regulation is represented by the pre-deregulation period, in which railroads were rated on strategy indicators as they were before the Staggers Act of 1980. Focused strategy frequency in this period is the indirect test.

Environmental variation is the shift from the regulated to the deregulated environment. Railroads were rated on strategy indicators for the period before and the period after the Staggers Act of 1980, giving 27 observations in each period.

variable_name: ownership structure categories (strong owner-controlled, weak owner-controlled, management-controlled)
description: Palmer's (1973) three ownership categories: a firm was categorized as strong owner-controlled if any single party owned at least 30 percent of its outstanding common stock, as weak owner-controlled if one party controlled at least 10 percent but less than 30 percent, and as management-controlled if less than 10 percent of common shares were owned by one party. In the Tobit models, MGMT is a 0/1 dummy for management control and WEAK is a dummy for weak owner control, with owner-controlled firms (both dummies equal to 0) as the omitted category.

variable_name: number of mergers of each type
description: The count of mergers of a given type made by each firm between 1961 and 1970, taken from the FTC large merger series of 1976, which classifies mergers as vertical, horizontal, product extension, market extension, or pure conglomerate. Following Amihud and Lev, the latter three categories were also aggregated into an 'all conglomerates' category. Each merger category is the dependent variable of a separate Tobit model.

Calculated for each firm by regressing its return on equity for each year on the average return on equity for all U.S. manufacturing firms for that same year, the average ROE coming from the FTC's Report to the President (1976). The measure is grounded in the assumption that the more businesses a firm holds in its corporate portfolio, the more closely its returns map to the all-market portfolio and the lower its unsystematic risk.

variable_name: Rumelt's five-level classification of diversification strategies
description: Rumelt's (1974) classification (single business, dominant vertical, related constrained, related linked, unrelated business) applied to the 160 firms that intersect Palmer's (1973) list of Fortune 500 firms and Rumelt's (1974) sample. Used in a chi-square test for independence of diversification strategies across ownership categories.

variable_name: standard deviation of the market model error term
description: Estimated from the capital market model using CRSP weekly returns, with 156 trading weeks (1964-66) used in keeping with standard conventions to ensure reasonably stable estimates of the market model's coefficients. The standard deviation of the error term reflects an estimate of the firm's unsystematic, or firm-specific, risk.

A 3-year average surrogate measure of Tobin's Q following the Fama and French (1993) definition, the ratio of market value to book value. Market-to-book is used rather than book-to-market because its interpretation is direct: the higher the market-to-book ratio, the higher the performance of the firm.

variable_name: percentage of shares held by large outside owners
description: Using stock ownership data from proxy statements, the number of shares held by each outside shareholder owning 5 percent or more of the outstanding shares is summed and then converted to a percentage of the firm's outstanding shares. Unlike Palmer's categories, the measure focuses exclusively on large outside shareholders.

The sum of two standardized components (mean = 0, standard deviation = 1): the percentage of outside directors on each board and the percentage of firm shares owned by outside directors. Directors who conduct business with the board either directly or through organizations they represent are not counted as outside board members.

Following Rumelt's (1974) five-level classification scheme, the relatedness of each of the 289 mergers was classified by two independent raters; inadequate or ambiguous data and nonreconciliatory classification differences reduced the usable sample to 149 buying firms. The classifications were converted into a ranked, ordinal variable assigning horizontal mergers a value of 1 and vertical, product extension, market extension and unrelated mergers values of 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Rumelt's (1974) five-level classification scheme was used to classify the diversification of each of the 289 buying and acquired firms using data from the year prior to the merger, with two raters independently evaluating each firm's diversification strategy. The classifications were converted into a ranked, ordinal variable assigning single business diversification strategies a value of 1 and dominant vertical, constrained, linked and unrelated strategies values of 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Estimated using the same source of data and methodology as Study 1, but over a 12-month time horizon ending 2 months before the day that the merger announcement first appeared in the Wall Street Journal, so that the measure is free of merger-related influences.
time_window: 12-month horizon ending 2 months before the merger announcement

description: Estimated as each firm's market-to-book ratio during the fiscal year prior to the year of the first public announcement of the merger.
time_window: fiscal year prior to the merger announcement

variable_name: type of acquisitions and level of diversification
description: Corporate strategy is operationalized through two variables. In Study 1, the type of merger (counts of horizontal, vertical, product extension, market extension, pure conglomerate and all-conglomerate mergers made 1961-1970, from the FTC large merger series) and the level of diversification (R-squared of ROE on average manufacturing ROE, and Rumelt's five-level classification). In Study 2, merger relatedness and diversification level were coded as ordinal Rumelt-based scores.

The measure, developed by Pugh, Hickson, Hinings, and Turner (1969), reflects the number of specialized roles across 16 functional areas. Organizational scores varied between 0 and 21, with a mean of 9.1 and a standard deviation of 5.1.

Measured by the number of departments in the organization, a department being defined as any unit having at least two persons and two levels, the head of which reported to the mayor, the administrator, and/or an alderman. The range was from 3 to 12 departments with a mean of 7.16 and a standard deviation of 2.22.

Measured by the number of levels in each department from the department head to the lowest level worker and then calculating the average for all departments. Organizational scores ranged from 2.50 to 6, the mean was 3.64, and the standard deviation was .87.

The degree of task routinization was based on six questionnaire items. Items 1, 3, and 5 were coded from 1 indicating strong agreement to 4 indicating strong disagreement, for items 2 and 4 the coding was reversed, and item 6 was coded as indicated (very routine = 4, routine = 3, nonroutine = 2, very nonroutine = 1). Respondents' scores were calculated by adding their responses and dividing by 6, and mean scores were then computed separately for the middle and lower echelons of each organization. Cronbach's alpha is .70 for middle echelon routinization and .73 for lower echelon routinization.

Each respondent was asked to report separately the number of contacts with persons in other organizations in the public sector and the number of contacts with persons in other organizations outside the public sector during a typical week. These were summed for each person, and level-specific scores were constructed by calculating the average for all department heads and the average for all subordinates in each organization. Cronbach's alpha is .78 for the middle echelon and .55 for the lower echelon.

Respondents were asked to report separately the number of contacts either in face-to-face meetings or by telephone with persons at the same level, at a lower level, and at a higher level in the organization in a typical week. For each respondent the number of such contacts was added, and level-specific averages were then computed for middle echelon department heads and lower echelon officials in each organization.

Measured on the basis of responses to five questionnaire items regarding perceived influence over several facets of the work environment. Response categories were none = 1, a little = 2, some = 3, and quite a bit = 4; the average response for each respondent was computed and then level-specific averages were calculated. The alpha coefficient of this scale was .90 for middle echelon officials and .87 for lower echelon ones.

All department heads (middle echelons) were automatically selected in the sample; within each department a simple random sample of other members (lower echelons) was selected, with the sampling ratio varying according to the size of the department (one-half in departments with fewer than 10 administrative staff, one-third in departments with 10 to 19, and one-fourth in departments with 20 or more). Middle echelon department heads perform vertical and horizontal coordination functions, whereas lower echelon officials directly supervise ongoing service delivery operations. Proposal measures and process scores were computed separately for the two echelons of each organization.

The percent of respondents in a particular echelon proposing the innovation in question, calculated from individual responses to the question: In the last ten years, have you ever made propositions or have you participated in the elaboration of formal propositions to change the technical equipment in this township administration, regardless of whether or not these propositions were accepted by your managers and whether or not they were put into practice? (No = 0, Yes = 1). Mean scores were computed separately for the middle and lower echelons of each organization.

Respondents were asked to briefly describe each of the propositions they had made, and a count of the number of proposals described furnished the data for calculating the average number of proposals. Requiring respondents to describe each of their proposals constitutes a check on the validity of these self-reports. Averages were calculated separately for the middle and lower echelons of each organization.

The percent of respondents in a particular echelon proposing the innovation in question, calculated from individual responses to the question: During the past ten years, have you made any propositions or have you participated in the elaboration of any formal propositions to your superior concerning changes in or modification in management methods, including techniques of leadership and other management techniques, regardless of whether these propositions were accepted or not by your management and whether or not they were put into practice? (No = 0, Yes = 1). Means were computed separately for the middle and lower echelons of each organization.

Respondents were asked to briefly describe each of the propositions they had made concerning management methods, and averages of the number of innovations proposed were based on a count of the proposals described. Averages were calculated separately for the middle and lower echelons of each organization.

variable_name: proposals for technical and administrative innovations (percent proposing, average number)
description: Self-reported proposals for innovation made by officials in the previous ten years, whether or not accepted or implemented. Measured for technical and for administrative innovations, each as the percent of respondents in an echelon who made a proposal (yes/no) and the average number of proposals described, computed separately for middle and lower echelons of each organization.

variable_name: role specialization, horizontal differentiation, vertical differentiation
description: Structural complexity is indicated by three organization-level structural measures: role specialization (number of specialized roles across 16 functional areas, Pugh et al. 1969), horizontal differentiation (number of departments) and vertical differentiation (average number of levels per department). The three indicators were entered as separate predictors.

Subsidiary royalty payments to parent firm operations, divided by total sales of the foreign operation. Royalties and licensing fees are paid to parent firms for the use of intangible property, such as patents, industrial processes, trademarks, copyrights, franchises, manufacturing rights, or other intangible assets or property rights. Because a measure specific to technology licensing fees is available only for 1989, the authors assume royalty payments provide a good proxy for technology transfer payments. The variable is lagged.
time_window: lagged one period (five-year lag between benchmark surveys)

description: Ratio of U.S. employees to total employees for each foreign operation, used to capture managerial knowledge transfers. Following existing literature, the authors created a variable that captures the ratio of U.S. employees to total employees for each foreign operation. Lagged values are used; because only benchmark survey data are used, the lag is five years.

Time-varying measure of foreign operation R&D intensity, created by dividing total country R&D expenditure by total country sales in each foreign country operation. The BEA collects data on the R&D expenditures for each foreign affiliate and parent firm. The variable is lagged.

Return on assets, used to measure subsidiary performance as an indicator of how profitable an operation is relative to its total assets, defined as net income divided by total assets. Return on assets is commonly employed to assess financial results and shows the amount of earnings generated from invested capital assets.

Survival time of the business in months. Respondents reported the month and year in which they commenced business activity and the month and year in which the activity was terminated. A firm still alive at the time of the survey is recorded as right censored.
time_window: from founding in 2001 to termination or to the spring 2005 survey

description: The intensity with which strategic issues were analyzed and planned prior to launch, measured through two survey questions (Zahra and Covin 1993). Founders were asked to assess how intensely they analyzed issues pertaining to (a) target market definition and (b) the attainment of competitive advantage. Responses to both questions were captured on five-point Likert-type scales, from 'not planned at all' to 'very thoroughly planned'; the two items have an alpha of 0.76.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (not planned at all to very thoroughly planned)

description: A dichotomous variable capturing whether or not a change was made to the firm's product or service offerings at any time between founding and the time the survey was administered (or termination of the business activity). Founders were asked to indicate if their product or service offering did not change (0) or if it changed (1) in any of the following ways: extension or new addition, reduction or deletion, or complete replacement.
time_window: between founding and survey administration (or termination of the business activity)

variable_name: Pre-entry knowledge of the business activity (log pre-entry knowledge)
description: Constructed as the highest value of two survey questions. The first asks the respondent to assess the extent to which the new business activity is related to their prior work experience on a five-point Likert-type scale; the second asks the extent to which pre-entry knowledge from prior work experience, education, and/or hobby or side activities was important in their decision to pursue the business opportunity, also on a five-point Likert-type scale. The highest score across both questions was used, rather than a sum or average, to avoid double-counting knowledge obtained through pre-entry work experience. Because the responses were slightly skewed, the log form of this measure was used in the analyses.
scale: highest of two five-point Likert-type items; log form used in analyses

description: Founders were asked to assess their level of management experience at the time they founded their business on a five-point Likert-type scale, from 'very low' to 'very high'. The measure indicates that founders had worked in a managerial capacity before they started the new firm.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (very low to very high)

description: The proportion of a firm's revenues that are attributable to its largest market category, industrial or consumer. CR ≥ 0.80 identifies uni-category firms, which concentrate their business activities in either consumer or industrial markets; CR < 0.80 identifies bi-category firms, which market significant proportions of their output to both consumer and industrial markets. The 0.80 break point was described as somewhat arbitrary but a reasonable compromise such that firms classified as unicategory were predominantly concentrated in one category but not exclusively so.

The proportion of a firm's revenues that are attributable to its largest product group, using the product group classification of durable goods, nondurable goods, industrial capital goods, components and raw or semi-finished materials, supplies or other consumable products, and services. PR ≥ 0.80 identifies single-group firms, which concentrate their activities in a single product group; PR < 0.80 identifies multi-group firms, which have significant proportions of their activities in more than one product group.

The proportion of a firm's revenues attributable to its largest single business. Firms with SR ≥ 0.95 are classified as single business, firms with SR between 0.70 and 0.95 as dominant business, and firms with SR ≤ 0.70 as diversified firms. Classifications for the market-based typology were made with 1979 data, and the three closest years were used to minimize the chance that a firm's category had changed.

Firm assignments under the Rumelt (1982) diversification scheme were performed by one of the authors employing a similar procedure to that of Rumelt and Montgomery (1982), and previous classifications where appropriate. Fifty percent of the sample was independently coded by a second coder; high reliability was obtained and differences were resolved by discussion. The scheme assigns firms to dominant-vertical, dominant-constrained, dominant-linked-unrelated, related-constrained, related-linked and unrelated-business categories.

Return on capital for the 3-year period 1978-80, based on data from Value Line, with the 3-year mean used. The formal definition is ROC = net profit + (interest on long-term debt)/(long-term debt + net worth), where net profit is net income before extraordinary gains or losses and net worth is common plus preferred stockholders' equity including intangibles.

Sales growth was measured as the percentage increase over the previous year. Two values, 1978-79 and 1979-80, were used, based on data from Value Line. Multiple years were employed to minimize the unreliability associated with a single year.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the licensor and licensee are partners in an equity joint venture at the time the license is initiated, and 0 otherwise. Joint venture agreements in effect at the beginning of the sample period were documented in the Toyo Keizai directories of foreign subsidiaries and matched to the licensing data. Only 27 of the 536 firm dyads have an equity joint venture in effect at the beginning of the sample period.
time_window: at the time the license is initiated

description: Dummy variable coded 1 if the focal alliance involves a cross-licensing agreement and 0 if it is a unilateral license only. NISTEP requires firms to indicate whether a particular license is part of a cross-license agreement, but the patents out-licensed by the Japanese firm to its U.S. counterpart are not observed.

Number of citations to any of the licensor's patents (1975-2002) appearing in the licensee's patents applied for after 1992, counting only cited patents that are in the same technology class(es) as the licensed patent(s). Patent citation counts in the empirical analysis are restricted to U.S. patents, and technology classes are the 118 classes defined in the International Patent Classification System. Where the license covers Japanese patents held by the U.S. firm, OECD triadic patent families are used to classify citations into related and unrelated categories.
time_window: cited patents 1975-2002; licensee patents applied for after 1992

description: Number of citations to any of the licensor's patents (1975-2002) appearing in the licensee's patents applied for after 1992, counting only cited patents that are not in any of the technology classes covered by the licensed patent(s). Citation counts are restricted to U.S. patents and use the International Patent Classification System technology classes.
time_window: cited patents 1975-2002; licensee patents applied for after 1992

description: Unrelated postlicense cites divided by total postlicense cites, where total postlicense cites is the number of cites to any of the licensor's patents (1975-2002) in the licensee's patents applied for after 1992. It captures whether changes in technology building under different alliance structures reflect symmetric changes in both related and unrelated technology areas or a change in the breadth of knowledge transfers.
time_window: cited patents 1975-2002; licensee patents applied for after 1992

description: The average age of the licensor's patents (1975-2002) cited in the licensee's patents applied for after 1992, where the cited patent is in one of the technology classes covered by the licensed patent(s). Higher values indicate a longer lag and therefore slower knowledge integration.
time_window: cited patents 1975-2002; licensee patents applied for after 1992

description: The average age of the licensor's patents (1975-2002) cited in the licensee's patents applied for after 1992, where the cited patent is not in any of the technology classes covered by the licensed patent(s). Higher values indicate a longer lag and therefore slower knowledge integration.
time_window: cited patents 1975-2002; licensee patents applied for after 1992

description: The dependent variable was the probability of franchisor failure. Entry occurs in the year Entrepreneur Magazine indicated that the franchise system was established; failure is exit from Entrepreneur Magazine's listing and nonreemergence in the listing at a later date. Firms that failed during the observation period were labeled events, and organizations that did not fail were treated as right censored.
time_window: 1979-1996, annual spells, with covariates tested against survival during the following calendar year

description: Age is operationalized as the log of the number of years since firm incorporation. The age of the franchise system and the age of the firm are correlated 0.97, so only one of the two could be included in a regression equation.
Size is operationalized as the log of the number of units in the chain.

Following Rao (1994), certification is operationalized as the log of the annual ranking of the franchise system by franchising experts in Entrepreneur Magazine. The ranking is based on a proprietary formula that incorporates the quantitative data reported in the magazine with the subjective assessment of the magazine's experts. The actual rank ranged from 1 to 501 and was reverse coded, with the best system receiving a rank of 501; all unranked franchisors were assigned a score of 1.
scale: reverse coded rank 1 to 501, best system = 501

description: Company is the percentage of total outlets that are company-owned; it captures the relative emphasis of the franchise system on company ownership of outlets.
Capitalization is the amount of money needed to open an outlet. A related change measure, Capitalization Growth, is the two-year change in the amount of capitalization necessary to open an outlet.
A dummy variable coded 1 if the franchise system was founded in a state in which franchisee termination laws exist and 0 otherwise.
A dummy variable coded 1 if the franchise system was founded in a state in which registration requirements exist and 0 otherwise.

Pay dispersion was measured with the gini coefficient, which measures the degree of inequality in a pay structure and ranges from 1, complete inequality, to 0, complete equality. The coefficient was computed for each firm and year from the total compensation of the managers reported in ExecuComp.
Pay dispersion was measured with the gini coefficient, computed for each firm and year on salary and bonus only, to parallel the compensation calculation used for the CAHRS data.

Pay dispersion was measured with the gini coefficient using salary and bonus data. Two subsets of managers were used: all managers within five reporting levels from the board of directors and all managers within ten reporting levels from the board (CEO = 1).
Average managerial tenure was computed for each firm and year. Tenure was computed from the recorded date of hiring and represents organizational, not job, tenure.
Average managerial tenure was computed for each firm and year. Tenure was computed from the recorded date of hiring and represents organizational, not job, tenure.
Turnover was coded as 1 if a manager left during the current year. Turnover data were available only in the COMPUSTAT sample.

Baber and colleagues' (1996) composite measure of investment opportunities, based on factor scores resulting from the analysis of four items measuring prior investment intensity, annual income and asset growth rates, and R&D expenditures. As in Baber et al., one factor was returned in the analysis.

Baber and colleagues' (1996) composite measure of investment opportunities, based on factor scores resulting from the analysis of four items measuring prior investment intensity, annual income and asset growth rates, and R&D expenditures. As in Baber et al., one factor was returned in the analysis.

Annual four-digit SIC industry sales over the previous five years (t-5 to t-1) were regressed onto a measure of time; the standard error of the slope coefficient was used as the measure of environmental instability.

Annual four-digit SIC industry sales over the previous five years (t-5 to t-1) were regressed onto a measure of time; the standard error of the slope coefficient was used as the measure of environmental instability.
Annual four-digit SIC industry sales over the previous five years (t-5 to t-1) were regressed onto a measure of time; the regression slope coefficient was used as the measure of munificence.
Annual four-digit SIC industry sales over the previous five years (t-5 to t-1) were regressed onto a measure of time; the regression slope coefficient was used as the measure of munificence.

A categorical measure of diversification following Hall and St. John (1994), based on the number of two-digit SIC codes a firm operates in. Firms were placed into one of four categories, and indicators for single-product, related-constrained, and related-linked diversification were entered, with unrelated diversification as the omitted category.

A categorical measure of diversification following Hall and St. John (1994), based on the number of two-digit SIC codes a firm operates in. Firms were placed into one of four categories, and indicators for single-product, related-constrained, and related-linked diversification were entered, with unrelated diversification as the omitted category.

The amount of scaled capital expenditures in a business unit with weak prospects is compared against the average scaled expenditure in all business units in the sample that have strong prospects; capital expenditures in a poor business that are greater than the average expenditure in stronger businesses are classified as overinvestment. Because scaled capital expenditures for a business unit may be tied to the capital intensity of its industry, the sum of this calculation was regressed on industry capital intensity and on the controls cost of capital, size, and industry ROA, and the saved residuals represent overinvestment. All measures are scaled by business unit size and constructed so that increasing numbers represent higher levels of overinvestment.
time_window: one year prior to the outcome variable (t-1)

description: The amount of scaled capital expenditures in business units with strong prospects is compared against the average investment in all businesses with weak prospects, based on the logic that capital expenditures in a strong prospect business should not be lower than the average investment in weaker business units. Residuals, representing underinvestment, are then calculated following the same approach as with overinvestment, regressing the calculation on industry capital intensity and on the controls cost of capital, size, and industry ROA. All measures are scaled by business unit size and constructed so that increasing numbers represent higher levels of underinvestment.
time_window: one year prior to the outcome variable (t-1)

description: Business unit performance is measured as ROA and calculated as the ratio of operating income to assets, following previous studies. In the sample description it is stated as annual business unit performance calculated as operating income divided by identifiable assets. Because year-to-year (transient) and average (stable) variation cannot be excluded ex ante, variance components of both types are estimated.

Market fragmentation is operationalized using the Herfindahl index (H), which, following Boyd (1990, 1995), takes into account both the number of firms in an industry as well as inequalities in market shares among those firms. The calculation is summed over j = 1, 2, … n, representing the number of firms in the industry, using the market share of each particular firm; the formula itself is not readable in this payload. The variable varied significantly over time and is introduced at the first (time) level.

Unrelated diversification is operationalized using the entropy measure of unrelated diversification (Jacquemin and Berry, 1979) and is calculated based on each firm's share of industry sales; in the formula Pi is defined as the proportion of firm sales in SIC code i for a firm with N different two-digit SIC business units. The formula itself is not readable in this payload. The variable mainly varies across firms and is aggregated and introduced as a stable effect at the corporate level.

The dependent variable is firm survival; the authors know the year in which failed ventures ceased operation, although the exact day of failure was missing for 80 percent of the firms. They therefore conducted a discrete time history analysis estimating the probability that firm i will survive during the period t1 to t2.

Constructed using a factor analysis post-estimation of two measures: annual regional homicides and annual regional extortive kidnappings. The two variables loaded onto a single factor with an eigenvalue of 1.10, and the item's values ranged from -1.133 to 2.509, with a mean of around zero.

Operationalized using the product of two variables. The first was a scale measure that captured the extent to which the entrepreneur monitored, updated, and compared production and sales activities to changes in the environment. The second was a binary variable that captured the extent to which an entrepreneur went into detail when appraising production and sales activities.

Measured using a series of nine questions that addressed the extent to which the entrepreneur made detailed future plans; these were aggregated into a single item using post-factor estimation to create a scale. The items loaded maximally and uniquely onto a single factor with an eigenvalue of 1.863, accounting for 93.1 percent of the variation, and a Cronbach's alpha of 0.702.
A squared term for comprehensive planning, created to capture any declining benefits of comprehensive planning at higher levels of engagement.

Content-analysis count based on the politics dictionary the authors built from an extensive literature review using the eight-step 'Weber Protocol', because no pre-existing dictionary existed. The authors summed the occurrences of each dictionary word at the organization-year level. The source texts are the internal minutes and decision lists of the board of directors' meetings of each individual water authority.
time_window: same year as the partnership outcomes (t)

description: Content-analysis count based on the procedural rationality dictionary, built from an extensive literature review using the eight-step 'Weber Protocol' since no pre-existing dictionary existed. The authors summed the occurrences of each dictionary word at the organization-year level. The source texts are the internal minutes and decision lists of the board of directors' meetings of each individual water authority.
time_window: same year as the partnership outcomes (t)

description: Computed in each partnership-year record by summing the respective values of Organization-level Politics for the participating water authorities. It therefore aggregates the partner organizations' content-analysis word counts at the level of the partnership.
time_window: same year as the partnership outcomes (t)

description: Computed in each partnership-year record by summing the respective values of Organization-level Procedural Rationality for the participating water authorities. It therefore aggregates the partner organizations' content-analysis word counts at the level of the partnership.
time_window: same year as the partnership outcomes (t)

description: The authors collected the total costs incurred by each organization on the laboratory and taxation activity respectively and calculated the change in these costs from t-1 to t; because value is created when costs go down, they took the opposite of this change as the value obtained by each organization. They then summed the value obtained by the partners to identify the total amount of value created in the partnership. The equations themselves are unreadable in the available text, but the construction is stated in prose.

Measured as the value obtained by the organization minus its relative size in the partnership multiplied by the total value created. Relative size is the organization's share of the partnership's cost driver: the total length of water canals in its region for laboratory partnerships and the total budgeted amount of tax to be collected for taxation partnerships. The measure is available only for organizations that were in the partnership at both t and t-1.

Bivariate indicator that takes a value of 1 if the firm has a foreign company as owner of some or all of its stock and 0 otherwise. It is measured at the level of the firm operating in Spain, that is, the subsidiary itself rather than the parent MNE.

Ratio of total expenditures in R&D to sales, measured at the level of the domestic firm or at the level of the subsidiary of the foreign MNE, not at the level of the parent firm. The authors state that there are no differences in how domestic firms and subsidiaries report their R&D expenditures.

The dependent variable is the number of new products introduced by the firm in the year. It is a count of the firm's product innovations and is measured at the level of the firm operating in Spain, either a subsidiary or a domestic firm.

Measured from the franchisor's litigation history in the past three years as disclosed in the offering circular. All lawsuits involving conflict with franchisees are used; each dispute is counted as one suit, regardless of whether several suits arose from a single dispute. Lawsuits that were not the result of an attempt at termination or enforcement of other contract provisions are not included.

The effect of tapered integration is measured by the number of units owned by the franchisor. If owned units do not create bargaining power, the number of franchisor-owned units would have no effect on litigation.
time_window: contemporaneous with the offering circular (in force during 1990 or 1991)

description: The length of the franchisor's training program through which each franchisee must pass, stated explicitly in the offering circular and measured in weeks.
An indicator variable employed to determine whether the franchisor requires previous industry experience of the franchisee.
The proportion of wholesale purchases by each franchisee that must be made from the franchisor.
An indicator variable measuring whether the franchisor has granted to the franchisee an exclusive territory.

Joint probability that the CEO and the analyst belong to the same caste, calculated as the sum over the caste categories of the product of the probability that the CEO belongs to caste j and the probability that the analyst belongs to caste j; the printed formula could not be extracted from the text. Each individual's caste probabilities were derived from the relative frequencies with which his or her last name mapped onto caste categories in the matrimonial database, and non-Indian CEOs were coded as having zero probability of belonging to a caste group.

Joint probability that the CEO and the analyst are proficient in the same Indian language, calculated as the sum over language categories of the product of the probability that the CEO belongs to language category j and the probability that the analyst belongs to language category j; the printed formula could not be extracted from the text. Language probabilities were derived from the relative frequencies with which a last name mapped onto language groups in the matrimonial database, and actors are assumed to be proficient in English in addition to the regional language coded.

Indicator coded 1 if the CEO and the analyst graduated from the same school, and 0 otherwise, based on undergraduate and postgraduate educational institutions attended. For the reported results, CEO and analyst were coded as drawn from the same school when both graduated from the same school system, irrespective of campus location or degree program; when educational background for either party could not be found, the dyad was conservatively coded 0.

Negative of the absolute difference between the analyst's forecasted annual EPS for firm j in fiscal year t and the firm's actual annual EPS, normalized by the share price at the end of the previous year; the sign is multiplied by -1 so that a higher score denotes greater forecast accuracy.

Dummy variable set to 1 if the CEO was born after 1967, the cutoff chosen because CEOs born in 1967 would have been around 24 years old, a typical age for finishing university education and entering the labor market, when the economic reform was launched in 1991; 1966 was used as an alternative cutoff with consistent results.

Dummy variable taking the value 1 if the controlling shareholder was foreign as per the Prowess ownership classification, and 0 otherwise; all MNC firms in the sample were Western MNCs operating locally listed Indian subsidiaries.

Business group affiliation based on the Prowess classification of ownership groups; the authors estimated BG size by adding the revenues of all firms affiliated to the focal BG, used its log-transformed version, and divided the variable by 10 so that coefficients could be reported to at least three decimal places. This continuous measure was interacted with the bases of affiliation, with the reasoning that the moderating effect was likely to be particularly strong for the largest BGs.
placeholder

Created by subtracting the firm's year of birth from 1880, the year of the first industry entrant. The variable is constructed so that higher values indicate that the firm entered earlier, which the authors say facilitates interpretation of the interaction effect that tests Hypothesis 4. Since early entry is expected to be negatively related to adoption of the dominant design, the variable is expected to have a negative coefficient.

Cumulative non-pneumatic safety models produced divided by firm age. A high value suggests that a firm has introduced and discontinued many products relative to the time that the firm has been in the market. The authors expect, following Hypothesis 3, that this variable will have a positive effect on the firm's introduction of the pneumatic safety.

variable_name: Founded with proximate technology (solid-tire safety producer)
description: Indicator variable for firms founded as solid-tire safety producers, the design most technologically proximate to the pneumatic safety bicycle in terms of having the most similar subsystems. Firms founded with this technology are treated as being founded with a technology that is proximate relative to what emerges later as the dominant design.

Variable that takes on the value 0 for every year that a firm has not yet produced a pneumatic safety bicycle, and then becomes 1 in the year in which the firm introduces its first pneumatic safety model. The event of transition to pneumatic safety production is an absorbing event, so standard event history models apply. Firms that initially produced pneumatic safety bicycles are excluded from this analysis.

variable_name: Firm was founded with distant technology (ordinary or high-wheel safety)
description: Firms are defined as being founded with distant technologies if they initially produced either the ordinary or the high-wheel bicycle models. In the mortality analysis the authors interact this variable with the firm's transition to production of the pneumatic safety bicycle (Hypothesis 6).

variable_name: Firm has made transition to dominant design
description: Variable that indicates that the firm has made the transition to the pneumatic safety bicycle, used in the mortality analysis and interacted with founding technology for Hypothesis 6 and with entry timing for Hypothesis 7.

variable_name: entry timing (years born prior to dominant design)
description: The firm's entry timing, interacted with the transition to the dominant design to test Hypothesis 7. The mortality analysis includes two variables that indicate the firm's timing of entry relative to the emergence of the model that becomes the dominant design: the first measures entry timing prior to the dominant design (1892 minus year of founding) if the firm enters up through 1891 and zero otherwise, and the second measures entry timing following the dominant design (year of founding minus 1892) if the firm enters after 1892 and zero otherwise; firms entering in 1892 are the excluded category.

Following standard practice in event history modeling, the variable is coded 0 for every year in which the firm operates until the firm's final year, when the variable changes to 1 to indicate the occurrence of an event. The event of interest is the firm's exit from the bicycle industry, and the hypothesis is tested using all firm-year observations.

The extent to which the supplier is successful in meeting the target price of the organization, measured on a 7-point Likert scale. If the supplier is a profit center, the question measures the degree to which the operating unit's current transfer price conforms to the assembly division's target price; if the supplier is in the market, it measures whether the supplier's current price matches the assembly division's objective. The measure combines achievement of the initial target price and accommodation of subsequent price changes.

The average of two indicators, each measured on a 7-point Likert-type scale: (1) the extent to which the production of the part requires technical labor skills that are relatively unique to the supplier and (2) the extent to which the production of the part requires manufacturing equipment that is relatively unique to the supplier. A confirmatory factor analysis found the two indicators created a single construct with a reliability of 0.912.
A dummy variable coded 0 if the part is produced by an in-house component division and 1 if it is produced by a market supplier.

The extent to which volume fluctuations are expected in the organization's relationship with the supplier, measured on a 7-point Likert scale. In Walker and Weber (1984) this variable was part of a two-variable construct measuring volume uncertainty with high validity; the correlation between the construct and the variable was 0.77.

The average of two variables, each measured on a 7-point Likert scale: (1) the extent to which the supplier possesses a scale advantage over other suppliers and (2) the extent to which the supplier possesses operating processes that give it a production cost advantage over other suppliers. A confirmatory factor analysis on the present data showed that these measures formed one construct with a reliability of 0.97.

The average of two variables, each measured on a seven-point Likert-type scale: (1) the age of the design technology of the input and (2) the age of the manufacturing process used to produce the input. A confirmatory factor analysis on the present data did not reject a single construct; the reliability of this construct was 0.95.
The extent to which the supplier's production technology is proprietary, measured on a 7-point Likert scale.

Measured as five stages ranging from the earliest possible stage of involvement in the design-to-production process to the latest possible stage. Managers in both organizations agreed that these stages accurately described the design-to-production process regarding supplier involvement.
scale: five stages (1 = earliest involvement, 5 = latest involvement)

description: The absolute difference between the BU's ideology and the ideology of the candidate location. A BU's ideology is calculated by identifying all of its existing establishments and the counties in which they are located and taking the average county ideology of those establishments, weighted by the total number of employees at each establishment. A county's ideology is the percentage of the population that voted for the Republican candidate in the previous presidential election, with missing years filled in by linear interpolation.
scale: absolute difference in the percentage voting Republican
level: county within a new-establishment location decision
time_window: county ideology from the previous presidential election

description: A binary dependent variable that takes the value of one in the location where the establishment is created and zero in the alternative counties. The risk set for each establishment includes only counties that already have at least one other facility engaged in the same SIC four-digit activity as the establishment the focal firm created. Control cases are chosen by choice-based sampling, taking a random draw of 5% of the nonselected counties as plausible alternatives.
level: establishment-county alternative within a location decision

description: Measured at the industry level using the number of approved patents from 2000 to 2014 for each industry in the PatentView database. The measure is standardised across industries after crosswalking the files from the USPTO to SIC four-digit codes.

A dichotomous measure categorising a firm as young if it first appeared in the NETS dataset less than 6 years before the current year. Firms are coded 1 when they are young and 0 when they are more mature.
time_window: 6 years since first appearance in NETS

description: Calculated from the American National Election Studies survey, which uses feeling thermometer questions on which respondents rate their sentiments toward ideological groups (conservatives/liberals) on a 0-100 scale. The measure is the difference between each respondent's feeling toward their own ideological group and their feelings toward the opposing ideological group, averaged across all respondents for each year of the survey.
scale: difference in feeling thermometer scores on a 0-100 scale

description: Board turnover is measured as the count of the total number of outside directors who exited the board in a given year. The measure does not distinguish between voluntary and involuntary director exits, because information detailing the various reasons for board turnover is generally limited and could not be consistently coded. The authors note that because their theorizing focused on mechanisms more likely to lead to voluntary exit, including involuntary exits makes the analysis a more conservative test.
time_window: each year of the five years following the IPO

description: Following prior research, the authors measured the amount of time directors had worked together using tenure overlap (TLAP), a measure of common historical experience. The measure equals the average of the pairwise overlaps in board service among each director; the formula block in the text is unreadable, but the authors state that N is the total number of pairwise comparisons and that u(i) and u(j) are the board tenures of the i-th and j-th directors. Individual director tenures in the sample range from 0 years to 15 years, and TLAP ranges from 0 to nine years.

Directors were classified into one of five occupational categories based on their primary expertise: business experts, support specialists, community influentials, private equity managers, and VCs. Expertise overlap was measured using the same formula as TLAP, calculating the average of the pairwise comparisons of directors' expertise, with each pairwise comparison coded 1 if the two directors had the same expertise and 0 if not. ELAP could therefore range from 0 to 1, with 0 representing no overlap at all and 1 representing a complete overlap in directors' expertise.

A director was treated as globally high status if he or she possessed at least one of three credentials: a degree from an elite educational institution on Finkelstein's list of prestigious institutions, experience as an executive at the level of vice president or above at an S&P 500 company, or experience as an outside director for an S&P 500 firm. Global status homogeneity for each firm-year was measured with the Blau index across the two director categories (high and non-high status). Because the index ranged from 0 to .5, the authors reversed it by deducting the values from .5, so that 0 represented complete status heterogeneity and .5 represented complete status homogeneity.
time_window: each year of the five years following the IPO, with a lagged year list of S&P 500 firms

description: Measured by examining the extent to which the two firms patented in the same technology classes. The authors identified all patents granted to each firm (the NBF and the pharmaceutical firm) during the period 1999-2002 and created a list of all patent classes to which these patents belonged. They then created a count of the number of patent classes in which both firms had patenting activities (overlap) during this window; a larger number of common patent classes was taken to mean a greater absorptive capacity of the pharmaceutical firm.

The authors identified the number of new drugs developed for each particular therapeutic area in the previous four years and then averaged these values across all therapeutic areas in which the pharmaceutical firm was active to create a firm-level measure. A higher value meant that the firm had deep development competences in the areas in which it was active.

The authors identified the number of new drugs developed in the previous four years in each therapeutic area and computed pharma therapeutic area diversity = [1 - sum(TAi x TAi)], where TAi was the proportion of drugs developed in the previous four years for therapeutic area i. A greater value meant that the firm had development competences across diverse therapeutic areas.

A patent-level measure counting the number of distinct therapeutic areas in which 'similar' active ingredients - those arising from knowledge bases that belong to the same patent class and subclass as the NBF's patent - had been applied in the past. Medtrack's Worldwide Patent Viewer links active ingredients to the patents that protect the know-how embedded in them, and each marketed drug is assigned to a specific therapeutic domain based on its therapeutic properties. For an NBF with more than one patent, the authors created a firm-level measure by calculating the average breadth of all its patents.

The dependent variable ALLij took a value of 1 if NBF i and pharmaceutical firm j established an R&D alliance in the 2003-2007 time window, and 0 otherwise. R&D alliances were defined as those with stated objectives (as reported in Medtrack) of R&D.

The Theil index computed from the set of dyadic (focal firm-partner) power imbalances. Power imbalance for each partner is first computed as the absolute value of the directional constraints, i.e., the absolute difference between the two actors' constraints, and the Theil index is then computed across the partners in the focal firm's portfolio. An index close to zero denotes that power imbalances between the focal firm and each of its partners are all similar, whereas an index close to one denotes that there exists a focal firm-partner dyad with a power imbalance significantly different from the remaining dyads.

The Theil index computed from the set of dyadic (focal firm-partner) mutual dependences. Mutual dependence for each partner is first computed as the product of the directional dyadic constraints, and the Theil index is then computed across the partners in the focal firm's portfolio. An index close to zero denotes that the focal firm's mutual dependences with its partners are uniform, whereas an index close to one denotes that the focal firm has strong mutual dependence with one partner but less so with the remaining partners.

The Burt (1992) redundancy measure normalized by the focal firm's portfolio size. For a given focal firm-partner dyad, partner j is redundant within the focal firm's portfolio if there is already a portfolio partner k that exchanges with partner j. Examining all other k partners in the dyad and all other j partners in the portfolio, the sum is divided by the number of firms in the focal firm's portfolio. A value close to one means that the focal firm's partners are redundant, i.e., substitutable with each other in terms of resources, whereas a value close to zero means that the partners are unique in terms of their resources.

The natural logarithm of the carrier's time t RevEx ratio, or ln(Operating revenue / Operating expense). RevEx is realized, per statutory requirement, when services are rendered, not when a ticket is sold. A RevEx ratio greater (less) than 1.0 indicates a profit (loss), so the log-transformed measure assigns positive (negative) values to profit (loss); RevEx is left censored, which is why it is logarithm transformed.
scale: log ratio (natural logarithm of the revenue-to-expense ratio)

variable_name: negative statements about firm leadership and strategy
description: All articles authored by journalists in the sample frame during the study period were identified and three coders independently evaluated each article; each sentence referring to a company or CEO in the sample was coded as negative, positive or neutral, and coders then determined whether the statement referred to firm leadership or strategy. For tests of Hypotheses 1-3 the authors totaled the number of negative statements by each journalist about the leadership and strategy of each firm in the sample over the 12-month period prior to the period for which distancing was measured; for tests of Hypothesis 4 the number of negative statements was totaled over the subsequent 12-month period, controlling for prior levels. Interrater reliability among the three coders was high (intra-class correlation coefficients ranged from .91 to .94).

variable_name: positive statements about firm leadership and strategy
description: Positive statements about firm leadership and strategy issued by the journalist, coded from the same content analysis of the journalists' articles as the negative statements, with the same three independent coders. For tests of Hypothesis 4 the authors totaled the number of positive statements over the subsequent 12-month period, controlling for prior levels of positive statements in the prior 12-month period.
time_window: subsequent 12 months, controlling for the prior 12 months

variable_name: friendship tie between focal CEO and alter
description: CEOs were prompted to list their personal friends and acquaintances among firm leaders in the sample frame. In the primary analysis, for each dyad (i.e., the focal CEO and another CEO who is a potential recipient of negative coverage) a dichotomous variable was created, coded 1 if the focal CEO rated the other ('alter') CEO as a friend. There was a high level of agreement (95%) between responding CEOs about the status of their personal relationship as friends, acquaintances, or neither.
level: CEO dyad (focal CEO and alter CEO)

variable_name: demographic similarity between focal CEO and alter
description: Demographic similarity was examined on four characteristics shown to be salient among corporate leaders: functional background (using Hambrick and Mason's typology), race (coded as White, African American, Hispanic, or Asian), gender, and age (CEOs were considered similar in age when they differed by less than one standard deviation). In the main analyses the four measures of demographic similarity were combined into a single index using discrete principal component analysis.
level: CEO dyad (focal CEO and alter CEO)

variable_name: CEO social identification with the corporate elite
description: A multi-item survey scale that has been validated across different samples of corporate leaders at different time periods; it includes items adapted from Mael and Ashforth's (1992) group identification scale. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated that the items loaded on the same factor without loading on other factors (factor loadings ranged from .84 to .90; Cronbach's alpha = .92), and the measure is a factor score estimated using the regression method.

Multi-item scales in the CEO and journalist surveys. CEOs were asked to indicate which journalists had tried to contact them during the prior six months and journalists were asked to indicate which CEOs they had tried to contact over that period; respondents then answered a series of questions about their interaction with each of these individuals, including the CEO's willingness to communicate and to interact with the journalist, whether the CEO had been available for interviews or meetings, the CEO's responsiveness to requests for information, comments and/or opinion, and the difficulty of getting in touch. In the main tests of Hypotheses 1-3 distancing was measured over the subsequent six months using CEO responses; for the main tests of Hypotheses 4-5 the average distancing experienced by the journalist from CEOs whom they had tried to contact during the prior six months was calculated using journalist responses.
time_window: subsequent six months (Hypotheses 1-3); prior six months, averaged across CEOs contacted (Hypotheses 4-5)

description: Survey measures that include five items for each career stage (early, middle, and late); examples of late career stage items are 'I am in the late stage of my career as a journalist,' 'I am in the latter phase of my career,' and 'To what extent are you getting close to retirement?'. Confirmatory factor analysis confirmed that the items loaded onto three factors as expected, without loading on other factors, and reliability was acceptably high (Cronbach's alpha values ranged from .86 to .88).

Following work by Martin and Salomon (2003), innovation activity is measured as the production of products incorporating a new lithography process technology. The authors count the number of new process technology generations that a single firm introduces over time and take the natural log of a firm's cumulative count to reduce skewness in the distribution. The counter is initiated at 1 for each firm. The specification formula itself was not recoverable from the text.
time_window: cumulative from the firm's first year of existence

description: Firm size is defined as the natural log of a firm's sales. The measure is lagged one year to avoid simultaneity.

The total amount of fabrication (production) experience accumulated by the focal firm's fabrication facilities in year t, measured at t-1, the year before the current year. The experience measure begins with the first year that a firm operated a production facility; for firms founded prior to 1990 the data imputes the production history of each firm's fabrication facilities. A discount equal to the age of the experience squared is applied to account for antiquation or decay of knowledge. The formula was not recoverable from the text.

The total amount of fabrication experience accumulated by all of the focal firm's codevelopment partners based on their fabrication (production) in year t, measured at t-1. The measure begins with the first year that a partner firm operated a production facility; for partner firms founded prior to 1990 the data imputes the production history of each partner's fabrication facilities. A discount equal to the age of the experience squared is applied and a natural log transformation of the sum is used to reduce skewness in the distribution. The formula was not recoverable from the text.

The total amount of fabrication experience accumulated by all of the focal firm's sourcing partners based on their fabrication in year t, measured at t-1. The measure begins with the first year that a partner firm operated a production facility, with imputed production histories for partner firms founded prior to 1990. A discount equal to the age of the experience squared is applied and a natural log transformation of the sum is used to reduce skewness in the distribution. The formula was not recoverable from the text.

Board gender diversity was measured using Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity, where i is the proportion of group members in each of the various categories. Blau's index is used to obtain a relative measure of diversity that is not skewed in favor of either gender. For board gender diversity the index can range from 0 (when there is only one gender on the board) to 0.50 (when there are equal numbers of men and women). Data for women on boards were gathered from the Investor Responsibility Research Center (IRRC) for the year 2002.

Firm performance was measured as return on assets, measured as net income divided by total assets, averaged over the years 2000-2002 using data from Compustat. Accounting-based performance was used because the theory concerns strategic leaders' responses to past and present performance.

Strategic change was proxied by resource allocations across six strategic resource dimensions. Change scores were created for each of the six resource indicators by subtracting the 2004 resource level from the 2002 resource level, and because change is indifferent to the direction of the change the absolute values of the change scores were used. Because the six change scores have different units of measurement, z-scores were created for each change score so that no single indicator would have a greater weight than any other, and the amount of strategic change was the average of the standardized absolute value differences in the six resource indicators from 2002 to 2004. All data were collected from Compustat for 2002 and 2004, with a two-year time lag between the predictors and the outcome.

Structural power was proxied as the average number of publicly documented board titles held by women on the board. Titles published in proxy statements publicly legitimize the director's role and the power that accompanies these titles. The mean power of all women on the board was used to measure the absolute power of women. The data were gathered from RiskMetrics, the Corporate Library, and proxy statements for 2002.

Prestige power was measured as the average number of high-status board committees to which women directors are assigned. The audit, nominating, compensation, and executive committees were coded as high-status committees because they are the most frequently used across companies and are an important tool for monitoring and reporting corporate activities. The mean power of all women on the board was used to measure the absolute power of women.

Ownership power was measured as the average percentage ownership of the firm's outstanding common stock held by women directors, because directors with large shareholdings are likely to influence the board. The mean power of all women on the board was used to measure the absolute power of women.

Expert power was measured as experience as business experts, community influentials, support experts, and insiders, coded using the biographical profiles of directors collected from the Corporate Library and supplemented with profiles within proxy statements or annual reports if missing. Business expertise was coded as the sum of two dichotomous variables indicating whether a director had experience as CEO or top executive at a for-profit firm and whether the director served on the board of a for-profit firm. Community influential expertise was coded as the sum of dichotomous variables indicating whether the director held a position in political office; as a clergy member; as a college or university leader; and/or as a leader of a nonprofit organization, foundation, or cultural organization. Support specialist expertise was coded as the sum of dichotomous variables indicating a position within banking, insurance, law, public relations, or consulting or in a government agency, and insider expertise was coded as a dichotomous variable representing whether the director is a current or former executive of the firm. The expert power measure is a formative construct, and the mean power of all women on the board was used to measure the absolute power of women.

variable_name: Number of canceled nuclear units within 100 miles
description: Count of previously proposed nuclear units that were canceled up to year t - 1 within 100 miles of the focal county. Distance is measured as the law-of-cosines great circle distance between the county's approximate center and the nuclear unit. The variable is coded in a cumulative rather than spot fashion, so that activism is modeled as a function of the community's entire history of success and failure.
time_window: cumulative up to year t - 1 (independent variables lagged 1 year)

variable_name: Number of completed nuclear units within 100 miles
description: Count of previously proposed nuclear units that were completed, i.e., reactors eventually connected to the grid and operating, up to year t - 1 within 100 miles of the focal county. Distance is measured as the law-of-cosines great circle distance between the county's approximate center and the nuclear unit. It is coded cumulatively rather than as a spot value.
time_window: cumulative up to year t - 1 (independent variables lagged 1 year)

description: Count of antinuclear protests in year t within the focal county, obtained by matching all protest events in the Dynamics of Collective Action dataset to their respective county and counting those reporting claim 0200, 'Anti-Nuclear (Power) Movement.'
Count of protests not targeting nuclear power in year t within the focal county, obtained by counting protests taking place within the county that do not report claim 0200.

variable_name: technological resource breadth (breadth of a firm's patent portfolio)
description: The breadth of a firm's patent portfolio is utilized as the indicator of the firm's breadth of technological resources. Patent data were obtained from the USPTO through Delphion's searchable database (1420 patents), matched to NBER patent data with additional searching by organization number (802 additional patents), and supplemented by direct USPTO database searches. Patents granted prior to 1975 were deleted to keep patents within their useful economic life. Breadth was calculated using a Herfindahl-type index analogous to Hall et al.'s (2001) approach, where Si is the proportion of n patents in USPTO class i; the formula itself is not readable in the text.

Firm actions were captured through structured content analyses of newspaper and trade publications identified in Lexis-Nexus, with articles classified by coders into preestablished competitive action categories. Competitive repertoire complexity measures the extent to which a firm's action portfolio for a given year consists of a broad variety of actions, capturing the within-firm diversity of actions. Following Ferrier (2001) and Ferrier et al. (1999) it is a Herfindahl-type index where Pi is the proportion of the ith category of competitive actions; higher values represent a broader range of actions and thus a more complex repertoire, lower values a narrower and simpler repertoire. The formula itself is not readable in the text.

Competitive repertoire deviance captures the extent to which a firm's portfolio of actions for a given year differed from those of its competitors. Similar to Ferrier et al.'s (1999) leader-challenger action dissimilarity, it is calculated as the sum of squared differences in proportions of categories of competitive action between the focal firm and the industry mean, where Pi is the proportion of the ith category of competitive action for the focal firm and the industry mean proportion excludes the focal firm. Actions were coded from structured content analyses of newspaper and trade publications identified in Lexis-Nexus.

Performance was measured as a firm's rate of return on assets (ROA). Because technological resources and competitive actions may not immediately affect performance, performance was measured across three separate periods: the most immediate effect using the subsequent year's performance (ROA1), the intermediate effect using the sum of ROA one to three years out (ROA3), and the longer-term effect using the sum of ROA one to five years out (ROA5). Performance data were collected from Compustat from 1996 to 2004.
time_window: t+1 (ROA1); sum of t+1 to t+3 (ROA3); sum of t+1 to t+5 (ROA5)

description: Measured as the fraction of team t's previous 20 opponents who picked hero h for role i in game g. The variable captures the degree to which the focal team's recent opponents used a given hero for the same role, and its coefficient estimates the focal team's propensity to imitate recent opponents' hero choices.

Binary measure equal to 1 if team t chose hero h to fulfill role i in game g, and 0 otherwise. Because each team includes five players who each fulfill one role in any game, the variable is predicted separately for five roles in each team; imitation is captured by examining the degree to which a team's choice of hero for a role is affected by recent opponents' use of this hero for the same role.

For each team, each role's interdependence with the other roles is characterized as a vector with four dimensions, each capturing the percentage of coordinated actions involving the focal role that also includes each of the other four roles. Coordinated actions are sequences of actions involving several players in which each action was performed 3 or fewer seconds after the previous one and within close geographical proximity, computed over the 20 games preceding the focal game. The measure is the average Euclidean distance between the vector representing the focal role and the equivalent role on each prior opponent team.

Captured as the number of pings per minute a team's players used during a match; pings are graphics and sound signals players use during a game to communicate with their teammates. The measure is captured at the team level as the average across all players on the team, and specifically as the team members' average number of pings during its past 20 games.

Computed for every pair of players in the team as the number of games they have played together on the same team; for each player, collaborative experience is the average of this measure across their four teammates. Unlike the communication variable, it varies within the same team depending on each player's experience with their teammates.

Indicator variable that distinguishes CFOs who received an MBA degree from those who did not; it takes a value of 1 if the CFO received an MBA degree and 0 otherwise. The degree information is recorded from the hand-collected educational profiles of the CFOs.

Indicator variable that takes a value of 1 if the CFO received an MBA degree ranked in top 25 programs of the US News & World Report 2011 rankings of the top 100 MBA programs, and 0 otherwise. It is one of four metrics of CFO characteristics based on the type of degree received and the perceived quality of the MBA program.

Indicator variable that equals 1 if the CFO received a professional accounting certification such as a Certified Public Accountant, Certified Management Accountant or Chartered Accountant certification, and 0 otherwise. It is used to proxy for accounting expertise.

Indicator variable that distinguishes CFOs who received a non-MBA master's degree (a master's or law degree) from those who did not; it takes a value of 1 if the CFO received such a degree and 0 otherwise.

Natural logarithm of total compensation (in 2008 dollars) for the first full year the executive was in the CFO position. Total compensation includes salary, bonus, options granted, restricted stock and other pay.
time_window: first full year in the CFO position

description: Natural logarithm of salary compensation, measured in 2008 dollars, used to examine the determinants of the cash component of the CFO pay package separately.
time_window: first full year in the CFO position

description: Natural logarithm of (1 + equity-based compensation), measured in 2008 dollars. Equity-based pay is computed as the value of option grants and the restricted stock owned by the CFO.
time_window: first full year in the CFO position

description: A five-item scale used to measure service adaptability, drawing on Heskett's (1986) description of service customization and Shostack's (1987) research on customization and service offerings. Respondents rated their firm relative to other firms in the industry. A confirmatory factor analysis indicated a good fit and all scale reliabilities reached the level Nunnally (1978) suggested.

A four-item scale constructed to measure the construct of service firm output specialization, which the authors use to capture the breadth of a firm's service offering relative to its competitors' offerings. Respondents rated their firm relative to other firms in the industry.

A four-item scale used to tap the level of customer coproduction involved in service firm output, where greater effort required of customers indicates a higher level of coproduction. Respondents rated their firm relative to other firms in the industry.

A three-item scale measuring the level of coordination required to produce a service. Both the number of steps a service firm uses to produce its service and the degree of interdependence among the steps can affect this level; the more steps required, or the greater the interdependence among steps, the higher the level of complexity.

Data were gathered on return on equity (ROE), return on investment (ROI) and respondent perceptions; the perceptual performance data came from a nine-item scale adapted from McGrath, MacMillan, and Venkatraman (1995) measuring top managers' perceptions of service quality, efficiency, productivity, sales growth, customer satisfaction, profitability, market share, stock performance and employee morale.
