ROE and ROI were collected from Compact Disclosure as two-year averages to reduce the potential for anomalous effects, and the nine perceptual items formed a single factor. A principal components analysis of the three variables produced a single factor, and this overall composite was used as the measure of firm performance.
time_window: two-year averages for ROE and ROI

variable_name: service adaptability, service focus (output specialization), customer coproduction
description: Strategic positioning is captured by three survey scales completed by the highest-ranking executive: a five-item service adaptability scale, a four-item service firm output specialization (service focus) scale and a four-item customer coproduction scale. Each scale was interacted with production complexity to predict performance.

A hospital-level measure created by CMS that is the average of the weights used to calculate financial payments to hospitals for each patient, representing the average clinical complexity of patients that a focal hospital has treated in a given year. The authors take the log of a given hospital's Case Mix Index to reduce skewness and use this logged value as the primary form of the variable across models. In addition, they create a categorized version in which hospitals are grouped into High, Medium, and Low Case Mix Index based on the top, middle, and bottom thirds of the distribution, used to examine the moderating effect of task requirements.

A count of competing hospitals within a focal health service area (HSA) that had adopted robotic surgery prior to the focal year. HSAs represent the geographically bounded markets from which a hospital draws its patient population, reflecting the local nature of competition in the hospital industry.
time_window: count of adoptions prior to the focal year

description: The models examine the hazard of Robotic Surgery adoption as the dependent variable. Each hospital reported the presence of robotic surgery each year, and Robotic Surgery is measured using a dichotomous variable that is 0 until the adoption event, after which it is reported as 1.

variable_name: Workstation revenue market share in each year
description: Dollar market share for each workstation for each year that the product is in the market, from 1988 to 1992. Revenue market share is used because it captures both the ability to sell more units as the innovation offers better value and the ability of product differentiation to allow the firm to charge premium prices. Profitability data were not available, so revenue market share is used as a proxy for the performance of a workstation maker adopting RISC technology; in the regressions the dollar market share enters in logarithmic form.

The variable assumes a value of 1 if the RISC microprocessor supplier had offered CISC microprocessors before, and 0 otherwise. Firms which supplied the old technology are more embedded in the systems, routines and procedures of CISC than new entrants; former CISC suppliers must unlearn the CISC skills and learn RISC ones while new entrants do not have to unlearn any.
The variable assumes the value of 1 if, in adopting RISC, a workstation maker switched from its supplier of CISC microprocessors to a new entrant supplier, and 0 otherwise.

Measured by whether the workstation maker was vertically integrated into CISC microprocessor design and development before adopting RISC or not. The variable assumes the value of 1 if a firm had been vertically integrated into CISC and 0 otherwise.

Measured by whether customers have to change from the operating system that they used with their CISC workstations to a new incompatible one when they buy RISC workstations. The variable assumes the value of 1 if a firm offered a new operating system with its RISC workstations, and 0 otherwise.

The proportion of individuals bound by a noncompete in each state-industry, constructed from survey respondents' reports of whether they had signed a noncompete. Only state-industries with at least 10 individuals in the survey are included in the sample.

An index from Starr (2019) that builds on Bishara (2011), which quantified each state's position in 2009, whether by statute or by case law, on seven dimensions of noncompete enforceability between 0 and 10, with 10 being the highest level of enforceability. The Starr (2019) measures incorporate the underlying Bishara scores and weight them using factor analysis, and the index is normalized to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 from a sample where each state is given a weight of 1.
scale: normalized index with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, built from dimensions scored 0 to 10

description: Indicator variable set to 1 if the worker has received a job offer in the last year and 0 otherwise.
Indicator variable set to 1 if the worker has received a job offer since their most recent change in employment and 0 otherwise.
time_window: since most recent change in employment

description: Observed tenure at the current firm in years, used as the measure of mobility because the cross-sectional data limit observation of mobility events over time. Tenure reflects a lack of prior mobility, since a worker who has stayed a long time at his or her job has not had a mobility event.
The worker's logged hourly wage, used as the dependent variable in the wage regressions.

Supplier performance is measured in terms of the supplier's average return on sales (profit before taxes divided by sales) regarding the OEM's business during 1993-1996. The return on sales data are gathered at the postinterest, pretax stage to capture the benefits that suppliers may reap because of any cheap loans or equity investment made by the OEM. The measure is continuous.

Physical asset specificity, measured as the supplier's investment in durable equipment, machinery, advanced design systems, operating procedures, R&D, and so on, to meet the specialized needs of the OEM customer. Suppliers responded to a multi-item construct measured on a Likert scale (1-5); the measure has a coefficient alpha of 0.74, indicating a high degree of internal consistency among the items. Also, exploratory factor analysis reveals only one eigenvalue in excess of 1.

Degree to which suppliers undertake detailed engineering and design activities, with OEM design of the component at the lower end of the scale and the supplier's proprietary technology on the higher end. It captures the OEM's technological dependence on the supplier and the credible commitment implicit in the practice of black-box designing.
The time, in months, it takes the OEM to replace this supplier successfully with an equally competent one. The variable measures the OEM's overall (managerial) dependence on the supplier.
The extent to which the supplier provides details of its production process to the OEM customer. The response is measured on a Likert scale ranging from 1 to 5.
Whether the supplier shares cost information with the OEM customer. The variable is binary in nature and takes the value 1 if the supplier shares cost information and 0 otherwise.

Incidence of cost-plus pricing or BPE clauses in supply contracts, captured both when the cost base is fixed and when it varies over time. The variable is binary in nature, coded 1 if cost-plus pricing is practiced and 0 otherwise. Because the two pricing variables are categorized from a common set of questions, the base-pricing category is the incidence of market pricing.

Incidence of target pricing, measured as a binary variable coded 1 if the supplier pursues target pricing and 0 otherwise, where the targeted time horizon could be fixed or varying. Because the two pricing variables are categorized from a common set of questions, the base-pricing category is the incidence of market pricing.
Contract duration is measured in terms of the number of months for which the parties (supplier and OEM) write a contract.
Quantity agreement has been measured, based on the feedback from industry experts at the pretesting stage of the survey, as the percentage of customer's requirements to be met by the contract.

Expectation of the duration of the relationship, measured by a ranked categorical variable with four categories: (1) less than a year, (2) between one and four years, (3) between five and ten years, and (4) more than ten years.
Volume stability has been measured in terms of the percentage of production schedules that remain unaltered by the OEM.
Binary variable indicating whether a firm signed at least one of the four progressive letter campaigns. A total of 118 firms in the dataset signed at least one letter.
Continuous variable measuring the total number of letters signed by a firm; the authors report an average of 0.14 and a standard deviation of 0.51.
Four separate variables for each letter, indicating if a firm signed that letter: 63 firms signed HB 2, 35 signed Low Carbon, 24 signed Travel Ban, and 63 signed DACA.

Derived from individuals' 2014-2015 political donation information from the FEC, following methods used by Chin et al. (2013) and Gupta et al. (2017): four different measures of 'organizational liberalism' were calculated by grouping individual data by employer and their average was taken to create an organizational ideology scale. The scale runs from 0, representing a conservative company, to 100, representing liberal. Firms with no political donations within a group were given an ideology value of 50.

Derived from individuals' 2014-2015 political donation information from the FEC, following methods used by Chin et al. (2013) and Gupta et al. (2017): four different measures of 'organizational liberalism' were calculated by grouping individual data by employer and their average was taken to create an organizational ideology scale. The scale runs from 0, representing a conservative company, to 100, representing liberal. Firms with no political donations within a group were given an ideology value of 50.

Derived from individuals' 2014-2015 political donation information from the FEC, following methods used by Chin et al. (2013) and Gupta et al. (2017): four different measures of 'organizational liberalism' were calculated by grouping individual data by employer and their average was taken to create an organizational ideology scale. The scale runs from 0, representing a conservative company, to 100, representing liberal. Firms with no political donations within a group were given an ideology value of 50.

Binary variable measuring whether both the CEO and the employees are on the liberal end of the political ideology scale. Three cut-off levels are used to compare degrees of liberalness in alignment: >50, >60, and >70; for instance, for a >60 alignment the variable equals 1 if both CEO and employee ideology within a firm are greater than 60.

Binary variable measuring whether both the TMT and the employees are on the liberal end of the political ideology scale; it does not include CEO ideology. Three cut-off levels are used to compare degrees of liberalness in alignment: >50, >60, and >70; for instance, for a >60 alignment the variable equals 1 if both TMT and employee ideology within a firm are greater than 60.

The FFM of personality was measured with the Spanish version of the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory 2, using 12 items for each factor. An example item is 'I am pretty good about pacing myself so as to get things done on time.' All items were scored on a 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) Likert scale; alpha reliability was 0.81. Personality data were collected from the CEO alone at the first time period.

Measured with 12 items of the Spanish version of the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory 2. An example item is 'I often feel inferior to others.' All items were scored on a 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) Likert scale, and the authors reverse coded the ratings on emotional stability to improve the interpretation of results. Alpha reliability was 0.79.

Measured with 12 items of the Spanish version of the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory 2. An example item is 'I like to have a lot of people around me.' Items were scored on a 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) Likert scale; alpha reliability was 0.74. Personality data were collected from the CEO alone.

Measured with 12 items of the Spanish version of the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory 2. An example item is 'I am interested in people.' Items were scored on a 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) Likert scale; alpha reliability was 0.72. Personality data were collected from the CEO alone.

Measured with 12 items of the Spanish version of the 60-item revised NEO Five-Factor Inventory 2. An example item is 'I spend time reflecting on things.' Items were scored on a 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) Likert scale; alpha reliability was 0.70. Personality data were collected from the CEO alone.

Respondents were asked to identify whether a change occurred in each of the four strategic initiation categories in the past two years. The measure (ranging from 0 to 5) was computed by adding the total number of categories in which the change occurred; the higher the initiation score, the more the initiated changes across many strategic categories. Respondents were instructed to include increases as well as decreases in activity in a particular category. CEO and top executive responses were averaged (single-measure ICC .72; average ICC .85).
time_window: past two years, reported at time 1

description: Respondents identified the changes in the five implementation categories they undertook to support and carry out initiated strategic changes in the past two years. The measure (ranging from 0 to 5) was computed by adding the total number of categories in which the change occurred; the higher the implementation score, the greater the efforts in supportive areas to facilitate and carry out the initiated changes. CEO and top executive responses were averaged (single-measure ICC .72; average ICC .85).
time_window: past two years, reported at time 1

description: Average performance ratings of the CEO and the top executive on a six-item scale adapted from Brouthers, Brouthers, and Werner (2003), rated on a 1-to-5 Likert scale; alpha reliability was 0.86. The scale was administered six months after collecting CEO personality and strategic change data. The authors averaged the z scores of CEO and top executives' responses to the six items (single measure ICC 0.75; average measure ICC 0.86).
scale: 1-to-5 Likert scale (ratings); composite is an average of z scores
time_window: six months after the first survey

description: Counting the number of prior contracts that were negotiated and signed by the focal licensing manager at the time of invention licensing. To improve its interpretation, the variable was rescaled by dividing it by 10.
time_window: prior contracts at the time of invention licensing

description: The licensing revenue earned by the TTO from an invention. Following standard procedures to correct for skewness, the natural log transformation of the dependent variable was used. For bundled contracts with multiple inventions, payments were divided according to the contract allocation rules (most of them specified equal sharing).

The fixed-fee payment paid by the licensing firm to the TTO upon licensing the invention. Following standard procedures to correct for skewness, the natural log transformation of the dependent variable was used. For bundled contracts with multiple inventions, payments were divided according to the contract allocation rules.

A percentage of annual sales based on the licensed invention. Following standard procedures to correct for skewness, the natural log transformation of the dependent variable was used. For bundled contracts with multiple inventions, payments were divided according to the contract allocation rules.
scale: percentage of annual sales, natural log

description: Based on the proportion of the number of backward citations to academic scientific articles out of the total number of backward citations (academic articles plus other patents) in the invention's patent. When the proportion is high, it indicates that an invention is science-intensive, drawing less heavily from the applied-scientific knowledge associated with published patent domains.
Measured by the average number of prior disclosed inventions among inventors.
Created based on the number of sub-classes into which the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) assigns the patent.

The DIR measure is defined as the change in the investment ratio across business units over time, using the firm's own capital allocation in the previous year as a benchmark, where CAPX is the capital expenditure of segment i in firm F in year t, AT is total assets of segment i in firm F in year t, and w is the asset share of each segment in firm F in year t. Firms that commit to maintaining stable allocations over time have low DIR, and firms that actively reallocate capital across their business units have a high DIR. The formula as displayed in the paper was not readable in the source text, so the exact specification is recorded as a gap.

A firm's profitability as measured by ROA is decomposed into industry and industry-adjusted profitability, where industry profitability is the profitability of a hypothetical firm that mimics the asset composition across industries of firm f, computed with the asset weight of each segment in year t-1 and the median ROA of single-segment firms in the segment's three-digit SIC industry. Industry-adjusted profitability is the difference between the profitability of firm f and its industry profitability, and it is used as the dependent variable in the analysis of the reallocation-performance link.
time_window: contemporaneous year t, with segment asset weights at t-1

description: AVA comes from Rajan, Servaes, and Zingales (2000), who measure a variant of internal allocation performance; in essence it measures the extent to which a firm is good at investing more (relative to the industry median) in businesses with higher future prospects (as proxied by Tobin's q) and less in businesses with lower future prospects. Following Rajan et al. (2000), AVA is defined by allocation, where j is each one of the firm's N business units, q is the estimated Tobin's q for business j, and capx/assets is the average investment ratio for the single-segment firms in segment j's industry. The displayed formula was not readable in the source text, so the exact specification is recorded as a gap.

The proportion of total compensation paid as stock options, which could theoretically range from 0 to 100 percent. Option values are based on the Black-Scholes method and were calculated by Execucomp. Because some firms award options periodically rather than annually, the measure used is the simple average percentage of stock option pay for the prior three years ([t - 1 + t - 2 + t - 3]/3).
time_window: three-year average of t-1, t-2 and t-3

description: Observations were divided into roughly equal thirds based on the percentage of a CEO's stock option pay. Cases in which stock options accounted for less than 20 percent of CEO pay were considered low stock option pay, cases between 20 and 49 percent were considered medium, and cases of 50 percent or more constituted high stock option pay.
time_window: three-year average of t-1, t-2 and t-3

description: Research and development expenditures coded as reported in COMPUSTAT. Values were logarithmically transformed after adding the constant 1 to all cases.
Capital expenditures coded as reported in COMPUSTAT. Values were logarithmically transformed after adding the constant 1 to all cases.
The sum of the transaction values for all acquisitions completed during the year, as reported in SDC. Values were logarithmically transformed after adding the constant 1 to all cases.

The sum of R&D investment, capital investment, and acquisition investment, used to allow parsimonious tests of the interaction hypothesis. Values were logarithmically transformed after adding the constant 1 to all cases.

Total shareholder returns, calculated as year-end stock price minus year-start stock price plus dividends paid, all divided by year-start stock price. Performance extremeness was derived in two steps: predicted performance was estimated by regressing performance on all control variables, and the absolute value of the residual (the difference between actual and predicted performance) in t + 1 was used as the indication of how extreme performance was, without regard to direction.

Return on assets, calculated as net income divided by year-end assets. Performance extremeness was derived in two steps: predicted performance was estimated by regressing performance on all control variables, and the absolute value of the residual in t + 1 was used as the indication of how extreme performance was, without regard to direction.

variable_name: Large losses relative to large gains
description: Residuals from the first-stage performance regression were retained with their direction, indicating how much better or worse performance was than predicted by all predictors except CEO stock options. Extreme performance was defined as greater than 1.5 standard deviations away from zero; the ratio of large losses to total cases of extreme performance (large gains and large losses combined) was calculated for each level of stock option pay. A multinomial logit analysis predicted three alternative outcomes: a big loss, a big gain, or neither, with big losses and big gains defined as performance 1.5 standard deviations below or above the value predicted from all control variables.

Manipulation of the degree of difficulty of the trivia quizzes used to rank entrants in each round. Each participant saw two simple-rank and two difficult-rank markets. For the interaction analysis, difficulty was coded difficult = -1 and simple = 1.

Participants indicated whether they would enter the market in each round of the game. The decision to enter resulted in either a gain or a loss of money depending on the participant's performance on the trivia quiz relative to seven other potential competitors. Each participant made one entry decision in each of four rounds.

Each participant provided statements about his or her market-entry decision process in each of the four rounds; 48 participants recorded verbal protocols and 48 recorded written protocols. Three trained research assistants rated each protocol on a three-point scale according to the degree of self-focus represented in the stated thoughts, where a code of 1 represented thoughts solely about factors external to the participant and a code of 3 represented thoughts solely about the participant. Where the coders disagreed, the three ratings were averaged to form a single measure of self-focus for each participant in each round. The rating was modestly correlated with use of self-referential pronouns and negatively correlated with references to others.

Manipulation of the number of entrants the market could sustain profitably. In a capacity 3 market, the top three entrants would earn $15, $10, and $5, respectively, and entrants ranked fourth through eighth would each lose $10. In a capacity 4 market the fourth-ranked entrant broke even.

variable_name: Estimate of the number of competitors who would enter
description: Participants estimated the number of other competitors who would enter the market in each round. Four participants were excluded because their estimates of the number of competitors who would enter the market in each round exceeded the maximum of eight in more than one round.

Transcriptions of the interviews were coded with a qualitative coding scheme; each participant's statements received as many codes as issues they mentioned. Mentions relating to the decision maker's abilities or experience were coded as ability factors, with confidence and concern subcategories.

Transcriptions of the interviews were coded with a qualitative coding scheme; each participant's statements received as many codes as issues they mentioned. Mentions about the business itself were coded as internal factors, with confidence and concern subcategories.

Transcriptions of the interviews were coded with a qualitative coding scheme; each participant's statements received as many codes as issues they mentioned. Mentions of factors within the external environment of the business were coded as external factors, with confidence and concern subcategories.

Fifteen compensation strategy scales based on 41 survey items were constructed, each scale calculated by averaging the respective item responses associated with that scale. The 15 scales were factor analyzed by a principal components method with ones in the diagonal, and only one factor reached an eigenvalue exceeding 1.0. A composite pay strategy score was calculated for each firm by averaging all 15 scales weighed by their respective factor loadings; a negative factor loading means that a high score on that scale represents a more algorithmic orientation and a positive factor loading signifies a more experiential orientation, so low composite scores are more algorithmic and high composite scores more experiential.

Four performance indicators were obtained from Compustat for the years 1982-1986: two profitability measures (average earnings per share and average return on investment) and two stock performance measures (average return on common stock and the average annual percent change in a firm's market value). A five-year average (1982-1986) was calculated for each performance measure, and a composite firm performance score was computed with each standardized measure weighed by its respective factor loading. The composite was used to categorize firms into performance quartiles and returned surveys were color-coded so that each firm received a score from 1 (lowest performance quartile) to 4 (highest performance quartile).

Extent of diversification was reported by participants according to Rumelt's (1974) typology of diversification, using the scale developed by Balkin and Gomez-Mejia (1990): single-product firm, dominant product firm, related product firm, and unrelated product firm (conglomerates). For each diversification category, firms were dummy coded for the regression equations, with 1 indicating the company falls into that category and 0 indicating it does not.

Respondents rated the extent to which the firm follows a 'steady state' or an 'evolutionary' diversification process. The measure follows Kerr's (1985) study of managerial rewards, which in turn was based on earlier work by Pitts (1976) and Leontiades (1980); the two ratings entered the regressions as separate variables.

Two forms of company-specific investments were measured: knowledge of the company's idiosyncrasies and knowledge of the company's product line. The measure consists of the mean response from a seven-item rating scale in which the response for each item was recorded on a seven-point strongly disagree/strongly agree format. Cronbach's alpha for this scale is 0.88.

The measure of customer-specific investments taps the extent to which the rep has made investments in forging a close relationship with customers. The measure is consistent with those used by Anderson and Schmittlein (1984) and Heide and John (1988). Cronbach's alpha for this scale is 0.82.

Respondents were asked to provide their best estimate (in terms of days, weeks, months, years, or combinations thereof) as to how long their selected manufacturer's representative had been selling the manufacturer's products in the sales district. The measure is the logarithm of the response. The logarithm was used on the assumption that the effect of length of prior relationship is not linear, with prior length having diminishing effects at higher levels.

The likelihood of terminating the relationship was computed as the maximum of the average from each of the two 'intentions to terminate' scales, so that a firm indicating a high intention to change reps and a low intention to integrate vertically is scored on the intention to change reps. The resulting dependent variable is coded such that high values mean a high likelihood of termination and low values mean a low likelihood of termination. The underlying scales are FLIPREP, a four-item scale tapping the manufacturer's seriousness about switching reps in the sales territory in the near term, and GODI, a six-item scale indexing the manufacturer's seriousness about dispensing with its rep and setting up a direct salesforce in the near future.

Nonexclusive 0-1 dummy variable recording whether the business had entered into at least one development-oriented collaborative relationship before the end of each record year. Development-oriented relationships comprise in-licensing of products or components from other businesses and technology agreements.
time_window: cumulative through end of current record year

description: Nonexclusive 0-1 dummy variable recording whether the business had entered into at least one marketing-oriented collaborative relationship before the end of each record year. Marketing-oriented relationships comprise marketing or distribution agreements and value-added relationships.
time_window: cumulative through end of current record year

description: The cumulative number of collaborative relationships that the business had established by the beginning of each record year. Because agreement termination was much less likely to be reported than agreement creation, the records report cumulative agreements created rather than the number of active agreements.
time_window: cumulative through beginning of current record year

description: Nonexclusive 0-1 dummy variable recording whether the business had established at least one other interfirm relationship before the end of each record year. This category covers out-licensing technology to other businesses and agreements whose primary purpose could not be identified.
time_window: cumulative through end of current record year

description: Dependent variable equal to 1 if the business was dissolved during the record year and 0 if it continued to participate at the end of the year. Dissolution exits occurred in 316 cases; each divestiture is treated as a nonexit (a right-censored case) in the analysis of dissolution.

Dependent variable equal to 1 if the business was sold by its parent to another firm during the record year, which is treated as having exited the industry, and 0 otherwise. Divestiture exits occurred in 233 cases; each dissolution is treated as a nonexit in the analysis of divestiture.

Fixed variable set equal to 1 for businesses operating in 1982 that had established at least one development-oriented collaborative relationship by that year, recorded for each year that the business operated between 1983 and 1991. In 1982, 20 businesses had formed development-oriented relationships.

Fixed variable set equal to 1 for businesses operating in 1982 that had established at least one marketing-oriented collaborative relationship by that year, recorded for each year that the business operated between 1983 and 1991. In 1982, 31 businesses had entered marketing-oriented relationships.

Fixed variable equal to 1 for industry incumbents operating in 1982 that had established no interfirm relationships by that year, recorded for each year that the business operated between 1983 and 1991. In 1982, 302 businesses had no collaborative relationships.

Businesses for which there was no public record of collaborative relationships were classed as taking independent commercialization approaches. Owing to data limitations the authors did not attempt to distinguish between independent approaches based on hands-off market relationships and those where businesses carried out most activities internally.

Business survival is the inverse of exit from the industry in a record year. Exit is coded 1 in the year a business is dissolved or sold by its parent (divested), and 0 while it continues to participate; logistic models predict the likelihood of exit and survival is reported as the businesses that remain to the end of the study.

variable_name: added product scope per time period
description: The measure captures the number and relatedness of the firm's expansion steps by the number and the products of newly created subsidiaries. Product relatedness is measured based on four-digit WZ industry codes, comparing the industry code of an expansion step to the closest industry code of the firm's business portfolio before expansion: a same four-digit code match is assigned 0, a three-digit level match 1, a two-digit level match 2, a one-digit level match 3, and no match 4. Scores are discounted (70 percent for the first year of the five-year expansion period, increasing linearly to 100 percent in the last year) and totalled for all steps undertaken in a five-year expansion period; the total score and its squared term are included.
scale: per-step scores 0 to 4, discounted and summed into a total score and squared term

description: Firm performance is measured as the firm's return on assets at the end of the expansion period. The authors chose an accounting over a market-based measure of performance because their model predicts realized performance, while market-based measures reflect shareholder expectations about the future, and state that ROA reflects the relative efficiency of the use of a firm's assets and the synergies gained through expansion.

Calculated using the algorithm developed by Thatcher et al. (2003) along organizational tenure, measured in years, educational specialization, coded using Hambrick, Cho, and Chen's (1996) categories, and level of formal education, measured using the state-approved degrees in the German educational system. For each possible pair of subgroupings, the strength of the respective faultline dividing them is the ratio of the variance of the relevant characteristics between the subgroups over the total variance in the entire team; the ratio can take values between 0 and 1, and the maximum value over all possible splits is the variable faultline strength. TMTs with more than three members are considered.
time_window: average over the five-year expansion period

description: Calculated using the same algorithm as task-related faultline strength, based on age and nationality. Nationality was coded as a dichotomous variable, German or non-German. Gender was considered as a possible bio-demographic attribute but not used because the number of women on the TMTs of the sample firms is negligible. For each possible pair of subgroupings the ratio of between-subgroup variance to total team variance is calculated and the maximum value over all possible splits is the variable.
time_window: average over the five-year expansion period

description: The coefficient on the female indicator in a semilogarithmic regression of log monthly pay on a constant, the female indicator, and pay-relevant observables. A negative value measures how much the firm's female employees are underpaid; this specification was explicitly recommended by regulatory authorities. In the case study the unadjusted pay gap is 30.1% and the adjusted gender pay gap is about one fourth of that amount.

Monthly pay for each employee. The dependent variable of the wage regression is a weakly increasing concave function of wages, most commonly log wages (yi equals ln wi), with untransformed wages (yi equals wi) as the alternative case.

The change in the gender pay gap coefficient from a marginal increase in employee i's wages. It is built from the elements c of the Moore-Penrose (pseudo) inverse of the matrix of wage determinants: when the dependent variable is log wages it equals ciF times wi, and when the dependent variable is untransformed wages it equals ciF.
A column vector whose element for employee i is one if the employee is female and zero otherwise.

The matrix of pay-relevant observables entered in the wage regression together with a constant. In the case study these are 40 dummy variables denoting job categories, six dummy variables denoting a job's general hierarchical level, nine dummy variables measuring the job's education requirement, and four dummy variables denoting other job qualifications, as well as variables for employee age and tenure; the accreditation organization requires the variables for hierarchical level, education, and other qualifications.

variable_name: fitted value from regressing the gender indicator on the observables (x̂iF)
description: The fitted value from a partial regression of the gender indicator on all the other pay-relevant observables and a constant. A low fitted value indicates that the observables do a bad job of predicting that a woman is female, or that they strongly predict that a man is male, i.e., that the employee resembles men on the observables; the lower this fitted value, the higher the employee's differential influence.

variable_name: ethics code use in strategic decision-making
description: A five-item scale. Senior financial officers were asked how helpful (1 = not helpful, 7 = very helpful) they personally found their firm's code of ethics to be in the listed decision areas. Each item was recoded on to a 0-6 scale and the item scores were averaged for the composite measure. Estimated reliability of this composite was alpha = 0.82.
scale: 1 = not helpful to 7 = very helpful, recoded to 0-6

description: Executives responded on unipolar scales to the stem 'In your opinion, how strong were the following forces in pressuring (1 = no pressure, 7 = intense pressure) your firm to adopt a code of ethics?' for market stakeholders. Each item was recoded on to a 0-6 scale and the item scores were averaged for the composite measure. The coefficient alpha was 0.85 for the six-item measure.
scale: 1 = no pressure to 7 = intense pressure, recoded to 0-6

description: Executives responded on unipolar scales to the stem 'In your opinion, how strong were the following forces in pressuring (1 = no pressure, 7 = intense pressure) your firm to adopt a code of ethics?' for non-market stakeholders. Each item was recoded on to a 0-6 scale and the item scores were averaged for the composite measure. The coefficient alpha was 0.87.
scale: 1 = no pressure to 7 = intense pressure, recoded to 0-6

description: Executives rated their agreement (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree) with a statement beginning 'A primary reason for a firm to have an ethics code is ...' that was completed by ways to deter unethical behavior. Each item was recoded on to a 0-6 scale and the item scores were averaged for the composite measure. The estimated reliability of this measure was 0.78.
scale: 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree, recoded to 0-6

variable_name: perceived benefit: create an ethical firm culture
description: Executives rated their agreement (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree) with a statement beginning 'A primary reason for a firm to have an ethics code is ...' that was completed by ways to create an ethical firm culture. Each item was recoded on to a 0-6 scale and the item scores were averaged for the composite measure. Internal consistency of this measure was alpha = 0.80.
scale: 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree, recoded to 0-6

variable_name: perceived benefit: promote a positive external image
description: Executives rated their agreement (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree) with a statement beginning 'A primary reason for a firm to have an ethics code is ...' that was completed by ways to promote a positive external image. Each item was recoded on to a 0-6 scale and the item scores were averaged for the composite measure. The coefficient alpha was 0.80.
scale: 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree, recoded to 0-6

description: Three questions assessed the extent of training undertaken by the corporation to implement their ethics codes, starting with the stem 'How frequently (1 = infrequently; 7 = frequently) has the firm resorted to the following efforts to secure compliance with the company code of ethics?'. The items concerned ethics training programs (e.g., classes, workshops, video, presentations) for different employee levels. The estimated reliability was alpha = 0.91.

Felt pressure from stakeholders to adopt an ethics code, measured with a single survey stem asking how strong each force was in pressuring the firm to adopt a code, rated 1 (no pressure) to 7 (intense pressure) for six market stakeholders and for non-market stakeholders. Item scores were recoded to 0-6 and averaged into two composites, market and non-market pressure, entered separately.

Dummy variable indicating whether a firm filed a material financial restatement during the study period. Firms filing restatements were coded 1 and their matched counterparts (control firms) were coded 0; restatement firms made up half of the total sample.

Dummy variable representing whether a restatement was prompted externally (by external auditors or the SEC) rather than internally (by a firm's officers or directors). Each subsample represented approximately half the total number of restatement firms.

Cumulative abnormal market-adjusted returns calculated with Eventus, using the CRSP equally weighted index. The market model was estimated over a 255-day window ending 46 days prior to the event, and the event window began the day prior to and ended the day after the restatement event. The day after restatement was included because some announcements may have occurred after stock market trading closed for the day.
time_window: event window from the day prior to the day after the restatement announcement; 255-day estimation window ending 46 days prior

description: Dichotomous dependent variable in the event history data set; individuals retaining their positions in a period were assigned a value of 0 and those who left were assigned a value of 1. Because the month of departure could be determined, CEO turnover was updated monthly and each executive was tracked for the 24-month period following each restatement announcement.
time_window: 24 months following the restatement announcement, updated monthly

description: Dichotomous dependent variable in the event history data set; individuals retaining their positions in a period were assigned a value of 0 and those who left were assigned a value of 1. Because the month of departure could be determined, CFO turnover was updated monthly and each executive was tracked for the 24-month period following each restatement announcement.
time_window: 24 months following the restatement announcement, updated monthly

description: Dichotomous dependent variable coded 1 for outside directors who left and 0 for those who retained their positions. Because the month of exit could not be identified, the data set was updated annually: board structure was recorded from the proxy statement preceding the restatement event and each outside director was tracked through three subsequent proxy statements.
time_window: three subsequent proxy statements, tracked for two to three calendar years after the restatement event

description: Dichotomous dependent variable coded 1 for audit committee members who left and 0 for those who retained their positions. Because the month of exit could not be identified, the data set was updated annually: audit committee structure was recorded from the proxy statement preceding the restatement event and each member was tracked through three subsequent proxy statements.
time_window: three subsequent proxy statements, tracked for two to three calendar years after the restatement event

description: Respondents ranked a set of criteria according to how they would use them in determining the overall merit of a department (10 = most important, 1 = least important). Two research-related criteria were used: the number of doctoral degrees awarded annually and the number and quality of faculty publications and papers presented. Rankings of these two criteria were averaged for the measure of research orientation.

variable_name: perceived criticality of support staff relative to faculty
description: Respondents evaluated, on a 9-point scale, the criticality of (1) faculty positions, (2) graduate assistants, and (3) classified staff in times of general scarcity of resources. A ratio variable was constructed by averaging each respondent's ratings of the criticality of graduate assistants and classified staff and then dividing this average by the criticality rating for faculty positions. Because the distribution of the ratio variable was highly skewed, the original scores were transformed to lognormal scores: transformed score = ln(ratio + 1).

Using university catalogs, the authors coded the longest chain of courses prerequisite to any single course for each academic discipline that contributed respondents, then ranked the disciplines from longest chain (high paradigm development) to shortest chain (low paradigm development). Each respondent received a paradigm development score equivalent to the rank score for that individual's discipline; lower numbers indicate higher levels of paradigm development. The rankings were validated against previous rankings, with correlations of .79 and .86.

Nine items, three for each of the elemental norms of flexibility, solidarity, and participation, all measured on seven-point rating scales (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). The elemental norms load on a single common factor, Norms. Cronbach's alpha for the battery of nine items is 0.88. Norms is the first-stage dependent variable of the two-stage model.

Evaluation measures the other party's performance through two items, the first of which is reverse coded. Cronbach's alpha for the battery is 0.82. Evaluation is one of the three exchange performance variables used as dependent variables in the seemingly unrelated regressions.

Satisfaction measures overall satisfaction with outcomes and is captured by three items. Cronbach's alpha for the battery of three items is 0.91. Satisfaction is one of the three exchange performance variables used as dependent variables in the seemingly unrelated regressions.

Future measures willingness to collaborate in the future and is captured by three items. Cronbach's alpha for the battery of three items is 0.96. Future is one of the three exchange performance variables used as dependent variables in the seemingly unrelated regressions.

A battery of four items assesses joint transaction-specific investments on seven-point rating scales. Cronbach's alpha for the battery is 0.77. Joint TSI is a primary covariate in the first-stage model predicting cooperative exchange norms.

Observability is identified by a battery of three items, the first of which is reverse coded. Cronbach's alpha for the battery is 0.89. Observability is a primary covariate in the first-stage model predicting cooperative exchange norms.

Low is a continuous variable constructed from the residuals of the first-stage cooperative norms equation; it equals the residual when the residual is negative and zero otherwise. It measures the degree to which a collaboration achieved an unanticipated low level of cooperative norms relative to the level expected from the exchange attributes. Higher values indicate a larger shortfall below the expected level. Low is an independent variable in the three performance equations.

High is a continuous variable constructed from the residuals of the first-stage cooperative norms equation; it equals the residual when the residual is positive and zero otherwise. It measures the degree to which a collaboration achieved an unanticipated high level of cooperative norms relative to the level expected from the exchange attributes. Higher values indicate a larger excess above the expected level. High is an independent variable in the three performance equations.

Percentage of common shares held by foreign corporations. The authors state that a single firm almost always holds the shares belonging to this category and that these shareholdings are primarily foreign collaborator holdings, representing substantial technical and managerial collaborations with Indian firms.

Percentage of common shares held by foreign institutional investors. The authors describe these holdings as small and dispersed relative to foreign corporate holdings, while accounting for a substantial proportion of the daily stock turnover of large and liquid stocks.

Percentage of common shares held by domestic Indian corporations, described as the largest component of equity ownership in Indian listed firms. An interaction variable, DOMCINT, multiplies domestic corporate ownership by the group dummy to represent domestic corporate ownership in firms affiliated to groups.
Percentage of common shares owned by domestic (i.e., Indian) financial institutions, which consist of development financial institutions, insurance companies, banks, and mutual funds.

Percentage of common shares owned by all directors (including relatives), described as the second largest category of owners in Indian listed firms. A squared term, DIR2, is used to test for a curvilinear relationship, and an interaction variable, DIRINT, represents director and other family member ownership in firms affiliated to groups.

A dummy variable adjusting for business group affiliation, built from the classification made by the Capitaline database, which determines group affiliation from a variety of sources including public announcements made by individual corporations and groups, regulatory filings, and stock exchange listings by corporations. The text does not state which value of the dummy denotes group affiliation.

Operating earnings before interest, depreciation, and taxes over the book value of total assets. Instead of dropping outliers, the authors cap the performance variables at their 1st and 99th percentile values.

The sum of the market value of equity and the book value of debt divided by the book value of assets. It is used as the stock market-based measure of firm performance, alongside ROA as the accounting-based measure.

Composite measure of the firm's provision of family-friendly practices. The authors transform each firm's response on each practice into a z-score by subtracting the sample mean and dividing by the standard deviation, sum the individual z-scores, and standardize the sum again, producing a 'double-z-score'. The practices entering the score are hours worked, holidays taken, childcare flexibility, working from home, job switching, job sharing, and childcare subsidy.
Natural log of sales per employee, used as the firm's labor productivity measure. Sales and employment come from company accounts and proxy statements.

Return on capital employed, used as the profitability measure of firm performance. The authors describe it as the broader performance measure because it includes the costs of implementing FFWP, unlike sales per employee.
The proportion of a firm's employees with a university degree, entered in the regressions as the natural log of the percentage. Collected in the HR interview alongside trainings and unionization.

Percentage of female employees as part of the total workforce, collected in the HR interview. The authors report that this variable is not significant in the FFWP regressions and was omitted from some specifications because of collinearity with the share of female managers.

Percentage of female managers as part of the management layer, collected in the HR interview. The authors argue it captures the presence of a group of key employees that places a comparably higher value on FFWP.

Composite z-score of management practice questions grouped into four areas: operations, monitoring, targets, and incentives. The practices are scored on a scale of 1-5 by trained interviewers during double-blind telephone interviews with plant managers, based on open questions about actual firm practices. The score is used as a control for the quality of management practices in the performance regressions.

Natural log of average imports over production by country/SIC pair, that is, import penetration, used to measure exposure to international competition. It is constructed at the three-digit industry level.

Three-digit industry Lerner index of competition by country, defined as one minus profits over sales, calculated as the average across the entire firm-level database excluding each firm itself. It is constructed for the period 1995-1999 to remove any potential contemporaneous feedback, and higher values indicate more competition.
Survey question on the number of competitors a firm faces, valued 0 for 'no competitors', 1 for 'less than five competitors', and 2 for 'five or more competitors'.

Managers' perceptions of their own firm's work-life balance versus that of other firms in the industry, defined as the response to the question 'Relative to other companies in your industry, how much does your company emphasize work-life balance?'. Responses are scored from much less to much more on a five-point scale.

variable_name: Number of fabless (specialized) and IDM (integrated) firms
description: Annual counts of publicly traded specialized (fabless) and integrated (IDM) firms active in the semiconductor industry, plotted from 1984 to 2008. The counts show that although the industry went through a significant period of vertical disintegration driven by the entry of fabless firms, integrated incumbents continued to persist and coexist with them, with only a small minority switching from vertical integration to specialization.

variable_name: Share of firms' patents corresponding to systemic innovations
description: The share of a firm's patents in a given year that correspond to systemic innovations. Patents in the Derwent technology classification sections covering semiconductors and related technologies are categorized as design or manufacturing based on an expert classification of the Derwent classes, and a patented innovation is systemic if it is categorized by both design and manufacturing classes. The analysis uses annual data on IDM and fabless firms' patent grants filed between 1993 and 2007, based on a total of 732,854 patent records assigned to fabless and IDM firms.

variable_name: Share of firms' patents corresponding to autonomous innovations
description: The share of a firm's patents in a given year that correspond to autonomous innovations, defined as patented innovations categorized by either design-only or manufacturing-only Derwent classes. For fabless firms the dominant category of patented innovation is design-based autonomous innovation, whereas for IDM firms design-only innovation represents about half of all patents and manufacturing-only innovation about 15%.

Firms are categorized according to whether they are vertically integrated or specialized, using the categorization provided in the GSA database, which lists all publicly traded semiconductor firms that competed in the industry between 1990 and 2008. Integrated firms are also known as integrated device manufacturers (IDMs), and specialized firms as fabless firms.

A dummy variable that distinguishes specialized fabless firms from integrated IDM firms in the regression of firms' annual return on invested capital. The estimate for this variable indicates whether the performance of fabless firms differs from that of integrated IDM firms.

The firm's annual return on invested capital, the dependent variable in the regression of the effect of firm- and industry-specific factors on firm performance from 1993 to 2007. The analysis is estimated by OLS with robust standard errors clustered by firm, and fails to reject the null hypothesis of no significant difference in performance between fabless and IDM firms.

variable_name: IDM firms using manufacturing services from foundries
description: The cumulative number of IDM firms that announced a shift in their manufacturing strategy from make to make and buy, i.e., IDM firms using external specialized foundry suppliers for a proportion of their manufacturing while retaining in-house manufacturing. The trend shows an increasing number of IDM firms using specialized foundries over time.

variable_name: IDM firms offering manufacturing services to fabless firms
description: The number of IDM firms offering their manufacturing services to specialized fabless firms in addition to internal use, plotted over time. The number of IDM firms participating in the intermediate market for manufacturing grew from 7 in 1997 to 39 in 2008.

Count of investment transactions made by U.S. firms in a country-industry-year. The authors describe it as a count-based measure of foreign investment—how many incremental investments are made a year in each of a multitude of different countries and their industries—and note it is nonnegative with a high frequency of zero and small integer values. The BEA data are disaggregated by industry and by investment mode (greenfield or acquisition).

Moving stock of patents for the host country-industry, built with the perpetual inventory method: the yearly patent flow in 1976 is the starting point and the existing stock is depreciated by 20 percent while each year's additional patents are added. Patents are assigned to industries using the USPTO SIC-USPC concordance and filing dates rather than grant dates are used to date the knowledge. The variable varies by country-industry-year and is entered in logs.
time_window: annual stock built from 1976 patent flows, measured 1989-1999

description: Patent stock for the U.S. industry-year, constructed the same way as the host stock with the perpetual inventory method and assigned to industries via the USPTO SIC-USPC concordance. It is industry-year varying rather than country-industry-year varying and is entered in logs. Together with the host count it captures the relative knowledge position between the home and host country-industries.
time_window: annual stock built from 1976 patent flows, measured 1989-1999

description: Uncentered correlation, following Jaffe (1986), between the vectors of patent stocks distributed across patent classes for a host country-industry-year and the corresponding U.S. industry-year. The authors use 313 separate patent classification categories, so each year vector has 313 dimensions, and construct the measure for each country-industry-year relative to the corresponding U.S. industry-year. Technical similarity varies from zero to one, with a value of one indicating that the two vectors are completely overlapped.

Dummy variable for country-industry-years with no technical overlap at all with the United States, that is, technical similarity equal to zero. The authors include it because numerous country-industry-years have zero overlap, a discontinuity a linear estimate would have difficulty reflecting.

Respondents indicated on a seven-point Likert-type scale the extent to which bilateral communication existed between the managers of head offices and subsidiary units involved in strategic decision making, head office managers applied consistent decision-making procedures across subsidiary units, subsidiary units could challenge and refute the strategic views of head office managers, subsidiary units received a full account of the final strategic decisions of head offices, and head office managers involved in strategic decision making were well informed about the local situations of subsidiary units. The five-item measure was developed in the authors' earlier study. The Cronbach's coefficient alpha for the five-item scale was .85 and the intraclass correlation was .94.
time_window: reflections on the strategic planning process just past

description: Subsidiary top managers rated the extent of their own compliance on four items measured on a seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree): following the final strategic decisions made by the head office with extreme care; accepting and fully implementing those decisions even if not parallel with the strategic interests of the individual subsidiary unit; a tendency, when given room for managerial discretion, to disregard and even subvert the corporate strategic decisions in the interests of the national unit (reverse-scored); and actions fully consonant with executing the strategic decisions to the letter and spirit with which they were set forth. The alpha for the four-item scale was .91 and the intraclass correlation was .91. To check for bias, individual scores were pooled within each national unit and correlated with head office managers' assessments of unit compliance; the correlation was positive and significant (r = .72, p < .01).
scale: seven-point Likert-type (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)
time_window: assessed just before the beginning of another annual strategic planning process, ten months after the first questionnaire

description: Organizational commitment was assessed using the nine-item short form of the Organizational Commitment Questionnaire developed by Mowday, Steers, and Porter (1979). Responses to the nine items were measured on a seven-point scale with scale anchors labeled 1, strongly disagree, and 7, strongly agree. The organization was defined as the multinational. Alpha for the overall nine-item scale was .90 and the intraclass correlation was .83.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)
time_window: within six weeks of the completion of the annual strategic planning process

description: Four items measured the trust subsidiary top managers had in head office management: how much confidence and trust they had in head office management; how much trust they had that the unit's current sacrifice would be justified by the head office's future support for the unit when decisions seemed against the unit's interests; how willing they were to accept and follow strategic decisions made by head office management; and how free they felt to discuss problems and difficulties faced by their unit without fear of jeopardizing their position. These items were measured on seven-point scales; alpha for the overall scale was .94 and the intraclass correlation was .81.
time_window: within six weeks of the completion of the annual strategic planning process

description: Respondents indicated on seven-point scales the extent to which they were satisfied overall with the content of the resulting strategy decisions and the extent to which they would prefer another strategy decision for their national unit; the second item was reverse-scored. The alpha for this measure was .84 and the intraclass correlation was .95.
time_window: within six weeks of the completion of the annual strategic planning process

description: Subsidiary top managers indicated the proportion of their unit's total sales accounted for by industry segments fitting three descriptions: toward the multidomestic, balanced between global and multidomestic, and toward the global. The three industry categories were coded 1, 2, and 3, respectively. The proportional breakdown of a subsidiary's industry-segment sales was multiplied by each industry category's code to derive a weighted-average measure of the type of each subsidiary unit's industries, with high values indicating a more global type and lower values a more multidomestic type. Ratings were consistent within units, and the scores correlated positively and significantly with head office managements' assessments of each unit's industry type (r = .71, p < .01).
scale: weighted average of category codes 1 to 3
level: subsidiary unit (reported by individual subsidiary top managers)

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 when a venture is part of a portfolio of multiple ventures and 0 otherwise. Any venture founded by an individual who concurrently owns another venture in a given year is considered a portfolio venture; to avoid contamination by branches of the same venture, portfolios are restricted to ventures that operate in multiple two-digit NACE Rev. 2 industries. Once a company is flagged as a portfolio venture, it is demarcated as such until it becomes the only venture in the portfolio, and periods when it is no longer part of a portfolio are removed from the control group.

The venture's number of staff employed at the end of the year (annual measure) and at the end of the month (monthly measure). In analyses using skill transferability as the dependent variable, the staff measure is a control to account for any potential differences in the level of skill transferability that are driven by differences in the number of staff between standalone and portfolio ventures.
time_window: end of year; end of month

description: Cross-industry skill transferability following Starr et al. (2018): each occupation-industry pair receives a value between 0 and 1 based on the estimated job availability for the occupation outside the focal industry. The estimate divides the share of employees of an occupation in the focal industry by the total number of employees in the occupation and subtracts this ratio from 1. Occupations are tracked with the two-digit Finnish Classification of Occupations 2010 code and industries with the two-digit TOL 2008 industry code, combined into a four-digit occupation-industry pair. For the main analysis the score is aggregated per venture by taking the average skill transferability of all the employees of a venture.

Natural logarithm of the previous year's annual revenue, used to proxy for a positive market signal. The coefficient of interest is its interaction with Portfolio Venture; the first year is excluded from the analysis because lagged values cannot be obtained for that year. The authors report a mean of 5 and a standard deviation of 1.77 for this variable.

Treatment dummy indicating the timing of adoption of the Employment and Growth Agreement: it equals 1 if the venture-month observation is in an industry where the agreement had already taken effect. Because adoption was staggered by month across industries, the specification is estimated at the month level with month, year, venture age, industry, industry-year and industry-month fixed effects, and the coefficient of interest is the interaction NewAgreement x PortfolioVenture.
time_window: 12 months before to 36 months after the agreement

description: Respondents were asked to indicate which one of two statements, both from Ouchi (1977), most closely reflected their superiors' actual approach to managing their business unit: focusing on the attainment of targets while allowing considerable discretion in how to achieve them, or monitoring decisions and actions on an ongoing basis. The first statement, representing output control, was coded 1 and the second, representing behavior control, was coded 2. The authors treat the variable as nominal.

Respondents indicated the importance of three functions - marketing-sales, manufacturing, and R&D - for the implementation of their SBU's strategy, and for each function whether their SBU shared resources and, if so, to what extent (for example, the percentage of the SBU's total sales handled by a common sales force). Using the data on the importance of the three functions as weights, the authors derived a weighted-average measure of resource sharing for each SBU.
scale: percentage of sharing; weighted average across three functions

description: Respondents indicated the percentage of their business unit's current total sales accounted for by products representing use of either Porter's low-cost or differentiation strategy. An overall cost-leadership strategy was assigned a value of -1 and a differentiation strategy a value of +1, and the percentage breakdown the SBU manager provided for each item was used to construct a weighted-average strategy measure. The strategy index is a continuous variable ranging from -1.00 to +1.00.

Effectiveness data were collected on ten performance dimensions: return on investment, profit, cash flow from operations, cost control, development of new products, sales volume, market share, market development, personnel development, and political-public affairs. On each dimension respondents rated their SBU's performance relative to corporate standards on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 'significantly below average' to 'significantly above average', and then rated each dimension on a 5-point scale ranging from 'not important' to 'extremely important' to indicate the degree of importance superiors attached to the criteria when determining the incentive bonus of an SBU manager. Using the importance data as weights, the authors obtained a weighted-average performance index for each SBU.
scale: 7-point Likert performance ratings weighted by 5-point importance ratings

description: Respondents chose which of two statements from Ouchi (1977) best described their superior's actual approach: monitoring decisions and actions on an ongoing basis was coded 2 and represented behavior control. The same nominal variable identifies output control (coded 1).

Respondents chose which of two statements from Ouchi (1977) best described their superior's actual approach: focusing on attainment of targets while allowing discretion in how to reach them was coded 1 and represented output control. It is the same nominal variable used for behavior control, read the other way.

For each house and each year in the sample period, the cumulative number of hectares of vineyards acquired in Champagne since 1998. The total number of hectares owned at any point in time was deliberately not used, because houses have owned vineyards for decades or even centuries and these vineyards do not antagonize growers; it is new acquisitions that are considered transgressions.

For each house and each year in the sample period, the number of winemaking subsidiaries opened outside of France since 1998. Subsidiaries in each house's corporate structure were tracked in the Diane and RCS databases and then checked against the various national registries of trade so that only subsidiaries dedicated to the production of wine were included, excluding those dedicated to mere distribution.

For each Champagne house in each year, the total number of supermarket brands it supplied in that year, taken as its natural logarithm because the difference between supplying 0 and 1 supermarket brands is perceived differently than the difference between supplying 4 and 5. Information on whether houses produced Champagne for supermarkets' private labels was collected from the annual Buyer's Own Brand Listing of Rayon Boissons.

A composite measure constructed as the sum of four binary variables, so that each feature is given equal weight: newcomer (reverse-coded, 1 for houses established before 1960), family CEO (1 if the CEO is a descendant of the founder by blood or marriage), traditional location (1 for traditional villages such as Reims, Epernay, and Les Riceys), and corporate group (reverse-coded, 1 for houses that do not belong to corporate groups). It ranges from 0, for a house that features none of the traditional characteristics, to 4, for a house that features all four; in the sample 6% scored 0, 33% scored 1, 25% scored 2, 25% scored 3, and 11% scored 4. Founding dates and family management were cross-checked with the French Who's Who and the Guide Curien, and corporate structures with the Diane and RCS databases.

The average price that a house paid for the raw materials used in its Champagne production in a given year, computed by dividing the annual purchase cost of raw material by the volume of grapes in kilograms for each house. The cost of grapes is not reported separately, but the only other raw materials that can be added are yeast and sugar, which are used in small quantities relative to the grapes and are commodities; because grapes are purchased from a large number of growers who can potentially charge different prices, the ratio averages the prices paid.

variable_name: Price (interview accounts of charging higher prices)
description: In the interviews, growers described charging role violators higher prices for their grapes as a way of punishing deviations from the institutionalized status quo, and described the satisfaction this brought them.

A self-reported informal legacy indicator derived from the World Bank Enterprise Survey. The survey asks respondents whether the firm was formally registered when it began operations. The variable takes a value of 0 if the firm was registered at the time of its foundation and 1 if it was not. All firms in the sample were formally registered at the time of the survey; 19.0% of them had an informal legacy.

A discrete, self-reported variable that measures whether a firm participates in export markets. It is set equal to 1 if a firm engaged in direct exports in the previous fiscal year and 0 otherwise. Of the firms in the sample, 12.0% participated in export markets, and the median exporting firm exported 30% of its total annual sales.

Takes the value of 1 in the first period our data indicates that a lobbyist changes employers, and 0 otherwise. The coefficient captures the initial change in the level of integration individuals experience when they join a new firm. Mobility events where the employee founds or joins a start-up firm, or works directly for a client, are excluded.

The level of employee utilization is measured in terms of revenue from lobbying activities an individual lobbyist has participated in. It is calculated as the dollar sum of all lobbying contracts a given lobbyist was associated with in a given period. LNRevenue is the natural log of lobbying revenue. This measure captures the amount of revenue the lobbyist participates in generating, not how much the lobbyist is compensated by the lobbying firm.

Measured with the unweighted Jaffe proximity measure, which captures the extent of issue overlap between the firm and the lobbyist. It computes the degree of overlap between a lobbyist's issue portfolio at time t−1 and the issues the firm lobbies at time t. The computation uses the firm's share in each of 78 predefined lobbying issues out of the firm's total revenue at time t and the employee's share in each issue out of the lobbyist's total revenue at time t−1.
time_window: lobbyist issues at t−1; firm issues at t

description: Measured by replacing the diagonal entries of the knowledge-relatedness matrix with zeros and using the off-diagonal entries to weight the calculation of firm–employee proximity, based on the same lobbyist and firm issue portfolios used for similarity. It captures how much of the issues covered by a lobbyist that do not overlap with the firm create more value for clients — the degree to which the issues covered by a lobbyist that do not overlap with the issues of the firm tend to be bundled together by clients. The knowledge-relatedness matrix is itself constructed from the issue co-occurrence patterns of clients' lobbying contracts.
time_window: lobbyist issues at t−1; firm issues at t

description: Created by counting the number of lobbyists who work with the focal lobbyist at time t who also worked with the lobbyist at the same firm in time t−1. By design, this reflects the number of lobbyists moving together to a new firm for mobility events. For periods of no mobility, the measure captures the number of coworkers at time t from the previous period.

The ratio of unique clients the lobbyist retained from period to period. It is an extension of the client transfer measure used by Raffiee (2017), extended to observations where employee mobility does not occur.

The pay program is represented by a dummy indicator of the treatment period, coded 0 for the pretreatment months and 1 for the posttreatment months at the treatment facility. In the quality model a treatment facility dummy and the treatment-by-facility interaction are also included, the interaction reflecting the net change at the treatment facility relative to the comparison facility. For the productivity and labor cost models the coefficient on the treatment variable is the estimated effect of the program.
level: production group-month; facility-month for labor cost

description: Quality was measured as the percentage of defective units (scrap) in the total units allowed through the production process. Because the data were pooled across heterogeneous production processes, outcome observations were standardized within groups. The treatment facility series covers the full period studied, whereas the comparison facility could provide comparable data beginning at month 16 of the treatment facility data. The test of interest is the interaction of treatment period and treatment facility, which reflects the net change in the treatment facility relative to the comparison facility.
time_window: monthly; treatment facility months 1-37, comparison facility from month 16

description: Productivity was assessed as labor hours per part. The series comes from the treatment facility only and is measured at the production group level, with group i observed at time t. Because the data were pooled across heterogeneous production processes, outcome observations were standardized within groups. The regression includes a dummy indicator of the treatment period and the control variables.

Labor cost was measured as actual wage expense divided by the number of good parts produced. Only facility-wide rather than group-level data were available, so there was one observation per month and the list of control variables was abbreviated to include only facility-wide measures. Two models were estimated, one controlling for the average hourly wage rate and one not controlling for it.

Our focal predictor variable, block-holding activism, took a value of one for firm-years following block-holding activism (including the year that a Schedule 13D was filed) for target firms and zero for other firm-year observations. Firm-year observations occurring more than 10 years after a campaign were excluded. For firms targeted more than once, only the first occurrence of block-holding activism was retained.
time_window: from the Schedule 13D filing year up to 10 years after

description: Lobbying expenditures equals the natural logarithm of one plus a firm's total lobbying expenditures in a year, taken from LobbyView. The log values were used to account for skewness in the right tail. In robustness checks a dummy for whether a firm lobbied in a given year was used instead.
scale: natural logarithm of one plus expenditures

description: Computed using BoardEx data to capture the ratio of directors with government work experience to the total number of directors on a board.
The proportion of busy directors with prior government experience relative to board size, where a busy director was defined as holding more than three board seats in a given year.

The proportion of nonbusy directors with prior government experience relative to board size, where nonbusy directors are those not classified as busy (i.e., not holding more than three board seats in a given year).

The percentage of a firm's shares owned by institutional investors with documented lobbying activity prior to the year in which block-holding activism occurred. Ownership data came from Thomson Reuters 13F Holdings and institutional investors' lobbying activity from OpenSecrets.
time_window: prior to the year in which block-holding activism occurred
