description: Ownership by lobbying-active institutional investors whose holding period in the focal firm was equal to or above the median of eight quarters, measured as the number of quarters the investor had been invested in the firm by the end of the previous year.
time_window: holding period ending the previous year

description: Ownership by lobbying-active institutional investors whose holding period in the focal firm was below the median of eight quarters, measured as the number of quarters the investor had been invested in the firm by the end of the previous year.
time_window: holding period ending the previous year

description: The complete 1997 Census of Manufactures is used to measure the total value sold in each industry and to calculate the share of total value shipped by each establishment. The relevant market is defined by the four-digit NAICS code reported as the primary product for each plant of interest. This value is logged to address the skewness of its distribution.

Indicator equal to 1 if the plant reports buying primarily over the Internet. Plants that report making purchases primarily over the Internet are coded as having adopted e-buying; establishments that merely experiment with Internet-based processes while relying primarily on a different network are excluded.

Indicator equal to 1 if the plant reports selling primarily over the Internet. Establishments that report accepting orders primarily over the Internet are coded as having adopted e-selling; those relying primarily on another network are excluded. The suppliers/customers on the other side of these transactions lie outside the manufacturing survey frame, so e-buying and e-selling concern separate transactions.

Indicator equal to 1 if the plant reports having adopted 'fully integrated' enterprise resource planning software. Some data for ERP adoption are missing in the 1999 CNUS survey, causing a change in sample size in that specification.

The authors' preferred measure of a plant's IT-related capabilities: an indicator equal to 1 if the plant reports using networked computers in two or more of the following activities. It was chosen because it is likely to pick up a degree of 'IT savvy' while being less codetermined with the e-buying and e-selling innovations. The adoption rate of this margin of IT use is roughly 13% of the population.

The Commodity Flow Survey is first used to determine the counties to which each focal plant ships its output, and each instance of a plant shipping to its own county is flagged for removal so that the measure is not contaminated by own-IT adoption choices. Population counts of plants reporting intensive internal use of IT are estimated by county using the CNUS and Census sample weights, restricting attention to counties with five or more CNUS plants. The plant-specific index purges population adoption counts of the focal plant, takes average adoption rates by county, and calculates the shipment-weighted average of IT adoption across all counties to which the focal plant ships output.

The authors construct an industry Lerner index of competitive pressure from a ratio of profits to sales, written in the text as 1 minus (sales minus cost of materials minus wages) over sales; the rendering of this formula in the text is partly unreadable. A higher Lerner index is assumed to represent a greater level of product market competition (and hence lower margins). To avoid bias from short-term fluctuations or outliers, the value-weighted average of this measure is taken for each industry over the past 10 years, with industry defined by four-digit SIC code. A plant is classified as being in a low-competition industry when the cutoff between the high and low categories (the mean Lerner index value) is not met.

Indicator equal to 1 if the plant's primary industry has 75% or more of the value in that industry transferred to 'final use' by consumers, according to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis input-output tables; such industries are treated as predominantly business-to-consumer. Results are said to be robust to raising the threshold up to 90%.

Innovation novelty is measured from a patent's recombination of knowledge components, proxied by the technological class-subclass combinations identified in the patent's backward citations. Using application dates, the authors took yearly panel counts of the cumulative number of times two patent class-subclass dyads had been combined. The prose states that z_ijc is the frequency with which class i has been cocited with class j, max(z_ijc) is the largest of i's reported ties with any other class, and Nc is the number of technology classes cited by patent c, but the algebraic rendering of the aggregation is not legible in the text. The resulting average degree of combination was subtracted from 1 so that patents that included previously uncombined classes achieved the largest values, and a firm's degree of novelty is a two-year moving average equal to the sum of the novelty scores of all of the firm's patents divided by the number of its patents.
level: firm-quarter (patent scores averaged to the firm)
time_window: two-year moving average using patent application dates (t)

description: Set to 1 when a new venture received VC funding and 0 otherwise, updated on a quarterly basis, so that a firm that received funding in quarter 11 is coded 0 in the first 10 quarters and 1 from quarter 11 onward. The authors relied on the BioScan, Knowledge Express, and SDC databases to determine if and when VCs invested in the sample ventures. A three-year lag is applied to all explanatory variables. About 33% of the firm-quarter observations in the first 5 years and 12% of the firm-quarter observations for firms older than 12 years had no VC funding.

The number of titles assigned to the CEO divided by the total number of titles of all TMT members, while correcting for the TMT's size; the adjustment for team size is designed to provide a lower bound for the effect of the CEO's structural power. A high degree of structural power reflects a more centralized decision-making process. Titles were taken from BioScan and Knowledge Express reports of executive titles. A three-year lag is applied to this explanatory variable.

Based on the number of patents on which the CEO served as a coinventor up to time t, accounting for industry tenure and impact on patents. The number of patents the scientist applied for by year t is divided by the scientist's industry tenure (number of years since the scientist's first patent application) and multiplied by the average forward citations received by the scientist's patents by year t. CEO names were matched to the names of patent inventors using inventor-level information provided by the NBER and USPTO. A three-year lag is applied to this explanatory variable.
time_window: three-year lag; cumulative to year t

description: Firms are classified by age: the first five years are considered the early stage because of the liability of newness, and firms older than 12 years are treated as late-stage ventures. The authors recognize that defining these cutoffs is somewhat arbitrary because ventures may vary in the time needed for maturity. The models are estimated on firms of all ages, on new ventures equal to or younger than 5 years, and on ventures equal to or older than 12 years.

CEOs engaged in the same decision-making task at two times (T1 and T2), separated by a distractor task that provided no new information, so any change in their strategic decisions is represented as erratic. Using metric conjoint analysis, a separate regression equation was calculated for each set of decisions for each individual, consisting of four main effects and three interaction effects, with the regression coefficients reflecting the weight given to a particular attribute. Each significant (p < 0.05) T2 beta weight was subtracted from the corresponding significant (p < 0.05) T1 beta weight, the absolute value of each difference was taken, and the scores were summed for each individual to form the dependent variable.
time_window: T1 and T2, separated by a distractor task of about eight minutes

description: A reduced version of the scale developed by Haynie and Shepherd (2009), measured with a six-item, seven-point Likert-type scale on which CEOs indicated the extent to which they strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (7) with statements regarding their experience with cognition (alpha = 0.74). The items capture the belief that one knows how to think about a task in order to successfully accomplish it.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: Slevin and Covin's (1997) six-item hostility scale, on which CEOs indicated on a seven-point Likert-type scale the extent to which they strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (7) with statements regarding the hostile nature of the environmental context of their principal industry (alpha = 0.65).
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: A variant of the Miller and Friesen (1982) dynamism scale, similar to that used by Green et al. (2008): a six-item measure on which CEOs indicated on a seven-point Likert-type scale the extent to which they strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (7) with statements regarding the stability/dynamism of their environmental context (alpha = 0.83). Responses were coded so that higher dynamism had higher scores.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: Measured using the Jaworski and Kohli (1993) scale with a standard Likert-type seven-point scale with anchors of 'strongly disagree' and 'strongly agree'. In the confirmatory factor model the construct represents a second-order factor, with the observed survey items representing first-order factors that in turn represent the second-order factor. Summated scores for each of the first-order constructs were used as indicators of the second-order construct.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale ('strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree')

description: Seven distinct market-related capabilities (product development, pricing, channel management, marketing communications, selling, market planning, and marketing implementation) were measured using existing scales. Respondents rated their business unit relative to major competitors on a seven-point scale with 'much worse than competitors' and 'much better than competitors' anchors. The construct is modeled as a second-order factor, with summated scores for each first-order construct used as indicators.
scale: seven-point scale ('much worse than competitors' to 'much better than competitors')

description: Respondents' subjective assessments of their firm's profitability, using a synthesis of items from previous scales, and of their firm's market effectiveness, using a scale tapping the degree to which the firm's market-related goals (e.g., sales, share) had been achieved. The construct is modeled as a second-order subjective performance factor.

The average return on assets for the two-year period covering the year of the primary data collection and the following year, calculated to allow for lagged effects and to minimize the impact of any short-run unobserved events. The data were collected from secondary sources for the 108 respondent firms for which secondary financial information was available.
time_window: two-year period covering the year of primary data collection and the following year

description: GDP by industry, representing an industry's contribution to overall GDP, was obtained for 51 broad industries for 1947-2000 and used as a measure of total industry demand. GARCH-in-mean models were fit to each individual industry time series; diagnostic checks indicated that a parsimonious GARCH-M(1,1) model provides excellent fit. The square root of the annual conditional variance generated from this model is the estimate of industry-specific uncertainty, capturing the uncertainty that is not predictable about any trend that might exist in each period of the series. Independent variables were computed for each year and lagged 1 year.
time_window: annual series 1947-2000; value lagged 1 year relative to entry

description: A firm may report up to 10 individual business segments, each with up to two primary segment SIC codes and four product SIC codes, so a firm may report up to 60 SIC codes in a year. Entry was detected where a firm listed a primary segment SIC code that did not match any of the possible 60 SIC codes reported by the firm in each of the 2 previous years, and the firm was in Compustat II in the prior year; that new primary segment SIC code was coded as an entry. All SIC codes were recoded from the 4-digit to the 3-digit level. 19,354 instances of entry were identified between 1981 and 1999, and in some instances firms have multiple entries in a given year.

Following precedent, irreversibility is approximated by the intangibility of the assets in which a firm invests, because intangible assets may have very little use outside their current application. Intangible is measured for each industry by the median value of the ratio of intangible assets to total assets for all firms in that industry in the previous year.

A second measure of irreversibility rests on the idea that assets with high salvage value can support high debt, so investments required to enter high-leverage industries should be more reversible. Inverse Leverage is computed by taking, for all firms competing in an industry, the median value of one minus the ratio of long-term debt to total book value of assets.

Industries with higher average market-to-book ratios should generally have more valuable growth options, since firms with a high market-to-book ratio are associated with a higher proportion of unexercised growth opportunities. Market-to-Book is the median industry market-to-book ratio, intended to capture expected future industry growth opportunities.

Growth is intended to capture expectations about the future growth rate of the industry, since firms targeting higher growth industries should have more valuable growth options. The GARCH model used to produce the uncertainty measure also produces an estimate of the predicted value of industry GDP for each year and industry; Growth is computed as the predicted value of industry GDP for the year that entry occurred, less the actual value of industry GDP in the previous year, all divided by the actual value of industry GDP in the previous year.
time_window: predicted year of entry relative to prior-year actual GDP

description: Preemption is a way in which firms can secure competitive advantages when the industry can only support a limited number of players, so target industries defined by larger scale economies should be stronger candidates for early entry. An estimate of each industry's minimum efficient scale (MES) was constructed as the median value of assets for all business segments that compete in each industry. Because it is MES relative to total industry size that influences the advantages of early entry, Scale Advantages is the estimated MES divided by total industry assets.
Past-Prod corresponds to the percentage of change in firm production over the last 2 years. It is the measure used for past variation of internal performance indicators (Hypothesis 1).

The difference between each firm's industry growth estimate (IGE) and the actual 1997 industry growth rate, which measures the forecast bias (i.e., the direction of the error). Firm estimates come from the Bank of France survey and the actual 1997 growth rates for the 36 industries from national statistics. The standardized value of this difference was used as a dependent variable.
The absolute value of straight errors, which measures the magnitude of the error (i.e., forecasting accuracy). The standardized value of this variable was used to test the hypotheses.
The difference between a firm's R&D expenditures expressed as a percentage of total sales and the calculated average percentage of R&D expenditures at the industry level (NACE 4-digit).

A weighted average of a firm's perceived strengths on identified industry key success factors, calculated as the ratio between the sum of the respondent's grades and the best grade possible, i.e., 5. The variable ranges from 0 to 1 and equals 1 when responses on the relative strength of the firm vs. its competitors are maximum and coincide with the industry key success factors identified by the firm.

The difference between the expenditures a firm devoted to gathering market information (expressed as a percentage of sales) and its competitors' expenditures, captured as the industry average at the NACE 4-digit level.

The difference between a firm's investments in education and training (expressed as a percentage of overall salary expenses) and the average expenditure made by other firms in the same industry at the NACE 4-digit level.

Organizational illusion of control is manifested by two variables: relative investment in dynamic resources (firm R&D expenditures as a percent of sales minus the NACE 4-digit industry average) and self-perception (weighted average of the firm's perceived strengths on the industry's key success factors, from 0 to 1). Both enter the models as separate predictors.

Organizational attention is measured by relative investments in external and internal information: firm marketing expenditures (percent of sales) minus the NACE 4-digit industry average (Rel-Market-Info), and firm education and training expenditures (percent of salary expenses) minus the industry average (Rel-Educ-Invst).

variable_name: Number of female directors on a board
description: The count of women serving on each company's board, taken from the ISS data for 2013 and from the RiskMetrics and ISS data for 2002 to 2013. The authors compare the actual distribution of boards with zero, one, two and so on female directors with the mean distribution produced by 10,000 simulations in which existing directors were randomly reassigned to existing board seats, holding the number of boards, the size of each board and the number of seats each director held fixed.

The number of media mentions of each S&P 1500 company in 2012 found in a LexisNexis search (mean media mentions of a company of 307), used as a proxy for visibility. Companies were ordered by mentions and grouped into deciles of 144 companies, and the logarithm of the average number of media mentions in a decile predicted the absolute difference between the observed and expected number of companies with exactly two women on their boards in 2013.

variable_name: Indicator for Two or More Women on Board
description: An indicator for whether the board already included at least two women when a new member was added, used as the primary predictor of a discontinuity in the likelihood of adding a woman. The number of women currently on the board entered separately as a control for increasing or decreasing marginal value of female directors.
scale: binary (1 = board already included at least two women)

description: The centered logarithm of the number of LexisNexis media mentions a company received in year t-1, gathered for each year starting in 2004, used to test whether more visible companies show larger discontinuities at the descriptive social norm. The logarithm was used rather than the raw number of media mentions because the distribution of media mentions is highly skewed.

variable_name: Original board has two or more women
description: An indicator for whether the hypothetical board participants saw included at least two female members; participants were randomly assigned to boards containing zero, one, two or three women. The number of women currently on the board was also included as a control in the regression predicting the choice of the female candidate.
time_window: at the time of the decision

description: Whether the participant chose the female candidate for the open board seat out of three candidates all described as qualified; which candidate had a female name (Jill Davis) and which qualification each name carried were randomized. The dependent variable of interest was the fraction of participants in each condition who chose a female candidate.

Participants saw images of five other seven-person panels: in the surpassed social norm condition four panels had one woman and one had no women (an average of 0.8 women), while in the unmet social norm condition four panels had three women and one had two (an average of 2.8 women). The participant's own panel already included two women.

Participants randomly assigned to the unscrutinized condition were told the review process was 'blind:' the names and photos of the panelists would not be submitted for evaluation. Participants randomly assigned to the scrutinized condition saw no such statement.

Participants rated their preference between the two candidates for the final panelist on a scale from 1 to 7, where 1 was labelled 'Strongly prefer Candidate A' and 7 was labelled 'Strongly prefer Candidate B.' The female candidate had 10 years of industry experience and a speaker rating of 4.6 and the male candidate had 12 years and a rating of 4.8; which candidate was presented first as Candidate A was randomized.

Participants randomly assigned to the surpassed social norm condition were told competitive intelligence suggested the other panel submissions would have 1.25 women on average; participants in the unmet social norm condition were told the other panel submissions would have 2.75 women on average.

As in Study 2A, participants in the unscrutinized condition were told the review process was blind, so the names and photos of the panelists would not be submitted for evaluation, while participants in the scrutinized condition saw no such statement.

Participants were offered a choice among three candidates for their final panelist. The female candidate had 10 years of industry experience, a speaker rating of 4.6, and cost $0.15 to select; the two male candidates had similar qualifications (11 or 12 years of experience; speaker ratings of 4.5 or 4.8) and cost $0.10 and $0.11. All participants were initially allocated a $0.25 bonus from which the cost of the selected panelist was deducted.

Participants randomly assigned to the surpassed social norm condition were told that other teams of their size included an average of 0.25 black people; participants in the unmet social norm condition were told that other teams of their size included an average of 1.75 black people.

Participants were randomly assigned to learn either that their team was 'not very important' in the company so there was a low probability that the HR department would review the composition of their team (low visibility), or that their team was 'very important' so there was a high probability that HR would review it (high visibility).

Participants chose between a black male candidate, who would come with a bonus of $0.03 if chosen, and a white male candidate, who would come with a bonus of $0.10; the incentives were set to place some cost on increasing diversity. Participants were told they would keep the bonus associated with the candidate they chose unless the HR department reviewed their team and chose to penalize it for a lack of racial diversity.

The number of alliance ties that a firm had with members of a focal alliance at time t - 1. All independent variables were lagged one year. Alliance ties are the stronger form of prior tie, involving direct social interaction and joint problem solving.

The number of arm's-length ties that the firm had with members of the focal alliance at time t - 1. Arm's-length ties are slot purchases or swaps that imply a transaction but not joint operation of a route, and they can be terminated more easily than alliance ties.

The absolute difference of the focal firm's fleet average ship age from that of the mean of the focal alliance's partners. Compatibility was assessed on three ship characteristics: age, maximum speed, and capacity, comparing the fleet average of the firm with those of the alliance partners.

The absolute difference of the focal firm's fleet average maximum ship speed (in knots) from that of the mean of the focal alliance's partners. Ships of unequal speed cause friction because the slowest ship determines the maximum speed of a route and fast ships are more expensive to operate.

The absolute difference of the focal firm's fleet average ship capacity (in TEUs) from that of the mean of the focal alliance's partners. Unequal ship sizes create friction because customers plan shipments with respect to the smallest ship, leaving larger ships underutilized.

The logarithm of the number of closed triads (i.e., common third-party ties) involving a focal firm and its alliance partners. Closed triads are developed either through closure of three dyadic alliances or through a single alliance containing three or more firms.

The difference between a firm's network constraint and the average constraint of its partners in a focal alliance. A more constrained firm is less powerful because it is more dependent on and controlled by its partners. Network constraint is measured with the Burt (1992) formula, in which pij, piq and pqj are the proportional strengths of i's relationship with j, with i's other contacts q, and of q's relationship with j; the payload does not render this formula, so the equation itself cannot be reproduced here. The number of alliances between two firms is used as the strength measure.

The proportional multimarket contact measure suggested by Baum and Korn (1996), calculated among firms participating in the market served by a focal alliance. It captures the potential for strategic interactions among all firms in a market as the average proportion of markets each focal firm has that is also occupied by each of its competitors. Market areas were defined as corresponding to trade routes.

Each firm's market overlap with other firms in the industry, regardless of whether they were members of the same alliance. Market overlap equals the sum of the firm density of the markets in which a firm participates, so firms operating in higher-density markets face stronger competition.

The logarithm of the months since an alliance was established, with new alliances set to have a tenure of six months. Time-varying effects were incorporated through interactions of the cohesion variables with this logarithm of tenure.

Coded 1 when a given member of an alliance operating a route at time t was no longer part of the alliance operating the route at time t + 1 and as 0 otherwise. The operationalization, which requires that the route still operated in the year after initial observation, distinguishes member withdrawal from route failure (alliance collapse).

Three-item self-report creative performance scale developed by Shalley, Gilson, and Blum (2009), designed to be suitable for a sample of employees in diverse occupations. The scale includes items such as 'The work I produce is creative' and 'The work I produce is novel' (alpha = .87). Self-reports were used because the sample was drawn from varied occupations across 34 highly dissimilar organizations. Reported by employees in the survey conducted 12 months after the initial survey.
scale: five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree)
time_window: time 2, 12 months after the initial survey

description: Five-item scale developed by Obstfeld (2005) that asked employees to evaluate their TI orientation (alpha = .84). Sample items include 'I introduce two people when I think they might benefit from becoming acquainted' and 'I will try to describe an issue in a way that will appeal to a diverse set of interests'. Collected in the initial survey of employees.
scale: five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree)

description: Five-item scale developed by Miller, Burke, and Glick (1998), used following Souitaris and Maestro (2010), asking managers to report agreement or disagreement with statements about how the firm decides courses of action (alpha = .81). It is a firm-level (level 2) construct, with assessments provided by managers aggregated at the firm level (on average, 5.6 managers per firm).
scale: five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree)

description: Three-item scale developed by Souitaris and Maestro (2010); one of the three original items was omitted because of its low item-to-total correlation (0.22) and because its inclusion would have produced inadequate reliability, leaving two items (alpha = .81). The two items are 'In our firm, we believe in making quick strategic decisions' and 'Please check the extent (1 being 'not at all' to 5 being 'to a great extent') to which your company emphasizes speed when planning or thinking about strategies'. Managers' ratings were aggregated at the firm level.
scale: five-point Likert scale (one item anchored 1 = 'not at all' to 5 = 'to a great extent')

description: The key independent variable reflects the extent to which a firm takes the interests of its primary stakeholders into account. It was constructed from Asset 4 items that map the extent to which management implements practices to attend to five categories of stakeholders: employees, customers, suppliers, local communities, and shareholders. Each stakeholder category score was normalized on a 0-1 scale, and stakeholder orientation is the average of the five normalized scores, so that it ranges from lower (the firm is attentive to fewer of its stakeholders) to higher (the firm is attentive to more of its stakeholders).
time_window: lagged one year relative to the dependent variable

description: The dependent variable used to test Hypothesis 1 is the number of divestitures that firms undertake each year. The underlying transactions are all divestitures (selloffs and spinoffs) announced and completed between January 1, 2002, and December 31, 2015 by the firms in the baseline sample, as recorded in SDC Platinum.

To distinguish between the two modes of divestiture, the authors define the number of spinoffs (Nspinoffs) and the number of selloffs (Nselloffs), using the 'spinoff' flag in SDC Platinum. These two counts are used as dependent variables in simultaneously estimated OLS regressions whose coefficients on stakeholder orientation are compared.

variable_name: N selloffs of unrelated businesses and N selloffs of related businesses
description: Selloffs are distinguished according to whether the divested business is unrelated or related to the divesting firm. Related businesses are those for which the primary SIC code of the divested business overlaps with that of the divesting firm by at least three digits; separate counts of selloffs of unrelated businesses and selloffs of related businesses are used as dependent variables.

variable_name: N selloffs of distant businesses and N selloffs of proximate businesses
description: Selloffs are distinguished according to whether the divested business is distant from or proximate to the divesting firm's headquarters. Proximate businesses are those for which the distance between the zipcodes of the divested business and the divesting firm's headquarters is less than the median distance in the sample (562 kilometers); separate counts of selloffs of distant businesses and selloffs of proximate businesses are used as dependent variables.

variable_name: N selloffs to alliance partners and N selloffs to nonpartners
description: Selloffs are distinguished according to whether the divested business was sold to an acquirer that is or was an alliance partner of the divesting firm. The authors count selloffs to nonpartners and selloffs to alliance partners, with any alliance relationship assessed within 15 years of any given selloff.
time_window: annual counts, 2002-2015; alliance relationship within 15 years of the selloff

description: Unit entry type is 0 for internal units and 1 for acquired units. Units entering as recombinations are not being tested in this hypothesis. The variable makes the distinction between acquired and internally developed units.
time_window: measured at unit entry into the firm

variable_name: time (in years) until a unit is reconfigured
description: Calculated as the period between when a unit enters a firm (either by internal development, acquisition, or recombination) and when it is reconfigured (recombined, divested, or dissolved). Because the sample is right censored, for units that are never reconfigured the calculation is the period from entry into the firm to 1997. Estimated in an accelerated event time model; the log-normal distribution was chosen based on the Akaike Information Criterion.
time_window: from unit entry into the firm until reconfiguration or 1997

description: Coded 0 for units that kept their original identity throughout their life at the firm, and 1 for units that were recombined with other units. It is the independent variable in the analysis of duration until divestiture. Because unit origin was related to reconfiguration, unit origin is also included as a control in those models.
time_window: lifetime of the unit within the firm

variable_name: time (in years) until a unit is divested or shut down
description: Calculated as the time between entry into the firm and when a unit and its activities are completely extracted from the firm. If a unit is recombined with other units it is not considered to be deleted from the firm, because its resources and activities are still within the firm. Estimated in an accelerated event time model; the log-logistic distribution was chosen based on the Akaike Information Criterion.
time_window: from unit entry into the firm until divestiture or 1997

description: A five-item scale adapted from Rempel and Holmes (1986) and administered to the purchasing manager. The final item pool consists of one item related to predictability, three items related to fairness, and one item that directly assesses interpersonal trust; items measuring the reliability element were eliminated after the assessment for unidimensionality. Items are rated on a seven-point scale anchored by 1 = strongly disagree and 7 = strongly agree.

A five-item scale adapted from Rempel and Holmes (1986), reported by the purchasing manager and by a second respondent in the purchasing organization. Two items reflect the fairness component of trust, one item directly assesses interorganizational trust, and the other two tap the reliability aspect; items measuring predictability were discarded after the assessment for unidimensionality. Items are rated on a seven-point scale anchored by 1 = strongly disagree and 7 = strongly agree.

A four-item scale operationalizing the costs of negotiation. Two items capture the ease and speed of negotiations over sharing the burden of costs when the business unit requests engineering changes, and two items measure the ease and speed of negotiations when the supplier's raw material costs increase. Items are answered on seven-point response scales.

Two items measuring the degree of conflict between the two organizations and the level of conflict between the two boundary-spanning individuals, adapted from Van de Ven and Ferry (1980). Respondents report how often during the past year there were significant disagreements, on a seven-point scale from 1 = never to 7 = very often.

A four-item scale reflecting the degree to which the supplier organization fulfilled the goals of competitive price, timeliness of delivery, high quality supply, and supplier flexibility. Respondents rate the supplier's performance on each goal on a seven-point scale from 1 = very poor to 7 = excellent.

Average pay was measured as the dollar amount specified in response to the question "On average, how much does a typical driver earn per year?" The item was answered by the key respondent for the firm.

The attractiveness of the benefits plan was assessed through three Likert-type agree/disagree items with seven response options. Items included in this and other multi-item scales are shown in Table 1.
Job stability was measured with two Likert-type agree/disagree items with seven response options. The items are listed in Table 1.
Training was measured with one item: "How many hours of formal training does a typical driver receive in a year?" Responses were transformed into logarithms for analysis.
Procedural justice included three Likert-type agree/disagree items with seven response options. The items are listed in Table 1.

Electronic monitoring consisted of three items asking respondents the percentage of trucks in their fleets with "on-board computers," "satellite tracking," and "on-board systems to communicate with dispatchers." The mean of these percentages served as the measure.
Time on the road was measured as the reverse of the number of times drivers were typically routed home each month.
The selection ratio was the number of drivers hired during the past year divided by the number of individuals who had applied for driving jobs in the past year.

A procedure was included in this measure if it had a validity coefficient of at least .25 in a meta-analytic or validity generalization study. This resulted in the inclusion of eight valid selection procedures. For each procedure, respondent companies were given a rating of 1 if they placed at least some weight on the procedure in the selection process and rating of 0 if the procedure was not used. The number of valid selection techniques used by the company was then counted.
Performance appraisal was measured as the number of times per year the company conducted formal performance appraisals for drivers.

Respondents reported measures of driver turnover expressed as percentages of total firm employment. These reports focused on drivers only, excluding other permanent or temporary employees. The driver quit rate, or voluntary turnover, was reported for the previous calendar year.

Respondents reported measures of driver turnover expressed as percentages of total firm employment. These reports focused on drivers only, excluding other permanent or temporary employees. The driver discharge rate, or involuntary turnover, was reported for the previous calendar year.

Staffing systems are indicated by the selection ratio (drivers hired divided by applicants in the past year), the number of valid selection procedures used (those with validity of at least .25) and training hours, entered as separate predictors; selection ratio and selection procedures were also interacted.
scale: ratio; count of valid procedures; hours (log)

variable_name: electronic monitoring and time on the road
description: Employer expectations are indicated by electronic monitoring (mean percentage of trucks with on-board computers, satellite tracking and on-board communication systems) and time on the road (reverse of the number of times drivers were routed home each month), both reported by the firm's HRM manager.

variable_name: pay, benefits, job stability, training, procedural justice
description: Direct HRM investment (average driver pay, benefits attractiveness scale) and indirect HRM investment (job stability scale, hours of formal training, procedural justice scale) were measured as separate survey-based variables and entered together as predictors of voluntary turnover.

Organizational monitoring systems are indicated by performance appraisal (number of formal driver appraisals per year) and electronic monitoring (mean percentage of trucks with on-board computers, satellite tracking and on-board communication systems), entered as separate predictors of discharge rates.

Coded as 1 if the government owned at least a 50 percent stake in the firm and 0 otherwise. The information for this key independent variable was gathered from the Global New Issues database maintained by SDC.

Coded as 1 if the acquisition was completed after the public announcement of a takeover attempt by the foreign firm and 0 otherwise. The information was obtained from the SDC M&As database. Of the 914 deals, 868 deals were completed.

The number of days for a foreign firm to complete an acquisition, calculated as the difference between the date when an acquisition was announced and the date when the acquisition was completed. The information was obtained from the SDC M&As database.
A dummy variable, coded as 1 if the target firm was publicly listed and 0 otherwise. The information for the moderating variables was obtained from the SDC M&As and Alliances databases.

Constructed as the number of R&D alliances a target firm formed in the U.S. during the three years prior to the focal acquisition announcement. The information for the moderating variables was obtained from the SDC M&As and Alliances databases.
time_window: three years prior to the focal acquisition announcement

description: Measured by the number of cross-border alliances a foreign firm formed in the U.S. during the three years prior to the focal acquisition announcement. The information for the moderating variables was obtained from the SDC M&As and Alliances databases.
time_window: three years prior to the focal acquisition announcement

description: Captured by the number of acquisitions a foreign firm completed in the U.S. during the three years prior to the focal acquisition announcement. The information for the moderating variables was obtained from the SDC M&As and Alliances databases.
time_window: three years prior to the focal acquisition announcement

description: Measured as the total number of directors serving simultaneously on the compensation and audit committees scaled by the total number of directors on the compensation committee. It is the focal independent variable of the study, measured for year t and related to compensation in year t + 1.
time_window: year t (compensation measured in year t + 1)

description: Dummy variable describing board contexts where there was no board committee overlap in year t - 1 but there was a board committee overlap in year t, coded 1 = yes and 0 = no. The omitted category is the case where there was no board committee overlap in year t - 1 and in year t.
time_window: change from year t - 1 to year t

description: Dummy variable describing board contexts where there was committee overlap in year t - 1, but no board committee overlap in year t, coded 1 = yes and 0 = no. The omitted category is the case where there was no board committee overlap in year t - 1 and in year t.
time_window: change from year t - 1 to year t

description: Total CEO compensation of the focal firm, measured in logged dollars for year t + 1. Salary and options contributed over 66 percent of executive compensation during the study period. The descriptive mean of total compensation in the sample is $4.683 million.
Salary divided by total compensation, used to assess reliance on behavioral compensation. In the sample, salary is on average 28 percent of total compensation.

Options divided by total compensation, used to assess the reliance on a particular type of outcomes based compensation. The authors focus on this ratio because the popularity of stock options, coupled with boards' limited understanding of option valuation, may have resulted in excessive compensation during the study time period. In the sample, options are on average 36 percent of total compensation.

An accrual-based measure of accounting conservatism computed as income before extra-ordinary items minus cash flows from operations plus depreciation expense, deflated by average total assets. This annual measure is averaged over a three-year period centered on year t and multiplied by negative one, so that positive values indicate greater conservatism. A dummy variable is then created and assigned the value of 1 if the firm is in the lower three quartiles of accounting conservatism, and 0 if the firm is in the highest quartile of accounting conservatism.
time_window: three-year period centered on year t

description: Dummy variable that receives the value of 1 for each firm whose name includes the name of its owner (eponymous ventures) and 0 for all other firms. It is coded with a string-matching algorithm that matches the firm name to the last name of its leading shareholder; the automated process compares both names, assigns a matching score and identifies exact matches. In the estimation sample 23% of firms are eponymous.

EBIT divided by assets. The variable is averaged within the firm over the years 2002-2012 so that the estimation data are cross-sectional. In the estimation sample the average firm has an ROA of 0.042 (median 0.019).

Computed as ln(Sales_t / Sales_{t-1}) and averaged within the firm over the years 2002-2012, giving cross-sectional values. The average firm in the sample has annual sales growth of 0.036 (median 0.016).

The region's absolute number of employees in financial credit institutions, taken from Structural Business Statistics; a credit institution is an undertaking whose business is to receive deposits or other repayable funds from the public and to grant credits for its own account. Firms are matched manually to NUTS level 1 regions using their physical addresses, and the analysis is performed within country with region fixed effects. The measure is entered in logs and interacted with ROA.
scale: number of employees, entered in logs

variable_name: Number of banks in a city (Bank Scope)
description: Number of banks located in the focal firm's city, constructed from Bank Scope bank locations. Higher values indicate greater financial development of the firm's local environment. The measure is interacted with ROA in the regressions.

Straight-line distance in kilometers between the focal firm and the closest matched Bank Scope bank in the same city, obtained by geocoding street addresses with the Google Maps Geocoding API. Higher distance means lower financial development, and the interaction of ROA with distance is accordingly expected to be positive.

Ratio between capital expenditures minus cash flow from operations and capital expenditures, following Rajan and Zingales (1999). It is computed from American Compustat firms, with values averaged over the pre-estimation period 1990-2001, and matched to the focal firm's industry; U.S. industries serve as the benchmark because American firms face the least friction in accessing external finance. Higher values indicate greater reliance on external finance.

Ratio between the net amount of equity issued and capital expenditures, computed from American Compustat firms with values averaged over the pre-estimation period 1990-2001 and matched to the focal firm's industry. It is used as an alternative measure of the industry's reliance on external finance.

For each firm the nearest bank is identified in Bank Scope, and the number of other firms that are closer to that bank than the focal firm is counted; the measure is entered as ln(1 + CloserFirms_i). Higher values mean greater density, that is, lower financier bandwidth in the firm's environment. Density counts all firms within the relevant distance, including out-of-sample firms for which financial or ownership information is unavailable, and the distance from the focal firm to its nearest bank is controlled for in all specifications.

The number of 'patent families' in successful telecom-related U.S. patent applications filed by supplier i in year t. Patent families group patents based on the same invention disclosed by a common inventor and patented in more than one country. Application dates are based on the year of the first patent application within the family.

An indicator variable marking the first introduction of one or more own-brand mobile handsets by supplier i. It takes a value of 0 in every year preceding the year in which supplier i introduces its first own-brand handset and changes to 1 in the year of introduction.
The total number of units of own-brand handsets sold by supplier i in year t. Sales data are available only for a subset of suppliers (34 firms) for the years 2004-2010.
The number of years from the first observation of a supply relationship for supplier i in our data to year t-1; i.e., how long supplier i has been supplying mobile telecom handsets up to year t-1.
The number of customers supplied in each year by supplier i, cumulated to year t-1.
The maximum number of patent families in the telecom-related patent applications of any one of supplier i's customers in year t-1.
The summation to year t-1 of supplier i's customers that are among the top five branded producers in terms of market share in mobile telecom handsets in a given year.
The summation to year t-1 of supplier i's customers that are mobile telecom operators.
A dummy variable equal to 1 if the supplier has successfully applied for one or more telecom-related patents prior to year t.
The count of ODM agreements (design and manufacturing) that a supplier has with customers in each year, cumulated to year t-1.
The count of OEM agreements (manufacturing only) that a supplier has with customers in each year, cumulated to year t-1.

Accumulation of capabilities is proxied by three dependent variables: PATENTS (count of telecom-related US patent families filed by supplier in year t) for technological capabilities, OWN BRAND (indicator for introduction of an own-brand handset) and BRANDED SALES (units of own-brand handsets sold) for marketing capabilities.

Respondents assessed knowledge transfer in six areas; an exploratory factor analysis using principal components extraction and Varimax rotation yielded a four-factor solution. Transfer of managerial capabilities, product and process design expertise, and research and development capabilities captured non-location-specific knowledge transfer in two directions, and N-LSKT to denotes the direction toward the acquired firm. The scale has a reported alpha of 0.79 and was used as the independent variable.

Measured using the sum of four items gauging profitability, market share, sales volume, and new product development. Principal component extraction with Varimax rotation showed a single factor (Eigenvalue = 2.80; explaining 70% of the variance; alpha = 0.86).
Industry-adjusted average return on assets (ROA) during the three years before the deal, following prior research. The text does not name the database from which the ROA figures were taken.

Measured with six survey items gauging the extent to which key functional areas of the acquired firm were integrated with those of the acquirer; reported alpha of 0.90. The individual items are not listed in the text.

A single survey item assessing the extent to which the acquirer made decisions about setting performance goals and competitive strategies of the acquired firm following the M&A. Coded 1 = acquired firm decides, 5 = parent firm decides.
scale: 1 = acquired firm decides; 5 = parent firm decides

description: Measured as the average amount of EPA fines a firm received in the three years prior to the focal spill. The EPA maintains detailed records of financial penalties issued to firms' facilities that violate federal and state environmental regulations, so the dollar amount captures the frequency and number of violations as well as the cumulative magnitude of a firm's environmental errors. To account for skewness the dollar amount was logged after being increased by 1 to address cases of zero fines.
time_window: three years prior to the focal spill

description: Measured as the cumulative number of oil spills the firm had caused since 1985. The variable was calculated as the log of this running total, increased by 1 to address cases of zero spills, in the year prior to the focal oil spill.
time_window: year prior to the focal spill; cumulative since 1985

description: Operationalized as the log of total oil spilled (gallons) recorded by the NOAA. The authors acknowledge the total may not be known for many weeks or months but argue the measure captures the observable characteristics of a spill in its immediate aftermath.

A dichotomous variable coded 1 if a spill received any coverage in Factiva within three months of its occurrence, and 0 otherwise. To search Factiva the authors used multiple synonyms for 'oil spill', together with the spill location, key characteristics, and all possible name variations of the culpable firm, and manually checked all search results.

variable_name: percentage of management positions filled by women
description: During the 1991 interviews, personnel-human resource managers were asked the percentage of management positions held by men at their workplaces in that year, and the authors subtracted this figure from 100. Respondents were instructed to include only employees with regular supervisory responsibilities in the management category, a definition consistent with that used by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. The average percentage of management positions filled by women was 26.6 and the distribution was highly skewed, so the authors transformed the variable to its square root.

variable_name: emphasis on development and promotion procedures
description: A seven-item scale developed from a factor analysis of eight items in the 1991 questionnaire and interview about procedures for the development, reward, and promotion of employees. In a single-factor solution, seven items had loadings of .40 or greater and were combined into one scale whose reliability is .72. One item was not included in the scale. Items were responses to a question about how accurate statements were concerning non-management employees, answered on a five-point scale. Data for these items were not collected in 1988.

variable_name: percentage of nonmanagement positions held by women
description: During the 1991 interviews, 232 personnel-human resource managers were asked the percentage of nonmanagement positions held by men at their workplaces in that year. The authors subtracted this figure from 100 to obtain the percentage of nonmanagement positions held by women. Data for this variable were not collected in 1988.

Using 1991 interview data, the annual average dollar amount of management pay was transformed to its natural logarithm to correct for skewness in the distribution. Data for this variable were not collected in 1988.

variable_name: difficulty in attracting and retaining employees
description: A four-item scale (alpha = .80) developed from a factor analysis of responses to the 1991 questionnaire rating the extent to which personnel-related and other issues made it difficult for an organization to achieve its goals. The scale items concern retaining and attracting nonmanagement employees and retaining and attracting management employees. Items were rated from 1, 'makes things very difficult,' to 5, 'does not make things difficult.' Data for these items were not collected in 1988.
scale: five-point scale (1 = makes things very difficult, 5 = does not make things difficult)

variable_name: percentage of management positions held by nonwhites
description: During the 1991 interviews, respondents provided the percentages of management jobs held by whites and by nonwhites at their workplace in that year. Data for this measure were not collected in 1988.

The authors calculated the rate of annual management vacancies as the sum of the average annual turnover and growth in management positions divided by the number of employees in each company. Respondents reported average annual management turnover during the interviews, and average annual growth in management jobs was calculated by subtracting the number of employees in management positions reported in 1988 from the number reported in 1991 and dividing by the number of years between the interviews. The variable was transformed to its natural logarithm to reduce skewness.

variable_name: percentage of professional or skilled employees
description: During the 1991 interviews, respondents classified employees as belonging to professional-skilled, management, clerical, or unskilled occupational categories. The authors reduced the skewness of the distribution of this variable with a square root transformation. Directly comparable information was not collected during the 1988 interviews.
The authors added three years to the age of each organization obtained in the 1988 interview. The square root of the variable was computed to reduce skewness in its distribution.

This variable was coded 1 for manufacturing work sites, where durable and nondurable manufacturing, mining, forestry, agriculture, and construction were carried out, and 2 for nonmanufacturing sites (services, transportation, and communication). The information was first obtained in the 1988 interview and confirmed during visits to each site in 1991.

Firms were clustered using the k-means algorithm on standardized values of starting salary, mentoring, developmental work experience, office and support services, promotion percentage, and up-or-out strictness. The procedure yielded a two-cluster solution; one group was interpreted as relatively options-based firms and the other as project-based firms.
The average starting salary of associates, determined directly from the NALP data. It was standardized by city for the cluster analysis.

A subscale derived from principal components analysis of ALMAS items, comprising feedback from partners, knowledge about partnership, treatment by partners, training and guidance, and how interesting work was. Responses were on 1-5 Likert-type scales, aggregated within firm.

A subscale derived from principal components analysis, comprising deal-making responsibility, client contact, role in client matters, and appearances before a judge. Responses on 1-5 Likert-type scales, aggregated within firm.
A subscale derived from principal components analysis, comprising office space and support services. Responses on 1-5 Likert-type scales, aggregated within firm.
Calculated as the ratio of the number of promoted associates to the number originally hired into each entering class, using NALP data for five previous entering classes.
Calculated as the ratio of the number of nonpromoted associates leaving a firm to the number of associates actually considered for partnership in each entering class.
Number of attorneys, determined directly from the NALP data.
The ratio of associates to partners, a prior HR strategy indicator.
A stand-alone measure from the ALMAS survey of the number of hours associates are expected to bill, on a Likert-type scale of 1 to 5.
Estimated as a firm's average profits per partner, multiplied (discounted) by the historical chances of making partner, divided by the partnership track.
Determined directly from the NALP data, in years.
Calculated as the ratio of the track's range to its lower bound.
A stand-alone ALMAS survey item assessing associates' intentions to remain with the firm, on a 1-5 Likert-type scale, aggregated within firm.
The rate at which associates leave the firm, computed from NALP data on associates leaving the firm.
Financial performance measure from Am Law 100, calculated as firm revenues divided by the number of lawyers.
Financial performance measure from Am Law 100, calculated as firm profits divided by the number of partners.
The ratio of profits per partner to revenues per lawyer, from Am Law 100 data.

variable_name: starting salary, mentoring, developmental work, office and support, promotion percentage, up-or-out strictness
description: Career mobility practices are measured by six firm-level indicators: average associate starting salary, mentoring, developmental work experience, office and support services, promotion percentage and up-or-out strictness. They were standardized and used to cluster firms into options-based and project-based groups.

variable_name: leverage ratio, target billable hours, firm size, expected partnership value, track length and variability, intentions to stay, turnover
description: Career-related outcomes and prior HR strategy indicators are measured by leverage ratio, target billable hours, firm size, expected value of partnership, partnership track length and variability, associates' intentions to stay and associate turnover, compared across the two clusters of firms.

Measured at the niche level for each product niche in which a company competes, as the ratio of sales in a focal product niche over two consecutive years in a specific country (Sales Growth = Salest/Salest-1). Values greater than 1 indicate sales growth; values less than 1 signal a sales decrease.

Sales growth over two consecutive years of a product niche that is separate from the niche that provides the input for the dependent variable but appears in the same firm portfolio. For every diversified firm the authors create a dyad of dependent-independent variables by linking the sales growth of every niche in which it sells products, excluding paired niche duplications but otherwise exhausting all possible combinations; the assignment of a niche as dependent or independent variable follows a matching algorithm.
Takes a value of 1 if, for two paired product niches matched, the firm uses the same brand, and 0 otherwise. It captures the presence of a scale free resource shared by the paired niches.
Counts the number of niches in the portfolio that use the same brand. The variable varies over time and firms.

Counts the number of niches in a firm portfolio that are not linked by the same brand. In the estimations it is interacted with Paired Niche Sales Growth to indicate whether the extent of non-scale free diversification has a positive or negative impact on the correlation between the sales growth of two niches in a firm portfolio.
Measured at the firm level as the ratio of sales over two consecutive years (Sales Growth = Salest/Salest-1), where sales are those of the firm's product portfolio.

The standard deviation at time t of sales growth across all product niches not linked by the same brand, divided by the number of non-scale free niches to address potential size effects. More redeployment should increase this intrafirm variance, because firms simultaneously invest more in growing sectors and decrease their investments in shrinking ones. The equation specifying the variance is not readable in the text as provided.

The standard deviation at time t of sales growth across all product niches linked by the same brand, divided by the number of scale free niches to address potential size effects. It is interacted with Scale Free Value in the firm-level regressions.

To measure brand value, the authors rely on their regressions from Analysis 1, extracting the fixed effect component estimated for each brand with the dummy, which represents the impact of a single brand on the sales growth in a focal niche-firm-country-year observation, and then averaging this component at the firm-country-year level. The measure varies across years, so that any dynamic movement of a new brand extension of a company across niches is taken into account.

Each chief planning officer was asked to give the percentage of time spent on four categories: corporate-level planning (planning re mergers, divestments and reorganizations), business-level planning (planning re existing operations), other planning activities, and nonplanning activities. The percent of time spent in each category indicates the relative importance of each activity; the percent allocated to corporate-level planning served as the dependent variable in the model. In the 16 firms where two CPOs were designated, only the questionnaire from the CPO who devoted the greatest percentage of time to corporate planning was used.

Each chief planning officer was asked to give the percentage of time spent on four categories of activity, one of which is business-level planning (planning re existing operations). The percent of time spent on business-level planning indicates the relative importance of that activity and was entered as the second independent variable in the model.

SR is Wrigley's specialization ratio, the percentage of total revenues accounted for by a firm's major or core business. The adjusted ratio (1 - SR) was used to simplify interpretation, so that the lower the number the less diversified the firm.
(N) represents the number of different lines of business for each firm. It was taken from the Value Line Investment Survey, 1977, or from the firm's annual report.

Log (N) uses the same definition of the number of different lines of business (N), except that the logarithmic value of (N) gives greater weight to initial diversification moves. The authors' premise was that initial decisions toward diversity would impact the corporate-level planning effort more than later diversification decisions, so that diversification moves 1, 2 or 3 are more influential than the nth decision to diversify.

A measure designed to combine Wrigley's (1 - SR) and (N) into a single variable: it squares the percentage of revenues from a firm's major lines of business and distributes the remaining revenues equally between the remaining number of lines of business. In the example given, a firm with four divisions and 70 per cent of total revenues from its major division gets a value of 0.48.

Respondents were asked to indicate on a seven-point scale the extent to which they agreed with statements about the discrepancy between their organization's position in the rankings and their own self-assessment of their school's positional status in the industry, first for Business Week's rankings and then for US News & World Report's. Two statements were used for each of the two rankings, one of which was reverse-coded, giving four items that factor analysis combined into a single factor; the four items were averaged into a score. Individual responses were aggregated to the school level after tests supporting aggregation.

Respondents were asked to indicate the extent to which they agreed with five statements about the validity of ranking criteria, comparison groups, stakeholders surveyed, and methods, first for Business Week's ranking and then for US News & World Report's. Factor analysis extracted a single factor with the items for the two rankings loading together, and the ten items were averaged to obtain a score. Responses were aggregated to the school level.

variable_name: Perceived strategic impact of the rankings
description: Respondents were asked to rate the impact of the rankings on each of eight listed items on a scale from 1 (no impact at all) to 7 (very high impact). Responses to the eight items were averaged to obtain a score for perceived strategic impact, and individual responses were aggregated to the school level.
scale: 1 = no impact at all; 7 = very high impact

description: Measured with a six-item scale used in prior research; respondents were asked to indicate on a seven-point scale their level of agreement with statements about the school's history, pride in its goals and mission, its unique place among graduate business schools, its goals and objectives, administrators' knowledge of its history, and enthusiasm in talking about the school. One item was reverse-coded. Responses were aggregated to the school level.

Measured using a five-item scale capturing the extent to which the school's identity was responsive to recruiters and students; respondents indicated on a seven-point scale the extent to which they agreed with statements describing their school. One item was reverse-coded, and responses on the five items were averaged to obtain a score. Responses were aggregated to the school level.

A list of changes that schools could undertake to their MBA program was generated based on telephone interviews, changes described in the press, and prior research, and was content-validated by administrators. Each change was rated by three administrators on a three-point scale of magnitude, and the ratings for magnitude were averaged for each change. For each potential change, respondents indicated whether or not their school had made the change during the study period; the variable was computed as the sum of all changes undertaken by the school, with each change weighted by its rating for magnitude of change.

A dummy variable that assumed a value of 1 if the specialty trade activity j in the project n was internalized by the building contractor and zero otherwise. For a single project, there were eight dummy variables, one for each specialty trade activity.
scale: 1 = internalized by the contractor; 0 = external subcontractor
level: specialty trade activity within a project

description: A composite measure of temporal specificity formed by multiplying three variables representing switching costs, the number of change orders, and the cost of delay. Switching costs are approximated by the market concentration of subcontractors of the various construction activities for each project type in each geographical region using the Herfindahl-Hirschmann Index; the likelihood of change orders is a dummy that takes the value of 1 if the project is not a housing complex, a residential building, or an office building, and 0 otherwise; the cost of delay is an ordinal measure of the activity's temporal position in the project.
level: specialty trade activity within a project, by region and project type

description: Measured by multiplying the number of Independent Reviewers of Construction Work (IRCWs) in a particular region and the average IRCW quality for that region, using June 2008 data from the centralized registry of IRCWs provided by the Chilean Ministry of Housing. The government determines the quality of the IRCW by classifying them according to a three-category scale. A project executed in a region with few and inexperienced IRCWs is more likely to feature vertical integration of its specialty trade activities.

A dummy variable that assumes a value of 1 for projects that started after August 2006, and zero otherwise, coinciding with the legislature approving the new subcontracting law on September 5, 2006. The change in legislation is treated as exogenous to individual firms because it was applied to all firms, industries, and geographical regions in the economy.

The differential in capabilities between the contractor and the subcontractors for each specialty trade activity is approximated by their relative accumulated outputs. The authors compiled the list of accumulated square meters built by subcontractors (for the entire period) for each of the eight trade activities and for each geographic region, and then computed a percentile for each contractor corresponding to the ranking that the accumulated square meters built by that contractor (for the entire period) would have if placed within each list. Thus, a higher percentile is associated with greater contractor capabilities in trade 'x' in region 'y' compared with the capabilities of the available subcontractors.

Measured by the period between the cartel's formation date and its termination date, sourced from the Official Journal of the European Commission. This period was split into multiple annual spells, resulting in 195 cartel-year observations. In the survival model, the dependent variable was the hazard rate of cartel termination, which combines both the likelihood of and the timing of a cartel termination. A positive coefficient means that the likelihood that the cartel will be terminated is increased, and therefore the probability of survival is reduced.

An entropy index of the firms' ages in a cartel, computed as the sum of pk times the natural log of pk, where pk represents the proportion of firms in the different age categories. The age of the firm was assessed as the number of years a firm has been in business. The age intervals used were [1-5], [6-10], [11-15] ... [46-50], and [51 and more]. Minimum variety occurs when all members belong to the same category and maximum variety when each member originates from a unique category.

The mean Euclidean distance between firms within a cartel, computed from the uncertainty avoidance values of the firms' countries. The mean Euclidean distance of one member i from all other members j is the root mean squared distance between each of those i, j pairs, where Si and Sj represent the uncertainty avoidance value for firms i and j and n is the number of firms in a cartel. Uncertainty avoidance values are the cultural values scores from the GLOBE study.

A Gini coefficient of the firms' size within a cartel, where the size of a firm is measured through the firm's total assets. The power disparity reflects both the distances between firms and the dominance of those of a larger size. In the numerator, Di and Dj represent the firms' size values for firms i and j, with D mean the mean firm size value and n the number of firms in a cartel.

The proportion of personnel in a CVC unit who had prior experience in independent venture capital (IVC) firms. IVC experience was coded person by person from job titles and employers in the reconstructed job histories, and annual panels of the proportion were created using CVC job start and end dates.
time_window: annual panels using CVC job start and end dates

description: The proportion of CVC personnel who were internal hires, that is, whose job immediately preceding their first CVC job was in the adopting firm. Annual proportions were created using the CVC job start and end dates for the managers.
time_window: annual panels using CVC job start and end dates

description: The proportion of CVC personnel who have engineering work experience or an engineering degree. Annual proportions were created using the CVC job start and end dates for the managers.
time_window: annual panels using CVC job start and end dates

description: The proportion of start-ups in a CVC unit's portfolio that resulted in an initial public offering or an acquisition by a firm other than the parent of the focal CVC unit. For each CVC unit and year the measure cumulates all IPOs and acquisitions and expresses this sum as a fraction of the cumulated entrepreneurial start-ups in the portfolio. Because traditional venture capital practices are financially oriented, a high fraction implies less modification of the original practice.
time_window: from the date of establishment of the unit up until 2008

description: The cumulated number of entrepreneurial start-ups acquired by the parent firm of a focal CVC unit as a proportion of all entrepreneurial start-ups in the CVC unit's portfolio since the unit's establishment. A higher fraction of start-ups acquired by the parent firm indicates divergence from the traditional financial goal orientation of independent venture capital firms.
time_window: from the date of establishment of the unit up until 2008

description: The number of investments in a CVC unit's portfolio classified by VentureXpert as 'seed' or 'early stage' expressed as a proportion of all start-ups in the portfolio. Early-stage investing is the standard IVC operational strategy, so a high proportion indicates less modification of the practice.
time_window: from the date of establishment of the unit up until 2008

description: A Herfindahl-Hirschman index of concentration of the CVC unit's investments across industry sectors, where the industry sector of each start-up is identified with the Venture Economics Industry Classification (VEIC) scheme. The index is an inverse measure of diversification and is recoded as (1 - HHI) so that higher values indicate a broader range of industry sectors invested in.
time_window: from the date of establishment of the unit up until 2008

description: A single 10-item scale developed for this study (Appendix A), consistent with Vogus and Sutcliffe (2007) and based on the five mindful processes of Weick et al. (1999). Respondents were asked to what extent the statements best represent their organization's use of HIS during the last year, with items covering preoccupation with failure, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience, reluctance to simplify interpretations, and deference to expertise. Items are aggregated into a latent construct in the structural equation model.
time_window: during the last year (survey administered April-June 2012)

description: A five-item construct on the degree to which providers adhere to established practices from hospital admittance through discharge, including how patient care and interactions should occur within and across units (Appendix A). Respondents rated their organization's efforts to meet standardized care requirements during the last year; specification refers to establishing the precise content, timing, and/or sequence of work practices. Items are aggregated into a latent construct in the structural equation model.
time_window: during the last year (survey administered April-June 2012)

description: A weighted aggregate of CMS 2013 Hospital Compare process measures that have specific time requirements, termed 'Timely Effective Care' in the CMS 2013 Hospital Compare database. For each care quality measure the proportion of patients who received the care in relation to all eligible patients who should have received it is computed, and the measures are combined into a hospital-level weighted aggregate. A logit transformation was performed on the weighted average prior to the analyses.
scale: proportion of eligible patients receiving the care (logit-transformed)

description: A weighted aggregate of CMS 2013 Hospital Compare process measures that do not have specific timing requirements. For each care quality measure the proportion of patients who received the care in relation to all eligible patients who should have received it is computed, and the measures are combined into a hospital-level weighted aggregate. A logit transformation was performed on the weighted average prior to the analyses.
scale: proportion of eligible patients receiving the care (logit-transformed)

description: Hospital-level IT adoption calculated from the 2009 HIMSS Analytics Database as the proportion of 87 types of live and operational technologies adopted by the hospital, covering categories such as cardiology and PACS, electronic medical record, laboratory, nursing, pharmacy, radiology and PACS, and revenue cycle management. Hospitals are designated as having low or high IT adoption in relation to the median proportion of IT adoption in the sample (57/87 or 0.66); 128 hospitals fall in the low group and 134 in the high group.

The firm's donation expenses divided by its total sales. The measure is adjusted for industry-specific trends by subtracting from a firm's donations-to-sales the median donations-to-sales of the firm's industry in the given year, with industries defined by the two-digit industry code of the China Securities Regulatory Commission. Donation data were obtained by combining three databases that collect data from the disclosure documents Chinese firms send to regulators.

The number of a firm's Chinese directors who have foreign experience divided by the total number of directors. A Chinese director has foreign experience if he or she has studied or worked outside mainland China; the biographies of directors were manually coded.

The fraction of returnees on the board who came back from high-donation countries, calculated at the firm-year level. High-donation countries are those foreign countries with World Giving Index scores above the median of all sample countries; directors with experience in multiple countries were associated with the average WGI scores of those countries.
