The fraction of returnees on the board who came back from low-donation countries, i.e., countries with World Giving Index scores equal to or below the median of all sample countries. Returnees with experience in a country whose WGI score was missing were assigned to this category.
The fraction of directors who are foreign nationals and come from high-donation countries, defined as countries with World Giving Index scores above the median of all sample countries.
The fraction of directors who are foreign nationals and come from low-donation countries, defined as countries with World Giving Index scores equal to or below the median of all sample countries.

variable_name: average overseas duration of returnee directors from high-donation countries
description: The average length of time spent abroad for returnee directors from high-donation countries, computed for firms with such directors and coded zero for firms without such directors.

variable_name: returnee directors from high-donation countries and on multiple boards
description: The number of interlocked returnee directors from high-donation countries divided by the total number of board members. Returnee directors from high-donation countries are categorized into those who serve on multiple boards in a given year, who are more embedded in the business network of the home institution, and those who serve on a single board.

The number of local directors who have political titles divided by the total number of directors. Political titles were coded from directors' biographies and include being a member of the National People's Congress, a member of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, or a Government Counselor appointed by the local government.

Per capita GDP of each province, taken from the CSMAR database, used to measure provincial-level economic development and interacted with returnee directors from high-donation countries. Lower values indicate less economic development and hence a greater field-level need for solutions.

An indicator variable coded one after 2008 and zero otherwise, accounting for the institutionalization of CSR practices in China after 2008, interacted with returnee directors from high-donation countries.

The Compensation level of the strategy each participant selected at the end of the training rounds as the one that would maximize long-term profits. Compensation could be set between $600 and $6,000 per month in increments of $200. Quality of learning is assessed by how close this choice is to the HR peak (c = $5,000/month), while adoption of inferior strategies is reflected in selections closer to the LR peak (c = $1,400/month).

The Work Structure value of the strategy each participant selected at the end of the training rounds as the long-term profit-maximizing choice. Work Structure ranges from specific tasks (zero) to broad tasks (one) and could be set in increments of 0.1. Quality of learning is assessed by how close this choice is to the HR peak (w = 1), while selections closer to the LR peak (w = 0) reflect inferior strategies.

Binary variable recording whether the final adopted strategy is in the basin of attraction of the LR strategy (coded as tL = 1) or the HR strategy (tL = 0). The two basins of attraction are demarcated by the dashed line through the saddle point at c = $2,000/month and w = 0.6. The variable provides an aggregate measure of bias in learning.

Expected profits from the final adopted strategy, PL = f(cL, wL), where f gives steady-state expected monthly profit of the simulated firm as a function of the two managerial decisions. Used as the measure of performance attained from learning; strategies in the vicinity of the LR and HR peaks can have equivalent expected performance despite very different Work Structure and Compensation.

variable_name: Variance of adopted strategies and performance across experimental conditions
description: Heterogeneity is quantified as the variance of the final adopted Work Structure, final adopted Compensation, and expected profits across participants, and the robust Levene test is used to assess whether the variance in these outcomes differs across the experimental conditions.

Breadth of search, measured as the standard deviations of Compensation and Work Structure over the 96 training periods; the Z-scores of these two components are added together for an overall measure of strategy coverage.
The mean number of evaluation periods (in quarters) that decision makers stay with each strategy to see its implications before making any changes.
The length of exploration segments, measured as the average normalized Euclidian distance traveled in each exploratory move during the training rounds.

The Compensation level of the strategy each manager selected at the end of the training rounds as the one that would maximize long-term profits. Compensation could be set between $600 and $6,000 per month in increments of $200. Quality of learning is assessed by how close this choice is to the HR peak (c = $5,000/month), with selections closer to the LR peak (c = $1,400/month) reflecting inferior strategies.

The Work Structure value of the strategy each manager selected at the end of the training rounds as the long-term profit-maximizing choice. Work Structure ranges from specific tasks (zero) to broad tasks (one) and could be set in increments of 0.1. Quality of learning is assessed by how close this choice is to the HR peak (w = 1), with selections closer to the LR peak (w = 0) reflecting inferior strategies.

Binary variable recording whether the final adopted strategy is in the basin of attraction of the LR strategy (coded as tL = 1) or the HR strategy (tL = 0). The two basins of attraction are demarcated by the dashed line through the saddle point at c = $2,000/month and w = 0.6. The variable provides an aggregate measure of bias in learning.

Expected profits from the final adopted strategy, PL = f(cL, wL), where f gives steady-state expected monthly profit of the simulated firm as a function of the two managerial decisions. Used as the measure of performance attained from learning.

variable_name: Variance of adopted strategies and performance across experimental conditions
description: Heterogeneity is quantified as the variance of the final adopted Work Structure, final adopted Compensation, and expected profits across participants, and the robust Levene test is used to assess whether the variance in these outcomes differs across the experimental conditions.

Breadth of search, measured as the standard deviations of Compensation and Work Structure over the 96 training periods; the Z-scores of these two components are added together for an overall measure of strategy coverage.
The mean number of evaluation periods (in quarters) that decision makers stay with each strategy to see its implications before making any changes.
The length of exploration segments, measured as the average normalized Euclidian distance traveled in each exploratory move during the training rounds.

Experimental manipulation with two levels: in the short delay condition the simulated firm's dynamics unfold four times as fast as in the long delay condition, which takes four times longer to reach steady-state performance after a change in Work Structure or Compensation.

Experimental manipulation of outcome uncertainty: a first-order autocorrelated, normally distributed noise term with standard deviation of 10% (noisy) or 20% (very noisy) of demand level was added to the demand function, versus no noise in the deterministic condition. Study 2 used only deterministic and very noisy conditions.

Partners were categorized according to whether their position was comparable to that of GE. The Directory of Multinationals, which lists the 250 largest multinational companies, was used to identify firms operating on a comparable scale; firms that were not listed were assumed not to be in the same 'league' as GE and hence not to pose a short-term competitive threat. For the logistic regression, the size of the partner was coded 1 for large global partners and 0 for small regional partners.

Each joint venture was categorized along two dimensions of scope: whether it was intended to serve global versus regional markets and whether it was designed to cover a broad versus narrow range of value-chain activities. Geographic scope was established by searching the agreement for references to a particular region; the agreement was regional if explicitly confined to one or two well defined markets such as Europe or South East Asia. Scope of activities was determined by references to particular types of value-chain activities; agreements were narrow if restricted to one or two specific activities such as R&D or marketing. For the logistic regression, a scope variable was coded 1 for alliances that were both broad and global and 0 for all other possible combinations.

The interaction between the partner-size dummy and the scope dummy, which identifies an alliance that is both broad in scope and formed with a large global partner, the situation the authors presume represents GE going against its own dominant logic.

variable_name: early success or failure of the alliance
description: Each joint venture was examined to determine whether it successfully made the transition from agreement to implementation. Of the 70 joint ventures that GE attempted, 17 were terminated within three years of the time they were first announced.

Dummy coded 1 if the firm appeared among the top 25 firms on either Fortune's 'Most Admired Companies' list or the Wall Street Journal/Harris Interactive 'Corporate Reputation' list in a given year, 0 otherwise. Fortune only listed the top 10 firms in an industry between 1997 and 1998 and only the top 20 firms between 1999 and 2005, and 22 of the 25 firms in Fortune's 1999-2005 top 10/top 20 list were also named in the WSJ/Harris top 25, which the authors take as validating the decision to combine the lists. The measure yielded 357 high-reputation firm-year observations.
time_window: annual, measured in a given year

description: Dummy coded 1 if the firm was in the top quartile for both media visibility and positive affective content in a given year, 0 otherwise. Media visibility was the total number of articles published about the firm each year in BusinessWeek, obtained from Lexis-Nexis, with top-quartile firms coded 1; their articles avoided false positives, tables of contents, firm listings, and stock reports. The affective component was measured by analyzing the positive and negative affective language of each article with the Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) program; an article was coded positive if positive affective content was at least 60 percent of total affective content and negative if 60 percent or more was negative. Overall affective resonance used the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance (P positive articles, N negative articles, V total articles), converted to a scale from -100 to 100 with 0 neutral, and firms in the top quartile of positive affective content were coded 1.
time_window: annual, measured in a given year

description: Dummy coded 1 if a firm experienced a positive material earnings surprise, 0 otherwise; because of the longitudinal, repeated-measures design firms could surprise more than once and could generate either type of surprise. Surprises were computed as the percentage difference between a year-end consensus estimate, based on the mean of analysts' last forecasts of firms' annual earnings, and firms' reported earnings. Material surprises were defined as the top and bottom quartiles of positive and negative surprises in a given industry in a given year, identified using the initial universe of Compustat firms in the same two-digit SIC industry segments for which earnings estimates were available rather than only the matched sample.

Dummy coded 1 if a firm experienced a material negative earnings surprise, 0 otherwise; firms could surprise more than once and could generate either type of surprise. Surprises were computed as the percentage difference between a year-end consensus estimate, based on the mean of analysts' last forecasts of firms' annual earnings, and firms' reported earnings. Material surprises were defined as the top and bottom quartiles of positive and negative surprises in a given industry in a given year, identified using the initial universe of Compustat firms in the same two-digit SIC industry segments for which earnings estimates were available rather than only the matched sample.

Cumulative abnormal adjusted return over the three-day (-1, +1) window surrounding the earnings surprise announcement for firms announcing a positive material earnings surprise. CARs are the sum of daily abnormal adjusted returns generated from a market model estimated over a period between 255 and 46 trading days prior to the earnings announcement, with the CRSP value-weighted index as the market return; the paper's regression equations were not readable in the provided text, so the exact formula cannot be quoted. CARs were calculated using EVENTUS, a program provided by Wharton Research Data Services, with the 'autodate-yes' command so that a nontrading date was replaced by the first subsequent business day. The measure is reported in percentage terms and compared across firm categories using paired t-tests of unequal variances.
time_window: three-day window (-1, +1) around the announcement; estimation period 255 to 46 trading days prior

description: Cumulative abnormal adjusted return over the three-day (-1, +1) window surrounding the earnings surprise announcement for firms announcing a material negative earnings surprise. CARs are the sum of daily abnormal adjusted returns generated from a market model estimated over a period between 255 and 46 trading days prior to the earnings announcement, with the CRSP value-weighted index as the market return; the paper's regression equations were not readable in the provided text, so the exact formula cannot be quoted. CARs were calculated using EVENTUS, a program provided by Wharton Research Data Services, with the 'autodate-yes' command so that a nontrading date was replaced by the first subsequent business day. The measure is reported in percentage terms and compared across firm categories using paired t-tests of unequal variances.
time_window: three-day window (-1, +1) around the announcement; estimation period 255 to 46 trading days prior

description: A nine-item team-level measure capturing three dimensions of behavioral integration: collaborative behavior (three items rated from 1 'strongly disagree' to 5 'strongly agree'), information exchange (three items rated from 1 'low effectiveness' to 5 'high effectiveness'), and joint decision making (three items rated as agreement). Respondents assessed TMT behavior over the past two years. Items were adapted from Mooney's behavioral integration scale, Eby and Dobbins's leader-member exchange scale, and Seers's quality of team member exchange scale, and the final nine-item measure was derived from a pilot survey of 110 senior executives; the overall measure's alpha was .85.

Respondents were presented with six actual situations and asked to assess the degree of appropriateness of the behavior described, from 1 'very inappropriate' to 5 'very appropriate'; two of the six situations were reverse-scored. The measure was developed as a values-based, situation-based assessment and its Cronbach's alpha was .80. Convergent validity was supported by a significant, negative correlation (r = -.42, p < .01) with Earley's (1989) statement-based measure of individualism among 54 evening MBA students.
Respondents indicated the number of years they had been CEOs.

A four-item measure of the extent to which TMT members had generally differed over the previous two years in risk taking, firm expansion, the importance of change, and goals in general, rated from 1 'rarely differ' to 5 'differ a lot'. Eight themes were initially identified from 35 senior executives and categorized with agency theory's view of goal preferences and goal alignment, then pilot tested on 110 senior executives; factor analysis revealed a single construct underlying all eight items, but only four had significant loadings above .40, and the remaining four were dropped.

Following Allison (1978), the coefficient of variation was used: each team's standard deviation of tenure was divided by the team's mean tenure, so higher scores indicated greater diversity and scores approaching zero indicated greater homogeneity.

Following Simons, Pelled, and Smith (1999), educational diversity was computed via the coefficient of variation: the highest degree attained was first transformed into years of formal education, and then each team's standard deviation of education was divided by the team's mean education level.

Respondents indicated the functional specialty of each team member, and a diversity score was calculated with Blau's (1977) index, which assesses the number of significant categories in a distribution and how individuals are dispersed over such categories.

Team tenure was measured as the average of the aggregate tenure of all team members, based on the demographic profiles CEOs provided for those who had been members of their TMTs over the past two years.
Team size was measured as the total number of individuals on a company's TMT, as reported by the CEO.

The reference point for the ith strategic variable for all firms within the jth strategic group at time period t+1. Because the group and industry reference point measures are unknown at time t, the mean value of each strategic variable for the strategic group at time t was used as a proxy for its value at time t+1, following the procedure of Lev (1969) and Frecka and Lee (1983). The deviation between the firm's current value and this reference point is the predictor whose coefficient B measures the speed of adjustment.

variable_name: distance between the industry and the group (D* - G)
description: The distance between the industry reference point and the current position of the strategic group, used as a measure of mobility barriers following Porter (1979) and Harrigan (1985). The distance between the industry and the group is used rather than the distance between groups to simplify the model formulation. Firms are treated as building barriers when the estimated adjustment coefficient is either greater than one or less than zero; values between zero and one imply that the distance narrows and that mobility barriers converge toward the industry average.

Eight strategic variables grouped into two strategic components: scope (product scope, product diversity, firm size) and resource deployment (production, finance, investment). The definitions of the variables for the insurance industry are given in Appendix 2. The dependent variable in the adjustment models is the year-to-year change in each of these strategic variables.

Binary measure of whether a technological opportunity has a mechanism of action already applied by the focal firm to the same therapeutic problem in the prior 10 years. Mechanisms of action were categorized for comparability by an expert with an industrial background in medicinal chemistry; mechanisms coded as 'unknown,' 'anticancer,' or immunostimulants were treated as invalid and those compounds excluded from the analysis. Coded 1 for opportunities with a familiar mechanism of action and 0 for those that are novel.
Binary dependent variable taking the value of 1 if an established firm in-sourced a technological opportunity to solve a problem in year t and 0 otherwise. Used to test Hypothesis 1.

Binary dependent variable taking the value of 1 if the firm in-sources a novel technology and 0 for all remaining observations, that is, either not in-sourcing a solution or in-sourcing a familiar solution. Used to test Hypotheses 2 and 3; familiarity is incorporated in this dependent variable and is therefore not included in these regressions.

Relative share of top management attention devoted to the therapeutic area addressed by the focal opportunity, measured from the established firm's annual report to shareholders, which includes the shareholder letter and outlook. Annual report texts were preprocessed by removing punctuation and numbers, lowercasing, eliminating stop words, and stemming; a keyword list was built for each therapy. The number of mentions of therapeutic area k in the annual report, Nk, was divided by the sum of mentions across all therapeutic areas in which the firm was active, giving values from 0 to 1.

Count of failures experienced by the established firm within the therapeutic area of the focal opportunity over a 2-year window. Failures are attempts to which the firm had already committed substantial resources and time but that ultimately failed to get launched on the market, counted from Phase 3 of the drug development process onward; the year of failure was coded using Pharmaprojects and Adis Insights.

Participants in the high responsibility condition chose one of two acquisition targets, Vista Video or Mix Music, designed to be as similar as possible to each other, equal in potential return to ABC and equally complementary to ABC's existing business, and they also decided on amounts to bid for the target, which was designed to reinforce the manipulation. Low responsibility participants were yoked to high responsibility participants and were told that, as the new president of ABC company, they had just taken over an acquisition from their predecessor, after which they saw an outline of the target choice and the bidding process of their yoked high responsibility counterpart.

Participants in the competition condition were told that there was someone else interested in acquiring the same target, and any bids rejected in this condition were said to have been rejected because the target was considering an alternative offer. Participants in the no competition condition were told that no one else was interested in acquiring the same target, and any bids rejected in this condition were said to have been rejected because the target considered the bid to be insufficient.

variable_name: public or private decision context manipulation
description: Participants in the public decision context condition were told that reports of their decisions would be sent over the computer network to the other participants in the simulation, and these reports were presented during the post-agreement period. Participants in the private decision context condition were told that their decisions were private and that no reports of their activities would be sent to the other participants.

variable_name: number of periods participants continued with the acquisition
description: The number of periods that participants continued with the acquisition. Participants had the option of staying from zero to three periods. Participants that stayed for fewer periods are less committed to the target than participants that stayed for more periods.

variable_name: participant estimates of annual income that the target would provide for ABC
description: After deciding whether to continue or withdraw, participants were asked to estimate the annual income that the target would provide for ABC; this measure was administered after each period that the participant continued with the acquisition and also at the point where the participant decided to withdraw. Negative estimates were accepted. The authors argue that participants who provide higher income estimates are likely to be more committed to acquiring the target, because individuals who are overcommitted distort information so that it supports their decision to remain committed.

The number of shares held by the CEO, identified from the proxy statements preceding the announcements of acquisitions, multiplied by the average daily closing share prices for the month prior to the month of the acquisition announcement. The value is adjusted for inflation. Actual dollar values are used rather than percentage ownership, because one percent of a very large firm is most likely a greater portion of a manager's wealth than one percent of a smaller enterprise.
time_window: proxy statements and share prices for the month prior to the acquisition announcement

description: The value of the CEO's option holdings estimated using data from proxy statements prior to the acquisition announcements. Options are valued with Kerr and Kren's (1992) modified version of the Black-Scholes (1973) model, chosen because volatility (variance in returns) is a key issue in the study and that model better reflects the underlying volatility in the sample firms' share prices.
time_window: proxy statements prior to the acquisition announcement

description: The covariance of returns to the investors of the merging firms over the sixty-month time period preceding their announcements, used as a proxy variable for risk-reducing or risk-enhancing corporate strategies. The variable captures the risk profile of an acquiring firm paired with a target and is subject to a portfolio diversification effect depending on the degree to which the two firms' returns are correlated.
level: acquiring firm paired with a target
time_window: sixty months preceding the acquisition announcement

description: Cumulative abnormal returns serve as the risk-adjusted measures for the returns associated with acquisition announcements. Using the event-study methodology, CARs are estimated for two event windows covering days -1 to 0 and days -3 to +3.
time_window: event windows of days -1 to 0 and days -3 to +3 around the acquisition announcement

description: Placeholder measure entry to satisfy one measure per construct; see cumulative abnormal returns measure.

Indicator variable that takes a value of 1 if a given recommendation was implemented, and is 0 otherwise. The IAC program tracks the adoption status of the recommendations over a two-year period; the DOE believes that if recommendations are not implemented within two years they are unlikely to be adopted in the future. The measure is constructed for each energy-saving recommendation made to an audited facility.

variable_name: Operational Characteristics, Standard Investment, Customized Investment
description: Energy-saving recommendations were classified into three increasingly disruptive categories of changes to routines: operational characteristics, standard investment, and customized investment. Two energy-efficiency experts blind to the hypotheses independently classified the 680 DOE sub-categories of recommendation types, with a kappa of 0.78, and differences were resolved jointly by the two raters. Three indicator variables were created from the classification; Standard Investment is the excluded category, so support for H1 is indicated by a positive coefficient on Operational Characteristics and a negative coefficient on Customized Investment.

The IAC recommendations include the adoption costs (equipment and installation) for the recommendation, and Cost represents all implementation costs associated with equipment, installation, training, etc. Following Anderson and Newell (2004), cost is normalized so that its mean equals 1, and the logarithmic form is used because it improves the model's fit with the data. The logarithm of cost is interacted with the disruption categories to test Hypothesis 4.

This represents the annual count of Sierra Club members in the state in which the facility operates, scaled by the state population. The authors use it as a time- and location-varying proxy for the strength of environmental norms in the area in which the firm operates; they note that more fine-grained data were not available for the length of the analysis period, and that the measure is similar to measures used in prior studies of institutional norms.

For a specific energy saving initiative recommended by an IAC, this is the cumulative count of the number of times a particular energy saving initiative has been implemented in the past when it was recommended by the same IAC. Support for H3 is indicated by a significant and positive coefficient on this variable.

Defined similarly to Prior Adopters Local but counts the number of times an initiative has been implemented when recommended by other IACs. It is used to show that local adopters matter and that the results do not simply reflect greater adoption across a wider area.

The number of services provided by each hospital in a given year, taken from the AHA survey, which asks each hospital to report all of the services that it provided in a given year. Services include trauma centers, emergency departments, orthopedics, oncology services, neurological services, intensity-modulated radiation therapy, outpatient surgery, transplant services, robotic surgery, and medical imaging. The authors use count-based measures because their arguments concern coordination and communication challenges stemming from a broad product offering. The independent variable is lagged by one year in the estimations.

Indicates a hospital's choice of governance mode with respect to physicians: it equals 1 for integration mode (employing their own physicians) and 0 for nonintegration mode (contracting with physicians as external service providers). The AHA survey identifies whether hospitals use an integrated or a nonintegrated governance mode. Nonintegrated mode hospitals include hospitals that coordinate their activities with physicians through arm's length or alliance-based arrangements. Approximately 20% of the hospitals changed their governance mode during the period of study.

Dependent variable of the co-employment analysis: it takes a value of 1 if individuals i and j were employed by the same firm and 0 otherwise. It was estimated over 32,809,050 unique, undirected individual ij dyads, of which 53,191 dyads were employed by the same firm in 2006. Coefficients and standard errors are adjusted for rare events bias.

Each educational affiliation was assigned the institution's overall score from U.S. News & World Report's 2011 worldwide rankings of the top 400 global universities; the maximum score is 100, the 400th ranked school received a score of 29.2, and unranked schools (24 percent of all affiliated schools) were assigned a score of 28.0. An individual's educational prestige is the median score among all prior educational affiliations held by that individual. For each individual-individual dyad the differential is the absolute value of the difference between the educational prestige scores assigned to individuals i and j.
scale: absolute difference in institutional scores, which range up to 100

description: Equals 1 if individuals i and j share a prior educational affiliation and 0 otherwise; 7 percent of all dyads do. It was constructed from an individual-by-school matrix whose rows are the 8,101 individuals and whose columns are all 1,081 prior educational institutions, transformed into an individual-by-individual matrix.

Equals 1 if individuals i and j share a prior employment affiliation and 0 otherwise; 1 percent of all dyads do. It was constructed from an individual-by-employer matrix whose rows are the 8,101 individuals and whose columns are all 12,143 prior employers, transformed into an individual-by-individual matrix.

Dependent variable of the co-investment analysis: it takes a value of 1 if firms i and j co-invested (i.e., participated in the same company-round of investment) in 2006 and 0 otherwise. It was estimated on 584,821 unique, undirected firm ij dyads with complete data; 6,981 of these dyads co-invested at least once in 2006, a co-investment rate of 1.19 percent. The dependent variable was coded dichotomously because only 331 of the 6,981 co-investing dyads formed more than two co-investment relationships in 2006.

Firm-level educational prestige differential computed using the same U.S. News & World Report institution scores used in the co-employment analysis. It is the absolute value of the difference between the median educational prestige score of all firm i employees and the median educational prestige score of all firm j employees.
scale: absolute difference in median institutional scores

description: Count of prior educational affiliations shared by the employees of firms i and j. Individual affiliation data were aggregated to a firm-by-school matrix whose rows are the 1,082 firms and whose columns are all 1,081 prior educational institutions, and both matrices were transformed into firm-by-firm matrices using Ucinet's cross-products method for valued data, which counted the schools jointly affiliated with two firms' employees. For example, if firm i has three employees who hold degrees from Emory University and firm j has two, the two firms share six prior educational affiliations to Emory.

Count of prior employment affiliations shared by the employees of firms i and j. Individual affiliation data were aggregated to a firm-by-employer matrix whose rows are the 1,082 firms and whose columns are all 12,143 prior employers, and both matrices were transformed into firm-by-firm matrices using Ucinet's cross-products method for valued data, which counted the prior employers jointly affiliated with two firms' employees. For example, if firm i has three employees who previously worked at Merrill Lynch and firm j has two, the two firms share six prior employment affiliations to Merrill Lynch.

The number of times over the previous five years that two firms invested in the same portfolio company. The five-year window was used because only 11 percent of firms in the sample are less than 5 years old but 52 percent are less than 10 years old. This variable was interacted with the number of shared prior educational and employment affiliations to test hypotheses 4a and 4b, and as a control it also accounts for cohesion produced by previous relationships and for unobserved dyad-level heterogeneity.

variable_name: (construct not measured in the co-employment analysis)
description: Not applicable: the co-employment analysis does not measure interorganizational relationship formation.

Measured as the number of patents that firm f held for the 5-year window preceding the make-buy sourcing decision for each component c, where c represents derailleur, freewheel, chain, and shifter. Patent count is based on data obtained from the USPTO and coded by a patent attorney reviewing every claim in each patent. Some patents held claims for multiple components, in which case the patent was counted for each component. Higher patent counts in the area of a particular component correspond to higher levels of absorptive capacity.
time_window: 5-year window preceding the make-buy sourcing decision

description: In the adoption timing model imitation speed is captured by Adoption_fst, a binary dependent variable set to 0 for each year t and then set to 1 in the year (and all following months) in which firm f first introduces index shifting in a gear-shifting set s. In the sourcing models the speed of imitation is captured by predicted probabilities constructed from probit first stages: P(Y_fst = 1), the likelihood that firm f adopted the index shifting innovation in a gear-shifting set s at time t during the early period (1985-1989), and P(X_fst = 1 and Y_fst = 1), the conditional probability that the firm adopted the innovation with a buy strategy in the early period. Market Growth Rate is included as an instrumental variable when obtaining these predicted values.
scale: binary; predicted probabilities ranging from 0 to 1
level: firm-gear-shifting set-year; firm-component-set-year for predicted probabilities
time_window: 1985-1995; predicted probabilities estimated for the early period 1985-1989

description: Opportunity costs associated with imitating slowly are measured by three co-variates. OC_Price is the number of months between Shimano's introduction of the Aerodynamics (AE) gear-shifting sets in 1981 and the date on which incumbents followed with a price increase; the shorter OC_Price, the faster incumbents are predicted to adopt. OC_MKS is the market share difference between Shimano and an incumbent the year before index shifting was introduced to the market; the smaller OC_MKS, the more head-to-head the competition. OC_Peer Group is set equal to 1 if an incumbent is among Shimano's peer group prior to the innovation shock, else 0.
time_window: 1981 price event and the year before index shifting was introduced; peer group status prior to the shock

description: Binary dependent variable set to 1 if the derailleur firm f produced internally the component c - freewheel, chain, and shifter - for gear-shifting set s, otherwise is set to 0. The sourcing decision is estimated separately for each of the three components in a seemingly unrelated regression framework, with all firms assumed to produce their derailleur internally.

Coded 1 if a component c from firm f's gear shifting set s was co-specialized so that it could be used only with one set, else 0. Coding is based on two criteria: using Bicycling's database the authors assessed more than 200 different offerings across firms and product lines as to whether a component for a derailleur firm was used for other derailleur firms, and they assessed component compatibility from Sutherland's Handbook for Bicycle Mechanics (6th ed.). Co-specialization is assumed if either a component is not used by other firms or if the component is not compatible with other index systems.

Fuel consumption, measured in miles per gallon (MPG), obtained by a focal car model with a hybrid carburetor, as measured by the EPA. MPG is used to measure the performance of the car model's carburetor through its theoretically relevant attributes, and it is the dependent variable in the tests of Hypotheses 1-3. The regressions explain MPG with a Hybrid dummy, the car's physical attributes, and the carburetor firm's patent measures interacted with Hybrid, so the hybrid portion of the estimate is the Hybrid x Patents term.

Firm-level measure of the annual over- or underperformance of a firm's hybrid carburetors relative to those of its competitors. Expected MPG values for each individual carburetor model are generated with the STATA postestimation command 'predict' following the pooled specification from the tests of Hypotheses 1-3 (Model 1 of Table 2) given the carburetor's observable attributes, and this predicted value is subtracted from the carburetor's actual measured MPG. These over- or underperformance values are averaged over model year by carburetor type (hybrid or not) and interacted with the manufacturer; the difference between these values provides a firm-level measure of the annual over- or underperformance of a firm's hybrid and standard carburetors relative to competitors. Values are calculated for lags of one through four years (HybridPerf t-1 through HybridPerf t-4).
time_window: lagged one to four years (t-1 through t-4)

description: Fuel consumption in miles per gallon, as measured by the EPA, of a firm's EFI-equipped car models; the dependent variable in the spillforward test of Hypothesis 4. In that test the MPG of EFI-equipped car models is regressed on the firm's lagged HybridPerf and StandardPerf and on the same controls used in Model 1 of Table 2. Relative EFI performance to competitor firms is used because it controls for variation (e.g., gas prices, government regulation) that might cause industry-wide changes in EFI performance.

Citation-weighted patenting activity associated with each individual car model's carburetor, in the standard carburetor technology area. Patents are counted when successfully applied for (i.e., subsequently granted) by the carburetor's manufacturer in the five years before the carburetor's sale to the public, and each patent is weighted by the number of patents granted to any inventor that subsequently cite it in the five years following its grant. The citation-weighted patent count is divided by 100 to make the regression coefficients more readable. Carburetor manufacturers are associated with patents through string searches in the 'Assignee' field of the NBER patent citation file, verified by manual checks for false matches. The formula for the measure is not readable in the supplied text.
time_window: patents applied for in the five years before the carburetor's sale; citations received in the five years after grant

description: Citation-weighted patenting activity associated with each individual car model's carburetor, in the electronic fuel injection technology area, constructed in the same way as CarbPatents. Patent classes are defined by the World Intellectual Property Organization's International Patent Classification system; 887 of the 9,506 patents in the relevant combustion-engine classification are specific to EFI. Patents are counted over the five years before the carburetor's sale and weighted by subsequent citations in the five years after grant, and the count is divided by 100. The measure is interacted with the Hybrid dummy to separate the effect on hybrids from standard carburetors.
time_window: patents applied for in the five years before the carburetor's sale; citations received in the five years after grant

description: Citation-weighted patenting activity in semiconductors, constructed in the same way as CarbPatents and EFIPatents, as a proxy for inventive experience in a technology domain related to the focal technology but not directly required to produce EFI. The semiconductor category is chosen because it is related to EFI (generic semiconductors are a component of EFI systems) and because it is comparable across all firms (all firms patented in semiconductors). A related technology category is preferred over more general measures such as all patents because firm diversification makes broad portfolios less comparable.
time_window: patents applied for in the five years before the carburetor's sale; citations received in the five years after grant

description: A dichotomous variable that takes a value of 1 if a candidate formally joined as a new director in a particular year and 0 otherwise. New outside directors who joined the specially treated firm in each year of the observation window were identified by comparing the firm's list of directors with that of the previous year.

The social capital of a director candidate in year t measured as their eigenvector centrality within the board-interlock network among all directors in year t - 1. The centrality scores of all upper echelons were standardized, and the squared term of the candidate's eigenvector centrality score was also calculated.

The average of the standardized values of four indicators of prior experience: accumulative experience as a top executive, accumulative experience as a director, accumulative experience in government, and accumulative experience in professional organizations. Candidates' experiences in government and professional organizations were extracted from their personal resumes disclosed in host firms' annual reports.

For each ST firm, the average of its standardized eigenvector centralities in three interfirm networks among public firms: the cross-shareholding network, the common institutional investor network, and the alliance or joint venture network. Relevant information was extracted from firms' announcements and annual reports.

Team members rated the frequency with which they interacted with each of 19 external parties as part of their jobs in the last six months on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all to 5 = very often). Responses of 3 or more were dichotomized to 1 and all others to 0; a source counted as a tie for the whole team if even one member had a tie to it, and the number of such ties across the 19 sources was summed. Higher scores mean greater breadth of external interactions.
time_window: last six months, rated at Time 1

description: Betweenness centralization of the team's problem-solving network. Each member was given a roster of all team members and asked 'How often do you go to [Name] for help when thinking through difficulties or problems at work?' on a five-point scale (1 = not at all to 5 = very often); responses of 3 or greater were dichotomized to 1 and all others to 0. Betweenness centrality was computed for each member in UCINET and the team centralization index was calculated following the Freeman (1978) formula, which is not readable in the text (the text states that c* is the maximum centrality observed in the network). Scores range from 0 (problem solving equally distributed) to 1 (star pattern with one primary hub); the mean was 0.12.

Team creativity was rated by team leaders at Time 2, four weeks after the Time 1 survey, using a three-item scale adapted from Madjar et al. (2011). Team leaders used a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) to rate their teams (Cronbach alpha = 0.85).

Team leaders rated three items adapted from Morgeson and Humphrey's (2006) measure of task complexity on a Likert-type scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree. All items were reverse-coded such that high scores indicated greater complexity (Cronbach alpha = 0.78).

The same procedure as in Study 1 was used to measure and operationalize this variable. All team members rated their frequency of interaction with each of the 19 external parties at Time 1, responses of 3 or greater were dichotomized to 1, a source counted as a team tie if any member had a tie to it, and the ties across the 19 sources were summed.
time_window: last six months, rated at Time 1

description: The same procedure as in Study 1 was used to compute betweenness centralization of the team problem-solving network from the sociometric roster ratings of how often members go to each other for help with problems. The mean centralization score in these teams was 0.40 with a standard deviation of 0.38.
Team creativity was rated by skip-level leaders at Time 2 using the same items as in Study 1. Skip-level leaders used a five-point Likert scale to rate their teams.

Similar to Study 1, team leaders rated three items adapted from Morgeson and Humphrey's (2006) measure of task complexity using a Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Cronbach alpha was 0.90.

All team members responded at Time 1 to a four-item scale adapted from Van Ginkel and Van Knippenberg (2008) and Hoever et al. (2012) using a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very often). Member responses were averaged to a team score, which had high interrater agreement (rwg = 0.87, ICC[1] = 0.38, ICC[2] = 0.98); Cronbach alpha = 0.90.

Measured using the index initially developed by Carter and Manaster (1990), constructed from the positions that investment banks occupy in tombstone announcements listing members of the underwriting syndicate. Banks that always appear in the highest bracket receive a ranking of 9, whereas investment banks receive lower rankings should their positions in successive tombstone announcements drop. The authors used the data on investment bank reputation from Loughran and Ritter (2004).
Equals 1 if the issuer was backed by a venture capitalist, and 0 otherwise. Data for this variable were obtained from the new issues module of the SDC database.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Dichotomous measure indicating whether the parties used a joint venture versus an acquisition as the market entry mode. Joint venture equals 1 for joint ventures with newly public firms and 0 for acquisitions of newly public firms. The governance structure for each transaction was obtained from the SDC database.
time_window: up to five years after the IPO

variable_name: Occurrence of a joint venture or an acquisition (selection equation dependent variable)
description: A sample selection equation distinguishes IPO firms that were either partnered with or acquired from firms that did not experience such transactions. In the ordered probit models the dependent variable assumes one of three values - no transaction (0), joint venture (1), and acquisition (2) - reflecting increasing levels of financial and other commitments by the exchange partner; four-category models add nonequity alliance (1).
time_window: up to five years after the IPO

description: Measures the euclidean distance between firms' industries based on their knowledge requirements, as proxied by their respective employment distributions. Data are provided from the Occupation Employment Survey from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which offers information on the distribution of employment across 823 occupational categories within industries at the three-digit SIC level. Continuous variables were standardized prior to the formation of multiplicative terms.
time_window: at the time of the transaction

description: The waste generation of the toxic chemicals is summed and each chemical is weighted by its toxicity to create a single waste generation total for each facility in each year. Because larger facilities generate more waste, the natural log of a facility's weighted waste generation is regressed on a quadratic specification of its size (number of employees) and its industry, with separate regressions run in each year. The standardized residuals from that prediction provide the measure of relative waste generation, i.e., the deviance from expected waste given size and industry. The value of the facility's relative waste generation in the year before it is acquired is used in the analysis.

The firm-level measure takes the average of the relative waste generation of the facilities owned by the acquiring firm. Because facility performance is rated relative to other facilities within its industry, facilities from different industries can be added together to arrive at a firm score. Although the underlying measure is continuous, the models require dichotomizing firms into those with higher and lower levels of capabilities: firms are designated 'clean' if they generate less than the median amount of waste and 'dirty' otherwise, and the effect of facility characteristics is modeled separately for clean and dirty firms.

Using the location (latitude and longitude) of each facility as reported in its TRI data, the geodesic distance in kilometers is calculated between each facility currently owned by a firm and each potential target. The measure is the average distance between a given potential target and the plants owned by the acquirer firm. The authors report that results do not change in robustness tests using the minimum distance instead of the average; interaction models use mean-centered variables and the figures display distance on a logarithmic scale.
level: acquirer firm-potential target pair within acquisition pool

description: Data on efficiency is from the second survey. In the empirical context, efficiency captures the extent to which a bank was able to reduce its costs of servicing customers through traditional channels by adopting online banking. The measure captures efficiency in terms of cost reductions while assuming constant service output in the form of customer transactions. Efficiency is the composite of three seven-point Likert-type items assessing the degree to which a bank has successfully leveraged online banking to reduce costs of customer service delivery.

Adaptability captures a bank's ability to respond swiftly to customers' changing needs. The variable captures two aspects: changes in a bank's online functionality and links to other channels in response to evolving customer needs, and the speed at which the bank is able to make those changes. Adaptability is the composite of four seven-point Likert-type items assessing the speed of response to changing market needs and technological environments, and is measured on data from the second survey.

Measured, similar to Pisano (1990) and Poppo and Zenger (1998), as continuous ranging from zero (all in-house) to 100 (all outsourcing). In the first survey, respondents indicated the percentage to which their bank relied on outsourcing versus in-house for the implementation of each of eight online service areas. Scope of outsourcing was calculated by summing the percentages of outsourcing across all service areas offered and dividing the sum by the total number of online service areas offered by a bank; because some services were not offered by some banks, the denominator differed across banks.

Operationalized as the proportion of operating income generated from nontraditional product markets. Nontraditional income refers to income generated from activities other than the traditional intermediation business of banks (taking deposits and making loans) and is an archival measure that regulators use to assess a bank's extent of activities in new product markets. The measure assesses not only a bank's attempt to enter new product markets but also its ability to realize revenues in these markets.

Participants were randomly assigned to a low or high construal level during problem framing and again during problem formulation. Construal levels were manipulated by adding different linguistic cues to the core task instructions; for the low construal level condition, participants were told to focus on concrete actions and details, whereas the high construal level condition asked them to take a big-picture view.
time_window: during problem framing and problem formulation

description: Construal levels were manipulated before the problem framing and problem formulation tasks by asking participants a set of how (to induce a low construal level) or why (to induce a high construal level) questions. Participants answered each question four times consecutively at increasing levels of abstraction or concreteness.
time_window: before problem framing and problem formulation

description: Respondents self-reported their construal level with which they formulated their strategic problems, using established measures from Burrus and Roese (2006). Cronbach's alpha was 0.63.

Two coders blind to the hypotheses counted the number of distinct symptoms participants identified during problem framing. Symptoms referred to information, facts, or data points that are directly observable in the experimental content; redundant statements were counted as one symptom. Interrater reliability per ICC(1) was 0.86.

Two coders blind to the hypotheses counted the number of distinct symptoms participants identified during problem framing after watching the video. Symptoms referred to information, facts, or data points directly observable in the video. ICC(1) was 0.91.

Two conference organizers blind to the hypotheses counted the number of symptoms respondents listed from their reports of symptoms they had noticed during 2020 that were preventing their firms from achieving performance aspirations. Rater counts were averaged; ICC(1) was 0.78.

Two coders counted the number of distinct causes participants theorized during problem formulation. A potential cause such as dementia was counted if participants had identified symptoms that plausibly pointed toward it. ICC(1) and ICC(2, 1) for comprehensiveness were 0.79 and 0.88, respectively.

Two coders blind to the hypotheses counted the number of potential causes participants identified during problem formulation after watching the video. ICC(1) and ICC(2, 1) were 0.88 and 0.94, respectively.

Two conference organizers counted the number of causes listed by each respondent. They were instructed to consider only causes that appeared plausible given the symptoms the respondent had listed. Rater counts were averaged; ICC(1) was 0.70.
time_window: during problem formulation at the conference

description: Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions formed by crossing construal level during problem framing (low versus high) with construal level during problem formulation (low versus high). The construal shift condition was the low-to-high combination; the other combinations were low-low, high-high, and high-to-low.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions formed by crossing construal level during problem framing (low versus high) with construal level during problem formulation (low versus high). The construal shift condition was the low-to-high combination; the other combinations were low-low, high-high, and high-to-low.

For multiple-unit operations, the number of rooms in a parent bank's current FX operations. Because banks typically have only one currency trading room in a country, it measures global dispersion. The natural logarithm of the variable is used in the expansion and contraction equations so that rates can plateau over the number of rooms; for single-unit operations the logarithm is zero. The text reports that between 1 and 23 trading rooms are associated with each parent bank.

Dummy variable that indicates if the current operation is not globally dispersed, coded 1 if the bank operates a single FX room and 0 otherwise. In the expansion and contraction analyses it distinguishes single-room from multiroom operations.

variable_name: PRD (proportion of rooms with the Reuters' Dealing System)
description: Firm-level information technology diffusion: the proportion of a bank's rooms that employ the Reuters' Dealing System. A room's dealing system is identified with a four to six character code that other banks use to contact the room. The variable is time-varying and was revised annually; if a bank closed a room, PRD was recalculated as the proportion of the bank's current rooms with the system.

Industrywide information technology diffusion: indicates whether historical time is after 1984. The Reuters' Dealing System was introduced in 1981 and widely adopted by 1984, so the period variable indicates whether the system is diffused industrywide.

variable_name: expansion rate (instantaneous rate of adding a room)
description: Dependent variable of the expansion model: the instantaneous rate at which the FX operation adds a room to its global configuration. Prob represents the probability that the parent bank will add a room, given it is "at risk" to do so at time t. The model is duration-based, using the duration that a room has not been added since either the study's beginning or the prior expansion event, and is estimated with the proportional hazards model of Cox (1972) using partial likelihood.
time_window: spells within 1974-1993; time-varying independent variables updated annually

variable_name: contraction rate (instantaneous rate of deleting a room)
description: Dependent variable of the contraction model: the instantaneous rate at which the FX operation deletes a room from its global configuration. Prob represents the probability that the parent bank will delete a room, given it is "at risk" to do so at time t. The model is duration-based, using the duration that a room has not been deleted since either the study's beginning or the prior contraction event, and is estimated with the proportional hazards model of Cox (1972) using partial likelihood. Contraction of a single-room operation is equivalent to withdrawing from market-making.
time_window: spells within 1974-1993; time-varying independent variables updated annually

variable_name: Net Change in Number of Rooms
description: Annual net change in the number of rooms, operationalized as a continuous variable that represents the combined effects of expansion and contraction and allows for multiple events in a single year. It is estimated only for multiunit operations with a fixed-effects model that includes dummy variables for each parent bank and dummy variables for each year. The dependent variable captures the change between years t and t-1, while the independent variables are calculated in year t-2.
time_window: annual, change between t and t-1; independent variables measured in t-2

description: Telephone respondents rated four selected DAX companies on six reflective indicators using a seven-point Likert scale: three affective indicators capturing likeability and three cognitive indicators capturing competence. A principal component analysis produced two orthogonal factor scores, and the reputation index used in the analyses resulted from a linear combination of these factor scores. Depending on the wave, reputation scores of 27-30 DAX companies with a minimum of 100 ratings per company were entered in the database.
scale: seven-point Likert scale for the indicators; scale of the resulting index is not stated
time_window: survey wave in December 2005 and every June/December from 2006 to 2011

description: The predicted value from a variant of Brown and Perry's financial halo model that regresses a company's total reputation score on return on assets, the market-to-book ratio, the natural logarithm of market value, mean market value growth, and beta, with period effects and firm-specific effects. Three variants of this model separate financial reputation by using between- and within-firm variances, only between-firm variances, or only within-firm variances in reputation. The equation itself is not readable in the text: the formula block was removed from the payload.

The residual term of the financial halo model, i.e., the part of the total reputation score that is not explained by return on assets, market-to-book ratio, market value, market value growth, and beta. As with financial reputation, three variants separate nonfinancial reputation using between-firm variance only, within-firm variance only, or both between- and within-firm variance in reputation. The equation itself is not readable in the text: the formula block was removed from the payload.

variable_name: monthly abnormal return of portfolio P (αP)
description: Portfolios are newly formed at the beginning of each six-month period from the most recent reputation data, with median splits classifying stocks into high (superior) and low (inferior) reputation portfolios; zero net investment strategies compare the performance spreads of the high and low portfolios, and the stocks are value weighted. The reported abnormal return is the intercept of a four-factor model that controls for market, size, value, and momentum risk factors, estimated with OLS and heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent standard errors; positive (negative) intercepts indicate outperformance (underperformance) of the benchmark. Total raw returns and annualized Sharpe ratios are also reported for the portfolios.

Corporate bankruptcy was a binary variable. All members of the primary group had filed bankruptcy over the period, but none of the matched group had done so. The bankruptcy variable is for the year in which a filing occurred; all other variables are lagged and represent circumstances five years prior to the filing of bankruptcy.

This variable is binary. The same individual either did or did not simultaneously serve as a firm's CEO and board chairperson. These data were collected from Standard & Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors, and Executives, and are lagged to five years prior to the bankruptcy filing.
time_window: five years prior to the filing of bankruptcy

variable_name: proportion of outside directors with "6b" affiliations
description: The measure relies on the distinction provided by Securities and Exchange Commission regulation 14A, item 6b, which sets forth the conditions under which directors' affiliation must be disclosed in proxy materials. Data were collected from the relevant proxy statements for both the bankrupt and matched firms, and the proportion of outside directors with "6b" affiliations is reported. Values are lagged to five years prior to the bankruptcy filing.
time_window: five years prior to the filing of bankruptcy

description: Dichotomous dummy variable coded 1 for failed launch attempts and 0 for successful launches. Most launches are clear failures (they blew up) or clear successes (they did not blow up). Partial failures, which reached earth orbit but significantly damaged the satellite, failed to obtain separation between satellite and launch vehicle, or deposited the satellite in the wrong orbit, were coded as failures because the launch vehicle did not properly perform its designed function.

Count of the number of an organization's prior failed launches. Each prior launch was depreciated using the best-fitting depreciation parameter lambda, determined by grid search, so that a prior launch is multiplied by lambda raised to the power of the number of years separating it from the current launch. For merged or acquired organizations, experience was constructed to account for all of the prior experience possessed by the merged organizations.
time_window: all prior launches, depreciated by year of launch

description: Count of the number of prior successful launches made by an organization. Depreciated in the same way as failure experience, with the depreciation parameter selected separately by grid search to maximize model fit. Merger and acquisition history was incorporated so that the merged organizations' prior successful launches were counted.
time_window: all prior launches, depreciated by year of launch

description: Count of an organization's prior partially failed launches, one of two additional independent variables partitioning failure experience by magnitude. Partial failures reached earth orbit but significantly damaged the satellite, failed to obtain separation between the satellite and the launch vehicle, or deposited the satellite into the wrong orbit. Depreciated in the same manner as the other experience counts.
time_window: all prior launches, depreciated by year of launch

description: Count of an organization's prior completely failed launches, one of two additional independent variables partitioning failure experience by magnitude. Complete failures are the clear failures in which the launch vehicle blew up. Depreciated in the same manner as the other experience counts.
time_window: all prior launches, depreciated by year of launch

description: Indexes the number of prior total failed launches made by organizations in the sample other than the organization attempting a given orbital launch. In practice constructed at the country level, indexing the prior orbital launch experiences of all other organizations located in the same country as the focal launch vehicle organization, because international knowledge sharing is highly problematic in launch vehicle technology.
time_window: all prior launches of other organizations, depreciated by year

description: Indexes the number of prior successful launches made by organizations in the sample other than the organization attempting a given orbital launch. Constructed at the country level, indexing the prior orbital launch experiences of all other organizations located in the same country as the focal organization.
time_window: all prior launches of other organizations, depreciated by year

description: Indexes the number of prior partially failed launches made by organizations in the sample other than the organization attempting a given orbital launch. Constructed at the country level together with the other vicarious experience variables.
time_window: all prior launches of other organizations, depreciated by year

description: Indexes the number of prior completely failed launches made by organizations in the sample other than the organization attempting a given orbital launch. Constructed at the country level together with the other vicarious experience variables.
time_window: all prior launches of other organizations, depreciated by year

description: The log of the hourly bill rate that the Agency charges the client for each project. The mean bill rate in the sample is $45 per hour, with a minimum value of $19.50 and a maximum of $150.
The Agency's margin measured as the difference between the bill rate and the pay rate, as a proportion of the bill rate. The average value is 0.40, with a minimum value of zero and a maximum of 0.6.

The total time in months that the worker has previously spent working on projects for the Agency at the start of the current project. Only time spent on projects with the Agency is counted, excluding spells when the worker was not working for the Agency. The variable is somewhat skewed, with a mean of 5.9 months and a maximum of 51.9 months.
time_window: up to the start of the current project

description: The number of months the worker previously spent on assignment with that specific client. The authors assume that the worker and the client had no relationship prior to the Agency placing the worker with that client. The measure has a mean value of 1.44, 60% of observations have a value of zero, and the maximum value is 36.23.
time_window: up to the start of the current project

description: Applicants completed the Kenexa Retail Associate Selector, a service-orientation battery containing three personality traits (conscientiousness, agreeableness, and emotional stability) with 15 items each, a 20-item situational judgment test, and a 5-item biodata-based measure of educational success. The overall predictor composite was formed by summing the standardized scales and then converting the composite score to a T-score, standardized values that have a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10.

Store-level mean of aggregate individual-level service-orientation KSA scores, nested within each store at each quarter; there were three repeated measures (quarters 1, 2, and 3) for each store. Each quarterly score was the mean service orientation score of all individuals who had applied to and were working at a store in a particular quarter, so an individual's score could contribute to a store's score for one to three quarters; the ICC(2) value was .87.

In the random coefficient growth model the repeatedly measured unit service orientation scores of the store were entered as a time-varying predictor of the sales criteria, with a change in unit service orientation term and a change in unit service orientation squared term; the regression weights estimate whether changes in unit service orientation lead to positive but decreasing changes in store sales criteria over time. Unit service orientation was the unit mean of individual scores, which were already standardized via T-scores and were not further standardized; the predictor was lagged one quarter relative to the criteria.
time_window: quarters 1-3, 2003 (predictor), lagged one quarter before the criteria

variable_name: between-store variance components for unit service orientation and unit service orientation squared
description: The interstore (level 2) model used variance components to estimate between-store heterogeneity among the intercept and slopes, representing the variability in the positive but decreasing relationship across stores. The variance component for the linear unit service orientation term estimates variability in the general strength of the linear trend, and the variance component for the squared term estimates variability in the inflection in the curve.
time_window: quarters 1-3, 2003 (predictor), lagged one quarter before the criteria

description: Store's quarterly sales divided by the average number of relevant employee positions for 2003, provided by the firm; service firms frequently use this measure as an index of productivity. Because the number of positions stayed highly consistent over the year, the measure was unaffected by turnover.
time_window: measured quarterly from quarter 2, 2003, through quarter 1, 2004, with unit service orientation lagged one quarter

description: Controllable profit represents a store's quarterly sales minus quarterly costs that are, to an extent, under the control of the staff (e.g., labor, utilities), an index of profitability the store management can be expected to have some control over. The firm did not want raw values presented, so the controllable profit figures were adjusted by multiplying them by a decimal constant, which reduced the numbers in consistent ways through all three quarters but had no effect on distributions, significance tests, standard errors, or the form of relationships.
time_window: measured quarterly from quarter 2, 2003, through quarter 1, 2004, with unit service orientation lagged one quarter

description: Percentage of sales growth for each store: quarterly sales minus quarterly sales for the prior year, divided by the quarterly sales for the prior year. The measure essentially uses each store as its own control variable, helping to minimize the effects of between-store differences.
time_window: quarterly, comparing a quarter in 2003 with the same quarter of the prior year

description: Number of a firm's business units that share at least one information dimension with a given market segment. Business units were identified from the lists of senior executives in the companies' annual reports, and every unit was coded on 25 information subcategories within Gulick's four categories of customer, product, function, and geography. A unit that shared at least one information dimension with a market segment in a given year was coded as a fit unit, and fit units were counted for each firm-market-year. The independent variables are lagged so that the number of units of each type precedes the entry decision.

Number of a firm's business units that share no information dimensions with a given market segment. Units were identified from senior executive listings in annual reports and coded on the same 25 information subcategories used for market segments. A unit sharing no dimensions with the market segment in a given year was coded as a nonfit unit, and nonfit units were counted for each firm-market-year. The independent variables are lagged relative to the entry decision.

Number of links between fit units for a given firm-year-market. Links were measured from the career paths of senior executives listed in annual reports: if an executive moved from one unit to another, a link was coded between those units for as long as the executive remained in the new position, and for managers who moved multiple times links were counted between the current division and any divisions where the manager previously worked. Symmetric links credit information linkages to a promoted executive's former and current units. The variable is lagged relative to the entry decision.

Number of links between fit and nonfit units for a given firm-year-market. Career paths of senior executives were used as the indicator of linkages, with a link coded between two units when an executive moved from one to the other and counted as long as the executive remained in the new position. Symmetric links credit information linkages to a promoted executive's former and current units. The variable is lagged relative to the entry decision.

Number of links between nonfit units for a given firm-year-market. Links were measured from executive career paths, with a link coded between two units when an executive moved from one to the other and retained for as long as the executive remained in the new position. Symmetric links credit information linkages to a promoted executive's former and current units. The variable is lagged relative to the entry decision.

Number of links between fit units and the corporate level of the firm for a given firm-year-market. Links were measured from the career paths of senior executives, so that a move between a business unit and the corporate offices created a link as long as the executive remained in the new position. Symmetric links credit information linkages to a promoted executive's former and current units. The variable is lagged relative to the entry decision.

Number of links between nonfit units and the corporate level of the firm for a given firm-year-market. Career paths of senior executives listed in the annual reports served as the indicator of linkages between a business unit and the corporate level. Symmetric links credit information linkages to a promoted executive's former and current units. The variable is lagged relative to the entry decision.

Coded 1 if the firm operates in the market segment in a given year and 0 if the firm remained out of the market. Entry was considered to have occurred if, in a given year, a firm offered a service that it had not offered in previous years; services and products were identified from the companies' SEC filings. The analysis for each firm excluded markets where the firm was active in the first year of the study, and potential entry began in the year that at least one firm established a market segment.

The number of active R&D alliances in year t, calculated by summing the number of R&D alliances that a firm formed over five years (t-4 to t). Active alliances were noted using the alliance termination data available in the Bioscan and Recap databases. To the extent that alliance termination data were not available, alliances were assumed to be active for a five-year duration.

The number of New Drug Approvals (NDAs) from the FDA captures NPI performance; the NDA counts exclude generic drug approvals. Actual NPI performance is measured as the average number of NDAs received over a two-year period: AvNPI_t = (New Products Introduced t-1 + New Products Introduced t)/2. The aspiration level NPI (ANPI) is a weighted average of past AvNPI values, with the later average weighted 0.6 and the earlier average weighted 0.4. Distance below aspiration NPI is AvNPI(t-4) minus ANPI(t-4), and an indicator variable equals 1 when AvNPI(t-4) < ANPI(t-4); only observations with the indicator equal to 1 are included in the analysis, so the variable is coded as a signed attainment value that is negative for below-aspiration firm-years.
time_window: t-4 (built from two-year averages at t-5 to t-7)

description: A composite slack index consisting of three categories of slack. Available slack measures liquid resources uncommitted to liabilities and is calculated by current assets divided by current liabilities. Absorbed slack is related to capital utilization and is measured by the working capital-to-sales ratio. Potential slack reflects the ability of firms to borrow further and is measured as the equity-to-debt ratio. Each slack category is standardized and the categories are summed to create the slack index.

Dummy coding, with 1 = the firm is located in an industrial cluster and 0 = otherwise. Cluster membership was treated as potentially endogenous; predicted values from a first-stage model were used in the second-stage regressions of product innovation.

Seven-item scale listed in Jansen et al. (2006: 1672). Mid-level manufacturing or marketing managers, who were knowledgeable about product innovation, indicated the extent to which they agreed with the scale items on a seven-point Likert-type scale ranging from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (7).
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale, 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree

description: Seven-item scale listed in Jansen et al. (2006: 1672). Mid-level manufacturing or marketing managers indicated the extent to which they agreed with the scale items on a seven-point Likert-type scale ranging from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (7).
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale, 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree

description: Senior managers indicated the extent to which their firms had managerial network ties with their suppliers within their clusters (in their regions for non-cluster firms) over the last three years, using a seven-point Likert-type scale ranging from very little (1) to very much (7).
