A composite score was created by averaging the items in each category. Network ties were treated as potentially endogenous and predicted values were used in the second-stage models.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale, 1 = very little to 7 = very much

description: Senior managers indicated the extent to which their firms had managerial network ties with their buyers within their clusters (in their regions for non-cluster firms) over the last three years, using a seven-point Likert-type scale ranging from very little (1) to very much (7). A composite score was created by averaging the items in each category. Predicted values of these ties were used in the second-stage models.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale, 1 = very little to 7 = very much

description: Respondents randomly assigned to the interpretive group read two short (no more than 300 words, about half a page) narrative texts that presented knowledge figuratively, combining abstract and concrete ideas, with a common theme across both texts. After reading they wrote a brief note about what was going on in the text, its key ideas, and the lessons that could be learned, which was intended to engage them in processing the material with the activated schema. The two texts differed from the general treatment in presentation, although judges found it hard to discriminate interpretive and general treatments on the figurative/literal rating scale.
time_window: phase 2, three weeks after the before phase

description: Respondents randomly assigned to the general group read two short texts that emphasized abstract knowledge which was less contextualized but presented the ideas literally, and that shared a common theme. After reading they wrote a brief note about the text and the lessons it contained, intended to reinforce priming. Self-report manipulation checks indicated the general treatments were perceived as significantly more abstract than either the interpretive or particular treatments.
time_window: phase 2, three weeks after the before phase

description: Respondents randomly assigned to the particular group read two short texts that presented highly contextualized ideas in a literal manner with higher concreteness, on the same two themes as the other treatments. After reading they wrote a brief note about the text and its lessons, intended to reinforce priming. Self-report manipulation checks indicated the particular treatments were perceived as significantly more concrete than the general treatments, and judges rated them as clearly more literal.
time_window: phase 2, three weeks after the before phase

description: One of four major categories of idea units identified by coders in respondents' open-ended decision recommendations (work process, professionalism in the organization, individual and personal concerns, and potential actions). Idea units were screened for appropriateness against eight key issues embedded in the case, and the two coders reached 68 percent agreement for this category before resolving discrepancies. Counts were normalized for group size and the difference between the after and before counts was used to display the treatment effect, with a constant added to obtain round positive numbers.
scale: count of idea units (normalized difference score)

description: One of the four major categories of idea units coded from respondents' open-ended decision recommendations, capturing issues such as methodology, cost estimates, project management guidelines, data adequacy, verification, and quality control. Coders worked independently and reached 75 percent agreement for this category before reconciling discrepancies; their consensual codings were analyzed. Counts were normalized for group size and before-after difference scores were used.
scale: count of idea units (normalized difference score)

description: One of the four major categories of idea units coded from respondents' open-ended decision recommendations, capturing issues such as a culture of honesty, open communication, professionalism, leadership, client relations, and ethics of data and method. Coders reached 82 percent agreement for this category before reconciling discrepancies; consensual codings were analyzed. Counts were normalized for group size and before-after difference scores were used.
scale: count of idea units (normalized difference score)

description: One of the four major categories of idea units coded from respondents' open-ended decision recommendations, capturing issues such as Bob's time management, career planning, personal integrity, priorities, and well-being. Coders reached 72 percent agreement for this category before reconciling discrepancies; consensual codings were analyzed. Counts were normalized for group size and before-after difference scores were used.
scale: count of idea units (normalized difference score)

description: Breadth was evaluated on the basis of the number of major categories included in a respondent's task response, using the technique for mapping responses in an ill-structured decision task of Boland, Greenberg, Park, and Han (1990). The before and after counts were normalized for group size, a chi-square statistic was computed using normalized after counts as observed and before counts as expected, and difference scores were used for graphical display.
scale: number of major categories (normalized difference score)

description: Depth was measured as the maximum number of appropriate idea units in a major category, adopting the technique of Boland, Greenberg, Park, and Han (1990) for mapping responses in an ill-structured decision task. Idea units had first to pass an appropriateness screen against eight key issues embedded in the case. As with breadth, normalized before and after counts and difference scores were used.
scale: maximum number of appropriate idea units in a category (normalized difference score)

description: Defined as per Sparks and Hunt (1998), the score is a weighted composite derived from the importance weights given to ethical issues, computed as the product of the number of ethical issues listed (0 to 3) and their corresponding importance weights (1 to 10). Three ethical issues were embedded in the case scenario (research integrity, fair treatment of vendors, and research confidentiality). The difference between the before and after measurements was the dependent variable.
scale: 0 to 3 ethical issues multiplied by importance weights of 1 to 10

description: Respondents rated their feelings about their decisions on three 7-point semantic differential scales with the endpoint pairs "very satisfied/not satisfied at all," "very confident/not confident at all," and "very pleased/not pleased at all." The Cronbach alpha reliability of the measure was .88. The difference between the before and after measurements was the dependent variable in the ANCOVA.

Intended to capture the diversity of ideas represented in respondents' decision recommendations, the measure used three 7-point semantic differentials with the endpoint pairs "many concepts/few concepts," "multiple perspectives/few focused perspectives," and "complex ideas/simple ideas" (alpha = .77). The difference between the before and after measurements was the dependent variable.

A self-evaluation of the decision recommendation the respondent had developed, using three 7-point semantic differential scales: whether the respondent tended to worry about interrelated versus unrelated issues, to consider trade-offs among different issues versus seek the best solution for each issue, and to take into account consequences of interacting versus separate issues (alpha = .75). A rich decision was reasoned to be characterized by interrelated issues requiring trade-offs and consideration of interactional consequences. The before-after difference score was the dependent variable.

variable_name: Access to relevant prior technological knowledge
description: Time-invariant dichotomous classification measured as of 1978: a firm is coded as having in-house access to relevant prior technological knowledge if it had prior experience in using electrical motors, potentiometers, rectifiers, and modulators in manufacturing other products. Of all the firms, 31 had such prior experience, including Fujitsu-Fanuc, Citizens Watch, Sony, Sanyo, and Seiko. Information was collected from secondary sources such as annual reports and trade magazines, validated with industry experts at the Robotics Industries Association, and corroborated with patent data: the listed firms had patents in at least one of the patent classes relevant for electrical robots (294/902, 294/907, 318, 356, 382, 414, 700, and 901) in 1970-1978. Together with access to in-house users this dimension forms the four quadrants used to construct the group dummy variables.

variable_name: Access to in-house users of the new product market
description: Time-invariant dichotomous classification measured as of 1978: dummy variable (1 = yes; 0 = no) if a firm had in-house users of robots in the new product market prior to entering it. Of the 141 manufacturers, 50 firms had access to in-house users of robots in the new product market prior to entering it; these firms assembled electronics, communication, and information technology-related products like computers, calculators, and other electrical and electronic gadgets, and 42 of them were from Japan. Information on whether a firm had in-house users was collected from various secondary sources and validated with industry experts at the Robotics Industries Association. Together with access to relevant prior technological knowledge this dimension forms the four quadrants used to construct the group dummy variables.

variable_name: Proximity to the product performance frontier in the new robotics product market—repeatability ratio
description: Time-varying measure for the period 1978-1987 defined as the ratio of (best repeatability achieved in the industry in a year)/(best repeatability achieved by the firm in a year). Repeatability is the precision with which a robot can return to the same position; the lower the value of a robot's repeatability, the better it is, so the inverted ratio rises as the firm's repeatability approaches the frontier. The best repeatability in a new robot introduced in a year is treated as the performance frontier in the new product market.

variable_name: Proximity to the product performance frontier in the original robotics product market—load capacity ratio
description: Time-varying measure for the period 1978-1987 defined as the ratio of (maximum load capacity achieved by a firm in a year)/(maximum load capacity achieved in the industry in that year). Load capacity is the maximum load that the robot's arm can carry, the critical performance feature in the original pre-CNC product market, and the maximum load capacity of a new robot introduced in a year is treated as the performance frontier. The higher the ratio, the closer is the proximity to the performance frontier in the original robotics product market in a given year.

variable_name: Proportion of products in a firm's portfolio targeted to the new product market
description: Time-varying measure for the period 1978-1987 measured as the ratio of (number of products manufactured by a firm in a given year in new applications of assembly, electronics assembly, arc welding, and inspection)/(total number of products manufactured by the firm in that year).

Proxy for the supplier's perceived probability of a switch, constructed by inverting the supplier's perception of its future with the customer and normalizing by the mean perception in the sample. It is built from EXPSUP, the number of years the supplier considers that there is 'a high probability that it will be supplying this customer', and its normalized version NESUP. The proxy is constructed so as to be bounded between zero and unity and is weighted towards zero. The exact formula appears in the Appendix but was not extractable from the text.

Second proxy for the supplier's perceived probability of a switch, constructed in the same way as PSWT1 by inverting the supplier's perception of its future with the customer and normalizing by the mean perception in the sample. It reduces the tendency of the first proxy to be weighted towards zero. The results for the two proxies are in extremely close agreement, so only the estimates of PSWT1 are presented.

Four variables represent the current competitive factors: COMP93, the number of firms supplying the same product to the same customer in 1993; BID93, coded -1 if other bids have been solicited by the customer, 0 if the supplier has no information in this area and 1 if no other bids have been solicited; MN93, the number of months required for the customer to replace the supplier with another supplier; and CON93, the length of the written contract with the customer. The authors describe these as measurable factors which could be seen as affecting incumbency, relating to the competition faced by the supplier, the degree of dependence of the buyer, and the buyer's contractual commitment.

Supplier's investment in equipment over the last four years to make the product, measured in U.S.$ '000s. The authors note that some of these investments may be redeployable, but that given the brand-specific nature of most OEM requirements there will almost certainly be costs associated with redeployment. These costs have been rated as 'substantial', which is all that is necessary to ensure that the variable does, in part, measure vulnerability associated with hold-up.

Three variables represent the technological complexity of the product: SKILPROC, the rating of skill in terms of incremental process improvements; SKILDE, the rating of skill in terms of design engineering; and COMPLEX, the technical complexity involved in manufacturing the product in 1992. The authors state that these variables relate to the engineering skills required in the production of the product and the product's overall complexity.

Two variables represent product characteristics: PRICE, the average piece price of the product in 1992, and ULAB, the percent of total costs accounted for by hourly wages and benefits. The authors state that even though the sample is relatively homogeneous these variables can be considered to normalize for firm-specific characteristics, specifically supplier technology and the buyer's purchase frequency.

Dummy equal to 1 if there is no other supplier for the same component to the buyer, i.e., the supplier is a single source, and 0 if there are other suppliers for the same component to the buyer. It is the first measure of trust, directly drawn from the buyer-supplier interface, on the claim that single sourcing has trust-building properties. The authors conclude that the subsamples defined by this proxy are insignificantly different from each other, so that SS89 does not function well as a proxy for trust.

Dummy equal to 1 if the supplier's own purchase/sales (PS) ratio exceeds the sample mean, i.e., the supplier has made itself too vulnerable to its suppliers, and 0 if the supplier's own PS ratio is below the sample mean. PS ratios in excess of 40% were specified to be high and those below this figure low; 40% was the mean PS ratio in the sample. The proxy is reported to work well as a measure of buyer-supplier trust by Mudambi and Schrunder (1996).

Dummy equal to 1 if the supplier's expectation of 'being treated fairly' by the buyer was scored at 4 or higher on a 5-point Likert scale, and 0 if this expectation was scored at 3 or lower. It is based on suppliers' own beliefs regarding the likelihood of being treated 'fairly' by the buyer, allied with the assumption that a 'fair' buyer will prove to be trustworthy.

Task complexity weighs a bank's online service portfolio by the interdependence of each service: the sum over services of xij si, where xij is '1' if bank j offered service i and '0' otherwise, and si is the technology vendors' rating of service i's interdependence with the bank's existing systems. Bank executives checked off their bank's online services from a list of 36 Internet banking services. Ten senior executives of technology vendors rated each of the 36 services on how heavy the demand imposed on back-end systems and the synchronization required between the bank's core processing systems and its Internet banking platform are. The raters' overall interrater reliability was alpha = 0.85.
scale: vendor service ratings on a one to seven scale
time_window: at the time the bank adopted Internet banking

description: For each of eight service categories, survey informants indicated the percentage of services implemented by in-house personnel versus external third parties. The variable is calculated by summing the percentages of services integrated across service categories and dividing the sum by the total number of service categories the bank offered, giving average integration across the service categories offered. It is a continuous variable ranging from zero (all external) to 100 percent (all internal).
scale: continuous, zero (all external) to 100 percent (all internal)
time_window: at the time of data collection in 2002

description: Dummy variable with a value of '1' for units that have both funding authority and task accountability and a value of '0' otherwise. Informants indicated which area head was ultimately accountable for e-business success and which area head controlled e-business funding, and the variable was coded '1' when both were held by the same area head. The measure presumes that units with funding control and accountability for a task are also likely to decide when to allocate what resources to task execution.
time_window: at the time of e-banking services adoption

description: Two one-to-seven scale items measuring the extent to which a bank had aligned its activities across channels and business units. Informants indicated the extent to which their bank had mechanisms in place to coordinate e-business activities across existing bank channels and across business units. The Cronbach alpha coefficient for the two items is 0.91.
time_window: at the time the bank decided to implement e-banking services

variable_name: educational background of the top executives (high prestige vs. average prestige)
description: Prestige of the educational background of the CEO and COO, manipulated by changing their undergraduate and graduate school alma maters. In the high-prestige condition the CEO and COO had attended schools ranked among the top 10 in the U.S. News & World Report (2004) rankings; in the average-prestige condition they had attended schools ranked between 50th and 75th. The educational background of the two least senior managers remained average prestige in all conditions.
scale: two levels: high prestige vs. average prestige

variable_name: race of the two most senior managers (CEO and COO)
description: Race of the two most senior executives, manipulated by changing the race of the CEO and COO to either African American or white in the photographs and short bios shown in the pitch book. The two least senior managers were white in all conditions, and all four team members were male in all conditions. Executives' names, professional experience, age, style of dress, and all other financial and descriptive information were held constant across all treatments.
scale: two levels: African American vs. white

variable_name: race of the two top executives (CEO and COO)
description: Race of the two most senior executives, manipulated by showing either African American or white pictures in the management bios. In a manipulation check, all of the participants responded correctly when asked to identify the race of the executive shown in the photo. The two least senior managers were white in all conditions.
scale: two levels: African American vs. white

description: Expectations of performance were operationalized by the valuation of the company's stock using the valuation tool provided. After reviewing the pitch book, participants entered a Price to Earnings multiple into a spreadsheet valuation tool, and the tool returned an estimate for the current price per share of stock.
scale: US dollars per share of stock
time_window: current value of the stock, based on projected earnings for the next year

description: As in the first study, stock price was used as a measure of expectations of performance. Participants entered a Price to Earnings multiple into a spreadsheet valuation tool that returned an estimate for the current price per share of stock.
scale: US dollars per share of stock
time_window: current value of the stock, based on projected earnings for the next year

variable_name: admissions policies (footnote manipulation: no preferential selection vs. ambiguous preferential treatment)
description: Manipulated through a single footnote on the third page of the pitch book describing the university's admissions process. In the condition where preferential selection was not practiced, the footnote stated that the university had changed its applications process to a double-blind procedure with no special consideration for gender, race, or ethnicity. In the ambiguous condition the footnote omitted any statement about admissions policies, so preferential treatment was not explicitly refuted. In both conditions the CEO's and COO's undergraduate and graduate school alma maters were top-ranked universities.
scale: two levels: no preferential selection vs. ambiguous preferential treatment

description: The dependent variable is a measure of the mode of foreign R&D activity that was initiated by an individual firm during the period 1980-92. Activities were categorized as sponsored, collaborative, or controlled based on their characteristics; sponsored research funds projects at a university or another firm without company research staff, collaborative research involves the participation of a firm's employees in the foreign research activity (including joint ventures), and controlled research is activity for which the firm establishes ownership. R&D was defined as any activities needed to synthesize, formulate, and test a pharmaceutical product prior to human clinical trials, and clinical activity for human trials was excluded.

variable_name: type of the first and subsequent foreign R&D activity
description: The dependent variables are the types of the first and subsequent foreign R&D activity that the firms undertook. Activities were ordered by the year in which each firm established them, and the second type of entry was tabulated given the first type, separately for established pharmaceutical firms and recent entrants.

The firms' domestic research competence was measured by the number of patents categorized in the two drug classes of 424 and 514. For each patent a class was counted only once regardless of the number of times it appeared, and patents that appeared in both drug classes were counted only once. Counts were based on the patent class assigned to each patent received by the firms during the 1975-80 period, in order to capture the skills possessed by the firms prior to the study period.

Complementary technical skills were measured by the count for the patent class for Molecular Biology and Biochemistry (435), which includes all patents related to fermentation. Where the Patent Office classified a patent in both a drug classification (424 or 514) and the Molecular Biology (435) classification, the patent was counted only in the Molecular Biology classification; this affected 60 of the 1040 patents included in the study. The counts are based on patents received by the firms during the 1975-80 period.

The number of years after 1979 that a firm undertook its first foreign research activity. The first firm undertook its first activity in 1980 and the last firm to begin foreign research in the sample initiated its research activity during 1991.

Foreign market presence was measured by whether a firm had a foreign sales office at the start of the study period, that is, prior to 1980. The information was collected from Japanese Overseas Investment: A Complete Listing by Firms and Countries 1992/1993. The variable serves to determine whether the prediction that R&D activities tend to follow marketing activities, based on product life cycle theory, provides greater explanatory power than the research competence and competitive pressure predictions of this study.
Where possible, the firm's export sales ratio in 1980 was also recorded. It correlates moderately strongly with foreign sales offices.

A 106 x 106 adjacency matrix containing information on the existence of supply relations between each pair of organizations in the sample. A unit entry indicates that the row organization is named as a supplier by the column organization, so that the row organization supplies the column organization. Supply and inventory managers of the key informant organizations were asked the names of their most important suppliers, in monetary terms, of mechanical parts and components operating in southern Italy, and a similar procedure was repeated at the level of first-tier suppliers. The matrix was left asymmetric to preserve the inherent directionality of supply relations.

The configuration in which a supplier is linked to multiple producers, that is, a supply out-star. The authors predict an increased likelihood of observing such out-stars, which in the random graph model for the supply network enter as a configuration with its own parameter.
level: network configuration (supplier linked to multiple producers)

description: Questionnaire item eliciting, for each organization cited as a supplier, information on equity arrangements (direct and indirect). Ownership ties are reconstructed as symmetric because the core organizations are subsidiary production units of larger industrial groups, so the question was posed in terms of comembership in the same group rather than direct ownership. This definition of equity relations in terms of comembership does not rule out the empirical possibility of observing nontransitive triads in the equity network.

Questionnaire item eliciting information on activities of technology transfer with each organization cited as a supplier. Relations defined in terms of technology exchange agreements are inherently symmetric because they are defined in terms of a joint involvement in product development and comanufacturing. The label technology transfer reflects the terminology used by the supply managers interviewed before the questionnaire was designed.

variable_name: Supply, Technology Transfer and Equity networks
description: Dyadic ties are recorded in three 106 x 106 adjacency matrices of 0/1 entries: supply relations (directed), technology transfer agreements and equity arrangements (both symmetric), from questionnaires to supply and inventory managers.

variable_name: configurations of ties to a common organization
description: Third-party ties are represented by network configurations in which two suppliers of a common organization are themselves tied by a supply or technology exchange relationship, estimated as parameters in the random graph models.

variable_name: Endogenous configuration parameters (reciprocity, stars, 2-paths, transitive triads)
description: Endogenous network processes are represented by the parameters for local network configurations in the Markov random graph (p-star) model fitted to each network separately, such as reciprocal ties, 2-in-stars, 2-out-stars, 2-paths, 3-stars and transitive triangles, estimated from the Supply, Technology Transfer and Equity adjacency matrices. Substantial positive parameters indicate that the status of a tie depends on neighboring ties.

variable_name: Multiplex configurations aligning Equity and Technology Transfer ties with Supply ties
description: Multiplexity is represented by multirelational network configuration parameters in the random graph model of the Technology Transfer and Equity networks conditional on the Supply network. These configurations align an equity tie or a technology transfer tie with a supply tie between the same pair of organizations (motifs e and f), and positive parameters indicate cross-network dependence.

The key dependent variable is the proportion of host inventors in a focal patent, Share, measured as the number of inventors from the host location divided by the total number of inventors listed in the patent. If the counts of host or total inventors for the same patent vary across the patent offices in which it was filed, the authors take the maximum. The variable is a proportion that varies between zero and one.

The primary method to identify the strength of the IPR is the location of the offshore patent, following the classification of Zhao (2006: 1189). The dummy weak equals 1 if the offshore patent was produced in a host country with a weak IPR and 0 otherwise; the dummy strong equals 1 if the offshore patent was produced in a host country with a strong IPR and 0 otherwise. Following the literature, patents are classified as originating from weak or strong IPR locations depending on whether the maximum number of inventors is from a weak or a strong IPR country.

variable_name: Filed only in the US / Filed only in Host / Filed in Both / Filed in Neither
description: The authors use the variation in filing location as a proxy for the country in which the focal patent is relevant. Conditional on a patent being offshore, four mutually exclusive dummies classify it: Filed only in the US equals 1 if the patent was filed exclusively with the US patent office and produced in a host country; Filed only in Host equals 1 if it was only filed in the same host country in which it was produced or coproduced; Filed in Both equals 1 if filed in both home and host locations; Filed in Neither equals 1 if filed neither at home nor at the host location. When the same patent was filed in multiple countries, the patent was included only once and classified as described.

Respondents indicated directly how extensively internetworking is used in the conduct of their firm's business operations. Four Guttman-type scales (Q1-Q4) calibrated reach, the degree to which customers, suppliers, partners, and employees utilized the Internet, with reach increasing as choices moved from top to bottom in each scale; three Guttman-type scales (Q5-Q7) and 34 statements (Q8) calibrated richness. The 34 statements covered online activities performed by the employee, customer, and supplier/partner communities plus financial management/budgeting/strategy formation, answered on a yes (1) or no (0) basis. Scores obtained for Q1-7 and the 34 item scales were summed to obtain an Internetworking Depth score per respondent firm, with a maximum of 68 points.

Two of the six change statements (the first and the last) measured Business Scope/Specialization. Respondents indicated their agreement (or otherwise) with each statement on a 5-point scale ranging from 'Strongly disagree—the opposite is true' to 'Strongly agree.' Strong agreement indicated a firm whose business scope was narrowing and specialization was deepening, with non-core activities being outsourced and lower value-added jobs being eliminated.
scale: 5-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree—the opposite is true to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Statements three and four of the six measured the effects on internal hierarchy. Respondents indicated their agreement (or otherwise) with each statement on a 5-point scale ranging from 'Strongly disagree—the opposite is true' to 'Strongly agree.' Strong agreement indicated a noticeable decrease in managerial levels, internal hierarchy, and bureaucracy, so higher values on this variable mean lower internal hierarchy.
scale: 5-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree—the opposite is true to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Statements two and five of the six measured partnering and alliance behaviors. Respondents indicated their agreement (or otherwise) with each statement on a 5-point scale ranging from 'Strongly disagree—the opposite is true' to 'Strongly agree.' Strong agreement indicated firms where in comparison to a few years ago many more external strategic partnerships/alliances/joint ventures were being entered into, and where mergers/acquisitions/disposals had also increased noticeably.
scale: 5-point agreement scale (1 = strongly disagree—the opposite is true to 5 = strongly agree)
time_window: compared with a few years ago

description: Scores given to sample firms directly by the Franklin Research and Development Corporation, based on criteria such as compliance records, expenditures, and other initiatives used to meet new demands, reduce waste, and support environmental protection organizations. The scale was reverse-coded to run from 1 to 5, so that high values reflect good environmental performance. The ratings are internally adjusted for industry conditions and were held constant for the two years because they were not systematically updated during that period.
time_window: 1991, held constant for both sample years

description: A company's return on assets, described by the authors as a generally accepted measure of firm performance and used as the dependent variable.

The average annual increase in sales for four years for 1991 observations or five years for 1992 observations, drawn from U.S. Bureau of the Census data at the three-digit SIC level. It was de-meaned (centered) before being used to build the interaction term.

We calculated the cumulative adjusted return (CAR) as the five-day firm cumulative return (from two days prior to the estimate until two days after the estimate) minus the cumulative return obtained by comparable firms' stocks in terms of market size (i.e., firms that were in the same decile of market capitalization at the beginning of the year). A CAR close to zero is indicative of a firm trading at close to what comparable firms trade for, suggesting little response from investors, while increasing positive or negative values suggest abnormal trading activity on the stock generated by investors' response to the analysts' forecast revision. The authors noted that the window typically includes days prior to the analyst's estimate to account for tipping.
time_window: five-day window from two days prior to the estimate until two days after the estimate

description: The current quarter's forecast minus the prior forecast, deflated by the stock price 10 trading days before the release of the revised forecast. It takes positive values when the analyst revises an estimate upward and negative ones when he or she revises an estimate downward. The authors used estimates only when an analyst issued both a current and a prior quarterly earnings forecast for the same firm and quarter, and when the current forecast was issued no more than 90 calendar days prior to the quarterly earnings announcement.

variable_name: treated analyst (gained All-Star status because of a category addition)
description: A dummy that takes the value of one when the forecast revision is issued by an analyst who was ranked at time t and who gained All-Star status because of a category addition (a newly created category or the splitting of an existing one) at time t + 1, and zero for revisions from the control group of analysts who were similarly ranked and similarly accurate at time t but operated in a category that Institutional Investor did not change. The authors characterized analysts' forecast revisions by whether they came from a treated analyst and by whether the revision was issued pre or post the category addition. The variable enters the models interactively with forecast revision and with the post category addition indicator.

variable_name: treated analyst (lost All-Star status because of a category removal)
description: A dummy that takes the value of one when the forecast revision is issued by an analyst who was ranked at time t and who lost All-Star status because of a category removal (a category disappearing or two categories merging) at time t + 1, and zero for revisions from the control group of analysts who were similarly ranked and similarly accurate at time t but operated in a category that Institutional Investor did not change. The authors characterized analysts' forecast revisions by whether they came from a treated analyst and by whether the revision was issued pre or post the category removal. The variable enters the models interactively with forecast revision and with the post category removal indicator.

The authors used latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic modeling to identify common topics in crowdfunding narratives and to represent each narrative as a probabilistic representation of these topics; the number of topics was specified to 100. Distinctiveness was calculated as the sum of absolute deviations between venture i's topic weights and the respective market category's average topic weight over 100 topics. Distinctiveness would be 0 if a given narrative used the same topic proportions as the average narrative in the respective market category. The equation spelling out the calculation is not readable in the text.

Computer-aided text analysis (CATA) was used to measure the number of contribution claims in each crowdfunding narrative. Following the multistep dictionary development process, the authors built a dictionary of 57 words using a theory-based approach and an inductive investigation of the 1,000 most frequently occurring words in the narratives, and executed the dictionary with the software package DICTION 7.1.3. The measure was validated by comparing it to manual coding by three graduate students of 500 crowdfunding campaigns.

Market category familiarity was operationalized through the volume of media coverage in leading newspapers, focusing on press articles published by The New York Times and The Washington Post that included the market category's label in their headline and mentioned the label of the basic category at least once in the article. The measure is the logged cumulative volume of news articles about a given market category in the mainstream media up until the month in which a given venture's crowdfunding campaign has ended, counting all articles published since January 1977.
time_window: cumulative since January 1977 up to the campaign end month

description: The dependent variable is the number of backers that pledge crowdfunding to a venture during its crowdfunding campaign. The authors use the natural logarithm of the number of backers to reduce the measure's relatively high degree of skewness. In robustness tests they used the log amount of pledged funding as an alternative dependent variable.

Dummy variable assigned a value of 1 if an adverse event was a fatal accident with one or more deaths (Severity category 4) and had an internal locus of control (Internal equals 1), and 0 otherwise. It captures the risk of event stigma through the combination of the two adverse event characteristics, event severity and event controllability.

Each adverse event was classified into four categories ranging from 1 (low severity) to 4 (high severity): (1) incidents with no injuries to crew or passengers; (2) incidents with minor injuries to passengers and/or crew; (3) non-fatal accidents; (4) fatal accidents with one or more deaths.

Dummy variable coded 1 if the FAA's preliminary investigation attributed the adverse event to the focal firm (e.g., pilot or maintenance errors) and 0 for external causes (e.g., collisions with birds, bad weather) or when cases were undetermined. Of the 1066 events analyzed, 52% were categorized as internal and 48% were external or undetermined.

The number of negative words appearing in media articles covering a specific adverse event on the event day and within the following 7 days, so that only event-specific coverage is considered. Negative valence of each article was assessed with the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) negative emotion dictionary. In the second stage the variable was log-transformed using the natural logarithm to reduce its skewness.
scale: count (words); natural log in the second stage
time_window: event day and the following 7 days

description: Binary dependent variable coded 0 for an ongoing alliance and 1 for an unplanned alliance dissolution. Alliance terminations were identified by reviewing airline companies' websites, corporate documents, media outlets and other online sources, which also provided insights into the reasons for dissolution. Predefined-duration alliances that ended as scheduled, alliances that ended due to mutually satisfying outcomes, and legally mandated dissolutions were excluded.

Measured as the number of stock market analysts following a focal firm, aligning with the concept of status as proportional to the recognition an actor receives. The number of analysts following each firm was obtained from the Institutional Brokers Estimate System (I/B/E/S). A natural logarithm transformation was applied to reduce multicollinearity and limit outlier influence.

Operationalized as the number of a firm's institutional owners, obtained from 13F filings in the Thomson Reuters database. Cases in which institutional investors reported holding more than 100% of a firm's outstanding shares were excluded to ensure data accuracy. A natural logarithm transformation was applied to reduce multicollinearity and limit outlier influence.
scale: count (number of institutional owners); natural log

description: The dependent variable measures the share of the requested funding that the panel awarded. Equals zero if the application is rejected and one if the application is fully funded, with partial funding lying in between. In the sample of 588 proposals, 28.7% are rejected and 37.8% are fully funded.

Dichotomous measure of the funding decision made before the focal decision, equal to one if the prior proposal received funding and zero otherwise. The variable is derived from the order in which projects appear in the secretary's booklet. If a decision on a project application was postponed, this is considered a decision not to fund, because postponing a project takes as much time and mental energy as rejecting it.
time_window: the decision immediately preceding the focal decision

description: The order in which the project was assessed during the panel meeting. Because the number of proposals in each meeting varies greatly, the authors used the log-transformed version of this variable to reduce the impact of outliers.

Binary variable for whether the client firm in each transaction is foreign. Following Kim (2019), a firm was designated foreign only if a foreign entity at the top of its ownership hierarchy-that is, a global ultimate owner-controlled the operations of the U.S. subsidiary, a strict measure the authors view as conservative in estimating the effect of the main explanatory variable. Because lobbying reports do not provide ownership or home-country information, firm identities were identified via multiple steps, beginning with Orbis and then researching remaining companies in the Capital IQ, Worldscope, and Zephyr databases, along with their websites, public disclosures, and historical press coverage.

A political-regime measure (v2x_regime) obtained from the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) project, whose classification scheme is based on the competitiveness of access to power (polyarchy) and liberal principles, on a scale from 0 to 3 (0 = closed autocracy, 1 = electoral autocracy, 2 = electoral democracy, 3 = liberal democracy). For ease of interpretation the authors inversed the measure to create Home-country autocracy, so that the higher a country's score, the more autocratic it is.
level: home country of the client firm

description: The natural logarithm of the lobbying fee in each transaction; because of the skewness of the dependent variable, the dollar amount of each lobbying contract was transformed to its natural logarithm. Exact amounts need not be disclosed if a given client's lobbying expenditure is less than $10,000 per half-year before 2008 and less than $5,000 per quarter since 2008, and the authors attributed the threshold amount to any lobbying expenditure whose exact amount is not reported.

Applying their own knowledge of nationalism and of the qualitative descriptions in each lobbying report, the authors classified at the individual issue level whether a foreign firm is likely to encounter U.S. nationalism during the sample period. Three senior political scientists in the Harvard University Government Department independently coded each issue area, and an issue area was coded as reflecting U.S. nationalism if at least three of the four independent codings agreed. Transactions were then split into subsamples that include at least one nationalism-classified issue and those that do not.
level: congressional issue area (used to split transactions into subsamples)

description: Tariff data downloaded from the U.S. Census and the U.S. International Trade Commission; the authors classified industries based on their 2-digit NAICS codes and calculated the average most-favored-nation tariffs based on harmonized import tariff schedules at the 2-digit NAICS level. Subsample analyses split industries with nonzero versus zero tariffs and industries whose average tariff was greater than or equal to the median versus lower than the median, on the assumption that protecting such industries may bolster policymakers' nationalistic credentials.
level: 2-digit NAICS industry of the client firm

description: The number of years that a given firm lobbied during the sample period. In the endurance models the authors also created interaction terms between the foreign-firm indicator (or home-country autocracy) and different years of lobbying experience, so that foreign and U.S. firms with identical lobbying experience are compared; given a 15-year sample period, 15 such interaction terms were created.

Innovativeness score from the Fortune Reputation Survey, obtained from Fortune magazine for 1998, 1999, and 2000, in which respondents (CEOs, top executives, and financial analysts) gave a subjective evaluation of each firm's overall innovativeness. The three yearly INNOV scores were used as indicators of the latent variable Innovativeness. Psychometric analyses showed strong construct and criterion-related validity for the attribute.

Quality of products/services score from the Fortune Reputation Survey, obtained from Fortune magazine for 1998, 1999, and 2000, reflecting respondents' subjective evaluation of each firm's overall product or service quality. The three yearly QUAL scores were used as indicators of the latent variable Quality of Products or Services. Although INNOV and QUAL were highly correlated, discriminant validity tests showed they represented two different constructs.

variable_name: compound annual growth rates of total assets, total revenues, and market capitalization
description: A firm's growth performance was measured by the three compound annual growth rates of total assets, total revenues, and market capitalization from 1998 to 2000. A compound annual growth rate measures the rate of movement between the first year and the last year and then compounds this rate over the period; observations between the first and the last are not considered. The three growth rates were obtained directly from COMPUSTAT and used as indicators of the latent variable Growth.

A firm's profitability performance was measured by three profitability ratios: ROA, ROE, and ROI, which are strongly related to one another and were therefore used together as indicators of the latent variable Profitability. Values were computed as three-year averages of the study variables, using mean substitution for missing values. The ratios were obtained directly from COMPUSTAT.

variable_name: market-to-book ratio and Tobin's q ratio
description: A firm's market performance was measured by two market-based measures of return: the market-to-book ratio and Tobin's q ratio, used as indicators of the latent variable Market Value. The market-to-book ratio is the ratio of stock price to book value per share and was calculated on COMPUSTAT with the formula provided by Standard & Poor's. Tobin's q is the ratio of the market value of a firm's debt and equity to the current replacement cost of its assets; the authors used the approximate Tobin's q formula of Chung and Pruitt (1994) with COMPUSTAT data.

variable_name: Change in the trust in the government
description: In both surveys respondents were asked to rate their trust in a list of institutions, including the government, on a 1 to 7 scale where 1 indicates 'do not trust at all' and 7 indicates 'fully trust.' The variable is the individual-level change in trust in the government between the pre- and post-impeachment surveys. Trust in government is used as the measure of trust in (regulatory) institutions because it is the closest to the broader concept of generalized trust in institutions and is correlated with trust in specific institutions within government such as the courts, politicians, or civil servants.
scale: 1 to 7 in each survey (1 = do not trust at all, 7 = fully trust); analysis uses the change between surveys
time_window: pre-impeachment survey March 1-7, 2017 and post-impeachment survey April 3-7, 2017

variable_name: Change in the probability of starting a business within 5 years
description: Respondents were asked the likelihood that they would start a business in 5 years and chose a response from 0 to 100% in 10% increments. The analysis uses the change in this response between the post- and pre-impeachment surveys. The average was 31.34% in the pre-impeachment survey, and the mean difference between the post and pre impeachment survey is -0.27% point and is not significantly different from zero.
time_window: pre-impeachment survey March 1-7, 2017 and post-impeachment survey April 3-7, 2017

description: Dummy variables indicating whether the respondent attended or was attending a top 5, top 7, top 10, or top 30 university, using university rankings based on the Times Higher Education Rankings averages over three years (2015 to 2017). Nine percent of the respondents graduated from or was attending a top 7 university, and 30% a top 30 university.

Respondents who selected college or above were asked the name of the institution and major, and majors were categorized into seven categories. The regressions use a dummy equal to one if the respondent is or was a STEM major. Humanities and Social Sciences majors comprise 39% of the sample followed by Engineering and Science majors at 31%, Business majors at 15%, Arts/Sports at 6%, Medicine at 5%, Education at 3% and Law at 1%.

The success of the group's initial investment decision was conveyed in a memo from the Board of Directors. In the success condition the memo stated that the decision had been a clear success and was accompanied by a table of sales and earnings showing clear performance improvements in the division that received the funding; in the failure condition the memo stated that the decision was a failure and was accompanied by a table showing clear performance declines in that division.
scale: two levels: success feedback, failure feedback

description: High or low perceived slack, as an attribute of the firm's current resource position, was conveyed in a memo from the Board. In the high-slack condition the memo stated that the courts had ruled in favor of the firm in a patent infringement lawsuit and that the firm would receive damage payments, so that $15 million would be available to the Committee. In the low-slack condition the memo stated that the courts had ruled against the firm, that it must pay damages, and that only $15 million would be available. All groups had $15 million available for reinvestment.
scale: two levels: high perceived slack, low perceived slack

description: In the positive frame condition the acceptable risk measure for the subsequent reinvestment decision was operationalized in terms of a success orientation, with the poles labeled 'lowest chance of success' (0 in 10) and 'highest chance of success' (10 in 10), and a memo from the Board stated that a major goal of the Planning Committee was to maximize total profits over time and that the reinvestment decision should be made with the goal of 'high future gains'. In the negative frame condition the acceptable risk measure was phrased in terms of chances of failure and the memo stated that a major objective was to minimize total losses over time and to limit financial loss and waste.
scale: two levels: positive frame, negative frame

description: After receiving the manipulations, each group was asked to decide what portion of an available $15 million should be reinvested in the division receiving the original investment. Each group discussed the decision, entered a dollar amount, and signed the group decision; uninvested funds reverted to the firm's general pool.
scale: dollars out of the $15 million available

description: Decision feedback and perceived slack were merged into one variable: half of the subjects received failure feedback on the initial decision together with the memo indicating low organizational slack, and the other half received success feedback on the initial decision together with the memo indicating high organizational slack.
scale: two levels: failure feedback/low perceived slack, success feedback/high perceived slack

description: Within each of the feedback/slack conditions, half of the subjects received the positive frame for the upcoming reinvestment decision and the other half received the negative frame.
scale: two levels: positive frame, negative frame

description: Each subject was asked to decide what portion of an available $15 million should be reinvested in the division receiving the original investment, and was informed that uninvested funds reverted to the firm's general pool. Each subject decided on a dollar amount and signed the decision.
scale: dollars out of the $15 million available

description: The piracy shock is the hacking event in which a group copied all of the files held on the major repositories of the cydia marketplace and released pirated versions of the entire population of applications for free, which was not expected by the content developers. Treated products are those sold at a nonzero price prior to the hacking event that had not previously been pirated. The effect is identified by the interaction of an indicator for the period after the piracy event (Post) with the treated indicator, which captures the difference in the response of the treatment group relative to the control group.
time_window: 12 months before and after the piracy event

description: Indicator for whether a given product was updated in a given month. If an update is released this indicates that a product had been revised, while if no updates were released this indicates that a product has been abandoned. A decline in the number of updates, or in the probability of an updating event each month, indicates a decline in innovation and a shift toward product abandonment.
time_window: 12 months before and after the piracy event

description: Indicator for the release of an incremental innovation, defined as minor tweaks released in order to correct minor issues or account for incompatibility issues, often referred to as bug fixes. Incremental innovations are distinguished by the version number, where a shift in the later numbers indicates only a minor change according to version numbering conventions, for instance shifting from Version 1.0.0 to Version 1.0.1.
time_window: 12 months before and after the piracy event

description: Indicator for the release of a substantial innovation, defined as feature updates or other major product revisions where the software application experiences a considerable improvement in quality or user experience. Substantial innovations are distinguished by a substantial shift in the first digit of the version number, such as a shift from Version 1.0 to Version 2.0.
time_window: 12 months before and after the piracy event

description: Count of new products launched, used as the outcome variable in a replication of the difference-in-differences regression. The data are aggregated to the firm (developer) level, including an indicator for whether the developer was affected by the piracy event.
time_window: 12 months before and after the piracy event

description: Average daily product downloads, used as a measure of product popularity. The variable is constructed as a single value at the time of piracy rather than varying over time, so that the regression uses one observation pre/post the piracy event.

The age of the product, included in the heterogeneity analysis together with other product and developer covariates. The value is collapsed to one observation pre/post the piracy event to avoid having multiple observations for a time-invariant variable.

A mean index of the ten HR practices, created in order to test the models of mediation and moderation. The index was transformed into a z-score and then interacted with the z-score for each customer segment variable. The authors note that the use of standardized z-scores in interaction terms allows them to be directly interpreted in relation to the mean of the interacted variable and reduces multicollinearity.

Created to capture the basic skill requirements of the customer service or sales job at each call center, it is the mean of two variables: the number of years of formal education of the typical (median) core employee and the number of years of formal and on-the-job training needed for a new employee to become proficient. The variables were transformed to z-scores.

The mean of four variables transformed to z-scores: two measures of individual discretion and two of employee collaboration in teams. The individual discretion scales used a 1-5 Likert response format, where 1 is 'little or no control' and 5 is 'complete control'; discretion over work methods included eight questions adapted from MacDuffie (1995) assessing influence over tasks, tools, work methods, pace of work, schedules, vacations, and technology design, and discretion over customer interactions used two additional questions on control over handling nonroutine requests and control over the pace of serving customers. Team participation included the percentage of employees that participated in regular off-line problem-solving groups and the percentage that participated in self-directed teams.

The mean value of four z-scored variables: ongoing training, employment security, pay level, and electronic performance monitoring. Ongoing training was measured by the number of weeks of training a typical core employee received each year; pay was the natural logarithm of the median annual base pay of the core workforce; employment security was the percentage of the core workforce that was permanent and full-time, as opposed to part-time or contingent; and electronic monitoring was measured as the percentage of the work performance of the typical employee that was electronically monitored, reverse-coded.

The dependent variable in the quit rate equations is the average annual quit rate. The measure of quits excluded discharges, retirements, transfers, and promotions. Because the dependent variable is 'left-censored' at zero, a Tobit model was estimated.

The natural logarithm of the percent change in the value of sales to the particular customer base served by the center, measured in the prior two-year period. Sales equations were estimated with OLS regression because there was no censoring of the data.

Establishments were dummy-coded as serving all customers in their market (these are called universal centers) or as serving a particular segment (large business, small business, or residential). If they served two segments, respondents were asked to answer all questions as they pertained to the segment with the largest volume of customers, and in all analyses universal center was the omitted category. Operator service centers were separated out because they provide a mass-market service likely to generate little or no revenue, so they were included in the analysis of quit rates but not in the analysis of sales growth.

New Domains is the total number of classes, new to the firm, in which the firm files for patents in the year. A domain is defined as the USPTO three-digit technology primary class, and a class is defined as new to the firm if the firm has not applied for patents in the class within the prior 5 years.
time_window: year t, with newness assessed over the prior 5 years

description: Binary version of the dependent variable used in the firm-year-technology class tests. It equals 1 if the firm i entered class j in year t and is 0 otherwise. For each firm-year the potential set of new domains is all USPTO technology classes in which the firm has not filed for patents during the prior 5 years and that fall within an NBER technology subcategory in which the firm has patented in the prior 5 years.
time_window: year t, with newness assessed over the prior 5 years

description: Coded 1 if the firm's primary law firm failed during the year and 0 otherwise. Because the law firms exited at different points in the year, the date of failure is mapped to the nearest year; for instance, a failure in December 2003 is coded 1 in 2004 and 0 in 2003. A value of 1 marks the loss of the firm's primary IP law firm, i.e., a reduction in its litigation ability.
time_window: year of the law firm's failure

description: Coded 1 if the firm's primary law firm failed during the year and 0 otherwise, with the date of failure mapped to the nearest year. The same treatment indicator is used in the firm-year-technology class sample that tests the contingency hypotheses.
time_window: year of the law firm's failure

description: For each nonfocal technology class k in which firm i had a patent filing within the past 5 years, the authors identify all inventors (including inventors outside the focal firm) with at least three patents in the prior 10 years, and count how many of these inventors in class k have also patented in the focal class j. That count is divided by the total number of inventors in k, and the resulting ratios are averaged across all technology classes k for firm i in year t.
time_window: year t, using firm patent filings in the prior 5 years and inventors with at least three patents in the prior 10 years

description: For each primary class j in year t, the authors identify all inventors with at least three patents over the prior 10 years that have patented in j. Within this list, an inventor is coded as having switched if she had been listed in more than one firm across patent filings, and Inventor Mobility counts the total number of inventors that switched during the period. The authors use the count as the primary measure and, in a robustness test, also scale it by the total pool of inventors.
time_window: year t, over the prior 10 years

description: The count of patent lawsuits the firm files per year, analyzed to show that the exit of the firm's primary law firm reduces the firm's litigation ability. It is modeled with negative binomial and fixed effect Poisson regressions of the count of lawsuits filed in a year.
Used in an additional analysis as a proxy for litigation ability instrumented by Law Firm Exit in a Poisson control function model of New Domains.

Respondents were asked whether the firm's employment practices were regulated by the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (1 = yes, 0 = no). This was one of three measures of EEO-AA intervention into an organization's personnel practices included in the survey.

Respondents were asked whether the firm had been the subject of an EEO-AA-related lawsuit in the last five years (1 = yes, 0 = no). The time frame on the lawsuits measure was restricted to the last five years to minimize the possibility that most of the respondents would reply in the affirmative, which would have resulted in a constant rather than a variable.

Respondents were asked whether the firm had ever been the subject of a compliance review (1 = yes, 0 = no). The time frame on the compliance review question was open ended to avoid the possibility that most of the respondents would reply in the negative, given the low probability of a company's being reviewed in any given year.

The survey form included 119 items describing formalized HRM structures, and respondents indicated whether or not their companies had adopted each structure. Two independent raters categorized each item as identity-conscious or identity-blind, and the 2 items on which the raters did not agree were eliminated. The index was created by taking the mean across the identity-conscious items, so the index score indicated the proportion of the listed identity-conscious structures adopted by each organization. Cronbach's alpha for the index was .93.

The survey form included 119 items describing formalized HRM structures, and respondents indicated whether or not their companies had adopted each structure. Two independent raters categorized each item as identity-conscious or identity-blind, and the 2 items on which the raters did not agree were eliminated. The index was created by taking the mean across the identity-blind items, so the index score indicated the proportion of the listed identity-blind structures adopted by each organization. Cronbach's alpha for the index was .88.

To assess top management's EEO-AA values, respondents were asked to respond to three survey items developed for the present research. The items were coded so that a high value indicated stronger support of EEO-AA. Cronbach's alpha for the three items was .89.

variable_name: percentage of employees who were women
description: Respondents were asked to estimate the percentage of employees in the company who were women. Five possible response options were given (0%, 1-10%, 11-25%, 26-50%, and 51% or more), and the midpoints of the ranges were used in the analysis (0, 5, 18, 38, and 51).

variable_name: percentage of managers who were women
description: Respondents were asked to estimate the percentage of managers in the company who were women. Five possible response options were given (0%, 1-10%, 11-25%, 26-50%, and 51% or more), and the midpoints of the ranges were used in the analysis (0, 5, 18, 38, and 51).

variable_name: percentage of employees who were people of color
description: Respondents were asked to estimate the percentage of employees in the company who were people of color. Five possible response options were given (0%, 1-10%, 11-25%, 26-50%, and 51% or more), and the midpoints of the ranges were used in the analysis (0, 5, 18, 38, and 51).

variable_name: percentage of managers who were people of color
description: Respondents were asked to estimate the percentage of managers in the company who were people of color. Five possible response options were given (0%, 1-10%, 11-25%, 26-50%, and 51% or more), and the midpoints of the ranges were used in the analysis (0, 5, 18, 38, and 51).

Each respondent was asked to indicate the number of layers of management or reporting levels between the lowest-level employee and the top executive, and then how many layers existed between the top executive and the highest-ranking woman. The ratio between the level attained by the highest-ranking woman and the top executive and the total number of levels in the organization was calculated; the variable had a potential range of 0 to 1, with a higher value indicating a higher management level attained.

Each respondent was asked to indicate the number of layers of management or reporting levels between the lowest-level employee and the top executive, and then how many layers existed between the top executive and the highest-ranking person of color. The ratio between the level attained by the highest-ranking person of color and the top executive and the total number of levels in the organization was calculated; the variable had a potential range of 0 to 1, with a higher value indicating a higher management level attained.

Respondents indicated whether their firm had adopted each of 119 formalized HRM structures. Two raters sorted items into identity-conscious and identity-blind sets, and each index is the proportion of structures in its set that the firm adopted.

The variable of interest in the difference-in-differences specifications is the interaction between Post-AIPA and U.S. patent. Post-AIPA equals one for licenses based on patent applications filed on or after November 29, 2000 (AIPA's effective date) and zero for applications filed before this date; U.S. patent equals one for licenses based on U.S. patent applications without foreign equivalents (the treatment group) and zero for foreign applications and U.S. applications with equivalent foreign applications. Before-and-after specifications use Post-AIPA alone as the variable of interest. Of the 440 licenses, 22.5% belong to the post-AIPA regime and 52.7% belong to the treatment group.

Binary variable that equals one if the licensing event occurs after patent grant and zero otherwise. It is the dependent variable in the probit regressions of the probability of licensing after patent grant and the reference outcome in the multinomial logit models of the licensing window. Among treatment-group patent applications, 56% of the pre-AIPA applications are licensed after grant, whereas only 28% delay until grant after AIPA.

Categorical dependent variable in the multinomial logit: one if licensing takes place before 18 months from application, two if licensing takes place after 18 months but before patent grant, and three if licensing takes place after grant (the reference outcome). In the panel-structured probit regressions the dependent variable equals one for the month in which the license was signed and zero otherwise, and Publication window equals one for months after 18 months but within 28, 30, or 32 months after application.
scale: three-category nominal; monthly indicator in the panel data

description: The number of months between the patent application date and the license date; the dependent variable in the Tobit regressions and the duration outcome in the Cox proportional hazard model of licensing. The authors report that the average patent is licensed 48.2 months after application.

Indicator of the licensor's organizational type in the license agreement. Thirty-two percent of the sample's licensors are nonprofit organizations (universities, hospitals, and research institutes), and among licensors 68.6% are for-profit entities, of which 66% are corporations and 2.2% individual inventors.

The number of deals captured by the RecapIP database (all types of deals, including those that do not contain contracts or identifiable IP information) that the licensor has undertaken as a seller prior to the focal agreement. For the heterogeneity analysis the licensor is defined as less experienced separately for the pre- and post-AIPA periods if its past number of deals is less than or equal to the respective median; 74% of the treatment-group licensors have at least one deal prior to the license, and the median is 3.5 before AIPA and four after AIPA.

The consumer's value rating was measured as the number of stars (out of five) assigned to the restaurant by the reviewer. Ratings are made individually by reviewers and can be filled out in whichever order relative to the text of the review. In the restaurant-month analyses, the outcome variable is the average rating the restaurant receives in a month.
time_window: review date; monthly aggregation in the restaurant-month panel, with value ratings at t+1 predicted from variables at t

description: Content analysis was conducted on the text of each review, with the goal of assessing whether the reviewer described the restaurant as authentic or inauthentic and to what degree. For each review the authenticity values of all the words that appear in the review and are also listed in the authenticity keyword list were averaged; restaurant-level analyses average these scores across reviews. Both the score from the focal review and the average authenticity score of all reviews prior to the focal review were used.
time_window: contemporaneous (focal review) and lagged (previous reviews; month t-1)

description: Whether the restaurant was affiliated with a larger chain, identified by determining the number of restaurants listed with the same name in the metropolitan area.

Whether the restaurant is family owned (or family operated), measured by searching for the term 'family-owned' (or 'family-operated') in the text of the reviews; those restaurants identified by reviewers as family owned or operated were flagged.

Category population was measured by the count of categories occupied by the restaurant. Each restaurant is categorized by the website into a particular cuisine such as American, Mexican, or Italian, sometimes in consultation with the restaurant; some restaurants are placed into a single category and others into multiple categories.

Participants were asked to estimate how much they would like the restaurant and its offerings, on a scale from 1 to 5, although half points were allowed. To resemble the online review system, the ratings panel used stars for its scale and asked respondents to click on the appropriate number.
time_window: elicited after the quality, price, and authenticity prompts

description: Participants were presented with a list of 30 keywords (the 10 highest and 10 lowest authenticity-related keywords plus 10 quality-related keywords) and asked to group them into 'words that are likely to appear in customers' reviews' and 'words that are likely not to appear in customers' reviews'. The authenticity score was calculated as the mean authenticity scores of the words the participant grouped as likely to be in reviews minus the mean authenticity value of the words grouped as likely not to be in the reviews.

Experimental condition: the vignette text described the restaurant as family owned. The text of the amplified conditions was very brief and straightforward, and the baseline conditions were created by removing the descriptive clauses.

Experimental condition: the vignette text described the restaurant as chain owned (e.g., founded by a company that owns and operates several restaurants throughout the Northeast). Ownership was manipulated with three conditions: family owned, chain owned, or a baseline with no information about ownership.

Experimental condition with two levels, single category or multiple category. The multiple-category condition added a sentence listing additional cuisines (e.g., 'They also serve a range of American favorites such as barbecue, hamburgers, and fries'); removing that sentence gives the single-category condition.

Coded 1 if the MNE's home nation has greater ties to Brazil than the rival MNE's home nation, and 0 otherwise. Ties is the sum of five indicators: whether the home nation shares a land border with Brazil, had colonial contact with Brazil, had marked immigration to or from Brazil, has a Portuguese or Latin root language, and has a 'civil code' legal system. The resulting ordering on ties to Brazil was Europe > Japan > United States, where Japan's ties exceed U.S. ties because of sizable immigration from Japan to Brazil and because geography was coded 1 only for a shared land border.
scale: binary (1 = greater ties, 0 = not greater ties)

description: Coded 1 if the MNE dominated its foreign rival in the latter's home market, and 0 otherwise. Only a handful of MNEs (five to be precise) entered the 'dominate' group coded 1; the rest were assigned to the 'contest' group coded 0. Instances of rivalry were thereby categorized as dominated or contested based on status in home-home rivalry.
scale: binary (1 = dominates rival in rival's home market, 0 = contested)

description: The dependent variable, foreign MNE leadership in Brazil, coded based on MNE sales shares in Brazil. Within each of the four cells formed by relative TECH and relative TIES, the authors state the ratio of lead to total MNEs and use these sample proportions to specify the logit model; the underlying unit of analysis was an individual MNE headquartered in Europe, Japan, or the United States.
scale: binary (lead vs. not lead); group proportions used in the logit model
level: individual MNE, aggregated into four groups for estimation

description: The independent variable in the difference-in-differences regressions is the interaction Treatment x Post-activism. Treatment receives a value of one if the firm is targeted by institutional investor activists and zero for control firms. Post-activism receives a value of one for the three years following an activism event, including the event year, and zero for the three years before the event.
time_window: three years before and three years after the activism event

description: TCR is computed as the number of work-related injuries and illnesses divided by the number of hours worked by all employees in a given establishment year. The value is multiplied by 1,000,000 to facilitate presentation. Data on TCR are obtained from OSHA, and the variable is measured at the establishment level.

The variable is measured based on the political ideology of the shareholder activist using political campaign contributions. The authors identify the political donations of all fund managers working for an institutional investor activist from the CRP database and follow Chin et al. (2013) to measure fund managers' political liberalism; the institution-level score is the weighted average of its fund managers' liberalism scores. An activist is classified as liberal if its liberalism score is higher than 0.5 and as nonliberal otherwise.

Each director's political campaign contributions are collected from CRP based on their primary employer's name and occupation, and the director's liberalism score is calculated using the same method as for activist liberalism. Directors who have not made any political contribution are assigned a value of 0.5. Board liberalism is the average of all the directors' liberalism scores; a firm is considered to have a liberal board if board liberalism is higher than 0.5 and a nonliberal board otherwise.

The dependent variable is Log (Tobin's q). Tobin's q is calculated as the ratio of the sum of market capitalization and total assets minus the book value of shareholders' equity over total assets for the focal firm in each year in the sample. Stock market data come from DataStream and accounting data from WorldScope.

Index of internal CSR actions built from 120 Thomson Reuters (ASSET4) data points that the authors independently classified, using a working decision rule that classified as internal those actions that are more internally oriented in terms of policies; the category includes corporate policy questions and several quantitative indicators of CSR implementation. Questionable items and items with a majority of missing data were dropped, and items with negative coefficients in the Cronbach's alpha test were dropped, leaving an index with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.75 (inter-item covariance of 0.06). The index is normalized on a 0-1 scale and divided by total (logged) assets, lagged one year.
