The measure was operationalized as the average responses to two items: relationships with officials in regulatory and supporting institutions (e.g., Internal Revenue Service, Environmental Protection Agency, etc.) and officials in investment and industrial institutions (e.g., Investment Board, Export Promotion Council, etc.).
scale: seven-point scale ranging from 1 'very little' to 7 'very extensive'

variable_name: social networking relationships with community leaders
description: Respondents assessed the extent to which top managers have developed and utilized personal and social networking relationships with community leaders for the three-year periods 1998-2000 and 2001-2003, on a seven-point scale ranging from 1 'very little' to 7 'very extensive'. The measure was operationalized as the average responses to two items: relationship with local kings, chiefs and/or their representatives, and leaders of religious organizations (e.g., pastors, traditional religious leaders, and imams). The Cronbach alpha was 0.84.
scale: seven-point scale ranging from 1 'very little' to 7 'very extensive'

description: The average top management tenure in a firm, i.e., the number of years that top managers have spent in a particular firm. It represents the experiential knowledge that is preserved at the top management of firms.

A dummy variable coded 1 for firms whose respondents answered 'yes' to whether the business is family owned, and 0 for firms whose respondents answered 'no'. Respondents also indicated with 'yes' or 'no' whether family members controlled the business and were involved in the business as directors or employees; all respondents who answered 'yes' to whether the business is family owned also answered 'yes' to the other two questions.

Ordinal measure of the outcome of the company's conflict minerals report: 0 when the company was unable to determine whether its products contain conflict minerals, 1 when it stated it had no reason to believe its products contain minerals originating from the Congo area, and 2 when it declared its products free from conflict minerals with a great level of certainty and evidence beyond reasonable doubt. Outcomes were first coded semi-automatically with regular expressions detecting outcome-related keywords, and then three research assistants blind to the hypotheses independently read each document; the semi-automated and manual codings differed in less than 5% of reports, in which case the Responsible Sourcing Network was consulted.

Entropy measure of total diversification that measures the extent to which a firm operates in a number of industries, using a weighted average of the proportion of a firm's sales made in each of the industry segments; each segment can have up to two four-digit SIC codes. The entropy formula is presented as an equation block that was not extracted, so the exact specification cannot be reproduced here. For companies that operate in only a single industry segment, this measure has the value of 0.

Calculated in the same manner as total diversification, except that segments are defined at the two-digit SIC level; the measure is calculated after first summing sales across two-digit SIC categories.
Calculated by subtracting unrelated diversification from total diversification.

A company's foreign sales divided by its total sales, used to measure the depth of international diversification and commonly used in the diversification literature to measure a company's multinationality.

Number of countries in which a company had at least one subsidiary, with the natural log taken of the total count to correct for its positively skewed distribution; used to measure the breadth of international diversification. Calculated from Compustat segment files and the LexisNexis Directory of Corporate Affiliations, which lists all current corporate affiliations of nearly 2 million companies; the corporate affiliations data as of June 30, 2016 were used, assuming the number of foreign countries with a subsidiary remains stable within the past 12-month window.
time_window: as of June 30, 2016, lagged one year relative to the 2015 reports

description: Total number of current suppliers with which the focal company has enduring business relations, with the natural log taken of the total count to adjust for its positively skewed distribution. Taken from the Bloomberg Supply Chain Function, which maps about 35,000 companies with their suppliers and buyers from public filings, announcements, and other proprietary data; the data as of December 31, 2015 were used, assuming the number of suppliers remains stable within the past 12-month window.
Percentage of a focal company's cost of goods sold that is spent on its five main suppliers. Based on the Bloomberg Supply Chain Function data as of December 31, 2015.

Cost of goods sold divided by the average inventory, used as a proxy of a firm's power over its direct suppliers; firms with power over suppliers can shift inventory tasks to suppliers and thereby show higher inventory turnover. Calculated from Compustat data.

Natural log of the number of news articles mentioning a given company during the 12 months leading up to the SEC filing due date. Articles were collected from four influential daily newspapers with nationwide circulation: New York Times, USA Today, Wall Street Journal, and Washington Post.
time_window: 12 months leading up to the SEC filing due date

description: Binary variable that takes the value 1 if a firm appeared on Fortune's Most Admired Companies top 50 list in 2014 and 0 otherwise. The annual list is based on a large-scale survey of executives, outside directors, and securities analysts rating the 10 largest companies in their operating industry on eight criteria.

Binary variable that had the value of 1 if a company participated in the Carbon Disclosure Project's survey in 2014 and 0 otherwise. CDP is a United Kingdom-based nonprofit that collects firm-level data on greenhouse gas emissions and climate change strategies, including Scope 3 emissions along the supply chain, on behalf of 767 institutional investors.

Technology similarity between the acquiring and target firms was operationalized using the number of patents in the same three-digit patent classes in 1996, considering all patent classes for a patent and not only the primary one. This measure captures the extent to which two firms develop technology in the same patent classes, hence using similar technological knowledge. It is calculated as the number of patents applied for by the target and acquirer that are in the same patent classes, multiplied by the total number of patents the acquirer has in all common classes divided by total acquirer patents.

Technology complementarity is operationalized as the number of patents in the same subcategory but in different patent classes in 1996. The measure mirrors the theoretical conceptualization of complementarity because it captures the integrative potential between two firms: if two firms' patents build on the subcategory 'Biotechnology' in the category 'Drugs and Chemical,' the extent to which they build on different technological classes (e.g., patent class 435 vs. patent class 800) captures their integrative potential.

The logic underlying this construct is that the degree of similarity in research publications of two firms' scientists reflects the degree of similarity in the firms' scientific knowledge. The science similarity variable was operationalized as the overlap in the research communities in which the acquirer and target publish, using the CRP indicator of a firm's membership in a research community. Science similarity is calculated differently than technology similarity (without the weights) because each research community is distinct for each firm.

Science complementarity is defined as the extent to which the target and acquirer build on the same science disciplines but not on the same research communities. It captures the extent to which two firms draw from related but different areas of science and is based on the number of unique (nonoverlapping) research communities in which each firm participates within the science disciplines that they share. Research communities and science disciplines are drawn from the CRP classification of firms' scientific knowledge.

Annual data from the USPTO on the number of patents for which the firm applied three years pre M&A (1994-1996) and three years post M&A (1999-2001). Three change measures (1999, 2000, and 2001) were created by subtracting the 1994-1996 value from the 1999-2001 value and then dividing that difference by the 1999-2001 value (i.e., the 1994 value was subtracted from the 1999 value for the 1999 change measure, etc.).

The number of citations for five years after the grant date on all patents for which a firm applied in the three-year pre-M&A window (1994-1996), divided by the total number of patents during each of those three years, producing an annual citations-per-patent ratio; the same was done for the 1999-2001 window. Three change measures for 1999, 2000, and 2001 were constructed using the procedure described for the invention quantity change measures. To test Hypothesis 1b, invention quality is operationalized as the number of citations to the acquirer's patents within the same classes pre and post M&A, weighted by the number of patents within each class.
time_window: five-year post-grant citation window; 1994-1996 pre-M&A and 1999-2001 post-M&A

description: An index of technological diversification similar to a Herfindahl index of concentration, where Sij denotes the percentage of patents that the ith firm holds in class j and the index is one minus the sum of the squared shares, with n the total number of patent classes the firm is involved in. If a firm is involved in a wide range of technologies the measure will be high, whereas if most patents are concentrated in a few fields it will be low (close to zero). The index was calculated for the three-year pre-M&A and three-to-five-year post-M&A windows, and the novelty change measures for 1999, 2000, and 2001 were created in a manner similar to the quantity and quality change measures.
scale: index, low (close to zero) for concentrated portfolios and high for broad portfolios

description: X-efficiency is computed on a country-by-country basis from an alternative profit function estimated with the stochastic frontier approach, which decomposes the error term into a random error and a time-invariant inefficiency component; the data are transformed using natural logarithms (translog) and the inefficiency components are averaged for each bank. Outputs are total loans and other earning assets; inputs are labor, physical capital, and funds, with the price of labor equal to salary expenses and fringe benefits over total assets, the price of physical capital equal to premises and fixed asset expenses over total assets, and the price of funds equal to total interest expenses over total funds. X-efficiency scores range from 0 < EFF ≤ 1, where 1 is the best-practicing bank in each country. Because efficient frontiers and accounting standards differ across countries, scores are normalized within each host country using its mean and standard deviation, so that a score greater (less) than zero indicates above (below) average X-efficiency in that environment. The exact translog specification is not readable in the text.
scale: X-efficiency score 0 < EFF ≤ 1; normalized scores centered on zero within host country

description: Banks are grouped into host country banks, which are headquartered in the particular host country, and foreign-owned banks, which operate in a particular host country with a parent's headquarters in a different country; all data represent the banks' operations in the host country. The authors used foreign-owned subsidiaries rather than foreign branches because subsidiaries face the same legal and regulatory requirements as host country banks and require separately capitalized charters in each host country. Banks that had operated in a host country for less than four years, and the initial two years of any new entrant, were removed. The two groups are compared on mean normalized X-efficiency.

The variable reflects the relative financial system efficiency score between a foreign-owned bank's home country and the host country. The underlying country score is Demirgüç-Kunt and Levine's (2000) measure of financial system efficiency, computed as total value added divided by net interest margin, where a high (low) score indicates an efficient (inefficient) financial system. If the difference between the home and host country scores is positive, the bank has relatively high financial system efficiency; if negative, relatively low financial system efficiency.
level: foreign-owned bank (home country relative to host country)

description: A dichotomous variable based on whether the home country of a foreign-owned bank has regulations similar to those of the host country in which it operates. Host countries are classified as low-regulation when banks may engage in securities-related activities within the bank, and high-regulation when such activities must be conducted in legally separate subsidiaries. If home and host regulations are similar the bank is categorized as low regulatory distance, otherwise high regulatory distance.

variable_name: Financial system distance (high/low financial system distance)
description: Host country financial system orientation is measured as the ratio of the sum of market capitalization and international bonds outstanding to the sum of market capitalization, international bonds outstanding, money supply (M2), and total bank claims, averaged over 1989-96; a high ratio indicates a capital market-oriented system and a low ratio a bank-oriented system. The six host countries with the highest ratios were considered capital market-oriented and the remaining seven bank-oriented. A foreign-owned bank is coded low financial system distance when its home country's financial system orientation is similar to the host country's, and high financial system distance otherwise.
scale: dichotomous (low vs. high financial system distance)

description: U.S.-owned banks are the subgroup of foreign-owned banks whose parent is headquartered in the United States and that operate in the sample host countries; the banking activity within the United States is excluded as a host country. The variable distinguishes these banks from other foreign-owned banks, which come from the other sample home countries. The two groups are compared on mean normalized X-efficiency.

A dummy variable coded 1 if there was an increase in the number of female directors at the firm from the prior year and 0 otherwise. Because a firm increasing the number of female directors by two or more in a single year happened in less than 1% of the cases, the variable captures any increase. To ensure that an increase was not a temporary arrangement, the authors checked the number of female directors in year t+1 and kept the coding as 1 only if the increase was maintained in year t+1.
time_window: prior year (t-1) to year t, confirmed in year t+1

description: One of three indicators used to capture the external pressure for a firm to increase female directors, based on the argument that proponents and advocacy groups for greater board gender diversity have largely targeted large firms in the Fortune 500 list. Measured as the logarithm of annual revenues.

One of three indicators used to capture the external pressure for a firm to increase female directors. Following Hillman et al. (2007), measured as the ratio of women in the workforce in the firm's industry at the two-digit SIC level.

One of three indicators used to capture the external pressure for a firm to increase female directors. Measured as the average number of female directors at firms that were within the same industry at the two-digit SIC level and listed in the same S&P large-cap, mid-cap, or small-cap index as the focal firm.

A dummy variable coded as 1 if the firm had two or more female directors on the board and as 0 otherwise. In robustness analysis the authors measured the presence of female directors as the ratio of female directors on the board and the findings were essentially the same.

variable_name: increase through addition of board seats
description: A dummy variable coded 1 if the increase in female directors was accompanied by an increase in board size (measured by the number of directors) at the firm from the prior year. When there was an increase in the number of female directors but no increase in board size, it indicated that the increase was done through substitution of male directors and was coded 0. To ensure that an increase in board size was not a temporary arrangement, board size in year t+1 was checked and the coding was kept as 1 only if the increase in board size was maintained in year t+1.
time_window: prior year (t-1) to year t, confirmed in year t+1

description: A dummy variable coded as 1 if a newly added female director served on any of the four major board committees (audit, compensation, nomination, and governance) during her first 3 years on the board. The observation period was limited to the first 3 years because direct interactions with male directors over time may weaken social categorization based on salient demographic attributes. The measure was also tested using membership during the first, second, and third year, respectively, with consistent results.

Indicator variable that takes a value of 1 for an investment recommendation submitted with a detailed justification and 0 if a simple justification was used. Detailed justifications thoroughly discuss the analysis leading to the recommendation, have a minimum of 600 words and average over 1,400 words, and their content is monitored by the platform to ensure a minimal level of quality and rigor. Simple justifications state support for the recommendation, have a maximum of 40 words and average 24 words, and their content is not strictly monitored other than the word limit.

Sum of the number of unique earnings estimates for the stock featured in the investment recommendation in each of the four quarters prior to that recommendation; the measure was not changed if estimates were updated within a given quarter. For example, three unique analysts covering a stock in each of the last four quarters and two other analysts covering it for two of the last four quarters gives a value of 16. Because buy-in uncertainty decreases as sell-side coverage increases, the reciprocal of the measure was used in the analyses.
time_window: four quarters prior to the recommendation

description: Calculated as the difference between the year the investment recommendation was submitted and the initial year the stock was covered in the CRSP database (most often the firm's initial public offering year), plus 1. The measure approximates the availability of historical data and information about a firm; as time passes there is more information and certainty about a firm's strategy, leadership, and performance. Because buy-in uncertainty decreases as firm age increases, the reciprocal of the measure was used in the analyses.

Number of articles in which a firm was discussed in the month preceding the investment recommendation, plus 1. These counts were hand-collected from a leading website focused on financial markets that aggregates and publishes news about stocks; a greater amount of media attention implies that a firm faces a higher level of scrutiny and attention. Because buy-in uncertainty decreases as media attention increases, the reciprocal of the measure was used in the analyses.

Ratio of the sum of shares of the firm's stock owned by each of the five largest institutional investors that file Form 13F to the total number of shares of the firm's stock outstanding, computed for each firm in the quarter preceding the investment recommendation. In the authors' example, if the five largest institutional investors collectively owned 60 of 100 outstanding shares, the measure takes the value 0.60.

Ratio of the total number of shares of the firm's stock owned by the remaining institutional investors (those outside the five largest) to the total number of shares outstanding, computed for each firm in the quarter preceding the investment recommendation. In the authors' example this equals (80 - 60)/100 = 0.20. For stocks that had fewer than five institutional investors, this measure took a value of 0.

Dichotomous variable that takes a value of 1 if the investment recommendation was to short sell the stock and a value of 0 if the recommendation was to buy and hold the stock. Short selling is a feature of the U.S. stock market and its presence offers an empirical opportunity to further test the main hypothesis because the costs of not achieving buy-in are much greater for a short-selling opportunity than for a buy-and-hold opportunity.

Cumulative abnormal return of a stock recommended with knowledge sharing, computed as the sum of the stock's abnormal returns over an event window, where the abnormal return is the stock's actual return minus its expected return. The expected return was estimated using an ordinary least squares regression of the stock's return on the market's return, here the value-weighted index of all stocks in the CRSP database, with coefficients estimated using a 239-day window prior to the start of the event window. The event window is 21 days, the 10 days prior to the submission of a detailed justification to the 10 days after, with the day of submission being day 0.
time_window: 21-day event window (10 days before to 10 days after submission)

description: Respondents were asked to estimate for their firm the value of investments (replacement cost) in computer automation and in total manufacturing outlay to compute IFA. The measure is the ratio of capital outlay in computer automation to total manufacturing outlay, both at replacement value. Comparatively higher proportions indicated a high IFA and lower proportions, a low IFA. Respondents were also asked which subtechnologies within FA were used and how long each had been in use, to confirm that both CAD and CAM were in place.

Managers were asked to objectively report sales for 3 years (1987-89). Average percentage sales growth over those years was used in the analysis. The performance implications reported in the results pertain to sales growth only since it turned out to be more significant than ROI.

Managers were asked to objectively report ROI for 3 years (1987-89), and average ROI was used in the analysis. Regression performed with ROI did not produce valid results; the IFA-moderator interactions were statistically insignificant for most variables. The authors attribute this to the absence of robust schemes for measuring the cost-profit impact of FA and to subjective assessment by respondents.

Three items on a 5-point Likert scale measured the importance the firm attached to scope flexibility competitive methods in comparison to direct competition. Group scores were summed and averaged. High scores indicated a high emphasis for this strategy construct.

Five items on a 5-point Likert scale measured the importance the firm attached to speed flexibility competitive methods in comparison to direct competition. Group scores were summed and averaged. High scores indicated a high emphasis for this strategy construct.

Four items on a 5-point Likert scale measured the importance the firm attached to quality leadership competitive methods in comparison to direct competition. Group scores were summed and averaged. High scores indicated a high emphasis for this strategy construct.

Five items on a 5-point Likert scale measured the importance the firm attached to cost leadership competitive methods in comparison to direct competition. Group scores were summed and averaged. High scores indicated a high emphasis for this strategy construct.

Four items on a 5-point Likert scale measured the importance the firm attached to cooperation between its operations and environmental constituencies pertinent to operations. Items were summed and averaged to determine the high-low emphasis.

A semantic differential scale of 11 items measured structure on task, authority, and coordination dimensions, with scales numerically anchored from 1 to 5 such that extreme scores indicated mechanistic or organic traits. High scores indicated organic traits and low scores, mechanistic traits. The summed scores on the 11 items were used in data analysis.
A semantic differential scale numerically anchored from 1 to 5 was used; three of its items measured shopfloor personnel skills. Item one, two, and three measured shopfloor personnel skills.

A single item of the manufacturing structure semantic differential scale, numerically anchored from 1 to 5, measured the design-manufacturing workflow. The authors note that the construct was measured using a single item.

Two items of the manufacturing structure semantic differential scale, numerically anchored from 1 to 5, measured the use of project teams and workgroups. Items five and six measured use of project teams and workgroups.
The natural logarithm of the total number of an organization's employees.

Each respondent was asked to indicate whether the proportion of total female employees was under 20 percent, 20-39 percent, 40-59 percent, 60-79 percent, or 80 percent or more, and a 1-5 scale was created from these responses with 1 = under 20 percent. Because establishment-level data were not collected in 1989, data from a follow-up 1991 survey were used, assuming that the demographic composition of these firms had not changed significantly during the two-year period 1989-91. The measure reflects the extent to which an organization depends on a single resource.
Respondents indicated the proportion of total employees who were parents of children under age 18. The variable was coded like the female employees measure.

Data provided by the Washington State Employment Security Department were used to identify employers associated with federal, state, or local governments. A public-private dichotomous variable was created to reflect this distinction between institutional sectors.
The proportion of employers in the same industry group and in the same county as a focal organization adopting both child care services and workplace flexibility benefits.
The proportion of employers in other industry groups but in the same county adopting both child care services and workplace flexibility benefits.
The proportion of employers in the same industry group but in other counties adopting both child care services and workplace flexibility benefits.

variable_name: Total business, professional, and membership organizations
description: Using data provided by the Washington State Employment Security Department, the number of business, professional (including labor unions), and membership organizations in a particular county was specified. Membership organizations included civic, social, and fraternal associations, political organizations, and religious organizations.

Each employer was asked to indicate the perceived effects of child care services with respect to nine different outcomes: recruitment, retention, absenteeism, tardiness, employee stress, employee morale, employee loyalty, employee training costs, and employee productivity. Responses were coded as positive effects = 3, uncertain effects = 2, no effects = 1, and negative effects = 0, and the responses were then summed to create a total benefits scale.

Employers were asked to indicate the extent to which concerns about expense or liability represented an obstacle to their adoption of child care services. The response categories were not an obstacle = 0, not sure = 1, minor obstacle = 2, and major obstacle = 3. A summary scale was created from these responses, built from the variables liability costs and expenses.

The measure was developed from information on adoption of child care services and options affording flexibility to employees. Adoption of a child care service was noted if an organization provided at least one of three benefits: on-site child care, financial assistance with child care expenses, or child care resource and referral services; adoption of flexibility was noted if it provided at least one of flextime, voluntarily reduced work time, job sharing, work at home, flexible leave, or parental leave. Organizations providing at least one child care benefit and at least one flexibility benefit were categorized as acquiescence, those offering only one major type of benefit but multiple options within that area as compromise, those offering only one work-family benefit as avoidance, and those offering neither as defiance. The dependent variable assigned these values: acquiescence 3, compromise 2, avoidance 1, defiance 0.

A dichotomous dependent variable distinguishing organizations categorized as pursuing an acquiescence strategy, that is, those providing one child care benefit or more and one flexibility benefit or more. Four dichotomous dependent variables were created and included in separate logit models.

A dichotomous dependent variable distinguishing organizations categorized as pursuing a compromise strategy, that is, those offering only one major type of work-family benefit but multiple options within that area. Four dichotomous dependent variables were created and included in separate logit models.

A dichotomous dependent variable distinguishing organizations categorized as pursuing an avoidance strategy, that is, those offering only one work-family benefit. Four dichotomous dependent variables were created and included in separate logit models.

A dichotomous dependent variable distinguishing organizations providing neither child care nor workplace flexibility benefits. Four dichotomous dependent variables were created and included in separate logit models.

variable_name: Institutional pressure factors (cause, constituents, content, control, context)
description: Strength of institutional pressures is not a single variable. It is represented by the measures of the five Oliver (1991) factors, entered together as separate predictors in the models of the four strategies: organizational size (cause), percentage of female employees and percentage of working parents (constituents), public sector status (content), the three industry and county diffusion proportions (control), and the number of business, professional and membership organizations in the county (context). Pressures are read as strong when an organization is large, public, dependent on women and parents, and located where many similar organizations have adopted.
scale: Set of variables (log count, 1-5 category scales, dichotomy, proportions, count)

variable_name: betweenness centrality of interunit social interaction
description: Two sociomatrixes of social interaction among the 15 business units were constructed from two questions, one on time spent together on social occasions and one on close social relationships. For each sociomatrix a standardized betweenness index was calculated, and the two standardized betweenness indexes correlated .86. The zero-order correlation across the two indexes indicates that the two matrices were combined as a measure of a unit's centrality in the interunit social interaction network.

Two questions on interunit trusting relationships were used to create two relational matrixes measuring trust and trustworthiness. Because trusting relationships were directional, the in-degree centrality of an actor (unit i) was the number of units that indicated that they trusted unit i; in-degree was used as the measure of trustworthiness, counting the number of nominations each business unit received. The in-degree measure was standardized for each of the two networks, and the zero-order correlation for the two in-degree measures (reliability and promise keeping) was .96.

A two-item measure of the level of shared vision in the different business units, assessed on a seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). The three responses within each unit were simply averaged to get unit-level data, and the zero-order correlation for the two-item measure was .71.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

variable_name: in-degree centrality of resource exchange and combination
description: Four questions covered the flows of information, products or services, personnel, and support among the business units; exchange and combination were dealt with together in these questions. The four resource networks were combined into a new matrix, and in-degree centrality was computed from the new matrix to yield a single-item measure of the level of resource exchange and combination a unit engaged in. An in-degree centrality measure was obtained for each network and a Cronbach's coefficient alpha based on the four in-degree measures was .87, showing a high level of correlation among the four resource networks.

A single item asked respondents, on average, how many product innovations per year were produced in their unit during the recent past (from 1993 to 1996). Only major product innovations were counted, with minor product changes and product facelifts excluded. The self-reported figures were validated by asking the company's headquarters managers to confirm the data, and no case was found in which these managers challenged the figures provided by the business units.

Dummy that takes the value of 1 if the start-up only received VC funding during the sample period, which ended January 2002. Data to code the variable are from the Venture Economics database. It is used in a three-way comparison whose excluded category is firms that only received SBIR funding, and its coefficient is interpreted relative to the omitted category.
time_window: during the sample period, ended January 2002

description: Dummy that takes the value of 1 if a start-up that was initially SBIR funded subsequently received VC funding by the end of the sample period. Data to code the variable are from the Venture Economics database. It identifies the third group of firms used in the three-way comparison.
time_window: by the end of the sample period, January 2002

description: Count of R&D alliances signed after the introduction of external funding, as of January 2002; the mean is 1.1. Cooperation events were counted using the year the firm received external funding as the dividing line between pre- and postfunding events. Extension announcements were excluded from the counts, as were alliance termination notices, and when the scope of a collaboration extended across type the primary function was coded, so that R&D alliances were separately coded from sales and marketing alliances. In the empirics logged transformations of the form log(1 + variable) are used, denoted by the prefix L.
time_window: after external funding, as of January 2002

description: Aggregate measure that counts the number of R&D alliances, sales and marketing alliances, and technology licenses following the introduction of external funding; the mean is 2.3. For technology licenses, the event was counted only if it was the target firm licensing out. The same pre/postfunding dividing line based on the year of external funding is used.
time_window: after external funding, as of January 2002

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 if an initial public offering was achieved as of January 2002; the mean is 0.37. IPO data come from SDC Platinum's Public Offerings database. It is used as the dependent variable in probit regressions whose reported coefficients are marginal effects.

Measure of investment bank underwriter reputation taken from Carter et al. (1998); the mean is 7.3. The variable ranges from a low of zero to a high of nine, and is based on underwriter placement in tombstone announcements. It is analysed in the subsample of start-ups that realized an IPO.

The number of companies a VC firm had taken public in the year prior to funding the target start-up; the mean is 43. The measure can only be constructed for the subsample that was VC funded. The authors argue that attaining a track record in bringing start-ups to the public market can contribute to VC reputation.
time_window: year prior to funding the target start-up

description: Centrality score based on the number and reputation of other VC firms with which the focal VC firm forms investment syndicates in the year before the focal start-up received VC funding; the mean is 0.14. The measure is based on a standard measure of centrality in the network sociology literature (Bonacich 1987). The authors interpret it as a measure of the information (and quality of information) available to the VC.
time_window: year before the focal start-up received VC funding

description: We trace, for each year, a firm's patents that include inventors with knowledge on antihypertensives, and count the ones listing more than one inventor. As this count may be confounded with a firm's overall inventive effort, the dependent variable is measured as a ratio of such count to a firm's total patents that include inventors with knowledge on antihypertensives in the year. It thus indicates a firm's extent of collaborative invention (with the alternative being individual invention) for a given amount of inventive effort.

Number of rival drugs building on the same mechanism of action underlying a firm's drug available in the antihypertensive market in the year preceding the observation year. By tracing these commercialized rival drugs rather than measuring rivals' knowledge similarity based on patents, the variable captures actual competitive threats rather than early outcomes of rivals' experimentation with similar knowledge. In cases where a firm had antihypertensives based on different mechanisms, the authors compute the average count of rival drugs across these mechanisms.
time_window: one year lag (year preceding the observation year)

description: Number of versions of a firm's antihypertensives that made it into the top 100 drugs generating the most sales in dollars in the U.S. prescription market in the year preceding the observation year. To ensure that the variable does not overstate commercial abilities by including duplicate versions with minimal technical advances, only a firm's distinct molecular entities are considered.
time_window: one year lag (year preceding the observation year)

description: The authors trace the order of a firm's antihypertensive within its respective mechanism; that is, whether its drug was the first, or second, or third (and so on) drug to appear in the market upon the introduction of this mechanism. They then calculate the inverse of this order (i.e., reciprocal, 1/n), such that higher values of this measure reflect greater technical abilities. When computing this measure for a firm that had antihypertensives based on different mechanisms, they used the average value for its drugs across mechanisms.

A binary variable indicating whether any of the focal incumbent firm's patents applied for in the observation year t (and subsequently granted) has cited the focal new venture patent; coded as 1 if so, and 0 otherwise. The unit of analysis is the incumbent firm–new venture patent dyad by year. Dyads were removed from the risk set once the incumbent cited the patent or once the incumbent acquired the new venture.

A dummy variable coded as 1 if a founder of the dyad's new venture had been previously employed by the dyad's incumbent firm, and 0 otherwise. Prior employment of founders who were also inventors was established through online searches of company websites, Businessweek executives' profiles and biography databases, and professional networking websites such as LinkedIn. If multiple founders had started a new venture, all of their employment histories were considered, and any founder who had worked for the dyad's incumbent firm made the dyad a spin-out relationship. Of the 370 new ventures, 132 had spun out from an incumbent in the sample of 41 incumbents.

A dummy variable coded as 1 if at least one non-founder inventor moved from the focal incumbent firm to the focal new venture in the five years prior to the observation year, and 0 otherwise. Inventors associated with the new venture's patents were identified in the U.S. patent inventor database and their patenting history was checked to see whether prior patents were assigned to incumbent firms in the sample, indicating prior employment. Inventor names were manually cross-checked so that a founder previously employed by the focal incumbent would not produce a false 1. Of the 14,267 incumbent firm–new venture dyads, 323 experienced such non-founding inventor mobility.
time_window: five years prior to the observation year

description: A cumulative count of unique patent infringement lawsuits that involved the incumbent as a defendant, computed over a five-year window including the observation year, using court docket data. Because the variable is highly skewed, a log transformation was used. Higher values indicate a greater history of possible knowledge misappropriation.
time_window: five-year window including the observation year

description: The venture's stage of development at the time of the investment round, a round-level variable. Building on VE definitions, four major stages are identified - seed, early, expansion, and later - and the value of Investment stage is set to 1, 2, 3, and 4, respectively. Seed-stage ventures engage in R&D and usually have no established commercial operations, whereas later-stage ventures exhibit increasing sales volume and may even be profitable; higher values are associated with less risky investment.

A count of the number of syndicate members who participate in a focal investment round, a round-level variable. Each unique investor is counted as one additional syndicate member, irrespective of whether it is an IVC or a CVC. For example, the variable equals four when a venture receives funding from four different IVC funds, or from one corporate program together with three IVCs.

Assigned a value of 1 if the focal round involves a corporate investor (e.g., a mixed CVC, IVC syndicate), and 0 if it consists solely of IVCs (e.g., an all-IVC syndicate). CVC investors are identified using VE's categories, and their identities are further confirmed via Lexis-Nexis. The authors exclude rounds in which two or more CVCs jointly participated.
Equal to 1 for corporate investors and 0 for IVC funds, used to distinguish corporate from independent investors in the fund-level performance regressions.

Equal to 1 if the consultant survey or press searches indicate a focal CVC awards carried interest, or if the CVC's score is above the median value of the LBS compensation index. The LBS index collapses responses about fixed salary, performance-based bonuses, and long-term outcome-based pay, and ranges from a low of 1 for programs that remunerate solely through fixed salary to a high of 4.4 for programs that employ IVC-like carried interest. The variable is colinear with CVC/IVC, which is dropped in specifications that include it.

Equal to 1 if the consultant survey or press searches indicate a focal CVC does not award carried interest, or if the CVC's score is below the median value of the LBS compensation index. It denotes programs that award low-powered incentives such as fixed salary.

The CVC-incentives-high definition used in the round-level models is carried over to the fund level: it equals 1 for CVC programs that award carried interest or score above the median of the LBS compensation index. It is used in the fund-level performance regressions together with CVC-incentives-low and CVC-other.

The CVC-incentives-low definition used in the round-level models is carried over to the fund level: it equals 1 for CVC programs that do not award carried interest or score below the median of the LBS compensation index. It denotes programs that offer low-powered incentives.

Defined as the fraction of portfolio companies that have successfully exited via an IPO or M&A transaction by 2006. Following Kaplan and Schoar (2005) and Hochberg et al. (2007), the authors analyze the incentive-performance association at the fund level using funds' exit rates because fund returns are unavailable due to strict data limitations. Investment practices enter the mediation models as the values of Investment stage and Syndicate size averaged across a fund's investment rounds.

A binary choice measure set equal to 1 for all observations where firm i expands either by adding a new greenfield plant (representing 25% of all major expansions) or by expanding one or more of its plant's production capacity by more than 10 percent, and 0 otherwise. De-bottlenecking was excluded from the total set of capacity expansions since it is carried out on an ongoing basis and does not represent a major, discrete investment. The dependent variable appears in the tables as the decision to add capacity.

Constructed as the percentage of rivals that invested simultaneously in a product-market during an observation year. The measure allows the authors to test whether firms are more likely to invest when they see more of their rivals investing, regardless of how much capacity they are adding. Its disadvantage is that it does not focus on preemption effects through the size of rivals' investments.

variable_name: RIVAL2 (percentage of capacity expanded by rivals)
description: Measures the percentage of total capacity that is added simultaneously by rivals. Its advantage over the first measure is that it directly measures the amount of capacity added by rivals and therefore focuses on preemption effects through the size of rivals' investments. Both indicators were used in the estimations.

A stock variable that accumulates the total number of expansion decisions that a firm made prior to the observation year. This cumulative measure is consistent with the operationalizations in the learning curve literature. Because of left censoring, the stocks were allowed to build up for 10 years before the estimations, so that the estimations employed the 1985-95 data.
time_window: accumulated prior to the observation year, with a 10-year stock build-up

description: The authors first calculated the difference between the actual and expected outcome of each expansion decision, using expected capacity utilization computed as the industry capacity utilization in the previous year plus any decrease in capacity utilization that a naive firm would anticipate because of its own expansion (based on a 4-year compound annual growth rate for the product-market). A poor outcome occurred when the actual industry capacity utilization during the observation year was lower than the firm's expected capacity utilization; good outcomes were ignored since it was assumed search would be reduced. The firm's poor outcomes were cumulated over time into the stock S PO.
time_window: accumulated over time prior to and including the observation year

variable_name: S RPO (stock of rivals' poor outcomes)
description: A measure that aggregates the stock of poor outcomes for each of the firm's rivals in its product-market. It includes the rivals' poor outcomes both when the firm expanded and when it did not expand.
time_window: accumulated over time prior to and including the observation year

description: A simple measure that counts the number of years from the previous capacity expansion in the product-market. Because capacity expansion decisions are infrequent, the authors did not estimate the decay with a constant depreciation rate or a geometric lag structure as studies of R&D stocks have done.
time_window: years since the previous capacity expansion in the product-market

description: The firm's original relative market share in 1975, employed as an indicator of its experience prior to 1975 to deal with the left censoring of the stock variables. The origins of these experiences are unknown as they could come from previous expansion decisions or the poor outcomes of those decisions.

Firm α's direct disadvantage relative to firms in industry j equals firm α's dependence on industry j minus the dependence of firms in industry j on firm α. Firm α's dependence on industry j is the importance of industry j's resources to industry i times industry j's concentration ratio times the firm's market share in industry i; the reverse dependence is the importance of industry i's resources to industry j times the firm's market share in industry i. When a firm operates in more than one industry, the proportion of the firm's sales generated from each involved industry is used as a weighting factor in a weighted sum.

Calculated for each industry the firm is involved with as the sum over all k of [industry k's dependence on industry j times firm α's dependence on industry k minus industry k's dependence on firm α times industry j's dependence on industry k], where k indexes intermediary industries. Industry j is treated as a significant partner industry when the absolute value of its direct advantage over the firm is greater than 0.01. When firm α operates in multiple industries, the percentage of the firm's total sales generated from each industry is used as a weighting factor in a weighted sum.

Calculated using the same formula used for a firm's indirect power disadvantage relative to industry j, except that industry j is limited to the firm's non-partners. An industry is considered a non-partner when the absolute value of its direct disadvantage relative to the firm is no larger than 0.01.

Measured through the firm's business in industry i as the sum of this business's indirect disadvantages relative to all other industries, then combined across the industries the firm operates in using the proportion of sales generated from each industry as a weighting factor. The authors note that this is a different variable from the firm–industry-level indirect disadvantage used in testing Hypotheses 1 through 3.

Equals 1 if the firm conducted at least one acquisition in industry j between years t and t + 4, inclusive, and 0 otherwise. Industry j is identified as a significant partner industry of the firm when the absolute value of industry j's direct disadvantage relative to the firm is greater than 0.01.

The total deal value of all acquisitions the firm conducted in industry j in a given year divided by its total sales, with the average value of this ratio during years t to t + 4 used as the final measure. The same calculation is applied to partner and non-partner industries.

Equals 1 if the firm conducted at least one acquisition in non-partner industry j between years t and t + 4, inclusive, and 0 otherwise. Industry j is considered a non-partner when the absolute value of industry j's direct disadvantage relative to the firm is no larger than 0.01.

The total deal value of the firm's acquisitions in non-partner industry j in a given year divided by its total sales, averaged over years t to t + 4; the likelihood and expenditure of acquiring partners and non-partners were calculated in the same way.

Calculated as a firm's ROA in year t minus the average ROA of the firm's primary industry in the same year. Because the distribution of this variable was highly skewed, the value was transformed so that the final measure equals log(ROA + 1,045.04).

The postaward period receives a value of '1' for the 4 years subsequent to witnessing the first CEO award and '0' for the 4 years prior to witnessing the first CEO award (including award years); periods are shorter when a competitor CEO turns over. Treatment receives a value of '1' if a firm is a superstar CEO firm's competitor and '0' if it is a control firm. Competitors are the superstar CEO firm's industry peers in the ExecuComp universe whose total assets lie within 75-125% of the superstar CEO firm's total assets, identified with TNIC-3 product similarity. Control firms are matched to treatment firms using a logit regression predicting treatment status from firm size (log assets), firm performance (ROA), Tobin's q, CEO age, CEO gender, CEO tenure, and number of acquisitions.
time_window: 4 years before and 4 years after witnessing the first CEO award

description: Acquisitions are classified by whether they were announced by a competitor CEO firm (treatment) or a control firm, and by whether they occurred in the postaward or the preaward period of the corresponding competitor CEO. The authors compare whether acquisitions by competitor CEO firms realize lower announcement returns in the postaward period than in the preaward period relative to acquisitions by control firms in the same periods.
time_window: 4 years before and 4 years after witnessing the first CEO award

description: Measured as the total number of majority-ownership acquisitions announced in a year, which will have been completed subsequently, as reported in SDC data. Only deals SDC codes as 'mergers,' 'acquisition of majority interests,' 'acquisitions of assets,' and 'acquisitions of certain assets' with a transaction value over $1 million are included. Firms that did not engage in any acquisition in a year receive a value of '0.' The authors take the natural logarithm of the number of acquisitions plus one to address skewness.

Measured as the total value of the majority-ownership acquisitions announced in a year, which will have been completed subsequently, as reported in SDC data. Only deals with a transaction value over $1 million are included. Firms that did not engage in any acquisition in a year receive a value of '0.' The authors take the natural logarithm of the value of acquisitions plus one to address skewness.

The product similarity score between two firms is obtained from Hoberg and Phillips (2010) and is based on the relative number of words in common that the firms' product descriptions contain. A higher product similarity score indicates a higher degree of similarity between two firms, and firm pairs with higher scores are nearer rivals. The score indicates the amount by which the pairwise score exceeds the similarity threshold for being included in the TNIC-3 database, so its range starts near zero. When a competitor CEO competes with multiple superstar CEOs, the average product similarity between the competitor CEO and all the superstar CEO firms is used.
level: competitor CEO firm-superstar CEO firm pair

description: Measured as the predicted probability that a (competitor) CEO wins an award in a given year, taken from a probit regression estimated on all CEO-year observations in ExecuComp during the sample frame. The binary dependent variable equals '1' if a firm's CEO won an award in a year and '0' otherwise, and the predictors are firm size (natural log of market capitalization at t-1), Tobin's q at t-1, industry-adjusted stock market returns at t-1 and t-2, firm advertising intensity, CEO gender, CEO age, CEO tenure at t-1, the total number of acquisitions by the CEO in the prior 2 years, and year and Fama-French 17 industry dummies.

Following Brown and Warner (1985), cumulative abnormal returns are computed as the returns over the event window minus the normal returns, which represent the expected returns if the event had not taken place. Abnormal returns for acquisition announcements are accumulated over a 3-day window surrounding the announcement of the deal [-1, +1], incorporating the day before and the day after the announcement. Windows of 5 days [-2, +2] and 2 days [0, +1] surrounding the announcement are also used.
time_window: 3-day event window around the acquisition announcement

description: Not applicable to the deal-level analysis of announcement returns; the deal-level models do not include product similarity.

Lagged sales of goods exported to parent operations divided by total sales of imported and exported goods with parent operations, built from the BEA data on transfers of goods across MNC operations located in different countries. The measure is intended to capture those operations that have the highest product export ratios for the MNC. All independent variables are lagged by 1 year in the models.

variable_name: Export ratio with third country t-1
description: Lagged sales of goods to third country MNC operations divided by total sales, built from the BEA data on transfers of goods across MNC operations located in different countries. It captures the product export ratio of the operation with third-country MNC operations. All independent variables are lagged by 1 year in the models.

Lagged imports from parent firm operations divided by total sales. The BEA does not collect information on third country goods sold to focal foreign operations, so third-country inflows could not be included. The measure captures product imports into the foreign operation separately from product exports.

Proportion of a foreign operation's patents that include a new technology domain for the MNC, relative to all innovations generated in that operation in each year. The measure compares the IPC codes of each foreign innovation with the list of MNC IPC codes in all years prior to the focal year; if a patent contains a new technology domain considering Section, Class and Subclass, that domain becomes part of the MNC technology domain list in the next year, and if a patent has more than one new domain all domains are included. The application date of the patent is used for all granted patents.

variable_name: Diverse tech diffusion - to home country
description: Indicator for whether an innovation that includes a new technology domain for the MNC was subsequently patented in countries that include the home country (the United States), using family patent information from the DWPI to track where an innovation has been patented after the priority filing. It is estimated at the patent level in a Heckprob model whose selection equation takes a value of 1 if the innovation includes a new technology domain.

variable_name: Diverse tech diffusion - to third countries
description: Indicator for whether an innovation that includes a new technology domain for the MNC was subsequently patented in countries that do not include the home country, using family patent information from the DWPI. It is estimated at the patent level in a Heckprob model whose selection equation takes a value of 1 if the innovation includes a new technology domain.

A dummy variable indicating whether any commercial relationship existed between Buyco and the supplier in the four quarters preceding the bid event. It is built from Buyco's central accounting database of monthly transactions with parts suppliers, which was aggregated to create a cumulative measure of each distinct supplier's quarterly dollar sales to Buyco. Coded 1 for bidders with prior exchange in the prior four quarters and 0 otherwise.
level: bidder (supplier) at the time of the bid event
time_window: four quarters preceding the bid event

description: The dollar value of sales from the supplier to Buyco during the four quarters preceding the bid event, a measure of relationship intensity, expressed in natural logs. The underlying dollar values are aggregated from Buyco's central accounting database of monthly part-level transactions from 2002 to midyear 2006. The natural log is shifted by a constant to avoid taking the log of zero when no relationship exists.
scale: natural log of U.S. dollars (shifted by a constant)
level: bidder (supplier) at the time of the bid event
time_window: four quarters preceding the bid event; underlying data 2002 to midyear 2006

description: The number of consecutive quarters in which the supplier and Buyco had an exchange relationship at the time of the bid event, a measure of relationship length, expressed in natural logs. Because the accounting database provides no historic exchange information prior to 2002, the measure is top-coded at 12 quarters. The natural log is shifted by a constant to avoid taking the log of zero when no relationship exists.
scale: natural log of quarters (shifted by a constant)
level: bidder (supplier) at the time of the bid event
time_window: consecutive quarters of exchange up to the bid event; top-coded at 12 quarters

description: The dependent variable takes on the value 1 if the bidder is awarded the contract to supply the bundle and 0 if the bidder places a valid bid for the item but does not win; if the bidder does not bid, the bidder-bundle pair does not form an observation. Bidder identities were manually extracted from Web pages generated by the application service provider that managed Buyco's online auctions and matched with a Buyco management database to ascertain the winning supplier. On average there are nearly 5.4 bidders per bundle, and the mean value of the dependent variable is 0.185.

Expert ratings of the degree to which the technology required to manufacture the products of a bid event had changed rapidly over the past five years. Each bid event was rated by procurement experts who were supplied with detailed descriptions and drawings of the bundles and who scored the products on a seven-point Likert scale relative to the universe of products sourced via reverse auctions. The measure used in the analysis is the z-scored average of the experts' ratings.
scale: seven-point Likert scale; z-scored average across raters

description: Expert ratings of how complex the parts in a bid event are, formed from three questions scored on a seven-point Likert scale relative to the universe of products sourced via reverse auctions. Raters were supplied with detailed descriptions and drawings of the bundles in each bid event. The measure used in the analysis is the z-scored average of the experts' ratings.
scale: seven-point Likert scale; z-scored average across raters

description: Expert rating of the extent to which supplying the parts requires the awarded supplier to make substantial investments in tooling and equipment that are specific to Buyco, scored on a seven-point Likert scale relative to the universe of products sourced via reverse auctions. The measure used in the analysis is the z-scored average of the experts' ratings.
scale: seven-point Likert scale; z-scored average across raters

description: Expert rating of the extent to which there can be a high level of variance month to month or season to season from the forecast demand for the parts, scored on a seven-point Likert scale relative to the universe of products sourced via reverse auctions; the authors label the measure demand predictability but the item is scored so that higher values indicate greater variance in demand. The measure used in the analysis is the z-scored average of the experts' ratings.
scale: seven-point Likert scale; z-scored average across raters

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if the bidder's headquarters is located in an English-speaking country, with the exception of the United States (classified as English-speaking); English-speaking countries are those in which one of the official languages is English. The location of the supplier's headquarters was identified from data provided by the auctioneer, augmented by online searches.

A dummy variable equal to 1 if the supplier's headquarters is less than the median distance from Buyco's headquarters, where distance is calculated with geomapping software. It is used in place of the continuous distance measure in the specifications that interact proximity with relationship history.

A dichotomous variable coded one when a firm's number of permanent employees (excluding contract and temporary workers) decreased by 5 percent or more between year t-1 and year t. The authors argue that changes of this magnitude are more likely to occur through concentrated efforts to reduce the workforce than through attrition and are more likely to attract publicity. Downsizing was accomplished through reductions in hiring, early retirements, sending employees to affiliates, and, in some cases, layoffs, which these data cannot distinguish. The authors preferred actual employment reductions to press announcements of downsizing.
time_window: between year t-1 and year t

description: Return on assets is profits before taxes and extraordinary items divided by total assets. It is lagged by one year.
Sales growth is the percentage growth in sales between year t-1 and year t.
time_window: between year t-1 and year t

description: The sum of years in the previous five years that a firm experienced losses. The authors use it to capture mounting years of poor performance, which further increased the likelihood of downsizing.

The deviation from industry mean of the ratio of a firm's operation profits to total employees. It is lagged by one year. The authors describe a low ratio of profits to employees as reflecting a high degree of redundancy.
Firm size is the log of total assets. In supplemental analyses the authors substituted the log of the number of employees in the previous year and found similar results.
Firm age is the number of years between a firm's founding and 1990.

The sum of the number of times that a firm appeared in Recruit's annual listing of the most attractive 50 firms for new graduates during the 1980s. The authors used rankings from the 1980s because frequent appearance in past rankings indicates an established reputation as an employer and because downsizing behavior could have influenced later rankings.

The deviation from industry mean of a firm's payroll expense divided by the total number of employees. It is lagged by one year. The authors treat high wage levels as reflecting high levels of firm-specific human capital.

The percentage of shares held by non-Japanese shareholders, lagged by one year. The authors examined the identities of these shareholders for a subset of about 700 firms and found that foreign shareholders were almost exclusively large American, European, or Australian corporations or institutional investors.

The sum of downsizings of all firms in the population, minus the focal firm, over the previous three years, divided by the total number of firms in the population, minus the focal firm, multiplied by three. It can be thought of as the percentage of firm-years in which a downsizing occurred over the previous three years. The authors chose a recent rather than cumulative measure because a safety-in-numbers effect depends on large numbers of recent downsizings.

Return on capital of a foreign firm relative to the average return on capital of British-owned firms in its 4-digit industry in the City of London. This relative performance is used as an indication of the foreign firm's liability of foreignness; higher relative performance indicates a weaker liability of foreignness.
Firms whose registered headquarters are located outside Britain are classified as foreign owned; British-owned firms are those with headquarters located in Britain.

A single compound measure created by combining the standardized values of multiple operations: intangible assets, financial strength (liquidity ratio and credit rating), size (total assets), and managerial skills (directors' remuneration as share of total remuneration).

A compound measure combining the standardized values of intensity of international activity (number of foreign offices a firm controls) and internal linkages (share of profits transferred by the affiliate to the parent, measured as a dummy variable with four levels).

A compound measure combining the standardized values of access to local information (number of local links in the City), preference of local customers (share of activity in British pounds in total activity), and reliance on local resources (share of expatriates among active directors and chief executives, measured as a dummy variable with four levels).
Operationalized by years since the establishment of the London office.

A composite index based on Hofstede's indices. It is calculated from the deviation along each of the four cultural dimensions (power distance, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity and individualism) of each country from the UK, corrected for differences in the variances of each dimension and then averaged across the four dimensions.
Dummy variable that gets the value 1 for entry via M&As; 0 for greenfield.
Dummy variable that gets the value 1 if the affiliate reports directly to the headquarters, 0 otherwise.
scale: dummy (1 = reports directly to headquarters, 0 = otherwise)

description: Coded 1 for franchise establishments and 0 for independents. It is used to test Hypothesis 1a, that franchisees have higher performance than independents, and in the probit models of practice use it captures the intrinsic motivation of the franchisee to use practices that it has paid for.

The sum of net owner income plus royalties in a given year, i.e., the total annual return available to the set of stakeholders (franchisor plus franchisee in the case of a franchise, owner in the case of an independent). Net owner income is the income to the owner alone and includes both salary and net income. The survey gathers five years of data on owner income and royalties and the observations are pooled across those five years.

For each of the 20 practices in the survey respondents report behavior: how frequently the entrepreneur uses the practice (daily, weekly, monthly, annually, biannually, and never). Hypothesis 1b decomposes the franchise advantage into a set of use dummies for each practice, with all remaining advantages of franchise association captured by the franchise dummy. Hypothesis 2 models the probability of use, P(use), of each practice as the dependent variable. The authors note they originally planned to use frequency of use to represent routine but opted not to because more use of a given practice was not uniformly better.

For each of the 20 practices, whether the entrepreneur is aware that industry experts recommend the practice (yes = 1, no = 0). Knowledge captures establishment capacity (information fidelity) to execute the prescribed routine and measures the establishment's effectiveness in gathering information not intended for it, and it enters the probit models of practice use.

For each practice, how strongly the entrepreneur agrees, on a scale of 1-5, that the practice will lead to higher profits (strongly agree = 1), so lower values indicate stronger agreement. Agreement measures the establishment's ability to interpret information it has gathered and enters the probit models of practice use.

For each practice, whether the franchise requires the entrepreneur to follow the practice (yes = 1, no = 0). Requirement captures the threat of franchisor sanctions for failure to use a practice and enters the probit models of practice use. The variable was added to each practice of the survey specifically to test for enforcement of the respective practice.

Each acquisition is classified by the F.T.C. into one of five mutually exclusive categories according to the primary economic relationship between the acquiring and acquired companies: horizontal, vertical, product extension, market extension and unrelated. In the tests, the first four categories (the related acquisitions) are combined and compared with the last category (the unrelated acquisitions).

The 1982 status of each acquired unit was determined through an extensive search of the Thomas Register, Moody's Industrials (1967-1982), and companies' annual reports and 10-Ks, and coded into categories: liquidated; sold (intact); sold (not intact); not sold (intact); not sold (not intact); the parent company was itself acquired; and insufficient information. In the tests the sold and liquidated categories are grouped together and compared with the two not-sold categories across acquisition types. Of the 434 acquisitions, 80 could not be traced and the remaining 354 were used in this comparison.

The number of simultaneous projects for the focal employee each month. The authors followed extant theoretical work and measured the MPW construct as the number of projects per employee, and employees were assigned to projects through a centralized, top-down allocation process. In the dataset, 58% of employees engaged in MPW and had, on average, 2.71 projects, with a maximum of 12 projects.

Operationalized as the difference between the most recent estimated completion date of the current gate and the gate's actual completion date. Project reports contained three timestamps of project advancement through the stage gates: the first report, from the beginning of the project, included the expected completion time for each gate, and changes in those estimates were reflected in the second monthly report; actual completion dates were taken from future project reports (month = 20). The measure traces deviations from both original expectations and later estimates.
time_window: most recent gate estimate versus actual completion date

description: For each employee, the cumulative number of months (across all projects) they have spent working in the same Program-Category combination previously to the current month. Each project belongs to one of four program categories and one of seven programs, and two projects in the same Program-Category combination proxy for the same project area. The full 20-month history of employee experience was observed from project reports across all projects.

The ratio of similar projects to the total number of projects for each employee/month. Two projects are considered similar if they belong to the same market segment (Building Services, HVAC, and Water Treatment). The metric ranges theoretically from 1 divided by the number of projects to a maximum of 1; empirically the observed range is 0.26 to 1.

The number of familiar project members with which the employee currently works or has worked in the past, measured for the focal project. An employee was classified as familiar if they were currently working or had previously worked with the focal employee, and the number of such monthly situations was counted for each employee.

The yearly innovative performance is measured as the number of successful patent applications filed during each year. All successfully granted patents of the focal firms were extracted from the Derwent patent database and recorded according to the date of application. The authors note that patent counts correlate highly with alternative measures of innovative performance.

A distinct count variable for each type of external business development activity, measured as the annually depreciated stock of past announcements of new investments with a 30 percent annual depreciation rate. The cumulative stock of CVC investments is included separately in each relatedness category (intra-industry, related, unrelated), and the three categories enter the regression jointly. All independent variables are lagged by one year.

A distinct count variable for alliances, measured as the annually depreciated stock of past announcements of new alliances with a 30 percent annual depreciation rate. The cumulative stock of alliances is included separately in each relatedness category (intra-industry, related, unrelated), and the three categories enter the regression jointly. All independent variables are lagged by one year.

A distinct count variable for joint ventures, measured as the annually depreciated stock of past announcements of new joint ventures with a 30 percent annual depreciation rate. The cumulative stock of joint ventures is included separately in each relatedness category (intra-industry, related, unrelated), and the three categories enter the regression jointly. All independent variables are lagged by one year.

A distinct count variable for acquisitions, measured as the annually depreciated stock of past announcements of new acquisitions with a 30 percent annual depreciation rate. The cumulative stock of acquisitions is included separately in each relatedness category (intra-industry, related, unrelated), and the three categories enter the regression jointly. All independent variables are lagged by one year.

A categorical measure based on the SIC code match between the venture and the focal firm. Ventures are classified as intra-industry when at least the first three digits of the SIC codes were identical, as related when at least the first digit matched between the venture and the focal firm, and all other ventures were classified as unrelated. The authors note that the SIC based relatedness information is the only information consistently available for all ventures in the sample.

variable_name: Stocks of CVC investments, alliances, joint ventures and acquisitions
description: External business development activity is measured as a distinct count variable for each governance mode (CVC investments, alliances, joint ventures, acquisitions), taken from announcements in SDC Platinum. Each is an annually depreciated stock of past announcements with a 30 percent depreciation rate, split by relatedness to the focal firm, and lagged one year.

Full-time employee turnover rate, calculated as the number of full-time employees who left the store during the period divided by the average number of full-time employees working at the store during that period. It is measured over the one-month period ranging from the 15th day of the prior month to the 15th day of the current month, and also over the prior three months. Employees engaged in office coordination or community relations activities and temporary employees are excluded.
time_window: one month (15th of prior month to 15th of current month); also prior three months

description: Part-time employee turnover rate, calculated as the number of part-time employees who left the store during the period divided by the average number of part-time employees working at the store during that period. It is measured over the one-month period ranging from the 15th day of the prior month to the 15th day of the current month, and also over the prior three months. Temporary employees are excluded.
time_window: one month (15th of prior month to 15th of current month); also prior three months

description: A single turnover measure combining full-time and part-time employees, given the similarity between the tasks performed by these two types of employees in this setting. It is calculated as the number of employees who left the store during the period divided by the average number of employees working at the store during that period, measured over the one-month period from the 15th day of the prior month to the 15th day of the current month and over the prior three months. The authors report subsequent results using this total turnover measure only.
time_window: one month (15th of prior month to 15th of current month); also prior three months

description: A subjective measure of store performance. Each store is shopped once a month by a mystery shopper who fills out a form that includes approximately 50 questions about the store environment and customer service interactions, and the store's overall customer service score is based on the mystery shopper's answers to these questions.

An objective measure of financial performance calculated as operating income divided by sales. The authors prefer it to total sales or total profit because those measures are affected by the absolute level of activity at the store, which depends on factors beyond the store manager's control.

A composite of two measures regularly tracked by Borders management.
