The first, store conditions, is a quarterly regional-manager inspection of conformance to a wide range of processes covering books, café, music and video, and store operations, scored by averaging item scores within sections and adding weighted section scores. The second, the returns pull list (RPL) score, is the number of units returned divided by the total number of units that were supposed to be returned in a monthly returns period. For each store and year the average store conditions score and the average RPL score are standardized by subtracting the yearly mean and dividing by the yearly standard deviation across all stores, and the standardized scores are combined. Stores are then ranked and divided into high-process-conformance and low-process-conformance categories.
scale: binary category (high vs. low process conformance)
time_window: yearly averages (store conditions quarterly, RPL monthly)

description: The legitimate positions were first determined by listing all the positions mentioned by the top 25 U.S. agencies in the years studied and keeping those mentioned by all of them in all years; these were 17 positions, regardless of whether or not the same person filled two positions. The variable is the proportion of these 17 legitimate positions mentioned by the focal agency in a year; an agency that listed a chair, art editor, and copy writer is coded 0.177 (3/17). All explanatory variables are lagged in the estimations.
time_window: lagged one year relative to growth

description: Coded one for a year if the agency submitted an entry to the Cannes Creativity Awards that year, and zero otherwise. Cumulated submissions were also considered, but because only 24 agencies had more than one submission over the years of observation, the variables were not very different. Only the Cannes Creativity Award was considered because it is the most prestigious award in the industry and receives the largest number of entries.
time_window: lagged one year relative to growth

description: Customer status is measured using annual advertising expenditure of the agency's customers, since data on the revenues of agency customers are not available. Two status levels are coded separately as continuous variables measuring the proportion of an agency's customers belonging to either the highest status level (the nation's top thousand advertisers listed in Ad $ Summary) or the next level (the largest advertisers, excluding the top thousand, listed in the Standard Directory of National Advertisers). Using the proportion rather than the total number of high-status clients eliminates the possibility that the observed effect is merely that of an additional client or an additional large client.
time_window: lagged one year relative to growth

description: Growth is measured as the change in the agency's gross billings compared with the previous year, estimated in the logarithmic form of Gibrat's law, a proportional growth model in which expected growth is proportional to size and the growth rate (size t+1/size t) is independent of size. The estimation uses pooled time series regression with firm-specific fixed effects, and all explanatory variables are lagged. The printed equation itself is not recoverable from the text.
time_window: annual change relative to the previous year

description: Growth is measured as the change in the number of agency employees compared with the previous year, estimated in the logarithmic form of Gibrat's law, in which expected growth is proportional to size and the growth rate (size t+1/size t) is independent of size. The estimation uses pooled time series regression with firm-specific fixed effects, and all explanatory variables are lagged. The printed equation itself is not recoverable from the text.
time_window: annual change relative to the previous year

description: Return on assets (ROA), chosen because it is the primary measure of firm profitability within the railroad industry and is tracked, evaluated, and publicized by the industry's governing body. A social aspiration level was constructed for ROA and equals the mean ROA across all organizations in the prior year. To examine performance below the aspiration level, spline variables were constructed by splitting ROA into two variables based on the aspiration level, and the coefficient estimates indicate the effect of performance below the aspiration.
time_window: aspiration level based on the prior year

description: Measure of installed capacity extracted through principal factor analysis with varimax rotation of miles of rail track, number of locomotives, and number of freight and passenger cars. Two factors were yielded but only the first was retained based on a comparison of eigenvalues, and all variables loaded highly on the retained factor. The score of this capacity factor is used as the first dependent variable, and the models estimate its growth rate.

Equals the total nondepreciated value of assets devoted to railroad operations, which includes facilities and structures as well as locomotives, cars, track, and other operating equipment, but excludes nonproduction assets such as administrative offices. It directly measures investment in railroad operations and is used as a second dependent variable, again modeled as a growth rate.

A logged measure of the cumulative number of train miles operated by each company through the year prior to the observation period, consistent with empirical research on learning curves; one train mile is equivalent to moving a train the distance of one mile. This variable accumulates each railroad company's experience beginning in 1978, when deregulation of the industry began, because radical changes such as deregulation diminish the impact of operating experience gained in the previous environment. The measure was standardized in final models (prior to constructing the interaction with performance) by centering it on its mean and dividing by its standard deviation.
time_window: cumulative through the year prior to the observation

description: Number of favorable articles minus the number of unfavorable articles about each company in each year, based on content analysis of print media pertaining to the company panel collected from the Factiva news media database; each article was given equal weighting. Coding units were rated as endorsing the railroad company, questioning its legitimacy, or neutral in content, and the net count reflects the volume as well as the tenor of media coverage. The values for this legitimacy variable were standardized.

A variable measuring the number of years since founding, similar to prior literature on organizational age. This variable was also standardized, and results using the unstandardized measure were identical.

The first principal factor of five regional indicators of informal institutional quality, attributed to sellers based on their home regions. The indicators were the average length of bankruptcy proceedings, the average length of judicial examination proceedings for civil trials in the first instance and in instances of appeals, the lack of corruption, and the lack of organized crime. The judicial efficiency indicators were standardized and then inverted by subtracting the standardized values from one; the provincial organized crime indicator was standardized, inverted in the same way and averaged across the provinces of each region. The factor was shifted such that the value for the Italian region with the lowest institutional quality equaled zero.
time_window: indicators for the year 2000; corruption data from the late 1990s; organized crime 1983-2009

description: Institutional quality scores attributed to buyers based on their home regions, using the same regional summary measure as for sellers.
time_window: indicators for the year 2000; corruption data from the late 1990s; organized crime 1983-2009

description: Calculated as the ratio of Seller institutional quality to Buyer institutional quality. A value of unity indicates that institutional quality in the home regions of the seller and buyer in a dyad are identical, while higher (lower) values indicate progressively higher (lower) institutional quality in a seller's home region relative to that of the buyer.
time_window: indicators for the year 2000; corruption data from the late 1990s; organized crime 1983-2009

description: Dummy variable taking a value of '1' if the seller was a limited liability company and '0' otherwise. Sellers that were sole proprietorships are the omitted category.
Dummy variable taking a value of '1' if the seller was a corporation and '0' otherwise. Sellers that were sole proprietorships are the omitted category.

Four dummy variables capturing a seller's legal status relative to the buyer, with Same legal status as the omitted category. Relative legal status seller lowest takes a value of '1' if the seller was a sole proprietorship and the buyer a corporation; Relative legal status seller low takes a value of '1' if either the seller was a sole proprietorship and the buyer a limited liability company, or the seller was a limited liability company and the buyer a corporation; Relative legal status seller high takes a value of '1' if either the seller was a limited liability company and the buyer a sole proprietorship, or the seller was a corporation and the buyer a limited liability company; Relative legal status seller highest takes a value of '1' if the seller was a corporation and the buyer a sole proprietorship.
Dichotomous variable taking the value of '1' if a buyer requested a quotation from a seller and '0' otherwise.

The number of formalized functions in a new venture divided by the potential maximum number of functional roles. The CorpTech database tracks common functional areas, and the measure was adapted from Dalton et al.'s (1980) definition of role formalization. The variable was orthogonalized with functional specialization, founding team size, and their interaction using a modified Gram-Schmidt procedure before being entered into the models.

The average number of functional assignments per founding team member, adapted from Pugh et al.'s (1963) definition of specialization. The variable was orthogonalized with role formalization, founding team size, and their interaction using a modified Gram-Schmidt procedure before being entered into the models.
The number of executives in a founding team divided by the number of total employees. The measure was adapted from Blau and Schoenherr's (1971) administrative ratio measure.

The number of executives in a firm. It was entered as a control variable and as the moderator of the effect of functional specialization on performance. The variable was orthogonalized with role formalization, functional specialization, and their interaction using a modified Gram-Schmidt procedure before being entered into the models.

The moving average of revenue (in millions of dollars) in years t and t + 1, adopted to shorten the lag time between the independent and dependent variables because the independent variables had a rapid impact on revenues in this sector. Revenue data were collected by CorpTech personnel.

The measure is based on the extent to which an acquiring firm's patenting efforts built on knowledge used in its previous patents. A list was created of the citations of all patents for acquiring firms filed up to five years before the focal acquisition; the degree to which the organization cited patents that had been cited previously is measured as the total number of duplicate citations. The total number of duplicates is divided by the total number of citations, and this ratio represents the degree of exploitation of acquiring firms, bound between 0 and 1.
time_window: five years before the focal acquisition

description: The degree of exploration is equal to 1 minus the degree of exploitation because the authors conceptualize exploitation and exploration along a continuum.
time_window: five years before the focal acquisition

description: Patents filed by acquiring firms for five years after a focal acquisition were identified and their citations analyzed. When a patent filed by the acquiring firm in the post-acquisition period cited at least one patent filed by both the target and acquiring firms prior to the acquisition, the patent was coded as evidence of integrated knowledge leverage. The aggregated number of integrated knowledge leverage patents over this period is used as the measure.
time_window: five years after the focal acquisition

description: Independent knowledge leverage is evident in post-acquisition patents that cite patents filed by the target firm but not the acquiring firm's patents. All patents that cite at least one patent of target firms but not acquiring firm patents, among the acquiring firm patents filed within the five years of the acquisition, were identified, and the total number was calculated. Any patent counted as integrated knowledge leverage was excluded from the calculation of independent knowledge leverage.
time_window: five years after the focal acquisition

description: Acquisition rate is measured as the average number of acquisitions that an acquiring firm undertakes during the focal and the preceding four years.
time_window: focal year and the preceding four years

variable_name: research and clinical trials alliance; research, clinical trials, and commercialization alliance
description: Alliance scope is measured as the number of value-generating activities that are covered by the alliance, building on Oxley and Sampson (2004) and refined for biopharmaceutical alliances by also accounting for the intermediate step of clinical trials and regulatory approval. Two binary variables are created: one for R&D alliances with clinical trials and another for R&D alliances with clinical trials and commercialization activities. Pure research alliances serve as the omitted reference category. The combination of research alliances with commercialization and no clinical trial activities did not occur in the data.

A binary variable that captures whether alliance activities are carried out jointly, replicating the measure proposed by Reuer and Devarakonda (2016). It relies on BioScience Advisors' classification of collaborative agreements designated as 'Co-Development,' and equals one if the alliance partners jointly develop the focal compound and zero otherwise. A binary indicator for sequential interdependence captures alliances in which partners independently perform certain upstream and downstream activities, and the omitted reference category is pooled interdependence, which includes pure licensing and commercialization agreements.

Calculated as the logarithmic sum of up-front payments, the maximum future milestone payments, and license fees. These contractually defined payments are specifically tied to the focal alliance and represent the client firm's commitment to compensate the research unit for past and future R&D investments. In this empirical context the investments are unilateral in the sense that the client firm finances the R&D activities of the research unit while the research unit contributes primarily intangible assets.

Based on the concentration of firms conducting clinical trials in the same disease area as the focal alliance. For each alliance the focal disease area targeted was identified and the concentration of firms undertaking clinical trials (industry sponsors) in that disease area in the five years prior to alliance formation was calculated. A Herfindahl-Hirschman-type index was inverted so that higher values in the range from zero to one indicate more intense rivalry. Disease names in the ClinicalTrials.gov database were standardized, and each alliance was classified using the list of diseases reported in that database.
time_window: five years prior to alliance formation

description: A binary variable that takes the value one if the steering committee is endowed with strategic decision-making authority over alliance activities and zero otherwise. For the main analyses the binary measure is one if the steering committee has decision-making authority over one or more of the alliance tasks; for example, a contract requiring the steering committee to approve an R&D plan counts as delegation, whereas a committee only allowed to review the R&D plan periodically is coded as no delegation. Every contract was coded by two independent coders unaware of the research question, with Krippendorff alphas for decision-making authority regarding research, clinical trials, and commercialization activities of 0.93, 0.98, and 0.93.

A binary variable that takes a value of one if final decision-making authority rests with one of the partners in case the steering committee faces a deadlock and zero otherwise, in which case partners routinely need to resort to trilateral dispute resolution such as arbitration or litigation. For the main analyses the binary variable is one if authority reverts for any of the alliance tasks. Krippendorff alphas for authority reversion regarding research, clinical trials, and commercialization were 0.97, 1.00, and 0.97.

A two-item Likert scale used to assess the extent to which the firm emphasizes having efficient-scale facilities and lower costs than major competitors. The overall coefficient alpha for the scale was .68 (Brazil, .60; Chile, .72; Mexico, .72). A composite score was calculated as an unweighted linear sum of the item scores.

A three-item scale adapted from Aulakh and Kotabe (1997) that captures the dimensions of quality standards, image, and general differentiation with respect to competitors. The overall coefficient alpha for the scale was .82 (Brazil, .77; Chile, .80; Mexico, .86). A composite score was calculated as an unweighted linear sum of the item scores.

A six-item scale developed to measure the extent of marketing standardization in foreign countries. Respondents indicated, on a five-point scale, the extent of their firms' standardization of product design, brand name, advertising messages, product positioning, pricing, and promotional techniques in foreign markets. The overall coefficient alpha was .82 (Brazil, .86; Chile, 73; Mexico, .84).

An adaptation of the entropy measure developed by Hitt, Hoskisson, and Kim (1997). Respondents were asked to indicate the extent of their export sales to six regions, and the entropy measure of export diversification is defined as export diversification = sum of [P sub i times ln(1/P sub i)], where P sub i is the sales attributed to each of the six regions and ln(1/P sub i) is the weight given to each region. It is a single-item measure.

A four-item scale assessing the overall role of exports in the firms' sales growth, market shares, and competitive positions, as well as the profitability of export sales. The overall coefficient alpha for the scale was .84 (Brazil, .78; Chile, .87; Mexico, .81).

Respondents indicated the percentages of their foreign sales in each of six regions. South America, Central America and Mexico, and Africa/Middle East were classified as developing countries; United States/Canada and Western Europe were classified as developed countries. For a firm to be categorized as having either a developed country or a developing country focus, 75 percent or more of its sales had to be in one of the groups; the dummy variable takes the value 1 for a developed country focus and 0 for a developing country focus.
scale: dummy variable (0 = developing country focus, 1 = developed country focus)

description: Indicator variable coded as 1 if the 'Attorney or Agent' field on the patent lists a law firm or external attorney and as 0 otherwise. Where the focal company's attorneys are listed, they are identified from the OED attorney roster and the patent is coded as not outsourced. All coding of the variable was done by hand because it was straightforward to categorize entries by visual inspection.

Measured for a given patent prosecution project by the number of 'backward' citations to patents of the same company that were also processed in-house. Because the authors expect diminishing returns and the variable is highly skewed, it is logged. It is measured over the five years prior to patent filing, differentiating firm-specific HC held by internal staff from prior outsourcing.
time_window: five years prior to patent filing

description: Measured by the logged number of prior patents processed internally by the firm in the same primary seven-digit International Patent Classification (IPC) as the focal patent. The IPC is used because of its unambiguous technological basis and nested structure, ensuring each class maps to a narrow but coherent technological subfield. The variable is measured with patents applied for or issued over the previous five years from the focal patent's filing date.
time_window: five years prior to the focal patent's filing date

description: Dummy variable coded as 1 if the focal patent cited a patent that was litigated in the past. Data on patent litigation were collected from the LitAlert database compiled by the USPTO and combined with patent cases from the Section 337 forum of the International Trade Commission.

Measures the number of patent attorneys employed by the focal firm, coded from the OED roster of registered patent attorneys. The variable has no variation among patents filed within the same firm-quarter, so the authors do not include its main effect and it enters the models only as an interaction with highly contested area. The authors use it as the firm's stock of internal occupational expertise, arguing a large internal staff can narrow the occupational HC gap with suppliers.

The dependent variable in the models is firm age at time of bankruptcy. Due to the highly skewed nature of the age distribution in the sample, age was log-normalized to better approximate a normal distribution. The mean age of the firms in the sample was 7.8 years (median 5.0).

A factor variable derived by principal components analysis from survey items in which bankruptcy trustees reported the extent to which the firm was affected by changes in market conditions, changes in technology, and legislative changes. Respondents used a five-point Likert-type scale to indicate the extent to which a given factor contributed to the bankruptcy. The items loaded strongly on a single factor with an eigenvalue of 1.84, and the derived factor serves as the proxy for the level of industry turbulence and change.
scale: five-point Likert-type items combined into a factor score

description: A composite factor variable derived with the principal components technique to test Hypothesis 3a, based on the manager's breadth of knowledge, depth of knowledge, and control. Breadth was defined as the level of knowledge across functional areas (e.g., marketing, finance, operations), while depth was the extent of knowledge within the functions. The derived factor variable serves as a proxy for general managerial abilities.

A two-item factor used to test for the impact of financial management resources and capabilities within the failed organizations. The relative contributions of unbalanced capital structure and poor capitalization are captured in this variable for H3b.
A composite factor variable for market development (H3c) that evaluated the impact of pricing strategy, product quality, and the establishment of market position.

variable_name: General management, financial management and market development factors
description: Resource and capability deficiencies are decomposed into three composite factor variables from the trustee survey, derived with principal components. General management covers breadth of knowledge, depth of knowledge and control. Financial management is a two-item factor on unbalanced capital structure and poor capitalization. Market development covers pricing strategy, product quality and market position.

variable_name: Trustee-reported causes of bankruptcy (four cause factors)
description: Causes of failure are measured from a survey of bankruptcy trustees who rated how much each factor contributed to the bankruptcy on five-point scales. The causes are summarized in four factor variables: industry change (market, technology and legislative changes), general management, financial management and market development. These are regressed on firm age at bankruptcy.

Five-item scale (alpha = 0.77) measured relative to competitors, capturing the degree to which customers participate in the design and delivery of the service offering. Items are on seven-point Likert scales and include whether the firm requires customers to perform functions similar to that of an employee, requires customers to become heavily involved in producing the service, minimizes the amount of time customers spend in the service production process, performs many tasks for customers, and is conveniently located near customers. Some appendix items are marked as reverse coded. The variable was centered (mean = 0) for the moderated hierarchical regression interaction tests.
scale: seven-point Likert (1 = not accurate to 7 = very accurate)

description: Two-item scale (alpha = 0.95) measured relative to competitors, capturing the degree to which customers and employees interact with one another during the service production process. Firms report whether most of their service production occurs out of customers' view (i.e., in the 'back office') or in full view of customers (i.e., in the 'front office'). Items are on seven-point Likert scales. The variable was centered (mean = 0) for the moderated hierarchical regression interaction tests.
scale: seven-point Likert (1 = not accurate to 7 = very accurate)

description: Five-item scale (alpha = 0.89) measured relative to competitors, capturing a firm's ability to alter service production in order to meet specific customer needs. Items include whether the firm changes how its service is offered for each customer, offers a service which is similar from customer to customer, allows customers to dictate how the service is offered, performs the same procedures for each customer, and requires a great deal of information from each customer before producing the service. Items are on seven-point Likert scales and some are marked as reverse coded in the appendix. The variable was centered (mean = 0) for the moderated hierarchical regression interaction tests.
scale: seven-point Likert (1 = not accurate to 7 = very accurate)

description: Composite selection and training scale consisting of five items (alpha = 0.85) assessing the level of human capital of employees directly involved in the service production and delivery process, measured relative to competitors. Items focus on whether firms select production employees with high levels of prior education, training, and experience, and how much time and money they spend on internal training activities. Items are on seven-point Likert scales. The variable was centered (mean = 0) for the moderated hierarchical regression interaction tests.
scale: seven-point Likert (1 = not accurate to 7 = very accurate)

description: Performance was measured using two variables, return on equity (ROE) and return on investment (ROI). A 2-year average of both ROE and ROI was used to reduce the potential for anomalous timing effects on performance, and the two were combined into one overall performance variable (alpha = 0.72). ROE and ROI data were obtained from Disclosure.

Each CEO was presented with all eight strategy-structure-environment combinations that result from strategy, structure and environment at two levels each, and assigned 100 points to the most desirable combination and rated the remaining combinations on a 0-100 point scale relative to the preferred combination(s) based on the likelihood of success for a manufacturing firm. Each CEO's ratings were regressed on the strategy, structure and environment variables and their interactions, using orthogonal polynomial effect codes in which differentiation strategy, organic structure and dynamic environment each received 1 and cost leadership, mechanistic and stable each were coded -1. The mean parameters from the two replications represent the CEO's judgment policy.
scale: 0-100 rating scale for the judgment task ratings

variable_name: Contingent vs noncontingent thinking cluster membership
description: The regression parameters from the CEOs' judgment models were standardized across the CEOs and clustered using Ward's minimum variance technique, with both the Pseudo-F and Pseudo-T criteria indicating a two-cluster solution and the cubic clustering criterion suggesting either two or five clusters; the two-cluster solution was selected. The clustering was validated by repeating it with K-means iterative partitioning, which matched Ward's classification for all but 3 of the 33 observations. Cluster 1 CEOs show below average preference strengths for particular strategies, structures and environments but above average recognition of bivariate contingencies and multivariate configurations, and were labeled contingent; Cluster 2 CEOs were labeled noncontingent.

The fit index was computed from the standardized (across firms) scores for environmental uncertainty (1 variable), the strategy variables (cost leadership and innovative differentiation) and the structure variables (formalization, centralization, specialization, controls and liaison devices). The raw score for each component of the index is divided by the number of pairs used in forming that component so that the same relative misfit within each component has the same contribution to the overall index; the total is made negative to convert the misfit index to an index of fit. To achieve the alignment specified by contingency theory, the innovative differentiation, environmental uncertainty, decentralization and liaison devices scales were reversed after standardization but prior to the fit calculation. The stated formula for the index appears in a formula block that is unreadable in this text.

variable_name: Performance compared to other similar firms
description: The CEO and the two non-CEO respondents were asked firm performance questions based on Dess and Robinson (1984); each was asked to rank his/her firm's performance compared to other similar firms on sales growth, after tax return on sales, after tax return on total assets, and overall performance/success, all for the previous five-year period. Five-year averages were sought to minimize the influence of short-term variations, and comparison to other similar firms provides a form of control for industry and strategic group effects. For the multivariate performance analyses the highly correlated return on assets and return on sales variables were combined to form an aggregate Return variable.
scale: rank compared to other similar firms

description: CEO background characteristics were determined by a questionnaire administered between replications of the judgment task. The questionnaire asked the CEO to report age, length of time with the firm, length of time in the industry, length of time as CEO, functional areas in which the CEO had previous experience, and level and types of educational experience.

The CEO questionnaire asked the CEO to report the functional areas in which he had previous experience, and the breadth of this past functional experience was used as a measure of CEO functional experience.

Three scales from Miller (1987) address perceptions of the firm's existing scanning, analysis, and planning processes, representing the degree of rationality in the firm's strategy making. Given their high intercorrelations, and consistent with previous work, the scanning, analysis and planning variables were summed to produce an aggregate rationality variable for use in subsequent analyses. The scales were answered by the two other top executives and were controlled for Log Size.

Count of the number of accidents experienced by an airline in a particular country during a particular year. Because accident reporting requirements and surveillance differ across countries, only fatal accidents (those that resulted in at least one fatality) are included in the accident counts.

Count of the number of fatal accidents experienced by all commercial airlines based in a focal airline's home country, excluding the focal airline itself. The variable was constructed over the three years prior to the year of a particular observation and discounted for the age of prior failure experience by dividing the number of passenger fatalities in a particular year by the number of years ago they had occurred. Independent variables were mean centered prior to being interacted.
time_window: three years prior to the observation year

description: Count of the number of fatal accidents globally experienced by all airlines based outside of the focal airline's home country. Like the within-country variable, it was constructed over the three years prior to the observation year and discounted for the age of prior failure experience by dividing the number of passenger fatalities in a particular year by the number of years ago they had occurred.
time_window: three years prior to the observation year

description: Measure of the regulatory strength of country-level aviation regulators, operationalized using data from regulatory audits carried out by the ICAO from 1999 to the present under the Universal Safety Oversight Audit Programme. Through these audits, the ICAO rates the effectiveness of aviation regulators on a 0-to-100 scale. Because audit data were available only from 1999, models including this variable were tested on the subset of the data from 1999 through 2011.

Dummy variables representing each of the 21 home countries of the airlines in the sample, included as fixed effects. Planned interactions between these country dummies and others' failure experience (within country) were constructed to test the influence of population-level (country-level) factors in driving vicarious learning from the experience of other organizations within a population; a country was the reference category.

Count of the number of fatal accidents experienced by a U.S.-based airline in a particular destination country during a particular year. Only fatal accidents (those that resulted in at least one fatality) are included, following the definition used in the global sample.

Count of the number of fatal accidents experienced by all commercial airlines based in a focal airline's home country, excluding the focal airline, constructed over the prior three-year window with the same discounting strategy. In the U.S. subsample this captures vicarious experience from other U.S.-based airlines.
time_window: three years prior to the observation year

description: Count of the number of fatal accidents globally experienced by all airlines based outside of the focal airline's home country, over the prior three years with the same discounting strategy. The U.S. subsample analysis includes this variable along with the independent and control variables from the global-level analysis.
time_window: three years prior to the observation year

description: Count of the number of rule changes enacted by the U.S. FAA over the prior three-year period, including any additions or changes to the FAA's policies regarding commercial airlines. There were a total of 507 changes to these rules made during the sampling period. This variable was included as an independent variable only in the analysis of the U.S. subsample because the FAA is a U.S.-based population-level actor, and it represents the compensating actions taken by the central population-level actor in the U.S. aviation population.

Count of the number of rule changes enacted by the U.S. FAA over the prior three-year period, entered in Model 2 of the U.S. subsample analysis. The coefficient for this variable is negative and significant, indicating that rule changes made by the FAA are associated with reductions in the number of subsequent fatal accidents experienced by U.S.-based airlines.

Binary variable equal to 1 if any of the individuals associated with that startup have previously worked for one of the established pharmaceutical firms on the list of the 50 largest pharmaceutical companies in the world by annual drug sales, and 0 otherwise. The underlying individual-level information was hand collected for the startups' senior management at the point at which they received investment. The definition and measurement derive from Chatterji (2009).

Binary variable equal to 1 if the startup has a senior manager who was previously employed at any incumbent firm in the industry other than the focal corporate investor, and 0 otherwise. It is used as the measure of generalized corporate experience in the decomposition of the corporate experience measure.

Binary variable equal to 1 if the startup has a senior manager who was previously employed at the incumbent firm that is the focal corporate investor in the dyad, and 0 otherwise. It distinguishes experience accrued at the specific investing firm from experience accrued at other incumbent firms in the industry.

Binary variable equal to 1 if the startup has a senior manager who was previously employed at an incumbent firm in a technology focused role, and 0 otherwise. Roles were classified by examining job titles and descriptions, using the types of roles in which the individual spent the longest duration in their pharmaceutical career, and, where duration information was not listed, the individual's summary or bio.

Binary variable equal to 1 if the startup has a senior manager who was previously employed at an incumbent firm in a commercialization focused role, and 0 otherwise. Commercialization focused careers commence within areas such as sales, marketing or business development, and individuals were classified according to the type of role in which they spent the longest duration.

Number of citations made by patents filed by the startup after the investment has been made to patents owned by the incumbent firm that is its corporate investor. Patent citations are used as a proxy for knowledge flows, following Jaffe et al. (1993), and are described as the most widely used measure of knowledge flows arising in interfirm partnerships, capturing informal interactions with employees of other organizations.

Count of downstream alliances formed between the startup and the established firm post-investment that are aimed at development or commercialization of the startup's technology. These are more targeted partnerships than CVC, typically focused on specific drugs or technologies, and their formation is the clearest indicator of the startup accessing these resources belonging to the incumbent firm.

A composite measure of the technological shock built from two yearly series: the yearly percentage increase in Internet hosts and the yearly change in semiconductor total factor productivity. Each measure was standardized using z-scores and the two were added together to create a single yearly index of the growth rate of the Internet and networking technologies.

Each firm's number of technology alliances formed for three-year windows leading up to and including the observation year, so that the observation for 1992 includes alliances formed in 1990-1992. The data were collected from SDC and log-transformed to improve their normality.
time_window: three-year windows leading up to and including the observation year

description: The sum of the reciprocal distances to every organization reachable from a given firm, i.e. the sum of 1/dij, where dij is the minimum (geodesic) distance from focal firm i to organization j. It increases with the size of the component in which the firm is embedded, the shortness of path lengths in that network, and the firm's centrality; the measure is based on the firm's position in the global technology collaboration network and was log-transformed because it is positively skewed.
time_window: three-year alliance windows used for the panel analysis

description: The number of successful patent applications for firm i in year t, collected from the Delphion database, with subsidiary patents aggregated up to the ultimate parent level. Patents were counted in their year of application and yearly counts were created for each firm for 1990-2005; because the measure has high variability across firms and is highly skewed, a log transformation of the counts is used. The minimum patent lag is one year, so the patent counts do not overlap with any of the independent or control variables.

Exposure to internal sources of new experiences was measured as the level of unexpected performance fluctuations in a given knowledge domain. Informants were asked to rate, for each knowledge domain, the degree of unexpected performance fluctuations. The resulting three measures were positively correlated, though no correlation was larger than .30 (alpha = .43), suggesting that performance fluctuations were domain-specific. The measure was used at the level of the knowledge domain without aggregating across the three domains.

Exposure to external sources of new experiences was measured as the level of innovation in the industry surrounding a knowledge domain of a subunit. Informants were asked how much processes (or products or conditions) in each area change as a result of innovation. Correlations between the resulting three domain-specific measures were between .40 and .50 (alpha = .71), and correlations were stronger within (.43-.51) than between (.00-.25) domains.

Measured as the degree of dissimilarity between a subunit's focus of operations and its peers' foci. Informants focused on those peer units (in the host country and worldwide) with which a unit had direct contact. A composite index of uniqueness of experiences was constructed from two items capturing the degree to which the operations of peers were dissimilar to or narrower than the focal unit's (alpha = .69).

A multi-item instrument asked informants to rate, for each of the three knowledge domains, the extent to which knowledge was stored as 'numbers and codes,' 'words and text,' or 'pictures and images.' Codification was not treated as a unidimensional construct but as an average index computed from formative indicators, so the average level of codification across the three forms was computed within each knowledge area. To establish construct validity, the measures were correlated with a measure of codifiability elicited with a separate instrument adapted from Zander and Kogut (1995); the correlations were moderate, between .30 and .33.

Outflows were measured with survey instruments that captured the overall volume of knowledge transmitted in each domain, an approach similar to the one used by Gupta and Govindarajan (1993). Knowledge outflows were measured with a multi-item instrument that asked informants to rate how much knowledge their subunit provided to other units, and the question was repeated for each combination of knowledge domain and flow direction. Informants were instructed to think about various channels through which knowledge might flow, including telephone conversations, e-mail, and regular mail. Informants provided ratings on five-point variables.

Outflows were measured with survey instruments that captured the overall volume of knowledge transmitted in each domain, an approach similar to the one used by Gupta and Govindarajan (1993). The multi-item instrument asked informants to rate how much knowledge their subunit provided to other units, repeated for each combination of knowledge domain and flow direction, thereby capturing assessments about the average level of knowledge sent from each knowledge domain to supervising units. Informants provided ratings on five-point variables.

Intensities of knowledge inflows were measured with a multi-item instrument that asked informants to rate how much knowledge their subunit received from other units, with a procedure analogous to the one for outflows. The question was repeated for each combination of knowledge domain and flow direction, capturing knowledge received from peer units.

Intensities of knowledge inflows were measured with a multi-item instrument that asked informants to rate how much knowledge their subunit received from other units, with a procedure analogous to the one for outflows. The question was repeated for each combination of knowledge domain and flow direction, capturing knowledge received from supervising units.

Detailed maps of wind speeds were projected onto a map of California counties, allowing measurement of the percentage of a county's area in each of seven wind speed classes; state and federal parks and national forest territories were excluded. A variable termed High Wind Energy Potential was created by multiplying the percentage of a county's land in Class 6 by its energy potential in kilowatts/acre and adding this to the percentage of Class 7 land multiplied by its energy potential. Preliminary analyses showed a clear break point between Classes 1 through 5 and Classes 6 and 7.

A summary variable for project economics built from two components: avoided cost information from the California Public Utilities Commission, converted to quarterly averages for each of the three major utilities and matched to counties (averaged where two service territories lay inside a county), and tax credits expressed as a decimal. A federal tax credit of 15 percent and a supplemental California tax credit of 25 percent of construction costs were in effect through 1985; in 1986 the California credit was reduced to 15 percent and no federal credit was offered; in 1987 and thereafter no credits were available. The index rises as avoided costs rise or tax credits rise; the formula is not readable in the text provided.

variable_name: Number of wind energy projects founded countywide in current quarter
description: The dependent variable is the number of projects sited in a county in a given quarter. Founding was tracked by the date on which the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission received an application from the project's proponents, since the certification FERC granted was necessary to qualify for PURPA benefits including avoided cost pricing. The data were scanned to remove duplicate applications and subsequent applications for new projects by existing developers, so each application could be treated as the founding of a new organization.

variable_name: Wind Energy Projects Founded in Prior 12 Months
description: To test Hypothesis 2, the sum of wind energy projects in a county during the 12 months previous to the start of a given quarter was computed and used as a variable.
time_window: 12 months prior to the start of the quarter

variable_name: Wind Energy Projects Founded in Adjacent Counties in Prior 12 Months
description: To test Hypothesis 3, the number of wind energy projects sited in counties that adjoined the focal county was tallied, using the 12 months prior to the start of a given quarter.
time_window: 12 months prior to the start of the quarter

description: Year-to-year change in the maximum potential unemployment insurance benefits in a firm's primary state of operation, calculated as the product of the maximum weekly benefit amount and the maximum regular duration. Firms are assigned to their state of firm headquarters as reported in Compustat. The nominal change is used.

Employment growth rate, measured as the net change in firm employment between year t and t−1 divided by the average of employment in the two years (0.5 × emp_t + 0.5 × emp_(t−1)). It captures a net change in firm employment that includes both layoffs and hiring, so lower values indicate more layoffs.

Binary variable equal to one if a firm's realized performance (return on assets) falls below the industry benchmark, calculated as the median ROA of the firm's primary four-digit SIC industry for each fiscal year. Firms with a ROA less than 100% and greater than −100% are excluded.

For each four-digit SIC code, the change in imports from China from the previous year, with the denominator equal to initial absorption measured as the sum of U.S. industry shipments and Chinese imports minus U.S. exports. Following Acemoglu et al. (2016), it is calculated for each year rather than for five-year intervals.

Binary variable equal to one if total value-add declines relative to the previous year for each four-digit SIC code, using changes in total value-add from the NBER-CES Manufacturing Industry Database.

Mean revenue growth rate of all public firms in Compustat for each four-digit SIC code, requiring at least 10 active firms in the industry. Used as an industry-level negative economic shock and also included in the control vector.

Binary variable equal to one if a respondent's employment status switches from employed to 'on indefinite layoff.' It isolates indefinite and involuntary layoffs of full-time workers without complications from voluntary exits and hiring.

Indicator based on whether the CEO made personal political donations to Senate, House, and presidential candidates who are Republican. Political donation data are collected from the Federal Election Commission and span the period 1993-2007; Republican CEOs represent 40% of the sample.

Indicator for a CEO promoted internally: an external CEO is identified as one whose first year as CEO is the year they join the firm, and internal CEOs are non-external CEOs. CEO-related information comes from the Execucomp database and the sample covers the period 1993-2007; external CEOs represent 36% of sample firms.

Population size of the headquarters' zip code, used to divide firms into the top 50%, bottom 50%, and bottom 25% of population size. Smaller population size proxies less social distance between managers and employees; the sample covers the period 1993-2007.

Family firm status from Anderson et al. (2012), who collect data on the 2,000 largest firms between 2001 and 2010; family firms with more than 5% ownership by family members comprise approximately one-third of the sample.

Binary variable equal to one if a business combination antitakeover law was adopted in a firm's state of incorporation by year t, following Giroud and Mueller (2010) and Keum (2021). The state of incorporation, which dictates corporate governance laws, differs from the state of a firm's primary operation; approximately 60% of public firms are incorporated in Delaware.
time_window: law in effect in year t

description: A firm's overall debt ratio (total debt divided by total assets); the sample is divided into high- and low-debt firms. Higher debt indicates greater financial pressure and less discretion.

Ratio of short-term debt to the industry median; the sample is divided into high- and low-constraint firms. Short-term debt that must be repaid within a year constrains managers' discretion to keep workers on the payroll.

The fraction of short-term debt that comes from currently maturing long-term debt; firms are split into high- and low-constraint firms based on the amount of long-term maturing debt, restricting the sample to firms with a total debt ratio above the median.

Attainment discrepancy is the difference between the firm's actual performance, measured as return on assets (net income divided by total assets) in period t-1 (the base year), and its aspiration level, obtained from its own performance in period t-2. ROA is the preferred performance proxy. The negative part of this discrepancy is entered in the models together with a quadratic term of the firm's negative attainment discrepancy, and the reported average marginal effect reflects the discrepancy and its quadratic term together.
time_window: performance in t-1 relative to aspiration in t-2

description: Attainment discrepancy is the difference between the firm's actual performance, measured as return on assets (net income divided by total assets) in period t-1 (the base year), and its aspiration level, obtained from its own performance in period t-2. ROA is the preferred performance proxy. The positive part of this discrepancy is entered in the models together with a quadratic term of the firm's positive attainment discrepancy, and the reported average marginal effect reflects the discrepancy and its quadratic term together.
time_window: performance in t-1 relative to aspiration in t-2

variable_name: Entry into new markets t (product and geographic)
description: A binary indicator equal to one if the firm adds at least one new market during a time window, and zero otherwise. To identify whether a firm added a new market, the authors manually compared the list of segments in its annual report for the last year of a given period with its list of segments in the base year of the period. Because the average number of new markets in a two-year window is relatively low, one or more entries during a period are coded as a single event.

This measure is mentioned only as an alternative coding of the dependent variable: for a robustness test the authors used the number of new markets as the dependent variable and re-estimated the models. No coding details beyond this are given in the prose.

Time-invariant dummy variable created to distinguish between charitable and non-charitable firms; it is coded 1 for firms rated and recognized for their charitable giving practices during the pre-treatment period (1990-1993). It is interacted with Post rating, a time-varying indicator variable coded as 1 for the post-treatment period (1994-1997). Because firm and year fixed effects are included, the authors focus on interpreting the Initial positive rating x Post rating interaction term.
time_window: pre-treatment period 1990-1993, interacted with the 1994-1997 post-rating period

description: The total amount of grants given to charity through a corporate foundation or given directly by the corporation divided by the level of pretax income for each firm. This transformation is consistent with KLD's evaluation of corporate philanthropic behavior and facilitates comparison of giving across firms of different size. Observations that generated negative values or extremely large values (greater than 10 percent) of pretax income were dropped.

A dichotomous variable coded as 1 for firms that experienced a downward recommendation during March 1994, the year firms were arguably most sensitive to their ratings due to increased media attention in the prior year. Firms that did not experience a downward recommendation were coded as 0.

A variable coded as 1 if the family (founder or founders' descendants) continued to own a 5 percent or greater stake in the company and/or have a presence on the board of directors, and 0 otherwise. Data were collected from a series of datasets produced by Anderson and colleagues, with non-matching observations supplemented by following their same methodology.

A local community was operationalized as a core-based statistical area (CBSA) established by the Office of Management and Budget. The variable is coded as 1 for CBSAs with tithing clubs and 0 otherwise; tithing clubs typically established recognition thresholds between 2 and 5 percent of pretax profits.

A dummy variable for firms involved in at least one of a set of industries characterized by significant negative social and environmental externalities. The variable distinguishes firms whose industry-specific risk profile leads them to donate more to charity.

variable_name: Ln (firm subscribers at the end of current year)
description: The dependent variable in the analysis of firm growth is the natural logarithm of subscribers for firm i at the end of year t. Growth is the increase in firm size, measured in total subscribers excluding those added through acquisitions in year t, between two consecutive years. The authors transform growth into the logarithm of subscribers in a given year, with the lagged values of the variable collected on the right-hand side of the model.

variable_name: N of new rookie executives from the focal firm
description: Count of new TMT members in year t-1 who were middle managers within the focal firm prior to entering the TMT. Rookies are executives without prior experience in a top management team. The counts are taken in the year prior to the growth measurement.

variable_name: N of new rookie executives from competitors
description: Count of new TMT members in year t-1 who were middle managers of wireless competitors prior to entering the TMT. Rookies are executives without prior experience in a top management team. The counts are taken in the year prior to the growth measurement.

variable_name: N of new rookie executives from outside the industry
description: Count of new TMT members in year t-1 who were middle managers in industries other than wireless telecom services prior to entering the TMT. In the few cases of an executive transfer from another business within a diversified firm, they were counted as a rookie from outside the industry. The counts are taken in the year prior to the growth measurement.

variable_name: N of new seasoned executives from competitors
description: Count of new TMT members in year t-1 who were top managers of competitors in wireless telecom services prior to entering the TMT. Seasoned refers to executives with prior experience in a top management team. The counts are taken in the year prior to the growth measurement.

variable_name: N of new seasoned executives from outside the industry
description: Count of new TMT members in year t-1 who were top managers in industries other than wireless telecom services prior to entering the TMT. Seasoned refers to executives with prior experience in a top management team. In the baseline analysis the study includes 114 executives categorized as seasoned outsiders because they came from outside the industry from positions ranked VP or above, of which 95 were confirmed as belonging to the top two levels of the firm.

variable_name: Average team tenure of existing TMT members
description: Measured, following other upper echelons studies, by the existing TMT members' average years of experience on the TMT of firm i in year t. The variable is used both as a control and as the moderator of the effect of new executives on growth.

Measured by the number of years since the first introduction of wireless communications service in the United States in 1983 in year t. The variable is used as a moderator of the growth effect of new executives from outside the industry.

variable_name: N of new rookie executives from competitors and from outside the industry
description: Outside rookies are measured by two yearly counts of new TMT members with no prior TMT experience who came from outside the focal firm: former middle managers of wireless competitors, and former middle managers in industries other than wireless telecom services. The counts are taken in the year before the growth measure.

variable_name: N of new seasoned executives from competitors and from outside the industry
description: Outside seasoned executives are measured by two yearly counts of new TMT members with prior top management experience who joined from outside the focal firm: former top managers of wireless competitors, and former top managers in industries other than wireless telecom services. The counts are taken in the year before the growth measure.

Survey-based, multi-item scales were used to measure each of the four aspects of the alliance learning process (articulation, codification, sharing, and internalization). For each firm, the score for each aspect was calculated as the mean of the scores it achieved on the items representing that aspect, and these mean scores were then aggregated across the four aspects to give an overall score for the firm's alliance learning process. Confirmatory factor analysis confirmed the alliance learning process as a second-order factor underlying the four first-order factors.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree) for the items

description: Multi-item survey scale measuring knowledge articulation as one aspect of the alliance learning process. The firm's score is the mean of its scores on the items representing articulation.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree)

description: Multi-item survey scale measuring knowledge codification as one aspect of the alliance learning process. The firm's score is the mean of its scores on the items representing codification.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree)

description: Multi-item survey scale measuring knowledge sharing as one aspect of the alliance learning process. The firm's score is the mean of its scores on the items representing sharing.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree)

description: Multi-item survey scale measuring knowledge internalization as one aspect of the alliance learning process. The firm's score is the mean of its scores on the items representing internalization.
scale: seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree)

description: Firms that had an alliance function were coded 1 and others were coded 0. The variable was also measured using a seven-point scale assessing the extent to which a firm's overall alliance activity was coordinated by a dedicated function or team.
scale: dummy (0/1) and seven-point scale (1 = Very Low, 7 = Very High)

description: A manager most closely associated with each specific alliance (a secondary respondent, different from the primary respondent) assessed that alliance on a multidimensional performance scale. Each alliance that scored four or more (above-average performance) on any three of the four performance dimensions was identified as 'successful or satisfactory.' The firm-level alliance success rate is the ratio of a firm's successful or satisfactory alliances to all its alliances during 1994-98.
scale: alliance-level items on a seven-point Likert scale; firm-level ratio (0 to 1)

description: The proportion of all active branch managers employed by the bank at time t who were hired from conventional banking, subtracted from 1 to capture purity. The variable was lagged by one-quarter prior to the focal branch's opening date.
time_window: lagged one-quarter prior to the focal branch's opening date

description: Dummy that takes the value of 1 if the branch manager came from conventional banking and had never worked in Islamic banking and 0 if the manager was appointed from an Islamic bank. It was estimated with random effects logit regression because the dependent variable is a dummy.

Computed as the bank's performance (return on assets) in a given quarter minus its historical aspiration level in that quarter. The aspiration level follows the standard aspiration-level adaptation formula with a four-quarter window and equal weight, because no very long historical window was defined. To capture asymmetric dynamics the variable was split with a spline: the above-aspiration component equals 0 when historical aspiration performance is at or below 0 and equals the value otherwise, and the below-aspiration component equals 0 when it is at or above 0 and equals the value otherwise. It was lagged by one-quarter in the estimations.
time_window: four-quarter window for the aspiration level; lagged one-quarter

description: Computed as a focal bank's performance (return on assets) in a given quarter minus its social aspiration level for that quarter, where the social aspiration level is the mean performance of the social comparison group. The comparison group consists of 25 banks identified as conventional banks specialized in retail banking. The variable was split into two categories: the above-aspiration component equals 0 when social aspiration performance is at or below 0 and equals the value otherwise, and the below-aspiration component equals 0 when it is at or above 0 and equals the value otherwise. It was lagged by one-quarter in the estimations.

Measured by the voting patterns in the town in which the new branches were opened: the number of votes for conservative political parties with an Islamic message divided by the total number of votes in that town. Both parliamentary elections (2002, 2007, 2011, 2015) and municipal elections (2004, 2009, 2014) were used to give a dynamic view of ideological tendencies. For years in which no elections were held, the average of the nearest two elections was taken.

The polarization index originally proposed by Esteban and Ray (1994), based on the Gini coefficient and taking into account both the size of the political party bases and the ideological distance between the political parties. Group sizes are the proportional number of votes that political parties received in each election at the town level, and the distance between polarized groups comes from the classification of all parties entering elections on a secular-religious scale ranging from 1 (extremely secular) to 10 (extremely religious). The authors set the multiplicative constant to 1 and gave a balanced weight to the size of and the distance between the subgroups; the equation itself is not readable in the provided text.
time_window: parliamentary and municipal elections during the study period

description: Operationalized at time t as the ratio of the number of transfers from conventional banking in the year before t that occurred in the focal town to the average density of local Islamic branches in the town during that year. The value was lagged a quarter prior to the opening of the focal new branch.
time_window: one year before t; lagged a quarter prior to the focal branch opening

description: Performance feedback is measured by two return on assets gaps. Historical aspiration performance is the bank's quarterly ROA minus its historical aspiration level from a four-quarter window. Social aspiration performance is the bank's ROA minus the mean ROA of 25 conventional retail banks. Each is split into above-aspiration and below-aspiration components with a spline.

Defined as the number of days elapsed between the date of the new product introduction and the date of each imitation. For example, a first mover's new product introduction is given a value of 1, denoting the introduction takes place on day 1, and an imitative response 100 days later is designated as day 101. Used as an independent variable in the cross-sectional regressions of shareholder wealth.

Defined as the temporal rank position of an imitator compared with the first mover and other imitators. The first mover is designated as order 1, the second mover as order 2, and subsequent laggards are designated in the same manner. Used as an independent variable in the cross-sectional regressions of shareholder wealth.

Cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) and standardized cumulative abnormal returns (SCARs) were computed for a 5-day trading period consisting of 2 days before to 2 days after the announcement. The market model regresses security returns against the overall return on the market (S&P 500) to generate expected returns, estimated over a 200-day period beginning with event day t = -260 and ending with event day t = -61. Abnormal returns are standardized by their standard deviation to compute SARs, and CARs are computed by summing abnormal returns over a particular time interval; the SCARs served as the dependent variable, with the 3-day event window (-1 to +1) used for hypothesis testing.
time_window: 200-day estimation period ending at t = -61; 3-day event window (-1 to +1) used for hypothesis testing

description: Identified from a structured content analysis of Predicasts F&S Index United States. The first article that reported the introduction of a product that was the same or imitative of an already existing competitor's product was considered the first imitation and the date of imitation (time) was recorded; these firms are designated as the second movers, and subsequent imitative responses were placed accordingly in response timing and order.

Number of foreign banks in each of the four strategic groups, counted for each year. Banks were classified into one of the four strategic groups for each year in which the bank had reported financial data, and changes in strategic group membership were considered for the purpose of calculating the density of banks in each group. All independent and control variables were time-lagged by one year.

Number of domestic banks in each of the four strategic groups, counted for each year. A bank was classified into one of the four strategic groups for each year in which it had reported financial data, and changes in strategic group membership were considered for the purpose of calculating the density of banks in each group. All independent and control variables were time-lagged by one year.

Number of new domestic bank entries each year into each of the four strategic groups. An entry was defined as the establishment of a new bank, or the acquisition of an existing bank by a foreign bank or an out-of-state domestic bank; mergers among California banks and acquisition by a local entrepreneur were excluded. For new banks, the loan portfolio in the first year determined the strategic group on entry. The number of domestic new bank entries totalled 302 over the 10-year period.

Number of new foreign bank entries each year into each of the four strategic groups. An entry was defined as the establishment of a new bank, or the acquisition of an existing bank by a foreign bank or an out-of-state domestic bank; mergers among California banks and acquisition by a local entrepreneur were excluded. For new banks, the loan portfolio in the first year determined the strategic group on entry. The number of foreign new bank entries totalled 61 over the 10-year period.

Each bank was classified into one of four strategic groups for each year in which the bank had reported financial data, using a combination of hierarchical and nonhierarchical cluster analysis on the bank's loan portfolio. The loan specialization of each bank was measured as the proportion of each of the three types of loans (real estate, personal, and commercial) in the bank's total loan portfolio. The four-cluster solution comprised one loan generalist category and three specialist categories: real estate loan specialists, personal loan specialists, and commercial loan specialists.
scale: proportion of total loans for each loan type

description: Each manager responded on five-point Likert-type scales, ranging from one for 'rarely' to five for 'almost always', about the extent to which the business unit shared seven sources with sister business units. No a priori information suggested differences in the relative importance of each function, so the seven measures were treated as equally important. A business unit was classified into the high relatedness group if the manager responded that one or more of the seven sources of relatedness were shared 'very often' or 'almost always' with sister business units, and into the low relatedness group otherwise. For the comparison with single businesses, business units were classified as single businesses using Rumelt's criteria: they were self-identified as a nondivisionalized company or a single division of the parent corporation accounted for 95 percent or more of corporate sales.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = rarely, 5 = almost always)

description: Market relatedness was captured using the questions about the extent to which customers, sales force, and advertisement and promotion were shared, answered on five-point Likert-type scales ranging from one for 'rarely' to five for 'almost always'. Whether the business unit had higher values on measures of market relatedness or production relatedness was used to classify the business units into one of the two types. The interaction between the two levels of extent of relatedness and the two types of relatedness was used to classify the businesses into four groups.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = rarely, 5 = almost always)

description: Production relatedness was captured by questions about the extent to which business units shared plant and equipment, research and development, or interdivisional product transfers, answered on five-point Likert-type scales ranging from one for 'rarely' to five for 'almost always'. Whether the unit had higher values on the market relatedness or the production relatedness measures classified it into one of the two types of relatedness.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = rarely, 5 = almost always)

description: Business unit managers self-assessed their strategic autonomy using a five-point Likert-type scale. A response of one indicated very little or no autonomy, while a response of five indicated complete or nearly complete strategic autonomy. Autonomy was considered to represent the extent of authority business unit managers exercise in making major strategic decisions, such as entering new product markets or changing product lines.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = very little or no autonomy, 5 = complete or nearly complete strategic autonomy)

description: The 362 initial respondents were sent a questionnaire asking for accounting data on their business unit sales and return on assets over the previous 5-year period. The dependent variable is the business unit's 5-year average after-tax return on assets.

The questionnaire asked for accounting data on business unit sales over the previous 5-year period, and the dependent variable is growth of business unit sales over that period. Growth was chosen together with profitability because the two have been theorized as two of the primary dimensions of business performance.

The paper's performance construct was operationalized with the business unit's 5-year average after-tax return on assets and growth of business unit sales over the same period. Profitability and growth were chosen because they have been theorized as two of the primary dimensions of business performance.

A count variable ranging from 0 to 3 that captures the number of CEMs implemented by founder-CEOs at IPO. The authors state that the effect of CEMs is cumulative: the larger the number of CEMs used by founder-CEOs, the more they can leverage control of the firm over and above retained equity. The variable therefore captures the extent of disconnection between equity ownership and voting rights.

The logarithm of firm market capitalization in million euros at the end of the first trading day, inflation adjusted to constant 1992 euros. It is the dependent variable of the OLS regressions predicting the effect of CEMs at IPO.
time_window: end of the first trading day

description: Abnormal buy and hold returns were obtained in two steps. First, simple buy and hold returns (BHRt) were computed by compounding monthly stock returns, including any dividends, over a given period t, representing the return on a hypothetical one euro investment held from the first to the last day of period t. Next, ABHRs were calculated by subtracting the BHRt of a benchmark portfolio (the SBF250 index) from the BHRt of the IPO firm over the same horizon, so that positive ABHRs indicate outperformance of the index. Up to five annual observations were computed per IPO firm, until delisting or CEO succession, resulting in an unbalanced sample; extreme values were winsorized at the 5th percentile on both tails.
time_window: up to five years post-IPO, annual observations

variable_name: distribution of domain and methodological expertise across sites
description: Site directors rated the expertise of 345 professionals who worked at their sites during 1996-2000 (97% of the total), designating whether each person on the list was an expert and what types of expertise that person had. Each professional's specialized expertise, if any, was coded zero or one in each of the nine domain and six methodological categories, with people having both types coded as one on both variables. The resulting distribution of experts across the six major sites was used to test whether experts were randomly distributed and whether their distribution matched site-level expertise requirements.

variable_name: proportion of projects requiring different types of domain expertise in each site
description: The expected distribution of expertise based on requirements for expertise at each site, derived from the coded expertise requirements of the projects carried out at that site. The proportion of domain experts available in each site corresponds to the proportion of projects requiring different types of domain expertise in each site. It served as the comparison distribution in chi-square tests of whether the distribution of experts across sites matched site requirements.

The number of domain experts on a project whose expertise is mentioned in the abstract as a requirement; for example, if a project abstract said the project requires expertise in education, then the number of education domain experts on the project was counted toward the project's total matched domain experts. Project abstracts were coded by the first and second authors (interrater reliability Kappa of 80%), with each project able to have up to nine domain expertise requirements.

The number of methodological experts on a project whose expertise is mentioned in the abstract as a requirement. Each project could have up to five methodological expertise requirements, coded from archived project abstracts by the authors.

Constructed for each member working on a project starting in year t from the person's collaboration history from 1996 to year t-1, and defined as the average number of other sites that project members with matched expertise had worked with in the past, normalized by the total number of connections a person could have had with all the other sites. Projects that started in 1996 (95 projects) had no work history collaboration data and were excluded from analyses including cross-site connection variables.
time_window: from 1996 to the year before project start

description: The cross-site work history network of unmatched experts, defined as the average number of other sites that project members without matched expertise had worked with in the past, normalized by the total number of connections a person could have had with all the other sites. It was constructed from each member's collaboration history from 1996 to year t-1 for projects starting in year t.
time_window: from 1996 to the year before project start

description: A dichotomous variable whereby a project was defined as dispersed if at least one project member's home site differed from the site where the project was managed. It was used as the dependent variable in logistic regressions of project staffing and as the moderator in regressions of project net earnings; the authors also examined whether the percentage of dispersed project team members had implications for coordination costs and financial performance.

The net of project revenue over project expenses, including all labor costs and overhead cost allocations, defined as AIR itself did. It is the dependent variable in the ordinary least squares regressions of project outcomes; a table note states that the dependent variable, year-to-date profit, was standardized.

Calculated using Blau's (1977) index (1 - ΣPi²), where P is the proportion of members in a specific gender category and i represents the number of categories. The computation includes the gender (1 = female, 0 = male) of the CEO and all TMT members.
