It is a continuous measure ranging from 0 (same-gender teams) to .50 (gender-balanced teams with equal female and male proportions).

Measured using the 7-item scale of Edmondson (1999), answered from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. Sample items are 'Team members are able to bring up problems and tough issues' and 'It is safe to take a risk on this team.' Individual ratings were aggregated to the team level on the basis of good interrater agreement and between-team variance.

Measured using the 8-item scale by He and Wong (2004), answered from 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree. Four items capture the exploration orientation (e.g., introduce new generation of products) and four items capture exploitation (e.g., improve existing product quality). Ratings were aggregated to the firm level, and the exploration and exploitation scores were multiplied to create a single index of ASO.
time_window: t3, with prior ASO measured at t1

description: Measured with Simsek et al.'s (2007) 4-item scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). An example item was 'Our firm has plentiful resources to produce our products or services.' TMT members' ratings were aggregated to reflect firm-level slack.

The main independent variable is the interaction term between the policy change variable Post-PC and the binary variable Jiangsu, which indicates whether a REB is located in Jiangsu province. Months up until November 2013 are treated as prechange (Post-PC = 0) and months starting in November 2013 are considered postchange (Post-PC = 1). The interaction term thus equals one if a business is located in Jiangsu province when the province has already passed the new migration policy.
time_window: May 2013 to April 2014, 6 months before and 6 months after the November 2013 policy change

description: The main dependent variable on business performance is a REB's monthly Sales. All monthly data on sales are normalized, meaning that the sales numbers are divided by one unknown number to ensure each entrepreneur's anonymity. Given the uncertainty of this approximation, the authors take the logarithm of all sales numbers, log(Sales), and interpret effect sizes in percentage terms.

Product innovation is measured as the number of distinct products a business displays. The authors report that Jiangsu REBs experienced a 5.8% greater increase in the number of new products relative to non-Jiangsu REBs after the policy change, and that substantial portions of the sales differences between Jiangsu and non-Jiangsu REBs in the postperiod months were mediated through an increase in product innovation.

Scores that customers assign to a business, of which the authors have three types: scores for logistics, services, and product descriptions, all scored out of five. The demand spillover test divides the sample by high versus low customer review scores for logistics/shipping prior to the policy change.

A variable distinguishing de novo from incumbent businesses. To define de novo versus incumbent businesses, the authors categorize all REBs that were registered before October 2013 as incumbent and those that were registered after that date as de novo. Because de novo businesses were founded, by definition, in the postperiod, the authors can only test the relative performance gains of Jiangsu versus non-Jiangsu de novo REBs in the postperiod.

A prefecture-level variable measured as the average wage of all employees in the urban parts of each prefecture, using data from 2014. It proxies returnees' financial endowments in each prefecture, on the assumption that it is more likely for rural migrants in a particular prefecture to be from and to return to a village in that prefecture than a village in another prefecture. The analysis divides the full sample into subsamples by the median wage level.

A dummy variable indicating whether a business is female-led, which enters the models as a triple interaction term with Jiangsu and Post-PC. The authors report that fifty-one percent of the entrepreneurs are female. Breaking the sample into subsamples, the female subsample and the male subsample are compared.

For each subcommittee and year, knowledge network ties between two firms were identified if at least one knowledge alliance between them was coded in the relevant five-year window. A degree centrality measure was then calculated for each firm using the number of such ties as edge-weights to account for the strength of these relationships. Knowledge ties were alliance announcements involving a new knowledge-generating agreement such as R&D or technology co-development, and the network was treated as undirected.

From the full NBER patent dataset, patents owned by member firms were extracted by matching on assignee names and filtered using technological categories relevant to the industry. A five-year moving window of cross citations between these patents defined the citation ties, and an in-degree centrality measure was calculated for every member firm. Because patent citations are unidirectional, the networks were treated as directed, and the patent application year was used for the time window.

For each subcommittee and year, commercialization network ties between two firms were identified if at least one commercialization alliance between them was coded in the relevant five-year window. A degree centrality measure was calculated using the number of such ties as edge-weights. Commercialization ties were alliance announcements based on existing technologies, including interoperability testing and certification, joint marketing, original equipment manufacturer/value-added reseller, licensing, or production, and the network was treated as undirected.

variable_name: Firm's vote on a ballot measure
description: All votes recorded in the standards subcommittee archival records for the 241 ballot measures were manually extracted and mapped to unique member firms based on the membership roster. The four voting choices were assigned ordinal values of 0 (yes), 1 (abstain), 2 (yes with comments/conditions), and 3 (no). The ordering reflects the level of effort required to address and resolve the objection, with a 'no' vote requiring more effort than a 'yes with comments' vote, which in turn requires more than an 'abstain' vote.

A composite index built from five stewardship variables. The investment aspect of stewardship was gauged by the R&D to sales ratio and by the capital expenditures to property, plant, and equipment ratio. Funding was assessed as cash holdings (cash plus short-term investments to property, plant, and equipment) and as 1 minus the dividend payout ratio (dividends to earnings). Unsystematic risk was assessed as idiosyncratic market risk for the firm's shares. All five stewardship variables were then standardized and summed to create the composite stewardship index, a formative index (Cronbach alpha 0.60) in which the components are intended to contribute collectively to the overall level of stewardship.
Family presence in the business was assessed according to the number of directors on the board who are family members. Data on individuals were aggregated to the firm level.
Family presence in the business was assessed according to the number of executives who are family members. Data on individuals were aggregated to the firm level.

Vote dispersion among family members was measured using the Herfindahl index with the polarities reversed, so that higher values indicate a greater breadth of dispersion of family votes across members of the controlling family.

For emotion/multigenerational involvement, the authors assessed whether two or more generations were present in the business. It is a binary variable indicating a family firm with family members present from multiple generations.

For power/family control, the authors measured the percentage of votes controlled by the family. Consistent with prior work, the focal family was designated as the one with the most votes, and in totaling family votes the shares of cotrustees of family trusts who were directly employed by the family were included. A squared term for family vote control was also entered in the regression to capture the curvilinear effect.

To gauge executive susceptibility to family influence, the authors employed dummy variables, one of which indicates the presence of a lone founder CEO, that is, a founder CEO with no other family members in the business.

variable_name: Family founder CEO and family founder chairman
description: To gauge executive susceptibility to family influence, the authors employed dummy variables indicating the presence of a family founder CEO and a family founder chairman, that is, the founder presides as CEO or chairman with other family members in the business.

variable_name: Family CEO-later generation (CEO2+) and family chairman-later generation (CH2+)
description: To gauge executive susceptibility to family influence, the authors employed dummy variables indicating the presence of a second-plus generation family CEO and a second-plus generation family chairman.

Performance was assessed as total shareholder returns, which the authors describe as a measure that reflects both growth and profitability and provides the most complete picture of how well shareholders have done with their investment. Market performance data were obtained from the Center for Research on Security Prices (CRSP).

The relative difference between the ideator's value forecast at Stage 1, defined as the idea's net economic benefit (resulting cost savings) over three years, and the true idea value as verified by accounting at Stage 5. The measure ranges continuously from undervaluation to overvaluation, with positive (negative) values indicating overvalued (undervalued) ideas and zero a correct evaluation. For non-implemented ideas the value cannot be determined and the measure is censored from above at 100%. For the regressions, values outside the 5th to 95th percentile range were Winsorized to those percentiles, so that the maximum of the overvaluation measure is capped at 1 (i.e., 100%) and its minimum at -6 (i.e., -600%).
scale: continuous relative measure, capped at 100% above and -600% below
time_window: net economic benefit over three years

description: Dummy variable denoting whether an idea was generated by employees of high (1) or low (0) rank. Lower-level employees (dummy = 0) include frontline workers and their first- and second-level supervisors, such as machine operators, foremen and production-line heads; higher-level employees (dummy = 1) include all upper-rank individuals according to the firm's formal organizational structure, such as production managers, quality managers and plant heads. The values were derived manually from existing organizational charts with the help of members of the firm, and lower-level employees are not guided by higher-level ones when it comes to ideation.

Dummy variable for the mode of idea creation (0 = individual ideation; 1 = collaborative ideation), indicated by the submission system's 'idea creator cell', which identifies a specific work unit or the precise names of multiple ideators. The authors dichotomize the variable because they do not always know the precise group size. In the sample, collaborative ideators were homogeneous in terms of hierarchy, so hierarchy levels could be assigned to collaboratively generated ideas.

TMT misfit was calculated by comparing the number of times each functional area was listed in any job title for the entire top team with the total number of managers with experience in those functional areas. TMT underqualification is a count of the roles listed for the TMT that include functional areas for which the group of top managers lack prior experience, summed across all 11 functional areas. Executives were considered to have prior experience in an area if their titles included that function in any of their previous three jobs, and were also considered to have experience in a function after they had held their current role for one year. The variable was lagged by 12 months (t-12).

TMT overqualification is a count of the prior experiences above those required by the current roles of the team across all 11 functions, for example when three top managers have operations experience but only two current job titles indicate an operations functional role. The count was summed across all 11 functional areas to give an overall measure of how much more experience the group of top managers had relative to the current roles listed for the team. As with underqualification, prior functional experience was coded from the managers' previous three jobs and from one year of on-the-job experience in the current role, and the variable was lagged by 12 months.

The authors dummy coded the firm's achievement of each of two developmental milestones—receiving venture capital funding and staging an initial public offering—at time t, and then summed across events to create an overall measure of level of firm development. The variable ranged from 0, in which a firm had no venture capital funding and no initial public offering, to 2, in which a firm had received venture capital funding and had staged an initial public offering. In the sample, 71% of the firms received venture capital funding and 53% went public.

TMT hiring is the sum of all top managers who appeared in month t but who were not employed by the firm in month t-1. This dependent variable comprises the number of hires in the TMT over a one-year period: TMT hiring measured at time t is the sum of the new hires within the TMT over the subsequent 12 months, but the variable is updated each month to reflect hiring at different times in the prior year.

New TMT roles were assessed as being added when a job title appeared that had never before existed in the firm; variations on a previously existing role (e.g., executive VP of sales, VP of North American sales) and splits of an existing role were not counted as new roles, and titles that existed during the founding month or the title 'founder' were not coded as new. The first author coded the job titles, and a second coder applied the coding scheme to half of the dataset with acceptable agreement (Cohen's kappa = .87). Of the 1,918 job titles in the dataset, 40% were considered new roles; new roles were counted over a one-year period but updated monthly.

The number of foreign countries in which the creative director had worked. It includes the breadth accumulated while this person was not yet a creative director, as well as the breadth accumulated following the person's promotion to the creative director's position. Home country was defined as the country where the person spent the most time before the age of 18. When a house was run by more than one creative director, the average across individuals was used.
level: creative director (averaged across a house's creative directors)

description: The number of years each director had worked abroad in their professional career. It includes the depth accumulated while this person was not yet a creative director, as well as the depth accumulated following the person's promotion to the creative director's position. When a house was run by more than one creative director, the average across individuals was used.
level: creative director (averaged across a house's creative directors)

description: An index of cultural distance between the home country and the countries in which the person has been working, built from Hofstede's cultural distance scores, with distances on the Hofstede dimensions aggregated using the Kandogan (2012) approach. The home country was compared to the foreign country in which the creative director has been working; when there were several countries, the absolute values of the cultural distances between the home country and each foreign country were added up.
level: creative director (averaged across a house's creative directors)
time_window: current exposure (countries in which the person has been working)

description: The ratings published by the French trade magazine Journal du Textile, in which industrial buyers evaluate the creativity of fashion collections in both fall/winter and spring/summer fashion shows. Buyers are asked to give 20 points to what they perceive as the most creative collection for the given season, and 0 points to collections considered not creative; each buyer can give points to a maximum of 20 houses. The points awarded by the buyers are summed to yield the final score, and the measure used in the analysis is the average number of points given to the fashion house by the raters in a given season. Inter-rater reliability (Cronbach's alpha) averages 0.97.

Market share data for the focal business are derived from the Trinet Inc. Large Establishment Data Base; market share of plants in the firm with the same primary SIC code are summed by firm to represent the market share of the focal business in the firm. The logistic transformation of market share is used because the distribution of market share is truncated at 0 and 1, and prevents predictions which are less than 0 or greater than 1. In this sample the logistic of market share correlates 19.70 percent with firm profitability.
scale: market share truncated between 0 and 1; logistic transform
level: business unit (four-digit SIC business of a firm)

description: The actual change in market share from period t+1 (1984) to t+2 (1986) for the businesses that changed ownership. For a group of businesses changing ownership in the same transaction, a sales-weighted average of the actual market share changes of the group is used.
level: business unit; sales-weighted group of businesses

description: Coefficients of Models 1 and 2, estimated within each industry, are applied to a business before and after its ownership change; the prediction of market share for time t+1 minus the prediction of market share for time t is the predicted change for the business. This net change in predicted market share is due to changes in interrelationships from the acquisition and is used as the measure of change in operational synergy. For groups of businesses changing ownership together, a sales-weighted average of the predictions of the businesses in the transaction is used.
level: business unit; sales-weighted group of businesses

description: Seven dimensions of relatedness are computed for each business by merging business-level sales from Trinet with flows between industries from the 1977 Input-Output tables, the 1977 FTC line of business expense-to-sales ratios, and Scherer's technology flow matrix. Flows from the firm's other businesses are weighted by the relative sales of those businesses, so flows in large firms receive less weight. In each industry the market share of a business is regressed on these variables; a significant positive coefficient identifies the existence of a type of synergy in that industry, and a significant negative coefficient identifies dissynergy.
level: business unit (focal business of a firm in a four-digit SIC industry)
time_window: business data for 1980 and 1984; industry flows and expense ratios from 1977

description: Business units which changed ownership between 1980 and 1984 are identified by selecting those business units which have a different parent company code in the Trinet data base in 1984 than they did in 1980. Business units in which not all plants changed ownership were dropped from the change of ownership sample.

Dichotomous variable for which a 1 indicates that a director left the board within three years of the year the independent variables were measured. A three-year window is the standard term for director service and ensures that a director has the opportunity to avoid reelection at least once.
time_window: three years following the year the independent variables were measured

description: Measured as the annual return on assets (ROA) of the focal firm. Alternative models using the total stock returns to the firm produced unchanged results.

A count of press reports in the business and general press that mentioned the firm in a given year, gathered from the LexisNexis database using keyword searches for the firm's name and ticker symbol in a selected set of major press outlets, including the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal. Because the measure is highly skewed, it was log-transformed; since many companies received zero coverage, a 1 was added to all observations before the transformation.

Dummy variable indicating if a director was not a corporate executive. Risk Metrics divides directors' occupations into eight separate categories (such as attorney, consultant, politician, academic, executive). The variable takes on a value of 1 when a director is not currently a corporate executive and 0 otherwise.
Dichotomous variable coded 1 if the focal director attended an exclusive secondary school as categorized by Domhoff (1970), and 0 otherwise. It is used as an indicator of elite social status.
Dichotomous variable indicating whether the director was the chair of the focal firm's audit committee, with 1 indicating holding the position and 0 indicating not holding it.
Dichotomous variable indicating whether the director was the chair of the focal firm's compensation committee, with 1 indicating holding the position and 0 indicating not holding it.
Dichotomous variable indicating whether the director was the chair of the board, with 1 indicating holding the position and 0 indicating not holding it.
Dichotomous variable coded 1 if a director was an active CEO and 0 otherwise.
A count of the total number of board appointments held by the director.

The total number of lawsuits filed by shareholders of a focal firm in the prior year, gathered from Institutional Shareholder Services. The authors describe shareholder lawsuits as a direct measure of the legal risk that directors face.

Dichotomous variable coded 1 if the focal firm announced a financial restatement that year, and 0 otherwise. Restatements made for routine reasons that were not conceptually related to observers' evaluative reactions were excluded.

Design quality of the developed component (output performance), based on multiple items, including performance, costs, conformance quality, and structural and functional coordination with other components. Each item was evaluated by the respondent in terms of his/her satisfaction with the outcome, and the relative position in comparison with the same type of component used for competing vehicle models in the market, to capture both engineering excellence and market competitiveness. The variable is the mean of the item scores.

The level of early, integrated problem-solving process with a supplier, built as the mean score of the survey items describing the project's development process. It scores high when, for example, the supplier's initial price/cost estimate was examined very carefully by the automaker from the beginning of the project, and the automaker examined the supplier's manufacturing process and design for manufacturing at the earlier stage. Some of the underlying items were reverse coded.

The frequency of face-to-face communication between the automaker and the supplier, measured as the mean number of days per year of mutual visits by the automaker's engineers and purchasing staff and the supplier's engineers and sales staff.
The knowledge level of the automaker's engineers about the component, defined as the mean of the two subcomponents engineers' component-specific knowledge (EKN1) and architectural knowledge (EKN2).
The level of knowledge specific to a component, including technology, cost, and manufacturing process. It is one of the two subcomponents averaged into EKN.

The level of knowledge about structural and functional coordination with other components and design for manufacturing; it indicates the level of knowledge about the component's coordination and linkage with other components and was named architectural knowledge. It is one of the two subcomponents averaged into EKN.

The level of the automaker's internal coordination, defined as the mean of three subcomponents: internal coordination within engineering departments (INC1), internal coordination between engineering and purchasing departments (INC2), and external consistency of the automaker's various engineering functions and purchasing department toward the supplier during the project (INC3).
Internal coordination within the automaker's engineering departments, one of the three subcomponents averaged into INC.

variable_name: INC2 (internal coordination between engineering and purchasing)
description: Internal coordination between the automaker's engineering and purchasing departments, one of the three subcomponents averaged into INC.
External consistency of the automaker's various engineering functions and purchasing department toward the supplier during the project, one of the three subcomponents averaged into INC.
The supplier's sales dependency on the automaker, constructed from industry data on component transactions in the Japanese auto industry.
A dummy variable set to 1 if the automaker owned a part of the supplier's stock; otherwise 0.

System variable constructed from combinations of the three aggregate change variables; a company is a member of System 1, taking the value 1, if the sum of Changing Structure plus Changing Processes and Changing Boundaries is equal to three, and is zero otherwise. Because the data are transformed into binary dummies, the mean can be read as the percentage of the sample that is high on all three dimensions.
Aggregate dummy variable constructed from the individual survey variables; a company takes the value 1 if it passes three of the four conditions under Changing Structure and zero otherwise.
Aggregate dummy variable; a company takes the value 1 if it passes four of the five conditions under Changing Processes and zero otherwise.
Aggregate dummy variable; a company takes the value 1 if it passes two of the three conditions under Changing Boundaries and zero otherwise.

Our measure of performance is a financial one. For the United Kingdom, performance data were obtained from the CD-database One Source and firms in the upper or lower quartile of their sector for adjusted return on capital employed were treated as high or low performers. For Continental Europe, scales for self-reported estimates of relative financial performance were used, high performers being those who reported their relative financial performance as 'a lot greater' than other firms in their sector and low performers those who answered 'lower'. The dependent variable in the performance models is relative firm performance.

variable_name: percentage of sales outside the company's domestic market
description: Internationalisation is measured by the percentage of sales outside the company's domestic market; the data are drawn from our questionnaire. It is entered in the probit equations on the individual design variables and on the change and system variables.

variable_name: R&D expenditure as a percentage of total sales
description: Knowledge intensity is proxied by R&D expenditure as a percentage of total sales; the data are drawn from our questionnaire. It is entered in the probit equations on the individual design variables and on the change and system variables.

U.K.-headquartered companies and German-headquartered companies were entered as the two largest groups of firms and as representing polar opposites in terms of capital market institutions, the first transaction driven, the second allegedly more long-term; the probit estimates control for business characteristics.

Measured with the International Monetary Fund's structural reforms index compiled by Sahay and Goyal (2006), which covers the period 1970-2005. The index captures economic liberalization and improvements in national governance, measuring the movement from high government intervention and domestic market protectionism toward low government control of a country's economy and market aperture. It ranges from 0 to 100, with higher values representing higher levels of promarket reforms. The measure was standardized and lagged one year in the analysis.

Profitability, the dependent variable, was measured as return on sales (ROS), a measure of profitability commonly used in research. ROS was chosen because the ratio includes two flow measures, which, compared to return on assets, tend to be less influenced by inflation and accounting standards. It was computed using data from AmericaEconomía.

Indicator of firm type based on the AmericaEconomía classification by majority ownership; it identifies firms whose capital is majority owned by the state in the home country. It serves as the base (omitted) category relative to which the other two firm types are compared in the moderation analysis.

Indicator of firm type based on the AmericaEconomía classification by majority ownership; it identifies firms whose capital is majority owned by private investors in the home country. It is interacted with the measure of promarket reforms to capture the impact of reforms on domestic private firms relative to domestic state-owned firms.

Indicator of firm type based on the AmericaEconomía classification by majority ownership; it identifies firms whose capital is majority owned by investors from another country. It is interacted with the measure of promarket reforms to capture the impact of reforms on subsidiaries of foreign firms relative to domestic state-owned firms.

Yearly individual worker fixed effects estimated from the company's production event data. The dependent variable is the log of the number of good units of an item produced on a date by the team working on a line and shift that included the worker, and the model includes worker × year fixed effects together with line, shift, item-type and month × year fixed effects and production covariates. The authors argue that this captures, at least directionally, supervisors' process of inferring workers' productivity from counterfactuals, net of teammate quality and the challenge of different types of production.

The numerical score each worker received on a yearly basis from his or her production supervisor. Supervisors developed the scores through an unstructured, qualitative process informed by their direct observation of workers' individual effort and ability on the shop floor; the firm did not use any production numbers in the evaluation process. Supervisors communicated the score to the employee through a short in-person meeting, and the score was highly influential in promotion and bonus decisions.

A continuous variable measuring the proportion of hours that a worker spent outside of her home team during the year. In some models the authors replace it with an indicator capturing observations above the median of this variable, which captures workers who spent more than 10% of their time on rotation beyond their home team.

A continuous variable ranging from 0 to 3, weighted by the percentage of working days in the year that a worker spent as crew, helper, assistant operator or operator. A worker who spent the entire year as an operator would have a job level of 3, and a worker who spent half the year as an operator and half as an assistant operator would have 2.5. In some models the authors replace it with an indicator equal to 1 for high authority workers (operators and assistant operators) and zero otherwise.

Causal assertions in the executives' annual letters to shareholders were content analyzed with a causal mapping protocol; a direct causal relationship between a type of competitive action and organizational performance was coded as 2, a second order mediated relationship as 1, and the absence of a stated causal link as 0. The measure was computed for each firm in each year, and executives' assertions were measured in the period preceding the year in which a rival's attack and the corresponding retaliation were observed.
time_window: one-year lag (frameworks measured in the year preceding the observed attack and response)

description: A firm was coded as responding (coded as 1) or not responding (coded as 0) to an attack, based on the structured content analysis of Aviation Daily. Responses ranged from immediate market-based reactions to immediate nonmarket-based reactions to announcements of longer-term initiatives.
Retaliation lag was defined as the number of days that lapsed before a response was reported in Aviation Daily. It was measured for the 369 discernable retaliations in the sample.
The amount of total assets owned by a firm in each year, as reported in Compustat. Used as one of two items capturing firm legitimacy.
The average return on assets (ROA) of a firm over the prior three years. Used as one of two items capturing firm legitimacy.

One minus the Euclidean distance between seven strategic dimensions that capture critical elements of strategy in the major airline industry. This resulted in a variable ranging from zero to one, with higher scores representing higher levels of organizational similarity. It was measured for each pair of firms, in each year.
Measured according to the methodology set forward by Baum and Korn (1999), for each pair of firms in each year, and coded from TransStats.
A binary variable indicating whether a firm's attack affected a geographic market in which a potential responder competed. Coded from TransStats.
Measured as the quick ratio for the focal firm in each year, consistent with prior research. Higher scores reflect an abundance of resources available for information processing routines.
Calculated as the average number of years of experience in the airline industry for TMT members. The TMT was defined as the top two tiers of management within the organization in each year.

Captured using the coefficient of variation, calculated as the standard deviation of the TMT's organizational tenure divided by the average organizational tenure. The TMT was defined as the top two tiers of management within the organization in each year.

variable_name: Likelihood of retaliation and retaliation lag
description: Competitive retaliation is measured by two variables from news coverage of airline attacks: whether the potential responder retaliated (1) or not (0), and the number of days before a response was reported for the retaliations observed.

variable_name: External cue variables (actor's size, actor's performance, organizational similarity, multimarket commonality, attack intensity)
description: Strength of external cues is represented by the array of cue variables in the model: actor's size (total assets) and actor's performance (three-year average ROA) as the two items of firm legitimacy, organizational similarity (one minus the Euclidean distance across seven strategic dimensions), multimarket commonality (Baum and Korn method), and attack intensity (a binary indicator that the attack affected a market in which the responder competed). H3 is tested through the interactions of these cue variables with the strategic importance measure.
scale: Continuous variables and one binary indicator, interacted with cognitive frameworks

description: The provision of contracted services was based on a question asking organizations whether they had provided such services in 1981. The absence of contracted services was coded zero and their presence was coded one.

Number of cars driven by employees, divided by the total to generate a percentage figure (e.g., employment/employment + leasing + ownership). The number of cars was used rather than the number of drivers because organizations generate revenues directly from utilization of their cars and car counts are not confounded with the length of shifts.

Number of drivers who were hourly employees, divided by the total number of drivers to generate a percentage figure (e.g., hourly/hourly + commission + leasing + ownership). Driver counts were used because separate numbers were provided for hourly and commission employees.

Number of drivers who were commission employees, divided by the total number of drivers to generate a percentage figure (e.g., commission/hourly + commission + leasing + ownership). Driver counts were used because separate numbers were provided for hourly and commission employees.

Number of cars driven by lessees, divided by the total to generate a percentage figure (e.g., leasing/employment + leasing + ownership). The number of cars was used rather than the number of drivers because organizations generate revenues directly from utilization of their cars.

Number of cars driven by owners, divided by the total to generate a percentage figure (e.g., ownership/employment + leasing + ownership). The number of cars was used rather than the number of drivers because organizations generate revenues directly from utilization of their cars.
Organization age was based on a question that asked the date the organization was established. It was calculated as 1981 minus the founding date.
Market share was assessed through a question asking the taxicab organization to assess what percentage of the business in its service area it had in 1981.

Multi-item scale based on established scales (Boyd and Reuning-Elliott, 1998; Hart and Banbury, 1994). Items were placed randomly in the final instrument, and the Likert method of summated ratings was used in scale construction. Respondents indicated the degree to which they agreed with statements about activities in their business unit.

Multi-item scale based on established scales (Boyd and Reuning-Elliott, 1998; Menon et al., 1999). Items were placed randomly in the final instrument, and the Likert method of summated ratings was used in scale construction. Respondents indicated the degree to which they agreed with statements about activities in their business unit.

Multi-item predictor scale listed among the four predictor scales of mission/goal clarity, situation analysis, strategic choice, and strategy formation process, based on established scales (Fredrickson, 1986; Menon et al., 1999). Items were placed randomly in the final instrument, and the Likert method of summated ratings was used in scale construction.

Multi-item scale based on established scales (Andrews and Smith, 1996; Hart and Banbury, 1994; Slevin and Covin, 1997). Items were placed randomly in the final instrument, and the Likert method of summated ratings was used in scale construction.

The criterion variable of the study, measured with a multi-item scale based on Jaworski and Kohli's (1993) measure. The Likert method of summated ratings was used in scale construction, and the criterion was regressed on the four predictor scales and the control variables.

Strategic orientation was assessed using the self-typing paragraph approach, the validity of which has been demonstrated in previous studies (Conant et al., 1990; James and Hatten, 1995; Shortell and Zajac, 1990). The descriptions are from Slater and Olson (2000), who discriminated between the Low Cost and Differentiated Defender types. Reactors account for a small proportion of the businesses and were not considered in either hypothesis development or analysis.

Coded one if the subsidiary had two or more subsidiaries that themselves belonged to the same multisubsidiary firm as its direct owners, and zero otherwise. The coding excludes subsidiaries with a single direct intrafirm owner and subsidiaries that were co-owned with other firms (joint ventures), and it also excludes cases in which the ultimate parent was one of the comanaging authorities. It is coded as a dichotomous variable because the theory distinguishes between single-managed and comanaged subsidiaries.

Sales-weighted average intrafirm complementarity of a subsidiary, built on the assumption that a subsidiary's relatedness increases with the similarity of its inputs and outputs to the inputs and outputs of the rest of the firm, captured by the correlation of input and output flows from industry input-output tables. The relatedness of a subsidiary to its firm is a function of the input and output similarity between its business and the other businesses in which the firm operates, and of how prominent each of these businesses is for the firm, with the importance of each industry weighted by the percentage of the firm's total sales from that industry. The paper's equation for this measure is not recoverable from the text.

A firm-in-market-level 'sales-at-risk' approach, calculated as the percentage of the sales of the subsidiary's firm in the markets (industries) in which the firm faces multimarket rivals that operate in the subsidiary's market. It captures the share of the firm's sales exposed to the potential negative externalities caused by the subsidiary's actions. The measure ranges from zero to one, with zero indicating no multimarket contact.

Industry production variability, following Dess and Beard (1984). The authors first estimated a linear growth model for each industry and year using the corresponding industry production data from industry input-output tables for the seven previous years, and then calculated the root mean square errors of the models, which serve as the measure of industry turbulence.
time_window: seven previous years, lagged one year

description: The severity index associated with all fires in the jurisdictions of the neighbors in the pair in a particular year. The index is calculated as the dot product of casualties and the ordinal assessment of seriousness for each casualty, ranging from least to most serious, where one indicates a minor injury and five indicates death. The measure uses the sum of casualties for both departments in a given year on all incidents, and in the casualties models a dummy variable is included for when casualties equal zero.
scale: index; each casualty coded 1 (minor injury) to 5 (death)

description: The U.S. deflated dollar value of property and contents at risk minus the value that was lost as a result of the fire or hazard. For each department-pair-year this is the collective total loss for each department in the pair, summed over both departments in a given year on all incidents.

Dummy variable in a vector of state-of-governance indicators for each department-pair-year, equal to one when the pair collaborates exclusively informally (no formal contract) and zero otherwise. The omitted state is no collaboration, and the coefficient on this indicator is the effect on performance of transitioning from no collaboration to an informal agreement.

Dummy variable in the vector of state-of-governance indicators, equal to one when the department-pair-year is in the formal state entered directly from no collaboration and zero otherwise. Its coefficient is the effect on performance of transitioning from no collaboration to a formal contract.

Dummy variable in the vector of state-of-governance indicators, equal to one when the department-pair-year is in the formal state entered from a prior informal arrangement and zero otherwise. Its coefficient is the effect on performance of transitioning from an informal agreement to a formal contract.

Within-team diversity of a destination firm captures the average dyadic diversity in technological fields between inventors within a given patent team. The author measures the angular distance between the knowledge experience vector of each pair of inventors within a team, where the vector contains the count of patents produced in each technology category and considers all technology experience gained throughout an inventor's career; R&D teams are identified as sets of inventors who file for the same patent application. The average of each patent team's team-level value gives the firm-level average within-team diversity, measured at the move year.

Across-team diversity measures the average dyadic diversity in technological fields between teams, showing how teams differ from one another in employees' knowledge experience. The author calculates the angular distance between the knowledge experience vector of each pair of patent teams within a firm, creating a team-level vector by adding up the teammates' experience in different technological fields throughout their careers. The firm-level average across-team value is the average of the pairwise distance between each pair of teams, measured at the move year.

Count of all patents produced after a mobility event, serving as a proxy for productivity at the destination firm. For external hires the count is measured throughout the hire's tenure at the destination firm, with pre-mobility number of patents at the departure firm controlled for.
time_window: post-mobility, throughout tenure at destination (from t+1)

description: Average number of forward citations received within the 5-year post-application period for each patent produced after the mobility event, calculated by taking the number of forward citations for each patent and then averaging the counts. It is used as a measure of the technological impact and the economic value of a patent invention.
time_window: 5-year post-application period for post-mobility patents; throughout the hire's tenure at the destination firm

description: Binary variable that takes a value of one if at least one of the patents produced at the destination firm is in the top 5% of 5-year forward citations in a given application year and technology class. It is used to capture 'breakthrough' innovations.
time_window: 5-year forward citation window; throughout the hire's tenure at the destination firm

description: Binary variable set to 1 if all of an inventor's post-mobility patents receive no citations. It captures inventions with minimal impact, the other end of the citation distribution.
time_window: 5-year forward citation window; throughout the hire's tenure at the destination firm

description: Number of new technological fields the inventor has entered after joining the new firm, used to examine the breadth of technological fields and the extent of learning at the destination firm.
time_window: post-mobility, throughout the hire's tenure at the destination firm

description: One minus the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) of concentration of post-mobility patents across different technological classes, measuring the degree of technological recombination and the novelty of patents. The value equals zero if all of the patents build on knowledge from one patent class and approaches one as the patents are spread across more technological fields; the formula block for the HHI-based measure is not legible in the text available.
time_window: post-mobility, throughout the hire's tenure at the destination firm

description: Firm-level average within-team diversity of the destination firm, capturing the average dyadic diversity in technological fields between inventors within a given patent team. It is computed as the average of each patent team's team-level value, where the team-level value is the average angular distance between the knowledge experience vectors of each pair of inventors in the team, measured at the move year.

Firm-level average across-team diversity of the destination firm, measuring the average dyadic diversity in technological fields between teams within the firm. It is computed as the average pairwise angular distance between the knowledge experience vectors of the firm's patent teams, measured at the move year.

Count of all patents produced by a teammate after a mobility event, serving as a proxy for productivity. For teammates the count is measured during the 2 years after the focal inventor joined the firm, controlling for the teammate's 2-year pre-mobility number of patents.

Average number of forward citations received within the 5-year post-application period for each patent produced after the mobility event, calculated by taking the number of forward citations for each patent and then averaging the counts. It measures the technological impact and economic value of the inventions produced by teammates after working with an external hire.
time_window: 5-year post-application window; 2-year period after the move year

description: Binary variable that takes a value of one if at least one of the patents produced after the mobility event is in the top 5% of 5-year forward citations in a given application year and technology class. It captures 'breakthrough' innovations by teammates.
time_window: 5-year forward citation window; 2-year period after the move year

description: Binary variable set to 1 if all of an inventor's post-mobility patents receive no citations, capturing inventions with minimal impact. For teammates it is measured over the 2-year period after the focal inventor joined the firm.
time_window: 5-year forward citation window; 2-year period after the move year

description: Number of new technological fields the teammate has entered after the focal inventor joined the firm, used to examine the breadth of technological fields and the extent of learning.

One minus the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) of concentration of post-mobility patents across different technological classes, measuring the degree of technological recombination and patent novelty. The value equals zero if all patents build on one patent class and approaches one as they spread across more technological fields; the formula block for the measure is not legible in the text available.

We measure firm performance as the firm's market share in each round. Depending on the competitive move of interest, Sonite market share or Vodite market share was used. Market share measures the relative success of firms by providing explicit comparison to rivals, and it allows comparison across simulation runs by controlling for industry size and other extraneous differences such as pricing. Interviewees discussed market share and related revenues at length in describing their competitive move strategies.
time_window: recorded at round r, predicting move frequency in round r + 1

description: A count of the market moves made by each firm in each round. Market moves were separated into three types: market probe, market entry, and market exit; specific market moves in each market and in each round were used to code them, and their number was counted. We summed these moves for each firm in each round to compute market moves.

A count of the R&D moves made by each firm in each round. R&D moves were separated into three types: R&D probe, R&D product, and R&D process; R&D moves in each market and in each round were used to code them, and their number was counted. We summed these moves for each firm in each round to compute R&D moves.

Measured as the diversification of the firm's market moves across customer segments in each round. Calculated using a Herfindahl index: 1 - ∑ (Na/NT)2, where Na equals the number of market moves made in segment a, and NT equals the total number of market moves made. The measure ranged from 0 to 1, where higher values indicate greater move diversity; the number of Sonite segments ranged from zero to five and Vodite segments from zero to three.

Measured as the diversification of the firm's R&D moves across customer segments in each round. Calculated using a Herfindahl index: 1 - ∑ (Na/NT)2, where Na equals the number of R&D moves made in segment a, and NT equals the total number of R&D moves made. The measure ranged from 0 to 1, where higher values indicate greater move diversity.

Coded 1 if the respondent answered yes to both 'Have you ever shared any knowledge based on your experience working in the U.S.?' and 'Did your company implement any of the suggestions you made as a routine procedure or repeated practice?'; otherwise 0. Open-ended responses were compared to the yes/no responses, and knowledge adoption was coded as 'no' for cases that did not reflect a change in organizational practices.
Indicator for whether the respondent reported sharing any knowledge based on experience working in the U.S. It is used as a dependent variable in the decomposition analysis.

Indicator for whether the returnee's company implemented any of the suggestions the returnee made as a routine procedure or repeated practice, asked only of respondents who reported sharing knowledge. Open-ended responses were used to validate and recode cases not reflecting a change in organizational practices.

Index combining breadth and depth of the returnee's U.S. professional experience. Breadth counts affirmative responses to five questions about prior U.S. work, a U.S. educational degree, at least weekly contact with coworkers, at least weekly contact with supervisor(s), and attending work-related conferences or workshops. Depth is the mean of years worked in the U.S. before the J-1 experience (scaled 0-5), frequency of contact with coworkers (0 = weekly or less, 5 = multiple times each day), and frequency of contact with supervisor(s) (same scale). The breadth score (b) and depth score (d) were combined as a coordinate pair, and the measure is the Euclidean distance of (b,d) from the origin.
scale: index based on Euclidean distance of (b,d) from the origin, with b and d each ranging up to 5
time_window: prior to and during the J-1 Visa experience

description: Index combining breadth and depth of the returnee's home-country professional experience. Breadth counts affirmative responses to five questions about prior home-country work experience, having worked for more than one company in the home country, having completed a post-secondary degree in the home country, having home-country coworkers during the J-1 experience, and communicating with home-country colleagues, friends, and family about professional or work-related matters. Depth is the mean of years worked in the home country before the J-1 experience (scaled 0-5), frequency of communication with home-country contacts about professional matters (0 = never, 5 = every day or more), and frequency of interaction with home-country coworkers (0 = weekly or less, 5 = multiple times each day). Breadth and depth were combined by Euclidean distance.
scale: index based on Euclidean distance of (b,d) from the origin, with b and d each ranging up to 5
time_window: prior to and during the J-1 Visa experience

description: Coded 1 if the primary industry of the returnee's current home-country organization was the same as the industry of the J-1 host organization in the U.S., using the survey and IntEx industry lists. Industries were classified into 25 broad categories.
Response to the survey question 'Do any of your current coworkers have U.S. career experience?'

From the World Values Survey item 'Of the following groups, whom would you NOT want as a neighbor?'; for each country, the proportion of respondents selecting 'foreigners' was calculated, and the variable was dichotomized so that 1 indicates the returnee's home country scored above the median of the xenophobia index among all countries included in the WVS.
time_window: latest wave available for each respondent's country

description: The relative prominence of a patent owner over a potential target is computed as the patent owner's prominence minus the potential target's prominence, where a firm's prominence is the log number of news articles covering a firm in the prior year. Articles were collected from the Factiva database across thirteen periodicals, yielding 76,648 distinct articles.

A firm's prominence is measured as the log number of news articles covering a firm in the prior year. For each company in the sample, all articles discussing the company published between 1979 and 2000 in the following periodicals were collected from the Factiva database: Wall Street Journal, New York Times, Boston Globe, Washington Post, Chicago Sun-Times, USA Today, San Francisco Chronicle, Houston Chronicle, Dallas Morning News, Electronics Times, Electronic Buyers' News, Electronic Engineering Times, and Electronic News. This yielded 76,648 distinct articles.

The dependent variable is the likelihood that a patent owner i sues a potential target j for patent infringement in a given year. For a dyad to enter the sample as being at risk of litigation, firm i must own at least one patent, and firm j must make at least one product in the given year.

Indicator for whether a patent owner is less prominent than a potential target, i.e., whether relative prominence is negative. It is entered as an interaction with relative prominence to test whether the negative effect of relative prominence is weaker in cases when the patent owner is less prominent than the potential target.

Tracks the elapsed time between the previous launch attempted by an orbital launch organization and a focal launch attempt by the same organization. Time is measured in days. The first launch attempted by an organization during the sampling period was excluded in order to calculate this variable's initial value.
time_window: elapsed time between the previous launch and the focal launch

description: A dichotomous indicator of launch failure, coded one when a launch attempt failed and zero when it succeeded, a negative indicator of performance. A launch attempt succeeded if the payload entered orbit and failed if the payload did not enter orbit; in the few partially successful cases, the launch was considered a success if the payload met more than half of its objectives and a failure otherwise.

A reverse index of the amount of previous experience an organization had with the components used in the launch vehicle for the focal launch. Prior experience with these components was calculated as the weighted average of the fraction of an organization's prior launches that had included each of the rocket stages also included on the focal launch vehicle, and novelty is one minus this index of prior experience with these stages. The measure ranges from zero, when all of an organization's previous launches had used all of the same components as the focal vehicle, to one, when the organization had never previously used any of the components of the focal vehicle.
An indicator variable that took a value of one when an organization's last launch before the focal launch had failed and a value of zero when the organization's last launch succeeded.

An indicator of the complexity of the launch vehicle used on a focal launch attempt, constructed as the number of stages contained in the focal launch vehicle. Launch vehicles are made up of one or more rocket stages, each stage containing fuel tanks, one or more rocket engines, and control systems, and increasing the number of stages increases the vehicle's complexity and the number of components that could fail.

We used recommendation revisions, not levels, because previous research showed that recommendation changes are more informative than levels. The I/B/E/S reports the number of upgrades and the number of downgrades across five recommendation categories (strong buy, buy, hold, underperform, and sell). We computed the recommendation changes as the net number up (the number of upgrades minus the number of downgrades) at the firm-month level.

Changes in the number of retweets that firm-initiated tweets directly related to growth have received in comparison to the prior month, proxied by the changes in retweets of firm-initiated employment tweets. Employment tweets include job posting messages and announcements about job fairs, and appear to directly indicate that the firm is doing well and growing; they also seem less subject to selective disclosure bias than investor-related tweets. The variable is in firm-month units.

The changes in retweets of firm-initiated customer-related tweets in comparison to the prior month. Customer-related tweets are those likely to be of interest to customers, including issues on bills, energy savings, and safety. The variable is expressed in firm-month units.

The changes in retweets of firm-initiated customer-related, CSR-related, and rapport-building tweets in comparison to the prior month. CSR-related tweets include employee benefits and firms' volunteering activities and donations; rapport-building tweets seem intended to build rapport, for example through greetings or messages on topics popular with the public without providing information regarding the firm. The variable is expressed in firm-month units.

variable_name: Unusually high volume of customer-initiated negative tweets (85th percentile)
description: We measured an unusually high volume of customer-initiated negative tweets using a binary variable. We first calculated changes in customer-initiated negative tweets compared to the prior month and then identified an unusually high volume based on a percentile threshold. The variable indicates 1 for changes greater than or equal to the 85th percentile in customer-initiated negative tweets compared to the prior month, and 0 otherwise. The authors report that the 85th percentile is the relevant threshold among the 70th, 75th, 80th, 85th and 90th percentiles examined.

variable_name: Unusually high volume of customer-initiated positive tweets (85th percentile)
description: We measured an unusually high volume of customer-initiated positive tweets using a binary variable. We first calculated changes in customer-initiated positive tweets compared to the prior month and then identified an unusually high volume based on a percentile threshold, coded 1 for changes greater than or equal to the 85th percentile and 0 otherwise. It is expressed in firm-month units.

For each firm, the extent to which customer satisfaction determines firm performance, estimated with a regression in which one-period-ahead ROA is the dependent variable and customer satisfaction, ROA, one-period-lagged ROA, stock returns, and one-period-lagged stock returns are the predictors; the variable corresponds to the coefficient for Customer satisfaction for each firm. Customer satisfaction was measured using the American Customer Satisfaction Index and firm performance using return on assets, with annual ACSI data from 2003 to 2011. The coefficient was estimated per firm using GLS regressions with corrections, OLS with the Newey-West variance estimator, and ARIMA dynamic regression models.

The presence of an institutional structure that supports consumer protection, calculated as the proportion of states with public consumer advocates among all states in which the firm's subsidiaries operate. Thirty-three states employ publicly funded consumer advocates who have rights to formally intervene in regulatory processes conducted by state PUCs, along with the right to appeal regulatory decisions to state courts. The data is state-specific and does not vary over time.

variable_name: Change in analyst stock recommendations (headline variable in Table 4)
description: Table 4 shows GLS regressions predicting changes in analyst recommendations, in which the dependent variable is the change in analyst stock recommendations.

variable_name: Control variables in the recommendation models
description: In addition, we controlled for firm size as measured by firm assets because analysts are likely to consider firms' financial resources in making evaluations of the firm. We also included growth and momentum factors as they are related to stock returns. Moreover, we included the number of competitors, market share, and residential sales over total sales because these variables may affect the extent to which securities analysts value consumer opinions.

Seven indicators capturing both the tangible and intangible aspects of investment in the OEM supplier–buyer transaction setting. Tangible investment was measured by three items describing the physical investment made by an OEM supplier in tooling, equipment, and engineering expenses that are specific to the requirements of an OEM buyer. Intangible investment was measured by four items describing the investment made by the OEM supplier in business processes and procedures, and in people that are specific to the requirement of an OEM buyer. All indicators were measured on a seven-point scale from 'extensive investment in terms of time and effort' to 'minimal investment'; Cronbach alpha for the construct is 0.897.
scale: seven-point scale from 'extensive investment in terms of time and effort' to 'minimal investment'
time_window: focal buyer relationship within the last five years

description: Operationalized as a single item reflecting the horizontal scope of an OEM-supplier relationship. The item was measured on a seven-point scale from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree.'
scale: seven-point scale from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree'

description: Measured as the logarithm of the number of activities along the value chain, such as global logistics and after-sales services, which the respondent had offered for the same OEM buyer. This item captures the degree of vertical scope of the exchange relationship.
scale: logarithm of the number of value chain activities offered for the same buyer

description: A capability upgrading scale was developed to describe the inter-project knowledge spillover effects with other transaction parties, measured by the extent to which an OEM supplier had experienced significant improvement in several aspects of capability after serving this OEM buyer. Five indicators were used to measure various types of capability improvement after serving this OEM buyer. All of the indicators were measured on a seven-point scale from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree'; Cronbach alpha for the construct is 0.92.
scale: seven-point scale from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree'

description: The reputation enhancement scale was developed to assess the positive spillovers that an OEM supplier can generate due to the endorsement effect of a good reputation of its buyer. Three indicators measure the benefits of being associated with a prominent buyer. All of the indicators were measured on a seven-point scale from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree'; Cronbach alpha for the construct is 0.92.
scale: seven-point scale from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree'
time_window: after doing business with the focal buyer

description: For each multipartner alliance in year t-1 the authors counted the number of prior ties formed by each dyad in the alliance, a prior tie being direct contact between a pair of firms through either a two-partner or multipartner alliance. A five-year moving window (t-6 to t-1) was used to identify prior ties, and each prior tie was weighted from 1 to 4 depending on the count of technology codevelopment, production, marketing, and technology licensing activities. The variance of tie strength across the multiple dyads within each alliance was computed for each year, so that a value of 0 indicates equal tie strength across all partner pairs and higher values indicate that tie strength is concentrated among a subset of partner pairs; a logarithmic transformation was used to enhance normality.
time_window: t-1, five-year moving window (t-6 to t-1)

description: Degree centrality was measured for all sample firms based on collaborative activities in the five years preceding the formation of each sample multipartner alliance, excluding any partners connected through the focal multipartner alliance, so that the count reflects ties with firms outside the focal alliance. The authors then calculated the variance in positional embeddedness among the partner firms within each multipartner alliance, and a logarithmic transformation was used to enhance the normality of the measure.

The dependent variable is a time-varying dummy variable set to 0 for every time period t in which alliance k existed at the end of the year and 1 otherwise. Dissolution dates were identified from archival and company sources, and the authors distinguished unplanned from planned dissolution events through in-depth media searches cross-referencing SDC deal-text statements, company press releases, and news stories; where no information was found and no tenure was specified, the termination was assumed to be unplanned. An alliance with a planned breakup was designated in the data set as censored.

A composite scale developed by Mayer and Davis (1999) to capture the dimensions of trustworthiness, measuring a CEO's belief that the TMT members of his/her firm wished to do more or less good to him/her. CEOs were asked to rate their TMTs as a group on each item, using a scale ranging from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 5, 'strongly agree.' A composite measure was created based on the factor loadings of each of the four items in the scale; the Cronbach's alpha coefficient was .87.
level: firm (CEO report on the TMT as a group)

description: Four items developed by Tosi and Gomez-Mejia (1989) used to measure the extent to which TMT employment contracts exhibited agent protection mechanisms. CEOs were asked the extent to which the evaluation and reward of TMT members were designed with each objective in mind, rated on the same 1 to 5 scale used for the benevolence items. A composite measure was created based on the factor loadings of the four items; the scale's Cronbach's alpha was .70.
level: firm (CEO report on the TMT as a group)

description: Dummy variable that took the value 1 when a CEO and most of a TMT's members belonged to a firm's owning family and 0 otherwise. Each CEO reported his/her personal family relationship to firm owners and that of TMT members; TMT family status was a continuous variable measuring the percentage of family members on a firm's TMT.
Measured as the percentage of a firm's equity owned by the owning family, available directly from the SABI database.

Dummy variable coded 1 when a CEO was a family member and 0 otherwise, based on each CEO's report of his/her personal family relationship to firm owners. In 91 percent of the cases in which the CEO was a family member, his or her last name corresponded with the last name of the owner family obtained from the SABI database.
CEO vulnerability was measured by his or her family status multiplied by the percentage of family ownership in the firm. A larger value for this variable represented lower CEO vulnerability.
CEOs were asked to indicate the percentage of total pay that TMT members on average received in the form of bonuses and long-term income.

Change in firm volatility, measured as the difference between the estimated volatility from 1 month to the next, Δ VOLi,t = VOLi,t - VOLi,t-1; positive values indicate an increase in firm volatility from the previous month to the current one, negative values indicate decreasing firm volatility. Firm i's volatility during month t is estimated from the natural logarithm of daily gross excess returns on the firm's stock within that month. The authors state that logarithmic returns mitigate skewness in the relation between returns and contemporaneous return volatilities. The exact monthly volatility formula is not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: monthly, current month and previous month

description: The difference between a firm's monthly returns and the monthly returns of a synthetic control firm competing in the exact same industries. The synthetic control's returns are the asset-weighted average of the industry returns of the firm's segments, where each segment's weight is the percentage of assets it contributes; an industry's average return is calculated from the returns of single-segment firms weighted by their relative market capitalization. Segments are matched on the most precise level of a segment's four-, three-, or two-digit SIC for which there is at least one single-segment firm in the industry-year.

Indicator variable equal to 1 if a firm reports two or more segments in a distinct four-digit SIC code, and 0 otherwise. These diversified firms are considered multi-business, and the variable serves as a first indicator for the presence of switching options.
scale: 1 = two or more segments in distinct four-digit SIC codes, 0 otherwise

description: The sum of segments having a unique four-digit SIC code, used to approximate the number of switching options inside a firm. In additional analyses industries are defined more broadly by aggregating segment-level data at the three-digit or two-digit SIC level.

Inducements to redeploy are approximated by sales growth correlations: the full-sample correlation of sales growth rates of single-segment firms is first calculated for each three-digit SIC industry pair. These correlations are then matched with the different segments operated in each multi-segment firm's portfolio and aggregated on firm level using a simple average. The sample is split into two subgroups: firms with positive average sales growth correlations in a given year and firms with negative average sales growth correlations.

Adjustment costs are approximated with several measures of portfolio relatedness, including resource similarity in occupational profiles, capital flows across tangible assets, firm-level product market relatedness, and the entropy measure. More related businesses are argued to require more similar resources and therefore to involve lower adjustment costs to redeploy.

A measure capturing concurrent increases and decreases in sales growth for at least one segment pair in a given year, used as redeployment experience. Using a 5-year rolling window, all such instances are counted and the number is divided by the number of years covered, that is, five, so the score ranges between 0 and 1 and increases with the amount of redeployment experience gained in the past. For example, 3 years with one segment's sales decreasing while a sibling segment's sales increased gives 3/5 = 0.6; the median redeployment experience in the sample is 0.4. Firms are split into high (above median) and low (below median) experience subsamples.

variable_name: extent of sales expansion and contraction
description: An additional measure of redeployment experience developed from Dickler and Folta (2020), who approximate redeployments by the relative difference between multi-segment and single-segment firms in the expansion and contraction of revenues. Redeployment expertise is examined by splitting the sample of multi-segment firms into subsamples based on the distribution of cumulative revenue redeployments over the previous 5 years.

Binary variable taking on the value of 1 if the firm dismissed the CEO in a particular year due to job performance and 0 otherwise, that is, if the firm did not change the CEO; if the CEO departed involuntarily due to illness, death, or policy-related issues; or if the CEO departed voluntarily due to retirement or the pursuit of new opportunities. The authors used the database compiled by Gentry et al. (2021) covering CEO dismissal events between 2010 and 2018 and coded dismissals for 2019 and 2020 themselves, adhering to the procedure outlined by Gentry et al. (2021).
time_window: 2010-2018 from the compiled database; 2019-2020 coded by the authors

description: Using data from Compustat, firm performance is the firm's ROA minus the median ROA within the firm's primary industry (four-digit SIC code, excluding the focal firm) for a given year. It is a continuous, industry-adjusted accounting performance measure.
time_window: measured yearly and lagged by 1 year relative to CEO dismissal

description: The number of military directors serving on a board each year. Directors were identified in three steps: inspection of the biographies of directors available in BoardEx; verification of directors not classified as military directors through content analysis of director biographies in proxy statements gathered via the SEC's Edgar platform, using the algorithm developed by Adams et al. (2018) and a dictionary including keywords such as 'military', military branches (e.g., 'army'), ranks (e.g., 'lieutenant'), or services (e.g., 'war'), with the flagged biographies read to minimize coding errors; and examination of director profiles in the Notable Names Database together with keyword searches of news coverage related to directors through LexisUni. Following these steps the authors identified 598 military directors.
time_window: measured for each board year and lagged by 1 year relative to CEO dismissal

variable_name: United Way influence over agency decisions
description: The executive director of each agency studied was asked to indicate the extent to which his/her agency's decisions were influenced by United Way over each of five items. These items were found to be highly intercorrelated and thus were combined into a single 5-item scale (mean interitem r = .50, Cronbach's alpha = .83).

Four measures reflect agency dependence on United Way for the three scarce resources of funding, information, and legitimacy; the four are financial dependence, agency-United Way interaction, initiation of United Way contact, and years in United Way. Fewer years in United Way, taken as demonstrating a stronger need for legitimacy, was treated as being related to greater United Way influence, so the coding of this indicator runs opposite to the others.

A group of variables focuses on agency linkages with organizations other than United Way, reflecting the extent to which an agency is able to modify its dependence on United Way for funding, information, and legitimacy by obtaining these resources from other sources. The variables are the number of other fund sources, interexecutive communication, interagency programs, and interagency board interlocks.

Time is used as the indicator of the increasing modularity of product architecture in the industry: a dummy variable, 'post-1925,' takes the value of 1 for the years 1925-1931 and zero otherwise. In a separate, preferred specification the post-1925 dummy is replaced by dummies for each year from 1920 to 1931, which allows year-by-year changes in vertical integration levels for the average car model year relative to the first year in the period to be assessed.

For each of nine major automobile components, a 1 was coded if the component was produced internally for a given car model year and a zero if it was bought; in the few cases in which some units of a component were made and some were bought, a value of 0.5 was coded. The make-buy values were summed across the nine components for each car model year, so that the measure ranges from 0 to 8. The unit of analysis is the car model year.

Because the vertical integration data were calculated for each car model, the value for each multimodel firm was obtained by computing the average vertical integration value across each firm's models in each year. The main independent variable for testing H3 is the interaction between this firm-level vertical integration measure and the time period dummy representing the post-1925 years.

The list price charged for each car model year in the sample; the assumption is that higher-priced car models tend to feature more differentiation in individual car components such as quality of interior, safety features, transmission performance and ignition performance than lower-priced models. Prices come from Lester-Steele (1960) and are available for 68% of the car model years listed in Kimes and Clark (1989). A squared term, car price squared, was added in some specifications with the idea that the effects of price on vertical integration may not appear until a firm moves higher up the quality ladder.
