Binary variable indicating the presence (coded one) or absence (coded zero) of market ties based on whether or not a firm had used a given bank as a lead manager or co-lead manager on bond or stock issues or as a merger and acquisition advisor in the last five years.

Bonacich's eigenvector measure used to calculate the status of banks in commercial banking. The measure is based on a symmetric network of agent ties in which each cell denotes how many times two commercial banks worked together as managers of a loan syndicate. Both measures of network status were based on yearly updated networks, lagged one year relative to the dependent variable, standardized to account for yearly differences in network size.

Bonacich's eigenvector measure used to calculate banks' network status in the asymmetrical networks of lead-manager/co-lead-manager ties based in the bond market. The network is yearly updated, lagged one year relative to the dependent variable, and standardized to account for yearly differences in network size.
Number of years banks had been present in investment banking, measured as the number of years passed since they first obtained investment-banking approval from the Federal Reserve Board.
Natural logarithm of the number of times firms had used the markets for bonds, stocks, and mergers and acquisitions in the prior five years.

The CEO of the spun-off firm was coded as an insider if he or she was employed in the combined firm in the prior year (it was also noted whether or not this person was the combined firm's CEO) and as an outsider if he or she was not. Three dummy variables are used in the analyses: outside CEO, inside CEO, and former CEO of the combined firm. Data are missing for two companies, leaving 76 CEOs.
time_window: year prior to the spin-off (combined firm) and first year after the spin-off (spun-off firm)

description: Indicator of whether the spun-off company's CEO has a compensation plan that includes an executive stock option contract, contrasted with the presence or absence of options contracts in the formerly combined firm. Options contract data were available for 77 companies. Option values used in the compensation estimates aggregate the dollar value of options exercised during the year, the value of new options granted during the year, and changes in the value of the outstanding options net of the first two option contract measures.
time_window: first full fiscal year subsequent to the spin-off completion

description: Performance-contingent compensation expressed as a percentage of the CEO's total annual compensation and as an absolute dollar amount. Total compensation is built from nine components; the first four (salary and bonus, thrift plan contributions, insurance payments, and other fringe benefits) are treated as nonperformance-contingent and the latter five as performance-contingent. The values of stock ownership, restricted stock, and ESOP shares are estimated by multiplying the number of shares or units in each component by the change in the value of the firm's common equity during the fiscal year, and new options granted are valued with the dividend-adjusted Black-Scholes option pricing model. All compensation variables are expressed in 1987 dollars.
time_window: fiscal year immediately prior to the spin-off announcement for the pre-spin-off organization; first full fiscal year after completion for the post-spin-off organizations

description: Percentage of the spun-off company's directors who are corporate insiders, that is, members of the board whose full-time employment is with the corporation. Directors are classified with a tripartite scheme into insiders, related outsiders (individuals such as consultants, lawyers, investment bankers, and retired insiders, who have some relationship with the firm that renders their independence from top management questionable), and executive outsiders (top-level executives of other companies).

Percentage of the members of the spun-off company's compensation committee who are executive outsiders, that is, top-level executives of other companies. Committee members are classified with the same tripartite scheme used for the board: insiders, related outsiders, and executive outsiders.

The mean standardized cumulative prediction error, computed with the market model, over the 2-day announcement period (days -1 and 0, where day 0 is the Wall Street Journal announcement date). The intercept term and slope coefficients were estimated over the 150-day interval beginning at day -200 and ending at day -51, and these parameters were used to calculate daily prediction errors and cumulative prediction errors for the interval beginning with day -50 and ending with day +20.

Voluntary corporate spin-off is the event that defines the sample rather than a variable. Spin-off announcements between 1972 and 1987 were found in the Dow Jones News Retrieval Service and kept if the pre-spin-off parent was on the CRSP file of NYSE and ASE firms, announcement and completion dates could be confirmed in the Wall Street Journal Index, the spin-off was voluntary (no bidder interest in the prior year) and a 100 percent stock distribution, and proxy statements were available, leaving 78 completed spin-offs. The governance hypotheses describe the spun-off firms after the event.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the UTSA was enacted in the state where the company is incorporated during the period between t buy (the year of its purchase by the PE company) and t sell (the year of its sale by that company to another firm), and 0 otherwise. Any regulatory change is coded 1 regardless of the intensity of the change. The target firm's state of incorporation is used as the relevant state.
time_window: between t buy and t sell

description: The internal rate of return deriving from acquiring a target, a standard measure of performance in the context of buyouts; it measures the target firm's percentage change in market value in any period, discounting any future cash flow by the IRR itself. The distribution is censored to account for outliers, defined as observations three standard deviations above and below the mean.
time_window: holding period of the private equity investment

description: The rate of inter-firm mobility of knowledge workers at year t sell in the industry in which the target company operates. Inventor mobility is identified when two consecutive patents were assigned to the same inventor but to a different firm in the same industry, defined by SIC at the two-digit level; patents are assigned to a public parent company using Bessen's (2009) concordance file. The measure is the proportion of inventors moving to rivals, computed as the number of inventors moving to rivals over the overall number of inventors in that year and that industry.

Computed from an industry profit forecasting equation: current industry profitability, measured as industry return on sales by SIC two-digit level, is regressed on the profitability of the previous two years plus a time trend, following Ghosal and Loungani (2000). The measure is the standard deviation of the residuals of that equation, which represent the unpredictable profit component, computed over the past five years of t sell.
time_window: past five years of t sell

description: An industry time-invariant measure that captures the proportion of investments by industry (SIC two-digit code) in the sample where PE firms lost all of their invested capital (IRR = -1). Because it is time-invariant it is captured by industry fixed effects in the models.

An indicator variable created for each restatement that captures whether bystander firms belong to the same four-digit SIC code industry in which the event occurred. Firms in the event industry are coded as 1 and all others as 0. It is used as the baseline independent variable and as the base term in the interaction terms testing the moderator hypotheses.
time_window: for each of the 84 restatement events in 2004

description: The CAR is the sum over the event window of the abnormal daily returns of each particular firm, where abnormal returns on a particular day are the difference between the actual return of the firm's stock and its expected return on that day. The expected return is computed using a market model whose parameters are estimated over a 'normal' period of -254 to -21 days prior to the restatement event. Following previous research on restatements, the event period is the day before the announcement and the day of the announcement (day -1 and day 0). CARs were estimated with the Eventus program (CRSP database) using the market-adjusted model based on an equally weighted index with dividends.
time_window: two-day event window (day -1 and day 0); estimation period of -254 to -21 days

description: Perpetrator firm familiarity was captured through the size of the perpetrator firm, measured by taking the natural log of each perpetrator firm's net sales in 2004 (the year of the event). Previous research has shown that familiarity is largely determined by firm size. An interaction term was created between this measure and the event industry indicator.

To determine whether someone was fired for the misconduct at the perpetrator firm, the authors examined the news coverage (via the Lexis-Nexis database) of the financial restatement event for the week following each event. Each restatement event was coded such that, if someone was fired, it was coded as a 1, and 0 otherwise. An interaction term was created between this measure and the event industry indicator.

The GAO Financial Restatement database captured whether there was an ongoing governmental investigation at the misconduct firm, and these data were used to create a categorical variable; each restatement event that was under investigation was coded as 1, and 0 otherwise. An interaction term was created between this measure and the event industry indicator.
time_window: at the time of the restatement event

description: Investors' familiarity with bystander firms was captured through the size of such firms. Bystander firm size was measured by taking the natural log of each firm's net sales in 2003. An interaction term was created between this measure and the event industry indicator.

Following previous research on corporate governance, board vigilance was captured through the proportion of independent directors on each bystander firm's board, calculated by dividing the number of independent directors by the total number of directors on the board. The RiskMetrics database classifies directors as either 'executive' (i.e., management), 'linked' (i.e., non-management but with a material relationship with the firm), or 'independent' (i.e., non-management with no material relationship with the firm), and this was used to obtain the number of independent directors on each firm's board. An interaction term was created between this measure and the event industry indicator.

The CEO duality at each bystander firm in the sample was measured via a categorical variable; firms with a CEO who was also the chair of the board of directors were coded as a 1, and 0 otherwise. An interaction term was created between this measure and the event industry indicator.

Spline variable set equal to zero for all observations in which the phone's performance is less than its historical aspiration level; when performance is above that level, the difference between actual performance and the historical aspiration level is used (divided by 1,000). Historical aspiration is an exponentially weighted moving average of past performance of the phone, with the adjustment parameter chosen by maximizing log-likelihood. The variable is lagged by three quarters.

Symmetric spline set equal to zero when performance is above the aspiration level and equal to the performance-aspiration gap when performance falls below that level; the absolute value is taken to facilitate interpreting the regression coefficients. A squared term of this variable is used to model the survival level as one of two approaches. The variable is lagged by three quarters.

Indicator variable used as the second approach to model the survival level; it is set equal to 1 when a device is in the lowest 20% of sales for all devices in the sample, based on evidence from firm-provided internal documentation. It is used as an alternative to the squared term of performance below aspirations. The variable is lagged by three quarters.

Two sets of coders (the authors and firm managers with extensive knowledge of product management) rated, on a 5-point Likert scale, the degree of centralization at each firm for each year of the sample. The ratings were motivated by the question of the degree to which product portfolio decisions must be deferred to someone higher up in the organization for approval, with 1 for decisions that never need approval at higher levels and 5 for every decision that must be deferred. The authors' ratings were built from an extensive review of public sources and case narratives, semistructured interviews with managers, and a formal survey sent to a primary senior interview subject from each firm; interrater agreement was 92%.

Phaseout is defined as the cessation of product shipments from the handset manufacturer to German retailers, indicated in the data by a discontinuous fall in monthly sales in Germany, since the manufacturer does not itself give an exact discontinuation date. All device phaseouts were coded manually by two individuals; for 94% of the devices the coded phaseout dates were within three months of each other, and disagreements were resolved by joint review and consensus. Devices already on the market at the beginning of the observation period were not coded.

Portfolio diversification is calculated with a modified formula of the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI) applied to the CVC portfolio rather than the firm. For each corporate investor the authors determined the number of active portfolio companies per year, adding companies first invested in and eliminating exited ones, and identified each company's industry on the basis of the Venture Economics Industry Classification (VEIC); industries were classified on the basis of 17 categories at the level of industry subgroup 1. Pi denotes the proportion of portfolio company counts from the i-th industry within the portfolio to the total number of portfolio companies, because sales data are not available for most start-ups. The higher the HHI, the more diversified the portfolio, and a value of 0 indicates that all portfolio companies are in the same industry.

Firm value is measured by Tobin's Q, a firm's market valuation over the replacement costs of its tangible assets. It is calculated with the simplified approximation formula of Chung and Pruitt (1995): firm equity value plus book value of long-term debt plus net current liabilities, divided by total assets. Because it incorporates growth values of equity, it captures investor expectations for future growth and the lag between CVC investment and realized benefits.
time_window: t+1 (next year's Q; regressions also run with Q t)

description: Current ratio is used to capture available slack, resources not yet committed to any specific purpose, which helps relieve corporate investors of financial constraints in making multiple CVC investments. The reversed value of the variable indicates the financial constraint that corporate investors face.

The debt-to-equity ratio is used to measure potential slack, future resources that can be generated externally through debt or equity financing. The reversed value of the variable indicates the financial constraint that corporate investors face.

The change in budgeted guided sales for each period and each branch. It is defined as the current year's budgeted guided sales minus the previous year's budgeted guided sales, divided by the previous year's budgeted guided sales, to account for differences in branch size. It measures the increase or decrease in a branch's target relative to its previous year's target.
time_window: year t relative to year t-1

description: Last year's actual guided sales minus the targeted guided sales, divided by the targeted guided sales. Actual sales refer to branch i in year t and targeted guided sales to the target set for the same branch-year. The variable is lagged one year relative to the target revision being explained.

The full formula is not readable in the provided text; the text states that n is the number of branches in branch i's region and that the measure compares last year's expected performance for a particular branch with the actual average performance of the branches in its region. It is normalized by employees to compare across branches with different numbers of employees. Expected performance is used to eliminate idiosyncratic risks associated with the actual realization of performance, and the average performance of branches in a region balances individual branch risks.

A dummy variable that takes a value of one for young branches, leaving mature branches as the reference group. Branches in operation for two to three years are young; branches in operation for more than three years are mature. One-year-old branches are not included because their opening year does not count as a full year.

A dummy variable that takes a value of one if last year's performance deviation was unfavorable, that is, below the target. It separates failure from success in the estimation of the weight placed on past performance.

A dummy variable for large performance deviations, both favorable and unfavorable. It takes a value of one for branch-year observations with a performance deviation larger than the 87.5 percentile or smaller than the 12.5 percentile of the performance deviation distribution.

Measured with the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ Form 5X-Short). Members of each TMT, except the CEO, evaluated how frequently their CEO engaged in the four components of transformational leadership, on a scale ranging from 1 ('not at all') to 5 ('frequently, if not always'). A one-way ANOVA using firm affiliation as the independent variable was significant for each item (p < .001) and the average intragroup reliability was .82, legitimizing aggregation of individual team member scores. The reliability for the overall transformational leadership score was .90.
scale: 1 ('not at all') to 5 ('frequently, if not always')

description: A nine-item scale developed and validated by Simsek, Veiga, Lubatkin, and Dino (2005), designed to capture a TMT's level of collaborative behavior, information exchange, and joint decision making. All TMT members, including the CEOs, assessed these team processes on a scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'). An ANOVA suggested individual scores could be aggregated to the team level (p < .001) and the average rwg for the scale was .80. The overall measure had a Cronbach's alpha of .90.

A seven-item scale adapted by Sutcliffe (1994) from a scale originally developed by Glick, Huber, Miller, Doty, and Sutcliffe (1990). The items captured the extent to which team members perceive they have responsibility and authority regarding seven aspects of day-to-day operations. All TMT members, including the CEOs, completed this scale, which was rated on the same five-point scale used for behavioral integration. ANOVA (p < .001) and rwg (average rwg = .87) results legitimized aggregation of individual team member scores, and the reliability of the measure was .92.

Following Gilley et al. (2002), the TMT's shared preference for risky growth opportunities was measured using six items, rated by all TMT members including the CEOs on the same five-point scale used for behavioral integration. ANOVA results supported aggregating individual scores to the team level (p < .001) and the average intragroup reliability was .86. The third item, 'Our team prefers to carefully analyze a situation before moving,' which was reverse-scored, had a low squared multiple correlation (.27) with other items and was dropped from further analyses, leaving a five-item measure whose reliability was .78.

Balkin and Gomez-Mejia's (1990) three-item measure. The three items asked TMT members, including CEOs, to evaluate the executive compensation in their firms, rated on the same five-point scale used for behavioral integration. ANOVA (p < .001) and rwg (average rwg = .84) results supported aggregating individual scores to the team level, and the overall measure reliability was adequate (alpha = .85).

Zahra's (1996) 16-item scale, which broadly measures a firm's entrepreneurial activities on three dimensions: innovation, venturing, and strategic renewal. Team members, including the CEOs, were asked to rate their firms' actual, rather than preferred, entrepreneurial activities. One strategic renewal item ('The firm has divested several unprofitable business units') was dropped because 33 percent of the cases lacked data, reducing the number of items from 16 to 15. An ANOVA confirmed that individual scores could be aggregated to the group level (p < .001), the average intragroup reliability was .83, and the overall measure had a reliability of .88.

Scale formed from four questionnaire items designed to capture the extent to which the knowledge could be articulated in documents and software, which may be substantive, e.g., in blueprints, or procedural. Respondents marked their answers on a seven-item scale. The responses were transformed into a standard normal deviate with zero mean and variance of one and the standard scores were summed to form a scale score. Cronbach's alpha for the final scale is 0.678.
scale: seven-item scale; scale score standardized to mean zero

description: Scale designed to capture the ease at the individual level by which knowledge, even when it cannot be formally articulated, can be taught to new workers. Five questionnaire items were used, with responses on a seven-item scale. The standardized item scores were summed into a scale score. Cronbach's alpha for the final scale is 0.785.
scale: seven-item scale; scale score standardized to mean zero

description: Variable developed by adding the scores on four items indicating the importance of four types of processes, as identified by Hayes and Wheelwright (1984). The authors decided upon this objective set of items to indicate the importance of different manufacturing methods, so that complexity is measured as the degree of multiple competencies used to manufacture a product.
scale: seven-item scale per item; summed scale score

description: Scale developed to capture at the organizational level the extent to which transfer or imitation of a capability is impaired due to dependence on many different (groups of) experienced people for its production, using items on the degree of dependence of manufacturing with other functions. Responses were given on a seven-item scale and summed as standardized scores; the scale includes one reversed item (that the product can be manufactured in a unit isolated from all other production without quality being influenced). Cronbach's alpha is 0.637.
scale: seven-item scale; scale score standardized to mean zero

description: Constructed from items concerning whether the manufacturing capability can be acquired by reversed engineering or from published reports. The construct is used only in the estimates for imitation, since a firm that voluntarily transfers its manufacturing does not need to resort to reverse engineering or generally available documents. Cronbach's alpha is 0.772.
scale: seven-item scale; scale score standardized to mean zero

description: Measured by the count of competitors perceived as engaged in parallel efforts aimed at developing a similar product at the time of the innovations' release. The questionnaire asked whether any of the competitors were engaged in developing products similar to the firm's at the time of the innovation, with the answers "No" or "Yes, # of competitors".
time_window: at the time of the innovation's release

description: Constructed from items indicating the extent to which machinery and software developed and kept within the company embody principal manufacturing capabilities. Cronbach's alpha is 0.61.
scale: seven-item scale; scale score standardized to mean zero

description: Indicates the extent to which machinery or software purchased from external vendors embody principal manufacturing capabilities. Cronbach's alpha is 0.97.
scale: seven-item scale; scale score standardized to mean zero

description: Derived from the question whether any of the firm's knowledgeable manufacturing employees had left the firm, coded as one or zero. The questionnaire item asks whether any skilled manufacturing people left the company to the benefit of competitors after the introduction of the product.
time_window: after the introduction of the product

description: Created by taking the maximum standardized value of how important subsequent modifications are perceived to be for preventing imitation. The items concern the importance of continuous modification of the product and of continuous development of the manufacturing process in preventing imitation of the product.

Dependent variable of the transfer models: the time to the transfer of the manufacturing capability to a new site, as measured from when manufacturing first started. The authors model the rate by which capabilities were transferred, expressed as the probability of transfer conditional on no previous event, using a partial likelihood specification that discards the baseline hazard and rank orders technologies in terms of the sequence of transfer times. Innovations not transferred by 1988, when the period of observation ended, are censored.
time_window: from when manufacturing first started until 1988 (observation end)

description: Dependent variable of the imitation models: the time to the first imitation of the innovation by a competitor, as measured from when manufacturing first started. The authors model the hazard of imitation, the probability of imitation conditional on no previous event, using a partial likelihood specification that discards the baseline hazard and rank orders technologies in terms of the sequence of imitation times. Innovations not imitated by 1988, when the period of observation ended, are censored.
time_window: from when manufacturing first started until 1988 (observation end)

description: Historiometric measure built from dossiers of publicly available information. Research assistants gathered content on each CEO until they had 10 pages of information or ran out of effective material; the dossier was then pared down to three to five pages of the most CEO-specific information, with CEO and firm names removed. Several hundred trained undergraduate coders, blind to the hypotheses, were each given a random set of 10 dossiers and rated the CEO's charisma on a five-point Likert scale, with five representing the highest level of charisma. Each CEO was evaluated by an average of 35 unique coders (529 coders participated), the individual assessments were aggregated into an overall mean evaluation, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC[K]) equaled 0.89.

The year-over-year absolute change in six strategic choice variables largely under the CEO's control: advertising intensity (advertising expense/sales), R&D intensity (R&D expense/sales), overhead efficiency (SG&A expense/sales), capital intensity (assets/sales), PP&E newness (net PP&E/gross PP&E), and leverage (debt/assets). The annual within-firm change in each of the six dimensions was calculated and standardized, the absolute values of the change scores were taken, and these were summed into a composite measure. The variable was natural log transformed to correct for skew. Missing values on a dimension were replaced with the industry mean of that variable for the focal year.

The extent to which a firm deviated from its S&P 500 industry peers on the same six strategic dimensions used in the strategic dynamism measure: advertising intensity, R&D intensity, overhead efficiency, capital intensity, PP&E newness, and leverage. Each indicator was first standardized; the absolute difference between the focal firm and the firm's industry average (excluding the focal firm) for that year on the given dimension was calculated; and these absolute difference scores were summed into a composite measure of deviation from industry central tendencies.

Following Hillman and Keim's (2001) approach, the five KLD categories most closely corresponding to the five primary stakeholder groups discussed in the CSR literature were aggregated: employee relations, diversity issues, product issues, community relations, and environmental issues. For each category KLD annually assesses the presence or absence of a number of strengths and concerns; net category scores equal the summed strengths minus the summed concerns for each category. After standardizing the five net category scores, they were averaged into an overall net score reflecting the level of emphasis on CSR in a given year.
A moderator variable in the analyses that reflected the time since becoming CEO. It was centered before being entered into the interaction terms with CEO charisma.

A count of articles reporting cases of abuse within the diocese during the previous decade, constructed from BishopAccountability.org records of every Catholic sex abuse case in the United States. Diocese-level information was then matched with the counties each diocese comprises. The variable correlates highly with both the total number of victims and the total number of accused priests within the same diocese, while ensuring that transgressions are known to both organizational members and the local community. It is logged in the models.

variable_name: Logged number of adherents to the Catholic Church
description: The logged number of adherents to the Catholic Church in each county, coded from the Religious Congregations and Membership Study carried out in 2000 and the Churches and Church Membership in the United States studies carried out in 1971, 1980, and 1990. These data sets are maintained by the Association of Religion Data Archives and include statistics for 149 religious bodies on the number of congregations within each county of the United States. County-level measures of church membership were constructed for 1971, 1980, 1990, and 2000.

variable_name: Logged number of adherents to (non-Catholic) denomination
description: The logged number of adherents to each of the 16 non-Catholic Christian denominations in the study, in each county, coded from the same church membership data sets as the Catholic measure. Denomination–county dyads are followed over time, retaining a variable for the number of Catholic adherents in each county to look for evidence of transfer between the Catholic Church and other churches at the local level.

The absolute value of the difference in strictness between the focal denomination and the Catholic Church, constructed from Iannaccone's (1994) strictness score. The variable is denomination specific and time invariant and is assumed to be stable and not to vary over time. It is orthogonalized in the models.
scale: absolute difference on the 1 to 6 strictness scale

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 if the focal denomination is stricter than the Catholic Church, 0 otherwise, built from Iannaccone's (1994) strictness score, which places Christian denominations on a strictness continuum. With a score of 3.0, the Catholic Church is fairly close to the center of the 1 to 6 scale. The variable is denomination specific and time invariant.
scale: dummy (1 = stricter than the Catholic Church)

description: Following Moody and White (2003), structural cohesion is defined as the k-connectivity of the most cohesive block in which the firm is nested in the annual board overlap network. Network data come from ISS board rosters and Execucomp corporate executive listings, joined by a string matching algorithm on individual names and birthdates; annual square firm-by-firm undirected adjacency matrices are built where cell i,j is 1 if firms i and j share a director or an executive from one firm sits on the board of another firm and zero otherwise. The cohesive blocking routine identifies the k-connectivity of the input graph, removes the k-cutsets that disconnect the graph, and repeats the procedure on each resulting subgraph until all subgraphs are either completely connected or trivial.
scale: k-connectivity of the most cohesive block (count)

variable_name: target of at least one governance related shareholder proposal
description: Dichotomous indicator of whether a firm was the target of at least one governance related shareholder proposal in a given year. Targets and nontargets are defined by comparing governance proposals listed in the ISS shareholder proposals database to firms in the larger ISS governance database. The procedure only includes proposals that were properly presented for a vote and were not withdrawn or omitted from the proxy materials.

Dichotomous dependent variable indicating whether the firm received at least one governance proposal sponsored by union funds in a given year. It is one of a series of disaggregated targeting indicators built from the sponsor type of governance proposals in the ISS shareholder proposals database.

Dichotomous dependent variable indicating whether the firm received at least one governance proposal sponsored by individual investors in a given year. It is one of a series of disaggregated targeting indicators built from the sponsor type of governance proposals in the ISS shareholder proposals database.

Dichotomous dependent variable indicating whether the firm received at least one governance proposal sponsored by public pension funds in a given year. It is one of a series of disaggregated targeting indicators built from the sponsor type of governance proposals in the ISS shareholder proposals database.

Dichotomous dependent variable indicating whether the firm received at least one governance proposal sponsored by other investment funds in a given year; this category includes mutual funds, hedge funds, university endowments, and other investment managers. It is one of a series of disaggregated targeting indicators built from the sponsor type of governance proposals in the ISS shareholder proposals database.

variable_name: implemented a proposal that passed a shareholder vote
description: Dichotomous indicator capturing whether the firm implemented a proposal that passed a shareholder vote. ISS does not provide data on proposal implementation, so this information is hand coded from company filings in the SEC EDGAR database up to two years following a passed proxy proposal. For the subset of proposals that passed under the relevant firm-specific voting threshold, the proposal is coded as having been implemented if the firm adopted the proposal or if management sponsored a proposal that would put the reform into effect. The relevant voting threshold is company specific and is recorded in the ISS database.
time_window: up to two years following a passed proxy proposal

description: The year of the observation, covering the study period. In the implementation analysis, model 2 tests whether the negative cohesion effect varies over time and introduces an interaction term between structural cohesion and year. Figure 3 plots predicted probabilities for proposal implementation for high and low cohesion firms across the study period.

Proportion of variance in firm-year performance attributable to individual CEOs, operationalized as a large set of dummy variables for individual CEO, with CEO contributions counted as distinctive to the extent that they differ from what contextual factors (year, industry, firm) predict and are consistent within tenures. Estimated separately for each 20-year period by sequential ANOVA, with predictors entered in the order year, industry, firm, and CEO, and by a four-level MLM with years nested within CEOs, within firms, within industries.
Return on sales, computed as net income divided by total revenues. Used as one of three firm performance metrics whose variance is partitioned among year, industry, firm, and CEO.
Return on assets, computed as net income divided by total assets. Used as one of three firm performance metrics whose variance is partitioned among year, industry, firm, and CEO.

Market-to-book ratio, computed as the market value of shareholders' equity divided by the book value of equity; the natural log of MTB was used because the variable was highly skewed. Used as one of three firm performance metrics whose variance is partitioned.

Performance panels are partitioned into three distinct 20-year periods: 1950-1969 (Period 1), 1970-1989 (Period 2), and 1990-2009 (Period 3). A second test uses a series of 41 overlapping rolling 20-year panels, each designated by its ending year.

Market space unconventionality is measured using a measure of structural constraint (Burt 1992). Market maps were built from the market category group information of all VC and private equity financed companies in Crunchbase, with firms represented as nodes and market group overlaps between firms represented as edges weighted by the number of overlapping categorical ties. Constraint was calculated for each firm at the time of its launch using the i-graph package in R; the formula for constraint is not readable in the text. Constraint scores were z-score standardized against other firms located in the market category group map at the time of the venture's birth and then multiplied by -1 because unconventionality is the conceptual opposite of constraint.
time_window: at the time of the venture's founding

description: The number of milestones passed, measured based on the completion of venture capital rounds and/or an initial public offering; the variable ranged from zero to four. Each of the first three formal rounds of venture capital finance (series A, B, and C) was coded as one, two, and three, respectively, and firms that had completed an initial public offering at time t were coded as four. The authors build on prior work that treats raising a round of VC financing and undertaking an IPO as incremental increases in development progress.

An index ranging from zero to three reflecting the degree to which the marketing & sales role has been developed within the firm. Firms were given one point for each of the following criteria met: presence of the role in the firm; at least one of the role holders having prior work experience performing that role; and the role being given status in the organization as reflected by its elevation to the top management team, measured as whether the job holder held a VP, C-suite, or founder title. Job titles were sorted into functional role areas by hand-coding and a maximum entropy model.

An index ranging from zero to three reflecting the degree to which the customer development role has been developed within the firm. Firms were given one point for each of the following criteria met: presence of the role in the firm; at least one of the role holders having prior work experience performing that role; and the role being given status in the organization as reflected by its elevation to the top management team, measured as whether the job holder held a VP, C-suite, or founder title. Job titles were sorted into functional role areas by hand-coding and a maximum entropy model.

An index ranging from zero to three reflecting the degree to which the accounting role has been developed within the firm. Firms were given one point for each of the following criteria met: presence of the role in the firm; at least one of the role holders having prior work experience performing that role; and the role being given status in the organization as reflected by its elevation to the top management team, measured as whether the job holder held a VP, C-suite, or founder title. Job titles were sorted into functional role areas by hand-coding and a maximum entropy model.

An index ranging from zero to three reflecting the degree to which the human resources role has been developed within the firm. Firms were given one point for each of the following criteria met: presence of the role in the firm; at least one of the role holders having prior work experience performing that role; and the role being given status in the organization as reflected by its elevation to the top management team, measured as whether the job holder held a VP, C-suite, or founder title. Job titles were sorted into functional role areas by hand-coding and a maximum entropy model.

An index ranging from zero to three reflecting the degree to which the finance role has been developed within the firm. Firms were given one point for each of the following criteria met: presence of the role in the firm; at least one of the role holders having prior work experience performing that role; and the role being given status in the organization as reflected by its elevation to the top management team, measured as whether the job holder held a VP, C-suite, or founder title. Job titles were sorted into functional role areas by hand-coding and a maximum entropy model.

Binary variable coded as 1 if the project was insourced and 0 if an independent contractor was involved in the project. All projects involved at least some Compustar employees, if only to monitor independent contractors, so the relevant question is whether independent contractors were used to fulfill the project.

The profit margin, expressed as a percentage, for each project. Because some projects incurred losses, Margin can be negative. Revenues are captured from customer billing and costs from project hours and expenses submitted by employees and contractors, with cost data using fully burdened labor rates for employees.

Coded as 1 if one or more of Compustar's proprietary technologies is required for a project and 0 otherwise. Compustar engineers and managers created the list of proprietary technologies that are important elements of the firm's competitive advantage, and no interviewees disagreed about their identity. If one of the proprietary technologies is used, it is typically at the center of the project.

Coded as 1 if Compustar personnel believed that, based on the technological description of the project, technology employed in the project made it difficult to verify quality upon an initial test or inspection of a project, and 0 otherwise. The variable was coded by two Compustar engineers with inter-rater reliability greater than 97%. Personnel used a binary scale because they did not feel they could accurately assess measurement cost using continuous or polychotomous scales.

Coded as 1 if persons outside the project team are directly involved in the execution of the project and 0 otherwise. The information is recorded in the deliverables and responsibilities sections of the contracts, and the variable is coded 1 only if the other party, either another supplier or customer personnel, is listed as responsible for some portion of the project deliverables.

Indicator variable for the treatment group, set to one for employees of acquired companies whose tenure crosses the month and year in which the acquisition of their employer transpired, and zero for matched, organically hired employees. Hired employees are workers who joined the same acquirers during the same year that an M&A occurs. Treatment and control observations are retained only if they inhabit a stratum defined by the coarsened matching covariates, and the observations in each stratum are assigned proportionate weights.
time_window: from the month and year of the acquisition or organic hire

description: Employee turnover is modeled as a hazard, with the risk of turnover commencing at the point of organizational entry at acquisition or organic hire. Observations are right censored for all workforce-active individuals that have not moved employers at the end of the observation window. Because individuals' full prior career histories are observed, there are no left censored observations.
time_window: from organizational entry to departure or right censoring

description: After cleaning up job titles, the authors use individuals' mobility from origin to destination job titles, either within or between companies, to create a seniority order of job titles, modeling each job switch as a game in which the destination job wins over the origin job. The ranking of each job is determined by an Elo rating system; jobs are matched in a five-quantile hierarchy in the Cox models.

Job titles are categorized with a bottom-up, unsupervised machine-learning algorithm that clusters the text LinkedIn members use to self-characterize their work roles, producing 150 job-role categories from the 30 million resumes. For the analysis, roles that are under-represented in the CEM sample are eliminated and job roles are joined by climbing the hierarchical tree from the clustering algorithm, leaving 28 'supra-job' categories, which are entered with their interaction with the AE indicator in a Cox regression.

Educational degrees on the resumes are manually categorized into three tertiary degree levels: bachelor's, master's, and doctoral. Individuals reporting secondary diplomas and associate degrees are dropped. In the models bachelor's degree holders are the omitted baseline group, and masters and doctoral holders are represented by indicator variables.

The number of shared markets between firms i and j in year t-1 divided by the sum of firm i's and firm j's numbers of markets in year t-1, computed when the numerator is greater than one. The variable takes the value of zero not only when the two firms in a dyad have no market contact, but also when they have just one market contact, because at least two common product markets are needed for two firms to engage in mutual forbearance.

In the shared markets between firm i and firm j, the authors compare the two firms' market shares and count the markets where each firm has a larger market share than the other. The markets where the firm with the smaller number of such markets has larger market shares are paired with markets where the other firm has larger market shares; those paired markets generate reciprocity and are counted as reciprocal. The count of reciprocal contacts is divided by the sum of each firm's number of markets to be consistent with the structure of the multimarket contact variable.

The remaining shared markets, in which no reciprocity can be generated because one firm has larger market shares in all of them, are counted as nonreciprocal contacts. The count of nonreciprocal contacts is divided by the sum of each firm's number of markets to be consistent with the structure of the multimarket contact variable.
Dichotomous variable coded one if firms i and j in a dyad form a new technology cooperation agreement in year t, and zero otherwise. Agreements are traced in the Thomson Reuters' Recap database.

Risk was measured as the ex ante uncertainty of a firm's earnings stream. For a company in a given year it is the standard deviation of securities analysts' forecasts of earnings per share, taken from the January IBES report. The forecasts, originally in earnings-per-share terms, were converted to ROA by multiplying by shares divided by total assets from the previous year.
time_window: For a given year; January IBES report

description: Performance was measured by return on total assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), and return on sales (ROS). Because the results agreed across the three measures, only the ROA results are discussed.
Industry performance was the average ROA of firms with a given two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code.

Expectations were measured by the mean of the earnings forecasts produced by securities analysts. The forecasts were originally in earnings-per-share terms and were converted to ROA by multiplying by shares divided by total assets from the previous year.
time_window: year; lagged one year in the performance equation

description: For firms with performance above the mean for their industry, aspirations were represented by multiplying past performance (ROA) by 1.05. For firms performing below their industry's mean, aspirations were set equal to that level of performance.
time_window: year; lagged one year in the performance equation

description: Following Bourgeois and Singh, indicators of three kinds of slack were used: the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities) represented available slack; selling, general, and administrative expenses divided by sales (SG&A/sales) represented recoverable slack; the debt-to-equity ratio, reflecting a lack of potential slack, and the interest coverage ratio (income before taxes and interest charges divided by interest charges), indicating potential slack, measured potential slack. The estimated equations included variables measuring kinds of slack and the squares of these variables to represent a U-shaped relation.
time_window: year; lagged one year in the performance equation

description: Percentage of the team's predetermined performance criteria on which the new product version failed to improve over the original in a performance episode. For each criterion the team compares user statistics for the new version with those for the original version; when the new version produces results that are worse than or the same as the original, the team deems it a failure on that criterion. Each criterion was coded 0 = non-failure and 1 = failure, and the failed performance criteria percentage was calculated for each performance episode.

Coefficient of variation (CV) of team member status, calculated by dividing the within-team standard deviation of status by the team mean. Individual member status was measured as degree centrality, the count of direct ties an employee has within the collaboration network comprising all product testing employees during the previous quarter. A higher number of direct ties indicates broader reach, instrumental social value and experience, and thus higher status.
time_window: performance episode N (network ties from the previous quarter)

variable_name: Team's willingness to add high-status members
description: Number of members added between two performance episodes who had higher status than all existing members of the team in episode N. The variable was created by comparing the membership information across performance episodes N and N+1.
time_window: between performance episodes N and N+1

description: Percentage of performance criteria that improve, i.e., the percentage of performance criteria in which the new product version outperforms the baseline, in performance episode N+1. For example, a performance score of 0.25 indicates that the new product version improves on the original in 25% of the criteria.

Participants were randomly assigned to a team failure or a team success condition through the ostensible ROI evaluation of their team's investment decisions. In the team failure condition participants read that their team's ROI failed to meet their goal, described as a disappointing result; in the team success condition they read that the ROI met the goal.

Manipulated through the team status hierarchy participants were shown after allocating respect points. In the high status differentiation conditions, teammates received investment acumen scores in the moderate and low range and the respect point figures placed the participant at the top or the bottom of the hierarchy; in the low status differentiation condition, participants and teammates all received moderate investment acumen scores and nearly equal respect points.

Participants were randomly assigned to a high or low individual status level condition within the status differentiation manipulation. Those in the high status level condition purported to have received an investment acumen score in the high percentile range and the most respect points, and were told they currently ranked high in their group; those in the low status level condition received the opposite information and were told they ranked low.

Three items measuring members' felt uncertainty about their status, reported after participants viewed the team performance feedback. A sample item is 'I feel that my status is at risk in this team.' All items were rated on a 1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree scale.

Three items developed by the authors regarding the potential benefits for collective performance that a new member could provide. A sample item is 'This person has abilities that can benefit our team.' Items were rated on a 1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree scale.

Five items developed by the authors regarding the potential cost to one's own status posed by the potential new member. A sample item is 'This person might threaten my status within the team.' Items were rated on a 1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree scale.

variable_name: Willingness to add a high-status member
description: After being shown the self-introduction, top-percentile investment acumen score and an AI-generated evaluation portraying a prospective member ('AH') as more experienced and likely to hold higher status than all current team members, participants indicated their own willingness to add AH. They responded to the question 'How likely are you to anonymously vote to add AH to your team?' on a 1 = extremely unlikely to 7 = extremely likely scale.

Teams were randomly assigned to a team performance failure or success condition using the same manipulation materials as in Study 2. The manipulation was reinforced by telling teams that if the team failed in the next round they would receive no bonus.

Teams were randomly assigned to a high or low status differentiation condition using the same materials as in Study 2. The manipulation was reinforced by a bonus distribution rule: teams in the high status differentiation condition were told that the high-status member would receive a larger share and low-status members a smaller share of a future bonus, whereas teams in the low status differentiation condition were told that all members would receive an equal share.

Within each team, participants were randomly assigned to a high or low individual status level condition using the same materials as in Study 2, such that each team consisted of one high-status and two low-status members. Status was operationalized as respect and admiration from the other team members.

Members of the interacting teams reported their status uncertainty using the same three-item measure as in Study 2. A sample item is 'I feel that my status is at risk in this team,' rated on the same 1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree scale.

Members of the interacting teams rated the potential benefit to collective performance that the new member could provide using the same three-item measure as in Study 2. A sample item is 'This person has abilities that can benefit our team,' rated on the same 1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree scale.

Members of the interacting teams rated the potential cost to their own status posed by the new member using the same five-item measure as in Study 2. A sample item is 'This person might threaten my status within the team,' rated on the same 1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree scale.

variable_name: Willingness to add the high-status member
description: Team members reported their own willingness to add the high-status new member using the same measure as in Study 2. Responses were given on the same 1 = extremely unlikely to 7 = extremely likely scale.

variable_name: Willing to invite a high-status member (team-level)
description: Teams were shown the same new member information as in Study 2, plus a researcher's note indicating that AH was likely to hold a higher status than all current members and that AH could receive the largest share of the team bonus if the next round succeeded. After the team discussed whether to invite AH, the high-status member submitted the team's final decision (0 = no, 1 = yes).

variable_name: Team random slope of willingness on perceived benefit
description: For each team, the Bayes estimate of the random slope relating members' perceived benefit to collective performance to their willingness to add the high-status member, from a multilevel model with random slopes. The slope is used as a team-level predictor of the team's decision.

variable_name: Team random slope of willingness on perceived cost
description: For each team, the Bayes estimate of the random slope relating members' perceived cost to individual status to their willingness to add the high-status member, from a multilevel model with random slopes. The slope is used as a team-level predictor of the team's decision.

Coded as the decision number at which subjects switched from the presumably safer option A to the riskier option B in the price list task. Option A had a possible high payoff of 300 CNY and a low payoff of 240 CNY, while option B had a possible high payoff of 580 CNY and a low payoff of 15 CNY, with the probability of the high payoffs increasing by 10% across the 10 successive decisions. Values range from 1 to 10, in line with the 10 decision steps, where switching points further down the list signify greater risk aversion; subjects who never switched were coded as 11.

Binary variable with a value of 1 if the switching point in the risk elicitation task is 6 or larger. It is used to construct interaction effects between guanxi activities and risk aversion in the performance models because a continuous measure of risk aversion would lead to multicollinearity problems and biased parameter estimates.

Simple average of three Likert items on reliance on guanxi in business-to-government transactions: with political government, with industrial authorities, and with other government authorities. Respondents were asked to circle the number that best describes the extent to which their firm utilizes guanxi with each counterpart on a scale from 1 ('very little') to 7 ('very much'). The three questions were embedded in separate modules of the survey questionnaire.

Simple average of three Likert items on reliance on guanxi in business-to-business transactions: with suppliers, with customers, and with competitors. Respondents were asked to circle the number that best describes the extent to which their firm utilizes guanxi with each counterpart on a scale from 1 ('very little') to 7 ('very much'). The three questions were embedded in separate modules of the survey questionnaire to reduce the risk of a method-response bias.
Measured as the number of years since registration as a private firm. It is used both as the contingency splitting the sample of young and established firms and as a covariate.

Measured as the average of a firm's local supplies in total supplies and local sales in total sales. Suppliers and customers located in the same community are defined as 'local', whereas 'nonlocal' suppliers and customers may be located in the same province but not the same locality, or in other provinces or overseas (including Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan).
Self-reported return on assets, calculated as the three-year average in order to smooth out performance variation over time.
Self-reported sales growth for the three-year period corresponding to the return on assets measure.

Each respondent named up to eight swine genetics firms with which they were familiar and rated each identified firm on a 10-point Likert scale across 16 competitive attributes (1 = least important/significant to 10 = most important/significant). The attribute list was elicited using the repertory grid technique from a group of 24 veterinarians. Based on the intersection of 11 firms common to all three respondent groups, the mean response for each firm's attribute was calculated for all 16 attributes within each respondent group. A case is one individual respondent's assessment of a swine genetics firm.
scale: 10-point Likert scale (1 = least important/significant, 10 = most important/significant)
level: individual respondent's assessment of a swine genetics firm, aggregated to firm means within respondent group

description: Cluster analysis placed firms into strategic groups on the basis of their degree of similarity, or dissimilarity, in the 16 competitive attribute ratings, performed on the mean attribute values for each firm of each respondent group. Hierarchical agglomeration with squared Euclidean distance (UPGMA) was followed by K-means analysis, with cluster cutoffs determined from large increases in Euclidean distance between clustering stages. Similarity between hierarchical and K-means solutions was assessed with the symmetric Goodman-Kruskal lambda statistic, and differences between respondent groups with the converted asymmetric G-K lambda statistic.

Respondents were members of three vertical segments of the swine genetics value chain: the TMT of the focal swine genetics company, veterinarians, and hog producers. The TMT was surveyed through one veterinarian who was a member of the team and administered the survey to five other members of his team; these six members constituted the TMT of the focal swine genetics company. The remaining veterinarian and hog producer respondent groups were asked to complete the survey form for up to eight swine genetics firms with which they were familiar.

Distance is given by the position of an industry participant in the value chain relative to the focal firm's TMT: the hog producer is the market's end customer and should receive the greatest information feedback, whereas the veterinarian is an intermediary user of swine genetics. Pairwise MANOVA comparisons of the TMT with each customer group used the F statistic as a measure of the degree to which the groups vary in their perceptions of the market's competitive attributes, and the converted asymmetric Goodman-Kruskal lambda measured the degree of divergence in competitive groupings between groups.

Dichotomous variable coded 1 when the test record indicates the vehicle passed and 0 when it indicates the vehicle failed. A vehicle passes only if it scores below a government-mandated threshold for all three constituents: hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, and nitrogen oxides. A higher average pass rate associated with a particular type of facility is interpreted as an indication of leniency.

Inspection facilities were categorized each year into one of three mutually exclusive industries based on the primary three-digit SIC code assigned that year by Dun & Bradstreet: car dealer (SIC 551 or 552), gasoline retailer (SIC 554), and service and repair facility (SIC 553, 753, or 769). Facility-years that could not be matched to D&B data were categorized from facility names or, for service and repair facilities, from whether the facility reported repair data to the state agency. Gasoline retailer is the omitted category in the models.

Logged number of facilities in the sample that shared the focal facility's parent company (after adding 1). A facility is considered a subsidiary in a particular year if its D-U-N-S number differs from that of its headquarters or if it shared its headquarters' D-U-N-S number with another facility that year; the designation is coded at the facility-year level and is not exclusive of branding. Independent facility is the omitted category in the models.

Logged number of facilities in the sample that shared the focal facility's brand (after adding 1). A facility is considered branded if its name includes a brand name associated with a gasoline retailer, a service/repair chain, or a vehicle make; the designation is coded at the facility-year level and is not exclusive of subsidiary status. Independent facility is the omitted category in the models.

Profit opportunity from cross-selling is represented by facility type, with car dealers and service and repair facilities assumed to have profitable cross-selling opportunities and gasoline retailers (omitted category) low ones. It is tested through the facility scope categories from D&B SIC codes.

A treatment dummy equal to 1 if the state has enacted the antidiscrimination law by year t, and 0 otherwise. Enactment is staggered across U.S. states, with the District of Columbia first passing such a law in 1977 and 15 treatments occurring between 1980 and 2006. The coefficient on this dummy (beta AD) is the coefficient of interest in the difference-in-differences model.

The total number of new, stand-alone establishments in a given U.S. state and year, taken from the Longitudinal Business Database (LBD). For each establishment the year of entry is defined, following Kerr and Nanda (2009), as the first year of positive employment. The LBD provides annual employment data for every U.S. private sector establishment with a payroll.

The number of patent applications filed by new assignees in a given state-year, normalized by the number of new entrants in that state-year; data retrieved from the USPTO Patentsview dataset. Patents were assigned to states based on both the location of the new assignee and the location of the first inventor, excluding patents for which the two locations do not coincide.

The average amount of venture capital funding a new venture received, computed as the total amount of VC investments in a given state-year (available from 1980) normalized by the number of new entrants in the same state-year. The VC data are by location of investee company and were retrieved from Thomson Reuters' VentureXpert.

The proportion of startups created in a given state-year that were able to survive for at least 5 years. Because the LBD ends in 2011, for firms founded in 2006 only a 5-year survival can be measured.

The total LGBT population present in a state, collected from the 2005 American Community Survey. Baseline models are re-estimated separately within two subsamples: states above and below the median levels of the U.S. LGBT population by state.

Litigation data on civil rights suits relating to jobs, available from the Federal Judicial Centre Integrated databases from 1970 to the present; for each state-year the count of civil suits was computed. To avoid endogeneity with the antidiscrimination legislation, the number of grievances between 1970, the first year information is available, and 1977, the year ENDA was first enacted (in DC), was used. States above the median annual number of civil right job suits are high-litigation states and states below the median are low-litigation states.

The construct was measured using eight items that asked respondents to assess the speed at which such things as product and service offer, branding strategy, prices, advertising activities, sales channels, and organizational structures in the field sales force were made similar during the integration process. The specific items were partly based on items used by Datta (1991).
time_window: during the integration process after the merger or acquisition

description: A single item adapted from previous M&A research asking the respondent to indicate how the return on sales has developed compared to the situation before the merger or acquisition, considering the sum of both companies.
time_window: before versus after the merger or acquisition

variable_name: Relatedness with respect to target markets
description: Measured by three items also used by Capron and Hulland (1999), capturing the extent to which the merging firms' geographical markets and customers are similar.

variable_name: Relatedness with respect to market positioning
description: Measured with five items that are based on previous research (Achrol, 1992), referring to the extent to which the merging firms' offers are similar in terms of the customer needs which they satisfy, quality, price positioning, etc.

variable_name: Relatedness with respect to strategic orientation
description: Constructs were measured separately for acquiring and target firms, and relatedness was computed for each construct as the average absolute value of the differences between the two firms' scores on the individual items. Strategic orientation covers cost orientation, product orientation and customer intimacy, with items based on previous work by Dess and Davis (1984), Nayyar (1993), and Treacy and Wiersema (1993, 1995).

variable_name: Relatedness with respect to management style
description: Management styles were assessed using seven items, the selection of which was guided by a comprehensive measure previously used in M&A-related research (Datta, 1991) and by previous research in the management literature (Khandwalla, 1977). The items describe management styles in terms of such dimensions as centralized/decentralized, short-term-oriented/long-term-oriented, and proactive/reactive. Relatedness was computed as the average absolute value of the differences between the two firms' scores on the individual items.

Measured by means of two items related to the merging firms' return on sales and market share, adapted from previous M&A research. Relatedness was computed as the average absolute value of the differences between the two firms' scores on the individual items.

variable_name: Relatedness in target markets and market positioning
description: External relatedness is measured by two survey scales answered by integration managers: target markets (three items on geographical markets and customers) and market positioning (five items on customer needs, quality and price positioning). Each is split at the median into high and low for the tests.

variable_name: Relatedness in strategic orientation, management style and performance
description: Internal relatedness is measured by three survey-based scores, strategic orientation, management style and performance (return on sales and market share). Each is the average absolute difference between the acquirer's and target's item scores, and is split at the median into high and low for the tests.
scale: Absolute difference of survey items; median split

description: Coded as 1 for Black executives and 0 for White executives. Race was coded from observers' perception rather than self-identification: two analysts independently coded each executive using all publicly available information and photos, and their comparison yielded an initial inter-coder reliability of 98%; after consulting additional sources for the discrepancies the final inter-coder reliability was 100%. Non-White and non-Black executives were excluded from the sample.

The sample of appointment announcements was divided into CEO appointments (1,662 announcements) and TMT appointments (2,626 announcements), and the hypotheses are tested by comparing the two subsamples. TMT positions comprise COO, CFO, President, and Executive Vice President.

Three-day cumulative abnormal return measured over the (-1, +1) window around the appointment announcement and used as the dependent variable. Shares had to be traded every day in the -240 to -20 day window to compute a beta for the market model; standard errors were obtained from the distribution across 500 bootstrap iterations. In the multivariate models the regressions are weighted by the standard error of the market model regression used to calculate the CARs.
time_window: -1 to +1 days relative to the announcement

description: Coded as 1 if the executive was promoted from within the company and 0 if the executive was not promoted from within the company. Several sources were used to determine this, such as the firm's announcement of the appointment, the firm's website, the executive's LinkedIn profile, and the executive's vita.
scale: 1 = promoted from within the company, 0 = otherwise

description: Summated score of the product dimension from KLD data, used to operationalize PSP. The aggregate score is obtained by differencing the scores on the strength and weakness dimension of each measure.

Summated score of the environment dimension from KLD data, used to operationalize ESP. The aggregate score is obtained by differencing the scores on the strength and weakness dimension of each measure.

Disaggregated PSP strength ratings from KLD, which capture the extent to which a firm's products or services can be deemed socially responsible (meet social concerns). Used together with PSP weakness to test H2a.

Disaggregated PSP weakness ratings from KLD, which capture violations of social responsibility, such as through fraud and recalls, which violate stakeholder expectations. Used together with PSP strength to test H2a.
Disaggregated ESP strength ratings from KLD, which capture the extent to which firms take actions to avoid waste and prevent pollution. Used together with ESP weakness to test H2b.
Disaggregated ESP weakness ratings from KLD, which capture violations of expected environmental norms. Used together with ESP strength to test H2b.

Firm performance is measured with Tobin's Q, computed using the formula proposed by Chung and Pruitt (1994). Tobin's Q is used because it is forward-looking and reflects future profitability. Current year Tobin's Q was used for the analysis.

IU is operationalized in terms of the imprecision of the firm's financial information. Following previous research in the accounting literature, IU is estimated from the unexplained portion of the regression of total accruals on cash flows. IU is estimated as the standard deviation of the residuals for a firm; the greater the standard deviation of the residuals, the higher is IU for the firm. The equation itself could not be read from the text as presented.

Labor productivity of a firm, constructed as value added divided by the number of employees, where value added is defined as the firm's total revenue minus its costs of nonlabor inputs. The figures for value added and for number of employees are provided by the EAE database, so they require no additional computation. Variables that take strictly positive values, including this one, are expressed in logarithms.

Indicator set equal to 1 at the date of a foreign acquisition and at one, two, and three years later, and set equal to 0 otherwise; the construction makes it easier to handle firms that make multiple acquisitions. Because the sample includes both acquiring and nonacquiring firms, the variable assesses the average effect of acquisitions on acquiring firms relative to nonacquiring firms. Acquisitions are majority acquisitions identified in the Thomson One Banker-Deals database.
scale: 1 = acquiring firm in the acquisition year and the three following years; 0 otherwise
time_window: Acquisition year and the three following years (acquisitions 1993-2001)

variable_name: Foreign acquisition MCC / Foreign acquisition LCC
description: The target countries are divided into two categories: those with a higher level of competitiveness than France (variable Foreign acquisition MCC, more competitive countries) and those with a lower level (variable Foreign acquisition LCC, less competitive countries). The level of country competitiveness is based on the overall rankings in the World Competitiveness Yearbook published by IMD, determined by four factors: economic performance, government efficiency, business efficiency, and infrastructure. Standard interactive dummy variables could not be used because such a dummy is not specified for nonacquiring firms.
time_window: Acquisition year and the three following years

description: The firm's investment rate, measured as its investments in tangible fixed assets divided by the sum of all tangible fixed assets. The variable is interacted with the acquisition variables and is lagged by one year.

Three-step content analysis of a combined yearly document built from letters to shareholders, MD&A sections of 10-K forms, and conference call transcripts. Coders identified statements specifying exact numerical past time horizons (dates or time spans), the sentences were rank-ordered by time horizon length in years, and three measures were computed: the longest, the median, and the shortest past date or time span cited. The composite is the average of the three items, with Cronbach's alpha of 0.71.

Three-step content analysis of a combined yearly document built from letters to shareholders, MD&A sections of 10-K forms, and conference call transcripts. Coders identified statements specifying exact numerical future time horizons (dates or time spans), the sentences were rank-ordered by time horizon length in years, and three measures were computed: the longest, the median, and the shortest future date or time span cited. The composite is the average of the three items, with Cronbach's alpha of 0.78.

Composite built from structured content analysis of news headlines in the LexisNexis online database; coders identified headlines representing competitive actions and 20,418 competitive actions were identified. Action volume is the total number of competitive actions initiated by a firm in a given year. Action speed is the average length of time lag between the focal firm's actions and rivals' immediately preceding actions in a given year, reverse coded by taking its inverse. The two standardized scores were averaged into a composite measure, and the yearly measure was lagged one year behind the executive temporal depth measures.
time_window: 1996-2000, lagged one year behind executive temporal depth

description: Computed as the average of the competitive actions (total competitive actions divided by number of firms) initiated by dominant firms in an industry in a given year. Dominant firms are those controlling the most market share (more than 80 percent), which the authors treat as setting the velocity for their industry.

Composite of two accounting measures of performance, return on sales (ROS) and return on assets (ROA), measured at the end of the same year as the competitive aggressiveness measure; the z-scores of the two measures were combined.

Categorical variable coded 1 if the participant was in the rational-analytic thinking condition during the attention allocation phase and 0 otherwise. Cognition was manipulated with formal instructions asking participants to think analytically and rationally, to provide logical arguments and/or concrete evidence, and not to make judgments relying on intuition. The manipulation was checked with three items ('I reasoned things out carefully,' 'I approached the task analytically,' and 'I arrived at my answer by carefully assessing the information') on a 1 = Strongly Disagree to 5 = Strongly Agree scale, which were averaged.

Categorical variable coded 1 if the participant was in the intuition condition during the judgment phase and 0 otherwise. Participants in this condition were instructed to rely on their gut feeling to formulate the needs or pain points, to use their intuition and write down what they personally felt was the right answer, and not to search for logical, rational explanations. The manipulation was checked with three items ('I relied on my sense of intuition,' 'I used my gut feelings,' and 'I trusted my hunches') averaged on a 1 = Strongly Disagree to 5 = Strongly Agree scale.

Two coders familiar with the industry evaluated the degree to which distant symptoms were identified during the attention allocation phase on a Likert scale from 1 = only common symptoms to 5 = included highly uncommon, distant symptoms. The final measure is the average of the coders' ratings; ICC(1) for agreement = .82 and ICC(2) for reliability = .90.
