Calculated as the fiscal year return to shareholders, in percentage terms, including stock price appreciation and monthly dividend reinvestment. It was transformed using the inverse hyperbolic sine method for the same reasons as CEO return.

For tests of Hypotheses 2-5, a firm-specific measure created by first estimating a within-firm regression of CEO return on shareholder return, controlling for firm size (assets), over each continuous three-year period (time t - 2 through time t). The resulting shareholder return regression coefficient was used as the financial alignment measure to predict subsequent performance for that firm.
Generated by calculating shareholder return for the subsequent three years: future shareholder return for period t was the shareholder return over the periods t + 1, t + 2, and t + 3.

Generated by calculating total net income before extraordinary items (earnings per share times shares outstanding) for the subsequent three years and dividing by 3. Future earnings for period t were the average earnings over the periods t + 1, t + 2, and t + 3.

Computed as the aggregate value at time t of the CEO's in-the-money options portfolio, restricted stock portfolio, and other equity portfolio, as well as net proceeds accumulated throughout the fiscal year from exercises and sales in the options portfolio, restricted stock portfolio, and equity portfolio. The distribution was skewed but did not take negative values; therefore it was transformed using a conventional logarithmic transformation.

Created by dividing the dollar value of a CEO's one-year return by the dollar value of one-year total shareholder return. This value represents the relative changes in wealth level for the CEO relative to all shareholders and, as a ratio, is interpretable in percentage terms. Because the distribution was highly skewed and included zero and negative values, it was transformed using the inverse hyperbolic sine method.

Estimates of the contribution of each originating industry to diversification events, given by the three-way interaction terms of country by industry by the incidence of diversification and transformed to be consistent with the assumptions of the p1 model following Wasserman and Iacobucci (1986, p. 62). The estimates are reported by industry for each of the five countries and are then correlated among countries.

Estimates of the tendency of an industry to be a target for diversification, given by the three-way interaction terms of country by industry by the incidence of diversification and transformed to be consistent with the assumptions of the p1 model following Wasserman and Iacobucci (1986, p. 62). The estimates are reported by industry for each of the five countries and are then correlated among countries.

Calculated as the difference between the predicted and observed cell counts in the array of diversification counts; the residual represents the interaction between originating and target industries, controlling for their relative expansiveness and attractiveness, and thus indicates the pattern of diversification between industry pairs within a country. The underlying array has four dimensions - the five countries, the 21 originating industries, the 21 target industries, and whether firms diversified - and its entries are the counts by country of firms in an industry that have diversified or not diversified into another industry.

Correlations between pairs of countries of the residual values of Equation (1), calculated for both diversification events and the absence of diversification. Positive correlations support the technological hypothesis, whereas a preponderance of negative intercountry correlations supports the institutional hypothesis.

Technological relatedness between industries is measured by a statistic similar to Teece et al. (1994), the residual of the log-linear model, defined as predicted minus observed counts of firms diversifying from each originating to each target industry, controlling for expansiveness and attractiveness.

Indicator of whether a mathematician is a specialist or a generalist at the time of the Soviet collapse. It is derived from an individual diversification index calculated as 1 minus the Euclidean distance in the multidimensional space of the 33 subfields (MSC codes) of theoretical mathematics, based on shares of publications in each subfield per mathematician. Generalists are mathematicians whose diversification index is in the top 10 percent of the distribution (above .290) and specialists are those with an index of 0 (published in only one subfield); the indicator is coded 1 for specialists.

Index of the degree to which a mathematician's area was affected by the Soviet collapse, i.e. how fast-paced the knowledge domain was. It is calculated as the sum of the shares of an individual's publications in each of the 33 subfields of theoretical mathematics, weighted by the rank order of the subfield, over the whole pre-collapse period. The higher the share of publications in subfields in which Soviets made greater contributions, the higher the index. Mathematicians whose index is in the top 10 percent of the range are coded 1 (fast-paced domain) and others are coded 0.
Count of publications per mathematician per year, used to measure the quantity of creative output.

Quality-adjusted count of publications per year in which each publication is counted as 1 plus the number of future citations it received in subsequent publications by 2014. For example, two publications in 1985, one with 10 future citations and the other with 20, give a quality-adjusted research output of 32 for that year.

Count of a mathematician's publications per year that belong to the top 5 percent of highly cited publications in the given year. Publications in the top 10 percent of highly cited publications were used for an alternative measure.
Number of collaborators of a mathematician, used as a dependent variable in the collaboration models estimated at the author-year level.
Number of unique collaborators of a mathematician, used alongside the total number of collaborators in the collaboration models at the author-year level.

TMT nationality diversity is calculated with a Blau index using the formula B = 1 - Sigma_i (p_i)^2, where p is the percentage of members in the ith group (i.e., nationality). The TMT is defined as the executive team listed in the company annual reports, and in Switzerland listed firms are required to file the nationalities of their top executives in these reports. TMT composition is measured in the beginning of the same year for which performance is measured.

The dependent variable firm performance is operationalized as return on assets (ROA) at the end of each calendar year. TMT composition is measured in the beginning of the same year, a lag structure chosen to ensure that the antecedent variables temporally precede the dependent variable and to avoid problems with causality of the studied relationship.
TMT tenure is measured as the median of the tenures of all TMT members.
Internationalization is the average of (1) foreign sales to total sales, (2) foreign assets to total assets, and (3) geographic dispersion of foreign sales.

Industry munificence is calculated as the rate of growth (regression coefficient of time on annual average sales for each industry) divided by the mean value of sales for the study period. Industry variables are measured based on two-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes.

Noncore business sales in 1997 minus noncore business sales in 1993, divided by total sales in 1993. The core business segment was identified as the segment with the largest sales in 1993 and 1997, and sales of the remaining segments were aggregated to arrive at noncore business sales. Normalizing by size in 1993 gives an indication of how rapidly firms grew in relative terms over 1993-1997. The variable is a dependent variable and is treated as endogenous in the estimations.

Foreign sales in 1997 minus foreign sales in 1993, divided by total sales in 1993. Foreign sales data were retrieved from Compustat for 1997 and 1993. Normalizing by size in 1993 gives an indication of how rapidly firms grew in relative terms over 1993-1997. The variable is a dependent variable and is treated as endogenous in the estimations.

A dummy variable indicating whether the firm is involved in an upstream strategic alliance, based on the survey question: Does your firm have a strategic alliance with any of your suppliers? The variable is coded 1 for firms with an alliance and 0 otherwise, and also serves as the selection-dependent variable in the self-selection probit model.

A scaled response measuring the average of the five performance-related scale measures (market share, ROA, product quality, competitive position and customer service), each of which rates the firm against its major industrial rivals. The authors report a Cronbach alpha for the scale.
An assessment of the firm's level of performance compared to its major industrial rivals in terms of market share, on a five-point scale where 1 = low and 5 = high.
An assessment of the firm's level of performance compared to its major industrial rivals in terms of return on assets, on a five-point scale where 1 = low and 5 = high.
An assessment of the firm's level of performance compared to its major industrial rivals in terms of overall product quality, on a five-point scale where 1 = low and 5 = high.
An assessment of the firm's level of performance compared to its major industrial rivals in terms of overall competitive position, on a five-point scale where 1 = low and 5 = high.
An assessment of the firm's level of performance compared to its major industrial rivals in terms of overall customer service, on a five-point scale where 1 = low and 5 = high.

The Inverse Mill's Ratio of the probit regression in step one of the self-selection model, included among the regressors of the performance equation; it estimates the correlation between the error terms of the selection and performance equations and is the ratio of the standard normal density function to the cumulative distribution function. The authors state that constituting the self-selection control, LAMBDA, are variables in the probit analysis measuring size (FirmSize), supply chain relationship commitment (SCM, Outsourcing, FirmasKeySupplier), and the SME's focus on supplier participation (SupplierParticipation).

Scores from the first stage of the self-selection model indicating the probability that an SME chooses UVA activity. The authors use a cut-off of 0.50 to classify SMEs as having strong or weak self-selection characteristics, and compare the scores of SMEs that perceived greater versus lesser UVA benefits.

An assessment of how much the upstream vertical alliance is helping the firm's market share, based on the survey question: How successful is your supplier alliance activity in terms of increasing your firm's market share? The response is on a five-point scale where 1 = low and 5 = high.

An assessment of how much the upstream vertical alliance is helping the firm's profitability, based on the survey question: How successful is your supplier alliance activity in terms of increasing your firm's profits? The response is on a five-point scale where 1 = low and 5 = high.

An assessment of how much the upstream vertical alliance is helping the firm's product quality, based on the survey question: How successful is your supplier alliance activity in terms of increasing your firm's quality level? The response is on a five-point scale where 1 = low and 5 = high.

An assessment of how much the upstream vertical alliance is helping the firm's cost level, based on the survey question: How successful is your supplier alliance activity in terms of lowering your firm's total costs? The response is on a five-point scale where 1 = low and 5 = high.

An assessment of how much the upstream vertical alliance is helping the firm's customer service, based on the survey question: How successful is your supplier alliance activity in terms of increasing your firm's customer service level? The response is on a five-point scale where 1 = low and 5 = high.

variable_name: number of patent citations by the parent company
description: For every patent in each of the three samples the authors determined every subsequent patent, up to 1995, that cited the sample patent in the overseas region of the parent company or alliance partner; a subsequent citation is interpreted as a case of knowledge building upon the original sample patent. In the negative binomial models the dependent variable is the number of patent citations occurring in the first five years after the patent application. In the regional-level analysis a citation by any firm in the home region (Japan, Europe, or the rest of Asia) indicates cross-border knowledge building.
time_window: first five years after the patent application; citing patents counted up to 1995

description: Dummy variable for the patents in Sample A, which consists of patents belonging to U.S. subsidiaries of foreign MNCs with recorded patenting activity both in the United States and in their home country (Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Italy, France, Germany, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom). Up to 10 patents filed before 1991 were selected for each of the 21 such MNCs, giving 146 patents. The dummy is entered together with the alliance dummy when Samples A, B, and C are combined, and alone when Samples A and B are combined.

Dummy variable for the patents in Sample B, consisting of patents belonging to the domestic units of United States firms that had a prior strategic alliance with the corresponding MNC in Sample A and did not themselves have a subsidiary in the home country of that MNC. For every patent in Sample A a matching Sample B patent of the same technology class and filing year was chosen, giving 146 patents. The dummy is entered together with the MNC dummy when Samples A, B, and C are combined.
time_window: same filing year as the matched Sample A patent (filed before 1991)

description: Sample C consists of patents having the same technology class and filing year as the corresponding patents in Samples A and B but assigned to firms in the United States with no formal links to the MNC or its home country; the total number of patents in Sample C is 146. These patents serve as the omitted reference category in the models that combine Samples A, B, and C.
scale: reference category (not entered as a dummy)
time_window: same filing year as the matched Sample A patent (filed before 1991)

variable_name: successor origin dummy variables (family successor, nonfamily inside successor, outside successor)
description: A series of dummy variables indicates the origin of the incoming chair, each coded 1 for the relevant type and 0 otherwise. A family successor was coded 1 if the incoming chair was related to the controlling family through marriage or family ties, and family successor and nonfamily inside successor were coded as mutually exclusive. A nonfamily inside successor was coded 1 only if a nonfamily executive who was currently an officer or a director of the focal firm was promoted to the position of chair. An outside successor was coded 1 only if an executive who was not an employee of the focal firm (or, for member firms of business groups, an employee of other affiliates in the same group) was hired to the chair position.

Return on assets (ROA) is the dependent variable used to capture firm performance, chosen as a widely used accounting measure of operational performance rather than market valuation. Because there is a time lag before the performance effect of succession becomes evident, the dependent variable is the average ROA in the two years after the year of the succession. For non-succession cases the dependent variable is also the average firm ROA in the subsequent two years.
time_window: average of the two years after the succession year

description: Family ownership is the percentage of shares owned by the controlling family, the family with the largest shareholding in the firm's ownership structure. Family shareholding is calculated by considering the pyramid structure in ownership using the methodology developed by La Porta et al. (1999), with family members owning shares directly or through other public and private firms under their control. For the interaction terms the authors centered and standardized family ownership.

Group membership was coded 1 only if a firm was a member of the top 100 business groups, and 0 otherwise. Because fixed-effects models were used, the main variable of group affiliates was dropped from the models; only the interaction terms with successor origin were estimated.

A dummy variable identifies firms in high tech industries, defined as the electronic and computer sectors. It was used to create interaction terms between industry type and the three types of successors. Because fixed-effects models were used, the main high tech industries variable was dropped from the models.

Foreign institutional ownership is the percentage of shares owned by foreign institutional investors. For the interaction terms with successor origin, the authors centered and standardized this variable.

variable_name: sample classification into the high diversity/high foreign sales quadrant
description: The 1978 Fortune list was pared to 256 firms required under FASB 14 to segment foreign operations. These firms were arrayed on a matrix bounded by the number of two digit SIC codes of operations and by foreign sales as a percentage of total sales, and divided as closely in half as possible along each axis. Seven or more SICs and 20 per cent or more foreign sales defined the high-diversity, high-foreign-sales quadrant, yielding a population of 93 firms, to all of which questionnaires were sent.

variable_name: number of two digit SIC codes of operations
description: The number of two digit Standard Industrial Classification codes of operations in which the firm operates, taken from the Standard and Poor's Compustat II tapes. This was the measure of diversity; seven or more SICs was the dividing point for high diversity.

variable_name: foreign sales as a percentage of total sales
description: Foreign sales as a percentage of total sales, taken from the Standard and Poor's Compustat II tapes. This was the measure of foreign dependence; 20 per cent or more foreign sales was the dividing point for high foreign sales dependence.

variable_name: research and development as a percentage of sales
description: Research and development as a percentage of sales, taken from the Compustat II tapes as the proxy for research intensity. It was measured for firms using global product and international division structures.

Forbes Industrial Classification was used to identify conglomerates; Forbes has a separate 'Conglomerate' category for firms which have diversified widely into unrelated businesses primarily by acquisition or merger. Eight of the 37 firms were in that category in 1980, and all but one of the rest were classified under one of the Forbes industry categories; the one remaining firm was placed in Forbes' 'Multiindustry' category.

Respondents, the chief financial officers, traced the path along which a typical non-North American production or processing facility reported up through the organization as financial results were consolidated, up to the level of chief operating officer, supplying for each level the kind of responsibility and the geographical domain (global, international or area). A firm's top-level structure was the responsibility of the last individual immediately below the chief operating officer; classifications were checked against organization charts and telephone interviews cleared up inconsistencies. A firm was coded as world-wide functional when top-level line executives had world-wide responsibility for separate functions.

Respondents traced the reporting path of a typical non-North American facility up to the chief operating officer, giving kind of responsibility and geographical domain at each level. Classification as a matrix required both a dual authority relationship and a power balance between the superiors to whom matrix subordinates report; two responses showing single line channels for consolidating financial data but dual lines in organization charts were treated as non-matrix after telephone interviews.

Respondents traced the path along which a typical non-North American production or processing facility reported up through the organization as financial results were consolidated, up to the level of chief operating officer, supplying the kind of responsibility and the geographical domain at each level. Top-level structure was the responsibility of the last individual immediately below the chief operating officer. A firm was coded as a global product structure when top-level line executives were responsible for one or more worldwide businesses.

Respondents traced the path along which a typical non-North American production or processing facility reported up through the organization as financial results were consolidated, up to the level of chief operating officer, supplying the kind of responsibility and the geographical domain at each level. Top-level structure was the responsibility of the last individual immediately below the chief operating officer. A firm was coded as an international division when all but one of the line executives reporting to the chief operating officer managed domestic activities and the remaining executive was in charge of all the company's foreign business.

Respondents traced the path along which a typical non-North American production or processing facility reported up through the organization as financial results were consolidated, up to the level of chief operating officer, supplying the kind of responsibility and the geographical domain at each level. Top-level structure was the responsibility of the last individual immediately below the chief operating officer. A firm was coded as an area structure when the executives reporting to the chief operating officer were responsible for all company businesses within specific geographic regions of the world.
Calculated by taking the percentage of applications the examiner approved before the submission of the focal patent application. Higher values indicate a more lenient examiner.
scale: percentage of prior applications approved (0 to 1)
time_window: before the submission of the focal patent application

variable_name: citation is in the original IDS
description: Binary variable that takes the value of 1 if the firm included that citation in the first IDS and 0 if it is a citation added by the firm in subsequent IDS or a citation known by the firm which is added by the examiner. Only citations the firm had previously cited before the current application are in the risk set.
Captures how crowded the field is in terms of other firms; measured as the number of assignees included in the list of citations in the same patent class as the application.
Captures how crowded the technological field is; measured as the average number of forward citations of the cites per active patents in the same patent class as the application.
Following prior work, the need to develop patent fences around high strategic stakes technologies is captured by looking at the number of self-citations included in the focal application.
Measured by dividing the number of patent litigation cases over the number of patents in the application's patent class, averaged over the previous 5 years.

The authors searched the Web of Science ISI database for journal publications appearing between 1974 and 2005 that had a keyword related to science research and could be unambiguously connected with one of the pharmaceutical firms in the sample, and tied each author back to firms based on affiliations. Star scientists are researchers who had both published and been cited at a rate of three standard deviations above the mean; to qualify, an individual must have published more than 28 papers during the study period and had to be cited at least 861 times. The authors identified 1,071 star scientists, representing only 0.63 percent of the total population of scientists in the sample. This measure was not lagged.
time_window: publications 1974-2005, measured annually and not lagged

description: Alliances with universities, research institutions, and biotechnology firms were documented from BioScan and Recap, and each alliance description was content analyzed to decompose a firm's total strategic alliances into upstream and downstream agreements. Grants, research and R&D alliances were coded as upstream alliances because they focus on the basic research oriented upstream knowledge discovery activities of the value chain; 2,041 upstream alliances were identified. Alliances were lagged by one year in the estimations.

Alliances with universities, research institutions, and biotechnology firms were documented from BioScan and Recap, and each alliance description was content analyzed. Manufacturing, licensing, development, and supply alliances were identified as downstream alliances because they focus on the downstream knowledge-leveraging activities of the value chain; 1,061 downstream alliances were identified. Alliances were lagged by one year in the estimations.

Forward citation-weighted patent information was collected for the sample firms following the procedure detailed in Hall, Jaffe, and Trajtenberg (2005), primarily through the National Bureau of Economic Research patent data, cross-checked and updated with the USPTO patent database. A five-year citation-weighting window was used, and the measure was created for 86 firms between the years 1974-2001. This is a count variable taking only nonnegative integer values.

The authors counted the number of new drugs annually that entered a firm's pipeline at the preclinical stage of development; these are so-called lead candidates that have overcome significant uncertainty, as only 2.5 percent of all drug compounds tested become lead candidates to enter preclinical testing in the laboratory and on animals before moving to phase I clinical trials. The average firm in the sample introduced just over six lead drug candidates into their pipeline per year. These data were obtained from PharmaProjects, a comprehensive database tracking new drug development in the pharmaceutical industry.

An equally weighted composite formed by summing three firm-level measures: industry experience, start-up experience, and venture capitalist directorships. Industry experience was the number of top management team members that had worked previously in the venture's primary industry or had had experience with its primary technology, with any amount of such experience counted. Start-up experience was the number of top managers that had previously started new businesses, and venture capitalist directorships was the number of venture capitalists who were on a firm's board. Because no theory exists to rank the measures by importance, equal weighting was used and the three measures were summed.

An equally weighted firm-level composite consisting of the sum of three proxies: business network, personal network, and underwriters. Business network was the number of arms-length relationships and alliances with Fortune 1000 clients and suppliers that a firm had at the time of its IPO. Personal network was a count of the number of top management team members and directors who were also directors of other firms with similar technologies or markets. Underwriters was the count of the number of underwriters that subscribed to an IPO, qualified by assigning a reputational weight to the lead underwriter based on the number of initial public offerings it had successfully completed.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Accumulated financial capital measured by adding a venture's assets during the quarter just prior to the date of its IPO to the proceeds from that offering, the latter being the much larger of the two components. Both liquid and hard assets were included in the calculation to control for the asset intensity of the firm's industry sector.
time_window: quarter just prior to the IPO date plus IPO proceeds

description: The two-year change in sales after the year of an IPO. The authors describe it as capturing a forward-looking trend in revenues, independent of the costs incurred to obtain them.
time_window: two-year change in sales after the year of the IPO

description: Profits over sales in the second year after the year of the IPO. The authors describe ROS as a static measure of the productivity of past investments and as a less biased performance statistic than return on assets in cross-sectional comparisons of firms that vary by asset intensity.
time_window: second year after the year of the IPO

description: The dependent variable was franchisor failure, defined as delisting of the franchisor from the Sourcebook. To be delisted, a franchisor had to have correspondence from the book's author returned by the post office with no forwarding address and a telephone number that the author confirmed was disconnected by the telephone company with no forwarding number available. Following Allison's (1984) recommendation, cases that withdrew from the study before the end of the period of investigation were treated as censored with the last date of covariates collected as the last period prior to the withdrawal.
time_window: covariates for each year tested against the outcome in the following year

description: Size, measured as the number of units in the chain. Where the descriptive statistics showed that some of the continuous variables were skewed, the variables were logged before analysis to normalize their distributions, and the regressions report the log of firm size.
time_window: measured annually; covariates tested against survival in the following year

description: The share parameter was operationalized as the percentage of sales that franchisees pay to the franchisor. Following Lafontaine (1992), this measure includes the royalty rate plus the advertising contribution. Where a range of royalties and advertising contributions were reported, the averages were used; where flat figures were reported, they were divided by the industry average level of sales to create a percentage.

Centralized services was operationalized as the number of centralized services that the franchisor provides to the franchisee as part of the franchise fee. This variable ranged from zero if no centralized services were provided to three if centralized purchasing, centralized data processing, and inventory control were provided.

Training was operationalized as the number of training services included in the franchise fee. This variable ranged from zero if no training services were provided to three if field training, field operations evaluation, and initial store-opening assistance were provided.

Communication services was operationalized as the number of communication services that the franchisor provides to the franchisee as part of the franchise fee. This variable ranged from zero if no communication services were provided to three if telephone hotline services, regional and national meetings, and franchisee newsletters were provided.
Term was the number of years for which the initial franchise agreement is operative.
Subfranchise agreement was operationalized as a dummy variable of one if the franchisor uses these agreements.

Registration was operationalized as the number of registration states and provinces in which the franchisor operates. The total number of states and provinces in which the franchisor operates is controlled for.
scale: count of registration states and provinces

description: International Franchise Association was operationalized as a dummy variable of one if the franchisor was a member of the industry trade association.
Site Selection was operationalized as a dummy variable of one if the franchisor offers site-selection assistance to franchisees.

Cash Investment was operationalized as the dollar value of the cash investment that a franchisee needs to make to purchase an outlet in the system. The log of cash investment is used in the regressions.

Composite index of previously validated measures of power for each co-CEO: salary, tenure at the focal firm, stock ownership, and an indicator variable for whether the co-CEO also held the title of board chair (or co-chair). Salary, tenure, and ownership were standardized; the board chair indicator was coded 1 if the co-CEO served simultaneously as board chairperson and 0 if not. For each dyad the difference in standardized scores was computed for each measure, leaving four index components, and the board chair component took a value of -1, 0, or 1 depending on which co-CEO(s) held the chair position. The four components were summed keeping the directionality of the power gaps intact, the absolute value of the sum was taken so that the index reflects the magnitude of the total power gap without reference to which co-CEO holds the advantage, and the final measure was standardized.

Operating return-on-equity, calculated as operating income divided by the book value of shareholder equity, consistent with recent research in strategic management. Because ROE reflects actual profitability outcomes and is thus a concurrent measure, the authors analyzed ROE in year t + 1.

The amount of monthly political campaign contributions made by an IOU or its parent company to state legislators and legislative candidates in the state in which the IOU operated. The data include contributions made by companies, political action committees, and individuals in the electric utility sector to election candidates for government office, assigned to a company and industry sector based on employer affiliation.
level: utility-month (in the state in which the IOU operated)

description: Indicator variable equal to one for each month in the 12-month period prior to the announcement of a merger/acquisition and zero otherwise. Two companion event indicators are defined in the same way: Review equals one in the months after the merger is announced and while the regulatory review is in progress, and Postreview equals one in each month of the 12-month period after the regulatory review is completed. In the estimated model Prereview enters interacted with Legislature Competition.

Legislature Competition = 1 - |Total Democrats - Total Republicans| / Total Legislators, computed for the state legislature where the IOU is located. The measure equals zero when one party controls 100 percent of the legislature (minimal competition) and equals one (maximum competition) when the Democrats and Republicans have an equal number of seats.

Estimated by fitting a continuous model of core/periphery structure (Borgatti and Everett 1999) to the nine time-varying affiliation matrices of film professionals using the continuous core/periphery procedure in UCINET VI. The algorithm attributes high values to core members and low values to periphery. A three-year moving window was used to define ties, so the adjacency matrix for a given year records collaborations formed in that year and in any of the previous three years.

Professionals were identified as peripheral or core depending on whether their coreness value was below or above the median. The variable is the ratio of team members closer to the core of the network to the total number of team members working on the same movie. For professionals working in two or more movies in a given year, the average team coreness was calculated by first summing the ratios at the movie level and then dividing by the number of movies in which the professional worked in that year. The variable varies from zero (a professional worked on movies in which all team members were peripheral) to one (a professional worked on movies in which all team members were core).

Number of awards and nominations the professional received in a given year from the ten professional societies considered (film critics and industry peers), as reported on the official websites of each organization. It is a count measure used to capture the degree to which individuals are creative, treating creativity as a continuous concept. The paper's primary data sources were the official websites of each organization.
The squared term of the Coreness variable, entered together with the linear term to test the predicted inverted U-shaped relationship between coreness and individual creative performance.
The squared term of the Team coreness variable, entered together with the linear term to test the predicted inverted U-shaped relationship between team coreness and individual creative performance.

KLD provides sector-specific analysts' ratings on firms' strengths on six aspects: union relations, cash profit sharing, employee involvement, retirement benefits, health and safety, and others. All six ratings are binary variables that equal one for firms rated as having a strength in the aspect and zero otherwise, and the six ratings are added to construct employee treatment. The ratings are matched in the year before loan initiation.

Measured as the natural logarithm of the drawn-all-in spread (i.e., interest rate) charged by the bank over the London Interbank Offered Rates (LIBOR) for the drawn portion of the loan facility. The unit of observation is the loan facility.

The proportion of the borrower's shares held by nontransient financial institutions. To ensure that investors can monitor the firm and provide banks with an alternative screen of trustworthiness, the measure focuses on the top five institutions ranked by their holdings of the firm's shares.

The number of suppliers whose sales to the firm make up at least 10% of their total sales. To minimize the influence of a focal (customer) firm's financial capability, supplier trust is set to zero if the firm's market share is above the sample median, so that dependence on industry leaders does not count as trust.
The strength of the prior relationship between the focal borrowing firm and the bank, estimated by the proportion of loans to the borrower in the last five years that are from the lead bank.

The level of social capital in the bank's home county, which reflects the banks' emphasis on social values. The NERCRD provides a social capital index for 1997, 2005, 2009, and 2014, and the variable is linearly interpolated for the missing sample years.
time_window: index years 1997, 2005, 2009, 2014, linearly interpolated for missing sample years

description: Employee treatment was manipulated as a composite rating of union relations, cash profit sharing, employee involvement, retirement benefits, and health and safety, consistent with the KLD items (except the 'other' dimension) used in the archival study. Three levels of treatment were distinguished: strong, equivalent to a KLD score of +1; no particular strengths or concerns, equivalent to 0; and weak, equivalent to -1.

For each scenario, subjects provided the interest rate they would require; the analysis uses the log-transformed interest rate as the dependent variable. The average interest rate was 9.43% (standard deviation = 4.55%).
For each scenario, subjects scored their willingness to extend a loan on a scale from one (very low) to five (very high). The regressions of this score include rater fixed effects.

Measured by averaging the ratings of the focal firm's benevolence and integrity (pairwise correlation: 0.700). Benevolence is agreement, on a scale from one (very low) to five (very high), with 'the company will have the best interests of its lenders at heart'; integrity is agreement with 'the company adheres to principles I find acceptable.'

Measured by averaging subjects' expectations of the firm's short-term profitability (after one year) and long-term profitability (after five years), each on a scale from one (very unprofitable) to five (very profitable); the pairwise correlation is 0.762.

Cumulative unit sales of the first independent aircraft introduced by the firm in the new business domain. Unit sales for the 27 aircraft projects for which production had not been terminated by the end of the study period were estimated with the yearly production schedule of the 86 programs that reached the end of their production life by 2000. Variables are estimated in the year before the first independent introduction in the business domain.
time_window: cumulative over the production life of the project

variable_name: Entry strategy dummies (independent entry, alliance entry, licensing entry)
description: Dummy variables record the entry strategy through which the firm entered the business domain: independent entry, licensing entry, or alliance entry. A firm was considered to have entered via licensing when it initially contracted to manufacture and commercialize another firm's product, and entry mode was based on the firm's first listing in each domain. Licensing entry is the omitted comparison category in the performance models.

Records the magnitude of the difference in complexity between the product(s) that a firm introduced in its pre-entry licensing phase and its first independently developed product; specifically the difference in complexity between the most complex licensed product and the first independent product. Product complexity is the log of the product of the aircraft's maximum speed, range, and takeoff weight. Large values indicate that the focal autonomous aircraft is much more complex than the licensed aircraft; low values indicate the reverse.
time_window: licensed product(s) versus first independent product

description: The number of citations made to a firm's digital imaging patent portfolio, summed for each application year. Total citations for each patent were adjusted based on its grant year using the truncation factor from the NBER database, year fixed effects were included, and the analysis stopped at the end of 2004 to allow forward citations to accumulate for an additional five years. Self-citations are included.

A count, for each year, of how many inventors currently at each firm have patented in both analog and digital classes. All inventors at the firm who had worked in both analog and digital classes were tagged, and each individual was labeled a bridge inventor two years before their first bridging patent. Because the exact departure date is unknown, inventors were assumed to have left a firm two years after their last patent application.

Citations from a digital patent to an analog patent are treated as representing the building of a bridge between the two technologies. The strength of each firm's technology bridges is calculated as the percentage of each digital patent's citations that were made to analog patents, averaged across each firm's digital patents applied for in a given year to obtain a firm-year measure.

Measured by summing the number of new APS cameras shipped by each firm in each year. APS cameras combined digital components with analog film, cameras, and film processing, and the APS system is the only industrywide hybrid.

To generate a performance measure that controls for the quantity of patenting, the authors divided the sum of citations made to the firm's analog photography patents applied for each year by the total number of analog photography patents applied for that year. The number of citations for each patent was adjusted based on its grant year using the NBER truncation factor.

variable_name: inventor, technology and hybrid product bridges (three bridge variables)
description: Intergenerational knowledge bridges were measured with three separate firm-year variables: inventor bridges (count of current inventors who patented in both analog and digital classes), technology bridges (strength of citations from digital to analog patents) and hybrid product bridges (number of new APS cameras shipped). Each was interacted with analog inventive performance to test the moderation.

Stock variable that switches from 0 to 1 in the year in which the academic engages in entrepreneurial entry and remains equal to 1 up to the end of the observation period or until the individual exits the panel. It indicates a more permanent change in an individual's conditions once that individual has become an entrepreneur, and is lagged by one year in the stage 2 and stage 3 models. Entrepreneurship is defined as being a director of a for-profit company at the time of foundation and a 'person with significant control' of that company.

Binary variable equal to 1 if, for any given year t, the scientist has published at least one article in an ISI journal category in which they have not published before, and equal to 0 otherwise. Journals labelled as multidisciplinary in the ISI categorization, which could confound the measure, are excluded.

Cumulative number of citations as reported by ISI Web of Knowledge, between years t+2 and t+4, to papers published by an individual in year t+1. Citations are used as an indicator of the intellectual debt citing authors are 'repaying' and hence of the worth the academic community attributes to the publication.
time_window: citations accrued between t+2 and t+4 to papers published in t+1

description: Captures, for each individual, the number of article coauthorships with academics affiliated with other Imperial departments between t-4 and t. The variable captures the degree to which an academic is routinely exposed to scientific disciplines different from the individual's own, ranges from 0 to 124, and is lagged by one year.
time_window: t-4 to t, lagged by one year

description: Reflects the similarity between the technology classes of the original patent and the citing patent. When both the original patent and the citing patent belong to the same technology class, the variable is assigned a value of one; otherwise it is zero.

Represents the public value to the industry of the original patent. Captured by the total number of citations the original patent received, not including self-citations, up to the application date of the particular citing patent. Patent citation counts have commonly been used to measure the commercial technical importance of an innovation.
time_window: citations accumulated up to the application date of the citing patent

description: Operationalized as the number of biotechnology patents filed for by the assignee of the original patent in 1990. Patent data have been used to measure technological capabilities of the firm in various high-technology industries.

The number of prior knowledge exchanges between the firms engaged in knowledge transfer. Measured as the number of citations by the citing firm of the same originating firm in the two years prior to the date of the citing patent. Prior citations of the same original patent were not considered.
time_window: two years prior to the date of the citing patent

description: A binary variable coded as one if the inventor locations for both the original patent and the citing patent were in the same MSA, indicating knowledge flow within a cluster; zero otherwise. Clusters are represented by 37 MSAs, following the approach of Jaffe et al. (1993).
A binary variable coded as one if the inventor location for the original patent was in a different MSA than that of the citing patent, indicating knowledge flow between clusters; zero otherwise.
A binary variable coded as one if the inventor location (country) of the citing patent was not the United States; zero otherwise. All originating patents were restricted to U.S. inventor locations.

The dependent variable is the steady-state performance of the process post transition to the offshore location, measured along four categories: cost savings, service quality improvements, rapid growth, and overall satisfaction with the service. Performance was measured on each category on a nine-point scale where -4 was 'complete failure', the midpoint 0 was 'meets expectations' and +4 was 'exceeds expectations'. The four items produced a single scale with Cronbach's alpha = 0.72, and all items loaded on a single factor with a CFI of 0.97.

Process interdependence was captured using two items that measured the intensity of interactions between the focal process with other processes, and the magnitude of cascading effects of process changes across its linked processes prior to transition. Respondents answered on a scale from -3 (strongly disagree) through 0 (neither disagree nor agree) to +3 (strongly agree). Because the two items capture different dimensions of interdependence, the authors created a composite measure by adding the scores on each item; the correlation between the two items is 0.4.

Five survey items measured the extent of investment in modularizing the process during transition, capturing the effort spent in reengineering the process, simplifying linkages between processes, creating well-specified interfaces, and portioning the process such that cross-location interdependencies were minimized. Items were rated on a scale from -4 (little or no effort) to +4 (intensive focused effort). The scale had a Cronbach's alpha of 0.88 and a confirmatory factor analysis CFI of 0.92.
scale: -4 (little or no effort) to +4 (intensive focused effort)

description: Four items measured the extent of investment in ongoing communication between the onsite and offshore locations, capturing the effort spent to create or adapt an IT network to enable distributed teams to communicate, to train in remote collaboration, and access to communication tools. Items were rated from -4 (little or no effort) to +4 (intensive focused effort). Cronbach's alpha for this scale was 0.75 and the confirmatory factor analysis CFI was 0.98.
scale: -4 (little or no effort) to +4 (intensive focused effort)

description: Six survey items captured the extent of investment in TCMs during and after transition, rated from -4 (little or no effort) to +4 (intensive focused effort). Prior studies as well as the authors' field research suggested that common ground is built tacitly by enabling mutual knowledge of respective decision-making procedures through shared work-related and/or cultural sensitivity training, enabling actions to be transparent across locations by investing in technology tools, enabling mutual knowledge of individuals' idiosyncrasies by leveraging shared work experience, and enabling easy interpretation of communications by using a shared vocabulary; the level of compensatory travel was also measured. Cronbach's alpha is 0.81 and confirmatory factor analysis indicated a single factor with a CFI of 0.87.
scale: -4 (little or no effort) to +4 (intensive focused effort)

description: CEO turnovers of publicly listed firms identified by following Farrell and Whidbee (2003) and Parrino (1997), using The Wall Street Journal as the primary information source and complementing it with a LexisNexis search. Turnover events are kept only when at least one rival firm can be identified and when the firm and its rivals pass the matching screens.
Dummy variable included in the regression analyses to test Hypothesis 2. The dummy variable equals 1 for a forced turnover, and 0 for a routine turnover.

Benchmark-adjusted buy-and-hold abnormal returns for each intra-industry rival, calculated for each trading day beginning 5 days before the turnover day and ending 250 trading days afterward. BHARs are computed with a four-factor model that includes Fama and French's size and valuation factors and Carhart's momentum factor, with factor coefficients estimated from the 255-through-5-trading day period before the turnover announcement. The regressions use the 100-, 150-, 200- and 250-trading day windows.
level: firm-event (rival firm relative to a turnover)
time_window: from 5 days before the turnover day to 250 trading days afterward

description: Return on assets, based on net income, measured as net income over total assets. For each accounting measure the authors compare the values for the turnover firms and their rivals for the 2-year pre- and postannouncement periods, ignoring the year of the turnover announcement, in a panel regression with a rival-firm dummy and a postperiod dummy.
time_window: 2 years before and 2 years after the turnover year (turnover year excluded)

description: Capital expenditures divided by lagged net property, plant, and equipment, with data from Compustat. It is used as an accounting measure in the pre- versus postturnover comparison of rivals and turnover firms and as a control variable in the BHAR regressions.
time_window: 2 years before and 2 years after the turnover year (turnover year excluded)

description: Depreciation, measured as log [EBITDA minus EBIT], analyzed for rivals and turnover firms for the 2-year pre- and postturnover periods together with the other accounting measures.
time_window: 2 years before and 2 years after the turnover year (turnover year excluded)

variable_name: stakeholder elements of the task environment
description: The problem description of FP7 call texts describes the task environment. A dictionary of 66 words such as 'civil society,' 'inclusive,' 'networking,' 'socioeconomic,' or 'transfer' indicating elements of stakeholder acceptance or support was developed through expert interviews and iterative validation. The software tool LIWC was used to count the occurrence of items from the dictionary in each of the 2,349 call texts, and this count is scaled by the length of the text. Two experienced evaluators rated a sub-sample of 30 call texts and achieved an intercoder reliability of .81 with the fractional word count obtained using the dictionary, so the fractional word count is used to measure differences across calls.

NAICS codes are used to identify advocacy groups on the basis of the activities in which organizations are engaged, defining organizations as potential advocacy groups if they are registered in the groups covering 'Religious Organizations,' 'Foundations,' 'Voluntary Health Organizations,' 'Human Rights Organizations,' 'Environment, Conservation and Wildlife Organizations,' 'Civic and Social Organizations,' and 'Business, Professional, Labor, Political, and Similar Organizations.' These organizations are then manually checked and coded to remove false positives. The first-stage probit predicts the likelihood that an advocacy group will be included in a consortium, and 1,284 consortia with at least one advocacy group included (3.64% of the sample) are observed.

To test Hypothesis 2, the number of advocacy groups included in a consortium is counted. This variable is interacted with knowledge dispersion and with a lack of experience to test Hypotheses 3 and 4. Consistency checks use alternative measures: a dummy for the inclusion of advocacy groups, the share of advocacy groups relative to the total number of consortium organizations, and the amount of funding allocated to advocacy groups in the application.

The likelihood of funding increases with the evaluation score assigned to each funding application by three to five independent experts for each call, who initially evaluate the applications individually before meeting in Brussels to determine the final scoring, a meeting moderated by a representative of the European Commission and an additional independent expert. The dependent variable is an ordinal measure, with the final score ranging from 0 to 100 and being assigned by experts on the basis of whether the application is likely to solve the underlying problem. The experts assess the technological and scientific excellence of the proposal, the quality and efficiency of the implementation and management, and the impact of the solution regarding exploitation and dissemination of the results and scientific outputs.

A Herfindahl index is used to calculate the concentration of International Patent Classification (IPC) classes of the patents held by all consortium members at the European Patent Office (EPO). Within the IPC, patented technologies can appear in 129 different technology classes at the three-digit level. To facilitate interpretation, the inverse Herfindahl index of IPC classes is used as a measure of dispersion, with a value of 0 representing full concentration and a value of 1 representing full dispersion.

A dummy variable for whether the organization leading a search consortium was participating in an FP7 application for the first time. The authors suggest that consortia particularly lack experience when the leader is inexperienced, because the leader ultimately submits the grant application and is particularly visible to the evaluating body. Alternative measures used in consistency checks include below-median participation experience, first-time participation in FP7 or its predecessor FP6, and the share of organizations in a consortium that participated in FP7 for the first time.

A binary switch that equals 1 rather than 0 under two conditions: school i is currently (in year t) more than five ranks worse than its school-specific, time-invariant mean rank, and school i previously (in a year p < t) ascended above that mean. The authors set the width of the boundary between perceived failure and success at ten ranks around the school's mean rank, so that being inside a ten-rank range around the mean denotes a region of relative indifference. All conditioning variables, including this one, correspond to the measurement year of the explanatory variables and are lagged one year relative to the tuition outcome.
time_window: t, with a look-back to any year p < t

description: A binary switch that switches from 0 to 1 when two mirror-image conditions are met: school i is currently (in year t) more than five ranks better than its school-specific mean rank, and school i historically (in a year p < t) fell beneath that mean. It is entered alongside status loss so that a status decline's effect on future price cannot be traced to a gain in status.
time_window: t, with a look-back to any year p < t

description: The natural logarithm of school i's tuition in year t + 1, where t ranges from 2005 to 2011. Tuition is the level published by U.S. News; values for which U.S. News printed an old or imputed tuition because the school did not report a current level were excluded from the models. Lagged tuition is included in the model so that the effect of a status decline is estimated conditional on the prior level of tuition.

Betweenness centrality computed each year from symmetric inter-school citation matrices built from U.S. News reports of the top five other schools to which each focal school's students also applied. In the matrix, a tie equals 2 if school i and school j jointly cited each other and 1 if either cited the other, and 0 on the diagonal; all private and public schools were pooled each year. Brandes' method was then applied to obtain betweenness centrality, which is a function of the number of shortest paths between two other nodes that pass through the focal node.

A weighted average of other schools' prior tuition, computed following Burt's structural-equivalence approach. The authors calculated two Euclidean distances in citation patterns between the focal school and every other school tracked by U.S. News in the focal year, defined proximity as the maximum distance minus the observed distance, normalized proximity into weights for each focal school, and then took the weighted sum of the peers' tuition values. The display equation for the measure was removed from the extracted text as unreadable, so the exact formula is not reproduced here.

The school's ordinal position in the annual U.S. News ranking. U.S. News takes a weighted average of component scores, normalizes the resulting overall score to 100 for the top-ranked college and top-ranked university, and converts the normalized scores into ordinal positions; ties are common, especially at larger ranks. For schools listed alphabetically outside the top tier, the authors followed Sauder and Lancaster's (2006) method and assigned the average rank, rounded to the nearest integer, of the reported range for that group.

The dollar value of construction loans for which no payment has been made for 90 days, divided by the dollar value of outstanding construction loans by the bank. Because the authors estimate a linear transformation of the learning model in the power form, they use the log of one plus the delinquency rate. Higher values indicate worse performance; average delinquency rates on construction loans are around 3% in the sample.

The accumulated sum of the bank's annual construction loan balances starting from the year a bank is first established. Loans from the preceding four years are excluded from the measure because the timing of recent loans has a direct effect on delinquency, and the estimating equations enter the logged stock lagged five years. Experience stocks are not depreciated. The authors interpret the measure as cumulative annual experience managing a loan portfolio of a given size rather than the accumulation of new loan commitments.
time_window: cumulative from bank founding (data available from 1976); measured over the 1991-2012 outcome sample

description: Experience accumulated during the same phase of the cycle as the phase in which performance is measured; aggregate experience Q is divided into Q s and Q a such that Q equals Q s plus Q a. Which stock counts as same versus alternate switches as the focal phase changes. Phases are identified from the direction and magnitude of change in building permit activity, categorizing each market-year as an upturn or a downturn using the worst 25% of downturns in permit applications relative to market size. The logged stock is entered lagged five years in the estimation.
time_window: cumulative from bank founding; entered lagged five years

description: Experience accumulated during phases other than the phase in which performance is measured; aggregate experience Q is divided into Q s and Q a such that Q equals Q s plus Q a. Which stock counts as same versus alternate switches as the focal phase changes. Phases are identified from the direction and magnitude of change in building permit activity, categorizing each market-year as an upturn or a downturn using the worst 25% of downturns in permit applications relative to market size. The logged stock is entered lagged five years in the estimation.
time_window: cumulative from bank founding; entered lagged five years

description: The bank's average annual loan volume in the same phase of the cycle up to the current date. Intensity is the amount of activity taking place, on average, within a period of time. Along with duration and transitions it is one of the three characteristics whose product equals a stock of organizational experience, and it is distinguished for the same and alternate phases of the cycle.

The bank's average annual loan volume in the alternate phase of the cycle up to the current date. Intensity is the amount of activity taking place, on average, within a period of time. Along with duration and transitions it is one of the three characteristics whose product equals a stock of organizational experience, and it is distinguished for the same and alternate phases of the cycle.

The average number of years a bank spent in one phase of the cycle before transitioning to the next phase, measured for the same phase as the current one. Duration is one of the three characteristics whose product equals a stock of organizational experience, and it is distinguished for the same and alternate phases of the cycle.

The average number of years a bank spent in one phase of the cycle before transitioning to the next phase, measured for the alternate phase relative to the current one. Duration is one of the three characteristics whose product equals a stock of organizational experience, and it is distinguished for the same and alternate phases of the cycle.

The total number of times that a bank has experienced a change from one phase to another, counting both upturn to downturn and downturn to upturn. Transitions are one of the three characteristics whose product equals a stock of organizational experience. Bank experience with transitions in any given year of observation ranges from zero to nine transitions, with a historical average of two.
scale: count (zero to nine transitions in a given year)

variable_name: Learning rates (coefficients on log experience stocks)
description: Organizational learning is operationalized as the estimated learning rate: the coefficient of the log construction loan delinquency rate on the bank's log experience stock, lagged five years, in a learning-curve model estimated with Arellano-Bond GMM. The classical single-stock rate (Model 1) is compared with separate rates for same-phase (lambda s) and alternate-phase (lambda a) experience (Model 2), and the stocks are further decomposed into intensity, duration and transitions (Model 3). Disruption of learning by cycles is read from the opposing signs of the same- and alternate-phase coefficients.

Cyclical change is captured by a binary indicator of upturn versus downturn phases for each state market-year, built from the direction and magnitude of change in building permits relative to the stock of permits issued over the previous 10 years. Market-years in the worst 25 percent of downturns in permit applications relative to market size are coded as downturns and all others as upturns. The indicator splits bank experience into same-phase and alternate-phase stocks and defines the phase in which performance is measured.

The centralization of environmental monitoring activities, i.e. those activities expected to be most important to the Prospector, was measured with a four-item index. The CEO was asked to indicate who was responsible for each of the activities, and each possible decision maker was assigned a weight ('3' corporate office; '2' regional/divisional office; '1' individual division) for the summed responses. An index was created that represented the summed responses for the four items, and a higher score indicates greater centralization than a lower score. The text as extracted lists only three of the four activities, so the fourth item is not readable.

A five-item index indicating who participated most in operational decisions. The first three items were measured on a six-point scale ('6' corporate board; '5' corporate management; '4' regional management; '3' division board; '2' division CEO; and '1' individuals below the division CEO); items four and five were measured using the three-point scale described above. To ensure comparability across the five items, the Z-score transformation of each of the five items was obtained and these five values were summed for each of the cases. A higher score indicates greater centralization.

variable_name: Centralization of the strategic planning process (CNTSP)
description: The CEO was asked to assign a score of '3' (most involved), '2' (second most involved), '1' (third most involved), or '0' (not involved) to the individuals involved in four aspects of the strategic planning process, with a 'no one' option available. An index was created that represented the summed responses for the four items; for this measure, as well as for the other centralization measures, a higher score indicates greater centralization than a lower score. The text describing how the decision-maker weights were combined into the index is partly unreadable in the extracted text.

Measures of profitability for 15 major inpatient and outpatient services were provided by senior management at each hospital, typically by the CEO in conjunction with the CFO. Because profit margin data were unobtainable across the sample, the CEO indicated the current profitability for the 15 services on a three-point likert-type scale ('1' not profitable; '2' operating revenues > operating expenses by between 1 and 10 percent; and '3' operating revenues > operating expenses by greater than 10 percent). It was thus possible to construct a variable measuring the overall profitability of the 15 services for each hospital.

Market share was measured for each of the 15 services on a five-point likert-type scale ranging from '1' (much less than other providers; at least one other provider has 1.5 times or greater market share than we have) to '5' (much more than other providers; we have 1.5 times or greater market share than any other providers), with a response category for services the hospital did not offer. The response for each value was multiplied by the number of hospitals in its local market area, data obtained from the Area Resource File, and the log transformation of the 15 responses was used, with the measure computed as the mean of the log transformed scores for the 15 services.

The CEO was presented with four characterizations of the strategic types (labelled Hospitals A through D) and was asked to indicate to which of the strategic types the division was most similar. The scale was designed such that a score of '1' represented a greater similarity to Hospital A (Defender), '7' to Hospital C (Prospector), and the midpoint to Hospital B (Analyzer); similarity to Hospital D (Reactor) was indicated by a score of '0', and the Reactors were excluded from the analyses due to their lack of a consistent strategy.
scale: 1-7 continuum from Defender (1) to Prospector (7), Reactor = 0. Direction: higher = more prospector (defender to prospector scale)

description: The independent variable is the number of corporate governance provisions that impose constitutional constraints on shareholder power. Following Bebchuk et al. (2009), the authors use the sum of four provisions: staggered boards, supermajority requirement to amend the charter, supermajority requirement to approve a merger, and supermajority requirement to amend the bylaw. Because the IRRC published corporate governance provision data every other year until 2005, missing alternate years in the sampling window without IRRC coverage were replaced with data from the immediately subsequent year. The variable is measured at time t-1.

A dummy variable that receives a value of 1 if a firm had a top manager who committed fraud in a year, and 0 otherwise. Misconduct cases were assembled from several sources: the ISS Securities Class Action database for top managers charged with fraud by investors, counting only settled lawsuits with settlement fees more than $2 million; material financial statement restatements from Audit Analytics that resulted in an SEC investigation; and SEC press releases covering stock option backdating, illegal insider trading, environmental law violations, bribery, and corruption. During the sampling window there were 349 instances wherein a top manager engaged in misconduct, occurring in 134 unique firms. The dependent variable is measured at time t.

Measured as the ratio of the total number of firms being acquired in a focal firm's primary two-digit SIC industry for a given year to the total number of firms in the same two-digit SIC industry. It is measured at time t-1.
A binary variable that receives a value of 1 if a CEO is also board chair, and 0 otherwise. It is measured at time t-1.

Dummy variable that takes value 1 if the hospital is affiliated with the Protestant Diakonisches Werk, and 0 if it is affiliated with the Catholic Caritas. The authors classified nonprofit hospitals into Protestant, Catholic, and other types by looking themselves at the hospital denomination and affiliation provided in each BQS report; in the regressions the dummy is equal to 1 for Protestant (not Catholic) hospitals.
The number of patients in each hospital, as reported in the BQS hospital quality reports. For the regressions on patients the authors take the natural logarithm of the original variable (lpatients).

A measure of the severity of the cases treated by a hospital: each theoretical case is assigned a severity level (Bewertungsrelation) such that the theoretical average case gets a severity score of 1.0, and the casemix of a hospital is the sum of its severity scores, so it depends on both severity and number of cases. The Krankenhaus-Reports provide only the range of the casemix of a hospital, and for each hospital the authors take the central value of the reported range; the natural logarithm is used in the regressions.

The casemix index, measuring the average severity of the cases treated in a hospital. For each case the reimbursement paid to a hospital equals the severity score times a base rate (Basisfallwert), so higher cmi corresponds to higher average complexity of treatments and to higher average revenues.

A measure of the total revenues of a hospital, obtained by multiplying the variable casemix with the base rate (Basisfallwert) taken from the Krankenhaus-Reports. Given the high correlation with casemix, the authors report the analysis of revenues in the online appendix.
The revenues per patient in each hospital, obtained by multiplying the casemix index (cmi) by the base rate (Basisfallwert).

Dummy variable that takes value 1 when the hospital is a teaching hospital linked to a university, and 0 otherwise. It is built from question A-5 of the BQS quality reports ('Academic teaching hospital (yes/no)? If yes, linked to which university?'), the dummy taking value 1 if the answer was 'yes'.
The number of doctors per patient in each hospital, computed from the number of doctors and the number of patients reported in the BQS quality reports.
The number of specialists per patient in each hospital, computed from the number of specialists (measured in full time equivalents) and the number of patients reported in the BQS quality reports.

The number of different medical fields in which the hospital is active. Fields are defined as the class of diagnosis at the one-digit level according to the 10th revision of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-10 classification, German modification); a hospital is considered active in a field if it had at least one diagnosis per week in that field in the given year.

The driving distance (in km) of a hospital to the closest neighboring hospital, irrespective of the ownership status of the latter. The authors assume that the smaller the geographic distance to the nearest hospital, the higher the competitive pressure to which the hospital is exposed, so higher values of distance mean lower competitive pressure.

The previous venture is coded as '1' (success) if it is an ongoing firm, typically still owned by the entrepreneur but managed by friends or close family members, and '0' otherwise (failure). For all entrepreneurs with a failed previous venture, they closed their earlier business before opening the current business. Five acquisitions were excluded from the coding because of their rarity and the uncertainty over perceptions of performance based on acquisition in China.

A dummy variable equal to '1' if the self-reported industries of the previous and subsequent ventures differ, and '0' otherwise. The Chinese government classifies firms into 11 industries. The authors report a full transition matrix between previous and current venture showing a large variety of transitions.

Founders assigned their previous and current venture to one of the following categories: the current company is the supplier of the last company, the distributor or consumer of the last company, does almost the same thing as the last company, is the complement of the last company, is a substitute for the last company, or no relationship. For analysis, a single variable was coded '1' if the new firm had any relationship to the prior (supplier, customer, competitor, complement, or substitute) and '0' otherwise, as no substantive differences between types of relationships were found.

Founders reported how central a differentiation or a cost-leadership strategy was to their previous and current ventures, using scales borrowed from Zott and Amit (2008): five items describe differentiation and four items describe low-cost strategy. The ratio of differentiation to cost leadership was taken for the previous (diff t-1) and current (diff t) businesses, and the change in strategy from the previous to the current business was calculated from these ratios; the equation rendering was unreadable in the text. The measure captured the normalized amount of change in strategy.

Planning style was measured with a 10-item scale borrowed from Falshaw, Glaister, and Tatoglu (2006) using a 1-5 Likert scale, designed to capture the formality of the strategic planning process within the firm, with higher values capturing more flexible and informal planning processes. D planning was calculated similar to D strategy to assess the degree to which the manager changed his or her planning style between ventures.

Decision-making style was measured with the decentralization scale borrowed from Miller and Droge's (1986) work: entrepreneurs were asked to identify which level in their company has the authority to make different decisions, coded 0 for board or owner, 1 for CEO, 2 for divisional or functional manager, 3 for sub-department head, 4 for first-level supervisor, and 5 for shop-level operatives. D management was calculated similar to D strategy to assess the degree to which the manager changed his or her management style between ventures.

Founders were asked about the three-year growth rate of their current ventures across a variety of measures, namely grow sales, grow profits, grow fixed assets, grow employees, and grow (market) share. In the results shown these responses are grouped as a single factor (growth); the authors note that results are consistent if each measure is treated separately.

In Study 1, analytic skill was measured with a financial-literacy questionnaire of 10 simple financial scenarios that asked a participant to name a price, for example the maximum price she would be willing to pay for a stock. The accuracy of a participant's responses was a measure of her ability to price assets, and for each participant a financial literacy score was calculated as the negative of squared errors in the questionnaire.
time_window: completed online before the trading session

description: Each participant was asked to pick a number between 0 and 100 so that her number would be closest to two-thirds the average of the numbers submitted by all other participants. The participant whose response was closest to the winning number won a prize, which was varied in $5 increments between $5 and $20; participants were not informed of their level of strategic intelligence. For each response the measure was calculated as the negative of the squared difference between the response and the winning number.

Each market consisted of six participants endowed with cash and assets, and the assets paid a dividend of 20 points or nothing with equal probability at the end of each trading period, so participants could earn profits from dividends and from trading. Trading consisted of one practice period and 10 real periods of 120 seconds each, after which each participant's profits were calculated and paid in cash together with a show-up payment. Performance was measured as profit from trading.

Study 2 measured analytic skills with four instruments: the financial-literacy questionnaire, The Race to 100 (a single-person version of a task solved by backward induction), the Cognitive Reflection Test, and the Need for Cognition scale.
