The first three instruments correlated highly with one another, and principal component analysis was used to aggregate them into a single measure of analytic skill. Need for Cognition did not correlate with the other measures and was excluded from further analysis.
time_window: completed online before the trading session

description: Participants completed two Guessing Games: one asked for a number between 0 and 100 closest to two-thirds the average of all numbers submitted, and one asked for a number between 0 and 360 closest to three-quarters of the average of all numbers submitted. For each response the score was the negative of the squared difference between the response and the winning number, and the two scores, which were strongly correlated, were averaged into a compound measure.

Performance was measured as profit from trading in an incentivized double-auction asset market in which each asset paid a dividend of 20 points or nothing with equal probability at the end of each trading period, and participants could earn from both dividends and trading. The authors also calculated for each participant earnings from dividends and profits from trading, so that luck (dividend earnings) could be separated from skill (trading profits).

Firms were located in the typology by dividing the summed collaboration and technology scores into high and low categories, creating four quadrants; problem-solvers are the firms high on both dimensions. The authors report that 65 firms are in the PS quadrant (III).

An index summing the 26 candidate collaboration variables selected from the Quickview survey, using equal weights. The constituent perceptual questions were answered on a 5-point ordinal scale ranging from 1 (never/not at all) to 5 (always/to a great extent). Firms were split at the median on this dimension to compare those above with those below.

An index summing the 22 candidate technology variables selected from the Quickview survey, using equal weights. The underlying multivariate structure was examined with maximum likelihood factor analysis using an oblique rotation.

The number of employees of the firm, used to test the size prediction. PSs have the largest number of employees (mean = 260), followed by collaborative specialists (mean = 150), technology specialists (mean = 44), and commodity suppliers (mean = 28); examination of the 95 percent confidence intervals for the means showed that all four quadrants were different from one another.

Total sales of the firm, the second indicator used to test the size prediction. Collaborative and technology specialists are not significantly different from one another, whereas the mean sales for both PSs and CSs differ significantly from the mean sales for collaborative and technology specialists.

The profitability indicator on which the authors report the typology results: firms in the PS quadrant have, along with CSs, the highest relative gross margins. The authors state that the PSs' profitability was expected as relational rents.
The share of a firm's sales that are exports, used to test the global market prediction. The authors report that firms in the PS quadrant have the highest percentage of export sales of any quadrant.
The wages paid by the firm, used to test the fourth hypothesis. The authors report that firms in the PS quadrant pay among the highest wages.

Indicator for having won any of 18 awards selected by the authors as the most prestigious in the field, on the basis of consultation with experts such as artists, critics, curators, and gallery owners; these awards are conferred on the basis of perceived artistic quality rather than commercial viability. Winners of these awards were coded over the 13-year period from 1998 until 2010. The variable takes a value of 1 beginning from the year the artist won any of the 18 awards until the end of the study period, and 0 otherwise. The indicator is lagged by one year before entering the estimation models.

Indicator for the appearance of an artist's name or artwork on the cover of any of 10 prominent magazines covering the field of contemporary art, selected in consultation with experts in the field. Media exposure is treated as primarily associated with the commercial value of an artist's work. The authors inspected and manually coded the names of artists or works by artists that appeared on the cover of each issue of these magazines for the 13-year period between 1998 and 2010. The variable takes a value of 1 beginning with the first year the artist appeared on a cover and continuing until 2010, and 0 otherwise, and is lagged by one year before entering the models.

Indicator variable capturing an artist's success with the museum audience in a particular year, assigned a value of 1 if the artist had at least one exhibition at a museum in the current year and 0 otherwise. An exhibition is assigned to the year in which it begins. The authors note that there are many artists and relatively few exhibition spaces, and that for emerging artists obtaining an exhibition at a museum is essential for a career in the art market.

Indicator variable capturing an artist's success with the gallery audience in a particular year, assigned a value of 1 if the artist had at least one exhibition at a gallery in the current year and 0 otherwise. An exhibition is assigned to the year in which it begins. This variable is the counterpart of Museum Exhibition and is used in the separate panel predicting gallery exhibitions.

Cumulative number of exhibitions an artist had at high-status museums. The 100 museums with the most visitors in 2010, identified from the annual exhibition attendance figures published by The Art Newspaper, are treated as high-status museums. The variable was log-transformed to adjust for its skewed distribution, lagged by one year, and mean-centered before being interacted with Award Won.

Cumulative number of exhibitions an artist had at high-status galleries. High-status galleries are the 100 galleries with the highest rankings assigned by ArtFacts.Net (the 2010 rankings, the only proprietary gallery ranking data provided by the consulting firm). The variable was log-transformed, lagged by one year, and mean-centered before being interacted with Magazine Cover.

Cumulative frequency of the artist's exhibitions at galleries, used in the models predicting an artist's success with the museum audience as the measure of interaction with the other (non-focal) audience. A log transformation was used to adjust for the skewed distribution, with one added to the value before taking the log to avoid missing values in the case of zeros, and the variable was lagged by one year. It was mean-centered before being interacted with Award Won or Magazine Cover.

Cumulative frequency of the artist's exhibitions at museums, used in the models predicting an artist's success with the gallery audience as the measure of interaction with the other (non-focal) audience. A log transformation was used to adjust for the skewed distribution, with one added before taking the log to avoid missing values in the case of zeros, and the variable was lagged by one year. It was mean-centered before being interacted with Magazine Cover.

variable_name: Award Won and Magazine Cover (two reputation signals)
description: Audience-specific reputation was captured with two indicator signals of an artist's attributes: Award Won, which takes a value of 1 from the year an artist won any of 18 prestigious awards given for artistic quality, and Magazine Cover, which marks appearance on the cover of prominent art magazines (commercial reputation).

Acquisition performance is the acquiring firm's abnormal return: the difference between the actual stock return and the return that would be expected given the performance of the market (market adjusted model). Abnormal returns are averaged over an event window running from three trading days before to three trading days after the announcement of the acquisition. The authors report that results were similar using the market and risk adjusted model, in which alpha and beta are estimated over the 240 days beginning 300 days before the event and ending 61 days prior to it; only market adjusted results are reported. The mathematical specification of the measure is not readable in the text.
time_window: three trading days before to three trading days after the announcement

description: A continuous measure of similarity built from four-digit SIC codes of the six main lines of business (by sales) in which the acquirer and target operated (all industries were used if a firm operated in fewer than six). Shared non-primary SIC codes were assigned a value of one at the two-digit level, two at the three-digit level, and three at the four-digit level; matches on the primary SIC codes were assigned two, four, and six respectively. A discrete alternative — similar if the acquirer and target had at least one of their top six four-digit SIC codes in common — correlated 0.89 with the continuous measure and yielded identical results, so only results for the continuous measure are reported.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: A variable distinguishing a firm's first and second large acquisition: first acquisitions were coded (1) and second acquisitions were coded (2). Acquirers that made both a first and a second large acquisition between 1970-1990 were included in the sample, and the 1948-1979 FTC large merger series was checked to ensure sample firms had made no earlier large acquisitions.

An acquisition pair is classified as similar when a firm's first and second targets were in the same industry, and as dissimilar when they originated in different industries. Because this classification is a discrete variable, subgroup regression analysis was performed on the similar-pair sample and on the dissimilar-pair sample.

Financial assets divided by total assets: of all the assets a firm owns, the proportion allocated to financial activities. Financial assets include both long-term and short-term financial investments such as mortgages, business and consumer loans, leases, certificates of deposit, commercial paper, and government and other marketable securities. The variable is entered lagged in the error-correction model.
Total liabilities divided by total assets, the common debt ratio formula, measuring the firm's dependence on debt. The variable is entered lagged in the error-correction model.

The sum of stock repurchases and dividends paid divided by total operating expense, a size-adjusted direct measure of income return to shareholders. Standardizing the amount with total expense measures how much a firm pays its shareholders in relation to other expenses; the variable is entered lagged in the error-correction model.

The firm's actual domestic employment size, based on a reliable count of domestic employment from the EEO-1 reports. The error-correction model estimates how the financialization variables influence the firm's future employment size relative to industry-year cell means, i.e. employment growth, rather than the absolute level of employment.

Total professional and managerial jobs, positions at the upper level of the corporate hierarchy that feature high autonomy, taken from the domestic employment counts in the EEO-1 reports and modeled as employment growth relative to industry-year cell means.

The sum of technicians, crafts, operatives, and laborer jobs, i.e. blue-collar, traditionally working-class positions that engage in industry-specific production, taken from the domestic employment counts in the EEO-1 reports and modeled as employment growth relative to industry-year cell means.

The sum of sales, clerical, and service jobs, positions that often require less formal skills and fewer educational credentials, taken from the domestic employment counts in the EEO-1 reports and modeled as employment growth relative to industry-year cell means.

Measured by subtracting the average performance rating of workers hired into a given job from that of those promoted into the same job. The performance rating was subjective, based on whether the employee had met his or her goals for the year, and was measured on a 1-5 scale. Average differences between promotees and hires were calculated in each year in each job, then averaged across all years to yield a single fixed value for the job. Transfers were excluded from the internal side of the measure so that it would not be sensitive to the ratio of transfers to promotees, and values for jobs entered exclusively by promotion or hiring were imputed from observable job and individual characteristics.

Calculated as the standard deviation of annual bonuses for workers in a given job in a given year, then averaged across all years to create a fixed value for the job. Bonuses were individualized and meant to reflect performance in the prior year, and the natural logarithm of bonuses was used because of their strong positive skew. Where individuals did not receive an annual bonus, a value of US$1 was substituted to allow calculation of a log value. The measure was calculated based only on the variability among those who had been promoted into the job, excluding external hires, in order to reduce concerns of reverse causality.

Calculated as the standard deviation of the subjective rating of employee performance for workers in a given job in a given year, then averaged across all years to create a fixed value for the job. The rating is based on whether the employee had met his or her goals for the year and was measured on a 1-5 scale. The measure was restricted to those who had been promoted into the job, excluding external hires, in order to reduce concerns of reverse causality.

Calculated as the number of workers in the job located one rank below the focal job, in the same division with the same O*NET title, divided by the number of workers in the focal job. The measure was averaged across all years, reflecting the argument that this ratio represents a structural feature of organizations.

variable_name: Mode of job entry (promotion, transfer, or external hiring)
description: The key dependent variable measures whether a move into a new job occurred through promotion, transfer, or external hiring. Each move into a new job represents a mobility event and serves as the unit of analysis. Hiring is the base category in the multinomial logit, so the coefficients on promotion and transfer indicate whether the various independent variables raise the probability of entry by either route relative to hiring.

Jobs were entered through promotion when a worker moved from a lower-ranked position during the prior year. Almost all promotions happened as part of an annual personnel process at the beginning of the year. In the data, 54% of job entry was by promotion, and promotion is estimated relative to hiring, the base category of the multinomial logit.

Jobs were entered through an internal transfer when a worker made a horizontal move from a job in the same vertical rank during the prior year, but from a different division or occupation. Those few moves across occupations or divisions that were accompanied by a change in rank were classified as promotions rather than transfers. In the data, 18% of job entry was by transfer.

Count of the number of fashion houses that adopted the stylistic element during the focal season. The number of occurrences of a stylistic element is the number of houses using it during a given season. The higher the number of houses using a given stylistic element during a given season, the more popular it is. Only stylistic elements that are used in a given season enter the analysis.

Burt's (1992) constraint measure computed on a one-mode network of stylistic elements that are affiliated through fashion houses. There is a tie between two stylistic elements if they were used simultaneously in at least one fashion house's collection, and the number of collections in which two elements were used together constitutes the strength of their tie. Ties were constructed from a four-season window (two spring and two autumn seasons) preceding the focal season, excluding the current season. A low constraint score is considered beneficial because it shows connections to otherwise unconnected others; a significant negative coefficient is expected to support Hypothesis 1. The constraint equation is printed in the paper but is not readable in this text.
time_window: four seasons (two spring, two autumn) before the focal season

description: Counting, for each element, the number of articles that covered the houses that adopted it in the year before the considered season; this number was then averaged. The number of articles was extracted from the comprehensive news database Factiva. All the 25 languages covered by Factiva were included in the search, but the search focused on magazines, newspapers, and blogs specialized in fashion or having sections dedicated to fashion.
time_window: one year before the considered season

description: An indicator distinguishing businesses headed by women from those headed by men. The models of survival and of growth in earnings were estimated separately for men's and women's businesses, and a gender indicator was also included in pooled models.

One data record was created for each year a firm was in business, and each record contains a dichotomous variable coded 0 if a firm was in business and 1 if it had dissolved by the end of the year. A company was defined as out of business at the time of the second or third wave of interviews if the telephone number used in the previous wave was no longer operative and no new, valid number could be found.
scale: 0 = in business, 1 = dissolved by the end of the year

description: Growth in the logarithm of gross earnings during the study period. In each wave of interviews, owner-operators reported their company's gross business earnings for the prior year, and gross earnings in later periods (1986 and 1987) were regressed on initial (1985) gross earnings; the coefficient of initial earnings represents the stability in earnings, and the coefficients of the other explanatory variables denote their impacts on changes in earnings.
time_window: prior year, reported in each wave, 1985-1987

description: A company's age in years since its founding. In 1985, the average age of the companies headed by men (13.2 years) was greater than that of those headed by women (10.5 years).
The logarithm of the number of a company's full-time employees.

The number of businesses with employees in a respondent's industry and county, lagged one year, so that wave 1 data represent 1984 values, wave 2 data 1985 values, and wave 3 data 1986 values. The counts include firms of all sizes, both incorporated and unincorporated, in each industry and each of the 12 counties represented in the data set.

The percentage of change in the number of businesses in Indiana in a respondent's industry, also lagged one year. This measure taps something different from the count of businesses, so the correlations between the two are low.

A perceptual scale averaging responses to four questions: how much competition there is in the market (1 = none to 4 = a great deal); whether the business has been affected by increased competition from large businesses (1 = yes, 0 = no); whether it has been affected by increased competition from small businesses (1 = yes, 0 = no); and how much of a problem competition is (1 = no problem at all to 5 = a great problem). The scale has a reliability (Cronbach's alpha) of .57, and less than 3 percent of the variation in it lies between industries.
The number of years a respondent had been in an industry.
Whether or not the respondent had been self-employed before acquiring the current business (1 = yes, 0 = no).

The measure is based on respondents' reports of which of six types of innovations they had engaged in during the two prior years; the number of types of innovations reported was averaged over each wave of the survey.
time_window: two prior years, reported in each wave

description: The sum of responses to two statements: 'I have a better idea about running my business than most of my competitors' and 'Compared to others, I feel I am very successful in my present business,' answered on a scale where 5 = agree, 3 = undecided, and 1 = disagree.

Responses to the statement 'I feel that outcomes of my business ventures are largely influenced by my own efforts,' made on the same scale as the confidence items (5 = agree, 3 = undecided, 1 = disagree).

Measured by applying the linguistic tool developed by Graf-Vlachy et al. (2020) to CEOs' spoken language during the question and answer portion of earnings calls. The tool consists of three dictionaries capturing three elements of cognitive complexity: differentiation, nuance, and comparison. Differentiation is the number of differentiation words used by the CEO divided by the total number of words attributed to the CEO; nuance is the number of weak words divided by the sum of weak and strong words used by the CEO; comparison is the sum of comparison words divided by the CEO's total number of words. The final measure is the average of standardized values of differentiation, nuance, and comparison, calculated on an annual basis.
Return on assets, calculated as net income divided by total assets. ROA is led by 1 year (t + 1) since it can take some time for CEOs' attributes and decisions to manifest in financial performance.

Measured as 1 - Herfindahl index, reflecting the sum of squared market shares of all firms that were listed in each two-digit standard industry classification (SIC) code during the year, using the entire Compustat database. The measure follows the method described by Connelly, Haynes, Tihanyi, Gamache, and Devers (2013).

Calculated using the regression of industry sales for the 5 years preceding the current year, using two-digit SIC codes. Industry munificence is the predicted value of that regression divided by average industry sales. The measure follows the method described by Connelly et al. (2013).

Calculated using the regression of industry sales for the 5 years preceding the current year, using two-digit SIC codes. Industry dynamism is the standard error of that regression divided by average industry sales. The measure follows the method described by Connelly et al. (2013).

Change in state-level noncompete agreement enforceability, coded as 1 for a decrease (favoring employees), 0 for no change, and −1 for an increase (favoring employers). The authors identified 14 states that experienced a significant change in NCA enforceability from four sources, classified each potential change as favoring employers or favoring workers, and compared across sources to confirm direction and significance; where sources contradicted, they relied on Malsberger et al. (2017). A positive value indicates a loosening of enforceability, that is, greater ease of worker mobility.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the establishment has adopted one of 31 enterprise data analytics software packages that incorporate ML technology, and 0 otherwise; the packages were identified by examining software functionality. Adoption in 2010 is assumed to be zero because ML became widely available in commercial software only in 2015, so the dependent variable is the change in adoption between 2010 and 2018. The overall ML adoption rate in the sample is 9.7% in 2018. The authors interpret a lower likelihood of adoption by 2018 as an increase in the time to adoption.

variable_name: Log number of site employees in 2010
description: Establishment size measured using the number of employees; because changes in this variable over time could be affected by the dependent variable, the authors use the base-year (2010) value and also report it as the log number of site employees in 2010. Hypothesis 2 is tested with split-sample regressions that estimate different NCA coefficients for large establishments (more than 100 employees) versus small establishments (50-100 employees), estimated separately to allow unrestricted effects of covariates.

The industry-level net benefits to ML adoption are proxied with the propensity to adopt predictive analytics technology. Lead user industries are identified as those with average predictive analytics adoption greater than or equal to 0.75, based on survey evidence reported in Brynjolfsson, Jin, and McElheran (2021). The sample of manufacturing establishments is split into industries above and below that threshold.

Indicator for whether the establishment is located in a large metropolitan statistical area, with large defined as MSAs having populations over 1 million, compared with establishments in other locations. Separate regressions estimate different NCA coefficients for the two groups.

variable_name: Log number of large establishments by MSA-SIC4 industry
description: Count of large (more than 100 employees) establishments in the same four-digit SIC code and the same MSA as the focal establishment, entered in logs and interacted with the NCA variable. The specifications progressively add controls for the number of small establishments in the industry-MSA, a sizable MSA dummy, and their respective interactions with the NCA variable.

Respondents indicated the level of emphasis placed on various areas in their corporate-level planning on a five-point scale ranging from 'no emphasis' to 'strong emphasis', with a 'not applicable' alternative available. Factor analysis of these items was used to develop an eight-item scale for planning openness, which produced a Cronbach's alpha of 0.75, and the summed scores of the eight items were converted to a five-point scale for planning openness. The planning horizon was divided into four categories based on the longest period for which a specific plan was prepared, and the two scales were used to categorize the firm's planning process as short-term forecasting, budgeting, annual planning, long-range planning or strategic planning.

Calculated from Fortune's published 10-year total returns to investors for companies in its list of the 1000 largest U.S. manufacturing companies, along with industry medians; the industry median was subtracted from the individual firm result to obtain a relative return. The total return figures include price appreciation and dividend yield to stockholders, with cash dividends, stock dividends, rights and warrants assumed to have been reinvested at the end of the year in which they were received, and the 10-year figures are annual averages compounded. Industry classifications corresponded to the greatest industrial sales volume for each company, and industry medians included only companies in the Fortune 1000.
time_window: 10 years; figures for 1979, 1980, 1981, 1982 and 1983 and the 1980-83 average

description: The firm's 10-year total return to investors as published in the Fortune lists, without subtracting the industry median. The total return figures include price appreciation and dividend yield to stockholders, and the 10-year figures are annual averages compounded. In the years after 1979 the 10-year performance figures are moving averages, so the 10-year total return numbers are in essence only one data point since the 10-year averages change only minimally from year to year.

variable_name: 1-year return on equity and 1-year total return to investors
description: Short-term performance figures taken from the published Fortune lists: the 1-year return on equity (absolute and relative) and the 1-year total return to investors (absolute and relative), tested for each year in the period 1979-83 and for the average of the years 1980-83. Relative return figures were calculated by subtracting the industry median from the individual firm's return, and total return includes price appreciation and dividend yield to stockholders with dividends and related receipts assumed reinvested at year end.
time_window: 1 year; each year 1979-1983 and the 1980-83 average

description: The first dependent variable is the initial capital at the time of the venture's establishment, in thousands of yen, logged. It is used in the difference-in-differences models; the authors note that the amount of capital an entrant raises is increasingly a test of legitimacy because it is seen as a signal of organizational prowess.

Binary variable that reflects whether a venture incorporated with initial capital of less than 3 million yen; such capital founding of less than 3 million yen is coded as one. The authors chose this level because it was possible to gain corporate certification with initial capital from 3 to 10 million yen under the old rules, so the variable captures ventures that adopted low capital after the 2003 regulatory reform. It is the dependent variable in the post-reform fixed effect logit analysis.

The treated emerging industry is coded as one if the venture lists 'custom software' as their primary SIC code. A new custom software venture is defined as those that develop and produce software not for retail sale but for customized requirements of customers, so ventures producing packaged software are excluded. The industry was classified as emerging using field interviews and market research reports and the rapidity of technological change.

Coded as one if a founding CEO is a graduate of one of the top universities and zero otherwise. The top universities include the seven former imperial universities (Tokyo, Kyoto, Hokkaido, Tohoku, Nagoya, Osaka, and Kyushu), the leading technical university (Tokyo Institute of Technology), and the two leading private universities (Keio University and Waseda University).

An unconventional founder is coded as one if the venture is either 25% or more owned by foreign entities and/or the CEO is a female. The measure reflects the unconventional nature of ventures with foreign owners or female founders in Japan.

Indicator of the first difference in the difference-in-differences design, namely before versus after the 2003 reform allowing for lower capital levels and founding at the lower capital level of one yen. In the intertemporal analysis the post-reform period is split into early years (2003-2005) and later years (2006-2007) following the reform.

Business model innovation was measured with the type II reflective-formative second-order measure of Von Delft et al. (2019). The measure includes four first-order constructs, customer value proposition, profit formula, key resources, and key processes, that make up the higher-level construct. Items with a standardized factor loading below 0.6 were removed from the final measurement model.

Coordination flexibility capabilities were measured with the scales developed by Kump et al. (2019) and Yuan et al. (2010), which the authors chose because they closely align with their definition of CFC. The authors describe CFC as an organization's capability to orchestrate assets, which includes both sensing and seizing capabilities.

Internal advice seeking capabilities were measured using a scale adapted from Borgatti and Cross (2003) and McDonald and Westphal (2003). The scale was designed to capture the various sources that managers use to obtain information, referring here to knowledge ties within an organization.

External advice seeking capabilities were measured with the same scale adapted from Borgatti and Cross (2003) and McDonald and Westphal (2003), capturing sources of information outside the organization. Building on Adler and Kwon (2002), the authors categorize external advice seeking into informal ties with a personal attachment (e.g., social club memberships and friendships) and formal network ties without a personal attachment (e.g., key suppliers, key partners and external consulting).

The authors developed a new measure to evaluate the extent of digitalization across eight functional areas in an organization as outlined by Porter (1985). They note that while measures such as the digitalization of products and services exist, a comprehensive measure of firm-level digitalization had not yet been introduced.

Total cash compensation consisting of salary, bonus, and miscellaneous earnings such as fringe benefits reported in the proxy, available for 110 company-years. All compensation and other dollar measures were expressed in 1983 dollars (deflated by the Consumer Price Index), and the logarithms of all compensation measures were used to reduce heteroscedasticity.

Salary reported separately in the proxy statements for a smaller number of observations than total cash compensation. It is expressed in 1983 dollars (deflated by the Consumer Price Index) and used in logarithmic form.

Bonus reported separately in the proxy statements for a smaller number of observations than total cash compensation. It is expressed in 1983 dollars (deflated by the Consumer Price Index) and used in logarithmic form.
Firm size was operationalized as the logarithm of total assets, in 1983 dollars. Financial data came from the COMPUSTAT data base, supplemented by Moody's Industrial Manual.

To ensure that the study was considering profit rates and not profit size, return on equity was taken as the measure of performance. Financial data came from the COMPUSTAT data base, supplemented by Moody's Industrial Manual.

Corporate complexity was operationalized as the number of four-digit SIC codes in a given year. SIC codes came from Standard & Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors and Executives. The authors note the measure lacks the subtlety needed for a study of the strategic aspects of diversity but is straightforward and sufficient for this project.

The CEO's experience in general management was coded as a dummy variable (1 = primarily general management experience; 0 = other). Information on managers' backgrounds was collected from the Dun & Bradstreet Reference Book on Corporate Management.
Tenure was operationalized as the number of years the executive has been CEO.
This variable was measured by the percentage of outstanding stock the CEO owned. Shares owned by the executive's spouse and children were considered part of his or her own shareholdings.

Family shareholdings was measured as the percentage of outstanding stock the CEO's family (but not the CEO) owned; shares owned by the executive's spouse and children were counted as part of his or her own shareholdings rather than the family's.

This variable was defined as the percentage of stock owned or controlled by outside directors. Since outside directors may be representatives of external organizations that owned stock, it was important to count controlling interests as well.
scale: percentage of stock owned or controlled

description: The sample was divided into three ownership classes: owner-managed, management-controlled, and externally controlled. The classes were determined by assessing who had effective control of firm stock; effective control was defined as 4 percent ownership of stock, and firms with ambiguous share distributions were eliminated.

A conjoint attribute varied at two levels. High: requirements necessary for success will not change radically during industry development. Low: requirements necessary for success will change radically during industry development. Attribute levels were chosen to represent variation that typically occurs in the decision environment of VCs.
A conjoint attribute varied at two levels. Pioneer: enters a new industry first. Late follower: enters an industry late in the industry's stage of development.

A conjoint attribute varied at two levels. Long: an extended period of monopoly for the first entrant prior to competitors entering the industry. Short: a minimal period of monopoly for the first entrant prior to competitors entering this industry.
A conjoint attribute varied at two levels. High: intense competition among industry members during industry development. Low: little competition among industry members during industry development.

A conjoint attribute varied at two levels. High: considerable resources and skills available to overcome market ignorance through education. Low: few resources or skills available to overcome market ignorance through education.

A conjoint attribute varied at two levels. High: venturer has considerable experience and knowledge with the industry being entered or a related industry. Low: venturer has minimal experience and knowledge with the industry being entered or related industry.

Respondents considered each conjoint venture description and provided a rating on an eleven-point scale with end anchors describing very low probability of survival and very high probability of survival. Survival is the probability that this venture will continue to participate in the market, and a ten-year time horizon was used in the task.

Count of joint partnerships firms i and j held in year t. The variable was logged to mitigate its skewed distribution across firms. It enters the models predicting whether the dyad forms a new collaborative or conflictual tie in year t+1.

Count of active patent infringement and antitrust lawsuits between firms i and j in year t. The variable was logged to mitigate skewness. It is used to predict new collaborative and conflictual ties in year t+1.

Binary dependent variable coded 1 if firms i and j entered into at least one partnership in year t+1, and 0 otherwise. The models estimate the likelihood of future collaboration (pcoll) for a given dyad. The residual probabilistic outcome (1 - pcoll - pconf) is the likelihood of no tie forming.

Binary dependent variable coded 1 if firms i and j initiated at least one lawsuit against each other in year t+1, and 0 otherwise. The models estimate the likelihood of future conflict (pconf) for a given dyad.

Count of third parties to which firms i and j were both linked through collaborative relationships in year t. The variable was logged to mitigate skewness. It captures the shared-collaborator triadic configuration.

Count of third parties to which firms i and j were both linked through conflictual relationships in year t. The variable was logged to mitigate skewness. It captures the shared-adversary triadic configuration.

Count of third parties to which firms i and j were linked through relationships of different types in year t (a collaborative tie for i and a conflictual tie for j, or vice versa). The variable was logged to mitigate skewness. It captures asymmetric third-party triadic configurations.

Index S = correlation between firms' participation in the collaborative segment (G1) and the conflictual segment (G2) of the dual network at the same time. Participation in each segment was coded 1 if the firm participated, and 0 otherwise. The average segregation of the real network over time was S = -0.520, confirming two distinct segments.

Average segregation E(S) of the simulated network measured across all 1,000 simulation runs for each test. The simulation's segregation was compared to the empirical segregation using z-scores. Test 1, using empirically estimated dyadic and triadic parameters, provided the best fit.

Count of patents filed by the firm as a sole assignee in year t in focused technology domains. A technology domain is focused if the firm filed a patent in one of 628 IPC-4 technology classes in the past five years (t-5 to t-1). The authors identified 7,445 patents in this category. Coding accuracy was checked on a random 10 percent of patents.
time_window: annual count in year t; domains classified over t-5 to t-1

description: Count of patents filed by the firm as a sole assignee in year t in diversifying technology domains. A technology domain is diversifying if the firm has not filed a patent in one of 628 IPC-4 technology classes in the past five years (t-5 to t-1). The authors identified 4,599 patents in this category.
time_window: annual count in year t; domains classified over t-5 to t-1

description: Count of patents filed by the firm in collaboration with another organization in year t in focused technology domains, based on coassigned patents. A technology domain is focused if the firm filed a patent in one of 628 IPC-4 technology classes in the past five years (t-5 to t-1). The authors identified 5,608 patents in this category.
time_window: annual count in year t; domains classified over t-5 to t-1

description: Count of patents filed by the firm in collaboration with another organization in year t in diversifying technology domains, based on coassigned patents. A technology domain is diversifying if the firm has not filed a patent in one of 628 IPC-4 technology classes in the past five years (t-5 to t-1). The authors identified 4,127 patents in this category.
time_window: annual count in year t; domains classified over t-5 to t-1

description: Firm failure defined as being delisted for negative reasons, such as failure to meet listing standards, financial distress, liquidation, insufficient capital, or lack of liquidity (delisting codes greater than 300 in CRSP). Firms still trading in 2010 were classified as survivors, and acquired firms were eliminated from the sample. The variable is coded 1 for failure and 0 for censored observations.

Absolute RoA was calculated by dividing a firm's earnings before interest by its average total assets; the median industry RoA was then subtracted from a firm's absolute RoA to provide the relative RoA measure. All time-varying covariates were lagged by one year until venture failure or 2010.

Tobin's q was measured by dividing the total market value of a firm by its book value, reflecting the firm's expected future profit determined by its market value. Market value information is compiled from CRSP and the balance-sheet information from COMPUSTAT.

Measured as the average rating received by a firm from survey respondents in a given year, the same way Vault's published prestige scores are computed. Because respondents are not allowed to rate their own firms, a firm's status is based only on ratings from respondents in other firms. For visualization, the continuous measure is discretized into integer ranges: greater than 2 and less than or equal to 3 (2,3], greater than 3 and less than or equal to 4 (3,4], and so on.
scale: average rating on a 1 to 10 scale

description: Respondent r's rating of firm i minus respondent r's rating of firm j. Only unique dyads, i < j, are included so that observations are not duplicated. The order of firms within a dyad is set by the firms' rank in a given year's Vault survey, so the sample represents every pairwise comparison of a firm and every lower-ranked firm. The authors report that they get the same results if status difference is computed as the absolute value of firm i's rating minus firm j's rating.

Pearson correlation coefficient between respondent r's and respondent s's ratings of the same set of firms i, where yri and ysi are the two respondents' ratings of firm i. Only unique dyads, r < s, are included because correlations are nondirectional. Dyads are constructed from respondents whose firms are in the same integer level of status: greater than two and less than or equal to three (2,3], greater than three and less than or equal to four (3,4], and so on. The authors report that they get the same results using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient.

A respondent-specific ordinary least squares regression of the respondent's prestige ratings is estimated for each individual respondent on the number of lawyers, revenue per lawyer (RPL), and profits per equity partner (PPEP) of rated firms, allowing respondent-specific coefficients. A firm's predicted rating by respondent r is X_i b_r and the residual rating is y_ri minus X_i b_r. The same Pearson correlation formula is then applied to residual ratings (and separately to predicted ratings) instead of raw ratings.

The number of observed deaths and total cases is used to calculate the observed mortality rate over the prior quarter for each surgeon. A probit regression on each patient's discharge status (alive or dead) estimates expected mortality from demographics (age, gender, race), preexisting health factors and other procedures undertaken during the admission, and year of admission, and the fitted values are aggregated for each surgeon. The quotient of the observed and expected mortality rates is standardized by multiplying by the quarter's overall panel average mortality, and the patient-weighted average of each hospital's surgeons is the focal independent variable for the prior quarter. Higher values mean poorer surgical resource quality; the percentage mortality figure ranges from 0 to more than 10 percent for high-risk cases.
scale: percentage mortality, 0 to more than 10 percent

description: For each patient admitted for cardiac surgery, the record documents attending and operating physician identifiers, showing whether the care team had focused (bundled resource deployment) or distributed (unbundled) leadership; this is a binary variable at the patient admission level. At the hospital level the patient-weighted average utilization of the bundled deployment form is computed for each hospital*quarter, ranging from 0 to 1, and the complement of this proportion (the proportion of unbundled teams) is used in the analyses. Higher values therefore indicate less bundled resource deployment.

Market share in cardiac surgical services is measured as the volume of patients admitted as a fraction of the volume performed by all hospitals in the 18 local HRRs in Florida. The HRR dimensions are computed from extensive analysis of Medicare travel patterns for tertiary health care. Measured at hospital*quarter level.
CABG patient volumes are used as an ancillary dependent variable to understand whether share changes were due to competitor effects or own effects. Measured at hospital*quarter level.

Average claimed hospital charges, which the authors state are deterministically related to actual costs for admitted cardiac surgery patients; reimbursements are almost always prospectively negotiated contractual payments or predetermined, which enforces rigorous cost control. Direct hospital costs typically contribute 62 percent of these costs, so variable decisions made during an admission have a meaningful impact on total charges. Measured at hospital*quarter level.

Patient-weighted average length of stay, included because it directly affects both patient experience and hospital costs and because minimizing the length of stay is a key hospital objective. Measured at hospital*quarter level.

variable_name: Average proportion of patients who required prolonged mechanical ventilation exceeding 96 hours
description: The average proportion of patients who required prolonged mechanical ventilation exceeding 96 hours in intensive care, usually the result of complications sustained intraoperatively or postoperatively or of preoperative illness severity. Measured at hospital*quarter level.

variable_name: Average proportion of live discharges who were not allowed home under self-care
description: The average proportion of live discharges who were not allowed home under self-care; live discharges may be transferred to a subacute hospital or skilled nursing facility for extended convalescence or rehabilitation, or allowed home only conditional on receiving skilled nursing help at home or visitations. Measured at hospital*quarter level.

24-month compounded holding period returns for the 24 months immediately following the IPO. HPRj represents the 24-month compounded return earned on a $1 investment in firm j made on the day following its IPO. When a firm was delisted because it was acquired, the HPR was estimated for the months prior to delisting; in the event of bankruptcy, the HPR was coded as a total loss.

The percentage of a board made up of executives actively involved with the business since its formation. An insider described in a prospectus as with the firm since its inception was classified as an original TMT board member. Biographical data came from prospectuses, 10Ks, and the Lexis-Nexis database.

Dummy variable coded 0 if a board was comprised of less than 50 percent original TMT member-board members and 1 if such directors represented 50 percent or more. The authors chose 50 percent as the point of transition to original TMT member control because boards generally had six to seven members, so original TMT members controlling three seats on a six-member board likely constitutes effective control.

The combined percentage of shares outstanding held collectively by directors who were original TMT members. Includes all 'in-the-money' options held at the time of the firm's IPO and exercisable during the subsequent two years.
time_window: at IPO and exercisable during the subsequent two years

variable_name: Original TMT member-board member ownership dispersion
description: Adapted Jacquemin and Berry's (1979) entropy measure of corporate diversification. The formula is not readable in the supplied text. The text states that OD is the level of ownership dispersion and Si is the percentage of total shares owned by original TMT member-board members held by the ith original TMT director. The value of ownership dispersion increases as ownership is spread more evenly across a given number of original TMT directors.

variable_name: Advice and counsel business expert board members
description: Dummy variable coded 1 if at least one board member was an advice and counsel business expert, such as the CEO of another firm, but did not own at least 5 percent of the IPO firm's outstanding shares or represent an organization with such ownership. Otherwise coded 0.

Dummy variable coded 1 if at least one outside director owned at least 5 percent of the IPO firm's outstanding shares or represented such ownership. This group excluded venture capitalists. Otherwise coded 0.
Dummy variable coded 1 if a board had at least one support specialist, such as an attorney. Otherwise coded 0.

Whether a store exits, determined from changes in a mall's layout between months: when a store was present in a month but gone the next, the store is coded as having exited during that month. This is the dependent variable of the survival analyses.

Dummy variable coded as 1 for stores in malls that had an HHGregg store, indicating a loss of an HHGregg store at the start of the data panel; stores in control malls have the treatment dummy variable coded as 0.

Store sizes are obtained directly from the DDR mall layouts, using the listed square footage for each store. The natural log value of store square footage is used so that coefficient estimates can be interpreted across the full range of store sizes in the data and because the log specification provided better model fit. The measure varies by store but is not time-varying.

Distance between a focal store and the HHGregg (actual or synthetic) in the same mall, measured from the DDR mall layouts. The distance is not 'as the bird flies'; it is the sum of the absolute difference along x and y dimensions using an x and y grid, consistent with customers walking along the sidewalks bordering the stores.

Relatedness between a focal store and the HHGregg (actual or synthetic), taken as the off-diagonal element of a relatedness matrix for the HHGregg's store category and the focal store's category. The matrix uses the difference between the observed frequency with which store categories appear together and an expected frequency benchmark generated by assuming randomly drawn pairs based on the count of stores in each category; observed frequency above the benchmark is consistent with relatedness. Store categories come from Google Maps listings.

The average size of stores in the mall excluding the focal store and HHGregg (in treatment malls) and the synthetic HHGregg (in control malls). The measure is store variant, as the focal store changes.
The average distance from the focal store to all other stores, excluding the actual or synthetic HHGregg. The measure is store variant, as the focal store changes.
The average relatedness of the focal store to all other stores, excluding the actual or synthetic HHGregg. The measure is store variant, as the focal store changes.

The level of new switching technology adopted by firms, measured by the percentage of electronic to total switches of a firm at each point in time. There are a number of multistate operating companies, and the adoption variable is at the aggregate network level; state-specific adoption data are not available from the data sources for the period of the study.

The absolute size of the network infrastructure, computed as the natural log of total miles of wire possessed by each company. Telephone network size can be expressed in the form of total miles of wire; the natural log is used because the distribution of total miles of wire is skewed.

A firm's share of the total switches in a given local market, computed as the percentage of a firm's installed base of switches in its operating area relative to the total number of all switches, inclusive of those of all other operating companies present in that operating area. For multistate firms SHARE is calculated as the ratio of their total switches across states relative to the total of all the switches in all of the states that they operate in, based on a simple averaging process. A squared term, SHARE 2, is also introduced to control for probable nonlinearities, with SHARE normalized in its mean deviation form before squaring.

For each state, the percentage of its urban population to the total state population is calculated, and an index is arrived at for each state. For each firm a simple average of the state indices is computed for all the states that it operates in; this index denotes the configuration of the urbanspace economy for each firm.

Calculated as the percentage of business lines to the total lines operated by each firm, used to proxy for customer variety. BUSINESS explicitly measures the business-residential customer mix of each firm.

For each firm a ratio is constructed with the proportion of the electronic switches possessed by its neighboring firm(s) as the numerator and the average proportion of electronic switches in the sector as a whole as the denominator. For single-state firms the comparator neighboring firm(s) may belong to the same territory or, if not, to the next territory, and aggregate revenue is used as a measure of size.

Dependent variable: the probability that a firm will adopt a CVC program at time t, estimated with a discrete-time event history model. Adoption years were drawn from the Corporate Venturing Directory and Yearbook for 2000, 2001, and 2002, with VentureXpert, IT firms' websites, and industry publications used for confirmation and missing data. Following corporate venture capitalists' advice in open-ended interviews, any firm making five or more direct investments within a single year was treated as having adopted a CVC unit in that year, and adoption was confirmed through company websites, Lexis-Nexis searches of business press articles and venture capital newsletters, and direct communication with business development executives. Each period in which a firm is at risk is treated as a separate observation.
scale: dichotomous (adoption event in a given year)

description: A weighted average of the number of miles from a firm's corporate headquarters to each of the three main VC clusters: Silicon Valley, New York, and Route 128. The weights are the density of VC funds targeting IT start-ups in each cluster, lagged by one year, and sum to one across the three clusters. Distance to a cluster is the number of miles from headquarters to the most proximate of the counties comprising that cluster, computed from zip codes with a spherical geometry formula; corporate headquarters zip codes were obtained from the Forbes lists. Higher values denote greater distance, i.e., lower proximity to the VC population.

Count of VC-backed IPOs tendered in the IT sector during the previous calendar year, obtained from the VentureXpert database. The authors argue that IPOs provide an unequivocal measure of private venture capitalists' value creation and that VC firms herald their investing acumen by highlighting portfolio firms that have gone public. The incidence of VC-backed IPOs is treated as indexing the returns generated by the venture capital model and as signaling to prospective IT adopters the potential effectiveness of VC practices.

The cumulated total number of CVC program adopters up to year t-1 within a single two-digit SIC industry sector of the focal firm. Prior adopters were defined as IT firms that had adopted a CVC program during or before the previous year. The authors limited the count to the two-digit SIC code in view of evidence that potential adopters pay greater attention to more comparable organizations.

The average sales of prior adopters of CVC programs in the same two-digit industry sector as the focal firm, used as a measure of the prominence of those prior adopters. The authors justify the measure by the argument that organization-level traits such as size and profitability are often used to infer social prominence and that large and profitable firms are imitated more frequently.

The cumulated number of CVC-backed acquisitions, counted since the year of adoption, used as a measure of the beneficial outcomes experienced by prior adopters. The authors obtained from SDC's Mergers and Acquisitions database a list of all private acquisitions by all CVC adopters in the sample for each year from 1992 to 2001, and matched these with the VentureXpert database to include only acquisition targets in which CVC adopters had invested; they identified a total of 94 CVC-backed acquisitions. Acquisitions are treated as a visible and tangible indicator of the benefits accruing from CVC programs.

For each firm at time t, the total number of adopters of CVC programs up to time t-1 in the same geographic region as the focal firm. The measure captures the availability of innovation-related information through observation of and interaction with industry peers, and it allows the authors to distinguish proximity to CVC adopters from proximity to the VC cluster.

variable_name: popularity, prominence, outcomes and proximity of prior adopters
description: Within-population contagion was captured by a set of four measures: popularity of the innovation (prior CVC adopters in the sector), prominence of prior adopters (their average sales), outcomes experienced by prior adopters (CVC-backed acquisitions) and number of proximate prior adopters in the same region. Prior adopters were IT firms that had adopted a CVC program by the previous year.

Measured by the percentage difference between the firm's value and the sum of the imputed values of its segments as single-segment firms. A firm's value is total firm capital, the sum of a firm's market value of equity, long-term and short-term debt, and preferred stock. A segment's imputed value is calculated by multiplying its sales by the median value for single-segment firms in the segment's industry (the most restrictive SIC grouping-four-digit, three-digit, or two-digit-that includes at least five firms), and the imputed value of the corporation is the sum of its segments' imputed values. The natural log of the ratio of a firm's value to its imputed value is the measure used as a dependent variable; firms with extreme excess values (more than 1.386 or less than -1.386) are eliminated from the sample.
scale: natural log of the ratio of a firm's value to its imputed value

variable_name: the natural log of Tobin's q
description: The second measure of firm value is the natural log of Tobin's q, which is more commonly used within the management literature. The authors state that using Tobin's q is an improvement over accounting measures as it incorporates forward-looking market valuations, but it is still limited in that the value of each segment within a firm is heavily dependent on the industry within which it competes, and it is difficult to adjust Tobin's q for industry because data are not available for segment-level market values or replacement values. Data for calculating this measure were obtained from Compustat.

An indicator variable equal to one if the firm operates in multiple industries. A firm is considered nondiversified (i.e., focused) if it operates in a single four-digit SIC industry, and diversified if it operates in more than one four-digit SIC industry. Data for calculating this measure were taken from the Compustat segments data. In the sample used for the analysis, 64 percent of the observations are nondiversified and 36 percent are diversified.

Among diversified firms, a firm is considered a related diversifier if it has any two segments in the same two-digit SIC industry. The authors note this approach is equivalent to classifying any firm as a related diversifier if it has a related entropy value greater than zero. Of the diversified firms, 47 percent of the observations are in related diversified firms.

Firms are categorized as unrelated diversifiers if they do not have any two segments in the same two-digit SIC industry. Of the diversified firms, 53 percent of the observations are unrelated diversified firms.

The hierarchical Bayesian model estimates a probability distribution of the diversification coefficient for each of the 838 firms, with firm-specific coefficients determined in part by firm characteristics. The long-term or persistent effect of diversification is computed as betaDi/(1 - rhoi), and this expected, long-term impact of diversification on performance enters the equation for the value the firm derives from diversification and thus the probability that the firm diversifies. Firm-specific coefficients are grouped into subdistributions for diversified and focused firms and further into related and unrelated diversifiers.

Calculated as the difference between the sum of institutional strengths and the sum of institutional concerns for each firm-year in KLD STATS, using Mattingly and Berman's (2006) factor split of the data into institutional (environmental, community, and diversity) and technical (employee, product, and governance) components. The human rights category is excluded because Mattingly and Berman do not analyze it, and the controversial issues screens are excluded. Netting the strengths and concerns is in line with prior work using KLD STATS and captures the net effect the indicator is intended to capture. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Count of nonhostile appearances in front of congressional committees for each firm-year, hand-coded from ProQuest's Congressional Hearings data set. A setting was defined as hostile when the witness knew ahead of time from the title of the hearing that her firm would be the subject of criticism; such appearances were excluded. Appearances in which the firm-connected witness testified as a representative of a trade association were also screened out. The count is measured at time t.

Captures the degree of Democratic control of Congress and ranges from 0 (minority party in both chambers) to 1 (majority party in both chambers). During the sample period the Democrats controlled the U.S. Senate between 2001 and 2002 (0.5 control) and both the U.S. Senate and House from 2007 through 2009. The authors code organizational control rather than the share of seats held by Democrats.

Contributions made by each firm's associated PAC to congressional candidates, coded using hand-matched data from the Federal Election Commission. Contributions to both parties are summed. The variable is log-transformed (C+1) because of a substantial right skew in its untransformed distribution, and it is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

A logged measure of each firm's annual federal lobbying expenditures, using hand-matched data from the Center for Responsive Politics. It is included to capture lobbying efforts and, on its own, to control for competing understandings of access related to campaign finance and information. It is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Measured from five waves of the European Values Study in 1981, 1990, 1999, 2008, and 2017. Respondents chose either 'Most people can be trusted' or 'Can't be too careful.' For each country, social trust is the number choosing 'Most people can be trusted' divided by the number who answered the question, combining all waves.

Calculated from Eurobarometer surveys from 1970 to 1997. Respondents rated trust in people from a list of countries on a four-point scale from 'lots of trust' to 'no trust at all.' Bilateral trust between countries X and Y is the average trust rating of individuals in country X toward people from country Y, aggregated across survey waves.

For each job posting, the average foundational score of all ESCO skills listed. Each ESCO skill's foundational score comes from a Prolific survey of 1,120 people with hiring experience, who rated 50 or 51 randomly chosen skills on a five-point scale where 5 indicates a highly foundational skill and 1 indicates a highly advanced skill; each skill was rated by 20 respondents and scores were averaged.

Four moderators measuring credential requirements: college degree, occupational certification, work experience, and job-preparation level. Education and work experience requirements are based on job postings; job preparation level is based on O*NET's coding of occupations. The variables are included as moderators in separate models.

JIT performance was measured as cycle time, defined as the total time from the receipt of raw materials by the plant until the product is received by the customer, in days, averaged across products. Lower cycle times represent better JIT performance. Six plants declined to provide information about cycle time, and the authors report that analysis of variance showed no systematic differences between respondents and nonrespondents, so all 42 observations were retained.

Quality performance was measured by a five-point Likert scale that asked managers to describe their own and their customers' perceptions of the quality of the goods produced by a plant, relative to competitors'. Responses were rated with 1 = strongly agree and 5 = strongly disagree, and reverse-worded items were reverse-coded, so a lower value indicates better quality performance. The appendix lists four items covering superior quality of product and service relative to competition, customer satisfaction with quality over the past three years, the plant's overall level of quality performance relative to industry norms (reverse-coded), and customer relations relative to competition. All responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant, and the variables were standardized to a standard normal distribution and by industry.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)
time_window: past three years (for the satisfaction and overall quality items)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which unique TQM practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Three items listed in the appendix; reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice. Items were collapsed into scales based on factor analysis and a panel of experts, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which unique TQM practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Seven items listed in the appendix, covering involvement of manufacturing and quality people in early design, design for producibility, part count minimization, and review of new product designs. Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which unique TQM practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Three items listed in the appendix covering close contact with customers, customer visits to the plant (reverse-coded), and customer feedback on quality and delivery performance. Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which unique JIT practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Four items listed in the appendix covering vendors filling kanban containers, supplier delivery in kanban containers, use of a kanban pull system for production control, and use of kanban squares or containers of signals. Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which unique JIT practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Three items listed in the appendix covering large lot sizes in the plant and in the master schedule (both reverse-coded) and aggressive work to lower lot sizes. Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which unique JIT practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Three items listed in the appendix covering aggressive work to lower setup times, crews practising setups, and low equipment setup times. Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant. Because of its relatively high degree of correlation with other independent variables, this measure was eliminated from further analysis.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which unique JIT practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Three items listed in the appendix covering the absence of time in the schedule for breakdowns or stoppages (reverse-coded), daily meeting of the production schedule, and schedule slack for catching up after stoppages. Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which infrastructure practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Four items listed in the appendix covering being told about job performance (reverse-coded), availability of quality performance information, manager comments about work quality (reverse-coded), and availability of productivity information. Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant. Because of its relatively high degree of correlation with other independent variables, this measure was eliminated from further analysis.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which infrastructure practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Five items listed in the appendix covering equipment readiness, pride in keeping the plant neat and clean, putting tools and fixtures in their place, keeping the plant clean, and the plant being disorganized and dirty (reverse-coded). Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which infrastructure practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Three items listed in the appendix covering plant management's personal leadership for quality, acceptance of quality responsibility by major department heads, and management outside the plant being primarily concerned with short-range financial performance (reverse-coded). Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which infrastructure practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Five items listed in the appendix covering striving for long-term supplier relationships, supplier involvement in new product development, quality as the number one supplier selection criterion, supplier certification for quality, and reliance on a small number of high-quality suppliers. Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

description: Respondents' perceptions of the extent to which infrastructure practices were employed, measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree). Nine items listed in the appendix covering direct labor technical competence, face-to-face contact, supervisory encouragement of teamwork and exchange of opinions, group incentives for quality improvement ideas, training for multiple tasks, group meetings, permanent production teams, and rewards for learning new skills. Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower scale rating indicates more extensive use of the practice, and all responses were aggregated into a single response per item per plant. Because of its relatively high degree of correlation with other independent variables, this measure was eliminated from further analysis.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree)

variable_name: Unique JIT practices (kanban, lot size reduction, setup time reduction, JIT scheduling)
description: Unique JIT practices are measured by four multi-item scales completed by plant respondents on five-point Likert scales (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree): kanban, lot size reduction, setup time reduction and JIT scheduling. Reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower rating indicates more extensive use of the practice; responses were aggregated to one response per item per plant and standardized by industry. Each scale entered the regressions as a separate variable; setup time reduction was dropped because of collinearity with other independent variables. The four scales are recorded separately as m_kanban, m_lot_size, m_setup_time and m_jit_scheduling.

variable_name: Unique TQM practice scales (statistical process control, product design, customer focus)
description: Unique TQM practices are measured by three multi-item perceptual scales completed by plant respondents: statistical process control, product design and customer focus. Items use five-point Likert scales (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree), reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower rating indicates better practice, responses were aggregated to one value per item per plant, and the scales were standardized by industry. Each scale enters the regressions as a separate variable.
scale: Multi-item 5-point Likert scales (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree), standardized

variable_name: Infrastructure practice scales (plant environment, management support, supplier relationship; information feedback and workforce management dropped)
description: Common infrastructure practices are measured by five multi-item perceptual scales completed by plant respondents, one per dimension: information feedback, plant environment, management support, supplier relationship and workforce management. Items use five-point Likert scales (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree), reverse-worded items were reverse-coded so that a lower rating indicates better practice, responses were aggregated to one value per item per plant, and the scales were standardized by industry. Each dimension enters the regressions as a separate variable; information feedback and workforce management were eliminated from the analysis because of high correlation with other predictors.
scale: Multi-item 5-point Likert scales (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree), standardized

description: The return on assets of a foreign subsidiary for a current year. ROA is described as a commonly used measure of bank performance in both strategy and finance research. Data were from the Call Reports database.
The natural logarithm of the number of banks in the metropolitan statistical area where a foreign subsidiary operated in a particular year, based on FDIC's Call Report data.

The difference between the first year of the study and the year when the foreign bank entered the local market in the United States, natural log transformed. Data were obtained from Bankersalmanac.com, Moody's, and BankScope; on several occasions a parent bank was contacted to confirm the entry year.
time_window: from entry year to study year

description: Based on Deephouse's (1999) measure of strategic deviation and similar to Finkelstein and Hambrick's (1990) concept of strategic conformity, the measure is based on bank asset strategies, reflecting the allocation of a bank's resources to certain product categories. Eight asset strategy variables, each adjusted for firm size and reported as a percentage of total assets, compare a foreign subsidiary's asset strategy with the mean of the corresponding asset strategy of local domestic banks in the same MSA, divided by the corresponding standard deviation for each strategy variable, and the sum of the absolute values is then multiplied by -1 to convert the meaning from strategic deviation to strategic conformity; the formula itself is unreadable in the text. The more negative the measure, the less a foreign subunit conformed to the strategy of local firms; the less negative this measure, the more it conformed to local firms' strategy.
