Dummy variable scored as either 0 or 1, equal to 1 for firms with diffused external shareholder ownership and no significant external shareholder or owner-manager. In the CEO rewards regression it is the omitted category: the coefficients for manager-controlled firms are those of the noninteractive independent variables when the dummies OC and OM both equal zero. The form of firm control was evaluated for each firm in the quarter of the acquisition announcement.
time_window: the quarter of the acquisition announcement

description: Dummy variable scored as either 0 or 1, equal to 1 for firms having a significant external shareholder owning at least 5 percent of the outstanding stock and no owner-manager. It enters the models directly and in interactions with SALES and CARs (the OC interactions in the regression equation).
time_window: the quarter of the acquisition announcement

description: Dummy variable scored as either 0 or 1, equal to 1 for organizations with senior executives who had at least 5 percent ownership but with diffused external stockholders; these executives held the position of CEO, president, chairman of the board, or some combination of the three. It enters the models directly and in interactions with SALES and CARs (the OM interactions in the regression equation).
time_window: the quarter of the acquisition announcement

description: Firm size was measured via total sales. SALES is one of the two independent variables entered in the CEO rewards regressions, alone and in interaction with the form-of-control dummies (OC x SALES and OM x SALES).

Changes in total cash payments, deferred compensation, and the annual changes in the values of CEO stockholdings, adjusted for inflation. Option values were not included owing to the imprecision and potential inaccuracy of available option-pricing tools. Total changes in inflation-adjusted rewards were measured for a 5-year period, beginning 2 years before the announcement of the acquisition and ending 2 years following the year of the announcement.
time_window: 5-year period beginning 2 years before and ending 2 years after the acquisition announcement year

description: Cumulative abnormal returns estimated for three periods surrounding the announcement of each acquisition: -1 to 0 days, -3 to +3 days, and -5 to +5 days. The event date (day 0) was defined as the day prior to an appearance for the first time of the acquisition announcement in the Wall Street Journal. The estimated CARs were used as dependent variables in separate regression models for each of the three time periods.
time_window: -1 to 0 days, -3 to +3 days and -5 to +5 days around the announcement

description: Lagged end-of-year stock of refining R&D capital divided by total firm sales. The capital stock is computed using a perpetual inventory approach: each start-of-year stock is the sum of the depreciated (10 percent rate) start-of-period stock and annual real R&D expenditures from 1974 through the end of the prior year, and the beginning-of-1974 stock is real 1974 R&D expenditures divided by the sum of a 10 percent depreciation rate and a 3.5 percent growth rate. Current-year R&D spending is excluded so that the stock reflects knowledge accumulated as of the start of each year. The variable is lagged 1 year.
time_window: end of prior year, lagged 1 year

description: Refining assets divided by total firm sales, lagged 1 year (lagged end-of-year value). Assets include the book value of property, plant and equipment adjusted for depreciation, depletion, amortization and write-offs, plus investments and advances to unconsolidated affiliates.

variable_name: Other synfuels R&D capital stock intensity (SYNRDCAP)
description: Lagged end-of-year stock of R&D capital on other synthetic fuels (oil shale and tar sands) divided by total firm sales. The stock is computed using the same perpetual inventory approach as the refining R&D capital stock variable. The variable is lagged 1 year.
time_window: end of prior year, lagged 1 year

description: Accumulated coal-related assets divided by total firm sales, lagged 1 year (lagged end-of-year value). Assets include the book value of property, plant and equipment adjusted for depreciation, depletion, amortization and write-offs, plus investments and advances to unconsolidated affiliates.

Annual firm coal gasification/liquefaction R&D expenditures divided by sales revenue for the entire firm. R&D is divided by firm rather than business unit sales because even the most advanced firms' coal conversion operations had not progressed beyond the pilot plant stage and therefore had minimal revenues. Sixty-six of the 156 coal gasification/liquefaction R&D observations are zero. The correlation between coal conversion R&D spending and total firm sales was 0.76 (significant at the 0.01 level) for the 1976-81 period.

The 1-year lag of coal gasification/liquefaction R&D intensity. The effects of cumulative learning in R&D and local search for new knowledge can be modeled as a first-order Markov process in which the cumulative impact of past R&D spending is embodied in last year's R&D activity, which in turn affects current R&D activity.

Lagged year-end value of total firm pre-tax operating income divided by firm sales, used as a proxy for financial resources. The FRS data base did not contain data on cash flows, an alternative measure, for 2 of the 6 years in the sample.

variable_name: Industry coal conversion R&D capital stock (INDRDCAP)
description: Lagged total FRS firm coal conversion R&D capital stock minus own-firm coal conversion R&D capital stock, divided by 1,000,000 to scale the coefficient estimate. The variable is not adjusted for firm size, since the extent of external knowledge spillovers or R&D rivalry would tend to vary with the total R&D capital stock rather than with the R&D intensity of other firms. It does not account for coal conversion R&D by non-FRS firms, nor for the size distribution of R&D spending among firms.
time_window: end of prior year, lagged 1 year

variable_name: Oil and gas recovery R&D capital stock intensity (OILRDCAP)
description: Lagged end-of-year R&D capital stock for oil and gas recovery divided by total firm sales. From 1976 through 1981 the FRS companies as a group spent more on oil and gas recovery R&D than on oil refining R&D.
time_window: end of prior year, lagged 1 year

description: Lagged end-of-year R&D capital stock intensity for the remainder of the firm's R&D (total firm R&D less that for coal conversion, refining, oil and gas recovery and other synfuels), divided by total firm sales. In the FRS data base petrochemicals R&D is not separated from other nonenergy R&D, so this variable includes petrochemicals R&D.
time_window: end of prior year, lagged 1 year

description: Market value of company i at time t, calculated by multiplying the stock price times the number of common shares outstanding and adding company debt. Shares outstanding and debt information are taken from the COMPUSTAT North America database. Measured quarterly over the period that the firms were publicly listed following the completion of their feasibility studies.

Built on the Cairns and Davis (1998) modified formulation of the Hotelling valuation principle for valuing hard-rock mineral properties, applied to each mine separately. The average forecast operating profit per unit of gold for the remaining period of operation is computed using the current price of gold minus the cost of extraction, multiplied by the quantity of proven and probable gold reserves and discounted with the Treasury bond yield with term equal to the remaining mine life. Data on cost of extraction, remaining quantity of proven and probable reserves, estimated mine life, and production start date were collected from company reports and filings.

Event-based measure built from over 50,000 media-reported stakeholder events coded from media documents that mention the mine or the parent company of the mine. Each article was read to identify stakeholder events, coded as source-verb-target triples, and the verb or verb phrase was scored on a modified Goldstein conflict-cooperation scale; over 11,000 verb phrases were mapped onto the scale through fuzzy matching of synonyms. Events are aggregated to the level of a company's conflict or cooperation with stakeholders at each mine in every quarter into a rolling stock computed as a moving average that weights past reports less than current reports (window of eight quarters and a discount rate of 0.8 in the main results).
scale: modified conflict/cooperation scale from -9 (extremely conflictual) to 10 (highly cooperative), neutral events valued 0

description: The credibility of the formal policy environment is measured with the Political Constraint Index (POLCON), which captures the number of veto players across the different independent branches of government in each country adjusted by the level of political alignment across the different branches.

The ratio of the backlog of orders in 1980 to the 3-year moving average backlog going back to 1974. A firm with a lot of excess plant and equipment is likely to have a low level of backlog. Given the hypothesis, the coefficient on BKLOG is expected to be positive.
RSL is the ratio of R&D expenses to sales in 1980. Following the theoretical arguments, the coefficient on RSL is expected to be negative because lower values of DELTADW indicate more related moves.

ASL is the ratio of advertising expenses to sales in 1980. Following the theoretical arguments, the coefficient on ASL is expected to be negative because lower values of DELTADW indicate more related moves.
DEMKT is the ratio of long-term debt to market value in 1980. Note that low values of DEMKT imply a low default risk; according to H3A, a negative sign is predicted on the coefficient of DEMKT.
CR is the ratio of current asset to current liabilities in 1980. According to H3A, a positive sign is expected on the coefficient of CR.

RLSTK is the ratio of average stock price, 1980-84, to average stock price, 1975-79. If this ratio is high, the market is willing to supply capital below historical averages; since the time periods are the same for all firms, this automatically corrects for market variation in stock prices. According to H3B the coefficient on RLSTK is expected to be negative.

The average return on assets (ROA) over the period 1984-86 to measure ex-post performance. Since the diversification moves were observed between 1981 and 1985, 1984 was chosen as the first point when the performance would show up. The mean ROA was used as the cut-off point for high and low performance.

A diversification index DW is computed at two points in time, 1981 and 1985. The formula block for DW is not readable in the provided text; the text states that din equals distance of industry i from that of the firm's largest business (h), and pij equals the fraction of firm i's sales which are in industry j, with din = 0 if i and h are in the same four-digit SIC code, din = 1 if they are in the same three-digit SIC code, and so on. DELTADW measures a longitudinal change in the degree of diversification between two points in time; large values indicate relatively unrelated diversification while small values indicate relatively related diversification.

Foreign ownership, the independent variable, is the percent shares held by foreign investors obtained from the Japan Company Handbook. It is used to predict strategic investments in interaction with growth opportunities.

Growth opportunity is a dummy variable with value 1 when Q exceeds 1 and 0 otherwise. Q is computed as the ratio of market value (sum of market value of equity, book value of preferred stock, and book value of debt) to total assets (Chung and Pruitt, 1994).
The dependent variable, strategic investments, was computed as R&D intensity, R&D expense to sales. It is the dependent variable of the R&D intensity panel model.
The dependent variable, strategic investments, was computed as capital intensity, capital expense to sales. It is the dependent variable of the capital intensity panel model.

The difference of a property's RevPar in the focal year from its RevPar in the prior year (RevPart0 subtracted from RevPart1). The authors create splines that differentiate between positive and negative deviations, and both splines are coded positively such that higher values signal higher (positive or negative) deviations from prior performance.
scale: continuous (RevPar deviation, splined to non-negative values)

description: For comparisons with reference others the authors use three alternatives: they subtract a hotel's RevPar from the average RevPar of all hotels in (a) its self-selected reference group, (b) the same class (e.g., luxury, economy), and (c) the same class and location. Class and location were selected because both are central parameters to the industry, and the overlap in these groups is limited so that statistical separation is still possible; for example, only 46% of the firms selected into reference groups were from the same class as the focal selecting hotel. Similar to prior performance, these variables are splined and re-coded to positive values only.
scale: continuous (RevPar deviation, splined to non-negative values)

description: A dummy variable equaling 1 if the reference firms selected into property i's reference group in t-1 differ from those in t0 and 0 otherwise. Because existing references continue until senior managers make an active decision to change them, the variable relies on managers' self-selected references, which are invisible to the outside and unaffected by impression-management motivations or by policy or regulation. The authors also construct a change-count variable detailing how many references were changed.

The ratio of references in the same class as the focal selecting hotel relative to all selected references; for example, if a hotel selects 10 references and 5 of them share the same class as the focal hotel, this ratio amounts to .5. In order to better understand the changes made to this ratio, the authors created count variables detailing the number of additions and deletions of same- or different-class references.
time_window: t0; one-year lag of the dependent variable included in the GLS model

variable_name: Reference additions and deletions of same- and different-class references
description: Count variables detailing the number of additions and deletions of same-class and different-class references in a property's self-selected reference group, used to examine the detailed adaptations behind the change in relative same class.

A dummy that equals one if there is a top 200 college in the focal city on break in the focal week. A location is considered to have a school break in a given week if there is a top 200 college within 5 miles of the city center and the college has a break that week. School break data were manually collected for the top 200 U.S. colleges.
The number of projects posted on the platform in city c during week t. It is the dependent variable of the main regression and the average city-week had 0.052 projects launched.
The total amount of funds raised by the projects posted in city c during week t. Because the distribution of funding is highly skewed, the authors also use log(Funding + 1) as a dependent variable.

Projects are divided into 15 bins based on the amount of funds they raise, from the lowest (bin 1) to the highest (bin 15); bins are defined by year to account for the growth of the platform. The dependent variable is the number of projects in a specific bin, and the unit of analysis is a city-week-bin.

The ratio between the share of projects with large target amounts (over $30,000) in the design and technology categories and the share of such projects in all other categories, for a given city-week. It is used in the difference-in-differences analysis of the May 2012 policy change.

The length of the text (in words) used to describe a project, one of three proxies for effort on the platform. The difference between break and work weeks is estimated for all projects and separately for value segments of the distribution.

The number of frequently asked questions (FAQs) the entrepreneur lists on the project page, one of three proxies for effort on the platform. The difference between break and work weeks is estimated for all projects and separately for value segments of the distribution.

The number of project updates posted to the crowd, one of three proxies for effort on the platform. The difference between break and work weeks is estimated for all projects and separately for value segments of the distribution.
The number of unique skills listed on a project, identified from the skills mentioned by creators in their biography pages (e.g., programming, photography), averaged for a city-week.
The number of unique skills divided by the size of the team, averaged for a city-week; the division is used to avoid a mechanical relationship between team size and the total number of unique skills.

The share of team projects among all projects for a given city-week. Team projects are captured by identifying the number of team members listed on the projects' biography pages; the share is also computed separately for relatively complex and relatively simple projects (split at the median of each complexity measure).

An indicator of the time periods after the May 2012 Kickstarter policy change, which disproportionately increased the requirement for posting projects in two categories (design and technology); it is interacted with breaks and with the affected categories in the difference-in-differences regressions.

The questionnaire related to 61 market-oriented behaviors representing seven market-oriented factors. Likert-type scales were used to measure market orientation profiles, and scores were compared between high performers and average performers within each competitive context.

The questionnaire related to 22 marketing strategy practices of the SBU representing four strategy orientations. Likert-type scales and semantic differentials were used to measure strategy profiles, and strategy orientation means were compared between high performers and average performers within each competitive context.

Actual and relative levels of ROI were probed in the questionnaire. ROI was used to bifurcate the sample in each competitive context, systematically separating high performers from average performers, and it was related to market orientation and strategy variables in zero-order correlation analysis.

The questionnaire included 15 situational context statements relating to three competitive context factors. These statements measured the competitive environment within which the SBU's market orientation and strategy profiles were assessed, and distinct clusters of contexts were identified from them.

Coalignment was assessed by identifying ideal profiles from a calibration sample: the sample in each competitive context was bifurcated by considering ROI and high performers were systematically separated from average performers. Profile analysis considered both the regression output and the zero-order correlations of all market orientation and strategy variables even if they were not specified in the initial profile solution; the coalignment proposition was further supported if the correlation coefficient of these variables was negative and statistically significant from zero.

In the level 1 model the performance of each firm is modeled as a function of a strategic group mean plus random error. The random firm effect measures the deviation of the firm's score from the strategic group mean; these effects are assumed to be normally distributed with a mean of zero and variance sigma-squared. Firm characteristics are modeled as latent factors rather than through direct measurement of variables.

Groups were defined through the deductive approach, in which a priori expectations exist about the specific nature of groups; a four-group solution was imposed in each industry based on an a priori theoretical framework drawing on strategic choice and organizational ecology. R&D intensity (average R&D expenditure divided by sales for 1991-95) measured the method of developing competitive advantage and the number of trademarks the firm holds measured breadth of operations. Ward's method was used to find cluster centroids and these were used as the starting point for K-means clustering.

Groups were derived empirically with no a priori expectations, and the number of groups was determined per industry by the largest percentage change in the agglomeration coefficient. Grouping variables covered scope of operations and resource deployment. Hierarchical clustering (Ward's method) identified group centroids, which were then used as the starting point for a nonhierarchical K-means procedure.

In the level 3 model the industry mean varies randomly around a grand mean. The random industry effect is the deviation of the industry's mean from the grand mean, assumed normally distributed with a mean of zero and variance tau-beta. Industry attributes are captured using common latent variables shared by members of the same industry.

Return on assets was used to indicate accounting-based (i.e., financial) performance, a short-term measure chosen to enhance comparability with the many previous variance decomposition studies that used ROA. In the HLM, the dependent variable is the average performance for a single dependent variable of firm i in strategic group j and industry k.

Market-based performance was assessed via Tobin's Q, described as the sum of the market value of equity, the book value of debt, and deferred taxes divided by the book value of total assets minus intangible assets. The dependent variable in the HLM is the firm's average performance on this measure.

The authors relied on Altman's Z, a measure of bankruptcy propensity, to capture prospects for firm survival. The likelihood of bankruptcy is described as an especially salient organizational-level measure of risk. The dependent variable in the HLM is the firm's average performance on this measure.

The cumulative number of awards won since the debut of an agency's first idol group in three major competitions: the Golden Disc Awards, the Seoul Music Awards, and the Gaon Chart Awards. Only the main prizes, awarded to the top 10-12 most popular and high-performing artists each year, and the grand prize, given to only one of the main prize awardees, are considered. The grand prize is weighted by multiplying it by the number of main prize awardees who were potential nominees for the grand prize. Finally the total number of awards at the agency level is log-transformed and rescaled from 0 to 10.
time_window: cumulative since the debut of the agency's first idol group

description: The alignment (similarity) between an idol group's newly released concept and the market-dominant concept, which is the concept that appeared most frequently among the songs released 6 months before the focal song; the 6-month window was chosen because the average interval between the releases of two songs is approximately 153 days in the data. Similarity between concepts i and j is calculated as the number of times both concepts co-occurred divided by the total number of occurrences of concept i in all songs. The formal equation for the co-occurrence-based similarity is not legible in the text provided.
time_window: 6 months before the focal song for the market-dominant concept

variable_name: Distance from idol group's previous concept
description: The distance between the idol group's current concept and their previous concept, calculated as the inverse of the similarity between the two concept categories. Concept distance is based on the cognitive distance between concept categories estimated from the co-occurrence of concepts across songs (Leung's, 2014, measure of category distance). The formal equation is not legible in the text provided. According to the measure, the most radical concept shift is, for example, a female idol group shifting from a 'naïve' concept to a 'sexy/revealing' concept.
time_window: relative to the idol group's previous song

description: A dummy variable assigned a value of 1 if all members of an idol group are female, and a value of 0 if they are male. Because of the small number of mixed-gender groups in K-pop, those groups were excluded from the main sample.

A four-item scale assessing employees' perceptions of the company's diversity climate, reflecting the equal and fair treatment, top leader support for diversity, and recognition of diverse perspectives facets of the construct. All items were measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree). For respondents with missing items (no more than 2.6% of the sample), person-mean imputation was performed using the within-person mean of completed items. The scale had an alpha of 0.82 and individual perceptions were aggregated to the store-unit level (ICC(2) = 0.78).
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Two items similar to those used in previous studies measured the extent to which employees felt that service was a strong priority in the work setting. Items were measured on the same five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree). The scale displayed substandard reliability at the individual level (alpha = 0.59), but the authors argue that between-store reliability is more important at their unit level of analysis (mean rwg = 0.64, ICC(2) = 0.74), and individual perceptions were aggregated to the store-unit level.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Minority representation was measured as the percentage of nonwhite employees working in a store unit, taken from company HR records.
Female representation was measured as the percentage of female employees working in a store unit, taken from company HR records.

Customer satisfaction data were collected in 2006 from respondents to a customer service survey completed on the Internet using a Web address provided on sales receipts. The measure was computed as the percentage of customers who indicated 'strongly agree' on a five-point Likert scale to the overall summary question 'I was satisfied with my overall experience at [the Company]'. Higher percentages represent greater customer satisfaction; on average, scores were based on 200 or more respondents per store unit.

Three questions assessed the extent to which issues management activities were a separate, formal activity in each firm. Two 5-point Likert-scale questions asked 'To what extent is the process of issues management a formalized and distinctly recognized function in your organization?' and 'To what extent does your company have staff that are formally assigned to conduct issues management activities?' A third question asked for the titles of the employees formally assigned to perform issues management activities, and the authors coded the number of managers with different formal responsibilities for issues management activities. Responses to the three questions were averaged to form one measure of formalization (alpha = .78).
scale: 5-point Likert scale plus a count of managers

description: Respondents indicated on a five-point Likert scale the total number of staff hours, measured as full-time equivalent hours (FTE), assigned to issues management activities. A second five-point Likert scale question asked respondents to identify a range of resources budgeted to issues management activities. The responses on these two questions were averaged to measure resources expended (r = .75).

This dimension assessed the extent to which firms used committees in their issues management activities. Respondents were asked to identify all the committees used in the issues management process and then to list the different organizational levels represented on each committee, the frequency with which it met, the functional departments represented, and the specific issues it addressed. Committees in firms with highly developed issues management structures were expected to have members from several different functional departments and organizational levels, to meet more frequently, and to address more issues. The Cronbach's alpha for the committee use questions was .92.

variable_name: Integration of issues management with corporate planning
description: Six Likert-scale questions measured the extent of a firm's integration of issues management into corporate planning, the frequency of public affairs involvement in planning and of issue introduction, the receptivity of the planning staff to public issues, the attention given to issues, and the degree of environmental scanning for issues by corporate planners.

variable_name: Integration of issues management and line functions
description: Five Likert-scale questions (alpha = .84) measured the use of formal and informal communication, the quality of the relationship between issues managers and line managers, the level of line managers' concern with public issues, and the extent to which line managers were rewarded for effectively managing public issues; a sample item was 'How often are formal written communications used between issues managers and line/division managers?' After factor analysis the authors dropped items and the final revised two-item line integration measure had a Cronbach alpha of .71.

Media exposure for each firm was measured by the number of issue-related articles appearing from January 1987 through May 1990 in a database including all articles published in ten major newspapers dispersed throughout the United States. An issue-related article was defined as one concerned with anything industry respondents mentioned as an important issue with which their firm was currently involved.

This variable was measured by a questionnaire item that asked how many interest groups had directly contacted the firm about its behavior regarding social and political issues in the last three years, with respondents asked to name each interest group. The number of groups that directly contacted a firm about their behavior on issues was used as the measure of interest group pressure.

Respondents were asked to list any crisis their firm had experienced in the last 20 years and the date of its occurrence, and they also rated the extent of the severity of the crisis on a scale ranging from minor (1) to severe (5). If more than one crisis was listed, the highest severity rating given was taken as the severity measure.
Size was measured as the mean of firm sales over the three years 1987-89. Sales data were acquired from annual reports.

A questionnaire item asked for the total number of hours per week a firm's CEO spent working on social and political issues. Survey respondents typically reported directly to their firms' CEOs, so they were in a good position to answer the question.

A content analysis of the letters to shareholders in the firms' 1989 annual reports, patterned after Bowman (1978, 1984). Each sentence was first coded as to whether or not it was issue related, issue-related sentences being those that mentioned an issue respondents identified on the questionnaire as currently important to their firms; the sentence was then coded as positively stated, negatively stated, neutral, or both positive and negative. The ratio of issue-related, positive sentences to the total number of sentences was the measure of top management commitment to social and political issues.

Total CEO compensation is the variable 'tdc1' from ExecuComp and consists of salary, bonuses, the value of restricted stock granted, the value of options granted, long-term incentive payouts, and other compensation. The authors use the natural logarithm of CEO total compensation to fit a log-linear model. They adjust CEO compensation by the average of compensation levels of other CEOs in the same industry (based on two-digit SIC codes) to partial out differences across industries. CEO compensation is measured at time t + 1.

Firm performance is measured as industry-adjusted stock returns. Annual stock returns are adjusted by industry averages: the average stock returns for all public firms, excluding the focal firm, in the same two-digit SIC code industry. Industry-adjusted stock return is therefore the difference between a focal firm's annual stock returns and the equally weighted industry returns. Stock returns are measured at time t.

Corporate strategic investment intensity is the ratio of summated R&D, acquisition, and capital expenditures to total sales revenues; the authors call it 'intensity' because it is scaled by firm size, measured as sales. Around 45% of firm-year observations have missing R&D values, which are coded as zero along with a dummy variable equal to 1 for these firm years. The variable is adjusted by industry average (based on two-digit SIC codes) to partial out the influence of industry peers' investment decisions on focal firms. It is measured at time t.

variable_name: CEO prestige (number of CEO certification contests won)
description: Awards are used as a proxy for the level of a CEO's prestige. The authors examine CEO certification contests conducted by a set of business magazines and organizations, and use the number of CEO certification contests that a CEO has won in a year to measure their level of prestige. Winners of CEO certification contests have a higher level of prestige than CEOs who did not win.

Board conservatism is measured from directors' donations to the two major parties in the United States, collected from the Federal Election Commission; the authors focus on directors' contributions to candidates for federal or state offices, their campaign finance committees, and political action committees. An index of director conservatism is built from four ratios, which are standardized and averaged to measure each director's conservatism. This is aggregated to the board level by averaging the scores of all directors on the board.

Group fear was measured at the end of each round after the financial results were announced and before the team decided to continue or terminate, using three sentences built from fear prototype words and rated on a five-point scale (1: not at all, 5: very much). The items were 'We fear for the future of our venture,' 'My team is scared of losing a lot of money at the end,' and 'My team is worried that we will not reach our goal in the game' (Cronbach's alpha = 0.79). Respondents reported how the team as a whole felt, and the data were aggregated to the team level for each of the 569 rounds (ICC(1) = 0.74).
time_window: end of each round, after financial feedback and before the escalation/termination decision

description: Group hope was measured at the end of each round and before the decision to escalate or terminate, using three items adapted from Snyder et al.'s State Hope scale and rated on a five-point scale (1: not at all, 5: very much). The items were 'My team feels hopeful that we will succeed in the game,' 'At the present time, we are energetically pursuing our goals in the game,' and 'Right now my team sees ourselves as being pretty successful in the game' (Cronbach's alpha = 0.80). Responses referred to the team as a whole and were aggregated to the team level for each round (ICC(1) = 0.72).
time_window: end of each round, before the escalation/termination decision

description: All team interactions were videotaped and coded by three trained video coders with the video silenced. Coders rated each team's nonverbal engagement on a five-point scale (1: bored, 3: neutral, 5: engaged), based on paying attention to teammates, leaning toward the laptop and focusing on the laptop versus not paying attention, leaning backward and looking away. The coding segments (minimum 30 s, maximum 5 min) were averaged into a round-level score, and the by-round scores were aggregated across the three coders (ICC(2) = 0.56), yielding 1,852 coding segments for 66 teams and 569 rounds.
time_window: coded across each round of the simulation

description: Team members responded to a question measuring their perceived relationship with each of the other two team members: how they would describe the relationship between them and their teammates, on a five-point scale (1: acquaintance, 3: somewhat close friends, 5: very close friends). The two scores correlated at 0.33 and were averaged to form a friendship score between each participant and the other two team members; the individual-level friendship strength data were then aggregated at the team level. Friendship data were available for 56 teams (470 team-round observations).
scale: 1-5 (1: acquaintance, 3: somewhat close friends, 5: very close friends)

description: Escalation of commitment to a currently failing venture versus termination was captured by a dummy variable ('quit') with a value of 1 for the round at the end of which the team terminated the virtual venture and 0 for all preceding rounds. The 66 teams participated in different numbers of rounds, ranging from 3 to 21, with a mean of 8.7 rounds; there was neither left-censoring nor right-censoring because all 66 teams quit the simulation, giving a final sample of 569 team-round observations.
time_window: each round until the team terminated the venture

variable_name: cumulative count of prior mergers of each type
description: A cumulative count was generated for each type of merger throughout the observed history of the firm, so each firm begins with a value of zero mergers for each type, receives a count of one after the first merger of that type, two after the second, and so on. The cumulative value at any given time is the independent variable used in the analysis of the effects of prior mergers on later mergers.
time_window: cumulative over the firm's observed history

description: Current product market diversification was measured with the classification system developed by Rumelt, which uses a computation of the firm's specialization ratio (the proportion of revenues derived from its largest single business) and its related ratio (the proportion of revenues derived from its largest single group of related businesses). The index contains nine ordered levels of diversification: 'Single Business' firms are not diversified and were assigned a value of 0, and the most diversified firms a value of 8.

Rumelt's structural categories were collapsed into four categories: functional firms were assigned a value of one, functional-with-subsidiaries a value of 2, divisionalized firms a value of 3, and holding companies a value of 4. Four rather than five categories were used because Rumelt's distinction between geographic and product division structures has no bearing on the proposed mechanisms and there were too few firms divisionalized by geography to make the distinction empirically useful.

Dependent variable: the rate of occurrence (instantaneous probability) of a product extension merger at time t, estimated simultaneously with the other three marginal merger rates in a multivariate point process model. Product extension mergers, together with conglomerate mergers, were defined as diversifying mergers because each involves the addition of distinctly new and separate product groups to the firm's prior activities.

Dependent variable: the rate of occurrence (instantaneous probability) of a conglomerate merger at time t, estimated simultaneously with the other marginal merger rates. Conglomerate mergers are one of the two types defined as diversifying mergers because they involve the addition of distinctly new and separate product groups to the firm's prior activities.

Dependent variable: the rate of occurrence (instantaneous probability) of a horizontal (including market extension) merger at time t, estimated simultaneously with the other marginal merger rates. Horizontal and market extension mergers involve the acquisition of a company that produces a product already produced by the acquiring firm, and are not counted as diversifying mergers.

Dependent variable: the rate of occurrence (instantaneous probability) of a vertical integration merger at time t, estimated simultaneously with the other marginal merger rates. Vertical mergers involve the acquisition of a customer or supplier (either actual or potential) and thus the extension of the firm's boundary along a processing chain.

A Herfindhal-Hirschman index based on the retained ownership of listed blockholders disclosed in each firm's prospectus, including VCs, BAs, founders, industry partners, non-founding directors, and others. The index equals the sum of the blockholders' squared ownership as a percentage of the total post-IPO block holding.

Calculated as (offer price - book value per share)/offer price, in line with Nelson (2003). The authors state it demonstrates the difference between the accounting and the market value and can measure intangible assets, monopoly control, investor overenthusiasm, or other factors that dislocate stock price from accounting-based figures.

Percentage of the total number of shares outstanding after the IPO date retained by venture capital investors. UK venture capital firms were identified from the British Venture Capital Association 2000/2001 Directory, the 2000 Pratt's Guide to Venture Capital Sources and the 2000/2001 Venture Capital Report Guide to Venture Capital in the UK, including venture capital trusts managed by established venture capital firms; French venture capital firms were identified from the AFIC Directory.

Percentage of the total number of shares outstanding after the IPO date retained by business angels. BAs were identified through the prospectus as those who had invested in the venture as private individuals not associated with founders, other board members, senior managers, and venture capital investors.

A dummy variable equal to one for the UK and zero otherwise, used to capture institutional differences between UK and French corporations in the sample. Country-specific hypotheses were tested with interactions between the UK dummy and three ownership variables: ownership concentration, VC retained ownership, and BA retained ownership.

Composite measure built from four dichotomous questions asked every 6 months, each coded 1 if the respondent answered yes and 0 if no: whether financial projections have been developed; whether the venture has gathered information about the market and competition; whether a business plan has been completed; and whether a formal, written business plan document has been prepared. In scoring, the venture received a score of one for gathering market and competition information and one for completing financial projections; if these two sections had been combined into a completed business plan it received an additional score of one; and it received another score of one if the business plan had been completed in a written form suitable for presentation to others. Because the score on this variable can increase over time, it captures ongoing maintenance and updating of plans.
time_window: measured at each survey wave (initial, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months)

description: Dichotomous measure based on the question 'Has a business plan been completed?', asked every 6 months, coded 1 if the respondent answered yes and 0 if no. The authors chose this item rather than 'Has a formal, written business plan document been prepared?' because business plans can be complete even if not presented in formal written form suitable for presentation to others, because the survey protocol used nested questions (the formal-plan question was asked only if a plan had been completed), and because a formal written document was much more likely to be prepared if the respondent was seeking outside capital.
time_window: measured at each survey wave (initial, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months)

description: Respondents were asked at each wave of the survey whether all parties pursuing the venture have ceased their effort to pursue it and, if so, in what month that effort ended. In the month that all members of the venture team ceased pursuit of the venture the venture is coded '1', otherwise it is coded '0'. Identifying the specific month of cessation allows monthly spells; ventures not disbanded by the end of the 30-month observation were treated as censored.
time_window: monthly spells over the first 30 months of venture life

description: Every 6 months respondents were asked, 'At what stage of development is the product or service this start-up will be selling?' The scale of responses was '1' equals 'No work has been done to develop a product or service;' '2' equals 'Work to develop the product or service is still in the idea stage;' '3' equals 'A model or procedure is being developed;' '4' equals 'A prototype or procedure has been tested with customers;' and '5' equals 'The product or service is completed and ready for sales or delivery.' Measuring the stage of product development repeatedly over time captures both improvements and decreases in product development.

Total score on eight dichotomous questions that prior research has shown are steps founders take to organize new ventures, asked every 6 months beginning with the initial survey, coded '1' if the respondent answered 'yes' and '0' if the respondent answered 'no'. Prior research has shown that these dimensions can be combined into an overarching measure. To mitigate the possibility that respondents would overstate completion, interviewers requested information that confirmed the respondents' statements; no information disconfirmed the statements.

Dummy variable that equals 1 when a firm has an owner-manager and 0 when a firm has a hired CEO. A firm has a foreign owner-manager when one of its foreign owners is also the CEO; owners are defined as shareholders with at least 20 percent of firm shares, and all hired CEOs in the sample are Russian.
Operating return on assets, the ratio of operating profit to the book value of assets. All monetary values are in nominal Russian rubles, with inflation captured by year dummies.

Operating costs of the firm, entered in logarithm form and used as the dependent variable in the cost regressions. The cost regressions are used to trace the underlying sources of the owner-manager's effect on firm performance.
Revenue of the firm, entered in logarithm form and used as a dependent variable alongside costs. The authors report no impact of foreign owner-managers on revenue.

Revenue growth of the firm, used as a dependent variable to examine whether owner-managers use extra profit to grow their firms at a higher rate. The authors report no impact of foreign owner-managers on revenue growth.

Natural logarithm of the distance between the city where the firm is located and the home country of the firm owners. The measure is used to capture the monitoring difficulty faced by nonmanaging foreign owners living in their home countries.

Annual regional unemployment rate of the Russian region in which the firm is located. Higher unemployment is used to indicate lower local competition for resources, which makes cost-efficient foreign resources less valuable.

Average management practice score of firms in the entrepreneur's home country, based on the management practices measure developed by Bloom and Van Reenen (2007). The score averages the quality of management practices across four areas.

Following the IR literature, political affinity is operationalized using the voting decisions of the home country i and the host country j made in the UN General Assembly in year t, leading to a time-varying variable. The variable captures in a given year t the similarity in the two countries' voting portfolios Vi and Vj and is equal to 1 - 2 Dt(Vi, Vj) / Dmax t, where Dt reflects the sum of (absolute) metric distances between votes in the two voting portfolios and Dmax t is the maximum possible distance for these votes. The vote distance between each country dyad is transformed such that the variable obtains its lowest score -1 for country dyads with a completely opposite voting pattern and its highest score of 1 when country dyads have an identical voting pattern in a given year.

The value of the initial acquisition premium, calculated as the ratio of the initial offer price to the target closing stock price four weeks prior to the original announcement date as reported by the Thomson ONE database. A four-week window is taken because information on the deal might leak prior to the official announcement and thereby distort the market price of the target firm. The premium data are trimmed by dropping the largest and smallest two percent of initial bids.
time_window: four weeks prior to the original announcement date

description: The (updated) measure of government fractionalization from the Database of Political Institutions. It captures the likelihood that two members of parliament-picked at random-from governing parties belong to different parties; a high fractionalization index indicates that the government consists of a large number of small parties, while a low fractionalization index indicates that the government consists of a small number of strong parties, possibly only one party.

An indicator of trade dependence computed as the sum of export and import flows between the home and host country divided by the GDP of the host country, taken from the Correlates of War Project Trade Data Set.

Product-level outcome based on independent expert ratings of three categories of LCD products (televisions, monitors, and laptop screens) from 1987 to 2005, drawn from Consumer Reports, CNet.com, PC World, PC Week, Government Computing News, and LCDTVBuyingGuide.com. As each source uses its own scale, each rating is normalized so the final variable is the number of standard deviations above or below the mean for that source. Where multiple ratings exist for the same product, the ratings are averaged to leave one rating per product. Composite ratings are used for monitors and televisions and the rating of the screen for laptops.
scale: standard deviations above or below the mean for each source

description: Count of the firm's early patents in the losing technology (plasma) applied for before 1983, derived from Derwent Innovation Index patent records; Derwent groups identical patents filed in multiple jurisdictions into a single patented innovation record. The variable captures the technological choices made by firms during the early, uncertain period in the industry's development.

Count of the firm's early patents in the winning technology (LCD) applied for before 1983, derived from Derwent Innovation Index patent records. Every pre-1983 LCD patent was missing at least one element of the dominant design (active-matrix amorphous silicon TFT), so the variable measures investment in an early LCD generation.

Dummy variable for firms with zero flat panel patents prior to 1983, included because firms with no pre-1983 patents systematically have zeroes for both early patenting variables, and to test H2 about the decision to wait for uncertainty to subside before initiating knowledge-creation investments.
scale: dummy (1 = no flat panel patents prior to 1983)

description: The Fortune reputation survey provides a list of the 10 largest companies per industry to over 8,000 executives, directors, and securities analysts, who rate the companies in their own industry along eight measures on a scale of 0 (poor) to 10 (excellent). Fortune aggregates the reputation scores for each of these criteria to create one overall reputation score. The authors standardized the reputation scores by industry.
scale: 0 (poor) to 10 (excellent) on each of eight criteria

description: Revenue is measured as the log transformation of annual sales for each firm. It is one of the two traditional measures of financial performance in the analysis.
Net income is calculated as a firm's total retained earnings, or gross revenue minus expenses. It is the second traditional measure of financial performance in the analysis.

EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, which indicates a firm's ability to carry debt. It is one of the two emerging measures of financial performance; in the results discussion the authors refer to the pro forma indicator of firm performance as the counterpart to free cash flow.

Free cash flow is the calculated aftertax cash flows from operations minus any incremental investments made in operating assets. The authors use Martin and Petty's definition of free cash flow as equal to cash flow from operations less any additional investments in working capital and long-term assets.

Overall CSR is the sum of a firm's scores on all 43 strength indicators minus the sum of its scores on all 37 concern indicators in the KLD data set. Strengths and concerns within each area are not complementary, so a firm can rate very high or low on both, and KLD concerns in certain areas are better proxies for actual behavior than strengths. The authors also used Overall CSR strengths (the sum of the strength indicators) and Overall CSR concerns (the sum of the concern indicators) as separate indicators of CSR behavior.

The weighted valence measure is the multiplicative product of the amount of attention that a performance variable gets in the media via article counts and the valence of the text in which the variable is used within the media articles: Weighted valence measure_ij = Article count_ij x Media coverage valence_ij. Article count is the annual sum of articles that mention the indicator, normalized by dividing by the total number of articles published in each periodical in that year, while media coverage valence is the mean measured valence of the text for each article in which the indicator is cited. The absolute value of the measure indicates whether the term is widely or scarcely used, and the sign is positive when positive emotion describes the indicator and negative when negative emotion does. Article counts for the financial indicators come from Fortune and Forbes and for CSR from the Wall Street Journal; valence was obtained through LIWC2007 content analysis of keyword-in-context lists of 101 words.

The registered capital of a foreign firm divided by the total registered capital of an IJV at the founding date. Because the sample is restricted to IJVs with a stable ownership structure, foreign equity share is constant over time. The sample excludes IJVs whose foreign equity shares fall outside the range of five percent to 95 percent of total equity.
scale: 5 to 95 percent of total equity (sample restriction)

description: Firm productivity is calculated as the ratio of value added (in terms of price in 1990) to the total number of employees in firm i at year t. Because industrial sectors differ in average productivity, the firm's productivity is divided by the average productivity of its four-digit industry sector, which is computed as the ratio of total value added to total employees in the industry.

A dummy variable coded one if FDI legitimacy is high and zero otherwise. FDI legitimacy in an industry is high once the ratio of employment by foreign firms (including IJVs and wholly foreign-owned subsidiaries) in that industry is above the industry average.

A dummy variable measuring FDI legitimacy in a metropolitan city and its surrounding area, coded one if the ratio of employment by foreign firms in a city is above the average ratio of foreign employment in all cities.

A standard Herfindahl measure for market concentration by utilizing the sales information reported in the annual census, computed for a given industry. A lower value of market concentration indicates a higher level of market competition, so the measure runs opposite to the level of competition. The formula itself is not readable in the provided text.

A dummy variable coded zero if the location of an IJV is in Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin, Liaoning, Shandong, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangzhou, or Hainan, and one otherwise. A value of one therefore indicates a less economically developed location.

Estimated with a proportional hazard model following Cox's partial likelihood approach because the dependence of subsidiary mortality on age is unknown and this semiparametric model does not require assumptions about that effect. The dependent variable is the instantaneous rate of subsidiary dissolution, based on whether or not an affiliate is still in existence and how long it has persisted. The tables report the survival rate of subsidiaries, the dissolution rate's logical converse, so a positive effect indicates that the variable enhanced the probability of survival of the observation (a subsidiary).

variable_name: Likelihood that an affiliate was an acquisition
description: Estimated with binomial logit models. The dependent variable captures the likelihood that an affiliate was an acquisition rather than a greenfield, using the expansions recorded for each firm over the window of analysis.

Tested with the same binomial logit models used for the propensity to acquire or establish a greenfield. Because the dependent variable captures the likelihood that an affiliate was an acquisition rather than a greenfield, the likelihood of a greenfield is the converse side of this dichotomous dependent variable.

The number of greenfields since 1966, counted from 1966 onwards, measured as the influence of preceding greenfields controlled for the number of acquisitions during the same period. The authors argue that the number of times a certain way of organizing has been reinstalled through a new subsidiary is relevant, and that what matters is the balance between preceding greenfields and preceding acquisitions rather than the absolute number of either.

The number of acquisitions since 1966, counted from 1966 onwards, measured as the influence of preceding acquisitions controlled for the number of greenfields during the same period. What matters for an observation at a certain point in time is the balance between the two variables rather than the absolute number of preceding acquisitions.

Measured in two ways. First, the number of greenfields that took place in an SBI code in which a firm was already present, the SBI code being the Dutch equivalent of the Standard Industrial Classification code. Second, the number of greenfields that took place in a country in which the firm had established a subsidiary earlier.
Measured in two ways: the number of greenfields that were the first in an SBI code and the number of greenfields that were the first in a country.
Measured in two ways: the number of acquisitions within two digits of the firm's prior SBI codes and the number of acquisitions in a country in which the firm had acquired earlier.
Measured in two ways: the number of acquisitions not within two digits of the firm's prior SBI codes and the number of acquisitions in a country not entered before.

Respondents rated the extent to which their firm focuses on each item in comparison to its major competitors on a 1 to 7 scale. A firm's score was derived by adding the responses for each item of the scale and then dividing by the number of items in the scale. The Appendix also presents a rating of the current product line or mix from low margin to high margin following these items.
scale: 1-7 (much lower to much higher than major competitors)

description: Respondents rated the extent to which their firm focuses on each item in comparison to its major competitors on a 1 to 7 scale. The mean response to the scale items was used as the firm's score on the measure.
scale: 1-7 (much lower to much higher than major competitors)

description: Respondents rated the extent to which their firm focuses on each item in comparison to its major competitors on a 1 to 7 scale. The mean response to the scale items was used as the firm's score on the measure.
scale: 1-7 (much lower to much higher than major competitors)

description: The scale contains a rated item on offering a broad line of products compared to major competitors and a rating of the firm's current product line or mix from limited variety to wide variety, both on a 1 to 7 scale. The mean response to the scale items was used as the firm's score on the measure.
scale: 1-7 (much lower to much higher than major competitors; limited to wide variety)

description: The scale asks about building a reputation for being first in the industry to try new methods and technologies, how the company's innovation efforts are classified (leader to follower), and the timing of entry (early to late), all on a 1 to 7 scale. The mean response to the scale items was used as the firm's score on the measure.

Respondents rated the extent to which their firm focuses on each item in comparison to its major competitors on a 1 to 7 scale. The mean response to the scale items was used as the firm's score on the measure.
scale: 1-7 (much lower to much higher than major competitors)

description: Respondents rated their firm's emphasis on new product development, the rate of new product introduction to market, and the number of new products introduced to market on a 1 to 7 scale. The mean response to the scale items was used as the firm's score on the measure.

Return on sales for the 3-year period following the survey data collection, collected from secondary sources (COMPUSTAT, Ward's Directory and company annual reports) and phone calls to companies. To control for industry variation the authors subtracted a firm's score from its industry average, divided the difference by the industry mean and multiplied the result by 100, so that the adjusted score reflects how well a company performs compared to its industry; the data were then standardized.
time_window: 3-year period following the survey data collection

variable_name: Aggressive technological posture, automation and process innovation, new product development scales
description: Technology policy was operationalized along three dimensions from the CEO questionnaire: aggressive technological posture, automation and process innovation, and new product development. The firm's score on each dimension was the mean response to its scale items.

Firms were grouped into business strategy clusters by Ward's hierarchical cluster analysis on the four business strategy scales (commodity-to-specialty products, marketing intensity, cost leadership and product line breadth). A five-cluster solution was chosen from changes in squared euclidean distance and the dendrogram.

To measure negative performance feedback, the authors first measured firms' aspiration level following Greve (2003). Historical aspiration is the exponential moving average of a firm's past ROA, and social aspiration is the average ROA of firms in the same industry; a firm's aspiration level is a weighted average of the two. Performance feedback variables, including Below aspiration, were then derived using a spline function based on the firm's aspiration level. The exact spline formula was not extracted in the text.

Expertise diversity is a composite measure built from three dimensions: industry experience diversity, functional experience diversity, and board experience diversity. Industry experience diversity averages the pairwise cosine similarity of directors' industry experience vectors and reverse-codes it; functional experience diversity does the same using seven functional experience categories based on BoardEx job role descriptions; board experience diversity is the standard deviation in the number of outside directorships held by directors on the board. The three scores are standardized as z-scores and summed.

Ascriptive diversity is a composite measure based on gender and racial background. Gender diversity is measured using a reverse-coded Herfindahl index of female directors; racial diversity is measured using a similar index that distinguishes white directors from all other racial groups, based on ISS/RiskMetrics race/ethnicity information supplemented by NamSor estimates. The two standardized scores are added to obtain the composite.

This measure captures whether chairs of the three important board committees (compensation, audit, and nomination) have expertise dissimilar to other directors. The authors retained pairs consisting of a chair and a non-chair director, computed average cosine similarity between chair-directors and other directors for industry and functional experience, subtracted these scores from one, and for board experience computed the absolute difference in average outside directorships between chair and non-chair directors. The three scores were standardized as z-scores and added; a higher score indicates that the chairs of the board have dissimilar expertise.

A dummy variable capturing whether women or directors from underrepresented racial groups hold any of the chair positions on the board (compensation, audit, or nomination committee). It is coded 1 when such a director holds a chair position and 0 otherwise.

A dummy variable indicating whether a venture participated in an accelerator. The focal group is startups that were selected and participated; the counterfactual group is startups that were selected but were not accelerated.

A binary measure that indicates whether a venture secured VC in the year following application to the accelerator program. The authors align this measure with prior research noting the importance of raising external capital for venture growth and scaling.
time_window: the year following application to the accelerator program

description: The amount of VC equity funding raised in the year following the accelerator program application, adjusted by taking the natural logarithm of the funding amount in thousands of US$. The adjustment accounts for the varying levels of funding and enables a more accurate comparison of funding amounts across ventures.
time_window: the year following the accelerator program application

description: The amount of capital that the venture aimed to raise in subsequent fundraising efforts for the year following the accelerator program application. The measure provides insights into the fundraising aspirations of the startups.
time_window: the year following the accelerator program application

description: The sales revenue of the startup (in thousands of US$) for the year after the accelerator program application. The authors describe this outcome as indicative of growth in a venture's customer or user base and the achievement of product-market fit.
time_window: the year after the accelerator program application

description: The number of full-time employees of the startup (other than the cofounders) who worked for the venture for at least 40 h per week in the year following the accelerator program application, adjusted by the natural logarithm of the headcount to correct for skew. The authors state that this measure reflects the venture's ability to scale its workforce.
time_window: the year following the accelerator program application

description: The natural logarithm of the value of wages paid in salaries to employees (in thousands of US$) in the year following the accelerator program application. The authors state that this measure provides insights into the startups' ability not only to scale employment but also to attract highly skilled employees and talent.
time_window: the year following the accelerator program application

description: A continuous index, mean centered at zero with a standard deviation of one, computed for each cohort in the sample. It was created using weights from factor analysis with orthogonal rotation based on three primary variables measuring the depth of peer knowledge.

A continuous index, mean centered at zero with a standard deviation of one, computed for each cohort in the sample using the same factor-analytic method as the depth index. Heterogeneity in operating models and industry sectors was measured as one minus the sum of the squared proportions of ventures in each category.

An indicator variable for whether the program features pitch nights or demo days, which are formal pitching opportunities that enable founders to obtain external feedback from a diversity of sources. The authors state that these events also increase a venture's visibility in the entrepreneurial ecosystem.

An indicator for whether the program provides seed funding to participants, in the form of financial grants or investments. The authors state that seed funding may help founders develop their products and engage in product-development and experimentation during acceleration.

An indicator for whether an accelerator program includes structured education comprising a paced, written curriculum that covers specific topical areas for startup development. The authors only consider whether programs provided a structured curriculum and do not have information about whether founders attended or completed sessions.

variable_name: Program has a specific industry sector focus
description: Identifies whether an accelerator is industry-agnostic, meaning it supports startups regardless of the industry they operate in, or has a specific sector focus, catering exclusively to startups within a particular industry such as healthcare, technology, clean energy, or finance.

The length of time that startups are actively engaged in an accelerator program. The authors argue that longer programs may provide more extensive support, more networking opportunities, and more chances to iterate on business models, products, or services.

Startup performance after acceleration was measured with six outcomes in the year after the accelerator application: whether the venture raised VC equity, the amount of VC equity raised, the planned VC equity raise, sales revenue, number of full-time employees and wages paid to employees.

CEO international assignment experience was gauged as the number of calendar years in which a CEO reported working in international assignments through 1993. The authors note that this measure has been used in prior studies of multinationals and international assignment experience.

variable_name: Top management team international assignment experience
description: This measure was calculated as the years of international assignment experience reported by the other members of a company's top management team, excluding the CEO. The results reported use all officers over the level of vice president, a definition that captured an average top team size of 9 and ranged from 3 to 24. The measure moderates the CEO experience-performance relationship in Hypothesis 1b and is a control in the compensation models.

A firm's 1993 global strategic posture was measured with a variation of Sullivan's composite measure of firm internationalization on three continuous dimensions: foreign sales (the ratio of foreign sales to total sales), foreign production (foreign assets as a percentage of total assets), and geographic dispersion (the number of country subsidiaries as a percentage of the highest number of country subsidiaries among firms in the sample). The three dimensions were summed to form the composite measure, which has a theoretical range of 0 to 3. The authors report that the items demonstrated high interitem reliability.

Firm performance was measured as return on assets, net profits divided by total assets. The authors state that ROA indicates the efficiency with which a firm employs its current asset base and is especially pertinent to this study, since firm internationalization is theoretically associated with the search for economies of scope and scale.

The market performance measure is stock market returns, the percentage change in stock price plus dividend yield. It is indicative of how effectively a firm is managing shareholder interests and the level at which it is providing shareholders an acceptable total stock market return.

CEO compensation level was measured as the logarithm of the total of all forms of compensation granted. Long-term forms of compensation, such as stock options, restricted stock, and long-term investment plans, were valued at their present value as provided by a company in its proxy statement. All stock options were valued with the SEC method: the option price is subtracted from the estimated stock price in ten years and the difference is discounted at 5 percent yearly to the present year, the estimated future stock price being the current price per share escalated by 5 percent per year for ten years.

Geographic scope of knowledge acquisition is delineated as the number of assignee countries found in the backward citations of a patent. The authors note that operationalization of geographic scope with inventor countries provides consistent results.

Innovation output is operationalized as the number of forward citations a patent receives, in line with extant studies. In order to address possible truncation bias, a five-year window is specified when calculating the number of forward citations.

Drawing on Zander and Kogut's insights on the speed of the transfer and imitation of organizational capabilities, the degree of isolating mechanisms is measured as the time to the first forward citation by other firms. It is measured by the length of time, in years, between the patent application and the first forward citation by other firms to the patent.

Innovation output is operationalized as the number of forward citations a patent receives, calculated as an annual average of the number of forward citations to the patents of a focal firm. This variable is an aggregation to the firm-year level of the dependent variable employed for Hypotheses 1 and 2b.
The time to first forward citation used in Hypotheses 2a and 2b is aggregated into the firm-year level to capture the degree of isolation used as the moderating variable in Hypothesis 3.

Financial performance is operationalized with return on assets (ROA) in its natural logarithm form (ln(1 + ROA)) as a measure of firms' profitability. A one-year time lag is specified between independent variables and dependent variables in order to incorporate into the analysis the time taken for the innovation to be realized in financial performance.

Calculated by determining the distance between the text descriptions of a developer's first and second apps using basic cosine similarity, a method for calculating the similarity between two text documents that measures the angular distance between two non-zero vectors. To create a word vector for each app's text description, Python was used to remove non-English words, remove punctuation and numbers, remove stop words, and stem words to their root, producing for each app a count of the number of times each word in its description is used. The search distance between two apps is calculated by subtracting the basic cosine similarity of their word vectors from one, because search distance is a measure of distance rather than similarity. The measure is continuous and ranges from 0.00 (identical descriptions, extremely local search) to 1.00 (no common words, extremely nonlocal search).
level: app (developer's first and second app pair)

description: Measures the logged number of installs a developer's second app had generated at the time it was last observed. Google Play provides data on how many times each app has been installed in ordered categorical format, with 19 categories of app installs; the lowest number in the categorical installs range is identified, one is added to correct for cases with zero installs, and this number is then logged to correct for skewness. For example, an app with 100-500 installs would be coded as log(100 + 1).
scale: logged installs (lowest value of a 19-category install range, plus one, logged)
time_window: at the time the second app was last observed

description: Measures the number of installs a developer's first app had in the month it was first observed. As in the case of app two installs, this measure is calculated by taking the log of the lowest number in the categorical installs range provided by Google Play, so the lower the installs of a developer's first app, the more negative the developer's initial performance feedback is assumed to be.
scale: logged installs (lowest value of a categorical install range, logged)
time_window: the month the first app was first observed

description: Percentage of revenue that a franchise outlet generated from nonstandard products, i.e., products that are not part of the original franchisor business model or product mix. Standard products are primarily services targeting the SOHO niche such as mailbox services, packing and shipping supplies and services, copy services, postal stamps and office supplies, whereas nonstandard products include greeting cards, passports, money wiring, phone messaging services, pager sales, and desktop publishing. Monthly data for this measure are available for all units of the franchise system over the entire 11-year period. The authors state the measure is likely conservative because only nine nonstandard products were measured in the firm archival data and only attempts that achieved nonnegligible sales volumes were reported.
time_window: Monthly, over the entire 11-year observation period

description: Percentage of an outlet's revenue generated from nonstandard products, which the authors use as their measure of deviation from the franchisor template and hence of local adaptation of the product mix. Nonstandard products are those not part of the original franchisor business model or product mix, such as greeting cards, passports, money wiring, phone messaging services, pager sales, and desktop publishing. Monthly data are available for all units of the franchise system over the entire 11-year period.
time_window: Monthly, over the entire 11-year observation period

description: Outlet-specific hazard of failure, the dependent variable of the analysis. Outlets are at risk of exit until the end of the observation period or until they have permanently closed down as indicated by the franchisor internal information system. Mere ownership transfers are not treated as exits, as long as the same outlet is operating at the same location within the same franchise system.

Dichotomous variable capturing whether a startup in the sample received a formal offer of admission to the accelerator. Admission offers are based almost entirely on the relative rank generated by average judge scores for a fixed number of slots. Distance from the admission threshold is characterized by normalizing the average judge score for each organization by the score of the 128th-ranked startup in that year's applicant class.

Dummy variable set to one when a startup received more than $500,000 in early-stage funding in the two years after the graduation of the cohort to which it applied, and zero otherwise. Financing data were downloaded from VentureXpert and Crunchbase and filtered to that window; where both sources existed, Crunchbase was used for rounds prior to the first VentureXpert round, and startups without any financing data were listed as having zero external financing. The threshold was chosen because investors report that contracts above it generally are more complicated and have clear milestones.
time_window: two years after graduation of the cohort to which the startup applied
