description: Log(1+x), where x represents the total amount of financing each startup raised in the two years after having applied to MassChallenge, constructed from the same aggregated external financing data used for the dichotomous funding measure.

Dummy variable set to one when a startup had 15 or more employees within the first two years after the graduation of the cohort to which it applied, and zero otherwise. Employment was collected from LinkedIn, counting only non-founder and non-intern workers listing employment in the startup. The threshold was chosen because the investors interviewed suggested it indicated when a firm was transitioning from exploring potential business models to executing a specific one that had shown promise.
time_window: two years after graduation of the cohort to which the startup applied

description: Log(1+x), where x is the total number of employees at the startup, counted from LinkedIn as non-founder, non-intern workers listing employment in the startup within the first two years after graduation of the cohort to which it applied.
time_window: two years after graduation of the cohort to which the startup applied

description: Indicator distinguishing accelerated startups founded in the same entrepreneurial ecosystem as the accelerator from those founded elsewhere. It was coded from the startup's location as given in its MassChallenge application, which allowed coding of geography; for startups that did not provide their location at the zip code level, web searches were conducted to supplement the information.

A distance-weighted count of distinct early-stage investors with headquarters near the startup's founding zip code, built from VentureXpert information on all investment activity in the three years before each application year to MassChallenge. Each startup's headquarters was geocoded to latitude and longitude based on the center of its zip code, counts of the resource were collected within one-mile bands from the startup, and more-distant resources were weighted less following the Sorenson and Audia proximity index. An increase of one in the index can come from one additional investor within a mile of the startup's founding headquarters, from two additional investors more than a mile but less than two miles away, and so on.
time_window: three years before each application year

description: A distance-weighted count of entrepreneurship networking meetings near the startup's founding zip code. Data on entrepreneurial meetup groups in the United States were collected from Meetup.com, capturing the number of entrepreneurship group meetings held in each U.S. zip code, and the proximity index was computed as the distance-weighted count of proximate opportunities using the Sorenson and Audia formula. An increase of one in the index can correspond to one additional networking event within a mile of the startup's founding headquarters, two events within two miles but greater than one mile, and so on.

KLD rates each company on eight attributes of CSP, using a five-step scale from 'major strength' to 'major weakness' for the first five attributes, which were converted to numerical values with +2 representing a major strength and -2 representing a major weakness; the last three attributes, on which KLD assesses only weaknesses, have values of -2, -1, or 0. A weighted average across the eight attribute ratings, using weights developed by Ruf, Muralidhar, and Paul (1993), yields a single-value CSP index for each company. The index ranges from -2.0, for companies rated lowest on all eight attributes, to +1.66, for those rated highest on all eight.

The number of institutions that held shares in each company. Institutional ownership data were taken from Standard & Poor's Stock Guides for mid-1991. This measure served as the dependent variable in models 1 through 3.

variable_name: Percent of shares owned by institutions
description: The percentage of each company's outstanding shares owned by institutions. Institutional ownership data were taken from Standard & Poor's Stock Guides for mid-1991. This measure served as the dependent variable in models 4 through 6.

PIMS questions about relative prices and relative direct costs per unit were used to define the strategy matrix and the 69 business units were categorized accordingly. PIMS expresses relative cost and price positions in percentage terms in comparison to the average for the three largest competitors, with 100 percent indicating parity. The median cut points were 100 percent for cost and 102 percent for price, giving roughly equal cells: pure cost, pure differentiation, cost and differentiation, and no competitive advantage. The measure captures realized rather than intended strategy.

Each business unit manager chose one of seven categories describing 'your role in determining what action has been taken' for each of 15 typical recurring business decisions affecting the business's strategic position, with categories ranging from 'My initiative/My decision' to 'Initiated by others/Not consulted'. These questions were designed to capture the degree of direct influence those outside the business unit (principally the corporate head office) have upon business decisions. A principal components analysis of the 15 autonomy variables was conducted and the factor score on the first principal component was used as the autonomy variable. The sample was then divided between those with high autonomy scores and those with low autonomy scores.
scale: seven response categories per decision; first principal component factor score

description: Respondents were asked 'How often are important aspects of this business's performance formally reviewed by your superiors?' and checked one of: day-to-day, weekly, monthly, quarterly, semi-annually, annually or longer. For the analysis the sample was split into frequent reviews, with an interval between reviews of 3 months or less, and infrequent reviews occurring at longer intervals, more than 3 months.
scale: seven response categories, from day-to-day to annually or longer

description: For each key function—manufacturing, applied research and engineering, sales force and marketing—the business unit head was asked to check one of the following: I or one of my managers (1) have direct (line) responsibility; (2) share responsibility with someone in another part of the company; (3) do not have direct line responsibility; (4) not applicable. Fifty-five percent of the business units indicated they had completely self-contained functional responsibility, responding with number 1 for all functions, while the remainder had, to some degree, shared functional responsibility; the sample was divided into those with self-contained and those with shared functional responsibility.
scale: four response categories per key function

description: Pretax return on investment, computed using PIMS definitions and taking a 4-year average for each business unit. In the analysis the average ROI of strategy classes is compared between subgroups of business units differing in organizational context.

Real sales growth, computed using PIMS definitions and taking a 4-year average for each business unit. In the analysis the average sales growth of strategy classes is compared between subgroups of business units differing in organizational context.

variable_name: Volume of wrongdoing associated with a negative event
description: Measured as the sum of legislative references associated with a major NCAA infraction by a focal university in a given year. A major infraction is defined as a violation of NCAA rules that results in significant recruiting, competitive, or other advantages for a university's athletic program. Each major infraction is associated with a number of legislative references, each of which refers to a specific NCAA rule that a university violated (e.g., recruiting violations, impermissible compensation, and impermissible financial aid awards to athletes). Information was obtained from the NCAA's Legislative Services Database; universities in the sample were cited for 803 legislative references.

Binary variable equal to one if the university was ranked among the top-50 universities by U.S. News and World Report in a given year, and zero otherwise. The authors used the top-50 cut-off because the top-50 universities were listed on the first page of the report and because visitors to the USNWR rankings webpage could view no more than 50 universities per page.

Binary variable equal to one if a university-year observation corresponded to undergraduate alumni donations and zero if the university-year observation corresponded to non-alumni donations. The authors used this proxy because, on average, alumni identification with a university is higher than that of non-alumni.

Measured as the natural logarithm of inflation-adjusted donations (based on 1999 U.S. dollars) by non-alumni, as well as by undergraduate alumni, to a given university in the year subsequent to an NCAA major infraction (t+1). Support from low-identification stakeholders is the donation amount given by individuals who do not have direct ties to the university (they did not attend the university, are not members of the faculty or staff, and are not parents of attending students). Support from high-identification stakeholders is the donation amount given to a university by its undergraduate alumni.

An objective proxy for the attributes of a firm's dynamic capabilities based on the technological sophistication of its seismic imaging and well drilling technologies used in full-scale projects. For drilling, firms with only vertical drilling received a value of 1, firms that also had directional drilling 2, firms with horizontal drilling 3, and firms with multilateral drilling 4. For seismic imaging, firms with only 2D imaging received a value of 1, firms with 3D technology 2, and firms with 4D technology 3. Once a firm started to deploy a technology in a full-scale application it was coded as having this attribute in the first year of full-scale use and all subsequent years. Because imaging and drilling work in concert, the two were combined into a single measure.
scale: imaging 1-3 and drilling 1-4 combined into a summary variable (observed range 2-7)

description: Annual expenditures on oil exploration, including up-front payments to lease a property or purchase land as well as costs of topographical, geographical and geophysical studies, drilling and equipment, and personnel. Expenditures in a given year are included regardless of whether they are capitalized or expensed for accounting purposes. Dollar values are converted to real 2000 dollars and then to natural logarithms; because some firms had zero expenditures, zero values were first converted to a value of one dollar before the log transformation.
scale: natural logarithm of US dollars (real 2000 dollars)

description: Annual expenditures on oil development, incurred in fields where exploration has been successful and companies have booked proved reserves. They include costs of seismic and land surveys, drilling of additional wells, and personnel and equipment. Values are converted to real 2000 dollars and then to natural logarithms, with zero values first converted to one dollar.
scale: natural logarithm of US dollars (real 2000 dollars)

description: The number of successful exploratory wells drilled, that is, wells for which proved reserves are booked because they are anticipated to contain economically viable amounts of oil. Because the distribution of successful wells is highly skewed and some firms have zero successful wells in some years, the counts were converted to natural logarithmic values using the same procedure as for expenditures.

The number of successful development wells drilled, that is, wells for which the presence of commercially viable amounts of oil is confirmed. As with exploratory wells, the skewed counts were converted to natural logarithmic values using the same procedure as for expenditures.

The breadth of a film's release, interpreted as indicating filmmakers' conformity to soficas' market finance logic: the more prints distributed (and thus screens occupied) in the first week of exploitation, the closer the release strategy is to the blitz model. It is the natural log of the number of prints distributed, chosen because print numbers are directly under filmmakers' control and illustrate concrete engagement by a production organization.

The natural log of the amounts invested by soficas, constructed by identifying production contracts involving soficas from the Film Public Register and retrieving the amounts invested from the contract details. When more than one sofica invested in a film, the amounts were summed. Total investment amount was used rather than the proportion of sofica investments in a film's total budget, and the variable was treated as endogenous and instrumented by a film's budget and the overall investments made via soficas in the production year.

A count of the number of "art & essai" movies a director had been involved with before directing the focal film. The "art & essai" classification was created during the Nouvelle Vague movement by directors, critics, and theater owners and signals directors' allegiance to the industry's established culturally oriented logic. The measure focuses on directors' track records because directors, not producers, are legally entitled to decide on the final cut.

The normalized value of a sofica's average degree centrality in the resource providers' network, computed by counting the number of ties to a given sofica over a three-year window; ties formed in projects that were never completed were included to avoid a common statistical bias. Ties were assumed to remain active for three years. Organizations not involved with soficas were assigned a value of zero, and normalized degree centrality was computed using UCINET 6.289.
The accumulated number of films financed by soficas as of the calendar month in which a focal film entered production, divided by 1,000.
time_window: as of the calendar month in which a focal film entered production

description: The total number of times a focal patent was cited by subsequent patents, excluding self-citations, counted over the period 1985-96. Patents cited in future developments by other firms are treated as more relevant, innovative, and important than patents that are disregarded. Forward citations are the paper's indicator of impact.

A count of the number of cited patents held by the same division as the focal patent, obtained by examining the focal patent's citation pattern. It is one of the three counts used to classify the source of the knowledge used by an invention.

A count of the number of cited patents held by another division in the same organization as the focal patent, obtained by examining the focal patent's citation pattern. It is one of the three counts used to classify the source of the knowledge used by an invention.

A count of the number of cited patents held by another organization, obtained by examining the focal patent's citation pattern. It is one of the three counts used to classify the source of the knowledge used by an invention.

variable_name: Capability constraints: distance from existing technical capabilities (ξ1)
description: Two survey items measure the extent to which respondents preferred internal development over external sourcing when their existing technical capabilities were close to the needed capabilities (capability closeness, item 1) and when they had a strong competitive position in the technical area (capability strength, item 2). Managers rated their agreement on a seven-point scale (1 = fully disagree, 7 = fully agree). The Cronbach alpha for ξ1 is 0.74.

variable_name: Capability constraints: distance from existing marketing capabilities (ξ2)
description: Three survey items measure the extent to which respondents preferred internal development to external sourcing when their existing marketing capabilities were close to the needed capabilities (capability closeness, item 1), when they had a strong competitive position in the marketing area (capability strength, item 2), and when they already knew the customers in the targeted capability area (capability strength, item 3). Items were rated on a seven-point agreement scale. The Cronbach alpha for ξ2 is 0.77.

variable_name: Internal social constraints: fit with systems (ξ3)
description: Three survey items report the extent to which respondents preferred internal development to external sourcing when the needed capabilities fit their firm's system of incentives and culture (item 1), when the firm's system of incentives suited hiring the needed people (item 2), and when their firm had systems in place to integrate newly hired people (item 3). Items were rated on a seven-point agreement scale. The Cronbach alpha for ξ3 is 0.71.

variable_name: Internal social constraints: social acceptance of targeted capabilities (ξ4)
description: Two survey items report the extent to which respondents preferred internal development to external sourcing when the needed capabilities triggered little or no internal competition (item 1) or created little or no internal resistance (item 2). Items were rated on a seven-point agreement scale. The Cronbach alpha for ξ4 is 0.81.

variable_name: Firm's effectiveness in creating new capabilities (η1)
description: Respondents assessed the effectiveness of their firms in creating new capabilities compared with that of their main competitors in three capability areas: R&D capabilities, information technology capabilities, and marketing capabilities (customer knowledge, branding, and pricing). The three items use a seven-point scale, with 1 for 'behind competition' and 7 for 'ahead of competition.' The variable is used as a mediating variable in the analysis of survival.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = behind competition, 7 = ahead of competition)

description: Denotes whether the responding firms continued to operate in 2005, five years after the survey. The dependent variable takes the value of 1 for dissolved firms, 2 for acquired firms, and 3 for surviving firms; the authors note that both dissolved and acquired firms typically were troubled firms but that they maintained the distinction because acquisition does not necessarily represent a negative economic outcome.

The number of key contacts a manager maintains, measured as the total number of unique direct ties reported. It has a possible range of 0-12 unique key contacts, and no respondent reported more than 11 key contacts, with an average of 6. Contacts were named in the ego-centered network assessment for the task-advice, idea-generation and social support networks.

A proportional density measure that calculates the number of indirect ties among contacts as the proportion of all possible ties, used to reduce the influence of direct ties. An indirect tie is said to exist if respondents indicate that the relationship between any two of their contacts was closer than simply 'arm's-length' (a 2 or higher on a 5-point closeness scale); no indirect tie is said to exist for a 0 (no relationship) or 1 (arm's-length relationship). The variable ranges from 0 (no or only arm's-length relations among contacts) to 1 (every contact interacts with every other contact, a closed network).
A variable for network closure coded 1 for fully closed networks, i.e. where Indirect ties = 1, and 0 otherwise, added to the regression models to test the closure argument.

Respondents were asked how close they felt to their contact in their working relationship, on a 1-5 Likert-type scale where 1 is 'distant: arm's-length' and 5 is 'very close', with emotional distance implied. Closeness takes the average level of closeness across a manager's key contacts.

Three Likert-type items comprise the scale for relational trust, covering perceptions of honesty and truthfulness in exchange (Integrity), perceptions of competence in ongoing interactions (Competence), and alignment of goals and values (Predictability); respondents agreed or disagreed with each item on a 1-5 scale. Factor analysis confirmed the existence of a single factor and a scale was constructed with an alpha of 0.68. Relational trust takes the average level of trust across contacts.

HR directors were asked to carefully consider a manager's product portfolio and rate the manager's contribution to the overall sales of those products in the past 6 months, taking into account factors such as the age of the products, market size and the regulatory environment, on a 1-7 scale from 'Weak' to 'Outstanding'. The assessments were made three months after the main questionnaire. Deviation scores (raw scores minus country means) were used to control for local setting differences.

HR directors were asked to carefully consider their managers' efforts in generating and implementing new ideas in their companies in the past 6 months and to comparatively rate the managers within their company on a 1-7 scale from 'Weak' to 'Outstanding'. Managerial innovation in this setting meant managers devising and implementing adaptations to local work practices and product/service offerings. Deviation scores (raw scores minus country means) were used.

Binary indicator that equaled 1 for firms that offered TQM as a consulting service and 0 otherwise. It was coded from the consulting services listed for each firm in the Kennedy directories, whose list of consulting services first included the category 'TQM' in 1992.

Binary indicator equaling 1 if the consulting firm was affiliated with the American Society for Quality (formerly the American Society for Quality Control) and 0 otherwise. It is one of three binary indicators of related expertise taken from the Kennedy Directories.
Binary indicator equaling 1 if a firm provided manufacturing advisory services and 0 otherwise. It is one of three binary indicators of related expertise taken from the Kennedy Directories.

Binary indicator equaling 1 if the firm was affiliated with the American Society for Training and Development and 0 otherwise. It is one of three binary indicators of related expertise taken from the Kennedy Directories.

Binary indicator variable for generalists that took a value of 1 for consultants that offered more than three service categories and 0 otherwise. The service categories are the ten high-level categories into which the Kennedy directory groups services offered by consulting firms.

A count, ranging from 1 to 10, of the total service categories that firms reported being active in. It is the alternate measure of generalism versus specialism used alongside the binary generalist indicator.

variable_name: Directory year (fashion boom versus fashion bust)
description: The five Kennedy directories published between 1992 and 2001 supply the time points, and coefficients from models estimated separately for each year are compared across the boom and the bust. The fashion boom ended in the early 1990s, with the volume of discourse peaking in 1993 (between the first and second data points), and the fashion bust extended and intensified through the rest of the study period; the dating of the cycle is taken from annual counts of TQM articles indexed by ABI/Inform.

Categorical variable set equal to one if firm i enters class j in year t, and zero otherwise. Firm i enters class j when it introduces its first product into that class; subsequent introductions of additional products into that class are not considered entries. Once a firm enters a class it is not at risk of entering that class again.

A count of the number of firms that enter class j in year t. It is the dependent variable of the negative binomial estimation of fringe firm entry into each class as a function of HP's presence, among other characteristics.

Indicator equal to one if HP competes in class j in year t, and zero otherwise. The authors state that it captures the initial (shift) effect of HP's entry on segment price, and it is used in the price, sales and class-level entry models.

Indicator equal to one if firm i is HP, and zero otherwise. It is entered in an augmented price model together with HPDum * HPClock to determine whether HP's printers are priced differently than those of fringe firms.

The price charged for printer k produced by firm i in class j in year t. The authors report models using the list price because the list price data are significantly more complete than the street price data. Results using the street price data are substantively the same.
Measured as the natural log of the number of printer units sold (plus 1) in class j in year t. Unit sales data, by printer model, is aggregated at the class-year level.

Categorical variable set equal to one if firm i exits class j in year t, and zero otherwise. Firm i exits class j when it ceases to ship any product in that class; withdrawing one or more products while continuing to sell at least one other product in the class does not count as an exit.

Growth of unit sales across all classes in which firm i competes, computed as the sum of unit sales across those classes at time t minus the sum of unit sales across the same classes at time (t - 1), divided by the sum of unit sales across the same classes at time (t - 1). The authors interact it with the HP dummy to test whether the dominant firm is more likely to enter a new class as sales growth in its existing classes falls.

Number of classes that firm i already competes in at time t that are in the same DPI row as class j, normalized. The authors argue that because laser printer firms' research capabilities are specialized to particular resolutions, entering new segments within an existing DPI range allows a firm to exploit its current technological capabilities.

Number of classes that firm i already competes in at time t that are in the same PPM column as class j, normalized. It is used as a comparison with SameDPI, because innovation along the speed dimension is generally undertaken by laser engine suppliers rather than by printer firms; the authors expected the DPI coefficient to be larger.

Indicator equal to one if, at time t, firm i already competes in at least one class that is directly adjacent to class j, and zero otherwise. It is interacted with the HP dummy to compare fringe and dominant firm entry into adjacent segments.

Indicator that identifies firms that precede HP into a class: one if firm i entered class j before HP has entered class j (if HP has not entered class j by 1996, then this is one for all firms in class j, zero otherwise). The authors note that this variable does not vary with time, hence it does not distinguish between time periods before and after HP's entry.
time_window: defined over the sample period (not time varying)

description: Time-varying indicator equal to one if firm i entered class j before HP has entered class j and HP has entered class j as of time t, and zero otherwise. Firms that follow HP into a class form the omitted category in the exit hazard model, so the coefficient compares preceders after HP's entry with followers.

Measured as the total amount of money awarded over the total amount requested, ranging between zero and one. The variable equals zero when an R&D project application is not selected for funding and equals one when an application is fully funded; partially funded projects take intermediate values. The authors confirm partial funding by analyzing the comments provided to the applicant by selectors. Over the sample period 244 (43%) applications were fully funded and 126 (22%) received no funding.

From the text of the expertise descriptions the authors derive the most frequently occurring words, pairs of words and triplets of words using a cut-off value of at least 10 occurrences, yielding a list of 574 keywords validated by senior managers. They examine which of these keywords appeared in the texts of the 556 project applications and construct all possible pairs of keywords that could occur in a proposal, then derive the proportion of these pairwise combinations that had never appeared in the company's expertise location system. The measure is new to the firm rather than new to the world. A squared term is included to test for curvilinearity.

Derived by counting the total number of characters in all project proposals evaluated in a given meeting and subtracting the character length of the focal R&D project proposal. Over the three financial years in the sample period the selection panels held 104 review meetings and evaluated a total of 913 project proposals, of which 556 were R&D proposals.

A cluster analysis using the Ward method with Euclidean distances on the co-occurrence matrix of the 574 keywords, derived from the entire set of 3,131 skill descriptions in the expertise location system, identifies 19 clusters of keywords describing different domains of engineering knowledge. Each selector's expertise profile is represented by a vector of 19 elements, and the Euclidean distance between each member's profile and those of all other panel members is calculated. The resulting panel expertise diversity variable is normalized by the number of possible dyadic combinations of the 19 expertise domains; the formulas are not readable in the supplied text.
A dummy variable equal to one if an R&D project applicant and at least one of the members of the selection panel work in the same location, and zero otherwise.
A dummy variable taking the value one if the director candidate up for election is female and zero if the director candidate is male. Gender information for directors was provided by ISS.

The percentage of votes that oppose the election of uncontested director candidates at the annual shareholder meeting. 'Abstain' votes are also considered expressions of shareholder dissent, and in plurality voting systems 'withheld' votes are considered dissenting votes; shares that are 'not voted' are not counted. The variable is log transformed because the vote distribution is skewed.
The number of female directors on the board divided by the number of all directors on the board in a firm-year.

Based on the rate of shareholder returns for the 12 months preceding the shareholder meeting, expressed as negative abnormal shareholder returns relative to the two-digit SIC industry benchmark. Negative abnormal returns are calculated by subtracting shareholder returns of the focal firm from the median shareholder returns in the two-digit SIC industry; positive values indicate firm underperformance relative to industry returns and negative values suggest firm overperformance.

Media controversies in environmental, social, and governance (ESG) matters that a company was exposed to in the year before the shareholder meeting, taken from the Thomson Eikon ESG database, which monitors global news sources for reporting that ties companies to controversial issues in 23 ESG domains. Curated controversies that materially impact the corporation are counted; for each firm and each year the authors summed up all media controversies reported by Thomson.

A dummy variable taking the value one if the director failed to attend at least 75% of board meetings in a given firm-year and zero otherwise. Firms report when a director does not attend at least 75% of board meetings, which indicates problematic board attendance.
A variable taking the value one if the director is nonindependent (e.g., the chief executive officer (CEO) or another executive holding a board position) and the value zero otherwise.
Return on assets, one of the two performance indicators. Performance data were supplemented by DataStream. Table 1 notes that the values are normalized using the Van der Waerden formula.

Tobin's q, the market performance indicator. Performance data were supplemented by DataStream. Table 1 notes that the values are normalized using the Van der Waerden formula, and the table note records that market capitalization was not available for one firm.

A 0/1 variable that distinguishes firms that have at least one woman on their boards from those that have none. The authors state that the measure of the presence of women on boards represents cumulative nominations over time, whereas the performance indicators are at one point in time, which introduces a time lag.
A 0/1 indicator of government ownership. It is entered in the models as a moderator of the relationship between women on boards and performance (Women x government).
A 0/1 indicator of family ownership. It is entered in the models as a moderator of the relationship between women on boards and performance (Women x family).

Ownership concentration, measured as the proportion of shares owned by the largest five shareholders. It is entered in the models as a moderator of the relationship between women on boards and performance (Women x ownership concentration).

Board ethnic diversity measured with the Simpson diversity index, D = 1 - sum of p_i squared, where p represents the proportion of individuals in category i and N is the number of categories. A diversity score equal to 0 means that all directors are of the same ethnic group.

Board independence, a board structure characteristic entered as a moderator of the relationship between women on boards and performance (Women x board independence). The paper describes independent boards as boards free of the demands of close relationships with management. Table 1 reports the variable together with its operation measure; the prose does not describe the coding further.

Two perceptual indicators were used to assess uncertainty, patterned after measures used in previous research on environmental uncertainty and adapted to the social and political dimensions of the environment. The first indicator measured perceived environmental complexity and consisted of the summed scale of five questionnaire items (alpha = .90), with a possible and actual range of responses from 5 to 35. The second indicator consisted of a summed scale of four questionnaire items (alpha = .79) assessing perceived environmental turbulence, with possible and actual responses ranging from 4 to 28. Each item was answered on a seven-point scale anchored by contrasting statements.

Buffering was conceptualized as being reflected in activities related to social stakeholders, political stakeholders, or both, and nine questionnaire items were used to assess the level of buffering activities carried out by the public affairs function. Six items assessed political buffering and three assessed social buffering; the items cover such issues as PAC contributions, advocacy advertising, and use of lobbyists. Respondents rated how active the firm was in each endeavor on a scale from 1, not at all active, to 5, extremely active. Overall, buffering scores ranged from 11 to 45.

Bridging was conceptualized as being reflected in activities related to social stakeholders, political stakeholders, or both, and six questionnaire items were used to assess the level of bridging activities carried out by the public affairs function. Three items assessed social bridging and three assessed political bridging, covering such matters as aggressive compliance with regulation and legislation and speed of adaptation to changing social expectations. Items were rated either on importance to firm success (1, of little importance, to 5, of great importance) or on how accurately statements described the firm (1, very inaccurate, to 5, very accurate). Overall, bridging scores ranged from 8 to 30.

Two indicators were used to capture the size construct: the value of firms' assets, which ranged from $285 million to $137 billion in this sample, and the number of employees (from 1,499 to 209,000). These data were collected from 10-K reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

This construct was measured according to the response to an item on the questionnaire. Each respondent assessed, on a scale of 1 to 7, whether the goods or services provided by his or her firm were best described as necessities or luxuries, with 1 representing the statement that the products or services provided are vital necessities in today's society and 7 representing that they are luxury items. Actual ratings ranged from 1 to 7.

The number of times a firm had been mentioned in the press was used to assess visibility. Mentions of each firm in five major newspapers (the New York Times, Washington Post, Los Angeles Times, Atlanta Constitution, and Boston Globe) over a 15-month period, from January 1991 to March 1992, were identified by an electronic search of article abstracts for company names. The number of mentions of each firm in each paper were summed to yield a visibility score, and scores ranged from 0 to 348.

Two indicators were used to capture the enterprise strategy construct: management's emphasis on collaboration and management's philosophy toward taking the initiative on social issues. Emphasis on collaboration was assessed by examining the latest two annual president's letters to shareholders for each responding firm, counting references to collaboration or cooperation with external stakeholders (such as competitors, the government, or local communities) with the level determined by summing the number of such references over the past two years; collaboration scores ranged from 0 to 7. Social initiative philosophy was captured using a questionnaire item on the firm's philosophy toward social issues, ranging from wanting to be a pioneer in complying with new social expectations to waiting until laws are passed and then complying.
scale: collaboration 0 to 7; social initiative questionnaire item
time_window: latest two annual president's letters to shareholders

description: The logged count of reviews for each app-month observation. The distribution of review counts is highly skewed, so a logged measure is used; 0.01 is added to all review counts before logging to account for apps that have not yet received a review. Review count and the download measure are highly correlated (0.79), and only users who have downloaded an app can give it a review score in Google Play.
time_window: each app-month observation from entry through the data collection period

description: Calculated by dividing the count of words in a focal app's text description that are also words from the category's top 50 words by the total number of words in the focal app's text description. The top 50 words are identified from the descriptions of all apps (not only de novo apps) in each of Google Play's 41 categories on a monthly basis, using the top 50 words used in the focal app's category the month before it was first published. A score of 0.0 indicates the focal app does not use any of its category's top 50 words; a score of 1.0 indicates an app uses only words from its category's top 50 words list.
time_window: the month prior to the focal app's first publication

description: The cosine similarity between the focal app's word vector and the vector of each of the top 100 most installed apps (the exemplar apps) in its category in the month before the focal app was first published; the single highest cosine similarity score (the nearest top 100 neighbor) is used as the measure. Vectors are lists of all words in an app's cleansed text description (stemmed words only, stop words removed, English descriptions only). A score of 0.0 indicates the focal app shares no words with any of the top 100 apps; a score of 1.0 indicates a text description identical to at least one of its category's top 100 apps.
time_window: the month prior to the focal app's first publication

variable_name: Japanese vs. U.S. venture capital firm
description: The sample consists of 20 Japanese venture capital companies with investments in the United States and 20 U.S. venture capital firms with similar investments. The Japanese group comprised 15 venture capital subsidiaries and 5 partnership funds, while the U.S. group consisted of 4 venture capital subsidiaries and 16 partnership funds.

Respondents reported the number of ventures in the firm's venture investment portfolio. The authors classify portfolios as small (fewer than 50 ventures) or large (more than 50 ventures) and control for the age of the venture capital investment program (young = started in 1981 or later; old = pre-1981). Japanese firms reported between 100 and 400 venture investments while only one U.S. firm had invested in more than 100 ventures.

Respondents reported the size of the firm's typical contribution to the total cost of a venture and its typical investment in a single venture over time. Responses were given as ranges; 18 Japanese firms reported a smallest investment between $100,000 and $300,000, and 12 U.S. firms reported a largest individual investment in the $5-20 million range.

Two sets of questions were used: one asked for the proportion of loss-making and negative cash flow ventures in the portfolio; the other asked for the proportion of ventures at break-even and in the profit and positive cash flow region.

An open-ended question asked firms to state their venturing objective. Responses were classified into categories such as ROI and technology; 14 U.S. firms reported ROI as their venturing objective while 17 Japanese firms reported technology.

Respondents reported their reasons for choosing target industries. Both groups reported similar reasons such as strategic directives, diversification, strategic fit, the search for future business relations, financial and market forecasts, and venture management's technical ability and managerial skills.

Respondents reported their reasons for selecting target ventures. Most U.S. firms used sales and profit forecasts and assessments of the venture management's technical and managerial abilities, while most Japanese firms chose ventures based on measures related to the investing firm.
Respondents reported the frequency with which they monitored or reviewed venture performance; the authors compared the frequency across the two groups.

Respondents reported the measures they used to evaluate venture performance. Categories include fit with existing technology and transferability of the new technology (measures related to the investing firm) and ROI and market growth (measures related to the venture).

Respondents reported whether they managed ventures at arms' length or provided supportive measures. Supportive measures include appointing executives to the venture's board of directors, transfer of managerial staff to the venture, and other administrative support.

An open-ended question asked how the firm culminated its venture investment. Japanese responses included retaining stock or transferring it to a sister firm in the keiretsu and commencing business relations such as joint ventures; U.S. responses included negotiated sale of stock to private investors, sale of stock to venture management and employees, and public sale of stock.

Total research and development expenditures divided by total sales. R&D expenditures were merged in from the Nikkei Economic Electronic Database Systems (NEEDS). The variable was Winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5th percentiles along with ROA, unabsorbed slack, growth opportunities, and advertising.

The firm's actual ROA subtracted from the aspiration level, where ROA is operating income divided by total firm assets. The aspiration level was constructed as AL = 0.8 × SA + 0.2 × HA, where historical aspiration HA is a weighted average of past performance (0.7 × ROA t-1 + 0.2 × ROA t-2 + 0.1 × ROA t-3) and social aspiration SA is the average ROA of all other firms in the focal firm's industry. In the spline regression this variable captures the slope of R&D on performance for observations below the aspiration level.
time_window: t-1 to t-3 for the historical aspiration component

description: A spline variable equal to ROA − AL if ROA > AL and zero otherwise. It was constructed to assess whether the slope of the relationship between R&D and performance relative to aspirations differs for performance above versus below the aspiration level. Setting the inflection point at ROA = AL was indicated because inflection points slightly above or below the aspiration level tended to reduce model fit.

The total number of shares owned by Japanese financial institutions and other Japanese business corporations divided by total shares outstanding. Larger values equate to more power and more influence for this type of owner. The measure combines financial and nonfinancial owners because prior research has shown that both act in ways consistent with a communitarian perspective.
time_window: end of the previous year (one-year lag)

description: The total number of shares owned by foreigners divided by total shares outstanding. Larger values equate to more power and more influence for this type of owner. Although foreign owners can come from various countries, the authors note that a majority of foreign owners in Japan are portfolio investors from the United States and the U.K.
time_window: end of the previous year (one-year lag)

description: The timing of entry into the ATM subfield, which the authors say reflects pioneering tendencies and captures differences between pioneers entering in the early years of the data period and those entering in later years. The variable is coded by years elapsed since entry: a firm entering in 1974 was coded 0,0,0,1,2,3,4,5,6 for the 9-year panel ending in 1979, a firm entering in 1971 was recorded as 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9, and nonentrants were recorded as zero for the entire panel. Higher values therefore indicate earlier entry.

Return on assets, described by the authors as the predominant measure of financial performance in the commercial banking industry and as the indicator most closely watched by bank analysts and bankers. The authors state that ROA has the advantage of permitting comparison across firms of varying size and of capturing the entry's overall impact on the firm.

Net income, used as a second performance measure in order to improve the reliability of the findings. The authors state that both ROA and net income have the advantage of being indicators of overall firm performance.

The bank's degree of specialization on a Specialist/Generalist continuum, defined in terms of its product mix, that is, the ratio of demand deposits to total deposits. Specialists had a higher ratio of demand deposits to total deposits, while Generalist banks had more diversified portfolios and lower values on the mix variable. The authors state that this mix of deposits is a meaningful indicator of niche width and that the measure may not be sufficient to capture the nuances of the true niche width construct.

Population density indicates the number of banks operating in each banking market. The authors note that the average market in the data consisted of 73 banks (S.D. = 100, minimum = 2, maximum = 408 banks).

PRIOR captures the proportion of market competitors that have entered the ATM subfield. The authors use it to represent the portion of the competitive population that had already entered the subfield when a bank entered.

A dummy variable reflecting the presence or absence of regulations mandating the sharing of ATMs with competing banks. The authors state that where mandatory sharing was instituted a new entrant could imitate competitors' entries with relative ease, whereas in markets where proprietary networks were protected entry was difficult to imitate and later entrants would have to spend heavily to match entrenched competitors' service levels.

Indicator variable coded = 1 if the license is exclusive and = 0 if nonexclusive. It was coded from details about the licensing alliance disclosed in press reports; two coders whose coding agreed approximately 82 percent of the time did the coding, with the authors exercising judgment in the remaining cases.
Indicator variable for one of four distinct types of licenses used in the multinomial logit models: licenses that are exclusive and unrestricted in scope (worldwide).

variable_name: exclusive licenses with product scope restrictions
description: Indicator variable for exclusive licenses whose scope is restricted by product (field-of-use). In the reported analyses licenses restricted by both geographic and product scope were coded as geographically restricted.

variable_name: exclusive licenses with geographic scope restrictions
description: Indicator variable for exclusive licenses whose scope is restricted by geography, always by country or region.
Indicator variable coded = 1 if the license required investments in any complementary assets by the licensee. Coding was done from careful examination of the news articles on each license.

Indicator variable coded = 1 if the licensee was expected to undertake R&D activities to complement, evaluate, or otherwise develop the licensed technologies. These investments are largely in intangibles, which are inherently quite technology-specific.

Indicator variable coded = 1 when investments usually related to building a plant, modifying existing production facilities, or developing production technologies relating to the licensed technology. These are mostly in tangible capital goods, which are arguably more redeployable despite being somewhat dedicated at the time of investment.

Indicator variable coded = 1 when investments related to obtaining regulatory and market clearances, as well as advertising, sales, or distribution for products developed from the technology. In the geographic scope analyses the authors also examine marketing-only investment, defined as marketing investment without R&D investment, and its interaction with international licensing.

Indicator variable coded = 1 if the licensed technology was early stage and = 0 otherwise, where an early stage technology is defined as one for which no proof of concept or prototype existed at the time of licensing; for therapeutic drugs, licensing before the second phase of clinical trials was coded as early stage. It was coded from news reports of the alliances.
Indicator variable that measures if the technology flows across national boundaries in the license.

Indicator variable capturing any additional formal relationships between the firms in a licensing alliance; most of these were equity relationships, with the rest being reciprocal trading relationships. It was included as a control in all analyses and interacted with early stage licensing to test Hypothesis 4.

An indicator of global equity offerings. It equals 1 if an issuing firm allocates sizable shares to be offered in the global capital markets at the IPO stage; if the issue is purely domestic, the indicator equals 0.

Tobin's q for IPO firms is calculated as the ratio of long-term debt plus the market value of equity to total book assets. The market value of equity is the offer price multiplied by the total number of shares outstanding after the IPO.

A dummy variable created for the probit model estimating a firm's propensity to conduct international diversification. It takes the value 1 if a company has foreign sales/income in the year subsequent to its IPO, and 0 otherwise.
time_window: the year subsequent to the IPO

description: An indicator variable that equals one for any treated university, that is, any university located within geographic proximity to any of the five major R&D locations identified in the study. Proximity is defined as 50, 100 or 150 miles as measured by geodetic distances between GPS coordinates, and the treatment is the colocated company's full-fledged entry into plant biotechnology R&D. Post-Entry switches to one in the year that follows the university's treatment, and each control university is assigned the same Post-Entry value as its matched treated university.

Count of a university's publications on scientific topics relevant to plant biotechnology R&D, identified in the Web of Science through a Boolean keyword search in two bodies of knowledge: basic plant physiology and in vivo breeding (mostly the Plant Sciences subject category) and plant molecular biology and genetics (subject categories such as Genetics, Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Biotechnology and Applied Microbiology, and Agronomy). Articles in irrelevant subject categories and field journals dedicated to paleobotany, taxonomy and nonagricultural vegetation were dropped. The dependent variable is a discrete, nonnegative count of publication output.

A quality-adjusted measure of publication output constructed by weighting each publication by its normalized citations, where citation counts are divided by the average of cumulative citations for articles in the respective Web of Science subject category published in the same year. A related outcome used in the same analysis is the average normalized citation per publication.
Count of plant biotechnology articles that include soybean, maize, wheat or cotton, the major cash crops in the United States, in their titles or abstracts.

Number of a university's publications coauthored with the local company, that is, the company located within the specified distance from the focal university. The variable is coded for both treated and control universities, and a control university's coauthorship with the focal company is coded as a local industry coauthorship so that it becomes the counterfactual outcome. Coauthorships with companies located outside the proximity boundary are coded as distant industry coauthorships.

Number of a university's publications that mention industry funding in the acknowledgments, collected from the Web of Science for the years 2008 and 2009. As with coauthorship, the variable is constructed separately for local and distant companies and is coded for both treated and control universities.

Number of a university's publications that cite publications by the local company, that is, the company located within the specified distance from the focal university. Publications of control universities that cite the focal company are also coded as local industry citations so that they serve as a counterfactual outcome, and citations to companies outside the boundary are coded as distant industry citations. Citations made by industry-coauthored university publications are excluded because they could reflect self-citations made by a corporate author.

Number of articles in the journal Plant Physiology that report a change in author address from university to any of the five anchor tenants in the study. The measure primarily captures instances where late-stage PhD and postdoctoral studies get published after these researchers move to industry jobs. The variable is constructed for a subset of universities that publish in the journal, separately for movement to a local company and to a distant company.

variable_name: Graduate student body in industry-relevant disciplines
description: Number of PhD and postdoctoral researchers in industry-relevant disciplines, used as a proxy for industry labor demand for the main panel data analysis. The industry-relevant disciplines are agricultural sciences, botany and entomology, while biochemistry and genetics departments were excluded because their sizes would primarily reflect demand for medical biotechnology.

variable_name: absolute change in aggregate industry specialization at the four-digit level for all incumbent firms
description: The absolute change in aggregate industry specialization at the four-digit SIC level for all incumbent firms between 1981 and 1989. Aggregate specialization for an industry is estimated in two stages: each firm's specialization to the industry is the ratio of its employees in that industry to all of its employees, and the industry value is the weighted mean of these ratios across firms. The measure is multiplied by 100 to give a potential value between 0 and 100.

variable_name: absolute change in aggregate industry specialization at the four-digit level for the largest four firms
description: The absolute change in aggregate industry specialization at the four-digit SIC level between 1981 and 1989 computed only for the largest four incumbent firms in each industry, measured in terms of employees. It is estimated in the same two-stage way as the measure for all firms. This measure is designed to capture the firms most affected by restructuring during the 1980s.

variable_name: absolute change in aggregate industry specialization at the two-digit level for all incumbent firms
description: The absolute change in aggregate industry specialization at the two-digit SIC level for all incumbent firms between 1981 and 1989. At this level the estimate captures the degree to which firms are focused on a group of related (as opposed to unrelated) industries. It is estimated in the same two-stage way as the four-digit measure.

variable_name: absolute change in aggregate industry specialization at the two-digit level for the largest 40 firms
description: The absolute change in aggregate industry specialization at the two-digit SIC level between 1981 and 1989 computed only for the largest 40 incumbent firms in each two-digit industry group. It is estimated in the same two-stage way as the other measures of change in aggregate specialization.

The proportion of industry employees in 1981 who worked in establishments which were sold off by firms which were incumbents in industry j in 1981, but which had exited that industry by 1989. An establishment present in the industry in 1981 and still there in 1989 is treated as sold off if its parent firm ownership changed; sales of entire firms, of lines of business and of parts of lines of business are included. The variable therefore measures the rate at which incumbent firms sold off their entire line of business in the industry.
scale: percentage of total industry employees, potential value between 0 and 100

description: The proportion of industry employees in 1981 who worked in establishments that were sold off by firms which remained as incumbents in industry j between 1981 and 1989. It measures the rate at which firms that stayed as incumbents sold off parts of their line of business in the industry during the period.
scale: percentage of total industry employees, potential value between 0 and 100

description: The proportion of industry employees in 1981 who worked in establishments in 1981 which were closed down by 1989 by firms which had exited industry j by 1989. An establishment is classified as closed if it was present in the industry in 1981 and was not present in that industry in 1989. The variable measures the rate at which incumbent firms shut down their entire line of business in the industry.
scale: percentage of total industry employees, potential value between 0 and 100

description: The proportion of industry employees in 1981 who worked in establishments that were closed down by 1989, and which were owned in 1981 by firms that remained as industry incumbents through 1989. It measures the rate at which incumbent firms closed down capacity in the industry between 1981 and 1989.
scale: percentage of total industry employees, potential value between 0 and 100

description: The proportion of industry employees in 1981 which were added to (removed from) establishments continuously owned by the same incumbent firms between 1981 and 1989. An establishment is classified as expanded if its number of employees increased (or decreased) over the period without a change in its parent firm ownership. If the variable is negative in an industry, incumbent firms reduced their involvement in that industry.
scale: percentage of total industry employees, potential value between 0 and 100

description: The proportion of industry employees who worked in establishments in 1989 that were added to that industry between 1981 and 1989 by firms which remained as industry incumbents between 1981 and 1989. An establishment is classified as added to an industry if it was not in that industry in 1981 but was in that industry in 1989. All restructuring variables are measured in terms of employees rather than numbers of establishments.
scale: percentage of total industry employees, potential value between 0 and 100

description: Company addition to the DS400 index announced between May 1990 and April 2007 for stakeholder-related CSR reasons, drawn from KLD's qualitative (Social Q) screen based on environment, social, and governance factors tied to primary stakeholder groups, such as strong employee relations, diversity strengths, beneficial products and services, and environmental strengths. Announcements related to KLD's exclusionary (Social E) screen, technical reasons, financial distress, or reasons that cannot be unambiguously related to primary stakeholder groups are excluded. The final sample contains 166 addition announcements.

Company deletion from the DS400 index announced between May 1990 and April 2007 for stakeholder-related CSR reasons, drawn from KLD's qualitative (Social Q) screen. Reasons for Social Q deletions include environment or product safety concerns, corporate governance issues or lack of transparency, marketing/contracting concerns, and issues with labor, diversity, or union relations. Announcements related to KLD's exclusionary (Social E) screen, technical reasons, financial distress, or reasons not unambiguously related to primary stakeholder groups are excluded. The final sample contains 28 deletion announcements.

Risk-adjusted excess returns for announcement firms around DS400 reconstitution announcements. A market risk-adjusted expected return for each firm is estimated by regressing daily stock returns on the return of an equally weighted CRSP market index over an estimation period of 255 days ending 46 days before the event. Daily abnormal returns are the differences between actual and expected returns, and cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) are computed for each event window and averaged across firms into cumulative average abnormal returns (CAARs) for the (-3,+3), (+1,+3) and (0,0) windows. Statistical significance is reported using a one-tailed Patell test statistic based on the precision-weighted CAAR.
time_window: 255-day estimation period (t = -255 to -46) and event windows (-3,+3), (+1,+3), (0,0)

description: The same risk-adjusted event study procedure applied to the industry rivals (peers) of each announcement firm. Rivals as of the event date are obtained from CRSP based on the focus firm's four-digit primary SIC code, retaining a peer only if its market cap is within the focus firm's market cap plus or minus 50 percent or if both firms are in the top 25 percent or both in the bottom 25 percent of industry market cap, and events are dropped when companies or industries repeat within a seven-day period. The final samples contain 2,104 peer companies for additions and 204 industry peers for deletions.

variable_name: Industry information opacity (opaque vs. non-opaque industry)
description: Classification of the focus firm's industry sector by information opacity. The nonfinancial services sector (SIC 7xxx-8xxx) is treated as opaque because it is characterized by information opacity stemming from both intangible products and from outcomes tied to intangible customer relationship management factors; the high technology manufacturing sector (SIC 28xx-39xx) is treated as opaque because firms there generally hold significant intangible assets related to R&D activities. The financial sector (SIC 60xx-66xx, excluding 'Holding and Other Investment Offices' 67xx) is singled out for its unique regulatory structure and is discussed within the group of opaque industries, although the authors suggest the regulatory safety net may mitigate information asymmetry for financial service firms. All other industries form the base, non-opaque group, and the opacity premium is measured relative to that group.

Count of patents that each firm had applied for and later received, collected annually for each firm. Patent counts measure technical innovation because patents are an especially strong defense against misappropriation of intellectual property in the medical device industry and are a major intermediate step in the creation of a new MIS device. In all, the sample firms received 2,647 patents during the study period.

Count of FDA product approvals obtained by each firm yearly, combining both types of device approvals. Devices substantively similar to previously approved ones qualify for a 510(k) approval, while radically novel devices require a PMA approval; PMA approvals are about 2 percent of product approvals in the sector. A new product introduction typically closely follows FDA approval. In all, the sample firms received 931 FDA approvals during the study period.

Binary variable set to one if the new firm received a venture capital investment in a year and zero otherwise. When there were missing data or discrepancies between the two fundraising databases, archival sources including Lexis Nexis were used to obtain data and resolve differences.

Binary variable set to one if the new firm received a corporate venture capital investment in a year and zero otherwise. Investment partners were coded as corporate if they provided equity (not loans or public offerings) and were non-financial firms.

Binary variable set to one if the new firm received federal funds from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in a year and zero otherwise. Both NIH research and Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) grants that the focal firm received are included, and their aggregate and separate effects were analyzed.

Firms were coded as '1' if the CEO was the only inside or affiliated member on the board; other board structures were coded as '0.' Across the final sample, boards were allowed to change structure as they adopted or abandoned lone-insider boards.

Excess pay was calculated as the residuals from an OLS regression where CEO total compensation was regressed on factors prior research shows predict CEO pay: firm size (market capitalization), prior performance (ROA), CEO equity ownership (%), CEO age, CEO tenure and tenure-squared, firm stock returns (compounded monthly), and industry and year dummy variables. Positive residuals reflect excess CEO pay and negative residuals reflect 'under-payment.'
The natural log of the difference between CEO total pay and the average total pay of the TMT, i.e., the next four top management team members after the CEO.
An indicator variable depicting instances of non-reliance restatements that were not due to clerical errors or minor accounting issues and are thus considered 'material.'
ROA was calculated as net income divided by total assets. It is one of the two measures used for firm performance.
Calculated as total assets minus deferred taxes plus the market value of equity less book value of equity, all divided by total assets. It is the second measure used for firm performance.
The number of analysts who follow the firm in a given year. It is used as the moderator of the relationship between lone-insider boards and firm outcomes.
The percent of outstanding shares held by institutions. It is used as the moderator of the relationship between lone-insider boards and firm outcomes.

The ratio of an MD's exploratory deals to total deals on that day. Exploratory deals are deals an MD initiates with a new product type he has never sold before and for which he has to build new product and marketing knowledge; in the database, deals with a new product type and deals with a previously sold product type are marked by an indicator variable created by the company. Deals are aggregated to the daily level for each MD, and days on which MDs posted no deals are dropped.
scale: ratio of exploratory to total deals

description: The average revenue of exploratory deals per day in U.S. dollars. For deals that spanned multiple days, the revenue was assigned to the first day and deal duration was controlled for. Monetary figures were converted to U.S. dollars.

A binary variable that takes the value of 1 for all daily observations relating to the period after the incentive change for a focal MD, and 0 for all daily observations relating to the period before. The incentive change replaced performance-based pay (baseline salary plus a monthly agreed-upon percentage of deal profit) with a much higher fixed salary and no performance-based bonus, and was implemented over four months in three waves affecting groups of 6, 30, and 11 MDs. The variable is coded 1 when a focal MD's performance-based pay incentives had been weakened.
time_window: daily observations before and after each MD's change date

description: The MD's average revenue per day before the change, interacted with incentive change to test H2. The variable is included in the individual fixed effects and is thus dropped from the reported results.

Measured by counting the total number of product categories that a focal MD dealt with in the past one week, and interacted with incentive change to test H4. In this context a product category refers to the types of goods sold by a team; for example, in the fashion/accessory team, examples of product categories are jewelry, sneakers, and T-shirts.

The number of contribution documents coauthored by a dyad within a quarter, calculated as a simple count of documents by a dyad in a given working group at a given quarter. Technical reports and proposals and discussion documents are included because they best capture new technical collaborations; change request documents are omitted because they are primarily backward looking and reflect prior cooperative efforts.

Treated dyads (plaintiff-defendant, co-defendant, and defendant-other dyads named in a standard-essential patent suit) are coded as 1 while matched untreated observations are coded as 0. Post-filing is set to 1 for quarters +1 to +4 and 0 otherwise; the treatment effect is captured by the interaction of the treated-dyad indicator with the post-filing indicator.
time_window: four quarters before through four quarters after the filing quarter

description: The Euclidean distance between the dyad members' technological profiles within a working group. A firm's technological profile within a working group is a vector of cumulative document counts, each vector element holding the cumulative number of documents authored by a firm in a technical specification assigned to the working group up to the given quarter. A dyad's technological distance can vary from one working group to another.
time_window: cumulative up to the given quarter

description: The defendant's degree centrality within a working group, calculated as the sum of coauthoring ties with other firms in the working group, excluding the plaintiff. A coauthoring tie has a value of 1 if the defendant had coauthored with the firm within the prior year and 0 otherwise. Because control observations do not have litigation attributes, the measure applies only to treated observations.

Calculated as 1-density, where density is the number of ties between a respondent's contacts (contact-to-contact ties) divided by the maximum number of possible ties between those contacts. The possible range is from 0 (all contacts know one another) to 1 (no contacts know one another); higher sparseness indicates a greater proportion of primary structural holes. The structural measures were calculated from a full structural network adjacency matrix constructed by combining ego network data and information from cited contacts. Sparseness was standardized to allow comparison of its relative impact with knowledge heterogeneity.

Derived from a knowledge distance matrix built from respondents' reporting of the knowledge contribution of each contact and the contact-contact knowledge distances collected on a four-point Likert scale. The uniqueness of each contact is a function of the uniqueness of that contact's own contacts and its distance from them, obtained as the eigenvector of the knowledge distance matrix; heterogeneity of knowledge is defined from contact distances to the respondent and contact uniqueness scores, with a 1/N term to compensate for the eigenvalue increasing linearly with network size. The measure increases linearly with the distance between contacts and with the distance between the respondent and her contacts, and is a monotonically increasing concave function of network size; the mean raw score was 8.98 (S.D. = 5.28). It was standardized.

Senior managers rated each respondent on four subjective items relating to general aspects of managerial task performance using a 7-point scale for the preceding 12 months. A principal component factor analysis of the four items yielded a single factor with an eigenvalue greater than one and a Cronbach alpha of 0.93; the standardized factor score generated by STATA's principal component factor analysis procedure is the measure.

Formed from the last two senior-manager rating items, an assessment of individual creativity and a measure of implementation effectiveness (correlation 0.29, p < 0.05). Because these are antecedent to the latent construct, a formative index was created rather than a reflective scale: the measure is the square root of the product of the two items, capturing the necessity of the joint presence of creativity and implementation skills. The measure was standardized to facilitate comparison of beta coefficients across performance models.

The total number of contacts a respondent cited; no upper limit was placed on the number of contacts respondents were asked to cite, to avoid censoring large ego networks. It was entered in the models as a measure of political opportunity, a cruder measure than sparseness.

Corporate giving was assessed as the amount of a firm's charitable contributions during a specific year, taken from the annual reports' listing of annual spending on charitable and sponsorship activities. The variable was highly skewed, so the authors computed its natural logarithm. The giving measure was taken for year t, and the dependent variable for t + 1.

ROA, calculated as net income over total assets, is a common accounting-based measure of financial performance. It is measured for year t + 1, following the year in which the charitable contributions were made.

The market-to-book ratio is calculated as the book value of a firm's equity divided by the year-end market value of its equity. The authors note it is theoretically and empirically equivalent to Tobin's Q. It is measured for year t + 1, following the year of the charitable contributions.

Firm advertising intensity was calculated as the ratio of selling, general, and administrative expenses to sales. It captures a firm's willingness to spend on marketing and selling-related activities in an effort to differentiate itself from competitors.

Market development was assessed from indexes developed by the NERI and computed using data from Chinese statistical yearbooks, reports from the administrations of industry and commerce, and surveys. The authors used one index, a province's GDP divided by its government's budget, to reflect the extent to which provincial resources are allocated by markets rather than through the government's redistribution system. The development score of the province where a firm operates was used, with the primary location used for firms operating in multiple provinces.

Past financial performance was measured as ROA and market-to-book ratio lagged by one year relative to the dependent variable. It was included in all second-stage models as a control as well as serving as a moderating variable.
Government ownership was a dummy variable coded 1 if the ultimate owner of a firm was the Chinese government and its agencies and 0 otherwise.

Following previous research on the political connections of China's listed firms, the authors used a firm's CEO's affiliation with government as an indicator of the firm's political connections, a dummy variable equal to 1 if the CEO was an official of the central or a local government, or of the military, and 0 otherwise. The information came from CEO biographical sketches in annual reports and from manually searched CEO profiles.

For each firm the authors identified who was appointed as the new CEO. For each potential candidate the variable is assigned a value of 1 if the candidate is appointed as CEO, and 0 otherwise. Candidates are all directors on the firm's board less than 69 years of age who do not hold the position of CEO, Kaicho, Komon, or Soudanyaku, which yields a total of 64,823 candidates.

Coded as a 1 if the candidate was born in the same prefecture as the CEO, and a 0 otherwise, similar to Faccio and Parsley (2009). Japan has 47 prefectures, and the distribution of candidates across them varies, with Tokyo having the most candidates in the sample. In the sample, 17% of the candidates have a geographic tie with the CEO.

Following Beckman (2006) and Chidambaran, Kedia, and Prabhala (2011), coded as a 1 if the candidate was previously employed at the same firm (other than the focal firm) as the CEO, and a 0 otherwise. In the sample, 12% of the candidates have an employment tie with the CEO.

Coded as a 1 if the candidate attended the same prestigious university or college as the CEO. The top schools in Japan include the former public imperial universities, top public universities in the field of social science and natural science, and the top two private universities. In the sample (N = 64,823), 7% of candidates attended the same prestigious university as the CEO.

Captures the number of years a candidate and the CEO have served on the board together. The authors also examine organizational tenure overlap and CEO tenure overlap, but report the results of board tenure overlap because it is the most relevant for capturing relational social capital, since it measures the extent of time the CEO and a candidate served concurrently as senior executives. The mean board tenure overlap in the sample is 4.4 years.
Measured by adding up geographic tie, employment tie, and prestigious university tie. This variable ranged from 0 to 3, with a mean of 0.38.

A dummy variable coded as a 1 if the CEO also holds the position of kaicho (the chairman of the board in a Japanese company), and a 0 otherwise. In 71% of the firms in the sample, the CEO has duality.
Firm financial performance is measured using industry-adjusted ROA for the three years prior to succession. In the tables, firm performance is displayed as industry-adjusted ROA.

Interaction of Post (coded 1 for the years after the State Match implementation) and Treat (coded 1 for firms in the states that ever had the policy, NC and KY). The noncompetitive State Match program approximates an exogenous follow-on certification from a different certifying institution. Post equals 1 on or after 2006 in the Atlantic region and on or after 2007 in the South region.
Time-varying binary indicator coded 1 if the firm has active SBIR Phase II awards, used as the measure of certification redundancy where the initial and follow-on certifiers are the same institution.

Acquisition of VC financing, including most prominently Series A-E rounds of financing and debt financing. Estimated in binary form (coded 1 if the firm secured VC financing after the State Match certification) and separately in continuous functional form (deflated and scaled in millions). Measured over five subsequent annual time periods following the public certification.
time_window: five subsequent annual time periods following the public certification
