description: The relative weight that the party assigns to the focal political issue, measured as the percentage of quasi-sentences allotted to it in the current election manifesto. This is the dependent variable used to test H1, H3A and H3B.

A binary variable coded 1 if the party has made any claim on the focal political issue, i.e., dedicated at least one quasi-sentence to it, and 0 if the party has not made any claim on this issue. This is the dependent variable used to test H2.

A dummy variable recording whether a specific issue belongs to the established identity of the focal party or not, according to the description of political ideologies provided by the Comparative Manifestos Project. In the case of the Liberals the coding was constructed based on the policy claims allotted to the 13 issues.

The sum of the investments made by the other political parties on the focal issue. The variable also controls for the popularity of a particular element in policy space and was square-rooted to reduce its skewness.
The sum of the percentage of coded sentences dedicated to an issue by the focal party in previous manifestos. The variable was square-rooted to reduce its skewness.

A dummy variable coded as 1 if the issue is unrelated to any of the party ideologies and 0 if otherwise. Its coefficient indicates how much the focal party invested in neutral issues compared with elements that are related to any other party identity.

A dummy variable coded as 1 if the issue belongs to the less oppositional ideological party identity and 0 if it belongs to the more oppositional party identity. For the Conservatives the more oppositional identity is defined by the Labour ideology and vice versa; for the Liberal ideology the more oppositional identity is defined by the Conservative ideology.

The omitted reference category for the element-type dummies: issues that belong to the more oppositional party identity, i.e., elements that are related to an identity oppositional to that of the focal party. Because this category is the least likely, it is used as the omitted category.

Cumulative annual rate of return on investment for each sample observation. Money invested by the PE firm in each portfolio company and the initial date of investment are aggregated on the entry side; money returned to the PE firm by the portfolio company and the final date of distribution are aggregated on the exit side. The authors state that this aggregation makes the measure lower than the true rate of return because holding time is exaggerated for money invested in follow-up rounds or returned early through partial exits. Investments not yet exited as of September 1, 2010 are assigned a return of -100 percent in the deal-level analyses, that is, they are counted as complete write-offs.
time_window: Initial investment to final date of distribution; not-yet-exited investments through September 1, 2010

description: Dichotomous variable taking a value of 1 if the PE firm is investing in its country of origin, and 0 otherwise. The authors report that only 7 of 25 PE firms with host country origins had invested outside their home country.

Dichotomous variable taking a value of 1 if, at the time of investment, the focal PE firm had previously raised PE funds to invest in the host country, and 0 otherwise. The authors use a dichotomous variable because of the high share of observations associated with firms on their first fund (74%) and the limited variation in the number of funds raised.

A continuous measure taken from the International Country Risk Guide's Investment Profile index. Countries are scored by ICRG analysts on a scale of 1 (weakest) to 12 (strongest) based on risks in three areas. The score for the year of initial investment is used, as it represents the information about the institutional context available to PE firms when they made the decision to enter.

The ratio of host country stock market capitalization to host country GDP for the year of PE investment. It is one of two commonly used measures, drawn from World Bank data, of host country financial development.

The ratio of host country domestic credit to host country GDP for the year of PE investment. Credit market development includes all domestic bank lending to the private sector and net lending to the government. It is the second of two commonly used measures, drawn from World Bank data, of host country financial development.

A formative index score for the firm's incentive bundle, calculated as an average of the firm-specificity score of each individual incentive across all incentives in the firm's bundle, excluding wages, cash bonuses, traditional benefits, and other incentives that are essentially cash equivalents. Key informants rated each incentive on how difficult or easy it is for software development professionals to find better options outside the company, using a five-point Likert-type scale anchored at the high end by 'very difficult to find better options' and at the low end by 'very easy to find better options'. Respondents could also write in additional incentives, which were categorized and, when common, added to the second wave of the survey. The measure captures the average difficulty of finding better options elsewhere for each incentive plus any additional incentives listed by the key informant.

Key informants indicated the total number of developers employed in the firm in the prior year, then the number of developers who 'left voluntarily' in the previous year, and then the number of those voluntary leavers who management would have preferred to keep. The measure focuses on undesirable turnover and was converted to a turnover rate: the number of dysfunctional voluntary leavers divided by the total number of developers.

The same formative index score for the firm's incentive bundle, computed as an average of the firm-specificity score of each individual incentive across all incentives in the firm's bundle, excluding wages, cash bonuses, traditional benefits, and other essentially cash-equivalent incentives. Key informants rated each incentive for how difficult or easy it is for software development professionals to find better options outside the company, on a five-point Likert-type scale anchored at the high end by 'very difficult to find better options' and at the low end by 'very easy to find better options'. In the multilevel wage models this firm-level measure predicts both the firm's intercept and its wage-tenure slope.

The natural logarithm of the total individual-level yearly cash compensation, computed as the sum of base salary and cash bonus; the authors note that results are robust to salary only. Culpepper collected the compensation data over a three-year window but shared them with the authors as a single-year cross section, aged to the current year to protect confidentiality. The developers covered are individual contributors, not leaders or managers.
time_window: single-year cross section (data collected over a three-year window)

description: Worker tenure in the organization, in years, taken from the worker-level compensation data and included as an individual-level predictor. In the multilevel model the coefficient on tenure is interpreted as the estimated wage-tenure slope within each firm, and this slope is allowed to vary with firm-level characteristics.

Dichotomous indicator of a succession event in a family firm in which an outgoing family CEO (founder or heir) is replaced by a professional manager CEO. Interim professional manager transitions and cases in which the controlling family went bankrupt and exited the firm are removed from the sample. It serves as the treatment indicator: firms that transitioned are matched, within the same two-digit SIC industry and year, with control firms that continue to be managed by family CEOs but had nearly identical propensity scores.
scale: dichotomous (1 = transition from family to professional CEO)
time_window: event year t of CEO succession

description: Operating income divided by the book value of total assets. Performance is compared as the cumulative change from the year prior to the transition event through three years after it, and the average treatment effect on the treated denotes the difference in cumulative performance change between the treatment and control groups.
time_window: t-1 through t+3 relative to the succession event

description: Percent of shares held by family members among the top 10 largest shareholders of the total outstanding shares. The median value at one year prior to the professional management succession event (12.8%) is used to classify firms into high and low family ownership subgroups for the post-succession performance comparison.
time_window: t-1 (one year prior to the succession event)

description: Percent of shares held by banks, insurance companies, corporations (excluding those related to founding families), and foreign investors among the top 10 largest shareholders of the total outstanding shares. The median value at one year prior to the succession event (26.18%) is used to classify firms into high and low institutional ownership subgroups.
time_window: t-1 (one year prior to the succession event)

description: Dichotomous variable that takes a value of 1 when outgoing family CEOs stay in the firm during the three years after CEO succession, as chairman of the board, advisor, or in any other senior position (high family legacy), and 0 when they leave the company after succession (low family legacy). It is used to split the professional manager succession sample into the two subgroups.
scale: dichotomous (1 = ex-family CEO stays in the firm)
time_window: three years after the succession event

description: Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if a firm bears the name of the founding family and 0 if not, reflecting an implicit form of family legacy. It is used to split the professional manager succession sample into high family legacy (family firm name) and low family legacy (no family firm name) subgroups.
scale: dichotomous (1 = firm bears the founding family's name)
time_window: t-1 (one year prior to the succession event)

description: Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the outgoing CEO is a founder and 0 if not. In the post-succession analysis, cases of transition to professional CEOs are divided into transition from founders and transition from non-founders, each matched with continuing family firms run by founders and non-founders, respectively.
scale: dichotomous (1 = outgoing CEO is a founder)
time_window: t-1 (one year prior to the succession event)

description: Professional manager succession cases are divided into two subgroups based on whether the professional manager graduated from an elite university, consistent with the classification of the seven former imperial universities (Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, Nagoya, Tohoku, Hokkaido, and Kyusyu) and Hitotsubashi and Kobe. The subgroups are compared with matched continuing family management firms.

Who's Who provided a birth date for each manager listed, and the editor of Who's Who was consulted to determine the date that the data was obtained; each manager's age was then determined. Ages were averaged for the managers of firms that changed strategy and of firms that did not.

Since a manager's career history was listed in Who's Who, it was clear how long a manager had been with his or her current railroad. A manager from a firm that participated in rail consolidation was not considered to have moved from one railroad to another.

Since a manager's career history was listed in Who's Who, it was clear how long a manager had been in the railroad industry. A manager from a firm that participated in rail consolidation was not considered to have moved from one railroad to another.

Managers were classified into one of six categories on the basis of their education history and assigned an estimated number of years of education, which allowed a calculation of years of education. The six categories, with estimated years of education in parentheses, are: No College (12); Some College (14); Bachelor's Degree (16); Master of Business Administration (MBA) (18); Other Graduate Degree (18); and Ph.D. (21).

variable_name: Percent of top managers with MBA
description: The education classification provided information on the incidence of MBAs, expressed as the percentage of top managers in firms that changed strategy and in firms that did not change strategy who held an MBA degree. The two percentages were compared with a chi-square test.
level: individual manager, aggregated as a percentage for each strategy-change group

description: A cluster analysis was run with a data set which combined both pre- and post-deregulation assessments to classify the 27 railroads into strategic groups, treating each railroad as if it were two firms (54 data points). If the same firm was found to be in two different clusters it was coded as having changed its strategy; firms in the same cluster at both periods were coded as not having changed. The underlying ratings came from a mail survey in which 104 shippers provided 245 usable responses (approximately nine per railroad) rating each railroad on strategic dimensions before and after deregulation.
scale: binary classification (changed vs. did not change strategy)
time_window: before and after the Staggers Act of 1980

description: A vacillation event is identified at time t when a firm's focus has shifted from one activity to another between time t-1 and time t, that is, when f it-1 and f it have an opposite sign. To build a yearly-updated measure, the authors count the number of vacillations performed by the firm over the last five years (from year t-4 to year t) and divide it by five. The time frame used to measure frequency must be more than two years because each vacillation event is identified yearly.
time_window: five-year moving window, from year t-4 to year t

description: The scale measure multiplies the absolute difference between a firm's focus ratio at t and at t-1 by an indicator of a vacillation event that takes the value 1 if there is a sign change between f it-1 and f it and 0 otherwise. The authors state that vacillation scale is measured by multiplying the difference between two consecutive time periods (i.e., |f it - f it-1|) by the vacillation-event identifier. The formula block in the paper is unreadable in the supplied text.

The dependent variable is Tobin's Q, a market-based value chosen because it reflects both short-term performance and long-term performance prospects and has the advantage of reflecting market expectations of competitiveness in terms of knowledge creation as measured by patents. Tobin's Q is measured for the year after the explanatory variables, Tobin's Q t+1.

variable_name: Rit (patents identified as exploration at time t)
description: The number of firm i's patents filed during a given year and in technical classifications for which the focal firm has not historically filed. Rit is one of the two patent counts entering the firm's focus ratio f it.

variable_name: Tit (patents identified as exploitation at time t)
description: The number of firm i's patents filed during a given year and in technical classifications for which the focal firm has historically filed. Tit is one of the two patent counts entering the firm's focus ratio f it.

The opportunity's common profitability potential is the difference between the market price and the cost of satisfactory inputs, divided by the market price, expressed as a unit gross margin percentage. The market price is the hourly bid of the winning individual and the cost of satisfactory inputs is the lowest nonwinning bid submitted by a platform-recommended bidder, as detailed in Barach et al. (2019); the platform's proprietary algorithm assigns a badge to recommended bidders. The figure is left censored so that all implied negative values equal zero. The authors state that the mean market price for an exchange is $13.76, the mean cost of satisfactory inputs is $7.61, and, accounting for left censoring, the mean exchange implies a common profitability potential of 37%.
scale: percentage unit gross margin, left censored at zero

description: The aggregated common value of profitability potential of each individual is the cumulative average of the common profitability potentials of the exchanges that individual has observed as of time t. It allows opportunities to be characterized in a way common to all individuals who observe the same set of exchanges and independent of their exploitation costs or of founding. To simplify interpretation and reduce sensitivity to a long right tail, the authors bin it by quartiles and report effects relative to the first quartile, which is all values less than 0.33; the second quartile ranges from 0.33 to 0.39, the third from 0.39 to 0.45, and the fourth contains all values greater than 0.45.
scale: quartile bins of cumulative average gross margin
time_window: cumulative average as of day t

description: The measure is the standard network measure of degree: the count of unique relationships that a seller has accumulated, through their job history, to platform buyers. Because the 25th percentile of this variable is 0 and the median value is 2, the authors do not coarsen by quartile; instead the first bin consists of individuals with no accumulated unique buyer relationships and the second bin consists of those with only one such relationship, while the third and fourth bins are defined by the third and fourth quartiles of the data. The third bin consists of individuals with two through six such relationships and the fourth consists of individuals with at least seven.
scale: four bins: 0, 1, 2-6, and 7 or more buyer relationships

description: A dichotomous measure that indexes an individual's founding of a new agency. The indicator variable is set to one on the day an independent contractor who is unaffiliated with any other digital agency registers a new agency and employs at least one subcontractor. Of the 32,274 at-risk individuals in the sample, 208 individuals (0.6%) make this fundamental transition from laborer to founder within the 3-year observation period.

Weighted overall clustering coefficient, computed as three times the number of triangles in the graph divided by the number of connected triples, where a triangle is a set of three nodes each of which is connected to both of the others and a connected triple is a set of three nodes in which at least one is connected to both the others. It represents the percentage of a firm's alliance partners that are also partnered with each other, weighted by the number of each firm's partners, averaged across all firms in the network. The variable ranges from zero to one, with larger values indicating increasing clustering.
time_window: three-year windows (six snapshots per industry, from 1990-1992 through 1995-1997)

description: Average distance-weighted reach, a compound measure that takes into account both the number of firms that can be reached by any path from a given firm and the path length it takes to reach them. In the prose the measure is described as the sum of the reciprocal distances to every firm reachable from a given firm, averaged across all firms in the network; the equation block in the paper is unreadable in this text. Larger values indicate higher reach.
time_window: three-year windows (six snapshots per industry, from 1990-1992 through 1995-1997)

description: The number of successful patent applications for firm i in year t, collected from the Delphion database, aggregating subsidiary patents up to the ultimate parent level. Granted patents were counted in their year of application, and yearly patent counts were created for each firm for the period 1993 to 2000.

Absolute difference between firm-level R&D intensity (R&D/total sales) and industry-level R&D intensity, averaged over times t-2, t-1, and t of the entry or exit event. Firm-level information on research expenditures as a percentage of sales was gathered from the Compustat data base.
time_window: averaged over t-2, t-1, t of the entry or exit event

description: Absolute difference between firm-level advertising intensity (advertising/total sales) and industry-level advertising intensity, averaged over times t-2, t-1, and t of the entry or exit event. Firm-level information on advertising expenditures as a percentage of sales was gathered from the Compustat data base.
time_window: averaged over t-2, t-1, t of the entry or exit event

description: Absolute difference between firm-level capital intensity (fixed assets/total sales) and industry-level capital intensity, averaged over times t-2, t-1, and t of the entry or exit event.
time_window: averaged over t-2, t-1, t of the entry or exit event

description: Dissimilarity in the percentage of type k human resources between an incumbent industry and a target industry is measured as the absolute difference in the shares of each occupational category; the overall distance is the square root of the sum of these dissimilarity measures. For the entry mode decision it is measured as the minimum of distances between the target industry and the industries the firm is already in; for the exit mode decision it is the sum of distances between a business and every other incumbent industry, weighted by the sales share of those other businesses.
level: industry pair (firm incumbent industry and target industry); line of business relative to the firm's other businesses

description: Product market relatedness is computed as the sales-weighted concentric diversification index. A weight takes the value 2 if the entered industry and another industry of the parent are within the same 3-digit SIC code, 1 if within the same 2-digit SIC, and 0 if in different 2-digit SIC industries; these weights are combined with the percentage of the firm's sales in each industry defined at the 4-digit SIC level. The measure reflects the product market relatedness between the entrant business and all the other industries in which its parent had operations.
level: line of business relative to the parent firm
time_window: at the time of the diversifying entry

description: The mode of entry is defined by a binary variable, denoted by one in the case of acquisition and zero in the case of internal development. If the establishment representing entry was listed as owned previously by another firm, the mode of entry was coded as acquisition; otherwise it was coded as internal development.

The mode of exit is defined by a binary variable, denoted by one in the case of sell-off and zero in the case of dissolution. If the exited establishment was listed as owned by another firm in a later time period, the mode of exit was coded as sell-off; otherwise it was coded as dissolution.
The number of years since the time of entry to the time of exit for each business. It thereby measures the years a business is associated with a particular firm.

A binary variable that equals to one if an original patent assignee sells a patent in force to another firm and zero if an original patent assignee does not transfer a patent to another firm. The authors call this variable patent trade. The main analysis estimates its likelihood with a rare events logistic regression because the dependent variable is a dichotomous variable in rare events.

The relative technological distance differential between a patent and the technology stocks of an assignee-buyer dyad. A firm's technology stock is a vector reflecting the distribution and composition of the firm's patents across patent classes, and the technological distance of a patent to a firm's patent portfolio is calculated by averaging the distance between the patent and every patent in the firm's 10-year patent portfolio. Two patent classes are considered distantly located if prospective patents do not frequently cite them, and the measure is time-weighted by applying a 15% depreciation rate per year. Technological relativity is computed by subtracting the technological distance between the patent and a potential buyer (d(B)) from that between the patent and the original assignee (d(A)).

Drawing on a Mahalanobis distance measure used by Bloom et al. (2013), the measure considers how much of any two firms' sales revenues overlap based on the four-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes. A firm's product-market activity is characterized by a vector of the average share of the sales revenue of the firm in each industry over the past four-year period. The product-market overlap between two firms is computed as the Mahalanobis distance between their two corresponding vectors, so that firms that are proximate in the product-market space are in intense product-market competition.

A firm's technological capability in year t is the accumulative citation-weighted number of patents in the previous 10-year timeframe (t-1 to t-10) with a 15% depreciation rate per year. For a patent granted in year T, the number of citations it receives throughout its lifespan is computed and multiplied by (1-delta)^(t-T), where delta equals 15%. These values are then aggregated for all patents in a firm's 10-year running patent portfolio, and in the regression analysis the citation-weighted patent counts are scaled down to 1/10,000.

variable_name: White source CEO and racial minority target CEO
description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if the source CEO was white and the target CEO was a racial minority. In the models of CEOs' internal performance attributions the reference category is the dyadic combination of white source CEO and white target. The variable is used to test hypothesis 1a.

variable_name: Male source CEO and female target CEO
description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if the source CEO was male and the target CEO was female. In the models of CEOs' internal performance attributions the reference category is the dyadic combination of male source CEO and male target. The variable is used to test hypothesis 1b.

An index of status in the corporate elite based on five indicators: the number of appointments held at corporate boards, the number of appointments held at nonprofit boards, elite education, the average stock rating of firms where the individual served as an outside board member, and memberships in prestigious social clubs. The indicators were combined into a single index using principal components analysis, a data reduction technique appropriate for combining causal indicators. Each indicator was measured in the year prior to the period for which performance attributions were measured. Standardized factor loadings ranged from .75 to .84.
time_window: year prior to the period for which performance attributions were measured

variable_name: Target CEO's status in corporate elite relative to source CEO's status
description: In the primary analysis, relative status was measured as the target CEO's status minus the source CEO's status. In separate analyses the effect of relative status was assessed by interacting the target CEO's status with the source CEO's status, controlling for the absolute status of each CEO. This variable is used to test hypotheses 2a and 2b.
time_window: year prior to the period for which performance attributions were measured

description: A count variable that indicates the number of internal attributions by the source CEO for low performance at the target CEO's firm over the two-week period following an earnings disclosure. It is based on a multi-item survey scale gauging whether a source CEO attributed low firm performance to the target CEO's leadership and to the target CEO's strategic decision making, how many times, when, and to whom; inter-item reliability of the scale was acceptably high (alpha = .88). In tests of hypotheses 3 and 4 the independent variable was measured with journalists' parallel reports of the number of instances in which other CEOs made internal attributions for low performance of the target CEO's firm in conversations with the focal journalist during the two-week period subsequent to an earnings disclosure.
time_window: two-week period following an earnings disclosure

variable_name: Internal performance attributions in journalists' reports
description: A count variable that indicates the number of internal attributions by the focal journalist for low performance of the target CEO's firm over the two months following the period for which performance attributions by CEOs were measured. All articles authored by journalists in the sample during the four-month period subsequent to that period that mention a firm or CEO in the sample were identified. Three coders independently assessed each article, judging whether each sentence referring to a company or CEO in the sample contained an internal attribution for low firm performance, using instructions based on Staw, McKechnie, and Puffer's (1983) procedure; the intraclass correlation coefficient across the three coders was .93.
time_window: two-month period following the period for which CEOs' attributions were measured; articles from the subsequent four months

description: A dichotomous indicator coded 1 if a firm's most recently reported quarterly earnings were below the median forecasted earnings for the same period among all analysts covering the firm, and 0 otherwise. It identifies the earnings disclosures following which internal performance attributions by CEOs and journalists were measured.

variable_name: Journalist and target CEO both racial minorities
description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if both the journalist and target CEO were racial minorities, used to test the moderating effect of journalists' racial minority status on the influence of CEOs' internal attributions. The reference category in models 1-3 is the dyadic combination of racial minority journalist and white target.

variable_name: Journalist and target CEO both women
description: A dichotomous variable coded 1 if both the journalist and target CEO were women, used to test the moderating effect of journalists' gender on the influence of CEOs' internal attributions. The reference category in models 4-6 is the combination of female journalist and male target.

A multi-item survey scale gauging envy of the more negative form toward target CEOs. Two items directly asked respondents whether they felt envy for a target CEO (e.g., 'To what extent do you feel envious of [CEO]'), and three other items asked about feelings of resentment toward the target CEO. Items were derived in part from survey measures developed by Smith and colleagues; inter-item reliability was acceptably high (alpha = .86).

For each of four role sets, the absolute difference in tie counts between the manager and the technologist is divided by the sum of their tie counts, so that a difference between 0 and 1 tie counts as more dissimilar than a difference of 6 and 7 ties. The four values are averaged and subtracted from 1 to give a measure of equivalence rather than dissimilarity. Individuals overlapping between the manager's and the technologist's ego network are excluded. The measure ranges from 0 for partners who have ties to none of the same role sets to 1 for partners who have the same number of ties to each of the four role sets.

The rating is taken from Neptune's HR records for the period covered by the survey and is allocated with a forced distribution across three rating categories, which are used as a categorical dependent variable. It is based on a multi-rater procedure: staff document their contributions using a formal template and a committee of line managers compares individual contributions within peer groups identified by seniority and career ladder. Technologists and managers are rated by the same committee but are in separate assessment pools.
time_window: the period covered by the survey; obtained six months after the survey

description: Respondents indicated all technical expertise areas in which they had relevant expertise and judged their depth of expertise in each area on a 5-point scale ranging from ''general awareness'' (1) through ''fairly competent'' (3) to ''leading expert'' (5). Shared technical expertise is the fraction of expertise areas in which the technologist is at least fairly competent in which the manager partner is also at least fairly competent. The areas held by the technologist are used as the reference point.

An individual's prominence was inferred from nominations by others: the number of times the individual is mentioned by fellow managers and technologists across the full sample of respondents as a source of advice or as a decision maker or opinion leader. All prominence counts were standardized by groups to account for differences between levels of seniority and career ladder. Prominence is expressed as the number of times the focal individual is nominated by others as knowledgeable or influential in the organization, normalized by role set.

The proportion of a developer's applications where the source code was listed on an open source site before the launch of the App Store. Making code publicly available requires additional effort and may have disadvantages, so the authors treat it as a good indication of open source affiliation. The authors note that listing source code on an open source site does not broadly prohibit commercialization.
time_window: before the launch of the App Store

description: Developer-level outcome with three states: Commercial (updated at least one application and charged for access to at least one application, 38 developers), Free (updated at least one application and kept all updated applications available for free, 18 developers), or Abandon (abandoned all applications and did not update them, 32 developers). A developer was coded Commercial if at least one application was listed for sale either on the App Store or through Cydia, or if the developer created a new paid application within two years after the launch of the App Store.
time_window: before and after the launch of the App Store, including new paid applications within two years of the launch

description: Dummy variable taking a value of 1 if the respondent reported in the second survey wave that, since August 2014, they had started a new business or started work as an independent contractor. This measures new commercialization activity after the first wave of the survey.
time_window: since August 2014 (first wave), measured in the second wave

description: Reverse coding of the five-point Likert item 'It is good that start-ups make money from FLOSS [free/libre open source software], provided they adhere to appropriate licenses,' taken from the first wave of the survey. Because it is reverse coded, higher values indicate stronger anticommercial attitudes.
scale: five-point Likert scale ('strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree')

description: Response to the five-point Likert item 'I believe software should be free,' taken from the second wave of the survey. It measures whether the respondent has adopted the OSS belief that all software should be free.
scale: five-point Likert scale ('strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree')

description: Four-item scale for the self-identity of OSS developers, modified by Daniel et al. (2011) from the work of Randel and Jaussi (2003), taken from the first wave of the survey. Each item uses a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'); Cronbach's alpha for the scale was 0.85. The items were asked with regard to a particular OSS project the developer was an active participant in and where there were at least three other developers.
scale: five-point Likert scale, 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree')

description: Mode of entry is captured by a dummy variable which takes a value of 0 if the Japanese parent made an acquisition and 1 if it established a greenfield joint venture. An acquisition takes place when a Japanese parent fully acquires an existing U.S. manufacturing company or parts thereof; a joint venture occurs when a Japanese investor establishes a new manufacturing facility and shares the ownership with an American partner, so partial acquisitions are excluded. The unit of observation is the entry.

A dummy equal to 1 if the U.S. partner who holds the desired assets is large, and 0 otherwise; a large U.S. partner is a U.S. firm with more than 5000 employees. Number of employees was obtained from the issue of the Directory of Corporate Affiliations published in the year before the corresponding Japanese entry. Size is measured by employees because postmerger difficulties arise from the need to integrate and motivate the acquired firm's labor force.

A dummy equal to 1 if the U.S. partner was divisionalized, and 0 if it was not. Whether the U.S. partner was divisionalized was ascertained by looking at the firm's organizational structure, as described in the Directory of Corporate Affiliations.

The Japanese investor's experience of the U.S. market at the time entry was made, measured by the number of years between entry and the establishment of the investor's first U.S. manufacturing subsidiary.

A dummy variable equal to 1 if the Japanese investor and its affiliate manufacture one common product, and to 0 otherwise. It proxies the difference in company culture between the Japanese parent and its subsidiary.

A dummy variable indicating whether the Japanese and the American partners were in the same industry, calculated by comparing the products manufactured by the Japanese investor and those manufactured by its U.S. partner. In the case of joint ventures the partner is the U.S. joint venture partner; in the case of acquisitions the partner is the parent firm of the acquired unit if the Japanese firm acquired a division or a part of a U.S. firm, or the acquired firm itself. It was coded 1 if at least one of the products produced by the American partner was also produced by the Japanese parent.

The concentration ratio of the U.S. industry entered, measured by the Herfindahl index for each 4-digit SIC U.S. industry, as published in the 1982 Census of Manufactures. The arithmetic average of the concentration ratio was used for subsidiaries active in multiple SICs.

GROWDEV is the absolute value of GROWTH's deviation from its sample mean divided by its standard deviation, with GROWTH equal to the 3-year average annual growth rate of shipments of the 4-digit U.S. industry 2 years before entry. The average industry growth rate was used for the few observations with multiple SICs; a high value of GROWDEV should encourage acquisitions.

INDIG captures the indigestibility of the assets coveted by the Japanese investor and is composed of SIZE, a dummy equal to 1 if the U.S. partner who holds them is large, and USSTRUC, a dummy equal to 1 if the U.S. partner is divisionalized. INDIG takes a value of 1 when the U.S. partner is not divisionalized (USSTRUC is 0) and large (SIZE is 1), and 0 otherwise.

Calculated as the aggregate number of continuing prestigious directors that served on a focal firm's board in a given year. A director was considered prestigious if he or she possessed at least one of three credentials: a degree from an elite educational institution on Finkelstein's list of 20 institutions, experience as an executive at the level of vice president or above at an S&P 500 company, or experience as an outside director in an S&P 500 firm. Prestige of prior employment and outside directorships was assessed against a lagged-year list of S&P 500 firms constructed for each year of the study. The square of this measure was also included to test the hypothesized curvilinear relationship.

Operationalized in the same manner as director prestige. Coded 1 if the CEO possessed any one of the three prestige credentials (educational, employment, or directorial prestige) and coded 0 otherwise.

A time-variant dichotomous measure coded 1 when a firm recruited a director who possessed any of the three prestige credentials in a given year and 0 otherwise. An average of 33.74 percent of firms in any given year reported adding at least one prestigious outside director to their boards.

A count variable ranging from zero to three that captured the number of prestige credentials a new director possessed. Sixty percent of the prestigious new directors in the sample had one source of prestige, 34 percent had two sources of prestige, and 6 percent had all three sources of prestige.

Calculated by summing the number of years each individual served as a director on a focal firm's board (director tenure) listed in the offering prospectus and the annual proxy statements and dividing the sum by the total number of directors on the board.
Coded 1 if a CEO was also the chairman of his/her firm's board in a given year and 0 otherwise.

Equal to the number of outside directors on a firm's board, defined as directors lacking any current or past executive positions in the firm and not related to any current employees, divided by the total number of directors on the board.

A dummy variable coded 1 if a firm's board had staggered elections and 0 otherwise. Companies sometimes stagger the elections of their directors so that only a minority of directors is up for reelection in a given year to reduce the likelihood of hostile takeovers.
Equal to the percentage of shares outstanding at the end of the year beneficially held by a firm's CEO.
Coded 1 if the CEO was the company founder and 0 otherwise.
A regulatory punctuation indicator that captures immediate effects. It takes an initial value of zero and shifts to one in 1983, the year after the punctuation occurred.
A regulatory punctuation indicator that captures immediate effects. It takes an initial value of zero and shifts to one in 1983, the year after the punctuation occurred.
A regulatory punctuation time clock that captures effects that emerge as time passes. It equals zero up to and including 1982; it shifts to one in 1983 and rises by one each subsequent year.
scale: year count beginning at zero in 1982

description: A regulatory punctuation time clock that captures effects that emerge as time passes. It equals zero up to and including 1982; it shifts to one in 1983 and rises by one each subsequent year.
scale: year count beginning at zero in 1982

description: Domain expansion measured as the one-year change in scope of operations. For hospitals, this is the count of services offered, out of 135 categories.
scale: services offered out of 135 categories, analysed as a one-year change

description: Domain expansion measured as the one-year change in the spread of investments in eight markets. The spread is computed from the proportion of assets firm i has invested in each market m, following Blau (1977); the formula as printed in the text is not legible.

variable_name: Activity in new lines of business
description: Activity in new lines of business measured as the proportion of assets invested in seven categories. The categories are nonresidential mortgages, consumer loans, commercial loans, mortgage-backed securities, real estate, investment securities, and service companies.

In the event-history analysis the dependent variable is the instantaneous rate of CEO succession. Any firm in the sample can experience multiple succession events, so a repeated-events framework is used in which the dependent variable incorporates information from all successions, not just the first; the process is modelled as semi-Markov with CEO tenure as the time clock.

In the event-history analysis the dependent variable is the instantaneous rate of CEO succession. Any firm in the sample can experience multiple succession events, so a repeated-events framework is used in which the dependent variable incorporates information from all successions, not just the first; the process is modelled as semi-Markov with CEO tenure as the time clock.

CEO succession measured with an indicator set equal to one year after a new top executive arrived and zero otherwise; in the year of a succession event the outgoing CEO was coded as being in office for the entire year. To test effects that emerge as time passes, a variable indicating the first post-punctuation CEO succession was set to zero up to and including the year of the first post-punctuation succession event and one afterward.

CEO succession measured with an indicator set equal to one year after a new top executive arrived and zero otherwise; in the year of a succession event the outgoing CEO was coded as being in office for the entire year. To test effects that emerge as time passes, a variable indicating the first post-punctuation CEO succession was set to zero up to and including the year of the first post-punctuation succession event and one afterward.

For hospitals, performance is measured as return on sales, gross patient-services revenue over net income. The authors state that it reflects both effectiveness (good choices about services to offer) and efficiency (low cost), and that it is preferable to return on assets because hospitals vary in their asset intensity, depending on the services they provide.

For savings and loans, performance is measured as return on assets. The authors describe this as the best measure of performance for this industry, which contains both joint-stock and mutual companies.

Customers who had implemented the electronic linkage with the supplier at least six months prior to the study period were classified as EDI customers. Each selected EDI customer was matched with a manual customer with comparable customer size (sales) and the same three-digit SIC code, giving 159 pairs in each set.

Indicator of whether the customer's orders arrive through an electronic linkage. These orders are transmitted via EDI from the customer's purchasing system to a customer service center where they are printed and keyed into the computer system by service representatives; once in the order-processing system, teletype EDI orders and manual orders are processed in the same manner.

Of the EDI customers, some were identified as initiators of the system and the rest had linkages initiated by the supplier. Customer-initiated EDI customers were compared with their matched manual customers, and the converse comparison was also examined.

Customers with a simple EDI linkage had their electronic orders printed and rekeyed into the order-processing system. The remaining customers had an enhanced EDI linkage, for which the supplier had implemented an integrated-EDI linkage and/or electronic invoicing.

Indicator of whether the customer's orders are transmitted via a fully integrated EDI link, which requires mapping between the customer's item identification code and the supplier's item code, so that orders are entered directly into the supplier's order-processing system without human intervention. This indicator is entered alongside the electronic order indicator for non-integrated EDI orders.

Indicator of whether the electronic invoicing transaction has been implemented with the customer. The probability of a delay is not affected for customers with a simple EDI linkage since the supplier has implemented only the purchase-order transaction, not the electronic invoicing function.

The probability that a customer's payment is delayed, observed over that customer's orders; for each customer there are multiple observations of the binary random variable. Because the fraction of customers with no delayed payments is small, the authors use a Probit model estimated by weighted least squares.

The probability of rework, that is, that an order generates a credit to the customer. Many customers have no credits, so the dependent variable takes the limiting value of zero and a Tobit model is used, estimated by maximizing the log-likelihood with the quasi-Newton method.

Sales volume is used as the key measure of strategic benefit, capturing the additional business the supplier obtains from a customer. The analysis compares the sales that EDI customers give to the supplier with the sales given by their matched manual customers.

EDI customers were classified in terms of the length of time for which they had an electronic linkage with the supplier: recently established linkages (between 6 and 18 months), medium-term linkages, and linkages in place for more than three and a half years.
scale: three duration categories (recent, medium term, long term)

description: Alignment dummy indicating a gender composition match between the venture's founder and mentor teams, with Alignment = 1 encompassing the aligned combinations of gender-diverse founders/gender-diverse mentors and male-dominated founders/male-dominated mentors and Alignment = 0 encompassing the misaligned combinations of gender-diverse founders/male-dominated mentors and male-dominated founders/gender-diverse mentors. It serves as the main predictor variable for the alignment model.

Binary measure of team gender diversity equal to one for gender-diverse founder teams with representation of 30.00% through 70.00% and equal to zero for the remaining male-dominated founder teams that had not yet reached a threshold level of representation. Gender was identified by matching Techstars-provided first and last names to Crunchbase profile data and cross-referencing self-reported binary gender against images and gender pronouns in submitted text.

Binary measure of team gender diversity equal to one for gender-diverse mentor teams with representation of 30.00% through 70.00% and equal to zero for the remaining male-dominated mentor teams that had not yet reached a threshold level of representation. Gender was identified by matching mentor names to Crunchbase profile data and cross-referencing self-reported binary gender against images and gender pronouns in submitted text.

variable_name: Founder Team Gender × Mentor Team Gender
description: Interaction term of founder team gender and mentor team gender delineating four groups indicating the presence or absence of gender diversity within each combination of founder and mentor teams: male-dominated founders/male-dominated mentors, male-dominated founders/gender-diverse mentors, gender-diverse founders/male-dominated mentors, and gender-diverse founders/gender-diverse mentors. For Hypothesis 2 the authors unpack this interaction term, observing the group means and comparing the pairwise contrasts of their predictive margins.

Count of investors associated with each venture, collected as Time 2 data on participating investor counts for each Techstars venture. Investor participation predominantly consisted of venture capital funds, seed funds, and early-stage investment from various angel investors and Techstars; counts ranged from 1 to 44 investors providing capital to a given venture across rounds. Crunchbase was the primary data source, verified against press releases and venture websites.

The dependent variable is firm profitability, measured through the firm's return on assets. The models shown are based on a 3-year moving average of return on assets, since firms are (to some extent) able to manipulate in which year they report profits or losses. Models based on 1-year observations of return on assets led to virtually identical results.

Measured yearly as the number of foreign affiliates of the firm. Affiliates had to represent a 'physical' foreign presence, ranging from a sales office to production facilities. The number of foreign subsidiaries relates to the size of foreign operations.

To measure speed, the average number of foreign subsidiaries per year was computed, i.e., the number of foreign subsidiaries divided by the number of years since the firm's first foreign expansion. A large (average) number of expansions per year indicates a fast-paced international expansion process.
time_window: since the firm's first foreign expansion

description: The product scope of a firm's expansion process is measured as the number of additional 3-digit SBI codes entered by the firm while internationalizing. The SBI code is the Dutch equivalent of the SIC code.
The number of countries in which a firm established subsidiaries during its international expansion is used to measure the geographic scope of the expansion process.

Regularity, or rhythm, of the internationalization process was measured through the kurtosis of the first derivative of the number of foreign ventures of the firm over time. This variable measures how concentrated in time the change in the number of foreign subsidiaries is. Large peaks in a firm's expansion pattern, combined with periods of inactivity, result in a relatively concentrated distribution and therefore a high kurtosis; a constant pace of foreign expansion results in a relatively flat distribution and therefore a lower kurtosis. The formula itself could not be read from the text; the text only states that n = number of observations, x_i = number of expansions in year i, and s = standard deviation of the number of expansions.

Inside ownership was defined as the sum of the percentage of equity shares owned by family members identified as the controlling shareholders of a business group and by other nonfinancial affiliates in the same group, measured at time t.

Family portion denotes what portion of inside ownership was held directly by the family. Higher values of this variable reflect the greater cash flow rights direct ownership confers, given the same level of inside ownership.

Profitability was measured as the return on invested capital (ROIC), defined as the sum of net income before taxes plus interest payments, deflated by total assets, measured at time t. It is an accounting-based performance measure intended to assess operating efficiency without being biased by the relatively high debt-to-equity ratios common in Korean firms.
Tobin's Q, measured at time t, as a proxy for firm value, using the algorithm originally proposed by Lindenberg and Ross (1981) and adapted by Kim, Kim, Park, and Chang (1996) for Korean firms.

The number of a conventional firm's interlocking companies, newly added within a year, that lie within the Internet sector. The unit of analysis is a conventional firm in a year. Only nonredundant ties were counted: a tie to an Internet company counted as a new initiation only if the focal firm was not connected to that Internet company during the previous year.

The product of the percentage of articles with positive tones toward Internet companies and the total number of articles in a year containing the keywords 'Internet company,' 'dotcom,' 'e-business,' 'e-commerce,' or 'new economy.' The number of articles was collected from the Factiva database; the valence was coded by two trained research assistants from 1,000 randomly selected articles in four leading business periodicals. It measures the total number of articles that manifest positive attitudes toward Internet companies in a year.
The percentage of other firms with the same three-digit NAICS code that in any one year were interlocked with Internet companies from among the S&P 1500 firms.

The percentage of other conventional firms headquartered within the same metropolitan statistical area (MSA) that in any one year were interlocked with Internet companies from among the S&P 1500 firms.

A dummy variable coded as 1 if the conventional firm had Internet interlocks in the previous year. It was interacted with media attention, adoption within an industry, and adoption within an MSA to test the attenuation of social influence on tie formation.

An interlock tie was coded as dissolved in a year if two firms shared at least one common director or executive in the previous year but not in the year in question. Ties that survived beyond 2006 were coded as right censored, and ties that failed but were reconstituted within the next three years were treated as unbroken. The instantaneous risk of failing is modeled as a hazard rate over one-year spells.

The product of the percentage of articles with positive tones toward Internet companies and the total number of articles in a year containing Internet-related keywords, as described for the formation analysis. It is entered contemporaneously to predict the hazard of tie dissolution.

The percentage of other firms with the same three-digit NAICS code that in any one year were interlocked with Internet companies from among the S&P 1500 firms, entered contemporaneously in the hazard models of tie dissolution.

The percentage of other conventional firms headquartered within the same metropolitan statistical area that in any one year were interlocked with Internet companies from among the S&P 1500 firms, entered contemporaneously in the hazard models of tie dissolution.

The media attention measure observed in the year in which the interlock tie was founded. It is interacted with a conventional firm's previous contact at tie founding to predict the hazard of tie dissolution, and it is available from 1997 onward because the IRRC database does not provide director data before 1996.

variable_name: adoption in industry at tie founding
description: The percentage of adoptions within the same industry observed in the year in which the interlock tie was founded, interacted with the conventional firm's previous contact at tie founding in the hazard models.

variable_name: adoption in MSA at tie founding
description: The percentage of adoptions within the same metropolitan statistical area observed in the year in which the interlock tie was founded, interacted with the conventional firm's previous contact at tie founding in the hazard models.

A dummy variable indicating whether the conventional firm had Internet interlocks in the year prior to the founding of the focal interlock tie. It is interacted with the three fashion variables measured at tie founding; this measure can only be observed for ties founded beginning in 1997.
time_window: year before the founding year of the tie

description: An 18-item scale measuring the extent to which a firm has implemented and integrated computer technologies for manufacturing (e.g., CAM, MRP II). One part of the scale asks the extent to which each technology is used in the plant, and another asks the extent to which transactions between pairs of production processes are accomplished using computers. Respondents were the plant and operations managers; given substantial interrater reliability, their responses were averaged to form the aggregated variable.
scale: technology use items: 1 = not at all to 5 = extensively; computer integration items: 1 = not computer integrated at all to 5 = completely computer integrated

description: A 10-item scale measuring the extent to which a firm uses techniques to promote continuous improvement, doing things right the first time, and devotion to fulfilling customer needs. Respondents were the plant and quality managers, whose responses were averaged to form the aggregated variable. Three items initially considered aspects of JIT (minimizing set-up times, performing preventive maintenance, and making accounting system changes) loaded onto the TQ factor and were aggregated with the other measures of TQ.
scale: 1-7 response scales (e.g., 1 = very little to 7 = a great deal)

description: A 10-item scale measuring the extent to which a firm attempts to cut costs through reduced inventories and lead times and by controlling such features as the number of suppliers, size of deliveries, and total number of parts. Respondents were the plant and production control managers, whose responses were averaged to form the aggregated variable. The items listed in the appendix ask how much each feature has changed in the past five years and were reverse-coded, with 1 = huge decrease, 4 = same, and 7 = huge increase.

A 7-item scale measuring the extensiveness of a firm's selection process, as demonstrated by the time and money spent and the number of people involved. Respondents were the three functional managers and the human resource manager from each plant. Because the zero-order correlations across functions were low, the measure was not aggregated to the plant level; within each function it is the mean response of the human resource manager and the relevant functional manager.
level: plant function (operations, quality, or production control)

description: An 8-item scale measuring the extensiveness of training and development opportunities, such as the frequency and variety of training, money spent, and the percentage of employees trained. Respondents were the three functional managers from each plant and their nonmanagerial employees. Interrater reliabilities showed convergence within functions but the correlations indicated independence across functions, so the measure is based on the mean responses of the functional manager and the nonmanagerial employee or employees within each department of each plant.
level: plant function (operations, quality, or production control)

description: A 9-item scale measuring whether performance appraisal was used for developing employees, as exemplified by diagnosing training needs, frequent feedback, problem solving, and discussing future issues. Respondents were the three functional managers from each plant and their nonmanagerial employees, and the measure is based on the mean responses of the functional manager and nonmanagerial employee or employees within each department. One item (fixed vs. flexible performance standards) was deleted because it cross-loaded on the appraisal and staffing factors, and one item (how closely raises and promotions are tied to performance appraisal) loaded on individually equitable rewards and was aggregated with those items.
level: plant function (operations, quality, or production control)

description: The 8-item equitable rewards scale was broken into two separate variables representing external and individual equity. Respondents were the three functional managers and the human resource manager, and within each function the measure is the mean response of the human resource manager and the relevant functional manager. The scale items concern the degree to which pay is competitive for the industry.
level: plant function (operations, quality, or production control)

description: The 8-item equitable rewards scale was broken into two separate variables representing external and individual equity. Respondents were the three functional managers and the human resource manager, and within each function the measure is the mean response of the human resource manager and the relevant functional manager. The items concern the degree to which pay is based on individual performance, and the item asking how closely raises and promotions are tied to performance appraisal loaded on this factor and was aggregated with these items.
level: plant function (operations, quality, or production control)

description: Integrated manufacturing was measured by three multi-item survey scales completed by multiple respondents per plant: advanced manufacturing technology (18 items), total quality (10 items) and just-in-time (10 items). Factor analysis confirmed three stable factors, and the facets were also interacted to test their joint effects.

Factor score obtained from a factor analysis of four COMPUSTAT-based measures of product strategy: R&D expenditures divided by net sales; the sum of advertising and administrative expenses over net sales; the moving average (up to ten years) of the difference between a firm's gross margin and the industry mean gross margin; and the market to book ratio (closing share price multiplied by the number of common shares divided by common equity). Higher scores indicate a greater emphasis on differentiation. The raw factor scores were standardized and rescaled to the range of -1 to 1 and used in the main analyses.
time_window: firm average across the sample years; relative gross margin uses a moving average of up to 10 years

description: Factor score obtained from a factor analysis of two COMPUSTAT-based measures of product strategy: new capital investment divided by net sales and asset utilization (total fixed assets divided by net sales), both reflecting the intensity of capital asset investment supporting the strategy. Higher scores indicate a greater emphasis on differentiation; lower values are associated with cost leadership. The raw factor scores were standardized and rescaled to the range of -1 to 1.
time_window: firm average across the sample years

description: Factor score obtained from a factor analysis of three CAPS benchmarking survey measures: organization form (degree of decentralization versus centralization of the purchasing management function), purchasing dollars per supplier (total purchase amount divided by number of suppliers) and supplier concentration (number of active suppliers accounting for 90% of purchases). A higher (lower) score denotes greater decentralization (centralization). The raw factor scores were standardized and rescaled to the range of -1 to 1.
time_window: firm average across the sample years

description: Factor score obtained from a factor analysis of two CAPS benchmarking survey measures: span of coordination, measured by the number of other functions that report to the purchasing management function divided by the total number of all applicable functions listed on the CAPS survey, and the percent of purchases through electronic data interchange (EDI) usage. A higher (lower) score denotes more (less) extensive coordination. The raw factor scores were standardized and rescaled to the range of -1 to 1.
time_window: firm average across the sample years

description: Return on assets, calculated as operating income before interest and extraordinary events divided by assets. In the main analysis the raw performance measure is first regressed on the industry- and firm-level environmental control variables and the residuals (renamed ROAa) are used as the dependent variable in the second-step regression on the strategy and design variables and their interactions.

A common factor extracted from all three measures of purchasing efficiency: purchasing amount per dollar of purchasing operating expenses (logged as the log of purchasing dollars per dollar of purchasing expense), purchase amount per purchasing employee (logged as the log of purchasing dollars per purchasing employee), and inventory turnover. Purchasing dollars per purchasing operating expense and the number of purchasing employees were obtained from the CAPS surveys, as was inventory turnover; COMPUSTAT data was used only when inventory turnover was not available from a survey. Firms were ranked by their common factor score and classified as high or low in purchasing efficiency relative to the median.
time_window: firm average across the sample years

description: Product strategy was measured from COMPUSTAT financial statements, as realized strategy, using six variables reduced by factor analysis to two scores: product uniqueness (differentiation) and capital intensity (cost efficiency).

Purchasing management design was measured from five CAPS benchmarking survey items reduced by factor analysis to two scores: organizational structure (degree of decentralization) and scope of activities (span of coordination).

variable_name: Change rhythm dummies (regular, focused, punctuated, temporarily switching, no change)
description: Strategic changes were coded from corporate reports for each firm-year; a diversification event was coded if a company entered a new country or business segment and a refocusing event if it withdrew from one, and the measure was transformed into a dichotomous variable coded 1 for years with one or multiple strategic changes and 0 otherwise. The change and stability event sequences of 1995-2001 were classified with the ClustalW multiple sequence alignment method and phase analysis into one regular change category and three irregular categories (focused, punctuated, temporarily switching); three companies that showed no change formed a control group. The categories were entered as dummies in the OLS regression, with the focused change rhythm dropped as the reference category, so the coefficients are interpreted in relation to the group of focused changers.

Measured as the total number of strategic changes between 1995 and 2001. The natural logarithm was used to convert the original, highly skewed distribution to a normal one, and the variable was mean-centered in the hypothesis 2 model to address potential multicollinearity; a squared frequency term was also entered.

ROE was calculated as net income divided by average equity, adjusting for industry effects by subtracting average industry ROE at time t from company ROE at time t. Average industry ROE was measured for each market region by computing the annual mean ROE of all companies in the sample headquartered in the same region. Performance was measured lagged three years from the end of the change period: because changes were coded for 1995-2001, performance was measured for 2002 to 2004 by summating the ROE of 2002, 2003, and 2004 and dividing this figure by three.

The Q ratio is computed as the sum of market value of equity and book value of debt divided by the book value of assets. It is used as the proxy for growth opportunities, with a high Q ratio indicating high growth opportunities. The dependent variable was capped at its 1st and 99th percentile values.

Group affiliation is identified through PROWESS's classification of firms into groups. It enters the models as an indicator variable for group affiliation; in the interaction plot the group dummy took the value of 0 for nongroup and 1 for group firms.

For each affiliate firm, group product access is calculated as the number of product markets that the business group operates in, apart from the focal affiliate firm, i.e., the sum of the firm product count of all other affiliate firms in the group. Product counts were built from the firm-product data in PROWESS, considering only products that contributed at least 10 percent of reported firm sales and dropping firms whose product sales summed to less than 90 percent of reported total firm sales. The natural logarithm of group product access was used for the analyses.

The MEC ratio is measured as a ratio of the number of companies in the business group to the number of product markets that a business group is present in. It is designed to parse the benefits of the organizational arrangement from the benefits of participating in multiple businesses, so that the impact of the organizational arrangement is examined for a given level of diversity. The higher the MEC ratio, the greater the multi-entity character of the business group.

The extent of pro-market reforms is captured using the reform index measure provided by Chari and David (2012). The index tracks the pro-market changes in the factor markets through an aggregate measure of foreign direct investment openness, tariff reductions, strengthening of intellectual property laws, strengthening of creditor and shareholder protection, and liberalization of labor laws and restrictions.

Five-item scale developed by Brett and VandeWalle (1999) used to measure individual core-knowledge employees' LGO. Response options ranged from 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree. Cronbach's alpha for LGO was .87.

Five items originally developed by Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Moorman, and Fetter (1990) and validated in the Chinese context by Wang et al. (2005). Cronbach's alpha for civic virtue was .88 and the ICC1 value was 0.23.

The CEO of each firm assessed the organizational AC using the 21-item scale developed by Jansen, Van Den Bosch, and Volberda (2005). Potential AC was measured with six items for acquisition and three items for assimilation. Cronbach's alpha for potential AC was .81.

The CEO of each firm assessed the organizational AC using the 21-item scale developed by Jansen, Van Den Bosch, and Volberda (2005). Realized AC was measured with six items for transformation and six items for exploitation. Cronbach's alpha for realized AC was .91.

Discounted sum of the total number of all banks that experienced near-failure in the focal bank's state between the bank's founding and the year before the bank was at risk of failure (t-1). Near-failure is defined as receiving a below-average CAMEL rating for at least two consecutive quarters and then recovering. Experience was discounted using age.

Discounted sum of the total number of all banks that experienced near-failure in the entire U.S. banking industry, excluding the state in which the focal bank was located, between the bank's founding and t-1. Experience was discounted using age.

Thrift near-failure experience variables were created using the same method as bank near-failure experience variables, measuring the discounted sum of near-failures in the focal bank's state between founding and t-1.

Thrift near-failure experience variables were created using the same method as bank near-failure experience variables, measuring the discounted sum of thrift near-failures outside the focal bank's state between founding and t-1.

Discounted sum of the total number of bank failures that had occurred in the focal bank's state since the bank's founding and until the year before the bank was at risk of failure. Experience was discounted using age.

Discounted sum of the total number of bank failures in the entire U.S. banking industry, excluding the state in which the focal bank was located, between founding and t-1. Experience was discounted using age.

Thrift failure experience variables were created using the same method as bank failure experience variables, measuring the discounted sum of thrift failures in the focal bank's state between founding and t-1.

Thrift failure experience variables were created using the same method as bank failure experience variables, measuring the discounted sum of thrift failures outside the focal bank's state between founding and t-1.

The dependent variable was the unobserved hazard rate for bank failure in the population of commercial banks chartered since 1984. Banks were considered to have failed if they were liquidated or merged with another bank with FDIC assistance. Mergers and acquisitions not associated with failure were treated as right-censored.

A factor score from an exploratory factor analysis with varimax rotation on z-scores of five environmental measures; a factor common to ST-TRITO, ST-TRITR, and KLD-ENVST was extracted and used as the measure of environmental risk management. The factor was the only one with an eigenvalue over 1.00 that had no cross loadings among observables and accounted for 43 percent of the variance in these data. Values were taken from 2001, a one-year lag relative to the 2002 reference year.

variable_name: ST-TRITO (total TRI emissions standardized by waste generation)
description: Total TRI emissions (TRI-TOTAL) standardized by WASTE-GEN to see what percentage of the firm's overall waste generation was being closely monitored through the TRI by public disclosure. The TRI values as compiled by IRRC are first standardized by dividing them by domestic revenues for the firm so that they are comparable across firms.

variable_name: ST-TRITR (TRI emissions treated on site standardized by waste generation)
description: Total TRI emissions treated on site to reduce their toxicity (TRI-TREAT) standardized by WASTE-GEN to see what percentage of the firm's discharges were being treated to reduce their toxicity. IRRC-standardized values dividing by domestic revenues are used.

variable_name: ST-TRIEN (TRI emissions reused or recycled on site standardized by waste generation)
description: Total TRI emissions reused or recycled on-site for energy (TRI-ERR) standardized by WASTE-GEN to see what percentage was being recycled for energy. IRRC-standardized values dividing by domestic revenues are used.

KLD examines seven 'strength' and seven 'concern' environmental dimensions ranging from pollution prevention programs or alternative fuel use to ozone depleting chemicals or hazardous waste generation. The authors averaged the strengths separately to create an average strength score for each firm.
Separate average concern score created by averaging the seven KLD environmental concern dimensions, consistent with Mattingly and Berman (2006), rather than subtracting concerns from strengths.

Each firm's WACC derived as in Equation 1, the weighted average of the cost of debt and the cost of equity. The cost of equity is estimated using the CAPM: the risk-free rate plus the firm's beta times the market risk premium. The risk-free rate used was the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond rate of 4.79 percent and the risk premium was set at 5.6 percent based on the Fama and French (2002) estimate of average returns over 1872-2000. The weight of equity is total market capitalization divided by debt plus market capitalization; the weight of debt is all debt issues divided by that debt plus market capitalization; the cost of debt is the firm's marginal cost of borrowing.

A factor score constructed from a factor analysis with varimax rotation on WACC-1, WACC-2, and WACC-3; a single factor accounting for 91 percent of the variance was extracted and the factor score was constructed from the factor weights times the original values. The alternative WACC estimates differ in the beta (weekly for Bloomberg versus annual for COMPUSTAT) and the risk premium (firm-specific versus the Fama and French average) used.

The firm's marginal cost of borrowing, based on estimates from the Bloomberg Financial dataset. The analysis was conducted with a before-tax estimate of the cost of debt; an after-tax version was also used as a dependent variable.

The authors' estimate of the cost of equity capital, equated to the risk-free interest rate plus the firm's beta times the market risk premium using the CAPM, with the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond rate of 4.79 percent as risk-free rate and a 5.6 percent risk premium.
The Bloomberg estimate of the firm's cost of equity capital, employed alongside the authors' own estimate in the cost of equity regressions.

The covariance of the market's return with the individual company's common stock return divided by the market's variance. An annual beta computed by Research Insight was used for each company found in the COMPUSTAT database.

The firm's level of long-term debt as reported in COMPUSTAT, standardized by market capitalization, consistent with the market-based perspective. It serves both as a control variable and as the dependent variable in the test of Hypothesis 1a.
The tax reduction associated with debt financing computed as TR = tax rate * cost of debt * leverage, regressed on environmental risk management with market capitalization and industry as controls.

The total number of shareholders at the close of 2002, used as the indicator of shareholder concentration: the higher the number of shareholders, the less concentrated the shares. Data came from COMPUSTAT's Research Insight database.
The published percentage of institutional holders of the firm's shares at the close of 2002, taken from COMPUSTAT's Research Insight database.

Firms were first sorted by stage of organizational life cycle on the basis of the information contained in the case reports. The binary distinction is between early and latter development, roughly paralleling the first two and the second two stages of a four-stage life cycle model. Each case report was reviewed and a subsequent sorting made by at least two authors, with disagreements referred to the third author.
