Firms were separately sorted by level of competition faced in their respective market using the case reports. The binary distinction is between little or no competition and intense competition, where intense competition means other organizations competing for the same customers with the same products or close substitutes have a clear, decisive impact. Sorting was done by at least two authors with disagreements referred to the third author.
scale: binary (little or no competition vs. intense competition)

description: Specific problem descriptions were taken verbatim from the case reports and categorized under major headings, producing 16 major categories for analysis. The percent of mentions was calculated for each subsample or quadrant by treating each cell in the matrix as an independent sample and calculating the proportion for each. The criterion for inclusion was the citing of the problem by at least 10 percent of the firms in at least one of the four quadrants.
scale: percentage of firms mentioning the problem
level: problem area within firm, aggregated to quadrant

description: Each firm was placed in one of four quadrants formed by crossing the life cycle distinction with the competition distinction: early development with little or no competition, later development with little or no competition, early development with intense competition, and later development with intense competition. The sample sorts by quadrant as 86 firms in Quadrant 1, 60 in Quadrant 2, 244 in Quadrant 3, and 255 in Quadrant 4. Each quadrant represents a different organizational task environment in which the firm must operate.

Proxy for the degree to which the value of a startup's patent assets is tied to the original venture and the inventors. Measured as the share of citations a startup's patents receive within 3 years from follow-on patents issued to the focal company, i.e., the share of self-cites. If no patents in the portfolio are cited within 3 years, the variable is set to zero. The measure is computed for the startup's portfolio and applied to its patents.
level: startup (patent portfolio), assigned to patent j
time_window: citations received within 3 years of patent grant

description: Based on trading activity in the secondary market for patents in the startup's sector and the issue years of its patents. The authors start with the population of patents issued in a calendar year in each sector using USPTO invention class-subclass lists, tally the number of US patents awarded in each set of classes and issue year, and compute the share involved in subsequent transactions at the exit year. The measure is averaged across patents in the startup's portfolio based on the issue year of the patents and the sector of the startup. The pool of potentially tradable patents is restricted to those issued 8 years prior to the exit year.
level: startup (sector and patent issue year), assigned to patent j
time_window: measured at the startup's exit year; patents issued in the prior 8 years

variable_name: Patent Sold as a Standalone Asset
description: Indicator for the patent being sold as a standalone asset. Set to one if patent j is involved in at least one change of ownership after the startup goes out of business and is sold without one or more of the inventors on the focal patent co-moving to the purchasing organization. The baseline category in the multinomial logit is the patent not being sold.

Indicator for co-mobility of a patent and an inventor. Set to one if the patent is sold and one or more of the inventors in the focal patent moves to the purchasing organization, as observed in LinkedIn employment profiles. The baseline category in the multinomial logit is the patent not being sold.
time_window: post-exit (employment histories after the startup fails)

description: Reference group in the multinomial logit regression. Indicates that no ownership changes are reported for the patent.

A latent construct measured by three observed variables: an asset dispersion entropy score, the number of countries in which the firm operates, and the number of foreign subsidiaries. The entropy score is defined as the sum over countries of the number of employees in a country times the natural logarithm of the inverse of the MNE's total employment, so it considers both the number of national markets in which a firm operates and the relative importance of these national markets to the firm. The number of countries is the dominant indicator.

A latent construct measured by four entropy measures of country-level conditions, calculated with the same entropy formula as asset dispersion. Economic conditions were estimated with a 5-year average of the Economic Freedom Index and a 4-year average of the Global Competitiveness Index, cultural boundaries with Hofstede's scores, and political systems with a 5-year average of the Political Constraint Index. Because the entropy measure requires categories, the economic freedom, global competitiveness and political constraint indices were categorized through hierarchical clustering, while Hofstede provided estimates of cultural categories; the elements are aggregated to the level of the MNE. The Global Competitiveness entropy score is the dominant element.

A latent construct defined by three market-based measures with all data for the fiscal year 1999 collected from Datastream: Jensen's alpha, the firm's excess return over and above that predicted by the Capital Asset Pricing Model; Sharpe's measure, the firm's average rate of return minus the risk-free rate divided by the standard deviation of returns; and the market-to-book ratio. The key measure appears to be the market-to-book ratio.

A network-based measure, the proportion of resource exchange weighted by concentration ratios (market power), following Casciaro and Piskorski (2005) as suggested by Burt (1983). The dependence of industry i on industry j is built from the proportion of goods industry i purchases from industry j and the proportion of goods industry i sells to industry j, measured at the six-digit NAICS level in the input-output accounts, together with the concentration ratio of industry j; the trade dependence of j on i is built symmetrically. Mutual dependence between the two industries combines both directional dependence terms. The functional forms are given in equation blocks that are unreadable in this payload, so the exact formulas cannot be restated.

The dependent variable is the hazard that an acquired subunit would be divested within a certain year. Time between the acquisition date and the divestiture date was split into annual spells for each subunit. It is a dichotomous variable coded 1 if the subunit was divested in a given year t and 0 otherwise. A positive coefficient in the Cox model indicates that the covariate increases the hazard of subunit divestiture and a negative coefficient indicates that it decreases the hazard.
time_window: annual spells from acquisition to divestiture

description: Measured by the three-year cumulative number of interindustry acquisitions completed by the subunit after it was acquired. Interindustry acquisitions are defined at the four-digit SIC level, and constraint absorption activities occurring in the subunit's own industry were excluded to reduce endogeneity. The variable was transformed with the log of one plus the count number to remedy significant positive skewness. The data were drawn from the SDC M&As database.

Measured by the three-year cumulative number of interindustry alliances formed by the subunit after it was acquired. Constraint absorption activities in the subunit's own industry were excluded, and interindustry alliances were defined consistently with interindustry acquisitions at the four-digit SIC level. The variable was transformed with the log of one plus the count number to remedy significant positive skewness. The data were drawn from the SDC Alliances database.

Market performance (i.e., sales and market share effectiveness) is measured with Babakus et al.'s (1996) 7-point measure. Values for the multi-item scale are computed as simple averages of the item scores because the number of items in each scale varies. The authors state that they did not discriminate between profitability and market performance in their hypotheses; a significant relationship with only one of the two dependent variables is characterized as partial support for the hypothesis.

Profitability is measured with Babakus et al.'s (1996) 7-point measure. Values for the multi-item scale are computed as simple averages of the item scores. The authors state that they did not discriminate between profitability and market performance in their hypotheses; a significant relationship with only one of the two dependent variables is characterized as partial support for the hypothesis.

Strategy type is assessed using the self-typing paragraph approach that is commonly used in strategic management and marketing strategy research. Respondents characterized their businesses as Prospectors, Analyzers, Low Cost Defenders, or Reactors by selecting the paragraph that described their business. The authors report that several studies have demonstrated that this is a valid measurement approach.
scale: categorical (Prospector, Analyzer, Low Cost Defender, Differentiated Defender, Reactor)

description: Selling strategy is assessed with Heide and Miner's (1992) 'Extendedness of Relationship' scale. This four-item 7-point scale assesses the seller's orientation towards the development of long-term relationships with buyers. A high score indicates a relationship selling strategy.

Internalization of selling activities is assessed with a single-item, 11-point scale that asks the respondent to indicate the proportion of sales revenues generated by members of the company's own sales force compared to the proportion generated by independent sales representatives. The scale goes from '0 percent by Company Sales Force/100 percent by Independent Sales Representatives' to '100 percent by Company Sales Force/0 percent by Independent Sales Representatives.' A high score indicates extensive use of an internal sales force.

Extent of supervision is assessed with Oliver and Anderson's (1994) eight-item 7-point scale, ranging from 'Strongly Disagree' to 'Strongly Agree.' A high score indicates high autonomy and low supervisory control, so the scale is reverse coded relative to the construct of supervision as named here. Values for the multi-item scale are computed as simple averages of the item scores.

Salesperson control system is measured with Babakus et al.'s (1996) seven-item 7-point 'Reward' scale that assesses whether sales people are evaluated and rewarded based on behaviors or on outcomes. A high score indicates outcome-based control while a low score indicates behavior-based control. Babakus et al. (1996) provided evidence of unidimensionality and discriminant validity in a confirmatory factor analysis.

Compensation is measured with an 11-point scale ranging from '0 percent by Commission/100 percent by Salary' to '100 percent by Commission/0 percent by Salary.' Respondents indicate the typical commission-to-salary compensation plan for members of the sales force in their business unit. A high score indicates a commission-based compensation system.

Technology intensity is measured as the research and development (R&D) intensity (R&D/sales) of the firm one year prior to the acquisition announcement, industry-adjusted by subtracting the industry average from the firm's R&D intensity using the firm's four-digit SIC code. Marketing intensity is similarly measured using the industry-adjusted advertising intensity (advertising/sales) of the firm one year prior to the acquisition announcement. The two variables are very highly correlated (r = 0.82), so the authors average the two values to get an overall technology and marketing-intensity variable.
time_window: one year prior to the acquisition announcement

description: The logarithm of total assets of the acquirer, measured one year prior to the merger announcement.
time_window: one year prior to the merger announcement

description: The organizational level of diversification measured with the entropy index for the organization (Palepu, 1985). The level of diversification is measured one year prior to the acquisition announcement.
time_window: one year prior to the acquisition announcement

description: Following Haunschild (1993), unabsorbed acquirer financial slack is measured in two ways. First, slack is operationalized as the debt-to-equity ratio, a conventional measure inversely related to slack. Second, the percentage of free cash flow is assessed, defined as (operating income - taxes - interest expense - depreciation - preferred dividend - common dividend)/equity. Both variables were measured at the end of the year before the acquisition year. The authors focus on unabsorbed slack because it is more closely related to major strategic actions such as mergers and acquisitions than absorbed slack.
time_window: end of the year before the acquisition year

description: The firm's return on assets (ROA), measured one year prior to the acquisition.
time_window: one year prior to the acquisition

variable_name: Timing of action in the wave
description: The number of days that each acquisition announcement occurred after the first acquisition in the wave, divided by the total number of days in the wave. The end score ranges from zero to one, with the first acquisition in the wave having the lowest value and the last acquisition in the wave having the highest value. If two or more acquisitions occurred on the same day, they carried the same timing value.

Answered questionnaire was a binary variable coded '1' if firms answered the CDP questionnaire in one particular year and '0' otherwise. The dependent variable came from the Carbon Disclosure Project, a U.K.-based nonprofit organization that works with institutional investors to persuade large corporations to disclose information on carbon emissions. The CDP addressed letters to the CEO of each firm asking the CEO to complete a questionnaire about climate change risks and opportunities, the firm's climate change strategy, and its greenhouse gas emissions.

MBA degree was created as a binary variable to capture the effect of business education. Educational background measures came from BoardEx, a comprehensive database containing profiles for more than 380,000 managers and directors worldwide, supplemented where necessary with Business Week's Executive Profile and Biography and company annual reports. CEO educational background was based on the current year.

Legal degree was created as a binary variable to capture the effect of legal education. Educational background measures came from BoardEx, a comprehensive database containing profiles for more than 380,000 managers and directors worldwide, supplemented where necessary with Business Week's Executive Profile and Biography and company annual reports. CEO educational background was based on the current year.

CEO tenure was measured as a binary variable: New CEO was coded '1' if the CEO had been in office for less than three years and '0' otherwise, since most CEOs take major actions within the first two and a half years of office. The tenure measure came from BoardEx, supplemented where necessary with Business Week's Executive Profile and Biography and company annual reports, and was based on the current year.

Computed in three stages following Fleming and Sorenson (2004). First, the average likelihood that an individual patent subclass was combined with other subclasses per patent was computed. Second, a patent-level score was created by averaging those likelihood scores over all subclasses on a patent and taking the inverse, so that a higher value indicates a patent that combines subclasses unlikely to be combined with each other. Third, these patent-level scores were averaged across all patents applied for by a focal subunit during a year. Patents were assigned to their primary subunit (home lab location) using the identity of the patent's first listed inventor, and inventors' subunit affiliations were identified from Motorola's annual employee directories. The dependent variable considers patent application date rather than issuance date.
time_window: patents applied for 1963-1998 used to construct the measure; outcome measured yearly 1974-1997

description: A corporate staff arrival rate: the total number of individuals who were absent from the corporate staff directory in year t − 1 but appeared in the corporate directory in year t, expressed relative to the number of corporate employees in year t. The authors state that Table 1 lists the formula used to construct each turnover variable.
time_window: year t, identifying arrivals relative to the year t − 1 directory

description: A corporate staff departure rate: the total number of staff members listed by the corporate staff directory in year t − 1 who were absent from the entire directory in year t, expressed relative to the number of corporate employees in year t. Because departure is identified from directory data, voluntary and involuntary turnover cannot be distinguished. The authors state that Table 1 lists the formula used to construct each turnover variable.
time_window: year t, identifying departures relative to the year t − 1 directory

description: A subunit member arrival rate: the total number of subunit members who were absent from the directory of subunit location i in year t − 1 but were listed by subunit i's directory in year t, expressed relative to the number of employees of that subunit in year t. The authors state that Table 1 lists the formula used to construct each turnover variable.
time_window: year t, identifying arrivals relative to the year t − 1 directory

description: A subunit member departure rate: all those who were listed by subunit i's directory in year t − 1 but were absent from the entire directory in year t, expressed relative to the number of employees of that subunit in year t. Departures are identified on the basis of directory data, so voluntary and involuntary turnover cannot be distinguished. The authors state that Table 1 lists the formula used to construct each turnover variable.
time_window: year t, identifying departures relative to the year t − 1 directory

description: Firm performance was captured with three measures: return on invested capital, return on equity, and return on assets, taken from year-end 1997 data in the Fintel database. Adjustments were made to these data to reduce the influence of outliers using the Winsor technique at the 5th and 95th percentiles. Calculations for ROIC and ROE were eliminated when invested capital and/or equity for a firm was negative, which left 144 firms with an ROIC measure, 142 firms with an ROE measure, and all 144 firms with an ROA measure.

Firm performance was captured with three measures: return on invested capital, return on equity, and return on assets, taken from year-end 1997 data in the Fintel database and adjusted with the Winsor technique at the 5th and 95th percentiles. Calculations for ROIC and ROE were eliminated when invested capital and/or equity was negative, which left 199 firms with an ROIC measure, 194 firms with an ROE measure, and all 200 firms with an ROA measure.

Firm strategy was measured via survey response, with eight questions on a six-point semantic-differential format about expected product and operational aspects, answered for firm operations during 1997. Seven of the eight questions loaded on a single factor and were summed, adjusted to a range of 0 to 35, with lower scores representing flexibility and higher scores representing efficiency; coefficient alpha was 0.86. Cut-off points classified firms scoring above 16 as efficiency firms.

The same survey strategy score, formed by summing seven six-point semantic-differential questions about firm operations in 1997 and adjusting the total to a range of 0 to 35. Lower scores represent flexibility, and cut-off points classified firms scoring below 11 as flexibility firms. Items one, three, four, and six of the original eight questions were reverse-scored.

The same survey strategy score, summed from the seven six-point semantic-differential questions on firm operations in 1997 and adjusted to a range of 0 to 35. Cut-off points established so that firms scoring between 11 and 16 were classified as mix firms, i.e., firms that offer both standard and made-to-order products.

Three raters examined every available page of each firm's website and gave their opinions on whether the firm was using an efficiency strategy, a flexibility strategy, or mixing strategies, using criteria specified in advance: efficiency firms only provide standard products. Based on the rater classifications the 200 firms were coded 1 = flexibility, 2 = mix, or 3 = efficiency, resulting in 84 efficiency firms; coefficient alpha between the three raters was 0.85.

Website-based classification of firm strategy by three raters, based on the principle that flexibility firms only provide made-to-order products. Firms were coded 1 = flexibility, 2 = mix, or 3 = efficiency based on rater classifications, resulting in 66 flexibility firms.

Website-based classification of firm strategy by three raters, based on the principle that mix firms provide both standard and made-to-order products. Firms were coded 1 = flexibility, 2 = mix, or 3 = efficiency based on rater classifications, resulting in 50 mix firms.

Alliance use was based on reports by the key managers regarding the firms' use or nonuse of alliance relationships, characterizing the firm rather than specific alliance relationships. Most firms reporting alliance use reported having multiple types of alliance relationships, and no firm held only less strategically motivated types such as outside contracting and purchaser-supplier relationships.

Subscale formed from the environmental perception scale, scored from the items loading on the general uncertainty factor; the scale comprised items from Miller and Friesen's environmental dynamism measures, Khandwalla's external environment measures, and original items developed by Schultz, Slevin, and Covin. Items used a five-point response scale and were worded to assess high levels of uncertainty.

Subscale formed from the environmental perception scale, scored from the items loading on the technological demand and volatility factor of the same item pool. Items used a five-point response scale and were worded to assess high levels of uncertainty.

Subscale formed from the environmental perception scale, scored from the items loading on the predictability of markets factor of the same item pool. Items used a five-point response scale and were worded to assess high levels of uncertainty.

Subscale formed from two additional items added to the environmental perception scale that assessed perceptions of the extent to which internationalization seemed needed for firm success. Items used a five-point response scale and were worded to assess high levels of uncertainty.

Subscale formed from the environmental perception scale, scored from the items loading on the potential for future growth and profits factor of the same item pool. The growth and profit questions, unlike the other items, were worded to reflect perceptions of a high level of certainty regarding the future, and they used a five-point response scale.

An eight-item, five-point scale drawn from the work of Covin and Slevin that assesses the tendencies of a firm's managers toward risk taking, innovation, and proactiveness toward competitors. A principal components factor analysis resulted in a solution in which all items loaded above 0.50 on a single factor with a factor eigenvalue of 3.56. The reliability estimate for the scale was .81.

Assessed via ten items developed by Erez and Earley; a factor analysis of data from the Norwegian questionnaire retained six items, four original items having cross-loaded or loaded below 0.50, and all remaining items loaded above 0.50 on a single factor with an eigenvalue of 2.49. The summate of these six items was used in the study, with a reliability estimate of .71.

Perceived environmental uncertainty was measured by a survey scale of the key manager based on Covin and Slevin and Schultz, Slevin, and Covin, plus two added items. Factor analysis produced five subscales: general uncertainty, technological demand and volatility, predictability of customers and competitors, demands for internationalization, and potential for growth and profits.

The Andersen survey measured sales growth as a five-year average using a six-point, nominal scale ranging from Decreased, No Change, Increased 1-5%, Increased 6-10%, Increased 11-20%, to Increased 21% or more. The authors argue the scale is appropriate because the construct is expected to be both right-censored and left-censored, and that sales growth is a more reliable measure of family-firm performance than income-based measures because privately held firms have incentive to minimize reported taxable income.
scale: six-point nominal scale from Decreased to Increased 21% or more

description: A dummy variable (1/0) from the survey that identifies firms offering pay incentives as annual and/or long-term cash bonuses to nonfamily employees. 72% of the firms in the sample indicated that they offer pay incentives to nonfamily agents.

A dummy variable (1/0) from the survey that identifies firms offering pay incentives as annual and/or long-term cash bonuses to family members. 75% of the firms in the sample indicated that they offer pay incentives to family members. A Dividends dummy is included to assure that cash bonuses paid to family agents are contingent portions of salary rather than dividend payments distributed as salary bonuses.

Measured by asking whether the firm has a strategic plan and how well these plans are known within the organization; the construct is coded as a three-level categorical variable: "No Strategic Plan," "Strategic Plan Exists but is Not Well Known to Company Management," and "Strategic Plan is Well Known by Company Management."

Measured with a 5-level scale ranging from "11 or more years until retirement" to "Semiretired," which the authors say conforms with other indirect measures of tenure available from the survey. The bivariate correlation between CEO tenure and CEO age is high (r = 0.62, p < 0.001).
Measured, like Finkelstein and Hambrick (1990), as the average number of years each member has served on the board.

A continuous variable identifying the number of outside directors (individuals who are neither family members nor employees) as a percentage of the total number of board directors. Only 19% of the sample placed outsiders on the board, and the average board has four members.

A dummy variable (1/0) that indicates whether the significant shareholders of the business know each others' estate and share transfer intentions. Share and estate transfer plans are not known in approximately one-third of the firms.

Cluster membership derived from a complete linkage cluster analysis of the seven independent variables used to test the first four hypotheses; dendograms were visually inspected to identify the number of clusters and cluster membership was confirmed with K-means iterative partitioning. Two profiles emerged, one showing generally high values for the seven governance variables and the other generally low values (N = 771 and 882 firms).

Automated content analysis of published news articles and newswires whose headline contains the name of a sample company. For each company-year the number of exploratory words is divided by the sum of exploratory and exploitative words. The exploratory and exploitative vocabularies were derived directly from March's (1991) definitions of the two concepts, and the program was revised to exclude irrelevant word occurrences identified in a key word in context analysis. The textual data were collected from the Reuters News archive in Factiva.
Market-based operationalization of Tobin's Q, computed as the market value of assets divided by the book value of assets. Financial data were collected from Compustat.

Calculated as the logarithm of the industry's total R&D expense divided by total industry sales. Industry R&D intensity is centered in the analysis to provide for the estimation in the model testing the average effects of the relative exploration variable.

Counts the number of clients shared by the acquiring firm and each potential target. The authors report the model using the simple logged count because it produced the best-fitting estimates; versions weighting each tie by the tenure of the acquirer-client relationship or by the time the two agencies shared the client produced equivalent patterns of results.

Binary dependent variable set to one for the actual mergers (the cases) and to zero for the unrealized combinations (the controls). Because acquirers essentially drive the selection of partners, the process was modeled as a conditional logit regression conditioned on the set of matched cases and controls.

Agencies were assigned to locations on the basis of their headquarters, and spherical geometry was used to compute the geographic distance in terms of the logged distance in miles between the acquiring firm and each potential target. The variable was centered prior to multiplying it with the count of common clients.

Created by assigning all clients to four-digit SIC codes and counting the number of codes in which both the acquirer and the potential target had clients. The variable was centered prior to multiplying it with the count of common clients.

The logged count of clients shared by the acquiring firm and each target before the merger. It enters the triple differences models together with its interactions with the merger and post-merger indicators.

Cumulative count of client accounts terminated for each post-merger year. Client accounts were tracked for three years before and three years after the merger, and an account was coded as dissolved in the first year the advertising firm no longer listed the client in its Redbooks record; these events were summed into cumulative annual counts of relationships lost. Post-merger, the measure counts the cumulative dissolutions of the accounts held by the target firm at the time of the merger, for both cases and controls. The models are Poisson regressions with the number of relationships included as an exposure term, so the estimates are rates of dissolution.
time_window: three years pre-merger to three years post-merger

description: Cumulative count of client relationships terminated, the relationship-level version of the client retention measure. If the authors observed a discontinuation of all of the accounts with the client, they also considered the relationship dissolved, and these events were summed into cumulative annual counts of relationships lost. The models estimate dissolution rates with the number of relationships as an exposure term.
time_window: three years pre-merger to three years post-merger

description: Post-merger, the logged total billings reported by the merged firm divided by the logged total number of clients listed across all of its subunits. Pre-merger, the billings of the acquiring firm and the acquired firm were summed, logged, and divided by the logged summed counts of clients listed by the two firms; the same construction was applied to the synthetic control mergers. Logging the numerator and denominator accounts for the fact that larger agencies tend to serve larger clients.

Two firms are coded as having an interlock tie when at least one officer or owner from firm A serves as an outside director at firm B, or vice versa. Ties are measured as directional and are created by individuals who are principally affiliated as officers or owners with the firms they connect. Data on board interlocks and board structure were collected for 1994-1995.

A multi-item scale from the CEO survey assessing behavioral elements of board control that have been theorized to entail board independence from management, including the board's tendency to monitor and evaluate CEO decision making and performance and the frequency with which directors challenge the CEO's position on strategic issues rather than deferring to the CEO's judgment. A confirmatory factor analysis with LISREL showed an adequate fit, and the control factor was estimated with the Bartlett method. Interitem reliability was acceptable, with an alpha of .88.

A multi-item scale from the CEO survey based on prior qualitative research about how CEOs may engage in ongoing collaboration with outside directors by seeking their advice and counsel on strategic issues. The cooperation factor was estimated with the Bartlett method after confirmatory factor analysis. Interitem reliability was acceptable, with an alpha of .89.

Indirect ties between CEOs and outside directors through third-party directors were measured for each dyad as the number of board appointments shared by the CEO and board members of the outside director's home company board, excluding the focal board. The product-term approach was used to test the hypothesized interaction effects between third-party ties and the focal CEO-board ties.

A dichotomous variable coded 1 if the two firms in a dyad entered into an alliance during the two-year period following the survey date (i.e., 1995-1996). The sample includes all interfirm partnerships that entail the creation of a new legal entity in which both partners hold equity, also referred to as joint ventures; only joint ventures that had actually been formed were recorded. These data were coded manually from the Funk and Scott Predicasts Index of Corporate Change and from Lexis/Nexis.

The average ratio of R&D to sales over the three-year study period for U.S. firms in industries producing the product of the alliance. The average was taken from information published in Business Week, which was based on COMPUSTAT data from that period. Only U.S. data were used, as U.S. and Japanese R&D data may not be directly comparable.
scale: ratio of R&D expenditures to sales

description: Evidence of an intention to conduct joint R&D was taken directly from the alliance announcements and coded as present if an announcement mentioned it and as absent if it was not mentioned.

A cooperation was considered as involving large firms when the consolidated total assets were greater than one billion dollars for the U.S. firm and one hundred billion yen for the Japanese firm. Assets data were taken from Moody's Industrial Manual and the Million Dollar Directory for U.S. firms and from the Japan Company Handbook for Japanese corporations.

An alliance was coded as a joint venture when its announcement indicated that the parents had formed a new legal entity with equity contributions. Informal arrangements, cooperative ties, developmental assistance programs, licensing arrangements, and marketing and supply arrangements were coded as agreements.

Average number of previous managerial positions that top management team members held in the medical and surgical instruments industry. The authors argue that with every managerial position held in the industry, managers become more knowledgeable about the key assets, strategies, players, and specific conditions in the industry.

Average number of managerial positions that outside directors previously held in the medical and surgical instruments industry. The measure is described as an indicator of the amount and breadth of industry-specific knowledge, because each additional managerial position held in the industry makes outside directors more familiar with the key assets and strategies of different industry players, and it serves as a proxy for the outsiders' level of industry-specific knowledge and ability to access industry networks.

Number of years since the firm's founding, used as a time-based, continuous indicator of the firm's entrepreneurial development and liability of newness. The authors state that the sample indicates sufficient variance in firm age and represents firms with different levels of exposure to the liability of newness, so that higher values indicate lower exposure to the liability of newness.

An entropy measure of international diversification that accounts for the extent of sales outside the domestic market and their distribution globally. Sales attributed to global market region i are weighted by the natural logarithm of the inverse of that region's sales; the measure considers both the number of global market regions in which a firm operates and the relative importance of each region to total sales. Foreign markets were classified into four relatively homogeneous global regions because country-level sales data were unavailable. The formula itself is not readable in the text.
time_window: three-year average, 1988-1990 (two-year average for a small subsample)

description: The entropy measure of product diversification strategy, in which sales attributed to segment i are weighted by the natural logarithm of the inverse of that segment's sales. The measure considers both the number of segments in which a firm operates and the proportion of total sales each segment represents. The formula itself is not readable in the text.
time_window: three-year average, 1988-1990 (two-year average for a small subsample)

description: Return on assets was chosen as the dependent variable from among three accounting-based performance measures. ROE was ruled out because it is more sensitive to capital structure differences; ROS was not used because ROS and the control variables in the regression equations are functions of total sales, so equations with ROS might reflect mathematical artifacts as well as true relations. ROA and ROS generated similar findings and were highly correlated (r = .91).
time_window: three-year average, 1988-1990 (two-year average for a small subsample)

description: R&D intensity was used as a proxy for innovation and was measured as the ratio of research and development expenditures to a firm's total number of employees. Use of this ratio avoided an artificial relationship with firm size measured with firm sales. The authors note the ratio is widely used in studies of innovation.
time_window: three-year average, 1988-1990 (two-year average for a small subsample)

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 when the patient has private insurance, with Medicaid as the omitted baseline. It is based on the primary payment method billed in NEMSIS; because insurance is collected only after the transport decision, the measure captures insurance information available to crews as they make en-route service decisions.
Count of unit-reported medical procedures performed by EMS personnel from initial contact until final dropoff. The variable is winsorized at the 99th percentile and transformed as log(x + 1).
scale: count, log-transformed and winsorized at the 99th percentile

description: Total time in minutes EMS personnel spent with a patient during a call. The variable is winsorized at the 99th percentile and transformed as log(x + 1).
scale: minutes, log-transformed and winsorized at the 99th percentile

description: Dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if an agency has a private call ratio above the median of all agencies in the sample, capturing long-term financial pressure based on the observed patient payment mix in each service area. Higher values indicate lower agency financial need.
scale: dummy (1 = above median private call ratio)

description: Measure of short-term agency financial need that uses the percentage of private insurance calls from a moving lagged 3-month window. Higher values indicate lower agency financial need.
Dummy variable equal to 1 if lights and sirens are used leaving the scene en route to a hospital and 0 otherwise. It is used as a proxy for call acuity.

Agency type classification provided by NEMSIS. Fire departments, community agencies, and governmental agencies are classified as nonprofits, while private (non-hospital) agencies are classified as for-profits. Hospital-affiliated EMS units are classified in multiple ways because hospitals cannot be classified cleanly as either nonprofits or for-profits.

variable_name: number of BT foundings in MSA-year
description: Event count of new dedicated biotechnology firm foundings in a metropolitan statistical area in a given year. The unit of analysis is an MSA-year treated as being at risk of experiencing spin-off companies from nearby firms of like kind. Founding events were identified by compiling biotechnology industry databases and directories.

IPO concentration, a distance-weighted measure of the local density of dedicated biotechnology firm IPOs. The contribution of each firm going public to each point in space is weighted by the inverse distance between the focal point and the location of the firm experiencing the event, and by the firm's market capitalization in constant (1995) dollars, computed as the number of outstanding shares multiplied by the share price at the close of the first day of trading. Summing these weighted contributions across all firms yields a distance-weighted measure of proximity to firms having an IPO in a chosen interval of time. Annual lags were created for each of the three years prior to the current one; the formal specification is given in an equation block that is unreadable in this rendering.
time_window: annual; one-year lag in the reported models, with two- and three-year lags also estimated

variable_name: local density of acquired BT firms
description: Acquisition concentration, a geography-specific, size- and distance-weighted measure of the local concentration of acquisition activity. The value of the acquired firm's equity, in constant (1995) dollars based on the price paid by the acquirer, is weighted by the inverse distance between the center of each MSA and the location of the acquired firm, and the weighted contributions are summed across all acquired firms. The measure was calculated including all acquired firms and was also decomposed into intraindustry and interindustry parts.
time_window: annual; one-year lag in the reported models, with two- and three-year lags also estimated

variable_name: local density of BT firms acquired by non-BT firms
description: The interindustry acquisition concentration: the acquisition concentration measure computed only from transactions in which a biotech firm is acquired by a non-DBF enterprise. Equity values are weighted by the inverse distance between the MSA and the acquired firm and summed across all such acquired firms. Interindustry transactions are mostly financed with at least some cash rather than exclusively with stock.
time_window: annual; one-year lag in the reported models, with two- and three-year lags also estimated

variable_name: local density of BT firms acquired by other BT firms
description: The intraindustry acquisition concentration: the acquisition concentration measure computed only from transactions in which one biotech firm acquires another. Equity values are weighted by the inverse distance between the MSA and the acquired firm and summed across all such acquired firms.
time_window: annual; one-year lag in the reported models, with two- and three-year lags also estimated

description: Dummy variable defined at the state level that takes the value of one if state law precludes or severely limits an employer's ability to enforce non-compete covenants, and zero otherwise. Ten states, including California, have enacted regulations that prevent employers from enforcing non-compete clauses. The variable is assigned to MSAs according to the state in which they are located.

Computed by summing a firm's strengths in the following KLD subdomains: environment, community, diversity, employee relations, and human rights. KLD rates the strengths and concerns that a firm's CSR practices and policies reflect using a binary system whereby '1' indicates the presence of a strength or concern in a particular area and '0' indicates its absence. The corporate governance and product quality subdomains are excluded from the measure.

Dichotomous variable equal to '1' if a firm had been targeted by an activist hedge fund in a given year and '0' otherwise. Only the first instance in which a firm was targeted by an activist hedge fund is included, to control for 'wolf pack' activism. Targeting was identified from Schedule 13D filings required by the SEC of shareholders who plan to actively influence a firm's management.
Computed as the average CSR score for all firms, excluding the focal firm, in an industry group classified according to two-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes.

Calculated as the total number of vague words and phrases divided by the total number of words spoken by managers during quarterly earnings conference calls, to control for the total length of each call. It is expressed as a percentage, whereby a value of 0.03 indicates that 3% of all words spoken during a call were characterized as 'vague.' Hiller's communication vagueness dictionary, containing 362 vague words and expressions classified along 10 dimensions of vagueness, was used to capture the vague terminology, and the dimensions were combined into an index measure of communication vagueness.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the firm-year observation is listed in Table 1 (an entry into renewable generation) and 0 otherwise. Probit models were used to test the proposed Hypotheses 1-5. Independent variables are lagged by one year to avoid potential endogeneity, and observations for years with no entries into renewables were dropped from the regressions.
time_window: 1992-2008 firm-years; independent variables lagged by one year

description: Heat rate is measured as the ratio of heat input of fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas to electricity generated (Btu/kWh), and thus represents combustion inefficiency. Firm-specific heat rate data were calculated by aggregating unit-level data obtained from the EIA (Form EIA-906/920/923) under a confidentiality agreement.

Actual renewable demand is proxied by the renewable fraction of the total electricity generation capacity at the state level. The electricity generation capacity data by fuel type was obtained from Form EIA-860. This variable was then weighted by the share of the company's electricity sales in each state to obtain a firm-specific variable.
level: firm-year (state-level measure weighted by the firm's state sales shares)

description: Because the paper focuses on variation across firms within the electric utility industry, variables that indicate the extent to which managers are insulated were used: CEO duality and percent of inside directors. These data were collected from Risk Metrics. CEO duality is one of the two measures of managerial discretion used in the entry regressions.

Because the paper focuses on variation across firms within the electric utility industry, variables that indicate the extent to which managers are insulated were used: CEO duality and percent of inside directors. These data were collected from Risk Metrics. Percent of inside directors is the second of the two measures of managerial discretion used in the entry regressions.

The presence of independent power producers in the renewable generation market was measured using the ratio of independent power producers' renewable capacity to total renewable capacity at the state level. The renewable capacity by producer type data at the state level was obtained from the EIA website. To calculate firm-specific values, this variable was then weighted by the share of the company's electricity sales in each state.
level: firm-year (state-level measure weighted by the firm's state sales shares)

variable_name: Renewable generation dummy at the utility level
description: Previous investments in renewables are indicated using a dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the firm has nonhydro renewable capacity in year t - 1, and takes 0 otherwise. This data was obtained from Form EIA-860.

To capture electric utilities' strategy towards renewables, the percentage of renewables in the firm's fuel mix portfolio was calculated. The share of renewables can be represented by the ratio of renewable capacity to total capacity; renewable capacity rather than renewable generation better captures electric utilities' strategy, since once renewable capacity is in place, renewable generation tends to be driven by weather conditions. Firm fixed effects and first-difference models were used to test Hypothesis 6.
Wholesale deregulation was an ordered categorical variable equal to 1 for 1992-1995, 2 for 1996-2000 and 3 for 2000-2008 if the electric utility operates in RTO/ISO regions.

variable_name: Regulatory order issued, deregulation legislation passed, actual start of retail access
description: Retail deregulation was measured by three state-year dummies (regulatory order issued, deregulation legislation passed, actual start of retail access) that equal 1 once the step is reached, built from EIA information. They were weighted for each firm by its sales across states and entered one at a time.
scale: dummies, weighted by share of sales

description: An index combining four measures of the CEO's power relative to the board, combined using principal components analysis. The four indicators are the CEO's tenure relative to the average tenure of board members, the portion of the board appointed after the CEO, board leadership structure (joint possession of the CEO and board chair positions), and director stock ownership. All four indicators loaded on a single factor with an eigenvalue greater than one.

Calculated as the number of shares repurchased in a given year divided by the total number of shares available for repurchase in that year under the plan. Repurchases are observed separately for each year in the implementation window following repurchase plan adoption (five observations per case of adoption). Higher values indicate greater implementation, i.e., less decoupling of the plan from practice.

variable_name: Decoupling of buyback programs at tied-to firms (one-step ties) and (two-step ties)
description: Extent of decoupling of buyback programs at other firms to which the focal firm is connected by an interlock tie. The paper states that P_i is the percentage of shares repurchased at tied-to firm i and N is the number of tied-to firms that adopted a repurchase plan within the past five years, but the formula itself was not extractable from the text and is not reconstructed here. Both one-step ties (directional and non-directional) and two-step ties through the board of a financial institution were measured separately.
time_window: tied-to firms that adopted a repurchase plan within the past five years

variable_name: Decoupling of LTIPs at tied-to firms (one-step ties) and (two-step ties)
description: Extent of decoupling of LTIPs at other firms to which the focal firm is connected by an interlock tie. P_i is the percentage of shares reserved for issuance under the LTIP that were actually granted under the plan and N is the number of tied-to firms that adopted a plan; the formula itself was not extractable from the text. Separate measures were created for one-step and two-step ties.

Calculated by taking the average percentage of shares repurchased under plans adopted during the previous ten years (i.e., prior to the current plan) and subtracting this value from one, so that higher values indicate greater decoupling.

Calculated by taking the percentage of shares reserved for issuance under a previously adopted LTIP that were actually granted under the plan and subtracting this value from one, so that higher values indicate greater decoupling.

JdT asks industrial buyers to evaluate the creativity of fashion collections in both Fall/Winter and Spring/Summer fashion shows. Buyers give 20 points to the most creative collection for the given season and 0 points to collections that they do not think are creative, and each buyer is able to give points to a maximum of 20 houses. The variable incorporates the average number of points that a given fashion house's collection received from all of the buyers for a particular season.

The number of houses across different countries to which the focal fashion house becomes connected through designers' outward mobility in a given six-year period. For example, if six designers left a U.S. house and joined two different houses in France, then the house's Foreign Mobility Out-Degree would be two. A linear and a squared term of this variable are entered in the regressions.

The number of houses within the same country to which the focal fashion house is connected through outward mobility of its past designers in a given six-year period. For example, if between 2000 and 2005 six designers left a U.S. house and joined four different U.S. houses, then the focal house's Domestic Mobility Out-Degree would be four. A linear and a squared term of this variable are entered in the regressions.

The number of competitors in the higher-status group to which the focal fashion house lost designers during the six-year window. Relative positions of houses in the status groups were determined based on status scores in the same year during which mobility events actually occurred, with the high-, medium-, and low-status groups identified from the 33rd and 66th percentiles of status in a given year. A linear term and, in some models, a squared term of this variable are entered in the regressions.

The number of competitors in the same-status group to which the focal fashion house lost designers during the six-year window. Status groups were identified by computing scores corresponding to the 33rd and 66th percentiles of status in a given year, and mobility events were evaluated with the status scores of the year in which they occurred. A linear term and, in some models, a squared term of this variable are entered in the regressions.

The number of competitors in the lower-status group to which the focal fashion house lost designers during the six-year window. Status groups were identified by computing scores corresponding to the 33rd and 66th percentiles of status in a given year, and mobility events were evaluated with the status scores of the year in which they occurred. A linear term and, in some models, a squared term of this variable are entered in the regressions.

Product differentiation was operationalized as the degree of advertising intensity in the industry, defined as advertising expenses as a percentage of sales. The average value for the 3 years prior to succession was used. The measure was obtained from the Troy Almanac of Key Business and Industrial Financial Ratios.

Defined as the average annual growth rate in value of shipments in the 3 years preceding the year of succession. The value of shipments data was adjusted for inflation using GDP implicit price deflators.
time_window: 3 years preceding the year of succession

description: Defined as the ratio of the industry's gross book value of assets to value of annual shipments, obtained from the U.S. Census of Manufactures. Because gross book value of assets data are provided only at 5-year intervals, the data available for the year closest to the year of succession had to be used (1977, 1982, and 1987 for this sample period).
time_window: year closest to the year of succession

description: Measured as the number of years the CEO had served in the firm prior to the year of succession. Data on this CEO successor characteristic were collected from Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management and Who's Who in Finance and Industry.

Measured as the number of years from the year of birth to the year of succession. Data were collected from Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management and Who's Who in Finance and Industry.

Measured on a 7-point scale based on the highest degree earned by the CEO: 1 = high school, 2 = some college, 3 = undergraduate degree, 4 = some graduate school, 5 = masters degree, 6 = attended doctoral program and 7 = doctorate degree. Data were collected from Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management and Who's Who in Finance and Industry.

A categorical measure that took a value '1' if the CEO successor was categorized as having a throughput functional background (dominant functional experience in production and operations, process R&D, and accounting) and '0' otherwise (nonthroughput). Data on CEO successor characteristics were collected from Dun & Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Management and Who's Who in Finance and Industry.

Measured as average relative firm ROA in the 3 years following succession minus average relative firm ROA in the 3 years prior to succession. Relative firm performance is the ratio of the firm's return on assets (ROA) to industry ROA; firm ROA was obtained from Compustat tapes and industry ROA from Dun & Bradstreet's Industry Norms and Key Business Ratios. Averaging ROA provides a more accurate picture of firm performance than ROA from a single year.
time_window: 3 years before versus 3 years after succession

description: Operationalized as the number of complementary product integrations completed by the firm in the 2 years starting from January 1998. Data on the number and type of CPI were collected from a comprehensive review of product data reported in three software industry trade publications and other public data forums, and were tallied with the same information requested from survey respondents; inconsistencies in figures relating to 11 firms were clarified, and 5 firms were dropped, leaving 78 firms.

Based on 12 generic design elements of a software development tool that play a critical role in tool integration. For each design element i, respondents indicated the total number of protocols implemented (xi) and the number of those protocols that were common with all of the relevant complementary technologies (yi); the ratio yi/xi indicates the proportion of protocols for design element i that are in common with relevant complementary technologies. The sum of such ratios over the 12 design elements is the measure.

Operationalized as the ratio between the total number of product design modules and the product size. Respondents were requested to indicate the total number of design modules of the first version of their product, and product size was reported in terms of the number of function points.

A six-item measurement scale reflecting the consideration of CPI in product modularity decisions, broadly focused on the nature of sharing data and functions with other products and the nature of coupling between core product modules and other modules. Respondents indicated their extent of agreement with the various items on a 7-point Likert scale, and an average of the scores of the six items was taken as the measure. Cronbach's alpha for the scale was 0.81 and the six items loaded on a single factor explaining 69% of the variance.

Operationalized as the number of new versions of the product introduced by the firm in the 2-year period starting in 1998. Respondents provided data on the release of new product versions (version number, release date), and this was cross-validated with data available from public data sources.

FDI is the total capital flow, including capital flow between parents and affiliates, intercompany loans, and reinvested earnings. The model is estimated on the totals of the inward and outward data, as the United States is the only country that publishes the data needed for this analysis. Major-owned (more than 50% owned) non-bank affiliates of non-bank parents are used for the outward analysis, and non-bank affiliates (more than 10% foreign ownership) for the inward analysis.

The cost of sales of affiliates as a share of total costs, used as an indicator of the extent of marketing and sales efforts directed to local markets. This cost-based operationalization was selected because local sales data are not available for inward FDI, to increase comparability between the inward and outward analyses; in the outward data the two measures were highly correlated (0.91, p < 0.01).
Local purchases by affiliates as a share of total costs. High shares of local purchases imply heavy reliance on the host economy for the acquisition of various resources.

Total exports by affiliates less exports to parents and exports to other affiliated bodies, divided by total sales of affiliates. It is a measure of the export propensity of affiliates that captures exports to unrelated bodies, and is thus distinguished from the intra-firm transactions used for the efficiency-seeking motivation.

A variation of Kobrin's index of integration, based on the magnitude of intra-firm transactions, which indicates the intensity of internal linkages within the MNE. The index combines sales of affiliates to parents, sales of affiliates to other affiliated bodies and sales of parents to affiliates over total sales of affiliates; the formula as printed is difficult to read. Kobrin's index also includes parents' exports in the denominator, which are not available for inward FDI.

Knowledge seeking is operationalized by two measures. The level of compensation per employee, computed as the average compensation per employee across all countries, where high pay levels indicate reliance on highly skilled employees. R&D intensity, measured by R&D investment by affiliates as a share of sales.

variable_name: Growth in the number of foreign affiliates
description: The number of new affiliates entering foreign markets each year, expressed as a share of the total number of affiliates in an industry; the measure is expressed in both linear and quadratic forms to account for the hypothesized non-linear impact. For outward FDI it is the growth in the number of U.S. affiliates overseas, operationalizing competitive pressure from home-country competitors; for inward FDI it is the growth in the number of all foreign affiliates entering the United States, measuring global industry pressure.

Investment in information and communication technology (ICT) in an industry, measured as the cumulated volume of investment in ICT between 1990 and 1999, expressed as a share of the total accumulated investment in the industry over the same period to adjust for industry size. Industries were ranked on this measure and the 15 with the highest and the 15 with the lowest ratios among 87 industries with FDI activity were selected as the high and low information-intensive groups.

Thematic text analysis of the first letter to shareholders signed by the newly appointed CEO. Each sentence of each letter was coded to one of three conceptual nodes (Past, Future, SEOC); search dictionaries built for each dimension were then applied within each node, and raw word counts were divided by the total number of words within the letter to obtain relative frequencies, which control for letter length. An overall CCV score was obtained for each CEO by summing the relative frequencies across all dictionaries.
time_window: first letter to shareholders after the CEO succession

description: All recommendations issued by each analyst covering each firm within one year after the release of the letter to shareholders were collected, and the 6-month and 12-month average recommendation was calculated for each analyst. I/B/E/S and FirstCall map recommendations onto a standard five-point scale.
scale: five-point scale (1 = strong buy; 2 = buy; 3 = hold; 4 = underperform; 5 = sell)
time_window: up to one year after the release of the letter to shareholders (6-month and 12-month averages)

description: For each firm, the standard deviation from the consensus (mean) recommendation across all analysts following the firm, the commonly used measure in previous studies. The variable was collected from I/B/E/S, where it is calculated on a monthly basis, thereby representing the monthly dispersion of recommendations for all analysts following each firm. It was examined at 6 months and 12 months after the release of the first letter to shareholders.
time_window: monthly, up to one year after the release of the letter to shareholders (examined at 6 and 12 months)

description: The absolute average forecast error of each individual analyst following the firm; the published formula could not be read from the text. The prose defines the error as the absolute average forecast error of analyst a following firm i for fiscal year t, where A is the actual EPS for firm i in year t and F is the forecast of analyst a of EPS of firm i for fiscal year t. All forecasts and actual EPS were collected from the release of the first letter to shareholders to one year after, and a single measure per analyst was obtained using six-month and one-year averages. Following previous studies, the measure was standardized by dividing each aggregate analyst score by the relevant firm stock price at the date the first letter to shareholders was filed.
scale: scaled absolute forecast error (divided by firm stock price)
time_window: up to one year after the release of the letter to shareholders (6-month and one-year averages)

variable_name: Industrial disaster incidents inside the host country outside the industry a focal firm operates (ID_HC)
description: Severity of industrial disasters in the host country measured by the number of incidents originating outside the industry in which the focal firm operates. The authors searched news articles from Dow Jones News Retrieval and Factiva for industry information on the disasters, which they found for 99% of disasters, and compared the industry information of disasters with focal firms' industries. Independent variables are one-year lagged.

variable_name: Industrial disaster incidents inside the host country within the industry a focal firm operates (ID_HC_WI)
description: Severity of industrial disasters in the host country measured by the number of incidents originating within the industry in which the focal firm operates. Built by comparing the industry information of EM-DAT disasters with the focal firm's industry to create the three geographic and industry dimensions. Independent variables are one-year lagged.

variable_name: Industrial disaster incidents outside the host country within the industry a focal firm operates (ID_WI)
description: Severity of industrial disasters measured by the number of incidents outside the host country that originate within the industry in which the focal firm operates. This dimension allows spillover effects across country borders to be tested. Independent variables are one-year lagged.

Technological capability is measured by the average number of citations and number of patents as these are common measures used in research on technological capability, innovativeness, and knowledge transfers. The measures are built from the NBER Patent Data Project, which contains detailed information on all utility patents granted in the U.S. between 1976 and 2006. A logarithm transformation was used for these measures to lower the skewness of the raw data.

Safety management capability is measured by the summation score of KLD's health and safety concern, product safety concern, and hazardous waste concern (all reverse coded) to consider different dimensions of safety in MNC operations. The original KLD ratings are binary variables indicating whether the company has recently been involved in major issues relating to health and safety, the safety of product and services, and waste management controversies. Concern ratings were used rather than strength ratings because the strength rating of health and safety is only available for recent years and product safety strength is not available. A logarithm transformation was used to lower the skewness of the raw data.

Philanthropic capability is measured by the annual amount of corporate foundations' donations, drawn from the Foundation Directory Online. A logarithm transformation was used to lower the skewness of the raw data. The authors note that firm-year level corporate foundation giving is used as a proxy for corporations' overall long-term philanthropic capability.

A binary variable which equaled one when the MNC invested in a wholly-owned subsidiary in a country for the first time and zero otherwise. Data recorded after the MNC entered the host country were treated as missing because only the initial entry information was of interest. Subsidiary locations were hand-collected from each firm's 10K annual reports, and only wholly-owned subsidiaries were included due to data availability limitations.

The number of wholly-owned subsidiaries in the host country after entry, counting the increase or decrease in the number of an MNC's WOS in a given host country. A selection parameter (inverse Mills ratio from a presence model) was included because of the possibility of self-selection bias in the expansion model. The variable was built from the hand-collected subsidiary locations in firms' 10K annual reports.

The dependent variable of the study, coded as 1 for a subsidiary-country dyad if subsidiary i was located in country j, and 0 for the dyads between subsidiary i and all other countries in the choice set. Only a firm's first entry into a foreign country was considered. The unit of analysis was the subsidiary-country dyad.

Measured as the natural logarithm of the physical distance between the capital city of China (Beijing) and the capital city of the foreign country. Following previous studies, the great-circle distance formula was applied to the latitude and longitude coordinates of the two capital cities, with the radius of the Earth r = 6,378 km and the latitude and longitude values converted into radians by dividing them by 180/pi. The formula itself is not readable in the supplied text.

The Euclidean distance index applied to Hofstede et al.'s six cultural dimensions, using each country's score on each dimension, China's score on that dimension, and the variance of the score on that dimension as a weight. Countries not included in Hofstede et al.'s report were assigned the mean cultural dimension scores of other countries in the same cultural block, based on the eight clusters of culturally similar countries identified by Ronen and Shenkar (1985), yielding scores on six cultural dimensions for 127 countries. The formula itself is not readable in the supplied text.

Measured as the natural logarithm of a firm's registered capital in the year prior to its FDI. The data on firm size were collected from China's State Administration for Industry and Commerce. Continuous variables were mean-centered prior to creating the interaction terms.

Measured as the age of a firm in the year prior to its FDI. The data on firm age were collected from China's State Administration for Industry and Commerce. Continuous variables were mean-centered prior to creating the interaction terms.

Coded as 1 if the controlling shareholder of a firm was the state and 0 otherwise. The data on state ownership were collected from China's State Administration for Industry and Commerce. SOEs do not include sovereign wealth funds in this study.

Indicator variable taking the value of 1 for firms that divest their legacy businesses and 0 for firms that retain these units, both measured in the divestiture year. No distinction is made between asset sales and spinoffs. It is the dependent variable in the first-stage regression of the Heckman selection model, and its predicted values serve as the key independent variable in the second-stage performance regression. Legacy divestitures were identified by matching the hand-collected historical information on firms' legacy businesses to the divestiture data.

Return on sales, used to quantify the operational consequences of legacy divestitures predicted in Hypotheses 3, 4, and 5. Measured in the year following firms' decisions to divest or retain their legacy businesses, and in years 2-9 after the legacy divestiture decision.
time_window: year following the divestiture decision; years 2-9 after the decision

description: The cumulative sum of abnormal returns. Daily stock returns were collected from CRSP within 250-day estimation windows before the announcement dates of each legacy divestiture; normal returns were predicted from these daily stock returns and the stock market's returns, and abnormal returns were then computed within three-day event windows surrounding the announcement dates. Announcement dates were identified from LexisNexis.
time_window: three-day event window surrounding the announcement date

description: The number of years a CEO has overseen a firm. Data on the characteristics of CEOs and boards of directors were collected from the Standard & Poor's Register.

The percentage of a firm's total business units that share a three-digit SIC code with the firm's legacy business. Larger values indicate that the firm's legacy business is more closely related to a greater proportion of the firm's other operations.

Indicator variable taking the value of 1 when Legacy Divestiture takes the value of 1 and the three-digit SIC code of the firm's legacy business is the same as that of at least one of its other business segments, representing divestitures of related legacy businesses. It takes the value of 0 when Legacy Divestiture takes the value of 0 and the firm's legacy business shares its three-digit SIC code with at least one other of its business segments, representing retentions of related legacy businesses.

Indicator variable taking the value of 1 when Legacy Divestiture takes the value of 1 and the three-digit SIC code of the firm's legacy business is not the same as those of any of its other business segments, representing divestitures of unrelated legacy businesses. It takes the value of 0 when Legacy Divestiture takes the value of 0 and there is no overlap in the three-digit SIC codes of a firm's legacy business and those of any of its other business segments, representing retentions of unrelated legacy businesses.

Indicator variable taking the value of 1 when Legacy Divestiture takes the value of 1 and the three-digit SIC code of the firm's legacy business is the same as the company's primary three-digit SIC code. It takes the value of 0 when Legacy Divestiture takes the value of 0 and the three-digit SIC code of the firm's legacy business is the same as the company's primary three-digit SIC code.

Indicator variable taking the value of 1 when Legacy Divestiture takes the value of 1 and the three-digit SIC code of the firm's legacy business is not the same as that of its primary industry. It takes the value of 0 when Legacy Divestiture takes the value of 0 and the three-digit SIC codes of a firm's legacy business and its primary industry differ.

Bilateral trade between the foreign partner's home country and the host country. The authors first define the trade dependence of firms in country i on other firms in country j from the proportions of the total dollar value of goods imported and exported between the two countries, weighted by the host country's import and export concentration ratios measured by Herfindahl indices, and define mutual trade dependence as the sum of the dependencies of the two countries on each other. It is a time-varying variable for each home country-host country-year segment, normalized by subtracting the mean and dividing by the sample standard deviation. The equations specifying the measure are unreadable in the available text.

Event history techniques split the time between the formation date and the termination date of each alliance into annual spells, producing 3,304 alliance-year observations. The dependent variable is dichotomous, coded 1 if the alliance was terminated in a given year t and 0 otherwise; a positive coefficient indicates that the covariate decreases the probability of the survival of the alliance. Termination events were coded by hand from Factiva and Lexis-Nexis.
time_window: 1990-2007, annual spells from formation to termination

variable_name: Additional alliance activities of the foreign partner
description: The total number of alliances formed by the foreign firm with other firms in the same industry after the focal alliance had been established in a given host country, regardless of the geographical locations where the additional alliances were formed. The count was logarithmically transformed to accommodate its skewed distribution.
time_window: after the focal alliance was established, time-varying

variable_name: Additional acquisition activities of the foreign partner
description: The total number of acquisitions completed by the foreign firm in the same industry after it had established a cross-border alliance in a given host country, regardless of the geographical locations where the target firms or businesses were acquired. Following Casciaro and Piskorski (2005), minority acquisitions and corporate restructuring activities such as self-tenders, repurchases, and acquisitions among a firm's business units were excluded. The count was logarithmically transformed to accommodate its skewed distribution.
time_window: after the focal alliance was established, time-varying

description: The number of other alliances established between the same foreign and local partners for each alliance-year observation before the focal alliance was terminated, regardless of their industries or geographical locations. All repeated alliances formed by the sampled firms were searched in the SDC Alliances Database, consistent with the coding scheme for repeated ties described by Gulati (1995). The count was logarithmically transformed to accommodate its skewed distribution.
time_window: before the focal alliance was terminated, time-varying

variable_name: total number of available eldercare benefits
description: Employers were asked to indicate whether they provided a range of 17 different eldercare benefits in three primary areas: education and referral, eldercare support services, and financial arrangements. A summary measure based on the total number of benefits provided by an employer was developed.

variable_name: employer involvement with organizations responding to work and family issues
description: Employers were asked whether they had become aware of employee eldercare needs through being members of business groups or coalitions or through association with other organizations involved in work-family issues. These data were used to create a dichotomous variable indicating involvement (1) or no involvement (0).
Degree of organizational exposure to eldercare issues was assessed using two measures assessed at the organizational level, one of which was the proportion of female employees.

variable_name: proportion of employees 40 years of age and older
description: Degree of organizational exposure to eldercare issues was assessed using two measures assessed at the organizational level, one of which was the proportion of employees 40 years of age and older.

Organizational assessment of eldercare needs was measured by asking employers whether they assessed employee eldercare concerns through focus groups or surveys. These responses were used to create a dichotomous variable for each employer indicating that there was (1) or was not (0) employee needs assessment.
scale: dichotomous: 1 = needs assessment conducted, 0 = not conducted
