variable_name: total number of other employer-provided work-family benefits
description: Respondents were asked to indicate whether they provided any of 15 benefits falling within three broad areas: childcare, alternative work schedules, and leaves. Organizational values regarding eldercare were measured on the basis of the total number of these other employer-provided work-family benefits.

variable_name: proportion of professionals in an organization
description: The proportion of professionals in an organization was measured. The GAO defined "professionals" in the survey as managers and administrators; professionals like attorneys and accountants; technical specialists; and sales representatives.

variable_name: perceived importance of eldercare benefits to employee productivity
description: Respondents were asked to indicate the importance of providing eldercare benefits to improving employee productivity, on a response scale from 1 (little or no) to 5 (very great).

Using DoD contracting records, a firm is coded as entering a product market in year t if it is awarded a contract in that market in year t and has not received a contract in that market in any earlier year within the observation window (1996 to t-1). Once a firm enters a market, subsequent observations for that firm-market pair are dropped from the risk set.

We measure Divisionalization using the count of units that operate without subordinates or subsidiaries. These units represent the lowest level of operational responsibility within the firm's hierarchy. The measure captures the degree to which a firm structurally differentiates its activities across organizational units rather than merely expanding the scope of markets in which it operates, and is interpreted as reflecting structural partitioning conditional on firm scope.

Adjacent markets are defined as those sharing the same initial 2-digit PSC code, using the hierarchical structure of the federal Product Service Code. The variable equals 1 if a firm was awarded a contract in an adjacent market during the pre-shock period (1996-2000) and 0 otherwise.

An organizational unit is coded as entering a market in year t if it is awarded a contract in that market in year t, provided that neither the focal organizational unit nor any other organizational unit within the same firm has previously received a contract in that market during the observation window. This definition ensures that we capture first-time entry by the firm rather than a reassignment of contracting activity across organizational units. Once entry occurs for any division within the firm, the division-market pair exits the risk set in subsequent years by construction.

Focal unit adjacent market experience equals 1 if the focal unit held contracts in markets adjacent to the focal market during the pre-shock period (1996-2000), and 0 otherwise. This variable captures experience embedded within the operating unit associated with the observed entry.

Sister unit adjacent market experience equals 1 if at least one other unit within the same firm, excluding the focal unit, held pre-shock contracts in markets adjacent to the focal market. This construction isolates experience located elsewhere in the organization.

Shared customer is an indicator equal to 1 when the focal unit and sister units with adjacent experience served at least one common customer prior to the shock, and captures a customer-based organizational linkage.

We calculate this variable as the total political contributions made by the parent firm to candidates, parties, and political action committees (PACs), as reported to the Federal Election Commission (FEC) and compiled by OpenSecrets, lagged by one year. It proxies for the salience of corporate-level external engagement.

Subsidiary managers were asked to indicate their level of agreement with four items on a scale from 1 to 5 (alpha = 0.70). The items cover the parent's challenging of the subsidiary's strategies and tactics, administrative relief, cost savings, and information received from the parent. High values for this variable indicate that the headquarters produced high additional value for the focal subsidiary through its activities. The scale was developed in a multistage process and validated in interviews with subsidiary and headquarters managers.

Informants were asked to rate the extent to which their headquarters maintained linkages to the same partners of the subsidiary's external network, using the same graphical six-point Likert-type scale used for subsidiary embeddedness. The approach emphasized that the strength of headquarters' relationships had to be indicated for the same set of subsidiary network partners rather than for the independent components of headquarters' external networks.

An adapted graphical scale based on a similar scale used by Ambos and Schlegelmilch (2007) was used. The survey instrument showed a range of possible partners in the subsidiary's external network, and respondents rated the strength of the subsidiary's relationships with each type of actor on a six-point Likert-type scale. The authors then derived the final measure of average subsidiary embeddedness.

Firm status is calculated from the ordering of investment banks on tombstone advertisements. Annual matrices of deference patterns were constructed in which cell Cij equals the number of times firm i appeared in a higher bracket position than firm j, divided by the number of deals in which both i and j were syndicate members. Bonacich's (1987) eigenvector measure was used to calculate firm status, with the weighting factor set to three-quarters of the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue. The resulting scores range between 0 and 1, with a firm's score indicating the fraction of status it holds relative to the highest-status firm.
time_window: annual status matrices; status collected at five-year intervals

description: Measured as the status of the postmerger firm less the status of the acquirer prior to a merger transaction. Postmerger status is operationalized as the firm's status in the first collection year following the merger, and the acquirer's premerger status is calculated using data from the last collection year preceding the transaction. The announcement date was used to determine the timing of the merger.
time_window: from the last collection year preceding the transaction to the first collection year following the merger

description: Operationalized as the acquiring firm's status prior to a sampled transaction minus the status of the target firm. The acquiring firm is socially superior to its target when this variable is positive. The square of the status difference (status difference squared) was also calculated to test for the nonlinearities anticipated in Hypothesis 1.
time_window: last measurement year prior to the merger

description: Takes a value of 1 if the merged firms are headquartered in different countries and is equal to 0 otherwise. Headquarters data for transactions that occurred prior to 1980 were gathered from media accounts of mergers in the ProQuest Historical Newspapers database; headquarters information for later years was available in the annual Securities Industry Yearbooks. In the sample, international transactions most often involve a merger between a U.S. bank and a European one.

Indicator variable that takes a value of 1 if one merging firm has its U.S. headquarters in New York City while the other does not, and 0 otherwise. The rationale is that firms headquartered in New York City share similar behavioral norms (e.g., dress, working hours) and beliefs (e.g., job insecurity builds character).

Indicator variable that takes a value of 1 when one of the firms involved in a transaction is a member of the bulge bracket, and 0 otherwise. Bulge bracket firms are those with particularly strong and idiosyncratic cultures, a moniker derived from the large type used to print firms' names in tombstone ads.

An index ranging from zero to six, calculated by adding one point for the presence of a provision protecting each of six representative shareholder rights in the country's commercial code or company law. Building on La Porta et al.'s cross-sectional index for 1996, the authors constructed a time-varying annual measure for 1988-1998 from full-text English-language translations of national corporate legislative codes and their revision dates, using additional sources where the primary reference was incomplete and, in some cases, the national laws in the original language. Coding rules were consistent with La Porta et al.'s description of each variable, and the two coauthors separately reviewed ambiguous provisions and reached perfect intercoder reliability.

The count of International Labour Organization conventions that each country had ratified and that were still in force in a given year. Only the 109 conventions in place throughout the study period were considered, and from these the authors limited attention to the 45 conventions that apply to all employees of publicly traded corporations, excluding standards pertaining only to narrowly defined special groups. Countries are permitted to denounce previously ratified conventions, so the measure varies over time.

A four-point scale of the restrictions on bank ownership of non-financial firms, traced over time to construct a time-varying measure. The original scale codes 1 as unrestricted ownership, 2 as permitted ownership, 3 as restricted ownership, and 4 as prohibited ownership, so higher original scores indicate greater restrictions. Because higher scores indicate greater restrictions, the authors multiplied the original variable by minus 1 so that it increases as banks' rights to participate in the ownership and governance of non-financial companies increases.

The count of announced hostile takeover bids in each country and year. The authors downloaded the complete listing of corporate takeover bid announcements, classified the records by year, by the attitude of the transaction (hostile or otherwise), and by the home country of the target firm, and aggregated them into country-year counts. SDC classifies a takeover as hostile when the target firm's board of directors officially rejects an offer but the acquirer persists with the takeover.

Event whereby a mutual fund manager exits the parent company in the mutual fund industry to launch a hedge fund. To identify hedge fund founders, the CRSP and TASS data are merged by the unique names of fund managers, including first and last names and middle initial, and the manager's appearance in the TASS database is checked against the appearance of a hedge fund. The variable varies monthly and equals 1 if the manager transitions to entrepreneurship and 0 otherwise.

Count of managers who shared a university affiliation with the focal manager and who founded a hedge fund. Managers who earned a degree (BBA, BA, BSc, MBA, MA, JD, or Ph.D.) from more than one academic institution shared several educational affiliations with others. For each manager, the count of same-university founders is aggregated over a period of 12 months, and the measure is lagged by one year; it varies annually and can take different values for each focal manager.

Count of other managers who are of the same gender as the focal manager, share a university affiliation with the focal manager, and launched a hedge fund. Gender is inferred from the managers' first names and coded 1 for male and 0 otherwise. The variable is observed annually and lagged by one year.
time_window: observed annually, lagged by one year

description: Average distance between the focal manager and each of his or her university peers, calculated from latitude and longitude converted from decimal degrees to radians. The CRSP data provide the zip codes identifying the geographic location of mutual funds, matched to longitude and latitude values from the U.S. Postal Service. Distances are computed using the principles of spherical geometry applied to curved surfaces and converted to miles using a constant based on the radius of the sphere (C = 3,437.9 miles); the exact formula for the distance between two points is not readable in the text supplied. The measure is observed annually.

Using the information on CEOs' contributions, the authors calculated four ratio-based indicators: (1) the number of donations to Democrats divided by the number of donations to recipients of both parties, (2) the dollar amount of donations to Democrats divided by the amount of donations to both parties, (3) the number of years in which the executive made donations to Democrats divided by the number of years donations were made to either party, and (4) the number of distinct Democratic recipients to whom the executive donated divided by the total number of distinct recipients of both parties. The four indicators respectively indicate behavioral commitment, financial commitment, persistence of commitment, and scope of commitment. Following Chin et al. (2013), the authors summed and then averaged these four ratio-based indicators and used it as the CEO liberalism index score (Cronbach's alpha 0.95). Scores range from 0 to 1; scores close to 0 indicate intensely conservative CEOs and scores close to 1 indicate intensely liberal CEOs.
time_window: the 10 years before the CEO's appointment (t-10 to t-1)

description: The authors first collected 10 years of donation records for each compensation committee member and calculated that member's individual liberalism index using the same donation-based index. They then took the mean of the individual members' indices and used it as the measure of compensation committee liberalism. Because membership changes were tracked, the variable could vary over time as committee membership changed during the sample period.
time_window: 10 years of donation records before the sample period

description: Horizontal pay equality was measured by the inverse of the coefficient of variation in the total pay of other TMT members, a measure of horizontal pay disparity used in previous studies. The coefficient of variation was calculated by dividing the standard deviation of other TMT members' total pay by the mean TMT's total pay. The pay data of the five highest paid executives were used, with total pay titled 'Total Compensation-As Reported in SEC Filings' in Execucomp, a sum of salary, bonus, the value of stock awards, the value of option awards, nonequity incentive, change in pension value and nonqualified deferred compensation earnings, and all other compensation.
time_window: each year a CEO was in office (t + n), excluding the year of appointment

description: Vertical pay equality was calculated as the log difference between the average pay of all other TMT members and the pay of the CEO, a transformed measure of vertical pay disparity used in previous studies. The pay data of the five highest paid executives were used, with total pay titled 'Total Compensation-As Reported in SEC Filings' in Execucomp, a sum of salary, bonus, the value of stock awards, the value of option awards, nonequity incentive, change in pension value and nonqualified deferred compensation earnings, and all other compensation.
time_window: each year a CEO was in office (t + n), excluding the year of appointment

description: Intervention type was recoded into a dummy variable representing multiple scenario analysis versus no multiple scenario analysis, combining participants in the control and strategic review conditions into one group and combining participants in the reading scenarios and creating scenarios conditions into a second group. A value of 0 indicates no multiple scenario analysis and 1 indicates multiple scenario analysis.
scale: 0 = no multiple scenario analysis, 1 = multiple scenario analysis

description: Change in pricing strategy in years 7-13, specifically the adoption of a price cutting strategy over this 7-year period. The authors calculated the number of price cuts made between years 7 and 13; the greater the number of price cuts made, the greater the incidence of strategic reorientation. Price-cutting was chosen as the indicator because alliance formation was common in the early rounds while price-cutting was rare.

The annual price change, calculated as the mean annual price change per year over years 7-13 inclusive. This measure of the extent of price cutting behavior (or, conversely, price increases) indicates the magnitude of strategic reorientation.

Computed at year 9 as the average of two items assessing participants' belief that increasing advertising expenditure and increasing the sales force would have a positive impact on their market share in future. Assessed on a percentage scale anchored at 0% = no confidence and 100% = certain.

Measured at year 9 as causal beliefs, by asking participants to rate the effectiveness of the four main strategies for increasing market share: increasing the sales force, increasing advertising, cutting call prices, and forming alliances, on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 = not effective to 7 = very effective. Belief in the effectiveness of cutting call prices was used to indicate belief in the new strategy because adopting this strategy was the most accurate indicator of strategic reorientation.

The level of market share, in percentage points, attained at the end of year six, that is, immediately prior to the experimental interventions. The label past performance reflects the authors' interest in how performance up to this point might moderate the effects of the interventions in subsequent rounds.

Measured as the absolute difference between an entrepreneur's rating of a VC and their actual quality based on the LPJ index. Entrepreneurs rate a VC's track record on a scale from 1 to 5, with 5 being the most positive score; because the LPJ index is a 100-point scale it was converted to a five-point Likert scale with the same distribution of ratings as the entrepreneur ratings of track record at TheFunded. For ease of interpretation, accuracy was then measured as 4 minus the absolute difference, so that positive values indicate greater accuracy. The result is an ordinal measure that ranges from 4 (highest accuracy) to 0 (lowest accuracy).

A variant of closeness centrality adapted to work on disconnected graphs, measured as 1/n * the sum of 1/path distance_i, where n is the total number of VCs investing during the focal year and path distance_i is the shortest path length between the entrepreneur and each VC (with 1/path distance set to 0 for disconnected entrepreneur-VC pairs). Ties were placed between an entrepreneur and each VC they met with (rated) up through the 90 days beyond the current rating, and the position of these VCs in the broader industry network was inferred from the network of syndication ties between VCs that had jointly invested in other ventures during the prior five years. Since reasons apart from network reach may influence the number of VCs an entrepreneur meets, closeness centrality was regressed on the number of ratings performed by the entrepreneur and the residual was taken as the measure. Higher values indicate more central entrepreneurs.

Motivation measured by whether the entrepreneur was presented with information on how other members of TheFunded have rated a VC, operationalized as whether there were no prior community ratings at the time the entrepreneur performed their rating. Takes a value of 1 when no such prior ratings were available (high motivation) and 0 otherwise (low motivation).
time_window: at the time of the rating

description: Binary variable with a value of 1 if an entrepreneur reported at TheFunded that they received an offer from the VC currently being rated. Coded from the optional additional information section where entrepreneurs indicated whether they had received an offer from that VC; where no such information was provided, the entrepreneur was conservatively assumed not to have received an offer.

The Lee-Pollock-Jin (LPJ) VC reputation index, a longitudinal, composite index that captures a VC's track record using a five-year moving average. The index captures a VC's performance and behavior by establishing values for six equally weighted factors using five-year moving averages: the total number of ventures invested in, the total dollar amount invested, the number of portfolio companies taken public, the total dollar amount of funds raised to invest, the average number of investment funds, and the age of the VC firm in the focal year. The index is a 100-point scale, with 100 indicating the highest quality.

Web traffic received by the VC firm in the 30 days preceding the evaluation (ending on the day prior to the evaluation). Measured as the 30-day average of daily page views of a VC's website, in millions, and logged to reduce skew.
scale: logged 30-day average of daily page views (millions)

description: Codes the answer to the Bank of France questionnaire question whether the firm is owner-controlled. The variable equals 1 for owner-controlled firms and 0 otherwise.
Codes the answer to the Bank of France questionnaire question whether agents report directly to the owners. The variable equals 1 if there is a flat organization and 0 otherwise.

Efficiency score assigned by data envelopment analysis, which uses linear programming to estimate the maximum potential efficiency for various levels of inputs based on each firm's actual inputs and outputs; the score conventionally termed θ ranges from 0 to 1 for the best use of the available inputs. Four inputs are used: total fixed assets, and expenditures in R&D, marketing, and education, all 2-year averages (1996-97) in French francs. Two outputs are used: gross profits and sales, 2-year averages (1997-98) in French francs. The dataset was separated into three by industry and efficiency scores were determined relative to firms in the same industry.

Geographic overlap between firms i and j is operationalized as the number of states in which both firm i and firm j have business operations. State-level operations were extracted from state mentions in Form 10-K filings (Items 1, 2, 6 and 7) obtained through the SEC's electronic filing system, and two research analysts validated a random sample of state mentions as related to business activity locations. The authors report that the average geographic overlap of firm pairs in the sample is 2, ranging from 0 to 35.

A dyad-level 1-0 dummy indicating whether the two firms within a dyad formed an acquisition in a given year. It is coded 1 for dyads in which the two parties constitute an actual acquirer–target pair, and 0 otherwise. It is measured for year t, while the independent and control variables are measured at time t-1.

Measured as the natural logarithm of the acquirer's total assets. The authors also alternatively measured acquirer size as the natural logarithm of the acquirer's total number of employees as part of the robustness checks.

A 1-0 dummy for whether an acquiring firm's business operations are geographically dispersed in a given year. It equals 1 if the number of states where the firm has business activities is greater than the sample median, and 0 otherwise.

Calculated as the actual miles between the acquirer's and target's HQ from a formula using the latitude and longitude of the two HQ locations, which are determined by the zip code of the firm's headquarters, with a constant C that converts the result to miles on the surface of the earth, for which the authors used 3,437; the formula itself is unreadable in the text. A natural log transformation of actual miles is then applied. To facilitate interpretation of the moderating effect, the variable is operationalized as a 0-1 dummy where 1 means the log distance between the two firms' HQs is larger than the sample median; as a robustness check the actual length between the two firms' HQs was also used.

Following Hoberg and Phillips (2010), a dictionary of unique words used in all product descriptions in Form 10-K Item 1 or Item 1A is built and a binary N-vector characterizing each firm's word usage is constructed; product similarity between firm i and firm j is the multiplicative product of their normalized N-vectors and is continuous between 0 and 1, with 1 representing high product similarity. The authors adopt the same approach for acquirer–target firms and then estimate product dissimilarity for each observation by multiplying the similarity measure by -1.

All citations in the focal firm's telecommunications equipment patents applied for in year t (and eventually granted) were classified and tabulated as 'new' or 'used.' A citation was classified as new if it was not to a patent developed by the firm during the seven years before the focal year; the seven-year window was chosen because the median age of cited patents in telecom technologies is about 6.5 years. The variable is computed as the number of new citations divided by total citations. Because it is a share of new citations rather than a count, it captures a firm's propensity to produce exploratory innovations independent of firm scale.
time_window: Patents applied for in year t; seven-year citation look-back

description: Built on Rodan and Galunic's (2004) measure of knowledge heterogeneity, it incorporates the knowledge distance between the focal actor and each partner and the distances among partners. For each firm-year, the distribution of the firm's patents across primary patent classes over a moving four-year window locates the firm in a multidimensional technology space. Technological distance between firms is measured at the dyad level with Jaffe's (1986) index; it is bounded between 0 (complete similarity) and 1 (maximum diversity) and is symmetric. The uniqueness of each partner is found in the solution of the eigen equation of the annual matrix of pairwise technological distances, and the network diversity available to the focal firm combines partner distances and uniqueness scores, with a 1/N term compensating for network size; the algebraic formulas were not readable in the text provided.
scale: Pairwise technological distance bounded between 0 (complete similarity) and 1 (maximum diversity)
time_window: Moving four-year patenting profile window; measured annually

description: Annual adjacency matrices for 1987-96 indicated the presence of a technology alliance, in existence at the end of a focal year, between all possible undirected pairwise combinations of sample firms. An alliance with more than two firms entered the adjacency matrix as separate dyadic combinations of all firms in the alliance. Ego network density was the percentage of all possible ties among an ego's alters that had been formed. Alliances were treated as present or absent: each tie value was set to 1 if a relationship existed and 0 otherwise, and the denominator term [N(N-1)] was divided by 2 to reflect that alliances are undirected ties.
time_window: Annual, 1987-96; alliances traced from 1980 to their dissolution or continuance

description: Density of the partner's external network, measured following Borgatti et al. (2002) for egocentric network data, where ties are the number of actual relationships among the contacts in the partner's network rated by the partner as being tied to one another and the denominator represents the number of possible ties among the contacts in the network. A high score indicates that the partner's contacts are highly interconnected. Separate density scores were calculated for external and internal networks.
time_window: measured at the time of the survey (November 1999-January 2000)

description: Density of the partner's internal network, measured following Borgatti et al. (2002) for egocentric network data, where ties are the number of actual relationships among the contacts in the partner's network rated by the partner as being tied to one another and the denominator represents the number of possible ties among the contacts in the network. A high score indicates that the partner's contacts are highly interconnected. Separate density scores were calculated for external and internal networks.
time_window: measured at the time of the survey (November 1999-January 2000)

description: When reporting their network contacts, partners were asked to give the main industry within which each contact worked; contact heterogeneity is measured as the count of different industries represented in each partner's external network. Separate contact heterogeneity scores were calculated for the external and internal networks.
time_window: measured at the time of the survey (November 1999-January 2000)

description: When reporting their network contacts, partners were asked to give the main industry within which each contact worked; contact heterogeneity is measured as the count of different industries represented in each partner's internal network. Separate contact heterogeneity scores were calculated for the external and internal networks.
time_window: measured at the time of the survey (November 1999-January 2000)

description: Partners were asked to indicate on a five-point Likert scale the combination of resources they used to build and maintain each relationship, with 5 indicating resources 'independent of formal' role in the firm and 1 indicating resources made available through their formal position in the firm. The authors then calculated the average score for all ties in the partner's external network, so higher values indicate greater informality of ties.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = formal, 5 = independent of formal)
time_window: measured at the time of the survey (November 1999-January 2000)

description: Partners were asked to indicate on a five-point Likert scale the combination of resources they used to build and maintain each relationship, with 5 indicating resources 'independent of formal' role in the firm and 1 indicating resources made available through their formal position in the firm. The authors then calculated the average score for all ties in the partner's internal network, so higher values indicate greater informality of ties.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = formal, 5 = independent of formal)
time_window: measured at the time of the survey (November 1999-January 2000)

description: Supervisors rated each partner in the sample on a five-point Likert scale, from 1 ('much better at implementing existing business') to 5 ('much better at new business development'), with a midpoint of 'equally good at both'. From this measure the authors constructed a dependent variable with three categories: partners who received a score of 1 or 2 were categorized as 'exploitation-focused', those receiving a 3 as 'ambidextrous', and those receiving a 4 or 5 as 'exploration-focused'. In this context 'new' refers to activity in which the firm has not yet engaged, as opposed to 'existing', which refers to an expansion or renewal based on existing practices with existing clients.
scale: five-point Likert scale recoded into three categories
time_window: collected shortly after the partners' official annual reviews

description: An ordinal indicator of the governance form used for the deal; higher values indicate higher degrees of integration along the market-hierarchies continuum. In the three-category ordered probit model the variable is set to two if the transaction involves a merger or acquisition (majority or minority), one if the transaction involves any kind of non-equity alliance or joint venture, and zero if the transaction involves a divestiture of any type; the other ordered probit models use a seven-value construction of the same variable. The ordering is similar in the binary probit models: the variable equals one for acquisitions and zero for alliances in the model of boundary expansion, and one for alliances and zero for divestitures in the model of boundary contraction. A positive coefficient on an independent variable is interpreted as a higher probability that the firm will choose a more integrative governance form.
scale: ordinal; three or seven ordered categories

description: The focal firm's R&D to sales ratio, used as a measure of its technological resources; higher values indicate richer technological resources.
The focal firm's advertising to sales ratio, used as a measure of its marketing resources; higher values indicate richer marketing resources.
The end-of-year percentage of common stock owned by insiders in the focal firm, taken from Compact Disclosure.
The end-of-year percentage of common stock owned by blockholders in the focal firm, taken from Compact Disclosure.
The end-of-year percentage of common stock owned by institutions in the focal firm, taken from Compustat.
The average number of acquisitions per year undertaken by the focal firm since 1990, computed from the SDC deal data; the count is cumulative up to the focal deal.
time_window: since 1990 up to the focal deal

description: The average number of divestitures per year undertaken by the focal firm since 1990, computed from the SDC deal data; the count is cumulative up to the focal deal.
time_window: since 1990 up to the focal deal

description: The average number of alliances per year undertaken by the focal firm since 1990, computed from the SDC deal data; the count is cumulative up to the focal deal.
time_window: since 1990 up to the focal deal

description: The number of segments in different SIC codes reported by the focal firm, taken from Compustat Business-Segment reports; higher values indicate a higher level of diversification.

Proximity in the SIC codes of the focal and target (or partner) firm. The value is highest when the primary SIC codes of the two firms are the same and declines as the match occurs at successively lower-order SIC codes (secondary, tertiary, and so on).
The ratio of the sales of the smaller firm to the sales of the larger firm, computed for the focal firm and its target or partner.
The average number of alliances per year between the focal firm and the target (or partner) firm between 1990 and the focal deal, taken from the SDC alliance data.

Proximity in the SIC codes of the focal firm and the deal, constructed in the same way as the focal-target firm relatedness variable. The deal SIC code is the primary SIC code of the target firm in acquisitions and divestitures, and of the joint enterprise in alliances.

The percentage of the focal firm's deals in the year that used the same governance form as the deal in question; it captures whether the firm shows evidence of pursuing a program of acquisitions, alliances, or divestitures.

The inverse of the number of years since the focal firm last engaged in a deal of the same type, so that higher values indicate a more recent same-form deal. It captures only the amount of time since the last deal of the same type, regardless of how specialized the firm is in that form.
The target (or partner) firm's R&D to sales ratio, used as a measure of its technological resources.
The target (or partner) firm's advertising to sales ratio, used as a measure of its marketing resources.

The variance of the target (or partner) firm's return on assets (ROA) over the preceding years, where ROA is operating income after depreciation over total assets. This variable is entered into the model interacted with asset specificity; the authors describe their measures as coarse proxies.

The number of engineers as a percentage of employees in the focal firm's industry, proposed as a measure of human asset specificity. The authors caution that this variable may also be indicative of the firm's knowledge capital and hence may proxy combined resource-based and transaction-cost arguments rather than transaction cost theory alone.
The number of managers as a percentage of employees in the target (or partner) firm's industry, used as a proxy for the internal organization costs of integrating the target into the focal firm.

An event is a federal cabinet-level appointment announcement or election to the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate by an individual who came from senior corporate management or from the board of directors of a publicly traded company. The firms involved had to be publicly traded on the NYSE, AMSE, or OTC stock exchanges and have stock price information reported in either the Wall Street Journal or on the CRSP data tape for the event days and pre-event period. The sample period was chosen to coincide with major elections and due to the availability of daily stock price data. During this time period there were 13 federal cabinet-level appointees and 14 elected members of Congress meeting the criteria, for a total of 31 companies, reduced to 30 companies from 27 elections/appointments after one firm was dropped because of a confounding event.

Cumulative abnormal returns estimated with Scholes-Williams event-study methodology, which compares changes in firm performance during the event window to those of the industry and market as a whole and against a pre-event window for the firm. The market model parameters (alpha hat and beta hat) are estimated over 255 trading days for each firm between 285 days and 30 days prior to the event, using the value-weighted return on the market portfolio consisting of NYSE, AMEX, and OTC securities on day t. Cumulative abnormal returns for the portfolio between days d1 and d2 are calculated by summing abnormal returns during that time period, and significance of the portfolio's abnormal return on a single day is tested by dividing the abnormal return by the estimated standard deviation of the forecast error (the statistic is distributed as standard normal). The event window is -1/+1, i.e., the day before the event, the actual event date, and the day following the event.
time_window: -1/+1 event window; 255-trading-day estimation period between 285 and 30 days prior to the event

description: Dates on which three major newspapers (Wall Street Journal, New York Times, Washington Post) announced the likely appointees for cabinet positions, analyzed as separate event studies with the same -1/+1 event window as the appointment announcements. Leak dates were broken down into two types: leak dates where the media coverage portrayed the eventual appointee as the 'likely' or 'favored' nominee, and leak dates where the media coverage portrayed an alternative candidate as the most likely or favored nominee. For three out of 13 appointees there were leakage dates; positive leakage dates involved two firms and negative leakage dates involved three firms.
time_window: -1/+1 event window around the leakage date

description: Hospital business strategy was characterized by eight archival variables: bed size, case mix index, scope of medical services, costs of medical education, proportion of Medicare and Medicaid discharges, and geographic location (east-west and north-south). A factor analysis yielded a reduced strategic space of three factors (Scope/Size, Payer Mix, Location) and cluster analysis of the factor scores produced five strategic groups. The group structure was validated with three ANOVAs, one for each archival factor, all significant at the 0.001 level, and a discriminant analysis of group identification with a total misclassification error of 1.3 percent.

Each respondent rated his or her own hospital along 16 attributes encompassing the medical and nursing staff, facilities, administration, and reputation of the hospital. Factor analysis of the ratings produced a structure with five dimensions (Nursing, Medical Facilities, Image, Support, Appearance) and cluster analysis produced six cognitive communities or groups, differentiated by nursing staff, support from the administration, and availability of medical facilities. The cluster solution was validated using ANOVA and discriminant analysis.

variable_name: networks of interacting firms from direct measures
description: Each of the 72 responding hospitals named its top two competitors. The 142 usable (in MSA) responses were coded into a lower diagonal matrix representation of an undirected bipartite graph, and pairs of institutions were iteratively linked to each other, a procedure algebraically equivalent to a block-diagonal partitioning through row and column interchange. There were three resulting unconnected networks, and a fourth small network of four hospitals on the periphery of the MSA.

Marketing performance was measured using the market share of admissions. Each hospital's market share was weighted by the HCFA Case Mix index to compensate for the fact that not all hospitals offer all possible services.
Operating performance was characterized by occupancy, a standard hospital industry measure.
Financial performance was indicated by return on assets.

variable_name: Archival strategy variables as mobility barriers
description: Mobility barriers were operationalized by the eight archival strategy variables used to form strategic groups: bed size, case mix index, scope of medical services, costs of medical education, proportion of Medicare and Medicaid discharges, and geographic location.

variable_name: Share of named competitors located in the target MSA
description: Geographic boundedness is established empirically from the competitor-naming survey. Each of the 72 responding hospitals named its top two competitors; of the 144 competitors named, all but two were located in the target MSA, and all 96 hospitals in the MSA were named at least once. The authors use this result to conclude that the competitive environment is geographically delimited. The sample itself was also restricted to nonfederal general hospitals in one MSA.
scale: count and proportion of named competitors inside the MSA

description: The equity stake held by the Japanese parent or parents in each joint venture as of December 31, 1980, classified into majority (over 50 percent), 50/50, and minority levels. Where a venture had more than one Japanese partner, the shares of the Japanese partners were combined. The authors note that combining the Japanese share has the effect of stacking the deck in support of the Trojan Horse hypothesis.

variable_name: Change in ownership level / change in status
description: Compares each venture's combined Japanese ownership level at December 31, 1980 with its level at December 31, 1989. The categories distinguish increases to 100 percent ownership, increases not reaching 100 percent, decreases not reaching zero, and Japanese ownership falling to zero - through sale to the 1980 U.S. partner, sale to another U.S. company, sale to a third country company, sale to another Japanese company, bankruptcy or liquidation - as well as unchanged shares.

variable_name: Reasons Japanese partners took over or sold their stakes
description: For each case in which the Japanese partner increased its stake to 100 percent or sold its stake, the authors ascertained the reasons through telephone interviews to the headquarters of Japanese parents and of their subsidiaries and through secondary sources such as Lexis-Nexis, and then judged whether the case fitted the Trojan Horse scenario. Information was obtained on 12 of the 13 cases of full takeover and on 12 of the 17 cases of full sell-off.

EO was measured in the 2007 survey Wave 1 using modified scales from Covin and Slevin's (1989) and Lumpkin and Dess's (2001) scale. The mean values of scale items for each construct were used in the path analysis model. The individual scale items and item loadings are listed in the online supporting information Table S1.

PACAP was measured in the 2007 survey Wave 1 using a modified version of the ACAP scale by Jansen, Van den Bosch, and Volberda (2005). The mean values of scale items for each construct were used in the path analysis model. The individual scale items and item loadings are listed in the online supporting information Table S1.

RACAP was measured in the 2009 survey Wave 2 using a modified version of the ACAP scale by Jansen, Van den Bosch, and Volberda (2005). The mean values of scale items for each construct were used in the path analysis model. The individual scale items and item loadings are listed in the online supporting information Table S1.

All patents approved for or filed by the venture during 2007 and 2009 were identified, and forward citations of all approved or filed patents (eventually granted) were counted until 2013. Because patent citation propensity varies across industry classes, the average forward citations of all patents in a given technology class year were subtracted from the total forward citations for a patent in the same technology class year. The technology class year adjusted forward citation values for each patent were used to calculate the standard deviation of the forward citations for all firm patents.
time_window: patents approved or filed 2007-2009; forward citations until 2013

description: The outcome variable is the compounded sales growth rate from 2010 to 2012, computed as (venture sales in 2012 / venture sales in 2010) raised to the power of one third. The median industry (at the six-digit SNI code level) compounded sales growth rate from 2010 to 2012 was subtracted from the firm's compounded sales growth rate.

A binary variable included in a logistic regression that captures the likelihood of CEO equity reduction. It equals one if CEO equity holdings have been reduced from end of 1997 to end of 1999, zero otherwise. When this variable equals one, CEOs sold more equity than those acquired through options exercise and firm grants, thereby reducing their equity position in the firm.

A continuous variable included in a Tobit regression for the magnitude of equity reduction. It is measured as the percentage reduction in equity holdings from end of 1997 to end of 1999, relative to equity holdings in 1997. It is continuous and positive for equity reduction, with a lower limit for censoring specified at 0%.

The total variance of monthly market returns for the previous sixty (60) months. The authors describe it as a total variance measure closely associated with measures of firm systematic and nonsystematic risk, which symmetrically captures the downside and the upside potential of firm equity.

In line with Miller and Reuer (1996), root-lower partial moment (RLPM_MKT) is used as a proxy for unsystematic downside risk; it reflects an expected target shortfall, i.e., the risk of underperforming a target return. RLPM_MKT uses the CRSP value-weighted market return as the target level. The parameter alpha reflects the investor's feelings about the relative consequences of falling short of the target; the value used in the calculations (alpha = 2) is consistent with risk-averse behavior. The formula itself is not readable in the text provided.
Return on assets over the period 1996-1997. The authors note that the use of accounting measures of firm performance complements the downside risk measures that rely on historical market returns.
The natural logarithm of the value of the shares owned by the CEO, evaluated at market price at year end of 1997.

Dichotomous dependent variable drawn from survey questions on new product/service activities; respondents were asked whether their firms had 'Developed successfully a major new product line/service' over the last 36 months (thus 2001-2003). Coded 1 if the firms indicated they had successfully deployed a new product line or service and 0 otherwise. The measure reflects whether the product or service is new to the firm and does not require that it be a new-to-the-world innovation.

Measured using the Heritage Foundation Index of Economic Freedom, described as a broad-based indicator of institutional development toward free markets. The authors used the average of the 2000 and 2001 values to capture the level of institutional development preceding the 2001-2003 period of interest.

Spending on research and development divided by sales revenue. The BEEPS survey does not provide exact sales revenues but categorizes sales in 13 levels; the midpoint of the category scales is used as the sales denominator, with 5,000 used for category 1 and 100,000,000 for category 13. The indicator is normalized (mean centered) by industry so that it is relative to the firm's industry.

The percent of employees who have some university education. The variable is reported at a point in time '36 months ago', thus at the beginning of 2001. The indicator is normalized (mean centered) by industry so that it is relative to the firm's industry.
time_window: 36 months prior to the survey (beginning of 2001)

description: Survey response to a question rating the importance of 'pressure from domestic competitors' with respect to developing new products or services, measured on a five-point Likert scale. Each type of pressure is modeled independently since factor analysis indicates that the variables are distinct.

Survey response to a question rating the importance of 'pressure from foreign competitors' with respect to developing new products or services, measured on a five-point Likert scale. Each type of pressure is modeled independently since factor analysis indicates that the variables are distinct.
Coded '1' if the firm is located in a transition economy and '0' in a nontransition economy. Transition economies are defined as post-Soviet, formerly-controlled economies.

Before tax income as a percentage of total sales. Sales was preferred over investment or assets as the denominator because of the varying effects of depreciation method and length of depreciation schedule on accounting investment figures, and the precision of sales reporting over investment or assets in the PIMS data; equity as a denominator was unavailable owing to the disaggregate, business specific (versus corporate specific) nature of the data.

A dummy variable, equal to one if at least one new competitor entered the market and claimed a market share of five per cent or more during the previous four years. In the ROS equation it represents potential entry barriers.
The percentage of total purchases made from the business's three largest external suppliers. The variable is used in the ROS equation and is not used in the ENTRY equation.
The sales of the three largest suppliers to the business as a percentage of the suppliers' total revenues. The variable is used only in the ROS equation.

A three level variable (no; yes, but with difficulty; yes, with no difficulty) defining the availability of good alternative sources of supplies. It is used in both the ROS equation and the ENTRY equation, where it is included as an entry barrier.

The proportion of the total number of immediate customers accounting for 50 per cent of the firm's total sales. Higher values indicate a more fragmented and diffused customer base, so the variable acts as a counter measure of customer concentration. It is used in the ROS equation and not in the ENTRY equation.

The approximate number of immediate customers served by the business. The authors note that the variable has been recoded to fit into a linear system. It is used in the ROS equation and not in the ENTRY equation.
The percentage of the typical immediate customer's total annual purchases accounted for by this type of product or service. It is used in the ROS equation.

The percentage of the typical user's total annual purchases accounted for by this type of product or service. It is used in the ENTRY equation, where a product important to the final consumer is treated as encouraging a pull distribution network.

A three level dummy variable measuring the importance of installation, repair, customer service, and other auxiliary services provided to the end user. It is not employed in the ROS equation and is used in the ENTRY equation.
Estimates the breadth of the firm's served market, relative to the average of its leading competitors, with respect to the number of customers. It is used in the ROS equation.
Estimates the breadth of the firm's served market, relative to the average of its leading competitors, with respect to the size of customers. It is used in the ROS equation.

The percentage of industry shipments that is accounted for by the shipments of the four largest firms in that four-digit SIC industry group; if the industry spans several SIC groups a weighted average using dollar shipments as weights is employed. The variable appears in both the ROS and the ENTRY equations.
The firm's sales in the industry expressed as a percentage of the top four firms' annual sales. It is used in the ROS equation and not in the ENTRY equation.
The average annual percentage change in the size, expressed in real dollars, of the industry group. It is used in the ENTRY equation and is not used in the ROS equation.

A dummy variable, equal to one if the business benefits to a significant degree from patents, trade secrets, or other proprietary methods of production or operations, reflecting benefits pertaining to products or services. It appears in both the ROS and the ENTRY equations.

A dummy variable, equal to one if the business benefits to a significant degree from patents, trade secrets, or other proprietary methods of production or operations, pertaining to processes. It appears in both the ROS and the ENTRY equations.

variable_name: Purchase and sales market condition variables
description: Relative firm power was expressed by a set of PIMS purchase market and sales market condition variables, such as supplier concentration, supplier dependence, availability of alternative sources, customer concentration and number, and importance of the product to customers, entered in the profitability equation.

Where Y is a style nested within genre Z, the label-to-label distance from the superordinate genre Z to the style Y at year t is used directly to measure the specificity of Y. The distance is built from the single-to-label Mahalanobis distance: it is the mean Mahalanobis distance from Z to the singles to which Y was assigned in the year before the focal categorization decision. Because membership in Y implies membership in Z, any distance from Z to Y represents extra information that Y adds to what is already encoded by Z. The variable is mean-centered and standardized before regression.
time_window: t-1 (labels' meanings inferred from singles categorized in the year before the focal decision)

description: Where Y and Z are styles nested within the same genre, which may also encompass other styles, pairwise label-to-label distances from Z, Z', Z'', ... to Y are computed and the mean of these distances is taken to measure the distinctiveness of Y at year t. The distance from Z to Y is the mean Mahalanobis distance from Z to the singles to which Y was assigned in the year before the focal decision, so the measure is a directed statistical distance. The variable is mean-centered and standardized before regression.
time_window: t-1 (labels' meanings inferred from singles categorized in the year before the focal decision)

description: Every product-label pair becomes an observation, with the dependent variable equal to one if the label was assigned to the product by the user, and zero otherwise. It is possible for the dependent variable to equal one for multiple product-label pairs within the same choice set, representing situations in which multiple style labels were assigned to the same product. Pairs are not formed for labels that were not yet available on Discogs at the time of the user's decision.

FilterAvailable equals one if the employer was assigned to the treatment group and has access to filters during the recruitment process, and zero if the employer was assigned to the control group. It does not indicate whether the employer chose to recruit workers or to use the filters. For average-treatment-on-the-treated models, UseFilter is set equal to one if the employer was assigned to the treatment group and used the filter, and zero if the employer was in the control group or was assigned to treatment but did not use the filter; the authors state these estimates are suggestive rather than causal because they conflate treatment take-up with selection into filter usage. The new filter functionality allowed the employer to narrow down the list of recruitable workers by characteristics such as amount earned in previous jobs, hourly rate stated on their profile, and previous job success.
level: employer (job postings inherit the assignment of the initial job opening)

description: Number of applicants interviewed by the employer for a job posting, recorded per job opening in the platform's stage-by-stage hiring funnel. The authors report the treatment-control difference in the number of applicants interviewed overall and separately for below- and above-median-experience applicants.

The mean interview probability of an applicant, plotted by machine learning algorithm score group and treatment status, with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors clustered at the employer level used for 95% confidence intervals. The authors also aggregate the application-level percentage-point changes in interview probability to the job level by dividing the change by the baseline interview rate for each tail group and multiplying by the average number of applicants per job in that group.
level: applicant application, aggregated to the job level

description: A continuous score between 0 and 1 generated by the platform's machine learning algorithm when a worker submits an application. The algorithm analyzes the job post, considering the skills, experience, and other requirements specified by the employer, compares these to the proposal, scanning for relevant keywords, skills, and past project experience, and a higher score indicates a better fit for the job. The score is never visible to employers; it determines the default sorting of applicants and marks applicants above a threshold as recommended. Because it is calculated only after a worker applies, it has no effect at the 'Recruited Freelancer' stage and no interaction with the recruitment filters.

The ratio of the offered worker's submitted bid to their publicly posted profile wage rate, estimated among candidates who received a job offer; the profile wage rate is a standing, publicly visible wage that workers update periodically and do not customize per application. The authors also report models of the log of the offered worker's bid and the log of their profile hourly rate.
level: offered applicant (worker who received a job offer)

description: An indicator for whether the candidate ultimately rejected the job offer, estimated for workers who received an offer. The authors report the average treatment effect (Panel A) and the average treatment effect on the treated (Panel B), and compare the change to the baseline rejection rate.

The natural log of the final contracted wage, conditional on a contract being formed; the authors report it for the average treatment effect and the average treatment effect on the treated, relative to a baseline contract wage rate.
scale: log of the hourly contract wage
level: contract formed by an offered applicant

description: Three outcomes capture post-contract performance: whether the employer reported the contract as successful to the platform, the public feedback score the employer left for the hired worker on a scale of 1 to 5, and the private feedback score the employer left for the hired worker on a scale of 1 to 10. Reported for both the average treatment effect and the average treatment effect on the treated.

The HR planning index was created from responses to two questions from the human resource survey. The first question asked whether or not the business unit formally plans for the number of workers and skills needed to run the business in the future; the second asked whether or not the human resource department formally evaluated its selection and staffing policies. The responses to both questions were coded 1 if the answer was yes and 0 if no, and added together to create the index, which therefore ranges in value from zero to two.

The hiring index measures the extent and sophistication of a firm's recruitment and selection practices. It is operationalized by adding the number of interviews per hire, the number of recruiting sources used, and whether or not selection testing is used, each weighted as described. Each component is a weighted sum over seven worker categories, with weights equal to the proportion of employees in each occupational category. The recruiting sources asked about include employee referrals, graduate and undergraduate institutions, search firms, private and government employment agencies, walk-ins and newspaper advertisements; the selection tests include skills tests, aptitude tests, drug tests and physical examinations.

The employee development strategy index measures how the business unit develops its employees. It is operationalized by adding the weighted number of formal training programs offered to employee groups and the extent to which promotions from within are used. The amount of formal training given is measured by a weighted sum of the number of job categories receiving formal training, and the use of internal promotions by the weighted percentage of nonentry-level job vacancies that are filled by internal sources.

The dependent variable, labor productivity, is measured by dividing the business unit's net sales (in millions of dollars) by the number of employees. The authors state that they thus compare the input of labor to the output of sales.

Capital intensity was measured by the ratio of assets to total employees. The natural log of this measure was used in analyses in order to smooth the skewness. The authors note that asset intensity is also likely to be related to such characteristics of the firm as degree of vertical integration.

The pay of the CEO (the only first-level executive) divided by the average compensation of all group members who were formally designated as second-level executives. Each executive's pay is the sum of short-term compensation (salary and bonus) and long-term compensation (stock options, restricted stock, performance share awards, performance units/cash awards, and dividend equivalents). The greater the value, the higher the differential between the CEO's compensation and the pay of those at the next level in the hierarchy.

The average compensation of all second-level executives divided by the average compensation of third-level executives. Each executive's pay is the sum of short-term compensation (salary and bonus) and long-term compensation.

A gauge of the degree to which a tournament pay scheme existed within the firm. It is computed by first taking the percentage differential in pay between the CEO and the average of Level 2 executives, then dividing that term by the percentage differential between Level 2 and Level 3 executives; the paper's worked illustration of the computation is not readable in the extracted text. The greater this ratio, the larger the pay disparity as one moves up the hierarchy.

The coefficient of variation of pay for all executives in the second level of the organization. The coefficient of variation is calculated by dividing the standard deviation of group members' compensation by the mean compensation of the group.

The coefficient of variation for all executives in the third level of the hierarchy, calculated by dividing the standard deviation of group members' compensation by the mean compensation of the group.
The coefficient of variation in pay of all members of the firm's top management group, calculated as the standard deviation of members' compensation divided by the mean compensation of the group.

The coefficient of variation in pay of all members of the top management group excluding the CEO. The authors included this measure because some unusually extreme CEO-compensation packages might mask the degree to which pay disparities existed among the other members of the TMG.

The R&D-to-sales ratio of each firm's industry, obtained from Schonfeld's R&D Ratios and Budgets. For firms in a single four-digit industry the R&D-to-sales ratio for that SIC was used; for firms in multiple four-digit industries within a single three-digit SIC the three-digit ratio was used; for vertically integrated firms the ratio of their primary three-digit industry was used. Schonfeld's calculates industry R&D/sales as a weighted average based on the sales of each company in the industry, so larger companies are weighted more heavily.

The average market value of the company's common stock divided by the book value of its common stock, for the two years following the year t of compensation data, using year-end data. The corresponding two-year average market-to-book value for the firm's two-digit SIC industry was then subtracted.

Share appreciation plus reinvestment of dividends for the two years following the year t of compensation data, divided by the stock price at the end of year t. The corresponding two-year average shareholder returns for the firm's two-digit SIC industry were then subtracted.

The sum of the stock of experience of rival entrant firms, where a firm's stock of experience is the number of years it has competed in the industry. For a focal entrant the measure aggregates the experience of the other entrants, while for an incumbent it aggregates the experience of the entire entrant cohort. All variables are time varying and lagged one year.
level: firm-year, aggregating over the entrant cohort

description: The aggregate postderegulation experience of the incumbent cohort, equal to the sum over incumbent firms other than the focal firm of the number of years each incumbent has competed in the industry since deregulation. All variables are time varying and lagged one year.
level: firm-year, aggregating over the incumbent cohort

description: The aggregate prederegulation experience of the incumbent cohort: for each incumbent firm, the number of years it competed in the industry before deregulation, summed over incumbent firms other than the focal firm. All variables are time varying and lagged one year.
level: firm-year, aggregating over the incumbent cohort

description: Firm size is defined as the log of firm operating assets reported on the ICC Form M. Aggregating log sizes across cohort members produces the mass variables, and each firm's log size multiplied by its experience produces the size × experience competitive intensity measures for entrants and incumbents. Incumbent firms with log(size) greater than the incumbent average log(size) at deregulation are classified as large at deregulation, those at or below it as not large at deregulation.
time_window: lagged one year; size at deregulation used for the large/not large classification

description: The exit rate of firms from the trucking industry following deregulation is estimated as the instantaneous rate of exit, the probability that a firm exits the industry in the interval (t, t+Δt) given that the firm is operating at time t, estimated over the change in t. A firm was considered to have exited the industry when it was absent from the industry, based on ICC filings, the Yellow Pages, the World Wide Web, and trucking-industry periodicals, for at least two years and never returned, and had not been acquired by another firm. Exit events used are failures by dissolution rather than by merger or acquisition.
time_window: 1980-1993; firms not exited by 1991 treated as right censored

description: The number of women borrowers served by an MFO in a year, logged. Data were collected from the Microfinance Information Exchange (MIX), a World Bank/CGAP initiative covering MFOs that account for roughly 85% of global microfinance loans; the data are based on MFO self-reports.
The proportion of an MFO's employees who are women, comprising managers and loan officers, as reported to the Microfinance Information Exchange (MIX).

variable_name: total amount of local funding received
description: The logged amount (USD) of local capital acquired per MFO year, as reported by the MIX. The models also include past foreign funding received (logged) as a control to account for interdependencies between types of funding.

A nation's factor score for patriarchy in the family and religion, calculated from a confirmatory factor analysis of standardized indicators coded so that higher values reflect greater patriarchy. Exploratory factor analysis showed that the family and religion indicators loaded onto one underlying factor. Indicators loading on this factor are patriarchal religions, religious restrictions, female testimony, female-headed households, and the male-to-female labor participation rate.

A nation's factor score for patriarchy in the professions, reverse-coded to ease interpretation of the contrast effects, so that higher values indicate greater gender equality. Indicators loading on this factor are professional training (the portion of women in a country employed in professional and technical occupations) and female tertiary education enrollment; contraceptive usage and fertility, which the authors expected to load with the family, also loaded with this factor.

A nation's factor score for patriarchy in the state, reverse-coded to ease interpretation of the contrast effects, so that higher values indicate greater gender equality. Indicators loading on this factor are the percentage of parliamentary seats held by women and years since a nation ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW).

A weighted summation of the acquirer's and the potential target firm's R&D pipeline scores, using the distances between the therapeutic areas their pipeline projects target on the Inteleos therapeutic tree. Pipeline scores are proxied by the clinical probability of FDA approval for the project's stage of development. The number of therapeutic areas treated by each drug serves as a proxy for its commercial value.

A weighted summation of the acquirer's and the potential target firm's R&D pipeline scores, computed from the distances between the therapeutic areas their pipeline projects target on the Inteleos therapeutic tree. Pipeline scores are proxied by the clinical probability of FDA approval for the project's stage of development. Distances on the therapeutic tree are used to identify which therapeutic areas are similar and which are distinct.

A weighted summation of the acquirer's R&D pipeline scores and the potential target firm's product scores, computed from the distances between the therapeutic areas their drugs and pipeline projects treat on the Inteleos therapeutic tree. Approved drugs are assigned a product score of 1, and approved drugs that lost patent protection and face heavy generic competition a value of 0.1. Pipeline projects are scored by the clinical probability of FDA approval of their development phase.

A weighted summation of the acquirer's R&D pipeline scores and the potential target firm's product scores, computed from the distances between the therapeutic areas their drugs and pipeline projects treat on the Inteleos therapeutic tree. Approved drugs are assigned a product score of 1, and approved drugs that lost patent protection and face heavy generic competition a value of 0.1. Pipeline projects are scored by the clinical probability of FDA approval of their development phase.

A weighted summation of the acquirer's and the potential target firm's product scores, computed from the distances between the therapeutic areas their approved drugs treat on the Inteleos therapeutic tree. Approved drugs are assigned a product score of 1, and approved drugs that lost patent protection and face heavy generic competition a value of 0.1. The number of therapeutic areas treated by each drug proxies its commercial value.

A weighted summation of the acquirer's and the potential target firm's product scores, computed from the distances between the therapeutic areas their approved drugs treat on the Inteleos therapeutic tree. Approved drugs are assigned a product score of 1, and approved drugs that lost patent protection and face heavy generic competition a value of 0.1. Distances on the tree identify which therapeutic areas are similar and which are distinct.

A weighted summation of the acquirer's product scores and the potential target firm's R&D pipeline scores, computed from the distances between the therapeutic areas their drugs and pipeline projects treat on the Inteleos therapeutic tree. Approved drugs are assigned a product score of 1, and approved drugs that lost patent protection and face heavy generic competition a value of 0.1. Pipeline projects are scored by the clinical probability of FDA approval of their development phase.

A weighted summation of the acquirer's product scores and the potential target firm's R&D pipeline scores, computed from the distances between the therapeutic areas their drugs and pipeline projects treat on the Inteleos therapeutic tree. Approved drugs are assigned a product score of 1, and approved drugs that lost patent protection and face heavy generic competition a value of 0.1. Pipeline projects are scored by the clinical probability of FDA approval of their development phase.

An indicator variable taking the value 1 when the potential target firm k is the actual choice (i.e., the chosen or acquired firm) of acquirer j at time t, and 0 otherwise. The indicator enters the log-likelihood of the maximum likelihood estimation of the choice model.

CEOs were asked to place their hospital on a scale of 1 (defender) to 7 (prospector), considering how the hospital currently operated, how it operated two years ago, and how it was likely to operate two years in the future. Letter anchors described a niche provider with a relatively stable set of services, a provider with a relatively stable base that selectively moves into promising new areas, a frequent changer that attempts to pioneer new services and markets, and a provider without a consistent pattern. Responses of 1 or 2 were collapsed into the defender category, 3 to 5 into analyzers, and 6 or 7 into prospectors.
scale: 1 (defender) to 7 (prospector), collapsed into three categories. Direction: higher = more prospector (defender to prospector scale)
time_window: both waves of data collection (1984-85 and 1986-87)

variable_name: emphasis on new services and new markets
description: For each of 15 service lines, ranging from general inpatient medical and surgical care to outpatient renal dialysis and health promotion, respondents assigned points from 0 to 100 (the total was to add to 100) across four categories: further penetrate current markets, develop new markets, refine current services, and develop new services. The measure is the degree of emphasis given to new service and new market development activity across the 15 service lines, which include 5 core business services (acute inpatient surgical care, medical care, obstetrics care, pediatrics care, and psychiatric care) and 10 noncore (diversified) services.

Count of diversified services offered by the hospital, selected from a 34-item services inventory that included ambulatory care, geriatric care, health promotion, home health-extended care, outpatient diagnostic services, and service delivery alternatives such as health maintenance organizations and preferred provider organizations. Values were adjusted for hospital bed size. The same count was taken at both data collections, including the number of such services provided at the time of the second collection.

variable_name: number of diversified services added in the past two years
description: Count of diversified services from the services inventory that the hospital added in the two years preceding data collection. In the second wave the variable captures the number of such services initiated over the interval between the two collections, which the authors also describe as the number of new services offered in the most recent two years.
time_window: two years preceding each data collection

variable_name: ratio of outpatient to inpatient services offered
description: Ratio of outpatient to inpatient services offered by the hospital, taken as the ratio of diversified to nondiversified services.

Count of high-technology services offered, drawn from a list of 15 services ranging from intensive care units to nuclear magnetic resonance imaging and various organ and tissue transplant services; the data came from the American Hospital Association. Values were adjusted for hospital bed size.

variable_name: number of new diversified services planned for the future
description: Count of diversified services from the services inventory that the hospital planned to provide in the future.

variable_name: percentage of services in high-growth areas
description: For each of the 15 services, respondents indicated the potential percentage of growth in the volume of patients seen or services provided using five response options: no growth potential (service may actually be declining), low growth potential (between 1% and 10% per year), moderate growth potential (between 11% and 50% per year), high growth potential (greater than 50% per year), and 'we do not offer this service'. The percentage of a hospital's services in high-growth areas was derived from these ratings and was measured on a scale of 0 to 100 points.

From a factor analysis of 19 items related to the planning process, four formality measures were obtained: agreement on goals, degree of formalization and discipline, degree of plan development, and extent of department directors' and division heads' involvement in planning. All four items had factor loadings above .50 and eigenvalues above 1.0 derived from principal components analysis with varimax rotation. The variable was measured on a 1 to 5 scale where 1 = low and 5 = high, and planning process information was gathered only in the second collection of data.

Measured by two items: degree of innovativeness compared to past strategies and degree of innovativeness compared with competitors; factor loadings were above .60 and eigenvalues above 1.0. The variable was measured on a 1 to 5 scale where 1 = low and 5 = high, and was gathered only in the second collection of data.

Measured by two items: the quality of market research and the ability to obtain market research information; factor loadings were above .70 and eigenvalues were greater than 1.0. The variable was measured on a 1 to 5 scale where 1 = low and 5 = high, and was gathered only in the second collection of data.

The count of U.S. drug patents granted to a firm in a given year. Drug patents are identified as any patent by the firm that is in patent classes 424 or 514, which the USPTO identifies as 'Drug, Bio-affecting and Body Treating Compositions.'
The count of drug patents in the 3-year period prior to a focal year, i.e., the sum of the three lagged years of the dependent variable. Used to measure firms' underlying research capabilities.

The count of firm patents in class 435 of the USPTO classification scheme, for the 3-year period prior to a focal year. Patent class 435 is the Molecular Biology and Biochemistry class and includes all patents related to fermentation. Used to measure firms' complementary research capabilities.

A dummy variable that records whether or not a firm had an international R&D activity within a given year. It takes the value of one for firms that engaged in international R&D activity, zero otherwise. International R&D includes sponsored, collaborative, and controlled research activities.
