The number of unique individuals that engage with a MOOC platform in a given month ('unique monthly visitors'), used as a direct indicator of customer demand in digital market contexts. The data point was gathered through Semrush, a commercial data provider that tracks unique monthly visitors for websites, and the organically acquired visitors were used to construct the variable. The measure was log-transformed to reduce skewness.

Calculated as the share of social impact keywords relative to the total number of words across all press releases made by the given venture in the most recent 3-month period. Keywords were counted with the Social Value Orientation wordlist of Moss et al. (2018), which contains 66 keywords and word stems, using the CAT Scanner software on cleaned press release texts. The measure was mean-centered using z-scores and the sample's minimum value was subtracted so that a value of zero indicates that no words indicating the frame appeared.

Calculated as the share of innovativeness keywords relative to the total number of words across all press releases made by the given venture in the most recent 3-month period. Keywords were counted with the Innovativeness wordlist of McKenny et al. (2018) consisting of 147 words and word groupings commonly used to indicate innovativeness, using the CAT Scanner software on cleaned press release texts. The measure was mean-centered using z-scores and the sample's minimum value was subtracted so that a value of zero indicates that no words indicating the frame appeared.

Operationalized as a decaying stock variable of news articles published in Factiva's 'Major News and Business Sources' that mention 'MOOC*' or 'Massive Open Online Course*' or at least one MOOC platform provider in the title or lead paragraph. Articles published in t are counted with a factor of 1.0, those in t-1 with 0.85, those in t-2 with 0.72, and so on, using a common decay factor of 0.15 per period. The natural logarithm of the number of news articles was used to reduce skew.

Measured as the natural logarithm of the total number of MOOCs offered across all MOOC platforms in a given month, including platforms excluded from the regression sample. It reflects both changes in the number of competing MOOC platforms and changes in the size of their MOOC portfolios. The variable was constructed by web-crawling Class Central archives of past MOOCs, including start dates and duration, to identify all months in which each MOOC was actively delivered.

A three-state categorical variable based on the three main categories identified by Institutional Investor: currently ranked as a star (recognized as one of the top three in his or her industry at the time of hiring), currently named as a runner-up, or excluded from the ranking (low status). The newcomer's status is identified at the moment of hiring, based on his or her first recommendation issued for the new employer.
time_window: at the time of the hiring event (first recommendation for the new employer)

description: A variable capturing whether the incumbent analyst is ranked as a star or a runner-up, or is unranked, at the time of the hiring event, computed following the same procedure as newcomer's status. The categorical status of the incumbent is interacted with the posthiring dummy and with newcomer status in the models.
time_window: at the time of the hiring event

description: Following Barber et al. (2007), the buy-and-hold abnormal return (BHAR) that would be obtained by creating a portfolio of stocks updated based on each analyst's stock recommendations, measured for both long positions (buy and strong buy) and short positions (sell and strong sell). The BHAR is obtained by going long or short in the recommended stock the day after the recommendation and holding the position up to 90 days, minus the expected returns, which are estimated with the Carhart (1997) four-factor model over a 30 to 150 trading day window prior to the recommendation date. A one-dollar investment is assumed for each recommendation, so the analyst's performance in a window is the average return per dollar invested following his or her recommendations in that window. The text presents the corresponding formulas in equations that were not readable in the extracted payload.
time_window: one year of data in each of the pre- and posthiring windows, excluding the quarter before and the quarter after the hiring event

description: Each four-digit SIC code defined a unique business and all businesses with the same first two digits of the SIC code were deemed related. Firms whose largest group of related businesses (two-digit SIC code) accounted for 40 percent or more of total firm sales were considered related diversifiers, and those with less than 40 percent were considered unrelated diversifiers. The 40 percent cut-off is an attempt to neutralize size effects of a single large group.

The percentage of total sales change resulting from mergers/acquisitions for each firm was first determined, representing utilization of the external mode; that percentage subtracted from unity represented use of the internal mode. If mergers/acquisitions accounted for 10 percent or more of the change in sales, the firm was classified as an external diversified firm, and less than 10 percent resulted in classification as an internal diversifier.

Firms classified by diversification breadth (related/unrelated) and mode (internal/external) were cross-classified into four combined categories. The number of firms in the four categories was 27, 26, 3 and 17.

Four accounting-based performance measures were used: return on equity (ROE), return on assets (ROA), return on invested capital (ROIC) and compound sales growth (CSG). The authors state that these are generally accepted performance measures used in one or more of the major studies in the field and that Table 1 illustrates the calculation of the four measures; the formula rendering is not readable in this payload.

variable_name: director experience with acquisitions in the same product market as the focal acquisition
description: Outside directors' prior experience with decisions about acquiring firms in the same product market as the focal acquisition. The prose states that A_s indicates an acquisition of a company that has the same primary two-digit SIC code as the acquired firm in the focal acquisition at the N firms where the individual served as manager or director in year y, and M indicates the number of outside directors on the board making the focal acquisition. The displayed equation could not be extracted from the text. Board-level experience was created by summing the relevant characteristics of individual members; separate analyses using mean, median and status- or performance-weighted aggregation reduced model fit.
level: focal acquisition (aggregated across outside directors of the acquiring firm's board)
time_window: prior years, at the firms where the individual served as manager or director

description: Directors' prior experience with decisions about related acquisitions. The prose states that A_r indicates an acquisition of a company that has the same primary two-digit SIC code as acquiring firm f at the N firms where the focal individual served as manager or director in year y, and M indicates the number of outside directors on the board making the focal acquisition. The displayed equation could not be extracted from the text. Aggregation across the board's outside directors was by summing individual members' experience.
level: focal acquisition (aggregated across outside directors of the acquiring firm's board)
time_window: prior years, at the firms where the focal individual served as manager or director

description: An analogous measure to the related-acquisition experience measure, developed to operationalize directors' prior experience with decisions about unrelated acquisitions. Because unrelated acquisitions are those not coded as related, the count of prior acquisitions is combined across outside directors in the same summing approach used for the other experience variables. The displayed equation could not be extracted from the text.
level: focal acquisition (aggregated across outside directors of the acquiring firm's board)
time_window: prior years, at the firms where the focal individual served as manager or director

description: A single index of board independence from management created from four widely used indicators by principal components analysis. The four indicators are the ratio of outside to inside directors; the portion of outside directors appointed after the CEO; separation of the CEO and board chair positions; and outside director stock ownership, measured as the percentage of total common equity held by outside directors. All four indicators were measured for the year prior to the acquisition announcement and loaded on one factor with an eigenvalue greater than one. Components of the interaction terms were centered to avoid multicollinearity.
time_window: year prior to the acquisition announcement

variable_name: excess stock returns from the acquisition
description: Excess stock returns, the difference between the acquiring firm's observed return and its expected return over a period surrounding the acquisition announcement. In the primary analysis excess returns were estimated over a two-day period (t - 1 to t 0). Parameters of the market model were estimated over a 238-day period (day t - 259 to day t - 21, where t signifies the announcement date), and heteroskedasticity was corrected for using the Jaffe-Mandelker portfolio method. The variable is computed as the difference between the observed return and the return expected given least squares estimates of the market model intercept and beta.
time_window: two-day event window (t - 1 to t 0); market model estimated over day t - 259 to day t - 21

description: Categorical grouping of respondents into four types used as the independent variable in the ANOVAs and as the dependent categorical group variable in the discriminant analysis. Of the 33 CEOs, 19 held business degrees (mostly undergraduate) and 14 did not. The MBA respondents were nearing the end of their capstone business policy class, and the nonbusiness respondents were in the final two weeks of graduate-level English and sociology classes.

A multiple regression was computed for each replication of the conjoint task by each respondent, regressing performance ratings on strategy, structure, environment and the double and triple interactions of the full model, and the mean parameters of the two replications represented each respondent's cause map. The parameters for the three double interactions were significantly intercorrelated and showed similar differences across respondent types, so they were summed to produce the composite contingency thinking variable. The larger the mean of the composite variable, the closer the cause map is to the prescriptions of business-level contingency theory.

variable_name: strategy attribute in the conjoint task
description: Strategy was an attribute of the 2 x 2 x 2 full factorial conjoint rating task, with differentiation strategy coded 1 and low cost strategy coded -1 in the regression of each respondent's performance ratings. Each respondent performed the task twice, and the mean of the two regression parameters estimated that respondent's utility for strategy.

variable_name: structure attribute in the conjoint task
description: Structure was an attribute of the 2 x 2 x 2 full factorial conjoint rating task, with organic structure (presented to respondents as "Type B") coded 1 and mechanistic structure ("Type A") coded -1 in the regression of each respondent's performance ratings. The mean of the parameters from the two replications estimated that respondent's utility for structure.

variable_name: environment attribute in the conjoint task
description: Environment was an attribute of the 2 x 2 x 2 full factorial conjoint rating task, with dynamic environment coded 1 and stable environment coded -1 in the regression of each respondent's performance ratings. The mean of the parameters from the two replications estimated that respondent's utility for environment.

Facilities' self-reported expenditure data, summed across the most common types of EMS adoption costs: staff time, consultants, travel and training, equipment, materials, corrective action, auditors and ISO 14001 certification. The summed cost data were logged to reduce the variability in the dependent variable. Sunk costs such as the expense of developing a pollution prevention plan were excluded.

Continuous dependent variable used in the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test to evaluate whether EMS adoption costs differed among the three types of ownership structures. The authors report average total cost per employee for publicly traded, privately owned, and government facilities.

variable_name: quality-based and inventory control management system experience
description: Facilities were asked whether they had implemented Total Quality Management (TQM) principles or ISO 9000 quality-based management systems prior to EMS adoption. They were also asked whether they had implemented Just-in-Time inventory management or materials accounting systems. Organizations that had implemented TQM, ISO 9000, JIT and materials accounting management systems were expected to have more quality-based and inventory control management system experience.

Facilities' pollution prevention practices were measured by whether they had participated in pollution prevention activities prior to adopting an EMS, where pollution prevention activities were defined as any materials substitution, process changes, or other activities that minimized waste production. Additionally, the authors accounted for whether or not the enterprise had adopted a pollution prevention plan or incorporated pollution prevention strategies into their future business planning. Organizations that indicated that they had implemented any one of these proactive environmental strategies were believed to have more pollution prevention practices.

The authors first determined whether facilities had parent organizations. They then assessed whether the parent organization provided financial support, technical support, or an EMS design template as assistance for EMS adoption. In additional estimation models, they examined whether parent-sponsored financial support, technical support, or support in the form of EMS templates reduced adoption costs.

To measure the extent to which facilities relied on government subsidies during EMS adoption, facilities were asked whether EPA or state-sponsored technical assistance influenced their EMS adoption decision. Facility managers responded by indicating whether this assistance had a high, medium, or low influence. Because of the ambiguousness between the 'low' and 'not applicable' classifications, these two responses were collapsed into the 'low' category.
Consultant assistance was measured by including a dummy variable indicating whether or not facilities relied on external consultants during EMS adoption.

Facility ownership was classified into three types: publicly traded, privately owned, and government enterprises. The Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test used ownership structure as the independent variable, with cost per employee as the dependent variable.

Facilities were classified into three ownership types: publicly traded, privately owned and government enterprises. Public ownership is the publicly traded category, with 20 publicly traded facilities among the 42 in the sample. It was the independent variable in the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney comparison of cost per employee.

Facilities were classified into three ownership types: publicly traded, privately owned and government enterprises. Government ownership is the government category of this classification, with six government enterprises in the sample of 42 facilities. It was the independent variable in the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney comparison of cost per employee.

Technological niche width is the range of engine capacity in terms of horsepower across all models produced by each firm at any given point in time, a realized niche. Producers define themselves by choosing an array of products: specialists offer products with a small range of variation on the dimension, generalists display a broad range. The measure implies that a firm is capable of producing engines for all values within its range, whether it actually does or not.
time_window: measured at each point in time

description: Distance of the focal firm's niche from the market center for firms whose niche contains a larger engine capacity than the center. It is the difference between the midpoint of the focal firm's technological product range and the midpoint of the market center, where the market center covers the range of the niches of the four largest firms in the industry.
time_window: measured at each point in time

description: Distance of the focal firm's niche from the market center for firms located below the center. It is the difference between the midpoint of the focal firm's technological product range and the midpoint of the market center, defined as the range of the niches of the four largest firms in the industry.
time_window: measured at each point in time

description: Count of firms whose niches overlap with the niche of the focal firm. The authors chose a density measure rather than a more complex alternative that would have weighted overlaps by the portion of the niche overlapping with that of competitors.
time_window: measured at each point in time

description: Dummy variable for size less than or equal to an annual production of 50 cars (size ≤ 50). This cutoff was used both to capture the compounded absolute-small-size disadvantage and to identify the subset of scale competitors and of very small firms that are treated as specialists on at least one unobserved environmental dimension.

Concentration-ratio measure defined as the ratio of the annual production of the four largest firms to the total industry output for that year. As the combined market share of the top four firms increases, concentration increases proportionately; the range of the four largest firms' niches is also used to define the market center. The authors note that if the market in any given year consists of four or fewer producers, concentration equals one, and they control for this feature of the early industry period.

Hazard rate of organizational life histories ending by disbanding of the firm or exit to another industry, defined to include events of unknown type. Firms known to have ended by merger or acquisition were treated as noninformatively censored on the right at the time of these events, following standard practice in event-history analysis. The rate is modeled as a piecewise exponential function of tenure in the industry with breakpoints at 0.5, 1, 3 and 7 years.

Aggregate distance of all larger firms from the focal firm, computed by first locating each firm at each point in time on a downward-sloping curve given by the inverse quadratic root of the size variable after adjusting for minimum size, and then summing the differences in scores between the focal firm and its larger competitors. The greater the number of larger competitors, the greater the competitive pressure, and a unit size difference creates more pressure when the focal firm is small; the estimated specification uses the exact formula as given in the paper, which is not readable in the supplied text. The variable is entered interacted with a dummy for firms with annual production above 50 cars.
time_window: measured at each point in time

description: TMT polychronicity was measured with a concise five-item version of the group polychronicity scale developed by Bluedorn and colleagues (Bluedorn et al., 1992, 1999). Items were measured along a five-point Likert scale (alpha = 0.96) and two items were reverse scored. Statistical checks indicated high interrater agreement for the two respondents (F = 13.4, p < 0.001; ICC[1] = 0.81; ICC[2] = 0.90; rwg = 0.87), and the values of the two respondents were averaged for the team variables.

The authors adapted and employed Schriber and Gutek's (1987) pace instrument to measure strategic decision speed, a three-item scale (alpha = 0.96). The instrument is a general one across decisions, intended to capture the organization's customary (average) speed in strategic decision making rather than the duration of one specific decision. High interrater agreement was found for the two respondents (F = 53.6, p < 0.001; ICC[1] = 0.93; ICC[2] = 0.96; rwg = 0.95) and the two responses were averaged.

Strategic decision comprehensiveness was measured with the Miller et al. (1998) five-point Likert scale items; scenario-based items were not used because they were perceived to be artificial, complex and harder to administer. High interrater agreement was found for the two respondents and the two responses were averaged.

variable_name: Standardised measure of financial performance (ROTA + ROS)
description: Financial performance was measured with two archival objective measures obtained from the FAME database: return on total assets (ROTA) as a measure of new venture efficiency and return on sales (ROS) as a measure of new venture profitability. The correlation between the two performance measures was 0.68; to increase parsimony the two indicators were standardized and averaged into a composite measure of financial performance. Performance data were collected one year after the instrument was administered (at t + 1).

We assessed whether a firm did or did not operate in each of nine markets served by firms in the electronics industry. The typology of markets evolved from existing typologies used by electronics analysts and industry associations and from interviews and a delphi process with a panel of industry experts. The markets served were assessed together with the business competencies used in each market.
scale: binary (did or did not operate in the market)

description: The same typology of nine markets served was applied to the Japanese family: each firm was assessed as to whether it did or did not operate in each market. The information was collected from the Japan Company Handbook and confirmed by telephone calls with each firm.
scale: binary (did or did not operate in the market)

description: The business competencies each firm drew upon to serve each market were measured. Combined with markets served, they form a matrix of markets served by business competencies that the authors and others use to characterize firm identity.
scale: binary (competency used or not used in the market)

description: For the Japanese family the same business competencies were recorded for each firm in each market it served. The information was taken from the Japan Company Handbook and confirmed by telephone calls with the firms.
scale: binary (competency used or not used in the market)

description: Firm size is one of the internal firm characteristics in the authors' elementary theory of organizational differences. In describing the populations, size is characterized by features such as the number of divisions, plants and facilities, and employees, and firms are described as smaller or larger on these size characteristics.

Firm size is one of the internal firm characteristics in the authors' elementary theory of organizational differences, applied to the Japanese family. Japanese populations are described in terms of the number of employees, divisions, plants and facilities, and firms are characterized as smaller or larger on these measures.

Macro productivity measures such as sales per employee are among the firm characteristics used as taxonomic characters. The population descriptions refer to ratios such as income per employee, sales per employee, and sales per total assets.

Macro productivity measures such as sales per employee are among the firm characteristics used as taxonomic characters for the Japanese family. The population descriptions refer to ratios such as income per employee, sales per employee, sales per total assets, and income per total assets.

Organizational diversification was measured by Rumelt's (1974) specialization ratio. The population descriptions characterize U.S. firms as more or less specialized overall and more or less specialized in electronics.

Organizational diversification was measured by Rumelt's (1974) specialization ratio for the Japanese family. The population descriptions characterize Japanese firms as specializing in electronics or not being specialized in electronics or overall.

Populations are groups of firms obtained by agglomerative clustering of 78 taxonomic characters per firm (markets served, business competencies, size, productivity and diversification measures). Resemblance matrices (distance and product-moment correlation) and joining methods (single linkage, group average and others) were compared; the distance matrix with group average clustering was judged best, with clusters defined at major jumps in fusion levels, giving 13 U.S. and 9 Japanese populations. Cluster significance was tested with cophenetic correlation, discriminant analysis, t-tests and F-tests, separately for the U.S. (s1) and Japanese (s2) families.

Following Lerner (1995), the variable is measured as the number of international patent classes that a patent has on its front page. It is a count of the classes listed on the patent, so a higher value indicates broader scope.

Following Ahuja and Lampert (2001), who use the lack of prior art to measure the pioneering nature of inventions created by firms, the variable is measured as the number of prior patents referenced by a patent. The authors note that the effect of pioneering nature is coded inversely, so more prior references indicate less pioneering inventions.
This is measured as time elapsed in years since the patent was granted. Both the age term and its square are included in the model to capture the predicted inverted U-shaped relationship.

The achievement of first sale of a product or service that makes use of the invention, measured as the receipt of the first dollar of revenue by the licensing firm. In the event history analysis a spell begins when an MIT patent is licensed by a particular firm and continues until a first sale is reported, and a licensed patent that does not lead to first sale is treated as censored.
time_window: from licensing of the patent until first sale, censored if no first sale is reported

description: Experimental treatment manipulated in the hypothetical market scenarios. Each of the four competitive forces used in the study was varied 'high' or 'low' to create a total of 16 scenarios; in the estimated equations the variable is set to 0 for low and 1 for high levels. Supplier power was held constant at the high level in all scenarios.

Experimental treatment manipulated in the hypothetical market scenarios. Each of the four competitive forces used in the study was varied 'high' or 'low' to create a total of 16 scenarios; in the estimated equations the variable is set to 0 for low and 1 for high levels. Detailed operational descriptions of 'high' versus 'low' settings were provided to respondents.

Experimental treatment manipulated in the hypothetical market scenarios. Each of the four competitive forces used in the study was varied 'high' or 'low' to create a total of 16 scenarios; in the estimated equations the variable is set to 0 for low and 1 for high levels. Detailed operational descriptions of 'high' versus 'low' settings were provided to respondents.

Experimental treatment manipulated in the hypothetical market scenarios. Each of the four competitive forces used in the study was varied 'high' or 'low' to create a total of 16 scenarios; in the estimated equations the variable is set to 0 for low and 1 for high levels. Detailed operational descriptions of 'high' versus 'low' settings were provided to respondents.

variable_name: Likelihood of pursuing the cost-leader strategy (Y1)
description: After reading each scenario, respondents indicated the chance that they would recommend pursuing the overall cost leadership strategy in that market, circling a percentage ranging from 0 to 100 percent in 10 percent intervals. The strategy questions were posed independently and respondents were not forced to choose among cost, differentiation or focus strategies.

variable_name: Likelihood of pursuing the differentiation strategy (Y2)
description: After reading each scenario, respondents indicated the chance that they would recommend pursuing the differentiation strategy in that market, circling a percentage ranging from 0 to 100 percent in 10 percent intervals. The strategy questions were posed independently and respondents were not forced to choose among cost, differentiation or focus strategies.

variable_name: Likelihood of pursuing the focus strategy (Y3)
description: After reading each scenario, respondents indicated the chance that they would recommend pursuing the focus strategy in that market, circling a percentage ranging from 0 to 100 percent in 10 percent intervals. The strategy questions were posed independently and respondents were not forced to choose among cost, differentiation or focus strategies.

variable_name: Differentiation or focus strategy likelihood (Y2 and Y3)
description: The authors analyze the differentiation (j = 2) and focus (j = 3) strategy likelihoods together as the 'differentiation or focus' competitive strategies when comparing countries and when interpreting the country interaction coefficients. Each constituent likelihood was elicited on the same 0 to 100 percent scale in 10 percent intervals.

Country of the respondent, used as a dummy in the multilevel equations: C = 1 for United States and 2 for Japan. The two samples were 316 usable questionnaires from U.S. firms and 459 from Japanese firms, drawn from sampling frames of medium-to-large firms listed in the World Business Directory.

The dependent variable was a dichotomous measure signifying whether a trade event occurred between two teams in a given year in the 17-year observation window; 1 indicated a trade and 0 indicated no trade. A few team dyads traded more than once during a given year, but less than 3 percent of the dyad-years at risk experienced more than one trade, and dichotomization prevented problems created by contagion within the dependent variable.
time_window: annual; study years began April 1 and ended March 31 of the following calendar year

description: Measure of prior exchange ties that involved both organizations and both of their current leaders. Each prior exchange is weighted by the number of players involved and by a decay function capturing memory loss, roster and personnel changes and other structural changes. A linearly decayed three-year window provided the best statistical fit for the interorganizational tie measures (OO, OOL, and OOLL). Coefficients indicate the degree to which a change in the decayed number of previously traded players changes the likelihood that a dyad of teams will trade players again at a given future time.

Measure of prior exchange ties that involved both organizations and only one of their current leaders. Each prior exchange is weighted by the number of players involved and by a decay function capturing memory loss, roster and personnel changes and other structural changes. A linearly decayed three-year window provided the best statistical fit for the interorganizational tie measures (OO, OOL, and OOLL).

Measure of prior exchange ties that involved one organization and both of the current leaders. Each prior exchange is weighted by the number of players involved and by a decay function capturing memory loss, roster and personnel changes and other structural changes. An undecayed five-year sliding window provided the best statistical fit for the other exchange tie measures (OLL, OL, and LL).

Measure of prior exchange ties between the two organizations when they were not led by their current leaders. Each prior exchange is weighted by the number of players involved and by a decay function capturing memory loss, roster and personnel changes and other structural changes. A linearly decayed three-year window provided the best statistical fit for the interorganizational tie measures (OO, OOL, and OOLL).

Measure of prior exchange ties between one organization and the leader of the other organization, isolating the influence of leader-organization ties. Each prior exchange is weighted by the number of players involved and by a decay function capturing memory loss, roster and personnel changes and other structural changes. An undecayed five-year sliding window provided the best statistical fit for the other exchange tie measures (OLL, OL, and LL).

Measure of prior exchange ties between the two current leaders of the dyad organizations when they were not leading their current organizations. Each prior exchange is weighted by the number of players involved and by a decay function capturing memory loss, roster and personnel changes and other structural changes. An undecayed five-year sliding window provided the best statistical fit for the other exchange tie measures (OLL, OL, and LL).

The year in which the FERC was notified that a proposed project was seeking QF status, aggregated by year within each state, with one observation recorded per state per year. Only the first project initiated by a QF was counted, with duplicate filings, later projects at other sites and projects with missing data deleted. Foundings were counted separately for alternative energy technologies and for cogeneration projects, which were treated as two distinct subpopulations.

A dummy variable capturing whether the term 'avoided costs' had been formally defined by the state commission. Without such a definition a wide range of avoided costs could be claimed, which could lead to disputes over payment terms once electricity was delivered to the utility grid. In the regressions this policy, together with the standard contract policy, was transformed into a set of mutually exclusive dummy variables, and the case of no contractual assurances was omitted.
time_window: policy adoption year reported by commissions; lagged one year

description: A dummy variable capturing whether standardized contracts for power purchase by utilities from QFs had been authorized by the state's regulatory commission. Use of a standardized contract was expected to deflate transaction costs. It was entered together with the avoided-costs policy as one of four mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive dummies (no contractual assurances, formally defined avoided costs only, approved standard contracts only, and both policies together), with no contractual assurances omitted.
time_window: policy adoption year reported by commissions; lagged one year

variable_name: Statewide industry association for QFs exists
description: A dummy variable for the presence or absence of a statewide trade association representing QFs. Such an association would advance the interests of independent power production by consolidating the power and presence of QFs, representing members using both alternative energy technologies and cogeneration through intervention in regulatory hearings, lobbying of legislators, and other collective action.

Summary ratings of the 'regulatory climate' for states provided by the Value Line Investment Service since the mid-1970s, using three categories: below average, average, and above average, in order of improving regulatory relations. Placement into categories reflects procedural and economic policies but is also closely tied to the political environment. Dummies for below-average and above-average rankings were included in the regressions, with the average category serving as the reference.
scale: three categories (below average, average, above average) entered as two dummies

description: Leniency multiplies the inverse of the category's contrast (the fuzziness of the category) by the natural log of the number of distinct other categories with which members identify. Contrast is the average grade of membership of member organizations, and grade of membership is the number of times an organization claims a category in its press releases divided by the number of times it claims any category in a given year. Leniency is measured for every year, and the models use the leniency of the category in the previous year.

A binary variable that equals 1 if the organization enters the category from the dyad in the current year and 0 if it does not. Market entry is coded 1 only if the organization has never previously been a member of that category, and the first year the organization is in the press release data is not coded as an entry.

A binary variable that equals 1 if the organization drops the category from the dyad in the current year and 0 if it does not. Exit is coded 1 in the last year that the organization from the dyad claims membership in the market category from the dyad. Organizational failures are not coded as a market exit, and because exit cannot be defined for 2002 the exit analysis covers 1990-2001.

variable_name: Leniency of the organization's categories (weighted average)
description: Computed as a weighted average of the leniency of the categories the organization is in, weighted by its grade of membership in each category. It is used as the moderator of the leniency of the target category in the entry models, and is also included as an organization-level control.

variable_name: Received VC funding (in the previous year)
description: A dummy variable that indicates whether the organization received venture capital funding in the previous year. It is interacted with the leniency of the target category to test H4.

Fuzziness is the inverse of the category's contrast, where contrast is calculated as the average grade of membership of member organizations and grade of membership is the number of times an organization claims a category in its press releases divided by the number of times it claims any category in a given year. A category is fuzzy if it has a high degree of overlap with at least one other category.

To measure across-niche product proliferation the authors use the Berry index of dispersion. For firm i at time t it is defined from Nist, the number of products offered by firm i in niche s at time t. The index varies theoretically from 100 (maximum APP) to 0 (firm sells in only one niche); it offers a precise, standard measure of dispersion.
To calculate within-niche proliferation the authors count the number of models that a firm is selling in a given time in the niche with the highest density of product models for that same firm.

Performance is defined as margins multiplied by the number of model units sold at time t for each brand i, where the set of products offered by firm i at period t enters the summation and price, marginal cost and units sold are taken per product. Margins are derived from a supply-demand structural model following Kadiyali et al. (1999): the demand function for each car model is specified with a random coefficient logit model, the equilibrium profit-maximizing price is derived from the first-order price condition assuming optimal multiproduct firm decisions in an oligopolistic market, and the equations are estimated simultaneously with the generalized method of moments. The final dependent variable is the aggregation, at the firm level, of the profits accrued for each model.

Following McEvily and Chakravarthy (2002), complexity is measured as the dispersion of product characteristics, keeping interdependence fixed. The authors identify 10 intervals of equal size for each attribute, from the minimal to the maximum value observed in the sample, then calculate for each period the proportion of models in each interval to compute a Berry index for each attribute; the Complexity variable equals the average of these attribute Berry indexes for each period, multiplied by 100 for scaling. Complexity uses the data for all competitors (European, U.S., and Asian) in the Spanish automobile industry.

A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if there is variation in the level of across-product proliferation by time and by firm. It is included to evaluate operational and management costs and negative customer reactions due to changes in the firm's fit with category schemas.

Market valuation measured as the firm's market capitalization, calculated as V = p * s, where V is the value of market capitalization, p is the price of the firm's shares on the last day of the year, and s is the total number of shares outstanding at that time. For market capitalization at the time of IPO the authors used the end of the first trading day. These values were log-transformed.
time_window: IPO model: end of the first trading day; longitudinal models: last day of the year

description: The proportion of total executive compensation granted in long-term forms (e.g., stock options). The measure is the average stock-based compensation of the top management team, using the estimated value of the awards on the date of grant rather than the eventual pay-off received; for stock options the Black-Scholes valuation method was used.
time_window: IPO model: time of the IPO; longitudinal models: end of the prior year

description: The percentage of company stock owned by executive officers of the firm.
time_window: IPO model: time of the IPO; longitudinal models: end of the prior year

description: A separate measure of the stock ownership of outside directors, calculated the same as executive stock ownership but for outside directors only.
time_window: IPO model: time of the IPO; longitudinal models: end of the prior year

description: The percentage of firm stock owned by parties with at least a 5 percent stake in the company who were not officers or directors and who had no business ties to the firm.
time_window: IPO model: time of the IPO; longitudinal models: end of the prior year

description: The total percentage of company stock owned by institutional investors (e.g., pension funds, mutual funds).
time_window: IPO model: time of the IPO; longitudinal models: end of the prior year

description: The percentage of firm equity owned by venture capital firms on the date of the IPO, taken from the registration forms that list beneficial shareholders both before and after the proposed offering.
time_window: date of the IPO (measured before the offering)

description: The percentage of company stock sold by venture capitalists during the IPO process, taken from the registration forms that list beneficial shareholders both before and after the proposed offering.
Board structure assessed by the traditional measure of board outsiders and insiders: the percentage of board members who were outsiders not otherwise employed by the firm.
time_window: IPO model: time of the IPO; longitudinal models: end of the prior year

description: The number of years since the firm was founded.

Computed as the product of the experience vector and the activity vector representing the innovation input requirements. The experience vector contains one element for each of 1,613 technologies used in biotechnology; each time a scientist creates a new patent using a technological category, he or she accumulates one unit of experience in that domain. The vector of individual experience in a team is then multiplied by the activity vector constructed using the unique categories corresponding to the technology subclasses listed on the patent.
time_window: cumulative from 1970 prior to focal patent

description: Relationship-specific knowledge RKij is defined as the number of times a given pair of scientists listed on a patent have worked together on a patent in the past, not including the present patent. Team experience is computed by summing this variable across all possible pairs of scientists on the team and dividing by the number of possible pairs.
time_window: past collaborations prior to the focal patent

description: Corresponding to prior learning curve studies, experience is accumulated each time a given task is completed. Each time a firm develops a new patent, it is considered to have accumulated one unit of experience. Firm experience is computed as the cumulative experience accumulated prior to the application date of a focal patent.

variable_name: Innovative productivity (inverse of unit labor requirement)
description: The inverse of the unit labor requirement (1/ULR). The unit labor requirement is the time in scientist man-days spent to successfully realize a patent. For a scientist i, the time spent on a patent (t_i) is defined as the number of days between two successive patent applications; the text says that if n scientists are listed on a patent, innovative productivity is defined by a formula that is not readable in the provided text.

The measure was derived by attaching a value of +1 to a build strategy, 0 to a hold strategy, -1 to a harvest strategy, and -2 to a divest strategy, then using the percentage breakdown of the SBU's current total sales across strategy descriptions to arrive at a weighted average strategy index. All 58 subject SBUs fell somewhere along the continuum from pure build to pure harvest. Higher values indicate a more build-like strategy.
scale: weighted average index, observed range -1.00 to +1.00 in this sample

description: Each respondent indicated on a 5-point scale the years of total experience accumulated by him/her in the marketing/sales function. Responses were coded as less than one year (=0), 1 to 3 years (=2), 4 to 6 years (=5), 7 to 9 years (=8), and 10 years or more (=11). Higher values indicate greater marketing/sales experience.

Constructed from two choice-dilemma cases framed in the Kogan and Wallach format and involving SBU-level strategic decision making situations. Scoring was identical to Kogan and Wallach's except that reverse scoring was used in order to arrive at a measure in which higher values imply greater willingness to take risk. Responses to the two cases were averaged. The interitem reliability estimate was coefficient alpha = .57.

Four items from the 7-item instrument developed by Lorsch and Morse (1974) were used. For each statement, respondents indicated on a 4-point scale whether they definitely agreed (=1), were inclined to agree (=2), were inclined to disagree (=3), or definitely disagreed (=4). Items 1 and 2 were reverse scored, and a straight average of the responses to the four statements was used. The interitem reliability estimate was coefficient alpha = .57.
scale: 1 to 4 response scale; average of four items

description: Effectiveness data were collected on 12 performance dimensions. On each dimension, each respondent rated on a 5-point Likert type scale, ranging from 'not at all satisfactory' to 'outstanding,' the SBU's performance as compared with his/her assessment of superiors' expectations from the SBU on that dimension. Using the data on dimensional importance obtained in an earlier question as weights, a weighted average effectiveness index was obtained for each SBU.
scale: 5-point Likert type scale per dimension; weighted average index

description: The number of unique subclasses (obtained from IPC codes) associated with the firm's patents filed by or granted to the firm over the 3 years prior to the post-TRIPS focal year. Scope in year t is the average of the number of unique subclasses the firm patented in during years t, t-1 and t-2. The measures of knowledge scope and specialization are based on prior process patents.

A Herfindahl index (HHI) based on the square of the share of process patents filed in each subclass over the rolling 3-year periods, following Hall, Jaffe, and Trajtenberg (2001) and Hall (2005), with the adjustment those authors suggest for firms with few patents made in constructing the variable. A high value means the firm is unbalanced across its knowledge assets and focused on a narrower set of innovation routines, while a low value means knowledge is distributed more equally across different classes.

The ratio of product patents to the total number of patents applied for, or granted to, a particular firm in each year. Patents were classified manually from the Title, Abstract and Description of the application; a product patent is one that specifies a new formulation, a new chemical entity (NCE), composition, molecule or method of delivery.

The ratio of the number of process patents relating to newly off-patent drugs applied for, or granted to, a particular firm in that year; the dependent variables are proportions with the denominator being the total number of patents applied for by the firm in each year. A patent is classified as an expiring patent when one of the diseases for which key drug patents were expiring in the USA between 1999 and 2013 is listed in the Title, Abstract and Description of the application.

The ratio of the number of process patents, exclusive of those targeted to newly off-patent drugs, applied for or granted to the firm in that year, with the total number of patents applied for by the firm in each year as the denominator.
Percentage change in breadth (Scope) over a time period, calculated for the early period 1995-2004 and for the later period 2005-2013.
Percentage change in specialization over a time period, calculated for the early period 1995-2004 and for the later period 2005-2013.
Percentage change in the proportion of product patents during the time period, calculated for the early period 1995-2004 and for the later period 2005-2013.
Percentage change in newly off-patent drug process patents during the time period, calculated for the early period 1995-2004 and for the later period 2005-2013.
Percentage change in process patents during the time period, calculated for the early period 1995-2004 and for the later period 2005-2013.

The outcome variable is the percentage of the change in income between the start and end of the time period; the early period is 1995-2004 (Panel A) and the later period is 2005-2013 (Panel B). Income in years 1995 and 2005 is controlled for in the respective estimations.

A Herfindahl-type quantitative index of product diversity based on the share of a firm's sales in each industry group, similar to the diversification index used by Berry (1975). The authors present PDIV and MDIV as continuous, quantitative measures that can identify and measure differences in diversity both between firms and across time. The index formula is not readable in the text provided.

An index of multinational diversity measured as the proportion of a firm's revenue derived from operations outside the United Kingdom. It is one of the measures of corporate diversity used by the authors, and like PDIV it is a continuous, quantitative measure that can identify differences in diversity both between firms and across time. The index formula is not readable in the text provided.

Pre-tax return on net assets, the authors' primary measure of firm profitability. For the static analyses the value used was the average over the period 1972-84, which the authors say minimizes the effects of short-term and cyclical influences on profitability. Asset values are based on company accounts data at historic cost. Other accounting measures (total operating profits, return on equity, return on sales) were used only to test robustness.

variable_name: Change in return on net assets
description: Simple differences were used to measure changes in profitability: the change over the period was measured as the difference between the average for the first three years of the period (1972-74) and the average for the last three years (1982-84).

Cash flow from operations over the period, which the authors consider the best indicator of the availability of internally generated investment funds. They describe current profitability, measured in terms of cash flow, as promoting diversifying investment.

variable_name: Change in product diversity (change in PDIV)
description: Change in the index of product diversity over the period, measured as a simple difference between the average for the first three years (1972-74) and the average for the last three years (1982-84).

variable_name: Change in multinational diversity (change in MDIV)
description: Change in the index of multinational diversity over the period, measured as a simple difference between the average for the first three years (1972-74) and the average for the last three years (1982-84).

Firms were allocated to one of Rumelt's strategic categories, using the classification system he devised; firms were classified into eight categories of corporate strategy according to the extent of their product diversity and the relationships between their different activities. Classification required a major element of subjective judgment about the boundaries of business activities and whether two activities were related, and relatedness was defined in terms of market and technological similarities. The categories were entered into the regressions as dummy variables.

Corporate diversity was measured by two indices of the spread of a firm's activities: a Herfindahl-type index of product diversity (PDIV) based on the share of sales in each activity, and an index of multinational diversity (MDIV) equal to one minus the UK share of total sales. Firms were also placed in Rumelt's strategic categories as a categorical alternative.

An aggregate measure of CSR computed from seven dimensions of the KLD data: community relations, corporate governance, diversity, employee relations, the environment, human rights, and product quality. A net score for each dimension is derived by taking the difference between the total number of strengths and concerns. To allow comparability across dimensions, each dimension is standardized by deriving its z-score, and the z-scores are summed across all CSR dimensions to create an equally weighted index that captures the firm's net CSR activities.

A composite measure of CEO narcissistic tendencies using a set of unobtrusive indicators extracted from archival data (Chatterjee & Hambrick, 2007, 2011), built as a four-item index: the prominence of the CEO's photograph in annual reports, the CEO's prominence in the company's press releases, and the cash as well as the non-cash compensation of the CEO relative to those of the other top executives at the same company. The two-year moving average of each narcissism indicator is taken, excluding observations pertaining to the first year of the CEO's tenure to avoid issues related to succession. The measure is computed by taking the mean of each indicator after standardization.

A media-based measure of CEO hubris following Malmendier and Tate (2008). News articles that mentioned the CEOs in the sampled firms were collected from major news sources such as The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Business Week, The Economist, and The Financial Times. For each CEO, the number of terms that suggested confidence (e.g., confident, confidence, optimistic, or optimism) and the number of terms that implied conservatism (e.g., reliable, cautious, conservative, practical, frugal, steady, not confident, or not optimistic) were counted, including counts only if the terms appeared within 10 words before or after the CEO's name. The measure subtracts the count of conservatism terms from the count of confidence terms and scales the difference by the sum of the two counts for each CEO in each time period.

The number of interlocked peer firms having a higher CSR score than the focal firm. Interlocked firms are the firms in which a focal firm's CEO or directors held a board position in each firm-year, identified from the BoardEx database. For each interlocked firm, data on its CSR score were collected and compared with the CSR score of the focal firm.

The number of interlocked peer firms having a lower CSR score than the focal firm. Interlocked firms are the firms in which a focal firm's CEO or directors held a board position in each firm-year, identified from the BoardEx database. For each interlocked firm, data on its CSR score were collected and compared with the CSR score of the focal firm.

A continuous measure of the similarity of a song's features to those of other genres, constructed as an average of the estimates of two machine-learning algorithms developed in the music information retrieval field. The algorithms compare a song's key audio components, such as rhythm and pitch, to predefined audio samples and estimate the song's genre similarity score as a probabilistic value based on feature distance. The theoretical range of the measure is between zero and one: a zero value implies that a song's features strictly abide by genre conventions, and a value of one indicates that a song's features bear no resemblance to its designated genre. The sonic features are shaped by production decisions such as composition, arrangement, and mixing.

The interaction of the treated market group dummy, Country, which is set to one for songs designated in the country market, and the Post democratization dummy, which equals one if a song is released after the date of the chart methodology change (Oct. 11, 2012). This interaction is the main variable of interest and provides an estimate of the impact of Billboard's chart experiment on the country market, an average treatment effect on the treated group.

Design Scope is a dummy that takes the value of 0 for relationships characterized by low levels of design scope and 1 for those characterized by high levels of design scope. It was coded from a set of four questions submitted to interviewees: at what point in the design process the supplier had been involved, who had been responsible for the development of the design concept, who had been responsible for the engineering of the identified solutions, and to what extent the supplier could have introduced changes without affecting other parts of the project. The answers were used to assign each relationship to one of four interaction types, and preliminary reports with this coding were validated with project managers and purchasing managers, with disagreement in only four of the 50 cases.

Level of Task Interdependency is a dummy that takes the value of 0 for relationships characterized by low levels of task interdependency and 1 for those characterized by high levels of task interdependency. It was coded from the same set of four questions submitted to interviewees about the supplier's involvement in the design process, its responsibility for the design concept and for engineering the identified solutions, and the extent to which it could have introduced changes without affecting other parts of the project. Together with Design Scope it assigns each relationship to one of four groups: Traditional Subcontracting, Integrated Subcontracting, Advanced Subcontracting, and Black-Box Subcontracting.

For each relationship, the project manager filled out an evaluation questionnaire containing items on a five-point Likert scale; six items were used to obtain a judgment of the supplier's performance in terms of measures of its "efficiency" (i.e., schedule deadline, cost objectives, quality levels, etc.). For example, one item asked the project manager to rate from one (never) to five (always) whether the identified supplier achieved during the project the targeted quality levels. The average correlation coefficient among the six items was 0.62, the items loaded strongly and positively on the first principal component, and Cronbach's alpha was 0.91. To create the Efficiency indicator, for each observation all the responses to the six items were summed, each weighted by its corresponding component loading on the first eigenvalue.
scale: six five-point Likert items combined into a weighted-sum indicator

description: Two items were used to capture the "learning" outcome of the relationship. One item assessed whether a project manager felt that his organization had learned something new from the interactions with the supplier; the other asked to what extent solutions developed during the specific interaction were later used by the manufacturer in other projects. The correlation between the two items was 0.57, they loaded strongly on the second principal component, and Cronbach's alpha was 0.72. To create the Learning indicator, for each observation all the responses to the two items were summed, each weighted by its corresponding component loading on the second eigenvalue.
scale: two five-point Likert items combined into a weighted-sum indicator

description: Dummy variable that equals 1 when any of the firm owners with at least 20 percent of the ownership stake is a firm CEO, and 0 when a firm has a hired local CEO. The 20 percent threshold is the most conservative ownership threshold in the literature, and it is also the smallest share owned by any firm CEO in the dataset. Firms with foreign hired managers are excluded from the analysis.

The firm's cost-to-revenue ratio: the sum of cost of goods sold and other operating expenses divided by operating revenue. For the analysis the authors removed observations with zero revenue. It is the dependent variable in the baseline model and in the difference-in-difference-in-differences models.

Industry labor intensity is the average labor intensity of all firms from that industry across all years of observation; firm labor intensity is proxied by the number of employees per 1,000 rubles of assets. The authors use both a continuous measure and a dummy variable for the top five percent of labor-intensive industries (recycling, hotels, restaurants, government, and social services). Industry is determined by the first two digits of the OKVED code.

The natural logarithm of GDP per capita in the firm owner's country, used as a proxy for the expensiveness of that country's native labor. At the time of data collection reliable GDP per capita data were available up to 2007, which limits the observation window for this part of the analysis to 1997-2007. In the retail ban analysis, countries are divided at the mean GDP per capita.

affected is a dummy variable that equals 1 if a firm has main operations in one of the areas affected by the 2007 labor ban (retail of liquor and pharmaceutical products, and retail sales in markets and outside of stores); post2006 is a dummy variable that equals 1 for all years after 2006. To be conservative, firms with secondary activities in any of the industries subject to the labor ban are excluded, and firms founded after the change are excluded from the sample. The coefficient for the three-way interaction with the owner-manager dummy is expected to be positive.

Cash stock is measured by cash and short-term investments divided by total assets. Cash stock is used rather than yearly free cash flow because additions to cash reserves occur when managers accumulate free cash flow rather than spending it, and Jensen focused on the cumulative cash balance. The operationalized measure ranges from 0 to 1 because it is scaled by total assets.

Tobin's q is the market value of the firm divided by total assets. Market value is the sum of calendar-year end values of the firm's common stock (PRCC_C times CSHO), the market value of the firm's preferred stock, the book value of the firm's long-term debt, and the book value of the firm's short-term debt with a maturity less than one year.

Firm size is measured by the natural logarithm of the number of total employees. The number of employees is preferred to sales or total assets because total assets are already used to scale Tobin's q and using them again as a proxy for size may introduce a spurious statistical relation between Tobin's q and size.

The KOF index of economic globalization, which accounts for the multidimensional nature of globalization. It measures economic globalization using actual economic flows (trade, foreign direct investment, portfolio investment, and income payments to foreign nationals, each measured as a percentage of GDP) and the absence of restrictions (hidden import barriers, mean tariff rate, taxes on international trade, and capital account restrictions). The index runs from one to 100, with a higher number indicating a higher degree of globalization, and the data were obtained from the website of the Swiss Economic Institute. Like all explanatory variables, it was lagged by 15 months.

Credit to the private sector as a share of GDP, a conventional metric in studies of banking; a greater value suggests that more abundant capital was provided to the private sector by the financial sector through loans, trade credits, and other accounts receivable that establish a claim for repayment. The data were obtained from the World Bank. The variable was lagged by 15 months, and it is a reverse indicator of local credit market failure.

The religion polarization index of Montalvo and Reynal-Querol, computed from the proportion of people affiliated to each religion in a given country at time i; the formula as printed in the paper is not readable in this record. Two categories were used, Muslims and non-Muslims. The index ranges from 0 to 1 and reaches its maximum when the two factions are of equal size; the authors multiplied the index values by 100 for ease of interpretation, and used data from the World Religion Data set.

The prevalence of windows across all countries that are in the same region as the focal country: for each country, the authors counted the number of Islamic windows operating in the neighboring regions. Countries' regional neighbors were determined using the geographical subregion definitions of the United Nations' Statistical Division (e.g., Africa: East Africa, Middle Africa, Northern Africa, Southern Africa, Western Africa).

The ratio of the Muslim population to the country's total population, used as the moderating variable in the models. The authors note that Muslims were a minority in 25 of the 58 countries in the risk set and that the average proportion of Muslim inhabitants in the population was 60%.

The dependent variable is the emergence of an Islamic window in a country at a given time. The authors construct monthly spells and model the hazard probability, that is, the conditional probability an Islamic window emerges at time t in a country, given that it has not emerged in the prior period. The study population is all Islamic windows that existed between 1975 and 2017, tracked through entries, exits, and mergers; Islamic investment banks were excluded.

Two researchers independently classified whether a 4-digit industry was loosely or tightly linked with all other manufacturing industries (codes 2011-3999), based on descriptions and product listings in the SIC manual. Tightly linked industries shared at least two of common raw materials, common science, or common processing technologies; loosely linked industries shared one; industries sharing none were manufacturing-unrelated. All forms of vertical integration were eliminated from the classifications, as were many 'not elsewhere classified' industries. Independent classifications reached 99.4 percent agreement, and disagreements were resolved through discussion.
scale: categorical: tightly linked, loosely linked, manufacturing-unrelated

description: ROS is operating-level return on sales for combined pairs of business units that were loosely or tightly linked. Within a firm portfolio each BU was compared to every other BU using both the primary and secondary SIC code; if two BUs showed linked SICs, their operating profit and sales were combined to calculate a weighted measure of ROS. ROS was the average for the combined units during 1986-92, and 1989 was selected as the basis for determining linkages across business units. Combined units with fewer than three years of data were excluded.

variable_name: performance category (high performers vs. low performers)
description: Firms that showed performance significantly higher (p < 0.05) than their industry mean were placed in the high-performing group (n = 15). Firms that showed performance significantly lower than their industry mean were placed in the low-performing group (n = 16).
scale: binary category: high performer, low performer

description: Evidence of managerial intent to create synergy was coded from public documents and, for participating firms, structured interviews. Firms were classified as '+', '0' or '-' on the dimension: '+' indicates evidence in the public documents that synergy was valued and encouraged, '0' indicates insufficient evidence to make a classification, and '-' indicates evidence that the firm did not believe in synergy creation. Interval scaling was not attempted because the data were too subjective to force further accuracy. When a firm had been assigned '0', the interview response was used to adjust the score to '+' or '-'.

Evidence of actual resource and activity sharing was coded from public documents and, for participating firms, structured interviews. Firms were classified as '+', '0' or '-' on the dimension: '+' indicates evidence of existing shared resources and activities, '0' indicates insufficient evidence to make a classification, and '-' indicates evidence that the firm clearly did not share resources. Interval scaling was not attempted because the data were too subjective to force further accuracy.

Evidence of use of administrative mechanisms to coordinate between business units was coded from public documents and, for participating firms, structured interviews, using the same '+', '0' or '-' scheme. Examples of the mechanisms observed were technology review committees, task forces, and combined strategic planning processes. Interval scaling was not attempted because the data were too subjective to force further accuracy.

A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if the home is located in the same ward or stake as the listing agent's home address, and 0 otherwise. Ward is the weekly congregation and stake is the larger unit in which wards are nested; boundaries are geographically assigned by church leaders without meaningful influence from members.
The log of the list price of the home listed by the agent; this is the dependent variable in the transaction value models. Control variables are measured using data from the initial listing.

variable_name: Log(number of homes listed for affiliates to date)
description: The log of the number of homes listed for affiliates to date. In the reputation models the unit is the agent/listing and the sample is limited to nonaffiliate transactions during the first 3 years an agent has listed homes; in the entrepreneurship hazard models the untransformed number of homes listed for affiliates to date is used.
time_window: to date; first 3 years for the reputation models

variable_name: Log(number of homes listed for nonaffiliates to date)
description: The log of the number of homes listed for nonaffiliates to date. Used alongside the affiliated-listing measure in the reputation models on the subsample of nonaffiliate transactions in the first 3 years, and as an untransformed count in the entrepreneurship hazard models.
time_window: to date; first 3 years for the reputation models

variable_name: Log(list price) of subsequent nonaffiliate listings
description: The log list price of the agent's nonaffiliated listings, used as the indicator of reputation for ability with nonaffiliates: a high average transaction value indicates that a professional is capable of providing work of sufficient quality to justify the cost, and a history of valuable transactions is associated with valuable current nonaffiliate transactions via the reputation signals it provides.
time_window: first 3 years of the agent's career

description: A dummy variable identifying whether the agent works for a major franchise brokerage such as RE/MAX, Coldwell Banker, or Prudential, which the authors treat as high-reputation firms and contrast with nonfranchise, low-reputation brokerages. In the reputation models the variables of interest are interacted with this dummy.

The hazard that an agent becomes a real estate broker, where entrepreneurship is defined as an agent starting a new brokerage that only employs one agent (themselves). The failure variable is set to 1 if the agent has opened a new brokerage before the focal listing and the time variable is the number of days since the agent's first listing; estimates come from Cox proportional hazard models.
time_window: days since the agent's first listing

description: Indicator for firm-year observations in the shooting range. The range is not imposed arbitrarily: the authors estimate abnormal revenue growth for firms in a moving range with a width of $15 million and select the range with the most positive abnormal rate of revenue growth. The primary approach bases the range on the predicted value of revenue in the next year from the firm's current-year revenue and average revenue growth rate over the last three years, which peaks at a range of $82 million to $97 million; the alternative approach based on current-year revenue peaks at $86 million to $101 million.

The firm's revenue growth rate from year t to year t+1, the dependent variable in Equation (4). The text reports the sample mean revenue growth rate as 20.4% and the standard deviation as 28%. The exact functional form of the equation as printed in the article is not available in the text provided.

The number of domestic acquisitions the firm makes, obtained from the SDC Platinum database for 1983 to 2014, examined in years t−1, t, and t+1 relative to the shooting range year. In the text, Table 4 is described as reporting OLS estimations of a variant of Equation (4) with acquisitions as the dependent variable.
The number of employees scaled by revenue, examined in years t−1, t, and t+1 relative to the shooting range year to capture hiring as a means of accelerating revenue growth.

The dollar amount of leasing scaled by revenue, examined in years t−1, t, and t+1 relative to the shooting range year, capturing leasing of assets as a means of increasing available productive assets.

The number of analysts covering the firm, obtained from the Thomson Reuters Institutional Holdings Database for 1976 to 2014. Because analyst coverage fluctuates within years, the maximum during each year is used. The variable is examined in years t−1, t, and t+1 around crossing the $100 million revenue threshold.

The number of newspaper articles that mention the company's name each year, obtained from LexisNexis; because Compustat abbreviates company names and automated searches generate excessive null results, the searches were conducted by manually entering names. The searches are restricted to three years before and after a firm crosses the $100 million revenue threshold, yielding 15,505 firm-year observations for 2,214 firms. Media coverage exhibits extreme right skewness and is winsorized at its 97th percentile.
time_window: three years before and after the crossing year; years t−1, t, and t+1

description: The percentage ownership of the firm's outstanding shares by institutional investors, obtained from the Thomson Reuters Institutional Holdings Database for 1980 to 2014. Because institutional ownership fluctuates within years, the maximum during each year is used. The variable is examined in years t−1, t, and t+1 around crossing the $100 million revenue threshold.

The number of institutional investors in the firm in year t+1, used to show that an influx of new investors attracted by increased visibility, rather than increased investment by existing investors, drives the increase in institutional ownership.
The number of block investors who hold more than 5% of the firm's outstanding shares in year t+1, used as a contrast in which no increase is expected.

Dichotomous variable for the pathway in which the salesperson entered the current sales position (0 = external, 1 = internal). An internal hire into sales is a job transition from any nonsales job within or across stores, and the authors are agnostic as to whether such switches are lateral transfers or vertical promotions. External hires include only new workers; rehires are omitted. Of these salespeople, 50,149 are internal hires (44,637 job switches within stores, 2,330 store switches within jobs, and 3,182 simultaneous switches of both) and 58,914 are external hires.

Dichotomous variable for the pathway in which the manager entered the current position (0 = external, 1 = internal), defined as for salespeople. Of these managers, 8,094 are internal hires (3,316 job switches within stores, 2,550 store switches within jobs, and 2,228 simultaneous switches of both) and 4,442 are external hires.

The chief performance measure in a given month is the logarithm of the salesperson's average sales per hour (SPH) divided by the SPH target in that month, winsorized at 1%. The company calibrates sales targets to the store, job, shift, day, and the worker's job tenure and does not adjust targets by internal hire status. Taking the logarithm yields a measure with mean zero and standard deviation 0.515.

The chief performance measure is the monthly profit (earnings before interest, taxation, depreciation, and amortization, or EBITDA margin) of the department the manager supervises, where the EBITDA margin divides those earnings by total revenues. Each department's margins are standardized so that they are mean zero with standard deviation one, so the dependent variable is essentially its z-score.
scale: standardized z-score (mean zero, standard deviation one)

description: Consecutive months of employment in sales jobs within the same store; tenure is not reset if workers change from one commissioned sales role to another. The models use the logarithm of job tenure. For the purpose of setting SPH targets, job tenure begins when a salesperson enters their first sales job and not at the point of internal hire.

Consecutive months of employment in manager jobs within the same store; tenure is not reset when a manager moves from managing one department to another. The models use the logarithm of job tenure. Department performance targets are tied to the position rather than the person and do not increase with the manager's job tenure.

Job exit for salespeople, modelled with a Cox proportional hazards model for turnover and promotions as competing outcomes, using salesperson-months as the unit of analysis and standard errors clustered by individual. Among salespeople, the mean annualized turnover rate is 0.403 (0.335 for quits, 0.068 for terminations).

Job exit for department managers, modelled with a Cox proportional hazards model for turnover and promotions as competing outcomes, using manager-years as the unit of analysis with district-year fixed effects. For department managers, the annualized turnover rate is 0.236 (0.195 for quits, 0.041 for terminations).

A move to department manager in a given month, modelled as a competing risk with turnover in the Cox proportional hazards model at the salesperson-month level. The promotion rate for salespeople is 0.004.

A move to either head store manager or district manager in a given fiscal year, modelled as a competing risk with turnover at the manager-year level. Promotion to trainee store manager is the precursor to a subsequent promotion to head store manager; the promotion rate for department managers is 0.026.
