Annual subjective ratings of a manager's prospects for future career advancement and promotion, explicitly forward looking, initially determined by the store manager and then potentially adjusted and approved by a committee that includes other head store managers in the district. To ensure anonymity the ordinal ratings are transformed onto a 100-point scale by dividing the rating by the scale's maximum and multiplying by 100, yielding evaluations for 38,651 manager-years.

The funding ratio of campaign i at time t (Funding i,t / Fundraising Goal i), minus 1. The measure is 0 when the goal has been reached and equals the funding ratio minus 1 when the goal has not been reached.

Measured in two steps. First, Euclidean distances between all campaign observations at a specific point in time are calculated on game genre, fundraising goal, and time remaining (as a percentage), each normalized to a 0-1 scale and weighted equally; the peer with the lowest distance score is selected. Second, the difference between the focal entrepreneur's campaign funding ratio and that peer's funding ratio is calculated. The measure is 0 when the focal campaign's funding ratio is at or above the peer's; when below, it equals the funding-ratio difference.
The number of days for which the campaign had been active divided by the total number of days of the campaign.

Coded extent of substantive change in the product offering between two subsequent observations of a given campaign. A codebook with conceptual definitions and empirical illustrations for each level of the extent of change was developed; 0 represents no change and 5 represents major changes. Each of the 6,758 observations was independently coded by two coders, and inconsistent ratings were resolved by discussion.

Content analysis of board meeting transcripts using a final list of words and phrases, focus questions, and guiding definitions of monitoring-related behaviors. Coders identified indicator words and phrases, judged whether surrounding sentences were relevant to monitoring, and measured the duration in minutes each board spent discussing monitoring topics; at least two coders coded each firm-year and differences were negotiated. The variable is the time spent discussing monitoring-related issues over the total meeting time for all meetings in a year, with both numerator and denominator coded as minutes, expressed as a percentage of yearly meeting time.
time_window: all meetings in a fiscal year

description: Deviation from prior performance is current performance compared with the average of the prior two years' performance. A spline function splits the single continuous deviation variable at the theoretically determined knot (the status quo) so that one variable models the relationship below the knot and the other above it; this variable captures the below-the-knot, negative side. Firm performance was measured with both return on equity and return on assets, analyzed in separate models.
time_window: current year relative to the average of the prior two years

description: Deviation from prior performance is current performance compared with the average of the prior two years' performance. A spline function splits the single continuous deviation variable at the theoretically determined knot (the status quo) so that this variable models the relationship above the knot, the positive side. Firm performance was measured with both return on equity and return on assets, analyzed in separate models.
time_window: current year relative to the average of the prior two years

description: A dummy variable used to code duality, with duality = 1 when the CEO also serves as chairperson of the board. These data, together with several control variables, were collected through publicly available corporate filings.

variable_name: Institutional Investor All-America Research Team rank (rank t + 1)
description: Analyst performance is measured as the analyst's rank in the Institutional Investor All-America Research Team poll in year t + 1. In each sector there are five levels of the dependent variable (categorical): the first, second, third, and runner-up ranks, and unranked. Respondents assign a single overall numerical score to each analyst in each industry sector, and votes are weighted based on the size of the voting institution.
scale: five ordered categories: first, second, third, runner-up, unranked
time_window: t + 1 (models also use t + 2 through t + 5)

description: Mover status is not a single variable; it is captured by the two dichotomous hiring-role variables (hired for exploitation and hired for exploration), each of which is 1 for an analyst-year in which a ranked analyst moved to a competitor's research department in that role. Star analysts who did not move ('stayers') form the omitted comparison group. Affiliations in the year subsequent to being ranked and the dates of moves were identified from Nelson's Directory of Investment Research, Lexis-Nexis, and Dow Jones News Service.

Dichotomous variable equal to 1 if the analyst was hired to begin coverage of a new sector not previously covered by the firm, 0 otherwise. Identification of whether analysts were hired for exploration came from a study of news releases at the time of hirings of ranked analysts and from Nelson's Investment Research Database.

Dichotomous variable equal to 1 if the analyst was hired to work in a sector already covered by the firm, 0 otherwise. Identification came from a study of news releases at the time of hirings of ranked analysts and from Nelson's Investment Research Database.

Moving with coworkers was tested with four dichotomous variables: hired solo for exploitation, hired as a team for exploitation, hired solo for exploration, and hired as a team for exploration. Each is 1 when the analyst switches to another sell-side research department, in that hiring role, either solo or together with a team of colleagues, and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: announcement of a star analyst's hiring
description: The event-study data set consists of 228 observations of analysts joining publicly quoted firms, excluding subsidiaries of larger diversified firms that generated less than 50% of those companies' revenues. Observations for analysts joining firms with confounding announcements in the event window and observations that overlapped in time and involved identical companies were deleted, leaving 101 announcements. The unexpected news of a star analyst's hiring is the event whose stock-market reaction is measured.

Daily excess returns around the announcement of a star analyst's hiring, cumulated over the event period of -1 to +1 days (the announcement date plus one day prior to and after the announcement date). Returns data were provided by the Center for Research in Security Prices. Abnormal returns are reported separately for hirings for exploitation and for exploration, and for solo versus team entries.

Announcements of hirings in which the star analyst was hired to establish brand new coverage of a sector, i.e., hired to explore. These hirings are separated from hirings to exploit in the event-study analysis.

Announcements of hirings in which the ranked analyst was hired into a sector already covered by the firm, i.e., hired to exploit. These hirings are separated from hirings to explore in the event-study analysis.

Abnormal returns are subdivided into four categories as hirings for either exploitation or exploration with solo or team entries by star analysts: hired solo for exploitation, hired as a team for exploitation, hired solo for exploration, and hired as a team for exploration.

Scale for the existence of a formal strategic planning process in the plant that aligns the manufacturing strategy with the business strategy by translating the business strategy into manufacturing terms. The authors define a formal strategic planning process as a necessary but not sufficient component of the manufacturing strategy process, since it is possible to do formal strategic planning without full implementation. This scale was answered primarily by the plant manager and chief superintendent, and plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale for communication of the manufacturing strategy throughout the plant so that it can guide decision making by plant personnel, since successful implementation is thought to be contingent upon the judgments of multiple decision makers. Other managers besides the plant manager and chief superintendent were included because the scale deals with the manufacturing strategy process for the whole plant. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale for the extent to which the manufacturing strategy focuses attention into the future, to anticipate the firm's needs and acquire manufacturing capabilities in advance of those needs. The business strategy is expected to provide general guidelines that allow manufacturing strategists to develop long-term goals in terms of plant capabilities. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale for the degree to which the manufacturing strategy is viewed as integral to reaching performance goals and providing competitive strength, so that plant decision makers recognize its existence and its use in focusing plant operations and monitoring performance. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale corresponding to Stage 3 of Hayes and Wheelwright's stages in the evolution of manufacturing's strategic role, in which manufacturing provides credible support to the business strategy and the business strategy is translated into manufacturing terms. Stage 3 plants are pursuing a manufacturing strategy in which manufacturing capabilities are crucial to achieving the organization's strategic goals. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale corresponding to Stage 4 of Hayes and Wheelwright's stages, in which the organization pursues a manufacturing-based competitive advantage and the business strategy is built on manufacturing capability. Stage 4 plants are pursuing a manufacturing strategy in which manufacturing capabilities are crucial to achieving the organization's strategic goals. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale, patterned after Georgopoulos and Mann (1962), measuring whether people and departments within the plant work together and coordinate their efforts. It is one of four scales used to assess the degree to which individuals perceive that practices representing individualism or collectivism are present in the plant. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale (Taylor and Bowers 1972) assessing whether supervisors encourage teamwork and exchange of information within groups. It is one of four scales used to assess perceived individualism or collectivism in the plant. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale measuring whether teamwork and group level results are rewarded, as one of four collectivism scales. Factor analysis indicated that the scale appears to capture an emphasis on rewards for teamwork as a separate factor rather than an overall emphasis on group versus individual rewards, but it was retained in the analysis because of its acceptable level of internal consistency. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.
Scale assessing whether teams are used for problem solving in the plant, one of the four collectivism scales. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale assessing whether managers and manufacturing engineers are present on the shop floor; more contact between plant management, technical professionals, line workers, and supervisors is expected to reflect a lower level of power distance. It is one of three power distance scales, and in the plant-level factor analysis it loaded on a second factor consisting primarily of the shop floor contact items. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale (Aiken and Hage 1966) measuring whether people perceive that they have the authority to make independent decisions; less centralization of authority, representing decentralization within the plant, represents a lower level of power distance. In the plant-level factor analysis it loaded strongly on the authoritarian factor of power distance together with the Hierarchical Index. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale that asked for objective information, assessing whether management and labor are distinguished by practices such as use of time clocks and uniforms; more egalitarian practices are expected to reflect less power distance. Because it asked for objective information it was assigned to two managers per plant rather than to all respondents. It loaded strongly on the authoritarian power distance factor at the plant level.

Scale (Mowday and Steers 1981) measuring whether people perceive their values to be similar to the organization's, whether they appreciate working for the organization, and whether they feel pride in the organization. A level of loyalty is indicative of a high level of shared values. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

Scale (Price and Mueller 1986) measuring the degree to which individuals believe that there is a recognizable set of beliefs embodying organizational wisdom present in the plant. A strong organizational philosophy signifies the presence of a distinctive homogeneous culture, or cultural congruency, although the scale does not indicate what the content of the plant's values and practices is. Plant scores are the mean of the respondents' scores.

variable_name: Organizational culture scales (collectivism, power distance, cultural congruency)
description: Organizational culture is represented by nine plant-level survey scales on three dimensions that distinguish hierarchical from clan cultures: four individualism/collectivism scales (Coordination of Decision Making, Supervisors as Team Leaders, Rewards for Group Performance, Small Group Problem Solving), three power distance scales (Shop Floor Contact, Centralization of Authority, Hierarchical Index) and two cultural congruency scales (Loyalty, Philosophy). Respondent scores were averaged to plant scores and the set of culture scales was related to the set of manufacturing strategy scales by canonical correlation. The individual scales are recorded separately under c_collectivism, c_power_distance and c_cultural_congruency.

The log of the miles between coordinates for the zip codes of the acquirer and target firm headquarters. The distance between two points is computed from their latitude and longitude, with a constant that converts the result to miles on the surface of the earth. Numerous typological errors and missing data in the zip code and city information within the SDC database were corrected manually by referring to individual company websites, directories, and the U.S. Census Bureau website.

A 0-1 dummy variable that indicates whether any dyad of two firms announced a deal in a given year; 1 denotes a target that was acquired and 0 denotes potential targets that were not acquired. Potential targets are firms that operate primarily in the same industry as the target that was eventually acquired and that are acquisition-worthy, identified by limiting potential targets to firms that were eventually acquired by chemical manufacturing firms during a five-year window around the focal acquisition. The endogenously stratified sample matches each acquisition that occurred with five other randomly drawn potential acquisitions that could have occurred but did not.
time_window: five-year window around the focal acquisition for identifying potential targets

description: A 0-1 variable indicating relatedness. In the first definition, this variable was 1 when the target operated in the same four-digit NAICS code and 0 when the target operated in a different four-digit NAICS segment. The broader definition, used in the reported results, also codes an acquisition as related if the acquirer had a prior acquisition in the focal target firm's industry, even if the target was in a different four-digit segment from the primary NAICS code of the acquirer.

A cumulative measure of the distance from prior acquisitions, which distinguishes distant from proximate acquisitions without making an arbitrary distinction—such as state boundaries—between 'distant' and 'close' acquisitions. The variable is interacted with acquisition distance to test H3A.

A 0-1 dummy variable that is 1 when the acquirer had previously acquired in the same state (other than the firm's headquarters state) as the focal acquisition. The variable is interacted with acquisition distance to test H3B.

A dummy variable indicating whether the acquirer is a parent with multiple subsidiaries. Among the 767 acquirers, 132 (17%) were parent firms with subsidiaries. The variable is interacted with acquisition distance to test H3C.

A dummy variable indicating whether the acquirer is a subsidiary itself. Among the 767 acquirers, 125 (16%) were subsidiaries themselves. The variable is interacted with acquisition distance to test H3C.

Density was measured as the total number of organizations in an environment. Following Barnett and Carroll (1987), who noted the need to control for potentially spurious effects of demand variables when measuring density, the authors divided firm density by state population, so density is the number of brewers per capita operating in each state for every year of the study. The information was available from Breweries Authorized to Operate, a report of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms.

To measure concentration, the authors used the four-firm concentration ratio for each state for each year of the study. This ratio represents the proportion of sales (volume) of the leading four firms in each state. The information was available from Keithahn and the Beer Institute.
Demand was measured at the state level as the total consumption of beer for each state in each year. This information was available for all years of the study from the Beer Institute.

Pricing regulation was examined in terms of price-posting laws, which regulate the length of price promotions and typically require a price promotion to remain in effect for three to six months. Since detailed information about the specific form of each regulation was not available, states could only be classified as to whether or not any form of price regulation existed for each year. States were coded as 1 in each year that price-posting laws were in effect and a 0 otherwise. The information was available from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms.

Taxation was measured as the proportion of the per barrel price of beer that consisted of state and federal excise taxes. This information was available from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms.

variable_name: change in the sales volume of national brewers
description: The dependent variable was the change in the total sizes of each of the three populations of brewers, measured as sales volume, by state for each year of the study. Total sales for all national, regional, and local brewers operating in each state were available from Keithahn and the Beer Institute.

variable_name: change in the sales volume of regional brewers
description: The dependent variable was the change in the total sizes of each of the three populations of brewers, measured as sales volume, by state for each year of the study. Total sales for all national, regional, and local brewers operating in each state were available from Keithahn and the Beer Institute.

variable_name: change in the sales volume of local brewers
description: The dependent variable was the change in the total sizes of each of the three populations of brewers, measured as sales volume, by state for each year of the study. Total sales for all national, regional, and local brewers operating in each state were available from Keithahn and the Beer Institute.

Binary variable set to 1 if there are multiple R&D groups reporting to separate heads within the top management team covering different pharmaceutical domains or to leads of business units, and 0 if the firm has a single integrated pharmaceutical R&D group. It is built in four steps from top management team data in company 10-K/20-F/DEF 14A SEC filings and annual reports, with roles coded using an established categorization, then validated against organizational descriptions in company filings and press releases and through interviews with managers from 28 of the 49 firms. 12.3% of the sample firm-years have R&D Decentralization = 1, with 18 out of the 49 firms changing their R&D structure at least once during the study period.

Established measure of patent originality, capturing the breadth of knowledge from which patents draw, built from the International Patent Classification (IPC) 4-digit technical categories of the citations made by a focal patent. Patents assigned in NACE2 category 21 (manufacture of basic pharmaceutical products) are used. The maximum originality patent in a patent family is assigned as the originality for that family, and these values are used to estimate an average originality per patent family for each firm-year. The larger the value, the more original a patent is, as it draws from a broader array of technologies.
scale: bounded between 0 and 1; observed range 0 to 0.936

description: The number of patent families in category (NACE2) 21 filed by firms annually is counted. Patent family counts are used to avoid double counting of patents filed in multiple jurisdictions, and the year in which a patent family is developed is defined as the earliest filing date of a patent in that family.

Measures the proportion of drug candidates in a firm's pre-clinical portfolio moving into Phase 1 per year. A panel dataset by drug-candidate year is developed from the Pharmaprojects clinical trials database in which parent firms are assigned to each drug candidate and the clinical phase a drug has reached at the end of the relevant year is captured; assigning candidates to parent firms uses the Pharmaprojects 'Overview' section and the Recap database. The initial risk set of drug candidates that can progress into development are those in pre-clinical trials, and drug candidates inactive for a period greater than 3 years are assumed to have been dropped by the focal firm and no longer contribute to the portfolio.
scale: proportion, spanning the full possible range of 0 to 1

description: Measures the proportion of a firm's preclinical development portfolio that are new chemical entities (NCE), which include no chemical component that has been previously approved by the FDA. The higher the value of Proportion NCE the greater the proportion of novel inventions in a firm's portfolio.

variable_name: Minority status (minority functional background, minority industry background, minority educational affiliation, minority degree type, minority race, minority gender)
description: Separate dichotomous measures of minority status were developed for five demographic characteristics and coded as 1 if less than 50 percent of the board members had the same characteristic as the focal director. For functional background, backgrounds were consolidated into output, throughput, and peripheral functions, and each director's primary functional area was the area in which he or she had the most experience. Industry minority status was coded as 1 if the focal director did not have prior management experience at another firm in the same industry while more than 50 percent of the other board members did. Educational background yielded two measures: minority degree type, coded as 1 if the director had an advanced management degree while more than 50 percent of the other board members did not, or vice versa, and minority educational affiliation, coded as 1 if the director had an Ivy League degree while more than 50 percent of the other board members did not, or vice versa. Dichotomous variables indicated minority status with respect to race and gender.

A multi-item director-influence scale assessed the degree to which directors feel they contribute to board discussions on strategic issues and their overall perceived influence on strategic decision making by the board, including the item 'To what extent do you influence strategic decision making?' Items used multiple response formats and were spread throughout the survey, and pretest interviews indicated that directors consistently interpreted them as referring to influence on corporate strategy. Cronbach's alpha for the scale was .89, and factor analysis using the iterated principal factors method yielded one common factor with all items loading as expected, so factor scores were estimated using the Bartlett method.

The measure aggregates, across all boards on which the director served as an outside director and across the demographic characteristics, the number of years the director had minority status on another board. Six indicators, one for each demographic characteristic, were added together into a single composite indicator, where higher values indicate more experience as an outside board member in a minority position. The composite was centered before the interaction terms were created.

An analogous composite measure of the focal director's prior experience in a majority role on other boards, parallel to the measure of prior minority-role experience. The variable was centered before the interaction terms were created.

Other majority directors' prior experience in a minority role, measured with the composite minority-experience measure and averaged across the majority directors on the focal board. The variable was centered before the interaction terms were created.
level: individual director; averaged across majority directors

description: The number of other boards in the larger sample frame on which the focal director and another, majority director both held an appointment. The number of shared appointments was calculated separately for each focal director/majority director dyad and then averaged across majority directors. The variable was centered before the interaction terms were created.

The number of ties between the focal director and each of the other majority directors such that the focal director sits on another board with a third director who also sits on a different board with that majority director, averaged across majority directors. The variable was centered before the interaction terms were created.

Following prior research, the authors measure lobbying in terms of whether lobbying for recall and/or recall-related safety issues was documented in the quarterly lobbying report on behalf of the manufacturer; they manually reviewed each lobbying report. Lobbying is reported under labels and keywords such as 'vehicle safety,' 'consumer product safety,' 'discussions with the NHTSA regarding automotive safety recall,' 'education and communication related to vehicle recall,' 'safety recalls/voluntary agreements,' and 'automotive safety issues.' Reports that mention whether the firm lobbied the NHTSA, the governing agency for recalls, are also included. Because issue codes such as 'Consumer Issues/Safety/Protection' also cover other matters, lobbying is measured in terms of whether recall and recall-related safety lobbying was reported, together with the NHTSA as the target agency.

Using Factiva, the authors identify for each manufacturer all unique US news articles classified by Factiva under the category 'Product Recalls' and download their text. Each article is scored with the LIWC program on the percentage of negative words; following Bae and Lee (2012), the sentiment score of an article is the percentage of positive words divided by that of negative words, and an article is classified as positive if the positive-negative ratio is larger than 1, otherwise negative. They aggregate the number of negative articles for the period of a month after each recall and take the natural log of the value to account for skewness. A random sample of high-negative-sentiment articles was manually examined to confirm the negative sentiment was directed at the focal company.

The authors download from Factiva all unique news articles published for the sample firms during the sample period containing the keywords 'lobby,' 'lobbying,' 'lobbies,' or 'lobbied,' and identify those that discuss firms' recalls as well as their lobbying. The text of each article is scored on negative sentiment using LIWC, and the authors compute an aggregate measure reflecting the amount of negative media coverage of recall-related lobbying in each period (a month after each recall). The measure is logged to account for skewness.

A dummy variable equal to 1 if the year is greater than or equal to 1996 and the company is incorporated in Delaware, and 0 otherwise. It measures the effect of the Delaware takeover regime shift on the treatment group relative to the control group. Historical state of incorporation was obtained from the IRRC database.

The share of backward self-citations made, calculated by counting all citations made in a firm's new patents in a certain year that cited the firm's own previous patents and dividing this number by the total number of citations made in all of the firm's new patents in that year. This share is multiplied by a weight, the extent to which the backward self-cited patents are subsequently cited by the focal firm (the fraction of total forward citations of these self-cited patents generated by the focal firm rather than by other firms). For the empirical analyses the share-based measure is further scaled by multiplying by 100.
time_window: focal year (citations made in that year, with forward citations observed subsequently)

description: The number of prior self-citations made, adjusted by the number of employees, multiplied by the same weight capturing the extent to which the backward self-cited patents are subsequently cited by the focal firm. A logarithm transformation of the count measure was performed because of its apparent skewness.
time_window: focal year (citations made in that year, with forward citations observed subsequently)

description: The fraction number (in percentage) of shareholding by all officers and directors. The information was collected from Compact Disclosure, which contains corporate governance data extracted from annual reports, 10Ks, and proxy statements.
The number of years for which a CEO has joined the firm, taken from the Execucomp database.

The value of stock options that were granted to the CEO during a firm's fiscal year. The variable was derived from the S&P ExecuComp database. The value of a stock option is determined using the standard Black and Scholes option valuation equation, one of the two alternatives approved by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to evaluate stock options; the authors made this choice because the Black and Scholes method is the most commonly used. The independent variables are lagged relative to the dependent variable.

variable_name: outside directors' stock option compensation (directors' options)
description: Determined by multiplying the number of stock options granted to an outside director during a firm's fiscal year by the average value of a firm's stock options granted to the company's executives during that fiscal year. The value of a stock option is determined using the standard Black and Scholes option valuation equation. Executable and unexecutable stock options were aggregated rather than studied separately. The independent variables are lagged relative to the dependent variable.

The ratio of a firm's book value of common equity to its market value, calculated on a yearly level at the end of each fiscal year. The authors chose it as their main measure of firm-level risk after reviewing a wide variety of risk measures used in prior research. They note that book equity to market equity has been shown to be a strong proxy for sensitivity to risk factors in returns and that its use has been proposed in finance research instead of beta. Higher values are treated by the authors as reflecting higher risk taking.

The number of new bridges built in a CBSA in a year, transformed with the inverse hyperbolic sine (IHS) to account for the declining marginal impact of higher numbers of new bridges built in the same year. The IHS is well defined at zero and does not require fudge factors such as are needed in log transformations. The independent and control variables are lagged one year.

A count of new startups founded in a CBSA in a year, where startups are defined as firms that received any angel or VC investment. Founding data were gathered from the Thomson Reuters VentureExpert or SDC Platinum data set, with the last data pull in 2014.

The total number of startup founders in a CBSA in a year, calculated using Crunchbase founder data for startups and aggregating unique founders by CBSA-year. This total was normalized by the existing number of startups in the CBSA to arrive at a founder entry rate.

The average number of early investors in the founded startups until the first round or earlier. Angels and other individuals comprise the majority; it also includes some smaller seed/early VC funds, which are included in calculating the average.

Textual descriptions of startups in Crunchbase were mined for words indicating recombination, including 'combining,' 'bridging,' 'spanning,' 'straddling,' 'fusion,' 'crossing,' and 'blending,' along with grammatical variants. A startup was identified as recombinative if it had one or more of these words in its description, and the average incidence of such recombinative startups in a CBSA-year cohort of startups was calculated. Startups in architecture, construction, general contracting, and real estate were excluded.
The average number of industry categories spanned by startups in a CBSA-year, based on Crunchbase classifications.

Difference in the value of the monthly biotechnology index for the target's subfield since initiation of the equity partnership. Four stock indices, one for each of the four subfields, were created from weekly returns of nine publicly traded, U.S. biotechnology firms specializing in the respective subfields. Each index ranges from April 1984 to December 1999; because of data limitations, any dates prior to 1984 were assigned the index value at its earliest point.
time_window: since initiation of the equity partnership; indices April 1984-December 1999

description: Difference in the number of public offerings since the initiation of the equity partnership, used as a proxy for the ability to attract capital from public markets. The authors argue this measure is appropriate in biotechnology, where burn ratios are high and raising capital to fund growth opportunities is a constant undertaking, so firms with larger growth opportunities should be able to raise more funds. The data came from S&P NetAdvantage.
time_window: since initiation of the equity partnership

description: 26-week standard deviation of weekly returns for each of the four biotechnology subfield indices, chosen because it provides enough history to produce a reliable measure of volatility without assuming constant variance over a longer period. Exogenous uncertainty was converted to a monthly measure by averaging the weekly standard deviations within any given month.
time_window: 26-week rolling window, averaged to a monthly measure

description: Log of the number of established firms with equity partnerships outstanding in the target firm in the previous month. The logarithmic transformation reflects the authors' belief in a declining marginal impact of competitive bidding with each additional partner. Higher values indicate a less proprietary (more shared) buyout option.

Total number of firms having stated their involvement in any of Bioscan's 123 biotechnology product areas. The variable is time-varying on an annual basis throughout the time horizon of the study. Higher values indicate a less unique growth option and a greater threat of technological preemption by rivals.

variable_name: hazard rate of acquiring a majority stake
description: Coded '1' when there were purchases that raised the ownership level to at least 50 percent of the biotechnology partner. The hazard rate is defined as the discrete probability of an event between t and (t + Delta t), conditional on the history of the process up to time t. Observations still in effect at the end of 1999 were right censored, and terminations by partnership dissolution, third-party acquisition of the target, or shutting down of the biotechnology firm were coded as distinct competing events.

variable_name: hazard rate of acquiring an additional stake
description: Coded '1' when there were any purchases of equity subsequent to the initial ownership stake in the partner, including purchases that raised the ownership to or beyond the 50 percent level. This definition allows for repeated events, where there are multiple purchases of equity in a single biotechnology firm by a single established firm. Right censoring and competing events were coded as for the majority-stake models.

Measure developed on the basis of Bierly and Chakrabarti (1996) and Moorman and Miner (1997); it assesses diversification in a firm's knowledge of customer portfolios, market segments, and technological background. Senior managers answered the questions about the characteristics of existing knowledge. For the analysis, the values used are residuals obtained by regressing knowledge breadth against market knowledge acquisition and knowledge sharing.

Measure developed following Moorman and Miner (1997) and Prabhu et al. (2005); it indicates the thoroughness of a firm's knowledge and technical expertise within its specialized fields. Senior managers answered the questions about the characteristics of existing knowledge. For the analysis, the values used are residuals from the stage-one estimation, as with knowledge breadth.

Measure adapted from Schulz (2001); it captures the extent of knowledge flow among individuals, decision makers, and units within the firm. The information was provided by middle managers, who reported on operational-level constructs.

Measured by three items adapted from Tsang (2002); it captures the amount and extent of knowledge the firm has acquired from external parties, such as customers, competitors, and suppliers. The information was provided by middle managers at the operational level.

Measure adapted from Atuahene-Gima (2005), Chandy and Tellis (1998), and Zhou et al. (2005); it reflects the degree of technological advances and performance revenue involved in radical innovation. The information was provided by middle managers at the operational level.

New measure of knowledge breadth adapted from De Luca and Atuahene-Gima (2007), used in Study 2 to refine the Study 1 measure. Collected in the first wave of the Study 2 survey from managers of high technology companies.
time_window: first wave, six months before radical innovation

description: New measure of knowledge breadth/depth adapted from De Luca and Atuahene-Gima (2007), used in Study 2 to refine the Study 1 measure. Collected in the first wave of the Study 2 survey from managers of high technology companies.
time_window: first wave, six months before radical innovation

description: Collected in the first wave of the Study 2 survey, which the authors describe as using a similar approach to Study 1. The same managers who reported knowledge breadth and market knowledge acquisition provided this information.
time_window: first wave, six months before radical innovation

description: Collected in the first wave of the Study 2 survey, which the authors describe as using a similar approach to Study 1. Reported by the same managers who provided knowledge breadth/depth and knowledge sharing.
time_window: first wave, six months before radical innovation

description: New scale of radical innovation developed based on Gatignon et al. (2002) and Smith and Tushman (2005). Collected six months after the knowledge variables, when the same managers were contacted by telephone.
time_window: six months after the knowledge variables

variable_name: Count of all firms in a regional network
description: Cumulative count of prior investments in a region at the time of each investment, comprising a focal firm's own entries, entries by firms affiliated with the same business group, and the count of all unrelated firms. The authors measure both the monotonic and the squared terms of this count in order to measure the joint effects of positive and negative network externalities.
time_window: cumulative count up to the time of each entry event

variable_name: Yit (choice made by firm i at time t)
description: A random variable that indicates a choice made by firm i at time t in a conditional logit model. Each observation (a firm choosing a location) has as many rows of data as there are regions in the choice set, each corresponding to a specific region, and the maximum likelihood method is used to estimate how the attributes of a region affect the probability that it is chosen.
time_window: at the time of each investment

variable_name: Count of a firm's own prior entry
description: The number of a focal firm's own prior entries into each region up to the time of an entry event. The authors treat this own prior experience as a source of network externalities for the firm itself.
time_window: cumulative up to the time of each entry event

variable_name: Count of entry by firms within the same group
description: The cumulative count of entries by firms associated with the same business groups in each region up to the time of each entry event. For firms with no group affiliation, this variable is coded as zero.
time_window: cumulative up to the time of each entry event

description: The number of Korean firms not associated with the same business groups that were operating in each region at the time of each entry. In some models this count is further classified into firms in the same industry and firms in different industries using the Korean 2-digit SIC code.
time_window: cumulative up to the time of each entry event

description: The number of manufacturing operations of non-Korean multinationals operating in each region at the time of each entry, taken from Dun & Bradstreet's Major Corporations in P.R. China 2001. In some models this count is split into foreign firms in the same industry and foreign firms in different industries, using the 2-digit SIC code.
time_window: cumulative up to the time of each entry event

description: The number of manufacturing operations of Chinese local firms operating in each region at the time of each entry, taken from Dun & Bradstreet's Major Corporations in P.R. China 2001. In some models this count is split into local firms in the same industry and local firms in different industries, using the 2-digit SIC code.
time_window: cumulative up to the time of each entry event

description: Newly developed scale to assess the ability of the firm to identify and access new markets, covering skills such as assessing the potential of new markets, building relationships in new markets, setting up new distribution and sales channels, and researching new competitors and new customers. Respondents rated how well or poorly they perceive their organization performs these marketing activities relative to competitors. All items are measured on seven-point Likert-type scales and scale scores are calculated by simple summation of item scores.
scale: seven-point Likert-type items, summed scale score

description: Newly developed scale to assess the ability of the firm to identify and incorporate new technologies, covering skills such as setting up new types of manufacturing facilities and operations, learning about technologies not used before, assessing the feasibility of new technologies, and recruiting engineers in unfamiliar technical areas. The scale has the same format as the marketing competence scale, with respondents rating their firm relative to competitors. Items are measured on seven-point Likert-type scales and scale scores are calculated by simple summation of item scores. The reliability of this scale is alpha = 0.89 at both T1 and T2.
scale: seven-point Likert-type items, summed scale score

description: An abbreviated version of the Chandy and Tellis (1998) scale, assessing the extent to which the firm is prepared to reduce the actual or potential value of its investments in assets and organizational routines. Items cover supporting projects that could take away sales from existing products, replacing one set of abilities with a different set of abilities to adopt a new technology, and willingness to sacrifice sales of existing products to improve sales of new products; two items are worded in the opposite direction. Items are measured on seven-point Likert-type scales and scale scores are calculated by simple summation of item scores. The reliability of this scale is alpha = 0.69 both at T1 and T2.
scale: seven-point Likert-type items, summed scale score

description: Scale adapted from existing measures of constructive conflict in groups to assess the extent to which interpersonal exchanges within the firm are characterized by constructive conflict, with items on useful give-and-take, constructive challenge of ideas, comfort in raising dissenting viewpoints, and mutual respect among people who disagree. Some items were newly formulated from descriptions of constructive conflict in the literature and others were adapted from group-level scales. Items are measured on seven-point Likert-type scales and scale scores are simple sums of item scores; one item was dropped at T2.
scale: seven-point Likert-type items, summed scale score

description: Measure newly developed for this study to assess the extent to which failure is seen within the firm as an opportunity to learn, with items stating that failure is understood as a necessary part of success, that failure is an inevitable byproduct of taking many initiatives, and that a mistake is seen as an opportunity to learn; one item is worded in the opposite direction. Items are measured on seven-point Likert-type scales and scale scores are calculated by simple summation of item scores.
scale: seven-point Likert-type items, summed scale score

description: Scale developed for this study to assess the extent to which the firm and its employees access outside information regarding technological and market trends through professional affiliation, conferences, and trade shows. It was derived by summing the extent to which the firm engages in various scanning activities, with items on participation in professional associations, attendance at scientific or professional conferences and trade shows, contacts with university researchers and the scientific community, and reading specialized journals; several items are worded in the opposite direction. Items are measured on seven-point Likert-type scales and scale scores are simple sums of item scores; two items were changed at T2, improving the scale.
scale: seven-point Likert-type items, summed scale score

description: Scale developed for this study to assess the extent to which slack resources are present within the firm, based on the informant's perception of the availability of slack resources, including financial and human resources. Items cover whether all available resources are locked up in current projects (worded in the opposite direction), resources held in reserve, ample discretionary financial resources, and available manpower for special projects. Items are measured on seven-point Likert-type scales and scale scores are simple sums of item scores. A squared term for slack was included in the regression models to test the hypothesized U-shaped lagged relationships.
scale: seven-point Likert-type items, summed scale score

variable_name: physical, human, and brand-name asset dummy variables
description: The relatedness of the restructured assets was measured in two steps. First, the assets were classified as existing within the restructuring firm's self-reported primary and related businesses (the four-digit SIC code designated as primary, plus all business lines sharing its two-digit SIC code) or in the secondary and unrelated business lines (those not sharing the primary two-digit SIC code), using company financial statements cross-referenced against published disclosures of the restructuring announcement. Second, separate dummy variables were computed for physical assets (machinery, facilities, technology), human assets (personnel, including specialized attached personnel and personnel-as-productive-assets in service industries), and brand-name assets (assets containing the restructuring firm's name) via a content analysis of published reports. Each dummy was coded 1 if the restructured assets resided in the primary and related business lines and 0 when they resided outside them. Interrater agreement after retest was 94 percent, raised to 100 percent after reconciliation.

The diversification of business lines variable was measured using Rumelt's (1974) classification typology, categorizing each restructuring firm on the basis of its specialization ratio (largest business segment in sales divided by total sales) and relatedness ratio (proportion of a firm's revenues attributable to its largest groups of related businesses). The variable was coded 1 for single businesses, 2 for dominant businesses, 3 for related-constrained, 4 for related-linked, and 5 for unrelated businesses. Two researchers coded each firm independently and the intraclass correlation of their codes was 0.96; data were gathered from financial statements and disclosures.

A variable called restructuring alternative was coded as a 1 for spin-offs and as a 0 for sell-offs. The classification of spin-off and sell-off was reported in the SDC's Merger & Acquisition Database and Mergerstat, and no restructuring events were a hybrid of the two alternatives.

Stock market value was the stock market returns associated with the restructuring announcement, measured with the standard event study methodology: a market model was estimated for each firm by ordinary least squares over an estimation period of 250 days (-300 to -50) before the restructuring announcement, daily abnormal returns were computed, and abnormal returns were cumulated over the two-day window around the announcement (day 0 is the announcement business day and +1 the next business day). Stock market data were taken from the Center for Research Security Prices data tapes.
time_window: two-day event window (day 0 to day +1); estimation period of 250 days from -300 to -50

description: The count of views of each article for each day, aggregated by month and scaled to a 31-day month equivalent so that months of different length are comparable. Because the number of article views is an integer count, it is transformed by taking the natural log.

The number of unique people who make at least one addition, edit, or deletion to an article in a given month. Activity made by automated software programs (bots) is removed using Wikipedia's list of approved bots, and discussions on comment and talk pages are not included.
Number of characters in the article, divided by 1,000; the natural log of article length is used in the statistical models.
The automated readability index (ARI), which estimates the U.S. school grade required to understand the article.
The number of header levels in the article; articles contain up to six levels of nested sections.
The number of external references cited; medical articles typically require citations to peer-reviewed medical journals.
The number of hyperlinks to other articles on Wikipedia, with the additive inverse (negative) used as the measure of independence.
The number of image, audio, or video files used in an article.

The age of the article content, measured in days elapsed and used in natural log form in the statistical models. The authors describe content age as the opportunity consumers have had to consume and contribute to the content.

KLD rates firms on nine dimensions of corporate social performance, five of which are typically used for research. Every firm is given a strength and a concern score for each dimension: an X for a moderate concern or strength, an XX for a strong concern or strength, or a blank to indicate no special concerns or strengths. Following prior research, the authors coded a blank as 0, a moderate strength as 1, a strong strength as 2, a moderate concern as -1, and a strong concern as -2. For each CSP dimension, a firm's score was the sum of its concern and strength ratings, so scores could range from -2 to +2.

Students (n = 75) in two sections of a senior-level strategic management course rated 189 companies in terms of their reputations on a five-point scale ranging from 1, 'very poor reputation,' to 5, 'very good reputation.' Respondents were also given a 'cannot judge' option, and an organization was retained only if at least one-third of the respondents actually rated it. Each organization's reputation score was the average rating for the respondents who rated the firm. Average reputation ratings ranged from 2.74 to 4.87.
scale: 1 = very poor reputation to 5 = very good reputation

description: Students in two sections of a senior-level strategic management course (n = 34) rated each of the 189 companies in terms of its attractiveness as an employer on a five-point scale ranging from 1, 'unattractive employer,' to 5, 'one of the most attractive employers.' Respondents were given a 'cannot judge' option, and an organization was retained only if at least one-third of the respondents actually rated it. Each organization's score was the average rating for the respondents who rated the firm, and such ratings ranged from 2.68 to 4.64.
scale: 1 = unattractive employer to 5 = one of the most attractive employers

description: The measure consists of three items developed from the conceptual works of Lewicki and Bunker (1996) and Rousseau et al. (1998). Two items assess the strength of rewards and punishments that sanction cooperative behavior in the interorganizational exchange, and one item captures the degree of exchange continuity, because according to the repeated game logic the expectation of doing business in the long run allows exchange parties to reward or punish prior moves. In the analysis the predicted values from the first-stage regression on transactional attributes, prior experience and guanxi importance are used to obtain a residual, and this residual is the indicator of calculative trust.

The measure has three items, each of which reflects the degree to which a shared identity exists and enables one party to trust the other to act on its behalf, shared identity being the highest level of relational trust. The items cover shared identification, shared understanding, and thinking like one another. As with calculative trust, the residual from the first-stage regression is used as the indicator of relational trust in the performance model.

Adapted from Cannon and Perreault (1999) and Zaheer et al. (1998), the measure examines supplier performance in the focal exchange relationship. The informant rates the supplier's performance on product quality, timeliness of delivery, after-sales support, and total value received.

Adapted from Cannon and Perreault (1999), the measure captures buyers' specific investments made or changes made specifically to accommodate the supplier. Respondents indicate the extent of investment or change in product features, personnel, inventory and distribution, and capital equipment and tools.

Adapted from Cannon and Perreault (1999), the measure examines the environmental changes in the supply market. Respondents report how frequently pricing, product features and specifications, vendor support services, technology used by suppliers, and product supply are changing for this supply market.
level: supply market of the buyer-supplier relationship

description: Developed on the basis of Brown, Dev, and Lee (2000), the measure assesses how difficult it is to evaluate the other party's activities. It asks whether it is difficult to evaluate if the supplier follows the buyer's recommended operating procedures and whether the buyer lacks accurate reports about the supplier's activities.

The dependent variable is a 0/1 variable that takes a value of zero if firm i has no foreign R&D labs at time t, and one if firm i has foreign R&D labs at time t. Foreign R&D labs are limited to foreign subsidiaries whose main purpose is 'information gathering' or 'research and development,' that is, labs creating new knowledge rather than adapting or exploiting knowledge from the home market. A native Japanese speaker consulted the Japanese language Toyo Keizai Shinposha Directory, which lists the main purpose of each firm's foreign subsidiary, to determine which firms have foreign R&D labs.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the firm is above the OECD industry average R&D intensity (R&D/sales). R&D intensity variables were created for each firm in each year, and the industry comparison is at the 2- or 3-digit industry classification depending on what is available from the OECD, which for most firms is the 2-digit level. The OECD data are only available starting in 1980, so the sample is reduced to 1980-94 when the global technology position is analyzed; the variable is one-year lagged.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the firm is the industry leader in the 3-digit industry at time t. The leader is determined using the R&D intensity variable (R&D expenditures/Sales) created for each firm in each year, and the position is assessed relative to all other publicly traded firms in the industry. The variable is one-year lagged.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the firm is in the top quartile of firms in terms of R&D intensity in the 3-digit industry, excluding the leader. When the models were run neither the 2nd nor 3rd quartile dummy variables were statistically significant, so the excluded category is firms in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd quartiles. The variable is one-year lagged.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the firm is the industry leader in terms of sales in the 3-digit industry at time t. Total sales of each firm are used to determine the leading market share firm in each 3-digit industry, comparing the domestic position of each firm to its domestic competitors. The variable is one-year lagged.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the firm is in the top quartile of firms in the 3-digit industry in terms of sales, excluding the industry leader. Similar to the technology variables, neither the 2nd nor 3rd quartile dummy variables were statistically significant when the models were run, so the excluded category is firms in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd quartiles. The variable is one-year lagged.
Performance was measured as the percentage of games each MLB organization won in a focal year. The variable was multiplied by 100 for scaling.
scale: percentage of games won, multiplied by 100 for scaling

description: Measured using the Gini coefficient for the dispersion of individuals' total pay in the organization as reported by the organizations, which includes all actual pay to a player by a team in a year. The Gini coefficient varies from a high of 1, indicating the highest amount of possible dispersion (absolute inequality), to a low of 0, indicating the lowest amount of possible dispersion (absolute equality). Pay dispersion was measured in the concurrent year.

Measured using the Gini coefficient for the dispersion of individuals' contributions to the performance of the organization, with the Gini coefficient ranging from 0 (absolute equality) to 1 (absolute inequality). An individual's value or contribution was assessed using the long-form method of adjusted player contribution outlined by Bill James, which combines offensive and defensive metrics into a single integer based on the marginal productivity associated with creating and preventing runs, adjusted for factors such as home field, league, and the strength of other players, and for positional differences. Players accumulating at least 10 at bats, or innings, or chances in the field for a team were included in proportion to their pay and contribution for each team.

variable_name: Congruence between pay and resource dispersions
description: Measured as one minus the absolute difference between the dispersions of resources and pay, so that a higher value indicates a greater degree of congruence between the dispersions of pay and resources. The authors analyzed whether the measure satisfies the four constraints noted by Edwards (2002) and report that the use of the difference score is justified. The dispersions of both pay and resource contributions were measured in the concurrent year.

Measured by dividing the sum of each organization's employee contributions by the average of all MLB organizations. Individual contributions were assessed with the adjusted player contribution measure outlined above.

Calculated as the average spending on player salaries for each organization, divided by 1 million for scaling. It was included to account for spending advantages, since organizations may spend more on salaries to obtain more talented employees or to motivate current employees.

Technology differentiation of firm i in year t is computed from the pairwise technology similarity between firm i and other firms active in year t. Firm technology portfolios are represented as tf-idf vectors whose dimensions are stemmed technical keywords and whose values are the share of a firm's patents containing the keyword offset by the share of all firm portfolios containing it; tech similarity is the cosine similarity between two firms' portfolio vectors. Only the top 10% of firms most technologically similar to firm i within year t are considered, so firms with more unique and less overlapping technology portfolios have higher values. The variable is measured in year t - 1 relative to deal announcement and is the main variable of interest.
time_window: patent portfolio uses patents filed between t-4 and t; measured at t-1

description: Tech differentiation of the target firm in the acquirer-target pair, computed from pairwise technology similarity in the same way as in the target analysis, based on the top 10% of most technologically similar firms. It enters the deal-level model together with its interactions with prod similarity and tech similarity. Measured in year t - 1 relative to deal announcement.
time_window: patent portfolio uses patents filed between t-4 and t; measured at t-1

description: Product similarity between firm i and firm j in each year, calculated as the overlap in the product descriptions found within the annual 10-K reports of the two firms. The measure is used to capture product market overlap and rivalry between prospective acquirer and target firms, and is available only from 1989 onward. It is measured in year t - 1 relative to deal announcement and is interacted with target tech differentiation.

Technological similarity between firm i and firm j in year t, calculated as the cosine similarity between the tf-idf vectors representing the two firms' patent portfolios. The metric captures the prospects for technology synergies between potential acquirers and targets. It is measured in year t - 1 relative to deal announcement and is interacted with target tech differentiation.

Binary outcome variable equal to one if firm i is the actual target in deal m in year t, and equal to zero in case of a matched pseudo-target firm. Estimated with conditional logit models that include deal fixed effects for the real target and its matched pseudo-targets, so that heterogeneity in tech differentiation between target and pseudo-target firms drives the probability of being a target.
time_window: deal announcement year t, firm characteristics at t-1

description: Binary outcome variable equal to one if firms i and j are the actual acquirer-target pair for deal m in year t, and equal to zero in case of matched pseudo-acquirer-target pairs. Pseudo-pairs include combinations of actual acquirers with pseudo-targets and pseudo-acquirers with actual targets. Estimated with deal-level conditional logit models including deal fixed effects.
time_window: deal announcement year t, firm characteristics at t-1

description: Dummy variable set to 1 if a client that a lobbyist works for in period p follows them to their new firm in period p+1. To ensure the client is following the employee and not simply returning to a firm in which they have prior ties, the client must not have enlisted the services of the lobbyist's new firm in prior periods.
time_window: period p+1, relative to mobility observed in period p

description: The number of periods a given lobbyist l lobbied for a given client c for lobbying firm f, prior to mobility. It captures the employee-client joint tenure at a focal firm, or the number of periods the client has enlisted the services of the given lobbyist at the focal firm.

The number of periods a given lobbying firm f lobbied for a given client c, prior to the mobility of lobbyist l. It captures the firm-client joint tenure, or the number of periods the client has enlisted the services of the given lobbying firm.

The total number of lobbyists at a given lobbying firm that are registered to lobby for a particular client in a given period. A value of 1 indicates that the client is exclusively tied to a single lobbyist, whereas a value of 6 indicates that six individual lobbyists (the focal lobbyist and five others) jointly lobby for the client in a given period.
time_window: given period (period p, prior to mobility)

description: An issue-based Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) computed from a lobbyist's lobbying history. Lobbying reports list the issues lobbied and a dollar value; that amount is divided by the number of lobbyists listed on the report and then by the number of issues listed, producing an issue- and lobbyist-weighted dollar value per report. Summing these values across issues by lobbyist yields the total lobbying revenue the lobbyist earned for a particular issue, adjusted for the number of lobbyists and issues on the report; these amounts are used to calculate an issue-based HHI for each lobbyist. The formula as printed in the article could not be extracted (the equation block is unreadable). The value is bound between 0 and 1, with higher values indicating specialists and lower values generalists; the average across all lobbyists who work with a given client in a given period captures the specialized expertise of the team.
time_window: lobbyist's lobbying history up to the given period

description: Diversification was measured by the entropy index of diversification (Palepu, 1985), decomposed into a related component (DR) and an unrelated component (DU) such that total diversification DT=DR+DU. DR was defined as diversification arising out of operating in several segments within an industry group, with two-digit SIC industries defined as industry groups and four-digit SIC industries as industry segments; each segment is weighted by (1/P_jt), where P_jt is the percentage of the firm's sales in industry j at time t. The change in diversification between two time periods was defined as diversification at the later date divided by diversification at the earlier date. Data to compute the measures came from the Trinet/EIS tapes, which were available for 1977, 1980, 1983 and 1986, with interpolation for intervening years.

Diversification was measured by the entropy index of diversification (Palepu, 1985), decomposed into a related component (DR) and an unrelated component (DU) such that total diversification DT=DR+DU. DU was defined as diversification across industry groups, with two-digit SIC industries defined as industry groups. The change in diversification between two time periods was defined as diversification at the later date divided by diversification at the earlier date. Data to compute the measures came from the Trinet/EIS tapes, available for 1977, 1980, 1983 and 1986, with interpolation for intervening years.

The level of the firm's diversification on the entropy index of diversification at the beginning of the time period over which the subsequent change in diversification is measured. Data to compute the measure came from the Trinet/EIS tapes.

Risk was measured by the asset beta as defined by Brealey and Myers (1988): Asset beta_t = debt beta_t · pD_t + equity beta_t · pE_t, where pD_t is the proportion of debt in the capital structure of the firm at time t and pE_t is the proportion of equity; the debt beta is assumed to equal zero. The equity beta is the beta of common stock, calculated from CRSP tapes on the basis of daily closing prices. The change in asset beta was defined as asset beta at the later date divided by asset beta at the earlier date.
The current ratio is a standard measure of liquidity and was calculated from COMPUSTAT data. A higher current ratio is taken to indicate that the firm is better able to afford diversification.

R&D intensity was adjusted for the extent to which the firm had diversified into industries with different R&D intensities, using Federal Trade Commission line of business data and EIS data. In the authors' notation RD_t is the corporate R&D expenditure of a firm at time t, S_t is total firm sales at time t, RDS_jt is the average R&D-to-sales ratio of all business units classified by the FTC into four-digit industry j, and pS_jt is the proportion of total firm sales attributed to industry j at time t. The equation itself appeared in a formula block that was not extracted, so the exact functional form of the adjustment is not readable here.

Advertising intensity was adjusted in the same manner as R&D intensity, using the average advertising-to-sales ratios of the industries in which the firm operates (Federal Trade Commission line of business data) and the proportion of total firm sales attributed to each industry (EIS data). The authors state that a similar measure to the adjusted R&D intensity measure was used to calculate advertising intensity; the formula block was not extracted.
Institutional holdings were measured by the percentage of stock held by the institutions. Data were taken from Standard and Poor's Stock Reports.
Management holdings were measured by the natural logarithm of the percentage of stock controlled directly and indirectly by managers. Data were taken from Standard and Poor's Stock Reports.
scale: natural logarithm of percentage of stock

description: The ratio of the firm's market to book value, calculated from COMPUSTAT data. The authors use it as an indication of how stockholders value a firm's assets under current management.

Profitability was measured by the return earned on stockholders' equity (ROE). The change in profitability was defined as return on equity at the later date divided by return on equity at the earlier date, with n = 1 to 3 depending on the performance interval examined. COMPUSTAT data were used to calculate profitability.

Risk-adjusted market returns were calculated using CRSP data and defined as the difference between the actual return earned on a stock and its expected return. The actual return R_jt was defined as (P_t - P_0)/P_0, where P_0 is the stock price on 1 January of year t and P_t is the capital gain on common stock plus dividend payments over year t. The beta used in the expected return is the annual beta based on daily closing prices, calculated on 31 December for year t-1; the expected-return equation appeared in a formula block that was not extracted.
time_window: 1977-1986; returns measured 1, 2 and 3 years after a change in diversification

description: We used a weighted measure to compute market share, defined as the sum of a firm's market share in each four-digit SIC industry in which it was active, weighted by the proportion of total firm sales generated in that industry; MS_jt is the market share of a firm in industry j at time t, and pS_jt is the proportion of a firm's total revenues generated in industry j at time t. Data to compute pS_jt came from the EIS tapes. The change in market share was defined as market share at the later date divided by market share at the earlier date, where n = 1 to 3 depending on the performance interval examined; the formula itself appeared in a formula block that was not extracted.

Leverage was measured by the debt to equity ratio, calculated from COMPUSTAT data. The change in leverage was defined as debt to equity at the later date divided by debt to equity at the earlier date, where n = 1 to 3 depending on the performance interval being examined.

variable_name: social distancing as reported by focal director
description: Eight-item scale adapted from Hollinger and Clark's (1982) measure and additional questions covering the aspects of distancing identified in the sociological and anthropological literature, including not being invited to informal board meetings, not having one's opinion or advice solicited in formal meetings, not having one's comments acknowledged or built upon, and exclusionary gossip. Multiple response formats were used (5-point Likert-type items, agree-disagree items, and counts of interactions over a specified period), and items were reverse scored so that higher values signify greater distancing. Factor analysis using the iterated principal factors method produced loadings greater than .5 on one factor and less than .2 on the others, Cronbach's alpha was .91, and factor scores were estimated with the Bartlett method.
time_window: past twelve months / most recent twelve-month period

variable_name: social distancing as reported by other outside directors
description: Assessments by other outside directors on the board of the extent of social distancing experienced by a given focal director, using the same eight items asked about each listed director; when responses were available from more than one director, one set of responses was randomly selected. Items were reverse scored where necessary so that higher values signify greater distancing, the distancing items loaded on one factor with loadings greater than .5, Cronbach's alpha was .91, factor scores were estimated with the Bartlett method, and the overall kappa for agreement between outside directors was .83.

variable_name: prior participation in elite-threatening actions-archival measure
description: Index calculated as the number of elite-threatening actions implemented by boards on which the individual served as an outside director during the two-year period prior to the survey. Each of the four actions was first coded dichotomously: CEO/board-chair separation coded 1 if the board-chair position was reallocated from the CEO to an independent director during the two-year period (temporary separations following a CEO succession were excluded); creation of an independent nominating committee coded 1 if the board had a nominating committee composed exclusively of outsiders in the current year and either had no such committee two years earlier or had one including insiders; poison pill repeal coded 1 if the board repealed a pill during the period, excluding repeals following a shareholder proposal and passing vote and repeals of defenses requiring a shareholder vote for renewal; CEO dismissal coded 1 if respondents indicated the CEO was replaced and that this change indicated independent board control over management. The equation for the index is not readable in the supplied text.
time_window: two-year period prior to the survey date

variable_name: prior participation in elite-threatening actions-survey measure
description: Index based on the director's perceived level of support for each elite-threatening action at each board where he or she served, as rated by other directors. Support was measured with three items ('To what extent did [the director] support the particular change?'; 'To what extent did [the director] make it clear that they were against this change?', reverse scored; 'The director was in favor of this change', agree/disagree); inter-item reliability was alpha = .90 and the overall kappa for the subsample rated by two or more board members was .81, with items loading on one factor. Factor scores indicate support for a particular change at a particular board and the index weights each elite-threatening action by that support. The equation for the index is not readable in the supplied text.
time_window: two-year period prior to the survey date

variable_name: subsequent participation in elite-threatening actions-archival measure
description: Dichotomous measure coded as 1 if one or more of the elite-threatening actions occurred on a particular board (other than the focal board) where the focal individual served as director during the subsequent two-year period. The unit of analysis is the director-firm. Data on CEO dismissal during the subsequent two-year period were obtained from the follow-up survey distributed in 2001, with very high interrater agreement about the occurrence of dismissal (93 percent).
time_window: two-year period following the survey date

variable_name: subsequent participation in elite-threatening actions-survey measure
description: Measure gauging the extent to which an individual director was perceived to have supported elite-threatening actions at a particular board where he or she served as director during the two-year period following the initial survey, built from follow-up survey data; the authors report acceptable inter-item reliability and interrater reliability for this scale.
time_window: two-year period following the initial survey

description: Factor score of four indicators of director status in the corporate elite: the number of board appointments held by the director; a dummy variable coded 1 if the focal director was CEO of a company in the Forbes 500 listing; the stock rating of the director's primary employer, obtained from Standard and Poor's Stock Survey, as an indicator of employer prestige; and a dummy variable coded 1 if the focal director had an undergraduate or MBA degree at an institution on Useem and Karabel's (1986) list of the most prestigious undergraduate institutions and MBA programs. The four measures loaded on one factor with loadings of .5 or greater and less than .2 on the other factors, Cronbach's alpha was .84, and factor scores were estimated with the Bartlett method. All of these variables were measured for the year prior to the survey.

Following a diffusion-based approach, the authors tracked year-to-year changes across all sample hospitals on an inventory of 135 separate service offerings reported to the state; each service was coded as available (1) or not available (0) within each hospital in a given year. Ratings for each of the 135 services were averaged annually across the industry, and the 40 services with the greatest rate of increase at the industry level were identified; a panel of ten California health care professionals ranked those 40 on a seven-point Likert-type scale and the 15 services at or above the median scale level in innovativeness formed the bundle studied.
