Each hospital's adoption score for each service in each year was adjusted for diffusion of that service within the hospital's market area (health services area), so that as a service became more diffused it became less innovative, and the adjusted scores were aggregated across the 15 service innovations into an overall hospital innovation score. The equation for this aggregate score is rendered as an unreadable formula block in the text and is not reconstructed here.

Structural links were tracked using data from the AHA annual survey of U.S. hospitals and were measured as a simple dummy indicator for hospitals that were a part of a multihospital system. About 49 percent of the sample hospitals were affiliated with systems.

A dummy variable indicating that a hospital contracted for management services with another hospital. Approximately 12 percent of the sample hospitals relied on contract managers over the study period, a figure generally consistent with national averages. The measure came directly from the data in CHFC disclosure reports.

Institutional links captured each hospital's involvement in important institutional or trade associations such as the AHA or Voluntary Hospital Association (VHA). The variable was measured as the total dollar value (in thousands) of contributions made by a hospital to such organizations. The measure came directly from the data in CHFC disclosure reports.

Resource links were measured as the total dollar value of major transactions (adjusted for hospital size) between a hospital and all other hospitals related through ownership or through key administrative personnel. Related hospitals were those in which ownership was shared, and related personnel were owners, board members, and managers who held interlocking administrative or ownership interests in both organizations; the presence of a relation was used as evidence of interorganizational governance. Aggregating these transactions yielded an indicator of the overall volume of network resource and equity flows. The measure came directly from the data in CHFC disclosure reports.

Interorganizational links were measured as four types: multihospital system membership (dummy), contract management of a hospital by another hospital (dummy), dollar contributions to trade and institutional associations, and the dollar value of transactions with related hospitals adjusted for size. Data came from the CHFC disclosure reports and the AHA survey.

Political ties took the value of 1 if at least one member of a firm's senior management held or previously held a senior government or political appointment, or if a senior government or political official currently or previously served as a senior manager in the firm. The authors focused on four key government and political organizations in China: the government, Communist Party, and two legislative bodies (the National People's Congress and the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference). Ties were identified from a variety of business and government sources and from an internet search by name for senior managers of the firms in the dataset; the authors identified 55 political ties among 33 firms, with no firm having more than three ties.
Local ties took the value of 1 for political ties at provincial, city, and county levels. Thirty-five of the identified ties were local.
Central ties took the value of 1 for ties at national levels of government and political bodies. Twenty of the identified ties were central.

A dummy variable took the value of 0 each year until a firm discontinued its operations in TV manufacturing or ceased to operate as a corporation, in which event Dissolution took the value of 1. Firms that survived until the end of the study had Dissolution = 0 for all years (i.e., were right-censored). The 26 firms that were acquired during the study period were also right-censored because acquisition exits are driven by substantially different dynamics; acquired firms remained in the dataset until the year they were acquired. The higher the likelihood of dissolution, the lower the likelihood of survival.

Measured as percentage change in TV sales revenue (US$ billion) each year (Sales t / Sales t - 1). The authors argue sales growth is a reliable performance measure because they focus on a single industry producing a narrow set of closely related products using common technologies, and because reliable profitability measures were more ambiguous in this period and limited for the 157 non-listed firms in the sample.
time_window: annual change from the prior year

description: Firm efficiency measured each firm's capabilities for converting resources into performance. Following Dutta, Narasimhan, and Rajiv (2005), the authors adopted stochastic frontier analysis to compute each firm's efficiency, using five indicators: number of employees, fixed assets, number of technicians, region dummies and year dummies. Firm efficiency was estimated for each firm as the ratio of its efficiency to that of the efficient frontier, which was based on the most efficient firm in the sample (i.e. efficiency equals 1). Data limitations prevented the use of a broader set of predictor variables and caused substantial missing data for one indicator, number of technicians.
scale: ratio to the efficient frontier, with 1 equal to the most efficient firm in the sample

description: A complementary measure of performance that measured sales growth over a one-year period, described by the authors as a consistent, current and measurable indicator of capabilities that captures product and quality differences across firms. Sensitivity testing used the quadratic terms of prior sales growth and firm efficiency to assess boundary conditions.

Percentage of knowledge test items answered correctly. The test comprised two sets of questions: one set tested inferences about bivariate causal relationships between pairs of simulation variables, covering the exhaustive set of actual relationships in each complexity condition plus items for which no relationship existed, with participants drawing a directed influence arrow and indicating polarity; 30 items were common to both conditions and high complexity participants answered a further 24 items. The second set presented graphs of one or two variables over time and asked participants to choose the evolution of another variable. Scores range from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates perfect knowledge of the tested aspects of causal structure and dynamic behavior.

Percentage of eleven knowledge test items answered correctly. Seven items involve inferred bivariate causal relationships about the key principles of the market diffusion process and four are graphical scenario questions covering a subset of the same relationships. Scores range from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates perfect knowledge of the tested aspects of the key principles of deep structure.

Cumulative profit at the end of the last decision trial for each of the nine trial blocks. Raw performance scores were divided by benchmarks for the high and low complexity conditions because the potential achievable cumulative profit differed between conditions. The benchmarks were found through a modified Powell search optimization, fixing marketing spend at five percent of revenue, determining capacity by a perfect foresight rule in which capacity always matched demand, and computing the single price level that optimized profits over the entire simulation; the benchmark is not a global optimum but a consistently calculated benchmark enabling comparison across the two complexity groups.
time_window: end of each of the nine trial blocks, including the delayed testing phase 15 weeks after the initial laboratory session

description: Task complexity was manipulated across two levels associated with either a monopoly market or a competitive market. The low complexity version had no competitor, two decision variables (price and target capacity) and 19 interdependent variables in the causal structure; the high complexity version included causal relationships for a competitor, three decision variables (price, target capacity, and marketing spend) and over 30 interdependent variables. Task complexity was coded such that 0 = low complexity and 1 = high complexity.

The level of apps market competition in a given console-platform j at time t is the overlap density for platform j on date t, borrowed from Venkatraman and Lee (2004) and Baum and Singh (1994). It sums over all developers the proportion of titles a developer released to platform j over all titles it developed, adjusted by the pairwise overlap weights between platforms (the extent to which two platforms attract the same set of game providers), measured through Sohn's (2001) overlap metric. The overlap density captures the total number of game producers for a given platform on a date as adjusted by the degree of market overlap these producers share across console platforms. The algebraic specification is not recoverable from the text as provided here because the formula block is unreadable.

The proportion of a platform's titles at time t that are exclusive. Following Corts and Lederman (2009), a title is defined as exclusive if it has never been released at any point in its whole life cycle (i.e., before and after time t) for any of the other rival platforms in the same technology generation. Only exclusive titles provided by third-party producers are counted.

Measured by comparing the proportion of games offered by a platform in each genre with the average figure for that genre at time t for rival platforms belonging to the same technological generation. The absolute values of these deviations from the mean are summed over the nine game genres. It takes a value of zero when the distribution of a platform's titles across genres coincides with that of its competitors, and positive values as the distance increases.

The console's unit sales in a given month over total unit sales of active consoles that month. This variable captures the monthly competitive dynamics of the industry and the overlap of incumbent and new generation consoles. A one-month lag is introduced to assess how the independent variables and controls in month t impact market share in month t + 1.

Computed as the coefficient of variation of bank size among the members of a clique, which equals the standard error of the focal variable divided by the mean and is larger for greater diversity when the mean is positive. Bank size is the inflation-adjusted dollar value of each bank's deals in that year: a solo deal was assigned 100 percent of the offering's dollar value, while for syndicate deals the lead bank was assigned 50 percent of the underwriting value and the remaining value was split equally among the co-lead banks. Values were assigned to the final year of each four-year network and lagged one year for model estimation. A positive coefficient would support Hypothesis 1.
time_window: four-year moving window assigned to its final year, lagged one year

description: Computed with the D-measure, the sum of squared differences between a focal member of a group and all other members, divided by the mean size of banks in the clique to get the scaled difference of size between the group member and the clique. The equation for the measure is unreadable in the available text. D is larger for greater distance and bounded at the lower end by zero. A positive coefficient would support Hypothesis 2.
time_window: four-year moving window assigned to its final year, lagged one year

description: The actual number of syndicate ties among the banks within a clique relative to the total number of possible ties among the banks, where d is density, T is the number of syndicate ties among banks, and n is the number of banks in a clique. The equation is unreadable in the available text. A negative coefficient would support Hypothesis 3.
time_window: four-year moving window assigned to its final year, lagged one year

description: Obtained by subtracting a bank's score for clique cohesion from its density of contacts within a clique, which is defined as the proportion of clique members to which the bank had syndicate ties. Bank cohesion is therefore higher for banks whose density of syndicate ties to other clique members exceeds the overall density of syndicate ties among clique members. A negative coefficient would support Hypothesis 4.
time_window: four-year moving window assigned to its final year, lagged one year

description: The diversity of lead role specialization among the banks in a clique, computed in the same way as clique size diversity, using the coefficient of variation. Bank lead role specialization is a bank's number of lead manager roles divided by the total number of syndicates in which it participated in each year: banks scoring 1 specialized in the lead role, and those scoring 0 specialized in the co-lead role. The measure was used to test Hypothesis 5, which would be supported by a negative coefficient.
time_window: four-year moving window assigned to its final year, lagged one year

description: The distance between a focal bank's lead role specialization and the lead role specialization of the other members of its clique, computed in the same way as bank size distance and scaled by the average role specialization of banks in the clique for compatibility with clique role diversity. The measure was used to test Hypothesis 6, which would be supported by a negative coefficient.
time_window: four-year moving window assigned to its final year, lagged one year

description: The average number of structural holes spanned by a clique's members. Each bank's structural holes were measured with Burt's network effective size, the number of partners a bank has minus the average number of ties its partners have (not counting ties to the ego) within the ego network, so that high network effective size means a bank's partners have few ties to one another and the bank spans many structural holes. A negative coefficient would support Hypothesis 7; the authors note they did not use Burt's network efficiency because they were concerned with the absolute and relative magnitudes of banks' overall network advantage.
time_window: four-year moving window assigned to its final year, lagged one year

description: A gini index of the network effective size of the banks in a clique, which operationally defines inequality as the average gain in network effective size an organization could get if given the choice of trading places with a randomly drawn other organization. The equation, which averages the differences in network effective size for all pairs of banks scaled by the average network effective size, is unreadable in the available text. The coefficient is larger for greater inequality and bounded by 0 and 1; a positive coefficient would support Hypothesis 8.
time_window: four-year moving window assigned to its final year, lagged one year

description: A bank's own structural holes (network effective size) minus the clique's structural holes, so that the value is larger for banks spanning more structural holes than the average clique member. A positive coefficient would support Hypothesis 9.
time_window: four-year moving window assigned to its final year, lagged one year

description: An indicator of a bank exiting its clique. Each bank was in the sample for the years in which it was a member of a clique and thus at risk of exiting that clique; the data covered 229 banks and 2,077 bank-year observations, and cliques experienced 290 member exits during the observation period. Observations for banks belonging to cliques that dissolved during a given year were removed from the data since there was no clique to exit from in that year.

Articles about the sample firms were gathered from a leading German daily paper (Die Welt) and two leading German business papers (Handelsblatt and Manager Magazin) and from several US news and business papers (The New York Times, Forbes, Los Angeles Times, Washington Post, and Financial Times) via the company search feature in LexisNexis. Only articles that mentioned the firm in the title, headline, or leading paragraphs and had at least 50 words were included. Each article was converted into a single text file and analyzed with LIWC2015, which calculates a score for negative emotion in each article from the percentage of negative emotional words; the average of all articles for each firm and year estimates the overall evaluation of the firm by the media within a year.
time_window: average per firm and year; explanatory variables lagged one year relative to firm action

description: The measure captures the difference between the firm's strategic actions in the focal year and the prior year, calculated as the Euclidean distance between the strategic actions of two years (the displayed equation is not readable in the text provided; A1-A8 represent the number of actions in each category). Strategic actions were identified from the RavenPack News Analytics database, which scans newswires for competitive actions and classifies the articles. The measures were standardized and the dependent variable winsorized at the 99% and 1% levels to mitigate the influence of outliers.
time_window: difference between the focal year and the prior year

description: Trained MBA student raters assessed the novelty-centered BMD using the scale suggested by Zott and Amit (2007), whose items are rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). The selected raters were unfamiliar with the hypothesized relationships and searched secondary data sources such as annual reports and websites to familiarize themselves with and assess the BMDs; 13 raters were selected, and BMDs were randomly assigned to two raters for comparison. Inter-rater reliability was validated pair-wise with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.64, and Cronbach's alpha for the novelty scale was .816.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: Trained MBA student raters assessed the efficiency-centered BMD using the scale suggested by Zott and Amit (2007), whose items are rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). The raters were unfamiliar with the hypothesized relationships and assessed the BMDs from secondary sources such as annual reports and websites, with BMDs randomly assigned to two raters for comparison; the Pearson correlation coefficient across rater pairs was 0.64. Cronbach's alpha for the efficiency scale was .755.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: TMT integrative complexity was assessed through the GDQ measure of intellectual flexibility, a construct analogous to integrative complexity and defined as 'seeing problems in multidimensional ways and changing one's mind in response to new evidence.' The dimension comprises 13 items that tap the evaluative differentiation and conceptual integration dimensions of integrative complexity. Each item consists of two opposite statements on a card, one at the top (upper statement) and one at the bottom (lower statement), and raters sort the cards into one of nine categories ranging from 1, 'upper statement is very characteristic of the group,' to 9, 'lower statement is very characteristic of the group,' under a forced distribution. At least two research assistants independently rated each TMT and their scores were averaged to create one Q-sort per TMT.
time_window: 1996-2002 (period covered by the firm's GDQ packet)

description: The GDQ measure of decentralization focuses on the degree to which employees at various organizational levels have decision-making power and comprises six items. Each item contrasts an upper statement (e.g., a top-down, pyramidal, and control-oriented style of management) with a lower statement (e.g., a bottom-up style of management that encourages initiative and self-control), and raters sort the cards into the nine forced-distribution categories. Scores from at least two research assistants were averaged to create one Q-sort per TMT.
time_window: 1996-2002 (period covered by the firm's GDQ packet)

variable_name: overall corporate social performance (aggregated KLD score)
description: Corporate social performance was measured with KLD scores based on performance on seven categories of stakeholder service (community relations, diversity, employee relations, environment, product, corporate governance, and human rights), each composed of several subindicators for which an organization receives a 1 or 0 for the presence (absence) of strength and a 1 or 0 for the presence of concern. Following Deckop and colleagues (2006), total concerns were subtracted from total strengths for each indicator, and the seven net scores were then averaged to obtain an overall corporate social performance score for a firm. The firm's industry was controlled for by subtracting the industry mean from the firm's overall score. Data from 2003 to 2005 were used and averaged to smooth the measure.

Dummy variable taking on the value 1 in the case of link alliances and 0 in that of scale alliances. Each alliance was classified by examining whether contributions came from one partner or overlapped, using three categories: (i) research, technology development, and product design; (ii) manufacturing facilities and capabilities; and (iii) marketing and sales networks and capabilities. When all the contributions of the partners overlapped across the three categories, the partnership was classified as a scale alliance; when in at least one of the three functional activity categories all contributions came from one partner, the alliance was considered to be of the link type. Three coders, including two authors and an industry expert, independently coded the variable, and three cases were dropped because of conflicting coding.

Absolute variation in relative market share 3, 7 and 10 years after the alliance was formed, corresponding to the percent growth or decline in relative market share. RCP3, RCP7 and RCP10 were calculated in the same way as relative competitive position when formed (RCP0), using unit volume outputs of the partners in the third, seventh, and tenth year after the alliance formation date. Relative competitive position when formed records the total global volume output of the smaller partner (measured in number of vehicles) divided by the total volume output of the larger partner.

Operationalized as the total decrease in net income of the focal firm following restatement divided by the firm revenue for the year prior to the restatement announcement. Since the matching firms have no restatement, they were assigned a value of zero for their severity measure, allowing the authors to fully capture the range of the severity measure.
scale: ratio (decrease in net income divided by prior-year revenue)
time_window: revenue in the year prior to the restatement announcement; net income decrease following the restatement

description: Takes the value of 1 if the successor CEO has been a chief executive prior to joining the restating firm, and 0 otherwise. Education and prior CEO experience were collected from proxy statements via SEC EDGAR and from focused web searches using Zoominfo, LinkedIn, Spoke.com, Forbes, Business Week, Fortune, and Google.

Takes the value of 1 if the successor CEO had experience as a CEO of returning a company which had experienced a severe loss back to profitability, and 0 otherwise. A severe loss was defined as operating return on equity greater than cost of equity for at least two consecutive years, immediately followed by at least a year of operating loss; all firms in Compustat from 1990 to 2006 that suffered a severe loss were identified, and CEOs who were put in charge during the severe losses and returned the firm to profitability were coded as turnaround CEOs.

Binary variable that takes the value of 1 if the successor has an elite educational degree at the undergraduate or graduate level and 0 otherwise. Graduates of Ivy League schools, public Ivy League schools (e.g., University of California, Berkeley), other elite private schools (e.g., Stanford, MIT), and elite service academies (e.g., the U.S. Naval Academy) were categorized as having an elite degree.

Binary variable that takes the value of 1 if the successor CEO's functional background is in finance or accounting, and 0 otherwise. Typical examples of financial or accounting backgrounds include Controller, Vice President for Finance, Chief Financial Controller, or Chief Accounting Officer. The information is available in the proxy statement and was triangulated with the other data sources.

Measured as the cumulative abnormal return surrounding the announcement of the successor CEO, from two days prior to two days after the announcement date, using financial event study analysis. The authors perused a firm's official SEC filings, usually Form 8-K, and relevant news articles to ensure they were using the precise announcement date, and the five-day window was used to capture prior leakage and any reaction not immediately reflected.
time_window: -2 to +2 days around the successor CEO announcement

description: Operationalized as the difference between the first earnings forecast made after the successor CEO was announced and the last forecast made prior to the announcement, using earnings-per-share forecasts for the same target forecast date. Observations in which the duration between the two consecutive forecasts was too great were dropped, with a duration span of up to two months (63 days) between the pre-succession and post-succession forecast.
time_window: up to 63 days between the pre- and post-succession forecasts; mean between-forecast duration of 31 days

description: Equal to the mean LIWC score for the positive tenor category from all articles about a sample firm, so the program calculates the percentage of positive content in each article. National and regional news articles were collected from Lexis-Nexis from two days prior to the successor CEO announcement to two days after, the firm name had to be included in the headline or title, and the article had to contain news about the succession announcement.
scale: percentage of words in the positive tenor dictionary
time_window: -2 to +2 days around the successor CEO announcement

description: Measured in the same way as positive coverage but for negative tenor, as the mean LIWC score for the negative tenor category from all articles about a sample firm, expressed as the percentage of negative content.
scale: percentage of words in the negative tenor dictionary
time_window: -2 to +2 days around the successor CEO announcement

variable_name: Technology performance (a given technology's performance in year t, CPWt)
description: A technology-level measure of core technical performance built on cost per watt (CPW), which is established as the standard measure for comparing performance across technologies and over time because it captures both cost and efficiency differences. Because historical CPW data is unavailable, the authors use CPW data for the final year of the sample, as reported by Greentech Media, as a baseline and then adjust the performance measure based on historical changes in efficiency and costs of materials, with a cost ratio for silicon for c-Si technology assumed equal to one for the other technologies. The formula is not readable in the text. For ease of interpretation the sign is inverted so the measure takes negative values, so a higher value implies higher performance of the technology.
scale: continuous, taking negative values where a higher value implies higher performance
time_window: year t (year of entry), with the final year of the sample as baseline

description: Operationalized based on the commercial availability of the deposition and contact manufacturing equipment, the upstream complementary assets specialized to a given technology. The variable takes a value of 2 if both the deposition and contact equipment were commercially available for a given technology prior to the year of entry, a value of 1 if either of the deposition or contact equipment were commercially available, and 0 if none of the deposition or contact equipment were commercially available. The time frame for commercial availability is identified from equipment suppliers' self-reported information in the Photon International annual equipment surveys as well as their product specifications; in almost all instances commercial availability implied the equipment was offered by at least three suppliers.
time_window: prior to the year of entry

description: A binary variable equal to 1 for the solar PV technology with which a firm chose to enter the industry, and 0 for the other technological alternatives that were commercially available in the year of entry. Given the large scale of technology-specific investments, all entrants chose to commercialize only one technology, although twelve firms did pursue other technological alternatives in later years. The variable is defined over the set of technology alternatives available to each entrant at entry.

An entrant was categorized as a diversifying entrant if it was an established firm operating in another industry before its entry into the solar PV industry, and as a start-up otherwise. For the main analysis, spinouts and incumbent-backed ventures, which represented a small proportion of the sample, were classified as start-up entrants.

variable_name: Diversifying entrants with related pre-entry capabilities
description: To classify diversifiers' pre-entry capabilities, the authors identify a diversifying firm's self-reported primary industry classification according to the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) and, based on the description for each NAICS code and following Helfat and Lieberman (2002), categorize each diversifying entrant as having pre-entry capabilities that were either related or unrelated to the commercialization of solar PV module technology. Related capabilities include semiconductor manufacturing capabilities as well as marketing and distribution capabilities related to the solar PV industry, such as customer relationships and understanding of customer preferences. The concordance between NAICS classification and the related versus unrelated categorization was discussed with solar PV industry experts, who agreed unanimously with the categorization.

For start-ups, the authors examine the background of the founder(s) and classify start-up entrants based on whether the founders' primary industry background was in related or unrelated industries based on the NAICS description. Founders with experience directly related to the technology's commercialization will be more likely to see opportunities to leverage their experience in combination with complementary assets. The concordance between NAICS classification and the related versus unrelated categorization was agreed unanimously by solar PV industry experts.

The posttreatment dummy representing the average treatment effect in difference-in-differences models. Treated equals 1 for individuals in states with no or partial pre-ACA regulations in individual insurance markets (the treated and moderately treated states) and 0 for individuals in states with the same or heavy regulations before the ACA reform. Post equals 1 for observations after the start of the ACA provisions (i.e., from 2014 onward) and 0 otherwise. The treated and control state classification builds on Heim and Yang's (2017) categorization; when the triple interaction Treated × Post × Female is included, Treated × Post estimates the treatment effect for men only.
time_window: Post from 2014 onward; pre-ACA before January 1, 2014

description: A binary indicator equal to 1 for women and 0 for men. It is the moderating variable in triple-difference models; when the triple interaction Treated × Post × Female is included in the regressions, it estimates the differential treatment effects for women relative to men.

Set to 1 if an individual was self-employed and declared a STEM occupational code at the time of the survey, and equal to 0 otherwise. The STEM occupational codes are based on the 2018 census STEM, STEM-related, and non-STEM-related code list. The measure is a broad self-employment indicator covering growth-oriented startups, sole proprietorships and bootstrapped unincorporated businesses.
scale: binary (1 = self-employed with a STEM occupational code)

description: An indicator for self-employed individuals with non-STEM occupational codes, used to evaluate the contingency of occupational field in the effects of the ACA reform.
scale: binary (1 = self-employed with a non-STEM occupational code)

description: A generic entrepreneurship indicator for self-employment regardless of occupational codes, used as an additional outcome to examine the effects of the ACA reform.

The coefficient of interest in the triple-difference regression, which represents the treatment effect difference between women and men - that is, the treatment effect on the gender gap in STEM entrepreneurship. A positive estimate suggests that the ACA reform encouraged more women than men to enter entrepreneurship, indicating a reduced gender gap. The gender gap itself is the difference between male and female STEM entrepreneurship rates.
time_window: 2011-2018, with 2013 as the event-study reference year

description: Occupational codes derived from the 2018 Standard Occupational Classification from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, with the Census 2010-to-2018 crosswalk used for linking CPS occupational codes prior to 2018 to the corresponding 2018 Census occupation codes for identifying STEM versus non-STEM categorization. A complete list of STEM versus non-STEM occupational fields is publicly downloadable from the US Census Bureau.

Equals 1 for individuals who were the policyholders of their recent health insurance plan that was purchased directly as an individual insurance plan (i.e., not related to current or past employment) and 0 otherwise. CPS ASEC respondents are asked about their last calendar year's health insurance information; the authors also use information on employment status in the last year and focus on individuals whose current employment/self-employment status is the same as last year.
scale: binary (1 = policyholder of a direct-purchase individual plan)
time_window: previous calendar year's health insurance information

description: Degree centrality of a firm's interlock network, calculated with the command 'Network . . . Centrality . . . Degree' in UCINET 6. The software estimates it by simply counting the number of other firms that are adjacent to the focal firm within the director interlocks network. Director data were collected annually and compiled into a list of directors to construct interlocking directorate networks. The published formula is unreadable in the text; the text states that a(pi,pk) equals 1 if and only if two actors are connected by a line and 0 otherwise, and that the degree centrality for an actor equals the total number of ties that actor is adjacent with for all other actors in the network.

Measured as a constraint using the command 'Network . . . Ego Network . . . Structural Holes' in UCINET. Following Burt (1992) the authors first obtained the effective size of the ego network, which is the number of contacts or alters minus the average degree of alters within the ego network, not counting the ties to the ego. Efficiency of the ego's network is the effective size divided by the number of alters; the higher the score, the richer the firm is in terms of structural holes. Fragmentation tests showed the average fragmentation level of the network across the six years was 0.48, suggesting the network is not highly fragmented.

The natural log of the annual cash compensation (salary and bonuses) that CEOs received between 2001 and 2006. It does not include long-term incentive plans such as stock options, consistent with previous compensation studies in China. The authors argue that cash compensation is directly controlled by boards and represents the closest conceptual match to 'compensation' in China.

Following Conyon and Peck (1998) the authors coded whether a firm has a CC (1) or not (0) as a dummy variable. It appears both as an independent variable predicting CEO compensation and as the dependent variable in the logistic models of setting up a CC.
scale: dummy: 1 = has a compensation committee, 0 = does not

description: Measured as the ratio of the number of founders who are active in the top management team to the size of the team. The authors state that this variable serves as a proxy for the level at which experiential knowledge of the original business model and the firm's capabilities are still preserved at the top management level. They conjecture that the higher the ratio of founders in the top management team, the stronger the influence of historical business premises and emphasis on new business development decisions.

Measured as the number of years of shared experience for the four managers with the longest tenure in the top management team. Because the mean team size in the sample is approximately six managers, the shared experience of four managers is treated as an appropriate proxy that incorporates the shared experience of the majority of managers on the team. The authors also calculate the variable as the years of shared team experience of the longest tenured three managers on the team.

Measured as the average number of managerial positions the managers previously held in the same industry. The authors state that this measure captures the breadth of industry-specific experience managers possess because, with every position in a specific firm in the industry, managers become familiar with the resources and strategies of an industry player as well as with the suppliers and buyers in the industry. Prospectus documents and proxy statements do not provide the number of years spent in each position or in total in the industry.
scale: average number of prior managerial positions

variable_name: Rate of entrepreneurial growth (rate of sales growth)
description: Measured as the annual rate of sales growth. The authors describe it as a critical indicator of performance for entrepreneurial firms that are in a stage of product commercialization and growth, and state that it reflects a firm's ability to increase its sales relative to its previous sales through innovative medical technology products. Data on firm performance are compiled from Compustat files.

Downsizing approaches were identified with a multistep analysis of historical patterns of resource reductions; downsizing by at least one firm was evident during each year and each firm had at least one downsizing event. Retrenchment was achieved by elimination of redundant resources and realignment of the administrative processes used to control and coordinate the resources. Downscaling consisted of resource reductions that lowered a firm's output without decreasing product/market scope, typically production facility idling, facility closure, and workforce reductions. Downscoping directed reductions at the resources underlying variety in a firm's activities; the horizontal forms product pruning and market withdrawal and the vertical form backward deintegration were observed.

Firm influences on choice of downsizing approach were based on an historical analysis of firm capacity expansion. If 3 of the 5 previous years showed evidence of a firm's 'substantial' investment in capacity, the firm's capacity investment was categorized as 'high'; otherwise capacity investment was categorized as 'low'. Lagged 5-year windows were used to reflect the payback period used by industry financial planners.

Firm influences on choice of downsizing approach were based on an historical analysis of firm product introductions. If 3 of the 5 previous years showed evidence of a firm's 'substantial' investment in products, the firm's product investment was categorized as 'high'; otherwise product investment was categorized as 'low'. The same lagged 5-year windows as for capacity investment were used.

variable_name: extent of recent firm investment in jointness (CAP * PRD)
description: The categorical level of each firm influence (extent of recent capacity investment, extent of recent product investment) and their interaction were used to explore the separate and combined influence of different levels and types of firm investment on choice of downsizing approach. The interaction term appears in the model as CAP * PRD.

variable_name: extent of recent competitor capacity investment
description: Measured as the average percentage of competitors who had engaged in 'substantial' capacity expansion in the 5 years prior to observation. It was expected that the greater competitor investment, the more likely a downsizing firm would retrench.

variable_name: extent of recent competitor product investment
description: Measured as the average percentage of competitors who had engaged in 'substantial' product expansion in the 5 years prior to observation. It was expected that the greater competitor investment, the more likely a downsizing firm would retrench.

variable_name: extent of recent competitor investment in jointness through contemporaneous investment
description: One of the measures used to explore the influence of the extent of competitor investment in firm-specific resources on a firm's choice of downsizing approach. It was measured as an interaction of the extent of competitor investment in capacity and products.

variable_name: extent of recent competitor investment in jointness through reconfiguration of resources
description: Measured as the proportion of competitors in the sample who had engaged in retrenchment in the 5 years prior to the year of observation. It was used to explore the influence of the extent of competitor investment in firm-specific resources on a firm's choice of downsizing approach.

Measured as a lagged 5-year average of annual demand changes in industry unit shipments of wheeled tractors (the dominant industry product). It was expected that industry demand decreases would increase managers' willingness to downscale or downscope.

The dimension along which the strategy of the firms was divided into broad vs. focused scope is similar to the concept of domain breadth. Firms characterize themselves and their competitors as 'full-line' (broad) or 'short-line' (focused) manufacturers; full-line competitors manufactured at least two types of engine-powered products - wheeled tractors and combines - as well as a wide array of implements and provided sales and financial support services to their dealerships, while short-line manufacturers focused on a limited, specialized line of equipment. Separate repeated-measures models were run for broad and focused firms.

An ego-centered network measure that asks respondents to identify the five most important external sources of advice and to report the extent to which these five sources know each other. The score is computed as (potential ties minus actual ties) divided by the number of advisors, where potential ties is the maximum number of ties that could exist among advisors (n(n-1)/2) and actual ties is the number of ties that do exist. The equation defines nonredundancy as a ratio of nonredundant ties per advisor, with low numbers indicating low nonredundancy and high numbers reflecting a network of ties that is entirely nonoverlapping.

Respondents reported the average number of conversations per month they have with each of their advisors about the business. An overall average infrequency of interaction score for each respondent is computed as one divided by the mean number of conversations per month.

Respondents indicated how far away each advisor was located in terms of travel time by car. These data were used to compute an aggregate geographic dispersion score for each respondent based on the average distance to an advisor.

A three-item scale capturing the use of the services available from the regional industrial extension center. A 7-point scale similar to the acquisition scale was developed to capture three primary decision-making stages: knowledge-awareness, evaluation-choice, and utilization.

The acquisition of competitive capabilities scale applied to pollution prevention, operationalized with three items measuring various product and process changes. The items were adapted from a national survey of pollution prevention conducted in one of the job shop industries selected for the study. The acquisition scale is based on the Assimilation of Innovation scale and captures the stages of awareness, evaluation, adoption, utilization and institutionalization.
Operationalized with three items that tap into the practices a firm uses to gather information about rivals. The items are based on the measurement instrument created and validated by Miller (1987).

Measured with three items capturing the use of statistical process control charts to provide operators with feedback, so that operators base their actions on the variability of the manufacturing process. The items are based on the measurement instrument developed by Flynn, Sakakibara, and Schroeder (1995). The authors report that this construct is marginal, at 0.61, on internal consistency reliability.

Total count of games from the publisher in the previous 8 years within the genre of the focal new game release, logged to deal with overdispersion. Each individual title release (not title-platform) is counted, so a game released on two platforms is not counted twice. The 8 year window equates to about 1.5 generations and broadly captures all experience in the current generation plus the previous generation. Genres are used to define the niche within which the experience is counted.

A Herfindahl index capturing the diversity of the games released by publisher i in the previous 8 years across genres. The share of a genre is the number of games that the firm has in a particular genre divided by the total number of games released by the publisher. This variable ranges between 0 and 1, where 1 represents maximum diversity. The formula as printed is not readable in the extracted text.

The natural logarithm of the revenues generated by a title-platform in the first 12 months of its release in constant 1995 dollars. Almost 75% of a game's sales occur within 12 months and the correlation between 12 month and lifetime sales is 0.99. Because video games is a hit driven industry, a log-transformation is used.

A binary measure distinguishing between transition (1) and stable (0) periods. The transition period covers the year of the first console's release in a new generation through the end of the year of the last console's release for that generation. In the sample, 22% of games are released in a transition period.
Count of years since 1994 (i.e., year of observation minus 1994) to capture broader industry evolution.

We used the log of per capita gross national income (GNI) in constant 2000 U.S. dollars. GNI was chosen because it is the primary criterion the World Bank uses to classify countries into income groups and determine aid allocation. For convenience in interpreting the results, the inverse of this measure was taken so that a higher number would be associated with greater income poverty.

A composite built from Kaufmann, Kraay, and Mastruzzi's Worldwide Governance Indicators. The governance index captures six individual dimensions of state capability, which were combined into a single measure of state fragility. In the index a higher score indicates a stronger state, so the inverse of the measure was taken so that a higher number is associated with a more fragile state. Because the variable was on average correlated with itself at 0.99 from one year to the next, the average measure of state fragility for each country across the study period was used.

variable_name: Commercial microfinance borrowers per thousand citizens
description: The number of borrowers registered to all commercial microfinance lenders in a particular country divided by the total population of that country. Because this created a very small number, the result was multiplied by 1,000. The variable was calculated for each country every year from 1998 to 2009, and taking the log of the dependent variable significantly improved model fit for Hypotheses 1 through 3.

variable_name: Proportion of total microfinance borrowers registered to commercial lenders
description: The total number of borrowers registered to for-profit microfinance lenders in a country divided by the sum of all microfinance borrowers in that country (those registered to both for-profit and nonprofit lenders). Because the resulting variable was a proportion bounded by one and zero, a logit transformation of the variable was used (ln(P/(1-P)), where P is the proportion of for-profit borrowers to total borrowers).
scale: proportion bounded by 0 and 1, logit transformed

description: The total operating costs a commercial microfinance lender incurs to make a single loan. MIX provides the median value of these costs per loan for each country each year, which was incorporated into the analysis. Operating costs include all personnel expenses (including salary and benefits), administrative expenses, depreciation and amortization, bank charges, insurance costs, and other expenses incurred to run the organization.

variable_name: Commercial capital (log of total capital invested)
description: The log of total capital invested into each country's microfinance sector that came from 'commercial' funders. 'Commercial' funders were defined as any organizations that MIX labels 'financial institutions' or 'funds', as opposed to 'development finance institutions' or 'governments'. Because MIX started reporting funding data only in 2007, the hypothesis was tested in cross-sectional data for the most recent year available.

The same operationalization as in the longitudinal analysis: the log of per capita gross national income (GNI) in constant 2000 U.S. dollars, with the inverse taken so that a higher number is associated with greater income poverty, used in the cross-sectional model for the most recent year available.

The same composite measure of state fragility built from the six dimensions of the Worldwide Governance Indicators, with the inverse taken so that a higher number is associated with a more fragile state, used in the cross-sectional model for the most recent year available.

variable_name: Revolving door pre-transition to in-house lobbying, decayed
description: A dummy assigned the value of one during all years of a USDA revolving regulator's tenure if that particular regulator subsequently took a position with the focal GE crop producer in the sample as its in-house lobbyist, and zero otherwise. The dummy is transformed by a time-decayed function, 1/t x revolving door dummy, where t is the minimum time distance in years to the transition from the USDA to the private sector, so that the farther the regulator is from the transition the closer to zero the value becomes. Where a given firm-year had more than one revolver associated with it, the minimum time distance across all associated revolving regulators is used; for regulators under a full year's time distance to transition the decayed value of the dummy is kept at its maximum value of one.

variable_name: Revolving door pre-transition to contract lobbying, decayed
description: A dummy that takes the value of one during all years of a USDA revolving regulator's tenure if that particular regulator subsequently took a position with a lobbying firm representing GE crop producers from the sample, and zero otherwise. It is transformed by the same time-decayed function, 1/t x dummy, where t is the minimum time distance in years to the regulator's transition from the USDA to the private sector.

variable_name: Revolving door post-transition to in-house lobbying, decayed
description: A dummy that takes the value of one for GE crop producers that have a former USDA regulator on their staff and zero otherwise, transformed by the time-decayed function 1/t x dummy, where t is the time distance in years from the regulator's transition from the USDA to the private sector. For example, DuPont has a value of one from 2009 onwards because it hired a former USDA regulator as its Director of Federal Government Affairs.

variable_name: Revolving door post-transition to contract lobbying, decayed
description: A dummy that measures one if the focal firm has retained as their lobbyist at least one former USDA regulator and zero otherwise, transformed by the time-decayed function 1/t x dummy, where t is the time distance in years from the regulator's transition from the USDA to the private sector.

For each crop, the authors have a date0 (the date when the planting request was received) and, for those approved, a date1 (the date when approval was issued); the time between date1 and date0 is the duration of the regulatory process, measured in days. The authors adopt an event history approach and estimate a log-logistic accelerated failure time model in which the dependent variable is interpreted as survival time, with negative coefficients indicating faster approval and positive coefficients indicating a slower regulatory process. Approval time varied from 0 to 852 days across crops.

Overall cognitive diversity was an aggregation of the two dimensions, preference diversity and belief diversity. It was assessed with four questionnaire items asking how strongly members of the top management team agree or disagree with each other about the best way to maximize the firm's long term profitability, what the firm's goal priorities should be, the best way to ensure the firm's long-run survival, and which organizational objectives should be considered most important. All cognitive diversity items were reverse scored.

Preference diversity was one of the two dimensions of cognitive diversity and was assessed with two of the four diversity questionnaire items. The items concerned preferred goals for the firm, and the text does not identify which of the four items these were. All cognitive diversity items were reverse scored.

Belief diversity was one of the two dimensions of cognitive diversity and was assessed with two of the four diversity questionnaire items. Belief items focused on one domain, the determinants of long-term organizational viability; the text does not identify which of the four items these were. All cognitive diversity items were reverse scored.

Comprehensiveness was assessed through three questionnaire items, each asking the chief executive to indicate how comprehensive the firm's approach is relative to descriptions of a very comprehensive and a very non-comprehensive firm. The items covered determining the cause of a major problem, generating alternatives to solve an important problem, and evaluating a particular action. These items were used by Fredrickson (1984), Fredrickson and Iaquinto (1989), and Fredrickson and Mitchell (1984) in their validity check procedures.

Each chief executive was asked to select the statement that best described his/her firm's approach to strategic planning. The first listed statement was indicative of a lack of formal strategic planning (coded as 1), the second was indicative of moderately extensive planning (coded as 2), and the third was indicative of extensive planning (coded as 3). The statements were developed by Robinson and Pearce, who provided evidence of some convergent validity.

A slightly modified version of the Study 1 measure, focused on the hospital sector. Five-point scales rather than seven-point scales were used for cognitive diversity. The measure combined preference diversity and belief diversity.
A slightly modified version of the Study 1 preference diversity measure, focused on the hospital sector, using a five-point scale. It is one of the two dimensions of cognitive diversity.
A slightly modified version of the Study 1 belief diversity measure, focused on the hospital sector, using a five-point scale. It is one of the two dimensions of cognitive diversity.
A slightly modified version of the Study 1 comprehensiveness measure, focused on the hospital sector. Five-point scales rather than seven-point scales were used for comprehensiveness.
A slightly modified version of the Study 1 extensiveness statement measure, focused on the hospital sector.

Assessed perceptually with the same four scale items and perceptual key informant methodology used in Studies 1 and 2, but each executive within a strategic business unit rated the level of diversity among the unit's executives rather than only the chief executive. The responses from executives within the same business unit were averaged to arrive at an aggregate score for the business unit as a whole.

One of the two perceptual key-informant diversity variables, based on the same four scale items used in Studies 1 and 2 but rated by each executive within the business unit, whose responses were then averaged to the business-unit level.

One of the two perceptual key-informant diversity variables, based on the same four scale items used in Studies 1 and 2 but rated by each executive within the business unit, whose responses were then averaged to the business-unit level.

Each executive was asked to rate the importance of 17 operative goals taken from a competing values model of organizational effectiveness. For each business unit, coefficients of variation were calculated for each of the 17 items; following factor analysis and other scale development techniques, these were summarized into preference diversity concerning human resource goals, system-maintenance goals, and profit goals.

Each executive was asked to rate how positively or negatively each of 22 business tactics would influence long-term profitability in their strategic business unit. Coefficients of variation were calculated for each business unit, factor analyzed, and summarized into a smaller set of dimensions of belief diversity concerning the efficacy of maintaining flexibility, low cost vs. differentiation tactics, innovativeness, and advertising.

Assessed through five questionnaire items developed by ogilvie and Glick (1990) and used in the CODE study, asking the extent to which the firm develops many alternative responses, considers many diverse criteria for eliminating possible courses of action, thoroughly examines multiple explanations for the problem or opportunity, conducts multiple examinations of any suggested course of action, and searches extensively for possible responses. Because all executives within a strategic business unit were asked the same questions, responses from executives within the same business unit were averaged to arrive at aggregate comprehensiveness data for the business unit.

The strength of market-supporting institutions is proxied by five items of the economic freedom index developed by the Heritage Foundation. The five categories selected as most closely reflecting the efficiency of markets are business freedom, trade freedom, property rights, investment freedom and financial freedom. Each category is reported on a scale of 0 to 100, and the time-series nature of the index allowed the authors to assign each observation the value pertaining to the year of entry. The index was interpolated for some missing years because it used to be published only every second year.

The survey asked subsidiaries to identify the three types of resources that were most important to the success of their business ventures, out of a list of 17 items, and to state the extent to which these resources were contributed by the parent MNE, the local subsidiary, overseas markets and the local market in percentage terms. Each resource was classified as tangible or intangible, and the share of resources sourced from the host country was defined as the sum of the shares sourced from the local partner and the host country market. The index reflects the relative contribution of local intangible resources to the overall package of resources the firm considers essential for its competitiveness, giving more weight to the resources ranked as more important; the weights are 3, 2, 1 and 0 for resources ranked first, second, third and not ranked, and the formula itself is not readable in the text.

The survey asked subsidiaries to identify the three types of resources that were most important to the success of their business ventures, out of a list of 17 items, and to state the extent to which these resources were contributed by the parent MNE, the local subsidiary, overseas markets and the local market in percentage terms. Each resource was classified as tangible or intangible, and the share of resources sourced from the host country was defined as the sum of the shares sourced from the local partner and the host country market. The index reflects the relative contribution of local tangible resources to the overall package of resources the firm considers essential for its competitiveness, giving more weight to the resources ranked as more important; the weights are 3, 2, 1 and 0 for resources ranked first, second, third and not ranked, and the formula itself is not readable in the text.

The dependent variable is categorical, based on the self-classification by respondents in the questionnaires and triangulated by other questions in the survey; it takes the value of 1 for greenfield, 2 for acquisition and 3 for JV. A multinomial logit model estimates the effect of the independent variables on the probability (differential odds) that one of the alternatives is chosen, and the reported coefficients are marginal effects of the probability that any of the three alternatives is chosen over the other two. The greenfield equation thus captures the probability of greenfield entry relative to the other two modes.

The dependent variable is categorical, based on the self-classification by respondents in the questionnaires and triangulated by other questions in the survey; it takes the value of 1 for greenfield, 2 for acquisition and 3 for JV. A multinomial logit model estimates the effect of the independent variables on the probability (differential odds) that one of the alternatives is chosen, and the reported coefficients are marginal effects of the probability that any of the three alternatives is chosen over the other two. The acquisition equation thus captures the probability of acquisition entry relative to the other two modes.

The dependent variable is categorical, based on the self-classification by respondents in the questionnaires and triangulated by other questions in the survey; it takes the value of 1 for greenfield, 2 for acquisition and 3 for JV. A multinomial logit model estimates the effect of the independent variables on the probability (differential odds) that one of the alternatives is chosen, and the reported coefficients are marginal effects of the probability that any of the three alternatives is chosen over the other two. The JV equation thus captures the probability of joint venture entry relative to greenfield and acquisition.

The need for local resources was measured by two survey-based indices, one for tangible and one for intangible resources. Each is the weighted share of the three most important resources of the venture that were sourced from the host country, with weights of 3, 2 and 1 for the first, second and third ranked resource.

Describes the pricing provision used in the focal contract to procure the engineered component or subsystem, adapted from Crocker and Reynolds (1993), Ghosh and John (2005), and Lo et al. (2012). Closed-price formats are agreements in which the OEM and the supplier agreed to either a fixed price or a price formula tied to objective, verifiable and exogenous criteria (e.g., inflation in commodity prices, producer price index). Open-price formats are those that either did not specify a price ahead of shipment, or did specify a price but allowed for negotiated adjustments. Price format is coded as a binary variable, with closed-price and open-price contracts assigned a value of 1 and 0, respectively.

The purchasing manager of each OEM rated on a six-item, 7-point Likert scale how extensively the supplier is required to invest in resources, efforts, and training to produce the component that fits the OEM's end product. The measure denotes a broad spectrum of tangible and intangible investments undertaken by the supplier. The authors note that the agreements do not usually describe in detail the specific investments to be made by the supplier, suggesting these investments are non-contractible in this context.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: A single-item scale that rates the complexity of the interface between the component and the end product. The more complex the interface among the end product's components, the more difficult it is to pre-specify all the architectural and technical interactions among them, so that modifications elsewhere in the system require unscheduled adaptation of the focal component. The authors describe interface complexity as primarily a function of the architecture and design features of the OEM's end product and hence an exogenous feature of the buyer–supplier relationship.

A five-item, 7-point Likert scale that measures how much customer value the OEM's end-product commands over competing products, adapted from Ghosh and John (2005). It measures how strong the OEM's product is in terms of price premium, customer perception, and its competitive advantage compared to products offered by its focal competitors, and thus captures the OEM's underlying preexisting resources and capabilities that a supplier may potentially appropriate.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: The key informant managers rated on a two-item, 7-point Likert scale the extent to which the procured component has helped to enhance the OEM's end-product performance and capture design and engineering synergies.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

variable_name: positive tone of a firm's news media coverage (mean positive words per article)
description: For each newspaper article in the sample, the authors used the Loughran and McDonald (2011, 2014, 2016) dictionary to obtain the number of words denoting positive emotion. Because the analyses are at the firm-newspaper-year level, they used the average of the number of positive words for each firm-newspaper-year combination as the dependent variable.

CSR is measured using data from the KLD database, which contains ratings of firms along several dimensions, including commitment to diversity, the environment, employees, the community, human rights, corporate governance, and product quality. Following previous research, the authors constructed a composite measure of CSR by adding the number of strengths for each firm in a given year for all KLD dimensions besides the corporate governance dimension and the product dimension.

Following previous research (e.g., Peake 2007), the authors used newspapers' endorsement of a Republican presidential candidate as a measure of newspaper conservatism. The variable is equal to one if the focal newspaper only endorsed Republican presidential candidates during the period of study (i.e., in the 2000, 2004, and 2008 presidential elections). The variable is equal to zero if the newspaper only endorsed Democratic candidates or if it endorsed Republican candidates in some elections and Democratic candidates in others.

CEO conservatism is measured using political donations data from DIME, which tracks political donations made by individuals. Based on the assumption that individuals prefer to donate to ideologically proximate politicians, DIME uses spatial models that capture patterns of who gives to whom to estimate a campaign finance (CF) score for each individual in the database; the higher the CF score, the stronger the individual's conservatism. Some CEOs made no political donations; the authors either treated nondonor CEOs as moderates and assigned them the median CF score or excluded the nondonor CEOs from the analyses.

Using data from Compustat, the authors captured stock market performance of a firm by the annual change of its stock price, accounting for stock splits. Because they are interested in poor stock market performance to test Hypothesis 3, they multiplied the measure by -1.

The percentage of the common shares of each firm that were owned by public pension funds holding at least $100 million in equity assets at the end of 2001 and therefore required to file 13-Fs with the SEC. The authors focused on public pension funds because they do not depend on the management of the corporations they invest in for other business. Data were reported in the Spectrum database for 2001.

The number of security analysts who issued earnings forecasts or investment recommendations for a given client in the last half of 2001. The natural logarithm of this number is used since analyst-induced demand for audit quality was expected to increase at a decreasing rate. Data on analyst coverage were obtained from I/B/E/S.
Two binary variables indicating whether a firm was traded on the NYSE or the NASDAQ, each coded 1 for yes and 0 otherwise.

A binary variable coded 1 if a firm decided to use a Big 4 auditor and 0 otherwise. The Big 4 are PricewaterhouseCoopers, Deloitte & Touche, KPMG, and Ernst & Young, the surviving members of the Big 5 that constituted the high-status bracket.

variable_name: choice of a particular Big 4 auditor
description: A binary variable with four observations for each firm, one for each firm-auditor dyad, coded 1 if a firm decided to use a particular Big 4 auditor and 0 otherwise.

Industry specialization measured as auditors' market shares within the client's two-digit SIC industry, calculated at the county level. Market share is the total sales of an auditor's clients in a particular industry divided by the total sales of firms within that industry, not including the focal firm's market share. The measure takes a value of 1 when all of a focal firm's competitors were audited by a particular Big 4 auditor and 0 if none of the competitors were audited by that auditor; a squared term is used to test the proposed curvilinear effect.

Industry specialization measured as auditors' market shares within the client's two-digit SIC industry, calculated at the national level. Market share is the total sales of an auditor's clients in a particular industry divided by the total sales of firms within that industry, not including the focal firm's market share. The measure takes a value of 1 when all of a focal firm's competitors were audited by a particular Big 4 auditor and 0 if none were; a squared term is used to test the proposed curvilinear effect.

The number of Wall Street Journal articles in 2000 and 2001 describing the involvement in audit failures of firms located in a particular county. Articles were retrieved by first collecting all WSJ articles referring to Big 4 auditors and then identifying, within that population, articles describing audit failures.

The number of Wall Street Journal articles in 2000 and 2001 describing auditors' involvement in audit failures, regardless of the location of the clients behind the audit failure. Articles were retrieved by first collecting all WSJ articles referring to Big 4 auditors and then identifying, within that population, articles describing audit failures.

Value derived by the high Tobin's q firm over the [ - 1,0] period, obtained by multiplying abnormal returns with market value. Prediction errors were calculated for the window [ - 1,0] from a market model estimated over the period - 250 to - 50 with the announcement date as day 0, using the CRSP equally weighted index as the market return; value created is the prediction error multiplied by the market value at the year-end preceding the formation of the JV.
time_window: [ - 1,0] announcement window; market model estimated over - 250 to - 50

description: Value derived by the low Tobin's q firm over the [ - 1,0] period, obtained by multiplying abnormal returns with market value. Prediction errors were calculated for the window [ - 1,0] from a market model estimated over the period - 250 to - 50 with the announcement date as day 0, using the CRSP equally weighted index as the market return; value created is the prediction error multiplied by the market value at the year-end preceding the formation of the JV.
time_window: [ - 1,0] announcement window; market model estimated over - 250 to - 50

variable_name: Tobin's q (HIQ, LOQ, industry adjusted q)
description: Tobin's q was measured as the sum of market value of equity, short- and long-term debt, preferred stock at liquidating value, and book value of convertible debt normalized by book value of total assets. Firms in each of the 344 JVs were assigned to a HI group (higher Tobin's q than the partner in the dyad) and a LO group (lower Tobin's q than the partner). The industry adjusted measure was calculated as the Tobin's q of the focal firm minus the average Tobin's q of all firms reporting the same SIC code in Compustat.

variable_name: absolute value of the difference between the SIC codes of the core business of the two partners
description: The authors calculated the absolute value of the difference between the SIC codes of the core business of the two partners, the logic being that the closer the SIC codes the more likely the partners are direct competitors. The hypothesis was tested in the subsample where the difference was below the median of the 344 JVs, and further in subsamples with distance values of less than 1,000 and 500.

JV experience was measured as a count of all prior JVs undertaken by a firm listed in the SDC database. The hypothesis was tested in the subsample where both the low Tobin's q firm and the high Tobin's q firm had above median JV experience.

Conflicts in a host country are measured for three types. Armed conflicts are contested incompatibilities that concern governments and/or territories where the use of armed force between two parties, of which at least one is the government of a state, results in at least 25 battle-related deaths in a year. One-sided violent conflicts are the use of armed force by the government of a state or a formally organized group against civilians that result in at least 25 deaths in a year. Nonstate conflicts are the use of armed force between two organized armed groups, neither of which is the government of a state, that result in at least 25 battle-related deaths in a year. All conflict data come from Uppsala University's Conflict Data Program.

This variable accounts for MNC experience with specific types of conflicts (armed conflicts, one-sided conflicts, and nonstate conflicts). Firm experience with each type of violent conflict is measured by counting the total number of subsidiaries that belong to a given MNC in countries that were affected by each type of conflict in which the MNC had operated in a previous year. The authors state this is consistent with the notion that experience can be measured in terms of the cumulative number of task performances.

This variable accounts for MNC experience with specific types of conflicts in a host country. To measure country-specific experience with each type of violent conflict the authors counted the number of subsidiaries in a host country that were affected by each type of conflict in the previous year. These count variables for corporate-level and country-specific experiences capture the intensity of international and host country activities.

MNC investment in a host country at the subsidiary level is measured as the number of wholly owned subsidiaries hand-collected from the annual reports of each sample firm. Only wholly owned subsidiaries are counted because many firms did not report partially owned subsidiaries or ownership information for subsidiaries, and because the establishment of a wholly owned subsidiary brings substantial responsibility, commitment, and higher risks to the MNC's headquarters. The second-stage expansion model considers only host countries in which a firm has already operated.

A dummy variable designating whether or not a RISC workstation maker had been vertically integrated into designing CISC processors for workstations prior to its use of RISC, coded 1 for yes and 0 for no. No vertical integration into CISC is the omitted category in the regressions, so a negative coefficient implies that incumbents that had been vertically integrated into CISC performed worse than those that had not been. The authors state that Hypothesis 1 suggests the coefficient of this variable should be negative.
time_window: prior to the firm's use of RISC

description: A dummy variable designating whether or not a RISC workstation maker was vertically integrated into designing RISC processors, coded 1 for yes and 0 for no. The authors state that Hypothesis 2 suggests the coefficient of this variable should be positive.

The technical performance of the resulting workstation, measured in SPECinteger, a calculation originated by SPEC that many firms settled on as the preferred unit of performance in terms of speed alone. Performance data for 1986 to 1988 came from Workstation Laboratories, and data from 1989 to 1993 came from SPEC. The measure was estimated in log-linear form because computer performance improved exponentially over the period.

The speed of a workstation divided by the price that the workstation maker charges for it, expressed as SPECintegers per $1,000. Many workstation developers touted price-performance as the measure of how well they were doing, since it represented what customers valued in workstations. It was estimated in log-linear form.

The revenue market share of the workstation maker, built from International Data Corporation market share and price data. The authors argue that if a firm is effective at product development, its products not only fetch a price premium but also attract more customers, so revenue market share captures whether a firm can pursue a low-cost or differentiator strategy. Profitability measures were not used because workstations were often only one division of the makers and many makers were private. It was estimated in linear form.

A dummy variable distinguishing new entrants from incumbents. An incumbent (1 = 'yes,' 0 = 'no') was a firm that developed and marketed CISC workstations before adopting RISC technology, and a new entrant was a firm that entered the workstation subfield using RISC technology; in the regressions the variable is reported as 'New entrant.'

Calculated by combining two measures from the performance evaluation survey, each scored by lead partners on a Likert scale from one to five. The first measure considered the partners' contribution to the firm in terms of new knowledge, from 'Meets minimum expectations for contributing to the firm's knowledge capital and assets' to 'Industry recognized thought leader whose ideas and assets have impact in the marketplace (ROI)'. The second measure looked at the partners' ability to create new knowledge and expertise, with anchors 'Much better at leveraging existing knowledge and expertise' and 'Much better at developing new knowledge and expertise'.
