Taking the average of these two measures creates the combined variable innovation performance; the two measures have a Cronbach Alpha of 0.78.
scale: 1 to 5 Likert scale for each item, averaged
time_window: annual review for 1999, collected at the beginning of 2000

variable_name: density between internal-local and internal-global ties
description: Density of connections between the internal-local and internal-global ties in the partner's network. It was calculated in the same way as the density within the categories of ties, except that the total number of possible ties between the two groups is the multiplication of the number of nodes in each group. The number of ties was counted and weighted by tie strength, which is the emotional closeness between each alter tie, rated on a scale from 'distant' to 'especially close' with 'neither distant nor especially close' in the middle; this number was divided by the total number of possible ties. The formula block for this measure is unreadable in the text.
time_window: at the time of the network survey (November 1999 to January 2000)

variable_name: density between external-local and external-global ties
description: Density of connections between the external-local and external-global ties in the partner's network, computed with the same procedure as the other between-category densities: ties counted and weighted by tie strength and divided by the total number of possible ties between the two groups, which is the multiplication of the number of nodes in each group. Tie strength is the emotional closeness between alters, rated from 'distant' to 'especially close'. The formula block is unreadable in the text.
time_window: at the time of the network survey (November 1999 to January 2000)

variable_name: density between internal-local and external-local ties
description: Density of connections between the internal-local and external-local ties in the partner's network, computed with the same procedure as the other between-category densities: ties counted and weighted by tie strength and divided by the total number of possible ties between the two groups. Tie strength is the emotional closeness between alters, rated from 'distant' to 'especially close'. The formula block is unreadable in the text.
time_window: at the time of the network survey (November 1999 to January 2000)

variable_name: density between internal-global and external-local ties
description: Density of connections between the internal-global and external-local ties in the partner's network, computed with the same procedure as the other between-category densities: ties counted and weighted by tie strength and divided by the total number of possible ties between the two groups. Tie strength is the emotional closeness between alters, rated from 'distant' to 'especially close'. The formula block is unreadable in the text.
time_window: at the time of the network survey (November 1999 to January 2000)

variable_name: density between internal-local and external-global ties
description: Density of connections between the internal-local and external-global ties in the partner's network, computed with the same procedure as the other between-category densities: ties counted and weighted by tie strength and divided by the total number of possible ties between the two groups. Tie strength is the emotional closeness between alters, rated from 'distant' to 'especially close'. The formula block is unreadable in the text.
time_window: at the time of the network survey (November 1999 to January 2000)

variable_name: density between internal-global and external-global ties
description: Density of connections between the internal-global and external-global ties in the partner's network, computed with the same procedure as the other between-category densities: ties counted and weighted by tie strength and divided by the total number of possible ties between the two groups. Tie strength is the emotional closeness between alters, rated from 'distant' to 'especially close'. The formula block is unreadable in the text.
time_window: at the time of the network survey (November 1999 to January 2000)

description: The log value of the number of workers in each state employed by firms with 10,000 or more workers nationally, derived from establishment-level EEO-1 reports. If a firm has 10,000 domestic workers, 5,000 in State A and 5,000 in State B, the measure in each state reflects the 5,000 workers employed there.

The Gini coefficient measures the percentage of area that lies between the Lorenz curve and a line of perfect equality. It varies between 0, which represents complete equality, and 1, which indicates complete inequality, and is expressed in percentage terms for ease of interpretation. The historical data were compiled from pre-tax income from IRS tax records by Frank (2009).

A Blau index of racial diversity, reflecting the chance that two randomly selected group members belong to different categories, was created for each large firm from EEO-1 reports using four race categories: white, black, Hispanic, and Asian. The index was standardized by dividing by its theoretical maximum of .75 to create the index of quality variation, and a weighted average across all large firms employing workers in each state in each year was multiplied by 100.

A Blau index was created to indicate how dispersed employment was in each large firm, based on establishment-level EEO-1 employment data. A weighted average of the Blau index for all large firms that employed workers in each state in each year gives a state-level index of establishment dispersion, which was multiplied by 100. Because there is no theoretical maximum for the number of establishments a firm can have, the measure was not standardized.
placeholder removed

Rover's share of gross transaction volume in a zip code, equal to Rover GTV divided by the sum of Rover and DogVacay GTV, with sellers' zip codes used for the market definition. Measured in 2016, the year prior to the acquisition. Zip codes are separated into groups with market shares below 20%, between 20% and 40%, between 40% and 60%, between 60% and 80%, and above 80%.
scale: 0 to 1, grouped into 20 percentage point bins
time_window: 2016, the year prior to the acquisition

description: Logged number of transactions in a zip code and month. For the platform-level tests the outcome is the (log) number of transactions of buyers whose booking inquiries in the prior calendar year were all made on Rover, or analogously all made on DogVacay. For the market-level test the outcome is the (log) total number of transactions in a zip code-month regardless of whether they were intermediated by DogVacay or Rover.
time_window: monthly, relative to February 2017, the month before the acquisition announcement

description: Number of successful transactions in a given month and zip code divided by the number of posted requests. Computed for the same buyer groups as the transaction outcomes (Rover-only buyers, DogVacay-only buyers, and market totals).
scale: ratio of stays to posted requests

variable_name: difference in outcomes between DogVacay and Rover buyers in symmetric markets
description: Estimated difference in outcomes between DogVacay buyers in markets with Rover market shares in (80% − s, 100% − s) and Rover buyers in markets with Rover market shares in (s, s+20%), i.e., markets where the two groups of buyers experienced the same change in platform size. The authors attribute any such difference in outcomes between Rover and DogVacay buyers in these symmetric markets to a reduction in platform differentiation.

A user is defined as multihoming if they transact at least once on both platforms over the five years before the acquisition. The share of multihoming users is computed separately for buyers and for sellers.

Buyers are classified as DogVacay buyers if all their booking inquiries in a given calendar year before the merger were made on DogVacay (Rover buyers are defined in the same way for Rover). Their outcomes, match rates and number of transactions, are then followed by zip code and month in the following calendar year. Multihomers with inquiries on both platforms are analyzed separately.

Text similarity between the patent portfolios of the outsider and the target in the year before the acquisition announcement. For each patent, a list of words is created by concatenating the title and abstract, eliminating stop words, single-character words and numbers, and restricting the list to nouns and stem words, then extracting unique keywords. Keywords are aggregated at the patent portfolio level using all patents filed in the five years before the announcement, and keywords appearing in a single portfolio or in more than 25% of the patent portfolios of firms in CRSP-Compustat each year are removed. For each firm and year a column vector is created whose element is the number of patents in the portfolio including a keyword divided by the total number of keywords in the portfolio, and TechProx is the cosine similarity between these vectors, calibrated to have the same level of coarseness as the three-digit USPTO technological classes.
level: outsider-target firm pair at the acquisition announcement
time_window: year before the acquisition announcement; patents filed in the 5 years preceding the announcement

description: Cumulative abnormal returns on the outsider's stock over a window starting two trading days before and ending two trading days after the acquisition announcement. The market model is estimated over 250 trading days ending 42 trading days before the deal announcement, with the CRSP value-weighted index as the market return, and abnormal returns are the residuals of that model. The cumulative abnormal returns are the sum of the daily abnormal returns over the 5-trading-day window; at least 100 days with nonmissing returns in the estimation period and nonmissing returns in all 5 event days are required, and CAR is winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles.
time_window: 250 trading days ending 42 trading days before the announcement (estimation); 5-trading-day window [-2, +2] around the announcement (event)

description: Return on assets is used as the measure of firm performance. It is obtained by dividing operating income by total assets, and both inputs come from COMPUSTAT. The authors describe ROA as the most widely used metric of accounting profitability and the most common performance variable in variance decomposition studies.

Each industry-year is classified into one of three latent regimes using Hamilton's regime switching model applied to the growth rate of industry sales, calculated by first differencing the logarithm of industry sales from value of shipments data. Transition probabilities are Markovian and parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood. Smoothed probabilities are computed for each state/year combination and the industry in that year is assigned to the stage with the highest probability.

The share of variance in ROA explained by industry membership, obtained from a four-way cross-classified and nested mixture model of ROA estimated separately for the growth, maturity, and decline subsamples. Repeated ROA observations are clustered by segment, which is simultaneously cross-classified by the respective industry and corporate parent.
scale: percentage of variance in ROA explained

description: The share of variance in ROA explained by the corporate parent, obtained from the same four-way cross-classified and nested mixture model of ROA estimated separately for the growth, maturity, and decline subsamples. Repeated ROA observations are clustered by segment cross-classified by industry and corporate parent.
scale: percentage of variance in ROA explained

description: The share of variance in ROA explained by the business-unit (segment) level, obtained from the same four-way cross-classified and nested mixture model of ROA estimated separately for the growth, maturity, and decline subsamples.
scale: percentage of variance in ROA explained

description: The authors aggregate the strengths and weaknesses ratings from KLD to create a net social performance score for each firm. Seven criteria (community, corporate governance, diversity, employee relations, environment, human rights, and product) are scored on an integer scale ranging from +1 (an area of strength) to -1 (an area of weakness), with 0 a neutral score; the remaining six criteria receive scores reflecting only whether the area represents one of weakness (-1) or a neutral score (0). Because testing for quadratics with a measure that can take negative as well as positive values distorts inference in multiple regression formats, the authors add 12 to each observation, so that 0 now reflects the least socially responsible firm and 27 the most socially responsible firm.
scale: 0 to 27 after the linear transformation (original net KLD score ranged from -12 to 15)

description: The net KLD score is an assessment of a firm's overall level of social responsibility and so proxies for stakeholder influence capacity; to achieve high net KLD scores, firms must have engaged in significant acts of social responsibility, and these acts are the flows that accrue into a firm's stock of SIC. The authors acknowledge that their KLD measure is an imperfect proxy for SIC in much the same way that R&D is an imperfect proxy for absorptive capacity, and that their measure captures relative differences in performance across firms at a given point in time rather than the dynamic, path-dependent construct.

Following Waddock and Graves (1997), the dependent variable is the return on assets for a given firm in a given year. ROA is defined as net income divided by total assets. The authors note that the use of ratio measures such as ROA as dependent variables may exaggerate relations of interest and confound the interpretation of results, which is why they complement it with an unscaled measure.

Net income is an unscaled measure of firm performance used as a complement to ROA. It is defined as the earnings (after interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) of a firm in a given year, expressed in millions of U.S. dollars. The authors include it because ratio measures may exaggerate relations of interest, and because each variable might reveal different aspects of performance.
An indicator that is equal to 1 if the investor is the LP of the focal firm's lead VC fund prior to the focal firm's IPO and zero otherwise.
time_window: prior to the focal firm's IPO

description: Event-time three-month holding risk-adjusted excess return to the focal firm's publicly traded stock, where the investment period starts at the end of the calendar quarter of the focal firm's IPO date. It is measured using Carhart's (1997) four-factor model alpha, which is the return above the expected return based on the investment's loadings on market, size, book-to-market, and momentum risk factors.
time_window: three-month holding period starting at the end of the calendar quarter of the IPO

description: The economic policy uncertainty index from Baker et al. (2016), which reports the frequency of articles in 10 leading U.S. newspapers that contain terms about economic policy uncertainty. The monthly index is averaged over the course of the year.

The Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index, an expected measure of S&P 500 index price fluctuations during the next 30 days. The average across monthly VIX measures for a particular year is used.

A dummy variable for the entrepreneurial firm's product stage, used as a proxy for information asymmetry. Firms with earlier-stage products have high information asymmetry regarding product development duration, cost, and termination, and investors have less understanding of the product's profit potential.

A dummy variable that takes on one if the entrepreneurial firm is in high-tech industries and zero otherwise, used as a proxy for information asymmetry. The technological landscape in high-tech industries can change rapidly, creating substantial uncertainty.

A dummy variable that takes one if the investor is within 100 km of the focal entrepreneurial firm and zero otherwise, used as a measure of low information asymmetry. If the focal entrepreneurial firm is local for the investor, the investor faces less information asymmetry.

The age of the focal entrepreneurial firm, used to operationalize the information asymmetry faced by the investor. Younger firms have less established track records and less established business relationships with other economic actors, so investors face higher information asymmetry when assessing a younger firm's stock.

Perceived strategic uncertainty was constructed for each of the six environmental sectors as a multiplicative combination of perceived sector importance and perceived sector uncertainty, where perceived uncertainty is the combination of perceived sector complexity and perceived sector rate of change. Importance, complexity and rate of change were each measured on five-point Likert scales. The algebraic formula for the score is not readable in the extracted text.

variable_name: task versus general environment sector membership
description: Customer, competitor and technological sectors were classified as task environment sectors because they have direct transactions with the organization; regulatory, economic and sociocultural sectors were classified as general environment sectors because these firms were not tightly regulated.

Scanning was measured with frequency questions that distinguished internal versus external and personal versus impersonal (written) sources. For each of the six sectors the executive indicated whether useful information was received on a daily, weekly, monthly, or less frequent basis, separately for written external, written internal, personal external and personal internal sources. The 'all modes' score combines the four source types.
scale: daily, weekly, monthly, or less frequent

description: A combined variable created to test Hypothesis 3, combining the personal internal and personal external scanning modes; the combination rule is presented in a table rather than in prose. Higher values indicate more frequent use of personal sources.

A combined variable created to test Hypothesis 3, combining the written external and written internal scanning modes; the combination rule is presented in a table rather than in prose. Higher values indicate more frequent use of written sources.

A combined variable created to test Hypothesis 4, combining the written external and personal external scanning modes; the combination rule is presented in a table rather than in prose. Higher values indicate more frequent use of external sources.

A combined variable created to test Hypothesis 4, combining the written internal and personal internal scanning modes; the combination rule is presented in a table rather than in prose. Higher values indicate more frequent use of internal sources.

Profitability was the measure of performance. ROA equals net income after taxes divided by total assets and was averaged over 1981 through 1983. The senior manager self-reported profitability on the category scale shown in Table 1, where the first category is the highest return and the last category the lowest, so higher codes indicate lower performance. Firms were classified as high-performing when their average three-year ROA was 9 per cent or greater and as low-performing when it was less than 9 per cent, 9 per cent being the median ROA in the sample.
scale: categorical profitability scale shown in Table 1

description: An eight-item Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree) covering the level of social interaction between the alliance partners; Cronbach's alpha for the scale was 0.82 and the ICC across the two firms was 0.49. To build comprehensive measures the authors took the average of within-firm scores (either Lilly or the partner) and averaged scores across firms where responses from both organizations were available. The aggregate score across the eight items can range from 7 to 56.

The proportion of patent collaboration ties between inventors within the partner firm, calculated as the ratio of observed collaboration ties to the total number of possible ties given the number of actively patenting scientists, where a collaboration tie is the common listing of two scientists on the same patent application. It is computed from all U.S. patent applications filed by the partner firm for the five years from the start of its alliance with Lilly. The value would be 1 if all inventors collaborated with each other at some point during the five-year observation window, or 0 if all firm scientists worked in isolation; because a proportional dependent variable in OLS creates challenges, the measure was log-odds transformed.
time_window: five years from the start of the alliance with Lilly

description: The count of inventor pairs listed on a patent application that had not collaborated in the period prior to the Lilly alliance, observed for all patents developed by partner firms with applications submitted to the USPTO in the five-year period following the start of their alliance with Lilly. Observation of new collaboration ties was limited to partner firm inventors employed prior to the alliance, based on their being listed on pre-alliance patents, which eliminated possible confounding effects from new-inventor hires. The data are over-dispersed, so a negative binomial model was employed.
time_window: five-year period following the start of the alliance

description: For a risk set of all pairs of partner firm inventors who were listed on patents prior to the alliance and who had not previously collaborated, the count of successful partner firm patent applications listing both dyad members as inventors for the five years following the onset of the Lilly alliance. The dependent variable has an overdispersed, nonnegative count distribution, making the negative binomial model the specification used.
time_window: five years following the onset of the Lilly alliance

description: The count of Lilly patents that are cited by the partner firm patent, used to indicate that inventors on that patent were more likely to be directly involved in the Lilly alliance.

Political liberalism index scored as the simple average of four donation-based indicators that respectively capture behavioral commitment, financial commitment, persistence of commitment, and scope of commitment to a political orientation (Cronbach's alpha = .92). The indicators are the number of donations to Democrats divided by the number of donations to recipients of both parties, the dollar amount of donations to Democrats divided by the amount given to both parties, the number of years donations were made to Democrats divided by the number of years donations were made to either party, and the number of distinct Democratic recipients divided by the total number of distinct recipients of both parties; .1 was added to all numerators and .2 to all denominators to handle zero values. Index scores ranged from zero to one, with scores above .50 representing degrees of liberalism and scores below .50 indicating degrees of conservatism. Contributions to individual candidates, party committees and party-affiliated PACs were included; other PACs were excluded. The worked numerical example of the four indicators is given in a formula block that is unreadable.
time_window: ten years before the CEO's appointment (t-10 to t-1), invariant during the CEO's tenure

description: Net CSR score for each year, calculated as the sum of all of the company's KLD strengths minus all of its concerns across six categories: product quality, employee relations, diversity, community relations, environment, and human rights. KLD annually rates the presence or absence of each of 40 strengths and 34 concerns under these categories. For instance, if a company in a given year had 8 strengths and 10 concerns, its CSR profile would be -2. KLD's governance and controversial businesses categories were excluded.
scale: count (net of strengths minus concerns; negative to positive)
time_window: each year the CEO was in office, excluding the year of appointment (t+n), through 2009

description: Formative index consisting of three variables that were standardized and then averaged: a dummy variable for CEO duality, coded as one if the CEO was also board chair; the CEO's relative ownership, measured as the difference between the percentage of stock owned by the CEO and the percentage owned by outside directors; and the proportion of outside directors appointed after the CEO. The index was logged.
time_window: updated for every focal year t+n

description: Market-to-book value of common equity (MTB) minus the mean MTB for the industry, logged. It was measured in the year prior to each focal year (t+n-1) and also served as the moderator for testing H3.
time_window: year prior to each focal year (t+n-1)

description: Number of control-related clauses in the contract, based on four of Parkhe's (1993) eight key contractual provisions (clauses 4, 5, 6, and 8), yielding an integer score ranging from 0 to 4. The coding scheme was revised on the advice of legal experts, who argued that the arbitration clause category was ambiguous as to its function. Coding was done by one of the authors and by a faculty member with a degree in law who was unaware of the hypotheses, and all coding of contracts was done prior to any analysis of dispute-related data; disagreements were resolved by discussion. The pairwise correlation among raters was r = .91 (p < .001) and Cronbach's alpha was 0.95.
time_window: T = 1, the contract in place at the outset of the dispute

description: Number of coordination-related clauses in the contract, based on two of Parkhe's (1993) eight key contractual provisions (clauses 1 and 2), yielding an integer score ranging from 0 to 2. The coding scheme was revised on the advice of legal experts, who argued that the audit clause category did not clearly represent a coordination function. Coding was done by one of the authors and by a faculty member with a degree in law who was unaware of the hypotheses; disagreements were resolved by discussion. The pairwise correlation among raters was r = .92 (p < .001) and Cronbach's alpha was 0.96. Unweighted composite indexes were used.
time_window: T = 1, the contract in place at the outset of the dispute

description: Ratio of goodwill-based trust messages to total messages exchanged between the disputing firms during the resolution process of the focal dispute. Every communication (paper or electronic) was analyzed and the failure to reply to a communication was also coded as a 'no reply' message; 2,293 messages were studied. Each message could be coded as signaling neither, one, or both types of trust, with messages coded for references to benevolence and/or integrity. The score could vary between 0 and 1. Coding followed Weber's (1990) procedure by two raters; the percentage of agreement was 95 percent and the pairwise correlation between raters was r = .93 (p < .01).
time_window: T = 2, during the entire dispute resolution process, after the onset of the conflict

description: Ratio of competence-based trust messages to total messages exchanged between the disputing firms during the resolution process of the focal dispute. Every communication (paper or electronic) was analyzed and the failure to reply to a communication was also coded as a 'no reply' message; 2,293 messages were studied. Each message could be coded as signaling neither, one, or both types of trust, with messages coded for references to skills, competencies, aptitude, training, and/or experience. The score could vary between 0 and 1. Coding followed Weber's (1990) procedure by two raters; the percentage of agreement was 97 percent and the pairwise correlation between raters was r = .94 (p < .01).
time_window: T = 2, during the entire dispute resolution process, after the onset of the conflict

description: Binary dependent variable based on the messages exchanged between the parties and the terms of the settlement/judgment recorded in the legal files, looking for indications of a willingness to continue with the relationship. Such intent was sometimes manifested in a direct communication between the firms and in other cases made evident through the crafting of a new agreement by the parties. Cases in which either or both parties explicitly stated no willingness to continue, and cases in which no indication of an intent to continue was present, were coded as 'no intent to continue'. Intent to continue the relationship was indicated in 29 cases out of 102.
time_window: T = 3, at the end of the dispute resolution process

description: A variable assigned a value of one for those car models in which either a unique engine was procured from outside suppliers or a standard engine was produced internally, and zero if a car model used a unique engine produced internally or a standard engine procured from an independent supplier. Values were assigned for each year covered by the data. For firms producing a single car model in a given year, the model-level value became the firm-level measure of misalignment for that year. For firms producing multiple car models, the firm-level measure is the unweighted average of the model-level misalignment values of the firm's models in that year. Because the measure relies on engine uniqueness defined by the upper tail of the cubic displacement distribution, most engines are defined as standard, so the measure captures primarily overintegration.
time_window: each year covered by the data, 1917-1933

variable_name: firm survival (hazard rate of firm failure)
description: The data consist of months and years of entry and exit by each member of the entire population of U.S. auto producers from 1917 to 1933. Only exits that represented unambiguous failure, i.e., liquidation, bankruptcy, or cessation of auto production by a unit of a multidivisional firm, were coded as exits; mergers and acquisitions were excluded. Firm survival is measured by the instantaneous rate of firm failure in the Gompertz hazard-rate models.

An indicator entered in the models as the period of shakeout/dominant design (1923-1933) and interacted with MISALIGNMENT. The authors use 1923 as their marker for the beginning of the shakeout period, a date they also take as marking the emergence of the dominant design in the U.S. auto industry.

The log of firm size measured by sales, included as an explanatory variable in all regressions. Because the firm size variable is highly skewed left in the data, the authors report regressions with the logged value of firm size. It is also interacted with MISALIGNMENT in Models 3 and 4.

Constructed from the distribution of cubic displacement (cc) values for all engines: these values were normalized for each year and a dummy variable was created indicating whether a given cc value was greater than two standard deviations above the mean. Engines in this upper tail of the cc distribution were assigned a value of one for engine uniqueness and zero otherwise. Cubic displacement is calculated using a standard industry formula that combines the number of cylinders of an engine and its bore and stroke values.
level: engine (applied to car models/firms by year)

description: A six-item measure pertaining to common, informal communication between engineers of the supplier and the buyer. Each item is a 5-point Likert scale and the measure is the average score provided by the respondent across the six items. Confirmatory factor analysis showed the measure is distinct from Technology Transfer.

A five-item measure describing the transfer of higher-level technological capabilities between the buyer and the supplier, including technology passing from the supplier to the buyer as well as in the reverse direction. Each item is a 5-point Likert scale and the measure is the average score provided by the respondent across the five items.

Measured as the number of years since the buyer and the supplier began their business relationship, reported by the respondent supplier. Two sets of estimates are reported, one using the untransformed value and one using its natural logarithm.
time_window: years since the relationship began, up to the 1996 survey

description: A four-item measure of the trend in the supplier's operational performance relative to its position 2-3 years earlier, using items on improvements in product design, process design, product quality, and lead time. Items are 5-point Likert scales and the measure is the average score across the four items. The four items loaded onto a single measure when factor analysed alongside the items making up the independent variables.
time_window: last 2-3 years relative to the 1996 survey

description: A six-item measure pertaining to common, informal communication between engineers of the supplier and the buyer. Each item is a 5-point Likert scale and the measure is the average score provided by the respondent across the six items. Confirmatory factor analysis showed the measure is distinct from Technology Transfer.

A five-item measure describing the transfer of higher-level technological capabilities between the buyer and the supplier, including technology passing from the supplier to the buyer as well as in the reverse direction. Each item is a 5-point Likert scale and the measure is the average score provided by the respondent across the five items.

Measured as the number of years since the buyer and the supplier began their business relationship, reported by the respondent supplier. Two sets of estimates are reported, one using the untransformed value and one using its natural logarithm.
time_window: years since the relationship began, up to the 1996 survey

description: A four-item measure of the trend in the supplier's operational performance relative to its position 2-3 years earlier, using items on improvements in product design, process design, product quality, and lead time. Items are 5-point Likert scales and the measure is the average score across the four items. The four items loaded onto a single measure when factor analysed alongside the items making up the independent variables.
time_window: last 2-3 years relative to the 1996 survey

description: Measured by the total number of deals an MD executes on a focal day. Executing each deal requires the MD to select the product, contact and negotiate with suppliers, create marketing images and messages, and go through internal approval to finally upload the product on the online platform. Observations are aggregated at the daily level for each MD.

Measured by the total number of suppliers shared by a focal MD to a team peer on a focal day. Peers can engage in commercial relationships with the focal MD's suppliers only when explicit permission is given by the focal MD. Sharing behavior is detected when a particular peer starts to execute a deal sourced from a supplier who has prior history of sourcing products to a focal MD; in some cases, a single MD shares the same supplier to up to two peers on a focal day.
Measured by the total number of suppliers shared by team peers to a focal MD on a focal day.

Measured as the proportion of team members (in percentage terms) that have been changed from pay-for-performance to fixed salary. Takes a value of 0 when all team members are still under the pay-for-performance system and 100 when all team members are switched to fixed salary; in the data the variable takes nine values: 0, 33.33, 40, 42.86, 50, 60, 66.67, 85.71, and 100.

variable_name: post x treatment / Focal MD's incentives change
description: For the difference-in-differences tests, post equals 1 for observations related to dates from April 1 onward and 0 otherwise, and treatment equals 1 for observations related to MDs who had their own incentives changed on April 1, 2013 and 0 for those who had their own incentives changed on May 1, 2013; the interaction post x treatment multiplies the treatment variable with the post variable and its coefficient represents the individual effect of the incentives change. In the analyses of the team's incentives change, the variable focal MD's incentives change takes a value of 0 if the focal MD is still paid according to the pay-for-performance system and a value of 1 if the focal MD's compensation scheme has been switched to fixed salary.
time_window: April 1, 2013 as the threshold for post and treatment

description: Two subsamples are used: individuals whose productivity (measured by average revenue per day) before the change was higher than the average productivity of all team members, and those whose productivity before the change was lower than the average productivity of all team members. The subsample for high performers included 3,255 observations for 15 MDs, and the subsample for low performers included 5,661 observations for 26 MDs.

An eight-item scale based on the work of Morrison et al. (2004) and extended by the authors, administered in the online survey. Items were answered on a Likert scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'); the scale was formed as the arithmetic mean of the different items and had an internal reliability of alpha = .75.
Measured from the web log as the total number of new threads started by the individual divided by the overall activity (total number of postings) of the individual.
Measured from the web log as the average number of responses received for each online posting of the individual.

Measured with a two-stage question in the online survey. Respondents were asked, 'Have you actively participated in other online communities NOT hosted by Propellerhead during the last three years?' and those who ticked 'yes' were asked for the names of other online communities. The names were identified and coded using Google and other search engines, with two of the authors coding the content independently and cross-checking. Only communities dealing with music production, recording and processing software, music editing, inspiration and sample downloading, or supporting software such as programming or sound track production were included; general social networks such as Facebook and Yahoo user groups were excluded.

A dummy variable coded 'yes' = 1 if (1) a respondent stated that he/she had 'made written plans to start a business' or 'looked for resources to start a new business (e.g., funding, business partners, business premises, etc.)' and (2) stated that 'my community experience was of importance' in that action. The items were adopted from the Panel Study of Entrepreneurial Development (PSED) and capture tangible evaluation activities signalling meaningful intent.

A dummy variable assigned the value 1 if an individual reported that he or she had 'sent invoices for products or services offered by your company,' 'done the paperwork and officially registered the company,' or 'sold products and services through my company' and that 'my community experience was of importance' in these actions. The statements focusing on sales and value creation capture a tangible validation that an opportunity actually exists to sell products and services.

variable_name: % of shares held by largest institutional owner
description: The percentage of a firm's outstanding shares held by its single largest institutional owner, identified using the detailed information in the CDA/Spectrum database. The authors measure the holdings of the largest, the second largest, and all other institutional owners separately. The variable is measured for each firm-quarter.

The percentage of a firm's outstanding shares held in aggregate by all institutional owners other than the largest institutional owner. In the models that add the second largest institutional owner, the variable is the total percentage owned by all institutions less the sum of the percentages owned by the largest and second largest institutional owners. It is measured for each firm-quarter.

The end-of-quarter bid-ask spread, computed by subtracting the bid price from the ask price and dividing by the midpoint of those bid-ask prices. Deflating by share price combats nonlinearity in bid-ask spreads. Bid and ask price data come from CRSP.
scale: ratio to the midpoint of the bid and ask prices

description: Number of markets outside the focal market in which the focal-market challenger meets the focal-market leader and in which the focal-market challenger is itself the leader. Four conditions must be simultaneously met: the focal firm is a challenger in the focal market, another firm is a leader in the focal market, the focal firm is a leader in another market, and the focal-market leader is present in that market; the product of dummies representing these conditions is summed over all other firms and markets. It is measured separately for each of the three dimensions (D) of territorial interests, market share dominance, market dependence and resource centrality. The specification is presented as a formula that is not readable in this text.
time_window: fourth quarter of each sample year

description: Number of markets outside the focal market in which the focal-market challenger meets the focal-market leader and in which the focal-market challenger is also a challenger. Together with reciprocal multimarket contact it sums to total multimarket contact, the total number of markets in which the focal-market challenger meets the focal-market leader outside the focal market. It is measured separately for each of the three dimensions of territorial interests.
time_window: fourth quarter of each sample year

description: Average of all pairwise reciprocal multimarket contacts of the focal-market leader with all of its focal-market challengers, where a pairwise contact is the number of markets in which the leader meets the focal-market challenger in other markets in which the focal-market challenger is a leader. The averaging is illustrated with an example: if a leader has two challengers in the focal market and has 100 reciprocal multimarket contacts with the first and 300 with the second, the average reciprocal multimarket contact equals 200. Measured separately for each of the three dimensions of territorial interests.
time_window: fourth quarter of each sample year

description: Average of all pairwise nonreciprocal multimarket contacts of the focal-market leader with its focal-market challengers, measured as the average number of markets in which the leader meets the focal-market challengers in other markets in which the focal-market challengers are also challengers. The sum of the reciprocal and nonreciprocal measures equals the total average multimarket contact of the leader. Measured separately for each of the three dimensions of territorial interests.
time_window: fourth quarter of each sample year

description: The average price level actually charged by the airline-route in a time period divided by the distance of the market; it is also known as revenue per passenger-mile. Lower yields indicate more intense competitive behavior and vice versa. The authors use this rather than information on actions or changes because they consider that firms behave competitively not just when they lower their yields, but also when they keep these yields low. Dividing price by distance homogenizes prices across markets of different distances and reduces possible heteroscedasticity. Actual prices are used rather than announced or advertised prices because airlines can change actual prices by changing seat availability across fare categories.
time_window: fourth quarter of the observation year

description: The market share of the airline-route measured as the passengers transported by the airline-route divided by all passengers transported in the market. Because equilibrium market shares are not directly observable, the market share equation uses a partial adjustment model in which observed changes in market share adjust actual market share toward the equilibrium market share, and the lagged value of market share is included; lagged market share is not a control variable in this equation.
scale: proportion of passengers in the market
time_window: fourth quarter of the observation year; lagged one period

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 if firm i is the market share leader in market m at period t, and 0 otherwise; the complementary dummy Challenger(MS) equals 1 if firm i is an incumbent in market m at time t but is not a leader. Market Share Dominance (MS) is operationalized as the market share of a focal airline-route in terms of passengers transported. The leader is the firm with the highest territorial interests in the market in terms of this dimension.
time_window: fourth quarter of the observation year

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 if firm i obtained a greater proportion of its revenues from market m at period t than any of its rivals, and 0 otherwise; the complementary dummy Challenger(MD) equals 1 if firm i is an incumbent but not a leader. Market Dependence (MD) is operationalized as the percentage of overall firm revenues obtained by the focal airline-route.
time_window: fourth quarter of the observation year

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 if the proportion of enplanements at both end cities of market m at period t is greater for firm i than for any of its rivals, and 0 otherwise; the complementary dummy Challenger(RC) equals 1 if firm i is an incumbent but not a leader. Resource Centrality (RC) is operationalized as the percentage of overall firm enplanements that take place at either of the two cities of the city-pair market, reflecting reliance on the firm's hub positions, which are costly to develop and difficult to redeploy.
time_window: fourth quarter of the observation year

description: Uses Baum and Korn's (1996) firm-in-market measure: the number of multimarket competitors (j) that focal firm i encounters in market m, where firm i and firm j must meet in at least one market other than m. Indicator variables denote whether firm i and firm j are active in market m at time t. The raw measure can vary from 0 (no multimarket contact) to 1 (the focal firm encounters all the other firms it meets in that market in all of its other markets) and was multiplied by 100 to scale it.

A composite measure based on two dimensions: competitive activity, the total number of competitive actions initiated by an MNC subsidiary in its host country during a given year, and competitive complexity, the extent to which that subsidiary carried out a broad rather than a narrow range of competitive actions in that host country during that year. Competitive complexity was calculated from the proportions of a subsidiary's actions falling in each of seven action categories (NTL is the total actions a subsidiary initiates in a given year and Na/NTL the proportion in the ath category; the formula itself was not readable in the extracted text). A factor analysis on the two dimensions produced a composite measure using the average of their standardized values, with a Cronbach's alpha of .91.

Following Curhan, Davidson, and Suri (1977) and Delios and Henisz (2000), the degree of subsidiary ownership is the percentage of each MNC subsidiary's equity held by its headquarters. Equity ownership data were collected from Who Owns Whom: The Directory of Corporate Affiliation.

variable_name: Cultural distance between home and host countries
description: Following Kogut and Singh (1988), cultural distance is measured with four primary dimensions of the Hofstede index: power distance, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity/femininity, and individualism. The measure compares the ith cultural dimension of country j with the ith cultural dimension of country k (the formula was not readable in the extracted text). The authors note they could not find a better alternative with complete coverage for their 27 countries.

Assessed with five variables from the World Economic Forum's Executive Opinion Survey, reflecting MNC managers' perceptions of host government regulatory restrictions on entry decisions and daily operations: access to credit, effectiveness of antitrust policy, ease of establishing cross-border ventures, freedom to acquire corporate control, and interest rate controls. Each variable is the average response to a statement about local capital markets, anti-monopoly policy, cross-border venture negotiation, foreign acquisition of control, and market-determined interest rates. The variables were reverse-coded to reflect perceived restrictions and factor-analyzed into a composite measure for host country constraints, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.85.

A dummy variable coded 1 when the local firms in a given country held over 30 percent of the market and 0 otherwise. Local firms are auto producers whose production and sales are limited to a single country, their home country. The authors note that the 30 percent threshold was used because their data appeared to be clearly demarcated at that point.

Each CEO's network is a matrix of symmetric connections with and among contacts, with connections scaled to vary from zero to one. Network constraint was computed from these values as a summary measure of network closure and multiplied by 100 to be discussed in points of constraint; a score of 100 indicates that a respondent's contacts were strongly connected with one another (no access to structural holes). The score decreases toward zero with network size (degree) and increases with density and with hierarchy (centralization through a central person).
time_window: at the time of the survey (2012), with contacts dated back to the firm's founding

description: Survey respondents were asked: 'In general, for how many years do you try to plan in advance in terms of the strategic or organizational development of your firm?' Five response categories were offered: no development plan, one to four months, four months to one year, one to three years, and three years or longer. Because only two CEOs said they planned three years or longer, those were combined with the 175 who responded 'one to three years' to define a long-run planning category, and the 13 with no development plan were combined with the 174 planning one to four months to define a short-run planning category; the remaining 336 CEOs formed a mid-range category (more than four months but less than one year).
time_window: at the time of the survey (2012)

description: Respondents were asked to specify the percentage of their management staff employed under each of the following contract terms: one-year contract, two-year contract, three-to-five-year contract, or other, where 'other' was selected by CEOs who did not have written contracts with their managers. The measure is the percentage of management staff employed under 'long-term', three-to-five-year contracts. On average, 37.6% of management staff were employed under such contracts, and the distribution was concentrated at the extremes.
time_window: at the time of the survey (2012)

description: Analogous to the long-run management contracts measure, respondents were asked for the percentage of technical staff employed under each contract term (one-year, two-year, three-to-five-year, other), using the same question and answer categories as for managerial staff. The measure is the proportion of technical staff who had three-to-five-year contracts, with a mean value of 34.6% and a bimodal distribution similar to that for management contracts.
time_window: at the time of the survey (2012)

variable_name: Firm employee training in last three years
description: Respondents were asked whether their company provided any in-house training for their employees during the last three years, a provision that signals future planning by the company. About two thirds responded that their companies had (67.7%). The variable is coded 1 if the firm provided in-house training during the last three years.

Business success was measured as a principal component analysis z score aggregating the value of annual sales, the number of full-time employees, and the number of patents at the time of the survey. The principal component described a large proportion of variance in the indicators (65%), and all three indicators had the expected negative association with closed networks.
time_window: at the time of the survey (2012)

description: The entrepreneur's total execution experience, measured as her number of projects prior to her current project and of the same subtype. Only projects that meet the funding threshold are counted, because they provide the entrepreneur with execution experience that exposes her to project interdependencies.

The total number of updates posted by the entrepreneur during project execution, after the fundraising campaign has ended and before the product is delivered, that cite unforeseen interdependencies. A member of the research team reviewed the most common words in updates relevant to unforeseen interdependencies and identified two categories of relevant words: words relating to issues being unforeseen and words relating to typical interdependence-related issues in the context. All updates containing words from either set are included in the measure.
time_window: after the fundraising campaign ended and before the product was delivered

description: A binary indicator equal to 1 if the product has the most features compared to the other products by the same entrepreneur (and 0 otherwise). The feature level of a product is identified relative to the other products by the same entrepreneur, using five independent reviewers who ranked each entrepreneur's set of products by number of features, with the rankings aggregated across reviewers.

The relative rank of the product compared to other products by the same entrepreneur. For example, if an entrepreneur completed two products, the product with the fewest features has a Features Rank of 1 and the product with the most features has a Features Rank of 2. Ranks come from aggregating the feature rankings of five independent reviewers across each entrepreneur's set of products.

The relative percentile of a project for an entrepreneur, for example, if an entrepreneur had three projects with Features Rank equal to 1, 2, and 3, the corresponding Features Percentile would be 0%, 50%, and 100%. Based on the aggregated feature rankings of five independent reviewers for each entrepreneur's set of products.

Set equal to 1 if the actual delivery date is after the predicted delivery date, or if the project has not yet shipped and the predicted delivery date is prior to the date when the sample was collected (and 0 otherwise). It is identified for 95% of projects in the sample.
The time (in days) between the actual delivery date and the predicted delivery date. It is identified for 89% of the sample.

The delay duration divided by the entrepreneur's predicted time, expressing the miss of the predicted timeline on a percentage basis so that projects of different predicted lengths can be compared. The analogous prior-project variable divides the prior project's Delay Duration by its Predicted Time.
The time (in days) between the end of the fundraising campaign and the predicted delivery date.
The time (in days) between the end of the fundraising campaign and the actual delivery date, that is, the sum of Predicted Time and Delay Duration.

Cultural distances from South Korea to other countries were measured with Kogut and Singh's (1988) index based on Hofstede's (1980) aggregate scores. The index has frequently been used in foreign entry studies and was applied here to afford comparability with prior work.
level: country dyad (South Korea to partner country)

description: Inward investment was dummy coded as '1' and outward investment as '0' for the analysis.

High control modes were coded as '1' and low control modes as '0.' In outward investment the modes were equity joint ventures or export distributorships; export distributorship implies handing over most sales rights to a foreign partner and thus represents less control from the Korean firm's perspective. In inward investment the modes were import distributorship, which retains more responsibility and control in the hands of the local Korean partner than an equity joint venture would provide, and equity joint venture. High control modes were therefore the equity joint venture in outward investment and import distributorship in inward investment, and the low control modes were export distributorship in outward investment and equity joint venture in inward investment.

Coded one for individuals whose immediate previous job spell is at a different company (external hires) and zero for individuals who move into the PM role from a different position within the same company (internal hires). Individuals hired directly after graduating from an educational institution are excluded from the analysis. The variable is the treatment indicator in the CEM procedure.

A binary variable set to one if the LASSO classifier mistakes the PM's job description for a venture-backed entrepreneur founding statement at a 75% probability threshold, and zero otherwise. The classifier is trained on 20,014 technology PM job descriptions retrieved from the LinkedIn data set and 33,324 VBE founding descriptions from Crunchbase; PMs whose job descriptions are falsely labeled as VBEs are considered intrapreneurial. Face validity was checked with feature weights and with human coders, and the binary version prioritizes precision.

Measured by counting the number of years to company departure following entry into the PM role, where the event is that the individual leaves the focal company as a product manager. Internal moves to a new job role within the firm and spells in which the employee still occupied the PM job role at the point of data collection are treated as right censored. The authors track job role tenure from entry into the focal PM role to avoid left censoring.

This measure is a composite construct constructed from four profitability ratios listed in the Analyst's Guide. The four ratios are: operating income to sales, recurring profit to sales, net income to sales, and industry ROE. The lowest interitem correlation was 0.715.

The product diversification measure is an entropy measure based on Palepu (1985), PD = the sum over industries of P x ln(1/P), in which PD is the extent of product diversification and P is the proportion of sales made in industry i. The Japan Company Handbook was the source for determining the industries in which a firm's sales occurred and the percent of sales in each segment. Three-digit SIC codes were used to classify diversification.

The measure was computed as the ratio of R&D expenditures to the firm's total sales, as reported at the corporate level. Two R&D terms were used: the Analyst's Guide was the source for one R&D term and the second R&D variable was from GlobalVantage. The measure was computed for the firm as a whole.
The measure was computed as the ratio of advertising expenditures to the firm's total sales, as reported at the corporate level. The Analyst's Guide was the source for the advertising measure.

The extent of geographic operations was measured by two counts: a count of the number of foreign direct investments the firm had made by 1996 and a count of the number of countries in which FDI had occurred. These data were gathered from Toyo Keizai (1997).

Data were compiled from GlobalVantage, a companion data set to CompuStat that lists accounting data for non-U.S.-based publicly listed companies. Three performance measures were used as items: return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), and return on sales (ROS). Each performance measure was computed as a 5-year average (1991-95). The measures had a high degree of correlation and a composite performance construct was modeled using the three measures as items.
Number of biopharmaceutical patents issued to a startup until 1989. The data were taken from the Technology Profile Report of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (1990).

Number of startup agreements with commercial firms until 1989. Any interfirm relationship listed in BIOSCAN (1989) was included; relationships from the three other sources were included only if they appeared in at least two of them.
Number of startup employees in 1988.
Number of years since startup founding until 1988.
Dummy variable indicating whether startup equity is offered to the public. Also labeled PUBLIC FUNDS in the descriptive statistics.
Number of biotechnology subfields (e.g., agriculture, human therapeutics) in which a startup has product development projects.

Network position was measured using the blockmodeling technique of Kogut et al. (1992). CONCOR was applied separately to the rows and columns of the matrix of relationships between startups and established firms to assign startups and established firms to groups whose members were structurally equivalent, and the separate partitions were then input to a refinement procedure called CALCOPT. The extent to which a group of firms contributes to the overall pattern of structural equivalence is the measure of its embeddedness in the network, assessed in 1987 to be temporally independent of the number of relationships in 1988.

The key variable, the internal employment mode of firms, was treated as a bi-modal variable and tested with seven Likert scale items; examples include 'In this organization, managers are mainly promoted from inside the organization rather than recruited from outside the organization' and 'People in this organization enjoy a long-term employment policy.' The items test the balance of the two modes: the lower the score, the more the firm is characterized by an internal employment mode; the higher the score, the more the firm is characterized by an external employment mode. The items were pretested in a class of MBA students in South China; the pretest showed a reliability alpha of 0.73 and intraclass correlations between the three sets of data from each firm ranging between 0.68 and 0.93. The score correlated with the proportion of long-term employed workers to all workers from the Chinese survey (-0.35; p < 0.05).

Joint venture was tested as a dummy, with a joint venture coded as 1 and a firm wholly owned by an overseas investor coded as 0. It was entered among the three institutional factors in the regression on the internal employment mode.
scale: dummy (1 = joint venture; 0 = wholly owned by an overseas investor)

description: An institutional factor representing the home country culture of the investing MNE, entered with Chinese institution and joint venture in the regression on the internal employment mode. The text does not state how this variable was coded.

Equipment per employee was tested by the ratio of the value of the equipment to the total number of employees. It was entered as one of the two strategic factors in the regression on the internal employment mode.

The nature of industrial competition was measured as a dummy variable, with electronic firms coded as 1 and clothing and footwear manufacturers coded as 0. It was entered as one of the two strategic factors in the regression on the internal employment mode.

Chinese institutional influence was tested by the share of a firm that was controlled by the Chinese party. It was entered as one of the three institutional factors in the regression on the internal employment mode, and its product with joint venture was entered as a controlled variable.

Middle managers responded to three items: (1) since 1995, the profit (or productivity) of this firm has (a) not changed, (b) decreased, or (c) increased; (2) since 1995, the market share of this firm has (a) not changed, (b) decreased, or (c) increased; and (3) since 1995, the number of employees who have been disciplined or fired has (a) not changed, (b) decreased, or (c) increased. These three items allowed the authors to create six dummy variables, three for improvement and three for deterioration.
scale: each item: (a) not changed, (b) decreased, (c) increased

variable_name: return on equity in the year prior to a succession
description: Presuccession performance was defined as return on equity in the year prior to a succession and taken from the COMPUSTAT tapes. In the split-sample models the firms were bisected at the median on this variable; the authors report that the mean return on equity in the year prior to succession was .17 and .06 for the good and poor performers respectively.
time_window: the year prior to the succession

description: For each firm the authors collected a vector of 401 daily returns, from 300 days before the announcement day to 100 days after it, together with corresponding equal-weighted daily market returns, from the CRSP tapes. The normal, or expected, return is modeled with an intercept specific to firm i and a regression coefficient specific to firm i (systematic risk) applied to the equal-weighted market return; the full equation is not readable in this extraction. Abnormal returns are actual returns minus expected returns, and cumulative abnormal returns reflect the net change in returns over a five-day interval surrounding the event (-2 to +2).
time_window: five-day interval from two days before to two days after the announcement; returns collected from 300 days before to 100 days after the announcement

description: Response to a survey item asking which of several options best describes the main reason for the change from the former to the current CEO: retirement of the former CEO because of age (customary), early retirement of the former CEO by his or her choice (CEO-initiated), early retirement not by his or her choice due to poor performance or skills no longer appropriate (board-initiated), or death or health problems of the former CEO (disability). Most 'other' responses were recoded into the four usable categories, and missing survey information was supplemented from unambiguous Wall Street Journal announcements. In the analyses, dichotomous variables representing each initiating force were used, with customary successions excluded as the reference category in the stockholder-reaction models.

Binary variable from the survey item 'Did the current CEO come from within the company: Yes or No?' coded 1 for insiders and 2 for outsiders. The authors relied on the key informants' own definitions of insiders and outsiders since they were examining the reactions of knowledgeable observers to the events.

Binary variable resulting from collapsing seven responses to a survey item about the role assumed by the former CEO after he or she was succeeded. Staying as active chairman of the board but not CEO, inactive chairman, member of the board, or consultant to the firm was coded 1; moving to another firm, completely retiring, or becoming incapacitated or deceased was coded 2. Missing survey information was supplemented from Wall Street Journal announcements when the latter were unambiguous.

A time-variant composite score of country-level corporatism drawn from Hicks and Kenworthy (1998) and Kenworthy (2003). Corporatism scores range from 0 to 1, with the lowest score of 0.01 assigned to the United States and the highest score of 0.99 assigned to Sweden. Because the Kenworthy (2003) measures are only available until 2000, the 2000 score was used for the years 2001 and 2002. Within countries there is only slight variation in the level of corporatism from year to year, leading to a stable rank ordering of countries.

Each partner's social value is measured by its degree centrality, calculated as the ratio of the partner's total number of alliances in year t and the total number of possible alliances in that year. The combined degree centrality of the dyad is the geometric mean of both partners' centrality normalized by the industry maximum in a given year. A five-year life span was assumed for every alliance to construct the alliance networks, so the age of alliances varied from 0 to 5 years.
time_window: year t, using five-year assumed alliance life spans

description: Calculated as the square root of the sum over the 35 patent subclasses (429/12-46) of the squared difference in the percentage assignment of partners' cumulative patents in subclass i up to year t. The measure ranges from 0 for identical patenting profiles to 1.41 (square root of 2) when there is no overlap in technology subclasses and hence maximum novelty.
time_window: cumulative patents up to year t

description: An alliance dummy assigned a value of 1 for the 171 dyads that saw a completed alliance and 0 for the remaining 336,985 dyads. Data on all fuel cell technology alliances specifically oriented toward joint technology development were collected from the LexisNexis database, which compiles publicly available archival sources such as news reports, industry journals and trade magazines.

Calculated as the sum of the lagged patent citations made to each partner by the other in the five-year window following alliance formation. For the purpose of the study, the citing of a partner's patents is regarded as evidence that the focal firm has successfully internalized and built on the partner's knowledge base.

Engine In-House took the value of 1 if the firm in question vertically integrated the production of the engine at the time of entry, and 0 otherwise. It is the dependent variable of the first-stage probit estimation of vertical integration choice. Very few entrants produced multiple models at their time of entry, and very few changed their engine integration choice over the studied period.

Parent Engine In-House took the value of 1 if the firm was a spinoff and its parent produced at least one type of engine in-house at the time of, or prior to, the spinoff's entry, and 0 otherwise. Parent Engine Outsourced took the value of 1 if the parent firm outsourced engine production, and 0 otherwise. The omitted category consists of nonspinoff firms. Hypothesis 1 predicted a positive and significant coefficient estimate for the Parent Engine In-House variable, and that this coefficient estimate would be significantly larger in magnitude than that for Parent Engine Outsourced.
time_window: at the time of, or prior to, the spinoff's entry

description: Log Price is the log of the price of the automobile in question. The authors use it as a proxy for strategic positioning because higher-priced cars were relatively insulated from direct competition against Ford's Model T, so that higher price segments reflect more defensible strategic positioning. The distribution of car prices in the sample is skewed to the right, and hence car prices were logged.

Log Survival Years is the log of the number of years the firm survived. Only three observations were right censored (due to acquisitions) and were dropped to accommodate this measure, reducing the sample to 60 entrants. Tobit estimation was used to analyze it because the variable is bounded below at 0.

A citation-weighted patent count in the lagged five-year window following an observation year. The expression is n + Σci, where n is the number of partners' patents a firm cited in the five-year window after the observation year, and ci is the value of patent i measured by the number of times it is cited by the firm in the same five-year window. Patents that are cited more frequently are likely to signify more value for the firm's knowledge-building efforts.
time_window: five-year window following the observation year (t+5)

description: Computed by pooling the patents of all alliance partners in each focal firm's portfolio using the formula 1 - Σ(ni/N)2, where ni represents the cumulative number of patents belonging to patent class i and N represents the cumulative number of fuel cell patents issued up to the observation year. A minimum value of 0 indicated that all partners concentrated their patents in one subclass, placing the least burden on the firm's latitudinal absorptive capacity, and a maximum value of 1 indicated no overlap among partners' technologies and the greatest burden on latitudinal absorptive capacity. Partners' patents belonged to 35 different patent subclasses representing aspects of the technology such as electrodes, electrolytes, catalysts, and hydrogen conversion and storage devices.

The technological distance between each focal firm and its alliance portfolio is calculated as 1 - Pij, where Pij is Jaffe's (1986) measure of similarity between a firm and its alliance partners' pooled technological capabilities; the printed formula is FiF′j / [(FiFj)(Fji)]1/2 (as printed, with F the vector of technological positions, represented by (F1, F2, F3, . . . Fk) where Fk is the cumulative proportion of patents assigned to patent subclass k). The measure ranges from a minimum value of 0 for identical patenting, representing the least technological distance and the lowest burden on longitudinal absorptive capacity, to a maximum of 1, where the firm and its partners' pooled patents are in nonoverlapping classes.

Coded as the order in which CEOs were born to their parents, taking the value of 1 for a first-born, 2 for a second-born, 3 for a third-born, and so on. Following prior studies, birth order was treated as a continuous variable in the regression models to allow interpretation of linear effects. Wald tests assessing deviation from linearity, using both a seven-category and a three-category operationalization, were not statistically significant, which led the authors to prefer the continuous treatment.

An aggregate risk-taking index of three risky spending categories: capital expenditures, R&D spending, and acquisitions. The authors aggregated the indicators instead of treating them separately because these spending categories often substitute for each other. Capital expenditures and R&D spending were obtained from the KLCA database, and acquisitions were measured as the transaction value of all completed acquisitions as reported in SDC Platinum. The index was formed by logging the sum of the three different types of risky spending.

Measured as the number of years between the focal CEO and their closest sibling. When the focal CEO was a first-born, the closest sibling was the immediate younger sibling; in cases where an individual had both a younger and an older sibling, the closest sibling was determined based on their birthdates. The variable was mean-centered prior to inclusion in the interaction terms.
Captured by subtracting the focal year from the CEO's birth year. The variable was mean-centered prior to inclusion in the interaction terms to mitigate multicollinearity problems.

A binary indicator that takes the value of 1 when a sibling of the focal CEO was simultaneously a CEO of another independently traded firm, which occurred for 37% of the CEO-year observations. This determination was made based on the executives list provided in the KIS database.

Measured by a 20-item scale developed by Kohli et al. (1993) tapping the three dimensions of the construct. Two items were deleted after factor analysis, and following Jaworski and Kohli (1993) the three dimensions were combined into a single scale. Identified by managers rather than inferred from resource allocations, and focused on the business unit or firm level.

Measured by six semantic differential items adapted from Covin and Slevin (1989). One item was deleted after factor analysis. The scale reflects the organization's degree of risk-taking propensity, proactiveness, and aggressiveness with respect to innovation, and is focused on the business unit or firm level.

variable_name: market/entrepreneurship orientation group (ME, EO, MO, CO)
description: Firms were arrayed in ascending order of market and entrepreneurship orientations and the sample was split at the median on both orientations into high and low groups to form the four groups of firms depicted in Figure 1. Firms with median scores were deleted to enhance discrimination, leaving 145 firms for analysis.

Measured by a four-item scale reflecting the extent to which the new product is perceived to have achieved its market share, sales and customer use, sales growth, and profit objectives since its launch. The measure pertains to a specific product innovation project.

Collected in a second survey of the original sample to validate the perceptual results. Three objective measures were used: the percentage of profits derived from new products less than three years old, the percentage of sales derived from new products less than three years old, and a three-year average of profits due to new products.

Respondents were asked to indicate whether the firm was first to market, an early follower, a late follower, or a late entrant with the new product. The measure pertains to a specific product innovation project.
scale: first to market / early follower / late follower / late entrant

description: Measured by three items that tap the new product's perceived benefits to customers and superiority over competing products. The measure pertains to a specific product innovation project.

Captured by three items measuring the fit of the new product project with the firm's market research skills, sales force skills, and customer service resources and systems. The measure pertains to a specific product innovation project.

Measured by three items pertaining to the effectiveness of market testing, evaluation of the launch procedures, and training of personnel for the launch. The measure pertains to a specific product innovation project.

Operationalized along two dimensions. Management involvement in product innovation was captured by four items reflecting the degree to which top management provides resources and encourages employee participation and teamwork during the project. Importance given to innovation in human resource strategy was measured by five items reflecting the extent to which innovation skills and experience are considered important by management in the recruitment, performance appraisal, and reward practices.
Measured by three items adapted from Covin and Slevin (1989) that tapped the perceived lack of control over the environment, risks facing the firm, and lack of marketable opportunities.
Measured by four items that tapped the perceived similarity of competitor offerings, price competition, and aggressiveness of the competitor's behavior.

Respondents rated an SBU's performance on each of twelve dimensions relative to superiors' expectations on a 5-point scale ranging from not at all satisfactory to outstanding. Using the data on dimensional importance obtained earlier for validating the strategic-context variables as weights, the author computed a weighted-average effectiveness index for each SBU. Observed values ranged from 1.46 to 4.80 with a mean of 3.21.
scale: weighted average of 5-point performance ratings; observed range 1.46 to 4.80

description: Each general manager indicated the percentage of an SBU's current total sales accounted for by activities in pursuit of five mission categories. All respondents entered 0 under category 5; the other four items were coded +1, 0, -1, and -2 respectively, and the percentage breakdowns were used to derive a weighted average measure, with low values indicating a harvest mission and high values indicating a build mission.

Using a 5-point scale ranging from significantly lower to significantly higher, respondents were asked to position their products relative to industry competitors in terms of performance and price.
