A five-item Likert scale measuring the extent to which a firm integrated its activities, strategies, and knowledge flows across its alliance portfolio. Summated scale scores were used in the analyses.

Measured on three items (alpha = 0.78) incorporating a firm's partnering reputation as a reliable network member, the quality of relationships the firm has accumulated over time, and the competitiveness of the firm's alliance network. Summated scale scores were used in the analyses.

The dichotomous alliance function scale is similar to Kale et al. (2002); respondents were asked whether their organization had a formal, dedicated program that was responsible for overseeing the firm's alliances. Sixty-five firms of the 235 firms reported that they had an alliance function, whereas 170 reported they did not have one.

Operationalized as a variation of Blau's index. Respondents were asked to note their number of alliances in each of the following areas: new product development, research and development/technology, marketing/distribution, supplier, manufacturing, and customer. Alliance portfolio diversity was then computed for each firm by adapting the network portfolio diversity measure of Powell et al. (1996); the formula itself is not readable in the available text.

A formative scale adapted from Venkatraman and Ramanujam (1986) measuring four aspects: market share, sales growth, market development, and product development. Respondents rated their performance relative to competitors to control for industry effects on a five-point scale with the anchors being 'much worse' and 'much better.'
scale: five-point scale anchored by 'much worse' and 'much better'

description: Dummy variable coded as one to indicate the presence of both radical and moderate tactics during a facility's licensing process, and zero otherwise. The authors construct it as a dummy rather than a multiplicative interaction between radical and moderate tactics because radical flank theory is premised on the presence of both radicals and moderates and says nothing about the relative magnitudes of each. Twelve percent of licenses experience a radical flank effect at some point during the licensing process. Radical tactics are protests reported in newspapers and moderate tactics are formal objections made by social activists during the public comment period.
scale: dummy (1 = both radical and moderate tactics present)

description: A weighted index of various private property rights acts (PPRAs) by state and year, borrowed from the political science literature (Hecht 2004). The index distills 20 different property rights acts into a single index that weights rules according to their severity; these acts are administrative procedures that limit the scope of regulatory decision making by discouraging regulations that limit the owner's use of private property. The index ranges from 0 to 100, where a high score indicates that regulatory agencies have little discretion and a low score indicates that agencies have a great deal of flexibility. For this analysis the authors reverse coded this variable.

License approval of hydroelectric power facilities, one if approved and zero otherwise; after a license is approved, withdrawn, or denied, the case is dropped from the data set. Because 94% of licenses are eventually approved and approval time can vary from 1 year to more than 20 years, the authors model the time to approval with accelerated failure time models, where coefficients are interpreted as accelerating or decelerating time to facility licensing.
scale: binary indicator; time to approval in days
time_window: time from application to license decision

description: The dependent variable, operationalized as the number of months between the sale/installation of the first minicomputer (or PC) and the month that the firm in question sold/installed its first minicomputer (or PC). Measuring entry timing in months has the advantage of more likely reflecting strategic decisions about the time period when a firm sought to enter the industry. Higher values indicate later entry.

The second operationalization of entry timing, reflecting the number of competitors that had already entered the industry when the firm entered the market. It also has the practical advantage of reducing the disparity in the mean and variance of the dependent variable across the two industries.

Technological resources measured as R&D expenditures divided by sales, as listed in Table 1. The authors state that the operationalizations of firm resources and organizational attributes are shown in Table 1.
Indicator variable coded 1 if the firm possesses a direct sales force and 0 if it does not, as listed in Table 1.
Current assets divided by current liabilities, as listed in Table 1. It is one of the two indicators the authors use for internal financial resources.
Long-term debt divided by owners' equity, as listed in Table 1. The authors predict that greater internal financial resources, indicated by a smaller debt-to-equity ratio, will lead to earlier entry.
Percent of firm sales attributable to a threatened industry, as listed in Table 1.

The natural logarithm of the number of employees, as listed in Table 1. The authors state that an organization's size refers to number of employees, a measure particularly relevant when considering influences upon the speed of decision making.

A weighted index (Caves et al., 1980) built from the proportion of the firm's sales in each industry, where industry is a 3-digit SIC code, and the 'distance' between industries: 0 if the industries are within the same 3-digit code, 1 if within the same 2-digit code but different 3-digit codes, and 2 if in different 2-digit codes. The formula itself could not be extracted from the paper. A value close to two signifies a highly diversified firm with many unrelated businesses and a value close to zero signals the opposite. The authors treat the 4-digit SIC code for computers and office equipment as if it were included in 367X (electronic components and accessories).
scale: index; close to two = highly diversified, close to zero = opposite

variable_name: expert ratings of first mover advantages
description: Experts were asked to assess the extent to which each of seven first mover advantages (learning curve advantage, brand name recognition, patents, preemption of key inputs, switching costs, preemption of market position, and technological certainty) affected the development of each industry, each on a 7-point scale (1-not influential; 7-very influential). Overall first mover advantages were reported as significantly higher in the minicomputer segment. No measure of this construct is entered in the regression models, which are estimated separately for each industry.

variable_name: technological, marketing and financial resource indicators
description: Firm resources were measured by R&D intensity as technological resources, possession of a direct sales force as marketing resources, and current ratio and debt-to-equity as internal financial resources. These variables were entered together in the entry timing regressions.

Senior managers from each partner firm rated the importance of their firm's contributions to the given joint venture in 10 areas of distinctive competence. The individual partner ratings in each functional area were then correlated to obtain a complementarity rating, where a correlation of -1 indicates that the partner firms have completely different distinctive competencies and a correlation of +1 indicates complete redundancy of distinctive competencies. Partner firm managers were also asked categorically whether complementarity was a characteristic of the joint venture in question.
scale: correlation ranging from -1 to +1; categorical yes/no item

variable_name: partner contribution in each functional area
description: Partner firm managers rated the importance of their firm's contributions to the given joint venture in 10 areas of distinctive competence on a 1 to 10 scale, where a rating of 1 means the area was the most important contribution by the given partner and a rating of 10 means the partner contributed little or nothing. For the regression analyses the contribution rating was set up as a 0/1 dummy variable, with a value of 1 if a partner firm rated a functional area as one of its top three areas of contribution and 0 if an area was rated as 4 or below.

variable_name: partner influence over each functional area
description: Partner firm managers were asked to rate on a seven-point Likert type scale their level of influence over each of the 10 different functional areas of the joint venture. Information on the number and types of reviews conducted by each partner was used to assess the validity of the perceptual measures. Separate regressions were performed for each functional area, with an interaction term between the partner's contribution and its influence in the area.

variable_name: dominant partner versus shared influence joint venture
description: A joint venture was classified as a dominant partner joint venture if one partner firm owned 51% or more of the joint venture and that partner was reported by all partners as being the most influential partner in the joint venture. A joint venture that was not a dominant partner joint venture was classified as a shared influence joint venture. Percentages of ownership participation and contracts and agreements specifying formal voting rights, board membership and the number of managers supplied by each partner were recorded.

Joint venture autonomy was measured by the number and types of decisions the joint venture is allowed to make on its own, with questionnaire items developed to measure decision making autonomy in each of the 10 functional areas. Most of the responses were on a seven-point Likert type scale, and open-ended questions and contracts and supplementary written agreements were used to corroborate the responses. For the analysis, joint ventures with mean response ratings of 5 or higher on a performance dimension were classified as high performers and those with mean ratings below 4 as low performers.

Statements about joint venture performance on a seven-point Likert scale were presented to the partner firm managers, who indicated the extent to which they agreed or disagreed with each statement; the statements covered the financial performance of the joint venture, how well the objectives of each partner had been met, and the level of satisfaction with the other partners. As an overall measure, managers rated on a seven-point scale how the joint venture compared with other such joint ventures with which they were familiar; they were also asked whether their firm would join the given joint venture again, and rated on a seven-point scale how well the given oil field had been developed thus far. A factor analysis of the measures produced four dimensions: relational performance, operational/technical performance, financial performance, and future performance potential.

Corporate parent density equaled the number of corporate parents whose PC businesses were alive in a given year. It is a count-based, industry-level measure of the number of multibusiness endorsers present in the new industry and was updated annually. Because density and mass are alternative measures of the same phenomenon, the effects of the two were estimated in separate models.

For each corporate parent the authors first measured net size, which equaled its total corporate sales minus the sales of its PC business, using formulas based on Barnett and Amburgey (1990) and Baum and Mezias (1992). Parental mass was then defined as the industrywide sum in a focal year of the net sizes of all corporate parents, excluding the net size of a focal business's corporate parent. For stand-alones the focal corporate parent's net size was 0, so parental mass was simply the sum of the net sizes of the other parents in the industry.

Stand-alone density equaled the number of freestanding PC businesses in a given year. It is a count-based, industry-level measure of the number of native start-ups in the new industry, updated annually. It was estimated in separate models from the mass-based measures because of collinearity.

Stand-alone mass equaled the industry sum in a focal year of all stand-alone PC business sizes minus the size of the focal PC business if it was a stand-alone. For corporate children, stand-alone mass was simply the sum of the sizes of stand-alone organizations.

Corporate parent age was measured as the number of years since a corporate parent had been founded, and the variable was logged to reduce heteroscedasticity in the models. Like all the independent variables, it was updated annually. For stand-alone PC businesses this variable, as well as the other measures of parental characteristics, took on a value of zero, with a corporate parent dummy marking those observations.

Business size was measured as the log of deflated annual sales of PCs in year t - 1, information obtained from the IDC database. Lagged sales were used because the authors wanted to assess the slack inherited from previous operations, not current-period sales performance. To avoid losing the first observation in each business's annual time series, they regressed logged PC sales at time t on business age at time t - 1 using observations in which business age was two years or more, and used those parameters to extrapolate the amount of slack a business had at its founding. A missing business size dummy was set to 1 when business age equaled one year.

Failure was defined as the death of an entire stand-alone business or the exit from the PC industry of a diversified corporation. A business was coded as failing in year t if it sold no PCs in year t + 1 and all subsequent years in the sample window. When mergers occurred, the authors tracked the separate survival of the acquiring and acquired entities' PC businesses.
time_window: year t, based on sales in t + 1 and all subsequent sample years

description: Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the hospital used any of the four different types of alliance with physicians - IPA, OPHO, CPHO, or MSO - and 0 otherwise. Hospital-physician organizational form was measured with dummy variables coded from the discrete categories used in the AHA survey, with the arm's-length relationship between hospitals and physicians as the base category.

Dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the hospital reported using an Integrated Salary Model (ISM), i.e., an integrated organizational form in which the hospital employs its own physicians, and 0 otherwise. The base category of organizational form is the arm's-length relationship between hospitals and physicians.

Separate categories of low, medium, and high alliance scope, based on the rank ordering of the extent of activities that hospitals and physicians carry out through the alliance as compared to their total set of activities. An IPA alliance was categorized as low alliance scope, an OPHO alliance as medium alliance scope, and a hospital that used either a CPHO or MSO alliance as having high alliance scope.

Dummy variable equal to 1 for the year the hospital invested in the technology. A hospital is assumed to have invested in the new technology during the first year that it reports the technology's availability in the AHA annual survey. The dependent variable is measured separately for the two imaging technologies, PET and MRI; hospitals that had invested in MRI prior to 1995 are left-censored and excluded from the MRI analysis.

Index built from the market context items that loaded on this factor in the factor analysis of the seven environment items. For each item respondents indicated the future probability of the event mentioned. Indices were constructed by applying the weights for each item obtained by principal components analysis and then summing the weighted items.

Index built from the market context items that loaded on this factor in the factor analysis of the seven environment items. Respondents indicated the future probability of the events mentioned, such as falling margins or sales volume. Indices were constructed by weighting each item with principal components analysis weights and summing the weighted items.

Index built from the market context items that loaded on this factor in the factor analysis of the seven environment items, relating to the emergence of new Internet-based supplier and distribution channels. Respondents indicated the future probability of the events mentioned. Indices were constructed by weighting each item with principal components analysis weights and summing the weighted items.

Index of the four 'core' items of the modularity scale; items were newly developed by the authors because they were unaware of previous attempts to measure the construct, and were informed by the field studies and by recent theorizing, in particular Sanchez and Mahoney (1996). The factor analysis produced a two-factor solution; four core items were combined into the main modularity variable and two items formed an 'advanced modularity' variable, but only the analysis for the core items is reported. Items with poor loadings were dropped.

The total number of models/variants offered by the firm, reported by manufacturing and marketing managers who, the interviews indicated, could easily identify such figures for their company or division. The strategic flexibility indicators were used directly after a log transformation, applied because the authors found clear departures from the assumption of equal variance.

The total number of new models/variants introduced during 1998, reported by manufacturing and marketing managers. The indicator was used directly after a log transformation because of departures from the assumption of equal variance.

The number of entirely new products introduced during 1998, reported by manufacturing and marketing managers. The indicator was used directly after a log transformation because of departures from the assumption of equal variance.

Perceived performance measured with three items developed by Powell and Dent-Micallef (1997), answered on a Likert-type scale. The authors argue that subjective measures of performance have been widely used and most studies find high convergent validity with objective measures such as publicly available accounting data.

Index of items adopted from Amabile et al. (1996) and Powell and Dent-Micallef (1997) asking respondents to assess the degree of shared vision and the encouragement of creativity in their firms. The items loaded on a single factor and were combined into an index using principal components analysis weights.

Index of three items asking respondents to indicate whether they had formulated plans to improve their product development processes, to use existing or new technology to develop new products, or to enter new markets with existing products. The items were combined into an index using principal components analysis weights.

Index of items about the existence of small, autonomous units and rotation of personnel between different product areas, newly developed by the authors. The reliability of this scale was the lowest of the constructs, with the authors reporting that alphas ranged from 0.56 for modular structure to 0.84 for firm performance.

Index formed from the seven items that loaded on the same factor, focusing on codification, standardization and reengineering of work processes, as well as knowledge management systems and knowledge transfer; two items with poor item-to-factor correlations were dropped from the scale. Items were developed on the basis of recent theorizing, in particular Sanchez and Mahoney (1996).

Market context was measured by seven survey items asking for the future probability of events in the industry. Factor analysis gave three indices, customer/competitor changes, margin/volume pressure and Internet channels, each a weighted sum of its items.

variable_name: model variety, new model and new product introductions
description: Strategic flexibility was operationalized with three counts reported by manufacturing and marketing managers: the total number of models or variants offered, the number of new models or variants introduced during 1998, and the number of entirely new products introduced during 1998. Each was log transformed.

Dollar sales (in millions of dollars) that mass-producing breweries derived from faux craft beer products within market j in year t. The variable is logged for analysis as it is skewed. This variable is used to test Hypothesis 1.
time_window: year t; lagged by one year in the models

description: The count of peripheral (or near-center) breweries that enter market j in year t. Entry is considered to have occurred when a brewery's first product logs a sale in a given market.
time_window: year t; lagged by one year in the models

description: The dollar sales by craft brewery i in market j in year t. This variable is logged as sales are skewed right. Because lagged sales are also controlled for on the right-hand side of the equation, the dependent variable represents year-over-year sales growth of craft breweries.
A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the brewery is headquartered in the focal market. It is used as the measure of a local identity in the growth models.
The number of unique beers offered by craft brewery i in market j in year t. It is used as the measure of a product proliferator identity in the growth models.

The density or count of the number of craft breweries in each market, which the authors describe as a measure of competitive rivalry. It also enters as the interaction term in Hypotheses 3 and 4. Firm density is excluded from the entry models because, aggregated at the market level and included with year dummies, it closely mirrors the entry count dependent variable.
time_window: year t; lagged by one year in the models

description: Dummy variable that takes the value 1 if an announced M&A was completed and 0 otherwise. The announcement date marks the beginning of the public takeover stage and the completion date its conclusion, both dates as reported in Thomson. Deals recorded as 'intent withdrawn,' 'withdrawn,' or 'rumored only' make up the abandoned category. Deals that were not completed by 2009 were considered withdrawn.

Sum of the acquirer's prior completed (successful) M&As, measured over a moving window of three years prior to the focal transaction and aggregated across all acquisition contexts. It is entered in the model together with its squared term.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior abandoned (failed) M&As, measured over a moving window of three years prior to the focal transaction and aggregated across all acquisition contexts. It is entered in the model together with its squared term.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior completed M&As classified as domestic, that is, deals in which the firms involved were headquartered in the same country according to Thomson. Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior abandoned M&As classified as domestic, that is, deals in which the firms involved were headquartered in the same country according to Thomson. Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior completed M&As classified as cross-border, that is, deals in which the firms involved were headquartered in different countries according to Thomson. Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior abandoned M&As classified as cross-border, that is, deals in which the firms involved were headquartered in different countries according to Thomson. Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior completed M&As classified as intra-industry, that is, deals in which both firms had SIC code 2711 (newspaper industry). Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior abandoned M&As classified as intra-industry, that is, deals in which both firms had SIC code 2711 (newspaper industry). Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior completed M&As classified as diversifying, that is, acquisitions of targets outside SIC code 2711. Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of all diversifying M&As, that is, acquisitions of targets outside SIC code 2711, that were abandoned in the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior completed M&As classified as friendly, based on a conservative classification of how a deal was presented publicly and reported in Thomson. Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior abandoned M&As classified as friendly, based on a conservative classification of how a deal was presented publicly and reported in Thomson. Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior completed M&As classified as hostile, based on a conservative classification of how a deal was presented publicly and reported in Thomson. Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Sum of the acquirer's prior abandoned M&As classified as hostile, based on a conservative classification of how a deal was presented publicly and reported in Thomson. Measured over the three years prior to the focal transaction.
time_window: three years prior to the focal transaction

description: Modularity degree of component i, following the measure introduced by Fine et al. (2005) as modified by Cabigiosu and Camuffo (2012); the algebraic specification is not readable in the text provided. The measure involves the number of functions the component performs (Fi) and the number of closed interfaces it has with other elements (Ini), with normalization scalars set to ζ1 = 1 and ζ2 = 1 so that modularity values range from 0 to 1, where 1 stands for perfect modularity. Only closed interfaces are counted, as the complementary and opposite category of open standard interfaces. Functions were listed and the number of functions performed by each component identified with the OEMs' chief engineers, and interfaces were counted and classified through a design structure matrix analysis covering spatial, energetic, material, and informative interactions.

Inverse proxy for organizational modularity, built from scales developed by Cabigiosu and Camuffo (2012) and earlier work on buyer-supplier integration. Ten questionnaire items measure the extent of information sharing between buyer and supplier in three interorganizational processes: new product development (3 items), contract and price negotiation (3 items), and logistics (4 items). The sample mean of these 10 items is used to obtain an overall measure of information sharing, and the reliability analysis is supportive (Cronbach's alpha is 0.81). Higher values indicate thicker relationships, i.e., lower organizational modularity.

Measure of the rate of component technological change referring to Brusoni et al. (2001) and Takeishi (2002) that encompasses both product and process technological changes. One item measures how frequently the underlying technology of the component changes over time, one item measures how frequently the component production process changes over time, and an extra item measures how important suppliers' technological innovativeness is as a criterion to choose and evaluate the suppliers of the analyzed component. The measure comprises three items adapted from previous studies, which show good reliability (Cronbach's alpha is 0.75).
The CEO's number of years in office. In the sample, CEOs had been CEO for 14 years (S.D. 8.52).

Measured using Miller and Friesen's (1983) 3-item, 7-point scale. The construct refers to the proclivity to engage in risky projects and preference for bold vs. cautious acts to achieve firm objectives. Cronbach's alpha was 0.77.

Following Zahra (1996), entrepreneurial initiatives were measured as a three-dimensional metaconstruct (innovation, venturing, and renewal activities) represented by 16 items on a 5-point scale, ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'). Respondents were asked to consider their responses over the last three years. Cronbach's alpha was 0.75.

Using items in Gupta and Govindarajan (1986), CEOs assessed their firms' performance relative to that of their competitors' on eight different dimensions (growth in sales, growth in market share, etc.) for the past year. Cronbach's alpha was 0.92.

The proportion of outlets franchised in a given year, used as a measure of the use of contractual forms of governance. The authors follow previous research (Lafontaine, 1992) in using this variable because franchisee outlets are operated by residual claimants and company-owned outlets are operated by salaried managers.

The number of years since the firm began to franchise. It is one of the two independent variables used to test the momentum hypotheses, and all independent variables in the analysis are lagged one year.

The difference between the numbers of franchised outlets at times t and t - 1. It is the second independent variable used to test the momentum hypotheses, and all independent variables in the analysis are lagged one year.

The five-year (1983-1987) average return on assets for the four-digit SIC industry in which the firm did the largest share of its business. Data came from Dun and Bradstreet's Industry Norms and Key Business Ratios.
The difference between a firm's average return on assets (ROA) and its industry's average ROA during the five-year period 1983-1987. Calculated using annual reports and Dun and Bradstreet data.
Based on data published by the Bureau of the Census, using the Herfindahl-Hirshman index, a figure calculated by squaring and summing the market shares of the 50 largest firms in an industry.
Average sales (in millions) for each firm during the period 1983-1987, using data from annual reports and Moody's Industrial News Reports.

Four questions on the structural questionnaire asked for information about vertical differentiation, horizontal differentiation, and spatial differentiation. Responses were verified as far as possible against information from 10Ks about number of sites and divisions, and then added together to yield a complexity index for each organization.

Collected with a questionnaire adaptation of the interview schedule used in the initial Aston study of structure. Forty-six questions asked informants to report the lowest hierarchical level responsible for making various kinds of decisions. Informants answered on a six-point scale (nonmanagerial employee = 0, nonmanagerial staff = 1, lower management = 2, middle management = 3, top management = 4, CEO = 5, board = 6). Responses were added together, yielding a range of possible centralization scores of 0 to 276. Summed scale scores were then reversed so that larger numbers indicated higher decentralization. Alpha coefficient was 0.81.
scale: 0 to 276 after summing; six-point response scale per item

description: Obtained by a 47-item mailed questionnaire based on the ethical practices questionnaire developed by Bentley College's Center for Business Ethics. The 47 items yielded a total possible score ranging from 0 to 65. Higher scores on the 65-point scale were interpreted as indicative of stronger levels of ethical climate. Alpha coefficient was 0.80.

Court proceedings among environmental enforcement actions under EPA and U.S. Coast Guard jurisdiction were designated serious violations. Data were obtained from government documents secured through Freedom of Information requests to the EPA and the U.S. Coast Guard Environmental Division, and from corporate 10K reports. The number of violations per firm was standardized by proportionalizing it by firm size (number of employees), producing the number of serious violations per 1,000 employees.

Administrative actions among environmental enforcement actions were designated nonserious violations. Data came from the same government documents and 10K reports. The number of violations per firm was standardized by proportionalizing it by firm size (number of employees), producing the number of nonserious violations per 1,000 employees.

Dummy variable for the fate of each 1977 unrelated acquisition tracked over a five-year period. Coded one if the acquired company was divested by the parent and zero if it was retained. Determinations were based on each parent's annual roster of subsidiaries and affiliates in Dunn and Bradstreet's Who Owns Whom and Standard & Poor's America's Corporate Families, cross-checked against annual activity reports in Mergers & Acquisitions, company annual reports, Wall Street Journal abstracts, and the Dow Jones Industrial Reporter.

Total cash and monetary contributions transferred from the acquired unrelated firm to the acquirer. Divided by the acquired unit's total sales to account for size differences. Recorded for the first year of the five-year tracking period from COMPUSTAT financial records.
time_window: first year of the 5-year tracking period

description: Proportionate change in the acquired unit's cash flow contributions calculated as (t2 - t1)/t1, where t1 is the value at the time of the acquisition and t2 the value at the time the acquisition was divested or the end of the five-year period if it had been retained. Built from COMPUSTAT data.
time_window: acquisition to divestiture or end of the 5-year period

description: The acquiring firm's debt-to-equity ratio, used as the measure of its debt capacity (higher debt-to-equity means lower debt capacity). Normed for industry effects by subtracting the acquiring firm's values from the primary 4-digit SIC industry average. Recorded for the first year of the five-year tracking period from COMPUSTAT financial records.
time_window: first year of the 5-year tracking period

description: Proportionate change in the acquiring firm's debt-to-equity ratio over the tracking period, calculated as (t2 - t1)/t1, with t1 the value at the time of the acquisition and t2 the value at divestiture or the end of the five-year period. A larger increase in debt-to-equity represents a larger reduction in debt capacity.
time_window: acquisition to divestiture or end of the 5-year period

description: Current assets divided by current liabilities, used to measure the acquiring firm's current slack. Normed for industry effects by subtracting the acquiring firm's values from the primary 4-digit SIC industry average. Recorded for the first year of the five-year tracking period from COMPUSTAT financial records.
time_window: first year of the 5-year tracking period

description: Proportionate change in the acquiring firm's current ratio over the tracking period, calculated as (t2 - t1)/t1, with t1 the value at the time of the acquisition and t2 the value at divestiture or the end of the five-year period. Built from COMPUSTAT data.
time_window: acquisition to divestiture or end of the 5-year period

description: Ratio of sales, general and administrative expenses to sales, used to measure the acquiring firm's potential slack (a higher ratio indicates lower potential slack). Normed for industry effects by subtracting the acquiring firm's values from the primary 4-digit SIC industry average. Recorded for the first year of the five-year tracking period from COMPUSTAT financial records.

description: Proportionate change in the acquiring firm's SGA/sales ratio over the tracking period, calculated as (t2 - t1)/t1, with t1 the value at the time of the acquisition and t2 the value at divestiture or the end of the five-year period. Built from COMPUSTAT data.

description: Concentric index of diversification (Caves et al., 1980), a continuous measure in which the fraction of the firm's sales in each industry is weighted by the distance of that industry from the firm's largest business; the distance is zero if the industries share a 4-digit SIC, one if they share a 3-digit SIC, and so on. Higher values reflect diversification away from the company's largest business. Computed for the first year of the five-year tracking period from Dunn and Bradstreet's Who Owns Whom and Standard & Poor's America's Corporate Families; the formula as printed in the text is not legible in this version.
time_window: first year of the 5-year tracking period

description: Number of employees (logged) of the acquired unrelated firm divided by the number of employees (logged) of the acquirer. Based on the year immediately preceding the acquisition, with values found in COMPUSTAT.

Difference in the standard deviation of the parent's sales before and after the acquisition, computed in three steps: the standard deviation of the parent firm's sales prior to the acquisition was computed, the standard deviation of the parent firm's sales for the years the acquisition was retained was computed, and the difference between the two was taken. That difference represents the parent's relative variability in sales after the acquisition. Data came from COMPUSTAT.
time_window: before the acquisition to the years the acquisition was retained

description: Dummy variable for the fate of each 1987 unrelated acquisition tracked over a five-year period. Coded one if the acquired company was divested by the parent and zero if it was retained. Determinations were based on each parent's annual roster of subsidiaries and affiliates in Dunn and Bradstreet's Who Owns Whom and Standard & Poor's America's Corporate Families, cross-checked against annual activity reports in Mergers & Acquisitions, company annual reports, Wall Street Journal abstracts, and the Dow Jones Industrial Reporter.

Total cash and monetary contributions transferred from the acquired unrelated firm to the acquirer, divided by the acquired unit's total sales to account for size differences. Recorded for the first year of the five-year tracking period from COMPUSTAT financial records.
time_window: first year of the 5-year tracking period

description: Proportionate change in the acquired unit's cash flow contributions calculated as (t2 - t1)/t1, where t1 is the value at the time of the acquisition and t2 the value at the time the acquisition was divested or the end of the five-year period if it had been retained. Built from COMPUSTAT data.
time_window: acquisition to divestiture or end of the 5-year period

description: The acquiring firm's debt-to-equity ratio, used as the measure of its debt capacity (higher debt-to-equity means lower debt capacity). Normed for industry effects by subtracting the acquiring firm's values from the primary 4-digit SIC industry average. Recorded for the first year of the five-year tracking period from COMPUSTAT financial records.

Higher values reflect diversification away from the company's largest business. Computed for the first year of the five-year tracking period from Dunn and Bradstreet's Who Owns Whom and Standard & Poor's America's Corporate Families; the formula as printed in the text is not legible in this version.

description: Number of employees (logged) of the acquired unrelated firm divided by the number of employees (logged) of the acquirer. Based on the year immediately preceding the acquisition, with values found in COMPUSTAT.

Difference in the standard deviation of the parent's sales before and after the acquisition, computed in three steps: the standard deviation of the parent firm's sales prior to the acquisition was computed, the standard deviation of the parent firm's sales for the years the acquisition was retained was computed, and the difference between the two was taken. That difference represents the parent's relative variability in sales after the acquisition. Data came from COMPUSTAT.
time_window: before the acquisition to the years the acquisition was retained

description: Calculated as the difference between a firm's innovation performance in year t, its number of successful patent applications, and its historical and social aspiration levels. Historical aspiration levels are exponentially weighted moving averages of historical performance, Ait = alpha*Ait-1 + (1 - alpha)*Pit-1. Social aspiration levels are the average patenting performance of other dedicated biotechnology firms in the panel in a given year. Spline variables are used: performance - aspirations (<0) equals the difference when performance is below the aspiration level and equals zero when performance is at or above it; performance - aspirations (>0) equals the difference when performance is above the aspiration level and equals zero when performance is at or below it.
Calculated as the ratio of a firm's selling, general, and administrative expenses to its sales in year t, consistent with prior research.
The share of all alliances in a firm's alliance portfolio in year t that include minority equity investments and/or are joint ventures.

The standardized monthly volatility of a firm's stock in year t. For each firm in each year, the coefficient of variation is obtained by calculating the standard deviation across the firm's monthly stock closing prices and dividing it by their average.

The count of alliances formed by a firm in year t + 1 involving a novel partner and exclusively focusing on resources already accessible through the firm's existing alliance portfolio. Partner identities and resources exchanged for each alliance were obtained from ReCap; a partner is novel when the firm had no active alliance with that partner in its existing alliance portfolio, and a resource is existing when the alliance did not include at least one technological area not already included in any alliance in the firm's portfolio.

The count of alliances formed by a firm in year t + 1 involving at least one new resource, with a partner already in the firm's existing alliance portfolio. Resources are identified and distinguished using ReCap's classification of alliances as pertaining to one or multiple of 53 possible technological areas, and an alliance focuses on new resources when it includes at least one technological area that was not included in any alliance in the firm's alliance portfolio.

The count of alliances formed by a firm in year t + 1 involving a novel partner and at least one new resource, where new resources are technological areas not already provided by an alliance in the firm's existing portfolio and a novel partner is one with which the firm had no active alliance in its existing alliance portfolio.

Measured as a firm's number of successful patent applications in year t, based on the patenting activities of the dedicated biotechnology firms in the sample. It is the basis for the historical and social aspiration levels used to construct performance relative to aspirations.

Annual average Goldstein conflict-cooperation score of all media-reported events between the home and host countries, taken from GDELT. Each event's impact is scaled from -10 (most conflictual) to +10 (most cooperative); the annual average for a country pair was reverse-coded so that higher values mean more conflictual events. The variable is lagged one year and mean-centered.
scale: Goldstein scale of -10 (most conflictual) to +10 (most cooperative), reversed

description: Annual ESG score of the foreign MNE's subsidiary in a given host country, supplied by Refinitiv Eikon. Refinitiv provides scores for each firm on the three pillars Environmental [E], Social [S], and Governance [G]; the aggregate ESG score is used as the dependent variable. Higher values indicate more ESG activity by the subsidiary in the host country.

Categorical coding built from interstate-conflict-and-crisis data in ICB v15. Country pairs whose home and host countries had been involved in serious interstate conflict with each other before the sample period (before 2002) but not during the sample period were coded 1. All other country pairs form the baseline reference group coded 0.

Categorical coding built from ICB v15. Country pairs whose two countries engaged in a serious interstate conflict or crisis identified in the database as main adversarial actors during the sample period were coded 2. All other country pairs form the baseline reference group coded 0.

Each case contained one of two alternative paragraphs that manipulated the decision motive as a problem or as an opportunity. The manipulation conveyed the motive in two ways: labeling (the heading 'The Problem' or 'The Opportunity' and a sentence stating that management 'was faced with an unusual problem' or 'an unusual opportunity') and the sign of the expected effects (negative consequences such as lost sales, lower flexibility, lower yields and higher costs versus positive consequences such as increased sales, flexibility and yields). Together with the performance manipulation this produced four combinations of conditions for each of the two cases.

Each case contained one of two alternative paragraphs that manipulated the hypothetical firm's performance level as poor or as excellent. Labeling was one means ('its recent performance had been poor' versus 'its recent performance continued to be excellent'); the second was numerical data placed above or below industry averages by the same amount in the two conditions, covering stock price change, returns on assets and equity, net income as a percentage of sales, and annual sales growth.

Participants indicated what they would do to decide whether to modify the manufacturing facilities or to develop a new product line, using Likert-type questions. Ten modified questions from two previous field studies were used: seven single-response questions that required a choice between the least and the most comprehensive of the actions previously presented as five or six alternatives, and three multi-item composites. All questions used 7-point scales; for the single-response questions 1 = strongly agree with the first, less comprehensive action and 7 = strongly disagree, recommending the more comprehensive action, whereas the composite questions were worded and scaled in the opposite direction and were rescaled for the data analysis, with Cronbach's alphas ranging from .83 to .94.

The same cases and the same problem/opportunity manipulation of the decision motive used in the first study were randomly assigned to the executives; the manipulation combined labeling of the motive with the sign of its expected effects, producing four combinations of conditions for each case.

The same manipulation of the hypothetical firm's performance level as poor or excellent, accomplished by labeling plus numerical data above or below industry averages, was used with the executive sample.

The executives responded to the same ten recommended-action questions (seven single-response questions and three multi-item composites) used in the first study, on 7-point Likert-type scales, with the composite items worded and scaled in the opposite direction from the single-response items and rescaled for the data analysis.

Measured as government-sourced contract revenue divided by total sales. Contract revenue comes from USASpending.gov and sales from Compustat. Predictors are measured at time t while dependent variables are measured at time t+1.

Calculated as the sum of the value of common stock, the liquidating value of preferred stock, the book value of long-term debt, and firm debt with maturity of less than one year, divided by the firm's total assets. It is used as a forward-looking measure of the market's valuation of the firm's future profit prospects and is measured at time t+1.

The log of capital expenditures, one of the two variables used to test the hypotheses focused on firm investment. It is a measure of investment of current resources in anticipation of future benefits and is measured at time t+1.

The log of R&D expenditures, the second variable used to test the hypotheses focused on firm investment. It is a measure of investment of current resources in anticipation of future benefits and is measured at time t+1.
The number of distinct major agencies of the U.S. government with which the firm contracts, measured at time t.
The number of new unique contracts a firm secured within the focal year, measured at time t.
The average number of years remaining for all ongoing and new contracts within each year, measured at time t.

A dummy variable indicating whether there were personal connections between a firm and the KMT in the pre-movement period. The authors considered both formal ties developed through politicians serving in firms and the informal ties of blood and marital relations, friendships, classmates, and hometown relationships, and membership in the same social clubs. Connections were identified by matching the names of corporate and political leaders, with political leaders defined as members of Central Committees, legislators-at-large, representatives of the National Assembly, and high-level government officials, and corporate leaders as directors, supervisors, senior executives, and shareholders with more than 10 percent of a firm's shares. The variable equals one if the firm had ties to the KMT and zero otherwise.

The dates, amounts, targets, and purposes of corporate philanthropic donations were collected and the amounts were aggregated for each quarter. A log transformation was applied to correct for skewed values, adding one to the raw values to handle zeros. Count and dummy variables were used as alternative measures only in the additional analyses.
The variable captures the occurrence of the Sunflower Movement and equals one for quarters after Q1 2014 and zero otherwise.

A dummy variable indicating whether political figures of the old regime had lost their positions. It indicates whether a focal firm was headquartered in a city that had a KMT mayor between 2012 and the fourth quarter of 2014 but elected a non-KMT mayor in the 2014 local election. The KMT administered 15 cities before this election and lost 9 of them.

The city-level per capita number of NGOs, measuring local engagement in citizens' groups. NGO registration information came from the Taiwan NGO Information Platform and demographic statistics from the Department of Household Registration. Data on 7,072 NGOs were collected, city-level NGO counts were aggregated based on their operation locations, and the variable was scaled by dividing by 10,000; the mean value in the pre-movement period was used.

Law firm growth is measured as a law firm adding associates in a given year. The authors report hazard models that estimate the probability of a law firm adding any associates in a given year, i.e. the 0/1 decision to add any associates rather than the number of associates added, because their baseline covariates only had significant effects on the 0/1 decision. The dependent variable is the instantaneous rate of a law firm adding one or more associates in a given year.

Freeman's betweenness centrality was computed for each partner from the yearly lawyer-by-lawyer coemployment matrix to determine the extent to which a focal lawyer is the only path through which other lawyers in the network are connected. The contemporaneous matrix for year t contains each lawyer's current affiliation and any movement of lawyers between firms that occurred only in the year t-1. Partners' betweenness centrality is aggregated to the firm level as the average betweenness of the partners in the law firm.

Betweenness centrality computed from the past-ties matrix, which for each year t contains each lawyer's current affiliation and any movement of lawyers between firms that occurred prior to t-1 (at least two years before the reference year). Partners' betweenness centrality is aggregated to the firm level as the average betweenness of the partners in the law firm.

Betweenness centrality computed from the imprinted-ties matrix, which for each year t contains each lawyer's current affiliation and the movement of lawyers at any point in the past (t-1 and prior) who had been imprinted in the formative stage of their careers. A tie was identified as imprinted when a focal lawyer early in her career (first four years of legal practice) worked with one or more lawyers late in their careers (five years or more of legal practice). Partners' betweenness centrality is aggregated to the firm level as the average betweenness of the partners in the law firm.

The firm's industry-adjusted annual stock return (including dividends), where industries were classified based on two-digit SIC codes. Stock returns were obtained from CRSP. The variable was lagged by one year in the regressions.

Calculated as the net strength and weakness rankings of five dimensions from KLD: employee, community, diversity, environment, and product. The authors assume that observable CSR ratings are positively correlated with CSR investment, which is generally unobservable. The variable was lagged by one year in the regressions.

Equals 1 if the CEO was fired, 0 otherwise. It was measured using Shen and Cannella's (2002) method to code involuntary turnover; 339 successions were evaluated using media articles from major U.S. newspapers in LexisNexis covering 1 year before to 1 year after the transition. Successions in which CEOs died, had health issues, were interim CEOs, accepted similar positions at other firms, or left due to a merger or acquisition were eliminated, and dismissals were identified from the remaining successions.
time_window: 1 year before to 1 year after the CEO transition

description: Directors rated their cognitive conflict with the CEO on two items adapted from Jehn (1995) and Jehn and Mannix (2001): 'How often do you have conflict of ideas with the CEO?' and 'How often do you have task-related disagreements with the CEO?' Responses were given on a seven-point scale (1 = never; 7 = always), and the Cronbach's alpha was .76. Ratings were aggregated to the board level, excluding the chair's rating because the chair would otherwise be rating their own leadership behavior.

The CEOs rated each focal outside director's engagement in monitoring using three adapted items from McDonald, Khanna, and Westphal (2008), with the name and surname of the focal director inserted in the item text. The items were measured on a seven-point scale (1 = minimally; 7 = very much so), and the Cronbach's alpha was .76.

The directors rated the participative leadership of the chair through six survey items following Arnold et al. (2000), adapted by Huang, Iun, Liu, and Gong (2010), for example 'The chair listens to directors' ideas and suggestions' and 'The chair gives all directors a chance to voice their opinions.' Items used a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree) and the Cronbach's alpha was .85. Ratings were aggregated to the board level, excluding the chair's own rating.

The directors provided ratings on board psychological safety using an adapted version of Edmondson's (1999) five-item measure of team psychological safety, in which the referent category 'team' was replaced by 'supervisory board.' Items included 'If you make a mistake on this supervisory board, it is often held against you' (reverse scored), 'Members of this supervisory board are able to bring up problems and tough issues,' and 'It is safe to express views within this supervisory board.' Items used a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree), the Cronbach's alpha was .78, and ratings were aggregated to the board level.

The yearly number of solar PV cell producers for each country in the dataset, based on counts of producers that resulted from triangulation of the annual lists of solar PV producers published by PV News and Photon International. The source lists include small producers with limited lifetimes, which the authors take as evidence that virtually all producers are captured. The independent variables were lagged by one year, and continuous predictors were centered prior to estimation.

Constructed as one minus the ratio of the number of producers with a contrasting identity over the total number of producers, so that it runs from zero (all producers have contrasting identity) to one (no producers with a contrasting identity). Contrasting identity was operationalized as having origins in the incumbent energy sector, i.e., companies with primary NAICS code 21 (Mining, Quarrying, and Oil and Gas Extraction), 22 (Utilities), or 324 (Petroleum and Coal Products Manufacturing). Because coherence is meaningful only for observations with non-zero density, an adjustment variable technique was used: a dummy takes the value of one when the independent variable is missing and the unconditional variable mean is substituted for those observations.

The concentration of the non-renewable energy industries sector in a country and for a given year, measured with the Herfindahl index (sum of the squared market shares) of nuclear, coal, oil, and natural gas, using data from the World Bank Database. A higher value indicates greater concentration. The variable was lagged by one year and centered prior to estimation.

A dummy variable, updated annually at the country level, capturing whether there was a feed-in tariff scheme in each country for all years up to 2012. Data were collected from the IEA Photovoltaic Power Systems Program Reports, the IEA ''Policies & Measures'' section, and reports by PV-ERANET; earlier years were collected from PV News by searching for the terms ''feed'' and ''tariffs,'' and recent years were corroborated using the Res-legal website.
scale: dummy (1 = FIT scheme present in the country for that year)

variable_name: family and lone-founder status dummy variables
description: Company web sites and Hoover's company histories were used to identify the founder or founding family, and proxy statements were then examined for beneficial owners of 5% or more of shares, officers, or directors sharing the founder's surname or with disclosed familial relationships. A family company was any firm with 5% or more beneficial (voting) ownership held by a family member or members, indicated by the dummy variable family. Lone-founder firms were coded when 5% or more beneficial ownership was held by a single person who was the company's founder and no other person related to the founder was a significant owner, director, or officer.
scale: dummy variables (regular public companies are the omitted category)

variable_name: links to family, lone-founder, and regular public companies
description: Received interlocks indicate the number of directors of each sample firm, each year, who were also officers or directors of another sample firm; neutral interlocks are the number of directors who were also directors (but not officers) of other sample firms; sent interlocks are the number of the focal firm's officers who were directors of other sample firms. Regardless of type, links to family firms represent the number of interlocks of any type that connected the focal firm to other family companies, and links to lone-founder firms (regular public companies) are the number of interlocks of any type that connected the focal firm to lone-founder firms (regular public companies).

For each director, the number of years that the director had served as an executive or director for one of the other companies in the sample; coded to 0 if the director had no such experience, and dynamic because it changes as the director's experience changes. For the firm-year panel, the number of years of family-firm experience was summed across all outside directors on the firm's board each year. The measure was log-transformed as log(1 + experience) because it was highly skewed and left-censored at 0.

For each director, the number of years that the director had served as an executive or director for one of the other lone-founder companies in the sample; coded to 0 if the director had no such experience, and dynamic because it changes as the director's experience changes. For the firm-year panel, the number of years of lone-founder experience was summed across all outside directors on the firm's board each year. The measure was log-transformed as log(1 + experience) because it was highly skewed and left-censored at 0.

The percentage of outstanding shares held by dedicated institutional investors in the fourth quarter of each firm-year, using Brian Bushee's institutional investor classification data. Because the data are quarterly, ownership was taken in the fourth quarter of each year, any institution with less than a 1% stake in the company was dropped, and institutional ownership was then summed across each category for each firm each year. Ownership information was not available for all sample firms and years, so the sample for the institutional investor analyses is smaller.

variable_name: family and lone-founder firm dummy variables
description: The same classification of sample firms into family, lone-founder, and regular public companies is used at the director level, so that each outside director's board is identified as a family-controlled, lone-founder-controlled, or regular public firm board. Regular public companies serve as the omitted category in the reported models.
scale: dummy variables (regular public companies are the omitted category)

description: A dummy variable coded to 1 if the director terminated his or her service during the year and to 0 otherwise. The dataset includes one observation per outside director per year, and all independent variables were updated each year; upon exit, the directorship was dropped from the dataset. Interpreted in the event-history model, exit = 0 is a censored observation.
time_window: annual, one observation per outside director per year

description: At the individual director level, the number of years that the director had served as an executive or director for one of the other sample family companies, coded to 0 when the director had no such experience. The measure is dynamic, is updated each year, and captures experience at other firms rather than the focal firm. It was log-transformed as log(1 + experience) because it was highly skewed and left-censored at 0.

At the individual director level, the number of years that the director had served as an executive or director for one of the other sample lone-founder companies, coded to 0 when the director had no such experience. The measure is dynamic, is updated each year, and captures experience at other firms rather than the focal firm. It was log-transformed as log(1 + experience) because it was highly skewed and left-censored at 0.

The dependent variable is a time-varying dichotomous measure for each firm-year, coded 1 when a firm divested its Burmese holdings in a given year and coded 0 otherwise. The data come from quarterly publications by the Investor Responsibility Research Center (IRRC) on multinational firm investments in Burma between 1996 and 2002.

A time-varying dummy variable coded 1 in years in which there was at least one documented anti-Burma protest event in the home country of the firms in the sample. Trained research assistants searched articles and press releases from around the world using keyword strings such as Burma + protest + 1996 or Myanmar + demonstration + 1998, and coded when and where a protest event took place.
scale: dummy (1 = at least one protest event)

description: An index of the level of political freedom constructed by Freedom House, based on ratings of political rights in a country from the 1996-2002 editions of the Freedom of the World Survey. It measures political rights in three main areas: electoral process, political pluralism and participation, and functioning of government. The index is measured on a 1-7 point scale, and the authors reverse-coded the original scale so that 7 represents the highest level and 1 the lowest level of political freedom.

The Corruption Perception Index compiled by Transparency International, a composite of surveys of country analysts and business people from multiple institutions worldwide, such as the Economist Intelligence Unit, IMD International, the World Bank and the World Economic Forum. The values of the index range from 1 to 10, where 1 = low transparency (high corruption) and 10 = high transparency (low corruption).

The divestment actions of other firms enter the heterogeneous diffusion model through the susceptibility, infectiousness and proximity vectors, which create in effect an interaction between the cumulative number of divesting firms and the firm- or country-level characteristic of interest. The susceptibility vector measures potential adopters' susceptibility to divestment by other firms, and the proximity vector captures how the actions of firms in a particular category affect other firms in that category.

A country's yearly mean number of economic ties to other countries via shared memberships in intergovernmental organizations, entered in the susceptibility vector. The authors expect that centrality in the economic IGO network reflects country-level business pressures that influence the decision to continue doing business in Burma.

A country's yearly mean number of social ties to other countries via shared memberships in intergovernmental organizations, entered in the susceptibility vector. The authors expect that centrality in the social IGO network reflects country-level social pressures that influence the decision to continue doing business in Burma.

Firm size is measured by the yearly logarithm of total sales. The variable is entered in the propensity vector as a firm-level control, in the susceptibility vector as a characteristic of potential adopters, in the infectiousness vector as a characteristic of divesting firms, and in the proximity vector as the basis for similarity between firms.

A composite of foreign sales as a percentage of total sales and foreign assets as a percentage of total assets, measured yearly, capturing access to foreign markets and ownership of foreign operations. The variable is entered in the propensity, susceptibility, infectiousness and proximity vectors of the diffusion model.

Similarity in internationalization was modeled in the proximity vector of the diffusion model using the yearly composite of foreign sales as a percentage of total sales and foreign assets as a percentage of total assets.

variable_name: firm size in the proximity vector
description: Similarity in size was modeled in the proximity vector of the heterogeneous diffusion model using each firm's yearly log of total sales, to test whether divestment spread among similarly sized firms.

The cumulative number of frequency changes that the newspaper had experienced so far, updated whenever a change occurred: if a change was registered in a certain subepisode, the following subepisodes were assigned the cumulative number of changes experienced so far. The natural logarithm of this variable was used, because some studies have revealed that the effect of prior changes is not linear.
time_window: monthly subepisodes, updated after each change

description: Dependent variable coded as 1 for a subepisode in which a frequency change occurred and 0 for all other subepisodes. A frequency change is a change in the weekly number of issues of a newspaper, which the authors treat as a market niche change because differences in the frequency of publication mean that different types of newspaper customers or preferences are addressed. The data were split into monthly subepisodes.

The logged number of prior coach replacements was taken as a covariate. Because the data provided the coach's name for each match of each team, a change of coach could be accounted for at each observation, and the count of prior changes was updated accordingly.
time_window: updated at each round of the Bundesliga

description: An observation was coded as 1 when a change of coach occurred and otherwise as 0. Each observation corresponds to a team's match in a round of the Bundesliga, which mostly take place in weekly intervals. A championship season consists of 34 rounds played by 18 teams.

The logarithmic formulation of the number of prior changes of a rule was included as a covariate in the analysis of rule change. Change events are alterations of an individual rule's content, and the count accumulates over the monthly subepisodes of a rule.
time_window: monthly subepisodes, accumulating over the observation period

description: When a rule change occurred, a subepisode was coded as 1, and otherwise as 0. A change event is defined as alteration of an individual rule's content. The history of each rule was split into monthly subepisodes.

Measured as the number of wineries in a CSD in a given year. The authors treat a CSD as a cluster of wineries and test the collocation effect on winery founding and mortality. Consistent with previous research, only CSDs in which at least one winery had been established during the observation period are included; in total 36 CSDs, or 36 industry clusters, are included in the study.

Counts of new winery establishments in a CSD in a given year, with the Census Subdivision as the unit of analysis. The analysis includes 142 founding events in 3,960 yearly observations spread out over 36 CSDs.

The hazard rate at which a winery perishes. The data involve 142 wineries over 109 years; only 8 wineries continued operating after 1974 and are therefore right censored, giving 1,673 winery-year observations at risk. Higher values indicate a higher chance of perishing, i.e., lower survival.

The life cycle of Ontario's wine production is divided into two stages using major exogenous, historic shocks rather than endogenous measures of entry: the growth stage from 1865 to 1928 and the mature stage from 1929 to 1974. The division follows a comprehensive historic analysis of the industry in which Prohibition (1916-1927) triggered a major boom and its end in 1927, together with the Great Depression beginning in 1929, initiated a long period of consolidation; the industry was reborn in 1975.

The influence of a dedicated M&A function is measured directly by following the measure of Markham, Bonjean, and Corder (1984). A five-point Likert scale is used to measure responses to the question of which organizational unit has which influence during the M&A process, including a 'not available' response. The variable is measured via the M&A departments at the corporate and business unit levels, and the dedicated M&A resources within other staff functions at the corporate and business unit levels. Since the variable is most likely determined by only one of the four indicators, the average of the existing units is calculated.

The operationalization is based on Kale and Singh's (2007) operationalization of alliance capabilities, slightly modified pursuant to the input of several pre-testers. An M&A capability builds on the articulation, codification, sharing, and internalization of knowledge, which are latent variables comprising several indicators. It is operationalized with a second-order model using a five-point Likert scale representing the level of consensus with each indicator, and the dimensions-related constructs are operationalized as constructs themselves rather than as observed variables. The first- and second-order models are both specified as reflective.

Following Datta and Grant's (1990) and Capron's (1999) operationalization, subjective evaluation criteria are used. Respondents were asked to assess the development of sales, market shares, operating margin, synergy realization, and overall satisfaction relative to the primary expectations on a five-point Likert scale. In addition, the respondents were asked whether, in retrospect, they would make the acquisition again.

One of the four deliberate learning mechanisms used to operationalize an M&A capability; it is specified as a reflective latent variable measured with several indicators (Appendix S1) on a five-point Likert scale representing the level of consensus with each indicator. The authors describe it as involving debriefing sessions and a formalized review process that make managers reflect on past activities and link their actions to associated outcomes, and as keeping a record of the status quo, the progress of the respective M&A, and the contact details of the relevant internal and external experts.

One of the four deliberate learning mechanisms used to operationalize an M&A capability; it is specified as a reflective latent variable measured with several indicators (Appendix S1) on a five-point Likert scale representing the level of consensus with each indicator. It refers to a well-defined, repeatable process that allows a larger number of personnel to gain acquisition knowledge and to collecting and understanding the reasons for the success and failure of past actions and decisions.

One of the four deliberate learning mechanisms used to operationalize an M&A capability; it is specified as a reflective latent variable measured with several indicators (Appendix S1) on a five-point Likert scale representing the level of consensus with each indicator. It covers formal ways of transferring and sharing knowledge via committees, task forces, meetings, seminars, and retreats, and informal ways via phone and e-mail, as well as incentives for employees to work together and share their personal M&A knowledge.

One of the four deliberate learning mechanisms used to operationalize an M&A capability; it is specified as a reflective latent variable measured with several indicators (Appendix S1) on a five-point Likert scale representing the level of consensus with each indicator. It covers the absorption of M&A knowledge through mentoring, training, and workshops, and access to codified M&A knowledge and best practices online via an intranet.

A dummy variable that takes the value 1 if a given top management position in a given firm in a given year is occupied by a woman, and 0 otherwise. A manager is coded as a woman if either ExecuComp coded the manager as a woman or the manager had the honorific 'Ms.' This variable serves as the equivalent of a dependent variable in the estimation methodology.
level: top management position in a firm in a given year

description: For each observation, a dummy variable that takes the value 1 if any of the other managers on the same top management team in the same year is also a woman, and 0 otherwise. It is described by the authors as the natural but econometrically problematic independent variable of interest for testing gender spillovers.
level: top management position in a firm in a given year

variable_name: Job category indicators (Chief executive officer, Line officer, Professional, Ex CEO, Miscellaneous)
description: Indicator variables for the job category of a top management position. Chief executive officer is coded using the CEO flag field in ExecuComp; line officer denotes senior managers with profit-and-loss responsibility such as the President, COO, or head of a division or subsidiary; professional denotes a manager with responsibility for a staff area; Ex CEO captures managers who served as CEO and subsequently shifted to an advisory capacity; all other managers are Miscellaneous, the omitted category, accounting for about 20 percent of observations. Titles that span categories are assigned to the highest category in the hierarchy Chief executive officer > Line officer > Professional.
level: top management position in a firm in a given year

description: Count of the owners of Scotch whisky distilleries whose headquarters are located outside the United Kingdom, measured annually. The count is entered together with an interaction with a dummy variable for the 1946-2009 period to capture the recent partitioning process. The number of non-Scottish UK owners is added as a control.

A Simpson index of concentration of the shares of distilleries controlled by each category of ownership. The index is entered with a main effect and an interaction with a dummy variable for the 1946-2009 period. The authors report that the concentration of distillery ownership by type of owner has a negative and significant overall effect but a positive and significant effect for the postwar period.

variable_name: Proportion of distillery owners in the categories beverage group, diversified, and other
description: Proportion of distillery owners in the least authentic ownership categories, interacted with the 1946-2009 period dummy. This specification replaces the interaction of concentration by type of owner and period in order to learn whether the entry process has been especially sensitive to the proliferation of these forms of ownership. The authors report that this effect is positive and highly significant.

Yearly count of cases in which a new or existing distillery, not controlled by a focused owner, comes under the ownership of an owner whose only business is malt whisky production. The counted events are building a new distillery, acquiring a distillery previously owned by an owner with a more diverse set of industrial activities, and taking a mothballed distillery back into production; transfers from one focused owner to another are excluded. The authors count 268 focused entries during 1826-2009.

For news articles during 1985-2010 containing a producer's name, a producer's name plus 'whisky', and a producer's name plus the nested 'malt whisky', each producer's grade of membership in the whisky category is the proportion of the articles that mention the firm that also mention whisky, and the grade of membership in the malt whisky category is the proportion of all articles mentioning the producer that also mention malt whisky. The authors slightly adapt the approach developed by Pontikes (2010) and present average grades by ownership type.

Team leaders were asked: 'Of what quality were the documents that the proposal team retrieved from the firm's databases?' Responses were given on a seven-point scale ranging from 1 'poor quality' to 7 'very high quality'. The authors describe it as a continuous variable measuring the quality of the documents' knowledge content.

Team leaders were asked: 'How much rework of the documents did the sales team have to do (rework includes rewriting parts of the slides, software, graphs etc. to use them for this proposal)?' Responses used a seven-point scale ranging from 1 'very little rework required' to 7 'a lot of rework required.' To test for possible curvilinear effects, the measure was mean-centered and then squared to create a second-order variable.
scale: 1 'very little rework required' to 7 'a lot of rework required'
