description: Team leaders responded to the statement: 'We (the sales team) were able to spend much less time on the proposal because we used existing knowledge in the firm' (time savings). Responses used a seven-point scale: strongly disagree (1), moderately disagree (2), somewhat disagree (3), neutral (4), somewhat agree (5), moderately agree (6), strongly agree (7).

Team leaders were asked: 'Did the people in the firm who helped the team have the experience that was needed for this particular proposal?' Responses used a seven-point scale ranging from 1 'did not have the needed experience' to 7 'had all the needed experience' to construct a measure of the quality of the knowledge content obtained from advisors.
scale: 1 'did not have the needed experience' to 7 'had all the needed experience'

description: Team leaders were asked: 'How much effort was exerted by the people in the firm who assisted the team?' Responses were reverse-coded from a seven-point scale ranging from 1 'exerted much less effort than average in the firm' to 7 'exerted much more effort than average in the firm,' so that a higher score indicated lower effort by the colleagues who advised the team. The measure was also mean-centered and squared to test for curvilinear effects.
scale: 1 'exerted much less effort than average in the firm' to 7 'exerted much more effort than average in the firm' (reverse-coded)

description: Team leaders were asked to assess the quality of the proposals delivered by their teams by responding to the statement: 'The proposal overall (solution, methods, value, presentation, and documentation) was among the best I have seen in the firm' (work quality). Responses used a seven-point agreement scale from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (7).

Team leaders were asked to respond to the statement: 'We (the sales team) were able to communicate the firm's unique competencies in the areas of the proposal to the client' (signal of competence). Responses used a seven-point agreement scale from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (7).

The dependent variable is a dummy equal to 1 if the assignees of the two patents in an observation are different. An observation is a pair of consecutive patent applications by the same inventor, denoted A1 and B2, restricted to cases where both assignees are on the ICE list, the two patents fall in one or more of the five semiconductor classes, and the inventor filed no patent with a firm not on the list between the two dates; if firm B acquired firm A, the first patent is treated as belonging to firm B so that no move is recorded. The descriptive mobility rate is the percentage of observations (A1, B2) in a period for which firms A and B differ.
time_window: Patents granted 1970-2002; first patent applied for by 1987

description: Equal to the number of spinoffs of firm A in the five years before date 1, the application date of the first patent of the observation; up to five years is allowed for the firm to complete its initial hires. Spinoffs and their parents were identified from the traced heritage of the ICE firms, where a spinoff is a firm whose main founder previously worked for another semiconductor firm.

variable_name: Number of SVEntrants x Silicon Valley
description: Number of SVEntrants equals the number of entrants in Silicon Valley in the five years prior to date 1 other than the firm itself and its spinoffs, and it is entered interacted with the dummy variable SV, which equals 1 if firm A in the observation is in Silicon Valley. A second version interacts Number of SVEntrants with (1 - SV) to allow Silicon Valley entry to affect the mobility of inventors elsewhere.

Equals 1 if firm A in observation (A1, B2) was based in Silicon Valley and equals 0 otherwise. An inventor is assumed to be at the location of the semiconductor operations of his employer; the authors checked this assumption against the inventor's location reported in patent filings and found that in almost all cases the two locations were the same.

variable_name: Share of initial hires from other local firms
description: Share of a spinoff's initial hires, other than those drawn from its parent, that came from other firms in the same region. Initial hires are the hires of a firm in its first five years, identified from inventor moves between ICE firms. The share is reported separately for the three early Fairchild spinoffs (National, Intel and AMD), the 34 later Silicon Valley spinoffs with parents in the sample, and the seven spinoffs outside Silicon Valley with parents in the sample.
time_window: First five years after the spinoff's entry

variable_name: Share of initial hires from the parent
description: Share of a spinoff's initial hires that came from its parent, where initial hires are the hires of a firm in its first five years identified from inventor moves between ICE firms. The share is reported separately for the three early Fairchild spinoffs (National, Intel and AMD), the 34 later Silicon Valley spinoffs with parents in the sample, and the seven spinoffs outside Silicon Valley with parents in the sample.
time_window: First five years after the spinoff's entry

description: Equals 1 for observations of inventors who previously moved from a parent to one of its spinoffs, and 0 otherwise. It is included in Model 6 alongside the other controls.
scale: 1 = prior move from parent to spinoff, 0 = otherwise

variable_name: Number of recent entrants outside of firm A's region
description: Count of recent entrants located outside firm A's region, one of the explanatory variables of the logit models; in the accounting exercise, all moves where firm A and firm B differ and are not in the same region and date 1 is within five years of the entry of firm B are removed from the count of moves.

Each of the four stakeholder category scores was first normalized on a 0 to 1 scale and the aggregate variable was then computed as the average of the normalized scores. The set of explanatory variables is calculated for the year before the acquisition took place. The variable was standardized in the regressions.

Measured as the sum of four dummy items included in the Asset4 'Employment quality' macro-category, which monitor whether a firm ensures good employee relations or has a policy for maintaining long-term employment stability, whether it describes the implementation of an employment quality policy, whether it monitors employment interests, and whether it sets specific employment development objectives. The measure is the sum of the four single constructs, so ranges from zero (low) to four (high). It was log-transformed in the separate-category models because of its skewed distribution.

Built from four Asset4 dummy items that assess a firm's commitment to treating suppliers as key business partners (presence of a policy; adoption of a code of conduct) and the existence of managerial practices to interact with suppliers (processes and communication tools to improve partnerships with suppliers). The construct ranges from zero (low) to four (high) and was log-transformed in the separate-category models because of its skewed distribution.

Assessed using Asset4's 'Customer loyalty' macro-item, which reflects a firm's capacity to maintain a loyal client base through communication, interaction, and satisfaction programs, together with its initiatives to enhance transparency in its dealings with customers. It is constructed by Asset4 analysts from 46 raw items and ranges from 0 to 100.

Measured using Asset4's 'Local communities' macro-variable, which assesses the extent to which a firm implements practices aimed at maintaining good relationships with the communities in which it operates and uses communication tools to interact with them. It is constructed by Asset4 analysts by aggregating 126 raw items and ranges from 0 to 100.

The acquiring firm's cumulative abnormal returns over the 36 months following the acquisition. The measurement process follows standard practices in corporate finance and strategic literatures. A long-term window was preferred so that information on the postacquisition phase would be included in the dependent variable measurement; the dependent variable represents a cumulative percentage.

Adapted from Finkelstein and Haleblian (2002) using both primary and secondary four-digit SIC codes. If any secondary SIC code of the acquirer matched any of the target's, one point was assigned for a two-digit match, two for a three-digit match, and three for a four-digit match; the same weighting was applied to primary SIC codes with the points doubled (two, four, and six). The sum of the matching scores yields a business relatedness score between zero and nine.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: Hand coded from company snapshots provided by Businessweek's public and private firms' database. If the snapshot reported the target firm as 'operating as a subsidiary,' integration was coded 0 (the firm remained a separate entity); if the snapshot reported the target as being 'acquired' with no further information, integration was coded 1 (the firm no longer existed as a separate entity). Validity was checked on a random sample of 200 acquisitions against the Lexis Nexis database, with 90% agreement between the two sources.

Coded one if, for any one of the positive items, a firm scores greater than zero on the Socrates social initiative participation measures, zero otherwise. The Socrates data contain 41 separate binary item measures of firm engagement along six social dimensions, with a firm scoring one for the observed presence of the measure, zero for its absence. Ratings were lagged by one year to insure that the ratings for each firm were public knowledge at the time of the event.

Following Mattingly and Berman (2006), coded one if the firm scored greater than zero on any of the positive items under the community or diversity dimensions of the Socrates data, zero otherwise. The measure was lagged by one year relative to the event.

Coded one if the firm scored greater than zero on any of the positive items under the governance, employee relations, or product relations dimensions, zero otherwise (Mattingly and Berman, 2006). The measure was lagged by one year relative to the event.

The cumulative abnormal stock return (as a percentage) accruing over the two-day event window; the unexpected percentage change in the stock price surrounding the event. Following Campbell, Lo, and MacKinlay (1997) stock returns were regressed against returns on a broad market portfolio for a period of 128 to eight trading days prior to the event window, and the CAR sums the day-to-day differences between the firm's actual and expected returns over the window. The Patell z test statistic suggested a two-day (t-1, t0) window.
time_window: two-day event window (t-1, t0); estimation period of 128 to eight trading days prior to the event

description: The natural logarithm of the market-to-book ratio of each firm the day before the event, collected from the Compustat data tapes. Market-to-book has been shown in the literature to correlate strongly with Tobin's q, the theoretical standard for measuring intangible assets (Villalonga, 2004).
Measured as the natural logarithm of sales for the fiscal year before the event, collected from the Compustat data tapes.
Calculated by summing the total negative individual item scores across the six major dimensions of the Socrates data.

One of three event categories, legal/regulatory actions arising from competitive behaviors, coded from keywords in the original Wall Street Journal articles describing the nature of the event. The initial classification of six event categories was collapsed into three broader categories to have samples large enough for meaningful analysis.

One of three event categories, health/safety violations, coded from keywords in the original Wall Street Journal articles describing the nature of the event. The initial classification of six event categories was collapsed into three broader categories to have samples large enough for meaningful analysis.

One of three event categories, integrity-based events, coded from keywords in the original Wall Street Journal articles describing the nature of the event. The initial classification of six event categories was collapsed into three broader categories to have samples large enough for meaningful analysis.

A firm's governance bundle is represented in the analysis by the set of governance mechanisms it adopts—board independence, CEO stock options, and venture capital backing. Fs/QCA identifies which combinations of these mechanisms are sufficient for high perceived value; solution configurations show firms achieving high premiums with one, two, or all three of these mechanisms.

Board independence approximates the extent of internal monitoring. Only directors with no prior professional or personal ties to the firm or its management, as indicated in the firm's prospectus, were classified as independent (nonmanagement) directors; VC-related board members were not counted as independent. Firms were coded 1, or fully in the set, if at least 70 percent of their board members were independent, and 0, or fully out, if 30 percent of their members were independent; the midpoint is the average of the two breakpoints.
A crisp set built as a proxy for executive incentives: a firm is coded 1 (fully in this set) if stock options were offered to the issuing firm's CEO prior to the IPO, and 0 otherwise.

A crisp set to indicate the presence of VCs among a firm's principal pre-IPO shareholders. Foreign IPOs backed by VCs prior to the date the firms went public are considered fully in the set, whereas those firms who were not backed by VCs are coded as out of the set.

Built from two indexes: La Porta et al.'s (1998) antidirector index, as revised by Djankov et al. (2008), which has six subindexes capturing de jure regulation, and the International Country Risk Guide 'law and order index,' which assesses both the legal system and the de facto law and order tradition of a country. After standardizing these indexes to a scale ranging from 0 to 1, values obtained from each were multiplied to combine de jure and de facto aspects of investor protection. Countries with scores above the sample median were classified as fully in the set of high minority investor protection countries and those below the median as out of the set.

Price premium was calculated as (offer price - book value)/offer price, where book value is the value of the firm's equity as reported in its financial statements. Firms were coded 0, or fully out of the set of highly valued foreign IPOs, if they did not receive a price premium of at least 66 percent, and coded 1, or fully in the set, if they achieved a 95 percent price premium; the midpoint was defined as the average of these two breakpoints.

A firm's financial performance assessed with prior ROA, calculated as operating return divided by total assets, with operating return indicated by EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization). To reflect poor financial performance, ROA was reverse-coded by adopting the scheme: Reversed ROA = ROA (maximum value) + ROA (minimum value) - ROA (original value). The reversed ROA ranged from -0.66 to 0.48.

A dummy variable indicating whether a turnover occurred in a firm in the year (t + 1) following the changes in the explanatory variables (t), that is, with a one-period lag. CEO turnover is defined as forced and voluntary CEO exits not due to sickness, death, retirements, or promotions; forced and voluntary turnovers are not distinguished because Taiwanese firms commonly disguise forced CEO dismissals with voluntary resignations.

The ownership percentage of all the non-family shareholders in the firm. In Taiwan the major types of non-family shareholders include the government and affiliated institutes, domestic and foreign individuals, domestic and foreign investment funds, domestic and foreign financial institutions, and related parties such as business groups. This variable ranged from 0.89% to 95% in the final sample.

A firm's information disclosure rating from the Information Disclosure and Transparency Rankings System (IDTRS) of Taiwan's Securities and Futures Institute. IDTRS provides seven grades (A++, A+, A, A-, B, C, C-) based on 113 corporate governance indices, including compliance with the mandatory disclosures, disclosure of financial forecasts, and reporting timeliness. To obtain a firm's ranking for all years from 1997 to 2011, the study averaged a firm's disclosure rankings from 2005 to 2011 and created a rating for each firm that was constant for all years; the rating was the mean of seven number values assigned to the rankings, with seven corresponding to A++ and one corresponding to C-. In the analysis, values above the median indicated high governance transparency and values at or below the median indicated low transparency.
time_window: rankings 2005-2011, averaged and held constant for 1997-2011

description: The proportion of control rights divided by the proportion of cash flow rights, built from information in the TEJ Corporate Governance Module for Taiwanese listed firms. The article illustrates the calculation with an ownership-chain example in which family A's control rights over company C are 30% while the cash flow rights generated from company C are 8%, giving a deviation of 4.25 (30%/8%). In the final sample, this variable ranged from zero to 413.

The main independent variable measures the degree of challenge that characterizes the locational context of an individual's posting, using the district's crime rate as a proxy. The crime rate is the annual number of penal code crimes per 100,000 district inhabitants averaged over the first four years of the individual's posting, and the log (base 2) of that rate is used as the independent variable so that the coefficient can be interpreted as the average change in the rate of career advancement. Crime rates are positively correlated with the prevailing degree of uncertainty and with threats to managerial goal attainment.
time_window: average over the first four years of the posting

description: Number of years it takes an individual to achieve a central posting in New Delhi, used to determine whether individuals from more challenging contexts are promoted faster. The data are cross-sectional and right-censored, so the authors use parametric survival analysis with a lognormal distribution. Because this is a survival model, a negative coefficient on crime is interpreted to mean that individuals exposed to higher levels of crime take less time to achieve central postings.

variable_name: Average Years Taken to be Promoted After Center
description: The average number of years it takes an individual to be promoted after transfer to a central posting in New Delhi; it is observed only for individuals posted to the center. The variable is analyzed as a function of the crime rate of the district of initial posting.

A dummy variable is created for each job title and a logistic estimation is conducted to estimate a difference in the likelihood of attaining it based on initial assignment. The reported estimation uses the dummy Joint Secretary, set to 1 when the individual achieves the rank of joint secretary to the government of India, an entry point into the upper echelons of the administration, which an officer typically achieves on the fourth promotion after being promoted to the center.

The total number of voluntary training courses an individual takes, observed prior to central posting. The authors estimate the association between this count and the crime rate of the individual's district to see whether individuals from high-crime districts take a higher number of courses.

A dummy set to 1 when an individual takes a course whose title specifies 'managerial decision making' or 'leadership training' and similar designations. The content of training courses is coded from their titles: courses that have 'leadership', 'decision making' or 'executive' in the title are considered to target leadership skills.

Estimated as the log of the number of units sold in all previous market niches in that year, with experience discounted over time using Baum and Ingram's (1998) method. The variable is expressed as a normalized deviation of experience by year, so that a value of 1.0 means the firm had 1 standard deviation more experience than the average firm in that particular year.

A dummy variable scored 1 if the firm had, prior to that year, entered a market niche other than its original niche, and 0 otherwise. For example, a firm that originally produced a 14" drive but had entered the 8" market then had experience with market entry.

The log of elapsed time since the firm last entered any market niche or since a disk-drive-related merger or acquisition occurred for that firm, following Amburgey et al. (1993). The authors also separated these two events into different clocks and repeated the analysis.

The dependent variable of the entry model: the probability that firm i will produce a drive in the focal category in the next year (t+1); for example, when examining the 8" category it is the probability that firm i will produce an 8" drive in the next year. A firm is at risk to enter as long as the new niche exists, industry-wide sales in the category have not peaked, the firm is still alive, and the firm has not yet entered.

The dependent variable of the performance model of the selection model: the future sales of the firm, predicted from the attributes of each incumbent firm in the first year of a market niche. The model is estimated on log sales; the authors use the median value of all variables in the appropriate sample to express the estimated effects in levels of sales.

Measured with the scale developed by Ungson and Schwab (1980), adapted from Miles (1975), which incorporates five categories of adjustments. Respondents indicated how often within the last three years their school had made a particular adjustment as a direct response to actions by environmental groups such as suppliers, teachers' organizations, and governmental regulatory agencies; responses for each adjustment variable ranged from 'never' to 'more than ten times' and were assigned weights from 1 to 5. A single composite overall measure of frequency of organizational adjustments (a = .74) was computed by averaging the unweighted score on each of the five adjustment variables, while the individual factor loadings and correlations were low enough to justify retention of each adjustment variable.

A 9-item, 5-point Likert measure adapted from the work of Duncan (1972) (a = .78). The questions require respondents to rate their ability to predict actions and changes in their schools' task environment sectors, including supplies of teachers and educational materials; relationships with teachers' unions, school boards, and state legislators; and regulatory control by state, federal, and local agencies. A factor analysis of the nine items with varimax rotation demonstrated that they all loaded substantially on one common factor with an eigenvalue of 2.65.

The measure of environmental resource scarcity was the percentage change in total enrollment reported for a three-year period. Enrollment change was used as a measure of resource availability or scarcity because, in the state in question, revenue allocations to primary and secondary schools depended, through a variation of formula funding, upon past enrollment levels. The 88 schools reported an average decrease in enrollment of 8.8 percent.

Organizational structure was determined by Hage and Aiken's (1969) three perceived measures of nonformalization: absence of rules and procedures, participatory decision making, and decentralization of the hierarchy of authority. The three measures consist of five items each; the reliability coefficients obtained in this study were .60, .80, and .91, respectively. A composite measure of organic structure (a = .84) was computed by averaging the unweighted mean scores on the individual measures.

variable_name: Five adjustment categories ordered by scope and cost
description: Scope and cost of adjustment is operationalized as a fixed ordering of the five adjustment categories of the Ungson and Schwab (1980) scale, from least to most costly: procedural, personnel, process, structural and strategic. Each category is defined by a set of changes (for example, procedural adjustments are changes in rules and work procedures; strategic adjustments are changes in basic instruction or services offered). The frequency of each category reported by school administrators over the last three years is compared across the ordering.

Within each firm, individual responses were averaged to give an overall department score for each item. The absolute value of differences across the 10 objectives were averaged to give an average difference on objectives, and the procedure was repeated for competitive strengths and trade-off decisions; the three highly intercorrelated measures were combined to form one overall measure of difference between marketing and manufacturing groups. High difference scores are referred to as low consensus scores, and signs for correlation coefficients between differences and co-ordinating mechanisms were reversed so that a positive coefficient indicated that use of that mechanism was related to consensus.
time_window: same year as the performance classification

description: Each company that was acknowledged by customers as one of the top 10 firms in at least one performance area was classified as having a high marketplace performance reputation; all other firms were classified as low marketplace performance reputation. The retailer-scored areas used here—style (products), quality, and service—are performance outcomes that parallel the order-winning criteria of Hill (1989) and are outcomes of interdependent marketing-manufacturing decisions. The performance classifications captured reputation in the same year that consensus was measured.
time_window: same year that consensus was measured

description: Participants were asked to indicate the frequency of use by their organization of the different co-ordinating mechanisms, and the measures of frequency of use were averaged across individuals within each firm. Planning processes included market forecasts, written strategic plans, and MBO linked to performance appraisal.

Participants were asked to indicate the frequency of use by their organization of the different co-ordinating mechanisms, and the measures of frequency of use were averaged across individuals within each firm. Decision rules/controls included statistical quality control, operations research-based scheduling and inventory control, and standard costing procedures.

Participants were asked to indicate the frequency of use by their organization of the different co-ordinating mechanisms; the measure was averaged across individuals within each firm. The authors also refer to this mechanism as direct contact/meetings between departments.

Participants were asked to indicate the frequency of use by their organization of the different co-ordinating mechanisms; the measure of this mechanism was averaged across individuals within each firm.

Participants were asked to indicate the frequency of use by their organization of the different co-ordinating mechanisms; the measure was averaged across individuals within each firm. The authors also refer to this mechanism as special interdepartmental committees and task forces.

Participants were asked to indicate the frequency of use by their organization of the different co-ordinating mechanisms; the measure was averaged across individuals within each firm. The authors also describe this mechanism as referral up the hierarchy, in which managers refer decisions to higher levels.

The authors calculated the average playing time of all batters, starting pitchers, and relief pitchers in the Major League, and from these averages determined the specific players in each of these roles whose participation in games over the past three years was more than one standard deviation above the mean. The measure of discrete productive knowledge available to a team is the number of players on each team that had such a high level of experience.

A count of the individuals on each team who had participated in playoff games at some stage during their professional career. The authors argue that postseason play offers unique learning opportunities because players face another high-performing team under more intense pressure and more severe competition, so the number of such players estimates the quality of productive tacit knowledge the team could draw upon.

The total number of years during which each of the managers in the sample had worked with a baseball team in the Major League. The authors focus on knowledge acquired about the best-possible use of players on a team rather than knowledge gained as a player.

The number of years during which each of the managers had taken his team into the playoffs. Managing teams during the postseason gives managers the opportunity to learn to use players in games played under higher pressure and against more intense competition.

The number of players on a team that had stayed continuously with that team for at least three years. The authors considered three years to be sufficient time for the individuals on a team to develop an understanding of each other.

Stability in starting lineups was measured game by game over the course of each entire season: each game's lineup was compared to the previous game's lineup, and if the set of players in the current lineup was not the same as the set in the previous game's lineup it was marked as a change in the lineup. Aggregated to the season level, this provided a measure of the number of lineup changes for each team each year; teams made as few as 16 and as many as 152 lineup changes.

A dummy variable equal to 1 when a manager was serving their third, fourth, or fifth season with a team. The authors believed it would take a manager the first two seasons to learn enough about the players to extract the best performance from the team, and they did not expect incremental learning effects after five years.
time_window: third, fourth, or fifth season with the team

description: A dummy variable equal to 1 to represent a midseason change in the manager of a team in a given year. The authors argue that in addition to the lack of tenure of the new manager, a change within the season can represent a significantly disruptive force because the new manager must quickly learn about the new players while games are being played.

The percentage of games won during the regular season, the measure of performance most widely used in studies of sports teams. It represents the degree to which a team has been successful over an entire season and is generally comparable over different teams and across different time periods.

Binary variable indicating whether the firm had and used defined steps, decision criteria, and checklists for partner selection (e.g., partner screening and fit analysis). Respondents answered which tools were used to support alliance management and indicated whether codified guidelines were available and used in the five-year period reported on. Defined as a single-item measure for this phase of the alliance process.

Binary variable indicating whether the firm had and used codified guidelines to manage partners (e.g., use of an implementation plan to manage partner characteristics and realize goals set). Respondents answered which tools were used to support alliance management and indicated whether codified guidelines were available and used in the five-year period reported on. Defined as a single-item measure for this phase of the alliance process.

Binary variable indicating whether the firm had and used codified metrics for partner termination (e.g., road maps, scorecard analysis, and termination templates). Respondents answered which tools were used to support alliance management and indicated whether codified guidelines were available and used in the five-year period reported on. Defined as a single-item measure for this phase of the alliance process.

Percentage of alliances in which the firm's goals were realized, measured at an ordinal level with a five-point scale (0-20%, 21-40%, ..., 81-100%). Respondents responsible for the firm's alliance portfolio answered the question: 'What is your company's overall success rate (i.e., percentage of strategic alliances where goals were realized) over the past five years?' The assessment is a subjective measure representing overall satisfaction with alliance portfolio performance and the extent to which objectives were met.

A dichotomous indicator of whether the firm used piece wages in a given year. Only firms in which more than 5% of total wages were paid as piece wages were coded as using this method of compensating workers, because the authors wanted to capture a commitment to using the strategy while not overlooking firms still experimenting with it.

A dummy variable, lagged one year, indicating whether the general manager was elected by the organization's workers. The authors note that an elected manager was not always the democratically elected official implied by this definition, but that there was no evidence of a relationship between this variable and either industry or size.

Coded one if the general manager was Communist Party Secretary, and coded zero if the manager did not hold this office. The authors measured party connections as holding the secretary office because party secretaries generally have a higher degree of commitment to the Communist Party than ordinary members.

A scale created from the quantitative data indicating the degree to which the manager is oriented toward market behavior, formed as the sum of positive responses to two series of questions about strategic management behavior. One was added if the manager indicated that her/his strategy was to improve production in order to be more competitive in securing state-controlled resources, and one was added if the strategy was to improve management practice to secure resources. One was also added if the manager indicated that demand, market forecasts, or a desire to maximize profits determined organization output.

A dichotomous indicator, lagged one year, of the degree to which labor markets were developed, coded from a direct question to managers asking whether each type of market was developed. It is coded one to indicate poor market development.

The exposure measure included in Model 2, computed in two steps. Predicted values of piece-rate use for each organization, given organizational and regional characteristics, were first obtained from Equation (1); for each pair of firms the predicted value for organization j was then divided by the geographic (greater circular) distance between the headquarters of organizations i and j, and these values were summed over all other organizations to give exposure for organization i. The measure uses the latitude and longitude of each firm and takes the curve of the earth into account.

One of two separate indicators of exposure created with the same two-step method, weighted by organization j's actual profits. The authors include only the profit-weighted variable because it is highly correlated with the exposure variable weighted by firm size, and substituting the firm-size-weighted exposure variable produces equivalent coefficient estimates.

Created as the residual of a generalized least-squares regression equation predicting profits as a function of lagged use of piece rates, along with the standard control variables included in the equations presented below. It indicates the degree to which the organization's profits differed from what would be expected by chance as a function of the use of piece rates in the prior time period (lagged one year), and can be interpreted as the benefit to financial performance of using piece wages.

Created as the residual of a generalized least-squares regression equation predicting profits as a function of lagged employment of state workers, along with the standard control variables included in the equations presented below. It indicates the degree to which profits differed from chance as a function of the continued employment of permanent, state-appointed workers in the prior time period (lagged one year), and can be interpreted as the cost of using state workers.

The hypothesis tests evaluated the effects of a set of covariates on the use of piece rates dynamically while allowing the effects to vary within three time periods. Separate logistic regression equations were estimated for 1978-1983, 1984-1986, and 1987-1989, using 1984 and 1987 as breaking points.

Time-to-build is calculated as the time in months from the date a firm first announced it would build a new plant until the plant achieved full capacity, i.e., reached its target yield and intended capacity. Plant-level statistics on the announcement date, construction start date, operations start date, and the date the plant achieved full-scale production were compiled from industry trade publications found in the Lexis/Nexis database. In some instances where the announcement date or the date when a plant achieved full-scale production was unavailable, the missing data were estimated using means for similar plants. The measure does not subtract construction delays.

The number of memory plants (other than the focal plant) built contemporaneously and with a feature size less than, or equal to, that of the focal plant. Smaller feature sizes indicate more advanced products resulting from more complex production processes. The measure was computed using the full sample of 571 memory plants.

Coded as a foreign investment where a firm held a share of at least 10% in a plant in another country; practically, if a plant had a foreign owner in these data, that owner always held at least 50% of the equity. Ownership data came from International Fabs on Disk for most joint ventures and otherwise from Lexis/Nexis searches and the Directory of Corporate Affiliations.

A count of the number of previous memory investments made by the firm in its home country. Because research shows that domestic expansion generates a different experience base than foreign expansion, own-firm experience was computed as two separate counts. Computed using the full sample of 571 plants.

The number of previous memory investments made by the firm abroad. It is the second of the two counts used to capture own-firm learning, because domestic and foreign expansion generate different experience bases. Computed using the full sample of 571 plants.

The cumulative number of plants built by the firm in the same foreign country as the current plant. This is one of the two components into which the foreign experience measure is disaggregated in the interaction models.
The cumulative number of plants built by the firm in other foreign countries. This is one of the two components into which the foreign experience measure is disaggregated in the interaction models.

A count of the number of memory plant investments made by other firms in the industry, in the same country, before the focal plant. The measure is at the country level because prior research shows that experience in a given country substantially affects subsequent investments in that country. Computed using the full sample of 571 plants.

The ratio of the focal facility's feature size to the average for all facilities built in the industry in the previous three years. Feature size measures the width of the conducting channels in a semiconductor chip, expressed in microns, and is reported in the IFOD database; the three-year window allows the technological frontier to evolve with contemporaneous practice. Because complexity increases with miniaturization, decreasing relative feature size indicates increasing complexity.
time_window: facilities built in the industry in the previous three years

description: Index built from 8 of the 23 HRM effectiveness items that loaded .40 or greater on the strategic HRM effectiveness factor. Respondents indicated how satisfied they were with "the results currently being achieved" using a scale from 1 (highly satisfied) to 5 (very dissatisfied); responses were reverse-coded, so higher values indicate higher perceived effectiveness. Cronbach's alpha was .75.
scale: 1 (highly satisfied) to 5 (very dissatisfied), reverse-coded so higher values indicate higher perceived effectiveness

description: Index built from 8 of the 23 HRM effectiveness items that loaded .40 or greater on the technical HRM effectiveness factor. Respondents indicated how satisfied they were with "the results currently being achieved" using a scale from 1 (highly satisfied) to 5 (very dissatisfied); responses were reverse-coded, so higher values indicate higher perceived effectiveness. Cronbach's alpha was .66.
scale: 1 (highly satisfied) to 5 (very dissatisfied), reverse-coded so higher values indicate higher perceived effectiveness

description: Index built from 11 of the 18 HRM capability items that loaded .40 or greater on the professional HRM capabilities factor. Respondents indicated "the extent to which HRM staff currently possess the capabilities and attributes listed" on a scale from 1 (applies to most) to 5 (applies to very few); responses were coded so that higher values indicated higher levels of perceived capability. Cronbach's alpha was .85.
scale: 1 (applies to most) to 5 (applies to very few), coded so higher values indicate higher perceived capability

description: Index built from 3 of the 18 HRM capability items loading on the business-related capabilities factor. Respondents indicated "the extent to which HRM staff currently possess the capabilities and attributes listed" on a scale from 1 (applies to most) to 5 (applies to very few); responses were coded so that higher values indicated higher levels of perceived capability. Cronbach's alpha was .61.
scale: 1 (applies to most) to 5 (applies to very few), coded so higher values indicate higher perceived capability

description: Employee productivity was defined as the logarithm of net sales per employee. The authors state that this measure tends to reflect employee efforts that are somewhat insulated from variations in the capital and product markets, and note that net sales per employee is an incomplete measure of firm performance because it does not reflect overall firm profitability.

variable_name: gross rate of return on assets (GRATE)
description: An accounting-based profitability indicator that reflects short-term (annual) profitability, calculated by dividing cash flow by gross capital stock. The authors state that it is superior to more traditional measures of accounting profits in that it is less sensitive to depreciation and other noncash transactions.

A future-oriented and risk-adjusted capital-market measure of performance that reflects both current and anticipated profitability, calculated by dividing the market's valuation of a firm's assets by their current replacement cost. Conceptually it is a measure of the value added by management.

A spline measure capturing the distance of a firm's return on assets above its social aspirations, where the relevant peer group is the S&P 500 firms in a given year with the same two-digit SIC code as the focal firm (excluding the focal firm). The variable is coded so that larger positive values represent greater distance from aspirations and takes the non-zero value only if ROA is greater than aspirations. The exact formula appears in the article but is unreadable in this record, so the specification is recorded only as the authors describe it in prose.

A spline measure capturing the distance of a firm's return on assets below its social aspirations, using the same peer group of S&P 500 firms in the same two-digit SIC code. The variable is coded so that larger values represent greater distance from aspirations and takes the non-zero value only if ROA is less than aspirations. The exact formula appears in the article but is unreadable in this record, so the specification is recorded only as the authors describe it in prose.

Positive abnormal returns equaled the value of the abnormal return if it was greater than 0, and 0 otherwise. Abnormal returns are the difference between a firm's observed and expected stock market returns, computed as firm returns minus the firm's intercept minus its beta times market returns, where the intercept and beta are least squares estimates obtained by regressing a firm's monthly returns on S&P 500 Composite Index returns for the prior 60 months. A new intercept and beta were estimated for each year in the observation period for each firm, and larger values represent greater distance above the level of external expectations.
time_window: abnormal returns lagged one year relative to the illegality measure (prior 60 months of monthly returns used for estimation)

description: Negative abnormal returns equaled the absolute value of the abnormal return if it was less than 0, and 0 otherwise, using the same abnormal returns calculation based on the difference between a firm's observed and expected stock market returns. Larger values represent greater distance below the level of external expectations.
time_window: abnormal returns lagged one year relative to the illegality measure (prior 60 months of monthly returns used for estimation)

description: A dichotomous variable that took the value 1 if a firm appeared on Fortune's Most Admired Companies list in a given year and 0 otherwise. The list is based on a survey in which executives, directors, and securities analysts are asked to identify and rate the ten largest companies in their industry. The variable was correlated .34 with another indicator of prominence, the number of analysts covering a firm.

A dichotomous variable coded 1 if a focal firm engaged in any incident of corporate illegality in a given year and 0 otherwise. Both convictions and settlements were coded as violations, and violations were coded according to the year in which they were committed rather than the year they were detected or reported. The illegal acts considered were environmental violations, anticompetitive actions, false claims, and fraudulent actions; the search identified 469 incidents, which yielded 270 firm-year observations coded 1.

Index built from CEOs' political donation records. Four ratio-based indicators measure commitment to a political orientation: behavioral commitment (number of donations to Democrat recipients over total donations to both Democratic and Republican recipients), financial commitment (dollar amount of donations to Democrats over total dollar donations to both parties), persistence of commitment (number of years of donations to Democrats over total years of donations to both parties), and scope of commitment (count of distinct Democratic donation recipients over total distinct recipients in both parties). The index is the simple average of the four ratios (Cronbach's alpha = .92), with scores ranging from 0 to 1; scores close to 0 indicate intensely conservative CEOs and scores close to 1 indicate intensely liberal CEOs. Contribution records cover the six to ten years before year t, ensuring at least three congressional election cycles and one presidential election.
time_window: six to ten years before year t

description: Indicator for whether an LGBT employee group formed in the focal firm. An LGBT group was deemed to have 'formed' when it had an explicit roster of members that was publicly available throughout the corporation, including to management. Some groups were formally recognized at founding, while others were simply known to managers and coworkers. Founding years were identified from the HRC contact database and a survey of the groups, giving precise founding years for 85 groups.

Formative index consisting of five variables, all measured in year t: CEO tenure in years, CEO duality (coded '1' if the CEO was also board chair), CEO founder status (coded '1' if the CEO was a founder of the firm), CEO relative ownership (ratio of CEO stock ownership to outside directors' ownership), and the proportion of the firm's directors who had been appointed after the CEO was appointed. The five components were standardized and averaged, and then combined into a formative index.

Organization-level measure of workplace climate based on FEC donation records of all donors who indicated the focal firm as their employer, typically including hundreds of individuals per firm per election cycle. Using four years of data prior to year t, it was calculated using the same procedure as the CEO liberalism index, except the numerator in the index item formulas was reversed-namely, donations to Republican recipients-to capture degree of workplace conservatism.
time_window: four years prior to year t

description: Number of corporate LGBT groups formed thus far, measured through year t-1. This type of variable has been widely used to capture the degree to which a social movement or a certain practice has diffused in a population.

For instances where succession occurred in the prior or current year, the authors computed the simple difference between the new CEO's liberalism score and the predecessor's liberalism score; for example, if a new CEO had a liberalism score of .80 and the predecessor's score was .20, the variable takes the value .60. The variable was coded '0' for cases where there was not a recent succession. The resulting variable ranged from -.82 (a much more conservative successor) to +.70 (a much more liberal successor).

Calculated using the cumulative number of patients treated by the focal ED. Experience is depreciated over time using an annual discount factor, based on the finding that approximately 42% of the impact of patient experience persists each year. The measure is log transformed to take into account diminishing returns to accumulated experience, so it incorporates diminishing returns over both time and quantity.
scale: log of depreciated cumulative patient count

description: Calculated as the number of patients who expired in the ED divided by the total number of ED visits in each year, scaled by 100. It is the primary measure of clinical performance, so a negative coefficient on this variable indicates higher clinical performance.

A binary variable that takes on the value of one if the hospital reports using CDSS each year and zero if not. Adoption is identified using the HIMSS Dorenfest Institute annual IT database, in which health and information technology managers are surveyed each year as to the systems and technologies present at their hospitals. It is used as a moderator of the cumulative experience-mortality relationship to capture the change in the slope of the learning curve following CDSS adoption.

An aggregate measure of the average level of patient severity seen within the ED, as reported by the California OSHPD. Patients are categorized into groups based on the severity of their condition upon arrival at the hospital by clinical staff. The sample is split at the median value of this aggregate measure into Low Difficulty and High Difficulty subsamples.

Measured using the degree of entropy in diagnoses or disease group categories treated within each ED, as reported by the California OSHPD data categories. Diagnosis Entropy is calculated from the proportion of patients in each diagnosis or disease category; the formula is not readable in the extracted text. The sample is split at the median value of Diagnosis Entropy into Low Variety and High Variety EDs.

Experiential learning is measured as the amount of performance improvement as a result of cumulative prior experience, that is, the slope of the relationship between an ED's cumulative experience and its clinical performance (mortality). The coefficient of interest in the second-stage model is the change in this slope, i.e., the Cumulative Experience x CDSS interaction, in response to CDSS adoption.

Operationalized from the Corptech Who Makes What? listings as a depth and breadth measure of a firm's product offerings, adjusted for the relative complexity of other firms in the same industry using vector algebra. Starting with the focal firm, the vector of the number of products in each product category was compared pairwise to another firm's vector in the same product categories, and cosine values were calculated for all K firms in the industry. The cosine values were summed and divided by the number of firms K to control for industry size and enhance interpretability; the weights in the vector indicate the depth, or number of products, in a given product class. The greater the number of products in a given product class and the more diverse the categories, the greater the complexity.

A multidimensional measure comprising sales growth, employee growth, and operating profit growth; the geometric mean of the three growth rates was used to develop the measure of performance. The compounded growth rate for each measure was calculated between 2007, 2008, and 2009. Operating profit growth was self-reported, while sales growth and employee growth were gathered from Dunn and Bradstreet (D&B) and Corptech.

Operationalized with latent congruence modeling starting from self-reported measures of exploration and exploitation from Lubatkin et al. (2006), which have six items each. LCM creates two second-order factors: the mean level of the two variables (level) and their difference (congruence); level represents the average of exploration and exploitation, whereas congruence represents similarity in the extent of exploration and exploitation. The latent factor for congruence was created by fixing the loadings for exploration and exploitation at 0.5. Because a higher congruence score implied a greater difference between exploration and exploitation, the congruence scores were multiplied by -1 so that increased balance relates to higher levels of ambidexterity.

Operationalized using an adapted scale originally developed by Jansen et al. (2005); the questions were originally based on a business unit level and were modified to fit the context of young firms. The items cover the acquisition, assimilation, transformation, and exploitation of external knowledge and were rated by the CEO. A second-order factor showed a better fit than the four correlated factors or the one-factor model, and item loadings, reliability, and discriminant validity were all at acceptable levels.

The percentage of a U.S. firm's equity that is owned by foreign (non-U.S.) institutional investors. It is measured as the sum of the holdings of all institutional investors domiciled outside the United States, divided by the number of shares outstanding. Ownership information is collected by FactSet directly from fund reports, regulatory authorities, fund associations in different countries, and fund management companies. All independent and control variables are measured at Year t, with the dependent variable measured at Year t + 1.

A firm's total corporate political spending in a year, combining the dollar amounts of its total annual lobbying expenditures and its contributions to PACs. The natural logarithm of the summated value is taken to mitigate skewness. The dependent variable is measured at Year t + 1.

A firm's exposure to government purchases, calculated as its revenue-weighted mean of the industry-level exposure measure. The industry-level measure is the ratio of federal purchase payments to total revenues in each three-digit SIC code by year, averaged over the period 2000-2013 to mitigate bias from lumpy contract awards. The measure is time invariant for each firm.

A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if a firm's main four-digit SIC industry is on the list of industries critical to national security in the 2008 CFIUS Annual Report to Congress, and 0 otherwise.

Subsidiary presidents were asked whether the subsidiary had any international responsibilities or world mandates and, if so, to estimate the approximate percentage of the subsidiary's revenues gained as a result of those international responsibilities. A value of 0 percent suggests that the subsidiary had no international responsibilities and 100 percent suggests that all revenues were gained from them. The measure records activities that are international in scope and recognized by the corporation, though it focuses on physical and technological resource flows.

An adapted scale from Roth and Morrison (1992) on which respondents rated five different subsidiary capabilities relative to other subsidiaries in the corporation. Although the activities are very different, they all loaded strongly onto a single construct, interpreted as the subsidiary's aggregate level of specialized resources.
scale: 1 = far below average, 7 = far above average

description: Eight questions were crafted to identify the various manifestations of subsidiary initiative, and three were dropped following a reviewer's advice because of questionable face validity. The remaining five questions ask the extent to which listed activities occurred in the subsidiary over the past 10 years, and all loaded strongly onto a single construct.

Three questions were used: the subsidiary's history of strong, internationally respected leaders; the credibility of the leadership with head office managers; and the leadership's efforts at developing middle management. The measures were only moderately correlated with one another, so the PLS program put most of the weighting on the first question only and the latter two were dropped from the analysis.

The five highest-loading items from Kuratko et al.'s (1990) intrapreneurial assessment index were used; the questions concern the openness of the subsidiary's working environment to entrepreneurship, risk-taking and innovation. All five items loaded strongly on a single construct.

A 7-item scale taken from Roth and Morrison (1992) that asked subsidiary managers to identify whether certain decisions were made in the subsidiary, at the divisional level, or at head office. During the PLS analysis four of the items were dropped because they loaded very weakly on the construct, leaving three items.
scale: 1 = decision made in the subsidiary company, 2 = decision made at the sub-corporate level, 3 = decision made by corporate headquarters

description: Ghoshal's (1986) measures of communication were used, specifically frequency of communication, frequency of business trips to head office, strength of working relations, and sharing of information. The latter two items were dropped in the course of the PLS analysis, leaving the former two, which reflected the frequency of communication between subsidiary and parent company.
scale: 1 = daily / twice a month or more, 5 = less than once a month / less than once a year

description: Beginning with the 7-item scale developed by Woodcock (1994), two strongly correlated items were extracted: 'domestic competition is intense' and 'competition in this country is extremely high'. Both loaded strongly onto the same construct, interpreted as the perceived level of local competition.

The scale used by Roth and Morrison (1992) was adopted. A factor analysis revealed one primary factor with eight items representing the extent to which the industry was global; these eight items were then reduced down to four items during the PLS analysis.

Firms are clustered into competitive interaction groups from the patterns of their competitive interaction. Action-response dyads (events) were identified by key-word search, and the number of competitive interactions among firms over the observation period was organized into matched pairs between firms, forming an action-response matrix whose rows represent initial actions and columns responses, with each cell giving the frequency of action-response events between the firms. Cluster analysis using the clique partitioning method with a tabu search optimization procedure was applied to this matrix; starting with the four-clique method, the three-clique and five-clique methods were also evaluated, and the four-clique solution provided the best-fit score.

Group heterogeneity is the amount of diversity within the TMT, measured in four ways: functional heterogeneity, educational heterogeneity, company tenure heterogeneity, and age heterogeneity. Functional background heterogeneity is measured by the Herfindahl index across nine functional background categories, where high values indicate that a TMT is heterogeneous; the formula block for this index is not readable in the available text. Education level heterogeneity and age heterogeneity are measured by the standard deviation (or coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean) across team members. Three types of tenure measures - years spent in the firm, years in the current company as a member of the TMT, and years in the current company at the current position - represent company tenure heterogeneity, denoted by the coefficient of variation as well as the standard deviation. To avoid multicollinearity, both the standard deviation and the Herfindahl index methods have been used.
scale: Herfindahl index takes values from 0 to 1; otherwise standard deviation or coefficient of variation

description: Euclidean distance measures capture the deviation of each firm's TMT characteristics from the dominant TMT characteristics (the group mean vector, or centroid) of the competitive interaction group to which the firm belongs; the formula block is not readable in the available text. The Euclidean distance scores for all the heterogeneity measures were factor-analyzed into two factors: the first factor, named experience heterogeneity, was composed of current tenure heterogeneity, age heterogeneity and education heterogeneity, and the second factor consisted of the single variable functional background heterogeneity. The two factors are the deviation variables entered in the regression models.
time_window: 1988-91 for TMT data; performance lagged 1 and 2 years

description: Performance of each airline was measured by the firm's load factor, the proportion of an aircraft's seating capacity that is actually sold or used, determined by dividing revenue passenger miles by available seat miles. Load factor is conventionally used as an efficiency measure directly associated with firm profitability. Two models were specified by time-lagging the dependent variable, the load factor, by 1 year and 2 years respectively.
scale: proportion of seating capacity sold or used

description: Gini coefficient of the distribution of bowl status among bowls, calculated by replacing y with status in the standard Gini specification; the coefficient ranges from 0, indicating absolute equality among all actors with the same value of y, to 1, indicating absolute inequality. The authors manually checked 84 status distributions over the study period for problematic distributions. For the analysis the variable was broken into two parts at the middle level of 0.5: bowl status inequality 1 (below the middle) and bowl status inequality 2 (above the middle). The Gini formula itself is unreadable in the extracted text.
time_window: annual; explanatory variables lagged by one year

description: Bowl status is built from bowls' exchange affiliations with football teams, using the teams' Associated Press (AP) Poll rankings. The end-of-season rankings were reverse-coded and unranked football teams were assigned a value of 0; the four-year average of a football team's reversed AP rankings from t-3 to t was calculated and then combined for the two contesting teams into the bowl's status. The combination formula is unreadable in the extracted text; the measure correlates positively with organizational size (stadium capacity) and past performance (stadium attendance).
time_window: four-year moving average, t-3 to t; lagged by one year in the models

description: The total number of spectators watching the annual game in a bowl's stadium, log-transformed to correct for distributional skewness. It captures buyers' judgment and choice of products, because watching a bowl game in a stadium requires much more effort from, and is much more costly for, football fans than watching on TV. TV ratings were considered but systematic data on TV ratings were not available over the study period, and stadium capacity limits are addressed because bowls expanded stadiums or added contingent seats.
time_window: annual; explanatory variables lagged by one year

description: Calculated as the difference between the current year and the founding year of a bowl, used as a proxy for uncertainty about a bowl's annual game: a track record can be established only by existence, so older bowls have a longer track record and thus less uncertainty about the quality of their product.

variable_name: Supplier worked for buyer the previous year
description: Dummy variable coded 1 for suppliers that worked for the buyer during the previous year, and 0 otherwise. It is the main independent variable of interest in the analysis of which supplier a buyer selects to fill a newly needed area of legal advice.

variable_name: Buyer choice of supplier for newly needed area
description: The dependent variable was coded 1 for the supplier selected by a buyer to fill a new need, and 0 otherwise. New needs are identified by comparing the areas of legal advice buyers list from year to year over four years, recording when a buyer first procured services in an area of legal expertise not previously required, as well as the supplier selected.

In the selection analysis, client-specific scope is included because the theory suggests that the level of client-specific scope economies matters to the choice of supplier, as it might be affected by adding a new area. In practice it is measured by counting the number of areas in which a supplier is providing services to a client.
The maximum number of areas in which services were sold by a single competitor, included to capture the potential influence of competitor entrenchment on the selection process.

The dependent variable was coded 0 if a relationship was still observed the following year, and 1 if it was not. Relationships were identified from the Chambers Client Report surveys and terminations are observed in 2003, 2004 and 2005.

variable_name: Number of areas with superior expertise relative to the set of competitors
description: A count of the number of areas in which a focal supplier's level of expertise is strictly superior to that of any supplier belonging to the set of relevant competitors. This reflects the idea that these competitors are construed to be alternatives by the client.
A count of the number of areas in which the focal supplier serves the buyer.
The maximum client-specific scope among competitors of the focal firm that serve the buyer.

Because the law firms in the sample are partnerships that distribute their profits (receipts from clients minus costs, including staff and associates' salaries) among equity partners, the dependent variable is profit per equity partner. PEP is the analogue of return on equity in the context of a professional firm and is the figure owner-managers want to maximize. The variable is expressed in thousand British pounds, and nominal monetary figures were translated into their year 2005 equivalents.

variable_name: Supplier expertise relative to the set of relevant competitors
description: This variable aggregates the position of a supplier relative to the set of relevant competitors for each of its buyers. For each supplier the authors computed the proportion of areas of service provided to a buyer in which the supplier had an advantage (defined as a strictly higher capability ranking) relative to suppliers in the relevant set of competitors, and then weighted each buyer proportional to the natural logarithm of its assets as a proxy for the amount of business the buyer represented. The final measure can take values between 0 (no superior expertise in any area of service for any given client relative to the relevant set of competitors) and 1.

For each law firm the authors calculated the proportion of clients for which it provided services in more than one area of law. The variable takes the value 0 if the law firm was not listed by a single client in the Chambers Client Report survey, and 1 otherwise.

For each law firm the authors calculated the proportion of clients for which at least one supplier in the set of relevant competitors provided services in more than one area of law. The variable takes the value 0 if the law firm was not listed by a single client in the Chambers Client Report survey, and 1 otherwise.

variable_name: principle-based agreement (combined coding of statements and chats)
description: Three research assistants independently coded the joint statements and the chat protocols of each pair for the presence of principles and rules; a principle was coded when a pair agreed on overarching, general guidelines for action rather than solely on a numerical quality and price. Both categories were coded only if there was clear agreement within the pair. A pair is counted as having a principle whenever a principle was agreed upon in the statement, the chat, or in both, and the analyses rely on this combined coding. Under the combined coding 30% of baseline pairs articulated a principle, compared with 85.2% (52 of 61) of pairs in the nudge treatment.
time_window: stage 2, before the first trading phase

description: Indicator for pairs randomly assigned to the nudge treatment. In that treatment the instructions and the communication screen displayed a message telling participants that they did not yet know the exact situation they would encounter in the second part of the study and that it might be helpful to think about the principles on which they would generally like to act. The manipulation was randomly assigned at the pair level within session (60 pairs in the baseline, 61 in the nudge).

For each of the three scenarios participants were asked what they should do and what their partner should do according to the agreement, and they were paid a bonus of 20 points for consensus with their partner. A pair exhibits normative consensus when the price–quality combination the buyer perceives as normatively appropriate corresponds with the seller's; efficient normative consensus additionally requires that both agree the seller should choose the efficient quality of 10. The measure captures in how many of the three scenarios a pair reached efficient normative consensus.
time_window: stage 4, before the shock was implemented

description: A party displays normative-behavioral consistency when it acts in accordance with what it thinks the pair's initial agreement implies: the buyer by choosing the price the buyer thinks the agreement indicates, the seller by choosing the quality the seller thinks the agreement indicates. The measure was elicited in each of the three scenarios, with the answer on first-period behavior binding if that scenario was later implemented in phase 2. Aggregated to the pair, it indicates the number of scenarios in which both parties displayed normative-behavioral consistency.
level: party, aggregated to pair (scenario level data)
time_window: stage 4, before the shock was implemented

description: An efficient equilibration score ranging from zero to three, constructed from the pairs' answers to the three scenarios presented before phase 2, where the answer about the first-period choice was incentivized by making it the binding first-period choice in phase 2 if that scenario was implemented. It captures in how many of the three scenarios a pair achieved efficient equilibration, that is, the buyer's chosen price met or exceeded the seller's price expectation, the seller's chosen quality met or exceeded the buyer's quality expectation, and the pair coordinated on the efficient quality of 10. The data are at the scenario level: 180 observations from 60 pairs.
time_window: stage 4, before the shock was implemented

description: The aggregate profits earned by a buyer–seller pair throughout trading phase 2, the repeated game after the environment changed, expressed in experimental points (25 points equal US$1). In this setting the seller's quality choice fully determines the joint profits of the relationship, so efficiency requires a quality of 10. Reported averages are 1,752 points for pairs with principles versus 1,348 points for pairs with rules only.
time_window: trading phase 2 (12 periods after the shock)

description: Blau's (1977) index of heterogeneity, calculated as one minus the sum of the squared proportions of group members in each racial category. Five categories of race were used in the Fortune survey (white, black, Hispanic, Asian, and American Indian), so the index ranges from 0 to 0.80: an index of zero suggests only one category of employees, while 0.80 implies that all five categories are equally represented. Taking a human capital approach, this firm-level measure assesses the level of overall organizational diversity rather than diversity within only one specific occupation or hierarchical level.
Revenue divided by number of employees, scaled by dividing it by 10,000 for ease of interpretation. The measure reflects employee efforts disassociated from variations in product and capital markets.

The ratio of the market value of a firm to the replacement value of its assets, using the measure proposed by Lee and Tompkins (1999): Q = (MKTVAL + PSVAL + DEBT)/TA. MKTVAL, the market value, is obtained by multiplying the number of shares outstanding by the share price; PSVAL is the liquidating value of the outstanding preferred stock; DEBT is long-term debt plus the difference between the value of the firm's short-term liabilities and its short-term assets; and TA is the book value of the total assets of the firm.

A dummy variable coded from each firm's standard industrial classification (SIC) code that differentiates between manufacturing (SIC code = 0 from 2000 to 3999) and service (SIC code = 1 if less than 2000 or greater than 3999). This approach preserves degrees of freedom and allows comparison of results between service and manufacturing firms.
A simple growth rate for each industry-year, calculated as the percentage change in industry revenues from the previous year, computed for all four-digit SIC codes included in the dataset.

Measured for the 6-year period 1997-2002 with the coefficient of variation (i.e., standard deviation divided by mean) as changes in power over time. Changes in power assess shifts in market share due to new entrants, exits, and consolidations.

A degree centrality measure, that is, the number of distinct interorganizational alliances of a focal firm within a given three-year rolling window, updated by month to align with the topic modeling periods. The alliances include R&D collaborations, technology licensing, comarketing, and software development agreements, and because bilateral interdependencies can occur in any part of the value chain the main analyses include measures based on all alliances by firms in the committee. The variable is mean centered and standardized in the regressions.
time_window: three-year rolling window, updated by month, lagged by one month

description: Built from the dyadic vertical relatedness measure of Fresard et al. (2020) by constructing a directed network graph with firms as nodes and relatedness as weighted edges. A firm's PFC is its centrality, defined as the weighted out-degree to other firms during a given period of standard-setting, reflecting how standards (upstream) influence downstream firms seeking complementarities. The measure does not leverage any actual data on existing interfirm relationships, and the variable is mean centered and standardized in the regressions.
time_window: during a given period of standard-setting, lagged by one month

description: Machine-learning-based content analysis (Latent Dirichlet Allocation, with 10 topics selected based on coherence scores and qualitative analysis) is applied at a monthly level to the technical documents and comments that firms submit to the standardization effort. Comment centrality is then defined as the position of each comment within this network of topics using a weighted degree measure, which accounts for heterogeneity even within a firm in the positioning of each comment within the overall emerging technical structure. The variable is mean centered and standardized in the regressions.

variable_name: Stock of Standard Essential Patent Claims
description: Counts the cumulative number of standard-essential patent claims submitted to the standards body by each firm over time. Standard-essential patent claims reflect patents critical to implementing mandatory or optional portions of the standard with no commercially or technically feasible non-infringing alternatives, thus indicating the ability of firms to capture future value from the emerging standard. The measure is multiplied with the interaction variables created to test H3 and H4 to obtain the three-way interaction variables.
time_window: cumulative over time, lagged by one month

description: An indicator variable on whether a comment proposed by a firm gets accepted (coded 1) or not (coded 0) into the standards draft by way of the comment resolution process. The ballot initiative in which each comment was introduced is also identified and used to address concerns over unobserved effects of comments from a specific ballot. A positive (negative) coefficient for an independent variable indicates greater (lower) success in shaping.

Using dummy variables, interim succession processes are coded as one and all non-interim succession processes as zero. Two criteria define interim successions: the incumbent CEO relinquishes the position and ceases to serve as CEO before a successor is named, and the board names a specific executive as 'interim CEO,' 'acting CEO,' or announces that he or she is serving as CEO 'until a search is completed.' The classification was made in three steps: comparing the last day of the incumbent's tenure to the first day of the successor's tenure in Execucomp, content analyzing press releases, news reports and company filings to determine the nature of each change and the date of the first public announcement of a permanent successor, and determining from company and press documents whether the board designated a specific executive as temporary CEO before the announcement of a replacement.

Accounting-based performance is measured as the average quarterly return on assets, measured over four progressively longer post-succession periods ending one, two, three, and four quarters after the departure of the incumbent CEO. ROA was averaged over subsequent quarters to reduce volatility and better reflect the firm's condition over the full period of time after the incumbent CEO departs the firm. This approach assures that the performance metric reflects the diminishing size of the treatment group of firms employing interim CEOs over time.
time_window: one to four quarters after the departure of the incumbent CEO
