description: Market-based performance is captured by examining the firm's Tobin's Q at the end of the first, second, third, and fourth quarters following the departure of the incumbent CEO. TOBINQ is defined as the adjusted market value of the firm's common equity, divided by the book value of its assets, thus capturing the premium that stockholders place on the firm's assets, which reflects investors' current sentiment regarding the firm's future prospects.
time_window: end of the first, second, third and fourth quarters following the departure of the incumbent CEO

description: Firm survival is coded as the length of time elapsed from the appointment of a permanent CEO until either the firm expires or the end of a seven-year period following the appointment. A firm is coded as expiring if it was delisted from its primary stock exchange with a delisting code between 500 and 585 in the CRSP database; these delisting codes indicate firm bankruptcy or the inability of the firm to otherwise maintain listing requirements such as market capitalization, a minimum number of shareholders, or minimum stock price.
time_window: seven years following the appointment of a permanent CEO

description: Industry dynamism is measured as the temporal variation in industry sales growth and employment growth at the four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code level. Sales growth instability was calculated as the standard error of the slope coefficient for sales growth divided by the mean value of sales in a three-year period beginning with the year that the CEO succession occurred; instability in employee growth was calculated using a similar procedure. The two scores were standardized and their mean was taken as a composite measure of overall industry instability.
time_window: three-year period beginning with the year of the CEO succession

description: Instances of CEO-chairman duality were dummy coded as one, and instances of non-duality as zero. The variable was coded for both interim CEOs and successor CEOs in the case of non-interim successions. Information was collected from the Reference Book of Corporate Managements, press releases, and SEC filings.

Second-order construct reflected by three first-order dimensions: ability, benevolence, and integrity. Ability was measured with two items adapted from Johnson et al. (1996), benevolence with three items based on Ganesan (1994) and Scheer, Kumar, and Steenkamp (2003), and integrity with two items based on Dyer and Chu (2003). All dimensions were measured on a seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree). The trustworthiness of the alliance partner is assessed by the trustor.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: The extent of contractual safeguards was measured with the index developed by Parkhe (1993) and validated by Reuer and Ariño (2007). Eight items described various deterrents to opportunism, and informants indicated which of these deterrents were explicitly included as a term in their alliance agreement. The eight items were arranged in order of increasing stringency and assigned a weight of 1 to the first item, 2 to the second, and so on; the weighted items were summed and divided by 36 to compute a composite score.

Four items introduced by Cameron and Freeman (1991) were used to measure the extent to which the trusted firm is characterized by a clan culture. The items contained brief scenarios describing the organization's general cultural characteristics, leadership style, institutional bonding, and strategic emphases. They were formulated as Likert-type statements anchored by a seven-point scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: Five items that Leonidou, Palihawadana, and Theodosiou (2006) used to measure the converse construct of distance were modified and recoded to capture familiarity. The items asked the informant in the trusting firm to assess his/her familiarity with various facets of the partner firm. They were anchored on a seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree).
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: The construct was captured using five items based on the measures used by Saxton (1997), rating the alliance partner relative to other firms in the industry on criteria such as producing high-quality products, retaining valuable employees, maintaining long-lasting customer relationships, and sustaining above-average innovativeness. The items were measured on a seven-point Likert scale (1 = much worse; 7 = much better).
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = much worse; 7 = much better)

description: Tobin's Q is estimated as the market value of total assets divided by the replacement costs of assets, with market values and replacement costs estimated following Yermack (1996). It is the authors' primary measure of firm performance. In the firm-level fixed-effects specification an industry-adjusted Tobin's Q is used as the dependent variable.

The number of independent directors divided by total board size, i.e., the fraction of independent directors. Independent directors are individuals whose only business relationship to the firm is their directorship. The authors describe this as their primary measure of independent director influence.

Binary variable that equals 1 when the family is present in the firm and 0 otherwise. Family firms were designated using the fractional equity ownership of the founding family and/or the presence of family members serving on the board of directors.

variable_name: Ratio of family directors to independent directors
description: The ratio of board seats held by family members to board seats held by independent directors. In the multivariate analysis the ratio is broken into three spline groups: 0.0 to 0.50, 0.501 to 1.00, and over 1.01.
Binary variable that equals 1 when family board control exceeds independent director control and 0 otherwise.

The fraction of total board seats held by affiliate directors, that is, nonemployee board members with existing or potential business ties to the firm, such as consultants, lawyers, financiers, and investment bankers.
The ratio of the number of independent directors to total board size, used as the dependent variable in the nominating committee analysis.
Binary variable that equals 1 when a family member served on the firm's nominating committee and 0 otherwise, gathered from corporate proxy statements.

Board control was measured using Boyd's (1994) multi-indicator factor model. The indicators are CEO duality, ratio of insiders to total board members, director stock ownership, representation on the board by ownership groups, and director pay; proxy statements were used to code these variables. CEO duality and director pay loaded negatively on this construct, while the other indicators loaded positively. A confirmatory factor analysis of the construct found all factor loadings in the expected direction and a unidimensional model provided the best fit.

Total diversification (Palepu, 1985) was separated into its components du (unrelated) and dr (related), using data from the Compustat Business Segment database and company 10-K filings. In the full model dr was used as the referent indicator of the common diversification dimension, and the loading for du on that dimension was positive and statistically significant. The authors tested and rejected an alternative model that treated dr and du as independent constructs.

To test Hypothesis 2 the authors constructed 12 additional LISREL models, reported as sets 2, 3a and 3b. In set 2 the confirmatory factor model for control was left unchanged but diversification was treated as a single-indicator construct (du in one model, dr in the other). In set 3 both board control and diversification were measured with single indicators, yielding five models based on du and each control measure (subset 3a) and five models based on dr and each board control measure (subset 3b). Path coefficients and explained variance of these models were compared with the full multiple-indicator model in Figure 1.

variable_name: BG dummy (1 if affiliated to BG, 0 otherwise)
description: A simple dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the firm is owned by a BG and 0 if it is not the case. The authors adopt CMIE's classification of firms to identify whether an individual firm belonged to a business group or was a stand-alone firm, based on continuous monitoring of company shareholding, new announcements, and a qualitative understanding of group-wise behavior. In the basic analyses the authors use a time-varying BG affiliation dummy, exploiting the small number of firms whose parent BG expands or shrinks around the two-affiliate threshold.

variable_name: Market participation dummy (1 if listed and actively traded, 0 otherwise)
description: A dummy variable for whether a firm is participating actively in the capital market and hence under market scrutiny in a given year. It takes a value of 1 if a firm is listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange under categories A, B, or T, which include firms that are regularly traded on the market (the Z category is excluded because those firms do not comply with listing requirements and are rarely traded), and a market price is available for the firm in that year; otherwise it takes a value of 0.

An index combining two widely considered indicators of capital market development with equal weights: market capitalization of listed companies as a percentage of GDP, and the domestic credit provided by the banking sector as a percentage of GDP. Both measures are made available by the World Bank. The authors also checked the robustness of the analyses using each measure separately.

Profit before interest and tax divided by total assets, adjusted for nonrecurring transactions. The authors use the industry-adjusted ROA after subtracting the average ROA for the firm's industry at the two-digit level from the firm's ROA.

Archival data gathered from the organization were used to establish the presence of top-down control and hierarchy in the traditional plants and greater self-control and collaboration for STS plants. These data included working papers and other documents prepared for plant use and archived by the Industrial Relations Division, articles and "CEO" columns gathered from the monthly house organs during the transition period of the conversion plants, and memorandums and reviews from IRD consultants written to conversion plant personnel during the transition period. Plants were classified as conversion plants (older plants with traditional, mechanistic histories that converted to self-managing teams) or start-up plants (organized with self-managing teams from their inception).
time_window: transition period of the conversion plants

description: Independent interviews were conducted with four of the parent company's Industrial Relations Division consultants who serviced the plants, and the consultants were asked to characterize the management style of all five plant managers in the study. There was 100% agreement in the characterization of three of the plant managers as "autocratic" and two of the plant managers as "participative."

Each message (a turn at talk) in each taped conversation received a three-digit code indicating the speaker, the message's grammatical form, and its response form; these codes were combined and translated into control moves according to Rogers and Farace's correspondence rules: one-up, one-down, and one-across. Sequentially ordered messages were then paired into "interacts," and the analysis used first-order transition matrices containing the probabilities that a particular control code at Time 0 is followed by a subsequent control code at Time 1, with the speaker (manager or subordinate) retained, yielding a 6 x 6 matrix. Differences in these transition probabilities were tested across plant history and plant manager style with the GSK procedure.
time_window: 30 minutes of interaction per dyad (first 30 minutes where conversations ran longer)

description: Sector PEU was computed with the formula PEU = Importance (Rate of change x Complexity), where the three components (rate of change, complexity, and importance) were each measured on a five-point scale from low (1) to high (5). PEU scores were computed for each sector of the environment, and the scores for the three task environment sectors and for the four remote environment sectors were averaged to obtain composite PEU scores for the task and remote environments.

Each respondent rated seven sectors of the environment separately: political/legal, economic, technology, socio-cultural, competitor/industry, customer/market, and sources of resources. The political/legal, economic, technology, and socio-cultural sectors constitute the remote environment; the competitor/industry, customer/market, and sources of resources sectors constitute the task environment.

Scanning frequency was measured using a six-point scale adapted from Hambrick (1982). The scale range is never (0), yearly (1), quarterly (4), monthly (12), weekly (52), and daily (365). Frequency scores for the task and remote environments were obtained by averaging the frequency scores for the three task environment sectors and the four remote environment sectors.

Scanning interest was measured using a five-point scale from low (1) to high (5). Interest scores for the task and remote environments were obtained by averaging the scores for the sectors in each of the task and remote environment categories.

variable_name: Frequency of use of external sources of information
description: The frequency of use of external sources of information was measured using a six-point scale adapted from Hambrick (1982). The scale range is never (0), yearly (1), quarterly (2), monthly (12), weekly (52), and daily (365). The text does not list which sources make up the external category or state how the score was aggregated.

variable_name: Frequency of use of internal sources of information
description: The frequency of use of internal sources of information was measured using a six-point scale adapted from Hambrick (1982). The scale range is never (0), yearly (1), quarterly (2), monthly (12), weekly (52), and daily (365). The text does not list which sources make up the internal category or state how the score was aggregated.

variable_name: Frequency of use of personal sources of information
description: The frequency of use of personal sources of information was measured using a six-point scale adapted from Hambrick (1982). The scale range is never (0), yearly (1), quarterly (2), monthly (12), weekly (52), and daily (365). The text does not list which sources make up the personal category or state how the score was aggregated.

variable_name: Frequency of use of impersonal sources of information
description: The frequency of use of impersonal sources of information was measured using a six-point scale adapted from Hambrick (1982). The scale range is never (0), yearly (1), quarterly (2), monthly (12), weekly (52), and daily (365). The text does not list which sources make up the impersonal category or state how the score was aggregated.

The dependent variable is a 0/1 dummy variable set equal to 1 in every year that an organization was acquired and 0 for every subsequent year in which acquisition did not occur. It was coded from all transactions listed in the Literary Marketplace section on mergers and acquisitions, which references the business press articles that describe these transactions in detail. All primary source articles were reviewed to distinguish the acquired from the acquiring firm.

The natural logarithm of the number of publishing imprints per firm as listed in the Literary Marketplace. An example of an imprint in higher education publishing would be an advanced mathematics series or a list of books on the sociology of culture. The variable is used to measure author-editor relational networks in production and, together with the count of divisions and subsidiaries, organization size and differentiation.

A 0/1 dummy variable set equal to 1 in every year that a publishing organization (supplier) has a contract for distribution of its books by another separately owned distributor or publisher. These contracts do not involve equity ownership sharing arrangements between firms, but represent the outsourcing of expenses for services such as advertising, selling, and fulfillment that are payable as a percent of sales.

A ratio measure of an annual count of potential competitors (all publishing organizations) and available resources (the number of college and university enrollments). College and university student enrollment data were obtained from the Digest of Education Statistics, published by the National Center for Education Statistics. The authors use the ratio measure because it is not highly correlated with other variables in the models and because it measures the direct effects of competition controlling for changes in market demand.

Observations were divided into two historical periods, 1958-1972 and 1973-1990, which correspond with the two ideal types of institutional logics. The cut point was selected from graphical analysis of time series indicators associated with changes in institutional logics and from interviews and historical research, and a sensitivity analysis of half-year cuts from 1967-1977 showed that the statistically significant differences between the two time periods remain for cut points between 1968.5 and 1976. In the piecewise exponential models the intercepts and the effects of covariates vary across the two historical periods.

variable_name: Period (before vs. after the d20 license)
description: The study compares the structure of the RPG sector between the 2-year period 1998-99, before the introduction of the d20 license, and the 2-year period 2000-01, after its introduction. The open license labeled the 'd20 system' was announced by the leader of the sector, Wizards of the Coast, in March 2000. The authors argue the two periods can legitimately be compared, as the U.S. market segment encompassing RPG products did not witness a drastic evolution over these 4 years.

Count of companies that entered the RPG sector in each of the two 2-year periods. The authors report 78 new entrants in the 2000-01 period against 20 new entrants in the 1998-99 period. The list of active companies in the sector was compiled from RPG publications and Internet websites.

Firms publishing RPGs in 2000-01 were classified as new entrants or as incumbents already present in the sector. The study compares the technological system adopted by the two groups. Firm data were collected from company websites.

For each firm, whether it adopted the open d20 system, relied on a proprietary system, or coupled the open system with the development of its own proprietary rules of play. Data on the technological system adopted were available for all 193 cases. The d20 license grants a perpetual, royalty-free, worldwide and non-exclusive right to use, modify, reproduce and distribute the open content of D&D's rules of play, while certain specific rules and the trademarks and logos remain proprietary.
scale: categorical (d20 system; proprietary system; both d20 system and proprietary system)

description: Number of employees of each firm, collected for 136 companies out of the population. The analysis compares the average size of firms in the industry between the periods, which the authors report as reducing from an average of 5.02 down to 2.76 employees after the diffusion of the d20 system.

For each sampled firm in each year, the total dollar amount of grants given to charity either through a corporate foundation or directly by the corporation, recorded from the National Directory of Corporate Giving. The variable includes charitable monetary donations but excludes political contributions and commercial sponsorships. To correct for skewed values, the authors log-transformed this variable (+ 1).

variable_name: Mega-event indicators (Olympics, Super Bowl, national convention)
description: Dummy variables indicating whether a given type of mega-event occurred in a company's community in the previous years, in the same year, or in the following years, created from the New York Times archives. Because the Olympics and national conventions always take place in even years, and the data consisted of even years only, their pre-event and post-event indicators used two-year lags, capturing whether these events occurred in year t + 2 or t-2. For the Super Bowl, one-year lags (t + 1 and t-1) were used in the main analysis.
time_window: t + 2, t, t-2 for the Olympics and national conventions; t + 1, t, t-1 for the Super Bowl

variable_name: Natural disaster indicators by damage category
description: Indicators built from impact estimates by the National Climatic Data Center and the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters. Disasters were categorized by the extent of economic damage in 2007 dollars: small-scale disasters had damages below $1 billion, medium-scale disasters damages above $1 billion but below $5 billion, and major disasters were the top 25 percent of billion-dollar disasters, corresponding to a $5 billion minimum threshold. The models include indicators for each damage category in the disaster year and in the following year (disaster at t-1 in the authors' lag notation).
time_window: year of the disaster and the following year

description: A company's annual average of charitable contributions (logged) at t-4 and t-2, used as the measure of its history of philanthropy. As sensitivity checks the authors used longer periods to define philanthropic history, only t-4 or only t-4 and t-6, and measures of past philanthropy adjusted for firm size.

A classification by Lev et al. (2010) that distinguishes industries in which the primary customer is the individual (e.g., consumer goods, personal services) from industries in which the predominant customer is industry (e.g., business services, capital goods). The categories are based on firms' four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes, which identify the line of business best representative of the company as listed in COMPUSTAT.

The reverse of the community's external-internal index, based on a network cohesion measure developed by Krackhardt and Stern (1988); the variable measures the ratio of locally headquartered firms' board interlocks within the community to their interlocks outside the community. Data on the interlock network of shared directors among corporate boards came from Compact D/SEC and were available for 1987, 1992, 1997, and 2002, yielding 152,466 director-year observations. Observations were given values from the closest year for which interlocks data were available.

Municipal revenues generated in the community, taken from the Census of Governments; this variable was used in the main analysis to capture the economic strength of communities. Total personal incomes in the community served as an alternative measure and yielded highly similar results.

Change in a firm's international presence measured by foreign sales changes between year t and the subsequent year, denoted in percentage. Since small changes are unlikely to spark significant effects, a sufficient change is defined as at least a 10% change in international presence. In the models the absolute value of Δ IP is included twice, interacted with a dummy that takes the value of 1 if Δ IP decreased by at least 10% and with the opposite dummy (decrease of less than 10%).

Change in a firm's business presence measured by noncore segment sales, denoted in percentage, between the reference year t and two years after the international contraction window (t + 3). In some models the dependent variable is a binary indicator that the firm's business presence at t + 5 is not lower than in the reference year.

Internal capital market value based on the measure developed by Billet and Mauer (2003) using COMPUSTAT segments data. It examines subsidies (capital provided to segments where expenditures exceed their cash flow) and transfers (capital provided by segments with excess cash flow), and evaluates efficiency by comparing a segment's return on assets or a fitted Tobin's Q to the firm's other segments. The ICM is the sum across a firm's segments of the product of each segment's subsidy or transfer and relative efficiency, weighted by the segment's assets.

A firm's technological knowledge is measured by counting the patent applications a focal firm has in year t + 4, the year after the change in business presence in year t + 3, and is denoted as a discrete variable. Patent application data are taken from the DISCERN 2 dataset, which mainly uses data from the US Patent and Trademark Office.

Binary dependent variable indicating the probability that a firm's international presence at t + 5 is higher than its level in the reference year t. The probability that the dependent variable will occur is interpreted from the linear probability model coefficients as a percent change in that probability.

The 'employee relations' construct provided by the KLD database measures the strength of a firm's relationship with its employees. Strength is measured using seven items, and a firm receives a score of 1 if it is judged to have strengths along each item and a 0 otherwise; the items are summed each year to create an aggregate measure. The lowest score is 0 and the highest is 7, and the highest score achieved by a firm in the sample was 4, so the measure ranges from 0 to 4 in the final sample. The variable is lagged by t-1, and because a nonlinear relationship is hypothesized both a linear and a squared term are included.
scale: 0 to 4 in the sample (possible range 0 to 7)

description: Local search is operationalized as the count of technological classes cited in year t if that technological class had been cited previously in the firm's accumulated citation base extending 5 years back. Technological classes are measured at the three-digit level categorized by the USPTO, and this measure counts the number of technological classes a firm cites each year and categorizes them as local from the firm's prior knowledge base. For firms entering the sample in 1992, the 5-year window extends to 1987.
time_window: 5-year look-back window (for firms entering in 1992 the window extends to 1987)

description: Distant search is operationalized as new additions to the firm's accumulated 5-year knowledge base in year t, i.e., the count of new technological classes cited in year t that the firm had not utilized in the previous 5 years. Technological classes are measured at the three-digit level categorized by the USPTO, and the measure counts the number of technological classes a firm cites each year and categorizes those distant from the firm's prior knowledge base.

The ratio of total sales of firms that belonged to business groups within each sector to the sales of all firms in that sector during a particular year. For South Korea it is calculated from the KIS database using the top 44 business groups; for Taiwan it is calculated from the BGT directory's top 100 groups together with sector sales from the Tian Xia survey. Values are measured at five points in time (1983, 1986, 1989, 1992, and 1995) for 21 sectors in each country.

The TRCA index measures the relative distribution of a country's inventive activity in each field compared to its own total patents and to the overall distribution of patents in the United States; it is the ratio of country i's share of total world patents in sector j to country i's share of total world patents. The index equals 1 if the country holds the same share of worldwide patents in a technology as in the aggregate, and is below (above) 1 if there is a relative weakness (strength). Patents granted to South Korean and Taiwanese residents are mapped onto 42 SIC-based industry groupings and aggregated into 21 sectors over three-year patenting windows.
time_window: five three-year periods following each group-share year, 1981-1995

description: A continuous industry-specific measure built from a South Korean survey that asked companies to select one of four stages of their main technology's life cycle: the Cradle, Growth, Maturity, or Declining stages. Responses were converted to a four-point scale, with one point for Declining, two for Maturity, three for Growth, and four for Cradle, and technological opportunity is the average of the points weighted by the response frequencies for each stage.

An industry's share of basic R&D, measured as the ratio of total private and government expenditure on basic R&D to total R&D expenditure by all private and public sources in Korea, using industry data from the Survey of Research and Development in Science and Technology.

Industry R&D intensity, used as the dependent variable in the multivariate kernel regressions on South Korean industry data in place of patents because it is more directly linked with the cost of R&D. The paper does not describe in prose how the ratio is constructed.

Availability of market-based innovation infrastructure is not measured with a separate variable. The authors treat Taiwan as the country with more varied, market-based infrastructure and South Korea as the country where chaebols supply most infrastructure, and compare the group share at which innovation peaks in each country.

Mix of patients served by a clinic, coded by group managers as a broad (heterogeneous) or focused (homogeneous) mix of patients. The study characterized patients of broad clinics as option seekers and those of focused clinics as relationship seekers. Used as an indicator of environmental complexity in the DEA model.

Change over time in a clinic's productivity attributable to its own endogenous efficiency, decomposed from the Malmquist Index. It is the change in the clinic's performance with respect to its peers of the same clinic type. Raw MI values have 1 subtracted, so positive values indicate an increase in efficiency and negative values a decrease.

Change over time in a clinic's productivity attributable to exogenous frontier policy or environmental shifts, decomposed from the Malmquist Index. It is the change in the clinic's performance with respect to all clinics in the sample. Values are raw MI components minus 1.

Mean of three items in an employee survey about the amount of influence in making decisions about what work is performed, how work is performed, and work policies and procedures. Survey questions adapted from Van de Ven and Ferry (1980).

Mean of five items in an employee survey about perceived interdependence and communications between individual clinics and group headquarters. Items cover dependence of clinic on group, group on clinic, communication frequency, work frequency, and meeting frequency.
Mean of four items in an employee survey about the clarity, degree, number, and enabling of work rules and procedures. Three items come from Van de Ven and Ferry (1980).

Mean of 10 items in an employee survey measuring the perceived degree of headquarters-subsidiary integration, including shared norms, culture, and integrative synergies. One item ('Get in each other's way') is reverse scored.
Number of full-time equivalent positions based on organization records. Used as the key input factor in the DEA model; labor costs account for approximately 80% of annual clinic operating costs.

Average of patient satisfaction (eight items), staff courtesy (four items), and clinical quality care (five items). Patient satisfaction and courtesy are from patient surveys conducted by an independent research firm; clinical quality is from a survey completed by clinic health-care providers. Used as a DEA output.
Average of clinic productivity (number of RVUs of care per provider) and clinic net income (net revenue per provider). Both are from organizational records. Used as a DEA output.

Macro-corporate control is represented by two employee-survey scales used together as predictors: work standardization (mean of four items on the clarity and degree of work rules and procedures) and headquarters-subsidiary integration (mean of 10 items on shared norms and culture). Both enter the regression on exogenous group frontier change.

Micro-subsidiary control is represented by two employee-survey scales used together as predictors: clinic autonomy (mean of three items on influence over what work is done, how, and work policies) and clinic-group interactions (mean of five items on interdependence and communication with group headquarters). Both enter the regression on endogenous clinic performance change.

A composite index following Kogut and Singh (1988), based on the deviation of a country from the U.S. ranking along each of four Hofstede cultural dimensions: power distance, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity/femininity, and individualism. The deviations were corrected for differences in the variances of each dimension and then arithmetically averaged. The algebraic formula printed in the text is garbled in this rendering, so only the verbal specification is reported here.

A dummy variable used to compare U.S.-Japanese with U.S.-U.S. joint ventures, coded 1 for U.S.-Japanese ventures and 0 for U.S.-U.S. ventures. In the same model, dummy variables for each other bloc of cross-border ventures, based on Ronen and Shenkar's synthesized country clusters, were compared with U.S.-U.S. ventures.

The absolute difference in the two partners' numbers of independent geographical and product subsidiaries, used to define each firm's scope of operation. The authors rejected the typical SIC-based diversification measure because it captures product diversification only and is not sensitive to growth by volume or geographical expansion.

The ratio of the logarithmically transformed three-year average sales of the larger partner to that of the smaller partner, used as a fair approximation of size distance. The authors note pitfalls in defining the boundaries of Japanese firms that may belong to larger industrial groups such as keiretsu.
The absolute value of the difference in the partners' life spans, calculated by subtracting the partners' founding years from 1995.

A dummy variable representing direct competition between partners, built from the partners' four-digit SIC codes: coded 1 when the parent firms' primary operations were the same and 0 when primary operations were different.

A dummy variable representing the relationship of the joint venture to the parent firms' operations, coded 1 if the primary operation of the joint venture overlapped with both partners' current product-market scopes and 0 otherwise.
A dummy variable representing joint ventures that involve technology transfer from the partners for venture operations (1 = technology venture, 0 = nontechnology venture).

Measured as the number of years and months from formation to dissolution of the joint venture. Liquidation or sale to a third party was used as the operational definition of dissolution, and surviving or acquired joint ventures were treated as censored cases. Joint ventures whose initial contracts specified a period of operation or included an option for governance change, such as acquisition by one of the partners, were excluded, and the unexpectedness of dissolution was confirmed by contacting managers in the U.S. parent firms.
time_window: formation to dissolution, observed through September 1995

description: A dummy that equals 1 in the period during which app i faces an increased entry threat to its app category but does not face Google's actual entry, and 0 otherwise. Entry threats are identified from Apple's release of its own apps or new iOS features into iOS app markets that Google had not yet entered on Android, following the pattern that Google entered 84% of the app markets Apple entered and entered before Google in 80% of the overlapped markets. The main analysis uses the three Apple entry events that occurred after 2012: Guided Access, Podcasts, and Flashlight.

A dummy that equals 1 after Google actually enters the app market and 0 otherwise. The authors use two time dummies to distinguish the entry-threat period from the period in which Google had entered, because app developers may behave differently under the two competitive environments.

The number of new versions released in month t by app i, log-transformed. Because a developer may update the same app multiple times in a month, the count captures all version releases; the authors argue that updates capture digital innovation as ongoing experimentation and product refinement and deliberately include both major and minor updates. The estimated coefficient of interest is the interaction Under Entry Threat x ADAA, where ADAA (affected developers' affected apps) equals 1 for the 378 apps of the 3,986 in the sample that would compete directly with the app Apple introduced, and 0 otherwise.

variable_name: number of new similar apps released in a month
description: The average number of new apps similar to the app Apple introduced that were released in a month, computed for the months before the threat, during the entry-threat period, and after the actual entry; similar apps are identified with Google's 'similar apps' search in the Google Play store, using the same procedure as for the ADAA dummy. The authors compare the means across periods with t tests. Taking the Flashlight market as an example, the average number of new Flashlight-related apps released per month was 38 before the threat, but only 10 during the entry-threat period, and only 7 after the entry.
time_window: monthly, before-threat, entry-threat, and actual-entry periods

description: The number of new versions released in month t by app i, log-transformed, measured for the unaffected apps published by affected developers. The estimated coefficient of interest is the interaction Under Entry Threat x ADUA, where ADUA (affected developers' unaffected apps) equals 1 if app i is not affected by the matched entry-threat event but has been developed by a developer with some app affected by the threat.

The number of new apps introduced by developer j in month t that are unrelated to any of the entry events, log-transformed because it is highly skewed. The unit of analysis is the developer-month; the coefficient of interest is Under Entry Threat x Affected Developer, where Affected Developer equals 1 if the developer has any app that is affected by the focal entry event. Each entry event is examined separately because a developer could face multiple entry events; developer fixed effects and month dummies are included and standard errors are clustered at the developer level.

The price of app i in month t; if an app's price changes within a given month, the authors use its price at the beginning of the month. Because Price is highly skewed, they use its log transformation in the regression analyses. The estimated coefficient of interest is the interaction Under Entry Threat x ADAA.

An app is considered popular if it had been ranked in the top 500 across all categories at any time prior to Google's entry threat. Within these popular apps the authors identify the popular apps affected by the entry threat (the ADAA group) and those developers' other popular unaffected apps (the ADUA group); the control group consists of the remaining popular apps by unaffected developers. The dataset provides the exact ranking for any app that was ranked in the top 500 in its category or among all apps.
time_window: any time prior to Google's entry threat

description: Tobin's Q, in the definition of Chung and Pruitt (1994), derived from a market value equation in which market value is the expected discounted future profits of the firm from tangible and intangible (knowledge) assets. The estimated dependent variable is the natural logarithm of Tobin's Q at the end of year t (month t in the monthly panel), and the dynamic specification lets growth in Tobin's Q depend on its lagged level. In the monthly panel market value is an end-of-month variable.
time_window: end of year t (end of month t in the monthly panel)

description: Count of new cross-border R&D investments announced by the focal firm in a year (or in a month). The model identifies the effect of new additions to the stock of knowledge assets, that is, the number of new R&D investments in a year (or month); the transformation of the knowledge stock function implies the scaling of the R&D variables by past market value V.
time_window: year t (month t in the monthly panel)

description: A weighted measure of the inverse of the (effective) patent protection the firm is confronted with in the destination countries of its R&D investments. The degree of effective patent protection is a composite index based on Ginarte and Park's patent rights index (GP) and a country's score on Impartial Courts (IC) in the Economic Freedom of the World report; both scores are normalized by the annual maximum value of each index, such that the composite index ranges from 0 to 1, and the GP index is multiplied by IC as a measure of enforcement. The measure of IP risk is 1 minus the index of IPR protection, summed over all destination countries of the R&D investments; in case of multiple R&D investments in a country, its IP risk enters the sum multiple times. The yearly panel aggregates IP risk over the countries of investment, whereas the monthly panel assesses the IP risk of a single country; the algebraic form of the specification is not recoverable from the text.
scale: composite protection index ranges from 0 to 1
time_window: year t (month t in the monthly panel)

description: Degree to which inventors based in different countries contribute to the firm's patents (cross-country inventor collaboration), identified from inventors' addresses. For each patent a Blau index of the country dispersion of inventors is computed (1 minus the Herfindahl index of the shares of inventors' resident countries listed on the patent), which increases when inventors of a patent are based in multiple countries. This dispersion score is multiplied by the highest IP risk score among the countries of the inventors, and the firm-level variable averages this weighted dispersion across all foreign invented patents of the focal firm. It is measured in year t-1 to reflect the firm's existing R&D organization and capabilities.
The Blau index of inventor dispersion but taking only positive values if the mean of the highest IP risk score among the countries of the inventors is above the sample median, else zero.
The Blau index of inventor dispersion but taking only positive values if the mean of the highest IP risk score among the countries of the inventors is below the sample median, else zero.

Six items (V1-V6) on a five-point Likert-type scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree. In their raw form the items are negatively coded such that the higher the response, the less valuable the resources and capabilities the firm controls; responses were recoded once the surveys were returned so that the higher the response, the more valuable the resources and capabilities to which the firm has access. Each capability value item (V1, V3, V5) was multiplied by the corresponding resource value item (V2, V4, V6), producing three preliminary value scores per resource/capability category, which were summed for each of the five categories (for example, V1a x V2a + V3a x V4a + V5a x V6a for financial resources and capabilities). A composite score reflecting the average value of all of the firm's resource-capability combinations was computed by averaging these five scores.
time_window: cross-sectional, at the time of the survey

description: Three items (R1-R3) on a five-point Likert-type scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree, assessing the degree to which a firm exploits unique resource-capability combinations as well as the degree to which it exploits common resources (or capabilities) with unique capabilities (or resources). The items are positively coded such that the higher the response, the rarer the firm's resource-capability combinations. Responses were summed for each resource/capability category, resulting in five scores (for example, R1a + R2a + R3a for financial resources and capabilities), and a composite score was computed by averaging these five scores.
time_window: cross-sectional, at the time of the survey

description: Three items (CA1-CA3) developed in accord with Barney's (1991) operational definition of competitive advantage as the degree to which a firm has reduced costs, exploited opportunities, and neutralized threats, on a five-point Likert-type scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree. Items are positively coded such that the higher the response, the greater the firm's competitive advantage. Responses to the three items were summed for each resource/capability category, resulting in five scores (for example, CA1a + CA2a + CA3a for financial resource-capability combinations), and a composite score reflecting the average level of competitive advantage across all resource/capability categories was created by averaging these five scores.
time_window: cross-sectional, at the time of the survey

description: Delaney and Huselid's (1996) market performance scale, comprising four items (P1-P4: marketing, growth in sales, profitability, market share) rated on a four-point Likert-type scale ranging from much worse to much better relative to other organizations that do the same kind of work, over the past 3 years. Items are positively coded such that the higher the response, the greater the firm's performance. The variable is operationalized by summing the responses to the four items.
scale: four-point Likert-type scale (much worse to much better)

description: Measured as the percentage reduction in the firm's level of diversification during the three-year period following the CEO succession event. For each firm an entropy index of diversification, as defined by Jacquemin and Berry (1979), was calculated from COMPUSTAT line of business data on the percentage of a firm's total sales in each segment. For the sample of non-diversifiers, values on this measure ranged from -0.01 to -1.61, of which the authors took the absolute value. Higher values indicate more corporate strategic change in terms of refocusing as measured by greater reductions in the firm's level of diversification.
scale: percentage reduction in level of diversification
time_window: three-year period following the CEO succession event

description: Operationalized as the length of time, if any, the incoming CEO was in the position of president and/or COO in the organization prior to being appointed as the CEO. The positions of president and/or COO were chosen because they represent the next highest executive-level positions to that of the CEO and are often the precursor positions to the CEO position. Values ranged from 0 (no experience) to 23 years. Data were gathered from the biographical data listed in Dun and Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Management and in Who's Who in Finance and Industry.
time_window: prior to being appointed as CEO

description: Number of titles held by the CEO at the time the CEO assumed the office, gathered from companies' annual reports and proxy statements. Because the CEO can hold the additional titles of board chair and president, values of this variable can and did range from 1 (CEO title only) to 3 (CEO, chairperson, and president). More titles indicates greater power; the number of titles is an indicator of formal authority.

Calculated by dividing the cash compensation of the CEO by the total cash compensation of the highest paid executive other than the CEO in the company. Total cash compensation was measured as the sum of salary and bonus. Values for the compensation measure ranged from .76 to 5.0 in the sample, and higher values indicate greater power. Data for this measure were gathered from proxy statements and the Execucomp database.

Calculated as the percentage of a firm's shares owned by the CEO as indicated on the firm's proxy statements: the number of shares owned by the CEO was divided by the total number of shares outstanding for the firm. Values on this measure ranged from 0 to 20 percent. Higher values indicate greater ownership power.

Coded 1 if any of the following conditions held: the CEO was the founder or was related to the founder(s), or the CEO shared the same last name as a firm founder; if both conditions held, then the variable was coded 2. The value of the measure ranged from 0 to 2, and higher values indicate greater ownership power. Data on this measure were gathered from the firm's proxy statements.

Calculated as the number of previous functional positions held by the CEO across her or his entire career, from the time the person graduated from college until he or she assumed the CEO position. Values of this measure ranged from 1 to 5, with higher values indicating higher degrees of expert power. Data on experience in different functional areas were gathered from the Dun and Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Management and Who's Who in Finance and Industry.
time_window: from college graduation until assuming the CEO position

description: Assessed as the number of degrees received by a CEO from universities or colleges rated as elite educational institutions, using the list of elite educational institutions developed by Finkelstein (1992). The value for the measure ranged from 0 to 3, with higher values indicating greater prestige power. The university degrees awarded to the CEO were identified from the Dun and Bradstreet Reference Book of Corporate Management and Who's Who in Finance and Industry.

Calculated by summing the total number of corporate boards of directors on which CEOs sat at the time they took office. The value for the indicator ranges from 0 to 13, and more boards indicate higher prestige power. Board membership was identified from company proxy statements and from Who's Who in Finance and Industry.

The authors number all advertisements in ascending order in each Vogue issue and calculate the average number of advertisements of prominent high-status fashion firms within a three-order difference. The list of prominent high-status fashion firms is built from Brand Z and Interbrand ranking reports. The variable is lagged one year.

Participants were randomly exposed to one of three conditions. In the Base condition they were shown an actual Vogue advertisement of the assigned firm alone; in the Mixed condition the advertisement was shown sequentially with advertisements of six other firms (two low-, two middle-, and two high-status); in the High condition the same was done with six high-status firms.

Logged-transformed average listed price of the products each fashion firm featured in Vogue. Prices are manually collected from the products' pages or from the index at the back of the magazine called 'In This Issue'. Jewelry and watches are excluded and only apparel, handbags, shoes, and accessories are included before calculating the average price. The price information is inflation-adjusted based on 2002.
time_window: products featured in the September issue of the year

variable_name: High Status, Middle Status, Low Status
description: Bonacich's centrality measure is calculated from a network of fashion firms that share the same fashion models during the major fashion weeks in a given year. Firms with centrality one standard deviation above the mean are classified as high status, those one standard deviation below the mean or not participating in fashion weeks as low status, and all others as middle status. Each status group dummy variable is multiplied by the proximity variable.

Participants were shown an actual Vogue advertisement of the assigned fashion firm and asked to rate its prestige. In the mixed and high conditions the same questions were answered after being exposed to the videos in which the focal advertisement appeared with advertisements of other firms. The status ratings of the three conditions are compared across low-, middle-, and high-status focal firms.

Component modularity is a modified version of the Fine et al. (2005) measure of component modularity and is used as an inverse proxy for the degree of coupling of product architectures. The authors state that F is the number of functions implemented by the component and I is the number of closed interfaces of the component; the equation itself is not readable in the extracted text. CM refers to a specific product component and is close to 1 when the component implements one or few functions and most of its interfaces are open standard, and close to 0 when it implements several functions and/or most of its interfaces are closed. The number of functions was gathered from a function breakdown structure for a generic high-precision air conditioning unit, and interfaces were identified and counted through a design structure matrix (DSM) analysis of the three analyzed products.

The firm-level test of the complementarity hypothesis uses the OEM-specific subsample means of CM shown in the descriptive statistics for the three firm-level subsamples, together with the three OEM-specific regressions. A firm's product modularity is therefore the average level of component modularity across the components of its analyzed product. The authors report that OEM1 has a mean modularity level higher than OEM3 but lower than OEM2, and that OEM2, which does the least information sharing, obtains the highest level of modularity.

Buyer-supplier information sharing is measured as the mean value of the interviewees' responses to the 10 items of the questionnaire dedicated to this variable, which ask how frequently detailed information is exchanged with the analyzed supplier in component development, logistics, and price/contract negotiation. Answers are given on a 1-5 scale where 5 is 'I completely agree' and 1 is 'I completely disagree'. The questions on information sharing were answered by the OEMs' buyers.

Supply relationship performance is measured as the mean value of the interviewees' responses to the nine items of the questionnaire dedicated to this variable, capturing the purchasers' perception of supplier performance. It expresses the degree of the OEM's satisfaction with its relationships with suppliers regarding component development, logistics, and price and contract negotiation. Answers are given on a 1-5 scale where 5 is 'I completely agree' and 1 is 'I completely disagree', and the questions on performance were answered by the OEMs' purchasing managers.

The variable equals the difference between an organization's operating cash flow and the sample mean operating cash flow for all MSOs in the same year. Constructing the variable on a relative basis provides an industry-specific way to mitigate the trend increase in cash flow over time, and by this definition it has a mean value of zero. All amounts are converted to constant 1984 dollars. The variable is lagged (year t-1) based on the theory that observed (prior year) performance influences the budgeting for and choice of investments in the focal year.

Calculated as the increase in the number of systems for each MSO between years t and t-1, whenever the difference is positive. The approach does not distinguish between newly constructed systems and acquired systems, because the payoff horizon for buying a cable system is similarly long either way. Adding systems is a long horizon investment because substantial upfront capital is needed to construct a headend facility and no subscriber revenue can be generated in the first one to three years after construction begins.

Dollar amounts for such investments are not reported, so the magnitude of an MSO's investments in new channels is captured based on the number of subscribers to each channel at the end of the study period as reported by Waterman and Weiss (1997). The eventual subscriber base of each network is attributed to an MSO's investment portfolio in the year the new channel was launched or acquired from another firm. The justification is that the cost to develop or acquire programming correlates with the number of eventual subscribers to the channel.
time_window: subscribers at the end of the study period, attributed to the launch/acquisition year

description: Measured as the increase in newly passed homes-homes that now have the ability to choose whether or not to subscribe to cable service but did not have such access one year earlier-within an MSO's franchised areas between years t and t-1. Technically, the authors compute the decrease in homes unpassed by cable from one year to the next to avoid contaminating this measure with the effects of new home construction and additional systems. Subscribers who previously had cable availability and elected to become paying customers are not captured in this measure.

Firm age is measured in years and is interacted with relative operating cash flow to test whether older organizations are less sensitive to performance feedback. Because of regulatory changes that substantially alter the cable industry at the start of the study period, firm age is calculated only from 1972 onward.

Measured as the aggregate in-the-money dollar value of options held by managers of organization i in year t, estimated based on the number of outstanding options and exercise prices reported in the footnotes to financial statements in each organization's annual 10K document. These data provide the intrinsic or redeemable value of options at the end of each fiscal year for all managers in aggregate; unlike proxy statement compensation data, the 10-K does not attribute option holdings to specific individuals. Out-of-the-money options are not considered because they have limited effect on managerial decisions in the present tense. Values are converted to constant 1984 dollars.

Measured as the aggregate in-the-money dollar value of unexercisable options held by managers of organization i in year t, estimated based on the number of outstanding options and exercise prices reported in the footnotes to financial statements in each organization's annual 10K document. The 10-K data provide the intrinsic or redeemable value of options at the end of each fiscal year for all managers in aggregate and do not attribute option holdings to specific individuals. Out-of-the-money options are not considered. Values are converted to constant 1984 dollars and are measured separately from exercisable options.

variable_name: Hierarchy of business unit of middle manager
description: Following Zhou (2009), the authors count the number of subdivisions and subsidiaries in each hierarchical layer in a given business unit and multiply this number by the rank of the layer in the business unit's overall hierarchy; the total hierarchy measure is the sum of these layerwise products. The measure thus captures both the number of hierarchical layers and the organization's top heaviness, and it is computed at the level of the business unit in which the mid-level manager works.

Within-subjects factor manipulated across the two blocks of the experiment: participants were told the number of direct superiors they had in each period. In the case where there was one superior, that superior reevaluated the ideas passed on to her from scratch; in the case where there were two superiors, the direct superior did as above and decided which ideas to pass further along to her own superior, who reevaluated them from scratch again.

Main dependent variable of the field study, taking a value of 1 if the idea was declared globally relevant by the local middle manager and 0 otherwise; it includes those cases in which she deemed the idea both locally and globally relevant, and thus captures the local manager's decision to pass information on to her superior in a typical hierarchy. Because predicting the fixed-effect residual is not feasible in the multilevel limited dependent variable model, the OLS specification of the first stage is used to compute the predicted residual for each middle manager, which serves as the dependent variable in the Stage 2 regressions on hierarchy.

variable_name: Number of ideas submitted (passed up) per period
description: For each of the ideas assessed in a period, participants could decide whether to pass the idea on to their superior or not. The outcome analyzed is the number of ideas passed up per period, which the authors also report as treatment averages.
scale: count of ideas passed up per period

description: In this between-subjects condition, participants were told that their superior(s) had the ability to determine whenever the participant made a commission error, in which case a participant's period earnings were reduced by 400 ECU. Evaluation apprehension was captured purely in terms of costs rather than in terms of actual behaviors.

In this between-subjects condition, participants were told that for each submitted idea they would face administrative costs of 200 ECU. These costs reflect the time the participant has to spend to deal with further evaluation requests by her superior(s), regardless of whether she correctly sends up a good idea or mistakenly passes up a bad one.

Four-item scale adapted from Strutton, Pelton, and Lumpkin (1995) that taps both task and interpersonal dimensions of cohesion. Following the referent-shift consensus model, franchisees reported their perceptions of franchisees' cohesion within their chain. A principal axis factor analysis produced a one-factor solution, all items loaded above 0.70, and Cronbach's alpha was 0.84. Chain-level scores were computed as the mean of franchisee perceptions for each chain, after establishing within-chain agreement (mean rwg(j) = 0.81) and between-chain variance (ICC(1) = 0.54; ICC(2) = 0.90).
level: individual franchisee, aggregated to the chain

description: Four-item scale specifically designed for the study, administered to franchisees as self-reports of their own behavior. Principal axis analysis with varimax rotation showed the items loaded on the expected factor with no cross-loading, and Cronbach's alpha was 0.80. A sample item is 'Within the context of my activities, I do more things 'my way' than according to my franchisor's recommended methods.'

Four-item scale specifically designed for the study, administered to franchisees as self-reports of their own behavior. Items loaded on the expected factor with no cross-loading and Cronbach's alpha was 0.75. A sample item is 'I hesitate to share with my franchisor information and know-how that I have gained myself.'

The same four items used in Study 1 were used to measure perceived cohesion between franchisees, administering the questionnaire to all franchisees in both chains. Cronbach's alpha for this scale was 0.82 in both samples.

The four-item measure from Study 1 was modified to reflect the franchise network manager's perception of a franchisee's deviation from standards rather than the franchisee's report of his or her own behavior. Network managers assessed franchisees' behavior approximately two weeks after franchisees provided data. Cronbach's alpha coefficients were 0.75 and 0.92 in Franchise Chain 1 and Franchise Chain 2, respectively.
time_window: manager ratings collected approximately two weeks after franchisee data

description: The four-item measure from Study 1 was modified so that franchise network managers assessed whether franchisees withhold information, rather than franchisees reporting their own behavior. Ratings were collected approximately two weeks after the franchisee survey. Cronbach's alpha coefficients were 0.94 and 0.92 in Franchise Chain 1 and Franchise Chain 2, respectively.
time_window: manager ratings collected approximately two weeks after franchisee data

description: A count of the total number of unique start-ups invested in by firm i in year t - 1. If a firm did not make any investments in a given year, a value of 0 was assigned. The variable was log-transformed because it was highly skewed and kurtotic.

The annual count of successful patent applications for firm i in year t. Application date (the date when a firm files a patent application) was used to assign a granted patent to a firm in a given year because it more proximally reflects the actual time of knowledge creation. Patents granted in the United States were used for consistency and comparability, and patents assigned to identified subsidiaries were aggregated to the parent firm. Prior studies have used patenting as a proxy for innovation rate.

The sum of all alliances formed with portfolio firms in a year plus the number of times the investor filled seats on portfolio firms' boards, divided by the investor's total number of CVC investments in that year. Alliances include all types, including those involving joint R&D, codevelopment, manufacturing, and marketing. The data were compiled through comprehensive searches by firm names and relevant keywords in Factiva and Lexis-Nexis.

variable_name: Technological knowledge diversity i(t-1 to t-4)
description: The inverse concentration ratio of the distribution of a firm's patents over the primary technology classes to which they had been assigned. It reflects the distribution of the corporate investor's patents across technology classes over four years (t - 1 to t - 4) prior to observation of the dependent variable. The authors write that Pj was the ratio of patents filed in patent class j, and 1 - Pj was the weight for patent class j; the algebraic formula itself is not readable in the text. A larger value of this measure represents greater diversity.

A binary variable equal to one if a firm or its founders were previously active in segments that adopted drones, including photography, motion pictures, real estate, energy and utilities, mining, insurance, telecommunications, geological surveying, agriculture, and retail. Firm and founder data come from firm websites, Crunchbase, LinkedIn, the AUVSI directory, industry reports, the FAA, and other news sources. For entrants lacking use experience, prior industries largely consist of aviation, electronics, robotics, and RC devices.
A binary variable that is equal to one if a firm was active in another industry before drone manufacturing and is equal to zero if the firm was founded as a drone manufacturer.

An HHI-type index calculated as one minus the summation of squared shares of the frequency counts of exemptions that a firm's drones received in each segment. The measure reflects the extent to which a firm's drones are distributed among numerous segments, rather than concentrated in one or few segments. Smaller values imply lower breadth.

Each drone is depicted with a vector in the 5-dimensional space of distinct segments, and the pairwise cosine similarity index is computed between each drone's vector of usage segments and that of every other drone in the firm's portfolio. Usage overlap is the average of the cosine similarity index across all drone pairs in the portfolio. Lower values indicate a greater divergence between targeted customer segments across products in a portfolio.

The firm's R&D expenditures divided by total sales. Using COMPUSTAT, R&D intensity could be matched for 59,510 of the events. In the reported analysis the observations are averaged by firm and year so that there are no observations of the same firm with the same financial controls, which reduced the sample to 18,462.

Cumulative abnormal returns computed with standard event study methodology over a (-15, +5) event window; a longer window is used because of the lag between the trade and the release of information about it. Cumulative abnormal returns (-15, +5) serve as the dependent variable in the regressions, with R&D intensity as the primary independent variable.
time_window: (-15, +5) around the date the trade is reported to the SEC

description: Cultural distance was measured with seven indicators, and a smaller set of items with loadings greater than 0.5 on the latent factor was retained for the measurement model. The indicators used 6-point Likert scales with coding ranging from one (strongly disagree) to six (strongly agree).
scale: 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree)

description: International experience was measured with five indicators, and a smaller set of items with loadings greater than 0.5 was retained for the measurement model. The indicators used 6-point Likert scales with coding ranging from one (strongly disagree) to six (strongly agree).
scale: 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree)

description: The relatedness of the strategic resources of the parent and the joint venture was measured with thirteen indicators, and a smaller set of items with loadings greater than 0.5 was retained for the measurement model. The indicators used 6-point Likert scales with coding ranging from one (strongly disagree) to six (strongly agree).
scale: 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree)

description: The relative contribution of each partner was measured on an interval scale ranging from zero to 100 percent with a composite index. The parent firm's relative contribution is the total of its contributions of resources minus the resource contributions of the other parent in each of several operational areas. This construct was measured with a single composite indicator rather than multiple indicators.
scale: interval scale from zero to 100 percent

description: The bargaining power of the parent was measured with nine indicators, and a smaller set of items with loadings greater than 0.5 was retained for the measurement model. The indicators used 6-point Likert scales with coding ranging from one (strongly disagree) to six (strongly agree).
scale: 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree)

description: The influence of government restrictions on equity share was measured with a single indicator on a 6-point Likert scale ranging from zero (no government restrictions) to five (strong government restrictions).
scale: 6-point Likert scale (0 = no government restrictions to 5 = strong government restrictions)

description: The level of equity held by the parent was measured as the percentage of total equity with a single indicator, using a continuous measure of percentage of equity holdings.

Control over specific activities was measured with eight indicators, and a smaller set of items with loadings greater than 0.5 was retained for the measurement model. The indicators are general statements about control of areas of special interest, on 6-point Likert scales ranging from one (strongly disagree) to six (strongly agree).
scale: 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree)

description: Overall control of the venture was measured with twelve indicators, and a smaller set of items with loadings greater than 0.5 was retained for the measurement model. The retained indicators are reversed statements about the partner's control over daily activities and overall managerial control, on 6-point Likert scales ranging from one (strongly disagree) to six (strongly agree).
scale: 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree)

description: Perceived performance of the joint venture was measured with nine indicators, and a smaller set of items with loadings greater than 0.5 was retained for the measurement model. The indicators are qualitative assessments of performance from the perspective of the Norwegian parent, on 6-point Likert scales ranging from one (strongly disagree) to six (strongly agree).
scale: 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree)

description: A count of the number of entries by a firm into 'new to the firm' niches measured at the patent main class level. The three-digit main classification followed by USPTO is used to identify technology domains. Corresponding to the two-year window for the dependent variables, it is the number of branching entries made by a firm in year t-0 and t-1. The mean branching with the two-year window is 0.7 and it has a maximum value of 9.

The number of years since incorporation. The data source for the founding year was Bioscan for the years 1988 to 2003; in a few cases where founding information was missing in Bioscan, company Web site information was used to find the year.

The number of new patents applied for in two subsequent years (t + 1, t + 2). Patent filing year, patent class, assignee names, number of subclasses, and number of claims were used to construct the patent data. The innovative output variable has an average value of 4.50 and standard deviation of 13.2.

The average number of citations, net of self-citations, received by patents filed by the firm in years t + 1 and t + 2, computed as citations received divided by count of patents, observed in five subsequent years (t + 2 to t + 6 and t + 3 to t + 7, respectively). The total citations received are divided by technology output to reduce the overlap with the innovative output measure. The impact variable has an average value of 4.2 and standard deviation of 14.2.
time_window: five subsequent years: t + 2 to t + 6, and t + 3 to t + 7

description: Unit-level measure of employees' collective motivation for NPD, rated by the NPD unit manager on a five-point Likert scale with two items, one for each key element of the construct: employees' willingness to work collaboratively toward common goals related to NPD and their willingness to take risks in developing, adopting, or implementing new ideas. Survey questions were framed in collective terms such as 'our employees' and 'different functional departments'. A key NPD engineer also rated the construct to validate the manager's responses; the correlation between NPD managers and key NPD engineers on this construct is 0.53 (p < 0.0001).

Unit-level measure of the coordinative ability among NPD personnel to carry out NPD tasks, rated by the NPD unit manager on a five-point Likert scale. Four survey items focus on the collective phenomena that constitute NPD capability, such as employees' understanding of each other's responsibility in the NPD process, their ability to carry out NPD procedures and routines, and cross-department coordination abilities. A key NPD engineer also rated the construct; the correlation between NPD managers and key NPD engineers on this construct is 0.65 (p < 0.0001).

variable_name: NPD performance (revenue generated from new products)
description: Firms' revenue generated from new products is used as a proxy for NPD performance. The data were collected by the Chinese Automotive Technology and Research Center in 2008, which is one year after the survey data were collected. The natural logarithm of this variable is employed in the analysis to ensure a normal distribution.

Firm-level construct measured with three items rated by a senior manager (the firm's top manager) on a five-point Likert scale, covering the strategic importance of new products and technology, expansion of product ranges and derivatives, and reduction of NPD cycle times. Top managers were chosen as informants because the construct describes the organizational direction of the firm.

variable_name: Reward and recognition practices emphasizing NPD
description: Unit-level construct measured with three items rated by the NPD unit manager on a five-point Likert scale. The items cover the extent of incentive, reward, and recognition practices that promote NPD activities and knowledge sharing, focusing on practices tied to employees' participation in NPD activities and NPD performance rather than on a general performance-based incentive policy. The NPD unit manager was chosen as informant because reward and recognition practices tied to NPD-related criteria are more likely to be adopted within an NPD unit.

variable_name: Staffing and training practices emphasizing NPD
description: A second-order construct combining two sub-constructs, staffing practices and training practices related to NPD employees, rated by the HR manager on a five-point Likert scale. HR managers were used as informants because staffing and training practices are usually managed centrally by HR managers in Chinese firms.

Faultline strength is measured based on educational background, dominant functional experience, outsider status, gender, and racial background using an algorithm developed by Meyer and Glenz (2013). Using a cluster-based approach, they develop a measure of faultline strength based on average silhouette width (ASW). The ASW faultline measure uses a clustering technique for finding a subgroup split associated with the team's strongest faultlines for teams that have two or more homogenous subgroups; it divides board members into subgroups based on their similarity so that the subgroups have the maximum internal homogeneity and maximum between subgroup heterogeneity. The resulting faultline strength is a number from 0 to 1, higher numbers representing stronger simultaneous alignments of demographic and human capital characteristics. It was calculated for the board excluding the CEO, for boards with at least three members.

Firm performance based on accounting returns was measured as 2-year average return on assets (ROA) after each observation. Accounting performance is considered more reflective of the actual contributions of board members than market related return measures.

Overlaps in personal range of functional experiences are operationalized as the average dyadic overlap in personal range for all possible dyads of CEO and demographic minority directors. The variable is based on data on CEO and demographic minority directors' personal range of functional experiences, which includes both dominant and nondominant functional experiences, that is, current and past professional experiences.
level: CEO-minority director dyads aggregated to firm-year

description: Overlapping tenure of the CEO with the demographic minority directors is measured based on a variable of common historical experience for teams, developed by Carroll and Harrison (1998). The variable measures the average dyadic overlap in tenure for all possible dyads of CEO and demographic minority directors. The published formula is not extractable from the payload, but the text states that N is the total number of demographic minority directors, and that mu_i and mu_CEO refer to the tenure in years of the i-th demographic minority director and the CEO, respectively.
level: CEO-minority director dyads aggregated to firm-year

description: Directors identified as women or racial minorities. Gender was measured using the BoardEx binary classification of woman vs. man, and racial background was collected using online biographies, websites, and press releases, categorized following US Census guidelines into White, Black/African American, Hispanic, Asian, Native American, and Multiracial. These directors define the dyads used for the CEO overlap moderators and the subsample of boards with at least one demographic minority.

A dummy variable coded one for UPC-year observations in which the product label included one of the combinations of text strings 'low/no/non/zero/free' and 'fat/saturated fat/salt/sodium/sugar', and zero otherwise.
