Egocentric claims emphasize the absence or small amount of unhealthy nutrients in a focal food product.

A dummy variable coded one for UPC-year observations in which the product label included one of the combinations of text strings 'fewer/reduced/less/half/lower/light' and 'fat/saturated fat/salt/sodium/sugar', and zero otherwise. Alter-centric claims emphasize the greater presence of unhealthy nutrients in a competing food product.

The yearly number of articles in which the media attacked a food category for its amount of any of the identified unhealthy nutrients, that is, sugar, salt, or fat. It is built from Factiva news database counts of mentions to sugar, salt, or fat together with mentions to each Nielsen food category for 2006–2015, covering both the online and paper versions of The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Los Angeles Times, The Chicago Tribune, and The Wall Street Journal.
Each UPC's annual sales in the U.S. territory in U.S. dollars (hundreds of thousands). Product sales are used to capture commercial performance and, indirectly, consumers' purchasing decisions.

The percentage of the firm's sales that occurred outside its home province. It is constructed from a survey question asking what percentage of sales occurred within the firm's home province (or home municipality under direct control of the central government) with respect to the firm's primary product. The authors argue that sales outside the home location indicate the geographic concentration of the firm's business operations and proxy for how 'local' the firm is in the eyes of the home-location government. The authors note that asset locations might be a superior measure but are not available in the survey.

The logarithm of the total amount of unauthorized levies (Tan Pai) that the firm paid in 1,000 yuan, used as the dependent variable measuring the overall level of state expropriation. The underlying survey question asked how much of the firm's earnings in 1999 (or 2003) were used to pay all kinds of Tan Pai. Unauthorized levies are described as common in the Chinese private sector and as a major financial burden on privately owned firms in addition to their tax obligations.
scale: logarithm of an amount in 1,000 yuan

description: An indicator of whether the firm's owner is a member of the Chinese Communist Party. Party members are argued to be more likely to have higher political status and to have accumulated greater political capital than nonparty members. The authors note that party membership is a widely used indicator of political capital in China in social science research.

An indicator of whether the firm's owner formerly served as a cadre in the party-state or in state-owned enterprises (SOEs), which were part of the bureaucratic system and included in the same cadre system for personnel management as government officials. Former cadres are described as having superior political capital in China.

An indicator of whether the firm's owner is a delegate of the People's Congress at any administrative level. Serving as a regular delegate of the congress is only a part-time job but is described as an important means for Chinese firms to build their political connections and political capital.

A standardized index from the NERI database that is reverse-constructed based on the province-level average of firms' extra-tax fees, plus unauthorized levies as a percentage of sales, with the underlying information collected by a separate survey. The index is negatively correlated with the amount of governmental discretion and power in a province that enable it to extract revenue from firms; it measures the degree to which the government refrains from using discretion and power to extract revenue from businesses.
scale: standardized index (standardized to a 0-10 scale as described in the text)

description: Dichotomous variable taking a value of 1 if a director departed a given focal board within three years of the restatement event and a value of 0 otherwise. The three-year departure window ensures that every director stands for reelection at least once following a restatement event. Whether the director departed was determined by examining the first focal firm proxy issued at least three years after the restatement event of interest.
time_window: three years following the restatement event

description: The percentage of the company's outstanding shares held by public pension funds. Data were collected from the 13F filings of PPFs, which all institutional investors managing over $100 million in assets are required to file with the SEC, as reported in the Thomson-Reuters Institutional Holdings database.

The logged number of unique analysts who issued earnings forecasts for the firm in the year prior to the restatement announcement. Collected from the Institutional Brokers Estimates System (I/B/E/S), a Thomson Financial database that compiles earnings forecasts and stock recommendations from analysts at hundreds of securities firms.
time_window: year prior to the restatement announcement

description: Dichotomous variable coded 1 if a focal board's activities were monitored and rated by The Corporate Library in the year of the restatement event and 0 otherwise. The Corporate Library covers over 3,200 North American companies, and firms it covered were expected to be followed by other agencies as well.

A composite measure of board human capital formed from three variables: the percentage of directors who were active CEOs, the total number of boards on which directors served, and the combined market capitalization of those boards. The three items were theoretically consistent and loaded highly on a single factor with an eigenvalue exceeding 1.0. A squared term, human capital, squared, was also included to test for a curvilinear relationship.

Each focal director's normalized degree centrality within the entire director population listed in Board Analyst for the year preceding the focal fraud event, defined as the number of unique ties that an individual had to other directors by virtue of sitting on the same board, divided by the total number of possible ties; these centrality scores were then averaged across all directors on a given focal board. The log of the resulting value was taken to correct for nonnormality and a constant was added so the variable is always positive. A squared term, social capital, squared, was also included.
time_window: year preceding the focal fraud event

description: A composite index based on four indicators, each measured for the two years prior to the focal year: the number of resolutions; aggregate support for resolutions; the number of distinct institutional investor sponsors; and the number of resolutions endorsed by ISS. The four indicators cohered strongly and were standardized and averaged to create the composite index.
time_window: two years prior to the focal year

description: A composite index based on four indicators, each measured for the two years prior to the focal year: the number of resolutions; aggregate support for resolutions; the number of distinct institutional investor sponsors; and the number of resolutions endorsed by ISS. The four indicators cohered strongly and were standardized and averaged to create the composite index.
time_window: two years prior to the focal year

description: The percentage change in the CEO's annual compensation, from year t 2 1 to t. Total CEO pay was measured with the TDC1 variable from Execucomp, which consists of salary, bonus, restricted stock, and stock options (using the Black - Scholes option pricing model), and other income paid to a CEO in a given year.

A binary indicator of whether the CEO was dismissed, based on data from Peters and Wagner (2014) and Jenter and Kanaan (2015) who, following Parrino (1997), triangulated media reports, executive profiles, and web searches. For CEOs over 60 years old, a departure was a dismissal when a media report described it as an act of ' dismissal, ' ' firing, ' ' removal, ' ' forced out, ' or ' resignation due to policy differences '; departures of CEOs under 60 not explicitly described as forced were coded as dismissals if the stated reason was not mandatory retirement, poor health, death, or attainment of another position.

A binary indicator of whether the CEO voluntarily departed, derived from the same coding used for dismissals. Cases in which departures were preplanned, such as long-announced and mandatory retirements, were excluded; departures were categorized as retirements if the CEO was 65 or older, and voluntary departures between ages 60 and 64 or with tenure over 7 years were manually inspected and recoded as 0 where retirement had been planned, as were departures due to the CEO's health, unexpected death, or care for a spouse or family member.

The TDC1 variable from Execucomp measuring the compensation awarded to a new CEO in his or her first year. In cases where CEOs joined the firm in the middle of a financial year, their annual compensation was imputed by prorating the reported compensation to the full year; interim CEOs were excluded.

The Fundación Empresa Pública collects information on the number of patents for which a focal firm applied in a given year. The variable captures the number of patent applications a firm filed for protection in Spain, whether via the Spanish Industrial Property Registry or the European Patent Office. It measures total patent applications regardless of whether they were granted, which likely upwardly approximates the number of patents a firm ultimately receives. Three lags of the variable are included as regressors to capture firm dynamics.
time_window: t; lags t-1 to t-3 as regressors

description: The export status of the firm was collected in the Fundación survey. This measure captures whether the focal firm sold to foreign markets in a given year. The variable takes the value one if the firm exported in a given period, zero otherwise. Because knowledge takes time to filter back to the focal firm, the variable is lagged one, two and three years.

The natural log of total export sales, expressed as thousands of Spanish pesetas plus one, so as to identify the measure for non-exporters. It complements the export status measure by capturing the volume of trade. The variable is lagged one, two and three years.
scale: natural log of thousands of Spanish pesetas plus one

description: An index that compares the focal firm to the average industry R&D expenditures in 21 OECD countries other than Spain. The R&D expenditures of firm i in industry j at time t are scaled by its sales at time t to eliminate size effects; R&D expenditure in industry j from country k at time t is scaled by gross production in that industry and year, and averaged across countries other than Spain. The industry average scaled R&D is then subtracted from the firm's scaled R&D. Increasing values of the index indicate that a firm is a technological leader in its industry whereas decreasing values indicate a technological laggard. The formal equation is unreadable in the provided text.

Calculated similarly to the OECD index, except that Spain's average R&D expenditure (scaled by gross production) in industry j at time t is subtracted from the R&D expenditure of firm i from industry j at time t. It captures the firm's technological standing in its home country. Again, increasing values of the index indicate that a firm is a technological leader in its industry, whereas decreasing values indicate a technological laggard. The formal equation is unreadable in the provided text.

Dichotomous measure coded 1 if the participant chose to donate any of an extra $1 bonus to the project and 0 otherwise. Participants were asked how much of the $1 they would like to donate; the authors note that operationalizing the outcome as the fraction donated within the unit interval yields similar results.

An established three-item measure based on McCroskey, Richmond, and Daly (1975), each answered on a Likert 7-point agree/disagree scale. The items are ''This person is like me,'' ''This person thinks like me,'' and ''This person is different than me'' [reversed]. In the primary experiment the alpha for the scale was .55.

A new three-item scale tapping, in terms of gender, shared group membership, belief that the founder faces shared negative inferences, and the belief that it is desirable to see those inferences overturned. Items are answered on a Likert 7-point agree/disagree scale; the three items are ''This person is representative of my gender,'' ''This person has to deal with some of the same gender stereotypes I face,'' and ''It is important for society to see people like this one succeed.'' The alpha was .71 in the primary experiment and a confirmatory factor analysis supported two separate scales.

Randomized experimental condition: participants were shown the same Kickstarter project with either a female (Jessica Smith) or a male (Michael Smith) founder. The two versions differed only in the name and picture of the founder, which were equated on race, ethnicity, attractiveness, pose, expression and clothing.

variable_name: At least one female, no males
description: Intersection effects representing each of three cells in a two-by-two table with one or more female or male founders in the row or column: at least one female founder and no male founder; at least one male founder and no female founder; and at least one male and at least one female founder. The omitted category is projects with no identifiably gendered founders, such as corporate entities, un-gendered avatars or mascots, which the authors treat as a strategic choice founders can make. Founder gender was coded by four research assistants from project images, with interrater reliability above .90.

A dummy variable that denotes that the project was successfully funded by meeting or exceeding the founder's fundraising goal. Because Kickstarter employs an all-or-nothing threshold, the measure quantifies whether a founder succeeded or failed to raise capital. Approximately 32 percent of all projects succeeded.

The proportion of a project's backers who are female (female backers/total backers). The authors scraped these data on over 250,000 backers from Kickstarter and coded them algorithmically with the genderize.io tool, comparing first names with a database of 86,710 distinct names across 81 languages with known gender distributions.

Dummy variables for the five Kickstarter categories from which projects were sampled: gaming, technology, film, fashion, and children's books. The categories were chosen based on the gender distribution of backers and founders; film is the omitted baseline category in the reported models.

A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if a firm has higher than industry average sales growth but lower than industry average profit in 2008, 2009 and 2010, and 0 otherwise. Sales growth is measured as the percentage of sales change from the previous year and profit as pretax ROA. A firm's values are compared with the average value of its sub-industry (four-digit SIC); sub-industries with fewer than 15 firms were deleted from the sample.

A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if a firm has higher than industry average profit but lower than industry average sales growth in 2008, 2009 and 2010, and 0 otherwise. Profit is pretax ROA, the net profit as a percentage of total assets in each year, and growth is the percentage of sales change from the previous year. A firm's values are compared with the average value of its sub-industry (four-digit SIC); sub-industries with fewer than 15 firms were deleted from the sample.

Failure is a dummy variable that has the value of 1 if a firm's legal status is coded as bankruptcy or liquidation, and the value of 0 if its legal status is coded as continuing operation. The end year is set to 2017 because it is the last year of the available information in ORIANA. It is the dependent variable in the hazard models, so higher values indicate a lower chance of survival.

TMT stability is defined as the ratio of current TMT members to the total number of TMT members (including both current and previous members). The authors use it as a proxy for managerial attention and non-scale free resources in a firm, reasoning that a stable top management team implies management's familiarity with company operations and thus a high stock of managerial attention.

A dummy variable indicating whether a firm belongs to an industry directly influenced by the stimulus plan in 2008-2009. The industries identified as more growth-oriented due to the stimulus plan are real estate, cement, steel, construction, medicine, transportation, non-ferrous metal, electricity, machinery, energy-saving, and environmental protection. Stimulus equals 1 if a firm belongs to one of these industries, and 0 otherwise.

Because the authors do not have direct observations on the stock of experience, the experiential acquisition of the firm's technological capability is captured by dummy variables for each subfield, equal to one if the firm was currently active in that area and zero otherwise. All variables are time-varying over the spells. Entry into the memory, ASICs, microcomponents, optoelectronics and telecommunication IC subfields is the focus of the tests.

The dependent variable is entry into a subfield at a given time and is set to one if the firm entered and zero otherwise. It is modelled as the conditional waiting time, or hazard, from the time a firm is first recorded as existing to the time of its entry into another field, with firms at risk in each annual spell until they enter. Separate binomial models are estimated for each of the subfields in which subsequent entries occurred in significant numbers.

The munificence of the selection environment is indexed by the growth of a subfield, measured by the yearly rate of changes in shipment volumes. It is a time-varying covariate in the hazard regressions and is the covariate used to capture market opportunity and the favorability of market conditions for entry.

Measured with nine items adapted from Floyd and Lane (2000) and Floyd and Wooldridge (1997) (Cronbach's alpha = .86). Respondents were asked 'To what extent do you perform the following activities?' A sample item reads as 'Search for new strategic opportunities.' The full list of items is presented in Appendix S1.

variable_name: organizational performance above- and below-historical aspirations (spline)
description: The company measured MCO performance as a composite score of underlying sales-volume growth and operating margins, and final MCO performance scores were obtained. Historical aspirations were the MCO's performance in the previous year, and the discrepancy was calculated as the difference between current and prior-year MCO performance. A spline specification splits this discrepancy into two variables: the performance above-historical aspirations variable is set to zero if current performance is below historical aspirations, and the performance below-historical aspirations variable is set to zero when current performance exceeds historical aspirations.
time_window: current year relative to previous year

variable_name: organizational performance above- and below-social aspirations (spline)
description: Social aspirations at the organizational level were the average performance of all other MCOs, since the firm had no global competitors and no market research data across MCO markets and because resources are allocated competitively across MCOs. As with historical aspirations, the discrepancy was split with a spline specification into separate variables measuring MCO performance above and below social aspirations, each set to zero on the other side of the aspiration level.
time_window: current year relative to other MCOs' average performance

variable_name: individual performance above- and below-historical aspirations (spline)
description: The organization's standardized performance management system annually assesses each manager's individual performance; the scores reflect several objective measures and individual development goals and have been normalized by accounting for MCO performance. Historical performance-aspiration discrepancy was calculated as the difference between current and prior-year performance, and a spline specification splits it into two variables allowing slopes to vary for above and below aspirations.
time_window: current year relative to previous year

variable_name: individual performance above- and below-social aspirations (spline)
description: To measure social aspirations, each manager's performance was subtracted from the average performance of other colleagues at the same MCO. As with historical aspirations, separate variables were calculated to gauge the discrepancy above and below the social aspiration level.
time_window: current year relative to peers at the same MCO

description: Five items adopted from Mael and Ashforth (1992) were used to measure the extent of a manager's organizational identification (Cronbach's alpha = .80). A sample item reads as 'When I talk about [the MCO], I usually say 'we' rather than 'they''.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the target CEO is retained by the acquiring firm in the year after the merger (t+1) and 0 otherwise. The individual occupying the position of CEO of the target firm in the fiscal year prior to the announcement date (t-1) is identified using the proxy statement filed with the SEC; in the first year following completion of the merger (t+1) the acquirer's proxy statement is analyzed to determine whether the target CEO is reported in any capacity (i.e., as an officer or director of the merged firm).

An industry-adjusted accounting measure from Compustat, defined as operating income divided by assets in t-1 and deviated from industry medians. For completeness and to avoid misclassifying performance due to outliers, three-year averages of this measure based on t-3, t-2, and t-1 are also calculated. In the interaction models all variables are mean-centered.

Total compensation as reported in ExecuComp in the year prior to the acquisition, which includes salary, bonus, and the value of stock options, restricted stock, and other forms of long-term incentives. The models use the logarithm of total compensation (compensation is reported in thousands of dollars).

The number of years in position as CEO, measured in the year prior to the acquisition, used as a proxy for the target CEO's firm-specific human capital. CEO characteristics come from proxy statements and ExecuComp.

An indicator variable equal to 1 if the acquiring firm's governance index (G-index) is in the top quartile of the index, i.e., greater than 12, and 0 otherwise; these acquirers are classified as firms that commit to maintaining managerial discretion. The G-index considers 24 different provisions in five categories, formed by adding one point if the firm has a specific defensive provision in place and zero otherwise, leading to values between 0 and 24, with larger values representing more restrictions on owners and in turn more support for managerial discretion.

The fraction of the firm owned by the acquiring CEO, calculated as the number of shares listed in SEC proxy statements in year t-1 divided by the total number of shares outstanding as reported directly in SEC filings.

Composite measure of the regulatory dimension of the host country's institutional profile, anchored in quality management. Items concern laws and rules about quality, enforcement, consumer protection, and regulatory bodies. The measure was developed through item generation, sorting, pretesting, and purification with exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, and aggregated across senior subsidiary managers for each country.

Composite measure of the cognitive dimension of the host country's institutional profile, anchored in quality management. Items concern shared social knowledge about quality and quality management. The measure was developed through item generation, sorting, pretesting, and purification with exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, and aggregated across senior subsidiary managers for each country.

Composite measure of the normative dimension of the host country's institutional profile, anchored in quality management. Items concern quality-related social norms and values. The measure was developed through item generation, sorting, pretesting, and purification with exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, and aggregated across senior subsidiary managers for each country.

Perceived dependence of the subsidiary on headquarters for major resources, measured with a seven-point scale from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree.' Respondents indicated whether their location was completely dependent on headquarters for each of six resource types. Responses from senior subsidiary managers were aggregated by subsidiary. Internal reliability alpha = .83.

Trust of the subsidiary in the parent, measured with a modified short form of the Organizational Trust Inventory. Eight positively worded items were rated on a seven-point scale from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree.' Some items were excluded because they were not relevant in the headquarters-subsidiary context and because the company insisted on only positively worded items. Responses from senior subsidiary managers were aggregated by subsidiary.

Identification of the subsidiary with the parent, measured with a six-item scale adapted from prior work. Items were rated on a seven-point scale from 1, 'strongly disagree,' to 7, 'strongly agree.' Responses from senior subsidiary managers were aggregated by subsidiary. Internal reliability alpha = .83.

Subsidiary implementation of the quality management practice, measured with a scale developed from the company's Chairman's Quality Award criteria. Senior managers assessed the level of implementation of the quality process at their location for eight items. Internal consistency alpha = .92, ranging across countries from .78 to .96. Responses were aggregated by subsidiary.

Internalization of the quality management practice measured with a seven-item scale adapted from the Organizational Commitment Questionnaire. One item is reverse-scored. Data were collected from nonmanagerial subsidiary employees and aggregated by unit as the average of the summated items. Internal consistency alpha = .92, ranging by country from .80 to .95. The measure was validated against psychological ownership (r = .74, p < .001).
Variation in internalization at each unit, measured as the coefficient of variation for each unit, calculated as the standard deviation divided by the mean.

Recipient units were classified by standardizing the implementation and internalization measures and using K-means clustering to determine group identification. The ceremonial adoption group was characterized by a relatively high level of implementation and a low level of internalization. Differences between groups on institutional and relational context variables were examined with one-way analysis of variance and Bonferroni multiple range tests.

Firm status is measured by the amount of sell-side security analyst coverage a firm attracts, weighted by the industry expertise of the focal analyst. To calculate analyst expertise, the authors count the number of firms that each analyst covers in a three-digit SIC industry; the analyst covering the highest number of firms in an industry gets an expertise score of 1, and the expertise of other analysts is the number of firms they covered in the focal industry divided by the number of firms covered by the analyst covering the most firms in that industry. Firm status is the aggregate of the industry expertise score of the analysts covering the focal firm. The status of firms not covered in the IBES database is assumed to be 0.

A firm was considered to be part of a scandal if the focal class action lawsuit complaint was related to the focal firm's involvement in one of the two scandals, the options backdating scandal and the subprime mortgage scandal. Scandal is a binary variable that is equal to 1 if a firm was part of the scandal, and 0 otherwise. A total of 40 firms in the sample were part of the backdating scandal and 91 were part of the subprime mortgage scandal.

An SEC enforcement action is a binary variable that equals 1 if the SEC files fraud charges against the focal firm and 0 otherwise. The authors hand-collected whether and when the SEC filed fraud charges against the firms in the sample by searching the Factiva database for the relevant newswires and press releases from the filing date of the lawsuit through the next seven years. They first recorded news items about all enforcement action announcements against the focal firm, and then assessed whether the focal enforcement action was indeed related to the focal lawsuit in the sample. The SEC took 112 enforcement actions against the firms accused of corporate fraud from 2006-2011, which amounts to 14% of the sample.
time_window: from the filing date of the lawsuit through the next seven years

description: Blau index of heterogeneity computed as one minus the sum of squared shares of TMT executives with each nationality in a firm in a given year. Nationality is taken from information on the country of origin of the top executives as stated in the BoardEx database. TMT members were identified from information in firms' annual reports, or, where these did not contain such a delineation, as individuals with at least the rank of Vice President or holding a board executive directorship.

The number of unique technology-country-sourcing mode combinations in a given firm-year. Technology alliances, technology-based M&As and corporate venture capital investments are first categorized by the geographic origin of the targets and by SIC industry or technology field, which are mapped into standard technology fields. For the innovation models, the CE activities during the prior 3 years are taken.
time_window: prior 3 years in the innovation models

description: Invention (patent) count used as the measure of firms' innovation output, using the patent application date as the first indication of new capabilities and invention. Patent applications are taken from the European Patent Office PATSTAT database. The authors argue that the EPO examination process is substantially more rigorous than the U.S. process, so that European patent applications are more likely to be representative of novel technologies with utility.

Measured at the TMT level by standardizing and averaging two indicators based on the presence of different hierarchical rank titles in TMTs. The first indicator is a count of title gradations per TMT in each year (e.g., CEO, Chief Financial Officer). The second indicator is the presence of a COO reflecting an additional hierarchical level in the TMT.

Country-specific score on national power distance from the Hofstede typology, corresponding to the country in which the focal firms have their headquarters. Because scores on German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland differ significantly in terms of power distance, different scores were assigned to firms headquartered in these regions.

The authors also report that the Hofstede score for the countries represented in the sample varies between 11 and 77, ensuring substantial between-firm variation in NPD. The variable is time-invariant and attached to the country in which the MNC has its headquarters.

The number of subject matter "expertises" (not the number of experts) that an organization registered during the standard's development. The ISO development process had seven categories of expertise that participants were encouraged to bring: industry, government, consumer, labor, nongovernmental organization, academic, and standards-based expertise. Organizations were permitted to have six experts represent them, and the authors created a single 1-6 scale capturing the number of types of expertise an organization had representing itself.

The number of representative members an organization had on the 13 working committees of the process, measured before the committee draft vote and from the committee vote until the final vote. These data were collected from the minutes and attendance sheets that were available for the various committees.

An organization's vote of yes or no on whether the developed draft content should be moved to the next development stage for approval. The first vote was on whether the committee draft standard should move into the last drafting stage and become a draft implementation standard, and the second vote was the final vote approving the standard. Votes to abstain and nonvotes were added to the votes of nonconsensus.
time_window: two votes (committee draft vote and final approval vote)

description: Two points in the standard development process at which proposed changes and votes were recorded. The data set for the first point comprised proposed changes to the first draft and votes on whether the draft should enter the draft implementation stage; the second data set comprised proposed changes to the draft implementation standard and voting records from the approval stage. Data on logic pluralism were not collected at both points in time because it remained the same by definition.

Organizations' proposed changes to the two drafts of the standard provided all data for coding how organizations framed changes; the Linguistic Inventory Word Count (LIWC) dictionaries were used in quantitative content analysis of the 4,887 proposed changes. Frames were operationalized for both rounds as percentages of framing; imposing frames were direct commands to alter the text justified by the assumed legitimacy of the proposing organization.

Coded from organizations' proposed changes to the two drafts using the LIWC dictionaries and qualitative coding, and operationalized for both rounds as percentages of framing. Normative framing covers appeals to shared norms, processes and social politeness as the basis for altering meaning.

Coded from organizations' proposed changes to the two drafts and operationalized for both rounds as percentages of framing. Supportive frames emphasize agreement with the text and keeping the text the same or preserving its meaning.

Operationalized as the act of not proposing changes during the two comment submission periods. A scale of 0 and 1 was created for both comment periods: an organization was coded 1 if it did not offer comments for that period and coded 0 if it did propose a change.

Coded from organizations' proposed changes to the two drafts and operationalized for both rounds as percentages of framing. Cognitive framing emphasizes cognition in proposing change, asking for reconsideration of meaning, and its language includes open-ended questions and the word "reconsider".

A second-order factor analysis structures a latent variable based on mutual trust, relational embeddedness and relational commitment, each of which is derived using principal components factor analysis. Mutual trust is measured with a five-item scale, relational embeddedness with a three-item scale, and relational commitment with a four-item scale; the items of each mechanism load on a single factor with eigenvalues ranging from 2.52 to 3.80, factor loadings ranging from 0.83 to 0.93, and scale reliability ranging from Cronbach's alpha 0.86 to 0.92. Items use a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree), with a single rater per alliance. The latent variable is derived when estimating the structural equations model.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: An eight-item scale referring to the extent to which an alliance (1) met its objectives; (2) increased revenues; (3) improved quality; (4) reduced time to market; (5) generated new customers, products or projects; (6) led to customer satisfaction; (7) received favorable recognition; and (8) could evolve into a long-term relationship. Principal components factor analysis yields a single factor with an eigenvalue of 4.96 and scale reliability of Cronbach's alpha of 0.91 with factor loadings greater than 0.5, and the factor score serves as the performance measure. Items use a 7-point Likert scale.

Organizational differences are measured along four domains: management style, organizational responsiveness, internal task routines, and marketing routines. For each variable, respondents separately assessed the characteristics of their firms and the partners, and the difference is the absolute value of the difference between the firm's and the partner's scores on each organizational characteristic, averaged across the items of the variable: Dijk = (1/Mk) sum |ki - kj|, where Mk is the number of scale items. Unit weights are assumed instead of factor loadings.
scale: 7-point Likert items (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree); absolute difference scores

description: Respondents separately assessed the characteristics of their firms and the partners. Management style is measured with four items referring to levels of (1) hierarchical control; (2) authoritative decision making; (3) formal communication; and (4) organizational politics. The difference score is the absolute value of the difference between the firm's and the partner's scores on each item, averaged across the four items. Items use a 7-point Likert scale.

The text describes a five-item scale for organizational responsiveness; the items named in the prose refer to a firm's tendency to (1) respond quickly to emerging needs; (2) have confidence in outsiders; (3) be open minded in its approach to problem solving and conflict resolution; and (4) demonstrate an unpretentious attitude towards external parties. Differences are computed as the absolute value of the difference between the firm's and the partner's scores on each item, averaged across the items of the variable.

The measure of internal task routines is based on four items representing the extent to which routines demonstrate (1) employees' achievement focus; (2) employees' work ethic; (3) their degree of autonomy; and (4) teamwork. Respondents separately assessed the characteristics of their firms and the partners, and differences are the absolute difference between the firm's and the partner's scores on each item, averaged across the four items of the variable.

Marketing routines are measured with a four-item scale referring to (1) a firm's approach for managing customer relationships; (2) the proactivity of its salespeople; (3) its salespeople's technical expertise; and (4) the extent to which its salespeople offer suitable products by considering alternatives. Respondents separately assessed their own firm and the partner, and differences are the absolute difference between the two scores on each item, averaged across the four items of the variable.

A three-item scale captures the tendency to recognize organizational differences, referring to (1) the parties' effort to acknowledge their differences prior to forming the alliance; (2) whether differences were identified or emerged over the course of the alliance; and (3) the extent to which the differences were openly discussed. The three items load on a single factor with an eigenvalue of 2.20, factor loadings ranging from 0.78 to 0.90, and scale reliability of Cronbach's alpha 0.82. Items use a 7-point Likert scale. This variable is a moderator of the association between relational mechanisms and organizational differences.
scale: 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: Score from LIWC sentiment coding of the media text segments that mention the focal firm. Articles whose meta-data contained the tickers of TSX member firms profiled in the Board Shareholder Confidence Index were selected, and the authors analyzed each sentence containing a governance, shareholder-value, or firm-performance keyword together with up to two sentences before and after in Factiva. The higher the score, the more negative words and expressions are used in the paragraphs of the media sources that also contain the name of the focal firm.

Score from LIWC sentiment coding of the same media text segments that mention the focal firm and a governance, shareholder-value, or firm-performance keyword. The higher the score, the more positive words and expressions are used in the paragraphs that discuss the focal firm. Positive and negative tone are treated as separate dimensions rather than two ends of one spectrum.

Obtained by summing up the negative coverage scores of the companies to which the focal firm is connected through shared directors. Interlocking relationships were identified as cases in which two firms share the same director.

Obtained by summing up the positive coverage scores of the companies to which the focal firm is connected through shared directors. Interlocking relationships were identified as cases in which two firms share the same director.

Binary indicator equal to 1 if the focal company adopted a given practice in a particular year and 0 otherwise. Eleven board reform practices are tracked from the Board Shareholder Confidence Index and each generates its own indicator; the single-practice diffusion matrices are pooled by stacking them into one large matrix, giving a series of firm-year-practice observations.

Logging the ratio of total compensation in year t divided by total compensation in year t - 1. Total compensation was equivalent to the TDC1 variable in Execucomp, which reflects the aggregate ex ante value of all salary, bonus, restricted stock grants, long-term incentive plan payouts, option grants (valued using Execucomp's Black-Scholes formula), and other income paid to a CEO in a given year. Pay revisions were examined for each CEO from the third year of tenure until departure or cessation of the panel, for a total of 2,319 CEO-years. This variable, as well as most of the continuous independent and control variables, was winsorized at plus and minus four standard deviations.
time_window: year t relative to year t - 1

description: Total shareholder return calculated as the compounded return to shareholders (assuming continuous reinvestment of dividends and adjusting for stock splits) for a given fiscal year. Because current TSR in t is already a change score, no modification was needed for this measure.

Constructed by calculating the difference in return on equity between t - 1 and t, where ROE is equal to net income before extraordinary items divided by year-end common equity. A change score was used because pay revision is the dependent variable and earlier performance was included in the analyses, so examining change in performance enabled a meaningful interpretation of how performance deviations from prior levels influenced pay revisions.

Measured as the monthly compounded return to shareholders from the start of a CEO's first year in office through the end of t - 1. It captured the cumulative return on an investment made at the beginning of the CEO's first year in office measured as a ratio (the value of the investment at the end of t - 1 divided by the value of the initial investment). This was subsequently log-transformed to correct for skew.
Measured as the average annual return on equity from tenure year 1 through t - 1.

Equals a focal CEO's regression residual in t - 1 from ordinary least squares models predicting (logged) CEO pay for all CEOs in the Execucomp database between 1996 and 2005 whose companies fit the sample-screening criteria; a first-year model was run for incoming CEOs (1,679 CEOs) and a second model pooled all other CEO-year observations. Predictors in the wage models included company size (natural log of sales in t - 1), recent performance (TSR and ROE for years t and t - 1), CEO tenure, CEO age, industry affiliation (24 GICS categories), year dummies, and a binary indicator for the CEO's last year in office. Positive values indicate gradations of overpayment, and negative values denote degrees of underpayment.

Equals the sum of a CEO's residuals from the pay models from the outset of his or her tenure through t - 2. Positive values indicate gradations of overpayment, and negative values denote degrees of underpayment. Recent and earlier overpayment were separated to acknowledge that boards may particularly focus on how much they paid CEOs in the immediate prior year.

CEO tenure as CEO of the current firm, included for each year. Tenure also structured the panel: the dependent variable, CEO pay revision, was measured annually from the third year of each CEO's tenure, and the sample was limited to CEOs who had served at least four years by 2005.

Examining the TSR of all firms in each industry, the authors determined whether a given firm was in the bottom quartile of its industry in terms of TSR during each of the most recent two years (t and t - 1). For any firms below these cutoffs, dummy variables for poor current TSR were created, and the other three-quarters of the sample received values of 0 for that year. This coding acknowledges that the relationship between current performance and CEO dismissal is not linear; only subpar performance is a meaningful predictor of dismissal.

Examining the ROE of all firms in each industry, the authors determined whether a given firm was in the bottom quartile of its industry in terms of ROE during each of the most recent two years (t and t - 1). For any firms below these cutoffs, dummy variables for poor current ROE were created, and the other three-quarters of the sample received values of 0 for that year.
Identical to the measure used in the pay analysis, measured as the compounded total shareholder return from the CEO's first year in office through two years prior to the focal year (year t - 2).
Earlier ROE also was measured as described for the pay analysis, that is, as the average annual return on equity from tenure year 1 through t - 2.

Calculated similarly to the earlier over(under)payment variable used in the pay revision analyses, with two changes. First, cumulative overpayment was measured up through and including year t - 1, rather than separating earlier and recent overpayment. Second, because overpayment likely becomes a meaningful predictor of dismissal only beyond a certain threshold, a binary variable was created indicating whether a focal CEO was in the top quartile of the sample in terms of overpayment during a given year of tenure (for example, a fourth-year CEO would be compared to all other fourth-year CEOs), with the remaining three-quarters of cases assigned a value of 0 (representing underpayment or modest overpayment).

A binary indicator coded 1 for exit in a given year and 0 otherwise. Cases in which a CEO's departure was clearly not a dismissal were not coded as dismissals: death or serious illness, the CEO left office but remained as a company director, the departure announcement was concurrent with appointment as CEO at another firm, or the company ceased to exist as a public firm (by merger or going private); in such instances the CEO's record was terminated in that year since he or she was no longer at risk of dismissal. Using this method, the authors identified a total of 145 dismissals in the sample.

Announcements of product recalls located by examining the Wall Street Journal Index over the 20-year period 1968 through 1987. To be included, the common stock of the recalling company had to be listed on either the New York or American Stock Exchange, and automobile and tire industry announcements were eliminated. Only the first announcement for a particular product was used, and companies were excluded if the Wall Street Journal printed another article about the company over the interval -1 to 1.

Using daily security return data, market model parameters are estimated from day -291 to day -91 in relationship to the initial Wall Street Journal announcement on day 0. Daily prediction errors are computed over the event time -90 to 90, averaged cross-sectionally, and summed across various subintervals of time to compute mean cumulative prediction errors (MCPEs). The test statistics described in Dodd and Warner (1983) are used to determine if the MCPEs are significantly different from zero.
time_window: estimation period day -291 to day -91; event time -90 to 90

description: Recalls are separated into announcements that replace the product or return the purchase price and announcements to repair and/or check a product. Of the announcements in the sample, 112 were to replace the product (or return the purchase price), and 21 were for product repairs.

A government-ordered recall includes any recall specifically ordered by the federal or state government or one of their agencies; a voluntary recall is one coming specifically from the producer of the product. Because announcements often conflicted and in some cases it was impossible to determine who initiated the recall, ambiguous cases were eliminated, leaving 31 government-ordered recalls and 20 voluntary recalls.

Announcements in which products are taken off the market with no apparent recall of the previously sold products, located in the Wall Street Journal Index. The authors found 27 such instances of problem products taken off the market.

Dummy variable set equal to 1 if the candidate declines an interview with Execo, and equal to 0 if the candidate does not decline an interview but either is formally interviewed or is rejected by Execo prior to the interview stage. The variable measures the lack of willingness to consider an opportunity and is therefore reverse coded with respect to the theoretical hypothesis. Declining an interview is clearly the candidate's own decision, which is the theoretical outcome the authors care about.

Dummy variable set equal to 1 if the focal candidate was ever rejected in a previous job consideration at any stage of the hiring process and set to 0 otherwise. Rejections may have occurred before interviewing with the search firm, after interviewing with the search firm, or after interviewing with the client, and the measure aggregates all past rejections into a single indicator. The authors use a dichotomous measure because the average number of jobs for which candidates have been rejected is small.
time_window: prior job considerations (interactions recorded from 2001 onward)

description: Dichotomous indicator of the candidate's gender, set equal to 1 for female candidates and 0 for male candidates. It is entered as one term of the predictor variable, an interaction effect between candidate was previously rejected and female candidate.

Respondents were asked to imagine that the company they wrote about approaches them about another role appropriate for their current career stage and asks them to apply for the role. Replies were given on a scale ranging from 1 (definitely will not) to 5 (definitely will). The variable is categorical and ordinal and is modeled with ordered logit.

Measured via seven items adapted from Colquitt and Rodell (2011). Respondents rated their agreement with the statements on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree); alpha = 0.85.
The predictor variable was the gender of the respondent, coded as 1 = female or 0 = male.

Participants were randomly assigned to either the rejection condition (candidate was unsuccessful at securing a position) or the acceptance condition (candidate was successful at securing a position). In the rejected condition the outcome of the application was noted as 'reject in favor of another candidate'; in the accepted condition it was noted as 'make offer'. A t-test confirmed that those who wrote from the unsuccessful candidate's perspective felt more rejected than those who wrote from the successful candidate's perspective.

Participants completed a 30-item 'executive sense of belonging' questionnaire adapted from Good, Rattan, and Dweck (2012); alpha = .96. Participants rated their agreement with each item on a Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). The scores were reversed to obtain a measure of belonging uncertainty in executive domains.

Participants were asked to put themselves in the shoes of the candidate about whom they had written and to indicate their perceptions of procedural justice. The authors used the same perceived procedural justice scale as employed in Study 2; alpha = .89.

Participants were asked to take the perspective of the same candidate and to consider being approached by the company about another executive-level position, then to indicate their likelihood of applying for this position (1 = definitely will not to 5 = definitely will). The authors used the same question as in Study 2.

Participants indicated their gender in the demographic questions. Participants' gender was matched with the applicant record they received, so men wrote about a male candidate and women wrote about a female candidate, and gender is entered in the model as the term female candidate and in the interaction rejection x female candidate.

Dummy variable set equal to 1 if the job function of the current position is different from the previous position for which the candidate was considered (for instance, a candidate previously considered for a CFO job now considered for a CEO job) and equal to 0 otherwise. It is estimated with a linear probability model because a logit specification with candidate fixed effects would omit all candidates with no variation in the dependent variable. The variable can be calculated only from the second job consideration onward.

The base salary, in British pounds sterling, that the client firm is willing to pay a hired candidate for the focal job. The logarithm of this value is used when it serves as the dependent variable, and the variable is rescaled to thousands of pounds when used as a control in the models predicting rejections. Salary varies within the same job function with level of responsibility and firm characteristics.
scale: GBP; logarithm used as dependent variable

variable_name: Search firm previously rejected the candidate
description: Dummy variable set equal to 1 only if Execo ever rejected the focal candidate, at any stage in the search process, in any previous job consideration. Three additional dummies indicate respectively whether the rejection occurred before interviewing with the search firm, after interviewing with the search firm, or after interviewing with the client. In the models predicting the search firm's decision to reject a candidate, this variable captures the search firm having rejected the other party in the past.

variable_name: Candidate previously rejected the search firm
description: Dummy variable that takes the value 1 only if the candidate ever rejected a job opportunity offered by Execo in the past, at any stage in the search process. Four additional dummies capture the stage at which the candidate rejected an opportunity. In the models predicting the candidate's decision to reject an interview, this variable captures the candidate having rejected the other party in the past.

variable_name: Search firm previously rejected the candidate
description: Dummy variable set equal to 1 only if Execo ever rejected the focal candidate, at any stage in the search process, in any previous job consideration, with three further dummies for the stage of that rejection. In the models predicting the candidate's decision to reject an interview, this variable captures the candidate having been rejected by the other party.

variable_name: Candidate previously rejected the search firm
description: Dummy variable that takes the value 1 only if the candidate ever rejected a job opportunity offered by Execo in the past, at any stage in the search process, with four further dummies for the stage at which the candidate rejected. In the models predicting the search firm's decision to reject a candidate, this variable captures the search firm having been rejected by the other party.

Dummy variable set to 1 if the candidate refuses to interview with Execo and 0 otherwise. The model is estimated as a linear probability model with candidate fixed effects, using as the base category candidates who go to an interview with the search firm, and excluding observations in which the search firm rejects the candidate and those whose status is unknown. Declining a formal interview, which lasts two to three hours, is a decision not to pursue matters.

Dummy variable set equal to 1 only if Execo decides not to conduct a formal interview with the candidate and 0 otherwise. Estimated as a linear probability model with candidate fixed effects using as the base category candidates who go to an interview, and excluding observations in which the candidate rejects the search firm.

variable_name: Search firm previously rejected the candidate; Candidate previously rejected the search firm
description: Past rejection is measured with two dummy variables built from the search firm's archives. One equals 1 if the search firm ever rejected the focal candidate in any previous job consideration, and the other equals 1 if the candidate ever rejected a job opportunity offered by the search firm, each at any stage of the search process, with further dummies for the stage of rejection.

Firms named in the New York Times on September 24, 2014 as contributors to the Republican Governors' Public Policy Committee (RGPPC), a 501(c)(4) nonprofit that makes independent political expenditures under the control of the Republican Governors' Association. The Times reported the names of 91 firms that contributed to the RGA's committee, 66 of which were publicly traded. Of the 66 contributing firms, 14 experienced at least one confounding event during the time period of interest or had already voluntarily disclosed their contributions to 501(c)4s, leaving a sample of 52 disclosed contributors in the market-wide event study.

Firm i's cumulative abnormal return, calculated by summing firm i's daily abnormal returns over a chosen event window. Daily abnormal returns are the prediction errors from a market model that regresses each firm's daily returns on the value-weighted returns of a market-wide index, estimated over all trading days in 2013 and 2014 (through August 31, 2014). The main analysis focuses on the [0,1] event window, and longer event windows of 5, 10, and 20 days post-event were also estimated.

Dummy variable coded 1 for firms in regulated industries and 0 for those not. Regulation is defined using Coates's (2012) mapping, which identifies the following Fama-French 48 industries as regulated: alcohol, tobacco, drugs, aircraft, guns, gold, oil, utilities, telecom, transportation, banks, insurance, and finance.

Dummy variable coded 1 for firms in Coates's more narrowly defined subset of heavily regulated industries (alcohol, tobacco, aircraft, drugs, utilities, telecom, transportation, banks, and insurance) and 0 otherwise. With the exceptions of aircraft and drugs, these industries are subject to substantial regulation at the state level in the United States.

Logged dollar amount (plus one) of contributing firms' federal PAC contributions, hand-matched to FEC data. Two windows are used: the last full election cycle prior to the disclosure event (2011-2012) and the three electoral cycles prior to the event (2007-2012).

Binary variable coded 1 if the firm faced a shareholder resolution regarding the disclosure of political activity made 'with corporate funds or assets,' whether 'direct and indirect,' during the 2013 proxy season and voted on, and 0 otherwise. Data were gathered from Institutional Shareholder Services and cross-checked using Si2 and Proxy Impact's Proxy Preview.

The absolute number of lateral transfers a given leader has accrued at that job level up to a given point in time. Lateral transfer rate was calculated as the number of lateral transfers a given leader received per year during his or her total time at that level. Cumulative lateral transfer rate was the rate up to any given year. Used as a time-varying predictor of promotion and job performance in stepping-stone positions.

The absolute number of lateral transfers a given leader has accrued at that job level up to a given point in time. Used as the dependent variable in regressions predicting transfers of unit leaders from cumulative average job performance.

Dichotomous indicator of whether a unit leader was laterally transferred in a given year. Used as the criterion in logistic regressions predicting likelihood of transfer and as a predictor of change in improved operational effectiveness.
time_window: yearly; 2004-2006 for transfer likelihood, 2005 for transfer predicting 2006 effectiveness

description: Leader job performance was evaluated on a yearly basis on a scale of one to five (with five being the highest level of job performance). Evaluations are made by immediate supervisors; in this organization job performance reflects a given leader's mastery of a set of competencies and achievement of several goals each year. When average job performance was used, it was computed for leaders over the course of their entire time at that level. Cumulative job performance represents the average job performance up to any specific year.
time_window: yearly; cumulative up to any given year

description: Dichotomous dependent variable in hazard analyses, indicating whether the leader was promoted in a given year. The authors report that 13% of leader trainees and 23% of assistant unit leaders are promoted in any given year.

Measured using unit leader bonuses in U.S. dollars. Unit leaders' bonuses are based on approximately 50% performance evaluation rating and 50% changes (defined as improvements) in several objective indicators of their unit's productivity (e.g., increased sales, decreased costs) during that year. Bonus data were only available for two years (2004-2005 and 2005-2006).

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three vignette conditions: a contraextrinsic rewards focus (free agency led to player movement but players later turned down lucrative contracts and sacrificed salary), a neutral condition (specialization had changed play on the field), and an extrinsic rewards focus (free agency, higher pay, strikes and lockouts). The conditions are coded in ascending order (contraextrinsic = 1, neutral = 2, extrinsic rewards = 3) to mirror the expected increase in attributions of inauthenticity and demand for traditional ballpark features. In the mediation models they are entered as two dummy variables with the contraextrinsic rewards condition as the reference.
scale: 1-3 ascending coding of the three conditions

description: After the assigned vignette, participants read a vignette in which a player said the game was about his team and that they loved to play, and were asked 'How likely is it that the player is representing his genuine feelings about the game and his team?' on a 1 (very unlikely) to 7 (very likely) scale. The item was then reverse coded to create a measure of perceived inauthenticity. It is the outcome variable for H1 and the mediator for H2.

Participants were told to choose three features from a list of eight MLB ballpark features. A pretest asked participants to evaluate the eight features on how authentic and traditional they were to Major League Baseball; the four features rated as more traditional were used to build the outcome. The dependent variable is the count of the traditional features each participant selected, i.e., between zero and three.

All ballparks in use during the observation years were coded by style using the standard era designations provided by baseball historians. A ballpark was coded as traditional (traditional = 1) if it was built during the classic era (1909-1922) or during the so-called retro era (1992-2006); if it was not built during these periods or did not have the key features it was coded as nontraditional (traditional = 0), and ballparks built after 2006 were coded as nontraditional.

variable_name: Difference in home and away capacity-controlled attendance per game, per year
description: Each game's attendance was divided by the total capacity possible for that game, creating a capacity-controlled attendance variable. Each team's annual away capacity-controlled attendance was then subtracted from the team's annual corresponding home capacity-controlled attendance to arrive at the value for each team and year. As a difference in percentages the variable lies between -1 and 1, and netting out away attendance identifies the component specific to home attendance.

A dummy variable for before (free agency = 0) and after (free agency = 1) the advent of free agency, capturing a leaguewide effect for the advent of free agency and used as an exogenous shock for the models comparing periods.

variable_name: Number of key free agents lost
description: A team-specific measure of exposure to free agency counting the key free agents each team lost in the off-season prior to the year in question; only free agents who signed with a team in that off-season were included. Key players were identified in two ways: a reputational measure noting whether a player had previously been an all-star, and a day-to-day involvement measure including players who played in more than 135 (83.3%) of the team's games in a year; the measure combines players fitting either criterion. It is used as a control in all models and interacted with the traditional ballpark variable in one model.
time_window: off-season prior to the year observed

variable_name: target company top management turnover rate
description: Cumulative percentage of the target company's top management team that had turned over at each of 5 years after the merger or acquisition date, computed from the departure dates provided in the parent company survey. Annual turnover rates are the differences between the cumulative yearly percentages. Top managers were identified from the companies' 10K or annual reports (mean 8.19 executives per team). The measure is available for 102 target companies.
time_window: 5 years after the merger or acquisition

variable_name: parent company top management turnover rate
description: Cumulative percentage of the parent company's top management team that turned over at each of 5 years from the point of initial observation. Each top manager's name was identified from the company's 10K or annual report and employment status was tracked in these 10Ks or annual reports. Matching parent company top management turnover rates are available for 77 of the 102 possible parents.
time_window: 5 years from the point of initial observation

variable_name: control company top management turnover rate
description: Top management turnover rates assessed by archival sources (10K or annual reports) for 75 companies not involved in merger and acquisition activity, computed as cumulative and annual rates at each of 5 years from the point of initial observation. Complete performance and turnover data are available for all 75 control companies.
time_window: 5 years from the point of initial observation

variable_name: preacquisition target company top management team turnover
description: Percentage of the target company's top management team that turned over over the 5 years prior to the merger or acquisition announcement. The top managers were identified from each company's 10K or annual report 5 years prior to the announcement date and their employment status was followed to the announcement. The 10Ks and annual reports were available for 59 of the possible 102 target companies.
time_window: 5 years prior to the merger or acquisition announcement

description: Cumulative abnormal returns for 1-year through 5-year periods ending 3 months before the acquisition announcement, where the monthly abnormal return is the excess return on the company's common stock over the return on an equal weighted market index. Five-year cumulative abnormal returns (assessed in the period 62 months through 3 months prior to the announcement) were available for 49 target companies and 34 parent companies. Stock price information was collected from CRSP.
time_window: 62 months through 3 months prior to the announcement

description: Cumulative abnormal returns for 1-year through 5-year periods ending 3 months before the acquisition announcement, where the monthly abnormal return is the excess return on the company's common stock over the return on an equal weighted market index. The intent was to obtain a performance measure unaffected by the typical rise in stock prices in the 2 months prior to a merger or acquisition announcement. Five-year cumulative abnormal returns were available for 49 target companies.
time_window: 63 months prior to the announcement through 2 months prior to the announcement

description: Cumulative abnormal returns computed over the same 1-year through 5-year time periods for the control companies, where the assessment began with the initial observation month of the top management team's employment status. The control companies were selected so that all 75 were listed on the New York Stock Exchange throughout the 63-month period preceding the observation of company turnover, so complete performance data are available for all 75.

variable_name: market reaction to the acquisition announcement
description: Two measures were collected. The first is the target company's abnormal return for the day the acquisition was announced, defined as the excess return on the target company's stock compared to the return on the equal weighted market index for that day. The second is the cumulative abnormal return for the period beginning 60 days before the merger announcement and ending with the announcement day (t = 0), the day the merger or acquisition was revealed in the Wall Street Journal; daily stock price information came from CRSP.
time_window: announcement day and 60 days prior to announcement

variable_name: target company versus control company classification
description: Companies merged with or acquired by U.S. companies with assets of at least $10 million were classified as target companies; the comparison group was 75 control companies not involved in merger and acquisition activity during the same period, drawn from the Standard and Poor's Stock Guide. Target and control companies were matched randomly by asset size but not by industry.

Degree centrality is the number of distinct alters with whom the actor corresponds, computed for each period from a symmetric matrix whose dyad-level entries are the total number of messages exchanged between i and j. The authors use the square root of degree in their models, a transformation that improves model fit. The measure is calculated with the StatNet package in R.
time_window: Time 1 (fourth quarter of 2006) and Time 2 (first quarter of 2008)

description: Structural constraint is an inverse measure of structural holes, built from the share of actor i's communication ties exchanged with each alter j and the indirect constraint imposed on i through connections among i's contacts. More connections among an actor's contacts means more constraint and therefore fewer structural holes. The natural logarithm of constraint is used in the models, a common transformation that improves model fit.
time_window: Time 1 (fourth quarter of 2006) and Time 2 (first quarter of 2008)

description: The matchmaker index is the proportion of all closed triads in which a focal actor participates with two other people from two different business units. A triad is closed when Ego communicates with both alters and the alters also communicate with one another; the numerator counts only those closed triads in which the two alters belong to different business units. A proportion is used to avoid excessive correlation between the index and measures of network size.
time_window: Time 1 (fourth quarter of 2006) and Time 2 (first quarter of 2008)

description: Dummy variable set to 1 for individuals with positions in the corporate headquarters. In interpreting the CHQ dummy, all comparisons are to otherwise similar members of the line organization.

Dummy variable set to 1 for individuals with positions in the corporate sales force. As with CHQ, the comparison group is otherwise similar members of the line organization, and regressions are estimated separately for each staff unit rather than on pooled data.

Dummy set to one if employee i transitioned to the corporate headquarters before Time 2, conditional on an origin job in the line. It serves as a dependent variable in the first-stage probit models and as the treatment indicator in the second-stage models of Time 2 network structure.
time_window: One-year interval between the fourth quarter of 2006 and the first quarter of 2008

description: Dummy set to one if employee i transitioned to the corporate sales force before Time 2, conditional on an origin job in the line; constructed analogously to Line-to-CHQ and used both as a first-stage dependent variable and as a second-stage treatment indicator.
time_window: One-year interval between the fourth quarter of 2006 and the first quarter of 2008

description: Dummy set to one if employee i transitioned to the line organization before Time 2, conditional on an origin job in the corporate headquarters. Used as a first-stage dependent variable and as a second-stage treatment indicator for the effect of exiting the corporate staff.
time_window: One-year interval between the fourth quarter of 2006 and the first quarter of 2008

description: Dummy set to one if employee i transitioned from the corporate sales force to the line organization before Time 2, conditional on an origin job in the corporate sales force; constructed analogously to CHQ-to-Line.
time_window: One-year interval between the fourth quarter of 2006 and the first quarter of 2008

description: Dummy variable indicating whether a paper was published in year t that included both members i and j of the dyad l as coauthors. It is the primary dependent variable and is used to assess the persistence of collaboration in the dyad. Dyads are kept in the sample while they are at risk for collaborating, that is, until either member has gone three years without publishing a paper, and they are then observed for every year they are at risk.
time_window: Every year the dyad is at risk for collaborating

description: Dummy variable indicating the years after the passing of k for the dyad l in which k was the third party: it is zero up to and including the year of k's passing and one for the subsequent years. For the dyads involved with control k's, the variable is always zero.
time_window: Annual, from the year of k's death onward

description: Helpfulness is measured by the number of acknowledgments k received by the treatment time, a fixed variable for each k. To simplify the interpretation of three-way interactions, k is classified as helpful if above the median on this count and as nonhelpful if below the median.
scale: 0/1 dummy (dichotomized at the median of acknowledgment counts)

description: Eigenvector centrality of k in the treatment year, calculated on a 10-year window of publications before that time. Because networks change over time, the measure is scaled so that at each point in time the most central scientist has a centrality measure of 1. It is a fixed variable for each k and is the authors' key measure of status.
time_window: 10-year window of publications prior to the treatment year

description: The number of acknowledgments that i and j received before the beginning of their triadic collaboration with k; the authors use the minimum of the acknowledgments the two individuals had received, and report similar results with the maximum or the average. It is a fixed variable for each dyad and enters the estimations as an interaction with the death of k.
time_window: Before the beginning of the triadic collaboration (fixed)

description: Dependent variable of the mechanism test: the logarithm of the number of acknowledgments scientist i had received by the time of k's death, with observations being ik pairs limited to the k's who passed away. The models control for full sets of dummies for the acknowledgments i received before the collaboration began, for i's career age when the collaboration began, and for the calendar year in which the collaboration started, as well as for the number of papers i published before the collaboration, the impact-factor-weighted number of papers, and the citations i had.
time_window: By the time of k's death

description: Coded as 1 when a given member of an alliance operating a route at time t is no longer part of the alliance operating the route in t + 1 and 0 otherwise. The unit of analysis is the firm-alliance-year. The authors impose the requirement that the route will still operate next year, to distinguish member withdrawal from route failure.

Count of firms in the market that are not in the focal alliance and that have higher complementarity with the focal firm than a threshold. The threshold is the complementarity of the firm with its partner(s) in the focal alliance, set at the lowest-complementarity firm in the alliance when there are multiple partners. Complementarity is calculated over markets defined by the International Transportation Handbook classification of routes into 16 regions.

A count of the number of complementary markets in which the two firms are represented divided by the union of the markets in which the firms are represented, using the International Transportation Handbook classification of routes into 16 regions. The formal expression is given in the paper as an equation block that is not legible in this text; the prose example states that if firm i is in four markets and firm j is in five markets, including two markets in which the other is also represented, the union of their market presence is seven markets, the complement is five markets, and the complementarity is 5/7.

variable_name: Outside options, no alliance in different market
description: Count of the focal firm's outside options with which it is not allied in a different market, i.e. options that offer access to new rather than existing market complementarities. The complementary variable, outside options with which the firm is partnered in a different market, is entered as a separate count in the same model.

variable_name: Outside options, not current alliance but past alliance
description: Count of outside options with which the focal firm has a past alliance but no current alliance, obtained by partitioning the outside options that have no alliance in a different market. The complementary count, outside options with neither current nor past alliances, is entered as a separate variable in the same model.

Count of the firm's outside options with clustering coefficients equal to zero, i.e. outside options that are not embedded in closed triads. Clustering coefficients are computed as the number of triads in which a firm is embedded divided by the maximum number of triads that a firm can potentially form with its partners, obtained for each firm in each year using the algorithm in UCINET 6. The complementary count, outside options with clustering coefficients greater than zero, is entered as a separate variable in the same model.

variable_name: Outside options, is in rival alliance
