description: Industry similarity is measured using a three-point ordinal scale, assigning a score of 2 if the core businesses of the acquiring and target firms share the same three-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code, 1 if they share the same two-digit but not the same three-digit code, and 0 otherwise. Deals based on similarity through vertical integration, as identified in the press releases, are also assigned a value of 2 since they can yield operating synergies.
The acquiring firm's payment method for a given acquisition is measured by means of a three-point ordinal scale: 1 for cash only, 2 for a combination of cash and stock, and 3 for stock only.
scale: 1 = cash only, 2 = combination of cash and stock, 3 = stock only

description: Involvement of advisors by the acquirer is measured through the number of stages or aspects of the deal process in which external advisors were actively involved, as reported in SDC Platinum.
This dummy variable takes on the value 1 if the acquirer had a stake in the target exceeding 10 percent prior to the current deal and 0 if not.
The use of defense tactics is measured as a dummy that equals 1 if the target deployed antitakeover defense mechanisms in reaction to the acquirer's bid and 0 if not, as reported in SDC Platinum.
The acquiring firm's current performance is operationalized through its profitability in terms of return on assets in the year in which the acquisition occurs.
time_window: year in which the acquisition occurs

description: The acquirer's capital structure is measured using its debt-to-equity ratio.
The acquirer's acquisition experience is measured using a cumulative count of all prior acquisitions completed by the focal acquirer from 1980 onward.
time_window: from 1980 onward, up to the focal acquisition

description: Within growing industries, trend firms have a fractional change in net sales over the 5-year period greater than the median value for their industry, and static firms have a fractional change in net sales below the median for their industry. Within declining industries, trend firms have a fractional change in net sales below the median for their industry and static firms have a fractional change in net sales above the median. The classifications are done separately for each 5-year period and each two-digit SIC code industry.
Returns are measured by return on assets. ROA is defined as income after tax but before extraordinary items divided by total assets.

Returns are measured by return on equity. ROE is defined as income after tax but before extraordinary items divided by stockholder equity. Stockholder equity is defined as preferred stock (liquidation value) plus tangible common equity.

Risk is measured by the variance in returns, computed separately for each firm over time and for both ROA and ROE. ROAVAR is a mean value of a sample of firm ROA variances calculated separately for each firm over time, and not the variance in ROA of a sample of firms. Simple variance in returns does not distinguish between variation about a trend and the trend itself.

The mean sum of squared errors from regressing returns for firm i in time t on a time variable that takes the values one, two, three, etc., depending on the year, with one being the first year in the sample on which the regression is being run. The estimates correct for serial correlation in the error term. Both ROA and ROE performance measures are used, giving two measures: MSE for the ROA equation and MSE for the ROE equation; the equations themselves are not readable in the text available.

Alliance network diversity is a latent variable with three observed indicators. The first two measure the extent to which an MNE has unique (i.e., not repeated) international joint venture partnerships with home country (Japanese) firms and with local firms in the host country, i.e., the number of unique Japanese partners and the number of unique local partners. The third focuses more directly on interfirm heterogeneity by measuring the number of different industries from which network partners originate.

Economic performance is a latent variable defined by three accepted measures: return on assets, return on sales, and return on capital. To avoid the potentially confounding effects of idiosyncratic asset valuation and local tax treatment, the return on sales and return on invested capital figures were based on operational profits rather than net, after tax profits. All data on MNE economic performance were collected from Compustat's Global Vantage.

A dummy variable operationalizing environmental munificence: the more munificent time period prior to March 2000 was coded as 0, and the less munificent time period after March 2000 was coded as 1. The coding corresponds to the timing of the environmental jolt to the technology sector that occurred on March 11, 2000. The measure was triangulated using expert judgment from eight e-commerce experts and validated with mean-difference tests on Internet sector indexes, bankruptcies, IPOs, and the NASDAQ stock market.

Cumulative abnormal stock returns during an event window of 3 days surrounding alliance announcements. CAR are the sum of daily percentage stock price changes after adjusting for general stock market movements and a focal firm's systematic risk, for each day in an event window. Day 0 is the first day investors could respond to an announcement; if announcements were made after trading hours, day 0 is adjusted accordingly. Residuals from a stock market model are used to yield predicted returns used to estimate abnormal stock returns.

variable_name: alliances with e-commerce or bricks-and-mortar partners
description: A dummy variable coded as 0 for e-commerce partners and coded as 1 for bricks-and-mortar partners. Firms were classified as e-commerce partners if they generate revenues by selling or providing products, services, and/or information exclusively through websites. Information about partners was collected from stock analysis sites, press releases, and SEC filings; 41 partners with both online and offline operations were classified as bricks-and-mortar partners.

A dummy variable coded as one if the alliance is for marketing-related activities and coded as zero if it is technology-related. Alliances involving product development and innovation activities were classified as technology-related. Multiple trained coders classified alliance types and 97 percent of alliance announcements were coded without discrepancies. Twenty-one alliances containing both marketing and technology activities were classified based on their main function.

A dummy variable equal to '1' if individual i is working in a municipality m that has enacted the entry deregulation 'On the Spot Firm' program by year t, and '0' otherwise. The program was officially launched in July 2005 and expanded over time across municipalities, so the treatment turns on for municipality-year observations at different moments.

A dummy equal to '1' if (a) in a given year an individual is associated with a firm different from their employer in the previous year, and (b) the individual becomes an employer at the focal firm (i.e., hires at least one other individual). Self-employment is excluded from the measure and only new ventures with at least one employee in addition to the founder are counted.

The monthly wage of the worker, constructed by adding up base pay (the gross amount of money paid in a given month to employees on a monthly basis for their normal hours of work), regular payments (e.g., tenure-related payments), and payment for extra work hours. The dependent variable in the wage regressions is the logged wage. The pay-for-performance component is excluded from the measure in these analyses.

A dummy variable equal to '1' for female employees, and '0' for male employees. Interacting this variable with the entry deregulation reform allows the authors to estimate the differential effect of the treatment for female versus male employees.

A variable equal to '1' for employees working in a managerial position in 2004 (the year before the deregulation was approved, to avoid any endogeneity issue), and '0' otherwise. An employee occupies a managerial position if she/he is a top or a middle manager; managerial position is coded from the firm's hierarchy, which records eight levels based on the autonomy individuals have in their jobs.

Residuals from a fixed-effects CEO wage equation predicting log CEO salary from education, firm tenure, job tenure, international responsibility, log firm sales, firm ROA and CEO/chair duality, with year dummies. The overpayment variable was constructed by setting the measure equal to the CEO residual term if the residual was positive and zero otherwise, so a positive value means the CEO's actual salary was higher than predicted.

Constructed by setting the measure equal to the CEO wage equation residual if the residual was negative and zero otherwise. In order to make interpretation more straightforward the sign was reversed so that larger positive values were associated with greater underpayment.

Compensation for the CEO and others in the sample, computed as the sum of base compensation and annual bonus. All compensation variables and sales data were inflation adjusted to a constant dollar basis and log transformed so that extreme values would not drive the results; the authors confined the analysis to annual compensation because information on stock options and other long-term incentives was not available from the survey.

A dummy variable that took on a value of one if there was no other executive at the firm with the title of chair, and zero otherwise. The authors note that they could not identify cases in which there is a separate chairman of the board who does not work for the company, but that this circumstance was relatively rare during the period.

Measured by subtracting the employee's wage equation residual from the CEO's wage equation residual. Because fixed-effects regressions were used, a positive residual means the actual change in salary in response to changes in the independent variables within the firm was larger than expected; if the CEO's residual is larger than an employee's, the CEO is overpaid relative to the employee and the employee should feel inequity.

Measured by subtracting the firm dummy variable estimated in the employee wage equation from the dummy variable estimated in the CEO wage equation. A high firm effect in either equation means the salary was high relative to the market, so a higher CEO firm effect than employee firm effect means the employee should feel inequity and be more likely to leave.

Individuals were recorded as exiting a company if they appeared in the survey for a given year but did not appear in the survey the following year. Survey instructions encouraged firms to drop people only if they left the firm, and individuals who left the sample in one year and returned later were excluded, which eliminated 624 observations out of more than 40,000.
time_window: annual, 1981-1984 (last year used to determine exits)

description: Firms provided data for individuals in the top five levels of the organization, with the CEO assigned as the only member of Level 1. The analyses were run separately for managers at Levels 2 through 5: the CEO over- and underpayment variables were inserted into wage equations for each of these levels, and the turnover models were estimated separately at each level.

Standard deviation of excess returns, the residual risk over and above the systematic market exposure a manager in an index fund would face. Excess returns are computed as the difference between raw returns and the benchmark risk-adjusted return predicted by the four-factor model for mutual funds (Fama and French three factors plus Carhart momentum) and the seven-factor model of Fung and Hsieh plus a liquidity risk factor for hedge funds. A 12-month moving-average standard deviation of excess returns measures time-varying risk exposure.
level: manager-fund-month (aggregated to manager or manager-fund in some tests)

description: Difference between raw returns and the benchmark risk-adjusted return predicted by the four-factor asset-pricing model for mutual funds (and the seven-factor model plus liquidity risk factor for hedge funds). Taking the difference every month and computing a moving average over time provides a time-varying performance measure.
Excess returns divided by idiosyncratic risk exposure.

Dichotomous variable equal to 1 when a mutual fund manager is/becomes a hedge fund manager and 0 otherwise. Manager transitions were identified by hand matching the CRSP mutual fund managers to hedge fund databases at the manager level.

A mutual-fund-to-mutual-fund transition (a transition to a new mutual fund) is coded as 2 in the multinomial logit analysis. The baseline case, coded as 0, is a manager who does not transition, and a mutual-fund-to-hedge-fund transition is coded as 1; an exit by a bottom-quartile performer is coded as 3.

The authors operationalize learning by measuring managers' risk-taking behavior, viewing excessive risk taking—the kind that reduces risk-adjusted performance—as an 'experiment' from which portfolio managers learn about themselves. Thus idiosyncratic risk taking serves as the proxy for experimentation.

Treatment indicator for the audit applications. For ex-founders the most recent job experience was listed as co-founder of a marketing- or HR-related start-up and the contact email address was listed as founder@..., while nonfounders listed a marketing/HR manager position at a midsized local firm and a name-based email. Résumés also indicated that the start-up employed 10-12 people to distinguish founding from self-employment.
time_window: most recent job listed on the résumé

description: The main predictor variable in the survey experiment, coded as '1' if the résumé belonged to an ex-founder, and '0' otherwise. Each participant was randomly shown one of the four conditions: male employee, male founder, female employee, or female founder.

Indicator for the gender of the audit applicant. To signal gender the authors altered the first name of the applicant and changed the listed interests to activities determined in a pretest to reflect similar socioeconomic status but be more associated with women than men (e.g., baseball to softball); names were selected via a pretest of 500 respondents.
The main moderating variable in the survey experiment, coded as '1' if the résumé belonged to a female job candidate, and '0' otherwise.

Binary outcome of the audit: whether the employer contacted the candidate (by phone or email) for a follow-up interview. Automated responses and follow-up requests for online skill-based tests were coded separately and not included as an interview request.

The principal outcome modeled in the survey experiment: the respondent's willingness to recommend the applicant to a prospective employer. Respondents were asked, 'Would you recommend this job candidate to a future employer?' and replied on a scale from '1' (definitely will not) to '7' (definitely will).
scale: 1 = definitely will not to 7 = definitely will

description: Perceived fit mediator: participants were asked to assess whether they believed the job candidate 'was a good fit for a more traditional/hierarchical organization,' with replies on a seven-point scale ranging from '1' (definitely no) to '7' (definitely yes).

Commitment measure: employers assessed the likelihood that the job candidate will 'quit their next job' on a seven-point scale ('definitely will not' to 'definitely will'), consistent with prior research that conceptualized commitment as a continuous relationship with an employer.
scale: 1 = definitely will not to 7 = definitely will

description: Because ex-founders might be seen as placing high value on autonomy and independence, the authors measured the perception that a job candidate was 'easy to manage' on a seven-point scale ('definitely not' to 'definitely yes').

Given that ex-founders might be perceived as unlikely to fit teamwork, the authors measured the perception that a job candidate was 'a team player' on a seven-point scale ('definitely not' to 'definitely yes').

Respondents were asked whether 'The candidate was a good fit for their last job (i.e., the job preceding the current job search),' with replies on a scale ranging from '1' (definitely was not) to '7' (definitely was).
scale: 1 = definitely was not to 7 = definitely was

description: Forward vertical relatedness coefficient between the segment industry and the core business industry. Fan and Lang (2000) normalize the interindustry use table by dividing the value of i's output to j by j's total output, which gives the forward relatedness coefficient F, ranging between 0 and 1. The degree of forward integration is defined as the dollar value of the segment industry's output consumed per dollar of the core business industry's output.
time_window: input/output data for 1982 used for 1979-1986, 1987 data for 1987-1991, and 1992 data for 1992-1997

description: Backward vertical relatedness coefficient between the segment industry and the core business industry. It is obtained by dividing the core business industry's dollar output consumed by the segment industry by the total output of the segment industry, or equivalently j's dollar output to i divided by total output of i. The degree of backward integration is calculated as the dollar value of the core business industry's output consumed per dollar of the segment industry's output.
time_window: input/output data for 1982 used for 1979-1986, 1987 data for 1987-1991, and 1992 data for 1992-1997

description: Forward complementarity coefficient between the segment industry and the core business industry, calculated as the correlation between the dollar values of outputs provided to various intermediate buyer industries by the two industries. The larger the correlation, the greater the overlap between the customers of the core business and the segment.
time_window: input/output data for 1982 used for 1979-1986, 1987 data for 1987-1991, and 1992 data for 1992-1997

description: Backward complementarity coefficient between the segment industry and the core business industry, calculated as the correlation between the dollar value of inputs procured by the two industries from various input industries. It captures the degree to which the segment and the largest business obtain inputs from the same supplier industries.
time_window: input/output data for 1982 used for 1979-1986, 1987 data for 1987-1991, and 1992 data for 1992-1997

description: Weighted forward relatedness coefficient at the firm level. To parallel the segment-level regression, the authors aggregated the four variables F, B, CF, and CB by weighting each variable by the proportion of segment sales and then summing the weighted coefficients. Because a larger core business accounts for a higher proportion of total firm sales, the weighted relatedness variables take lower values for the same levels of F, B, CF, and CB.

Weighted backward relatedness coefficient at the firm level, formed by weighting the segment-level coefficient B by the proportion of segment sales and summing across the firm's segments. WTDB is the fraction of the total output of the core business industry consumed by the industries of the various segments.

Weighted forward complementarity coefficient at the firm level, formed by weighting the segment-level coefficient CF by the proportion of segment sales and summing the weighted coefficients across the firm's segments.

Weighted backward complementarity coefficient at the firm level, formed by weighting the segment-level coefficient CB by the proportion of segment sales and summing the weighted coefficients across the firm's segments.

Relative core business size, measured as core segment sales divided by total firm sales, included at the firm level to control for the effects of a large core business independent of its overlap of transactions with the segment.

Segment productivity, measured as the sales of a segment less the sales of an average single-business firm in the same four-digit SIC code with comparable assets, normalized by firm size. It is equivalent to subtracting the segment's expected sales from its actual sales, assuming the same asset turnover ratio as single-business firms, and then normalizing by firm size; normalization takes into account that a given deviation in productivity in sales implies a greater distortion in a smaller firm. Single-segment firms serve as benchmarks and are not included as observations in the segment-level regressions.

Core business productivity, calculated similarly to segment productivity. For every firm in the sample there is one core business productivity observation, and single-segment firms are not included because they serve as benchmarks in calculating core business productivity.

Firm value measured by Tobin's Q, measured as market to book, used as the dependent variable in the firm-level instrumental variable regression. It is one of the variables for which summary statistics of the firm-level regression are reported.

Shareholder return calculated by compounding the daily returns to shareholders from the CRSP tapes over each fiscal year, adjusted for stock splits and dividends, so that the measure represents shareholder returns at the end of the fiscal year from a $1.00 investment made on the first day of the fiscal year. The variable is then standardized at the four-digit SIC code of the spin-off firm, that is, the market performance of the firm is divided by the average market performance of all firms at that four-digit SIC for that year.
time_window: each fiscal year, up to five years after the spin-off

description: The percentage of ownership retained by the parent firm in the child after the spin-off event. The variable varies from zero to 20 percent, and only eight percent of parent firms retained an ownership stake in the child.

The list of directors from the proxy statement for the child was examined to determine if the parent organization retained any seats on the board. The variable is coded 1 if the parent organization retained at least one seat on the board (other than the chairman) and 0 otherwise.

Proxy statements were examined to determine if the chairman of the board is affiliated with the parent firm (i.e., CEO of the parent, top manager, etc.). The chairman of the board variable is coded 1 if this is the case and 0 otherwise.

To test the hypothesis about excessive monitoring, the interaction between board representation and board chair variables is included, which divides firms into four groups: board member from the parent, chairman of the board from the parent, both, and neither. Monitoring is considered disproportionately high when the parent firm retains both the chair of the child firm's board and at least one other regular board seat.

variable_name: Prior parent-child relationship (unrelated, vertically integrated, horizontally related)
description: Three expert raters classified each parent-child relationship according to business descriptions, SIC codes, and buyer/supplier relationships as unrelated, vertically integrated, or horizontally related. The unrelated variable was set to 1 if the relationship was determined to be unrelated and 0 otherwise; the vertically integrated variable was set to 1 if the relationship was determined to be vertically integrated and 0 otherwise; the horizontal related variable was set to 1 if the relationship was determined to be related and 0 otherwise. Initial interrater reliability was 0.75 and discrepancies were resolved by discussion and mutual agreement.

Calculated as the ratio of live births resulting from IVF treatment done at the focal clinic, divided by the total number of female patients who had IVF treatments at the focal clinic in year t. The measure does not discriminate between singleton, twin, or multiple births, and is a standard measure to assess clinical performance in this field.
scale: ratio of live births to patients

description: Coded as 1 if the clinic reported the availability of a 'patient liaison' during treatment in the Annual Patient Guides to IVF; coded as 0 if no liaison role for the patient was reported. Almost none of the clinics changed their integrator status throughout the duration of observation.
time_window: time invariant over the observation window

description: Coded as 1 if both options of a dedicated physician and a named nurse were reported by the clinic, and 0 otherwise. Reported terminology in the patient guides allows this distinction from 1999 onward.

Coded as 1 if only the option of a dedicated physician (i.e., 'one physician throughout treatment') was reported, and 0 otherwise. Doctor-integrators are generally known to exercise stronger informal authority than nurses.

Coded as 1 if only the option of a named nurse (i.e., 'named nurse system') was reported, and 0 otherwise. Nurse-integrators add a layer of informational richness and ease of communication with and about the patient that is superior to that of doctor-integrators.

Binary variable indicating whether the observation occurred after (i.e., equal to 1) or prior to (i.e., equal to 0) the policy change regarding multiple embryo transfers. Its interaction with the integrator measures is used to test whether the use of integrators enables or impedes clinic-level adaptation to the interdependence shift.

A dummy variable that took a value of one if one or more PVC investments were made in a complementor with apps in the subcategory during the previous three months and was coded zero otherwise. To operationalize it, the authors identified the subcategories in AppExchange in which an investee complementor had apps by the time the PVC investment became public. All independent and control variables were lagged by four months in the app introduction analyses and by one month in the app withdrawal analyses.

A dummy variable capturing a complementor's decision to introduce one or more apps in a subcategory in a given month. It took a value of one for each complementor-subcategory-month observation where a complementor chose to introduce apps, and zero in all other cases. It was collected from monthly observations of all apps on AppExchange.
time_window: monthly observations from April 2013 to June 2014, with independent variables lagged four months

description: A dummy variable that took a value of one in the app-month where a complementor decided to permanently withdraw the app from AppExchange and a value of zero otherwise. It was observed in an unbalanced panel data set at the level of the app-month, with independent and control variables lagged by one month.
time_window: monthly observations, with independent variables lagged one month

description: Measured as a function of both the size and age of a complementor's app portfolio. The authors computed the sum of the number of months between the time of observation and the time of introduction over all apps by a complementor, and then log-transformed this variable to reduce skewness and to account for possible diminishing returns to learning. It is measured at the level of the complementor.
time_window: time-varying, measured at the time of observation

description: A dummy variable taking a value of one when a complementor built its business exclusively on the Salesforce platform and zero otherwise. It was hand-coded using the information complementors provided about their business on AppExchange along with information retrieved from their websites, coding for whether complementors centered their business entirely on the Salesforce platform as opposed to also providing other products and services, being active on other platforms, or similar. The variable is time-invariant.

A five-year cumulative count of the number of unique patent infringement lawsuits launched by a source firm between 1973 and a focal observation year. The authors screen out duplicative listings of a dispute and exclude instances in which a firm is defending against lawsuits filed by others. The measure captures the litigious activity of a source firm against all defendants rather than against a particular recipient.
time_window: five-year cumulative window between 1973 and focal year

description: Cumulative count of inventors hired from a given source firm by a recipient firm over the preceding five years, measured by the application year of a mobile inventor's first patent at the recipient organization. Mobility events are identified through an inventor name matching algorithm applied to patent records. The authors identify 1,166 mobility events from 28,123 unique inventor names.

Count of citations made by patents of a recipient firm to patents of a source firm in a given year. More (fewer) such citations are interpreted as evidence of higher (lower) knowledge spillovers. Self-citations and citations made by firms outside the focal sample are not included.

Dummy variable set to one if, in the focal year, the recipient firm is privately owned, has less than 100 employees, or is less than five years old; zero otherwise. A firm is coded as private when it is not listed on the New York or NASDAQ stock exchanges; small means fewer than 100 employees (the 60th percentile of the size distribution); young means the first five years after founding.

Dummy variable set to one if, in the focal year, the source firm is privately owned, has less than 100 employees, or is less than five years old; zero otherwise. A firm is coded as private when it is not listed on the New York or NASDAQ stock exchanges; small means fewer than 100 employees; young means the first five years after founding.
Dummy variable set to one if the source firm has headquarters in California; zero otherwise. Information about headquarters location was compiled from Hoover's, Compustat, and VentureOne.

The event is the firm's public announcement of a switch to the M-form structure, identified in the Wall Street Journal or the New York Times. An announcement had to indicate that at least two of three changes were taking place: formation of a corporate office with associated staff; decentralization to semiautonomous divisions; and indication of appropriate M-form controls such as cash flow allocation. Day 0 is defined as the day of the article in the financial press.

variable_name: average abnormal return (AR) and cumulative average abnormal return (CAR)
description: Abnormal return for security i on day t is defined against the expected return generated by the market model, with the S&P 500 as the market proxy; the equation block itself is not readable in this payload. Security-specific parameters are estimated by running the market model on three independent sets of data: before, during and after the switch to the M-form. The day t average abnormal return is the equally weighted average of the abnormal returns for the individual securities, and average abnormal returns are summed over intervals to produce cumulative average abnormal returns. Because it is unclear whether the article reports an announcement made before or after the market closed on day -1, both days -1 and 0 comprise the event period.

Each sample firm was classified into one of three major diversification strategies using Rumelt's (1974) methodology: vertically integrated firms (primarily dominant vertical firms), related diversifiers (primarily the related constrained category) and unrelated diversifiers (the unrelated acquisitive category). For the event study the data were broken into two portfolios, one of vertically integrated and unrelated firms and one of related diversified firms, because the small sample size made three portfolios impossible.
scale: three categories: vertically integrated, related diversifier, unrelated diversifier

description: Longer-term performance is measured with the Sharpe and Treynor portfolio performance measures, and the reported figures are mean differences between the portfolio measure and the market measure (firm measure minus the market, T - Tm and S - Sm). These mean differences are computed for the two groups of firms (vertically integrated and unrelated diversifiers versus related diversifiers) for three time periods: before, during and after the M-form announcement. The mean differences have been transformed as explained in Jobson and Korkie (1981).
time_window: before, during and after periods around the announcement

description: Teachers reported on the school as a whole rather than on their individual experiences, using survey items based on Nahapiet and Ghoshal's three facets of social capital. Information sharing (six items, Cronbach's alpha = 0.89), trust (six items adapted from Pearce et al., Cronbach's alpha = 0.88) and shared vision (six items, Cronbach's alpha = 0.93) were each measured on a multi-item Likert scale. The internal social capital measure was created by averaging the level of information sharing, trust, and shared vision reported by teachers within each school.

Measured through principal time diaries as the relative amount of time on the job that principals spent interacting with stakeholders outside the school, computed as a proportion of each principal's total hours so as to capture relative effort rather than overall hours worked. Activities counted as external were those centered on bringing extra resources into the school, parent relations, and community relations. On average principals spent 13.7% of their time on external relations (sd = 7.5%).

An average quality of instruction score for each school built from the district's parent survey, using three items: parental satisfaction with the methods used to teach their child, with the materials used to teach their child, and with opportunities for learning for their child. The average parent rating on these items was 3.9 (sd = 0.28) on a five-point scale ranging from 1 = very dissatisfied to 5 = very satisfied, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.94.
scale: five-point scale from 1 = very dissatisfied to 5 = very satisfied

description: The percentage of students in the school attaining scores that meet or exceed state standards for achievement in mathematics, the method of reporting used by the state and mandated as part of NCLB. Tests were uniformly administered and mandated by the state: for elementary schools to all 5th graders, for middle schools to all 8th graders, and for high schools to all 11th graders. On average, fewer than 40% of each school's students met or exceeded state standards in any given year.

The percentage of students in the school attaining scores that meet or exceed state standards for achievement in reading, the method of reporting used by the state and mandated as part of NCLB. Tests were uniformly administered and mandated by the state: for elementary schools to all 5th graders, for middle schools to all 8th graders, and for high schools to all 11th graders. On average, fewer than 40% of each school's students met or exceeded state standards in any given year.

variable_name: Proportion of responses to strategic actions
description: The 191 actions were comprised of 16 different action types, which were classified as strategic or tactical by six professors with expertise in the airline industry; of the actual observations, 158 were classified as tactical and 33 as strategic. For each organization for each year, the number of times a firm responded to a strategic action was divided by its total number of responses. A firm's tactical score was the complement of its strategic score.

The externality of a firm's orientation was inferred from how many of its vice presidents were in marketing and customer relations, with information drawn from the World Aviation Directory. The two measures were summed to form a single scale labeled external orientation.

The total number of departments and the total number of officers in each company were obtained from the World Aviation Directory and each was divided by organizational size. Size was measured by total revenue passenger miles, the total number of miles an airline's passengers travel, excluding passengers who do not generate revenue. The two totals were standardized and summed into a single scale, structural complexity.

Absorbed slack was the amount of selling, general, and administrative expenses divided by total revenue, a measure reflecting slack that is absorbed by costs. Information on airlines' annual expenses came from Air Carrier Financial Statistics.

Unabsorbed slack was measured by the extent to which current liabilities covered the sum of cash and marketable securities for a year. This measure, the quick ratio, reflects a company's uncommitted liquid resources, and information for it was taken directly from Standard and Poor's COMPUSTAT tapes.

Data on the educational levels of the chief executive officer and seven other randomly chosen corporate executives were gathered for each airline for each year. These data were averaged; an average of 22 corporate executives were listed in the Dun and Bradstreet directory for each airline.

Data on the years of industry experience of the chief executive officer and seven other randomly chosen corporate executives were gathered for each airline for each year. These data were averaged across the executives.

Response imitation, or the degree to which a response imitated an action, was measured in terms of the concurrence of the type of action and the type of response. A binary variable captured the degree of duplication involved in each response, with a value of 1 when the type of response was the same as the type of action and a value of 0 when the types differed. These values were averaged for each airline for each year to obtain an imitation score, with a high score indicating a propensity to mimic a competitor's action.
scale: binary per response (0/1); averaged into a firm-year score

description: Response likelihood was calculated by summing the number of times each airline responded to competitors' actions during a given year and dividing that figure by the number of times the firm had an opportunity to respond. Opportunities to respond were counted airport-by-airport, with no double counting, as the number of actions that potentially affected a focal airline. Firms that score high on this scale are likely responders.

Response lag was measured by the amount of time it took a firm to respond to a competitor's action, that is, the difference between the date of the first report of a specific competitive action in Aviation Daily and the date a response was reported. Average response lags were calculated by averaging the amounts of time it took a given airline to respond to competitors' actions for each year.

Response order was measured as the rank position in time of a responding firm among all responders, calculated by averaging each airline's actual rank position in the order of responders for each action for each year.
Performance was measured in terms of net profit after taxes divided by total revenue. Data for this profitability measure came from Air Carrier Financial Statistics.

Percentage of Yale's endowment allocated to venture capital, gathered annually from Yale's reports and the NACUBO Endowment Study. The authors used the percentage rather than the absolute amount because informants emphasized the percentage as the key signal of Yale's support for venture capital relative to other asset classes. The measure was lagged one year in the models.

Dummy variable equal to one if at least one venture-capital-backed company went public and experienced a run-up—a doubling or greater of the offering price on the first day of trading—during the quarter. Data on IPOs came from the Securities Data Corporation's new-issue database. The measure was lagged one year.

Event count of the number of U.S. venture-capital foundings in each quarter, calculated using the primary sample from VentureXpert. The count variable takes only discrete, nonnegative values and was lagged one year in the models.

The real manufacturing wage index is the nominal wages index corrected for changes in purchasing power measured by the consumer price index (100 x nominal wage index / consumer price index). The authors subtract the wage index of the previous year from the wage index of the present year for each location and calculate the mean across all existing production locations of the MNC in a year. All variables including the controls are lagged by one year relative to the expansion.

An autoregressive conditional heteroskedastic (ARCH) process is used to estimate the degree to which the current wage index could not be expected looking at the past development. To obtain a measure of uncertainty in the entire portfolio, the authors compute the mean volatility across all locations in a year. The variable is lagged by one year.

The authors calculate the variance in real manufacturing wage growth of the current set of host countries within a year, reflecting the heterogeneity of labor cost developments across the locations of the production network. The variable is lagged by one year relative to the expansion decision.

Dummy variable that takes the value of 1 in the year in which an investor establishes a new production subsidiary abroad, and 0 otherwise. Establishments of subsidiaries that compensated for subsidiary closures in the same country and year were ignored to avoid a bias from in-country firm restructuring. Within the period between 2002 and 2007, 245 of the 352 investors established a new subsidiary.

Absolute change in the average labor cost growth rate of the existing production locations effectuated by the establishment of the new production subsidiary, i.e., the level of the network after the expansion compared with the level before the expansion. It indicates whether the chosen location lowers the average wage growth of the network. Computed for the 245 network expansions.

variable_name: change in uncertainty of labor costs
description: Absolute change in the uncertainty of labor costs of the existing production network effectuated by the establishment of the new production subsidiary, i.e., the level of the network after the expansion compared with the level before the expansion. Used to check whether the chosen location increases the labor cost volatility of the network. Computed for the 245 network expansions.

variable_name: change in diversity of labor cost developments
description: Absolute change in the diversity of labor cost developments of the existing production network effectuated by the establishment of the new production subsidiary, i.e., the level of the network after the expansion compared with the level before the expansion. Used to check whether the chosen location raises the diversity of labor cost developments in the network. Computed for the 245 network expansions.

Indicator variable for CEOs whose family's socioeconomic situation while growing up was upper or upper-middle class. CEOs answered the question 'Which of the following best describes your family ' s socioeconomic situation while you were growing up?' with five response choices: lower, lower-middle, middle, upper-middle, and upper. The upper and upper-middle categories were aggregated into a single upper social class origins category, which is contrasted with the middle class baseline in the regressions.
time_window: childhood, reported in the August 2012 survey

description: Indicator variable for CEOs whose family's socioeconomic situation while growing up was lower or lower-middle class. CEOs answered the question 'Which of the following best describes your family ' s socioeconomic situation while you were growing up?' with five response choices: lower, lower-middle, middle, upper-middle, and upper. The lower and lower-middle categories were aggregated into a single lower social class origins category, which is contrasted with the middle class baseline in the regressions.
time_window: childhood, reported in the August 2012 survey

description: Composite of three variables: research and development (R&D) expenditures, capital expenditures, and the value of the firm's long-term debt. The unscaled versions of the variables were used, with firm size explicitly controlled to avoid spurious correlations common to ratio measures. Principal components factor analysis returned a single factor, with a 1.58 eigenvalue, explaining 53% of the variance; the factor loadings were 0.66 for R&D, 0.81 for capital expenditures, and 0.71 for long-term debt, justifying aggregation into a single composite indicator of firm risk taking. Strategic risk taking was measured at time t+1, one year after the predictors.
time_window: t+1 (one-year lag between predictors and the dependent variable)

description: Degree of elite education, measured using a modified version of the index used by Tihanyi and colleagues (2000). Coded '0' if the CEO did not complete a formal four-year degree, '1' if he or she had an undergraduate degree from a nonelite university, '2' if he or she had an undergraduate degree from an elite university, and '3' if both degrees were from elite universities. The list of elite universities reported in Finkelstein (1992) was used.

Each CEO's career functional background was coded following Hambrick and Mason's (1984) classification scheme into throughput functions (R&D, operations, engineering), output functions (marketing and sales), and peripheral functions (law, finance, accounting). A functional background that did not fit into one of these categories was coded as general management functional background, resulting in four functional background indicators. Peripheral background was used as the baseline in the analyses.

Count of protest events in the relevant metropolitan area in the five years preceding the year of the union election, logged. The count is built from the Dynamics of Collective Action coding of every protest event reported in the New York Times; strikes and other protests specific to labor unions are not recorded in that series. The natural log is taken because the effect of the level of protest activity is probably multiplicative and because it helps resolve the skewness of the count variable.
time_window: five years preceding the year of the union election

description: Votes for the union divided by the votes cast in the NLRB-supervised representation election. The NLRB records the number of eligible voters, the number of votes cast, and the number of votes in favor of unionizing. Elections in which the union received none or all of the votes were excluded from the trimmed variable used in the analyses, because small bargaining units make unanimous outcomes common and their uneven distribution across cities could bias the estimated effect of protest; robustness checks were conducted with the non-trimmed measure.

Natural log of the count of protest events in the metropolitan area over the previous five years that were coded as making politically progressive claims. The variable was built by relying on the claims made by each protest as recorded in the DoCA dataset.
time_window: five years preceding the year of the union election

description: Natural log of the count of protest events in the metropolitan area over the previous five years whose claims were related to Civil Rights. For the test of H3 the models are estimated only on elections held through 1981 and thus influenced by protest activities through 1976.
time_window: five years preceding the year of the union election

description: Natural log of the count of protest events in the metropolitan area over the previous five years whose claims were made by the women's movement on employment-related issues. Models are estimated separately for elections held through 1981 and from 1982 on.
time_window: five years preceding the year of the union election

description: Unions were classified into progressive, neutral, and conservative subclasses as described in Online Appendix B. Separate submodels were fitted for each union and a weighted average effect of protest was estimated for each subclass. Progressive unions represent 52.6 percent of the organizing efforts studied, neutral unions 33.1 percent, and conservative unions 14.3 percent.

The data are split into elections held through 1981 and elections held from 1982 on, so that the protest measures capture protest activity through 1976 and after 1976 respectively. The authors treat the years before 1982 as earlier in these data for historical reasons, motivated by the break in the protest and union-organizing time series and the change in the vote-share series.

Firms were originally classified into six groups using Rumelt's (1974) classification, based on proportion of revenue from a product and general relatedness: single-product, vertical, dominant, related, unrelated and conglomerate. They were later reclassified into three groups for simpler analysis: single-product and vertical firms were considered 'low' diversifiers, related firms 'medium' diversifiers, and unrelated and conglomerate firms 'high' diversifiers. Dominant firms were dropped from analysis because of limited response, leaving 44 firms.

Executives rated, on a five-point Likert scale, the importance of five performance goals: financial, production, marketing, personnel-related goals and coordination among same-level executives. Objective goals were taken to be those which are more readily quantifiable, e.g. financial measures; subjective criteria included personnel-related goals and coordination among managers.
Executives' estimates of the percentage they receive as base vs. bonus pay. The low, medium, and high diversifiers' bonus means were 25.14, 36.25, and 33.50 percent respectively.

Measured on a five-point Likert scale with two questions, e.g. the extent to which bonus distribution was based on (1) a formula, such as a certain percentage increase in profit generating a bonus of a certain amount, or (2) judgement of evaluators, such as the President or board of directors.

The natural logarithm of the stock of immigrants from country j in region r in year t. It was built from Russian Federal State Statistics Service data on the number of foreigners that entered region r in year t as permanent residents, constructing a stock by adding the numbers from previous years starting in 1997. Permanent residents were used because the regional distribution of permanent residents, but not of temporary foreign workers, was reported for the observation window.

Operating return on assets, calculated by dividing earnings before interest and taxes by the book value of assets, used as the dependent variable in all models. The results are robust to using ROA instead. Outliers were removed by eliminating the top and bottom 1% of observations on OROA.

Dummy variable that equals 1 when a firm has an immigrant CEO and 0 when it has a Russian CEO. CEO nationality was listed in the database for 19% of firm-years; for the remaining observations the authors used the uniqueness of Russian names to identify whether the CEO had a Russian name or a name typical of the firm's home country, dropping firms from countries with names similar to typical Russian names unless manager nationality was listed in Ruslana.

Dummy variable that equals 1 when a firm is founded by one or more foreign individuals and 0 when it is founded by a foreign company (MNC). Independent firms are thus operationalized as foreign entrepreneurial ventures, such as a pizzeria started by an Italian entrepreneur.

Average score by region on the 2005 World Values Survey question 'What brings success in life - hard work or luck and connections?', on a scale ranging from 1 at the 'hard work' extreme to 10 at the 'luck and connections' extreme. Regions were then split at the median value of the scale.
level: region (lowest geographic unit in the WVS is a federal district)

description: Share of respondents in a region who answered 1 (trust completely) or 2 (trust somewhat) on the 2005 World Values Survey four-point scale of how much individuals trust people of another nationality, out of the total number of respondents in that region. The sample was split into regions with above-median trust and below-median trust.
level: region (lowest geographic unit in the WVS is a federal district)

description: Firms are classified by industry, with industry dummies at the two-digit level included in the models. For the industry comparison, the sample is limited to retail trade and service firms in one model and to manufacturing firms in another. The sectoral distribution of the sample is reported in the text.

Natural logarithm of the employment of the subsidiary's MNC parent. The model uses firms with available data on parent-firm employment, and subsidiaries with more than one parent firm are excluded because it is unclear how resources of multiple parent firms would combine; using parent-firm assets provides similar results.

variable_name: top 2.5% sales rank / top 2.6%-20% sales rank / bottom 80% sales rank
description: Games' first-month unit sales, taken as the percentage rank at the platform-year level and broken up into three dummy variables: top 2.5% sales rank (market-leading sales), top 2.6%-20% sales rank (good initial sales), and bottom 80% sales rank (poor initial sales, the base category). The 20% cutoff reflects the Pareto principle that 80% of sales come from 20% of products, and the 2.5% cutoff is restrictive enough to identify the very top games. First-month unit sales are used because they account for more than 40% of cumulative unit sales and because they avoid including sales that occur after the endorsement decision.
scale: percentage rank split into three dummy categories

description: Percentage rank of all genres by total unit sales for each year and platform. All genres are first rank ordered by the sum of first-month unit sales of all games released in that genre, in that year, on that platform; the percentage of genres with lower sales than a given genre is its percentage rank, so higher percentage ranks reflect more valuable genres. The measure is calculated separately for each game and excludes the focal video game, and it is a within-platform rather than a between-platform measure.
level: game-platform (genre-year-platform value assigned to each game)
time_window: same year as the game's release

description: A dummy that takes the value of 1 if there is no top 20% ranked video game measured by first-month unit sales in the same genre and platform of a game under consideration, measured over a one-year rolling window prior to a game's release.
time_window: one-year rolling window prior to the game's release

description: A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 if a game is launched only on the focal platform. It is built by looking at the population of video game releases and counting the number of platforms on which a game is released.

A dummy that indicates whether a video game has a Metascore of 75 or higher. Metacritic produces a numerical score ranging from 0 to 100 based on expert reviews, most of which are published prior to a game's release. The base group includes games with Metascores below 75 and games with missing Metascores; 90 games in the sample have no Metascore registered on Metacritic.
time_window: reviews published prior to a game's release

description: A dummy variable that takes the value of 1 when a video game is endorsed and rereleased through a platform sponsor's selective promotion; the moment of endorsement and a game's rerelease coincide, and in the sample all endorsed games are rereleased and only endorsed games are rereleased. The unit of analysis for this measure is the game-platform level.
The count of endorsed video games that are released on a platform at the platform-genre-month level, traced from the start of the data in 2007 up to the last month of 2011.
The number of new games that are released within a particular genre per month on a platform, counted at the platform-genre-month level.

Five items rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all and 5 = very much). Respondents rated the extent to which their ventures were successful relative to their major competitors in terms of (1) frequently introducing new products, (2) being first in new product introductions in the market, (3) quickly launching new products into the market, (4) developing new products with superior quality, and (5) using new products to penetrate markets. Items were averaged to create the construct score.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

description: Composite measure created by averaging four items asking respondents to indicate the extent to which their ventures had close relationships with (1) technology service firms (i.e., technology commercialization and brokering), (2) accounting and financial service firms, (3) law firms, and (4) talent search firms. Each item was rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all and 5 = very much).
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

description: Single item from the ties-with-service-intermediaries question. Respondents indicated the extent to which their ventures had close relationships with technology service firms (i.e., technology commercialization and brokering), rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all and 5 = very much).
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

variable_name: ties with accounting and financial service firms
description: Single item from the ties-with-service-intermediaries question. Respondents indicated the extent to which their ventures had close relationships with accounting and financial service firms, rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all and 5 = very much).
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

description: Single item from the ties-with-service-intermediaries question. Respondents indicated the extent to which their ventures had close relationships with law firms, rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all and 5 = very much).
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

description: Single item from the ties-with-service-intermediaries question. Respondents indicated the extent to which their ventures had close relationships with talent search firms, rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all and 5 = very much).
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

description: Three items adapted from McDougall et al. (1994). Respondents were asked to indicate the extent to which they agreed with statements regarding their principal industry in the last three years: (1) There has been high growth in demand in this industry; (2) This industry offered many attractive opportunities for future growth; and (3) Growth opportunities in this industry have been abundant. Items were rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all and 5 = very much) and averaged.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

variable_name: adoption of agency business for foreign firms
description: Dummy variable indicating whether the venture has been involved in any business as an agent to market and distribute a foreign firm's products and services in China. Coded 1 = yes and 0 = no.
Dummy variable indicating whether the venture has exported products out of China. Coded 1 = yes and 0 = no.

Our survey of executives asked respondents to assess, on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 'never' to 'very often', how often they get advice from executives at each of the other fund companies. The responses were mapped onto a knowledge matrix recording the flow of knowledge among executives in different firms in the industry. Cell ij equals 0 when the executive at fund company i received no knowledge from any executive in fund company j, and 4 when the executive in fund company i received knowledge from someone at fund company j very often. When responses were received from more than one executive at a given firm, the highest of the values was used as the level of knowledge flow.
scale: 0 to 4 (five-point Likert scale from 'never' to 'very often')

description: The 77 × 77 geographic proximity matrix measures geographic colocation, coded 1 if firms i and j shared the same geographic area and 0 otherwise. Firms were measured as located in the metropolitan area where the head office is located. In the two cases where fund management activities took place other than at the head office, the firm was deemed to be located in both of the distinct geographic locations where the major activities took place.

The 77 × 77 institutional ties matrix assesses common membership on the IFIC Board of Directors, the IFIC Management Committee and the IFIC Retail Council, which comprise the Investment Funds Institute of Canada's committee structure. Two firms have a tie when each firm has a member on the same board or committee; firms do not have a tie if one has a member on the Management Committee and the other on the Retail Council. Cell ij equals 0 when there are no institutional ties from fund company i to fund company j and 1 when there is an institutional tie between them.

The 77 × 77 matrix of organizational ties was created from the interfirm management ties and interfirm ownership ties and then dichotomized. Cell ij equals 0 when there is no organizational tie between fund company i and j and 1 when there is an organizational tie. Because the authors had no ex ante expectation about the direction of knowledge flows, the matrix was symmetrized.

The survey question 'I have a friend at (Fund Company X)' was used to create the 77 × 77 friendship matrix. Cell ij was coded 1 if any of the respondents from firm i indicated that he or she had a friend at fund company j.

Institutional tie proximity measures institutional ties between firms in the same geographic area. To do this we multiplied the variables institutional ties and geographic proximity. In the resulting 77 × 77 matrix, cell ij equals 1 when there is an institutional tie between i and j and firms i and j are in the same location; it is coded 0 either when there is no institutional tie between i and j, or if i and j are in different locations, or both.

Organizational tie proximity measures organizational ties between firms in the same geographic area and was generated the same way as institutional tie proximity. In the 77 × 77 matrix, cell ij equals 1 when there is an organizational tie between i and j and firms i and j are in the same location; it is coded 0 when either there is no organizational tie between i and j, or i and j are in different locations, or both.

Friendship proximity measures friendships between executives in the same geographic area. To do this we multiplied each of the cells in the matrices representing the variables friendship and geographic proximity. In the resulting 77 × 77 matrix, the value of cell ij is 1 when there is a friendship between executives at firms i and j and firms i and j are in the same geographic location; it is coded 0 either when there is no friendship between executives at firms i and j, or if i and j are in different geographic regions, or both.

Density of past collaboration ties among the members of each project network, obtained by applying a block density procedure to the entire network of past collaboration among the 4,793 specialists. Five square 4,793 x 4,793 matrices of past ties were computed, one for each five-year moving seven-year window, in which cell xij was the number of projects on which specialists i and j had worked together over the prior seven years. A 4,793 x 249 binary matrix recorded which specialists worked on which production, and the density of ties among a project's members was then calculated on the basis of their past relations.

Calculated in the same way as past internal network closure but using the network of current ties as the input to the block density procedure. The current-tie networks are square 4,793 x 4,793 matrices in which xij is the number of projects on which specialists i and j were currently working together.

Average across a project's members of individual members' constraint in the broader network of past ties, excluding ties among current project members. Constraint is the extent to which all of a specialist's relations are directly or indirectly invested in his or her relationship with a contact, summed across contacts. The constraint value was multiplied by -1 in order to capture structural holes, the opposite of constraint.

Computed using the same procedure as the past structural holes measure but with the network of current ties as the input for the constraint index procedure. Individual constraint scores were averaged to the level of the project network.

The size of the audience that watched each TV production, measured as the natural logarithm of the number of people that watched the production. Audience data are collected by Auditel, which monitors the Italian broadcasting market with a panel of 5,101 families and more than 14,000 individuals stratified by areas' residential populations. Because audience numbers are highly skewed, the natural logarithm of the number of viewers was used.
scale: natural logarithm of number of viewers

description: Founders were identified as the set of top managers reporting to the firm's chief executive (and including the chief executive) at the time of a firm's founding; for the 78 semiconductor firms there were a total of 431 founders at risk of departure. The dependent variable is the likelihood of a founder leaving a new venture, estimated as a hazard rate with continuous-time event history analysis on quarterly observations. Right-censoring of the data, owing for example to firm failure, was taken into account.
Measured quarterly in two ways: sales, using a logarithm, and number of employees.
Measured as the number of quarters since a company's incorporation.

variable_name: Firm growth (employee growth; sales growth; squared terms)
description: Measured as both employee growth and sales growth, each entered with a squared term in the models. Employee growth was the proportionate increase in employees in the two quarters preceding data collection. Sales growth compared a firm's revenue growth to revenue growth for other firms in the semiconductor industry competing in the same product categories over the prior two quarters: the authors identified 20 specific product-market segments, derived the proportion of sales in each category for each firm, weighted revenue growth by the specific product categories the firm competed in, and compared it to the average revenue growth rate in that category for other firms in the sample. Because all firms start with no sales, the measure of sales growth began four quarters after incorporation.
time_window: prior two quarters (sales growth beginning four quarters after incorporation)

description: Assessed as the proportion of total firm ownership held by the founders of a company.
Measured as the proportion of ownership held by the top four owners of a firm.
Measured as the proportion of board members who were employed by the firm.
Dummy variable coded 1 if the founder's primary responsibilities in the new venture were in research and development.
A founder's number of years of employment in the semiconductor industry prior to founding the new venture.
Dummy variable coded 1 for each founder who was the chief executive.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two scenario conditions: a typical long-short equity (LSE) fund, whose manager employed a combination of investments very common among the LSE fund class, or an atypical LSE fund, whose manager employed a unique combination of investments compared to most other LSE funds. The manipulation was assessed by asking participants how many other LSE hedge funds exist that have similar portfolios and use similar trading strategies as their fund. In the regressions, a dummy variable is equal to one for the atypical fund condition.
scale: binary (0 = typical fund condition, 1 = atypical fund condition)

description: Binary indicator set to one when a participant indicated that the LSE index was the most important reference group for making an evaluation, zero otherwise. Participants were shown the filled-in data table with index performance and instructed to 'Click on ONE area of the table that, in addition to the performance data associated with your investment, you referenced the MOST while analyzing the data and evaluating the performance of the fund in which you are invested.' Performance evaluation theory suggests participants should have chosen the long-short equity index, and this index was selected far more than any other.
scale: binary (1 = LSE index chosen as most important referent, 0 = another referent chosen)

description: Takes the value of one when a participant indicated that the fund's past, systematically worse performance was 'Very Important' to consider when making their performance evaluations, zero otherwise. On a final screen participants indicated on a four-point scale ranging from 'Very Important' to 'Not at all Important' how important the fund's prior performance was in making their evaluations. All participants were told that the returns they experienced were slightly better than the returns generated by the fund over the two quarters prior to their investment.

Participants indicated how committed they felt to their investment, assessed on a seven-point scale. In the models a dummy variable is equal to one when participants reported above average commitment prior to knowing the performance outcome of their investment. Commitment was not systematically related to fund typicality versus atypicality, and it proved uncorrelated with participants' gender, age, race, and financial acumen, as well as with assignment to the typical or atypical experimental condition.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = 'Not at all committed' to 7 = 'Very committed')

description: Fund performance is captured by way of four dummy variables where the omitted performance category is the middle one. At random, participants were assigned to one of five returns outcomes ranging from a high two-year net return of 27.23% to a low two-year net return of 4.67%. Index returns were identical across all participants but participants' individual investment returns varied.
scale: five randomly assigned two-year net return levels, entered as four dummy variables

description: Combined three-item measure (alpha equal to 0.87) of participants' performance evaluations. The three previously validated questions were: 'On a scale of 1-7, with 1 being the worst, how would you evaluate the performance of the hedge fund in which you are invested?'; 'Would you invest any additional money in the hedge fund?'; and 'Would you suggest that your friends and family members also invest in the hedge fund?' The latter two evaluation questions used a seven-point response scale ranging from 'Very Unlikely' to 'Very Likely.' The measure had a mean of 3.89 and standard deviation of 1.61 across all participants in all waves.

Return on sales (ROS) used as a measure of performance. Past performance was calculated for the five years preceding the deregulation; it was assumed that managers used the average performance of the industry as a reference point, so a firm's deviation from the industry median was computed in each of the five years and then averaged.

Stability of financial and operational ratios that express the strategic position of a company. For each strategic indicator the variance was calculated over the five years following the deregulation; the variance scores were standardized and multiplied by -1 so that positive scores indicate greater persistence; the standardized indicators were summed to yield an overall measure.

variable_name: change in performance after the environmental change
description: Performance in the five years after the deregulation was calculated with the same ROS measure used for past performance. A difference measure was then computed by subtracting performance before deregulation from performance afterward.

Return on sales (ROS) used as a measure of performance. Past performance was calculated for the five years preceding the deregulation; it was assumed that managers used the average performance of the industry as a reference point, so a firm's deviation from the industry median was computed in each of the five years and then averaged.

Stability of financial and operational ratios that express the strategic position of a company. For each strategic indicator the variance was calculated over the five years following the deregulation; the variance scores were standardized and multiplied by -1 so that positive scores indicate greater persistence; the standardized indicators were summed to yield an overall measure.

variable_name: change in performance after the environmental change
description: Performance in the five years after the deregulation was calculated with the same ROS measure used for past performance. A difference measure was then computed by subtracting performance before deregulation from performance afterward.

The experimental treatment consisted of three levels of task knowledge provided at the beginning of the simulation that led to different levels of success. The three conditions were coded 1, low success; 2, moderate success; and 3, high success.
scale: 1 = low success, 2 = moderate success, 3 = high success

description: Because the effective strategies were predetermined in the simulation and identical for all participants, persistence was measured by summing the standardized variance of advertising expenditure and sales force per million people served between years 8 and 13. A high score indicated high persistence with the old strategy, and a low score indicated low persistence.

variable_name: change in performance after the environmental change
description: The measure was change in operating profits between decision period 8 and decision period 13. In exploratory analyses the authors also used change in return on sales between the same two periods, and since the two measures produced the same pattern of results they used change in operating profit for the main analyses.
time_window: between decision period 8 and decision period 13

description: Measured by computing the means of responses (1 = not at all, 7 = totally) to two questions (alpha = .94): 'I am very satisfied about last year's market share' and 'I am very satisfied about last year's overall performance.'

Measured as the mean of two items expressing confidence (0-100; alpha = .78) that increasing the sales force and increasing advertising expenditures would have a positive impact on market share in the future.

The sum of the standardized responses to two items (alpha = .97): assessing confidence in achieving thirteen levels of market share or higher in the next year by rating yes for each level, and assessing confidence in achieving the same thirteen levels by giving a number between 0 and 100 for each level.
scale: yes/no answers (range of total number of yes answers, 0-13) and 0-100 ratings

description: Measured by the sum of responses to two items (alpha = .96): 'Indicate the level of market share that you are trying to attain next year' and 'What is the minimum acceptable level of market share for the next year?' These items were filled out at the end of year 9 because that was when the deregulation started to affect the rules of competition.
The total amount of information was obtained by summing the information requests made between years 9 and 13.
The amount of information sought between years 9 and 13 from executives who had been supportive in the past.
The amount of information sought between years 9 and 13 from executives who had been critical in the past.

An index of five measures: CEO tenure divided by average tenure of all directors on the board; the sum of the number of external board seats the CEO holds divided by the average number of outside board seats for each director; a count of outside board members whose current title is CEO at another for-profit firm; board dependence, measured as one minus board independence (independent directors divided by board size); and industry-adjusted return on assets, calculated as net income divided by total assets with median two-digit SIC ROA subtracted. Each of these measures was standardized and summed to produce a standardized index of CEO power.

An index of five indicators: director tenure, measured as the difference between the current year and the year the director was initially appointed to the board; the sum of a director's seats on outside boards; whether the director is a business expert, coded 1 if the individual's primary employment title was an executive title (e.g., CEO, COO, CFO, President, Vice-President) at another for-profit firm; whether the director received a degree from an elite educational institution; and whether the board designated the director a financial expert. Each variable was standardized and summed for each director-year observation to produce an index of director power.

A binary variable measured '1' if the CEO and board chair positions remained combined but an independent board member was appointed to the lead independent director position in a given year, and '0' otherwise. In the models for Hypothesis 1 this outcome is one of three mutually exclusive categories of board leadership change, alongside separation of the CEO and board chair positions and the base case of no change (CEO duality). Firms leave the risk set once they either separate the CEO and board chair positions or appoint a lead independent director, and a contemporaneous separation is given priority over a lead director appointment.

variable_name: Separation of CEO and board chair positions
description: Measured as '1' if another individual besides the CEO is appointed board chair in the current time period and '0' otherwise, determined by examining whether the CEO and board chair positions were occupied by the same individual in the current year or if an independent director had assumed the role of board chair as listed by the BoardEx database. For the models of the likelihood of future separation following a lead independent director appointment, the variable is measured as '1' if CEO–board chair separation occurred following the appointment of a lead independent director and '0' otherwise.

A binary variable measured '1' if the focal director is appointed to the lead independent director position and '0' otherwise. It captures the likelihood that an independent director currently serving on the board at time t-1 is appointed to the lead director position at time t, is measured at the level of the individual director, and is examined only for boards that appointed a lead independent director during the sampling time frame. Only the initial lead independent director appointment is examined.
time_window: director on the board at t-1, appointment at t

description: Calculated as the year-end share price minus initial share price plus the stock's dividend yield, all divided by initial share price, to capture the return on a firm's stock from the beginning to the end of a calendar year.
