time_window: moving three-year window ending in year t

description: Measured as the standard deviation of members' tenures in the firm, observed in t -1. The variable was centered in the multivariate analysis.
The number of members who left the TMT in year t. It is a low base-rate count variable and was modeled with a Poisson distribution.
Return on assets in year t, or the ratio of net income to total assets, adjusted for operating leases. ROA was normally distributed and was modeled with a Gaussian distribution.

Created by standardizing and averaging two indicators for each TMT each year: functional structure, whether the team was based entirely on functional posts (coded 1) or consisted of multiple general managers (coded 0), and functional titles, the proportion of executives with titles indicating they were primarily functional managers.

Created by standardizing and averaging two indicators for each TMT each year, and reversing it so that higher scores reflected greater interdependence: the number of distinct hierarchical levels, counted as the number of title gradations in the TMT each year, and presence of a COO, reflecting whether there was this additional level in the TMT.

Created by standardizing and averaging three indicators for each TMT each year: co-movement of bonuses, the extent to which members' bonuses move up and down in unison (reversed from the coefficient-of-variation formula); co-movement of noncash pay, captured similarly but using the value of stock options and restricted stock grants; and proportion of noncash pay, the ratio of the TMT's sum of noncash pay to total pay.

Measured as the average age of the funds held by VCs on the board. If a VC firm invested in the same venture from multiple funds, the youngest fund age was used; if a VC firm has two representatives on a venture board, its fund age is used twice. The average is therefore a weighted average incorporating the number of board seats that each VC firm holds.
Measured by the proportion of independent directors on the venture board. Independent directors are directors who are not venture managers/founders and do not represent investors.

Dependent variable for one of the four types of venture exit, coded as one if the event occurred; otherwise zero. Exit data were tracked until 2018 and in-process ventures were checked for active status.

Dependent variable for one of the four types of venture exit, coded as one if the event occurred; otherwise zero. M&As were categorized by deal value: an M&A joined the low-value category if its value was lower than either the total amount raised or the latest valuation, so high-value M&As are those not classified as low-value. For ventures with undisclosed acquisition values, exit outcomes were evaluated based on their valuation records, past fundraising performance, and the tone of the news reports.

Dependent variable for one of the four types of venture exit, coded as one if the event occurred; otherwise zero. An M&A was categorized as low-value when its value was lower than either the total amount raised or the latest valuation. For ventures with undisclosed acquisition values, exit outcomes were evaluated based on their valuation records, past fundraising performance, and the tone of the news reports.

Dependent variable for one of the four types of venture exit, coded as one if the event occurred; otherwise zero. Exit data were tracked until 2018, and in-process ventures were checked to confirm active status.

For establishment i, the count of establishments from the same parent firm j in the same MSA g in year t. It measures the intensity of internal agglomeration because it captures the physical scope of a firm's presence within a market, as measured by discrete operating units. The baseline specification uses the level of this count; the logarithm of firm-MSA establishments is used as an alternative explanatory variable.

Labor factor productivity for establishment i in year t, estimated as the residual from the period-by-period pooled cross-sectional regression of log revenue on log payroll across all establishments; this residual is then used as the dependent variable in the difference-in-differences regressions. The authors argue the high correlation between sales and payroll suggests this one-factor measure is a strong proxy for multifactor productivity.

For establishment i, the average productivity of all other establishments in the same MSA g in year t. It is included in the vector of controls in the baseline specification and is interacted with internal agglomeration in the reflection test.

A dummy variable equal to one if the establishment is in a firm with all of its hotels in the same MSA in a particular year, and zero otherwise. It is interacted with Firm-MSA establishments to compare the marginal effect of internal agglomeration in single-market firms with that in multi-market firms.

Positive treatment is a dummy variable equal to one when firm j increases the number of establishments in establishment i's MSA g in year t, and zero otherwise; negative treatment is a dummy equal to one when firm j decreases the number of establishments in that MSA. Positive treatment captures contemporaneous and persistent benefits, while negative treatment only picks up a reduction in the net contemporaneous effects, so comparing the two coefficients separates contemporaneous from persistent effects of internal agglomeration.

Same measure applied to the restaurant sample: the count of establishments owned by the same parent firm in the same MSA, used as the key explanatory variable in the restaurant replication with establishment fixed effects and year x MSA fixed effects.

The dependent variable in the restaurant replication, with the same tests applied as in the hotel sample: increases in the intensity of internal agglomeration by one unit are associated with a precisely estimated improvement in productivity.

Following Kim, et al. (1998), the authors measured liquidity as a firm's cash and equivalents (e.g., cash and marketable securities) in a specific year divided by the book value of total assets in that same year. It is the outcome variable of the liquidity analyses, and its one-year lagged value is used as the predictor in the R&D analyses.
time_window: same year as the outcome; one-year lag used in the R&D analyses

description: For each year, the authors calculated R&D intensity by dividing the firm's yearly R&D expenses by total assets in that same year. It is a predictor in the liquidity analyses and the outcome measure of R&D investments in the R&D analyses.
time_window: same year as the outcome in the liquidity analyses; outcome year in the R&D analyses

description: The authors count the number of times each of a firm's patents is cited in the years following the date of patent filing; the count of subsequent citations ends after 2002 because the NBER Patent Citations database contains data through 2002. Each patent's citation count is divided by the mean patent citation count for all patents produced by all U.S. publicly traded biotechnology firms the authors identified in that patent's year of filing and technological class. For each year the firm's standardized patent citation values are added together to represent the patent 'flow' created in that year, and the previous four years' flows are added to generate a 'stock' of patent value. Patents are assigned to a year using the patent application filing date rather than the grant date.
time_window: current year plus the previous four years (five-year stock)

description: Using Windover Information Inc.'s RX Deals database, the authors identified all alliances formed by firms in the sample during the sample period. For each year they counted all alliances formed in that year that focused on marketing, licensing, and commercialization of an existing technology.
time_window: single year (count formed in that year)

description: The authors also used Windover Information Inc.'s RX Deals database to calculate the exploration alliance variable, first identifying all alliances formed by firms in the sample during the sample period and retaining only alliances whose primary focus was the discovery of new technology. Alliances whose partners later engaged in exploitation activities were still considered exploration alliances since discovery would precede commercialization. They counted the number of exploration alliances formed in each year for each firm.
time_window: single year (count formed in that year)

description: The cumulative years of experience that the focal firm has operating fabs within a given host country. One year is added to the sum before logging to avoid the indeterminacy of logging zero experience. The variable is logged because the incremental value of an additional year of experience is greater for lower levels of experience than for higher levels of experience. The metric is based on the full history of surviving fabs.
time_window: cumulative history of surviving fabs through the sample year

description: The cumulative years of experience that the focal firm has operating fabs in other foreign countries (internationally) outside the home country. The sum is incremented by one year before logging and then logged, for the same reasons as the other experience measures. The metric is based on the full history of surviving fabs.
time_window: cumulative history of surviving fabs through the sample year

description: The cumulative years of experience that the focal firm has operating fabs in its home (origin) country. The sum is incremented by one year before logging and then logged. The metric is based on the full history of surviving fabs.
time_window: cumulative history of surviving fabs through the sample year

description: Technology generations in semiconductor manufacturing are defined by manufacturing process linewidth or process geometry, the minimum size of the smallest circuit feature that can be produced reliably. The technological sophistication of a facility in a given year is the leading-edge process linewidth divided by the facility's process linewidth, with numerator and denominator adjusted according to the most sophisticated product manufactured by the facility using the product listing provided by SMA. The technological sophistication of a firm in a given year is the average technological sophistication of the most recent five fabs the firm has established, which eliminates archaic or legacy fabs. The measure ranges from 0.02 (technologically lagging) to 1 (technologically leading).
time_window: given year; most recent five fabs

description: A time-varying index of the political hazards in a host country that measures the extent to which a change in the preferences of any one actor can lead to a change in government policy. It identifies the number of independent branches of government with veto power over policy change in a given year, assumes the preferences of each branch and the status quo are independently and identically drawn from a uniform unidimensional policy space, and derives a quantitative measure from a spatial model of political interaction. The measure is modified for alignment across branches using party composition data and for preference heterogeneity within aligned or opposed legislative branches. Possible scores range from 0 (minimal hazards) to 1 (extremely hazardous).

The technological environment of a given country in a given year is measured using the average technological sophistication of the last five fabs opened within the country by either foreign or domestic firms. The five-fab window eliminates archaic or so-called legacy fabs.
time_window: last five fabs opened in the country; country-year

variable_name: Foreign firms (different home country) host-country experience
description: The natural log of the number of years of host-country fab operating experience by other foreign semiconductor firms whose home countries are different from the focal firm's home country, calculated in each sample year.

variable_name: Foreign firms (same home country) host-country experience
description: The natural log of the number of years of host-country fab operating experience by other foreign semiconductor firms that come from the same country as the focal firm, calculated in each sample year.
The natural log of the number of years of host-country fab operating experience by domestic semiconductor firms in each sample year.

The dependent variable for the negative binomial and zero-inflated negative binomial specifications is a count of foreign investments by semiconductor firm x in country i at time t. A foreign investment is defined as the construction of a new fab. Greenfield construction in the semiconductor industry represents a significant capital expenditure commitment in both equipment and infrastructure development.

Retention at the room level is defined as a change in a room's experience ratio that moves a room to a position that is less than one standard deviation away from its parent-bank's organizational template (average experience ratio) in the previous year. The retention event counts are summed across each parent bank annually to define a bank's retention intensity in year t. A natural log transformation of a bank's retention intensity is used to account for differences in the distribution.

A trader's cumulative industry experience (the number of years a trader worked in the industry) from 1973 to 1993 is calculated by an algorithm that compares a trader's last name, first initial, and second initial across years; the experience counter is not reset when a trader moves. A room's experience ratio equals the total amount of trader experience in a room divided by the number of traders in a room. Each parent bank's average room-experience ratio is calculated annually based on the trading rooms operated by each parent bank.

An intrafirm personnel inflow event occurs when a trader moves between two rooms of the same parent bank over consecutive years. For each event the amount of industry experience that the trader brings into a recipient room is defined. The amount of trader experience that flows into a room annually is summed for each source, aggregated to the parent-bank level annually, and the natural log of the experience sum is taken.

An interfirm personnel inflow event occurs when a trader moves from a room of one parent bank into a room of a different parent bank over consecutive years. For each event the amount of industry experience that the trader brings into a recipient room is defined. The annual experience sums are aggregated to the parent-bank level and the natural log is taken.

A cross-border personnel inflow event is defined as a trader moving from one room into another room, and the rooms are located in different countries. For each event the amount of industry experience that the trader brings into a recipient room is defined. The annual experience sums are aggregated to the parent-bank level and the natural log is taken.

A local personnel inflow event is defined as a trader moving from one room into another room and the rooms are located in the same country. For each event the amount of industry experience that the trader brings into a recipient room is defined. The annual experience sums are aggregated to the parent-bank level and the natural log is taken.

A cross-border intrafirm personnel inflow event is defined as a trader moving between two trading rooms of the same parent bank over consecutive years, and the trading rooms are located in different countries. For each event the amount of experience that a trader brings to a room is defined. The annual sums are aggregated to the parent-bank level and the natural log is taken.

A local intrafirm personnel inflow event occurs when a trader moves between two trading rooms of the same parent bank over consecutive years, and the trading rooms are located in the same country. For each event the amount of experience that a trader brings to a room is defined. The annual sums are aggregated to the parent-bank level and the natural log is taken.

A cross-border interfirm personnel inflow event occurs when a trader moves between the trading rooms of different parent banks over consecutive years, and the trading rooms are located in different countries. For each event the amount of experience that a trader brings to a room is defined. The annual sums are aggregated to the parent-bank level and the natural log is taken.

A local interfirm personnel inflow event occurs when a trader moves between the trading rooms of different parent banks over consecutive years, and the trading rooms are located in the same country. For each event the amount of experience that a trader brings to a room is defined. The annual sums are aggregated to the parent-bank level and the natural log is taken.

The firm's ranking on the American Lawyer's annual ranking of the 200 largest U.S. law firms on their commitment to pro bono activities, based on firm-reported survey data, used as the authors' primary measure of a firm's commitment to CSR activities. Two-thirds of the ranking comes from a firm's average number of pro bono hours per lawyer, and the remaining third comes from the percentage of lawyers at the firm who have completed 20 or more hours of pro bono work. Firms whose pro bono rankings are higher numbers have 'better' pro bono programs.

Dichotomous variable that takes a value of 1 when an attorney is no longer affiliated with a law firm in the Martindale data at the beginning of the following year, meaning that s/he made a move at some point during the focal year. The attorney must remain absent for two years to ensure that data errors are not mischaracterized as exits. The sample is limited to attorneys under the age of 65 to avoid the influence of death on the results.

Dichotomous variable that takes a value of 1 when the attorney founds a new law firm in the following year. The attorney must appear in a newly created law firm within three years of his/her exit from the current organization, and must be a 'name partner,' meaning that his/her last name appears in the name of the law firm in the firm's first appearance in the data. A size cap of 25 attorneys is placed on these new firms, and 'new' firms whose workforce constitutes 50% or more of the workforce of a prior employer are eliminated.

variable_name: Leaves the firm for an established law firm
description: Dichotomous variable that takes a value of 1 when the attorney appears in a listing for a different law firm in the following year and the attorney is not a founder of this different firm. Together with occupation change and founding a startup law firm, it is collectively exhaustive of alternative employment destinations.

variable_name: Leaves the firm for any destination
description: Dichotomous outcome equal to one when an attorney leaves the firm for any destination; it is the union of the three mutually exclusive destinations of occupation change, founding a startup law firm, and joining an established law firm. The authors estimate in a logit model the correlation between a firm's pro bono ranking and the probability that an attorney leaves the firm for any destination.

The firm's yearly pro bono ranking. In the 9/11 analysis the authors split the sample into firms with pro bono rankings that are above the median ranking of 100 ('better' pro bono firms) and below the median ranking of 100 ('worse' pro bono firms).

Dichotomous indicator of a move out of the legal occupation, taking a value of 1 when the attorney is no longer affiliated with a law firm in the Martindale data at the beginning of the following year. In the 9/11 analysis the multinomial logit has two outcomes, joining a different law firm or occupation change, against the reference group of staying with the current firm.

Dichotomous outcome that combines mobility to established law firms and mobility to startup law firms into one category, because of the infrequency of startup mobility events in the 9/11 sample. The authors report that results are the same if foundings are instead included in the occupation change outcome.

Interaction of NYC metro birth with year indicators, used to capture the mortality-related shock of the September 11, 2001 terror attacks. NYC metro birth is coded 1 for attorneys whose self-reported place of birth matches a place located within CBSA #35620, 'New York – Newark – Jersey City,' or one of the five boroughs of New York City. The treatment group is all NYC metro-born attorneys working for AmLaw 200 firms in 1999 and the comparison group is their 1999 officemates who were born outside the NYC metro area.

Intensity of original search, measured as the number of first-ever combined subclass pairs contained in the patents cited by the focal patent. The authors used the entire corpus of patents to identify every incidence of the first-time introduction of any pair of subclasses and then counted, for each sampled patent, the number of these new subclass pairs in its cited patents. Because of the high skewness of this main independent variable, it was log-transformed along with other count-based control variables in the analysis. It is the main independent variable in the tests of Hypotheses 1a and 1b.

Continuous measure of search boundary constructed as the technological proximity between the focal patent and the patents it cites, using Jaffe's (1986) patent class-based proximity measure, in which the focal patent and all patents cited by it are represented as dimension vectors of USPTO patent classes. Because Class 977 can only be assigned as a secondary class, 977 was merged with the patent's primary class and treated as an element of the dimension vector. The formula itself is not legible in the available text. This measure is included in the tests of Hypotheses 1a and 1b.

Count, among all backward citations, of the number of first-ever recombined subclass pairs in the nanotechnology patent class (i.e., within Class 977), normalized by the number of backward citations to patents in that domain. It captures the intensity of search targeting original knowledge within the local domain and is one of the measures used to test Hypotheses 2a and 2b.

Count, among all backward citations, of the number of first-ever recombined subclass pairs in non-nanotechnology patent classes (i.e., outside Class 977), normalized by the number of backward citations to patents in that domain. It captures the intensity of search targeting original knowledge outside the local domain and is one of the measures used to test Hypotheses 2a and 2b.

Count, among all backward citations, of all recombined subclass pairs in the nanotechnology patent class except the first-ever recombined subclass pairs in that class, normalized by the number of backward citations to nanotechnology patents. It captures the intensity of local search targeting ordinary knowledge.

Count, among all backward citations, of all recombined subclass pairs in non-nanotechnology classes except the first-ever recombined subclass pairs in those classes, normalized by the number of backward citations to patents in that domain. It captures the intensity of boundary-spanning search targeting ordinary knowledge.

A second set of search-type measures constructed in three steps: for each search type, the search proximity between the focal patent and the cited patents containing the target knowledge was calculated; this search-type-level proximity was normalized by dividing it by the overall search proximity between the focal patent and all cited patents; and the corresponding search intensity was multiplied by this normalized proximity. These joint-effect measures were used, together with the intensity-based measures, in the tests of Hypotheses 2a and 2b.

Dummy variable indicating the incidence of the first combination of two subclasses that a nanotechnology patent established across the entire patent population by the grant year 2006. Subclasses represent fine-grained classifications of a technology, and the first recombination of a pair of subclasses is treated as a path-breaking novelty.

Dummy variable indicating that the patent belongs to the top 5% of the citation distribution. The authors first generated the citation distribution of the population of U.S. patents (about 3.9 million) granted during the period 1976-2010; to account for differences in the citation hazard due to timing and technology they used the residuals recovered from regressing the number of forward citations on patent class, application year and grant year; they then computed a z-score for each patent using these normalized forward citations and coded the top 5% as high-impact breakthroughs.

Dichotomous variable indicating the termination of a relationship between a lobbyist and client. A dissolution is defined as a market tie that existed in year t but not in any year between t + 1 and the end of the observation period (2009); a gap in years between lobbying activity was not coded as a dissolution because the Texas legislature meets biennially. Thus only the final occurrence of the lobbyist-client dyad was coded as dissolved and prior occurrences were coded as ongoing. All 2009 entries were right censored, and the final dataset contained 9,600 dissolutions.

Dichotomous variable indicating when a lobbyist left one firm and joined another. It equals 1 for the last year that a lobbyist worked for a particular firm before appearing in the dataset associated with another firm, as a sole practitioner, or with any other entity captured in the dataset. All 2009 entries were right censored and no departures were coded in that year; each firm, including self-employment, was coded with a unique identification number as the basis for comparison.

Duration of the relationship between each lobbyist-client dyad, used to measure the potential impact of the depth of the relationship between lobbyist and client. If a lobbyist-client dyad first appears in 2002, relationship tenure is coded 1 for that year, and if the next appearance is in 2004, it is coded 3 for that year.

Number of unique clients a lobbyist services in a given year. Double counting was eliminated because the Texas Ethics Commission source material contains only one record per year for each lobbyist-client relationship. The natural log of the client count was computed to accommodate an uneven distribution.

Accounts for the level of time and attention each client receives from its lobbyist in any year when compared with other clients. For each lobbyist a client relationship focus measure was created for each year by computing the percentage of each client's fees of the focal lobbyist's total fees for that year; a higher percentage in a year indicates that the client received a higher share of the lobbyist's time and attention.
scale: percentage of the lobbyist's total fees

description: Lobbyists were coded as working on a team when more than one lobbyist from the same firm was serving the same client in a focal year. Team composition did not matter, as teams may change members over the course of a firm's relationship with a client. This was judged the most direct measure of relationship sharing because lobbyists file activity reports and registration forms on an individual basis.

Measures whether an incubator assists sponsored organizations in building external relations by hosting networking events and conferences that provide access to suppliers, customers, and potential funding sources. Coded 1 if specific networking activities were reported, and 0 otherwise, based on coding of incubators' program descriptions and practices.

Measures the degree to which an incubator sponsors similarly focused organizations, capturing sponsorship specialization. The authors relied on 1 minus the Blau diversity index (similar to Herfindahl's index), calculated for each incubator by year using the three-digit NAICS industry classification for sponsored organizations; p is the proportion of incubated organizations in industry k. The formula was not readable in the text. The index ranges from a maximum of 1, for a high level of industry specialization or field-building efforts, to a minimum of 0, which indicates a low level of industry specialization among sponsored organizations.

Captures whether an incubator engaged in management service and training activities. When an incubator listed a schedule of management training workshops, courses, and certifications for its tenants, the variable was coded 1, and 0 otherwise, based on coding of incubators' program descriptions and practices.

A count of the number of organizations in the same three-digit NAICS code at the county level in the organization's founding year, using annual data from the County Business Patterns database. The authors argue this localized measure better approaches an identity-based view in which competition is recognized as increasing with geographic proximity. The variable is mean-centered in the interaction terms, consistent with Aiken and West (1991).
level: county-industry founding year matched to the entrant

description: The exit variable is equal to 1 if the last year of activity reported for an entrant occurred on or before 2007, the last year of observation in the data, and 0 otherwise; exits represent 7.7 percent of observations. Subsequent closing of a business because of a change of ownership is treated as exit in the year in which that business was last known to have operated in a particular establishment. Businesses that relocated by 'graduating' out of the incubator or ceased to exist were recorded.

The dependent variable in the hazard model is a hazard rate that denotes a likelihood of a firm to form an R&D consortium (or R&D consortia) at each time period. It takes 1 if firm i forms an R&D consortium (or R&D consortia) in year t, and 0 otherwise.

The number of establishments in the three-digit industry classification is used as a proxy for the degree of industry competition. It is constructed from industry-level data on the number of establishments.

The average of the scores to the questions 'how effective are patents to protect a firm's product innovations?' and 'how effective are patents to protect a firm's process innovations?' in percentage reported in Cohen et al. (1997), used as the appropriability conditions of industries. The measure is taken from the 1994 Carnegie Mellon survey and used for the whole period.
The difference between a firm's R&D intensity (R&D expenditure/sales) and the R&D intensity of the industry to which the firm belongs.

variable_name: Net number of firms met in past consortia
description: The net number of firms a firm has met in the past R&D consortia, one-period lagged. It is a proxy for the extent of the technological network a firm forms through its participation in R&D consortia.
The cumulative number of R&D consortia in which a firm has participated, one-period lagged. It is a proxy for the depth of a firm's experience in R&D consortia.

variable_name: Encounter with other firms in product markets
description: Calculated from Market Share in Japan (1990) of the Yano Research Institute, which tracks the market shares of the top Japanese firms in 591 distinct, disaggregated product markets. The data are used to count the number of firms a particular firm encounters in these product markets; the 'net' number of firms each firm meets in product markets is a proxy for the extent of a firm's network in product markets, or the degree of diversification. The data in 1990 are used for the entire analysis.
The number of years passed after the establishment of the firm.

Index of a firm's ideology built from the political donations of its employees. Gifts of $200 or more to the two parties, their candidates, campaign committees, and associated PACs were identified from Federal Election Commission records by searching for donors who named the sampled firm as employer; donations by the CEO and other corporate officers were excluded. Four indicators were computed for each two-year election cycle: (1) total dollars given to the Democratic Party divided by the total given to both parties; (2) number of donations to the Democratic Party divided by the number given to both parties; (3) number of unique employee donors to the Democratic Party divided by the number of employee donors to both parties; and (4) number of unique Democratic donation recipients divided by the number of all unique recipients. The four indicators showed high convergence (Cronbach alpha = 0.96) and were averaged into a liberalism score for each election cycle; for the regression analyses the measure was averaged over the two most recent election cycles.
scale: continuously scaled, roughly 0 to 0.85; higher values indicate greater liberalism
level: firm-election cycle, aggregated to firm-year for analysis
time_window: 1998-2012, two-year election cycles; averaged over the two most recent election cycles for the regressions

description: A firm's CSR profile computed from KLD data as the sum of all strengths minus all concerns across five KLD categories: product quality, employee relations, community relations, environment, and human rights. Under these categories companies are rated annually on 32 strengths and 31 concerns indicated in binary terms. The KLD diversity category was excluded because two of its items overlap with the other dependent variables.
scale: sum of strengths minus concerns (net count)

variable_name: Representation of women in top management
description: The count of company officers (vice presidents and higher) who were female. Lists of officers were obtained from Compact Disclosure and Standard and Poor's Register of Corporations, Directors, and Executives, which reproduce the information companies provide in their annual reports and filings with the SEC.

Whether and when each company adopted domestic partner benefits. The authors first used data from Briscoe and Safford (2008) for firms overlapping with their sample, originally provided by the Human Rights Campaign, which kept records on benefit adoptions among Fortune 500 firms, and then expanded the dataset to all additional firms and years using company press releases and media coverage. The dependent variable is 1 in the year of adoption and 0 otherwise.
scale: binary (1 in the year of adoption, 0 otherwise)

description: The average CSR score of two-digit SIC peer firms, used as the industry-pressure moderator for the omnibus CSR analysis and measured in t-1.

variable_name: Percent of female executives in industry
description: The average proportion of female executives among two-digit SIC peer firms, used as the industry-pressure moderator for the female executive representation analysis and measured in t-1.

variable_name: Prior adoption of benefits in industry
description: The number of peer firms that had adopted domestic partner benefits thus far, used as the industry-pressure moderator for the domestic partner benefit adoption analysis and measured in t-1.

Assumed to be predominantly a function of the industry task environment and proxied using data on average worker pay at the two-digit-SIC industry level, computed for the universe of Compustat firms by dividing 'staff and related expenses' by 'number of employees' following Connelly et al. (2016). Measured in t-1.
The number of years a given CEO had worked in the firm, measured in t-1 alongside the other moderators and controls.

The natural log of sales from the supplier to Buyco in the prior four quarters plus a constant, built from monthly transaction values in Buyco's central accounting database and aggregated from part-level data to a cumulative measure of each supplier's quarterly dollar sales to Buyco. The authors use this as their measure of repeated exchange between Buyco and supplier j at the time of competitive bid event m; the dollar value of sales between Buyco and j at the time of the CBE is also used as h_j in constructing the concentration measures.

variable_name: logsales rivals ijm (and, alternatively, fraction of experienced j rivals for item i)
description: Two measures of competing bidders' exchange histories constructed from the same transaction data: the log of the mean sales of rivals bidding for item i, and the fraction of rivals for item i who sold to Buyco in the prior year. These are the variables interacted with logsales_jm in the bid regressions.

The natural logarithm of the final bid offer by bidder j for item i, drawn directly from the auctioneer's records. The bid value is the product of the unit price offered by the bidder and the number of units that Buyco anticipates purchasing.
time_window: at the time of the CBE

description: Calculated as the percent difference between bidder j's bid and the lowest bid for item i (elsewhere described as j's bid for item i divided by the lowest bid for item i). It is used as the dependent variable in the repeat-bidder regression that tests H2.
time_window: at the time of the CBE

description: The ratio of the number of contracts won by bidder j in its kth CBE in the sample to the total number of items bid upon by j in that kth CBE. It is constructed only for bidders who appear in three or more CBEs, and the first observation for each bidder is dropped because it provides the lagged independent variable.

A dependent variable for each bidder-bundle pair that takes on the value 1 if bidder j is awarded the contract for item i and 0 if j places a bid for item i but does not win. It is modeled with a discrete choice conditional logit in which the utility Buyco obtains for selecting bidder j depends on the bid price, the bidder's exchange history and other bidder and bid-strategy controls.
time_window: at the time of the CBE

description: The normalized difference between the two highest levels of exchange history among bidders for item i, (h1 - h2)/(h1 + h2), where h1 and h2 are the highest and second-highest exchange histories. The measure is 0 when the top two bidders have identical exchange histories and 1 when only bidder 1 possesses an exchange history; it is computed at the time of the CBE and prospectively at a time one year after the exchange.
time_window: at the CBE and one year after the exchange

description: An entropy measure following Jacquemin and Berry (1979) that captures the distribution of relational capital among all bidders for item i, where s_ij is the share of relational capital possessed by bidder j. It equals 0 when all relational capital is concentrated in the hands of a single supplier and increases both in the number of suppliers with exchange histories and in the relative similarity in exchange histories among suppliers with nonzero exchange histories; it is computed at the time of the CBE and prospectively one year after the exchange.
time_window: at the CBE and one year after the exchange

variable_name: weight placed on logsales_jm (β2) estimated by quarter
description: Coefficients on logsales_jm from a conditional logit model of the probability that supplier j is awarded the contract for item i, estimated separately for each of six distinct quarters of the sample period. Buyco places a large weight on logsales_jm during three of the six quarters and a small weight, not significantly different from zero, in the other three; tests of joint equality of the quarterly coefficients are rejected.
time_window: six quarters of the sample period

description: Blau's index of heterogeneity calculated as 1 - ∑ pi², where p is the proportion of employees in each of six racial categories (white, Hispanic, African American, Asian American, Native American, and other races). The racial composition data were taken from the culture audit survey completed by a management representative. The theoretical range with six categories is 0 (no diversity) to 0.83 (theoretical maximum).

A dummy variable that indicated whether at least 50% of existing employees received stock options in the culture audit survey; 1 = stock options to 50% of existing employees or more, 0 = not. The majority-coverage criterion is presented as a reasonable standard for determining inclusive adoption of stock options.

Operating profit divided by total assets at t + 1; operating profit and total assets data came from the Compustat data set. Operating profit (profit from normal business operations) is used rather than net profit because net profit reflects extraneous factors outside the influence of the workforce.

The number of full-time employees who voluntarily left the company divided by the number of total full-time employees each year as reported by a management representative in the culture audit survey. The turnover rate was transformed by taking the natural log because it was highly skewed.

Employee responses to two items that assessed levels of affective commitment to the firm, with Likert-scale response options ranging from 0 to 5. The two items directly capture core elements of affective commitment such as pride in organizational membership and desire to maintain membership and involvement in the company.

R&D expenditures divided by sales, used as a proxy for search intensity. The authors restricted the sample to firms with R&D intensity less than or equal to 1 because about 8 percent of the sample firms spent more on R&D than their total sales; the resulting sample has median R&D intensity at 0.048, mean at 0.096, and a standard deviation of 0.146.
scale: ratio, restricted to values less than or equal to 1

description: The gap between the firm's past performance and its aspiration level, entered separately for underperforming firms (I1 = 1) and for outperforming firms (1 - I1), where I1 equals 1 if the firm's past performance falls below aspirations. Performance is return on assets lagged one year relative to the dependent variable. Two aspiration proxies are used in separate models: firm aspiration is the focal firm's performance one year prior to past performance (t-2), and industry aspiration is the median performance of firms in the same 4-digit SIC industry one year prior to past performance (t-2).
time_window: t-1 for performance; t-2 for aspirations

description: Altman's (1983) Z, defined in the text as a weighted combination of the following ratios: working capital divided by total assets, retained earnings divided by total assets, income before interest expense and taxes divided by total assets, market value of equity divided by total liability, and sales divided by total assets. A lower Z value means a higher likelihood of bankruptcy. The variable is lagged relative to the dependent variable.

Following Bourgeois (1981) and Singh (1986), the authors selected the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities) and the working capital to sales ratio as proxies for available slack. They standardized and summed these variables to form a composite slack index, lagged relative to the dependent variable. The correlation between the two ratios was 0.40.

All models included indicator variables for firms (and all but one years); the firm and period effects were entered as a baseline whose coefficients are not reported. The authors interpret the significant firm fixed effects as idiosyncratic search determinants for individual firms that persist over time, i.e., institutionalized search, and find that most of the explained variance in R&D intensity is due to firm effects.

Average R&D search intensity of firms in the same 4-digit SIC industry, computed by deleting the observation firm's data so that there are no own-firm effects on the industry average. It is measured contemporaneously with the dependent variable.

First-day closing price minus the offer price, divided by the offer price. Offer prices were obtained from the final prospectuses and first-day closing prices from the CRSP data tapes. A positive return represents underpricing by an IPO's underwriter and indicates value that was not appropriated by the new venture.

The number of firm officers serving as board members divided by the total number of board members. The authors note that a high value indicates a board can face an underwriter with a strong, unified voice.
The total equity owned by insiders divided by the total equity of a new venture as reported in the prospectus.

A count measure of the number of other boards on which insiders sit, based on information directors are required to report in an IPO's prospectus. The authors describe it as a measure of the experience and information levels of inside directors.
Operationalized as the average tenure of all insider directors. Together with insider age, the authors describe it as a proxy for the amount of risk insiders perceive themselves as bearing.
The average age of all insiders on a board. Together with insider tenure, the authors describe it as a proxy for the amount of risk insiders perceive themselves as bearing.
The percentage of all pre-IPO ownership by venture capital firms.

The existence of a prior link between the primary venture capitalist for an IPO firm and the IPO underwriter. The primary venture capitalist was defined as the largest owner among all venture capital firms investing in a given IPO that had investments in prior IPOs, and a tie was defined as any investment by the primary venture capital firm in any IPO underwritten by one of the tombstone underwriters in the previous three years. Coded 1 for a tie and 0 otherwise.

Following Grullon et al. (2012) and Lee et al. (2018), the measure is computed in two stages. In the first stage, a firm's volatility on a weekly basis is the standard deviation of daily stock returns for that year, month and week, and the change in volatility is the difference between the current and the previous week. In the second stage, the firm's weekly excess return is regressed on the change in volatility and the control variables; a total of 11,570 separate regressions were run and the estimated coefficient on the change in volatility (beta) is the firm-year real options intensity used as the dependent variable. A firm whose stock value increases more per a given firm-level volatility is defined as having greater real options intensity.

Calculated as in Campbell et al. (2011). CEO confidence is the value per exercisable option divided by the average strike price, where the value per exercisable option is the total value of the exercisable but unexercised options scaled by the number of those options, and the average strike price is the average stock price at the time the option value is determined minus the value per exercisable option. Using a cutoff ratio of 100%, the variable is an indicator that equals 1 from the first year in which the CEO's level of confidence is greater than 100% in two or more years, and 0 otherwise. CEOs who hold options too long before exercising them are considered overconfident.

The degree of variation in the focal firm industry's performance, measured by gross sales. In each quarter, the average of firm gross sales within the industry, defined by the SIC two-digit number, was calculated as industry-level performance; the standard deviation of industry-level performance over the past 20 quarters was then divided by the mean value of industry-level performance over the same period. An industry with a high ratio is viewed as having a high degree of market uncertainty.

Coded as 1 if a business group was ranked 5th, 11th, or 31st (top of tiers 2, 3, and 4, respectively) in the KFTC business group rankings, and 0 otherwise. The authors chose one business group at the top of each tier because these business groups are most likely to perceive the opportunity of moving up to the next higher tier by a single spot change in the ranking.

Coded as 1 if a business group was ranked 4th, 10th, or 30th (bottom of tiers 1, 2, and 3, respectively) in the KFTC business group rankings, and 0 otherwise. The authors chose one business group at the bottom of each tier because these business groups are most likely to perceive the threat of falling into the lower tier by a single spot change in the ranking.

The number of firms the business group acquired during the observation period. It is the dependent variable for Hypotheses 1a, 2a, and 3a and is estimated with fixed-effects negative binomial models because the number of acquisitions was over-dispersed.

Calculated as the logarithm of the total monetary amount (in Korean Won) a business group spent on acquisitions during the observation period. It is estimated with unconditional fixed-effects Tobit models censored at zero.

Coded using industry input-output tables from the Bank of Korea, based on the idea that two industries are less related when there are fewer inter-industry transactions as suppliers and buyers. The authors calculated the ratio of the monetary value of industry i's output used by industry j over the total output of i and the ratio of industry j's output used by industry i for each year, took their average, and used its negative value plus one as the measure so that a higher value indicates a higher level of vertical unrelatedness in acquisitions.

Based on the idea that two industries are less related when there are fewer business groups having the two industries in their business portfolios. The authors created an industry-by-industry matrix for each year in which each element is the number of business groups having both industries i and j in their portfolios, divided each element by the sum of the row (the number of business groups having industry i in their portfolio in a year), and used the negative value plus one so that a higher value indicates a higher level of portfolio-based unrelatedness in acquisitions.

The relative growth in total assets between the focal business group i and the business group j in the next rank, based on their total assets in year t and year t-1; the formula as printed in the paper is not readable in the text provided. A positive value indicates that the business group at the top of the lower tier is growing faster than the business group at the bottom of the higher tier, whereas a negative value indicates the opposite.

Dichotomous indicator variable for the use of cooperative arrangements in the marketing function, coded as '1' for use of a cooperative arrangement. Identification of key phrases in the IPO documents served as the basis for this codification; for example, an agreement with a supplier for the distribution of a product was indicative of a firm engaged in marketing cooperative arrangements.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Dichotomous indicator variable for the use of cooperative arrangements in the R&D function, coded as '1' for use of a cooperative arrangement. Identification of key phrases in the IPO documents served as the basis for this codification.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: Dichotomous indicator variable for the use of cooperative arrangements in the manufacturing function, coded as '1' for use of a cooperative arrangement. Identification of key phrases in the IPO documents served as the basis for this codification.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The adjusted summation of total years of marketing experience possessed by members of the management team. The adjustment technique involved adding the years of experience to the mean of the subsample; each year beyond one standard deviation from the mean was proportionally adjusted so that the years falling one standard deviation from the mean equalled zero, and all subsequent years were also assigned a value of zero. The adjustment was intended to reduce the bias of managers possessing considerably more years of experience.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: An 'average' measure of marketing experience, calculated by dividing the team's total years of marketing experience by the number of management team members. This second measure was intended to correct for the number of members in each management team.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The adjusted summation of total years of technical (R&D) experience possessed by members of the management team. The adjustment technique involved adding the years of experience to the mean of the subsample; each year beyond one standard deviation from the mean was proportionally adjusted so that the years falling one standard deviation from the mean equalled zero, and all subsequent years were also assigned a value of zero.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: An 'average' measure of technical (R&D) experience, calculated by dividing the team's total years of technical experience by the number of management team members, in order to correct for the number of members in each management team.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The adjusted summation of total years of production (manufacturing) experience possessed by members of the management team. The adjustment technique involved adding the years of experience to the mean of the subsample; each year beyond one standard deviation from the mean was proportionally adjusted so that the years falling one standard deviation from the mean equalled zero, and all subsequent years were also assigned a value of zero.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: An 'average' measure of production experience, calculated by dividing the team's total years of production experience by the number of management team members, in order to correct for the number of members in each management team.
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: A firm's choice of competitive strategy was coded after a thorough review of the IPO statement, with special attention given to the information contained in the IPO document's 'Market' and 'Strategy' sections. Key phrases in the IPO documents were used to identify a firm's choice of competitive strategy, and firms were classified as emphasizing marketing differentiation, technical differentiation, or cost leadership. A second coder independently classified a subsample of 52 new ventures; the two researchers agreed on the strategic emphasis classifications in nearly 90 percent of the cases and the interrater agreement produced a Cohen's kappa = 0.83, with disagreements resolved by reexamining the IPO documents.
scale: categorical (marketing differentiation, technical differentiation, cost leadership)
time_window: at the time of the IPO

description: The 3-year compounded annual rate of sales growth for each firm. Annual sales included all annual income generated for the provision of goods and services, not including liquidation of assets and other extraordinary items. The measure used the annual sales of the firm at the time of the IPO and the annual sales 3 years prior to the IPO; the formula as printed is garbled in the text and was not reconstructed. A natural logarithmic transformation of the dependent variable was applied.
time_window: 3 years prior to the IPO to the time of the IPO

description: It captures a firm's liquid assets and is measured as a firm's cash and short-term securities in year t-1. Unscaled variables are used, as they reduce the possibility of spurious associations due to correlation between denominators of both right- and left-side variables. The variable is winsorized at the one percent level and standardized with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1.

Since a CEO's temporal orientation when making investment choices cannot be measured directly, asset durability is used as a proxy. Asset durability is measured as the annual investment in property, plant, and equipment (PP&E) divided by depreciation expense; the paper calculates useful life, or asset durability, by dividing gross PP&E by total depreciation expense for firms using straight-line depreciation. The average life of the assets is referred to as asset durability. The variable is winsorized at the one percent level and standardized with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1.

Calculated using a variable from Execucomp: the product of number of options from each option grant and their corresponding spread (the market price minus the exercise price, the latter being the price at which the CEO can purchase the stock) for options that have a market price above the exercise price (are in-the-money) on the final day of the fiscal year. The resulting values are reported annually in the firm's proxy statement. The variable is winsorized at the one percent level and standardized with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1.

An estimate of future increases in the CEO's current wealth due to successful (yet risky) strategic investments that uses the average Dow increase during the period of the study, 7.0 percent. The present-day stock price is deducted so that only the additional wealth from future stock price increases is included, and the calculation is multiplied by the number of options held to capture total gains from stock price increases. The paper's formula block for this calculation is unreadable in the text, so the exact specification cannot be recorded from the paper. The number of options held is calculated as the sum of unexercisable and exercisable stock options in Execucomp, and average time to expiry is estimated using the Core and Guay (2002) estimation.

The interaction of CEO current wealth with available slack, entered in the interactions model predicting temporal orientation. The main effects of current wealth and slack are also entered, and the interaction is standardized like the other non-binary variables.

The interaction of CEO prospective wealth with available slack, entered in the interactions model predicting temporal orientation. The main effects of prospective wealth and slack are also entered, and the interaction is standardized like the other non-binary variables.

Indicator variable set to 1 if the respondent's current position requires at least a college degree, and 0 otherwise. The authors use college degree requirements as their primary measure of high skill because they want results to reflect firm occupational job requirements rather than misallocated high-skill individuals. Approximately 51% of respondents indicate that their job requires at least a college degree.

Indicator variable set to 1 if the respondent indicates that they are a frequent (weekly or daily) user of the online job platform LinkedIn, and 0 otherwise. The authors use it as a proxy for the visibility of the worker, and therefore for the firm's cost of finding and reaching that candidate. Approximately 42% of respondents stated that they use LinkedIn frequently.

Indicates whether the respondent was hired by their present employer through outbound recruiting, that is, whether they were 'hunted.' It is coded 1 if the respondent indicated that a recruiter from the employer reached out and invited them to apply, or that a headhunting firm reached out and invited them to apply, and 0 if the respondent applied directly for the role, hired a headhunter, or was referred by an existing employee. Approximately 14.3% of respondents were hired through this mode.

Indicator marking whether the firm ever posted for a recruiter in the data, based on either the job title or the job's skill requirements. A posting is classified as recruiting-focused if the raw text of the job title includes the words 'recruit,' 'talent,' or 'candidate sourcing,' or if any of the job's skill requirements include those words. The sample is restricted to firms that posted for at least one HR role.

variable_name: Average number of skills listed in a firm's job posts
description: The authors average the number of skills listed in all non-HR job postings by the firm, using it to measure whether a firm demands higher- or lower-skilled workers. The larger the number of skills listed, the higher the skill requirement of the job.

variable_name: Share of MSA-Industry workers who frequently use LinkedIn
description: Share of Qualtrics survey respondents in a given MSA-Industry who use LinkedIn at least once a week. The measure is constructed by aggregating the worker survey to MSA-Industry cells (dropping cells with one or fewer survey responses) and then merging the aggregated market-level statistics onto each firm using the firm's MSA and industry codes.
time_window: Survey responses from March 2022 merged with firms' 2010-2020 postings

variable_name: Share of MSA-Industry workers who have a college degree
description: Share of Qualtrics survey respondents in a given MSA-Industry cell who have a college degree, calculated from the aggregated worker survey and merged onto firms in the same MSA-Industry cell. The authors interpret a lower share as indicating that higher-skilled workers are fewer in number and so harder to find.
time_window: Survey responses from March 2022 merged with firms' 2010-2020 postings

description: The degree assortativity of a firm's intra-firm network, constructed only from patent coauthorship ties between inventors employed in each firm, excluding collaborations that occurred outside the firm boundaries. Following Newman (2003), the extent to which similar nodes are connected with each other is captured by r, estimated using the Pearson correlation coefficient; the value of r is 0 when mixing is random, 1 in case of perfect assortativity and -1 when the network is perfectly disassortative. The value of r ranges between -1 and 1, with negative values representing disassortative structures and positive values indicating assortative structures.
The total number of patents a firm produced in a year. Because of the count nature of this variable, a fixed-effects Poisson estimator is used.

Built from the USPTO-assigned technological subclasses that a patent combines. The familiarity of a subclass is estimated following Fleming (2001), capturing (a) the extent to which the subclass was combined with other subclasses in prior patents and (b) the recency of these patents, using a time constant of a knowledge base of 5 years to reflect 18% knowledge decay per year. The measure of familiarity of each subclass is subtracted from one to measure novelty; the novelty of a patent increases with the novelty of the subclasses on the patent. The dependent variable is the average of the novelty values of all patents granted to a firm in the focal year. The variable takes values between 0 and 1 and is modeled with a fractional logit method.

Measured as the average number of forward citations to a firm's patents. At the firm-year level, the number of forward citations received by a firm's patents granted in a given year, normalized using the total number of patents granted in that year. It is a continuous variable modeled with OLS.

A count of the number of unit boundary changes (expansion or contraction from moved resources and activities) that occur in a firm within a time period. Combining two units counts as two recombination events because both units' boundaries were altered, and moving product market activities from one unit to another also counts as two events. Unit acquisitions and divestitures during the period are not recombination events, though an acquired unit that is later folded into another unit is counted in that later period. The variable is observed for five periods: 1978-1983, 1983-1986, 1986-1989, 1989-1993 and 1993-1997.

Industry growth is measured with Dess and Beard's (1984) munificence operationalization: each industry variable is regressed against time (the past five years) to obtain a slope, and munificence is the time coefficient estimate (b1) divided by the variable's mean value. The equation itself is not readable in this text; the prose gives only the slope-over-mean formula. The authors use industry sales alone rather than the four-variable Census sum, collecting sales data from Compustat to match their study periods. Munificence is calculated for each of the 28 four-digit NAICS market segments and then averaged for each firm-period across all markets in which the firm is active, with a market's value counted once for each of the firm's product markets that falls in it.

Dynamism (i.e., turbulence) is the standard error of the time coefficient (b1) from the regression of the industry variable on time, divided by the variable's mean value. Values are computed for each of the 28 four-digit NAICS market segments and then averaged for each firm-period using the same product-market weighting as munificence. The underlying industry data are industry sales collected from Compustat.

Amount dynamism reduction (p) = dynamism(p-1) - dynamism(p): the difference between dynamism in an earlier period and dynamism in a later period. A positive value means that dynamism is declining (it was higher before and is less now); a negative value means that dynamism is not declining but actually increasing.
time_window: change from period p-1 to period p

description: Management is examined as corporate executives at headquarters (HQ), and the number of executives at HQ represents corporate team size. Actual HQ turnover at period p is the count of the number of executives who were added to and removed from the TMT from period p-1 to p. The authors follow Romanelli and Tushman (1994), who operationalized changes in power distribution within organization design as executive turnover.

variable_name: amount increase in corporate team size
description: The change in the total number of corporate executives in headquarters from period p-1 to p. A positive value indicates an increase in the team size by that amount, and a negative value indicates a decrease in the team size by that amount.

Blau's index of heterogeneity computed for the categorical variable nationality within each team. The index can vary from zero (indicating all team members are the same) to a high of one (indicating all team members are different).

Blau's index of heterogeneity computed for the categorical variable functional background within each team. The index can vary from zero (indicating all team members are the same) to a high of one (indicating all team members are different).

Calculated for each team as the coefficient of variation (i.e., standard deviation divided by the mean) of team members' ages. The coefficient of variation is described as a scale-invariant measure judged superior in its psychometric properties to other measures such as the standard deviation.

Team-level coefficient of variation of members' responses to a single seven-point questionnaire item asking approximately how specialized the members of the MARKSTRAT organization were. The scale was anchored with the phrases 'No person has a specialized role to play' and 'Each person has a specialized role to play'.
time_window: Administered early (end of second decision period) and late (end of second from last decision period) in the game

description: Team-level coefficient of variation of members' responses to a single seven-point questionnaire item asking managers to estimate how easy it would be to challenge the decision-making power of the dominant members. The scale was anchored with the phrases 'Very easy to challenge decision-making power of dominant members' and 'Very hard to challenge decision-making power of dominant members'.
time_window: Administered early (end of second decision period) and late (end of second from last decision period) in the game

description: Team-level coefficient of variation of members' responses to a single seven-point questionnaire item: 'How much agreement was there in your MARKSTRAT organization about the causes of your market share results during the last decision period?' The scale was anchored with the phrases 'Everybody stuck to a different explanation' and 'All members agreed'. The greater the variation in members' responses to this question, the more interpretative ambiguity the team was assumed to exhibit with respect to attributions about past performance.
time_window: Administered early (end of second decision period) and late (end of second from last decision period) in the game

description: Team-level coefficient of variation of members' responses to a single seven-point questionnaire item: 'Think about how difficult or easy it is for your MARKSTRAT organization to make decisions.' The scale was anchored with the phrases 'Very difficult to make decisions' and 'Very easy to make decisions'.
time_window: Administered early (end of second decision period) and late (end of second from last decision period) in the game

description: Team-level coefficient of variation of members' responses to a single seven-point questionnaire item asking about participation in the organization's decisions in the last session and whether the participant felt they should agree with the decisions reached by the MARKSTRAT organization. The scale was anchored with the phrases 'No—I felt that I could disagree' and 'Yes—I felt that I should agree'.
time_window: Administered early (end of second decision period) and late (end of second from last decision period) in the game

description: Team-level coefficient of variation of members' responses to a single seven-point questionnaire item asking each manager whether there were some obvious ways in which the MARKSTRAT organization could be run more effectively. The end points of the scale were anchored with the phrases 'Yes there are many ways to increase effectiveness' and 'No there are few ways to increase effectiveness'.
time_window: Administered early (end of second decision period) and late (end of second from last decision period) in the game

description: Net marketing contribution at the start of the second period divided by the net marketing contribution at the start of the game. The measure was greater than one for firms that improved their performance during the first period, and less than one for firms that suffered performance decreases as a result of decisions made during the first period. It was used to assess how well firms were doing early in the simulation.

The market share result at the end of the simulation. Market share was expressed as a percentage of the total market captured by the focal firm in competition with the other four firms in its industry.

The profitability result at the end of the simulation. The net marketing contribution was the basic measure of profitability and was defined as total revenues from sales minus expenses (cost of goods sold, research and development, inventory holding costs, etc.).

Percent change in market share for each firm from early in the game (end of second period) until the end of the game. This measure was used to capture performance increase and decrease over the course of the game.
time_window: From early in the game (end of second period) until the end of the game

variable_name: Team-level coefficient of variation on six questionnaire items
description: Cognitive diversity is measured with six single-item seven-point questionnaire measures (specialization, power, ambiguity, decision difficulty, decision pressure, effectiveness), each converted to a team-level coefficient of variation across team members' responses. The items follow questions used by Zucker (1977) to measure cognitive variability.
scale: Coefficient of variation of seven-point items

description: Quantifies the level of company access specified in the contract as the sum of the number of the six sponsor-access content terms found across the sample contracts. The value of ACCESS ranged from 0 to 5, with a mean of 1.43.

Codes reporting requirements detailed in the contract, calculated as the sum of the reporting terms present. Contracts varied by whether it was explicitly stated that the PI needed to maintain records documenting project activities, that a final report was required, or that interim progress reports were called for in a specific number with dates for report delivery, and whether content elements to be included in the reports were outlined. REPORT ranged from 0 to 5, with a mean of 2.17.

Measures the attention paid in the contract to the specification and allocation of IP rights for inventions resulting from the sponsored research, constructed by summing the scores from four categories. The scores for the option expansiveness, licensing framework and unobstructed rights categories simply count the presence of each element, whereas the score for the exercise/negotiation period category is determined by the total exercise/negotiation period granted, with one point given per three-month interval. ALLOCATE ranges from 0 to 11, with an average of 5.57.

A measure of the publication constraints included in the agreement, which vary in four respects. Specified review/delay periods are coded as 1 for periods up to 90 days, 2 for periods between 91 and 120 days, 3 for periods between 121 and 150 days, and 4 for periods greater than 150 days; the score is increased by one for each of the remaining three variations. The value of the PUBLICATION variable ranged from 1 to 7 with an average of 1.68.

A count of the number of sponsored research agreements that the individual principal investigator has conducted with the same company prior to the current contract. The number of previous contracts between an individual PI and a specific company ranges from 0 to 4.

Measures the contracting experience between parties in the university-company dyad via the log of the number of previous sponsored research interactions between these two parties. To capture past interorganizational relationships rather than concurrent activities, only agreements signed more than 12 months prior to the focal agreement are counted; the variable is calculated using the full population of contracts signed by the university between 1994 and 2005.
time_window: agreements signed more than 12 months prior to the focal agreement

description: A single-item proxy, scaled from 1 to 7, capturing the need to develop new technology to complete the project. The extremes are projects that score a 1 that 'require no innovation to complete' versus projects that score a 7 that 'cannot be completed without a technological breakthrough'; the authors note that no project was coded 7 and the actual range is from 1 to 6. The coders, experienced Compustar engineers, judged the radicalness of task innovation straightforward to determine and uniformly coded.

A count variable ranging from 0 to 3 identifying the extent of exchange hazards affecting a particular transaction, formed from three types of contractual hazards in the IT services industry: measurement cost, proprietary technology, and interdependency. Measurement cost is a dummy coded 1 if a quick inspection/test could not verify the quality of the deliverable after project completion; proprietary is coded 1 if the project required any of Compustar's proprietary technologies; interdependency is coded 1 for projects in which Compustar depends on the buyer taking some action before Compustar can complete its project. Hazard was treated as a continuous variable when analyzing the interaction effects.

A categorical variable coded 0 if the contract involves a hybrid payment structure (i.e., T&M with a cap), 1 if the payment is a 'pure' T&M, and 2 if the payment is a fixed fee. Fixed-fee contracts involve Compustar completing a well-defined project for a fixed price, and T&M contracts involve the buyer paying an hourly (or possibly daily) rate until the job is done. Estimated with multinomial probit models treating Hybrid as the base level.
scale: categorical: 0 = hybrid, 1 = pure T&M, 2 = fixed fee

description: Coded by the engineers on a Likert-type scale ranging from 1 to 7, in which 1 indicates that the contract contains very few details about the DR on roles and deliverables and 7 indicates an extensive description of the roles and/or deliverables. Contracts providing an engineer at the buyer's discretion with no details on requirements were coded 1, whereas a detailed help desk system project was coded 6. Treated as an ordinal variable and estimated with ordered probit models.

Coded as 1 if processes were included to address contingencies and 0 if no contingencies were mentioned. Forty-one percent of the contracts did not contain any contingency planning, and the vast majority that did plan for contingencies did so using processes to address possible contingencies. Estimated with probit models.

variable_name: country of the firm (China vs. Russia)
description: The sample was split by the firm's home country and separate hierarchical linear models were estimated for the Chinese and Russian firms. There were 1,890 observations for Chinese firms and 1,740 observations for Russian firms. The coefficients obtained in the two country models were compared using the adjusted-standard-error technique for comparing coefficients across regression equations.

One of the 14 partner selection criteria presented to managers in the case scenarios. The levels of the criteria were varied randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high), so that respondents evaluated 30 prospective alliance partners on this criterion at varying levels. The randomized assignment of levels was recalculated several times until each of the 14 variables had a variance relatively equal to that of the others.

One of the 14 partner selection criteria presented to managers in the case scenarios. The levels of the criteria were varied randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high), so that respondents evaluated 30 prospective alliance partners on this criterion at varying levels. The randomized assignment of levels was recalculated several times until each of the 14 variables had a variance relatively equal to that of the others.

One of the 14 partner selection criteria presented to managers in the case scenarios. The levels of the criteria were varied randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high), so that respondents evaluated 30 prospective alliance partners on this criterion at varying levels. The randomized assignment of levels was recalculated several times until each of the 14 variables had a variance relatively equal to that of the others.

One of the 14 partner selection criteria presented to managers in the case scenarios. The levels of the criteria were varied randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high), so that respondents evaluated 30 prospective alliance partners on this criterion at varying levels. The randomized assignment of levels was recalculated several times until each of the 14 variables had a variance relatively equal to that of the others.

One of the 14 partner selection criteria presented to managers in the case scenarios. The levels of the criteria were varied randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high), so that respondents evaluated 30 prospective alliance partners on this criterion at varying levels. The randomized assignment of levels was recalculated several times until each of the 14 variables had a variance relatively equal to that of the others.

One of the 14 partner selection criteria presented to managers in the case scenarios. The levels of the criteria were varied randomly over five levels, from 1 (low) to 5 (high), so that respondents evaluated 30 prospective alliance partners on this criterion at varying levels. The randomized assignment of levels was recalculated several times until each of the 14 variables had a variance relatively equal to that of the others.

A two-item scale on which executives rated each of the 30 potential partners described in the cases.
