The items were (1) the attractiveness of the firm as an alliance partner and (2) the probability of recommending an alliance with the firm, each rated on a seven-point Likert-type scale. The two items were averaged to form the dependent variable, and the scale had a correlation of 0.89 between the items.

Return on sales (ROS) and return on assets (ROA) ratios were collected for 2001 to 2003 and averaged over the three-year period. Since the measures of ROS and ROA were highly correlated, they were combined to create a composite measure of financial performance.

Four Likert-scale items (1 = 'strongly disagree' to 7 = 'strongly agree') adapted from Combs and Ketchen (1999b) and Erramilli, Agarwal, and Dev (2002), asking respondents to compare their chain to competitors over the past three years: brand name recognition was strong, the chain had a good reputation for quality and service, the chain was well respected, and the brand name was one of the chain's most precious assets. The measure was obtained by computing the average score provided by the respondents across the relevant items.

Three Likert-scale items (1 = 'strongly disagree' to 7 = 'strongly agree') adapted from Hansen (1999, 2002), Szulanski (1996) and Zander and Kogut (1995): business practices were precisely described in manuals (reversed-coded), business practices were not particularly well documented, and operational procedures describing what people working in outlets should do were available (reversed-coded). The measure was obtained by computing the average score provided by the respondents across the relevant items.
Data on the proportion of franchised outlets were collected from various issues of Toute la Franchise for 2001 to 2003 and averaged over the three-year period. The variable varies between 0 and 1.
Using the eight industry segment dummy variables from Toute la Franchise, the author created a variable that took the value of 1 for service-type chains and 0 for retail-type chains.

Lobbying breadth focused on the number of government entities and issues in which a firm attempted to exert influence. The authors used the number of legislative acts and the number of federal agencies/entities directly targeted by lobbying activities on behalf of the firm over the course of a year. The number of entities and acts were standardized and summed to give an aggregate measure of total breadth of the firm's lobbying efforts.
time_window: year t (dependent variables measured at t+1)

description: Political connectedness is the ability to access and influence government officials through prior relationships. The measure combines the number of revolving door lobbyists employed (individuals formerly employed in federal government, including former members of Congress, Congressional staffs, White House staff, or specific federal departments), the number of board members with current or prior government employment, and the number of congressional campaigns to which the firm donated, with multiple donations to the same campaign counted only once. Each measure was standardized and summed, and each was scaled by the number of operating segments within which the firm operates.
time_window: year t (dependent variables measured at t+1)

description: Government contracts was measured as the logarithm of the total value of all contracts between the focal company and the U.S. federal government throughout the year. The measure is left-censored because not all firms receive government contracts in a given year, with approximately 39% of observations left-censored at zero.

Firm performance was measured as Tobin's Q, calculated as market value of the firm divided by total assets. Market value was calculated as the value of the firm's common stock, liquidating value of preferred stock, book value of long-term debt, and firm debt with maturity of less than one year.

A composite measure created annually for each firm. Its first component is the Shannon index, a diversity index computed from the proportions of competitive actions belonging to each of eight competitive action categories, ranging from a high of ln(R) when all action types are equally common and approaching zero as actions become concentrated. The second component is the Euclidean distance between the firm's action repertoire in the prior year and the focal year. The third component counts the number of action types in which a firm engaged at time t but not at time t - 1. Z-scores of the three assessments were summed to create the composite measure.
time_window: year t, with change measured from t - 1 to t

description: Return on assets (ROA) expressed as a percentage at the end of the focal year under investigation. Both competitive complexity and ROA were measured at the end of the focal year to capture the actions' immediate impact.

The slope of the regression of ROA over three years, beginning with the focal year of analysis, using four data points (t, t + 1, t + 2, and t + 3). The three-year period was selected to calculate a relatively long-term trend without getting too temporally removed from the competitive action repertoires under investigation.

The percentage of a firm's total shares held by dedicated institutional investors, accounting for shareholders with at least one percent equity in a focal firm. Each institutional owner was categorized in accordance with Bushee's (1998) classification system as dedicated, transient, or neither for each year, based on past trading behavior described by portfolio diversification, portfolio turnover, and trading sensitivity. Dedicated institutional investors have low portfolio diversification, low portfolio turnover, and low trading sensitivity.
time_window: annual, measured at the end of year t - 1

description: The percentage of a firm's total shares held by transient institutional investors, restricted to shareholders with at least one percent equity in the focal firm. Owners were classified using Bushee's (1998) system based on portfolio diversification, portfolio turnover, and trading sensitivity. Transient institutional investors have high portfolio diversification, high turnover, and high trading sensitivity.
time_window: annual, measured at the end of year t - 1

description: The difference between the CEO's total compensation and the average total compensation of the TMT's four highest-paid members other than the CEO. Because CEO-TMT pay gap is not normally distributed, it was monotonically transformed by taking the natural logarithm of the difference, plus a constant that made all observations positive.
time_window: annual, measured at the end of year t - 1

variable_name: environmental strategy cluster (reactive, pollution prevention, environmental leadership)
description: All variables were standardized so as to give all criteria an equal weight, and the 10 items measuring environmental practices were subjected to a cluster analysis using the SPSS Quick cluster routine, with the number of clusters specified ex ante. A four-cluster solution separated two intermediate groups only by the application of LCA and was rejected; a three-cluster solution yielded a clear separation among the clusters along all 10 items and was retained, giving reactive (67 firms), pollution prevention (95 firms) and environmental leadership (35 firms). Items 2, 3, 8, 9 and 10 were measured on Likert scales with possible scores ranging from 1 to 5, and items 4, 5, 6 and 7 on a binary scale.
scale: items on 1-5 Likert scales and binary scales; firms assigned to three clusters

description: Managers rated on a Likert scale of 1 to 5 the impact of each stakeholder pressure on decisions related to environmental management, with 1 denoting no influence at all and 5 a very strong influence. The 14 stakeholder influence items were entered into a principal component analysis; the fourth factor represents government regulators at the national (and subnational) and local levels, and factor scores were computed to replace the original set of variables in the subsequent analyses.
scale: factor score computed from 1-5 Likert ratings

description: Factor score computed from the principal component analysis of the 14 stakeholder influence items, each rated on a Likert scale of 1 to 5 for its impact on environmental management decisions. The first factor captures most 'external' primary stakeholders, namely domestic and international customers and suppliers; factor scores were computed to replace the original variables in the analyses.
scale: factor score computed from 1-5 Likert ratings

description: Factor score computed from the principal component analysis of the 14 stakeholder influence items rated on a Likert scale of 1 to 5 for their impact on environmental management decisions. The third factor includes mainly 'internal' primary stakeholders, namely employees and shareholders, and also financial institutions.
scale: factor score computed from 1-5 Likert ratings

description: Factor score computed from the principal component analysis of the 14 stakeholder influence items rated on a Likert scale of 1 to 5 for their impact on environmental management decisions. The second factor includes the secondary stakeholder influences, namely domestic and international competitors, international agreements, ENGOs, and the media.
scale: factor score computed from 1-5 Likert ratings

description: The number of local standards-based certification organizations operating in state i at time t. Local organizations operate at the state or city level and have no formal affiliations with other organizations. The count was compiled from the National Organic Directory and three additional directories, supplemented by telephone contacts for founding dates.

The number of affiliates or chapters of a federated standards-based certification organization operating in state i at time t. The count was compiled from the National Organic Directory and three additional directories, supplemented by telephone contacts for founding dates.

A count of the number of provisions for a given state-year that had never appeared in any previous laws passed by any other state. Legal code was coded into provision categories to obtain a vector of ones and zeros for each state-year indicating the presence or absence of particular provisions.

The absolute value of the difference between the average similarity score for all states at year t and the similarity score for each state at year t. Similarity to the first state law, Oregon 1973, was computed with the Sorenson-Dice binary similarity measure, excluding co-absences; the absolute deviation captures deviation in either direction from the yearly mean.
Operationalized as the number of amendments passed or changes made through bureaucratic processes. Cosmetic changes, such as renumbering, were excluded from the analysis.

Percentage of aggregate ownership held by pressure-resistant institutions, defined as public pension funds, mutual funds, and endowments and foundations. Institutional ownership information came from Compact Disclosure, and the 1,622 institutional investors were classified using the Money Market Directory, Moody's Bank and Finance Manual, and Nelson's Directory of Investment Managers.

Percentage of aggregate ownership held by pressure-sensitive institutions, defined as insurance companies, banks, and nonbank trusts. Institutional ownership information came from Compact Disclosure, and the 1,622 institutional investors were classified using the Money Market Directory, Moody's Bank and Finance Manual, and Nelson's Directory of Investment Managers.

Percentage of aggregate ownership held by pressure-indeterminate institutions, a residual category, such as corporate pension funds, brokerage houses, and investment counselors, whose motives and actions could not be clearly defined. Institutional ownership information came from Compact Disclosure, and the 1,622 institutional investors were classified using the Money Market Directory, Moody's Bank and Finance Manual, and Nelson's Directory of Investment Managers.

The level of compensation was the sum of total salary, bonus, and long-term compensation in a year. Long-term compensation comprised grants of restricted stock, stock options, stock appreciation rights, and performance plans, valued using the Black-Scholes options-pricing model. Compensation data were obtained from proxy statements, and the variable was entered in the regressions as the dependent variable for the level of pay.

The proportion of long-term incentives was the ratio of long-term compensation to total compensation. As the distribution of this variable was skewed, a logarithmic transformation was applied. Compensation data were obtained from proxy statements.

The entropy index of diversification was used to measure the change in diversification; the total level of diversification (DT) is a continuous measure that considers the number of segments in which a firm operates and the relative importance of each segment for firm sales, with unrelated diversification (DU) arising from businesses in different 2-digit industry groups. The difference in the 1981 and 1982 indexes, obtained from COMPUSTAT business segment tapes, measured the change in unrelated diversification. The entropy formula itself is not readable in the text.

The entropy index of diversification was used to measure the change in diversification; related diversification (DR) is the diversification resulting from businesses in 4-digit segments within a 2-digit industry group (based on SIC code). The difference in the 1981 and 1982 indexes, obtained from COMPUSTAT business segment tapes, measured the change in related diversification. The entropy formula itself is not readable in the text.

COMPUSTAT provides two variables from the annual flow of funds statement: the sale of common and preferred stock, and long-term debt issued; their sum represents total new financing in that year. The measure is long-term debt issued in 1982 as a proportion of total new financing in 1982.

Total new financing for 1982 was computed from COMPUSTAT as the sum of the sale of common and preferred stock and long-term debt issued. The Directory of Corporate Financing was used to identify all public issues, both debt and equity, by the sample firms in 1982; the amount of financing not identified as public was from private sources. The amount of public financing as a proportion of total new financing in 1982 was used as the measure of the source of financing.

The number of acquisitions completed in 1982 was used to measure mode of entry strategy. Because the sample is limited to diversifying firms, firms that scored high on this variable are adopting an acquisitive entry strategy, and firms with a low (or zero) score a direct entry strategy.

Dichotomous variable that takes a value of one when a solo practitioner who competes in the same CBSA and legal specialty as the focal attorney dies unexpectedly in the current year. Solo practitioners are defined as attorneys who are the only individuals affiliated with their firm in the Martindale data. Deaths are classified as unexpected if the person is under the age of 65 and the obituary describes the death as sudden or unexpected, such as from a heart attack, accident, or sudden illness; suicides are excluded. Deaths are identified from the list of attorneys Martindale knows to have died, cross-checked against the Social Security Administration Death Master File, and from searches of ObituaryData.com.

Dichotomous variable that takes a value of one when the attorney founds a new law firm in the following year, which effectively lags all independent variables by 1 year. The attorney must appear in a newly created law firm within 3 years of her exit from the current law firm without appearing in another organization, and she must be a 'name partner', meaning that her last name appears in the name of the law firm in the firm's first appearance in the data. Recodes and mergers are scrubbed using flows of employees and a 25-attorney cap on the size of a new firm; nonfounders who work for the firm in its first year are not counted.

variable_name: % of partners in practice area from attorney's law school
description: Calculated as the percentage of partners in the attorney's office and legal specialty who obtain their law degree from the same law school as the focal attorney. The law school an attorney attends is used as a marker of shared educational affiliation, and these partners are the individuals most likely to affect the focal attorney's promotion and compensation.

Ratio of associates to partners who share the same office and legal specialty as the focal attorney, used as an approximation of the average number of competitors vying for a given promotion opportunity. Partners also compete with each other to advance to higher levels of the partnership, but these gradations cannot be observed in the Martindale data, so the analyses for H2b focus only on associates.

Log of cash compensation, the sum of base salary and cash bonuses, of the focal employee. The focal employee is the median-paid employee of each unique firm-occupation-skill level-region-year group, yielding 177,540 focal employees drawn from the full set of employee records.

Log of average cash compensation (the sum of base salary and cash bonuses) of the focal employee's internal reference group, defined as all employees who work at the same firm as the focal employee, are at the same skill level, in the same year, but outside the focal employee's functional area. The coefficient on Internal Pay estimates the sensitivity of employee pay to the internal pay benchmark.

Log of average cash compensation of the market reference group for each focal employee: all employees in the data set who work at the same skill level and in the same occupation and region in the same year, but at firms other than the focal employee's employer. The coefficient on Market Pay estimates the sensitivity of employee pay to the market pay benchmark.

A standardized cardinal measure of skill provided by the consultancy that ranges from level 1 to level 22. It increases with job level within the organization but varies within hierarchical levels and occupations with the tasks required, and the consultancy refers to it as the 'reference level' because it is the basis for pay comparisons within and across firms. Employees are divided into deciles of Skill Level for parts of the analysis.

Industry-average knowledge capital intensity, defined as the accumulated sum of past spending on research and development, calculated following Peters and Taylor (2017). The 18 industries in the sample are split into terciles of six industries each: low-knowledge industries (e.g., retailers and restaurants) average less than 1%, moderate-knowledge industries (e.g., construction and insurance) range from 1% to 4%, and high-knowledge industries (e.g., chemicals and high technology) exceed 4%.

A binary indicator that equals one if the combined score on the complex problem-solving index is above the median and zero otherwise. The index is the average of scores across three Hay Group job components; the occupation-level scores were produced by prompting ChatGPT-4.0 to map each occupation to the nine Hay components.
A binary indicator built from a collaboration index that averages scores on four Hay Group job components; the binary indicator distinguishes above-median from below-median collaboration intensity.

For each patenting firm-year, the coefficient on Internal Pay estimated using a three-year rolling window relative to nonpatenting firms; because nonpatenting firms are pooled as the base group, the coefficient represents the three-year average firm-year pay sensitivity relative to nonpatenting firms. A positive coefficient denotes higher sensitivity to the internal benchmark than the average nonpatenting firm. The variable is z-scored for interpretability.

The corresponding firm-year coefficient on Market Pay estimated with a three-year rolling window relative to nonpatenting firms; a positive coefficient denotes higher sensitivity to the market benchmark than the average nonpatenting firm.

The dependent variable is the sum of z-scored innovation measures: the number and stock of patents and publications, forward citations by the most cited patent, and the breakthrough index (Consolidation-Disruption index) of the most breakthrough innovation.

Patent counts based on patent application dates for each firm year across all patent classes constituting the five components. The ratio of patents in a particular component to the total patents across all components is computed for each firm year to capture the relative allocation of inventive effort to a particular component. The proportion was logit-transformed and used as the dependent variable. The system board was the omitted component category, so the proportions in a firm year do not sum to one.

The constraint component identified in each year from product reviews was coded as a dummy variable taking a value of 1 for the component with a 1-year lag. The 1-year lag was motivated by Moore's law technological cycles and by interviews indicating that R&D budget cycles usually lasted 12-14 months. Three to four reviews per year were used to triangulate the primary bottleneck, and the set of components identified as constraints reflects unanimity among three coders.

The primary component product market domain of each firm in the sample was identified, and a variable was coded 1 if the firm did not produce the component that was identified as a constraint in the given year and 0 otherwise. This variable was interacted with the constraint component dummy to test Hypothesis 2.
time_window: same year as the constraint (1-year lag relative to the outcome)

description: A stock of firm knowledge in the slack component was created by cumulating the firm's stock of patents in its primary slack component. This stock was interacted with the S-firms dummy and the constraint component dummy to test Hypothesis 3. The main effect of firm knowledge stocks in each component technology, lagged by 1 year, is included as a control.

Four anchored 5-point Likert scale items suggested by Eisenberger et al. (1986) assessing how much the organization cares about employee wellbeing, about ample and fair pay, about satisfaction at work, and about sharing profits. The most senior vice president of each organization completed this scale. The Cronbach alpha for the OCE1 measure was 0.82 and factor analysis showed the four items loading on one factor.

Two 5-point Likert scales asking the CEO of the firm to rate his organization relative to its principal competitors on how much the company invested in education and competence development for its employees, and how much the company invested in total compensation, including benefits and vacation. The topmost executive of each organization completed these scales. The Cronbach alpha for the OCE2 measure was 0.71.
scale: 5-point Likert (much less to much more than principal competitors)

description: Return on assets, based on figures on sales, total assets and before-tax earnings that top executives supplied from their financial statements. For the 30 public companies, published financial reports were obtained to confirm the figures provided by the top managers; ROA computed from published figures correlated at 0.98 with ROA computed from data supplied by the managers.

Dedication to cost leadership assessed with three anchored Likert items from a Korean translation of Miller's (1988) scales, gauging the use of efficient inventory management techniques, cost reduction efforts, and just-in-time manufacturing. A confirmatory factor analysis showed the items loaded highly only on their own strategy factor, and the items were averaged into a composite score reflecting the vigor and thoroughness with which the strategy was pursued.
scale: anchored Likert items averaged into a composite score

description: Dedication to marketing differentiation assessed with three anchored Likert items from a Korean translation of Miller's (1988) scales, gauging the use of advertising, the promotion of brand identification, and attractive design or packaging. The items loaded highly only on their own strategy factor and were averaged into a composite score reflecting the vigor and thoroughness with which the strategy was pursued.
scale: anchored Likert items averaged into a composite score

description: Dedication to innovative differentiation assessed with four anchored Likert items from a Korean translation of Miller's (1988) scales, measuring new product development, product R&D, the creation of state-of-the-art products, and the continual refinement of product lines. The items loaded highly only on their own strategy factor and were averaged into a composite score reflecting the vigor and thoroughness with which the strategy was pursued.
scale: anchored Likert items averaged into a composite score

variable_name: Dedication to cost leadership, marketing differentiation and innovative differentiation
description: Dedicated positioning strategy is measured with three composite scores from a Korean translation of Miller's (1988) anchored Likert scales: cost leadership (three items), marketing differentiation (three items) and innovative differentiation (four items). Items are averaged within each strategy to reflect the vigor and thoroughness of its pursuit, and each strategy interacts with OCE.

Subsidiary presidents indicated whether their subsidiary became a part of the corporation as a result of an acquisition/merger (coded as 1) or whether the subsidiary was created as a greenfield operation (coded as 0). The authors argue that, relative to greenfield subsidiaries, acquired subsidiaries on average have a knowledge stock that is less duplicative vis-a-vis the rest of the corporation and should therefore have a larger pool of relevant knowledge to offer the global network.

This variable was measured in terms of the number of employees in the subsidiary. In order to dampen the high variability in size and achieve a more normal distribution, the natural logarithm of the number of employees was used to indicate subsidiary size in the analyses.
scale: number of employees (natural logarithm used in analyses)

description: This variable was computed by dividing the per capita income for the host country (where the subsidiary is located) by that for the home country (the country-of-origin of the parent corporation). For each country, data on per capita income (gross national product per capita adjusted for purchasing power parity) were obtained from the World Development Report.
scale: ratio (host per capita income divided by home per capita income)
level: subsidiary (host country relative to home country)

description: Subsidiary presidents were asked how their annual incentive bonus was actually determined for the most recent year, indicating the percentage of the bonus based on their subsidiary's performance and the percentage based on the performance of a cluster of subsidiaries (answers totalling 100%). Responses to the cluster-of-subsidiaries item were used as a measure of the extent to which the incentive system was network-focused rather than subsidiary-focused.

This variable was measured through a 3-item Likert-type 7-point scale (ranging from 'used rarely' to 'used very frequently') that asked respondents to indicate the extent to which their subsidiary used liaison personnel, temporary task forces, and permanent teams to coordinate decisions and actions with sister subsidiaries. The final measure was a weighted average of responses to the three items where the most complex mechanism (permanent teams) was given a weight of 3, the intermediately complex mechanism (temporary task forces) a weight of 2, and the least complex mechanism (liaison personnel) a weight of 1.

Adapted from Ghoshal and Bartlett (1988). Respondents were asked to provide 'yes' or 'no' answers to two questions: (1) whether they had worked for one or more years in other subsidiaries of this corporation, and (2) whether they had participated in executive development programs involving participants from several subsidiaries. For each respondent, the total count of 'yes' responses was treated as a measure of participation in lateral socialization.

Adapted from Ghoshal and Bartlett (1988). Respondents were asked to provide 'yes' or 'no' answers to two questions: (1) whether they had worked for one or more years at corporate headquarters in this corporation, and (2) whether they had a mentor at corporate headquarters. For each respondent, the total count of 'yes' responses was treated as a measure of participation in vertical socialization mechanisms.

The same incentive-bonus question posed to subsidiary presidents: the percentage of the annual incentive bonus based on the performance of a cluster of subsidiaries was used as a measure of the extent to which the incentive system was network-focused rather than subsidiary-focused. In the context of knowledge inflows, the authors argue that subsidiary-focused (rather than network-focused) incentives create a stronger disposition to learn from any and all sources.

Computed by dividing the per capita income (gross national product per capita adjusted for purchasing power parity) for the host country by that for the home country, using World Bank data. In the context of knowledge inflows, the authors expect that the lower the level of economic advancement of the host country vis-a-vis the home country, the more eager subsidiary personnel would be to learn from the parent corporation.
scale: ratio (host per capita income divided by home per capita income)
level: subsidiary (host country relative to home country)

description: Following Vancil (1980), respondents were given a list of nine strategically relevant decisions. Using an approach similar to Hofstede (1967), for each decision each respondent indicated on a 5-point Likert scale the typical influence they had in affecting the outcome of the decision, ranging from (1) 'your opinion not asked but decision is explained to you' to (5) 'proposal by you, followed by consultation with superior, with your opinion prevailing'. Responses on the nine questions were averaged to create an index of headquarters-subsidiary decentralization; higher values indicate higher decentralization.

Subsidiary presidents indicated whether their subsidiary became a part of the corporation as a result of an acquisition/merger (coded as 1) or whether the subsidiary was created as a greenfield operation (coded as 0). In the context of absorptive capacity, the authors argue that the novelty of acquired subsidiaries' knowledge base implies a lower absorptive capacity for intra-corporate knowledge relative to greenfield subsidiaries.

variable_name: Proportion of local nationals in the subsidiary's top management team
description: For managers heading each of seven positions, subsidiary presidents indicated the nationality of each particular person on a four-point scale: 'local national', 'home country expatriate', 'third country expatriate', and 'not applicable' implying that there was nobody heading such a position. The percentage of applicable positions that were headed by local nationals was regarded as a measure of the extent to which the subsidiary top management team was localized; a greater proportion of local nationals implies lower homophily and hence lower absorptive capacity.

Knowledge flow data were collected on seven items of largely procedural knowledge. For each item the subsidiary president was asked to indicate on a 7-point scale (ranging from 'not at all' to 'a very great deal') the extent to which the subsidiary engaged in transfers of 'knowledge and skills' by 'provides knowledge and skills to sister subsidiaries'. Responses across the seven items were averaged to yield a composite measure of KO-S.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = not at all to 7 = a very great deal); composite mean of seven items

variable_name: Knowledge outflows to the parent corporation (KO-P)
description: For each of the seven items of largely procedural knowledge, the subsidiary president was asked to indicate on a 7-point scale (ranging from 'not at all' to 'a very great deal') the extent to which the subsidiary 'provides knowledge and skills to parent corporation'. Responses across the seven items were averaged to yield a composite measure of KO-P.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = not at all to 7 = a very great deal); composite mean of seven items

description: For each of the seven items of largely procedural knowledge, the subsidiary president was asked to indicate on a 7-point scale (ranging from 'not at all' to 'a very great deal') the extent to which the subsidiary 'receives knowledge and skills from sister subsidiaries'. Responses across the seven items were averaged to yield a composite measure of KI-S.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = not at all to 7 = a very great deal); composite mean of seven items

variable_name: Knowledge inflows from the parent corporation (KI-P)
description: For each of the seven items of largely procedural knowledge, the subsidiary president was asked to indicate on a 7-point scale (ranging from 'not at all' to 'a very great deal') the extent to which the subsidiary 'receives knowledge and skills from the parent corporation'. Responses across the seven items were averaged to yield a composite measure of KI-P.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = not at all to 7 = a very great deal); composite mean of seven items

description: Weighted network density among the set of the acquirer's components, computed as the average tie strength among these components normalized by the maximum tie strength. Ties measure how many e-commerce websites use two components jointly for at least 3 months during the year. If the acquirer has only one component, local component interdependence is set to 1. For each potential target the target's component is included in the acquirer's set of components, and the expected change is the proportional change calculated as (post-acquisition measure minus pre-acquisition measure) divided by the pre-acquisition measure.
level: acquirer–potential target pair within an acquisition choice set
time_window: quarterly moving windows of one year before the acquisition

description: The ecosystem network is decomposed into clusters using a unipartite modularity algorithm, partitioning components into groups with as many internal and as few external linkages as possible. Concentration within clusters is then computed as a Herfindahl–Hirschman Index over the number of clusters in a given network; the printed formula could not be read because it was removed as unreadable. The pre-acquisition measure is computed on the acquirer's components, and the expected change is constructed for each potential target by including the target's component in the acquirer's set of components.
level: acquirer–potential target pair within an acquisition choice set
time_window: quarterly moving windows of one year before the acquisition

description: The eigenvector centrality of each component is computed in the ecosystem matrix, and the pre-acquisition measure is the average eigenvector centrality across the acquirer's components. For each potential target the post-acquisition average centrality is computed by including the target's component, and the expected change is the proportional change from the pre- to the post-acquisition measure.
level: acquirer–potential target pair within an acquisition choice set
time_window: quarterly moving windows of one year before the acquisition

description: Binary dependent variable set to one for the actual targets and to zero for the potential targets of unrealized acquisitions. The model is conditioned on the set of matched cases and controls per acquisition, so the estimates capture variation in attributes between potential targets and predict the likelihood of acquirer i choosing a particular target j. The sample includes 186 cases and 2116 controls.
time_window: quarterly moving windows of one year before the acquisition

description: For each patent, the authors tabulated the list of cited patents and counted the number of citations the patent made to prior patents belonging to the focal firm's CV spinouts. Citation count variables have a Poisson distribution, and therefore in the main models the count is used in logarithmic transformation to correct for skewness.

For each patent, the authors tabulated the list of cited patents and counted the number of citations the patent made to prior patents belonging to the focal firm's employee spinouts. Citation count variables have a Poisson distribution, and therefore in the main models the count is used in logarithmic transformation to correct for skewness.

For each patent, the authors counted the number of citations the patent made to prior patents belonging to the firm's CVC portfolio ventures (ventures that received CVC funds from the 20 firms between 1990 and 2009 and that earned patents from the USPTO). The citation count is used in logarithmic transformation in the main models to correct for skewness.

For each patent, the authors counted the number of citations the patent made to prior patents belonging to the firm's allied partners (partners of alliances completed by the 20 firms between 1990 and 2009 that had patent records with the USPTO). The citation count is used in logarithmic transformation in the main models to correct for skewness.

A weighted index of the number of claims awarded to the patent, forward citations that the patent received in the five years after its granting, and the number of backward citations that the patent made to prior patents. For each patent, the NBER technological category was identified from the Marco et al. (2015) data set, and the coefficients developed by Lanjouw and Schankerman (2004) for that technological category were used to weight the patent's claims, forward citations, and the inverse of its backward citations. Patent quality index is a linear combination of the three weighted indicators.
time_window: forward citations received within five years after grant

description: For each firm-year item, the firm's core U.S. patent classifications (USPCs) were identified as those in which the firm's patenting frequency was higher than its mean patenting frequency in all other USPCs. For each patent, the authors derived a list of inventors who moved from the citing firm to the cited CV spinouts and counted the number of patents these spun-out inventors applied for in the parent's most frequent USPCs during their corporate employment. Because the count is highly skewed, it was transformed into a dummy variable equal to one if the focal patent cites CV spinouts that employ inventors with any experience in the parent's most frequent USPCs and zero otherwise.
scale: dummy (1 = cited CV spinout inventors have experience in the parent's most frequent USPCs)

description: Following Fleming (2001), the authors derived the list of all subclassifications assigned to the patent by the USPTO, which proxy for the knowledge components recombined in the focal patent. For each inventor listed on the patent, familiarity with the patent's components was measured as the number of times that he or she used such components in the past, multiplied by a decay coefficient over five years to account for time-constant knowledge loss, and the average component familiarity of all inventors was taken. This average was transformed into a dummy variable equal to one if the average component familiarity in the patent was null (the patent recombined components unfamiliar to its inventors) and zero otherwise; patents are split into familiar and unfamiliar components samples.
scale: dummy (1 = average component familiarity is null, i.e. unfamiliar components)

description: The number of franchises awarded in each specific origin- and host-country group prior to the focal decision date. The authors note that conventional distribution-correction procedures (e.g., log and root) were employed where indicated because some variables were highly skewed, and that standardized variables were used to compute interactions. A squared term for accumulated experience is included in the model to capture the curvilinear relationship.
time_window: prior to the focal decision date

description: The long-term performance of a given franchisee, measured as the Daily Transaction Volume that the franchisee had on February 3, 2015. The authors argue the metric reflects the extent to which sales agent recruitment and selection of franchisees improves with experience, and that it is relatively unbiased by short-term franchise-level variance associated with differences in learning, motivation, or other peer-level effects. Franchise Age (days elapsed between February 3, 2015 and the date the franchise was awarded) is included as a covariate to ensure comparability.

A moving average of the days between the three decisions prior to the focal decision. The authors illustrate: if 30 days elapsed between franchise 6 and 5, two days between franchise 4 and 5, 458 between franchise 4 and 3, 52 between franchise 3 and 2, and 100 days between franchise 2 and 1, the moving average is 163 for franchise 6 and 186 for franchise 5.
time_window: three decisions prior to the focal decision

description: Computed with the same moving-average approach as pace: the moving average of the Daily Transaction Volume for the three decisions prior to the focal decision. The authors discuss it as the variance in the prior decisions' outcome, indicated by variance in franchisee revenues, which they associate with the information content of early decisions.
time_window: three decisions prior to the focal decision

description: The dependent variable is the total number of exploratory deals that a focal SE initiated on a focal day. Exploratory deals are those that require the sourcing of completely novel products that have not been sold by any SE to date from completely new suppliers that have not engaged in any business transactions with the company previously. Because the entire history of deals for all SEs in the company can be tracked, the authors state there is no left-censoring issue with this measure.

The main independent variable is the interaction between treatment (coded as one if the focal individual was moved into a common workspace with a previously separated peer; zero otherwise) and post (coded as one if the observation was related to the time period after the workspace reconfiguration; zero otherwise). Increased spatial proximity to a previously separated peer was not measured as the actual dyadic distance between individuals but as whether a focal individual was moved into a common workspace with previously separated peers. The coefficient on this interaction captures the difference in exploration between the treatment and control groups caused by the treatment.

Measured as the accumulated number of deals that an SE had sold so far within the company at the time of the move. The authors state that this variable approximates the level of capability an individual has to learn new knowledge and apply it to novel and useful means. The median value of this variable was used to split the sample into individuals with above median and below median prior organizational experience (30 individuals each).
time_window: at the time of the move

description: Coded as one if a focal individual had a tie with a previously separated peer; zero otherwise. In this context the tie was defined based on whether the individuals constituting a tie joined the company together and were therefore part of the same cohort, because interviews indicated that starting in the same cohort created exceptionally strong and long-lasting ties and that cohort members met regularly outside of the workplace. The sample was split into a subsample of individuals with such ties and one without.

A Java-based language parser accesses patent texts on the USPTO Web site and codes the dependence-independence nature of all individual claims, using the heuristic that a dependent claim always contains a reference to an earlier claim number within the same patent and coding all other claims as independent. The coding is aggregated at the patent level and patents are mapped to R&D locations based on inventors listed in the patents; one patent is assigned to more than one R&D location when it involves inventors residing in multiple locations. Scopeijt is constructed as the average number of independent claims per patent that firm i in R&D location j applies for in year t.

Inventors are compiled at each R&D location j in a given year t. For each inventor k, the authors trace the patent applications the inventor is involved in for year t and their assigned main technology classes, and calculate a concentration ratio of technology classes for all patents involving that inventor, reflecting how focused the inventor is on particular technological areas. Inventor Specializationijt is the average of this concentration ratio across all inventors in firm i at R&D location j in year t.
time_window: year t (predicted value lagged by one year in the second stage)

description: The CEO's base salary, one of the four categories of CEO compensation examined as a dependent variable. The compensation data were drawn from the Execucomp database and measured with a 1-year lag after the stakeholder management and financial performance measures.

The CEO's bonus compensation, one of the four categories of CEO compensation examined as a dependent variable. The compensation data were drawn from the Execucomp database and measured with a 1-year lag after the stakeholder management and financial performance measures.

The value of stock options granted to the CEO, valued using the Black-Scholes options pricing model. It is one of the four categories of CEO compensation examined as a dependent variable, drawn from the Execucomp database.
The CEO's total compensation, one of the four categories of CEO compensation examined as a dependent variable, drawn from the Execucomp database.

KLD rating of the firm's stakeholder management performance in the area of community relations. Analysts at KLD determine each firm's performance on this dimension after extensive investigation of public records, surveys, and even facilities visits; firms are then given ratings on 5-point Likert-type scales.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale from -2 (poor social performance) to +2 (superior social performance)
time_window: year prior to the CEO compensation measure

description: KLD rating of the firm's stakeholder management performance in the area of diversity (including diversity initiatives, to the extent that certain diversity initiatives are directed toward suppliers). KLD analysts assign ratings on 5-point Likert-type scales after extensive investigation of public records, surveys, and facilities visits.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale from -2 (poor social performance) to +2 (superior social performance)
time_window: year prior to the CEO compensation measure

description: KLD rating of the firm's stakeholder management performance in the area of employee relations. KLD analysts assign ratings on 5-point Likert-type scales after extensive investigation of public records, surveys, and facilities visits.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale from -2 (poor social performance) to +2 (superior social performance)
time_window: year prior to the CEO compensation measure

description: KLD rating of the firm's stakeholder management performance in the area of environmental impact. KLD analysts assign ratings on 5-point Likert-type scales after extensive investigation of public records, surveys, and facilities visits.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale from -2 (poor social performance) to +2 (superior social performance)
time_window: year prior to the CEO compensation measure

description: KLD rating of the firm's stakeholder management performance in the area of product safety/quality (customer related). KLD analysts assign ratings on 5-point Likert-type scales after extensive investigation of public records, surveys, and facilities visits.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale from -2 (poor social performance) to +2 (superior social performance)
time_window: year prior to the CEO compensation measure

description: Return on assets, measured following Berman et al. (1999) and drawn from the Compustat database for the year prior to the CEO compensation measure. It is used to test the interaction effects between stakeholder management and financial performance.
time_window: year prior to the CEO compensation measure

description: Total returns to shareholders, one of the two measures of financial performance used to test the interaction effects between stakeholder management and financial performance. It was drawn from the Compustat database for the year prior to the CEO compensation measure; the regression tables label it as the 1-year return.
time_window: year prior to the CEO compensation measure

description: A count of the players from the same source high school or junior college that preceded each player into the focal FBS team within the previous 4 years. The window corresponds to the length of a typical high school or college career, providing reasonable indication that a potential recruit and a current college player from the same source were teammates or had shared teammates. The mode value was 0, indicating that the majority of players matriculated from a source without a dyadic pipeline in the previous 4 years; 10.9% of players followed a single preceding player, 3.3% came after two, 1.3% followed three, and 1.4% followed four or more. The analysis is limited to recruited players in years 2009-2014 so that this variable can look back 4 years without any data censoring.

A third-party rating of each recruit's potential as an FBS player provided by 247Sports, which assigned scores from 70 (minimum) to 100 (maximum) for the most sought-after recruits. Unrated players, who make up part of every roster, were randomly generated a value between 60 and 69 to indicate a level of human capital sufficient to make an FBS team but lower than the minimum rating of 70. Players were ranked within their team according to their human capital rating to standardize for differences in teams' attractiveness. The rank was transformed so that all values are positive and higher values indicate higher pre-entry human capital (multiplying initially by -1 and then adding the maximum number of players for a team in the dataset).
scale: 70 to 100 for rated recruits, 60 to 69 for unrated players; transformed within-team rank

description: The average number of games started per year in the player's college career, a count variable. Averaging games started standardizes variation in college career lengths, as some careers are truncated by injury, quitting, or leaving early for professional football while others are extended past 4 years with redshirt seasons. The variable is founded on a discrete count with few denominator possibilities, a Poisson-like distribution, and an overdispersion parameter alpha greater than zero, which motivated the negative binomial specification.

Indicator of whether a declining firm achieved a successful performance turnaround. A firm was considered successful if it had at least two years of increasing ROA after the two declining years of ROA and had achieved and maintained positive ROA by at least the sixth year after the base year before decline started. Firms that continued in existence but failed to achieve or maintain the upturn in ROA, and firms that declared bankruptcy, were liquidated, delisted by stock exchanges, or acquired while still unprofitable, were classified as nonturnarounds.
time_window: through the sixth year after the base year

description: Count of new product introductions reported for each sample firm in newspaper and trade articles covering the first three years of decline. Two coders performed a structured content analysis of each article and classified it into pre-established action categories, with a third coder classifying actions on which the two coders did not agree.

Count of new alliances reported for each sample firm in newspaper and trade articles covering the first three years of decline, coded by two coders through a structured content analysis with a third coder resolving disagreements.
Indicator variable for whether or not the firm engaged in an acquisition, coded from newspaper and trade articles covering the first three years of decline through a structured content analysis.

Indicator variable for whether or not the firm engaged in layoffs in years 1-3 of decline, coded from newspaper and trade articles through a structured content analysis. Layoffs are defined as wholesale reductions in employees. The authors used an indicator variable because insufficient information existed to create a continuous variable, as in most layoff cases it was impossible to ascertain the proportion of the workforce let go.

Indicator variable for whether asset reduction occurred, coded from newspaper and trade articles through a structured content analysis. Asset reduction occurred when a firm sold or closed any of its physical assets.

Indicator variable for whether a product withdrawal occurred, coded from newspaper and trade articles through a structured content analysis. Product withdrawal occurred when a firm closed or sold product lines. An indicator variable was used because the same conditions as for layoffs applied to product withdrawals, with insufficient information to create a continuous variable.

Ratio of the firm's investment in external knowledge acquisition (extramural R&D activities) in 2000 and the total amount invested by the firm in both internal and external R&D activities (intramural plus extramural R&D activities). Extramural R&D involves creative work related to product development performed by another entity for a fee and excludes expenditure on the acquisition of non-R&D-related external knowledge or equipment. To test the curvilinear relationship hypothesized in H1, the squared term of extramural R&D is used. The measure emphasizes the degree of extramural R&D relative to the firm's total R&D expenditure.

Innovation performance due to new-to-market products measures the share of turnover in 2006 from products that were new to the firm's market and were introduced by the firm during 2004-2006. It is operationalized based on the innovativeness of the firm's product(s) and taken from the latest survey. The dependent variable is a proportion that takes values between 0 and 1.

Dummy variable based on questions about specific knowledge protection activities during the period 2002-2004. It takes the value 1 for firms that undertook special efforts to retain skilled employees. Linear and squared interactions of this term with the variable extramural R&D and its square were created to assess its moderating influence.

Dummy variable based on questions about specific knowledge protection activities during the period 2002-2004. It takes the value 1 for firms that used secrecy. Linear and squared interactions of this term with the variable extramural R&D and its square were created to assess its moderating influence.

Dummy variable based on questions about specific knowledge protection activities during the period 2002-2004. It takes the value 1 for firms that made use of design complexity. Linear and squared interactions of this term with the variable extramural R&D and its square were created to assess its moderating influence.

Self-reported measures of ten dimensions of new venture performance relative to competitors: sales growth, employment growth, market share, gross profits, net profit margin, innovation in products and services, speed in developing new products and services, quality of products and services, cost control, and customer satisfaction. Respondents used a scale ranging from 1, 'much worse,' to 7, 'much better,' to rate these items (alpha = .80).
time_window: performance relative to competitors at the time of the survey

description: An objective performance measure, sales growth was measured as the percent change in total sales over the previous year. The authors were successful in obtaining sales growth data for a subsample of 72 firms.

Covin and Slevin's (1989) nine-item scale, with all items on a seven-point semantic differential scale with a neutral midpoint. The question asking whether a firm prefers to 'undo competitors' or to 'live and let live' was replaced with an item from Lumpkin and Dess asking whether a firm 'has a strong tendency to follow the leader' or to 'be ahead of other competitors' in introducing new products and services. All items loaded above 0.60 on a single factor with an eigenvalue of 4.04, and the nine items were combined into a single scale (alpha = .84).
scale: seven-point semantic differential scale with a neutral midpoint

description: Respondents were presented with a roster of all firms in their industry and asked to 'check off those firms where you regularly exchanged information with the CEO or someone else from the board over the past year.' Responses were recorded in a 90 by 90 data matrix in which cell ij was coded 1 when any founder of firm i reported an information tie with firm j; the matrix was symmetrized using the union rule. From the symmetrized data matrix, each firm's closeness centrality was calculated in UCINET VI, computed as the reciprocal of the sum of the shortest path distance to each other firm in the network (both direct and indirect ties taken into account).
scale: reciprocal of the sum of shortest path distances

description: Adapted from the managerial ties scale developed by Peng and Luo (2000). Entrepreneurs were presented with a list of 13 different kinds of organizations, distilled from the expert interviews and expected to be important sources of resources and legitimacy for open source companies, including research institutes, financial institutions, law firms, open source development communities, and foreign companies. Respondents assessed the extent to which the founders of their firm maintained personal contact with each type of organization, and responses were averaged into a composite measure (alpha = .88).
scale: 0 = no contact to 7 = very extensive contact

description: An equally weighted composite measure of three commonly used measures: industry experience, measured as the number of years of IT industry experience on a firm's founding team; start-up experience, measured as the number of start-ups that a founding team had founded; and managerial experience, measured as the number of years that team members had worked in senior management functions prior to founding the current venture.
time_window: prior to founding the current venture

description: Person-year work histories were constructed from the PSID question 'Head/Wife works for self or others?', which classifies individuals as self-employed, unemployed, or employed by an employer. Wage/salary earners were confirmed to be working full time by cross-checking total annual hours of work and total annual hours of unemployment against a threshold of 1,200 hours, which led to reclassification from employed to unemployed for less than 0.5% of the sample. Entry into entrepreneurship is treated as a transition, and observations after the first transition are deleted. The dependent variable is the hazard rate of entrepreneurship from the time the individual leaves full-time education.

A categorical variable for whether the individual is employed in the private or the public sector or is unemployed in any given year, built by merging the individual work history file with the PSID question 'Work for government?' and, as a backup, PSID data on industry affiliation (which classifies government). In the hazard model the authors include a two-level categorical variable indicating whether the individual was a public or a private employee in the previous year, using private employment as the benchmark category.

The endogeneity correction term obtained by extending the proportional hazard model with an equation for public employment; the covariation between the error terms of the hazard equation and of the public employment choice equation indicates the extent to which the model suffers from unobserved heterogeneity in the form of self-selection. It is estimated with a bivariate probit specification using instrumental variables for sectoral choice. A significant negative estimate is interpreted as evidence that nonentrepreneurial individuals are matched with public sector job opportunities.

Length of public sector employment, generated from the categorical variable for private employment, public employment, or unemployment. The tenure clock is reset to zero every time the individual switched between these states, so tenure shows the duration in either of the two states.
Dummy variable coded 1 for Black respondents; White respondents are the reference group. A second dummy identifies respondents of other races excluding White.

Part of a categorical venture-creation variable coded 0 for no venture creation, 1 for intrapreneurial entry, and 2 for entrepreneurial entry. Intrapreneurs were identified by the screening question asking whether the respondent, alone or with others, was currently trying to start a new business or a new venture for their employer, an effort that is part of their normal work.

Part of the same categorical venture-creation variable coded 0 for no venture creation, 1 for intrapreneurial entry, and 2 for entrepreneurial entry. Entrepreneurs were identified by the screening questions asking whether the respondent was currently trying to start a new business, including any self-employment, or was the owner of a business they help manage.
Time-varying dummy variable for whether a new venture has earned revenue, coded 1 for 'yes' and 0 for 'no'. The PSED II identified whether and when a new venture earned revenue.
Time-varying dummy variable coded 1 when a business received monthly revenue exceeding monthly expenses for more than 6 of the past 12 months, and 0 otherwise.

Dummy variable coded 1 for high-discriminatory states that had no fair housing law until federally mandated by the Fair Housing Act of 1968 and 0 for other states, following the long-standing tradition in research on entrepreneurship and race.

Dummy variable equal to 1 for high-discrimination states and 0 for other states. States in the bottom half of a ranking based on the overall number of discrimination complaints filed with the Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity divided by 100,000s of residents are considered high-discrimination states; states in the top half are low-discrimination states.
Dummy variable indicating whether respondents hold a college degree; this variable is set to 1 for no college degree and 0 otherwise.
Dummy variable indicating a high growth orientation, that is, aspiring for a business to be as large as possible.
Continuous variable indicating entrepreneurs' aspirations for future business growth, that is, the expected number of managers or employees working for the new business when it is 5 years old.

The dependent variable in all analyses is the percentage ownership of the Japanese parent(s) in the foreign investment. When more than two Japanese firms possessed equity in the foreign investment and were part of the same keiretsu, the dependent variable was the sum of the equity holdings of the keiretsu affiliated firms; otherwise the dependent variable was the percentage ownership of the main Japanese parent. ToBIT analysis was used because the dependent variable takes a maximum value of 100 percent ownership.
scale: percent, truncated at a maximum of 100

description: Industry-level measure of the degree of proprietary content in the firm's marketing assets, calculated as the ratio of advertising expenditure to total sales. The ratio was computed from yen expenditure and sales values for the 2-year period prior to 1994 (1992 and 1993) and was coded by Daiwa's 5-digit industrial classification.

Industry-level measure of the degree of proprietary content in the firm's technological assets, calculated as the ratio of R&D expenditure to total sales. The ratio was computed from yen expenditure and sales values for the 2-year period prior to 1994 (1992 and 1993) and was coded by Daiwa's 5-digit industrial classification.

Firm-level advertising intensity minus industry-level advertising intensity, where firm-level intensity is the ratio of advertising expenditure to total sales. The normalized term identifies firms that had marketing assets with a greater proprietary content than the industry mean. A dummy version of the variable was also created, assigned a value of one when a firm-level intensity was greater than the corresponding industry-level intensity.

Firm-level R&D intensity minus industry-level R&D intensity, where firm-level intensity is the ratio of R&D expenditure to total sales. The normalized term identifies firms that had technological assets with a greater proprietary content than the industry mean. A dummy version of the variable was also created, assigned a value of one when a firm-level intensity was greater than the corresponding industry-level intensity.

Dummy variable coded as 1 to identify investments made in resource-based industries such as food and beverages, textiles, wood, petroleum, rubber, primary metals, and pulp and paper. Such entries indicate the foreign firm's need for raw material inputs supplied in noncompetitive local markets, which a local joint venture partner is better placed to provide.

Dummy variable comparing the main line of business of the Japanese parent with the affiliate's industry as described in Toyo Keizai (1994). Unrelated entries were coded as 1 in this dummy variable and related entries as 0; an unrelated entry indicates a greater need for new knowledge and assets on entry.

Size of the investment as compared to the parent firm, computed as the ratio of total employment in the investment to total employment in the parent. A similar ratio computed from sales values was also constructed; the two were moderately correlated and exhibited identical effects, and the employment-based variable was used in all reported models because it had fewer missing values.

Measure of the level of host country political and economic risk in 1993, derived from the host country risk index published in Euromoney in 1993. Euromoney's risk index has been shown to be replicable using objective host country economic and political factors.

Measure of the extent of restrictions on foreign ownership, constructed from the World Competitiveness Report, 1994. The yearbook provided information on the openness of 47 countries, including the nine host countries in this study, to foreign equity participation in domestic enterprises in 1993.

Measure of the degree of intellectual property protection in the host country environment, taken from the World Competitiveness Report, 1994. That report contains information on 81 criteria used to assess a nation's international competitiveness, developed from statistical indicators of international organizations and national institutions and from responses by 2850 executives worldwide to questionnaires concerning perceptions of the international business community.
Measure of the extent of a firm's international trade activity and its international experience, computed as the ratio of foreign sales (exports) to total sales for the years 1992 and 1993.

Measure based on the extent of the firm's international investment activity, computed as the log of the count of the number of foreign direct investments in which the firm is involved either as a majority or minority equity partner. The log form reflects the assumption that the incremental value of more international experience is greater when a firm has fewer international investments.

Measure of host country experience based on the firm's international investment activity, computed as the log of the total number of firm-years of experience in the host country. A firm-year represents 1 year of operating experience in the host country for one foreign investment, and the number of years of operating experience for each of the firm's investments in the host country were summed.

Three items measure the degree to which the assets used to produce an information service were custom-tailored to the buying firm: (1) to what degree must individuals acquire company-specific or division-specific information to adequately perform the IS function (AS1); (2) to what degree is the approach to this function custom-tailored to the company (AS2); and (3) how costly would it be to switch outsourcing vendors (SW). Items were measured on a 7-point scale (Cronbach alpha = 0.83).

Key informants indicated on a 7-point scale (1 = very difficult, 7 = very easy) the degree to which it is easy to measure the collective performance of those individuals who perform this function (Meas). We reverse scored this item to create a measure of measurement difficulty.

Two items measure the degree of change in both skills and technology: (1) to what degree are the underlying skills associated with this IS function rapidly changing (CH1); and (2) to what degree is the optimal configuration of hardware and software required to perform this function rapidly changing (CH2). Items were measured on a 7-point scale (Cronbach alpha = 0.84).

Key informants indicated their level of agreement on a 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree) with the statement that the formal contract is highly customized and required considerable legal work. The construct is measured by a single item. The survey also requested the length of the contract in pages, and the correlation between the two items was significant (rho = 0.65), but a lower response rate precluded its use as a second indicator.

Relational governance is viewed as a composite factor with the following underlying norms and dimensions: open communication and sharing of information, trust, dependence, and cooperation. Key informants indicated agreement on a 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree) with three statements: the buyer has an extremely collaborative relationship with the vendor (RG1); both parties share long- and short-term goals and plans (RG2); and the buyer can rely on the vendor to keep promises (RG3) (Cronbach alpha = 0.78).

The degree of satisfaction was measured using a 7-point scale in which '1' represented 'dissatisfied' and '7' represented 'satisfied.' Buyers reported satisfaction with: (1) the overall cost of the service; (2) the quality of the output or service; and (3) the vendor's responsiveness to problems or inquiries (Cronbach alpha = 0.84). The composite measure captures satisfaction with exchange performance rather than governance costs.

Key informants indicated agreement on a 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree) with the statement that the buyer has worked with the vendor for years and years. This measure is used as an identifying instrument in our equation predicting relational governance.

Our measure of resource scale is the natural log of size of the operating budget for IS (Budget). Firms with larger IS budgets are also likely to have in-house legal counsel with experience in drafting complex contracts. The measure is used as an identifying instrument in the equation predicting contract complexity.

Our measure of experience is the job tenure in years (ln) of the IS executive (Tenure), which proxies for firm knowledge about outsourcing. The measure is used as an identifying instrument in the equation predicting contract complexity.

variable_name: Asset specificity, measurement difficulty, technological change
description: Exchange hazards are represented by three hazard variables used together as predictors of contract complexity and relational governance: asset specificity, measurement difficulty, and technological change (uncertainty). Each is measured from key informant survey items on 7-point scales, and the hazards also enter as interaction terms.

Composite strategic choice and environmental determinism scores were created to identify each hospital's choice situation. Hospitals were classified into the minimum, differentiated, maximum or incremental choice situation. A majority of the sampled hospitals were in minimum and maximum choice situations.

Five measures of strategic choice were used: three measures of size, one of market power, and one of bargaining power. The measures were standardized and composite strategic choice scores were created to identify each hospital's choice situation.

Three environmental determinism measures were used: county population, total county income, and total number of physicians on active staff in the county. These measures attempted to capture the levels of local resources available to the hospital in potential patients, revenue, and doctors. To adjust for differences in the size of markets served, the measures were divided by the number of beds in the market, then standardized and reverse coded, where high scores reflected high resource constraints or determinism, and combined into composite scores.

Each hospital's strategy was classified as differentiation, cost leadership or muddling using three measures of differentiation and three measures of cost orientation. The differentiation indices were technological sophistication of service offerings, breadth of service offerings, and number of rare service offerings. Low cost orientation was based on total expenses divided by the average number of occupied beds for each hospital, cost adjusted per patient day, and salary adjusted per patient day.

Based on consultations with industry experts at the State of Florida's Hospital Cost Containment Board, five performance measures were chosen. The industry experts considered the set of indicators useful in discriminating between the high and low performing hospitals in the state, and the measures are consistent with previous research on hospital performance.

Following Bertrand et al. (2014), the level of specialization is measured with a Herfindahl-Hirschman Index of the issue areas in which the lobbyist lobbies, built from cumulative lobbying revenue by issue. The specification is given as a formula that is not readable in the provided text; the text states that s it-1 is cumulative lobbying revenue for lobbyist i until period t-1, s imt-1 represents cumulative lobbying revenue for lobbyist i for the specific issue area m until period t-1, and 78 denotes the number of pre-defined issue areas. By construction, the HHI can vary from 0 to 1, with larger numbers indicating a higher specialization.
time_window: cumulative from career start through period t-1

description: Natural log of a lobbyist's lobbying revenue reported in semiannual lobbying disclosure reports, calculated by aggregating the dollar amount of lobbying contracts each lobbyist is involved in each time period. In the revolving door lobbyist sample mean revenue is $863,948 and median revenue is $420,000. Given the highly skewed distribution, a natural logarithmic scale is used.

Dummy variable coded 1 for observations after the first period a connected politician is no longer assigned to one of the four powerful committees in Congress (Senate Finance and Appropriations, House Ways and Means and Appropriations) and 0 otherwise. Politicians who leave one powerful committee to simultaneously enter another are excluded.
time_window: from the period after the politician leaves the powerful committee

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 when a politician connected to a lobbyist is first assigned to one of the four powerful committees and until the politician exits the committee, and 0 otherwise. Only politicians newly assigned to powerful committees during the sample period are considered.
time_window: from the period of first assignment to the powerful committee until exit from it

description: Dummy variable coded 1 for observations after a politician connected to a lobbyist leaves office and 0 otherwise. These exits of connected politicians are largely due to defeats at reelection or voluntary retirement; cases in which the connected politician exited the House to become a Senator are excluded.
time_window: from the period after the politician leaves office

description: Dummy variable coded 1 for the years when a politician connected to a lobbyist is selected to be the chair of a standing committee in Congress and 0 otherwise. Only events in which a non-chair politician newly becomes a chair during the sample period are considered.
time_window: years in which the connected politician serves as committee chair

description: Environmental pressure from each of 14 stakeholder groups as perceived by managers, measured through seven-point Likert scales where a value of 1 indicates 'not at all important pressure' and a value of 7 indicates 'extremely important pressure'. Confirmatory factor analysis of the 14 variables retained five first-order dimensions (corporate government stakeholders, internal economic stakeholders, external economic stakeholders, regulatory stakeholders, and external social stakeholders) plus a second-order factor summarizing the five dimensions.

Self-classification variable constructed from four descriptions of environmental management shown to respondents in the questionnaire: passive response, attention to legislation response, attention to the stakeholders' response, and total environmental quality response, with assigned proactivity values from 1 to 4 respectively. The names of the categories were omitted and respondents were told that identifying with one of the four descriptions required complying with at least three of its characteristics, and they were asked to choose the most appropriate description for their firm. Convergent validity of the variable was examined with 14 indicators of environmental activity (E1 to E14) measured on seven-point Likert scales.

The first dependent variable is an indicator of whether the partner firms establish a joint steering committee to govern the alliance. Steering committee equals 1 when the contract specifies the establishment of this committee and 0 otherwise. The authors reviewed each contract to determine whether the partners devised a steering committee to support the alliance's governance.

The authors analyzed the text of termination provisions and relied on the number of unique words used to define termination provisions after excluding common grammatical forms, such as articles and prepositions. For each contract they calculate the proportion of the number of elements in the set of words present in the termination clause of the contract to the number of elements of the set of words from termination clauses across the sample. The variable takes the value of 1 if the proportion of unique words falls above the sample mean of this ratio.

Built from patent and geographic information in a disambiguated patent inventor database. The authors identify patents classified at the three-digit level under classes that include core subject matter related to the biopharmaceutical sector and count the number of distinct cited-citing patent pairs that belong in the same MSA in a five-year window before the focal year.
