This count is divided by the number of establishments that belong to the biopharmaceutical sector, so higher values reflect a greater degree of localized knowledge spillovers in the MSA in which the R&D firm is located.
time_window: five-year window before the focal year

description: A measure based on the Herfindahl-Hirschman index using information about the geographic distribution of funding to research projects from grants awarded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health. Using an organization's share of total awards at the MSA level, the authors calculate a Herfindahl index and subtract it from 1 to get the degree of dispersion. The variable ranges between 0 and 1, and higher values indicate greater intensity of R&D rivalry within the regional unit.

The authors use the number of employees that belong to the pharmaceuticals sector (North American Industry Classification System code 3254) or biotech and other research services (NAICS code 54171) and calculate the variable as a share of the total employment in the aggregated regional unit (MSA) of the R&D firm's location. Data were provided by the U.S. Census Bureau.

Membership data from the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB) are used to develop the measure. FASEB is an umbrella organization covering 27 U.S. societies in the field of biological and medical research with more than 120,000 members. The authors obtained the geographic distribution of FASEB members and matched it with U.S. Census Bureau data, measuring FASEB membership as a share of the biopharmaceutical sector employment in the MSA.

Computed as one minus the normalized Freeman et al. (1991) flow-based betweenness centralization index of the carrier's task system (the valued digraph of tasks and aircraft flows, Figure 6). In the equation CF denotes the degree to which resource flows pass through a task and CF* the most central (largest flow) task, so the measure is one minus the average difference between the most central task and all other tasks in the carrier's task system. The range is zero to one; a large value suggests that a carrier's task system is highly decentralized.

Computed as the weighted average cycle length of the tasks found in the carrier's task system. For each task, the cycle length is the length (task count) of the cycle that the task most often completes, and the weight is the proportion of task departures accounted for by that task. The shortest cycle length is two, indicating a simple roundtrip of two tasks; a large value suggests that a carrier's task system is complex.

Computed as one minus the weighted sum of the carrier's distance-based concentration index of its aircraft, 1.0 - sum_k p_ik RangeHerfindahl_ik. The weight p_ik is the proportion of departures performed with aircraft type k, and RangeHerfindahl_ik is the sum of squares of the proportion of that aircraft type's departures falling into each 250-mile range increment (with a maximum of 5,250 miles). The Range Herfindahl is one if the aircraft type is used in a single distance range and near zero if it is used across many distance ranges; the fungibility measure is bounded between zero and one, where large values suggest that a carrier's aircraft are more fungible.

Computed as one minus the weighted sum of the ratio of total aircraft ramp-to-ramp time (in use) divided by total time the aircraft is available for passenger service, 1.0 - sum_k p_ik (RampToRamp_ik / Available_ik). The weight p_ik is the proportion of departures performed with aircraft type k; RampToRamp is the total time between an aircraft pushing back from the origin gate and turning the engine off at the destination gate. The measure is bounded between zero and one, where large values suggest that aircraft are available but not in use.

Carrier i's quarterly departure OTP at time t is the proportion of departures that actually departed within 15 min of the carrier's scheduled departure time. Because the variable is bounded between zero and one, the authors apply a natural logarithm-odds transformation; a larger value denotes higher carrier departure OTP.

Using an established protocol from applied linguistics, both coders identified the frequency of figurative language across each transcribed pitch, treating as figurative those words and expressions whose contextual meaning differs from their basic and most conventional meaning. Frequency was calculated as a percentage for each transcribed text and its total length, and the coders then judged whether such usage was systematic and high versus more incidental and low. The alpha coefficient for the coding of figurative language was 0.85.

Both coders divided the movements of the entrepreneur's hands into gestures and non-gestures (self-adapting hand motions with no communicative role), described the shape, motion, placement, and orientation of the hands in each gesture, and categorized gestures into ideational gestures (subdivided into metaphoric, iconic, and deictic) and beat gestures that mark points of emphasis but present no discernible meaning. Frequency of gesturing was calculated based on the number of gestures per minute. The alpha coefficient for the gesture coding was 0.90.

Figurative language was manipulated by creating video pitches in which, in the low figurative language conditions, the entrepreneur delivered the pitch without figurative language, providing a literal and technical description of the venture focused on facts associated with the product and business. In the high figurative language conditions, the pitch included the same basic information but also a range of figurative expressions, including an anecdotal story linking the product's origins to the entrepreneur's own embodied experience of treating an injury sustained while playing soccer, likening the venture to the progression from analog to digital communication technologies, and metaphorical expressions describing the market penetration strategy as a 'targeted' and controlled 'top-down' movement into a series of markets.

Gesturing was manipulated in the video pitches. In the low gesture conditions the entrepreneur used no explicit hand or overt bodily gestures, with hands and body remaining static and hands clasped in front of the body. In the high gesture conditions the actor delivered the pitch using frequent beat gestures, including a rhythmic beating of the arms and hands to emphasize the pattern and cadence of the speech and single beats to mark important points, and a series of ideational gestures including iconic gestures (e.g., simulating the product compressing the entrepreneur's knee joint) and metaphoric gestures (e.g., moving the arms and hands away from the body in a forward motion to represent the growing market for the product).

A measure of communication-evoked imagery originally developed by Bone and Ellen (1992) and refined by Babin and Burns (1998) was used, focusing on imagery quantity and imagery elaboration. Three items assessed the quantity of imagery experienced (e.g., 'Many images came to mind') and three items assessed imagery elaboration, concerning viewers' bodily responses evoked by the imagery experienced (e.g., 'I imagined what it was like to use the product,' 'I imagined the feel of the product'). All items used a seven-point Likert style scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree), and responses to the six items were summed.

Four items measured investment intentions, asking whether, based on the pitch, respondents would take the opportunity further with a view to investing by finding out more information about the business, doing further research into the industry and/or market of the business, meeting with the entrepreneur again, and finding out more information about the entrepreneur/management team, rated on a Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree); responses were averaged into a single score. A further single item asked how likely participants would be to invest in the business, using an 11-point scale anchored at 0 (0% chance) and 10 (100% certain). The measures of investment intentions and investment likelihood were standardized and combined into a single summative indicator termed 'propensity to invest'.
scale: four items 1-5 plus one item 0-10, standardized and combined

description: Perceptions of the passion displayed by the entrepreneur were measured with the six items of the 11-item scale developed by Chen et al. (2009) concerning body language (e.g., 'The presenter had energetic body movements') and verbal delivery (e.g., 'The presenter talked with varied tone and pitch'). All items were measured on a five-point scale (1 = not at all to 5 = very much).
scale: five-point scale (1 = not at all to 5 = very much)

description: Perceptions of the preparedness of the presenter were measured with the five items of the 11-item scale developed by Chen et al. (2009), including 'The presentation content had substance' and 'The presentation was thoughtful and in-depth'. All items were measured on a five-point scale (1 = not at all to 5 = very much).
scale: five-point scale (1 = not at all to 5 = very much)

description: Ratio of cash and short-term investments to the book value of total assets. All values of cash below 0 and above 1 are dropped. It is the main explanatory variable in the models.

Tobin's q denotes the market value of a firm's assets relative to replacement costs, and is proxied by the market-to-book (M/B) ratio. The numerator is the market value of the firm, defined as the book values of long-term debt and debt in current liabilities plus the market value of equity plus preferred stock liquidation value minus deferred taxes and investment tax credit; the denominator is the book value of the firm's assets. Fiscal year-end prices are used to compute the market value of the firm, and observations where the M/B exceeds 10 are dropped.

Operationalized using the Herfindahl Index, defined as the sum of squared market shares of firms in an industry, where firm sales are used to compute market shares. Since the Herfindahl Index measures industry concentration, this measure is subtracted from 1 so that higher values equate to greater competition. Industries are defined at the four-digit SIC level.

Defined as the mean R&D intensity of all firms in the focal industry. Firm R&D intensity is calculated as R&D expenses divided by sales; missing R&D values are replaced with zeros and the upper limit for R&D intensity is capped at 1. Industries are defined at the four-digit SIC level.

A dummy variable that is equal to 1 if an industry's median M/B exceeds 1.08, and 0 otherwise. The authors first computed the median M/B ratio of each industry, the median of which across all industries was 1.08. Industries are defined at the four-digit SIC level.

The G-index is a summative index comprising 24 antitakeover provisions that assess the degree of restriction on shareholder rights. The authors state that '[a] higher G-index is assumed to mean weaker shareholder rights and lower governance quality.' Missing G-index values are replaced with those from the most recent prior period.

Palepu's entropy measure of diversification, constructed from the COMPUSTAT Segments database. The authors report that results are substantially similar if the entropy measure is replaced with either a count-based or a Herfindahl-type diversification measure.

Measured using the opacity index developed by Anderson et al. (2009), built from four proxies for firm-level opacity: trading volume, bid-ask spread, analyst following, and analyst forecast errors. Trading volume is the natural logarithm of the daily dollar trading volume for the year; bid-ask spread is the ask price less the bid price divided by the average of the bid and ask prices, averaged across all trading days in a year; analyst following is the natural logarithm of the number of analysts following each firm in a year; analyst forecast error is the square of the difference between the mean analysts' earnings forecast and actual firm earnings, scaled by the firm's stock price. These four proxies are individually ranked into deciles, with the most opaque firms taking a value of 10 and the least opaque assuming a value of 1; the four rankings are summed and scaled by a factor of 40 to provide an index that ranges from 0.1 to 1.0, where lower values denote more transparent firms and higher values denote more opaque firms.

A time-changing variable that takes the value of 1 starting in the year in which retail deregulation was enacted or a regulatory order was issued, and 0 otherwise. Because 17 percent of the utilities operate in both regulated and deregulated states, the variable was weighted based on the percentage of electricity sold by the utility in each state. Information on state retail deregulation came from the U.S. Department of Energy (2000).
scale: 0/1, weighted by share of electricity sold per state
time_window: takes the value of 1 from the year of enactment onward

description: The League of Conservation Voters index counts the number of times each representative or senator in Congress votes in favor of the environmental agenda and ranges from 0 to 100, with 100 representing a record of voting with the environmental agenda in all cases. Following Kahn (2002) and Levinson (1999), the raw variable is calculated as the average of the environmental scores of members of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate. This average was then weighted by the total number of Congressional representatives in each state and by the percentage of generation of each firm in each state.
level: utility-year (state-level score weighted to the utility)

description: Using EGRID, the authors calculated the percentage of electricity generated by coal for each utility. The variable enters the regressions lagged one year and de-meaned before the interaction term is computed.

Productive efficiency was estimated using Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA). The DEA technique uses linear programming to convert multiple input and output measures into a single measure of relative efficiency for each observation. Further details of the DEA calculation are reported by the authors in the Appendix.

variable_name: Change in percentage of generation from renewables
description: This variable represents the yearly changes in percentages of renewable generation as a percentage of the electricity generated by a utility. Using information from the EGRID database, the authors calculated the difference between the percentages of renewable generation in two consecutive years. The equation for this difference is not readable in the text provided.

Assessed with a structured perception questionnaire administered to the top management of the acquired firms. The final measure consists of seven dimensions of three to five items each, 29 items in total, and each item elicits responses concerning cultural differences on a five-point scale ranging from very similar to very different. Responses were deemed reliable when a minimum of 80 percent of the perceptions demonstrated an acceptable level of agreement, and the seven dimensions were collapsed into a single index by summing the scores for all 29 items and then taking their average.
scale: five-point scale ranging from very similar to very different
time_window: up to 3 years after the merger

description: A questionnaire of 23 items asked the top management of the acquired firm to report, on a five-point scale, the extent to which their goals and decisions were imposed on them by the buying firm. The authors assume that control mechanisms represent the primary means by which buyers transfer their own culture to the sellers, so the more controls, the less the tolerance. The two dimensions were collapsed into a single index by taking the average score for all 23 items.
level: firm (top management team of the acquired firm reporting on the buying firm)

description: Historic parameters were obtained by longitudinally regressing 150 trading days of data beginning 200 trading days before the merger announcement day, and these parameters were used to compute abnormal returns, the firm's returns in excess of its expected market returns. The estimates of the standardized abnormal returns were cumulated over a 16-day interval, beginning 10 trading days before the first public announcement and continuing to 5 days after the announcement day; a 7-day interval was also used. The formal equation for the market model is not readable in the text provided.
time_window: 16-day interval from 10 trading days before to 5 trading days after the first public announcement (and a 7-day interval)

description: Ten items of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule adapted into Spanish rate on a five-point scale the extent to which the CEO generally experiences each affect. The measure used is the factor score from a principal component analysis with varimax rotation; the component comprised all the positive affect items and Cronbach's alpha was 0.820.
scale: five-point response scale per item; factor scores

description: Ten negative affect items of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule adapted into Spanish rate on a five-point scale the extent to which the CEO generally experiences each affect. Nine of the ten items loaded on the negative affect component and the remaining item, distressed, showed a loading of 0.292, so the principal component analysis was rerun excluding it; the measure used is the factor score of that component and Cronbach's alpha was 0.859.
scale: five-point response scale per item; factor scores

description: Each asset strategy is measured as the proportion of a given asset type to total assets, and is assumed to represent service to different market segments. Each asset strategy is compared to the industry mean for that strategy and expressed as a standard deviation; the measure of global strategic deviation sums the absolute values of the standard deviations for all the asset strategies and is multiplied by minus one to convert its meaning to conformity. The Cronbach alpha across the deviations of all asset categories was 0.740.

Three measures frequently employed to evaluate bank performance are used: ROA, the standard return on average assets, and gross operating profit margin and net operating profit margin, the ratios of gross income to total assets and net income to total assets respectively. The authors state that the measures of typical performance were calculated like that of strategic conformity, i.e., from the deviation of the institution from the industry mean expressed as a standard deviation.

The total percentage of stock held by shareholders that owned at least 3 percent of a firm's stock, for both U.S. and Japanese firms. The authors used 3 percent to capture the influence of large owners, including pension funds, which customarily hold less than 5 percent of a single firm's stock. U.S. ownership data came from Compact Disclosure, and Japanese ownership data came from the Japan Company Handbook, which provides information on the identity and ownership position of each major shareholder.

The ratio of R&D investment to sales in 1995. For the U.S. sample these data come from COMPUSTAT; for the Japanese sample they come from the Japan Company Handbook. The authors note that U.S. firms are required to expense investments in R&D in each period whereas Japanese firms are allowed to capitalize R&D expenditures, but they argue that this difference in accounting standards would not bias results and that, to the extent Japanese firms underreport R&D, the reporting bias works against their results.
A dummy variable for country, coded 1 for Japanese firms and 0 for U.S. firms. It was included in the pooled regression to allow a test of differences between the U.S. and Japanese samples.

Two indicators for 1990: the percentage of equity owned by pension funds and the number of pension funds owning a firm's stock. The percentage of equity owned was calculated as the sum of their ownership divided by common shares outstanding. Institutional ownership data were collected from the Spectrum III database, and public pension funds were identified from Pensions and Investments.

Two indicators for 1990: the percentage of equity owned by investment manager funds and the number of investment manager funds owning a firm's stock. The percentage of equity owned was calculated as the sum of their ownership divided by common shares outstanding. Mutual funds were identified from the Investment Company Institute's Directory of Mutual Funds, and securities brokers and banks by comparing the list of investors on Spectrum III with firms included in the COMPUSTAT tapes in the securities and banking industries (SIC codes 60 and 62).

Two indicators measuring different aspects of the construct: firm R&D intensity and new product intensity. R&D intensity, measuring inputs to innovation, was the average of a firm's reported R&D per $1,000 of sales in 1991 and 1992. New product data, measuring innovation outputs, came from Dialog's PTS New Product Announcements database; the mean of new product announcements over the two years was divided by mean firm sales as an adjustment for size effects in the number of announcements.

Three survey items assessing the importance of external innovation to a firm in 1991: external acquisition of new products, external acquisitions to develop new processes, and external acquisitions to build new markets. Items were rated on a seven-point Likert scale (alpha = .73). The interrater reliability correlation for the external innovation factor, based on duplicate surveys sent to a different top executive, was .81.

Two indicators collected for 1991 for inside directors: equity and stock option valuation. The percentage of equity owned by inside directors was calculated as equity holdings divided by common shares outstanding. Inside directors' stock options, valued with the Black-Scholes method, were collected directly from the Standard & Poor's Executive Compensation Data Set.

Two indicators collected for 1991 for independent outside directors: outside director ratio and outside director equity. The outside director ratio was the number of independent outside directors divided by board size. The percentage of equity owned by outside directors was equity holdings multiplied by outside directors divided by common shares outstanding. Affiliated outside directors, defined according to SEC regulation 14A item 6b as including relatives, customers, suppliers, former employees, lawyers, and bankers, were removed from the sample.

Calculated for each county-year from the richness/variety indices proposed by Shannon and Weaver; the Shannon index is calculated as the negative sum over types of pi log(pi), where n is the total number of types, pi is the proportion of the ith type in the community, and log is the natural logarithm. Exponentiating the Shannon index produces 'true' diversity and makes it directly comparable across communities. Voluntary associations are identified based on their NTEE categorization. The kind of diversity measured is closest to what Harrison and Klein (2007) call 'variety'.

variable_name: Number of foundings of human services organizations
description: The count of human service organizations founded in a county-year, based on foundings of local non-branch, non-religious, non-foundation human services organizations from 1991 to 2010. Organizations are identified on an annual basis by their unique employer identification number and include both incorporated and unincorporated nonprofit organizations. An organization is considered newly founded if it has not filed 990 forms in the previous three or more years in a row. Only non-branch, non-religious organizations are counted, excluding hospitals and healthcare providers and specialist disaster preparedness and relief organizations.

A dummy variable set to 1 if there was a disaster declaration in a particular county in that year, gathered from the FEMA website. 'Assistance declarations,' such as for fire management assistance, were excluded. In the models the disaster shock for period t-1 predicts foundings in period t.

variable_name: Dummy for more unexpected (more novel) disaster event
description: Novelty of a disaster event is calculated as the ex-ante probability of the disaster being of a particular kind given that a disaster of any kind has happened, based on the proportion of past disasters of the focal kind among all disaster events in the previous 30 years in the county. The continuous measure is split across the median to create two conditional dummy variables, one indicating whether a lower-probability (more novel) disaster event happened and the other indicating whether a higher-probability (less novel) disaster event happened.

variable_name: Dummy for multiple kinds of disaster in a county-year
description: Disaster events are classified in six categories: earthquakes, flooding (including from tidal waves), storms (including coastal storms and hurricanes), wildfires, extreme snowfall and freeze, and drought. In testing H3 the disaster dummy variable is replaced by two dummies, one representing a single kind of disaster having happened in a year and the other for instances of multiple kinds of disaster occurring in the community in the same year.

variable_name: Dummy for natural disaster event in 5-year period before last year
description: A control dummy variable that is set to 1 if there was a disaster or mass emergency declaration in the five years preceding the previous year. It captures the very recent history of natural disaster events in an area.
time_window: five years preceding the previous year

description: Measured with a relational approach considering each dyad of founders identified from the bank application documents. For each dyad the length of time the two founders overlapped in their career histories in the same prior banking institution was captured as Tij; the sum of Tij for all dyads was divided by the total number of dyads in the founding team. For example, a three-member team with a four-year shared dyad yields a value of 1.33 (four divided by three).

New bank performance measured as return on assets (ROA) at the end of the bank's first full calendar year (e.g., a bank that began operations in 1999 uses ROA of 2000). Expressed as net income as a percentage of assets. ROA information was collected from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). The authors note that performance is highly volatile during the start-up year and that most banks stabilize by the end of their second year, and that most banks sustain negative earnings in their early tenure.
time_window: end of first full calendar year of operation

description: Because performance was measured for the first full calendar year, teams had varying amounts of shared current experience before that period. The authors counted the number of months that the team operated during its initial (partial) year as a proxy for current shared experience. The variable ranged from 1 (the team began working together in the prior December) to 12 (the team began working together in the prior January).
time_window: initial partial year before the performance measure

description: Using a dyadic approach, for each dyad of founders with PSE the prior experience was coded 1 if it occurred in a bank charter type that did not match the new bank's charter type, and 0 if the charter types matched; the values were summed and divided by the total number of PSE dyads in the founding team. The variable ranges from 0 (total match) to 1 (total mismatch); for example, three mismatched dyads and one matched dyad give (3 + 0)/(3 + 1) = 0.75.

For each PSE dyad in a founding team the last calendar year of shared experience was recorded; the difference between that last calendar year and the year the new bank was chartered was taken, summed across dyads, and divided by the total number of PSE dyads. The authors illustrate with Bridge Bank, established in 1996, whose gap since PSE was 1.36 years.
time_window: between last year of shared experience and founding year

description: Indicator variable that takes the value of one if, according to the CDP survey, the firm is exposed to physical climate risk, and zero otherwise. The CDP asks firms annually how their company is exposed to physical risks from climate change, with the possible answers 'we consider our company to be exposed to physical risks', 'we do not know the answer to this question', and 'we do not consider our company to be exposed to physical risks'. The measure captures firm managers' perception of climate impact on their firms' operations.

Subsidiary-weighted average number of climate-related natural disasters that occurred in the states where the firm's subsidiaries are located, scaled by 100. Disaster events are obtained from SHELDUS and aggregated by state and year; subsidiary locations are identified following the approach of Dyreng, Lindsey, and Thornock (2013). Higher values indicate greater exposure to physical climate risk.

The price term of the loan, measured as the rate of interest and fees paid in basis points in excess of LIBOR or its equivalent, adopting its natural logarithmic form. Loan contract information is retrieved from DealScan. Higher loan spread indicates a more stringent loan contracting term.
scale: basis points over LIBOR, natural logarithm

description: Equals one if the facility has secured assets, and zero otherwise. Secured status is a non-price term indicating that the loan is collateralized and therefore more stringent.
The number of covenants in the loan contract, used as a non-price term. A larger number of covenants indicates more stringent loan contracting terms.
Indicator variable that equals one if the firm integrates climate change into its overall business strategy, and zero otherwise, based on CDP survey information.

Indicator variable that equals one if the highest level of direct responsibility for climate change issues in the firm is with the board of directors, and zero otherwise, based on CDP survey information.

Indicator variable that equals one if the firm has set up a specific climate change risk management process or if climate risk is integrated into a multi-disciplinary company-wide risk management system, and zero otherwise, based on CDP survey information.
Indicator variable that equals one if the firm possesses potential opportunities related to climate change, and zero otherwise, based on CDP survey information.
Indicator variable that equals one if the firm engages in activities that could directly influence public policies on climate change, and zero otherwise, based on CDP survey information.

One-year ahead return on assets, calculated as income before extraordinary items divided by total assets. It is used to proxy for the borrowing firm's operational performance in the channel test. Firm accounting information is retrieved from Compustat.
One-year ahead cash flow from operations, used together with one-year ahead ROA to proxy for the borrowing firm's operational performance in the channel test.
One-year ahead probability of default, estimated following Bharath and Shumway (2008), used to measure the borrowing firm's loan default risk in the channel test.

Indicator variables for CEOs who earned an MBA degree before the 1970s (MBA60), in the 1970s (1971-1980; MBA70), or after the 1970s (MBA80). Data on CEOs' MBA education and the year the degree was received came primarily from the Who's Who database, supplemented by BusinessWeek's executive database and newspaper articles. Undergraduate business degrees and certificates of executive programs for senior managers were not considered.

Rate of acquisition deals announced by the firm, taken from SDC Platinum's Mergers and Acquisitions database. Deals are counted as diversifying when the acquiring firm's industry differs from that of the acquired firm or asset at the two-digit SIC level. The timing of announcements is used, so some announced deals may not have been completed. The duration metric is day and the clock is reset to zero once a firm made an acquisition announcement (gap-time spells).

Percentage of outside directors-those directors not employed by the firm (e.g., senior executives)-on the board, used to measure the effectiveness of board monitoring. Information was collected from Standard & Poor's Register.

Percentage of a given firm's stock owned by all blockholding institutional investors, each of whom held at least 5 percent of the firm's stock; used to measure the effectiveness of institutional-investor monitoring. Information was collected from Thomson Financial's institutional ownership database.

Indicator variable for CEO duality: when the same person holds both the CEO and board chair positions. Described as a common measure of CEO power in previous studies; data collected from Standard & Poor's Register.

The CEO's tenure in the position, used as a measure of CEO power because the longer a CEO stays in the position the more intra-organizational power he or she accumulates. Data collected from Standard & Poor's Register.

Measured in months, taking the license date as the onset of risk and the date of application for the first patent filed after the signing of the license agreement as the transition time. For the matched non-licensee the onset of risk is the time when the matched licensee signed the license agreement (t=0). Application dates rather than grant dates are used so that results are not biased by differences in patent office procedures.
time_window: months from license signing (or matched t=0) to first patent application, censored at May 2008

description: A dummy generated by the matching procedure that distinguishes licensees from non-licensees and is used to test Hypothesis 1. It takes the value one for firms that signed the license agreement of reference and zero for their matched non-licensees.

A dummy variable indicating inclusion of a grant-back clause, created by going through the license agreements one by one. Non-licensees are attributed a value of 0 because by definition there is no grant-back clause without a licensing contract.

A dummy for unfamiliarity: a technology is regarded as unfamiliar to the licensee if the licensee's prior patent history (previous six years) did not include any patent grants in the International Patent Classification (IPC) code listed in the patent(s) included in the license agreement. Because unfamiliarity relates to the patents included in the license agreements, the variable is calculated only for licensees.
time_window: previous six years before the license agreement

description: A naive Bayesian machine-learning classifier trained on hand-coded sentences scores all relevant annual report sections. The software assigns each sentence a probability that each of 21 themes is present, based on word co-occurrences learned from the training set, and these probabilities are aggregated across the sentences of a report and adjusted by the number of sentences to provide measures of relative theme presence or 'density'. Reports with fewer than 25 sentences with a score on one or more themes were excluded, and theme scores were standardized across reports.

variable_name: principal component scores on seven strategic factors
description: Principal components analysis (SPSS factor-principal components method) with Varimax rotation reduced the 21 theme scores for each annual report to a smaller number of higher-order indicators of patterns of strategic cognition. Seven components with eigenvalues greater than one were retained, capturing 55% of the variance, and were labelled on the basis of the theoretical origins of the coding scheme and the pattern of loadings.

variable_name: cluster membership in six cognitive strategic groups
description: The Mclust package in R, a model-based clustering algorithm, was applied at the individual report level and suggested a six-cluster solution for model VVV as optimal (Bayesian Information Criterion = 69,563.89). Clusters were given interpretive labels on the basis of average factor scores by cluster and their theoretical origins.

ROE is calculated by dividing net profit before abnormals by shareholders' equity, and is set to null where shareholders' equity is less than or equal to zero. ROA is a fiscal year's earnings divided by total assets, that is, shareholders' equity as well as other borrowings. PER is a valuation measure that divides the company's closing share price on the last day of its financial year by pre-abnormals earnings per share. The first two are accounting-based indicators of the efficiency with which a firm applies its resources, while the third is a market-based measure generally viewed as reflecting investors' expectations and judgments about the quality of a firm's future performance.

Sampled companies were classified by the top-level Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) sector. The top-level GICS includes 10 sectors: Consumer Discretionary, Consumer Staples, Energy, Financial, Health, Industrial, Information Technology, Materials, Telecommunications, and Utilities; the last two were excluded owing to the small numbers of firms, leaving eight sectors used in the analysis.

variable_name: Annual report sections attributed to a top-level executive
description: The top team is operationalized as the top-level executives whose statements are analyzed: only sections of annual reports whose titles identify the source of the content as a top-level executive, typically the message to shareholders from the CEO or managing director, were content analyzed. The paper has no variable describing the team itself (composition, size or characteristics); the top team is the assumed author of the text from which attention is measured.

variable_name: return on assets before tax and exceptional items
description: Return on assets before tax and exceptional items, averaged over three years with 1983 and 1993 as midpoints to smooth any irregularities. For the United Kingdom, financial data were taken from Datastream, with the few gaps filled on a consistent basis from annual reports; for France, data were taken direct from annual reports; for Germany, data were taken from annual reports, the Wegweiser durch deutsche Unternehmen, and the official governmental publication Der Bundesanzeiger. The authors note the limitations of accounting performance measures, including their susceptibility to managerial manipulation, but state that the high proportion of French and German firms not actively traded on financial markets made financial market-based measures inappropriate.
time_window: three-year average with 1983 and 1993 as midpoints (1982-84 and 1992-94)

description: Indicator of firms following a related-constrained strategy, that is firms drawing more than 30 percent of their turnover from businesses related in terms of technologies and markets and having tightly clustered relationships between all businesses in their portfolio. Strategies were coded following Rumelt (1974) from annual reports, business directories and other publicly available sources, classified independently by two judges with a third judge helping resolve disagreements (initial agreement 93.4 percent), and checked against interviews with senior managers in a subset of firms.

Indicator of firms following a related-linked strategy, that is firms drawing more than 30 percent of their turnover from businesses related in terms of technologies and markets but having a series of limited relationships between businesses. Coded with the same procedure as the other Rumelt types, from annual reports, business directories and other publicly available sources, independently by two judges with a third resolving disagreements, and checked by interviews with senior managers in a subset of firms.

Indicator of firms following an unrelated diversification strategy, one of the four Rumelt types used, coded from annual reports, business directories and other publicly available sources and classified independently by two judges with a third judge helping resolve disagreements. The authors contrast unrelated diversifiers with related diversifiers, which are held to enjoy operational synergies and knowledge transferability.

Rumelt's single and dominant business strategies combined into a single 'undiversified' category, coded with the same procedure as the other strategy types from annual reports, business directories and other publicly available sources with two independent judges and a third resolving disagreements. The reported results concern the performance effects of the other strategy types.

Dummy variables identifying the firm's home country among France, Germany and the United Kingdom in the aggregate regression, with the United Kingdom as the omitted reference variable. In the disaggregated analysis, separate regressions are run for each country. The authors report that the negative coefficient for Germany suggests that levels of financial performance are typically lower than in the United Kingdom.

The analysis covers two time periods, 1982-84 and 1992-94, with 1983 and 1993 as midpoints, and performance is averaged over the three years of each period. The aggregate regression indicates that performance does not vary significantly over the period; the disaggregated regressions are run separately for each time point.

Domestic commercial performance was measured by the logged (due to the skewed distribution of commercial performance) number of admissions in the domestic country. It is a film-level variable based on yearly domestic admissions reported in LUMIERE.

Artistic acclaim was measured by a binary variable that indicates whether or not a film was selected to open in (main) competition at Cannes, Berlin, or Venice. These three festivals are the most prestigious and important film festivals worldwide, and films open in them before opening to the general public, so the measure is not affected by commercial performance.

Cultural distance between the film-producing country and the market country was measured using Hofstede's (1980) widely accepted measure of cultural distance. Following Kogut and Singh (1988), the measure takes the difference between the two countries' scores on the four key cultural dimensions, corrects for the variance differences of each dimension by dividing the squared difference in the scores by the variance of each dimension, and then arithmetically averages the four numbers.

A binary variable was used to distinguish between major and independent distributors. For each market country, all major distributors were identified using Lange and Newman-Baudais' (2007) comprehensive description of film distribution companies in Europe: subsidiaries of U.S. distributors, such as United International Pictures, 20th Century Fox, and Warner Brothers, and large European distributors distributing films for the major U.S. studios were defined as major distributors. Independent distributors are defined as all the non-major distributors in the film's domestic market.

A binary variable was used to distinguish between major and independent distributors in each foreign market country. Major distributors were identified using Lange and Newman-Baudais' (2007) description of film distribution companies in Europe, defining subsidiaries of U.S. distributors and large European distributors distributing films for the major U.S. studios as major distributors, and all non-major distributors as independent distributors.

The unobserved likelihood that a film will be exported to a given foreign market country. Film exports are modeled as a sequential process: once produced, a film can be exported to each of the 32 other market countries, which creates 32 film-market country dyads per film, and observations are at the film/market country/year level, observed until the film is exported to the focal market country or until 2009 if it is not exported within the timeframe.
time_window: Observed until exported to the focal market country or until 2009

description: Foreign commercial performance was measured in terms of the logged (due to the skewed distribution of commercial performance) number of admissions in the foreign country. Only exported film/market country dyads are included in these models, and the inverse Mills' ratio for each film estimated by the Cox proportional hazards model is included to account for selection bias.

Our main independent variable is same-NPI-mode experience, which we captured by counting the number of times a firm has used a mode since its entry into a particular area of business (fighter, helicopter, jet, or turboprop). This measure corresponds to the traditional measure of experience based on cumulative output. Same-NPI-mode experience ranges from 0 to 9, with an average of 1.81.
time_window: cumulative since the firm's entry into the area of business

description: Our dependent variable is NPI performance, which we assessed by the cumulative unit sales of each aircraft. Sixty-four of the aircraft included in our sample were still being produced in 2000; to avoid midprogram bias, we estimated the unit sales for these projects based on the production schedule of those projects whose production was terminated in 2000. Overall, cumulative unit sales range from 3 to 8,584, with a mean of 575.

We classified as internal developments all aircraft listing a single firm under the Contractor heading. When at least two firms are listed under the Contractor heading, we classified the aircraft as a joint development. We coded as licensing when a firm acquired for a lump sum and royalties the right to manufacture and commercialize an aircraft that was initially developed by another manufacturer, in which case the name of the licensee appears under the Licensee heading. The data include 169 introductions of internally developed aircraft, 56 introductions of jointly developed aircraft, and 53 introductions of licensed aircraft.

As is common in studies of the aircraft industry, we estimated an aircraft's technological complexity by the logarithm of its maximum speed, range, and takeoff weight. It is entered in the performance models as a control and interacted with same-NPI-mode experience.
scale: logarithm of maximum speed, range, and takeoff weight

variable_name: Coefficient of same-NPI-mode experience within each mode
description: The speed of experiential learning is the marginal performance benefit of experience, taken as the coefficient of same-NPI-mode experience on cumulative unit sales in separate regressions for internal development, joint development and licensing (Models 3a, 4a, 5a). Coefficients are compared across modes with seemingly unrelated estimation (suest) and a Wald test. It is a derived quantity from regression coefficients, not a separate variable.

variable_name: Inflexion point of the same-NPI-mode experience-performance curve
description: The experience threshold is the level of same-NPI-mode experience at which benefits level off, taken as the inflexion point of the quadratic relationship between same-NPI-mode experience (main and squared terms) and cumulative unit sales, estimated separately for internal development, joint development and licensing. The inflexion points (6.47 in internal development, 1.64 in joint development; no experience benefits in licensing) are compared across modes with seemingly unrelated estimation and a Wald test. It is a derived quantity from regression coefficients, not a separate variable.

Market coverage was measured as the ratio of the number of individual branch facilities that a bank established in a given county to the total number of branches that all banks operated in that county. The mean score of each bank on the measure was first computed for the period 1984-86. The difference measure is the absolute value of the difference between the bidder's score and the target's score on the variable, so higher values indicate greater dissimilarity between the merging banks.

Operational efficiency was measured as the ratio of overhead expenditure to total bank revenues (overhead/revenues), an indicator often used in banking studies. Mean scores of each bank for 1984-86 were computed, and the difference measure is the absolute value of the difference between the bidder's and the target's scores. Higher values indicate greater dissimilarity in operational efficiency between the merging banks.

Emphasis on marketing activity was measured as the ratio of marketing expenditure to total bank revenues (marketing expenditure/revenues). The mean score of each bank on this element of strategy was computed for 1984-86. The difference measure is the absolute value of the difference between the bidder's and the target's scores, with higher values indicating greater dissimilarity in marketing emphasis.

Client mix was captured by the ratio of business loans to consumer loans, which distinguishes wholesale from retail banking. Mean scores for each bank were computed over 1984-86, and the difference measure is the absolute value of the difference between the bidder's and the target's scores on the ratio. Higher values indicate greater dissimilarity in the client mix of the merging banks.

Risk propensity was measured as the ratio of core capital to loans outstanding, an indicator used by bank analysts of a bank's degree of aggressiveness. Mean scores of each bank for the period 1984-86 were computed, and the difference measure is the absolute value of the difference between the bidder's and the target's scores on the ratio. Higher values indicate greater dissimilarity in risk propensity between the merging banks.

variable_name: Change in performance following the merger
description: Performance was measured with accounting profitability, using return on assets (ROA), which is the accounting measure least sensitive to the estimation bias induced by changes in leverage or bargaining power resulting from a merger. Ex ante performance is the revenue-weighted mean of the ROA of both the target and the bidder over the three years (1984-86) preceding the merger, and ex post profitability of the bidder was computed similarly for 1988-90, with the merger year dropped. The dependent variable is the difference between premerger and postmerger performance.

Market reaction is measured as the cumulative abnormal returns earned by shareholders around the adoption announcement; the abnormal return is the difference between the observed return and the normal return predicted by the capital asset pricing model. Daily security market rates of return are taken from the CRSP daily file, and the abnormal returns are standardized for use as the dependent variable in the cross-sectional regression. The proxy statement mailing date is used as the estimate of the date of the first public announcement, except for 36 announcements located earlier in the Wall Street Journal Index and for poison pills with no corresponding proxy statement, for which the date reported in Corporate Control Alert is used. The event window runs from 50 days before to 5 days after the announcement date.
time_window: -50 to +5 days around the announcement date

description: The first measure of the independent monitoring of the board is the proportion of outsiders on the board, where outsiders are directors who are not current or previous executives of the firm or its subsidiaries. Data on board composition were obtained from proxy statements.
level: firm board at the provision announcement

description: The second measure is the proportion of outside members who were not appointed during the incumbent CEO's tenure on the corporate board, used as a more fine-grained measure of outsiders' independence, because the independence of outside members can depend on who appointed them to the board. Data were obtained from proxy statements.
level: firm board at the provision announcement

description: Leadership of the board is coded as a dummy variable: 1, if the CEO and chairperson of the board are held by the same individual, and 0, if they are held by different individuals. Data on board composition and leadership were obtained from proxy statements.
level: firm board at the provision announcement

variable_name: ratio of royalties earned from licensing to unaffiliated foreigners over sales revenues from subsidiaries
description: The dependent variable is the ratio of royalties earned from licensing to unaffiliated foreigners over sales revenues from subsidiaries. Royalties from unaffiliated foreigners are payments of royalties and license fees in return for the use of intangible property or rights to firms in which the seller has less than a 10 percent ownership interest; sales revenues of subsidiaries are gross sales less adjustments exclusive of taxes of firms in which the parent company has a majority ownership (greater than 50% of the voting stock). Because initial examination showed the data were not normally distributed, N-scores for the dependent variable were calculated according to the DATADESK normalization procedures, and regressions were run on the normalized variable.
level: 2-digit SIC manufacturing industry investing in a host country

variable_name: ratio of royalties earned from licensing to unaffiliated foreigners over sales revenues from subsidiaries
description: The dependent variable is the ratio of royalties earned from licensing to unaffiliated foreigners over sales revenues from subsidiaries. Royalties from unaffiliated foreigners are payments of royalties and license fees in return for the use of intangible property or rights to firms in which the seller has less than a 10 percent ownership interest; sales revenues of subsidiaries are gross sales less adjustments exclusive of taxes of firms in which the parent company has a majority ownership (greater than 50% of the voting stock). Because initial examination showed the data were not normally distributed, N-scores for the dependent variable were calculated according to the DATADESK normalization procedures, and regressions were run on the normalized variable.
level: 2-digit SIC manufacturing industry investing in a host country

description: The power distance index is taken from Hofstede (1980), who surveyed over 116,000 employees in more than 40 overseas subsidiaries of IBM to create ordinal scales for countries on four cultural dimensions based on a standardized factor analysis of questionnaires. In the development of the indices, Hofstede controlled for bias for differences in occupational positions among subsidiaries.

The integration scale was taken from a study by the Chinese Culture Connection (1987), in which Chinese social scientists administered a questionnaire to 50 male and female undergraduates in 20 countries; integration was one of the dimensions that resulted from a factor analysis of the data. Integration includes questions that discuss trustworthiness, harmony with others, tolerance of others, solidarity with others, and noncompetitiveness—in other words, interpersonal trust.

Dichotomous variable set to 1 for alliances meeting ReCap's definition of an equity agreement, alliances involving the issuance of a minority share of less than 50% of legal ownership interest in an entity, and set to 0 for alliances not involving the issuance of legal ownership interest. Equity investments were by the client firm in the target firm. The data included only eight joint ventures, which the authors treated as equity alliances.

Dichotomous variable set to 1 for alliances that ReCap characterized as Collaboration (two or more parties perform research and/or development activities in a single R&D program) or Co-Development (both parties participate to some degree in the clinical development of a compound or project), either of which describes parties coinvolved at the same stage of the innovation process. Set to 0 for alliances ReCap characterized as Research or Development, in which a sponsoring party engages another party to perform R&D services. The variable applies the link-versus-scale alliance distinction to innovation alliances.

Number of alliances the target firm had initiated in the last five years. Following Sampson (2005), the authors assumed that coordination skills are gained from any type of alliance and therefore did not distinguish between prior alliances with and without pooled R&D activities in measuring alliance experience.

Number of alliances the client firm had initiated in the last five years. As with the target firm, the authors did not distinguish between prior alliances with and without pooled R&D activities in measuring client alliance experience.

variable_name: Combinations of target and client firms' alliance experience
description: The sample is split into subgroups based on the median values of the target and client firms' alliance experience, and models are estimated separately for each combination of high and low experience for the two partners. The coefficient for pooled R&D activities is then compared across groups using the Wald chi-square statistic and the ratio of the pooled R&D coefficient to the alliance scope coefficient.

Participants were randomly assigned to a decision-maker or control condition. Decision-makers were told their evaluations would be the final word and would determine whether the idea advanced; control participants were told their ratings would be averaged with others' ratings. The variable distinguishes the decision-maker role from the control role.

variable_name: percentage of time in a decision-making role
description: Participants rated the percentage of time they spend in decision-maker roles, defined as responsible for resourcing or funding ideas.

A three-item scale with the stem 'While making this decision, to what extent, did you:' followed by 'focus on economic concerns,' 'care about whether this decision made business sense,' and 'focus on the economic consequences of the decision' (α = .86).

Participants described their main role and its main goals and function. Three independent coders blind to the study's hypotheses rated the extent to which participants described the main goals of their role using terms from prior research priming economic mindset, such as profitable, efficient, and cost-benefit analysis, on a 1-4 scale (mean pairwise α = .75).
scale: 1-4 (1 = no economic mindset, 4 = strong economic mindset)

description: Participants saw a video pitch with either high or low social approval cues. In the high social approval condition, the idea had received 178% of its requested funding from 396 contributors on Kickstarter and 22,000 Facebook likes; in the low social approval condition, the idea had amassed 22% of funding from 12 funders and 31 Facebook likes.

Participants rated the password pill idea on a mock Kickstarter.com page. In the high social approval condition, the idea had 268 backers and was 94% funded; in the low social approval condition, 22% of funding had been amassed from 12 funders. Participants were told the campaign had been on for over 30 days.
Participants assessed how 'creative' and 'innovative' they thought the dirty diaper recycling idea was (α = .90) on a 7-point scale.
Participants rated the password pill idea using the same creativity scale used in Study 1 (α = .84).
Participants assessed idea usefulness with a three-item measure, specifically how 'practical,' 'feasible,' and 'useful' the idea was (α = .84).
A two-item usefulness scale including the words 'useful' and 'practical' (α = .70) on a 7-point scale.

variable_name: Performance rank group of ISV i,t+1
description: An ISV's market share is computed as a weighted sum of the ISV's market shares in all software product markets in which it operates, where the weights are the percentages of the ISV's total revenues coming from the different product markets. Performance rank is obtained by ordering all ISVs' time t+1 weighted market share scores from highest to lowest. Using this ordering, the ISVs are classified into five performance groups: (1) lowest 20 percent; (2) low-mid 20 percent; (3) mid 20 percent; (4) mid-high 20 percent; and (5) highest 20 percent. Each performance group is numbered from 1 to 5, with 5 denoting the highest 20 percent, and the computations are repeated for all years.

Hypercompetitiveness of the software industry is measured with annual changes in the performance rank orders of ISVs. In Model 1 all year dummies are included and their significance indicates whether the performance rank orders of the ISVs changed significantly every year. The covariates are set to their yearly means and the coefficients of the year dummies are used to plot the time t+1 probability of an ISV being classified into one of the five performance rank groups, using year 1991 as the baseline.

Computed as a weighted sum of all pairwise complementarity scores in the ISV's existing product portfolio, in which the double sum captures the asymmetric complementarity relationships between all product market pairs. Larger values denote higher levels of complementarity within the product portfolio. Pairwise complementarity of two product markets is inferred from the extent to which customers purchase and use the products of the two markets together, measured with a cosine similarity metric on the sales data of all ISVs offering products in those markets; the values range from 0.0, denoting independent product markets, to 1.0, denoting highly complementary product markets.

Computed with the same approach as the complementarity within the existing portfolio, applied to the portfolio of newly entered product markets at time t. Higher levels of Complementarity of N entry i,t are observable manifestations of the firm's ability to enter strongly complementary product markets in the constantly shifting web of complementarity relationships among product markets in the industry.

Computed with the same approach as the complementarity within the existing portfolio, applied to the portfolio of product markets exited at time t. Higher levels of Complementarity of N exit i,t indicate that the firm is not able to recognize some of the strongly complementary product markets in the industry and, hence, it exits them and forgoes their potential performance advantages.

variable_name: Industry position of N existing i,t
description: Computed as the revenue weighted sum over all of the ISV's product markets in N inside i,t with all other product markets j' in N outside i,t, i.e., all other product markets in the industry in which the ISV does not participate. Large values are observable manifestations of the firm's ability to reposition its portfolio to a more central, complementarity position in the industry.

variable_name: Industry position of N entry i,t
description: Computed with the same approach as the complementarity position of the existing portfolio, applied to the product markets the ISV entered at time t. It captures the strength of complementarity relationships between the entered products and all other product markets in the industry in which the ISV does not participate.

variable_name: Industry position of N exit i,t
description: Computed with the same approach as the complementarity position of the existing portfolio, applied to the product markets the ISV exited at time t. It captures the strength of complementarity relationships between the exited products and all other product markets in the industry in which the ISV does not participate.

variable_name: Resource reconfiguration in N existing i,t
description: For each pair of product markets in the ISV's existing portfolio, the direction of change in the strength of complementarity from t - 1 to t is measured as the log of the ratio of the two pairwise complementarity values, and the direction of change in the firm's resource allocation between the product markets is measured as the change in emphasis, i.e., the log of the ratio of the ISV's revenue proportions in the two product markets. The two terms are multiplied for each product market pair and summed over all product market pairs in the ISV's existing portfolio. A net positive sum indicates that the firm is making coherent resource reconfigurations, whereas a negative sum indicates that the firm is not making coherent reconfigurations to its portfolio in response to the changing product market complementarities in the industry.

Four items adapted from Xin and Pearce (1996). The scale indicates the extent to which the venture's senior management over the past 3 years has spent much effort in cultivating personal connections with officials of government and its agencies, maintained good relationships with officials of state banks and other governmental agencies, devoted substantial resources to maintain good relationships with officials of administrative agencies, and spent a lot of money on building relations with the top officials in government. Cronbach's alpha for the scale is above the 0.70 threshold.

Following McGee et al. (1995), functional experience was measured with five items that reflect the extent to which members of the senior management had functional experience in the listed areas. This measure indicates the overall experience of a venture's senior management across the various functional areas.

New venture performance was measured by eight items. The respondent was asked to rate his or her venture's performance relative to its principal competitors over the last 3 years on the eight listed dimensions.
State ownership was coded 1 for state-owned ventures and 0 otherwise. Because it is a dummy variable, it took the values of zero and one when the interaction effect was plotted.

Four items were used to measure dysfunctional competition (Li and Atuahene-Gima, 2001). They indicate the extent to which the venture's principal industry (i.e., the industry that accounts for the largest percentage of the venture's sales) has experienced the listed conditions in the last 3 years.

The primary dependent variable. CEOs identified which of four entities - corporate board, corporate management, local (hospital) board, or local management - made decisions in each of 14 decision areas. Responses were scored 0 when local management or the local board made decisions exclusively, 1 when local and corporate authorities shared decision making, and 2 when corporate management or the corporate board made decisions exclusively; scores were totaled for each area and divided by the highest possible cumulative score. Change was computed by subtracting the 1983 score from the 1985 score, so negative differences indicate increasing decentralization and positive scores increasing centralization.
scale: items scored 0, 1, or 2; index divided by the highest possible cumulative score

description: A system's 1983 score for overall centralization, computed the same way as the dependent variable from CEO responses on which entity made decisions in each of 14 areas, scored 0 (local management or local board exclusively), 1 (shared), or 2 (corporate management or corporate board exclusively), totaled and divided by the highest possible cumulative score. The 1983 centralization score was used as the measure of initial control strategy, and the corresponding 1983 subcategory scores were used for the four decision areas.
scale: items scored 0, 1, or 2; index divided by the highest possible cumulative score

description: Index of the locus of decision making in the management accountability and control decision area, built from the individual measurement items falling under that category and scored with the same scheme (0 = local management or board exclusively, 1 = shared, 2 = corporate management or board exclusively), totaled and divided by the highest possible score. The item on the appointment of local board members was omitted from this index because removing it raised the alpha coefficients over .60. Scores were computed for 1983 and 1985 and differenced.
scale: items scored 0, 1, or 2; index divided by the highest possible score

description: Index of the locus of decision making for resource allocation decisions - the transfer, sale, pledging, or purchase of the assets of a corporation or its divisions - built from the individual measurement items falling under that category and scored with the same 0-2 scheme (local, shared, corporate), totaled and divided by the highest possible score. Scores were computed for 1983 and 1985 and differenced.
scale: items scored 0, 1, or 2; index divided by the highest possible score

description: Index of the locus of decision making for operating policy decisions, covering decisions affecting the operating policies of divisions in their local markets such as changes in hospital bylaws, granting medical staff privileges to admitting physicians, and hospital operating and capital budget processes. Items were scored with the same 0-2 scheme (local, shared, corporate), totaled and divided by the highest possible score, and scores for 1983 and 1985 were differenced.
scale: items scored 0, 1, or 2; index divided by the highest possible score

description: Index of the locus of decision making for local strategy decisions, covering decisions affecting divisions' competitive positioning in local markets through planning, diversification, and service and product mix, such as formation of new companies, strategy formulation at a hospital level, and hospital service additions and deletions. Items were scored with the same 0-2 scheme (local, shared, corporate), totaled and divided by the highest possible score, and scores for 1983 and 1985 were differenced.
scale: items scored 0, 1, or 2; index divided by the highest possible score

description: The authors did not explicitly measure environmental uncertainty; they captured it for the time period studied, assuming that environmental conditions exist as relative rather than categorical states for key decision makers and that adaptation occurs by increments. A three-year period was employed on the assumption that key decision makers used recent environmental conditions as a referent; the period brackets the implementation of Medicare's prospective payment system in October 1983, which the authors assumed to be a major contributor to environmental uncertainty.

The size of a multihospital system, measured as the number of hospitals it owned, leased, or sponsored. Contract-managed hospitals were excluded because the authority relations between these hospitals and multihospital systems do not conform to the divisionalized form or to the continuum of decision-making authority used in the study.

Based on the number of states in which a system operated hospitals, and intended to reflect geopolitical disparities in hospitals' operating environments as well as the approximate physical distances among hospitals in a given system. To adjust for the effects of system size on dispersion, the number of states in which a system operated hospitals was divided by the square root of the number of hospitals in the system.
Number of years a system had been incorporated as of 1983; if the date of incorporation was not available, the affiliation date of the second oldest hospital in the system was substituted.

A series of four binary variables corresponding to ownership by a state or local government, investors, a secular not-for-profit entity, or a religious entity. For the multivariate analysis the religious category was designated the reference group and was omitted.

Each statement in the protocols was coded according to whether it made an explicit reference to superficial features of the technology or of a market context, that is, the objects, their attributes and characteristics. The occurrence of these statements was summarized by the number of participants who made at least one (and two or more) such statements and by the percentage of the average protocol length devoted to them. In the logistic regressions each statement formed the superficial side of the structural-versus-superficial contrast.

variable_name: structural alignment statements (first- and higher-order relationships)
description: Each statement was coded according to whether it explicitly referenced one of two types of structural relationships: first-order relationships (how a technology operates and its aims; how a market works and the aims of market actors) or higher-order relationships (the benefits and problems of a technology and of market activities, with their causes). The two forms of structural relationships were combined for the quantitative analyses. Their occurrence was summarized as the number of participants making at least one (and two or more) statements and as the percentage of average protocol length, and each statement formed the structural side of the structural-versus-superficial contrast in the logistic regressions.

Each statement was coded for the level of prior knowledge that anchored the reasoning it expressed, distinguishing low, medium and high levels, where high levels were mostly concerned with prior knowledge of markets. In the logistic regressions prior knowledge was entered with linear and curvilinear terms. As a post-experimental control, participants also reported the prior knowledge they had of the specific technologies presented, of the markets they discussed and of the problems affecting individuals in those markets, on nine-point scales anchored 1 = 'minimal knowledge'.

Voice mail was implemented for one year in two of the firm's five sales regions, with the other regions serving as non-voice-mail counterparts. Dealerships located in a sales region having access to voice mail are contrasted with dealerships located in sales regions not having such access. A field representative worked solely in a voice mail or a non-voice mail region; there was no crossover.

The number of new trucks sold by each dealership, obtained from archival sources for the year of the voice mail trial as well as for the prior year. These sales amounts were each standardized for the prior year and the trial year through the application of the Buying Power Index, reflecting the demographic and economic profile of each dealership's sales territory. The performance index is formed by dividing the actual number of trucks sold in a market by the sales measure for that territory; an index above 1 indicates that actual sales have exceeded the sales potential and conversely for results below 1.
scale: performance index; above 1 indicates actual sales exceeded sales potential
time_window: year of the voice mail trial and the prior year

description: Each respondent was asked to indicate the extent to which various media were used in communicating with a dyadic partner, answering on a five-point scale of extent of use. The verbal form combines the items for face-to-face contact, the telephone, and voice mail (the voice mail item being used only in the regions with voice mail). Factor analysis of the responses resulted, as expected, in two media forms, verbal and written. Separate verbal media use scales were formed for the field representative and for the sales manager, and their internal consistency is reported by the authors.

Each respondent was asked to indicate the extent to which written media were used in communicating with a dyadic partner, answering on a five-point scale of extent of use. The written form combines the items for facsimile and for written or printed documents. Separate written media use scales were formed for the field representative and for the sales manager, and their internal consistency is reported by the authors.

Satisfaction with the dyadic partner's interaction was determined using five-point Likert scales, with distinct items used to reflect the perspectives of the field representatives and of the sales managers. The items reflect the national sales manager's performance objectives for his field representatives and dealerships, and their face validity was assessed in a pretest. The internal consistency of the two sets of items is reported by the authors.

Cohesion is operationalized as the average network constraint of the inventors associated with a given patent. Two inventors are connected by a collaboration tie if they co-authored at least one patent within the last 3 years. The ego network constraint of each inventor is the sum of contact-specific constraints c_ij = (p_ij + sum p_iq p_qj)^2 over all contacts. All network measures were computed with the igraph R-package.
time_window: ties within the last 3 years; inventor network at the time of the patent grant

description: For each patent, the average geodesic distance of each inventor's location from the corporate headquarters in thousands of kilometers, computed with the STATA command 'geodist'. These distances were divided by the mean distance between headquarters and inventors for all patents of the assignee firm granted in the same year, allowing comparison across firms with varying degrees of geographic diversification. Inventors' locations were retrieved from the Harvard Patent Database, and headquarters' locations were ascertained using Compustat and Factiva.
time_window: at the time of the patent grant

description: A renewal decision is classified as a commission error if the patent was renewed at a given point in time but it should not have been renewed based on the first-stage quality model and the selected predicted-probability threshold. The threshold was selected as corresponding to the median predicted renewal probability in the sample based on Model 3. The first-stage logit estimates the probability of renewal from objective quality indicators plus technology, geographic and maintenance year fixed effects.
time_window: renewal decisions in the 4th, 8th and 12th year after the patent was granted, patents granted 1990-2010

description: A renewal decision is classified as an omission error if the patent was not renewed at a given point in time but it should have been renewed based on the first-stage quality model and the selected predicted-probability threshold. The threshold was selected as corresponding to the median predicted renewal probability in the sample based on Model 3. The first-stage logit estimates the probability of renewal from objective quality indicators plus technology, geographic and maintenance year fixed effects.
time_window: renewal decisions in the 4th, 8th and 12th year after the patent was granted, patents granted 1990-2010

description: The 'regulatory commission expenses' of the utility, limited to those costs directly attributable to the home state's PSC, and exclusive of all costs for other regulatory bodies, such as those at the federal level and other states. A three-year moving average of costs, each placed in 1986 dollars, was used to measure regulatory monitoring. Because regulatory costs are partly a function of firm size, an initial regression estimates baseline regulatory costs as a function of firm size and employees, and the difference between actual costs and these baseline values is used as the independent variable.

The absolute dollar amount of equity (in $1986) held by the parent in subsidiaries that do not represent vertical integration. Since subsidiaries that do not represent backward integration generally are not regulated, all represent diversity with respect to that critical dimension. A change version of the variable, the one-year change in diversification, is used in the second equation.
