The absolute dollar amount of equity (in $1986) held by the parent in all subsidiaries engaged in the location, procurement, and transportation of natural gas to the electric utility and its gas distribution affiliates. A change version of the variable, the one-year change in backward integration, is used in the fourth equation.

Constructed in two steps: for each month in the life of the focal investment the authors tallied the number of ongoing investments, and then computed the average of this count across all months of the focal investment's life. The measure captures the activity load faced by the private equity firm during the management of the focal investment and indicates the number of similar projects carried out in parallel. The variable was log-transformed and mean-centered before entering the models.
time_window: over the months of the focal investment's life

description: The internal rate of return measures the gross return earned by investors from the acquisition of the company until it is sold, and corresponds to the annually compounded discount rate that would make the net present value of all cash flows related to the investment equal to zero. It is calculated using monthly cash flows for each company. Because the data include significant outliers, the authors Winsorized the dependent variable at the 95th percentile (i.e., 191%).
time_window: from acquisition of the company until it is sold

description: The stock of experience is measured as the number of investments completely sold by the private equity firm prior to the starting date of the focal investment. Including only exited investments means the measure reflects only deals for which the firm observed the entire buyout process from investment to exit, and it separates experience stock from activity load, which includes ongoing investments. The variable was log-transformed.
time_window: prior to the starting date of the focal investment

description: The homogeneity of experience measures the extent to which a private equity firm's accumulated experience before the focal investment was concentrated in specific industries, with buyout industries classified following the 48-industry Fama-French classification. To measure it the authors used the Herfindahl index, where s_i is the percentage of buyouts done by the private equity firm in the i industry for a total of N industries (i.e., 48 industries); high values indicate high experience homogeneity. The OCR rendering of the Herfindahl formula in the payload is unreadable, so the exact specification is not recorded from the equation.
time_window: accumulated experience before the focal investment

description: Pacing is measured as the mean time interval between acquisition of one buyout and acquisition of the subsequent buyout, taking into account the entire investment history of the private equity firm before the focal buyout. It is constructed by dividing the number of months between the focal buyout and the first acquisition in the history of the firm by the total number of investments acquired by the private equity firm. High values of this variable (long time intervals) indicate a slow pace, whereas low values indicate a fast pace.
time_window: entire investment history of the firm before the focal buyout

description: Prior success is calculated by averaging the IRR of all investments done by the private equity firm prior to the focal investment. To compute past success the authors averaged IRRs Winsorized at the 95th percentile (i.e., 191%) to avoid outliers leading to an overestimation of mean past performance. The variable was log-transformed.

The index is the number of product divisions plus 1.5 times the number of major manufacturing subsidiaries, divided by total revenues. The number of divisions and major manufacturing subsidiaries reported by large firms in the sample was counted from corporate annual reports and Moody's Industrial Manual, using 1976 data representing 1975 organization; the sales figure is for 1975 as reported in the Fortune 500 Directory. A greater weight (1.5) was assigned to major subsidiaries because subsidiaries are generally understood to operate more independently than divisions. Firms with very many and very few patents were excluded so that more variance could be carried by the numerator.

A concentric measure of diversification calculated from patent applications for the period 1974-81. The 55 technical fields in the data were divided into 15 groups, the fields corresponding to 3-digit SIC categories and the groups to 2-digit SICs. The index measures the distance between patents concentrically by comparing each patent with every other patent in the firm's portfolio, adding one point if the two patents are in the same technical field (same 3-digit SIC) and two points if they are in different technical fields (same 2-digit SIC); patents assigned to more than one technical field were treated as different applications. The index ranges from 0 to 2 and is increasing in diversity; because it is assumed to be uniformly distributed on [0,2], it was transformed into a standard normal using a transformation used in industrial organization studies of industry concentration based on Herfindahl indices.

A dummy representing less technologically progressive firms. The sample was simply divided into two groups: those with fewer than 100 patent applications in the period and those with more than 100; the LOW dummy identifies firms in the former group.

The total number of moves a player carried out, equivalent to the number of rooms she visited before finding the treasure. Participants were told to minimize the number of moves. Performance over trials on this indicator is the basis of the moves learning curve.
time_window: each trial; trials 1-20 before the treasure moved, trials 21-40 after

description: The total amount of time in seconds a player used to find the treasure in each trial. Participants were told to minimize their total time as well as their number of moves. This is the second indicator of performance.

The average number of moves to reach the treasure predicted by the credit assignment model, based on an average of 1,000 simulated organizations playing the game. The predicted series is plotted against and compared with the observed moves of the participants.

The cumulative number of periods or units, X, in the power law learning curve, which in this study is the number of trials played. Analyses of learning in a stable environment use only the first 20 trials before the treasure is relocated.
time_window: trials 1-20 (stable environment); trials 21-40 after the change

description: Estimated by regressing the logarithm of performance (time or moves to treasure) on the logarithm of the cumulative number of trials; a significant and positive b indicates a learning curve. The related progress ratio is calculated as 2 to the power minus b and indicates the percentage of previous performance reached with each doubling of experience.

Participants were randomly assigned to two conditions that differed in the amount of information displayed after each trial. In the baseline condition only the room of the treasure is displayed; in the three-step condition the three rooms the participant visited just before finding the treasure are also shown. The manipulation aims to direct attention to one-step, two-step, and three-step neighbors and thereby to manipulate the depth of credit assignment.

The parameter that specifies the number of preceding state-action pairs to which credit is assigned, which was varied in the simulation while other parameters were held constant. The value producing the smallest root mean square deviation between observed and predicted average moves was taken as the best fit.

variable_name: mean ranking of rooms by perceived proximity
description: After every five trials a message box asked participants to rank order four rooms in terms of their perceived proximity to the treasure; unknown to them, the rooms were one, two, three, and four steps away, respectively. The mean ranking of each room over time indicates how accurately subjects valued rooms at different distances from the treasure.

variable_name: distance of rooms from the treasure
description: The four rooms presented for ranking were chosen such that they were one, two, three, and four steps away from the treasure, respectively. Rooms physically proximate to the treasure represent important subgoals that allow the problem to be broken down into smaller, intermediate steps.

The treasure was kept fixed for the first 20 trials and then changed to a room four steps away from the initial location for the last 20 trials. Participants were told in the beginning that the location of the treasure would shift to an unknown location in the 21st trial.

The total number of moves a team carried out in a trial, equivalent to the number of rooms visited before finding the treasure. This is the same performance indicator used in the individual experiment, with other experimental details kept the same.
time_window: each trial; trials 1-20 before the treasure moved, trials 21-40 after

description: The total amount of time in seconds a team used to find the treasure in each trial. As in the individual experiment, teams were instructed to work together to get as good at the game as possible, and both time and moves were recorded.

The exponent b estimated from the log-log regression of team performance (time and moves to treasure) on the cumulative number of trials. Progress ratios for the teams were also computed from these estimates and their distribution compared with that of simulated organizations.

Teams were randomly assigned to the baseline condition or the three-step condition, the same information manipulation used in the individual experiment. Twenty-three teams were assigned to the baseline condition and 24 teams to the three-step condition.

variable_name: depth of credit assignment parameter (team simulation)
description: Organizations varying in the depth of credit assignment were simulated and compared with the team data, keeping other parameters the same. The authors assumed that the two team members share a common value function and make joint decisions, and the best-fitting depth of credit assignment for the teams was much higher than for individuals.

variable_name: mean ranking of rooms by perceived proximity (teams)
description: The mean ranking of rooms over time for the teams, based on their periodic rank ordering of four rooms according to perceived proximity to the treasure. As in the individual data, rooms closer to the treasure were learned earlier than those far away.

Estimated as the coefficient on lagged normalized profit in the autoregressive profit model (Equation 1). The estimate indicates the rate at which abnormal profits converge upon long-run levels; the higher it is, the more persistent are the abnormal profit outcomes, and an estimate not significantly different from 1 indicates that convergence is forestalled. It is estimated first with α and B forced to be the same across all firms and then in regressions in which α and B are allowed to vary across firms. A variant of the model is estimated using only those observations for which lagged normalized profit is greater than zero.

Obtained from the autoregressive profit model by combining the intercept and the persistence parameter as α/(1-B); it is the level upon which firm profits converge in the long run. When the estimate is not significantly different from zero, high and low profits converge upon normal levels in the long run, while an estimate significantly greater than zero indicates that firms earn relatively high profits even into the long run. Firm-specific estimates are calculated by combining each firm's own α and B estimates.

The firm's relative profitability in year t is its profit rate less the average profit rate earned across all firms, divided by that average. Firm profitability is measured as ROA, defined as the ratio of net income to total assets. The measure of normal profitability used is an intraindustry one: the asset-weighted average ROA across the sampled firms. Annual accounting data on net income and total assets describing publicly traded pharmaceutical firms are taken from the Compustat and GlobalScope data bases.

In each year the authors compute the ratio of innovative product sales to total pharmaceutical sales for each firm and subtract the corresponding industry average. The firm's innovative propensity is the average of this ratio calculated across the years for which the firm is in the sample, so a value of zero indicates average innovative propensity. Innovative products are those introduced with initial market shares in excess of 15.6 percent, the 90th percentile of the initial market share distribution; 145 of the 1070 products introduced by the sampled firms are categorized as innovative.
time_window: averaged across the years for which the firm is in the sample

description: For each new product the authors calculate the slope of the regression line relating market share to elapsed time, where elapsed time is the number of years between the year and the product's first full year on the market. Firms with greater average slope estimates for their innovative products are considered better at avoiding competition, so higher values indicate less intense competition. The firm-level variable is built from the slopes of the firm's innovative products; coefficients are not available for products with less than two years of data.
time_window: over each product's term on the market

description: Status is operationalized as Bonacich's beta centrality in VC syndication networks, calculated from one-year adjacency matrices of coinvestment networks based on five-year moving periods beginning with the VC firm's founding year; for VC firms less than five years old all available data were used. Data on all VCs in the TBO database, not just the sample, were used, and the measure was calculated with UCINET. Beta was set to 75 percent of the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue. The measure was standardized so that its effect size could be compared with the effects of reputation.

A modified version of the Lee, Pollock, and Jin (2011) LPJ reputation index, a multi-item, time-varying index reflecting a VC firm's ability to raise investment capital and develop start-ups. Five formative indicators were standardized and aggregated using a five-year moving average, and firm age was excluded from the index because the authors used it as a moderator. The index was rescaled so that within-year differences are maintained while cross-year variance due to market conditions is eliminated and converted to a 100-point scale, and the final measure was standardized.
time_window: five-year moving average of prior years

description: VC firm age was calculated as the focal year minus the year a VC firm raised its first fund. It is the moderator used in tests of H1a, H1b, H2, H3a, and H3b.

The number of blockbuster IPOs a VC invested in as of the year before the current year. Each IPO's underpricing (percentage change in stock price on the first day of trading) was weighted by its IPO value to allow for size effects, and blockbuster deals were defined as those whose weighted underpricing was above the 75th percentile of IPO underpricing for all IPOs that year. The measure is a count that increases only when a VC participates in a blockbuster deal.

SUMDIR is the simplest measurement of board diversity in terms of the sum of directorships in financial institutions and industrial companies held by nonexecutive directors. It was constructed from information in the IPO listing prospectuses.

NEO represents an 'intensity' of outside links of nonexecutive directors measured by the total number of nonexecutive directorships in financial institutions and industrial companies, and partnerships/memberships in professions, firms, and 'stakeholder' organizations divided by the total number of nonexecutives. The partnerships and memberships were identified from the listing prospectuses.

ENT is an entropy measure constructed to provide a direct evaluation of the diversification of board composition. The entropy formula is not recoverable from the text (the equation was not readable in the source), and the authors state only that Diri, i = 1,...,4, represents the number of outside directorships in financial, industrial, and professional firms and 'stakeholder' organizations respectively held by nonexecutive directors.

NEB > 33 percent is a dummy variable, constructed to verify the firm's compliance with the LSE's 'Combined Code on Corporate Governance' principles, that was assigned a value of one if the percentage of board members which are nonexecutives is greater than 33 percent, and zero otherwise.

NECHAIR is a dummy variable that was assigned a value of one if a company has a nonexecutive chairman, and zero otherwise, constructed to verify the firm's compliance with the LSE's 'Combined Code on Corporate Governance' principles.

Executives' experience is defined as the management positions and board memberships held over the last 5 years before the IPO, derived from the career histories of the CEO and other executive directors of the young firm reported in the listing prospectuses. In the analysis the authors use CEO experience and other executives' experience both separately and in combination, the latter providing a measure of the 'collective experience' of the top management team.

ESHAR represents the executive share ownership stake, measured in terms of the percentage of the total number of ordinary shares retained by executive board members after the IPO, as reported in the listing prospectus.

NESHAR represents the nonexecutive share ownership stake, measured in terms of the percentage of the total number of ordinary shares retained by nonexecutive board members after the IPO, as reported in the listing prospectus.

The size of underpricing was measured as the percentage difference between the offer price and the price at the end of the first day of trading adjusted for market movements. Share prices for this measure were obtained from the LSE Share Monitoring Service and Datastream.
time_window: end of the first day of trading

description: For each focal individual and year, the authors identify every workplace the individual worked in and all of the individual's coworkers there. For each coworker they compute the number of years the colleague had been self-employed in the preceding five years, and the measure is the average of these values across the focal individual's peers. The maximum possible value is five and the minimum is zero, and the measure is calculated at the establishment level so that only physically colocated coworkers count.
time_window: preceding five years, calculated for each year 1990-1996

description: Individuals are classified as entrepreneurs if they found a business, with or without employees. Because founders of incorporated ventures cannot be identified directly, the authors treat employees of new firms with fewer than three employees as entrepreneurs, and in larger firms only individuals who are top managers or directors are considered to be founders. All three types of entrepreneurial entry are pooled into a single transition.

Information on parental occupation in the database is used to identify whether either one of an individual's parents were entrepreneurs in a given year; the variable indicates whether the individual's parents were self-employed in the past. The authors note that its main effect is not reported in the interaction models because it is a fixed individual attribute absorbed by the individual fixed effects.

To calculate the level of entrepreneurship across regions, the authors compute the prior entrepreneurial experience (in the prior five years) for all individuals in the labor market in 1989. They then average these individual-level entrepreneurial measures by county and create a dummy variable that takes a value of one if the county is one with above median rates of entrepreneurship. Its main effect is not reported because it is absorbed by the county fixed effects.

The absolute difference in equity share between the foreign parent and the primary Hungarian firm measured at time 1. Sixty-five percent of the IJV sample had a dominant foreign parent and 12 percent had split ownership. It is the single indicator of the ownership control imbalance construct.

IJV general managers evaluated the influence that the Hungarian parent, foreign firm, and IJV managers had over seven issues by dividing 100 percent influence across the three groups. The difference between the foreign parent influence and the Hungarian parent influence was calculated for each issue, and the natural logarithm of the absolute value was computed to enhance the normality of each of these dimensions.

A three-item measure including the level (1 to 5, low to high) of mistrust between the parents, conflicting goals of parents, and conflict over the original agreement. Composite reliability for the construct was reported as 0.78.
A three-item measure assessing the degree to which the IJV received product- and manufacturing-related technology from the foreign parent.
A four-item measure assessing the extent the IJV received sales, managerial, administrative, and emotional support from the foreign parent.

A five-item scale appraising the extent to which the venture had learned technological expertise, marketing expertise, product development, managerial techniques, and manufacturing processes. Composite reliability for the construct was reported as 0.89.

IJV survival was coded as a dichotomous variable (0 = dissolved, 1 = survived). Of the usable sample of 121 IJVs, 83 remained operational as IJVs and 38 had been dissolved at the time of the second survey in 1996.

Identically worded, multiple-item, seven-point scale measure reflecting the view of the focal firm, adapted from past research in interorganizational relations and indexing the idiosyncratic investments made by both parties to the exchange. It was measured at time 1, together with the other relationship safeguards and ex post opportunism. The authors report that estimated reliabilities for the constructs average 0.84, with a range of 0.76 to 0.91.

Identically worded, multiple-item, seven-point scale measure reflecting the view of the focal firm and adapted from prior research in interorganizational relations, capturing the extent to which the firms perceive compatible objectives. It is an organization-level attribute measured at time 1. Construct values exhibited a five- to six-point range on the seven-point scale, indicating substantial heterogeneity across relationships.

Identically worded, multiple-item, seven-point scale measure adapted from prior interorganizational research; unlike the other measures, it is captured at the interpersonal level of the individual respondents and refers to the respondent's relationship with the individual contact at the counterpart firm. It was measured at time 1. The authors report estimated reliabilities for the constructs averaging 0.84 (range 0.76 to 0.91).

Identically worded, multiple-item, seven-point scale in which respondents report not on their own but on their counterpart's ex post opportunistic behavior in the exchange, an approach chosen because selfish motivations and guile are difficult to study directly and self-reports are subject to social desirability bias. The construct is organizational and behavioral, depicting the activities of the counterpart firm after the transaction is underway. It was measured at time 1 and used to split the sample at its median.
level: focal firm reporting on its counterpart

description: Identically worded, multiple-item, seven-point scale reflecting the focal firm's holistic evaluation of the counterpart's performance, adapted from past research in interorganizational relations. It is an individual, short-term outcome reflecting the view of the focal firm alone and was measured at time 2, one year after the predictors.
time_window: Time 2 (one year after the time 1 predictors)

description: Identically worded, multiple-item, seven-point scale reflecting the focal firm's assessment of strategic benefits that the pairing has gained over competing firms, adapted from past research in interorganizational relations. Because strategic performance cannot be captured by accounting-based concepts alone, the measure goes beyond financial outcomes. It was measured at time 2, one year after the predictors.
time_window: Time 2 (one year after the time 1 predictors)

description: Identically worded, multiple-item, seven-point scale reflecting the focal firm's view of the financial outcomes generated jointly in the dyad, designed to reflect aspects of the dyadic relationship between the firms rather than one player's own results. It was measured at time 2, one year after the predictors.
time_window: Time 2 (one year after the time 1 predictors)

description: Identically worded, multiple-item, seven-point scale reflecting the focal firm's perspective on the long-term viability of the relationship. Although confidence in the future of the relationship is not a performance outcome, the authors treat it as an important exchange outcome because without it firms adopt a short time horizon. It was measured at time 2, one year after the predictors.
time_window: Time 2 (one year after the time 1 predictors)

description: Exchange outcomes are the set of four outcome measures: evaluation of the counterpart's performance, achievement of competitive advantages, joint profit performance, and expectations of relationship continuity. Each is a multiple-item seven-point scale from the buyer survey, and each is modeled as a separate latent outcome.
Time varying measure of firm age, operationalized as the time elapsed in years since a firm first applied for a patent. Older firms are argued to have engaged in patenting prior to younger firms.

Organizational knowledge is represented as a vector of expertise across USPTO four-digit technologies, computed as the sum of the skill vectors of the firm's scientists. Core knowledge is the subset of the top 5 technologies in which the organization possesses the most expertise. A core change is recorded when the composition of this top 5 group changes. Whether change took place is determined for the period between the application dates of two successive patents of the firm; repeated changes may occur to a given firm.
time_window: between application dates of two successive patents of the firm

description: Count of the number of hires in an organization in the two years prior to the application date of a patent, divided by the number of scientists present in the firm. Hiring is inferred by comparing the firms listed on two successive patents of a given scientist: if the firm names differ, hiring is assumed and dated at the mid-point of the two application dates. The normalization is necessary because firms with a larger mass of scientists are more likely to recruit more people.
scale: count normalized by the number of scientists
time_window: two years prior to the patent application date

description: The knowledge new hires bring is computed by summing their skill vectors. Hire knowledge similarity is the angle between the expertise of hires and that of the organization, computed as the product of the hire and organizational knowledge vectors divided by their respective magnitudes, and is bounded between 0 and 1. Hire knowledge distance is then computed by subtracting similarity from 1 (θd = 1 - θs).

For each hired scientist, experience is the number of patents the scientist had already worked on prior to the application date of the focal patent, including patenting experience accumulated in organizations worked in prior to joining the hiring organization. Hire experience is the average of the experience of all new hires that a firm recruited in the two years preceding the application date of a given patent.
time_window: two years preceding the application date of the focal patent

description: Blau (1977) heterogeneity index computed over functional categories: one minus the sum of the squared proportions of the total team that each functional category represents. Functional assignment was based on the titles reported in the secondary data sources; individuals whose function could not be assigned were classified as general, and the CEO was also classified by functional background where possible.

Blau (1977) heterogeneity index computed over functional categories: one minus the sum of the squared proportions of the total team that each functional category represents. Functional assignment was based on the titles reported in the secondary data sources; individuals whose function could not be assigned were classified as general, and the CEO was also classified by functional background where possible.

Coefficient of variation of team tenure, the standard deviation divided by the mean. It was calculated by using all the executives active on the team year by year, so that the tenures of the members of a firm in a particular year entered the mean and standard deviation of the team tenure.

Coefficient of variation of team tenure, the standard deviation divided by the mean. It was calculated by using all the executives active on the team year by year, so that the tenures of the members of a firm in a particular year entered the mean and standard deviation of the team tenure.

The numbers of executives entering and exiting the team each year, standardized by total team size to give percentages. Executives who were not on the team the previous year were identified and counted as entering the team for the current year; executives listed in the previous year but not in the current year were counted as exiting in the current year.

The numbers of executives entering and exiting the team each year, standardized by total team size to give percentages. Executives who were not on the team the previous year were identified and counted as entering the team for the current year; executives listed in the previous year but not in the current year were counted as exiting in the current year.

Pfeffer and Moore's (1980) ranking index, first used to assess the relative weight of each rank on the team; it gives the weighted average of the ranks of individual members, so that teams top heavy in titles have high values of the index. The formula for the index is not readable in the text as provided. Thirty-four titles were grouped into one of six levels.

Pfeffer and Moore's (1980) ranking index, first used to assess the relative weight of each rank on the team; it gives the weighted average of the ranks of individual members, so that teams top heavy in titles have high values of the index. The formula for the index is not readable in the text as provided. Thirty-four titles were grouped into one of six levels.
The average of the individual members' tenures on the team. As no measure of organizational tenure was available for individual members, no average organizational tenure was available.
The average of the individual members' tenures on the team. As no measure of organizational tenure was available for individual members, no average organizational tenure was available.

Change in return on assets calculated over two years, representing growth from time t through t + 2. ROA was appropriate for the cement industry because there is an extremely high investment in plant and equipment which acts as a barrier to entry for the industry.

Change in return on assets calculated over two years, representing growth from time t through t + 2. ROA was appropriate for the minicomputer industry because efficient use of production facilities is an important factor in that industry along with technological superiority.

The year in which a jolt (environmental or technological) occurred and the four following years were defined as turbulent years for the cement industry, and years that were five or more years past a jolt were defined as stable. The categories of jolts were technological discontinuities, legislative, judiciary, or regulatory changes affecting the industry, oil shocks, and the world wars.
time_window: jolt year and four following years versus five or more years past a jolt

description: Number of two digit SIC codes in which the MNC participates, which identifies the broad product lines of a particular company. Consistent with prior research, this study used SIC codes for measuring product/service diversity. The two digit SIC codes for the MNCs for 1987 were provided by the 'Compact Disclosure' data disc by Disclosure Inc.
scale: count of two digit SIC codes

variable_name: Foreign sales as a percentage of total sales
description: Percentage of total sales or revenue earned from foreign operations, the operationalization of the extent of foreign market involvement. The measure provides an overall level of foreign operations for the MNC, although it does not identify each foreign market separately. Foreign sales as a percentage of total sales were collected from the 1987 annual reports and/or 10-K forms of each MNC in the sample; for banks and financial institutions within the service MNC category total sales indicated the aggregate of interest income, non-interest income, and other income.

Classification of the MNC structure based on the type and geographical domain of managerial responsibility of the executives immediately below the CEO level; responsibility was categorized as functional (production, marketing, sales etc.) or product/service, and geographic domain as global, international, or regional. Where the responsibility for a particular function or product/service line was traced to more than one executive the structure was identified as a matrix structure, and where the responsibility pattern differed from one executive to another it was classified as a mixed structure. Corporate titles listed in annual reports and/or 10-K forms for 1987, the 'Reference Book of Corporate Managements' by Dun and Bradstreet, organizational charts gathered in a survey of the sample MNCs and selected telephone interviews were consulted. Worldwide functional and international division structures were combined for all statistical analysis because their generalized squared distances were not only the lowest but also nominal.
scale: categorical; four structure types treated as dummy variables

description: Following Venkatraman's framework, two types of fit were analyzed, fit as matching and fit as moderation. Fit as matching was assessed with discriminant analysis that used the two strategy variables (product/service diversity and foreign sales) as independent variables and the type of structure as the classification variable, so that the fit (match) between MNC strategy and structure could be judged from the predicted versus observed structure. Fit as moderation was analyzed as the joint or interaction effect of strategy and structure on performance, and MNCs were classified as fit or non-fit according to whether their structure matched the structure prescribed for their strategy combination.
time_window: 1987 for strategy and structure; 1987-1988 for performance

description: ROA was recorded for 1987 and 1988 and averaged over the two consecutive years to smooth the profit variance. Industry ROA for each MNC, based on the primary two digit SIC code, was also collected, and the final performance measure was the difference between the average MNC ROA and the respective industry ROA, which shows the relative performance of the MNC compared to the industry. The 'Compact Disclosure' data disc by Disclosure Inc. provided the MNC ROA figures while the Dun and Bradstreet 'Industry Norms and Key Business Ratios' for 1987 and 1988 provided industry ROAs.
scale: difference between MNC ROA and industry ROA

description: For the purpose of this research, MNCs which derived more than 50 percent of their sales from manufacturing and/or mining were defined as manufacturing MNCs, and MNCs with more than 50 percent of their revenues from non-manufacturing and/or non-mining operating businesses were defined as service MNCs. Examples of such service MNCs are banking, insurance, retailing and transportation firms. The sample contained far more manufacturing MNCs than service MNCs, so additional directories were used to increase the size of the service group.

A discrete variable that classifies as owner-controlled those firms in which at least 5 percent of the outstanding stock is in the hands of one individual or organization that was not involved in the actual management of the company, did not deny beneficial ownership, did not report only disposition rights, or was not an employee benefit plan. Otherwise, firms were designated as management-controlled, unless there was a manager with a 5 percent holding, in which case they were designated as owner-managed.

Base pay is the average of all surveyed managers' base salaries. All variables were analyzed at the firm level, and average variable values were computed for the number of years a firm was in the CAHRS database.
time_window: averaged over the years a firm appeared in the database (1981-1988)

description: Base and bonus is the average of all surveyed managers' salaries plus bonuses they received. All variables were analyzed at the firm level, and average variable values were computed for the number of years a firm was in the CAHRS database.
time_window: averaged over the years a firm appeared in the database (1981-1988)

description: Measured by the average base and bonus in year t minus the average base and bonus in year t - 1, all divided by average base and bonus in year t - 1, for all surveyed managers for all years available. Change scores were computed for the variables used in the test of pay's sensitivity to changes in performance.
time_window: year t relative to year t - 1

variable_name: percentage of managers eligible for long-term performance incentives
description: Calculated by dividing the number of surveyed managers who are eligible for long-term performance incentives by the total number of surveyed managers in each firm.

variable_name: percentage of employees eligible for bonus
description: Calculated by dividing the number of employees eligible for bonus by the total number of employees per company.

variable_name: bonus to base and bonus ratio
description: Calculated by dividing the average bonus of surveyed managers by the average base and bonus of surveyed managers in each firm.

Financial performance is a composite index constructed from standardized values of return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE). The change variable was calculated for year t as the variable in year t minus the variable in year t - 1, all divided by the variable in year t - 1, for all years available. All financial data were adjusted to December 1992 dollars using the Consumer Price Index.
time_window: year t relative to year t - 1

description: Organizational size is a composite index constructed from a factor analysis of the standardized values of assets, sales, and number of employees, weighted by item loadings to obtain the size measure. The change variable was calculated for year t as the variable in year t minus the variable in year t - 1, all divided by the variable in year t - 1, for all years available.
time_window: year t relative to year t - 1

description: The measure of firm-level competitive activity was expressed quantitatively as the annual sum of each firm's moves. Competitive actions were identified by a structured content analysis of published articles, examining citations of the sample firms in the Predicasts F&S Index for the 1983-1991 period; coded moves were product introductions, product announcements, and marketing/promotion campaigns. The method identified a total of 1,903 rivalrous actions in the computer software industry.

The industry-level measure of competitor activity was expressed as the aggregation of firm moves to the industry level minus the focal firm's own competitive activity. The authors state their approach is consistent with that of Kwoka (1979), who aggregated sample market share data to construct industry concentration values.

Each Predicasts F&S Index citation of a horizontal cooperative move in the software industry was counted as one cooperative mechanism for each of the participating firms in the sample; only cooperative moves that create mechanisms for interfirm communication but are not directly tied to a competitive activity were included. Cooperative moves were defined as equity arrangements, mergers, technology licenses, and participation in trade associations and technology consortia.
The industry-level measure of cooperative mechanisms was expressed as the aggregation of firm-level cooperative mechanisms to the industry level minus the focal firm's own cooperative activity.

One of two commonly accepted financial measures of firm performance used in the study. The data were collected from annual SEC filings as reported by the Disclosure database; the authors state that because the legal requirements associated with SEC filings mandate accurate reporting, that data source is highly reliable. Return on assets was the dependent measure of firm performance in the first performance model.

One of two commonly accepted financial measures of firm performance used in the study, taken from annual SEC filings as reported by the Disclosure database. Return on sales was used as the dependent measure of firm performance in the second performance model.

An eight-item scale measuring the frequency and unpredictability of environmental change, with four items from the market environment and four from the technological environment and a hypothesized second-order factor structure. Items were adapted from Heide and John (1990) and other similar scales, and each dimension was weighted equally following purification in the final scores. Items were rated on a scale ranging from 1, 'completely inaccurate,' to 7, 'completely accurate.'

A five-item ambiguity scale adapted from Daft and Macintosh (1981). The items measured the extent of uncertainty in the perception of environmental conditions and events, in keeping with the authors' definition of ambiguity. Items were rated on a scale ranging from 1, 'completely inaccurate,' to 7, 'completely accurate.'

An eight-item supplier opportunism scale adapted from John (1984), with items added explicitly addressing strategic (noncooperative) bargaining to better tap overt actions. Informants rated the items on a scale ranging from 1, 'completely inaccurate,' to 7, 'completely accurate,' and following purification the final items were summed to form the scale.

Measured by the type of development agreement used in a relationship. Informants were asked to indicate whether their development agreements were governed by firm fixed-price contracts, prespecified price and prespecified adjustment formulas, negotiable adjustments, fully negotiable prices, or no specification. Responses were then categorized into the fixed-price contract and negotiable price contract regimes, coded as 1 and 0 respectively.

Single-item measure of the degree of the shadow of the past: how long the manufacturer had worked with the supplier, in years. Because the variable had a positive skewness value, the authors transformed the measure by taking its logarithm; following the transformation the skewness value was close to zero.

Measure adapted from Heide and Miner (1992) that captures the manufacturer's expectation of continuity regarding future interaction with the supplier. Measured on a seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree).
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: Five-item measure consistent with Zaheer et al. (1998), consisting of three components: reliability, predictability, and fairness, plus a general indicator of trust. One item directly assesses interorganizational trust, one reflects the reliability component, two indicate predictability, and one reflects fairness. Measured on a seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree).
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: Composite construct with two first-order factors, one on the buyer side and the other on the supplier side, operationalized as parties' dependence in the relationship and switching costs to alternative partners. Measured with the seven-point Likert scale used for all scales unless otherwise indicated.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: Measure adapted from Noordewier et al. (1990) capturing the manufacturer's perceptions of uncertainty associated with the supply market, i.e. unanticipated changes in circumstances surrounding the product exchange in the marketplace. Measured with the seven-point Likert scale used for all scales unless otherwise indicated.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: Measured using the WES question 'has your workplace experienced the implementation of TQM in the prior 12-month period?' The question was coded for each year as yes (1) or no (0), and the five years of responses were aggregated, so the variable ranged from 0 to 5. The cumulative measure is intended to capture the organization's commitment and investment of time and resources to an ongoing TQM program.

Summed response scores of four WES items asking respondents to rate organizational activities with respect to their relative importance in the workplace general business strategy. The items are rated on a scale from 1 = 'not important' to 5 = 'crucial', and the year-specific summed values were averaged over the sampling frame. A confirmatory factor analysis verified that the seven strategy items loaded on the two strategic orientation dimensions.
scale: four items each rated 1 = 'not important' to 5 = 'crucial'

description: Summed responses on three WES items asking respondents to rate organizational activities with respect to their relative importance in the workplace general business strategy. The items are rated on a scale from 1 = 'not important' to 5 = 'crucial', and the year-specific summed values were averaged over the sampling frame.
scale: three items each rated 1 = 'not important' to 5 = 'crucial'

description: Operating margin, calculated as operating revenues minus operating expenditures divided by operating revenues. The variable was calculated using data from the 2003 survey.

Binary variable equal to one for all of the observations of the treated firms and zero for all of the other observations; in the cross-section it is equal to one for the treated firms. Treated and control startups received the same ten sessions of training, but only the treated startups were taught to frame and identify the problem, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test them rigorously with valid and reliable metrics, and set thresholds for concluding whether a hypothesis is corroborated.
time_window: all 16 periods (training administered over the first 8 periods)

description: In the panel regressions, this is a binary variable that takes the value zero until the firm exits (abandons the program and ceases the startup), one in the time period in which the firm drops out, and a missing value thereafter. In the cross-section regressions, this is a dummy equal to one if the firm exits at any point and zero otherwise. Firms that exit had not yet made heavy investments in their company.
time_window: up to the period in which the firm exits

description: In the panel regressions, this is a binary variable that takes the value one in the exact time period in which the firm made a major change to its business model and zero whenever the firm does not pivot; firms that made more than one such major change take the value one at any time in which a major change occurs. In the cross-section, this variable is equal to the total number of major changes of the firms during our timeframe.
scale: 0/1 in the panel; count of major changes in the cross-section

description: In the panel regressions, this is the firm's revenue flow in euros between any 2 of our 16 time periods; in the cross-section, it is the cumulative revenue over the 16 time periods of our sample. To control for outliers, along with the absolute value the authors show results using revenue winsorized at 99% and the revenue's hyperbolic sine transformation.
time_window: 16 time periods over about one year; cross-section accumulated over the same 16 periods

description: Star exit was calculated by tracking the patenting activities of stars across different firms. The star exit dummy variable equals one for firm i in year t if a star inventor stops patenting for firm i in year t and subsequently patents in another firm. Stars who stopped patenting but did not subsequently patent at another firm were not counted as exits. There were a total of 328 events of a star exit between 1985 and 2010, involving 135 firms.

Innovation performance is the cumulative number of forward citations to patents granted to the firm in the three years immediately following the star's departure. The three-year postexit window was selected to account for the path-dependence and longer gestation periods of R&D activities. Star exits were observed from 1985 through 2010, allowing enough time to accumulate forward citations until 2020 and reducing concerns about right-censoring.
time_window: three years immediately following the star's departure

description: Coinventors' performance is the cumulative number of forward citations to patents granted to all coinventors from the firm in the three years immediately following the star's departure. The coinventors considered are those working in the same firm as the star. The three-year postexit window accounts for the path-dependence and longer gestation periods of R&D activities.
time_window: three years immediately following the star's departure

description: Coinventors' mobility is the number of coinventors who also exited their firms within two years of the departure of stars. The coinventors considered are those working in the same firm as the star.
time_window: two years following the star's departure

description: The authors first identified subclasses of the star's patents in year t − 1. They then counted the subclasses in which the star had at least one patent in the five years before t − 1 (between t − 7 and t − 2), which they refer to as previously used subclasses. Search depth of star s at firm i and time t was calculated by dividing the number of times these subclasses appeared in different patents by the total number of subclasses of the star's patents in t − 1. A high value suggests that the star's patents are largely limited to technological areas with which the star has experience; the formal equation is not readable in the text provided.
time_window: subclasses of patents in year t − 1; prior use counted between t − 7 and t − 2

description: Search breadth was calculated as the sum of the proportions of a star's patents in each subclass relative to the total number of the star's patents, subtracted from one. A higher value indicates that the star produced patents in a diverse set of technologies. Patents granted in the previous five years were used to calculate breadth. N is the total number of patents of a star from firm i between years t − 7 and t − 2, n is the number of the star's patents in subclass j in the same period, and k is the total number of subclasses assigned to the N patents; the formal equation is not readable in the text provided.
time_window: patents granted between t − 7 and t − 2

description: Positional embeddedness was measured as the centrality of the star in the coinventor network. The centrality of stars was calculated using their degree centrality, which captures the number of inventors with whom the star collaborated as a proportion of the total number of inventors in the firm.

The structural embeddedness of the coinventors was captured in terms of the density of the network of the star's coinventors. It was measured using the number of ties between coinventors as a proportion of the number of possible ties.

Standard deviation of the daily returns of the target from 275 to 30 days prior to the earliest acquisition announcement date, winsorized at the 5% level. The authors state that the average standard deviation of stock returns of targets in the sample was 4.5 percent. Higher volatility is interpreted as more idiosyncratic target resources and greater ex-ante and ex-post acquisition risk, and such targets are described as 'lottery-like' in nature.
time_window: 275 to 30 days prior to the earliest acquisition announcement date

description: The absolute dollar value of the abnormal return surrounding the prior acquisition announcement, interacted with an indicator D1 that takes on a value of 1 when the prior abnormal dollar returns are negative and 0 otherwise. Abnormal returns were obtained by first regressing acquirer daily returns on market returns over the period t = -250 to -50 and then cumulating the residuals over the (-5, +5) day window around the previous announcement; the cumulated returns were multiplied by the market value of the acquirer to obtain the dollar value.
time_window: (-5, +5) days around the previous acquisition announcement; estimation window t = -250 to -50

description: The absolute dollar value of the abnormal return surrounding the prior acquisition announcement, interacted with an indicator D2 that takes on a value of 1 when there is a prior abnormal gain and 0 otherwise. Abnormal returns were obtained by first regressing acquirer daily returns on market returns over the period t = -250 to -50 and then cumulating the residuals over the (-5, +5) day window around the previous announcement; the cumulated returns were multiplied by the market value of the acquirer to obtain the dollar value.
time_window: (-5, +5) days around the previous acquisition announcement; estimation window t = -250 to -50

description: The dependent variable is a hard drive producer's highest areal density in any of its form factors in a given year; areal density is the number of bits that can be stored on a square inch of disk. Improvement in areal density is described as the central technological metric in the evolution of the industry. The authors use a natural log transformation of maximum areal density at time t in their growth models.
Indicator variable for whether a hard drive firm has had a spin-off (0 or 1). This variable becomes 1 once a firm has a spin-off and remains at that value thereafter.

variable_name: average technology of the spin-offs (spin-off frontier ratio)
description: Constructed to measure the proximity of the focal firm's spin-off to the technological frontier, calculated as the spin-off's maximum areal density in a given year divided by the highest areal density in the industry in that year. For firms with more than one spin-off present in the industry, the authors compute the average frontier ratio of all of a firm's spin-offs at each point in time. In additional models they assume that the technology effect fades at 25% or 50% per year, or becomes zero, after all of a firm's spin-offs leave the industry.

Captures the amount of time (in years) that has lapsed since the progenitor has had that spin-off. If a hard drive producer had more than one spin-off, the spin-off clock was reset to zero and began counting until its next spin-off. In the Maxtor illustration, spin-offs in 1990, 1991 and 1992 kept the clock at zero and it began to increase annually from 1993.

The dependent variable: the ordinal stratum of the business unit's relative performance. In each 5-year period the longitudinal ROA distributions of the entities at that level were compared by iterative application of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov two-sample method, clustering entities into statistically significantly different performance strata; strata above the modal stratum were combined into a single superior stratum and those below into an inferior stratum. This yielded three strata ranked in ordinal fashion (superior performers, modal performers, and inferior performers).
scale: three ordinal categories: inferior, modal, superior

description: The business unit's performance stratum in the prior period, obtained by lagging the business unit performance strata, which lost the first period for all business units. It enters the ordinal regression as the lagged business-level factor.
scale: three ordinal categories: inferior, modal, superior

description: The corporate-level relative performance stratum for the corporation the business unit belonged to, obtained from the iterative Kolmogorov-Smirnov stratification of corporate-level ROA. Operating profit and assets for business units that were part of corporations were aggregated to the corporate level and formed into a ratio to give corporate ROA. It enters the ordinal regression as the corporate-level factor.
scale: three ordinal categories: inferior, modal, superior

description: The industry-level relative performance stratum for the primary industry in which the business unit operated, obtained from the iterative Kolmogorov-Smirnov stratification of industry-level longitudinal ROA data. It enters the ordinal regression as the industry-level factor predicting the business unit's performance stratum.
scale: three ordinal categories: inferior, modal, superior

variable_name: Cumulative hazard of exiting the superior performance strata
description: Estimated with Cox regression, the cumulative hazard rate of exiting the superior performance strata over the entire period studied, compared across industries, corporations, and business segments; higher hazard rates would be associated with lesser persistence, and vice versa. The authors report that industry had the lowest hazard rate (0.374), followed by the corporate cumulative hazard rate (0.456) and then the segment hazard rate (0.566), which indicates the least persistence.

An adapted version of the instrument developed by Khandwalla (1977) comprising 17 items measuring differences in the risk-taking propensity of the management groups, extent of participation encouraged in decision-making, approach to decision-making, and emphasis placed on formality. Respondents indicated the extent of perceived differences in management styles between the acquiring and acquired firm management along each item using a five-point Likert-type scale (1 = very similar, 5 = very different). Principal-components factor analysis with varimax rotation extracted a single factor, and the aggregate measure was calculated by averaging the scores on all items. The Cronbach-alpha value for the scale was 0.92, and the composite correlated highly with a separate overall-difference question (r = 0.82, p<0.001).
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = very similar, 5 = very different)

variable_name: Differences in reward and evaluation systems (DIFREW)
description: A scale identified by Kerr (1982) with eight items covering differences in the evaluation criteria and in the administration of rewards. Respondents indicated the extent of perceived differences on a Likert-type five-point scale (1 = very similar, 5 = very different). Principal-components factor analysis indicated that all eight items loaded on a single factor, and the Cronbach-alpha value for the scale was 0.90. A composite measure was calculated for each acquisition by taking the mean of the item scores, which correlated highly with the overall measure provided by respondents (r = 0.78, p<0.001).
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = very similar, 5 = very different)

description: Respondents indicated the extent of post-acquisition integration or consolidation of operations along items covering manufacturing/R&D and marketing activities, using a scale from 1 = very low integration to 5 = very high integration. Principal-component analysis identified two factors, with manufacturing items loading on one and marketing items on the other; Cronbach-alpha values were 0.91 and 0.90 respectively. Individual scores were used to calculate composite indexes of manufacturing and marketing integration, and these two composite scores were used to categorize acquisitions into a high integration subgroup (both composite scores greater than 3.0, the midpoint of the scale) and a low integration subgroup (both scores less than 3.0).
scale: five-point scale (1 = very low integration to 5 = very high integration)

description: Respondents assessed the extent to which the acquisition was able to achieve prior expectations in terms of its impact on the performance of the acquiring firm, rating the acquisition along each of five criteria on a five-point Likert-type scale and assigning weights to each criterion according to its perceived importance. The importance scores were used to weight the performance scores so that a weighted average acquisition performance index could be established for each acquisition. A separate question asked for an opinion of the overall performance of the acquisition; the two scores were highly correlated (r = 0.89, p<0.001). Perceptual measures were used because accounting measures are typically available only in aggregate form and market measures reflect only a priori expectations rather than acquisition performance as an outcome.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale, weighted by importance scores
time_window: at least 2 years after completion of the acquisition

description: Composite measure of the level of highest status of minority players per team, built from five status indicators collected for each player: salary, awards, tenure, starting games, and celebrity profile. Each indicator was scaled by dividing the individual player's value by the maximum value within the player's team, and the five scaled indicators were summed, so the composite status ranges from zero (lowest status) to one (highest status in the team); the highest score among a team's minority players is the team-level predictor. Tenure is the number of years the player had been in the league until a given year since debut (T - T0 + 1), and awards is a weighted sum of six MLB awards.
time_window: year t, predicting hiring in year t+1

description: Each team's annual hiring outcome, calculated as the change in the number of minority players by subtracting the current number of minority players from the number of minority players in the following year. For the subgroup analyses the authors computed the analogous changes in the number of Black players and in the number of Hispanic players.

Whether the highest-status minority player per team was a pitcher or not (1 = pitcher, 0 = nonpitcher). The authors treat pitcher positions as commonly perceived as more prototypical for White players and nonpitcher positions, such as shortstops and fielders, as more prototypical for minority players; being a pitcher therefore indicates a less prototypical role for a minority member.
level: team-year (attribute of the highest-status minority player)
time_window: same year as the status measure

description: The authors created separate highest-status variables for Black players and for Hispanic players, and the outcome was the change in the number of players of that same subgroup; the highest status of non-Black minority players and of non-Hispanic minority players served as the different-subgroup comparisons. Players in other minority groups were included as non-Black and non-Hispanic minority players because there were not enough of them to be split into their own categories.
time_window: year t, predicting hiring in year t+1

variable_name: Executive status profile (high versus low status)
description: Participants reviewed executive team profiles in which the female executive of Company A had relatively high status and the female executive of Company B relatively low status: the high-status executive received a high salary, won multiple awards, had a long tenure, and had a large number of LinkedIn followers, whereas the low-status executive received a relatively low salary, won no awards, had a short tenure, and had a small number of followers. The starting-games indicator from Study 1 was not used, and the average values of salaries, awards, tenures, and followers of the four executives were held constant between the two companies. As a manipulation check, participants rated each executive's status on a seven-point scale (1 = 'lowest status'; 7 = 'highest status').
level: individual executive, as rated by participants

description: Participants indicated the extent to which the company should invest its resources to hire more female executives, using three items on a seven-point scale (e.g., 'How much more or fewer resources do you think Company A [B] needs to invest in hiring a female executive in the future?'), which were averaged into a composite measure. Participants in the high-status minority condition rated Company A, the company with a high-status female executive, and those in the low-status minority condition rated Company B. The questions were asked indirectly about what the company should do in the situation to reduce social desirability bias.

Functional generalism (F) for artist i in year y is 1 minus the sum of the square of proportional membership, defined by the count of credits X in category n divided by the total number of credits T. Every credit an artist received in a given year across the eight most common job functions was counted; the credit count is the sum of all credits from the start of the sample through year y for each skill category. Using a proportional measure in the Herfindahl constrains the measure between 0 and 1, with a higher score indicating greater generalization. The formula block in the text is unreadable and was not reconstructed.
time_window: cumulative from the start of the sample through year y

description: A Herfindahl index that sums the squared proportional membership in each of the principal music genres; market breadth (M) for artist i in year y is 1 minus the sum of the artist's squared proportion of claims C (out of all the claims the artist had made T across the genres considered) for each genre g. The measure is constrained between 0 and 1, where a lower score indicates a narrower market experience (i.e., greater concentration). Genre identification was collected from the label and from Allmusic.com, where audience members generate tags; each tag was treated as a single vote for a subgenre and subgenres were aggregated into principal genres recognized by the National Endowment for the Arts. The formula block in the text is unreadable and was not reconstructed.

An indicator variable that captures whether an artist launched a new, independent record label in a given year. Individuals who founded a record label but lacked a track record in the industry because their previous jobs lay outside the music industry, they did not classify as music artists, or they had never worked before were excluded, as were non-artist founders.

Commercial success measured with record sales obtained from the Nielsen SoundScan database; for each record album in the sample the corresponding commercial sales were identified. A time-varying, cumulative sum of record sales from time t0 through time ty was constructed for each artist, and a natural logarithm was taken to mitigate the influence of outliers.

Whether any given artist's work was published in a compilation album, made up of tracks by various artists (such as soundtracks, label samplers, and theme albums) or by a single artist. The measure computes a time-varying cumulative count of compilation albums between time t0 and time ty for any given artist, and the natural logarithm was taken to mitigate the influence of outliers.

For each of the eight functional categories, artists were given a binary score indicating whether they had (1) or had not (0) been credited with that function on any albums from t0 through ty. Each functional combination F was then calculated to determine the frequency with which it appeared across all observations N; the measures were updated annually. A higher score indicates greater typicality, constrained between 0 (no one else demonstrated this combination in any year) and 1 (every other artist demonstrated this combination in every year). The formula block in the text is unreadable and was not reconstructed.

Audience receptivity to breadth was proxied with income and education, specifically the percentage of a given genre's audience that was college-educated or high-income (over median U.S. income). For artists who span multiple genres, the average income and education for any given audience was calculated. Data on audience education and income were drawn from the 2012 Survey of Public Participation in the Arts. The formula block in the text is unreadable and was not reconstructed.

A natural logarithm of the yearly count of articles that provide nonnegative information on city i serves as a proxy for media coverage of city i in year t. The count is based on an automatic double-mention search through the Dow Jones Factiva database of periodicals, counting all articles where a city name was mentioned at least twice in the article body, excluding obituaries, sports, and calendars; articles where the most frequent negative words were associated with the city name were excluded. The article counts are based on four English-language newspapers, and the data collection window for media coverage was widened from 1996-2005 to 1992-2005. Media coverage enters the model with a four-year lag (k = 4), and the variable ranges from 0 to 1,284 articles with a mean of 77.8.
scale: article count (0 to 1,284 in the sample)

description: The dependent variable, entry, is the number of foreign firms that entered industry j in city i in year t for the count model and a natural log of this number for the 2SLS model. Only firms with 100 percent foreign ownership and only first-time foreign entries are counted. The sample covers cities with populations over 100,000 in 1995 and with at least one foreign entry during the observation window, and industries with at least one foreign entrant during 1996-2005. The variable ranges from 0 to 386 entrants per year, with a mean of 1.16.

Firm home region is indicated by a dummy variable, NIS, which equals 1 if a firm is coming from a NIS (Newly Independent State, i.e., former Soviet Union republic) country and 0 otherwise. NIS firms are geographically and socially closer to Russia than the rest of the world and are therefore expected to have better private information about Russian cities. Media coverage is interacted with the NIS variable and the coefficient is expected to be negative.

A foreign entrepreneurial firm is a firm directly owned by one or several foreign individuals. The ownership type is indicated by a dummy variable entrepreneur that equals 1 if all firm owners are individuals and 0 if at least one owner is a firm; twenty percent of foreign firms in the main sample are owned by entrepreneurs. Multinational firms are expected to have better private information than foreign entrepreneurs, so the sign for the interaction between media coverage and the entrepreneur variable is expected to be positive.

Number of software packages a developer maintained in 2002, collected from the project's bug-tracking database. A package is a discrete unit of software code that can be maintained independently of the rest of an operating system but has a standardized interface that allows integration with other packages. To maintain a package is to manage the receipt and review of code contributions from other contributors and to 'package' these smaller contributions into a discrete module. The authors report the descriptive statistics in the original scale by taking the exponential of the value in the reported model.

Popularity of the packages a developer maintained, computed as the sum of the votes for all the packages maintained by the developer. Since early 2001, Debian users have been able to install a 'popularity-contest package' that automatically calculates the number of people that download, install, and use a particular package. The popularity count is akin to a citation count in academic circles: it signifies how many people in the community use or rely upon your work. The authors report the descriptive statistics in the original scale by taking the exponential of the value in the reported model.

Number of e-mail postings a developer made to the 'debian-devel' mailing list, the one list to which all developers subscribe. Debian has over 100 different mailing lists, focused on different subgroups of developers and specific technical issues. The number of e-mails a developer posted on this mailing list provided a reasonable proxy for his or her propensity to communicate publicly with the rest of the community. The authors report the descriptive statistics in the original scale by taking the exponential of the value in the reported model.

Count of the number of other community members the developer had met as of January 1, 2003, based on keys signed by dyads in the Debian keyring from 1994 until January 1, 2003. Since each key signing is dated and requires a face-to-face meeting, these data indicate when project members met each other. The measure only counts each single face-to-face meeting and is considered a very conservative measure.

Coded for developers who held a position on the community's full leadership team in 2003: project leader, project secretary, software release coordinator, developer accounts manager, and members of the technical committee. Release coordinators shepherd the project to closure and developer account managers are responsible for allocating account rights to the project's code repository. The technical committee (selected by the project leader) has the constitutional right to resolve technical disputes.

Each subject is assigned to one of six treatment conditions defining the organizational structure: solitary agent (A), hierarchy of two members (H), polyarchy of two members with individual payoffs (P), coordinated polyarchy of two members with shared payoffs (CP), random-position hierarchy of two members (RH), and fixed-position coordinated polyarchy of two members (FCP). Assignment of subjects to treatments is random, and in the two-member treatments subjects are permanently and anonymously paired by the server software. These pairs (or individuals in treatment A) are the independent units of observation.

Estimated from a mixed logit model of the accept/reject decision as a function of image quality, in which the reservation parameter equals (alpha minus R) divided by sigma and is estimated jointly with the slope by maximum likelihood; because the noise scale sigma is indeterminate, the estimated parameter has the opposite sign relative to the reservation level R. Marginal effects of interest are computed as average marginal effects, with standard errors computed based on clustering by pairs and with random effects defined over pairs (individuals in treatment A). The parameter is estimated at the aggregate organizational level, at the group level and at the individual level.
time_window: last 50 periods of the performance stage

description: Estimated jointly with the reservation parameter by maximum likelihood in the same mixed logit model of the accept/reject decision, where the slope parameter equals beta divided by sigma and a higher value implies higher screening capability. It is estimated at the aggregate organizational level, at the group level and, using the stacking approach, for each individual position (first and second agent) within an organization.
time_window: last 50 periods of the performance stage

description: The fraction of decisions that are correct, calculated as 1 minus the type I error rate minus the type II error rate, where the type I error rate is the ratio of false positives (rejected good) to total images and the type II error rate is the ratio of false negatives (accepted bad) to total images.
time_window: last 50 periods of the performance stage

description: Index of the extent to which a focal firm's partners controlled large shares of their respective telecommunications markets, computed as the sum of squares of the market shares of the firm's partners, where each partner's share is of its primary market (local, long-distance, or wireless services). The squared functional form assumes that a partner's market power and nonsubstitutability increase at an increasing rate with its market share. High values indicate that a firm's alliance partners had relatively large resource endowments and would be difficult to replace.

Index computed as the proportion of a firm's alliance partners that were incumbent local exchange carriers in a given year. It is an industry-specific measure of the market power that arises from these carriers' monopolist or quasi-monopolist control over access lines or local loops: the higher the proportion of incumbent local exchange carriers in a firm's alliance network, the less substitutable its partners are.

Calculated as the ratio between the observed and the maximum possible number of alliances for a given number of partners, capturing the presence or absence of ties among alliance partners. The measure was computed using UCINET. It is treated as an adequate measure of both the absence of structural holes in an alliance network and of its closure.

Measured as yearly net income divided by invested capital, where invested capital is the sum of common equity, long-term debt, and preferred stock. It is one of two measures used to capture organizational profitability.

Measured as yearly net income divided by average total assets for that year. Unlike ROI, its calculation does not take into account how the firm finances its assets. It is the second measure used to capture organizational profitability.

The percentage of pie-splitting (PS) control rights won by the pharmaceutical firm. Ten PS control rights were identified from a review of the literature on R&D alliances and alliance contractual design combined with input from industry practitioners; for each agreement the authors counted the number of PS control rights allocated and calculated the percentage won by the pharmaceutical partner. The rights were coded from the point of view of the pharmaceutical firm, and some rights are binary while others are cumulative.
The amount pharmaceutical firms spent annually on biotechnology R&D alliances, in billions of dollars, measured using data from Recap.
The percentage of alliances in a period that were late-stage alliances, calculated from the sample of alliances.
The total amount of money raised in biotechnology IPOs in the previous quarter, in billions of dollars, obtained from the SDC database.

The number of patents assigned to an early-stage biotechnology firm as at the time of signing an alliance, minus the number of patents assigned to the early-stage biotechnology firm with the fewest patents in that period. Patents were identified from U.S. Patent and Trademark Office data.
