The percentage formed by dividing the equity of the subsidiary by the stockholder's equity of the parent and multiplying by 100. The authors note that the average relative size of individual subsidiaries is about 1.6 percent of the size of the core business.
Coded 1 for multidivisional structures, 0 otherwise.

A subsidiary was judged to be related when common skills, resources or a common purpose applied to each of the businesses, including similarities in day-to-day operation, technological and infrastructure inputs, applicability of human skill, and similarities in end-markets or channels of distribution. Two senior managers, one from an electric utility and one from a regulatory commission, coded the business descriptions, and the author categorized the cases on which they disagreed.

The time elapsed from the birth date of the subsidiary to its termination or to censoring, used as the time dimension in the hazard models. Age was measured in years rather than decades, a choice the authors note matters for whether evidence of a liability of newness would be found.

Death was defined to include dissolution of the subsidiary and the sale of its operations to other companies, following the view that exiting a business line constitutes strategic failure. Information on birth and termination dates was used, subsidiaries that were merged or folded into other operations were deleted, and the remaining observations were treated as right-censored.

Five closed-ended Guttman type scales measuring ends specificity were developed. Statements ranging in choices from unspecified to very specific were presented, and in every scale but one respondents indicated which one statement best described their firm. Individual scale scores were summed to obtain the overall ends specificity score, with low specificity scores indicating ends typical of the Incremental Model and high specificity scores denoting ends characteristic of the Synoptic Model.

Four closed-ended Guttman type scales measuring means specificity were developed. Statements ranging in choices from unspecified to very specific were presented, and in every scale but one respondents indicated which one statement best described their firm. Individual scale scores were summed to obtain the overall means specificity score, with low specificity scores indicating means typical of the Incremental Model and high specificity scores denoting means characteristic of the Synoptic Model.

A Guttman type scale was developed to measure planning flexibility because no prior research measuring the construct was located. Respondents indicated how often their firm's ends are changed or altered. Planning flexibility is scaled so that higher scores indicate greater inflexibility, so a negative coefficient means high specificity with high flexibility.

A Guttman type scale was developed to measure planning flexibility because no prior research measuring the construct was located. Respondents indicated how often their firm's means are changed or altered, using the same scale statements as for ends flexibility. Planning flexibility is scaled so that higher scores indicate greater inflexibility, so a negative coefficient means high specificity with high flexibility.

A subjective perceptual measure capturing overall firm performance data relative to competitive peers and firm market share change over the past 5-10 years, described by the authors as an externally anchored performance measure. OFP scores were obtained by summing the three industry peer comparison scores with the market share change score. In the peer comparison scales a 'Not Applicable' box was included for firms that did not have listed securities, or for divisions/business units that did not have any stock performance to rate; when this box was checked the average of the other two factors was used as a proxy for stock price performance.

A subjective perceptual measure capturing the planning performance of respondent firms, described by the authors as an internally anchored performance measure evaluating planning capabilities and effectiveness. PP scores were obtained by summing the six individual item ratings provided by respondents.

Respondents self-selected one of four industry/business environments that most closely described their firm's industry/business environment, ranging from a mature, stable context to a young industry in which the rules of competition are still emerging. Because of the relatively few respondents who selected the third and fourth choices, these were merged into a single 'high instability' category, giving a trifurcated categorization of environmental stability: Mature/Stable, Mature/Unstable, and Very Unstable.

In another section of the questionnaire respondents rated the stability of their firm's primary industry across ten industry stability factors using a seven point rating scale, and indicated which word of two in three pairs best described the business environment of their firm: slow or rapid change, stable or unstable, and predictable or unpredictable. Where slow change, stable, or predictable was chosen a score of -1 was given, where rapid change, unstable, or unpredictable was chosen a score of 1 was given, and a 'not applicable' choice scored 0. The industry stability ratings and the respective -1, 0, 1 scores received for the three pairs of words were summed to obtain Industry Stability scores for each firm.

Respondents reported the period of time their firms had been conducting the planning in one of five choices: less than one year; 1-3 years; 4-7 years; 8-15 years; and more than 15 years. Comparing data obtained on firms with a planning duration of three years or fewer with firms reporting a planning duration of four years or more tested the impact of planning duration.

A count of the number of subsidiaries a firm divested in each year in its home market, the United States. The measure was created by consulting the Directory of Corporate Affiliates for each firm for each year from 1981-2000 and tracking subsidiaries, defined as businesses owned by the company 50% or more; divisions and affiliates were not included, and no weighting of subsidiaries was possible because size, employees, and sales are not consistently reported.

The total number of new foreign investments for each firm in each year in developing countries, based on subsidiaries (parent owns more than 50%) listed in the Directory of Corporate Affiliates. The location choice proxies for lower-cost production opportunities, on the argument that U.S. manufacturing firms are more likely to invest in developing countries to gain access to cheaper inputs. Developing countries include Mexico, most Asian countries (not Japan), Central and South American countries, Eastern European countries, ex-Soviet bloc countries, Russia, and African countries.

The total number of new foreign investments for each firm in each year in industrialized countries, based on subsidiaries listed in the Directory of Corporate Affiliates. The location choice proxies for new market opportunities, on the argument that U.S. manufacturing firms are more likely to invest in industrialized countries to exploit knowledge created in their home country. Industrialized countries include the United States, Canada, Western European countries, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand.

Total product diversification measured with an entropy index calculated from Compustat segment tapes; the formula is unreadable in the extracted text, so only the prose description is recorded. The measure takes into consideration both the number of segments in which a firm operates and the relative importance of each segment in the total sales of the firm, and is described as a weighted average of the shares of the segments, the weight for each segment being the logarithm of the inverse of its share. The variable was mean centered before being interacted with new foreign investment.

To examine different levels of a firm's foreign investment activity, a firm's total number of foreign subsidiaries was used to separate firm years into quartiles. The quartile splits were made by observation, not by firms, so firms can and do change quartiles over the time period. The first quartile contains firms with no foreign subsidiaries, and these benchmark firms were included in the second, third, and fourth quartile subsamples.

In weeks 4 and 5 of a 10-week strategy course each subject constructed detailed scenarios concerning his or her chosen strategic variables, over a time frame of 1 to 5 years, and received graded feedback from the instructor on completeness, coherence and scope. Part (iii) of the exercise then repeated the initial estimates and ranges.

Subjects chose strategically important issues and a few quantitative target variables (for example profit margins, sales, market share, budget size, returns on investment, salary and personal wealth) and gave a best estimate plus a 50 percent and a 90 percent confidence range for each, anchored at a future date; a friend or colleague familiar with the issue did the same. The same measures were collected again after scenario construction, and the after/before ratios of range widths served as the measure of stretching.
time_window: before: weeks 2-3; after: weeks 6-7 of the course

variable_name: high and low scenarios at 30 percent or 50 percent
description: Each subject developed both a 'high' and a 'low' scenario for the assigned variable such that the target would be 30 percent (in one condition) or 50 percent (in the second condition) above or below his or her best guess, each typed on one page. The control group did not construct scenarios for the question it rated in stage II.

Upon completing the two scenarios, subjects wrote down a best guess and a 50 percent and a 90 percent confidence range for the assigned variable, with the note that the ranges should be as symmetric as possible around the best guess. In stage II the 50 percent and 90 percent ranges for all three questions were collected from all subjects, permitting a scenario vs. control contrast and a 30 percent vs. 50 percent contrast within the scenario group.
time_window: one week take-home exercise followed by stage II collection

description: Each subject received six outcomes in a fixed order and assigned each a subjective probability from 0 percent to 100 percent of occurring sometime before the end of 1990; two of the six outcomes were conjunctions. Group A received the conjunctions of the interest-rate question with the Democrat-president question and of the Dow Jones question with the oil-price question, while group B received the conjunctions of the economic-growth question with the trade-surplus question and of the Central America question with the apartheid question, so that each group served as the other's control.
time_window: fall 1986; outcomes assessed to the end of 1990

description: The same 0 percent to 100 percent probability assignment was elicited for the elemental, non-conjunctive outcomes, such as U.S. GNP growth of at least 4 percent per annum by the end of 1990, short-term interest rates exceeding 13 percent, election of a Democrat as U.S. president, a U.S. trade surplus with Japan, direct U.S. military involvement in Central America, the Dow Jones falling below 1500, oil prices exceeding $30 per barrel, and the fall of the South African apartheid regime.
time_window: fall 1986; outcomes assessed to the end of 1990

description: For each subject the 5 by 5 matrix of subjective correlations was sliced into six triplets, and each triplet was submitted to an upper and lower bound test derived from the statistical requirement that absolute partial correlations do not exceed unity, so that a total of 12 inequalities could be tested per matrix. The consistency index is the percent of inequality tests passed out of the total permissible tests; where matrix elements were blank or marked with a question mark the tests assumed either a missing value or a zero correlation.

After reading a Stanford case on Apple Computer, each subject identified the five most important strategic uncertainties facing Apple and assessed their interrelationships using subjective correlations ranging from -1 to +1, completing a 5 by 5 matrix on the answer sheet.

A binary indicator of HD Radio adoption by a station in a given quarter, drawn from digital broadcast registration dates in the FCC Media Bureau's Consolidated Database System. The variable is equal to 0 for all station-quarters prior to adoption and 1 in the quarter of HD Radio adoption; the station exits from the sample after that. No stations abandoned the technology during the study and there is no left censoring of the data.

A dichotomous variable that indicates the legal transfer of more than 50 percent of the station's equity. Sale data are taken from the Consolidated Database System for the FCC's Media Bureau and cross-referenced against press releases and other media reports. The variable captures any sale in the nine-month period including the observation period, after sensitivity tests of three-, six-, nine-, and 12-month linearly decayed and undecayed windows.
time_window: nine-month period including the observation period

description: A count of the number of stations in the referent group that adopted HD Radio in the six months prior to the spell at risk of an adoption event. Geographically proximate adoptions are captured using a count of adopting stations that share a local market. The six-month window was selected because sensitivity tests showed it provides the best statistical fit.
time_window: six months prior to the spell at risk

description: A count of adopting stations with a common corporate parent, measured over the six months prior to the spell at risk of an adoption event.
time_window: six months prior to the spell at risk

description: A count of adoptions by stations with similar broadcast formats (i.e., rock music, sports talk, classical music), measured over the six months prior to the spell at risk of an adoption event.
time_window: six months prior to the spell at risk

description: Binary explanatory variable set to 1 for those alliances that were exposed to an acquisition event (the main sample of alliances) and 0 for those alliances in the matched control group that were not exposed to an acquisition event. A control alliance had to be functional ('alive') on the date at which the treated alliance was exposed to an acquisition, after which treated alliances were matched with up to 10 control observations using nearest-neighbor matching on propensity scores.

Binary measure that captures whether an alliance was terminated within a 24-month window following an acquisition event; coded 1 if the alliance's termination date fell within the window and 0 if it fell outside. Termination dates were extracted from Factiva press releases covering each alliance; for alliances whose termination was not explicitly covered by a press release, the year and month of the alliance's last press release were recorded as its termination date. For control alliances the 24-month window was measured from the acquisition date of the matched treated alliance.

variable_name: stress on the acquirer's alliance capacity
description: Measured as the ratio of the number of inherited alliances (the additional number of target alliances the acquirer must now manage post acquisition) to the number of the acquirer's preexisting alliances (the number of alliances to which the acquirer's existing alliance management capacity is allocated). The treated group is then split into a high-stress group (stress greater than the sample median) and a low-stress group (stress less than or equal to the sample median), with matched control alliances allocated to the corresponding subgroup.

Binary variable that identifies the alliances inherited from the target. It equals 1 for alliances inherited from the target firm (T-TP) and 0 for the acquirer's preexisting alliances (F-FP); its coefficient estimates the average probability of termination of alliances inherited from targets compared to the termination probability of the acquirer's preexisting alliances.

Count of the number of partners that either TP or FP shares with the acquirer's or the target's alliance portfolio, respectively, depending on whether the alliance in question is an inherited alliance or an acquirer's preexisting alliance. For a target alliance it indicates the number of common partners between this alliance partner's portfolio and the acquiring firm's preexisting alliance portfolio; for an acquirer's preexisting alliance it indicates the number of common partners between this alliance partner and the target firm's alliance portfolio. For the calculation, the authors consider the pool of alliances entered into by the alliance partners themselves, tracking ties from formation to termination and using the sample average tie duration of 4 years where termination data were unavailable.

Count of the number of partners that the alliance partner (either TP or FP) has collaborations with that are nonoverlapping with both the target's and the acquirer's portfolio of alliances; it is the count of firms outside the combined (i.e., union of) relationships of the acquirer and the target. It is built from the pool of alliances entered into by the alliance partners themselves, tracked from formation to termination, using the sample average tie duration of 4 years where termination data were unavailable.

Divestitures in the sample are classified either as spinoffs or as management buyouts. A spinoff distributes pro rata the shares of a subsidiary to the parent firm shareholders, creating a publicly traded company that continues the operations of the division or subsidiary; a buyout sells a subsidiary to an investor group that includes the managers of that organization, creating a private company that continues those operations. Only divestitures whose announcement reports an innovation opportunity for the divested unit, identified from divestiture announcements using a dictionary of innovation-related terms, enter the sample. The models contrast buyouts with spinoffs over the five years after divestiture.

We measure strategic emphasis as the difference between R&D and marketing expenditures divided by the firm's assets, in order to account for firm's size (Mizik and Jacobson, 2003). The paper states that the measure is then specified to account for the industry in which a firm competes, but the equation giving that specification is not readable in the text provided. Data on R&D expenditures, marketing expenditures and assets are collected from the same sources used for the paper's other accounting data, and TNS Media is used to supplement data on marketing expenditures.
scale: ratio (difference between R&D and marketing expenditures over assets)
time_window: first through fifth year after the divestiture

description: Products introduced by each divested unit each year are identified through announcements of new product introductions, coded independently by a research assistant and one author. Two ten-point scales measure the extent to which a new product (1) incorporates a substantially different core technology and (2) provides substantially higher customer benefits. We multiply the score of the two scales to get a measure of radicalness. The radicalness of a divestiture at time t is calculated as the mean of the radicalness of all the products that it introduced during the time period.
scale: product of two ten-point scales, averaged across products
time_window: first through fifth year after the divestiture

description: Performance is measured with profits, and specifically return on asset (ROA). Data are collected from the Wharton Research Data Service and supplemented with the Edgar SEC database, which provides copies of the firms' annual reports.
time_window: first through fifth year after the divestiture

description: The acquirer's bid minus the target's pre-announcement market value divided by the target's pre-announcement market value, expressed as a percentage. The reported analysis uses the announcement-day premium in order to reduce the effect of distracting events without excluding the stock market's pre-announcement anticipation; premia determined over longer time periods are analyzed in robustness tests.

The target firm's R&D investment over the four previous fiscal years, divided by the target firm's pre-acquisition market value. The authors note that the R&D-to-sales ratio is a problematic measure of R&D in growing firms that may not yet have generated much sales revenue, and therefore scale R&D by pre-acquisition market value instead.
time_window: four fiscal years prior to the acquisition

description: The growth of the target firm's R&D investment measured over the four years prior to the acquisition.
time_window: four years prior to the acquisition

description: The target firm's pre-acquisition market value divided by its book value of equity. The 14 firms that had negative equity were excluded from the analyses because the ratio has a different meaning when its sign is reversed.

A market model was created for each acquiring firm's stock by regressing 200 daily dividend-corrected returns from day -240 to -40 against the index; the model was then used to determine expected returns. Differences from the model were regarded as abnormal returns for acquirer shareholders and were summed up over the chosen window to form the cumulative abnormal returns. Results for the acquisition time window from -1 day to +1 day are reported formally, with other windows discussed in robustness tests.
time_window: day -1 to +1 relative to the acquisition announcement; market model estimated from day -240 to -40

description: The dependent variable is the amount of time elapsed between the emergence of the networking switches market and a firm's entry event, or censoring. The entry event is the first appearance of a firm being listed as a producer of networking switches in the CorpTech Directory. The hazard rate of entry is estimated with a piecewise exponential specification in which the rate stays constant within each period t(j) to t(j+1) but varies arbitrarily between periods.

Network density, defined as the degree to which a firm's contacts are connected between each other, is calculated by dividing the number of actual ties by the number of all possible pairs, multiplied by 100. The measure is based on relationships with horizontally linked partners, is updated annually, and is lagged one year in the analytical model. One assumption in constructing the measures is that the duration of alliances is only one year and the alliances terminate 12 months after the announcement.

Network constraint is an index that measures the extent to which a firm's contacts are separated by structural holes, where the holes are like buffers that separate the contacts into groups; more constraint means more network closure and constraint is higher if there are fewer holes in a firm's social structure. The measure is built from relationships with horizontally linked partners, computed with UCINET 6, updated annually, and lagged one year.

Used as a measure of brokerage opportunities: in a dense network, the direct connections between contacts eliminate opportunities to broker information, so the authors expect a negative relationship with the rate of entry and a high value indicates fewer brokerage opportunities. The measure is built from relationships with horizontally linked partners, updated annually, and lagged one year.

Used as a measure of brokerage opportunities: more constrained networks have fewer brokerage opportunities because there are fewer structural holes separating the sources of information, so the authors expect a negative relationship with the rate of entry and a high value indicates fewer brokerage opportunities. The measure is built from relationships with horizontally linked partners and is computed with UCINET 6.

Network degree is the number of directly linked contacts and measures the extent to which a firm is positioned at the crossroads of information flow; the more direct connections a firm has, the larger the size of its network and the more central (degree centrality) its hub-like position is. The measure is built from relationships with horizontally linked partners, computed with UCINET 6, updated annually, and lagged one year.

The ratio between the number of alliances and the number of partners, capturing the extent to which a firm has multiple ties with the same partner; the higher the alliance-per-partner ratio is, the more repeated interactions there are with direct contacts. The measure is based on relationships with horizontally linked partners.

variable_name: Standard deviation of the alliance-per-partner ratio over 2-year windows (horizontal relationships only)
description: The standard deviation of the alliance-per-partner ratio between the prior year and the current year, calculated over 2-year moving windows. For the same number of alliances, the higher the standard deviation is, the more likely that the network configuration changes over time.

variable_name: Count of alliance partners (and its square)
description: The count of alliance partners, which includes both horizontally linked and vertically linked partners, entered together with its square to estimate the inverted-U-shaped relationship between network size and the rate of entry. The total count of partners prior to entry is also used as a normalizing control variable.

Blau's heterogeneity index measures a firm's aggregate network composition prior to entry and captures the distinction between partners of dissimilar operational context; it has a higher value when the composition is more heterogeneous, and its value is 0 for a completely homogeneous network. The proportion is computed based on all alliances prior to entry; the equation for the index is not readable in the text provided.

variable_name: Number of firms already entered (and its square)
description: The count of firms operating in the market, used as a proxy for the level of legitimation and competition in the emerging product market and entered with its square. The net effect is expected to shift from legitimation at low density to competition at high density.
Corporate risk of firm i, defined as the variance of ROA over the 5-year period 1977-81. It is the dependent variable of the risk equation.

Industry risk (IRK) is measured at the four-digit SIC code level as the relative variation of industry demand. The firm-level WIRK weights each industry's risk by the square of the weight of that industry, the weight being the fraction of the firm's total net sales generated from it. Because of the square effect, WIRK decreases as the number of businesses increases, so the variable proxies both industry and diversity effects.
The logarithm of the mean assets of firm i over the 5-year period 1977-81. Asset data are drawn from Compustat I for the years 1977-81.
The total count of three-digit SIC code industries in which the firm operates. The data are drawn from Compustat II using 1979 as the base year.
Corporate return of firm i measured by the mean ROA over the 5-year period 1977-81. It is the dependent variable of the return equation.

Industry profitability is measured by the price-cost margin at the four-digit SIC level, computed as the gross margin of a four-digit industry divided by the total value of shipments of that industry, where gross margin is value added minus total payroll minus rental payments. For non-manufacturing industries a proxy is computed from the ratio of the total gross margin of all firms under the same industry code in Compustat I to their total net sales. The mean industry profitability (MIP) across 1977-81 for each industry in which the firm operates is multiplied by the fraction of the firm's total net sales generated from that industry to form WIRN; where a segment has two SIC codes the segment sales are split equally.

Two dummy variables represent generic diversification strategy: RL equals 1 for related-linked firms and 0 otherwise; UR equals 1 for unrelated firms and 0 otherwise, so related-constrained firms are the omitted reference category. The categories of the sample firms were determined by Rumelt (1974) and updated by Bettis and Hall (1982); the authors note that dummy variables only provide rough estimates of diversification strategy effects because the degree of relatedness among business segments is not homogeneous within a strategy category.
The ratio of the mean ROA over 1980/84 to the mean ROA over 1977/81. It belongs to the set of variables used in the analyses of the causal relationship between diversification and performance.

The change in product diversity from 1978 to 1983. Product diversity PDIV(78) is estimated by a Herfindahl formula in which w is the fraction of total corporate sales contributed by a four-digit industry of the firm. The formula itself is not readable in the text.
The change in geographic diversity from 1978/80 to 1981/83. Geographic diversity is estimated as the ratio of mean international sales over mean corporate sales, both over a 3-year period.

Team-level Gini coefficient of individual player salaries on team j, computed separately for each team and each year, with salaries arranged in decreasing order of size. The maximum gini coefficient is unity, indicating the greatest degree of dispersion (absolute inequality), and the minimum is zero, indicating the lowest degree of dispersion (absolute equality); organizations with higher gini coefficients have more hierarchical pay dispersions. The algebraic formula is not readable in the extracted text.

Coefficient of variation of pay on a team, used as an alternative variation measure of the entire pay distribution (Pfeffer & Langton, 1993). A larger coefficient of variation indicates greater pay dispersion. Team ginis and coefficients of variation were correlated at .72.

variable_name: Maximum pay on team - player's pay
description: A ratio measure of pay dispersion computed as the simple difference between the maximum pay on a team and a player's pay, based on upward comparisons only, since people judge their pay against those who are higher in the organizational hierarchy. Larger values indicate greater dispersion.
A ratio measure of pay dispersion computed as the ratio of a player's pay to the maximum pay on the team, based on upward comparisons only. Smaller values indicate greater dispersion.

Rank of a player's pay on his team, with the rank of the highest-paid player equal to 1; a lower value indicated a higher position in the dispersion. The rank of a player's pay rather than actual pay was used because the study concerned the interaction between relative pay and pay dispersion. An interaction term was created by multiplying the rank by the team gini coefficient.

A standard measure of offensive performance: how many points (runs) a player contributed to his team over the course of a season, where a higher score indicates better player performance. It is a composite of several different indicators intended to capture the variety of ways a player can contribute points offensively, with coefficients from Palmer's analysis of all major league games over a 77-year period. Batting runs are normalized and adjusted for characteristics of home baseball parks, allowing comparisons of player performance across time periods. The formula is not readable in the extracted text.

Defensive performance converted into run equivalents: efforts a player makes to prevent an opposing team from scoring runs are treated as if they contributed points to his own team. Like adjusted batting runs it is a composite of several different indicators of defensive performance, with coefficients from Palmer's 77-year analysis, and it is adjusted for a player's defensive position; the league average for fielding runs at the player's position enters the formula. Higher scores indicate better performance. The full formula as printed is only partly readable in the extracted text.

A composite of several measures that assess a player's overall offensive and defensive performance. It assesses a player's performance relative to the performance of all other nonpitchers in major league baseball in a specific year. Higher scores indicate better performance.

Earned runs times nine divided by innings pitched; it reflects how many of an opposing team's points result from hits made while a particular pitcher was performing and is adjusted for the home baseball park. A higher value indicates poorer pitcher performance since it indicates opposing teams scored more points while the pitcher was pitching.

Computed as innings pitched divided by nine, multiplied by the difference between the individual earned run average and the league-average earned run average. It treats efforts a pitcher makes to prevent opposing teams from scoring runs as points contributed to the pitcher's team. Higher scores indicate better performance.

A composite measure that reflects a pitcher's overall performance relative to that of all other major league baseball pitchers in a specific year; it measures overall pitching and fielding performance.
On-field performance measured as wins divided by games played.
On-field performance measured as total home attendance divided by the product of stadium capacity and home games.

The number of games behind the division leader the team was at season's end, which measures the team's performance relative to its most important competitors, division rivals. The higher this value, the poorer the performance.

All team revenue and valuation data were obtained from Financial World and are not available for years prior to 1990. Gate receipts included all gate and club receipts but excluded sales taxes; media income included national, local, and cable television and radio revenues; total income was the sum of gate, media, and stadium receipts, the stadium receipts component including suites and luxury seat fees, concessions, parking fees, venue advertising, and licensing and merchandising income; franchise value was the assessed value of a team franchise computed by researchers at Financial World on the basis of total revenues, the team's playing venue, associated leases, and other information.
time_window: from 1990 onward (data not available for years prior to 1990)

description: Binary variable indicating that a hospital employed unit managers in its inpatient units (1 = employed, 0 = not employed) at some point during the study period. The questionnaire asked hospital administrators whether they had ever adopted unit management, defined as the presence of unit managers, administrators, or coordinators in hospital inpatient units, and in what years they adopted it. These data were used to compute the probability of adoption.

Administrators who reported adopting unit management were asked whether they had discontinued the program and in what years they adopted and abandoned it. The survey information on the time of abandonment was used to compute the probability of abandonment among hospitals operating the program.

Number of emergency department visits divided by total hospital admissions, reflecting the diversity of clients treated. Values were measured at the four panel points and linearly interpolated to annual values for the event-history analyses.
time_window: measured in 1961, 1966, 1972, and 1978; interpolated annually and lagged one year

description: Outpatient visits divided by total hospital admissions, reflecting the diversity of clients treated. Values were measured at the four panel points and linearly interpolated to annual values for the event-history analyses.
time_window: measured in 1961, 1966, 1972, and 1978; interpolated annually and lagged one year

description: Composite of two indicators of functional diversity, the presence of an affiliation with a medical school (1 = affiliation, 0 = no affiliation) and the size of the hospital's teaching program (number of residents). Principal components analysis was used to combine the indicators, and the measure was constructed from the factor loadings of the first principal component extracted (74 percent of common variance explained).
time_window: measured in 1961, 1966, 1972, and 1978; interpolated annually and lagged one year

description: Composite of three indicators, the number of hospital beds, the volume of hospital revenues, and the volume of hospital expenses, combined using principal components analysis. The measure was constructed from the factor loadings of the first component extracted (81 percent of common variance explained).
time_window: measured in 1961, 1966, 1972, and 1978; interpolated annually and lagged one year

description: Total hospital revenues minus total expenses, multiplied by 100,000.
time_window: measured in 1961, 1966, 1972, and 1978; interpolated annually and lagged one year

description: Composite of the academic reputation and visibility of the medical school with which a hospital was affiliated. Reputation came from a study in which a national sample of medical school faculty members ranked the reputations of medical schools on the perceived quality of their medical faculties (distinguished = 6, poor = 1); visibility was the percentage of all respondents who felt they had sufficient information to rate a school. The two ratings were combined using principal components analysis (one factor extracted; 99 percent of common variance explained), and prestige was measured once, in the mid-1970s, and assumed constant throughout the panel period.
time_window: measured in the mid-1970s and assumed constant over the panel period

description: Number of reports of matrix programs appearing each year in health administration research and trade journals between 1961 and 1978. A content analysis of the reports revealed that only 3 percent dwelt on any negative aspects of the focal matrix program.

Percentage of hospitals in the same geographic region adopting matrix management by the year prior to a survey point. Nine geographic regions were specified using the classification scheme of the American Hospital Association.
time_window: cumulative by the year prior to each survey point

description: Percentage of hospitals in the same Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA) adopting matrix management by the year prior to a survey point, measured in the same manner as the regional force of adoption.
time_window: cumulative by the year prior to each survey point

description: The regional proportion of hospitals discontinuing matrix management by a prior measurement period.
time_window: cumulative by a prior measurement period

description: The cumulative force of abandonment in the local network, the Metropolitan Statistical Area, before a given measurement period.
time_window: cumulative by a prior measurement period

description: MSAs were split in half using data from the later period and classified as the acceptance group or the nonacceptance group. The acceptance group comprises MSAs that had a hospital using matrix management in 1971 and a cumulative experience of at least ten program-years, a program year being one year of a hospital's operating a matrix program; all other MSAs form the nonacceptance group.
time_window: experience prior to 1972, used to split the late-period (1972-78) analyses

variable_name: Center-periphery influence (adoption after a higher-prestige hospital in the local area)
description: In each local area with two or more adoptions, every second and later adoption was classified by the prestige of the adopting hospital's medical school network relative to earlier adopters: same network (structural equivalence), less prestigious network (center-periphery), or more prestigious network (periphery-center). High-prestige prior adoption is captured by the center-periphery category: adoption by a hospital in a less prestigious network than a hospital that had already adopted. The share of adoptions in each category is compared, and dummy variables for the three network effects are added to the adoption regression.

variable_name: Entrepreneurial strategy making (factor score for Entrepreneurial SMP)
description: Measured using a modification of Hart's (1991) instrument, which relates to strategy-making practices and processes, CEO style, and general management orientation, and consists of 25 items with associated 5-point Likert scales ranging from 1 'Strongly Disagree' to 5 'Strongly Agree'. Factor scores for the ESM factor developed in Phase 1 were used in the regression analysis; Cronbach's alpha for the variables loading on the entrepreneurial SMP factor was 0.64. CEO responses were used to represent the entrepreneurial strategy-making variable to minimize common method variance.
scale: 5-point Likert (1 = Strongly Disagree to 5 = Strongly Agree)

variable_name: Firm performance (sales growth; profitability/ROI; overall company performance)
description: Performance was measured by obtaining individual responses to three performance indices assessed with a 7-point Likert type scale ranging from 1 'Low Performer' to 7 'High Performer'. The three categories include sales growth, profitability and return on investment, and overall company performance. The questionnaire asked executives to 'assess your organization's performance OVER THE PAST FIVE YEARS relative to your competitors'. Responses of other executives were averaged to obtain a firm-level score.
scale: 7-point Likert type (1 = Low Performer to 7 = High Performer)

description: The environment portion of the survey used Miller's (1983) measures of dynamism, unpredictability and heterogeneity. The three dynamism and two unpredictability items used 7-point semantic differential-type scales anchored by descriptive phrases. Since unpredictability and dynamism are the key components of the overarching construct of uncertainty, the dynamism and unpredictability variables were combined into a composite index of environmental uncertainty. Responses of other executives were averaged to a firm-level score.

The heterogeneity portion consisted of three items relating to customer buying habits, competition, and technological requirements, and used a 7-point scale. Managerial perceptions of the environment were used, as supported by prior studies on their relevance to strategy formulation and their accuracy with respect to objective measures. Responses of other executives were averaged to a firm-level score.

The measure of Porter's generic strategies used a 7-item scale similar to the scale developed by Miller (1988), asking questions regarding the importance of specific competitive tactics; it includes two cost leadership items, two innovative differentiation items and three marketing differentiation items. The scale is a 5-point Likert-type scale with responses ranging from 1 'Not At All Important' to 5 'Extremely Important'. Responses of other executives were averaged to a firm-level score.
scale: 5-point Likert-type (1 = Not At All Important to 5 = Extremely Important)

description: Three of the 7 items of the Porter generic strategy scale, similar to Miller's (1988) scale, ask about the importance of specific competitive tactics associated with marketing differentiation. The scale is a 5-point Likert-type scale with responses ranging from 1 'Not At All Important' to 5 'Extremely Important'. Responses of other executives were averaged to a firm-level score.
scale: 5-point Likert-type (1 = Not At All Important to 5 = Extremely Important)

description: Two of the 7 items of the Porter generic strategy scale, similar to Miller's (1988) scale, ask about the importance of specific competitive tactics associated with innovative differentiation. The scale is a 5-point Likert-type scale with responses ranging from 1 'Not At All Important' to 5 'Extremely Important'. Responses of other executives were averaged to a firm-level score.
scale: 5-point Likert-type (1 = Not At All Important to 5 = Extremely Important)

description: Factor score from the exploratory factor analysis (principal factors method with promax rotation) of the 25 strategy-making process variables. The factor includes variables indicating a participative management style, and two variables with significant negative loadings that were considered the opposite of participation.

Factor score from the exploratory factor analysis of the 25 strategy-making process variables. The factor suggests an external orientation focused on adapting to customer needs and responding to cues and feedback from the environment.

Factor score from the exploratory factor analysis of the 25 strategy-making process variables. The factor indicates a well-established but limited strategy-making process, corresponding to a routine way of conducting business or a narrow focus on a dominant element of strategy.

variable_name: Percent of variance in business-unit ROA attributed to stable and unstable effects
description: The total variance in business-unit ROA is partitioned in each 4-year moving window into stable and unstable economy, industry, corporate-parent, and business-unit effects, and each effect is reported as a percentage of that total. Random effects assumptions are applied and the estimation uses the SAS VARCOMP procedure with the ANOVA method, also known as Henderson's Method II. Because of computational limitations each 4-year window is randomly subsampled into 4000-observation subsamples and weighted average variance components estimates are calculated.
scale: percentage of total variance in ROA

variable_name: 1-year lagged ROA (ROA it-1) and its interaction with the year counter (ROA it-1 * YEAR t)
description: Business-unit ROA is regressed on a constant, the 1-year lagged value of ROA, a year counter ranging from 1 (in 1979) to 19 (in 1997), the interaction of lagged ROA and the year counter, annual GDP growth, annual inflation, and an error term. The lagged ROA coefficient generally falls between 0 and 1.00, with a value near 1.00 indicating little if any decay in abnormal returns from the last to the current year; the interaction coefficient indicates whether the rate of decay in abnormal returns exhibits a linear time trend. The analysis includes all businesses from 1979 to 1997 that reported financial data in the previous year.

A dummy taking the value of 1 if the business unit does not survive in the following year. It is modeled with a proportional hazard rate model explaining the likelihood that a business will disappear (exit) from an industry in the next year. The sample includes all businesses from 1978 to 1996, excluding observations from 1997 because survival in the following year cannot be determined.

Industry sales, capital expenditures, and assets are each regressed on a variable representing the years in the 5-year panel. The standard error of each regression is divided by the mean value of the dependent variable, and the average of these three resulting numbers yields a composite measure of the level of dynamism in the industry in each year of the four 5-year periods examined.

Munificence is measured using the regression coefficients for each of the regressions of industry sales, capital expenditures, and assets on the years in the 5-year panel. The coefficients for the three indexes are averaged to construct a composite measure of the level of industry munificence in each year of the four 5-year periods examined, providing an indication of the degree of growth or decline within an industry over that period.

Increasing hypercompetition is operationalized as the passage of calendar time over the 1978-97 panel: a year counter running from 1 (1978) to 20 (1997) in the mortality model and from 1 (1979) to 19 (1997) in the autoregressive model, and indicator variables for three of four 5-year windows in the industry dynamism and munificence regressions. Trends in performance stability (successive 4-year windows), durability, mortality, dynamism and munificence over this period are read as evidence for or against a hypercompetitive shift.

We measured Speed of Scaling as the number of outlets an area unit opened in their area in a given month. The measure is defined at the area-unit month level for the areas into which the franchise chain partitions the United States, each managed by an area unit.

The measure is calculated as the number of required products/services that are not implemented by a focal outlet in a given period (month, in this case). The franchisor designated the provision of thirteen products and services as required products/services that all outlets of the chain should implement; these represent the routines that the franchisor sought to replicate consistently across all outlets. Monthly data for the implementation of required product/services are available for all outlets of the franchise system.
scale: count of required products/services not implemented

description: We measured Adherence-Related Failure Experience as the total number of outlet failures experienced by an area unit up to the focal period (month). We focused on outlet failures, that is, permanent closures of outlets, and counted outlet failures in which outlets' mean adherence to required routines over their lifetime was at least one standard deviation lower than the mean adherence to required routines of all outlets under the supervision of the focal area unit.
time_window: cumulative up to the focal month

description: Measured as a time-variant variable, using the standard deviation of the Speed of Scaling of an area unit over the period commencing from the start of the period of observation in 1991 to the focal period (i.e., month).

To measure Outlet Operating Experience, we used the time elapsed since the inception of the focal unit, that is, the number of months an outlet had been in operation. Then, we divided this measure by twelve to express it in years.

The authors examined whether the keywords of the destination market appeared jointly with the keywords of the origin market(s) in the same news article. Cxjt is the number of news articles that contain the keywords of destination market x and the keywords of origin market j. The volume measure is the mean article count across a firm's products. The authors used the mean rather than the sum because the number of origin markets in which a firm was a producer differed by firm and by year.

Four raters independently evaluated the tenor of each article as positive, negative, or neutral. Positive tenor was coded when an article described the relationship between the two product-markets as complementary or synergistic; negative tenor when they were described as competing or conflicting; neutral when no relationship was specified. The tenor of associative rhetoric was measured with the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance, which measures the relative proportion of articles that have positive versus negative tenor each year. It reaches a maximum of 1 when tenor is all positive and a minimum of -1 when tenor is all negative.

Four raters independently evaluated the source of each article. Associative rhetoric was considered to stem from a firm if an article transcribed that firm's press release, and from journalists/analysts if the content was predominantly a journalist's opinion or an analyst's forecast without interview transcriptions and without a company contact person as source; articles reporting journalists' interviews with firm managers were coded as having a mixed source. The measure adapts the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance to the counts of firm-source versus journalist/analyst-source articles. It reaches a maximum of 1 when firms were an article's only source and a minimum of -1 when only journalists/analysts were the source.

Four raters independently evaluated the focus of each article. Focus reflected generalizations if an article reported broad industry trends and general principles; multiple examples if it reported the actions of three or more firms; and one or two examples if it reported the actions of one or two firms. The measure again adapts the Janis-Fadner coefficient of imbalance to the counts of generalization versus multiple-case articles. It reaches a maximum of 1 when the focus reflects only generalizations and a minimum of -1 when it reflects only multiple cases.

Each firm observation was split into annual spells. The dependent variable is a categorical variable coded as 1 if the firm entered the destination market in year t, and 0 otherwise. The hazard of market entry was estimated with a proportional-hazard specification (Cox model) applied to the event history data.

variable_name: Articles associating an origin market with the destination market
description: Figure 1 reports the total amount of associative rhetoric by year for each of the five origin markets, based on the count of news articles containing both destination-market and origin-market keywords. This is the article count on which the volume measure is built.

ROA, net income divided by total assets, was selected because much prior strategic management and economic research has employed a measure of accounting returns. A rolling five-year window was used to create up to 22 distributions of returns for each firm. Firms that did not have at least four out of five years of performance data in a period were excluded from the analysis for that period. Superior performers were those firms whose performance distribution was statistically significantly different from the industry distribution using the Iterative Kolmogorov-Smirnov stratification technique.

Tobin's q was operationalized as the ratio of market to book value, the ratio of firm market value to the replacement cost of its assets. This ratio has been shown to be theoretically as well as empirically equivalent to Tobin's q, with a correlation greater than 0.92 with all alternative operationalizations. It was used as the economic performance measure alongside the accounting measure ROA, and was stratified with the same Iterative Kolmogorov-Smirnov technique over rolling five-year windows.

Sustained superior economic performance was operationalized as superior economic performance that lasted six or more consecutive windows (i.e., ten years), since that period contained two nonoverlapping five-year windows, thus eliminating any potential bias due to the effect of a single outstanding performance year. For the event history models, a separate observational record was created for each time period in which a firm is not in (or enters) the PSP stratum, and for each firm period the dependent variable is coded 1 if the firm entered the PSP stratum in that period and 0 otherwise.
scale: dichotomous (1 = entered the PSP stratum in that period, 0 = otherwise)
time_window: six or more consecutive five-year windows (ten or more years), 1974-1997

description: Industry four-firm concentration ratio was operationalized by dividing the combined total revenues of the four largest firms in each industry by the total revenues of all firms in the industry. It was entered into the event history models to test Hypothesis 2a. Models were also estimated using the two-firm concentration ratio.
time_window: five-year windows matched to the dependent variables, 1974-1997

description: Market share was operationalized as the ratio of each firm's total revenues to the total revenues of all firms in the industry. It was entered into the event history models to test Hypothesis 2b.
time_window: five-year windows matched to the dependent variables, 1974-1997

description: Computed OTSA transition matrices report the frequency of transition shifts among the ordered strata of the superior-performance stratum, the modal-performance stratum, and the inferior-performance stratum. The matrices give the frequency of a firm moving from the row stratum in the prior period to the column stratum in the subsequent period. These observed transition incidence matrices were compared to expected-value matrices in which the above-average stratum is completely stable, via the G' statistic. Matrices were computed for the entire sample for each of the two performance measures.

Personal attachment was measured by the average of the responses, on a 7-point Likert scale, to four items: the extent to which interpersonal relations have been developed to date between each party's boundary spanners since the ICV was formed; the extent to which interpersonal relations had been developed between these boundary spanners through previous trade, investments, or negotiations before the ICV was formed; the extent to which foreign boundary spanners have provided Chinese boundary spanners with needed personal skills and knowledge; and the extent to which Chinese boundary spanners have provided foreign boundary spanners with needed personal skills and knowledge. In each question, boundary spanners were defined as the ICV's resident board members and senior managers from each party, and each respondent answered as the venture's leading manager. Because the effects of some items multiply in interaction, the items were averaged with a geometric rather than an arithmetic approach.

The length of tenure overlap between boundary spanners was measured by the arithmetic average of tenure overlap between (1) the two parties' resident board members and (2) the two parties' top managers (general or deputy general managers). This overlap was defined as the number of years working together in the venture with a counterpart in a similar position. A respondent from each ICV was asked to report this tenure overlap in his or her ICV.

The education difference between boundary spanners was measured by the difference between the average number of years of schooling of foreign boundary spanners and that of local boundary spanners, as reported by one respondent per ICV.

Goal congruity was measured by asking each respondent, on a 5-point Likert scale, to assess the overall congruity of the strategic goals behind the establishment of the ICV set by foreign and local parents before the commencement of ICV operations. Its content validity was validated by a covariance structure analysis that reported a significant path correlation between this congruity and the mean of specific goal differences (profitability, risk reduction, local market expansion, and knowledge sharing) between parent firms, reverse coded.
time_window: strategic goals set before the commencement of ICV operations

description: The cultural distance between parties from different countries was computed following Kogut and Singh's composite index (1988) and based on the data from Hofstede (1984) and Huo and Randall (1991). The index measures deviation along each of four cultural dimensions (uncertainty avoidance, individuality, power distance, and masculinity-femininity) from the score of a given focal country for each foreign country; the formula itself is not readable in the text as provided. The name of the foreign country involved in each ICV was identified from MOFTEC's database, and when the nationality of the key foreign boundary spanner differed from that of the foreign parent, the boundary spanner's nationality from the survey was used in computing the distance.

Market disturbance was measured as the geometric average of the standard deviations of five structural market attributes—an industry's total sales, profit after tax, output, capital investment, and the number of firms—between 1994 and 1997. The authors argue that standard deviation is a common measure of volatility, that market structure is a multidimensional construct, and that a geometric average prevents a skewed distribution. Information about the industry in which an ICV participates was obtained from MOFTEC's database, while the five structural attributes came from the China Statistical Yearbook.

Information on regulatory deterrence was obtained from The Orientation Directory of Industries for FDI, compiled by the State Council, China, which explicitly states that governmental priorities and institutional support are given to industries as categorized by priority from 5 to 1. Using the directory's categories, regulatory deterrence was coded 5 for an ICV's industry in the most restricted category, 4 in the next restricted category, 3 in the newly opened category, 2 in the encouraged non-technological category, and 1 in the encouraged technological category; the higher the number, the greater the regulatory deterrence. This objective measurement correlates highly with overall regulatory deterrence as perceived by senior ICV managers on a 5-point questionnaire item.

Process performance was the mean of managerial satisfaction, on a 5-point Likert scale, with ICV performance in ten areas of operation. Respondents were asked to refer to the recent three years as the time frame for answering these items, and each was asked to represent the venture in his or her capacity as its leading manager. Cronbach's alpha (.79) validates the internal consistency of this construct.
Return on investment was calculated as the total profit before tax divided by total investments, using information from the MOFTEC database (1994-1996).

Cumulative number of biotechnology patents assigned to the firm during 1981-91, defined in terms of classification 935 (genetic engineering: recombinant DNA technology, hybrid or fused cell technology, and related manipulations of nucleic acids). Patents associated with companies acquired by the focal firm during the period and patents accessed through licensing agreements are excluded, since these reflect purchases of existing technology.

Cumulative number of biotechnology products that the firm had on the market, or under review by regulatory agencies, as of 1991. Products were counted if they were in any of the three phases of development at the FDA, if applications for approval had been submitted or were pending, if they were in human clinical trials, or if they had received final approval by the FDA. Products were included only when the firm was named as the developer, so products associated with acquired companies were not included.

variable_name: Reputation for possessing expertise in biotechnology (REP)
description: The firm's overall reputation for possessing expertise in biotechnology, measured by peer evaluation using the survey instrument. Respondents were given a list of firms active in biotechnology and rated each firm's current level of expertise in human health care applications of biotechnology on a 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = very low level of expertise; 5 = very high level of expertise), considering indicators such as patents, new drug applications, products, dedicated facilities, and alliances. The measure is the mean score for each firm across all survey respondents; the authors report high interrater reliability for all experts.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = very low level of expertise; 5 = very high level of expertise)

description: Proportion of the firm's biotechnology R&D expenditures allocated to internal R&D during 1981-85, where internal R&D is biotechnology R&D conducted in-house by the firm at either the corporate or the divisional level. Respondents estimated how expenditures were allocated between internal and external R&D so that the total allocation adds to 100 percent. Because of the heterogeneity of responses within multi-respondent firms, only the response of the individual responsible for R&D at the most senior level was included in the analysis.
scale: percentage of R&D expenditures (allocations sum to 100 percent)

description: Proportion of the firm's biotechnology R&D expenditures allocated to internal R&D during 1986-91, where internal R&D is biotechnology R&D conducted in-house by the firm at either the corporate or the divisional level. Respondents estimated the allocation between internal and external R&D such that the total adds to 100 percent. As with INVEST1, only the response of the most senior individual responsible for R&D was included where multiple responses were received.
scale: percentage of R&D expenditures (allocations sum to 100 percent)

description: Count of the number of biotechnologies that the firm reported using, taken at the end of the study period from Biotechnology in the U.S. Pharmaceutical Industry. The report distinguishes between eight technologies, including hybridoma, liposome, protein engineering, recombinant DNA, tissue culture, fermentation, and large-scale cell culture. The measure is a count of the absolute number of technologies listed by the firm.
time_window: measured at the end of the study period (1991)

description: Count of how many of five different types of alliances were used by each firm for alliances undertaken during 1981-91. The five types are two nonequity forms (research contracts and licenses) and three equity-based modes (acquisitions, minority equity investments, and joint ventures). The variable is a count of the number of different types of linkages, similar to network-level measures of diversity but taken at the level of the organization set.
scale: count of up to five alliance types

description: Count of the number of times the sample firm used research contracts during the period 1981-91, taken from Biotechnology in the U.S. Pharmaceutical Industry. The data were not fine grained enough to determine the status, start and termination dates of the firm's alliances, so change over the period could not be explored.

Count of the number of times the sample firm used licenses during the period 1981-91, taken from Biotechnology in the U.S. Pharmaceutical Industry. Licenses are nonequity forms of technology sourcing linkages. The data did not permit tracking when individual alliances started or ended.

Count of the number of acquisitions undertaken by the sample firm during the period 1981-91, taken from Biotechnology in the U.S. Pharmaceutical Industry. Acquisitions are one of the three equity-based modes of technology sourcing linkages.

Count of the number of joint ventures formed by the sample firm during the period 1981-91, taken from Biotechnology in the U.S. Pharmaceutical Industry. A joint venture is defined as a new venture created by the equity contributions of two or more partners, and is one of the three equity-based modes of technology sourcing linkages.

Count of the number of minority equity investments made by the sample firm during the period 1981-91, taken from Biotechnology in the U.S. Pharmaceutical Industry. Minority equity investments are one of the three equity-based modes of technology sourcing linkages.

Proportion of Syrian households in each governorate, based on 2015 Jordanian census data, used to quantify the refugee influx. It is interacted with a post indicator for the years after refugees began entering.

Binary variable equal to 1 if the venture's initial funding comes from family, and 0 otherwise. The control group is ventures that received their initial funding from other types of sources such as government grants and non-governmental organizations.
Binary variable equal to 1 if the venture's initial funding comes from a bank or other formal market institution, and 0 otherwise.
Indicator that takes the value of one if a firm fails within 2 years of founding, and zero otherwise. It is the dependent variable in the difference-in-differences and triple-differences models.

Dummy variable produced for each pair of firms, equal to one if firms i and j are members of the same group and zero otherwise. Membership is taken from the affiliation list maintained by Chile's Superintendencia de Valores y Seguros (SVS), which tracks groups so that regulators can spot lending to affiliates. The authors checked the SVS list against the opinions of other knowledgeable sources, independent published sources, and group annual reports.

Indicator of family overlap among directors, equal to one if there are distinct (i.e., not the same individual) directors of firms i and j with the same surname, and zero otherwise. Family affiliations of each owner and director were identified with the assistance of a graduate student in Chile, and the analyses focus on paternal links only.

Degree of family overlap among directors: the number of individuals serving on the board of firm i with a distinct director of the same surname serving on firm j's board, plus the number on j's board with a distinct director of the same surname on i's board, divided by the total number of board members for i and j. The continuous variables range from zero (no family overlap of boards) to one (full overlap).

Indicator of family overlap among owners, equal to one if there are distinct major owners of firms i and j with the same surname, and zero otherwise. Family affiliations of owners and directors were identified using paternal surnames only.

Degree of family overlap among owners: the number of major owners of firm i with a distinct major owner of the same surname associated with firm j, plus the number of major owners of firm j with a distinct major owner of the same surname associated with firm i, divided by the total number of major owners for i and j. The continuous variables range from zero (no family overlap of ownership rolls) to one (full overlap).
Indicator of overlap among board directors, equal to one if at least one individual serves on the boards of both firms i and j, and zero otherwise.
Degree of overlap among board directors: the number of individuals serving on the boards of both firm i and firm j divided by the average number of board members for i and j.

Indicator of overlap in major individual owners, equal to one if firms i and j have a major owner in common, and zero otherwise. Ownership data identify as many as 20 of the largest individual owners of each widely held firm.

Degree of overlap in major individual owners: the number of individuals appearing on the ownership rolls for both firm i and firm j divided by the average number of individual owners listed for i and j.

Indicator of a direct equity relationship, equal to one if firm i directly holds a stake in firm j or vice versa, and zero otherwise. Equity stakes as small as 1% are reported with precise figures, and even smaller stakes are denoted by special symbols.
Size of the direct equity relationship: the maximum of two figures, the fraction of firm j's shares directly held by firm i and the fraction of firm i's shares directly held by firm j.

Indicator of an indirect equity relationship, equal to one if firm i holds a stake in firm j through a third company or vice versa, and zero otherwise. Indirect interlocks arise when, for instance, firm i owns part of firm k, which in turn owns part of firm j.

Size of the indirect equity relationship: the maximum of two figures, the fraction of firm j's shares held by firm i through third companies and the fraction of firm i's shares held by firm j through third companies. To account for such holdings the authors calculate firm i's total stake in j by all direct and indirect routes and then subtract out any direct holding.

Visible ties are the five types of interfirm ties the authors can observe in Chile: family connections (among directors and among major owners), common owners, director interlocks, direct equity holdings and indirect equity holdings. For every pair of firms each type is coded as a presence dummy and as a degree measure, and together they form the vector Tie. Tabulations of Tie for within-group and nongroup dyads test the nonnecessity and nonsufficiency hypotheses. The individual tie measures are recorded under c_family_ties, c_owner_overlap, c_director_interlocks, c_direct_equity and c_indirect_equity.
scale: dummy and continuous degree per tie type

description: The authors measured hiring directors using the number of directors who were serving on the board when the CEO was hired. They confirmed this measure using the proportion of hiring directors to total board members as well as the proportion of independent outside hiring directors to total directors.

Respondents were shown a list of 20 randomly ordered attributes - the 6 attributes of their selected candidate, the 6 attributes of the other candidate, and 8 additional attributes not associated with either candidate at the time of selection - and indicated whether each attribute describes their candidate, the other candidate, or neither. The score follows Mather et al.'s established formula: the sum of positive features attributed to the selected CEO plus negative features attributed to the nonselected CEO minus the sum of negative features attributed to the selected CEO plus positive features attributed to the nonselected CEO. Positive asymmetry scores indicate favorable bias toward the selected candidate, and negative scores indicate favorable bias toward the nonselected candidate; an average score of zero would indicate general memory loss rather than bias.
time_window: approximately 12 minutes after the candidate preference was expressed

description: Following Seo et al. (2015), the authors first calculated annual CEO excess pay as the residuals from the regression of CEO total pay on important determinants of CEO total pay. The determinants were firm size (natural log of firm sales and firm assets), firm performance (ROA and shareholder returns), human capital (CEO tenure measured as years in the position), a squared value of CEO tenure, and indicator variables for industry (two-digit SIC codes), S&P indices, and year. Using these yearly figures, they then operationalized change in pay as the year-to-year (t-1 to t) change.

The authors created a 0/1 indicator equaling 1 when the CEO was replaced. Potential dismissals were identified as turnover events involving CEOs under age 65 who did not continue on the board. Major media outlets were then used to identify cases where the CEO died, had health issues, were interim CEOs, accepted similar positions at other firms, or left due to a merger or acquisition, and these were coded as nondismissal events.

Using BoardEx, the authors identified the total number of years of board service across all boards other than a focal firm's board among the firm's independent and affiliated directors over the 5 years (inclusive) prior to the focal year. For example, a director who served on four other boards from 2005 to 2010 contributed 24 years to a focal firm's board experience measure for 2011.
time_window: 5 years (inclusive) prior to the focal year

description: Dummy designating dyad-market-year observations in the treatment group at t+1, t+2 and t+3, where t is the marriage year. A companion dummy, Married (ij), is set to 1 for each dyad-market-year observation of chaebols that were involved in a marriage tie between t-3 and t+3 and 0 otherwise, and the same two dummies are used in all datasets.
time_window: marriage year t, observed from t-3 to t+3

description: Dummy identifying whether the focal observation belonged to a chaebol whose family married its son (coded 1) or its daughter (coded 0). In the entry and exit analyses the husbands' chaebols are the actors in Datasets 1 and 2, where the marriage involved their child as the husband and their chaebol could enter the wife's chaebol's markets or exit markets shared with the wife's chaebol.
scale: dummy (1 = married a son, 0 = married a daughter)

variable_name: Husband's Chaebol (read for the wife's chaebol)
description: The same dummy identifying whether the focal observation belonged to a chaebol whose family married a son (1) or a daughter (0), read with the wife's chaebol as the focal actor. In the entry and exit analyses the wives' chaebols are the actors in Datasets 3 and 4, where the marriage involved their child as the wife and the wife's chaebol could enter the husband's chaebol's markets or exit markets shared with the husband's chaebol.

Coded 1 when the focal chaebol entered, in a given year, a 4-digit SIC market of the partner chaebol, and 0 otherwise; the presence of affiliates of a chaebol in a specific 4-digit market in a given year was coded as 1 and the absence as 0. In Dataset 1 the markets are those in which the wife's chaebol was present and the husband's chaebol was not present prior to marriage; in Dataset 3 they are markets in which the husband's chaebol was present and the wife's chaebol was not present prior to marriage.
time_window: t-3 to t+3 around the marriage

description: Coded 1 when the focal chaebol exited, in a given year, a 4-digit SIC market that it shared with the partner chaebol, and 0 otherwise. Dataset 2 covers markets in which both the husband's and the wife's chaebols were present prior to marriage and from which the husband's chaebol was at risk of exiting after the marriage; Dataset 4 covers the corresponding common markets of the wife's chaebol.
time_window: t-3 to t+3 around the marriage

description: The personal wealth of chaebols' owner-CEOs, published annually by the Korean government in the form of a ranking in which a lower number (i.e., 1) illustrates a higher wealth rank and a higher number (i.e., 30) an inferior wealth rank. The wealth of the owner-CEOs is highly linked to the overall financial performance of the chaebol, so it is used as a proxy for the chaebol's performance. The data were reorganized from the dyad-market-year structure to a chaebol-year structure covering the chaebols that had marriage events.
time_window: same period as the main analyses

description: Coded 1 if the focal mayor joined the party before 1978, and 0 if the focal mayor joined in the economic reform era after 1978. The coding reflects the authors' argument that mayors joining the party during the Mao era, before the economic reform, were imprinted with a strong communist ideology.
scale: 1 = joined the communist party before 1978; 0 = joined after 1978

variable_name: Ratio of private firms' political appointment
description: Political appointment was coded at the firm level as a continuous variable by considering both the CEO's and the chairman's service, ranging from 0-2 for each firm. The total number of deputyships obtained by all private firms in the focal city in a given year was summed and divided by the total quota of deputyships in the focal city. The ratio of private firms' political appointment varies from 0 to 6% of total deputyships, with an average of 0.12%.

Coded 1 if the focal mayor was born between 1950 and 1959, and 0 otherwise. Historians have identified this cohort (7 to 16 years old when the Cultural Revolution started in 1966) as having been most influenced by such an extreme institutional environment.

Measured by the timing of each province's liberation by the People's Liberation Army, coded as the number of months liberated before (or after) the founding date of the PRC in October 1949. The higher the number of months before the founding, the earlier a province had been liberated, and hence the stronger its communist legacy; provinces liberated after the founding have negative values. This variable ranges from 23 months before the founding of the PRC to 19 months after.
scale: months liberated before or after October 1949 (23 to -19)

description: Measured by the focal city's gross domestic product (GDP) in a given year. City-level institutional and economic development data were acquired from the China City Statistical Yearbook published annually by the National Statistics Bureau of China.
