A dummy variable with a value of one if the firm is a piece of a firm broken into multiple firms. It has a value zero if it is the original unrestructured firm. It is the key independent variable in the regressions for Hypothesis 1a.
time_window: 1991 firm data; restructuring identified from the privatization plans

description: Log of number of restructured units from original firm. Because the dependent variables are also logged (log of total demand and log of share price), the coefficient is interpreted as an elasticity.

Log of total share demand in Round I of the Voucher Scheme divided by total number of available shares in the firm. Demand is taken as a measure of investor valuation because Czech authorities set the prices of all shares at 33.33 voucher points in the first round.
time_window: Round I of the voucher scheme (1992)

description: Log of share prices set during the auction on July 8, 1993, in the RMS (Registracni Misto System). It is used as a second dependent variable to assess the investor value of shares.
Percentage of ownership by banks in 1991. It enters both as a control for all firms and as an interaction term with the restructuring dummy for the restructured firms.

Percentage of fund ownership in 1991. Fund ownership was determined through the voucher process, so its effect on the value of restructured firms can be assessed only by measures of firm value following the completion of the voucher scheme, such as subsequent share prices.
Percentage of foreign ownership in 1991. It enters both as a control for all firms and as an interaction term with the restructuring dummy for the restructured firms.
Percentage of management ownership in 1991. Czech law did not permit managerial ownership to exceed 5 percent. It enters both as a control and as an interaction term with the restructuring dummy.
Percentage of government ownership in 1991. It enters both as a control for all firms and as an interaction term with the restructuring dummy for the restructured firms.

In the 1996 questionnaire survey respondents reported the units with which they communicated frequently, selecting from a list of all business units provided in the questionnaire. From this item the author constructed an adjacency matrix of interunit communication among the 36 business units, symmetrized the matrix to focus on bilateral communications, and calculated the degree centrality index for each business unit. The degree centrality index was chosen because it is held to be relatively the most suitable centrality measure for capturing an individual actor's visibility, information access, and potential communication activity.
time_window: 1996 survey, before the new unit was officially established

description: Interunit trusting networks were examined by asking two questions: which units the respondent's unit was confident would do what it required without a written contract, and which units could provide reliable information or service. Based on the responses the author created two sociomatrices and calculated indegree for each unit in each matrix, indegree counting the number of nominations a unit received in the interunit trusting network; the higher the indegree, the more trustworthy the unit. The indegree measure was standardized for each of the two interunit trusting networks, and Cronbach's coefficient alpha for the two indegree measures was 0.89. The 1996 survey data were used for this measure.

Following Verdin and Williamson (1994) and Markides and Williamson (1996), the author operationalized strategic relatedness based on five broad categories of strategic assets, and respondents rated the importance of these assets to their units' operations using a scale of high, low, or moderate. The author then compared responses across all units and considered two units strategically related if they highlighted the importance of the same category or categories of strategic assets, creating a variable counting the number of categories for which two units had the same responses. The variable was coded from 0 (two units had nothing in common in their responses) to 5 (exactly the same responses to the five categories). For each of the 36 original units the author calculated the degree of its strategic relatedness with the newly formed unit based on the 1998 survey data.
level: dyad between an existing unit and the newly formed unit

variable_name: duration until creation of first linkage with the new unit
description: In the second questionnaire survey the directors of the original 36 business units indicated when their units started exchanging resources with the newly formed unit, distinguishing tangible exchange (transfer or sharing of tangible resources such as special input materials or specific product components) from intangible exchange (transfer or sharing of intangible resources such as technical skills or knowhow) and reporting initial dates for each type. To verify the responses the author provided a different questionnaire to the new unit asking when it started exchanging resources with all other units, and consistency was found after double-checking during follow-up interviews. For each unit the author calculated the duration in months that passed until the creation of its first linkage with the newly formed unit, coding the data from 1 to 24 since the second questionnaire was administered 24 months after the new unit was formed; durations with no ending date (no linkage had yet occurred) were treated as right-censored. Using event history techniques the rate of new linkage creation was modeled as the instantaneous probability that an existing unit would create a linkage with the new unit given that it had yet to do so.
level: existing business unit (dyad with the new unit)
time_window: 24 months after the new unit was formed (1996-1998)

description: Coded '1' for boycotted firms and '0' for the matched firms. Boycotted firms were identified by a manual content analysis of the six largest U.S. newspapers from 1990 to 2007, searching for all articles mentioning 'boycott,' 'boycotted,' 'boycotts,' or 'boycotting,' and then matched with company-specific quarterly and yearly financial data from COMPUSTAT. Control firms were matched 1:1 using coarsened exact matching on two-digit SIC industry, size (by assets), and status (by ranking in Fortune's 'Most Admired Companies').
time_window: quarter before and quarter after the boycott event

description: The proportion of all contributions dispersed from a firm's affiliated PACs that were reported as refunded in a given quarter, indicating that they were rejected by the recipient politicians. Built from the Federal Election Commission's transaction-level data for corporate PACs and aggregated into quarterly data (proportion refunded = total refunds / total non-netted contributions); where a firm had multiple linked PACs, contributions were aggregated across all of these PACs in each quarter. The variable is bounded between 0 and 1 and is modeled with a fractional logit model.

The number of times that a representative of a given firm testified in congressional hearings in a given quarter, hand-collected and aggregated from ProQuest's Congressional Hearings data archives. Hostile appearances, in which the committee compelled the testimony of a company as part of an investigation into a scandal or crisis, and appearances by firm representatives on behalf of a trade organization rather than their home firm were culled. The variable ranges from 0 to 7 and is an overdispersed count modeled with a negative binomial regression.

The total number of unique government procurement contracts assigned to each sampled firm by quarter, collected from the Federal Procurement Data System by searching for all contracts assigned to each boycotted and matched firm in the quarters prior to and after a boycott's announcement. The authors focused on the count of contracts, as opposed to their dollar value, because the simple act of awarding contracts creates a concrete, public tie between a firm and policymaker. The variable ranges from 0 to 5,560 and is modeled with a generalized linear model with a log-link function and negative binomial errors.

The proportion of refunded PAC contributions described above, used as a dependent variable in the second-stage within-boycotted-sample models, measured in the post-boycott quarter. Estimated with a fractional logit model with robust standard errors clustered by firm.

The count of invited appearances in congressional hearings used as a dependent variable in the second-stage within-boycotted-sample models, measured in the post-boycott quarter. Estimated with a negative binomial model with robust standard errors clustered by firm.

The count of awarded government procurement contracts used as a dependent variable in the second-stage within-boycotted-sample models, measured in the post-boycott quarter. Estimated with a generalized linear model with a log-link function and negative binomial errors, with robust standard errors clustered by firm.

variable_name: amount of media attention attracted by the boycott
description: Constructed by collecting all articles from the six largest U.S. newspapers related to the boycotts in the sample and summing the total number of articles written about each boycott. The amount of media attention ranged from 1 article to 18 articles, with a mean of 1.77; for the majority of the sample (70 percent) the boycott appeared in the media only once, on the day of the boycott's initial announcement.

A binary variable coded '1' if the primary issue underlying the boycott corresponds with one of the issues reported in Gallup's 'Most Important Problem' poll in the quarter preceding the boycott, and '0' otherwise. In that poll, Gallup asks a randomized sample of American voters open-endedly to name 'the most important problem facing this country today,' and the data report each individual problem listed along with the proportion of polled individuals who chose it.

A proxy for corporate status using Fortune magazine's annual 'Most Admired Companies' index, a ranking of corporate prestige based on surveys of the executives of an organization's peer firms, in which firms are ranked on a scale ranging from 0 to 10 and the firms scoring highest in their industry are reported in the annual list. The measure is the raw score reported for each firm surveyed, with all firms not included in the rankings assigned a score of 0. The rankings have a natural one-year lag, so the reported score in the year in which the boycott occurred is used, and because lower-status firms were expected to experience more disruption the variable is reverse coded by multiplying the raw scores by -1.
time_window: year of the boycott (rankings based on prior-year surveys)

description: The same reverse-coded Fortune 'Most Admired Companies' score used as a moderator in the second-stage within-boycotted-sample models, where a one-standard-deviation decrease from the mean in the status of a boycotted firm is interpreted as lower status.
time_window: year of the boycott (rankings based on prior-year surveys)

description: Number of heroes selected by the team in the focal game that were never picked by the team in its previous ten games. The author uses the word experimentation rather than search because teams engage in online search by directly experimenting with new choices. The measure may vary over time even in periods with no game updates, so that coefficients reflect whether teams increase their experimentation with heroes as a response to environmental change.
time_window: focal game, relative to the previous ten games

description: Strategies are captured through their materialization as collective sequences of actions. For each game, all sequences of actions involving several of a team's players were recorded, in which each action was performed less than three seconds after and within close geographical proximity of the previous action. For each game, the rate of change is computed as the average distance between all sequences recorded in the team's focal game and the sequences recorded in its ten previous games. Distances were computed through optimal matching, the cost of turning one sequence into the other by substituting, deleting or inserting elements.
scale: average distance between sequences of actions
time_window: focal game, relative to the previous ten games

description: Indicator variable equal to one if the game happened within two months of a game update that affected only the abilities of heroes. These game updates modify the mapping from players' actions to their outcomes and thereby change which heroes and which strategies are viable.
time_window: two months after a game update

description: Number of pings per minute among all members of a team during a game. Pings are graphic-and-sound signals that players generate by clicking a specific location on the game's map and constitute a major means of communication between players during games. The variable was measured as the average over the last ten games before the last game update.
time_window: average over the last ten games before the last game update

description: Percentage of pings emanating from the captain relative to the total number of pings within the team during the focal game. Teams allocate the captain role to one of their members, and Valve Corporation requires every professional team to formally report the player occupying that role, whose function is to facilitate coordination among team members. The variable was measured as the average over the last ten games before the last game update.
time_window: average over the last ten games before the last game update

description: Captures the percentage of the total population of state s born in home country c. The proportion of co-national immigrants relative to the total state population is small in most cases, but the measure varies significantly across states for immigrants of the same nationality, preserves relative differences within states across different nationalities, and reduces the bias of states with very large populations present in raw counts of immigrants. Because the immigration data come from the 2000 decennial U.S. census and do not change yearly, the measure is time invariant.

Coded as 1 if an entry by parent company p occurred within state s in industry i, and 0 otherwise. Each firm had a choice set of up to 50 states, and the choice set for each company is composed of states in which it has no prior subsidiaries; the mean choice set size is 47.93 (median of 49). Industries are assigned based on the activities of the subsidiary—not the parent—so entries into different industries are treated as separate choice sets; repeated investments in the same state are not accounted for.

Coded as 1 if subsidiary j continued to be operated by parent company p eight years after its initial establishment, the maximum period for which the survival of a subsidiary established in 2003 could be observed. The authors verified the timing and reason for exit of each entry and removed nine exits that occurred for 'positive' reasons. The survival rate was 61.8 percent.
time_window: eight years after initial establishment (through the end of 2011)

description: Measured as the number of states in which the parent firm had subsidiaries prior to the year of entry. To test the hypotheses, the sample was divided into firms with low and high experience based on whether the number of states they entered was below or above the sample mean, respectively.
time_window: prior to the year of entry

description: The intensity of industry activity measured as the share of total U.S. employment in each subsidiary's industry by state. The measure serves as a control in all models and as a contingency variable when testing H4a and H4b. To test the hypotheses the sample was split into low and high industry concentration based on whether the state's share of industry employment was below or above the sample mean.

Each firm was categorized as high or low technology based on the parent's primary SIC code, relying on the Bureau of Labor Statistics 1999 classification of three-digit SIC codes, which was published during the period of observation and relied on objective, knowledge-related data. According to that study, industries are considered high tech if employment in both research and development and in all technology-oriented occupations accounted for a proportion of employment that was at least twice the average for all industries in the U.S. Firms in high-technology industries are considered more knowledge intensive than those in low-technology industries.

The sample was split at the mean level of prior experience in the U.S. into firms with low and high experience; H3a and H3b were tested by comparing the marginal effects of immigrant concentration across these subsamples.

One of the withholding influence strategies measured in the facility-level survey. Each respondent was asked to denote to what extent these influences were important in shaping their company's sustainability policies/practices, on a scale from 1 = no impact to 7 = complete influence. The authors interpret directors'/officers' liability as the influence of regulations and regulators on firm practices.

variable_name: Withholding influence strategies (environmental group and local community)
description: Set of withholding influence strategy items in the facility-level survey, each rated by respondents on how important the influence was in shaping their company's sustainability policies/practices (1 = no impact to 7 = complete influence). The items capture environmental group protests, disruption of operations, media reports, lobbying of the provincial government, and local community protests and disruptions. Environmental group protests at customer sites, environmental groups disrupting operations, environmental group participation in environmental reviews and local disruptions of operations were dropped from the final analysis because they were found not to have an impact on sustainability practices.

Usage influence strategy items in the facility-level survey that capture demands made by customers on the firm. Each respondent was asked to denote to what extent these influences were important in shaping their company's sustainability policies/practices, from 1 = no impact to 7 = complete influence.

variable_name: Usage influence strategies (economic stakeholders and employees)
description: Set of usage influence strategy items from the facility-level survey, each rated by respondents on how important the influence was in shaping their company's sustainability policies/practices (1 = no impact to 7 = complete influence). The items cover customer demands, employee information and suggestions, and information obtained through trade conferences and seminars; local community and environmental group participation in environmental reviews were also examined but were not included in the final analysis because they had no impact on sustainability practices.

variable_name: Stakeholder withholding and usage influence strategies (all items)
description: All of the withholding and usage influence strategy items collected in the facility-level survey, each rated by respondents on how important the influence was in shaping their company's sustainability policies/practices (1 = no impact to 7 = complete influence). The withholding items include customer order cancellations, directors'/officers' liability, environmental group protests, disruption, media reports and lobbying, and local community protests and disruptions; the usage items include customer demands, community and environmental group participation in environmental reviews, employee information and suggestions, and trade conference information.

Factor of sustainability practices reported by companies, derived from a content analysis of annual reports, environmental reports and company websites in which specific reported actions were categorized and coded for each facility. In the factor analysis of items reflecting the early phases of sustainability practices, pollution control is captured by detoxification and synthetic reduction.

Factor of sustainability practices derived from the content analysis of company documents, coded for each facility. In the factor analysis of early-phase practices, eco-efficiency is captured by fuel efficiency and energy efficiency.

Factor of sustainability practices derived from the content analysis of company documents. In the factor analysis of practices requiring organizational investments, the recirculation factor includes durable design, de-packaging and internal recycling.

Factor of sustainability practices derived from the content analysis of company documents. In the factor analysis of practices requiring organizational investments, the eco-design factor includes designing products for easy disassembly or reuse and the use of product life-cycle analyses.

Factor of sustainability practices derived from the content analysis of company documents. In the factor analysis of practices requiring organizational investments, sustainable harvesting includes sustainable yield management, access restriction and reforestation. The authors use sustainable harvesting practices as the proxy for ecosystem stewardship.

variable_name: Use of alternative fibers (business redefinition proxy)
description: Factor of sustainability practices derived from the content analysis of company documents. In the factor analysis of practices requiring organizational investments, the last factor consisted of one practice, the use of alternative fibers, which the authors use as the proxy for business redefinition practices.

Count of new services a hospital added in each year. The CHFC survey included data on the availability of 162 services, and an addition was noted when a hospital indicated the availability of a service not previously provided in the prior year. An addition could occur either by the hospital directly providing the new service or by establishing a contractual relationship with another provider. For each year, the authors determined the number of new services each hospital added and summed them to create the dependent variable.

Count of services a hospital no longer provided in each year. A service divestiture was noted when the survey indicated that a hospital no longer provided a service either it or an external provider had previously offered. For each year, the authors developed a summary measure of the total service divestitures based on the 162 services included in the CHFC survey.

Changes in ownership involving the transfer of control from one individual, group, or organization to another individual, group, or organization. Comparing the names of owners from year to year allowed the authors to see if a change had occurred. The exact nature of each ownership change could not be determined from the CHFC data; for example, they knew that an ownership transfer had occurred but not whether the new owner was a sole proprietor, a group of physicians, or a large, integrated multihospital system.

Proportion of new members on a board of directors as a result of turnover from one year to the next. The authors note that the turnover measure may in part reflect changes due to the expiration of terms of service, because hospitals adopting a corporate board structure tend to limit the number of consecutive terms a board member may serve whereas hospitals with a philanthropic board structure tend to have no limits.

variable_name: Change in the proportion of inside members
description: Changes in the proportion of management staff members on boards of directors from year to year. As the initial distribution of this variable deviated significantly from normal assumptions, a square root transformation was used to make the distribution conform more closely to conventional statistical assumptions.
CEO successions were coded for each year in the study. Because the authors lacked data on the origins of new CEOs, they were not able to distinguish between internal and external succession.

Change in hospital bed capacity in the Standard Metropolitan Statistical Area, used as a measure of market competition. The authors argue that excess capacity in a market increases competition and that growth in bed capacity puts pressure on hospitals to use facilities and services efficiently. Although regulation of bed capacity in California might reduce the likelihood of excess, hospitals can use a multitude of exemptions to expand their numbers of beds.

A dummy variable included to capture the 1983-85 period, during which the Medicare Prospective Payment System was introduced and implemented. The PPS established ceiling rates on specific medical procedures, shifting the burden of cost control to hospitals.

Change in hospital occupancy, included as a measure of hospital performance. The authors expected variations in hospital performance associated with changes in hospital occupancy to exert direct effects on strategic change, and Hypothesis 9 concerns declines in hospital occupancy. The paper does not describe how the change in occupancy was computed.

The degree of asset specificity for supplementary services was measured using three items: the level of major investments and training, the level of professional skills, and the level of specialized know-how required in providing the services. These three indicators were adapted from Erramilli and Rao's (1993) study and measured by 5-point scales (5 = very high, .... 1 = very low). Cronbach's alpha = 0.85 for supplementary services.

Capital intensity measures the major investments made in providing the supplementary services. It is measured by two items: the degree of capital intensity of the supplementary services, and the level of one-time cost involved in switching from one service provider to another if the firm were to change service providers. The levels of these two indicators were measured by 5-point scales (5 = very high, .... 1 = very low); Cronbach's alpha = 0.78 for supplementary services.

Inseparability of supplementary services was defined as the degree of which production and consumption of the services would occur simultaneously. It was measured using a 5-point scale (5 = very high, .... 1 = very low).
The demand uncertainty of supplementary services was assessed using a single item on a 5-point scale (5 = very high, ..., 1 = very low).

Transaction frequency of supplementary services was defined as the frequency with which transactions involved in sourcing the same supplementary services recurred (Williamson, 1985). It was measured using a single item on a 5-point scale (5 = very high, .... 1 = very low).

variable_name: Extent of global sourcing of supplementary services
description: Measured as a percentage of total value of supplementary services that were procured inside the corporate system on a global basis (both from domestic and foreign sources). Consistent with Lovelock (1992), supplementary services were those services that facilitated and enhanced the use of core services and provided competitive advantages over the firm's competitors.

variable_name: Extent of domestic sourcing of supplementary services
description: Measured as a percentage of total value of supplementary services that were procured from domestic suppliers inside the corporate system.

variable_name: Extent of global sourcing of core services
description: Measured as a percentage of total value of core services that were procured inside the corporate system on a global basis (both from domestic and foreign sources). Core services were defined as those services that fulfill customers' needs for a basic benefit, which were similar to the competitors' offerings.

variable_name: Extent of domestic sourcing of core services
description: Measured as a percentage of total value of core services that were procured from domestic suppliers inside the corporate system.

The extent of foreign sourcing of supplementary services, entered in the market performance models together with internal sourcing. The measures section does not report how this variable was constructed.

Strategic market performance included market share and sales growth rate. They were measured relative to the three largest competitors over the last 3 years in the U.S. market using 5-point scales (5 = much higher, .... 1 = much lower); Cronbach's alpha = 0.83.

Financial market performance included return on sales, return on investment, and return on equity. These three variables were measured relative to the three largest competitors over the last 3 years in the U.S. market using 5-point scales (5 = much higher, ..., 1 = much lower); Cronbach's alpha = 0.84.

An inverted Herfindahl index of team members' geographic locations, identified from patent data, used to measure dispersion instead of concentration. The score reflects both the number of locations and the proportion of members in the same location, and it allocates a higher weight to teams dispersed across multiple countries; the index accounts for the number of countries from which R&D members for a given patent were sourced. The squared term of the index was included in addition to the linear effect to test the proposed nonlinear relationship. The formula as printed in the paper was not readable in the extracted text.

Built from the technological class-subclass combinations identified in a patent's backward citations as a proxy for the patent's underlying knowledge elements. Using application dates, the authors took yearly panel counts of the cumulative number of times two patent class-subclass dyads had been combined, and then averaged the level of combination between any two patent classes in a patent (the averaging formula as printed was not readable in the extracted text). They subtracted this number from 1 so that patents that include previously uncombined classes attain the largest values. The variable varies from 0 (knowledge elements previously and frequently combined) to 1 (knowledge components never previously combined).
time_window: yearly panel counts through patent application dates up to December 31, 1999

description: Modeled as network density, the average level of collaboration between any two members of team k, where the frequency with which member i collaborated with member j is scaled by the largest of i's ties to anyone on the team and by the number of members in the team. Relational strength varies from 0 (no coinvention) to 1 (a high level of relational strength, where all team members have previously collaborated on a patent). The value was updated after every new patent application. The formula as printed in the paper was not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: updated after every new patent application

description: Operationalized as the degree to which the innovative productivity of a team centers on just one or a few key scientists, calculated as a weighted Herfindahl index of inventors' patenting activity. Inv_i is the proportion of previous patents inventor i earned prior to joining his or her current team relative to the total number of patents issued by all of the scientists on the team. The value of the Herfindahl index was increased for teams with fewer scientists to correct for possible bias; a higher score indicates a higher degree of status asymmetry. The formula as printed in the paper was not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: patents earned prior to joining the current team

description: Count of the total number of individuals in the top management team, including directors, with a doctorate degree, as reported in the IPO prospectus. Medical doctors, dentists, and holders of other academic degrees where the emphasis is on the mastery of the application of specific bodies of knowledge rather than the generation of new knowledge are excluded. The variable is mean-centered in the regressions.

Coded to 1 if one or more founder sold secondary shares in the IPO, and coded 0 if no founders sold secondary shares in the offering. The information comes from the 'Principal and Selling Shareholders' table included in filing 424b submitted by each company to the SEC.

Assigned a value of 1 if one or more VCs sold secondary shares in the IPO, and assigned a value of 0 if no VCs sold secondary shares in the offering. The information comes from the 'Principal and Selling Shareholders' table included in filing 424b submitted by each company to the SEC.
Coded to 1 if the IPO included any secondary shares at all, and coded to 0 if it had no secondary shares, as reported by SDC.
Calculated for each firm as the natural log of annual sales in the year of the IPO as reported by Compustat. Sales is mean-centered in the regressions.

variable_name: failure to disclose known relevant prior art
description: Count of the inventor's previously granted patents listed as prior art of the focal patent and added by the patent examiner. The inventor's inventory of previously granted patents is limited to those granted during the 10-year window prior to the focal patent's application year, so all of this prior art was known to the inventor yet was not subsequently disclosed by the inventor. The measure does not account for known relevant prior art that was withheld but never discovered by the examiner, making it a conservative estimate.
time_window: prior art granted in the 10-year window prior to the focal patent's application year

description: Total number of patents granted to the inventor before the application year of the sample patent, counted going back to 1975. Measured at the time of application for the sample patent. Log transformed for the models.
level: inventor at the time of the focal patent application
time_window: from 1975 to the application year of the sample patent

description: For each applicant firm connected to a sample patent, firm ROA for the year prior to the application year of the focal patent is subtracted from the industry average ROA (based on four-digit primary SIC) if firm ROA was below the industry average; if firm ROA was greater than the industry average, performance below aspirations is coded as 0. A more positive value indicates greater underperformance relative to aspirations. Log transformed for the models.
scale: continuous, 0 when firm ROA exceeds the industry average
time_window: year prior to the application year of the focal patent

description: Determined by examining the 'law firm' field within the 'Agents' section of the Google database; if a name of a law firm appeared in this field, the counsel was deemed to be outsourced legal counsel. Dummy variable set to 1 if outside legal counsel was used, and 0 otherwise.

Our dependent variable is the date on which each college or university in our sample applied sanctions on Russell by terminating and agreeing not to renew its licensing contract without the firm ceding to the specified activist demands. Dates were coded from information found in college and university press releases, in newspaper articles, and on the United Students Against Sweatshops website. There were 75 supplier-sanction events that occurred over time in our sample of schools.

Time-varying variable constructed to indicate the schools that did not experience any activist tactics but still adopted the practice, counted within the network of the focal school. There were 52 such adoption events that were not associated with any visible signs of activism. We confirmed the absence of activism from our interviews with activists and administrators.

Time-varying count of prior adoptions within a school's network that were coupled with disruption-based tactics, included in the propensity vector. We coded the presence and timing of disruption-based tactics by tracking anti-sweatshop protests that incorporated a more confrontational approach. There were 27 such events staged by student activists, and six of those events were successful, based on adoption occurring after the event.

Time-varying count of prior adoptions within a school's network that were coupled with evidence-based tactics, included in the propensity vector. The presence and timing of the evidence-based tactics were coded using detailed information on the victim-testimonial events organized by USAS, obtained from media reports and corroborated with key informants from USAS. There were 23 victim-testimonial events altogether, 18 of which were successful based on adoption occurring after the event; only one school experienced both disruptive and evidence-based tactics.

Measure based on organizational participation in a private regulatory initiative involving the Fair Labor Association (FLA) Code of Conduct at the time of the Russell campaign. Through their FLA memberships, affiliated schools had made public commitments to the issue of fair labor and workers' rights in their procurement and licensing of collegiate-branded merchandise. Data on college and university participants were made available by the FLA.
time_window: at the time of the Russell campaign

description: Time-varying count of peers within the focal school's network that had experienced disruptive tactics, irrespective of those peer schools' response to the practice. This count is based on tactic deployment dates, whereas the disruption-linked adoptions variable is based on the dates that universities adopted supplier sanctions.

We coded whether each school had a USAS chapter at the start of the study time window. These data were obtained from a USAS website and triangulated with information from media reports and key informants associated with the movement. Of the 355 sampled schools, 99 had activist groups present during the study.
time_window: start of the study time window

description: Whether and when the focal school experienced disruption-based tactics, entered in the propensity vector. We coded the presence and timing of disruption-based tactics during the study period by tracking anti-sweatshop protests that incorporated a more confrontational approach. Examples include holding large gatherings outside the university president's office, occupying and shutting down administrative buildings, and holding picketing demonstrations at retail apparel stores on or near campus; 27 such events were staged by student activists.

Whether and when the focal school experienced evidence-based tactics, entered in the propensity vector. The presence and timing of the evidence-based tactics were coded using detailed information on the victim-testimonial events organized by USAS, which brought aggrieved workers into direct contact with members of the organizational community. Information about these worker testimonial events came from media reports and was corroborated with key informants from USAS; there were 23 victim-testimonial events altogether.

Time-varying measure that includes all adoptions by schools within the network of the focal school, entered in the contagiousness vector of model 1. It tests whether practice adoption in the organizational field was fueled through the general diffusion process among network-proximal organizations.

The dependent variable identifies the ith firm's choice of accessing the jth R&D project through minority investment, joint venture, or acquisition. A minority investment is defined as an equity position in a biotechnology firm of less than 50 percent, a joint venture is the formation of a child by two parent firms (one of which is a biotechnology firm), and an acquisition is cumulative ownership of 50 percent or more of a biotechnology firm, essentially giving the investor control. Because the authors did not theoretically specify how preferences for joint ventures and minority investments should differ, a binary logit collapses equity collaborations (minority investments and joint ventures) into one choice mode contrasted with acquisition.
scale: three categories (minority investment, joint venture, acquisition); binary version is equity collaboration vs. acquisition

description: A dummy variable coded '1' if a biotechnology firm transacted with a large established firm having a core business outside of biotechnology, and coded '0' if the transaction involved two biotechnology firms.

The value of project j's technology was measured as the value of the biotechnology index for its subfield at the announcement of the project. Four stock indices were created from weekly returns of nine U.S. biotechnology firms specializing in each of the four subfields; the indices are equally weighted, have a base value set at 100, were adjusted for inflation, and their values were averaged within a month to get a monthly index value. Firms were selected for each index using BioScan and, where detail about strategic focus was lacking, the PaineWebber Health Care Group lists of firms. Number of Rivals and Technological Value were transformed by taking their natural logarithm to correct for positive skewness.
time_window: value at the announcement of the project (index values from October 1983 to December 1992)

description: It is calculated from the 26-week standard deviation of the log of (inflation-adjusted) weekly returns for each biotechnology subfield index, using a formula the authors describe as consistent with option pricing models in finance; the formula itself is not readable in the extracted text. The 26-week measure was chosen because the authors believed that volatility one-half year prior to the transaction accounts for most of the influence on the governance choice decision, and the measure was converted to a monthly value because transaction announcement dates are monthly.

The number of biotechnology firms with R&D programs in subfield m at time t, based on annual data on the number of biotechnology firms in each subfield available from the Office of Technology Assessment (1984) and the Ernst & Young surveys. The variable was transformed by taking its natural logarithm to correct for the positive skewness.

The measure of asset specificity is the R&D intensity (the ratio of R&D expense to total expense) of the technical subfield to which the target firm belongs, calculated for five different years from data reported in the Ernst & Young annual surveys; because there was little variance over time, the 5-year average of the ratio was used. Total expenses include cost of product sales, general and administrative expenses, marketing and selling expenses, R&D expenses, interest expense, and miscellaneous expenses. Because Williamson advocated a curvilinear relationship between asset specificity and governance choice, R&D Expense was transformed by taking its exponential; the coefficients and standard errors for this variable are reported multiplied by 10 to the negative eleventh power.
scale: percentage (ratio of R&D expense to total expense)

variable_name: previous exit-, retrenchment-, entry- and deepening-target category similarity
description: Pairwise similarity between two product categories is computed from the 286 product attributes in CAPSU: the sum of the relevancy scores of the attributes commonly used in both categories divided by the sum of the relevancy scores of all active attributes for both categories, where an attribute's relevancy score is the number of product families in the category with valid information on that attribute divided by the total number of product families in the category. For each hypothesis the variable is the revenue-share-weighted average of similarity between the businesses the focal firm exited, retrenched, entered, or deepened in year t - 1 and a potential target category, weighted by revenue shares when there are several such businesses. Incumbent business-target category similarity is the analogous weighted average over the firm's incumbent businesses.

Dichotomous variable with a value of one when there is a first product-family released in year t in a product category in which the focal firm did not previously participate, and zero otherwise. To ensure that entry represents a genuinely new product category, all product histories from 1966 to date in CAPSU are cross-referenced.

Number of new product families introduced in year t in an incumbent product category, subtracted by the absolute value of the average number of new product families in the past 3 years. Deepening takes a value of zero if the resulting value is negative.

Dichotomous variable that takes a value of one when the firm stops producing new product families across 3 consecutive years, that is, from year t to t + 2, and zero if not. If the firm restarts new product generation at time t + 3, the variable switches back to nonretrenchment status.

Dichotomous variable that takes a value of one if the firm stops producing new product families in a product category from time t until the end of the observation time period, that is, 2016, and zero if not.

Firms are classified as fabless firms, which focus only on design and subcontract chip production to foundries, or as integrated device manufacturers (IDMs), which integrate from design to production. All models are estimated separately for the two groups, so the classification enters as the grouping dimension of the analysis; pure-play foundries are excluded from the sample.

variable_name: market hazard rate of adopting each new format
description: The diffusion process was modeled as an event history with adoption of the four formats as dependent variables, using data on the timing of adoptions to estimate the instantaneous transition rate of adopting each format. The market hazard rate is the sum of the hazard rates of the stations in the market, so the logged number of stations in the market is included as a covariate. The analysis models the diffusion of the different formats as constrained competing risks, treating entry into each destination format as competing with entry into all other destinations.

variable_name: station hazard rate of adopting each new format
description: The diffusion process was modeled as an event history with adoption of the four formats as dependent variables, using data on the timing of adoptions to estimate the instantaneous transition rate of adopting each format given a set of covariates. The model used was specified by Strang and Tuma (1993) and separates propensity to adopt, susceptibility to influence, and social proximity between actors. The analysis models the diffusion of the different formats as constrained competing risks.

Geographical distance was captured through a discrete measure of region, with six regions specified: Pacific, Southwest, Northwest, Great Lakes, New England, and South. The regions are based on Walker (1969), but modified to capture geographical rather than political groupings of states. A difference indicator in the social proximity vector was set equal to 1 if the potential and previous adopter were in different regions, and zero otherwise. Because it is a difference measure, a negative coefficient will support the hypothesis.

Difference in market size was captured by grouping markets into ranks by population: the top 25 markets were one group, markets 26 through 100 were another, and markets below 100 were the lowest. The market ranks were collected from Arbitron (1991). An indicator was set to 1 if the previous and potential adopter was in different categories, making the measure one of difference in market size. A negative coefficient supports the hypothesis.

The influence of adoptions by corporate counterparts was captured by coding lists of all corporate contacts. The estimation procedure matches this list with the previous adopters and sets an indicator variable equal to 1 for each adopter in the list, allowing correct computation of the sum of influence in the diffusion model. Corporate counterparts are owned by the same corporation as the focal station, and the hypothesis predicts a positive coefficient because adoptions by contacts are more influential than adoptions by others.
scale: indicator (1 = adopter is a corporate counterpart)

description: The influence of adoptions by market contacts was captured by coding lists of all market contacts. The estimation procedure matches this list with the previous adopters and sets an indicator variable equal to 1 for each adopter in the list, allowing correct computation of the sum of influence in the diffusion model. Market contacts are owned by different corporations than the focal station, and the hypothesis predicts a positive coefficient because adoptions by contacts are more influential than adoptions by others.
scale: indicator (1 = adopter is a market contact)

description: The total number of conflict-laden structural holes within the firm's ego network in a given year, where such a hole is a case in which the focal firm maintains concurrent alliance ties with two partners, j and k, who are engaged in an ongoing patent lawsuit with one another. The resulting values ranged from 0 to 13 and the variable was logged because of a right-skewed distribution.
time_window: focal year, with alliance ties traced five years backward

description: The average market value of the firm's successfully filed patents, defined as the absolute change in stock market valuation associated with new patent grants and derived using the two-step approach proposed by Kogan et al. (2017). In the first step the effect of a new patent on the firm's stock price is observed within a narrow three-day window following the USPTO's announcement of the patent grant; in the second step a formal market model filters out other events that might influence the stock price during this window. Because the dependent variable was right-skewed, its natural logarithm was applied, and a one-year lag was implemented.
time_window: three-day window around the patent grant announcement; dependent variable lagged one year

description: The total number of structural holes within the focal firm's ego network that do not involve interalter conflict. The values of this variable ranged from 0 to 6,248, with an average of approximately 36 across all brokering firms, and a logarithmic transformation was applied because of its right-skewed distribution. The variable was mean-centered and interacted with Tertius Dolens Brokerage, and its standalone term was included in all models to control for its direct impact on innovation.

Operationalized using the eigenvector centrality concept, which assigns higher status values to network actors who are linked to other central actors. Firm i's network status is expressed as (1/lambda) times the sum of the degree centrality of each alter j, where lambda is the largest eigenvalue of the network; eigenvector centrality values were computed in Stata using the 'netsis' command and subsequently log-transformed. An interaction between the mean-centered values of Tertius Dolens Brokerage and Network Status was estimated.

Defined as the mean number of distinct types of collaborations maintained by the brokering firm with its conflicting alters in a given year, expressed as Mi = (1/2n) sum (mj + mk), where mj and mk denote the number of different collaboration types (both vertical and horizontal) between broker i and each conflicting alter j and k, and n represents the number of conflict-laden structural holes held by broker i. The Recap database identifies 15 distinct alliance formats in the biopharmaceutical sector, encompassing R&D collaborations, licensing, manufacturing, marketing, and sales agreements. The resulting values ranged from 1 to 10, with an average of around two distinct alter ties per broker, and were logged to address their skewed distribution; mean-centered values were interacted with Tertius Dolens Brokerage.
scale: count of distinct collaboration types, 1-10, average about 2 (logged)

description: Employees rated how often coworkers in their work unit notice peers' behavior and results, praise good work, correct coworkers who make mistakes, report dishonest coworkers, and discuss how everyone performs. The confirmatory factor analysis retained 14 items forming five first-order factors, and the variable score was computed by averaging the means of the five factors to weight them equally (coefficient alpha of 0.88 for the 14 items). The response choices were 1 = almost never, 2 = rarely, 3 = sometimes, 4 = often, and 5 = almost always. Employee ratings were aggregated into work-unit scores (mean interrater agreement index of 0.86).

Employees rated how often coworkers in their work unit gossip about coworkers who perform poorly, gossip about coworkers and their performance, refuse to socialize with poorly performing coworkers, and avoid coworkers who perform poorly. The five retained items formed two first-order factors (gossip and avoid), and the variable score was computed by averaging the means of the two factors (coefficient alpha of 0.90 for the five items). The response choices were 1 = almost never to 5 = almost always. The ratings were aggregated into work-unit scores, but the mean interrater agreement index was 0.54, lower than the 0.70 value used to support aggregation.

Employees rated the level of supervisory monitoring in their units on seven items (coefficient alpha of 0.88). The response choices ranged from 1 (almost never) to 5 (almost always). The measure averaged the means of the ratings on two dimensions, the degree to which supervisors observe and ask about employee performance. Ratings were aggregated into work-unit scores (mean interrater agreement index of 0.77).

Employees rated the level of cohesiveness in their units on six items (coefficient alpha of 0.80) using a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The measure averaged the means of the ratings of task and interpersonal cohesiveness, as indicated by Mullen and Copper (1994). Ratings were aggregated into work-unit scores (mean interrater agreement index of 0.86).

Managers and assistant managers rated the task interdependence of their units using a five-point scale (1 = almost always true, 5 = almost never true); the data were then reverse-coded so that higher values indicate greater task interdependence. The measure used four items from Mohr (1971), Pearce and Gregersen (1991), and Campion et al. (1993) (coefficient alpha of 0.85). Ratings were aggregated into work-unit scores (mean interrater agreement index of 0.84).
scale: 5-point scale, 1 = almost always true to 5 = almost never true, reverse-coded

description: Managers and assistant managers rated how frequently six problems occurred in each of their units over the past month on a scale ranging from 1 (always) to 7 (never), such that higher values represent fewer problems and therefore better unit performance. The items were absenteeism, tardiness, disciplinary problems, mistakes and accidents, employee bickering, and overall frequency of problems (coefficient alpha of 0.91). Ratings were aggregated into work-unit scores (mean interrater agreement index of 0.91).

Peer monitoring is measured by an employee survey scale with two forms: direct peer monitoring (noticing, praising, correcting, reporting and discussing) and indirect peer monitoring (gossiping about and avoiding poorly performing peers). Employee ratings are averaged within factors and aggregated to work-unit scores.

Measured as the total number of media citations to the initial lead VC in Belgian national newspapers between 1995 and the year of investment. Constructed using the Mediargus database. The number of citations to a VC ranges from zero to 654. The measure used is the natural logarithm of media citations plus a constant equal to 1.
scale: Count of media citations ranging from zero to 654; log-transformed

description: Measured as the total number of investments made by the initial lead VC in the same industry (two-digit industry code) as the focal firm prior to the VC's investment in the focal firm. Multiple databases were triangulated to reconstruct all prior investments made by the initial lead VC. Cumulative industry deal experience ranges from one to 26 investments with a median value of two. The natural logarithm of industry experience is used.
scale: Count of prior industry investments ranging from one to 26; log-transformed
time_window: prior to the VC's investment in the focal firm

description: Measured as the natural logarithm of the total amount of financing that VC-backed firms hold at various points in time. This measure includes both equity and debt financing.

Includes only debt and excludes subsequent equity investments. Measured as the natural logarithm of the total amount of debt financing that VC-backed firms hold at various points in time. The measure was constructed so that repeat equity investments by VCs participating in the initial round are not included and to mitigate the impact of information flows within VC networks.
scale: Log-transformed amount of debt financing held

description: Measured as the natural logarithm of the total number of persons (on a full-time equivalent basis) that VC-backed firms employ at various points in time.
scale: Log-transformed number of full-time equivalent employees

description: Measured as the natural logarithm of the number of employees that are primarily involved in intellectual labor and, accordingly, work under the more favorable employment contract. This measure draws on the distinction in employment contracts between employees primarily involved in manual labor and employees primarily involved in intellectual labor.
scale: Log-transformed number of employees under the more favorable employment contract

description: Event indicator for a dyad of an organization and a market category that the organization is not in. A dyad enters the risk set the first year both the organization and the target market category are observed in press releases; when the organization enters the target market, an event occurs and the dyad is removed from the risk set. Only the first entry is counted as an event, and the category the organization is already in when it first appears is not counted as an entry.

Event defined as the last consecutive year the organization is in the market category since entry; the first observed exit is used, after which the dyad is removed from the risk set. Organizations that exit the data altogether are censored observations, and exits are undefined for 2002, so the exit analysis runs for 1990 through 2001.

Number of venture capital funding events in market category k in the prior year. Each funding event is weighted by the organization's grade of membership in the market, calculated as the number of times organization A claims market category k in press releases divided by the number of times it claims any other market; for organizations in multiple categories the measure is averaged, weighted by grade of membership. Independent and control variables are lagged by one year.

Number of bankruptcies in market category k in the prior year, weighted by the organization's grade of membership in the market. The bankruptcy counts come from Thomson Financial, augmented with organizations coded as ''defunct'' by Venture Economics; the authors refer to all negative events as bankruptcies.

Weighted number of bankruptcies in market category k at the time of organization A's entry into the category. The effect is allowed to vary over the time the organization has been in the market, to test the argument that the enduring effects of entry conditions take time to materialize.

Average number of prior-year venture capital fundings across all categories k that organization j is in for the given year, weighted by j's grade of membership in each category k. The models include this variable with a quadratic and with a piecewise specification to allow for nonlinearities in the functional form of the effect.

variable_name: VC fundings in market(s) at round 1 funding
description: Number of VC investments in category k in the year that firm j was funded, weighted by the funded organization's grade of membership in the market category and averaged over its categories. It is calculated in two ways: as the funding count in the year the organization receives its first round of funding, and as the mean of that count over all years in which the organization receives funding.
time_window: year of funding (and mean over all funding years)

variable_name: No. categories entered after 2+ VC fundings (2-year window; logged)
description: Number of markets organization j entered for which weighted VC funding events are greater than or equal to 2 in the previous two-year moving window. The natural log is taken to reduce skew.

Event that organization j receives venture capital financing. Funding is a repeat event: when a firm is funded it reenters the risk set as a new observation. The risk set is privately held companies including the years a company was private before it went public, restricted to organizations less than 15 years old.

Event that organization j transitions from private to public ownership through an IPO. The risk set includes organizations 20 years and younger or those whose founding date is not known; firms that enter the press release data in the year they go public are excluded because their funding histories are not available.

The number of travel agencies with a vendor's computerized reservation system in the origin city of a city-pair, lagged one year (t - 1) because agencies need time to train personnel and integrate the system into workflows. Each carrier's installed base variable in the multinomial logit model is built from its number of locations in the origin city at time t - 1, and the number of locations is then adjusted by the arithmetic mean of all carriers' locations in the market.

The number of travel agency locations using each computerized reservation system vendor's system in each year of the study, measured at the national level. The variable is lagged one year following the same logic as the city-pair model, so that it is treated as predetermined.

Each carrier's percentage of revenue passenger miles between an origin and destination city, computed with reference to the origin-destination data of the Department of Transportation's ODIA database for each city-pair. For estimation, the raw market share value is divided by the arithmetic mean market share and the logarithm of that expression is taken (log-centering), and the independent variables are centered on their arithmetic means.

The total number of miles flown by paying passengers on the airline each year, measured in millions of miles as a measure of revenue generation. A revenue passenger mile is defined as a paying passenger flying one mile on the airline; it is not a direct measure of revenue as it only shows the fact that the passenger was paying, not how much was paid.

The average percentage of seats filled with paying passengers during the year, a measure of efficiency. If a plane has 100 paying passengers and a capacity of 200 passengers, the load factor for that flight is 50%.

Operating revenues minus expenses, measured in thousands of dollars, a short-term measure of financial performance. Expenses related to aircraft depreciation and leasing have been removed as they are not considered controllable in the short run, and the firm's own computerized reservation system fees were excluded by subtracting the Miscellaneous Revenue account on Form 41 from revenues so that the assessment of computerized reservation system impacts was not confounded by this highly direct measure.

An indicator for a lease being offered by a captive lessor, equal to one when the lessor is a captive and zero when it is an independent lessor. It is the dependent variable in the linear probability model, and the fitted probability is interpreted as captive market share in the relevant lease market.

The share of leases written by independent lessors. Because every lease in the data is written either by a captive or an independent lessor, independent market share is the complement of the captive indicator, and the authors describe results in terms of independents being more or less likely to have written a lease on a given vehicle.

A credit risk score calculated for each lessee by taking the average interest rate on car loans sold at the same dealership where the lease was originated. The authors describe this as a rough proxy for the credit risk of a dealership's customers, and it assumes that the relative creditworthiness of lessees across dealerships parallels that of borrowers.

Consumer Reports assigns overall reliability scores based on the number of major problems reported in owner surveys, with the highest score meaning few problems. Vehicles also receive component reliability scores for the engine, transmission, and electrical and braking systems, and the analysis disaggregates the overall score into these component scores.
scale: overall reliability scores of 1-3; component reliability scores of 1-5

description: Inventory quantities were manually collected from the Automotive News and were available for cars covering 27,770 of the leases. The models use the log of inventory; high standing inventory evidences a vehicle that is less demanded than predicted.

An indicator for whether the vehicle is in the first year of a new body style, that is, the first year after a body style refresh, the period in which the risk that the model will be refreshed within the lease term is least problematic.

The dependent variable in the tests of the AMC3 and AMC4 predictions: the share of a captive lessor's leases that are of its own manufacturer's make. The authors use it to show that captive competitive intensity is due to the captive's relationship with its own manufacturer rather than to a general taste for those classes of leases.

Whether a leased vehicle is of the captive lessor's own manufacturer's make. The analysis separates leases on vehicles from the captive's own manufacturer from leases on non-own-manufacturer vehicles, which are excluded when estimating captive market share on the remaining leases.

Lessor type is coded as a dummy for a lease written by a captive lessor (a manufacturer's financial subsidiary) equal to one, versus an independent lessor equal to zero, for each lease in the California lease data.

A dummy variable indicating whether the organization was using an employee ownership plan. The dummy was available from the organizational survey in which HR managers reported whether the organization used an employee ownership plan (1 = yes; 0 = no) in each wave.
Net sales divided by the total number of employees, with a logarithm taken. The measure follows prior employee ownership and strategic HR research.

Each firm's total sales were log-transformed and averaged for each industry for each year. The industry average value was regressed on the year over a 12-year period (2000-2011); the regression slope coefficients were antilogged and standardized, with higher values indicating higher industry growth. Industry was defined by the two-digit level of the Korean Standard Industry Classification code.

From the same industry-level regressions of industry average log sales on the year over 2000-2011, the standard errors of the slope coefficients were antilogged and standardized and used as environmental instability. The higher the standard error, the higher the industry instability. Industry was defined by the two-digit level of the Korean Standard Industry Classification code.

The percentage of employee owners in a firm, computed as the number of employee owners divided by the total number of employees, with the total number of employees available from Global Compustat. The percentage measure was then standardized.
Measured as a log of net sales per employee, consistent with Study 1 and prior employee ownership research.

Measured in the same way as in Study 1. A regression of the log of sales for each industry for each wave on the year was run over a nine-year period (2006-2014) and the standardized antilogged slope coefficients were used as environmental growth. Industry was defined by the three-digit level of the North American Industry Classification Code.

Measured in the same way as in Study 1: standardized antilogged standard errors from the regressions of industry-level log sales on the year over 2006-2014 were used as environmental instability. Industry was defined by the three-digit level of the North American Industry Classification Code.

variable_name: Technological complexity (high-, medium-, and low-complexity firm)
description: In line with most studies of complexity, technological complexity was measured relatively. Using common industry classifications, 13 hospital software product-classes were identified, including one 'other' category, and a panel of 18 industry experts rated their complexity on a four-point scale (not complex, limited complexity, significant complexity, extreme complexity); 15 usable questionnaires were returned. As no product-class was regarded as noncomplex, each was categorized by the experts' modal rating into one of three complexity classes: low, medium, and high. Each firm was classified as participating in one or more of these complexity categories: firms commercializing one or more high-complexity systems in any year were high-complexity businesses, firms with at least one medium-complexity product but no high-complexity products were medium-complexity businesses, and firms with no high- or medium-complexity products were low-complexity businesses.
scale: three complexity classes (low, medium, high), derived from a four-point expert rating scale

description: Survival was measured as a firm's participation in the industry. A dummy variable recorded each firm's participation in the industry; for each year, it was coded 1 for industry exit and 0 for no exit. Failure was recorded when a business discontinued operations and ceased to operate as an entity, and the logarithmic odds of exiting the industry in a year were modelled as linearly affected by the covariates. Cases in which a business sold a majority of its equity to another firm but continued to operate in the industry were treated as divestments, not failures, and firms still in the industry in 1991 were treated as censored.
scale: dummy variable (1 = industry exit, 0 = no exit)

description: A dummy variable indicating the period in which a significant technological shock occurred, chosen as 1982-84 because of the government-mandated introduction of the Prospective Payment System for reimbursement of medical fees, which imposed new reporting and operating constraints on hospitals and required vendors to undertake major software systems modification and development.

variable_name: New product; new product, one-year lag; new product, two-year lag
description: Technological expansion was measured with three indicator variables: new product, new product lagged one year, and new product lagged two years. These variables indicated when a business first entered a new product-class and each of the following two years, allowing the effects of technological expansion to be detected over a three-year period.
time_window: year of entry into a new product-class and the following two years

variable_name: Number of high-, medium-, and low-complexity systems
description: Technological diversity was measured by the total number of high-, medium- and low-complexity product-classes each business commercialized in each year of the study period, measured at the end of each year, as diversity in high-complexity technologies is likely to have greater impact on survival than variety in low-complexity technologies.
time_window: each year, 1961-1991, measured at year end

variable_name: Technology and nontechnology alliances by complexity class
description: Alliances were identified from announcements of cooperation between firms; 693 collaborative relationships between 248 businesses were recorded. The primary purpose of each alliance as reported by the cooperating businesses was recorded, and each alliance was categorized as a technology, licensing, marketing and distribution, value-added reseller, or other alliance; alliances related to joint R&D, development of interfaces, or other technological issues were classified as technology alliances, and all others as nontechnology alliances. The multiplication of the two types of alliances with the three complexity variables created six indicator variables; ten cases in which businesses created freestanding joint ventures were omitted. The approach measures the establishment rather than the current existence of alliances.

Dummy variable equal to 1 when the article-page counterpart to the focal discussion page is restricted, and 0 otherwise. Page restrictions can be semi-protection (restricting unregistered users) or full protection (restricting all users).

variable_name: Entries per month on focal page
description: Number of monthly discussion entries by a user on the talk page of the focal restricted article page. Used as the dependent variable in Analysis 1 to measure contributor effort on a specific problem.

variable_name: Discussion entries per month on nonfocal pages
description: Number of monthly discussion entries by a user on nonfocal pages—pages other than the focal restricted page on which the user had been active around the time of the restriction. Used as the dependent variable in Analysis 2 to measure reallocation of effort.
time_window: one month pre and post restriction

description: Dummy variable indicating whether the article page has been classified by the Wikipedia community as more likely to be disputed by users (e.g., intelligent design or climate change).
Ratio of deletions to overall edits on the article page in the month prior to the protection.
Relative number of times a previous article entry has been turned back and deleted.
Difference between the number of barnstars an administrator has received and the number a given organizational member has received. Aggregated at page level for tests of H2a.
Difference in years between the time an administrator has spent with Wikipedia and the time another organizational member has spent.
A person's absolute tenure with the organization. Used to test how a member's tenure affects her response to authoritative intervention.
Herfindahl index of each user's activity across pages. The more users distribute their effort to many pages, the lower their Herfindahl index.

An annual time-varying measure obtained from Henisz (2000b) that quantifies the extent to which any one institutional actor, such as the executive or a legislative chamber, in a given country is unconstrained in its choice of policies in a given year. It is constructed using a spatial model of political interaction that incorporates data on the number of independent veto players and their party affiliations. Each additional veto player provides a negative but diminishing effect on the level of hazards, and hazards decline in the homogeneity of party preferences within an opposed veto player. In the interactions the measure is mean-centered and lagged one year.
time_window: annual, lagged one year (t-1) in the interactions

description: An indicator variable that took a value of 1 if firm x made an entry in country i at time t, otherwise it was zero. An entry was a foreign direct investment, not a portfolio investment, that resulted in a firm's first establishment of a foreign subsidiary in the focal host country. Observations started in 1980, continued until an entry occurred, or were right-censored in 1999 if the variable was zero in every year t for firm x in country i.
A firm's experience gathered in all national settings and by all types of entry, computed from all data compiled on the history of a firm's investment activity in all years.
time_window: full history of a firm's investment activity

description: The logarithm of a firm's years of experience in the operation of subsidiaries in countries with above mean levels of political hazards. In the interactions the measure is mean-centered and lagged one year.
time_window: annual, lagged one year (t-1) in the interactions

description: The logarithm of a firm's years of experience in the operation of subsidiaries in countries with below mean levels of political hazards.
The logarithm of a firm's years of experience in the operation of subsidiaries in countries in the same cultural block. In the interactions the measure is mean-centered and lagged one year.
time_window: annual, lagged one year (t-1) in the interactions

description: The logarithm of a firm's years of experience in the operation of subsidiaries in countries in another cultural block.
The logarithm of a firm's years of experience in the operation of subsidiaries in manufacturing entries. In the interactions the measure is mean-centered and lagged one year.
time_window: annual, lagged one year (t-1) in the interactions

description: The logarithm of a firm's years of experience in the operation of subsidiaries in distribution entries.

Following Barkema et al. (1996), countries were coded into Ronen and Shenkar's (1985) cultural blocks, and these blocks were then ordinally ranked in terms of their comparative distance from Japan. The nearest cultural block to Japan was scored one, the next most proximate two, and so forth. Results were similar if a cultural distance measure was used.

The moderator variable of interest is measured by the total years of IT experience for each participant. The authors use years of IT experience as their best proxy for domain experience because it measures exposure to solving domain-relevant problems, citing Mithas and Krishnan (2008) who validate that the technical competencies of IT professionals are reflected in their on-the-job IT experience.

Ticket Resolved is a binary variable set to 1 if ticket k was resolved by participant i and 0 if it was not resolved; it is the standard measure of performance for IT support work at TECHCO. The comparison of algorithm-augmented to self-performance is captured by the binary Is AutomateIT Ticket indicator (1 for the AutomateIT tool, 0 for the manual system), and the effect of interest is the quadratic fit of years of IT experience on solving AutomateIT tickets relative to manual tickets. Because each participant resolved the same tickets in both modes, the comparison is made within participants.

In the questionnaire each respondent circled the number (7-point Likert scale, from 1, 'very little/low', to 7, 'very extensive/high') best describing the extent to which top executives (general and deputy general managers) at his or her firm had utilized personal ties, networks, and connections during the past 3 years with six types of external actors. The level of managerial networking was measured using the average of the above six items. Cronbach's alpha for this variable is 0.73, suggesting a reasonable level of internal consistency.
scale: 7-point Likert scale, 1 = very little/low to 7 = very extensive/high

description: Structural uncertainty was defined as the geometric average of standard deviations (1996 through 1998) in output, sales, and profit of the industry in which the firm participates (i.e., [S.D.(output) x S.D.(sales) x S.D.(profit)]^1/3). It is constructed from archival industry data in the China Statistical Yearbook.
Industrial growth was measured by the compound growth rate (%) of the respective industry's sales from 1996 to 1998. It is constructed from archival industry data in the China Statistical Yearbook.
