Industrial regulation level was measured by the arithmetic average (1996-98) of an industry's tax and fiscal charges intensity (i.e., [sales tax and fiscal charges + value-added tax] divided by an industry's sales). The authors argue this is an appropriate proxy for the degree of regulation because in China governmental regulation in a particular industry is reflected in this industry's burden of VAT, sales tax, and various fiscal charges.
Competitive pressure was the compound growth of the number of firms during the 3 years from 1996 to 1998. It is constructed from archival industry data in the China Statistical Yearbook.

An industry's production capacity utilization was operationalized as the arithmetic average (1996-98) of utilization rate (%) reported in the Yearbook. Capacity utilization was positively skewed and was thus transformed by taking its logarithm.

Strategic proactiveness was measured by the average of five items, each on a 7-point Likert scale (1, strongly disagree, to 7, strongly agree). The reliability and dimensionality of this construct was confirmed by Cronbach's alpha (0.83) and communality estimates (0.82-0.92). The survey information was framed within the most recent 3 years.
scale: 7-point Likert scale, 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree

description: Based on the earliest action taken by a rival in response to a focal firm's announcement. The competitive action announcements of the two duopoly firms were temporally ordered starting with the first announcement in the time frame; a rival's actions between a focal firm's two successive announcements were deemed responses to the first announcement, and the absence of such actions was deemed a nonresponse. Two coders used competitive keywords to confirm that the rival's actions were responses against the focal firm. The hazard of the rival's response was then estimated with event history analysis: response is a dichotomous variable indicating whether a response occurred and time delay a continuous variable indicating the time span, evaluated on a daily basis since the focal firm's announcement, with right censoring if no response was observed.
time_window: between a focal firm's two successive action announcements

description: An ordered categorical measure created for each press release: 3 (most vague) = only qualitative cues and no numeric cues, 2 (moderately vague) = mix of numeric and qualitative cues, 1 (least vague) = only numeric cues and no qualitative cues. Cues were extracted from the focal firms' press releases by a customized automated content analysis program based on a dictionary of dates, numeric time frames, and nonnumeric temporal descriptors; coding was manually checked for 10% of the press releases.

Measured by the total number of qualitative cues in the press release. Qualitative cues were identified from the dictionary of nonnumeric temporal descriptors (e.g., soon, quickly, long term, short term, in the coming days) using the customized automated content analysis program.

Measured as the number of days between the date of the press release and the latest date (e.g., August 22, 2013) or time frame (e.g., in the next three years, in the coming years) cited in the press release. For press releases with no numeric cues, temporal distances were derived from nonnumeric temporal descriptors: three coders blind to the hypotheses categorized the nonnumeric descriptors into proximal, distal, and medium-term distances, and proximal descriptors were assigned the minimum temporal distance, distal descriptors the maximum distance, and medium-term descriptors the median temporal distance found in all the press releases of that focal firm in the data.

Measured by the number of times the longest time frame was repeated in a press release. The longest time frame was identified from the numeric and nonnumeric temporal cues extracted by the customized automated content analysis program.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the percentage change in net income exceeds the industry average, and 0 otherwise. Values are used for the restructuring year (t0) and for each of the two prior years (t-1, t-2). In the logistic regressions COM is ranked as the most important predictor of downsizing and of upsizing.
time_window: restructuring year and prior two years

description: Return on assets, computed as 100 x (net income / total assets), measured at fiscal year-end for the restructuring year (t0) and for the two preceding years (t-1, t-2).

ROA of firm i minus the ROA of the industry in which firm i falls, reported for the restructuring year and the two prior years. The authors report that the patterns they find for industry-adjusted returns also hold for this measure.

Industry-adjusted return, the difference between a corporation's stock return and the equally weighted average return on the corresponding Global Industry Classification Standard stocks represented within the S&P 500; the return is the standard measure based on stock price and annual dividends. The authors report IAR for the event year (t0) and for the two years before restructuring (t-1, t-2) and describe it as their key metric.

Average industry-adjusted return over fiscal years t+1 and t+2 following restructuring in year t, also estimated separately for IAR t+1 and IAR t+2. The estimates come from dummy-variable regressions in which the employee, asset and combination decile dummies are the explanatory variables and the intercept is suppressed, so that the estimates are simple mean values of average returns for each dummy.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the percentage change in dividends exceeds the industry average, and 0 otherwise; abnormal dividend changes serve as the proxy for managerial foresight, and managerial perceptions of a company are treated as positive (negative) if the percentage change in dividends is greater (less) than the average in the company's industry. Values are used for the restructuring year and its two lags.
Dummy variable equal to 1 if the percentage change in GDP exceeds 2.3%, and 0 otherwise, measured for the restructuring year and its two lags.
Dummy variable equal to 1 if the intrayear standard deviation of the Partisan Conflict Index exceeds 13, and 0 otherwise, measured for the restructuring year and its two lags.
Dummy variable equal to 1 if excess industry return exceeds 0, and 0 otherwise, measured for the restructuring year and its two lags.

Trend variable equal to the year, taking a value of 1 in year 1, 2 in year 2, and so on; it is not ranked with the other antecedents but its significance is noted. The authors deploy it to capture possible long-run tendencies in restructuring relating to technology changes such as the adoption of computer technology.

Using a 5% cut-off on year-over-year changes, companies are classified as employee downsizers (decline in employees greater than 5% but decline in plant and equipment less than 5%), asset downsizers, combination downsizers (declines in both employees and plant and equipment greater than 5%), employee upsizers, asset upsizers, combination upsizers (increases in both greater than 5%) and stable employers (none of the above). In the logistic regressions the dependent variables are Cat3 = 1 for combination downsizers versus Cat7 = 0 for stable firms, and Cat6 = 1 for combination upsizers versus Cat7 = 0.

Firms are sorted year by year into deciles of percentage changes in employees and into deciles of percentage changes in total assets; deciles 1-4 are treated as downsizing, deciles 7-10 as upsizing and deciles 5-6 as stable. Standalone employee (asset) restructuring is conditioned on asset (employee) changes falling within the fifth or sixth decile, and combination restructuring requires the unconditional employee and asset changes to fall in the identical decile.

Each firm's prestige score from Vault.com's annual law firm rankings. Thousands of associates rate firms on a scale of 1 to 10 based on how prestigious they believe working for each firm would be; respondents do not rate their own firms and are asked not to rate firms with which they are not familiar. Rankings are based on each firm's average rating in these surveys. Prestige scores were obtained directly from Vault for all firms identified in Vault's survey exercise, including unranked firms.

The absolute value of the difference between the Vault prestige scores for hiring firm i and source firm j in that year. It is partitioned into Status_differential_ij, Si>Sj (hiring firm higher in status) and Status_differential_ij, Si<Sj (hiring firm lower in status), each the absolute value of the prestige score difference in the relevant case.
Total firm profits divided by the number of firm partners with residual claims, a common industry profitability metric obtained from American Lawyer surveys.

The absolute value of the difference in PPEP (in U.S. dollars) between hiring firm i and source firm j. It is partitioned into Profitability_differential_ij, Pi>Pj (hiring firm more profitable) and Profitability_differential_ij, Pi<Pj (hiring firm less profitable), each the absolute dollar profitability difference in the relevant case.

variable_name: Organization i hires from competitor j (0/1)
description: Indicator of whether Am Law 200 firm i hires a partner from another Am Law 200 firm j in a given year. Data on lateral hiring were obtained from the Lateral Partner Moves database, which summarizes hiring information from the American Lawyer's annual Lateral Partner Survey of Am Law 200 firms, industry publications, firm websites, and press releases. Between 2000 and 2009, 9,465 partners transitioned between two Am Law 200 firms.

CEOs evaluated their firm's financial performance in the prior half year on a five-point scale (1, 'a large loss'; 3, 'breaking even'; 5, 'a large profit'). Objective performance was ROS during the same period as reported in the survey. Both values were industry-adjusted by subtracting the respective industry mean, converted to z-scores, and hubris was measured by the z for subjective evaluation minus the z for ROS; the greater the difference, the greater the hubris. A score of less than zero was recoded as zero.

CEOs were asked whether their firms had 'invested in projects involving high and new technologies.' Responses were coded 1 for having invested in new technologies and 0 otherwise. Nine categories of high and new technology were suggested.
Measured as the average growth in industry sales over the prior five years, based on a firm's primary industry, using data from the Chinese Statistics Yearbook.

Measured as the number of competitors (in thousands) in an industry. The number of rivals was counted for each year from the Chinese Statistics Yearbook and averaged over the five years prior to the survey date.

Measured as the instability of industry sales over the prior five years; industry sales were regressed against time and the standard errors of the regression slope coefficients were divided by the mean sales. Larger values indicated greater environmental uncertainty.
Coded as the number of years from the founding of a firm to 2000, using data obtained from the CEO survey.
Measured as the logarithm of the firm's total assets, using data obtained from the CEO survey.
Measured as the ratio of R&D expenditure to sales, using data obtained from the CEO survey.
A dummy variable coded yes when duality was present, that is, when a firm's CEO also chaired its board.
A dummy variable for state ownership; about 46 percent of the sampled firms were wholly state-owned or state-controlled.
Political appointment of the CEO was flagged with a dummy variable; about 48 percent of the CEOs in the sample had been politically appointed.

Calculated as the difference between a firm's risk-taking level and the average risk-taking level of peer firms in the same industry; the score could range between -1 and 1. A firm with a score below -0.5 was a lagger, above 0.5 a pioneer, and between -0.5 and 0.5 a follower.

The HCCP listed 12 selection practices. HR managers were asked to rate which selection practices their firms used in 2004 to select full-time employees on a dichotomous response (use = 1, nonuse = 0). Internships were excluded from the composite, so the authors added up the 11 individual selection practices to operationalize a composite index of selection practices.
Firm productivity measured as sales divided by the total number of employees, averaged over 2004-2007. The monetary unit of all firm performance metrics is 1,000 won.

Firm productivity measured as operating profit divided by the total number of employees, averaged over 2004-2007. This measure recognizes operating expenses such as labor costs, so it is related to but different from sales per employee.

Profit operationalized as revenue minus costs of products sold and administrative and selling costs related to firm operations, averaged over 2004-2007. EBIT is very similar to operating profit but further includes non-operating income (or losses) in the calculation.

Prior firm performance computed as the average firm performance during 2000-2003, using the average sales per employee and average operating profit per employee (and EBIT) over that period. We used firm performance data in 2004 to operationalize subsequent firm performance variables, and computed average firm performance during 2000-2003 as the independent variable.

Overall turnover ratio in 2004. In the 2005 survey, HR managers reported the number of full-time leavers and the number of full-time employees in 2004; collective turnover is the total number of full-time leavers divided by the total number of full-time employees in each firm, multiplied by 100.

Total number of selection screening stages (or hurdles) in the hiring process. In the 2005 survey, HR managers rated selection stages on a 5-point scale by asking how many selection stages (from application stage to final selection decision) their firms used to select new employees in 2004.
scale: 1 = one stage, 2 = two stages, 3 = three stages, 4 = four stages, 5 = more than five stages

description: Industry sales were collected as additional data sets during eight time periods using the KISVALUE database on the basis of Korean SIC codes. Industry sales were first regressed on a TIME variable; industry growth is computed by the regression coefficients divided by the mean values of industry sales during 2000-2003 and 2004-2007.

Industry sales were collected during eight time periods using the KISVALUE database on the basis of Korean SIC codes. Industry sales were first regressed on a TIME variable; industry dynamism is computed by the standard errors of the regression coefficients divided by the mean values of industry sales during 2000-2003 and 2004-2007.

Identity elements were coded from the identity statements in the annual school report cards, covering three facets of the charter school identity. Ten substantive themes were coded, seventeen kinds of resources and services emerged in the coding, and target population was coded as three grade levels (high school, junior high, elementary) plus four specific types of students (at-risk, gifted, ethnic identity, at-home). The grade levels were not mutually exclusive categories, as a school could serve all three levels.

Each organization was treated as a matrix of element co-occurrences, and the population-level co-occurrence count matrix was transformed into a binary matrix indicating whether the actual count exceeds the expected count of co-occurrences. Stochastic blockmodels estimated with the BLOCKS program using Gibbs sampling were fitted to two-, three-, four- and five-block structures for each year, with 10,000 Gibbs sequences per structure. Goodness of fit was assessed with Hx, where a higher value indicates more indeterminate block positions and a value near zero indicates a highly structured pattern, and the representation with the lowest Hx is preferred.

The dependent variable is the number of FSP elements present in each charter school, tallied annually. It ranges in value from zero to eight, and no organization ever had all nine elements at the same time. Rather than requiring a specific number of elements for membership, the authors maintain that schools fluctuate along a continuum of inclusion in the cluster.

The number of FSP elements (other than those belonging to the focal school) in the focal school's district. The variable is mean-centered before the interaction effect is calculated in order to reduce multicollinearity.

A dummy variable indicating the presence of an existing magnet school in the focal school's district. The main effect of magnet school presence is included in the model as well as its interaction with the district FSP count.

A 4-item index, adapted from Chatterjee and Hambrick (2007), averaged across four unobtrusive indicators: (1) prominence of the CEO's photograph in the company's annual report on a four-point scale; (2) the ratio of the number of times the CEO's name was mentioned in all company press releases to the number of times the second-highest-paid executive was mentioned; (3) the CEO's relative cash compensation (salary and bonus) divided by that of the second-highest-paid executive; and (4) the CEO's relative non-cash compensation (deferred income, stock grants, and stock options) divided by that of the second-highest-paid executive. The four indicators were calculated using data from the second and third years of each CEO's tenure averaged together, so each CEO had an invariant narcissism score. A fifth indicator, the CEO's use of first-person singular pronouns in interviews, was dropped because the data were not available before 1997.
time_window: second and third years of each CEO's tenure

description: Content analysis of articles about health-related biotechnology published between 1980 and 2008 in the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal. Five trained coders selected statements that referred to biotech in evaluative terms, either conveying a positive outlook (enthusiasm or excitement) or portraying biotech as challenging, difficult, or risky; the coders identified a total of 1,957 such statements. The final measure is the average number of evaluative statements in both newspapers combined for the focal year and the prior year.

Following the content analysis approach of Kaplan, Murray, and Henderson (2003), the number of biotech-related words (e.g., 'biotech,' 'monoclonal antibody') in each firm's annual letter to shareholders for year t-1 was counted and divided by the number of paragraphs in the letter; the ratio was multiplied by 100 to allow more interpretable regression coefficients. The authors extended the list of biotech-related words to 61 search terms.

The degree of biotech adoption was measured by summing the number of new strategic initiatives in biotech for each year (t) of a given CEO's tenure: formations of biotech alliances, acquisitions of biotech companies, and launches of organic biotech R&D projects. Results were similar when the indicators were standardized and averaged.
time_window: each year t of a given CEO's tenure

description: Calculated as the sum of the squares of the minority board members' percentage share of votes divided by the square of the largest shareholder's percentage share of the votes. Following Tabachnick and Fidell (1989), the authors based the calculation on the total shares held by the five largest shareholders who served on a board and dropped observations with more than five board members from the primary analyses. Values of 1:1 or less indicated the distribution of ownership favored the largest shareholder, and values higher than this indicated that the dispersion of ownership favored the minority shareholders; ownership favored the largest shareholder in 73 percent of the cases and minority shareholders in the remaining 27 percent.

A six-level indicator of a firm's debt-to-equity ratio; codings from 1 to 6 were "no debt," "1-25%," "26-50%," "50-100%," "101-200%," and "over 200%." The mean debt-to-equity ratio among the sample group of mature firms was 2.57, which interpolates to about 18 percent. The measure was self-reported and, as is the case with virtually all privately held firms, objective measures were not available.

A dummy variable coded 1 if the mean of the reported growth in sales for the industry category was greater than the median ratio for all industry categories, and coded 0 if mean growth was below the median. The authors note that, although coarse-grained, this measure distinguishes industries that enjoyed high levels of sales growth during this period (for instance, manufacturing and telecommunications) from those that did not.

For each article about the sample firms, the content of 'negative emotion' was measured using the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software program. Articles that mentioned more than four firms or in which the focal firm was not mentioned in the first 25% of the article were excluded. The measure was aggregated by firm-year using the average of all articles' negative valence scores in a given firm-year, and was lagged one year.

variable_name: resource development relative to resource access
description: Ratio of the dollar amount invested in resource development (drilling and bringing into production of wells) divided by the dollar amount invested in resource access (exploration). All development and access investment values were incremented by 1 to eliminate zero values and log-transformed to normalize the distribution, and then a ratio of investment in development activities to investment in access activities was created. The measure captures the firm's relative focus on the two core activities, that is, strategic decision-making relating to investing in one activity in relation to the other.

The number of times a set of development-related word segments appeared in each news article was counted and divided by the overall word count for the article. The article-specific development-focused content scores were then averaged within firm over the calendar year and lagged by one year.

The aspirational performance level was computed using the 'switching model' of aspiration level: when the firm's performance, captured as ROA, in the prior period (t - 2) fell short of the industry average performance in that period, the firm's aspirational level in the next period (t - 1) is set equal to the industry's average performance in the prior period (t - 2); when the firm's performance exceeded industry performance, the aspirational target is the firm's prior performance at time t - 2 multiplied by 1.05. Aspiration-relative performance is the firm's actual performance in t - 1 minus the aspirational level in period t - 1, winsorized to the 99th or 1st percentile. The printed formulae were not readable in the extracted text.
time_window: aspirations set from t - 2 performance; performance measured at t - 1

description: Firm size was measured via the natural log of total assets. Because initial models suggested possible multicollinearity due to high variance inflation factors, the variable was orthogonalized using a modified Gram - Schmidt procedure.

Volatility of industry stock market indices. The authors first computed monthly value-weighted market returns for each industry using data from the Center for Research in Security Prices, then specified a Fama and French three-factor model to forecast monthly industry returns recursively from 1950 to 2005, with a GARCH(1,1) process modeling the variance of the error term. For each estimated monthly return they obtained the conditional variance from the GARCH model, annualized the variance by averaging the conditional variance over the past 12 months for an investment occurring in the current year, and took the log of the average variance. Industries were recorded at the three-digit SIC level.
time_window: past 12 months, lagged relative to the focal investment

description: Dichotomous dependent variable indicating whether an investing firm used CVC or acquisition as the investment mode. The variable CVC takes the value one if an investment is structured as a CVC investment, and zero if structured as an acquisition.

Asset intangibility measure of irreversibility, calculated as the median value of the ratio of intangible assets to total assets for all firms in the industry in the previous year. Intangible assets are used because they are likely to suffer from market failure, making their trading much more difficult compared to tangible and physical assets.

The median market-to-book ratio of the investee's industry at the three-digit SIC level in the previous year, used as a proxy because industries in which firms have a higher average market-to-book ratio should present a higher level of growth opportunities in general.

One minus the industry concentration ratio. The concentration ratio was calculated as the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index of the investee's industry at the three-digit SIC level, the sum of the squares of the market shares of all of the companies in the industry in the previous year. One was subtracted from the HHI so that the higher the value of the measure, the higher the level of competition in the industry.

A dummy variable equal to 1 if the business markets industrial/commercial capital goods, components for incorporation into finished products, or consumer durables, and equal to 0 otherwise. The authors state the measure distinguishes products likely to entail high versus low information search and has been used in previous PIMS studies. About 53% of businesses in the sample market goods that entail high information search.

Built from key informants' responses to the question: 'Have there been major technological changes in the products offered by the business or its major competitors, or in methods of production, during the last 8 years?' The Yes/No responses were coded as a dummy variable with a '1' indicating an exchange condition of a major technological impact and '0' otherwise. The authors call the measure broad but the most pragmatic feasible, and conservative because respondents were asked to answer 'No' if in doubt. About 28% of businesses faced this exchange condition.

Constructed by multiplying the percentage of a business's output sold to OEMs with a measure of the importance of the product to customers. The former was obtained via a corresponding direct question; the latter is based on the proportion of annual purchases accounted for by the types of products sold by the business. The larger the value of the variable, the more critical are the business's products to customers.

The dollar outlay of customers is measured as the average dollar amount of transactions over a 10-year period, constructed by multiplying the average transaction amount with the average number of purchase orders over 10 years and expressing the result in billions of dollars. The authors do not give the numeric values in prose.

Measured by a dummy variable which equals '1' if the business's products are designed or produced to order for individual customers, and '0' otherwise. The authors note this measure has been employed in previous studies to indicate whether a business offers customized products. About 22% of the businesses entail exchange conditions with customized products.

Key informants were asked whether auxiliary services such as customer education, installation, repair, and other product-related services were of great importance, of some importance, or of little or no importance. The responses were captured via a three-point scale and serve as a measure of exchange conditions with varying importance of auxiliary services.

variable_name: Percentage of sales made directly to end-users
description: A continuous measure of the percentage of sales that are made directly to end-users, constituting the utilization of direct channels. Sales to channel intermediaries such as wholesalers, distributors, and retailers represent the use of indirect distribution channels. A value of 100% signifies that the firm relies solely on direct channels, while 0% signifies the use of indirect distribution channels only. Among the 2569 businesses, about 32% utilize direct channels only, about 23% utilize indirect channels only, and about 45% use a combination of the two.

variable_name: Family firm pairing indicators (NFF Acquirer-NFF Divester; NFF Acquirer-FF Divester; FF Acquirer-NFF Divester; FF Acquirer-FF Divester)
description: Four indicator variables represent whether the acquiring and divesting firms in a given transaction are family or non-family firms. NFF Acquirer-NFF Divester takes the value one when both the acquiring and divesting firms are non-family firms, NFF Acquirer-FF Divester when the acquirer is a non-family firm and the divester is a family firm, FF Acquirer-NFF Divester when the acquirer is a family firm and the divester is a non-family firm, and FF Acquirer-FF Divester when both firms are family firms; each is zero otherwise. To test Hypothesis 1, FF Acquirer-NFF Divester is the omitted category and the other three are entered; to test Hypothesis 2, NFF Acquirer-FF Divester is the omitted category and the other three are entered.
time_window: year in which each transaction took place

variable_name: Family CEO pairing indicators (NFC Acquirer-NFC Divester; NFC Acquirer-FC Divester; FC Acquirer-NFC Divester; FC Acquirer-FC Divester)
description: Four indicator variables represent whether the acquiring and divesting firms in a given transaction are managed by family or non-family CEOs. Non-family CEO (NFC) Acquirer-NFC Divester takes the value one when both firms are managed by non-family CEOs, NFC Acquirer-FC Divester when the acquirer has a non-family CEO and the divester a family CEO, Family CEO (FC) Acquirer-NFC Divester when the acquirer has a family CEO and the divester a non-family CEO, and FC Acquirer-FC Divester when both firms are managed by family CEOs; each is zero otherwise. FC Acquirer-NFC Divester is the omitted category for the acquirer regressions and NFC Acquirer-FC Divester for the divester regressions.
time_window: year in which each transaction took place

description: Cumulative abnormal returns to the acquiring firm, computed from the announcement dates identified by SDC Platinum. The acquiring firm's normal returns are predicted from its daily stock returns and the stock market's returns within a 250-day estimation window of [-800, -551] before the announcement date, and abnormal returns are then computed within a 2-day event window [-1, 0] surrounding the announcement date; the CAR is the sum of these abnormal returns over that event window. Acquirer CAR was available for the 2,178 transactions in which the acquiring firms were publicly traded.
time_window: event window [-1, 0] around the announcement date; estimation window [-800, -551]

description: Cumulative abnormal returns to the divesting firm, computed from the announcement dates identified by SDC Platinum. The divesting firm's normal returns are predicted from its daily stock returns and the stock market's returns within a 250-day estimation window of [-800, -551] before the announcement date, and abnormal returns are then computed within a 2-day event window [-1, 0] surrounding the announcement date; the CAR is the sum of these abnormal returns over that event window. Divester CAR was available for all 6,504 transactions in the sample.
time_window: event window [-1, 0] around the announcement date; estimation window [-800, -551]

description: We use the pre-spin-out earnings of the founder of the spin-out team as a reflective measure of the individual's performance or underlying attributes. We use the earnings of the individual that had the highest earnings while employed at the source firm among all individuals in the departing team. For parent firms that experienced more than one spin-out event in a year, we compute an average of the earnings of the founders across these events.

We use the pre-spin-out earnings of the founder of the spin-out team as a reflective measure of the individual's performance or underlying attributes. We use the earnings of the individual that had the highest earnings while employed at the source firm among all individuals in the departing team.

This measure is a count of all individuals who moved from the parent firm to the focal spin-out in a year. For parent firms that experience multiple spin-out events in a particular year, we average the team size across the different spinouts for that year.
This measure is a count of all individuals who moved from the parent firm to the focal spin-out in a year.

The team's organizational experience is measured by the average number of years that the departing team members were employed at the parent firm. For parent firms experiencing multiple spin-outs in any one year, we use the average across all spin-out events for that year.
time_window: employment at the parent firm prior to the spin-out event

description: The team's organizational experience is measured by the average number of years that the departing team members were employed at the parent firm.
time_window: employment at the parent firm prior to the spin-out event

description: We use the firm's revenue per employee to measure parent firm performance in the year following the spin-out event. The firm's revenue is obtained by aggregating the taxable income paid to everyone on the firm's payroll (all earnings of partners, associates, paralegal, and administrative staff). The measure is net of noncompensation costs and set-asides for future years, and allows comparison of the productivity of firms of different sizes. To avoid estimating a spurious relationship caused due to denominator changes, we include replacement hires in our measure.

We construct a dummy for 'failure' that takes the value of '1' if the spin-out exits in the next year. Survival is used because income-based measures may not reflect true performance and exhibit high variance and noise, and because analysis of spinouts using revenue per worker would condition the estimation on better-surviving firms.

Dependent variable taking the value of 1 if at least one career move was observed from contrada i (sender) to contrada j (receiver) in year t, and 0 otherwise. The unit of analysis is the neighborhood-dyad year. For the stochastic actor-oriented models, career moves were aggregated into five 50-year time windows, normalized into z scores between -1 and 1 and dichotomized using 0 as threshold, yielding five 17 x 17 mobility networks.

Key independent variable set to 1 if a formally declared rivalry between contrada i and contrada j existed in each period t, and 0 otherwise. Rivalries are formally voted by the contrada assembly and can be reciprocated or terminated.

Variable identifying configurations in which one contrada is a rival of the other's allies, obtained in a given period t by multiplying the alliance network by the rivalry network. All matrices were directed and nonsymmetrical.

Variable identifying configurations in which one contrada is an ally of the other's rivals, obtained in a given period t by multiplying the rivalry network by the alliance network. All matrices were directed and nonsymmetrical.

Counts the number of alternative historical horse races each year that employ jockeys from Siena, described as the first of two related ways to capture the development of the jockeys' labor market over time. Based on interviews, four races - in Asti, Ferrara, Fucecchio and Legnano - were identified as opening their doors to jockeys in Siena, granting them legitimacy and further remuneration opportunities.

Count of active regulatory constraints on jockeys' activity, described as the second way to capture the development of the jockeys' labor market. Based on expert evaluation, four regulatory dimensions of jockeys' activity were identified. The rulebook of the Palio originated in 1721 and was revised repeatedly.

Indicator of assignment to pitch training. Participants agreed to be randomly assigned to five different training treatments delivered by video, four of which provided detailed training on how to pitch to investors (pitch training) and one of which provided training on venture finance without any information on pitching (the null). The authors collapsed the treatments into two categories: pitch training and null. Random assignment to treatment was stratified by gender and prior experience pitching.

Six undergraduate students, who did not know the participants' identity, their treatment, or whether a draft was initial or final, coded the presence or absence of six dimensions of content, six dimensions of style, and the three basic elements common to all treatments in both the initial (pretraining) and final (posttraining) drafts. The measure is the average number of elements present across all coders for each participant's first and final draft. The intraclass correlation of the average number of elements measured by the six coders was 0.82.
scale: count of elements present, out of 15
time_window: first (pretraining) and final (posttraining) drafts of the same pitch

description: After the pitch and question period, judges scored the pitch using seven-point Likert-scale questions from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree.' Four items were used: whether the judge would pursue a follow-up meeting to learn more about the venture, would be interested in seeing the business plan, would recommend the opportunity to a co-investor, and would initiate due diligence. Responses were aggregated into a score that ranges from 4 to 28.

Three undergraduate students who had taken and received a grade of 'A' in an upper-level entrepreneurial finance class, and who had not coded the first and final drafts for presence of the elements, each read each of the first-draft pitches and coded them for the quality of the business described using a 10-point Likert scale. The quality measure used in the analysis was the sum of the three evaluators' quality scores, and the intraclass correlation of the average evaluations of the three coders was 0.73.
scale: 10-point Likert scale per evaluator; sum of three evaluators in the analysis

description: The authors identified the number of early-stage deals in which each judge had been involved, as measured by CrunchBase, and created a dummy variable equal to one for those at or above the median.

variable_name: venture capitalist, business angel, or startup mentor
description: A dummy variable equal to one for judges who indicate being a venture capitalist, business angel, or startup mentor as part of their professional identity, as indicated by their LinkedIn profile.

Annual federal spending on renewable energy research and development programs in a state, taken from the U.S. Census Bureau's Consolidated Federal Funds Report. The measure includes annual spending in thousands of dollars on renewable energy research and development, regional biomass energy programs, and two programs that have been eliminated (solar energy partnership support and barrier elimination) but had some spending during 1983-present. The final measure is based on thousands of dollars distributed annually to a particular state and was subjected to a log transformation as a result of a pronounced positive skew in its distribution.

Number of registered 'alliances and advocacy' nonprofit organizations within the 'environmental and conservation' group for a given state and year, constructed from NCCS data. The NCCS classification is defined as including organizations whose activities focus on influencing public policy within the Environment major group area, from influencing public opinion to lobbying national and state legislatures. This classification is distinct and does not overlap with the 'Renewable Energy and Energy Conservation' category.

A count of the number of TSMOs registered in a state for a given year, created by coding the National Center for Charitable Statistics category 'Renewable Energy and Energy Conservation'. To ensure that this category was made up of clean energy TSMOs, the authors investigated the goals, strategies, knowledge, capabilities, scope, and funding of the Colorado, Minnesota, and Oregon organizations in the category through Internet searches, analysis of organizations' websites, and primary interviews in Colorado.

The growth of the wind energy industry in a state, measured through the total number of megawatts of wind energy installed capacity in that state for a given year. Data from the National Renewable Energy Laboratories were used to construct this measure.

An annual count of articles on wind energy found in the top circulated newspaper in each state for all 48 states, expressed as a proportion of the average circulation of the newspaper. Articles were identified using keywords selected based on a detailed assessment by five renewable energy experts, including terms such as 'wind power,' 'wind energy,' 'wind turbine,' and 'wind farm,' and were verified through manual inspection of abstracts to confirm that they covered subjects related to wind power. Because of limited accessibility of local newspaper content data, the measure is available only up to the year 2007.

The sum of the cumulative state-level incentives that increase the attractiveness of wind power markets. These include financial rewards such as sales, income, and property tax credits toward the purchase and/or use of wind energy technology, the availability of state programs offering low-interest loans for wind energy investments, and government incentives in the form of corporate tax exemptions and grants designed as short-term measures to support industries in their early stages. Data from the Database of State Incentives for Renewables and Efficiency (DSIRE) were collected to construct this measure, and the final variable required a log transformation.
time_window: annual, cumulative, measured at time t

description: Measured along seven demographic characteristics: age, gender, ethnicity, education level, Ivy League background, functional area of expertise, and industry background. Diversity along each dimension except age was measured with Blau's index (1-Σ(Pi)2), where Pi is the proportion of directors in the ith category; age diversity was measured with the standardized coefficient of variation in age. The measure is the focal board's average diversity along a dimension during the new CEO's tenure (up to three years since appointment) minus the average diversity of the other boards on which the CEO served in the previous five years, with the standardized scores of the seven dimensions summed into an index. When a new outside CEO had no prior board experience, the focal board's diversity level after standardization was used.
time_window: focal board: CEO tenure up to three years; other boards: five years prior to succession

description: Coded as 1 if the new outside CEO was replaced within the first three years and 0 otherwise.
A binary variable coded as 1 when one or more outside directors left the board during the new CEO's tenure (up to three years since the initial appointment) and 0 otherwise.
time_window: up to three years since the CEO's initial appointment

description: The firm's annual ROA minus the average ROA of the firm's primary industry (based on three-digit SIC), averaged over the new CEO's tenure, up to three years since the initial appointment.
time_window: up to three years since the CEO's initial appointment

description: Target CSR was measured on the basis of the five dimensions of KLD data: environment, employee, community, diversity, and product. Each dimension consisted of two components, strengths and concerns, and each item was a binary indicator showing whether a firm fulfilled a certain criterion. Because the KLD dimensions are not comparable with each other, the strength and the concern scores in each dimension were standardized for each target firm by subtracting the sample mean and dividing by the sample standard deviation. Target CSR is the sum of the standardized strength scores minus the sum of the standardized concern scores.
time_window: one year prior to the acquisition (data period 1999-2011)

variable_name: Acquirer announcement return (acquirer cumulative abnormal return, CAR)
description: Three-day cumulative abnormal return around the deal announcement date with the event window [-1, 1]. The abnormal return on day t is the actual daily stock return minus the expected daily stock return, where the expected return is based on the daily value-weighted stock market return estimated over the window [-210, -11], requiring at least 100 days of available stock returns. Acquirer CAR is the sum of the abnormal returns in the three days and was multiplied by 100 for better coefficient manifestation. CAR was calculated with Eventus using the 'autodate-yes' option.
time_window: three-day event window [-1, +1] around the announcement; estimation window [-210, -11]

description: Measured as the degree to which the stakeholder portfolios of the acquirer and target were similar, operationalized as the Mahalanobis distance (MD) between the merging firms' stakeholder portfolio, multiplied by -1. The stakeholder portfolio of a firm is a column vector comprising 10 elements that combine the five dimensions of KLD data (environment, employee, community, diversity, product) and the two indexes (strength and concern). The distance is computed with the inverse of the pooled covariance matrix.
time_window: one year prior to the acquisition (moderators lagged by one year)

description: A composite measure computed as the average of the standardized scores of three indicators: similarity in product market, similarity in human capital, and similarity in technology resource, with a higher score representing greater business similarity between merging firms. Similarity in product market was based on the four-digit SIC code industries in which the merging firms participate and was measured as the reverse value of the sum of the numbers of the acquirer's and the target's four-digit SIC industries minus the number of overlapped four-digit SIC industries. Similarity in human capital is the reverse value of the Mahalanobis distance between the merging firms' occupation portfolios, where the occupation scalar is the proportion of firm employees in an occupation computed from industry segments. Similarity in technology resource is the reverse value of the Mahalanobis distance comparing the merging firms' patent-class portfolios from the United States Patent Classification system.
time_window: one year prior to the acquisition (moderators lagged by one year)

description: Cumulative abnormal return of each firm covered in each CSI disclosure, retrieved with the event study method to measure market reactions. An estimation period of 255 days ([-284, -30]) before the focal event date, defined as the date of the CSI news disclosure, is used, and CARs are calculated over a two-day event window (-1, 0). CAR is expressed as a percentage. The text does not state the source of the stock return data.

CSI disclosure type equals 1 when the media report disclosing a focal firm's CSI activities also covers other firms' CSI activities (i.e., multi-violator CSI disclosure) and 0 otherwise (i.e., single-violator CSI disclosure). The variable was hand-coded from the source news articles corresponding to each CSI disclosure record in the dataset.

Calculated as the total number of media CSI disclosures of a firm from year t - 3 to t - 1. Each past CSI disclosure of a firm is weighted by the reach of the news outlet, with numeric values set as {High, Medium, Low} = {1, 1/2, 1/3}, and by the novelty of that CSI disclosure, with {Novel, Not Novel} = {1, 1/2}. This weight measure accounts for the possibility that investors' attention to CSI disclosures differs depending on the reach of the news outlet and the novelty of the news information.

Captured by the diversity of the domains/categories (i.e., environmental, social, or governance) that a firm's past CSI behaviors fall into, calculated with an entropy measure over a 3-year period (t - 3 to t - 1). The printed entropy formula is the sum over the firm's n (up to three) different types of CSI disclosures of p_k ln(1/p_k), where p_k is the percentage of CSI disclosures of this firm in each category, and the formula as printed is partially garbled. A larger value indicates that a firm has acted irresponsibly in multiple contexts. Each news disclosure is weighted by source reach and novelty, similar to the calculation of past CSI frequency.

Dummy variable coded as 1 (or full acquisition) when a firm acquired a 95-100% equity stake in a target, and 0 otherwise. The acquirer's equity ownership level was obtained from the SDC database. This operationalization reflects the modal distribution of the data, in which 77.7% of the acquisitions are full acquisitions.

Norway's SWF investments in a host country were calculated as the cumulative equity investments up to the observation year, obtained from the electronic archival records of the SWF's global equity holdings. To correct for the skewed distribution, the authors computed the natural log of the SWF investment plus 1, so that countries with no SWF investment took a value of 0.
time_window: cumulative up to the observation year

description: A dummy variable that took a value of 1 if the acquirer was headquartered in Norway, and 0 if its headquarters was in Sweden.

The number of IGOs in which the home and host countries in the cross-border acquisition dyad jointly participated in the observation year, retrieved from Pevehouse et al. (2004). Only IGOs whose core mission overlapped with the ESG mandate of the Norwegian SWF were counted: all 495 IGOs were manually coded and 79 IGOs met the criteria. To address the skew toward high IGO membership, the authors calculated the natural log of the count of IGOs plus 1 so that country pairs with no joint membership took a value of 0.

The share of self-citations made, calculated by counting all citations made in a firm's new patents in a certain year that cited the firm's own previous patents, then dividing this number by the total number of citations made by all the firm's new patents in that year. It is further adjusted by a weight, the extent to which the self-cited patents are subsequently cited by the focal firm, which is the fraction of the total forward citations of these self-cited patents that are generated by the focal firm versus by other firms. The authors infer that the higher the percentage of internal knowledge accumulation as represented by self-patent citations, the more likely that the firm's knowledge assets are firm specific.
Restricted stock was defined as the value of restricted stock granted to the CEO during the year divided by the total annual compensation.

A dummy variable coded as 1 if there was a forced turnover in a firm's CEO in a particular year according to the classification procedure described, and 0 otherwise. A turnover event was identified if there was a change in a firm's CEO in a particular year based on Execucomp, and the Factiva news database was searched for the announcement date and whether the turnover was forced or voluntary.
The number of different businesses in which the firm operates. To test the interaction effect between firm-specific knowledge and diversification, this variable was mean-centered.

One minus the Herfindahl index, where the index is calculated as the sum of squares of segment sales divided by the square of firm sales, so a greater score suggests a higher level of diversification. To test the interaction effect between firm-specific knowledge and diversification, this variable was mean-centered.

Our primary measure is prior year industry-adjusted stock return, computed as the firm's stock return minus the median industry stock return. The median industry return is calculated using all CRSP firms in the focal firm's two-digit Standard Industrial Classification industry (excluding the focal firm).
Return on asset (ROA) similarly adjusted by industry, included because it is a very commonly used accounting-based measure of firm financial performance.

Participants were randomly assigned to either a CSR, CSI, or control condition in a one-factor design. In the CSR and CSI conditions they read about 'Company X,' a fictitious company that engaged in either fair or unfair manufacturing processes overseas, using a vignette established in prior literature. The control condition contained no information on CSR.

Immediately following the CSR manipulation, participants rated whether they believed Company X to possess four warmth attributes: tolerant, warm, good natured, and sincere. These items were randomly embedded in other, unrelated attribute items. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a two-factor solution, with the four warmth items loading onto Factor 1 with loadings ranging from .80 to .85 and a Cronbach's alpha of .93.

Participants rated whether they believed Company X to be competent, confident, independent, competitive, and intelligent, using the same randomly embedded attribute items as the warmth measure. The five competence items loaded onto Factor 2 with loadings ranging from .77 to .84, and the Cronbach's alpha was .86.

After rating the firm on warmth and competence, participants rated their perceptions of the firm's reputation on four items: favorable, good, pleasant, positive. The reliability of the reputation scale, measured using Cronbach's alpha, was .97.

Participants indicated their purchase intentions by answering: 'If the products from Company X were available for purchase, what is your likelihood of purchasing a product from Company X?' The response scale ran from 1 (not at all likely) to 7 (very likely).

Participants were randomly assigned to a CSR state (CSR, CSI, or control) and read the same vignettes as in Study 1, modified to manipulate warmth and competence via country of origin. A pure control condition without country-of-origin manipulation was also run but was not included in the final analyses.

Warmth of the firm's country of origin was manipulated between subjects at two levels (high, low) by changing the name of the organization in the vignette to include the country of origin. Based on previous research, the in-group (the United States) represented the high-warmth, high-competence country, Portugal the high-warmth, low-competence country, Germany the low-warmth, high-competence country, and Pakistan the low-warmth, low-competence country.

Competence of the firm's country of origin was manipulated between subjects at two levels (high, low) through the country name included in the organization's name in the vignette. Germany and the United States represented high-competence countries and Portugal and Pakistan low-competence countries, following prior mappings of countries on the warmth - competence dimensions.

After rating the firm on the dimensions of warmth and competence, participants answered the same questions constituting the reputation dependent variable as in Study 1, that is, ratings of the firm's reputation.
Participants answered the same purchase-intention question as in Study 1, stating their likelihood of purchasing a product from the firm.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three experimental conditions (CSR, CSI, control) and received background information about each of the four pen manufacturers. Embedded within neutral performance information was information on environmental impact and labor practices: in the CSR condition the manufacturers promoted strong environmental protection and repair as well as employee standards, in the CSI condition they were poor in environmental standards and labor practices, and in the control condition neutral information was provided.

Country of origin was manipulated within subjects by labeling the pens as 'Made in Sweden,' 'Made in Germany,' 'Made in Portugal,' and 'Made in Pakistan' in a 1-millimeter font, with each participant receiving and rating each of these four pens. Sweden represents the high-warmth, high-competence country, Germany the low-warmth, high-competence country, Portugal the high-warmth, low-competence country, and Pakistan the low-warmth, low-competence country.

The within-subjects country-of-origin manipulation also varied the competence stereotype of the pens' origin. Sweden and Germany were used as high-competence countries and Portugal and Pakistan as low-competence countries, following prior classifications of countries on the warmth and competence dimensions.

Participants were told that the pens were prototypes and that the organizations would like feedback on the pen designs, and they were encouraged to try out each pen. They were given a blank essay box to provide feedback to the organization on their pen design, and the number of words written was measured as a measure of helping (adapted from Porath & Erez, 2007). Each participant completed this measure for each of the four country-of-origin pens.

As part of the feedback task, participants rated the subjective quality of each pen with the items 'The pen is of high quality' and 'The pen is desirable'. The reliability of the two-item scale ranged from .72 to .76 across the pens, and each participant rated each of the four country-of-origin pens.

In a purchasing task using the Becker-DeGroot-Marschak method, participants were given an additional dollar and told they could use this money to purchase the pens and keep whatever money they did not use. Participants stated a purchase price for each of the four pens on a sliding scale between $0.01 and $1.00; the mean price was $0.33.

variable_name: Reputation, purchase intentions, subjective quality, purchase price, helping
description: Organizational outcomes are the participant responses after the CSR, CSI or control manipulation: firm reputation and purchase intentions (Studies 1 and 2), and in Study 3 subjective quality, purchase price in a Becker-DeGroot-Marschak task, and number of words written as helping. Penalties and rewards are the differences between the CSI or CSR conditions and control.
Percentage of foreign sales to total sales, a measure of foreign market dependence. The variable was reported by Senior Vice Presidents-International responding to a questionnaire.
Percentage of foreign assets to total assets, a measure of foreign production dependence. The variable was reported by Senior Vice Presidents-International responding to a questionnaire.

Mean number of years of international experience of the top management team. The international experience of each executive was measured as number of years spent abroad on assignment and/or higher education, or spent in the international division, from Dun and Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Managements (1986).
Proportion of top managers who had international experience. Based on the international experience data from Dun and Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Managements (1986).

Homogeneity of international experience among top management team members, based on the international experience data from Dun and Bradstreet's Reference Book of Corporate Managements (1986). The variable is a homogeneity measure, so it is reverse coded relative to the heterogeneity construct as named.

Both buyers and sellers were asked to assess the success of the acquisition. Success was assessed on five scaled questions relating to the economic performance post-acquisition and to the success or failure of implementing the buyer's strategy. In the sample of 40 cases 55 per cent were very successful or successful and 45 per cent were either disappointing or very unsuccessful as assessed several years later by the people involved. On the criteria used for assessing success the buyers and sellers had to agree.
time_window: several years after closure, on average 3.6 years after completion

description: Acquisitions were classified using Ansoff's classification into horizontal diversification (staying within the same business but acquiring markets), concentric marketing (same markets, different technology), concentric technology (same technology, different markets) or conglomerate diversification. In the British sample 20 years after Kitching only 25 per cent were diversifying using the concentric marketing or concentric technology strategies, and the 40 cases produced only three cases of diversification through conglomeration.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

variable_name: size mismatch, seller's turnover as a percentage of the buyer's
description: The relative size of buyer and seller was measured as the seller's turnover relative to that of the buyer, and a size mismatch was recorded when the turnover of the seller was less than 2 per cent of that of the buyer. In the British sample the mismatch failure rate at 2 per cent of buyer turnover was 67 per cent.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: Whether the organizational format — either the reporting relationships or the extent of autonomy allowed — was changed by the buyer after the acquisition was legally completed. In 22 per cent of the cases of failure, changes to the organizational form were an issue; of these nine cases, seven seller respondents reported that changes to the format were a major problem, while only one-third of the buyer respondents knew that structural changes were an issue in these cases.
time_window: after legal completion of the acquisition

description: Whether the acquisition was buyer-initiated or seller-initiated. In the sample 70 per cent of the bids were buyer-initiated and 30 per cent were seller-initiated, and the behavioural process from targeting onwards was influenced by who initiated the deal.
time_window: at the time of the bid

description: Buyer and seller respondents were asked to rank, on a five-point scale, the seller's corporate performance before the bid on profitability and three capabilities: general management, marketing management and technical advantage. There was a high level of correlation between the ranking of the buyer and seller respondents (0.83); of the 40 cases 18 per cent were ranked unhealthy, 42 per cent fairly healthy and 40 per cent healthy.

variable_name: clear growth strategy versus opportunistic buying
description: Whether the buyer's strategy was a clear strategy of growth through acquisition rather than unclear, opportunistic buying. Of the 40 cases only 8 per cent were opportunistic, compared with up to 60 per cent of the American acquisitions in the 1960s acquisition boom.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: The behaviours of the negotiators and implementers across the four phases of the acquisition process: targeting the seller, negotiating, post-acquisition implementation and converting the seller's staff to the buyer's way. Targeting variables include who initiated the deal, the time frame and secrecy; the tone of negotiations may be friendly, contested or hostile; implementation ranges from a 'hands-on' to a 'hands-off' strategy.
time_window: from targeting the seller to post-acquisition implementation

description: The contextual variables of the paradigm: clear strategy, industry (staying within the industry), ownership of the seller, health of the seller, relative size, the acquisition experience of the buyer and access to audit information. Of these contextual variables, success in the British cases correlates positively with clear strategy, horizontal diversification, a healthy seller and not massively different size of buyer and seller.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: The change in shareholder value is the unexpected percentage change in the stock price surrounding the event, i.e., the abnormal return, which is the error term of a market model whose coefficients are estimated by ordinary least squares. The benchmark market index is an equally weighted portfolio of all Canadian firms with non-missing returns in Datastream, used because the SEC rule affects all U.S. firms. The coefficients are estimated over the period beginning 130 days prior to the event and ending 10 days before the event date, and the event window is restricted to the single day of the announcement. The average of all firm abnormal returns in the sample represents the market reaction.
time_window: One-day event window (25 August 2010); estimation window from 130 days before to 10 days before the event

description: A count variable of the total number of owners holding at least three percent of the firm's outstanding stock at the end of 2009 (the previous calendar year). It represents the potential number of discrete share owners who would receive the benefit of proxy access for the purpose of director nomination, and is proxied using data on institutional investor ownership.
A dummy variable identifying a staggered or classified board, which limits the number of directors up for election in any given year.
Board independence is measured as the ratio of outside directors appointed before the CEO assumed the position to the total number of directors.
Measured as the percentage of the firm's outstanding stock owned by the CEO at the end of the firm's 2009 fiscal year (last year available).

Measured based on firm characteristics using the firm's capital intensity as a proxy, calculated as the ratio of net property, plant, and equipment to the total number of employees at the end of the previous year; because it measures the lack of discretion it is multiplied by -1 to ease interpretation. In the absence of a prespecified theoretical threshold, a spline function with the knot set at the seventy-fifth percentile of the sample creates two variables from the single continuous variable: low discretion (below the knot) and high discretion (above the knot).
Following Surroca, Tribó, and Waddock (2010), resource intangibility is measured as the ratio of research and development expenses to the total number of employees.

Abnormal bond returns calculated using the returns to similarly rated bonds as the benchmark, adjusted for whether the firm has a rating of A or above or a BBB and below rating. The returns were further adjusted based on comparable bonds in the Canadian market, and the proper method for calculating bond abnormal returns is not a regression-based technique, so the Patell and Boehmer et al. tests are not available.

Greater shareholder influence over director nomination is the SEC's adoption of the proxy access rule on 25 August 2010, treated as a natural experiment that applies to all sample firms. The market reaction is measured in a one-day event window around the announcement.

Indicator variables code each firm's participation/non-participation in five microcomputer industry value chain activities (1 = activity pursued in-house). To obtain a vertical integration score at the firm level, the five scores were summed into an aggregate measure; because all sample firms manufacture microcomputers in-house, the minimum score is 1 and the maximum score is 5 (full vertical integration). Coded from the Computer Select database; a second researcher independently coded business press coverage from Lexis/Nexis and the intersource reliability was r = 0.68 (p < 0.001).

Count of the strategic alliances in which a firm engaged in year t whose content mapped onto a value chain activity that the firm pursued in-house. Alliance data were obtained from the SDC Platinum strategic alliance database, while a second researcher independently coded press coverage of the firms' alliance activity from Lexis/Nexis; the intersource reliability was r = 0.86 (p < 0.001). The 1,205 alliances in the sample include 852 taper alliances (71%).
time_window: each year t during the study period

description: Count of the strategic alliances in which a firm engaged in year t whose content did not map onto a value chain activity that the firm pursued in-house, capturing quasi integration. Alliance data were obtained from SDC Platinum and independently coded from Lexis/Nexis press coverage (intersource reliability r = 0.86, p < 0.001). The 1,205 alliances in the sample include 353 quasi alliances (29%); approximately 36 percent of the sample firms engaged in quasi integration and about 22 percent simultaneously pursued both taper and quasi integration.
time_window: each year t during the study period

description: Number of microcomputer products that a firm offered in each year between 1994 and 1997. The measure includes all microcomputer products that the firms sold during each year, rather than limiting it to the products that were newly introduced and reviewed in computer publications. During the study period, all sample firms combined had a total of 13,125 products in their portfolios, an average of 27 products per year for each firm.

Firm-level aggregation of individual new product evaluations taken from microcomputer product reviews in the top-ten computer industry publications contained in the Computer Select publications database; reviews had to include at least four products and to provide a competitive evaluation. Each reviewed product was coded clear winner = 4, runner-up = 3, neutral = 2, loser = 1, and an adjusted review score corrected for the selectivity of each review was computed as ARS = RS × (1 - p), where RS is the assigned review score and p equals the number of winning products divided by the total number of products in the review, so that scores vary between zero and four. The annual adjusted review scores were averaged for each firm, with the denominator k equal to the number of products reviewed per firm in each year t. Three measures were developed: a composite score for the full sample, a desktop-only score, and a laptop-only score; the 148 server/workstation and handheld evaluations were dropped, leaving 3,411 product evaluations.

Total annual revenues, with all revenue data converted into U.S. dollars corresponding to the historic dollar value and a logarithmic transformation applied because of skewness in the revenue data. Revenues were used as the proxy for overall firm performance because products that succeed in the marketplace capture higher revenues, and because revenue data were more readily available than net income or return on assets for a sample that was mostly privately held. Firm revenues lagged by one time period are included in the regression model as a control.

A nine-item scale to measure a firm's level of corporate entrepreneurship intensity (alpha = 0.87). The scale was developed and validated by Covin and Slevin (1986) based on previous scale development work by Khandwalla (1977) and Miller and Friesen (1982) and contains items that measure a firm's tendency toward innovation, risk-taking, and proactiveness. Items 1a, 2a, and 2b measure innovation; items 1b, 1c, and 4a measure risk-taking; items 3a, 3b, and 3c measure proactiveness. The mean score, calculated as the average of the nine items, assesses a firm's position on a conservative-entrepreneurial continuum, the higher the score the more the firm demonstrates an entrepreneurial orientation. A separate one-item, 7-point Likert scale assessing the respondent's position on the conservative-entrepreneurial continuum served as a second measure of the construct (r = 0.62).
scale: 7-point Likert items; mean of nine items

description: A 12-item scale developed specifically for this study to measure scanning intensity (alpha = 0.83), made up of two six-item subdimensions. The first set of six items was a modified version of Miller and Friesen's (1982) Effort Dedicated Towards Scanning scale, rating the extent to which listed scanning devices are used to gather information about the business environment; the second set of six items measured scanning comprehensiveness by asking how thoroughly the firm scans elements of its task and societal environments. The mean score, averaged across the 12 items, assesses a firm's degree of scanning intensity.

A nine-item scale developed for this study to measure planning flexibility (alpha = 0.80). The scale asked the respondents to assess how difficult it is for their firms to change their strategic plans to adjust for each of nine theoretically relevant environmental contingencies. The mean score on the scale, averaged across the nine items, assesses a firm's level of planning flexibility.
scale: 7-point scale anchored 1 = very difficult to 7 = not at all difficult; mean of nine items

description: A four-item multipart scale developed specifically for this study to measure planning horizon (alpha = 0.90). The scale asked the respondent to assess the degree of emphasis his or her firm places on business strategies or firm investments for each of four predetermined time periods (less than 1 year; 1-3 years; 3-5 years; and more than 5 years) and to make this assessment for each of four hierarchical levels (board of directors, top management, middle management, and lower-level management). Only a portion of the data captured by this scale was of interest: the amount of emphasis placed on planning horizons of more than 5 years, averaged across the four hierarchical levels.
scale: 7-point scale anchored very little emphasis to considerable emphasis
time_window: emphasis on horizons of more than 5 years

description: A five-item multipart Likert scale developed specifically for this study to measure locus of planning (alpha = 0.89). The scale measures the extent to which employees from different hierarchical levels in a firm are involved in their firm's strategic planning process. The scale items represent the basic steps in the strategic management process: goal formation, environmental scanning, strategy formulation, strategy implementation, and evaluation and control. Locus of planning was determined by averaging the scores for middle management, lower-level management, and rank-and-file employees across the five steps in the strategic management process.
scale: 7-point Likert items; mean across three employee levels and five planning steps

description: A three-item scale modified from a scale used by Johnson, Hoskisson, and Hitt (1993) to measure strategic controls (alpha = 0.64). The scale asks how important each of the listed factors is in making sure that the firm's employees and business strategies meet predetermined objectives. The mean score, calculated as the average of the three items, assesses a firm's emphasis on strategic controls.
scale: 7-point scale anchored unimportant to important; mean of three items

description: A three-item scale modified from a scale used by Hitt et al. (1996) to measure financial controls (alpha = 0.77). The scale asks how important each of the listed factors is in evaluating the performance of business unit or functional area personnel. The mean score, calculated as the average of the three items, assesses a firm's emphasis on the respective type of control.
scale: 7-point scale anchored unimportant to important; mean of three items

description: Participants were randomly assigned to a high or low evaluation criteria consensus condition in a one-factor two-level between-subject design. In the high-consensus condition they read that academic and industry experts have agreed on the appropriate metrics and that there is great consensus about what metrics should be used for evaluating image classification algorithms; in the low-consensus condition they read that the experts do not agree. Perceived consensus was checked with three items such as 'There is consensus about the proper metrics to evaluate image classification algorithms' (alpha = 0.89).

The scenario and manipulation were the same as in Study 1: participants were randomly assigned to a high or low evaluation criteria consensus condition in a one-factor two-level between-subject design. Perceived consensus was checked with the same three items as in Study 1 (alpha = 0.96).

Operationalized as the overall similarity among criteria proposed for evaluating the same technology across different competitions, calculated following Hsu et al. (2012). The evaluation metrics proposed in all competitions were obtained and two computer scientists calibrated different expressions of the same metric; each competition was compared with all other competitions involving the same technology in each year to calculate pair-wise Jaccard similarity scores (number of shared metrics divided by number of shared and distinct metrics). Pair-wise scores were summed and divided by the number of pair-wise comparisons to get the average Jaccard score for each technology, and for each firm the scores for the technology(ies) it identifies with were summed and divided by the number of claimed technology(ies). The variable was lagged one year.

Same construction as in the U.S. sample: pair-wise Jaccard similarity scores across competitions involving the same technology in each year, averaged per technology and per firm across the technology(ies) the firm claims, matched to firms using keywords identified by JuziIT. The variable was lagged one year.

Three items adapted from Larsen and Newton-Smith (2001) measured intention to invest in the firm. Participants rated the extent to which they agreed or disagreed with statements such as 'I am willing to invest money in this firm' on a seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). Cronbach's alpha = 0.95.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: Participants were asked, 'How much of the Y2,000,000 will you invest in this firm?' The number reported was the measure for investment amount, out of a possible Y2,000,000.
The items were the same as in Study 1, with participants rating agreement with statements about their willingness to invest in the firm on a seven-point scale. Cronbach's alpha = 0.96.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: The question was the same as in Study 1, with available funds of $200,000.

Participants rated the extent to which they agreed or disagreed with three scale items, such as 'This firm has demonstrated extraordinary technology competence', on the seven-point scale used throughout the paper. Cronbach's alpha = 0.88.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: Participants indicated the extent to which they agreed or disagreed with three scale items, such as 'Other people in my field (e.g., my boss, colleagues, and other investors) will be willing to invest money in this firm', on the seven-point scale used throughout the paper. Cronbach's alpha = 0.95.
scale: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

description: Following previous studies (Pontikes 2012, Wry et al. 2014), investment in a firm was measured with a binary variable, investment, with 1 indicating that the firm received investment(s) in a particular year and 0 otherwise. The authors decided not to use investment amount because these figures tend to be inaccurate and exaggerated.
Same measure as in the U.S. sample: a binary variable, investment, with 1 indicating that the firm received investment(s) in a particular year and 0 otherwise, based on JuziIT records.

Unit head narcissism was measured using the self-report Narcissistic Personality Inventory 16-item scale (NPI-16). Unit heads were presented with 16 pairs of statements and chose which statement best fit them; narcissism-consistent responses were coded as 1 while narcissism-inconsistent statements were coded as 0.
