Two pairs of items with lower loadings on the first unrotated factor than those reported by Ames et al. (2006) were removed, leaving a 14-item scale (Cronbach's α = .7). The rating was provided by each unit head in the first survey wave.

A three-item scale adapted from Williams (2007) assessed the degree of knowledge transfer to the focal unit from other units; an example item is 'We learned a lot from other units.' Because narcissistic unit heads might underrate the degree of knowledge transfer, the deputies of the unit heads in each focal unit provided the rating. Responses used a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree); Cronbach's alpha was .90.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree)

description: A four-item scale adapted from Miller and Friesen (1982) captures the environmental heterogeneity and range of a unit's activities. A sample item is 'There are great differences among the products/services your unit offers, with regard to customers' requirements' (α = .7). Unit heads rated the complexity of their local market in the first survey wave.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: The five-item scale from Jansen, Van Den Bosch, and Volberda (2006) captures the rate of change and the instability of the external environment. An example item is 'In your unit's local market, changes are taking place continuously' (α = .90). Unit heads rated the dynamism of their local market in the first survey wave.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: A single item adapted from Hansen, Mors, and Løvås (2005) asked each unit head to respond to the question 'How would you describe the competitive nature between your unit and other units in the corporation?' The item used a seven-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (noncompetitive: never compete for status, performance evaluation, and resources in the corporation) to 7 (strongly competitive: frequently compete for status, performance evaluation, and resources in the corporation).
scale: seven-point Likert scale (1 = noncompetitive; 7 = strongly competitive)

variable_name: change in the number of physicians per capita in a county
description: Change in the number of physicians per capita in the hospital's county. County boundaries were used to define hospitals' environments, and changes in county environments were measured for each year of the study as the proportionate change from the level of the same variable in the previous year. Data were obtained from the California Health Facilities Commission's area resource file for 1980-86.

variable_name: change in the number of beds per capita in a county
description: Change in the number of beds per capita in the hospital's county, measured for each year of the study as the proportionate change from the previous year. County boundaries were used to define hospitals' environments. Data were obtained from the California Health Facilities Commission's area resource file for 1980-86.

variable_name: change in the number of health maintenance organizations per capita in a county
description: Change in the number of health maintenance organizations per capita in the hospital's county, measured for each year of the study as the proportionate change from the previous year. County boundaries were used to define hospitals' environments. Data were obtained from the California Health Facilities Commission's area resource file for 1980-86.

Board composition was contrasted at two points in time: two years prior to PPS implementation (1981) and one year following it (1984). The time lags and comparison method are similar to those Zajac and Shortell (1989) used to examine strategic change in hospitals in response to the implementation of PPS.

variable_name: annual change in the proportion of physicians on the board
description: The dependent variable was measured as the annual change in the proportional representation of each group on each board, calculated as the change in the proportion of board members that are physicians divided by the proportion of that same group one year earlier. On average, for all years of the study, hospital boards consisted of approximately 27 percent physicians.

variable_name: annual change in the proportion of business executives on the board
description: The dependent variable was measured as the annual change in the proportional representation of each group on each board, calculated as the change in the proportion of board members that are business executives divided by the proportion of that same group one year earlier. On average, for all years of the study, hospital boards consisted of approximately 25 percent business executives.

variable_name: annual change in the proportion of hospital executives on the board
description: The dependent variable was measured as the annual change in the proportional representation of each group on each board, calculated as the change in the proportion of board members that are hospital executives divided by the proportion of that same group one year earlier. On average, for all years of the study, hospital boards consisted of approximately 22 percent hospital executives.
time_window: annual change, 1980-1986; for the PPS test, proportions in 1981 and 1984

description: Profitability was measured as the annual net profits to a hospital divided by its revenues. This information was available for the years 1980 through 1986 from the California Health Facilities Commission data base. In the tests of interactions, performance was measured as an exponential function, e to the power x, where x equals performance.

The occupancy rate for each hospital in each year of the study. This information was available for six years only, 1980 through 1985, from the California Health Facilities Commission data base. In the tests of interactions, performance was measured as an exponential function, e to the power x, where x equals performance.

A five-item scale adapted from a measure developed and validated by Westphal (1999), asking a respondent director how often during the past year he or she provided input or advice on strategic issues at the request of the CEO, information about the strategic actions, policies, and/or practices of other firms, information or expertise on a strategy or policy issue at the CEO's request, answers to a question from the CEO about a specific strategy or policy issue, and the extent to which he or she acted as a kind of consultant or counsel to management. In a factor analysis with promax rotation the advice and information items loaded on a single factor (loadings greater than .5 on that factor and lower than .2 on the monitoring/control factor), with Cronbach's alpha of .87. Factor scores were estimated with the Bartlett method.
time_window: the past year (12 months) prior to the survey

description: A five-item scale that captured key elements of decision control, as conceived of by Fama and Jensen (1983), and adapted from a measure of board monitoring developed by Westphal and colleagues. Items asked how many times during the past year the director requested information from the CEO or another inside director for the purpose of evaluating management's progress in implementing the firm's corporate strategy, the extent to which he or she sought information for the purpose of evaluating the performance of top management, how many times he or she constructively criticized a strategic proposal put forth by management, how many times he or she suggested revisions to such a proposal, and the extent to which he or she exerted control over management decision making. The monitoring and control items loaded on a separate factor from the advice and information items (loadings greater than .5 on the first factor and lower than .2 on the second), with Cronbach's alpha of .91. Factor scores were estimated with the Bartlett method.
time_window: the past year prior to the survey

description: A nine-item scale about the respondent's behavior toward each of the other directors on a focal board, covering the three kinds of ingratiatory behavior identified in the literature on social influence: opinion conformity, other enhancement, and favor rendering. Items were adapted from measures of ingratiation developed by Kumar and Beyerlein (1991) and Westphal (1998) and refined using pretest feedback. In a factor analysis with promax rotation the ingratiation items all loaded on a single factor (loadings greater than .5 on the ingratiation factor and lower than .2 on other factors), with Cronbach's alpha of .91; factor scores were estimated with the Bartlett method. Interrater reliability against peer directors' reports was assessed with weighted kappa coefficients, which exceeded .75 for all items but one.
time_window: the past twelve months prior to the survey

description: A dichotomous variable was created to indicate minority status with respect to ethnicity, set to 1 if a focal director was an ethnic minority and 0 otherwise. A second dummy variable was set to 1 if the focal director was a woman and 0 otherwise. Data on director gender and ethnicity were obtained from a large management consulting firm.

A dichotomous measure indicating whether a focal director received an appointment as an outside director of the board of a particular firm where another director served on the nominating committee or as CEO. Board appointments subsequent to the survey were examined at all firms in the Forbes listing of large and medium-sized companies for which data on board membership were available (906 companies), over the two-year period subsequent to the survey date.
time_window: two years subsequent to the survey date

description: The authors chose to measure employee growth because firms might invest in employees ahead of other measures of growth, such as sales growth. Growth is measured as the relative growth rate in employees (Zt) from year t-1 to year t-2, computed as the difference between employees in t-1 and employees in t-2 divided by employees in t-2. Both the linear and the squared term of growth enter the hazard models.

Firm failure was coded as 1 if the firm ceased to exist in a given year and as 0 otherwise. Technically, failure was identified when a firm stopped having employees or stopped filing a tax return. The authors checked that exits were related to poor performance by analyzing the conditions of equity, assets, and sales reported in the T2SUF database.

The authors use the Ellison-Glaeser measure, which proxies for the presence of knowledge spillovers, labor-market pooling, input sharing, product shipping costs, and natural advantage. In the reported decomposition, T = sum over rings of (xr - sr) squared, where xr is ring r's share of total employment in all manufacturing sectors and sr is the ring's share of employment in a particular three-digit SIC sector, and H is a Herfindahl index of the K firms in the sector with zk representing the employment share of the kth firm. The geographic boundaries are determined empirically with concentric rings of various radii around the geographic centroid of each census subdivision that experienced an entry in a given year, and all covariates are updated annually.
level: three-digit SIC sector x ring x year

description: The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index based on sales, calculated at the local level, is used as the measure. It is computed as the sum of the squared market shares of firms in sector j, location l, in year t-1, where the market shares are shares of sales of firm i in sector j based on the sales of all firms located in the same boundary ring as the focal entrant. Low values indicate a large number of small competitors; high values indicate fewer, relatively large firms. To resolve cases where the HHI misrepresents competition, the authors dropped 2.5 percent of the right tail of the empirical distribution of the HHI.
level: three-digit SIC sector x location x year

description: A dummy variable in which 1 indicates that the franchisor allows passive ownership.
The dollar value of the cash investment that franchisees need to make to purchase an outlet in the system.
A dummy variable of 1 if the franchisor requires franchisees to have prior experience.
The ongoing percentage of sales (including advertising fees) that franchisees pay to the franchisor.
The number of outlets per state in which the franchisor is operating.
A count of the number of different support services that the franchisor contracts to provide to the franchisee as part of the franchising package.
A dummy variable in which 1 indicates that the franchisor uses master franchise agreements.
The term of the franchise agreement in years.
The dollar value of the cost of creating a franchise outlet.

The event of cessation of franchising was operationalized as the delisting of the franchisor from all of the following sources: Sourcebook of Franchise Opportunities, Franchise Annual, IFA's Franchise Opportunities Guide, and Entrepreneur Magazine's Franchise 500. The cessation of franchising was modeled as the instantaneous rate of cessation, with the data divided into yearly spells. The sample contains 114 exits, 43 censored cases and 1078 organization years.
time_window: yearly spells from entry into franchising forward in time

description: We categorized a player as a star if and only if in the previous season, he was above the 90th percentile of league-wide performance per the VORP statistic, and played in a majority of games for his team. VORP measures a player's performance over and above the performance of a fictitious replacement player that a team could hire at minimal cost. Players who were not stars are non-stars.

variable_name: PreAbsence Phase, Absence Phase, and Return Phase indicators
description: Three within-season indicator variables: a PreAbsence Phase for games when the star is present in the team, an Absence Phase for games when he is absent due to injury, and a Return Phase for games when he returns to the team after recovery. PreAbsence Phase is the reference category and is omitted from the empirical specification. Injuries are unpredictable and beyond anyone's control, so they are treated as exogenous shocks.

Absence duration is measured in number of games and is included as a control variable in the model. The return-phase indicator variables are created as mutually exclusive short, medium, and long return-phase indicators based on whether the absence duration was short, medium, or long.

Equals one if the focal team won the game and zero if it lost. This is the dependent variable in the specifications testing H1, H2, and H3, where the team's performance in the pre-absence phase is the reference for performance in the absence and return phases.

The change in win percentage between the return and the pre-absence phases. Δ denotes taking the mean of the game-level values of each variable in the return and pre-absence phases and computing the difference. This is the dependent variable in the analysis of routines as a mechanism explaining increased team performance.

Shot balance is given by a formula based on the proportion of shots (s_i) and the proportion of minutes (m_i) of player i in a game; the rendering of the formula in the text is only partly readable. The authors state that shot balance captures how evenly shots are distributed across players, is minimized at zero when one player takes all shots, and is maximized when all players take the same number of shots. A positive change in shot balance from the pre-absence to the return phase is interpreted as an improvement in routines. The variable is used as the change in average team-level shot balance between the return and pre-absence phases.

The variable Innovation is the cohort-adjusted number of citations received by patents applied for by the firm in the period immediately following the completion of structural recombination, i.e., between time t and t+1. Patents are counted in the year that they are applied for, although only patents that are eventually granted are included. Each patent's citations are adjusted by the average citations received by any patent in that same year and within that same patent class, and patents that receive no citations take the value of 0 and are effectively not counted. These adjusted citation counts are then added together for all patents applied for by the firm between t and t+1.

A count, for a firm, of the number of events in which a business unit was merged into another business unit (thus losing its original identity), either through the creation of a new (combined) unit or the absorption of a unit by another, for the lagged time period t-1 to t.

The average relatedness between a firm's patents, where p_i is the stock of firm patents in patent class i and R_ij is the relatedness between class i and class j. R_ij is calculated as (C_ij + C_ji)/(C_i + C_j), where C_ij is the total number of citations from patents in class i to patents in class j across all patents successfully filed with the U.S. patent office, and C_i is the total number of citations from all patents in class i. The equation printed for combining these terms is unreadable in the available text and is not reproduced here. Patent stocks are constructed using a 15% depreciation rate.

The percentage of self-citations in the total number of citations received by the firm, calculated following the prior literature. The inclusion of this self-citation percentage also implicitly controls for the extent to which intrafirm knowledge synergies are already being realized through transfers of knowledge between units.

For a firm in a given period, the average number of citations it has received per patent, where the number of citations is adjusted for the average citations in the focal patent's year and patent class. Values greater than 1 imply that the firm's patents are, on average, of higher quality than those of other firms, whereas a value less than 1 implies that they are of lower quality. The measure is calculated using depreciating stock measures.

In the first stage of the interview the names of 13 competitors in the four traditional industry segments - commercial banks, thrifts, brokerages, and credit unions - were presented three at a time in seven predetermined, random trials, and the informant was asked which two of the firms were most similar in terms of their strategies in Arizona. The ratio of expected (traditional segment) pairings provided by each informant to the total possible was calculated. Of the 141 triadic comparisons, 127 reflected traditional industry segments, a proportion significantly different from the one-third predicted under the null.

Each informant rated the 13 focal competitors on seven-point scales anchored by the similarities and contrasts he or she had just provided, supplying on average 14.5 dimensions. Rating grids of informants who provided adequate data (n = 20) were evaluated with the average linkage cluster analysis method in SAS, and the four-cluster solution was compared with the four traditional categories. The average hit rate was 72%, significantly different from the null expectation of 25%.

variable_name: Environmental turbulence of the research site
description: The three research projects were conducted in markets differing in the rate and amount of environmental change: New York in 1981, where traditional boundaries were only beginning to erode (low); Chicago in 1986, after Illinois began phased deregulation and authorized regional interstate banking (moderate); and Arizona in 1989, after full interstate banking and a real estate crisis (high). These research sites represented high, moderate, and low environmental change, respectively.

variable_name: Categories of constructs represented across informants
description: Elicited strategic dimensions were content analyzed into categories by three independent raters using a modified Delphi procedure; categories and dimensions on which all three raters agreed were retained, and dimensions without complete agreement after the final iteration were removed. Walton's classification scheme was adopted, with strategy and organizational structure added, and the results were compared across the three studies. The number of categories considered by managers in the industry doubled over the decade.

variable_name: Mean number of dimensions per informant
description: The strategic dimensions each informant supplied through the repertory grid interview were counted and averaged within each study. The mean number of constructs per individual increased only slightly across the studies and not significantly (Chicago mean = 13.79; Arizona mean = 14.5; n.s.). Walton did not report the average number of constructs per informant, so statistical comparison with his data was not possible.

variable_name: Cumulative profit over eight simulated years
description: Total accumulated profit over eight simulated years in the strategic decision-making task, the online 'Strategic Innovation Simulation' (Christensen and Shih 2008). Participants manage R&D portfolios over eight simulated years (eight trials) and must decide which of several market opportunities to pursue, with the objective of maximizing cumulative profit. The measure is suggested as comprehensive by the creators of the simulation.

variable_name: Routinization propensity (average response time in the four-armed bandit task)
description: The time it took participants to complete each of the 300 trials in the four-armed bandit task. To exclude the very early trials in which participants had not yet had the chance to develop any routine, the average response time was calculated for trials 5-75 of each of the four sessions and then averaged across the four sessions to obtain a single measure. A high routinization propensity implies a low response time.
time_window: trials 5-75 of each of four sessions

description: Five tasks produced 18 variables, which were grouped by an exploratory factor analysis (principal component analysis, varimax rotated solution) into six factors used as the proxy for the level of CCCs. Each factor groups variables corresponding to a functional component of the CCCs, with two components represented by two factors each, one for performance and one for speed of response.

Constructed for firm i in year t - 1 using patent citation data. All patents applied for and assigned to firm i in the ten years prior to, but not including, year t - 1 (i.e., t - 2 to t - 11) form the focal firm's patent stock; the universe of U.S. patents applied for in year t - 1 and subsequently granted was identified, patents assigned to firm i were removed, and the remaining patents containing a citation to any of firm i's stock of patents were identified as firm i's forward-citing patents. All prior art (backward) citations contained in those forward-citing patents were then identified and all citations to patents owned by firm i were removed. The two lists were joined, all redundant patent numbers removed, so that the pool contains only unique patents from firms other than firm i.
time_window: year t - 1 (from a ten-year patent stock)

description: This variable was measured as the total number of unique patents in firm i's spillover knowledge pool at year t - 1. This variable was log-transformed because of skewness.

An index developed by Jaffe (1986) was used. For each firm-year, an index measures the distribution of a firm's patents across primary patent classes and the distribution of a firm's spillover knowledge pool across primary classes, using a moving ten-year window to establish each firm's patenting profile. The firm is located in a multidimensional technology space by a J-dimensional vector Di = (di1 . . . dij), where dij is the fraction of firm i's patents in patent class j, and the pool by a J-dimensional vector Ei = (ei1 . . . eij), where eij is the fraction of the pool's patents in class j. The measure is bounded between 0 and 1, with larger values representing increasing similarity; the formula block in the paper's text is unreadable in this payload and is not reproduced here.

Measured as the proportion of prior art patents contained in firm i's patents of year t that belonged to its spillover knowledge pool in year t - 1. Because this measure is a share rather than a count of citations, it captures a firm's propensity to build on knowledge in its spillover knowledge pool. For estimation it was transformed using a logit (i.e., log odds) transformation, ln(knowledge integration / 1 - knowledge integration), with values of 0 and 1 recoded as 0.0001 and 0.9999.

Measured as the number of successful patent applications for firm i in year t. Patents were counted in the year of application to capture the precise timing of knowledge creation. It is a count variable that can take on only nonnegative integer values.

Average industry return on assets for the year 1984, a weighted average of the profitability of all of the four-digit industries in which the sample firm participated. The weights are the proportions of the firm's sales in each four-digit industry, and the return on assets is taken for each four-digit industry. The equation printed for this measure could not be read in the text, so only the prose description is recorded.

A continuous entropy measure using Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes, assessed for the year 1985, that identifies and evaluates the extent of diversification. It is computed from the proportion of firm i's sales in four-digit industry j and the proportion of firm i's sales in two-digit industry j. The equation printed for this measure could not be read in the text, so only the prose description is recorded.

The ratio of R&D expense to sales for each firm i, measured for the year 1986 and adjusted for industry membership by subtracting the weighted average industry ratio. The industry mean is the mean ratio of R&D expense to sales in each four-digit industry j, weighted by the proportion of the firm's sales in that industry; the authors state that they controlled for industry differences in R&D levels in this way. The printed formula for the adjustment could not be read in the text, so only the prose description is recorded.

The ratio of capital investment to sales for each firm i, measured for the year 1986 and adjusted for industry membership by subtracting the weighted average industry ratio. The industry term is the mean ratio of capital investment to sales in each four-digit industry j, weighted by the proportion of the firm's sales in that industry; the authors state that they controlled for industry differences in investment levels in this way. The printed formula for the adjustment could not be read in the text, so only the prose description is recorded.

A weighted average of the operating margins of each firm's business units adjusted for industry membership, intended as a relative measure that reflects the value of outputs relative to the value of inputs. The weights are the proportion of firm i's sales in four-digit industry j in 1987, and the adjustment subtracts the operating margin in four-digit industry j in 1987 from the operating margin of the firm's business units in that industry. The equation printed for this measure could not be read in the text, so only the prose description is recorded.
The dependent variable used to test H1-H5 is categorical and captures the alliance governance structure. It is set to 1 when the R&D alliance is equity-based and 0 when it is contract-based.
The independent variable takes the value of 1 if an R&D alliance is formed between three or more partner firms and 0 if an R&D alliance has two partner firms. It is used in tests of H1 and H4.
scale: 1 = three or more partner firms; 0 = two partner firms

description: Net is set to 1 when the trilateral R&D alliance is net-based and 0 when it is chain-based. The variable was coded from synopses of alliance activities provided by the SDC database (supplemented by company 10-Ks, the LexisNexis database, and the RDS Business Reference Suite) by two independent coders not aware of the theoretical arguments or hypotheses; initial agreement was 82% and Cohen's kappa was 0.87, and disagreements were discussed and resolved by the two raters. The variable is used in tests of H2 and H5.

Scope reflects the vertical scope of alliance activities. It is set to 1 when alliance activities involve operations such as manufacturing and/or marketing in addition to R&D (broad scope) and 0 when alliance activities involve R&D activities exclusively (narrow scope). It is used in tests of H1-H5.
Alignment takes the value of 1 if the governance structure is as predicted and 0 if the governance structure diverges from the predicted. It is used to test H6.
Alliance duration is the dependent variable used to test H6 and is measured in years. Multiple archival sources were used to identify the sample alliances' termination date.

Binary variable coded one if the user indicated they already had a startup idea they wanted to work on (selecting 'Yes, I want a cofounder who can help me build it') and zero if they indicated they were open to helping a cofounder with an existing idea or to exploring new ideas together.

The Brysbaert Concreteness Index, created from ratings of 40,000 commonly used word lemmas on a scale of one (abstract) to five (concrete). A score was computed for each profile using the Recursive Inspection of Text (RIOT) scan, representing the mean concreteness of each word in the text. This score was reverse-coded and standardized to arrive at a score for construal level.

An index variable ranging from zero to three, built from three standardized profile questions about what the user is looking for in a cofounder: (1) the responsibilities they could perform, (2) whether they are technical, and (3) their industry interests. For each item the user indicated whether they 'prefer' or 'require' the criteria, and the index adds one for each of the three criteria marked as 'require,' so zero indicates the user marked 'prefer' on all three.

Text analysis of each user's description of what they are looking for in an ideal cofounder. A dictionary of resource seeking words was developed through a deductive, inductive, and validation process, and the final dictionary included 243 words or word roots. The dictionary was imported into the Linguistics Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software, which produced a score for each observation representing the ratio of dictionary words to total words in the description.

Text analysis of each user's description of what they are looking for in an ideal cofounder. A dictionary of interpersonal attraction words was developed through a deductive, inductive, and validation process, and the final dictionary included 207 words or word roots. The dictionary was imported into the Linguistics Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software, which produced a score for each observation representing the ratio of dictionary words to total words in the description.
Equals one if the respondent received the 'Lead Entrepreneur' manipulation and zero if they received the 'Potential Cofounder' manipulation.

Three seven-point Likert questions measuring construal level related to finding a cofounder (alpha = 0.86), adapted from Venus et al. (2019) and focused on whether the respondent is looking for specific or general traits. A sample item is 'I care more about what they are like overall rather than about their specific characteristics.' The responses were averaged and standardized.

Four items measuring utilitarian and instrumental motives, drawn from scales used in marketing and social psychology and adapted to entrepreneurial team formation, selected after an online pilot study (n = 200) showed sufficiently high loadings on a single factor and high interitem reliability (alpha = 0.82). A sample item is 'This person could be used to accomplish goals.' The responses were averaged and standardized.

Attribute importance scores from a hierarchical Bayesian multinomial logit model of responses to 12 choice tasks in which respondents chose among three cofounder profiles (or 'none of the above'); profiles varied in rated levels (high, medium, or low) of skillset, experience, personality, and familiarity. The importance scores sum to 100 and represent the percent of variation in utility influenced by each attribute. The scores for skillset and experience were added to obtain an overall importance score for resources, which served as the dependent variable.

Attribute importance scores from a hierarchical Bayesian multinomial logit model of responses to 12 choice tasks in which respondents chose among three cofounder profiles (or 'none of the above'); profiles varied in rated levels (high, medium, or low) of skillset, experience, personality, and familiarity. The importance scores sum to 100 and represent the percent of variation in utility influenced by each attribute. The scores for personality and familiarity were added to obtain an overall importance score for interpersonal attraction, which served as the dependent variable.

Two independent raters who were blind to the study hypotheses and other variables coded each conversation after reading it in full, rating on a scale ranging from zero to seven the extent to which lead entrepreneurs discussed nonventure related topics, such as hobbies, shared group memberships, personal background, and common friends. Interrater agreement was acceptable (ICC(2) = 0.65, p < 0.001), and interpersonal content was calculated as the mean score across both raters.

The same two independent raters coded each conversation on a scale ranging from zero to seven based on the extent to which lead entrepreneurs discussed venture-related topics, such as aspects of the venture and its development, as well as the professional experience or educational qualifications of either the lead entrepreneur or potential cofounder. Coding was done concurrently with the interpersonal attraction coding. Interrater agreement was acceptable (ICC(2) = 0.76, p < 0.001), and resource content was calculated as the mean score across both raters.

Tie formation was operationalized based on whether the potential cofounder and the lead entrepreneur agreed to work together, as indicated in the official team roster for the incubator program; dyads in which they decided to work together were coded as one and those that did not were coded as zero. For the test of Hypothesis 7 the authors categorized each dyad as hybrid if the standardized dyadic resource seeking score and the standardized dyadic interpersonal attraction score were both positive (n = 85), with all other ties categorized as nonhybrid.

Dummy variable that takes value 1 if at least 10% of the firm is owned by a family or a private person and zero otherwise. The authors note that 10% is a common cutoff point to identify family ownership, especially among listed companies.

Dummy variable that takes value 1 if the patent was licensed or sold and 0 otherwise. It is built from the survey questions about the status of the patent at the time of the survey, that is, whether the patent was commercially exploited internally or externally.
time_window: patent status at the time of the survey

description: Dummy variable that takes value 1 if the patent was internally commercialized and 0 otherwise. It is built from the survey questions about the status of the patent at the time of the survey, that is, whether the patent was commercially exploited internally or externally.
time_window: patent status at the time of the survey

description: Dummy variable for the inclusionary hierarchy dominant design period, defined as the period from the emergence of the dominant design in the catalytic converter architecture in 1981 to the emergence of digital control technology in 1994 (1981-1993). The authors also define the inclusionary hierarchy dominant design era as 1970-1993, the period that captures the enactment of the technology-forcing Clean Air Act of 1970 until the emergence of digital control technology in 1994, and use that time frame for the analysis of architectural innovation in the inclusionary hierarchy.
scale: binary (1 = the inclusionary hierarchy dominant design period)

description: Dummy variable for the digital control hierarchy technology-shift period, the period following the emergence of the advanced onboard diagnostic electronic control module in 1994 (1994-1998). In the digital control hierarchy analysis the authors used the period from 1981 to 1998.
scale: binary (1 = the digital control hierarchy technology-shift period)

description: Dependent variable in the logistic regressions on component innovation, coded 1 for component innovation and 0 for architectural innovation. It is built from the firms' successful U.S. patent applications in automobile emissions control technology; patents that capture the identifiable physical part of the product represent component innovation. Coding used the generic definitions of component and architectural innovation provided by Henderson and Clark (1990; see also Ulrich 1995) and was cross-checked by an independent coder.

The same coded dependent variable, innovation type, where architectural innovation is the reference category (0) and component innovation is coded 1. Patents that address the interfacial problems among components and how the components can be linked together into a whole system were coded as architectural innovation. Coding used the generic definitions of component and architectural innovation provided by Henderson and Clark (1990; see also Ulrich 1995) and was cross-checked by an independent coder.

Dummy variable distinguishing automakers (OEMs) from suppliers of components. The authors generated interaction terms between this dummy and the two technology-shift period variables to examine whether automakers' propensity for different types of innovation is related to the two technological shifts; in the fixed-effects specification the OEM dummy is subsumed within the firm fixed effects.

variable_name: Anticipation of social interaction with alter
description: Multi-item survey scale measuring the extent to which a focal director anticipates social interaction with an alter, together with a causal indicator that is simply the amount of time before the next meeting in minutes, inverted so that higher values indicate less time before the meeting. Directors answered at five points in time around each meeting: over the prior day (time 1), since the prior survey (times 2, 3 and 5), and since the meeting (time 4). CFA showed the time indicator and the survey items loaded together on one factor.
time_window: over the prior day, since the prior survey, and since the meeting (five points in time around each meeting)

variable_name: Alter's relative social status in the corporate elite
description: Built from four indicators of social status in the corporate elite: the number of corporate board appointments held, the number of nonprofit board seats held, elite education, and whether the individual is CEO of a Fortune 500 firm. CFA indicated that all four variables loaded on the same factor with acceptable reliability. In the primary models, relative status was measured as the alter's status in the corporate elite minus the focal director's status.

Dissimilarity between the focal director and the alter on five characteristics that provide a salient basis for personal and/or social identification among corporate leaders: functional background, age, gender, ethnicity, and primary industry of employment. The indicators were combined into an index using principal component analysis, which the authors describe as appropriate with causal or formative indicators; because four of the variables are dichotomous, tetrachoric correlations were used in the analysis.

variable_name: Reflection on characteristics held in common with alter
description: Count variable indicating the number of times the focal director had reflected on a characteristic held in common with the alter during the relevant time period. Directors indicated whether they had thought about a characteristic of the alter, which one(s), and on how many occasions; a subsequent survey asked them to indicate whether they possessed each of these characteristics. Two other survey items asked respondents more directly how many times they had reflected on a characteristic or attribute of the other director that they also possessed. In models of recommendations the variable is cumulated from the day before the meeting to the time of the meeting and averaged across interactions.
time_window: from the day before the meeting to the time of the meeting (reported at five points in time)

variable_name: Reflection on characteristics not shared with alter
description: Count variable indicating the number of times the focal director had reflected on a characteristic not shared with the alter during the relevant time period. Directors indicated whether they had thought about a characteristic of the alter, which one(s), and on how many occasions; a subsequent survey asked them to indicate whether they possessed each of these characteristics. Two other survey items asked respondents more directly how many times they had reflected on a characteristic or attribute of the other director that they did not possess. In models of recommendations the variable is cumulated from the day before the meeting to the time of the meeting and averaged across interactions.
time_window: from the day before the meeting to the time of the meeting (reported at five points in time)

variable_name: Self-regulated cognition (reflection on characteristics held in common; low reflection on characteristics not shared)
description: In the primary models the pattern of self-regulated cognition is captured by the two count variables, reflection on characteristics held in common with the alter and reflection on characteristics not shared with the alter, which are entered separately in the models. A second-order factor analysis showed that the survey measures loaded onto two first-order factors corresponding to the two kinds of reflection, which in turn loaded onto a single second-order factor representing self-regulated cognition. In separate models director cognitions were measured using factor scores, and the hypothesized results were unchanged.
time_window: five points in time around each meeting

description: Multi-item survey scale measuring the alter's report of the focal director's expressions of liking during the meeting, including items on the frequency with which the focal director smiled at the alter and items gauging verbal expressions of liking such as stating that they enjoy working with the alter. Items drew on measures developed by Kumar and Beyerlein (1991), Provine and Fischer (2010), and Westphal and Stern (2006) and were revised and added to based on the literature and preliminary interviews. In the primary analysis the alter's responses were used; the hypothesized results were unchanged using self-report measures. Intra-class correlations for the items ranged from .85 to .93 and the scale alpha was .89.
time_window: during the meeting (and averaged across meetings for the recommendation models)

description: Multi-item survey scale measuring the alter's report of the focal director's expressions of admiration during the meeting, including questions about complimentary remarks and items asking whether the focal director conveyed (or tried to convey) their admiration for the alter, in order to capture both verbal and nonverbal communication. Items drew on measures developed by Kumar and Beyerlein (1991), Provine and Fischer (2010), and Westphal and Stern (2006) and were revised and added to based on the literature and preliminary interviews. In the primary analysis the alter's responses were used; the hypothesized results were unchanged using self-report measures. The scale alpha was .93.
time_window: during the meeting (and averaged across meetings for the recommendation models)

description: Dichotomous variable indicating whether the focal director was recommended by the other director in their dyad (alter) for a board appointment where the alter serves on the nominating committee. Three months after the meeting, participating directors were asked whether they had recommended anyone for a board appointment in the prior three months, and if so whom and for what position; other directors serving on the same nominating committees were asked whether the directors with whom they served had suggested someone for a board position. Inter-rater agreement about whether participating directors recommended the other director in their dyad was 96%.
time_window: three months after the meeting; predictors measured over the six months prior

description: Each CEO was rated on items adapted from a validated scale of CEO charisma by three trained raters who watched edited video clips of at least 2.5 minutes; the videos had identifying information about the CEO and his/her employer firm removed and omitted sections in which the camera focus was not on the CEO. Interitem reliability was 0.87 (Cronbach alpha), interrater reliability ICC1 = 0.58 and ICC2 = 0.81, and interrater agreement rwg = 0.91. Scores based on two different videos of the same CEO recorded at least one year apart correlated at 0.57, and the authors treat charisma as a highly stable attribute that does not change meaningfully during a CEO's tenure. In the imitation models these peer CEO scores were used as weights on peer firms' recent strategic actions.
level: CEO (entered at the focal-firm-year level as a weighted average over peer firms)

description: Three trained raters rated each CEO on items of a third-party adapted version of the Narcissism Personality Inventory (NPI-16), using the same edited video clips of at least 2.5 minutes as for charisma. Interitem reliability was 0.90 (Cronbach alpha), interrater reliability ICC1 = 0.52 and ICC2 = 0.77, and interrater agreement rwg = 0.87. Scores based on two different videos of the same CEO recorded at least one year apart correlated at 0.65, and narcissism is treated as a highly stable attribute of CEOs. In the imitation models these peer CEO scores were used as weights on peer firms' recent strategic actions.
level: CEO (entered at the focal-firm-year level as a weighted average over peer firms)

variable_name: Recent CSR actions by peer firms
description: Computed as the average recent CSR actions of industry peers (firms in the same 4-digit GICS industry, excluding the focal firm) from year t-3 to t-2 and year t-2 to t-1: the mean of each peer firm's recent actions was first taken and then averaged across all peer firms in the industry. Each firm is treated both as a focal firm and as a peer firm for other focal firms, and the measurement of independent variables temporally preceded the dependent variable. To form the key independent variables, these peer actions were weighted by the peer firms' CEO attributes (recent strategic actions by charismatic CEOs and by narcissistic CEOs).
level: industry peer group per focal firm-year

variable_name: Recent international diversification actions by peer firms
description: Computed as the average recent international diversification actions of industry peers (same 4-digit GICS industry, excluding the focal firm) from year t-3 to t-2 and year t-2 to t-1, by first taking the mean of each peer firm's recent actions and then averaging across all peer firms. Peer CEO attributes were used as weights to create the key independent variables (recent international diversification actions by charismatic CEOs and by narcissistic CEOs).
level: industry peer group per focal firm-year

variable_name: Recent product-market diversification actions by peer firms
description: Computed as the average recent product-market diversification actions of industry peers (same 4-digit GICS industry, excluding the focal firm) from year t-3 to t-2 and year t-2 to t-1, by first taking the mean of each peer firm's recent actions and then averaging across all peer firms. Peer CEO attributes were used as weights to create the key independent variables (recent product-market diversification actions by charismatic CEOs and by narcissistic CEOs).
level: industry peer group per focal firm-year

description: Firms' CSR profiles were measured from KLD ratings of CSR strengths and concerns, indicated in binary terms, as the sum of all the strengths minus concerns under each of five categories; the five scores were then standardized and averaged. Because the interyear comparability of the data becomes tenuous after 2008, CSR profiles were examined during 2001-2008. The firm's prior year CSR was controlled in all models.

A ratio measure of the firm's international revenues divided by its total revenues in each year between 2001 and 2012, obtained from the Compustat segment database. The prior year's international diversification was controlled in all models.

Palepu's (1985) entropy measure, computed as the sum over segments of Pi × ln(1/Pi), where Pi is the sales emanating from segment i and ln(1/Pi) is the weight assigned to each segment. Data were obtained from the Compustat segment database. Because the variable had a significant negative skew, it was first log transformed and then used with the same model specifications as the other two dependent variables; the prior year's product-market diversification was controlled in all models.

Measured by first regressing the annual industry averages of three firm performance variables - the growth in sales, the growth in operating income, and the growth in total employment - over the years in the study period (2001-2012), and then assessing the volatility of each industry as the dispersion about the regression line by dividing the standard error of the regression slope coefficient by the mean value of each variable. The composite index resulting from a principal components analysis of these three measures is the measure of industry dynamism, and it was standardized before entering the regressions.

Measured by first regressing the annual industry averages of three firm performance variables - the growth in sales, the growth in operating income, and the growth in total employment - over the years in the study period (2001-2012), and then assessing the volatility of each industry as the dispersion about the regression line by dividing the standard error of the regression slope coefficient by the mean value of each variable. The composite index resulting from a principal components analysis of these three measures is the measure of industry dynamism, and it was standardized before entering the regressions.

Measured by first regressing the annual industry averages of three firm performance variables - the growth in sales, the growth in operating income, and the growth in total employment - over the years in the study period (2001-2012), and then assessing the volatility of each industry as the dispersion about the regression line by dividing the standard error of the regression slope coefficient by the mean value of each variable. The composite index resulting from a principal components analysis of these three measures is the measure of industry dynamism, and it was standardized before entering the regressions.

The focal firm's CSR profile in the prior year (t-1), which was controlled for in all models and then used as the measure of the focal firm's prior strategic experience in the CSR domain for the moderation tests.

The focal firm's international diversification in the prior year (t-1), which was controlled for in all models and then used as the measure of the focal firm's prior strategic experience in the international diversification domain for the moderation tests.

The focal firm's product-market diversification in the prior year (t-1), log transformed, which was controlled for in all models and then used as the measure of the focal firm's prior strategic experience in the product-market diversification domain for the moderation tests.

A binary variable to reflect whether or not the CEO either possessed an Ivy League degree or had gained admission to an Ivy League school. The variable was hand collected for each CEO-cover observation along with the other CEO attributes.

Average valuations were examined for three-, two-, and one-year intervals pre- and post-cover, that is, for seven-, five-, and three-year market valuation averages centered on the publication year. Changes in Tobin's Q were assessed for three-, two-, and one-year intervals after the cover (relative to the year before the cover). The dependent variables were Winsorized at the 5 percent level to remove outliers.
time_window: Seven-, five-, and three-year windows centered on the cover year; changes from the year prior to the cover to one, two, and three years after

variable_name: degree level, Master and above versus Bachelor and below
description: The sample was split according to whether a CEO had obtained a graduate or an undergraduate Ivy degree, with the subsamples labelled 'Master and above' and 'Bachelor and below'. The subgroup findings were also checked with interaction analyses on the total sample using a product of Ivy and a dummy that distinguished education at, above, or below the Master's level.
The age of the CEO, hand collected with the other CEO attributes. Subsamples were defined by median bifurcation according to CEO age.

The number of employees, reported in thousands in the descriptive statistics and entered as a logarithm in the regressions. Subsamples were defined by median bifurcation according to firm size, producing small-firm and big-firm groups.

The year in which the CEO graduated, used to divide the sample according to the 1960 year of graduation into an early cohort (graduation year before 1960) and a later cohort (graduation year 1960 or after).

For each stock an analyst covered, the authors calculated the proportion of the portfolio of stocks the analyst covered that were covered jointly by each other analyst who also covered the focal stock, and then computed the average proportional overlap among analysts (Baum & Korn, 1996). The formal definition is given in an equation that is unreadable in the provided text; only its prose explanation could be recorded. Cocoverage is examined over 12-month moving windows updated quarterly, so each quarter's measure uses all joint stock coverage in the prior 12 months, and the measure is recomputed at the time of each estimate using the appropriate quarterly network.

Dummy variable coded 1 for analyst estimates that differed from the current mean, or consensus, estimate for a stock by more than 1.5 standard deviations above the consensus, and 0 otherwise. The consensus estimate for each stock was calculated by averaging all active earnings estimates for that stock the day prior to a focal estimate. The authors used the standard deviation of analyst estimates rather than a numeric distinction to capture boldness more consistently across stocks and estimates over time.

Dummy variable coded 1 for analyst estimates that were more than 1.5 standard deviations below the consensus estimate for the stock, and 0 otherwise. The consensus estimate for each stock was calculated by averaging all active earnings estimates for that stock the day prior to a focal estimate. The same standard-deviation band was applied to capture boldness consistently across stocks and estimates over time.

Variable defined for estimates that have positive boldness and are closer to actual earnings than the analyst consensus. It is one of the four outcomes estimated in the simultaneous system of equations.

Variable defined for estimates that have negative boldness and are closer to actual earnings than the analyst consensus. It is one of the four outcomes estimated in the simultaneous system of equations.

Measured from an analyst's history of Institutional Investor All-Star rankings since 1990. The authors summed each year an analyst had been listed as an All-Star, weighted by its recency (i.e., 1/(year t - year of listing)), which gives more weight to recent rankings to account for the enduring, but weakening, effect of being ranked. In additional analyses they found better fit with a dichotomous indicator of whether an analyst was ranked, but the weighted measure was used in the reported models.

Dichotomous variable coded 1 for all dates after October 1, 2000, and 0 otherwise. Although Reg-FD was announced in August 2000, it was not ratified until October 23, 2000; the authors allowed for an adjustment period and set October 1, 2000 as the start of the Reg-FD period. It is interacted with multipoint contact and with analyst status.

Language vagueness is proxied with the Linguistic Inquiry & Word Count (LIWC) 'certitude' dictionary, which measures the degree to which language is specific and clear about the state of the thing being discussed. The certitude index for each pitch transcript is calculated as a percentage of the total words in the pitch that can be found in the certitude dictionary; because the opposite of this construct is being measured, this amount is subtracted from 100 to capture the percentage of the language that is not from the certitude dictionary, and the variable is then rescaled for interpretability so that the vagueness measure starts at just over zero.
scale: percentage of total words, rescaled to start at just over zero

description: For each founder, rhetoric-oriented skills are flagged from educational keywords such as 'literature,' 'rhetoric,' and 'journalism' and from job titles generally associated with those backgrounds, such as 'editor' and 'writer,' supplemented with top-scoring jobs on O*Net's cognitive-ability categories of oral expression, oral comprehension, written comprehension, and written expression. Skill is a binary variable at the individual level and a ratio at the firm level; a firm with three founders, one of whom has any education or experience tagged as rhetoric-oriented, has a rhetoric-oriented skill ratio of 0.33.

A binary variable that takes the value of zero if the firm does not receive a formal indication of interest from the judges and a value of one if it does. Contestants have one opportunity to pitch, after which judges determine a list of finalists and then select a runner-up and a winner, and they also announce Audience Choice Award recipients; the binary measure captures whether the focal firm advances to the next stage of the competition immediately following the pitch.

Five items from the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire developed by Bass and his colleagues; items 2, 3, and 5 represent contingent reward behavior and items 1 and 4 represent active management-by-exception behavior. Each participant rated his/her CEO on a five-point scale (1, 'not at all' to 5, 'frequently, if not always'). One overall measure of transactional leadership was formed with an alpha coefficient of .81, and managers' perceptions were combined into an averaged, aggregated score for each firm.
scale: 1, 'not at all' to 5, 'frequently, if not always'

description: Seven items from the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire: items 6, 9, 11, and 12 describe leader behaviors that help maintain a charismatic relationship, and items 7, 8, and 10 represent consequential or attributional aspects of the relationship. Each participant rated his/her CEO on a five-point scale (1, 'not at all' to 5, 'frequently, if not always'). The charisma measure displayed an alpha coefficient of .90, and managers' perceptions were combined into an averaged, aggregated score for each firm.
scale: 1, 'not at all' to 5, 'frequently, if not always'

description: Four items from an instrument developed by Khandwalla (1976), similar to the measure Singh (1986) labeled 'environmental turbulence'. Responses were on a five-point scale with anchors ranging from 'strongly disagree' (1) to 'strongly agree' (5). The alpha coefficient was .63, and managers' perceptions were combined into an averaged, aggregated score for each firm.

Net profit margin (NPM), computed as net income divided by net sales, corrected by subtracting the average industry (two-digit SIC code) NPM from a firm's own net profit margin. Industry-adjusted NPM data from 1990 through 1994 were averaged for each firm to form a composite measure, which the authors argue helps guard against random fluctuations and anomalies and reflects long-term performance effects. Data were extracted from COMPUSTAT for 90 percent of the firms, and Compact Disclosure was used when a firm had missing values for at least one of the years, in which case all five years were obtained from Compact Disclosure.

Measured as the duration in years in the CEO's initial employment contract. The authors hand-collected the data from CEO employment agreements, usually available on Form 8-K (the Material Definitive Agreement or Employment Agreement) and Form 10-K or 10-Q (filed under Exhibit 10), searched through the S&P Capital IQ company filing database. The analyses focus only on firms and CEOs with fixed-term contracts.

The average number of acquisitions per year within the initial contract duration; the period for which the variable is constructed starts at hiring and ends at initial contract termination. Deals are taken from SDC Platinum and limited to completed deals by U.S. acquiring firms, with disclosed and undisclosed values, acquirers holding fewer than 50% of target shares before the announcement and 100% after completion, and transaction values of at least $10 million.
time_window: from hiring to initial contract termination

description: The number of private targets divided by the total number of corporate acquisitions made during the initial contract period.
The number of targets that are divested business units divided by the total number of corporate acquisitions made during the initial contract period.

The average relatedness score of all M&A deals during the initial contract duration. Following Laamanen et al. (2014), a relatedness score of 2 is assigned if the detailed 4-digit SIC of the acquirer is the same as that of the target and a score of 1 if the broader 2-digit SIC of the acquirer is the same as that of the target.
The average value of transactions (in billion dollars) across all M&A deals during the initial contract period.
The average cash payment value proportion out of the total value of M&A transactions for all M&As performed during the initial contract period.

The annual value of government contracts classified as fixed-cost from the DOD in the U.S. federal government procurement system, based on type-of-contract information obtained from USAspending.gov. The variable was logged to account for skewness and mean-centered to minimize multicollinearity and ease interpretation.

The annual value of government contracts classified as cost-plus from the DOD in the U.S. federal government procurement system, based on type-of-contract information obtained from USAspending.gov. The variable was logged to account for skewness and mean-centered to minimize multicollinearity and ease interpretation.

The total number of OSHA inspections a firm received, subtracting the number of accidents, complaints, and follow-up inspections, so that only discretionary inspections remain. Inspections recorded at the establishment level in the OSHA Enforcement data set were manually consolidated to the firm level by matching establishment names and locations with their respective firms.

Contract duration was computed from the period_of_performance_start_date and period_of_performance_current_end_date columns for each contract, as the number of days between the start and end dates; contracts with unresolved inconsistencies were excluded. Individual durations were then grouped by firm and calendar year and averaged to a firm-year measure of the mean contract duration. A dummy variable distinguishes firms with spot contracts from firms with no contracts, both of which have a duration value of zero.

variable_name: negative media coverage of labor issues
description: The number of incidents involving a firm under negative media coverage in the United States over the past five years, counted only from high-reach information sources. RepRisk categorizes employee relations incidents into less severe, severe, and very severe levels. The measure is a weighted sum constructed using inverse probability weighting, assigning weights to each incident based on the inverse of its probability of inclusion so that rarer, more severe incidents receive greater emphasis. A higher value indicates more negative incidents and a worse reputation for regulatory compliance.

Measured with the LIWC psycholinguistic text analysis program. The score is the percentage of words from the LIWC past dictionary (145 words such as 'had,' 'did,' 'was,' 'were') in the CEO information set, which was constructed separately for each year by pulling texts from four archival sources into a single document and was normalized by the total length of the text. Two coders manually checked a randomly drawn subsample of 50 firms for misclassified or spurious words.
scale: percentage of words from the LIWC dictionary

description: Measured with the LIWC psycholinguistic text analysis program. The score is the percentage of words from the LIWC present dictionary (169 words such as 'is,' 'does,' 'are') in the CEO information set, which was constructed separately for each year by pulling texts from four archival sources into a single document and was normalized by the total length of the text. Two coders manually checked a randomly drawn subsample of 50 firms for misclassified or spurious words.
scale: percentage of words from the LIWC dictionary

description: Measured with the LIWC psycholinguistic text analysis program. The score is the percentage of words from the LIWC future dictionary (48 words such as 'will,' 'may,' 'might,' 'shall,' 'going to') in the CEO information set, which was constructed separately for each year by pulling texts from four archival sources into a single document and was normalized by the total length of the text. Two coders manually checked a randomly drawn subsample of 50 firms for misclassified or spurious words.
scale: percentage of words from the LIWC dictionary

description: A composite of two measures. Rate of environmental change was measured as the average yearly changes in industry sales value and units between 1996 and 2000. Unpredictability of environmental change was measured by regressing industry values of shipment over five years against time and dividing the standard error of the regression coefficient on the time dummy by the average value of the industry's shipments, yielding a standardized index. Because the two measures were highly correlated and loaded on a single factor, they were aggregated into a composite measure of environmental dynamism.

Counts of new product introductions reported in newspapers, magazines, and journals, identified through the Factiva and Lexis-Nexis Academic databases. Two coders independently checked every headline to confirm that it concerned a new product introduction and to remove multiple headlines reporting the same product launch. A three-year average of new product data was used, and the rate of NPI was lagged by one year.

Five of Goudreau's (1984) ratios, which measure how extensively savings and loans had adopted the liberalized powers granted to them during industry deregulation, were factor analyzed with orthogonal varimax rotation and loaded on one factor; they were used as indicators of adaptation. The five ratios were calculated for each savings and loan over the years 1980-83 from Federal Home Loan Bank Board financial data tapes. For each ratio a savings and loan was assigned plus one if it was in the upper third of all savings and loans, minus one if it was in the bottom third, and zero if it was in the middle, and each savings and loan was assigned an 'adaptation value', the arithmetic sum of these values over all five of the ratios; the adaptation values ranged from a minus five to a plus five. Savings and loans with an adaptation value ranging from plus 1.7 to plus five (the top third) were classified as having a high-level of adaptation while those with adaptation values less than minus 1.7 were classified as having a low-level of adaptation.

Hage's (1965) instrument measuring organic and mechanistic structures, which includes two items for each of four variables (formalization, stratification, complexity, and centralization), was rewritten to conform with the savings and loan industry. Study participants were asked to indicate the extent to which these structural variables best described their savings and loan, with responses measured using a 5-point, appropriately anchored Likert scale. The eight structural items loaded on one factor using a factor analysis with an orthogonal varimax rotation and were highly correlated, and an average structure mean was used to compare organizations; organizations with low structural means are more organic while those with a high structural mean are more mechanistic.

Snow and Hrebiniak's (1980) procedure describing the strategy types of the Miles and Snow (1978) typology was used to measure strategy. Study participants were asked to check the type best describing the strategic behavior of their savings and loan. Twenty-eight of the 37 high-level adaptation savings and loans reported the use of a prospector strategy while 52 of the 62 low-level adaptation savings and loans indicated that they had been using a defender strategy; no savings and loan reported having a reactor strategy and the remaining 19 that indicated an analyzer strategy were not included in subsequent data analysis.
scale: categorical (strategy types of the Miles and Snow typology)

description: The value ratio determines the net worth of a savings and loan; industry analysts argue that such a ratio gives a clear picture of a savings and loan's 'real health'. The ratio was calculated for each savings and loan in the sample for the period 1980-83.
The profitability ratio measures profitability using total assets rather than owner's equity. The ratio was calculated for each savings and loan in the sample for the period 1980-83.

The risk ratio measures the extent to which assets have been repossessed and provides an index of the quality of a savings and loan's loan portfolio. The ratio was calculated for each savings and loan in the sample for the period 1980-83.

Responding savings and loans with similar strategy-structure arrangements were clustered, and three clusters were identified in each adaptation state. Using Hage's (1965) argument that his structural variables provide a continuum, the cluster with the lowest structural means in the high-level adaptation state (Cluster 1) was identified as having the best strategy-structure 'fit' because it had the best type of organic structure, and the cluster with the highest structural means in the low-level adaptation state (Cluster 3) was identified as having the best strategy-structure 'fit' because it had the best type of mechanistic structure.

The dependent variable of the mean regressions is the natural logarithm of the growth rate of firm stock market value, where SMV denotes stock market value. Growth rates are computed as one-year and ten-year changes and averaged across the firms in the industry, so that the industry mean for a single year is the unit of analysis.
time_window: one-year growth from 1959 to 1991 and ten-year growth from 1968 to 1991

variable_name: natural logarithm of the squared residuals from the mean regression
description: The dependent variable of the variance regressions is the natural logarithm of the squared residuals from the associated mean regression of stock market value growth. The mean and variance regressions are estimated together, so that the estimated variances correct for the non-uniform and non-normal nature of the dependent variable.
time_window: matching the one-year and ten-year growth regressions

description: To allow for the hypothesized secular trend, key rivalry variables are interacted with a linear time variable: (year-59) for the one-year changes and (year-68) for the ten-year changes. All estimation also includes fixed effects for years, whose coefficients are not of interest and are not reported.

One-year and ten-year growth rates of industry shipments, used in natural-logarithm form. Together with prices and unit costs it is one of the core independent variables that drive industry cashflows and measure the challenge from rivalry. The data come from the NBER industry dataset.
time_window: one-year growth from 1959 to 1991 and ten-year growth from 1968 to 1991

description: One-year and ten-year growth rates of industry wholesale price indices, used in natural-logarithm form; the study's proxy for the price instrument of rivalry. A reduction of prices ceteris paribus signals escalating challenge, so price growth measures the reverse of escalating rivalry. The data come from the NBER industry dataset.
time_window: one-year growth from 1959 to 1991 and ten-year growth from 1968 to 1991

description: One-year and ten-year growth rates of unit cost of goods sold, computed for firms and drawn from Compustat, used in natural-logarithm form. Increases in unit costs ceteris paribus signal greater competition and challenge to industry cashflows.
time_window: one-year growth from 1959 to 1991 and ten-year growth from 1968 to 1991

description: One-year and ten-year growth rates of unit selling, general, and administrative expense, computed for firms and drawn from Compustat, used in natural-logarithm form. SGA expenses aggregate marketing and R&D activities and represent the instrument of rivalry most likely to trigger the creation of new strategic assets.
time_window: one-year growth from 1959 to 1991 and ten-year growth from 1968 to 1991

variable_name: percentage of final demand to consumers
description: For each 4-digit SIC industry, the proportion of final demand due to consumers rather than to business or government demand, taken for the single year 1987 from the Annual Input-Output Tables of the United States. It is used as a proxy for the inelasticity of demand and hence for transactor dynamism, a determinant of dynamic resourcefulness.

variable_name: percentage of inputs from raw materials
description: For each 4-digit SIC industry, the proportion of inputs coming from agriculture and mining, taken for 1987 from the Annual Input-Output Tables of the United States. It is an inverse proxy for the technical sophistication of suppliers, and thus expected to work against dynamic resourcefulness.

variable_name: percentage of the workforce that is professional
description: The percentage of workers in an industry who are professional, taken for 1989 from the Current Population Survey. It proxies the knowledge base of the industry and the capacity of its workers to innovate.

Industry productivity growth, measured as growth in constant-dollar shipments per worker, used in natural-logarithm form as a rather direct measure of innovative activity and as part of the knowledge-base proxy set for dynamic resourcefulness. The data come from the NBER industry dataset.
time_window: one-year growth from 1959 to 1991 and ten-year growth from 1968 to 1991

variable_name: growth in the industry concentration ratio
description: Growth in the industry concentration ratio, taken from Salinger (1990) and used in natural-logarithm form. It is an inverse proxy for ease of entry, and thus a negative indicator of dynamic resourcefulness.
time_window: one-year growth from 1959 to 1991 and ten-year growth from 1968 to 1991

description: Outlet managers were asked in a survey to predict their sales targets for the following month for four products; the authors compare the predictions with the actual targets and separate managers into high- and low-prediction ability groups according to their average prediction error (results are based on the 'raw' prediction error). Accurate predictions are interpreted as superior knowledge of how the organization works. The measure was validated against independent ratings of interview transcripts: the prediction-based measure of FSHC matched the interview-based ratings in 15 out of 17 cases for the full transcript group and in 14 out of 17 cases for the partial transcript group.
scale: binary, high vs. low prediction ability
time_window: interviews conducted 1 month before, and predictions elicited 3 months after, the 13-month observation period

description: Average daily value and average daily number of primary loans sold by an outlet. The units of the value measure have no economic interpretation because the bank rescaled the data; the number measure is the count of loans sold per day.

Value-weighted interest rate on primary loans sold by outlet u on day t. Because of confidentiality concerns the bank did not release the exact interest rate of each loan; loans were aggregated into groups of similar size and price and the data contain the loan interest rate category on a scale of 1 to 5, with category definitions stable over time and equidistant from one another. The authors interpret managers' discounting behaviour - in particular the responsiveness of the interest rate to the outlet's plan position, i.e. its cumulative sales with respect to the monthly target, time-adjusted using week-of-month dummies - as incentive gaming: using the interest rate as a substitute for effort in selling loans.

Lost profits are defined as the difference between observed profits and the profits that would have been earned under a benchmark. Benchmark 1 ('fourth-week effect') assumes that managers maintained loan prices in week 4 at the levels observed in weeks 1-3; Benchmark 2 ('monopoly pricing') assumes pricing as a monopolist under the estimated demand function. Because the bank provided transformed data, profit levels have no economic meaning and so only the ratio of actual to theoretical profits is reported; the lost profits measure used in the learning analysis is 1 - (actual profits / theoretical profits).
scale: ratio of actual to theoretical profits
level: outlet (and outlet-month in the learning analysis)

description: Time measured in months elapsed since the introduction of the new incentive regime. It enters the learning model together with high FSHC and the interaction of the two.

Calculated as the mean number of ESG concerns among publicly traded companies within a focal organization's state, using MSCI STATS for 2012. For example, the measure for Pennsylvania was based on ratings of 109 companies headquartered in the state. The measure captures the difference between the average ESG concerns of public companies and the essentially negligible ESG concerns of the prototypical B Corp member within the regional context. Mean centered to facilitate interpretation of the interaction terms.

Calculated as the mean number of ESG concerns among publicly traded companies within a focal organization's industry, as defined by its SIC division, a widely accepted classification of 10 industrial groups. Examples of ESG concerns include toxic emissions and waste, product quality and safety, workforce diversity, and controversial investments.
